This exclusion, far from being a deficiency, reveals a powerful conceptual coherence to Shmuel's reading of the *mishna*: it contains only *nizkei mamon* — property damages — and only categories that are *muad* from the start.

### Rav Adam Included

The Gemara now turns to examine Rav's reading, which holds that *maveh* is *adam*, the human tortfeasor, and that *shor* encompasses all three aspects of ox-damage. The question is then: according to Shmuel, why not read *maveh* as Rav does, as *adam*? Shmuel answers: *ha-ketani seifa: shor ha-muad ve-shor ha-mazik be-reshut ha-nizak ve-ha-adam* — a later *mishna* explicitly lists *adam* among those who pay full damages at the outset. Shmuel does not want *adam* to appear in the first *mishna* when it already appears — more appropriately, in his view — in the later one.

The Gemara presses: but why couldn't *adam* appear in both? And Shmuel's deeper answer is: *be-nizkei mamon ka-miyri, be-nizkei gufo lo ka-miyri* — the first *mishna* is discussing damage to property, not damage by a person's own body. When a human being personally causes harm, that is a conceptually distinct category. The *mishna*'s subject is *mamon ha-mazik* — one's property causing damage — not one's own person doing so.

Rav, for his part, has no difficulty with *adam* appearing in both *mishnayot*. When *adam* appears later in the *mishna* listing those who pay full damages, it is not introducing the category anew — *adam* was already introduced as an *av nezikin* in the first *mishna*. The later *mishna* is merely restating the case in the context of listing full-payment categories; it adds no new information about what is *chayav*, only about the measure of payment.

### Shor Darko Lehazik

The Gemara then raises a pointed question that applies to Rav's reading in particular: *ve-chi shor darko lehazik* — is it really the way of an ox to cause damage? The *tzad ha-shaveh* of the *mishna* states *she-darkan lehazik*, that it is their way to damage. For Shmuel, who excludes *keren* from the *mishna*, this phrase applies comfortably to *shen* and *regel*, which are the natural, constant behaviors of an animal. But for Rav, *shor* includes *keren* — intentional goring — which is decidedly not the ordinary way of an animal. Goring is exceptional, aberrant behavior.

### Muad Question

The Gemara suggests: *be-muad* — the *mishna* is referring to the case of a *muad*, an animal that has been warned three times. At that point, surely, goring has become its established pattern. But the Gemara does not let this pass easily: *u-muad darko lehazik* — even a *muad*, is goring really its *derech*? This is a striking moment. The Gemara entertains the possibility that even three incidents of goring do not make goring the animal's normal behavior; it remains an exceptional act. Ultimately the Gemara affirms: *keivan de-i'ad orchei hu* — once it has been established through repeated incidents, that is now considered its *derech*. But the question itself reveals that the category of *keren*, even as a *muad*, sits uneasily alongside *shen* and *regel* in a *mishna* premised on *darkan lehazik*.

### Shmiratan Alecha

A parallel question arises regarding *adam*: *adam darko lehazik* — does a person go about normally causing damage? The Gemara answers *be-yashen* — when asleep. A sleeping person tosses and turns and can damage things nearby. The Gemara presses further: *yashen darko lehazik* — is that really a person's ordinary way? And the Gemara replies: *keivan de-kayif u-fashit orchei hu* — since one stretches out and moves in one's sleep, yes, there is a genuine propensity to cause inadvertent damage in that state.

The *mishna*'s *tzad ha-shaveh* then says *u-shmiratan alecha* — watching them is your responsibility. The Gemara observes that this phrase is awkward when applied to *adam*. The formulation *shmiratan alecha* implies that the hazard is something external to the person, something one must watch over as a separate entity. When the tortfeasor *is* the person himself, the more appropriate phrase would be *shmirat gufo alav* — the responsibility to watch his own person rests upon himself.

### Muad Question

The Gemara resolves this by citing Karna's *brayta*: *arbah avot nezikin ve-adam echad mehen*, a *brayta* that lists *adam* among the *avot nezikin* and explicitly uses the phrase *adam shmirat gufo alav* — confirming that the appropriate formulation for the human tortfeasor is indeed that one bears responsibility for one's own body, not the general *shmiratan alecha* formula.

### Rabbi Abahu

Rabbi Abahu teaches explicitly: the *tanna* who included *adam* in the *mishna* would not use *shmiratan alecha* when describing *adam*, but rather *shmirat gufo alav*. The phrase *shmiratan alecha* in the *mishna*'s *tzad ha-shaveh* describes all the other cases — ox, pit, fire — where there is something external that one must supervise. When *adam* is described, the formulation shifts: you are responsible for yourself. So the *mishna*'s general *tzad ha-shaveh* phrase, while not perfectly calibrated to *adam*, is understood to carry that adjusted meaning when applied to it.

What this entire discussion brings into relief is the conceptual tension in Rav's reading. Shmuel's exclusion of *keren* and *adam* from the primary *mishna* preserves a tight, coherent category: things that are one's property, that have a genuine *darkan lehazik*, that are *muad* from the outset, and for which the responsibility-to-watch rationale applies naturally. Rav's inclusion of *adam* — and *keren* — forces one to extend the concepts of *darkan lehazik* and *shmiratan alecha* considerably. The notion that a human being failing to watch himself is analogous to a negligent animal owner is, by any measure, a striking claim. Yet that is the implication of Rav's reading that *maveh* is *adam*.

---

## Maveh Alternatives

### Water Suggestion

After resolving the dispute between Rav and Shmuel, the Gemara entertains two additional proposals for the meaning of *maveh* before closing the discussion. Rav Mari raises the possibility: *ve-eima maveh zeh ha-mayim* — perhaps *maveh* refers to water. He cites the *pasuk*: *ke-kadoch eish hamasim mayim tivei eish* — as fire kindles, it melts things, and the fire causes water to bubble. The verbal root *tivei* could link to *maveh*.

### Fire Suggestion

The Gemara rejects this: *mi-ksiv mayim nivu* — the *pasuk* does not say the water bubbled; *tivei eish ksiv* — it is the fire that causes the bubbling. Water is not the subject of the verb. Next, Rav Zvid proposes: *ve-eima maveh zeh ha-eish* — perhaps *maveh* means fire, based on the same root *tivei* as applied to fire.

### Four Categories

The Gemara dismisses this immediately: if *maveh* means fire, then what is *hav'er*? *Hav'er* already means fire. The *mishna* lists four *avot nezikin*; if *maveh* and *hav'er* are both fire, that collapses two categories into one.

### Distinct from Esh

One might respond that *shor* already encompasses two things — say, *shen* and *regel* — and that *maveh* and *hav'er* together form what is really *esh*, so the four are really only three. The Gemara rejects this: *ei hachi lo zeh ve-zeh she-yesh bahen ruach chayim, eish mai ruach chayim it bei* — the *mishna* explicitly says that *maveh* and *shor* share the characteristic of *ruach chayim*, living breath. Fire has no *ruach chayim*. Moreover, the *mishna* states that *maveh* is not like fire — the two are contrasted as distinct categories. It is therefore clear that *maveh* and *esh* are categorically separate, and water and fire are definitively ruled out as identifications for *maveh*.

---

## Thirteen Avot

### Thirteen Categories

The Gemara now introduces a *brayta* of Rabbi Oshaya, which dramatically expands the list of *avot nezikin* from four to thirteen. The structure of the tractate has devoted its opening pages to the conceptual architecture of the four *avot*; Rabbi Oshaya's *brayta* asks how much broader the category of primary damage-obligations might be.

### Four Shomrim

The first addition Rabbi Oshaya makes is the four *shomrim* — the four types of bailee. *Shomer chinam* is the unpaid watchman, who bears liability only for negligence; *sho'el* is the borrower, who pays even for accidents; *nosei sachar* is the paid watchman; and *socher* is the renter. The latter two pay for *geneiva va-aveidah* — cases of theft and loss where some degree of negligence is involved — but are exempt for complete accidents. These four categories cover the full spectrum of custodial responsibility under Torah law and together form a coherent sub-unit within Rabbi Oshaya's expanded list.

### Five Payments

Rabbi Oshaya then adds the five payments owed by a human who wounds another human: *nezek*, *tzaar*, *ripuy*, *sheves*, and *boshes* — damages, pain, medical expenses, lost work, and humiliation. Together with the four *shomrim*, this brings the total to nine additional categories beyond the *mishna*'s four, yielding thirteen in all.

### Mishnah Limitations

*Ve-tani didan mai ta'ama lo tani hani* — why did the *tanna* of our *mishna* not include these? According to Shmuel, the answer is clean: *be-nizkei mamon ka-miyri, be-nizkei gufa lo ka-miyri* — the *mishna* deals exclusively with property damage, not personal injury. All of Rabbi Oshaya's additions either involve personal injury (*chavalah* and its five payments) or fall under a different framework (the *shomrim*). The *mishna*'s scope is the damages caused when one's property harms another's property.

According to Rav, who includes *adam* in the *mishna* and reads it as encompassing all human-caused damage, the explanation is: *tanna adam be-chol milei de-adam* — the *mishna*'s reference to *adam* is itself comprehensive, subsuming all the cases Rabbi Oshaya lists explicitly. Rabbi Oshaya's *brayta* was needed not because the *mishna* failed to cover these cases, but because Rabbi Oshaya wished to articulate them distinctly and explicitly.

---

## Chavala Distinct

### Two Types Adam

The Gemara now works through the question of why exactly each of Rabbi Oshaya's additions was necessary — that is, why they could not have been absorbed by inference from the *mishna*'s existing categories. This discussion brings the fundamental distinction between property damage and personal injury into sharp relief.

There are two types of *adam* in the world of *nezikin*: *adam d'azik shor* — a person who damages property — and *adam d'azik adam* — a person who injures another person. The *mishna* is exclusively concerned with the first. The *mishna*'s *adam* is the person whose conduct damages another's property, analogous in form to the ox that damages property. But *chavalah* — wounding — is conceptually distinct. When one human being injures another, the law does not merely assess the market value of the harm and require payment of *nezek*. It recognizes *tzaar*, *ripuy*, *sheves*, and *boshes* as independent heads of liability, each requiring separate payment and each reflecting a different dimension of the injury. This is not a quantitatively larger version of property damage; it is a qualitatively different legal category.

### Shor Damages Human

The Gemara then asks: if the distinction is between property-object and human-person as the thing harmed, why not similarly distinguish between an ox that gores property and an ox that gores a human being? Should we not expect a separate category for *shor d'azik adam*? The Gemara's answer is instructive: *hai mai* — what is the comparison? When a human injures a human, the difference is categorical: *adam d'azik shor — nezek hu de-meshalem; adam d'azik adam — meshalem arba devarim*. The difference is not merely in how much is owed but in what *kind* of liability attaches. The five-payment framework for *chavalah* is a fundamentally different halachic structure from simple *nezek*.

By contrast: *shor d'azik shor — nezek hu de-meshalem; shor d'azik adam — nezek hu de-meshalem*. Halachically, when an ox injures a human being, the law still treats it as property damage. You assess the harm and pay *nezek*. There is no *tzaar*, no *boshes*, no *sheves* as independent obligations. The ox and the human victim are both treated as objects of property valuation. The damage is compensable, but it is compensated on the property-damage model, not the personal-injury model. There is therefore no halachically distinct category of *shor d'azik adam* that needs separate listing.

### Direct vs. Negligent

This brings the Gemara to Rabbi Oshaya's inclusion of the four *shomrim*. These are not cases of direct damage — *hezek de-be-yadayim* — but of indirect damage — *hezek de-meila*, damage that occurs on its own while the person is responsible through negligence or custodial obligation. The *mishna*, even for Rav who reads *adam* broadly, is discussing cases where the person directly performs an act of damage. Rabbi Oshaya needed to list the *shomrim* separately precisely because their liability arises from a different structural basis: not because they *did* something damaging, but because they were responsible for something that was damaged.

### Negligence Concept

This raises a conceptual question that the Gemara leaves open but which resonates throughout the tractate. When a *shomer* is *chayav*, is it because we conceptualize his negligence as having itself been the damaging act — treating him, in legal terms, as the *mazik*? Or is the framework simply that property was damaged and we are assessing who must bear the loss, without needing to characterize anyone as having committed an act of damage? The question is whether negligence is a species of *mazik*-liability or an independent basis for payment. The answer may vary depending on the degree of negligence — whether it is *peshiah* (clear negligence) or a more attenuated failure — and may even depend on whether the *shomer* in question is a *sho'el*, who pays even in cases of complete accident. Whether the liability of *shomrim* belongs in the same conceptual universe as the *avot nezikin* of property-damage, or merely in the same practical universe of "who pays," is a question that will continue to unfold in the pages ahead.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 5

## Intro & Categories

### Opening

We pick up today on daf 4b, approximately ten lines from the bottom, at the words *tani Rabbi Chiya*.

### Mishna Review

By way of orientation, we have by this point worked through the different explanations of the *mishna*'s four categories: *shor*, *bor*, *ma'aveh*, and *hev'er*. Along the way, we discussed that when an animal walking kicks up stones, it pays half damages, since that is a form of *kocho* — the animal's indirect force — and is incidental rather than the animal's primary damaging act. We also discussed the *mishna*'s inclusion of *adam*, a person who causes damage, and the two competing frameworks for understanding that liability: strict liability by virtue of the act itself, or negligence as the operative basis. A parallel question arises regarding animal liability — whether the owner pays because of what the animal did as such, or because of a failure to watch it adequately.

### Rabbi Oshaya List

Following the *mishna*'s four categories, the *gemara* now presents several *braisot* that expand the list of *avot nezikin*. Rabbi Oshaya's expanded *braisa* brought the total to thirteen categories, moving beyond the *mishna*'s four by incorporating personal injury cases — where the tortfeasor pays not only for the damage itself but for pain, lost labor, medical expenses, and related items — and by incorporating the laws of *shomrim*, the various categories of bailee, who do not directly cause damage but who bear liability through negligence or, in the case of a *sho'el*, even without negligence. This gives us thirteen distinct categories. The *gemara* now introduces a still broader enumeration.

## Rabbi Chiya 24 Categories

### 24 Categories Listed

*Tani Rabbi Chiya esrim v'arba avot nezikin* — Rabbi Chiya's *braisa* enumerated twenty-four categories of *nezikin*. That is eleven more than Rabbi Oshaya's thirteen, and the *gemara* proceeds to identify them.

The first additions are *tashlumei kefel* — the double payment in cases of theft — and *tashlumei arba v'chamisha* — the fourfold and fivefold payments when the thief additionally slaughters or sells the stolen animal, applicable specifically to an ox or a sheep. Then *haganav v'hagazlan* — the principal payment by a thief (without the double) or a robber, who also pays only the principal. That brings us to four new categories. Fifth is *eidim zomemim* — conspiratorial false witnesses who, when they are exposed, pay what they had sought to extract from the defendant. Sixth through eighth are *v'ha'ones v'hamifateh u'motzi shem ra* — the rapist, the seducer, and the husband who falsely libels his bride as having committed adultery. Ninth through eleventh are *v'hametameh v'hamedameh v'hamenasech* — one who renders another's *terumah* ritually impure, one who mixes *terumah* with *chullin*, and one who pours another's wine as a libation to *avoda zara*, rendering it worthless. These last three derive not from *psukim* but from rabbinic teaching and are instances of *hezeik she'eino nikar* — damage that is not visibly apparent. Adding these eleven to Rabbi Oshaya's thirteen yields the total of twenty-four.

### Kanasim & Mamona

The *gemara* now asks: why did Rabbi Oshaya not include these additional categories in his own list? The answer is *bemamona ka'mar uveknasa lo ka'mar* — Rabbi Oshaya was dealing exclusively with compensatory monetary obligations, *mamona*, and not with *knasot*, fines. Many of the items on Rabbi Chiya's expanded list are not true compensation but rather punitive or arbitrary assessments, and therefore fell outside Rabbi Oshaya's conceptual scope.

The *gemara* proceeds to examine which of Rabbi Chiya's additions are in fact *mamona* rather than *knas*. It notes that *ganav v'gazlan* — when paying only the principal amount — would seem to be straightforward compensation. Why then did Rabbi Oshaya not include them? The answer is that Rabbi Oshaya's list already included the *shomrim*. The connection is this: if a *shomer* falsely swears that an item was stolen or robbed, he is treated legally as a *ganav* or *gazlan* respectively. The *gemara* then turns the question around and asks why Rabbi Chiya lists both *shomrim* and *ganav v'gazlan* separately, if the former subsumes the latter. The answer is *tana mamona d'atei liyadei b'heter ukatani mamona d'atei liyadei b'issur* — Rabbi Chiya deliberately distinguishes between money that came into one's possession legitimately at the outset, as in the case of a *shomer* who then betrayed his charge, and money that was taken unlawfully from the very beginning, as in the case of an outright thief or robber. These are conceptually distinct categories, and Rabbi Chiya wished to enumerate both.

## Mamona vs. Knas

### False Witnesses

The *gemara* then turns to *eidim zomemim*, asserting that this is *mamona* — genuine compensation rather than a fine. This claim warrants close attention. On its surface it is surprising: the Torah's rule is *ka'asher zamam v'lo ka'asher asa l'achiv* — the conspiratorial witnesses are punished for what they plotted, not for what they actually accomplished. By definition, then, the false witnesses are punished only when they did not succeed. If there was no actual loss to the intended victim, in what sense can the payment be called compensation?

### Rashi Criteria

Rashi explains the criteria for distinguishing *mamona* from *knas*. Any payment that exceeds the actual damage caused is by definition a *knas* — the excess beyond the harm is clearly a punitive addition and not compensatory. He cites *kefel* and *tashlumei dalet v'hei* as examples. Alternatively, even where the payment does not exceed the harm, if it is a fixed statutory amount rather than a direct function of the damage caused, that too constitutes a *knas*, since it is arbitrary and symbolic rather than truly compensatory. As examples, Rashi mentions the fifty *shekel* payment by the rapist or seducer, and the payment by the husband who libels his bride — and he notes that *motzi shem ra* shares this character. A cleaner example, one might add, is the thirty *shekel* payment when an ox gores a slave: there is a real loss — indeed a loss of life — but instead of assessing the actual value of the slave, the Torah fixes a statutory sum of thirty *shekel*. That is the mark of a *knas*.

On these criteria, *eidim zomemim* qualifies as *mamona*: they pay an amount equivalent to the damage they attempted to cause, not more, and it is not a fixed arbitrary sum but proportionate to the specific harm they schemed to bring about. The payment is equivalent to the intended loss — *ka'asher zamam* is precisely calibrated. Rashi is explaining why, despite the fact that the plot did not succeed and there was no actual loss, the payment is still classified as *mamona* rather than *knas*: it is neither in excess of the damage nor arbitrary in amount.

### Tosafot Analysis

Yet one might still object: if *mamona* requires that there be an actual loss, how can *eidim zomemim* be classified as *mamona* when, by the rule of *ka'asher zamam v'lo ka'asher asa*, they pay only when the intended victim suffered no actual loss?

Tosafot on daf 4b addresses this directly, citing the explanation of the Riva. Tosafot argues that in monetary cases, *eidim zomemim* are liable even when they did succeed — that is, even when the intended victim was actually made to pay based on their false testimony. The reason is *delo shayach b'mamona ka'asher zamam v'lo ka'asher asa d'efshar b'hazara* — the principle of *ka'asher zamam v'lo ka'asher asa* does not fully apply in monetary matters, because monetary outcomes are always reversible. If a court issued a ruling based on false testimony, that ruling can be undone and the money returned. It is therefore never truly a case of *ka'asher asa* in monetary matters — the damage is never final the way, say, corporal punishment is final. The witnesses are therefore always in the position of having plotted, not having irreversibly accomplished, and accordingly the Torah does impose the payment — but because it applies even when the victim did pay, there is a real loss being compensated, which is why it is *mamona*.

The Riva then adds a second, independent approach: one need not rely on this argument at all. *Degabei mamon mechayavinan lei bekal vachomer* — in monetary matters, we can impose liability by *kal vachomer* even in the absence of an explicit verse. The Torah says *ka'asher zamam*, and we derive by *kal vachomer* that if they pay when they only plotted, they should certainly pay when they actually succeeded. In capital and corporal cases one cannot punish on the basis of a *kal vachomer* — *onshin min hadin* is forbidden — but in monetary matters this restriction does not apply, and *onshin min hadin* is permitted. Thus, even according to this approach, the false witnesses pay in the case where there was an actual loss, and the payment is therefore genuine compensation — *mamona*.

This analysis reveals the essential requirement of Tosafot's position: for a payment to constitute *mamona*, it is not sufficient that the amount be equivalent and non-arbitrary; there must also be an actual loss being compensated. If *eidim zomemim* paid only when the intended victim suffered no loss, Tosafot would apparently classify that as *knas*. The *gemara*'s classification of *eidim zomemim* as *mamona* therefore implies, for Tosafot, that they pay in the case of actual loss as well.

The *gemara* continues: *savar lah kerabi akiva de'amar ein meshalmin al pi atzman* — Rabbi Oshaya's list may reflect the position of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that *eidim zomemim* do not pay if they confess to their own false testimony. According to Rabbi Akiva, even in monetary cases, the self-incriminating admission does not obligate payment, which is the hallmark of a *knas*. That is why *eidim zomemim* appears on Rabbi Chiya's expanded list of *knasot* and not on Rabbi Oshaya's list of pure *mamona*.

The *gemara* then raises a further question: if we are operating within Rabbi Akiva's framework and treating *eidim zomemim* as *knas*, then according to Rabbi Akiva there is another distinct category of ox — namely, an ox that gores a person — which Rabbi Akiva holds pays full damages rather than the standard half, even for a *tam*. *Af tam shechaval b'adam meshalem bemotar nezek shalem* — even a *tam* ox that injures a person pays full damages for the excess of harm over the countervailing harm. Should this not be added as a separate category, making twenty-five?

The *gemara* responds: *hatam Rabbi Akiva legaziziah* — Rabbi Akiva blunted the force of his own ruling. Even though he holds that a *tam* ox pays full damages when it injures a person, he also holds that the payment is limited to the body of the animal itself: *miguf meshalem v'eino meshalem min ha'aliyah* — you pay from the animal's body, not from general assets, even though the payment is nominally full rather than half. As a result, this is not a standard unrestricted payment that would belong on a list whose purpose is to declare that all enumerated categories require payment from the best property. Tosafot makes this precise: since the distinctive purpose of these lists is to establish the rule of *meitav* — that payment from land must come from the best land — Rabbi Akiva's special case of *tam* goring a person is excluded because it is categorically limited to the body of the animal and cannot invoke the *meitav* rule at all.

## Personal Injury & Hidden…

### Ones & Mifateh

The *gemara* next addresses why *ones*, *mifateh*, and *motzi shem ra* — rape, seduction, and libel — appear on Rabbi Chiya's list but not on Rabbi Oshaya's. The answer is straightforward: *mamma nafshach* — whatever payment in these cases is *mamona*, it is already subsumed within the categories Rabbi Oshaya did enumerate. If we are speaking of *nezek* — the basic loss of value — Rabbi Oshaya's list included *nezek* under personal injury. If we are speaking of *tza'ar* — pain — that too was on his list. If *boshet* — humiliation — again it was included. And *pagam* — the stigma — *hainu nezek*, that is essentially subsumed in *nezek* as well, as will be analyzed more fully when these cases are treated directly.

The only element of *ones* and *mifateh* that is not a personal injury payment is the *knas* — the statutory fine. Rabbi Oshaya does not deal with *knasot*; Rabbi Chiya does. *Motzi shem ra* is similarly classified primarily as *knas*, since one might question whether a payment for reputational harm constitutes genuine monetary compensation in the way that tangible injury does. Rabbi Chiya includes all three because he is cataloguing *knasot* as well.

### Hidden Damages

The final three categories — *hametameh*, *hamedameh*, and *hamenasech* — are compensatory: making someone's *terumah* impure, mixing *terumah* with *chullin*, or pouring wine as a libation to *avoda zara* all cause concrete loss, rendering the affected produce either worthless or worth significantly less. The *gemara* asks why these were not on Rabbi Oshaya's list if they are genuine *mamona*.

### Visibility Question

The *gemara* raises a dilemma: *ei hezeik she'eino nikar shemeih hezeik* — if non-visible damage is considered real damage in the legal sense, then these cases would have been covered under the *nezek* category already on Rabbi Oshaya's list, and they need not have been enumerated separately. *Ei hezeik she'eino nikar lo shemeih hezeik* — if non-visible damage is not legally cognizable damage, then it is only a rabbinic imposition, functioning more like a *knas*, and Rabbi Oshaya would have excluded it from his *mamona*-only list.

The *gemara* resolves that this is not a decisive inference either way. Rabbi Chiya may well hold that *hezeik she'eino nikar shemeih hezeik* — that non-visible damage is real damage — and yet still list these categories separately in order to distinguish between two varieties of *nezek*: visible damage, which is the paradigm, and non-visible damage, which, though equally real, is a distinct type and deserves explicit mention. Just as the *gemara* earlier explained that Rabbi Chiya separately enumerates *shomrim* and *ganav v'gazlan* not because they are legally unrelated, but to underscore that they are conceptually distinct varieties of the same broad category, so too here: *tana hezeka de-minchar v'tana hezeka de-lo minchar* — he teaches visible damage and he teaches non-visible damage, not to resolve the question of whether the latter is legally cognizable, but to ensure that both types are explicitly covered.

A related question arises in the course of this discussion: could reputational harm itself not be characterized as a form of *hezeik she'eino nikar*, particularly when it directly affects one's livelihood? The absence of such a framework in *halacha* is notable, and the question of why defamation is not abstracted into a broader category of non-visible damage — especially when the harm is economically concrete — is an interesting one that the *gemara* here does not directly address.

## List Purpose & Exclusions

### Moser & Mefagel

The *gemara* now turns to what Rabbi Chiya's number of twenty-four is designed to exclude — the logic being that if a count is stated, it implies that something is being left out. Two candidates are identified: *moser* and *mefagel*.

*Mefagel* refers to a *kohen* who, at the moment of *shechita*, entertains the intention to eat the offering at the wrong time or in the wrong place, thereby rendering the sacrifice *pigul* and worthless. This case is straightforwardly excluded from Rabbi Chiya's list because *bekodashim lo ka meiri* — these lists are not dealing with the domain of sacred offerings. The *kohen* does pay in such a case — that is not in question — but it falls conceptually outside the scope of the *masechet*.

*Moser* refers to an informer who discloses another person's property or affairs to the authorities, causing the government to seize that property. The informer does pay. The question is why this case is also excluded from Rabbi Chiya's list.

### Words & Action

The *gemara*'s answer is *shani moser d'dibura, u'vidibura lo ka meiri* — the case of the informer involves damage caused purely through speech, and the lists here are not dealing with damage caused by words alone.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: what about *motzi shem ra*, which is on the list and also involves speech? The response is that *motzi shem ra* as it appears in the *parsha* is not pure speech. The *parsha* in the Torah addresses the specific case of a husband who first has sexual relations with his bride and then spreads the false claim that she was not a virgin. There is thus an act — the marital relations — behind the verbal libel. The words do not stand alone. If the husband had spread the same libel without the prior act, he would not fall under the *parsha* at all and would not be liable.

The *gemara* then challenges further: *eidim zomemim* is on the list, and that involves no act at all — it is pure testimony, pure speech. The answer is *rachmana karyei ma'aseh* — the Torah itself characterizes it as an act, as it is written, *v'asitem lo ka'asher zamam la'asot le'achiv* — you shall do to him as he schemed to do to his brother. The Torah describes the conspiratorial testimony using the language of *asiyah*, of doing. Even though the false witnesses did nothing but speak, the Torah treats their speech as equivalent to an act, and that is what allows it to appear on the list. Something so purely a matter of words as informing, without such a textual re-characterization, remains outside the list's scope — even though, as noted, the informer's liability is a genuine topic addressed later in the *masechet*.

## Avot & Best Property

### Abbahu's Approach

The *gemara* now turns to a more fundamental question: what is the purpose of calling these categories *avot* at all? For the *tanna* of our *mishna*, the answer is clear — *avot* implies *toldot*, that is, the four concrete cases in the Torah are abstract categories with conceptual offspring, other scenarios that share their essential features and are governed by the same rules. But for Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Chiya, whose expanded lists include *eidim zomemim*, *motzi shem ra*, and the like, what could *avot* possibly mean? There is no abstracted category of *eidim zomemim* that includes related sub-cases; there is just the one scenario. Why call these *avot*?

Rabbi Abbahu answers: *kulan k'avot l'shaleim m'meitav* — all of these function like the four classic *avot nezikin* in one crucial respect: they require payment from the best property. The rule of *meitav sadeihu u'meitav karmo yeshaleim* — that payment from land must come from the best land — is established in the Torah specifically in connection with *shen v'regel*. The four *avot nezikin* of the *mishna* are understood to be linked to one another, and therefore the *meitav* rule derived from *shen v'regel* applies to all four — to *keren*, *bor*, and *eish* as well. Now, by placing all of Rabbi Oshaya's and Rabbi Chiya's additional categories on the same list and calling them *avot*, the point is that they too share this rule: any of these payments, if made from land, must come from the best land.

### Key Terminology

The *gemara* then explains how this connection is established: *asya tachas tachas nesina yishalem kesef*. Each of the four classic *avot nezikin* contains one of four key terms — *tachas*, *nesina*, *yishalem*, or *kesef* — and these words serve as the lexical hooks by which the derivation from *shen v'regel*'s *meitav* rule is extended to all of them. *Tachas* appears, for instance, in *shaleim yeshalem shor tachas hashor*; *yishalem* appears in *meitav sadeihu u'meitav karmo yeshaleim*, the direct source of the *meitav* rule; *nesina* appears in *kesef shloshim shekalim yitein la'adonav* in connection with the ox that gores a slave; and *kesef* appears in *kesef yashiv l'va'alav*. Having established that all four classic *avot* are linked by this vocabulary to the *meitav* rule, the broader lists declare that everything they enumerate likewise contains one of these key terms and is therefore likewise subject to *meitav*. The reader may verify which term appears in each of the enumerated categories by consulting Rashi's explanation directly.

The conceptual upshot is twofold: the four concrete cases in the Torah are abstracted into categories with *toldot*, and then the four categories themselves are grouped into a single network in which the *meitav* rule circulates across all of them and, by extension, across all the additional categories that carry the relevant terminology.

## Four Categories Necessity

### Mishna Position

The *mishna* states that one cannot derive all four categories from fewer — *lo ha-rei ha-shor k'harei ha-mav'eh* and so on. The *gemara* asks what this assertion means operationally. Why does the *mishna* require all four? Could the Torah not have written fewer and allowed us to derive the rest?

The *gemara* explains this through the structure of *Zevid* and *Mesharshaya*'s respective readings of the *mishna*. The *mishna* is saying: the Torah could not have written just one category and expected us to derive the rest, because each has some feature the others lack. Could it have written two? No — any two share a feature that makes them inapplicable to everything else. Could it have written three? Consider *shen*, *regel*, and *eish*: all three are things that go out and cause damage, whereas *bor* stays in one place and the damage comes to it. One could not have learned *bor* from the other three. So why not just write three plus *bor*, and derive everything from the four minus one?

### Rava's Analysis

Rava intervenes with a sharpened analysis: in truth, *d'shadita bor beineihu asu chulhu b'ma hatzad* — if you insert *bor* alongside any one of the other categories, you can derive everything from that pair by *ma hatzad*, the common denominator. Here is the reasoning. *Bor* is the weakest of the categories: it does not go out to damage, it does not have *ruach chayim*, and its whole hazardous character consists in the fact that its creation is itself the beginning of the hazard — *techilat asiyato lenezek*. If you are liable for *bor*, which has none of the features that make the other categories obviously dangerous, surely you should be liable for those others which do possess those features. Conversely, *bor* lacks the feature of going out to damage, which *shen*, *regel*, and *eish* all share — but if you add any one of those alongside *bor*, the common denominator eliminates both distinctive features and yields a pure principle: anything that is my property and that I have an obligation to guard, if it causes damage, I am liable. That principle captures *shen*, *regel*, *eish*, and *bor* together.

The one thing that *bor* plus one other category cannot derive is *keren*.

### Keren Exception

Why can *keren* not be derived? Because *keren* is weaker than all the others in one critical respect: *mu'adin mitichlatan* — all the other categories have an inherent propensity to cause the damage they cause from the very outset. *Shen* naturally eats; *regel* naturally tramples; *eish* naturally spreads. Even *bor* is, by its nature, a hazard. *Keren* — goring — is not the natural behavior of an ox. A normal ox does not gore. Therefore, if the Torah had only given me the other categories and had not separately addressed goring, I might have concluded that the first three instances of goring were so unanticipated as to create no obligation at all — complete exemption. I would never have inferred from the other categories that you pay even half damages for completely unexpected behavior. *Keren* had to be stated independently.

Rava's conclusion is therefore: you needed *bor* plus one other category, and you needed *keren* independently. You did not need all four distinct categories. What the *mishna* says is strictly true — you cannot learn one from the other — but the *gemara* here is sharpening that claim: the impossibility is not between every pair, but between the *keren* case and everything else.

## Keren Characterization

### Below vs. Above Line

The *gemara* then introduces a dissenting position: *u'leman d'amar adrabba keren adifa she-kavanato lehazik* — according to the one who says, on the contrary, that *keren* is actually the stronger and more obviously liable category, because the animal acts with intention to injure, *afilu keren nami atie* — even *keren* could have been derived. If *keren* is in fact above the threshold of expected liability because goring does reflect a real propensity for harm that an owner ought to anticipate, then you could have learned *keren* from *bor* plus one other: if you are liable even for something with no propensity to damage (*bor*), you are certainly liable for something with a propensity (*keren*). The Torah's inclusion of *keren* would then serve a different purpose entirely — not to create liability where none was expected, but to limit it, by telling us that the first three times you pay only half.

Rashi notes — significantly — that this *maan d'amar* is not identified anywhere, and Tosafot fills in the gap by connecting it to a debate that will emerge later in the *perek*: is *keren* fundamentally below or above the line of expected liability?

### Keren: Fine or Compensat…

The question can be framed in two ways. One approach holds that ordinary animals do not have a propensity to gore — *stam shor bechezkat shimur*, a standard ox is presumed to be watched and not dangerous. If an ox gores, it is essentially an *ones* for the owner; strictly speaking, the owner should be fully exempt. The Torah, however, imposes a half-payment as a kind of incentive to be more vigilant. On this reading, the half-payment of *keren* is a *knas* — the owner is technically not negligent, and the payment is not compensation for recognized harm but rather a punitive imposition.

The opposing approach holds that there is just enough inherent risk in an ox — animals are occasionally prone to this behavior — that an owner does have some baseline obligation of care. The ox is technically just above the line of required vigilance. Therefore, strictly speaking, the owner should pay full damages. But because it is so close to the line, the Torah goes easy on the owner the first three times and requires only half. On this reading, the half-payment is *mamona* — the owner is genuinely negligent, the damage is real, and the reduced payment reflects leniency applied to a borderline case.

This debate — which will be treated fully at the end of the *perek* — governs the present discussion. If *keren* is below the line, it cannot be derived from the other categories, because those categories all involve clear liability; *keren* would be a special imposition of its own. If *keren* is above the line — if it really is the case that an owner ought to anticipate goring — then the *tzad hashaveh* argument would have reached it, and the Torah's explicit mention of *keren* comes only to narrow its scope.

## Category-Specific Laws

### Keren Laws

Once the *gemara* establishes that the four categories nonetheless stand as distinct *avot*, it enumerates the unique *halachot* that attach to each one and that justify the separate enumeration. For *keren*: the half-damage rule and the distinction between a *tam* — an ox that has not yet established a pattern of goring, for which only half damages are paid — and a *mu'ad* — an ox that has gored three times and has been formally warned, for which full damages are paid.

### Shen & Regel Laws

For *shen* and *regel*: the exemption in the public domain — *patur b'reshut harabim*. When an animal eats or tramples in the public domain, the owner is exempt. This may reflect a public policy consideration that people must be permitted to move their animals through public spaces, or it may reflect the principle of *pechitat hanizek* — contributory exposure, the idea that one who leaves produce in a public thoroughfare where animals are expected to pass has assumed the risk.

### Bor Laws

For *bor*: the exemption for vessels. If a camel falls into a pit and vessels carried on its back are broken, the one who dug the pit is exempt for the vessels. And according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that one is liable even for vessels damaged in a pit, *bor* carries a different distinctive rule: exemption when a person is killed by falling into the pit. The distinctive contours of liability in each case justify *bor* as a separate category.

### Adam Laws

For *adam* — a human being who directly injures another person: the obligation to pay the four additional elements beyond *nezek* that apply when the victim is a person rather than property — *tza'ar*, *ripui*, *shevet*, and *boshet* — pain, medical expenses, lost labor, and humiliation.

### Eish Laws

For *eish*: the exemption for concealed objects. If a fire spreads and burns a haystack, and within the haystack there was something buried — a hidden object not exposed to view — the one who sent the fire is exempt from liability for that concealed item. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one liable even for buried objects, the special *chiddush* of the *eish* category is the rule that one is liable even when the fire charred rather than fully consumed — *lichacha niro v'sichacha avanav*. If a fire singed the surface of another's plowing or charred stones, though it did not fully destroy the underlying material, liability still attaches. Since this is not the paradigmatic manner in which fire destroys, one might have thought it falls outside the category — the *chiddush* is that it does not.

## Concrete & Abstract

### Summary & Open Q

Each of the four *avot nezikin* thus carries its own distinctive *halachot* that apply specifically when a case is categorized within it. The *mishna* required all four to be stated independently because these distinct laws — the half-damage rule for *keren*, the public domain exemption for *shen* and *regel*, the vessel and person exemptions for *bor*, the personal injury payments for *adam*, and the concealment rule for *eish* — could not be derived from one another or collapsed into a smaller number of categories.

But this generates a question that will carry the discussion forward: having established four concrete categories with their own specific laws, the *gemara* has also identified a broad abstract principle that encompasses all of them and more.

### Preview Tomorrow

That principle is *kol she-darko lehazik u'shemirasan alecha chav hamazik leshaleim* — anything that has a propensity to cause damage and whose guarding falls upon you obligates payment if it damages. This *tzad hashaveh*, the common denominator across all four categories, is itself a *halachic* proposition. The question that opens tomorrow's discussion is: when a case fits neatly under this abstract rule but cannot be placed precisely within any one of the four concrete categories, what *halachot* govern it? Does it inherit the specific rules of whichever category it most resembles — the half-damage rule, the public domain exemption, the concealment exemption — or does the abstract category operate with its own distinct set of rules, independent of the four concrete ones? The challenge of holding both a set of specific concrete categories and a single broad abstract principle simultaneously, and of applying them coherently to novel cases, is the agenda for the discussion ahead.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 6

## Hatzad Hashaveh

### Intro: Principle & Categ…

The sixth daf opens with the *mishna*'s statement of the *hatzad hashaveh shebahen* — the common denominator shared by the four primary categories of damage. At this stage in the *mishna*, we have already established the four *avot nezikin*, abstracted and defined what is included in each, and examined specific cases such as *regel*'s liability for thrown stones. The *mishna* now articulates the overarching principle: because no single category could have been derived from any other, once we have all four together, there is a common denominator that captures a more general standard of liability.

As *Rava* demonstrated in yesterday's *gemara*, this general principle did not strictly require all four categories to be stated — *bor* plus any one other would have sufficed to derive it. The reason the *Torah* nonetheless defined four (or six, depending on how one categorizes them) distinct categories is, as the *gemara* answers emphatically, that each category carries its own *halachot*: *shen* and *regel* are exempt in *reshus harabim*; *keren* pays only half for the first three occurrences; *eish* is exempt for damage to buried objects; *bor* is exempt for the breaking of vessels; and a person who directly causes injury is liable for the four additional payments of *arba devarim*. It matters greatly, therefore, which category a given case falls into.

This generates an important question that will occupy the *gemara* from this point forward: if categorization is so consequential, what purpose does the general principle serve? One possibility is that certain cases genuinely do not fit neatly into any single category and must be placed in some overarching catch-all — but then which special *halachot* apply to them? Does the catch-all carry none of the restrictions of the individual categories, making it in some ways more stringent? Alternatively, perhaps everything must ultimately be assigned to one of the existing categories, and the *tzad hashaveh* merely provides flexibility in defining the boundaries of those categories. These are the questions the *gemara* now turns to address.

### Mammon & Shmiratan Alecha

The *mishna* states the common denominator as follows: *shemamoncha* — it is your property; *v'darkan lehazik* — it has a propensity to cause damage; *ushmiratan alecha* — you bear the obligation to watch it; and when it damages, the damager is obligated to pay *tashlumei nezek* from the best of the land.

This raises two interconnected questions. First, the requirement of *mamoncha* — of ownership or some proprietary connection — is not straightforwardly satisfied by every one of the four categories. Is a *bor* dug in *reshus harabim* considered *mamoncha*? Is *eish* considered *mamoncha*? The *gemara* will grapple with precisely those questions. More broadly, what is the nature of the connection to an object that makes one the responsible party? If a random cow is wandering the street, there clearly needs to be some link to a particular person before that person can be held liable.

The second question concerns the role of *shmiratan alecha*. Is the obligation to watch the object a criterion that must be independently established before liability attaches — meaning one must demonstrate that the object is one's property, that it has a propensity to cause damage, *and* that one bears a duty of care — or is *shmiratan alecha* rather the *consequence* of establishing the first two elements? If ownership and propensity are shown, the duty to watch follows automatically as the legal consequence. The distinction matters because if *shmiratan alecha* is a separate criterion, one must ask how to determine whether it applies in a given case, which is itself not always obvious.

### Textual Variants

*Tosafot* raises the question of whether the word *mamoncha* even belongs in the *mishna* at all. If one holds that *adam* — personal liability — is included within the *mishna*'s framework, then *mamoncha* cannot be a universal criterion, since a person is not their own property. More broadly, since the printed text of the *gemara* often reflects the editorial interventions of *Rashi* and *Tosafot*, and since different manuscript traditions (*nuschaot*) vary on this point, the presence or absence of *mamoncha* in the *mishna* cannot be determined with certainty without consulting the parallel manuscripts — a task that was not undertaken here. What is clear is that *Tosafot* argued for its removal, and the standard printed edition appears to reflect that position.

What remains true regardless of the textual resolution is that something must constitute the relevant connection between the responsible party and the hazardous object. Whether that connection is ownership, creation, or ongoing control, some such link must exist to identify the party who bears responsibility.

### Abstract Principle

The abstract principle of the *hatzad hashaveh* thus functions as follows: we know there is a shared denominator across the categories, but the cases that require it are precisely those that do not fit neatly into any single box. The *gemara* will now ask, *le'atuyei mai* — what does this general principle actually include that could not have been derived from one of the individual categories alone?

There are two ways of understanding the answer. On one view, the *tzad hashaveh* creates a genuine residual category into which anomalous cases are placed, with the consequence that those cases carry neither the exemptions nor the restrictions of any one category. On another view, every case must ultimately be assigned primarily to one of the existing categories, and the *tzad hashaveh* merely permits us to avoid being overly rigid about which characteristics define that category's boundaries — one learns from the other categories that certain features are not disqualifying. As will become apparent, the latter approach seems closer to what the *gemara* is doing in practice, though the question deserves continued attention.

---

## Abaye: Roof Cases

### Setup: Wind Blown Objects

*Abaye* answers the question of what the *hatzad hashaveh* includes: *le'atuyei avno sakino umaso she'nichan berosh gago venaflu beruach metzuya vehiziku* — to include a case where a person leaves a stone, knife, or bundle on the roof of their house, and a common wind blows them off so that they cause damage. Such a case does not fall neatly into any single category of the *mishna*.

### During vs. After Fall

The *gemara* immediately asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the scenario? If the objects damaged someone in the process of falling — that is, *behadi deka azli kamazki*, as they were traveling through the air — then this *does* fall into an existing category.

### Eish: Koach Acher

Specifically, it falls into the category of *eish*, fire. The defining characteristic of *eish* is *koach acher meurav bo* — another force is mixed into the act of damage. In the case of fire, that other force is the wind spreading the flame. Here, the other force is similarly the wind blowing the object off the roof. The *gemara* notes that this case also satisfies *mamoncha ushmirasan alecha* — it is your property and you bear the obligation to watch it. So if the damage occurs during the fall, it is a variant of *eish* and requires no *hatzad hashaveh* to justify liability.

### Eish & Bor Comparison

The *gemara* therefore redirects: *ve'ela batar denaychi* — rather, suppose the objects have already fallen and are now lying in the street, and someone subsequently trips on them. In that scenario, if the owner renounced ownership (*afkerinu*), then *bein l'Rav bein l'Shmuel* — whether one follows *Rav* or *Shmuel* — this constitutes a *bor*. It is a hazard in *reshus harabim* in the most basic sense. The question of why the *hatzad hashaveh* is needed at all for such a case will be addressed in the following section.

---

## Afkerinu & Bor

### Hefker in Public Domain

The *gemara* establishes that when objects are renounced and come to rest in *reshus harabim*, both *Rav* and *Shmuel* agree that the case constitutes a *bor*. The similarity to *bor* is clear: there is a stationary hazard in the public domain over which people may trip. Whether this is legally *mamoncha* when ownership has been disclaimed is a subtle point the *gemara* returns to — in fact, even in cases of *afkerinu*, the *gemara* continues to use the language *mamoncha ushmirasan alecha*, suggesting that the initial ownership connection may be sufficient to generate the ongoing duty, even after formal renunciation.

### Bor Definition

The *gemara* then identifies what distinguishes a classic *bor*: *techilat asiyaso lenezek* — from its very inception, the *bor* constitutes a hazard. When one digs a pit in *reshus harabim*, the act of digging is simultaneously the act of creating the danger. The *gemara* suggests that the objects that fell from the roof similarly satisfy this criterion once they have landed: once the knapsack is lying in the street, it now has the identity of a hazard, even if the object itself was not inherently dangerous when manufactured.

However, the *gemara* goes on to identify why even the *hefker* case is not a simple *bor* and therefore requires the *hatzad hashaveh*: *mah lebor she'ein koach acher meurav bo* — a classic *bor* was created directly by the person who dug it. Here, the hazard in *reshus harabim* was created not through direct action but through the combination of the owner's negligence and the wind. The wind is a *koach acher* — another force — that participated in creating the danger. One might therefore argue that the person's act is too attenuated to generate full *bor* liability.

The *gemara* resolves this through the *tzad hashaveh*: *esh tochiach* — *eish* demonstrates that even when another force contributes to the damage, the person remains liable. But one cannot simply categorize this as *eish*, because *mah le'eish sheken darko leilech ulehazik* — *eish* characteristically spreads and moves, whereas this object sits stationary in *reshus harabim*. So *bor tochiach* — *bor* demonstrates that a stationary hazard generates liability even without active movement. Since neither category alone accounts for this case — *eish* captures the *koach acher* element, *bor* captures the stationary hazard element — the *gemara* applies *v'chazar hadin*, the back-and-forth argument: the common denominator of both categories establishes liability.

The practical takeaway seems to be that the case is fundamentally a type of *bor* — one learns from *eish* not to exclude it merely because a *koach acher* was involved in its creation. This illustrates the broader analytical point: the *tzad hashaveh* may not create a free-floating generic category so much as it prevents any single distinguishing feature of one category from serving as a ground of exclusion, by showing that another category shares liability despite that feature being absent.

### Tosafot: Rav Excluded

At this point, *Tosafot* intervenes in a significant textual matter. The *gemara* as standardly printed does not include a line stating that according to *Rav*, the case where the owner did *not* renounce ownership would constitute a *shor*. *Tosafot* explains that such a line presumably appeared in earlier manuscripts, but it was removed — because according to *Rav*, the case of a knapsack that one still owns, lying in *reshus harabim*, is precisely the type of case that *requires* the *hatzad hashaveh*. It cannot simply be called a *shor*, and therefore the *gemara* cannot use it as a case where the category is already determined.

Why not? Because *shen* and *regel* — the classic manifestations of *shor* that involve movement — are *patur* in *reshus harabim*. One cannot say this stationary knapsack is a *shen* or *regel* case. And if one says it is *keren*, the response is that *keren* involves *kavanato lehazik* — intentional or habitual goring — and an inanimate object cannot be characterized that way, nor does the distinction between *tam* and *mu'ad* apply to inanimate objects (*delo shayach lechalek ela bevaalei chayyim*). So according to *Rav*, this case genuinely does not fit neatly into *shor*, and the line stating that it is a *shor* was rightly removed.

### Tosafot: Shor-Bor Hybrid

*Tosafot* then offers its own positive characterization of the case, citing *Rashbam*: the knapsack lying in *reshus harabim* that one still owns is a hybrid — *mishor umibor*, from both *shor* and *bor*. It resembles *bor* because it is stationary and presents a hazard in *reshus harabim*. It resembles *keren* — as a variant of *shor* — because unlike *bor*, it is *mamoncha*, the owner's property. A classic *bor* is specifically not the owner's property in the same sense. The combination of these two elements — owned property (*shor* dimension) sitting stationary as a hazard in *reshus harabim* (*bor* dimension) — is precisely what requires a *tzad hashaveh* to justify liability.

This clarifies *Rav*'s position substantially. When *Rav* says *kulan mishor lamadnu* — all of these cases can be derived from *shor* — he does not mean a plain *shor*. He means something that partakes of *shor* (insofar as it is owned) but must be analyzed through the *hatzad hashaveh* incorporating *bor* as well.

The contrast with *Shmuel* is equally important. *Shmuel* holds that whether one owns the object or not is not dispositive — the case is fundamentally a *bor* in either event. *Shmuel* brackets the significance of ownership; for *Shmuel*, the hazard in *reshus harabim* is the defining feature. For *Rav*, ownership is central: it pulls the case toward *shor* and away from simple *bor*, which means that for *Rav*, the owned-but-stationary case genuinely requires a *tzad hashaveh* in a way it does not for *Shmuel*.

The *nafka mina* between these positions is concrete: if one's knapsack, still owned, is lying in *reshus harabim* and breaks someone's vessels, according to *Shmuel* the case is a *bor* and the owner is exempt (*bor* is exempt for damage to vessels). According to *Rav* the case is a *shor* — and therefore the owner may be liable even for vessels. The category to which one primarily assigns the case determines which special *halachot* apply, even when the *hatzad hashaveh* is invoked to establish basic liability.

### Hatzad Hashaveh Logic

The overall logical structure is now apparent. For cases where the objects were renounced (*afkerinu*), both *Rav* and *Shmuel* agree the case is a *bor*, but it still requires the *hatzad hashaveh* because the *bor* was not created through direct action but through negligence combined with a *koach acher* (the wind). The *tzad hashaveh* between *eish* and *bor* establishes that such indirect creation does not exempt the owner. For cases where ownership was retained, *Shmuel* still characterizes the case as *bor*, while *Rav* characterizes it as a *shor-bor* hybrid requiring the *tzad hashaveh* between those two categories.

In either configuration, it is not that the *gemara* is placing the case in some generic overarching category. Rather, it is assigning the case primarily to one existing category and using the *tzad hashaveh* to prevent a distinguishing feature of another category from serving as grounds for exclusion.

---

## Rava: Bor Hamisgalgel

### Case Setup

*Rava* offers a second example of what the *tzad hashaveh* includes: *le'atuyei bor hamisgalgel beraglei adam u'vraglei beheima* — to include a *bor* (hazard) that is being kicked around by the feet of people and animals. The scenario is essentially the same knapsack left in *reshus harabim*, but now, rather than someone tripping on it where it initially landed, passersby have been kicking it around so that it comes to rest in a different location within *reshus harabim*, and ultimately someone trips and is injured there. The location of the hazard at the time of injury was not created directly by the owner, but by the accumulated movement of other people and animals.

### Renounced Status

The *gemara* asks: *heichi dami*? If the owner renounced ownership (*afkerinu*), then according to both *Rav* and *Shmuel* it is already a *bor*. The criteria for *bor* are satisfied: *techilat asiyasan lenezek* — the object's placement in *reshus harabim* constituted an original hazard — and *ushmiraso alecha* — the obligation to protect against damage attaches. Here again, notably, the criterion *mamoncha* is absent from the *gemara*'s formulation, precisely because the owner renounced ownership. Yet the analysis proceeds as if the case is a *bor* nonetheless, suggesting that the prior ownership connection — the fact that this was originally *mamoncha* — suffices to generate the duty even after *hafkara*.

### Koach Acher Issue

Even so, the case is not a simple *bor*, and the *tzad hashaveh* is needed. The reason: *mah lebor sheken ma'asav garmu lo* — by a classic *bor*, the person directly created the hazard, whether by digging the pit or by placing the knapsack. Here, the owner did not directly create the location of the hazard at the time of injury. The location was produced by others — the people and animals who kicked it. Just as the wind was a *koach acher* in *Abaye*'s case, here the feet of people and animals function as a *koach acher*: another force that moved the object to the place where it eventually caused harm.

### Shor & Bor Learn

The *gemara* applies the same *tzad hashaveh* structure: *shor yochiach* — *shor* demonstrates that liability can attach even when the owner did not perform the damaging act directly; the ox walked and gored on its own, and yet the owner is liable for his negligence. But *mah leshor sheken darko leilech ulehazik* — *shor* characteristically goes out and does active damage, whereas here someone trips on a stationary object. So *bor tochiach*, and *v'chazar hadin*: the back-and-forth between *shor* and *bor* establishes that even a hazard that was moved to its current location by others remains the owner's *bor*, and negligence in leaving the object in *reshus harabim* in the first place is sufficient. The *koach acher* of other people's feet does not sever the causal chain.

The pattern here is consistent with *Abaye*'s case. The case is fundamentally a *bor*; one learns from *shor* that even the indirect manner in which the hazard came to occupy its final position does not exempt the owner.

---

## Tosafot: Dual Liability

### Textual Variant

At this juncture, *Tosafot* addresses an important textual and conceptual question: what happens when two parties may both bear responsibility for a single act of damage? The specific scenario is: suppose someone kicks the knapsack lying in *reshus harabim* and it strikes a passerby. Is that kick the damager's *adam hamazik*, or is it the owner's *eish* — with the kicker serving as the *koach acher*, like the wind in *Abaye*'s formulation?

*Tosafot* notes that in all standard manuscripts, the *gemara* contains the line: if a person kicked the knapsack and it struck someone, *kocho hu* — it is that person's *koach*, and it constitutes an *adam hamazik*. *Rashi* apparently crossed out this line (*u'peirash b'kuntres d'lo garsinan lai*), reasoning from a later *gemara* (*b'hamaniach*) that *ein darchan shel b'nei adam l'hisbonen b'drachim* — people do not normally watch where they are going — and therefore the kicker cannot be held responsible. Under this reasoning, the kicker is analogous to the wind: a natural, expected force that the owner of the knapsack should have anticipated, making the case the owner's *eish*. *Tosafot* disagrees with *Rashi*'s deletion, arguing that *d'inyan k'dei shelo yeilchu kol kach b'chozek she'ya'iziku v'yaziku* — one should be careful enough not to kick something with such force that it injures another, and *darko l'hisbonen shapir* — a person can reasonably be expected to pay that degree of attention.

### Conscious Agent Principle

The deeper conceptual point *Tosafot* is making goes beyond the textual question. Even if both parties might theoretically bear some responsibility, *Tosafot* articulates a principle about what happens when a conscious agent — a *bar deia* — enters the picture. When a *bar deia* intervenes and through his action causes the damage, his agency eclipses the background causal role of the original owner. The act becomes entirely his.

### Dog vs. Human

*Tosafot* illustrates the contrast by reference to the famous case of a dog that takes a burning wafer (*charara*) and carries it to a haystack, igniting a fire. There, the *gemara* holds both parties liable: the owner of the fire for his *eish*, and the owner of the dog for the *shen v'regel* variant. But that is because *d'kelev lav bar deia hu* — a dog is not a *bar deia*, a conscious agent. The dog's action does not fully constitute an independent volitional act that can absorb and extinguish the other party's causal role. By contrast, *aval hacha hamikalkel o hamisgalgel bar deia hu* — here the person who kicked or moved the object is a *bar deia*, and that changes everything.

*Tosafot* makes the point vivid with an extreme illustration: if someone digs a pit and another person comes and deliberately pushes a third party's ox into it, one would not say the pit owner bears liability — the person who pushed the ox is entirely responsible. Similarly, if someone makes a fire and another person deliberately throws someone's garment into it, one cannot apportion the liability to the fire-maker. The conscious, volitional act of the second party entirely assumes the causal role.

### Adam Overrides Mamon

*Tosafot*'s conclusion follows from this: once a *bar deia* is involved, *adam hamazik* eclipses *mamon hamazik*. Even if the kicker was not acting intentionally — even if he was merely negligent — the fact that he is a conscious agent means that his action is the dominant causal event. The owner of the knapsack no longer remains a co-participant in the *nezek*; the entire act is attributed to the kicker. The *mamon hamazik* dimension of the owner's responsibility disappears in the face of the *adam hamazik* of the one who intervened.

---

## Rav Acha: Drainage Case

### Drainage Setup

*Rav Acha bar Abba* offers a third example of what the *tzad hashaveh* includes, citing a *beraita*: *kol eilu she'amru potkin bivoseihen v'gorfin meiaroseihen biyemos hachama ein lahem reshus biyemos hageshamim yeish lahem reshus* — those who open their drainpipes and sweep out their refuse pits: in the summer months, when the streets are dry, they have no right to do so; in the rainy winter season, they do have permission. This special case — where someone causes damage through an action they were *permitted* to do — is what requires the *tzad hashaveh*.

### Active vs. Static Damage

Again the *gemara* asks: *heichi dami*? If the person is actively pouring and the water or refuse strikes someone in the process (*behadi deka azlei mazikei*), that is *kocho* — direct personal force — and constitutes *adam hamazik*. The *hatzad hashaveh* is not needed for that scenario. Rather, the case of concern is where the water landed in *reshus harabim*, settled, and then someone later slipped on it. If the owner renounced his interest in it, the case becomes a *bor*: *bein l'Rav bein l'Shmuel haynu bor*, because the water settled in the public domain and created a hazard. The *gemara* again invokes *mamoncha ushmirasan alecha* even for the *afkerinu* scenario, reinforcing the notion that the original proprietary connection generates the ongoing duty.

### Permission ≠ Exemption

What genuinely requires the *tzad hashaveh* in this case is the element of *reshus* — permission. The drainpipe scenario is distinctive because the person acted with authorization. When one digs a *bor* in *reshus harabim* without permission, it is perhaps unsurprising that liability follows: not only did one create a hazard, one acted unlawfully. But this case involves someone who was explicitly permitted to pour refuse into the public domain in winter. Could that permission carry with it an implicit waiver of liability for resulting damage?

The *gemara* says: *shor yochiach* — *shor* demonstrates that liability exists even when no improper act was committed. The ox owner did nothing prohibited; his negligence in failing to watch his animal is what creates liability. But *mah leshor sheken darko leilech ulehazik* — *shor* does active damage, whereas this is a stationary hazard. *Bor tochiach*, and *v'chazar hadin*. The *hatzad hashaveh* establishes that permission to perform an act does not automatically generate exemption from damage caused through negligence as a result of that act. Even when one has the legal right to pour refuse into *reshus harabim*, one must ensure that no one is injured as a consequence. This is a striking ruling, and perhaps the most intuitively challenging of the cases discussed.

### Shor & Bor Learn

The broader principle it establishes is genuinely important. *Reshus* — whether legal permission or communal authorization — does not translate into a waiver of liability for foreseeable harm. One may always have a *takana* or explicit communal override, but absent such a special provision, the fundamental principle is that creating a hazard, even with permission, requires one to prevent damage; and if through negligence one fails to do so, liability follows.

---

## Ravina: Wall & Tree

### Mishna Rule

*Ravina* offers the final example: *le'seifa detnan* — to include what is taught in the *mishna* itself: *hakotel veha'ilan shenafelu l'reshus harabim vehiziku patur milishalem* — if a wall or tree fell into *reshus harabim* and caused damage, the owner is exempt. But if authorities had warned the owner (*natnu lo zman*) — telling him he must cut down the tree or demolish the wall within a set period — and it fell within that allotted time, the owner is still exempt (since he had not yet been negligent in failing to act). If it fell *le'achar zman* — after the allotted time expired — he is liable.

### Case Setup

Once again the *gemara* asks: *heichi dami*? We again assume the scenario involves someone tripping on the fallen debris (not being struck during the fall, which will be addressed separately). If the owner renounced ownership (*afkerinu*), the case resembles a *bor*: *hanami hezeika matzui ushmiraso alecha* — here too damage is prevalent and the obligation to prevent it applies.

### Techilat Asiyaso Issue

Here, however, a crucial distinction emerges. In the earlier cases, the *gemara* could characterize the fallen objects as having *techilat asiyasan lenezek* once they were positioned in *reshus harabim* — their very placement there constituted their identity as a hazard. But a wall or a tree is different. When the owner originally built the wall or planted the tree, there was nothing hazardous about it. The object only became a hazard later, through deterioration or some other change in circumstances. Therefore, the *gemara* deliberately shifts its language away from *techilat asiyaso lenezek* and instead uses *hezeika matzui* — damage is prevalent — as the operative description.

When the *gemara* then tries to characterize this as a *bor*, the objection arises: *mah lebor sheken techilat asiyaso lenezek* — a classic *bor* starts life as a hazard. *Tomar behani she'ein techilat asiyatan lenezek* — but here the object did not start life as a hazard.

### Shor Learns

So: *shor yochiach* — *shor* demonstrates that an object need not start life as a hazard in order to generate liability. The ox was not born as a *keren*; it only became dangerous later. Yet the owner is liable for failing to prevent damage once the dangerous propensity manifested. *Mah leshor sheken darko leilech ulehazik*, and *bor yochiach*, and *v'chazar hadin*. The *hatzad hashaveh* establishes that even an object that did not originate as a hazard — a wall that stood peacefully for years before becoming dangerous — can generate *bor*-style liability once it presents a foreseeable hazard and the owner is negligent in failing to address it.

What is particularly striking about this series of cases is that all the examples generated by the *hatzad hashaveh* turn out to be variants of *bor*: a *bor* created through *koach acher*; a *bor* displaced by *koach acher*; a *bor* created with permission; and now a *bor* whose hazardous character emerged only after its initial creation. The exception, for *Rav*, is the owned knapsack in *reshus harabim*, which he characterizes as a *shor-bor* hybrid. But the dominant pattern is that the *tzad hashaveh* is being used to expand the operative scope of *bor* in cases where one of its defining characteristics — direct creation, stationary placement from the outset, absence of permission, or *techilat asiyaso lenezek* — is absent.

### Tosafot: Fall Damage

*Tosafot* raises one additional question at the bottom of *vav amud aleph*: what is the status of damage that occurs *during* the fall of the wall or tree, before it comes to rest? Should this not be characterized as *eish*, given the involvement of another force (gravity) in motion? Interestingly, *Tosafot* suggests that even damage during the fall could be characterized as *bor* rather than *eish*. The reasoning: *eish* characteristically spreads, moves through the medium of wind, and generates damage over a wide area. Gravity is not a *koach acher* of the same type as wind; it merely causes the object to fall within a limited vertical space, not to spread across *reshus harabim*. *Tosafot* therefore describes the falling tree as a moving *bor* — *af al gav d'bor ein holech umazzik v'elu holchim umazikin* — even though a classic *bor* does not move, one can learn from the stationary *bor* (which causes damage to those who come to it) that even a moving object that damages within its confined trajectory constitutes a *bor* variant rather than an *eish*. This is perhaps the most genuinely hybrid characterization of all the cases discussed.

*Tosafot* also raises the question of timing in the case of debris that has already fallen: must the owner be held immediately liable once it lands in *reshus harabim*, or is there a reasonable period during which he cannot yet be considered negligent in failing to clear it? *Tosafot* suggests that even after the wall falls, there may be some allowance of time for the owner to act before liability attaches — a point that connects directly to the broader question of how negligence is assessed circumstantially.

---

## Liability & Payment

### Damager's Obligation

The *mishna* concludes the section on the common denominator with the statement that when damage occurs, *chav hamazik leshalem tashlumei nezek* — the damager incurs a debt to pay the damages.

### Chav vs. Chayav

The *gemara* notes a linguistic peculiarity: the *mishna* uses the word *chav* rather than the more standard *chayav*. *Rav Yehuda* says in the name of *Rav*: *hai tanna Yerushalmi hu d'tani lishna kalila* — this *tanna* is from Jerusalem, and they speak a lighter, more refined dialect. *Tosafot* observes that *chav* is not unheard of elsewhere — it appears in contexts like *hamagbi'ah metziah l'chaveiro b'makom shechav l'acheirim* — but that *chav* specifically denotes incurring a debt, while *chayav* denotes being obligated. The *mishna*'s use of *chav* signals the creation of a monetary obligation.

### Meitav Sadeihu

The *mishna* specifies that payment is from *meitav ha'aretz* — the best of the land. The *gemara* will now investigate where this standard is derived from the verse and what it precisely means. The verse in question is *meitav sadehu umeitav karmo yeshalem* — he shall pay the best of his field and the best of his vineyard — and the dispute between *Rabbi Yishmael* and *Rabbi Akiva* turns on how to read that verse in relation to the injured party and the damager respectively.

---

## Yishmael vs. Akiva

### Yishmael: Nizak Standard

*Rabbi Yishmael* rules: *meitav sadehu shel nizak umeitav karmo shel nizak* — the payment is measured against the best of the *nizak*'s field and the best of the *nizak*'s vineyard. In other words, the quality benchmark for collection is set by the injured party's own property, not the damager's.

### Akiva: Mazik Standard

*Rabbi Akiva* disagrees: *lo ba hakatuv ela ligbot lenizakin min ha'idit* — the verse comes only to teach that damages are collected from the highest quality land. For *Rabbi Akiva*, this refers to the highest quality of the *mazik*'s own land. The amount of the debt is fixed by the damage actually caused — one hundred dollars is one hundred dollars — but that sum is to be extracted from the best grade of *Reuven*'s (the *mazik*'s) property. *Rabbi Akiva* adds: *vechol shekein lehekdesh* — certainly when *hekdesh* (consecrated property) is the collector, it collects from the highest quality available.

### Initial Interpretation

The *gemara* initially reads *Rabbi Yishmael*'s position in a striking way. When he says one pays the best of the *nizak*'s land, the plain reading might suggest that whatever quality the animal actually ate is irrelevant — the *mazik* must always compensate as if the animal ate from the finest crop. If the animal ate from a poor quality field, one might still owe compensation at the rate of the best. This reading makes *Rabbi Yishmael*'s position seem quite severe.

### Rav Idi Clarifies
