One might have assumed that only the intervening act of a fully competent *ben da'at* could break the causal chain between an owner's negligence and resulting damage. Rabbi Yochanan holds that even the act of a legally incompetent individual suffices — the human act itself, not the actor's legal status, is what matters.

The *sugya* of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on this point will be addressed more fully in a later section of *Gemara*; here it is introduced only in the context of the *Baraita*. What the *Mishnah* ultimately emphasizes, however, is the centrality of the owner's negligence as the grounding of his liability. The *mazik* is called a *mazik* not because his property mechanically caused harm, but because he — in failing his duty of supervision — effectively brought that harm about.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 10

## Meitav & Negligence

### Opening Context

We arrive at Daf 10 having just completed several pages devoted to the concept of *meitav* — the form of payment required when one owes compensation for damages — and we now turn to what will occupy the bulk of the *masecheta*: the direct question of *mamon hamazik*, when one's property or one's own actions cause damage and under what circumstances liability follows. The previous *mishna* was notably cryptic, its language archaic and seemingly quite old, and it concluded by repeating the refrain of the very first *mishna* of the tractate: *kshe-hizik chav hamazik leshalem tashlumei nezek mimeitav ha'aretz* — when animals or property cause damage, one pays with the best of the land.

### Negligence Principle

The *mishna* framed this principle with a striking formulation: *chavti bishmirato hichsharti nizko* — when I was obligated to watch and I was negligent and did not watch, it is as though I laid the groundwork for the damage that would occur. This framing bears on a fundamental conceptual question that runs throughout the *masecheta*: is one liable because one's animal or property did the damage, or is one liable because one's negligence brought it about? The *mishna* clearly seems to emphasize the latter — that one has ultimately prepared and enabled the damage.

### Fire Exemption Debate

The *Gemara* used this emphasis on negligence as an occasion to examine a related question: the case in which one gives over an ox or a well, or a fire, to a *cheresh shoteh ve-katan* — a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor — as custodians. In such a case, one is more liable for the ox and the well than for the fire. This was the subject of a debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, which we will encounter more fully in approximately two weeks in a dedicated *sugya*. For now, the brief summary is that Reish Lakish holds the *cheresh shoteh ve-katan* is adequate custodianship for fire because if given only an ember, it will die out on its own — the inadequate custodian neither improves nor worsens the situation, and the fire extinguishes itself. Rabbi Yochanan, however, holds that even where the fire is a live flame, one would be exempt, a position we will explore in greater detail later.

---

## Avot Nezikin Comparison

### Shor vs Bor Setup

With that background in place — and keeping in mind the distinction that fire carries a more lenient rule in the *cheresh shoteh ve-katan* case — the *Gemara* proceeds to a *braita* that compares and contrasts the different *avot nezikin*, much as we have done earlier in the tractate. The *braita* opens: *chomer bashor mibabor ve-chomer babor mibashor* — there are respects in which *shor* (the ox, specifically in the context of goring) is more stringent than *bor* (the pit), and respects in which *bor* is more stringent than *shor*.

### Shor Weightier Points

The ways in which *shor* is weightier than *bor*: first, *she-shor meshalem et hakofer* — if a *mu'ad* ox gores a person and that person dies, the owner pays *kofer*, an atonement payment. By contrast, if a person falls into a well and dies, there is no *kofer* payment; the *kofer* applies only when an ox or similar animal kills a person, not when a person dies in a pit. Second, *ve-chayav bishloshim shel eved* — if the ox kills a slave, the owner pays the fixed penalty of thirty *shekel* of silver. Again, this does not apply when a well causes a slave's death. Third, *nigmar dino asur behana'ah* — there is the category of *shor haniskal*: if an ox has been judged by a court to have killed someone, it is forbidden in benefit even before it is stoned, from the very moment its judgment is rendered. This status of *shor haniskal* does not apply to any other category.

### Shor Characteristics

In terms of its character, *shor* is also weightier because *darko leilech ulehazik* — it goes out and creates damage; damage does not merely come to it, as is the case with the stationary pit.

### Bor Weightier Points

The ways in which *bor* is weightier than *shor*: *shehabor techilat asiyato lenezek* — the well, from the very moment it was created, is a hazard. An ox is born as a harmless calf; its entire identity is not from the outset that of a danger. Furthermore, *umuad mitechilato* — in contrast specifically to the goring category, where a *tam* ox does not have an established propensity to gore and therefore pays only half-damages because the harm is unanticipated, the well from its very beginning has the propensity to cause damage, and the harm it causes is to be expected. *Techilat asiyato lenezek* thus captures both that the well's identity is inherently hazardous and that the damage it causes is foreseeable. None of these things are true of *shor*.

### Shor vs Fire Setup

The *braita* now turns to comparing *shor* to *esh* (fire), examining both directions: *chomer bashor mibe'esh* and *chomer be'esh mibashor*.

### Shor Fire Penalties

The ways in which *shor* is weightier than *esh*: as established, these will always be the monetary payments triggered by death — *kofer* for a free person, the thirty-*shekel* payment for a slave, and the status of *shor haniskal*. All of these apply only to the *keren* category and not to fire. In addition — and here the *braita* introduces something new that ties back to our earlier discussion — *mesaro lacheresh shoteh vekatan chayav*: if one gave an ox to a *cheresh shoteh ve-katan* to watch, one remains liable, because even if the ox is bound, it is likely to struggle free, and such custodianship is therefore insufficient. This is not so for fire — *ma she'ein ken be'esh* — where the *cheresh shoteh ve-katan*'s custody is deemed adequate. The characteristic *darko leilech ulehazik* was not listed as a distinction here because fire too has the character of *darko leilech ulehazik* — it spreads and creates damage — and so that cannot serve as a point of contrast.

### Fire Weightier Fire

The ways in which *esh* is weightier than *shor*: *she'esh mu'edet mitechilatah* — fire has a propensity to cause damage from its very inception, *ma she'ein ken beshur*, which is not true of *shor* in the goring category. An ox is not presumed from the outset to have the propensity to gore; the first time it gores it pays only half-damages. Fire, by contrast, is considered *mu'ad* from its very first occurrence.

### Bor vs Fire Setup

Having compared *shor* to *bor* and *shor* to *esh*, the *braita* now addresses the one remaining pair: *bor* versus *esh*.

### Bor Fire Inherent

The ways in which *bor* is weightier than *esh*: *shetechilat asiyato lenezek* — the pit, from its inception, is a hazard. Lighting a fire in one's own property is not analogous to placing a pit in the public domain; the pit's very placement constitutes the danger. And again, *mesaro lacheresh shoteh vekatan chayav* — one remains liable when handing over custodianship of a well to a *cheresh shoteh ve-katan*, because even a covered well requires responsible oversight to ensure the cover does not break. By contrast, for fire — *ma she'ein ken be'esh* — one is exempt when giving a *gachelet* (ember) to a *cheresh shoteh ve-katan*.

### Fire Unfit Items

The ways in which *esh* is weightier than *bor*: *she'esh darchah leilech ulehazik* — fire goes out and creates damage, unlike the pit to which things must come. And further, *umu'edet le'echol bein davar hara'ui lah bein davar she'eino ra'ui lah* — fire has a propensity to consume both things that are fit for it and things that are not fit for it, which is *ma she'ein ken bebor*, not the case by the pit. The meaning of *davar she'eino ra'ui lah* will require unpacking, and the *Gemara* will return to it shortly.

---

## Keilim Exemptions

### Keilim Omission

At this point the *Gemara* raises a challenge: why did the *braita* omit a significant distinction between *shor* and *bor*? The *Gemara* asks: *u'litnei chomer beshor mibabor she-shor chayav bo es hakeilim ma she'ein ken bebor* — an ox is liable for damages to *keilim* (vessels), whereas a well is exempt from liability for *keilim*. This exemption derives from the famous *derasha* on the verse *venafal shamah shor o chamor*: *shor velo adam, chamor velo keilim* — the Torah's specification of "ox or donkey" teaches that one is liable for animals but not for persons (in the death context), and for donkeys but not for vessels. The *shor velo adam* is less intuitive — if a person is injured by falling into a well, one would of course be liable for injury — and that passage concerns the exemption from *kofer* in the death case. But the more commonly discussed exclusion is *chamor velo keilim*: if vessels are damaged in a pit, the owner of the pit is exempt. Since *shor* is liable for *keilim* and *bor* is exempt, why was this not listed as a way in which *shor* is weightier?

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

The *Gemara* answers: *ha mani Rabbi Yehuda hi* — this *braita* reflects the view of Rabbi Yehuda, *de-michayev al nizkei keilim bebor*, who holds that one is in fact liable for vessel damage caused by a pit and rejects the *derasha* that would exempt *keilim*. According to Rabbi Yehuda, there is no exemption for *keilim* in *bor*, and so the distinction cannot be listed.

### Unfit Definition

But the *Gemara* now uses this to probe the meaning of *davar she'eino ra'ui lah*. The line in the *braita* says fire is weightier than *bor* because it consumes things unfit for it, *ma she'ein ken bebor*. The *Gemara* asks: *davar hara'ui lah mai nihu* — what is normally fit for fire? *Eitzim* — wood and ordinary fuel. *Davar she'eino ra'ui lah mai nihu* — what is unfit? *Keilim* — vessels. Fire does not normally burn vessels in the way it burns wood, yet if it does, one is liable. And this is in contrast to *bor*, where *keilim* are exempt. So this line is understood to be making the same *keilim* distinction: one is liable for vessel damage caused by fire, exempt for vessel damage by a pit. If the *braita* is going according to Rabbi Yehuda, however, and Rabbi Yehuda holds that even *bor* is liable for *keilim*, then that distinction disappears and this line no longer makes sense.

### Incomplete List Theory

The *Gemara* therefore offers an alternative: *ella lerabbanan vetannei veshayar* — the *braita* follows the Rabbanan, and *davar she'eino ra'ui lah* does refer to *keilim*, but the list is simply incomplete. It omitted the *keilim* distinction in the *shor-bor* comparison even though it existed. The *Gemara* then immediately asks, as it always does when told a list is incomplete: *mai shayar de-hai shayar* — what else did it leave off? Because one cannot posit an incomplete list that omitted only a single item.

### Tamun Omission

The *Gemara* answers: *shayer tamun* — it also omitted *tamun*, buried or hidden items. This is a useful occasion for a brief review: each category of *avot nezikin* has its own special exemption. *Shen veregel* is exempt in the public domain. *Bor* is exempt for *keilim*. *Esh* is exempt for *devarim hamitmanim* — things that are buried or hidden. If a fire burns something concealed in a haystack, the owner of the fire is exempt, whereas if an ox walks on something buried in a haystack, the owner is liable. So *shor* is weightier than *esh* in the *tamun* case as well, and this too was omitted from the list. The list thus left off at minimum both *keilim* and *tamun*, which justifies characterizing it as incomplete.

### Tosafot Unlikely Damage

The *Gemara* also — in a second answer, *iba'it eima leolam Rabbi Yehuda* — returns to the possibility that the *braita* follows Rabbi Yehuda. In that case, since Rabbi Yehuda holds one is liable for *keilim* even in *bor*, *davar she'eino ra'ui lah* cannot refer to *keilim*. What then does it mean? The *Gemara* explains: *lav le'atuyei keilim ella le'atuyei likhukha d'niro vesikhsukha d'avnav* — it comes to include a case where fire scorches someone's fallow field or singes their rocks. This is *she'eino ra'ui lah* — unfit for it — in the sense that it is an unlikely thing for fire to damage significantly.

This raises two questions, both of which Tosafot addresses. First, why is damage to a fallow field or rocks considered *she'eino ra'ui lah*? Second, what is the contrast with *bor* — what is the *ma she'ein ken bebor*?

On the first question: Tosafot explains that it is not that fire cannot spread to a fallow field, but that it is very unlikely for fire to cause meaningful damage to rocks or to a field that lacks standing produce or significant fuel. A fallow field may contain incidental growth from dropped seeds or other random vegetation, but there is little for a fire to catch onto in a serious way, and rocks by their nature absorb little damage. Yet even in such a case, if fire does cause damage, one is liable.

On the second question, Tosafot addresses the contrast with *bor*. Rashi appears to suggest the comparison is that a fallow field cannot fall into a well — but Tosafot dismisses this as an absurd basis for comparison. One could say the same of countless things that cannot fall into a well; you do not compare liability in possible cases to liability in impossible ones. Instead, Tosafot explains the contrast as follows: if a well is only nine *tefachim* deep, it is not categorized as capable of causing death, only damage. If an animal nonetheless dies in a nine-*tefach* well, one is exempt — because one is not liable for damage that was not normally to be anticipated from that particular pit. By contrast, fire is liable even for unlikely damage — damage to rocks and fallow fields that fire would not normally affect. Thus *ma she'ein ken bebor*: the pit exempts for unanticipated damage, whereas fire does not. This resolves the difficulty without needing to invoke *keilim* at all, and it allows the *braita* to work even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *bor* is liable for *keilim*.

### Psulei Mukdashim

Rav Ashi raises a further challenge. He notes an additional distinction that was omitted: *she-hashor chayav bo shor psulei hamukdashim ma she'ein ken babor* — an ox is liable if it gores an ox that was once consecrated as a *korban* but became disqualified and was redeemed, known as *shor psulei hamukdashim*. Such an animal remains one's property — one may slaughter and eat it, though with certain restrictions — and if another ox gores it, the damaging owner is liable. Yet if this same animal falls into a pit, the owner of the pit is exempt. Why was this not listed as another way in which *shor* is weightier than *bor*?

The *Gemara* responds that if the *braita* follows the Rabbanan — as in the earlier answer — this presents no difficulty: *aidi de-shayer hacha shayer nami hacha*, since we have already established the list is incomplete, having omitted *keilim*, *tamun*, and now *psulei hamukdashim* as well. The list is simply abbreviated and there is no need to account for every omission. But if the *braita* follows Rabbi Yehuda, this becomes problematic, because Rabbi Yehuda not only accepts liability for *keilim* in *bor* but also — as the *Gemara* notes — rejects the exemption for *tamun* in *esh*. Under Rabbi Yehuda's view, the only thing actually omitted is *psulei hamukdashim*, and one cannot posit an incomplete list that left off only a single item.

The *Gemara* considers whether *dash binira* — an ox that inadvertently plows a fallow field — might serve as another omitted item to justify an incomplete list under Rabbi Yehuda. Rashi characterizes this as *keren*, describing it as intentional-type damage because the ox is habituated to plowing. However, the *Gemara* rejects this answer: *de-tana she-ken darko leilech ulehazik* — the distinction that an ox goes out and creates damage, while the pit can only damage things that come to it, already encompasses the idea that an ox damages things incapable of moving to it, such as a field. The *dash binira* case is already subsumed within *darko leilech ulehazik* and adds nothing new. The *Gemara* therefore concludes that the *braita* does not work according to Rabbi Yehuda; the *maskana* is that it follows the Rabbanan.

---

## Partial Negligence

### Partial Preparation

The *Gemara* now turns to the second cryptic phrase in the *mishna*: *hichsharti bemiktzat nizko chavti betashlumei nizko ke-hachshar kol nizko* — even if I prepared only part of the damage, I am liable for all of it, as though I had prepared the entire damage. This is the principle of partial preparation carrying full liability.

### Two Diggers Case

The *braita* that fleshes out this principle is as follows: *ha-chofer bor tisha* — Reuven digs a pit nine *tefachim* deep. A nine-*tefach* pit is liable for damage but not for death, as we have established. *U-va acher ve-hishlimo le-asara* — Shimon then comes and digs the tenth *tefach*, completing the pit. If an animal dies in the well, it is obviously only Shimon's responsibility, since Reuven's nine-*tefach* pit was not capable of causing death. But the *chiddush* concerns damage: one might reasonably assume Reuven and Shimon should split the liability for *nezek*, since Reuven already created something capable of causing damage. The *braita* teaches otherwise: *ha'acharon chayav* — the last one is fully liable, even for *nezek*. This ruling is *v'd'lo k'Rabbi* — not in accordance with Rabbi.

### Rabbi vs Rabbanan

A separate *braita* records Rabbi's position: *achar acharon l'misa, v'achar shneihem l'nezikin* — the last one is indeed fully liable for death, but for damage they are both liable. The *tanna kamma*, by contrast, holds that the last one is fully liable even for *nezek*. The *Gemara* cites Tosafot's reference to a *pasuk*: *ki yichre ish bor* — one person digs the pit — *echad ve-lo shnayim*, one and not two, meaning that even when two people dig, there are cases in which only one bears the full liability.

### Transformation Principle

Why should the last person bear full liability for *nezek*, rather than sharing it proportionally with Reuven? The key, as Tosafot explains, is the concept of *transformation*. The liability falls entirely on Shimon not simply because he did the last act, but because his act qualitatively transformed the nature of the pit. Reuven created a *bor* of *nezek* — a pit categorized as capable of causing damage. Shimon transformed it into a *bor* of *misa* — a pit categorized as capable of causing death. Because Shimon changed its fundamental identity, the pit is now entirely identified as his, and he is liable for everything it does, including *nezek*.

This contrasts with a case where two people each dig equal amounts that remain within the same category. If one person digs four *tefachim* and another adds four more, both contributing to a *bor* of *nezek* without either transforming it into a different category, they would both be liable. The *chiddush* applies only when the last person changes the pit's identity from one legal category to another. This is the only scenario in which the principle *ki yichre ish bor — echad ve-lo shnayim* operates to assign sole liability to the last actor.

One might ask about intermediate cases — say, one person digs eight *tefachim* and another adds one. The answer to this connects to the deeper conceptual models underlying the entire discussion. If one understands liability as rooted in *ownership* of the *bor*, then once both parties participate in digging, they are like joint owners and would split equally regardless of proportion, just as joint owners of an ox each bear liability for what that ox does. If, however, one understands liability as rooted in *negligence and fault*, then proportional contribution becomes relevant, and one who dug eight *tefachim* might bear greater liability than one who dug only one. These models — ownership versus negligence — are precisely the two frameworks the *mishna* has been gesturing toward throughout, and they carry real practical consequences for how liability is distributed in joint-causation scenarios.

### Liability Levels

Rav Pappa offers a clarification: *lemisa divrei hakol* — with respect to death, all agree that the last person who deepened the pit to ten *tefachim* is fully liable, even though Reuven's nine *tefachim* laid the groundwork. This is less of a *chiddush* since Shimon is the one who created the death-capable pit, though it is still noteworthy that even the partial groundwork Reuven laid does not make him share in the death liability at all. For *nezikin*, that is where the debate lies: the *tanna kamma* holds the last one is fully liable, while Rabbi holds they split it.

---

## Contributory Cases

### Zeira Challenge

Rabbi Zeira challenges: *v'tu leka* — are there really no other cases where one does only a little and is nevertheless fully liable for everything? He proposes cases that should also fit the *mishna*'s principle, and then subjects them to scrutiny.

### Five Watchers

The first case: *masar shor le-chamisha bnei adam* — one entrusts an ox to five people to guard together. *U-pasha bo echad mehen* — one of the five is negligent, and because of his negligence the ox escapes and causes damage. Is the one negligent party fully liable? The *Gemara* deconstructs this into two scenarios. If *bilav ihu lo havi mintar* — without him, the remaining four would not have been sufficient to guard the ox — then *peshita*, of course he is liable; his negligence was entirely responsible for the lapse in guarding. That is not a novel case. If, on the other hand, *bilav ihu nami mintar* — actually one person would have been sufficient and the five were simply redundant — then *ma ka'avid*, what has the negligent one actually done? His departure did not genuinely expose the ox to danger, since four capable people remained. In that case, the departure cannot be characterized as *peshi'ah* at all, because the effective level of guarding was not diminished by his absence. Either scenario thus fails to generate the interesting case the *mishna* contemplates — it is either obvious or it is simply not a genuine case of liability.

### Fire Addition

Rav Sheshet offers a second case: *ha'ika marbe be-chavila* — what about one who adds a bundle of wood to someone else's fire, and the fire then spreads and causes damage? The same analysis applies. If *bilav ihu lo azla* — without the additional wood the fire would not have spread — *peshita*, it is obviously his fire now. But if *bilav ihu azla* — the fire would have spread regardless — *mai ka'avid*, what did he actually contribute?

### Tosafot Fire Analysis

Tosafot pushes back on the simple reading of *mai ka'avid* as meaning the additional party is entirely exempt. Tosafot holds that one cannot simply say: the fire was going to spread anyway, so I bear no responsibility for having thrown more wood on it. Tosafot cites the case from the next *perek* where one person digs a pit to ten *tefachim*, a second deepens it to twenty, and a third deepens it to thirty — all are liable, even though the animal would have died at ten. So too, one who adds fuel to a spreading fire should bear some liability.

Yet Tosafot is genuinely uncertain about the threshold. He asks: *v'chi bishvil she-hishlich ish etz be-toch esh gedola yitchayev* — if Michael has a huge bonfire and I throw my toothpick into it, does it become equally my fire? That is clearly not the intent. Tosafot observes that this is analogous to one person digging a pit to ten *tefachim* and another deepening it to ten thousand; the trivial contribution cannot generate equal liability. But Tosafot does not resolve where the threshold lies — at what point does one's addition of fuel make it sufficiently "one's fire" to generate full or proportional liability? These questions are left open. The underlying tension, as noted above, is between an ownership model — who owns this fire? — and a negligence model — whose act actually brought about the damage? By *bor*, the ownership model is more tractable because a pit stays in place and can be quantified; by fire, which spreads dynamically, the negligence or causation model may be more appropriate, and causation analysis is sensitive to whether the damage would have occurred regardless of one's contribution.

---

## Bench Weight Case

### Six on Bench

Rav Papa introduces a *braita* rather than a thought exercise: *chamisha she-yasvu al safsal echad ve-lo shivruhu, u-va echad ve-yashav alav ve-shivruhu* — five people sat on a bench and it did not break; a sixth person sat on it and it broke. *Ha'acharon chayav* — the last one is fully liable. Rav Papa notes the case is like *Papa bar Abba*, evidently a notably weighty individual, whose additional mass caused the bench to collapse.

### Bench Conditions

The *Gemara* poses the familiar challenge: what exactly is the scenario? If *bilav ihu lo itbar* — without him the bench would not have broken — then *peshita*, obviously the sixth person is liable, he exceeded the weight limit. If *bilav ihu nami itbar* — the bench was already going to break with just five people — then *ma ka'avid*, what did the sixth person do?

### Acceleration Principle

The *Gemara* resolves this: *de-bilav ihu hava itbar bi-trei sha'ei ve-hashta itbar be-chada sha'a* — without the sixth person the bench would have broken in two hours, but with him it broke in one hour. He accelerated the damage. Now this is a genuine *chiddush*: one might argue that the first five people, by sitting on an overloaded bench, were already doing something wrong and bear responsibility. The sixth person sat down in circumstances where damage was already foreseeable. Why should he bear full liability? The *Gemara* explains that the five could argue: *ilu lav at haveinan yasvinan tutei purta ve-kaiman* — had you not arrived, we would have gotten up before the bench broke. During that first hour, nothing would have happened; only because you came did the break occur within this hour. So it is your *nezek*, not ours.

The sixth person might counter: *ilu lav atun bididi lo hava itbar* — if not for you being here with me, it would not have broken. The *Gemara* accepts this counter-argument as valid, and reverses itself: since the first five were already in a situation where the bench would eventually break, and they were not getting up, they too bear responsibility. The *Gemara* understands their continued sitting — even in the first hour where nothing would yet break — as participatory in the eventual damage, because they are sitting in circumstances under which breakage could occur. The bench is, in a sense, being damaged incrementally with every moment of excess weight. All parties are therefore liable.

### Holding Down

The *Gemara* then presents a distinct case: *de-samach behu tavar* — what if one does not sit on the bench but instead leans on or holds down one of the five people, preventing them from rising, so that the bench breaks under the weight of the five? Here the principle invoked is *kocho kegufoy dami* — one's force or energy is equivalent to one's body. The person who prevented another from rising is liable, even though it was not his own body weight that broke the bench, but rather the weight of the person he restrained. The *chiddush* is that preventing someone from getting up — rather than adding one's own weight — is treated as an exercise of force legally equivalent to one's own bodily action. There is genuine uncertainty in the *rishonim* about whether Rashi means the person was actively pushing down or simply blocking the other from standing; if the latter, the case is a more dramatic *chiddush* because the restraining person added no weight at all.

### Kocho Principle

The principle is articulated as follows: *de-heikha de-gufey tavar, kocho nami tavar* — wherever one's body would have broken it, one's *koach* — one's force or energy — also breaks it. One is liable through *kocho* in the same way one is liable through direct bodily action.

---

## Multiple Beatings

### Ten Beatings Setup

The *braita* presenting the final case: *hiku'u asarah b'nei adam be-asarah maklot, bein be-vas achas bein be-zeh achar zeh, u-met, kulam peturim* — ten people beat a victim with sticks, either simultaneously or sequentially, and the victim dies. All are exempt. Since each person contributed only a partial, non-lethal blow, no individual can be held fully liable for the death.

### Sequential Causation

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira dissents: *be-zeh achar zeh ha'acharon chayav mipnei she-keirev misaso* — if the beatings were sequential, the last person is liable because he brought about the death. Everyone else had beaten the victim to within an inch of his life; the last blow closed that final gap. The last person is therefore the proximate cause of death. This is the principle of *keirev misaso* — bringing about death — as a basis for sole liability even when others contributed.

### Gemara Resolution

The *Gemara* clarifies why the *mishna*'s earlier case — the tenth *tefach* of the pit — need not be seen as reflecting Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira's minority view. The *mishna* there concerns *nezikin*, financial liability, not capital punishment; the *masechet* is not *b'ktala ka mairy*, not dealing with the death penalty context in which Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira's ruling would be relevant. Furthermore, *d'plugta lo ka mairy* — the *Gemara* will not establish a *mishna* as following a minority position. The earlier ruling that the one who dug the tenth *tefach* is liable even for *nezek* follows the Rabbanan against Rabbi; establishing that ruling requires invoking a majority position. But to have the *mishna* follow Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira against the Rabbanan — *lo mukminan* — that we will not do.

### Contributory Summary

These final *sugyot* bring to a close a recurring theme throughout the first *perek*: the problem of contributory negligence and last-actor liability. When are all parties equally exempt, as in the ten-beatings case? When is the last party alone fully liable, as in the tenth-*tefach* case? When should liability be distributed proportionally, and when equally? When does a trivial contribution trigger no liability at all, and when does even a small act — the sixth person on the bench, the one who deepens a pit by a single *tefach* — carry full responsibility? These questions recur in various forms throughout the *masecheta* and will receive much fuller treatment in the *sugyot* to come.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 11

## Tashlumei Nezek

### Mishna: Tashlumei Nezek

The *mishna* that enumerates the *avot nezikin* concludes with the phrase *chavti betashlumei nizko* — "I have incurred the obligation of *tashlumei nizko*," the compensation for the damage. The *gemara* immediately notices a subtle but significant linguistic choice: the *mishna* does not say *chavti benizko*, "I am liable for the damage itself," but rather *betashlumei nizko*, for the *payment* of the damage. This leads directly to a *beraita* that explicates the phrase.

### Owners & Carcass

The *beraita* teaches: *tashlumei nezek melamed shehabealim metaplin benevelah* — the phrase "payment of damage" comes to teach that the owners, meaning the owners of the animal that was killed or injured, retain responsibility for and ownership of the carcass. The practical illustration is straightforward. If a bull gores a cow worth one hundred dollars, and the carcass is now worth ten dollars, the owner of the bull pays ninety dollars — the loss in value — and does not "buy" the dead animal. The original owner continues to own the carcass. It is not a case of "you break it, you buy it." The *mazik* caused a one-hundred-dollar cow to become a ten-dollar carcass; he pays the ninety-dollar difference, and the *nizak* retains the carcass.

### Makeh Behema Source

The *gemara* asks: *mina hani milei* — from where is this derived? Perhaps the *mazik* would have to pay the full one hundred dollars and take the carcass in return. Rabbi Ami answers from the *pasuk* in Shemos: *makeh nefesh behemah yeshalmena* — one who strikes and kills an animal shall pay for it. The *gemara* reads this through the lens of *al tikrei yeshalmena ella yashlimena* — do not read "shall pay for it" but rather "shall complete" or "shall supplement" the value. That is, if a person kills a cow worth one hundred that is now worth ten, he does not pay the full hundred; he supplements the difference, paying ninety. The object itself remains with its original owner; the *mazik* pays only for the damage his actions caused.

### Shomer & Hatreifah

Rav Kahana offers a different *pasuk* as the source. In the case of a *shomer* whose animal was killed by a wild beast, the *pasuk* reads: *im tarof yitaref yevi'eihu ed hatereifah lo yeshalem* — if it is torn up he shall bring testimony, and for the *tereifah* itself he shall not pay. Rav Kahana understands *yevi'eihu ad hatereifah yeshalem* — he pays up to the value of the dead animal — but *tereifah atzmah lo yeshalem* — for the carcass itself he does not pay. The *shomer* pays the difference between what the animal was worth and what the carcass is worth now, but the carcass itself belongs to the original owner and remains his.

### Goring & Ownership

Chizkiyah derives the same principle from a third *pasuk*, concerning an ox that gores another ox: *shallem yeshalem shor tachat hashor vahamet yihiyeh lo* — he shall pay an ox for an ox, and the dead animal shall be his. The question is: who is the *yihiyeh lo*, who gets the carcass? The *gemara* reads this as *hamet yihiyeh lo lanizak* — the carcass belongs to the *nizak*, the damaged party. This is admittedly a strained reading. The plain sense of *shor tachat hashor* sounds like full replacement — you break it, you buy it, you pay the whole ox and take the carcass. Chizkiyah and the *gemara* read it differently: pay for the damage you created, and the *hamet yihiyeh lo* tells us the carcass stays with the *nizak* rather than reinforcing the simple reading of complete replacement.

The *gemara* defends this reading through an argument raised by Abaye. If one were to understand *vahamet yihiyeh lo* as meaning the *mazik* takes the carcass and pays the full value, then the *pasuk shor tachat hashor* would have sufficed. Why add the phrase *vahamet yihiyeh lo* at all? The fact that it adds this phrase signals that it is not reinforcing the simple reading of full payment but rather modifying it — informing us that the carcass stays with the *nizak* and the *mazik* pays only the difference.

### Three Cases Logic

The *gemara* then asks: *utzricha* — is it really necessary that all three cases be stated? Could one not have been derived from another?

The *gemara* works through each possibility. The first *pasuk*, concerning a person who directly kills an animal (*makeh behemah*), involves a rare act. One might have thought that because it is uncommon, the Torah went easy on the *mazik* and left the carcass with the *nizak*, but that perhaps in the more common case of a *shomer* whose animal is torn by a wild beast, the Torah would be more protective of the *nizak* and require the *mazik* to pay everything, absorbing the carcass. The *tereifah* case therefore needed to be stated. Conversely, had only the *tereifah* case been stated — where the harm is indirect, *mimayla*, the *shomer* being passively rather than actively responsible — one might have thought the Torah goes easy on the *shomer* precisely because his culpability is passive. But when a person directly kills an animal *biyadayim*, perhaps the *mazik* should bear full responsibility for the carcass. Thus the *makeh behemah* case was also necessary.

Even granting both of those cases, there would still be need for the *pasuk* of the goring ox. Each of the first two cases has one mitigating factor: the *makeh behemah* is direct but rare; the *shomer* case is common but indirect. One might argue that in each, the Torah's leniency toward the *mazik* was a product of that particular mitigating factor. But an ox that gores another ox presents both aggravating features simultaneously — it is common (*shechicha*) and it is a direct act of the *mazik*'s property. One might then conclude that in such a case, with no mitigating factor present, the *mazik* should take the carcass. It needed to be stated explicitly that even here, the carcass remains with the *nizak*.

Similarly, had only the goring-ox case been stated, one might have thought that the principle applies specifically because the *mazik* in that case acts through his property — *mamona kamazik* — rather than through his own body. But when the *mazik* himself causes the damage, whether as a *shomer* or as an *adam hamazik*, one might think the personal nature of the culpability changes the result. All three cases were therefore indispensable, and the principle emerges comprehensively: regardless of whether the harm is common or rare, direct or passive, caused by the person himself or through his property, the *nizak* retains ownership of the damaged object and the *mazik* pays only the loss of value.

### Carcass as Payment

Rav Kahana poses a sharp challenge to Rav. Given everything we have established — that *baalim metaplin benevelah*, the owners retain the carcass — one can ask: why does any of this matter? The *gemara* has taught from *yashiv l'rabbos shaveh kessef afilu subbin* that a debt for damages may be paid with any object of value, even something as base as dross. So if the *mazik* owed the full one hundred dollars and owned the carcass, he could simply hand over the carcass as the first ten dollars of payment. The question of whether he owes ninety or one hundred, or who owns the carcass, would seem to dissolve practically if the carcass can always be deployed as partial payment regardless of theoretical ownership. Why did the Torah need to spend such effort on this point?

### Depreciation Matter

The *gemara* answers: *lo nitzrecha ella lephat nevelah* — the principle is necessary because of the depreciation of the carcass. When the animal is killed, the carcass is worth ten dollars. But by the time the case reaches *beis din* and a payment is assessed, the carcass has continued to deteriorate and may now be worth only five dollars. If we say the *mazik* fundamentally owes one hundred dollars and owns the carcass, then when he tenders the depreciated carcass as partial payment, he has paid only five, and must still make up the balance. The *nizak* absorbs none of the loss from the carcass's deterioration. But if we say from the outset that the *mazik* owes only ninety dollars and the *nizak* owns the carcass, then any further decline in the carcass's value is the *nizak*'s loss to bear. The conceptual distinction thus has real practical consequences wherever the carcass depreciates between the moment of damage and the moment of payment.

---

## Carcass Ownership

### Tannaim Dispute

The *gemara* now raises the possibility that the question of *p'chas neveilah* — who bears the cost of the carcass's depreciation — is itself a *machlokes tanna'im*. This would mean that the underlying principle of whether the *mazik* owes ninety or one hundred is disputed at the *tanna'ic* level.

### Tarof Pasuk

The vehicle for this discussion is a *beraita* that interprets the *pasuk* cited earlier by Rav Kahana: *im tarof yitaref yevi'eihu ed hatereifah lo yeshalem*. Two readings are offered. The first, that of the *tanna kamma*, reads the *pasuk* straightforwardly: *yavi edim shenitrefa b'ones upatur* — the *shomer sachar* brings witnesses that the animal was torn by a wild beast due to complete *ones*, entirely beyond his control, and he is exempt. This is simply the basic *halacha* that a *shomer sachar* is exempt from an *ones*. Abba Shaul, however, offers a strikingly different reading. He reads *yevi'eihu*, "he shall bring it," as referring to the carcass itself: *yavi adudah l'beis din* — he must bring the carcass to *beis din*. On this reading, the *mazik* or *shomer* is required to bring the dead animal before the court so it can be assessed, and the *shomer* pays the difference. The *gemara* initially suggests that these two readings reflect a dispute about who owns the carcass and who bears its depreciation.

### All Agree Owner

The *gemara* resists this reading of the dispute, however. It insists: *d'chuli alma d'nizak* — everyone agrees that the carcass belongs to the *nizak*. The principle of *baalim metaplin benevelah* is not in dispute between the *tanna kamma* and Abba Shaul. The *gemara* refuses to allow that any *tanna* would hold the *mazik* is fundamentally owed the full value of the object.

### Bringing Carcass

If everyone agrees that the *nizak* owns the carcass, then what exactly is the dispute between the *tanna kamma* and Abba Shaul? The *gemara* answers: *b'torach neveilah kamiflegi* — they disagree about who bears the burden of transporting the carcass. Abba Shaul's language — *yavi adudah l'beis din*, bring the carcass to *beis din* — is his *chiddush*: it is the *mazik*'s responsibility to bring the carcass to court, or more broadly, to bring it from the field to the city where it can be sold and the *nizak* can realize its value. A *beraita* is cited in support: *acheirim omrim minayin she'al ba'al habor l'haalos hashor miboro* — from where do we know that the owner of the pit must bring the dead ox up from the pit? The verse teaches: *kesef yashiv l'ba'alav vehamet* — money he returns to its owner, and the dead animal as well. He must return the carcass to the owner in a state where it can actually be sold, meaning he must extract it from the pit and bring it to a useful place.

### Effort & Debt

This raises a practical question. If at the bottom of the pit the carcass is worth one dollar, and once brought to the top it is worth four dollars, then who cares whether the *mazik* is required to bring it up? If he brings it up, his debt diminishes accordingly — he still owes the *nizak* the difference between the original value and the current value, accounting for the improvement. If he doesn't bring it up, he owes more. Either way the math adjusts. Why does it matter who has the formal obligation?

The *gemara* resolves this by positing a case where the value of the carcass is the same at the bottom of the pit as at the top — one dollar either way. Is such a case realistic? The *gemara* affirms: *de'amri inshi kashura be'mata be'zuza kashura be'dabra be'zuza* — people say, a beam in the city costs a dollar and a beam out in the field costs a dollar, even though you would need to transport it. Sometimes the effort invested in transportation does not translate into a corresponding increase in the sale price — much as home improvements often do not fully recoup their cost in resale value. In such a case, if the *mazik* is required to bring the carcass to a place where it can be sold, he may expend three dollars of effort but only reduce his debt by one dollar. It therefore matters significantly who bears the obligation to transport it. The conclusion is that the *mazik* bears that responsibility, even at a cost to himself.

---

## Shmuel Ganav/Gazlan

### Shamin Principle

The *gemara* now introduces a teaching of Shmuel that both confirms and sharpens what has been established: *ein shamin lo leganav velo legazlan ella lenizikin* — this principle of *shamin*, of assessing the loss in value and paying only the difference, applies exclusively to cases of damage, *nezikin*, and not to cases of theft (*ganav*) or robbery (*gazlan*).

### Possession vs Damage

The conceptual basis for this distinction is compelling and is explained by Tosafos. In a case of damage, the *mazik* never took possession of the object. He broke it, diminished it, made it worth less — but it remained the *nizak*'s object throughout. The *mazik* therefore pays only for the damage he created: the difference between the object's original value and its current value. The object itself stays with the *nizak*. A thief or robber, however, *took* the object. That act of *geneiva* or *gezeila* made him liable for the full value of the cow the moment he took it. He owes one hundred dollars. If the cow subsequently dies, the question of what he can tender in payment — whether he can use the carcass as partial payment under the principle of *yashiv l'rabbos shaveh kessef afilu subbin* — is a separate discussion. But his fundamental liability is for the full value of the object he took, not merely for a diminution of value. Conceptually, he owes one hundred dollars, and the carcass may or may not serve as a means of discharging part of that debt, but it does not change the underlying obligation.

### Shoel Full Amount

Shmuel adds a further teaching — though a textual dispute affects how precisely it should be read. Tosafos preserves a *girsa* in which Shmuel says: *va'ani omer af leshoel* — and I say, even for a *shoel*, a borrower. His father, who is identified here as Rav, agrees with him on this point as well. The question is in which direction: does Shmuel mean that a *shoel* is like *nezikin* and one assesses only the damage, or that a *shoel* is like a *ganav* or *gazlan* and pays the full amount?

The conceptual tension here is genuine. A normal *shomer*'s liability arises from negligence — something went wrong on his watch and he is responsible for the resulting damage. This closely parallels *nezikin*, and accordingly a *shomer*'s liability should be measured by the diminution of value. A *shoel*, however, borrows the object and uses it as if it were his own. There is an argument that this taking-for-use creates a form of liability resembling *geneiva* — he has, in a sense, taken the object into his domain, and his obligation is to return the whole object. If the object breaks, he owes its full value, not merely the loss in value.

### Axe Case

A practical case is brought to test the question. A man borrowed an axe from his friend and broke it. He came before Rav, and Rav told him: *zil shalim leih narga ma'alya* — go pay him for a complete, full-value axe. This appears to support the reading that a *shoel* pays the full amount, not merely the assessed diminution — and that when Shmuel said Rav agreed with him, he meant they both hold a *shoel* pays like a *ganav* or *gazlan*.

### Challenge to Rav

The *gemara* pushes back. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged Rav directly, asking *dina hachi* — is that truly the *halacha*? Should it not be that the *shoel* pays only the assessed difference? Rav was silent. The *gemara* draws the inference: *shema mina shamin* — from Rav's silence it appears he conceded, and the *halacha* is that a *shoel* is assessed like other cases of damage, paying the diminution of value, not the full amount.

---

## Liability Categories

### Ulla's Version

The matter is then stated as a formal ruling. Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar taught: *shamin leganav ulegazlan* — one does assess the difference even for a *ganav* and a *gazlan*. This contradicts Shmuel's teaching.

### Rav Pappa Halakha

Rav Pappa rules explicitly: *ein shamin* — one does not assess the difference for a *ganav* or *gazlan*. The *hilchisa*, the accepted *halacha*, follows Shmuel: *ein shamin lo leganav velo legazlan* — neither for the thief nor the robber does one merely assess the loss in value. Both owe for the full object they took.

### Shoel Halakha

The *halacha* further specifies: *aval leshoel shamin*, but for a *shoel* one does assess the damage, following the position of Rav Kahana and Rav Assi, whose challenge to Rav was met with silence. Even though there is a conceptual argument that a *shoel* resembles a *ganav* or *gazlan* — having taken the object and used it as his own — the *halacha* does not follow that logic. A *shoel* is treated like other *shomrim* and like *nezikin*: his liability is for the diminution of value he caused, not for the full original value of the object. The *nizak* retains the damaged object, and the *shoel* pays the difference.

---

## Ulla's Teachings

### Birth Timing

Having cited a ruling of Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar, the *gemara* now strings together a series of additional teachings in that same name. The first concerns a case where the amniotic sac (*shilya*) containing the embryo emerges partially on one day and partially on the next — for instance, some emerges on Sunday just before nightfall and the remainder after nightfall, which begins Monday. Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar rules: *monin lah min harishon* — she counts the seven or fourteen days of *tumas leida* beginning from Sunday.

### Rava Challenge

Rava challenges this. Starting the count from Sunday seems like a *chumra* — being strict because she might have been *tamei* on Sunday. But it is a *chumra de'asi lidei kula hu* — a stringency that leads to a leniency. By counting from Sunday, the fourteen days may end earlier than if she had counted from Monday, and she could erroneously be declared *tehorah* while she is still in her period of *tum'ah*. Rava therefore rules: from Sunday she is concerned she may be *tamei* and acts accordingly, but she only begins counting the fourteen days from Monday, ensuring full coverage on both ends.

### Fetus Presence

The *gemara* then asks what *chiddush* is being conveyed by Ulla's teaching, since Rava has revised it. The answer is: *de'ein miktzas shilya belo velad* — the *chiddush* is that even when only part of the sac emerges, we assume some of the fetus was present within it. If it were possible that the partial emergence of the sac contained none of the fetus, there would be no basis for concern that childbirth began on Sunday. It is only because we assume the fetus was at least partially present in what emerged on Sunday that we are concerned at all. This is the novel principle.

The *gemara* challenges this as well, suggesting the principle might already have been taught in a *mishna*: *shilya sheyatza miktzasah asurah ba'akhilah* — if part of the amniotic sac of an animal emerged before *shechita*, what is within the sac is forbidden, because *shilya* is a sign of a *velad*. But the *gemara* deflects: one could read that *mishna* as a *gezeira* — a rabbinic fence — forbidding even the case where no fetus was in the partial sac, to prevent people from permitting cases where a fetus was present. It would not necessarily prove the underlying assumption that a fetus is always present with a partial sac. The *chiddush* of Ulla's teaching therefore stands.

### Bechor Treifa

Another teaching of Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar: if a firstborn son (*bechor*) suffered a wound rendering him a *treifa* within the first thirty days of his life, *ein podin oso* — one does not perform *pidyon haben* when day thirty arrives. Even if the child was healthy at birth and even if he is still alive on day thirty, since he has become a *treifa* — his death is now inevitable from the wound — he does not have the status of a fully viable living person, and the *mitzva* of *pidyon haben* does not apply. A *beraita* corroborates: the verse says *padoh tifdeh*, "you shall surely redeem," which one might think applies even to a child who became a *treifa* within thirty days; the word *ach* — "however" — limits the obligation and excludes such a case.

### Animal Meshicha

Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar further teaches: *behema gassa nikneis bemeshicha* — a large animal such as a cow acquires a new owner through *meshicha*, pulling it toward oneself. The *gemara* notes a tension with what was taught in Kiddushin, where acquisition of a large animal is said to occur through *mesira*, handing over the reins. Ulla follows the view of the *Chachamim* in the *beraita* who hold that both large and small animals are acquired through *meshicha*. Rabbi Shimon in the same *beraita* holds that both types of animal require *hagbaha*, lifting.

### Estate Division

Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar rules: when brothers who have been living jointly off an estate come to divide it, *ma she'aleihem shamin* — one assesses the value of the clothing they themselves are wearing, counting it toward their respective shares. However, *ma she'al beneihem uvnoteihem ein shamin* — one does not assess the clothing worn by their children, even if those garments were paid for from the estate. Bringing all the children before *beis din* to have their clothing appraised would be undignified, and the brothers are presumed to have waived any claim on that point.

Rav Pappa adds a qualification: *pa'amim af ma she'aleihem ein shamin* — there are circumstances in which even the brothers' own clothing is not assessed. This applies when one of the brothers has been serving as the representative of the estate, managing business dealings on behalf of all of them. In that case, the others are presumed to have implicitly consented to his using estate funds for clothing appropriate to his representative role, for the benefit of all. Since he acted in their collective interest, his higher clothing expenditure is not counted against his share.

### Shomer Transfer

Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar teaches: *shomer shemassar l'shomer patur* — a *shomer* who transfers an object to another *shomer* does not thereby incur additional liability. If Reuven was given an object by Fred to watch, and Reuven asks Shimon to watch it in his place, this act of transfer does not make Reuven more liable than he was before. If Reuven was a *shomer chinam* he remains liable for *pshiah*; if he was a *shomer sachar* he remains liable for *geneiva v'aveida*. But the transfer itself does not constitute a new act of liability.

It goes without saying, says the *gemara*, that if Reuven was a *shomer chinam* and he paid Shimon to watch it as a *shomer sachar*, one would not fault him for raising the standard of *shmira*. More significantly, Ulla's ruling covers even the case where Reuven was a *shomer sachar* and transferred the object to Shimon as a *shomer chinam* — where one might expect the lower standard of care to constitute a form of negligence on Reuven's part. Even so, Reuven is *patur*. The reason: *sheharei masar l'ben da'at* — he transferred the object to a responsible adult, and that does not by itself violate the terms of his guardianship.

### Rava Liable

Rava disagrees sharply: *shomer shemassar l'shomer chayav* — a *shomer* who transfers to another *shomer* is liable. The act of transfer is itself a form of negligence or violation of the original agreement, and once a *shomer* has shirked his responsibility in this way, he becomes liable even for an *ones* that subsequently occurs — analogous to the principle of *techilato b'fshiah v'sofo b'ones*.

Rava's ruling likewise covers both directions. It goes without saying that if the *shomer sachar* transferred to a *shomer chinam* — thereby reducing the expected standard of care — that is negligence. Rava's ruling covers even the case where the *shomer chinam* transferred to a *shomer sachar*, where the *shomer* might argue he actually improved the *shmira*. Even so, he is *chayav*.

### Trust & Oath

The reason Rava gives is fundamental: *at meimnat li bishvua hai lo meimnat li bishvua* — the owner trusted *you*, and by placing his object with you, he implicitly agreed he would accept *your* oath if something happened to it. He never agreed to accept the oath of whoever you might subsequently choose to entrust it to. If the object is now in Shimon's hands and something goes wrong, Shimon's *shvua* is simply not one the owner agreed to credit. The *shomer* who transferred it has therefore violated the very basis of the trust placed in him. The *gemara* notes that in Bava Metzia an additional and perhaps more fundamental reason is given: *ein ritzoni she'yehei pikdoni b'yad acher* — the owner never agreed that anyone other than the original *shomer* should hold it. Regardless of whether the substitute would do better or worse, the original *shomer* had no right to make the transfer at all.

### Slave Collection

Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar further rules: *hilchata govin min ha'avadim* — the *halacha* is that one may collect a debt from slaves. This implies that slaves have the status of real estate (*karka*) for purposes of debt collection, meaning creditors hold a lien over a debtor's slaves just as they hold a lien over his land.

### Nachman Challenge

Rav Nachman challenges Ulla directly: *amar Rabbi Elazar afillu b'yasmi* — did Rabbi Elazar really mean this applies even when collecting from orphans? Tosafos notes that in this context, the discussion of orphans is effectively equivalent to the question of *lakuchos* — third-party purchasers who acquired the property after the debt was incurred. The question is whether a lien on a slave follows the slave even after it is sold, so that the creditor can collect from the new owner or the heirs. Did Rabbi Elazar really go that far? Ulla withdraws: no, he meant only that one may collect from the debtor's own slaves. But Rav Nachman presses: *miminei? afilu miglima d'al katfei* — from the debtor himself? You can take the shirt off his back! Obviously one can collect from all of a debtor's assets directly. That is not a *chiddush* requiring a ruling.

### Slave Apotiki

Under this pressure, Ulla revises the statement a second time: *hacha b'mai askinan she'asao apotiki* — the case we are discussing is where the debtor explicitly designated the slave as an *apotiki*, a formal lien. In that case, even if the slave is subsequently sold or passes to heirs, the creditor may collect from it. This is supported by Rava's ruling: if one makes his slave an *apotiki* and then sells the slave, the creditor may collect from the purchaser. This is distinct from the general case of slaves, which without explicit designation do not carry automatic liens the way real estate does.

### Slave Publicity

One might ask: if an explicit *apotiki* designation works for slaves, why does it not work equally for other chattel? If a person designates his ox as an *apotiki* and then sells the ox, can the creditor collect from the purchaser? The answer is no: *mai ta'ama hai it lei kala v'hai leit lei kala* — the reason is publicity. Slaves are known individuals. People know which slaves belong to whom, and if a lien is placed on a slave, that information can be known and the potential purchaser can investigate and protect himself. Real estate similarly carries publicly knowable liens, which is why automatic liens on real estate are enforceable against purchasers. Ordinary chattel — like a cow — is anonymous enough that nobody could reasonably be expected to know whether a particular animal carries a lien, and therefore even an explicit *apotiki* designation on chattel cannot be enforced against a third-party purchaser. Slaves occupy an intermediate position: they do not carry automatic liens like real estate, but an explicit *apotiki* on a slave is sufficiently public to be enforceable, because slaves are individuals whose status and encumbrances can be known. The discussion continues on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 12

## Liens on Slaves

### Gobvin min ha-avadim

We pick up at the very top line of Bava Kamma 12a, in the midst of a series of statements transmitted by Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar. The most recent of these is the ruling of *gobvin min ha-avadim* — that debts may be collected from slaves. The claim is that just as there exists a lien on real estate, there is similarly a lien on slaves: if a debtor sells his slave to a third party, or dies and his heirs inherit, the creditor may nonetheless collect from that slave. This stands in contrast to ordinary chattel, from which no such collection may be made.

### Rav Nachman's objection

This position was challenged by Rav Nachman, who rejected the idea that any general lien could attach to a slave. Under the pressure of that challenge, Ulla appeared to retreat, saying that he was speaking only of a case involving an *apotiki* — an explicit lien formally placed on the slave through a document. Without such an explicit designation, he seemed to concede, the general rule is that liens apply only to land, not to slaves.

### Ulla's real position

However, when we pick up at the top of 12a, we discover that this was not Ulla's genuine position. *Le-basar de-nafak* — after Rav Nachman had left — Ulla said to those present: know that this is truly what Rabbi Elazar taught, namely that one may collect *afilu mi-yasmei*, even from the heirs, because there is a real lien on slaves just as there is a lien on real estate. Rav Nachman, hearing of this, remarked that Ulla had been *ishtamititen* — evading him, declining to state his true position directly rather than confront Rav Nachman's strong opposition. Ulla's authentic tradition from Rabbi Elazar maintains that liens on slaves are real and operative.

### Neharde'a and Pumbedita…

The weight of practice appears to support Ulla's view. There was a case in Neharde'a — the seat of Shmuel's authority and the city where Rav Nachman himself held sway — in which the judges of Neharde'a were prepared to collect a debt from slaves, treating a loan as conferring a lien not only on land but also on slaves. They followed the ruling of Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar. Similarly, *hava uvda be-Pumbedita* — there was a case in Pumbedita in which Rav Chana bar Bizna permitted a creditor to collect from slaves that had either passed to heirs or been sold to a third party. The principle was being applied consistently: slaves are fully analogous to landed property for the purpose of liens.

### Rav Nachman's threat

Despite this, Rav Nachman remained entirely unconvinced. He instructed the judges — *zilu ahadureh* — to go and reverse their rulings, returning the slaves to the purchasers. There is no lien on slaves, he insisted. And if the judges would not comply, he declared, *magbinan lechu apandaichu* — he would seize their very castles from them, treating their erroneous rulings as actionable judicial misconduct. His opposition was fierce and unambiguous.

### Rava's challenge

Rava then pushed back directly. He enumerated the authorities: Ulla holds there are liens on slaves; Rabbi Elazar holds it; the judges of Neharde'a ruled on it; Rav Chana bar Bizna in Pumbedita ruled on it. *Mar keman svara lei* — like whom exactly does Rav Nachman hold, that he dismisses all of these positions?

### Rav Nachman's defense

Rav Nachman's reply is disarming in its simplicity: *ana matnita yedana* — I know only the *braita*. It is not that he is unaware of the distinguished chain of authorities; it is that his anchor is a specific *braita* taught by Avimi, and that *braita* is the basis upon which he stands.

---

## Pruzbul and liens

### Pruzbul on land/slaves

The *braita* to which Rav Nachman refers is the teaching of Avimi: *pruzbul chal al ha-karka ve-eino chal al ha-avadim* — a *pruzbul* takes effect when the debtor possesses land, but not when the debtor possesses only slaves. The *pruzbul*, it will be recalled, is the rabbinic mechanism enacted by Hillel permitting the collection of debts even after the *shemita* year, which would otherwise annul outstanding loans.

### Pruzbul principle

The logic underlying this rule is as follows. Ordinarily, *shemita* annuls debts because the creditor cannot compel collection. But when the creditor holds a lien on the debtor's land, it is as though the debt is already effectively secured — the creditor can seize that land at any moment. The land is stable, fixed, and accessible, and the lien upon it is therefore meaningful. On that basis, the *pruzbul* can be written when the debtor owns land: the lien is real and the debt is effectively under the creditor's control. But if the debtor has only a slave, the *pruzbul* does not work — apparently because, on Rav Nachman's reading, there is no lien on slaves to begin with.

### Kinyan Agav principle

The same *braita* continues with a second principle: *metaltelin niknim im ha-karka ve-einam niknim im ha-avadim* — chattel may be acquired together with land, but not together with slaves. This refers to the principle of *kinyan agav* established in tractate Kiddushin: when one takes formal possession of land, the seller may simultaneously transfer ownership of movable property located anywhere — even at a great distance — by stipulating that the chattel is acquired along with the land. This mechanism works when the anchor is *karka*, but the *braita* states it does not work when the anchor is a slave.

### Slaves third category

In both of these rules, slaves diverge from land: there is no *pruzbul* on a slave as there is on land, and *kinyan agav* does not operate with a slave as the vehicle. Yet the second clause of the *braita* also distinguishes slaves from ordinary chattel — because one does not say that taking possession of slaves automatically carries along with it possession of *metaltelin*. Slaves appear, in both dimensions, to stand in a category of their own.

### Tosafot's distinction

Tosafot notes that throughout *Shas*, the standard assumption is that *avda ke-karka'ei* — a slave is like land. Slaves and land are grouped together in numerous exemptions: from the laws of theft and robbery (*gneiva ve-gezeila*), from the obligation against overcharging, from the requirement of an oath, and so forth. So what is the controversy here?

Tosafot answers that the question is specifically whether we extend the equation of slaves with land to *rabbinic* law. Both *pruzbul* and *kinyan agav* are rabbinic enactments. The Torah-level equation of slaves with land is established and uncontested; the question is whether we carry that equation into the rabbinic sphere, where the rationale might differ.

One way to understand why the equation might not hold for these particular *halachot* is by attending to their underlying logic. Liens attach to land rather than chattel because land is fixed, identifiable, and its ownership can be precisely recorded — factors that make it fair to third-party purchasers who can research the record. A slave, despite being legally analogous to land in many ways, does not share those characteristics in the same fashion. Similarly, the concept of *kinyan agav* — using land as a vehicle to simultaneously transfer chattel — may depend on land functioning as a stable repository for property, a stable location to which things are conceptually anchored. That rationale does not translate straightforwardly to a human being who moves. These considerations help explain why, within the domain of liens and *kinyanim*, the question of whether slaves are treated like land or like chattel becomes live, even though in other domains the equation is settled.

---

## Two conflicting braitot

### First braita details

With this backdrop established, the *Gemara* proposes that the dispute between Ulla and Rav Nachman may correspond to a *tannaic* debate — *leima k'tana'ei*. It turns to a *braita* that works through several combinations of property types. If someone sold slaves and land to another person: if the buyer took possession of the slave, he did not thereby acquire the land; and if he took possession of the land, he did not thereby acquire the slave. Each stands alone.

### Kinyan Agav explained

The *braita* then clarifies the rule for land and chattel: if one takes possession of land (*karka*), one simultaneously acquires *metaltelin* — that is *kinyan agav*. But the reverse does not hold: taking possession of chattel does not confer possession of land.

### Slaves and chattel

When it comes to slaves and *metaltelin*, the *braita* states that taking possession of the slave does not confer possession of the chattel, and taking possession of the chattel does not confer possession of the slave. Slaves do not function as a vehicle for *kinyan agav* in either direction with respect to chattel.

### Second braita intro

However, a second *braita* is then cited that teaches the opposite regarding this last case: *hechezik ba-avadim kanah metaltelin* — if one takes possession of slaves, one does acquire the chattel along with them.

### Slaves like land or chat…

The *Gemara* proposes that this is the crux of the *tannaic* dispute. The first *braita* holds that slaves are like *metaltelin* — chattel — and therefore taking possession of a slave no more carries along other chattel than taking possession of one piece of chattel carries along another. The second *braita* holds that slaves are like *karka* — land — and therefore taking possession of a slave can serve as the vehicle for *kinyan agav*, conferring possession of chattel just as taking possession of land does. This appears to map directly onto the debate between Ulla (slaves are like land, liens apply) and Rav Nachman (slaves are like chattel, no liens).

---

## Rav Ika's first view

### Everyone agrees like land

Rav Ika son of Rav Ami intervenes to argue that the two *braitot* need not reflect a dispute about whether slaves are fundamentally like land or like chattel. On his first explanation, *de-chulei alma avadim ke-mika-rke-dami* — everyone agrees that slaves are like land. The *braita* that says *kinyan agav* works with slaves follows naturally from that premise. But the *braita* that says it does not work — that also can be reconciled without disagreeing about the underlying status of slaves.

### Biblical basis Kinyan Ag…

The *Gemara* has already established the scriptural basis for *kinyan agav*. The *mishna* in Kiddushin states that property without liens (i.e., chattel) may be acquired along with property that has liens (i.e., land), through the same modes by which land is acquired — money, deed, or *chazaka*. The verse underlying this, as taught by Chizkiyah, is from Chronicles: *va-yiten lahem avihem matnot rabot le-kesef u-le-zahav u-le-migdanot im arei mitzurot bi-Yehuda* — their father gave them many gifts of silver, gold, and precious things together with the walled cities of Judah. The act of taking possession of the walled cities carried along the transfer of all the movable gifts simultaneously.

### Stability requirement

From this verse, Rav Ika derives a qualification: *kinyan agav* requires *karka dumya de-arei mitzurot bi-Yehuda* — land that resembles the walled cities of Judah. The essential characteristic of those cities is stability: they do not move. The *kinyan agav* mechanism is predicated on something fixed and immovable serving as the vehicle.

### Slaves move, don't work

A slave is a human being who walks about. Even if we agree that a slave is juridically equivalent to land in the standard sense, a slave is not the kind of stable, unmoving property that the verse envisions as the vehicle for *kinyan agav*. Therefore, even on the view that slaves are like land, using a slave as the vehicle for acquiring chattel through *agav* does not work. The *braita* that denies it is not disagreeing about the fundamental status of slaves — it is simply applying the more specific requirement that *kinyan agav* demands actual, rooted property that does not move. Ulla's position that there are liens on slaves, and the broader equation of slaves with land, can therefore remain intact; the failure of *kinyan agav* is a separate and narrower rule.

---

## Rav Ika's second view

### Slaves like chattel

The *Gemara* then presents an alternative version of Rav Ika's reasoning — attributed there to Rav Ika son of Rav Idi — proceeding from the opposite premise: *de-chulei alma avdi ke-metaltelin dami* — everyone agrees that slaves are like chattel. On this reading, the *braita* that denies *kinyan agav* for slaves follows straightforwardly. But the *braita* that seems to permit it requires an alternative explanation.

### Kinyan chatzer concept

The *braita* that says taking possession of slaves confers possession of chattel is, on this reading, not describing *kinyan agav* at all. Rather, it describes a case *be-oden alav* — where the chattel is physically resting on the slave. When you take possession of my slave, and my watch happens to be on that slave's person, you acquire the watch — not through *agav*, but through *kinyan chatzer*: just as taking possession of one's courtyard can effect acquisition of objects placed within it, so too, when the slave enters your possession, anything resting on the slave comes along with it.

### Chatzer mehalechet

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *chatzer mehalechet hi* — a moving yard. The whole premise of *kinyan chatzer* is that the courtyard is a stable enclosure under the owner's control. A slave walks around freely; how can a slave function as a *chatzer* for purposes of acquisition?

### Conditions for chatzer

Rava addresses this: *kol she-illu mehalekh lo kana omed ve-yoshev lo kana* — any entity that, were it walking, would not serve as a *chatzer* for acquisition, does not serve as one even when standing or sitting. A slave who has the capacity to walk is, by that very fact, not analogous to a stationary courtyard, even when momentarily still. The only way this can work, therefore, is if the slave is bound — physically restrained so that he lacks the ability to walk. Tosafot adds that the slave may also need to be asleep, so that the object is kept in place solely by the owner's domain and not by the slave's own volition.

### Limited explanation

This is a deeply constrained explanation. It applies only in a narrow circumstance — the slave is physically bound, the chattel is resting upon him — and it operates through *kinyan chatzer* rather than *kinyan agav*. On this entire approach, slaves are categorically like chattel, there are no liens on them, and the appearance of *agav* in the second *braita* is an illusion to be explained away.

---

## Slaves with land

### Land acquires slaves

The *Gemara* now turns to a further *braita*: *hechzik be-karka kanah avadim* — if one takes possession of land, one acquires slaves along with it. This seems to stand in tension with the first *braita* cited earlier, which stated that taking possession of land does not yield possession of slaves. The *Gemara* resolves the apparent conflict: the *braita* that says it works is referring to a case *be-omdim be-tokhah* — where the slaves are physically standing within the land being acquired. The *braita* that says it does not work refers to slaves who are not standing on the land at the moment of acquisition.

### Distinction if chattel

The *Gemara* then explores whether this distinction holds together on either view of slaves' status. If slaves are like chattel (*ke-metaltelin*), one might understand why their physical presence in the land matters: it would be a case of either *kinyan agav* (chattel being acquired together with the land) or *kinyan chatzer* (the land functioning as a courtyard that draws in what is physically present within it). On this view, the presence of the slave within the land makes the acquisition operative, and the absence of the slave from the land leaves it inoperative.

### Kinyan Agav problem

But the *Gemara* immediately presses: even if slaves are like chattel, the requirement of physical presence should not matter for *kinyan agav*. The established principle is *de-lo ba'inan tziburin* — we do not require the chattel to be physically piled up in the land being acquired. *Kinyan agav* works even if the chattel is entirely elsewhere. So why should it matter whether the slave is standing in the land or not?

### Moving vs. non-moving

The *Gemara* answers: *shani metaltelin de-naydi mi-metaltelin de-lo naydi* — there is a distinction between property that moves and property that does not. Tosafot clarifies that "moves" here means moves like a human being, not simply like a cow. The mechanism of *kinyan agav* — by which the seller mentally packages all of his property together and the buyer's acquisition of the land carries the rest — works when the ancillary property is inanimate or even an animal without its own will. In those cases, the seller's intent is sufficient to unite them conceptually. But a slave has intellect and will of his own; he is not conceptually fused with the land unless he is physically present on it.

### Moving land concept

If, alternatively, slaves are treated as land (*ke-karka*), the same structural problem arises in a different form. Shmuel teaches that if someone sells ten fields in ten different countries, the buyer's act of taking possession of any one of them acquires all of them simultaneously — one act of *chazaka* on one piece of land works for every other piece of land the seller intends to transfer. If slaves are like land, why should it matter whether the slave is physically standing on the particular parcel being acquired? One piece of land should suffice for all others. The *Gemara* answers: *shani mi-karka'ei de-naydi mi-mi-karka'ei de-lo naydi* — even on the view that a slave is like land, there is a difference between land that does not move and land that does. A slave is, on this view, *mi-karka'ei de-naydi hu* — moving land. Being *koneh* a stationary field in one location does not extend to acquiring a slave, even if that slave is conceptually in the category of land, because the slave is a fundamentally detached and independent entity.

### Land as one unit

The reason Shmuel's principle works for fields in distant countries is captured by the phrase *sadna de-ara chad hu* — the crust of the earth is one unit. All land, however distant, is somehow connected as part of the same continuous ground; taking possession of any piece of it is, at some level, taking possession of the same fabric of earth. A slave — even if categorized as a form of land — shares no such connection. He is ambulatory and independent, not part of the unbroken crust of the earth. And therefore, taking possession of a parcel of land in one place does not reach out to acquire a slave who happens to be somewhere else.

---

## Summary of discussion

### Liens as central

Stepping back, the central question animating the entire discussion is whether liens apply to slaves as they do to land. Ulla, transmitting from Rabbi Elazar, and supported by the practice of the judges of Neharde'a and Rav Chana bar Bizna of Pumbedita, holds that they do. Rav Nachman, anchored in the *braita* of Avimi concerning *pruzbul*, holds that they do not.

### Exceptions for kinyanim

When it comes to *kinyanim*, the picture is more nuanced. Even if one accepts that slaves are fundamentally like land — as is the standard position throughout *Shas* for Torah-level rules — there may be exceptions in the domain of *kinyanim*. A slave may not serve as the vehicle for *kinyan agav* because the relevant verse requires stable, non-moving property.
