And even when one begins with a piece of land, that act of *chazaka* may not extend to a slave, because the slave is moving land — detached from the earth's continuous fabric. These are specific features of *kinyan* law that may operate differently even when the slave's general legal status is settled.

---

## New topic: me'ila

### Me'ila principle

We now move to the next section of the *Mishnah*, which states a general principle: one is liable for damages done to property for which there is no *me'ila* obligation — *nechasim she'ein bahem me'ila*. The point is that the exemption from damage liability applies to *hekdesh* — consecrated property — and specifically to property that carries the *me'ila* obligation. But there exists a category of sanctified property for which there is no *me'ila*, and for such property one remains liable for damages as one would be for ordinary property.

### What is me'ila?

*Me'ila* is the offense of misappropriating consecrated property — making improper use of something dedicated to *hekdesh* — which triggers both a financial penalty and the obligation to bring a special *korban asham*. The *Gemara* asks: what is the category of property that is sanctified and yet carries no *me'ila* obligation?

### Kodshim Kalim example

The paradigmatic answer is *kodshim kalim* — sacrifices of lesser sanctity, such as a *shelamim*. A *shelamim* is brought by an individual, the blood is sprinkled on the *mizbeach*, but the meat is eaten by the owner and his household in Jerusalem, and the *kohanim* receive the breast and thigh. There is no *me'ila* on the *shelamim*'s meat; *me'ila* applies only to the *eimurim* — the fats and innards burned entirely on the *mizbeach*, which belong wholly to God. The rest, being eaten by humans, carries no *me'ila* obligation. The implication of the *Mishnah* is therefore: if one's ox gores another person's *shelamim*, one is obligated to pay, since the victim's *shelamim* is in a category of sanctified property that nonetheless triggers damage liability.

---

## Rabbi Yosi's view

### Attribution

Rabbi Yochanan identifies the *tanna* whose position underlies this *Mishnah*: it follows Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, and it applies specifically to *kodshim kalim*.

### Mammon ba'alim

The cornerstone of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's position is the principle that *kodshim kalim* is *mammon ba'alim* — it remains the owner's property. Even though the animal is sanctified and will be brought as a *korban*, its status is akin to that of a person who owns a *sefer torah* or *tefillin*: the object carries sanctity, but ownership has not been transferred away from the individual. Unlike *kodshei kodashim* — the most sacred offerings such as a *chatas* or *olah*, which belong entirely to *hekdesh* — *kodshim kalim* remains in the owner's domain.

### Damage liability

The practical consequence follows directly: if your ox gores my *shelamim*, you owe me damages, just as if it had gored an ordinary cow. The fact that the animal is sanctified does not shield the tortfeasor from liability, because the property is still mine — *mammon ba'alim*.

### Oath braita

The *Gemara* brings a *braita* in support of this from the law of false oaths. The Torah describes a case in which a person denies under oath having received a deposit from his fellow and thereby commits a *me'ila* against God — *u-ma'ala ma'al b'Hashem*. The *braita* derives from this that *l'Hashem l'rabot kodshim kalim she-hein mamono* — the phrase "against God" comes to include *kodshim kalim*, which is the owner's property. Even though the object has sanctity, the denial of it to one's fellow constitutes a wrong against that fellow — *v'kichash b'amito* — and the laws of denial and false oath apply. This is the express teaching of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili.

### Me'ila extension

Rabbi Yosi HaGlili thus extends the full range of consequences that flow from *mammon ba'alim* to *kodshim kalim*: the owner's property rights are real, the standard laws of torts apply, and the laws of oaths and denial apply as well.

---

## Kiddushin contradiction

### Priest kiddushin case

The *Gemara* now raises an apparent contradiction from a *Mishnah* in Kiddushin. The *Mishnah* states: *ha-mekadesh b'chelko* — if a *kohen* attempts to betroth a woman using his portion of a *korban*, whether from *kodshei kodashim* or from *kodshim kalim* (specifically the *chazeh v'shok* — the breast and thigh that the *kohen* receives), she is *eina mekudeshet* — the betrothal does not take effect.

### Not his property

The reason the *kiddushin* fails is that the *kohen*'s portion is not considered his property in the relevant sense. *Kiddushin* requires that the groom give the woman something of value that belongs to him. If the item does not truly belong to him, the *kiddushin* is invalid.

### Mishulchan gavoa

The phrase the *Gemara* invokes to capture this is *mishulchan gavoa k'zachu* — he has acquired this food by virtue of eating from God's table. The *kohen* is invited to partake; he does not own what he is partaking of. He eats the breast and thigh not as an owner consuming his own property, but as a guest at God's table. Therefore, it cannot serve as the instrument of *kiddushin*.

### Contradiction emerges

But this seems to contradict Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's position. The *kohen*'s portion of a *shelamim* is *kodshim kalim*. Rabbi Yosi HaGlili says *kodshim kalim* is *mammon ba'alim*. If so, why can't the *kohen* use it for *kiddushin*? The *Gemara* asks: *leima d'lo Rabi Yose HaGlili* — is this *Mishnah* in Kiddushin simply not following Rabbi Yosi HaGlili?

---

## Rabbi Yosi limited

### Living vs. slaughtered

The *Gemara* answers that the apparent contradiction can be resolved even within the framework of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili. *Ki amar Rabi Yose HaGlili michayim* — when Rabbi Yosi HaGlili says that *kodshim kalim* is *mammon ba'alim*, he is speaking specifically about the living animal. While the animal is alive, it is still the owner's *korban*; the owner is bringing it, the owner will eat it, it is his in every meaningful sense. At that stage, Rabbi Yosi HaGlili says it remains *mammon ba'alim*.

### After slaughter change

But once the animal has been slaughtered and offered as a *korban*, and the portions are being distributed and eaten, the character of the property changes. At that point, *aval le'achar shechita afilu Rabi Yose HaGlili modeh d'ki k'zachu mishulchan gavoa k'zachu* — even Rabbi Yosi HaGlili agrees that when one is partaking of the meat after *shechita*, one is eating from God's table. The *kohen* who receives the breast and thigh after the animal has been brought as a *korban* receives it as a *matnas kehuna* — a divinely ordained gift dispensed from God's bounty — not as his own property. The *kiddushin* therefore fails, and this is entirely consistent with Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's position, which applies only to the living animal.

### Rashi-Tosafot debate

Rashi and Tosafot disagree about the scope of this ruling. Rashi holds that the principle of *mishulchan gavoa k'zachu* applies even to the owners when they eat their portion of the *shelamim* after *shechita*. On Rashi's reading, Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's *mammon ba'alim* is operative only while the animal is alive; once slaughtered, everyone — owners and *kohanim* alike — is eating from God's table, and the practical implications of *mammon ba'alim* are extinguished. Tosafot draws a sharper distinction: the owner's portion is different from the *kohen*'s portion. The *shelamim* began as the owner's animal; the owner raised it, consecrated it, and is now eating his own animal — just in a sanctified context, in Jerusalem. According to Tosafot, Rabbi Yosi HaGlili would say that the owner is eating *his own* portion of the *shelamim* even after *shechita*, and if the owner were to use that portion for *kiddushin*, it would be considered *mammon hedyot* and the *kiddushin* would work. The *kohen*, by contrast, never owned the animal; the *kohen*'s portion was carved out of someone else's offering and given to the *kohen* as God's dispensation. The *kohen* is always, on Tosafot's reading, eating *mishulchan gavoa*, even according to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili.

---

## Bechor case test

### Bechor sales

The *Gemara* now tests Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's position against a *braita* concerning a *bechor* — a firstborn animal, which the Torah requires be given to a *kohen* and brought as a *korban*. If the animal has a *mum* — a blemish — it cannot be offered on the *mizbeach* and the *kohen* may simply slaughter and eat it outside the Temple precincts. The *braita* teaches: *mochrin oso tam chai* — if the *bechor* is unblemished and must be brought as a *korban*, nevertheless the *kohen* may sell it to another *kohen* who will bring it. *U-va'al mum chai v'shachut* — if it has a blemish, it may be sold whether alive or after slaughter, since it is no longer destined to be brought as an offering. *U-m'kadshin bo es ha-isha* — and one may use it to betroth a woman, demonstrating that it is considered the *kohen*'s actual property.

This *braita* appears to confirm that even an unblemished *bechor* — a *kodshim kalim* animal alive and theoretically destined for the *mizbeach* — is treated as *mammon ba'alim* by the *kohen*. This would vindicate Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's principle in its fullest form: the living *korban* is the owner's property.

### Rav Nachman limit

However, Rav Nachman qualifies this sharply. *Lo shanu ela b'bechor b'zman hazeh* — the *braita*'s permission to sell and use the *bechor* for *kiddushin* applies only nowadays, when there is no *Beis HaMikdash*. Without a Temple, the *bechor* cannot in fact be brought as a *korban*. It may be unblemished in principle, but since it will never be sacrificed, the *kohen* is simply waiting for a blemish to appear so he can eat it. In that circumstance, it is on the path toward being ordinary meat, and it is therefore considered *mammon ba'alim* in an unqualified sense.

### With Beis HaMikdash

When the *Beis HaMikdash* exists and the *bechor* could genuinely be brought as a *korban*, the ruling is reversed: *aval bi-zman she-Beis HaMikdash kayam d'chazi l'hakrava, lo* — when it is destined for the *mizbeach*, it is not considered the *kohen*'s property in that sense, and neither the sale nor the *kiddushin* would be valid. The *bechor*'s status as *mammon ba'alim* is contingent on it not being genuinely on the path toward *hakrava*.

### Rava's challenge

Rava challenges this construction. According to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, *kodshim kalim* is *mammon ba'alim* while alive — why should that not apply to a living *bechor* even when the *Beis HaMikdash* stands? The *bechor* is alive, it is *kodshim kalim*, and Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's principle should make it *mammon ba'alim* straightforwardly, regardless of whether a Temple exists. Why does Rav Nachman insist on the special circumstance of no *Beis HaMikdash*, or on the *bechor* being outside of *Eretz Yisrael*, rather than simply applying Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's rule?

The *Gemara* here introduces a further wrinkle. Ravina proposes that the *braita* about the *bechor* should be read as referring specifically to a *bechor* in *chutz la'aretz* — outside of *Eretz Yisrael* — and following the position of Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Shimon holds that *im ba'u temimim yikrevu* — if unblemished *bechorot* from outside *Eretz Yisrael* are brought to the Temple, they are sacrificed, but *lechatchila lo* — there is no obligation to bring them. Outside of *Eretz Yisrael*, the *bechor* is not truly on a path toward *hakrava*, and it is therefore effectively equivalent to the case of no *Beis HaMikdash*. On this reading, Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's general principle that a living *kodshim kalim* is *mammon ba'alim* would not, after all, cover a standard *bechor* in *Eretz Yisrael* when the Temple stands.

---

## Matnas kehuna resolution

### Matnas kehuna

The *Gemara* now provides the definitive resolution. The challenge to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's position — why does the *bechor* not function as *mammon ba'alim* even while alive, given his principle — is answered with a fundamental distinction: *shani matnas kehuna d'ki ka zachu meshulchan gavoah ka zachu* — *matnas kehuna* is categorically different, because when the *kohen* acquires it, he acquires it from God's table.

### Owner's portion only

Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's principle of *mammon ba'alim* applies specifically to the owner's *korban*. The paradigm is a *shelamim*: I own a cow, I sanctify it as a *shelamim*, I bring it as my offering, and I eat the meat. Throughout this process, it started as mine; it remains, in the sense Rabbi Yosi HaGlili means, mine. The laws of torts apply; the laws of oaths apply; it is *mammon ba'alim*. This is the case Rabbi Yosi HaGlili is addressing.

### Bechor as matnas

A *bechor* given to a *kohen* is categorically different. It was never the *kohen*'s own animal. The animal was born, became *sacred* automatically by virtue of being a firstborn, and was handed over to the *kohen* as a *matnas kehuna* — a divinely prescribed gift. The *kohen* did not start with this as his sheep. God gave the *bechor* to the *kohen* as part of the priestly entitlement; the *kohen* receives it from God's table. Just as the *kohen*'s portion of the breast and thigh of a *shelamim* — though *kodshim kalim* — is *mishulchan gavoa*, because it flows to the *kohen* from God's dispensation rather than from the *kohen*'s own prior ownership, so too the *bechor* in its entirety is *mishulchan gavoa k'zachu*: the *kohen* acquired it from God's table.

### Not usable kiddushin

The conclusion follows: the *bechor* cannot be used for *kiddushin* because it is not the *kohen*'s actual property. It is a *matnas kehuna*, and as such it always has the character of something received from God rather than something owned outright. Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's *mammon ba'alim* principle does not extend to it — not because the animal is slaughtered or because there is no *Beis HaMikdash*, but because the *kohen* never possessed this animal as his own from the outset. The *matnas kehuna* distinction cuts across the entire analysis and leaves the *bechor* outside the scope of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's ruling, regardless of whether the animal is alive or dead, in the Temple era or outside it.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 13

## Kodshim Kalim Debate

### Opening & Dedication

Today's *daf* is Bava Kamma 13. We pick up four lines from the top with the word *gufa*, and this learning should be in the *zechus* and protection of our *chayalim* and *chayalot* who are right now in the middle of very heavy fighting in Gaza. *Hakadosh Baruch Hu* should protect them and all of *Am Yisrael*.

### Gufa: Full Baraita

The Gemara now returns to a *Baraita* that was cited earlier concerning the position of Rabbi Yose Haglili. Rabbi Yose Haglili held that *kodshim kalim* — lesser holy offerings that may be eaten throughout Yerushalayim — are considered *mamon ba'alim*, still under the proprietary ownership of their owners. This position was invoked to explain a clause in the *Mishnah* stating that the laws of *nezikin* apply only to property that carries no liability for *me'ilah* — *me'ilah* being the *korban* brought for the misappropriation of *hekdesh*. At first glance, this formulation seems to imply that there exist items possessing a degree of sanctity yet falling outside the domain of *me'ilah*, to which *nezikin* would nonetheless apply. Rabbi Yose Haglili identifies those items as *kodshim kalim*: they carry *kedushah*, yet since they are essentially consumed by their owners throughout Yerushalayim and are not regarded as wholly dedicated to God, *me'ilah* does not apply to them. Consequently, if such an animal — say, a *shelamim* ox — were to gore another animal, the laws of *nezikin* would govern the case.

The Gemara now presents the full text of the *Baraita*: *"Umal-ma bashem"* — four lines from the top of 13a — *"lirbos kodshim kalim shehem mamonot, divrei Rabbi Yose Haglili."* The *pasuk* in question concerns one who, while serving as a *shomer* for his fellow's property, denies holding it and takes a false oath, obligating him to bring an *asham*. The Torah characterizes this as a trespass against God. Rabbi Yose Haglili derives from this that even if the object denied was a *shelamim* or other *kodshim kalim* held for one's fellow, the denial still constitutes *v'kichash b'amito* — a wrong against one's fellow — because the *kodshim kalim* remain *mamon ba'alim*, the owner's property.

## Ben Azzai Position

### Shelamim Specifically

Ben Azzai's position in the *Baraita* is formulated similarly but with a notable narrowing: *"lirbos es ha-shelamim"* — to include not *kodshim kalim* in general, but specifically *shelamim*, the paradigmatic form of *kodshim kalim*. This immediately raises the question of what Ben Azzai intends to exclude, and how his position differs from that of Rabbi Yose Haglili.

## Kodshim Kalim Debate (II)

### Gufa vs. Amar Mar

This passage offers a textbook illustration of two Talmudic analytical terms that are frequently encountered but are here juxtaposed in a way that clarifies their distinct functions. *Gufa* — "the body of the matter" — is the signal to step back and examine the full text of something that was previously cited only in excerpt. Earlier, only the Rabbi Yose Haglili clause regarding *mamon ba'alim* was quoted; now the Gemara says *gufa*, let us look at the entire *Baraita*, which also includes the positions of Ben Azzai and Abba Yossi Ben Dostai. *Amar Mar*, by contrast, is nearly the inverse movement: having now placed the complete text before us, the Gemara zooms in and examines each line individually. Having already addressed Rabbi Yose Haglili's position, the Gemara now turns to analyze the Ben Azzai line in detail.

## Ben Azzai Position (II)

### Shelamim Demands

The Gemara asks: *"Amar Mar: Ben Azzai omer lirbos es ha-shelamim — l'maite mai?"* If Ben Azzai specifies *shelamim*, what is he excluding? One possibility raised is that he is excluding *bechor* — the firstborn animal — which is the position that will ultimately be articulated by Abba Yossi Ben Dostai. The logic would be that *bechor* is less *mamon ba'alim* than *shelamim*. But the Gemara challenges this: *"Hashtah u-mah shelamim she-te'unim semichah ve-nesachim ve-tenufah ve-chazeh ve-shok — shelamim amarta mamon ba'alim, bechor mi-ba'ya?"*

*Shelamim* carries a substantial array of *halachos*: the owner must perform *semichah* — the laying on of hands — bring *nesachim* of wine, flour, and oil, and wave the *chazeh ve-shok*, the breast and thigh. The multiplicity of these ritual obligations would seem to reflect a diminished degree of owner control and an elevated sanctity. Yet if even *shelamim*, with all its demands, is nonetheless *mamon ba'alim*, then *bechor*, which carries far fewer such requirements, is obviously *mamon ba'alim* as well. Ben Azzai cannot therefore be excluding *bechor*.

### Ma'aser Exclusion

Rather, says Rabbi Yochanan, Ben Azzai's *shelamim* formulation comes to exclude *ma'aser* — the animal tithe. *Ma'aser* is also a form of *kodshim kalim* eaten throughout Yerushalayim, but it cannot be considered *mamon ba'alim*.

### Bechor vs. Ma'aser

The *Baraita* cited in support makes the distinction precise. Regarding *bechor* the Torah states *"lo yipadeh"* — it cannot be redeemed, meaning its sanctity cannot be transferred to a monetary substitute — yet *venimkar*, it can still be sold. An unblemished *bechor* may be sold by one *kohen* to another *kohen* who will bring it as a *korban*; a blemished *bechor* may be sold alive or after *shechita*, to be eaten outside Yerushalayim. The very fact that *bechor* can be sold is powerful evidence that it remains *mamon ba'alim* — the capacity to sell is a hallmark of ownership.

Regarding *ma'aser*, however, the Torah states *"lo yiga'el"* — a term the Gemara derives to prohibit sale entirely. *Ma'aser* cannot be sold, whether unblemished or blemished, whether alive or slaughtered. Since the owner lacks the power to sell it, it is not *mamon ba'alim*. This is why Ben Azzai, in saying *shelamim*, means to include *shelamim* and *bechor* but exclude *ma'aser*.

One might recall that at the close of the previous *daf*, an argument was introduced that *bechor* is not truly *mamon ba'alim* because the *kohen* receives it not from the owner's voluntary dedication but as a *matnat kehunah* — a priestly gift — such that his stake in it derives *mishulchan gavoah kazachu*, from the table of Heaven, not from any transfer by the owner. The Gemara acknowledges this but notes — as Rashi explains — that we are speaking either of *bechor bechutz l'aretz* or of *bechor* in a time when there is no *Beis HaMikdash*, circumstances that neutralize the *matnat kehunah* dimension of *bechor* and leave it genuinely in the owner's domain.

Now Ravina offers an alternative: he reads this entire discussion — the comparison between *bechor* and *ma'aser* — not as commentary on Ben Azzai's statement about *shelamim*, but rather on the closing statement of Abba Yossi Ben Dustai, who said that Ben Azzai spoke only of *bechor*. According to the first reading, Ben Azzai said *shelamim* (including *bechor*) but not *ma'aser*; Abba Yossi Ben Dustai then contracted that to *bechor* alone. Ravina re-anchors the *bechor*-versus-*ma'aser* analysis at Abba Yossi Ben Dustai's statement instead.

## Abba Yossi Position

### Bechor Only

Abba Yossi Ben Dustai states: *"Lo amar Ben Azzai ela b'bechor bilvad"* — Ben Azzai's ruling applies only to *bechor*. The question immediately arises: *"lemeimra demai?"* — what is this formulation coming to exclude? If the intention is to exclude *shelamim* — to say that *bechor* is the most obviously *mamon ba'alim* because *shelamim* carries heavier obligations like *nesachim* and *tenufah* — the Gemara objects to that logic.

### Alt. Reading

There is an alternative way of ordering these categories. One could argue that *shelamim* is in fact the most obviously *mamon ba'alim* of all: it begins as an ordinary *chullin* animal and only subsequently is sanctified by the owner's deliberate act of dedication. *Bechor*, by contrast, is sanctified from the very moment of birth — *"kadosh merechem"* — and never passes through a stage of being *chullin*. Moreover, from the *kohen*'s perspective, it is received as *matnat kehunah*, *mishulchan gavoah kazachu*. If so, *shelamim* is the clearest case of *mamon ba'alim*, and *bechor* is a more ambiguous case.

### Bechor Paradox

This is the crux of the tension: which is more obviously *mamon ba'alim* — *bechor*, because it carries fewer ritual demands, or *shelamim*, because it originates as the owner's own property freely dedicated? The Gemara entertains both readings.

According to the first reading: *bechor* is the easiest case because of fewer demands; then *shelamim*; then *ma'aser* is excluded entirely. According to the second reading — which is conceptually the more compelling — *shelamim* is the most obvious, *bechor* is less so (due to its innate sanctity and its character as *matnat kehunah*), and *ma'aser* is excluded.

Rabbi Yochanan endorses the second reading, citing the same *Baraita* about the sellability of *bechor* and the non-sellability of *ma'aser* as the basis for Abba Yossi Ben Dustai's exclusion: he is excluding *ma'aser* on the grounds that it cannot be sold. The Gemara observes, however, that this reading creates a textual difficulty: *"hai b'bechor bilvad ka'amar"* — the language "only by *bechor*" implies that *shelamim* is excluded, not that *shelamim* and *bechor* are both included while only *ma'aser* is excluded. The Gemara concludes: *"kashya"* — this is difficult, and the tension is left unresolved.

The conceptual progression, however, remains elegant: *shelamim* is the most *mamon ba'alim*; *bechor* is one degree less so; *ma'aser*, which cannot be sold at all, is the least *mamon ba'alim* of the three and is thus excluded by those who narrow the ruling.

## Rava's Reinterpretation

### Lay Property Reading

At this point the Gemara has completed its treatment of the question of which *kodshim* fall within the domain of *nezikin*. Rava now offers a fundamentally different reading of the *Mishnah*'s language. *"Mai nechasim she'ein bahem me'ilah?"* — what does the *Mishnah* mean by "property in which there is no *me'ilah*"? Rava says it means *"nechasim she'ein bahem din me'ilah"* — property that is entirely outside the discussion of *me'ilah* altogether, that is, non-sanctified lay property. *"U'mani ninhu? Dehedyot"* — what property is that? Ordinary property owned by a layperson. According to Rava, the *Mishnah* is simply distinguishing between lay property and *hekdesh*, and even *kodshim kalim* would be outside the realm of *nezikin*.

### Language Question

The Gemara objects: *"ve'lisni dehedyot"* — if that is the intent, why not simply say "lay property" rather than "property without *me'ilah*"? The Gemara answers *"kashya"* — it is difficult. The *Mishnah*'s terminology remains somewhat awkward on Rava's reading; it might have said "non-*hekdesh*" or "lay property" more directly. It is worth noting that *hedyot* may not have been the standard Tannaitic term for this concept, which could account for the more roundabout formulation. In any case, Rava's interpretation makes the *Mishnah* straightforwardly about the *hekdesh* / non-*hekdesh* divide, without granting any special status to *kodshim kalim*, and would presumably reflect a position not in accordance with Rabbi Yose Haglili.

## Shelamim Gores Case

### Meat vs. Innards

Having established the framework, the Gemara now turns to practical applications. Rav Abba states: *"shelamim she'iziku govin mibesaram ve'eina govin me'imureihen"* — if a *shelamim* animal causes damage, the damaged party collects from the meat of the animal but not from the *imurim*, the sacrificial innards that are burned on the altar.

The scenario runs as follows: Reuven has dedicated an ox as a *shelamim*, and it gores Shimon's cow. According to Rabbi Yose Haglili, *nezikin* applies, so there is an obligation to pay. Since the animal is a *tam* — a non-habitual gorer — Shimon does not collect out of pocket from Reuven; rather, a *tam* obligates payment from the body of the goring animal itself. Shimon therefore acquires rights in the physical body of Reuven's ox up to half the value of his damages. Reuven then brings the animal to the *Beis HaMikdash*, the blood is sprinkled, and Reuven receives credit for having brought his *shelamim*. But then Shimon claims the meat — that meat is effectively his payment, and he eats it. One should bear in mind that the value of the ox is significantly diminished by its status as a *shelamim*: what might have been worth a thousand as a *chullin* animal is worth far less, since the recipient must consume it within two days. Nevertheless, Shimon's claim is to the meat.

### Altar Restriction

Rav Abba further specifies that Shimon cannot collect from the *imurim*. The Gemara immediately asks: *"peshita"* — is that not obvious? The *imurim* ascend to the altar; how could one even imagine that Shimon might collect from them?

### Proportional Division

The answer is that the ruling is necessary for the following case: *"lo tzricha legavo mibsara kneged imurim"* — it is needed to tell us that Shimon may not collect from the meat in lieu of the *imurim*. Consider a scenario where the meat and the *imurim* are each worth a hundred, and Shimon is entitled to a total of a hundred. One might reason: Shimon's claim is to a hundred dollars from the cow; the *imurim* are inaccessible; therefore he should be able to collect his full hundred from the meat. This is precisely what the ruling rejects. The principle established here is one of proportional division: Shimon's rights are distributed proportionally across all parts of the animal. If the meat and *imurim* are each worth half, he has a fifty-dollar claim on the meat and a fifty-dollar claim on the *imurim*. Since the *imurim* go to the altar, his fifty-dollar claim on them is simply lost — he cannot redirect it and collect that additional fifty from the meat.

This is a genuine *chiddush*. The intuition that one ought to be able to collect one's full entitlement from whatever assets are available is a natural one, and the ruling runs squarely against it.

### Two Parties Distinction

The Gemara now asks according to whose view this ruling is stated. *"Ee aliba derabbanan pshita"* — if it is according to the Rabbanan, it is obvious. The Rabbanan hold the principle *"ki leka leishtalumei mehai lo mishtalam mehai"* — when you cannot collect from one party, that does not entitle you to collect the remainder from another. The Gemara illustrates this with a well-known case: an ox pushes a person into a pit and the person dies. In principle, both the owner of the ox and the owner of the pit share causal responsibility for the damage. Yet the owner of the pit is legally exempt — the pit-owner's liability attaches only when an animal falls in on its own, not when it is pushed in by another animal. The Rabbanan say: the initial allocation of liability is fifty-fifty; the fact that one party has a legal exemption does not shift his share onto the other.

The underlying conceptual framework, as Rashi and Tosafos explain on this *daf*, is that both the ox and the pit each caused one hundred percent of the damage — they are not viewed as contributing fifty percent apiece to a shared total. Given that both caused it fully, the damages are allocated fifty-fifty between them. Once that allocation is made, each party's case stands on its own. The pit-owner's exemption is a *get-out-of-jail-free* circumstance that relieves him of his fifty — but it does not transfer that fifty to the ox-owner, who already had a separate, fully adjudicated obligation. The Rabbanan's rule is thus clear: *ki leka leishtalumei mehai lo mishtalam mehai*. Applied to the *shelamim* case, it is therefore obvious that Shimon cannot redirect his claim from the *imurim* to the meat — and so according to the Rabbanan, Rav Abba's ruling is no *chiddush* at all.

### One Animal Case

If so, the ruling must be according to Rabbi Noson. Rabbi Noson holds the opposite principle: *"ki leit lei l'ishtalumi mehai mishtalem mehai"* — when you cannot collect from one, you may collect from the other. And indeed, according to Rabbi Noson, Shimon should be entitled to collect his full hundred from the meat. So why does Rav Abba rule otherwise?

The Gemara offers two answers: *"iba'it eima Rabbanan, iba'it eima Rabbi Noson"* — one can maintain the ruling according to either view.

If one wishes to say it is according to the Rabbanan: their principle of *"ki leka leishtalumei mehai lo mishtalam mehai"* applies specifically *"betrei gufei"* — when there are two distinct bodies, meaning two separate parties being sued. The initial allocation separates the liability between them, and one party's exemption cannot be transferred to the other. But here we are dealing with *"behad gufa"* — one single animal, one single *mazik*. In that case, the Rabbanan would agree that one can say *"mikol heikha d'beina mishtalemna"* — I will collect my full payment from wherever in the animal I can. There is no conceptual basis for pre-dividing a claim within the parts of a single animal.

### One Owner Paradox

This makes the case genuinely surprising. We have one owner and one animal, and yet the ruling still holds that Shimon cannot collect the full hundred from the meat. If we are according to the Rabbanan's rule as just explained — that for a single animal you collect from wherever you can — then Rav Abba's ruling seems to cut against it.

Alternatively, if one wishes to say it is according to Rabbi Noson: Rabbi Noson's allowance to collect from the second party rests on a specific argument available to the damaged party. As the Gemara explains, Rabbi Noson's position is that *"ba'al hashor l'ba'al habor ana torai bevirecha ashkachtei"* — the owner of the ox can say to the owner of the pit: I found my animal in your pit; what I cannot collect from the *tam* ox, I will collect from you, because the pit-owner bears the ultimate underlying responsibility. Rabbi Noson's rule thus derives from the special culpability of the pit-owner as the site where the animal came to rest. But *"aval hacha"* — here, in the *shelamim* case — *"mi matzi amar besra azik imurim lo azik?"* — can one say that the meat did more of the damage than the *imurim*? Of course not. No part of the animal bears greater causal responsibility than any other. The head or horns that gored bear no more guilt attributable to the meat than to the *imurim*. Without that asymmetry of culpability, Rabbi Noson's logic does not apply, and the proportional division stands.

The result is striking: whether one holds like the Rabbanan or like Rabbi Noson, the conclusion is the same — Shimon cannot collect more than fifty from the meat of this *shelamim* ox. The intuitive argument that "I should collect my full entitlement from whatever is available" is rejected on both accounts.

## Toda Gores Case

### Toda Meat/Bread

Rava now presents a parallel case involving a *toda* — a thanksgiving offering. The *toda* is a species of *shelamim* but with the distinctive feature that forty loaves of bread are brought alongside the animal offering. If a *toda* animal causes damage, *"govin mibsara ve'ein govin lachma"* — the damaged party collects from the meat but not from the bread.

### Bread Obligation

The Gemara asks: *"lechem peshita"* — is it not obvious that the damaged party has no claim to the bread? The bread was not the *mazik*; even if it is part of the same *korban*, one only collects from the animal that did the damage. The Gemara answers that the *chiddush* lies in the closing clause: *"nizak ochel basar u'mitkaper meivi lacham"* — the damaged party eats the meat as his payment, while the *mitkaper* — the one on whose behalf the *toda* was brought, the owner of the goring animal — must still bring the bread. It is his *korban* and therefore his obligation.

One might have thought otherwise: since the bread accompanies the meat as part of a single integrated *korban*, and since the bread is *"hechshera dezevach"* — a prerequisite for the validity of the offering — whoever eats the meat should bear responsibility for the bread. The *mitkaper* might argue: you ate the meat, so you bring the bread. The ruling teaches that this is not so. The bread obligation is *"chiyuva debe'alim"* — the owner's obligation, irrespective of who eats the meat. Even though Shimon eats the meat as his damages payment, the bread remains Reuven's responsibility. It is still his *korban*; the damaged party acquires only the meat, not the whole of the *korban* with its attendant obligations.

## Property Status Rules

### Designation Requirement

The Gemara returns to the *Mishnah*'s criteria for *nezikin* liability, now examining the requirement that property be *"nechasim meyuchadim"* — designated property. The question *"lema'utei mai"* — what does this exclude? — is posed, and Rav Yehuda answers: it excludes a case of *"ze omer shorcha hizik veze omer shorcha hizik"* — where two oxen from two different owners both ran after a third animal and one of them gored it, but neither party knows which ox was responsible, each pointing at the other. In such a case, both owners are exempt. The property is not *meyuchad* — not identifiable as belonging to a specific, determinable *mazik*.

### Ambiguity & Exemption

The Gemara notes that this very rule appears explicitly in a later *Mishnah*: *"hayu shnayim rodfim achar echad... ze omer shorcha hizik veze omer shorcha hizik — shneihem peturim."* Here, as earlier, the Gemara observes *"tana vehadar mefareish"* — the *Mishnah* first presents general criteria in terse form, and later *Mishnayot* elaborate on each principle individually. This is characteristic of the early *Mishnayot* at the opening of Bava Kamma, which are composed in a compressed, list-like format.

### Hekdesh/Hefker Exempt

A *Baraita* offers an alternative explanation of the *meyuchad* requirement: *"prat lenichsei hefker"* — it excludes ownerless property. The Gemara then asks: *"heichi dami?"* — what exactly is the case? If an owned ox gored an ownerless ox, of course there is no one to sue. The case must therefore be an ownerless ox that gored a person's ox. Here one might imagine the damaged party could simply seize the goring ox and take it. But if another party came first and took possession of that *hefker* ox before the damaged party could act, does the damaged party now have a lien on it? The answer is no. Just as *hekdesh* is exempt from *nezikin*, *hefker* is equally exempt. If the ox was ownerless at the moment of goring, there is no owner whose negligence grounds the *nezikin* obligation, and no valid claim attaches to the animal — even once someone else takes possession of it.

### Status Consistency

Ravina adds a further dimension: *"nagach ve'achar kach hikdish, nagach ve'achar kach hifkir"* — the *meyuchad* requirement also addresses cases where an ox gored while it was owned, but the owner subsequently declared it *hekdesh* or *hefker* before the damaged party could bring him to *beis din*. One might think that since the ox was fully owned and fully liable at the moment of goring, the damaged party retains rights against it regardless of the subsequent change of status. The ruling is that this is not so: the status must be consistent throughout.

### Anti-Avoidance Rule

An owner cannot strategically change the status of his animal after the damage event in order to escape liability. The requirement of *meyuchad* — consistent, designated ownership — forecloses this avenue.

### Shor Haniskal

The Gemara cites a *Baraita* in support: Rabbi Yehuda states that this consistency requirement extends even to the case of a *shor* that gored and killed a person, which would ordinarily be subject to stoning. If the owner sanctified or renounced ownership over the ox at any point between the act of goring and the final judgment, the ox is exempt from stoning. The derivation: the *pasuk* links *"vehu'ad biva'alav... vehemit... vehashor yissakel"* with connecting *vav*s, indicating that all elements — the warning to the owner, the death, and the judgment — must occur while the animal is in the same status. The Gemara adds that *"vegmar din lo ba'ei?"* — surely the final judgment (*gmar din*) must also be included? The answer is yes: the text *"vehashor yissakel"* implies a stoning that follows a completed judgment, so the consistent status must be maintained all the way through *gmar din*. Thus: *"ad she'tehei misah ve'ha'amadah badin vegmar din shavin ke'echad."* The same principle applies by analogy to standard *nezikin* cases: an owner cannot alter the status of his property at any point prior to the completion of judgment in order to evade liability.

## Reshut Hameyuchedes

### Domain Exemption

The final clause of the *Mishnah* under discussion establishes another exemption: *"chutz mereshut hameyuchedes lamazik"* — damage occurring in the *mazik*'s exclusive domain exempts the *mazik*. Rav Chisda citing Rav Avimi explains: *"de'amar lei torcha birshusi mai ba'ei"* — because the *mazik* can say to the damaged party: what was your ox doing in my property? If your animal entered my private domain without authorization and was gored there by my ox, I bear no liability. The damaged party had no right to be there, and therefore the *mazik* is entirely exempt when the damage occurs within his exclusive *reshut*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 14

## Nechasim Hamiyuchadim

### Mishnah Introduction

The *mishnah* introduces the concept of *nechasim hamiyuchadim* — designated or assigned property — as one of the conditions for liability in *nezikin*. The first order of business is to determine what this phrase excludes. Picking up approximately twelve lines down on 13b, the *gemara* asks: *lemautei mai* — what does it come to exclude?

### Two Oxen Case

*Amar Rav Yehuda lemautei zeh omer shorcha hezik vezeh omer shorcha hezik* — Rav Yehuda explains that *nechasim hamiyuchadim* comes to exclude the case where it is not clear whose ox caused the damage. Two oxen were running after a third ox, the third was gored, and now Reuven and Shimon are each pointing the finger at the other. The *gemara* immediately challenges this reading: that case is already taught explicitly later in the *mishnah* — *hayu shenayim rodfim achar echad*, two oxen chasing one, *zeh omer shorcha hezik vezeh omer shorcha hezik*, and the ruling is *shenayim peturin*, both are exempt, by the classic principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya*. The *gemara* resolves this by saying the *mishnah* first states the abstract principle and then later makes it explicit — *tani ve'ader mefaresh*. That is one reading of the *mishnah*.

### Hefker Ox Analysis

A *baraita* offers a second interpretation: *prat lenichsei hefker* — *nechasim hamiyuchadim* excludes ownerless property. The *gemara* then probes what case this refers to.

If our ox gored a *hefker* ox — *denagach tora didan letora dehefker* — obviously one is exempt. There is no plaintiff; *man tavei lei*, who would even bring the matter to *beis din*? That is trivial.

The more interesting case is the reverse: an ownerless ox gored one of ours. One might think the solution is simple — just go ahead and take possession of the ox, since it is ownerless. Whatever damage it did to you, you can simply recoup by claiming the *hefker* animal. But the *gemara* refines the case: *beshekadam vezacha bo acher* — what if someone else, say Reuven, got there first and took possession of the *hefker* ox before you could? Now, one might reason that since the *halacha* in a case of a *tam* ox (one that has not gored before) is that payment comes from the body of the ox itself, perhaps you automatically acquired a partial ownership in that ox from the moment it did the damage — a lien, as it were, of one hundred dollars' worth of an ox that caused you a hundred dollars of damage.

The *chiddush* is that this is not so. Without an owner, no liability is triggered at all. You do not acquire any partial ownership in an ox that gored yours if that ox had no owner at the time of the goring. This is not merely an arbitrary exemption. The entire framework of *nezikin* presupposes a person who is liable — either because of negligence or because their property caused the damage. It does not operate as some metaphysical mechanism by which the damaging animal itself becomes partially owned by the victim. Without an owner, the process never begins.

### Ravina's Reading

Ravina offers an even more striking *chiddush* as a third reading of *nechasim hamiyuchadim*: *nagach ve'achar kach hikdish, nagach ve'achar kach hefkir* — my ox gored, and after it gored and I am already liable, I sanctify the ox to the *beis hamikdash* (*hekdesh*), or I renounce ownership (*mafkir*), and thereby escape payment. The idea that one can exit an existing liability through a post-damage transfer of ownership is quite a remarkable claim.

A *baraita* confirms this position: *af illu nagach ve'achar kach hikdish nagach ve'achar kach hefkir patur* — even if after the goring you sanctify or renounce ownership, you are exempt.

## Kofer & Ownership Transf…

### Rav Yehuda on Kofer

The *baraita* cited by Ravina deals specifically with the *kofer* payment — the atonement payment owed when a *shor ha-mu'ad* kills a person. Rav Yehuda teaches that if after the ox kills someone the owner sanctifies or renounces the ox, he is exempt from paying *kofer*. The *pasuk* the *gemara* invokes is *vehu'ad beva'alav vehameis ish* — the ox was warned against the owner and it killed a man or a woman — followed by *ha-shor yisakeil*, the ox shall be stoned.

### Same Status Requirement

The *derasha* is *ad she-tehei misa ve-ha'amada ba-din shavin* — the killing and the adjudication must occur in the same legal context, with the same status of ownership. More precisely, the *gemara* clarifies: from the moment of the killing through the *gmar din* — the issuance of the final verdict — the ox must remain in the same ownership status. *Shavin ke-echad*: the two events must be aligned. If I transfer the ox to *hefker* or *hekdesh* before the *ha'amada ba-din*, I have transferred it into a status that would have exempted me from liability had the ox been in that status at the time of the goring. And so I am off the hook.

The *gemara* raises an obvious question: does it suffice to transfer to *hefker* or *hekdesh* and then reclaim? That is left as an open question. The exemption appears to apply when the ox is in that exempt status at the moment of *ha'amada ba-din*, but whether reclaiming it afterwards reimposes liability is not resolved.

### Extension Beyond Kofer

What is striking is that the *gemara* does not explicitly derive from any *pasuk* how the *kofer* rule — with its requirement that ownership status remain consistent from goring through adjudication — extends to ordinary cases of property damage. There is no textual bridge. And the extension produces a profound injustice: my ox causes a thousand dollars of damage; the ox is worth a hundred dollars; I simply *mafkir* it and escape paying a thousand dollars in damages.

Some *acharonim* suggest, and this resolution is compelling even if the *gemara* does not make it explicit, that the *gemara* may intend to limit this rule to *keren tam* — the case of an unhabituated ox goring for the first three times, where only half-damages are paid.

### Knas vs. Monetary Obliga…

Two reasons converge to make this rule work specifically for *keren tam*. First, there is a debate — to be addressed later — as to whether half-damages for *tam* is a *knas* (a fine) rather than genuine compensation (*mamon*). If it is a *knas*, then the liability does not arise automatically at the moment of the event. In ordinary cases of damage — where my ox tramples your produce or falls into your pit — I owe you money from the instant the damage occurs; *beis din* merely clarifies what already exists. A *knas*, by contrast, is imposed by *beis din*; I do not owe anything until the court imposes it. Accordingly, if the ox is in a legally exempt status — *hefker* or *hekdesh* — at the time *beis din* adjudicates, *beis din* cannot impose the fine because the ox's status has changed.

Second, and just as importantly, this limitation dissolves the injustice problem. When my ox gores for the first three times, my liability is capped at half-damages and is further limited by the value of the ox itself. I never pay more than what the ox is worth. So *mafkir*-ing the ox does not save me any money — indeed, I may lose by renouncing it. The perverse incentive to escape a large damage obligation by abandoning a small ox does not arise if my liability was already capped at the ox's value.

By contrast, applying this rule to full compensatory damages — where an ox worth a hundred dollars could shield me from a thousand-dollar judgment — would be both technically incoherent and deeply unjust. The *gemara* leaves this gap unexplained, and this is one of those moments where the reasoning works compellingly only when we confine the principle to its natural domain. As noted, *ein danin dinei kenasos be-Vavel* — courts in Babylonia do not adjudicate *kenas* matters at all — which adds another dimension to why the *beis din* must be involved for the fine to take effect.

## Own Domain Exemption

### Tosafot's Principle

The *mishnah* states *chutz me-reshut ha-meyuchedet la-mazik* — the damager is exempt when the damage occurs in his own domain. Tosafot articulates this as a broad principle: there is no liability for damage that occurs within the damager's own property when the victim's animal or produce entered without permission.

### Risk & Freedom Logic

The logic is straightforward. If your ox wanders into my property without permission, I can say to you: *torcha bi-reshuti mai ba'ei* — what is your ox doing on my property? You came here of your own accord. I have the right to do whatever I wish on my own property. I am not obligated to police my own animals in my own space to protect a trespasser. You assumed the risk by entering.

This is worth pausing over. The exemption is not merely technical — it reflects a deep principle that a property owner retains freedom of action within his domain, and that a victim who enters without authorization cannot impose liability on the property owner for events that occur there. The *rishonim* make explicit what the *gemara* does not spell out: this applies only when the victim entered without permission. If the damager invited the victim in, the calculus shifts entirely — the invitation removes the predicate for the exemption.

## Shared Domain Debate

### Mishnah Reading

The *mishnah* then presents what turns out to be a genuinely ambiguous line. After establishing the exemption for the damager's own domain, the *mishnah* says *ve-reshut ha-nizak ve-ha-mazik* — the domain of both the damagee and the damager — and then concludes *ke-she-hizik chav ha-mazik le-shalem* — when damage occurs, the damager is obligated to pay.

The question is how to parse this. Is *ve-reshut ha-nizak ve-ha-mazik* part of the *chutz* clause — meaning one is also exempt in a shared domain — and the final phrase is simply restating the general principle of liability? Or does the sentence structure mean that in a shared domain, unlike in the damager's own domain, one is liable to pay?

This ambiguity generates a significant *machloket* among the *amora'im*.

### Rav Chisda's View

Rav Chisda citing Avimi says: *chatzar hashtufin chayav bah al ha-shen ve-al ha-regel* — in a shared domain, one is liable for *shen* and *regel*. It is worth noting why the debate about a shared domain is confined to *shen* and *regel* and does not extend to *keren*. By *keren*, one is liable in *reshut ha-rabim*; the only exemption is when the victim's animal entered the damager's exclusive domain without permission. A shared domain by definition is one where the victim has a right to be — so there is no question one is liable for *keren* in a shared domain. The interesting question is only *shen* and *regel*.

For *shen* and *regel*, the Torah establishes liability in *sadeh acher* — the other person's field — and exemption in *reshut ha-rabim*. A shared domain sits between these poles. From one angle: the exemption in *reshut ha-rabim* is a special case driven by the need to preserve freedom of use of public thoroughfares and by *pshiat ha-nizak* (the victim's own negligence in placing property in a high-traffic area); anything that is not a *reshut ha-rabim* should generate liability, including a shared domain. From the other angle: liability in *shen* and *regel* is specifically tethered to *sadeh acher*; without the quality of "another's domain," there is no liability, and a shared domain where both parties have rights is not *sadeh acher*.

Rav Chisda adopts the first reading: a shared domain is not a *reshut ha-rabim*, so one is liable. The *mishnah*'s final phrase — *ke-she-hizik chav ha-mazik le-shalem* — according to Rav Chisda is the *mishnah*'s affirmative ruling about a shared domain. According to this reading, *ve-reshut ha-nizak ve-ha-mazik* establishes that in a shared domain the damager pays. And the general principle at the end — *ke-she-hizik chav ha-mazik* — is read, according to Shmuel, as coming to include *keren*, while according to Rav, who understands *shor* in the first *mishnah* to already include *keren*, it comes to include the case of a *shomer* — a watchman — whose animal causes damage, a topic the *gemara* develops in a substantial digression.

The *gemara* addresses the *shomer* case at length. The *baraita* states that when an animal under a *shomer*'s care does damage in his domain, a *tam* pays half and a *mu'ad* pays full; but if the animal broke out at night or bandits breached the fence — cases of *onnes* — the *shomer* is exempt. The *chiddush* is not merely that a *shomer* bears responsibility for damage the animal he is watching causes to third parties, which is intuitive enough. The *gemara* pushes into harder cases.

If the ox the *shomer* was watching gored the *shomer*'s own ox, why should the original owner pay? The *shomer* would ordinarily pay for damage the ox causes to third parties, so why should the original owner compensate the *shomer* for damage his own watched ox inflicted on the *shomer*? The reverse case is equally puzzling: if the *shomer*'s own ox gored the ox he was watching, one might think he owes full compensation as a *shomer* — since a *shomer* bears full liability for damage to the item he is guarding, regardless of the cause — not merely half as a *mazik*. The *gemara* resolves these difficulties by introducing a case of stipulation: the *shomer* accepted responsibility for guarding the animal from harm (*shmiras gufo*) but explicitly did not accept responsibility for damage the animal causes (*shmiras nizko*). In such a case, if the watched ox — with no liability resting on the *shomer* for its actions — gores the *shomer*'s own ox, the original owner remains liable. And conversely, the *shomer*'s ox goring the watched ox is addressed by distinguishing between *shomer* liability and *mazik* liability based on what was stipulated.

### Rabbi Elazar's View

Rabbi Elazar takes the opposite position: *patur al ha-shen ve-al ha-regel* — in a shared domain, one is exempt from *shen* and *regel*. According to Rabbi Elazar's reading, *chutz me-reshut ha-meyuchedet la-mazik ve-reshut ha-nizak ve-ha-mazik nami patur* — the exemption clause encompasses both the damager's exclusive domain and a shared domain. The only context in which one is liable for *shen* and *regel* is *sadeh acher* — the victim's domain exclusively. The final phrase *ke-she-hizik chav ha-mazik* then, according to Rabbi Elazar, does not refer to a shared domain at all but is a separate clause — and the *gemara* explains it comes to include *keren*, on the theory that one is liable for *keren* even in a shared domain.

### Baraitot Contradiction

The *gemara* now confronts a direct conflict between two *baraitot*. Rav Yosef cites a *baraita*: *chatzar hashtufin ve-hapundak chayav bahen al ha-shen ve-al ha-regel* — a shared domain and an inn, one is liable for *shen* and *regel*. This appears to be a flat refutation of Rabbi Elazar.

Rabbi Elazar responds that there is an equal and opposite *baraita*: the four categories articulated by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in *nezikin*. First category: it is exclusively the damagee's domain (*reshut le-nizak ve-lo le-mazik*) — liable for everything, *chayav bakol*, including *keren*. Second: exclusively the damager's domain (*le-mazik ve-lo le-nizak*) — fully exempt, *patur mikol*, because *torcha bi-reshusi mai ba'ei*. Third: a shared domain (*laze u-laze*), exemplified by *chatzar hashtufin* or a *bika* (valley) — *patur bahen al ha-shen ve-al ha-regel*, exempt from *shen* and *regel*, but liable for *keren* (half-damages for *tam*, full for *mu'ad*). Fourth: neither party's domain (*lo laze ve-lo laze*), described as a domain belonging to neither of them — *chayav al ha-shen ve-al ha-regel*, liable for *shen* and *regel*.

This *baraita* says precisely the opposite of Rav Yosef's *baraita* regarding a shared domain: one is liable according to Rav Yosef's source, exempt according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. We have an outright contradiction between *baraitot*.

## Reconciling Baraitot

### Rav Yosef's Distinction

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction by introducing a crucial distinction: *ki tanya hi be-chatzer meyuchedet laze u-laze bein la-peiros bein li-shvarim* — the *baraita* that exempts applies to a shared domain in which both parties have full rights: the right to bring their oxen *and* the right to keep their fruit there. *Hahi de-Rav Yosef be-chatzer meyuchedet la-peiros ve-eina meyuchedet li-shvarim* — the *baraita* that creates liability applies to a domain where one has the right to bring fruit but not to bring oxen.

This is the key: what does it mean to have a "right" to be in a given domain? The *gemara* is drawing a distinction between the right to deposit fruit and the right to bring cattle. In the case of Rav Yosef, the victim has a right to have their fruit in this shared courtyard, but the damager has no right to bring their ox there. From the perspective of the ox, it has entered a space it has no right to occupy — and that is functionally equivalent to *sadeh acher*. In the case of the *baraita* that exempts, both parties have the right to bring their oxen, so the ox's presence is entirely legitimate, and there is no basis for liability in *shen* and *regel*.

The *gemara* observes that this reading is confirmed by the language of the two sources themselves: the *baraita* that rules liability spoke of a case comparable to an inn (*pundak*) — one brings luggage to an inn, not oxen; the inn grants rights over fruit and belongings, not over animals. The *baraita* that rules exempt spoke of a *bika*, a valley — a space where one has an unquestioned right to bring one's animal to graze.

### Zevid-Abaye Exchange

Rav Zevid challenges this reconciliation: if the victim has rights to the domain for fruit, can one really say it is *sadeh acher*? The *pasuk* requires *u-vi'er bi-sdei acher*, and here the victim has some rights. Abaye responds: *keivan de-eina meyuchedet li-shvarim, sdeh acher karinan beih* — since the domain is not designated for oxen, we call it *sadeh acher* from the ox's perspective. The victim may have a right to bring fruit there; the ox had no right to be there at all. The ox's right of entry — or lack thereof — is the operative question.

### Mixed Rights Scenario

With the *baraitot* reconciled, the *gemara* asks whether the *amora'im* — Rav Chisda and Rabbi Elazar — were also just talking about different scenarios and do not in fact disagree. The *gemara* answers: possibly. If we are generous, Rav Chisda was speaking about a case where only fruit rights exist (no ox rights), which is functionally *sadeh acher*, and Rabbi Elazar was speaking about a case where both ox rights and fruit rights exist, which is not *sadeh acher* — and both would agree on both cases.

Or, says the *gemara*, if we say they do genuinely disagree, their disagreement is confined to the *kushya* of Rav Zevid and the resolution of Abaye: the case where one has rights for oxen but not for fruit. One position says this is *sadeh acher* because the ox had no right there; the other says you cannot call it *sadeh acher* when the victim has some right in the domain, even if it is only a fruit right.

### Core Principle Extraction

What the *gemara* is doing conceptually throughout this entire discussion is decisive and important. The operative question is never whether a domain resembles *reshut ha-rabim* closely enough to generate an exemption. The *pasuk* does not say: exempt in *reshut ha-rabim*, liable elsewhere. The *pasuk* says *u-vi'er bi-sdei acher* — liable specifically in *sadeh acher*. Accordingly, you are liable in *shen* and *regel* only when you can define the location as *sadeh acher*. And *sadeh acher* requires, at minimum, that the ox had no right to be in that domain. Any time the ox had a right to be there, we cannot call it *sadeh acher*, and liability in *shen* and *regel* is off the table.

The *bika* is in the exempt category precisely because, even if it is technically ownerless, one's ox has a right to be there — it is the kind of space where animals graze freely. The *pundak* is in the liable category because, even though one may have rights to store property there, one does not have a right to bring an ox into an inn.

## Four Categories Analysis

### Damagee's Domain Only

Returning to the *baraita* of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, the *gemara* now unpacks each of the four categories in detail. The first category — *kol she-reshut le-nizak ve-lo le-mazik*, the domain is exclusively the damagee's — generates liability for everything: *chayav bakol*. The *gemara* emphasizes that the *baraita* does not say *al ha-kol* (for all the types of damages) but *bakol* (fully, completely). This reads as: one pays full damages, even for *keren*. This follows Rabbi Tarfon's position: *meshuneh keren be-chatzer ha-nizak nezek shalem meshalem* — when an unusual act of *keren* occurs in the damagee's domain, full damages are owed even if the ox is a *tam*. When the ox invaded a space it had absolutely no right to enter and committed an act of damage there, the elevated circumstance justifies full payment.

### Damager's Domain Only

The second category — *le-mazik ve-lo le-nizak*, exclusively the damager's domain — is *patur mikol*, fully exempt. The victim's property entered without right; *torcha bi-reshusi mai ba'ei*, the damager is under no duty of care.

### Shared Domain Breakdown

The third category — *laze u-laze*, shared domain, exemplified by *chatzar hashtufin* and a *bika* — is *patur* for *shen* and *regel* but liable for *keren*: *tam* pays half, *mu'ad* pays full. As established above, in a shared domain where both parties have rights to bring their oxen, the ox's presence is legitimate and *sadeh acher* cannot be invoked. But *keren* — which is liable even in *reshut ha-rabim* — applies in any domain that is not exclusively the damager's, so liability for *keren* persists.

### Neither's Domain

The fourth category — *lo laze ve-lo laze*, neither party's domain — initially appears to refer to a third party's domain: my ox enters Reuven's yard and eats Shimon's fruit. But the *gemara* rejects this reading: the *pasuk* of *u-vi'er bi-sdei acher* would not be satisfied, because the fruit consumed must belong to the person whose domain was entered. If my ox is in Reuven's yard eating Shimon's fruit, Shimon's property is not in Shimon's domain.

The *gemara* therefore reinterprets *lo laze ve-lo laze* not as "neither party," but as "not both" — meaning it is one person's domain, namely the damagee's. It is *lo laze* (not the damager's) *ve-lo laze* (and not both of theirs) — it is only the damagee's. And therefore one is liable for *shen* and *regel* as in the first category.

This creates an apparent redundancy: the first and fourth categories seem identical. The *gemara* resolves this by noting that the final category carries a different ruling for *keren* — *tam* pays half and *mu'ad* pays full — which follows *rabbanan*, who hold that even in *chatzer ha-nizak* a *tam* pays only half for *keren*. The beginning of the *baraita* followed Rabbi Tarfon (who rules full payment for *keren* in *chatzer ha-nizak*), and the end follows *rabbanan*. Shmuel advised Rav Yehuda: *shevok matnitin*, do not try to reconcile the *baraita* as a unified position — the *reisha* is Rabbi Tarfon and the *seifa* is *rabbanan*.

Ravina citing Rav offers an alternative: the entire *baraita* follows Rabbi Tarfon. The fourth category is not the damagee's domain but rather a domain that is *lo laze ve-lo laze la-peiros ela de-chad, lazeh ve-lazeh li-shvarim* — neither party has exclusive rights to the fruit (only one of them does), but both have rights to bring their oxen. According to this reading, both are permitted to bring oxen, so from the perspective of *keren* it resembles *reshut ha-rabim* (the ox had every right to be there), and the *tam* pays only half. But since only one party has the right to keep fruit there, from the perspective of *shen* it constitutes *chatzer ha-nizak*, and the damager is fully liable.

## Fruit vs. Ox Rights

### Mixed Rights Setup

This brings us to the final and most complex scenario — the one the *gemara* did not explicitly adjudicate but which generates a *machloket* between Rashi and Tosafot. The case, as read by Rashi from the *girsa* of Ravina citing Rav: both parties have rights to bring their oxen to this domain, but only the damagee (not the damager) has the right to keep fruit there. My ox therefore enters a space where it has every right to be — but it eats your fruit, which is in a space where you have a right to keep it and I do not.

### Rashi's Approach

According to Rashi, this scenario splits the liability. With respect to *shen* — the eating of the fruit — it is considered *chatzer ha-nizak*, the damagee's domain. Even though my ox had a right to be there, the absence of my right to keep fruit there means it is, to that degree, *sadeh acher*: the domain is "another's" with respect to what was consumed. Rashi thus holds that *sadeh acher* is satisfied whenever any element of the domain is exclusively the other person's — it need not be that the ox had no right to be there; it is enough that I had no right to the fruit that was consumed. Accordingly, the damager pays fully for *shen* and *regel*.

With respect to *keren*, however — since both parties have the right to bring their oxen — it resembles *reshut ha-rabim*, and a *tam* pays only half.

### Tosafot's Objection

Tosafot rejects this. Rabbeinu Tam's reading reverses the critical variable: the relevant question for *sadeh acher* is always and only whether the ox had a right to be in the domain. If my ox had a right to be there, no element of "another's field" is present, and *shen* and *regel* cannot generate liability. For Tosafot, *sadeh acher* requires that the ox itself had no right of entry — the fruit rights of either party are secondary. Accordingly, Rabbeinu Tam reads *lo laze ve-lo laze* as: neither party has rights to bring their ox there — and then, with respect to *shen*, it is *chatzer ha-nizak*; with respect to *keren*, because both ox rights are absent, it resembles *reshut ha-rabim*.

The divide is thus fundamental. For Rashi, *sadeh acher* is a function of the rights to the property consumed: as long as the victim has a right to the fruit and the damager does not, it is sufficiently "another's domain" to generate liability in *shen*. For Tosafot, *sadeh acher* is solely a function of the ox's right of entry: if my ox had a right to be there at all, the domain cannot be called *sadeh acher*, whatever my rights to the fruit. This sharp disagreement about the precise definition of *sadeh acher* will carry forward into subsequent discussions.

# Bava Kamma 15

## Mishna Overview

### Archaic Mishna Language

The daf begins at the top of 14b, where we continue with a series of *mishnayot* that are notably cryptic, written in what one can only describe as an archaic layer of Tannaitic language. One wonders about the scholarly consensus: the assumption is that these *mishnayot* are among the earliest in the *mishna*. It is, in a way, a testament to the remarkable editorial achievement of Rebbe in organizing and standardizing *Shas* that most *mishnayot* do not read like this. The opacity here is striking precisely because it stands apart from the more discursive style that characterizes most of the *mishna*.

### Shum Kesef Mishnah

The *mishna* reads: *shum kesef, shaveh kesef, bifnei beis din, ve-al pi eidim, bnei chorin bnei bris, ve-nashim bikhlal ha-nezek, ve-hanizak ve-hamazik betashlumin.* Assessment of money, monetary equivalent, before a court, through witnesses, free persons, members of the covenant, women are included in damages, and both the damaged party and the damager participate in the payment. It reads almost as a legal poem, and the *gemara* will now work through each phrase methodically to determine what it actually means.

---

## Para and Talit

### Rav Yehuda's Read

The *gemara* opens with the first phrase: *mai shum kesef?* What does "assessment of money" mean? Rav Yehuda explains: *shum zeh lo yehei ela bekesef* — when you assess the loss, you do so in terms of the monetary value, the dollar amount. The *gemara* then notes that we have already learned this teaching, since a *braita* elaborates on it more explicitly.

### Cow/Garment Case

The *braita* presents the following scenario: *para she-hizika talit ve-talit she-hizika para* — a cow and a garment got into a kind of altercation and damaged one another. Tosafot works out precisely how this could occur: if the *talit* caused the *para* to slip, that would function like a *bor birshut harabim*; if the *para* ate the *talit*, that would need to occur in *reshut hanizak* and would be a form of *shen*. Perhaps the cow gored the garment, or consumed it in an unusual manner. Regardless of the precise mechanism, the *braita* rules: *ein omrim tze para be-talit ve-talit be-para* — we do not simply declare a swap, saying that the cow covers the garment's damage and the garment covers the cow's damage and the whole matter is settled. Rather, *shamnin otan bidamim* — you assess each loss in monetary terms, determine the difference, and whoever holds the balance pays that difference.

### Tosafot Chidushim

This ruling may seem self-evident, yet Tosafot identifies two distinct *chidushim* embedded here. The first concerns the case where the *para* damaged the *talit*. If the ox gored and was a *tam* — an animal that has not yet established a pattern of goring — the well-known rule is that the owner pays half the damage, capped at the value of the goring animal itself. One might have thought that rather than merely owing money, the injured party automatically acquires a proprietary interest in the goring ox itself. The second *chidush* addresses the reverse scenario: the *talit* functioned as a *bor* and caused the cow to slip. One might have thought that even though the owner of the *talit* owes money for the damage to the cow, the injured party of the cow should at least be able to seize the *talit* itself that caused the harm — especially in a case where the owner of the *talit* has since died and left no landed property from which a lien could be exercised. The *braita* teaches that this too is incorrect. What is owed in both cases is a monetary obligation, not a proprietary claim on the damaging object.

### Rabbi Akiva's Ownership

The first *chidush* speaks directly to a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael. Rabbi Akiva holds the position of *yuchlaf hashor*: as soon as your ox gores my animal, I automatically become a part-owner in your ox. It is not merely that you owe me money; I now own a percentage of your animal as of the moment of the goring. This *mishna*, according to Tosafot, rules against Rabbi Akiva. When the *braita* says we do not simply declare a swap — *ein omrim tze para be-talit* — it is teaching that you do not acquire ownership of the goring ox. The owner of the ox owes you money, limited to the ox's value, but your claim does not translate into direct ownership of the animal.

The second *chidush* is perhaps less intuitive. By ordinary principles, one can only collect debts from landed property on which there is a lien. If the owner of the *talit* that caused the slip has died and left no land, the injured party might argue: surely I should at least have rights to the *talit* itself, the very object that caused my loss, even if I cannot collect from the orphans' other assets. The *braita* says no. The obligation here is purely monetary. How one pays is a separate question — one can pay in chattel, not necessarily in cash — but the nature of the obligation is defined as an amount of money owed, and not as any proprietary claim on the damaging object itself.

---

## Shaveh Kesef

### Chattel Payment

The *gemara* now turns to the next phrase: *shaveh kesef*, monetary equivalent. The natural reading would seem to be that one need not pay in actual cash; any chattel equivalent in value will suffice — even *subin*, bran, as the *gemara* uses as its example. This is how the term is most classically understood.

### Braita's Land Read

What the *gemara* actually does with this phrase is, however, surprising. A *braita* interprets *shaveh kesef* in a completely unexpected way: *shaveh kesef melamed she-ein beis din nizkakin ela le-nekhasim she-yesh lahem achrayus* — *shaveh kesef* teaches that *beis din* will only deal with, that is to say seize or levy, property that bears liens, which means land. According to this reading, *shaveh kesef* refers not to chattel as a payment medium but specifically to real property.

This is genuinely puzzling on two levels. First, why should *shaveh kesef* mean land, when it most naturally means chattel equivalent in monetary value? Second, why would *beis din* be limited to seizing land when the *mazik* is alive and directly obligated? The *braita* adds a further clause: if the *nizak* went ahead and physically seized chattel from the *mazik* on his own, *beis din* will allow him to keep it. Why? If *beis din* cannot officially levy chattel, why would a unilateral seizure by the *nizak* be validated?

The *gemara* resolves the second question: the rule applies specifically *be-yasmei*, where the *mazik* has died and we are dealing with orphans. The heirs are not directly obligated in their father's debt; collection from the estate is limited to landed property on which liens had been established. And liens, the *gemara* clarifies, are created automatically — the moment one causes damage, the injured party holds a lien on the *mazik*'s land. *Beis din* does not create the lien; it assists in exercising it.

The case of unauthorized seizure during the *mazik*'s lifetime is resolved by reference to the principle of *shetafas mechayim*: if the *nizak* seized chattel while the *mazik* was still alive, at a moment when the debt was directly owed by a living obligor, *beis din* will validate that seizure retroactively as payment. One might note, as was raised in the course of the *sugya*, that this bears resemblance to the principle of *avid inish dina le-nafshei* — taking the law into one's own hands — a topic that receives fuller treatment later in the *gemara* at 27b.

### No Fixed Price

The *gemara* then circles back to the primary puzzle: since when does *shaveh kesef* mean land? Rabba bar Ulla offers an explanation: *davar ha-shaveh ke-kesef* means something that can be worth an unlimited sum, with no fixed market price — and that is land, because land is formally excluded from the *parasha* of *ona'ah*, the prohibition of overcharging. Since there is no fixed price for land, it can be said to be equivalent to any amount of money, and hence is called *shaveh kesef*.

The *gemara* objects: slaves and documents of debt also lack the prohibition of *ona'ah*. Rabba bar Ulla then reformulates: *davar ha-nikneh be-kesef* — something acquired with money. Land is acquired through a monetary transaction, whereas chattel is acquired through *meshikha* and *hagbahah*, physical acts of acquisition. The *gemara* presses again: slaves are also acquired with money. Rashi and Tosafot note that the inclusion of *shtaros* — loan documents — in this category is itself not straightforward, since transferring debt obligations does not clearly follow the same rules. Regardless, the objection stands at least for *avadim*.

### Like Money Not Money

Rav Ashi then proposes an altogether different reading: *shaveh kesef ve-lo kesef* — something that is *like* money but is not money itself. And who is *like* money? *Ve-hani kulu kesef ninhu* — all chattel is considered money. This follows from a point established earlier in the *gemara* regarding *meitav*: when one pays with chattel, even low-quality chattel, it can serve as payment, because movable property is presumed to be readily liquidable and therefore functionally equivalent to cash. What is genuinely *like* money but not quite money is land. Hence *shaveh kesef* designates land, because land is the one category that approximates but does not equal cash in terms of its acquisition and transfer mechanisms.

As the *gemara* itself acknowledges, this is not the straightforward reading of *shaveh kesef*. The most natural interpretation — and indeed the one that governs its use throughout *halakha* — is simply that payment can be made in any chattel equivalent in value to money. But the *braita* reads it as land, and the *gemara* works through various attempts to explain how that reading is derived.

---

## Bifnei Beis Din

### Court Requirement

The *gemara* next addresses *bifnei beis din* — assessment and payment must occur in the presence of a court. One might have thought that this refers to the situation where one sold off all one's property before going to court, leaving the plaintiff with nothing to collect. But the *gemara* immediately objects: if any of the sold property was land, the injured party should still be able to collect based on the existing lien. *Beis din* does not create liens; liens arise automatically at the moment of damage or borrowing. The court's role is to assist in enforcing them, not to generate them. Selling one's land before appearing in court should therefore make no difference to the plaintiff's ability to levy on those properties.

### Semicha Authority

The *gemara* therefore reinterprets *bifnei beis din*: *prat le-beis din hedyotos* — it excludes a court of commoners, a *beis din* that lacks the ordained authority traced back to Moshe Rabbeinu. This *semikhah* — distinct from the modern rabbinical ordination that bears the same name — empowers judges to adjudicate capital cases and *knasot*, monetary fines. A court empowered only to handle standard monetary litigation (*dinei mammonot*) cannot adjudicate the types of claims present here. The reason is that some of the obligations arising from the laws of damages — as the *gemara* is about to elaborate — are classified as *knas*, punitive fines rather than compensatory payments. Imposing a punishment requires a court that holds a level of divine authority, conceptually linked to the verse *ad ha-Elohim yavo devar shneihem*. A court of *hedyotos* lacks that standing.

### Valid Witnesses

The *mishna* continues: *al pi eidim* — through witnesses. This seems obvious; of course adjudication requires witnesses. The *chidush*, the *gemara* explains, lies in the phrase that follows: *prat le-modeh be-knas ve-achar kach ba'u eidim she-hu patur* — to exclude the case where one admitted to a fine and witnesses subsequently arrived. Since we are dealing with cases of *knas*, the rule of self-admission — *modeh be-knas patur* — comes into play.

---

## Modeh Beknas

### Self-Admission Exclusion

The underlying principle here is that self-admission cannot create an obligation to pay a fine. This distinguishes a *knas* fundamentally from *mamon*, ordinary civil liability. In matters of compensation, self-admission suffices and even obligates. In matters of fine, it does not.

### Fines as Punishment

The reason for this distinction is structural. A fine is conceptually a punishment imposed through monetary means, analogous to lashes — a punishment imposed through the body. Just as lashes require objective testimony and cannot be self-imposed, so too a monetary fine requires objective testimony. The principle of *ein adam meisim atzmo rasha* — a person cannot render himself wicked — functions here not merely as a procedural protection but as a substantive rule: the court's authority to punish depends on externally established guilt. Self-incrimination does not supply that foundation.
