Moreover, the court imposing the fine must possess the requisite *semikhah*, since the fine represents not compensation but a divinely authorized sanction.

### Witnesses After Admission

There is a further debate referenced in the *gemara*: if one admits to a fine and witnesses subsequently arrive, is one obligated? One opinion holds that subsequent witnesses do render one liable — the initial admission is simply irrelevant but does not permanently foreclose the obligation. A second opinion holds that having admitted first, the person is permanently exempt, even if witnesses later corroborate the event. The *gemara* notes that if one follows the second view, the *chidush* of *al pi eidim* is that witnesses alone create the fine obligation. If one follows the first view — that subsequent witnesses do create liability — then *al pi eidim* is needed for a different purpose, which leads into the next clause: *bnei chorin bnei bris*.

---

## Bifnei Beis Din (II)

### Bnei Chorin Bnei Brit

Valid witnesses must be *bnei chorin* — free persons — and *bnei bris* — members of the covenant. *Bnei chorin le-mautei avadim*: free persons to exclude non-Jewish slaves, who are not valid witnesses, even though they bear a partial obligation in *mitzvot*. *Bnei bris le-mautei ovdei kochavim*: members of the covenant to exclude non-Jews. The *gemara* establishes that both exclusions are necessary. One might have thought that excluding slaves — who occupy a diminished societal standing because *halakha* does not recognize their family relationships — is straightforward, whereas non-Jews, who do possess recognized family relationships and are of equal standing in society, might be includable. Conversely, one might have excluded non-Jews on account of their greater distance from the obligations of *mitzvot*, while thinking slaves, who are partly obligated in *mitzvot*, might qualify. Each exclusion is therefore necessary to convey that neither category is valid.

One notable observation arises here: the list of valid witnesses mentions *bnei chorin* and *bnei bris* but not women — even though the *mishna* explicitly mentions women in its subsequent clause. Women are in practice excluded from serving as witnesses, yet the *braita* does not include that exclusion in this list. A possible explanation is that it is simply taken for granted, though the asymmetry is noteworthy.

This raises the question, engaged in medieval practice, of how women's testimony might be handled in *dinei mammonot*. In medieval Ashkenaz, where women were frequently active participants in commerce, the *rishonim* developed a framework of accepting women's testimony not as formal *edut* but as *birur davar* — a form of circumstantial evidentiary weight that operates outside the technical framework of witness law. This approach sidestepped the formal disqualification while addressing the practical needs of a community where women were often central economic actors.

The related question of women serving as *dayanim* — judges — is taken up by Tosafot in the context of the verse *asher tasim lifneihem*, which the *gemara* elsewhere reads as referring to the judges before whom cases are brought, rather than the litigants. If *lifneihem* there includes women as parties to litigation, could it also be read to include women as judges? Tosafot notes that the general principle — *kol ha-kasher ladun kasher le-ha'id* — would seem to foreclose this, since women are disqualified as witnesses and therefore disqualified as judges. But Tosafot reframes the principle: it applies to men who are qualified to judge being qualified to testify. A woman might, on this reading, be a qualified judge even though she cannot serve as a witness. The case of Devorah is raised and then somewhat set aside: *shema hayu mekabelim otah aleihem mipnei Shekhinah* — perhaps they accepted her authority on account of her prophetic status, which constitutes a form of consensual arbitration rather than a demonstration of women's formal judicial standing. Tosafot leaves the question of whether a woman can serve as a *kasher dayan* as genuinely open.

---

## Women in Damages

### Women Included

The *mishna* states: *ve-nashim bikhlal ha-nezek* — women are included in the laws of damages. The *gemara* asks: *mena hani mili?* From where is this derived?

### Masculine Language Defau…

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, and similarly the school of Rabbi Yishmael, derive it from the verse *ish o isha ki ya'asu mikol chatot ha-adam* — if a man or woman commits any of the sins of a person. From this, *hishvah ha-katuv isha le-ish le-khol onashim she-ba-Torah* — the Torah equates women to men with regard to all punishments in the Torah. The reason such a verse is needed, as Tosafot explains, is that the entire Torah is written *be-lashon zachar*, in the masculine gender. As in classical legal drafting, the masculine formulation is presumed to function as a gender-neutral default unless explicitly stated otherwise. But this raises the question of whether women are automatically included or whether explicit inclusion is required in each domain.

### Textual Proofs

Multiple verses are brought to cover different domains. The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from *ish o isha* that women are included in all punishments. The school of Rabbi Elazar derives from *ve-eileh ha-mishpatim asher tasim lifneihem* — the word *lifneihem* is not specifically masculine, and from it we learn *hishvah ha-katuv ish le-isha le-khol dinim she-ba-Torah*: civil law applies equally to men and women. The school of Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yose Ha-Gelili derive from *ve-nigach ish o isha* — an ox that gores a man or a woman — that with respect to being the injured party, the victim of a goring, men and women are treated identically: *hishvah ha-katuv ish le-isha le-khol mitot she-ba-Torah*.

All three are necessary.

### Women's Hava Amina

### Not Bar Mitzvah

### Women Judges Question

Had only the first verse been stated — that women bring *korbanot* for sins — one might have said the Torah showed *rachmanus* on women so that they could achieve *kaparah*, but that this does not extend to civil law, where women, presumed not to be primary actors in commerce (*ish de-var masa u-matan*), might not be subject to the full framework of litigation. Had only the civil-law inclusion been stated, one might have inferred it was necessary only to ensure that women could function in economic life (*ki heichi de-tehavi lah chiyusa*), but that when it comes to *kaparah* — atonement — a woman, *de-lav bat mitzvah* in the sense of being less comprehensively obligated in *mitzvot*, perhaps does not fully access the atonement mechanism in the same way as a man who is more completely obligated. Had only these two been stated without the verse about the gored victim, one might — and here the *hava amina* becomes genuinely disturbing — have thought that if an ox kills a woman, the owner need not pay *kofer*, because *kofer* is linked to the gravity of the life taken, and a life with fewer *mitzvot* obligations might be seen as less fully within that calculus. The *gemara* closes this *hava amina* by pointing out that *kofer* is paid because *ika ibbud neshama* — there is a loss of life — and therefore of course it applies to a woman equally. All three verses are necessary, and the *maskana* is that women are included in all domains of Torah law — as agents, as litigants, and as victims — unless explicitly excluded.

The *gemara* here is, as the *hava amina* stage reveals, working with certain presumptions about women's status that are difficult for the modern reader. The conclusion is unequivocal in equalizing women across the board in tort law, but the very structure of the *tzricha* — needing proofs in each domain — reflects underlying assumptions that the rabbis themselves were working to address through the exegetical process.

---

## Both Parties Pay

### Joint Participation

The *mishna* concludes: *ha-nizak ve-ha-mazik be-tashlumin* — both the injured party and the damager participate in the payment of damages. The *gemara* will now examine what this phrase means in light of the central dispute about the nature of *palga nizka*, half damages by *keren*.

---

## Half Damages Debate

### Rav Papa Compensation

*Palga nizka* — half damages in the case of a *tam* ox that gores — is the subject of a famous *itra'mar* between Rav Papa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua. Rav Papa holds: *mamona* — it is genuine compensation. His reasoning: *kasvar stam shvarim lav be-chezkat shimur kaimi* — ordinary oxen are not presumed to be inherently self-restrained; even an ox that has never gored still requires supervision. If an ox has not been watched and it goes out and gores, there is an element of negligence on the owner's part. Strictly speaking, therefore, the owner *should* pay full damages. *U-ve-din hu de-ba'ei le-shlumai kulei* — by strict logic he should pay everything. But the Torah has *rachmanus* on him — *de-akhti lav ya'ad*, the ox has not yet established a pattern of goring, has not gone through the *muad* process, and so the owner stands right at the edge of negligence. Because the negligence is borderline, the Torah goes easy on him and requires only half. But it remains genuine *mamon*: the owner was genuinely negligent, and what he pays is real compensation for real damages attributable to his failure.

### Rav Huna Fine

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua holds: *knasa* — it is a fine. *Kasvar stam shvarim be-chezkat shimur kaimi* — ordinary oxen *are* presumed to be naturally restrained and not in need of close supervision. Therefore the owner was *not* negligent. *U-be-dino de-lo le-shalem klal* — by strict logic he should pay nothing at all. But the Torah fined him anyway — *ki heikhi de-lintrei le-torei* — to incentivize a higher level of care. By knowing that even a *tam* goring will cost half the damage, every ox owner is pushed to maintain vigilance beyond what strict negligence liability would demand. The half payment is not compensation for actual fault; it is a punitive incentive to prevent harm.

### Borderline Agreement

Both positions, when placed side by side, agree on one thing: the *tam* goring occupies a genuine borderline. That is precisely why the Torah set the payment at half, not full and not zero. Rav Papa reads the halved payment as the Torah moderating a genuine obligation downward; Rav Huna reads it as the Torah imposing a liability where none strictly existed. One says it is slightly above the threshold of negligence with the Torah being lenient; the other says it is slightly below that threshold with the Torah being strict. The disagreement is about which side of the line the *tam* goring falls on.

---

## Mamona or Knasa

### Incomplete List

The *gemara* now attempts to resolve the *machloket* between Rav Papa and Rav Huna from Tannaitic sources. The first attempted proof: the *mishna* that enumerates the differences between *tam* and *muad* does not include *modeh be-knas* — self-admission — among those differences. If *palga nizka* were a *knas*, one would expect the list to mention that a *tam* cannot be paid on self-admission while a *muad* can. The omission suggests it is *mamona*. The *gemara* deflects: *amar tana ve-shayer* — the *tanna* taught an incomplete list.

---

## Both Parties Pay (II)

### Compensation Model

Returning to the *mishna*'s phrase *ha-nizak ve-ha-mazik be-tashlumin*: if *palga nizka* is *mamona*, the meaning is elegant and precise. The *mazik* genuinely owes full compensation, but pays only half; the *nizak* effectively absorbs the other half of his own loss. Both parties thus participate in the payment: the *mazik* pays half, and the *nizak* bears half. They each lose an equal portion of the damages.

### Fine Model

If *palga nizka* is *knasa*, the framing is different. The *mazik* technically owes nothing, yet receives a windfall of half the damage's value. The *nizak*, meanwhile, is out the full loss of his animal. In what sense can one say the *nizak* "participates in payment"? What *tashlumin* is the *nizak* paying when the entire amount is a fine that the *mazik* did not truly owe?

### Carcass Depreciation

The *gemara* answers: *lo nitzrecha ela le-pichut neveila* — the phrase teaches that the *nizak* bears the depreciation of the carcass. When the animal is gored and killed, the carcass immediately begins to lose value. The *nizak* suffers that ongoing loss and cannot pass it to the *mazik*. That is how the *nizak* "participates in the payment" even under the *knasa* model: not by paying for half of what is owed, but by absorbing the diminishing value of what he was left with.

---

## Mamona or Knasa (II)

### Counter Incomplete

The *gemara* notes that the teaching about carcass depreciation appeared already in an earlier *mishna* — *tashlumei nezek melamed she-ha-bealim metaplin be-neveila* — and asks whether the earlier *mishna* and the current one overlap or address different cases. The answer: *chada be-tam ve-chada be-muad* — one addresses goring by a *tam* and the other goring by a *muad*. Both cases need to be stated: in the *tam* case one might have thought the *nizak* is partly spared since the *mazik* pays only half; in the *muad* case one might have thought the *mazik*, paying full, should also absorb the carcass depreciation. Each case requires explicit teaching.

Returning to the first proof attempt: the *mishna* listing differences between *tam* and *muad* omitted *modeh be-knas*. The *gemara* says this does not prove the list is complete, since another difference was also omitted: *kofer*. A *muad* pays full *kofer* and a *tam* pays none. The *gemara* responds: *ha mani Rabbi Yosei Ha-Gelili hi de-amar tam meshalem chatzi kofer* — this *mishna* may follow Rabbi Yosei Ha-Gelili, who holds that a *tam* does pay half *kofer*. If so, the distinction between *tam* and *muad* on *kofer* does not exist according to that opinion, and there is nothing left off the list with respect to *kofer*. So the first proof remains inconclusive; the list may simply be incomplete.

### Self-Admission Proof

The *gemara* then brings a *braita*: *heimit shori et ploni o shoro shel ploni, harei zeh meshalem al pi atzmo* — if I admit that my ox gored and killed a person or gored another's ox, I pay based on my own admission. The *gemara* asks: is this not speaking even of a *tam*? If so, it shows that half damages by a *tam* is *mamona*, since the owner pays on his own admission. The *gemara* deflects: perhaps the *braita* speaks only of a *muad*. But then, the *gemara* responds, what would the ruling be for a *tam*? If *palga nizka* is *knasa*, then by a *tam* one should not pay on self-admission. Why does the *braita* not tell us that explicitly — contrasting *muad* with *tam* — rather than contrasting the case of goring a person or animal with the case of goring a slave? *Liflog ve-litni bididah* — let the *braita* divide the *tam/muad* distinction internally. The *gemara* answers: the *braita* is speaking entirely of *muad* cases and has no occasion to address *tam* goring at all.

### The Key Rule

The *gemara* advances what appears to be a decisive *braita*: *ze ha-kelal, kol ha-meshalem yoter al mah she-hizik eino meshalem al pi atzmo* — here is the general rule: anyone who pays *more* than the actual damage does not pay on self-admission. Payment in excess of actual damage is the hallmark of *knas*. The implicit counterpart: if you pay *less* than the damage, it would seem to be *mamon*, compensation. And half damages is less than full — so it should be *mamona*.

### Resolving Exception

The *gemara* immediately presses: does paying *less* than the damage always mean it is *mamon*? The *braita*'s formulation says if you pay *more* you cannot pay on self-admission — implying that if you pay less, you can. But should one say that if you pay less it is *always* compensation? That would mean one should have stated the rule differently: *kol she-eino meshalem kamah she-hizik* — anyone who does not pay the *exact* amount of the damage does not pay on self-admission. That broader formulation would capture both more and less than exact damage as potential *knas*. The fact that the *braita* said only "more" seems to prove that paying less is *mamon*. This appears to be a strong proof — *tiyuvta*.

### Tzerorot Example

The *gemara* responds: *lo psika lei* — the rule cannot be stated in that broader form, because there are cases where one pays *less* than the full damage and it is nonetheless *mamona*, genuine compensation. The example: *chatzi nezek tzerorot* — the half damages paid for pebbles kicked by an animal in the public domain. In that case, the animal's owner was fully negligent; the indirect causation through the pebbles simply means the law reduces the payment to half as a matter of *halakha*, not as a punitive measure. It is *mamona*, but it is less than full damage. Because this exception exists, the *braita* could not formulate the rule as "any amount other than exact damages is *knas*" — that would have incorrectly classified *chatzi nezek tzerorot* as a fine. Hence the rule was stated only for the "more than" case, leaving "less than" ambiguous. The attempted proof from this *braita* therefore fails to establish definitively that *chatzi nezek keren* is *mamona*.

---

## Final Ruling Knasa

### Ruled as Fine

After systematically deflecting every Tannaitic proof that would have established *palga nizka* as *mamona*, the *gemara* delivers its ruling: *ve-hilkheta palga nizka knasa* — the *halakha* is that half damages of a *tam* goring is a *knas*, a fine. This is remarkable. The *gemara* just concluded *tiyuvta* — a definitive refutation — of the *mamona* position, and then immediately rules as *knasa*. The *gemara* acknowledges the tension: *tiyuvta ve-hilkheta?* It responds: *ein* — yes. The reason the *tiyuvta* was considered so powerful was because the *braita* said "more than the damage" — implying less than the damage is *mamona*. But in fact that implication does not hold universally, since *chatzi nezek tzerorot* is *mamona* while paying less than full. The *braita*'s formulation was not meant to be exhaustive in the other direction. With that resolved, the *gemara* is free to rule that *chatzi nezek keren* is *knasa*, in accordance with Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua.

### Implications Pending

The practical consequences of classifying *chatzi nezek* of a *tam* as *knasa* are substantial and will be taken up in the *gemara* that follows. Among the most significant: from what source does one pay the *knas*? The *gemara*'s resolution of that question — touching on the rule of payment from the body of the animal, the principle of *modeh be-knas patur*, and related issues — will be the subject of the continuation.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 16

## Keren Half-Damages: Knas

### Knas Status Established

The discussion opens by revisiting the central question of the previous session: when an ox gores for the first three times and the owner pays *chatzi nezek*, half-damages, is that payment a form of *mamon* — genuine compensation reflecting some degree of negligence — or is it a *knas*, a fine? The evidence had seemed to point toward *mamon*, and one *baraita* had implied as much, reasoning that any payment exceeding actual damages is a *knas*, while a payment that falls *short* of full damages must be *mamon*. The *gemara*, however, rejects this inference. It distinguishes between two types of half-damages: *chatzi nezek tzerorot*, where the animal kicks pebbles that indirectly cause damage, is *mamon*, since the owner bears full negligence and the reduction to half reflects only the indirect nature of the act; whereas *chatzi nezek* of *keren* is *knas*. The conclusion, then, is that half-damages for *keren* constitutes a *knas*, and this determination carries significant practical consequences — most immediately, the rule that a *knas* is not collected upon the tortfeasor's own admission.

### Meshuneh Animal Acts

With this conclusion in place, the *gemara* draws an immediate application before turning to the next *mishnah*. The passage begins: *de-hashta de-amart palga nizka knasa* — now that we have established that half-damages for *keren* is a *knas* — *hai kalba de-achal imrei ve-shunra de-achal tarnigola*, if a dog ate sheep or a cat ate a chicken, *meshuneh hu*, that is unusual behavior, *ve-lo magbinan be-Bavel*, and we do not collect it in Bavel. The underlying principle, not stated explicitly in the *gemara* but implicit in its reasoning, is that an animal that causes damage in an unexpected, *meshuneh* fashion is treated as a type of *keren*.

### Shen vs. Keren Question

This classification raises a sharp analytical question, which the upcoming *mishnayot* will develop: when an animal eats something not natural to it — a sheep that chews on a garment, for instance — is that an unusual form of *shen*, eating that falls outside its normal pattern, or is it a type of *keren*? The *nafkamina* between these two characterizations is not merely taxonomic. One might raise the question of whether the act could ever become a *muad* through repetition, or whether it would be a *knas* or *mamon*. But the most immediate and decisive *nafkamina* is: *patur bi-reshut ha-rabim*. If the act is classified as *shen*, the owner is exempt for damage caused in the public domain; if it is *keren*, the owner is liable even there.

### Reshut Harabim Status

This distinction — *patur bi-reshut ha-rabim* for *shen* versus *chayav bi-reshut ha-rabim* for *keren* — is thus the critical practical question when determining whether unusual eating is a form of *shen* or *keren*.

### Rishonim: Unusual=Keren

Most *rishonim* assume that unusual eating is classified as a type of *keren*. Their reasoning proceeds from the logic of the *knas* ruling itself. If half-damages were *mamon* — reflecting genuine but partial negligence — one could extend that rationale by analogy to other categories such as *shen* and *regel*, creating a parallel form of reduced liability. But *knas* is inherently more arbitrary; fines are not derived by analogy in the same way. Therefore, once we conclude that *chatzi nezek keren* is a *knas*, and we wish to impose half-damages in other analogous scenarios of unexpected damage, the only way to derive that liability is to fold those scenarios into the category of *keren* itself. This leads to a striking conceptual revision: *keren* is not defined solely by *kavana le-hazik*, a deliberate intent to cause harm, but more broadly by the fact that the animal causes damage in an unexpected, unusual manner. Any act that is *meshuneh* — unpredicted and out of character — is, by virtue of that quality alone, a *keren*.

This is a significant conceptual shift. The possibility remains open that unusual eating is simply *shen*, with the same reduction to half-damages applied by analogy rather than by reclassification. But the dominant *rishonic* position treats such acts as genuine *keren*, with full liability in *reshut ha-rabim* and all the attendant consequences.

### Knas & Bavel Restriction

Returning to the case of the dog that ate sheep or the cat that ate a chicken: since the act is *meshuneh* and classified as *keren*, and *chatzi nezek keren* is a *knas*, it follows that *lo magbinan be-Bavel* — we do not collect this payment in Bavel. Courts in Bavel lack the *semikhah* necessary to adjudicate *dinei knasos*; the authority to impose fines, like the authority to administer lashes or capital punishment, requires ordination traceable to Eretz Yisrael. The *gemara* adds a qualification: *ve-hani mili be-ravrevei* — this applies only to a large sheep or large chicken, where such eating is genuinely unusual. *Aval be-zutrei*, if the animal ate something small, *orcheih hu*, that is within its normal range and would not be *meshuneh*.

But this creates a practical problem. The victim has been injured and receives nothing, since the court cannot adjudicate a *knas* in Bavel. The *gemara* addresses this: *ve-i tafas lo mafkinan minei* — if the victim seizes property from the tortfeasor, we do not force him to return it. He deserves at least half compensation, and while the court cannot affirmatively impose the *knas*, it will not dispossess someone who has helped himself. Additionally, the victim may request that the court set a date for him to travel to Eretz Yisrael, compelling the tortfeasor to appear before a court there with proper authority. If the tortfeasor refuses to attend such proceedings, *meshamtinan leh* — we place him in *nidui*. And in any event, *meshamtinan leh ad de-masalek hezika* — we subject the tortfeasor to *nidui* until he removes the dangerous animal from his possession.

### Dangerous Animal Removal

This last provision connects to a broader obligation articulated by Rabbi Natan. The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *Rabbi Natan omer minayin she-lo yigadel adam kelev ra be-toch beito ve-al yamid sulam ra'ua be-toch beito* — how do we know that one may not keep a dangerous dog in one's home or maintain a rickety ladder in one's home? The verse states, *lo tasim damim be-veitecha*, do not bring blood upon your house — meaning one may not maintain any condition that creates danger for others. The *rishonim* debate the precise threshold: at what point is an animal dangerous enough to require removal, and does "removal" mean confining it or physically eliminating it? Tosafot distinguishes between animals that can be adequately restrained with a chain and those whose danger cannot be so neutralized. These parameters remain a subject of discussion among the *rishonim*.

### Tosafot: Tafas Limits

The principle of *tafas lo mafkinan minei* — that we do not dispossess a victim who has seized property to satisfy a *knas* we cannot adjudicate — is subjected to an important qualification by Tosafot, citing *Rabbeinu Tam*. Tosafot rules: *davka i tafas ha-mazik atzmo ke-gon kelev o shor* — the permissible seizure applies only if what the victim seizes is the damaging animal itself, such as the dog or the ox. The concern driving this limitation is that if we allowed *tafas* of any property without restriction, a bad actor could fabricate a *knas* claim, seize someone's property, and then shield himself behind the argument that Bavel courts cannot hear *dinei knasos* and therefore cannot order the return of the seized property. That, says *Rabbeinu Tam*, *yavo lidei takala* — would lead to grave abuse, as one could effectively confiscate anything and render the courts powerless to respond.

This connects to another observation implicit in Tosafot: because *keren* liability attaches to the body of the animal itself, there is a conceptual basis for the victim to seize specifically the damaging animal, insofar as the animal is the very object from which *keren* damages are normally collected.

### Tafas & Gezela Debate

Many *rishonim* take a different approach to the problem entirely. They argue that when a victim seizes another's property, that act does not begin as a *din knas* at all — it begins as a potential *gezeilah*. The court is not thereby being asked to adjudicate a fine; it is being asked to determine whether the seized item must be returned. That is a question of *dinei gezeilah*, and Bavel courts are fully competent to hear such matters. The court will examine the facts sufficiently to determine: was there in fact a damaging act? Is the value of the seized property equivalent to or greater than the damage sustained? If the seizure exceeds the damage, the excess must be returned; if it is equivalent, the seizure stands. According to this view, the prohibition on adjudicating *dinei knasos* in Bavel does not prevent the court from engaging with the facts at all — it simply means the court is resolving a *gezeilah* question rather than affirmatively imposing a fine. This debate has ramifications far beyond goring oxen, extending to cases of personal injury where certain components of the damages — such as pain and suffering — may themselves be classified as *knas*. How much of a victim's entitlement can be vindicated through *tafas* and the resulting *gezeilah* inquiry becomes a significant question in the *rishonic* literature about the scope of judicial authority in Bavel.

---

## Five Tam, Five Muad

### Five Tam Types

The *mishnah* enumerates five categories in which an animal is classified as *tam* — an innocent first-time offender paying only half-damages: *lo ligach*, not to gore; *ve-lo ligof*, not to push or butt; *ve-lo lishoch*, not to bite; *ve-lo lirvots*, not to crouch on something and break it; and *ve-lo livot*, not to kick. Each of these represents a form of *keren* behavior for which the animal has not yet been forewarned.

### Shen Muad (Natural)

The *mishnah* then turns to the five *muad* categories. *Ha-shein muedes le-echol et ha-ra'uy lah* — the tooth (*shen*) is *muad* to eat things that are natural for the animal to eat. Each animal is assessed according to its own species: what is normal for a goat differs from what is normal for an ox. The implication of specifying natural eating is, of course, that unnatural eating occupies a different legal space — presumably a *tam* version of *shen*, as the *mishnah* is laying the groundwork for that distinction.

### Regel Muad

*Ha-regel muedes li-shbor be-derech hiluchah* — the foot (*regel*) is *muad* to break things in its normal way of walking. Whether there exists a *tam* version of *regel* is less clear from this formulation, though the *mishnah* does not address it here.

### Shor Muad & Keren

The *mishnah* continues: *ve-shor ha-muad* — an ox that has been formally forewarned three times and is now *muad* for *keren*; and *ve-shor ha-mazik bi-reshut ha-nizak* — an ox that causes damage in the victim's domain. The term *muad* here carries a dual meaning: sometimes it denotes habitual behavior, and sometimes it simply means that full damages are paid. The ox goring in the victim's domain is no more habitually inclined to gore there than elsewhere; rather, *muad* in this context means the legal consequence is full payment. This is the position of Rabbi Tarfon. *Ve-adam* — a person is also always *muad* in the sense of always paying full damages for whatever harm he causes, whether awake or asleep. Here too, *muad le-olam* does not mean a person is habitually disposed to cause damage; it means that in all circumstances, the legal consequence is complete liability.

### Wild Animals Muad

*Ha-ze'ev ve-ha-ari ve-ha-dov ve-ha-namer ve-ha-bordelis ve-ha-nachash — harei elu muadim* — the wolf, lion, bear, leopard, *bordelis*, and snake are *muad* from the outset. One immediately notices that this list contains six entries, not five. The deeper question — what kind of *muad* are these animals? Is their characteristic violence a form of *shen* and *regel*, given that they act from natural instinct and appetite, or is it a form of *keren*, reflecting a kind of intentional destructive act? Instinct might suggest *keren*, since these animals seem deliberately aggressive. But stepping back, when a lion attacks a sheep for food, it is engaging in exactly what an ox does when it eats grain — it is satisfying a natural appetite. That would make it *shen*, not *keren*.

One student raised the interesting point that animals also attack out of territorial instinct — not for food at all, simply to drive away intruders. A bear, for example, when it feels threatened, will attack without any intent to eat. This kind of violence is not *shen* and is not obviously *regel*; it may genuinely constitute *keren* in the sense of purposeful harm. This point actually reinforces the reading of Rashi, who comments that these animals are *muad* for all forms of damage — *afilu bi-neshikha be-khol nezikin* — even biting, in all categories of damage. According to Rashi and, by implication, the Rambam, the *chiddush* of the *mishnah* is that for these animals, all manner of violence — whether for food or otherwise — is classified as *keren muad* from the outset.

Tosafot takes a more restrictive view, attempting to confine the lion's characteristic acts to the categories of *shen* and *regel* — natural behavior for which the animal simply has no *tam* phase — and correspondingly ruling that a lion eating in *reshut ha-rabim* is *patur*, since *shen* in a public domain generates no liability. The Rambam, by contrast, does not draw this distinction, treating the lion as *muad keren* across the board. The discussion remains instructive: one must resist the anthropomorphic temptation to read violence as inherently malicious when it may simply be instinctive, while also recognizing that certain kinds of attack — territorial aggression, for instance — may genuinely belong to the *keren* category regardless of whether food is the motive.

---

## Animal Identity & Lo (II)

### Domestication Doctrine

Rabbi Eliezer offers an optimistic counterpoint to the general rule that these animals are *muad* from the outset: *bi-zeman she-hem benei tarbut einam mu'adin* — when they are domesticated, they are not *muad*. A trained lion, in Rabbi Eliezer's view, can have its legal status reversed. Normally the trajectory runs from *tam* to *muad* through three acts of forewarning; for these animals, the reverse trajectory is possible — from *muad* to *tam* — through domestication. One might note that practical experience raises doubts about how fully any apex predator can be domesticated, but that concern lies outside the *halacha*'s formal framework.

The one exception is absolute: *ve-nachash muad le-olam* — a snake is permanently *muad* and can never be domesticated. Whether this reflects a purely naturalistic assessment that snakes are simply incapable of domestication, or whether it carries metaphysical resonance given the snake's role in the garden of Eden and the symbolism pervading rabbinic literature, the *gemara* leaves implicit. The text moves on without extended comment, though as will be seen, the snake's eternal *muad* status is woven into a remarkable aggadic passage later in the *sugya*.

---

## Muad Categories Debate

### Rabbanan vs. Tarfon

The *gemara* now turns to a structural problem in the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* appears to enumerate five *tam* and five *muad* categories, contrasting them in parallel. But the *shen* liability seems to presuppose the victim's domain (*chatzer ha-nizak*), while the *keren* as *tam* seems to be paying only half — which, according to Rabbi Tarfon, should not be possible in the victim's domain where *keren* pays full. Can the entire *mishnah* be attributed to the Rabbis, who hold that even in the victim's domain *keren* pays only half? Or to Rabbi Tarfon? The difficulty is that the later portion of the *mishnah*, which lists *shor ha-mazik bi-reshut ha-nizak* as a *muad* category, seems to reflect Rabbi Tarfon's position. So: is the first half Rabbanan and the second half Rabbi Tarfon?

### Rashi's Reshut Solution

Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav attempts to resolve this by arguing that the *mishnah* is entirely Rabbi Tarfon, by positing a divided domain: *reisha be-chatzer ha-meyuhedet le-peirot le-echad u-le-zeh u-le-zeh le-shorim* — the first section speaks of a courtyard where each owner has the right to bring his ox, so from the perspective of the oxen it is like *reshut ha-rabim* and *keren* pays only half; but only the victim has the right to store fruit there, so from the perspective of the fruit it is *reshut ha-nizak* and *shen* pays full. On this reading, *shen* pays full because only you have the right to store fruit there, while *keren* pays only half because we both have the right to bring our oxen there, rendering it quasi-public for that purpose. This is the reading that Rashi adopts.

### Kahana-Zebid Challenge

Rav Kahana reported that when he presented this explanation to Rav Zebid of Nehardea, Rav Zebid challenged it sharply: *mi matzit mokimat lah kulei ke-Rabbi Tarfon?* How can you possibly attribute the whole *mishnah* to Rabbi Tarfon in this manner? The *mishnah* states that *shen* is *muad* only when it eats *ra'uy lah* — things natural to it — and by implication, not when it eats something unnatural. Now, the *mishnah* teaches this *shen* liability in the victim's domain. Unnatural eating in the victim's domain would generate half-damages — classifying it as a type of *keren*. But Rabbi Tarfon holds that *keren* in the victim's domain pays full damages. So if we attribute the entire *mishnah* to Rabbi Tarfon, any unnatural eating in the victim's domain should trigger full damages, not half — yet the *mishnah* implies only half. The reading therefore cannot be coherently assigned to Rabbi Tarfon throughout.

### Later Mishnah Evidence

Ravina presses this point further using a later *mishnah*. The later *mishnah* introduces the phrase *shor ha-mazik bi-reshut ha-nizak keitzad* and then explicitly presents the debate: Rabbi Tarfon says full damages, while the Rabbis say half. This later *mishnah* makes plain that the phrase *shor ha-mazik bi-reshut ha-nizak* refers specifically to *keren* in the victim's domain and is a point of disagreement between Rabbi Tarfon and the Rabbis. Therefore, if the earlier *mishnah* counts that phrase among the five *muad* categories, it is adopting Rabbi Tarfon's position that such a case pays full. But we have shown that the *mishnah* cannot be entirely Rabbi Tarfon. So we appear to be back to a divided *mishnah* — first half Rabbanan, second half Rabbi Tarfon — which is formally awkward when the *mishnah* is structured as an explicit contrast of five against five.

---

## Five Tam, Five Muad (II)

### Ravina's Rewrite

Ravina ultimately proposes a thoroughgoing rewrite of the *mishnah*: *chasurei mechasra ve-hachi katani* — the *mishnah* is missing text and should be read as follows. The five *tamim* and five *muadim* are not two separate lists of five distinct categories; rather, the five *muadim* are simply those same five *tamim* if they were formally forewarned. *Chamisha tamim hem ve-im hu'adu chamishtan muadin* — there are five *tam* types; if they were forewarned, all five become *muad*. What follows in the *mishnah* — *shen*, *regel*, *shor ha-muad*, *shor ha-mazik bi-reshut ha-nizak*, and *adam* — is not a separate list of five *muadim* but rather a continuation of the *mishnah* discussing other legal categories. Specifically, *shen* and *regel* are *muad* from the outset; the phrase *shor ha-mazik bi-reshut ha-nizak* is the subject of the explicit debate between Rabbi Tarfon and the Rabbis and is not being declared *muad* by this *mishnah* — it is simply mentioning the category as a contested case; and *adam* is indeed *muad* always. Then the *mishnah* adds a further clause: *ve-yesh muadin acherim ka-yotzei ba-elu* — and there are other *muadim* analogous to these, namely the wolf, lion, bear, leopard, *bordelis*, and snake.

This is acknowledged to be a forced reading of the *mishnah*. The phrase *shor ha-mazik bi-reshut ha-nizak* does not naturally read as introducing a debate rather than as a declaration of *muad* status, and the suggestion that the *mishnah* is "missing words" (*chasurei mechasra*) is always a difficult move. Nevertheless, this is the resolution with which the *gemara* is most satisfied.

### Baraita Support (Questio…

A *baraita* is then cited that appears to support Ravina's reading exactly, restating word for word: *chamisha tamim hem ve-im hu'adu chamisha muadin; ve-shein ve-regel muadin mi-techilatan; ve-zehu shor ha-muad; ve-shor ha-mazik bi-reshut ha-nizak — machloket Rabbi Tarfon ve-Rabbanan; ve-yesh muadin acherim ka-yotzei ba-elu: ha-ze'ev ve-ha-ari ve-ha-dov ve-ha-namer ve-ha-bordelis ve-ha-nachash*. The *baraita* thus seems to confirm that *shor ha-mazik bi-reshut ha-nizak* is a debate and not a declaration, and that the dangerous animals form a separate additional category.

It is worth noting, however, what scholars have observed about such *baraitot*: occasionally a *baraita* cited as *tanya nami hachi* — "so too it was taught in a *baraita*" — appears only in the Babylonian Talmud, has no parallel in the Yerushalmi or any other tannaitic source, and is worded identically to the *amora*'s preceding statement. Since *amoraim* often formulated their legal rulings in Hebrew — the same language used by *baraitot* — it is at least possible that some such passages began as *amoraic* statements that were subsequently remembered and transmitted anonymously, eventually coming to be regarded as *baraitot*. The *gemara* itself takes the *baraita* as genuine corroboration, but the observation is worth registering.

### Five / More Muad Problem

A formal objection is then raised against the *mishnah* itself: the *mishnah* says *chamisha tamim va-chamisha muadim* — five *tamim* and five *muadim* — and yet includes wolves, lions, bears, leopards, *bordelis*, and snakes, which is six animals. How can it claim to enumerate five *muadim* and then produce six? The *gemara* resolves this by returning to Ravina's reading: the word "five" in the *mishnah* refers only to the five *tam* categories and their *muad* counterparts when forewarned; the dangerous animals form a separate additional list introduced by *ve-yesh muadin acherim*, and are not counted as part of the five.

---

## Crouch & Vessels

### Large vs. Small Vessels

The *mishnah*'s inclusion of *lirvots* — crouching on something to break it — as a *tam* act now receives further analysis. Rabbi Elazar rules: *lo shanu ela pachim gedolim aval pachim ktanim orcheihu* — this category of *tam* applies only to large vessels; it is not in the animal's way to crouch on those. But small vessels, like the delicate perfume flasks one sees in museum collections, are small enough that an animal might naturally sit or lie down on them without any deliberate act of destruction — *orcheihu*, that is within its normal behavior.

### Walking Crush (Darko)

A *baraita* is cited that states: *ha-behema muedes la-halech ke-darkah u-le-shaber* — an animal is *muad* to break things in its normal way of walking — *u-le-ma'och et ha-adam ve-et ha-behema ve-et ha-kelim* — and to crush a person, another animal, or vessels. This seems to indicate that crushing vessels through some normal form of movement is indeed considered *darko*. The *gemara* initially treats this as relevant to the *lirvots* question, but then reconsiders.

### Side Impact Theory

The *gemara* resolves the tension: *dilma min ha-tzad* — crushing here means not crouching on an object but catching it from the side. The animal is walking along a wall, for example, and a person or object is pressed between the animal's body and the wall, or a vessel protrudes and the animal's flank strikes it as it passes. That lateral crushing is *ke-darkah* — its normal way of moving. Crouching upon a stationary object intentionally, by contrast, is *she-lo ke-darkah* and thus *tam*. Rashi raises the question that on this reading, the references to crushing *adam* and *behema* in the *baraita* would need to refer to very small individuals — a small child or a small animal — but the *gemara*'s essential distinction is between lateral impact while walking versus deliberate crouching.

---

## Animal Identity & Lo (II)

### Bordelis Identity

The *gemara* now asks: *mai bordelis?* — what exactly is this animal? *Amar Rav Yehuda nafreza* — Rav Yehuda says it is a *nafreza*. The *gemara* then asks *mai nafreza?* and Rav Yosef identifies it as an *apa*. The precise identification remains uncertain; the Soncino translation suggests something like a cheetah or hyena, and while these are biologically distinct — a cheetah is a large cat, a hyena more canine — they occupy adjacent conceptual territory in this context.

### Tzavoa Addition

Rabbi Meir adds to the list: *af tzavoa* — including the *tzavoa* as well. Rav Yosef identifies the *tzavoa* as also being an *apa*. This creates an apparent problem: if both *bordelis* and *tzavoa* are the same animal, why does Rabbi Meir need to add it separately? The *gemara* resolves that the two terms refer to different variants — one to the male, the other to the female of the species. The significance of distinguishing male and female here becomes immediately apparent.

### Transformation Sequence

A *baraita* teaches a remarkable sequence of transformations. *Tzavoa zachar*, a male hyena, *le-achar sheva shanim na'aseh atalef* — after seven years becomes a bat. *Atalef le-achar sheva shanim na'aseh arpad* — the bat after seven years becomes an *arpad*, another variety of bat. *Arpad le-achar sheva shanim na'aseh kimosh* — after seven years that becomes a type of thorn bush. *Ve-kimosh le-achar sheva shanim na'aseh choach* — after seven years that becomes a different type of thorn bush. *Ve-choach le-achar sheva shanim na'aseh shed* — after seven years that becomes a demon. The progression descends through increasingly lowly and sinister forms of existence: a despised animal, a creature of darkness, a thorny and barren plant, a demonic spirit. The word *shed* also plays on *shidro shel adam*, a person's spine, and the passage continues: *shidro shel adam le-achar sheva shanim na'aseh nachash* — the spine of a person, seven years after death, turns into a snake. This is followed by the qualification: *ve-hani mili de-lo kara be-modim* — this applies only to one who never bowed during *modim* in prayer, never lowering himself in gratitude before God, and thus in death his very backbone is transformed into the primordial serpent.

The imagery converges with the *gemara* in *Berachot* about bowing like a snake during *modim*, and with the deeper symbolism of the snake in *Gan Eden*. The descent through these forms has also been understood through the lens of *gilgul*, transmigration, as the *gemara*'s claim that these transformations literally occur across the life cycle of the animal evokes parallel ideas about the soul's passage through different forms of existence.

### Snake Eternal Muad

Rabbi Eliezer adds: *af nachash* — even the snake belongs on the list of dangerous animals. The *gemara* notes the apparent tension: in the *mishnah*, Rabbi Eliezer himself argues that domesticated animals can revert to *tam* status — yet in this *baraita*, he seems to concede that all the other animals are *muad* (which is why he needs to add the snake separately). The *gemara* resolves this by reading *af nachash* simply as *nachash* — Rabbi Eliezer is saying only that the snake is *muad* and cannot be domesticated, while the other animals on the list can be, and he is not conceding their permanent *muad* status. The snake stands alone as eternally and irreversibly *muad*.

---

## Lion Behavior Analysis

### Dras = Shen

*Amar Shmuel: ari bi-reshut ha-rabim — das ve-achal patur.* Shmuel rules: a lion in the public domain that *dras* and ate — that is, that trampled living prey and ate it while still alive — is exempt. Since this is *orchei le-midras*, the natural way for a lion to consume its prey, it is classified as *shen*. Just as an ordinary animal eats fruit or grain and is exempt in *reshut ha-rabim* because that is *shen*, so too a lion eating in this manner: *hachi nami ke-man de-achlah peirot ve-yerakot* — it is precisely like one who eats fruits and vegetables. The natural predatory consumption of living prey is, for a lion, its *shen*.

### Taraf = Keren

*Taraf ve-achal chayav* — but if the lion first killed the prey and then ate it, Shmuel rules it is liable. According to this ruling, killing before eating is *lav orchei* — not the natural way — and therefore constitutes an act of *keren*, generating liability in *reshut ha-rabim*. Whether that *keren* liability is *tam* or *muad* remains bound up in the earlier discussion, but it is *keren* nonetheless. Empirically, one might observe that lions typically do kill their prey before eating, raising the question of how "unnatural" such behavior truly is. The *gemara* will address this.

### Psalms Evidence

The *gemara* raises a scriptural challenge: *umi amart de-tarfah lav orchei hu? Ve-ha-ketiv "aryeh toreif bedei gurotav"* — and does it not say in Psalms that a lion slashes prey for its young? This suggests that *terifah*, killing prey, is indeed the lion's natural way. The *gemara* answers, following Rashi's reading: *bishvil gurotav* — when the lion is hunting for its cubs, it will kill the prey and transport it back. The verse continues: *u-mechaneik le-leviotav* — it strangles prey for its lionesses — again, *bishvil leviotav*, it kills to bring food home. And *va-yemalei teref chorav, u-me'onotav treifah* — it fills its cave with prey, it stores carcasses in its dwelling. *Bishvil chorav, bishvil me'onotav* — when bringing food for storage or for dependents, it kills first. But when eating on the spot for itself, it eats while the prey is still alive. That on-the-spot killing-then-eating is therefore anomalous — *keren* — while eating living prey is *shen*.

### Baraita: Full Payment

A *baraita* apparently contradicts Shmuel's ruling: *ve-chein chayah she-nichnesah le-chatzer ha-nizak ve-tarfah behemah ve-achalah basar — meshalem nezek shalem* — a wild animal that entered the victim's domain, slashed an animal, and ate it — the flesh already dead (*basar*) — pays full damages. This seems to indicate that *terifah* followed by eating is normal lion behavior, since the *baraita* treats it matter-of-factly and assesses *nezek shalem* based on the domain, not on any abnormality of method.

### Changed Mind Scenario

The *gemara* first attempts to explain the *baraita*: *ha-cha be-mai askinan she-tarfah le-hani'ach* — perhaps the lion killed the prey intending to store it, and only later ate it on the spot. The *gemara* objects: *ha achalah katani* — the *baraita* says it ate it, implying immediately after killing. The *gemara* then suggests *be-shinuyah* — the lion changed its mind: it killed with intent to store, then decided to eat on the spot. A further challenge is raised: *umi yadeinan?* — how could we ever know whether the lion intended to store and then changed its mind? And by that logic, perhaps even in Shmuel's case, where the lion killed and ate on the spot, we should say it planned to store and then changed its mind, rendering it *shen* as well.

### Domesticated Lion Theory

At this point Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes a different resolution of the *baraita*: the passage must be read as referring to two separate cases — *metzodadim katani* — it is presenting paired scenarios. In one, the lion killed for storage and did not eat; in the other, it ate the prey alive (*darsa ve-achlah*). Full payment applies to either. This preserves Shmuel's ruling intact.

Rav Yeimar then offers a different framework altogether: Shmuel's ruling — that killing before eating is *lav orchei* — applies only to a *domesticated* lion, *ari tarbut*. A wild lion's every act of predation, including killing before eating, is entirely natural — all *shen*. This would mean that Shmuel's rule is aligned with Rabbi Eliezer's position that domestication transforms the animal's legal character: the domesticated lion, no longer behaving as a wild predator, finds that certain predatory acts are now classified as *lav orchei* relative to its tamed nature. The *gemara* challenges this: if a domesticated lion's killing is *lav orchei*, then even eating living prey should be *lav orchei* for a domesticated animal — why does Shmuel distinguish between the two modes? The *gemara* then suggests that Rav Yeimar's statement was not explaining Shmuel at all, but explaining the *baraita* about the animal entering the victim's domain: *ki tanya matnitin be-ari tarbut ve-aliba de-Rabbi Eliezer* — that *baraita* speaks of a domesticated lion and follows Rabbi Eliezer's view. The *gemara* then raises the difficulty that if it is domesticated and Rabbi Eliezer applies, it should pay only half until warned three times, then full. The *gemara* replies that it had already been warned three times (*de-iyad*), making it fully *muad*. A further difficulty arises: if the lion went through the process of domestication and then renewed violence, the *baraita* categorizes this under *toldah de-shen* — a derivative of *shen* — whereas it should properly be categorized under *toldah de-keren*, given its history of becoming a *muad* through warning. The *gemara* concludes: *kashya* — this remains difficult.

### Rambam: Muad Keren

It is notable that the Rambam completely ignores Shmuel's ruling. When the Rambam rules that a lion is *muad*, he does not distinguish between *taraf* and *daras*, does not differentiate *reshut ha-rabim* from *reshut ha-nizak*, and does not limit any acts to *shen*. He treats the lion as *muad keren* in all circumstances, returning to the straightforward *peshat* of the *mishnah* — these dangerous animals are *muad* from the outset, full stop.

### Shen vs. Keren Unresolved

The *sugya* thus ends without a clean resolution to the question of whether a lion's eating constitutes *shen* and therefore generates no liability in *reshut ha-rabim*. One student raised a pointed observation: since when does a person have the right to bring a lion into *reshut ha-rabim* in the first place? If one has no right to bring such an animal into the public domain, perhaps one can never invoke the *shen* exemption at all, because the exemption presupposes a legitimate presence in that domain. This framing would align naturally with the Rambam's position: since the lion should never be in *reshut ha-rabim*, all its acts are *keren muad*, and the *shen* framework simply never applies. The question remains instructive and the sources leave it, ultimately, unresolved.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 17

## Tam vs. Muad

### Opening

We begin today's daf, 17b, by picking up with the *mishna* in the middle of the page. The first *perek* of *Bava Kamma* has, up to this point, been remarkably well organized: it opened with concrete cases from the *Torah*, abstracted them into general principles, identified the categories of *tamim* and *muadim*, and now turns to the *halachic* implications of that distinction. Compared to other *masechtot*, this one is extraordinarily well laid out, and that architectural clarity is worth appreciating before diving into the substance.

### Mishna on Tam/Muad

*Ma bein tam lemuad?* — What is the difference between a *tam* and a *muad*? The *mishna* answers: *ella shehatam mishalem chatzi nezek migupo* — a *tam* pays half damages, and that payment comes from the body of the goring animal itself. The cost cannot exceed the value of the damaging animal. The full significance of this rule — including the debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon over whether the injured party automatically acquires a share in the animal's body — will be treated later in the tractate. *Umuad mishalem nezek shalem min ha-aliya* — a *muad*, by contrast, pays full damages from *aliya*, from "the best." The *Gemara* will immediately address what *aliya* means.

### Meaning of Aliya

*Mai aliya?* — What does *aliya* mean? *Amar Rabbi Elazar bimeula shebinichasav* — the best of one's property. This does not necessarily mean *meitav*, the finest-quality land, in the technical sense developed elsewhere in the tractate. Rather, the essential point is that payment is not limited to the body of the damaging animal; the owner must pay from his own assets. If he pays willingly, he may choose what to pay — whether land or *metaltelin*. If *beis din* must seize assets, the *Gemara* earlier suggested that *beis din* would make that determination, and there are relevant *mishnayot* in *Erchin* on those procedures. The running theme in the *Gemara* of *afilu suvin* — that one must pay even with bran, i.e., even the least valuable property — comes from a *braita* that the *Gemara* treats as authoritative, though one could ask whether an alternative reading of *meula min hanechasim* might yield a different approach.

### Chizkiyahu Burial

To support his reading of *aliya*, Rabbi Elazar cites the verse: *vayishkav Chizkiyahu im avosav vayikberuhu bemaaleh kivrei bnei David* — Chizkiyahu lay down with his fathers and they buried him in the *maaleh* of the graves of the sons of David. *Veamar Rabbi Elazar bemaaleh etzel meulim shebamishpacha* — he was buried near the most prestigious members of the family, that is, near David and Solomon. The word *maaleh* thus denotes elevation and excellence, and that same sense of *meula* is what characterizes *aliya* in our *mishna*: payment comes not from the animal but from the owner's own assets, with no upper limit tied to the animal's value.

---

## Aggadic Digression

### Zanim & Spices

Since the *Gemara* cited a verse about Chizkiyahu's burial, it now transitions — by means of an adjacent verse — into an extended *aggadic* excursus that will carry us through to the end of the *perek*. The connecting verse describes the burial of Asa, king of Yehuda: *vayashkivuhu bemishkav asher maleh besamim uzeinim* — they laid him in his resting place which was filled with spices and *zeinim*. The *Gemara* asks: *mai besamim uzeinim* — what does this mean?

### Fragrances Dispute

Rabbi Eliezer interprets *zeinim* as *zinei zinei* — many different types of spices, all different kinds of fragrances. *Rashi* explains that *zanohei* is the Aramaic equivalent of *min*, a species or kind, so the verse means an abundance of varied fragrances. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani offers a strikingly different reading: *kebesamim shekol hamariach bahem ba lidei zimah* — these were erotic fragrances of such a nature that anyone who smelled them would be driven to an act of sexual impropriety. This leads into a question about what exactly Asa's attendants suspected him of.

### Zona & Pit

Rabbi Elazar says: *shechashdu mizona* — they suspected him of consorting with a prostitute. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says: *shechashdu meishet ish* — they suspected him of adultery. The word *zeinim* triggers an associative connection to *zenut* and *zona*, and the *Gemara* then draws in a verse from Yirmiyahu: *ki shucha lachadeni* — for they have dug a pit to trap me — *upachim tamnu leragli* — and traps were laid for my feet.

*Bishlama* according to the opinion that they suspected him of a prostitute, the verse works well: *ki shucha amuka zona* — a prostitute is like a deep pit, a trap that ensnares. But according to the opinion that they suspected him of adultery, *mai shucha* — what is the pit? The *Gemara* resolves this: *atu eishet ish minafka miklal zona* — does a married woman fall outside the category of *zona* in this metaphorical sense? The image of a pit captures any forbidden sexual entanglement, and so the verse applies to adultery as well. Tosafot further notes that Yirmiyahu was a *Kohen*, and thus the suspicion of consorting with a *zona* carried an additional dimension: a *zona* is forbidden to a *Kohen* in marriage — though whether the prohibition extends beyond marriage was itself a question discussed at the end of *Kiddushin*. By contrast, *eishet ish* is the more severe sin of adultery, which is why Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani preferred that reading.

The *Gemara* continues: *bishlama* according to the opinion that they suspected him of adultery, the verse *ve'ata Hashem yadata et kol atzatam alai lamut* — You, God, know all their plots against me to kill me — fits naturally, since adultery is a capital offense. But according to the opinion that they suspected him of a prostitute, *mai lamut* — what does "to kill me" mean? There is no capital punishment for that. The answer is *dehishlichuhu lebor hatit* — they literally threw him into a pit filled with mud, as recounted explicitly in the *pesukim*. So there are also literal pits in the world that people construct against one another.

### Stumbling Blocks

*Darash Rava* — Rava expounded: *maid dechtiv veyehyu muchshalim lefanecha* — what is the meaning of the verse, "Let them stumble before You; at the time of Your anger, act against them"? Yirmiyahu said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the Universe, *afilu besha'at she'osim tzedakah hachshilem bivnei adam she'einam mehuganim* — even when they are performing *tzedakah*, cause them to stumble by directing their gifts toward people who are not of proper character, *kedai shelo yekablu aleihem sachar* — so that they receive no reward for it, since those recipients will use the money for improper purposes.

This raises an interesting *halachic* question: the *halachot* about vetting recipients of *tzedakah* are largely designed to protect the giver from an obligation that may not be genuine. But if one chooses not to vet and the money is misused, does that mean the *mitzvah* was not fulfilled? Presumably one did fulfill the *mitzvah* — at least when the scam was not obviously apparent. The *Gemara* here suggests, at minimum, that the quantum of *sachar* one receives when a recipient uses the money for drugs is less than when it is used for food. This is left as an open *halachic* question. On *Purim*, the practice of *matnos aniyim* is deliberately structured so that one does not vet — that is its characteristic quality.

The aggadic role this passage plays in the broader context of the *perek* is also worth noting. Just as one can dig a pit that is not a literal excavation — through slander, allegations, and plots, as in the case of Yirmiyahu — one can also create *michsholim*, stumbling blocks, through the people one encounters or enables. A *michshol* is not only a physical obstacle in the street; it can also be the moral environment one creates around others.

### Sefer Torah Honor

*Ukvodo asu lo bemoso* — and they did honor for him in his death. This verse refers to Chizkiyahu. *Milamed shehoshivu yeshiva al kivro* — this teaches that a *yeshiva* studied Torah at his grave. Tosafot notes that one of Chizkiyahu's central achievements — attested in other *Gemarot* — was spreading Torah throughout Israel to an extraordinarily high level of knowledge. The practice of Torah study near the graves of great rabbis continues to this day.

### Grave Learning Duration

*Pligi Rabbi Natan verabanan* — Rabbi Natan and the Sages dispute the duration of this *yeshiva* at the grave: one opinion says three days, another says seven, and a third says thirty. These correspond to stages of mourning: *shiva* and *shloshim* are familiar, and the tractate *Moed Katan* establishes that even three days constitute a primary unit within *shiva* for certain *halachot*.

### Chizkiyahu Procession

*Tano rabanan* — the Sages taught: *zeh Chizkiyahu melech Yehuda sheyatzu lefanav shloshim veshisha elef chalutzei katef* — this was Chizkiyahu king of Yehuda, before whom went 36,000 people with their shoulders uncovered. Rashi understands this as a reference to *kriya*, such that the garment was torn and the shoulder exposed. Tosafot reads the number 36,000 as encoded in the words *asu lo* — *lamed vav* equals 36, multiplied by a thousand for rhetorical weight.

This is the view of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Nechemiah objects: *velo le'achiv asu kein?* — did they not do the same for his brothers? A king always receives an enormous funeral procession, and Tosafot references another *Gemara* that reads the verse *kemisped Hadad-rimmon ben Tabrimmon* as an allusion to Achav's enormous funeral. So what was distinctive about Chizkiyahu's honor? *Ella* — the distinctive honor was that they mentioned his righteousness explicitly, not merely his status as king.

### Sefer Torah Honor

The distinctive honor was this: *shehinichu sefer Torah mitato ve'amru kiyem zeh mah shekasuv bezeh* — they placed a *sefer Torah* on his funeral bier and declared in the procession: "This one fulfilled what was written in that." He was being honored as an embodiment of the *sefer Torah* itself.

The *Gemara* asks: *ha'idna nami avdinan hachi* — do we not do this today for great rabbis? What is uniquely remarkable about Chizkiyahu? The *Gemara* answers: *apukei mapkinan anuchet lo manchinan* — perhaps today we carry a *sefer Torah* in the procession, but we do not actually place it on the bier. And if you prefer, perhaps we do place it on the bier — *kiyam lo amrinan* — but we do not make the explicit verbal declaration. What was distinctive about Chizkiyahu was that they articulated it: they said outright that this man fulfilled everything written in it. That explicit declaration of fulfilled embodiment was the singular honor.

### R. Yochanan Story

*Amar Rabbah bar bar Chana*: I was once following Rabbi Yochanan in order to ask him *halachic* questions. When Rabbi Yochanan would emerge from the bathroom, he would not give us a *psak* until he had first washed his hands, put on *tefillin*, and recited the *beracha* — and only then would he answer. The *Gemara* notes the interesting detail that the *beracha* is mentioned after the putting on of the *tefillin*, though that question is left aside. After performing all of this, Rabbi Yochanan then taught them Torah.

### Learning vs. Doing

At first glance this story seems parenthetical — a colorful anecdote whose real purpose is to convey what Rabbi Yochanan told them regarding Chizkiyahu. One reading, however, understands the story as substantive in itself, and we will return to that shortly.

What Rabbi Yochanan told them was: *afilu kiyam amrinan* — even today we would be prepared to say that someone fulfilled the *sefer Torah*. So what was uniquely honorable about Chizkiyahu? *Limadei lo amrinan* — that he taught others Torah, that is something we do not say today. The distinctive achievement being commemorated was not merely that Chizkiyahu embodied the *sefer Torah* himself, but that he spread Torah to others, making him a teacher of the entire nation.

The *Gemara* then introduces: *ve'amar mar gadol limud Torah shelimud meivi lidei ma'aseh* — great is learning, for learning brings about action. Now the *Gemara* does not initially distinguish between learning and teaching. The question it raises is: why is saying that someone taught Torah a higher honor than saying he fulfilled it? Based on the principle that learning brings about action, one might conclude that doing is the greatest achievement. If so, saying he did is better than saying he learned or taught. Why, then, is it treated as a greater honor to say he taught?

Rashi reads the *Gemara* accordingly: the hierarchy of religious value, from lowest to highest, is learning, then doing, then teaching. Learning is celebrated because it leads to action, but that means action itself is the higher value. Teaching is highest of all because it spreads action to others. This raises a profound question that lies at the heart of how we define religious achievement: is the doctor who spends his life saving people and performing practical *mitzvot* of greater religious worth than the *talmid chacham* who sits and learns? Rashi would seem to say yes — doing ultimately surpasses learning.

### Teaching Hierarchy

Tosafot disputes Rashi's reading of the *Gemara* in *Kiddushin*. For Tosafot, the conclusion of that *sugya* is not that doing is greater, but that learning is greater — precisely because it brings about action. Learning subsumes doing; it is the superior category. On this reading, the question here is different: if learning is already the greatest value, why is it a higher honor to say that Chizkiyahu taught rather than that he learned? Tosafot answers: because saying that someone did *mitzvot* already implies that he learned — *ein am ha'aretz chasid*, one who has not learned cannot truly fulfill a life of doing. So if we were praising his doing, we would already be implying his learning. What Chizkiyahu was honored for was not just learning or doing but *teaching* — spreading Torah to others. In the end, both Rashi and Tosafot agree on the conclusion: teaching stands at the top of the hierarchy. But their disagreement about the relationship between learning and doing is a genuinely important question about how to read the *Gemara* in *Kiddushin* and about which achievement our tradition ultimately prizes more.

The *Sheiltos* offers an entirely different reading of the passage about Rabbah bar bar Chana. On his reading, the story of Rabbi Yochanan coming out of the bathroom is not parenthetical at all. The point is that Rabbi Yochanan first washed his hands, then put on *tefillin*, then taught Torah — and the *Gemara* asks why he did it in that order. If *limud mevi lidei ma'aseh* — learning brings about action — then should he not have taught Torah before performing the action of putting on *tefillin*? The *Gemara* answers: *lo kashya, ha lemigmar ha le'agmorei* — there is no contradiction; one distinction applies to learning for oneself and another to teaching others. If it is between learning and doing, you learn first. If it is between teaching and doing, you do first — because by doing first you are modeling the hierarchy. You learn first, then act, then teach, thereby demonstrating through your own conduct the correct sequence of religious life. This reading transforms the entire passage: it is not about what was said at Chizkiyahu's funeral but about the order in which Rabbi Yochanan structured his own actions.

### Torah & Chasadim

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai*: What is the meaning of the verse *ashreichem zor'ei al kol mayim meshalechei regel hashor vehachamor* — praised are you who scatter seeds on all waters, who send forth the foot of the ox and the donkey? *Kol ha'osek baTorah uvigmilus chasadim* — anyone who engages in Torah and *gmilus chasadim*, *zocheh lenachalas shnei shevatim* — merits the inheritance of two tribes. The verse's imagery is decoded: *zeri'ah* means *tzedakah*, as in the verse *zir'u lachem letzedakah vekitzru lefi chesed* — sow for yourselves in righteousness and reap according to kindness. And *mayim* means Torah, as in *hoi kol tzameh lechu lamayim* — all who are thirsty, come to the waters.

One who plants seeds — acts of *tzedakah* — and draws on living water — Torah — *zocheh lechilah keYosef* — merits a bridal canopy like Joseph, derived from *ben porat Yosef banot tza'adah alei shur*, where young women ascended upon the wall to gaze at him. *Vezocher lenachalas Yissachar* — and merits the inheritance of Issachar, *Yissachar chamor garem* — Issachar is a bony donkey, understood as one who bears the weight of Torah. Another reading: *oyevav noflim lefanav keYosef* — his enemies fall before him like Joseph's, from *bechor shoro hadar lo vekarnei re'em karnav bahem amim yenagach yachdav afsei aretz* — the honor of the firstborn ox is his, with the horns of a wild ox he gores nations to the ends of the earth. And *vezocher levinah keYissachar* — and he merits wisdom like Issachar, *umivnei Yissachar yodei vinah le'itim lada'at mah ya'aseh Yisrael* — for the sons of Issachar knew how to read the times and knew what Israel should do.

The connection back to the opening of the *perek* is worth drawing out: *meshalechei regel hashor vehachamor* — sending forth the foot of the ox and the donkey — is the *pasuk* of *regel*, of *nezikin*. But as this *aggadic* passage suggests, sending forth one's foot can be an act of destruction or an act of building. Negligence allows one's animals to go out and damage; intentional devotion to Torah and *gmilus chasadim* sends forth forces that benefit and uplift. *Hadran alach arba'ah avos* — we conclude the first *perek*.

---

## Perek Two: Regel

### Perek Structure

The second *perek* is devoted specifically to *shein* and *regel*. If the first *perek* offered a presentation of primary principles — and it is hard to find another *masechet* that opens with such clarity — the second *perek* moves to *pratim*, to the specific cases. The structure is consistent throughout: each category is introduced with a *keitzad*, a "how so?", followed by the general rule, and then a set of exceptions that clarify the boundaries of liability.

### Regel Muad Definition

*Keitzad haregel mu'edet leshabber bederech hilucha?* — How is the *regel* *mu'edet*? In what way is *regel* considered *muad*, and in what situations does it pay full damages? The answer: when the damage is caused in the normal course of the animal's walking, that constitutes the *muad* of *regel*, and full damages are owed. The second line of the *mishna* restates this: *ha-behema mu'edet lalechet k'darkah u'l'shaber* — the *behema* is *muad* to go normally and to break. The *Gemara* will later address the apparent redundancy of these two formulations.

### Regel Examples

The *mishna* then offers examples of departures from the basic rule. *Hayetah meva'etet* — if the animal was kicking, that is not *regel* but *keren*, and *chatzi nezek* is paid. *O she'hayu tzerorot menatzin mitachat ragleiha* — or if pebbles were scattering from under its legs, that too pays half damages — but for a different reason: *tzrorot* is the indirect force of *regel*, a *kocho* rather than a *gufo*, and is therefore reduced to half. *Darsah al hakli veshibarto*, *venafal hakli veshibaro* — if it trampled on a vessel and broke it, and the broken vessel then struck another vessel and broke that too, the first vessel pays full (classic *regel* in the *reshut hanizak*), and the second pays half, since the second damage was caused through *tzrorot*, indirect force.

### Behema & Chickens

*Hatarnagolim mu'adin lalechet k'darkan u'l'shaber* — chickens are *muad* to walk normally and break. The *mishna* adds an exception: *haya d'li kashur beraglav* — if a bucket was tied to its leg and was bouncing around and breaking vessels, that pays half damages, as another case of *tzrorot*. Strikingly, the language used for chickens is essentially identical to the language used for the general *regel* and the *behema*. The apparent redundancy among all three formulations will be the subject of the *Gemara's* opening question on this *mishna*.

---

## Av & Toladah Debate

### Redundancy Question

*Amar lei Ravina l'Rava*: *Hainu regel hainu behema* — what did the second line add to the first? You said *regel* is *muad* to break in walking, and then you said *behema* is *muad* to walk and break. They are the same thing.

### Av vs. Toladah

*Amar lei tana avos v'katanei toladot* — Rava answers: the *Tanna* teaches an *av* and a *toladah*. Rashi explains: the *av* is *regel mamash*, the leg itself; the *toladah* is *lalechet k'darkah*, which includes any part of the animal's body — its tail, its side, anything that bumps into something in the normal course of its movement. The first line establishes the leg as the primary category; the second line generalizes to the whole animal as a derivative category.

### Follow-up Questions

The *Gemara* presses further: if that is the structure — *av* and *toladah* — then look at the equivalent structure for *shein* in the next *mishna* (19b): *keitzad hashen mu'edet le'echol et hara'ui lah*, followed by *ha-behema mu'edet le'echol peirot veyerakot*. There the second line does not introduce a new part of the animal — it simply specifies that *ra'ui lah* means fruits and vegetables. The exceptions there are *ksut vekelim*. So what is the *av* and *toladah* in the *shein* structure? The *Gemara* notes that Rava's answer does not obviously extend to *shein*.

### Chaya vs. Behema

*Amar Rav Ashi*: the solution is different for *shein*. There, the first line concerns *chaya*, an untamed animal, and the second line concerns *behema*, a domesticated one. One might have thought that the rule of *uvi'er biseh acher* — the verse from which *regel* liability is derived — applies only to *behema*, as the word *behema* appears there explicitly, and not to *chaya*. Therefore the *mishna* teaches: *ka mashma lan de-chaya bichlal behema* — the category of *behema* in the verse includes *chaya* as well, so both are liable.

### Literary Structure

This raises a further question about ordering. If that is so, the first line concerns *chaya* and the second concerns *behema*, which would mean the *toladah* — inferred from *drasha* — is placed before the *av*. Why lead with the derived case? The *Gemara* answers: *hai de-atya mi-drasha chaviva leh* — the *Tanna* prefers to open with what must be derived, because it is the more novel teaching. But then why not apply the same logic to *regel*, leading with the *toladah* (any body part) before the *av* (the leg itself)? The *Gemara* responds: *hatam eidi de-avot ninhu* — there, *chaya* and *behema* are not in a true *av*-*toladah* hierarchy with respect to each other; they are parallel instances of the same *av*, and so the derived case can lead. But when there is a genuine hierarchy of *av* and *toladah*, you begin with the *av*. Alternatively: *eidi de-salik me-regel patach be-regel* — since the preceding *mishna* concluded with the word *regel*, this *mishna* naturally opens with *regel* as well, even though it would otherwise prefer to begin with the derived case. None of these answers is entirely satisfying as *pshat* in the *mishna*, but that is the *Gemara's* resolution.

---

## Gufo vs. Tzrorot

### Direct Body Cases

*Tano rabanan* — the Sages taught: *behema mu'edet lalechet k'darka lishabber*. The *braita* then specifies in detail which components of an animal's movement are classified as *gufo* — direct body damage — and which are *tzrorot*. If a *behema* entered the *chatzer hanizak* and caused damage *begufa derech hilucha*, through its body in the normal course of walking, that is *gufo*. The list of components that count as *gufo* is extensive: the animal's body itself, its hair or tail (*sa'ara*), the saddle on its back (*ukaf*), the saddlebags (*shlif*), the bit in its mouth (*pumbia*), and the bell around its neck (*zug*). The logic is consistent throughout: so long as the damaging element has not left the animal's body and continues to be directly moved by the animal, it remains *gufo* and not *tzrorot*.

The bell (*zug*) might appear to raise a difficulty. A bell swings when the animal moves, and one might think that its oscillation resembles the chicken's bucket (*d'li*) tied to its leg, which the *mishna* classifies as *tzrorot*. The distinction will become clearer when the *Gemara* examines the chicken cases: the bucket, unlike the bell, is not in continuous contact with the animal and does not move in direct proportion to the animal's body motion. The *braita* lists all the above items as *gufo* unambiguously.

### Donkey Burden

*Vechamor bemasso'o* — and a donkey bearing its burden — *meshallem nezek shalem*, pays full damages. The burden on the donkey's back is treated as part of its body for purposes of liability, not as *tzrorot*.

### Sumchus Disputes

*Sumchus omer tzroros vechazir shehaya nover be'ashpah vehitiz vehizik meshallem nezek shalem* — Sumchus says: in the case of *tzrorot* and in the case of a pig rooting in a dung heap and scattering material that causes damage, one pays full damages. The *Gemara* initially asks: but if the pig directly damaged, of course it pays full — that is obvious. The *Gemara* therefore corrects the reading: the case of the pig is specifically one where it was rooting and that caused things to scatter and strike another object — it is a case of *tzrorot*. The pig is rooting presumably in search of food; its motion scatters debris that then causes damage, making this a *regel* case.
