The Gemara brings a new case: *gamal ta'un pishtan ve'over bireshus harabim* — a camel carrying flax is passing through *reshus harabim*. *Nichnas pishtano letoch chanut* — the flax extends into a store. *Vedalka benero shel chanvani* — it is ignited by the storekeeper's candle. *Vehidlik es habirah* — and the fire then ignites the entire building. The straightforward ruling: *ba'al hagamal chayav* — the camel's owner is *chayav*. But if the *chanvani* left his candle outside the store in a place where passing animals would be likely to brush against it — *chanvani chayav* — the storekeeper is *chayav*, since it was effectively his fire, his negligence with his candle having set the whole sequence in motion. Rabbi Yehuda adds: *be-ner Chanukah patur* — if it was a *Chanukah* light, the storekeeper is *patur*, because he had a right to light his *Chanukah* candles outdoors. That case will be addressed later in a separate *mishna*.

The question the Gemara focuses on is the first scenario — why is the *ba'al hagamal chayav*, and what is the nature of that *chiyuv*?

### Rav Yochanan Problem

*Bishlama le-man de-amar mishum chitzav, chitzav de-gamal hu* — according to Rav Yochanan, the camel's action is like its arrow: its flax caught fire and the fire spread, so this is the camel's *chitzav*, and the owner is *chayav*. But here too the difficulty immediately presents itself: this should then be *chatzi nezek*, since the camel's spreading fire is analogous to *tzroros*. The *mishna* says *chayav* without qualification, which sounds like full payment — a difficulty for Rav Yochanan's position as it stood in the earlier case.

One might also wonder whether the analysis can be pushed further: I have flax, I know people have fires in their homes, I know my camel is overloaded with flax — does this knowledge make the flax itself into something like "my fire" heading toward an anticipated flame? This would be a way of treating the camel owner as directly negligent with respect to fire. But the Gemara does not pursue this line. The assumed framework is that the owner's negligence was in overloading the camel, and whatever *chiyuv* flows from that negligence is at most *tzroros*-level — *chatzi nezek*.

### Reish Lakish Problem

*Ella le-man de-amar mishum mamono, hai eish lav mamono de-ba'al gamal hu* — according to Reish Lakish, the same problem as in the dog case arises: this is not the camel owner's fire. The *chanvani* lit the candle; it is the *chanvani*'s fire. The camel owner was negligent with the flax, but once the flax caught fire, he had no ability to intervene — he is an *ones* at that point. He is not liable for the *chanvani*'s fire, and it never becomes his own *mamono*. He should therefore be exempt.

### Direct Contact Requireme…

The resolution for Reish Lakish, as with the dog case, depends on the distinction between direct contact and spreading. *Di-mesachseches kol ha-birah kullah* — the key is that the animal was not merely the source of ignition from which fire then spread; rather, the camel itself, carrying the burning flax on its back, was directly moving through and coming into contact with the entire building. This is not fire spreading on its own — it is the camel's body (or the flax attached to it) directly burning the structure. This falls into the category of *mekom gechelet* extended: it is all treated as direct contact, *kocho* of the animal, not the spreading of fire.

### Oness via Urination

But then the Gemara confronts a new difficulty: if the animal is directly causing the burning by moving through the building — *mistachseches* — why is the *chanvani* the sole liable party when he places his candle outside? If it is the camel's direct contact that matters, then even when the *chanvani* was negligent with his candle, the camel owner should share liability, since it is the camel's direct presence that is burning the building.

The Gemara's answer: *beshe'amdah* — the animal had stopped. *Amar Rav Huna bar Manoach mishmeih de-Rav Ika hacha bemai askinan kegon she'amdah lehatil mayim* — the specific scenario is one where the animal stopped to urinate. Once an animal is urinating, it cannot be moved. This is the key: the owner is now an *ones* with respect to his ability to intervene. He cannot control the animal's position at this moment.

### Negligence + Oness Logic

This allows the Gemara to account for both halves of the ruling. *Reisha ba'al gamal chayav delo ibai lei le'afushei bete'inah* — in the first scenario, the owner is *chayav* because he should not have overloaded the camel with flax. His negligence was the overloading; everything that followed — the flax entering the store, catching fire, and directly burning the building while the camel stood and urinated — is a direct consequence of that negligence. The burning is by direct contact, not spreading, so it falls within the scope of *chiyuv* even for Reish Lakish.

*Seifa chanvani chayav delo ibai lei le'anuchei nero mibara'i* — in the second scenario, the storekeeper is *chayav* because he should not have left his candle outside. His negligence began the sequence. The camel owner, meanwhile, was not negligent in overloading — the scenario posits that the flax entered the store because of the *chanvani*'s negligently placed candle, not because of any excess load on the camel. By the time the fire starts, the camel owner cannot intervene because the animal is urinating. His *ones* is established: he did not begin negligently, and now he physically cannot stop it. The *chanvani*'s negligence started the chain; the camel owner bears no *chiyuv*.

The overall picture for Reish Lakish is now coherent: one can never be *chayav* under the *mamono* framework when one's animal ignites a fire and the fire spreads on its own — that spread is the animal's fire, not the owner's *mamono*. The only basis for *chiyuv* is when the animal itself is in direct contact — *mistachseches* — with what it burns. And even then, if one cannot intervene because of an *ones* (here, the animal urinating), the liability shifts to whoever was negligent at the outset of the causal chain.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 23

## Esh: Chitzav vs. Mamono

### Intro: Rabbi Yochanan &…

We pick up in the middle of a very rich *sugya* concerning why one is liable for *esh* — fire. The core question is: is liability *mishum chitzav*, treating fire as if you acted directly, like shooting an arrow? Or is it *mishum mamono*, treating fire as your property or responsibility that caused damage, analogous to your ox going out and injuring someone? Rashi consistently emphasizes that you own the fire, you own the coal. Tosafot pushes back: ownership may not be the relevant criterion — what matters is that you bear responsibility for the fire, and once it spreads, it is like your ox going out and causing damage.

This is the conceptual landscape of the debate. Rabbi Yochanan holds *esh mishum chitzav*; Reish Lakish holds *esh mishum mamono*.

### Animal-Caused Fire & Hal…

The *Gemara* now focuses the dispute on the case of an animal that causes a fire. If fire is *mishum chitzav*, the concept can be transferred to the animal: the animal lit a fire, it is like the animal's *koach* — its force — and therefore one pays half damages, analogous to the rule of *tzroros*, where an animal propels a projectile and the owner pays half. This fits naturally with the *mishnah* and coheres with Rabbi Yochanan's position.

### Reish Lakish: Fire as Ma…

According to Reish Lakish, the animal's fire cannot generate liability through the *mishum mamono* framework, because an animal cannot bear responsibility for another piece of property, and you yourself cannot be considered responsible for a fire that your animal lit outside your awareness or control. Unless you saw the fire developing and could have stopped it, making it yours in a more direct sense, the fire that your animal ignites is not yours to be held liable for — and the result would be that you pay nothing. The *Gemara* reconstructs certain cases to explain how half-damages are nonetheless paid, but the straightforward reading of those cases aligns with Rabbi Yochanan: the animal lit a fire, it is treated as the animal's *koach*, and half is paid. This in turn illuminates how we think about *esh* in general.

---

## Burning Haystack: Goat &…

### Scenario Setup

The *Gemara* now presents an entirely different application: *hamadlik et hagadish* — one who sets fire to a stack of grain — and alongside that stack there is *gedi kafut lo*, a goat bound to it, and *eved samuch lo*, a slave standing nearby. The question is whether the one who lit the stack is liable for the death of the goat or the slave when everything burns up. The *Gemara* rules *chayav* — liable — and now we must work out the precise conditions under which that liability applies.

It is notable that this case seems to involve intentionally setting the stack alight. This raises the question of whether Reish Lakish would concede to Rabbi Yochanan when the spreading of fire is deliberate and intended. The *Gemara* implies that the debate between them remains consistent whether the spreading was negligent and unintentional or fully intentional — it appears to be the same disagreement in either case.

### Slave Death & Civil Liab…

The Torah never assigns a monetary value to a human life when a person kills another person directly. This is distinct from the case of an ox that gores a person, where one does pay *sheloshim shel eved* for a slave. When a person takes a human life — even unintentionally — the Torah addresses it criminally but not civilly. This means there is simply no monetary claim for the slave's death as against the one who started the fire. One cannot pursue a civil case for a human life taken directly, unlike in the *ox-gores* scenario.

### Goat Bound, Slave Free

Given this framework, why must the goat be bound and the slave be free? The answer has two parts. First, why must the slave be unbound? If the slave is bound and cannot flee, the person who lit the fire may have committed an act tantamount to killing — even if unintentional, it remains a capital offense — and the principle of *kim lei b'drabba minei* would apply, exempting the tortfeasor from all monetary liability incurred during the commission of a capital act. Since the slave is free and could have run away, there is no murder, no capital offense, and no *kim lei* to speak of — hence liability attaches for the goat.

Second, why must the goat be bound? Rashi offers one explanation, but Tosafot's reading is more compelling: of course the goat must be bound, because an unbound goat would naturally flee from fire. Animals instinctively escape flames, arguably more reliably than humans. If the goat was free, one would not be considered negligent toward it — the goat should have run — and one would be exempt. The goat must therefore be bound, unable to escape, for liability to attach.

To summarize: if either condition is not met — if the slave was bound (triggering *kim lei*) or if the goat was unbound (since it could have fled) — one is exempt. Tosafot reads the conjunctive in the text as disjunctive: either condition, if absent, causes the exemption.

### Kim Lei Principle Explai…

*Kim lei b'drabba minei* operates as follows: when one commits an act that constitutes a capital crime — or even a capital sin, such as *mechalel Shabbos* — any monetary liability arising from the same act is not prosecutable. The principle does not concern the inherent value of a human life, which is a separate and independent question. Rather, it holds that once one faces execution or the highest degree of divine punishment, one cannot simultaneously be brought to court for civil damages arising from that same act. To use a vivid analogy: if one kills someone and burns that person's garments in the process, one cannot be separately sued for the garments. The *kim lei* principle wipes away those collateral monetary consequences.

### Direct Torching & Kim Lei

The *Gemara* presses a difficulty: if fire is *mishum mamono*, analogous to one's property causing damage, why should *kim lei* apply at all? When an ox kills a slave, you still pay *sheloshim shel eved*, and if the ox simultaneously destroyed the slave's property, you would pay for that as well — *kim lei* does not apply because killing via your ox is not a capital act on *your* part. Why, then, should fire be different?

The *Gemara* answers in the name of Reish Lakish: *hacha b'mai askinan shehitzis b'gufo shel eved* — we are speaking here of a case where one directly torched the body of the slave, not merely where fire spread. In that case, one has committed an act of killing directly, and *kim lei* does apply.

### Different Owners & Kim L…

The *Gemara* then asks: if one directly torched the slave, what is the *chiddush* — the novel ruling? Surely that is no different from any direct act of killing. The answer is that the novelty lies in the case where the goat belongs to one person and the slave to another — *gdei d'chad v'eved d'chad*. The question is whether *kim lei* applies when the capital crime was committed against one litigant (the slave's owner) and the civil damage was suffered by a different litigant (the goat's owner). Does *kim lei* collapse multiple claims from different parties, or do we treat them as fully separate proceedings?

The general question can be framed as *misa l'zeh u'mamon l'zeh*: if you are liable to execution for what you did to Reuven, and civilly liable for damage caused to Levi by the same act, do we say *kim lei* and wipe out Levi's claim as well? There is extensive discussion in Tosafot about how this *sugya* and the related *sugya* in Sanhedrin resolve, and what the final *halacha* is. Our *Gemara* appears to be asserting that *kim lei* does apply even across different litigants — that is the *chiddush*: you are exempt from paying Shimon for his goat because of what you did to Reuven's slave.

---

## Pasuk & Braisa Support

### Pasuk: Spreads & Pays

Rava states that both a *pasuk* and a *braisa* support Rabbi Yochanan. The *pasuk* in Exodus reads *ki tetzei eish* — if fire goes out, meaning it spread on its own through negligence, unintentionally — and yet the Torah declares *shaleim yeshaleim hamavir et hab'eirah*, the one who kindles the conflagration shall pay. The spreading was unintentional, yet the person is identified as the one who effectuated the burning — *hamavir*, the burner. The *pasuk* thus equates your fire with your act. *Shma mina isho mishum chitzav*.

### Braisa: Property to Doer

A *braisa* states the point even more explicitly: *patach hakatuv b'nizkei mamono v'siyem b'nizkei gufo* — the Torah opens by framing fire damage in the language of property damage (*mamono*), as when one's ox escapes, but concludes by identifying you as the doer — *hamavir et hab'eirah*. The *braisa* derives from this that *eish mishum chitzav*: the Torah is telling you that you are liable as though your fire were your own direct action. By this point in the *sugya*, one observes that virtually all the evidence has accumulated on Rabbi Yochanan's side: the dog-fire case paying half, the *kim lei* discussion by the slave, the *cheresh shoteh v'katan* case, the *pasuk*, and now the *braisa*.

---

## Buried Items & Chitzav P…

### Buried Item Exemption

Despite this weight of evidence, Abaye raises a purely logical challenge. *Tamun ba'eish d'patar Rachmana* — the Torah exempts one from liability when fire burns something buried in a haystack. If fire is truly *mishum chitzav* — treated as your direct action, like shooting an arrow — how can this exemption exist? If one directly lights a haystack and there happens to be a wallet buried inside, one would certainly be liable for the wallet. Why then, when fire spreads to a haystack and burns a buried wallet, is one exempt? This exemption makes sense only if fire is in some category other than direct action. One can tolerate arbitrary exemptions for damage caused by property (*mamono*), analogous to an ox being exempt for certain things in the public domain, but you cannot coherently maintain arbitrary carve-outs for something treated as your own direct action.

### Fire's Trajectory & Wall

Abaye resolves his own question. The case of *tamun* within this framework refers to the following scenario: the fire spread from the tortfeasor's domain to a neighbor's field — call it Reuven's field — and was stopped by a wall. Then the wall collapsed *shelo machmas deleika*, not because of the fire itself, and the fire crossed into a second field — Shimon's. The key insight is that when one negligently allowed the fire to escape, the trajectory of one's "arrow" extended only as far as the wall. The original negligence, the original act as it were, had a natural stopping point. Beyond the wall, where a new event caused the spread, the fire is no longer acting within the range one set for it. *Kalu lei chitzav* — the arrows have run out. In that second field, the fire burning something buried is no longer your direct action.

### Wall Falls, Liability Co…

The *Gemara* asks: if the *chitzav* ends at the wall, why are you liable for anything at all in Shimon's field — even for things that are not buried? The *Gemara* answers: *lema'an d'is lei mishum chitzav is lei nami mishum mamono* — whoever holds *mishum chitzav* also holds *mishum mamono*. Rabbi Yochanan does not replace the *mamono* framework; he layers *chitzav* on top of it. Beyond the wall, it is no longer your direct action, but it remains your fire — your property in the sense of negligence — and you are still liable as the one who should have guarded it. *Kegon shehaya lo ligdor v'lo gadar* — you could have contained it after the wall fell and did not.

This means your continued liability in Shimon's field is grounded in *mamono*: you could have intervened once the wall came down and the fire crossed over, and you failed to do so. At that point it is like an ox you could have restrained but did not — *d'azal she'ura lo tapach b'apei* — you did not close the gate in front of your ox. But since the fire's reaching Shimon's field was not the product of your original negligent act — some independent event, the wall's collapse, intervened — that spread is no longer *chitzav*. The *tamun* exemption kicks in for that second field precisely because the fire there is only *mamono*, not *chitzav*.

---

## Both Chitzav & Mamono

### Dual Nature of Fire

The *Gemara* now states the conclusion explicitly: *d'man d'is lei mishum chitzav is lei nami mishum mamono* — according to Rabbi Yochanan, fire carries both categories simultaneously. The *chitzav* dimension does not displace the *mamono* dimension; they coexist. The *chitzav* applies within the anticipated scope of the original negligent act — the fire spreading as far as one could have foreseen — and *mamono* applies beyond that, wherever the fire spreads due to a new, intervening event after one had an opportunity to stop it and did not.

The *Gemara* then asks: now that Rabbi Yochanan holds both, what is left between them and Reish Lakish? The answer is that there is in fact a great deal separating them — the dog-fire case, the *kim lei* case, the *cheresh shoteh v'katan* cases all represent additional obligations generated by *chitzav* that Reish Lakish does not recognize. The *Gemara* is simply searching for yet another *nafka mina*, an additional practical difference to articulate.

According to Tosafot, the structure of the debate is somewhat different. Rather than framing it as two separate ontological categories layered upon one another, Tosafot understands the distinction as one of degree of negligence: to trigger *mishum chitzav* — to treat one's fire as one's own direct action — requires a very high degree of negligence, while *mishum mamono* requires only moderate negligence. The *Gemara*, on this reading, is not asserting two simultaneously operative frameworks, but rather two thresholds of culpability. Other *Rishonim* hold what may be a more faithful reading of the *Gemara*'s language: it is not about degree of negligence at all, but about whose action, categorically, the fire represents — and the *mamono* framework applies whenever it ceases to be one's direct action.

### Personal Injury Four Dam…

A crucial and previously unstated *nafka mina* emerges: *ika beinaihu lechayvo b'arba'ah devarim* — the practical difference between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish includes liability for the four additional categories of personal injury damages. Throughout this *sugya*, the discussion of *esh* has focused entirely on *nezek* — property damage. But if one's fire spreads and burns a person — injuring but not killing them — the question of what one owes is suddenly transformed. If an ox gores a person, the owner pays only *nezek*. But if a person directly injures another, they owe not only *nezek* but also *tza'ar*, *shevet*, *ripui*, and *boshet* — pain, lost work, medical expenses, and humiliation. According to Rabbi Yochanan, since fire is *mishum chitzav* — treated as one's own direct action — if one's fire burns a person, one pays all four categories as though one had personally inflicted the injury. This is a major and independent *nafka mina* for the *chitzav* position.

---

## Hagra: Negligence & Prop…

### Negligence = Direct Liab…

The Vilna Gaon offers a fundamentally different reading of the *sugya*'s *maskana*. He draws attention to the word *ela* in the *Gemara* — marked in the text with a notational symbol — and argues that the *Gemara* there is not combining two frameworks but rather completely rejecting the falling-wall resolution and returning to the *braisa*: *patach hakatuv b'nizkei mamono v'siyem b'nizkei gufo*. On the Hagra's reading, this does not mean that fire is both *mamono* and *chitzav* as two separate categories. Rather, the *mechayev* — the basis for liability — is always and fundamentally *mamono*: you were negligent with your property. But once that negligence is established, the Torah treats you *as though* you had done it directly, and payment is assessed accordingly.

### Foundation: Should Have…

The Hagra reads *kegon shehaya lo legodrah v'lo gadrah* not as a special case but as the very foundation of the obligation. The entire reason the Torah makes you liable is *shehaya lo legodrah v'lo gadrah* — you should have guarded against this and did not. *D'azal she'ura lo tapach b'apei* — you did not close the gate in front of your ox. The *chiyuv* is rooted in failure to guard; once that failure is established, you pay as though you had committed the act yourself. This explains, elegantly, why you are exempt for *tamun* in ordinary cases without needing the falling-wall construction: since the *chiyuv* is fundamentally that of *mamono hamazik*, one can accommodate the *tamun* exemption naturally, the same way one accommodates exemptions elsewhere in the *shor hamazik* categories. You did not truly do it; the Torah holds you liable as though you had — and therefore certain exceptions remain.

This reading also brings two *Rambam* rulings into alignment. The Rambam rules like Reish Lakish in the *cheresh shoteh v'katan* case — you are exempt only when you gave a *gachelet*, a coal, but liable if you gave a *shalhevet*, a flame — and separately rules that the *tamun* exemption applies in ordinary cases without requiring the falling-wall scenario. On the Hagra's reading, this is coherent: the *chiyuv* must begin as a *chiyuv* of *mamono* — you were negligent with your property — and once it is established you pay as though you acted directly. The dog-fire case paying half remains a difficulty that must be worked through separately, but the overall structure holds.

---

## Dog Takes Coal to Sh (II)

### Scenario & Damages

The *Gemara* now turns to the case where a dog takes its owner's coal and carries it to someone else's grain sheaf, causing a fire. The owner of the dog pays full value for the grain sheaf burned — or rather the *Gemara* is working out who pays what. The dog's owner pays for the sheaf's destruction, and the question arises whether the owner of the coal also bears responsibility. After all, it was the coal-owner's fire that ultimately caused the damage — why should this not be treated as a combination of the coal-owner's *esh* and the dog's *tzroros*?

### Coal Owner's Defense

The *Gemara* answers: *b'sheshimar gachalto* — the coal-owner was watching the coal carefully and guarded it properly. Since the coal-owner satisfied the required standard of care, one cannot hold that person liable for the fire. The coal-owner's negligence is not established.

### Dog Digging Under Fence

The *Gemara* then asks: if the coal-owner was truly watching the coal carefully, how did the dog get it? The answer is *bechatar* — the dog dug under the fence. Rav Mari son of Rav Kahana derives from this: *stam dlatot chatar einan l'kelev* — an ordinary wall or fence is the kind that a dog can dig under. If a normal fence cannot prevent a dog from tunneling beneath it, then the coal-owner who erected only a normal fence has not truly guarded against dog intrusion. And if the coal-owner is not fully protected, one might argue the coal-owner shares in the negligence. But conversely, the same logic demonstrates the dog-owner's negligence: it is foreseeable that an unrestrained dog will dig under a normal fence.

---

## Dog Takes Coal to Sh (II)

### Different Standards of C…

Tosafot raises a crucial distinction that applies here and carries broader significance. In the *Tosafot* entry beginning *l'chayev ba'al hagachelet*, Tosafot articulates the principle: *d'yoteir yeish l'adam l'hazaher atzmo shelo yazik acherim mishelo yuzak* — a person bears a higher degree of responsibility to ensure that they do not injure others than to ensure that their own property is not damaged by others. The standard of care required to avoid causing damage to a third party is higher than the standard required to protect one's own goods from being damaged by that third party. The coal-owner, therefore, may have satisfied the lower threshold required to protect one's own coal from being taken, even though a dog could dig under a normal fence; the responsibility for ensuring one's dog does not run loose and cause damage is higher, and falls primarily on the dog-owner.

---

## Mouth as Domain Question

### Third Party Field Eating

The *Gemara* asks: *d'achlah heicha* — where exactly did the dog eat the biscuit? If it ate it in a third party's grain sheaf — not in the coal-owner's domain — then why is the coal-owner liable for the biscuit? The biscuit was not eaten in the coal-owner's field; it was consumed in someone else's domain entirely. This brings the fundamental question of *reshut* into sharp relief. The assumption embedded in the question is that liability for *shen* — for an animal eating — requires that the eating take place in *reshut hanizak*, the victim's domain. If the dog took the biscuit from the coal-owner's area and ate it in a third person's domain, one would be exempt from the cost of the biscuit.

### Mouth = Victim's Domain

The *Gemara* resolves: *lo tzricha d'achlah b'gidish d'charara* — actually, the dog ate the biscuit within the domain of the biscuit's owner (the coal-owner's own domain, since that is where the coal and the biscuit were). And from this, the *Gemara* derives: *pi parah k'chatzer hanizak dami* — the mouth of the animal is treated as the domain of the victim, not the domain of the animal's owner. The eating takes place, legally, in the victim's domain, and that is why liability attaches.

### Contradiction Resolved

This conclusion is striking, because it seems to contradict everything the *Gemara* assumed until this point. Earlier cases — an animal eating a garment in an open marketplace, eating within a shop — all appeared to proceed on the assumption that wherever an animal eats, the owner is liable, without any special concern about whether the eating occurred in *reshut hanizak* or *reshut hamazik*. The *Gemara* never paused to ask whether the animal's mouth constitutes the victim's or the tortfeasor's domain. How does this newly announced principle cohere with all those earlier cases?

### Tosafot: Location of Eat…

Tosafot offers a penetrating answer. Until this point, the *Gemara* implicitly assumed that it does not matter where the animal eats — what matters is where the animal *took* the food. If an animal entered your domain, took your fruit, and then wandered into the public domain and ate it there, you would think liability should clearly attach: the animal violated your domain, took your property, and the owner was negligent. Who cares where the actual eating occurred? The *taking* should be the operative moment, and it occurred in *reshut hanizak*. On this assumption, the mouth is irrelevant — it could be *chatzer hamazik* or *chatzer hanizak*, it makes no difference.

But in the dog case, the *Gemara* implicitly asserts something different: it is not sufficient that the animal *took* from your domain. The eating must also occur in your domain for full *shen* liability to attach. If the dog took the biscuit from the coal-owner's property and ate it in a third party's field, the coal-owner would be *patur* for the biscuit. This is what the *Gemara* is asserting in the course of resolving the case. And once one accepts this — once the location of the eating, not merely the taking, becomes determinative — then the conclusion follows inescapably: the mouth of the animal must be considered *chatzer hanizak*, the victim's domain. Otherwise, whenever an animal ate anything at all, the eating would be occurring in *chatzer hamazik*, and liability for *shen* would never arise. The only *shen* cases on this view would be the animal rubbing against a wall or rolling in fruit for pleasure — not eating at all. Since this cannot be the intent of the Torah's laws of *shen*, the mouth must be regarded as *chatzer hanizak*. Tosafot's insight is that the *Gemara* is implicitly asserting a principle about the location of eating — not merely a rule about the mouth — and that the *chatzer hanizak* conclusion about the mouth is the logical entailment of that prior, implicit assertion.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 24

## Inciting Animals

### Dog/Snake Attack Case

The *gemara* opens with a *tashma* — an attempt to bring a proof — appearing approximately ten lines into 23b. The passage reads: *shissa bo et ha-kelev, shissa bo et ha-nachash, patur* — if a person incites a dog or a snake to attack a third party, that person is *patur*, entirely exempt from liability. The case involves someone who encourages another's animal to attack a bystander; the inciter is not the owner, and the owner is not the one who actively caused the attack. Because liability appears to be split between two different parties, the question immediately arises: who, precisely, is *patur*?

### Liability Question

The *gemara* poses the question directly: *man patur* — who is the one who is *patur*? The initial reading suggests that the inciter (*mashse*) is *patur*, and the owner of the dog (*ba'al ha-kelev*) is *chayav* — after all, it was the owner's animal that caused the damage. If a dog is already *mu'ad*, the owner would owe *nezek shalem*. This reading makes straightforward sense: the owner's animal attacked someone, so the owner bears responsibility.

### Open Mouth Theory

However, the *gemara* introduces a counterpoint: *ve-ee bayit eima de-afkalan niveiha ve-sarteh* — an alternative reading in which the dog bared and thrust its teeth outward. This *iba'is eima* proposes that when a dog opens its mouth and attacks, the teeth are no longer entirely within the dog's body in a way that could be considered the owner's private domain. The relevance of this point connects to the broader question being debated in the *sugya*: is the mouth of an animal considered *kechatzer ha-mazik* — like the property of the person causing the damage? If so, then just as one is *patur* for damage caused in the *mazik*'s own domain, the owner might similarly be *patur* when the dog bites, since the mouth is treated as his domain. The *iba'is eima* offers a way to maintain the owner's *chiyuv* even according to that view: if the dog lunged outward with open jaws, the mouth is no longer functioning as a contained domain.

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi explains the *iba'is eima* precisely: *she-hotzi shinav ve-sarto de-lo hichnis yado le-toch piv* — the dog jumped out and attacked rather than the person inserting their hand into the dog's mouth. This distinction matters because the entire exemption under the *kechatzer ha-mazik* theory rests on the victim having, in effect, entered the *mazik*'s domain voluntarily. When the dog attacks outward with an open mouth, that framework no longer applies, and the *ba'al ha-kelev* becomes *chayav*. Importantly, as one might observe, the *iba'is eima* is not simply another answer to the same question — it is an alternative explanation of the same ruling, representing a genuine *machlokes* between the two readings of the *braisa*.

---

## Snake Bite Liability

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

The *gemara* brings a second *tashma* concerning a case of directing a snake to bite someone. *Rabbi Yehuda mechayev* — Rabbi Yehuda holds the person *chayav* — while the *chachamim* hold the person *patur*. Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: *eres nachash bein shinav hu omed* — the venom of a snake sits lodged within its fangs at all times. According to this view, a snake is already a preloaded lethal weapon; its venom does not need to be voluntarily expelled. Consequently, one who takes a snake and has it bite another person is treated as if they struck someone with a poisoned blade, and the *halacha* is that such a person is executed by the sword (*machish be-sayaf*) for having committed an act of killing. The snake itself is *patur*, since the act of biting was entirely in the control of the human who deployed it.

### Chachamim's View

The *chachamim* dispute this understanding of snake physiology and, accordingly, the legal conclusion. In their view, *eres nachash me-atzmo makya* — the venom of the snake is expelled by the snake's own volition. The snake decides whether to inject its venom when it bites, and therefore one who forces a snake to bite another person can never be certain that the bite will be lethal. Because it is never *vadai* — certain — that the snake will release venom, one cannot be held criminally liable for murder. The snake, having caused a death through its own volitional act, is executed by *skila*, but the person who wielded it is *patur* from capital liability. This raises the pointed question of whether such a person could at least be liable for *nezikin* — civil damages — but the *gemara* does not fully resolve it in this context, and the question of *kim lei be-drabba minei* (that the more severe penalty absorbs lesser liability) complicates any definitive answer.

### Capital Crime Exception

The *gemara* raises an apparent difficulty: if we say that the mouth of the animal is *kechatzer ha-mazik*, why would the owner of the snake be *chayav* at all, even according to Rabbi Yehuda? The *gemara* answers: *le-inyan katla lo amrinan* — we do not apply the *kechatzer ha-mazik* principle in cases of capital crimes. That rule, which would permit the owner to say "why did you put your hand into the mouth of my animal," operates only in the realm of civil damages.

### Unauthorized Entry

A *braisa* is cited to support this distinction: if someone enters another's *chatzer* without permission and is gored to death by the owner's ox, the *halacha* is that the ox is executed by *skila* — because it caused a death — but the owner is *patur min ha-kofer*, exempt from the monetary penalty of *kofer* that would normally accompany a killing by a *mu'ad* animal. The owner's defense is: *be-reshuti mai bayis* — what were you doing in my property? However, this same argument cannot save the ox from execution. *Le-inyan katla lo amrinan* — for the purposes of capital punishment of the animal, we do not extend the "it was my domain" argument. The animal must be destroyed regardless of whether the victim had permission to be on the premises.

---

## Rav Yosef's Goats

### Goat Damage & Fence

The *gemara* presents a vivid practical case. There were goats belonging to a family called Beit Tarbu (*hanehu izi de-vei tarbu*) that were causing ongoing damage to Rav Yosef's property. Rav Yosef instructed Abaye to go and tell the owners to confine their animals. Abaye pushed back: why must you issue a formal demand? The owners will simply say that the goats went and did as goats do, and that they bear no additional liability. Furthermore, Abaye raises the *halachic* challenge: if you are going to require owners to fence in their animals, then how can you ever have a case of liability for *shen* — damage caused by grazing? If an animal is always required to be locked up, and an animal escapes, the escape itself is *ones*, an unforeseeable circumstance, and the owner would have a defense. The *gemara* responds that *shen* liability can be found in a case where the animal dug under the fence (*ke-she-chatrah*), but this opens further questions about the scope of the owner's responsibility.

### Public Warning

Rav Yosef — or possibly Rava, as the *gemara* offers an alternative attribution — issued a public proclamation directed both to those traveling up to *Eretz Yisrael* and those coming down to *Bavel*, covering both communities. The announcement concerned goats taken to the marketplace (*hanei izei de-shuka*) that were causing damage. Rav Yosef declared that he was treating the owners as though they had already been warned two and three times (*trei u-tlata zimnei*), effectively establishing *mu'ad* status for these animals by public decree. He was not addressing any single owner individually; rather, he was using his authority to put all goat-herders on notice that their animals had achieved a presumptive status of *mu'ad* with respect to marketplace damage.

### Forced Slaughter

Beyond the proclamation, Rav Yosef went further: if the owners did not comply, he declared that they would be told to go and slaughter (*shecht*) their animals immediately. This meant selling the animals before the market day, when there would be fewer buyers and the price would be lower, causing the owners a real financial loss. This was a deliberate legislative measure — Rav Yosef was personally affected by the damage, and he used rabbinic authority to impose real economic consequences on those who refused to control their animals. The episode reflects the broader concern documented throughout *Bava Batra* as well, where *Chazal* expressed strong opposition to raising *behema daka* — small livestock such as goats and sheep — in *Eretz Yisrael*, precisely because such animals tend to wander and graze on others' property, which amounts to *gezel*.

---

## Tam vs. Muad

### Mishna Definition

The next *mishna* takes up a foundational question: *eizehu tam ve-eizehu mu'ad* — what constitutes a *tam* (innocent) animal and what constitutes a *mu'ad* (forewarned dangerous) animal? The *mishna* establishes that any animal about which testimony was given on three separate days (*kol she-he'idu bo shlosha yamim*) becomes *mu'ad*. Conversely, a *mu'ad* animal can revert to *tam* status (*ve-tam mi-she-yachzor bo shlosha yamim*) — after three days of not goring. This reversion cannot be based on mere passivity; it must involve some circumstance that would normally provoke the animal, where the animal nonetheless demonstrates restraint. This is the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda.

### Rabbi Yehuda & Counting

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'amei de-Rabbi Yehuda* — what is the reasoning behind Rabbi Yehuda's position that three separate days are required? Abaye explains by parsing the *pasuk*: *temol* — yesterday, represents one day; *mi-temol* — meaning not merely yesterday but the day before, represents a second day; and *shilshom* — the day before that — represents a third day. The key textual detail is that *shilshom* means two days before today, which corresponds to three distinct calendar days. And *ve-lo yishmerenu ba'alav* — "and its owner did not guard it" — introduces the owner's responsibility only *after* those three days of testimony, meaning it is the fourth goring that triggers full *chiyuv* as a *mu'ad*.

Rava disagrees with Abaye's parsing: in Rava's reading, *temol mi-temol* together count as a single unit of one day, and *shilshom* provides the second. The phrase *ve-lo yishmerenu* then brings the owner into liability at the third goring rather than the fourth. This is the classic tension between Abaye and Rava: is the third occurrence itself the point of *chiyuv*, or does *chiyuv* begin only with the fourth, after three completed warnings?

### Rabbi Meir's View

Rabbi Meir takes a different approach entirely: *mu'ad mi-she-he'idu bo shlosha pe'amim* — an animal becomes *mu'ad* after being testified against three times, without requiring that those occurrences span three separate days. And for reversion to *tam* status, Rabbi Meir holds that it suffices for children to be playing around the animal without it goring — even if that happens in a single day.

Rabbi Meir's reasoning is presented as a *kal va-chomer*: *richak negichotav chayav* — if the gorings were spread out over multiple days, he is certainly *chayav*; *kirav negichotav* — if they were even closer together, is that not *kal she-ken*, all the more so? The *chachamim* challenge this with the case of *zava*: a woman whose three irregular flows occur on a single day does not achieve the halachic status of *zava gedola* and is not required to bring a *korban*. *Zava* requires three separate days. If Rabbi Meir's *kal va-chomer* were correct, one would expect *zava* to apply even more stringently when the occurrences are clustered; yet it does not.

### Zav/Zava Comparison

Rabbi Meir responds by distinguishing between *zav* and *zava*. He cites the *pasuk*: *ve-zot tihyeh tum'ato be-zovo* — this shall be his impurity in his discharge — and argues that the Torah explicitly distinguished between the two cases. For *zav* — a man with an irregular discharge — the count is by *re'iyot*, individual occurrences, meaning three times even on one day can qualify. For *zava* — a woman — the count is by *yamim*, separate days. The word *ve-zot* functions as a *mi'ut*, an exclusion, to separate the two regimes.

The *gemara* then asks: why apply the *mi'ut* to exclude *zava* from the *re'iyot*-based count, rather than to exclude *zav* from the *yamim*-based count? The answer is drawn from a subsequent *pasuk* that compares *zav* and *zava* as equivalent — *la-zachar ve-la-nekeva* — which creates a *hekesh* equating male and female. The *gemara* reasons that the *hekesh* applies in the context where the exclusion is made: where the text deals with *re'iyot*, the *mi'ut* excludes *zava* from that regime, and where the text deals with *yamim*, the *hekesh* brings *zav* in to require three separate days as well. Thus *zav* can achieve his status through three occurrences even on one day, but *zava* requires three consecutive days.

The *Rambam* in *Sefer Ha-Mitzvot* reflects precisely this distinction: he counts the *korbanot* for *zav* and *zava* as two separate *mitzvot*, because their underlying laws differ substantially, whereas the *korban* for *metzora* is listed as a single *mitzva* applying equally to men and women, since the laws of *tzara'at* apply identically to both.

### Mixed Positions

A *braisa* then presents the opinions of Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Yose's position is a hybrid: his *reisha* mirrors Rabbi Yehuda in requiring three separate days for *mu'ad* status, but his *seifa* mirrors Rabbi Meir in that the standard for reverting to *tam* status is whether children can play with the animal without it goring. Rabbi Shimon holds that *mu'ad* status requires three occurrences (*shlosha pe'amim*) like Rabbi Meir, but limits the three-*pe'amim* rule to *chazara* — reversion to *tam* status — while applying different criteria to becoming *mu'ad* in the first place.

### Rav Nachman's Psak

Rav Nachman rules, citing Rabba bar Avuha: *halakha ke-Rabbi Yehuda be-mu'ad*, because Rabbi Yose agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on that point, making it two against one. *Ve-halakha ke-Rabbi Meir be-tam*, because Rabbi Yose agrees with Rabbi Meir on the reversion standard, again two against one. In effect, Rav Nachman is *paskening* like Rabbi Yose, who happens to align with different *tanna'im* on each half of the question.

Rava challenges this: one could equally argue that Rabbi Shimon agrees with Rabbi Meir for *mu'ad*, making it two against two for that side, and that Rabbi Shimon agrees with Rabbi Yehuda for *tam*, making it two against two the other way — leaving the *psak* in the opposite direction. Rav Nachman's response is direct: *ana ke-Rabbi Yose sevira li* — I hold like Rabbi Yose because *Rabbi Yose nimuko imo*, Rabbi Yose always has well-grounded, well-developed reasoning. This invokes a general principle in the *klalei ha-psak*: when Rabbi Yose argues a position, his reasoning is typically the most fully articulated. It is worth noting the contrast with Rabbi Meir, about whom *Chazal* understood that his arguments were often so intellectually sophisticated that his colleagues could not always follow them — he was, in a sense, too creative for his own good.

---

## Muad Status Question

### Muad Definition

With the *psak* established, the *gemara* opens a new *she'eila*: the three days that the *mishna* requires — are they *le-i'udei tora* or *le-i'udei gavra*? That is, are the three days of testimony meant to establish a legal *status* for the animal itself — that this ox is now a known *mu'ad* — or are they meant to inform the owner, placing on him a personal obligation to act, so that his subsequent failure to contain the animal generates full liability?

The *nafka mina* is clarifying. At first the question may seem obscure, but the *gemara* focuses it with a concrete case.

### Single-Day Witnesses

The *nafka mina* is: what if three separate groups of witnesses came to court regarding the same ox, all on the same day? The ox gored three times in rapid succession, and three independent pairs of witnesses testified accordingly, all on that single day. If the requirement is *le-i'udei tora* — about establishing the ox's status — then the ox is indeed *mu'ad*, because three independent acts of testimony have been rendered. But if the requirement is *le-i'udei gavra* — about notifying the owner with enough time to act — then the owner can truthfully say: *hashta hu de-kamsa'adi bi* — only now are they informing me. He had no meaningful opportunity to respond to the information before the next goring occurred.

### Beit Din Requirement

A *tashma* is brought: the ox cannot become *mu'ad* until the witnesses testify both in the presence of the owner and in the presence of *beit din* simultaneously. If testimony was given before *beit din* but without the owner present, or before the owner but not in court, it does not count toward establishing *mu'ad* status.

### Multiple Witnesses

The *braisa* continues with a more complex scenario: two witnesses came the first time, two more the second time, and two more the third time — six witnesses in three separate groups. The *braisa* notes that this constitutes three distinct *eduyot*, and that if any one group is later disqualified, it invalidates only that group's testimony while leaving the others intact. However, for the purpose of *hazamah* — if the witnesses are found to be *edim zomemim* — all six are treated as a single unit: *edut achat la-hazamah*.

### Third Group Hazama

The *braisa* then explores what happens when each successive group is found to be *zomemim*. If the first group is disqualified, there remain only two valid testimonies, the animal is not *mu'ad*, and both the defendant and the disqualified witnesses are *patur*. If the second group is disqualified, there remains only one valid testimony, and again both are *patur*. But if the third group is found to be *zomemim*, then *kulan chayavim* — all of them are liable. The logic is that it is only the third group whose testimony creates the *mu'ad* status, and therefore only at the moment of the third group's testimony does the *hazamah* have real monetary consequence — shifting liability from *chatzi nezek* to *nezek shalem*. The *edim zomemim* must pay what they sought to impose: the additional exposure that comes with *mu'ad* status.

The question emerges regarding how the six witnesses split liability. The *braisa*'s formulation that they function as *edut achat la-hazamah* might suggest they all split it equally. But the *gemara*'s *shakla ve-tarya* points toward the conclusion that only the third group bears sole responsibility, since it is their testimony alone that completes the *mu'ad* determination, while the first two groups' testimony, standing alone, achieved nothing.

### Rav Kahana's Challenge

Rav Ashi recounts that he presented this *braisa* before Rav Kahana, who challenged the *le-i'udei tora* interpretation sharply. Rav Kahana's objection: even if you say that it is all about establishing the ox's status, how can you make the last group of witnesses liable as *edim zomemim*? They arrived at court having seen an ox gore another animal, and they came to testify that the owner should pay *chatzi nezek* — they believed they were dealing with a *shor tam*. They had no way of knowing that two prior groups had already testified before them, rendering their testimony the decisive third strike. *Anan le-chayuvei gavra palga nizka asinan* — we came only to make him pay *chatzi nezek*, they could say. How can they be held responsible for creating *mu'ad* status if they were unaware that their testimony was the one that achieved it?

This challenge applies even if the *mu'ad* determination is purely about the animal's status and not the owner's notification. Even within the *le-i'udei tora* framework, the final witnesses acted without any knowledge of what their testimony would accomplish. Rav Kahana's point is that for *edim zomemim* liability to attach, the witnesses must have had some awareness of the consequences their false testimony would create.

### Conspiracy Evidence

Rav Ashi offers a resolution: *ke-she-ba'u retzufim* — the case of *edim zomemim* liability applies when the witnesses arrived one right after another in rapid sequence. Consecutive appearances in court serve as circumstantial evidence of a coordinated conspiracy. Ravina offers a different indicator: the case involves witnesses who could identify the owner of the ox (*makirin ba'al ha-shor*) but could not identify the specific ox (*ve-ein makirin et ha-shor*). Such witnesses came and said, in effect, "your ox gored someone" — but had they been asked to pick the ox out of a herd, they would not have been able to do so. This is evidence that they were fabricating testimony. Both of these markers — consecutive appearance or inability to identify the animal — can establish the conspiracy that would make the *edim zomemim* framework applicable.

---

## Friend's Animal Inciteme…

### Third-Party Attack

The *gemara* now takes up a related *she'eila*: *ha-mshaseh kalbo shel chaveiro be-chaveiro mahu* — what is the law when someone incites his friend's dog to attack a third party? The inciter is not the owner; he has used another person's animal as a weapon against someone else entirely.

### Owner's Defense

One possibility is that the owner can claim: *ana mai avidna leh* — what did I do? I was not present, I did not direct my animal, I am not responsible for what someone else caused my dog to do.

### Knowledge & Prevention

The counter-argument is that the owner may nonetheless bear responsibility: *keivan de-yadata be-kalbecha de-mashseh leh u-mishtaseh* — since you knew that others were inciting your dog and that the dog was in fact being incited and attacking, *lo iba lach le-ashuyei* — you should not have kept the dog around. That is, once an owner is on notice that his animal is being used as a weapon by others, his failure to take protective measures may itself constitute culpable negligence.

### Tam Challenge

An attempt is made to resolve this from the *mishna*'s standard for reverting an animal to *tam* status: *be-tam she-hayu tinokot me-shamshin bo ve-eino noge'ach* — if children were playing around the animal and it did not gore, the animal is *tam*. The implicit inference is: *ha nogei'ach chayav* — if it did gore when the children were playing around it, that act of goring creates *chiyuv*. Since children playing around an animal constitutes a form of incitement, this might serve as a precedent for holding the owner liable when someone else incites his dog.

### Abaye Response

Abaye rejects this inference. *Mi ke-tani nagach chayav?* — did the *mishna* actually say that if it gored in that circumstance it is *chayav*? All the *mishna* says is that if the animal did not gore when children played with it, that is the standard for reverting to *tam* status. If it did gore, the consequence is simply that it does not revert to *tam* — *dilma ha nagach lo havi tam u-be-hai negicha lo mechayev* — but for that particular act of goring it is not *chayav*, because it was provoked by the children. One cannot prove anything about the incited-dog case from this *mishna*.

---

## Tashma Proof

### Braita Statement

The *gemara* returns to the original *tashma*: *shissa bo et ha-kelev, shissa bo et ha-nachash, patur* — one who incites a dog or a snake to attack is *patur*.

### First Inference

The first possible reading of this *braisa*: *patur ha-mashse ve-chayav ba'al ha-kelev* — the inciter is *patur* but the owner of the dog is *chayav*. This is the straightforward reading that exonerates the inciter while placing responsibility on the animal's owner.

### Counter-Inference

The alternative reading is: *eima patur af mashse* — perhaps the *braisa* means that the owner is obviously *patur* (because the mouth of the animal is *kechatzer ha-mazik*, and one can ask why the victim put their hand into the dog's mouth), and even the inciter is *patur* — the less obvious case. On this reading, both parties are exempt.

### Rava's Analysis

Rava sharpens the analysis: *im timtzi lomar ha-mshaseh kalbo shel chaveiro be-chaveiro chayav* — if you say that one who incites another's dog against a third party is *chayav*, then *shisseihu hu be-atzmo patur* — if the person incited the dog against himself, the owner is *patur*. That is, if the victim was himself responsible for provoking the attack by engaging with the animal, the owner cannot be held liable.

### Change Principle

The underlying principle is: *kol ha-meshaneh, u-va acher ve-shinah bo, patur* — if one person introduces a change in the normal situation, and then another person comes and introduces a further change, the second party is *patur*. In the context of the dog: the inciter altered the normal situation by provoking the animal, and then the dog itself responded — one change layered upon another. Once the initial change is introduced by someone other than the owner, the owner's responsibility is displaced. This principle will recur shortly in the discussion of the two cows in the public domain.

---

## Cows Kicking Case

### Reish Lakish

Rav Papa brings a *mimra* from Reish Lakish that aligns with Rava's earlier analysis. Reish Lakish states: if two cows are in *reshut ha-rabim* and one is crouching (*revutza*) while the other is walking (*mahalechet*, and the walking one kicks the crouching one, the walking cow is *ptura* — exempt. The reason is that the walking cow is simply doing what cows do in the public thoroughfare; this is the normal and permitted use of *reshut ha-rabim*, and it falls under the category of *regel*, ordinary walking damage. But if the crouching cow kicked the walking cow — *revutza be-mahalechet* — the crouching cow is *chayavet*, liable. By kicking from a resting position, the crouching cow departed from normal behavior (*kol ha-meshaneh chayav*).

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges Reish Lakish's ruling on the walking cow. Even if a cow has the right to be walking through *reshut ha-rabim*, that does not include the right to kick other animals. Kicking is not part of the normal walking motion; it is an independent act of damage. Therefore, Rava argues, even the walking cow should be *chayav*.

### Rights Analysis

The distinction Rava draws is conceptually precise: *ki it lach reshuta lisgu'ei alai, limva'at bi leit lach reshuta* — you have rights to walk past me in the street, but you do not have rights to kick me while doing so. The right of transit in *reshut ha-rabim* covers walking, not striking. Kicking is a *tolada* of *keren* — analogous to a horn-type damage — not a *tolada* of *regel*, since it is not the ordinary and inevitable consequence of the animal's movement through public space.

---

## Property Domain Effects

### Mishna Payment Rates

The next *mishna* addresses the rates of payment owed when an animal causes damage in the *reshut ha-nizak* — the victim's private property. The *mishna* enumerates the relevant types of damage: *nagach, nagaf, nashach, ravatz, ba'at* — goring, pushing, biting, sitting on something, or kicking — and notes that when such damage occurs in *reshut ha-rabim*, the owner of a *tam* animal pays *chatzi nezek*.

### Rabbi Tarfon vs. Chacham…

The *machlokes* is over what happens when a *tam* animal causes *keren* damage in the *reshut ha-nizak*. Rabbi Tarfon holds that the owner pays *nezek shalem* — full damages — because the logic that reduces liability to *chatzi nezek* in *reshut ha-rabim* does not apply when the animal has trespassed onto the victim's property. The *chachamim* hold that *keren tam* always pays only *chatzi nezek*, regardless of domain — it is simply the *Torah*'s rule.

### Rabbi Tarfon's Logic

Rabbi Tarfon makes a *kal va-chomer* argument. *Shein* and *regel* are entirely *patur* in *reshut ha-rabim*, yet in *reshut ha-nizak* they pay *nezek shalem*. *Keren* in *reshut ha-rabim* — where *shein* and *regel* are *patur* — still requires the owner to pay *chatzi nezek*. Therefore, in *reshut ha-nizak* — where *shein* and *regel* pay *nezek shalem* — should *keren* not pay *nezek shalem* as well?

### Chachamim Response

The *chachamim* respond with the principle of *dayyo la-ba min ha-din lihyot ka-nidon* — it is sufficient for the conclusion of a *kal va-chomer* to equal its premise, not to exceed it. *Mah bi-reshut ha-rabim chatzi nezek, af bi-reshut ha-nizak chatzi nezek* — just as *keren tam* pays *chatzi nezek* in the public domain, so too it pays *chatzi nezek* in the victim's domain. The *kal va-chomer* cannot generate a more stringent outcome than the rule from which it derives.

### Rabbi Tarfon Clarifies

Rabbi Tarfon responds that he was not comparing *keren* to *keren* — he was comparing *keren* to *regel*. His *kal va-chomer* is constructed from *regel*, not from *keren* itself: *u-mah bi-mkom she-heikel al ha-shein ve-al ha-regel bi-reshut ha-rabim, hechmir be-keren, makom she-hechmir al ha-shein ve-al ha-regel bi-reshut ha-nizak, eino din she-nachmir be-keren* — in the place where *shein* and *regel* are treated leniently (i.e., *patur* in *reshut ha-rabim*), *keren* is treated stringently (*chatzi nezek*); in the place where *shein* and *regel* are treated stringently (*nezek shalem* in *reshut ha-nizak*), should *keren* not also be treated stringently, paying *nezek shalem*? The *chachamim* apply *dayyo* once more and hold firm: *chatzi nezek* for *keren tam* applies in all domains.

---

## Tosafot Analysis

### Counting Gorings

With the *mishna*'s dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and the *chachamim* established, the shiur turns to a *Tosafot* on 24a that addresses the question of how gorings are counted toward establishing and triggering *mu'ad* liability. *Tosafot* raises the question: when exactly does the owner become *chayav* to pay *nezek shalem* as a *mu'ad* owner? Is it on the third goring, or only on the fourth? The *Tosafot* notes the view that the answer might be the fifth goring, and explains why.

### Tosafot's Position

*Tosafot* argues: *i le-i'udei gavra lo she-yehei mu'ad la-avor be-hatra'ot, de-im ken lo haya mechayev ad negichah shel chamishit* — if *mu'ad* is about the owner having been warned (*le-i'udei gavra*) and then violating that warning, one would expect *chiyuv* not until the fifth goring. The reasoning: the first goring generates the first warning; the second goring is a violation of the first warning and generates the second; the third goring violates the second warning and generates the third. At that point, the owner has been warned three times. But the fourth goring is the first one that violates all three accumulated warnings — and yet, that fourth goring is itself also the occasion of being told "this has now happened a fourth time." So the violation of the third warning, strictly speaking, would only become actionable at the fifth goring. 

*Tosafot* uses this reductio to reject the *le-i'udei gavra* framework: the rule cannot be about warning, because that would produce an absurd and unsupported result. Instead, *Tosafot* maintains that *mu'ad* is a *status* — it is about what kind of animal this has proven itself to be, not about whether the owner has violated a specific admonition. The gorings establish the status; the owner's consequent liability follows automatically from that status.

### Contradicting Tosafot

Yet, notably, another *Tosafot* in *Bava Batra* reaches precisely the opposite conclusion — the one that the *Tosafot* on 24a was rejecting. That *Tosafot* in *Bava Batra* holds that the owner does not become fully *chayav* until the fifth goring, because only at that point has he genuinely violated the complete set of three warnings. This represents the *le-i'udei gavra* position in full, and it directly contradicts the reasoning of *Tosafot* here. It is a striking internal tension within *Tosafot* across the two *masekhtot*, leaving the two approaches to *mu'ad* status — as a quality of the animal versus as a violation of the owner's informed duty — in genuine dispute, even within the *Rishonim*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 25

## Tarfon: Full Damages

### Tarfon's Kal Vachomer

The *mishna* opens with the dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and the *Chachamim* regarding an ox that gores in the *reshut hanizak* — the property of the injured party. Rabbi Tarfon argues that even on the first offense, when the animal would ordinarily be liable for only half-damages (*chatzi nezek*), the owner must pay full damages when the goring occurs in the *reshut hanizak*. He derives this through a *kal vachomer* from *shen* and *regel*: in the *reshut harabim*, *shen* and *regel* are entirely exempt; yet in the *reshut hanizak*, they are liable for the full amount. *Keren*, which pays half in the *reshut harabim*, should certainly — *kal vachomer* — be liable for the full amount in the *reshut hanizak*.

### Rabbis' Dayo Response

The *Chachamim* respond with the *dayo* principle: *dayo l'avo min hadin lihyot k'nidon* — it is sufficient that the conclusion derived from the *kal vachomer* equal the case from which it was derived. Since Rabbi Tarfon's *kal vachomer* derives *keren* in the *reshut hanizak* from *keren* in the *reshut harabim*, and *keren* in the *reshut harabim* is half-damages, the most the *kal vachomer* can establish for the *reshut hanizak* is half. The greater severity of the *reshut hanizak* is acknowledged, but *dayo* prevents the conclusion from exceeding its source.

### Tarfon's Second Approach

Rabbi Tarfon then shifts his framing. Rather than comparing *keren* in one domain to *keren* in another — which immediately invites the *dayo* limitation — he focuses on the domains themselves. The *reshut harabim* is a place where one sometimes pays nothing (*shen* and *regel*) and sometimes pays half (*keren*). The *reshut hanizak* is a place where one pays the full amount for *shen* and *regel*. It therefore follows that *keren* in the *reshut hanizak* should also be full, since the *reshut hanizak* is inherently a place of full liability. The comparison is between *shen* and *regel* in the *reshut hanizak* — where the payment is full — and *keren* in the *reshut hanizak*, which should likewise be full. On this framing, *dayo* need not constrain us, since we are not comparing *keren* to *keren*.

### Rabbis' Rebuttal

The *Chachamim* reject this reformulation. At its core, they argue, the *kal vachomer* is still fundamentally a comparison of *keren* to *keren*, and therefore *dayo* applies regardless of how the argument is framed. That is the scope of the debate as presented in the *mishna*.

---

## Tarfon & Dayo

### Dayo Question

The *Gemara* now steps back from the *mishna* itself and probes the underlying structure of Rabbi Tarfon's reasoning. The *Gemara* asks: *v'Rabbi Tarfon leise lei dayo* — does Rabbi Tarfon simply not accept the *dayo* principle? The question arises because in his original formulation, Rabbi Tarfon appeared entirely unbothered by *dayo*, arguing directly that *keren* which pays half in the *reshut harabim* should certainly pay full in the *reshut hanizak*. Only when the *Chachamim* pressed him did he shift to the second approach. This implies that in his own view, the *kal vachomer* could simply produce a result beyond its source without any constraint.

### Dayo Principle

This prompts a further challenge: *v'ha dayo de-oraita hu* — the *dayo* principle is itself a biblical law. Beyond the logical problem of knowing how far a *kal vachomer* can extend (since it establishes only a minimum, not a maximum), the principle is grounded in the *Torah* itself. The *Gemara* cites a *braita* from the list of the thirteen hermeneutic principles (*Yud Gimmel Middot*) through which *halacha* is derived from the *Torah*, and demonstrates that *dayo* is one of them with an explicit scriptural basis.

### Miriam Case

The *braita* sources the *dayo* principle from the episode of Miriam's *tzara'at*. The *pasuk* states: *v'aviha yarok yarak b'faneha halo ticalem shivat yamim* — if her father were to spit in her face, would she not be embarrassed for seven days? The *pasuk* then concludes: *tisager michutz lamachaneh shivat yamim* — let her be closed outside the camp for seven days. When Miriam contracted *tzara'at* through divine displeasure, a *kal vachomer* would seem to argue: if a father's spitting causes seven days of isolation, then God's rebuke should certainly produce *arba-asar* — fourteen days. Yet in practice, Miriam was confined for only seven.

### Dayo Limits Kal Vachomer

The *braita* explains: *ela dayo l'avo min hadin lihyot k'nidon* — it is enough that the conclusion of the *kal vachomer* equal the case from which it was derived. Since the source case (the father's spitting) involves seven days, the *kal vachomer* regarding divine displeasure cannot produce more than seven. Even though the case of God is weightier, *dayo* limits the result to seven. This is the scriptural grounding of *dayo* as a *de-oraita* principle.

### Tarfon Rejects Dayo

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction in Rabbi Tarfon's position with a precise formulation: *ki leise lei dayo heicha de-mifrach kal vachomer* — Rabbi Tarfon rejects *dayo* only in cases where applying *dayo* would entirely undermine the *kal vachomer*. Conversely, *heicha de-lo mifrach kal vachomer, isay dayo* — where the *kal vachomer* still yields a meaningful result after applying *dayo*, Rabbi Tarfon accepts *dayo*.

### Tarfon Principle Explained

The logic of this distinction requires careful unpacking. In most *kal vachomers*, one is deriving from a known case (A) and applying to an unknown case (B). The *kal vachomer* establishes that whatever is true of A is certainly true of B. Even when *dayo* is applied and prevents going beyond A, the *kal vachomer* still "bore fruit" — it established that the law of A applies to B, even if B cannot exceed A. In the case of Miriam, we had no independent source establishing that divine displeasure produces seven days of isolation. The *kal vachomer* from the father's spitting was what brought us to the number seven. Even after *dayo* limits the result (preventing us from going to fourteen), the *kal vachomer* still accomplished something: it taught us that the law of seven days applies in the divine case. *Dayo* removed the additional seven but preserved the base seven — *apik shiva ve-okei b'atrah*.

In the case of the goring ox, however, the situation is entirely different. The *Torah* explicitly establishes that a goring ox pays half-damages — *aval hacha chatzi nezek ksiv*. There was never any reason to think this rule was limited to the *reshut harabim*; half-damages applies universally, regardless of where the goring occurs. So even before the *kal vachomer* is applied, we already knew that *keren* in the *reshut hanizak* is half-damages. The *kal vachomer* from *shen* and *regel* attempts to elevate this to full damages — *ve-asa nezek shalem* — by showing that the *reshut hanizak* is a more stringent domain. But if *dayo* is then applied, it collapses us right back to what we already knew: half-damages. The *kal vachomer* would produce nothing — *ei darashta dayo, ifrach leh kal vachomer*. Since *dayo* would entirely destroy the *kal vachomer*, Rabbi Tarfon holds that in this case *dayo* does not apply. In its place, one may draw on other evidence — such as the fact that *shen* and *regel* pay full damages in the *reshut hanizak* — to determine how far the *kal vachomer* extends.

### Rabbis Defend Dayo

One might then ask: how can the *Chachamim* apply *dayo* even in the Miriam case, given that they appear to already know seven days applies to God — since the *pasuk* itself concludes with *tisager shivat yamim*? The *Gemara* explains the *Chachamim*'s position: a second *pasuk* states *v'tisager Miriam* — and Miriam was sealed up — for seven days, repeating the number. The *Chachamim* argue that this repetition teaches that God's displeasure warranted seven days *independently* of the *kal vachomer*. Since seven days was already established for the divine case, the *kal vachomer* still "bore fruit" even after *dayo* — it confirmed what we already knew rather than leaving us with nothing. Therefore, *dayo* applies and limits the result to seven, and we do not go to fourteen.

### Tarfon's Response

Rabbi Tarfon, however, reads the second *pasuk* differently. He does not understand the repetition as establishing an independent source for seven days in the divine case. Rather, *hahu d'afilu b'alma darshinan dayo* — the repetition is there to teach that *dayo* is a general principle applicable in all cases, not one that was invoked here merely as a special concession to Moses. The concern the *pasuk* is preempting is this: one might have thought that ordinarily *dayo* is not applied at all, but that God made an exception here out of honor for Moses — limiting Miriam's punishment to seven rather than fourteen so as not to distress Moses excessively. The *pasuk* therefore repeats the seven-day limit to signal that *dayo* is a universal hermeneutic rule, not a one-time accommodation. *V'lo tomar hacha mishum kvodo shel Moshe, aval b'alma lo, kamashma lan* — lest one say that this principle only operates here because of God's regard for Moses, the *Torah* clarifies that *dayo* applies universally whenever the *kal vachomer* would otherwise bear fruit.

The upshot is that Rabbi Tarfon fully accepts *dayo* and accepts it in all cases — but only when applying *dayo* still leaves the *kal vachomer* with something to show for itself. Where *dayo* would nullify the *kal vachomer* entirely, Rabbi Tarfon holds that *dayo* does not apply.

---

## Pappa's Challenge

### Keri B'Zav Case

Having established Rabbi Tarfon's principle, the *Gemara* raises a challenge. *Amar lei Rav Pappa l'Abaye*: Rav Pappa said to Abaye that there exists a *tanna* who does not apply *dayo* even in a case where the *kal vachomer* would bear fruit — that is, even where *dayo* would still leave the *kal vachomer* with a meaningful result. The *Gemara* cites a *braita* asking: *keri b'zav minayin* — from where do we derive that the seminal emission (*keri*) of a *zav* is *tamei*?

### Semen Kal Vachomer

To appreciate the question, one must understand the underlying *halachot*. A *zav* is a person who has experienced a discharge (*ziva*) from the male organ on three occasions of sufficient quality to render him severely *tamei* — he is an *av hatumah* whose *tumah* persists for seven days and whose bodily fluids carry significant *tumah* as well. The *Torah* explicitly states that if a *zav* spits upon a *tahor* person, that person becomes *tamei* — *v'chi yarok hazav al hatahor* — establishing that a *zav*'s spit is itself an *av hatumah*. The question is how we extend this to his semen (*shichvat zera*).

The *braita* constructs a *kal vachomer*: spit, which is ordinarily *tahor* when it comes from a *tahor* person, becomes *tamei* when it comes from a *zav*. Semen (*shichvat zera*), which is *tamei* even when it comes from a *tahor* person, should certainly be *tamei* when it comes from a *zav*. This is the *kal vachomer*: *ma tahor b'tahor tamei b'tamei, tamei b'tahor eino din shehei tamei b'tamei* — that which is *tahor* when it comes from a *tahor* person becomes *tamei* when it comes from a *zav* (spit), then that which is *tamei* when it comes from a *tahor* person (semen) certainly becomes *tamei* when it comes from a *zav*.

### Tamei by Carrying

But the *braita* does not stop there. It goes further and applies the resulting law — that the *keri* of a *zav* is *tamei* — not merely by touch (*maga*) but also by carrying (*massa*): *v'kameisi la bein l'maga bein l'massa*. The distinction matters because the *ma'ayanos* of a *zav* — his bodily fluids, including his spit — are *tamei* in the weightier sense that even carrying them (without direct contact) conveys *tumah*. The ordinary *keri* of a *tahor* person, by contrast, conveys *tumah* only through touch, not through carrying. The *braita* is thus applying the *kal vachomer* to establish not only that the *keri* of a *zav* is *tamei*, but that it is *tamei* in the more stringent manner — like the spit — through carrying as well.

### Dayo Question 2

This is where Rav Pappa's challenge bites. The *Gemara* asks: *ve-amai neima hanei kal vachomer lemaga* — why is *dayo* not applied? Even granting that *dayo* would limit the *kal vachomer*, the *kal vachomer* would still bear fruit. If *dayo* were applied here, we would know that the *keri* of a *zav* is *tamei* by touch — *lemaga* — which is something we supposedly did not know before the *kal vachomer*. *Dayo* would then preclude the additional stringency of *tumah* through carrying. The *kal vachomer* would not be undermined; it would still teach us something meaningful. And yet the *braita* does not apply *dayo* and goes all the way to *tumah* through carrying. This appears to contradict Rabbi Tarfon's principle — this *tanna* seems to reject *dayo* even where the *kal vachomer* is not destroyed by it.

### Source Pasuk

The *Gemara* addresses the challenge. The assumption underlying Rav Pappa's question is that *dayo* would still leave the *kal vachomer* with something to teach — namely, that the *keri* of a *zav* is *tamei* by touch — and therefore *dayo* should apply. But the *Gemara* responds: *vechi teima lemaga lo itztrich kal vachomer* — perhaps no *kal vachomer* was needed at all for *tumah* by touch. *Dila gara migavra tahor* — the *keri* of a *zav* is no less *tamei* than the *keri* of a *tahor* person, and we know the *keri* of a *tahor* person is *tamei* by touch from the *Torah*. Since there is no reason to think the *keri* of a *zav* would be less *tamei* than that of a *tahor* person, we already know it is *tamei* by touch without any *kal vachomer*.

One might push back: *salka daitcha amina*, I might have thought that the *Torah*'s law of *tumah* for seminal emission — *mikreh laylah ksiv* — applies only to one whose seminal emission is what *causes* him to become *tamei*, *mi shekeiryo gorem lo*. It would then exclude a *zav* — *yatza zeh she-ein keiryo gorem lo* — since his semen does not cause his *tumah* (his *ziva* does). The *kal vachomer* is therefore needed even for *tumah* by touch. And if so, *dayo* should limit us to touch alone, and the *braita*'s extension to carrying would be unwarranted.

### Semen Tamei by Touch

The *Gemara* dismisses this reasoning. *Midei velo davar acher ksiv*? The *Torah* does not say that only the semen caused the *tumah* and nothing else. The *pasuk* speaks of semen causing *tumah*, but this does not exclude cases where *some other factor* also causes *tumah* — *ela davar acher gorem lo*. The original *pasuk* about *ba'al keri* therefore already includes both a *tahor* person and a *zav*; the *keri* of a *zav* was already known to be *tamei* by touch through the original *pasuk* itself, not through the *kal vachomer*. The *kal vachomer* serves only to elevate the *keri* of a *zav* to the status of the *zav*'s spit — *tamei* even through carrying.

This now maps perfectly onto Rabbi Tarfon's structure. We already knew that *keri* is *tamei* by touch for all people, including a *zav*. The *kal vachomer* pushes us toward a higher level of *tumah* — *tumah* through carrying — by analogy with the spit. If *dayo* were applied, it would collapse us back to *tumah* by touch, which we already knew. The *kal vachomer* would produce nothing. Precisely as Rabbi Tarfon holds, *dayo* does not apply when it would entirely nullify the *kal vachomer*.

### Tanna Identity

Having established that the *braita* operates according to Rabbi Tarfon's principle, the *Gemara* asks whose position it represents. *U-man tanna de-shamiesh lei d'amar shichvat zera shel zav metamei be-massa* — who is the *tanna* who holds that the *shichvat zera* of a *zav* is *tamei* by carrying in this intrinsic sense? The *Gemara* answers: *lo Rabbi Eliezer ve-lo Rabbi Yehoshua* — it is neither Rabbi Eliezer nor Rabbi Yehoshua.

### Kelim Mishna

A *mishna* in Kelim makes the positions of these two *tanna'im* clear. Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *shichvat zera* of a *zav* is *tamei* only by touch and not by carrying — *metamei be-maga ve-eino metamei be-massa* — entirely rejecting the *braita*'s conclusion. Rabbi Yehoshua does hold that the *shichvat zera* of a *zav* is *tamei* by carrying, but only because *lefi she-i efshar belo tsichtsuchei ziva* — it is impossible for the semen to be emitted without some trace drops of *ziva* mixed into it. Those drops of *ziva* are themselves *tamei* by carrying, and their presence in the semen causes the whole to be *tamei* by carrying.

The *Gemara* therefore notes: *ad kan lo ka-amar Rabbi Yehoshua hatam ela lefi she-i efshar belo tsichtsuchei ziva* — Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling is grounded entirely in the physical admixture of *ziva*; *ha lav hachi, lo* — were it not for that admixture, Rabbi Yehoshua would not hold that the semen is intrinsically *tamei* by carrying.
