The point is that this profile of risk is less foreseeable than the profile in the carpenter case with permission, where — as *Tosafos* emphasizes — the permission was recently granted, meaning the person might walk in at any moment.

### Alternative reading

Rav Pappa, citing Rava, then offers an entirely different reading of the *baraita*. Rather than placing the *baraita*'s entire discussion in the realm of *nezek*, he now teaches the ruling on the *first* part of the *baraita* — the case where the person entered without permission. On this reading, the *baraita* is not primarily about *nezek* at all; it is about *galus*. The case of entering without permission yields exemption from *galus*; entering with permission yields liability for *galus*. This is the *baraita*'s subject throughout.

This reading comes with its own difficulty, however: without permission, the carpenter is *patur* in *galus*, but what is the rule for *nezek*? Rabbi Yose bar Abba Chanina clarifies: *chayav b'arba'ah devarim* — he is still *chayav* in the four payments for bodily harm. This requires explanation, since without permission one might have thought there is no liability at all. Both Rashi and *Tosafos* explain that the carpenter was aware the person had entered even without permission, and that awareness establishes sufficient grounds for *nezek* liability even absent formal *reshus*.

### Galus focus

The *gemara* closes by drawing out the two readings' implications for one another. The one who teaches the *baraita*'s ruling on the second clause — that with *reshus* one is *patur migalus* because the negligence is too great — will certainly also teach that without *reshus* one is *patur migalus* by simple logic. But the one who teaches the *baraita* as addressing the first clause — that without *reshus* one is *patur migalus* — holds that with *reshus* one is in fact *chayav galus*: *keivan d'v'reshus chayav galus*.

The clean formulation that emerges from the second reading: without *reshus*, *patur* in *galus*; with *reshus*, *chayav* in *galus*. And in both cases, for *nezek* proper, the rule tracks *adam muad l'olam* — without *reshus* one is *patur* in *nezek*, with *reshus* one is *chayav* in *nezek*. The first reading's *chiddush* — that even with permission the carpenter is *patur migalus* because of excessive negligence — is rejected by the second reading, which restores the intuitive symmetry: *reshus* is the operative factor for *galus* liability just as it is for *nezek*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 33

## Reshut & Negligence

### Permission ≠ Exemption

The earlier *mishnayot* in this chapter discussed cases of people colliding in the *reshut harabbim* and ruled that the one who caused the damage was *patur*, because both parties were operating with *reshut* — with permission to be doing what they were doing. This created an impression that an *adam hamazik* who acts with *reshut* enjoys a broad exemption from liability. But the *mishna* we have just studied refutes that impression decisively: a person chopping wood in his own private domain, where a splinter flies off and injures someone on adjacent private property, is *chaiyav*. He was entirely permitted to chop wood in his own yard; the splinter flew not even into the *reshut harabbim* but into someone else's private domain — and yet he is liable.

The *reshut harabbim* exemption, then, is not a blanket rule that permission equals exemption. One might have supposed that the exemption there rested on something like contributory negligence — a principle that when everyone is using the public thoroughfare, everyone bears responsibility for watching out for themselves, so that being injured by another's act in the *reshut harabbim* is partly *pi ha-nizak*. The *Gemara*, however, emphasizes a different logic: in those earlier cases, both parties were in motion simultaneously, and when that is so, one cannot isolate a single *mazik* and a single *nizak*. If both people are moving, the question of whose beam struck whose pitcher — or whose fist met whose face — becomes indeterminate. That is the specific logic of the *reshut harabbim* exemption, and it does not extend to the case of the carpenter whose splinter injures a bystander, nor to cases analogous to *bor*, where even disposing of garbage or water in the *reshut harabbim* with permission leaves one liable.

### Carpenter's Splinter

With this framework established, the *Gemara* now addresses the central problem of the section. The *mishna* and *braita* discuss scenarios in which someone is killed by a flying piece of wood from a carpenter's work, and the question is whether the carpenter is liable for *galus* — the exile that replaces capital punishment in cases of unintentional killing — and whether he owes the *arba'ah devarim*, the four monetary payments for injury (*nezek*, *shevet*, *tza'ar*, and *ripuy*).

Rav Pappa in the name of Rava taught the relevant ruling specifically about the first clause of the *braita*: if someone enters a carpenter's workshop without permission (*shelo birshut*) and is struck and killed by a flying splinter, the carpenter is *patur* from *galus* but *chaiyav* in *arba'ah devarim*. Rabbi Yose bar Chanina states this ruling explicitly.

This combination of rulings generates an immediate tension. *Adam muad l'olam* — a person is always considered forewarned with respect to *nezek*. But the additional payments of *arba'ah devarim* — the payments for lost work, pain, and medical care — require *peshiah*, actual negligence. Payment for *boshet* requires intent to damage. So if the ruling states *chaiyav be-arba'ah devarim*, that concedes negligence was present. And if there was negligence — if the carpenter was aware of the person in the workshop — why is he *patur* from *galus*? The earlier discussion had suggested that exemption from *galus* could result from the carpenter being *shogeg karov l'meizid*, negligent to the point of near-intentionality. But that reading is now being challenged.

### Rashi's Formal Exclusion

Rashi resolves the difficulty not through the lens of degrees of negligence — neither too much nor too little — but through a formal distinction rooted in the structure of the *Torah*'s cases. The paradigm case for *galus* in the *Torah* is two people chopping wood together in a forest (*dumya d'yaar*): both have permission to be there, and the killing is genuinely accidental. Rashi argues that being obligated in *arba'ah devarim* does not preclude exemption from *galus* — the exemption from *galus* in this case is not because negligence is absent, but because the situation is formally dissimilar from the *yaar* case. If the victim entered without permission, that formal disanalogy is sufficient to remove the carpenter from the domain of *galus* liability, regardless of whether he was in fact aware of the victim's presence.

The *Gemara* then presents the structural contrast: according to the one who teaches the ruling about the *reisha* (the case where the victim entered without permission), exemption from *galus* follows naturally in that case, and when one turns to the *seifa* — the case where the victim entered *bireshut*, with permission — one would say the carpenter is *chaiyav galus*, since the formal condition of the *yaar* parallel is now met. According to the one who teaches the *seifa* case, the exemption from *galus* even with permission follows, and the *reisha* case of no permission is all the more clearly *patur*.

The *Gemara* then introduces a *braita* about a metalworker's shop: someone enters the ironworker's premises and is killed by a flying spark — and the *braita* rules *patur* even though he entered *bireshut*, with permission. This seems to flatly contradict the reading that permission triggers *galus* liability.

### The Apprentice

The *Gemara* resolves this by recharacterizing the case. We are dealing, it says, with a *shulya d'napcha* — an apprentice of the metalworker. The *Gemara* itself immediately objects: is the fact that he is an apprentice sufficient grounds to render his death the owner's *reshut*-exempt? Does mere employment create a license to be killed?

The *Gemara* refines: the case is one where the master has been repeatedly telling the apprentice to leave — *mesarhev bo latzet* — and the apprentice refuses to go. But again the *Gemara* objects: just because the master is urging him to leave, does that expose him to be killed without liability?

The final resolution is: *kasavar yatza* — the master concluded that the apprentice had in fact listened and left. This reframes the case as one of no negligence: the master, having told his apprentice to go and reasonably assuming the apprentice obeyed, was genuinely unaware of his continued presence. The *Gemara* then asks why this same logic cannot apply to any stranger who entered. The answer: *acher leit lei eimata d'rabbeih* — a stranger has no particular deference to the carpenter's authority, so one cannot assume he left simply because he was told to. But an apprentice, who has *eimata d'rabbeih*, fear of his master, may be assumed to have complied. This is a very narrow *ukimta*, limiting the exemption to the specific circumstance of an apprentice who was ordered out and reasonably presumed to have obeyed.

The net result of this section is that the *Gemara* has offered two competing frameworks for understanding exemption from *galus*: one in which excessive negligence (*shogeg karov l'meizid*) disqualifies the perpetrator from the formal category of unintentional killing, and another in which *Rashi*'s reading prevails — no exemption based on degrees of negligence, but rather formal disqualification when the case is not *dumya d'yaar*, such as when the victim entered without permission. The case of the metalworker's apprentice ultimately rests on factual absence of negligence: the master did not know the apprentice was still there.

## Rock & Trajectory

### Flying Axe Head

Razid in the name of Rava taught that the ruling about exemption from *galus* applies to yet another category of case — not the question of whether the victim had permission to be present, but rather the question of causation and trajectory. The *Torah* uses the language that the axe-head "found" (*u-matza*) the victim, which the *Gemara* takes to exclude the case of *mamtzi et atzmo* — the victim who "causes himself to be found," who moves himself into the path of the flying object.

### Moving Into Path

The *Gemara* illustrates this with a *braita* in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov: one throws a rock into the *reshut harabbim* — or perhaps it slips from his hand — and while the rock is in mid-flight, another person emerges and extends his head into the rock's trajectory. The rock strikes him and he dies. The thrower is *patur* from *galus*.

This is, notably, not an exemption based on lack of negligence. Throwing an object into the *reshut harabbim* is unambiguously negligent — people are present and moving in the public thoroughfare, and one must anticipate that someone may be struck. But the victim, while not himself negligent, has actively participated in the causal sequence that brought the rock to his head. The *Gemara* draws an analogy to the cases of two people moving simultaneously in the *reshut harabbim*: when the victim is an active participant in the event, even if not blameworthy, there is a formal ground for exemption from *galus*, since this too is not *dumya d'yaar*.

Rabbi Yose bar Chanina then states: in this case as well, the thrower is *patur mi-galus* but *chaiyav be-arba'ah devarim*. The thrower was negligent — he threw something into the public thoroughfare — and that negligence is sufficient to generate monetary liability for injury. The exemption from *galus*, again, is formal rather than substantive: the case does not fit the paradigm of the *yaar*, because the victim moved into the path.

The *Gemara* then notes the structural interplay between the two teachings. According to the one who teaches the exemption specifically in this *mamtzi et atzmo* case, one can argue *kol sheken* that the monetary obligation of *arba'ah devarim* certainly applies in the earlier cases, where the carpenter's negligence was more straightforwardly present. But according to the one who teaches the *arba'ah devarim* obligation in the earlier cases, one might say that in the *mamtzi et atzmo* case the thrower is *patur legamre* — fully exempt — because perhaps here, given that the victim walked into the rock's path, one cannot attribute sufficient negligence to the thrower to ground even the *arba'ah devarim*. The *Gemara* is candid that this reasoning is not entirely transparent: it is not obvious why the negligence in the *reshut harabbim* case should be treated as categorically less than the carpenter's negligence. The *Gemara* seems to be working with assumed degrees of negligence that depend on the particular circumstances of each case, and it acknowledges that a general framework based purely on the facts would simply ask what the individual circumstances warrant.

The takeaway of these sections is the distinction between the requirements for *arba'ah devarim* — which require negligence (*peshiah*) — and the requirements for *galus* — which are subject to formal exclusions based on the structure of the *Torah*'s paradigm cases, independent of the degree of negligence actually present.

## Workers & Wages

### Implicit Right to Enter

The *Gemara* now presents another *braita* along these lines. Workers come to demand their wages (*po'alim she-bau litvo'a scharam mi-ba'al ha-bayis*) from their employer. They enter his property and are gored by his ox or bitten by his dog; the *braita* rules *patur* — the owner is exempt. The employer's exemption in cases of injury in his *reshut* normally requires that the victim entered without permission. The implicit question is therefore whether workers who come to collect wages have an inherent right of entry that would constitute *reshut*, or whether they need explicit permission.

The *Gemara* then cites *Acherim*, who argue that workers indeed have an implicit right to enter to demand payment, and the employer would not be exempt.

### Ambiguity of 'En'

The *Gemara* asks: what is the actual case being debated? If the employer is regularly found in the town, the workers have no right to enter his property unannounced — they should wait to find him in the public domain. If he is virtually never found anywhere but his home, then obviously the workers must enter his property to get paid — there is no practical alternative — and the first opinion's exemption would be difficult to sustain. The debate must therefore concern an intermediate case: a man who is sometimes found in town and sometimes not.

And there is a further wrinkle. The workers knock on the gate and call out, and the employer responds: *in* — yes. The dispute is over what that word means. One opinion holds that *in ul* means "come in" — permission has been explicitly granted. The other holds that *in kum be-duchtach mashma* — "yes, stay where you are, I'll come to you." *En* is intrinsically ambiguous, and which interpretation one adopts determines whether the workers had *reshut* to enter.

### Reinterpretation

The *Gemara* then brings a *braita* that appears to rule the owner *patur* even where the worker entered *bireshut* — with permission — and treats this as confirming the reading that *in* means "stay where you are." The *braita*'s description of the worker as having entered *birshut* is accordingly reinterpreted: it is not that he had actual permission, but rather that he *thought* he had permission — he entered believing he was invited in, when in fact the employer's *in* was merely an acknowledgment of his presence, not a grant of entry. The *braita* thus calls it *nichnas birshut* loosely, meaning he entered with an expectation of permission that was not, in fact, conferred.

The broader lesson the *Gemara* draws from this section is consistent with the preceding analysis: the *braitot* had appeared to make sweeping statements — that being on someone's *reshut* is sufficient for the owner's exemption regardless of circumstances — but the *Gemara* systematically presses each case back to its specific factual foundation: either the victim was genuinely without permission, or there was a genuine absence of negligence, or the employer's acknowledgment did not actually constitute permission. No broad general rule emerges beyond the case-by-case inquiry into whether *reshut* was actually granted.

## To Goring Ox

The *Gemara* now transitions — and it is worth pausing to appreciate the structure of these chapters. The first chapter established the *klalim*, the general principles. The second chapter addressed *shen ve-regel*, and concluded with the *mishna* introducing *adam muad l'olam*. The intervening *sugya* has been devoted entirely to *adam hamazik* — liability of persons for harm they cause. Now the *Gemara* pivots decisively to *shor hamazik* — liability arising from a goring ox — which will be the subject of the remainder of the tractate's discussion.

Yet before leaving *adam hamazik* entirely, the *Gemara* introduces a *mishna* about two oxen goring one another that requires careful analysis in terms of both ox liability and, subsequently, the parallel case of two people who injure one another.

## Two Oxen Goring

### Two Tame Oxen

The *mishna* presents several configurations of two oxen that gore one another. When two *tam* oxen — oxen that have not yet established a pattern of goring — injure each other simultaneously, each pays half of the *difference* in damages (*bemotar chatzi nezek*). If one inflicted a hundred dollars of damage and the other inflicted eighty, the one that did more pays half of the twenty-dollar difference, that is, ten dollars. When both are *muad* — established habitual gorers — each pays the full difference: twenty dollars.

### Tame & Muad Mixed

The *mishna* then addresses mixed cases. If the *muad* inflicted more damage than the *tam*, the *muad* pays the full difference. If the *tam* inflicted more damage than the *muad*, the *tam* pays half of the difference. *Tosafot* notes that at first glance this *mishna* seems entirely obvious — whatever the difference is, you pay it at the appropriate rate — and one wonders what the *chiddush* could possibly be.

### Rosh: Net Difference

The *Rosh* explains that the *chiddush* is significant, and it is specifically the mixed case of *tam* and *muad* that reveals it. Consider: the *tam* inflicted a hundred dollars of damage, and the *muad* inflicted eighty. If these were two independent acts, one would first calculate the *tam*'s liability — half of a hundred, fifty dollars — and separately calculate the *muad*'s liability — full eighty dollars. Netting those two obligations against each other, the *muad* would actually owe the *tam*'s owner thirty dollars, not ten. Yet the *mishna* says the *tam* pays half the difference of twenty, that is, ten. That is a striking and counterintuitive ruling.

The *Rosh* furthermore establishes a critical precondition for the entire *mishna*: this scenario only applies where both oxen started simultaneously. If one ox attacked first and the other reacted, the entire framework changes — the reacting ox's owner is *patur* entirely, under the principle of *kol hamishaneh b'acher v'shinah bo* (one who provokes another and the other responds is not held liable for the response). An ox that is gored cannot be blamed for goring back.

Given that both started simultaneously, the *chiddush* of the *mishna* is that we do not treat this as two separate acts of damage. We look at the *net* outcome. Everything that cancels out between the two sides is treated as though it never happened. Only the difference in damages — the residual harm — is the actual damage recognized by *halacha*. This has a further consequence for *Tosafot*'s analysis, which anticipates a debate we will encounter shortly. According to the view that when a *tam* gores an ox, the injured party does not merely have a monetary claim against the owner but actually acquires a percentage ownership interest in the goring ox, the *mishna*'s approach again follows: we do not say each party now owns a stake in the other's ox. We say only the net difference creates any ownership transfer or obligation. This is a *chiddush* of enormous scope, and the *Gemara* does not explicitly explain why this netting principle applies, but the *Rosh* establishes it as the foundation of the *mishna*'s ruling.

## Two People Fighting

### Payment by Difference

The *mishna* continues: *v'chen shenei anashim shechavlu zeh bazeh* — and similarly, two people who intentionally injured one another pay the difference in full (*bemotar nezek shalem*). The *mishna* also addresses cases of a person fighting a *muad* ox, and of a person fighting a *tam* ox. When a person inflicts more damage on a *tam* ox than the *tam* inflicted on the person, the person pays the full difference. When the *tam* inflicted more on the person, the owner of the *tam* pays half the difference — not half the *tam*'s damage calculated independently and then netted against the full human liability, but half of the net difference.

Rabbi Akiva then introduces his well-known position: even a *tam* that gores a person pays full damages. This anticipates a *braita* that the *Gemara* will now analyze through the relevant *pesukim*.

The *Gemara* brings the relevant *braita* interpreting the verse *kamishpat hazeh ye'aseh lo* — "as this law shall be done to him" — which the Torah uses when discussing an ox that gores a child. The rabbis understand this to be referring not to a killing but to an injury, specifically when the ox injures a person, and they debate what law applies. The *Tanna Kamma* argues: *kamishpat shor beshor kach mishpat shor be'adam* — just as an ox goring another ox is subject to the standard rules of *tam* (half payment) and *muad* (full payment), so too an ox injuring a person. And the phrase *kamishpat hazeh* also serves to exclude the additional payments that apply when a *person* injures another person: the *arba'ah devarim* of *nezek*, *shevet*, *tza'ar*, and *ripuy* do not apply when an ox injures a person, since those derive from the verse *ish ki yiten mum be'amito* — a person who inflicts a blemish on his fellow — and an ox is not a person.

Rabbi Akiva reads *kamishpat hazeh* differently. The *Torah*'s structure in these *parshiyot* is as follows: first, an ox kills a person in a *tam* scenario; then, an ox kills a person in a *muad* scenario (where *kofer* is paid); then, an ox gores another ox in *tam* and *muad* configurations. When the *Torah* says *kamishpat hazeh ye'aseh lo* — do like *this* law — it refers to the most proximate precedent, which is the *muad* case. Therefore, *ketachton v'lo ke'elyon* — like the lower case and not the upper — when an ox injures a person, one applies the law of *muad* and pays full damages. However, *yigach yaaseh lo* — the phrase "it shall be done *to it*," the ox — indicates that one pays from the body of the ox (*migufo*), not from the owner's general assets, even though the amount is full damages. It is an unusual hybrid: the full rate of a *muad* but the collection mechanism of a *tam*.

The *Gemara* then asks how Rabbi Akiva knows that an ox injuring a person is exempt from *arba'ah devarim*, since the verse he is using for his *muad* reading cannot also serve to exclude the additional payments. The answer: Rabbi Akiva derives the exclusion of *arba'ah devarim* from the verse *ish ki yiten mum be'amito* — *ish be'amito* and not *shor be'amito*, these payments apply only when a *person* injures another person.

The rabbis, for their part, could not have derived the exclusion of *arba'ah devarim* from that verse alone, because they would have said: perhaps we only learn the exclusion of *tza'ar* from there, but *ripuy* and *shevet*, which are derived from different verses, might still apply when an ox injures a person. It is *kamishpat hazeh* that tells us the law of an ox injuring a person follows the standard goring-ox framework entirely, excluding all such additional payments.

### Self-Defense Rights

Now, before fully departing the topic of *adam hamazik*, there is a critical ruling of the *Rosh* in *Siman* 13 of the third *perek* that bears directly on the *mishna* about two people who injure one another. The *Rosh* begins by applying the principle of *kol hamishaneh b'acher v'shinah bo* to the human case as well: if Reuven and Shimon started fighting simultaneously, or if Reuven beat up Shimon and later Shimon came back and beat up Reuven, the net difference rule applies. But if Reuven started hitting Shimon and Shimon fought back, Shimon is *patur* — he was defending himself. This is true even though the principle of *kol hamishaneh* does not technically apply to people as it does to oxen, because the right to self-defense provides an independent basis for exemption. And this right extends, the *Rosh* notes, even to using physical force to protect property — drawing on the principle of *avid inish dina l'nafshei* discussed earlier in the tractate, where even violence was permitted to prevent an immediate, irrecoverable loss.

### Force Limitations

The *Rosh* then introduces the critical limiting principle. The right of self-defense is not unlimited. He cites the case of the woman in the *Torah* who grabs a man's private parts while defending her husband from an attacker: she is liable for *boshet* if she had an alternative, but exempt if she had no other means of stopping the assault. The *Rosh* extrapolates from this: if one could have protected oneself with lesser force but instead inflicted greater injury, one is *chaiyav* for the excess. The *Gemara*'s standard from *rodef* applies — only the force necessary to stop the threat is authorized. Once the attacker is incapacitated, or once a lesser measure would have sufficed, continued or disproportionate force becomes its own tortious act.

### Extended Protection

The *Rosh* then extends the analysis outward. If a person sees someone beating his father, his children, or his brother, and intervenes physically to protect the family member — and there was no other means of stopping the assault — he is *patur*, analogous to the woman who had no alternative to physical intervention to save her husband. The same right that exists for self-protection extends to protecting one's immediate family members.

The *Rosh* then turns to an even broader case: if a person witnesses one Jew physically attacking another, and cannot stop it except by striking the attacker, is it permitted to intervene even though this is not self-defense and not protection of family? The *Rosh* rules that it is permitted — but notably, the *halachic* mechanism he invokes is not an extension of *avid inish dina l'nafshei*, but rather the principle of *l'hafrisho me-issura*: one may use force to stop a person from committing a transgression. This framing is meaningful. *Avid inish dina l'nafshei* is explicitly *l'nafshei* — for oneself — and the *Rosh* does not extend that principle to third-party protection. Instead, he grounds third-party intervention in the obligation to prevent another person from perpetrating a sin.

This distinction has practical implications that the *Rosh* himself acknowledges. Framing the right of intervention around the *aveirah* of the aggressor rather than the protection of the victim raises difficult questions. What if the aggressor is a *katan*, who is not halachically culpable for his actions? Can one use force to stop a non-culpable aggressor on the basis of preventing a transgression? The *Rosh*'s framework does not straightforwardly accommodate that case.

One might have wished to say instead that any case of physical injury to a person is, by its nature, a *pesida* — an irreversible harm — and therefore the logic that permits immediate action without waiting for the courts (*avid inish dina l'nafshei* where *ika pesseida*) should extend to protecting third parties from physical harm, just as one may intervene to prevent a *rodef* from killing. The *Rosh* is effectively reaching the same practical destination, but through a different halachic mechanism, and it is worth flagging that the grounding in *l'hafrisho me-issura* rather than in protection of the victim creates a different structural framework with different outer limits. This is a very significant *Rosh*, and it serves as an important complement to the earlier discussion of *avid inish dina l'nafshei*.

## Ox Goring Ox

### Takes Entire Ox

The *mishna* at the bottom of 33b now introduces the case of an ox worth a *maneh* (one hundred *zuz*) that gores and kills an ox worth two hundred *zuz*, where the carcass is worthless. Since the *tam* pays half of the damage — here, one hundred *zuz* — and that equals the full value of the goring ox, the *mishna* rules that the injured party simply takes the entire goring ox. The *chiddush* is not merely that payment is capped at the value of the goring ox (*migufo*). The deeper *chiddush* is that the injured party takes the ox itself, not merely its equivalent value in cash. The question — how literally do we mean *migufo*, from its body — will drive the debate between Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva.

### Mistaken Attribution

The *Gemara* establishes that this *mishna* reflects the position of Rabbi Akiva, not that of the rabbis generally. This is demonstrated from a *braita*.

### Creditor vs. Partner

The *braita* records that Rabbi Ishmael says: *ve-yusham ha-shor be-veit din* — the ox should be assessed by *beit din*. Rabbi Akiva says: *huchlat ha-shor* — the ox is directly transferred. The *Gemara* identifies the root of their dispute. Rabbi Ishmael holds that the injured party (*nizak*) is merely a *ba'al chov* — a creditor. The injuring party owes him money, and the ox is the mechanism through which that debt is satisfied, but Shimon does not own any part of Reuven's ox. Rabbi Akiva holds *shutfin ninhu* — they become partners. The moment Reuven's ox gores Shimon's ox, Shimon acquires a partial ownership interest in Reuven's ox.

The dispute is anchored in the reading of the verse *u-machru et ha-shor ha-chai v'chatzu et kaspo* — they shall sell the living ox and divide its value. The *Torah*'s paradigm case has two oxen of equal value, one of which kills the other and renders it worthless. The injured party is therefore owed half the value of the goring ox. Rabbi Ishmael reads *u-machru* as addressed to *beit din*: the court sells the ox and distributes the proceeds. The injured party is a creditor; *beit din* is the agent that liquidates the ox to satisfy the debt. Rabbi Akiva reads *u-machru* as addressed to the two parties themselves: *you* — the *nizak* and the *mazik* together — sell the ox and divide the proceeds. If both parties are selling the ox, it follows that both are already owners of it. From the moment of the goring, Shimon became a co-owner.

The *Gemara* identifies one obvious practical difference (*mai beineihu*): if the *nizak*, Shimon, consecrates the goring ox (*hikdisho nizak*), does the consecration take effect? According to Rabbi Akiva, Shimon owns the ox, and his *hekdesh* is valid. According to Rabbi Ishmael, Shimon owns nothing; he is merely a creditor, and a creditor cannot consecrate someone else's property. *Tosafot* notes that many further differences could be listed — the *Gemara* is content to cite one illustrative example, but the structural divergence between "creditor" and "partner" ramifies through any legal relationship involving the ox.

## Sell Ox or Pay Cash

### Rava's Question

Rava poses a question to Rav Nachman: according to Rabbi Ishmael, if Reuven — the owner of the goring ox — sells the ox before Shimon collects, what is the result? According to Rabbi Akiva, this question is easy: Reuven cannot sell what is no longer fully his; Shimon already owns a portion of the ox. But according to Rabbi Ishmael, Reuven is simply a debtor who owes money. In ordinary cases, a debtor can sell his assets and pay his creditor cash. Is that true here, or does Shimon's relationship to *this specific ox* constrain Reuven's ability to alienate it?

### Sale & Collection

Rav Nachman's answer: *eino machur* — it is not fully sold. Even though Shimon does not own the ox under Rabbi Ishmael's view, Shimon's right to *this ox specifically* is strong enough that Reuven cannot unilaterally sell it away from him. The *Gemara* then cites a *braita* that appears to say *machur*, the sale stands. The *Gemara* reconciles: the sale does stand insofar as Levi (the buyer) acquires the ox — it was Reuven's to sell. But *chozer v'goveh* — Shimon can go and collect it from Levi. Reuven sold encumbered property, and Levi bought it with Shimon's lien attached. The sale is valid as between Reuven and Levi; it does not extinguish Shimon's right.

The *Gemara* then asks: if Shimon can collect the ox even after the sale to Levi, what exactly did Levi acquire? The answer: *l'radya* — Levi may use the ox to plow his field. He owns the ox in the interim; he can work with it and derive benefit from it. Until Shimon chooses to exercise his lien and come collect it, Levi's ownership is fully operative. This is analogous to any purchase of property that carries a prior lien: the buyer acquires real ownership and can use the asset, but must surrender it if the lienholder comes to collect.

### Lien Mechanism

This raises a difficult technical problem. The mechanism by which Shimon can collect the ox even after Reuven has sold it to Levi is that of a lien — *meshubad* — on the ox. But standard *halacha* holds that liens operate on land, not on *metaltelin*, movable property including cattle. If Reuven owes money and sells his cattle, a creditor normally cannot pursue those cattle in the hands of a third-party buyer. How, then, can Shimon collect the ox from Levi?

The *Gemara* initially suggests we might derive a general principle that a creditor can collect *metaltelin* from a third-party purchaser. Rava pushes back: this is not the general rule. His proof: if one makes an *apotiki* — an explicit lien — on one's slave and sells the slave, *beit din* will enforce that lien and allow collection from the buyer. But if one makes an explicit *apotiki* on one's ox and sells it, *beit din* will not enforce the lien against the buyer. The difference is that a slave has the legal status closer to land (*karka*) for certain purposes, whereas ordinary cattle do not. An explicit *apotiki* on ordinary cattle cannot be collected from third-party purchasers.

### Notorious Goring Ox

If ordinary cattle with an explicit *apotiki* cannot be collected from buyers, why can Shimon collect the goring ox from Levi, given that Shimon's right under Rabbi Ishmael is merely that of a creditor with an implicit *Torah*-granted lien?

The *Gemara*'s answer is elegant and grounded in practical reality. The reason explicit liens on slaves are enforceable against buyers (*apotiki* on *eved*) is *mishum d'is lei kala* — because information about enslaved persons becomes widely known. Slaves are significant enough pieces of property that encumbrances on them circulate as public knowledge, so buyers are on notice and the legal maxim of *lav kol keminei* — the seller cannot unilaterally strip the creditor's rights — applies. Ordinary cattle, by contrast, are commonly bought and sold without any public notice of encumbrances, so liens on them cannot be enforced against purchasers.

But a goring ox is different: *keivan d'nagach kala is lei* — since it has gored, the word gets out. *Tora nagchana karu lei* — people call it "Reuven's goring ox." A goring ox is notorious; its status becomes public knowledge. Therefore, even though it is cattle and not land, the *kala* — the public awareness — that attaches to a goring ox is sufficient to treat it like property on which an effective lien can be maintained and collected even from a third-party purchaser.

The *Gemara* is thus careful not to generate a *gezeiras hakasuv* where a principled explanation is available. Rather than simply saying the *Torah* granted this right and that is that, the *Gemara* fits the ruling back into the existing framework of lien law: the goring ox's notoriety makes it function like property on which an effective *apotiki* can operate, and Shimon's *Torah*-granted right to that specific ox is therefore enforceable even against Levi. The debate between Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva — creditor versus partner — will continue to generate further practical differences that the *Gemara* will explore in the coming *daf*.

# Bava Kamma 34

## Akiva vs. Ishmael

### Ownership vs. Lien

The sugya on 33b opens with the fundamental dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Ishmael concerning the nature of the *nizak*'s claim against the *tam* ox that gored. According to Rabbi Akiva, once a *tam* gores, the *nizak* immediately becomes a co-owner of the ox itself — the ox passes directly into the *nizak*'s possession. According to Rabbi Ishmael, by contrast, the *nizak* is owed money, but his claim is limited in recovery to the value of the ox: he may collect from the ox itself, but he remains fundamentally a creditor rather than an owner. The Gemara describes this as an *apoteiki* — a focused lien — on the ox. The *mazik* still owns the animal; the *nizak* simply holds an unusually powerful security interest in it.

### Machro/Hekdesho

The Gemara records that Rav Tachlifa bar Marava taught the following *baraita* before Rabbi Abahu: *machro ein machur, hekdesho mukdash* — if he sold the ox, the sale does not hold; but if he sanctified it, it takes effect as *hekdesh*. The immediate question is: who is the subject of these actions — the *mazik* or the *nizak*? And why the apparent inconsistency between the two rulings?

The Gemara first considers whether we are speaking of the *mazik* who sells or sanctifies the ox. If the *mazik* sells it and the sale is invalid, that fits Rabbi Akiva's position that the *nizak* already owns the ox outright — but then why would the *mazik*'s sanctification take effect? Conversely, if we say the subject is the *nizak*, then the rule that his sale is ineffective fits Rabbi Ishmael — the *nizak* does not own the ox and therefore cannot sell it — but then why does his sanctification work, since under Rabbi Ishmael he has no ownership?

The Gemara resolves the difficulty: *le-olam mazik* — we are speaking throughout of the *mazik*, and the ruling operates according to both positions simultaneously.

### Lien Interpretation

The Gemara explains *machro ein machur* as follows: even according to Rabbi Ishmael, who holds that the *mazik* retains ownership of his ox, the sale is not fully valid — not in the sense that it is wholly void, but in the sense that it is not permanent. The *nizak* retains his lien and can retrieve the ox from the purchaser. The sale allows the buyer to use the ox for plowing (*le-radya*) until the *nizak* exercises his lien, but the *nizak*'s right to recover it remains intact. *Machro ein machur* thus does not mean the sale is entirely without effect; it means the sale cannot permanently defeat the *nizak*'s claim.

That said, the plain sense of the *baraita* — as the Gemara acknowledges — is considerably more permissive: it seems to say that before the court case, the *mazik* can fully remove the ox from the *nizak*'s reach. The Gemara is deliberately strengthening the *nizak*'s lien beyond what the surface reading of the *baraita* would suggest.

### Bedek Habayis

As for *hekdesho mukdash* — that sanctification takes effect — the Gemara explains this as well. Even according to Rabbi Akiva, who says the *nizak* already owns the ox, the *mazik*'s act of sanctification has a degree of legal force, because of the principle taught by Rabbi Abahu.

Rabbi Abahu rules that there is a rabbinic concern that *hekdesh* not appear to dissolve without a proper act of *pidyon* — lest people say that *hekdesh yotzei belo pidyon*, that consecrated property can be removed from its sacred status without redemption. Now, when property subject to a creditor's lien is sanctified to *bedek habayis* — to the Temple maintenance fund, as opposed to being consecrated as a *korban* — the sanctification is treated like a sale to a third party. The *hekdesh* of *bedek habayis* represents the Temple's proprietary ownership, and therefore, just as a *nizak* can retrieve an ox from a third-party purchaser by exercising his lien, so too he can retrieve it from *hekdesh*. His lien trumps even the Temple's claim.

Nevertheless, because the ox was genuinely held as *hekdesh* in the interim, the *nizak* must perform some nominal act of redemption — he gives a small amount to *hekdesh* — so that it does not appear as though sacred property simply loses its *kedusha* automatically. Under Rabbi Akiva, the *nizak* truly owned the ox from the moment of the goring, and the sanctification never really took hold; yet even so, the Gemara applies Rabbi Abahu's principle, requiring a token *pidyon* so as not to create the appearance of *hekdesh* dissolving without redemption. Under Rabbi Ishmael, the *nizak*'s lien genuinely yields to the *hekdesh* during the interim period, making the *pidyon* all the more clearly necessary before the *nizak* retrieves it.

---

## Mishnah: Tam Rules

### Amad Ba-Din

The *baraita* restates the governing framework. In the case of a *tam* that caused damage, the rules turn critically on whether the matter has come before *beit din* — *amad ba-din*, literally "stood in judgment." The *baraita* distinguishes sharply between what the *mazik* may do before and after that moment.

### Pre-Court Actions

Before *amad ba-din*, the *baraita* rules: *makhar machur, hekdesho mukdash* — if the *mazik* sells the ox, the sale is effective; if he sanctifies it, the sanctification holds; if he slaughters it and gives it away as a gift, what he has done is done. As noted above, the Gemara significantly limits the plain reading of these rulings. The sale is "effective" only in the interim sense that the buyer may use the ox for plowing until the *nizak* exercises his lien. The sanctification works, but the *nizak* may still retrieve the ox from *hekdesh* after performing a nominal act of *pidyon* in keeping with Rabbi Abahu's principle.

What of slaughter? The *baraita* states that if the *mazik* slaughtered the ox and gave it away, *mah she-asa asui* — what he did stands. The Gemara asks: why should this be final? Let the *nizak* come and collect from the meat. A *baraita* supports this: the verse says *umachru et hashor hachai* — sell the *living* ox — which might suggest the *nizak*'s rights expire upon slaughter. But the continuation, *umachru et hashor*, without the word *hachai*, teaches that the *nizak* still has rights even to a slaughtered animal.

Rav Shizbi therefore explains that *mah she-asa asui* in the case of slaughter does not mean the *nizak* loses his claim entirely. Rather, it refers to *pachat shechita* — the depreciation caused by the act of slaughter itself. If after slaughter the carcass is worth only eighty of an original hundred-dollar value, the *nizak* may collect eighty but not the full hundred.

This leads to the principle stated by Rav Avuya, son of Rav Yehoshua: *ha-mazik shibudo shel chaveiro patur* — one who damages property upon which another holds a lien is exempt. I owe you a hundred dollars; you hold a lien on my plot of land; I go and destroy that land — I am not liable for the indirect loss to your security interest. The land was mine when I damaged it. Similarly, when the *mazik* slaughters the ox, it is still legally his at that moment, so the *nizak*'s resulting loss is treated as an indirect consequence, not a direct act of damage.

The Gemara notes that this same principle was already derivable from a ruling of Rava — *ha-soref shtaro shel chaveiro patur*: one who burns another's debt document is exempt. He destroyed a piece of paper; the underlying debt still exists; the loss of the ability to prove it in court is indirect. The Gemara works through why neither of these prior cases would have been sufficient to generate the full principle, and why the case of slaughter adds something: slaughtering an animal and reducing it to a carcass is, in terms of real destruction, equivalent to digging ditches into a field held under lien — and yet even in that case one is exempt. These acts fall under the broader principle of *grama* and *dinei de-garmi* — indirect causation — a topic the Gemara will address more fully later in the tractate.

### Post-Court Control

Once there has been *amad ba-din*, the *baraita* rules differently: *makhar eino machur, hekdesho eino mukdash* — a sale by the *mazik* is invalid, and a sanctification does not take effect. At this point the *nizak*'s rights have been fully established by the court, and the *mazik* can no longer act unilaterally to undercut them.

It is worth pausing here to note a point raised by *Tosafot* and debated extensively among the *rishonim* and *acharonim*. According to the normative ruling that *chatzi nezek knasa* — that the half-damages paid by a *tam* are a fine rather than ordinary compensation — a fine does not take on legal reality until there is *ha'amadah be-din*. Normally, the moment I borrow money from you or break your property, I owe you money as an objective fact; the court merely clarifies and enforces a pre-existing reality. A *knas*, however, is different: the court does not merely identify the obligation, it creates and imposes it. Before the court acts, I owe you nothing.

Given this, one might have expected that even according to Rabbi Akiva — who says the *nizak* becomes an immediate co-owner — the ownership should not arise until *ha'amadah be-din*, since the underlying debt is a *knas*. Nevertheless, the Gemara understands that according to Rabbi Akiva the *nizak* becomes a co-owner automatically, without any court action. This may be because the verse *umachru et hashor hachai* frames the arrangement as an immediate operative reality. The *baraita* before us, which draws a distinction based on *amad ba-din*, is accordingly read by the Gemara as functioning within the framework of Rabbi Ishmael, who attributes greater rights to the *mazik* before the court acts.

### Creditors vs. Nizak

The *baraita* then addresses the claim of the *mazik*'s general creditors. *Kidmu ba'alei chovot ve-higbiu* — if the creditors came and collected the ox — *bein chav ad she-lo hizik bein hizik ad she-lo chav*, regardless of whether the debt to the creditors arose before or after the damage to the *nizak*'s ox, *lo asu velo klum* — what they did has no effect — *lefi she-ein meshalem ela migufo* — because the *nizak*'s collection is from the body of the ox itself.

This is striking, and the Gemara presses the point. If the *mazik* owed the creditors money before the damage occurred, the creditors held an earlier lien — *ba'alei chov kodem* — so why should the *nizak* be able to displace them? And even if the damage preceded the loan, perhaps the creditors, as the first to actually seize the ox, should be entitled to keep it. The Gemara raises the general question of whether a later creditor who seizes property first is allowed to retain it — and in ordinary circumstances, the answer may well be yes.

The Gemara responds: *le-olam eima lach mah she-gava gava* — ordinarily, what a creditor seizes he may keep. But this case is different, because the *nizak* can say to the creditor: *ilu gabakh havei lav minach havah gavina lei* — had the ox always been in your possession, I would still have had the right to collect from it, since it is the very ox that damaged me. *De-hai tora de-azkin minei mishtalamna* — it is from this ox, the ox that gored mine, that I collect.

*Tosafot* notes that this argument is ultimately just a sophisticated articulation of the *baraita*'s own conclusion — *lefi she-ein meshalem ela migufo*. The *nizak*'s lien is focused specifically on the body of the ox, not on the *mazik*'s assets generally. The creditor's lien, by contrast, attaches to all the *mazik*'s property indiscriminately. Because the *nizak* has this uniquely focused claim on the specific ox, he has a superior right to that animal over any general creditor, regardless of the order in which the debts arose or the property was seized. The creditor is not left without recourse — he may turn to the *mazik*'s other assets — but he cannot hold this particular ox against the *nizak*'s focused claim.

---

## Damage Assessment

### Shevach Mazik

The Gemara turns to a *baraita* that explores the principles governing how damage is assessed when the value of the animals changes between the moment of the goring and the time the case reaches court.

The case: an ox worth 200 gores an ox worth 200, causing 50 worth of damage. Afterward, the *nizak*'s injured ox appreciates — it is now worth 400, and had it not been damaged it would have been worth 800. How much does the *mazik* pay? The rule is *noten ke-sha'at ha-nezek* — payment is assessed at the moment of the damage. The damage was 50 at the time of the goring, so the *mazik* pays 25 (half of 50, as this is a *tam*). One cannot claim that because the ox would have been worth 800 but is now only worth 400, the damage amounts to 400 — that increased loss is treated as indirect, a loss of anticipated profit that does not enter into the assessment.

The Gemara identifies this ruling as consistent with Rabbi Ishmael's position that the *nizak* holds only a lien, not a share of ownership. Were the *nizak* a co-owner according to Rabbi Akiva, one might expect him to share in the ox's appreciation — his percentage stake would grow along with the animal's value. But the rule here is that he receives only the fixed amount assessed at the moment of the goring, suggesting he is a creditor owed a sum, not a partner in the animal.

### Pachat at Amad

The *baraita* then addresses the reverse: *kachash ke-sha'at ha-amadah ba-din* — if the *nizak*'s ox depreciated by the time of the court case. Suppose it was worth 200 at the time of the goring, the damage was 50, but by the time of *amad ba-din* it had fallen further in value to 100. In that case, the *mazik* pays based on the depreciated value — effectively 50 now constitutes proportionally greater damage, and payment is calculated accordingly.

This asymmetry is notable. When the ox goes up in value, the *nizak* gains nothing from the increase — but when it goes down, the *mazik* must pay based on the lower value, as though the continued decline is part of the original injury. This seems inconsistent: if the *nizak* holds a percentage of the animal (à la Rabbi Akiva), he should gain when it rises and lose when it falls. If he is only owed a fixed sum (à la Rabbi Ishmael), he should always recover that fixed sum regardless of subsequent fluctuations.

The Gemara asks of the *seifa* — the depreciation case — that it seems to operate like Rabbi Akiva (the *nizak* bears a percentage interest), while the *reisha* — the appreciation case — seems to operate like Rabbi Ishmael. Does the *baraita* split between the two opinions? The Gemara answers: *lo kula Rabbi Akiva hi* — the entire *baraita* is according to Rabbi Akiva. Both rules operate on the premise that the *nizak* is a co-owner.

### Continued Injury

The reason for the asymmetry lies in the specific circumstances of each case. The *baraita*'s statement that the *mazik* pays only the original 50 even when the ox appreciated to 400 refers to a case where the *mazik* fattened the animal — *ke-she-pitmu*. The increase in value resulted from the *mazik*'s own investment and effort. Even if the *nizak* is a co-owner, he cannot fully claim the benefit of appreciation that was generated by the *mazik*'s expenditure. The Gemara adds via Rav Pappa that the *reisha* also teaches a separate *chiddush* for cases of natural appreciation: even if the ox simply became worth more on its own, the *mazik* is not excused from paying the original 50 on the theory that the animal is now worth more than it was originally — because the gap between 400 and 800 demonstrates that real damage was done. *Tosafot* notes, however, that this resolution is not entirely clean: even partners in a field, when one improves it unilaterally, generally cannot exclude the other partner from all benefit, and the precise allocation remains a subject of discussion among the *rishonim*.

As for the depreciation case: the Gemara asks, *kachash machmat mai* — what caused the ox to decline in value? If the *nizak* himself worked the animal into decline, the *mazik* could reasonably say: you diminished it yourself. Rav Ashi answers that the case in view is *kachash machmat makah* — the ox declined because of the original wound. The injury kept worsening. In such a case, the *nizak* can say *kurna de-torach kevira beh* — the horn of your ox is still embedded in my ox, meaning the original injury is the ongoing cause of every subsequent decline. This is not *grama* — it is not treated as an indirect consequence that falls outside the *mazik*'s liability. Rather, it is how the full extent of the original injury is properly assessed. The damage is not capped at the 50 measured at the moment of the goring; it is measured by how much worse the injury ultimately became.

The overall principle that emerges: appreciation of the *mazik*'s ox generates no windfall for the *nizak* — that is an indirect matter of lost profit. But continued depreciation of the *nizak*'s ox as a direct result of the original wound is part of the damage itself, assessed at the time of *amad ba-din*. Under Rabbi Akiva, the *nizak* as co-owner loses when the animal loses value, but gains from the original owner's investment only to a limited degree. These are the practical *nafka minas* between the two positions — and the Gemara has significantly strengthened the *nizak*'s lien even under Rabbi Ishmael, against what the plain reading of the *baraita* would suggest.

---

## Torah Case Debate

### R. Meir Position

The Gemara now turns to the *baraita* that parses the precise scriptural case in the Torah. The verse (*Shemot* 21:35) reads: *umachru et hashor hachai vechatzu et kaspo vegam et ha-met yechetzun* — they shall sell the live ox and split its proceeds, and they shall also split the dead one. The question is: what scenario does the Torah envision?

Rabbi Meir says: *al zeh ne'emar* — the Torah is speaking to the case of an ox worth 200 that gores an ox worth 200, where the *neveilah* — the carcass — is worth nothing at all. In that case, the debt is 100 (the full value of the dead animal), and since it is a *tam*, chatzi nezek is 50. The verse *umachru et hashor hachai vechatzu et kaspo* addresses this case directly. But then how does Rabbi Meir read *vegam et ha-met yechetzun*? He explains: this does not mean physically divide the carcass. Rather, *pachat she-pichas'o mitah machatzin be-chai* — the depreciation caused by the death is split within the context of the live ox. *Vegam et ha-met yechetzun* refers to splitting the loss, not splitting the carcass.

### R. Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees. He says: yes, the ruling you describe is correct, and yes, that is the *halacha* — but that is not the case the Torah is addressing. The Torah speaks of an ox worth 200 goring an ox worth 200 where the *neveilah* is worth 50. In that situation, the *mazik* and *nizak* each take half of the live ox and half of the carcass, walking away with 125 each. Each lost 75 from an original holding of 200. The total damage was 150, and chatzi nezek is 75 — perfectly consistent with half-damages. The verse *vegam et ha-met yechetzun* means exactly what it says: they divide the carcass.

Rabbi Yehuda's objection to Rabbi Meir's case is pointed: if the *neveilah* is worth nothing, why does the Torah bother saying *vegam et ha-met yechetzun* — why legislate a division of a worthless object? The scriptural instruction to split the dead animal implies the dead animal has value. Hence the Torah must be speaking to the case where the carcass is worth 50.

### Pachat Neveilah

What is actually at stake between them? The Gemara notes that in the case Rabbi Yehuda describes — the *neveilah* worth 50 — both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree on the arithmetic: each party walks away with 125 and absorbs a loss of 75. *Mai beinaihu* — what do they actually dispute?

Rava answers: *pachat neveilah ika beinaihu* — the question of who bears the depreciation of the carcass. If after the goring the carcass continues to lose value, who absorbs that loss — the *nizak* or the *mazik*? Rabbi Meir holds *pachat neveilah de-nizak havei* — the depreciation of the carcass falls entirely on the *nizak*. The *mazik* pays for the loss at the time of death, but the carcass itself and any further decline in its value belong to the *nizak*. Rabbi Yehuda, insisting that the Torah says *vegam et ha-met yechetzun*, holds that the carcass is actually split between them, making the *mazik* a part-owner in the carcass — and therefore *pachat neveilah de-mazik havei palga*: the *mazik* absorbs half of any subsequent depreciation.

### Tam vs. Muad

Abaye immediately raises an objection: *matzinu le-Rabbi Yehuda tam chamur mi-muad* — according to Rabbi Yehuda, a *tam* would be stricter in this respect than a *muad*. In every other category of damage — *bor*, *muad*, and so forth — the *nizak* takes the carcass and the *mazik* pays for the loss. The *mazik* never bears the depreciation of the carcass. A *tam*, which is universally the most lenient category of payment, would according to Rabbi Yehuda uniquely impose on the *mazik* a share of the carcass's ongoing decline.

One might respond: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda holds that a *tam* is indeed stricter in certain respects. After all, elsewhere Rabbi Yehuda rules — as will appear later in the tractate — that the minimum level of *shemira* required to be exempt from liability is actually higher for a *tam* than for a *muad*. Perhaps Rabbi Yehuda accepts that a *tam* can impose greater obligations.

The Gemara rejects this parallel. Rabbi Yehuda's stringency regarding *shemira* for a *tam* is derived from specific scriptural verses — *dikesivei kra*. But one has never heard Rabbi Yehuda apply greater stringency to a *tam* in the domain of *tashlumin*, of the actual payments. Payment by a *tam* is always more lenient. The *baraita* itself confirms this: Rabbi Yehuda says there — *tam ha-kal kol she-ken* — if a *muad* pays only the actual loss without any windfall from the split, then a *tam*, which is the more lenient category, certainly cannot produce a result that benefits the *nizak* beyond his actual loss. Rabbi Yehuda explicitly rejects the possibility that a *tam* would ever be more burdensome for the *mazik* than a *muad* in terms of what is owed.

### Shevach Neveilah

Rabbi Yochanan therefore proposes a different resolution of the dispute. The argument between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is not about *pachat neveilah* — both agree the depreciation of the carcass falls on the *nizak* alone. Rather, the dispute concerns *shevach neveilah* — appreciation of the carcass.

If after the goring the carcass increases in value — perhaps hides became more valuable, or the meat fetched a better price — who benefits from that increase? Rabbi Meir holds that *shevach neveilah de-nizak havei* — the appreciation belongs entirely to the *nizak*, who holds the carcass. Rabbi Yehuda holds that *shevach neveilah de-mazik havei palga* — because the *mazik* is a part-owner in the carcass (per the verse *vegam et ha-met yechetzun*), he shares in any increase in value. Crucially, this means the *mazik* benefits from the appreciation: his effective payment is reduced, since the *nizak* must now credit the *mazik* with his share of the increased carcass value. This is a leniency for the *mazik* rather than a stringency, which is precisely why Rabbi Yehuda embraces it — it is consistent with the principle that a *tam* never imposes greater payment than a *muad*.

*De-mar savar de-nizak havei u-mar savar palga* — one holds the appreciation belongs entirely to the *nizak*, the other holds it is split. This is what prompted Rabbi Yehuda's analysis: the Torah goes easy on the *mazik* in the case of a *tam*, making him a part-owner of the carcass not to burden him with its depreciation but to allow him to benefit from its appreciation — thereby reducing what he effectively pays. The verse *vegam et ha-met yechetzun*, on this reading, extends a leniency: it gives the *mazik* a share in the upside of the carcass, ensuring that chatzi nezek in a *tam* is never more burdensome than full payment in a *muad*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 35

## Live/Dead Split

### Mishnah Setup

Today's daf is 35. We pick up in the middle of 34b, dealing with the debate in the *mishnah* between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir about how to read the *pesukim* in the Torah concerning the division of the live and dead animal. Rabbi Meir reads the verse as indicating that the dead animal is worth nothing — it does not literally mean that you split the dead animal, but rather that you split the depreciation due to death. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, reads the verse more literally: you actually split both the live and the dead animal.

### Rabbi Meir's View

According to Rabbi Meir, then, the division of the *neveila* is not a literal transaction but a formulaic way of expressing that the *mazik* pays half the loss attributable to the animal's death. The carcass itself belongs entirely to the *nizak*, and the *mazik* bears no ownership interest in it whatsoever.

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

Rabbi Yehuda insists on a more literal reading: each party takes half of the live animal and half of the dead one. This reading, however, can only work out equitably when the animals are of equal value, as the *gemara* has begun to illustrate. When the animals are worth the same amount, the arithmetic of splitting both produces exactly the right result — each party absorbs half the loss.

### Equal Value Requirement

The condition that makes Rabbi Yehuda's reading coherent is that the two animals must be of equal value at the time of the goring. When they are, a literal split of the live animal and the carcass yields precisely half-damages, no more and no less.

### Mazik Ownership Scope

One might think that if the *mazik* is a part-owner of the carcass, he would also suffer if the carcass depreciates further after the goring. But that would make *tam* more severe than *muad* and other categories of *nezek*, since in all other cases it is the *nizak* who fully owns the carcass and bears all subsequent loss or gain. There is no reason why *tam* should uniquely burden the *mazik* with depreciation risk. The resolution is that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the *mazik*'s partial ownership of the carcass functions only in one direction: if the value of the carcass appreciates, the *mazik* benefits from that appreciation. The ownership does not cut against him if values fall.

---

## Appreciation Theory

### Yochanan's Principle

The *gemara* now introduces Rabbi Yochanan's resolution of the dispute. *Shvach neveila ika beinaihu* — the practical difference between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerns a case where the carcass increases in value after the goring. That is the crux of their disagreement.

### Depreciation Agreement

In cases where the carcass depreciates further, both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree that the *nizak* absorbs that loss. This follows naturally from the rule applicable to *muad* and other forms of *nezek*, where the *nizak* is the sole owner of the carcass. There is no reason for *tam* to differ on this point.

### Appreciation Dispute

Where the carcass appreciates after the goring, the two *tanna'im* diverge. Rabbi Meir holds that even this appreciation belongs entirely to the *nizak* — the *mazik* has no stake in the carcass at all. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the *mazik*, as a partial owner of the carcass, gains half of any appreciation, and that this gain offsets the payment he owes. *De-mar savar denizak havei* — one holds the appreciation belongs to the *nizak*; *u-mar savar palga* — and the other holds the *mazik* takes half. This is the fulfillment, according to Rabbi Yehuda, of the verse that they split the carcass.

---

## Unequal Value Problem

### Compassion Question

Having established Rabbi Yehuda's position that the Torah shows compassion on the *mazik* by granting him a share in the carcass's appreciation, the *gemara* now follows a logical challenge Rabbi Yehuda himself raises. *Hashta de-amarta chas Rachmana ilvei de-mazik* — now that you say the Torah goes easy on the *mazik* and lets him gain from the appreciation of the carcass, a question arises: why can't this principle extend to cases of unequal-valued animals?

### Unequal Case Setup

Consider the following scenario: a *shor shaveh chamesh sela'im* — an ox worth twenty — gores a *shor shaveh maneh* — an ox worth a hundred. The carcass then depreciates to fifty. The actual damage was fifty. Under a straightforward application of the rule, the *mazik* should pay half the damage, which is twenty-five — meaning the entire goring ox would effectively be transferred to the *nizak*. But what happens if we apply the verses literally?

### Profit Problem

If you read the verse as written — *zeh notel chatzi chai ve-chatzi meis ve-zeh notel chatzi chai ve-chatzi meis* — then each party splits the live animal and each party splits the dead one. The *mazik* takes ten from his half of the live ox and twenty-five from his half of the carcass. He walks away with thirty-five. But his ox was worth only twenty to begin with. He has gained fifteen — a clear profit from an act of damage.

### Absurdity Stated

The absurdity is stark: the *mazik* would profit from the goring rather than pay for it. *Heichan matzinu mazik niskar?* — where have we ever found that a *mazik* walks away with a profit? The principle underlying the entire law of *nezek* is that the damager compensates the damaged party, not that he enriches himself through the act of damage.

### Exclusionary Verse

The verse itself closes this door: *shalem yeshalem ba'alim meshalmim ve-ein ba'alim notlin* — the owner of the goring ox pays, he does not take. The *mazik* is the one who pays out of pocket. He cannot walk away having received more than he started with.

---

## Equal Value Only

### Loss Prohibition

The *gemara* clarifies: the case where a *mazik* profits at the *nizak*'s obvious expense — the hundred-shekel ox gored by the twenty-shekel ox — is so clearly unjust that no verse is even needed to rule it out. That case was not the reason a verse was necessary. *Hani mili heicha de-ika pseida le-nizak* — this is obvious when there is a clear loss to the *nizak*.

### Mutual Gain Case

The more interesting case requiring a verse is where there is no loss to the *nizak*. Consider two oxen each worth twenty, and the carcass appreciates to thirty after the goring — perhaps because the market for dead oxen has risen. If you split literally: the *mazik* walks away with twenty-five and the *nizak* also walks away with twenty-five. Everybody gains something. The *nizak* is not actually out money compared to what he had before the goring — at least not in absolute terms, even if his ox would have been worth more had it not been gored. One might argue: in such a case, since the Torah anyway grants the *mazik* partial ownership of the *neveila*, perhaps he should own it fully enough to even walk away with a profit.

### Offset Principle

The verse *shalem yeshalem ba'alim meshalmim ve-ein ba'alim notlin* resolves this. The *mazik*'s ownership of the *neveila* is real, but it is instrumental: it exists to *offset* the payment he owes, not to generate a profit. Even in the mutual-gain scenario where the *nizak* does not suffer an absolute loss, the Torah does not permit the *mazik* to hold the carcass as an asset beyond what is needed to cover his payment obligation. His ownership cancels debt; it does not create wealth. He gains from appreciation to offset his liability, but he cannot gain so much that he actually walks away ahead.

A more concrete illustration: suppose that at the time of damage, the carcass was worth ten, each party owned five, but the market later rose and that five dollars grew to fifteen. Rabbi Yehuda's principle says yes, the *mazik* gains from appreciation of the *neveila* — but only enough to offset payment. He cannot gain past the point of full offset into actual profit.

### Fundamental Agreement

At this point the *gemara* addresses a further challenge. *Amar lei Rav Acha bar Tachlifa le-Rava*: if Rabbi Yehuda is going to read the verses literally, what happens in a middle case — say a fifty-shekel ox that gores a forty-shekel ox, and the carcass goes down to twenty? In this case, applying the literal split: the *mazik* walks away with thirty-five, and so does the *nizak*. Neither profits from the other's loss. But the problem is that the *mazik* is paying more than half damages — he loses thirty-five and he only owed twenty shekels' worth of half the depreciation. How can that be, given that Rabbi Yehuda's entire approach was meant to be easier on the *mazik*, and the verse *ve-machru et ha-shor ha-chai ve-chatzu et kaspo* implies a straight split?

The *gemara*'s answer is decisive: *eis lei le-Rabbi Yehuda pachat she-pachtah mitah machatzin be-chai* — Rabbi Yehuda also agrees that in the end, the *mazik* pays only half of the depreciation from live to dead. This is learned from *ve-gam et ha-meit ye-chetzun* — the word *ve-gam*, "also," teaches two things simultaneously. On the one hand, *ha-meit ye-chetzun* — they split the carcass, from which Rabbi Yehuda derives that the *mazik* has a partial ownership in the *neveila* and gains from its appreciation. On the other hand, the *ve-gam* tells you that the fundamental principle remains intact — the payment is half the depreciation, no more and no less.

This is why the literal verses only apply when the animals are of equal value. When they are equal, the arithmetic of splitting both the live and dead animal works out to exactly half the loss. When they are unequal, applying the verse literally produces wildly different results — the *mazik* might profit, the *nizak* might receive more than half, or the *mazik* might pay more than half. None of those outcomes is acceptable. Therefore the verses can only be read in a context where both animals are worth the same.

At the bottom of this entire analysis, everyone agrees: no one reads the *pesukim* literally across all scenarios. Both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree that the fundamental obligation is to pay half the depreciation due to death, and that the *nizak* holds the carcass or a lien on the goring ox based on that half-damages figure. The one and only practical difference between them is Rabbi Yehuda's principle that the *mazik* holds a partial ownership in the *neveila* such that if it appreciates, that appreciation offsets his payment. The *nizak* retains the carcass; but if it rises in value, that rise reduces what the *mazik* must pay out of pocket.

---

## Payment/Exemption Cases

### Mishnah Cases

The *gemara* now turns to a new *mishnah* that presents cases where the liability of an ox's owner and the liability of a human being for the same type of act diverge — in some cases, the ox creates liability while the human is exempt; in others, the human is liable while the ox creates no liability for its owner.

### Embarrassment Case

The first case: if an ox causes embarrassment — *shoro she-bi'eish, patur* — the owner is exempt. Payment for *boshes* is a form of personal-injury compensation, equivalent to *tza'ar*, *ripuy*, and *sheves*. These additional payments for personal injury apply only when a human being directly inflicts harm, not when his animal does so. If my animal gores someone, I pay damages only — no hospital bills, no pain and suffering, no embarrassment. *Ve-hu she-bi'eish chayav* — but if the person himself caused embarrassment, he is obligated to pay.

### Eye/Tooth Case

The second case: if an ox knocks out the eye or tooth of the owner's slave — *shoro she-sima es ein avdo ve-hipil es shino, patur* — the owner is exempt. The Torah's rule that knocking out a slave's eye or tooth liberates the slave applies only to direct action by the master, not to the master's animal acting on his behalf. *Ve-hu she-sima es ein avdo ve-hipil es shino chayav* — if the master personally does so, the slave goes free.

### Parent Injury Case

Now the first of the reversed cases: *shoro she-chaval be-aviv ve-imo chayav* — if an ox wounds the owner's father or mother, the owner is liable and pays the father or mother damages. *Ve-hu she-chaval be-aviv ve-imo, patur* — but if the owner personally inflicts a wound on his parent, he is exempt from monetary payment because *chavala*, a wound that draws blood, when inflicted on a parent, makes the offender *chayav misa*. The gravity of the capital crime overrides any monetary liability.

### Shabbat Fire Case

The parallel case: *shor she-hidlik et ha-gadish be-Shabbat chayav* — if the owner's ox lights a pile of grain on fire on *Shabbat*, the owner is liable for the damage. *Ve-hu she-hidlik et ha-gadish be-Shabbat, patur* — but if the owner himself did so, he is exempt, because he has committed *chilul Shabbat*, a capital offense, and therefore we say *kimlei* — the capital liability overrides the monetary one. *Mipnei she-mitchayev be-nafsho* — because he has incurred liability to his own life.

---

## Kimlei Principle

### Abbahu's Teaching

The *gemara* now examines the principle of *kimlei* in depth. *Tani Rabbi Abbahu kammai de-Rabbi Yochanan* — Rabbi Abbahu taught the following *braita* in the presence of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol ha-mikalkelim peturim chutz me-chovel u-mav'ir* — all who perform a *melacha* on *Shabbat* in a destructive manner are exempt from the prohibition's consequences, with the exception of wounding and making a fire. The general principle is that a *melacha she-einah tzricha le-gufah* — a destructive labor — does not incur liability. But Rabbi Abbahu's *braita* carves out exceptions: wounding and fire remain violations even when done purely destructively. One can appreciate the intuition: *shechita* is a form of wounding that ultimately produces meat, and fire is paradigmatically productive, but both also have a fundamentally destructive dimension — enough to retain their character as *melacha* even in purely destructive form.

### Yochanan's Rejection

Rabbi Yochanan rejected this *braita* entirely: *puk tani le-vara* — go teach that outside. *Chovel u-mav'ir eino mishnah* — this is not a valid teaching. Even wounding and fire incur no *Shabbat* liability when performed purely destructively. *Ve-im timtza lomar mishnah* — and if you insist it is a legitimate source, it must be referring only to a case where there is an element of constructive purpose. *Chovel ve-tzarich le-kabbo* — you wound an animal because you want to extract blood to feed your dog. *Mav'ir ve-tzarich le-afro* — or you burn down a fine table because you want its ashes. In each case, the act is destructive in the macro sense — you have ruined something of value — but you have a constructive purpose. That constructive element, however partial, is what defines the act as *melacha* on *Shabbat* and makes it a capital crime. A purely destructive act — *mikalkel* in the full sense — would not constitute *chilul Shabbat* and therefore would not trigger *kimlei*.

### Intent Debate

The *gemara* now presses this point by looking at the *mishnah* case of the ox that burns the grain pile on *Shabbat*. *Ve-katani hu dumya de-shoro* — the *mishnah* presents the human case as parallel in scenario to the ox case. *Mah shor de-lo kaba'i lei* — just as when an ox burns a grain pile it is not interested in the ashes, it is acting purely destructively, *af hu nami de-lo kaba'i lei* — so too when a person does it in our *mishnah*, presumably they are not interested in the ashes. And yet the *mishnah* says *patur*, exempt — because it is *chilul Shabbat*. This would prove that even a purely destructive burning constitutes *chilul Shabbat*, against Rabbi Yochanan's position.

The *gemara* responds: no — read it the other way. *Shor dumya dideh* — the ox's act in the *mishnah* is analogous to the human act, not the human act to the ox. The *mishnah* is in fact describing a case where the human *did* want the ashes, and similarly the ox case in the *mishnah* should be understood as a case where the ox also had some constructive intent. But *shor heichi mishkachas lah* — how would you ever find a case where an ox burns a grain pile in order to get the ashes?

### Clever Ox Example

*Amar lei Rav Acha: hacha be-mai askinan — be-shor pikeach* — we are dealing with an unusually clever ox. The ox had a bite or sore on its back, *she-asa lo neshicha be-gavo*, and wanted to burn down the grain pile and roll in the ashes to soothe the irritation. *U-mina yad'inan* — and how would we know that was the ox's intention? *De-le-vasar de-kalyei kamitnafia be-kitmei* — because after burning the pile down, we saw it rolling in the ashes. Such behavior reveals the ox's intent.

*U-mi shecheicha hai gavna* — is this really a realistic scenario? Does an animal ever act with that kind of purposive intelligence? *In* — yes. There was an ox in the house of Rav Papa whose gums were bothering it. *Ayeil pitka le-niza'isa* — it found and uncovered a barrel of mead, *ve-shati shichra* — and drank it, and that soothed its gums. Animals can indeed exhibit remarkably purposive behavior.

The *gemara*'s conclusion regarding the *mishnah* is therefore that even its straightforward scenario must be understood as one in which the human had some constructive intent — namely, wanting the ashes — for it to constitute *chilul Shabbat* and thus trigger *kimlei*. A purely destructive burning does not rise to that level.

### Rava's Resolution

*Rava amar matnisin be-shogeg* — Rava offers a different resolution: our *mishnah* is not talking about an intentional violation of *Shabbat* at all. It is talking about an unintentional one — *shogeg* — meaning the person was not a willful violator. Perhaps he forgot it was *Shabbat*, or did not know that this act was forbidden on *Shabbat*. And this opens up the crucial question: do we say *kimlei* even when somebody committed a capital-worthy act without being willful about it, such that *Beis Din* could never actually impose the death penalty?

### Chizkiya Teaching

The answer comes from the famous teaching of *Dei Chizkiyahu*: *makeh adam u-makeh behemah*. The Torah juxtaposes two verses: *makeh behemah yeshalmena* — one who strikes an animal pays for it — and *makeh adam yumos* — one who kills a person is put to death. The teaching of *Bei Chizkiyahu* draws an analogy: just as the law of striking an animal makes no distinctions — *lo chalakta bo bein shogeg u-vein meizid, bein miskaven le-she'eino miskaven, bein derech yerida le-derech aliya* — whether willful or unintentional, whether directed or misdirected, whether on the downstroke or the upstroke — and the payment applies in all cases, so too for striking a human.
