No distinctions are made — but in the opposite direction: *ela le-potro mamon* — in all those cases, you are exempted from monetary payment. The weight of the act of taking a human life, or committing any capital crime, permanently displaces any monetary liability — not because a punishment is being imposed, but because the nature of the act itself is so weighty.

### Kimlei with Capital Crime

This teaches a fundamental distinction between two categories of *kimlei*. One category, derived from the principle of *ke-dei rishato* — that *Beis Din* imposes one punishment, not two — applies when *Beis Din* is actually inflicting a punishment. In that case, the simultaneous imposition of *malkus* and monetary payment is precluded because you do not punish someone twice for one act. But that form of *kimlei* requires that the punishment actually be imposed.

The *kimlei* of *Bei Chizkiyahu* is categorically different. When it comes to a capital crime, the exemption from monetary payment has nothing to do with whether *Beis Din* can or will punish the person. A person who committed *chilul Shabbat* entirely *be-shogeg* — who could never be executed — is nonetheless exempt from monetary payment. The gravity of having committed an act that is in the category of capital crime erases all monetary liability, regardless of circumstances.

The *gemara* therefore explains: *keivan de-be-meizid nitan be-nafsho* — since were the person to have done this intentionally they would be deserving of the death penalty, and *hashta be-shogeg patur* — even though in this instance it was unintentional and no death penalty could be imposed, nevertheless the act is one that by its nature belongs to the category of capital crime, and that is sufficient to exempt from payment.

### Rashi/Tosafot Debate

This raises a subtle but important question. Rava's answer establishes that *kimlei* applies even *be-shogeg*, without willful violation. But one might ask: is constructive intent still required to *define* the act as *chilul Shabbat* in the first place? After all, Rava's point was that intent to willfully violate *Shabbat* is unnecessary for *kimlei* to apply. But is the intent to achieve something constructive — wanting the ashes — separately required not as an element of culpability, but as an element of what makes the physical act an act of *chilul Shabbat* at all?

Rashi's reading of Rava's answer seems to be that once we establish *kimlei* applies even *be-shogeg*, intent does not matter. Whether or not the person wanted the ashes, since the physical act of burning a grain pile is the kind of act that can constitute *chilul Shabbat*, and since with the right intent under the right circumstances it would be a capital crime, *kimlei* applies. The act's potential to be capital-level is sufficient.

Tosafot reads it differently. Tosafot insists that constructive intent — the intent to want the ashes, or some other productive purpose — is still required to define the act as *chilul Shabbat* in the first place. What Rava is saying, according to Tosafot, is that you do not need to be a willful violator — you do not need to know and accept that you are transgressing *Shabbat*. But the intent that gives the act its character as a Shabbat-violating *melacha* — the intent to achieve something constructive through the act — is still necessary. Without that, it is simply not *chilul Shabbat*, and *kimlei* cannot apply. To burn a grain pile for purely destructive purposes without wanting the ashes is, according to Tosafot, not *chilul Shabbat* at all, regardless of how the act looks from the outside.

This dispute touches on a deeper conceptual question: at what point does the absence of intent mean not merely that you are not culpable, but that you have not even performed the relevant act? And the extreme case makes the issue vivid: if someone was gesticulating and his hand inadvertently knocked over a torch that started a fire — is that *mechallel Shabbat be-shogeg*, exempting from monetary payment via *kimlei*? Or is the absence of intent so complete that we cannot say he performed an act of *chilul Shabbat* at all, only that something happened through his physical movement?

It is also worth noting, as one might observe, that the precise term *kimlei* does not appear in this *sugya*. The concept operative here — that the weight of a capital crime wipes out monetary liability entirely, even without the punishment being imposed — may in fact be a broader principle than the classic *kimlei* formulation, which is more narrowly about *Beis Din* not imposing two punishments simultaneously.

---

## Burden of Proof

### Ambiguity Cases

The *gemara* now turns to the final section of the *mishnah*, which presents a series of cases governed by the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* — the one who seeks to extract from his fellow bears the burden of proof. These cases all share the feature that the facts are ambiguous: something clearly happened, but who or what caused it cannot be established with certainty.

### Single Pursuing Ox

*Shor she-hayah rodeif achar shor acher* — one ox was running after another ox. The owners found one ox on the ground, injured. One party says: *shorkha heizik* — your ox gored mine. The other says: *lo ki al sela lakah* — no, it tripped over a rock; my ox had nothing to do with it. *Hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* — the one seeking payment bears the burden of proof. The point is that circumstantial evidence — even if it looks very much like goring occurred — may not suffice. The claimant must prove his case.

### Two Pursuing Oxes

*Hayu shnayim rodfin achar echad* — two oxen, owned by Reuven and Shimon respectively, were both running after Levi's ox. A witness at a distance saw one of the oxen gore Levi's ox but could not tell which one. Reuven says it was Shimon's ox; Shimon says it was Reuven's. *Shneihem peturin* — both are exempt, because Levi cannot prove from either which one is liable. Each owner points to the other, and neither can be established as the responsible party.

### Single Owner Both Oxes

*Im hayu shneihem shel ish echad* — if both goring oxen belong to one owner, Reuven, then *shneihem chayavim* — both oxen are liable, meaning Reuven is liable. Even though Levi cannot prove which of Reuven's oxen specifically gored his animal, he can prove that one of Reuven's oxen did it. Reuven cannot escape liability by pointing to ambiguity between his own animals. Note that if we rule like Rabbi Akiva that the goring creates a lien on the specific ox that gored, there is a further complication: Levi knows he owns half of one of Reuven's oxen but cannot identify which one. Nevertheless, he knows Reuven holds his property, and some satisfaction can presumably be obtained on that basis.

### Large and Small Oxes

*Im haya echad gadol ve-echad katan* — one of Reuven's oxen is large and one is small, both are *tam*. Since for a *shor tam* the payment is limited to the value of the goring ox, the identity of the goring ox is financially significant. *Ha-nizak omer gadol heizik* — Levi claims the large ox gored, so he can recover his full half-damages from the large ox. *Ve-ha-mazik omer lo ki ela katan heizik* — Reuven says the small one gored, so Levi's recovery is limited to the value of the small ox. *Hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* — Levi must prove his version; he cannot simply demand recovery based on the large ox.

### Tam and Muad

Similarly, *echad tam ve-echad muad* — one of the oxen is *tam* and one is *muad*. *Ha-nizak omer muad heizik* — Levi claims the *muad* gored him, entitling him to full damages. *Ve-ha-mazik omer lo ki ela tam heizik* — Reuven says only the *tam* gored, so only half-damages apply. Again, *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* — Levi bears the burden.

### Multiple Damages/Damagers

The *mishnah* extends this to more complex configurations: two damaged oxen (one large, one small) and two goring oxen (one large, one small) belonging to Reuven and Levi respectively; or one *tam* and one *muad* among the goring oxen. Levi claims the arrangement most favorable to his recovery — the large gored the large, the small gored the small; or the *muad* gored the large and the *tam* gored the small. Reuven claims the opposite arrangement in each case. All of these scenarios are governed by the same principle: *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya*. The claimant must prove his preferred version of events and cannot collect on the more favorable scenario without doing so.

---

## Admitted Claim Debate

### Anti-Sumchos Position

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba observes that this *mishnah* as a whole is formulated as a refutation of Sumchos. *Cholkim alav chaverav al Sumchos* — Sumchos' colleagues disagree with him. *De-amar Sumchos: mamon ha-mutal be-safek cholkim* — Sumchos holds that whenever there is a genuine monetary doubt, you split the disputed amount between the parties. Sumchos does not require the objective doubt to arise from nothing — there must be some basis for it, some observable ambiguity that a neutral observer would recognize. In our *mishnah*, clearly something happened, and it is objectively uncertain which ox is responsible. Sumchos would say: ignore the claims and counterclaims, ignore *hamotzi mechavero*, and simply split it. The *mishnah* rejects this and insists that the claimant must prove his case.

### Sumchos Splits Even Bari

*Amar lei Rav Abba bar Mammal le-Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: amar Sumchos afilu bari ve-bari?* — Would Sumchos apply his splitting principle even when both parties are making definite claims — *bari ve-bari* — not merely saying "I don't know what happened" but actively asserting that they know exactly what occurred? Perhaps Sumchos's principle applies only when the parties themselves acknowledge uncertainty. When the *mazik* is making a firm, definite claim that he does not owe money, perhaps even Sumchos would respect the *mochezek* position and apply *hamotzi mechavero*. *Amar in: amar Sumchos afilu bari ve-bari* — the answer is yes: Sumchos applies his splitting principle even when both parties are making definite claims in direct contradiction of each other.

### Challenge to Recovery

This raises the question: since the *mishnah* is established as a case of *bari ve-bari* — as evidenced by the language *zeh omer shorkha heizik* and *zeh omer lo ki* — is the *mishnah*'s position simply that the *nizak* recovers nothing, or does the *nizak* at least recover something?

### Lesser Claim Recovery

*Matkif lah Rav Pappa* — Rav Pappa raises a challenge. If the *mishnah* is dealing with *bari ve-bari*, then consider its end section: the *nizak* claims the large ox gored him and seeks full half-damages from the large ox; the *mazik* claims the small one gored and argues the *nizak* is limited to the small ox. *Hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* — fine, the *nizak* cannot prove his larger claim. But can the *nizak* at least recover based on what the *mazik* himself conceded? After all, the *mazik* has admitted that one of his oxen gored — he is only disputing *which* one. Shouldn't the *nizak* be entitled to at least collect based on the *mazik*'s own concession?

### Wheat/Barley Analogy

Here the *gemara* introduces the case of *ta'ano chittin ve-hoda lo be-se'orin patur* — if I claim you owe me a pound of wheat and you admit only to a pound of barley, you owe me nothing. The logic is that my definite claim for wheat was an implicit rejection of barley as an acceptable substitute. I did not say "you owe me wheat, or barley, or anything of equivalent value." I said "you owe me wheat," which means "not barley." When you concede barley, you are admitting to something I never claimed, something I implicitly denied owing me. My *bari* claim for wheat actually forecloses my recovery of barley.

The same logic applies here. If the *nizak* says definitively that the large ox gored — and in the *tam* scenario, this is a claim about which specific property of the *mazik* he now has a lien on — he is implicitly saying the small ox did not gore. When the *mazik* concedes the small ox gored, he is conceding exactly what the *nizak* implicitly denied. Just as in the wheat-and-barley case, the *nizak*'s definite claim may preclude collection even on the *mazik*'s concession.

### Bari v'Bari Question

This leads to the question with which the *sugya* closes: is our *mishnah* in fact dealing with *bari ve-bari* — both parties making definite, mutually exclusive claims — or might it be dealing with *bari ve-shema* — the *mazik* making a definite claim while the *nizak* only claims it is possible? If the *nizak*'s claim is framed as *shema* — "perhaps" the large one gored — rather than a definite assertion, then the dynamic is entirely different, and the *nizak* may well be entitled to recover based on the *mazik*'s concession without running into the wheat-and-barley problem. We leave off here and will take up tomorrow the question of whether the *mishnah* is indeed *bari ve-bari* or *bari ve-shema*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 36

## Hamotzi vs. Sumchos

### Intro: Burden of Proof

The present sugya continues from the bottom of 35b and engages a *mishna* that establishes the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya*: the *nizak* who seeks to claim that a higher liability applies bears the burden of proof. The *gemara* notes that this ruling stands in direct tension with the position of *Sumchos*, who holds that in any case of objective doubt — *safek* — the disputed amount is split between the parties. The *gemara* therefore asks whether *Sumchos* would maintain his position of *chokim* even in a case of *bari ve-bari*, where both the *nizak* and the *mazik* each make definite, unequivocal claims — no, that happened; no, this happened — and concludes that he would. Even in *bari ve-bari*, *Sumchos* says you split, because the *safek* is objective regardless of how confident each party sounds. Our *mishna*, which insists on *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya*, is therefore in direct conflict with *Sumchos*.

### Bari vs. Shema

Once the *gemara* establishes that the *mishna* opposes *Sumchos* even in *bari ve-bari*, it turns to a related implication of the *mishna*'s language. The *mishna* seems to suggest that even if the *nizak* cannot prove his larger claim, he is at least entitled to collect whatever the *mazik* concedes. The *gemara* asks: if this is a case of *bari ve-bari* — where each party flatly rejects the other's account — why would the *nizak* be entitled to anything at all? If the *nizak* is claiming the *mazik*'s larger ox gored his ox, and the *mazik* says it was definitively the smaller one, then the *nizak* is actively rejecting the *mazik*'s own admission. This leads directly to the principle of *tanu chitin ve-hodo lo bise'orin*.

### Chitin v. Se'orin

*Rava bar Natan* teaches: if a claimant says "you owe me wheat" and the defendant says "I owe you only barley," the defendant is entirely exempt — *patur* — even from paying barley. The *gemara* here applies this principle: since the claimant is rejecting the defendant's concession, he cannot then turn around and collect based on it. The *tanu chitin ve-hodo lo bise'orin* case is taught explicitly in a *braita*, and *Rava bar Natan*'s innovation is that the defendant is *patur le-gamri* — completely exempt. One might have thought the ruling only meant the claimant cannot collect the wheat; he should still be entitled to the barley which was conceded. *Rava bar Natan* teaches that this is not so: since the claimant denied that he was owed barley, his concession is rejected and nothing is owed.

### Shor Tam Application

The *gemara* applies this logic to the *shor tam* cases in the *mishna*. If the *mazik* claims it was his smaller ox that gored and the *nizak* says no, it was definitely the larger one, the *nizak* cannot collect the smaller amount because his *bari* claim constitutes a rejection of the *mazik*'s admission. The *mishna*'s implication that the *nizak* collects at least based on what the *mazik* conceded must therefore be read as applying only when the *nizak* himself is making a *shema* claim — an uncertain claim — rather than a definite one.

The *gemara* asks: if the *mishna*'s implication of entitlement to the lesser amount requires the *nizak* to be saying *shema*, then who is saying *bari* and who is saying *shema*? The *gemara* considers and rejects the possibility that the *nizak* is saying *bari* and the *mazik* is saying *shema*, because in that configuration the *nizak* would still be saying definitively that he is owed the larger amount, while the *mazik* says only "maybe" — and in that case the *chitin ve-se'orin* problem resurfaces: if the *mazik* is saying *shema* about the large ox, has he truly conceded anything about the small one that the *nizak* can collect?

The *gemara* concludes: the case where the *mishna* implies the *nizak* collects at least the smaller amount must be where the *nizak* is saying *shema* — "I don't know, perhaps it was your larger one" — and the *mazik* is saying *bari*, definitively claiming it was the smaller one. In that configuration, the *nizak* is not rejecting the *mazik*'s admission; he is only uncertain about whether he is owed more. He therefore does not trigger the *chitin ve-se'orin* exemption and may collect based on what the *mazik* concedes.

A further wrinkle: the *gemara* notes a *braita* that states the *nizak* collects — *mishtalem al ha-katan min ha-gadol* — and resolves this with the answer *de-tafas*: the *nizak* had seized the ox. This is a somewhat difficult resolution. If *tefisa* — seizure — is sufficient to switch who is considered the *muchzak*, one might expect the *nizak* to be entitled to his full larger claim. The *gemara* limits recovery to the smaller conceded amount even after *tefisa*, which raises the question of precisely what *tefisa* accomplishes here.

### Sumchos Extreme Case

Having established that the *mishna*'s *seyfa* — where the *nizak* collects the lesser conceded amount — involves a case of *nizak shema* and *mazik bari*, the *gemara* asks whether *Sumchos* would say *chokim* even in this configuration. This is actually a more extreme version of the *Sumchos* position: the *mazik* is the *muchzak* — he has the money in his possession — and he is making a definite claim, while the *nizak* who seeks to extract money from him is only saying *shema*, he is not even certain of his own claim. Would *Sumchos* really say to split the disputed amount in a case where the claimant himself is uncertain and the one in possession is confident? That is a striking and counterintuitive position.

The *gemara* says yes, *Sumchos* would go that far. And the argument makes sense within *Sumchos*'s framework: if the *safek* is objective, the relative confidence of the parties is irrelevant to the question of how to distribute property in doubt.

### Mishna's Position

The *gemara* now resolves the full picture. The *mishna* contains cases in both directions: some where the *nizak* is saying *shema* and the *mazik* is saying *bari* (*nizak shema, mazik bari*), and others where the *nizak* is saying *bari* and the *mazik* is saying *shema* (*nizak bari, mazik shema*). The *gemara* notes that these are not two entirely different genres — in each, one party is *bari* and the other is *shema* — they are the same genre with the parties reversed, and *chada milta hi*, it is one type of case.

The *mishna*'s purpose in spanning both configurations is to make the most powerful possible case against *Sumchos*. The *reysha* — where the *nizak* is *bari* and the *muchzak* is saying *shema* — is precisely the scenario where *Sumchos*'s position has the strongest logical support: the *nizak* makes a definite claim, the person in possession is only uncertain, and yet the *mishna* still rules *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya*. Even there, the *nizak* bears the burden of proof and gets nothing if he cannot meet it.

At the same time, the *mishna*'s implication that in some cases the *nizak* does collect the lesser amount — where he himself was saying *shema* and is not rejecting the *mazik*'s concession — is preserved. The *mishna* thus navigates between rejecting *Sumchos* on one end and avoiding the full harshness of *chitin ve-se'orin* on the other, with the key variable being whether the *nizak*'s own claim is *bari* or *shema*.

---

## Shnayim Chayavim

### Both Oxen Present

The *mishna* states: if both oxen belonged to one person, *shnayhem chayavim* — both are liable. At first glance the meaning seems obvious: the owner of both oxen is clearly liable for the goring. But the precise phrasing — *shnayhem chayavim*, both of them are *chayav* — is curious, since in this case we do not know which of the two oxen actually gored. Saying both are liable requires explanation, because at most one of them did the damage.

The *gemara* draws a *diyuk* from the phrase *shnayhem chayavim*: the *mishna* is not simply saying the owner owes money. *Chayavim* refers to the oxen themselves, implying that both oxen must be present and available in order for the *nizak* to collect. *Tosafot* notes the *diyuk* — that the *mishna*'s language points to a rule about requiring both oxen to be on hand, even though in this particular case it is not literally true that both gored.

### Tam vs. Muad

The *gemara* raises the question of whether this case involves *tamim* or *muadim*. The *gemara* initially considers whether the *mishna* might be discussing *muad* oxen in the opening case. However, this is rejected: the *seifa* of the *mishna* debates whether the big ox or the small ox gored, and that debate would be irrelevant if the oxen were *muad*, since a *muad* owner pays full damages regardless of which ox caused the harm — what matters for a *muad* is the size of the damage suffered by the *nizak*, not which ox caused it. Since the *mishna* clearly cares which ox gored, it must be discussing *tamim*. The *gemara* therefore reads the opening case as *muadim* and the later case as *tamim*, then ultimately concludes the whole *mishna* addresses *tamim* oxen and invokes Rabbi Akiva's *shutfin* model.

### Akiva's Logic

The *gemara* concludes: *ela le-olam be-tamim ve-Rabbi Akiva hi de-amar shutfin ninhu* — the *mishna* always speaks of *tamim* oxen, and it follows Rabbi Akiva who holds that the *nizak* becomes a *shutaf* — a partner — in the goring ox. *Ve-taama de-itnayhu le-tarvayhu*: the reason the *nizak* is entitled to collect at all is because both oxen are still present. If both are alive and available, the *nizak* can say to the owner: one of these is partially mine, I have rights to one of them — you decide which one to give me, but you cannot deny that one of them is mine.

This is the correct reading of *shnayhem chayavim*: it is not that both oxen are each independently *chayav*. Rather, the presence of both together is what generates the obligation. If one of the oxen died or ran away, the *mazik* can say: perhaps the one that is gone was the one that gored you, and your lien — your partnership interest — was in that one. Since you cannot prove otherwise, *matzi amar lei zil ayisi raya de-hai tora azikach ve-ashalem lach* — go and prove that this living ox is the one that gored you, and I will pay. Without that proof, the *nizak* cannot collect.

### Yishmael vs. Akiva

The *gemara*'s attribution of the *mishna* to Rabbi Akiva rather than Rabbi Yishmael flows from a fundamental structural difference between their positions. Rabbi Yishmael holds that the relationship between the *nizak* and the *mazik* is one of *ba'al chov* — creditor and debtor. The *nizak* has a monetary claim, and the goring ox serves as the vehicle through which that claim is collected; the *nizak* holds a lien focused on the ox. Rabbi Akiva holds that the *nizak* becomes a *shutaf* — an actual co-owner — in the goring ox itself, up to the value of the half-damage owed.

The question of why the *mishna* cannot follow Rabbi Yishmael is sharpened here. If the *nizak* has a debt claim against the *mazik* — not merely an interest in the ox — then even if one of the two oxen dies or disappears, the debt remains. Why should the *nizak* lose his claim? The *mazik* still owes him money. The *gemara* therefore says the *mishna* must be Rabbi Akiva: under the partnership model, the *nizak*'s entire entitlement is tied to his co-ownership of a specific ox, and if that ox is gone, there is nothing left to collect from.

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* engages a significant dispute here with *Rashi*. *Rashi* understands that according to Rabbi Yishmael, the *nizak* is not limited to collecting from the ox alone; since the relationship is one of debt, the *nizak* retains the right to collect money from the *mazik* even if the ox is no longer available. Under *Rashi*'s reading, losing the ox does not extinguish the *nizak*'s rights — he can simply demand payment.

*Tosafot* disagrees and marshals a powerful proof from elsewhere in the *gemara*, which states that according to Rabbi Yishmael, if the *mazik* slaughtered the goring ox — *shachto* — the act stands and the *nizak* loses his money. *Tosafot* asks: if the *nizak* truly has an independent debt claim under Rabbi Yishmael, why is he left empty-handed when the ox is slaughtered? Let him simply demand cash payment instead. The fact that the *gemara* does not propose this answer indicates that under Rabbi Yishmael as well, the *nizak*'s right is fundamentally tied to the ox. The *mazik* may choose to pay cash in order to buy out the *nizak*'s lien, but the *nizak* cannot independently demand cash — his right runs against the ox and only against the ox.

*Tosafot* therefore concludes that it is *pashita* — self-evident — that under Rabbi Yishmael, if one of the two oxen is gone, the *nizak* loses out, because the *mazik* can simply assert that the departed ox was the one that gored. The *gemara*'s attribution of the *mishna* to Rabbi Akiva is needed not because Rabbi Yishmael would produce a different result in this case, but because Rabbi Akiva's *shutfin* model might have suggested a different outcome — namely that the *nizak*'s established co-ownership creates a *chazaka* — a presumption — entitling him to collect even if one ox is gone. The *mishna* therefore needs to specify that Rabbi Akiva's rule too requires both oxen to be present.

---

## Multiple Gorings

### R. Meir: Last First

A new *mishna* introduces a case of sequential gorings: an ox gores four or five oxen one after another — *ze achar ze*. The *tanna kamma*, identified as Rabbi Meir, rules *acharon acharon nishkar*: the last victim collects first. Whatever remains in the value of the goring ox after the last victim is paid goes to the second-to-last, then to the one before that, and so on, working backward. The logic and structural justification of this position become the subject of extensive *gemara* analysis below.

### R. Shimon: Partners

Rabbi Shimon takes a fundamentally different approach, one rooted in the partnership model of Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Shimon presents the case numerically: an ox worth 200 gores an ox worth 200, and the carcass of the victim is worth nothing. The *nizak* takes 100 — half the damage — and becomes a partner in the goring ox to the extent of 100. Now this jointly owned ox — belonging to both the original owner and the first victim — turns and gores another ox worth 200. The last victim takes 100 from the jointly owned ox. Whatever remains of the joint ownership is split proportionally. The second goring is collected equally from both co-owners of the ox at the time of the second goring. And so on: each subsequent goring is distributed proportionally according to each party's ownership share in the ox at the moment of impact.

Concretely, in a case of three sequential gorings where all oxen are worth 200 and all carcasses are worth nothing: the third victim gets a full 100; the second victim, who owns half the ox, and the first victim and original owner who each own a quarter, each receive 50 and 25 and 25 respectively from the third goring's distribution — but accounting as well for what each had already collected. The *mishna* states that after three gorings the last victim takes 100, the one before him takes 50, and the first two each take a *dinar zahav* — 25 *zuz*.

### Awareness Caveat

*Tosafot* raises an important qualification to Rabbi Shimon's model. The *mishna* presents a situation where each successive *nizak* automatically becomes a part-owner of the ox and thereby assumes responsibility for its future conduct. But *Tosafot* asks: how can a person become liable for an ox's future gorings if he had no knowledge that he had become a co-owner, or if he had no practical ability to watch the animal?

*Tosafot* admits this creates a *teima* — a difficulty — and offers a somewhat forced answer: since the new co-owner has the ability in principle to bring witnesses and prove his ownership and win in court, his responsibility for the ox begins from the moment the goring occurs. This is so even though the court case has not yet been adjudicated and the co-ownership has not yet been formally established — *kivan she-yesh be-yado le-havi edim le-altar*, since he has the capacity to bring witnesses immediately, his liability attaches now. The retroactive legal establishment of ownership creates retroactive liability.

Crucially, however, *Tosafot* makes clear that this reasoning applies only when the new co-owner had actual knowledge of what occurred and had the practical ability to watch the ox. If he was not in a position to guard it — if he was elsewhere, or unaware — then the subsequent goring cannot be charged to his portion. In that case, the full liability falls on *Reuven*, the original owner. The new co-owner is in the position of an *oneis* — someone facing an unavoidable circumstance — and bears no liability for what he could not have prevented.

### Attribution to Amoraim

The *gemara* asks whose opinion is reflected in the opening case of the *mishna* — the *acharon acharon nishkar* rule of Rabbi Meir. It observes that this case fits neither Rabbi Yishmael nor Rabbi Akiva cleanly. Under Rabbi Yishmael's debt model, the first victim should have the earliest lien and therefore the strongest priority claim — *rishon rishon nishkar* would be the expected rule, not *acharon acharon nishkar*. Under Rabbi Akiva's partnership model, whenever there is a remainder after paying the most recent victim, it should be distributed to all prior co-owners proportionally — not funneled entirely to the immediately preceding victim.

*Rava* resolves this by saying the opening of the *mishna* — Rabbi Meir's position — follows Rabbi Yishmael, but with a specific mechanism: *tafas nizak ligbot heimenu ve-na'asa lo ke-shomer sachar le-nezikin*. Each *nizak*, upon being damaged, seizes the goring ox in order to secure his lien — analogous to a creditor taking collateral. By taking possession of property in which he has a monetary interest and from which he benefits by being able to secure his debt, the *nizak* becomes a *shomer sachar* — a paid watchman — with respect to the ox. As a *shomer sachar*, he bears liability for damage the ox causes while under his watch.

The closing of the *mishna* — Rabbi Shimon's position — follows Rabbi Akiva: the victims become actual partners, and the distribution flows accordingly.

### Seizure & Shomer

The mechanism *Rava* describes requires careful unpacking. Under Rabbi Yishmael's model, when *Shimon*'s ox is gored by *Reuven*'s ox, *Shimon* acquires a lien on *Reuven*'s ox. *Shimon* then physically seizes that ox — *tafas* — to prevent *Reuven* from removing it before *Shimon* can collect. By holding a piece of property in which he has a legal interest and from which he derives the benefit of secured collection, *Shimon* takes on the legal status of a *shomer sachar*. A *shomer sachar* is liable for damage the object under his care causes to others.

When the seized ox subsequently gores *Levi*'s ox, *Levi* collects his full amount from *Shimon* — who, as *shomer sachar*, was responsible for the ox at the time of the second goring. Whatever portion of the ox's value *Shimon* held by virtue of his lien, *Levi* collects from that. Then *Levi* seizes the ox, becomes the new *shomer sachar*, and when the ox gores *Yehuda*, *Yehuda* collects from *Levi*.

The *gemara* challenges this account: if there is any remainder after *Levi* collects, why does that remainder go to *Shimon* (the immediately preceding victim) rather than all the way back to *Reuven* (the original owner)? The *gemara* answers — as articulated by *Ravina* — that the remainder goes back to whoever held it. The original 150 that *Reuven* owned and was never seized by *Shimon* always belonged to *Reuven*. But the 100 that *Shimon* seized — that is what gets swapped through the chain. Each successive victim collects his portion from the immediately preceding party's seized share, and any excess of that seized share returns to the party who held it, not to *Reuven*.

### Remainder Rules

To fully appreciate the distribution mechanics, one must track carefully the size of each victim's damage relative to the ox's value. When each goring produces the same damage, the shares simply pass down the chain and any remainder flows back in strict sequence. When damages differ — when, say, the first goring entitles the *nizak* to 150 and the second goring entitles the subsequent *nizak* to only 100 — then the second *nizak* takes his 100 from the first *nizak*'s 150, and the first *nizak* retains the remaining 50. The third *nizak* then collects from whoever holds shares at the moment of the third goring, and any leftover from their portions returns to them.

The critical point *Ravina* adds is that *im yesh motar be-nizakav yachzir le-shel lifanav* — if there is a leftover within the damage distribution, it returns to the one who preceded. This is because the chain of *tefisa* and *shomer sachar* liability creates a sequential trail of ownership: each *nizak* takes over the seized portion from the one before him, and excess beyond what was owed returns to the source. Whatever *Reuven* owned and was never touched in the *tefisa* chain returns to *Reuven* throughout.

The *gemara* concludes by confirming that the *reysha* of the *mishna* reflects Rabbi Yishmael via the *tefisa*-and-*shomer sachar* mechanism, while the *seifa* reflects Rabbi Akiva's partnership model. Although it is slightly surprising that Rabbi Meir — himself a student of Rabbi Akiva — sides with Rabbi Yishmael's framework, and Rabbi Shimon — also a student of Rabbi Akiva — sides with Rabbi Akiva, *Shmuel* already anticipated this kind of difficulty: *shevok masnisin ve-ta batrai* — set aside the expectation that students must follow their teacher's framework, and follow the analysis as it leads.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 37

## Boshet & Coin Values

### Mishna Boshet

The Gemara opens by citing a *mishna* from *Hachovel*: *hatokeia lachaveiro notein lo sela* — one who strikes his friend (near the ear, according to Rashi) must pay a *sela* as the assessment for *boshet*, for the embarrassment and shame. Any distinct damages — loss of hearing, medical expenses, and the like — would be assessed separately. This *sela* represents the standard *mishna*ic figure for *boshet*. Rabbi Yehuda then cites Rabbi Yose HaGlili, who assesses it at a *maneh*, which is 100 *zuz* — twenty-five times the amount of the *tanna kamma*, who assessed it at four *zuz*. Tosafot suggests that perhaps the *tanna kamma* was speaking of the minimum assessment for a person of low social standing, while Rabbi Yose HaGlili was addressing a person of high social standing. That distinction, however, is not the focus of the Gemara here.

### Sela Tzori v. Medina

The Gemara presents a case: a certain person struck his friend. Rashi notes immediately that *boshet* is a *knas* and is not adjudicated in Bavel, so Rashi understands the case as one involving *tofas* — seizure of the payment — though the details are not fully clear. Rav Tuvia bar Matna sent the matter before Rav Yosef and posed the following question: when the *mishna* says *sela*, does it mean *sela Tzori* or *sela Medina*? This is a genuinely confusing question because the same coin names were used across two different monetary systems. A *sela Medina* is one-eighth of a *sela Tzori* — which is itself four *zuz* — making a *sela Medina* worth only half a *zuz*. The difference between the two systems is thus a factor of eight in terms of the *sela*, or equivalently, a factor of two in terms of the *zuz*. Rav Yosef responds: we can infer the answer from the *mishna* about the goring ox.

### Ox Mishna Evidence

In the *mishna* about the goring ox, the damages are distributed in amounts denominated in *dinar zahav*, a gold *dinar* worth twenty-five *zuz*, with amounts breaking down as one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, and twenty-five. The Gemara asks: if a *tanna* were ever prepared to employ the coinage of *sela Medina*, why did the *mishna* not include the case of the ox goring a fifth time? In that scenario, the distribution would eventually yield a figure of twelve and a half *zuz*. If *sela Medina* — a half-*zuz* — were an acceptable denomination in Tannaic discourse, the *tanna* could have expressed that amount as "twelve *zuz* and a *sela*," avoiding fractional language. The presumption is that the *tanna* did not wish to speak in halves, which would mean he would never use *sela Medina* language at all, since its value is precisely a half-*zuz*. If one is in the currency system of *Tzur*, the only way to express a half-*zuz* is to say "half a *zuz*." If one were operating in *Medina* terms, one could say "a *sela*" to mean that amount — but if such language is never used, it proves that the Tannaim always refer to *sela Tzori*.

The Gemara entertains a challenge: *tanna ki rochla lisne v'leizel* — is the *tanna* like a merchant who must enumerate every possible case? The fact that the *mishna* stopped after four gorings does not mean the *tanna* committed himself to covering all possibilities.

### Tzori vs. Medina

The resolution is drawn from a ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *kol kesef ha'amur ba-Torah kesef Tzori* — whenever the Torah specifies a monetary amount, it is denominated in *sela Tzori*. And rabbinic assessments — *shel divreihem* — are denominated in *kesef Medina*. The *mishna*'s assessment of *boshet*, being a rabbinic assessment of damages rather than a Torah-mandated sum, is therefore expressed in *sela Medina*, which equals half a *zuz*. The answer to Rav Tuvia bar Matna's question is accordingly that the *mishna* is using *sela Medina*, and the actual payment is only half a *zuz* — not four *zuz*.

This distinction carries significant practical implications. The Torah, for instance, requires *mohar habetulot* of fifty *kesef*, which on the *Tzori* system yields 200 *zuz*. Yet there is a well-known debate in the Gemara in Ketubot regarding whether *ketubah* is *d'oraita* or *d'rabanan*. Those who held *ketubah* to be rabbinic — a widespread position in Sfarad — interpreted the fifty *kesef* through the *Medina* lens, arriving at a *ketubah* worth only 25 *zuz*. Those who held *ketubah* to be biblical maintained it at 200 *zuz*. The result was that the value of the *ketubah* in Sfarad was one-eighth what it was in Ashkenaz. The HaRosh, who came from Ashkenaz and lived in Sfarad, faced the tension acutely: Ashkenazic *ketubot* include the phrase *d'chazi lichi mid'oraita*, while Sfaradic *ketubot* omit *mid'oraita*. The HaRosh resolved this by arguing that even if the *ketubah* is *d'rabanan*, the term *mid'oraita* is intended to signal that the amount is denominated in *kesef Tzori* — 200 *zuz*, not 25. Tosafot, by contrast, argues that the biblical origin of the fifty *kesef* figure determines the denomination regardless of the *d'oraita*/*d'rabanan* debate.

### Chanan Bisha Case

Following the ruling that *boshet* is assessed in *sela Medina*, the Gemara presents the case of *Chanan Bisha* — "Chanan the wicked" — who struck a man and was ordered by Rav Huna to pay half a *zuz*. Chanan Bisha had a *zuz* that was worn and rubbed down, and he sought to exchange it for the required payment. No merchant would accept the degraded coin. So he simply struck the man again and handed him the whole *zuz*. The punchline is pointed: when the penalty for striking someone amounts to only half a *zuz*, it may not be worth the trouble of finding change.

### Tosafot Transfer

The preceding case raises a prior legal point that Tosafot addresses. When the victim in the first case declared "give it to the poor," Rav Yosef responded: *kvar zachu bei ani'im* — the poor have already acquired it. But this is puzzling. The money was still in the pocket of the *mazik*; no physical transfer had taken place. How do the victim's words effect a transfer?

Rav Yosef's answer is *yad ani'im anan* — we, the rabbis, stand as the hand of the poor. Rashi clarifies that Rav Yosef himself was a *gabbai tzedakah*, and since the matter was adjudicated before him, when the victim said "give it to the poor" in Rav Yosef's presence, Rav Yosef could act as the representative of the poor and acquire it on their behalf. This is grounded in the principle stated by Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name that orphans do not require a *pruzbul*, because *beis din* is always presumed to act in their interests — as the Baraita of Rami bar Chama states, *Rabban Gamliel u-veiso aviahem shel yesomim hayu*, Rabban Gamliel and his court were as fathers to orphans.

Tosafot presses further. Why is *yad ani'im anan* even necessary? If a person announces he will give *tzedakah*, that itself becomes like a *neder* and should obligate him. Once he said "give it to the poor," why could he retract?

Tosafot answers by drawing an analogy to *hekdesh*: just as a person cannot consecrate something that has not yet come into his possession — *ein adam makdish davar she'lo ba l'olam* — so too one cannot transfer *tzedakah* obligations over money that is not yet in one's possession. The half-*zuz* had not yet been paid to the victim; it was still owed by the *mazik*. The victim therefore lacked the capacity to effect a transfer of ownership to the poor. What the words *could* do, says Tosafot, is create a personal obligation: had the victim said "when I receive this payment I will give it to *tzedakah*," that would function as a *neder* and bind him. But the victim did not say that. He said *tnahu la-ani'im* — "give it to the poor" — intending to transfer the money directly, not to assume a personal pledge. Since the money was not yet in his possession, the words had no transferring effect. This is why *yad ani'im anan* was needed: only because Rav Yosef, as *gabbai tzedakah*, could stand in as the representative of the poor and effectuate the acquisition on their behalf.

---

## Muad Framework

### Muad Mishna

The Gemara now turns to a *mishna* concerning the *muad*, the habitually vicious animal. The *mishna* states: *shor she'haya muad shehu muad l'mino ve'eino muad l'she'eino mino* — an ox that has become *muad* for goring its own kind is not necessarily *muad* for goring other kinds. Similarly, something that is *muad* for goring people is not necessarily *muad* for goring animals; something *muad* for goring small animals is not necessarily *muad* for goring large ones. For whatever category it has established a pattern, it pays full damages; for whatever category it has not established a pattern, it pays half damages. Something can gore a hundred times across a broad range of targets and yet only be *muad* for specific categories — a question the Gemara will explore at length.

### Shabbat Question

The *mishna* records that the students said to Rabbi Yehuda: suppose an animal gored on *Shabbos* and not on the weekday — what is the law? The question, at its core, is how formalist the system is. Is it sufficient that three gorings occurred on *Shabbos*, even though there is no obvious reason why an animal would confine its viciousness to one day of the week? Or do we require some causal logic?

Rabbi Yehuda ruled: *l'shabbasos meshalem nezek shalem, v'liyamos hachol meshalem chatzi nezek* — for *Shabbos* goring it pays full damages, for weekday goring it pays half. Rashi and Tosafot, however, are not entirely comfortable with pure formalism here. Rashi explains that *Shabbos* is genuinely different: the animal has a day off, is idle, and grows restless — *batel mimmellacha v'zacha da'ato alav*. Tosafot cites the Yerushalmi, which explains that on *Shabbos* people wear unfamiliar fine clothing, making them less recognizable to the animal and thus more likely to provoke it. In other words, Rashi and Tosafot understand Rabbi Yehuda's ruling not as pure pattern-formalism but as grounded in a real behavioral distinction between *Shabbos* and weekdays.

The *mishna* then addresses reversion: *eimasai hu tam?* — when would such an animal revert to *tam* status? The answer is *misheyachzor bo gimmel yemei Shabbosos* — once it has been given three opportunities, three *Shabbosos*, in the same circumstances that habituated it, and has not gored. This mirrors the *Rambam*'s understanding of *ba'al teshuva*: one confronts the same situation and does not repeat the transgression. The *shor* performs, as it were, its own *teshuva* by demonstrating restraint under identical conditions three consecutive times.

### Vav Question

A textual dispute now surfaces. *Rav Zevid amar ve'eino muad tnan; Rav Pappa amar eino muad tnan* — Rav Zevid holds that the *mishna* reads *ve'eino muad* (with a *vav*), making it descriptive; Rav Pappa holds that it reads *eino muad* (without a *vav*), making it prescriptive.

### Zevid v. Pappa

The dispute is not merely textual — it reflects a fundamental disagreement about how *muad* status generalizes.

According to Rav Pappa, reading *eino muad* without the *vav*: the *mishna* is stating a legal rule. If an animal gored three oxen, it is *muad* only for oxen, not for other animals. One identifies the evidenced pattern and limits *muad* status to precisely what has been demonstrated. There is no generalization. The animal is *muad* only for what it has concretely habituated itself to.

According to Rav Zevid, reading *ve'eino muad* with the *vav*: the *mishna* is describing a specific scenario. The standard rule is that once an animal gores three times — regardless of what it gored — it becomes *muad* for everything. The *mishna* is presenting an exceptional case: an animal that happened to be *muad* for its own kind and happened not to be *muad* for other kinds, because it actually encountered other animals on multiple occasions and refrained from goring them. The *vav* signals that the *mishna* is telling us a description of a case, not a rule limiting the scope of *muad*.

The practical stakes are significant. Under Rav Pappa, the scope of *muad* is always limited to the specific pattern evidenced. Under Rav Zevid, *muad* is presumed general unless actively rebutted by demonstrated restraint.

### Mishna Structure

The Gemara attempts to determine from the *mishna*'s structure which reading is correct.

Rav Zevid derives his position from the *seifa* of the *mishna*, which states that something is *muad l'ketanim ve'eino muad l'gedolim* — *muad* for small animals and not for large. On his reading, the *mishna* is describing a specific case in which the animal happened not to gore large ones when it had the opportunity. The implicit teaching is that in a standard case, even if an animal only gored small animals, we would assume it becomes *muad* for large ones as well — a *chiddush*, since one might have thought that a bully picks on the weak but not the strong. The *mishna* is telling us that the default is always generalization, and this particular case is an exception where the animal had demonstrated it would not attack large ones.

Rav Pappa responds: that *chiddush* is necessary even on his reading. One might have thought that once an animal has shown a predisposition within a category — say, goring small oxen — it would generalize at least within that *min*, attacking large oxen too. The *mishna* tells you it does not. Even the jump from small to large within the same species requires concrete demonstration. So the *seifa* is informative regardless of which reading one adopts.

Rav Pappa's own evidence comes from the *reisha*, which states *muad l'adam eino muad l'behema* — *muad* for goring people is not *muad* for goring animals. On his reading this is a legal rule: *muad* for one category does not extend to another. This is a striking *chiddush*, because one would reason by *kal vachomer* that an animal willing to gore a human being would certainly gore an animal, which it has less reason to fear. The *mishna* is telling us that no such generalization operates.

Rav Zevid responds: if the *mishna* were merely describing an exceptional scenario with a *vav*, one would not need to specify *muad l'adam ve'eino muad l'behema*. Since under his reading the standard case already generalizes from *behema* to *behema*, the case of generalizing from *adam* to *behema* would be obvious — it requires far less logic. The only reason the *mishna* mentions it is to address the case of *reversion*: an animal that had been *muad* for both *adam* and *behema*, then saw three animals and refrained, may have reverted its *muad* status for *behema* while remaining *muad* for *adam*. The *mishna* is telling us that such partial reversion is valid — that *hazara b'behema hazara hi*, even without demonstrated reversion from *adam*.

### Sumchus Baraita

A *baraita* is now introduced: *Sumchus omer muad l'adam muad l'behema mikal vachomer* — Sumchus says that if something is *muad* for goring humans, it is certainly *muad* for goring animals, by *kal vachomer*. The logic is self-evident: if it will gore a person, it will certainly gore an animal. The *baraita* implies that the *tanna kamma* of the *mishna* held the opposite — that *muad l'adam* does not make it *muad l'behema*. This seemingly confirms that the *tanna kamma* is reading *eino muad* without the *vav*, as a legal rule, in line with Rav Pappa.

### Teshuva Focus

Rav Zevid deflects: Sumchus is not disputing the initial establishment of *muad* status, which both agree generalizes. The dispute is over *reversion* — specifically, the scenario established earlier, where an animal was *muad* for both *adam* and *behema*, then encountered animals three times without goring. The *tanna kamma* holds that *hazara b'behema hazara hi* — reversion demonstrated for animals is valid reversion, even though the animal has not reverted from goring people. Sumchus disagrees: *mikal vachomer*, since it has not reverted from goring people — the harder thing — it has not truly reverted from goring animals. *Hazara d'behema lav hazara hi*. The reversion is not sincere if the more aggressive impulse remains unreformed.

Under Rav Zevid's framework, the initial establishment of *muad* always generalizes; the debate between *tanna kamma* and Sumchus is thus narrowly about the mechanism of reversion.

### Shabbat Revisited

The Gemara adduces evidence from the *Shabbos* case in the *mishna*. The text reads: *harei zeh muad l'shabbasos ve'eino muad l'yamos hachol* — he is *muad* for *Shabbosos* and not for weekdays. *Rav Zevid amar ve'eino muad tnan* — with the *vav*, it is descriptive: the students are presenting Rav Yehuda with a scenario (the animal gored on *Shabbos* and not on the weekday) and asking the *halacha*. Rabbi Yehuda confirms it. This reading makes sense: the *shayilu* — they were asking — and *hu nami ka mehadar lehu* — he was responding to their question.

But if the *mishna* reads *eino muad* without a *vav*, as Rav Pappa would have it, then the students are not posing a question — they are already stating a ruling: *muad l'shabbasos eino muad l'yamos hachol*. And then what is Rabbi Yehuda responding to? *Agmurei hu d'ka megamrei lei* — are they teaching *him* a *halacha*? That makes no sense. The structure of the *mishna* as a dialogue between students and Rabbi Yehuda strongly supports Rav Zevid's reading: with the *vav*, it is a question; without the *vav*, there is no question to answer.

Rav Yannai adds that one can also infer this from the *reisha*. After enumerating all the cases — *muad* for this and not for that — the *mishna* concludes: *es shehu muad lo meshalem nezek shalem v'es she'eino muad lo meshalem chatzi nezek*, the thing it is *muad* for pays full, the thing it is not *muad* for pays half. If the preceding clauses were already prescriptive rulings — *muad l'adam eino muad l'behema*, etc. — then this concluding line adds nothing. By daf 37 of this tractate, no reader needs to be told that a *muad* pays full and a *tam* pays half. But if the preceding clauses describe behavior, this final line is necessary: it tells you what follows legally from the pattern that was described. Thus the *mishna*'s structure as a whole corroborates Rav Zevid.

The Gemara notes, however: *ve'im timtzi lomar nami isa l'Rav Pappa* — even so, the Gemara does not abandon Rav Pappa's framework entirely, because it is Rav Pappa's position that generates all the interesting questions about pattern identification that follow.

---

## Pattern Scope

### Mixed Animals

Granting Rav Pappa's framework for the purposes of inquiry, the Gemara proceeds: *nagach shor chamor vegamal na'aseh muad lakol* — if an ox gored a *shor*, a *chamor*, and a *gamal*, it becomes *muad* for all animals. The principle under Rav Pappa is to identify the smallest level of abstraction that contains all the observed gorings as a common denominator. Here the three animals are of distinct species, and the common category encompassing all of them is simply *behema*, or perhaps all large animals. One might ask whether this would extend to *adam* as well, or whether it would apply to small animals — and the answer would depend on whether the three observed victims were of comparable size and whether people had been gored as well.

The *Rif* rules on the basis of these discussions that the *halacha* follows Rav Pappa, because all the subsequent cases of pattern identification work most naturally within his framework.

### Alternating Gores

A *baraita* teaches: if an animal saw an ox and gored, saw an ox and did not gore, saw an ox and gored, saw an ox and did not gore, saw an ox and gored, saw an ox and did not gore — *na'aseh muad l'sirugin l'shorim* — it becomes *muad* for goring every other ox. The pattern of alternation is itself recognized as a *muad* pattern. If it then gores two oxen in a row, only the second goring triggers full liability — the first, as an "off" event in the alternating cycle, is still only *chatzi nezek*. A second *baraita* extends this: if the alternating pattern involves six different animals — ox, donkey, horse, camel, mule, wild ass, alternating gore and no-gore — *na'aseh muad l'sirugin l'khol*, it becomes *muad* for alternately goring any type of animal. The level of abstraction again captures the full breadth of what was observed.

### Teiku Cases

The Gemara raises a series of unresolved questions. Suppose an animal gored: ox, ox, ox, donkey, camel. Does the first three gorings — all oxen — fix its *muad* status as *muad l'shorim*, such that the subsequent donkey and camel gorings are insufficient to upgrade it to *muad lakol* (since two additional species are not yet three)? Or do we look at the last three — ox, donkey, camel — and declare it *muad lakol*?

The reverse is also asked: chamor, gamal, shor, shor, shor. Do we take the first three — chamor, gamal, shor — yielding *muad lakol*, and disregard that the last three are all oxen? Or are we drawn to the grouping of three oxen, establishing it as only *muad l'shorim*?

The Gemara applies the same uncertainty to days of the week. Suppose the animal gored on *Shabbos*, *Shabbos*, *Shabbos*, then Sunday, Monday. Does the first three establish *muad* for *Shabbos* alone, leaving Sunday and Monday insufficient for a pattern of their own? Or do we take the last three — *Shabbos*, Sunday, Monday — and declare it *muad* for all days? The reverse is similarly posed: Thursday, Friday, *Shabbos*, *Shabbos*, *Shabbos*. Do we take the first three, establishing *muad* for all days of the week? Or are we drawn to the grouping of three consecutive *Shabbasos*, yielding *muad* only for *Shabbos*?

All of these remain unresolved — *teiku*. The underlying question of whether the determining grouping is the first three gorings or the last three is not settled.

One should note that for any of these cases involving interim days, the analysis assumes the animal had no opportunity to gore on those days — that is, it was not presented with an ox on Sunday through Friday. If it encountered animals during those intervals and refrained, that would separately bear on its reversion from *muad* status for those days.

### Monthly Dates

The Gemara now presents a case that reveals just how thoroughly formalist the system becomes: an ox gored on the 15th of one month, the 16th of the next, and the 17th of the following month. Here there is no intuitive behavioral explanation for the pattern — unlike *Shabbos*, for which Rashi and Tosafot offered reasons involving the animal's idleness or the unfamiliar clothing of people. Nevertheless, the *muad* framework apparently applies even to such arbitrary-seeming date sequences.

The specific question raised is whether the pattern of "plus one day each successive month" — fifteenth, sixteenth, seventeenth — constitutes an established *muad* pattern, and if so, what it predicts for the following month. The problem is that while three data points exist, the "plus one" increment has only been observed twice: between the fifteenth and sixteenth, and between the sixteenth and seventeenth. The Gemara notes that this parallels a debate between Rav and Shmuel in the laws of *vesset* in *Niddah* — a woman's established cycle for the onset of her period. *Ra'ata yom tes-vav be-chodesh zeh, yom tes-zayin be-chodesh zeh, yom yod-zayin be-chodesh zeh* — she saw on the fifteenth of one month, the sixteenth of the next, the seventeenth of the next. Rav holds *kave'ah lah vesset* — she has established a cycling pattern, and next month she anticipates the eighteenth. Shmuel holds *ad she-teshalesh b'dilug* — she needs three instances of the incremental shift, meaning four months total, before the pattern is fixed. The same dispute applies to the goring ox.

### Shofar Example

Rava teaches: if an animal heard a *shofar* blast and gored, heard a *shofar* and gored, heard a *shofar* and gored — *na'aseh muad l'shofaros* — it is now *muad* to gore every time it hears a *shofar*. One might have thought this is obvious. But the Gemara raises a possible objection: perhaps the first time should not count, since the *shofar* blast was so startling and disorienting that the goring was essentially a reflexive fright response — *siyuta b'alma* — and does not yet establish a pattern of habituated vicious behavior. The Gemara rejects this: we still count all three instances, and three times is three times.

### Formalist Conclusion

By the end of the *sugya*, the system has moved decisively toward formalism. The question of *Shabbos*, which Rashi and Tosafot explained on behavioral grounds, gives way to a framework in which patterns of goring on specific calendar dates — the fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth of the month — are treated as legally constitutive *muad* patterns without any causal explanation. The analysis under Rav Pappa's framework is not asking *why* the animal gores in a given pattern; it is asking only *what* pattern the evidence supports, and identifying the smallest level of abstraction that captures the observed data.

As one might ask: what counts as a pattern? It cannot be that any three numbers constitute one. There must be some criterion of simplicity or describability — a pattern like *n*, *n*+1, *n*+2 is recognizable; a sequence like 15, 117, 34 is not. The Gemara does not spell out this criterion explicitly, but the cases it considers — same-day-of-week gorings, consecutive monthly dates, alternating gorings — all share the quality of being simply and uniformly describable. That implicit standard of what constitutes a recognizable pattern appears to be the unspoken logic underlying the entire formalist approach.

---
