# Bava Kamma 38

## Hekdesh Exemptions

### Overview & Context

Daf 38 is a particularly central page of Talmud, devoted in large part to the discussion of legal obligations between Jews and non-Jews. But the daf opens — on 37b — with a *mishna* concerning *hekdesh*, Temple property, and its relationship to the ordinary laws of goring. What follows is a daf that moves from technical hermeneutics to broad questions of theology, universalism, and the moral complexity of particularistic law.

### Mishna: Hekdesh Cases

The *mishna* states: if the ox of a layperson (*hedyot*) gores an ox belonging to *hekdesh*, or if an ox of *hekdesh* gores that of a layperson, both parties are exempt from payment — *patur* in both directions. The verse cited is *shor re'ehu* — "the ox of his neighbor" (Shemot 21:35) — which the *mishna* reads as excluding *hekdesh*: the Temple is not your *re'ehu*, not your fellow, and therefore the entire *parasha* of liability does not apply. One might have assumed that *hekdesh* would always enjoy a privileged position and be entitled to compensation. Nevertheless, on the basis of this *pasuk*, the exemption runs in both directions.

A practical question presents itself: what does the *beit hamikdash* do with an ox that has been killed? It sells it — the ox passes out of *hekdesh* status, is redeemed into *chulin*, and the proceeds go to the Temple treasury. Not every ox belonging to the Temple is a *korban*; oxen might be donated or held as an asset of the Temple's estate.

### Censorship & Terminology

Before proceeding to the *mishna*'s second case, a note on textual history is essential. The printed *girsa* of the *mishna* uses the word *kena'ani* — "Canaanite" — where the original text almost certainly read *nochri* or *goy*. The standard term for non-Jew in the Talmud is either *nochri*, drawn from the *Torah* itself (*m'chor l'nochri*), or *goy*, a more rabbinic term, both of which are simply neutral words meaning "foreigner."

The word *akum* — an acronym for *ovdei kochavim u'mazalot*, worshippers of stars and constellations — entered the Talmud through a process of self-censorship. In the Middle Ages, when Jewish converts to Christianity informed the Church about passages in the Talmud that were unfavorable to non-Jews, the Church began censoring and burning the Talmud. To preempt further persecution, Jewish communities replaced sensitive terms like *nochri* and *goy* with *akum*, allowing the argument that such passages referred only to ancient pagan star-worshippers and not to contemporary Christians. The Church, of course, eventually reinterpreted *akum* as a reference to their own sacred figures and did not accept the explanation.

Crucially, the word *kena'ani* — "Canaanite" — is a signal of an even deeper layer of censorship. If a passage uses *kena'ani* rather than *akum*, it marks a text that was considered especially problematic. The original sources, as attested throughout the *Rishonim*, consistently have *nochri* or *goy*. What is printed is a medieval gloss. This context matters enormously for understanding the *sugya* that follows.

### Non-Jew Cases in Mishna

The *mishna* continues: if a Jew's ox gores the ox of a non-Jew (*nochri*, in the original text), the Jew is *patur* — exempt from payment. But if a non-Jew's ox gores that of a Jew, whether the ox is a *tam* (an ox that has not yet gored three times and thus has no established pattern) or a *mu'ad* (a habitual gorer), the non-Jew pays full damages (*nezek shalem*). This assumes the non-Jew is living under Jewish jurisdiction and subject to the court system.

This asymmetry is striking and troubling in two respects. First, it is simply unfair: one party pays nothing, the other pays in full. Second, it departs from the ordinary graduated rule under which a *tam* ox pays only half-damages. The non-Jew pays full in either case. Both of these anomalies will receive sustained attention in the *Gemara*.

## Hekdesh Gemara Analysis

### Tanna Kamma vs. R. Shimon

The *Gemara* opens by noting that the *mishna*'s position — full mutual exemption between *hedyot* and *hekdesh* — is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya. A *beraita* records the dispute explicitly. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that both are *patur* in both directions, derived from *shor re'ehu* — the ox of your fellow — which excludes *hekdesh* categorically. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya disagrees: if *hekdesh* gores a layperson's ox, *hekdesh* is exempt; but if a layperson's ox gores that of *hekdesh*, the layperson pays full damages — *nezek shalem* — whether the ox is *tam* or *mu'ad*.

The *Gemara* immediately raises the logical problem: *mai kasavar Rabbi Shimon* — what exactly is Rabbi Shimon's position? The difficulty is one of internal consistency. If the word *re'ehu* is being read in a precise, limiting sense (*davka*) — such that only transactions involving a fellow layperson generate liability — then both directions should be *patur*. This is exactly the *Tanna Kamma*'s position. If, on the other hand, *re'ehu* is *lav davka* — not technically precise, merely a general expression — then liability should flow in both directions.

This is worth pausing over. We are trained to read words like *re'echa*, *amitecha*, and *re'ehu* as technically limiting terms that exclude non-members of one's legal community — typically understood to mean non-Jews, or here, *hekdesh*. But in the *peshat* of the *pesukim*, this is far from obvious. The word *achicha* — "your brother" — is clearly used in contrast to *nochri* in some places (as in *lanachri tashich u'le'achicha lo tashich*), but *re'echa* and *amitecha* in their plain meaning appear simply to mean "another person." Indeed, *ve'ahavta l're'echa k'mocha* — love your neighbor as yourself — clearly includes everyone. The *Gemara*'s willingness here to raise the possibility that *re'ehu* is *lav davka* is therefore significant: it acknowledges that sometimes such terms are not meant in a technically exclusive sense, even while the halakhic tradition generally reads them as exclusive.

The *Gemara* presses the logical problem further. The *Tanna Kamma* has a coherent position: *re'ehu* excludes *hekdesh* in both directions. But Rabbi Shimon reads it asymmetrically. The *Gemara* proposes that even if *re'ehu* is *davka* — and thus *hekdesh* is excluded from the *parasha* entirely, making *hekdesh* exempt when it gores — one might still derive a *chiyuv* on the layperson who gores *hekdesh* through a *kal vachomer*: if a layperson's ox is liable when it gores another layperson's ox, how much more so when it gores the property of *hekdesh*. The *Gemara* then invokes the rule of *dayo* — it is sufficient for the law derived by inference to be equivalent to its source — meaning that such a *kal vachomer* would yield only the same measure of liability as applies in the ordinary *hedyot*-to-*hedyot* case, namely half-damages for a *tam*. This does not produce "full damages always," which is what Rabbi Shimon requires.

### Reish Lakish Solution

The *Gemara*'s resolution comes from Reish Lakish: *hakol hayu bichlal nezek shalem* — the original default is that everyone always pays full damages. This requires understanding the structure of the *pesukim*. In the verse dealing with the *tam* ox (*ki yigach shor ish et shor re'ehu*), the word *re'ehu* appears — "his neighbor's ox." The *pasuk* for *mu'ad*, by contrast, does not contain *re'ehu*; it reads simply that if the ox is known to be a gorer, the owner pays in full (*shaleim yeshalem*).

Reish Lakish argues as follows: the baseline rule, before any scriptural qualification, is full damages for everyone in every case. The *Torah* then introduced the word *re'ehu* specifically in the context of the *tam* — to teach that when you gore *your neighbor's* ox and it is a first offense, you pay only half. This qualification applies only to *re'ehu*: only when goring the ox of a fellow layperson do you receive the concession of half-damages. When you gore *hekdesh* — which is not your *re'ehu* — you revert to the default of full damages, even for a *tam*. Similarly, because *hekdesh* is not included in the *re'ehu* framework at all, it never benefits from the reduction to half — it always starts and stays at full.

The difficulty that remains, however, is this: if the logic is that one reverts to full damages when dealing with *hekdesh*, why doesn't *hekdesh* also pay full when it gores a layperson? Reish Lakish's argument, as the *Gemara* frames it, explains the asymmetry in the direction of the layperson paying *hekdesh*, but not in the reverse. The *Gemara* notes that if the *Torah* had wanted to exclude liability entirely — including full damages — it should have written *re'ehu* by the *mu'ad* rather than by the *tam*. Since it placed *re'ehu* only by the reduced liability case, the implication is that the default of full payment remains operative for all cases not covered by *re'ehu*.

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi's answer addresses the remaining difficulty — why *hekdesh* does not pay full when it gores a layperson — by focusing on the word *ish* at the opening of the *parasha*: *ki yigach shor ish*. The verse says "if a man's ox gores." When a layperson's ox gores *hekdesh*, the ox belongs to an *ish* — a person — and it has not gored *shor re'ehu*, since *hekdesh* is not *re'ehu*. Because the ox has not gored *re'ehu*, the layperson does not receive the reduction to half-damages and must pay full. Now consider the reverse: when *hekdesh*'s ox gores, the verse's opening condition — *shor ish*, the ox of a person — is not even met, since *hekdesh* is not an *ish*. If the ox does not even enter the threshold of the *parasha* through its opening clause, then the entire framework of liability simply does not apply. There is nothing to start from — not full, not half — and therefore *hekdesh* pays nothing at all. Rashi's reading is somewhat compressed, and the asymmetry it produces is admittedly difficult. Nevertheless, the logic is that a layperson's ox can enter the *parasha* (as a *shor ish*) and then be denied the half-damages reduction (because it gored *hekdesh*, not *re'ehu*), whereas *hekdesh*'s ox cannot enter the *parasha* at all.

## Non-Jew Liability Rules

### Rav Yosef's Logic

The *Gemara* now turns to the parallel problem regarding the non-Jew, and the same structural difficulty arises. If *re'ehu* is *davka*, excluding the non-Jew, then the non-Jew's ox goring a Jew's should also be exempt. If *re'ehu* is *lav davka* — a general term — then a Jew who gores a non-Jew should also be liable. The pure logic of the *pasuk* cannot yield the asymmetric result the *mishna* states. Rav Yosef, therefore, abandons the attempt to derive the asymmetry from *re'ehu* alone and instead brings a different verse entirely to ground the rule. The *pasuk* in Habakkuk (3:6) reads: *amad vayimoded eretz ra'ah vayater goyim* — God stood and measured the earth, He saw and scattered the nations. Rav Yosef reads *vayater goyim* as meaning that God rendered the property of the nations permissible to Israel.

The reading is as follows: God measured the earth — meaning He assessed the moral state of the nations — saw that they had accepted upon themselves the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach* and had not fulfilled them, and therefore declared their property free, in effect imposing a divine fine. Since they forfeited their obligations under the moral law they had accepted, Israel is not required to pay compensation when their animals cause damage to non-Jewish property.

This raises an important question about the scope of *hitir mamonam l'Yisrael* — rendering their money permissible. Does this mean outright license to steal from non-Jews? Tosafot is explicit that the *peshat* of this *sugya* gives no such license. The permission operates specifically within the domain of damage law — the question of whether one is obligated to pay or entitled to demand compensation — not as a general authorization for theft. Indeed, Tosafot notes that according to the position that *gezel nochri assur* — stealing from a non-Jew is forbidden — one understands immediately why a special *pasuk* is needed here and why its application is limited to these damage cases. According to the opposing position that theft from non-Jews is permitted, the *pasuk* would be superfluous — which is itself a difficulty.

### Rav Abbahu & Sheva Mitzv…

Rav Abbahu derives the same rule from a different verse: *v'hofia me-Har Paran* — God revealed Himself from Mount Paran (Devarim 33:2). On Rashi's reading, this refers to the tradition that God offered the *Torah* to the nations at *Har Paran* and they refused — specifically because it contained prohibitions against violence and theft. The nations' refusal to accept the *Torah* demonstrates not merely that they declined additional obligations, but that they were unwilling to accept even the basic moral law. It is this that rendered their property permissible.

There is a question of what the underlying logic of *hitir mamonam* actually is. Is it simply a divine fine — a punishment, with Israel as the incidental beneficiary — or is there a deeper rational justification? A more substantive reading understands the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach* as something like the Jewish conception of natural law, the foundational conditions of civilized society. If the nations are not fulfilling those obligations, they are, in effect, not participating in the social order that generates mutual legal obligations. The *Gemara* was written under Roman rule in *Eretz Yisrael*, and the context of oppression and lawlessness is not incidental. From this perspective, the rule is not an arbitrary ethnic privilege but a response to the practical reality that those who do not participate in civil society cannot claim its protections. This reading — that the nations are not careful (*zehirim*) about causing damage and do not maintain the systems of accountability that make civil compensation meaningful — appears to inform the Rambam's position.

### Rambam's Rationale

Returning to 37b, in a marginal note on the lower right side of the page, there is a citation from the Rambam in *Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon* (chapter 8, *halacha* 5): since non-Jews do not hold a person liable for damage caused by his animal, we follow their law with them — *harei anu danim imahem kedineihem* — and this is sourced in the Yerushalmi. This grounds the exemption from paying them in a principle of reciprocity: they themselves do not impose this form of liability, so we need not pay them under it.

The Rambam then adds, in the same location, that the reason non-Jews pay full damages to Jews — the fine imposed upon them — is because *einam zehirim b'mitzvot v'einam mesalkim hanezek*: they are not careful about their obligations and do not remove the source of damage. This is not merely a statement about ritual noncompliance with *sheva mitzvot*; the Rambam is saying that their failure to maintain orderly protection of others' property and persons — their broader disregard for the conditions of civil society — is what justifies the imposition of full liability against them. This appears to be a rationalization of Rav Abbahu's position, framing the asymmetric rule not as pure ethnic privilege but as a response to a structural failure in how the non-Jewish nations govern civil life.

### Later Qualifications

The discomfort this *sugya* generated is visible in subsequent *Rishonim*. Looking at the *Shita Mekubetzet* on 38, lower left, the following is cited: *ra'ah sheva mitzvot* — the *pasuk* says God saw the *sheva mitzvot* — *mashma dechol shemekaymim sheva mitzvot dinam etzlenu kedinenu etzlam*: this implies that any nation that does observe the *sheva mitzvot* would be treated by us as we are treated by them, with full legal parity. From this it follows that for nations governed by religious and ethical law — *omot hagedurot bedarkhei datot venimusim*, in the language of the Meiri — these distinctions would not apply. The Meiri's position, that nations which are bound by civilized norms of law and ethics are outside the scope of these discriminatory rules, finds its justification here.

The *Shita Mekubetzet* further explains the phrase *vayater goyim* as referring specifically to those who are cruel and wicked and who pay no regard to the suffering of others — *achzarim velev ra lahem* — and who are suspect with respect to all seven Noahide commandments. The point is not generic: it is specifically their disregard for causing damage and their indifference to others' welfare that justifies the fine. *Lefikach knasam hakatuv kedei sheyishmeru shoroteihem* — the *Torah* fined them in order that they should guard their animals. The *Shita Mekubetzet* then adds that *vechol zeh lo dibru ela al sheva umot* — all this was said only regarding the seven Canaanite nations — which is, of course, a further attempt to distance the rule from any general application to contemporary non-Jews. That this gloss ultimately found its way into the printed text itself, replacing *nochri* with *kena'ani*, reflects how deeply uncomfortable later authorities were with the rule's apparent scope.

Two things are significant here. First, there is a clear apologetic motivation — an awareness of how this rule would appear to outsiders and perhaps also an internal moral discomfort. But second, and more importantly, what these authorities are attempting is not merely apologetics but a genuine rational reconstruction: the rule is not simply "they are *reshaim*, so we can take advantage of them." Rather, it is that their failure to participate in the structures of civil and legal accountability is what generates the asymmetry. This makes the rule comprehensible in a way that pure ethnic privilege does not.

## Rabbi Meir's Universalism

### Tanya on Non-Jew Cases

A *beraita* records the rule regarding the non-Jew's ox in precisely the form stated in the *mishna*: *shor shel nochri shenagach shor shel Yisrael bein tam bein mu'ad meshalem nezek shalem* — whether *tam* or *mu'ad*, full damages. Two *pesukim* are cited as the source: *amad vayimoded eretz ra'ah vayater goyim* (Rav Yosef) and *v'hofia me-Har Paran* (Rav Abbahu / Rabbi Yochanan). The *Gemara* asks: why are two verses needed? If the first is sufficient, why cite the second?

The answer is that the first *pasuk* — *amad vayimoded eretz* — is needed for two other entirely different teachings, attributed to Rav Matna and Rav Yosef respectively, and thus cannot also serve as the source for the damage law. Therefore a second *pasuk* is required.

### Rav Matna & Rav Yosef

What does Rav Matna read from *amad vayimoded eretz ra'ah vayater goyim*? He reads it as a statement of divine punishment through exile. God saw the *sheva mitzvot* they had been commanded (*sheva mitzvot shenitzvu aleihen Bnei Noach*), saw that they did not fulfill them (*v'lo kiyemum*), and therefore exiled them from their land (*amad v'higlah osam me-al admasam*). On this reading, *vayater goyim* means not "made their money permissible" but "scattered them," "sent them into exile" — the same way Israel is exiled for its sins, the nations are exiled for theirs. The verbal support is from a *gezerah shavah*: the root *n-t-r* appears elsewhere in connection with jumping or leaping across the land (as with the locust, *l'nater bahen al ha-aretz*, rendered by the Targum as "to leap upon the land"), implying movement from place to place.

Rav Yosef offers a still more surprising reading of the same *pasuk*. God saw the *sheva mitzvot* the nations had accepted (*sheva mitzvot shekiblu aleihem Bnei Noach*), saw that they were not fulfilling them, and therefore *amad v'hitiram lahem* — released them from their obligation entirely. He revoked their commandment.

The *Gemara* immediately objects: *ishtari ishtra* — are you serious? *Im kein matzinu choteh niskar* — if that is so, the sinner is rewarded! The more flagrantly you violate, the more you are released from your obligations. Mar, son of Rav Avina, resolves the paradox: the release does not mean freedom from punishment when they violate. It means that even when they do fulfill the *mitzvot*, they no longer receive reward. Having demonstrated such categorical disregard for their commandments, they have severed the relationship of *metzuveh v'oseh* — the status of being commanded and acting accordingly — and now, when they happen to do the right thing, they do so without the orientation of commandedness. They therefore receive only the lesser reward of *eino metzuveh v'oseh*. But violation is still punished.

### Reward for Non-Jews

The resolution through the category of *aino metzuveh v'oseh* raises a deeper question: do non-Jews receive any reward at all for doing *mitzvot*? And Rabbi Meir's statement provides an answer.

### Rabbi Meir on Goy & Torah

*Minayin she'afilu nochri v'osek baTorah harei hu k'kohen gadol* — how do we know that even a non-Jew who engages in Torah is like a *kohen gadol*? From the verse *asher ya'aseh otam ha'adam v'chai bahem* (Vayikra 18:5): it does not say *kohanim*, *leviyim*, or *Yisraelim* shall do them and live — it says *ha'adam*, any human being. The universalist implication is explicit: any person (*adam*), regardless of people or station, who performs the commandments of the *Torah*, attains life through them — and the measure of reward is that of a *kohen gadol*.

It is important to note that *v'osek baTorah* here, in its original Tannaitic context, means performing the *mitzvot* of the *Torah*, not studying *Torah*. Although Tosafot later applies this to *Talmud Torah*, connecting it to a different *drasha* in *Sotah* about Torah being more precious than pearls (*yekarah hi mipninim m'kohen gadol hanichnas lifnai v'lifnim*), that reading reflects Tosafot's own framework and is not the *peshat* of this *Gemara*.

What is remarkable here is that Rabbi Meir's statement appears to go even further than the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach*: it seems to say that a non-Jew who performs *mitzvot* from the full *Torah* of Israel receives reward commensurate with a *kohen gadol*. The Rambam, elsewhere, states that a non-Jew who performs any *mitzvah* from the *Torah* receives reward like an *eino metzuveh v'oseh*, and he applies this principle even to *bris milah*.

### Aino Metzuveh Resolution

The *Gemara* reconciles the apparent contradiction with Rav Yosef's reading — which seemed to imply no reward — as follows: *ein mekablim aleihem sechar mitzvah k'metzuveh v'oseh ela k'mi she'eino metzuveh v'oseh* — they do receive reward, but not at the level of one who is commanded and fulfills. They receive reward only at the reduced level of *eino metzuveh v'oseh*. And *Rabbi Chanina* taught: *gadol metzuveh v'oseh yoter m'mi she'eino metzuveh v'oseh* — it is greater to act under the compulsion of commandment than out of pure volition.

This resolution applies on two levels. With respect to the *taryag mitzvot* of Israel, non-Jews are genuinely *eino metzuveh v'oseh* — they were never commanded in those *mitzvot* — so their reward is naturally at the lower level. But with respect to the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach*, the additional element introduced by Rav Yosef's reading is that even these commandments, which they *were* obligated in, they have severed themselves from through persistent violation. So even when they do fulfill them, they no longer experience them as the acts of a *metzuveh*, and their reward reflects that diminished orientation.

What is striking about this entire unit is the way the *Bavli* has structured it. Immediately after establishing the harsh asymmetric rule — non-Jews pay full damages and receive nothing — the *Gemara* introduces Rabbi Meir's universalist teaching: *asher ya'aseh otam ha'adam*, any human being who performs Torah is rewarded like a *kohen gadol*. The principle that humanity as such (*adam*) is the relevant category, and that no specification of *kohanim*, *leviyim*, or *Yisraelim* was written, directly counterweights the particularism of the preceding rule. The *Gemara* does not abandon the *halakha*, but it complicates the picture immediately and forcefully.

A related universalist passage appears in the *Sifra*, cited by Tosafot in the first wide line of the *tosafot* on this *daf*. There an extended passage notes multiple *pesukim* that use non-particularistic language — *pitchu shearim veyavo goy tzaddik* ("open the gates, let the righteous nation enter," Yeshayahu 26:2), read as referring to any righteous nation; *hetiva Hashem latovim*, God does good to the good, where it does not say *kohanim, leviyim, v'Yisraelim* but *latovim*, to the good — all converging on the same principle: *afilu nochri v'osek baTorah harei hu k'kohen gadol*. The *Sifra* extends this across numerous verses, building a sustained universalist counterweight.

Tosafot discusses this passage because other *gemarot* create the opposite hermeneutical move — reading the word *adam* specifically as *excluding* non-Jews. This is, as the *Gemara* here implicitly acknowledges, the inverse of the thrust of this passage. Tosafot works through the tension; it may reflect a genuine dispute among *Tana'im* over how to read those terms. But the juxtaposition within our *daf* itself is deliberately constructed: the *Bavli* places this universalist counterweight immediately adjacent to the most exclusionary-seeming *halakha*, not merely to qualify it but to fundamentally complicate the picture of how one ought to view the non-Jew.

## Roman Sardiytot Story

### Roman Officers & Torah

The *Gemara* records that the Roman government — the original *girsa* was *malkhut harasha*, "the evil government," subsequently altered — had already sent two *sardiytot* to the sages of Israel. Saul Lieberman notes evidence that Rome had a practice of sending legal scholars to study the laws of subject nations, and he understands *sardiytot* in that sense, though the term is more commonly understood to mean officers. The officers studied *Torah* with the sages of Israel thoroughly: *kara veshanu veshilshu* — they read, reviewed, and mastered the material three times over.

### Officers' Critique

When they came to depart, they told the sages: *dikdaknu bechol Torat-chem ve'emet hu* — we have gone through your entire *Torah* with great precision, and it is true — *chutz midavar zeh*, with one exception. That exception is precisely the rule at issue: the Jew's ox that gores the non-Jew's ox is *patur*, while the non-Jew's ox that gores the Jew's pays full damages whether *tam* or *mu'ad*. Their objection is framed in terms of the *mimah nafshach* argument: if *re'ehu* is *davka*, exemption should run in both directions; if *re'ehu* is *lav davka*, liability should run in both directions. The rule as stated is internally inconsistent.

### Officers' Discretion

Having stated their critique, the officers add: *vedavar zeh einu magidim oso lamalchut* — this thing we will not report to the government. They chose not to inform Rome of this discriminatory rule.

### Bavli vs. Yerushalmi

Several observations about this story deserve attention. First, the *mimah nafshach* argument — the logical inconsistency framing — is a later Aramaic gloss, borrowed from the earlier discussion in this very *sugya*. The original text of the story almost certainly said only: here is the one thing we cannot accept, the asymmetric damage rule. And the reason they could not accept it was not logical inconsistency but moral offense — it is discriminatory. The *Bavli* by inserting the *mimah nafshach* argument transforms their objection from a moral one into a merely logical one, thereby understating the depth of their critique. The rule is framed as *all your Torah is true* (*ve'emet hu*) — a logical problem, not an ethical scandal.

The Yerushalmi's version of the story is instructive by contrast. There, the officers describe the *Torah* as *na'eh umeshubachat* — praiseworthy and beautiful — and say this one thing is *not* praiseworthy. That is a moral objection, not merely a logical puzzle. Furthermore, in the Yerushalmi's version, the officers had disguised themselves as Jews in order to study *Torah*. The *Bavli*'s version has them come openly as Romans — consistent with the immediately preceding statement of Rabbi Meir that the *Torah* is open to all; they can come from Rome and we will teach them *Torah*. The Yerushalmi is more protective of *Torah* as specifically Israel's, while the *Bavli* has deliberately contextualized the story within a universalist frame. The Yerushalmi also adds that on their return journey, God made them forget everything they had learned, so they could report nothing to Rome. The *Bavli* contains no such epilogue — the officers are left in possession of their knowledge and choose, on their own, not to report.

The *Maharsha* and the *Yam Shel Shlomo* raise the question: why did the sages not simply misrepresent the *halakha* to the officers, or simply decline to teach this rule? Given that disclosure might lead to Roman reprisal, was there not a *pikuach nefesh* justification for concealment? The *Maharsha*'s answer: from this story we learn that it is forbidden to misrepresent *Torah* even where one might argue that doing so could prevent danger to life. One may decline to teach; one may not falsify.

## Divine Compassion Stories

### Ulla's Theology

The *Gemara* introduces Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, whose daughter had died. The rabbis said to Ulla: let us go and comfort him, let us pay a *shiva* call. Ulla declined to join them, saying: *mai li gabei nichuma d'Bavla'ei* — what do I want with the Babylonian style of *nichum aveilim*? *D'gidufa hu* — it is blasphemy. His reasoning: when Babylonians offer condolences, they say *mai efshar l'me'evad* — what could have been done? And the implication of that phrase is that if something *could* have been done, one would have tried to do it — thereby suggesting a readiness to subvert the divine decree. Ulla went alone. His approach to *nichum aveilim* reflects a theology that is, by any measure, harsh: complete submission to divine judgment, with no comfort offered beyond that submission.

### Kal V'Chomer Logic

Ulla went to Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda and offered the following comfort. He cited the verse from Bamidbar (21:16): *al tatzar et Moav v'al titgar bam milchama* — do not distress Moav and do not wage war against them. Ulla frames this through a *kal vachomer* that Moshe himself had reasoned: if regarding Midyan — who came only to assist Moav in hiring Bilam and were the secondary party to the hostile design — the *Torah* commands *tzor et haMidyanim v'hikitem osam*, to fight and strike them — then regarding Moav itself, which instigated the entire plot, *lo kal vachomer* that we should wage war? Yet God told Moshe: *lo k'sh'alta datcha al datchi* — My thinking is not like yours. God had a reason to preserve Moav: *shtei preidot tovot yesh li l'hotzi mehem* — I have two beautiful doves to bring forth from them — Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite.

### Ruth & Na'amah

The logic Ulla applies to the bereaved father is this: if, on account of two righteous descendants, God had compassion over two entire wicked nations and did not destroy them — *v'lo hechrivam* — then your daughter, *im keshera hi v'rauya hi l'atzeit mimena davar tov*, if she was righteous and worthy for some good to descend from her, *al achat kama v'khama d'hava chaya* — how much more so would she have lived. Therefore, since she died, one may conclude that nothing good would have come from her progeny in any case. Accept God's decree.

This is, to put it plainly, not pastoral counseling. The logic is as brutal as it is tidy. What is theologically significant, however, is what the story establishes about divine providence: even a completely wicked nation — one that actively tried to destroy Israel — is preserved by God on account of the potential for righteous descendants. The calculus of divine compassion is entirely indifferent to present wickedness when future goodness is possible.

### God's Reward System

The *Gemara* continues with Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ein Hakadosh Baruch Hu mekappea sechar kol berya* — God does not withhold the reward of any creature, however small the good deed. *Afilu sechar sicha na'ah* — even for a pleasant manner of speech, reward is given.

### Daughters' Merit

The illustration comes from the daughters of Lot. The older daughter, who slept with her father and named her son Moav — *me-av*, from the father — was explicit and perhaps immodest in her language. God's instruction to Moshe was *al tatzar et Moav v'al titgar bam milchama* — do not afflict Moav and do not wage war, with the added nuance that even *angarya*, forced labor or tribute, is permitted against Moav. The younger daughter, who named her son Ben Ammi — "son of my nation" — was less explicit and more *tzanua*, more modest in her choice of words. For this modest speech — a single small *mitzvah* — she received a greater reward from God: *al tatzar* and *al titgar* with no qualification, meaning not even *angarya* may be imposed upon the Ammonites.

The *Gemara*'s handling of this narrative is significant. In many *midrashim*, the story of Lot's daughters is deployed as evidence of the licentiousness and depravity of the nations that descended from them. Here it is reframed entirely: the daughters are credited with performing a *mitzvah* — indeed a great one — and their *tzniut* is highlighted as meritorious. The very story that elsewhere serves as a negative exemplar is turned into a story of righteousness, divine reward, and the value of modesty.

### Genealogical Merit

The final word of the *sugya* is Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: *le'olam yakdim adam l'dvar mitzvah* — a person should always hasten to perform a *mitzvah*. The illustration again comes from the daughters of Lot. The older daughter was the first to act — she preceded her sister by one night in the incestuous act undertaken (in their understanding) to preserve humanity. As a result of that one night's priority in performing the *mitzvah*, her progeny entered the genealogy of Israel four generations earlier. The line from Moav runs: Ruth married Boaz, and their line continues through Oved, Yishai, David, and Shlomo — four generations of the royal lineage. Naamah the Ammonite married Shlomo, and so the younger daughter's lineage entered only at that later point, through Rechavam her son, four generations after Ruth. *Kadmasa arba dorot b'Yisrael* — the older daughter preceded in the Jewish royal line by four generations — all because she was one night quicker to the *mitzvah*.

The *sugya* closes, then, in a remarkable place. Beginning with one of the most legally and morally challenging rules in the entire tractate — a rule that is discriminatory, asymmetric, and defended through *pesukim* that require considerable hermeneutical work — the *Bavli* has built a sustained counterweight. Rabbi Meir's universalism (*asher ya'aseh otam ha'adam*, any human who performs Torah is like a *kohen gadol*), the *Sifra*'s extended universalist passages, the story of the Roman officers who acknowledge *kol Torat-chem emet*, the divine preservation of wicked nations for the sake of two righteous descendants, and finally the reframing of the mothers of Moav and Ammon as exemplars of *mitzvah* and *tzniut* — all of this sits deliberately adjacent to, and in tension with, the asymmetric *halakha* that opens the discussion. The *Bavli* does not retract the *halakha*. But it will not allow it to stand without complication.

# Bava Kamma 39

## Samaritans & Knas

### Mishna: Jew/Samaritan Go…

We continue from 38b, picking up with the *braita* beginning *shor shel Yisrael*. The broader theme of the *mishna* — that an ox of a Jew that gores an ox of a non-Jew is *patur*, while a non-Jew whose ox gores a Jew's ox pays full damages — has already been addressed by the *gemara*. We now turn to how these rules operate with respect to Samaritans (*kutim*).

The *braita* reads: *shor shel Yisrael she-nagach shor shel Kuti patur* — if an ox of a Jew gores an ox of a Samaritan, it is exempt — *ve-shel Kuti she-nagach shor shel Yisrael, Tam meshalem chatzi nezek, u-Muad meshalem nezek shalem* — but if a Samaritan's ox gores a Jew's ox, a *tam* pays half damages and a *muad* pays full damages.

This is immediately puzzling. If the Samaritans had the legal status of non-Jews, their ox goring ours would produce full liability regardless of *tam* or *muad* status. But since the *braita* applies the standard *tam*/*muad* framework — the very framework that governs Jewish-on-Jewish cases — the implication is that Samaritans are treated halachically as Jews. Why, then, are we exempt when our ox gores theirs?

### Chachamim: Knas Rationale

The *gemara* does not directly analyze the position of the *chachamim* here. However, Rashi and Tosafot both understand this asymmetry as a *knas* — a punitive measure designed to create social and legal distance between Jews and Samaritans. Even if Samaritans are halachically Jewish, their religious practice diverged significantly, and there were concerns about intermarriage and assimilation. The *knas* therefore operates in one direction: when our ox gores theirs, we are not required to pay, producing a kind of second-class status that reinforces separation.

The asymmetry in the other direction — that we do not actively demand *more* from them than the law requires — reflects a different logic: we will not take money from them beyond what the law obliges, but we will exempt ourselves from payment in order to maintain those barriers. That is the position of the *chachamim*: no payment when our ox gores theirs, but standard *tam*/*muad* liability when theirs gores ours.

### Rabbi Meir: Gerei Arayos

Rabbi Meir's position goes further: *shor shel Yisrael she-nagach shor shel Kuti patur* — like the *chachamim*, our ox goring theirs is exempt — *ve-shel Kuti she-nagach shor shel Yisrael, bein Tam bein Muad meshalem nezek shalem* — but when their ox gores ours, they pay full damages whether *tam* or *muad*.

The *gemara* infers from this that Rabbi Meir holds *Kuti'im gerei arayos hen* — that the Samaritans are converts due to lions. This refers to the account in *Melachim* 2, where Nevuchadnezzar settled various nations in the land of Israel following the destruction of the first *Beis Hamikdash*. Among them were people from Kuta — the origin of the name "Kutim." The text relates that they continued worshipping their foreign gods until God sent lions against them, after which they accepted the worship of the God of Israel. The question raised by the *gemara* is whether this constitutes a sincere conversion (*gerei emes*) or merely a coerced and insincere one (*gerei arayos*).

As Tosafot notes, the accepted *halacha* is that motivation alone does not invalidate a conversion — what matters is whether the convert's commitment was ultimately sincere. So the question about the Samaritans is not whether their initial motivation was fear of lions, but whether they genuinely embraced Judaism at the end of the process. If they did, they are *gerei emes*; if not, they remain *gerei arayos* and are treated as non-Jews. Rabbi Meir, it seems, holds that their conversion was not sincere — they are non-Jews — and therefore the full-payment rule applicable to a non-Jew's ox goring a Jew applies to them.

### Blood Stain Purity Debate

This reading of Rabbi Meir, however, is immediately challenged. The *gemara* cites a ruling regarding *ktzamim* — blood stains found on garments in *Rekem*: *kol ha-ktzamim ha-baim mi-Rekem tehorin* — all stains that come from *Rekem* are *tahor*.

Some background: a woman who menstruates is a *niddah*. If a bloodstain is found on her garment without direct bodily discharge, it produces only rabbinic impurity and is called a *ketzem*. If such a stained garment is found in a public space, the question is whether we assume it originated from a Jewish woman — and is therefore *tamei* — or from a non-Jew, whose menstrual blood carries no such impurity. Since the population of *Rekem* is predominantly non-Jewish, such stains are presumed *tahor*. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *metamei* — he rules them *tamei* — because he holds that the inhabitants of *Rekem*, though they think themselves non-Jews, are actually descendants of converts who have simply forgotten their origins, and therefore their blood stains are those of Jews.

The key passage for our purposes follows: *mi-bein Yisrael u-mi-bein ha-Kutim, Rabbi Meir metamei* — stains found among Jews or among Samaritans, Rabbi Meir rules *tamei*. It is clear from this ruling that Rabbi Meir considers *kutim* to be halachically Jewish — otherwise their stains would be no different from those of non-Jews. *Ve-chachamim metaharim* — the *chachamim* rule *tahor* — not because the stains of Samaritans would be inherently *tahor* if their origin were known, but because Samaritans are presumed to be careful about not discarding stained garments in public, so stains found in the street cannot be attributed to them with confidence.

The upshot is that both Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* treat *kutim* as halachically Jewish in the context of *niddah* law. This is the *gemara*'s challenge: *alma kasavar Rabbi Meir Kutim gerei emes hen* — we see that Rabbi Meir holds the Samaritans are true converts. How then does his position in the goring case reflect the law of non-Jews?

### Knas vs. Seduction Cases

The resolution is provided by Rabbi Abba: *knasu she-knas Rabbi Meir be-mammonam* — Rabbi Meir applies a *knas* to their money. Even though he holds that Samaritans are halachically Jewish, he imposes a financial penalty — exempting us from paying them and requiring them to pay us at the rate of non-Jews — *shelo yitame'u bahem*, so that Jews do not intermingle and intermarry with Samaritans. Rabbi Meir thus goes further than the *chachamim*: whereas the *chachamim* impose only a one-directional exemption (we do not pay when our ox gores theirs), Rabbi Meir also requires them to pay us as if they were non-Jews.

This resolution immediately raises a question from Rav Zeira, who cites the *mishna* in the context of seduction and rape fines: *ve-eilu naaros she-yesh lahen knas* — the following women are owed a *knas*. The *mishna* lists several categories: a woman who is a *mamzeret*, a *nesina* (from the Canaanite nations brought into servitude by King David, who converted), and *ve-al ha-Kutit* — a Samaritan woman. This is a *stam mishna*, which is attributed to Rabbi Meir. And indeed, the *knas* applies to her because she is halachically Jewish.

The challenge: if Rabbi Meir imposes a *knas* on Samaritans' money in the goring context *shelo yitame'u bahem*, why not apply the same principle here and declare that a man who seduces or rapes a Samaritan woman need not pay the *knas*? That would similarly create barriers and separation.

### Abaye & Rav Mari: Liabil…

Abaye answers: *kedei shelo yehei chotei niskar* — so that the wrongdoer should not profit from his sin. If a man seduces or rapes a Samaritan woman and we exempt him from the *knas* in the name of communal separation, he faces no consequences for profoundly harmful behavior. The concern about *yitame'u* — intermingling — is real, but it cannot come at the price of allowing a perpetrator to act with impunity. The imperative that a wrongdoer face consequences outweighs the goal of social distancing in this case, and therefore the *knas* is paid as the *halacha* demands.

One might still ask: why not require the man to pay, but direct the money to the poor rather than to the Samaritan woman? Rav Mari responds: *mishum de-havay mammon she-ein lo tove'in* — because it would be money with no one to sue for it. The man cannot be compelled to pay unless there is a plaintiff asserting a claim in court. Without the Samaritan woman as a plaintiff, there is no mechanism to extract payment at all. Therefore we allow the *knas* to be paid to her as the *halacha* requires, and we do not treat it like the goring case where payment is simply withheld.

## Cheresh/Shoteh/Katan Ox

### Mishna: Liability & Exem…

We now turn to the top of 39a and a new *mishna*. The *mishna* states: *shor she-pikeach she-nagach shor she-cheresh shoteh ve-katan chayav* — if a normal person's ox gores the ox of a *cheresh* (a deaf-mute, who lacks full legal competency), a *shoteh* (one with mental illness who does not process reality normally), or a *katan* (a minor), the owner of the goring ox is liable. *Ve-shel cheresh shoteh ve-katan she-nagach shor she-pikeach patur* — but if the ox of a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan* gores the ox of a competent adult, it is exempt, because these individuals bear no legal responsibility for their actions or negligence.

### Apotropus Mechanism

The *mishna* continues: this situation creates a public safety problem. An ox that has gone out and gored remains dangerous, yet its owners cannot be held accountable. The *mishna* therefore provides a mechanism: *shor she-cheresh shoteh ve-katan she-nagach beis din ma'amidin lahen apitropas* — if their ox gores, the court appoints an *apitropas* for them, a custodian. Normally an *apitropas* is appointed to protect the property interests of orphaned minors. Here the role is somewhat different: this is an *apitropas* appointed primarily to protect the community by ensuring someone takes responsibility for the ox and prevents further goring.

*U-me'idim lahen bifnei ha-apitropas* — and one testifies against the ox in the presence of the *apitropas*. Each goring incident is formally witnessed before the *apitropas*, so that after three such incidents the ox achieves the status of *muad*, with the full legal consequences that follow.

### Reshus Meshaneh Debate

What happens if the *cheresh* recovers his hearing, the *shoteh* recovers his sanity, or the *katan* comes of age? The ox was warned three times before the *apitropas* and achieved *muad* status. Now that the formerly incapacitated owners are competent adults, does the ox revert to *tam*?

*Chazar le-tumuso divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir says yes, it reverts to being a *tam*. *Rabbi Yosi omer harei hu be-chezakaso* — Rabbi Yosi says no, it retains its *muad* status. This principle is called *reshus meshaneh* in the *gemara*: does a change of possession or control alter the ox's legal status?

### Yi'udei Debate Framework

One straightforward way to understand this debate is through the question of *yi'udei tora* versus *yi'udei gavra*. What is the purpose of warning an ox three times? If the purpose is *yi'udei tora* — to establish the ox itself as a habitual gorer — then once that is established, the fact of the ox's dangerous nature is fixed. Changing owners changes nothing about the ox's character, and the new owner (now a competent adult) takes it as a *muad*. This is Rabbi Yosi's position.

If, however, the purpose is *yi'udei gavra* — the warnings establish the owner's negligence — then the warnings apply specifically to the person who was warned. Once control passes to a new person, the three warnings do not transfer, and the ox reverts to *tam*. This is how Rabbi Meir can be understood: the *muad* status is personal to the responsible party, not inherent to the animal.

This framework can also apply more broadly: if one purchases an ox already classified as *muad*, does it revert to *tam*? What if the ox was in the care of a *shomer* when it became *muad* and the owner then reclaims it? In the case of a *shomer*, one might argue the possession never truly changed because the *shomer* acts as an agent of the owner — a *ben da'as* — and so it remains the same *reshus* throughout. But the question remains open in many configurations.

### Payment Phase of Liabili…

The *gemara* now identifies an internal contradiction within the *mishna* itself. The opening clause states that when a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan*'s ox gores a competent person's ox, it is *patur* — exempt. This implies, as the *gemara* reasons, that even with an *apitropas* in place, as long as the ox is still a *tam*, one does not collect from its body. The *mishna* makes a point of going straight to the testimony before the *apitropas* and the creation of *muad* status, implying that collection only begins once the ox is *muad*.

Then the *gemara* looks at the second half of the *mishna* — the appointment of the *apitropas* and the testimony before him — and suggests that this might imply collection even from a *tam*. There is thus an apparent internal tension: the opening seems to preclude collection from a *tam*, while the continuation seems to permit it.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava resolves the difficulty with a close reading of the *mishna*: *im huchzeku nagchanim* — if the ox has established itself as a gorer. Tosafot notes that this does not require three prior gorings; it simply means that the ox has demonstrated a vicious nature and it is apparent that steps must be taken to protect the community. Once that condition is met, *ma'amidin lahem apitropas* — the court appoints an *apitropas* — *u-me'idim bifnei ha-apitropas* — and testimony is given before him — *u-mashvinan lei muad* — and the ox is then established as a *muad*. Only thereafter — *d'chi hadar ve-nagach lishalem me'aliyah* — does payment become due, out of pocket and not merely from the body of the ox.

Rashi and Tosafot observe that the *gemara* does not explicitly spell out why collection from a *tam* in this context is precluded. The underlying logic seems to be that *chatzi nezek* (half damages for a *tam*) already represents an attenuated liability — whether understood as a pure *knas* with no real obligation, or as a genuine liability in which the *Torah* nonetheless treated the owner leniently given the absence of prior warning. Either way, the *Torah* shows leniency toward a *tam*, and this leniency extends to the case of a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan*: since the *Torah* has already gone easy on a fully competent owner of a *tam*, it will certainly go easy on those who lack full legal competency. The *apitropas* is therefore appointed to protect society and facilitate testimony, but actual collection awaits *muad* status.

## Apotropus Payment Debate

### Orphans vs. Apotropus

Once the ox does achieve *muad* status and then gores again, who pays? *Me'aliyas man* — from whose resources? *Rabbi Yochanan amar me'aliyas yesomim* — Rabbi Yochanan says the orphans pay. *Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina amar me'aliyas apitropas* — Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina says the *apitropas* pays, since it was his negligence that allowed the goring to continue.

It is worth noting that although the *mishna* speaks of *cheresh*, *shoteh*, and *katan*, the *gemara* frames the discussion in terms of *yesomim* — orphans — because the institution of the *apitropas* is most naturally associated with orphaned minors who have inherited an estate. The case in view is precisely that: minors who possess this ox.

### Orphan Protection Princi…

A significant objection is raised against attributing the position "orphans pay" to Rabbi Yochanan. Rabbi Yehuda cites Rav Assi: *ein nizkakim le-nichsei yesomim ella im ken ribis ocheles bahem* — the court does not intervene in matters involving the property of orphaned minors, except where interest is accruing on a loan. The concern is that a non-Jewish creditor to whom the deceased father owed money with interest should not continue accruing that interest indefinitely — so the court steps in to discharge the debt and stop the ongoing loss. Similarly, Rabbi Yochanan himself had held that the *kesuba* of the father's widow could be paid out in order to stop the ongoing expense of her maintenance from the estate. But apart from such cases of ongoing loss, the court categorically protects orphan property while the heirs are still minors and does not allow claims to be processed against the estate until they come of age.

Given that Rabbi Yochanan himself stated this protective principle, how can he simultaneously hold that orphans pay from their estate for their ox's goring? The *gemara* initially proposes reversing the attributions — giving the "orphans pay" position to Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina and the "*apitropas* pays" position to Rabbi Yochanan — so as to make Rabbi Yochanan consistent.

### Mazik Exception

But the *gemara* rejects this reversal. *Ve-ha Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina dayna hu ve-nachis le-umka de-dina* — Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina is a judge of depth and precision; he would never stake out a position that directly contradicts the established principle that orphan property is not touched while the heirs are minors.

The *gemara* therefore maintains the original attributions and explains the apparent inconsistency in Rabbi Yochanan's view: *u-mazik shani* — the case of a *mazik* is categorically different. It is not like a debt owed to a creditor — an obligation that arose from a prior transaction or loan. Here, the orphans' ox went out and actively caused damage. That is a distinct legal category that justifies an exception to the general protective rule. Rabbi Yochanan thus holds both positions simultaneously, without contradiction: ordinarily, orphan property is protected, but when the orphans' property itself becomes the instrument of harm, payment follows from that property.

### Incentive Structures

With this established, the *gemara* returns to explain the full logic of each position. *Ei amarta me'aliyas apitropas, mimna ve-lo avid* — if you say the *apitropas* pays from his own resources, no one will agree to take the job. The *apitropas* receives no compensation for this role — no fee, no stipend. What he does receive is a degree of communal trust and status, the fact that *beis din* relies on him to protect the estate. But if in addition to performing this thankless service he faces personal financial exposure every time the ox gores, the position becomes untenable. Since the community *needs* someone to fill this role, Rabbi Yochanan concludes that payment must come from the orphans — even now, during their minority — or no one will ever accept the appointment.

Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina disagrees. He says the *apitropas* does pay initially — it is his negligence that allowed the goring — but *ve-chozer ve-nifra min ha-yesomim le-che-she-yigdelu* — he then recovers the payment from the orphans once they come of age. This arrangement reconciles all the interests: the *apitropas* faces immediate consequence, protecting against negligence; the victim is compensated promptly; and ultimately the financial burden falls on the true owners of the ox once they achieve legal majority. Critically, on both views, the final cost is borne by the orphans — the debate concerns only the timing and mechanism of payment.

### Two Apotropus Types

Tosafot raises a further complication. The *gemara*'s suggestion that we cannot impose liability on the *apitropas* — because it would deter anyone from taking the position — seems to imply a blanket exemption from negligence liability. Yet another *gemara* indicates that an *apitropas* who is negligent is indeed liable. How are these reconciled?

Tosafot distinguishes between two fundamentally different types of *apitropas*. The *apitropas* appointed here, to oversee a goring ox, functions essentially as a community watchman — a kind of policeman tasked with ensuring the ox does not harm others. There is no real trust relationship, no delegation of estate management, and no incidental benefit that might accrue to him from the position. In order to get someone to fill this low-status protective role, we must exempt him from liability; otherwise the appointment is meaningless. By contrast, an *apitropas* appointed to manage the estate of orphaned minors occupies a position of genuine trust and prestige. Being known as someone whom *beis din* relies upon to steward an estate confers real reputational benefits. In that high-status role, says Tosafot, the *apitropas* is indeed liable for negligence.

## Tanaim: Apotropus Power

### Sumchus vs. Chachamim

The *gemara* now establishes that the question of whether the *apitropas* enables collection from a *tam* is itself a dispute among *Tanaim*. The *braita* reads: *shor she-nitcharshu ba'alav ve-she-nishtatshu ba'alav ve-halku ba'alav li-medinah ha-yam* — an ox whose owners became *cheresh*, became *shoteh*, or simply departed overseas and left the ox without anyone assigned to watch it. Yehuda ben Nekusa says in the name of Sumchus: *harei hu be-tamuso ad she-yo'idu bo bifnei ha-ba'alim* — it remains a *tam* until testimony is given before the actual owners. The *chachamim* say: *ma'amidin lahem apitropas u-me'idim lahem bifnei apitropas* — you appoint an *apitropas* and testify before him, allowing the process of establishing *muad* status to proceed.

The opening of the *braita* presents what looks like a simple binary: either you appoint an *apitropas* or you do not. But a closer reading complicates this picture.

### Temimus = Full Tam

What does Sumchus mean when he says the ox *harei hu be-tamuso* — remains a *tam*? The *gemara* presses this. If Sumchus is saying no *apitropas* is ever appointed and the ox never becomes *muad*, then what is the content of the second clause in the *braita* — the clause about what happens when the *cheresh* recovers and the owners return — where Sumchus says *chazar le-tamuso*, it returns to being a *tam*? For the ox to return to *tam* status, there must have been a prior process by which it became *muad*. This shows that Sumchus agrees the *apitropas* mechanism operates and the ox can become *muad*. So what exactly is Sumchus debating with the *chachamim* in the first clause?

The *gemara* answers: *harei hu be-tmimuso* — the phrase does not mean "it remains a *tam*" in the sense of never having been made *muad*. It means it remains *complete* and *whole* — *de-lo mechasrina lei* — you do not diminish it. Sumchus concedes that an *apitropas* can be appointed and that testimony before the *apitropas* can make the ox a *muad*. But he insists that during the period when it is still a *tam* in the process — before the three warnings have accumulated — the ox's body is not subject to collection. *Ein ma'amidin apitropas le-tam ligvot mi-gufo* — the *apitropas* does not enable collection from the body of a *tam*. Collection only becomes available once it achieves *muad* status. The *chachamim*, by contrast, are read here as holding that the appointment of the *apitropas* does enable collection from the body even while the animal is still a *tam*.

### Seifa: Reshus Meshaneh

In the second clause — the *seifa* — both Sumchus and Rabbi Yosi address what happens when the owners return to competency or majority. Sumchus says *chazar le-tamuso* — it reverts to *tam* status — invoking the principle of *reshus meshaneh*: changing ownership or control resets the ox's status. Rabbi Yosi says *harei hu be-chezakaso* — it retains its *muad* status regardless of the change in ownership. Thus the *seifa* of the *braita* maps cleanly onto the *mishna*: the debate over *reshus meshaneh* — whether a change of possession reverts a *muad* to *tam* — is the same dispute we saw between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi in the *mishna*.

## Rabbi Yaakov: Half Damag…

### Rabbi Yaakov Braiта

A *braita* introduces a new ruling: *shor she-cheresh shoteh ve-katan she-nagach, Rabbi Yaakov meshalem chatzi nezek* — the ox of a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan* that gores; Rabbi Yaakov says one pays half damages. The *gemara* immediately interjects with characteristic wit: *Rabbi Yaakov mai avidteih* — what did Rabbi Yaakov himself do wrong that he is paying half damages? The answer is obvious — *ella eima Rabbi Yaakov omer meshalem chatzi nezek* — clearly the *braita* means Rabbi Yaakov rules that half damages are owed. The playful clarification noted, the *gemara* turns to the substantive question.

### Hermeneutic Question

*Be-mai askinan* — what is the case under discussion? If the ox is a *tam*, the answer is self-evident: of course a *tam* pays half damages — that is the universal rule. The *chiddush* might be that even for a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan*'s ox there is liability at all, but then the *braita* should simply say *chayav* — liable — rather than specifying *chatzi nezek*. Specifying *chatzi nezek* implies that one might have supposed the payment would be *more* than half, and Rabbi Yaakov is telling us it is only half.

If, on the other hand, the ox is a *muad*, the problem cuts the other way. A *muad* that was properly guarded should be entirely exempt; a *muad* that was not properly guarded should pay full damages. What scenario produces exactly half?

### Rava: Hybrid Muad-Tam

Rava answers: *le-olam be-muad* — the case is indeed one of a *muad* — *de-avad leih shemirah pechusah ve-lo avad leih shemirah me'ulah* — where B-level *shmirah* was performed but not A-level *shmirah*. And Rabbi Yaakov holds like two related principles both associated with Rabbi Yehuda.

### Shmirah Level Threshold

The first principle: *muad sagi leih be-shemirah pechusah* — for a *muad*, B-level *shmirah* is sufficient to be exempt. The second principle: for a *tam*, A-level *shmirah* is required.

This is a striking and counterintuitive position. One's initial instinct is that a *tam*, which carries only half liability, should be easier to become exempt from — requiring equal or lesser *shmirah* than a *muad*. Rabbi Yehuda inverts this: a *muad*, despite being the more dangerous and more heavily sanctioned animal, only requires B-level *shmirah* for the owner to be exempt; but a *tam*, despite its lighter penalty, requires A-level *shmirah*. One way to understand this is that for a *tam*, the owner had no prior warning at all, yet the *Torah* still imposes liability — suggesting the liability attaches not to negligence but to the mere fact of ownership. For such a liability to be fully excused, the owner must demonstrate truly excellent *shmirah*. A *muad*, by contrast, operates through the lens of negligence: the owner was warned, and as long as he is not grossly negligent, he is exempt.

### Synthesis: Half Liability

The second principle Rabbi Yaakov adopts is *tzad tamus bi-mekomah omedes* — associated here with Rabbi Yehuda — which holds that even after an ox has been warned three times and officially declared *muad*, the *tam* dimension of its nature persists. The animal is, in a sense, half *tam* and half *muad*.

Combining these two principles produces Rabbi Yaakov's ruling. The ox is a *muad* — but Rabbi Yehuda holds it is simultaneously half-*tam* half-*muad*. The owner performed B-level *shmirah*. With respect to the *muad* half: B-level *shmirah* is sufficient, so the owner is exempt for that portion. With respect to the *tam* half: B-level *shmirah* is insufficient — A-level was required — so the owner remains liable for that portion. The result is *chatzi nezek*: half damages. The *chiddush* is not simply that a *tam* pays half — that is obvious — but that this *muad* animal, because of its hybrid nature under Rabbi Yehuda's doctrine, pays only half even though it has been warned three times.

There is a further *chiddush* folded into the ruling as well: even though this is a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan*'s ox — entities whose owners ordinarily would not pay — because an *apitropas* was appointed and the ox became *muad*, there is liability. This reflects the position of the *Rabbanan* (*de-amri ma'amidin apitropas le-tam ligvot mi-gufo*), who hold that the *apitropas* mechanism does allow for collection. And the specification of *chatzi nezek* rather than simply *chayav* signals, as Rashi and Tosafot explain, that you might have thought full damages would be owed — but because this is a hybrid *muad*-*tam* and only B-level *shmirah* was performed, only the *tam* half remains, and therefore the payment is exactly half.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 40

## Apotropus & Reshus

### Guardian Setup

The daf under discussion is 40a, though the sugya picks up from the middle of 39b. The *mishnah* there addressed the case of a goring ox owned by a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan* — individuals who lack the legal competency to be held responsible for their animal. Because they cannot be held liable, the community is nonetheless left unprotected, and so *beis din* appoints an *apotropus*, a guardian, to oversee the animal.

### Two Types Guards

This *apotropus* is importantly distinct from the ordinary *apotropus* appointed to serve the interests of the incompetent person or the minor — to manage their affairs and protect their wellbeing. The *apotropus* appointed here is installed for the sake of the community. His role is not to serve the *cheresh shoteh v'katan* but to protect those who might be injured by the animal.

### Warning & Muad

By appointing such a guardian, the *mishnah* establishes that this *apotropus* can receive formal warnings on the owner's behalf. If the ox gores three times and the *apotropus* is warned on each occasion, the ox acquires the status of a *muad* — a confirmed habitual gorer.

### Tam Payment Query

The *gemara* raises the question of whether payment would be imposed for the first three gorings. The general principle is that the *torah* treats the first three incidents with leniency, making the *tam* payment — half damages — more akin to a *knas*, a penalty imposed only under specific conditions. The question is whether, given the unusual nature of this situation, anyone would pay even the *tam* half for those initial incidents. The specific formulation is *ma'amidin apotropus l'tam ligvos migufo* — whether a *beis din*-appointed guardian enables collection of *tam* payment from the body of the ox.

### Owner Liability

A further question concerns who bears liability once the ox becomes a *muad*. The *cheresh shoteh v'katan* are never liable even for damages they cause directly, which would suggest they should bear no liability here either. On the other hand, the *apotropus* has taken on responsibility for the animal and functions in some respects like a *shomer* — a guardian who has assumed custodial duties. Yet the *gemara* never suggests transforming the position into a paid arrangement. The conclusion reached is that the *cheresh shoteh v'katan* must pay — either directly from their own assets or by reimbursing the *apotropus*.

### Reshus Meshaneh

The final topic introduced from the prior session is the principle of *reshus meshaneh* — the puzzling idea that when the ox changes possession, its *muad* status may revert to *tam*. This applies even in a case where the *apotropus* had the ox warned and declared a *muad*, and then the *katan* grew up and the ox was returned to him. Even more strikingly, the *gemara* will shortly explore whether this reversion applies even when the ox is merely returned from a *shomer* to its original owner — a case in which there is no change of ownership at all, since it was always the owner's animal being watched on his behalf.

The conceptual underpinning of this principle, though the *gemara* never makes it explicit, seems to be that *muad* status is not primarily a statement about the animal's habitual temperament, but about the *owner's* habitual negligence. It is the owner who has repeatedly ignored warnings. If the person receiving the warnings is not the current owner, the negligence cannot be attributed to the new possessor — even if that new possessor is the original owner receiving his ox back from a *shomer*.

---

## Yaakov Half Payment

### Half Payment Intro

The *gemara* now takes up the statement of *Rabbi Yaakov*, who rules that for the ox of a *cheresh shoteh v'katan*, one pays *chatzi nezek* — half damages.

### Muad Context

The *beraita* supplies the context: the case involves a *shor tam* that became a *muad* while under the oversight of the *apotropus*.

### Half-Tam Status

This is where the unusual position of *Rabbi Yehuda* becomes relevant. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds *tzad tamuso bimkomo omedes* — the *tam* dimension of the ox remains in place even after it becomes a *muad*. In other words, the ox is viewed as half-*muad* and half-*tam*: it pays the additional half as a *muad*, but the original half it was always paying is treated as if it remains a *tam*. *Rabbi Yaakov*'s ruling of half damages is therefore understood as a *pesak* consistent with *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position.

### Shmira Paradox

This gives rise to a genuinely counterintuitive result. The levels of *shmirah* — watchfulness — produce a paradox. A *shmirah me'ula*, a superior level of guarding, exempts entirely. A *shmirah p'chusa*, a minimal level of guarding, paradoxically exempts from liability for the *muad* half of the animal, yet does not exempt from the *tam* half. The result is that a *muad* ox with inadequate but minimal *shmirah* still incurs half-payment — because minimal *shmirah* is insufficient for the *tam* dimension, even though it suffices for the *muad* dimension. This is the strange consequence of *Rabbi Yehuda*'s framework, and it is part of what *Rabbi Yaakov*'s statement encapsulates.

### Abaye's Challenge

*Abaye* challenges *Rava*: do *Rabbi Yaakov* and *Rabbi Yehuda* in fact disagree? The *beraita* records them debating — *Rabbi Yehuda* says *chayav*, fully liable, and *Rabbi Yaakov* says *chatzi nezek*, half — which implies a real dispute. If *Rabbi Yaakov* were merely clarifying *Rabbi Yehuda*, there would be no dispute at all.

### Rava's Read

*Rava bar Ulla* resolves this by saying that *Rabbi Yaakov* is indeed only explaining *Rabbi Yehuda*. When *Rabbi Yehuda* says *chayav*, he means liable for half — specifically, the half that results from the interplay of *tam* and *muad* status under the conditions of *shmirah p'chusa*. *Rabbi Yaakov* is spelling out what that liability amounts to.

### Abaye Disagrees

*Abaye* rejects this harmonizing reading and insists they do genuinely disagree. The actual dispute, on *Abaye*'s reading, concerns whether an *apotropus* for a *cheresh shoteh v'katan* enables collection of *tam* damages at all — the principle of *ma'amidin apotropus l'tam ligvos migufo*.

---

## Debate Clarified

### Apotropus Authority

On *Abaye*'s reading, the *beraita* presents a case where the ox received no *shmirah* whatsoever — *b'muad v'lo natru klal*. In that scenario, the owner ought in principle to pay fully, both for the *muad* half and the *tam* half.

### Tam Collection

*Rabbi Yehuda* says full payment is owed. This is because he holds *ma'amidin apotropus l'tam ligvos migufo* — the *apotropus* arrangement enables collection even for the *tam* portion of the ox belonging to a *cheresh shoteh v'katan*. Since there was no *shmirah* at all, one pays the full *muad* half and also the *tam* half, which under *Rabbi Yehuda* is collectible via the *apotropus*.

*Rabbi Yaakov*, by contrast, agrees with *Rabbi Yehuda* on one point — that the ox retains its *tam* dimension (*tzad tamuso bimkomo omedes*) — but disagrees on the other: he holds *ein ma'amidin*, that no *apotropus* arrangement enables collection of *tam* damages from an ox of a *cheresh shoteh v'katan*. Therefore, the only payment owed is the *muad* half — which is the *chatzi nezek* he rules. Notably, in this reading, when *Rabbi Yaakov* says half, he means the *muad* half, not the *tam* half — a more coherent result for property belonging to those who are not legally competent.

### Rav Acha Q

*Rav Acha bar Abaye* then challenges *Rava*'s reading. If *Rava* is correct that they do not disagree, *Rava* has constructed an unnecessarily elaborate scenario — a *muad* ox whose owner performed a partial level of *shmirah*, such that he is exempt from the *muad* half but still liable for the *tam* half. This is a complicated and multi-layered case.

### Tam Simplification

Why not simply present the straightforward case? Make it a *tam*, and say the reason for half-payment is *ma'amidin apotropus l'tam ligvos migufo* — we appoint a guardian who can collect from the body of the *tam* ox, and that is the *chidush*. For *Rabbi Yehuda*, the scenario would be that the owner performed a *shmirah p'chusa*, which is insufficient for a *tam* and therefore he is liable. For *Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov*, who rules that minimal *shmirah* suffices even for a *tam*, the case would be no *shmirah* at all. In either scenario, there is no need to introduce the complicated *muad* framework.

The *gemara* responds on *Rava*'s behalf: the reason the *beraita* constructs the more elaborate case is that it teaches us multiple things simultaneously — that *ma'amidin apotropus l'tam ligvos migufo*, that *tzad tamuso bimkomo omedes*, and that *shmirah p'chusa* exempts from the *muad* portion but not the *tam* portion. The *beraita* prefers to communicate a greater *chidush* even at the cost of complexity.

### Ravina Reshus

*Ravina* then offers an entirely different framework for understanding the dispute between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Yaakov*. On his reading, their debate is not about *ma'amidin apotropus l'tam ligvos migufo* at all, but about *reshus meshaneh*. The case is where the ox was declared a *muad* under the *apotropus*, and then the situation of the *cheresh shoteh v'katan* changed — the deaf-mute was cured, the mentally ill person recovered, the minor came of age — and the animal was returned to its now-competent owner. Does the ox retain its *muad* status or revert to *tam*?

*Rabbi Yehuda* holds *harei hu b'chezkas muad* — it remains presumed a *muad*. *Rabbi Yaakov* holds *reshus meshaneh* — the change of possession reverts it to *tam*, and consequently only half is paid.

---

## Apotropus Payment

### Payment Source

Having mapped the contours of the dispute, the *gemara* proceeds to a *beraita*: an *apotropus* pays *min ha'aliyah* — from quality property — but does not pay *kofer*.

The *min ha'aliyah* ruling raises the underlying question of who exactly is paying. The conclusion from the prior session was that the *cheresh shoteh v'katan* must bear the financial burden — either directly from their assets or by reimbursing the *apotropus*. When the ox is a *muad* and damages must be paid, payment comes from the highest-quality assets available, not merely from the body of the ox.

### Kofer Exempt

The second ruling — that the *apotropus* does not pay *kofer* — requires explanation. If the *apotropus* system enables collecting even full damages when the ox kills property or injures someone, one might expect that when the animal kills a person and the more severe obligation of *kofer* would apply, certainly some payment should be imposed. Yet the *beraita* rules that no *kofer* is paid.

### Kofer Concept

The *gemara* explains this by identifying the nature of *kofer*. *Kofer* is not simply a form of compensation assigned to represent the value of a human life. Rather, it functions as *kapparah* — atonement. The *pasuk* is explicit: the owner of the ox is described as one who deserves to die, since his animal killed a person through his negligence, and the *kofer* payment is the mechanism by which he redeems his soul. It is, in effect, a monetary substitute for a *korban*. The owner pays the family of the deceased not as compensation for their loss, but as the vehicle through which he achieves *kapparah* for his own culpability.

If that is the case, the *gemara* reasons, then *yesomim lav b'nei kapparah ninhu* — orphans and incompetent individuals are not in the category of those who require or are capable of achieving *kapparah*. They are not *bnei mitzvos*, and the entire framework of atonement and accountability that *kofer* addresses does not apply to them.

One might ask: why not impose *kofer* on the *apotropus* himself, as the one exercising custodial responsibility? The *gemara* does not press this point, apparently treating the *apotropus* as a representative of the *cheresh shoteh v'katan* rather than as independently liable in his own right. Since it is the orphans' *kapparah* at stake, and they are not subject to such obligations, the system cannot impose *kofer* at all.

### Kofer Self-Value

*Rav Hisda* identifies the ruling that *kofer* is *kapparah* as the position of *Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka*. A *beraita* presents a dispute on the quantum of *kofer* payment: the *pasuk* states *v'natan pidyon nafsho k'chol asher yushat alav* — he shall give the redemption of his soul according to what is assessed upon him. The *tanna kamma* rules that payment is assessed based on the value of the *nizak*, the person killed — calculated in market terms as one would assess a slave. *Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka* rules that payment is assessed based on the value of the *mazik*, the owner of the ox — his own life's worth in the same terms.

---

## Kofer Debate

### Kofer Source

The *gemara* initially assumes this is a deep conceptual dispute: the *rabbanan* hold *kofra mamona* — *kofer* is fundamentally compensation — and therefore they assess it by the life of the one who was killed, the *nizak*. *Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka* holds *kofra kapparah* — *kofer* is atonement — and therefore it is assessed by the life of the one who must atone, the *mazik*. If the payment is about expiation, it must correspond to the value of the one expiating, not the one lost.

The logic of the *kapparah* reading emerges directly from the *psukim*. The verse immediately preceding the *kofer* provision states explicitly that the negligent owner of a *muad* ox is deserving of death: *v'gam b'alav yumas*. The *kofer* is then introduced as an alternative — the owner redeems his soul rather than forfeit his life. *Pidyon nafsho*, the redemption of *his* soul, is the phrase the *torah* uses, which is why *Rabbi Yishmael* concludes that the assessment must be based on the owner's own worth.

This reading, the *gemara* notes, also has bearing on the general principle of *ayin tachas ayin*. Several *rishonim* understand that *ayin tachas ayin* means monetary payment, but the framing of "an eye for an eye" implies that what is owed is not the value of the victim's eye, but the value of the perpetrator's eye — because the underlying logic is that the perpetrator deserved the same injury but is instead paying money as a substitute.

### Kapparah Consensus

*Rav Pappa* intervenes to clarify that the dispute between the *tanna kamma* and *Rabbi Yishmael* need not be understood as a disagreement about whether *kofer* is *kapparah* or *mamona*. In fact, says *Rav Pappa*, *kulei alma kofra kapparah* — everyone agrees that *kofer* is *kapparah*.

### Nizak vs Mazik

The actual dispute, on *Rav Pappa*'s reading, is only about how *kapparah* is achieved. *Rabbanan* hold *b'de'nizak shayminan* — atonement is attained by paying for the life of the one killed. *Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka* holds *b'de'mazik shayminan* — atonement is attained by paying the value of one's own life.

### Pidyon Value

The *rabbanan*'s textual basis is a *gezeirah shavah*: the same word *yushat*/*yushas* appears both in the *kofer* verse and in a verse concerning the miscarriage case, where the payment is assessed based on the value of what was lost — the life of the fetus. Therefore, the parallel usage indicates that *kofer* too is assessed by the value of what was lost, i.e., the *nizak*.
