*Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka* counters from the plain reading of *v'natan pidyon nafsho* — he shall give the redemption of *his* soul, meaning the *mazik*'s soul — which indicates that the payment is calibrated to the *mazik*'s own worth.

The *rabbanan* reply that *pidyon nafsho* does indeed mean he redeems his soul, but the manner in which he does so is by paying for the life of the other — *mihu ki shayminan b'nizak shayminan*. The vehicle of atonement is the valuation of the victim.

With this clarified, the *gemara* returns to reinforce the exemption from *kofer* for the orphans. If everyone agrees that *kofer* is *kapparah*, and if *kapparah* is inherently inapplicable to those not subject to *mitzvos* and personal accountability, then *kofer* cannot be imposed on them under any reading of the dispute, whether the quantum is assessed by the *nizak* or the *mazik*.

---

## Partners & Kofer

### Scholar Meeting

The *gemara* now narrates that *Rava* spoke highly of *Rav Acha bar Yaakov* to *Rav Nachman*, praising him as a great *talmid chacham*. *Rav Nachman* instructed *Rava* to bring him over, and when *Rav Acha bar Yaakov* arrived, *Rav Nachman* challenged him: ask me something — effectively inviting a scholarly examination.

### Partner Division

*Rav Nachman* then posed his question. If an ox is owned by two partners — *shor shel shnei shutfin* — and it gores and kills a person, how is the *kofer* paid?

### Payment Problem

The problem is as follows. If each partner pays a full *kofer*, one might object: *kofer echad amar Rachmana v'lo shnei kofrin* — the *torah* prescribed one *kofer*, not two. If each partner pays half a *kofer*, one might object: *kofer shalem amar Rachmana v'lo chatzi* — the *torah* prescribed a complete *kofer*, not a partial one.

The tension here runs deep. In ordinary damage law, when an ox injures someone's property, the concern is compensation — and two half-payments that together make the victim whole are entirely satisfactory. Here, however, *kofer* is *kapparah*, and atonement presents a different logic. By analogy, when two people jointly perform a *chilul Shabbat*, the obligation is not discharged by each bringing half a *korban*; each has a full sin requiring full atonement. That would argue for each partner paying a full *kofer*. Yet the *kofer* is paid not to the *beis hamikdash* but to the family of the deceased, and there is no evident reason the family should receive double payment simply because the ox has two owners.

As *Tosafos* notes: were *kofer* directed to the *beis hamikdash*, one could argue that both partners bring a full payment, as each has a full obligation of *kapparah*. But since the *kofer* goes to the *nizak*'s family, doubling the payment seems incoherent. Conversely, halving the payment seems to undercut the essential nature of the obligation. The question thus remains genuinely unresolved.

### Seizing Property

While *Rav Acha bar Yaakov* was still turning over the first question, *Rav Nachman* posed a second. *Chayvei erchin memashkin osan* — if someone has pledged a donation to the *beis hamikdash*, such as an *erech*, and has not paid, the *beis hamikdash* can seize his property as collateral. *Chayvei chataot va'ashamot ein memashkin osan* — but if someone owes a *korban chatas* or *asham*, the *beis hamikdash* does not seize his property, relying instead on the debtor's own sense of urgency about achieving *kapparah*.

The conceptual basis for this distinction may go beyond mere motivational psychology. One line of reasoning is that the obligation to bring a *korban* is a matter between the individual and God — it is not a debt to the *beis hamikdash* as an institutional creditor, and therefore it may not be appropriate for the *beis hamikdash* to exercise the coercive powers of a creditor. This parallels the broader question of *kofin oso ad she'yomar rotzeh ani* — whether someone can be compelled to bring a *korban* at all.

### Korban vs Debt

*Rav Nachman*'s question is: what is the rule regarding one who owes *kofer*? Two possibilities present themselves.

On one hand, *kofer* is *kapparah*, structurally similar to a *chatas* or *asham*, and the debtor therefore feels the weight of his obligation pressing upon him. He will pay without compulsion, and no seizure of property is necessary — *belo ba'i mashkunei*.

On the other hand, unlike a *chatas* or *asham*, the *kofer* is paid to a human being — the family of the deceased. Since the payment goes to another person rather than being brought to the *mizbeach*, the debtor may treat it psychologically as an ordinary monetary debt, without the same urgency. Moreover, since the owner himself did not directly kill anyone — his ox did — he may feel less personal guilt and less internal compulsion to pay. In that case, the *beis din* would need to seize his property to ensure payment.

### Unresolved Q

*Rav Acha bar Yaakov* was unable to answer either question. He was, as the *gemara* says, still sealed within the first one when the second was presented. *Rav Nachman* had effectively demonstrated that even a celebrated *talmid chacham* could be presented with genuinely unresolved questions.

*Tosafos* notes a further nuance regarding the *mashkon* question: since the *kofer* is paid to the *yorshei ha'nizak* — the heirs of the victim — rather than to the *beis hamikdash*, the question of seizure involves not the *beis hamikdash* acting as institutional creditor, but whether the *yorshei ha'nizak* themselves can directly seize property. Some *meforshim* understand *Tosafos* as suggesting that once a judgment has been issued by *beis din*, the question of whether the debtor feels internally motivated becomes irrelevant — *beis din* enforces the judgment regardless of the nature of the underlying obligation. The question of *mashkon* without a prior court judgment is a separate issue, and it is specifically whether the *yorshei ha'nizak* can act on their own initiative, without waiting for the court's enforcement apparatus, that remains open.

---

## Borrowed Ox

### Borrow Setup

The *gemara* returns to the case of the *shomer* and *reshus meshaneh*, now with competent owners and a genuine borrowing arrangement. A *beraita* presents the following: one borrowed an ox presumed to be a *tam* — *sha'alah b'chezkat tam* — and it turned out to be a *muad*.

### Half Payment Case

The *beraita* rules: *ba'alim meshalem chatzi nezek v'shoel meshalem chatzi nezek* — the owner pays half damages and the borrower pays half damages. The logic is that even had the ox been a *tam*, the borrower, as a *shoel*, would have been liable for half the damages if the animal gored. Since the animal is a *muad* and the total damage payment is full, the borrower pays the half he would have owed in any case, and the owner — who knew it was a *muad* — pays the remaining half.

### Borrower Claim

The *gemara* challenges this: why should the *shoel* pay at all? He should be entitled to say to the owner: *tora sha'ali, arya lo sha'ali* — I thought I was borrowing an ox, not a lion. I borrowed what I understood to be a docile animal unlikely to gore; if it was a *tam*, it would not have gored. The fact that it turned out to be a *muad* and caused damage should be the owner's problem entirely.

### Owner Counter

The *gemara* answers: the scenario is one in which the borrower could see from the animal's temperament that it was aggressive. He recognized it was the kind of animal that would gore. Given that he accepted it with this knowledge, his claim that he was merely borrowing an ox and not a lion rings hollow. He knowingly accepted a potentially dangerous animal, and with it the risk of paying the half he would have owed had it been a *tam*.

### Borrower Escalates

The borrower might still argue: fine, I knew it was aggressive, but I thought it was technically a *tam* — it had not yet been warned three times or formally declared a *muad*. I expected to pay at most half, and I expected that payment to be limited to the body of the animal itself — *migufo*. Now that it turns out to be a *muad*, the liability structure has changed entirely and I should not be held to it.

### Tam Payment Rule

The *gemara* resolves this directly: *sof sof*, in the end, had it been a *tam* you would have paid half. The fact that it is a *muad* does not reduce your obligation below what you would have owed in the best-case scenario for you. You pay what you would have paid as a *tam* — half, up to the value of the animal — and the owner pays the balance.

The *gemara* then works through a series of further claims the *shoel* might raise. He might say: as a *tam*, I could have been *modeh* and thereby avoided the *knas* payment — *modeh b'knas patur*. Or he might say: I could have brought the animal to a swamp — *mavrikna lei l'agma* — and denied the victim access to it, using it as leverage to negotiate a lower settlement.

On the *modeh* claim, the *gemara* answers that the scenario assumes *beis din* seized the animal immediately, so the option of being *modeh* before the court would not have been available in any case.

On the swamp claim, *Tosafos* raises an objection: what kind of argument is this? Hiding the animal from the *nizak* would be *gezeila* — the *nizak* has a legal right to it. *Tosafos* explains that what the borrower means is not that hiding the animal would have been legally permissible, but rather that the threat of making recovery difficult would have given him leverage to negotiate a lower settlement from the *nizak*. The victim, anticipating difficulty in enforcement, might have accepted less. Since the ox is now a *muad* and any property can be seized directly, that leverage is lost. The *gemara*'s final resolution is that *beis din* seized the animal immediately, so this leverage would not have existed in any event — had it been a *tam*, the same immediate seizure would have occurred.

The *gemara* then turns to the owner's perspective. Why should the owner pay only half? Could he not demand full compensation from the *shoel*, arguing that the *shoel* caused the loss of his ox by letting *beis din* seize it? The *shoel* responds that even if he had returned the ox, *beis din* would have seized it from the owner as well. The owner counters: I would have hidden it. The *shoel* counters: you still would have had to pay the full damage from your own funds — *sof sof me'alya havei mishtalem* — so the seizure of the ox caused you no additional net loss. The *gemara* notes that this logic holds only if the owner has other assets; if the ox was his only property, then the seizure did cost him leverage he could have used in negotiating. In that case, the *shoel* invokes the principle of *Rabbi Nosson* — *d'tanya Rabbi Nosson omer: minayin l'nosheh b'chaveiro maneh v'chaveiro b'chaveiro* — whereby one can pay a creditor's creditor directly, and the chain of obligations collapses: the *shoel* owed the ox to the owner, but the owner owed the ox to the *nizak*, and therefore paying *beis din* on behalf of the *nizak* was a legitimate discharge of the *shoel*'s obligation.

---

## Return & Reversion

### Return Case

The *beraita* then presents the second case: *hu'ad b'veit shoel* — the ox became a *muad* while in the borrower's possession, and *v'hechziro l'ba'alim* — it was returned to the owners. The ruling is: *ba'alim meshalem chatzi nezek v'shoel patur miklum* — the owner pays half and the *shoel* is completely exempt.

### Inconsistency Q

The *gemara* identifies a striking inconsistency. In the first case, when the owner gave the ox to the *shoel* and it was already a *muad*, it retained its *muad* status — possession change to the *shoel* did not revert it. In the second case, when the *shoel* returns it to the owner, it does revert — becoming a *tam* again, with the owner paying only half. Why would giving it to the *shoel* not trigger *reshus meshaneh*, while returning it to the owner does?

### Tavra Position

*Rabbi Yochanan* responds with *tavra* — these two rulings cannot both come from the same authority. The first part of the *beraita* assumes that *reshus meshaneh* does not apply — changing possession does not change status. The second part assumes the opposite. They are irreconcilable.

### Rabba Consistent

*Rabba* offers a different response. He reads the *beraita* as consistent throughout: *reshus meshaneh*, the change of possession, does always revert the status. Therefore, consistent with the second part of the *beraita*, the *seifa* is correct that returning it to the owner reverts it to *tam*.

But then why, in the *reisha*, does giving it to the *shoel* not revert it back to *tam*?

### Fairness Argument

*Rabba* explains: *lav kol kaminach d'me'adas lei l'torai* — the owner can say to the *shoel*, you have no power to impose this change on my ox. The *shoel* took the animal with knowledge of its status — he willingly accepted it. But when the *shoel* returns it, the owner has no choice but to accept it back. The ox was always his; it must come back to him. If the *shoel* has, in the meantime, allowed it to become a *muad* — by receiving the warnings and failing to act upon them — and then simply hands the animal back, the owner finds himself stuck with a *muad* ox through no act of his own. He never chose to accept a *muad* in place of the *tam* he parted with.

This principle runs deeper than a simple fairness argument. Since the *shoel* knew the animal would necessarily return to the owner, the status of *muad* that was established under the *shoel*'s watch cannot, in fairness, be imposed on a party who had no say in that process. The owner had no ability to oversee the warnings, respond to them, or contest them — the *muad* status was created by someone who was temporarily custodian of property that was always going to revert. Therefore, upon return, the status reverts as well.

The converse applies to the *reisha*: when the owner initially gives the ox to the *shoel*, the *shoel* is a willing recipient. He accepts it knowingly, with full information. That voluntary acceptance is why the *muad* status is retained in his hands — he made a choice to take on responsibility for this animal as it stood.

This framework may also explain the broader application of *reshus meshaneh* discussed earlier. When an *apotropus* turns an ox into a *muad* and then returns it to the now-competent owner, the same logic applies. The reversion occurs not because of some inherent characteristic of the ox changing, but because of the unfairness of imposing a legal status — established by a custodian whose tenure was by definition temporary — onto a party who had no agency in the matter.

By contrast, *reshus meshaneh* does not apply when an ox changes hands through a voluntary sale. A purchaser who knowingly buys a *muad* assumes that status. He has made a choice to acquire this animal as it is.

### Rav Pappa Q

*Rav Pappa* raises a further question: if the *seifa* demonstrates that *reshus meshaneh* applies — that returning the ox to the owner reverts it — can we use the *seifa* to shed light on the *reisha*? The *gemara* explores whether the cases are truly parallel or whether a principled distinction between them is available.

### Shomer vs Ownership

The *gemara* ultimately identifies a clean distinction among three scenarios. The first is a full transfer of ownership, as when Reuven buys the ox from Shimon. Here, the ox genuinely changes its legal identity and there is a genuine question about whether it should revert — the new owner willingly accepted it, which suggests it should retain its status, but the change of ownership is real. The second scenario is that of a *shomer* who takes the ox to watch: here the ox formally remains the owner's property the entire time — *kol makom sheholech shem be'alav alav* — wherever it goes, the owner's name goes with it — so there is the least basis for reversion, and the *shoel*'s willing acceptance reinforces this. The third scenario is when the *shoel* returns it to the owner against whom the *muad* status was created by someone else's custodial relationship: here the case for reversion is strongest, because the owner is involuntarily receiving back property whose status was altered without his participation.

---

## Stadium Ox

### Stadium Status

The *gemara* now turns to the *mishnah* concerning a *shor itstadyon* — a stadium ox, an animal forced into combat in an arena. Such an ox, the *mishnah* rules, is not subject to the death penalty even if it kills a person.

### Sacrifice Q

The *gemara* raises the question: *mahu legabei mizbeach* — may such an ox be used as a sacrifice? Even where there are not two witnesses sufficient to impose the death penalty — for example, where the killing was established through the owner's own admission or a single witness — the ox might nonetheless be halachically disqualified for the *mizbeach*, on the grounds that it is an animal through which an *aveirah* was committed. The question is whether an ox that was forced to gore — provoked and not acting from its own inclination — carries the same stigma.

### Rava Shmuel

*Rava* says *kasher* — the ox is valid for the *mizbeach*. *Ones hu* — the ox was compelled; it did not act willingly. Since it was essentially used as a tool by another agent, the act does not stigmatize the animal. *Shmuel* says *pasul* — invalid. *Harei ne'evdah bo aveira* — an *aveirah* was performed through this animal, and that fact alone disqualifies it, regardless of whether the animal was willing or coerced.

### Korban Exclusions

The *gemara* challenges *Rava* from a *beraita*. The *torah*'s phrase *min habeheima* — from the animal — is interpreted as an exclusion: not all animals may be brought. Specifically, *lehotzi et harov'ea v'et hanirva* — to exclude an animal that engaged in an act of bestiality, whether penetrating or penetrated. *Min habakar* — from the cattle — *lehotzi et hane'evad*, to exclude an animal that was worshipped as an idol. *Min hatzon* — from the flock — *lehotzi et hamuktzeh*, to exclude an animal that was designated for idolatrous worship even without actually being worshipped. *U'min hatzon* — the additional *vav* — *lehotzi et hanogeach*, to exclude a goring ox. All of these categories are disqualified from use as a *korban*.

### Rabbi Shimon Q

*Rabbi Shimon* asks: if we already know that a *rov'ea* is excluded, why must the *torah* also state that a *nogeach* is excluded? And conversely, if we know the *nogeach* is excluded, why state the *rov'ea*? Both are cases where the animal committed an *aveirah* for which the ox would be stoned — seemingly the same category.

### Different Factors

*Rabbi Shimon* answers his own question: *yesh barov'ea she'ein banogeach v'yesh banogeach she'ein barov'ea* — each has a feature the other lacks. By *rov'ea* — an act of bestiality — *asa bo ones keratzon* — the *torah* treats a coerced act the same as a willing act. Whether the animal was the active or passive party, it is disqualified. By *nogeach* — goring — *lo asa bo ones keratzon* — the *torah* distinguishes: only voluntary goring disqualifies; a provoked ox is not treated the same way. On the other hand, a *nogeach* triggers the obligation of *kofer*, while a *rov'ea* does not.

### Korban Unresolved

The *gemara* considers whether this *beraita* supports *Rava*'s position. The *beraita* says that by *nogeach*, a coerced act is not treated the same as a willing act — which seems to suggest that a provoked ox is *kasher* for the *mizbeach*. However, the *gemara* pushes back: this distinction about *ones* vs. *ratzon* in the *beraita* refers to the question of whether the ox is stoned, not to whether it is disqualified for a *korban*. In the context of stoning, it is well established that a provoked ox is not stoned. The *beraita*'s statement that *nogeach lo asa bo ones keratzon* describes this rule about the death penalty — it cannot be taken as establishing the *korban* rule, since that is precisely the open question. To use the *beraita* to resolve the *korban* question would be circular.

The result is that neither side has been proven. The disanalogy between *rov'ea* — where coercion and volition are treated identically — and *nogeach* — where they diverge for purposes of stoning — cannot be cleanly extended to the *korban* question. Whether a provoked *nogeach* is valid for the *mizbeach* thus remains *teiku* — unresolved, to be continued.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 41

## Intro & Kofer

### Opening

We pick up on daf 41b, four lines from the bottom. The *mishnah* had been treating the case of *nezek* caused by an ox, but with an appendix concerning the *apotropus* — whether an ox that becomes a *mu'ad* under a legal guardian acquires that status in the usual way. What the publishers of the Vilna Shas appended to the close of that *mishnah* is really the beginning of a new *mishnah*, one that shifts the focus to *kofer*. The transition is clean: the previous *mishnah* had discussed a stadium ox, one provoked into goring, and established that such an animal is not stoned. Before moving to the new *mishnah* proper, the *gemara* had asked whether the ox could still be used on the *mizbe'ach* — whether the fact that it committed an *aveira*, however forced upon it, creates the stigma of *ne'evad ba'aveira* sufficient to disqualify it. That question was left unresolved. We now return to the more central discussion of stoning and *kofer*.

### Stoning vs Kofer

The *pasuk* is explicit: *shor nogeach hu mi-tmol shilshom ve-hu'ad bi-ve'alav ve-lo yishmerennu ve-hemit ish o ishah ha-shor yisakkel ve-gam be'alav yumat im kofer yushas alav* — a *mu'ad* ox that kills is stoned, and its owner is liable to death, redeemed by payment of *kofer*. The first instance of goring carries the *sekilah* of the ox without *kofer*. The interplay between these two consequences — *sekilah* and *kofer* — is what the *gemara* now undertakes to analyze.

## Rovia vs Nogeiach

### Basic Distinction

The *gemara* cites a prior discussion in which animals are disqualified for the *mizbe'ach*: among them, an ox that gored (*nogei'ach*) and one that participated in an act of bestiality (*rovei'a*). Both, with sufficient witnesses, would be stoned; even without sufficient testimony they remain *pasul* for the *mizbe'ach*. The *gemara* notes a distinction in their relative gravity: *nogei'ach meshaleim et hakofer, rovei'a eino meshaleim et hakofer* — a goring ox obligates *kofer*; a *rovei'a* does not.

### What Case?

The *gemara* immediately interrogates this distinction: *heichi dami* — what is the case? If the *rovei'a* killed the woman through the act of bestiality — *ilima de-rava ve-katla* — then *ma li katla bekarna ma li katla birvi'ah*: what difference does it make whether it killed with its horns or through the act itself? Death is death; why would *kofer* not be owed? Conversely, if the *rovei'a* did not kill — *de-rava velo katla* — then the exemption from *kofer* is simply because no death occurred, and that would be a perfectly natural reading: *kofer* is owed when a life is taken, so of course there is none here. Indeed, that seems to be the plain sense of the *baraisa*: in one case the animal killed, in the other it committed a grave *aveira* but took no life, and *kofer* attaches to life-taking.

The *gemara*, however, resists this simple reading, insisting that there must be a legal distinction between the categories, not merely a factual one about whether death occurred.

### Abaye's View

*Amar Abaye l'olam de-rava velo katla* — Abaye maintains that the *rovei'a* did not kill the woman directly. Yet because the act of bestiality subjects her to capital punishment by *beis din*, and because she was in fact executed for her participation, one might have thought: *keman dkatla dami* — perhaps the act of *revia* is treated as if it took a life, since it caused the execution of the woman through the machinery of *beis din*. The *gemara* therefore teaches: no, we do not say that.

*Tosafos* presses a sharp question here: if the woman is being stoned, that implies she was a willing and active participant in the transgression. In that case, the ox did not bring about her death — she brought it upon herself. How then can we even entertain the *havamina* that the ox bore responsibility? The question is acknowledged as stronger than the answer given.

### Rava's View

*Rava amar le'olam de-reva ve-katla* — Rava holds that the *rovei'a* did in fact kill the woman through the violent act itself. So why no *kofer*? Because *keren kavanato lehazzik* — *keren* acts with intent to damage, while *hai kavanato la-hana'at atzmo* — this act was performed for the animal's own gratification, not with intent to harm.

### Shen ve-Regel

This leads directly to a striking question: does *kofer* apply in the category of *shen ve-regel* when a person is killed? Is *kofer* limited exclusively to *keren* — to *kavanato lehazzik* — or does it also apply to categories where no such intent is present?

The parallel case the *gemara* raises is *regel she-darsa gabei tinok be-chatzer hanizzak* — a foot that trampled an infant in the domain of the injured party. Since we are dealing with *shen ve-regel*, liability follows the parameters of those categories, including the territorial restrictions — there would be no liability in *reshut harabbim*, though one might question whether an act of bestiality against a person could ever be analogized to normal *shen ve-regel* activity that people are expected to guard against in a public domain.

The upshot: *ve-Abaye meshallem kofer, le-Rava lo meshallem kofer* — according to Abaye, *kofer* is owed even in the *shen ve-regel* case; according to Rava, it is not. Remarkably, this significant question does not emerge from a dedicated *mishnah* or *baraisa* on the topic. It arises as a byproduct of interpreting the contrast between *nogei'ach* and *rovei'a* in the context of *mizbe'ach* disqualifications.

The *gemara* then cites a supporting *baraisa*: *tanya kevattei de-Rav* — a *sitia* ox (one to which something was done) is not *chayav mita* and may even be used on the *mizbe'ach* because it is *ke-anusah*, treated as though coerced; it did not choose the act. This further clarifies the issue of *shen ve-regel* and *kofer* independently of the *mizbe'ach* question.

The lecturer flags a further pair of questions that hover over this entire analysis and remain, at this stage, unresolved: In the case of the stadium ox, where the animal is not stoned, would its owner pay *kofer*? And in the *shen ve-regel* case where Rava says no *kofer* — would the animal even be stoned? The logic seems clear enough in the latter case: if an animal acted without *kavanato lehazzik*, there is less grounds for treating the death as a culpable killing and therefore less basis for *sekilah*. But the question of whether *kofer* and *sekilah* can come apart — one present without the other — is precisely the tension the *gemara* is mapping, and it remains open whenever only one side of the pair is addressed.

## Tam to Mu'ad

### The Paradox

The *mishnah* states: *mu'ad meshalem kofer ve-tam patur min hakofer* — a *mu'ad* pays *kofer* and a *tam* is exempt. Yet both are *chayav mita* — *zeh va-zeh chayavim misa*. This last point the *mishnah* derives from the *pesukim*, which speak of stoning from the very first goring: *sakol yisakel hashor velo yeachel et besaro uva'al hashor naki* — the ox shall be stoned and its flesh shall not be eaten and its owner shall be clean.

This raises an acute logical problem: *vechi me'achar demitam katlinan lei mu'ad heichi mashkachat lei* — if we stone the *tam* after the first killing, how does an ox ever live long enough to become a *mu'ad*? If the *Torah* is followed literally, the ox is executed the first time it kills. How does it accumulate the three prior gorings necessary to reach *mu'ad* status?

### Rav Ashi

The *gemara* first considers an answer attributed to *Rabba*: *she'amdu lishelosha bnei adam* — three people were seriously threatened; based on assessment (*umdna*) they would have been killed had they not escaped at the last moment. But Rav Ashi rejects this: *umdna lav klum hu* — an assessment does not count for anything. You cannot establish *mu'ad* status on the basis of a near-miss.

Rav Ashi's own answer is: *kegon shesiken lishelosha bnei adam* — the ox critically injured three people. Because the victims had not yet died, the ox could not yet be executed — *sekilah* requires an actual death, and the court case must await that outcome. But the owner can be warned based on the critical injuries: the ox has demonstrated both the capacity and the propensity to kill fatally. That is sufficient to establish a warning and begin the process of rendering it a *mu'ad*, even if the full status with attendant *kofer* liability awaits the actual deaths.

Rashi's formulation — *l'kach lo niscal b'shem harishon u'kshenagach shlishi metu kulam hilchach meshalem alav et hakofer* — requires that all three victims die. It is not entirely clear from the *gemara* why that is necessary if even one death would suffice to trigger *kofer* liability on a *mu'ad*. It is worth noting that Rashi consistently assumes that the full *mu'ad* payment, including *kofer*, is triggered at the third goring. *Tosafos* points out that the plain sense of the other *sugyot* is that the first three gorings establish *mu'ad* status, so that it is the fourth goring where *mu'ad* liability and *kofer* apply. Rashi's reading runs against this in a consistent and notable way.

### Rav Zevid Rejected

Rav Zevid proposes: *kegon sheharag shelosha behemot* — the ox killed three animals. Michael raises this question, and the *gemara* immediately rejects it: *u-mu'ad livehema havai mu'ad l'adam*? Being a habitual killer of animals makes it a *mu'ad* with respect to people? The *gemara* treats this as unacceptable.

This rejection is significant. In an earlier *sugya*, there was a debate between Rav Zevid and Rav Ashi about whether *mu'ad* status extends across categories — whether an ox habituated to goring one type of victim is considered *mu'ad* for another. Rav Zevid had read the relevant text as *v'imu'ad*, suggesting that once *mu'ad* status is established, we presume it applies broadly unless the evidence clearly limits it to a specific type. The *stama d'gemara* here clearly finds the extension from *behema* to *adam* absurd, treating it as self-evidently wrong. This in turn supports the position that we read *mu'ad* status as narrowly as the evidence of the three prior acts warrants. The formalist approach dominates: the *mu'ad* character is defined by what the ox was actually seen to do, not abstracted into a general propensity for violence.

### Victims & Status

*Rav Shimi* then suggests: *kegon she'harag shelosha ovdei kochavim* — the ox killed three non-Jews. The original text used *goyim*, though that has been censored in standard printings. The logic is clear: a *shor* is not stoned for killing a non-Jew; therefore the ox could not be executed after those three deaths, yet it has demonstrated a propensity for fatal violence that suffices to establish a warning and *mu'ad* status. The *gemara* rejects this too: *u-mu'ad le'ovdei kochavim havei mu'ad le'Yisrael*? — just because it kills non-Jews makes it *mu'ad* for Jews?

The question of whether there is a principled reason for the distinction, or whether this is purely formalist — the ox has only done what it has done — runs through all these cases. The *gemara* may be assuming some substantive difference, perhaps that Jews and non-Jews present different circumstances to a goring animal. But the formalist reading is equally available: if the three prior acts involved only non-Jewish victims, that is the only identity the ox has established as a *mu'ad*.

*Resh Lakish* then proposes: *kegon she'harag shelosha benei adam tereifa* — it killed three people who were *tereifa*, i.e., who had internal injuries rendering them halachically in a category such that killing them does not constitute capital murder. For a human murderer who kills a *tereifa*, there is no capital punishment — the victim is not *shalem* in the relevant sense, though this is not merely a question of life expectancy. A *goses* — someone actively dying — does not carry this exemption; it is specifically the halachic category of *tereifa*, defined by a particular type of internal injury, that changes the status of the killing. By the same logic applied to the ox: it is not stoned for killing *tereifos*, so it survives. But the *gemara* again rejects the extension: *u-mu'ad le-tereifa havei mu'ad le-shalem*? — perhaps a *tereifa*, for whatever reason, attracts violence from animals in a way a healthy person would not.

### Rav Pappa

*Rav Pappa* cuts through all of this: *de'katal ve'arak le'agma de'katal ve'arak le'agma* — each time it killed, the ox fled to the swamp. The court was unable to capture and execute it, but the owner was warned three times. There is no need to construct exotic categories of victims. The ox did kill, the owner was warned, but the physical impossibility of apprehending the animal prevented the court from carrying out *sekilah*. On the fourth goring the animal is finally caught, it can be stoned, and the owner — having been warned three times — owes *kofer*.

A subtle question arises: if *sekilah* requires the court case to be conducted in the presence of the ox, can the testimony of witnesses even be received — for purposes of warning the owner — without the ox present? It may be that the warning can proceed on the basis of witness testimony even when the ox is not before the court, while the formal judgment of *sekilah* remains suspended until the animal is apprehended.

### Zommin Case

*Rav Acha brei de-Rav Ika* offers a further scenario involving *zommin*: *kegon she-huzmu zommei zomemin* — those who invalidated the witnesses were themselves invalidated. Here is the sequence: a first pair of witnesses testifies that the ox gored and killed; their testimony is accepted in court and *sekilah* is ordered. A second group then appears and says: *immanu hayisa b'oso hayom* — you were with us that day, you could not have witnessed the goring. The first testimony is thrown out. This happens a second and third time. Then a third group of witnesses comes and says the same thing to the second group — that *they* could not have been where they claimed to be. The second group is thereby invalidated, and the original testimony of the first group is retroactively resurrected.

The *gemara* asks: does this work? *Haneicha i-leyudei tora ba-inan* — if what we need is simply to establish that the ox has a history of goring (*yedi'at tora*), then yes: we now know that the first group's testimony was always true, and the ox did in fact gore three times. *Ella i-leyudei gavra ba-inan* — but if we require that the *owner* be meaningfully warned and personally violate that warning, then the owner can say: I relied on the second group's invalidation of the first witnesses; I genuinely believed my ox had not gored.

The *gemara* resolves this by stipulating that the first group's testimony included that the owner himself was present at each goring: *kol eimas de-katil tora gabei havai kai* — every time your ox gored, you were standing there. Given that the owner was present, his claim of ignorance fails: he cannot say he did not know. He knew, or should have known, that the first group was telling the truth because they were testifying to something he personally witnessed.

The distinction between two formulations of warning is important: *yedia tori* — knowing the ox's history — versus *yedia gavra* — knowing the owner knew and failed to act. In the simplest case, a single pair of witnesses before *beis din* testifying that the ox gored three times would establish *mu'ad* status without requiring the owner to be warned after each individual incident. But the present scenario is specifically designed to show how the owner's personal presence allows the warning to function even when intermediary testimony had temporarily invalidated it.

### Ravina

*Ravina* proposes yet another scenario: *bemakirin es baal hashor ve'ein makirin es hashor* — the witnesses know one of the owner's oxen gored, but they cannot identify which ox it was. The ox cannot be stoned because the court cannot identify it. But the owner can be warned: you have a goring ox among your cattle. *Ibayi lach linterei kulei bakra* — you are obligated to watch all of your cattle. The owner cannot excuse himself by saying he did not know which ox to restrain. Eventually, on the last occasion, the witnesses recognize the ox; it can now be stoned and the owner is liable for *kofer*.

The *gemara* asks — *mai hava lei lemevad*, what was the owner supposed to do if he did not know which ox it was? — and gives the answer just stated: his obligation, once warned that a killer is among his herd, is to restrain the entire herd.

## Mishnah Analysis

### Lo Yochel

Before turning to the *mishnah* itself, the *gemara* derives from the *Torah* when the prohibition on the ox's meat and benefit begins. The *baraisa* says: from the verse *sakol yisakel hashor*, we would know it becomes *neveila* — but *neveila* is obviously forbidden to eat. Why then does the *Torah* say *lo yeachel et besaro*? This teaches that once judgment has been passed on the ox — even before *sekilah* has been carried out — if the owner were to shecht the animal, its meat remains forbidden. *Leachar shenigmar dino asur ba'achilah* — the prohibition attaches at the conclusion of the legal judgment, not at the moment of execution.

### Mishnah Text

The *mishnah* itself: *shor shenagach es adam vames — mu'ad meshalem kofer ve-tam patur min hakofer, zeh va-zeh chayavim misa* — a *mu'ad* pays *kofer*, a *tam* is exempt, but both are liable to *mita*. *Ve-chein be-ven ve-chein be-vat* — the same applies if the ox kills a child. This is obvious as a matter of law but the *mishnah* is working through the *pesukim* systematically: the *Torah* says *o ven yigach o vat yigach kamishpat hazeh yei'aseh lo* — if it gores a son or a daughter, the same law applies. The next *pasuk* addresses the case of a slave: *im eved yigach hashor*, and the *mishnah* follows accordingly.

*Nagach eved o amah noten shloshim sla'im* — if it gores a slave or maidservant, the payment is thirty *shekel, bein shehu yafeh me'ah maneh bein she'eino yafeh ela dinar echad* — whether the slave is worth a hundred *maneh* or only one *dinar*, the payment is always the fixed amount of thirty *shekel*. This is the irony of the slave *pasuk*: whereas *kofer* varies with the value of the victim — assessed by the slave market value of the person killed — the payment for a slave is counterintuitively fixed regardless of that slave's market value.

### Ba'al Naki

The *gemara* then derives from the phrase *uba'al hashor naki* — and the owner of the ox is clean — that the owner may not derive any benefit from the ox, not merely that he cannot eat it.

The *baraisa* begins the derivation: once we learn from *lo yeachel et besaro* that the meat may not be eaten, we know this applies even when the ox was shechted after judgment. But how do we know there is also an *issur hanaah* — a prohibition on benefit? *Talmud lomar uba'al hashor naki.* The owner is "cleaned out" — *shimon ben zoma omer keadam sheomer lechavero yatza ish ploni naki mikhasav ve'ein lo vo hana'ah klum* — like one who says of another that he has been completely cleaned out of his property and has nothing left. The owner of the ox is similarly stripped of any benefit from the animal.

But a question arises: if *lo yeachel et besaro* tells us that you cannot eat it even after shechting, and if — following the principle of *Rabbi Abbahu* in the name of *Rabbi Elazar* — *lo yeachel* always includes *issur hanaah* unless the *Torah* explicitly permits benefit (as it does by *neveila*, where it says to give to the stranger or sell to the foreigner), then *lo yeachel et besaro* already tells us both *issur achilah* and *issur hanaah*. What then remains for *uba'al hashor naki* to add?

The *gemara* answers: *lehana'at oro* — to prohibit benefit even from the hide. One might have thought *besaro* — the flesh — is what is restricted, but the leather, being commercially valuable, might remain permitted. *Uba'al hashor naki* teaches that the owner is stripped entirely, including of the hide.

A further question: why not derive the prohibition on the hide from the word *et* in *et besaro*? Following the hermeneutic principle of *Shimon HaAmsuni* — who interpreted every instance of *et* in the *Torah* as including something adjacent to the named object — the word *et* would teach that *hatafeil lebesaro*, what is secondary and attached to the meat, namely the hide, is also included. The *gemara* answers that this *tanna* does not derive legal content from the word *et* at all, following a different hermeneutic approach.

This occasions the famous *aggadic* passage: *Shimon HaAmsuni* had interpreted every *et* in the *Torah* until he reached the *pasuk et Hashem Elokecha tira* — you shall fear the Lord your God. Unable to identify what could be "appended" to God as an object of comparable fear, he withdrew from the entire interpretive enterprise. His students asked: what of all the *drashot* you have delivered over the years? He responded: the same reward I received for deriving those teachings, I will receive for withdrawing now — *keshem shekibalti sachar al hadrisha, kach kibalti sachar al haprisha*. This is a striking statement of intellectual honesty: a scholar willing to abandon decades of work upon recognizing an insuperable difficulty in the underlying premise.

*Ad sheba Rabbi Akiva velimmed* — until Rabbi Akiva came and taught that *et Hashem Elokecha tira* extends to include *talmidei chachamim*, who are to be revered in a manner comparable to the fear of Heaven. *Tosafos* observes that elsewhere the *gemara* does draw a comparison between fear of parents and fear of Heaven — *ish immo ve'aviv tira* is paralleled to *et Hashem Elokecha tira* — without discomfort. *Tosafos* distinguishes: there the *Torah* draws an analogy between two separate *mitzvos*. Here, however, to say that the *mitzvah* of fearing God intrinsically *includes* another category of beings would be to place them far too close to the divine — a qualitatively different and far more fraught claim, which is precisely why *Shimon HaAmsuni* was unwilling to say it.

On the broader question of whether *drashot* carry the weight of *Sinai* transmission: the *gemara* does not assume that the content of exegetical derivations was transmitted from Sinai. The most that can be said of *masora* as obligating content applies primarily — and even then not absolutely — to *gzera shava*, where the Ramban already shows that the *gemara* itself debates which terms to pair. The Rambam's position, developed against the Karaite critique, is that very little content was handed down intact; rather, the hermeneutic capacity — the empowerment of rabbinic courts to derive and rule — is what was transmitted, and those derivations, properly made, carry *d'Oraisa* force.

## Half-Kofer Debate

### Eliezer vs Akiva

The *gemara* then presents a tannaitic dispute over the *drasha* on *uba'al hashor naki*. *Rabbi Eliezer* reads: *naki michatzi kofer* — the owner of a *tam* is clean from having to pay half *kofer*. The argument is by analogy: if a *mu'ad* pays full *kofer*, one might reason that a *tam* — by the same logic that it pays half-damages for ordinary *nezek* — should pay half *kofer*. *Rabbi Eliezer* reads *uba'al hashor naki* as foreclosing that analogy.

### Akiva's Logic

*Rabbi Akiva* objects: who needs a special *drasha* for this? *V'halo hu atzmo ein mishtalem ela migufo* — the *tam*'s payment of half-damages is collected from the body of the ox itself. So if you were to reason by analogy that the *tam* owes half *kofer*, the payment would similarly come from the animal. But the animal is stoned and its body is forbidden for any benefit. *Yavou l'veit din v'yisalku lach* — let the owner tell the claimant: come to court and take your half *kofer* from the body of the ox. The body is worthless. There is nothing to pay. No *drasha* is needed; the halacha enforces itself automatically.

### Eliezer Clarifies

*Rabbi Eliezer* responds: *kach ani b'einecha shedanti b'zeh?* — is that what you think of me? That I was discussing a case where the ox is stoned? Of course in that case there is nothing to pay. *Ein dini ela k'shehe'emidu et ha'adam al pi ed echad o al pi be'alim* — my case is where the testimony establishing that the ox killed came from a single witness or from the owner's own admission, which suffices to obligate *kofer* as a *kapara* payment but is insufficient to bring about *sekilah*, which requires two witnesses as in a capital case.

*Rabbi Akiva* raises a further objection: if the owner is admitting, that is an admission to a *knas* — a fine — and one who voluntarily admits to a fine is exempt from it. *Rabbi Eliezer* replies: *kasvar kofer kapara* — he holds that *kofer* is not a *knas* but a *kapara*, an atonement payment. An admission to a *kapara* obligation — analogous to admitting one owes a *korban* — is fully effective. The owner admits liability, the liability stands, and *sekilah* is not triggered because two witnesses are lacking.

## Kofer No Stone

### Intended Beast

A second *baraisa* clarifies *Rabbi Eliezer*'s position still further. When *Rabbi Akiva* pressed him — how can there be *kofer* from a stoned ox? — *Rabbi Eliezer* answered: *kach ani b'einecha shedanti b'zeh shechayav mita? Ein dini ela b'mitkavein laharog et habeheima v'harag et ha'adam* — I am not dealing with a case where the ox is deserving of *sekilah* at all. My case is where the ox intended to kill an animal and instead killed a person. In such a case, since the intent was not to kill a human being, the ox is not executed: this was not murder in the full sense. Yet a human life was lost, so *kofer* is owed. The animal is not subject to *sekilah* — it is not wicked enough to be stoned — but the death of a human being generates a *kofer* obligation.

### Examples

*Rabbi Eliezer* elaborates: *sheniskaven laharog et habeheima veharag et haadam* — it intended to kill an animal and killed a human. Or where it intended to kill a non-Jew (*le-goy*) and killed a Jew — no *sekilah*, but *kofer*. Or where it intended to kill a *nefil* — a fetus — *veharag ben kayama* — and killed a viable person. In each of these cases the ox lacks the criminal intent that would warrant *sekilah*, but a human life was taken and *kofer* applies.

These cases also bear on the question raised earlier about *shen ve-regel* and *kofer*. There, the animal acts without *kavanah le-hazik* at all — it is not intending to harm. Here, the animal does have *kavanah le-hazik*, but that intent is directed at a category of victim whose death would not trigger *sekilah*. The parallel structure strengthens the case that *kofer* and *sekilah* can come apart, and that *kofer* is triggered by the fact that a human life was lost, while *sekilah* is reserved for acts of killing that satisfy the full criteria of culpable homicide.

### Big Fish Parable

The *gemara* closes with a dispute about the order in which *Rabbi Eliezer* offered his answers. *Rav Kahana* in the name of *Rava* says *niskaven amar lehu bereisha* — he gave the "intended to kill the animal" answer first. *Rav Tavyumi* in the name of *Rava* says *hen meisu amar lehu bereisha* — no, he gave the single-witness / owner-admission answer first.

Each position is illustrated by the parable of the fisherman: *mashal letzayad sheshola dagim min hayam* — like one pulling fish from the sea. According to *Rav Kahana*: first he pulls up big fish, takes them, then pulls up small fish, and takes those too. That is: *Rabbi Eliezer* led with the stronger answer — the ox intended to kill the animal and killed the person, a case where *sekilah* is simply inapplicable — and then added the weaker, supporting case of single-witness testimony. The better answer is the "big fish," the case where the animal is fundamentally not *chayav mita*; the single-witness case is the small fish, added as supplementary support.

According to *Rav Tavyumi*: first the fisherman pulls up small fish and keeps them not knowing what else he might find; then he pulls up big fish and throws the small ones back. That is: *Rabbi Eliezer* first offered the single-witness answer, then realized he had a far stronger response — the case of intended animal homicide — and discarded the first answer in favor of the better one.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 42

## Ba'al HaShor Naki

### Overview & Applications

The discussion in today's daf opens at 42a, five lines from the top, at the *baraita* introduced by the formula *tanya idach*. We are in the middle of a series of teachings derived from the phrase *ba'al hashor naki* — the owner of the ox shall be clean — which appears in the context of the goring ox. When an ox gores a person to death for the first time, the ox is stoned, but the owner bears no personal liability. After three such incidents, the verse *gam ba'alav yumat* — also his owner shall die — is interpreted as *misah bidei shamayim*, divine death, and the owner atones through the payment of *kofer*. In the first three instances, however, *ba'al hashor naki* — the owner is clean — and *Chazal* derive additional teachings from this phrase beyond the simple peshat.

The first two applications had already been covered. The first is that one is forbidden to derive any benefit whatsoever from the gored ox — the animal is *assur be-hana'ah*, including its hide. The second is that Rabbi Eliezer derived from *ba'al hashor naki* that the owner of an innocuous ox (*shor tam*) is not liable to pay *chatzi kofer* — half the *kofer* — when his ox gores to death for the first time. Rabbi Akiva challenged this, arguing that the model of a *tam* is payment from the body of the animal (*migufo*), and since the animal is condemned to be stoned, it is worth nothing; the very concept of *chatzi kofer* is therefore incoherent in this context. The remainder of today's daf continues to explore what else is derived from *ba'al hashor naki*.

### Assur be-Hana'ah

As noted, the first teaching derived from *ba'al hashor naki* is that the condemned ox is *assur be-hana'ah* — one may not benefit even from its leather or hide. The phrase *ba'al hashor naki* signals the owner's complete disengagement from the animal and its value.

### No Chatzi Kofer

The second teaching is that there is no *chatzi kofer* for the owner of a *shor tam* when it gores a person to death. Since a *tam* pays *migufo* — from the body of the animal — and the body of the animal is condemned to stoning, there is nothing from which to collect. Rabbi Akiva's critique of Rabbi Eliezer was that no *pasuk* was needed to reach this conclusion, since it follows logically. This dispute, and the final *drasha* on exemption from *chatzi kofer*, set the stage for all that follows.

---

## Dmei Vlodot Exemption

### R. Yose HaGelili

Another *baraita* is introduced: *ba'al hashor naki* — Rabbi Yose HaGelili says — means the owner is exempt from *dmei vladot*, the payment for fetal loss. The case in view is one where an ox gores a pregnant woman and she miscarries. Separately, the Torah in *Mishpatim* establishes that when men fight and one strikes a pregnant woman causing a miscarriage, the assailant pays *dmei vladot* to the husband. One might therefore have thought that the same payment should apply when an ox causes a miscarriage. Rabbi Yose HaGelili teaches that *ba'al hashor naki* exempts the owner of the ox from this payment.

This *halakha* requires some unpacking, because it is genuinely puzzling. When an ox gores a woman, we do pay *nezek* — damages for injury to her body. The method of assessing that injury is to ask how much the woman's value on the hypothetical slave market has decreased as a result. One might expect that if a pregnant woman miscarries, her body is worth less — a pregnant slave fetches a higher price than a non-pregnant one, because the buyer also acquires the future value of the offspring. Yet the *halakha* treats the fetal loss as a separate category, *dmei vladot*, rather than as part of the *nezek* calculation for the woman's body. The very fact that a distinct *pasuk* is needed to impose liability for *dmei vladot* — and a separate *pasuk* to exempt the ox's owner — indicates that the straightforward *nezek* assessment of the woman's body does not automatically account for the lost fetus. This is admittedly strange, but it is the *halakha*.

### R. Akiva's Critique

Rabbi Akiva challenges Rabbi Yose HaGelili. The verse in *Mishpatim* introducing *dmei vladot* already says *ki yinatzu anashim* — when men fight. From this phrase we derive *anashim velo shevarim* — the law applies to people, not to oxen. If the Torah itself already excludes oxen from *dmei vladot*, why does Rabbi Yose HaGelili need to derive the exemption from *ba'al hashor naki*? The Gemara acknowledges that Rabbi Akiva's critique is well-taken: *shapir ka'amar Rabbi Akiva*. So what would Rabbi Yose HaGelili respond?

### Muad vs. Tam

Rav Ulla the son of Rav Idi answers that both *pesukim* are indeed necessary. Without *ba'al hashor naki*, one would reason as follows: *ki yinatzu anashim* — *anashim velo shevarim*, people and not oxen — but more precisely, people insofar as people are always treated as *muad*, fully liable. The derivation *anashim velo shevarim* would then exclude only a *shor muad*, which is comparable to a human being always liable. However, a *shor tam* — which is the ox we are discussing throughout the passage of *ba'al hashor naki* — would not be excluded by that reasoning, because a *tam* is not analogous to the fully liable human. One might therefore have concluded that the *tam* must pay *dmei vladot*. Hence *ba'al hashor naki* comes to exclude even the *tam*.

Rava, however, raises a sharp objection. If the reasoning is that *anashim velo shevarim* excludes the *muad* — since people are always *muad* — then I would have derived from *kal va'chomer* that the *tam* is likewise exempt: if the *muad*, which is more culpable, is exempt, how much more so the *tam*. I therefore already know both are exempt from *anashim velo shevarim* alone. So why does *ba'al hashor naki* need to address this at all? Rava answers by reversing the logic. Perhaps *anashim velo shevarim* — understood in the direction of comparability — would have led us to exempt the *muad*, and then to infer the *tam* as well. *Ba'al hashor naki*, then, does not come to teach exemption; rather, it comes to restrict the exemption to the *tam* alone and to affirm that the *muad is actually liable* for *dmei vladot*. This yields a striking conclusion: a *shor muad* that causes a miscarriage pays *dmei vladot*, while a *shor tam* does not.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges this approach. If we are prepared to use *ba'al hashor naki* to modify the implication of *anashim velo shevarim* in the case of *dmei vladot*, the same move could be made for *boshet* — the payment for indignity. The passage describing *boshet* also uses the phrase *ki yinatzu anashim*, and similarly one could apply *anashim velo shevarim* to derive that oxen are exempt. By the same reasoning Rava employed, one would then use *ba'al hashor naki* to teach that only the *tam* is exempt and the *muad* must pay *boshet*. Abaye's point is that Rava's method yields an absurd result if applied consistently: why does it produce an obligation to pay *dmei vladot* but not *boshet*? There is no principled reason to apply the method selectively.

The Gemara takes Abaye's challenge seriously. If we were genuinely prepared to derive an obligation for a *shor muad* to pay *boshet*, the *baraita* presenting Rabbi Yose HaGelili's teaching should have stated explicitly that the owner is exempt from both *dmei vladot* and *boshet*. The fact that only *dmei vladot* is mentioned signals that something is wrong with the general approach, and a different reading is needed.

### Anashim Resolution

Abaye and Rava together — *amarei tarvaihu* — offer a resolution that abandons the previous approach and reads *anashim velo shevarim* entirely differently. The *pasuk* in question reads: *ki yinatzu anashim venagefu ishah harah veyatzu yeladeiha velo yihyeh ason anosh ye'anesh* — when men fight and strike a pregnant woman and her children come out, and there is no tragedy, the striker shall be fined. *Ve'im ason yihyeh venasata nefesh tachat nafesh* — but if there is a tragedy, you shall give a life for a life.

The reading offered by Abaye and Rava is this: *anashim ein ason be'ishah ye'anshu* — by men, if there is no loss of life involving the woman, they pay all attendant damages including *dmei vladot*. *Yesh ason be'ishah lo ye'anshu* — but if the woman dies, they do not pay monetary damages for the lesser injuries. This is an expression of the principle *kim leh bederabbah mineih*: when a person incurs a capital or severe criminal liability, lesser monetary obligations are subsumed and forfeited. The death of the woman renders the attacker liable to the more severe sanction, and the financial payment for *dmei vladot* is absorbed.

*Velo shevarim* — and not oxen: by oxen, even if the ox kills, the owner does not say *kim leh*. The ox causes a death, the ox is stoned, but the owner's financial liabilities — for damages other than the loss of life itself — are not absorbed. It is important to note that the absence of payment for *loss of life* by an ox is not itself an expression of *kim leh*. As *Tosafot* stresses, there is no civil monetary compensation for loss of life in halacha; that is simply not a category of financial liability. *Kim leh* is a separate principle by which a person who incurs a capital obligation is released from lesser monetary obligations that would otherwise apply. By oxen, this principle does not operate.

The contribution of *ba'al hashor naki* is then to exclude *dmei vladot* specifically. Since *anashim velo shevarim* now teaches the inapplicability of *kim leh* by oxen, there is no longer a *pasuk* exempting oxen from *dmei vladot* — one might think an ox should pay *dmei vladot* since it does not say *kim leh*. It is precisely *ba'al hashor naki* that comes to say: nevertheless, an ox does not pay *dmei vladot*. The two *pesukim* thus work in tandem: one teaches there is no *kim leh* by oxen, the other teaches there is no *dmei vladot* by oxen.

---

## Kim Leh Principle

### R. Ada bar Ahava

Rav Ada bar Ahava challenges this framework. Is the exemption from payment by people really contingent on *ason* — on a loss of life triggering *kim leh*? He argues it is rather *bkavanah talya milsa* — it depends on intention. According to Rashi's reading of Rav Ada bar Ahava's position, he holds a remarkably narrow view of *kim leh*: it applies only when one performs a direct, intentional act of murder toward the very person who was killed. Accidental homicide, in his view, does not trigger *kim leh* at all. Furthermore, he holds — strikingly — that there is in fact a financial payment for loss of life, at least in certain circumstances.

### Intention Doctrine

On Rav Ada bar Ahava's reading, the *pasuk* is structured as follows. *Ki nishkavnu zeh la-zeh* — when people are fighting intending to harm each other — *af al gav she-asa'un be'ishah ye'anshu* — even if in the course of their fighting they cause injury or even death to a woman, they will still pay, because *kim leh* attaches only to the act directed at the intended target. If Reuven is trying to kill Shimon and accidentally strikes a woman who dies, *kim leh* operates only with respect to what was done to Shimon — not with respect to the collateral harm to the woman. Therefore, the attacker remains liable for whatever injury or loss of life befell the woman.

The one case where payment is not made is when the fighters *nishkavnu le'ishah atzmah* — when they actually intended to kill the woman herself. In that case, *kim leh* does attach to the woman, and neither payment for her life nor payment for the fetus is made. *Velo shevarim* — but not by oxen: even if the ox intentionally gored a woman — the paradigm case of *shor haniskal* — one does not say *kim leh* for the ox's act, and the owner remains liable. According to Rav Ada bar Ahava, who holds there is a financial payment for loss of life, the owner would even pay that financial penalty — not *kofer*, but some form of monetary liability — since *kim leh* is simply not invoked for oxen. *Ba'al hashor naki* then comes to exclude *dmei vladot* specifically.

The Gemara notes that a *baraita* is brought in support of Rav Ada bar Ahava's position, and similarly that Rav Chaggai, upon arriving from the south, brought a *baraita* consistent with Rav Ada bar Ahava's view.

### Reconciliation

To summarize the resolution achieved: from *anashim velo shevarim* we derive — according to the dominant view of Abaye and Rava — that *kim leh* does not apply to oxen. From *ba'al hashor naki* we derive that an ox is exempt from *dmei vladot*. According to Rav Ada bar Ahava, the reading differs in its mechanism but arrives at the same place: *anashim velo shevarim* teaches that there is no *kim leh* by oxen even when they intentionally kill, while *ba'al hashor naki* teaches exemption from *dmei vladot*.

The cumulative list of what is derived from *ba'al hashor naki* now stands at three: the prohibition of benefit (*assur be-hana'ah*) from the condemned ox; exemption from *chatzi kofer* for the *shor tam*; and exemption from *dmei vladot*. We turn next to a fourth derivation.

---

## Dmei Eved Exemption

### R. Akiva Slave Exempt

A further *baraita* introduces Rabbi Akiva's teaching: *ba'al hashor naki* — the owner is exempt from *dmei eved*, the thirty-*shekel* payment owed when an ox gores a slave to death. The relevant verse in the Torah reads: *im kofer yushat alav... im eved yigach hashor o ama kesef shloshim shekalim yitein la'adonav* — if the ox gores a male or female slave, thirty silver *shekalim* shall be given to the master. When an ox is a *muad* and kills a slave, the owner pays this fixed sum of thirty. The question is whether a *shor tam* would also be liable for this payment.

The cases discussed up to this point — *dmei vladot*, *assur be-hana'ah*, *chatzi kofer* — were all directly associated with the killing of a person, making them naturally proximate to the *shor haniskal* scenario. The slave case is similar: it involves a loss of life, even if not the life of a free person. The *hazmana* — the proximity — to the stoning context is maintained.

### Internal Contradiction

The Gemara immediately raises a pointed question: why does Rabbi Akiva need a *pasuk* to reach this conclusion at all? Rabbi Akiva himself previously challenged Rabbi Eliezer on the *chatzi kofer* question by saying: bring the ox to court and they will pay you — meaning, the *tam* pays *migufo*, from the body of the animal, and the condemned ox is worth nothing. That same argument should have applied here. If the ox is condemned, there is nothing to pay from; why does *ba'al hashor naki* need to exempt the owner from *dmei eved*?

### Pre-Court Slaughter

Shmuel bar Abba Yitzchak answers: the scenario contemplated is one where the owner slaughtered the ox before the *gmar din* — before the court issued its final judgment condemning the animal. Once the court's sentence is pronounced, the ox becomes a *shor haniskal* and is *assur be-hana'ah* even if subsequently slaughtered. But if the owner slaughtered it before *gmar din*, the animal was never formally condemned; it never assumed the status of *shor haniskal*, and its meat remains *mutar*. In that case, there would be genuine value in the animal's body from which payment could theoretically be made. One might then have said: let him pay *dmei eved* from the meat of the animal he slaughtered before *gmar din*. It is this scenario that *ba'al hashor naki* comes to exclude. Since the ox was fundamentally deserving of death — *bar katla* — even though the owner circumvented the process by slaughtering it early, we do not say he should pay from its value. He has beaten the system, but the Torah does not then impose *dmei eved* upon him.

### R. Eliezer's Answer

The Gemara asks a further question: if this pre-*gmar din* slaughter scenario is a valid answer for Rabbi Akiva, why could Rabbi Eliezer not have given the same answer when Rabbi Akiva challenged him over *chatzi kofer*? Rabbi Eliezer's scenario was different: he was discussing a case where the ox had intended to gore an animal but accidentally struck a person. In that case, the ox never becomes a *shor haniskal* at all, because stoning applies only to an ox that intentionally killed a human being. An ox that accidentally killed while targeting an animal is not condemned. Here, the ox has genuine legal standing, is not condemned, retains its value, and there is therefore a real *hava amina* that the owner would pay *chatzi kofer* from it. This is why a *pasuk* — *ba'al hashor naki* — was needed to exclude that payment.

By contrast, the pre-*gmar din* slaughter scenario is weaker, because the animal was fundamentally *bar katla* — it was deserving of death from the outset. The Torah would not naturally have been understood to impose payment in a case where the standard outcome would be stoning; the pre-*gmar din* slaughter is an aberration. Rabbi Eliezer's scenario, where the animal was never deserving of stoning at all, is a stronger *hava amina* and therefore requires a *pasuk* more obviously. The Gemara states explicitly: Rabbi Akiva himself would have agreed that Rabbi Eliezer's scenario is fundamentally stronger — *vadi hachi hava* — and he challenged Rabbi Eliezer precisely hoping Rabbi Eliezer would produce a better answer than the one Rabbi Akiva had in mind.

### Akiva's Doctrine

Rav Assi then introduces an entirely different explanation for why Rabbi Akiva needed a *pasuk* to exclude *dmei eved* from the *tam* — and it is a striking one. He says he heard this from a great man, namely Rabbi Yose the son of Rabbi Chanina. The insight turns on a position unique to Rabbi Akiva: Rabbi Akiva holds that when a *shor tam* injures or kills a *person* (as opposed to an animal), the payment is full damages, not half. This is in contrast to the standard rule that a *tam* pays half damages. Rabbi Akiva derives this from the verse *k'mishpat hazeh ye'aseh lo* — this law shall be done to him — and holds that in human cases, the *tam* pays full.

Now, Rabbi Akiva's *hava amina* comes into focus. If a *tam* that kills a person pays full — not half, not *migufo* from the condemned body — then perhaps the *tam* should pay the full thirty *shekel* of *dmei eved* as well, and it would not be paying *migufo* but rather from cash (*min ha'aliyah*). This is why Rabbi Akiva could not say to himself what he said to Rabbi Eliezer — "the animal isn't worth anything" — because in Rabbi Akiva's own system, the payment for killing a person is not necessarily tied to the value of the animal's body.

The Gemara, however, deflates this answer. Rav Zeira points out to Rav Ashi that Rabbi Akiva already blunted his own position elsewhere. A *baraita* records Rabbi Akiva himself saying: one might have thought a *tam* that injures a person pays from liquid assets (*min ha'aliyah*); the verse says *k'mishpat hazeh ye'aseh lo* — this law shall be done to it — teaching that even when the *tam* pays full, it pays only *migufo*, from the body, not from cash. So Rabbi Akiva's own ruling reintroduces the *migufo* limitation even in the context of injury to people, and the question of the condemned ox's worthlessness reasserts itself.

### Arbitrary Payment

Rava therefore provides the definitive explanation. The *hava amina* — the assumption that would have led us to impose *dmei eved* on the *tam* — is based on the apparently arbitrary character of the thirty-*shekel* payment itself. For a free person killed by a *muad*, the owner pays the actual assessed value: if the person was worth one *sela*, one pays one; if thirty, one pays thirty. *Ben chorin yafeh sela nosein sela, shloshim nosein shloshim*. But for a slave, the payment is always thirty *shekel*, regardless of the slave's actual worth: *eved yafeh sela nosein shloshim*. The Torah fixes a flat rate.

This flat, somewhat arbitrary payment gives rise to a *hava amina*: since the Torah is being arbitrary about the quantum — paying thirty regardless of the slave's value — perhaps it is also being arbitrary about the form of payment, dispensing with the *migufo* limitation and requiring payment even from cash, even when the ox is a *tam* and would normally pay only from its body. And since the payment is arbitrary in one dimension, perhaps it is also arbitrary in another: it does not matter whether the ox is a *tam* or a *muad*, it always pays thirty. This is a genuine *hava amina*, rooted in a reasonable reading of the *pasuk* that seems to treat the slave case as categorically distinct. Therefore, a *pasuk* — *ba'al hashor naki* — is needed to say: no, the owner of the *tam* is clean even from *dmei eved*.

### Final Resolution

The Gemara confirms: *tanya k'vosei d'Rava* — a *baraita* is brought consistent with Rava's explanation. The *baraita* records Rabbi Eliezer saying *naki mi-dmei eved* — the owner is clean from the payment of *dmei eved* — and then walks through precisely the *kal va'chomer* arguments in both directions. On one hand, since by a free person killed by a *muad* you pay the exact assessed value, and yet you exempt the *tam*, so too by a slave you should exempt the *tam*. On the other hand — and this is the counter-argument that necessitates the *pasuk* — one could argue the opposite: the Torah is stricter, or more precisely more arbitrary, by the slave, since the slave always costs thirty even if he is worth only one *sela*. That arbitrariness might suggest the thirty-*shekel* payment is regime unto itself, applicable regardless of *tam* or *muad*, and payable from cash rather than from the body. It is this counter-argument that *ba'al hashor naki* comes to rebut.

The final tally of teachings derived from *ba'al hashor naki*: prohibition of benefit from the condemned ox; exemption from *chatzi kofer*; exemption from *dmei vladot*; and exemption from *dmei eved*.

---

## Vehemit Ish

### New Derivation

With the *drasha* on *ba'al hashor naki* concluded, the Gemara moves to a new verse. The *baraita* opens: *vehemit ish o ishah* — and it kills a man or a woman. This is a distinct phrase in the passage of the goring ox, and the Gemara now mines it for its own legal teachings.

### Woman-Man Linkage

Rabbi Akiva asks: what does the Torah intend by specifying both a man and a woman? If the purpose is simply to establish that one is equally liable for the life of a woman as for the life of a man, that has already been stated earlier: *ki yigach shor et ish o et ishah vamet* — when an ox gores a man or a woman and they die. Rabbi Akiva therefore reads the second mention as establishing an analogy: *hikish ishah le'ish* — the Torah links the woman to the man. Just as a man, when killed, has his *kofer* paid to his heirs, so too a woman, when killed, has her *kofer* paid to her heirs.

This might seem obvious, but the subtle question is: who are her heirs? A woman's husband normally inherits her estate. Yet here Rabbi Akiva appears to direct the *kofer* to her children, not her husband. The Gemara asks: does Rabbi Akiva not hold that a husband inherits from his wife? Surely Rabbi Akiva himself derives from the verse *veyarash otah* — in the laws of inheritance — that a husband does inherit his wife's estate, and that this is a biblical rule, not merely rabbinic. So why does the *kofer* go to her children and not to him?

### Post-Mortem Obligation

Reish Lakish resolves this cleanly. The rule directing the *kofer* to the woman's children rather than her husband is limited to *kofer* specifically, because *kofer* is paid only *le'achar mitah* — after death. The *kofer* obligation crystallizes only once the person is dead. At the moment of death, the woman is no longer this man's wife in the ongoing sense. A husband inherits property that was in his wife's possession and control at the time of her death — property she *had*. But property that comes to her only after her death is a different matter.

### Inheritance Timing

The Gemara elaborates on the underlying principle. The obligation of *kofer* accrues from the moment of goring — *chovin mish'at negichah* — but is not paid until death — *lemitah*. It was therefore *ra'uy* to come to the woman — fit to come to her estate — but had not yet come into her actual possession. The rule is *ein haba'al notel b'ra'uy k'b'muchzak* — a husband does not inherit property that was merely fit to come to his wife in the same way he inherits property that was already in her control. He takes only what she actually held at the moment of death, not what was destined to arrive afterward.

The rationale is intuitive. The husband's right of inheritance is grounded in the marital bond. Once the wife dies, that bond dissolves. The children, by contrast, descend from their mother regardless of her death; their biological connection to her is permanent. Money that flows to her estate *after* her death therefore passes to her children — her blood heirs — not to the husband whose legal bond to her ended at the moment of her death. The *kofer* therefore belongs to the children, as Rabbi Akiva's derivation of *mah ish nizkak leyorshav af ishah nizkaket leyorsheiha* indicates. The Gemara will continue from here in the next session.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 43

## Husband's Inheritance

### Pasuk Repetition

The daf begins at the very bottom of 42b, in the course of a broader *darshanung* of the *pesukim* governing the goring ox. The question arises: why does the *pasuk* repeat the phrase *ish o isha* — "man or woman"? The Torah first states *ki yigach shor ish o isha vamet*, and then again *vehemit ish o isha*. What is the purpose of this repetition?

### Rabbi Akiva's Position

Rabbi Akiva explains that the repetition comes to teach us something about who collects the *kofer*. Since the victims are dead by the time payment is made, the *kofer* is necessarily paid to their heirs. One might have assumed that the *kofer* for the woman should go to her husband, since a husband ordinarily inherits his wife. Rabbi Akiva's *chidush* is that this is not the case: the payment goes to the woman's own heirs, not to her husband.

The underlying rationale is that a husband inherits his wife only with respect to money she had, or was entitled to, during her lifetime — because it is that bond of marriage-during-life that causes the inheritance to flow to him. But money she becomes entitled to only *after* her death carries no such bond, and therefore descends instead to her natural heirs.

### Debt After Death

The *Gemara* probes: according to Rabbi Akiva, where would he *not* apply this rule? That is, where would a woman's heirs fail to collect damages owed to her? The implication is that if money was owed to her during her lifetime — a genuine *nezek* debt incurred while she lived — that money should logically pass to the husband upon her death, since it was a pre-existing obligation. Rabbi Akiva, the *Gemara* assumes, would agree with this. But is it actually so straightforward?

### Miscarriage Case

A *braita* complicates the picture. The *braita* presents the Torah's case of a man who strikes a woman and she miscarries: *hika et isha veyatz'u yeladeha*. The ruling is that *nezek* and *tzaar* — the injury and the pain suffered by the woman — are paid to the woman herself, while *demei veladot*, the monetary value of the fetus, goes to the husband: *nosay nezek vetza'ar le'isha udmei veladot leba'al*. So far, this reflects the standard division.

The *braita* then addresses what happens when one of the parties is no longer living at the time of payment. If the husband is deceased, the *demei veladot* are paid to his heirs. And if the woman is deceased — *ein ha'isha, nosay leyorsheha* — the *nezek* and *tzaar* go to *her* heirs. But this creates a problem: the woman suffered this injury during her lifetime, meaning the debt of *nezek* and *tzaar* was incurred while she was alive. Why, then, do her heirs collect rather than her husband? This appears to contradict our assumption that pre-existing debts pass to the husband.

### Divorce Solution

Rabbah and Rav Nachman both offer the same resolution: *begerusha* — the case in the *braita* is one where she was divorced. Rashi explains that at least initially, we understand this to mean she was divorced *after* the injury occurred. At the time of the injury, the *demei veladot* were rightly owed to the husband — he was the husband then, and that is what the Torah specifies. But the *nezek* and *tzaar* were owed to the woman herself, and after their divorce she died unmarried, so those payments now pass to her heirs rather than to her former husband. That is why the *braita*'s ruling is perfectly coherent.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this, however: if the case is one of a *gerusha*, why does the *braita* still award the *demei veladot* to the husband? The *Gemara* assumes that the *demei veladot* are connected to the wife in some way — perhaps through *ma'aseh yadeha* or a similar principle — so if the injury occurred after the divorce, the husband seems entirely out of the picture. Why should he receive anything?

### Father vs. Husband

Rav Pappa resolves this: *haTorah zachta demei veladot leba'al* — the Torah awarded the *demei veladot* to the husband, but the critical word is *ba'al*. The *pasuk* uses the term *ka'asher yashis alav ba'al ha'isha*, and the word *ba'al* carries the connotation of *boel* — the one who had sexual relations with her. The award, therefore, is not contingent on being the husband at the time of the injury; it goes to the biological father of the lost fetus. Even if the couple was divorced at the time of the *nezek*, and even — as an extreme extension — *afilu ba l'beiznus*, even if the conception occurred entirely outside the context of marriage, the *demei veladot* still go to the biological father.

Why? Because the Torah's use of the term *ba'al*, which linguistically emphasizes the sexual relationship rather than the formal marital bond, signals that it is the father — not the husband — who is awarded these damages. This, indeed, reflects the deeper assumption of *halacha* that children are fundamentally seen as the father's. According to basic *halachic* principle, in a case of divorce where children already exist, they are regarded as belonging to the father unless the children are very young and require the mother's care.

This is in itself a striking *gemara*. The *demei veladot* go not to the husband but to the biological father — and not only in a case of legitimate marriage, but even in a case of conception outside marriage.
