The *gemara* asks how this can be: if the *shomer* performed adequate *shmira*, he should be exempt in both directions; if he did not, he should be liable in both. The resolution — offered by Rava — is that the case involves a *shomer* who knew the ox had a propensity to gore and accepted it for guardianship. In such a case, *stama d'milsa d'lo azil ihu umazik achrina kabil alay* — the presumed purpose of the *shmira* arrangement is to prevent the ox from harming others. That is what the owner was worried about, and that is what the *shomer* implicitly accepted liability for. That the ox might itself be harmed, *lo asik ada'atei* — was not something the *shomer* would have considered as part of the arrangement. Hence the asymmetric outcome.

---

## Judgment Without Ox Pres…

### Rabbanan: Presence Requi…

Having established the general framework of the *baraita*, the *gemara* now returns to examine the deeper logic of the *rabbanan*–Rabbi Yaakov dispute about whether *gmar din* can occur outside the ox's presence, and what consequences that has for the *shomer*'s liability.

According to the *rabbanan*, who hold *ein gomrin dino shel shor ela befanav*, the ox must be physically present for *gmar din* to be issued. This makes the *shomer*'s failure to return the ox before the court obtained it a direct cause of the *gmar din* itself. The owners can legitimately argue: *ei ahadrateih nihali, havena mivrachna leh l'agma* — had you returned my ox in time, I would have taken it away and the judgment could never have been issued. Because the *rabbanan* hold that *beit din* cannot proceed without the ox, the *shomer*'s negligence in allowing *beit din* to gain possession is precisely the act that enabled the *gmar din*. The *shomer* therefore cannot discharge the obligation through *harei shelcha lefanecha* — the damage is not merely inferred from the ox's presence in court; it is *caused* by that presence.

### Rabbi Yaakov: Presence N…

Rabbi Yaakov, who holds *gomrin dino shel shor shelo befanav* — that *gmar din* can proceed without the ox present — can therefore instruct the *shomer* to respond: *sof sof migmar havei gamri leh l'dineih* — in the end, the court would have issued its judgment regardless. The ox's presence in *beit din* did not cause the *gmar din*; the *gmar din* was going to occur no matter what. The damage therefore does not flow from the ox being in the hands of *beit din*, and seeing it there does not constitute *hezek nikar*. The *shomer* may therefore say *harei shelcha lefanecha* and be discharged.

### Rabbi Eliezer on Muad

Rav Huna bar Chinana had already offered his resolution above: the *baraita* follows Rabbi Eliezer's position that *ein lo shmira ela sakin* — for a *muad*, no *shmira* ever suffices, making the *shomer* always liable for *kofer*, regardless of what level of *shmira* was performed.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye resolves the difficulty differently: the *baraita* in fact follows Rabbi Meir, but the transmitted tradition reverses the standard attribution of positions on the *socher*. Under this reading, the minimum *shmira* performed by the *shomer chinam* is sufficient to discharge his obligation to the owner — the ox becoming a *shor haniskal* was not a result of his gross negligence — while the others, held to a higher standard, remain liable for reimbursing the owner. The *kofer* obligation, meanwhile, persists because minimum *shmira* for a *muad* is still insufficient to exempt one from liability for the damage it caused, under Rabbi Meir's framework.

---

## Tam vs Muad Watchfulness

### Four Positions on Shmira

The *gemara* now turns to the *mishna* that has been repeatedly referenced throughout this discussion — the one that spells out explicitly what level of *shmira* is required to be exempt when an ox goes and damages. *Kesharo be'alav bemosira* — the owner tied it up with a standard rope — *vena'al befanav kera'uy* — and locked it in the normal way — and it still went out and caused damage. *Echad tam ve'echad muad chayav* — this is the ruling of Rabbi Meir: both a *tam* and a *muad* require a higher level of *shmira* to be exempt; standard minimum *shmira* is insufficient. Rabbi Yehuda presents a striking inversion: *tam chayav umuad patur* — minimum *shmira* exempts the owner of a *muad* but not the owner of a *tam*. Rabbi Eliezer says: *ein lo shmira ella sakin* — for a *muad*, there is no *shmira* short of slaughter that suffices.

### Rabbi Meir: High Shmira

Rabbi Meir holds that both *tam* and *muad* require maximum-level *shmira*. His reasoning proceeds as follows. The *gemara* explains: *stam shorim lav bechezkat shmira kaymi* — Rashi reads this to mean that in the ordinary course of life, people do not bother carefully watching their oxen, since they are normally tame. Yet the *Torah* says *tam meshalem* — you pay for a *tam* — which implies you were expected to do more than the standard non-existent watching. You needed at least minimum *shmira*. Then the *Torah* adds, concerning the *muad*, *velo yishmerenu ba'alav* — "and the owner did not guard it" — suggesting that for the *muad*, you needed an even higher level still. Finally, the *gezerah shavah* of *negicha* and *negicha* — the word for goring appears in both the *tam* and *muad* contexts — links them together and raises the standard for the *tam* to match the *muad*. The result: both require maximum *shmira*.

### Rabbi Yehuda: Inverse

Rabbi Yehuda's position is precisely the opposite, and deliberately so. He holds *stam shorim bechezkat shmira kaymi* — the *Torah* presumed that people do watch their oxen. When it nonetheless made you liable for a *tam*, it was already requiring you to do *more* than what everyone normally does, i.e., the highest level of *shmira*. Then when it added *velo yishmerenu* for the *muad*, one might expect an even greater demand — but since you were already at the highest level, this creates a *ribui achar ribui*, an amplification upon an amplification, and the rule of *ribui achar ribui* is to restrict rather than expand. The additional mention therefore comes to reduce the standard: for a *muad*, minimum *shmira* suffices. This is deeply counterintuitive — more dangerous ox, less stringent watchfulness requirement — but there is a powerful underlying logic to it. The *gezerah shavah* of *negicha-negicha* would bring the *tam* down to the *muad*'s level, but the *gemara* notes that Rabbi Yehuda can resist this: *lo yishmerenu* is written specifically regarding the *muad* — *lizeh velo l'acher* — and limits the leniency to the *muad* alone. Thus the *tam* retains the higher standard.

### Rabbi Eliezer: Slaughter…

Rabbi Eliezer holds the most extreme position: for a *muad*, *ein lo shmira ella sakin* — the only true *shmira* is slaughter. No fence, no chain, no enclosure suffices. Once an ox is *muad*, the owner is always liable for whatever damage it causes.

### Scriptural Derivation

The *gemara* derives these positions from two key textual features. The first is *yigach* — the word for goring appears in both the *tam* and *muad* passages, enabling a *gezerah shavah* that links the legal standards for the two. The second is *lo yishmerenu ba'alav* — "and its owner did not guard it" — which each opinion reads differently. For Rabbi Meir, it signals a heightened demand of maximum *shmira* for a *muad*, which via the *gezerah shavah* is then extended to the *tam*. For Rabbi Yehuda, the presence of *lo yishmerenu* after the maximum *shmira* was already required generates the *ribui achar ribui* logic, reducing the *muad* to minimum *shmira*.

### Tam vs Muad: Liability T…

The underlying conceptual tension that makes Rabbi Yehuda's position so striking is the question of whether payment for a *tam* is fault-based or strict liability. Rabbi Yehuda's view can be understood as holding that payment for a *tam* is a *knas*, a penalty — arbitrary in the sense that you were not truly at fault. Ordinary oxen do not gore. *Stam shorim bechezkat shmira kaymi* can be read to mean not merely that owners normally watch their oxen, but that oxen can be presumed to be self-contained — they do not go out and attack. Nevertheless, if your ox gored, you pay half. The payment is not based on fault; it is simply imposed. If that is so, then no degree of watchfulness short of maximum can get you out of it — because the payment is not responsive to fault in the first place. The only exemption is when the event was a complete *ones*, an act of God that you truly could not have prevented — which requires the highest *shmira*.

A *muad*, by contrast, is fault-based. You knew your ox was dangerous. You should have watched it. If you did at least the minimum required of a reasonable person, your fault is discharged and you are exempt. This is the normal logic of negligence liability: once you have fulfilled the duty of care, you bear no further obligation.

The apparent absurdity — that it is easier to be exempt for a more dangerous animal — dissolves once one grasps this distinction. The *tam* imposes strict liability; strict liability cannot be waived by reasonable care. The *muad* imposes fault liability; fault liability can be waived by reasonable care.

### Tam Half-Payment Remains

This logic leads directly to Rav Adda bar Ahava's clarification: *lo patar Rebbi Yehuda ela tzad ha'ad she'bo* — when Rabbi Yehuda exempts the owner of a *muad* who performed minimum *shmira*, he exempts them only from the *muad* component of payment, that is, the additional liability that flows from fault. But *aval tzad tamut bimkomo omedet* — the *tam* dimension of liability remains in place. Even when an ox has become *muad*, the original strict-liability half-payment of a *tam* has never been waived. It was never fault-based to begin with, and therefore minimum *shmira* cannot discharge it. The owner who performed only minimum *shmira* for a *muad* will still owe *chatzi nezek* — half payment — as though the animal were still a *tam*.

The *gemara* indicates there is one further point to be made about *tzad tamut bimkomo omedet*, which will be picked up in the next session.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 46

## Right/Left Horn

### Rav's Position

The daf opens at the bottom of 45b with a ruling of Rav: *muad le-keren yamin eno muad le-keren smol* — an animal that has been established as a *muad* for goring with its right horn is not thereby a *muad* for goring with its left horn. If the ox gored three times and on each occasion used its right horn, it has not become habituated with respect to the left.

As both Rashi and Tosafot observe, Rav cannot merely be stating the obvious point that a *muad* for one type of goring is not a *muad* for another type. That general principle is already well established throughout the *mishnayos* and *Gemara* — if an animal is *muad* for goring cows, it is not thereby *muad* for goring sheep, and so on. It goes without saying that an ox that gores habitually with its right horn should not be assumed habitual with the left, and so if it then gores with the left, only half damages (*chatzi nezek*) would apply. Rav clearly does not need to teach us that. The presumption, therefore, is that Rav's ruling carries a specific implication about *shemira* — supervision — and that in some configuration, a difference in *shemira* obligations can produce a scenario where the owner is liable for one horn and exempt for the other.

### Gemara's Query

The *Gemara* asks: *aliba de-man* — according to which authority does Rav's distinction about right and left horns become halachically interesting in terms of *shemira*? The *Gemara* surveys the positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, which were the subject of the preceding discussion.

### Rabbi Meir's View

According to Rabbi Meir, both a *tam* and a *muad* require *shemira meula* — a high standard of supervision — for the owner to be exempt from liability. If that is so, then whether the animal gores with its right horn or its left horn makes no difference from a *shemira* standpoint: insufficient *shemira* renders the owner liable in either case, and sufficient *shemira* exempts him in either case. The distinction between right and left horns would carry no practical implication under Rabbi Meir's view.

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

According to Rabbi Yehuda, the situation is more nuanced — and famously ironic. Rabbi Yehuda holds that a *muad* requires only a low level of *shemira* to exempt its owner, while a *tam* requires the higher standard. This opens up an interesting possibility with Rav's ruling. If an owner performs only a minimal level of *shemira* and the animal gores with its right horn — the horn for which it is *muad* — he is exempt. But if it gores with the left horn — for which it remains a *tam* — he would be liable, having failed to provide the higher standard of *shemira* required for a *tam*. Here, then, the right/left distinction generates a real and practical difference in liability.

### Gemara Objection

The *Gemara* raises an objection, however. If the goal is to demonstrate a scenario where a single level of *shemira* produces different outcomes for different aspects of the animal's status, one need not introduce two separate horns at all. Rabbi Yehuda's own position already contains a built-in mechanism for exactly this, through the principle of *tzad tamus be-mekoma omedes* — the *tam* aspect remains in place even within a *muad*. According to that doctrine, even an animal that has become fully *muad* retains an inner dimension of *tam* status, and so even for the right horn itself, a low level of *shemira* would still leave the owner liable for the *tam* component. There would be no need to invoke the distinction between two horns at all.

### Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves this by confirming that Rav is indeed proceeding according to Rabbi Yehuda — but emphatically not according to the doctrine of *tzad tamus be-mekoma omedes* associated with Rav Adda bar Ahava. Rav rejects that principle entirely. In his view, once an animal is fully *muad*, it is *muad* through and through — there is no residual *tam* aspect lurking within it. The only genuine case where a single animal simultaneously presents a *muad* dimension and a *tam* dimension is precisely the situation of right horn and left horn: the right horn being *muad* and the left remaining *tam*. That is why Rav found it necessary and meaningful to articulate the distinction.

## Tam Aspect Debate

### Rav vs. Rav Adda

The *Gemara* makes explicit that Rav's ruling is a direct response to — and rejection of — the position of Rav Adda bar Ahava. Rav Adda bar Ahava had maintained the doctrine of *tzad tamus be-mekoma omedes*: that even within a fully *muad* animal, the *tam* dimension endures. This had the practical consequence that even for a full *muad*, performing only a low standard of *shemira* would still leave the owner liable for the residual *tam* component, and a variety of intermediate liability scenarios could arise.

### Full Muad Status

Rav flatly rejects this. *Ve-hachi ka'amar* — what Rav is really saying is: if you want to find a genuine case where an animal is simultaneously *muad* for one thing and *tam* for another, producing a scenario where *shemira* at a low level generates liability for one aspect but not the other, then the right horn and the left horn are the only scenario that achieves this. At the top of 46a, Rav states the principle: if an animal is a *muad legamrei* — fully and completely *muad* — there is no *tam* dimension embedded within it. The thing for which it is *muad* is one hundred percent *muad*. You cannot speak of a *tam* wrapped within every *muad*. The only way to obtain an animal that is half *tam* and half *muad* is through something structurally distinct — like a right horn established as *muad* and a left horn remaining *tam*. This is a sharp pushback against Rav Adda bar Ahava's conceptual framework.

## Rabbi Eliezer

### No Shemira Rule

The final portion of the *mishna* presents Rabbi Eliezer's striking position: *ein lo shemira ela sakin* — for a *shor muad*, there is no effective supervision except the knife. The only way the owner of a *muad* ox can free himself from liability is by performing *shechita*. Short of slaughter, the owner will always be considered liable when the animal causes damage.

### Rava's Reading

The *Gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Eliezer* — what is the reasoning behind Rabbi Eliezer's position? Rava answers by pointing to the verse *velo yishmrenu* — "and he did not watch it." Rava reads this phrase not as a description of negligent behavior but as a statement of ontological impossibility: once an animal has become a *muad*, it is in principle no longer watchable. The owner is therefore always in a state of fault — he can never be said to have genuinely supervised it. The only exit from this perpetual liability is to remove the animal from existence entirely through *shechita*.

### Pit Comparison

Abaye challenges Rava's reading. If *velo yishmrenu* means the ox is inherently incapable of being watched, then by the same token one should say *velo yichasenu* — the parallel language about a *bor*, a pit — means that covering a pit provides no exemption either, since covering it is similarly "impossible." Yet we have an explicit *mishna* ruling that if one covered the pit properly and an animal nevertheless fell in and died, the owner of the pit is exempt. We find no record of Rabbi Eliezer disputing this ruling. The analogy therefore breaks down: the textual logic Rava applies to the ox cannot extend uniformly to the pit.

### Hazard Principle

Abaye therefore offers an alternative grounding for Rabbi Eliezer's position, derived from a *braita* in the name of Rabbi Natan. The *braita* states: how do we know that one must not keep a vicious dog in his home, nor maintain a rickety ladder? From the verse *velo tasim damim beveitecha* — you shall not place blood in your house. The verse, which appears in the context of the obligation to build a parapet on one's roof, is read more broadly to prohibit maintaining any hazard in one's domain that could lead to another person's injury or death.

### Rashi's Logic

Rashi explains how this *braita* transforms the reading of *velo yishmrenu*. In isolation, the verse *velo yishmrenu* by the *shor muad* — or *velo yichasenu* by the *bor* — might simply mean: one failed to watch it, or failed to cover it. Read in that neutral descriptive sense, one who does watch it, or cover it, would be exempt. But once we know from *velo tasim damim beveitecha* that the Torah imposes an affirmative obligation to remove the *muad* ox entirely — not merely to supervise it — the language *velo yishmrenu* takes on a different meaning. Since the owner was under an obligation to eliminate the hazard and failed to do so, we read *velo yishmrenu* as expressing an impossibility: there is no form of supervision that discharges his duty. He remains liable until he performs *shechita*. The obligation to remove, in other words, interacts with the verse to rule out supervision as a viable defense.

The obvious follow-up question is why the same logic does not apply to a *bor*. A pit in one's domain is also a hazard under *velo tasim damim beveitecha*, and one should arguably be obligated to fill it — not merely cover it — in which case covering should provide no exemption either.

### Tosafot Answer 1

Tosafot's first answer draws a fundamental distinction between a living ox and a covered pit. An ox is a living creature; no matter how rigorously it is guarded, it will always strive to break free. The owner of a *muad* ox can never truly be said to have neutralized the danger in any lasting or definitive way. A covered pit, by contrast, can be rendered genuinely inert: once properly covered, it effectively ceases to exist as a pit at all. The hazard has been neutralized in a real sense. Starting from the obligation of *velo tasim damim beveitecha*, the *muad* ox therefore remains a perpetually present danger regardless of supervision, while the covered pit does not.

### Tosafot Answer 2

Tosafot's second answer operates on a different level entirely, distinguishing between civil liability and religious obligation. Tosafot observes that when Rabbi Eliezer states *ein lo shemira ela sakin*, we might initially have understood him to mean that one who fails to slaughter the *muad* ox is always civilly liable for its damages, regardless of how well he supervised it. But Tosafot suggests that once we ground the ruling in the *braita* of Rabbi Natan and the verse *velo tasim damim beveitecha*, Rabbi Eliezer may not actually be speaking about civil damages at all. Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer would concede that an owner who performs a genuinely high standard of *shemira* is exempt from civil liability in damages. What *velo tasim damim beveitecha* establishes is a separate religious obligation — an *issur* — to remove the hazard. Similarly, by a *bor*: covering it may fully exempt one from civil damages, yet one might still be under an independent obligation to eliminate it. The two tracks — civil liability and religious duty — need not rise and fall together. This second answer, though analytically elegant, does stretch the imagination somewhat when applied to pits in one's own home.

## Pregnant Cow Case

### Case Setup

With the declaration *hadran lach* marking the transition, the *Gemara* opens a new *perek*, still within the domain of goring. The *mishna* presents the following scenario: an ox gores a pregnant cow, and afterward one finds the fetus lying dead beside the cow. The goring clearly took place — there is sufficient evidence to establish the ox's liability for the cow. But a critical fact is unknown: *ein yadu'a im ad shelo nagcha yalda im mishe-nagcha yalda* — did the cow give birth before it was gored, or was it still pregnant at the time of the goring?

The practical stakes are evident. If the cow gave birth first and the fetus was already delivered when the goring occurred, the owner of the ox bears no responsibility for the fetus: the fetus was a separate entity, never struck by the ox, and its death cannot be attributed to the goring. But if the cow was still pregnant when gored, then the ox caused two losses simultaneously — the injury to the cow and the death of the fetus — and the owner owes damages for both.

### Mishnah Rule

The *mishna* rules: *meshalem chatzi nezek la-para u-reviah nezek la-vlad* — he pays half damages for the cow and a quarter of the damages for the fetus. The half damages for the cow is straightforward: this is a *shor tam*, and a *tam* pays half the damage it causes. The quarter damages for the fetus requires explanation. Had it been certain that the ox gored the fetus — i.e., that the cow was pregnant at the time — the owner would owe half the value of the fetus. Since there is genuine doubt as to whether he owes anything at all for the fetus, we take half of what he might owe: half of a half, yielding a quarter.

This ruling, as we shall see, reflects the position of Sumchus. But before exploring the *Gemara*'s analysis, it is worth appreciating the full structure of the case. The *mishna* also presents the reverse scenario — a cow gores an ox — but the mechanics of that case are considerably more complex and will require Abaye's clarification.

### Sumchus Principle

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel identifies the source of the *mishna*'s ruling: *zu divrei Sumchus* — this is the position of Sumchus. Sumchus maintains the principle of *mamon ha-mutal be-safek cholkin* — money suspended in doubt is divided. When there is a genuine and balanced uncertainty as to whether a financial obligation exists, and no external fact can resolve it, the parties split the difference rather than assigning the full loss to one side. Applied here: it is fifty-fifty whether the ox owes for the fetus, so the obligation is split — the owner pays half of the half he might owe, yielding the quarter the *mishna* specifies.

### Burden of Proof

The *Chachamim* disagree and articulate their opposing position in terms of a foundational principle: *ze klal gadol ba-din, ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya* — this is a great rule in adjudication: the one who seeks to extract money from another bears the burden of proof. Under this principle, the uncertainty does not produce a split; instead, the owner of the ox retains his money unless and until the other party proves his liability. The owner of the cow wants to be paid for the fetus: he must prove the cow was pregnant when gored. Since he cannot, the claim fails entirely.

## Hamotzi Principle

### Principle Scope

The *Gemara* asks why the *Chachamim* found it necessary to introduce their ruling with the words *ze klal gadol ba-din* — "this is a great rule in adjudication" — rather than simply stating *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya*. The answer is that the expanded formulation signals the breadth of the principle's application: it applies even in circumstances that might seem like obvious exceptions, and the *Gemara* now enumerates several such cases.

### Bari vs. Shema

The first extension: *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya* applies even in a case where the *nizak* — the injured party — says *bari*, meaning he asserts with certainty that the cow was still pregnant when gored, and the *mazik* — the damaging party — says *shema*, meaning he is uncertain whether it was pregnant or not. The *Chachamim* rule that *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya* still governs: the certainty of the plaintiff's claim does not in itself constitute proof.

This invokes the broader *sugya* of *bari ve-shema* — whether a definite claim (*bari*) overcomes an uncertain response (*shema*) in monetary litigation, without any additional evidence. The question is a serious one: if I claim with certainty that you owe me one hundred coins and you respond that you simply do not remember whether you borrowed from me, does my confident assertion carry enough weight to obligate you? The *Gemara* here rules that *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya* applies even in such a configuration — the plaintiff's certainty is not a substitute for proof.

Tosafot develops this analysis at some length, introducing the categories of *bari tov* and *bari garu'a*, and *shema tov* and *shema garu'a*. A *bari tov* — a strong *bari* — is a case where the defendant would know if the plaintiff were lying, and yet the plaintiff asserts the claim anyway: there is a check on fabrication. A *bari garu'a* — a weak *bari* — is where the defendant has no way of verifying the claim, so the plaintiff's certainty carries less epistemic weight. Similarly, a *shema tov* — a strong uncertainty — is where the defendant had no particular reason to know one way or the other; a *shema garu'a* — a weak uncertainty — is where the defendant should have known and his uncertainty is therefore suspect. A claim of certainty against someone who would know if they were lying, combined with a *shema garu'a*, may well tilt the analysis toward the plaintiff even under *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya*. These distinctions carry significant practical implications, though the general principle holds.

### Money vs. Rov

The *Gemara* introduces a further extension: *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya* applies even in the face of *rov* — majority. In many areas of *halacha*, factual questions are resolved by *rov*: we follow the majority to determine the status of an object, an act, or a situation. One might have thought that if a statistical majority supports the plaintiff's position, that majority should function like evidence and shift the burden back to the defendant. The *Gemara* rejects this.

The discussion arrives through the case of *ha-mocher shor le-chavero ve-nimtza nagchan* — one who sells an ox to another and the ox turns out to be a habitual gorer. Rav rules that this is a *mekach ta'ut*, a sale in error, on the grounds that buyers generally purchase oxen for plowing, not slaughter, and had the buyer known about the goring nature he would not have bought it. Shmuel disagrees: the seller can say he assumed the buyer intended *shechita*, and since nothing was explicitly stated, the buyer has no recourse. Rav's reasoning rests on *rov* — the majority of ox purchases are for plowing — while Shmuel holds that in monetary matters we do not follow *rov*; the buyer must prove his expectation was betrayed.

The *Gemara* notes several layers of circumstantial evidence one might consult before even reaching this debate. Is this seller known to deal primarily with farmers or with butchers? What was the price of the ox? If plowing oxen command a higher price than slaughter animals, the sale price might indicate what both parties implicitly understood. The *Gemara* posits the case as one where no inference can be drawn from either the seller's identity or the price — because, for example, the market price of meat had risen to the point where slaughter animals were being sold at the same price as plowing oxen. In this situation of total ambiguity, the dispute between Rav and Shmuel is fully engaged.

Rav follows *rov*: the majority of ox sales are for plowing, and so the buyer had a legitimate expectation that gives rise to *mekach ta'ut*. Shmuel rules that *rov* does not apply in monetary cases: *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya*. This is explicitly offered as a separate *chidush* beyond the earlier cases. The earlier cases involved factual uncertainty about what actually happened. This case involves a question about the implicit meeting of minds in a transaction — a meaningfully different terrain. Shmuel's position is effectively a form of *caveat emptor*: unless the parties made explicit representations, no one bears a duty to disclose, and the buyer cannot extract money on the basis of unstated assumptions.

The *Gemara* distills the principle cleanly: *hanei milei ki azlinan batar ruba be-issura, aval be-mamona lo azlinan batar ruba* — the rule of following the majority applies when we are determining the halachic status of something in a domain of *issur*, but in monetary matters it does not. When one party seeks to extract money from another, *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya* governs, and statistical majority does not discharge the burden of proof.

### Verse Source

Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani seeks a Biblical source for the principle of *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya*. He cites the verse *mi ba'al devarim yigash aleihem* — Moshe, upon ascending Har Sinai, instructed the people that whoever has a matter, *yigash aleihem*, let him bring it to Aharon and Chur. The *derasha* reads *yigash* not merely as "come forward" but as "bring his evidence" — *yagish ra'ayah aleihem*. The litigant, the *ba'al devarim*, is the one who must produce the proof.

### Sevara Basis

Rav Ashi challenges this derivation: *lamah li kra, sevara hu* — why do I need a verse? This is a matter of pure logic. As he puts it: *de-khaiv leih kevi azil le-vei asya* — the one who is in pain is the one who goes to the doctor. The party who wishes to collect, who is pressing the claim, is the one who bears the natural responsibility to substantiate it. The principle of *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya* is an expression of basic rationality and does not require Scriptural support.

This observation itself carries some conceptual weight: the suggestion that a *sevara* carries no less force than a verse — that logical necessity is a source of law in its own right — is a significant methodological point in the structure of *Torah she-be'al peh*. The force of the *sevara*, to be sure, is not entirely self-evident: one might ask, once the plaintiff has brought his claim to court, why does the pressure to produce evidence not equalize? But Rav Ashi's intuition is that the natural asymmetry of the situation — the plaintiff goes to the defendant, not the other way around — carries through to the burden of proof.

Rav Ashi therefore holds that the verse *mi ba'al devarim yigash aleihem* teaches something else entirely: the ruling of Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha, which holds that when two litigants each have claims, the court first attends to the suit and only afterward to the countersuit — *nizkakin le-toveiah techilah*. The verse *mi ba'al devarim yigash aleihem* signals that the *ba'al devarim*, the one actively pressing a claim, comes first.

### Litigation Order

The scholars of Neharde'a add a qualification: *pe'amim she-nizkakin le-nitba techilah* — there are circumstances in which the court would first attend to the one being sued, even before the primary suit. Specifically, if the defendant's property is being devalued or his assets are being seized by creditors as a consequence of the delay in resolving his countersuit, the court may attend to his claim first in order to prevent irreversible loss. The basic order — suit before countersuit — is therefore a presumptive rule, not an absolute one.

A genuine analytical difficulty lurks here, as Rashi and Tosafot discuss: how exactly do we define which claim is the "suit" and which is the "countersuit"? From the perspective of the countersuit's plaintiff, he is every bit the *toveiah* and the other party the *nitba*. The designation of priority is not self-evidently determined merely by the sequence in which claims were filed. The basic principle is nonetheless clear, even if its precise application requires careful determination.

## Cow Gores Ox

### Parallel Setup

The *mishna* then presents the reverse of its opening case: *ve-chen para she-nagcha et ha-shor ve-nimtza vladah betzidah* — a cow gored an ox, and you find the cow's fetus lying beside it. This was a pregnant cow. The uncertainty mirrors the first case: did the cow give birth before the goring, or was it still pregnant when it gored? If it had already delivered the fetus, then the victim — the owner of the ox — can only collect from the cow itself, since only the cow was the gorers. But if the cow gored while still pregnant, the fetus was co-present within the cow at the moment of goring, and the question arises whether the fetus bears a share of the liability.

### Problem Stated

The *mishna* rules *chatzi nezek min ha-para u-reviah nezek min ha-vlad* — half damages from the cow and a quarter damages from the fetus. But this ruling is immediately puzzling. In the first case, the ambiguity concerned liability: perhaps the ox owes nothing for the fetus. Here, by contrast, the owner of the damaged ox is entitled to collect half damages from the cow without any doubt — the cow gored. The doubt is only about whether the fetus was also a contributing party to the goring, and therefore whether the fetus's value should also be available for collection. Why then does the *mishna* speak of collecting only *chatzi nezek* from the cow, as though even that amount were somehow uncertain?

### Abaye's Read

Abaye resolves this with a reconceptualization of what *chatzi nezek* and *reviah nezek* mean in this context. *Chatzi nezek — echad me-arba ba-nezek*: what the *mishna* calls "half damages" actually means one quarter of the full damages. And *reviah nezek — echad mi-shmoneh ba-nezek*: what the *mishna* calls "a quarter damages" actually means one eighth of the full damages.

To understand Abaye's reading, consider a concrete case: the ox was worth 200, and the owner is entitled to collect half damages — 100. Now, if the fetus was indeed present within the cow at the time of the goring, we would treat the cow and the fetus as two gorers who together caused the damage. Tosafot notes that in reality the division would be proportional — if the cow weighed ninety percent of the combined mass and the fetus ten percent, one would assign liability accordingly — but for simplicity the *mishna* treats them as equal contributors. So the cow accounts for half the goring and the fetus for the other half: of the 100 the victim is entitled to, 50 is attributable to the cow and 50 to the fetus.

Since there is now doubt whether the fetus was present at all, the victim can collect the full 50 from the cow — there is no doubt about the cow's role — but from the fetus only 25, splitting the 50 he might be owed because of *mamon ha-mutal be-safek cholkin*. So the victim collects 75 total: 50 from the cow and 25 from the fetus. Translating into the *mishna*'s language: *chatzi nezek* from the cow means half of the 100 he is entitled to, i.e., 50 — which is one quarter of the total damage of 200. And *reviah nezek* from the fetus means a quarter of the 100, i.e., 25 — which is one eighth of 200.

### Same Owner

This analysis, however, only applies when the cow and fetus belong to different owners. If they have the same owner — *paru ve-vlad de-chad ninhu* — the victim need not subdivide the goring between them at all. He can address the cow owner directly and say: your cow definitively gored me, and I am entitled to collect my full half damages from you. The cow and fetus together are simply one large animal under your ownership; I need not attribute separate fractions of the goring to each part. The victim can collect the entire 100 from the cow without any reduction.

### Equal Gorers

The logic of treating the cow and fetus as two equal gorers, then, only operates when they are held by separate owners. When the fetus has been sold and is the property of a different person — say, Reuven owns the cow and Shimon owns the fetus — it becomes necessary to divide the responsibility between them. The victim cannot collect his full 100 from Reuven alone while ignoring Shimon's potential involvement, nor can he simply extract everything from whichever party he chooses. The two are treated as co-gorers whose respective obligations must be assessed individually, and the doubt about the fetus's presence introduces the *mamon ha-mutal be-safek* analysis for Shimon's share.

### Separate Owners

When the cow belongs to Reuven and the fetus to Shimon, the victim faces a choice: whom does he approach first? The answer turns out to matter significantly for what each party can be made to pay.

### Defense Strategy

The *Gemara* considers whether the victim might simply go to Reuven first and demand the full 100. One could argue: Reuven, your cow definitely gored me. I am entitled to 100. If you want to claim that Shimon's fetus shares responsibility and you should only owe 50, you bear the burden of proving that the fetus was present. Since you cannot prove that, you owe me the full 100. This would be a straightforward application of *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya* — though of course in this case we are operating under Sumchus's framework, since the *mishna* reflects Sumchus's view that *mamon ha-mutal be-safek cholkin*.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes that the scenario of *chatzi nezek* from the cow and *reviah nezek* from the fetus must reflect a situation where the victim went to Shimon — the fetus owner — first. Shimon naturally claims the fetus was delivered before the goring, so we split: the victim collects 25 from Shimon. He then goes to Reuven, who argues: *galeit da'atach de-shutafa it li* — by going to Shimon first, you have already revealed that you concede Shimon was involved. You collected from Shimon as though he were a co-gorer. Therefore, I owe you only the remaining half — 50 — not the full 100.

*Ika de-amri* — some say — an alternative reading holds that even if the victim went to Reuven first, Reuven can still limit his liability. Reuven could argue: *meida yad'ei de-shutafa it li* — it is established that I have a partner in this matter, namely the fetus owner. Since I know Shimon was involved, you cannot demand more than half from me, regardless of the order in which you pursued your claims. The victim cannot use the sequence of litigation to extract more than 50 from Reuven. On this reading, *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-raya* works in Reuven's favor: the victim cannot prove that Reuven was responsible for more than half the damage.

The *sugya* closes here with Abaye's analysis in place. As will emerge on the following daf, Rava will offer a substantially different reading of the *mishna* — one that challenges the entire framework Abaye has constructed.

# Bava Kamma 47

## Pregnant Cow Damages

### Safek Pregnancy Intro

We open the fifth *perek* picking up at the bottom of 46b. The previous *perek* was focused heavily on *shor tam* and *shor mu'ad*; now we move into more general issues connected to the goring ox, as well as cases we will encounter in the upcoming *mishnayot*. The central concern of the first *mishnah* of this *perek* is *safek* — doubt. The case is one in which it is unknown whether a cow was pregnant at the time it was gored. Does the owner of the goring ox owe damages for the fetus? The position of Sumchos is to split the payment for the fetus, since it may or may not have been gored. The *chachamim*, by contrast, invoke *hamotzi mechaveiro alav hara'ayah* — the burden of proof rests on the claimant.

We are now dealing with the second case of the *mishnah*, which is less straightforward: the cow gored, and it is uncertain whether it was pregnant at the time. The *mishnah* states that one pays half damages from the cow and a quarter from the fetus — which at first glance appears to yield three-quarters total damages, a perplexing result.

### Abaye's Half Damages

Abaye explains the difficulty by positing that the fetus belongs to a different owner. Because of this ownership division, you cannot simply collect everything from the goring cow. You take half of what you should have been owed — half of the half-damages — from the goring ox, since that ox was definitively one of the perpetrators. As for the other half of the half-damages, if you knew for certain the fetus was part of the goring animal, you would collect that from the fetus. Since you do not know, you split it: you receive half of the half, which is a quarter.

Two important observations from Tosafot accompany this position. First, even if the fetus was indeed part of the cow, it presumably contributed only a small proportion of the total force of the goring. Tosafot notes that speaking of "half" is merely a representative number; the real principle is that the fetus's responsibility is proportional to its contribution, and since that is unknown, you receive only half of that proportional share. Second — and this will resurface later — even when there are multiple participants in causing damage, if you cannot collect from one party, you cannot transfer that uncollected portion onto the other. If, say, it is a ninety-ten split and the ten-percent party is unavailable, you may not collect more than your ninety percent from the other.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges Abaye's reading directly. The *mishnah* says *chatzi nezek u-revi'a nezek* — a half and a quarter. Abaye's interpretation forces us to read "half" as meaning a quarter of the total, and "quarter" as meaning an eighth of the total. But that is not what the *mishnah* says. The *mishnah* did not say a quarter and an eighth; it said a half and a quarter.

### Same Owner Sequential

Rava therefore offers his own explanation. The cow and the fetus are owned by the same person — there is no separate ownership at all. So what is the problem? Why not simply collect everything from the cow? Rava's answer is that the *mishnah* is not describing simultaneous collection from two sources. Rather, it describes sequential collection rights: *ita le-parah mishtalem chatzi nezek mi-parah* — if the cow is available, you collect your full half-damages from the cow. The cow is definitively the *mazik*; you are entitled to collect completely from it. *Leita le-parah* — but if the cow is not available, whether because it died, fled, or is worthless, and all you have is the fetus, then since you do not know whether the fetus was part of the goring, you can only collect half of the half-damages — a quarter — from the fetus. This is a clean and straightforward reading: "half and quarter" refers not to simultaneous payments but to two alternate scenarios.

### Fetus Presence Doubt

The *gemara* then clarifies the underlying reason for this division: *ta'ama de-la yad'inan i hava valad bahadah ki nachah i lo* — the reason for the split is the uncertainty about whether the fetus was present together with the cow when it gored. But it follows from this that if it were absolutely clear the fetus was present during the goring, you would be entitled to collect your full half-damages from the fetus alone: *mishtalem kulei chatzi nezek meivlad*. Why not? It was part of the goring animal.

### Full Fetus Payment

The *gemara* notes that this last point aligns with Rava's own stated principle elsewhere: *parah shehizikah goveh meivladah* — if a pregnant cow gored, you may collect the entire damages from the fetus if there is sufficient value there to collect from. The same logic applies here: if it is known the fetus was present, you collect fully from the fetus; if not, you collect only half.

### Fetus Body Unity

The *gemara* then asks: *mai ta'ama?* — what is the reasoning behind this? The answer: *gufah hi* — it is all one body. The fetus is part of the mother's body.

Tosafot observes that the *gemara* appears to be reaching for the familiar phrase *ubar yerech imo* — the fetus is considered a limb of the mother — and discusses why it does not use that formulation, since the applicability of *ubar yerech imo* varies depending on context. But before arriving at Tosafot's analysis, it is worth pausing on what is at stake conceptually. What would the *halachah* be if we did *not* say *gufah hi*? Suppose instead we treated the fetus as a separate entity. Consider the case where two oxen gore a cow together, causing one hundred dollars of damage, each ox worth one hundred dollars, and one of the two oxen is unavailable. Could you collect the entire hundred dollars from the available ox? As we saw in yesterday's discussion: if the two oxen are owned by two different people, you divide responsibility — fifty dollars from Reuven, fifty from Shimon. If Shimon's ox is unavailable, you cannot collect the remaining fifty from Reuven. They are truly each liable only for their proportional share.

What if both oxen belong to the same person, Reuven — could you then collect the full amount from one? The *gemara*'s implicit assumption is still no: even then, each ox is only liable for its proportional portion, and if one is unavailable, you cannot recover the balance from the other. Therefore, the only reason Rava can say you are entitled to collect all of the half-damages from the fetus — when you know it was present — is because we do *not* treat the fetus as a separate animal at all. It is one body. And when part of one body dies or is removed, you are still collecting from different parts of the same animal, not from two separate *mazikim*. This is a meaningful chiddush: even under single ownership, two separate goring animals create proportional, non-transferable liability. Only the principle of *gufah hi* — treating them as one body — permits full recovery from one part of that body.

### Chicken Egg Contrast

The *gemara* now introduces a contrast. *Tarnegolet shehizikah einah govah mibeitzatah* — if a chicken caused damage, you cannot collect from the egg that was within it at the time of the damage. *Mai ta'ama? Pirsha b'alma hu* — it is merely like refuse; it is not considered part of the body.

This is interesting, because in other contexts the egg *is* considered part of the hen. Tosafot addresses this by distinguishing stages of development: while the egg is still forming within the hen, it is considered part of the hen — if the hen is a *treifah*, the egg is too. But once the egg is fully developed and merely awaiting laying, it is considered separate from the mother. At that final stage, it would not be classified as a *mazik* at all.

One might ask why we do not at least treat the egg as a partial *mazik* and collect proportionally from it. The likely answer is that a fully-formed egg is not a live being — it is not an independent entity in the way a fetus is. The fetus can be observed as its own creature within the mother; an egg at the stage of ready-to-be-laid is something categorically more distinct and inert. A fetus, even if born dead or miscarried, is recognizably its own form; the egg, perhaps because it has not been fertilized and hatched, does not achieve that independent identity. As one might note in passing: the question of when something counts as "separate" and "alive" enough to be an independent *mazik* is itself a genuinely complex one that the *gemara* does not fully resolve.

### Valuation Method

Rava now introduces a second principle: *ein shamin leparah bifnei atzmah ulevlad bifnei atzmo ela shamin levlad al gav parah* — you do not assess the cow independently and the fetus independently; rather, you assess the fetus as part of the cow. This principle is relevant not only here but will resurface when we later encounter the *sugya* of *dmei vladot*, the assessment of damages when a woman is struck and miscarries.

The question being addressed is: when an ox gores a pregnant cow and causes a miscarriage, how do we calculate the damages owed for the lost fetus? One might think to assess separately: how much is this fetus worth on its own? How much for a cow about to give birth in two weeks? Rava rules this is incorrect. Instead, we look at the cow as a whole: how much would you pay for this pregnant cow, and how much is it worth now, having lost its fetus? The fetus is evaluated as a component of the pregnant cow, not as an independent item.

The reason given is *nimtza attah machlish et hamazik* — this prevents unfairly burdening the *mazik*. The point is not merely that he would pay more with separate assessment, but that it would be fundamentally unfair, because what he actually damaged was a pregnant cow. You assess what he damaged, not its constituent parts. This is analogous to someone who destroys a field: you do not say "he destroyed one pound of grain worth such-and-such," you say "how much was the field worth before, and how much is it worth now?" The damaged object is the field as a whole, not its component grain.

---

## Pregnant Cow Valuation

### Parallel Damage Cases

The *gemara* supports this principle with parallel cases. *Vechein attah motzei bekotei'a yad avdo shel chaveiro* — the same approach applies if one cuts off the arm of another's slave. Rashi explains that the alternative — assessing the arm independently — would mean asking how much someone would demand to be paid to allow his slave's arm to be cut off. Obviously no one would agree to such a thing for any ordinary market price; the figure would be artificially inflated and meaningless as a legal metric. The correct assessment is: how much was the slave worth before, and how much is he worth now?

Similarly: *u'vi'er b'sadeh acheir, shamin otah al gav sadeh acheir* — if an animal enters a field and destroys grain, you assess the damage as a field before and after, not as the raw value of however many pounds of grain were consumed. The damaged object is the field. One might raise the question of *kol ha'omed liktzor k'katzur dami* — grain that is ready to be harvested might, at that late stage, be valued more like harvested grain than like field. That is a legitimate consideration and there likely is a point at which the grain has effectively separated in status from the field. But as a general principle, you look at the whole object that was damaged.

### Unified Object Principle

Rav Adda bar Abba poses the question to Rav Ashi: if the law is simply that it is fairer to assess the fetus as part of the cow, that is one thing — but why *must* we do it this way? Why not assess the fetus independently and let the *mazik* absorb the higher liability?

The answer: *mishum d'amar lei parah me'ubertah aziktech, parah me'ubertah shamna lach* — because the *mazik* can say: "I damaged a pregnant cow; assess for me a pregnant cow." What he damaged was the pregnant cow as a single object. You cannot take that object and artificially separate it into components that he never engaged with as separate items. The pregnant cow is the object of the tort, and it must be assessed as such.

### Separate Valuation Problem

This creates a practical challenge. If the cow and fetus are owned by different people — say, the cow belongs to one person and the fetus has been sold or transferred to another — we must determine how to divide the total assessed damage between the two owners. The intuitive approach would be to ask: what would the cow be worth without the fetus? The difference between that figure and the total value of the pregnant cow represents the fetus's contribution, and that amount goes to the owner of the fetus.

### Fatness Analysis

But Rashi identifies a complication. A pregnant cow may have gained weight and become *fatma* — fattier and more valuable — during the pregnancy. Does that additional value belong to the cow's owner or to the fetus's owner? *Mah she'shamnu'u she'hayah yafeh mipnei shumno, havei d'ba'al parah, d'velad machmato lo ati shumno* — the additional weight and fat belong to the cow's owner, because the weight gain, whatever its biological cause, accrues to the cow's body, not the fetus's. So when you try to imagine what the cow would be worth without the fetus, you imagine it without the fetus but *with* its current weight — not as it was before the pregnancy began.

### Bulk Appearance

Rav Acha raises a further nuance: *nafcha mai?* — what about the appearance of bulk? Even if the weight itself belongs to the cow, the visual volume of the cow — the fact that it looks larger — may be attributable to the fetus. Buyers may pay more for an animal that appears physically larger, regardless of actual weight. Does that increment in price go to the cow owner or the fetus owner?

### Bulk to Cow

Rav Papa holds that the bulk increment goes entirely to the owner of the cow. One would assess what the cow would be worth with its current weight *and* its current volume, as though no fetus were present — and that entire figure belongs to the cow owner.

### Split Bulk Value

Rav Acha brei deRav Ika disagrees: *cholkin* — you split the increment attributable to the appearance of bulk, since that visual enlargement is genuinely connected to the fetus's presence and the fetus owner has some claim to it.

### Halacha Split

*Vehilchata cholkin* — the *halachah* follows Rav Acha brei deRav Ika: the bulk-value increment is split between the two owners. With that ruling, the discussion of the pregnant cow concludes.

---

## Potter's Pots Case

### Pots Without Permission

We now make a significant shift. The next *mishnah* moves beyond goring cows into a broader set of questions about liability for damage that occurs in someone else's domain. *Hakadar shehichnis kedeirotav lachatzar ba'al habayit* — a potter who brought his pots into the yard of the homeowner *shelo birshut* — without permission. He is a door-to-door salesman who simply walked in. *Veshivra behemto shel ba'al habayit* — and the homeowner's animal broke the pots. *Patur* — the homeowner is exempt. This is effectively a case of *regel*, and *regel* is only *chayav* in *reshut hanizak*. Since the potter entered without permission, this is *reshut hamazik*, and there is no liability: *shurcha birshuti mai ba'ei* — what right did your pots have to be on my property?

### Animal Injury Liability

*Ve'im huzka bahen ba'al hakedeirot chayav* — if the homeowner's animal slipped on the pots and injured itself, the potter is liable. This is akin to a *bor*: he left his pots — his hazard — in a place where he had no right to leave them, and the homeowner's animal was damaged as a result.

### Permission Implies Liability

*Ve'im hichnis birshut* — but if the homeowner explicitly gave permission for the potter to enter, then *ba'al hachatzer chayav* — the homeowner is liable if his animal then tramples and breaks the pots.

### Host Liability Puzzle

Why is the homeowner liable? The most natural answer would be *regel* — his animal trampled the pots. But *regel* is only *chayav* in *reshut hanizak*. The potter's pots are in the homeowner's yard; it is at most a shared space. Can the homeowner's yard become *reshut hanizak* merely because he invited the potter in? That seems strained. The *gemara* will resolve this differently: when the homeowner says "you may come in," he is implicitly accepting responsibility for anything that happens to his guest's property. It is not a matter of domain-status; it is a matter of implicit *kibul* — acceptance of liability. As will become clear, it is as though the homeowner has declared himself an insurer of his guest's belongings.

---

## Fruit and Oxen Cases

### Fruit Without Permission

The *mishnah* continues with parallel cases. *Hichnis perotav lechatzer ba'al habayit shelo birshut* — the guest brings fruit into the homeowner's yard without permission. *Ve'achaltan behemato shel ba'al habayit* — the homeowner's animal eats it. *Patur* — the homeowner is exempt. Again, this is *reshut hamazik*; who gave you permission to leave fruit in my yard?

### Host Liable Shen

*Ve'im hichnis birshut* — if the homeowner gave permission and the animal then eats the fruit, *ba'al hachatzer chayav* — the homeowner is liable. This is a case of *shen*, but again, not technically *reshut hanizak* — the liability is rooted in the homeowner's implicit acceptance of responsibility upon granting permission.

### Ox Without Permission

*Hichnis shoro lechatzer ba'al habayit shelo birshut* — the guest brings his ox into the homeowner's yard without permission. *Unegacho shoro shel ba'al habayit* — the homeowner's ox gores the guest's ox, *o shenashcho kalbo shel ba'al habayit* — or the homeowner's dog bites it. *Patur* — the homeowner is exempt. This is *keren*, but even *keren*, which is ordinarily *chayav* regardless of domain, is exempt when the victim's animal was present *shelo birshut*: *shurcha birshuti mai ba'ei*.

### Well Contamination

The *mishnah* then considers the reverse. If the guest's ox gores the homeowner's ox, the guest is obviously *chayav* — it is *keren* in the homeowner's domain. *Nafal leboro* — if the guest's ox falls into the homeowner's well and *hev'ish meimav* — contaminates the well water with the stench of the animal carcass — the guest is also *chayav*. The guest's ox has no right to be here; whatever damage flows from its unauthorized presence falls on the guest.

### Kofer Question

*Hayah aviv o beno letocho* — if the homeowner's father or son was in the well and was killed by the falling ox, *meshallem et hakofer* — the guest pays *kofer*. A difficulty immediately arises: *kofer* is normally the liability of a *mu'ad*, a forewarned animal. Why is *kofer* owed here? This requires further examination, particularly in light of the position that when an animal gores in *chatzer hanizak*, it may owe full damages even as a *tam* — and whether that elevated liability extends to *kofer* is a live question that the *gemara* will need to address.

### Host Liable Keren

*Ve'im hichnis birshut* — if the homeowner gave the guest permission to bring his ox in, and then the homeowner's ox gores the guest's ox — *ba'al hachatzer chayav*. Once the ground of *shelo birshut* is removed, the homeowner's ox goring the guest's ox is straightforward *keren*, and of course the homeowner is *chayav*.

### Rabbi Disagrees

*Rabbi omer bechullan eino chayav ad sheyekabbel alav lishmor* — Rabbi holds that in all these cases, the homeowner is not liable unless he explicitly declares that he will guard and take responsibility for the guest's property. Granting mere permission to enter does not, for Rabbi, constitute an implicit acceptance of liability. Without a verbal declaration of responsibility, *shen* and *regel* remain exempt because it is not *reshut hanizak*, and there is nothing else to generate liability.

It seems, then, that the *tanna kamma* holds that granting permission constitutes implicit *kibul*, and Rabbi disagrees. Rabbi's position equally implies the converse: even the guest is not implicitly accepting liability for the host's property simply by virtue of having been granted permission. The question of what exactly "permission" generates — for whom, and in which direction — is what the *gemara* will now analyze.

---

## Implicit Responsibility

### Permission Reversal

The *gemara* examines the structure of the *mishnah*. *Ta'ama deshelo birshut* — when the guest is there without permission, the homeowner is exempt for damage to the guest's pots, and the guest is liable if the homeowner's animal is injured by the pots. *Ha birshut* — but if there *is* permission, the *gemara* infers, *lo mechayev ba'al hakedeirah benizkei behemto d'ba'al hachatzer* — the potter would not be liable if the homeowner's animal were injured by the pots. We do not say that because the homeowner granted the guest permission, the guest implicitly accepted liability for any damage to the homeowner. Nor — *velo amrinan kibulei kibal ba'al hakedeirah netirosa d'behemto d'ba'al hachatzer* — do we say that the guest's receipt of kindness from the host generates some reciprocal obligation to protect the host from harm.

The *gemara* notes the logical structure. When the guest has no permission and places his pots, he has created a *bor shelo birshut* — an unauthorized hazard — and is liable for the animal that slips on it. Once he has permission, his pots are a *bor birshut* — a hazard he was authorized to create — and he is not liable if the animal slips on them. But one might have thought: the homeowner was gracious enough to let the guest in; perhaps that reception generates a reciprocal implicit acceptance of liability. The *gemara* rejects this.

*Mani? Rabbi hi, de'amar kol bistama lo kibal alav netirosa* — this is Rabbi's position: there is no implicit acceptance of responsibility in either direction. Granting permission to enter says nothing about who accepts liability for damage.

But then, says the *gemara*, examine the end of the *mishnah*: *hichnis birshut, ba'al hachatzer chayav* — when the homeowner grants permission and the animal damages the guest's pots, the homeowner *is* liable. So the homeowner is impliedly accepting responsibility. *Atya k'Rabbanan, d'amri bistama nami kibulei kibal alav netirosa* — this accords with the Rabbis, who hold that granting permission to enter constitutes an implicit acceptance of liability for what happens to the guest's property. The *mishnah*'s *reisha* and *seifa* thus reflect different positions: where the homeowner is not impliedly liable, that is Rabbi; where he is, that is the Rabbis.

Rav Zeira observes: *man deshuna zo lo shuna zo* — whoever taught one clause did not teach the other; these positions are simply inconsistent and come from different authorities. But Rava offers a more coherent account: *lo kula Rabbanan hi* — the entire *mishnah*, except for Rabbi's explicit statement, reflects the Rabbanan's view. *Uvireshut, shemirat kedeirot kibal alav bechatzer* — when I invite you in, I am implicitly accepting custodial responsibility for your pots. *Va'afilu nishberu beruach* — even if they broke due to wind, with no action of mine. This is not incidental. If you are a guest in my home with permission, I am the host, and the role of host carries with it general responsibility for the wellbeing of the guest's belongings. It is not that a specific tort was committed; it is that I have taken on the position of the responsible party.

### Host-Guest Asymmetry

This generates the obvious question: why does the host accept implicit liability for the guest, but the guest does not implicitly accept liability for the host? If my granting you permission creates my implied responsibility toward you, why doesn't your receiving that permission create your implied responsibility toward me?

The answer lies in the fundamental asymmetry of the host-guest relationship. When the homeowner extends an invitation, he is, by the nature of hospitality, taking on the role of the responsible party. This is his domain, his property; welcoming someone in means placing yourself in the position of the one who oversees and bears responsibility for what occurs. The guest's role is not to take responsibility for the host — the guest is the beneficiary of the hospitality, and the host is the protector. The logic of the institution runs in one direction only.

One might push back and say this analysis fits true hospitality, but not every case of "permission" is hospitality in that sense. A door-to-door salesman who is allowed to step in with his wares is not quite a guest in the same sense as a person who is welcomed into one's home. The salesman brings his goods into your space for commercial purposes. The moral intuitions of host responsibility may not map cleanly onto every scenario involving granted permission. This is a genuinely interesting question that the *gemara* implicitly leaves open.

### Accident vs. Eating

The *gemara* introduces an important distinction. *Lo shanu* — the rule that the guest is liable when the host's animal is damaged by the guest's objects applies specifically when *shehuchleka bahen* — the animal slipped on them. *Aval achla patur* — but if the animal ate the fruit and became ill, the guest is exempt.

This creates a striking asymmetry. In *reshut harabbim*: if I leave fruit in the street and an animal slips on it, that is a *bor* and I am *chayav*. But if the animal eats the fruit and becomes sick — is that also a *bor*? In a classic *bor*, the damage occurs because the victim encounters the hazard through inattention or accident. Here, the animal actively sees the fruit and consciously consumes it. The victim is not passively injured; it participates in its own injury. Even if one might fault me for leaving the fruit there, the animal's conscious ingestion introduces a break in the causal chain that makes it very difficult to classify this as a *bor*. It becomes something closer to *grama* — indirect causation — for which one is exempt.

### Active Participation

Tosafot addresses this directly. One might be tempted to say the animal is exempt on grounds that it is unusual (*lo shechich*) for an animal to eat the fruit and injure itself — as though it were an unlikely occurrence. But Tosafot rejects that explanation; the *gemara* makes clear elsewhere that an animal eating fruit is an entirely expected event. Tosafot instead explains: *keivan shebimechaven mevi alav davar shemaziko* — the animal knowingly brings upon itself the thing that injures it. It is a form of *pi hanizak* — active participation in one's own damage. When the victim is actively complicit in the harm, you cannot make the depositor of the fruit responsible. The *avot nezikin* presuppose a structure of actor and passive victim; when the "victim" consciously acts in a way that produces the harm, the classic framework no longer applies.

This is not limited to a narrow technical point. The broader principle that Tosafot articulates is that all *avot nezikin* require a clear distinction between the perpetrator and the one upon whom the damage was perpetrated. When the damaged party is itself the agent of the damage — even if another party created the conditions — the liability framework breaks down. At most, one might be *chayav bidinei shamayim* — morally culpable — but exempt in human courts.

### Sheshet Challenge

Rav Sheshet objects: *ki nayim veshachiv Rav amrah leha shemeitata* — Rav must have been half-asleep when he said this ruling. The *gemara* brings a *beraita*: *hanosein sam hamaves lifnei behemas chaveiro* — one who places poison in front of another's animal is *patur midinei adam vechayav bidinei shamayim* — exempt in court but liable in heaven. Rav Sheshet reasons: since the *beraita* addresses poison and exempts the depositor, it implies that in the case of fruit — which an animal would naturally eat — you *should* be *chayav* in human courts. Why would Rav rule otherwise?

### Self-Inflicted Damage

The *gemara* resolves the challenge. *Sam hamaves hu, delo avida de'achla* — poison is a case where the animal would not normally eat it; normal animals avoid poison. That is precisely why the *beraita* must tell us you are still *chayav bidinei shamayim* even though the animal consumed something abnormal. But fruit, which an animal would naturally eat — surely you would be *chayav* there. The *gemara* responds: *hu hadin afilu peiros nami patur midinei adam* — the same exemption applies to fruit. You are exempt in human courts in both cases. The reason the *beraita* chose to illustrate with poison is that it carries the more surprising teaching: even with poison, where the animal is arguably even more responsible for eating something it should have recognized as dangerous, there remains *chiyuv bidinei shamayim*. This tells us that moral liability persists even in extreme cases. But in both cases — poison and fruit alike — the depositor is *patur midinei adam* because the animal brought the harm upon itself.

An alternative reading is offered as well: *ve'iba'is eima sam hamaves nami ba'afarzata dehainu peiros* — "poison" in the *beraita* might refer to a particular type of grass that is toxic but which animals would naturally eat without recognizing as harmful. In that reading, both cases involve something the animal would plausibly consume, and both are exempt in human courts for the same reason: the animal, by consuming it, was the proximate cause of its own injury.

---

## Grain Mill Entry

### No Permission Entry

The *gemara* introduces a further case to probe these questions. *Ha'ishah shenichnesah litchon chitin etzel ba'al habayit* — a woman entered a homeowner's mill to grind her grain. Tosafot notes that the novelty here is precisely that one might have assumed a customer has implicit permission to enter a place of business; the *gemara* is telling us that even a customer must obtain explicit permission. She entered *shelo birshut*. *Ve'achaltan behemato shel ba'al habayit* — the homeowner's animal ate the grain. *Patur* — the homeowner is exempt, because she was there without permission.

### Injury Liability Same

*Im huzak* — if the animal was injured by the grain, she is liable. This is the direct parallel to the pot-slipping case. The question arises: does *huzak* here mean the animal slipped on the grain (the *bor* scenario), or does it mean the animal ate the grain and became ill? The *gemara* notes that the word *bahen* — "by them" — was used in the pot case (explicitly indicating slipping), whereas in this case the text simply says *huzak* without specifying *bahen*. This suggests the case here might involve eating and injury from consumption, which would make the woman liable despite the general principle of *pi hanizak*.

### Rava Clarifies

Rava clarifies: the question of permission is determinative. The two scenarios — *shelo birshut* and *birshut* — are governed by entirely different logics and cannot be compared to one another. *B'reshut shelo birshut ka ramit* — you are conflating a case of permission with a case of no permission. The principles that operate in one setting do not transfer to the other.

### General Responsibility

*Birshut* — when permission has been granted, *shemirat shoro kibal alav* — the homeowner has accepted general custodial responsibility for the guest's animal. *Va'afilu chanak et atzmo* — even if the ox strangles itself. Whatever happens to the guest's animal while it is on the premises, having been welcomed in, falls within the scope of the homeowner's implicit acceptance of liability. So the case of the ox eating grain and dying in the *birshut* scenario is not an instance of *pi hanizak* canceling liability; rather, the homeowner has independently accepted liability for everything, including harms that the animal brought upon itself. The two legal logics operate independently and must not be confused.

---

## Third-Party Liability

### Third-Party Question

*Iba'ya lehu* — the *gemara* now raises an unresolved question. When the homeowner has accepted responsibility — implicit or explicit — for the guest's belongings, does that acceptance extend to damage caused by a third party? *Dinafshei hu dekibel alei o dilma afilu netiruta de'alma kibel alei* — does the homeowner accept liability only for things that his own property or domain causes, or does he accept responsibility even for damage inflicted by a third party's animal that happens to enter his yard?

### Third-Party Ox Case

The concrete scenario: a guest brings fruit into the homeowner's yard *birshut* — with permission. A third party's ox then enters and eats the fruit. Is the homeowner liable to reimburse the guest for the loss caused by this third party?

### Borrowed Domain

A *beraita* is cited: *hichnis peirotav lechatzer ba'al habayit shelo birshut* — fruit brought without permission, eaten by an ox from elsewhere — the homeowner is exempt. *Ve'im hichnis birshut* — with permission — *chayav*. The question is who is *chayav* and who is *patur*. One possibility is that we are speaking of the homeowner being liable for the third party's act. Another possibility is that we are speaking of whether the third party — Reuven, the owner of the ox that ate the fruit — is directly *chayav*.

### Third Party Liable

The *gemara* clarifies: if the homeowner gave permission for the fruit to be there, then the fruit has a *reshut* to be there. When Reuven's ox comes and eats it, that is *shen birshut hanizak* — the *shen* damage occurred in the domain of the victim, because the guest, having been granted permission, possesses a temporary *reshut* in that space. *Shen* is *chayav birshut hanizak*, and therefore Reuven is directly *chayav* to the guest.

### No Permission Exempt

*Shelo birshut* — if the fruit was there without permission, it has no right to be there. Reuven's ox eating it is effectively *shen birshut harabbim* — eating in a domain where the victim had no standing — and *beshen birshut harabbim paturah*. Reuven is exempt. So the question of whether the fruit had permission determines whether the direct tortfeasor — Reuven — is liable.

### Host Reimbursement

But this still leaves open the original question: even in the *birshut* case, where Reuven is directly liable, does the homeowner *also* accept liability toward the guest for third-party damage — such that the guest could collect from the homeowner instead of, or in addition to, pursuing Reuven? Does the homeowner's implicit acceptance of responsibility when welcoming the guest in extend to covering losses caused by outside parties whose actions the homeowner did not control?

This question remains unresolved — *teiku* — and we will continue examining it in the next session.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 48

## Animal in Chatzer

### Tashma: Third Party

The *gemara* opens with a *tashma* beginning on the fourth line of 48a. The case runs as follows: someone brought his animal into another person's property without permission — *hechnish shoro l'chatzer ba'al habayit shelo birishut* — and then a third party's animal entered the property and gored the first animal. The *gemara* declares that someone is *patur*. The immediate question is: who? If one party is *patur*, presumably another is *chayav*. Is it the owner of the third animal who caused the damage, or is it the owner of the *chatzer*?

The *gemara* then states: *ve'im hechnish birishut*, if the animal was brought in with permission, then *chayav* — again leaving unspecified who bears the liability. The *gemara* sharpens the difficulty: *man patur man chayav?* Are we really saying that the *ba'al hachatzer* is *patur* when he gave no permission, but *chayav* when he did? That seems extreme — the property owner did nothing, so why should the mere fact of granting permission make him responsible for damage caused by some third party? The *gemara* resolves the ambiguity: *patur ba'al hashor vechayav ba'al hashor* — it is the third-party animal owner who is either *patur* or *chayav*. But this raises a further question: if the third party obviously had no permission regardless, why should it matter whether the first animal-owner had permission or not?

### Rabbi Tarfon View

The *gemara* answers: *ha mani Rabbi Tarfon hi* — this must be according to the position of Rabbi Tarfon. Rabbi Tarfon holds that even a *shor tam*, which normally pays only *chatzi nezek*, pays *nezek shalem* — full damages — if it caused damage in *reshut hanizak*, the private domain of the injured party. According to Rabbi Tarfon, *chatzi nezek* for a *shor tam* applies only in *reshut harabim*.

The key move here is that the granting of *reshut* — permission to bring the animal into the *chatzer* — functions not as a matter of simple courtesy, but as a legal determination of domain status. When the property owner grants permission for another's animal to be present, the domain effectively takes on characteristics of *reshut harabim* from the perspective of the animal owner. Without that permission, the animal's presence is unauthorized, and the *chatzer* retains its status as *chatzer hanizak* — making it a case where the third party's goring animal would owe *nezek shalem* under Rabbi Tarfon's rule. With permission, it becomes more like *reshut harabim*, and the third-party owner pays only *chatzi nezek*.

One might object that technically *chatzer hanizak* should mean the property of the person who suffered the loss — and here it is not the first animal-owner's property at all. The *gemara* acknowledges the force of this point. The resolution is that the grant of *reshut* confers a kind of partial ownership, somewhat analogous to having been granted the right to place produce in another's domain, which itself resembles a form of *shutafut* — partnership. The *rishonim* also note the distinction between *chatzer hashutfim* where one partner damages another, versus this case involving a third party's animal operating in jointly-used space.

It is worth noting, of course, that Rabbi Tarfon's position was ultimately rejected. The fact that this *braita* can only be made sensible by reading it through Rabbi Tarfon's *shitta* is itself a difficulty. According to the *Rabbanan* who disagree with Rabbi Tarfon — holding that a *shor tam* pays only *chatzi nezek* even in *reshut hanizak* — there would be no difference between permission and no permission: in either case the third party pays *chatzi nezek*, and the distinction drawn in the *braita* would be meaningless.

### Woman Baking Bread

The *gemara* transitions to a related case: *hahi itteta de'alata lemifa behahu beita* — a certain woman went to a house in order to bake bread there. The goat belonging to the owner of that house came, ate her dough, became ill, and died — *chavil umit*. Rava ruled that she must pay for the goat: *chiyava Rava leshalumei dmei barcha*.

One might ask whether Rava is here disagreeing with Rav, who had said *havaya lah shelo tochal* — the animal itself bears some responsibility for overeating, and a person who leaves food out cannot be held liable if an animal eats to excess and perishes. The *gemara* answers: in the case Rav discussed, the person had come *shelo birishut* — without permission — and therefore *lo kibla aleiah netiruta*: she had not accepted upon herself any responsibility for the homeowner's property or animals.
