On one side: *davar she'tzaddik nitzta'er bo* — that which a righteous person devoted himself to will not become his stumbling block. On the other: God is exacting with those nearest to him, and his son died precisely of thirst. Tosafot works to reconcile this tension by arguing that the principle about the *tzaddik* does not cover every misfortune — it is only the specific instrument of one's devotion that will not be the cause of one's destruction. The daughter would not die by falling into a well; but the son dying of thirst is a different form of misfortune, not the same instrument. It is a fine distinction — a hair's breadth, as it were — but Tosafot requires it to maintain the principle.

Yet what is perhaps most refreshing about this *Gemara* is its refusal to remain comfortable with a tidy theological narrative. Even if Tosafot's reconciliation is technically valid, the *Gemara* inserts the son's death precisely to puncture the easy consolation of *hashgacha pratit* operating in perfectly neat ways. Tragedy and irony are woven into the world, and the *Gemara* insists we sit with that.

The *Gemara* then cites Rabbi Chanina himself — the same Rabbi Chanina who predicted the daughter's rescue — asserting that God is *erech apayim l'tzadikim v'la-rashaim* — long-tempered with both the righteous and the wicked. And Rabbi Chanina further warns: *kol omer hakadosh baruch hu vatran yivatru chayav* — whoever says that God is easy-going and overlooks things will have his own life treated leniently in the same manner, meaning without careful protection. *Ha-tzur tamim po'alo ki kol derachav mishpat* — the Rock is perfect in his work, for all his ways are justice. Nothing is forgotten; everything is accounted for. The *Mesilas Yesharim* grapples with the apparent tension between this exacting divine justice and the Torah's characterization of God as *chanun v'rachum*, compassionate and gracious. His resolution: the compassion expresses itself precisely in the provision of *teshuvah*; where *teshuvah* has been done, God forgives fully. Where it has not, the justice is exact. The two attributes do not contradict — they operate in different registers.

## Stones/Justice Narrative

### Stone Throwing Rule

The *Gemara* now introduces a related ruling: *lo yisakel adam meirshuto l'reshut harabim* — one should not clear stones from his private property by throwing them into the public domain. The principle on its face seems self-evident; throwing debris into a public thoroughfare creates an obvious hazard. The *Gemara* illustrates this with a narrative.

### Man & Chasid Story

A certain person was clearing stones from his property and tossing them into *reshut harabim*. A *chasid* — and here, as elsewhere in Bava Kamma, the word *chasid* carries the specific connotation of one who is especially careful about causing harm to others; recall the *chasidim harishonim* discussed earlier in the tractate in connection with the disposal of broken glass — encountered him and rebuked him. *Reika*, he said — empty one, low life — *mipnei ma ata mesakeil meirshut she'eino shelcha l'reshut shelcha?* Why are you removing stones from a domain that is not yours and placing them in the domain that is yours? The man laughed him off. What do I care about the public domain? I am cleaning out my own yard. The *chasid*'s remark seemed absurd to him — the street was not *his*.

### Karmic Reversal

The *Gemara* then describes what happened next. *Liyamim* — in time — the man was reduced to poverty and was forced to sell his property. Now he walked the streets himself. *Venichshal be'otan avanim* — and he stumbled over those very stones he had thrown there. At that moment he said: *yafeh amar li oto chasid* — how right that righteous person was. *Mipnei ma ata mesakeil meirshut she'eino shelcha l'reshut shelcha* — why do you remove from what is not yours and put it into what is yours? What had been the anonymous public street had become, through his reversal of fortune, his domain — the space in which he now lived and walked. And what he had blithely discarded there as someone else's problem became his own hazard.

The story captures something important about how self-interest distorts our perception of communal obligation. It is easy to be meticulous about one's own property and dismissive about harms to others in shared space. The *chasid* of Bava Kamma is precisely the person who resists this distortion — who treats *reshut harabim* with the same care as *reshut hayachid*, recognizing that the public domain is, in a deep sense, everyone's domain including one's own. The story also echoes the preceding discussion about Nechunya: there, the mechanism of divine justice was that the *tzaddik*'s merit in a particular domain protected those he loved in that domain; here, the man's negligence in that same domain ultimately returns to injure himself in kind.

## Rav vs. Shmuel: Pit Dama…

### Ten-Tefach Rule

The *Gemara* returns to the laws of *bor* proper. The *mishna* had established that all types of excavations — *bor*, *shiach*, *me'ara*, *charitzin*, and *ne'itzin* — carry liability. The word *bor* in the Torah is not meant to exclude other forms of excavation; rather, it establishes the parameters of the classic case: just as a *bor* must be ten *tefachim* deep in order for one to bear liability in the event an animal is killed, so too any other pit-like excavation must be ten *tefachim* deep to carry that level of liability. If the pit is less than ten *tefachim* deep, one is *patur* in the event of a death, though still *chayav* if the animal was merely injured, since even a shallow pit can cause damage.

### Rav: Hevel Theory

Rav now introduces one of the most striking theoretical positions in this *sugya*: *bor shechiiva alav Torah l'hevlo v'lo l'chavato* — the *bor* for which the Torah made one liable is the *bor* of its *hevel*, its vapor or noxious air, and not its *chavatah*, the physical impact of hitting the ground. The liability of *bor*, according to Rav, is grounded not in the fact that one exposed ground and an animal struck that ground, but in the fact that one created a space in which a heavy or toxic air accumulates — an *hevel* — which itself causes injury or contributes to death.

This position seems initially bizarre. When a donkey falls into a pit and breaks its leg, the intuitive cause of injury is the physical impact with the ground, not the air quality in the pit. But Rav's position makes more sense when examined against the conceptual background of the *sugya*. The problem Rav is solving is this: when one digs a pit in *reshut harabim*, the ground at the bottom of that pit is not one's ground — it is public ground, ground that existed before one's digging, ground that one does not own. The Torah says *ba'al habor*, the owner of the pit is liable. If an animal's injury is caused by impact with ground that belonged to the public all along — ground that one merely exposed — then one's connection to that injury is attenuated. Rav resolves this by locating the liability not in the ground itself, but in the *hevel* — the heavy air — which is something the digger genuinely created, something that did not exist before the excavation and that is properly the digger's creation. It is the *hevel* that connects the owner to the damage, even when the physical impact is with *karka olam* — the eternally existing ground.

### Shmuel: Both Elements

Shmuel disagrees. For Shmuel, one is *chayav* for both the *hevel* and the *chavatah*. The ground impact is itself a consequence of the pit the person created, and there is no reason to exempt the digger from the consequences of the impact simply because the ground itself pre-existed.

### Mound Hypothetical

The practical difference between Rav and Shmuel emerges clearly in the following case: one who creates a mound (*govah*) in *reshut harabim*, and a person trips over the mound and strikes the flat ground — not the mound itself. For Rav, one is *patur* in this case. There is no *hevel*; the person did not create a pit with accumulated heavy air; and the injury from striking the flat ground is *karka olam heizikato* — the eternally existing ground caused the injury, not the mound-maker. For Shmuel, one is nonetheless *chayav*, since the mound caused the fall and the injury is a direct consequence of one's creation. The mound-maker cannot disclaim responsibility simply because the final impact was with ground that preceded his action.

Rav's position on the mound should be distinguished from the liability for stones and knives left in *reshut harabim* that was discussed earlier in the tractate. If a person trips over a mound and strikes the mound itself, Rav would presumably hold the person *chayav*, since the injury is then from the thing one created. The exemption is specifically when the fall results in impact only with the flat ground — the *karka olam* — and there is no *hevel* establishing the digger's connection to that ground.

### Wool Cushion Proof

The *Gemara* adduces proof that the Torah's liability for *bor* is indeed grounded in *hevel* rather than, or at least in addition to, *chavatah*: *ha-Torah heidah al ha-bor ve-afilu malei spurgin shel tzemer* — the Torah declares one liable for a *bor* even if it is filled with cushions of wool. If the basis of liability were solely the physical impact with the ground, then a pit stuffed with soft wool cushions would produce no injurious impact, and there should be no liability. Yet the Torah makes one liable regardless. This demonstrates that *hevel* — the noxious air that can build up in an enclosed space and cause death or harm — is itself a recognized source of liability, entirely independent of physical impact. This also means, as pointed out to the class, that *hevel* cannot be reduced to the mere conceptual act of "exposing the ground" — it is something distinct, something the creation of the pit brings into being.

The proof cuts against the earlier suggestion that *hevel* could be understood simply as a metaphor for the exposed ground now constituting a danger. If that were all *hevel* meant, there would be no liability in the wool-cushion case, since the exposed ground is entirely buffered. The Torah's liability in that case proves that *hevel* is a real, independent factor.

### Pit Types & Hevel

The *Gemara* then asks why the *mishna* needed to enumerate all the different types of pits and excavations if a single general term would have sufficed. The answer is that each type of excavation has different physical characteristics, and one might have thought the *hevel* requirement is only met by some of them. A classic round *bor* of ten *tefachim* — *katin v'karich*, narrow and deep — clearly generates *hevel* through the compression of air in a confined vertical space. A *shiach*, a long trench, is not as narrow and might be thought insufficient to trap *hevel* at the same depth. A *me'ara* — a cave-like excavation, square and covered — is wide in both horizontal dimensions, and one might have thought that its greater width prevents the accumulation of *hevel*; yet its covered top compensates, trapping the air. *Charitzin* are not covered and are wide in both directions; one might have thought their openness dissipates any *hevel* entirely. *Ne'itzin* are funnel-shaped — wider at the top than at the bottom — which might also seem to mitigate the accumulation of heavy air in their depths. The *Gemara* asserts that all of these, when ten *tefachim* deep, do in fact generate *hevel* sufficient to create liability for a killed animal, and the enumeration of each type is necessary to establish this across all the variations in shape, width, and coverage.

It must be emphasized that no one — not Rav, not the *Gemara* — actually imagines that *hevel* alone breaks an animal's leg or snaps a human bone. Rather, as Rashi makes clear, the *hevel* functions as the conceptual link between the pit-owner and the injury caused by the ground impact. Without *hevel*, the impact with the ground is simply *karka olam heizikato* — the eternal ground did it — and the pit-maker bears no responsibility. With *hevel*, the pit-maker has created something new in that space that ties him to whatever injury occurs within it. The real-world dispute between Rav and Shmuel, then, is whether that conceptual link — *hevel* — is necessary to establish liability for ground-impact injuries, or whether one is *chayav* for such injuries regardless, simply by virtue of having created the excavation.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 51

## Rav vs. Shmuel: Hevel

### Rav-Shmuel Intro

The daf opens by returning to the debate between Rav and Shmuel concerning whether *hevel* — the thick, pressurized air that accumulates within a *bor* — is a necessary condition for liability. To briefly recap the stakes of this dispute: Rav holds that *hevel* is the operative mechanism through which the owner of a pit is liable, while Shmuel holds that *chavata* — the blunt impact of striking the ground or wall — is an independent basis for liability. The practical difference emerges in a case such as a raised mound on which someone trips and strikes the ground: since no enclosed cavity is involved, there is no *hevel*, and Rav would therefore exempt the owner, while Shmuel would hold him liable based on the impact alone.

### Mishnah Analysis

The Gemara now turns to analyze the Mishnah in light of this debate. The Mishnah states: if the *bor* was less than ten *tefachim* deep and an ox or donkey fell into it and died, the owner is exempt — *patur*. However, if the animal was merely injured, the owner is liable — *chayav*. The Gemara initially presumes that the difference between a pit that can cause death and one that cannot is simply a function of the severity of the *chavata*: the shallower the pit, the less violent the impact. If so, the concept of *hevel* would seem irrelevant, since the Gemara assumes *hevel* does not vary with depth. But if *hevel* were sufficient on its own to create liability, the owner should be liable for death even in a shallow pit — since both Rav and Shmuel agree that *hevel* generates liability for death in a sufficiently deep pit.

### Hevel Levels

The Gemara resolves this tension by rejecting the premise that *hevel* is all-or-nothing. Rather, the Gemara explains: *ein hevla le-mita ve-yesh hevla le-nezikin* — there is not enough *hevel* in a shallow pit to cause death, but there is enough to cause injury. The difference between death and damage, then, is not solely a function of impact force; it is also a function of the intensity of the *hevel*. Even according to Rav, who insists that *hevel* is the operative mechanism, the Mishnah's distinction between death and injury can be maintained: a pit shallower than ten *tefachim* generates insufficient *hevel* to be lethal, yet sufficient *hevel* to cause damage. This is a striking position, because it means that *hevel* is not binary but admits of degrees — a conceptually unusual claim that the Gemara treats as settled.

### Student Q&A

One might reasonably ask: how does a pit ten *tefachim* deep cause the death of an ox, given that the animal's head stands well above that height? The Gemara does not resolve this difficulty directly, and the precise physiological mechanism of *hevel* remains opaque throughout the sugya. One reading is that *hevel* is not merely a mysterious lethal vapor but rather a conceptual device that connects the person who dug the pit to all damage caused within it — that is, the *hevel* establishes causal ownership over the *chavata*. However, the Gemara does not seem to pursue this reading. Instead, the Gemara treats *hevel* as a genuinely distinct factor whose lethality depends on its own intensity within the cavity, independent of impact. This makes the discussion somewhat counterintuitive, but it is the framework the Gemara operates within.

---

## Ox in Canal Case

### Story Setup

The Gemara introduces a narrative: an ox fell into an *arista de-dilai* — an irrigation canal known to be a standard *ama* wide, which is six *tefachim* deep. The owner of the ox, seeing that his animal had fallen in, immediately performed *shechita* rather than waiting, presumably fearing it would die.

### Treifa Ruling

Rav Nachman declared the animal a *treifa*. The basis for this ruling is the halachic concern of *risuk evarim* — a loosening or shattering of the internal organs caused by blunt impact. Even when no external wound is visible, an animal that has suffered a significant fall must be presumed to have sustained potentially fatal internal injuries and is considered a *treifa* unless it survives for twenty-four hours or demonstrates normal ambulatory behavior. Since the owner slaughtered the animal immediately, without allowing the requisite time to pass, the animal retained the status of *treifa*.

### Moral Teaching

The Gemara records Rav Nachman's additional observation: had the owner of this ox expended a modest effort — taken a measure of flour's worth of coin to the *beis midrash* and studied the relevant *halacha* — he would have learned that *im shasta me-es le-es kesheira*: if the animal survives twenty-four hours, it is kosher. By acting in haste out of ignorance, the man forfeited the full value of his ox, which was worth far more than the cost of acquiring the knowledge that would have saved it. The Gemara's point is not merely moralistic; it illustrates the concrete, practical stakes of Torah study in the domain of everyday life.

### Challenge Analysis

The narrative raises a serious challenge to the framework established thus far. The canal was only six *tefachim* deep, yet Rav Nachman treated the impact as potentially fatal — sufficient to create a concern of *risuk evarim*. This appears to conflict directly with the Mishnah, which requires a pit to be ten *tefachim* deep before its impact can be considered lethal. Thus, *alma kasavar Rav Nachman yesh chavata be-pachos me-asara* — Rav Nachman appears to hold that an impact from a fall of less than ten *tefachim* can be fatal. The Gemara proceeds to press this tension.

---

## Execution Height

### Execution Site

Rava challenges Rav Nachman on the basis of this apparent position. The Gemara cites a *baraita*: *beis ha-sekila* — the platform from which a condemned person was pushed during the execution of *sekila* — was required to be two stories high, *ve-koma shelo*, plus the height of the condemned person himself. This yields a fall of effectively three human heights. Rashi translates *komos* as stories, though given the phrasing *koma shelo*, the likely intent is the equivalent of three persons' heights, amounting to something on the order of ten *amos* — a considerable distance, far exceeding ten *tefachim*. Rava's challenge: if Rav Nachman holds that a fall of less than ten *tefachim* can cause death, why does the law require such an extreme height for execution? Even a modest fall could produce death.

### Height Necessity

The Gemara itself deflates this challenge somewhat by noting that the question applies equally against either position. Even according to those who require ten *tefachim* as the threshold for lethality, the execution platform is vastly higher than ten *tefachim*, so the question of excessive height arises regardless. The Gemara's real answer is not about the minimum required for death but about the degree of certainty and the character of the death required.

### Merciful Execution

The Gemara cites the principle taught by Rabbah bar Abbuha: *ve-ahavta le-re'acha kamocha* — love your neighbor as yourself — includes even the condemned. From this the Rabbis derive *beror lo mita yafa*: one is obligated to choose for the condemned person the most merciful available form of death. The condemned individual remains one's neighbor and friend even in the moment of execution. Therefore, the greater the height, the more instantaneous and painless the death — and the execution method must be calibrated accordingly to maximize mercy within the constraints of the law.

### Balance Required

However, the Gemara raises a counterpoint: if greater height yields more merciful death, why not make the platform arbitrarily high? The answer is *mishum deminuvel* — an excessive fall would disfigure and desecrate the body. There is thus a precise balance required: high enough to ensure swift, certain death; not so high as to cause grotesque disfigurement. The law's specification of two stories plus the person's height reflects this calibrated equilibrium.

---

## Bayit Definition

### Fence Obligation

The Gemara introduces a *baraita* concerning the obligation of *ma'akeh* — the Torah's requirement to build a parapet around one's roof. The *baraita* states: if the *reshut ha-rabim* is ten *tefachim* higher than your rooftop, such that a passerby in the public domain might fall *onto* your roof rather than *off* it, you are exempt from building a fence. Conversely, if the *reshut ha-rabim* is ten *tefachim* lower than your rooftop — meaning a person on your roof could fall down into the public domain — you are obligated to build a fence. The case of the overpass is illustrative: your building is below the level of the street, and someone walking above might fall down onto your roof. In that scenario, no fence on your roof would help anyway. The operative case is where your rooftop stands above the public space below, creating a potential fatal fall.

### Exterior vs. Interior

This *baraita* prompts a challenge to Rav Nachman's position. If it is true that a fall of less than ten *tefachim* can be lethal, why does the *ma'akeh* obligation only attach when the fall is ten *tefachim* or more? Presumably, the Torah only mandates the fence where the fall presents a genuine risk of death — and if even a shallow fall can be fatal, the threshold should be lower. Rav Nachman responds: the ten-*tefach* requirement here has nothing to do with the minimum height needed for a fatal fall. Rather, it is a definitional criterion: *kol pachot me-asara lav bayit hu* — anything whose interior height is less than ten *tefachim* does not attain the halachic status of a *bayit*. The *ma'akeh* obligation applies only to a *bayit*, and a structure lacking the requisite interior dimension simply does not qualify — even if its roof could theoretically produce a dangerous fall.

The Gemara immediately pushes back: if the ten-*tefach* requirement is really about defining a *bayit* as a structure with sufficient interior living space, then the measurement must refer to the *internal* height of the cavity. Yet the *baraita* speaks of a ten-*tefach* fall, which is measured from the *exterior* — from the level of the rooftop to the ground below. Subtracting the thickness of the ceiling and its plaster (*tikra ve-aziva*), the interior height would necessarily be less than ten *tefachim*. So how can an exterior fall of ten *tefachim* satisfy an interior-based definition of *bayit*?

### Interior Measurement

The Gemara resolves this by positing a specific architectural scenario: *kegon de-dachak migavai* — the house has been dug into the ground on the inside, so that the interior floor is below the exterior ground level. In such a structure, the interior height can be ten *tefachim* even while the exterior roofline stands at ten *tefachim* above the surrounding terrain. The Gemara then points out that this resolution cuts too far: if we are imagining a house where the interior is dug down, the exterior height of the rooftop could be *less* than ten *tefachim* while the interior still measures ten *tefachim* — *de-havei migavai asara kegon de-chachak bitfei*. This means that the *ma'akeh* obligation would apply even to a structure whose rooftop stands fewer than ten *tefachim* above the public domain. And if so, we are back to the conclusion that the real operative factor is not the *bayit* definition at all, but the height of the fall itself — and less than ten *tefachim* on the outside is not enough to be lethal. The *pshat* of the Mishnah is thus reinstated: ten *tefachim* is genuinely required for a lethal impact.

---

## Impact Calculation

### Dimensions

The Gemara now provides Rav Nachman's actual reasoning for the *treifa* ruling on the ox that fell into the six-*tefach* irrigation canal. It is not that Rav Nachman holds that a fall of less than ten *tefachim* is independently lethal. Rather, Rav Nachman's calculation is as follows: *michreisa de-tora le-ar'a kama havei* — from the underside of an ox's belly to the ground, what is the distance? The Gemara answers: four *tefachim*. And the depth of the irrigation canal was six *tefachim*.

### Total Impact

The total impact experienced by the falling ox is therefore four plus six — ten *tefachim*. The animal begins with its underside four *tefachim* above the ground; when it topples into a six-*tefach* canal, the effective fall traverses ten *tefachim* from its natural position to the floor of the canal. *Ishtakach de-chi ka-machbat me-asara ka-machbat* — it turns out that when it sustains the impact, it sustains an impact of ten *tefachim*. Rav Nachman's ruling is therefore entirely consistent with the Mishnah's threshold. He did not deviate from the principle that ten *tefachim* is required for a potentially fatal impact.

### Mishnah Context

The Gemara draws a further distinction to close the apparent tension: the Mishnah's case is one of *igandar le-bor* — an animal that *rolled* into the pit from ground level. In that scenario, the animal was already lying on the ground before it rolled in, so the effective fall is simply the depth of the pit itself, and ten *tefachim* of pit depth is required. But in the case of an animal falling from a standing position, the height of the animal's underside above the ground must be added to the depth of the pit. In that situation, a pit of only six *tefachim* suffices to generate a ten-*tefach* impact. While this conclusion may seem to depart from a simple reading of the Mishnah, the Gemara treats it as the correct technical understanding.

---

## Two Partners Well

### Mishnah Setup

The Gemara now turns to a new Mishnah: *bor shel shnei shutafin* — a pit owned jointly by two partners. The Mishnah describes a case in which the first partner passed by without covering the pit, and the second partner also passed by without covering it. The Mishnah's ruling — at least according to the textual version familiar to Rashi — is that the second person is *chayav*. (The *girsa* of the Rif and Rambam has it the other way, holding the first partner liable — a point that will require examination, as it goes to the core ruling of the Mishnah.)

### Joint Ownership Q

Before reaching the substantive ruling, the Gemara asks a threshold question: *bor shel shnei shutafin heichi mishkachat lah* — how does one even arrive at a scenario of joint ownership of a pit for purposes of liability? This question is nontrivial because liability for a *bor* flows in different ways depending on one's theoretical framework.

### Liability Scenarios

The Gemara notes that according to the view of Rabbi Akiva — that liability for a *bor* derives from ownership, not only from the act of digging — the case is easily constructed. Two partners could own a field jointly, with a pit situated within it; they then relinquish ownership of the field but retain joint title to the pit. In that scenario, both remain liable as owners. However, according to the competing view that ownership alone does not generate liability, and that liability flows only from the act of digging in the *reshut ha-rabim*, the question becomes more difficult. How can two people be jointly and equally responsible as diggers?

One might propose that they both appointed an agent to dig on their behalf — *shavvu shliach tarvaihu*. The agent digs, and both principals are treated as having dug. The Gemara rejects this: *ein shliach le-dvar aveira* — one cannot appoint an agent for a transgression. The transgression attaches to the one who actually performs it, not to the one who commissioned it.

### Agency Principle

The Gemara's invocation of *ein shliach le-dvar aveira* here is notable. It raises the underlying question — left largely implicit — of whether digging a *bor* in the *reshut ha-rabim* constitutes an *aveira* in the first instance. A number of *Rishonim* identify the operative prohibition as *lifnei iver lo titein michshol*, understood in its literal sense of placing a stumbling block before others. However, regardless of the precise prohibition, the Gemara's point is applicable both in the domain of religious transgression and civil liability: the agent who chooses to dig the well is the responsible party. One cannot transfer civil liability through an agency instruction any more than one can transfer criminal culpability through an emissary. The company that orders a worker to dig is not, under this framework, the liable party — the worker who performs the act bears the responsibility.

The alternative scenario for joint liability is that both partners each dig a portion — Reuven digs five *tefachim*, Shimon digs five *tefachim*, together reaching ten. However, as the Gemara will explain, this generates complications in light of the principle of *nistalku maaseh rishon* — that when the second person transforms the pit into a full, lethal *bor*, his act effectively supersedes and displaces the first person's act. This principle, and its precise scope, is what the next section addresses.

---

## Rabbi vs. Rabbanan

### Baraita Setup

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: one person digs a pit nine *tefachim* deep, and another comes and completes it to ten. *Ha-acharon chayav* — the last person is liable. This sets out the basic framework: the person who transforms a non-lethal pit into a lethal one bears primary responsibility for any death that occurs within it.

### Rabbi Position

Rabbi qualifies this ruling. *Achar acharon le-mita* — the last person alone is liable for death. But *achar shneihem le-nezikin* — both are equally liable for damages. Rabbi's reasoning is that even the initial nine-*tefach* pit was a *bor* capable of causing injury, so the first digger retains liability for that dimension of harm. Only for death — which requires the full ten-*tefach* threshold — does the last person's transformative act take exclusive ownership.

### Rabbanan Position

The Rabbis disagree. In their view, once the second person completes the pit to ten *tefachim*, he becomes solely liable for both death *and* damages. The act of making the pit lethal is so qualitatively significant that it wholly displaces the first person's contribution. The first digger's nine *tefachim* are, in effect, subsumed into the second person's *bor*.

### Source Analysis

The Rabbis derive their position from the verse's phrasing: *ki yiftach ish bor, ki yichre ish bor* — whether a person *opens* or *digs* a pit. The inclusion of both terms might seem redundant — surely if one is liable for digging, all the more so for merely opening. The Rabbis read the apparent redundancy as a substantive teaching: *le-havi kore achar kore* — to include a digger who digs after a previous digger has already dug. This teaches that the subsequent digger can bear full and exclusive liability, *she-silak maaseh rishon* — because his act displaces the first act entirely. Additionally, the phrase *ki yichre ish bor* — singular *ish*, one man — teaches that there are situations where two people dig yet only one bears liability: specifically, the one who transforms the pit into something lethal.

### Redundancy Debate

Rabbi disputes this reading. He maintains that both phrases in the verse — *ki yiftach* and *ki yichre* — are genuinely necessary and not redundant, each addressing a distinct legal scenario: the first addresses liability for one who merely opens an existing pit without digging, and the second addresses one who digs. Since neither phrase is extraneous, no additional inference about *kore achar kore* can be drawn from them. Moreover, Rabbi reads *ish bor* differently: it serves to exclude a case where an ox, rather than a person, digs the pit — *ish bor ve-lo shor bor* — teaching that if an ox excavates a cavity, its owner is not liable for resulting injuries as a *bor* tortfeasor.

The Rabbis counter that the word *ish* appears *twice* in the relevant verses — once in *ki yiftach ish bor* and once in *ki yichre ish bor*. The first occurrence teaches the exclusion of an ox as digger; the second teaches that one person can be fully liable even when two have dug. Rabbi responds that the repetition of *ish* is not informative — *aidi de-katav ha katav ha*, once the Torah wrote it in one clause, it simply wrote it again in the parallel clause, without intending an additional teaching.

The Gemara then asks: even granting the Rabbis' position that the last digger bears sole liability, what identifies the *last* person as the liable party rather than the first? The verse *ve-ha-mes yihyeh lo* — the carcass shall be his — identifies the tortfeasor as the one whose act rendered the pit lethal: *hahu de-ka-avid mita*. The person who gave the pit its death-causing capacity is the one who owns it, and the carcass belongs to him as compensation for the liability he bears.

The Gemara notes, however, that the same verse *ve-ha-mes yihyeh lo* is also needed for a separate teaching of Rava: that if the animal that fell into the pit was a *shor psulei ha-mukdashim* — an ox that had been consecrated as a *korban*, subsequently became blemished, and was redeemed — the owner of the pit is exempt from liability. The reason is that the carcass of such an animal cannot be used by its owner, since it was once sanctified property. The verse *ve-ha-mes yihyeh lo* — the carcass shall be *his* — implies liability only where the carcass is the property of the owner and has usable value. Where the carcass cannot benefit the owner, there is no compensable loss and therefore no liability. The Gemara resolves the double use of the verse by noting that both teachings can be derived from it: it establishes the principle that liability attaches to the one who made the pit lethal, and simultaneously teaches the exemption in the case of *psulei ha-mukdashim*.

Tosafot adds an important clarification: even according to the Rabbis, there are scenarios where both diggers remain jointly liable without any question. If Reuven digs three *tefachim* and Shimon digs three *tefachim*, neither has qualitatively transformed the pit into a *bor* of *mita* — they have each contributed equally to a pit that remains non-lethal, and both are liable for any damages. Equally, if one person digs ten *tefachim* and another digs an additional ten, the second person has not transformed a non-lethal pit into a lethal one; the first already made it lethal, and the second merely deepened it further. Both therefore remain *chayav*. The Gemara's discussion focuses on the paradigmatic case of a standard ten-*tefach bor* where one digs nine and the other completes it — because in that scenario the question of qualitative transformation is sharpest.

---

## Plastering Case

### Baraita Text

The Gemara cites a second *baraita*: one person digs a pit to ten *tefachim*, and another comes and plasters it (*siyado*) and engraves or carves it (*kiyado*). The *baraita* rules: *he-acharon chayav* — the last person is liable. This is striking. The first person already dug the pit to the full lethal depth of ten *tefachim*. Under the framework we have developed, once the first person creates a *bor* capable of causing death, his act should not be displaced. Yet the *baraita* gives sole liability to the one who merely plastered and carved. Why?

### Hevel Increase

The Gemara considers whether this *baraita* reflects the position of Rabbi alone (who distributes liability) or of the Rabbis alone (who concentrate it in the last person), or whether both opinions are represented across the two *baraitot*. The initial answer offered is that of Rav Zvid: *ha va-ha Rabbanan* — both *baraitot* reflect the position of the Rabbis, and there is no contradiction. The Rabbis say the last person is fully liable only when the first person had not yet created *shiur mita* — a pit meeting the threshold for lethality. When the first person *had* already created *shiur mita*, the Rabbis agree with Rabbi that all subsequent diggers remain jointly liable alongside the first.

The resolution of the *baraita* about plastering, then, must be that the first digger's ten-*tefach* pit did not in fact reach *shiur mita* — it lacked sufficient *hevel* to be lethal, even though it met the depth requirement. Rashi explains: *she-mitechila rechavo lo haya bo hevel kol kach ve-zeh siyado ve-kiyado* — at the outset, the width of the pit was such that it did not generate sufficient *hevel*; the second person, by plastering and narrowing the interior walls, increased the *hevel* to the level required for lethality.

### Alternative: Rabbi

An alternative version (*ika de-amri*) has Rav Zvid saying instead: *ha va-ha Rabbi* — both *baraitot* reflect the position of Rabbi. In that case, the *baraita* where all are liable (the one who digs ten, the one who deepens to twenty, and so on) is straightforwardly Rabbi, who distributes liability broadly. The *baraita* where only the last person is liable — the plastering case — is also Rabbi, but in a scenario where the first digger's pit had no effective *hevel* at all, neither for death nor for injury. In that case even Rabbi agrees that the first person did nothing of legal significance, and the entire liability rests with the one who transformed it into a functional *bor*.

### Alternative: Width

Tosafot develops this second explanation further. Although the Gemara previously established that even pits with different proportions possess *some hevel*, a pit that is substantially wider than it is deep may generate so little *hevel* that it creates no cognizable liability at all. The first digger dug a deep but extremely wide pit — effectively an open sloping depression rather than a true enclosed cavity. Such a pit lacks the concentrated *hevel* necessary for liability even for damages. The second person, by plastering the walls and narrowing the cavity, created the first genuine *bor* with effective *hevel*, thereby assuming full and sole liability. This understanding draws an analogy to a swimming pool with a graduated incline: the gradual slope removes the quality of an enclosed pit even if the deepest point meets the depth requirement.

---

## Reversing Acts

### Filling Question

Rava poses a new question that emerges directly from the framework of the preceding discussion. Suppose the second person — who had dug the tenth *tefach* and thereby assumed ownership of the entire *bor* — subsequently filled in that tenth *tefach*, restoring the pit to nine *tefachim*. Alternatively, suppose the second person had placed a stone at the edge of the pit (to raise the effective fall height to ten *tefachim*) and then removed that stone. In both cases, the second person has reversed his own act. The pit now looks exactly as it did after the first person finished — a nine-*tefach* excavation. Whose *bor* is it?

### Two Approaches

Two possibilities present themselves. The first: *mai de-avad shaklei* — he has undone what he did, and we treat the situation as though he had never intervened. The pit reverts to being the first person's responsibility. The second: *keivan de-istatam istallek maaseh rishon* — once the pit was filled in, the first person's act was already displaced and nullified. Now, when the second person removes the fill material and leaves a nine-*tefach* opening, he has himself created a nine-*tefach* pit. It is entirely his, even though it is non-lethal. The question has practical implications: if the first reading is correct, the first person resumes liability; if the second is correct, the second person owns a nine-*tefach* pit whose halachic status must be assessed independently. This is analogous — as noted in the discussion — to the question of the tenth *tefach*: just as digging the final *tefach* can transfer ownership of the entire *bor*, reversing that act raises the symmetric question of whether ownership transfers back.

### Teiku

*Teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

---

## Water Lethality

### Water Ratio

The Gemara introduces a teaching in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Shmuel bar Marta: a *bor* that is eight *tefachim* deep, of which the bottom two *tefachim* are filled with water, renders the owner *chayav* for death — as though it were a full ten-*tefach* dry pit.

### Water Power

The underlying principle is: *kol tefach de-maya ke-trei de-yavsha dami* — each *tefach* of water is as injurious as two *tefachim* of empty space. Thus, an eight-*tefach* well with two *tefachim* of water at the bottom effectively functions as a ten-*tefach* pit: six *tefachim* of air cavity plus two *tefachim* of water, which count as four, yields the equivalent of ten. Rashi explains this through the lens of *hevel*, noting that water contributes additional *hevel* — whether understood as vapor, toxicity, or some quality of the air — beyond what a simple air-filled cavity of the same depth would produce. Whether one prefers to understand the water's additional danger in terms of drowning, asphyxiation, or the concentrated *hevel* of a damp enclosure, the halachic equivalence is two-to-one: water is twice as dangerous as an equivalent depth of dry air.

### Nine Plus One

The Gemara raises a series of unresolved questions about the limits of this principle. The first: what is the law concerning a pit that is nine *tefachim* deep with one *tefach* of water at the bottom? One *tefach* of water counting as two would bring the total to ten — making the owner liable. But perhaps there is a minimum threshold of water required before the two-to-one ratio applies: with only one *tefach* of water, there may be insufficient water to generate the enhanced *hevel*, and the pit should be treated as simply a nine-*tefach* dry pit, below the threshold for death. Alternatively, even one *tefach* of water counts as two, in which case the pit reaches the equivalent of ten. The further consideration is that a nine-*tefach* pit is deeper than an eight-*tefach* pit, and the greater depth might itself contribute to *hevel* in a way that supplements the water's contribution — *keivan de-amik tefei it beih havla*. The question is left unresolved.

### Seven Plus Three

The second unresolved question: what of a pit seven *tefachim* deep, of which three *tefachim* are water? The arithmetic is: four *tefachim* of air plus three *tefachim* of water (counting as six) yields the equivalent of ten. On this accounting, the owner should be *chayav*. But one might argue the opposite: because the air cavity begins only four *tefachim* down, the pit does not achieve sufficient depth to generate meaningful *hevel* regardless of the water — *keivan de-lo amik kuli hai leit beih havla*. Moreover, the ratio of water to air is now higher — three to four — but the overall structure is shallower. Whether the water's enhanced lethality can compensate for the reduced depth, or whether the reduced depth undermines the *hevel* framework entirely, remains unresolved.

---

## Well Expansion

### Expansion Effect

Rav Shizbi poses a question to Rava: *hirchiva mahu* — what is the law if the second person widened the pit? The first person dug a *bor*, and the second person came and expanded it — opening it wider without changing its depth. From one perspective, widening the pit appears to be a public service: it reduces the *hevel* within the cavity, since *hevel* is more concentrated in a narrower space. From another perspective, widening the pit increases the surface area exposed to the *reshut ha-rabim*, making it easier for people or animals to fall in — thereby increasing the hazard.

### Rav Ashi View

Rava's initial response — that the widener reduced the *hevel* and should receive credit — is immediately challenged by the rejoinder that widening brings the danger closer (*kireiv heizeika*). Rav Ashi cuts through this impasse with a practical resolution: *nachzi anan* — let us look at the actual circumstances. The question is not purely theoretical; its answer depends on what actually occurs.

### Cause of Death

If the animal or person died as a result of *hevel* — some form of asphyxiation or toxic air — then the one who widened the pit is exempt, because his act reduced the *hevel* and thus diminished rather than increased that particular hazard. If the victim died by impact — *chavata* — then the one who widened the pit is liable, because his act increased exposure to the risk of falling.

### Location-Based

A second formulation of Rav Ashi's *nachzi anan* resolves the question by the physical location of the fall rather than the cause of death. If the victim fell into the portion of the pit that was expanded by the second person — the newly opened section — then the second person is liable, because the victim fell into territory he created. If the victim fell into the original portion of the pit dug by the first person, then the second person's widening actually reduced the *hevel* in that area, and he is exempt.

---

## Pit Proportions

### First Opinion

The Gemara records a dispute transmitted in the name of Rabbah bar bar Chanah, citing Rabbi Mani, concerning the relationship between a pit's depth and its width and how this affects the presence of *hevel*. One opinion holds: *l'olam yesh bo hevel ad she-rachvo yater al omko* — there is always *hevel* in a pit as long as its width does not exceed its depth. Under this view, a pit whose width equals its depth still qualifies as having *hevel*; only when the width exceeds the depth does the *hevel* dissipate.

### Second Opinion

The opposing opinion holds: *l'olam ein bo hevel ad she-omko yater al rachvo* — there is no *hevel* in a pit until its depth exceeds its width. Under this view, a pit of equal depth and width lacks sufficient *hevel*; only when the depth strictly exceeds the width does the confined air generate *hevel* capable of creating liability. The case of exact equality is thus the point of contention between these two opinions — a structural question somewhat analogous to the Talmudic class of *i efshar le-tzamtzem* disputes, where a boundary condition admits of no easy resolution.

---

## Shared Well Mishnah

### Mishnah Text

The Gemara now turns to the Mishnah's core ruling: the first person passed by the uncovered pit and did not cover it; the second person passed by and did not cover it. According to Rashi's textual version, the second person is *chayav*.

### Exemption Q

The Gemara asks: *ve-rishon eimat miptar* — at what point does the first person become exempt? The question assumes that the first person was once liable — he passed an uncovered pit without covering it and bore some responsibility at that moment. Something subsequently occurred that shifted full liability to the second person. What was that event?

### Opinion One

One opinion holds: the first person is exempted from the moment the second person begins using the well — *mishemenicho mishtamesh*. Once the second person actively draws water or otherwise makes use of the pit, there is an implicit transfer of responsibility. The first person, seeing the second party take over, is reasonably understood to have been relieved of his obligation to cover. This requires no formal transaction; the practical assumption of control suffices.

### Opinion Two

The second opinion is more demanding: the first person must physically hand over the cover — *misheyimsor lo dalyo* — or more precisely, the covering implement or bucket, as Rashi interprets *dalyo* to mean the *kisui ha-bor*. A mere assumption of use by the second party, without an explicit transfer, does not exempt the first. Until there is a concrete, tangible handover, the first person remains liable alongside the second.

---

## Water-Drawers

### Baraita Setup

The Gemara grounds this dispute in a *tannaic* debate. The *baraita* describes: one person is drawing water from a pit; a second person comes and says, *hanach li va-ani edleh* — leave it to me, I'll draw. *Keivan she-henicho mishtamesh patur* — once the first person leaves and the second takes over the drawing, the first is exempt.

### Stricter View

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disagrees: *misheyimsor lo dalyo* — the first person is exempt only from the moment he physically hands over the bucket (or cover) to the second. A verbal declaration of assumed responsibility by the second party, followed by the first person's passive withdrawal, is not sufficient to transfer the obligation.

### Breira Question

The Gemara analyzes the underlying conceptual disagreement. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds *yesh breira* — that there is retroactive determination. Under the principle of *breira*, the division of responsibility between the two parties can be retroactively clarified based on what actually unfolds: *hai mideidieh ka-memalei ve-hai mideidieh ka-memalei* — each one is understood to have been drawing from his own portion, as it were. Because the two parties' responsibilities are conceptually separable and retroactively determinable, a verbal agreement to transfer is not enough; a concrete physical act of handover is required to mark the precise moment of transfer. The first opinion, which exempts the first person upon the mere assumption of use, presumably holds *ein breira* — that no such retroactive determination is possible, and therefore we must look to conduct and circumstances to determine when responsibility effectively passed. The precise working-out of this *breira* analysis is left for the following session.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 52

## Liability Transfer

### Intro & Core Dispute

Daf 52 continues the sugyot related to the *bor* — the uncovered pit — and picks up at the bottom of 51b. The *mishnah* there established that when a first owner passed over a well without covering it and a second owner then failed to cover it as well, one of them bears liability. Depending on the textual version, either the second owner is liable or the first remains so. But this creates an immediate difficulty: if both simply passed by and neither did anything, then each was negligent, and both should be liable. The *gemara* must therefore construct a scenario in which the first owner can genuinely transfer his liability to the second — a point at which his own obligation ends.

### Implicit vs Explicit

The *gemara* offers two versions of how this transfer occurs. The first version holds that once the second owner came and began using the well, that act of usage was sufficient to make him implicitly responsible. The second, more demanding version holds that it is not enough for the second owner merely to use the well; rather, the first owner must actively hand over the cover of the well to the second owner — only then does responsibility formally pass. The *gemara* now turns to identify what underlying dispute drives these two positions.

### Tannaim Debate

The *gemara* introduces a parallel *tannaitic* dispute with the phrase *ke-tanai* — this mirrors a debate among the *tannaim*. The case: someone is drawing water from a well, and his fellow says to him, "Leave off and I will draw." Once the first person steps aside and the second begins using the well, the first is exempt — he has, by stepping aside, renounced his responsibility. That is the position of the first *tanna*: usage alone by the second party is sufficient to transfer liability.

### R. Eliezer Position

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disagrees. Mere usage is not enough; the first owner remains responsible until he explicitly hands over the cover to the second. Only that formal act of transfer — physically giving over the cover — constitutes a genuine handover of responsibility.

## Breira Concept

### Breira Defined

The *gemara* asks: *b'mai kamipalgi* — what is this dispute actually about? The answer turns on the concept of *breira*, which concerns whether shared ownership in jointly held property can be retrospectively individuated. When two people jointly own a well and each uses it in turn, are they each drawing on a common, undifferentiated resource — or can we say that when one uses it, he is accessing only his own portion, and when the other uses it, he is accessing only his?

### Yesh Breira

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds *yesh breira* — there is distinguishability. When I use the well, I am using my half; when my partner uses it, he is using his half. The practical consequence follows directly: when the second owner drew water, he was only ever accessing his own portion of the well. He never took over my portion, and therefore he never assumed responsibility for my half. The only way my half can be transferred to him — and my responsibility along with it — is if I explicitly hand over the cover. That physical act is the unambiguous statement: "You are now responsible for this well." The *gemara* notes, in passing, that *breira* pertains to the act of using, not to the moment an animal falls in; an animal falling in does not choose which half to fall into, and liability for that event would be shared accordingly.

### Ein Breira

The *rabbanan*, by contrast, hold *ein breira* — there is no distinguishability. When either partner uses the well, he is using the undivided whole, the portions of both owners together. Consequently, when the second owner begins using the well, he is accessing the entire resource, including the first owner's share, and thereby assumes full responsibility for it.

### Field Prohibition

Ravina notes that this same dispute appears in another *tannaitic* context. If two partners in a jointly held field each took a vow that the other may not derive benefit from him — so that my half of the field is forbidden to you and your half to me — the *rabbanan* rule that neither may enter the field at all, since each necessarily benefits from the other's portion by entering. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, however, says that when I enter, I enter my own portion, and when he enters, he enters his own portion — *yesh breira*, each use is attributed to one's own share, and therefore neither violates the other's *neder*.

### Ravina Summary

Ravina draws the two disputes together: the debate about watching the well and the debate about the jointly held field are expressions of the same underlying question — when you use something owned jointly, to what degree are you accessing something that belongs to the other person, or are you only ever accessing the portion to which you have rights?

## Handing Over Keys

### Selling Well

Since the *gemara* has been discussing the handing over of a cover as an act of transferring responsibility, it now pivots to examine this gesture as a potential act of *kinyan* — formal acquisition. Rabbi Elazar rules: if one sells a well to another and hands over the cover (*dalyo*), the buyer takes possession. The simple reading of *dalyo* is the bucket, but the *gemara* will treat it as the cover. At first glance, this appears to introduce an entirely new mode of *kinyan*: handing over that which symbolically controls access to the property — a kind of "handing over the keys to the kingdom."

### Authorization Model

The *gemara* resists this reading. Land is acquired only through *kesef*, *shtar*, or *chazakah*, and it asks: if money was paid, that should be the act of acquisition; if a *chazakah* was performed, let that suffice. What work is the handing over of the cover doing? The *gemara* resolves: the *kinyan* is always effected through *chazakah*, but for a *chazakah* to be valid the seller must authorize the buyer to perform it — he must say *lech chazek u-knei*, "go, take possession and acquire." The handing over of the cover is not itself the *kinyan*; it is the equivalent of that authorization. Once you hand over the cover, it is as though you have told the buyer: go ahead and perform the act of *chazakah*. The *gemara* thus reinterprets Rabbi Elazar's ruling: not a new form of *kinyan*, but an authorization that enables the established form.

### House Keys

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi offers a parallel ruling at the top of 52a: one who sells a house to another — once the seller hands over the key, the buyer acquires it. The *gemara* raises the same objection: if there was already payment or a *chazakah*, why does the key matter? And it gives the same answer: *le'olam b'chazakah* — the *kinyan* is through *chazakah*, and handing over the key is the equivalent of saying *lech chazek u-knei*. It is an authorization, not an independent act of acquisition.

One might note, as *Tosafot* does, that the *Rashbam* in Bava Batra appears to take the simpler reading of these statements at face value — that handing over a key actually constitutes a form of *kinyan* — which creates tension with the *gemara*'s reinterpretation here. *Tosafot* also points to a *sugya* at the beginning of Pesachim, where the *gemara* discusses whether a landlord has handed over keys to a tenant in the context of who bears responsibility for *bedikat chametz*. *Tosafot* explains, however, that the issue there is not when the *kinyan* of rental takes effect, but the practical question of whether the renter yet has physical access to the house. A person cannot be obligated to check a house for *chametz* if he has not yet been given the means of entry. So there the key is significant, but for reasons of practical access rather than as an act of *kinyan* — a distinction that preserves the *gemara*'s general framework.

### Flock & Goat

Reish Lakish, citing Rabbi Yannai, extends the same pattern: one who sells a flock to another — once the seller hands over the *mashchuchis*, the buyer acquires. The word *mashchuchis* derives from the root *mashoch*, to lead or draw, suggesting something that causes the flock to follow. The *gemara* raises its now-familiar objection: if you actually moved the animals, that is *meshichah* and should be the act of *kinyan*; if you handed over something attached to the animal, that approaches *mesirah*, which works precisely because it is connected directly to the animal itself. The *mashchuchis*, however, is not attached to any individual animal in that direct sense. So again the *gemara* redefines: the *kinyan* is through *meshichah*, and handing over the *mashchuchis* is tantamount to saying *lech meshoch u-knei* — the authorization to perform the act.

### Mashchuchis ID

What exactly is the *mashchuchis*? The *gemara* reports two identifications. The local interpretation is that it is a bell — a ringing bell that the flock is trained to follow. Rabbi Yaakov says it is the lead goat, the animal that walks at the head of the flock and which all the others follow, functioning somewhat like a sheepdog in its role. Indeed, goats naturally fulfill this function as leaders of sheep, and the arrangement of a different species — a goat — leading sheep reflects a well-known feature of how flocks were managed.

### Locks & Punishment

A certain Galilean expounded before Rav Chisda: when a shepherd grows angry at his flock, he blinds the lead animal. The *derashah* carries a homiletic point — when the Holy One wishes to punish the Jewish people, He strikes the leaders. *Tosafot* addresses a further point arising from this entire section: while the *Rashbam* in one place seems to entertain the possibility that handing over keys constitutes a genuine *kinyan*, the *gemara* here consistently drives toward the authorization model. And separately, the *sugya* at the beginning of Pesachim, though it also invokes the handing over of keys, operates on a different plane — one of practical halachic access rather than formal acquisition.

## Second Owner Liable

### Mishnah Setup

The *gemara* now proceeds to the next *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states: if the first owner covered the well and the second owner subsequently found it uncovered and did not cover it, the second owner is liable. This *mishnah* differs from the preceding one. The previous *mishnah*, as Rashi explains, assumed that the second owner either used the well or was handed the cover — thereby assuming full responsibility. The present *mishnah* begins from the premise that if the first owner had not covered it, both would share responsibility, since both passed over it without covering. Here, the first owner has done his part by covering it; the second owner then finds it exposed and fails to act. The second owner therefore becomes fully liable.

The *mishnah* continues: if the owner covered it properly (*k'ra'uy*) and an ox or donkey nonetheless fell in and died, he is exempt. If he did not cover it properly and an animal fell in and died, he is liable. It is not sufficient merely to place something over the well — the covering must be adequate to withstand animals walking over it.

The *mishnah* further records: if an animal fell forward into the pit because it was startled by the sound of digging within the well, the owner of the well is liable even if the person digging is not the owner. This is striking: one might have argued that the digger should be exempt because the harm is only *grama* — indirect causation — and that the owner of the well should be exempt because it was not the well itself but the sound that caused the animal to fall. Yet the law holds the well owner liable.

Conversely, if the animal fell *backwards* into the well — that is, it was startled and fell in the opposite direction, back into the pit — the well owner is exempt. The *mishnah* then addresses the case of an ox together with its implements: if the ox fell in and its yoke broke, or a donkey fell in and its saddlebags tore, the owner is liable for the animal and exempt for the implements — consistent with the established rule of *shor v'lo adam, chamor v'lo kelim*.

The *mishnah* concludes with two further distinctions. If an ox that is deaf, mute, or a minor (*cheresh shoteh v'katan*) fell in, the owner is liable. But if a son or daughter, a slave or maidservant fell in, he is exempt. The *chiddush* in both parts is notable. One might have thought that since the well owner is generally exempt for human injuries on the grounds that people bear responsibility for themselves, a child — who cannot fully look out for himself — might generate liability. Similarly, one might have considered treating a slave as property and therefore assigning liability as for damaged property. The *mishnah* teaches that neither exception applies: both children and slaves remain within the general exemption for human beings.

### When Does Liability Return…

The *gemara* now raises a question about the first part of the *mishnah*: at what point does the first owner, having properly covered the well and thereby exempted himself, have his liability reignite? He is not exempt forever. If word reaches him that the cover has been removed or has failed, at some stage he becomes obligated to respond. The question is: when?

### Three Duration Views

Three *amoraim* offer distinct positions. Rav says: *bichedei sheyeda* — there must have been enough time for him to have found out about it. As *Tosafot* explains, this does not require proof that the person actually heard; once sufficient time has elapsed that one would normally expect the information to have reached him through ordinary channels, he is again liable. Shmuel says: *bichedei sheyodi'uhu* — it is not enough that word could have trickled through informally; there must have been enough time, or in fact an actual occurrence, of someone going and directly informing him. Hearing a rumor does not create the same sense of imperative to act as being directly told. Rabbi Yochanan says: *bichedei sheyodi'uhu v'yiscor v'yichros arazim v'yechasenu* — there must have been enough time not only for him to be informed, but to hire workers, obtain timber, and construct a proper new cover. The *chiddush* is not that he need do nothing in the interim: even Rabbi Yochanan would agree that before the full cover can be prepared, the owner must arrange temporary supervision — placing watchers by the pit, for example — until a permanent solution can be installed. Rabbi Yochanan's ruling addresses only the question of when full liability attaches, not whether any interim obligation exists.

## Proper Covering

### Proper Cover

The *gemara* proceeds to examine the clause: if the well was covered properly and an ox or donkey nonetheless fell in, the owner is exempt. This is clear in principle — if you fulfilled your obligation, you bear no liability. But the *gemara* presses: if you covered it properly, how did anything manage to fall in at all?

### Rotting Exception

Rav Yitzchak bar bar Chana answers: *shehitlia mitocho* — it rotted from within, literally became infested with worms from the inside. If the owner placed on a cover that appeared sound but had been eaten away internally — by termites, say — with no external indication of its weakness, then his covering was indeed *k'ra'uy* at the time it was placed, and what subsequently caused the failure was something he had no reason to anticipate. The *gemara* will later note the possibility that a responsible owner ought to perform periodic inspections, tapping the wood to detect internal hollowness. But at this stage, *hitlia mitocho* is treated as a genuine *ones* — an unforeseeable accident — even for an owner who otherwise fulfilled his duty.

### Camel Weakening

A new question is now posed: suppose the owner placed a cover that could withstand oxen but was not strong enough to withstand camels. Camels came and weakened it. Then oxen came and fell in. Is the owner liable? The *gemara* asks: what are the circumstances?

### Common Animal Test

If camels are common in that area (*shchichei gemalim*), then the owner is clearly a *poshea* — negligent. He should have known that a cover inadequate for camels in a place where camels regularly pass is not a responsible cover; he could have anticipated that the cover would be weakened and that oxen would then fall in. On the other hand, if camels are entirely uncommon (*she'einam metzuyim*), he is an *ones* — he had no reason to guard against them, and his covering was appropriate given the realistic conditions. The more challenging case, and the one the *gemara* is actually pursuing, is where camels come only occasionally (*l'prakim*) — not regularly, but not never.

### Unresolved Vigilance

The *gemara* frames the question precisely: do we say that since camels come occasionally, the owner should have anticipated it — *de'ibei lei asukei ada'atei* — and therefore he is a *poshea*? Or do we say that since camels are not currently present and their appearance is not a reliable expectation, the owner is an *ones* and bears no liability? The question is genuine because it is not simply an objective actuarial matter — it is also a question of what we can realistically demand that a person think about. A common person tending a well does not sit and calculate that a camel might pass once in some period. The *gemara* is asking whether that failure of anticipation itself constitutes negligence.

This question is structurally parallel to the familiar framework of *ruach metzuyah* and *ruach she'einah metzuyah* — the common wind versus the uncommon wind — and the standard three-tiered framework of *poshea*, intermediate care, and *ones*. What the *gemara* is doing here is applying that same continuum to camels as a type of external force: a common camel is a *ruach metzuyah*; a never-present camel is a *ruach she'einah metzuyah*; an occasional camel is the difficult middle case. The *teyku* — the *gemara*'s unresolved suspension — reflects that this middle category genuinely resists easy classification.

## First Mishnah Proof

### Fit Oxen/Unfit Camels

The *gemara* now attempts to resolve the open question from a reading of the *mishnah* itself. *Ta shema* — come and hear: if the well was covered properly (*k'ra'uy*) and an ox or donkey fell in, the owner is exempt. The *gemara* asks: what is the case? If the cover was fully adequate for both oxen and camels, how did anything fall in at all? That seems to leave only one possibility that generates a genuine *chiddush*: the cover was fit for oxen but not for camels.

### Proof from First Part

From this reading, the *gemara* attempts to identify the case of the *mishnah* as one where camels occasionally come (*d'atu l'prakim*), they came and weakened the cover, and oxen subsequently fell in. If so, the *mishnah*'s ruling that the owner is exempt (*patur*) would demonstrate that occasional camel visits do not generate an obligation to reinforce the cover — the owner is an *ones*, not a *poshea*. This would resolve the open question in favor of the lenient position.

### Rebuttal: Rotting

The *gemara* rejects this reading. In fact, the cover may have been fully adequate for both oxen and camels, and the *chiddush* of the *mishnah* is supplied by the statement of Rav Yitzchak bar bar Chana: *shehitlia mitocho* — it rotted from within. The case is one of internal decay that could not have been detected or anticipated. On this reading, the question of occasional camels remains unresolved, and the *mishnah* proves nothing about it.

## Second Mishnah Part

### Improper Setup

The *gemara* now turns to the second clause of the *mishnah*: if the cover was not *k'ra'uy* and an animal died, the owner is liable. Once again the *gemara* probes: what is the case? If the cover was obviously inadequate by any measure — neither fit for oxen nor for camels — it is entirely obvious that the owner is liable. There is nothing to teach.

### Case Reading

For the second part of the *mishnah* to constitute a genuine *chiddush*, the *gemara* reads it as a case where the cover was fit for oxen but not fit for camels, and camels were common in that area. In that scenario, the owner was clearly negligent for not providing a cover adequate to the realistic conditions, camels came and weakened it, and oxen fell in. The *gemara* then suggests that if this is the case, and the *mishnah* declares the owner liable, perhaps the *chiddush* is different: perhaps the cover was fit for oxen but not for camels, camels were common, but in the end it was *hitlia mitocho* — internal rot — that caused the failure. The *mishnah* would then be teaching: since you were negligent with respect to camels, you are liable even for the rot — *migu d'havei poshea l'inyan gemalim, havei poshea l'inyan hatla'ah*. Because you were negligent in one direction, your negligence extends to and covers the unrelated cause of the failure.

### Migo Question

The *gemara*, however, declines this reading as well. The case of the second clause of the *mishnah* is simply one where the cover was fit for oxen but not for camels, camels were common, the camels came and weakened it, and the oxen fell in — straightforward and fully connected negligence throughout. The response to the objection that this seems obvious is the same as before: since the *mishnah* stated the case of a proper cover in the first clause, it balanced it with an improper cover in the second clause, even though the liability in the second clause follows as a matter of course.

The *gemara* then attempts the same reading of the *mishnah* in reverse — trying to derive from the first clause that *migo* does apply, and from the second clause that it does not — and reaches the same impasse. Each time, the *gemara* is able to reread the *mishnah* in a way that makes the case obvious on its own terms, without invoking *migo* in either direction. The *mishnah* therefore proves nothing about whether negligence in one domain transfers to an unrelated cause of harm. The question of *migo* remains open through this entire extended analysis.

The underlying conceptual tension can be framed as follows. One view holds that liability is always scenario-specific: you are liable only for what actually resulted from your negligence, and if the actual cause of injury was something unrelated to where your negligence lay, you are exempt for that specific outcome. The opposing view holds that once you have established a zone of negligence — you left a dangerous pit inadequately covered — you bear liability for whatever happens within that zone, even if the precise mechanism of harm differs from the one you were negligent about. The *gemara*'s sustained effort to read the *mishnah* either way, always finding an alternative explanation, indicates that neither position can be decisively established from the *mishnah* text alone.

## Blind Ox Proof

### Vulnerable Animals

The *gemara* now reaches what it presents as a stronger proof. It returns to the clause of the *mishnah* dealing with an ox that is deaf, mute, or a minor (*cheresh shoteh v'katan*), or blind (*suma*), or walking at night — in all such cases the owner of the pit is liable.

### Smart Ox Exempt

This leads to a startling implication, which the *gemara* now makes explicit. If a normal, sighted ox falls into an uncovered pit in the daytime, the owner of the pit is actually exempt. The reasoning: an ox in normal conditions looks where it is going. A sighted ox walking in daylight should have seen the pit and avoided it. The fact that it did not is attributed to the ox itself rather than to the hazard. Only when the ox cannot be expected to see or avoid the hazard — because it is blind, or because it is nighttime, or because the animal lacks ordinary awareness — does the pit owner bear liability.

### Migo Argument

This creates a *migo* question directly parallel to the one that has been under discussion. The pit owner has an open, uncovered well. He is clearly negligent and liable with respect to a blind ox, a *cheresh shoteh v'katan* ox, and a nighttime scenario. Should we not then say: since he is a *poshea* in all those respects, he should be liable *across the board* — including for the normal daytime sighted ox? His negligence in leaving the pit uncovered is a general negligence, and perhaps it should generate a general, undifferentiated liability?

### Migo Rejected

The *gemara* answers: no. *Shema mina lo amrinan migo* — we do not apply *migo* in this way. The owner is exempt for the normal sighted ox in daytime, and the fact that he is negligent in other respects does not change that. *Shema mina*.

### Tosafot Critique

*Tosafot*, however, objects to the *gemara*'s use of this case as a proof regarding *migo*. *Tosafot* argues that the exemption for a normal sighted ox in daytime has nothing to do with the owner's negligence or its absence. The reason you are exempt is not "I was not negligent for this type of ox." The reason is that the ox did it to itself. The concept of *bor* as a tortious hazard means that the pit served as the instrument of harm — the animal tripped into it, was drawn in by it. But a normal sighted ox that walks into an open pit in broad daylight is, in the *gemara*'s framework, attributed as acting upon itself. The well was not the active cause of harm; the ox was its own cause. My well was not the *mazik* of that ox.

This is categorically different from the *migo* question that has been debated throughout the *sugya*. In the camel-weakening and rotting scenarios, the pit genuinely was the *mazik* — an animal fell in and was harmed by the pit — and the only question is whether the precise pathway of harm matches the owner's negligence. That is a *migo* question. In the case of the normal sighted ox, there is no *migo* question at all; the ox simply is not treated as a victim of the pit. *Tosafot* therefore regards the *gemara*'s proof as conceptually imprecise, even as it accepts the *gemara*'s ultimate conclusion.

## Liability Framework

### Negligence-Specific

The *gemara*'s conclusion, toward which the entire extended discussion has been building, is that liability for a *bor* is not automatically across-the-board once any negligence is established. The traditional view emerging from the *sugya* is that you are liable only for those scenarios for which you were in fact negligent, and an unrelated cause of harm — even one occurring against a background of negligence — does not automatically draw in your liability.

### Strict Liability View

An alternative framework, however, presents itself as conceptually coherent and was raised toward the end of the discussion. On this view, the act of digging a pit creates a strict liability that persists until the danger is completely neutralized. The owner's obligation is not simply to exercise reasonable care in each individual scenario; it is to eliminate the hazard entirely. Until he does so, he remains liable for whatever harm the pit causes, regardless of whether the specific mechanism of harm corresponds to a direction in which he was individually negligent. The *mishnah*'s language of *k'ra'uy* — proper covering — then becomes the test for whether the danger has been fully neutralized, not merely a standard of reasonable care with respect to foreseeable animals.

### Causation Requirement

Even on the strict liability model, however, a causation requirement remains. The *gemara* never suggests that the pit owner is liable for harms entirely disconnected from the pit. What the strict liability model requires is not that the owner be negligent for the specific mode of injury, but that the injury itself must still be causally connected to the pit — that the pit was in fact the *mazik*. The debate, ultimately, is about whether the owner's liability is determined scenario by scenario, matching negligence to outcome, or whether it is determined globally once the underlying dangerous condition has been established and not remedied. The *gemara* leaves this framework-level question open, having demonstrated through the *mishnah* analysis that the text does not decisively resolve it in either direction.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 53

## Nafal Lifanav

### Case Setup

The daf opens at the very last line of 52b with the term *nafal lifanav* — the animal fell forward. The *mishna* had established that if someone is digging in a pit and the noise startles a passing animal, causing it to fall forward into the pit, the owner of the pit is liable; if the animal fell backward, the owner is exempt. The question the *gemara* immediately confronts is: what precisely does "fell backward" mean? After all, we understand well enough what it means for an animal to fall face-first into the pit. The other direction requires elaboration.

### Rav's Hevel Theory

Rav explains the *mishna* in the most literal sense: *lifanav lifanav mamash, l'acharav l'acharav mamash, v'zeh v'zeh b'bor* — "forward" means literally face-first into the pit, and "backward" means that the animal fell into the pit with its back facing downward, its mouth and face pointing upward, and it descended in that orientation into the well. At first glance this seems puzzling: either way the animal is in the pit — why would the direction it was facing matter for the owner's liability?

Rav's answer flows from his foundational position established a few days earlier: *bor shechiyva alav torah l'havalo v'lo l'chavato* — the category of *bor* in which the Torah imposes liability is based on the *hevel*, the stagnant air within the pit, and not on the impact with the ground.
