The reasoning, though initially counterintuitive, is that the ground itself is *karka olam* — the earth has always been there and the pit owner did not create it. What the digger did create is the cavity, the absence of ground, and therefore the air within it. Accordingly, the pit owner bears responsibility specifically for the danger posed by that air. If the animal falls in with its face pointing upward, the argument is that it is breathing the air outside the pit rather than the hazardous *hevel* within it, and therefore the pit owner is absolved. One might push back that even a face-up animal receives some of the pit's *hevel*, but that is how Rav accounts for the *mishna*'s distinction.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel disagrees: *b'bor bein milifanav bein mil'acharav chayav* — if the animal fell into the well, it makes no difference whether it fell face-first or face-up; the owner is liable in either case. Shmuel holds *l'havalo v'chol shekein l'chavato* — while the Torah did indeed obligate the pit owner on account of the *hevel*, it certainly also obligated him for the impact against the ground. The pit was not a hole before he dug it. Even though the ground was always there, the walls of the pit and the opportunity to strike the ground at depth are all the pit owner's creation. Therefore, even a face-up fall still results in liability.

### Resolving Mishna

For Shmuel, then, how does the *mishna*'s exemption for *l'acharav* make sense? The *gemara* explains: *kigon shenitkal b'bor v'nafal l'achorei habor chutz labor* — the case of the *mishna* where the owner is exempt is not one where the animal fell backward into the pit, but rather one where the animal tripped over the edge of the pit and then fell *outside* of it — behind the pit, not into it. *Lifanav* means it fell into the pit; *l'acharav* means it fell to the ground outside the pit.

One might ask: even if it fell outside, shouldn't the pit owner still be liable? After all, the pit was the hazard that caused the trip, and this is analogous to the *gemara*'s case of *avno sakino umaso* — if one places a stone in the *reshus harabbim* and someone trips and hits the ground, liability attaches even though the ground itself caused the injury, not the stone. Why should this be different?

The answer is that in the *mishna*'s case, the tripping was caused not by the pit itself but by the person digging — the noise of the digging startled the animal. The digger, not the pit, is the proximate cause of the stumble. Unless the owner of the *bor* can be identified as the party who caused the damage, he is exempt. The ground outside is public ground, and the tripping was the digger's doing. In summary: according to Rav, the pit owner is exempt when the animal falls in face-up because *hevel* never reached it; according to Shmuel, it never matters which direction the animal fell *into* the pit, but if it fell *outside* the pit due to the digger's noise, the pit owner is fully exempt because a third party caused the stumble.

---

## Defending Rav

### Baraisa Challenge

The *gemara* now challenges Rav directly. A *baraisa* states: *b'vor bein milifanav bein mil'acharav chayav* — if the animal fell into the pit, the owner is liable whether face-first or backward. This appears to be an explicit contradiction of Rav's position. The *gemara* initially declares *tiyuvta d'Rav* — a refutation of Rav.

### Bor BiReshuto

Rav Chisda resolves this: *modeh Rav b'bor bireshuso d'chayav* — Rav concedes liability in the case of a pit dug within one's own property. The standard *bor* liability in the public domain exempts the owner from *chavata*, the impact, because the ground belongs to *reshus harabbim* and is *karka olam*. But if the pit is on the owner's own property — even if the public has a right of passage through it — then the ground at the bottom belongs to the pit owner as well. In that case, *mima nafshach*: whether the animal died from the *hevel*, that air is his; and whether it died from the impact, that impact is his too. The *baraisa*, then, is speaking of a *bor bireshuso*, and Rav's position for the standard public-domain pit remains intact.

### Rava's Flipover Case

Rava offers a second resolution. The *baraisa* is speaking of a case where the animal initially fell face-first — *nafal al apei* — and then flipped over mid-fall — *ve'ishapech* — and ultimately struck the ground back-first — *venafal al gabei*. In this scenario, the animal did inhale the *hevel* in the initial descent, and since that *hevel* contributed to the outcome, the pit owner bears full liability despite the fact that in the end the back struck the ground. It is a strained reading of the *baraisa*, which seemed to be making a categorical statement about the direction of the fall, but it does resolve the apparent contradiction on Rav's terms.

### Water Damage Theory

Rav Yosef proposes an entirely different reading of the *baraisa*. The *baraisa* is not discussing the pit owner's liability for damage to the ox at all. Rather, *hacha b'nizkei bor b'shor askinan* — we are speaking of the damage caused by the ox to the pit. Specifically, *she'hiv'ish meimav* — the animal fell in and fouled the water in the well. In that case, the direction in which the animal fell is entirely irrelevant, because what matters is that the owner's ox trespassed onto someone else's property — *reshus hanizak* — and spoiled the water there, which is a form of *shen varegel*. This is why the *baraisa* makes no distinction between *lifanav* and *l'acharav*: neither direction bears on the question of whether the ox fouled the water. The *baraisa* thus poses no challenge to Rav's ruling on pit liability for the animal's injury.

### Derech Nefilah

Rabbi Chanina teaches a *drasha* that affirmatively supports Rav. The verse states *v'nafal shama shor o chamor* — an ox or donkey "falls" into the pit. The *drasha* derives: *ad sheyipol derech nefilah* — the verse requires that the animal fall in the natural manner of falling, which is face-first. From this, the *halacha* is stated explicitly: *nafal lefanav mikol hakriyah chayav, l'acharav mikol hakriyah patur* — if the animal fell forward because of the sound of the digging, the owner is liable; if backward, exempt. Furthermore, the source adds *v'zeh v'zeh b'bor* — both cases are speaking of the animal falling into the pit itself. Rabbi Chanina's source thus directly confirms Rav's reading: the direction of the fall into the pit is determinative, and falling backward, even into the pit, exempts the owner.

---

## Stumbling Debate

### Digger's Causation

The *gemara* now turns to the deeper structural question embedded in the *mishna*. We have established that when an animal falls forward into the pit due to the sound of the digging, the pit owner is liable. But the *gemara* asks: *ve'amai? nema kol garam leh* — why? Cannot the owner of the pit argue that it was the sound of the digger that caused the animal to stumble, and that this should absolve him of liability?

This question highlights the dual function of a *bor* as a hazard: it both creates the stumbling condition — analogous to placing a stone in *reshus harabbim*, violating *lifnei iver lo titein michshol* — and it then inflicts the actual damage through impact. When these two functions are separated — when the stumble is caused by one party and the damage by another — what is the rule? Must the pit itself cause the stumble for the pit owner to be liable?

### Rabbi Noson Intro

Rav Shimi bar Ashi resolves this: *ha meni Rabbi Natan hi* — this *mishna* follows the position of Rabbi Natan. Two principles characterize Rabbi Natan's view. First, *ba'al habor heizeika avid* — the owner of the pit causes the damage, and that alone is sufficient for liability, even without having caused the stumble. Second — and this addresses the concern about the digger — *kol heicha d'lo efshar le'ishtalumi mei'hai mishtalem mei'hai*: wherever one cannot collect from the party that caused the stumble — because, for example, causing a stumble through sound is a *grama*, indirect causation, for which one is exempt — the full liability can be collected from the owner of the pit. These two principles together explain why the *mishna* holds the pit owner liable even though the digger caused the trip.

### Ox Pushes Ox

The *gemara* now identifies the *tannaic* source for Rabbi Natan's position. The *baraisa* states: *shor sheda'chaf et chaveiro labor* — an ox pushed a fellow ox into a pit. The *tanna kamma* rules *ba'al hashor chayav, ba'al habor patur* — the owner of the pushing ox is fully liable, and the owner of the pit is exempt. The reasoning of the *chachamim* is clear: liability for a *bor* requires that the *bor* itself create the hazard that caused the stumble. Since here an ox — not the pit — caused the other animal to fall in, the pit owner bears no responsibility. The pushing ox constitutes an act of *keren*, and the ox owner pays full damages. As a consequence of this view, in the case of our *mishna* — where the digger's sound caused the stumble — the pit owner would also be exempt according to the *chachamim*, and since the digger acted only as a *grama*, no one would be liable at all.

### Chachamim vs. Noson

Rabbi Natan disagrees: *ba'al hashor meshalem mechtza u'va'al habor meshalem mechtza* — the owner of the pushing ox and the owner of the pit split the payment equally. The pit inflicted the damage and is therefore jointly liable regardless of whether it caused the stumble. The fundamental dispute, then, is whether *bor* liability requires the pit to have generated the hazardous condition that caused the animal to fall in, or whether it is sufficient that the pit was the instrument of the actual damage. The *chachamim* focus on the stumble; Rabbi Natan focuses on the damage. It follows that in the case of the digger's sound, where the *grama* of the digging cannot be made to pay, Rabbi Natan imposes full liability on the pit owner.

---

## Liability Division

### 3/4 vs 1/2 Split

The *gemara* now notes an apparent internal contradiction in Rabbi Natan's rulings. In one *baraisa* he divides liability equally — the ox owner pays half and the pit owner pays half. But a second *baraisa* attributes three-quarters of the liability to the pit owner and only one quarter to the ox owner. How can Rabbi Natan maintain both positions?

### Tam vs Mu'ad

The *gemara* resolves this simply: *lo kashya, ha b'tam, ha b'mu'ad* — there is no contradiction, because the two *baraisos* address different cases. Since we are dealing with *keren*, the distinction between a *tam* — a non-forewarned ox, which pays only half-damages — and a *mu'ad* — a forewarned ox, which pays full damages — changes the arithmetic of the split. In the case of a *mu'ad*, where both parties bear full individual liability, the split is 50/50. In the case of a *tam*, the numbers work out differently, producing the 3/4 and 1/4 division. The *gemara* then unpacks the conceptual machinery that generates these figures.

### Conceptual Models

The key question is how we conceptualize joint liability. Rava explains that Rabbi Natan was a *dayan* who penetrated to *umka de'dina* — the very depth of the law. Rabbi Natan's view is *le'olam kasavar hai kulei heizeika avid v'hai kulei heizeika avid* — each party is considered to have caused 100% of the damage. Since the victim cannot collect double the value of his animal, the parties divide the payment — but they begin from full individual liability for each.

The alternative conceptual model would hold that each party caused only 50% of the damage. Under this model, in the case of a *tam*, the ox owner caused 50% and pays half of that — a quarter — and the pit owner pays his 50%, leaving the victim out one quarter. This yields a 50/25 split with a 25% loss to the victim, which does not match either *baraisa*.

### Ox's Complaint

Under the 100/100% model, in the case of a *mu'ad*, each party starts at full liability; the payment is divided 50/50. But in the case of a *tam*, the *gemara* explains the resulting 75/25 division through a compelling argument: *mishum d'amar lei ba'al hashor l'ba'al habor, shutafutai mai ahanei li* — the owner of the ox says to the owner of the pit: what benefit did this partnership bring me? Had my ox gored alone, as a *tam* I would owe only 50. Now that my ox and your pit both caused the full damage, why should I still pay 50? You are also in the equation. The argument is arithmetically persuasive. The pit owner, had he acted alone, would owe 100. The ox owner, had he acted alone, would owe 50. Their combined "debt" is 150 against a single payment of 100. A fair allocation proportionate to their individual liability yields 100/150 to the pit owner — that is, two-thirds of 100, or approximately 67 — but the *gemara* arrives at 75 and 25. The core logic is that the ox owner's 50% share gets divided in half once the pit owner enters the equation, so that the ox owner pays 25 and the pit owner pays 75.

This framework also clarifies the case of the digger: since each party holds 100% liability, and the digger cannot pay because his contribution was *grama*, the full obligation rests on the pit owner. You collect from the party from whom you *can* collect.

### Deductible Liability

The *gemara* then presents an alternative formulation: the pit owner bears full liability — 100% — and the ox owner's liability is calculated separately and is deductible from what the victim recovers from the pit owner. *Mai d'leisa lishalumi mei'hai mishtalamna mimach* — whatever I cannot collect from the ox owner, I collect from you. As *Tosafos* notes, this language suggests not a 50/50 conceptual split but rather that the pit bears 100% liability and the ox's share — half of 50% for a *tam*, i.e., 25% — is deducted, leaving 75% owed by the pit owner. Anything that cannot be collected from the ox owner falls entirely on the pit. This is the meaning of *kol heicha d'leika le'shalumi mei'hai mishtalama mimach*, and it fully explains why the *mishna*'s pit owner pays even when the stumble was caused by the digger.

---

## Stone at Pit Edge

### Rock Case

Rava introduces a new scenario five lines from the bottom of the page: *hiniach even al pi habor, ba shor v'niska bo v'nafal b'abor* — someone placed a stone at the entrance of a pit, an ox came, tripped on the stone, and fell into the pit. The question is how liability is allocated between the owner of the stone and the owner of the pit. Rava states that this case falls within the debate of Rabbi Natan and the *rabbanim*: the *rabbanim* would hold the stone owner fully liable as the one who caused the stumble, and Rabbi Natan would split it between stone and pit.

### Stone's Dependency

The *gemara* objects: *peshita* — isn't this obvious? Isn't the stone analogous to the ox that pushed the other ox into the pit? The *gemara* responds: no, one might have thought that this case is categorically different. In the ox-pushes-ox scenario, the pit owner can say to the ox owner: *ilav bira didi, tora didach hava katil lei* — even without my pit, your ox would have killed; the ox was goring on its own and the pit was incidental. That is why both the *rabbanim* and Rabbi Natan apply liability to the ox owner. But in the stone case, the stone owner might argue the reverse.

### Pit Owner Defense

The owner of the stone can say to the owner of the pit: *ilav bura didach, avna didi mai havai avda* — had it not been for your pit, my stone would have done nothing at all. *I havai miskel bah, havai nafal v'ka'i* — even if the animal tripped on my stone, had there been no pit, it would simply have fallen and gotten back up. My stone, standing alone, caused no lasting damage. On this reasoning, the stone owner might be completely exempt, and perhaps the *rabbanim* would hold both parties exempt while Rabbi Natan would — as always — impose liability on the pit for the damage it caused.

### Both Necessary

The *gemara* rejects this escape: *ka mashma lan* — the case teaches us that this reasoning does not succeed. The counter-argument is symmetrical: *ilav even, lo havai nafal l'bira* — had it not been for the stone, the animal would never have fallen into the pit. Yes, the stone needed the pit to cause injury, but equally, the pit needed the stone to cause the stumble. Both parties were necessary causes, and therefore the debate of Rabbi Natan and the *rabbanim* applies here just as it does in the ox case. For Rabbi Natan, the two split liability; for the *rabbanim*, the stone owner bears full liability as the cause of the stumble, even though without the pit no damage would have occurred.

---

## Multiple Actors

### Sanctified Ox Case

At the top of 53b the *gemara* introduces a new scenario involving *pesulei hamukdashin* — animals consecrated for sacrifice that were later disqualified and thus retain a degree of sanctity while being permitted for ordinary use. A gloss in the text, attributed to Rav Hai Gaon in *Halachos Gedolos*, clarifies that the specific case here involves a firstborn ox with a blemish that was never redeemed. Such an animal retains sufficient sanctity that its owner falls outside the category of *shor rei'eihu* — "the ox of his fellow" — the phrase the Torah uses to define the subject of *keren* liability. Accordingly, the owner of such an ox is exempt from payment when it causes damage.

The case: this sanctified-but-disqualified ox and a normal ox jointly gore another animal. Abaye rules that the owner of the normal ox pays *chatzi nezek* — half damages. Ravina rules *revia nezek* — a quarter.

### Tam/Mu'ad Explanation

One way to understand this dispute is that both Abaye and Ravina are discussing a *tam* and arguing about whether the case follows the *rabbanim* or Rabbi Natan. According to Rabbi Natan's 100/100% model: the exempt ox did 100% and cannot be made to pay; the normal ox did 100% and, being a *tam*, pays half — that is, 50% of the full value. According to the *rabbanim*'s 50/50% model: each ox caused half the damage, and the normal *tam* ox pays half of its half — a quarter — with the remaining quarter unrecoverable. Thus Abaye's ruling of half reflects Rabbi Natan's model and Ravina's ruling of a quarter reflects the *rabbanim*'s model.

### Rabbanim Explanation

Alternatively, both Abaye and Ravina follow the *rabbanim*, and the difference between them is whether the normal ox is a *mu'ad* or a *tam*. Under the *rabbanim*'s 50/50 model: if it is a *mu'ad*, the normal ox caused 50% of the damage and pays its full 50% — hence Abaye's *chatzi nezek*. If it is a *tam*, the normal ox caused 50% but pays only half of that — hence Ravina's *revia nezek*. A third formulation in the *gemara* holds that both follow Rabbi Natan's 100/100% model and the difference is simply *mu'ad* vs. *tam*: for a *mu'ad* the normal ox pays 100%; for a *tam*, 50%.

### Rava's Example

Rava then presents a comprehensive illustration — an ox and a person who together push a victim into a pit — that draws all these threads together. *Tosafos* notes that the human must have acted *shelo b'kavana*, without intent, because a person acting intentionally would be the dominant cause and the other parties would be treated as instruments of his action, as in the case of someone who throws another's *tallis* into a fire and uses the fire as his instrument. Assuming unintentional action and following Rabbi Natan's 100/100% model, all three parties — ox, person, and pit — share liability for the full damage.

### Four Categories

Rava maps liability across four payment categories. For *nezek* — the straightforward damage payment — all three are liable, and it divides among them equally under Rabbi Natan's framework. For the four additional payments imposed when a human is injured — *tza'ar, rippui, shevet, boshet* — and similarly for *demei veladot* in cases of miscarriage, only the human is liable; the ox and the pit owner are exempt, as the Torah assigns these categories exclusively to human actors. Since each party holds 100% liability, the human pays full for these categories. For *kofer* — the ransom payment when an ox kills a person — and for the *shloshim* of an *eved* when a slave is killed, only the ox is liable, as the Torah imposes *kofer* solely on the *ba'al hashor* and never on a person who causes a death or on a pit. Accordingly, the ox's owner pays full for these. For *kelim* — vessels broken in the incident — the human and the ox are liable but the pit owner is exempt, as the Torah explicitly exempts a pit from liability for vessels. Therefore, the human and ox divide this payment between them.

One of the entries in Rava's table specifies an ox of *pesulei hamukdashin* in connection with *kelim*, noting that the pit owner is exempt there as well. This prompts the *gemara* to examine the source of the pit's exemption regarding *pesulei hamukdashin* — which leads to the final section.

---

## Invalid Sacrifices

### Exemption Question

Rava's neat table assumes that the pit owner is exempt when an ox of *pesulei hamukdashin* falls into the pit. But the *gemara* notes that Rava himself had earlier raised this as an open question — *iba'i Rava*, Rava asked — *shor pesulei hamukdashin shenafal l'bor mahu*: if a disqualified consecrated animal falls into a pit, what is the law? If this was Rava's own unresolved question, how could he take the exemption for granted in his illustrative table?

The *gemara* answers: *batar d'ba'i, hadar pashtei* — after raising the question, he subsequently resolved it. The table reflects Rava's concluded position: the pit owner is indeed exempt when an animal of *pesulei hamukdashin* falls in and dies.

### V'Hameit Meaning

The substantive question Rava had raised was the proper interpretation of the verse *v'hameit yihyeh lo* — "and the dead animal shall be his" — which appears in the Torah's passage about pit liability. Two readings are possible. The first: *b'mi shehameishehameit shelo*, the verse speaks of a case where the dead body has some usable value; *yatza zu she'ein hameit shelo* — excluded is a case where the dead body belongs to no one or cannot be used, as with a consecrated animal that cannot be redeemed after death and whose carcass has no permitted utility. On this reading, where there is no usable carcass, the pit owner is categorically exempt. The second reading: *b'alim metaplin b'neveilah hu d'ata* — the verse is teaching the rule discussed earlier in the tractate, that it is the original owner of the dead animal who retains the carcass and the pit owner pays only the depreciation. On this reading, the verse says nothing about an exemption for *pesulei hamukdashin*.

### Categorical Exemptions

Having resolved his question in favor of the first reading — an exemption for *pesulei hamukdashin* by the *bor* — the *gemara* now asks: where does the *b'alim metaplin b'neveilah* principle come from, if not from this verse? The answer: *nafkah lei mi'v'hameit yihyeh lo d'shor* — the same phrase appears in the context of one ox goring another, and *there* it teaches the principle of *b'alim metaplin b'neveilah*. The verse appears twice, and each instance teaches a different rule.

### Why Not Ox

The *gemara* then asks why we not reverse the assignments — let the verse by the *bor* teach *b'alim metaplin b'neveilah* and the verse by the *shor* teach the exemption for *pesulei hamukdashin*. The *gemara* responds: *mistabra p'tor gabei bor, ho'il u'patar bo et hakelim* — it is more logical to locate the exemption for *pesulei hamukdashin* with the *bor*, because the *bor* already has other categorical exemptions built into it. The pit is exempt from liability for *kelim* and in some contexts for human death as well. It is therefore fitting to add the exemption for *pesulei hamukdashin* to the *bor*'s list of categorical exemptions.

The *gemara* considers one final objection: *adderaba, p'tor gabei shor shekein patar bo chatzi* — on the contrary, assign the exemption to the *shor*, since the *shor* already exhibits leniency by paying only half-damages as a *tam*. The *gemara* rejects this: *kulei nezek mi lo ashkachan* — we never find that an ox is completely exempt from a whole category of objects. By contrast, we do find that a *bor* is categorically exempt from *kelim*. The *bor*, not the *shor*, is the category that features total exemptions for specific types of damage, and therefore it is the *bor* that carries the exemption for *pesulei hamukdashin*.

### Framework Conclusion

With this resolved, Rava's illustrative table is fully vindicated. The framework in which ox, person, and pit each carry 100% liability under Rabbi Natan's model allows the *gemara* to map which party pays for which category: *nezek* is divided three ways, the four human payments fall entirely on the human, *kofer* falls entirely on the ox, and *kelim* — and the analogous case of *pesulei hamukdashin* — fall entirely on the human and the ox, with the pit categorically exempt. Whatever cannot be collected from one party due to categorical exemption or inability to pay is recovered in full from those who remain liable.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 54

## Vessel Exemption

### Mishna Overview

The daf opens by returning to a principle that has been invoked since the beginning of the masechta but never fully analyzed: the exemption of a *bor* from liability for *keilim* damaged within it. The *mishna* states that if an ox and vessels fell into a well — *nafal l'tocho shor ve-kelav venishbaru* — the owner of the well is liable for the ox but exempt for the broken vessels. The *gemara* immediately notes that our *mishna* follows the *rabbanan* and not Rabbi Yehuda: *matnisin d'lo k'Rebbi Yehuda*. A *braita* specifies the point of dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds the owner of the well liable for damage to *keilim* as well — *Rebbi Yehuda mechayev al nizkei kelim ba-bor*.

### Hermeneutics

What is the *rabbanan*'s reasoning? The verse states *ve-nafal shammah shor o chamor* — an ox or a donkey falls therein. The *rabbanan* apply the hermeneutical principle: *shor v'lo adam, chamor v'lo kelim* — "ox" (excluding a person) and "donkey" (excluding vessels). Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, reads the word *o* — "or" — as coming to include *keilim*: *o l'rabot et ha-keilim*. In other words, the disjunctive "or" in the verse is not merely distinguishing between ox and donkey, but extending liability to things carried by the animal, namely vessels.

It is worth noting that Rabbi Yehuda's resistance to categorical exemptions in the *arba avot nezikin* is a broader pattern: in the next chapter on *esh*, he similarly rejects the exemption for *tamun* — objects that were concealed and thus not exposed — a position parallel to his rejection here of the *keilim* exemption.

The *rabbanan* respond that the word *o* is not available to perform that inclusion, because *o* is necessary for a different purpose: *l'chaleik* — to establish that the two animals, ox and donkey, are treated as independent cases. You need not have both an ox and a donkey fall in to incur liability; either one suffices. Rabbi Yehuda counters that this function could have been served by the word *ve-nafal* alone — written in the singular, the verse implies each animal independently — and so the *o* is free to include *keilim*. The *rabbanan* respond that *ve-nafal* written in the singular can nonetheless refer to multiple objects falling simultaneously, and Rashi provides the support: *kemo ve-ata Betzalel v'Oholiav... u-va ha-ot v'ha-mofet* — instances where the Torah uses a singular verb with multiple subjects. Therefore, without the word *o*, we would not know to read the verse disjunctively, and *o* is indispensable for that purpose, leaving nothing to include *keilim*.

### Rationale

Before proceeding to the *gemara*'s deeper analysis, it is worth pausing on the underlying logic of the *keilim* exemption. The exemption for *adam* — a person who falls into the well and dies — is in some ways not even a special *halakha* of *bor*. As Tosafot has noted from early in the masechta, there is a fundamental principle that civil payments are not assessed for the death of a human being; the verse *ha-meit yihyeh lo* speaks of property, not persons. Rabbi Yehuda does not dispute this aspect of the law.

The more genuinely puzzling exemption is that for *keilim*. One way to understand it is through a degree of causal indirectness: the well constitutes a direct hazard to anything moving autonomously through its vicinity — animals, people — but it is only an indirect hazard to vessels, which do not come to the well on their own; they must be brought there by an animal. The owner of the well has created a *michshol* for moving beings; the *keilim* are, so to speak, one step removed from the hazard. This is not to say there is some independent reason to be *chayav* that must be overcome — the Torah's exemption speaks for itself — but this framing at least gives some conceptual texture to why the *rabbanan* might have read the verse as excluding *keilim*.

### Klal u'Prat

At the top of 54a, the *gemara* raises a prior question: before we even get to the debate over *keilim*, how do we know that the *bor* creates liability for anything beyond an ox and a donkey? One might read the verse as a *klal u'prat* — *ve-nafal* as a general term, *shor v'chamor* as the specific — and conclude: *ein ba-klal ela mah she-ba-prat*, only an ox and a donkey.

The *gemara* answers: *ba'al ha-bor yeshalem* — "the owner of the well shall pay" — constitutes a *chazarah v'chalal*, a return to the general. We thus have a *klal u'prat u'klal*: a general, a specific, and then a general again. The rule for such a hermeneutical structure is *klal u'prat u'klal ee ata dan ela k'ein ha-prat* — you include anything similar to the specific. Since the specific (*shor v'chamor*) is *ba'alei chayim* — living creatures — we include all living animals. This in itself explains the exclusion of *keilim* through a more familiar hermeneutical path, without requiring the technical readings of *shor v'lo adam, chamor v'lo kelim*.

But the *gemara* presses further: even within the *klal u'prat u'klal* framework, should we not limit liability to animals whose carcass conveys *tumah* by touching and carrying — *davar she-neveilatah metama b'maga u-v'masa* — since that is what *shor v'chamor* share? This would exclude birds, since the carcass of a bird does not convey *tumah* in the same way. The *gemara* then counters: if so, why write both *shor* and *chamor*? Had the Torah written only *shor*, one might have thought liability applies only to animals fit for sacrifice; had it written only *chamor*, one might have limited it to animals that have the sanctity of a firstborn (*kadosh bivchora*). The need to write both *shor* and *chamor* tells us we are not dealing with such narrow categories. Yet even granting this, birds remain potentially excluded. The *gemara* therefore concludes that the broadening phrase is *ha-meit yihyeh lo* — "the dead animal shall be his" — which includes any creature that can die. That is the foundational basis for liability.

### Breaking = Death

This leads to a pointed question: if *ha-meit yihyeh lo* is the ultimate source of liability — covering everything that dies — why did the *rabbanan* need a special *derashah* to exclude *keilim*? And why did Rabbi Yehuda need the word *o* to include them? *Keilim* do not die. They should be categorically excluded from *ha-meit yihyeh lo* without any additional derivation, and there would then be nothing for the word *o* to include.

The *gemara* answers: *shvirasam zo hi misasam* — the breaking of vessels is considered, in this legal framework, equivalent to their death. And this is consistent with what Rashi explains throughout: the exclusion of *shor v'lo adam* applies only to *mita* — death — since the operative phrase is *ha-meit yihyeh lo*. For injury to a person, one remains *chayav*, as injury is not covered by that exclusion. Vessels, however, are excluded even for damage short of total destruction, because any damage to a *keli* is conceptually its *mita*. Hence *keilim* fall within the scope of *ha-meit yihyeh lo* and do require active exclusion by the *rabbanan* and active inclusion by Rabbi Yehuda.

### Hevel Theory

A further complication arises from the position of Rav, who holds that the *bor* obligation established by the Torah is *l'hevelo v'lo l'chavato* — for the noxious air (*hevel*) within the well, not for the physical impact of striking the ground (*chavata*). According to Rav, the real hazard is inhalation of the bad air. But how could *keilim* be harmed by *hevel*? One cannot speak of a vessel inhaling toxic air. If *keilim* are simply not susceptible to *hevel*, they would have been automatically excluded without any need for a *derashah*, and there would have been nothing for Rabbi Yehuda's *o* to include.

The *gemara* answers: *b'chadti d'mifka'ei mehavla* — new, freshly-made vessels can actually shatter from the concentrated *hevel* within a deep well. New vessels, not yet hardened by use or time, are susceptible to bursting when exposed to the compressed noxious air. This is surprising — one might have expected old vessels to be more fragile — but the *gemara* apparently understands that newly fired pottery, for instance, retains a kind of internal sensitivity before it has fully set. This explains why the *keilim* exemption was necessary even according to Rav: new vessels genuinely could be affected by *hevel*, so without the *derashah* of *chamor v'lo keilim*, one might have been *chayav* for them.

### General Verse

The *gemara* now determines which verse provides the comprehensive basis for liability. One candidate is *ha-meit yihyeh lo*, but Rava's teaching forecloses this: *shor psulei ha-mukdashin she-nafal l'bor pattur*, an animal that was consecrated as a sacrifice, became blemished, was redeemed, but whose carcass may not be used by the owner — for such an animal the owner of the *bor* is exempt, because *ha-meit yihyeh lo* applies only *l'mi she-ha-meit shelo*, where the carcass belongs to the owner. If *ha-meit yihyeh lo* is reserved for Rava's ruling, what is the source for the general principle of broad liability?

The answer is *kesef yashiv liv'alav* — "he shall pay money to its owners" — which is read inclusively: *l'rabot kol d'isa ba'olam*, to include anything in the world that has owners. This general verse establishes the scope of liability, and then *shor v'lo adam, chamor v'lo keilim* carves out the exemptions. For Rabbi Yehuda, the word *o* then restores *keilim* to liability, but it remains unclear what work the word *chamor* itself is doing in his reading. The *gemara* acknowledges the difficulty by raising a parallel: the word *seh* in the context of *aveidah* — lost property — appears similarly redundant given the phrase *al kol aveidah*. The *gemara* concludes: *kashya* — both difficulties stand unresolved.

---

## Animal Intelligence

### Mishna Case

The *mishna* teaches a seemingly peculiar rule: *nafal l'tocho shor cheresh shoteh v'katan chayav* — if a *cheresh* (deaf-mute), *shoteh* (imbecile), or *katan* (minor) ox fell in, the owner of the *bor* is liable. The *gemara* immediately challenges the formulation: what exactly is a "*shor cheresh shoteh v'katan*"?

### The Paradox

If it means an ox *owned by* a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan*, the *gemara* asks: why would anyone think you would be *patur* for damaging the property of such owners? Their property is no less protected. And more startlingly, the *gemara* observes, does this imply that if the ox belonged to a person of full capacity — *shor shel pikeach* — you would be *exempt*? That seems counterintuitive to the point of being absurd.

### Animal Not Owner

Rabbi Yochanan therefore explains: *shor she-hu cheresh, shor she-hu shoteh, shor she-hu katan* — the *mishna* is speaking not about who owns the ox, but about the ox itself, which displays the behavioral characteristics associated with a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan*. The animal itself is, in some sense, deficient in its capacity to perceive and navigate its environment.

### Braita Contradiction

This explanation, however, immediately generates a difficulty from a *braita*: *nafal l'tocho bar da'at pattur* — if an intelligent being fell in, you are exempt. If *bar da'at* describes the animal itself, this would mean that an ox possessing full perception is *patur*. That is indeed striking: one of the primary cases of *bor* liability — an animal falling in — would be exempt when the animal is a fully functioning creature in daylight.

### Bar Da'at

The *gemara* offers one resolution: *bar da'at* in the *braita* simply means a human being — *min bar da'at*, a species characterized by intelligence — and thus the *braita* is merely restating the established *halakha* that the owner of the *bor* is exempt for the death of a person who falls in. The term is categorical, not descriptive of the individual's mental state. This is confirmed by the verse *shor v'lo adam ketiv* — the exclusion of persons from *bor* liability is absolute, not dependent on whether any given person happened to be alert or mentally competent.

### Rava Position

Rava, however, accepts the more radical reading directly. He rules: *shor ve-hu cheresh, shor ve-hu shoteh, shor ve-hu katan davka* — the *mishna* is precise: you are *chayav* only for an ox that was itself a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan*. But if the ox is a *pikeach* — a fully aware animal — you are *patur*. The reasoning is *d'ba'ei lei ayyunei u-mazal* — a normal, perceptive animal in an exposed, visible well should have seen the hazard and avoided it. The well was not, in legal terms, a hazard to such an animal. It only constitutes a genuine hazard to animals that lack the perceptual or developmental capacity to recognize and sidestep the danger.

This is a striking *gemara*. The owner of the *bor* creates a public hazard, and yet his liability for the paradigmatic case — a normal animal in daylight — is exempt. The law functions only at the edges: animals that cannot see, cannot perceive, or have not reached maturity are the ones whose fate is attributed to the *bor*.

### Examples

The *gemara* confirms this with a *braita*: *shor cheresh shoteh v'katan chayav* — plus a blind animal (*suma*) or one traveling at night — these are cases of *chiyuv*. But a *pikeach* traveling in the daytime — *patur*. These cases where the animal's natural capacities would have been adequate to detect and avoid an exposed well yield exemption.

### Rambam

The Rambam, apparently troubled by the growing narrowness of liability, limits the exemption to the case of death (*mita*). His reasoning: *mipnei she'derech ha-behema lirot velasur min ha-michsholim* — it is the nature of a normal animal to see and avoid obstacles. Only for death — where we presume the animal walked directly to its end despite full capacity to detect the danger — would we say the *bor* was insufficient a hazard to hold the owner accountable. But if the animal was merely injured, even a *pikeach* animal in daylight can be injured by a *bor*, and the owner remains liable: *ve'im huzak bah adam o ha-behema ha-pikchit chayav nezek shalem*. This also resolves the question about persons: an intelligent adult person injured by the *bor* — the owner is *chayav* for that injury, since injury does not require the same degree of reckless inattention as death would. The Rambam thus preserves a meaningful scope of liability: all injuries, and deaths of animals that were incapacitated in some way, while exempting only the death of a fully perceptive animal in conditions where it plainly should have seen the danger.

---

## All Animals

### All Animals Principle

The next *mishna* opens with the inclusive declaration: *echad shor ve'echad kol behema* — not only an ox but all animals are subject to the laws of the *bor*, as well as to *hafrashat Har Sinai*, *tashlumei kefel*, *hashavat aveidah*, *perika*, *chasimah*, *kilayim*, and *shabbat*. Wild animals (*chaya*) and birds (*of*) are included as well. One might have expected that wherever the Torah specifies *shor v'chamor*, the law is limited to those two species. The *mishna* teaches otherwise.

The *mishna* acknowledges the question directly: *im ken lama ne'emar shor v'chamor?* — if so, why does the Torah say "ox and donkey" in these contexts? The answer: *shediber ha-katuv be-hoveh* — the Torah speaks of common cases. The specification of ox and donkey is descriptive, not restrictive.

This is, however, in evident tension with the earlier *gemara*, which read *shor v'lo adam, chamor v'lo keilim* as active exclusions derived from those very words. The *mishna* here appears to treat the same words as merely illustrative. The *gemara* will need to work out how these two approaches coexist.

### Multiple Sources

The *gemara* now traces the individual sources for inclusion across the various laws. For the *bor*: *kesef yashiv liv'alav ketiv kol d'it lei be'alim* — "he shall pay money to its owners" is the general verse, as established at the end of the previous *sugya*, and it encompasses any creature or object with an owner.

For *hafrashat Har Sinai*: the verse says *im behema im ish lo yichyeh* — the word *behema* in its broad sense includes wild animals, and *im* serves to include birds. For *kilayim* in the sense of crossbreeding: *behemtecha lo tarbi'a kilayim* — the generic *behemtecha* encompasses all animals. For *kefel*, the double payment: *al kol devar pesha* — all matters of transgression — is naturally inclusive, and requires no special derivation for animals since the verse does not limit itself to living creatures at all. Similarly, *hashavat aveidah*: *lechol aveidat achicha* — all lost property of your fellow — is broadly inclusive, even beyond living creatures.

### Shabbat Source

For *perika* (unloading a collapsing animal) and *chasimah* (muzzling): the *gemara* derives these through a *gezerah shavah* from *shabbat*. *Perika* is stated with the word *chamor* — *ki tir'eh chamor achicha rovetz tachat mas'o* — and is linked to *shabbat* where *chamor* is shown to include all animals. *Chasimah* uses the word *shor* — *lo tachsom shor bedisho* — and is likewise linked to *shabbat* where *shor* includes all animals. Once both *shor* and *chamor* in the context of *shabbat* are read broadly, the same broadening applies wherever those words appear throughout the Torah.

### Klal u'Prat 2

The source for this broad reading in the laws of *shabbat* itself comes from Rabbi Yose in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, who notes the contrast between the two sets of the *Aseres Ha-Dibros*. The first *dibros* mention *avdecha va'amatecha u'vehemtecha* — your servant, maidservant, and animal (general). The second *dibros* mention *ve-shorecha va'chamorecha ve-chol behemtecha* — your ox, your donkey, and all your animals (both specific and more broadly general). The question then arises: *vehalo shor v'chamor bi-khlal kol behema hayu* — ox and donkey were already included within "all your animals." Why were they singled out? The answer: *lomar lach mah shor v'chamor ha'amur kan chaya ve'of kayotzei vahen* — to teach that wherever the Torah specifies ox and donkey, we should understand it as including all living creatures, just as it does here.

But can we read the two *dibros* together as a *klal u'prat u'klal*? The *gemara* explores this possibility: *behema* of the first *dibros* as a *klal*, *shor v'chamor* of the second as a *prat*, and *ve-chol behemtecha* of the second as a return to the *klal*. The rule of *klal u'prat u'klal* would then extend liability to all creatures similar to the *prat*. The *gemara* again raises the challenge: perhaps limit it only to animals whose carcass conveys *tumah* — *davar she-nevilatam metame be-maga u-ve-masa* — which would exclude birds. And the response mirrors the earlier discussion: had the Torah written only *shor*, one might have limited rest on *shabbat* to animals eligible for sacrifice; had it written only *chamor*, one might have limited it to animals sanctified as firstborns. The pairing of *shor v'chamor* prevents both over-restrictions. Yet even so, birds might remain excluded under a *klal u'prat u'klal* analysis.

### Kol Inclusive

The resolution lies in the phrase *ve-chol behemtecha* itself — specifically, the word *ve-chol*. Tosafot draws the distinction: *ba-kol* (as in the phrase used at *maasar sheni*) functions as a normal *klal*, while *ve-chol* — with the preceding *vav* — functions as a *ribuy*, an affirmatively inclusive term. This is the better reading of the *gemara*'s point: the *ve-chol* was not needed, since the *dibros rishonot* had already said *u'vehemtecha*; the extra *ve-chol* in the *dibros acharonot* is thus a *ribuy*, explicitly extending the category beyond what a *klal u'prat u'klal* would yield, to include birds as well.

The *gemara* puts it plainly: had the Torah wished merely to include domesticated and wild animals, it could have written *u'vehemtecha*, as in the first *dibros*. The choice of *ve-chol behemtecha* in the second *dibros* is a deliberate expansion. *Shema minah ribuyah* — learn from this that it is an inclusive formulation.

### Shor Chamor Link

Given that *ve-chol behemtecha* already does the work of including all animals, the *gemara* asks: what then is the purpose of specifying *shor v'chamor* in the second *dibros*, since they were already included? The answer: each word carries a function beyond the *shabbat* context itself. *Shor* is specified in order to link the *shabbat* ruling to *chasimah* elsewhere in the Torah — teaching that "ox" in *lo tachsom shor bedisho* is not limited to an ox. *Chamor* is specified to link to *perika* — the obligation to unload a collapsing donkey is not limited to donkeys. *U'vehemtecha* of the *dibros rishonot* is specified to link to *kilayim* — the prohibition of crossbreeding applies not only to domesticated animals but to *chaya* and *of* as well. In each case, the specification enables a *gezerah shavah* to the corresponding law elsewhere, extending inclusion.

### Human Inclusion

This raises a sharp question: if *shabbat* links all the laws to all animals, and human beings are also included in the *shabbat* prohibition — indeed, *shabbat* says *lema'an yanuach avdecha va'amatecha ka-mocha*, and servants and laborers are explicitly mentioned alongside animals — then should human beings also be included in *kilayim*? Should it be forbidden for a person to plow together with an animal, since the same inclusionary logic that extends animal laws to all species should extend them to humans? The *mishna*, in fact, explicitly states the opposite: *adam mutar im kulam lachrosh v'limshoch* — a person may plow alongside any animal.

### Rav Pappa

Rav Papa resolves this by citing Rav Acha bar Yaakov of Pappuna. The verse in *shabbat* states: *lema'an yanuach avdecha va'amatecha ka-mocha* — "so that your servant and maidservant may rest like you." Rav Acha bar Yaakov reads this precisely: *le'hanacha hikishtiv v'lo l'davar acher* — the Torah linked human beings to animals exclusively for the purpose of rest (*hanacha*). For all other purposes — *kilayim*, and by extension the other laws of the *mishna* — human beings remain categorically distinct from animals. The inclusion of human laborers in *shabbat* does not draw them into the broader framework of animal-related prohibitions.

---

## Tablets & Tet

### Tov Question

A striking *aggadic* passage follows, occasioned — as Tosafot notes — by the *gemara*'s discussion of the two versions of the *Aseres Ha-Dibros*. There is indeed a second set of *luchos*, and the *shivre luchos* carries its own significance. The specific question posed here: *mipnei ma ba-dibros ha-rishonos lo ne'emar bahem tov u-va-dibros ha-acharonos ne'emar bahem tov*? Why does the word *tov* not appear in the first *dibros*, while it does appear in the second? The reference is to *Kibbud Av Va'em*, which in the second *dibros* contains the phrase *lema'an yetav lach*, but not in the first.

### Dismissal

Rabbi Chanina's response to the questioner is itself memorable. Rather than answering, he says: before you ask me *why* it says *tov* in one place and not the other, ask me *whether* it says *tov* in the first *dibros* at all — *she'eini yodea im ne'emar bahem tov im lav*. I don't even know that! The point is not feigned ignorance but principled demarcation: this is *aggadata*, and that is not my field. Go to Rabbi Tanchum ben Chanilai — *she'ragil etzel Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, she'hayah baki ba'aggadah* — who spent time with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and is expert in *aggada*. The exchange is the mirror image of the famous case where Rabbi Akiva offered an *aggadic* explanation and was told to return to *Nega'im ve'Ohalos* — his proper domain is *halakha*, not *aggada*. Here the dynamic is reversed: a *halachic* authority declines to venture into *aggada* and directs the questioner to a specialist.

### Breaking Tablets

The questioner proceeds to Rabbi Tanchum ben Chanilai, who reports not his own explanation but one he heard from Shmuel bar Nachum — described as a relative of Rav Acha the son of Rabbi Chanina, though the precise relationship is uncertain in the *gemara*'s transmission. The explanation: *ho'il ve-sofan lishhtaber* — since the first tablets were destined to be broken, it would not have been fitting for the word *tov* — "good" — to appear in them. The *gemara* challenges: *ve-chi mishhtaber mai havi?* So they were broken — what of it? Many momentous things were contained in the first tablets, including *Anochi Hashem Elokecha*, and their breakage was of cosmic significance.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi explains the concern: *chas ve-shalom paskah tovah mi-Yisrael* — God forbid that *tov* — goodness — should have been severed from Israel. The breakage of the other commandments, however tragic, was one thing. But had the word *tov* itself broken, it would have symbolized symbolically that good had ceased among Israel. That symbolic rupture would have been too severe a portent. So *tov* was held back from the first tablets, preserved for the second ones, where it could endure unbroken.

### Tet in Dreams

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi then teaches a related teaching: *ha-ro'eh tes be-chalomo siman yafeh lo* — one who sees the letter *tet* in a dream has a favorable omen. The *gemara* asks: is this simply because *tet* appears in the word *tov*? But surely there are many words beginning with *tet* that carry negative connotations — *ve-tet'ei'ah be-matatei ha-shmad* — "I will sweep them with the broom of destruction" — or *tum'atah be-shuleiha* — her defilement is on her skirt — both *pesukim* associated with destruction and *churban*. The *gemara* clarifies: seeing a single *tet* in a dream refers to the word *tov*, specifically; these other verses contain multiple instances of *tet*, which reads differently.

### First Tet

The deeper reason for the association: *ho'il u-fatach bo ha-katuv le-tovah techilah* — the *tet* first appears in the Torah in a context of goodness. From the very beginning of *Bereishit* until *vayar Elokim es ha'or ki tov* — "and God saw the light, that it was good" — the letter *tet* does not appear in the Torah at all. Its inaugural appearance is in the word *tov*. Therefore, the letter *tet* is fundamentally associated with goodness; when it appears in a dream, the omen is favorable regardless of other possible associations.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi also teaches a final teaching: *ha-ro'eh hesped be-chalomo, chasu alav min ha-shamayim u-fduhu* — one who sees a eulogy in a dream was subject to a heavenly decree that was then commuted through divine compassion. This applies, according to Rashi, specifically when the word is seen written, as if on a page — *be-chtava*. The daf concludes here, with the parameters of *kilayim* to be resumed on the following day.
