The disagreement between Rabba and Rav Yosef may thus be much narrower than it first appears — not whether there is any *hana'ah*, but whether the *hana'ah* is financially significant enough to trigger the status of *shomer sachar*.

### Rav Yosef: Obligation

The *Gemara* records a second explanation for Rav Yosef's position, attributed to some authorities — though certain *acharonim* note that this version does not appear in parallel *sugyot* and may have been added by the Geonim. According to this reading, *keivan d'Rachmana shabdei b'al karchai* — because God has obligated him against his will to perform this *mitzvah*, he is in effect contractually bound by the Torah itself. That compelled obligation places him in a different category from a person who voluntarily undertakes a favor, and therefore makes him more like a *shomer sachar*.

### Pnei Yehoshua

The Pnei Yehoshua offers yet another approach, directly addressing the point that intrinsic religious reward can constitute *hana'ah* for halachic purposes. Because God will compensate a person for performing *mitzvot*, the *shomer aveidah* has in some sense "been paid" for his efforts — and that reward is sufficient to classify him as a *shomer sachar*. Other *acharonim* frame this more conceptually: having accepted — even involuntarily — the terms of a *mitzvah* obligation creates a qualitatively different level of responsibility and involvement with the object than a freely chosen act of kindness. The contrast they draw is instructive: a *shomer chinam* is doing another person a favor; a *shomer sachar* is doing a professional job; and a *shoel* — the borrower, who has the highest liability — is receiving the favor himself. The *shomer aveidah*, by this logic, more closely resembles the engaged professional than the gratuitous volunteer.

---

## Tosefta Challenge

### Proof from Tosefta

Rav Yosef now challenges Rabba directly from a *Tosefta*. The *Tosefta* teaches: *hechezira limkom sheyirena* — if the *shomer aveidah* returned the lost object to a place where its owner will come across it and find it, *eino chayav letapel bah* — he has no further obligation to be involved with it. But if *nigneva o avda* — if it was subsequently stolen or lost — *chayav be-achrayuta* — he bears responsibility to pay.

Rav Yosef reads this as proof for his position. A *shomer chinam* is exempt from paying if an object is stolen or lost — that is precisely one of the defining features of the *shomer chinam*'s reduced liability. If the *shomer aveidah* is liable when the returned object is stolen or lost, this suggests he has the higher liability of a *shomer sachar*.

Rabba, however, defends himself. The liability in the *Tosefta*, he argues, is not because the *shomer aveidah* is generally a *shomer sachar*. Rather, the case is one where the *shomer* returned the object to an unusual location — outside the normal context of *shmira*. That act of displacement is itself a form of *peshia*, negligence, and even a *shomer chinam* is liable for negligence. Read this way, the *Tosefta* does not prove elevated liability but rather a specific instance of negligence within the framework of the lower-level *shomer*.

### Morning vs. Afternoon

The *Gemara* then clarifies the *Tosefta*'s precise teaching. *Betartei katani* — the *Tosefta* is in fact teaching two distinct cases. If the *shomer aveidah* returned the object in the morning — *shacharit* — before the owner leaves for work, this is a reasonable time for return. The owner will naturally be going in and out of his home and will come across the object. In such a case, *eino chayav letapel bah* — the *shomer* has no further obligation, and if the object is subsequently stolen, he is exempt, consistent with the rules of *shomer chinam*.

But if the object was returned in the afternoon — *batzohorayim* — after the owner has already left for the day, then even if it was placed where the owner would theoretically see it, the owner is not going in and out and will not encounter it. In that case, if it was subsequently stolen or lost, *chayav be-achrayuta* — the *shomer* bears responsibility, because leaving it at that time and in that manner constitutes *peshia* for even a *shomer chinam*.

### Yam Shel Shlomo

The Yam Shel Shlomo makes an important observation here. All of these *halachot* in the *Tosefta* are grounded in reasonable presumptions about normal patterns of behavior and are not fixed universal rules. Someone who comes home for lunch, someone who leaves for work later in the morning, someone who works a night shift — all of these individual circumstances will affect how the ruling applies to any particular case. What the *Tosefta* is ultimately measuring is the degree of negligence: how foreseeable was it that the object would be lost or stolen in the interval between when it was left and when the owner would be able to retrieve it? The categories of morning and afternoon serve as heuristic defaults, but the underlying principle is one of reasonable care given the actual circumstances.

---

## Rabba Defends

### Always Liable

A new challenge from the *Tosefta* now confronts Rabba. The *Tosefta* states: *l'olam hu chayav ad sheyachzirenu l'reshuto* — the *shomer aveidah* is always liable until he returns the object to the owner's domain. Rav Yosef presses: what does *l'olam* — "always" — mean if not even when the object is in the *shomer*'s own house? If liability exists even at that stage, this implies that theft or loss in the *shomer*'s home triggers obligation — the very mark of *shomer sachar* liability, since a *shomer chinam* would be exempt in such a case.

### Animals Exception

Rabba responds: *modina lach b'ba'alei chayim* — I concede to you, Rav Yosef, with respect to animals. In the case of animals, the *shomer aveidah* does bear a higher level of liability. But the reason, Rabba explains, is not that the *shomer aveidah* is categorically a *shomer sachar*. Rather, it is because these animals are known to wander — *keivan d'nakti nigrei b'raita ba'u netiruta yetirta* — they habitually go out, and their nature is to stray. Rashi explains: *keivan she-ra'ah she-melumadot hen latzeit* — once the *shomer* knows that these animals are accustomed to leaving on their own. An animal that wanders away is therefore not simply "lost" in the ordinary sense — it is something the *shomer* should have anticipated and guarded against. That failure to take adequate precautions is *peshia*, and a *shomer chinam* is liable for *peshia*.

### Animals vs. Objects

The critical distinction Rabba draws is between animals and inanimate objects. For *metaltelin* — ordinary movable objects — a *shomer chinam* retains his standard exemption for theft and loss: *patur mi-gneivah u-me-aveidah*. The liability that attaches to animals in the *shomer aveidah* context does not reflect a general elevation of the *shomer*'s status to that of *shomer sachar*; it reflects the specific heightened duty of care that animals require by virtue of their mobility, such that a failure to provide that care constitutes negligence even under the lesser standard of *shomer chinam*. Tosafot frame this precisely: even a *shomer chinam* is liable in the animal case — not because he is elevated to *shomer sachar* status, but because the animal's known tendency to stray means that losing it is, in practical terms, an act of *peshia*.

---

## Hashavat Aveidah

### Torah Language

Rabba now challenges Rav Yosef with a *drasha* from the Torah. The *pasuk* uses the word *hashev* — "return." From this alone, *ein li ela b'beito* — one might conclude that the obligation to return a lost object is fulfilled only by returning it to the owner's house. *L'ginato u-l'churbato minayin* — how do I know that returning it to his garden or to his *churva*, his ruin, also satisfies the obligation? The Torah therefore adds *tashivem*, yielding the double formulation *hashev tashivem* — an emphatic repetition that *mikol makom* extends the *mitzvah* to include additional places of return beyond the house proper. Once obligated to return, the Torah gives the *shomer* broader latitude in how that return is accomplished.

### Unenclosed Properties

Rabba develops his reading: the additional *drasha* of *tashivem* comes to include even an unprotected garden, even an unenclosed *churva*. His reasoning is that a *shomer aveidah* operates at a low level of obligation. Once the object is back on the owner's property — even unenclosed, even where the animal could wander away — the *shomer* has discharged his duty. This reading is consistent with Rabba's view that the *shomer aveidah* is a *shomer chinam*: having placed the object anywhere on the owner's premises, even in an exposed location, the *shomer*'s responsibility ends. Rabba reads the word *beito* not as a literal reference to the house alone, but as an abstracted principle representing any enclosed protected space — but then the additional teaching of *tashivem* extends even beyond that to unenclosed properties.

### Enclosed vs. Awareness

Rav Yosef responds with a different reading entirely. He maintains that the *drasha* of *tashivem* comes to include only properties which are *mishtameret* — enclosed and protected — whether a walled garden or a secured ruin. The extension from house to garden or ruin is meaningful only when those alternative properties offer the same degree of protection as the house. Rav Yosef then addresses Rabba's objection that this would simply be equivalent to returning it to the house: *ha kamashma lan d'lo ba'inan da'at ba'alim* — the teaching comes to tell us that one does not require the owner's awareness. The difference between the house and these other enclosed spaces is not in the level of protection but in whether the owner necessarily knows the object has been returned. From properties other than the house, one might have thought that *da'at ba'alim* — the owner's knowledge — is required for the return to take effect. *Tashivem* comes to teach that it is not.

This is in line with the position of Rabbi Elazar: *ha-kol tzrichim da'at ba'alim chutz me-hashavat aveidah* — all cases of return require the owner's knowledge except for *hashavat aveidah*. Rabbi Elazar's reasoning is that *sheharei rivta bo Torah hashavot harbeh* — the Torah multiplied the expressions of return in this context, signaling that there are many valid modes of returning a lost object and that the owner's awareness is not a prerequisite. Even according to Rav Yosef, who demands a higher standard of *shmira* and requires an enclosed location, the *mitzvah* is complete once the object is placed in a secured part of the owner's property — the owner need not know it has been returned.

---

## To'en Ta'anat Ganav

### Abaye's Source

Abaye now challenges Rav Yosef directly. He cites a statement of Rabbi Yochanan transmitted through Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: *ha-to'en ta'anat ganav ba-aveidah meshalem tashlumei kefel* — a *shomer* watching a lost object who falsely claims it was stolen — *to'en ta'anat ganav* — must pay *kefel*, the double payment. Abaye's challenge to Rav Yosef is pointed: if a *shomer aveidah* were a *shomer sachar*, as Rav Yosef maintains, this ruling would make no sense. As Abaye reasons: *v'ei salka da'atach shomer sachar havei, amai meshalem tashlumei kefel* — why would he pay *kefel*? The *kefel* payment is associated specifically with cases of *gneivah* — theft — where a *shomer chinam* can claim exemption from liability by asserting the object was stolen, take an oath to that effect, and subsequently be proven to have lied. The mechanism of *to'en ta'anat ganav* and its *kefel* consequence is structurally embedded in the *shomer chinam*'s framework. A *shomer sachar* who is liable for theft has no comparable claim to make — the claim that it was stolen does not exempt him, so he would not make such a claim in the first place, and *kefel* would never arise. The case makes sense only if the *shomer aveidah* is a *shomer chinam*, as Rabba holds.

### Definition of Claim

This requires pausing to explain the mechanics of *to'en ta'anat ganav*. When a *shomer*'s liability is contested in court, the *shomer chinam* has certain defenses available to him. If the owner accuses him of *peshia* — negligence — while the *shomer* claims the object was simply stolen, the Torah provides that he may take a *shevuat hashomrim* to exempt himself from payment: *shevuat nishba ve-niftar*. If, however, witnesses subsequently establish that he lied — that the object was not stolen but rather that the *shomer* had himself misappropriated it — he has violated his *shevuat hashomrim* and attempted to acquire the owner's property through a fraudulent court claim. The Mishnah coming up at the start of the next *perek* establishes that such a *to'en ta'anat ganav* must pay *kefel*, the same fine imposed on a *ganav*.

It is worth noting a crucial distinction: claiming that the object was stolen (*ta'anat ganav*) triggers *kefel* liability if the claim is proven false. Claiming that it was merely lost (*ta'anat avad*) does not. At first glance, this seems to reward the more artful liar — one might as well claim loss rather than theft to avoid the *kefel* penalty. The full discussion of these distinctions belongs to the next *perek*, but the underlying logic of why *ganav* specifically triggers *kefel* is rooted in the classical distinction between *ganav* and *gazlan*: a *ganav* acts covertly, demonstrating fear of human judgment while disregarding divine judgment, which is the conduct the Torah subjects to a special fine.

For a *shomer sachar*, the analogous exemption is not *gneivah* but *ones* — circumstances beyond his control. A *shomer sachar* is liable for theft and loss but exempt when the damage was truly unavoidable. The theoretical question arises whether there is a parallel category of *to'en ta'anat ones* for a *shomer sachar* — a *shomer* who falsely claims unpreventable loss and is subsequently proven to have lied — analogous to *to'en ta'anat ganav* for a *shomer chinam*.

### Armed Robbers

Rav Yosef responds to Abaye's challenge: *hacha b'mai askinan, kegon she-ta'un ta'anat listim mezuyan* — the case in Rabbi Yochanan's ruling must involve a *shomer* who claims that armed robbers, *listim mezuyan*, took the object. This is precisely a claim that would be available to a *shomer sachar*: an armed robbery, being beyond anyone's ability to prevent, is tantamount to *ones* and would exempt even a *shomer sachar* from liability. So the *shomer aveidah*, even if he is a *shomer sachar* as Rav Yosef maintains, could make this claim in order to get off the hook. When he is then discovered to have lied, he pays *kefel* — exactly what Rabbi Yochanan describes.

### Ganav vs. Gazlan

Abaye challenges this solution: *listim mezuyan gazlan hu* — an armed robber is a *gazlan*, a robber who operates openly by force. A *gazlan* is not subject to *kefel*; only a *ganav* — one who steals covertly — incurs that fine. If the *shomer* claims armed robbers took the object, that is a claim of *gezeilah*, not *gneivah*, and the word *ganav* used by Rabbi Yochanan would be inapt.

Rav Yosef responds: *sha-ni omer listim mezuyan, keivan d'mitamar mei-inshei, ganav hu* — armed robbers are nevertheless classified as *ganavim* because they are afraid of people. Despite their weapons, they conceal themselves or take precautions to avoid exposure, and that element of concealment or fear of human detection is precisely what defines the *ganav* as distinct from the *gazlan*. The defining characteristic of *gneivah* and its associated *kefel* penalty is not the absence of force but the absence of brazenness — the *ganav* fears people while disregarding God, whereas the *gazlan* fears neither. Because *listim mezuyan* act in a manner that displays fear of people — they are masked, they operate in concealment even while armed — they retain the halachic character of *ganavim*. This allows their robbery to be classified as *ta'anat ganav* while the armed character of the attack makes it more like *ones* for the *shomer sachar*, who thus has the very claim Rav Yosef requires.

---

## Shomer Sachar

### Baraita Rule

Abaye presses further with a *baraita*: *im amarta be-shomer chinam she-kein meshalem tashlumei kefel, tomar be-shomer sachar she-eino meshalem tashlumei kefel* — if you say that a *shomer chinam* pays *kefel* (because there is a class of cases where *ta'anat ganav* applies to him), can you say the same of a *shomer sachar*? The *baraita* states flatly that a *shomer sachar* never pays *kefel*. Since *kefel* is the direct consequence of *to'en ta'anat ganav*, and since *to'en ta'anat ganav* requires a case where the *shomer* has a plausible exempting claim of *gneivah*, the *baraita* implies that no such case exists for a *shomer sachar* — there is no scenario in which a *shomer sachar* could claim *gneivah* to get off the hook. But this directly contradicts Rav Yosef's solution, which posited exactly such a case: *listim mezuyan* as a *ganav*-type claim available to a *shomer sachar*. If Rav Yosef is correct that *listim mezuyan* is a *ganav* and that a *shomer sachar* can make this claim, then a *shomer sachar* could be found to pay *kefel* — contradicting the *baraita*.

### Limited Exception

Rav Yosef refines his position in response: *lo, im amarta be-shomer chinam she-kein meshalem tashlumei kefel be-chol ta'anotav, tomar be-shomer sachar she-eino meshalem tashlumei kefel ella be-to'en ta'anat listim mezuyan* — the *shomer chinam* is broadly defined by the quality of *to'en ta'anat ganav* paying *kefel* across the full range of his claims. The *shomer sachar*, by contrast, pays *kefel* only in the single, highly specific case of *ta'anat listim mezuyan* — and even there, only when the armed robbers are shown to have acted covertly enough to qualify as *ganavim*. This one narrow exception does not define the *shomer sachar* as a category. The *shomer chinam* is characterized by *to'en ta'anat ganav* and the resulting *kefel* in a broad and general sense; the *shomer sachar* has only this one anomalous case, which falls outside his normal liability structure entirely. The *baraita*'s statement that *shomer sachar* never pays *kefel* is therefore accurate as a general characterization, with *listim mezuyan* remaining a limited and exceptional case.

---

## Socher Case

### Immediate Payment

The *Gemara* now introduces a case involving a *socher* — a renter, who constitutes the fourth category of *shomer*. The case: a person rented a cow from another and the cow was subsequently stolen. The *socher* appears in court and declares: *hareni meshalem ve-eini nishba* — I will pay you now and I will not take an oath. This is a striking choice. Normally, a *shomer* in this position would take a *shevuat hashomrim* to establish his claim and exempt himself from payment, especially if the claim is truthful. The *socher* here is instead opting for immediate payment, forgoing whatever defense a *shevuah* might have provided.

One might ask whether this reflects a theological motivation — a reluctance to invoke God's name even in a truthful oath — or simply a pragmatic preference for a quick settlement. Both possibilities are plausible. The Talmud attests to the gravity of *shevuot* even when truthful, and many people would naturally prefer to settle a financial matter directly rather than bring it into the register of sacred oaths. It is also worth noting a less innocent possibility: the *socher* may know exactly where the thief is, be concealing that information, and be acting quickly to acquire the rights to the animal before the thief is found — thereby positioning himself to collect the *kefel* payment.

### Thief Found Later

What follows is a remarkable legal consequence. *Ve-achar kach nimtza ha-ganav* — after the *socher* has paid, the thief is subsequently discovered and brought to account. *Meshalem tashlumei kefel la-socher* — the thief pays *kefel* to the *socher*, not to the original owner. The logic is that by choosing to pay immediately and unconditionally, the *socher* effectively purchased the rights to the animal outright. Having fully compensated the owner, the *socher* is now treated as having acquired the animal's full legal standing, and when the thief is held liable for his theft, the *kefel* goes to the *socher* as the party who bore the loss.

### Machloket

The *Gemara* then identifies a prerequisite assumption embedded in this case. *Savruha ke-Rabbi Yehuda de-amar socher ke-noseh sachar dami* — this *baraita* was initially understood to follow the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a *socher* has the same liability as a *shomer sachar*. The reasoning: the fact that the *socher* said *hareni meshalem ve-eini nishba* implies that he could alternatively have taken a *shevuah* to exempt himself. *Michlal de-ei ba'ei patar lei le-nafsheih bi-shevuah* — the very option of paying instead of swearing presupposes that a *shevuah* would have been available to exempt him. What oath would have exempted him? It must be *ta'anat listim mezuyan* — the armed robbers claim — which, as Rav Yosef has argued, is a *ganav*-type claim available to a *shomer sachar*. And since Rabbi Yehuda holds that *socher* is like *shomer sachar*, the *socher* has exactly this claim available. The *socher*'s choice to pay rather than swear, and the subsequent *kefel* he collects, therefore makes sense within Rabbi Yehuda's framework.

The *Gemara* then questions whether the case must follow Rabbi Yehuda at all. Perhaps it follows Rabbi Meir, who according to one version of the *machloket* holds that *socher* is like *shomer chinam*. If the *socher* is a *shomer chinam*, he is exempt from paying when the object is stolen — and if he pays anyway, it is simply a choice to settle conveniently rather than take a *shevuah*, with no implications about what claim he could have made. The payment in this reading is voluntary, not the product of a specific legal defense strategy.

The *Gemara* notes further that Rabba bar Avuha transmitted this *machloket* in the exact reverse: in his version, Rabbi Meir is the one who says *socher* is like *noseh sachar*, and Rabbi Yehuda is the one who says *socher* is like *shomer chinam*.

### Rabbi Zeira

Rabbi Zeira resolves the difficulty by reframing the case entirely: *be-to'en ta'anat listim mezuyan ve-nimtza listim she-eino mezuyan* — the case involves a *socher* who claimed that armed robbers took the animal, but the robbers were subsequently found to have been unarmed. An unarmed robber does not qualify as a *ganav* under Rav Yosef's framework. The claim therefore fails regardless of whether the *socher* is classified like *shomer sachar* (Rabbi Meir's version) or like *shomer chinam* (Rabbi Yehuda's version): in either case, the *socher* made a false claim that does not provide exemption, was proven wrong, and therefore paid and subsequently collected *kefel*. This reading resolves the case in a way that does not depend on which position in the *machloket* the *baraita* follows — it is consistent with both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda as each *machloket* is formulated.

---

## Rashi's "I Don't Know"

### Intellectual Honesty

At this point in the *sugya*, Rashi notes that he does not know the source of a particular teaching: *matnitin hi ve-lo yadana heichi tanya* — it is a *Mishna* or *baraita*, but he does not know where it appears or exactly what it contains. Rabbi Akiva Eiger, in his *Gilyonei Ha-Shas* on Berachot 25, compiled a list of all the places in *Shas* where Rashi explicitly says *eini yodea* — I do not know. That Rashi — one of the greatest teachers in Jewish history — would commit such acknowledgments to writing is itself a significant *mussar* point. *Le'olam yilmad adam piv lomar eini yodea* — a person must train his mouth to say "I do not know." Intellectual honesty toward one's students and toward oneself is not a sign of weakness but a hallmark of genuine scholarship.

### Why Kefel?

A conceptual question lingers about *to'en ta'anat ganav* more broadly. When a *shomer chinam* makes a false claim of theft and is proven to have lied, he pays *kefel*. But what is the underlying rationale for this *kefel* payment? Is it because through his fraudulent act he has transformed himself into a *ganav* — having sought to appropriate the owner's property through a false court claim — and since a *ganav* pays *kefel*, so does he? Or is there a distinct and special *din* in the laws of *shomrim* that prescribes *kefel* for this particular violation, independent of the general *ganav* framework? This is a genuinely conceptual question, with limited practical difference between the two approaches, but it goes to the heart of how one understands the structure of *to'en ta'anat ganav*.

---

## Shoel Exemption

### Owner Present

The *Gemara* turns to the case of *ba'alav imo* — the exemption that applies when the owner is present during the *shoel*'s use of the borrowed item. The *shoel* normally carries the highest level of liability among the *shomrim*: even injury or death to the borrowed animal that occurs without any negligence on the *shoel*'s part renders him liable. But if the owner is present and working alongside the *shoel* at the time of the damage, the *shoel* is exempt.

### Ralbag Logic

This exemption is difficult to explain. Why should the owner's mere presence matter? One might think it is simply *gezirat ha-katuv*, an arbitrary Torah decree without further explanation. The Ralbag, however, in *Mishpatim*, offers a strikingly conceptual rationale: one object cannot have two *kings* — two sovereigns — ruling over it simultaneously. If the owner is present with his animal at the moment of use or damage, there has been no true transfer. The *shoel* has not genuinely taken possession of the object in the way that creates *shoel* liability, because the owner remains present with it. The animal is still, in the relevant sense, with its owner. The *shoel* is simply alongside — he has not assumed the exclusive dominion that generates the heightened responsibility of *shoel*. This is not merely an exemption but a reconceptualization: when the owner is present, there is no *shoel* relationship to speak of.

---

## Animal in Garden

### Cushioning Benefit

The *Gemara* turns to a Mishnah case: *nafela l'gina ve-nehenit, meshalemet mah she-nehenit* — if an animal fell into a garden and benefited from what it landed on, it pays back whatever benefit it received. The context here is that the animal's fall was cushioned by vegetation in the garden, reducing the force of its impact. The owner of the animal effectively received a benefit — his animal was protected from greater injury — at the expense of the garden owner's produce that was crushed. The measure of payment is *mah she-nehenit*, whatever the animal benefited from the cushioning.

### Rav's Position

Rav introduces a qualification: *be-nachvata* — the Mishnah's payment of *mah she-nehenit* applies only to the case of the fall itself, where the vegetables cushioned the animal's impact. But *aval achla, afilu mah she-nehenit einah meshalemet* — if the animal then ate from the garden, it does not pay back even what it benefited from eating. The *Gemara* suggests this may reflect Rav's broader principle: *hayah lah she-lo tochal* — the animal should not have eaten. That is, if the animal consumed produce and was subsequently damaged — by eating too much, for instance — the owner of the produce can say that the damage resulted from the animal's own choice to eat, not from any act of the produce owner. The animal should have known better than to eat.

### Damage Direction

The *Gemara* draws a critical distinction between the direction of harm. The principle *hayah lah she-lo tochal* was articulated in an earlier context involving an animal that broke into property and overate, dying from the excess — in that case, the owner of the food is not liable for the animal's death. In that scenario, it is the animal that got damaged; it could have refrained from eating. Here, however, the analysis shifts. The *Gemara* clarifies: *ela lo mibaya achla de-meshalemet mah she-nehenit* — in fact, if the animal ate, it does pay back what it benefited. The question then becomes about the case of cushioning rather than eating. The distinction that ultimately emerges is between a case where the animal itself suffered damage (*itzika hee*) versus a case where the animal caused damage to others. *Hayah lah she-lo tochal* is the owner of the produce's defense when the animal was damaged — arguing that the animal's own eating caused its harm. But when the animal caused damage to the garden by eating from it, that defense is unavailable to the garden owner; the animal caused the loss to others, and the measure of liability is *mah she-nehenit*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 58

## Hana'ah vs. Nezek

### Nafela L'Gina

The daf opens by returning to a core *Bava Kamma* concern: an animal that enters another's field and causes damage. The *mishnah* uses the phrase *nafela legina v'nehenis* — a sheep fell into a garden and derived benefit — and concludes *meshalemes mah she'nehenis*: the owner pays only for the benefit received, not for the *nezek*.

The underlying principle is the concept of *hana'ah*. Even if the animal's entry into the field would otherwise constitute *shen* or *regel* — categories of actionable damage — the fact that the animal fell in as an *ones* (force majeure) exempts the owner from liability for *nezek*. Nevertheless, a concrete transfer of value has occurred: the animal benefited from the owner's property. That benefit, as it were, remains "held" by the animal's owner, and must be returned. The logic parallels a case where money was transferred from one person's bank account to another's inadvertently — no theft occurred, no *aveidah* was created, but the value must be restored. So too here: the owner pays *mah she'nehenis*, no more.

### Cushioning Fall

On this, *Rav* says a single word: *benachbeta* — the case concerns an animal whose fall was cushioned by the fruit. The *hana'ah* in this instance is not a meal consumed but rather the physical cushioning of the animal's impact. Assessing that *hana'ah* is genuinely difficult: the fruit may have been worth ten dollars, yet it may have prevented the animal's death, in which case the benefit received far exceeds the market value of the fruit. The Gemara does not resolve precisely how one would calculate *hana'ah* in such a case.

### Eating Exemption

What follows is striking. The Gemara introduces: *aval achla afilu mah she'nehenis eino meshalemess* — but if the animal ate, it does not pay even *mah she'nehenis*. This is puzzling in the extreme. The animal fell in as an *ones*, which explains the exemption from *nezek*. But why should the owner be exempt from paying for the meal? The animal ate someone else's food and derived clear, quantifiable benefit. Why is there no obligation to restore even the *hana'ah*?

### Hayah Lah Shelo

The Gemara attempts to connect this ruling to Rav's position elsewhere: *d'amar Rav hayah lah shelo tochal* — the animal should not have eaten so much. This refers to a case in which Reuven brought fruit into Shimon's domain without permission, and Shimon's cow ate it and suffered a stomach ache. There, Rav says Reuven need not pay for the cow's injury, reasoning that the cow should not have eaten to excess and thereby harmed itself. The Gemara suggests that perhaps the rule about the eating animal also follows this logic — *hayah lah shelo tochal*, it should not have eaten, and therefore the owner is exempt.

But this reasoning is immediately counterintuitive. *Hayah lah shelo tochal* means the animal brought harm upon itself by overeating — the point being that the damage was self-inflicted. To apply that principle here, where the animal is consuming someone *else's* property and causing *them* a loss, inverts the logic entirely. If the animal should not have eaten, that is all the more reason to require payment to the one whose food was consumed. The Gemara senses this immediately.

### One Word Only

A further complication: as a sharp reader points out, Rav said only one word — *benachbeta*. The formulation *aval achla afilu mah she'nehenis* is the Gemara's own inference, not Rav's ruling. This observation is significant because once we recognize that Rav limited his statement to *benachbeta*, the framing of the entire discussion shifts. The word *benachbeta* is not meant to be *davka* — it is not limiting the *mishnah*'s ruling to cases of cushioning only. Rather, it highlights the *chiddush* of that case.

### Lo Mibaya Achla

The Gemara now resolves the apparent paradox with the principle of *lo mibaya ka'amar* — the *mishnah* is stating its ruling by way of the less obvious case. It goes without saying (*lo mibaya*) that if the animal fell as an *ones* and then ate, *meshalemes mah she'nehenis* — the owner pays for the benefit of the meal. That is the classic *mah she'nehenis* case: no liability as a *mazik*, but an obligation to restore the value of a meal received. The *chiddush* is specifically about *benachbeta* — that even in the case of cushioning, where the *hana'ah* is not a consumed meal but a prevented injury, one still pays *mah she'nehenis*. That is what Rav came to teach with his single word.

---

## Mavriach Ari Debate

### Lion Chase Hypothetical

Having established that one pays *mah she'nehenis* even in the *benachbeta* case, the Gemara asks: why? After all, the animal's fall cushioned by the fruit presents an unusual configuration — the owner's property passively intervened to prevent harm to another's property. This raises a comparison to the classic case of *mavriach ari minichsei chaveiro*: chasing a lion away from a friend's field. Is such a benefactor entitled to reimbursement for the value of the benefit conferred?

### Mitzvah Exemption

The Gemara's initial concern is this: performing a *mitzvah* does not entitle one to payment. A doctor or a rabbi, strictly speaking, is not permitted to charge for services that constitute the performance of a *mitzvah*; whatever compensation is permitted operates under the rubric of *sechar batala* — opportunity cost, payment for what one could have been doing otherwise, not for the *mitzvah* act itself. If chasing the lion was a *mitzvah*, perhaps no reimbursement is warranted. The benefited party might simply say: a good deed is its own reward.

This framing generates a tension. On one hand, if the benefactor performed a *mitzvah*, he cannot collect. On the other hand — and this is a distinct conceptual point — there is a question whether there was any *hana'ah* at all in the technical sense. The person whose property was saved has not gained additional value; his property simply was not lost. Preventing a loss and conferring a benefit are different things. If the *hana'ah* concept requires that value be transferred from one party to another, then merely preventing destruction may not qualify as *hana'ah* at all.

### Mida'ato Distinction

The Gemara draws a key distinction. *Mavriach ari minichsei chaveiro mi-da'ato hu* — when a person consciously acts to chase the lion, he does so of his own volition. In that case, the act is framed as a *mitzvah*, and the conscious choice to perform it carries an implicit understanding that one is acting selflessly, without expectation of payment. *Hai lav mi-da'ato hu* — in the *benachbeta* case, the person is not acting at all. His property acted on its own. There was no conscious decision, no *mitzvah* framing, and therefore no implicit waiver of the right to reimbursement. The irony is notable: the less deliberate the act, the stronger the claim to compensation.

This distinction carries a further implication. When the owner's property passively cushioned the animal's fall, the situation is not framed as *mavriach ari* — it is simply: I suffered a loss because of your animal, and I am entitled to recover something. The absence of conscious agency removes the *mitzvah* overlay entirely.

### Loss-Based Rationale

The Gemara offers a second rationale: *mavriach ari minichsei chaveiro leit lei pesida* — when a person consciously chases the lion, he incurs no loss. He cannot collect payment for his personal service. But *hai it lei pesida* — in the *benachbeta* case, there is an actual loss. And where there is a loss, the party who suffered it is entitled to at least recover expenses.

Importantly, this does not mean full *nezek* compensation. One cannot be paid for personal service and cannot receive more than the *hana'ah* conferred. The entitlement is likely limited to the lesser of the actual loss and the *hana'ah* received by the other party — which, practically speaking, in most such cases will be equivalent. If $10 worth of fruit was destroyed while saving a sheep worth considerably more, the *mah she'nehenis* is at least $10, and the owner of the fruit can recover that amount. The illustration is apt: if in saving someone's property one ruins a suit in a puddle, one cannot charge for the *mitzvah* of saving the property, but one is entitled to recover the cleaning bill — to the extent that it overlaps with the *hana'ah* conferred.

### Hefsed & Psida

The Gemara's analysis thus yields a coherent framework. The *mavriach ari* who acts consciously and incurs no loss cannot collect anything — neither for service nor for *hana'ah*. The owner of property that passively intervenes and sustained a loss occupies a different position: because there was no conscious *mitzvah* act and because there was genuine *hefsed*, the owner can recover, but only to the extent of the *hana'ah* conferred — not as full *nezek*. The entitlement is recovery of loss, bounded by *hana'ah*, not payment for service.

This framework implicates numerous other *sugyot* throughout *Shas* — including the case of the barrel of wine spilled to collect another's honey — which *Tosafot* addresses at length. The present Gemara only touches the surface of those broader questions about conscious intervention, selfless acts, and the limits of compensation for benefit conferred.

---

## Ones & Pshiah

### Slipping in Urine

Having established the framework of *mah she'nehenis* and *ones*, the Gemara turns to the definitional question: what exactly constitutes *ones* when an animal falls into a field? *Rav Kahana* says: *she'huchleka b'meymei ragleha* — it slipped on its own urine. That is clearly *ones*.

### Single File Requirement

*Rava* says the *ones* case is where *dchaftah chavertah* — a fellow animal from the same herd pushed it down. According to the one who holds that being pushed by a fellow animal constitutes *ones*, being slipped in its own urine is certainly *ones* as well — it is the easier case. But according to the one who limits *ones* to slipping in urine, being pushed by a fellow animal may actually constitute *pshiah* on the owner's part. Why? *D'amar lei* — because the owner of the field can say: *iba'ei lach le'avorei chada chada* — you should have led them through single file. If you are walking your animals past a slope or ledge from which they could fall into someone's property, basic responsible ownership requires that they pass one by one.

### Cliff Case Limitation

*Tosafot* introduces an important limitation. The cases of *ones* described by Rav Kahana and Rava — slipping in urine or being pushed by a fellow animal — apply only where the animal could not have descended into the field on its own. If the path adjacent to the field is a cliff that the animal could not have walked down independently, and it fell in, that is *ones*. But if the animal was capable of walking down into the field on its own, then even a fall constitutes *pshiah*, because the relevant negligence is *techilato b'pshiah* — the owner was negligent from the outset in walking the animal where it could freely enter another's domain.

This raises a pointed question: must an animal owner refrain from walking his flock near any field into which they could stray? The *Riva*, cited by the *Gra* in a marginal note, pushes back strongly. He rules that walking one's sheep past another's yard does not constitute *pshiah*. As he puts it: *v'chi ochezna biznava v'yeilech?* — is the owner supposed to hold the sheep by the tail wherever he walks? The requirement cannot be so sweeping. What the Gemara identifies as negligent — not going single file, not attending to an animal's known propensity to stray — is distinguishable from the ordinary act of shepherding a flock through the landscape.

### Row-to-Row Movement

Returning to the Gemara proper, *Rav Kahana* addresses the duration of the *ones* status once the animal has fallen in. *Lo shanu ela b'osah arugah* — the *ones* classification applies only while the animal remains within the same row or garden patch into which it fell. Once the animal moves from one *arugah* to another — *aval me'arugah l'arugah meshalemet mah shehizikah* — the owner's *ones* is exhausted and he is now a *poshea*. The logic is that sufficient time and opportunity to intervene have passed; at the point of moving between patches, we define the owner as negligent for having failed to act.

### No Time Limit

*Rav Yochanan* disagrees. Even moving from one patch to another does not automatically convert the *ones* to *pshiah*. *V'afilu kol hayom kulo* — even if the animal was eating the entire day, the owner remains exempt *ad sheteitzei v'tachzor l'daas* — until it leaves and returns with knowledge. The Gemara declines to set any objective time threshold. Rather, the question is entirely case-by-case: the owner is not liable until he is aware of what is happening and has a genuine opportunity to intervene. Six hours of eating, if the owner was distant and ignorant, still falls within the *ones* category.

### Heightened Liability

*Rav Papa* adds a further dimension. Even within *Rav Yochanan*'s framework, once the owner knew that his animal had been in the field and had left, he is liable even if it subsequently re-enters without his knowledge — *af al pi shechazrah shelo l'daas*. The reasoning is *keivan d'yalfa* — since the animal has now demonstrated a habit of going to eat in that field, the owner bears a heightened level of *shmira* going forward. Every time the animal breaks away, it is likely to run back to that field. Knowing this, the owner is negligent if he does not take precautions — up to and including keeping the animal restrained — to prevent recurrence.

*Rashi* interprets the term *l'daas* throughout this discussion not as literal knowledge alone, but as a proxy for negligence: one can be aware and still be an *ones* (if one is distant and cannot intervene), and one can be ignorant and still be a *poshea* (if the ignorance itself reflects negligence). The operative question is always whether the owner was acting responsibly given what he knew and what he could have done.

### Birthing in Field

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* poses a related question. Suppose the animal descends normally — without *ones* — into another's field, and rather than eating, it gives birth there, and the birthing fluids ruin the owner's produce. This would presumably be *regel*. Is the owner liable?

The question is framed in terms of the dispute about *techilato b'pshiah v'sofo b'ones*: where an act begins with negligence but ends in something unexpected. According to the view that *techilato b'pshiah v'sofo b'ones* renders one *chayav*, the case presents no difficulty — the owner was negligent in allowing the animal into the field, and liability extends to all damage that resulted. The question arises according to the view that such a combination normally exempts. Does the fact that the animal was about to give birth count as part of the same act of negligence, such that the owner should have anticipated and prevented it?

The Gemara answers: *keivan d'chazya d'karva l'meylad* — since the owner knew the animal was close to giving birth, *ibaei lach l'naturei* — he was obligated to guard it against going into the field precisely for this reason. Birthing is a foreseeable consequence of the negligence; it is not an independent *ones* but part of the same nexus of negligence. The Gemara leaves this as *teiku* — unresolved.

---

## Shishim Standard

### Ubiyeir B'Sdei

The Gemara now turns to how one calculates *mah shehizikah* — the payment for damage. The established principle is that one does not simply pay the market value of the fruit consumed. Rather, one assesses the depreciation of the field: how much was the field worth before, and how much is it worth now? The source for this is the *pasuk*: *ubiyeir bisdei acheir* — it consumed in another's field.

*Rav Masna* derives from this verse that assessment is based on the field rather than the fruit: *melamed sheshamin al gav sadeh acheir* — we assess against the backdrop of another field.

### Acheir Analysis

The Gemara challenges this: surely the phrase *ubiyeir bisdei acheir* is needed to establish the basic *halacha* that liability for *shen* applies only in a private domain — *la'apukei reshus harabim* — and not in the public domain. The word *acheir* (another's) is doing that work. How can it simultaneously teach the assessment standard?

The Gemara responds: if the verse meant only to exclude the public domain, it could have said *bisdei chaveiro* — in a friend's field. The specific word *acheir* — another, implying a standardized model — signals something additional: *sheshamin al gav sadeh acheir*, we assess based on a standardized other field. Furthermore, there are two verses that address this: the verse describing the act of damage (*ubiyeir*) and the verse describing payment (*meitav sadeihu umeitav karmo yeshalem*). From their combination, the Gemara derives *tarti* — two things: first, liability is limited to damage in a private domain; second, the assessment is conducted based on the framework of another field.

The conceptual point underlying this discussion is one that *Rav Lichtenstein* once developed around the letter *beit*: the question is whether *bisdei acheir* means the damage occurred *in* another's field (a locative reading), or whether it means the animal *consumed another's field* (an objective reading, as in *ubiyeir es sadeh acheir*). If the field itself is the object of the damage, then the natural unit of assessment is the field — not the individual fruits consumed. This reading appears consistent with the parallel verse: *meitav sadeihu umeitav karmo yeshalem* — the *pasuk* speaks of paying for the *field* and the *vineyard*, not for the *fruit*.

### Seah B'Shishim

*Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina* gives the operative standard: *seah b'shishim se'in* — for every *seah* consumed, one assesses it within a field of sixty *se'ah*. This is the *shishim* standard, analogous to the principle of *bittul* applied elsewhere in *halacha*.

The practical import is this: the same *seah* of grain consumed will produce a very different damage calculation depending on the size of the field it was part of. If someone has a two-*seah* field and half of it was consumed, the depreciation is enormous. If someone has a thousand-*seah* field and one *seah* was consumed, the depreciation is trivial. Rather than allowing the size of each individual farmer's field to determine the award — which would be both unpredictable and potentially unjust — the *shishim* standard creates a uniform benchmark: assess the damage as if it occurred within a sixty-*seah* field.

This is the *chiddush* of *sadeh acheir* — not merely that the field is the unit of assessment rather than the fruit, but that a standardized, hypothetical field size is used for every case.

### Per-Acre Pricing

*Rabbi Yannai* states: *tirkav b'shishim tirkavim* — a *tirkav* (half a *seah*) is assessed among sixty *tirkavim*, which corresponds to a thirty-*seah* field. Superficially, this seems identical to Rabbi Yose's position. But *Rashi* explains the difference: the per-acre cost of a field varies with its size. A smaller field commands a higher per-acre price because small fields are scarcer and more specialized. By assessing a *tirkav* within sixty *tirkavim* — a smaller field than sixty *se'ah* — Rabbi Yannai applies a higher per-acre valuation, which produces a larger award for the *nizak*. This represents a more stringent position for the damager.

### Alternative Standards

*Chizkiyah* departs from the field-based model entirely: *kelach b'shishim kelachim* — one stalk assessed among sixty stalks. Rather than asking how much the field depreciated, Chizkiyah assesses the damage to the fruit directly: what is the value of sixty stalks compared to fifty-nine stalks? This is a radical departure, reintroducing the fruit itself as the unit of measurement. Chizkiyah still uses the *shishim* multiplier, but he applies it to the crop rather than to the field.

### Kav Prohibitions

A *baraita* is cited: *ein shamin kav mipnei shemashbichah v'lo beit kor mipnei shepogmah* — one does not assess by a *kav* because that is too favorable to the *nizak*, and not by a *beit kor* because that is too harmful to the *nizak*. The Gemara is initially puzzled by the wording, noting the asymmetry between *kav* (a unit of measure) and *beit kor* (a unit of field size). After reanalysis, the *baraita* is reread as: one does not assess a *kav* of damage on its own (*bifnei atzmo*) — because assessing the raw value of a *kav* of grain inflates the award unfairly — and one does not assess a *kav* within a *beit kor* — because the per-acre depreciation of such a large field would be negligibly small, short-changing the *nizak*.

### Fair Middle Ground

*Rav Papa* synthesizes the *baraita* with the prior discussion: the answer is *b'shishim* — the sixty-fold standard is precisely the middle path that avoids both extremes. Assessing the damage in terms of the fruit itself overpays the *nizak*; assessing it within a field too large makes it vanishingly small. A standardized field of sixty times the damaged area represents a calibrated and fair benchmark.

---

## Adam Hamazik

### Palm Tree Case

A practical case is now presented. A person cut down a palm tree belonging to his neighbor. The matter came before the *Reish Galuta*, who told the parties: I personally saw that plot — there were three palm trees growing from a single base (*kina*), the entire cluster was worth 100 *zuz*, you cut down one of the three, so pay thirty-three and a third *zuz*. The defendant protested: this is Persian law, not *halacha*. He brought the case to Rav Nachman.

### Rav Nachman Position

*Rav Nachman* ruled: assess it *b'shishim* — apply the *shishim* standard. Rather than simply dividing the value of the palm cluster by three, one should determine how much the loss of one palm tree depreciates the value of a standardized larger grove of palm trees assessed at sixty times the unit.

### Rava Challenge

*Rava* challenged Rav Nachman: *im amru b'nizkei mamon yomru b'nizkei gufo?* — just because this principle applies to damage caused by an animal (*shen*) does not mean it applies when a person personally causes damage. The *shishim* standard was derived from the verse *ubiyeir bisdei acheir*, which speaks specifically to animal damage. Perhaps it is a special *halacha* for *shen*, and when *adam hamazik* — a person acting intentionally or negligently — destroys property, we assess the damage differently, without the *shishim* overlay.

### Vineyard Baraita

*Abaye* responds to Rava's challenge: what do you suppose the law would be by personal damage? A *baraita* states that if someone destroys another's vineyard when the grapes were *smadar* (unripe), one assesses *kamah hayta yafa kodem lachen v'kamah hi yafa l'achar mikan* — how much was the vineyard worth before and how much is it worth after. That language describes a field-depreciation model, not assessment of the fruit directly. And crucially, *v'ilu b'shishim lo katani* — the *baraita* does not explicitly say *shishim*. Does that mean *shishim* does not apply here?

### Vineyard Baraita

The *baraita* presents a spectrum of views on how to assess damage to unripe fruit. *Rabbi Yossi HaGlili* holds that one looks at *mishuyar sheba* — the value at harvest: what would the crop have been worth when brought to market? *Rashi* explains this as assessing future value — the full ripened worth of the produce — which may seem unfair but reflects the loss of a realized agricultural investment. The *chachamim* disagree: *ro'in osah kamah hayta yafa v'kamah hi yafa* — one looks at the actual current value of the vineyard before and after the damage. Assessment is based on present market value of the field, not projected fruit value.

### Unripe Fruits

A parallel dispute concerns *smadar* — unripe grapes. *Rabbi Yehoshua* says one looks at the grapes as if they were already ripe and ready for harvest. The *chachamim* again apply the field-depreciation model. These positions span a range: raw fruit value, projected ripe value, current field value — each representing a distinct theory of what was actually damaged and how that damage should be measured.

### Maturity Standard

*Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon ben Nedra* introduces a maturity-based distinction. If the animal ate *lulavei gefanim v'chorei te'einim* — the earliest stage, before blossoming — then the *chachamim*'s field-depreciation standard applies. But if it ate *pagim o boseir* — fruit that has already begun to develop, even if still unripe — then *ro'in osan k'ilu hen anavim omados l'hibatzeir*: one assesses as if the grapes were fully ripe and ready for market. Once development has begun, even partial maturity is treated as full ripeness for purposes of assessment.

### Shishim Applies

*Abaye* now draws the inference. The *baraita* about animal damage — which describes the field-depreciation model without explicitly mentioning *shishim* — is universally understood to imply *shishim* as the operative standard. We read *shishim* into it even without explicit textual support because we know that is how field depreciation is calculated. By the same token, when the *baraita* about personal damage (*adam hamazik*) describes a field-depreciation model, *shishim* should equally be implied there as well. *Hacha nami b'shishim* — here too, by personal damage, the *shishim* standard applies.

The debate between Rav Nachman and Rava — and the analysis contributed by Abaye — thus produces a live question: is the *shishim* standard a *halacha* specific to *shen* and animal damage, derived from the particular verse of *ubiyeir bisdei acheir*, or is it a general principle of how field depreciation is assessed whenever a field is the unit of damage, applicable equally to *adam hamazik*? The Gemara will continue to develop this question on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 59

## Shaminu al Pi Sadeh

### Field vs. Fruit

The daf opens in the middle of an expansion of the concluding line of the first *mishna* in the sixth *perek*, which established that when assessing damage done by *shein v'regel*, one employs the principle of *shaminu al pi sadeh acher* — the damage is assessed against another field. This principle contains two essential ideas. First, the focus falls on the depreciation of the field itself, not on the value of the fruit that was eaten — a figure that is substantially lower than what one would calculate by simply valuing the consumed produce. Second, the question arises of how to conduct that assessment, since the answer will differ depending on whether the owner's entire plot consists of the one patch where the animal ate, or whether that patch is but a small portion of a far larger holding.

The *gemara* responds to this second question with the formulation *shaminu al pi sadeh acher* — one assesses the damage against a reference field. This introduces the *shishim* calculation, though the precise mechanics of that figure — sixty *se'ah*, sixty *tirkav*, and how the arithmetic works — remain somewhat involved.

### Rashi's Sixty Model

Rashi understands this to mean that one imagines what the depreciation would have been had the damage occurred within a standardized field that is sixty times the size of the patch consumed. From Rashi's presentation, it sounds as though one constructs a generic model — a kind of hypothetical benchmark — rather than anchoring the calculation to the owner's actual field.

### Tosafot's Actual Field

Tosafot, however, emphasizes that the *mishna* itself reads *shamin beis se'ah be-osah sadeh* — one assesses a *beis se'ah* within *that* field. What Rashi's explanation loses, Tosafot argues, is precisely the word *be-osah sadeh*: the *chiddush* of the *mishna* lies in the insistence on the actual damaged field. One asks how much *this* person's field was depreciated. The *shishim* model still applies, but the reference field used in the calculation is imagined as sixty *se'ah* of this very field — with its particular location, soil quality, and market value — not some generic abstraction. The calculation thus becomes proportional: if the animal ate a half *se'ah*, one pays half the assessed depreciation; if it ate a quarter *se'ah*, one pays accordingly. The *chiddush* of *be-osah sadeh* is that one envisions this field expanded to sixty *se'ah*, not an interchangeable generic plot.

---

## Tannaic Fruit Valuation

### R. Yosi: Market Value

The *gemara* now proceeds on 59a. Abaye states that Rabbi Yosi HaGelili and Rabbi Yishmael *amru davar echad* — they said the same thing. Rabbi Yosi HaGelili appears in a *beraita* introduced earlier: *nidon be-mishuyar she-ba* — the damage is assessed based on the value of the produce at the time it will be brought to market. According to this approach, if an animal ate a bushel of unripe grapes that would eventually sell for one hundred dollars per bushel, the owner pays one hundred dollars. The focus here shifts from the field's depreciation to the value of the fruit destroyed, and the mechanism for valuing unripe produce that has no current market price is to assess it according to what it will eventually fetch when fully ripened.

### R. Yishmael: Best Field

Rabbi Yishmael, as derived from a separate *beraita*, expounds the verse *meitav sadehu u-meitav karmo yeshaleim* — "the best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay." Rabbi Yishmael reads this as *meitav sadehu shel nizak* — the best of the *victim's* field. Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, reads the verse as addressing the *mazik*'s obligation to pay from the best of his own holdings: when the *nizak* comes to collect the assessed damages, he may collect from the *mazik*'s best-quality land. If the *mazik* destroyed a hundred dollars' worth, the *nizak* collects that sum from the choicest field available. This reading is clear enough. But what does Rabbi Yishmael mean when he says one pays based on the best of the *nizak*'s field? Does it mean that if the animal destroyed a low-grade acre one must reimburse the owner as though a prime acre were destroyed — a position without precedent?

One reading was proposed by Rav Idi bar Avin: the case involves a situation where the animal ate from a patch positioned at the boundary between average and prize produce, and it is genuinely unknown whether it consumed from the inferior section or the superior one. In that situation of *safek*, the *Torah* tips the doubt in favor of the *nizak* and one pays as though the best were destroyed.

### Hamotzi Principle

The *gemara* rejects this reading — *de-hachi lo amrinan* — on the grounds that it violates a fundamental principle: *hamotzi me-chaveiro alav ha-ra'ayah*, the burden of proof lies with the one seeking to extract money. The *gemara* is willing to accept a *chiddush* in the *Torah*, even an arbitrary ruling, so long as it does not collide with a general operative principle of law. A ruling that tips the *safek* in favor of the *nizak* would do precisely that, and while it is not impossible for the *Torah* to legislate such an outcome, the *gemara* prefers not to read Rabbi Yishmael that way.

### Future Value Approach

The correct reading of *meitav sadehu*, the *gemara* concludes, is *be-meitav de-lekamei* — in its best state, meaning its future state when it will be ready for harvest. Rabbi Yishmael is thus aligned with Rabbi Yosi HaGelili: when unripe produce is destroyed, one pays based on what it will eventually be worth when brought to market. The phrase *meitav sadehu* refers not to the best-quality location within the field, but to the produce at its optimal future stage — when it will have reached full ripeness.

This reading is striking in its own right. The damage to the *mazik* consisted in the destruction of produce that at the moment of the act was unripe and had no straightforward market value, yet he is made to pay based on a significantly higher figure — the mature crop's market price. One might argue, however, that since there is genuinely no available method to put a dollar value on an acre of unripe grapes — no one purchases bare unripe produce; one either buys the land or the finished goods — the *Torah* directs us to the future value as the only workable mechanism of assessment. Even so, the question of fairness to the *mazik* remains, not least because no deduction is yet made for the labor, irrigation, and other costs that would have been required to bring the produce to that eventual state of ripeness.

---

## Ripening Stages

### R. Shimon: Pre-Emergence

The *gemara* returns to a *beraita* in which Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda rules in the name of Rabbi Shimon: *bameh devarim amurim she-achlah lulavei gepanim ve-ikhrei te'einim* — when does one pay based on the depreciation of the field? When the animal ate what amounted to budding vine-shoots or budding fig-shoots, meaning the fruit had not yet meaningfully emerged at all.

### Smader Threshold

This implies that once the produce reaches the stage of *smadar* — when the fruit has just barely begun to emerge and ripen — one shifts to the future-value assessment rather than the field-depreciation model. Rashi clarifies that *lulavei gepanim* describes the very first emergence of the fruit, while *smadar* denotes a slightly more advanced stage of early ripening, though still far from completion. So if the animal ate produce at the *smadar* stage, one presumably applies the principle of *ro'ina oso ke-ilu anavim omdos le-vatzer* — one views the grapes as though they were already ready to be harvested.

The *gemara* then probes the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's statement: *achlah pagim o boser* — if the animal ate produce at the *pagim* (unripe figs) or *boser* (unripe grapes) stage. These terms describe a stage more advanced than *smadar*, closer though still not at full ripeness. At this stage, one pays as though the produce were already ready for harvest. The implied tension is that the *beraita* addressed two extremes — before any emergence and close to ripeness — without addressing the intermediate stage of *smadar*, the classic problem of the excluded middle.

### Ravina's Unification

Ravina resolves the ambiguity: *krukh ve-tani* — wrap them all together. The field-depreciation model applies only when the animal ate before the fruit had meaningfully begun to emerge (*lulavei gepanim* and *ikhrei te'einim*). But once the produce has entered any stage of ripening — whether *smadar*, *pagim*, or *boser* — one applies the future-value model and treats it as though the grapes were already ready for harvest. The *smadar* stage, even though it precedes *pagim* and *boser*, belongs in the second category.

### Position Comparison

This leads the *gemara* to observe that if Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda places *smadar* in the second category, his position is identical to that of Rabbi Yehoshua, who appears at the very top of 59a: *achla smadar Rabbi Yehoshua omer ro'in otah ke-ilu anavim omdot le-vatzer* — if the animal ate at the *smadar* stage, Rabbi Yehoshua says one views the grapes as ready to be harvested. If we are incorporating *smadar* into the future-value category for Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda as well, then the two positions are identical. The *gemara* answers: *ika beinayhu kachash gufna* — there remains a point of difference between them, concerning the question of *kachash gufna*.

---

## Kachash Gufna

### Nutrient Depletion

The issue of *kachash gufna* introduces a significant complication into the future-value framework. When one pays the *mazik* as though the produce were already ripe and ready for harvest, does one deduct from that payment the degree to which the process of ripening — specifically the drawing of nutrients from the vine — would have depreciated the vine itself? Rashi explains: *u-menakes min ha-tashlumim mah she-yachishu ha-anavim ba-gephanim im ya'amdu sham ad ha-batir* — one deducts from the payment what the grapes would have drained from the vines had they remained on them until harvest, since the grapes continuously draw on the vine's nutrients and leave the vine somewhat depleted. The *gemara* focuses specifically on this cost to the vine as the representative carrying cost of bringing the produce to market. While one might also imagine factoring in the costs of labor or other agricultural inputs, the *gemara* specifically identifies the depletion of the vine's nutrients — *kachash gufna* — as the operative consideration. The idea is that the payment for future value must be offset by the costs the *mazik* would have saved the owner from incurring.

The *gemara* notes that while one of the two positions — Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda or Rabbi Yehoshua — must account for *kachash gufna*, it is not immediately clear which one does. Abaye asserts that it can be identified: *mesaymi* — the positions can be sorted out.

### R. Shimon ben Menasya

To demonstrate which *tanna* is the one who factors in future costs to be deducted, Abaye invokes a *beraita*: *Rabbi Shimon Yehuda omer mishum Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya* — Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda rules here in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya. And in a separate case we know Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's approach to deducting costs that would have arisen in the future.

### Rape Case Parallel

The *beraita* adduced is deeply challenging. A rapist (*ones*) is obligated under *halacha* to pay damages — including *nezek* assessed as the diminution in value of the woman as a slave-market commodity (comparing the price of a virgin to a non-virgin), and *boshet* for humiliation. What he does *not* pay, according to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, is *tzaar* — pain and suffering — and the stated rationale is *she-sofa le-hitztayer tachat ba'ala*: she would have suffered this same pain in any case when she eventually had marital relations with her husband, and therefore no additional *tzaar* payment is owed for the loss of virginity.

The *gemara* responds that the rabbis objected to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's position on *tzaar*: *eino domeh nivalet be-ratzon le-nivalet be-ones* — the pain of a willing participant is categorically different from the pain of rape. The objection is obviously and entirely correct, and this is the accepted position. The reason the *gemara* invokes this deeply disturbing case at all is not to endorse Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's reasoning about *tzaar*, but to demonstrate that he operates on the principle that one deducts from a damage payment any cost of a similar nature that would have been incurred in the future in any event. It is this principle — deducting future-arising costs from present damage payments — that links him to the *kachash gufna* question.

### Miscarriage Costs

The *gemara* further extends the comparison. In the case of striking a pregnant woman and causing a miscarriage, the *Torah* mandates payment of *dmei vladot* — compensation for the loss of the unborn child. The question is how this sum is assessed. The reference point appears to be what an unborn child would have been worth on the slave market — or more precisely, the difference in value between a pregnant slave and a non-pregnant one — which amounts to compensating the husband for a future asset not yet realized. This is analogous to the unripe fruit scenario.

A dispute then emerges. Rabbi Yose says one deducts *nechi chaya* — the cost of the midwife. Ben Azzai says one deducts *nechi mezonot* — the cost of the additional food the woman would have consumed during pregnancy. The *gemara* establishes that whoever holds one must deduct midwife costs *a fortiori* would also require deducting food costs, since the food cost is more certain. But the reverse does not follow: Ben Azzai, who requires only deducting food costs, would not require deducting midwife costs, because the husband can credibly argue *itteta didi pekicha hi* — my wife is skilled and capable and would not have needed a midwife. An uncertain future cost that the husband might have avoided cannot be subtracted from what the *mazik* owes, whereas the cost of the extra food during pregnancy is a certainty.

---

## Palm Tree Assessment

### Aramean Palms

The *gemara* reports: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua ruled in practice like Rav Nachman that even when it is an *adam ha-mazik* — a person who destroys a *dekel* — one assesses the damage not solely by the tree's intrinsic value but in relation to the field, employing a *shishim*-style method. An alternative version of this ruling states that they assessed the value of a palm tree *agav katina d'ara* — in conjunction with a small parcel of land — which may not require the precise *shishim* model but still grounds the assessment in the depreciation of the land rather than isolating the tree as an object. The underlying question is when one destroys something growing on land, does one look to the diminution in the land's value, or does one focus on the thing destroyed? The answer may depend on whether the growing object is perceived in the market as integral to the land or as possessing independent significance.

The *halacha* is stated: one rules like Rav Pappa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua for *dikla d'Armia* — an Aramean palm tree.

### Persian Palms Exception

However, the *halacha* is like the Reish Galuta for *dikla d'Parsa* — a Persian palm tree. Rashi explains that a Persian palm tree is sufficiently *chashuv* — significant and imposing — that people do not perceive it as merely a feature of the surrounding land. When they see it, they focus on the tree itself as the primary object of value. Accordingly, one assesses the damage to the Persian palm directly as the value of the tree, not as the depreciation of the surrounding field. This recalls the earlier complaint that the Reish Galuta was *dan dina d'Parsa* — judging by the Persian standard — which now proves to have been correct in the case of the *dikla d'Parsa* specifically.

---

## Eliezer Zeira Story

### The Black Shoes

The *gemara* introduces a short narrative that connects to the Reish Galuta and to the theme of assessing future value. Eliezer Zeira — the younger or smaller Eliezer — *hava sayem masanei uchmei*, was wearing black shoes. He was standing in the marketplace of Nehardea when members of the Reish Galuta's household came upon him. They asked why he was wearing these unusual shoes. Tosafot notes some difficulty here, since other *gemarot* suggest black shoes were in fact the common practice, and Tosafot therefore suggests that perhaps it was the combination of black shoes with black laces that was distinctive. Whatever the precise nature of the practice, it evidently carried symbolic weight.

### Mourning Jerusalem

Eliezer replied: *de-ka-m'aveilna Yerushalayim* — because I am in constant *aveilus* over the loss of Jerusalem. He was not formally an *avel* in the technical sense, but he maintained a constant state of mourning for the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Yuhara Accusation

The members of the Reish Galuta's household were unimpressed. *At chashivta l'is-avulei al Yerushalayim?* — You are so important that you walk around in perpetual mourning for Jerusalem? They regarded this as *yuhara* — religious pretentiousness, presenting oneself as a great *chasid* who is continuously distressed over the destruction. One might also speculate that displaying such conspicuous mourning for Jerusalem carried an implicit critique of the present political condition — an awkward posture before the household of the Reish Galuta, who served as the lay political head of the Jewish community in Babylonia. Whatever the precise reasoning, they threw him into prison.

### Dates Question

From jail, Eliezer proposed to demonstrate his caliber as a *talmid chacham*: either they would pose him a *halacha* question, or he would pose one to them. They told him to ask. He asked: *hai man d'katatz kufra mai m'shalem* — if someone cuts down a *kufra*, an unripe date, what does he pay? They answered: *m'shalem dmei kufra* — he pays the value of an unripe date. As Rashi notes, that value is essentially nothing, since no one purchases unripe dates. Eliezer then pressed: *hava tamrei* — but it would have been a ripe date; the owner has lost what would eventually have been a mature fruit. They responded: fine, pay the value of a ripe date. He countered: *ve'ha lav tamrei shakil minei* — but he didn't take a ripe date from him. The full tension of the assessment problem is exposed: the owner lost something real, but what was taken was not yet worth very much, and what it would have been worth lies in the future.

### Shishim Answer

They asked him to provide the answer. He replied: *bishishim* — one applies the *shishim* computation. Rashi explains: if one cut an entire acre of unripe dates, the field's value — which is assessed in part by the quality of its produce — reflects a portion of that future value, and the *shishim* method captures this. The precise mechanics of how *shishim* resolves the ripe/unripe tension for a single date are not spelled out fully, but the principle is that the field-based computation provides a coherent framework for valuing something not yet at its mature stage.

When they asked who confirms this ruling, he cited Shmuel: *hashmua chai uveit dino kayam* — Shmuel is alive and his *beis din* is in session; go ask him. They sent to Shmuel, who confirmed: *shappir ka'amar lachon, bishishim* — he spoke correctly, it is *shishim*. Eliezer was released. The story is a vivid one, though the connection between demonstrating *Torah* scholarship and the right to wear unusual shoes as a sign of mourning remains somewhat elusive. What is clear is the narrative's integration of the *shishim* theme and the broader question of valuing future produce.

---

## Complete Fruit Rule

### R. Shimon's Rule

The *gemara* returns to the final ruling in the *beraita*: Rabbi Shimon holds that *achal peirot gemurim* — if the animal ate fully ripened fruit ready for harvest — one assesses the damage not by the field-depreciation method but by treating the produce as already-harvested fruit. The field-valuation model applies only so long as the fruit has not yet reached full completion.

### Independence Rationale

The *gemara* asks for the rationale: *amar Rachmana uvi'er b'sadeh acher melamed she-shamin al gav sadeh* — the verse establishes that one assesses in relation to the field context. But this holds only for produce that still requires the ground — *midi d'tzarich l'sadeh* — produce still drawing on the field's nutrients in order to ripen. Once the fruit is fully ripe and no longer needs to draw on the field's resources, it is considered as though already detached from the ground — *be-einayhu ba'ei shulumi* — and one pays for it as for harvested produce, without reference to the field at all.

### Rav's Ruling

Rav Huna bar Chiya reports in the name of Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba that Rav once ruled in an actual case like Rabbi Meir — and separately that he stated in principle, to his students, that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon on the question of *peirot gemurim*.

### Ketuba Case

The ruling *dan Rav ke-Rabbi Meir* is then elaborated through a *beraita*. A husband who wishes to sell a field over which his wife holds a *ketuba* lien would normally need her consent, expressed by her signing the *shtar mechira*. However, *halacha* assumes that a wife who signs a document transferring property at her husband's initiative may be doing so merely to please him, not out of genuine acquiescence, and therefore her rights are not thereby extinguished.

Rabbi Meir holds that if the husband wrote a deed to a first buyer and the wife refused to sign, and the husband then wrote a deed to a second buyer and she did sign, she has lost her lien — *avda ktuvata*. The fact that she refused to sign for the first and only agreed when a different buyer was proposed demonstrates that her signature here was genuine, not coerced deference. Rav ruled in a real case in accordance with this position. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: even in that scenario she may argue *nachat ruach asiti le-va'ali* — I only did it to give my husband peace of mind — and her lien remains intact.

---

## Stacking Grain

### No Permission Case

The *mishna* concludes the discussion of *shein* with a case that recapitulates themes encountered before. *Ha-magdish be-toch s'deh chaveiro shelo bi-reshus* — if one stacks grain in a neighbor's field without permission, and the owner of the field's animal then eats it, the owner is *patur*. This is straightforward: *shein* liability attaches only in *reshus ha-nizak*, the victim's domain. An animal eating in its own owner's field — which is effectively *reshus ha-mazik* — is certainly not *chayav*.

### Animal Damage

The *mishna* continues: *ve-im huzka va-hen* — if the animal was injured by the piled grain, then the owner of the grain pile is *chayav*. The grain pile, placed without permission on someone else's property, constitutes a hazard analogous to a *bor*, and the one who created it bears liability for resulting injuries.

### Permission Case

*Ve-im higdish bi-reshus* — if, however, he stacked the grain with the field owner's permission — *ba'al ha-sadeh chayav* — the field owner is now *chayav* if his animal eats it. The *chiddush* here requires explanation: granting permission does not by itself transform the field into *reshus ha-nizak*. Even in *reshus ha-rabim*, where a person has a full right to be present, *shein* liability does not apply. Why should permission to stack grain in one's field be different?

One approach within the *shein* framework would be to say that by granting permission the field owner has effectively leased that portion of the land to the grain owner, temporarily making it *reshus ha-nizak*. Another framing, which several students raised, is that the owner by granting permission accepted *shmira* — a duty to watch the produce — which itself generates the obligation.

### Threshing Floor Context

The *gemara* raises the objection: this *mishna* would then contradict the view of Rabbi, who holds that one is not liable until one has explicitly accepted *shmira*. Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty: *hacha bi-natrei bei darei askinan* — here the *mishna* is speaking about the context of grain-watching arrangements at threshing floors, where it was standard practice for field owners to accept communal grain and store it for threshing.
