In that institutional context, *keivan de-amar lei ayyel ve-agdash*, once the owner says "come in and pile your grain," it is tantamount to saying "come in and I will watch it" — the acceptance of *shmira* is implicit in the nature of the arrangement. Rabbi's requirement of explicit acceptance is thus not violated; in the *bei darei* setting, the invitation itself constitutes the explicit acceptance.

---

## Fire Exemption

### Mishna Statement

The *gemara* now transitions to the third major *av nezek* of this *perek*: *esh*, fire. The *mishna* states: *Ha-meshale'ach et ha-be'eirah be-yad cheresh shoteh ve-katan* — one who sends a fire — or sends it via an errand — in the hands of a *cheresh* (deaf-mute), *shoteh* (mentally incompetent individual), or *katan* (minor) — *patur be-dinei adam ve-chayav be-dinei shamayim* — is exempt in human courts but liable in the court of Heaven.

### Action Detachment

The question is why. These individuals are not *bnei da'at* in a full legal sense — they lack full legal responsibility. One might expect the sender to be treated as though he had introduced a force like *ru'ach metzuyah* that carried the fire to someone else's field, which would render him liable. The answer, the *gemara* implies, is that even though a *cheresh shoteh ve-katan* lacks full legal competence, he still makes choices and acts. This is sufficient to sever the causal attribution from the sender: it becomes *their* fire, not the sender's fire. Since they cannot be held liable — being exempt from consequences — the result is an unjust outcome, which is addressed by the pronouncement of liability *be-dinei shamayim*. Notably, this ruling implicitly ascribes a form of agency to the *cheresh shoteh ve-katan*: they are not treated as a mere natural force analogous to wind. Their holding of the fire constitutes an act, which transfers ownership of the fire to them.

### Competent Person

*Shol'ach be-yad pikei'ach ha-pikei'ach chayav* — if one sends the fire through a legally competent adult, the adult is liable. The fact that the sender instructed him provides no defense: *divrei ha-rav ve-divrei ha-talmid, divrei mi shom'im* — when the master's command and the student's action conflict with law, whose words does one heed? The agent who carries out the unlawful instruction bears personal liability.

---

## Fire Spreading

### Wood Bringer Liable

*Echad heivi et ha'or ve-echad heivi et ha'eitzim, ha-meivi et ha'eitzim chayav* — if one person brought a fire and another brought the wood, the one who brought the wood is liable. The fire existed before the wood arrived; it was the addition of the wood that made the blaze capable of spreading and causing damage.

### Fire Bringer Liable

The *mishna* then reverses the order: *echad heivi et ha'eitzim ve-echad heivi et ha'or, ha-meivi et ha'or chayav* — if the wood was already there and one person came and set it alight, the fire-bringer is liable. The interesting question not fully addressed by the *mishna* is what happens in borderline cases: where the pre-existing fire was not entirely negligible and Michael's wood enhanced the blaze to a new level of danger, is there any shared liability, analogous to the case of digging a well nine *tefachim* deep and a second party completing it to ten? The *mishna* does not address these intermediate cases.

### Blower Liable

*Ba acher ve-libah, ha-melabeh chayav* — if a third party came and blew on an existing fire, the one who blew it into a larger flame is *chayav*. Again, the *mishna* does not specify whether this applies only when the fire could not have spread without the blowing, or whether the last actor to materially enhance the fire always absorbs all liability.

### Wind Exemption

The most challenging case: *libata ha-ru'ach, kulam pturim* — if the wind blew the fire and spread it, all parties are *patur*. This presents a difficulty: if the *ru'ach* was a *ru'ach metzuyah* — a foreseeable, naturally occurring wind — how can anyone be *patur*? The entire principle of *esh* liability is premised on the owner being responsible for foreseeable spreading of fire.

---

## Wind Foreseeability

### Substantive Fire

Tosafot raises precisely this question and offers a first interpretation: the case involves a *ru'ach metzuyah*, and the reason all are *patur* is that what was in place before the wind arrived was not yet a genuine *aish* capable of spreading. It was a small, nascent fire that would have extinguished itself. The wind transformed it into a spreading fire, making it the wind's fire rather than the originator's. Even though the wind was foreseeable, the sender cannot be liable because he never created a hazard in the first place — an *aish* is defined as a fire capable of spreading, and this was not that.

### Unforeseeable Standard

Tosafot, however, rejects this first interpretation based on other evidence elsewhere in the *gemara*. Even if one started a fire too small to spread on its own, if a *ru'ach metzuyah* then spreads it, one is still *chayav* — it is still one's *aish*. Therefore, Tosafot concludes, the *mishna*'s case of *libata ha-ru'ach ve-kulam pturim* refers specifically to a *ru'ach she-eina metzuyah* — a wind that was unforeseeable and unusual. When an extraordinary wind unexpectedly converts a fire into a spreading blaze, one is indeed *patur*. But where the wind was of the ordinary, foreseeable variety, one remains *chayav* regardless of the initial size of the fire.

---

## Ember vs. Flame

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish said in the name of Chizkiya: *lo shanu ela she-masar lo gacheles ve-libah* — the exemption granted when fire is handed to a *cheresh shoteh ve-katan* applies only when one handed them an ember (*gacheles*) and they blew it into a flame. In that case, the *cheresh shoteh ve-katan* truly takes ownership of the fire — they transform a dormant coal into a live flame, and so it is genuinely their fire.

### Force Transfer

*Aval masar lo shalheves, chayav* — but if one handed them a live flame, the sender is *chayav*. *Mai ta'ama? Masrah koach gorem lo* — because the sender's own force and action are the direct cause: the fire was already active and capable of spreading when he transferred it. This is analogous to the principle underlying *ru'ach metzuyah* — when you introduce an already-operative hazardous force, the intermediary does not break the chain of causation. Handing a live flame to a *cheresh* is close enough to directly setting the fire that the sender remains liable.

### R. Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *afilu masar lo shalheves, patur* — even if one handed them a live flame, the sender is *patur*. 

### Holding Intervenes

*Mai ta'ama? Tzafta d'cheresh ka garim lei* — it is the holding of the *cheresh* that caused the fire to spread. Even where the fire was already live, the act of the *cheresh* — however limited his legal capacity — constitutes an intervening act sufficient to break the sender's causal chain. The *cheresh*'s physical possession and handling of the flame is what ultimately brings about the spread, and therefore the fire becomes attributed to him rather than to the sender.

---

## Asha Obligation

### Act vs. Property

The *gemara* connects this dispute to a deeper conceptual question: *asha mishum chitzav* versus *asha mishum mamono* — is fire liability grounded in the category of a personal harmful act (like an arrow shot from one's bow, *chitzav*), or is it a property-based obligation, akin to liability for one's ox or *bor*?

### Agent Competence

This underlying conceptual question directly bears on the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan. The more fire liability is conceptualized as a personal act — *asha mishum chitzav* — the more one requires a direct, uninterrupted causal connection between the sender and the resulting harm. The interposition of another agent, even a legally incompetent one, severs that connection and removes the sender's liability. The more fire liability is conceptualized as a property obligation — *asha mishum mamono* — the less important it is that the causal chain passes through another agent. One's *mammon* (property or force) caused damage, and that alone suffices for liability, regardless of who physically carried it to the point of impact. Thus Rabbi Yochanan, for whom even a live flame transferred to a *cheresh* results in *petur*, may be working from a *chitzav*-oriented model in which the *cheresh*'s holding constitutes a genuine intervention. Reish Lakish, who holds one liable for transferring a live flame, may be working from a *mammon*-oriented model or from the intuition that a live flame leaves too little meaningful intervening action for the *cheresh* to perform.

---

## Ember vs. Flame (II)

### Minimal Acceleration

Rabbi Yochanan's exemption, even in the case of a live flame, has a limit. *D'la mechayaves ela she-masar lo guza silta sharga* — one is only *chayav* when one hands the *cheresh* something that amounts to flax, combustible material, and a flame together — essentially a conflagration already fully prepared to burst forth, where the *cheresh* need do almost nothing for it to cause damage. In that case, *d'hu vadai ma'aseh didei garmi* — it is unquestionably one's own act that causes the harm. The term *ma'aseh didei* itself resonates with the *chitzav* conceptualization of *asha*: when the sender's act is so complete and decisive that the *cheresh* contributes nothing beyond minimal transport, the fire remains the sender's act in the fullest sense, and liability is unambiguous.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 60

## Fire & Blowing

### Mishna: Adding Wood/Fire

The *mishna* establishes that when a fire exists but is too small to sustain itself — presumably one that would have gone out on its own — and someone intervenes to make it substantial, that intervening party bears liability. Three cases are given: one who adds wood to an existing fire, one who lights wood that is already present, and one who blows on a small fire and thereby turns it into a substantial and potentially dangerous flame. In each case, it is the person who transformed the fire into something dangerous who is considered its maker and who is held responsible.

This framing resonates with discussions we have seen around the *bor*: the essential question is not merely negligence in the abstract, but whose fire it is — who made it into a potential danger. That question connects directly to the broader debate of *eisho mishum chitzav* versus *eisho mishum mamono*: whether liability for fire flows from the person as an extension of himself, analogous to an arrow he shot, or from his fire as his property that caused damage.

### Liba vs. Niba

The *Gemara* opens with a textual observation from Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak. The *mishna* contains a verb meaning "to blow on" the fire, and there are two legitimate manuscript traditions for this word. *Man d'tani liba lo mishtabesh u-man d'tani niba lo mishtabesh* — whoever has the version *liba* is not in error, and whoever has the version *niba* is not in error. The version *liba* derives from *labbat esh*, the flame of fire, meaning to turn the fire into a flame. The version *niba* derives from *borei niv sefatayim*, God who creates the utterance of the lips, meaning the blowing produced by the lips. Both readings are linguistically grounded and textually valid.

### Blowing & Wind

The *mishna* rules that if a person blew on a fire but the wind, rather than the blowing, was what actually turned it into a substantial flame, all parties are exempt — *libta ruach kulem patur*. This raises an immediate difficulty. It is worth noting that had the fire been left in one's possession and became dangerous, a question of responsibility to extinguish it might arise, akin to one who leaves a broken vessel in *reshut harabbim* and fails to clean it up, rendering it equivalent to his *bor*. But the *Gemara* proceeds on the assumption that the fire was left in a public space and the subsequent wind was one that could not have been anticipated.

A *braisa* then addresses the specific case where a person blew on a fire at the same time the wind was also blowing — a collaborative causation. The *braisa* rules: *im yesh belibta k'dei le-labbta chayav v'im lav patur* — if the person's blowing, considered on its own, was sufficient to create a substantial flame, he is liable; if not, he is exempt. The *Gemara* finds this troubling. If a person knowingly blows on a fire while the wind is simultaneously present, he is in effect combining his action with the forces at hand. Why should this not be treated like *zoreh* — winnowing — where a person throws grain into the air, the wind carries away the chaff, and he is fully liable for that act of *melacha* on *Shabbos*? He is using the wind as a partner in his act, and it achieves his desired result. Why, then, is he exempt in the *nezikin* case?

### Abaye: Separate Actions

Abaye answers that the *braisa* is speaking of a case where the person's blowing and the wind's blowing act from opposite sides: *k'gon she-liba mitzad echad v'libta ruach mitzad acher*. If one imagines the fire divided in half, what the person did on his side had no meaningful effect, and the wind, operating entirely independently on the other side, is what created the flame. The two forces did not combine; they acted in parallel on separate vectors. The person's contribution was entirely inconsequential to what the wind achieved.

### Rava: Wind Predictability

Rava offers a different answer. The case involves a person who blew on a fire under conditions of *ruach metzuya* — ordinary, predictable winds — and even accounting for those normal winds, his blowing was insufficient to create a flame. Then *ruach she'eina metzuya*, an extraordinary, unpredictable gust, arrived and turned it into a flame. Since the person could not have anticipated this unusual wind, he cannot be said to have harnessed the forces at his disposal. He did something insubstantial, and something entirely unrelated to and disconnected from his actions then created the danger. The question of whether he bears any responsibility to extinguish it if he is still present when this happens — given that the fire seems to develop simultaneously — is not directly addressed, though it remains an ever-present concern lurking beneath all of these *sugyot*.

### R. Zeira: Minimal Blow

Rabbi Zeira provides a third answer: the case involves blowing so faint as to be essentially negligible — *d'tzamra tzimurei*, the sort of breath one exhales on one's hands to warm them. Rashi understands it similarly. This was not a real blowing at all, certainly not in partnership with the wind. The wind is simply doing its own thing, and the person's act was entirely insubstantial by any measure. None of these three answers, however, embrace the straightforward reading of the *braisa*: that in every case where one's blowing was insufficient on its own, one is exempt, regardless of the wind's role.

### Rav Ashi: Winnowing

Rav Ashi takes a fundamentally different approach and offers the answer that does engage the plain meaning. *Ki amrinan zoreh v'ruach mesayato hainu l'inyan Shabbos* — when we say that winnowing with the wind's assistance makes one liable, that rule belongs specifically to *Shabbos*. The reason is *d'melechet machshevet asra Torah* — the Torah's prohibition on *Shabbos* was derived from the *mishkan* and requires intentional action directed toward a defined result. 

This application of *melechet machshevet* is striking, because ordinarily *melechet machshevet* functions as a limiting principle — if one intended one act and performed a slightly different one, there is no *chilul Shabbos*. Here, however, Rav Ashi invokes it in an expansive direction: since the person's entire intention is to separate chaff from wheat, we look past the specific mechanics of the throw and the wind's assistance and evaluate the intentional end result, which was achieved. The act of *zoreh* just is this: one throws the grain and the wind does the separating. Similarly, the act of cooking on *Shabbos* consists of placing food on a flame; the food then slowly cooks over an hour, and the person is liable even though he did not transform the food with his own hands — because that is what cooking means. One could say Rav Ashi means that *zoreh* is defined precisely as an act that uses the wind, whereas creating fire by blowing must be accomplished entirely by the person alone.

### Grama in Nezekim

For *nezikin*, however, Rav Ashi concludes: *aval hacha grama b'alma hu v'grama b'nizikin patur* — here it is merely *grama*, indirect causation, and indirect causation in the area of damages exempts the tortfeasor. This conclusion is genuinely surprising. One would expect the reverse: that *issurin* — violations of prohibition — focus narrowly on whether the precise prohibited act was performed, while *nezikin* — tort liability — is driven by negligence, and negligence clearly exists here. The person knew the wind was present and knew his action would combine with it to produce a dangerous fire. Yet he is exempt from *nezikin* liability while he would be liable for *Shabbos* violation. 

If one adopts the position of *eisho mishum chitzav*, the rationale can perhaps be understood: the fire must be traceable entirely to the person's act, and since it is not, we cannot call it his fire. If one adopts *eisho mishum mamono*, the irony deepens, though perhaps one could argue that since he did not fully create the fire — unlike the person who digs a *bor* entirely on his own — we cannot deem him the owner of this fire. Still, the broader asymmetry between *Shabbos* and *nezikin* liability remains a striking feature of this *sugya*.

### Tosafot: Two People

Tosafot press the logic further in their comment *v'hacha grama b'Nezikin*. Tosafot ask: if we replace the wind with a second person, do we reach the same result? Imagine two people who each blow on a fire, where neither blowing alone would be sufficient to create a flame, but together they are. Are we to say they are both exempt because no single one of them did it alone? Tosafot themselves find this conclusion difficult — it would be extraordinary to say that two people can together create a genuinely dangerous fire and bear no liability for it whatsoever. The resolution seems to lie in the difference between a *shutafus* — a joint enterprise — and the role of the wind. When two people each contribute half, they are equal partners and joint owners of the resulting fire. But when a person and the wind together create a fire, the wind cannot be a co-owner. One would have thought this means the person must claim full ownership of the fire he helped create using the available wind. Instead, the *Gemara* concludes the opposite: since the wind cannot be his partner, the fire is simply not his at all. It is, as Tosafot acknowledge, a bizarre result.

---

## Sending Out Fire

### Mishna: Sending Fire

The following *mishna* declares: *hashole'ach es hab'eira v'achla etzim o avanim o afar chayav* — one who sends out a flame and it consumed wood, stones, or dirt is obligated. Even if the fire did not fully destroy its target but merely scorched or blackened it, that constitutes fire damage sufficient to impose liability. The *mishna* then cites the verse: *ki seitzei eish u-matza kotzim v'ne'echal gadish o hakama o hasadeh shalem yeshalem hamav'ir es hab'eira* — when fire goes out and finds thorns and consumes a haystack, or standing grain, or a field, the one who kindled the fire shall pay.

The *mishna*'s choice of the verb *hashole'ach* — one who sends out — is worth noting. In Parshat Mishpatim there is a *pasuk* that reads *v'shillach es b'eiro*, which the *Gemara* interprets as referring to *shen v'regel*, but whose plain meaning suggests intentionally sending forth one's flame. This contrasts with the next verse, *ki seitzei eish* — the fire escaped — which describes an unintentional release. This distinction may track the difference between *eisho mishum chitzav* and *eisho mishum mamono*, and notably the *pasuk* of *v'shillach es b'eiro* is followed by *meitav sadehu u-meitav karmo yeshalem*, the obligation to pay from the best of one's property — a consequence that does not appear in the case of the fire that merely escaped. A related distinction between igniting fire on one's own property versus on another's will emerge shortly in the *Gemara*.

### Gemara: Multiple Examples

Rava asks: *lama li d'chsav Rachmana kotzim gadish v'kama v'sadeh* — why did the Torah need to enumerate all of these examples? Could a single case not have sufficed? The *Gemara* answers: *tzrichi* — each example is necessary, because each one teaches something the others cannot.

### Common vs. Uncommon

Had the Torah mentioned only thorns and thistles — *kotzim* — one might have thought liability attaches specifically there *mishum deshachiach esh bahu*, because kindling is the sort of material that fire readily catches, making negligence on the part of the one who sent the fire highly likely. But one might have thought that if the fire traveled an unusual distance and consumed a *gadish* — a mound of grain — *d'lo shachiach esh beh*, since fire does not commonly spread that far, the person could argue that no one could have foreseen such damage, and therefore be exempt. The Torah tells us he is nonetheless liable even in that case.

Conversely, had the Torah mentioned only the *gadish* — the mound of grain — one might have thought liability is imposed there because *dehefsed merubeh*, it represents serious financial loss, and therefore the Torah holds the tortfeasor responsible. But perhaps for the minor loss of thorns and thistles one might be exempt. The Torah must therefore also explicitly include the thorns to establish that even minimal damage gives rise to liability.

### Standing Grain

The Torah then mentions *kama* — standing grain. Why is this necessary? *Ma kama begalui af kol begalui* — just as standing grain is exposed and open, anything that is similarly exposed is included in the liability. This simultaneously establishes the exemption of *tamun ba'esh*: property that is hidden within a haystack, not visible and exposed, is exempt from fire liability. The question immediately follows: according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that one is liable even for *tamun ba'esh* — property hidden within the haystack — what does the mention of *kama* come to teach? The answer is *lerabos kol baalei komah* — to include all property that stands upright, not limited to crops growing from the ground. Rashi understands this to encompass even animals and other types of property.

Where do the *Rabbanan*, who disagree with Rabbi Yehuda on *tamun ba'esh*, find the inclusion of *kol baalei komah*? They derive it from the phrase *o hasadeh* — "or the field" — where the word *o* signals an expansion beyond what was previously stated. Rabbi Yehuda, for his part, reads the *o* of *o hakama* and the *o* of *o hasadeh* as each carrying an expansive function, even though one *o* would suffice — which sets up the need to explain what each teaches.

### Field: Charring

This brings us to the final term: *sadeh* — the field. *Latuyei lechniro vesichsicho avanav* — to include even one whose field was plowed but left charred, or whose stones were scorched by the fire. This appears to be the *chiddush* of the *mishna* itself: that fire damage short of actual destruction — the mere charring of plowed ground or blackening of stones — is nonetheless compensable. One might ask: if the Torah had mentioned only the field, could we not have inferred that all the other cases of actual destruction are certainly included? The *Gemara* responds that without the earlier examples, one would have interpreted *sadeh* to refer to its contents — the grain, the haystack, everything within the field — not the ground itself. Only after the earlier items are listed explicitly can *sadeh* be understood to mean the very ground of the field, establishing liability even for charring alone.

---

## Theodicy & Fire

### Suffering & Wicked

The *Gemara* transitions into an extended *aggadic* section, prompted by the verse *ki seitzei eish u-matza kotzim*. Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ein puraniyos ba l'olam ela bizman she-resha'im ba'olam* — suffering does not come to the world except at a time when there are wicked people in the world. But the statement does not end there. *V'eina matchala ela min ha-tzadikim techila* — yet when suffering arrives, it begins with the righteous first.

The verse is read as the vehicle for both claims. *Eimasai esh yotzei? Bizman she-ha-kotzim metzuyin la* — when does the fire go out? When thorns are present to catch it. The wicked are the thorns; their presence in the world is what unleashes destructive forces. And yet *vene'echal gadish* — the haystack, representing the righteous — is consumed. Notably the Torah says *vene'echal*, not *ve'achal*: the haystack was already consumed, as though it is the first thing taken. The Rabbis here are grappling honestly with the reality of *tzadik vera lo* — the righteous who suffer — not precisely explaining why it is just, but acknowledging it as part of how the world operates.

### Destruction Indiscrimina…

Rav Yosef taught: *mai dikhtiv ve'atem lo tetze'u ish mipetach beito ad boker?* — what does it mean when Moshe tells the people on the night of *makat bekhorot* not to go out of their homes until morning? It might seem as though God's protection makes it safe and the warning is merely precautionary. No — *keivan she-nitan reshut la-mashchit eino mavchin bein tzadikim le-resha'im* — once destructive forces have been granted permission to operate, they do not distinguish between the righteous and the wicked. Innocent people get caught up in the destruction. *Velo od ela she-matchil min ha-tzadikim techila* — and beyond that, it actually begins from the righteous first. The proof text is *vehikhrati mimekha tzadik varasha* — I will destroy from you both the righteous and the wicked — with the *tzadik* mentioned before the *rasha*.

### Rav Yosef Weeps

Upon hearing this, Rav Yosef wept. *Kulei hai nami la'ayin dumin?* — are all of these righteous people worth nothing? They receive no protection at all, and it even starts with them? Abaye responded: *tivuta hu legabbeihu* — it is actually a kindness for them. For it is written *ki mipnei hara'a ne'esaf ha-tzadik* — because of the coming evil, the righteous person is gathered in. They are taken first so that they do not have to witness the suffering that is to come upon the world. The *Gemara* does not offer a full theodicy — there is no explanation of why the righteous deserve this fate — but it recognizes these realities and attempts to locate some measure of meaning within them.

---

## Pestilence Laws

### Day Travel

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *le'olam yikanes adam bechi tov v'yetze bechi tov* — a person traveling should always enter a city while it is still light and leave while it is still light. The verse cited is *vayar Elohim et ha'or ki tov* — God saw the light, that it was good. When you arrive at a destination or depart on a journey, do so in the light of day; traveling after dark exposes one to bandits, wild animals, and other dangers.

### Pestilence vs. Famine

A *braisa* teaches: *dever ba'ir knas raglecha* — if there is pestilence in the city, pull in your feet and stay home. The source is the verse from the night of *makat bekhorot*: do not go out of your house until morning. Additional support comes from *lekh ammi bo vakhadarekha usgor daltekha ba'adekha* — go, my people, enter your chambers and close your doors — and from *michutz teshakel cherev u-mikhadarim eima* — from outside is the sword, and from inside is fear.

The *Gemara* explores why multiple verses are needed. Perhaps the initial verse applies only at night but not by day — the subsequent verse, which speaks generally of going in and closing one's doors, establishes the requirement even by day. And perhaps one could argue that if a person feels fear inside the house as well — *eima migavai* — he should go out and be among people, since social company might be more beneficial than isolation. The third verse addresses this: *michutz teshakel cherev u-mikhadarim eima* — even if there is fear inside, the sword makes people bereaved outside, and one is better off remaining indoors. This exchange resonates with the experiences of more recent times, including the deliberations many faced during periods of pandemic.

Rava's practice is cited: *be'iddan ritcha hava sakhar kavei* — in a time of divine wrath, which Rashi understands as plague or pestilence, Rava would seal the windows. The supporting verse is *ki ala mavet be-khaloneinu* — death has arisen through our windows.

The *braisa* then turns to famine: *ra'av ba'ir pazer raglecha* — if there is hunger in the city, spread out your feet and leave. The proof text is *vayehi ra'av ba'aretz vayered Avram Mitzrayma* — there was a famine in the land and Avram went down to Egypt. He did not stay where he was; one should seek sustenance elsewhere.

### Lepers' Choice

Additional support for leaving the city during famine comes from the episode of the *metzora'im* who were outside the city during the Aramean siege. They reasoned: *im amarnu navo ha'ir vehara'av ba'ir vamasnu* — if we go into the city, the famine will kill us; let us rather throw ourselves on the camp of Aram, *lechu venippela el machaneh Aram im yechayunu nichyeh* — if they let us live, we live; if they kill us, well, we are going to die here of starvation anyway. This second verse is needed because one might have argued that the instruction to leave during famine applies only when no other danger awaits outside — *heicha de-leka sofek nefashot* — but if leaving the city also risks one's life, perhaps it is better to stay. The verse about the lepers establishes that even when one faces mortal risk on the road, one should still leave and try one's fortune, rather than remain and starve with certainty.

### Angel of Death

Another *braisa* instructs: *dever ba'ir al yehalech adam be'emtza haderech* — if there is pestilence in the city, do not walk in the middle of the road. The reason: *mipnei she-malach hamaves mehalech be'emtza haderachim* — the *malach hamaves* walks straight down the middle of the road. Since *keivan she-nitan lo reshut maskei lehadiya* — once he has been given permission to bring death to the world, he moves openly and directly, and the center of the road is his domain. One might also observe that this is practically where other people are congregating, so the advice carries a secondary practical dimension even if its stated rationale is metaphysical.

### Peace: Center Road

The converse rule follows. When *shalom ba'ir* — there is peace in the city and no destructive force is operating — *ayeilech be-tzidei drachim* — one should not walk at the edges of the road. *Keivan de-lis lei reshut* — since the *malach hamaves* has not been given permission to act in public — *maskei u-mechabi chibuwei* — he hides himself and moves along the margins. Walking at the edges thus exposes one to those marginal, hidden forces. The implicit guidance: when things are good, walk the straight path and do not veer into marginal activities.

### Synagogue Safety

A further *braisa* teaches: *dever ba'ir al yikanes adam yachidi leveit ha-knesses* — during pestilence, do not enter the synagogue alone. The reason given is that *malach hamaves maskei sham kelav* — the *malach hamaves* keeps his instruments there. This may reflect the reality that the *beit ha-knesses* functioned not merely as a house of prayer but as the central communal gathering place — the site from which decrees affecting the entire community would emanate. Entering alone, without the protective presence of a congregation, leaves one exposed.

This rule is qualified: *vehani mili heicha delo karu bei dardekei velo matzlu bei asara* — this applies only when there is no *cheder* with children learning there and no *minyan* present. When those conditions are met and people are present, one is protected even within the *beit ha-knesses*.

### Dogs as Omens

Finally, a *braisa* offers signs carried by dogs: *klavim bochim malach hamaves ba l'ir* — if dogs are howling and crying, the *malach hamaves* is coming to the city, animals sensing that something terrible is about to occur. *Klavim mesachakim* — if the dogs are playing and excited, *Eliyahu hanavi ba l'ir* — Elijah the prophet is coming to the city. The *Gemara* adds a qualification: *vehani mili delo is behu nekeiva* — this applies only if there is no female dog among them, since in that case the excitement may have an entirely mundane explanation.

---

## Parable & Zion

### Two Wives Parable

Rav Ami and Rav Assi were sitting before Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha. One asked for *halacha*, the other for *aggadta*. Unable to satisfy both simultaneously, Rabbi Yitzchak said: let me give you a parable. *Le-adam she-yesh lo shtei nashim, achat yelada ve-achat zekena* — a man had two wives, one young and one old. The young wife would pluck out his white hairs, not wanting him to look old. The old wife would pluck out his dark hairs, not wanting him to look young. *Nimtzeu kereach mikan u-mikan* — he ends up bald on both sides, bald of his white hairs and bald of his dark hairs, entirely bald either way. The phrase *kereach mikan u-mikan* captures a situation of being pulled in opposite directions with no winning outcome.

So, Rabbi Yitzchak concluded, let me tell you something that is good for both of you — a blending of *aggadta* and *halacha*, which was in fact a classic form from the time of the *Gemara* and the early *Geonim*. The *Sheiltos* of Rav Achai Gaon exemplifies this structure: a *drasha* that opens with a *halacha* question and, in the course of homiletic exposition, arrives at its resolution. What follows here does precisely that.

### Fire as Divine

The verse is *ki tetze esh u-matza kotzim*. The word *tetze* — it went out — implies the fire escaped of its own accord. Yet the verse then concludes *shalem yeshalem ha-mavir es ha-beirah* — the one who kindled it shall pay — using the word *mavir*, which refers to one who deliberately lit a fire. Rabbi Yitzchak reads this as a statement about divine punishment. *Ki tetze esh* — when destruction goes forth into the world — *tetze me-atzmah*, it goes out as though on its own, as when the *Beit HaMikdash* was destroyed: it happened because of our sins, it was not a direct divine intervention in the simple sense, and in that way it escaped, so to speak. *Shalem yeshalem ha-mavir* — and yet God treats himself as the *mavir*, the one who deliberately kindled it, and accepts responsibility.

### God's Rebuilding

*Amar HaKadosh Baruch Hu: alai leshalem et ha-beirah she-hivarti* — it is upon Me to pay for the fire that I lit. *Ani hitzati esh be-Tzion* — I lit the fire against Zion — as the verse says *va-yatzet esh be-Tzion va-tochal yesodoteha* — it consumed the foundations. And as a consequence and compensation, *ve-ani atid livnotah be-esh* — I will build it again with fire, a new *Beit HaMikdash*. The proof text is *ve-ani ehyeh lah chomat esh saviv u-chavod ehyeh be-tochah* — I will be for it as a wall of fire round about, and for glory in its midst. This is the *aggadta* portion of Rabbi Yitzchak's combined teaching.

### Esho Mishum Chitzav

Now the *halacha*. The verse begins by describing fire damage as though it were a property tort — the fire escaped, analogous to an ox that went out and caused damage — but concludes by calling the responsible party the *mavir*, the one who lit it, implying personal culpability. *Patach ve-chatav bi-nizkei mamon ve-siyem bi-nizkei gufo* — it opens with language of property damage and closes with language of bodily act. *Lomar lach esho mishum chitzav* — this teaches that the liability for fire is understood as *eisho mishum chitzav*, an obligation rooted in the person's act as an extension of himself, rather than *eisho mishum mamono*, the liability of one whose property caused damage. This serves as a proof text in the larger *sugya* we encountered earlier on that foundational question.

---

## Tamun Ba'esh

### David's Water

The *Gemara* brings an episode from the wars of David against the Philistines. *Vayyisaveh David vayomer mi yashkeni mayim mi-bor Beit Lechem asher ba-sha'ar* — David expressed a longing for water from the well of Beit Lechem that is in the gate. *Va-yifke'u sheloshet ha-gibborim be-machaneh Plishtim va-yish'avu mayim* — three of his mighty men broke through the Philistine camp and drew the water. At the surface this reads as a literal thirst, but the *Gemara* will interpret it through the classic rabbinic metaphor in which water signifies Torah and *sha'ar* — the gate — signifies the place where the elders sit and teach, so that the desire was for a *halacha* ruling from the sages of Beit Lechem.

### Hidden Property

*Mai ka miba'ei lei?* — what precisely was David asking? Rava said in the name of Rav Nachman: *tamun ba-esh ka miba'ei lei* — he was asking about *tamun ba-esh*, property hidden inside a haystack that is consumed by fire: does the one who caused the fire bear liability for the hidden contents? The debate was whether the ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one liable for *tamun ba-esh*, or the *Rabbanan*, who exempt. *U-pashtulei mai de-pashtulei* — they sent him an answer, but since the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Rabbanan* was never resolved, we cannot know what the answer was. The reason this episode was associated with *tamun ba-esh* at all will become clearer as the surrounding verses mention *gadishim* — mounds of grain — provoking a connection to this *halacha*. Rashi suggests it is possible the question arose practically, from an actual burning of a grain pile, prompting inquiry into liability for hidden objects.

### Barley Mounds

Rav Huna offers an entirely different reading of what David's question was. *Gedishim di-se'orim di-Yisrael havu de-havu mitmurei Plishtim behu* — there were mounds of barley owned by Israelites in which Philistine soldiers were hiding. *Vekamiba'ya lei mahu lehatzil atzmo bemamon chaveiro* — and David's question was: is it permissible to save oneself by destroying another person's property? Could he order the burning of this barley — owned by a fellow Israelite — in order to flush out or destroy the Philistines hiding within?

### King's License

*Shalchu lei assur lehatzil atzmo bemamon chaveiro* — the reply was that it is forbidden to save oneself by means of another's property. This is a striking ruling. After all, the only acts one may not perform even to save one's life are the three cardinal sins: *avoda zara, gilui arayot, ve-shpichut damim*. Property damage does not fall in that category, and one might expect that destroying someone's barley to save lives would be straightforwardly permitted, especially given the expectation of compensation. Tosafot note that Rashi seems to read the *Gemara*'s question as literally asking whether it is permitted at all. But in light of the difficulty — since it is hard to argue that property destruction for *pikuach nefesh* is actually prohibited — the overwhelming view of the *Rishonim* is that the underlying question was about liability: if you destroy another's property in the course of *pikuach nefesh*, must you compensate him? And the answer is yes, you are liable.

As to David specifically: *aval atah melech atah melech poretz la'asot lo derech* — you are a king, and a king has special license; a king may break through another's field to make a path and *ein mochin beyado* — no one can restrain him. The king's license here means that even if such an act would normally entail liability, the king operates under different legal conditions. There is also a broader question lurking here: do the ordinary civil laws governing property and compensation apply the same way in wartime as they do in peacetime? That question is raised but not resolved.

### Taking Barley

The *Rabbanan* — and some attribute this version to Rabba bar Mari — offer a different account altogether. There were *gedishim di-se'orim di-Yisrael* — mounds of barley owned by Israelites — and *gedishim di-adashim di-Plishtim* — mounds of lentils owned by Philistines. David's question was: *mahu litol gedishim shel se'orim di-Yisrael liten lifnei behemto* — may we take the Israelite barley without permission to feed our animals during the military campaign, *al menat leshallem gedishim shel adashim di-Plishtim* — with the intention of compensating the Israelite owner afterward with Philistine lentils captured in battle, which would actually be worth more? So in the end the Israelite owner would profit — but at the moment of taking, the act is one of unauthorized seizure.

### Barley & Lentils

The answer sent back was: *chaval yashiv rasha gezeila yeshallem* — even if one repays the stolen property, *rasha hu* — one is still wicked for having stolen it. *Af al pi she-gezeila meshallem* — paying back does not retroactively transform the act of theft into something permissible. And again the response adds: *aval atah melech umelech poretz la'asot lo derech ve'ein mochin beyado* — but you, as king, have the special license that permits what would otherwise be restricted.

A textual question then arises: one verse in *Divrei HaYamim* describes the field as full of lentils, while a parallel verse in *Shmuel* describes it as full of barley. According to the version of Rav Huna — that the question involved Israelite barley in which Philistines were hiding — both verses can be accounted for: there were piles of barley and David was asking about them, which explains one verse, and presumably there were also lentil piles, which explains the other. According to the *Rabbanan*'s version — that the question involved taking Israelite barley to feed the animals and repaying with Philistine lentils — the two crops are both part of the narrative: the barley was Israelite property that was taken, and the lentils were Philistine property with which compensation was to be made. The two verses record each commodity in turn, and both are necessary to the full account.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 61

## David & Water

### David's Water Story

The *daf* opens in the middle of the final section of the sixth *perek*, which addresses the *chiyuv* of *eish* — the liability for fire damage. We arrive in the midst of a remarkable *agadata* drawn from verses in Shmuel and Divrei HaYamim, concerning a strange episode in the life of David HaMelech. David declared, "Who would give me water to drink?" — whereupon some of his soldiers broke through the camp of the *Plishtim* to retrieve water. When they returned, David refused to drink it and instead poured it as a libation to God. The episode is puzzling on its face: what was actually going on?

One version of the story mentions that the *Plishtim* were hiding in a field filled with lentils; another says barley. The *Gemara* interprets the "water" as a metaphor for the *Sanhedrin*, and David's request as a quest for a *psak halacha*. Three possible versions of what he sought are offered. First, he wanted to know the *halacha* concerning property that was buried or hidden — *tamun* — in a fire, which is precisely why this *agadata* is cited here in the context of fire liability. Second, he wanted to know whether one is permitted to burn down stacks of grain in which *Plishtim* are hiding in order to save oneself, even though this means destroying another person's property — *ba lehatzil atzmo b'mamon shel chavero*. Third, he wanted to know whether he could take one pile of grain to feed his animals with the intention of repaying with another pile.

### Three Inquiries

According to the latter two versions, the ruling he received was that technically a commoner is not permitted to save himself using another's property, nor may one steal with the intention to replace — but as a king, David would be permitted, since a king may exercise prerogative over people's property.

This raises a genuinely difficult question. In Judaism the general principle is that one may transgress virtually any prohibition to save a life, with the sole exceptions of *avodah zarah*, *gilui arayot*, and *shefichat damim*. Theft is not among those three. Why, then, would saving one's life by damaging another's property be considered problematic? This prompts *Tosafot* and many *rishonim* to reframe the question: of course one may damage another's property to save a life, but one is obligated to compensate afterward. The question, then, is whether one may do so without having to pay. This can perhaps be reframed further as involving a distant rather than immediate threat to life.

There is, however, a deeper issue. When we normally speak of violating a prohibition to save life, the question concerns only the *sin* dimension. But here we are speaking of actually injuring someone else — and that may operate by different logic. We do say one cannot commit murder even to save oneself, so there must be some threshold. Would one be permitted to blind someone to save one's own life? Property, being entirely replaceable, would seem to be the clearest case where we should say yes — which is why the simple reading of this *Gemara* that forbids it is so strange, and why *Tosafot* feels compelled to reread it.

A further dimension worth noting is the question of whether normal rules apply at all during wartime. War is, by definition, an enterprise of destroying property and person. If David was fighting the *Plishtim*, does the question of compensating one's countrymen for their grain stacks even arise? When an army drives through a field or confiscates property to feed its troops, it seems anachronistic to read that as a simple question of personal liability. Perhaps the scenario was understood as a local skirmish rather than a full-scale war, but it is striking that the *Gemara* treats it at such an intimate, personal level rather than as a question of war powers.

### King's Prerogative

The *Gemara* now says: *bishlama l'man de'amar hani tartei* — according to those who say David's question was one of the two other matters (either the saving-oneself-with-another's-property question or the taking-of-one-pile-to-repay-another question), the story works well. The ruling was that technically such acts are forbidden, but David as king was permitted. The verse then records that *ve-lo ava David lishtotam* — David refused to drink the water, meaning he refused to act upon the permissive ruling. He said: *keivan de'ika issura, lo nikha li* — since the act is fundamentally forbidden for a commoner, I have no desire to avail myself of the king's prerogative.

But according to the version in which David's only question was about *tamun* — buried property destroyed by fire — what does the phrase "he refused to drink it" mean? If it was merely a legal inquiry with no personal stake in the ruling, why would he refuse?

### Anonymous Tradition

The *Gemara* explains: *zu amrinuhu mishmaya hi* — in this version, the "water" is a Torah teaching brought back to David by his valorous soldiers, who literally broke through the *Plishtim* encampment to reach the *Sanhedrin* and retrieve the ruling. David then chose not to transmit the *psak* in the names of those men. One would think this deprives them of deserved honor. Why did David not attribute the ruling to them?

### Martyrdom Principle

David said: *kach mekubalni mi-beit dino shel Shmuel HaRamati* — this is the tradition I received from the court of Shmuel HaRamati (not to be confused with the *amora* Shmuel): *kol hammoser atzmo lamut al divrei Torah, ein omrin devar halacha mishmo* — anyone who risks their life for the sake of Torah is not cited as the source of a *halacha*.

This is striking. One would expect such a person to receive all the more honor. But the *Maharsha* reads this as a critique. The phrase *zot hatorah adam ki yamut ba'ohel* — this is the Torah, a person who "dies" in the tent — and the principle that *ein hatorah niknet ela b'mi shemeimet atzmo aleha* — Torah is only acquired by one who "kills himself" over it — are meant as metaphor, not literally. One is not supposed to actually risk one's life simply to obtain a *psak halacha*. Torah study is not among the things for which one is literally required to give one's life. If the honor of having one's teaching cited *maivi geula la'olam* — brings redemption to the world — then someone who risked their life for an unnecessary purpose is not worthy of that merit.

This reading actually fits remarkably well with the plain sense of the Biblical narrative: David made an offhand wish for water, his soldiers took it literally and risked their lives, and David's pouring it out as a libation was his way of expressing that he felt they had done something pointless and even reckless. The *Gemara* maps this onto a discussion of Torah — *vayisech osam l'Hashem*, he poured it to God, meaning he gave the teaching to the anonymous tradition, making it "God's water" rather than theirs.

---

## Barriers & Exemptions

### Exemption Rules

With that striking *agadata* concluded — a discussion of water interleaved into a section about fire — the *Gemara* turns to the next *Mishnah*, which addresses the technical question of what constitutes a sufficient protective barrier against spreading fire.

The *Mishnah* states: *avar geder sheguvo'ah arba amot* — if a fire crossed a wall that is four *amot* high — or if it crossed a *derech harabbim*, a public thoroughfare (understood to be sixteen *amot* wide), or *o nahar*, a river, *patur* — the person who started the fire is exempt. The underlying principle is *shmira*: if one has made an adequate protective measure such that a *ruach metzuya* — an ordinary wind — cannot be expected to cause the fire to spread, then the hazard has been adequately contained.

Four *amot* is roughly six feet. Whether a six-foot wall actually contains a large fire is a fair question, and the *Gemara* will address the details of how and from where that measurement is taken.

### Baraitot Reconciliation

A *baraita* appears to contradict the *Mishnah*: *avar geder sheguvo'ah arba amot chayav* — if the fire crossed a wall four *amot* high, one is *chayav*. This seems to say that four *amot* is never sufficient for exemption.

Rav Pappa resolves the tension: *tanna didan k'chashi mil'ma'ala l'mata* — our *Mishnah*'s *tanna* counts from the top downward. That is, starting from a very tall wall, once you get down to four *amot*, you are still exempt — *patur* applies all the way down to four *amot*, and only below four *amot* does liability begin. *Tanna bara*, the outer *tanna* of the *baraita*, counts *mil'mata l'ma'ala* — from the bottom upward. Saying you are *chayav* at four *amot* means you are *chayav* up to four *amot*, and above four *amot* you are *patur*. Both sources agree that more than four *amot* exempts and less than four *amot* creates liability — the ambiguity only concerns exactly at four *amot*, and each source reads that borderline case from its own direction.

Rava then adds: *arba amot she'amru d'patur afilu b'veit kotzim* — even if your field is filled with thorns and thistles, which constitute excellent kindling — dry, thin, and highly flammable — you are still exempt if the wall is four *amot* high. This seems counterintuitive: if there is more fuel, shouldn't the standard be higher? Rav Pappa refines this: *umisfas kotzim ul'ma'ala arba amot* — the four *amot* must be measured not from the ground but from the top of whatever fuel material sits on the ground. If there is a pile of thorns, the wall must be four *amot* above the top of the thorns. If there is a woodpile, the four *amot* is measured from the top of the woodpile.

*Tosafot* confirms this reading explicitly in a note at the bottom of the sugya (*s.v. avra*): the *Mishnah*'s four *amot* is measured from the height of the wood used for the fire. This reflects a practical logic: the concern is where the base of the fire would be when it reaches the wall. One cannot measure from the height of the flame itself, because no one can predict how high the flame will be by the time the fire reaches the wall. The fuel source on the ground is the more determinate and measurable baseline.

### Fire Orientation

Rav introduces an important distinction. All of the foregoing — the four-*amot* wall, the exemptions, the measurements from the fuel source — applies only to a *kolachas*, a fire that rises straight upward. *Aval b'menasheves* — but if the fire is slanted, bending in the wind — *afilu ad me'ah ama chayav* — even if the distance is a hundred *amot*, one is still *chayav*.

*Rashi* understands this as referring to the horizontal distance the fire traverses: a fire that bends and moves at an angle can spread across an enormous area. *Tosafot* understands it as referring to the height of the wall: even a wall a hundred *amot* high will not stop a slanting fire, because the fire bends over it. A subsequent *baraita* (*tani kivatei de-rav*) supports the reading in terms of distance, using the phrase *afilu ad me'ah mil chayav* — even up to a hundred *mil* one is *chayav*, and a *mil* is approximately a kilometer. No wall is a hundred kilometers thick, so Tosafot's reading that this refers to the thickness of the wall is clearly an exaggeration used for rhetorical effect, even by Tosafot's own admission. The distance reading is more naturally supported by the language.

The *baraita* also specifies an additional condition for the *menasheves* case: *ha-etzim metzuyim lo* — there must be available fuel for the fire to spread along. This makes physical sense: a slanting, wind-driven fire will continue indefinitely as long as it has fuel, but it cannot cross a gap where there is nothing to burn.

A question arises naturally: when do we assess whether a fire is *kolachas* or *menasheves*? When you are still tending the fire, you may not yet know which it will become. The implication seems to be that if one is intentionally setting a fire that is already of the *menasheves* type — perhaps deliberately burning brush — then one is already on notice that no distance will exempt them. If you set a fire with the potential to become *menasheves*, the question of what standard governs it is precisely the critical unresolved issue.

Shmuel offers an alternative formulation: our *Mishnah* actually describes the *menasheves* case, and says that in that case, even a small wall exempts one if the fire is straight — *aval b'kolachat, afilu kol shehu patur* — because a straight-rising fire is not expected to spread. Shmuel thus inverts Rav's formulation, taking the *Mishnah* as speaking of the slanted case and the leniency as applying to the straight one.

### Water Barriers

The *Mishnah* continues: *avar nahar o shelulit she-hem rechavim shmoneh amot, patur* — if the fire crossed a river or a *shelulit* (a water channel) that is eight *amot* wide, one is exempt. The *Gemara* then asks whose opinion underlies the *Mishnah*'s reference to *derech harabbim* as an exempting factor. Rabbah answers: it is Rabbi Eliezer, *detnan rabbi eliezer omer shesh esrei amot kederech reshut harabbim* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that the width of a *reshut harabbim* is sixteen *amot*, and that this width constitutes a sufficient break to exempt the fire's originator. We will see this figure again in the next *Mishnah*.

Regarding the river: Rav says *nahar mamash* — an actual river, even if it contains no water at the time, presumably provides sufficient width or residual moisture to constitute a break. Shmuel says even an *arisa de-diluy* — an irrigation canal — suffices, but only *if it beit maya in* — if it actually contains water at the time, since otherwise there is nothing stopping the fire.

### Shelulit Definition

The *Gemara* explores the term *shelulit*, citing its usage in the tractate of *Pe'ah*, where the question is what features divide a single field into two, each requiring its own *pe'ah* contribution. The list includes *ha-nachal* (a wadi), *ha-shelulit*, and both a private path and a *derech harabbim*.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines *shelulit* as *makom she-mei geshamim sholelim sham* — a place where rainwater streams or collects. This might indicate a naturally low area where runoff flows, or a shallow ditch worn over time by repeated drainage. For it to function as a divider in the field — either for *pe'ah* or for fire liability — it must be some semi-permanent feature of the terrain, not merely a transient puddle that appears during rain.

Rav Bibi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan defines it differently: *amat ha-mayim she-mechaleket shalal le-agafeha* — a water channel that distributes its overflow to its banks, like a ditch that fills with water and spills over. The word *shelulit* on this reading derives from *shalal*, meaning booty or spoil — the water "distributes its spoil" to the surrounding banks.

The two opinions diverge in their implications for *pe'ah*: if a *shelulit* means merely a place where rainwater naturally collects, then *a fortiori* a man-made channel would also divide the field. But if *shelulit* means specifically a man-made channel, then a natural low-lying area where rain puddles would *not* be considered a sufficient division — *dehanu bagnei de'ara mikru* — those are simply called puddles in the ground, and do not rise to the level of a field boundary.

---

## Distance Standards

### Beit Kor Standard

The next *Mishnah* takes up the question of open-field fire: if you light a fire in your own property and there is no wall — just flat, open land between your field and your neighbor's — how far must the fire travel before you are exempt from liability for what it destroys? The *Mishnah* presents four positions.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says: *ro'in oto ke'ilu hu be'emtza beit kor* — we view the person as if standing in the center of a *beit kor*, a field measuring 274 by 274 *amot*. If placed at the center, that means 137 *amot* of open land in every direction. Only after traversing that distance would the fire be considered beyond the range of normal accountability, and anything past that threshold would render the fire-starter exempt.

### 16-Cubit Rule

Rabbi Eliezer says: *tet-zayin amot kederech reshut harabbim* — sixteen *amot*, corresponding to the width of a *reshut harabbim*, is sufficient. This now explains why, in the previous *Mishnah*, the ruling that a *derech harabbim* constitutes an exempting barrier was attributed to Rabbi Eliezer: because Rabbi Eliezer equates the width of a *reshut harabbim* with sixteen *amot*, and holds that this distance is adequate to break liability for spreading fire. Once the fire has traveled sixteen *amot* beyond where it was set, it is no longer the originator's legal responsibility.

This is a notably lenient position. Sixteen *amot* is roughly twenty-four feet — a rather short distance for an open-field fire. One would intuitively feel that only Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's 137-*amot* threshold reflects the real potential of fire to spread. The width of a road, however wide it may be for foot traffic, does not feel like a natural boundary against fire in an open field the way a river or a high wall does. Yet Rabbi Eliezer anchors his position in that standard.

### 50-Cubit Rule

Rabbi Akiva says *chamishim ama* — fifty *amot*, roughly seventy-five feet. This represents a middle position between Rabbi Eliezer's sixteen and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's 137.

### Context-Dependent

Rabbi Shimon says: *shallem yeshallem hamav'ir et hab'era, hakol lefi hadleika* — the verse simply says "the one who kindled the fire shall pay," and everything depends on the particulars of the fire. He rejects all arbitrary numerical thresholds. How can one say sixteen *amot* or fifty *amot* without knowing how large the fire was, how much fuel was on the ground, what the wind conditions were? The only rational standard is case-by-case assessment.

The *Gemara* observes that one reason the *rishonim* may have preferred fixed numbers is practical: how does a court retroactively determine wind conditions, fuel volume, and flame size? There is something to be said for a workable legal standard, even an imperfect one. And yet Rabbi Shimon's critique stands — those numbers are simply arbitrary.

Notably, the *psukim* on fire never include the formula of exemption for adequate *shmira* that appear by other *nezikin*. By the *shor* it says *velo yishmerennu* — if he did not guard it; by the *bor*, *velo yechassennu* — if he did not cover it. But by fire, the verse says only *ki tetzei esh* — fire goes out — *shalaim yeshalem* — he shall pay. No exemption is stated. This could support reading Rabbi Shimon as saying that one always pays for fire, no matter what. The *Gemara* does initially read him that way, before concluding otherwise.

When the *Gemara* pushes back and asks whether Rabbi Shimon holds that there is truly no level of *shmira* that can exempt one from fire liability, it cites the subsequent *Mishnah* about oven placement, in which Rabbi Shimon himself says that the precautionary measures prescribed are precisely what *create* the exemption if damage occurs. Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha therefore explains Rabbi Shimon's position in the field case as follows: *hakol lefi govah hadleika* — everything depends on the height and character of the fire itself. Rabbi Shimon is not saying you always pay; he is saying the correct standard is the particular fire, not an arbitrary number. Rav Yosef in the name of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules: *halacha k'Rebbe Shimon*. Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel likewise: the *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon.

This ruling is in one sense relieving. The fixed numbers of the other opinions always had an arbitrary quality. At the same time, it leaves unresolved the practical question of exactly how the fire is to be assessed. Is it measured based on the fire's current state when one lights it, or based on its potential — what it could become under foreseeable conditions? By analogy, recall the discussion of a well cover: if the cover can protect against oxen but not camels, and camels are commonly found in the area, the cover is inadequate. Similarly, a *shmira* adequate for the fire as it currently stands may be inadequate for the fire as it is likely to develop given prevailing winds and available fuel. The *halacha* demands anticipation of the reasonably foreseeable, not merely the present state.

---

## Oven Safety Rules

### Oven Clearances

The *Mishnah* here addresses the placement of ovens and hearths in shared residential structures — a question not of after-the-fact liability (*bava kamma*) but of before-the-fact prevention (*bava batra*). This distinction is important: *Bava Batra* addresses the right of neighbors to demand that you configure your property so as not to create hazards for them. The rules of *harchakat nezikin* — distancing to prevent damage — allow a neighbor to compel you to move a hazardous installation even before any damage occurs, whereas Bava Kamma governs what you owe after damage has been done.

The *Mishnah* states: *lo ya'amid adam tanur betoch habayit ela im kein yesh al gabav gavo'ah arba amot* — one may not install an oven inside a house unless there is four *amot* of clearance between the top of the oven and the ceiling. If the oven is on the upper floor — *hayah ma'amido b'aliyah* — in addition to the ceiling clearance, the floor below the oven must be *shlosha tfachim* thick so that the heat does not break through the floor. For a *kira*, a type of oven with less concentrated heat, one *tefach* suffices. *Rashi* notes that this is not merely a neighborly arrangement — it functions more like a municipal fire code, with the residents of the city collectively able to impose these requirements on any individual.

### Post-Damage Liability

Despite full compliance with all these precautionary standards, the *Mishnah* adds: *im hizik meshalem mah shehizik* — if the oven nonetheless causes damage, one remains liable. Compliance with the preventive requirements does not automatically generate an exemption after the fact.

### Shimon's Distinction

Rabbi Shimon disagrees. *Lo ne'emru shiurim halalu ela she'im hizik patur milshalem* — the entire reason these specific measurements were prescribed is precisely to tell you that if damage occurs after you have complied with them, you are exempt. This is why the *Gemara* earlier cited this *Mishnah* against the suggestion that Rabbi Shimon holds one always pays for fire: Rabbi Shimon himself establishes that adequate protective measures create exemption from liability. The difference between this case and the open-field discussion is that here we are speaking of a contained fire with defined precautions, whereas there the debate concerned what measures constitute adequate *shmira* for a fire burning in an open field.

Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha, as noted above, reads Rabbi Shimon's open-field position as consistent with this: Rabbi Shimon is not eliminating the possibility of exemption, but insisting that the standard for exemption must track the actual characteristics of the fire in question. Both rulings of Shmuel — transmitted through Rav Yosef and through Rav Nachman — confirm: *halacha k'Rebbe Shimon*.

---

## Buried Property

### Core Dispute

After the extended discussion of *shmira* and measurement, the *Gemara* finally turns to the question of *tamun* — buried or hidden property destroyed by fire — which was the first thing raised in the David narrative at the opening of the *daf*. The *Mishnah* addresses a case where someone lit a stack of grain (*gedish*) on fire, and there were vessels (*keilim*) concealed within it that were destroyed.

Rabbi Yehuda holds: *meshalem mah shebetokho* — one must pay for whatever was in the stack, including things that were hidden there. The *Chachamim* disagree: *eino meshalem ela gedish chitim o shel seorim* — one pays only as if the stack contained what would normally be expected — wheat, or barley, as the case may be. One does not pay for unexpected hidden objects.

At first glance, it is tempting to read the *Chachamim* as saying there is simply no exemption based on what could or could not have been expected — just an arbitrary rule that *tamun ba'eish*, hidden property in a fire, creates no liability. But the simpler reading of the *Mishnah* resists that. The *Chachamim* seem to be saying something eminently sensible: if you could not reasonably have known that something precious was buried in that haystack, you cannot be held accountable for it. If you were making a fire in the middle of a field surrounded by what appeared to be wheat, and it turns out someone had buried something valuable in that wheat — that is not a foreseeable consequence of your negligence.

The *Mishnah* also records that the *Chachamim* agree with Rabbi Yehuda in the case of *madlik et habirah* — one who burns down a large house. In that case, *meshalem kol mah shebetokho* — one pays for all the contents, *shekein derekh bnei adam lehaniach b'vatim* — because people normally keep things in their houses. Here the rationale is plain: burning someone's house makes you responsible for all ordinary contents, because that is entirely foreseeable.

Before the *Gemara* explores the detailed mechanics of this debate, it pauses on another clause of the *Mishnah* — the case of a goat (*gedi kafut lo*) bound near the stack, and a slave (*eved samukh lo*) positioned nearby. If both caught fire and burned, one is *chayav*. The reason is subtle: one is liable despite the slave's death because the principle of *kim leih bid'raba minei* — by which a greater punishment subsumes a lesser monetary one — does not apply, since the slave was not bound and therefore could have fled. The *Gemara* is careful to specify: one is *chayav* only if the *gedi* was bound (so it could not escape) and the *eved* was unbound (so *kim leih* does not apply). If the *eved* was bound — effectively meaning one committed an act of murder — then *kim leih* does apply, and one is *patur* on everything. Likewise, if the *gedi* was unbound and should have run away, one is *patur* for the *gedi* on grounds that it should have escaped.

### Own vs. Friend's

Rav Kahana introduces a crucial structural observation: *machlokes bemadlik betoch shelo vehalcha betoch shel chaveiro* — the entire debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* about *tamun* applies only when the fire was started in one's own domain and spread into another's. When it starts on one's own property, there is a question whether one must pay for hidden objects in the neighbor's domain that the fire reaches. Rabbi Yehuda says *chayav*; the *Rabanan* say *patur*.

*Aval bemadlik betoch shel chaveiro* — but if one started the fire in the friend's property, *dekuli alma meshalem kol mah shebetocha* — everyone agrees one pays for everything. The act of originating a fire on another's property is fundamentally more culpable, and no exemptions apply.

### Spreading Fire

Rava challenges Rav Kahana's reading with a pointed textual argument. If the debate is only about fires that start on one's property and spread, why does the *Mishnah* settle the house-burning case by appealing to the general principle that *people normally leave things in houses*? If someone is burning their friend's house from the outside, the exemption or liability should not hinge on what people generally store in homes — it should simply hinge on the fact that you set fire to your friend's property, in which case everyone agrees you pay for everything. The appeal to normalcy only makes sense if we are distinguishing between expected and unexpected contents in a case where the fire *originated* on one's own property and spread to the house. But in that case, the *Mishnah* should have made that distinction explicitly within the haystack case, rather than introducing the house as a separate illustration.

*Ella amar Rava bitartei pligi* — Rava therefore concludes that the debate operates on two separate fronts simultaneously, and this reading preserves both the notion of an arbitrary *tamun* exemption and the role of reasonable expectation.

### Started in Friend's

The first front is when the fire starts on one's own property and spreads. There, Rabbi Yehuda holds one is *chayav* for *tamun ba'eish*, and the *Rabanan* hold one is *patur* — and this exemption is *arbitrary*. When it spreads from your domain, the *Chachamim* exempt you for anything hidden, regardless of whether it was something one could have expected or not. This is a genuinely striking ruling: it means that if one is negligent with a fire and it spreads to a neighbor's property and burns down the neighbor's house, one would — according to the *Chachamim* — be liable for the structure but potentially exempt from paying for its contents, since those contents are *tamun* relative to the fire-starter who was in a different domain.

### Permission Limits

The second front of the debate is when the fire starts in the friend's property. There too Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* disagree, but the operative principle shifts. Rabbi Yehuda says one pays for everything — *afilu arneki*, even a wallet. The *Chachamim* say one pays for *keilim she'darkan lehatmin b'gadish* — objects that are normally stored in or near a grain stack, such as farm implements and animal equipment — because those were reasonably foreseeable. But *keilim she'ein darkan lehatmin b'gadish* — objects not normally stored in a stack — *lo meshalem*, one does not pay for those.

This is why the *Mishnah*'s ruling about the burned house makes perfect sense: when you burn your friend's house, you started the fire in his domain. You pay for everything that could normally be expected to be in a house — because that is the standard that applies when the fire originates on the friend's property.

A supporting *baraita* confirms Rava's analysis. *Bameh devarim amurim bemadlik betoch shelo v'halcha v'dalka betoch shel chaveiro* — the exemption for *tamun* applies when one lit on one's own property and the fire spread. *Aval madlik betoch shel chaveiro, meshalem kol mah shehayah betocha* — if one started in the friend's property, one pays for everything (meaning: everything that was reasonably foreseeable to be there).

### Grain Swap Cases

The *Mishnah* then records a case in which Rabbi Yehuda agrees with the *Chachamim*. If one granted a neighbor permission to stack grain in one's field — *mashreh makom le-chaveiro le-hagdish gadish* — and the neighbor stacked grain and also buried objects within it, one is liable only for the grain itself, not for the buried objects. Here the property owner can say: I gave you permission for your grain. I did not authorize you to hide your vessels here. Since one's permission extended only to grain, the presence of hidden objects in excess of that permission means those objects are, from the property owner's perspective, there without authorization. Just as a person who enters one's property without permission cannot recover for injuries that occur there, items stored beyond the scope of permission fall outside the scope of liability.

The *Mishnah* then works through a series of *grain swap* cases. If one granted permission to store wheat and the neighbor stored barley, one pays only for barley — that is the easy case. If one granted permission for barley and the neighbor stored wheat, one also pays only for barley — the more valuable wheat was stored without permission, so one is liable only up to the value of the permitted barley. The rationale is analogous to the rule that if an ox gores someone on one's property whom the owner told not to enter, the owner is *patur*. Since the wheat was present without authorization, the loss of wheat is treated as if only barley had been there.

What of wheat covered with a layer of barley, or barley covered with a layer of wheat? In every such case, *eino meshalem ela dmei seorim bilvad* — one pays only the value of barley. In every permutation, the liability is capped at whatever the explicitly permitted grain was worth. A subtle point emerges: even in the case where one had permission only for barley and the neighbor brought wheat, one is not entirely *patur* — one still pays the equivalent of barley, because the neighbor *could* have brought barley, and at minimum one bears liability as if they had. Just as when the *keilim* are present and one does not pay for them but does pay *as if the space were filled with grain*, the principle here is that the scope of permission defines the ceiling of liability, but not a complete exemption. As one student observes, the relative flammability of wheat versus barley — one grain may burn more readily than the other — could also factor into the practical calculation, though the *Gemara* does not explicitly develop this point.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 62

## Rava's Guardianship Case

### Intro: Tamun Machlokes

The daf opens amid a series of cases that work through the finer implications raised by the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* had established a *machlokes* between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim* concerning *tamun* — items concealed within a haystack that is subsequently destroyed by fire. The person who lit the fire is clearly liable for the damage to the haystack itself; the question is whether liability extends to items hidden inside, which the person who set the fire presumably was unaware of and could not reasonably have been expected to anticipate. This dispute opens into a broader discussion of the levels of *shemirah* — guardianship — that a person accepts upon himself, and what consequences flow from those differing levels of accepted responsibility.

### Golden Coin Case

Rava presents a case that illustrates this principle in a guardianship context: a person gave a golden coin to a woman and said to her, "Be careful with it — it is made of silver." In fact, this description was false or deliberately misleading. The coin was gold, worth substantially more than silver — the *gemara* assumes throughout that gold is worth approximately twenty-five times the value of silver, though the shiur notes that exchange rates between silver and gold have shifted considerably since the time of the *gemara*, and whether this was understood as a fixed or variable ratio is itself an interesting question.

### Damage Type Liability

Rava rules that if she damaged the coin directly — for example, she threw it into a fire or struck it with a hammer — she must pay back the full value of a gold *dinar*. The reasoning is straightforward: since she went ahead and actively destroyed the object, she bears full liability for whatever it actually was, regardless of what she was told. The fact that she did not know its true composition does not exempt her from liability for her own destructive act.

However, if the damage occurred through negligence while she was in the role of *shomeres* — that is, she failed in her duty of guardianship in some way that led to damage — she pays back only the value of a silver *dinar*. She can argue: *netirusa d'chaspa kabili alai, netirusa d'dahava lo kabili alai* — I accepted upon myself only the level of *shemirah* appropriate for something made of silver; I never accepted the level of *shemirah* required for something made of gold. Since she believed the item to be silver and acted accordingly throughout her guardianship, her accepted level of liability is calibrated to silver alone.

### Mordechai's Sword Case

The Mordechai applies Rava's ruling to a striking practical case rooted in a recognizable historical reality: Jews were frequently in possession of collateral on loans to non-Jews, since they were heavily involved in moneylending and mercantile trade. The case is: Reuven borrowed a sword that Shimon held as collateral (*mashkon*) on a loan he had extended to a non-Jew. While borrowing it, Reuven lost the sword. Later, the non-Jew returns and claims the sword was actually an extraordinarily valuable antique heirloom — worth far more than a standard sword — and Shimon accordingly attempts to extract that inflated value from Reuven.

The Mordechai rules that Reuven cannot be held liable for more than the value of an ordinary sword, since that is what he understood himself to be borrowing and what he accepted *shemirah* over. However, the Mordechai himself adds *tzarich iyun* — he is uncertain whether the case is fully analogous to Rava's.

### Deception Distinction

The Yam Shel Shlomo (the Maharshal) explains the distinction that underlies the Mordechai's hesitation. In Rava's case, the person handing over the coin explicitly stated that it was silver — he actively described the item and thereby defined the scope of *shemirah* the woman would reasonably accept, even if his description was intended to mislead. In the Mordechai's sword case, by contrast, Reuven simply borrowed the sword with no explicit representation about its nature or value. There was no deception, no stated description — he simply took the sword at face value. The absence of any explicit communication about the object's value creates a *machlokes* between the Mordechai and the Yam Shel Shlomo as to whether the same principle applies.

---

## Baraita Challenge
