The *Gemara* answers with a parallel logic: *mah li kullah katlah mah li palga katlah* — whether you destroyed it entirely or partially, the diminution in value is attributable to the *ganav*'s own actions. He should not be able to reduce his fine liability through damage he himself caused. The principle thus has a symmetry: value the *ganav* added does not increase the fines he must pay; value the *ganav* destroyed does not decrease them.

### Wine Barrel Case

Rava introduces a case that probes the boundary between the principal and the fines under conditions of market change. A *ganav* stole a barrel of wine worth one *zuz*. By the time the case reaches court, the wine is worth four *zuzim*. The question is whether the principal — the *keren* — is assessed at one (the value at theft) or at four (the value at the time of standing in court).

### Active Destruction

Rava rules: *tavrah sha'at* — if the *ganav* actively destroyed the barrel when it was worth four, he pays four. *Itbar mimeila* — if it broke on its own, he pays one. The reasoning is that when the *ganav* actively destroys an object worth four, he incurs a new and independent act of liability at that moment. It is no longer merely the original *gneiva* that is being assessed; the act of destruction at the higher value constitutes a fresh *chiyuv* for that higher value. The principal is assessed accordingly. Where the barrel breaks on its own, no new act of liability is incurred, and the principal reverts to the value at the time of theft.

### Active Destruction

One might ask why the *ganav*'s active destruction raises the *keren* to the higher value rather than simply adding a *chiyuv* for *nezek*. The answer is that this is not a case of *shinui koneh* — the *ganav* did not acquire the barrel through transformation. The object still belongs to the owner, and the obligation to return it persists. But by actively destroying it at a point when it is worth four, the *ganav* generates a liability for four — not as a *shomer* who was negligent, but as someone who committed a fresh act of damage to the owner's property.

### Liability Breakdown

The distinction that emerges is between passive changes in value and active intervention. The three components of payment — *keren*, *kefel*, and *arba'ah ve'chamishah* — are each calibrated to a different moment and a different type of event. The *keren* is assessed at the time of theft, because that is when the transgression creating the principal obligation occurred. The *kefel* and *arba'ah ve'chamishah* are assessed at the time of *ha'amadah badin*, because these are penalties imposed by the court at the moment of adjudication. Neither category is adjusted for value changes attributable to the *ganav*'s own actions — whether increases or decreases. But if the *ganav* actively destroys the object when it carries a higher value, the *keren* itself is recalculated upward because a new independent act of liability has been committed.

### Ganav vs Shomer

A question arises from the comparison with a *shomer*. If a *shomer* holds an object given to him when it was worth one, and the value rises to four, and through negligence the object is destroyed when it is worth four, the *shomer* pays four. His liability is rooted in the ongoing obligation of *shmira* — he was responsible for the object when it was worth four, he was negligent, and an object worth four was lost. By contrast, if a *ganav* holds the same object and it is destroyed *mimeila* — on its own, without any active intervention — even through what would constitute negligence in a *shomer*, he pays only the value at the time of theft. This is not a leniency for the *ganav* in all respects; it reflects a difference in the nature of the liability. The *shomer*'s obligation is an ongoing custodial responsibility; damage during that custody triggers liability based on current value. The *ganav*'s obligation, by contrast, is generated by the original act of theft and is assessed at that moment. He never accepted the obligations of *shmira*, and therefore his liability for passive deterioration or passive destruction is calibrated to the original moment of taking.

The converse illustrates the same principle from the other direction. A *shomer* whose object is destroyed by *oness* — unavoidable accident — is exempt, because his liability is conditioned on negligence. A *ganav* whose object is destroyed by *oness* is *chayav*, because his liability is unconditional, rooted in the act of taking regardless of what subsequently occurs. The *ganav* pays not because of negligence or because of ongoing responsibility, but because he stole. That original act carries the obligation forward regardless of how the loss ultimately occurs.

### Final Synthesis

The full picture that emerges from this *sugya* is as follows. The *keren* is assessed *ke'ein sheganav* — at the value of the stolen object at the moment of theft, because that act is what generates the principal obligation. The *kefel* and *arba'ah ve'chamishah* are assessed *k'sha'at ha'amadah badin* — at the value at the time the *ganav* stands in court, because these are court-imposed penalties activated at the moment of adjudication. Neither category is inflated by value the *ganav* himself added, nor reduced by value the *ganav* himself destroyed. Where the *ganav* actively destroys the object at a point when it carries a higher market value, the *keren* is assessed at the higher value — not because the rule of *ke'ein sheganav* has been abandoned, but because the act of active destruction constitutes a new independent act of liability assessed at the time it occurs.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 65

## Kefel vs. Keren Payment

### Rav's Principle Stated

The daf begins at the bottom of 65a with the statement of Rav, which will occupy much of today's discussion. The governing question is: when do we assess the value of the object for purposes of payment — at the time of the theft or at the time of the court case?

The distinction turns on the nature of the obligation. *Kefel* — the double payment — together with the four-and-five payments for slaughtering or selling a stolen ox or sheep, is a *knas*, a court-imposed financial penalty. It is not a natural debt that accrues automatically; it requires the court to impose it. Indeed, if the thief admits to the theft, he is exempt from the *knas* entirely. Rav therefore rules that the *kefel* and four-and-five payments are assessed based on the value of the object at the time the court adjudicates the case, whereas the *keren* — the principal — is assessed based on the time of the theft, since that is when the fundamental liability was incurred.

### Limitations on Rav

The Gemara had already introduced certain qualifications on Rav's ruling. If the animal became fatter or thinner during the period of the theft, this does not shift the baseline — the thief neither benefits from an increase he contributed nor bears additional liability for a decrease in market value he did not cause. What Rav is addressing is a straightforward change in market value. If the thief slaughtered or sold the animal — both acts which independently trigger additional liability — then the principal payment for that subsequent act is assessed at the higher value, since a new debt is being incurred at that moment. But for a simple holding of the object without slaughter or sale, the split applies: the *keren* is assessed at the time of theft, and the *kefel* at the time of the court case, whether the value rose or fell in the interim.

## Rabbi Chanina's Baraita

### False Oath Scenario

The Gemara now cites a *baraita* of Rabbi Chanina brought specifically to support Rav's ruling. The case involves a *shomer* — a bailee — who, when asked about an object entrusted to his care, claims it was stolen (*ta'anat gannav*) and swears to that effect. This is the precise scenario that occupied the opening *dappim* of this chapter. Such a false oath creates two distinct and overlapping liabilities: on the one hand, if witnesses later establish that the object was not stolen but was kept by the *shomer*, he would owe *kefel*, since a *ta'anat gannav* with a false oath triggers the double-payment penalty when witnesses contradict it. On the other hand, the act of falsely swearing to keep another's property and then admitting to it triggers the obligation to bring an *asham gezeilot* — the special sin offering for theft through oath — and to pay back the principal plus a *chomesh*, a fifth.

The critical asymmetry is this: *kefel* is triggered by witnesses; the *korban* and *chomesh* are triggered by admission. The *baraita* now distinguishes three scenarios based on the timing of each.

### Admission Before Witnesses…

If the bailee admitted to his false oath before witnesses arrived, he is exempt from *kefel* — since admission to a *knas* exempts one entirely, and crucially, according to this *baraita*, this exemption persists even if witnesses subsequently arrive. He pays only the *keren*, brings the *asham*, and adds the *chomesh*. The *kefel* is simply off the table.

### Admission After Witnesses

If witnesses arrived first and the bailee admitted afterward, both liabilities are now active. The witnesses established the *kefel* before the admission could forestall it, and the subsequent admission — even if it cannot affect the *kefel* — still carries weight for purposes of the *asham* and *chomesh*. There is something striking here: one might have thought that an admission made only after witnesses have already exposed the wrongdoing should count for nothing. Yet the tradition recognizes that the act of admitting guilt retains moral and legal significance even at that stage, for the purposes of *kapparah* and *teshuvah*.

### Oath Then Admission

The third case introduces a three-way dispute. Where witnesses came and the bailee later admitted, he pays *kefel* and brings the *asham*. The question is whether he also separately pays the *chomesh*. Rabbi Yaakov holds that the *chomesh* is subsumed within the *kefel* payment — conceptually, one counts toward the other. The *chachamim* disagree: their position, which they derive from the phrase *b'rosho v'chamishito* ("its principal and its fifth"), is that the *chomesh* obligation applies only when the base payment is the *keren* — the principal. When one's primary payment is *kefel*, no *chomesh* is added. The practical result for Rabbi Yaakov and the sages may be similar — no *chomesh* payment is made independently — but their reasoning differs: Rabbi Yaakov says it is conceptually absorbed into the *kefel*, while the sages say there is simply no obligation of *chomesh* in a *kefel* case. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai goes further still: not only is there no *chomesh* when the payment begins with *kefel* rather than *keren*, but there is no *asham korban* either.

## Chomesh in Kefel Debate

### Constant Value Problem

The Gemara now turns to interrogate Rabbi Yaakov's position. The notion that the *chomesh* can be said to be subsumed within the *kefel* presupposes that the two amounts are somehow equivalent or identifiable. But if the value of the object remained constant — say it was worth four throughout — then the *kefel* is four (the extra amount beyond the principal) and the *chomesh* is only one (a fifth of five, or equivalently a quarter of the principal). One cannot plausibly say that the one-*zuz chomesh* is subsumed within the four-*zuz kefel*, since they are manifestly distinct amounts.

### Value Decrease Solution

The Gemara resolves this by proposing a case in which the value of the object decreased between the time of the theft and the time of the court case. If it was worth four when stolen but only one by the time of adjudication, then — on Rav's ruling that *kefel* is assessed at the time of the court case — the *kefel* would be only one *zuz*, while the *chomesh* is also one *zuz* (a fifth of the principal of four, since the *chomesh* is based on the principal). Now the two amounts are equal, and it is intelligible to say the *kefel* and the *chomesh* overlap. This, then, is simultaneously a demonstration of how Rabbi Yaakov's position works and a support for Rav: the only way to construct a case where *kefel* and *chomesh* are the same amount is if *kefel* is assessed at the later, lower value — exactly as Rav holds.

### Rava's Multiple Oaths

Rava objects that this need not be a proof for Rav at all. He proposes that the case can be read even where the value remained at four throughout. How? If the bailee took four separate oaths — pressed to swear repeatedly by the owner — then upon admission he would owe a *chomesh* for each oath separately. The verse uses the plural *chamishisav* — "its fifths" — indicating that multiple *chomeshim* can accrue on a single principal. In such a case, four *chomeshim* of one *zuz* each would total four *zuzim*, equaling the *kefel* of four. Hence Rabbi Yaakov's position can be explained without any change in the object's value and without reference to Rav's principle. The apparent proof for Rav is therefore dissolved.

### Principal Triggers Chome…

The upshot of the exchange is that all opinions agree: the *chomesh* obligation is triggered only when the base payment is the *keren*, not the *kefel*. Whether the *kefel* "subsumes" the *chomesh* (Rabbi Yaakov) or the *chomesh* obligation simply does not arise in a *kefel* case (the *chachamim*), the practical result is that no additional *chomesh* is paid.

### Asham Korban Dispute

The debate between the *chachamim* and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai concerns the *asham korban*. Both hold that no *chomesh* is paid when the primary liability is *kefel*. The *chachamim* derive this from *b'rosho v'chamishito* — the *chomesh* is linked to paying the base principal. If, however, the *asham* is mentioned in the very next verse — *v'es ashamo yavi la'Hashem* — one might have thought the *asham* retains its independence even in a *kefel* case. The *chachamim* read the intervening text as severing the connection: the *asham* in the following verse stands on its own and is not similarly conditioned on the payment being a *keren*. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai disagrees, arguing that the word *v'et* reconnects the *asham* to the preceding conditions, so that just as the *chomesh* applies only when one begins with a base *keren* payment, so too the *asham* is brought only in such a case. The *chachamim* counter that *et* serves to demarcate rather than connect — the word separates the monetary payment owed to a person from the *korban* brought to Heaven, since it would be inappropriate to speak of both in a single breath. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, for his part, holds that *et* was necessary precisely to make that separation explicit, but that the substantive conditionality — beginning with *keren* — still governs both.

## Kinyanei Gneivah Models

### Two Models Explained

Having concluded the discussion of *kefel*, *chomesh*, and the *asham*, the Gemara now pivots to a topic that will occupy much of the remainder of the chapter: the various ways in which a thief acquires ownership of a stolen object. This framework of *kinyanei gneivah* is worth introducing with some conceptual clarity before examining the specific cases.

There are two distinct theoretical models for how a thief can take legal possession of something that was not given to him. The first model treats it as an affirmative act of *kinyan*: just as a normal buyer acquires through *meshichah* or *hagbahah*, a thief who performs some sufficiently transformative act on the object is understood to have forcibly taken possession of it, turning it from something belonging to the original owner into something that is now his. The act of physical change is itself the mechanism of acquisition.

The second model is grounded not in an act of taking but in the removal of an obligation to return. The Torah states *v'heshiv et hagezeilah asher gazal* — that one must return the stolen object as it was. If the object is no longer in its original state, the thief is no longer obligated to return the object itself; he need only pay its monetary value. According to this model, it is not that the thief actively acquires the object — rather, once his obligation to return it falls away, he naturally retains it, since he already had some measure of possession from the moment of the theft.

### Shinuy Ma'aseh

The clearest and most uncontested form of *kinyan* through transformation is *shinuy ma'aseh* — a physical act that changes the object. The thief steals wood and fashions it into a box; he steals wool and weaves it into a garment. This kind of transformation satisfies both conceptual models simultaneously: the thief has actively done something to make the object his own, and the object is now so different that the Torah's obligation to return "what was stolen" no longer applies to this new thing. *Shinuy ma'aseh* thus has the strongest claim to effect acquisition.

### Shinuy Hashem

*Shinuy hashem* — a change of name — refers to a natural transformation that the thief did not actively cause. A lamb grows into a ram; a calf becomes an ox. This differs from *shinuy ma'aseh* in a critical respect: no act of the thief produced the change. The object evolved on its own. One might argue that this still results in a new object with a new name — and therefore triggers acquisition — but one might equally argue that since nothing was done to it, it is simply the same thing at a later stage of its natural development. This is precisely the debate that will be explored below.

### Yeush Concept

*Yeiush* — the owner's despair of ever recovering the lost or stolen object — represents yet another model. When an owner gives up hope, his psychological and practical connection to the object is severed. If the thief continues to hold the object after *yeiush* occurs, there is a tradition that acquisition takes effect. This is more akin to the first model of an act of *kinyan* — not a transformation of the object, but a combination of the owner's abandonment and the thief's continued possession. The important question, however, is whether *yeiush* by itself is sufficient, or whether some additional element is required.

### Yeush & Shinuy Reshut

A final category combines *yeiush* with *shinuy reshut* — a change of domain. The thief steals an object, the owner despairs, and then the thief transfers the object to a third party. From that third party's perspective, the object came into his possession after *yeiush* had already occurred, and this combination — *yeiush* followed by a genuine change of hands — is widely accepted as effecting acquisition. The dynamics of each of these models will now be examined through the cases that follow.

## Calf-to-Ox Case

### Rabbi Ila's Position

Rabbi Ila states: if one stole a lamb and it became a ram, or a calf and it became an ox, a *shinuy* has occurred in the thief's possession and he has thereby acquired it. The consequence is significant: if the thief then slaughters or sells the animal, he is doing so with something that already belongs to him. Therefore, he would not be liable to pay four or five, since the four-and-five penalty applies only to slaughtering or selling a *stolen* animal — one that still belongs to its original owner.

### Baraita Challenge

Rabbi Chanina challenges this from a *baraita*: if one stole a lamb and it became a ram, or a calf and it became an ox, one pays *kefel* and the four-and-five payment as of the time of the theft. This *baraita* poses a double difficulty. First, it contradicts Rav, since it assesses the payment at the time of theft rather than at the time of standing in court. Second, and more directly relevant here, it contradicts Rabbi Ila — for if the thief had already acquired the animal when it changed, why is he paying four or five at all? You cannot be penalized for slaughtering your own property.

### Rabbi Ila's Response

Rabbi Ila responds: even accepting the *baraita*, ask yourself — what does *shinuy hashem* accomplish in this case? He argues that the natural change is indeed *not* sufficient for the thief to acquire the object; it happened by itself, without any act on the thief's part, and therefore does not constitute the kind of transformation that effects acquisition. However — and this is Rabbi Ila's crucial move — the very same naturalness that prevents acquisition also prevents the *kefel* and four-and-five from being assessed based on the *current* value of the now-grown animal. For the thief can say: did I steal an ox from you? Did I steal a ram from you? No — I stole a calf, I stole a lamb. Just as the Gemara noted earlier that the thief does not pay *kefel* for the added value from fattening an animal (since he did not steal that added value), here too the thief pays *kefel* based on the value of what was actually stolen. The *kefel* is a double of the stolen object — and what was stolen was a calf, not a cow. Hence the *baraita* says you pay based on the time of the theft, meaning based on the object as it was when stolen, not based on the current transformed animal.

### Mutual Rejection

The exchange ends in a striking way. Rabbi Chanina said to Rabbi Ila: *Rachmana litzlan me'hai da'ata* — "Heaven save us from such an opinion." Rabbi Ila responded in kind: *addaraba, Rachmana litzlan mida'ata didach* — "On the contrary, Heaven save us from *your* opinion." This kind of direct and symmetrical rhetorical rejection is unusual. The underlying logic of each rejection, however, is intelligible. From one side: if you concede that the animal has become sufficiently different that you will not pay four or five based on its current form — acknowledging it as a distinct object — then you should equally concede that the thief has acquired it. From the other side: recognizing an object as different enough to anchor the calculation of the penalty does not mean the thief has performed a *kinyan* on it; a natural change he did not cause cannot simultaneously exempt him from returning the object and from the penalty. Both positions remain coherent, and the Gemara treats the impasse as genuine.

## Rabbi Zeira Challenge

### New Name Question

Rabbi Zeira now presses from a different angle. Granted that the transformation from calf to ox happened naturally — does it not at least constitute a *shinuy hashem*, a change of name sufficient to effect acquisition? Even if one argues that the thief's lack of active involvement prevents the change from functioning like *shinuy ma'aseh*, the simple fact that the animal is now called by a different name — no longer a *egel* but a *shor*, no longer a *taleh* but an *ayil* — might independently suffice.

### Rava's Name Response

Rava addresses this by challenging the premise that there has been a genuine change of name at all. He cites two prooftexts. First, the verse *shor o chesev o ez ki yivaled* — "an ox, a sheep, or a goat when it is born" — indicates that an animal is called *shor* from the moment of birth. Second, from *ve'eilei tzonecha lo achalti* — Yaakov's statement to Lavan that he did not eat his *eilim* — Rava infers that *ayil* likewise applies from birth, for surely Yaakov did not mean he refrained from eating rams but helped himself to lambs. Thus, a one-day-old ox is already called an ox, and a one-day-old ram is already called a ram. The calf and the ox share the same categorical name from birth; the growth from young to mature does not introduce a genuinely new name. Without a new name, there is no *shinuy hashem*.

### Contradiction Remains

Yet this answer, while resolving the *shinuy hashem* question in principle, does not dissolve the tension with the *baraita*. Even after Rava's response, the contradiction against Rabbi Ila remains: the *baraita* says one pays four or five even after the animal has grown, which — on Rabbi Ila's view that natural change effects acquisition — should never happen. The Gemara notes: *mikol makom kashya* — regardless of Rava's point about names, the contradiction to Rabbi Ila stands.

## Rav Sheshet Resolution

### Beit Shammai Position

Rav Sheshet resolves the difficulty by identifying the author of the *baraita*. The *baraita* that imposes four-and-five liability even after the animal changes reflects the position of Beit Shammai, who hold *shinuy bimkomo omedes* — a change stays in its place. Beit Shammai simply do not recognize transformation as creating a new object. For them, the changed object is still, legally and conceptually, the original object. Therefore, there is no acquisition through *shinuy*, and the animal remains the owner's property regardless of its growth, requiring the full payment.

### Prostitute Fee Debate

Where do we find that Beit Shammai hold this principle? The Gemara turns to a *baraita* concerning *etnan zonah* — the fee given to a prostitute — which cannot be brought as a *korban*. The question is whether this prohibition applies to a transformed version of what was given. If one gave wheat as the fee and she ground it into flour, or gave olives and she made them into oil, or grapes made into wine — is the transformed product still forbidden? One *baraita* rules it forbidden, another permits it. Rav Yosef cites a tradition that this is precisely the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: Beit Shammai forbid the transformed product; Beit Hillel permit it.

### Beit Shammai's Proof

Beit Shammai derive their position from the word *gam* in the verse: *ki so'avat Hashem Elokecha gam sheneihem* — "for they are both an abomination before your God." The word *gam* serves to expand the prohibition and includes the transformed versions of these objects — *le-rabbos shinuiyyehem*, to encompass their changed forms. What was given retains its forbidden status through any transformation.

### Beit Hillel's Counter

Beit Hillel read the same verse differently. The operative word is *hem* — "they" — embedded in *sheneihem*: it is *they* that are an abomination, *velo shinuiyyehem* — but not their transformed versions. The changed object is a different object and is no longer included in the prohibition. Additionally, *hem velo veladoseihem* — the prohibition does not extend to offspring, since offspring too are a different category. Thus, Beit Hillel derives two exclusions from *hem*: transformed products are permitted, and offspring are permitted.

The word *gam*, which seems to favor Beit Shammai, poses a difficulty for Beit Hillel. The Gemara acknowledges: *gam le-Veit Hillel kashya* — that word is a problem for Beit Hillel's reading.

## Foundation Principles

### Changed Object Principle

Before the question of *kinyan gneivah* can even be addressed, there is a prior and more fundamental question: are we willing to look at a transformed object as a new object at all? This is the conceptual threshold that must be crossed before discussing whether a thief acquires through *shinuy*. If the answer is no — if we insist the object, even after transformation, is still the original object — then there is no basis on which to speak of a new entity that the thief might acquire.

### Recognition Framework

This is precisely the divide between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Beit Shammai, by refusing to recognize a transformed object as new, eliminate the entire discussion of *kinyan* through *shinuy* at the threshold. There is nothing to acquire; there is only the original object, still in its original legal identity, regardless of what has been done to it. Beit Hillel, by contrast, acknowledge the transformed object as a genuinely new entity. That recognition is the first step — once a transformation is acknowledged as producing something new, then one can proceed to ask whether a *ganav* has acquired it.

It is important to note, as one might fairly observe, that Beit Shammai's underlying position in the *etnan* debate need not have been intended as a universal principle about all transformations throughout *halacha*. The *baraita* is about a specific prohibition, and the *gam* could have been interpreted narrowly. It is the Gemara that reads from Beit Shammai's ruling a broader conceptual stance — namely, that they never recognize an object as genuinely new after transformation. Whether that is what Beit Shammai originally intended is a separate question, but it is the Gemara's reading, and it is what makes Rav Sheshet's resolution work: the *baraita* requiring payment of four and five even after the animal's growth is Beit Shammai's, who refuse to see the grown animal as anything other than the original stolen animal.

## Rava's Identity Answer

### Four-Word Answer

The Gemara now returns to the direct challenge to Rav from the *baraita* that says *kefel* and four-and-five are paid *ke-sha'at hagneivah* — as of the time of the theft — which seems to contradict Rav's view that *kefel* is assessed at the time the case is adjudicated. Rava offers a terse resolution: *sheit kide'mei ikara, damim k'shel achshav* — the object is assessed according to its original identity, but the monetary value is assessed as of now.

### Tosafot's Explanation

Tosafot explains this answer by invoking the principle that already emerged in the exchange between Rabbi Ila and Rabbi Chanina. The *kefel* and four-and-five are always multiples of the *object that was stolen* — not of whatever object happens to be present at the time of the court case. If a calf was stolen and it has since grown into an ox, the four-and-five is four or five times the calf, not the ox. That is what *ke-sha'at hagneivah* means: you are paying based on the identity of the stolen object. However, once we have established that we are paying for a calf, we can still ask: at what price do we value a calf — the price when it was stolen or today's market price for calves? Here, Rav's principle applies: the monetary valuation of the *kefel* is assessed at the time of the court case. Thus, *ke-sha'at hagneivah* addresses the identity of the object — what unit are you multiplying — while *ke-sha'at amida badin* addresses the market price assigned to that unit.

### Rashi's Alternative

Rashi offers a somewhat different reading. Rather than a question about whether the object has changed, he frames the issue as a question about the units of payment. If the thief wishes to repay in kind — returning the same type of object he stole — then the payment is assessed at the original value. But if he wishes to pay in cash, the assessment is at today's market price. The conceptual foundation is similar — is one paying back an object or a monetary obligation? — though the application differs. Tosafot's explanation has the advantage of connecting most naturally to the reasoning already developed in the Gemara, and it makes the most intuitive sense given the cases examined: you owe four times the sheep you stole, not four times the ram now standing before the court.

## Shinuy Acquisition Proof

### Biblical Source

Rabbah now steps back to establish the very foundation of *kinyan* through *shinuy* — that it is supported both by a biblical source and by Tannaitic tradition. The Torah states *v'heshiv et hagezeilah asher gazal* — one must return the stolen object as it was stolen. The phrase *asher gazal* is interpreted to mean: you must return it *in the way in which you stole it*, i.e., in the same condition. If the object is *ke-ein shegazal* — in the same form — then you return the object itself. But if it is no longer in that form — because the thief has transformed it — then the obligation to return the object falls away, and the thief pays money but keeps the transformed object. The object has, in effect, become his.

### Mishnaic Source

The Talmudic tradition supports this as well. A later *mishnah* in the tractate states: if one stole wood and fashioned it into vessels, or stole wool and wove it into garments, he pays the value of what he stole — *ke-sha'at hagezeilah* — but he does not return the now-finished product. The owner receives the monetary value of the raw materials; the thief retains the box, the garment, the completed object. This is the practical expression of *kinyan* through *shinuy ma'aseh*.

### Dyeing Wool Source

An additional source is drawn from a different area of *halacha* entirely. When one shears his flock, he is obligated to give *reishit hagez* — the first of the shearings — to a *kohen*. If one sheared the requisite amount and thereby incurred the obligation but then dyed the wool before transferring it, he is exempt from giving it to the *kohen* — *patur*. The dyed wool is no longer considered the same object. This is presented as further evidence that *shinuy* effects acquisition, or at minimum that transformation severs the object from its prior legal status. One might note that the degree of transformation here — dyeing and presumably processing raw wool into marketable colored threads — is not trivial, and likely encompasses more than a mere change of color.

## Yeush Acquisition Status

### Yeush Status Question

Rabbah acknowledges that *yeiush* works — there is a rabbinic tradition to that effect — but he is uncertain whether its basis is biblical or rabbinic. The question matters greatly for the strength of the acquisition and its downstream consequences.

### Lost Object Parallel

The natural comparison is to *motzei aveidah* — finding a lost object. If an owner loses an object and despairs of recovering it, and a finder then picks it up, the finder is permitted to keep it. The reasoning is that the owner's *yeiush* severs whatever remained of his psychological and practical connection to the object. His ownership, already weakened by the object's having left his physical control, is finally dissolved when he mentally abandons it as well. At that point, the object is available for the finder to take into his possession.

### Key Difference

The obvious difference between *aveidah* and *gneivah* is the timing of the *yeiush* relative to when the object entered the second party's possession. By a lost object, the *yeiush* must occur *before* the finder picks it up. Once a finder has taken the object with the intent to return it, he holds it on the owner's behalf — it is, as it were, back in the owner's domain through the finder's custodial role. *Yeiush* that occurs *after* this point does not help the finder, because the finder's holding is not adverse to the owner's interest; it is in service of it. The analogy offered is striking: if someone believed their wallet was lost on the street and gave up hope, yet all along it was sitting in their own backyard — and then someone walked into the backyard and picked it up, pointing to the *yeiush* — that would obviously not suffice, because the object was effectively within the owner's sphere all along.

### Yeush Analysis

The case of the thief is structurally different. From the moment the thief takes the object, every second of his holding is actively adverse to the owner's interest. He is not a custodian; he is an adversary. Therefore, when the owner subsequently has *yeiush* — gives up hope of recovering the object from this active adversary — the situation is not comparable to *yeiush* occurring while a finder holds it benevolently. In that sense, one might argue that *yeiush* by a thief is effective even though it occurs after the taking, because the thief's possession has always been a form of drawing the object away from the owner rather than preserving it for him.

### Rabbinic Yeush

Alternatively, the Gemara proposes, perhaps *yeiush* by a thief is only rabbinic — not because the logic of *yeiush* fails, but as a considered policy decision. The Rabbis allowed the thief to keep the object and merely pay its value, as a *takkanat hashavim*, an enactment to encourage those who have stolen to come forward and make restitution. If the law required returning the actual object no matter what, thieves would be reluctant to confess, since by doing so they would lose whatever they had made of the stolen goods. By allowing the thief to keep the transformed or long-held object and pay the original value, the Rabbis made the path of repentance easier.

## Rav Yosef's Position

### Yeush Alone Fails

Rav Yosef disagrees with Rabbah's entire framing. In his view, *yeiush* by itself does not effect acquisition — not even rabbinically. The thief who has stolen an object and whose owner subsequently despairs must still return the original object if it remains intact; he has not acquired it through *yeiush* alone.

### Yeush With Transfer

What *does* work, according to Rav Yosef, is *yeiush v'shinuy reshut* — *yeiush* combined with a transfer to a third party. If the thief steals the object, the owner has *yeiush*, and then the thief sells or gives the object to someone else, *that* third party acquires it fully. From the third party's perspective, the object came into his hands after *yeiush* had already occurred — analogous to the finder who picks up a lost object after the owner has despaired. The acquisition is clean. This is the position accepted by most *rishonim* as the normative ruling.

### Thief's Prior Possession

The logic is that the thief's pre-*yeiush* possession prevents *yeiush* alone from severing the owner's claim. The thief came into possession of the object through an act of violation — *be'issura ata l'yadei* — and that tainted beginning is not cleansed simply by the owner's subsequent despair. The *yeiush* occurred too late, in the wrong sequence, to do the work it does by a lost object. Only when the object moves to a third party who received it after *yeiush* does the acquisition take hold. Tomorrow's discussion will develop the practical implications of this debate between Rabbah and Rav Yosef.

# Bava Kamma 66

## Rabbah vs. Rav Yosef

### Ye'ush Acquisition

The daf opens in the midst of a *machlokes* between Rabbah and Rav Yosef on whether *ye'ush* — the despair or relinquishment of hope by the original owner — effects a *kinyan* for a *ganav*. Rav Yosef holds that *ye'ush* has no effect whatsoever: the *ganav* does not acquire the stolen object through the owner's despair alone. Rabbah, by contrast, holds that *ye'ush* does create a *kinyan* for the *ganav*. The discussion that preceded this point also touched on *shinui ma'aseh* and *shinui hashem* — physical transformation and change of name — as additional mechanisms that might, independently or in combination with *ye'ush*, effect an acquisition.

### Chametz over Pesach

Rav Yosef, who holds *ye'ush* has no effect, raises a challenge against Rabbah, who holds that it does. The case is *gazal chametz v'avar alav ha-pesach* — someone stole another's *chametz* just before Pesach, and the holiday came and went while the *chametz* remained in the *ganav*'s possession. The relevant background is the rabbinic *knas* governing *chametz she'avar alav ha-pesach*: if one possessed *chametz* throughout Pesach without selling it, declaring it ownerless, or otherwise disposing of it, the *chametz* becomes completely worthless after the holiday — forbidden for consumption, sale, or any use. The penalty applies regardless of fault.

In this case, as Pesach approaches, the original owner despairs of recovering his stolen *chametz*. He does not want it back; even if it were returned at that moment, it would be of no use. There is *vadai ye'ush* — certain, unambiguous despair. Rav Yosef's challenge runs as follows: if *ye'ush* is *koneh*, then the *ganav* acquired the *chametz* through the owner's despair, and the *ganav* must therefore pay its value — he cannot simply return it with *harei shelcha lefanecha*, "here is yours before you." Yet in practice, the *ganav* can say *harei shelcha lefanecha* and discharge his obligation by returning the object. This suggests that *ye'ush* is not *koneh*, for if it were, the object would have become the *ganav*'s property and he would owe *damim* rather than being permitted to return the thing itself.

### Neither Wants It

Rabbah responds that this case is atypical and cannot serve as a challenge to his general position. In a normal case of theft, he explains, there are effectively two parties to the event: the *ganav* actively wants to possess the stolen item — that is why he stole it — and at some point the owner despairs of recovering it. The *ye'ush* of the owner combines with the desire of the *ganav* to complete the acquisition. The *chametz* case, however, is entirely different. Not only does the owner not want the *chametz* back — it would be useless to him — but the *ganav* himself does not want it either, since possessing *chametz she'avar alav ha-pesach* would render him in violation of a Torah prohibition. Neither party wants the object, and so the normal dynamic of *ye'ush* cannot operate. The case is therefore sui generis and provides no general proof against Rabbah's position.

### Stolen Korban

Abaye raises a separate challenge, this one from the laws of *korbanot*. The verse states *korbano v'lo ha-gazul* — one may only bring his own sacrifice, not a stolen one. The question is: what case does this verse address? If it speaks of a case *lifnei ye'ush* — before the owner has despaired — then it is entirely obvious that a stolen animal cannot be brought as a *korban*. Would God accept such a thing? No verse would be necessary to teach this. The verse must therefore be speaking of a case *achar ye'ush* — after the owner has already despaired. And yet even then, the verse teaches that the *korban* is invalid, implying that *ye'ush* does not effect a *kinyan* and the stolen animal remains the owner's — which is a direct challenge to Rabbah.

### God's Domain

Rava responds on Rabbah's behalf. He points to a parallel formulation: *mishkavo v'lo ha-gazul* — the bed of a *zav* transmits impurity only if it is his own bed, not a stolen one. What case does *this* verse address? If the *ganav* took someone's raw wool and wove it into a blanket — a classic *shinui ma'aseh* — there is no dispute that it is now his; everyone agrees that a real physical transformation acquires the object for the thief. The verse cannot be addressing such a case. Rather, it must be addressing a case where someone stole an actual bed — no transformation at all — and then lay on it in a state of *tumah*. The verse teaches that this does not convey *tumah* to the bed, because the stolen object is not truly *his*. So too with *korbano v'lo ha-gazul*: the verse is not speaking about someone who stole an ordinary *chullin* animal and attempted to bring it as a *korban* after *ye'ush*, but rather about someone who stole a *korban* that was already consecrated and attempted to offer it. A consecrated animal is already, in a sense, in God's domain — *b'gaza deRachmana* — and the concept of *ye'ush* simply does not apply there. God does not relinquish ownership in the manner that a human owner does. These cases therefore tell us nothing about whether *ye'ush* is *koneh* in ordinary circumstances.

---

## Tumat Orot

### Thief's Machshavah

Having defended Rabbah's position against challenges, the Gemara now turns to challenge Rav Yosef, who holds that *ye'ush* is not *koneh*. Abaye raises a challenge from the laws of *tumah* as they apply to hides — *tumat orot*.

A raw piece of leather is not *mekabel tumah* in its unprocessed state. Whether it becomes susceptible to *tumah* depends on what the owner intends to use it for and how finished it is. The relevant *mishnah* teaches: *oros shel ba'al ha-bayit machshavah metam'asan* — the hides of a private householder: his *machshavah*, his intention, renders them susceptible to *tumah*. If he decides the hide is finished and ready for use, that thought is sufficient. *Veshel avdan ein machshavah metam'asan* — but the hides of a professional tanner: his *machshavah* does not suffice, because the final determination belongs to the customer who will use the hide, not the craftsman who processed it.

Then comes the critical ruling: *shel ganav machshavah metam'asan* — if a *ganav* stole a hide, his *machshavah* does render it susceptible to *tumah*. *Shel gazlan ein machshavah metam'asan* — but a *gazlan*'s *machshavah* does not. The reasoning offered is that a *gazlan* robs openly and is known; the original owner can identify him, pursue him, and may well recover the stolen property. The owner therefore has not despaired, and since *ye'ush* has not occurred, the property has not been acquired by the *gazlan*, and his *machshavah* carries no legal weight. The *ganav*, by contrast, steals secretly; the owner does not know who took the object, despairs of recovering it, and *ye'ush* has occurred.

Rabbi Shimon reverses the ruling: *shel gazlan machshavah metam'asan* — the *gazlan*'s *machshavah* does render it susceptible to *tumah*, because the owner sees how brazen and powerful the robber is and despairs immediately. *Veshel ganav ein machshavah metam'asan* — the *ganav*'s *machshavah* does not, because the owner has not yet despaired; he hopes the investigation will uncover the thief and the object will be recovered.

The challenge to Rav Yosef is clear: according to both the first *tanna* and Rabbi Shimon, *ye'ush* occurs for at least one of the two — *ganav* or *gazlan* — and in that case the thief's *machshavah* is effective. This presupposes that the thief has acquired the object through *ye'ush*, and his intention consequently carries legal force. But Rav Yosef maintains *ye'ush* is not *koneh* at all. *Shema mina ye'ush kaneh* — one ought to conclude from this *mishnah* that *ye'ush* is indeed *koneh*.

### No Trimming Needed

Rav Yosef attempts to deflect the challenge by arguing that the case in the *mishnah* is not one of pure *ye'ush* alone, but involves a *shinui ma'aseh* as well. Specifically, he suggests the case concerns *kitze'an* — the *ganav* trimmed the hide a little. The trimming constitutes a minor act of transformation; combined with *ye'ush*, this is what renders the acquisition effective and the *machshavah* operative.

Rabba bar Rav Chanan objects: the *mishnah* about the hides follows immediately upon a longer discussion involving a specific object, an *itzba* — a type of tray or mat. The earlier *mishnah* states the principle: *kol makom she-ein chisron melachah machshavah metam'asan* — wherever no further work remains to be done on the hide, *machshavah* alone renders it susceptible to *tumah*. *Yesh chisron melachah ein machshavah metam'asan* — if work remains to be done, *machshavah* is insufficient. The exception is an *itzba*, which does not require any further *melachah* even where a *chisron melachah* would otherwise be relevant.

The force of the objection is this: Rav Yosef proposed that the case involves trimming — a minor *shinui ma'aseh* — combined with *ye'ush*. But the preceding *mishnah* teaches that for an *itzba* specifically, no *melachah* at all is needed. The case of the *ganav* is drawn from this context, meaning no trimming is required. *Itzba lo tzericha kitzu'a* — the *itzba* needs no trimming. Therefore, *ye'ush* alone appears to be operative, and Rav Yosef's deflection fails.

### Shinui Hashem

Rava then reports a remarkable detail: this very difficulty had been pressing Rav Yosef for twenty-two years — *esrin ve-tartein shanin* — and he had no answer. Only when Rav Yosef became *Rosh Yeshiva* was he finally able to resolve it, suggesting, as the Gemara implies, that his elevated position brought with it a corresponding elevation in *siyata de-shamaya*.

The answer Rav Yosef ultimately gave is: *shinui hashem ke-shinui ma'aseh dami* — a change of name is legally equivalent to a physical change. The case of the *itzba* may require no trimming, but it does involve a *shinui hashem*. Before the *ganav* stole the hide, it was simply a piece of leather — *mashka*, as the Gemara puts it. Now, in the hands of the *ganav*, it is being used and designated as a tray or mat, and is called something different: *arveza*. This change of designation, even without any physical transformation, constitutes a recognized *shinui*. Combined with *ye'ush*, it is sufficient to render the *ganav* the owner and give his *machshavah* legal effect.

The distinction being drawn is precise. If the *ganav* stole a sheep and it is still the identical sheep two days later — same adult ram, same appearance, nothing done to it — there is neither *shinui ma'aseh* nor *shinui hashem*, and Rav Yosef would say *ye'ush* alone accomplishes nothing. But in the case of the hide, even without physical alteration, the object now bears a different name and serves a different function in the household context. That suffices to qualify as a *shinui*, and it is *ye'ush* together with this *shinui hashem* — not *ye'ush* in isolation — that accomplishes the acquisition. The challenge from the *itzba* therefore does not undermine Rav Yosef's core position, because that case was never a case of pure *ye'ush* to begin with.

---

## Reversible Shinui

### Stolen Beam Case

Having established that *shinui hashem* functions like *shinui ma'aseh*, the Gemara probes the limits of this principle. If a *shinui hashem* is sufficient to effect acquisition together with *ye'ush*, one would expect it to work consistently. But there is a famous case that creates a difficulty — *mareish ha-gazul she-bano be-vira*: a stolen beam that one has built into the roof of one's house.

The Gemara notes that in this case, before Pesach even enters the picture, there is an apparent *shinui hashem*: what was previously a *keshura* — a beam in its raw state at the lumberyard — is now a *tafala*, a rafter integrated into the roof of a building. That is a change of name and function. And yet the well-known *takanah* — *takanat ha-shavim* — presupposes that absent this special enactment to facilitate repentance, the *ganav* would be required to demolish his house and return the actual beam. The *takanat ha-shavim* is needed precisely because the law would otherwise demand the return of the object itself; we relax that requirement only so as not to discourage *baalei teshuvah* from making restitution at all. This implies that *shinui hashem* alone did not transfer ownership to the *ganav* — the beam still belongs to the original owner — which stands in tension with Rav Yosef's answer that *shinui hashem* suffices.

Rav Yosef responds: the beam has not actually undergone a *shinui hashem*. A beam is still called a beam even when it is installed in a roof. The Gemara supports this from the book of Yechezkel, whose description of construction in the third *Beit HaMikdash* uses the term for beams — *marei shem* — even in the context of a completed structure. So the two by four that was at the lumberyard is still called a beam after it is placed in the roof. The name has not changed. Therefore, the beam case does not challenge the position that *shinui hashem* is effective, because in the beam case there is simply no *shinui hashem* to speak of. The case of the *itzba* and the tray, by contrast, does constitute a genuine change of name.

### Reversible Shinui

Rav Zeira offers an alternative resolution. Rather than arguing that the beam case involves no *shinui hashem* at all, Rav Zeira distinguishes between reversible and irreversible changes of name. The principle he articulates is: *shinui ha-chozer le-veryato be-shinui hashem lo havei shinui* — a *shinui hashem* that can revert to its original state is not a valid *shinui*. In the case of the beam, if the house were to collapse, the beam would simply be the same beam as before. Nothing was done to alter it permanently — it was not dyed, shaped, carved, or molded. It was simply placed in a supporting role. Since the *shinui* is reversible, it is not a legally cognizable *shinui*, and this is why the *takanat ha-shavim* is necessary: without it, the *ganav* would have to return the beam because he never truly acquired it through a reversible change of name. The case of the *itzba* or the tray that is genuinely repurposed and given a new designation, particularly where some work has been done to it, involves an irreversible *shinui hashem* and thus does qualify.

### Pipe Case

The Gemara then tests Rav Zeira's formulation: if a reversible *shinui hashem* does not qualify, is it conversely true that an irreversible *shinui hashem* always does? The Gemara raises the case of a *tzinor* — a wooden pipe. If one takes a block of wood, hollows it out to make a pipe, and then attaches it to the ground so that rainwater flows through it into a pit serving as a *mikveh*, the pipe is *posel* — it invalidates the *mikveh* — because the water passes through a vessel that carries *torat keli*, the legal status of a vessel, and is thus considered *mayim she'uvim*, drawn water. However, if one first plants the block of wood into the ground and only afterward hollows it out, the resulting pipe does not invalidate the *mikveh*.

The question posed is: if an irreversible *shinui hashem* always effects acquisition — since a hollowed wooden pipe cannot simply un-hollow itself — then in the second case, where the block was first planted in the ground and then hollowed out, there has been an irreversible *shinui hashem* from block to pipe. Should this not also be *posel* the *mikveh*? Why does the order of operations matter?

### Kelli Status

The response distinguishes the two cases not on the basis of *shinui hashem* but on the basis of *torat keli*. The prohibition of *mayim she'uvim* in a *mikveh* is itself rabbinic in origin, and even within that rabbinic framework, the determinative question is whether the object had the status of a *keli* at the relevant moment. In the first case — where the block was hollowed out first and then attached to the ground — before it was affixed to the ground it was already a *keli*, a completed vessel. Water flowing through a *keli* is *she'uvin*. In the second case — where the block was first planted into the ground and only then hollowed out — at the moment of affixing it to the ground, it was still just a block of wood, not a *keli*. It never had *torat keli* at the time it was attached, and therefore the water flowing through it is not considered *she'uvin*.

The upshot is that the *tzinor* case is resolved not by challenging or refining the principle of *shinui hashem*, but by reference to the independent legal category of *keli* status. The position of Rav Yosef remains intact: a case of pure *ye'ush* alone does not transfer ownership, but *ye'ush* combined with a genuine *shinui* — whether *shinui ma'aseh* or an irreversible *shinui hashem* — is effective. The challenges raised from these various cases have all been addressed, and the Gemara affirms that no one has yet mounted a successful challenge against the core of Rav Yosef's position.

---

## Consecration Cases

### Thief Consecrates

The Gemara raises another potential challenge to Rav Yosef. The *mishnah* states: *ha-ganav ve-ha-gazlan ve-ha-annasin — hikdishan hekdesh, u-terumatan terumah, u-ma'aseratan ma'aser* — a thief, a robber, or one who takes by force: if they consecrate stolen property, it is *hekdesh*; if they separate *terumah* from it, it is valid *terumah*; if they separate *ma'aser*, it is valid *ma'aser*. Prima facie, this is a challenge to Rav Yosef: if *ye'ush* is not *koneh*, how can the *ganav* consecrate or separate *terumah* or *ma'aser* from property that is not his?

### Status Change

Rav Yosef answers: these cases all involve a *shinui hashem*. When one steals *tevel* — untithed produce — and separates *terumah* from it, the *tevel* before separation is called *tevel*, and afterward it is called *terumah*. It is a different legal category entirely, governed by its own rules of sanctity and restriction. When one steals an ordinary *chullin* animal and consecrates it as a *korban*, the animal was *chullin* before and is *hekdesh* afterward — a genuine and irreversible *shinui hashem*. These are therefore not cases of pure *ye'ush*; they are cases of *ye'ush* combined with a *shinui hashem*. Rav Yosef's position remains that in a case of pure *ye'ush* without any *shinui* whatsoever, no acquisition takes place.

---

## Rav Yonatan Teachings

### Shinui Koneh

The Gemara now presents two teachings transmitted in the name of Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Yonatan, which are striking because they are diametrically opposed — and both are derived from the very same verse.

The first teaching: *minayin le-shinui shehu koneh* — from where do we know that *shinui* effects acquisition for a thief? The source is the verse *ve-heshiv et ha-gezelah asher gazal* — he shall return the stolen object which he stole. The question is: what does the phrase *asher gazal* add? It would seem self-evident that one returns the stolen object that one stole rather than something else. The answer is that the verse is establishing a condition: only if the object remains in the state in which it was stolen — *ke-ein she-gazal* — must it be returned in kind. If not — *ve-im lav* — monetary compensation suffices. The verse is thus teaching that *shinui* creates a new legal reality; the object need not be returned because the *shinui* has transferred ownership, and the *nigzal* receives *damim* instead.

### Shinui Lo Koneh

The second teaching: *minayin le-shinui she-eino koneh* — from where do we know that *shinui* does not effect acquisition? Also from the same verse: *ve-heshiv et ha-gezelah* — he returns *the* stolen object, in any condition, regardless of transformation. The *ganav* must always return the object itself because *shinui* carries no acquisitive power. The phrase *asher gazal* in this reading is not limiting the return to cases of unchanged objects; rather, it is the source for the law that the heirs of a thief who return stolen property on behalf of their deceased father are not required to add the *chomesh* — the one-fifth surcharge — that the father himself would have owed upon voluntary confession. The verse thus exclusively informs the *chomesh* law, leaving *ve-heshiv et ha-gezelah* to teach an unrestricted obligation to return the stolen object. As the Gemara notes, both sets of laws can be derived simultaneously from the two clauses of the verse, depending on which reading one adopts.

### Ye'ush Irrelevant

Ulla now advances an independent proof that *ye'ush* is not *koneh*. He derives it from the verse: *vahasatem gazul ve-et ha-pisach ve-et ha-choleh* — you bring before God that which is stolen, lame, and sick. God rejects all of these as unfit *korbanot*. Ulla argues that *gazul* must be understood *dumya de-pisach* — by analogy to *pisach*, the lame animal. A lame animal has no remedy; as long as it is lame, it cannot be brought as a *korban*, regardless of any circumstance. So too a stolen animal: it cannot be brought as a *korban* regardless of circumstances — *velo shna lifnei ye'ush velo shna le-achar ye'ush*. Whether *ye'ush* has occurred or not makes no difference. The stolen animal can never be offered, which implies that *ye'ush* does not transfer ownership.

### Rava Counter

Rava articulates a competing position from a different verse: *korbano v'lo ha-gazul* — his offering, but not a stolen one. The question is again what case the verse is addressing. If it speaks of a case before *ye'ush*, it is entirely obvious — no verse is needed. The verse must therefore be addressing a case after *ye'ush*. And from the fact that even after *ye'ush* the stolen animal cannot be offered, one derives: *shma mina ye'ush lo kani* — *ye'ush* does not effect a *kinyan*.

One might ask: did not Rava earlier explain *korbano v'lo ha-gazul* differently — as referring specifically to a case where the *ganav* stole a consecrated animal (*korban dechavreih*) rather than a *chullin* animal that he later tried to consecrate? The Gemara acknowledges this tension and resolves it either by saying that Rava retracted his earlier position — *hadar beih* — or that one of these two contrary opinions attributed to Rava was in fact stated by Rav Pappa. In any event, what the Gemara is establishing through these latter two teachings is a reinforcement of the view that *ye'ush* is not *koneh*.

---

## Arba'ah V'Chamishah

### Only Shor/Seh

The *mishnah* states that the law of multiple payments — *tashlumei arba'ah va-chamishah*, paying four or five times the value — applies exclusively to an *ox* and a *sheep*, and to no other animal. One who steals a donkey, a goat, or any other animal and slaughters or sells it does not incur these multiplied payments. The question is why the law is restricted in this way.

One might have thought to derive a broader principle by analogy to *Shabbat*. The verse in *Shabbat* mentions *shorcha va-chamorcha* — your ox and your donkey — but the *Shabbat* prohibition of labor extends to all animals. Similarly, the verse here mentions *shor o seh* — ox or sheep — and perhaps the law of multiple payments should extend to all animals by the same reasoning. Why is *arba'ah va-chamishah* restricted to these two?

### Mentioned Twice

Rabbah offers the textual basis for the restriction. The Torah writes *shor* and *seh* twice in the passage governing these payments. The verse begins: *ki yignov ish shor o seh* — if a man steals an ox or a sheep — and then concludes: *chamisha bakar yeshalem tachat ha-shor ve-arba tzon tachat ha-seh* — he shall pay five cattle in place of the ox and four sheep in place of the sheep. Both the beginning and the end of the *pasuk* specify *shor* and *seh*. *Shor va-seh in, midi acharina lo* — ox and sheep yes, anything else no. The doubling is legally significant; it functions as a limitation.

### Pasuk Analysis

The Gemara does not simply accept this argument without scrutiny. If the verse could have been written differently and still conveyed the same laws, then the repetition of *shor* and *seh* is not truly significant — it is merely the most natural way to write the verse, and one cannot derive a limiting principle from it. The Gemara therefore examines whether an alternative formulation would have been both linguistically and legally sufficient.

The Gemara first asks: could the Torah have omitted the second mention of *shor* and *seh* and written simply *chamisha bakar yeshalem tachtav ve-arba tzon tachtav* — five cattle in its place and four sheep in its place — using the pronoun *tachtav* rather than naming the animal again? The answer is no, because *tachtav* referring back to an earlier mention of both *shor* and *seh* would be ambiguous: one might think that for either a stolen *shor* or a stolen *seh* one must pay both five cattle and four sheep — a total of nine — rather than understanding that five applies to the *shor* case and four to the *seh* case separately. Although the Gemara considers whether using *tachtav* twice might solve this ambiguity, it concludes that such a double usage of *tachtav* would itself be needed for a separate *derashah* — teaching that the payments must be made with quality animals, not inferior ones. Thus the end of the verse cannot be reformulated, and the repetition of *shor* and *seh* there is required.

The Gemara then asks: could the Torah have omitted the first mention of *shor o seh* and begun the verse as *ki yignov ish* without specifying the animal, letting the end of the verse clarify what was stolen? The answer is again no: without the opening *shor o seh* and its disjunctive *o* — "or" — one might have thought the law applies only when one steals both an ox and a sheep together, never when one steals either animal alone. Even if one would not think one must slaughter both or sell both, there remains a plausible reading that one must steal both before the multiple-payment law is triggered. The opening specification of *shor o seh* is therefore also necessary.

### Exclusion Proven

Since both the opening *shor o seh* and the concluding *tachat ha-shor... tachat ha-seh* are each independently required to prevent misreadings, neither is simply redundant. The Gemara ultimately concludes that the Torah could alternatively have written the verse using the opening *shor o seh* together with *tachtav* at the end, dispensing with the specific mention of *shor* and *seh* in the concluding clause, and the law would have been adequately conveyed. The fact that the Torah instead chose to repeat *shor* and *seh* explicitly in the concluding clause — beyond what was strictly necessary — constitutes the basis for the limiting *derashah*: *shor va-seh in, midi acharina lo* — only an ox and a sheep incur the multiple payments; no other animal does. Whether one finds the *derashah* fully compelling or not, the underlying *halacha* is clear: *arba'ah va-chamishah* is categorically restricted to *shor* and *seh* alone.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 67

## Shinuy & Acquisition

### Mari Shemeh Lav

The Gemara opens by rejecting a proposed *shinuy hashem* — a change of name — in the case of a stolen beam incorporated into a roof. The objection is *mari shemeh lav*: simply calling something by a new name does not constitute a genuine change if the object itself remains substantively the same. The Gemara supports this from a *baraita* in Yechezkel regarding the construction of the third *Beit HaMikdash*, where the term *uvim* (groups or structures) is explained as *marshin* — beams. Even when a beam serves as part of a roof, it is still identified as a beam. The name has not truly changed.

This stands in contrast to a piece of leather fashioned into shoes: there, looking at the object, one would say "those are shoes," not "that is a piece of leather." The *shinuy hashem* is genuine. But looking up at a roof, one might readily say, "there's a 2x4" — the beam hasn't shed its identity. So there is no real *shinuy hashem* in the beam case, and the objection from that case falls away.

### Shinuy Hachozer

Rabbi Zeira offers a different approach. His principle is: *shinnuy hachozer livriyato beshinnuy hashem lo havei shinnuy* — a reversible *shinuy hashem* is not a genuine *shinuy* at all. If the transformation can be undone, it lacks the halakhic weight needed to effect acquisition.

Applied to the beam case: even granting that there is some *shinuy hashem*, since the beam could in principle be removed from the roof and restored to its original state — it was never cut, trimmed, dyed, or sculpted, merely placed among other beams — the change is reversible, and therefore insufficient to be *koneh*. This is the position that supports Rav Yosef's broader claim that without a genuine, irreversible *shinuy*, acquisition through the thief cannot occur. The only reason the thief is not required to physically dismantle the roof and return the beam is *takanat hashavim* — the rabbinic ordinance enacted to encourage penitent thieves to make restitution without facing impossibly burdensome demands. Without that ordinance, the reversibility of the change would require the beam's actual return.

### Shoes & Trays

Rabbi Zeira's principle can be sharpened by contrast with cases of irreversible *shinuy ma'aseh*. If stolen leather has been fashioned into shoes, the former owner cannot demand "give me back my leather" — the object has undergone a genuine *shinuy ma'aseh* and a genuine *shinuy hashem*. The leather is now shoes; the transformation is complete and irreversible. Similarly with a tray that has been warped, stitched, or otherwise worked: if the change is a *shinuy ma'aseh*, the thief acquires through it. The principle thus operates with precision: a mere *shinuy hashem* that is reversible does not confer acquisition; an irreversible *shinuy ma'aseh* does.

### Pipe Case

The Gemara now challenges the premise that a reversible *shinuy hashem* does not count as a *shinuy*, while an irreversible one does. The challenge comes from the law of *mayim she'uvim* — drawn water — which invalidates a *mikvah*. The case involves a wooden pipe: a block of wood is hollowed out to form a pipe and then affixed to the ground, channeling rainwater into a pit that serves as a *mikvah*. The ruling in a *baraita* is as follows: if one first hollowed out the wood (creating the pipe as a *kli*, a vessel) and then affixed it to the ground, the *mikvah* is invalid because the water passed through a vessel. But if one first affixed the block of wood to the ground and then hollowed it out, the *mikvah* is valid.

The Gemara's challenge: if we say that an irreversible *shinuy hashem* (the wood becoming a pipe, which is not reversible) constitutes a genuine *shinuy*, then even in the second case — where the wood was affixed and then hollowed — there has been an irreversible *shinuy hashem*, and it should still invalidate the *mikvah*. Why does the second case produce a valid *mikvah*?

The Gemara attempts to deflect: the laws of *mayim she'uvim* are themselves rabbinic, so perhaps the *shinuy* here only matters in a rabbinic context. But this response immediately invites a follow-up challenge: if it is all *de-rabbanan*, why are we making any distinction at all? Either the rabbinic rule applies in both cases, or it applies in neither. Why is the first case problematic while the second is not?

### Kli Presence

The Gemara resolves the problem by distinguishing based on the presence of a *kli*. The relevant question is not merely whether a *shinuy hashem* occurred, but whether the object had the status of a *kli* at the moment it was in its detached (*talush*) state, before being affixed to the ground. In the first case — hollow it out, then affix it — the wood was a *kli* (a pipe) while it was still detached. That *kli*-status in its *talush* state is what triggers the rabbinic stringency. In the second case — affix it, then hollow it out — the wood was still a plain block when it was detached and affixed; it only became a pipe-shaped form after being fixed in the ground. Since it was not a *kli* in its *talush* state, the rabbinic strictness does not apply.

This resolution preserves the underlying framework: the Gemara is not abandoning Rabbi Zeira's position, nor is it abandoning the distinction between reversible and irreversible *shinuy*. The *mikvah* case is governed by an independent rabbinic criterion — *kli*-status at the time of detachment — that does not disturb the core *shinuy* analysis. Rav Yosef's position that straight *yeush* without any *shinuy* does not confer acquisition therefore remains intact.

---

## Rav Yosef Defense

### Yeush Alone

With the *shinuy* discussion concluded, the Gemara returns to the core position requiring defense: Rav Yosef holds that *yeush* alone — the owner's despair of recovering his stolen property, without any accompanying *shinuy* — does not render the thief *koneh*. Every challenge to this position has, to this point, involved a case where some form of *shinuy* was also present, whether a *shinuy hashem*, a *shinuy ma'aseh*, or a reversible variant thereof. Rav Yosef can consistently respond: you are not challenging me on a pure *yeush* case; there was always a *shinuy* involved. The core claim — that *yeush* by itself has no effect — has not yet been directly refuted.

### Ganav Challenge

A challenge is now raised from a *baraita*: a *ganav*, a *gazlan*, or one who takes by force — if they consecrate an animal (*hikdisho hekdesh*), the *hekdesh* takes effect; if they separate *terumah*, the *terumah* is valid; if they separate *ma'aser*, the *ma'aser* is valid. This appears to demonstrate that even without an obvious *shinuy*, the thief has acquired the object sufficiently to effect these religious-legal changes. If *yeush* alone does not confer acquisition, how can the thief's *hekdesh* or *terumah* be valid?

### Shinuy Hashem Answer

Rav Yosef's response: there is in fact a *shinuy hashem* present in every one of these cases. When stolen wheat was *tevel* (untithed produce with no separated portions) and the thief separates *terumah*, the object is now called *terumah* — a fundamentally different legal category with its own body of laws. When stolen *chulin* is consecrated as *hekdesh*, it is no longer *chulin* — it carries an entirely different name and legal status. In each case, the object before and after bears a different name. This is precisely a *shinuy hashem*, and Rav Yosef's position is that *yeush* combined with *shinuy hashem* — even one that is arguably reversible — may suffice to confer acquisition, depending on the details. What he insists upon is that *yeush* alone, without any *shinuy* whatsoever, accomplishes nothing.

One might note, as indeed the question arose in the shiur, that using a stolen object for a *mitzvah* raises its own difficulty — for a stolen species, for instance, is invalid for use in a *mitzvah*. The Gemara returns to this matter subsequently.

---

## Two Yonatan Teachings

### Shinuy Koneh

Rav Chisda transmits a teaching in the name of Yonatan: how do we know that *shinuy* is *koneh* — that a change of form effects acquisition? From the verse (*Vayikra* 5:23): *vehishiv et hagezeilah asher gazal* — "he shall return the stolen object which he stole." The phrase *asher gazal* seems superfluous; of course the returned object is the one he stole, not one he didn't steal. The *drasha* is: *im ke'ein shegazal yachazir ve'im lav damim be'alma ba'ei shilumei* — if it is in the same state as when he stole it, he returns the object itself; if not — because it has undergone a *shinuy* — he pays its monetary value. The requirement to return the *gezeilah* applies only when it remains *asher gazal*, in its original form. If it has changed, he owes *damim*, implying that the *shinuy* has effected acquisition and he can no longer return the object itself.

One might then object: if *asher gazal* is doing this work, there is another law that also needs this phrase — the rule that one who confesses a theft and makes voluntary restitution must pay the *keren* plus a *chomesh* (an additional fifth), but if the *thief's heir* makes restitution, no *chomesh* is required. This too is derived from *asher gazal*: the obligation to add a *chomesh* falls on the original thief — *al gezeilo shelo* — not on his heirs. Since one phrase cannot serve both purposes, we might think we must choose. The Gemara resolves this by demonstrating that both *drashos* can coexist: the Torah could have written simply *vehishiv et hagezeilah* (without *asher gazal*) if only the *chomesh* exemption were needed, or it could have written *vehishiv et hagezeilah asher gazal* without separately specifying *gezeilah*. The redundancy of having both allows us to learn both laws — *shma mina tarti*.

### Shinuy Lo Koneh

Immediately thereafter, the Gemara presents a second tradition, also attributed to Rav Chisda in the name of Yonatan — but reaching the opposite conclusion. *Menayin leshinuy she'eino koneh* — from where do we know that *shinuy* does *not* confer acquisition? From the same verse: *vehishiv et hagezeilah* — he must return the *gezeilah* in all circumstances, regardless of what state it is in. *Shinuy* does not help; he still owes the object.

And what then is *asher gazal* doing? It is entirely devoted to the *chomesh* exemption for heirs — *al gezeilo shelo hu shemosif chomesh* — and carries no implication about the state of the object. The same verse, the same phrase, yields diametrically opposed conclusions in the two versions of this teaching. The fundamental *machloket* between Rav Yosef and Rava — does *yeush*, does *shinuy*, effect acquisition? — remains unresolved even at the level of these *Amoraic* teachings, and pointedly, both versions derive from the selfsame *pasuk*.

---

## Ulla & Rava

### Yeush No Effect

Ulla now offers a proof that *yeush* does not work — supporting Rav Yosef's position. The verse in Malachi (1:13) states: *vahasaitem gazul ve'et hapise'ach ve'et hacholeh* — you bring to God what is stolen, lame, or sick. God rejects such offerings. Ulla derives: *gazul dumya de-pise'ach* — the case of a stolen animal is compared to a lame one. Just as a *pise'ach* — a lame animal — has no remedy as long as it remains lame (one cannot reattach a missing limb), and its disqualification is absolute, so too a stolen animal offered as a *korban* has no remedy. And this is true *velo shna lifnei yeush velo shna le'achar yeush* — whether before or after the owner's *yeush*, the stolen *korban* remains unacceptable. *Yeush* effects nothing.

### Rava Korban

Rava offers a parallel teaching: the verse (*Vayikra* 1:2) says *korbano* — his offering, implying the *korban* must be his own and not stolen: *korbano velo gazul*. The Gemara asks: when does this apply? If before *yeush* — obviously the stolen animal cannot be offered; no verse is needed to tell us that. Rather, the verse is addressing the case *after yeush*, and it is teaching that even then the stolen animal is invalid. *Shma mina yeiush lo kani* — we learn from here that *yeush* does not confer acquisition.

### Case Distinction

At this point the Gemara raises an internal tension. Earlier in the discussion, when Rava's position was being examined, the question of a stolen *korban* was addressed with a different answer — that Rava's statement *korbano velo gazul* was specifically about a case where one stole the animal *in its already-consecrated state* as a *korban*, not a case where *chulin* was stolen and then consecrated. That earlier resolution distinguished those two scenarios. Now Rava appears to be using the verse to prove that *yeush* has no effect in a general sense, which would seem to contradict his earlier position that *yeush* does effect acquisition in the case of stolen *chulin*.

The Gemara notes the tension: *shinuyei smi mikan* — has Rava retracted? Or, as Rav Papa clarifies: these are in fact different rulings from different authorities, and the two positions attributed to Rava may not both be his. At a minimum, we now have two clear teachings — Ulla's and the teaching associated with Rava — both establishing that *yeush* does not confer acquisition, in alignment with Rav Yosef's position. The earlier case involving stolen *chulin* made into a *korban* remains a matter the Gemara acknowledges it has not fully resolved, possibly distinguishing along the lines of whether the theft occurred before or after the animal's consecration, or whether different *Tannaitic* sources are in play.

---

## Arba V'Chamisha

### Exodus Pesach

The Gemara now turns to a different topic: the law of fourfold and fivefold restitution, *arba v'chamisha*. The *Mishnah* has already established that this obligation applies exclusively to a *shor* (ox) and a *seh* (sheep or goat) — not to other animals, such as a *chamor* (donkey). The question is: what is the biblical basis for this restriction?

The relevant verse is Shemot 21:37: *ki yignov ish shor o seh* — if a man steals an ox or a sheep — *u'tvacho o mecharo* — and slaughters or sells it — *chamishah vakar yishalem tachat hashor v'arba tzon tachat haseh* — he shall pay five cattle in place of the ox, and four sheep in place of the sheep. Two things are immediately notable: first, the verse specifies *shor o seh* explicitly in its opening clause; second, the closing clause specifies the payment again as *tachat hashor* and *tachat haseh*, naming the animals a second time.

### Shabbat Parallel

A challenge presents itself: why not derive from the laws of *Shabbat* that *arba v'chamisha* should apply to all animals?
