The *pasuk* in Shemot 23:12 requires that one's *shor* and *chamor* rest on *Shabbat*; and the verse in Devarim (5:14) expands this — *l'ma'an yanuach shorecha vachamorecha* — so that all one's animals and dependents rest. Just as *Shabbat* rest is not restricted to an ox and a sheep but extends to all animals in one's possession, so too the fourfold and fivefold restitution should extend beyond *shor v'seh* to all animals. By analogy, stealing any animal and slaughtering or selling it should incur the enhanced penalty.

### Rava Double Mention

Rava responds: *kra shor v'seh shor v'seh shtei pe'amim — shor v'seh in, midi achrina lo* — the verse mentions *shor v'seh* twice, and this double mention constitutes a deliberate exclusion of all other animals. Mentioning *shor v'seh* at the beginning and *tachat hashor* and *tachat haseh* at the end signals that the law is specifically and exclusively limited to these two species. The repetition is meaningful and restrictive.

The force of Rava's answer depends, however, on the claim that this repetition is truly surplus — that the verse could have been formulated differently and still conveyed the same information. If the verse had no choice but to name the animals twice for structural reasons, then the double mention teaches nothing and the *Shabbat* comparison would stand unchallenged. The Gemara therefore proceeds to examine whether either mention of *shor v'seh* could have been omitted.

### Pasuk Formulation

The Gemara works through the possibilities systematically. Could the Torah have omitted the second mention — *tachat hashor* and *tachat haseh* — and written instead *chamishah vakar yishalem tachtav v'arba tzon tachtav*? The term *tachtav* ("in its place") would refer back to the *shor o seh* mentioned at the opening, and we would understand that five *bakar* are paid for the *shor* and four *tzon* for the *seh*. If so, the closing *tachat hashor v'tachat haseh* is surplus and could serve as the restrictive teaching.

The Gemara rejects this: had the verse written *tachtav* without specifying the animal, one might have thought the obligation was *nine*-fold — that for stealing either a *shor* or a *seh*, one owes *both* five *bakar* and four *tzon*, since *tachtav* in the singular refers ambiguously to whatever was stolen. The payment formula would then apply collectively: steal any one of these animals, pay nine. Therefore the verse must specify *tachat hashor* and *tachat haseh* separately to make clear that the five *bakar* go for the *shor*-case and the four *tzon* go for the *seh*-case.

But then, the Gemara asks: is *tachtav* even available to be used this way? The term *tachtav* itself is needed for an independent *drasha* — that the repayment must be *in kind*, of comparable quality. One who stole a healthy ox worth a *maneh* cannot pay back weakling oxen at death's door. *Tachtav* teaches that the quality must be equivalent. Since *tachtav* is already claimed for this teaching, it cannot simultaneously serve to distinguish between the *shor* and *seh* payments — making the repetition of *tachat hashor v'tachat haseh* doubly necessary.

Could the Torah have omitted the opening *shor o seh* instead? Could the verse have read simply *ki yignov ish u'tvacho o mecharo chamishah vakar yishalem tachat hashor v'arba tzon tachat haseh*, with the closing clause alone identifying the animals? The Gemara considers this and concludes it would fail: without the opening *shor o seh*, one might think the law applies only when both animals are stolen together — that the thief stole a *shor and* a *seh*, slaughtered one and sold the other, and only then does the fivefold and fourfold obligation arise. Every argument that it applies to one animal individually (*u'tvacho* in the singular, *o mecharo* in the singular) is deflected: the Gemara pushes through each iteration — slaughter both, sell both, slaughter one and sell one — showing that some ambiguity remains unless the opening clause explicitly states *shor o seh* as alternative cases.

### Both Needed

The conclusion is that both mentions of *shor v'seh* — at the opening and in the closing payment clause — are independently necessary. The opening is needed to make clear that the law applies to either animal stolen individually, and the closing is needed to prevent the misreading that nine animals are owed or that the quality of repayment is unconstrained.

Since both mentions are required for their own purposes, neither is truly surplus. How, then, does Rava's argument work? The Gemara arrives at a subtler formulation: *ela shor d'seifa v'shor d'reisha miat* — it is the combination of *shor* at the end and *shor* at the beginning together that effects the limitation. The Torah could theoretically have written the verse in an asymmetric form — mentioning *shor* in the opening and then using *tachtav* in the closing for one of the animals, or some analogous construction — which would have accomplished the necessary clarifications without doubling the explicit mention of both species. The fact that the Torah chose to name *shor v'seh* prominently in both positions, when the verse could have been formulated otherwise with one implicit reference, is what signals the deliberate exclusivity. *Shma mina shor v'seh in, midi achrina lo* — only an ox and a sheep, nothing else.

Whether this *drasha* fully satisfies one's sense of the argument or not, the underlying *halakha* — that *arba v'chamisha* applies only to a *shor* and a *seh* — is in any case the received rule, and the Gemara's analysis here serves to anchor that intuition in a textual basis. With this the discussion on this *daf* concludes.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 68

## Second Theft & Yeush

### Mishna Setup

Daf 68 opens by returning to the *mishna* that began the seventh *perek*. The *mishna* establishes that a second thief who steals from a first thief (*ganav*) does not pay *tashlumei kefel* — the double payment — because the first *ganav* did not own the stolen item. Similarly, if the second thief slaughters the animal, he does not pay the fourfold or fivefold penalty (*tashlumei arba'ah v'chamisha*) to the first *ganav*, again because ownership had not transferred to the first *ganav*.

### Rav's Position

*Amar Rav* — Rav qualifies the *mishna*'s ruling: *lo shanu ela lifnei ye'ush* — the exemption of the second *ganav* applies only when the theft occurred before *ye'ush*, the owner's despair of recovering the stolen item. But *aval l'achar ye'ush kano ganav rishon* — after *ye'ush*, the first *ganav* acquires ownership of the stolen item. This reflects the position that *ye'ush lechudei kanei* — *ye'ush* alone is sufficient to transfer ownership — and consequently the second *ganav* would owe *tashlumei kefel* to the first *ganav*, who is now the legal owner.

### Rav Sheshet Challenge

Rav Sheshet objects sharply, introducing a *beraita* that appears to contradict this position. The *beraita* asks: why did the Torah say that one who slaughters or sells a stolen animal pays four or five? Rabbi Akiva answers: *mipnei shenishtares b'cheit* — because the thief has driven his sin deeper, setting further roots into the transgression. The act of slaughter or sale deepens the original sin of theft.

---

## Nishtaresh B'Cheit

### R. Akiva

Rabbi Akiva's principle of *nishtaresh b'cheit* — deepening or entrenching the sin — serves as the rationale for the obligation of *tashlumei arba'ah v'chamisha*. By slaughtering or selling the stolen animal, the thief goes beyond the original act of theft and compounds his wrongdoing.

### Timing Question

The *Gemara* then presses on the timing: when, precisely, does this deepening of sin occur? If we say it refers to a sale before *ye'ush* — *iyleima lifnei ye'ush* — the question arises: *mi ika nishtares*? In what sense has the sin deepened? The animal has merely been transferred to another person, but it has not been taken any further from the owner's sphere; the owner has not yet despaired of recovering it. The sin has not truly gone deeper in any meaningful sense.

Therefore, the *Gemara* concludes, it must be referring to a sale *after* *ye'ush* — *ela l'achar ye'ush*. At that point, *ye'ush* alone has not yet transferred ownership, but now the *ganav* sells it, creating *ye'ush v'shinui reshus* — despair combined with a change of domain — which genuinely removes the object from the owner's legal ownership. That is when the sin has truly been entrenched.

The critical inference follows: *v'ei salka da'atach ye'ush lechudei kanei* — if *ye'ush* alone were sufficient to transfer ownership to the first *ganav*, then when he subsequently sold the animal after *ye'ush*, he would be selling something already his. *Shelo tovach v'shelo mocher* — he would be slaughtering or selling his own property, for which there can be no *chiyuv* of four and five. The fact that the Torah obligates him for the sale therefore demonstrates that *ye'ush* alone is not *koneh* — it does not transfer ownership.

### Rava's Reinterpretation

The *Gemara* responds on behalf of Rav's position: *k'd'amar Rava* — as Rava explained, the phrase *nishtaresh b'cheit* need not be interpreted as "deepening" the sin. Rava reads it as *shana b'cheit* — the thief has repeated his sin. Even if the sale did not push the stolen object further from the owner's legal grasp, the thief has once again demonstrated his brazen disregard for the owner's ownership by treating the animal as his own to dispose of as he wishes. This repetition of the original transgression is sufficient grounds for the obligation, even before *ye'ush*.

Under Rava's reading, the obligation for *mechira* falls *before* *ye'ush*, consistent with Rav's position that *ye'ush* is *koneh*. Under the alternative reading of *nishtaresh b'cheit* — genuine deepening of the sin — the obligation falls *after* *ye'ush*, which simultaneously demonstrates that *ye'ush* alone is not *koneh*.

---

## First Beraita

### Slaughter/Sale

The *Gemara* now brings a *beraita* as further evidence. The *beraita* states: *u'tevacho u'mecharo* — if one slaughters or sells the animal — *mah tevicha she'eina chozeres af mechira she'eina chozeres* — just as slaughter cannot be undone and the object cannot be restored to its original state, so too the *mechira* must be one that cannot be undone and restored. The *Gemara* asks: when does this apply? If before *ye'ush* — *iyleima lifnei ye'ush* — why would the sale be irreversible? The owner can simply recover the object from whoever holds it; it has not truly changed status. It must therefore be that the *beraita* is speaking of a sale *after* *ye'ush* — *ela l'achar ye'ush* — at which point the purchaser legally owns it, and the matter cannot be undone. This parallels slaughter, which likewise cannot be reversed.

The inference follows immediately: if *ye'ush* alone transferred ownership to the *ganav*, he would be selling his own property and could not be obligated for four and five. The *beraita*'s requirement of *she'eina chozeres* — irreversibility — implies that the *mechira* occurs after *ye'ush* while the *ganav* still does not yet own the object, proving *ye'ush* is not *koneh*.

### Rav Nachman's Intent

The *Gemara* deflects this proof by invoking Rav Nachman's interpretation. Rav Nachman explains *she'eina chozeres* as referring not to whether the object physically returns to the original owner, but to the *intention* with which the sale is framed: *prat l'shehikna lishloshim yom* — excluding a sale made explicitly for thirty days. The Torah's obligation of four and five applies only when the *ganav* sells the animal in the framework of a permanent transaction. If Reuven the *ganav* sells to Shimon saying "I sell this to you for thirty days," that is not the kind of *mechira* for which the Torah imposes liability. *She'eina chozeres* thus characterizes the nature of the sale's intent, not its actual legal effect. Under this reading, the *beraita* offers no proof about *ye'ush* at all, and the challenge is neutralized.

---

## Sequential Theft Cases

### Simple Theft Chain

The *Gemara* advances to a second *beraita* containing a series of sequential theft scenarios. The first case: *ganav uva acher ugnavo* — Reuven stole an animal, and Shimon came and stole it from Reuven. The *beraita* rules that Reuven pays *tashlumei kefel* to the original owner, while Shimon pays only *keren* — the principal — to Reuven, and nothing more. Shimon does not pay *kefel* because Reuven does not own the animal; one cannot incur the double payment penalty by stealing from someone who is not the true owner.

### Theft-Sale-Theft

The second case introduces a sale: *ganav u'machar uva acher ugnavo* — Reuven stole the animal, sold it to Shimon, and then Levi came and stole it from Shimon. The *beraita* rules that Reuven pays *tashlumei arba'ah v'chamisha* — four and five — and Levi pays *tashlumei kefel* to Shimon. Reuven is liable for four and five because he stole and sold; Levi is liable for double because he stole from Shimon, who legitimately owns the animal.

The third case: *ganav v'tavach uva acher ugnavo* — Reuven stole and slaughtered the animal, and then Levi came and stole it from Reuven. Reuven pays four and five, but Levi pays Reuven only *keren*, not *kefel*.

### Middle Case Proof

The *Gemara* focuses on the middle case — *katni meihas metzi'ata* — and brackets the problematic third case for the moment. Why does Levi pay *kefel* to Shimon in the sale scenario? *Iyleima lifnei ye'ush* — if there was no *ye'ush* — how does Shimon own the animal such that Levi's theft from him triggers *kefel*? *Shinui reshus belo ye'ush mi ika man d'amar dekani* — there is no opinion holding that a mere change of domain without *ye'ush* confers ownership. Therefore, *ela pishita l'achar ye'ush* — it must be that *ye'ush* occurred before the sale to Shimon, so that Shimon owns the animal through *ye'ush v'shinui reshus*, and Levi's theft from Shimon triggers *kefel*.

But then, *v'i salka da'atach ye'ush koneh* — if *ye'ush* alone transferred ownership to Reuven — why would Reuven be obligated for four and five for selling to Shimon? *Didei hu d'zavin* — he would be selling his own property. The inescapable conclusion: *shema mina ye'ush lo konei* — *ye'ush* alone is not *koneh*. This creates a contradiction for Rava's position as well: the first case of the *beraita* — simple theft from a *ganav* — establishes that the second thief pays only *keren*, not *kefel*. Yet we have now established that *ye'ush* must be present for the sale case to make sense. If *ye'ush* occurred in the hands of the first *ganav*, why does the second thief pay only *keren* in the simple theft scenario? The answer again: *ye'ush* alone is not *koneh*, and consequently the first *ganav* does not own the animal merely because of *ye'ush*.

### Theft-Slaughter-Theft

The third case presents a genuine difficulty. Reuven slaughtered the animal and then Levi stole it. Reuven pays four and five, but Levi pays only *keren* to Reuven. This is puzzling: slaughter is a *shinui ma'aseh* — a physical transformation of the object — which should confer ownership on Reuven. If Reuven now owns the animal carcass, Levi who steals it ought to pay Reuven *kefel*. Why does Levi pay only *keren*?

Rava points out that there is no reading of the *beraita* that makes all three cases internally consistent. The problematic third case cannot simply be set aside.

### Textual Solutions

One resolution: *v'eipoich seifa l'mitziata u'mitziata l'seifa* — the second and third cases in the *beraita* have been transposed due to a scribal error, and the correct reading is the reverse of what appears. In the corrected version, the slaughter case is the one where the subsequent thief pays *kefel* — because *shinui ma'aseh* gives Reuven ownership, and Levi steals from an owner — and the sale case is the one where the subsequent thief pays only *keren* — because the sale was before *ye'ush* and Shimon therefore does not own the animal. Under this reading, the entire *beraita* discusses cases *lifnei ye'ush*, and the apparent difficulty dissolves.

Rav Pappa offers an alternative that avoids reversing the *beraita*'s text: *seifa Beit Shammai hi d'amar shinuy bimkomo omed* — the third case, in which Reuven slaughtered the animal yet Levi pays only *keren*, reflects the position of Beit Shammai. Beit Shammai holds that even a *shinui* — a physical transformation — does not confer ownership on the thief; the transformation remains in its place legally. Hence Reuven does not acquire the carcass through slaughter, and Levi's theft from him triggers no *kefel*. The middle case then reflects the standard view — *ye'ush* plus *shinui reshus* transfers ownership to Shimon — and the first case involves no *ye'ush* at all. Whether this creates a difficulty for Rav's position remains to be explored.

---

## Rav Zvid's Resolution

### Yeush Timing

Rav Zvid offers a comprehensive reconciliation of the *beraita* without reversing any cases and without invoking Beit Shammai. He proposes that all three scenarios in the *beraita* are set *lifnei ye'ush* as far as the first *ganav* is concerned, but that *ye'ush* occurred after the animal passed into the purchaser's hands — not while it was still in the possession of the first *ganav*.

### Both Obligations

This resolves both obligations simultaneously. Since *ye'ush* had not yet occurred while the animal was in Reuven's possession, Reuven never acquired ownership through *ye'ush*. That is why Levi, who stole from Reuven in the simple theft scenario, pays only *keren* — Reuven is not the true owner. And that is why Reuven, who sold the animal to Shimon, is still obligated for four and five — he was selling something not yet his. As for Levi who stole from Shimon: *ye'ush* occurred after the animal reached Shimon's hands, so Shimon acquired it through *ye'ush* combined with *shinui reshus*, and Levi's theft from Shimon triggers *kefel*.

### Yeush Alone Koneh

One might ask: if we needed *ye'ush* plus *shinui reshus* to give Shimon ownership, why not simply have *ye'ush* occur while the animal was still with Reuven? Then Reuven would be the owner and the second thief would owe him *kefel*. The answer: *afilu b'ye'ush lechudei nami kani gabei ganav* — *ye'ush* alone would indeed be sufficient to transfer ownership to Reuven. However, the *beraita* specifically constructs the scenario to yield *both* obligations — Reuven's four and five *and* Levi's *kefel* — simultaneously. *D'lo meshkachat d'mishalem tarvaihu ganav rishon v'ganav sheini ela b'hachi* — you cannot get both obligations at once except in precisely this configuration, where *ye'ush* occurs in the purchaser's hands rather than in the first *ganav*'s hands. The scenario is designed this way not because *ye'ush* alone is insufficient, but because it is the only arrangement that produces both liabilities at once.

---

## Three Positions

### Rav Nachman

Having traced the debate through the *beraita*, the *Gemara* now articulates three distinct positions on when the obligation for *mechira* applies. *Itmar* — it was stated: Rav Nachman rules *chayav* — obligated — for a sale made before *ye'ush*. His reasoning: *u'mcharo amar Rachmana v'azvin* — the Torah says "and he sold it"; it does not require that the sale actually effect a transfer of ownership. The act of sale itself suffices. Therefore *lo shena lifnei ye'ush v'lo shena l'achar ye'ush* — it makes no difference whether the sale occurs before or after *ye'ush*. Rav Nachman holds that *ye'ush* is not *koneh*, so a post-*ye'ush* sale does give rise to *ye'ush v'shinui reshus*; but he equally maintains liability before *ye'ush*, where the act of sale, even without effect, is sufficient.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet disagrees: you are *patur* — exempt — if you sold before *ye'ush*. *Chiyuva l'achar ye'ush hu* — the obligation falls only after *ye'ush*, *de'ahani maasav* — because only then does the act of sale actually accomplish something legally, actually transferring ownership through *ye'ush v'shinui reshus*. Before *ye'ush*, the sale has no legal effect; *lo ahani maasav* — the thief's act accomplished nothing. The comparison to slaughter is instructive: just as slaughter produces a genuine, irreversible physical change — *dumya d'tevichah d'ahani maasav* — so too the *mechira* must produce a genuine legal change. That genuine change occurs only after *ye'ush*.

### Missing Position

The *Gemara* has now identified a logical gap. If *ye'ush* is *koneh*, the obligation can only arise *before* *ye'ush* — since after *ye'ush* the *ganav* is selling his own property. If *ye'ush* is not *koneh*, there is a further debate between Rav Nachman, who obligates both before and after *ye'ush*, and Rav Sheshet, who obligates only after *ye'ush* when *ahani maasav*. All three logical possibilities have now been mapped.

---

## Rabbi Akiva Revisited

### Proof Structure

The *Gemara* returns to Rav Sheshet's position in greater detail. *Mena amina lah* — where does Rav Sheshet derive his ruling? From the *beraita* of Rabbi Akiva: *mipnei mah amra Torah tavach u'machar meshallem arba'ah v'chamisha mipnei shenishtaresh b'cheit* — the Torah mandated four and five because the thief entrenched himself in sin. As established earlier, this entrenchment — *nishtaresh b'cheit* — cannot refer to a sale before *ye'ush*, where the sin has not genuinely deepened; it must refer to a sale after *ye'ush*, where the sale genuinely removes the stolen object from the owner's legal ownership. Therefore, *chiyuva l'achar ye'ush hu*.

The *Gemara* then rehearses Rava's counter: *mipnei sheshanah b'cheit* — Rabbi Akiva may mean only that the thief repeated his sin, which would support an obligation before *ye'ush* as well. And again the *beraita* on *she'eina chozeres* is cited — *u'tevacho u'mecharo mah tevichah she'einah chozeres af mechira she'einah chozeres* — and the response attributed to Rav Nachman's interpretation, that the requirement of permanence refers to the framing of the sale as a permanent transaction, not to an actual change in legal ownership. These arguments track what was established above and lead into the position of Rabbi Eliezer.

### Counter Question

At this point a natural question arises: even granting that the obligation for *mechira* requires *ye'ush*, how do we know that *ye'ush* is always present in a standard theft case? Perhaps in any given instance there was no *ye'ush*, and the *ganav* who sells cannot be held liable. Why should the Torah's formulation of four and five be assumed to apply to every case of theft?

### Slaughter Comparison

The *Gemara* responds by pressing the comparison to slaughter: *dumya d'tevichah mah tevichah d'ahani maasav af mechira d'ahani maasav* — just as slaughter has a genuine irreversible effect, so too *mechira* must actually accomplish something. The Torah does not attach a special precondition to slaughter; it obligates immediately upon the act. Since the obligation for *mechira* is placed on the same footing as slaughter — *u'tevacho u'mecharo*, as an immediate obligation — we cannot require that *ye'ush* be separately demonstrated in each case. It must be built into the standard assumption.

### Yeush Assumption

This leads Rabbi Eliezer to his explicit ruling at the top of 68b: *teda she-stam gneiva ye'ush be'alim hu* — you should know that a standard case of theft carries with it the assumption that the owners have despaired. The proof: the Torah says one who slaughters or sells pays four and five — *she-harei amra Torah tavach u'machar meshallem tashlumei arba'ah v'chamisha*. Since the obligation for *mechira* requires *ye'ush* (as Rav Sheshet and Rabbi Eliezer assume), and the Torah speaks of this obligation without requiring any additional showing of *ye'ush*, the Torah must be assuming that *ye'ush* accompanies every standard theft.

One might still ask: perhaps the Torah is simply telling us the law in a case where we happen to know *ye'ush* occurred. Rabbi Eliezer responds with the temporal logic: *dumya d'tevichah mah tevichah l'alter af mechira l'alter* — just as one who slaughters is obligated immediately, so too one who sells is obligated immediately. The Torah treats both as arising from the act alone, with no additional required condition. This can only be the case if *stam gneiva ye'ush be'alim* — standard theft is accompanied by the owners' despair.

*Tosafot* notes that *l'alter* cannot be taken literally as absolutely instantaneous, since the rule of *ye'ush shelo m'da'at lo havai ye'ush* — despair without the owner's knowledge does not constitute valid *ye'ush* — means the owner must actually become aware of the theft before *ye'ush* can occur. *Tosafot* therefore reads *l'alter* as "shortly thereafter" — by the time the *ganav* has brought the animal home and is ready to slaughter it, it can be assumed the owner is already aware of the theft and has despaired. The Torah requires no separately articulated condition of *ye'ush* because the assumption is that it will be present in virtually every case.

---

## Gneivat Nefesh

### No Yeush Case

Rav Yochanan now challenges the view that the obligation for *mechira* falls only after *ye'ush*. His challenge comes from a striking case: *gneiva b'nefesh tochi'ach* — the case of kidnapping proves the point. As Rashi notes explicitly — particularly poignant in our own times — *she'ein adam mitya'esh al atzmo*: a person never despairs of his own redemption. *Ye'ush* by the owner is simply impossible in a case of *gneivat nefesh*, yet the Torah obligates the kidnapper who sells his victim. This demonstrates that an obligation for *mechira* exists even without *ye'ush*.

### Torah Obligation

The structure of the argument is transparent: the Torah writes *gonev ish u'mecharo* — one who kidnaps a person and sells him — and the *chiyuv* is clear. Since there can be no *ye'ush be'alim* in such a case — a person is always his own *be'alim* and never gives up hope of being freed — the Torah's obligation must operate *lifnei ye'ush*. This implies that the obligation for *mechira* can arise even before *ye'ush*.

### Yochanan-Reish Lakish

The *Gemara* draws out the further implications. From Rav Yochanan's argument it is clear that he holds *lifnei ye'ush chayav* — one is obligated before *ye'ush*. What is the status *after* *ye'ush*? The positions diverge: *Rav Yochanan amar chayav* — Rav Yochanan holds one is obligated both before and after *ye'ush*, since *ye'ush* is not *koneh*; there is therefore always a basis for liability. *Resh Lakish amar patur* — Reish Lakish says one is *patur* after *ye'ush*, because for Reish Lakish *ye'ush* is *koneh* — the thief acquires the stolen item through *ye'ush*, and any subsequent slaughter or sale is of his own property: *shelo hu tovei'ach shelo hu mocher*.

---

## Sanctification Proof

### Sanctification Case

Rav Yochanan now presses his challenge to Reish Lakish's position directly. A *beraita* states: if someone stole an animal, sanctified it (*hikdish*), and then slaughtered it — *meshalem tashlumei kefel v'eino meshalem tashlumei arba'ah v'chamisha* — he pays *kefel* but not four and five. The reason for the exemption from four and five is that once the animal is *hekdesh*, it no longer belongs to the *ganav*'s victim in the relevant sense — *re'eihu v'lo hekdesh* — and slaughtering *hekdesh* does not trigger the four and five penalty.

### Cannot Sanctify

The question is: when did the *ganav* sanctify the animal? *Iyleima lifnei ye'ush* — *mi kadosh*? Can the *ganav* sanctify before *ye'ush*? The *Gemara* invokes the rule: *ish ki yakdish et beiso kodesh amar Rachmana mah beiso shelo af kol shelo* — the Torah says a person may sanctify his house; just as his house is his own, so whatever he sanctifies must be his own. A *ganav* who has not yet acquired ownership cannot sanctify. Therefore the sanctification must have occurred *l'achar ye'ush*. This means *ye'ush* plus the sanctification — which constitutes a *shinui reshus* or *shinui hashem* — together confer ownership upon the *ganav*, enabling the sanctification to take effect. Accordingly, when the *ganav* slaughters the animal, *d'ki katavach d'hekdesh katavach* — he is slaughtering something that belongs to *hekdesh*, and therefore he does not pay four and five.

The critical inference follows: *v'i salka da'atach ye'ush kanah* — if Reish Lakish is correct that *ye'ush* alone is *koneh* — why would the *ganav* owe anything at all? Once *ye'ush* occurred, the animal was already his before the sanctification; he would be slaughtering his own property and would be exempt without any need for *hekdesh* to intervene. The fact that the *beraita* requires the sanctification to explain the exemption from four and five demonstrates that *ye'ush* alone is not *koneh*. That is Rav Yochanan's proof.

### Owners Sanctify

Reish Lakish responds: *hacha b'mai askinan k'gon shehikdishu be'alim beyad ganav* — the case is not one in which the *ganav* sanctified the animal; rather, the original owners sanctified it while it was still in the *ganav*'s possession, before *ye'ush*. Since the owners sanctified it, when the *ganav* slaughters it he is slaughtering *hekdesh* and therefore does not pay four and five. The *ganav* himself never needed to be the one who sanctified; the scenario does not implicate *ye'ush* at all.

---

## Reish Lakish Defense

### Pidyon Analogy

The *Gemara* immediately challenges Reish Lakish's alternative reading: *u'mi kadosh* — can the original owners actually sanctify something that is no longer under their control? And Rav Yochanan himself is on record stating: *gezel v'lo nityashu habe'alim shneihem einam yecholim l'hakdish* — if something was stolen and the owners have not yet despaired, *neither party* can sanctify it. The *ganav* cannot sanctify because *it is not his*; the owner cannot sanctify because *it is not in his domain*. How, then, can Reish Lakish propose that the owners sanctified it?

Reish Lakish responds by pointing to the ruling of the *tznuin* — the scrupulously pious — as a source of analogy. The *mishna* teaches that those who were careful about transgressions would, when their orchard was in its *neta revai* year, set aside coins and declare: *kol hanilkat mizeh yehei mechulal al hamaos ha'elu* — whatever anyone takes from this tree shall have its sanctity transferred onto this money. Since passersby would take fruit without permission — effectively in an act of *gezilah* — the owner could not restore the fruit to his possession, yet he was nevertheless able to effect a transfer of *kedushah* through this *pidyon*. This demonstrates, argues Reish Lakish, that an owner retains some ability to act legally with respect to stolen property even when it is out of his domain.

*Tosafot* notes that the analogy is imperfect. *Pidyon* — redemption — is fundamentally different from *hakdash*. When one redeems something, the *kedushah* is already present and one is merely transferring it to a different object; moreover, the *tznuin* who perform the *pidyon* are acting to benefit the unwitting sinners who take the fruit (*zochin l'adam shelo b'fanav*), so the ability to perform *pidyon* here is explained by that consideration. Sanctifying something that is already stolen — taking an object out of the domain of its rightful owner and dedicating it to *hekdesh* — is an altogether different act and arguably cannot be derived from the *pidyon* case. Nonetheless, the *Gemara* accepts that Reish Lakish would press this analogy in defense of his position.

### Beit Din Case

The *Gemara* continues to press Reish Lakish: even if the owners could sanctify the stolen animal, if the owners sanctified it, doesn't that mean they reasserted control over their property? The *ganav* could argue that when he comes before *beit din*, the sanctification by the owners is tantamount to their having retrieved the animal — *chazra keren l'be'alim* — the principal has effectively returned. And if the principal returned before *beit din* issued its ruling, the *ganav* would not owe *kefel*. Why then does the *beraita* say he pays *kefel*?

Reish Lakish answers: *k'amad b'din* — the case is one where the *ganav* had already stood before *beit din*, and *beit din* had already obligated him in *kefel*, before the owners sanctified the animal. Only thereafter did the *ganav* slaughter it. Since the *kefel* obligation was established before the sanctification, it remains in force; and since the owners sanctified it before the slaughter, the slaughter is of *hekdesh* and the *ganav* is exempt from four and five.

### Obligation vs. Command

The *Gemara* refines the scenario further by invoking Rava's important distinction. If *beit din* issued an actual command — *tzei ten lo*, "go and pay him" — then, as Rava rules, *tavach u'machar patur*: if the *ganav* subsequently slaughtered or sold the animal, he would be exempt even without the *hekdesh* intervening, because *keivan d'paski l'milta* — the matter has been concluded. The *ganav* is no longer operating within the framework of the original *geneivah*; he has been ordered to pay and his continued withholding constitutes something closer to *gezilah*. Any subsequent slaughter is therefore not a continuation of the original theft and does not trigger four and five. Since even without *hekdesh* the *ganav* would be exempt in such a case, the *hekdesh* would be doing no work.

Rava therefore distinguishes: the relevant case is *chayav atah litten lo* — where *beit din* declared the *ganav obligated* but had not yet issued the operative command to go and pay. In that intermediate state, *keivan d'lo paski l'milta* — the matter has not been fully concluded — and *achti ganav hu* — the *ganav* remains within the original framework of his theft. If he slaughters in that state, he would normally pay four and five. It is only the sanctification by the owners that exempts him. This, concludes the *Gemara*, is the precise scenario Reish Lakish is describing: *beit din* has declared the obligation (*chayav litten lo*), the owners have then sanctified the animal, and the *ganav* subsequently slaughters it — obligated for *kefel* by virtue of the *beit din*'s prior declaration, yet exempt from four and five by virtue of the *hekdesh*. With this clarification, Reish Lakish's account of the *beraita* is fully resolved.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 69

## Prior Discussion Review

### Kinyanim & Ye'ush

The opening of our discussion on daf 69 requires briefly revisiting the terrain covered in the preceding days, as the current sugya builds directly upon those foundations. The central question animating the earlier discussion was: which types of *kinyanim* are effective in the context of *geneiva*? Specifically, the *gemara* examined the distinction between *shinui ma'aseh* — a change in the physical nature of the stolen object — and *shinui hashem* — a change in its name or designation, without a corresponding physical transformation. The question of *chozer livriyaso*, whether the object reverts to its original state, bears directly on whether such a change constitutes an effective *kinyan*.

Woven through this discussion was the role of *ye'ush* — the owner's despair of recovering the stolen item. The *gemara* addressed whether *ye'ush* and *shinui hashem* must operate in tandem, or whether *ye'ush* merely serves as a precondition enabling the *shinui hashem* to take effect. On this reading, the *ganav*'s act of designating the stolen leather for a particular use would only carry legal significance once the owner had already despaired — the *ye'ush* licenses the *ganav*'s designation. The *kinyan*, however, is ultimately effected through the *shinui hashem* itself, not through the *ye'ush* alone. The broader question of whether *ye'ush* operates independently as a *kinyan* was also explored at length, though from an indirect angle.

### Shechita vs. Mechira

The discussion then pivoted to a parallel question: under what circumstances is a *ganav* liable for slaughtering or selling a stolen animal? For *shechita*, the liability is essentially universal — slaughtering the stolen animal in any circumstance triggers the fourfold or fivefold payment. The more contested question concerns *mechira*, selling the animal. Here the *gemara* offered two conceptual frameworks. The first is *shana bacheit* — the *ganav* has repeated the sin; the act of selling mirrors the original act of theft in its defiance of the owner's rights. The second is *nishtarsha bacheit* — the sin has been given roots, made more permanent; the sale has now placed the object beyond the owner's reach.

### Mechira Timing

These two rationales carry different implications for the timing of liability in *mechira*. If the reason for the additional payment is that the *ganav* has simply repeated the sin, then liability could attach even before *ye'ush*, since the act of selling already constitutes a repetition regardless of whether the owner has despaired. If, however, the reason is *nishtarsha bacheit*, then the liability attaches only after *ye'ush*, because only at that point has the sale genuinely placed the object beyond the owner's recovery. A third possibility — that liability attaches both before and after *ye'ush* — was also on the table. The viability of these options depends in part on the antecedent question of whether *ye'ush* by itself operates as a *kinyan*. If *ye'ush* alone is *koneh*, then after *ye'ush* the *ganav* already owns the object, and the question of the *mechira* liability must be reframed entirely. This was the terrain of the prior discussion.

---

## Ganav's House Theft

### Keplal Exemption

We now turn to the *mishna* at hand, which addresses what happens when a second thief steals an object from the house of the first *ganav*. The *mishna* establishes that the second thief does not pay *kefel* — the double payment — to the *ganav*, since the *ganav* does not own the object. This is straightforward. What is the *chiddush* of the *mishna*, however, is that the second thief does not pay *kefel* even to the original owner. The source for this is the *pasuk*: *v'gunav mibeis ha'ish* — the theft must be from the person's own domain, his house. "House" here is understood figuratively, meaning the owner's sphere of control. Since the object has been stolen away and is now in the *ganav*'s possession, it is no longer within the owner's *reshut*, and the *kefel* obligation does not arise.

### Shomer Chinam

A related question emerges regarding a *shomer chinam* — an unpaid guardian. If one deposits an object with an unpaid guardian, and the object is subsequently stolen due to the guardian's negligence, the guardian bears liability for that negligence. The *ganav* who stole from the *shomer chinam* pays *kefel* — not to the original owner directly, but effectively into the network of obligations surrounding the object. The precise mechanics of who ultimately receives the *kefel* in various scenarios is acknowledged as a discussion belonging to tractate *Bava Metzia* rather than to the present context.

### Cannot Sanctify

This now brings us to the *gufa* of the discussion, which centers on a ruling of Rabbi Yochanan: *gezel velo nityashu habalim* — if an object was seized and the owners have not yet despaired, *sheneihem einam yecholim lehakdish* — neither party can sanctify it. The *gazlan* cannot sanctify it *lefi she'eino shelo* — because it is not his. But the owner also cannot sanctify it *lefi she'eino birshuto* — because, while it remains legally his, it is not within his control. Rabbi Yochanan is drawing a significant inference: the same logic that denies *kefel* when an object is outside the owner's domain — the requirement of *mibeis ha'ish* — implies a broader principle that an owner's capacity to exercise ownership rights is impaired when the object is not under his control.

---

## Field Markers

### Marking Practice

The *gemara* then pivots to a *mishna* from *Ma'aser Sheni* that will ultimately create a difficulty for Rabbi Yochanan's principle. The *mishna* describes the practice of marking different areas of one's field with distinct symbolic markers. A *kerem revai* — a vineyard in its fourth year, whose fruit must be brought to Jerusalem or redeemed — would be marked with clumps of earth, *tzrorot adamah*. An area bearing *orlah* — fruit of the first three years of a tree's growth, which is entirely prohibited — would be marked with pottery shards, *charsit*. A portion of the field that contained graves would be marked by pouring plaster, *sid*, around the perimeter.

### Symbols Explained

The *gemara* explains the symbolic logic behind each marker. The clumps of earth marking *kerem revai* evoke the nature of the ground itself: just as the earth yields produce from which one derives benefit, so too *kerem revai* — once redeemed — is permitted for consumption and benefit. The pottery marking *orlah* conveys the opposite: a broken shard yields no benefit, signaling that the fruit in that area is entirely forbidden in benefit. The plaster marking a grave is white, evoking the whiteness of bones — a visible warning to *kohanim* who must avoid ritual contamination through proximity to the dead.

### RSBG Position

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then qualifies this practice. He asks: when does the obligation — or at least the propriety — of such marking apply? His answer is: *beshvi'it*, only in the *shmita* year. The *gemara* explains: during *shmita*, the produce of the land becomes *hefker*, and people have a legal right to enter fields and take fruit. In such circumstances, it is genuinely important to alert passersby that what they are about to take is *kerem revai* or *orlah*, since their entry is lawful and their taking permitted. But during the other years of the seven-year cycle, the situation is different.

### Ethical Obligation

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel invokes the principle *haliteihu l'rasha v'yamot* — pour it down the wicked person's throat and let him die. This is a striking moral position. If someone is already committing the sin of stealing from your field, you bear no responsibility to provide them with information that would prevent them from compounding that sin by consuming *orlah* or eating *kerem revai* outside of Jerusalem. The ethical question this raises is genuinely challenging. The principle seems to say: when a person is already engaged in a transgression, the obligation to prevent them from committing a secondary transgression is diminished or eliminated.

This does not mean that any harm that befalls them is to be wished for — it is more a statement about the limits of one's obligation to facilitate another's compliance. If someone is stealing from your property, you are not required to label your stolen goods for their convenience. The message embedded in marking the field under such circumstances might even be seen as tacitly condoning the theft — as if the only *aveira* that matters is the *bein adam l'makom* dimension of eating *orlah*, while the *bein adam l'chavero* violation of theft is passed over in silence. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position, then, is that you do not paper over a more serious wrong by accommodating the sinner in a lesser matter.

### Chasidim Extra

The *mishna* then introduces the *tzenuim* — the pious ones, those who go beyond the letter of the law in their concern for others. The *mishna* describes what the *tzenuim* would do in a case involving *kerem revai*: *manichin et hamaot*, they would set aside money, and declare: *kol hanilkat mizeh mechulal al hamaot halalu* — anything taken from this vineyard shall be transferred, redeemed, onto this money. In other words, even if a thief ignores the marker and takes the *kerem revai*, at least the *kedusha* has been transferred to the money and the thief will not be eating *kerem revai* outside of Jerusalem.

---

## Tzenuim/Dosa Puzzle

### Challenge to RY

Here the *gemara* raises a sharp question against Rabbi Yochanan. If Rabbi Yochanan holds that an owner cannot exercise ownership rights over an object that is out of his control — and in particular cannot be *makdish* it — how can the *tzenuim* redeem the *kerem revai* once it has already been taken? Once the fruit has been stolen or taken out of the owner's domain, it is no longer *birshuto*. The act of redemption the *tzenuim* are performing — transferring the *kedusha* from the fruit to the money — would seem to be precisely the kind of exercise of ownership rights that Rabbi Yochanan says cannot be done when the object is outside the owner's control.

Moreover, the *gemara* notes that Rabbi Yochanan himself ruled that *halacha* follows a *stam mishna* — an anonymous, unattributed *mishna*. And if the *tzenuim* passage is a *stam mishna*, Rabbi Yochanan would be bound to rule accordingly. One might argue that the passage about the *tzenuim* falls within the quoted opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and is not truly a *stam mishna*. However, the *gemara* neutralizes this escape route by citing the well-known ruling — transmitted by Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — that wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel appears in *mishnatenu*, *halacha k'moto*, we rule like him, with only three exceptions: *arev*, *Tzidan*, and *ra'aya acharona*. So even if the *tzenuim* passage is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view, Rabbi Yochanan would follow it.

### Breira Solution

The *gemara*'s first attempt at resolution is to reread the *tzenuim*'s declaration. Instead of reading *kol hanilkat mizeh* — anything that was already taken — read it as *kol hamitlaket mizeh* — anything that will be taken. On this reading, the *tzenuim* are making their declaration in the morning, before anyone has entered the vineyard, while the fruit is still entirely under the owner's control. The redemption thus takes effect now, based on whatever fruit will subsequently turn out to be taken. This is a classic *breira* — the designation is made now but its object is determined retroactively by future events. In this reading, there is no *aino birshuto* problem at all, because the owner is acting while the fruit is still in his possession.

*Tosafot* raises two observations here. First, one might wonder why the owner does not simply redeem the entire vineyard at once. *Tosafot* suggests that the owner wishes to bring the fruit to Jerusalem and eat it there, and therefore prefers not to redeem it; or that additional fruit may grow later and the blanket redemption would not cover it, so he prefers to redeem only what is necessary. Second, this reading requires the *gemara* to assume that fruit can be redeemed while still attached to the ground — normally a problematic assumption — since the declaration is being made in the morning when the fruit has not yet been picked.

### RY No Breira

However, this resolution immediately generates a new difficulty: Rabbi Yochanan himself does not hold of *breira*. The *gemara* cites the ruling transmitted by Rabbi Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ha'achim shechalku lekuchos hen* — brothers who divide an inherited estate are treated as purchasers of one another's shares. This means that when *yovel* arrives, those divisions revert, just as any sale reverts at *yovel*. This ruling reflects a rejection of *breira*: Rabbi Yochanan does not accept the retroactive determination that each brother's share was "always" destined to be his. Instead, the division is viewed as a transactional exchange, subject to the laws of *yovel*. If Rabbi Yochanan does not hold of *breira*, he cannot explain the *tzenuim*'s practice as a morning declaration that takes effect retroactively.

At this point the *gemara* has exhausted its initial avenue of escape. Whether the *tzenuim*'s declaration is read as occurring after the fact — in which case it runs afoul of Rabbi Yochanan's principle of *aino birshuto* — or as occurring in the morning as a *breira* — it runs afoul of Rabbi Yochanan's rejection of *breira*. The same problem applies to Rabbi Dosa's ruling about the *baal habayit* and the *aniyim*. In the version of the *braita* as initially presented, Rabbi Yehuda says the *baal habayit* declares in the morning — *shacharit* — that whatever the *aniyim* will pick shall be *hefker*, and Rabbi Dosa says the declaration is made toward evening — *le'itotei erev* — covering what the *aniyim* have already picked. The *gemara* attempted to reverse the names so that Rabbi Dosa would be the one declaring in the morning, and thus his position would align with the *tzenuim* as understood through *breira*. But this reversal was itself necessitated by the need to reconcile Rabbi Yehuda's stated position with the fact that he is elsewhere known not to hold of *breira* — and it is noted that in the *mishna* concerning one who purchases wine from Samaritans on *erev Shabbat* at *bein hashmashot*, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Shimon all forbid the *breira*-dependent solution that Rabbi Meir permits.

*Rashi* notes, however, that there is another *gemara* indicating that Rabbi Yehuda does in principle hold of *breira*, and that his objection in the *maaser* case stems from a different concern — the possibility that the wine might all be consumed or the barrel might break before the designation can be carried out, leaving the separation retroactively invalid. On this reading, it is not necessary to reverse the names in the *braita* at all: Rabbi Yehuda may genuinely hold of *breira* and be the one who says the declaration in the morning; Rabbi Yosi is the one who says it in the evening; and the *tzenuim* align with Rabbi Yosi, not with Rabbi Dosa.

### Other Stam

With the *breira* solution foreclosed for Rabbi Yochanan, the *gemara* reaches its resolution. *Rabbi Yochanan stama d'matnitin ashkech* — Rabbi Yochanan found another *stam mishna*, one that in his view reflects the governing principle and takes precedence. That *stam mishna* is precisely our *mishna* here: *eino gonev achar ganav meshalem tashlumei kefel* — a second thief who steals from the first *ganav* does not pay *kefel*. The *gemara* asks: why not? Clearly the second thief cannot pay *kefel* to the *ganav*, since the *ganav* does not own the object — *v'gunav mibeis ha'ish*, not from the *ganav*'s house. But why not pay the original owner? The answer the *gemara* derives is: *zeh lefi she'eino shelo v'zeh lefi she'eino birshuto* — this one because it is not his, and the other because it is not under his control. Rabbi Yochanan reads this *stam mishna* not as an arbitrary scriptural limitation (*gezeirat hakatuv*), but as reflecting a substantive legal principle: when an object is outside the owner's *reshut*, the owner's legal capacity to exercise ownership rights is impaired.

### Impaired Rights

The *gemara* then asks why Rabbi Yochanan chooses to follow this *stam mishna* rather than the *stam mishna* of the *tzenuim*. The answer is that there is a *pasuk* that supports Rabbi Yochanan's principle specifically in the domain of *hekdesh*: *v'ish ki yakdish et beito kodesh l'Hashem* — a man who sanctifies his house. The *gemara* infers: *mah beito birshuto, af kol birshuto* — just as his house is under his control, so too any sanctification must be of something under his control. The language of *beito* in the *hekdesh* verse parallels the language of *mibeis ha'ish* in the *geneiva* verse, and both converge on the same principle: it is *reshut*, control, that enables the exercise of ownership rights.

Rabbi Yochanan's original stated ruling was limited to *hekdesh* — that neither the *gazlan* nor the owner can be *makdish* an object that is not in the owner's control. But the *gemara* abstracts this further. If the owner cannot be *makdish* the object — an act that transfers its status — the underlying reason must be that any meaningful exercise of ownership requires the object to be within one's domain. This abstraction extends, in principle, to selling, giving, being *mafkir*, and redeeming.

---

## Rishonim Answers

### Abaye View

The *gemara* now presents three *amora'im* — Abaye, Rava, and Ravina — each of whom proposes what he would have said, had Rabbi Yochanan not equated the *tzenuim* with Rabbi Dosa. Abaye's position is motivational rather than doctrinal. He says: had Rabbi Yochanan not linked them, I would have said that the *tzenuim* agree with Rabbi Dosa's general principle — that one can be *mafkir* something even when it is taken by the *aniyim* and out of one's control — but that Rabbi Dosa would not necessarily agree with the *tzenuim* in their case. Why? Because the *tzenuim* are animated by a concern for the *ganav* who has stolen the *kerem revai* — an entirely uninvited guest, a wrongdoer. One might wonder whether any act of piety on the owner's behalf would extend to protecting such a person's spiritual welfare. But in the *leket* case, the Rabbis enacted a *takanta* on behalf of the *aniyim* — they have a recognized right to be in the field, and protecting them from inadvertent violation of *halacha* is clearly within the spirit of the institution. *U'ma be'ganav avdu rabanan takanta, ani'im tzarich l'meimar* — if the Rabbis made accommodations even for the case of a *ganav*, certainly for the *aniyim*. But the reverse does not follow: *aval ganav, lo avdu lei rabanan takanta* — by the case of a *ganav*, they made no such accommodation. So Abaye would have kept the *tzenuim* and Rabbi Dosa's cases conceptually separate, each motivated by different considerations.

### Rava View

Rava's alternative solution operates on an entirely different plane. He says: had Rabbi Yochanan not linked them, I would have said *man tana tzenuim — Rabbi Meir hi* — the *tzenuim*'s practice follows the opinion of Rabbi Meir. And therefore the *tzenuim*'s case presents no contradiction to Rabbi Yochanan at all.

### Redemption Kodesh

The relevance of Rabbi Meir is as follows. Rabbi Meir holds that *ma'aser sheni mammon gavoha hu* — *ma'aser sheni* is not the owner's money. The fruit designated as *ma'aser sheni* must be brought to Jerusalem and eaten there; technically, it belongs to God, not to the individual. The owner has certain rights regarding it, but does not fully own it. *Kerem revai* is halachically linked to *ma'aser sheni* and carries the same sanctified status. If one follows Rabbi Meir, then the *kerem revai* was never fully the owner's to begin with.

### Ma'aser Precedent

Yet the Torah allows the owner to redeem *ma'aser sheni*. The *gemara* cites the verse: *v'im gaol yigal ish mi-maasro, chamishito yosef alav* — if a person redeems his own *ma'aser*, he adds a fifth. The fact that the Torah uses the possessive — *his* tithe — and that the owner adds a fifth when others who redeem it need not, shows that the Torah treats the owner as having a special proprietorial relationship to the *ma'aser sheni* for purposes of redemption, even though he does not fully own it in the ordinary sense.

### KR-Ma'aser Link

The *gemara* extends this logic to *kerem revai* through a *gezeira shava*: the word *kodesh* appears both in the verse relating to *kerem revai* (*kodesh hillulim*) and in the verse relating to *ma'aser* (*kodesh l'Hashem*). Just as by *ma'aser sheni*, even though it is *mammon gavoha* — God's money — the Torah nevertheless treats the owner as the owner *le'inyan pidyah*, for purposes of redemption, so too by *kerem revai*, even though it is sanctified and technically not his, the Torah treats him as the owner *le'inyan achlolei* — for purposes of consumption, or more broadly, for purposes of exercising redemption rights over it.

### Redemption vs. Mafkir

The crucial distinction that Rava's analysis implies is between *pidyon* — redemption — and *mafkir* — renouncing ownership. Redemption is an act of a particular kind: it does not require full ownership, because even by *ma'aser sheni* where full ownership is absent, the Torah enables the owner to redeem. In fact, any person, not just the owner, can redeem someone else's *hekdesh*. The ownership requirement for redemption is thus attenuated from the outset. Since the Torah considers the owner as having proprietorial standing for purposes of redemption even when the object is *kodesh* and therefore not fully his, the argument from *aino birshuto* is simply inapplicable: the owner's "control" was already legally theoretical before the object was stolen, and the Torah granted him redemption rights anyway.

But *mafkir* — renouncing ownership of one's own property — is categorically different. This is an act that presupposes full, ordinary ownership. *Ki itei birshuto hu d'matzei mafkir lei, v'ki leitah birshuto lo matzei mafkir lei* — when it is under your control you can renounce it, but when it is not under your control, you cannot. *Mafkir* involves transferring title away from oneself. That is a full exercise of ownership, and it cannot be done when the object is outside one's domain.

*Tosafot* engages with the question of why one cannot argue the reverse — that *hefker* should be *easier* to effect when an object is already partially out of one's control, since one is simply completing the process of severance that has already begun. The *gemara*'s position, however, is that the act of *mafkir* is precisely an active exercise of ownership, and this is what it requires in full.

---

## Ravina Identification

### ID as Dosa

Ravina offers yet another alternative. He says: had Rabbi Yochanan not stated that the *tzenuim* and Rabbi Dosa said the same thing, I would have said *man tana tzenuim — Rabbi Dosa hi* — the *tzenuim* of the *mishna* are none other than Rabbi Dosa himself. The passage describing the *tzenuim*'s practice would not be a separate, anonymous tradition, but rather a direct expression of Rabbi Dosa's own teaching. If so, it is not a *stam mishna* at all — it is a statement of a single *tanna*, Rabbi Dosa, recorded in the *mishna* without attribution.

### Stam Yachida

The *gemara* then concludes with an important general principle: *stam mishna l'Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Yochanan ki stam yachida lo amar* — even for Rabbi Yochanan, who rules like *stam mishnayot*, this rule applies only when the anonymous formulation genuinely represents a broadly accepted view. If the anonymous voice of a *mishna* turns out to reflect only a single opinion — a *stam yachida* — Rabbi Yochanan does not defer to it. Had Ravina been correct that the *tzenuim* passage is simply Rabbi Dosa's individual opinion, Rabbi Yochanan could have dismissed it on those grounds. The fact that Rabbi Yochanan made the effort to equate the *tzenuim* with Rabbi Dosa is what creates the difficulty — it reveals that Rabbi Yochanan himself treated the *tzenuim* as distinct from Rabbi Dosa, and thus as a genuine *stam*, rather than as an expression of a minority position.

---

## RY Logic Chain

### Logic from Keplal

With all of these alternatives presented, the *gemara* now pulls back to articulate the underlying logic of Rabbi Yochanan's position in its final, consolidated form. Rabbi Yochanan's starting point is the *stam mishna* that exempts the second thief from paying *kefel* to the original owner when he steals from the *ganav*'s house. This exemption is not treated as an arbitrary *gezeirat hakatuv*. Rather, Rabbi Yochanan reads it as reflecting a substantive principle: that once an object is outside the owner's *reshut*, the owner's legal status is impaired. He cannot collect *kefel* — and not merely because of a technicality, but because his *ba'alut*, his ownership, is somehow diminished in its practical force.

### Ownership Rights

From there, Rabbi Yochanan extends the principle to *hekdesh*. He cites *v'ish ki yakdish et beito* — sanctification must be of something within one's domain. If you cannot be *makdish* an object out of your control, this is not an isolated rule about *hekdesh*; it reflects the underlying principle that meaningful exercises of ownership require the object to be within the owner's sphere of authority. The *ganav* cannot be *makdish* because it is not his. The owner cannot be *makdish* because it is not within his *reshut*. Both limitations flow from the same root: *ba'alut* without *reshut* is an impaired form of ownership.

### Gemara Extends

The *gemara* then extends this principle further. If the owner cannot sanctify the object, it follows that he cannot sell it — that is the most obvious extension. But the *gemara* also applies the principle to *mafkir* and to *pidyon*, redemption. These are the cases that are less intuitive, and which the sugya has spent considerable effort analyzing. The *tzenuim*'s redemption of the *kerem revai* and Rabbi Dosa's *mafkir* of the grain taken by the *aniyim* — both represent attempts to exercise ownership rights over objects outside one's domain. Rabbi Yochanan rules against them, preferring the *stam mishna* of *kefel* and the *pasuk* of *yakdish et beito*, which together provide both the logical and textual grounding for the principle.

---

## Ye'ush vs. Hefker

### Process Difference

The sugya concludes by returning to a conceptual question that underlies the entire discussion: what is the relationship between *ye'ush* and *hefker*? A student raises the intuitive observation that *ye'ush* — the owner's despair — seems to render the object *hefker*, ownerless. If that is so, is *ye'ush* simply another form of being *mafkir*? The answer requires distinguishing the two processes carefully.

*Ye'ush* operates through a weakening of the owner's connection to the object. The object is physically out of his possession, and his despair reflects the psychological and practical severing of his hold on it. The question of whether *ye'ush* renders the object technically *hefker* — so that it is no longer the owner's property at all — or merely weakens the owner's control to the point where others may acquire it, is itself a debate among the *rishonim*; the *acharonim* frame it as such. But in either case, *ye'ush* is a *passive* process: it is the registration of a loss of control that has already occurred.

### Full Control Need

*Hefker*, by contrast, is an *active* exercise of ownership. The owner who declares *hefker* is not recording a loss — he is affirmatively pushing the object out of his ownership, transferring it to no one. This active declaration requires the full, unimpaired status of ownership. Herein lies what is admittedly a somewhat counterintuitive result: *ye'ush*, even if it leads to the same end-state as *hefker*, does not require the owner to possess full control. It works precisely because the object is already outside his domain. *Hefker*, however, cannot be accomplished in that state — the very act of declaring *hefker* presupposes that the owner retains full title and authority, and it is that authority he is choosing to divest. If the object is already half-removed from his *reshut*, he lacks the standing to execute that divestiture.

### Ye'ush Limits

The point extends to the redemption case as well. Even if *ye'ush* produces an outcome similar to *hefker*, *ye'ush* itself could not serve as the operative act by which the *kerem revai* is redeemed or by which the *aniyim*'s grain is rendered *hefker*. Those require deliberate acts of the owner — *pidyon* and *mafkir* respectively — and those acts themselves, as the sugya has established, cannot be performed when the object is outside the owner's control. *Ye'ush* is the weakening; *hefker* is the severing. And it is the severing that requires the owner to still be in a position to sever.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 70

## Harsha'ah Overview

### Rabbi Yochanan & Harsha'…

The daf opens by returning to the principle of *Rabbi Yochanan* — *gezel velo nityashu hab'alim sheneihem einam yekholim lehakdish* — that once an item has been stolen and the owners have not yet despaired of recovering it, neither party can sanctify it: the thief because it is not his, and the owner because it is not under his control. The Gemara had extended this principle broadly to cover selling, gifting, redeeming, leasing (*maskir*), and declaring ownerless (*mafkir*). The core insight is that ownership alone is insufficient to exercise the full rights of an owner; the item must also be under one's actual control (*birshuto*).

With that principle firmly established, the Gemara now draws out a striking implication — one that introduces a legal instrument most readers would otherwise barely know existed: the *harsha'ah*, a form of power of attorney.

### Harsha'ah vs. Agency

The Gemara introduces the *orchata* (also written *adrachta* in some *Rishonim*) — a written power of attorney, derived from *leharshot*, to authorize or give permission. This instrument is fundamentally different from ordinary *shelichut* (agency). Appointing an agent to buy or sell something on one's behalf is a recognized *halakhic* institution. But a power of attorney is something qualitatively distinct: it confers the right to litigate in court, to represent one's interests, and to render decisions that are binding on the principal. This resembles in some respects the institution of *apotropus*, but the *harsha'ah* raises its own pressing question: what is the *halakhic* mechanism that makes it operative?

### Standing Problem

The practical problem the *harsha'ah* is designed to solve is the problem of standing. If Reuven claims that Shimon is wrongfully holding his iPhone, Reuven might wish to authorize David to litigate on his behalf. But Shimon can simply turn to David and say: *lav ba'al devarim didi at* — you are not my litigant; this is not your dispute. In secular court, we would call this lack of standing. The only way David can bring Shimon to court is if he has some personal stake or ownership interest in the property. This is the crux of how the *harsha'ah* must work: Reuven must somehow transfer to David a degree of ownership — at least a fiction of ownership — so that David can claim the matter as his own.

Why, then, would land present no problem while *metaltelin* (chattel) does? Because land, even if contested, is always "there." The concept of *eino birshuto* — not under one's control — does not apply to land in the same way. But chattel held by a denier is effectively in the other party's possession, and Reuven cannot grant what is not under his control.

---

## Harsha'ah on Chattel

### Kafrei Restriction

The *Nahardai* academy ruled: *lo kasvinan orchata amitaltelin* — we do not write a power of attorney on chattel. If the dispute concerns land, one may write a *harsha'ah*, because land is never truly removed from one's *reshut*. But for movable property — the iPhone in Shimon's pocket — such a document cannot be issued. The reason invoked is Rabbi Yochanan's principle: since Reuven cannot freely transfer something that is not under his control, the *harsha'ah* over *metaltelin* would be halakhically inoperative.

### Michzi Kesikra

A second version (*ika d'amri*) of the Nahardai position refines this significantly: *lo kasvinan orchata amitaltelin dekafrei* — we do not write a *harsha'ah* on chattel only when the other party is *denying* (*kafrei*) that the item belongs to Reuven. If Shimon says "I know it's yours, but I'm holding it as collateral for a debt you owe me" (and Reuven denies the debt), that is not *kafrei* — Shimon concedes the underlying ownership, and in that case a *harsha'ah* may be written. But if Shimon says "it's mine, not yours," then writing a document that says "I hereby transfer my iPhone to David" looks like an outright fabrication — *michzi kesikra* (appearing as a lie). Even if Reuven is telling the truth, the document on its face is absurd: the item is in Shimon's pocket and Shimon claims it is his. Courts would refuse to recognize such a document.

### Rishonim Challenge

This refined position, however, immediately draws a challenge from the *Rishonim*. The second version of the Nahardai ruling states: *aval lo kafrei, kasvinan* — but if Shimon is not denying ownership, we do write the *harsha'ah*. Yet the *Rabbi Yochanan* problem of *eino birshuto* presumably applies here too! Even when Shimon admits the item is Reuven's but refuses to return it, the property is still not under Reuven's control. How can Reuven transfer it to David?

The *Rishonim* answer that this concession is telling: fundamentally, the *harsha'ah* really cannot work perfectly within Rabbi Yochanan's framework. It is, at its core, a *takkanah d'rabbanan* — a rabbinic enactment, a legal fiction. The Sages recognized that the legal system requires such an instrument, and they permit it despite the technical problem. The next section of the Gemara will go further in clarifying exactly what kind of fiction is being constructed.

---

## Ownership Fiction

### Written Harsha'ah

The Gemara now presents the Nahardai academy's second statement: *orchata d'la ksiv bei zil dun v'zachi v'apik l'nafshach* — a *harsha'ah* document that does not contain the clause "go litigate and extract the property for yourself" is worthless (*leit bei mashasha*). Why? Because Shimon can respond to David with *lav ba'al devarim didi at* — you are not my litigant. Without the clause authorizing David to act on his own behalf, David has no claim against Shimon; he is merely Reuven's messenger, and Reuven's dispute is not David's to press.

The only thing that grants David standing is a degree of transferred ownership, coupled with the framing that he is acting in his own interest. Yet the paradox is obvious: if Reuven had truly and fully transferred ownership to David, there would be no need to write "do it on your own behalf" — David would simply be suing for his own property and would have no obligation to return anything to Reuven. The *harsha'ah* is thus walking a tightrope: enough transferred ownership to grant standing, but not so much that David is the true and exclusive owner.

### Abaye: Partial Ownership

Abaye refines this. He says: *i katav lei lemachatza leshlish uleravia* — if the *harsha'ah* document stipulates that David is entitled to keep half, a third, or a quarter of whatever he wins (analogous to a contingency fee arrangement), then the clause "do it on your own behalf" is unnecessary. David clearly has his own stake in the matter, and his interest in his portion gives him standing to press the entire case: *migo demishtayei dina apalga, mishtayei dina akula* — since he can litigate for his own portion, he can litigate for the whole.

Abaye's formulation makes explicit what was already implicit: in most real-world uses of the *harsha'ah*, David does not actually pocket the proceeds. He is paid a fee, or nothing beyond the principal's gratitude, and returns whatever he recovers. The fiction of acting "on one's own behalf" is therefore largely just that — a fiction. And this actually helps dissolve the Rabbi Yochanan problem: since Reuven is not truly transferring ownership, the principle that one cannot transfer what is not under one's control is not genuinely being violated. The *harsha'ah* functions as rabbinic fiction of ownership just sufficient to confer standing.

One might ask: could Reuven simply give David a token share — a *perutah's* worth — to establish his ownership stake minimally? This is a reasonable question, and it is not directly resolved here, but it sharpens the underlying principle: at some point the ownership stake becomes so nominal that it looks like a farce rather than a genuine transfer.

### Ameimar: Retention Risk

Ameimar draws out the uncomfortable logical consequence of the ownership fiction. If the *harsha'ah* works by genuinely (even if partially) transferring ownership to David — if the document says "go litigate on your own behalf" without any contingency clause — then if David wins the case and simply keeps the money, Reuven is stuck. *I tafas, lo mapkinan mineih* — if David seizes the proceeds, we do not remove them from him, because the fiction of ownership that enabled him to litigate also entitles him to retain what he won.

This is a sobering consequence: whoever is named in a *harsha'ah* must be deeply trusted, because the legal mechanism that empowers him also enables him to retain the proceeds against the principal's wishes. The practical response — and this is a reasonable one — is to execute a separate written agreement alongside the *harsha'ah* by which David commits to returning whatever he recovers. The *harsha'ah* says "take it for yourself," and the side agreement creates the enforceable obligation to return it. This dual-document structure was indeed part of how the institution functioned in practice.

---

## Rav Ashi: Agent Only

### Court Judgment Clause

Rav Ashi offers a resolution to Ameimar's concern. He says: *keivan dikhtiv lei kol dimistanei mindina kabileti alai* — since the *harsha'ah* document contains the clause "any judgment rendered by the court I accept upon myself," this language proves that the arrangement is not a true transfer of ownership. If Reuven had really transferred the property to David, why would Reuven declare that he accepts the court's judgment? The court's judgment would be David's concern, not Reuven's. The very fact that Reuven declares his acceptance of the outcome reveals that this is still fundamentally Reuven's case, and David is his agent — *shaliach shaveih* — not a new owner.

Therefore, Rav Ashi concludes, even if David were to attempt to keep the recovered property, Reuven could retrieve it. The court judgment clause in the *harsha'ah* is the textual signal that David has been constituted as an agent, not an owner.

### Teiku & Compromise

The Gemara records a middle position: *shutaf shaveih* — David has been made a partner (*shutaf*), not merely an agent. This corresponds to the *machatza, shelish, u'revia* formulation of Abaye — David has been given a genuine partial ownership stake, which entitles him to his portion but not to the whole. The practical question distinguishing *shutaf* from *shaliach* is *lemitpas palga* — could David seize his half? As a partner he could claim his share; as a mere agent he could not retain anything.

### Final Halakha

The *halakha* is *shaliach shaveih* — David is constituted as an agent only. Significantly, if one reads the *Rif*, he transmits that this final ruling was not actually found in the Gemara text itself but was a ruling of the *Geonim* — specifically attributed to Rav Hai Gaon — and was recorded in the language of the Gemara by the *Hilkhot Gedolot*, from which it was absorbed into the Gemara text. This is a well-known phenomenon: the *Geonim* quote Aramaic *sugyot* in Geonic works, append their rulings in the same style, and later readers assume the ruling is part of the original Gemara.

The ruling that David is *shaliach* solves the concern about retention — David cannot keep the property — but it reopens the original standing problem. If he is only an agent, how does he have standing? Shimon can again say *lav ba'al devarim didi at*. The answer the *Rishonim* give is that the *harsha'ah* is ultimately a *takkanah*, a juridical fiction: David is fundamentally an agent (*shaliach*), but the *harsha'ah* document creates a fictional element of ownership just sufficient to grant him standing. Since it is only a fiction — not a true transfer — we need not worry overly about Rabbi Yochanan's principle of *eino birshuto*, because no genuine ownership transfer is occurring. And since he remains fundamentally an agent, he cannot retain the proceeds.

What the *harsha'ah* creates, then, is a new legal instrument that does not exist natively in *halakha*. *Halakha* knows *shelichut* and it knows ownership; it does not natively know power of attorney. The *harsha'ah* blends the two — fundamentally an agency relationship, with a dash of fictive ownership to resolve the standing problem — and the *takkanah* framework legitimates this construct.

---

## Tosafot Practice

### Kafrei Expansion

Rabbeinu Chananel records, and Tosafot cites approvingly, that in the practice of subsequent generations the *harsha'ah* was written even on *metaltelin dekafrei* — chattel that the opposing party denies. This directly contradicts the Nahardai ruling as initially understood, which prohibited the *harsha'ah* in exactly such cases due to *michzi kesikra*. Rabbeinu Chananel himself acknowledges that he does not know the reason for this expanded practice; Rabbeinu Tam provides the explanation.

### Agency Rationale

Rabbeinu Tam argues that the operative *halakha* follows the second version (*lishna batra*) of the Nahardai position — the one that anchors the restriction in *michzi kesikra* rather than in Rabbi Yochanan's principle. And then, as Tosafot proceeds to demonstrate from another Gemara in Ketubot, *ulmichezi kesikra lo chaishinan* — we are ultimately not concerned with something that merely *appears* to be a fabrication, as long as it is not actually false. Since Reuven genuinely claims the property is his, writing the *harsha'ah* is not a *sheker*; it only superficially resembles one. Moreover, since the Gemara has concluded that the *harsha'ah* is fundamentally *shelichut* — agency — the ownership-transfer element is a minor technical fiction, not the core mechanism. One need not worry so much about appearances when the underlying legal structure rests on agency rather than a contested ownership claim.

### Malve Extension

The expansion of *harsha'ah* practice raised a further question in the era of the *Rishonim*: can a *harsha'ah* be written for a loan (*malve*) case, where there is no tangible property to transfer at all, even fictively? If Reuven lent Michael a thousand dinars and Michael denies the debt, there is no object to "give" to David as a way of conferring standing. The entire fictive-ownership mechanism seems unavailable.

The *Rishonim* debate this, and in practice — particularly as the need expanded with communities living at great distances and parties unable to appear in court themselves — many *Rishonim* permitted the *harsha'ah* even for *malve* cases. The reasoning is that if the *halakhic* foundation is ultimately *shelichut* sustained by a rabbinic *takkanah*, and the *takkanah* is enacted to accommodate a genuine systemic need, then the *takkanah* can extend even to cases where the ownership-transfer fiction is formally unavailable. The *harsha'ah* as an institution, in other words, outgrew its original mechanical justification and came to rest on its *takkanah* foundation alone.

---

## Mishnah: Two Witnesses

### Standard Cases

The Mishnah on 70a opens: *ganav al pi shnayim vetavach umachar al pihem* — if someone broke in and stole, as established by two witnesses, and then slaughtered or sold the animal, also witnessed by those same two, he pays the fourfold or fivefold penalty. Remarkably, the Mishnah adds: *o al pi shnayim acherim* — the testimony of slaughter or sale may come from an entirely different pair of witnesses. The two sets of witnesses combine to produce liability for the enhanced penalty.

### Exemption Cases

The Mishnah then catalogues a series of cases in which the thief is *chayav* to pay the fourfold or fivefold penalty, alongside implicit contrasts with cases in which he would be exempt. Several need brief explanation.
