# Bava Kamma 72

## Timing of Shechita

### Mishnah Setup

The current daf continues a rich series of sugyot within the perek of *mrubba*, each one yielding substantive halachic questions. The preceding discussion addressed cases of *shechita she'eina re'uya* — an act of slaughter that cannot produce permitted food — including scenarios of *shechita* on Shabbos, the principle of *kim lei b'derabba minei*, slaughter of a *shor haniskal*, and slaughter intended for *avoda zara*. In all those cases, either the animal is *assur b'hana'ah* or otherwise removed from the owner's domain, precluding liability for four and five.

The Mishnah now continues directly in that vein. The *tanna kamma* holds that one who slaughters *chullin ba'azarah* — non-consecrated animals in the Temple courtyard — or slaughters an animal that turns out to be a *treifa*, is still liable for four and five, since a valid act of *shechita* was performed. Rabbi Shimon disagrees: in his view, both cases constitute *shechita she'eina re'uya*, a *shechita* whose product cannot be eaten, and the thief is therefore exempt.

The case of a *treifa* is straightforward — the animal cannot be eaten, but it is still permitted in *hana'ah*, so the question of ownership and liability is coherent. The case of *chullin ba'azarah*, however, poses a deeper problem, since that *shechita* is presumed to render the animal *assur b'hana'ah*. Why, then, would anyone hold the thief liable? Once the animal is forbidden in benefit, it is as though it no longer belongs to its owner. This is the question the Gemara now takes up.

### Ein Lah L'Shechita

The Gemara opens four lines from the top of 72a. Rav Chaviva of Mechuzna said to Rav Ashi: we can infer from this Mishnah the principle of *ein lah l'shechita ela l'sof* — the act of *shechita* is considered to occur only at its final moment. *Shechita* consists of severing the majority of both the trachea and the esophagus. Everything done up to that point — say, forty-nine percent of the cut — is not yet the act of *shechita*. The act itself is the final passage from fifty percent to fifty-one percent. This stands in contrast to the position of *yeshno l'shechita mitechila v'ad sof*, which holds that the process of *shechita* begins from the very first moment of cutting, and the entire process constitutes the act.

### Shechita Start Problem

The Gemara now articulates why the position of *yeshno l'shechita mitechila v'ad sof* creates a problem in our context. If the act of *shechita* begins from the first stroke of the knife, then the moment one begins cutting, one has performed an act of *shechita* of *chullin ba'azarah*. That initial act renders the animal *assur b'hana'ah* immediately. Every subsequent stroke — from a few percent all the way to fifty-one — is then performed on an animal that is already forbidden in benefit and, by extension, no longer considered to belong to its owner. The slaughter at that point is not *shechita* on the owner's animal, and the thief cannot be liable for four and five.

Tosafot notes an important nuance: if one were to stop in the middle of the cutting without completing the *shechita*, retroactively no act of *shechita* would have occurred at all — merely a nick. But if the *shechita* is completed, we say in hindsight that it began from the first cut, and it is from that moment that the animal becomes *chullin ba'azarah*.

Rav Ashi also notes a *nafka mina* for this question in the laws of *kodashim*: Rashi observes that the question of when the *shechita* begins determines when a disqualifying intent — such as *she-lo lishma* — is operative. If intent is only effective at the final moment (*ein lah l'shechita ela l'sof*), a thought formed earlier in the cutting process would not affect the *korban's* status. If the process begins from the outset (*yeshno l'shechita mitechila v'ad sof*), any intent formed at any point during the cutting is legally significant.

### V'Tavcho Kulo

The Gemara proposes a resolution: since the act of *shechita* begins from the first cut, one is already liable for four and five from that initial moment — simultaneously with when the animal becomes *assur b'hana'ah*. Rav Acha son of Rava articulates this: *ki kemichayev v'hu purta* — when one becomes liable, it is also from that small beginning.

Rav Ashi rejects this. *Lo tidcheih* — do not deflect the difficulty in that way. *Utvacho kulo ba'inan v'leika*: when the Torah says "and he slaughtered it," the word *utvacho* — and Rav Ashi reads it as requiring the complete act of slaughter — implies that liability for four and five is triggered only at the conclusion of the *shechita*, not at the beginning. The *chiyuv* comes only when the animal has been fully slaughtered.

This understanding makes intuitive sense as well: the liability for four and five reflects the full realization of the wrongdoing, the *nishtana b'chet*, the change effected through the transgression. That change is only complete at the end of the act. Therefore, if the *shechita* process begins at the outset and renders the animal *assur b'hana'ah* from that first moment, the animal is already alienated from its owner before the moment of liability arrives. The *chiyuv* never attaches.

### Walking Animal In

The Gemara declares the difficulty unresolved — *ela kashya* — and then offers a practical resolution attributed to Rav Gamda in the name of Rava: *kegon she-shachat miktzat simanim bachutz u'gamran bifnim* — the case of the Mishnah is one where the *shochet* began cutting the animal's *simanim* outside the *azarah* and completed the cut once inside. In such a configuration — however physically awkward to envision, perhaps involving the *shochet* walking alongside the animal as it crossed into the *azarah* — the act of *chullin ba'azarah* only occurs at the final moment, precisely when the *chiyuv* for four and five is triggered. Both events — the forbidden status of *chullin ba'azarah* and the liability for four and five — arrive simultaneously at the conclusion of the cut, so the *chiyuv* is never preempted.

This is admittedly a peculiar scenario, and the Gemara notes as much. But it stands as a viable explanation for how one who performs *shechita she'eina re'uya* of *chullin ba'azarah* might nonetheless be held liable by the *tanna kamma*.

### Yochanan vs. Shimon

The Gemara now introduces an alternate version of the same debate, taught not in the context of the Mishnah but as a freestanding dispute between Amoraim. Rabbi Shimon — citing Rabbi Levi the elder — holds *eino l'shechita ela l'sof*: the *shechita* occurs only at the end. Rabbi Yochanan holds *yeshno l'shechita mitechila v'ad sof*: it runs from beginning to end.

### Chullin B'Azarah Status

Rav Chavivi of Chuzao said to Rav Ashi: from the position of Rabbi Yochanan — *yeshno l'shechita mitechila v'ad sof* — we can infer that Rabbi Yochanan holds *chullin shenishchatu ba'azarah lav de'oraisa*: that the prohibition of *chullin ba'azarah* is not biblical in origin. This is the only way to reconcile Rabbi Yochanan's view with our Mishnah. If the *shechita* begins at the outset and the animal thereby becomes *assur b'hana'ah* from the Torah from that first moment, the same problem recurs: by the time the *chiyuv* of four and five arrives, the animal is already forbidden and effectively ownerless. To maintain Rabbi Yochanan's position alongside the *tanna kamma*'s ruling, one must conclude that the *issur hana'ah* of *chullin ba'azarah* is not a Torah-level prohibition.

A word on what that means is warranted. There is a *drasha* derived from the verse *ki yirchak mimcha hamakom* — that one may slaughter non-*kodashim* animals only at a distance from the Temple, not near it. This is generally understood as prohibiting *chullin ba'azarah* on a Torah level. But the question is not whether the act is prohibited; the question is what the consequences are for the animal. There is no explicit *pasuk* that declares such an animal *assur b'hana'ah*. When the Gemara says the prohibition is *derabbanan*, it means that the Rabbis never enacted that the animal becomes *assur b'hana'ah* — or at minimum, that the Torah did not impose that consequence. Through the lens of Torah law, the animal remains in the owner's possession and permitted in benefit.

### Derabbanan Clarification

This leads to a precise and important clarification that Tosafot addresses. One might ask: if something is *assur b'hana'ah midrabbanan*, does that not still affect civil liability? After all, the Gemara elsewhere treats rabbinic prohibitions as operative realities — for instance, *chametz* forbidden only rabbinically on *Erev Pesach* cannot effect a valid *kiddushin*. So why should the *derabbanan* status of *chullin ba'azarah* not prevent liability for four and five?

Tosafot draws a careful distinction. In cases like *tikroves avoda zara* — where some opinions hold the prohibition of *hana'ah* is only rabbinic — we would still say the thief is exempt from four and five, because the rabbinic prohibition is a real and operative status. Everyone agrees the animal is *assur b'hana'ah*; it is only the source of that prohibition that is debated. Rabbinic law defines our reality, and we do not bracket it simply because it is rabbinic.

The case of *chullin ba'azarah* is categorically different. To say *chullin ba'azarah* is *derabbanan* in this context is to say that the Rabbis never enacted *issur hana'ah* at all — not from the Torah and not rabbinically. They may have prohibited the act of slaughtering *chullin ba'azarah*, but they did not render the resulting animal forbidden in benefit. Accordingly, "the prohibition is *derabbanan*" here effectively means: there is no *issur hana'ah* operative in any domain, and the animal therefore remains the owner's property for purposes of the *chiyuv* of four and five.

Tosafot on 72b makes this explicit: if *chullin ba'azarah* is *derabbanan* in this sense, a bill of sale signed by witnesses to such a transaction would be valid, and *kiddushin* effected with the proceeds would take effect. It is treated as permitted in benefit for all practical purposes. The Gemara thus preserves the Mishnah's ruling by reading Rabbi Yochanan's position as holding that *chullin ba'azarah* simply does not carry *assur b'hana'ah* at all.

To summarize the three answers the Gemara has generated: first, reject *yeshno l'shechita mitechila v'ad sof* and hold that the *shechita* occurs only at the end — then both the *issur* and the *chiyuv* coincide; second, maintain *yeshno l'shechita mitechila v'ad sof* but hold that *chullin ba'azarah* is not *assur b'hana'ah*, thus the animal never leaves the owner's possession; third, the case of the Mishnah involves physically walking the animal into the *azarah* during the final stroke, making the *issur* and *chiyuv* simultaneous. Each answer is a coherent resolution to the underlying tension, and together they illuminate the interplay between the act of *shechita*, the moment of liability, and the *issur hana'ah* of *chullin ba'azarah*.

---

## Edim Zomemim

### Edim Zomemim Intro

Having worked through the laws of *shechita she'eina re'uya* and its relationship to the *chiyuv* of four and five, the Mishnah turns to a closely related topic that will dominate the remainder of the daf: *edim zomemim*, conspiring or plotting witnesses. While the tractate of Makkot addresses what punishment is administered once witnesses are found to be *zomemim*, and Sanhedrin treats the procedural mechanism by which the *hazama* is established, our Mishnah's focus is a more conceptually acute question: *when* do witnesses become *zomemim*, and what are the downstream consequences of that moment?

Before examining the Mishnah, it is worth clarifying precisely what *edim zomemim* means. It does not mean witnesses who are shown — even by incontrovertible evidence — to have testified falsely about the underlying facts. Even if the alleged murder victim walks into court alive (*ba harug b'raglav*), those witnesses are not *zomemim*. In such a case the testimony is contradicted and discarded, but the witnesses themselves do not bear the special status of *edim zomemim*. Likewise, if two witnesses testify to a theft and two others testify to the contrary, we discard both sets of testimony because they are evenly opposed — but neither group is *zomemim*.

*Hazama* — the act that makes witnesses *zomemim* — occurs specifically when a second pair of witnesses comes and testifies not about the facts but about the first witnesses themselves, saying: you could not possibly know what you claim to have seen on that day, because you were with us elsewhere. The second pair says, in effect, *imanu heyitem b'oto hayom*. Their testimony is about the person, not the event. The halachic result — believing the second pair over the first and administering the punishment of *ka'asher zamam*, as they intended to do to others — is the great *chiddush* of *edim zomemim*, since it is two witnesses against two, and there is no obvious logical basis for preferring one group over the other.

One *rishon* suggests a framework for understanding why the second pair is believed: just as witnesses who are *psulei edut* — say, relatives or known criminals — can be disqualified by testimony about their personal status (which is a separate matter from the facts they are testifying to), so too the second pair is testifying about the personal status of the first pair, saying in effect, "you could not have been there." This creates an asymmetry: the first pair spoke about the events; the second pair speaks about the first pair. And in that sense the second pair's testimony, touching directly on the witnesses rather than the underlying facts, is credited — and produces the consequences of *ka'asher zamam*.

### Mishnah Cases

The Mishnah presents several scenarios of *edim zomemim* in the context of *ganav v'tavach u'machar* — theft followed by slaughter or sale. In the baseline case, one group of two witnesses testified that a person stole an animal (*al pi shenayim*), and a separate group of two witnesses testified that the same person slaughtered or sold it (*al pi shenayim acherim*). Subsequently, a third pair appears and establishes that all four of these witnesses — both groups — were *zomemim*, since they were with the third pair at the time they claimed to have witnessed these events.

The ruling: the first group pays double (*tashlumei kefel*) to the victim of the alleged theft, since their false testimony would have caused the payment of *kefel* — and that is what they pay in return. The second group pays three times (*tashlumei gimmel*), since their testimony added the incremental liability of four and five above the *kefel* — specifically three additional units of payment — and that incremental portion is what they are required to pay.

### Payment Scenarios

The Mishnah then considers partial *hazama*. If only the second group is found *zomemim* (*nimtze'u acharonim zomemim*), the first group's testimony stands, and the original thief pays *kefel* to the owner. The second group, having attempted to add the further liability of four and five through false testimony, pays *tashlumei gimmel* — three times — to the thief, since their *hazama* was directed against him. The thief pays twice to the owner; the *zomemim* pay three times to the thief.

If only one member of the second group is identified as a *zomem* — not both — the entire second group's testimony is voided, but the rule of *ka'asher zamam* does not apply, since that rule requires both witnesses to be *zomemim*. Accordingly, the *ganav* pays only *kefel*, no further payment is extracted, and the second group is not penalized.

If one member of the first group is identified as a *zomem*, the consequence is more sweeping: *batla kol ha'eidus* — the entire testimony collapses. Since the foundation of the case is the testimony that this person was a *ganav* — the theft — without which neither *kefel* nor four and five can be applied, voiding the first testimony removes any basis for liability. The alleged thief may claim he owned the animal legitimately, having purchased it from the original owner, and without testimony establishing the theft, no payment is due. No group was fully established as *zomemim*, and the entire case is nullified.

### Payment Scenarios

The Mishnah then considers partial *hazama*. If only the second group is found *zomemim* (*nimtze'u acharonim zomemim*), the first group's testimony stands, and the original thief pays *kefel* to the owner. The second group, having attempted to add the further liability of four and five through false testimony, pays *tashlumei gimmel* — three times — to the thief, since their *hazama* was directed against him. The thief pays twice to the owner; the *zomemim* pay three times to the thief.

If only one member of the second group is identified as a *zomem* — not both — the entire second group's testimony is voided, but the rule of *ka'asher zamam* does not apply, since that rule requires both witnesses to be *zomemim*. Accordingly, the *ganav* pays only *kefel*, no further payment is extracted, and the second group is not penalized.

If one member of the first group is identified as a *zomem*, the consequence is more sweeping: *batla kol ha'eidus* — the entire testimony collapses. Since the foundation of the case is the testimony that this person was a *ganav* — the theft — without which neither *kefel* nor four and five can be applied, voiding the first testimony removes any basis for liability. The alleged thief may claim he owned the animal legitimately, having purchased it from the original owner, and without testimony establishing the theft, no payment is due. No group was fully established as *zomemim*, and the entire case is nullified.

### Abaye vs. Rava

The Gemara (*itmar*) now turns to the central Amoraic dispute of this sugya: what is the temporal status of an *ed zomem*? When, precisely, does a witness become disqualified?

To understand the question, one must picture a timeline. At some point in the past — call it the first date — the two witnesses appear in court and give their testimony, claiming to have witnessed the theft and slaughter of an animal on an earlier occasion. Months later — call it a later date — a second pair of witnesses establishes that the first pair were *zomemim*: they could not have seen what they claimed because they were elsewhere. Between the first date and the later date, the original pair may have signed *shtaros* (documents), testified in other cases, and been relied upon by the public as valid witnesses.

Abaye holds: *l'mafrei'a hu nifsul* — the disqualification is retroactive. Once the *hazama* is established, we now know that on the earlier date, these witnesses bore false testimony. The Torah teaches that a *rasha* — one who transgresses the prohibition against false testimony — may not serve as a witness (*al tashet yad'cha im rasha lihyot ed chamas*). Since they transgressed that prohibition at the first date, they have been *resha'im* since then, and any testimony they gave in the intervening period must be retroactively invalidated.

Rava holds: *mikan u'l'haba hu nifsul* — disqualification applies only from the later date going forward.

### Abaye's Logic

Abaye's position flows from the premise that the *hazama* reveals a truth about the past. The Torah instructs us to believe the second pair of witnesses — and if we believe them, we now know that the first pair testified falsely. That false testimony made them *resha'im* from the moment they stood in court and lied. Since the disqualification status of a *rasha* attaches at the moment of the transgression, and the transgression occurred at the first date, the *nifsul* — the disqualification — must run from that moment. The testimony given between the first date and the later date was therefore given while they were already *psulim*, and it must be voided.

Crucially, this is not an evidentiary claim about the credibility of those intermediate testimonies. Perhaps every one of those intermediate testimonies was entirely accurate. But just as a *karov* — a relative — cannot testify even when he is telling the absolute truth, because his personal status renders him *pasul le'eidus*, so too these witnesses, having become *resha'im*, are disqualified regardless of the veracity of what they said in the interim.

### Rava's Chiddush

Rava's position begins from a fundamental observation about *edim zomemim*: the entire framework is a *chiddush*. *Trei u'trei ninhu* — it is two against two. Why do we listen to these witnesses over those? There is no logical basis for preferring the second pair's account. The *chiddush* of the Torah is to say: in this specific procedural context — where the second pair testifies not about the facts but that the first pair was elsewhere — we follow the second pair. But since the entire enterprise is a *chiddush*, one should not extend its consequences beyond its own scope. *Ein lecha bo ela mishat chidusho v'eilach*: one applies the *chiddush* only from the moment it is invoked, going forward.

Conceptually, Rava's position is striking. It implies that even after the *hazama* is established, we do not necessarily *know* that the first pair lied. We know that the Torah's procedure designates them as *edim zomemim* and that we apply *ka'asher zamam*. But that procedure is a *chiddush* — a legal mechanism — not necessarily a factual determination about who told the truth. If we could truly say that the Torah is revealing to us that the first pair lied, Abaye's retroactive logic would be compelling. But if the *chiddush* is a procedural mechanism — "in this configuration, these witnesses bear this status" — then extending it retroactively goes beyond what the *chiddush* licenses. The status applies from the moment the Torah's procedure activates it: *mikan u'l'haba*.

This reasoning resonates with a broader observation about the punishments associated with *edim zomemim*. The Torah applies *ka'asher zamam v'lo ka'asher asah*: punishment for what the witnesses *intended*, not what they actually accomplished. This is itself disproportionate by any conventional logic. The Ramban, in his commentary on the Torah, notes that this category of punishment — along with *ben sorer u'moreh*, *zaken mamre*, and *navi sheker* — is characterized by the Torah's statement *v'chol Yisrael yishme'u v'yira'u*: all of Israel shall hear and be afraid. In each of these cases, the punishment exceeds what the individual strictly deserves, but society requires a severe deterrent to protect foundational institutions — the courts, parental authority, the authority of the *sanhedrin*, the authority of God. The disproportionate punishment is thus not about individual desert but about systemic integrity. This is deeply consistent with Rava's view that *edim zomemim* is a *chiddush*: the Torah is not primarily making a factual finding; it is protecting the court system by making the consequences of attempted *hazama* severe and categorical.

### Pesida D'Luchochos

The Gemara reports a second version of Rava's position. According to this view, Rava in principle agrees with Abaye — once the *hazama* is established, one recognizes retroactively that the witnesses were *resha'im* from the moment of their false testimony. But Rava holds *mikan u'l'haba* for a different reason: *mishum pseida d'luchochos* — to protect innocent parties.

Consider the practical consequences of retroactive disqualification. The two witnesses who gave false testimony in court may have, in the intervening months, signed numerous *shtaros* — loan documents, bills of sale, contracts. Creditors and buyers relied on these witnesses in good faith, seeing that the courts had accepted them as valid. To retroactively invalidate all those documents would cause devastating losses to innocent third parties who had no reason to doubt the witnesses' reliability. To prevent this injustice, Rava rules that as a practical rabbinic measure, the disqualification is applied only going forward.

This version of Rava's position is more limited than the *chiddush* formulation. It concedes Abaye's theoretical framework — the witnesses really were *resha'im* from the earlier date — but overrides the practical consequence for civil documents in order to protect the innocent *luchochos*. Importantly, however, this protection extends only to monetary documents. Where the intervening testimony touched on matters of personal status — a woman's marriage, a divorce, an adulterous act, capital punishment, *kiddush hachodesh* — those testimonies would be retroactively voided even according to the *pseida d'luchochos* rationale, because the injustice of allowing such testimony to stand exceeds the benefit of protecting innocent third parties. Tosafot makes this explicit, listing cases of *dinei nefashos*, *gittin*, *kiddushin*, and *eidus hachodesh* as instances where the *pseida* rationale would not override the need to invalidate the prior testimony.

### Chiddush vs. Pesida

The Gemara asks: what is the practical difference between the two versions of Rava — the *chiddush* reasoning and the *pseida d'luchochos* reasoning?

The Gemara offers the following scenario: two witnesses say one of the *zomemim* was with them, and two other witnesses say the other one was with them — each witness is challenged individually (*d'asi bei trei l'chad u'bei trei l'chad*). In this configuration, each individual challenge is two against one, not two against two. If the only basis for applying *mikan u'l'haba* is the *chiddush* — namely, that the Torah makes a special allowance for two against two — then where there is no *chiddush* (because it is two against one and no special allowance is needed to believe the challengers), disqualification would be retroactive. But if the reason is *pseida d'luchochos*, we still want to protect innocent buyers and sellers, so we apply *mikan u'l'haba* even here.

Alternatively (*ei nami*), where the second pair disqualifies the first pair not through *hazama* — "you were with us" — but by testifying that they are *gazlanim* and therefore *psulei eidut*, that is also not a *chiddush* since there is a straightforward reason to believe testimony about personal status. According to the *chiddush* rationale, there would be no basis for limiting the disqualification to *mikan u'l'haba*, and it would apply retroactively. According to the *pseida d'luchochos* rationale, we would still protect innocent *luchochos* and apply it only going forward.

### Halakha L'Abaye

The Gemara concludes decisively. Rav Yirmiya of Difti reports that Rav Pappa ruled in practice like Rava — disqualifying the witnesses only going forward. Rav Ashi counters: *hilchesa k'vasei d'Abaye* — the *halacha* follows Abaye, and disqualification is retroactive.

The Gemara then states its final ruling: *v'hilchesa k'vasei d'Abaye b'Ya'al Kagam*. This is the well-known mnemonic encoding the cases in which the halacha follows Abaye against Rava — an exception to the general rule that the halacha follows Rava in their disputes. The *ayin* stands for *edim zomemim*, our case. The other letters of the mnemonic encode: *yud* for *yeush she-lo m'da'as*, *lamed* for *lechi ha-omed me-elav*, *kuf* for *kiddushin she-lo nimseru l'via*, *gimmel* for *giluy milsa b'gita*, and *mem* for *mumar ochel neveilos l'teiavon*.

The sugya thus closes with the halacha firmly in Abaye's camp: once witnesses are established as *edim zomemim*, their disqualification runs retroactively to the moment they bore false witness. Any testimony they gave between the date of their perjury and the date of the *hazama* is invalidated as well. The debate between Abaye and Rava — whether that retroactive disqualification is a principled truth about their status from the moment of the transgression, or merely the outer limit of a *chiddush* that licenses only prospective consequences, or a concession to practical justice for innocent third parties — remains one of the Gemara's most penetrating discussions of the nature of the law of *edim zomemim*, and the discussion will continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 73

## Edim Zomemim Retroactive

### Intro: Edim Zomemim

We find ourselves squarely in the middle of one of the most analytically intense *sugyot* in *Shas* concerning *edim zomemim*. The preceding discussion established the great debate between Abaye and Rava over whether *edim zomemim* are disqualified *lemafre'a hu nifsul* — retroactively from the time of their false testimony — or only *mikan ule-haba* — prospectively from the moment they are exposed.

### Abaye: Lemafrea

Abaye's position is in many ways the intuitive one. Once the *zomemim* are proven to have lied, and we accept the testimony of those who contradict them, we can conclude that back at the moment they testified they were already lying. This retrospective recognition stamps them as *resha'im* — or more precisely, as *edim zomemim* — which formally disqualifies their witness status even for that earlier period. Importantly, this does not mean that a person who has lied once will necessarily lie again; rather, the act of bearing false testimony categorically labels one a *rasha* and invalidates one's standing as a witness, even if, as a matter of fact, what was said in some instance happened to be true.

### Rava: Mikan Ule-Haba

Rava's response is that disqualification takes effect only from this point forward. One compelling explanation he offers rests on a fundamental conceptual point about the nature of *edim zomemim*: logically speaking, there is no compelling reason to believe the later group over the original witnesses. If the *Torah* instructs us to accept the *hazama* process, we comply — but the degree to which we can say that this *proves* the original witnesses were lying is limited. We do not know as a fact that they lied; the *Torah* imposes a legal status upon them. That status, therefore, properly attaches from the moment it is declared, not retroactively. On another reading, Rava may genuinely agree with Abaye that the disqualification is logically retroactive — but introduces a sweeping practical consideration: if *lemafre'a* applies without qualification, then anyone who has ever testified in court is potentially a liability. Witnesses who signed a *get* two years ago might later be proven *zomemim*, rendering the *get* retroactively invalid. The practical consequences, particularly for monetary documents, would be catastrophic.

### Practical Consequences

The *halakha* is one of the well-known cases in which we rule like Abaye: *lemafre'a hu nifsul*, the disqualification is retroactive. Even Rava's pragmatic concession extends only to monetary documents — for matters of personal status, the retroactive invalidation stands with full force. The possibility that witnesses trusted for years might be unmasked as *zomemim* long after the fact is genuinely disquieting. Rava's position limits the damage for monetary instruments but cannot wholly resolve it for *issurei* matters.

### Teshuvah Discussion

One might ask whether an *ed zomem* can ever restore his witness status through *teshuvah*. The *Gemara* in Masechet Sanhedrin addresses this directly: the answer is yes, but the standard is demanding. It is not sufficient to *klop al chet* on Yom Kippur. What is required is visible, practical change — communal recognition that the person has genuinely altered his conduct. Abstract inner repentance does not suffice; the community must be able to observe tangible evidence of transformation before its confidence in the witness is restored.

---

## Ganav, Tavach, Machar

### Mishna Overview

The *Gemara* turns to a *mishna* that presents a case directly relevant to the Abaye-Rava debate. The *mishna* reads: *ganav al pi shenayim* — someone was convicted of burglary on the testimony of two witnesses; *ve-tavach u-machar al pihen* — the very same two witnesses testified that he subsequently slaughtered or sold the stolen animal; *ve-nimtzu zomemim* — and they were proven to be *edim zomemim* on the entire matter. The ruling is *meshalmim et hakol* — they pay the full amount corresponding to the fourfold or fivefold penalty they had sought to impose.

The natural reading of this scenario assumes a sequence: the witnesses first testified about the theft, and subsequently testified about the slaughter or sale. This makes procedural sense — no one simply walks into a *beit din* and testifies that someone sold an animal without first establishing that the animal was stolen.

### The Kashe

The *Gemara* now raises a sharp difficulty against this natural reading. If we rule like Abaye that disqualification is retroactive, a serious problem emerges. Let us place these events on a timeline. Suppose the witnesses testified about the theft at noon on Sunday and about the slaughter at noon on Monday. Later, a group of *hazama* witnesses came and declared: you could not have seen the theft on Sunday, for you were with us that day. Then another group — or the same group at a different point — declared: you could not have seen the slaughter on Monday either.

Now: according to Abaye, the witnesses became *psulei edim* retroactively from the moment of their false Sunday testimony. That means that by Monday at noon, when they testified about the slaughter, they were already disqualified witnesses. But if they were already *pasul* at the time they gave the *tavichah* testimony, that testimony was never validly received — not as false testimony but as *invalid* testimony, testimony that should never have been credited at all. A disqualified witness cannot become an *ed zomem* for that very act, since the status of *ed zomem* presupposes a legally valid act of testimony that is then proven false. Consequently, they should pay only *kefel* — the twofold penalty associated with the theft alone — but not the additional payment for slaughter or sale, since that testimony was void from the outset. This is the *Gemara*'s *kashe*.

The *Gemara* attempts a first answer: perhaps the *hazama* came first on the *tavichah* testimony, so the witnesses became *pasul* only from that later point, leaving the original *geneivah* testimony intact. But the *Gemara* immediately rejects this, noting that ultimately the *geneivah* testimony will also be undone, and *igalai milta* — it will retroactively emerge — that even at the moment they testified about the *tavichah*, they were already *pasulim*. The order in which the *hazama* groups come to court is immaterial; at the end of the day, both testimonies will be nullified.

### Bevat Achat Solution

The answer, which in retrospect may seem obvious, is that the testimony was given *b'vat achat* — all at once. The witnesses did not come on Sunday to testify about the theft and return on Monday to testify about the slaughter. They delivered the entire testimony — *ganav ve-tabach* — in a single court session.

This requires some unpacking. Even within one court session, testimony takes time to process. Witnesses do not speak simultaneously; there is cross-examination, clarification of dates and locations, and so on. So the question is not merely whether they entered the building on the same day, but whether the entire testimony is legally regarded as a single unit. The *Gemara* affirms that it is, because it was delivered within *toch k'dei dibbur* — within the halakhic span of a single speech act.

The key insight is this: if the entire testimony is one unit, then the retroactive *pesul* that attaches when the *zomemim* are exposed attaches to the whole unit simultaneously. One cannot say that "at the first instant of the testimony the witnesses were kosher, and only at the second instant they became *pasul*," because halachically there is no first and second instant — it is all one moment. Therefore, the same testimony that renders them *pasul* is also the testimony upon which they are judged as *edim zomemim*, and they pay for the full amount.

### Toch K'dei Dibbur

This solution raises the further question of what exactly *toch k'dei dibbur* means and why it renders the entire testimony a single unit. Tosafot explains the connection: within *toch k'dei dibbur*, one retains the ability to retract or correct a statement. If you pronounce a *bracha* over the wrong food and correct yourself within *toch k'dei dibbur*, the correction stands. This is why the entire speech act — even if it spans several sentences — is considered legally undivided: it remains open to self-correction and therefore constitutes one coherent act of speech rather than a series of distinct acts.

One might ask: even if all the witnesses arrived in court together, surely the testimony about the theft and the testimony about the slaughter take more than a single breath to deliver. Is it truly the case that a testimony spanning perhaps a minute of description counts as *toch k'dei dibbur*? The answer, as we shall see, involves a more nuanced examination of what *toch k'dei dibbur* actually measures — but the *Gemara*'s position at this stage is that it indeed encompasses the relevant span of time, and therefore the entire testimony is one unit.

An interesting adjacent question arises: if witnesses had their testimony accepted by the court, and it were subsequently discovered that they were relatives or otherwise disqualified — not *zomemim* — yet it is also known that their testimony was false, would their disqualification as valid witnesses carry any moral or legal consequence of its own? They would not be *chayav* for *hazama*, since *hazama* requires valid testimony that is proven false, and their testimony was never legally valid. Whether the bare fact of knowingly bearing false witness, even under a technical procedural invalidity, carries independent consequences is a genuinely difficult question.

---

## R. Yosi: Part Negates Wh…

### Sh'tei Eduyot vs. Edut A…

The *Gemara* now introduces a *tanna'ic* debate and asks whether it maps onto the Abaye-Rava dispute. The *baraita* presents two scenarios. In the first, two witnesses testify that someone stole an animal (*geneivah*) and that he subsequently slaughtered it (*tavichah*). They are then proven *zomemim* only on the *geneivah* — but not on the *tavichah*. In this case, *edut she-batlah miktzatah batlah kullah* — because the theft testimony is void, the slaughter testimony becomes meaningless (one cannot be liable for the enhanced penalty of four or five without the predicate theft), and nobody pays four or five. The witnesses pay *kefel* for the false theft testimony alone.

In the reverse scenario, the witnesses are found *zomemim* only on the *tavichah*. Here the *ganav* pays *kefel* for the theft, since that testimony stands, and the witnesses pay three additional parts — the difference between fourfold or fivefold and twofold — because they were *zomemim* on the slaughter.

Rabbi Yosi then introduces his qualification: *bameh devarim amurim* — when does this hold? Only *bi-shtei eduyot*, when the testimony was delivered in two distinct testimonies. But *b'edut achat*, when it was one unified testimony, *edut she-batlah miktzatah batlah kullah* — if any part of the testimony is void, the whole is void.

The novel implication here is that Rabbi Yosi applies this principle in the reverse direction from what one might expect. The *Rabbanan* already established that invalidating the *geneivah* portion nullifies the *tavichah* portion — that is the straightforward reading of the principle. Rabbi Yosi extends it: invalidating the *tavichah* portion also nullifies the *geneivah* portion, even though the *geneivah* testimony logically preceded it in time. This is the surprising move — because even under *lemafre'a*, the *geneivah* testimony was delivered *before* the false *tavichah* testimony. How does a later falsehood retroactively poison an earlier valid statement?

### Gemara Challenges

The *Gemara* seeks to clarify what Rabbi Yosi means by *shtei eduyot* versus *edut achat*. One reading: *shtei eduyot mamash* refers to two separate groups of witnesses — Group A testifies about the theft, Group B testifies about the slaughter. *Edut achat* would then mean one group, testifying on two occasions.

But this reading immediately creates a problem. If *edut achat* means one group testifying first about the *geneivah* at noon and then about the *tavichah* an hour later, how can finding them *zomemim* on the *tavichah* void their earlier *geneivah* testimony? *Me-heicha teisi hach* — where does that come from? They testified about the theft at noon and were valid witnesses. Their subsequent falsehood about the slaughter happened an hour later. There is no obvious mechanism by which a later falsehood retroactively corrupts an earlier valid testimony.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes that *shtei eduyot* means one group testifying sequentially — first about the theft and then, some time later, about the slaughter. *Edut achat* means one group testifying about both in a single utterance, *b'vat achat*, within *toch k'dei dibbur*. The dispute between Rabbi Yosi and the *Rabbanan* must therefore be about whether *toch k'dei dibbur k'dibbur dami* — whether something stated within the span of *toch k'dei dibbur* is treated as a unified single statement.

### Debate Focus Refined

The *Gemara* now proceeds carefully. It first assumes that *kulei alma* — both Rabbi Yosi and the *Rabbanan* — would agree that the disqualification of *edim zomemim* is *lemafre'a*, retroactive. Given this shared assumption, the question of whether invalidating the *tavichah* throws out the *geneivah* turns on whether we treat the testimony as one unified statement or two. If it is one unified statement (because *toch k'dei dibbur k'dibbur dami*), then retroactive invalidation reaches back through the entire statement and voids the *geneivah* portion too, since at the moment of the unified act of testimony, the witnesses were *pasulim*. If, however, the two parts are treated as distinct statements — even if delivered within *toch k'dei dibbur* — then the *geneivah* portion was validly given and is not undermined by the later *pesul*.

On this reading, the *Rabbanan* hold *toch k'dei dibbur lav k'dibbur dami* — even within that brief span, the two conceptually distinct testimonies about theft and slaughter are treated as separate. Thus only the portion upon which they are *zomemim* is void; the prior portion stands. Rabbi Yosi holds *toch k'dei dibbur k'dibbur dami* — the entire utterance is one statement, one moment in time, and voiding any part of it voids the whole.

The *Gemara* then revises this picture. It notes that if *kulei alma* held *lemafre'a* and *kulei alma* held *toch k'dei dibbur k'dibbur dami*, everyone would agree to throw out everything, and there would be no dispute. The debate must therefore itself be about *toch k'dei dibbur*. The *Rabbanan* deny that *toch k'dei dibbur* can unify two conceptually distinct testimonies into one statement; Rabbi Yosi affirms it. And since everyone by this point is understood to hold *lemafre'a*, it follows that Rabbi Yosi's position that it is all one statement also entails retroactive invalidation of the *geneivah* testimony. This is how Rabbi Yosi's ruling maps cleanly onto Abaye: *lemafre'a hu nifsul*, retroactively they were *pasul*, and therefore the unified testimony is entirely void.

The *Gemara* then raises a striking challenge against Rabbi Yosi himself. Does Rabbi Yosi truly hold *toch k'dei dibbur k'dibbur dami*? The *mishna* in the laws of *tmura* records a dispute: if someone says *harei zo tmurat olah tmurat shelamim* — "this animal shall be an exchange for a burnt-offering, an exchange for a peace-offering" — Rabbi Meir holds that we follow the first part of the statement; the animal becomes a *tmurat olah*. Rabbi Yosi says: if the person intended from the outset to designate it for both, since it is impossible to pronounce two words simultaneously, we do not coerce the statement to follow only the first word — *devarav kayyamim*, both designations are upheld and the animal is treated as half of each. But if the person said *tmurat olah* and then *nimlach* — changed his mind — and said *tmurat shelamim*, then *harei zo tmurat olah*: he is bound by his first declaration.

This seems to say that Rabbi Yosi *does not* hold that you can amend a statement within *toch k'dei dibbur* — if you clearly changed your mind, you are bound by the first word. But then how does he say, in the *edut* case, that the entire testimony is one unified statement and voiding the *tavichah* voids the *geneivah*? He seems to be treating the two halves as bound together, which should require him to hold *toch k'dei dibbur k'dibbur dami*. Yet the *tmura* case suggests he does not allow a statement made within *toch k'dei dibbur* to undo a prior statement. The cases seem to pull in opposite directions.

One could draw various distinctions: between amending a statement and appending to one; between the speech-act context of a *korban* designation, where speech creates immediate metaphysical change, and the context of court testimony, which unfolds through a process of examination; or between a correction that goes backward and a continuation that adds forward. There is also the issue of *devarim she'ba-lev* — Rabbi Yosi's ruling in the *tmura* case appears to depend on what the speaker intended, raising questions about when we rely on the speaker's declared intent.

The *Gemara*, however, resolves the tension with a technical rather than conceptual distinction, introduced by Rav Pappa.

---

## Two K'dei Dibur Measures

### Rav Pappa's Distinction

Rav Pappa explains that there are in fact two distinct measures subsumed under the term *toch k'dei dibbur*. The first is *k'dei she'elat talmid le-rav* — the time it takes a student to greet his teacher: *shalom alecha rabbi u-mori*. This is the longer measure, equivalent to roughly a full breath's worth of speech. The second is *k'dei she'elat ha-rav le-talmid* — the time it takes a teacher to greet a student: simply *shalom alecha*, which is half the length.

On this basis, Rav Pappa explains Rabbi Yosi's apparently contradictory positions. In the *tmura* case, where Rabbi Yosi says that changing one's mind within *toch k'dei dibbur* does not help — *nimlach* within *toch k'dei dibbur* still leaves you bound by your first statement — he is referring to the longer measure, *k'dei she'elat talmid le-rav*. That longer span is long enough that a change of mind partway through constitutes a genuine interruption and a distinct act of speech. But in the *edut* case, where he treats the entire testimony as a unified statement, he refers to the shorter measure, *k'dei she'elat ha-rav le-talmid* — within that briefer interval, he does hold *toch k'dei dibbur k'dibbur dami*.

This is an admirably economical solution, though one may be forgiven for finding it somewhat mechanical. There are many richer distinctions one might have drawn — between amending and extending a statement, between the immediate performative effect of a *korban* designation and the processual nature of court testimony, between a corrective reversal and a continuous elaboration. The *Gemara* sets all of these aside and resolves the tension on the basis of a quantitative difference in the span of *toch k'dei dibbur*.

### Rabbeinu Tam's Theory

Tosafot cites Rabbeinu Tam, who addresses a more foundational question: why is *toch k'dei dibbur* measured by a greeting at all? What is the relationship between the measure of a salutation and the legal unification of speech acts?

Rabbeinu Tam's answer is distinctively pragmatic. When a person is in the middle of a transaction or giving testimony, it can happen that a friend or teacher greets him. The *Gemara* in Berakhot establishes that one who is greeted and fails to return the greeting is called a *gazlan* — he has withheld something owed. Therefore, anyone in the course of a transaction or testimony may find himself compelled to interrupt and respond to a greeting. Since this interruption is not voluntary but socially and halachically obligatory, the Sages ruled — using the language of *tiknu chachamim* — that such an interruption shall not be counted as a *hefsek*, a legal break in the speech act. The measure of the greeting thus defines the maximum obligatory interruption that is considered invisible to halacha.

### Two Conceptions

Tosafot itself notes a tension in Rabbeinu Tam's formulation. The language *tiknu chachamim* — "the Sages enacted" — is an unusual way to describe what might seem like a definitional or conceptual ruling. Rabbeinu Tam acknowledges that this explanation sits uneasily with the *Gemara* in the final chapter of Nedarim, where *toch k'dei dibbur* is applied to the laws of *kriah* — a mourner who tears his garment believing his father has died, but the father actually dies a moment later: if the death occurs within *toch k'dei dibbur* of the tearing, the *kriah* is valid. This has nothing to do with social interruptions or obligatory greetings. Rabbeinu Tam offers only a tentative answer to this difficulty.

The deeper theoretical issue is this: there are really two distinct conceptions of *toch k'dei dibbur* operating in halachic literature. One conception, which resonates with Rabbeinu Tam's framing, treats *toch k'dei dibbur* as defining the natural unit of a *speech act* — the period during which an utterance remains open, correctable, still part of the living breath of a single declaration. The other conception, perhaps better suited to the *kriah* case, treats *toch k'dei dibbur* as defining a *moment in time* — the halachic precision with which simultaneity is measured. Two events that occur within *toch k'dei dibbur* of one another are treated as having occurred *at the same time*, regardless of their content or any speech involved.

Both of these conceptions are at play in our *sugya*, and distinguishing which applies in a given case is itself a significant analytical task.

---

## Hachasha v. Hazama

### Rava's Principle

Rava now introduces a separate but related ruling. *Edim she-huchkhashu u-le-vasof huzmu* — witnesses who were first subjected to *hachasha* (contradictory testimony) and who were subsequently made *zomemim* — *neheragin*, they can still be executed. The *hachasha* does not prevent the *hazama* from taking legal effect. The reason: *de-hachasha techilat hazama hi* — a contradiction is considered the *beginning* of the process of *hazama*, not an independent competing process that forecloses it.

To understand this, one must recall the distinction between *hachasha* and *hazama*. *Hachasha* occurs when another group of witnesses contradicts the testimony — saying, for instance, that Reuven was not at the scene, or offering a different account of events. This does not prove that the first group lied; it creates an impasse, and the court cannot rely on either group. *Hazama* is categorically different: the contradicting witnesses say "you could not have seen what you claim to have seen, because you were *with us* at a different location at that time." This is not merely contradictory — it is *disproof*. The *Torah* applies specific consequences to *hazama* that do not apply to mere *hachasha*.

Rava's ruling is that if witnesses are first *mochachash* — their testimony is contradicted and thrown out — and then *later* the same witnesses are *muzzam* (proven *zomemim* by a subsequent group who says they were with them elsewhere), they are still liable as *edim zomemim*. One might have thought that because the testimony had already been discarded, there was no longer a legally operative testimony against which the *hazama* could function. Rava says no: *hachasha* is the opening stage of the same process that culminates in *hazama*. The testimony is attacked, not resolved, by *hachasha*, and the *hazama* completes the attack.

### Eye and Tooth Case

Rava then asks: *mena amina lah* — from where do I derive this? He cites a *baraita*. The case involves a slave owner who is said to have blinded his slave's eye and then knocked out his tooth. The background rule is that a master who destroys any limb of his slave must free him — *ayin tachat ayin*. Crucially, if the tooth was knocked out first, the slave becomes free from that moment, and then the destruction of the eye entitles the now-free slave to the full monetary value of an eye as compensation. If the eye was blinded first, the slave becomes free from that point, and the later loss of the tooth entitles him only to the (much smaller) value of a tooth. The order thus dramatically affects the financial consequences.

The *baraita* describes witnesses who testify: first the eye was blinded, then the tooth was knocked out. And the *baraita* notes: *harei ha-rav omer kein* — the master is satisfied with this order of testimony. The *Gemara* asks: why would the master be satisfied? If this group of witnesses were the *first* to come to court, their testimony would be making the master *liable* — they are forcing him to free the slave and then pay the value of the tooth. That is worse for the master than if no testimony had been given.

The only way the master is *satisfied* with this testimony is if there was already a different testimony in place — specifically, the *opposite* order. If a prior group of witnesses had testified that the tooth came first (freeing the slave) and then the eye was blinded (now entitling the free man to the full value of an eye), the master faced a vastly larger payment. The *second* group then comes and says: no, it was the eye first, then the tooth — which means the slave became free only when the eye was blinded, and the tooth was knocked out while he was still a slave, entitling him only to the value of a tooth. The master pays far less under this order. That is why *harei ha-rav omer kein* — relative to the first testimony, the master benefits enormously from this second testimony.

### Hachasha = Beginning

Now the crucial point. The second group testified in a context where the first group had already testified to the opposite order. The second group's testimony is therefore *mochachash* — contradictory — from the very moment it is given. There is no stage at which the second testimony was simply accepted by the court; it entered into an immediate conflict with the prior testimony. And yet, the *baraita* says *ve-nimtzu zomemim* — and they were found to be *zomemim*. A third group came and said: you couldn't have witnessed what you claimed, for you were with us. And the ruling is *meshalmin dmei ayin le-eved* — the *metziai*, the middle group of false witnesses, must pay the slave the value of an eye (net of the tooth).

This proves Rava's principle. The middle witnesses began their career as *mochachashim* — their testimony was in immediate conflict with the prior group and could not be simply accepted. Yet they were ultimately processed as *edim zomemim* and paid accordingly. The *Gemara* confirms: *shema mina hachasha techilat hazama* — this case demonstrates that contradiction is the beginning of the *hazama* process, not a bar to it.

### Abaye's Counter

Abaye, however, challenges this reading of the *baraita*. He argues that the case does not require a backdrop of prior contradictory testimony. Rather, the sequence was: the middle group came first and testified that the eye was blinded and then the tooth was knocked out. *On this original testimony alone*, the master was being made liable — forced to free the slave and pay for the tooth. The master was *not* happy; they were hurting him.

Then a later group came and made the middle group *zomemim* — saying you were with us, you could not have seen what you claim. But they simultaneously testified to the true order of events: in fact, it was the tooth first and then the eye. Only now, with this later testimony in court, do we understand the true state of affairs. Retroactively, we see that what the middle witnesses had actually accomplished — had their false testimony been relied upon — was not to hurt the master but to hurt the slave, preventing him from recovering the much more valuable compensation for the eye. Their *kavana* aside, the *objective effect* of their false testimony, once the true facts emerge, was to deprive the slave.

On Abaye's reading, there is no *hachasha* at all — the *hazama* stands alone. The later witnesses do double duty: they prove that the middle witnesses were *zomemim*, and they supply the true testimony that reframes the financial impact of the falsehood. Abaye thus rejects Rava's proposed proof, denying that the *baraita* involves a case of *hachasha* preceding *hazama*. Rava's principle may or may not be correct, but this particular proof text, Abaye argues, does not establish it. The *sugya* will continue on the next *daf*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 74

## Hachasha v. Hazama

### Dispute Overview

The sugya opens in the final lines of 73b with the dispute between Abaye and Rava over whether *hachasha techilat hazama* — whether contradiction (*hachasha*) constitutes the beginning of the process of *hazama* (the invalidation of witnesses as *eidim zomemim*). The practical stakes are significant. If witness group A testifies that Reuven committed a crime on Monday, and group B contradicts them by saying Reuven was with us on Monday — that is *hachasha*, which neutralizes group A's testimony. But can group B then go further and say "and you, group A, were also with us on Monday" — completing the process of *hazama*? Rava holds that *hachasha hi techilat hazama*: contradiction is merely the opening stage of a process that can lawfully culminate in *hazama*. Abaye disagrees: once testimony has been neutralized by *hachasha*, it is no longer live, and *hazama* cannot follow.

### Rava's Braita Proof

Rava attempts to establish his position from a *braita* dealing with witnesses who testify about injuries a master inflicted on his slave — specifically, whether the eye was knocked out first or the tooth. The order matters enormously: since knocking out either the eye or the tooth obligates the master to free the slave, the second injury would carry no such consequence, and only a monetary payment would apply. A master who has already lost his slave due to the tooth would naturally prefer testimony that the eye came second, so that he owes only the monetary value of the tooth. The *braita* describes a case where witnesses testify in the order the master prefers — eye then tooth — and are subsequently found to be *zomemim*. They must then pay the master the value of the eye, since their false testimony was aimed at depriving him of that amount. Rava argues that this *braita* presupposes the existence of prior contradicting testimony about the reverse order, and that the *zomemim* testimony followed and overrode it — demonstrating that *hazama* can succeed *hachasha*.

### Abaye's Two-Group Model

Abaye rejects this reading entirely. He argues that there were never three groups of witnesses — only two. The *eidim* who carried out the *hazama* were themselves the ones who provided the alternative account of events. The Gemara introduces this with the phrase *lo d'hafchinun v'hazminun*: the very witnesses who reversed the story are also the ones who performed the *hazama*. How does Abaye know that the *seifa* of the *braita* involves only two groups? He infers it from the *seifa* itself. In the *seifa*, the case is that witnesses testify in the order favorable to the slave — tooth then eye — and the *eved* is happy with this. But the *eved* would be happy with this testimony even without any prior contradicting testimony, simply because it promises him his freedom and a monetary payment. There is therefore no textual signal in the *seifa* that a separate prior group testified to the reverse. Since the *seifa* is definitively a two-group case, Abaye argues, so too is the *reisha*.

### Eye/Tooth Cases

The Gemara then works through the mechanics of how such testimony operates. The key constraint, noted by Rashi, is that in the *seifa* — where the *zomemim* are testifying that the eye came last — their testimony could never have stood unopposed if a prior *kat* had already testified that the eye came first. Testimony demanding greater payment (the eye) would not have been accepted had a contradicting account already been on record. Since such testimony was apparently accepted and acted upon, there was no prior *kat*, and the reversal must have come from the *mazimim* themselves.

The *reisha* operates differently. There, the *zomemim* testified that the tooth came last — a lesser obligation. Had a prior *kat* testified to the tooth and then a second *kat* testified to the eye, the court would follow the lesser of the two competing claims (since that represents the overlap), meaning the first *kat*'s testimony about the tooth would still have been operative rather than neutralized. This is consistent with three *kitot*: the first *kat* testifying tooth-then-eye, the middle *kat* testifying eye-then-tooth, and the *mazimim* then invalidating the middle *kat*.

The Gemara then addresses a subtle question posed by Rav Zeira: perhaps when a slave sustains both injuries, the Torah only provides for his freedom — once for the eye and once for the tooth — with no monetary payment at all? Abaye responds from the verse: *tachas eino*, "in exchange for his eye" — but not in exchange for his eye *and* his tooth. The Torah grants freedom for one injury; the other must be compensated differently, i.e., monetarily.

### Hamarah B'Din

A further complication is introduced: even granting the structure of the case, the *braita* cannot be describing a situation in which the contradicting testimony refers to events that occurred *after* the first group's testimony was given. If the *batra'i* say the real events occurred on Monday (whereas the first group claimed Sunday), then when the first group testified about Sunday, the master had not yet been obligated to free the slave — so the false testimony was attempting to impose a full monetary liability for the slave's value, not merely to alter the order of injuries. That cannot be the *braita*'s intent.

Similarly, it is not enough that the master committed the act on an earlier date unless he had already appeared in *beis din* — since freeing a slave on account of an injury is a *knas*, and a *knas* is not a self-executing obligation. It is imposed by *beis din*. Consequently, the scenario must be that: (a) the second group's contradicting testimony refers to events that preceded Sunday, and (b) there had already been *hamarah b'din* — a court ruling — before the date the first group claimed the injury occurred. Only then can the first group be characterized as falsely shifting the monetary consequence, rather than falsely creating an obligation wholesale. This requirement for *hamarah b'din* applies equally to both the *reisha* and the *seifa* of the *braita*, and stands independently of the Abaye-Rava dispute.

### Rav Acha's Challenge

Rav Acha b'rei d'Rav Ika challenges Rava's inferences directly, focusing first on the *reisha*. He asks: what is actually the source of Rava's proof that the *reisha* involves three *kitot*? The *reisha* says the master is pleased with the testimony. While this does suggest a prior adverse account, Rav Acha points out that the middle *kat* — the one ultimately found to be *zomemim* — is not actually *neutralized* by the first *kat*. Because their testimony asserts the lesser obligation (the tooth rather than the eye), the principle of *d'is biklal meah masayim* — that the lesser is included in the greater — means the court will actually follow the second *kat*'s ruling. Their testimony prevails; it is the first *kat* whose position is set aside. So where is the *hachasha*? If the testimony of the *zomemim* was never truly contradicted, then the *reisha* does not demonstrate that *hazama* can follow *hachasha*.

### Rava's Response

Rav Ashi, responding on behalf of Rava, explains the source of Rava's inference differently: Rava draws his proof not from the *reisha* alone but from the interplay between *reisha* and *seifa* considered together. Since the *reisha* clearly involves three *kitot* — as signaled by the master's satisfaction with the testimony — Rava infers that the *seifa* must also involve three *kitot*. And in the *seifa*, the *zomemim* are the group that claimed the eye came last. Their testimony *was* genuinely neutralized — the court followed the other group's testimony that the tooth came last, since that was the lesser obligation. Nevertheless, those neutralized witnesses can be found *zomemim* and made liable. This, Rava argues, proves *hachasha techilat hazama*: the fact that testimony was contradicted and set aside does not prevent it from subsequently being subject to *hazama*.

### Abaye's Concession

Abaye accepts the argument regarding the *reisha*. When the *braita* states that the master is pleased with the testimony, there must indeed have been a prior account on record — a prior *kat* — for that pleasure to make sense. Abaye concedes: *bishlama reisha lo sagi delo shalosh kitos* — admittedly, the first case requires three *kitot*. But he disputes the inference to the *seifa*. The *seifa* states that the *eved* is pleased with the testimony, and Abaye argues this is uninformative. A slave would naturally prefer any testimony that promises his freedom, regardless of what came before. The *eved*'s pleasure does not signal the existence of a prior adverse *kat*. Therefore, the *seifa* is consistent with only two groups, and the *mazimim* themselves provided the reversal. Since the *seifa* — the case where genuine neutralization would be most pertinent — does not require three *kitot*, it offers no proof that *hazama* can follow *hachasha*.

---

## Theft/Slaughter Case

### Rav Idi's Teaching

Rav Idi bar Avin introduces a *tanna* teaching that appears to bear on the *hachasha-hazama* debate. The teaching addresses a case where two witnesses testified that someone stole an animal, and those same witnesses also testified that he subsequently *shechted* or sold it — and then both testimonies were found to be *hazama*. The ruling is *meshalmin lo es hakol*: the false witnesses must pay the accused the full four-or-five-times amount (five for an ox, four for a sheep). This is because their false testimony attempted to saddle Reuven with the penalty for theft plus the additional penalty of *tashlumei arba v'chamishah*.

### Application to Case

The natural reading of this *baraita* is that the theft was attested to have occurred on one day and the *shechita* on a second day. Witnesses came and invalidated the theft testimony as *hazama* — "you were with us on Sunday, you could not have seen the theft" — and then separately invalidated the *shechita* testimony. The question is: once the theft is invalidated as *hazama*, does the *shechita* testimony not become effectively neutralized — since if he didn't steal it, he couldn't have *shechted* it? And yet the *baraita* says the full four-or-five must be paid. This seems to prove that even after *hachasha* (the neutralization of the *shechita* testimony), *hazama* can still follow. However, the Gemara deflects this proof: the *mazimim* could have invalidated the *shechita* testimony *first* — "you couldn't have seen the *shechita* on Monday, you were with us" — leaving the theft testimony intact at that point, and only then invalidating the theft testimony as well. In that sequence, there is no *hachasha* preceding *hazama*, and the case is fully resolved without implicating the Abaye-Rava dispute.

### Rabbi Elazar's View

The Gemara now identifies the underlying Tannaitic dispute behind the Abaye-Rava disagreement. The debate is between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar regarding witnesses who were first contradicted (*huchashu*) and subsequently found to be *zomemim* in a capital case. One holds they are executed; the other holds they are not. The Gemara concludes that it is Rabbi Elazar who holds they are *not* executed — i.e., *hachasha* is *not* the beginning of *hazama*, consistent with Abaye's position.

### Malkus Rule

The proof for this attribution is striking. Rabbi Elazar is recorded as holding that witnesses who testify falsely in a capital case and are subsequently contradicted (*huchashu b'nefesh*) receive *malkus* — lashes — for transgressing the *lav* of *eidus sheker*. The Gemara reasons: if Rabbi Elazar held that *hachasha* is the beginning of *hazama*, then such witnesses could potentially face execution if *mazimim* were subsequently to appear. In that case, the *lav* of *eidus sheker* would be a *lav she'nitan l'azharas misas beis din* — a prohibition whose violation is subject to the death penalty — and by the well-established rule, one does not receive *malkus* for such a transgression. The very possibility that the testimony could ultimately lead to their execution would preclude *malkus*. The fact that Rabbi Elazar does award *malkus* in this scenario must therefore mean he holds that once witnesses have been contradicted (*huchash*), the process *cannot* culminate in *hazama*. Accordingly, the *lav* of *eidus sheker* retains its ordinary *malkus* consequence.

One might ask: how can the witnesses be proven to have lied if they have merely been contradicted by an equal number of witnesses? The Gemara answers by invoking the case of *ba harug b'raglav* — the "murdered" victim walks into *beis din* on his own two feet. In that scenario, there is irrefutable proof that the testimony was false, yet no *hazama* is involved. Rabbi Elazar — who holds that *hachasha* cannot be the beginning of *hazama* — can therefore posit a case of unambiguous *eidus sheker* that carries *malkus* without any risk of the proceeding eventually escalating to a capital punishment of the witnesses themselves.

Tosafos raises a pointed question about the application of *lav she'nitan l'azharas misas beis din* here. Ordinarily, this principle requires not merely that the act sometimes leads to capital liability, but that this *specific lav* serves as the warning for an offense punishable by death. Why, then, should the mere possibility that a subsequent *hazama* might follow suffice to categorize *eidus sheker* as such a *lav* in this case? Tosafos answers that since we know from an explicit *pasuk* that *eidus sheker* independently carries *malkus*, the general capacity of false capital testimony to lead to execution is not itself sufficient to displace the *malkus* — but if this *specific* testimony could terminate in the witnesses' execution, then the *lav* as applied to this testimony carries the character of *azharas misas beis din*, precluding *malkus* entirely.

---

## Mishna Payment

### No Four/Five Cases

The Mishnah enumerates circumstances in which a thief pays the double payment (*tashlumei khefel*) but not the four-or-five-times penalty (*tashlumei arba v'chamishah*). The general principle at work is that *tashlumei arba v'chamishah* is a *knas*, and various conditions that undermine the *knas* liability — either because the testimony is insufficient or because the act was performed under circumstances that affect the legal categories — will reduce the obligation to *khefel* alone.

### Special Cases

The first category involves theft established by two witnesses, but *shechita* or sale attested by only a single witness or by the thief's own admission: the double is paid but not four-or-five, since a *knas* requires two witnesses and cannot be self-imposed through admission. A second category is where someone steals and then *shechts* on *Shabbat*, or steals and *shechts* for *avodah zarah*. In both instances, the act of *shechita* renders the actor *chayav misa*, and the principle of *kim lei b'deraba minei* — that the greater penalty subsumes the lesser monetary obligation — exempts the thief from the payment. A third case is one who stole from his father, and his father died before the *shechita* or sale occurred: by the time the *shechita* took place, the animal had already passed into the thief's inheritance, and one does not pay four-or-five on one's own property. Finally, one who stole and then consecrated (*hikdish*) the animal before *shechting* or selling it: once the animal is *hekdesh*, it no longer belongs to the original owner in the conventional sense, and the four-or-five liability does not attach.

### Rabbi Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon introduces a further distinction within the *hekdesh* category. He holds that *kodashim she'chayav b'achrayusam* — consecrated animals for which the donor retains a replacement obligation — are still considered sufficiently "his" to generate the four-or-five liability. But *kodashim she'ein chayav b'achrayusam* — consecrated animals for which the donor bears no replacement obligation — are considered fully removed from his domain, and he is therefore exempt. The Gemara will elaborate on these distinctions.

---

## One Witness Analysis

### One Witness Rule

The Gemara begins its analysis of the Mishnah by noting that the case of a single witness is obvious — since *tashlumei arba v'chamishah* is a *knas*, it requires two witnesses and a single *eid* is plainly insufficient. The real *chiddush* of the Mishnah, the Gemara explains, is the case of the thief's own admission. The Mishnah teaches that self-admission (*al pi atzmo*) is analogous to the testimony of a single witness. Just as a single witness's testimony, while insufficient to impose liability, does not prevent subsequent witnesses from doing so, so too a thief's admission: it does not impose liability, but neither does it preemptively exempt him if two witnesses subsequently appear.

### Rav Huna Position

This reading stands in direct tension with the position of Rav Huna citing Rav: *modeh b'knas v'achar kach ba'u eidim — patur*. Rav Huna holds that if someone admits to a *knas* and witnesses subsequently come, he is exempt from payment. The question is whether an admission to a *knas* functions like a form of *teshuvah* that permanently shields the confessor, or whether it is merely insufficient on its own to generate liability. The Mishnah's implication, as noted by the Gemara, cuts against Rav Huna's position — but the Gemara will now probe this dispute through a famous narrative.

---

## Rabban Gamliel Story

### The Admission

The Gemara records the celebrated incident of Rabban Gamliel and his slave Tevi. Rabban Gamliel blinded Tevi's eye — under what circumstances the text does not specify — and was overjoyed, because this meant Tevi would finally be able to go free. He encountered Rabbi Yehoshua and told him the news. Rabbi Yehoshua, however, informed him that nothing would come of it, because there were no witnesses.

### Rav Chisda Challenge

Rav Chisda raises this narrative as a challenge to Rav Huna. The story implies that *had* there been witnesses, Tevi would have gone free — despite the fact that Rabban Gamliel had already admitted the act. This suggests that the master's admission does *not* exempt him from the *knas* of freeing the slave, and that if witnesses subsequently appear, the slave is indeed freed. This reading directly contradicts Rav Huna's position that admission to a *knas* followed by witnesses yields exemption.

### Rav Huna Response

Rav Huna responds that Rabban Gamliel's case is categorically different: *shani Rabban Gamliel delo bifnei beis din hoda'ei* — Rabban Gamliel's admission was not made before *beis din*. He disclosed the information to Rabbi Yehoshua in an informal encounter, not in the context of a judicial proceeding. An admission of a *knas* is only legally operative — whether to exempt or to simply remain non-obligating — when made before *beis din*. An offhand statement to a colleague, even a distinguished one, does not qualify.

The Gemara anticipates the objection that Rabbi Yehoshua served as *av beis din*, and responds by clarifying — at the opening of 75a — that Rabbi Yehoshua was simply not *sitting in beis din* at the time. Institutional standing does not convert a casual conversation into a judicial admission.

### Two Baraita Versions

The Gemara then notes that two different versions of this same incident appear in *braitot*. The first version records Rabbi Yehoshua's response as: "there are no witnesses" — implying that had there been witnesses, the slave would have gone free even after the admission. This version appears to contradict Rav Huna's position, consistent with Rav Chisda's challenge. The second version records Rabbi Yehoshua's response as: "you have already admitted" — implying that the admission itself is the barrier to the slave's freedom, because admission to a *knas* exempts the admitter even if witnesses subsequently appear. This version strongly supports Rav Huna.

### Dispute Resolution

The Gemara considers whether these two *braitot* reflect an underlying *tannaic* dispute about the substantive law of *modeh b'knas*. However, it ultimately resolves the contradiction differently. Both *tanna'im* may in fact agree that admission to a *knas* before *beis din* exempts the admitter even if witnesses later appear. The dispute between the two versions of the story is not about the underlying law but about the facts of the case: one *tanna* understood that Rabban Gamliel's admission occurred *outside beis din* and was therefore not legally operative — hence Rabbi Yehoshua's response focused on the absence of witnesses. The other *tanna* understood the admission to have taken place *before beis din* — and therefore Rabbi Yehoshua pointed to the admission itself as the operative factor preventing Tevi's freedom.

On this reading, the *braita* that records *shekvar hodaita* — "you have already admitted" — clearly supports the position of Rav Huna amar Rav that *modeh b'knas v'achar kach ba'u eidim patur*. The *braita* recording *ein lecha eidim* is ambiguous: it can be read either as implying that witnesses would obligate him (against Rav Huna) or as reflecting a case where the admission was outside *beis din* and thus non-operative (consistent with Rav Huna). The Mishnah's *diyuk* against Rav Huna's position remains on the table, but the *braita* of *shekvar hodaita* stands as a clear tannaic endorsement of his ruling.

# Bava Kamma 75

## Rav vs. Shmuel: Modeh B'…

### Admission vs. Obligation

The *sugya* opens with a formal statement of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel concerning the rule of *modeh b'knas* — the case in which a person admits to an act that carries a *knas*, a monetary penalty, and witnesses subsequently arrive to corroborate that admission. The controlling principle under discussion is whether such an admission actively exempts the defendant from liability, or whether it merely fails to obligate him in the first instance.

Rav's position is stated directly: *modeh b'knas achar kach ba'u edim — patur*. If one admitted to a *knas* and witnesses thereafter came to testify, the defendant is nonetheless exempt. The admission itself generates the exemption. The underlying intuition is that a *knas* functions as a punitive measure for wrongdoing; one who comes forward voluntarily is, in some sense, no longer the proper target of that punishment, whether because the admission demonstrates a reformed disposition or because the legal system seeks to incentivize such confessions.
