Shmuel's position is the converse: *modeh b'knas achar kach ba'u edim — chayav*. The witnesses' subsequent testimony renders the defendant liable. According to Shmuel, the admission merely fails to obligate — it does not create an exemption.

### Knas vs. Mammon

To appreciate Shmuel's position, one must understand the structural distinction between *knas* and *mamon*. An ordinary monetary obligation — say, a loan — exists from the moment the act occurs; admission by the debtor simply confirms what is already legally his burden. *Knas*, by contrast, is not an obligation that inheres in the act itself. It requires *beis din* to impose it. The verse explicitly conditions the payment on a judicial finding: *asher yarshi'un elohim yishalem shnayim lerei'ehu* — those whom the judges declare guilty shall pay double. It follows that one cannot obligate oneself in a *knas* merely by confessing, because the obligation depends on an external determination of guilt by the court. Admission to a *knas* therefore neither obligates the confessor nor — according to Shmuel — exempts him.

### Rabbah bar Ilai on Rav

Rabbah bar Ilai undertakes to explain Rav's reasoning from the *pesukim*. The verse concerning the *shomer* who claims *to'en ta'anas gannav* — a watchman who falsely claims that the deposited item was stolen — states: *im himatzei timatzei beyado hagnivah... shnayim yishalem*. Rabbah bar Ilai reads this as encoding two distinct teachings: *im himatzei* — "if it is found in his hand" — refers to discovery through witnesses (*be'edim*), while *timatzei beyad hadayanim* — "found by the judges" — means that the judges impose the double payment on the basis of witness testimony. The exclusion *prat le'modeh b'atzmo* follows: one's own admission will not lead to a *knas* obligation.

But Rabbah bar Ilai presses further. The verse *asher yarshi'un* already teaches that *knas* requires judicial imposition and therefore cannot be self-imposed by admission. If so, why is the exclusion stated a second time in the verse about the *shomer*? The doubling of the teaching, Rabbah bar Ilai argues, can only be explained if the second instance is carrying an additional message — namely, that admission not only fails to obligate but actually exempts. Thus: *shema mina modeh b'knas achar kach ba'u edim patur*.

### Shmuel's Counter

Shmuel is unpersuaded. He reads the two appearances of the exclusion differently: one verse addresses the *shomer* who claims *to'en ta'anas gannav*, and one addresses the ordinary *gannav*. One might have thought the *Torah* is stricter with an actual thief and that even his admission could obligate him in *knas*; the second verse disabuses us of that notion. Both instances therefore teach only that admission does not obligate — neither teaches that admission exempts. Shmuel associates this reading with the position of the *Tanna de'bei Chizkiyahu* cited earlier, and concludes that the textual argument does not compel Rav's position.

---

## Baraitah: Admitting Befo…

### Case Setup

Rav then challenges Shmuel from a *baraitah*. The case: a man saw witnesses making their way to court — he recognized them, understood that they were coming to testify against him for theft and subsequent *shechita u'mechira* — and he raced ahead of them. Before the witnesses could testify, he declared: *ganavti* — I admit I stole — *aval lo tavachti ve'lo macharti* — but I did not slaughter or sell the animal. The witnesses then arrived and testified to both the theft and the *shechita u'mechira*.

The *baraitah* rules: *eino meshalem ella keren* — he pays only the principal. He does not pay *kefel*, and consequently he does not pay four or five times, since the Torah's obligation of four and five presupposes *kefel* and cannot be computed without it.

### Rav's Proof

Rav reads this *baraitah* as a direct proof for his position. The witnesses did arrive and testify to the *shechita u'mechira*, yet the defendant's earlier admission to the theft exempts him from *kefel*. Since the removal of *kefel* collapses the four-and-five calculation entirely — the additional multiple is predicated on the double payment — the result is that the defendant pays only the principal. This, Rav argues, demonstrates that *modeh b'knas patur af al pi sheba'u edim*: admission to a *knas* is an exemption even when witnesses subsequently testify.

### Shmuel's Defense

Shmuel deflects the proof with a pointed reinterpretation of the *baraitah*'s facts. He contends: *shechazu edim me'achorav* — when the defendant admitted, the witnesses who had been heading to court simply turned around and went home. Because he had already confessed, they saw no purpose in testifying. The *baraitah* is therefore not describing a case in which witnesses testified despite a prior admission and the admission nonetheless exempted; rather, it is a case in which the admission caused the witnesses to forgo testifying altogether. The *chiddush* is different: that other witnesses who testified to the *shechita u'mechira* do not render him liable once the *kefel* obligation has been removed. This is a notable concession to Rav's framing of the factual narrative, even though it does not constitute a concession to the legal principle.

### R. Elazar's Opinion

The *gemara* challenges Shmuel's reinterpretation from the *seifa* — the concluding clause — of the same *baraitah*. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon offers a dissenting view within that text: *yavo'u edim ve'ya'idu* — let the witnesses come and testify. In the very case under discussion, where the defendant has raced ahead of the witnesses and confessed, Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon insists that the witnesses should nonetheless proceed to testify and render him liable in *kefel*.

### Tana Kama vs. R. Elazar

The implications of this dissent are significant. *Michlal* — by inference from Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's position — the *tana kama* must hold the opposite: that once the defendant admitted, there would be no point in the witnesses testifying, because the admission has created an exemption. Thus the *baraitah* encodes a dispute between the *tana kama*, who holds *modeh b'knas patur*, and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, who holds *chayav* even with a prior admission.

For Shmuel, this is perfectly acceptable: *l'didi k'Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon d'ka'i k'vasi* — he is aligned with Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon. The *tana kama* reflects an opposing tannaitic view, and there is a genuine *machlokes tana'im* on this question, which Shmuel acknowledges comfortably.

The *gemara* then asks whether Rav is similarly compelled to acknowledge a *machlokes tana'im* — whether Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon necessarily represents a view that contradicts Rav's principle. This leads to the next refinement.

---

## Sincere vs. Fear-Motivat…

### Rav's Refinement

Rav offers a nuanced response: *ana d'amri afilu k'Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon* — he can hold his position while still being consistent with Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon. The key is that in the *baraitah*'s case, the defendant's admission was made specifically because he saw the witnesses approaching the courthouse. That context matters enormously. Rav argues that Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's ruling — that witnesses may come and obligate despite the admission — is limited precisely to that scenario.

### Demodei Me'Anfsheih

The distinction Rav draws is between two categories of *hoda'ah*. An admission that is *demodei me'anfsheih* — from one's own initiative, with no external pressure motivating the confession — is a genuine *hoda'ah* and warrants the exemption. An admission made *machmat bisusa d'edim* — out of fear or awareness that witnesses are about to arrive — is a strategically motivated act, not a sincere expression of contrition or legal obligation. Such an admission is aimed at preempting the *kefel* liability and has no genuine character as a confession. It neither obligates the defendant in *knas* nor earns him the exemption that a true *hoda'ah* provides.

The *baraitah*'s case — where the defendant saw the witnesses boarding their transportation to court and raced ahead — is paradigmatically an admission *machmat bisusa d'edim*. That is precisely why Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon says the witnesses should proceed; the admission was not genuine.

### R. Elazar Concedes

On Rav's reading, therefore, Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon is not a dissenter from the general principle of *modeh b'knas patur* but rather an authority who identifies this particular case as falling outside the principle's scope. In any normal case — where a person comes forward *demodei me'anfsheih*, admitting without strategic motive — even Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon would agree that the admission serves as an exemption. The dispute in the *baraitah* is thus confined to the special scenario of fear-motivated admission, and Rav can maintain his general position without conflict.

For Shmuel, by contrast, this resolution is unavailable. He must accept that the *tana kama* and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon dispute the general principle, even in cases of sincere admission.

---

## Rav Hamnuna: Chiyuv Atzm…

### Obligation in Principal…

A further refinement of Rav's position is offered by Rav Hamnuna. Even granting Rav's general principle, Rav Hamnuna argues that *mistabra milta deRav* — the reasoning of Rav's view is most coherent — only in a case where the admission itself obligates the confessor in the *keren*, the principal. The case he specifies is: *omer ganavti u'va'u edim sheganav — patur, dechayev atzmo bekeren*. When someone says *ganavti* — I stole — that admission, while not creating an obligation in *kefel* (which remains a *knas*), does obligate him to restore the principal amount of what was stolen. He has genuinely assumed a monetary burden through his confession.

### Incentive Theory

The logic underlying Rav Hamnuna's position operates on two levels. Conceptually, a true *hoda'ah* involves the confessor incurring an obligation — he is giving something up, acknowledging a real debt. An admission that carries no monetary consequence is not, in the full sense, an admission; it is merely a statement. On an instrumental level, the exemption from *knas* may serve as an incentive for wrongdoers to at least make the victim whole with respect to the principal. That incentive structure only makes sense when the admission entails paying the *keren*. Where the admission carries no monetary obligation whatsoever, neither the conceptual nor the instrumental rationale supports awarding an exemption.

### Theft vs. Shechita U'Mec…

Rav Hamnuna illustrates by contrasting two cases. In the first, a defendant says *ganavti* — I stole — and witnesses come to confirm the theft. This admission obligates him in the *keren* even though it spares him from *kefel*, and therefore, on Rav's principle, the admission exempts him from *kefel* even when witnesses subsequently arrive. In the second case, witnesses have already established the theft — so the *keren* obligation is no longer created by the admission but by the witnesses — and the defendant then separately admits to *tavachti u'macharti*, I slaughtered or sold the animal. At the moment of that second admission, there is nothing of monetary consequence that the confession is adding. The *shechita u'mechira* carries only the additional penalty of four and five times, which is entirely *knas*. Since the admission to *tavachti u'macharti* obligates the defendant in nothing — *depatar nafsheih mikula*, it only exempts him — it does not qualify as an *hoda'ah* that earns the exemption. If witnesses come after and testify to the *shechita u'mechira*, he is *chayav*.

---

## Rava Challenges Rav Hamn…

### Rabban Gamliel & Tavi

Rava challenges Rav Hamnuna's formulation — *kapcheinhu sabei d'vei Rav*, he claims he has bested the elders of Rav's academy — by pointing to the case of Rabban Gamliel discussed on the previous *daf*. Rabban Gamliel admitted that he had blinded the eye of his servant Tavi. The legal framework for injuring a Canaanite servant is that the master must free the servant; this remedy is conceived entirely as a *knas* — there is no *mamon* component, no principal obligation that the master assumes through his admission. His admission was, in Rav Hamnuna's terms, *poter atzmo mikula* — it exempted him from everything while obligating him in nothing.

### Pure Exemption Problem

Yet the discussion on the previous *daf* — in which Rav Chisda challenged Rav Huna — treated that case as potentially relevant to whether Rabban Gamliel's admission served as an exemption from liability or merely failed to obligate him. Rava's argument is that had Rav Hamnuna's principle been operative, Rav Huna would have had a simpler answer available to him in that exchange: he could have said that in the case of Tavi, there was no *chiyuv b'keren* whatsoever, and therefore the admission could never function as an exemption regardless of any other consideration. The fact that Rav Huna did not employ this answer — and instead gave a different response — suggests that Rav Huna, speaking in the tradition of Rav, did not accept Rav Hamnuna's condition.

### Rava's Position

Rava concludes accordingly that Rav's position does not require *chiyuv atzmo b'keren* as a condition for the exemption to apply. Even where an admission purely exempts the confessor — where he assumes no monetary obligation through the confession — Rav would maintain that the admission generates an exemption. Rav Hamnuna's refinement, while logically coherent, does not accurately represent Rav's view.

---

## R. Yochanan's Middle Pos…

### Admission + Principal

The *gemara* then records a statement transmitted by Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, which precisely tracks the distinction Rav Hamnuna articulated. Rabbi Yochanan rules: *ganavti u'va'u edim sheganav — patur, she-harei chiyuv atzmo b'keren*. If one says *ganavti* and witnesses come to confirm the theft, he is exempt from *kefel* because his admission obligated him in the *keren*. The principal obligation is present; the admission is substantive; the exemption applies.

### Admission Without Princi…

In the contrasting case, the defendant denied stealing — *lo ganavti* — witnesses then established the theft, and subsequently the defendant admitted *tavachti u'macharti*. Witnesses then arrived to confirm the *shechita u'mechira*. Rabbi Yochanan rules: *chayav*. In that configuration, the admission to *tavachti u'macharti* — given that the *keren* obligation was already imposed by witnesses to the theft — creates no new monetary burden on the defendant. *She-harei patar atzmo mikolum*: the admission only serves to exempt, not to obligate. Such an admission does not function as an *hoda'ah* warranting exemption from the subsequently corroborated *knas*.

### R. Yochanan's Authority

Even if Rava is correct that Rav himself does not require *chiyuv b'keren* as a condition, Rabbi Yochanan's position is an independently authoritative ruling. His distinction — between an admission that carries a *keren* obligation and one that does not — represents a coherent middle ground between Rav and Shmuel, and remains a live *halachic* principle regardless of whether it precisely tracks Rav's own view.

---

## Rav Ashi's Textual Proof

### Mishnah's Specificity

Rav Ashi adds that this same distinction — between an admission that obligates in the principal and one that does not — is actually embedded in the *mishna* and the *baraitah* themselves, as demonstrated by close textual reading. The *mishna* states: *ganav al pi shnayim ve'tavach al pi ed echad o al pi atzmo — meshalem tashlumei kefel ve'eino meshalem tashlumei arba'a ve'chamisha*. He stole as established by two witnesses, and the *shechita u'mechira* was established by one witness or by his own admission — he pays *kefel* but not four or five.

Rav Ashi asks: why did the *mishna* specifically construct the case so that the *geneivah* was established by two witnesses while only the *shechita u'mechira* was admitted to? If the *mishna* simply wanted to convey that one's admission does not obligate in *knas*, it could have presented all the variables together — one who admitted to both the *geneivah* and the *shechita u'mechira* and should pay only the *keren*. Why limit the illustration to admission at the stage of *shechita u'mechira*?

### Admission = One Witness

The *mishna* had earlier paired *al pi atzmo* with *al pi ed echad* — one's own admission alongside the testimony of a single witness — as parallel cases producing the same outcome. This comparison was previously examined by the *gemara* and carried a significant implication: just as a single witness does not exempt but merely fails to obligate (such that a second witness arriving later would render the defendant liable), so too one's own admission may not exempt but merely fail to obligate.

### No Principal = No Exempt…

Rav Ashi now explains why the *mishna* constructed the case specifically around *shechita u'mechira*: it is precisely because in that configuration — where witnesses have already established the *geneivah* and the defendant admits only to the *shechita u'mechira* — the admission does not obligate him in the *keren*. That is the scenario where *al pi atzmo* is genuinely parallel to *al pi ed echad*: in neither case is there an exemption, and subsequent witnesses can impose liability. The *mishna* taught the rule specifically where it applies — namely, where the admission carries no *keren* obligation — and used the parallel to *ed echad* to convey that the admission, like a single witness, neither obligates nor exempts.

### With Principal = Exempts

By contrast, had the *mishna* constructed a case where the defendant admitted to the *geneivah* itself — *ganav ve'tavach ve'machar al pi ed echad ve'al pi atzmo* — it would not have said that *al pi atzmo* is parallel to *al pi ed echad*, because in that case the admission to the *geneivah* does obligate him in the *keren*. There, his admission would earn him an exemption: if witnesses later arrived to confirm the *geneivah*, he would be *patur* from *kefel*. The admission would not function merely like a single witness awaiting corroboration; it would function as a genuine *hoda'ah* warranting exemption.

The *mishna*'s deliberate choice to illustrate the rule only at the stage of *shechita u'mechira* — and not at the stage of *geneivah* — is thus not incidental. It reflects the principle of Rabbi Yochanan precisely: the comparison between one's own admission and *ed echad* holds, and the absence of exemption applies, only when the admission does not obligate in the *keren*. When the admission does carry a *keren* obligation, the dynamics shift entirely, and the admission warrants the exemption. This, Rav Ashi concludes, is encoded in the *mishna*'s own careful architecture.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 76

## Hoda'ah & Kenas Debate

### Rav's Position

The Gemara on 75b is engaged with the question of *modeh b'knas v'achar kach ba'u eidim* — what is the legal effect of admitting to a *knas* when witnesses subsequently arrive to testify to the same offense? Three positions have been presented, or more precisely, two positions together with a significant nuance on one of them.

Rav holds that if a person admits to a *knas* and witnesses come afterwards, he remains exempt. His admission not only fails to obligate him — since the principle of *modeh b'knas patur* means that one who admits to a fine does not pay — but it actively exempts him, so that even if witnesses later appear, the *knas* cannot be imposed.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel disagrees. In his view, the admission does not obligate the defendant, but neither does it exempt him in a durable way. If witnesses subsequently arrive, they do obligate him, and he must pay the *knas*. The Gemara's discussion appears to come down strongly in favor of Rav's position.

### Principal Requirement

Within Rav's position, however, there is a further nuance: not every type of admission is sufficient to exempt a person when witnesses come later. The qualifying condition is *chiyev atzmo b'keren* — the admission must be one that simultaneously obligates the defendant in the *keren*, the principal amount owed. That constitutes a genuine admission. But if the admission relates only to the *knas* element, without any corresponding self-obligation in the principal, then it lacks the legal weight to produce exemption. In short, no admission ever creates an obligation in a *knas*, but the admission that exempts from a *knas* is one that carries with it a real obligation in *keren*.

---

## Brayta d'Tanya

### Scenario Setup

The Gemara now seeks to demonstrate this position from a *brayta*. The *brayta* in question describes the following scenario: a person sees witnesses making their way toward the *beis din*, moving in to testify against him, and decides to get ahead of them by admitting. He declares *ganafti* — I committed the theft — but adds *aval lo tavachti v'lo macharti*, I did not slaughter or sell the animal. The rule is *eino meshalem ela keren*: he pays only the principal.

The *chiddush* of this *brayta* is that even though the defendant admitted only because he saw witnesses approaching — hardly a spontaneous or entirely voluntary admission — it is still legally treated as an admission. And because it is treated as an admission, even if the witnesses actually arrive in court, he is exempt from the *kefel*. Since *kefel* is one component of the four-and-five payment (four for a sheep, five for an ox), his exemption from *kefel* carries with it exemption from the additional payments as well.

### Brayta Logic

How does this *brayta* support the position that admission must come with an obligation in *keren* in order to exempt? The Gemara asks: why does the *brayta* specifically present the example of admitting to the theft (*ganafti*) while denying the slaughter and sale? Why not simply give one of two cleaner examples — either admitting to the *gneivah* alone, which would exempt from *kefel* and thus automatically from four-and-five, or admitting to the *tevicha u'mechira* alone, which would exempt from that component?

The answer, the Gemara suggests, is that the second option simply does not work. An admission only to the *tevicha u'mechira*, made after witnesses to the *gneivah* have already appeared, does not obligate the person in anything — it obligates him in no *keren*, since the *gneivah* has already been established by others. Therefore the *brayta* specifically gives the example of admitting to the *gneivah*, because that admission obligates him in the principal and thereby qualifies as the kind of admission that can exempt. This seems to be a sound proof: *hoda'at tevicha lav hoda'ah hi* — an admission to the slaughtering alone is not a real admission, because it comes with no self-obligation.

### Gemara's Challenge

The Gemara, however, rejects this inference. The reason the *brayta* chose the example of admitting to *gneivah* rather than admitting to *tevicha* is not to teach that only the former counts as a valid admission. Rather, the *brayta* chose this case in order to teach a remarkable *chiddush* about the case itself.

### The Novelty

The *chiddush* is this: the defendant admitted to the theft but denied the slaughter and sale. He was lying about the denial, as witnesses later came to testify to the *tevicha u'mechira*. Yet despite having denied it and despite witnesses proving the *tevicha u'mechira*, he is still exempt from paying the additional penalty. *Uva'u eidim she'tavach u'machar — patur*: even when witnesses come to prove the slaughter and sale, he pays nothing beyond the *keren*. This is a remarkable and extreme result: an admission made only because witnesses were already on their way, accompanied by a lie about the *tevicha u'mechira*, still suffices to remove the obligation for everything beyond the principal.

### Torah's Language

Why? *Tashlumei arba'a v'chamisha rachmana*, the Torah declared that one pays four or five — not four and three, not some other combination. Once the defendant admitted to the *gneivah* and thereby obligated himself in the *keren*, one unit of the *kefel* payment is removed. And the Torah's language of "four and five" means that the payments stand together: remove one component, and the entire structure of the penalty collapses. You cannot have a payment of four without the full complement of components, and you cannot have a payment of five without it either. So the reason the *brayta* chose this example was to teach the dramatic *chiddush* of this specific case — not to exclude the possibility that an admission to *tevicha* alone might also work. The *brayta*, on this reading, is silent about that question, and so it does not prove our position.

---

## Alternative Brayta Readi…

### Tana'im Debate

Since the *brayta* fails to resolve the question definitively, the Gemara proposes a different approach. Perhaps the debate about whether an admission that does not obligate in the *keren* is a valid admission is itself a *tannaitic* dispute — that is, perhaps the positions of the *amora'im* reflect earlier debates between *tanna'im*. All may agree with Rav that an admission can exempt a person; the question is whether that exemption extends even to an admission that carries no obligation in *keren*. To explore this, the Gemara turns to a *brayta* involving *edim zomemim*.

### Witnesses Discredited

The *brayta* presents the following scenario. Two witnesses testify that a defendant committed *gneivah*, and two additional witnesses testify that he performed the *tevicha u'mechira*. If the witnesses to the *gneivah* are subsequently proven to be *zomemim* — their testimony is discredited — then by the principle of *eidut shebatla miktzatah batla kulah*, once part of the testimony falls, it all falls. Since one cannot establish that the defendant was a *ganav*, the testimony to the *tevicha u'mechira* becomes meaningless. Perhaps he was slaughtering his own animal. Accordingly, the discredited witnesses pay him *kefel*, and the defendant pays nothing, even though there remain witnesses to the *tevicha u'mechira*.

### Slaughter Witnesses Discredited

In the reverse case, where the witnesses to the *tevicha u'mechira* are proven *zomemim*, the result is different. The *gneivah* still stands, so the defendant pays the owner *tashlumei kefel*, and the discredited witnesses pay the defendant three (the extra component beyond *kefel* that constitutes the "four" for a sheep or "five" for an ox).

### Sumchus Position

Then the *brayta* adds: in the name of Sumchus, the witnesses pay *tashlumei kefel* (two) and the defendant pays *tashlumei shlosha* (three). This is a perplexing position on its face. Why would the witnesses pay two and the defendant pay three? This formulation makes sense only in the first case — where the witnesses to the *gneivah* are discredited — since at least numerically the figures of two and three correspond. But in the first case, it seems impossible: if you cannot establish that there was a *gneivah*, how can the defendant be paying three to the owner?

The Gemara works through the possibilities. *Ileima reisha* — if Sumchus is addressing the first case, the problem is clear: he would be contradicting himself by holding that only part of the testimony is discredited while the rest remains. *Ella seifa* — perhaps Sumchus is addressing the second case, where the witnesses to the *tevicha* are discredited. But in that scenario, it is the *Rabbanan's* position — that the defendant pays *kefel* and the witnesses pay three — that makes the most sense, and Sumchus's reversal seems inexplicable.

Because neither reading of Sumchus coheres naturally with the cases described, the Gemara concludes that a completely different underlying scenario must be constructed to render Sumchus intelligible.

---

## Zomemim Scenario

### Setup & Proof

The Gemara reconstructs the case as follows. Two witnesses, call them Michael and David, come to court and testify that the defendant committed *gneivah*. The defendant responds: yes, I admit — *ganafti v'tavachti u'macharti*, I stole and I slaughtered and I sold — however, *lo bifneichem ganavti*, I did not steal it in your presence. You were not there. You are lying about having witnessed it. The defendant then produces his own witnesses who prove that Michael and David were elsewhere at the time — they are *edim zomemim*. They must therefore pay him *kefel*.

Now, in the meantime, the owner of the stolen animal brings ראובן and שמעון (*Reuven* and *Shimon*), who come to court and testify that they witnessed the defendant commit the entire *gneivah*, *tevicha*, and *mechira*. The question is: what does the defendant now owe the owner?

### Rabbanan View

The *Rabbanan* hold that the defendant's admission — *ganafti v'tavachti u'macharti* — counts as a valid *hoda'ah*, even though it was made in response to witnesses who subsequently turned out to be *zomemim*. It was a double admission: an admission to the *gneivah* and an admission to the *tevicha u'mechira*. Since it counts as a genuine admission, and since *modeh b'knas patur*, the defendant is exempt from the *kenas* component. He pays the owner only the *keren*, and no more, even when *Reuven* and *Shimon* come to confirm the *tevicha u'mechira*. The admission stands as a valid *hoda'ah* that prevents the *kenas* from being imposed. The *zomemim* pay the defendant two, and he remains exempt beyond the *keren*.

### Sumchus View

Sumchus holds that this admission does not qualify. His reasoning is subtle and precise. The defendant's admission to the *gneivah* — *ganafti* — was made in direct response to Michael and David's accusation. Even though they turned out to be *zomemim*, the defendant did not know at the moment of admission that he would be able to disprove them. His *ganafti* was not a free and spontaneous *hoda'ah*; it was a reaction to their presence in court. An admission made under that kind of pressure, *machmat eidim*, is not a genuine *hoda'ah*.

Furthermore, Sumchus identifies a critical asymmetry within the double admission. The defendant said *ganafti v'tavachti u'macharti*. Michael and David accused him only of *gneivah* — they said nothing about *tevicha u'mechira*. So when the defendant added *tavachti u'macharti*, that portion of the admission was entirely volunteered and not driven by their testimony. It was, in that sense, a sincere *hoda'ah* to the *tevicha u'mechira*. But according to Sumchus, that admission to *tevicha u'mechira* is precisely the kind of admission that does not obligate in any *keren*, because at the time of that admission, the *gneivah* itself had not been established — the *ganafti* portion was driven by the *eidim* and therefore does not count. An admission to *tevicha u'mechira* in isolation, without a corresponding obligation in *keren*, is not a valid *hoda'ah*.

Therefore, Sumchus concludes, the defendant's admission affords him no protection. When *Reuven* and *Shimon* come to confirm the entire sequence of events, the defendant is obligated for the full amount. Since Michael and David are *zomemim* and must pay him two, and since he owes the owner the full four or five, the practical result is that Michael and David's payment of two flows to the owner via the defendant, and the defendant pays the remaining three directly from his own funds. Hence: they pay two, he pays three.

The *Rabbanan*, by contrast, hold that even though the *ganafti* was in reaction to the *eidim*, the admission to *tevicha u'mechira* added on top of it remains a valid *hoda'ah* and exempts from the *kenas*.

### Rav Acha's Reading

Rav Acha bar Rav Ika objects to this entire construction. He argues that it is not necessary to build the case around *eidim* who are subsequently proven *zomemim* in order to explain Sumchus's position. On his reading, *dechulei alma hoda'at tevicha lav hoda'ah hi* — everyone agrees that an admission to *tevicha* alone, without an accompanying obligation in *keren*, does not constitute a valid *hoda'ah*. This is not the point of the *tannaitic* dispute. Rather, the real dispute concerns *edut she'ei atah yachol lehazimah* — testimony that structurally cannot be subjected to *hazamah*, the procedure by which witnesses are discredited.

### Real Witnesses

The scenario Rav Acha constructs is closely parallel in its opening but diverges decisively in what follows. Two witnesses accuse the defendant of *gneivah*. He again says *ganafti v'tavachti u'macharti* while denying that those particular witnesses were present. He again proves them *zomemim*. But this time, rather than the owner producing entirely independent witnesses, the defendant himself has named *Reuven* and *Shimon* — saying, in effect, "it was before them that I stole." The owner then calls *Reuven* and *Shimon*, who duly testify to the *gneivah*, *tevicha*, and *mechira*.

---

## Undisproven Testimony

### Rabbanan Position

The *Rabbanan* hold that the testimony of *Reuven* and *Shimon* in this scenario is disqualified, because it constitutes *edut she'ei atah yachol lehazimah*. Ordinarily, the principle that testimony incapable of *hazamah* is inadmissible exists because witnesses who cannot be proven *zomemim* have no fear of lying — the threat of being found *zomemim* is what makes testimony trustworthy. Here, the defendant himself has asserted that *Reuven* and *Shimon* witnessed his actions, which means he is effectively supporting their testimony. Testimony that the accused himself corroborates cannot be subjected to *hazamah* in the ordinary way, for it would be bizarre to go ahead and try to prove that *Reuven* and *Shimon* were elsewhere when the defendant himself said they were present. This creates a situation where the testimony is formally protected against *hazamah*, and therefore, paradoxically, it is inadmissible under the principle of *edut she'ei atah yachol lehazimah*.

The practical consequence, according to the *Rabbanan*, is that since *Reuven* and *Shimon's* testimony is invalid, it cannot obligate the defendant. The *zomemim* pay him two, and he pays the owner nothing beyond the *keren* — not because of any *hoda'ah* exemption, but because the testimony that would have obligated him is inadmissible.

### Sumchus Position

Sumchus holds that *edut she'ei atah yachol lehazimah* is still valid testimony. He maintains that such testimony, though it cannot be subjected to *hazamah*, is not thereby disqualified. On this view, *Reuven* and *Shimon's* testimony stands, and the defendant is obligated for the full four or five. The *zomemim* pay him two, and he pays the owner the remaining three.

### Conclusion

The Gemara then moves to dismiss this entire reconstruction by invoking the accepted principle: *v'kayma lan* — it is established that *edut she'ei atah yachol lehazimah lo havya edut*, that testimony which cannot be subjected to *hazamah* is not valid testimony. Since this is the accepted ruling, Sumchus's position — which requires that such testimony be valid — cannot stand as the *Gemara* has described it. Any reading of the *brayta* that forces us to attribute to Sumchus the view that such testimony is valid is therefore untenable. One should note that this principle applies where the testimony is rendered incapable of *hazamah* because of a structural defect — not merely because it happens to be difficult to disprove, as when witnesses are vague about the time or place of the event.

---

## Sanctification Issue

### Mishnah Case

The Gemara now moves forward to the *Mishnah*. The case presented is: *ganav v'hikdish v'achar kach tavach u'machar* — a person stole an animal, sanctified it as a *korban*, and then subsequently slaughtered or sold it. The *Mishnah*'s ruling is that he does not pay four and five for the *shechita* or *mechira* performed after the *hekdesh*. The reason is straightforward: when he slaughtered or sold it, he was dealing with an animal that belonged to *hekdesh*, not to the original owner. *De'ki tavach de'hekdesh tavach, v'lo de'marei tavach* — he slaughtered *hekdesh's* animal, not the owner's.

### Gemara Question

The Gemara, however, raises a pointed question about the *Mishnah*. Granted, once the animal has been sanctified and the defendant then slaughters it, there is no liability — he is not slaughtering the owner's animal. But what about the act of sanctification itself? Why is *hekdesh* not treated as an act of *mechira*? *Mah li machar l'hedyot mah li machar l'shamayim* — what difference does it make whether you sold it to a private individual or to *shamayim*? The thief took this stolen animal and transferred it to *hekdesh*, to the ownership of the *Beis HaMikdash*. Why does that not constitute a sale that would obligate him in the four-and-five payment?

### Rabbi Shimon Answer

The Gemara answers: *ha manni Rebbi Shimon hi* — this is the view of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that *kodshim she'chayav b'achrayutan birshutei de'marei kamei*, that *kodshim* for which the owner bears liability for replacement are still considered to remain under the owner's domain — in the present context, under the *ganav's* domain. What does this mean in practice? If a person has accepted upon himself a *neder* of an *olah* or is obligated to bring a *chatat*, and he designates this stolen animal to fulfill that obligation, then if the animal is lost, he must replace it. Because its loss causes him a financial loss, it is treated as though the animal is still under his control. This is analogous to the principle of *davar hagorim l'mamon k'mamon dami* — something whose loss generates a monetary obligation is treated as though it remains within one's possession.

Accordingly, in Rabbi Shimon's framework, the act of sanctification in such a case is not a full *mechira*, because the animal is treated as still under the *ganav's* control. It is, however, no longer the owner's animal — it belongs to *hekdesh*. This creates an interesting intermediate status: the act of sanctification does not constitute a *mechira* that would obligate in four-and-five, because the animal is considered still under the *ganav's* auspices; yet when the *ganav* subsequently slaughters it, he is not liable, because at that point he is slaughtering *hekdesh's* animal, not the owner's. Rashi notes the irony: the sanctification did not transfer the animal far enough away from the *ganav* to create liability for *mechira*, yet it transferred the animal far enough away from the owner that subsequent *shechita* creates no liability.

### Types of Kodashim

The Gemara then proposes an alternative approach that does not require relying on Rabbi Shimon. The *Mishnah's* ruling could reflect the position of *kodashim kalim* according to Rabbi Yose HaGalili. Rabbi Yose HaGalili holds that *kodashim kalim*, lighter sacrifices such as *shelamim*, are considered *mamon ba'alim* — still the property of the owner — because the owner retains the right to eat the meat. Since the animal is still considered the *ganav's*, the act of sanctification is not a *mechira*. Yet because it is *hekdesh*, subsequent *tevicha* does not create liability. This is another pathway to the same intermediate result.

The Gemara then asks: what would the rule be for *kodshei kodshim*, the most sacred sacrifices, where neither Rabbi Shimon's *chayav b'achrayutan* nor Rabbi Yose HaGalili's *kodashim kalim* reasoning applies? Would the act of *hekdesh* then constitute a *mechira* and obligate in four-and-five? If so, the *Mishnah* should have made a distinction: for *kodashim kalim* no liability for *hekdesh*, but for *kodshei kodshim* liability for *hekdesh*. The fact that the *Mishnah* makes no such distinction suggests that neither type of *hekdesh* is ever treated as a *mechira*.

---

## Status vs. Ownership

### Association Remains

The Gemara, pressed to explain why the act of *hekdesh* is universally not considered a *mechira* regardless of the type of *korban*, offers the following principle: *me'ikara tora d'Reuven v'hashta tora d'Reuven* — when one sells to a private individual, the ox that was Reuven's is now Shimon's. The association of the animal with the original person is severed. But when one sanctifies an animal as a *korban*, it is still referred to as Reuven's *olah* or Reuven's *chatat*. The animal may be sanctified, it may belong to *hekdesh*, but it is still associated with the person who sanctified it. This persistent association is what distinguishes *hekdesh* from *mechira*: a genuine *mechira* severs the connection entirely, whereas sanctification as a *korban* does not.

### Kedusha vs. Ownership

This observation points to a deeper distinction. When a person sells an animal to another person, the transaction is fundamentally about transferring ownership. The question is: who is the owner? The answer changes cleanly from seller to buyer. But when a person sanctifies an animal as a *korban*, the transaction is not primarily about transferring ownership — it is about conferring *kedusha*, about changing the animal's status so that it may now function as a vehicle for the *avodah*. The *korban* is still referred to as the person's *korban*. The purpose of sanctification is not to give the animal to some other legal entity but to invest the animal with holiness, with a capacity for sacred service. That is why even *kodshei kodshim*, where the owner has no remaining proprietary interest in the meat, still does not constitute a *mechira*: the question of ownership is simply not what sanctification is about.

### Types of Sanctity

This distinction carries important implications when one considers *kodshei bedek habayit* — donations made to the Temple treasury for the upkeep of the *Beis HaMikdash*. Tosafot, as noted below, identifies *kodshei bedek habayit* as a category of *hekdesh* that does function like a *mechira*. The conceptual difference is precisely this: when one donates an animal to *bedek habayit*, the animal passes into the ownership of the *Beis HaMikdash* as an institution. The *gizbar* takes possession; the animal is now the *Beis HaMikdash*'s asset. No one refers to it as the donor's animal — at most, they say the donor gave it. By contrast, a *korban* remains associated with the person who brought it, because the entire purpose of a *korban* is precisely this personal relationship between the *makriv* and the *avodah*.

This also maps onto two distinct ways of conceptualizing *me'ilah* — the prohibition of deriving benefit from *hekdesh*. One can understand *me'ilah* as a form of *geneivah* or *gezeilah*, taking something that belongs to another (in this case, *hekdesh*). That conception fits naturally with *kodshei bedek habayit*, where the animal is genuinely owned by the Temple. Alternatively, one can understand *me'ilah* as an *issur hana'ah* — a prohibition against using a sanctified object for non-sanctified purposes, based not on ownership but on the object's sacred status. That conception fits naturally with *kodshei korbanos*, where the prohibition is rooted in the animal's *kedusha* rather than in a transfer of title. The two ways of thinking about *me'ilah* thus reflect two fundamentally different concepts of *kedusha*: one about ownership, and one about status.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot addresses an apparent difficulty in this framework. If the act of sanctifying an animal as a *korban* leaves the animal still associated with the *ganav*, one might think that no *shinui* at all has occurred — and if no *shinui* has occurred, the entire discussion of *hekdesh* as a potential *mechira* would never have gotten off the ground in the first place. Tosafot therefore clarifies that a *shinui hashem* — a change of name or designation — does unquestionably occur when an animal is sanctified as a *korban*, since it is now called a *korban* rather than simply an animal. Moreover, Tosafot invokes the possibility of *shinui reshut*, noting that once something becomes a *korban*, it is indeed considered under the auspices of *hekdesh* and is not purely and entirely the *ganav's*. It is not, as one might oversimplify, that sanctification leaves the animal wholly within the *ganav's* domain with only its *kedusha* added on. Rather, the animal genuinely passes to some degree into the domain of *hekdesh*. But because it remains associated with the *ganav* — it is still his *korban* — this *shinui reshut* is incomplete, and it is precisely this incompleteness that prevents the act of sanctification from rising to the level of a full *mechira*.

---

## Rabbi Shimon's Rule

### Seeming Contradiction

The *Mishnah* at the end cites Rabbi Shimon's statement that *kodashim she'chayav b'achrayutan* — sacrificial animals for whose replacement the owner is liable — do obligate in four-and-five, while those for which the owner is not liable do not. This seems, at first glance, paradoxical. Rabbi Shimon himself, as quoted above, holds that *kodashim she'chayav b'achrayutan* are still considered under the owner's control. If that is true, then *chayav b'achrayutan* means the animal is still considered the *ganav's*, and therefore sanctification is not a *mechira*. But then why would Rabbi Shimon say that in the case of *chayav b'achrayutan* one must pay four-and-five? And if *she'eino chayav b'achrayutan* means the animal has left the *ganav's* control entirely and passed to *hekdesh*, that would seem to be more like a *mechira* — yet Rabbi Shimon says in that case one is exempt.

### Different Case

The resolution is that Rabbi Shimon in the *Mishnah* is not addressing the same scenario that the earlier discussion addressed. He is not speaking of a case where the *ganav* stole an animal and then sanctified it himself. Rather, Rabbi Shimon is addressing a different case entirely: someone steals a *korban* that was already sanctified from the owner's house.

### Liability = Ownership

In this scenario, the question is whether the law of *v'gunav mibeis ha'ish* — theft from the house of a person — applies to a sanctified animal. Rabbi Shimon holds: if the owner is *chayav b'achrayutan*, meaning that if this *korban* is lost he must replace it at his own expense, then the animal is considered his in a meaningful economic sense. Its loss is his loss. Therefore, the law of *v'gunav mibeis ha'ish* does apply, and a *ganav* who steals such a *korban* from the owner's house and slaughters it must pay four-and-five. *Karina bei v'gunav mibeis ha'ish* — it qualifies as being stolen from the house of that person.

### No Liability = Exemption

Conversely, if the owner is not *chayav b'achrayutan* — if this particular *korban* is not his financial responsibility should it be lost — then the animal is not considered his in the relevant sense. Stealing it from his house is like stealing from *hekdesh* itself, and the rule of *v'gunav mibeis ha'ish* does not apply. The *ganav* pays no four-and-five. *D'lo karina bei v'gunav mibeis ha'ish.*

---

## Shechicha Outside Beis H…

### Problem Setup

Having established that in the case where a *ganav* steals a *korban* that is *chayav b'achrayutan* he must pay four-and-five, the Gemara identifies a serious difficulty. Rabbi Shimon himself holds that *shechita she'einah re'uyah lo shma shechita* — a *shechita* that does not render the animal permissible for consumption is not considered a *shechita* for the purposes of the four-and-five obligation. But if the *ganav* steals this *korban* from the owner's house and slaughters it in his backyard, outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, this is a classic case of *shchutei chutz* — slaughtering a *korban* outside the Temple — and the animal is *assur b'hana'ah*. One cannot benefit from it. How then can such a *shechita* be the basis for a four-and-five payment?

### First Answer: Brought to…

Rav Dimi, citing Rabbi Yochanan, provides the first answer. The case is one where the *ganav* felt remorseful and, recognizing that the animal is a *korban*, brought it to the *Beis HaMikdash* and slaughtered it there on the owner's behalf — *l'shem ba'alim*. In this setting, the *shechita* is entirely proper and the animal could be eaten. It qualifies as *shechita re'uyah*. The *ganav* has, in effect, brought the owner's *korban* on the owner's behalf — which might seem like an act of restoration rather than an act of *geneivah*. How can this be the predicate for a four-and-five payment?

The Gemara resolves this: *she'harei chazar keren l'ba'alim* — it would appear that the *ganav* has returned the principal, the animal itself, to the owner's account. And indeed, at the moment of *shechita*, had everything proceeded normally, it would have been credited to the owner. But then the blood was spilled — *k'she'nishpach hadam* — the *kohen* spilled the blood before it could be thrown on the altar, and the *korban* was never actually credited to the owner's account. In hindsight, therefore, this was not an act of restoration — the owner received nothing. We now see that the *shechita* was an act of furthering the *geneivah*. Yet the *shechita* itself, at the moment it was performed, was fit and proper: the animal was inside the *Beis HaMikdash*, slaughtered in the correct manner, and the meat would have been permissible had the blood been sprinkled. It was therefore a *shechita re'uyah*, and the four-and-five obligation applies.

There is something striking in this analysis: we assess the validity of the *shechita* as of the moment it was performed — at which point it was indeed *re'uyah* — while we assess the *geneivah* character of the act retrospectively, based on the spilled blood revealing that the owner received no benefit. The two assessments are, in a sense, made at different moments in time.

### Second Answer: Not For O…

Ravin, also citing Rabbi Yochanan, offers a second answer that does not require the *ganav* to be so well-intentioned. In this version, the *ganav* brings the animal to the *Beis HaMikdash* and slaughters it inside — but *shelo l'shem ba'alim*, not on the owner's behalf. He claims it as his own *korban*. The owner therefore receives no credit — the *korban* is not attributed to him — so there is no act of restoration. At the same time, the *shechita* is performed inside the *Beis HaMikdash* and the meat is fit to be eaten, either by the *kohanim* or, if it is a *shelamim*, by others as well. It is thus unambiguously a *shechita re'uyah*, and the four-and-five obligation follows. The *ganav* did not return the animal to the owner and did advance the *geneivah*, and the *shechita* was a proper one — both conditions for liability are satisfied.

### Third Answer: Animal Had…

Reish Lakish proposes a third approach. The animal had a *mum* — a blemish — and was slaughtered outside the *Beis HaMikdash*. An animal with a *mum* cannot be brought as a *korban* in any case, and therefore slaughtering it outside the *Beis HaMikdash* does not violate the prohibition of *shchutei chutz*, which applies only to animals that could have been offered inside. Accordingly, the *ganav* has not transgressed *shchutei chutz*, and the animal is not *assur b'hana'ah* on that basis.

However, a question remains: even though the *ganav* has not violated *shchutei chutz*, the animal still carries *kedushat korban* — it was sanctified as a *korban* even if it could not be offered in its current state. Does slaughtering it outside, while it still has *kedushat haguf*, render it a *shechita she'einah re'uyah*? After all, a blemished *korban* that has not been redeemed cannot be eaten — it retains its sanctity even in its disqualified state. If the meat cannot be eaten, then by Rabbi Shimon's own principle, this *shechita* should not qualify as *shechita re'uyah* for the purposes of four-and-five. The Gemara leaves this as an opening for further discussion, noting the three distinct proposed answers and their respective resolutions — or unresolved difficulties — in accounting for how a *shechita* of a stolen *korban* can qualify as *shechita re'uyah* and give rise to the four-and-five obligation.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 77

## Three Answers Intro

### Core Problem Setup

The sugya before us opens with a fundamental difficulty rooted in Rabbi Shimon's own position. The Mishnah addresses a case where a thief steals a cow or sheep that is *kodshim* — a sanctified animal. Because the thief bears *achrayus*, financial responsibility to replace the animal should it be lost, the animal is treated as if it were his own for purposes of the theft law, making him liable for *kefel* (double payment). All of this is straightforward. The difficulty arises when the thief proceeds to slaughter or sell the animal, triggering the four-and-five penalty. How can one be liable for *tvicha* — slaughter — of a *kodshim* animal?

Rabbi Shimon himself is the very authority who rules that a *shechita* which does not render the meat permissible for eating does not qualify as a valid act of *shechita* (*shechita she'eina re'uya*). And here, if the animal is *kodshim* slaughtered outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, it is *assur behana'ah* — forbidden to derive any benefit from — making the slaughter apparently invalid. So how does one ever arrive at a case of four-and-five involving a stolen *kodshim* animal?

### Yochanan Answer 1

Rabbi Yochanan's first answer is that the thief slaughtered the animal inside the *Beis Hamikdash* as a *korban* on behalf of the animal's owner. At first glance, this seems to undermine the premise of the case entirely — bringing the animal as a *korban* for the owner would be a form of returning it, such that the theft obligation would dissolve. The Gemara therefore qualifies the scenario: the thief slaughtered it with that intent, but then the blood was spilled before *zerika* — the blood-sprinkling on the *mizbe'ach* — could be performed. As a result, the owner never received the benefit of the *korban*, and the thief's act remained one of ongoing *geneiva*. Yet since the slaughter was performed in a context where the blood could have been sprinkled — which would have made the meat permissible — it is considered a *shechita re'uya*, a valid act of slaughter. That this is so even though the blood was ultimately never thrown is precisely what the Gemara will now have to establish.

### Yochanan Answer 2

Rabbi Yochanan's second answer is more direct. The thief slaughtered the animal inside the *Beis Hamikdash* not for the sake of the owner — *shelo lishmo*, not for the owner's obligation. Since the *korban* was brought *shelo lishmo*, it does not discharge the owner's obligation (*lo oleh labaalim lishum chova*), so there is no concern that this constitutes a return of the stolen animal. And yet the slaughter is undeniably valid, the meat is permissible — it will be eaten by the *kohanim* or by those who brought a *shelamim* — making this unambiguously a *shechita re'uya*.

### Reish Lakish Answer

Reish Lakish offers a third scenario entirely. Rather than situating the slaughter inside the *Beis Hamikdash*, Reish Lakish says the thief slaughtered the animal outside, but it was a *ba'al mum* — a blemished animal. Because the animal had a blemish, there is no violation of *shechutei chutz* (slaughtering sanctified animals outside the Temple), since such an animal is not *ra'uy lepetach ohel moed* — it could not have been brought to the altar. More importantly for our purposes, a blemished *kodshim* animal can be redeemed. Because it is not fit for the *mizbe'ach*, it is eligible for *pidyon* — redemption — through which its sanctity transfers to the redemption money, rendering the animal itself ordinary and permissible for consumption. It is precisely this potential for redemption, Reish Lakish argues, that qualifies the slaughter as a *shechita re'uya*.

---

## Kol Ha'omed Doctrine

### Elazar's Challenge

Rabbi Elazar was unsatisfied — the Aramaic term used is *toyba*, which Rashi reads not as wonder but as something that didn't pass the "sniff test," in the spirit of *tohey bat tiha*. His challenge cuts across both Rabbi Yochanan's first answer and Reish Lakish's answer: in each case, is it the *shechita* alone that renders the meat permissible? For Rabbi Yochanan's first scenario — where the blood was ultimately spilled — you need *zerika*, the throwing of the blood, to permit the meat. For Reish Lakish's scenario, you need *pidyon* — redemption — to permit the meat. In neither case does the *shechita* itself complete the process. So how can either be called a *shechita re'uya*?

Tosafot add an important clarification here. Regarding Rabbi Yochanan's second answer — the animal slaughtered in the *Beis Hamikdash shelo lishmo* — Tosafot do not consider this to be problematic at all. If the blood is eventually thrown, we look back retroactively and treat the entire sequence — *shechita* followed by *zerika* — as the act that rendered the meat permissible. The *shechita* was part of a complete process that culminated in the meat becoming *muttar*. The genuine difficulty, Tosafot explain, is only in the two scenarios where the second step was not completed: either because the blood was spilled, or because the animal was a *ba'al mum* slaughtered outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. In those cases, the meat never actually became permissible, and it may be too late to do anything about it — Tosafot raise the question of whether one can even redeem an animal post-slaughter. For it is one thing to say the *shechita* initiated a process that was completed; it is another to say the *shechita* initiated a process that was never completed, and call the *shechita* valid nonetheless.

The Gemara's response is that Rabbi Elazar had forgotten a principle of Rabbi Shimon: *kol ha'omed lizrok kezarok dami* — anything that was in a position to have its blood sprinkled is treated as if the blood was sprinkled. And the parallel: *kol ha'omed lifdos k'padui dami* — anything that was in a position to be redeemed is treated as if it was redeemed.

A clarification is essential here: these principles do not mean that one achieves *kappara* without actual *zerika*, or that one may benefit from *hekdesh* without actual *pidyon*. The scope of the principle is narrower and precisely defined: it is asking whether the meat may be considered *ra'ui la'achila* — fit for eating, even in a notional sense. *Ra'ui*, fitness, is by its nature a hypothetical category — was this meat in a position to become edible? If there existed a path by which it could have been rendered edible, then it is considered food, and that status is what underlies both the law of *tumas ochlin* (food-related impurity) and the definition of *shechita re'uya*.

### Kol Ha'omed Principle

Rabbi Elazar is told that he had overlooked a teaching of Rabbi Shimon — a different Rabbi Shimon, though as the Gemara proceeds, all the Rabbi Shimons converge beautifully. The principle: *kol ha'omed lizrok kezarok dami* — if the blood was in a position to be thrown on the *mizbe'ach*, it is treated as though it was thrown. This does not mean one obtains atonement without the actual *zerika*; it means specifically that for the purpose of evaluating whether the meat can be considered food — whether it is *ra'ui la'achila* — we apply this principle. Since the word *ra'ui* itself is inherently hypothetical (was the meat *fit* to be eaten?), it is sufficient that there existed a realistic possibility of the meat becoming edible.

### Notar Food Status

The Gemara now grounds the principle in a concrete case from a *Baraisa*. Rabbi Shimon teaches: there is a type of *notar* — leftover sacrifice meat — that can contract *tumas ochlin*, the impurity of foodstuffs, and there is a type that cannot. The question is when *notar* qualifies as food. *Notar* does not begin its existence as *notar*; it begins as valid sacrificial meat and becomes *notar* only once it has overstayed its permitted time. So the question is: was this meat ever in a state where it could have been eaten? If it was, then even though it is now *notar* and may no longer be consumed, it retains the legal status of food and can become *tamei* with *tumas ochlin*.

### Notar Before/After Zerika

The *Baraisa* draws the distinction as follows. If the meat *lan lifnei zerika* — spent the night before *zerika* was performed — it does not contract *tumas ochlin*. If it became *notar* after *zerika* — *le'achar zerika* — it does.

The Gemara then clarifies what *lifnei zerika* and *le'achar zerika* mean in practice. They do not refer simply to whether the blood was literally thrown before or after. Rather: *kodem shenir'eh lezerika* — the meat spent the night before it ever had an opportunity for the blood to be thrown, versus *le'achar shenir'eh lezerika* — after there had been at least one moment during which the blood could have been thrown.

The paradigm case of meat that never had a moment for *zerika*: the animal was slaughtered just before sunset, right at the edge of nightfall, at a point when there was simply no time left in the day for the *avoda* to be performed in the *Mikdash*. The blood was caught, but the moment the day ended there was no longer an opportunity for *zerika*. Such meat never had *sha'as hakosher* — a window of fitness — and therefore is not considered food. It cannot become *tamei* with *tumas ochlin*.

Contrast this with meat where the animal was slaughtered with sufficient daylight remaining that the blood could have been thrown. In that case, even if the *zerika* was never performed, the meat had its moment of potential fitness. And that moment suffices to categorize it as food.

### Elicit Kol Ha'omed

The Gemara draws its conclusion: *alma kol ha'omed lizrok kezarok dami* — you see from this that anything which was in a position to have its blood sprinkled is treated as though the blood was sprinkled — at least for the purpose of determining whether the meat is considered food. This is precisely the operative principle for *shechita re'uya* as well. The goal of *shechita re'uya* is to establish that the act of slaughter produced edible meat. Since the blood could have been thrown at the moment of *shechita*, we treat the meat as though it were edible. Accordingly, even in Rabbi Yochanan's first scenario where the blood was ultimately spilled, because at the time of slaughter the blood could have been thrown, this qualifies as a *shechita re'uya*, and the thief is liable for the four-and-five payment.

---

## Kol Ha'omed Redemption

### Para Aduma Impurity

The Gemara now extends the parallel principle — *kol ha'omed lifdos k'padui dami* — through an analogous *Baraisa*. The case involves a *para aduma*, the red heifer. It should be noted that the *para aduma* occupies a fascinating hybrid status: it is *kodshei bedek habayis* rather than *kodshei mizbe'ach*, not technically a *korban* in the conventional sense, though sharing many similarities with one. The question posed is whether the slaughtered *para aduma* can contract *tumas ochlin* — food-related impurity.

This raises an immediate puzzle: the meat of a *para aduma* is never intended to be eaten. It is *kodshim*, entirely *assur*, and destined to be burned. How could it ever be considered food? Tosafot engage at length with a further complication — the *para aduma* is itself a source of *tuma*, so why discuss it acquiring *tuma* from outside? — but the straightforward resolution is that the *para aduma* generates *tuma* specifically in the context of the purification process, not through ordinary contact.

The *Baraisa* states: *para metame'a tumas ochlin ho'il v'hayesa la sha'as hakosher* — a *para aduma* can contract *tumas ochlin* because it had a moment (*sha'as hakosher*) of fitness. What moment could that be?

### Para Redemption Window

Reish Lakish transmits a teaching in the name of Rabbi Shimon — and once again, all the same figures converge: *amar Reish Lakish amar Rabbi Shimon*, Rabbi Shimon used to say: *para nifdeis al gabei maarachta* — a *para aduma* can be redeemed even while its carcass sits atop the pyre, right up until the moment the blood is sprinkled. Even at that ultimate last moment before burning commences, one could declare: we will redeem this *para aduma* and begin the process again, perhaps with a better animal or with improved intentions. Tosafot note that presumably this window closes once *zrikas hadam* has been performed, but until that point, redemption remains available.

### Fitness for Redemption

This teaching establishes that the *para aduma*, between the moment of slaughter and the moment of *zerika*, had a window during which it could have been redeemed and its sanctity transferred to the redemption money, rendering the meat theoretically permissible. That window of fitness — *sha'as hakosher* — is sufficient to classify the meat as food, even though no *mitzva* requires one to redeem it, and even though no one ever would. Indeed, this case is an even more striking *chiddush* than the *zerika* case: by a *korban*, there is an affirmative *mitzva* to perform *zerika*. Here, there is no *mitzva* to redeem the *para aduma* — redemption is merely a theoretical option. And yet the mere theoretical possibility of redemption, the fact that it *could have* been eaten after redemption, confers upon the meat the status of food.

The Gemara therefore states: *alma kol ha'omed lifdos k'padui dami* — anything that was in a position to be redeemed is treated as though it was redeemed, for the purpose of determining whether it is considered food.

### Reish Lakish Vindicated

The application to Reish Lakish's original answer follows directly. When a thief slaughters a blemished *kodshim* animal outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, the meat was never actually eaten and the animal was never actually redeemed. But because it *could have* been redeemed — because, as Reish Lakish himself taught, redemption remains available right up until the last moment — the slaughter is treated as a *shechita re'uya*. The thief is therefore liable for the four-and-five penalty.

---

## Yochanan vs Reish Lakish

### Yochanan's Reasoning

Having established that both Rabbi Yochanan's and Reish Lakish's scenarios are internally coherent, the Gemara turns to an equally important question: why did each *amora* not simply adopt the other's scenario?

The Gemara begins with the easier case. *Bishlama* Rabbi Yochanan did not employ Reish Lakish's *ba'al mum* scenario — *d'kabai l'okme masnisin afilu b'tamimim* — because he did not want to limit the Mishnah's ruling to blemished animals. Rabbi Yochanan did not dispute Reish Lakish; he acknowledged that a blemished animal slaughtered outside the *Beis Hamikdash* would indeed be a valid case. But the Mishnah's law should apply even to unblemished animals brought inside the *Beis Hamikdash*, and Rabbi Yochanan therefore framed his answers to account for that broader scope.

### Tvicha u-Mechira Princip…

The more substantive question is why Reish Lakish did not adopt Rabbi Yochanan's scenarios. Here the Gemara introduces a new principle — *tvicha u-mechira*. The verse states *u'tvacho o mechoro* — "and slaughtered it or sold it" — and Reish Lakish derives from this juxtaposition a rule of structural symmetry: *kol heicha de-isa bi-mechira isa bi-tvicha* — wherever there is liability for *mechira* (sale), there is liability for *tvicha* (slaughter); *ve-chol heicha de-leisa bi-mechira leisa bi-tvicha* — wherever there is no liability for *mechira*, there is no liability for *tvicha*. The two forms of liability are interdependent.

### Unblemished Sale Impossi…

This principle explains why Reish Lakish cannot accept Rabbi Yochanan's scenarios. An unblemished *kodshim* animal cannot be sold. If the thief attempted to transfer the animal to a third party, no valid sale could occur — one cannot acquire a *kodshim* animal through a standard commercial transaction, because the animal's sanctity cannot be transferred by sale. Consequently, since the thief could not have been liable for *mechira*, he cannot be liable for *tvicha* either. This is not a disagreement with Rabbi Yochanan about whether the *shechita* was technically valid — Reish Lakish may well agree that slaughtering an unblemished *kodshim* inside the *Beis Hamikdash* constitutes a *shechita re'uya*. Rather, his objection is structural: the Torah's four-and-five penalty operates through a linked framework where liability for sale and liability for slaughter stand or fall together.

### Both Sages Consistent

The Gemara confirms that this dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is not ad hoc; they are each applying their own consistently held positions. *Ve-azdu le-ta'amaihu* — and they have gone each according to his own reasoning — meaning this is a known, independent debate between these two *amoraim* about the relationship between *shechita* and *mechira* within the four-and-five framework.

### Reish Lakish Interdepend…

Reish Lakish's position is stated with full symmetry: *kol heicha de-isa bi-mechira isa bi-tvicha ve-chol heicha de-leisa bi-mechira leisa bi-tvicha*. The liability for slaughter and the liability for sale are perfectly interdependent. Being unable to incur liability for one necessarily precludes liability for the other. It is this principle that drives Reish Lakish to require the *ba'al mum* scenario: a blemished *kodshim* animal can in principle be sold — through redemption, the sanctity transfers and the animal can change hands — and therefore the *tvicha* liability can also attach.

---

## Treifa Case Test

### Treifa Baraita

The Gemara now introduces a *Baraisa* that puts this debate to the test. *Ganav kilayim u-tvacho, tereifa u-mechoro, meshalem tashlumei arba ve-chamisha* — if one stole a *kilayim* (crossbred animal) and slaughtered it, or a *tereifa* and sold it, he pays four-and-five. The Gemara immediately flags this as significant: why does the *Baraisa* specifically cite *selling* a *tereifa*, rather than *slaughtering* it? This is surprising if, according to Rabbi Shimon, *shechita* of a *tereifa* is not valid — since the meat of a *tereifa* is never permissible, the slaughter does not render it edible, and therefore it is not a *shechita re'uya*.

### Yochanan's Challenge

Rabbi Yochanan presses the point. The very fact that the *Baraisa* chooses to discuss *selling* a *tereifa* and not *slaughtering* it suggests that the *Baraisa* is operating according to Rabbi Shimon's position. Under Rabbi Shimon, *shechita* of a *tereifa* generates no liability because it is not a *shechita re'uya* — so the *chiddush* of the *Baraisa* is that even though you cannot be liable for slaughtering a *tereifa*, you can be liable for selling it. This directly supports Rabbi Yochanan's view that the two forms of liability — *tvicha* and *mechira* — are independent, and that one can be liable for sale even without potential liability for slaughter.

### Reish Lakish Response

Reish Lakish responds: the *Baraisa* follows the *Rabanan*, not Rabbi Shimon. According to the *Rabanan*, *shechita* of a *tereifa* is perfectly valid and does generate liability. So the *Baraisa* is simply presenting one illustrative scenario per case: it mentions *slaughtering* a *kilayim* and *selling* a *tereifa*, but this is not meant to be exhaustive — the same liability would apply in either scenario for either animal. The *Baraisa* chose one case for each; it does not mean to exclude the other.

### Gemara Counterargument

The Gemara is unpersuaded. *Hai mai* — what kind of answer is this? If the *Baraisa* follows the *Rabanan*, then there is no reason to structure it the way it does. If we are going to mention a *tereifa* under the *Rabanan*, and *shechita* of a *tereifa* is fully valid and generates liability just like any other case, then the *Baraisa* should have combined both animals into a single statement: *ganav kilayim v'tereifa, tavchan u-mecharan, meshallem tashlumei arba'ah ve-chamisha* — if you stole a *kilayim* or a *tereifa*, whether you slaughtered them or sold them, you pay four-and-five. The fact that the *Baraisa* deliberately separates the two animals and assigns different scenarios to each — *shechita* for *kilayim* and *mechira* for *tereifa* — is inexplicable under the *Rabanan*'s view, where the distinction carries no significance.

Moreover — though the Gemara does not press this point explicitly — if the *Baraisa* truly follows the *Rabanan* and is simply picking one scenario per animal for stylistic reasons, why pick *selling* a *tereifa* at all? Under the *Rabanan*, the *chiddush* would be *slaughtering* a *tereifa*, since that is where they disagree with Rabbi Shimon. Selecting the *mechira* scenario for the *tereifa* case only makes sense if the *Baraisa* is telling us that *shechita* of a *tereifa* is *exempt* — i.e., it is operating according to Rabbi Shimon — and the *chiddush* is precisely that liability attaches through *mechira* even when it would not attach through *tvicha*.

### Unresolved Status

The Gemara concedes: *kashya*. The difficulty stands. The *Baraisa*'s structure remains awkward and unexplained on Reish Lakish's reading. The Gemara does not resolve the tension, and the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding the interdependence of *tvicha* and *mechira* remains unresolved.

---

## Kilayim Interpretation

### Kilayim Included

Having introduced the case of *kilayim* in the *Baraisa*, the Gemara pauses to explain the legal basis for the four-and-five liability in that case. The Torah's formulation — *ki yignov ish shor o seh* — "if a man steals an ox or a *seh*" — is the source of the law. But is a crossbred animal a *seh*? The Gemara establishes that it is, and explains why through an analysis of how the word *o* ("or") functions in different biblical contexts.

### Rava's Principle

Rava introduces the analytical framework. As a baseline: *kol makom shene'emar seh eino ela l'hotzi et hakilayim* — wherever the Torah uses the word *seh* on its own, it signifies to the exclusion of crossbreeds. This is Rava's stated default position. However — and this is the crux of the analysis — whether the word *o* that follows confirms or overrides this default cannot be determined by the word alone. It depends entirely on context.

### Theft Law Analysis

In the law of theft, the verse reads *shor o seh* — an ox or a *seh*. Now consider the default assumption absent the word *o*: an ox and a sheep cannot interbreed. The very pairing of these two animals in the same verse would, on its own, suggest that crossbreeds are excluded — because no crossbreed of an ox and a sheep is possible, the category defined by their conjunction implicitly excludes hybrid animals. If the default without the *o* is already that crossbreeds are excluded, then the *o* must be serving the opposite function: it comes to *include* crossbreeds (*o l'rabos kilayim*). Thus in theft law, *kilayim* — a crossbreed of, say, a sheep and a goat — is included in the four-and-five penalty.

### Kodshim Law Analysis

The situation is reversed when we turn to *kodshim*. The verse concerning sacrificial animals reads *shor o chesev o ez ki yivaled* — "an ox or a sheep or a goat when it is born." Within this verse, the relevant pairing for our purposes is *chesev* and *ez* — sheep and goat. Unlike an ox and a sheep, a sheep and a goat *can* interbreed (as was established in Masechet *Chullin*). Therefore, the juxtaposition of sheep and goat in the same verse, without the word *o*, would naturally suggest that crossbreeds are *included* — because a crossbreed of these two is a real biological possibility, and mentioning them together implies coverage of the full range. Since the default assumption — absent the *o* — would be that crossbreeds are included, the *o* must be serving the opposite function here: it comes to *exclude* (*o l'ma'utei kilayim*).

But there are two *o*'s in this verse. The first (*o chesev*) excludes *kilayim* — genuine crossbreeds of sheep and goat. The second (*o ez*) excludes something even further: *nidmeh* — an animal that is biologically a purebred offspring of sheep but happens to look like a goat, or vice versa. Such an animal is also disqualified from being brought as a *korban*, despite being genetically pure.

### Why Two Or's

This explains why two *o*'s are required. If the *o*'s were serving an *inclusive* function, one *o* would suffice — once you have included *kilayim*, there is no remaining category left to include, since *nidmeh* (which is biologically pure) would *a fortiori* be included. But if the *o*'s are serving an *exclusive* function, then two *o*'s make perfect sense: the first excludes *kilayim* — genuine hybrids — while the second is needed to extend the exclusion to *nidmeh* — animals that are genetically pure but look different from their parents. These are two distinct categories, each requiring its own exclusion. The logical structure thus forces us to read both *o*'s as exclusionary, confirming that the verse in *kodshim* limits eligible animals to those that are genuinely typical specimens of their species.

### Default Principle Questi…

This raises a pointed question that the Gemara leaves open. Rava articulated a principle — the word *seh* by itself defaults to excluding *kilayim*. But as the preceding analysis has shown, the entire interpretive exercise was driven not by this default but by the surrounding context: in each case, the *o* was read against the background assumption created by the other animals mentioned in the verse, not against any free-standing default meaning of *seh*. One might therefore ask: does Rava's stated default ever actually do independent work? In every case we have examined, the direction of the *o* — whether inclusive or exclusive — was determined entirely by contextual considerations. The Gemara does not resolve this question. We will resume from this point in the next shiur.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 78

## Kilayim & Seh

### Hybrid Theft

Today's daf is 78, and we continue in the middle of a digression regarding whether the word *seh* in the Torah functions to exclude *kilayim* — a hybrid animal. The issue arose because of a practical question: if someone steals a hybrid sheep-goat, does he pay four and five upon slaughtering or selling it? The answer is that he does pay, because the verse uses the phrase *o seh* — the *vav* serving to include *kilayim* — whereas by *korbanot*, that same *o* functions to exclude *kilayim*. In fact, in the context of sacrifices, not only is a hybrid excluded, but even a *nidmeh* — an animal that does not resemble its parent — is excluded as well.

### Rava's Rule

With that established, the *gemara* turns to a general principle attributed to Rava: *kol makom she'ne'emar seh, eino ela l'hotzi et hakilayim* — wherever the Torah uses the word *seh*, it comes to exclude *kilayim*. This is formulated as a *binyan av*, a paradigm applicable across the Torah. The immediate difficulty, however, is that the cases we have seen do not seem to operate on a simple default; each requires an explicit textual signal pointing one way or the other. So the *gemara* presses: when, in practice, is Rava's principle ever independently relevant?

### Is It Relevant?

The *gemara* poses the question directly: *l'mai hilchata?* — for which *halacha* does Rava's general rule actually do any work?
