How can Rav prohibit cats entirely? The *gemara* resolves the tension: *lo kashya — ha be-uchma ha be-chivra* — the distinction is between black cats and white cats. Black cats are permissible to keep; white cats are the dangerous ones and subject to Rav's prohibition.

### Cat Colors Explained

But a further difficulty arises: the cat that attacked the baby in Rav's story is identified by the *gemara* as black. If black cats are safe, how does Rav's ruling emerge from that incident? The *gemara* responds: *hasam uchma bar chivra hava* — that particular cat was black but born from a white parent, and therefore retained the dangerous qualities of the white lineage.

This generates a secondary question: Ravina himself had asked — and not resolved — the status of *uchma bar chivra*, a black cat born from a white one. If Ravina's question was open, how can the *gemara* treat Rav's case as settled? The *gemara* distinguishes: Ravina's unresolved question concerned *uchma bar chivra bar uchma* — a black cat whose parent was white but whose grandparent was black, raising uncertainty about whether the black lineage reasserts itself. The cat in Rav's incident was *uchma bar chivra bar chivra* — black, but born from a line of white cats, making the dangerous character much more clear-cut. The *gemara* acknowledges, however, that how one is meant to know the precise lineage of a particular cat is not entirely clear. The bottom line is that black cats from a stable black lineage are permitted for pest control, while white cats and their offspring — even when black in appearance — are dangerous, forbidden to keep, and may be killed.

---

## Opportunity & Welfare

### Boils & Doors

A chain of teachings attributed to Rabbi Acha bar Papa in the name of Rabbi Abba bar Papa in the name of Rabbi Adda bar Papa (with variant traditions substituting Rabbi Chiya bar Papa and Rabbi Chanina bar Papa) introduces several apparently disparate rulings that are linked by thematic association. The first: *matri'in al ha-chichuch be-Shabbat* — one may sound an alarm (*matri'in*) or call out even on *Shabbat* on account of *chichuch*, a spreading blister or boil, out of concern that a contagious outbreak may be developing in the community. According to *Rashi*, *matri'in* refers to sounding a *shofar*; according to *Tosafot*, the distinction between *matri'in* and *tzo'akin* may have more to do with the day on which one calls out than with the instrument used. This discussion is more fully developed in *Masechet Ta'anit*.

The second teaching: *ve-delet ha-ne'elet lo be-meheira tiftach* — a door that has been closed will not quickly open again. One must seize opportunity when it presents itself.

A *baraita* seems to challenge the first ruling: certain plagues — including *chichuch*, locusts, flies, hornets, gnats, snakes, and scorpions — would not warrant *matri'in* but only *tzo'akin*. The *gemara* resolves: *lo kashya — kan be-lach kan be-yavesh* — the distinction depends on whether the affliction is moist or dry. The moist, weeping type of boil is more dangerous and warrants the stronger response even on *Shabbat*. This is supported by a teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: the *shchin* that God brought upon Egypt was moist on the outside and dry on the inside — the worst possible combination — as implied by the verse describing it as *shchin av'bu'ot* (Shemot 9:9), boiling and sprouting sores. That type of affliction can be the occasion for calling out even on *Shabbat*.

### Door Metaphors

The teaching about the closed door that does not quickly open is then interpreted in several ways by various Amoraim. Mar Zutra says it refers to *smicha*: the chain of rabbinic ordination stretching back to Moshe Rabbeinu was at certain periods in acute jeopardy of being broken, and if one had the opportunity to receive *smicha* and missed it, that door might not open again soon. Rav Ashi gives a more general formulation: *kol ha-marei'in lo lo be-meheira meitivin lo* — one to whom things have gone badly will not quickly find them going well again. Rav Acha mi-Difti gives the most pessimistic version: *le-olam ein meitivin lo* — one who has missed the opportunity will never find it again. The *gemara* notes, however, that *lav hi* — that is not the authoritative formulation; it represents Rav Acha mi-Difti's personal experience. *Tosafot* observes that in the story underlying Rav Acha mi-Difti's remark, he himself initially said the door would not *quickly* reopen — and only after he never did recover the lost position did he revise his teaching to "never." It is a quietly poignant footnote about how experience colors one's rulings.

---

## Deeds on Shabbat

### Writing Deed

The *gemara* now arrives at the ruling most directly relevant to the broader theme of *yishuv Eretz Yisrael*: *ha-lokeach bayit be-Eretz Yisrael kosvin alav ono afilu be-Shabbat* — one who purchases a house in Eretz Yisrael may have the deed written even on *Shabbat*. This is the reason the preceding teaching about closed doors was cited here: if an opportunity to acquire property in Eretz Yisrael presents itself and one hesitates, it may not present itself again.

### Settlement Priority

The *gemara* immediately questions the ruling: *be-Shabbat salka da'atach*? Can you literally write on *Shabbat*? Writing is a *melacha de-oraita*. The answer, as *Rava* stated in a parallel context, is: *omer le-nochri ve-oseh* — one instructs a non-Jew to write the deed, and the non-Jew performs the act. Normally, *amira le-nochri* — instructing a non-Jew to perform *melacha* on *Shabbat* — is itself a rabbinic prohibition (*shvut*). But here, *mishum yishuv Eretz Yisrael lo gazru bah rabanan* — for the sake of settling Eretz Yisrael, the rabbis did not apply the usual *gezeira*, and the *amira le-nochri* is permitted.

### Amira Exception

This ruling opens a broader halachic question: under what conditions is *amira le-nochri* permissible? The *Bahag* (*Ba'al Halachot Gedolot*), quoted by *Tosafot*, takes a radical position: *amira le-nochri* is permitted even for a *de-oraita* in the context of *mitzvot* such as *bris milah* — or at least for *machshirei bris milah*, the preparatory acts surrounding a *bris*, on the grounds that *bris milah* itself overrides *Shabbat*. Some opinions extend this further to *tzorchei rabim* — communal needs. The opposite extreme would not permit *amira le-nochri* even for a *shvut de-shvut be-makom mitzvah*. The normative consensus is that *amira le-nochri* is permitted for a rabbinic prohibition (*de-rabanan*) when a *mitzvah* is at stake, but not for a *de-oraita* prohibition — and the case of *yishuv Eretz Yisrael* is treated as a specific exception to that rule.

---

## Town Pathways

### Four Directions

The *daf* closes with a teaching of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: *ha-lokeach ir be-Eretz Yisrael kofin oto likach lo derech me-arba ruchoseha* — one who purchases an entire town in Eretz Yisrael is compelled to also acquire pathways leading to and from it in all four directions, *mishum yishuv Eretz Yisrael* — for the sake of settling the land. The underlying concern, it seems, is that if the roads and paths surrounding the town are held by others who might close them off, the town becomes inaccessible — which would undermine the very purpose of Jewish settlement. By compelling the purchaser to acquire the pathways as well, the rabbinic enactment ensures that the town remains genuinely viable and connected to the surrounding landscape, and that the settlement cannot be strangled by a hostile neighbor who controls the access routes.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 81

## Yehoshua's Ten Stipulati…

### Ten Takkanot Overview

The *gemara* on Bava Kamma 81b opens with a *baraisa*: *asarah tenayim hitna Yehoshua* — Yehoshua made ten stipulations when the Jewish people entered the land of Israel. These were conditions assumed to have been agreed upon at the time of the conquest, governing the entire society going forward. What is immediately striking is how different these *takkanot* are from the mishna's preceding discussions of tort law. Rather than restricting behavior to prevent damage to others, these stipulations grant the public a degree of freedom even with respect to the private property of others.

### Grazing & Gathering

The first stipulation is *she-yehei mar'in b'chorshin* — that people may graze their animals in the forests, including privately owned ones. As noted earlier in the tractate, one is permitted to own sheep and goats provided they are grazed in forests rather than in fields. Here Yehoshua extends this principle to allow grazing even in someone else's private forest. The presumption seems to be that the vegetation poses no real concern to the owner — the forest is not being used for crops, and the vegetation will grow back.

The second and third stipulations allow gathering sticks and grasses from others' property. One may collect *etzim* — sticks — from another person's fields, presumably for firewood or fodder. One may also collect *asavim* — grasses — from anywhere, to feed one's animals. Yehoshua's logic throughout seems to be that wherever the owner suffers no real loss, the public cannot rightfully be excluded. The *gemara* will qualify each of these substantially, because there are plainly situations where the owner does stand to lose something.

### Water & Fishing Rights

The fourth stipulation concerns *mayan ha-yotzei ba-techilla* — a wellspring that emerges on its own. Even though the spring surfaces on private land, the townspeople have a right to use it. This is described as a remarkable ruling: water was a desperate public necessity, and Yehoshua declared that even a naturally occurring spring on private property is subject to public usage rights. The owner may retain some form of ownership — Rabba bar Rav Huna argues that one must pay for the water — but the *gemara* rejects this view and holds that no payment is required. The precise scope of this right (how much water, for what uses) is left open, but the principle is clear: the private owner cannot simply exclude the public.

The fifth stipulation permits *mechakin b'yama shel Tverya* — cast hook fishing in the Sea of Tiberias — even from shores that border private land. The qualifier is *bilvad she-lo yifros kela ve-ya'amid et ha-sefinah* — one may not spread out box traps or similar devices that would obstruct the boats. Nets, however, are permitted.

### Paths & Privacy Rights

The sixth stipulation, *niftin le-achorei ha-geder* — one may relieve oneself behind a stone fence — applies even in a field full of saffron, the most precious commodity of the ancient world. The allowance is clearly grounded in *kavod ha-briyot*, human dignity, and perhaps the recognition that necessity admits of no argument.

The seventh stipulation concerns *shvilei ha-reshut* — either paths that private owners have designated for passage or simply paths on privately owned land — which the public may use until the second rainfall. The background is that after the harvest, a field lies fallow and passage causes no harm. Once the second rain falls after seeding, however, the growing crops are at risk, and the right of passage lapses. Rashi interprets *reshut* as referring to paths that owners have explicitly permitted; others understand it simply to mean privately owned paths.

The eighth stipulation, *u-mistalkin le-tzidei ha-derachim mipnei yesados ha-derachim*, permits walking onto private property at the edges of a road when the hardened mud of the path — having dried into sharp, uneven ridges after the rainy season — makes the center of the road difficult to traverse.

### Lost in Vineyard & Meis…

The ninth and tenth stipulations complete the list. *Ha-to'eh bein ha-keramim* — one who is lost among the vines of a vineyard — may cut his way out, whether upward or downward, *mafaseg ve-oleh mafaseg ve-yored*, until he reaches a road or a town. And *meis mitzvah koneh mekomo* — an unidentified corpse acquires, as it were, its place of death. Wherever an unknown person dies, he has the right to be buried there, regardless of whose property it is.

---

## Grazing Qualifications

### Animal Size & Forest Den…

The *gemara* now unpacks each stipulation in detail. Regarding the first — grazing in forests — Rav Papa qualifies: *lo amran ela daka b'gasah* — this was only said of small animals (*daka*), such as sheep and goats, grazing in a thick, densely wooded forest (*gasah*). Three other combinations are excluded. Small animals in a thin forest (*daka b'daka*) — not permitted, because the sparse vegetation could be significantly damaged. Large animals in a dense forest (*gasah b'gasah*) — also not permitted, because even dense growth cannot withstand large animals without real harm to the owner. And *kol she-kein gasah b'daka* — certainly large animals in a thin forest are not permitted. All of this, of course, applies only to someone else's forest; an owner may do as he pleases on his own land.

### Gathering Sticks Rules

Regarding gathering sticks, the *gemara* layers qualification upon qualification. *Lo amran ela b'hizmei ve-higni* — it applies only to thornbushes, not to other wood, which the owner may well want for firewood. Even for thornbushes, the allowance applies only to *mechubarim* — things still attached to the ground — because detached thornbushes (*telushin*) may already have been pulled out by the owner for his own use. And even if the thornbushes are still attached, the allowance is only for *lach* — moist ones — not dry ones, since dry thornbushes are much more readily usable as firewood and the owner may have plans for them. Finally, even in permitted cases, *u-vilvad she-lo yesharesh* — one may not uproot the thornbush in a way that damages the soil.

The pattern here is instructive. Most of Yehoshua's stipulations are operative only where the owner suffers no real loss. The moment a genuine loss to the owner comes into view, the permission evaporates. The exceptions are the cases that override even tangible damage — the meis mitzvah, relieving oneself — and those are grounded in overriding concerns of dignity or the sacred.

### Fenugreek & Grasses

Regarding grasses, the *gemara* notes the exception of *tiltan*, fenugreek: grasses may be gathered everywhere *chutz mi-sdeh tiltan* — except from a fenugreek field. This prompts a question: are we saying that grasses actually benefit fenugreek? But a *baraisa* implies the opposite — if fenugreek grows up alongside other grasses, we do not require the owner to uproot either the fenugreek or the grasses on account of *kilayim*, the prohibition of mixed species, precisely because the mixture arose on its own without deliberate planting. The implication of that *baraisa* is that the grasses actually harm the fenugreek, not help it.

Rav Yirmiyah resolves the tension: *lo kashya, kan le-zera, kan le-zirin* — no difficulty. It depends on whether the fenugreek is being grown for its seeds or for its stalks. For the seed, the grasses are harmful — *kashu leh asavim de-machchesh lah* — they weaken the seeds. That is the case in the *baraisa*, where the mixture arose incidentally; since the grasses damage the fenugreek-for-seed, the owner does not want them growing together, and there is no *kilayim* concern. But for the stalk, *ma'alu leh* — the grasses are beneficial, because when the fenugreek grows up amid grasses, *mirkava*, it spreads across the surrounding vegetation and the stalk develops more robustly. In that case the grasses are wanted, and removing them would hurt the owner.

Alternatively, the *gemara* offers a second distinction: *kan le-adam, kan li-vhemah* — whether the fenugreek is grown for human consumption or for animal consumption. If it is grown for animals, then *de-zara asavim nami miba'ei leh* — the grower wants the grasses too, as additional feed. In that case, gathering the grasses hurts the owner and Yehoshua's *takkana* does not apply. Rav Papa adds a practical marker: if the fenugreek is planted in rows, it is grown for human consumption; if not in rows, it is for animals.

---

## Branch Cutting Rules

### Olive Tree Branches

Regarding the fifth item in the original list — *ve-kotmim neti'ah be-chol makom chutz mi-grufiyot shel zayit* — the public may break off a small twig anywhere, from any tree, except from the shoots of an olive tree. Rav Tanchum and Rav Birai, citing an elder, specify: for an olive tree the relevant threshold is *ke-beitzah* — egg-sized. The precise application of this measurement is itself debated, but one reading is that a twig of up to that size may be taken, though the surrounding prohibition on olive shoots makes this complicated.

### Other Tree Branches

For other trees — reeds and grapevines — one may cut from *min ha-paka u-le-ma'alah*, from the knuckle-like joint upward. For all other trees, one must cut from *ovyo shel ilan ve-lo me-chudo* — from the inner, less exposed part of the tree, not from the tip or the top. Rashi explains this as meaning one must take from the interior side.

Two further restrictions apply regardless of tree type. One may only cut a *chadash* — a new twig that is not yet bearing fruit — and not from a branch that is actively producing. And one must take from a location that is *eino ro'eh et ha-chamah* — not exposed to sunlight — since sun-exposed growth produces the best fruit and is exactly what the owner would wish to preserve. The *gemara* cites the verse *u-mi-meged tevu'ot shamesh* — from the sweetness of the produce of the sun — as the basis. The aggregate principle is plain: the twig may be taken only in a manner that causes the owner no meaningful loss.

---

## Water & Fishing

### Wellspring Rights

*U-ma'inah yotzei techilat benei ha'ir mistapkim mimenu* — if a new wellspring emerges naturally on someone's land, the townspeople have a right to draw from it. Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that payment must nonetheless be made to the owner. The *gemara* rejects this ruling: *v'leit hilchata ke-vateih* — we do not rule in accordance with his position. The owner retains some formal ownership, but the public's right of use is not conditioned on payment. The exact parameters of this right — how much water, for what purposes — are not spelled out, but the underlying principle reflects the ancient understanding of water as a communal necessity that private ownership cannot fully obstruct.

### Fishing Methods

The *gemara* elaborates on the fishing stipulation. Tosafot explains that there are three tiers of access. Cast hook fishing — ordinary line fishing from shore — is available to anyone, even on shores that front private land. The large box traps, *kela*, which would catch passing boats, are prohibited to everyone, even the landowner whose shore it is. Net fishing — *reshatot u-michmeret* — occupies the middle tier: permitted only to the landowner.

### Kinneret Ownership

A *baraisa* records that from the outset, the tribes made a mutual condition among themselves not to use the *kela* traps, but that net fishing was freely permitted.

A further *baraisa* provides the historical background: the Sea of Tiberias fell within the tribal portion of Naftali. Moreover, Naftali received an additional strip — *melo chevel cherem bi-droma* — a measured section of the southern shore, even though his primary territory lay to the north and east, in fulfillment of the verse *yam ve-darom yerashah* — he shall inherit the west (i.e., the western shore of the Kinneret) and the south.

On a related point, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches: detached objects found in the mountains — *telushin she-be-harim* — were held collectively in the presumptive ownership of all the tribes, while attached things — *mechubarim* — belonged to the specific tribe in whose territory they lay. Rashi understands this broadly: movable property seized in the conquest of the land was distributed equally among all Israel regardless of where it was found, while land and its attachments were divided by tribal portion.

The *gemara* adds that every tribe received a portion encompassing the full range of landscapes: *har*, *shefela*, *negev*, and *emek* — mountains, lowlands, dry terrain, and valleys. The verse in Devarim supports this: *ba-aravah ba-har u-va-shefela u-va-negev u-va-chof ha-yam* — in the plain, in the mountain, in the lowland, in the south, and at the shore of the sea. Not every tribe received coastal access literally, but the distribution was designed to give each tribe a variety of terrain. The *gemara* notes that this pattern preceded Israel as well, having characterized the holdings of the Canaanites, Perizzites, and Emorites before them, as the verse implies: *ve-el kol shecheinav* — and to all its neighbors.

---

## Relief & Passage

### Relieving Oneself

*Ve-niftin le-achorei ha-geder* — one may relieve oneself behind a fence — *va-afilu bi-sdeh she-mlei'ah karkom* — even in a field full of saffron. Rav Acha bar Yaakov observes that the core *chiddush* here is not the obvious permissibility of relieving oneself (whether obvious because of *kavod ha-briyot* or because the act arguably fertilizes the field), but rather that one may *take a stone from the stone wall* to use for wiping. That — removing a stone from another's fence — is the genuinely novel ruling.

### Kavod Habriyot on Shabbat

Rav Chisda extends this further: *va-afilu b'Shabbat* — even on Shabbat. The stone is *muktzeh*, yet *kavod ha-briyot* overrides this *de-rabbanan* restriction. Mar Zutra Chasida, being a *chasid*, would take the stone, use it, and then return it to the wall. He would then instruct his attendant — naturally, not on Shabbat itself — to plaster over that section, so that the used side would not remain exposed to others.

### Paths of Reshut

The stipulation *u-mehalchin bi-shvilei ha-reshut ad she-teired reviah shniyah* — one may walk through the private paths until the second rainfall — reflects the agricultural calendar. After the harvest the field lies fallow; passage causes no harm and is therefore permitted. Once the second rain falls after sowing, the seedlings are vulnerable and the right lapses.

### Hardened Mud Paths

Rav Papa qualifies this for Babylonian conditions: *va-hadidan afilu talya di-kashla* — in their fields, even a light dew suffices to make crossing damaging. The underlying principle is the same: passage is permitted only when it causes no harm. If the field is in any condition where crossing would injure it, the right does not apply. The stipulation about hardened mud — *yesados ha-derachim* — concerns the summer months when the path itself becomes treacherous: dried into sharp, uneven ridges, the center of the road is difficult and potentially injurious to walk on. In that situation, one may step off the road onto the private field margin.

---

## Walking on Field Edges

### Shmuel & Rav Yehuda

A narrative illustrates this. Shmuel and Rav Yehuda were walking along a road, and Shmuel stepped off to the side — onto private land — to avoid the hardened, treacherous mud of the path in the dry season. This is, of course, a stipulation Yehoshua made for the Land of Israel. But here we are outside of Eretz Yisrael, in Babylonia.

### Outside Eretz Yisrael Qu…

Rav Yehuda challenged Shmuel directly: *tenayim she-hitna Yehoshua afilu b'Bavel?* — are you claiming that the conditions Yehoshua stipulated apply even in Bavel? Yehoshua's conditions were manifestly limited to Eretz Yisrael. Shmuel replied: *sha'ani omer afilu b'chutz la-aretz* — I say they apply even outside the land. Whether Shmuel is claiming that Yehoshua himself intended universal application, or that any organized Jewish community operates with these implicit norms, is left somewhat open. It is worth noting that the *gemara* earlier applied the restrictions of the *mishna* regarding small animals to Babylonia as well, so there is a broader tendency to treat Babylonian Jewish society as operating by similar principles.

### Rebbi vs. Ben Kenusa

A parallel episode is related involving Rebbi — Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi — and Rebbi Chiya, who were walking together in Eretz Yisrael and similarly moved to the side of the road. Coming toward them, moving directly through the middle of the road, was Rebbi Yehuda ben Kenusa, navigating the difficult terrain by hopping from one stable spot to the next rather than stepping onto private property.

Rebbi turned to Rebbi Chiya and asked: *mihu zeh she-mapgin gedulah b'faneinu?* — who is this person displaying his greatness before us? The implied affront was clear: here stand Rebbi, the foremost rabbinic and political leader of the generation, and Rebbi Chiya, alongside him — both walking on the side of the road — and this person ostentatiously refuses to do so, implicitly casting their practice into question.

Rebbi Chiya responded: perhaps it is Rebbi Yehuda ben Kenusa, my student — *ve-chol ma'asav le-shem shamayim* — and all his actions are *le-shem shamayim*. He is not performing. He is simply that careful. When they drew close and saw who it was, they confirmed this was indeed the case. In Rashi's reading, Rebbi's initial remark was sufficiently sharp that had it been anyone else, it would have warranted *nidui* — excommunication. But given that it was Rebbi Yehuda ben Kenusa, and his intentions were transparently pure, no such measure was appropriate.

---

## Lost in Vineyard

### Self-Rescue in Vineyard

*Ha-to'eh bein ha-keramim mafaseg ve-oleh mafaseg ve-yored* — one who is lost among the vines may cut his way upward or downward through the vineyard until he reaches a town or a road. A *baraisa* extends this explicitly to two scenarios.

### Rescuing the Lost

The first scenario is a bystander who sees another person lost in the vineyard: *ha-ro'eh chaveiro to'eh bein ha-keramim mafaseg ve-oleh mafaseg ve-yored* — he too may cut a path in and out in order to extract the lost person and bring him back to a town or a road. The second scenario is the lost person himself: he may likewise cut his own way out.

One might ask why the *gemara* needs to tell us the second case separately — if even a bystander may cut through the vineyard to rescue someone, surely the person himself may do the same. The *gemara* anticipates this: one might have thought the difference matters. The bystander, coming from outside, knows where he is going — he can cut a relatively direct and limited path. The lost person, by contrast, has no idea of his orientation, and granting him the right to cut in any direction he imagines correct might lead to far greater destruction. Perhaps we should have required him to make his way to the edges of the vineyard and follow the perimeter out, even if that seems to him to be a far longer route. The *gemara* rules against this: *ka mashma lan* — the stipulation applies to the lost person as well, and he may cut in the direction he judges best.

### Deoraisa vs. Drabanan

The *gemara* then raises a pointed question: is this stipulation even necessary? Rescuing a person is a *de-oraisa* obligation. A *baraisa* teaches: *hashavat gufo minayin* — how do we know there is an obligation to return a person to himself, in the same manner as one is obligated to return lost property? From the verse *va-hashevoto* — you shall return him. So there is already a biblical obligation to rescue the lost. Why does Yehoshua's *takkana* add anything?

### Yehoshua's Tikkun

The *gemara* answers: *de-oraisa hu de-kai be-metzarei* — the biblical obligation is satisfied by having the rescuer go along the edges of the vineyard, without causing destruction to the vines. The *de-oraisa* obligation of *hashavah* does not, by itself, permit cutting through and damaging another's property. What Yehoshua came to establish — *atah tikken de-mafaseg ve-oleh mafaseg ve-yored* — is that even destructive passage through the vineyard is permitted in order to effect the rescue. That is Yehoshua's *takkana*: to authorize a form of rescue that would otherwise constitute prohibited damage to private property.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 82

## Ten Conditions

### Joshua's Takanos

The daf opens in the middle of the list of *eser takanos* — the ten conditions that Yehoshua stipulated with the Jewish people upon their entry into the land. These *takanos* represent a compromise of individual property rights for the benefit of the larger community. The list appears at the bottom of 81b, just before the lines widen on the page.

### Mes Mitzva

The final condition on the list is *mes mitzva koneh mekomo*: wherever one finds an unattended corpse with no obvious family, it may be buried in that very spot. The *Gemara* then raises a contradiction from another source: *hamotzei mes mutal ba'esratya* — if one finds a corpse lying across an *esratya*, a major road (the word is Greek), one does not bury it right in the middle of the road. Instead, one moves it to the right or left, to a nearby field. The *Gemara* then sets out a hierarchy: between an unplowed lot (*sadeh bor*) and a plowed-but-unplanted lot (*sadeh nir*), one brings it to the *sadeh bor*; between a *sadeh nir* and a planted field (*sadeh zera*), one brings it to the *sadeh nir* so as to cause the least possible damage. If both sides offer equivalent options, one simply chooses whichever seems best.

Rav Bibi resolves the contradiction: the case of the *esratya* involves a corpse lying stretched across the full width of the road — *mutal al hametzar* — which makes burial in place impossible regardless. Since the body must be moved in any case, one makes a considered choice about where to bring it, and if the options are equivalent, one uses whatever sensible principle is available. That explains how this condition of *mes mitzva* coheres with the *braita* about the road.

### Counting Issue

Having completed the list, the *Gemara* observes: *hanei chad asar havyen* — if one counts the items, there are eleven, not ten. The *Gemara* therefore must account for the discrepancy.

### Shlomo's Teaching

The *Gemara* answers that one of the items — the rule that people may walk through a neighbor's field via its footpaths (*shvilei ha-reshus*) during the off-season when nothing is growing — is not actually a *takanas Yehoshua* at all. Rather, it derives from a principle associated with Shlomo, and so it does not count toward the ten. A *braita* elaborates: if someone's produce has already been harvested and he nonetheless refuses to allow people to cut through his field, people will say of him, *mah hana'ah l'ploni u-mah habriyot mazikos lo* — what benefit does he get from it, and in what way are people harming him? Standing on one's legal rights in a case of *zeh ne'eneh v'zeh eino chaser* — where others benefit and you lose nothing — is technically permissible but morally indefensible.

The *Gemara* quotes a verse to that effect: *al timna tov miba'laiv biheyos le'el yadecha* — do not withhold good from those who deserve it when you have the power to give (Mishlei). One might have thought this was a different verse, perhaps from *Ben Sira*, but the *Gemara* identifies a proper *pasuk* from Mishlei that conveys the same sentiment.

### Additional Takanos

The *Gemara* then asks whether there are yet additional conditions beyond the ones enumerated. Several are introduced.

Rabbi Yehuda teaches that during the season of removing dung, one has the right to bring fertilizer out into the public domain and leave it there for thirty days — *b'sha'at hotza'at z'valim* — so that it can be trodden upon and turned into usable material. This too was a condition of Yehoshua.

Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka teaches three further conditions, all framed as *tnai beit din* — a stipulation of the court. First, if my bees swarm onto a branch in my neighbor's property, I may cut off that branch to retrieve the swarm, paying my neighbor for it. Second, if I spill my wine to save your honey when your barrel is breaking, you must compensate me — you cannot claim you never asked me to do so. Third, if I unload my firewood from my donkey to transport your flax when your animal breaks down, you must pay me for my wood. A question naturally arises: why do these require a formal *tnai beit din* at all? Surely simple logic would demand reimbursement. *Tosafot* notes a tension with another *Gemara* that seems to limit the obligation to paying a fee rather than the full value of the wine. *Tosafot* resolves this by distinguishing a case where the honey-owner himself physically compelled the other person to spill the wine — in that case full reimbursement is owed.

The *Gemara* deflects these additional teachings by noting *be-yachidai lo ka-amina* — the list of ten *takanos* claims only conditions taught unanimously, not those transmitted in the name of individual authorities. Whether this means others actually dispute these conditions or merely that they lack unanimous transmission is not entirely clear.

The *Gemara* then cites Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a tree that leans over a neighbor's field or stands near a boundary line — one may still bring *bikkurim* from it. This is because there is an opinion in the *Gemara* that such a tree, since it damages a neighbor's field, has no legal standing in its current location, and therefore one should not be able to bring *bikkurim* from it. Rabbi Yochanan rules that Yehoshua's conditions explicitly permitted this. Rashi notes that this teaching is a *baraita*, raising the question of why it is not included in the canonical list of ten. The *Gemara* resolves this by revealing that the original list of ten conditions is not an anonymous *baraita* at all. *S'fuyai* — it is in fact the teaching of an *amora*, Yehoshua ben Levi specifically, and therefore other *amoraim* or *tannaim* may well offer different or additional formulations. Rav Geviah of Bei Kasil teaches this explicitly, and Rav Tanchum and Rav Beris transmit it in the name of a certain *zakein* — identified as Yehoshua ben Levi — that he listed exactly ten conditions. So the list of ten is a specific formulation of that authority, not a universally binding enumeration.

---

## Ezra's Takanos

### Leadership Shift

The *Gemara* transitions from the *takanos* of Yehoshua to those of Ezra. The shift is thematically significant. Yehoshua's conditions were framed as *hinchil Yehoshua et ha'aretz* — he bequeathed the land — reflecting his role as political sovereign, setting up the economic and social structure of Jewish life in the land. Ezra, by contrast, operated under foreign rule; the Jews in his time had no political sovereignty, returning to the land only because the Persian king Koresh granted permission. The first taste of genuine sovereignty would come only later, with the Chashmonaim. Ezra's leadership was religious rather than political — he was, in a sense, the first rabbi — and his *takanos* reflect that character entirely.

### Torah Readings

Two of Ezra's ten *takanos* concern the public reading of the Torah. The *Gemara* lists them together: *shekorei b'mincha b'shabbos*, that there should be a Torah reading at Shabbos Mincha, and *shekorei b'sheni u'v'chamishi*, that there should be readings on Mondays and Thursdays.

The reason for the Shabbos Mincha reading, as Rashi explains, is *mishum yoshvei chanuyos kol yemei hachol* — for the sake of the shopkeepers who are occupied with business throughout the week and have no opportunity to hear the Torah reading on market days. Rather than reading for those who are already present on Monday and Thursday, this gives the storekeepers an additional opportunity. It also provides anticipation of the coming week's *parsha*.

Regarding the Monday-Thursday reading, the *Gemara* asks: was this Ezra's institution at all? A *braita* reveals that it goes back much further — to the generation that left Egypt. The *pasuk* records that they walked three days in the desert and found no water — *vayelechu shloshet yamim bamidbar v'lo matzu mayim*. The *Gemara* interprets this *midrashically*: *ein mayim ela Torah* — water here means Torah. They had gone three days without Torah and had become spiritually weary, *nil'u*. The Maharsha connects this to the verse *vayorehu Hashem etz* — the wood thrown to sweeten the water — as an allusion to *etz chayim*, the Torah. At that moment, *sham sam lo chok u'mishpat*, a standing ordinance was established: one should never go three days without Torah. The prophets among them — Moshe, Aharon, and Miriam — therefore instituted reading on Shabbos, Monday, and Thursday, skipping Sunday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday, so that the gap between readings never exceeds two days.

### Ancient Source

This ancient institution addresses the concern that Ezra could not have "instituted" something already in place from the time of the Exodus. The *Gemara* clarifies the nature of Ezra's contribution.

### Ezra Expansion

Originally, the institution consisted of one person reading three *pesukim*, or alternatively three people each reading one *pasuk* — a total of three *pesukim* — corresponding to *kohen*, *Levi*, and *Yisrael*. Ezra came and expanded this: three people should receive *aliyos* and together they should read a total of ten *pesukim* — *k'neged asara batlanim*, corresponding to the ten *batlanim*, the community members who are regularly present in *shul* to ensure a *minyan* and attend to communal needs. Rashi explains these *batlanim* as people of good standing who set aside their own affairs to be available for *tzorchei tzibur* and to be present in the *beit knesset*. So Ezra's contribution was both the expansion of the number of *pesukim* and the institutionalization of the *asara batlanim* — the concept of a standing *minyan* of ten. One wonders whether Ezra's reform also reflects the emergence of the synagogue as a more ritualized institution, with a formal structure of being called up to the Torah and a *minyan* of ten.

*Tosafot* asks why specifically Monday and Thursday were chosen; other day combinations could have served equally well. *Tosafot* cites a *midrash* that when Moshe ascended to receive the final *luchot*, he went up on a Thursday and came down on a Monday — making those days an *et ratzon*, a time of divine favor. *Tosafot* also notes the connection to fast days, which were historically observed on Mondays and Thursdays as days of divine receptivity — and naturally, if people are gathering to read the Torah, those same days would be chosen for fasting.

### Court & Laundry

The *Gemara* records that courts sat on Mondays and Thursdays — *danin b'sheni u'v'chamishi* — because that is when people gathered in town for the Torah reading. Whether the courts preceded the Torah readings or vice versa is a kind of chicken-and-egg question, but the practical integration is clear: by concentrating communal activities on the same days, attendance at one event ensures presence for the other. *Tosafot* raises the question that another *Gemara* suggests that before Ezra, *beit din* sat every day. *Tosafot* resolves this by proposing that Ezra specifically instituted the practice for smaller towns and villages, while major centers may already have had daily courts. Alternatively, focused, less frequent sessions can actually be more productive than daily sittings — just as designating a specific laundry day ensures the task gets done.

The laundry ordinance — *mechabsin b'chamishi b'shabbat*, doing laundry on Thursday — is *mishum kevod Shabbat*, in honor of Shabbos, so that fresh clothes are ready for the holy day.

### Garlic & Onah

Another *takana* of Ezra is eating garlic on *erev Shabbat* — *mishum onah*, in order to fulfill the *mitzvah* of marital relations. A *braita* lists five properties of garlic: it satisfies, it warms the body internally, it gives a pleasant glow to the complexion, it increases semen, and it destroys intestinal parasites. Some add that it fosters love and dispels jealousy, contributing to the general wellbeing that makes garlic something of an ancient superfood. The *Gemara* derives the connection to Friday night from the verse *asher piryo yiten b'ito* — he gives his fruit in the proper time — which is applied to one who fulfills *onah* from *erev Shabbat* to *erev Shabbat*. The *Gemara* presents this teaching through a chain of possible attributions: Rav Yehudah, or alternatively Rav Nachman, or alternatively Rav Kahana, or alternatively Rabbi Yochanan. It is worth noting that certain sects during the *bayis sheni* period considered marital relations on Shabbos to be forbidden, viewing the holy day as incompatible with physical pleasure. The ruling of *Chazal* is precisely the opposite: *Oneg Shabbat* includes the *mitzvah* of marital relations, representing an explicitly anti-ascetic religious posture.

### Women's Takanos

Three of Ezra's *takanos* concern women specifically. First, a woman who bakes should bake early in the morning — *isha mashkemet v'ofah* — so that bread will be available for the poor who pass through during the day. Bread being the staff of life, early baking ensures that the poor have access to food. Second, a woman should wear a *sinar* — some type of undergarment, though the word more literally means an apron — *mishum tzniutah*, for the sake of modesty. Third, a woman should comb her hair before immersing in the *mikvah* — *isha chofefet v'tovelet*.

A question arises: why does this *takana* specifically address women when men too were immersing regularly in that era, before the temple service became inaccessible to most? The answer, as a student suggests, is that the concern about hair pertains to those with long hair, and that describes women in the typical case. The *Gemara* presses further: is not combing the hair before immersion a biblical obligation in any event? The verse says *v'rachatz et besaro bamayim* — one's flesh must be in direct contact with the water, and the extra word *et* includes *hatafel l'besaro*, what is attached to the body, namely the hair. Thus hair must also be in direct contact with water. The *Gemara* responds: *d'oraisa*, the biblical requirement is satisfied by mere inspection — running one's fingers through the hair or visually checking for obstructions, since the concern is *chatzitza*, an interposition preventing contact between the hair and water. What Ezra added was the requirement of actual combing — *chafifa* — rather than simple inspection.

*Tosafot* raises an interesting point here: the elaborate bathing and full-body preparation that women perform before *mikvah* immersion today appears to be an ancient practice with roots in the *Gemara*, but it does not seem to have been formally part of Ezra's *takana*. The *takana* addressed specifically the hair, since hair is harder to inspect and prone to knotting; the full body, being more readily visible, was not given the same formal ordinance, though the practice of thorough bodily preparation developed later. Even regarding the hair, a question remains: does the obligation require combing alone, or combing together with washing?

### Peddlers

Ezra further ordained that fragrance sellers and peddlers should have the right to travel through the various towns and villages — *rochlin machzirin ba'ayarot* — and communities may not bar them. The purpose is *mishum tachshitei nashim*, to enable women to purchase jewelry and fragrances, *k'dei shelo yitganu al ba'aleihen* — so that they not become unattractive to their husbands. This *takana* is less obviously religious in character, but it connects to the same concern for domestic harmony that underlies the *sinar* ordinance. The running theme in Ezra's women's *takanos* is the stability and quality of family life.

### Tevilah Ba'alei Keri

Finally, Ezra ordained immersion in the *mikvah* for a *ba'al keri* — a man who has had a seminal emission. The *Gemara* notes that *d'oraisa*, such a man is already obligated to immerse — the Torah says *v'ish ki tetze mimenu shichvat zera v'rachatz bamayim et kol besaro*. The biblical obligation, however, concerns only his status with regard to *terumah* and *kodashim* — without immersion he may not eat *terumah* or participate in sacrificial service. What Ezra added — *afilu l'divrei Torah* — was that a *ba'al keri* is prohibited from learning Torah or *davening* until he has immersed. He was not formally reinstituting the immersion itself but rather extending its implications to Torah study and prayer.

This is the source of the practice among certain *chassidim* of immersing in the *mikvah* every morning. Since a man who had relations the night before would be required to immerse before *davening*, and since attendance at the *mikvah* each morning would advertise what transpired the previous night, the practice developed of immersing every single morning, removing any inference. *Tosafot*, however, rules that we do not follow Ezra's *takana* in this regard. Rather, we rule in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira — *divrei Torah ein mikablin tumah*, words of Torah cannot become impure — and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira effectively overrode Ezra's extension. A question naturally arises about the authority of a later *amora* to abrogate a *takana* of Ezra, but the practical factor was that the community was simply unable to abide by it. The *takana* thus effectively fell away, though certain communities preserved it — giving rise to the morning *mikvah* practice that persists in some circles today.

---

## Jerusalem Laws

### Jerusalem Property

The *Gemara* now presents ten laws specific to Jerusalem. The first is *ein bayis chalut bah*: a house sold in Jerusalem cannot become permanently transferred to the buyer. In all other walled cities, if a house is not repurchased within the year, the buyer acquires it permanently. In Jerusalem, the seller retains the right to repurchase until the *yovel*. The second is *ein mevia egla arufa*: if a murdered victim is found outside Jerusalem, the *egla arufa* — the calf whose neck is broken in a special ceremony — is not brought for Jerusalem. Third, *v'eino na'asit ir hanidachas*: if the entire city worships idolatry, the law of *ir hanidachas* that mandates total destruction does not apply to Jerusalem.

### Urban Restrictions

The *Gemara* continues: *ein motzi'in bah zizin u'gezustra'ot* — no beams or balconies may protrude over Jerusalem's streets. *Ein osin bah ashpatot* — no garbage dumps may be made in Jerusalem. *Ein osin bah kivshonot* — no kilns for firing pottery may operate in Jerusalem. *Ein osin bah gannot u'fardesot* — no gardens or orchards may be planted in Jerusalem.

The prohibition on protruding beams is explained on two grounds: *mipnei ohel hatuma*, because a protruding beam above a street would spread *tumah* from a corpse to people far removed from the body, and Jerusalem's proximity to the temple service makes any expansion of *tumah* particularly undesirable; and *mishum olei regalim*, because the pilgrims who flood Jerusalem for the festivals would risk striking their heads on protruding structures. The prohibition on garbage dumps is *mishum shekatzim* — garbage attracts rodents, and dead rodents are themselves a source of *tumah*. The kilns are prohibited *mishum kutra* — because of smoke and air pollution. The gardens and orchards, counterintuitively, are prohibited *mishum sircha* — because they emit unpleasant odors, particularly rotting fallen fruit; apple orchards are especially notable in this regard, and the requirement for fertilizer adds to the problem.

### Animal & Death Rules

*Ein migdalin bah tarnegolim* — no chickens may be raised in Jerusalem. This is *mishum kodashim*: chickens forage freely and might pick up small pieces of bone and deposit them on someone's *terumah* or *kodashim*, rendering them *tamei*. *Ein malinin bah et ha-meis* — a corpse may not remain overnight in Jerusalem. The *Gemara* notes that no formal textual source is cited for this; it is simply a tradition, though it evidently connects to the *kedushah* and *taharah* of Jerusalem.

### Scriptural Sources

The *Gemara* then provides the scriptural basis for those laws that derive from the principle *lo nitchalka Yerushalayim l'shvatim* — Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes and therefore does not belong to any single tribe.

For *ein bayis chalut bah*, the verse reads *vekama habayis asher lo chomah lakone oto l'dorotav* — the house in a walled city passes to the buyer *l'dorotav*, for his generations, implying permanent ancestral inheritance. But Jerusalem, having never been apportioned to a tribe, lacks that sense of owned ancestral land being transferred.

For *ein mevia egla arufa*, the verse reads *ki yimatze chalal ba'adamah asher Hashem Elokecha noten lecha lerishtah* — "the land which Hashem gives you to inherit." The word *lerishtah* carries the connotation of inheritance and private possession. Since Jerusalem was never "given" in that tribal-inheritance sense, it falls outside the ordinance.

For *v'eino na'asit ir hanidachas*, the relevant term is *irecha* — your city — implying a city that is possessed and owned. Jerusalem was not parceled out to be anyone's possession in that sense.

For *v'einah metame'ah b'nega'im*, the verse says *venatati nega tzara'at beveit eretz achuzatchem* — I will place the affliction of *tzara'at* in a house of the land of your *achuzah*, your holding. Since Jerusalem was not apportioned as anyone's *achuzah*, the law of a house afflicted with *tzara'at* does not apply there.

---

## Pig Raising Ban

### Transition

The *Gemara* now departs from the structured list of Jerusalem laws and returns to the broader *mishnah*, which lists prohibitions that apply more generally. The *mishnah* had already discussed restrictions on grazing animals in the land of Israel, but the next prohibition is more sweeping: *ein migdalin chazirim b'chol makom* — one may not raise pigs anywhere at all.

### Siege Account

A *baraita* narrates the historical event that generated this prohibition. During the period of the Chashmonaim, the royal house fell into civil war — *beit Chashmonai zeh al zeh*, one faction against another. Horkanus was inside Jerusalem and Aristobulus was besieging it from outside. Despite the hostility between the factions, both parties observed Jewish practice: each day the besieged city would lower a basket of *dinarim* — coins — to the besiegers, who would in return send up animals for the daily *tamid* sacrifice.

Among the besiegers was an elder who possessed *chochmat yevanit* — Greek wisdom. What this means is somewhat puzzling, since what this elder is about to say seems essentially religious in content. A note in the edition suggests it refers to a kind of coded or allusive language, perhaps cryptic speech used within the royal household that would not be understood by the masses. Some at the shiur suggest it may indicate a Hellenist perspective on divine protection through temple worship — an interesting possibility, though the details of the historical conflict between the religious and Hellenist factions within the Chashmonaim would require more research to confirm. This elder warned the besiegers: *kol zeman she'oskin ba'avodah ein nimtsarim beyadechem* — as long as those inside are able to perform the divine service, you will not be able to conquer them.

### Pig Incident

The next day, instead of lowering the usual animals in exchange for the coins, the besieged city received back a pig. As the pig was being hauled up partway along the wall — *keivan shehigia lachatzi hachomah* — it dug its claws into the stones, because, as Rashi notes, that is what pigs do when forcibly dragged somewhere against their will. At that moment, *venizda'aza'ah Eretz Yisrael arba me'ot parsa al arba me'ot parsa* — the entire land of Israel, assumed to span four hundred *parsangs* by four hundred *parsangs*, shook with the sacrilege of the act.

### Curse Enacted

At that moment a declaration was made: *arur ha'ish sheyegadel chazirim* — cursed be anyone who raises pigs. And alongside it: *arur ha'adam sheyelamed et beno chochmat yevanit* — cursed be anyone who teaches his son Greek wisdom. The *Gemara* records that the *mishnah* in *Menachot* notes a consequence of the siege: the *omer* offering had to be brought from the gardens of *Tzrifin* — a distant location — and the *shtei halechem* from the valley of *Ein Socher*, because the besieged city had insufficient local wheat for these sacrifices.

### Tosafot Questions

*Tosafot* raises two significant questions about this narrative. The first concerns the prohibition on pig-raising itself. We already have a general principle that one may not engage in business with non-kosher items — *asur la'asot schora b'chol devarim hateme'im*. If so, why was a special *takana* needed? *Tosafot* responds that the general prohibition on commerce in non-kosher items applies only when those items are being dealt with as food. One might raise pigs for other purposes — their hides, their fat (such as lard), and other by-products — and in such a case the business prohibition would not apply. Hence the need for the specific *gezerah* against raising pigs at all. An alternative answer is that the general rabbinic prohibition on such commerce had not yet been enacted at the time, though by the era of the *mishnah* it was already in place, which raises its own question about why the *mishnah* still needed to state the pig prohibition separately.

The second question *Tosafot* raises is temporal: the curse against *chochmat yevanit* was proclaimed at this moment of the Chashmonaim, yet another *Gemara* records a prohibition against learning *chochmat yevanit* that was enacted at the time of the destruction of the *beit hamikdash*. *Tosafot* resolves this by distinguishing between a curse — which was declared in the Chashmonaean period and left individual compliance voluntary, if morally censured — and a formal rabbinic prohibition, which was enacted only at the time of the *churban*. The earlier declaration was an imprecation; the later enactment was binding legislation. *Tosafot* acknowledges that there remains some apparent overlap and redundancy in these formulations.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 83

## Greek Wisdom

### Opening

Daf 83 of Bava Kamma opens on the very last line of 82b. The previous portion of the *gemara* had already noted that a *gezeira* was instituted — either during the Hasmonean period or perhaps later, around the time of the *churban* under Roman rule — prohibiting the teaching of *chochmat yevanit*, Greek wisdom, to one's child. The *gemara* now turns to examine what exactly that prohibition entails and whether it is valid at all. *Tosafot* addresses the question of when this *gezeira* was instituted and observes that if the public was unable to keep it, the *Sanhedrin* would not have had the power to institute it to begin with — the principle being *gezeira she'ein hatzibur yachol la'amod bah*. *Tosafot* also flags a textual variant: one *girsa* reads *arur ha'adam she'ylamed et bno chochmat yevanit* — cursed is the person who teaches his child Greek wisdom — while another reads *asur l'adam she'ylamed bno chochmat yevanit* — it is prohibited. Whether the act is merely cursed or actually forbidden will prove to be a *nafka mina* shortly.

### Pigs & Greek

The *mishna* had discussed the prohibition on raising pigs, and the *gemara* now transitions to *chochmat yevanit* by posing a sharp question: *chochmat yevanit mi asar?* — who said that Greek wisdom is actually forbidden? This question is particularly pointed given what the *gemara* itself records elsewhere: several *amora'im* quote from Aesop's fables, a *sefer Torah* may be written in Greek, and the *gemara* in *Megillah* derives from the *pasuk* *yaft Elokim l'Yefet v'yishkon b'oholei Shem* that the Greek language has a legitimate place in relation to Torah study. The broader rabbinic tradition was clearly familiar with Greek culture and did not uniformly condemn it.

### Language vs. Wisdom

The *gemara* cites a *braita*: *amar Rabbi* — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declared — that in *Eretz Yisrael*, there is no reason to speak *lashon sursi*, the Aramaic dialect of the Land of Israel. One should speak either *lashon hakodesh*, biblical Hebrew, or *lashon yevanit*, the Greek language. *Rashi* understands *lashon sursi* as a confused or inelegant mode of speech, while *Tosafot* identifies it as Palestinian Aramaic — the dialect of the *Yerushalmi* and the *Targum* — as distinct from the eastern Aramaic of the *Talmud Bavli*. The key point is that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi regarded Greek as a perfectly legitimate language.

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing: *lashon yevanit lachud, chochmat yevanit lachud* — the Greek language is one thing, Greek wisdom is another. One may speak Greek; it is something else entirely — philosophy, literature, or some specific body of knowledge — that is subject to the *gezeira*. The *gemara* does not define precisely what *chochmat yevanit* encompasses, and this ambiguity appears deliberate.

### Lashon HaKodesh

The mention of *lashon hakodesh* prompts a brief but significant digression. Why is Hebrew called *lashon hakodesh*, the holy tongue? There is a famous *machloket* between the *Rambam* and the *Ramban* on this question. The *Rambam* in *Moreh Nevuchim* argues that Hebrew is called *lashon hakodesh* because it lacks vulgar or explicit terminology — it speaks only in euphemism. Even the sexual act is described merely as *biah*, entering, without explicit description. Other languages have direct words for such things; Hebrew does not. The *Ramban*, writing in *Parshat Ki Tisa*, disagrees entirely: Hebrew is *lashon hakodesh* because it is the language in which God gave the Torah, the language of angels, the language of creation itself. Its holiness is intrinsic, not merely a function of its lexical modesty. The *Rambam*, of course, would resist attributing human language to God in any direct sense — which is precisely why the *Ramban*'s formulation imbues the language with a more direct and anthropomorphous divine holiness.

### Aramaic & Persian

Rabbi Yosi makes a parallel statement regarding *Bavel*: *lashon arami lama?* — why do they speak Aramaic in Babylonia? One should speak either *lashon hakodesh* or *lashon parsi*, Persian. This is somewhat striking given that elsewhere *Chazal* speak highly of Aramaic — it is the only language besides Hebrew that appears in the Torah itself (when Lavan uses *Yegar Sahaduta*), and the *Talmuds* and *targumim* were composed in Aramaic. Rabbi Yosi's point seems to be that Greek and Persian, as the languages of the ruling dynasties in their respective locations, are useful, clear, and elegant — perfectly reasonable to know. Aramaic, by contrast, occupies an awkward middle position. The broader implication is that the prohibition, where it exists, is not on the Greek language but on something else entirely.

### Shimon ben Gamliel

The *gemara* then cites *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel* in the name of *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, who offers a *midrash* on the *pasuk* in the third chapter of *Eicha*: *eini olela linafshi mikol benot iri* — my eye weeps most for myself out of all the daughters of the city. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: there were one thousand children in my father's household — understood to include students and members of his broader community. Five hundred studied Torah, and five hundred studied Greek wisdom. Of all one thousand, only he and his cousin living in *Asya* survived the *churban*; nine hundred and ninety-eight perished. This sounds like a powerful indictment of *chochmat yevanit* — and yet the *gemara* immediately offers a justification: *shani beit Rabban Gamliel she'hayu krovim lamalchut* — Rabban Gamliel's household was different because they were *kerovim lamalchut*, close to the ruling class, and needed to be able to engage in diplomatic conversations with the Roman government. Their study of Greek wisdom was therefore permitted as a communal necessity. This principle — that proximity to governmental authority creates exceptions to certain restrictions — runs throughout *halacha*, from Yosef shaving in Pharaoh's court to Esther's conduct in the Persian palace.

### Karov Lamalchus

A *braita* is then cited: if one gets a *kumi* haircut — a style associated with *midarchei ha'Emori*, the ways of the Amorites, which is the rabbinic code for practices connected to *avoda zara* or pagan identification — that is prohibited. Similarly, a *bularit* haircut is prohibited. However, *Avtulumos ben Reuven* was permitted by the rabbis to get such a haircut *mipnei she'hu karov lamalchus* — because of his proximity to the Roman government. (The *gemara* in *Me'ilah* notes that his son Reuven ben Avtulumos was likewise involved in dealings with Rome.) The parallel case follows: the family of Rabban Gamliel was permitted *lesaper be'Chochmat Yevanis* — to engage with Greek wisdom — for the same reason.

There is a delicate question lurking here. If the *kumi* haircut falls under *be'chukoseihem lo seleichu*, the *de'oraysa* prohibition on following non-Jewish practices, how can *karov lamalchus* function as an exception to a biblical prohibition? The *Kesef Mishneh* addresses this by arguing that the Torah's prohibition is formulated in broad terms — *masro hakasuv lachachamim* — and that the rabbis themselves are authorized to define the contours of what falls under that prohibition and what does not. This is a far-reaching principle with significant implications.

### Maharik Framework

This question connects directly to the *Maharik* — Rabbi Yosef Colon of Cologne, writing in the fifteenth century — whose *teshuvah* on a related question became foundational. The *Maharik* was asked whether a Jewish scholar attending university could wear academic robes. His answer introduced a crucial framework: there are two categories of non-Jewish practices. Practices that are entirely irrational and serve no purpose other than to identify one as a non-Jew or to blend into non-Jewish society — those are prohibited under *be'chukoseihem*. But practices that have a clear rational basis — professional attire worn as a marker of one's occupation or academic achievement — are not prohibited, because one is not adopting the practice as an act of identification with non-Jewish ways but rather for an objectively intelligible reason.

The *Maharik*'s framework, codified in the *Shulchan Aruch*, addresses the academic robes question but does not, by itself, address the *kumi* haircut problem. For that, the *Kesef Mishneh*'s principle — that the rabbis have the authority to define and limit the scope of even the *de'oraysa* prohibition — is still required.

### Bechukoteihem

The *Maharik*'s *teshuvah* became the foundation for a much broader ongoing discussion of *be'chukoseihem lo seleichu* in later generations. One of the most significant modern applications appears in the *Seridei Esh*, which addresses the *bat mitzvah* celebration. The question there is not whether non-Jews celebrate *bat mitzvahs* — obviously they do not — but rather whether certain forms of celebration developed by non-observant Jewish communities constitute an imitation of non-Jewish practice and thus raise concerns of *bechukoseihem*. The *Seridei Esh* uses the occasion to develop a broader analysis of the principle as a whole. This represents a striking extension of the original *sugya*: from a *tanna*'s observation about the household of Rabban Gamliel, through the *Maharik*'s Renaissance-era analysis of university robes, to twentieth-century debates about communal religious celebrations.

---

## Dogs & Border

### Dogs Unchained

The *gemara* continues with a *braita* related to the next section of the *mishna*: *lo yegadel adam et hakelev ela im kein kashur beshalshelet* — a person may not raise a dog unless it is fastened with a chain. The *braita* then introduces an exception: *aval megadel hu be'ir hasmucha lesefar* — one may raise a dog in a city adjacent to the border, *sefar*. Even if the dog is not always chained, it is permitted in border towns.

### Border Defense

The justification for the border-town exception is the same logic that prevents declaring a city *ir hanidachat* at the border of *Eretz Yisrael* — reducing border territory is itself harmful to the collective. A vicious dog roaming the border at night deters encroachment on Jewish-held territory. Accordingly, the *halacha* is *dekoshro bayom umatiro balaila* — the dog must be chained during the day but may be released at night, precisely to deter intruders.

The *gemara* then adds that *Rav Yosef bar Minyumi* in the name of *Rav Nachman* rules: *Bavel ke'ir hasmucha lesefar dami* — Babylonia is treated like a border city for purposes of this *halacha*. *Rashi* specifies that this refers to the city of Nehardea, which was also called Bavel. *Rashi* draws out two criteria that qualify a city for this status: *yishuv kavua*, a permanent settlement, and *Yisrael harbe*, a substantial Jewish population. These two criteria — permanence and communal density — are what allow a diaspora city to be treated, at least for this purpose, as a border settlement of *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Rabbi Eliezer

*Tanya* — it is taught in a *baraisa* — *Rabbi Eliezer Hagadol omer: hamegadel kelavim kemegadel chazirim* — one who raises dogs is like one who raises pigs. Raising pigs in *Eretz Yisrael* carries the formulation *arur hamegadel chazir*, cursed is one who raises pigs. Rabbi Eliezer Hagadol now extends that comparison to dogs.

The *gemara* asks: *lemai nafka mina?* What practical difference does Rabbi Eliezer's comparison make? After all, the *mishna* already prohibits raising an unchained dog. The answer: *lemekayeim alav be'arur* — the *nafka mina* is whether one who raises a dog in violation of the *mishna* also incurs the curse. According to the *mishna* alone, the act is *asur* — forbidden — but one does not necessarily incur a curse for it. According to Rabbi Eliezer, one who raises dogs as the *mishna* forbids also receives the *arur*, the curse, just as one who raises pigs does.

This connects interestingly to the earlier *Tosafot* about the *gezeira* of *chochmat yevanit*: there *Tosafot* noted that a *girsa* reading *arur* rather than *asur* might actually soften the prohibition — something cursed is not necessarily something forbidden. Here, the logic runs in the opposite direction: the act was already forbidden under the *mishna*, and Rabbi Eliezer adds the additional dimension of the curse.

Regarding the practical *halacha* of dog ownership today: the relevant considerations remain that a *kelev ra*, a vicious dog, is unambiguously prohibited, and that a dog must be restrained in public spaces — this *halacha* continues to apply. The distinction between a working animal and a pet is a modern one that *Chazal* did not contemplate, and contemporary *poskim* have addressed it accordingly.

### Shechina & Dogs

*Darash Rabi Dostai demin Biri*: the *pasuk* states *uvnucho yomar shuva Hashem rivvot alfei Yisrael* — when the *aron* rested, the cry went up that God should return to the *rivvot alfei Yisrael*, the tens of thousands and thousands of Israel. *Tosafot* points out that this cannot be a multiplication — ten thousand times one thousand yields ten million, far exceeding the six hundred thousand present in the desert — and therefore it is an addition: *rivvot* as twenty thousand (two tens of thousands) plus *alafim* as two thousand, yielding twenty-two thousand.

The *derasha*: *ein Shechina shora al Yisrael pachot mishnei alafim ushnei rivvot* — the *Shechina* does not dwell among the Jewish people unless twenty-two thousand are present. This is the threshold for the *Shechina*'s full dwelling. Smaller groupings carry their own levels of divine presence: ten for a *minyan*, three for a *zimmun*, two for *chavruta*, and even one person learning alone is joined by God. But twenty-two thousand is the threshold for the *Shechina* to dwell in a communal sense.

Now the *gemara* brings a strikingly vivid application. What if there were twenty-one thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine Jews, and a pregnant woman was present — *har'uya lehashlim*, she would complete the count, because the *ubar* she carried would have been the twenty-two thousandth person? *Venavach bah kelev* — and a dog barked at her — *vehipila* — and she miscarried. *Nimtza zeh gorem lash'china shetistalek miYisrael* — that dog caused the *Shechina* to be removed from Israel. This is the aggadic underpinning of Rabbi Eliezer Hagadol's position: the presence of a dangerous, unrestrained dog is not merely a civil hazard but can have cosmic consequences.

### Woman's Retort

A related narrative: a woman came to bake at a neighbor's house — as was customary, since women would share millstones and ovens, going to one another's homes for different stages of food preparation. The dog in the house snapped at her. The owner of the dog reassured her — the Aramaic is *lo tid'chali minei*, do not be afraid of it — and offered to have the dog's canine teeth removed. She replied: *shekuli tivutach veshadei achizrei* — take your good wishes and throw them to the pigs. *Kevar nad velad* — the child had already moved in her womb, meaning she knew she was going to miscarry.

*Rashi* frames her response with remarkable emotional depth: *netulah hi tovat'cha umutelet al hakotzim* — your good wishes are stripped away and thrown onto the thorns. *Ma atah menachameni havel* — why are you consoling me with emptiness? The *havel* echoes the *Kohelet* register of futility. There is, in fact, a *kinah* in the Ashkenazic *Kinnot* that opens with the phrase *ma atah menachameni havel*. The *aggadic* principle underlying the narrative is also connected to the *mishna* in *Pirkei Avot* regarding *meto mutal lefanav* — there are moments when a person is simply not yet ready to receive *tanchumin*, and to offer consolation at the wrong time is worse than silence.

---

## Dove Traps

### 30 Ris Rule

The final section of *Perek Meruba* deals with dove traps. The *mishna* states: *ein porsin nishvin leyonei* — one may not spread nets to trap doves within thirty *ris* of the city. Thirty *ris* equals four *mil*, which is approximately the distance a person walks in seventy-two minutes — slightly less than four of our miles. The concern is that people who live in cities keep their dove-cotes within a manageable distance of their homes. Spreading nets near the city therefore risks catching doves that belong to other people.

### Hungry vs. Satiated

The *gemara* asks: *umi azlei kulei hai* — do doves actually travel that far? After all, the *mishna* elsewhere states that a dove-cote must be placed only fifty *amah* from the city — implying that doves do not fly very far. *Abaye* resolves the apparent contradiction: *mishat shat yatvu karsaihu bechamishim amah* — when they are hungry, doves settle within fifty *amah*, looking for food. But *umishloshim ris* — once they are full and their crops are satisfied, they will fly as far as thirty *ris*. The two figures describe two different behaviors: the doves forage within fifty *amah* of their cote, but when not eating they may range up to four *mil*. The prohibition on trapping must therefore extend to the full range of their flight.

### 100 Mil Rule

Another *braita* is then cited: *be-yishuv, afilu me'ah mil lo yifros* — within a settled area, one may not spread nets even one hundred *mil* away. One hundred *mil*, at approximately eighteen minutes of walking per *mil*, represents a journey of many days. This is a dramatically different number. The *gemara* treats this as a genuine difficulty requiring resolution.

### Vineyards/Cotes

*Rav Yosef* explains: the hundred-*mil* rule applies specifically to *be-yishuv kramim* — a settled area with vineyards. Doves can stop and rest in the vineyards along the way, and then resume flying, effectively covering vastly greater distances in stages. *Rabba* offers an alternative: *be-yishuv shovachin* — an area with many dove-cotes. The doves can rest at intermediate dove-cotes along their route, using them as way-stations, and thereby travel much farther than they otherwise would.

### Ownership Status

The *gemara* then offers further alternatives. One reading distinguishes between non-Jewish dove-cotes and Jewish ones: perhaps a greater distance is required regarding Jewish dove-cotes — reflecting a higher standard of *lifnim mishurat hadin* within the Jewish community — while regarding non-Jewish dove-cotes only the basic fifty *amah* applies. Another reading (*be-hefker*) suggests the rule differs depending on whether the doves are ownerless, in which case the concern of theft is reduced. A third reading (*be-didai*) addresses one's own doves: if you are spreading nets near your own dove-cote, you will only ever catch either wild doves or your own, and you pose no risk of stealing from anyone else.

The underlying concern throughout is theft — not noise or nuisance. The question of how much *lifnim mishurat hadin* one must observe regarding non-Jews, as opposed to fellow Jews, is the subtext of several of these distinctions.

---

## Chovel Intro

### Five Obligations

With *Hadran alach Meruba*, we turn the daf to 83b and begin *Perek Ha-chovel*, the chapter on bodily injury. The first six chapters of *Bava Kamma* dealt primarily with *nizkei mamon* — damages caused by one's property — with some discussion of *adam ha-mazik*, a person who directly causes damage. *Perek Meruba* addressed *gneiva*, theft, and a wide range of additional topics. Now the *masechta* returns to *adam ha-mazik* directly.

The *mishna* opens: *ha-chovel be-chaveiro chayav alav mishum chamisha devarim* — one who strikes another person is liable under five categories. These are: *nezek* (actual damage), *tza'ar* (pain and suffering), *ripui* (medical expenses), *shevet* (lost wages), and *boshet* (embarrassment). Each of these five categories requires its own method of evaluation, and the *mishna* will now address each in turn.

### Nezek

*Be-nezek keitzad?* — How is *nezek* assessed? If one blinds another's eye, severs a hand, or breaks a foot, we apply the slave-market standard: *ro'im oto ke'ilu hu eved* — we consider what this person would have fetched at the slave market before the injury and what he would fetch now. The difference in value is the *nezek*. We do not attempt to place an absolute monetary value on a hand or a foot; we measure the relative diminution of the person's overall market value. This valuation is itself a *kula* — an attempt to arrive at a figure that is defensibly objective and avoids inflating the sum extracted from the tortfeasor.

There is a *machloket* between *Rashi* and the *Rosh* about which slave-market standard is meant. *Rashi* holds that the reference is to the *eved Ivri* — the indentured Hebrew servant who sells his labor for six years. The *Rosh* objects: an *eved Ivri* is not even a full *mechira*, a sale of the person, but only of his labor; he does not represent the true market value of a person's body. The *Rosh* therefore holds that the standard is the *eved Kena'ani* market, which valued the person as a commodity.

### Tzaar

*Tzaar* addresses pain and suffering without permanent injury. The *mishna* gives the example of burning someone with a spit or a nail — or stabbing them even on the fingernail, a place that does not leave permanent injury. The method of assessment: *omdin kama adam kayotzei baze rotze litol l'hiyot mitzta'er kach* — we estimate how much a person of similar circumstances would require to be paid in order to willingly undergo such pain. This is the *halacha*'s mechanism for monetizing pure suffering: a willing-participant model, not unlike modern game-show logic, but applied judicially.

Whether *tzaar* encompasses only immediate physical pain or also encompasses ongoing trauma is a *machloket rishonim* that bears on questions of psychological injury.

### Ripui

*Ripui* covers medical expenses. *Hikahu, chayav l'rapoto* — if you struck someone, you are obligated to heal that person, meaning to bear the cost of competent medical care. The *mishna* then addresses complications: *alu bo tzmachim, im machamat hamaka chayav* — if a disease or secondary condition develops as a result of the initial injury, the tortfeasor remains liable. If the complication is wholly unrelated to the original injury, he is exempt.

*Chayeta v'nistara* — if the injury healed and then worsened again, the tortfeasor remains liable, since the recurrence is presumed to be a continuation of the original damage. Only if the injury healed completely — *chayeta kol tzorka* — does liability for subsequent deterioration end: *eino chayav l'rapoto*, the tortfeasor may then plausibly argue that the new condition is independent of the original injury.

The *Rosh* adds an important practical note: if the injured party failed to follow the doctor's instructions and thereby caused or worsened a complication, that is the injured party's own responsibility. The tortfeasor's medical liability does not extend to self-inflicted complications arising from non-compliance with medical treatment.

### Shevet

*Shevet* addresses lost wages during the period of incapacitation. *Ro'im oto k'ilu hu shomer kishu'im* — we evaluate the injured party as if he were doing the minimum possible job, that of a watchman over a cucumber or squash field. This is the *halacha*'s equivalent of a minimum wage floor. The reason the assessment is pegged at this minimal figure rather than at the injured party's actual earning capacity is that the tortfeasor has already compensated for the actual injury to the limb through *nezek*. Since the *nezek* payment accounts for the permanent loss of the limb's productive capacity — evaluated via the slave-market differential — it would be double-counting to also pay the full wage that the limb would have earned. The *shevet* payment covers only the period of recovery at a baseline rate.

### Boshet

*Boshet* — embarrassment — is assessed differently from all the others: *boshet hakol lefi ham'vayesh v'hamit'bayesh* — everything depends on the relative status of the person who caused the embarrassment and the person who was embarrassed. If a person of high standing humiliates me, that is a greater indignity than if someone of low standing does so. Social rank thus enters the calculation on both sides of the equation.

---

## Ayin Tachat Ayin

### Kashya Amai

With the five categories of liability established, the *gemara* poses a striking *kashya*. The entire *mishna* — all five obligations — seems to be undermined by the *pasuk*: *ayin tachat ayin*, an eye for an eye. If the Torah mandates literal physical retaliation, why does the *mishna* prescribe five categories of monetary payment? The *kashya* is not merely a question about the scope of compensation; it challenges the legitimacy of the entire chapter. *Eima ayin mamash* — perhaps the Torah means that you literally extract the wrongdoer's eye in return. The full force of the question is: *lo salka daitach* — this surely cannot be entertained, and yet the *gemara* insists on working through the scriptural derivation carefully.

### Animal Parallel

The first *tanna'itic* source the *gemara* brings: *makeh behema yeshalmena, umakeh adam yumat* — one who strikes an animal pays monetary compensation, and one who strikes a person faces death.
