That would seem to answer Rava's question directly, proving that *shevet* applies even to a temporary injury. But the *gemara* deflects: *kegon shechersho* — the case is where one rendered the parent deaf. And indeed Rava himself had stated that causing one's father deafness is a capital offense — *hacheresho le'aviv neherag* — because it is impossible for deafness of this kind to occur without a drop of blood entering the ear (*tipat dam nafla leh be'ozneh*), and that internal bleeding constitutes a wound even if no external bruise is visible. So the case of "no bruise" in the *braita* is not a case of a healing injury — it is a case of internal injury causing permanent damage. That reading does not resolve Rava's question.

The *gemara* then proposes a different case: *kegon she-gilcho* — perhaps the case is where one shaved the parent's head. But hair grows back — *mehadar hadar* — so that too seems temporary and self-correcting.

### Baldness & Job Loss

The *gemara* ultimately resolves the case by explaining: *amrei hacha bemai askinan kigon she-sacho nashra* — the case involves applying a depilatory resin or cream that destroys the hair follicles permanently, effecting lasting hair removal analogous to what we today would recognize as permanent depilation. With that, all five categories can be identified. *Tzaar* — *de-it lei kartufnei be-reishei* — because the victim had fissures or cracks in his scalp, and applying the caustic substance to those wounds caused genuine pain. *Ripui* — *de-baei asuyei* — because those wounds require medical treatment. *Shevet* — *de-hava markid bei kuvei* — because this person was a juggler or jester who earned his living by performing at taverns, and *de-baei mechavei gunei a-reisha velo mechavei me-hanei kartufnei* — because his act required vigorous head movement that he can no longer perform on account of the wounds to his scalp. And *boshet* — *ein lach boshet gadol mi-zeh* — there is no greater embarrassment than being forcibly and permanently stripped of one's hair. Some *acharonim* note that the *boshet* from baldness is not inherent to baldness itself — many people lose their hair naturally and gracefully — but rather derives from the sudden, involuntary, and premature nature of the loss, compounded by whatever cultural context one inhabits. In *Chazal*'s milieu, at least, such a forced disfigurement was considered a grave public humiliation.

The *shevet* here is notably subjective and occupation-dependent: this person's *shevet* is calculated not based on the generic "watchman of the cucumber patch" standard but based on the gap between his skilled, specialized employment and whatever lower-paying work he can perform in the interim. The case makes vivid that *shevet* carries an inherently variable, context-sensitive quality that the more abstract examples can obscure.

---

## Abaye vs Rava

### Abaye's Two Shevet

The *gemara* observes that what was a genuine unresolved question for Rabbah was obvious to Abaye and Rava in opposite directions — a phenomenon entirely recognizable in a *yeshiva* setting, where a *rosh yeshiva*'s open question can become the settled position of two leading students who each embrace a different side. The case before them: *hikehu al yado vetzimtah vesofo lachzor* — someone struck another on the hand, causing a severe bruise or swelling that rendered the hand unusable, but the hand will eventually heal.

Abaye rules: *noten lo shevet gedola ushevet ketana* — he pays both a *shevet gedola* and a *shevet ketana*. Rashi is essential here. *Shevet gedola*, according to Rashi, is *d'mei yado* — the value of the hand — meaning the lifelong, permanent-type assessment of the kind we have been calling *nezek*. *Shevet ketana* — *kol yamim sheyipol lemishkav vero'in oto ke'ilu hu shomer kishu'in* — is the day-by-day compensation for the period of incapacitation, assessed at the minimum-wage baseline corresponding to the injury.

Abaye's conceptual move is striking: he reconceptualizes what the *mishnah* calls *nezek* as a form of *shevet*, a lifelong reduction in earning power. For Abaye, both the permanent dimension and the temporary dimension of an injury's economic consequences are properly categorized under *shevet*, one large and one small. This reflects a deeper view that the underlying principle of *shevet* — compensation for impaired earning capacity — encompasses both temporal scales.

### Rava's Daily Shevet

Rava disagrees sharply: *eino noten lo ela d'mei shivto shebechol yom vayom* — one pays only the day-by-day *shevet* for each day of incapacitation. For Rava, there is no such thing as *shevet gedola*. *Nezek* and *shevet* are categorically distinct: *nezek* applies only when there is permanent damage, and *shevet* compensates only for temporary lost wages. Since the injury here will heal, *nezek* does not apply at all; only the temporary *shevet ketana* is owed.

### Eved Ivri Case

The dispute is then applied to a case involving an *eved Ivri* — a Hebrew indentured servant — whose hand has been severed by a third party. An *eved Ivri* is not owned in the full sense; he is a free person who has contracted his labor to a master. The question becomes: when a third party injures the *eved* in a way that impairs his ability to work, who receives the *nezikin* payment, and for which components?

### Eved Ivri Payments

Abaye rules: *noten lo shevet gedola la'eved veshevet ketana larav* — the *shevet gedola* goes to the *eved* himself, since it pertains to the permanent value of his person, while the *shevet ketana* — the temporary loss of labor during recovery — goes to the master, since the master holds the contractual right to the *eved*'s labor during the term of service.

Rava rules: *hakol yinaten la'eved* — everything goes to the *eved*. The assessment of *nezikin* is not about who purchased the rights to someone's labor; it is about who suffered the injury. Furthermore, *veyilakach bahen karka* — the *eved* should use the money to purchase land — *veharav ochel peirot* — and the master is entitled to the produce of that land. This reflects the *halakhic* structure of the master-*eved* relationship more precisely: the master does not own the *eved*'s labor outright, but rather functions as *ochel peirot* — he benefits from the fruits of the labor. This is structurally parallel to the relationship between a husband and wife regarding landed property in a marriage. Therefore, the *nezikin* payment goes to the *eved*, the land is purchased with it, and the master draws his entitled benefit through the produce.

The *gemara* raises a challenge against Rava: *peshita pichat eitzel atzmo ve'eitzel rabbo lo pichat* — obviously the *eved* himself was devalued; but was he devalued relative to his master? And it clarifies that the dispute between Abaye and Rava is confined to cases where the injury actually affected the *eved*'s capacity to work — *pichat eitzel rabbo* — whereas if the injury was to a peripheral location such as an earlobe or nostril (*lerish udna o lerish nechira*), that injury affects his personal valuation but not his productive output, and all agree that the *nezikin* payment goes to the *eved* himself, who buys land with it and from which the master then takes *peirot*.

---

## Boshet Mishnah

### Assessment Standard

The *mishnah* rules: *boshet hakol lefi hamivayesh vehamitbayesh* — embarrassment is assessed entirely according to both the one who caused the embarrassment and the one who was embarrassed. The standard is thus thoroughly subjective and bilateral.

### Tanna Identity

The *gemara* immediately asks: *mani matnitin*? Whose position does the *mishnah* represent? It cannot be Rabbi Meir, it cannot be Rabbi Yehuda; it must be Rabbi Shimon.

### Rabbi Meir Standard

The *braita* records Rabbi Meir's position: *vekulan ro'in otam ke'ilu hem bnei chorin sheyardu minechaseihem shehem bnei Avraham Yitzchak veYaakov* — we assess every Jewish person's *boshet* as if they were free people of noble lineage who have simply lost their wealth, because all Jews are descendants of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, and that ancestry confers equal stature on all. Rabbi Meir applies a single, flat, universal standard. This clearly cannot fit the *mishnah*, which explicitly varies the assessment based on the identity of the parties.

### Rabbi Yehuda Standard

Rabbi Yehuda takes the opposite approach, fully subjective: *hagadol lefi godlo vehakatan lefi katno* — the more prominent or wealthy person is assessed at the higher level, the less prominent at the lower. Greater prominence means greater *boshet* when embarrassed. This too cannot fit the *mishnah*, as the next *mishnah* — to be addressed shortly — rules that one is liable for embarrassing a blind person, whereas Rabbi Yehuda holds that a blind person has no *boshet*.

### Rabbi Shimon Standard

Rabbi Shimon occupies a middle position: *ashirim ro'in otam ke'ilu hem bnei chorin sheyardu minechaseihem* — wealthy people are assessed as free people who have lost their money, meaning we reduce even the wealthy to a modest baseline and do not take full account of their prominence. *Aniyim kepchutim shebahem* — poor people are assessed at the lowest level of poverty. Two tiers, both bumped downward. The rationale connects to the procedural principle of *hamotzi mechaveiro alav hara'aya* — the burden of proof falls on the one seeking to extract money, and courts must therefore be conservative in imposing liability. The *gemara* concludes that the *mishnah* follows Rabbi Shimon.

The *gemara* considers whether the *braita* describing wrong-target embarrassment — *nitkaven livayesh et hakatan uvayesh et hagadol* — can be attributed to any of the three *tannaim*. It concludes after extended analysis that it fits Rabbi Yehuda, provided one reads *ein la'avadim boshet* narrowly: Rabbi Yehuda means that slaves do not have the *right* to collect their *boshet* — *lemishkal minei* — but they can still serve as the basis for a *boshet* assessment — *le-meisham sha'iminan behu*. Hence if one intended to embarrass a slave and instead embarrassed a free person, the free person collects the amount that would have been assessed for embarrassing the slave. Alternatively, the *gemara* suggests *gadol* and *katan* in the *braita* may simply refer to an adult and a child respectively, not to wealthy and poor, in which case the *braita* could even fit Rabbi Meir, since Rabbi Meir's equalization of standing among adults would not necessarily extend to equalizing adults with children.

---

## Intention Requirement

### Sleeping Person

The *mishnah* had stated: *veyashen she'biyyesh patur* — a person who is asleep and who while asleep embarrasses someone else is exempt from paying *boshet*. The exemption turns on intention: *boshet* requires *kavana livayesh*, an intention to cause embarrassment. Unlike the general rule of *adam muad le'olam* — that a person is always liable for the physical damage they cause regardless of intent — *boshet* does not follow this principle. Without purposeful intent, no *boshet* liability attaches.

### Wrong Target Case

The *gemara* asks: whose position is the rule that *nitkaven livayesh et hakatan uvayesh et hagadol noten lagadol miboshto shel katan* — if one intended to embarrass a child and ended up embarrassing an adult, one pays the adult the amount assessed for embarrassing the child? And similarly *livayesh et ha'eved uvayesh ben chorin* — intended to embarrass a slave and embarrassed a free person, one pays the free person the assessment for embarrassing the slave. The *gemara* works through the three positions of the *tannaim* to determine whose view this represents.

### Murder Comparison

The *gemara* draws an illuminating comparison: *mai ta'ama de-katla mah katla ad de-michavein lei* — why should *boshet* require intention directed at the specific victim? Because it is analogous to the law of killing. The difference between murder and manslaughter turns entirely on premeditation and directed intent — *dich'tiv ve-arav lo ve-kam alav*, the verse speaks of lying in wait *for him*, meaning you had to have had that specific person in mind. Just as murder requires intent directed at the actual victim, *boshet* requires that the embarrassment was directed at the person who ends up collecting. This is a striking comparison that *Chazal* develop elsewhere as well: *hamalbein penei chaveiro barabim chayav mitah* — publicly embarrassing someone is compared to taking their life, *zeh shofech damim*, because the blood drains from a person's face in embarrassment just as it drains from a body in death.

### Struggle Source

The *scriptural* source for the *kavanah* requirement in *boshet* is *dich'tiv ve-shalcha yadah ve-hechezika bi-mivushav* — the passage describing a woman who extends her hand during a brawl to grab the attacker in the genital area in defense of her husband. The verse emphasizes the deliberate extension of her hand — *ad de-michavein lei* — she had to have specifically intended to do that act. From here the *gemara* derives that *boshet* liability requires intentional, purposive action directed at the specific form of embarrassment caused.

---

## Special Cases Mishnah

### Liable Cases

The *mishnah* states: *hamevayesh et ha'arum* — one who embarrasses a naked person is liable; *hamevayesh et hasuma* — one who embarrasses a blind person is liable; *vehamevayesh et hayashen* — one who embarrasses a sleeping person is liable.

### Sleeping Exemption

*Veyashen she'biyyesh patur* — but a sleeping person who embarrasses others is exempt, since the sleeping person lacked any intention to cause embarrassment.

### Roof Fall Rule

*Nafal min hagag vehizzik uviyyesh* — a person who fell from a roof and thereby caused both damage and embarrassment is *chayav al hanezek upatur al haboshet ad sheyehe mitkavven* — liable for the *nezek* but exempt from *boshet* unless there was intention. This follows directly from the principle already established: *adam muad le'olam* applies to physical damage and requires no intent, but *boshet* demands *kavanah*. The *gemara* notes that this rule had already appeared in the discussion of *nezek* at 27a and resurfaces here in the context of *boshet*.

---

## Comparative Embarrassment

### Naked Less Serious

The *braita* teaches: *biyyesho arum hayyav, ve'eno domeh biyyesho arum le-biyyesho lavush* — one who embarrasses a naked person is liable, yet there is no comparison between embarrassing a naked person and embarrassing a clothed person. Embarrassing someone who is already unclothed is less serious than embarrassing someone who is clothed and then revealed. If a person is partially exposed already and then exposed further, the *boshet* is real but diminished compared to having one's clothing removed when one is fully dressed.

### Location Difference

Similarly: *biyyesho beveit hamerhatz hayyav, ve'eno domeh biyyesho beveit hamerhatz le-biyyesho bashuk* — one is liable for embarrassing someone in the bathhouse, but the embarrassment in the bathhouse is nowhere near as serious as the same embarrassment in the marketplace. In a setting like a bathhouse or locker room, partial or full undress is expected and normalized; the same public exposure in a marketplace or open street carries far greater humiliation. This gradation reflects the *gemara*'s attentiveness to social context as a genuine variable in calculating *boshet*.

The discussion of bathhouse embarrassment occasions a *sugya* on *kevod haberiyot*, which is only briefly touched upon here. The *halakhic* principle that *kevod haberiyot* overrides a rabbinic prohibition is often misapplied. The more precise reading, as many *rishonim* explain, is that *kevod haberiyot doheh lo ta'aseh sheba-torah* refers to one specific biblical prohibition — the *lo ta'aseh* of *lo tasur*, the obligation to follow rabbinic enactments — meaning that *kevod haberiyot* can suspend a rabbinic rule in the narrow situations where *Chazal* applied it: clothing oneself in the street, basic bodily needs on *Shabbat*, and comparable cases of intimate human dignity. The category is not a broad license to override rabbinic law whenever something is inconvenient or embarrassing.

### Wind Case

Rav Pappa addresses the ruling that embarrassing a naked person still incurs liability, raising the obvious question: *arum bar boshet hu*? Is a naked person really someone who can be embarrassed? He answers: *mai arum? da'ati zika vekarchei lemanei* — what does it mean that the person was "naked"? The wind came and blew up his garment, since men of that era wore long robe-like smocks without undergarments. Then *ve'ata hu vedalineihu tefei uveisho* — someone came along and pulled the garment up further, compounding what the wind had begun. The person was not freely walking around naked; he was caught in an embarrassing moment by the wind and then made worse by another person's deliberate act. That is when liability for *boshet* attaches even to a "naked" person.

### Bathhouse Clarification

Similarly, Rav Pappa explains that *biyyesho beveit hamerhatz* does not mean embarrassing someone in a closed, private bathhouse — where everyone is undressed and there is no particular *boshet* to speak of — but rather *shebeisho al gav hanahar*, embarrassing someone who was bathing by the river in a semi-public setting. The riverbank is neither fully private nor fully public, and there a person retains some expectation of dignity. Exposure or embarrassment in that context is humiliating precisely because of that intermediate status.

---

## Asleep Then Died

### Death Question

Rabbi Abba bar Memel poses a question: *beisho yashen umet* — what if someone was embarrassed while asleep and then died before waking? The person never experienced the embarrassment themselves. Is the tortfeasor nonetheless obligated to pay *boshet* to the deceased's heirs?

### Two Frameworks

Rav Zvid explains that the question hinges on the underlying rationale of *boshet*. Is *boshet* grounded in *kisufa* — the victim's own subjective emotional experience of humiliation? Rashi glosses *kisufa* as *chapiyat panim*, the personal distress and internal hurt felt by the person who was embarrassed. Or is *boshet* grounded in *ziluta* — something broader, the societal degradation of the person's standing, independent of whether they personally felt anything? Rashi glosses *ziluta* as *demizalzel bei bifnei rabbim* — the act of publicly diminishing someone in the eyes of others.

### Dead Person Analysis

If *boshet* is rooted in *kisufa*, the dead person's claim is weak: *veha mit lei deleit lei kisufa* — once a person dies, they can no longer experience the emotional hurt. But if *boshet* is rooted in *ziluta*, the claim survives: *veha ozlei* — you still diminished this person's standing while they were alive, regardless of whether they were aware of it, and that degradation already occurred as a social fact.

---

## Deaf Child Fool

### Rights Assignment

A *braita* is introduced: *Rabbi Meir omer cheresh vekatan yesh lahem boshet* — a deaf person and a child have *boshet* rights, meaning one is liable for embarrassing them. *Shoteh ein lo boshet* — but a *shoteh*, a person with severe mental disability characterized by total unawareness of social reality, does not have *boshet* rights. The *gemara* is careful to note that the *halakhic* category of *shoteh* — one who acts in a completely irrational way and has no awareness of their place in society — is quite distinct from what we today recognize as mental disability or special needs. Most people with disabilities or special needs retain a robust sense of their own identity and social standing and can manifestly be embarrassed; they would not fall under the *gemara*'s definition of *shoteh*.

### Ziluta Test

The *gemara* tests the *ziluta* framework against the *braita*. If *boshet* is about societal standing, why does the *braita* specifically mention *katan*? A child's position in society is already of lesser significance than an adult's, so it makes sense that the *braita* would need to affirmatively teach that children too have *boshet* — because without that teaching, one might have thought the child's diminished social standing means no *boshet* is owed. That fits *ziluta* well: the *braita* teaches that even with a lower social profile, children still have a protected standing that others are not permitted to degrade.

### Maximum Embarrassment

But the *ziluta* framework runs into difficulty with the exclusion of *shoteh*. If *boshet* is about societal standing, then even the family of a *shoteh* has a standing that could be further damaged by someone embarrassing the *shoteh* in public. The *gemara* responds: *shoteh ein lach boshet gadol mizo* — being a *shoteh* is already the maximum possible embarrassment for the family. There is no incremental *boshet* to be calculated, since the family's standing has already been reduced to the lowest point by virtue of having a *shoteh* in the household. Any additional embarrassment would be subsumed within that already-existing condition.

### Rav Pappa Kisufa

Rav Pappa then offers a *kisufa*-based account of why children have *boshet*: *demachlimu lei umichlam* — we are talking about cases where you say something to a child and the child actually feels embarrassed, where the child actually experiences the hurt. This is a contextual and developmentally sensitive standard. A two-year-old is different from an eight-year-old, who is different from a twelve-year-old; what rolls off one child's back may genuinely wound another. The *boshet* of a child is calibrated to whether the particular child, at their particular age and development, actually experiences the humiliation.

---

## Boshet Basis

### Kisufa vs Family

Rav Pappa raises what the *gemara* presents as his own open question: *mishum kisufa didei* — is the basis of *boshet* the victim's own personal embarrassment, the inner hurt they experience? *Vahamis lei* — but what if the person has died? Or is it *mishum boshet mishpacha* — for the embarrassment of the family unit, a wider circle of those whose standing is affected by the degradation?

### Child Test

The *gemara* tests the family-embarrassment thesis against the case of *katan*. If *boshet* is for the family, it makes sense to include children, because embarrassing a child embarrasses the family even if the child does not personally process the humiliation in the way an adult would.

### Fool Test

But the *mishpacha* thesis again runs into the *shoteh*. If *boshet* is for the family, then embarrassing a *shoteh* should embarrass the *shoteh*'s family — and the *gemara* gives the same answer as before: *shoteh ein lach boshet gadol mizo* — the family already endures the maximum possible embarrassment from having a *shoteh*, and there is no further degradation that can be added.

### Rav Pappa Reconsidered

The *gemara* concludes by returning to Rav Pappa's own position: *amar Rav Pappa, ain, demachlimu lei umichlam* — even at the personal *kisufa* level, children can have *boshet*, because it is assessed contextually based on whether this particular child, at this stage of development, would actually feel the hurt. A child's *boshet* need not be explained through the broader *mishpacha* framework; it can be grounded in the child's own experiential capacity for embarrassment, provided that capacity is present. The assessment of what a given child can feel scales with age and circumstance, creating a sliding, developmentally sensitive standard. The *gemara* leaves the ultimate resolution of Rav Pappa's framing open, closing with the observation that this is how far we have reached on 86a, with the continuation to follow on the next *daf*.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 87

## Suma & Boshet

### Mishnah Overview

The *mishnah* on 86b, beginning with the words *hamvayesh et hasuma*, establishes that one who embarrasses a blind person or a naked person is still *chayav* in *boshet* — embarrassment damages are owed regardless of the victim's condition. The only exemption the *mishnah* articulates in its second clause is for one who causes embarrassment while asleep, because *boshet* requires *kavanah*, and a sleeping person lacks the requisite intent. By mentioning only the sleeping person as exempt, the *mishnah* implies that all other actors — including a blind person who embarrasses someone — remain liable.

### Suma Embarrassing Others

The *gemara* picks up on this implication and asks whether everyone agrees that a blind person who embarrasses another is *chayav*. Both Rashi and Tosafot understand the *gemara*'s question not to be whether one is liable *for* embarrassing a blind person — that much is clear from the *mishnah* — but rather whether a *suma* who himself causes embarrassment would be *chayav* or exempt. The *gemara* answers: *matnisin d'lo k'Rabbi Yehuda* — our *mishnah*, which implies that a blind person who embarrasses is liable, does not accord with the view of Rabbi Yehuda. For as a *baraisa* teaches: Rabbi Yehuda says that a blind person has no *boshet* — he is exempt when he causes embarrassment. Moreover, Rabbi Yehuda would similarly exempt a *suma* from *galut* if he killed someone unintentionally, from *malkut* if he violated a negative prohibition, and from *mitas beis din* if he committed a capital offense. This is a sweeping, categorical exemption — not a case-by-case inquiry into whether this particular blind person could have been more careful.

### Gezeirah Shavah Source

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama d'Rabbi Yehuda* — what is the scriptural basis for his position regarding *boshet*? The answer is a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *einecha* ("your eye") appears both in the passage concerning *eidim zomemin* (conspiring witnesses) and in the passage concerning *boshet* — the verse *vekatzota kapa lo tachos einecha*. This verbal parallel links the two laws. And since the entire *parshah* of *eidim zomemin* applies only to witnesses who can see — for the simple reality is that a blind person cannot serve as a valid witness — so too the obligation of *boshet* applies only to one who can see. The shared language of *einecha* creates the link, and the structural logic of *eidim zomemin* being categorically closed to the blind imports that same categorical exclusion into *boshet*.

### Broader Exemptions

The *gemara* then works through the rest of Rabbi Yehuda's exemptions. His exclusion of the *suma* from *galut* is derived from the verse *belo re'ot* — "without seeing" — in the context of one who kills another in the forest. Rabbi Yehuda reads this to mean that the *parshah* of exile applies only to one who normally could have seen his victim but on this occasion did not; a blind person, who categorically cannot see, is therefore excluded entirely. Rabbi Meir disagrees and reads *belo re'ot* as *including* the blind person — meaning even one who cannot see is liable for *galut*. Since another verse uses the phrase *bivli da'at* ("without awareness"), which could also be read as excluding the *suma*, Rabbi Meir invokes the rule that *mi'ut achar mi'ut* — two consecutive exclusions — actually serves to *include*. Tosafot notes the peculiarity here: removing both exclusions merely returns one to the default position of inclusion, so the double *mi'ut* seems to accomplish nothing new. Regardless, for Rabbi Meir the *suma* is included in *galut*. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, holds that *belo re'ot* genuinely excludes the blind, and *bivli da'at* serves the separate and more obvious purpose of excluding the intentional killer — who faces execution, not exile.

The exemption from *mitas beis din* is derived through a *gezeirah shavah* of *rotze'ach rotze'ach* — the word appears both in the context of *galut* and in the context of capital liability, linking them so that the *suma*'s categorical exclusion from one extends to the other. The exemption from *malkut* is then derived through a *gezeirah shavah* of *rasha rasha* — the verse by *mitas beis din* reads *asher hu rasha lamut*, and the verse establishing *malkut* uses the same word *rasha*. Since a *suma* cannot be executed, by the verbal parallel he also cannot receive lashes.

### Rabbi Meir Disagrees

The full structure of Rabbi Meir's position becomes clear from his reading of *belo re'ot*. For Rabbi Meir, no blanket categorical exclusion of the *suma* follows from that phrase; he reads it as including the blind person. The double-exclusion argument is his mechanism for restoring the *suma* to the default of liability. Rabbi Yehuda, however, uses each scriptural peg — *belo re'ot* for *galut*, the *gezeirah shavah* of *einecha* for *boshet*, the *rotze'ach rotze'ach* for capital liability, and the *rasha rasha* for *malkut* — to build a comprehensive categorical exclusion from all court-administered penalties.

### Total Exemption

A second *baraisa* extends this even further. Rabbi Yehuda not only exempts the *suma* from all punishments but, as the *gemara* on 87a begins, declares: *vechen haya Rabbi Yehuda potro mikol dinim shebatorah* — Rabbi Yehuda would exempt him from all civil law as well. This is a qualitatively different category. The earlier exemptions concerned intentional conduct and court-administered penalties; civil law governs monetary obligations that do not depend on intention in the same way. The scriptural basis offered for this expansion comes from the verse in the context of *galut*: *veshaftu ha'edah bein hamakeh uvein go'el hadam al hamishpatim ha'eleh* — the congregation shall judge between the killer and the blood-redeemer according to "these laws." The *gemara* derives: whoever is in the category of *galut* — that is, subject to exile — is also in the category of civil *mishpatim*; whoever is excluded from *galut* is excluded from *mishpatim* as well. For Rabbi Yehuda the *suma* is excluded from *galut*, and therefore excluded from civil law entirely.

A third *baraisa* takes the final step: *vechen haya Rabbi Yehuda potro mikol mitzvos ha'amuros batorah* — Rabbi Yehuda would exempt him from all *mitzvos* in the Torah. Rav Sheshes the son of Rav Idi supplies the scriptural basis: the verse *ve'eleh hamitzvos hachukim vehamishpatim* links *mitzvos* and *mishpatim* in a single formulation. Whoever is in the category of *mishpatim* is in the category of *mitzvos* and *chukim*; whoever is excluded from *mishpatim* — as Rabbi Yehuda has shown the *suma* to be — is excluded from *mitzvos* as well. Tosafot, struck by the radical sweep of this position, maintains that *Chazal* must have obligated the *suma* at least *miderabbanan*, and that other *gemaros* make clear that a *suma* may recite *Krias Shema* and daven. But the position of Rabbi Yehuda at the level of *de'oraisa* is nevertheless a sweeping categorical exemption that functionally places the blind person in the same legal category as a *cheresh* and *shoteh*.

### Rav Yosef's Stance

The *gemara* then records a poignant personal statement by Rav Yosef, who was himself blind. He said: initially I would say that if anyone holds the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda — that a *suma* is exempt from *mitzvos* — I would make a *yom tov* for the rabbis. Why? Because I am not commanded yet I do, and I assumed that performing *mitzvos* without being obligated would be regarded as an act of exceptional voluntarism deserving great reward. But now, having heard the teaching of Rabbi Chanina — that greater is one who is commanded and does than one who is not commanded and does — I have reversed course. Now I would make a *yom tov* if someone tells me the *halacha* does *not* follow Rabbi Yehuda, because if I am commanded, my reward is greater.

### Metzuve vs. Eino Metzuve

The principle of *metzuve ve'oseh* versus *eino metzuve ve'oseh* that Rabbi Chanina articulates is well established, and two distinct reasons are given for why the commanded one receives greater reward. Rashi's approach is psychological: if you are obligated, the *yetzer hara* is more active, the pull to find an exemption is stronger, and therefore overcoming that resistance to fulfill the command is a greater achievement. A second approach is theological: if God commanded certain people to perform a given act and did not command others, this reflects that performing it is more fully aligned with *ratzon Hashem* for those who are commanded. If God had wanted the voluntary performer's act to be equally fundamental to His will, He would have commanded it. This theological framework has direct implications for how the *rishonim* of Ashkenaz understood women's *brachos* on *mitzvos asei shehazman gerama*: just as Rav Yosef, even if exempt, would have continued performing *mitzvos* and reciting the *bracha* of *asher kidshanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu*, so too women who are exempt may recite that *bracha* when performing those *mitzvos*.

---

## Five Damages

### Adam vs. Shor

The *gemara* transitions to the next *mishnah*: *zeh chomer b'adam mibshor* — this is a stringency by a human over an ox. A human who injures another human must pay all five standard categories of damage: *nezek* (permanent injury), *tza'ar* (pain), *ripui* (medical expenses), *sheves* (lost work), and *boshet* (embarrassment). Furthermore, a human who caused a woman to miscarry must pay *dmei velados*, an assessed value for the fetuses. By contrast, an ox that gores a human pays only *nezek*, and if it causes a woman to miscarry, it pays nothing for the lost fetuses.

### Kiyum Lei Doctrine

The *mishnah* then introduces cases touching on the principle of *kim lei b'drabba minei* — when one's conduct simultaneously incurs capital liability, the lesser monetary obligation is subsumed. The *mishnah* presents: one who struck his father or mother but did not actually draw blood (*chavurah*) — which is required for the capital offense — and one who wounded another on *Yom Kippur*, which carries *kares* but not *mitas beis din* — in both these cases the injurer is *chayav b'kullan*, obligated in all five payments, because neither case triggers actual capital liability. The principle of *kim lei b'drabba minei* does not apply where the more severe liability (*mitas beis din*) is absent; *chiyuv kares* alone does not displace the monetary obligation.

### Eved Ivri Injury

One who injures a *eved ivri* must pay all five payments — *nezek*, *tza'ar*, *ripui*, *boshet*, and *sheves* — with one exception. An *eved ivri* is a full Jewish person; the master holds only rights to his labor, not to his person. Therefore *nezek*, *tza'ar*, *ripui*, and *boshet* all go to the slave himself. The sole exception is *sheves*, the compensation for time out of work: if it is your own *eved ivri*, that payment is exempt, because the master is the one losing the benefit of the slave's labor during his recovery — paying *sheves* would simply be paying oneself. If, however, it is someone *else's* *eved ivri* who is injured, the third-party injurer must pay *sheves* to the master, because the master is the party actually sustaining the loss of labor.

### Eved Kena'ani Injury

A *Canaanite slave* is legally the full property of his master, not merely his labor. Therefore one who injures another person's *eved kena'ani* must pay all five damages, but pays them to the master, who owns the slave entirely. Tosafot discusses at length the question of the medical bill: since payment for *ripui* goes to the master, the master remains obligated to ensure the slave is actually healed, or alternatively that sum is paid directly to the slave for his treatment. The *mishnah* also records that Rabbi Yehuda holds *ein l'avadim boshet* — slaves do not collect *boshet*. Rather than examining case by case whether a particular slave experienced embarrassment, Rabbi Yehuda applies a categorical exclusion: slaves do not collect embarrassment damages.

---

## Categorical Exempts

### Cheresh Shoteh Katan

The *mishnah* states: *cheresh shoteh v'katan pgi'atan ra'ah* — it is bad to have a violent encounter with a deaf-mute, a mentally ill person, or a minor. If you injure them you are fully *chayav*: they can suffer, they incur medical expenses, they experience pain and embarrassment. But if they injure others, they are exempt — *patur* — because they do not bear legal responsibility for their actions. The *cheresh* as understood by the *gemara* is one who, lacking hearing and speech, did not develop full intellectual capacity; the *shoteh* is one with mental illness; the *katan* is a minor. None of them are held liable for their tortious conduct.

### Woman & Slave Exempt

A woman and a slave (*eved kena'ani*) present a related but distinct case. *Ha'eved v'ha'ishah pgi'atan ra'ah* — it is also bad to have a violent encounter with them, because if you injure them you are *chayav*. But if they injure others, they are *patur* — not because they lack legal capacity, as the *cheresh shoteh v'katan* do, but because they have no collectible property. A woman's property is largely under her husband's control; a slave owns nothing, as *mah she'kanah eved kanah rabo* — whatever a slave acquires is acquired by his master. There is therefore nothing to collect from them, even though in principle they bear legal responsibility.

### Future Liability

Nevertheless, this exemption is not permanent. *Aval m'shalmim l'achar zman* — they will pay at a later time. Once a woman is divorced (*nitgarshah ha'ishah*) and comes into her own property, and once a slave is freed (*nishtachrer ha'eved*), they become *chayavim l'shalem* — obligated to pay for damages they caused while exempt.

The *mishnah* then loops back in a chiastic structure to a case implicating *kim lei b'drabba minei*: one who strikes his father or mother and actually draws blood (*asah bahen chavurah*), or one who wounds another on *Shabbos* and draws blood — in those cases the injurer is *patur mikulan mipnei shehu nidon b'nafsho*: exempt from all monetary payments because he faces capital liability, and *kim lei b'drabba minei* applies. Similarly, one who injures his own *eved kena'ani* — since he owns the slave entirely, there is no one to pay; he is *patur mikulan*.

---

## Minor Daughter

### Father's Rights Query

Rav Elazar posed a question to Rav: *ha'chovel b'vas ktanah shel acherim chavalah le'mi* — if someone injures the minor daughter of another man, who collects the injury payments? The question turns on the nature of the father's rights over his minor daughter. On one hand, the Torah granted the father *shevach neurim* — the benefits of his daughter's minority. He may sell her as a slave and he may betroth her, even to someone entirely unsuitable, such as one covered with boils. Since he may thus extract significant monetary benefit from her person, perhaps the *Torah*'s grant of *kol shevach neurim le'aviah* is broad enough to encompass the proceeds of an injury to her as well — for what is such a payment but compensation for reducing her value, *afchata mi'kaspa*, diminishing her worth? On the other hand, perhaps the father's rights are limited precisely to what he can achieve through the powers the Torah explicitly granted him: selling her or betrothing her. He cannot lawfully injure her himself, and therefore the Torah's grant of rights over her does not extend to the proceeds of another's wrongful injury to her body. Her body, at some fundamental level, remains her own.

Tosafot approaches the question at the *derabbanan* level: to the extent that the father receives benefits beyond the explicit biblical ones — for example, when his daughter finds a lost object — that is a rabbinic enactment designed to prevent ill-will between father and daughter, lest he grow resentful and marry her off to someone harmful. The question then becomes whether the Rabbis extended that same enactment to cover injury payments. But the *gemara* itself frames the issue in more fundamental conceptual terms: is the Torah's grant to the father structural and limited, or sweeping and categorical?

### Rav's Answer

Rav answered: *lo zichsah Torah le'av ella shevach neurim bilvad* — the Torah gave the father only ordinary *shevach neurim*, and did not include *chavalah*, injury payments, in that grant. He receives the money from selling her as a slave and from betrothing her, but does not receive the proceeds of injury to her body. This makes intuitive sense: despite the remarkable power the Torah grants a father over his minor daughter, rights to the consequences of injury done to her own person are, at their core, hers.

### Eved Ivri Challenge

The *gemara* challenges Rav's ruling from the *baraisa* concerning a *eved ivri*. That *baraisa* states: one who injures a *eved ivri* pays all five payments — except for *sheves* when it is your own *eved ivri*, because the master is entitled to the slave's labor and therefore the lost work time is a loss the master has already absorbed. The implication is pointed: just as the master who owns the labor rights is exempt from paying *sheves* because he is entitled to that labor, the father — who can sell his daughter into servitude and is therefore entitled to her labor — should likewise not have to pay *sheves* when he injures her. And correspondingly, if others injure her, they should pay *sheves* to the father. This seems to undercut Rav's ruling that all injury payments go to the daughter.

### Abaye Resolves

Abaye resolves the tension: Rav's ruling was never intended to address *sheves* at all. *Modeh rav besheves dema'aseh yadeha ad sha'as bagrus de'avuha havei* — Rav concedes that with respect to *sheves*, the father does collect. The father can sell his daughter into servitude until she reaches *bagrus* — approximately twelve and a half years of age. Therefore, the compensation for lost work during the period she would have been in that service belongs to the father. But *nezek*, *tza'ar*, *ripui*, and *boshet* — the payments that concern her body itself — go to the daughter. Rav's ruling thus stands, appropriately narrowed: only *sheves*, reflecting the labor rights the Torah granted the father, goes to him; all other payments remain hers.

---

## Minor Daughter (II)

### Second Challenge

The *gemara* raises a second challenge from a *baraisa* that states: one who injures his own minor daughter is *patur* — exempt; and not only that, but if others injure her, they are *chayavim liten le'aviha* — obligated to pay the father. This sounds like a blanket ruling granting the father all injury proceeds: he pays nothing when he himself injures her, and everyone else must pay him. This would seem to entirely negate Rav's position that *nezek*, *tza'ar*, *ripui*, and *boshet* belong to the daughter herself.

### Sheves Only

The *gemara* reinterprets this *baraisa* in a remarkably narrow fashion. *Hachi nami besheves* — here too, the *baraisa* is speaking only about *sheves*, only about lost labor. The father's exemption when he injures his daughter, and others' obligation to pay him when they injure her, refers exclusively to *sheves*. The payments tied to her own body — permanent injury, pain, medical expenses, embarrassment — remain hers. The *gemara*'s reading is striking: an apparently sweeping statement about the father being exempt and others being *chayav* to pay him is compressed entirely into the single category of labor compensation.

### Unsupported Daughter

One further complication arises: what if the father is not supporting his daughter? The *gemara* observes that if he does not feed her, *ledida baei lemeisav lah debaei mezonei* — he should give her the *sheves* payment because she needs food. If he will not support her, she retains rights to her own earnings. The *gemara* draws on the analogy of an *eved ivri*, for whom the Torah requires equality — *imach bema'achal imach bemishteh* — and concludes that a *kol sheken* applies to the father's daughter: one cannot demand labor while refusing sustenance.

However, the *gemara* resolves this through the principle stated by Rava the son of Rav Ulla in a different context: *lo nitzrecha ela le'adafa* — we are speaking only about the *surplus* labor beyond what the daughter needs to feed herself. Even if the father does not support her, she retains the right to earnings sufficient for her own food; everything beyond that still belongs to the father. So if she earns substantially more than her food costs, the excess goes to the father — and therefore, with respect to the *sheves* corresponding to that excess, he remains entitled: he is *patur* when he injures her, and others pay him when they injure her. The portion covering her own sustenance, however, she keeps.

---

## Sons & Daughters

### Sons Payment

A *baraisa* addresses the case of sons. One who injures his adult son must pay him immediately — *yiten lo miyad*. One who injures his minor son must set aside the funds as a *segulah* — a trust or sacred investment held for the child's benefit, since paying immediately risks the child squandering the money. One who injures his own sons and daughters, whether adult or minor, is *patur* — exempt.

### Contradiction

This creates an immediate difficulty: how can a father be exempt for injuring his own children, whether minors or adults? There is no principle comparable to *kim lei b'drabba minei* at work here, and the blanket exemption seems inexplicable.

### Support = Rights

The *gemara* resolves: *lo kashya — kan keshemuchim al shulchano, kan keshein smuchim al shulchano*. It depends entirely on whether the father is supporting his children. When they eat at his table — *smuchim al shulchano* — he is exempt. When he does not support them, he is *chayav*. The entire framework, as Tosafot explains, concerns only *sheves*. It would be unthinkable to suggest that just because a father feeds his children, he need not pay for the pain, suffering, embarrassment, or permanent injury he causes them. The operative question is whether he has rights to their labor.

### Father's Labor Rights

The logic proceeds as follows. When a father supports his children, he is — as a *Chazal*-structured reciprocity — entitled to their *ma'aseh yadayim*, their labor. He is also entitled to their *metziah*, any found objects they discover. If someone else injures his supported children, their *sheves* payment technically belongs to him, since he holds rights to their work. But if *he* injures them, he does not pay *sheves* because paying *sheves* would simply mean paying himself — he would receive the labor compensation that is already his.

### Unsupported Daughter

The underage daughter presents a special case even when the father does not support her. As established above, when he does not feed her, she is entitled to retain her earnings up to the cost of her own sustenance. But the father retains rights to the *surplus* beyond her food costs. He is therefore still *chayav* in the role of a *gavra kapdana* — a demanding person who insists on his rights even from the outside — because those surplus earnings are genuinely his. Correspondingly, others who injure her pay the *sheves* of that surplus to him, not to her.

### Windfall Exception

The *gemara* then asks: if the father is supporting his children and is therefore entitled to their labor and their *metziah*, why do *others* who injure them pay *sheves* to the *children* rather than to the father? The answer: *ki ka kapid bemidi dekachasar, bemidi de'ati me'alma lo kapid* — the father demands and is *makpid* when it requires him to reach into his own pocket. When he injures his children, he does not pay *sheves* because doing so would mean paying out of his own funds for something he is owed. But when the money comes from the outside — from a third party who injured them — and his children are suffering physical pain, he is not *makpid*. He lets them keep it. In that case, even though he is technically entitled to their labor, he relinquishes the *sheves* payment because it is both a *windfall* and compensation for their personal suffering.

The *gemara* then confronts an apparent inconsistency: we know that when a father supports his children, he also takes their *metziah* — found objects — even though those too are windfalls from the outside. If he takes a *metziah* even though it comes from the outside, why does he yield on *sheves*? The *gemara* answers: *revacha dekati me'alma veleit lehu tza'ara degufaihu begavah kapid* — for a pure windfall that involves no suffering on their part, such as finding a lost object, the father demands and receives it. *Aval chavala de'it lehu tza'ara degufaihu* — but for injury payments, where they are themselves suffering bodily pain, and the money is coming from the outside, *lo kapid* — he does not demand it, and they keep it.

The full picture thus resolves into three distinct situations. First, when the father does not support his children: for adult children and sons generally, they are fully independent and collect everything themselves; if he injures them, he pays them fully. For his minor daughter, even without supporting her, he retains rights to her surplus earnings; he does not pay *sheves* for the surplus, and others pay him that *sheves* — because this father, having abandoned his support obligation, is indeed a *gavra kapdana* who insists on what is his even when it is a windfall and his daughter is suffering. Second, when he supports his children: if he injures them, he pays nothing in *sheves* because he owns their labor — paying himself would be circular. If others injure them, the children keep the *sheves* payment because the father, who is generous enough to support them, is not *makpid* on a windfall that accompanies their suffering. Third, the *metziah* distinction: found objects, being pure gain with no associated suffering, the father does insist on receiving.

### Segula Definition

Finally, the *gemara* turns to the question of what precisely constitutes the *segulah* — the trust arrangement used when a minor child is to receive an injury payment. Rav Chisda says: a *Sefer Torah*. A *Sefer Torah* retains its value, carries religious significance, can be used for learning, and represents both a sound spiritual and financial investment. Rabba bar Rav Huna offers a more practical alternative: *dikla de'achil minei tamrei* — a palm tree from which they can eat the dates. This is essentially a productive asset: the principal is preserved and generates ongoing income. Reish Lakish concurs with this latter approach.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 88

## Father & Daughter Injury

### Shevach Neurim Only

The daf opens by completing a *sugya* that began toward the end of the previous page. The *Gemara* had been exploring the question of whether a father collects compensation payments when his daughter is injured. The conclusion reached is that the *Torah* gave the father only *shevach neurim* — the ordinary benefits of his daughter's minority, namely the right to betroth her, to sell her as a Hebrew slave if she is a minor, and rabbinically to collect any lost item she finds — but not the payments for the injury itself.

*Reish Lakish* states this explicitly: *lo zachata Torah l'av ela shevach neurim bilvad* — the *Torah* gave the father no more than the benefit of her youth. *Rabbi Yochanan*, by contrast, holds that the father would collect even for a *ptziah*, a minor wound that does not rise to the level of a serious injury.

The *Gemara* immediately questions this: what payment could there possibly be for such a minor wound? After all, even the foundational question raised by *Rabbi Elazar* that launched this entire *sugya* concerned a genuine injury (*chavala*) that reduced the daughter's monetary value — her attractiveness as a prospective bride or her worth as a Hebrew slave. *Rabbi Yose bar Chanina* resolves the difficulty: the case *Rabbi Yochanan* envisions is where someone struck her in the face, causing a wound that, even if not permanent, temporarily diminishes her desirability and thus her father's ability to marry her off advantageously or sell her into service.

This resolution sharpens what is genuinely at stake in the *sugya*. The underlying assumption, now made explicit, is that payments for *tzaar* (pain), embarrassment, and suffering go to the daughter herself — those belong to her alone. What might conceivably flow to the father is only loss tied directly to his financial interests: specifically, the diminution of her value as a bride or slave. The debate was never about general compensation payments; it was always about that narrow category of harm that strikes at what the father himself stood to gain. With this clarification, the *sugya* concludes.

### Chovel B'Eved Knaa'ni

The *Gemara* now turns to a new *mishna*: *hachovel b'eved knaani shel acheirim chayav* — one who injures another person's Canaanite slave is liable. The slave is considered the master's property, and the tortfeasor must pay the full range of damages to the master.

### Boshet for Slaves

*Rabbi Yehuda*, however, holds that the payment for *boshet* (embarrassment) is not included. There is no *boshet* owed for injuring a slave. Notably, *Rabbi Yehuda* had similarly excluded a blind person categorically from the *chiyuv* of *boshet* in an earlier passage; there the *Gemara* traced the categorical exclusion through a broader analysis of areas where *Rabbi Yehuda* considers a blind person outside the scope of certain *mitzvot* obligations. An analogous analysis will now unfold for the slave.

## Eved: Achvah vs. Mitzvot

### Eved Lo Ba'Achvah

What is *Rabbi Yehuda*'s reasoning? The *Gemara* cites the *pasuk*: *ki yinatzu anashim yachdav ish v'achiv* — "when men fight together, a man and his brother" (Devarim 25:11). From this verse, the obligation of *boshet* is derived. *Rabbi Yehuda* reads the phrase *ish v'achiv* restrictively: *b'mi sheyeish lo achvah* — the laws of *boshet* apply only to one who possesses *achvah*, brotherhood. *Yatza eved she-ein lo achvah* — a slave is excluded because he has no brotherhood.

What does it mean that a slave has no *achvah*? Two distinct explanations emerge from the *Rishonim*. *Rashi* explains that a slave is not *ba b'kahal* — he cannot marry into the Jewish community and is therefore not part of it in the relevant sense. One might immediately ask: should a *mamzer* likewise be excluded from *boshet*, given that a *mamzer* is also barred from marrying into the broader community? The *Gemara* therefore turns to a different explanation. A slave has no *achvah* because *mutar ba-achoto uv'eishet achiv* — he is permitted to marry his own sister and his brother's wife. The recognized structures of family and kinship simply do not apply to him. While non-Jews are bound by the *sheva mitzvot b'nei Noach*, which includes the prohibition against incest, *Chazal* understood that the Canaanite slave occupies a distinct legal status in which no family structure is recognized at all. He has no *achvah* because there is no legally cognizable family relationship.

*Tosafot* formulates this point somewhat differently: *ein yotzei chalatzav k'ruyim achim* — the slave's own children are not considered siblings to one another. The family ties do not run laterally either. Whether this functions as a *gezeirat hakatuv* or reflects a more substantive principle about the nature of *boshet* as a form of communal embarrassment requiring some recognized community — that remains to be explored.

### Achiv Hu B'Mitzvot

The Rabbis respond to *Rabbi Yehuda* with the principle *achiv hu b'mitzvot* — a slave is one's brother in *mitzvot*. Even if no family structure is recognized, a Canaanite slave who has been immersed in the *mikveh* becomes obligated in *mitzvot* at the level of a Jewish woman. If he is subsequently freed, he becomes fully obligated as a Jewish male. He is therefore part of the religious community, and that community membership is what the word *achiv* captures.

### HaMeiri: Achiv B'Mitzvot

A striking extension of this principle appears in the *HaMeiri*, who in several places advances the view that non-Jews who abide by the moral tenets of their own religion — who live according to a framework of *din* and *mussar* — may be considered *achiv b'mitzvot* relative to Jews in certain areas of *halacha*. This is a bold and controversial position, but it flows from the same conceptual structure: the category of *achvah* may be constituted not only by biological kinship but by shared religious obligation and moral framework.

### Zomemim & Eved

The *Gemara* now presses *Rabbi Yehuda* with a consequence of his position. If a slave is not within the category of *achiv*, then *zomemim* — conspiratorial false witnesses — who testified against a slave should not be put to death. The relevant verse prescribes that *eidim zomemim* receive *kegamam lazot l'achiv* — whatever they sought to do to their brother. If a slave is not one's brother, the punishment of *eidim zomemim* would not apply to testimony against him.

The *Gemara* treats this consequence as untenable. *Tosafot* notes that if this were correct, testimony against a slave could never function at all: valid testimony requires the possibility of *hazamah*, and if *hazamah* can never apply to witnesses against a slave, those witnesses can never be qualified. Yet we know that testimony against slaves is accepted. How then does *Rabbi Yehuda* resolve this?

## Eved & Eidus

### Rav Sheishes on Zomemim

*Rava* citing *Rav Sheishes* resolves the problem by invoking a broader verse: *uvi'arta hara mikirbecha* — "you shall destroy the evil from your midst." This phrase provides an independent, expansive basis for the punishment of *eidim zomemim* that is not limited by the word *achiv*. Therefore, even according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, *zomemim* who testified against a slave are subject to punishment. The exclusion based on *achvah* pertains specifically to *boshet*, not to the general category of *eidim zomemim*.

### Meluchah: Mikerev Achecha

The *Gemara* now raises a parallel difficulty, this time pressing the Rabbis. If the Rabbis hold that a slave is *achiv b'mitzvot* — a religious brother — why cannot a slave serve as king? The verse states *mikerev achecha tasim alecha melech* — "from the midst of your brethren you shall appoint a king over you" (Devarim 17:15), and the *Gemara* understands this to exclude a slave and even a *ger* (convert) from the monarchy. But if a slave is considered a religious brother, the word *achecha* should include him.

The *Gemara* responds by reframing the question. Rather than answering on its own terms, it notes that a *ger* would pose the same difficulty for *everyone* — for *Rabbi Yehuda* as much as for the Rabbis. A *ger* has family relations after conversion (his children are related to him) and according to *Rabbi Yehuda*'s own criteria, a *ger* ought to qualify as *achiv*. Yet a *ger* too cannot be king. The answer, the *Gemara* concludes, is that *mikerev achecha* for the purposes of kingship is read through a heightened lens: *mimuvchar shebe'achecha* — from the most distinguished among your brethren, the most naturally integrated. Kingship requires a qualitatively deeper form of communal belonging that excludes both the *ger* and the *eved*, regardless of their *mitzvot* obligations.

### Four Categories Excluded

The *Gemara* then raises yet another challenge for the Rabbis: if a slave is *achiv b'mitzvot*, why is he disqualified from *eidus* (testimony)? The disqualification of testimony is derived from the verse *vehinei ed sheker he'ed sheker ana be'achiv* — the false witness testified falsely against his brother. If a slave is one's religious brother, the word *achiv* should include him and his testimony should be admissible.

*Ulla* responds that the disqualification of slaves from testimony cannot rest on *achvah* at all. Rather, it flows from a *kal vachomer* from a woman: a woman is excluded from testimony on the basis of *shenei ha'anashim* — "the two men" — and if a woman, who *is* eligible to enter the Jewish community through marriage, is excluded, then certainly a slave, who is not eligible to enter the community through marriage, should be excluded.

The *Gemara* then subjects this *kal vachomer* to rigorous scrutiny. Perhaps the exclusion of women is specifically because women do not undergo *milah* — in which case a slave, who does undergo *milah*, should not be excluded by analogy. The *Gemara* counters with a *katan* (minor): a minor is also circumcised but is disqualified from testimony. Perhaps then the operative factor is the minor's youth — but a slave is not a minor. A woman (*ishah tochiach*) — a woman is obligated in *mitzvot* yet excluded from testimony, so *mitzvot* obligation alone is not the qualifying criterion for testimony.

### Shoresh Ha'Psul

The *Gemara* applies the standard *talmudic* methodology: since neither a woman nor a minor by itself captures the full principle of exclusion, one seeks the common denominator — *hatzad hashaveh shebahen* — and that is *einam b'chol hamitzvot*: they are not fully obligated in the entire range of *mitzvot*. A minor is not yet obligated in any *mitzvot*; a woman is exempt from *mitzvot aseh shehazman gerama* (time-bound positive commandments). Since neither is fully obligated, and both are excluded from testimony, the operative principle is incomplete *mitzvot* obligation.

A slave, even a male slave, is obligated in *mitzvot* only at the level of a woman — not fully obligated as a Jewish male. Therefore he too falls under this principle and is excluded from testimony.

The *Gemara* pushes back once more: perhaps the common denominator of woman and minor is not *mitzvot* obligation but *eino ish* — neither is fully a man in the legal sense. A slave is a man (*ish*). The *Gemara* then considers whether adding a *gazlan* (robber) to the mix helps: the *gazlan* is disqualified because his own actions rendered him a *rasha* — this disqualification stems from personal conduct, not from any categorical deficiency. A slave did nothing to earn his disqualification.

Combining *gazlan* with woman or minor, the *Gemara* seeks a principle that explains all three. It cannot be *eino ish* (since the *gazlan* is a man), and it cannot be *ma'asav garmu lo* (since the woman and minor did nothing wrong). The only common denominator that works for all three — *ishah*, *katan*, and *gazlan* — is that none of them is fully performing all *mitzvot*. The *gazlan* is not observant; the woman is exempt from certain *mitzvot*; the minor is not yet obligated. And a slave, obligated only at the level of a woman, falls squarely within this category.

### Lo Yumtu Avot Al Banim

*Mar brei deRavina* offers an entirely different scriptural derivation for the exclusion of a slave from testimony. The verse states *lo yumtu avot al banim* — "fathers shall not die for their sons, nor sons for their fathers" (Devarim 24:16). Ordinarily this is understood to mean that relatives may not testify against each other. But *Mar brei deRavina* reads it differently: *lo yumtu al pi avot she-ein lahem chiyus banim* — no one may be put to death on the testimony of fathers who have no legally recognized relationship to their children. And such a father is precisely the Canaanite slave, who is not considered related to his offspring.

The *Gemara* asks: why does the *Torah* use the generic *banim* rather than *bnehem* (their sons)? Had it said *bnehem*, we would know only that sons cannot testify against their specific fathers. By using the more open *banim*, the verse teaches that the disqualification extends to a category of person whose relationship to children is altogether unrecognized.

### Ger vs. Eved

One might think this same derivation would disqualify a *ger* from testimony — after all, a *ger* is also not related to his father. The *Gemara* refutes this. The verse contains two parallel clauses: *avot al banim* (fathers who have no relation to their sons) and *banim al avot* (sons who have no relation to their fathers). The first clause — *avot al banim*, a father who is not related to his children — applies uniquely to a slave, because a slave has no recognized relationship either upward to his own parents or downward to his children. A *ger*, by contrast, has no relationship upward (his father is not halachically his father after conversion) but does have a relationship downward — once he converts, his children are his children. He is a *banim* who lacks *avot*, not an *avot* who lacks *banim*.

The *Torah*'s inclusion of both clauses is thus deliberate and precise: *avot al banim* excludes the slave (who lacks relation in both directions), while *banim al avot* is written only to create a stylistic parallel, not to exclude the *ger*. Had the *Torah* wanted to exclude the *ger*, it would have written only *banim lo yumtu al avot* without the possessive suffix, which would have been sufficient to invalidate both *ger* and *eved* — the *ger* directly, and the *eved* via a *kal vachomer* (since an *eved* lacks both upward and downward relation, he is certainly to be excluded if a *ger* who lacks only one direction is excluded). The fact that the *Torah* instead used *avot al banim* — the clause that uniquely fits only the slave — signals that the *ger* is *kasher le-eidus*.

The parallel *banim lo yumtu al avot* is present purely because the *Torah* writes in balanced, parallel language, mirroring the structure of the first clause. Its presence carries no additional legal exclusion. The conclusion stands: a *ger* is fully valid as a witness; it is only the slave — who has no *yichus* either upward or downward — who is disqualified.

This prompts *Tosafot* to raise a broader concern: how far does *Rabbi Yehuda*'s exclusion of the slave from *achvah* actually reach? If *achvah* is the operative word in laws of *ribbis*, *ona'ah*, *gonev nefesh*, and even *tzedaka*, are all of these to be understood as inapplicable to a slave? *Tosafot* acknowledges the difficulty without fully resolving it. He notes that *gonev nefesh* may be categorically limited to Jews based on the phrase *b'nei Yisrael* even for the Rabbis. As for *ribbis* and *ona'ah*, there is a technical point that a slave has no independent property and therefore these prohibitions simply have no application. But the question of *tzedaka* is pointed: is a slave not included in *achicha he'ani* — your poor brother? There may be a hint from the first chapter of *Gittin* that the obligation of *tzedaka* toward a slave is qualitatively different, though this is not fully demonstrated. What *Tosafot* leaves us with is the sharp recognition that once we accept *Rabbi Yehuda*'s categorical exclusion, its ramifications ripple through a remarkable range of interpersonal obligations.

## Gift of Melog Property

### Ketivatah L'Nechsa

The *Gemara* now introduces a case study that will anchor the remainder of the daf. The mother of *Rav Shmuel bar Abba* from Hagronia was married to *Rabbi Abba*. Before her death, she wrote over — gifted — all of her property to her son, *Rav Shmuel bar Abba*. The purpose of this transfer was to ensure that her property would pass to her own son rather than be inherited by her husband and then divided among his heirs. After she died, *Rav Shmuel bar Abba* brought the matter before *Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba*, who ruled that the property was indeed his — the mother's transfer was effective and the son was entitled to the property. (That *Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba* may himself be a stepbrother of the claimant goes unremarked by the *Gemara*.)

*Rabbi Abba* — the husband who stood to lose — then went and related the facts to *Rabbi Hoshaia*, who in turn reported them to *Rav Yehuda*.

### Samuel's Psak

*Rav Yehuda* responded with a ruling in the name of his teacher *Shmuel*: *ha'isha she'makhrah b'nichsei melog b'chayei ba'alah u'meitah, haba'al motzi miyad halakochos* — a woman who sold or transferred her *nichsei melog* property during her husband's lifetime, and then died, the husband may reclaim it from the purchasers.

The concept of *nichsei melog* requires explanation. This is property the wife brings into the marriage over which the title (*kinyan haguf*) remains hers, while the husband receives the right to benefit from the property's produce (*kinyan peiros*). To use a concrete illustration: if she brings an orchard into the marriage, she owns the orchard itself, but he collects the fruit each season. Alternatively, if she brings an apartment building, she holds the title while he collects the rent.

*Shmuel*'s ruling is that she cannot unilaterally transfer or sell this property while her husband is alive, because his *kinyan peiros* gives him a stake in it. Therefore the transfer the mother made to her son is ineffective, and *Rabbi Abba* should be able to recover the property.

### Mishnah: Kotev Nechsav

*Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba* was not moved by this challenge. He cited a *Mishna* that he regarded as directly on point. The *Mishna* (in *Ketubot*) discusses a case of *hakotev nechsav livno le'achar moto* — a father who writes his property over to his son to take effect "from today and after I die." The legal effect of this language is that the son acquires the title (*kinyan haguf*) immediately, while the father retains the right to the *peiros* until his death.

The structure is perfectly parallel to *nichsei melog*: the son holds the *kinyan haguf* while the father holds the *kinyan peiros*, exactly as the wife holds the *kinyan haguf* of her *melog* property while the husband holds the *kinyan peiros*.

The *Mishna* states:

- *haben eino yakhol limkor mipenei shehen bireshut av* — the son cannot sell the property, since the father still controls the *peiros*.
- *ha'av eino yakhol limkor mipenei shehen ketuvin laben* — the father cannot sell, since the title is written over to the son.

Neither party can complete a sale on their own. However, if the father goes ahead and sells his rights, the purchaser acquires the *peiros* until the father dies. If the son sells his title, the purchaser acquires nothing until the father dies — but the sale of the title itself is effective.

The crucial inference is: *ki meit av miha itei lalokeiach* — when the father does eventually die, the purchaser from the son does receive the full property. This is true even *af al gav de'meit haben b'chayei ha'av* — even if the son dies while the father is still alive, so that the full possession never passed through the son's hands during his lifetime. The son's sale of his title worked even then.

This case maps directly onto the mother's situation: she transferred her title to *Rav Shmuel* even while her husband retained the *kinyan peiros*. The *Mishna* demonstrates that such a transfer of title is valid.

### Kinyan Peiros & Guf

The *Mishna*'s conclusion — that the purchaser from the son receives the property when the father dies, even when the son predeceased the father — is the subject of a fundamental dispute between *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Resh Lakish*.

### Resh Lakish: Lav K'Kinya…

*Rabbi Yochanan* holds *lo kana lokeach* — the purchaser from the son does not acquire. His reasoning: since the father holds *kinyan peiros*, the father is considered a co-owner or even the primary owner. The son cannot sell a title while the father's rights effectively prevent the son from exercising any ownership. *Kinyan peiros ke-kinyan haguf dami* — the right to benefit from the produce is legally equivalent to title ownership. The sale the son attempted while the father was alive and active is therefore void. The purchaser could only receive the property if the father died first, allowing full possession to pass to the son before the sale took effect.

*Resh Lakish*, by contrast, holds *kana lokeach* — the purchaser does acquire. The son's title is real and transferable independent of the father's *kinyan peiros*. *Kinyan peiros lav k'kinyan haguf dami* — the right to the produce does not constitute ownership of the property. The father's retention of *peiros* does not impair the son's ability to convey title. Therefore, even if the son sold his title while the father was alive and then predeceased the father — so that full possession never passed through the son's hands — the purchaser (*Reuven*) will receive the property once the father dies.

The *Mishna*'s ruling that the purchaser from the son does receive the property when the father eventually dies, even in the scenario where the son died first, aligns with the position of *Resh Lakish*.

### Analogous Transfer

The relevance to the mother's case becomes explicit. The *Gemara* notes that both *Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba* (who ruled in favor of *Rav Shmuel*) and *Rav Yehuda* (who initially challenged that ruling on the basis of *Shmuel*'s opinion) in fact both hold like *Resh Lakish* — that *kinyan peiros lav k'kinyan haguf dami*. This is the accepted principle in *halacha*.

*Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba*, in invoking the *Mishna*, was therefore pressing *Rav Yehuda*: if you hold like *Resh Lakish* — as everyone does — then you must accept that the son's sale or the mother's transfer of title works even while the party with *kinyan peiros* is still alive. The father's (or husband's) *kinyan peiros* does not prevent the transfer of title. Therefore *Rav Shmuel*'s mother's gift was effective, and *Rav Shmuel* is entitled to the property once *Rabbi Abba* dies.

The *Gemara* makes this reasoning explicit: if one were to hold *kinyan peiros ke-kinyan haguf dami*, then even the *Mishna*'s case would be incoherent — why would the purchaser from the son ever get the property, even when the father dies first? The answer is that the son's sale was void ab initio. Yet the *Mishna* clearly validates the purchaser's eventual acquisition. This can only be consistent with *kinyan peiros lav k'kinyan haguf dami*. Since everyone accepts the *Mishna* and everyone holds like *Resh Lakish*, the mother's transfer to her son should be fully effective.

### Zu Eina Doma L'Mishnasenu

When this counterargument was reported back to *Rav Yehuda*, he responded in the name of *Shmuel*: *zu eina doma l'mishnasenu* — this case is not analogous to our *Mishna*. *Shmuel* maintained that the mother-to-son transfer is categorically different from the father-to-son scenario the *Mishna* addresses. The precise nature of that distinction — why the mother-son transfer cannot be resolved by the same principle that governs the father-son case — is left to be elaborated in the continuation of the *sugya* on the following daf.
