## Takanas Usha Debate

### Woman's Sales Rights

The *Gemara* now turns to the question of *takanas Usha* and the rights of a woman with respect to her *nichsei milugs*. The relevant issue is whether a woman can sell her *nichsei milugs* — property she owns within the marriage over which her husband enjoys the *peiros*, the usufruct. The husband's position is defined by *kinyan peiros*: he has the right to the produce or benefit of the property. The woman holds title, *kinyan haguf*. The question is whether *kinyan peiros kekinyan haguf dami* — whether ownership of the *peiros* is tantamount to ownership of the body of the property.

If *kinyan peiros lav kekinyan haguf dami*, as Reish Lakish holds, then in principle the woman should be able to sell her *nichsei milugs*, since she holds title and the husband's interest is merely usufructuary. But *takanas Usha* — an enactment attributed to the rabbinic convocation at Usha, shortly after the period of Kerem beYavneh — ostensibly grants the husband greater rights over his wife's property than he technically deserves under the law, potentially blocking the wife from such sales. The question driving the *Gemara* here is whether the disagreement we find in the sources is really a debate about *takanas Usha* or about the underlying principle of *kinyan peiros*.

### First Braita

The first *braita* teaches: *avdei milugs yotzin b'shein v'ayin l'isha* — slaves held as *nichsei milugs* go free if the woman knocks out their eye or tooth, but not if the husband does so. The implication is clear: the woman is considered the halachic owner of these slaves, and it is the owner's act of knocking out an eye or tooth — the *halacha* of *shein v'ayin* — that triggers manumission.

### Second Braita

A second *braita* teaches the opposite: *lo l'ish v'lo l'isha* — neither the husband nor the wife can free such slaves through *shein v'ayin*. This creates an apparent contradiction that the *Gemara* must resolve.

### Gemara Analysis

The *Gemara* begins its analysis with an assumption: *savruha de'kulei alma kinyan peiros lav kekinyan haguf dami* — let us assume that everyone agrees with Reish Lakish that *kinyan peiros* alone does not constitute ownership of the object itself. Given that starting point, what is the debate between the two *braisos* about?

The first suggestion is that this is a dispute about *takanas Usha* itself. The *braita* that allows the wife to free the slave through *shein v'ayin* represents the view that holds there is no *takanas Usha* — the wife has title, the husband has only *peiros*, and the wife may therefore exercise full ownership rights including the ability to free the slave. The *braita* that denies this power to both husband and wife represents the view that accepts *takanas Usha*, which grants the husband a blocking power over the wife's disposition of the property. Under *takanas Usha*, the wife cannot unilaterally free the slave because the husband can veto it, and the husband cannot free it because the title belongs to the wife. The result is that neither party can effect manumission.

The *Gemara* considers whether this debate might instead be attributed to different historical periods — one *braita* reflecting the law before *takanas Usha* and the other after. It further entertains the possibility that both *braisos* reflect the post-*takana* reality.

### Rava's Principle

This leads to the key question: if we accept *takanas Usha* and the husband accordingly has the power to block the wife from alienating the property, how could the wife still free the slave through *shein v'ayin*? The *Gemara* answers: *k'de'Rava*, invoking Rava's principle that *hekdesh, chametz, ve-shichrur mafki'in midei shibud* — sanctification to the Temple, the transformation of *chametz* into something *assur behana'ah*, and the freeing of a slave each operate to sever a lien or encumbrance.

The principle requires elaboration. The ordinary rule is that a lien-holder's interest survives the transfer of property. If Michael holds a lien on my ox and I sell the ox to Dov, Michael can repossess it from Dov, just as he could have from me. If I donate the ox to the Temple treasury as *bedek habayis* — a straightforward transfer of ownership — Michael can likewise recover it from the Temple, since the Temple treasury acquired it subject to his lien. The transfer does not extinguish the lien.

However, if I consecrate the ox as a *korban* — as an *olah*, for instance — something fundamentally different has occurred. This is not merely a transfer of ownership but a transformation of identity. The ox is now a sanctified object of a distinct ontological category. To say that Michael can simply "take it" from this new status would be to say that his assertion of a proprietary lien can undo a *kedusha* — and that is not how liens work. The lien attaches to an object as it is; when the object undergoes a fundamental change of identity, the lien has no purchase on the new thing.

Similarly with *chametz*: if a non-Jew holds a lien on my *chametz* and it remains in my home over *Pesach*, becoming *assur behana'ah*, the non-Jew cannot simply assert his lien and take it, because the thing that now exists — something forbidden in all benefit — is a categorically different object from what he originally held a lien on. One qualification must be noted: as the *Yerushalmi* observes, the *assur behana'ah* argument cannot apply straightforwardly to the non-Jewish lien-holder, since *chametz* is not *assur behana'ah* to a non-Jew. The stronger version of the principle is the *hekdesh* case, where the identity transformation is absolute.

The most vivid illustration, however, is *shichrur* — the freeing of a slave. If Michael holds a lien on my slave and I free him, the slave becomes a *ben chorin*, a free person. How could Michael now assert his lien? To "take" the slave would require reducing a free person back to servitude. There is no mechanism by which asserting a monetary lien accomplishes that. The free person is a new legal and human reality; the lien, which attached to an *eved*, cannot follow him into his freedom.

### Shichru & Identity

This is precisely the *Gemara*'s answer to our question. The woman is the halachic owner of the *nichsei milugs* slaves. When she knocks out the eye or tooth, the act of *shichrur* that follows is not a mere alienation of property — it is a transformation of identity. The husband's interest, however robust under *takanas Usha*, is in the nature of a lien or blocking power. But that blocking power cannot prevent what *shichrur* does, because *shichrur* does not merely change ownership — it changes the very being of the slave. The slave is no longer property at all; he is a free man. The husband's lien or veto right, like any *shibud*, is severed by the identity transformation.

A question arises: could the husband, by analogy, knock out the slave's eye and achieve the same result? The answer is no, because the husband is not the owner. The *Gemara* is careful to say that the mechanism of *shichrur mafki'a midei shibud* presupposes that one begins from the position of owner. The woman starts as owner; she knocks out the eye; the *halacha* is the slave goes free; the husband's interest cannot block that. But a random person — or the husband, who holds no title — cannot invoke the same principle because the identity-transforming act of *shichrur* can only be performed by the master.

The *Gemara* then asks whether Rava's principle is itself a subject of *tannaitic* debate — *leima de-Rava tanna'ei hi?* — since if everyone agrees with *takanas Usha* and the *braisos* diverge, the second *braita* must apparently reject the *shichrur* argument. The *Gemara* answers: no, everyone can agree with Rava. The second *braita* may hold that the Rabbis made the husband's interest under *takanas Usha* so powerful as to constitute something like partial ownership, not merely a lien — and if he is effectively a co-owner, the wife's act of *shichrur* might be blocked not as the assertion of a lien against an identity-change, but as the exercise of a co-owner's veto against a co-owner's decision. The exact parameters of that position — in particular, whether a co-owner who knocks out a slave's eye can effect manumission — would need to be explored separately.

### Kinyan Peiros Debate

The *Gemara* then offers yet another resolution of the two *braisos*: *kulei alma leit lehu lehani tanna'ei takanas Usha* — perhaps neither *Tanna* holds of *takanas Usha* at all. There is no *Usha*, no enactment, no blocking power granted to the husband beyond what he possesses under the basic law. Under this reading, what the *braisos* debate is the classic dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish: *be-kinyan peiros kekinyan haguf dami plugi* — whether *kinyan peiros* is equivalent to *kinyan haguf*.

Under this framework, *takanas Usha* is needed only if one accepts Reish Lakish's position that *kinyan peiros lav kekinyan haguf dami* — for only then does the husband lack ownership, and only then must some additional enactment shore up his rights. But if one holds like Rabbi Yochanan that *kinyan peiros kekinyan haguf dami*, then the husband is already, by the basic logic of the *halacha*, an owner. No *takanas Usha* is required to block the wife's disposition of the property — the husband's *kinyan peiros* already suffices.

This debate is then shown to parallel a *tannaitic* dispute of broader scope. The *braita* discusses the case of one who sells his slave to another but stipulates that the slave shall continue to serve the seller for thirty days. The seller, for those thirty days, holds *kinyan peiros* — he receives the service of the slave — while the buyer holds *kinyan haguf*, the title. Now suppose one of these parties beats the slave so severely that the slave dies. The *halacha* of *yom o yomayim* — the Torah's provision that a master who beats his slave is not executed if the slave survives for a day or two — applies only to the master. Who is the master in this divided arrangement?

Rabbi Meir holds that the first man — the seller who still has the slave's service for thirty days — is the one governed by *yom o yomayim*, because the slave is *tachasav*, directly under his control. The *Gemara* reads Rabbi Meir as formally holding *kinyan peiros kekinyan haguf dami*: his *kinyan peiros* makes him the full halachic master, more than the one who holds mere title. This is indeed a stronger version of the principle than encountered previously — here, *kinyan peiros* does not just give the *peiros*-holder equal standing with the title-holder; it actually displaces the title-holder entirely, rendering him irrelevant to the *yom o yomayim* calculus.

Rabbi Yehuda holds that the second man — the buyer who holds title — is subject to *yom o yomayim*, because *she-hu kaspo*, he is the one for whom the slave represents capital. The *Gemara* reads Rabbi Yehuda as holding *kinyan peiros lav kekinyan haguf dami*: the *peiros* rights are insufficient to constitute ownership; it is the title-holder who is the master.

Rabbi Yossi holds that both are subject to *yom o yomayim*. The *Gemara* declines to read this as Rabbi Yossi affirming that *kinyan peiros* creates a second, co-equal *kinyan haguf*; rather, the *Gemara* reads Rabbi Yossi as holding the matter *be-safek* — he is uncertain whether *kinyan peiros* rises to the level of *kinyan haguf*. Since we do not know who the master is, we would not execute either party. Crucially, the *Gemara* is not prepared to treat *kinyan peiros* as an equal form of *kinyan haguf* that simply adds a second owner; it insists the question is binary.

Rabbi Eliezer holds that neither is subject to *yom o yomayim*: the seller cannot invoke *yom o yomayim* because the slave is no longer *tachasav* — he does not hold title; the buyer cannot invoke it because the slave is not yet *kaspo* in the active sense — he is not yet working for him. The *Gemara* asks *mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Eliezer* — what is Rabbi Eliezer's source? The verse uses the language *ki kaspo hu* — because he is his property. From the extra word *hu*, the *Gemara* derives *kaspo ha-meyuchad lo* — property that is fully and exclusively his. For *yom o yomayim* to apply, one must have both title *and* active control. This mirrors the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan discussed elsewhere that neither the *gazlan* — who has possession but not title — nor the original owner — who has title but not possession — can be *makdish*, because the *halacha* requires both that the object be one's own and that it be within one's domain.

There is, it should be noted, something that feels somewhat artificial about making the *yom o yomayim* debate entirely dependent on the abstract *kinyan peiros* question rather than on the practical question of who has the right to discipline the slave at any given moment. The *Gemara*, however, insists on framing it formally, and this framing is itself significant.

### Ameimar Teaching

The *Gemara* then asks: *keman azla ha de-amar Ameimar* — whose view is reflected in the teaching of Ameimar? Ameimar rules: *ish ve-isha she-machru be-nichsei melog — lo asu ve-lo klum* — a husband and wife who jointly sell *nichsei milugs* have accomplished nothing; the sale is void.

One might have thought that since between them they hold all interests in the property — she has title, he has *peiros* — their combined signature would suffice to constitute a complete transfer. Why is this not the case? Rashi explains the distinction from ordinary *shutfin*: if two partners each own fifty percent of a property, each is the full and exclusive owner of his fifty percent. Either may independently sell his share, and together they can convey the whole. But in the case of *nichsei milugs*, the division of interests is not quantitative but qualitative. She holds title to the entire property; he holds *peiros* over the entire property. He cannot sell what he does not own — the *guf* of the property — and she cannot sell what would, absent a disposition of his *peiros* rights, leave the buyer with a property burdened by his usufruct. There is no mechanism by which two people, each lacking sufficient ownership standing, can pool their deficiencies to create a valid sale. For that to work, one party would need to first transfer his or her interest to the other — so that one person holds both *kinyan peiros* and *kinyan haguf* — and that person could then convey the whole.

### Full Ownership Req.

This connects directly to the *shein v'ayin* analysis. A further *braita* is cited: *mi she-chetzio eved ve-chetzio ben chorin* — a slave who is half-free and half-enslaved — *ve-chen eved shel shenei shutafin* — or a slave owned by two partners — does not go free through *shein v'ayin*. The requirement is not only qualitative but quantitative: one must be one hundred percent the owner, not merely the qualitative form of owner appropriate to the *halacha* of *shein v'ayin*.

The *Gemara* asks whose view this represents, and Rav Mordechai cites in the name of Rava: *Rabbi Eliezer hi* — this is the position of Rabbi Eliezer, who derives from the same *pasuk* — *ki kaspo hu* — that full, exclusive ownership is required. Just as *yom o yomayim* requires a *kaspo ha-meyuchad lo*, so too *shein v'ayin* requires an *avdo ha-meyuchad lo* — his slave, fully and exclusively. Even if a partner owns one hundred percent of one half of the slave, that half-share of ownership does not suffice to free the slave through *shein v'ayin*. The *Gemara* acknowledges, through *Tosafos*, that this is a special *derashah* in the *pasuk* applicable to the specific *halachos* of *shein v'ayin* and *yom o yomayim*, not a general principle applicable to all areas of law, where ordinary partnership rules would of course apply.

---

## Boshet Damages

### Boshet Principle

The *Gemara* now transitions to a new *mishna* dealing with *boshet* — the payment for embarrassment. The transition brings with it a striking irony. Throughout Bava Kamma, the framework for assessing damages has been inherently flexible and case-specific: one assesses the reduction in market value caused by an injury, the reasonable cost of medical treatment, the earning capacity lost, the pain and suffering that the victim would require compensation to endure. For *boshet*, the same logic would seem to demand a case-by-case assessment — how embarrassed was this particular person by this particular act? How much would he or she require to have willingly undergone this experience? The *mishna* immediately before our passage states the principle explicitly: *hakol lefi ha-mivayesh ve-ha-mitbayesh* — everything depends on the nature of the embarrassor and the one embarrassed.

Yet what we find, counterintuitively, is that *Chazal* attempted to set fixed amounts for *boshet*. Perhaps because subjective assessment of embarrassment was too difficult or too susceptible to manipulation, the tradition established a schedule of set payments for specific humiliating acts.

### Fixed Amounts List

The *mishna* sets out the following: *ha-tokeia le-chaveiro* — one who strikes his friend on the ear — pays one *sela*, equivalent to four *zuz*. Rabbi Yehuda, citing Rabbi Yossi HaGlili, says the payment is a *maneh* — one hundred *zuz*, which is twenty-five times the *tanna kamma*'s figure.

To calibrate the magnitudes: a *kesubah* was two hundred *zuz*, an amount understood to represent roughly what was needed to sustain a person for a year. A *maneh* is therefore half that sum — a very substantial payment for a single act of striking someone's ear.

*Sotra* — slapping someone in the face — carries a payment of two hundred *zuz*, equal to the full value of a *kesubah*. This is for a slap in the face, presumably in public. Striking with the back of the hand — which carries a connotation of contemptuous dismissal — costs four hundred *zuz*, double the *sotra* payment. *Tzarmo b'ozno* — yanking him by the ear — is similarly enumerated. *Talash be-searo* — pulling his hair. *Rakak ve-higi'a bo roko* — spitting on him, with the spit reaching him. *He'evir taliso mimenu* — pulling off his cloak, leaving him exposed. And *para rosh isha ba-shuk* — uncovering a woman's hair in the marketplace — also carries a payment of four hundred *zuz*.

The *mishna* then appends: *ze ha-klal — hakol lefi kevodo* — this is the principle: everything depends on the person's honor.

### Rabbi Akiva's Dignity

The tension is obvious. The *mishna* has just set fixed amounts, and then immediately declares that assessment depends on the individual's standing. The *Gemara* resolves this through Rabbi Akiva: *afilu aniyim she-be-Yisrael ro'im osam ke-ilu hem bnei chorin she-yardu min-nachaseihem she-bnei Avraham Yitzchak ve-Yaakov* — even the poor of Israel are viewed as if they were members of the free upper classes who have fallen from their wealth, being descendants of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov.

Rabbi Akiva is drawing a distinction between class and wealth. One may be financially impoverished while belonging, in terms of lineage and social standing, to the nobility. The analogy is apt: there exists such a thing as the impoverished aristocracy — people of distinguished lineage living in straitened circumstances. Their poverty does not diminish their *kavod*, their honor and standing. Rabbi Akiva argues that every Jew, as a descendant of the Patriarchs, is in exactly this position: even the poor are *bnei chorin she-yardu min-nachaseihem*, free people of noble lineage who have come upon hard times. Since the *boshet* assessment is keyed to *kavod* rather than to wealth, and since everyone's *kavod* is, as a matter of halachic principle, maximum, the fixed high amounts specified in the *mishna* apply universally. *Hakol lefi kevodo* and the fixed amounts are not in tension — the fixed amounts represent what *kavod* demands for everyone.

### Hair Uncovering Story

The *Gemara* illustrates this principle with a remarkable story. *U-maaseh be-echad she-para rosh isha ba-shuk* — there was an incident in which a man uncovered a woman's hair in the marketplace. The woman came before Rabbi Akiva, who obligated the man to pay her four hundred *zuz*. The man requested a week to pay, and Rabbi Akiva granted the extension.

The man then devised a scheme. He observed the woman standing at the entrance to her courtyard, the opening of her yard facing the *reshus ha-rabim*, the public domain. He contrived to drop a small flask of oil — worth about a *issar*, a trivial amount — in front of her. The woman, seeing the oil, uncovered her own hair, used her hand to collect the oil, and applied it to her hair right there in the public domain. The man had arranged witnesses to observe this. He then appeared before Rabbi Akiva: *l'zo ani nosen arba me'os zuz* — for this type of woman I am paying four hundred *zuz*? She uncovered her own hair for a dollar's worth of oil.

### Objective Value

Rabbi Akiva was unmoved. *Lo amarta klum* — you have said nothing. The response draws on an established legal principle: *ha-chovel be-atzmo — af al pi she-eino rashai — patur* — one who injures himself, even though he is not permitted to do so, is exempt from payment. *Acherim she-chavlu bo — chayavim* — others who injure him remain liable. Similarly: *ha-kotzetz netiotav — af al pi she-eino rashai — patur* — one who cuts down his own saplings is exempt, yet *acherim she-chavlu bo — chayavim*. The objective fact of the injury or degradation does not change based on whether the victim was willing to inflict it upon himself or herself.

The parallel is exact. The woman may have been willing to expose her hair for a trivial amount of oil — she may, in that moment, have not felt the shame to be significant. But *boshet* as assessed by *halacha* is not a purely subjective phenomenon. It has an objective value rooted in the person's inherent *kavod*, which is, in Rabbi Akiva's framework, always at the maximum. The same way a severed arm represents an objective injury regardless of whether the owner cut it off himself, an act of public humiliation represents an objective degradation of a person's dignity regardless of whether the victim was willing to participate in a similar act for personal benefit.

The deeper insight in this ruling — noted in the discussion — is its close relationship to the debate between Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai. Rabbi Akiva famously holds that *ve-ahavta le-reacha kamocha* is the *klal gadol ba-Torah* — love your neighbor as yourself is the great principle. Ben Azzai counters that *zeh sefer toldos adam* — this is the book of the generations of man — is a greater principle, because one's obligation to respect another person does not derive from self-love but from the other person's status as a human being. If you do not respect yourself, the *ve-ahavta le-reacha kamocha* principle might suggest your obligations to others are proportionally diminished. Ben Azzai insists this cannot be so. Interestingly, Rabbi Akiva here — in the case of the woman — is making a parallel argument: it does not matter that this woman does not respect herself in this moment. The objective *kavod* that belongs to every descendant of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov remains intact, and the person who violated it must pay its full price.

---

## Witness as Judge

### Core Problem

The *Gemara* has been discussing the payment of a *maneh* for striking an ear, and the question arises whether this is a *maneh Tzori* — the larger denomination — or a *maneh medinah*, one-eighth that value. A story is cited: a man who struck another's ear was brought before Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, the grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The judge declared, *ha ana v'ha Rabbi Yossi HaGlili* — here am I, and here is Rabbi Yossi HaGlili — and ordered payment of a *maneh Tzori*. The *Gemara* derives from this that when the *mishna* states a *maneh*, it means *maneh Tzori*, the higher value.

But a deeper question immediately presents itself. The *Gemara* initially reads *ha ana v'ha Rabbi Yossi HaGlili* as the judge saying: "I witnessed what you did" — combining his personal testimony with Rabbi Yossi HaGlili's legal ruling to order payment. The difficulty: this would mean that the judge who witnessed the event is also adjudicating it. *Le-meimra de-eid na'aseh dayan* — does this imply that a witness may become a judge in the same case?

### Tarfon vs Akiva

A *baraita* bears directly on this question. A *Sanhedrin* out walking witnessed a murder. Rabbi Tarfon rules: *miktzatan na'asu eidim u-miktzatan na'asu dayanim* — some of them become witnesses and some serve as judges; one cannot do both. Rabbi Akiva rules: *kulam eidim hein ve-ein eid na'aseh dayan* — they are all witnesses, and a witness cannot become a judge. For Rabbi Akiva, the mere act of seeing something — even if one never formally testifies — disqualifies one from adjudicating the case. The *Sanhedrin* would have to convene a different court. This is feasible since capital cases require only twenty-three judges rather than seventy-one.

### Day vs Night Rule

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent tension as follows. Rabbi Tarfon does not say that the judge can use his own sighting as a basis for ruling — he says only that some members of the *Sanhedrin* may formally testify while others judge; being a witness does not inherently disqualify one from judging, but one cannot do both in the same proceeding. What the *Gemara* needs to establish is whether the judge's direct sighting can function like the receipt of testimony.

The resolution: *ki tanya hi ke-gon she-ra'u ba-layla* — the *baraita* deals with a case where they saw the murder at night, when a court cannot be in session. Since testimony can only be received during the daytime, a judge's nocturnal sighting cannot be treated as the equivalent of receiving testimony. The formal witnesses must testify in court during the day, and once those witnesses have testified, they cannot turn around and serve as judges.

But if the sighting occurred during the day, a judge who personally witnessed the event has effectively "received" the testimony directly. There is nothing epistemically inferior about direct observation compared to hearing witnesses; indeed, one might argue the opposite. If the judge saw it himself during the day — during the hours when a court would be in session — that sighting is analogous to testimony formally received, and he may then adjudicate.

### Alt Explanation

The *Gemara* offers an alternative reading of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's statement that requires no *ed na'aseh dayan* analysis at all. *Ve-i ba'it eima, hachi ka'amar leh* — perhaps *ha ana* means not "I witnessed you" but "here I am as *dayan*, holding like Rabbi Yossi HaGlili, who rules a *maneh Tzori*" — *ve-ha sahadi de-mesahadei bach* — and there are witnesses who have testified against you. Under this reading, the judge was not personally testifying; he was simply identifying his ruling with Rabbi Yossi HaGlili's position. The witnesses are separate persons who gave testimony in the ordinary fashion.

### Instrument Rule

The discussion of *ed na'aseh dayan* concludes, and the *Gemara* transitions to a related topic: the requirement to assess the instrument of injury. Shimon HaTeimani derives from the verse — *ve-chi yakeh ish et re'ehu be-even o be-egrof* ("and if a man strikes his fellow with a stone or a fist") — that just as a fist can be examined and assessed by both the *eidah* (the court) and the *eidim* (the witnesses), so too any instrument used to inflict injury must be assessable by both. The *perat* — the exclusion — applies to instruments that left the possession of the witnesses: if the *eidim* can no longer produce and show the instrument, the defendant is acquitted.

### Akiva Objection

Rabbi Akiva objects to Shimon HaTeimani's formulation. His objection is pointed: *ve-chi bifnei beis din hikah* — did the assailant strike in front of the *beis din*? The *beis din* can look at the defendant's fist, but it did not see how many times he struck, at what part of the body, with what force. Assessing a fist in the abstract tells you little. More strikingly: *harei she-dofahu me-chaveiru me-rosh ha-birah* — what if he pushed his friend off the top of a tower or castle and the victim died? Should *beis din* take a field trip to inspect the building? *Ha-birah holechet etzel beis din* — should the castle come to the court? *Ve-od im naflah ha-birah* — what if the castle has since fallen down? *Chozer u-voneh et ha-birah* — rebuild the building so the court can inspect it? The requirement that *beis din* directly assess the instrument is physically and practically impossible in many real cases.

### Witness Assessment

Rabbi Akiva therefore reformulates the principle: *ela mah egrof meyuchad she-masur le-eidim* — rather, a fist is paradigmatic of things that can be assessed by the *witnesses*. The requirement is not that *beis din* see and assess the instrument, but that the *eidim* be able to assess it. *Af kol she-masur le-eidim* — any instrument assessable by the witnesses suffices. *Perat she-yatza even mitachat yado shel makeh* — the exclusion is when the stone left the striker's hand before the witnesses had a good visual on it, such that even the *eidim* cannot assess it. In that case, the defendant goes free.

The relevance to the *ed na'aseh dayan* discussion is then made explicit. The *baraita* attributes to the court the question *ve-chi bifnei beis din hikah she-yod'im kamah hikah* — as if to say, if *beis din* had directly witnessed it, they would know the specifics. This implies that if *beis din* had witnessed the event directly, they could use that knowledge. But does this not contradict Rabbi Akiva's view that witnessing an event disqualifies one from judging? The *Gemara* answers: *aliba de-Rabbi Shimon HaTeimani ka'amrei leih ve-lo sevira lei* — Rabbi Akiva is merely arguing from within Shimon HaTeimani's own framework to expose its absurdity. He is showing that the *beis din*-assessment requirement leads to impossible demands. Rabbi Akiva himself does not hold that a *beis din* witnessing an event can ever serve as judge; as soon as they become witnesses, they must recuse themselves entirely.

---

## Shor Tam & Mu'ad

### Judgment Order Rule

The final *baraita* of our daf deals with the sequencing of judgments when an ox has both killed a person and inflicted property damage. The *baraita* rules: *shor tam she-hemit ve-hizik — danin oto dinei nefashot ve-ein danin oto dinei mammonot* — a *shor tam* that killed and caused damage is tried first for the capital offense (*dinei nefashot*), and the monetary case (*dinei mammonot*) does not proceed. Conversely, *mu'ad she-hemit ve-hizik — danin oto dinei mammonot ve-chozrin ve-danin oto dinei nefashot* — a *mu'ad* that killed and caused damage is tried first for the monetary obligation, and only then for the capital offense.

### Tam Ox Rule

The logic for the *shor tam* case is clear. A *shor tam* pays for damages from the body of the ox itself — *mi-guf ha-shor*. But an ox condemned as a *shor nesakel* becomes *assur be-hana'ah*: the stoned ox may not be used for any benefit. If the capital judgment is rendered first, the ox becomes a *shor nesakel* and there is nothing left from which to collect the monetary damages. The injured party loses his recovery. Hence, for the *shor tam*, the capital case takes priority and the monetary case simply cannot proceed; the order of judgment is not merely a sequencing preference — it is determinative of outcome.

### Mu'ad Problem

For the *mu'ad* ox, however, the question is less obvious. A *mu'ad* owner pays the full damages out of his own pocket, not from the body of the ox. Whether the ox becomes a *shor nesakel* before or after the monetary judgment is rendered, the owner can still be compelled to pay. Why should the order of proceedings matter at all? If the *dinei nefashot* case were adjudicated first, condemning the ox, why couldn't *beis din* then proceed to the monetary case and order the owner to pay?

### Rava's Source

Rava found the scholars of the *beis medrash* debating this very question and offered his analysis. They proposed that the *baraita* follows the position of Shimon HaTeimani: *de-amar mah egrof meyuchad she-masur le-eidah u-le-eidim* — the *beis din* must assess the instrument of injury. For an ox, the ox *is* the instrument of injury. Before any judgment can be rendered in the monetary case, *beis din* must assess the ox — examine it and determine whether, under the circumstances, it had the capability and characteristics to inflict the damage that occurred. *Alma ba'inan umdana de-veis din* — we require a direct assessment by *beis din* of the instrument.

### Execution Delay

But here is the problem: *ve-ha keivan de-gamruhu le-dineih le-katla, lo mashghinan beih le-umdana de-veis din* — once the ox has been condemned to execution as a *shor nesakel*, one cannot delay the execution to allow *beis din* to conduct its assessment for the monetary case. The reason is *lo ma'aninan le-dineih* — we do not cause an affliction of justice by making the ox wait for its execution.

This principle is deeply parallel to the rules governing human capital punishment. Throughout Bava Kamma we have encountered the *shor nesakel* as an analogue to a human convicted of a capital offense — the ox is processed with many of the same procedural requirements as a human murderer. Here, too, the parallel holds: just as one does not delay the execution of a person convicted of a capital crime — because the certainty of impending death combined with an indefinite wait constitutes a form of torment — so too one does not delay the execution of a *shor nesakel*. Once the ox is condemned, it must be executed without delay. The *beis din*'s need to assess the ox for purposes of the monetary judgment cannot justify holding the condemned animal in suspension. Since the *umdana* required by Shimon HaTeimani's position cannot be performed post-condemnation without causing this unacceptable delay, the monetary case must precede the capital one. The *Gemara* notes that Rava's response to this explanation will be taken up on the following daf.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 91

## Murder Weapon Inspection

### Stone or Fist Dispute

The daf opens in the midst of a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Shimon HaTeimani regarding whether the *beit din* must directly inspect the murder weapon. The source for this debate is the *pasuk*, *ve-chi yakkeh ish et re'ehu be-even o be-egrof* — "if a man smites his fellow with a stone or a fist." It is worth noting at the outset that the *pasuk* itself is addressing not murder but bodily injury; nonetheless, the debate between Rabbi Akiva and Shimon HaTeimani centers specifically on the murder context and on whether the *beit din* must personally examine the implement used.

### Direct Inspection View

Shimon HaTeimani reasons as follows: just as the *beit din* could directly inspect the man's fist — which is always present and available for examination — so too must they be able to directly inspect any weapon used to kill. The logic is that if direct inspection of the fist is the standard, then whatever object serves as the instrument of killing must likewise be physically examined by the court itself.

### Witnesses Suffice

Rabbi Akiva rejects this position on practical grounds. One could never expect the *beit din* to observe all the circumstances under which a murder was committed. Since the court relies on *edim* — witnesses — for everything else regarding the act, it may similarly rely on the witnesses' testimony regarding the murder weapon. The *beit din* need not see it directly.

## Ox Murder & Injury

### Shor Tam & Mu'ad

The *gemara* then introduces a *baraita* that, in some respects, belongs thematically in the earlier portions of Bava Kamma but is brought here for its connection to the preceding discussion. The case: an ox has both murdered a person and caused injury to another. If the ox is a *shor tam* — an ox without prior warning — the injured party will simply not be able to collect, because a *shor tam*'s liability for damage is paid only from its own body (*mi-gufo*), and the ox itself will become a *shor haniskal*, sentenced to execution, rendering it worthless for collection purposes. In such a case, only the *shor haniskal* judgment needs to be carried out, and the injured party loses his claim.

However, if the ox is a *shor mu'ad* — a forewarned ox, whose owner pays cash for damages — one might think the order of adjudication is irrelevant. Yet the *baraita* insists that even here, it is essential to first adjudicate the payment case and only afterward adjudicate the *shor haniskal* case. Reversing the order, the *baraita* says, prevents the injured party from collecting.

### Reversed Order Problem

This prompts the *gemara*'s question: why should reversing the order prevent collection? Once the ox is declared a *shor haniskal*, it will be stoned — but the owner's obligation to pay cash for the injury of a *shor mu'ad* remains. The cash obligation does not depend on the ox's continued existence. So what precisely is lost by adjudicating the *shor haniskal* first?

### Rava's Explanation

Rava reports that he found the scholars of the *beit midrash* explaining this *baraita* as reflecting the position of Shimon HaTeimani. According to Shimon HaTeimani, just as the *beit din* must directly inspect the murder weapon, so too must it directly inspect the object that caused the injury — and this applies not only when a person inflicts injury but even when an ox does so. The court must physically bring the ox before it and determine: could this ox, under ordinary circumstances, have caused the kind of damage it did? The question is not whether it in fact caused the damage — that is established — but whether such damage was to be expected from this ox.

This is the key link. Once the ox has already been declared a *shor haniskal*, you cannot ask the court to hold off on executing it for a week while it handles the separate injury case. And that is why, according to Shimon HaTeimani, the order is critical: the injury case must be tried first, before the *shor haniskal* judgment is entered, so that the *beit din* can still directly examine the ox.

## Order & Payment Logic

### Immediate Execution

The *gemara* explores a further dimension of why the order matters. Once an ox has been declared a *shor haniskal*, it must be executed without delay. One cannot say: "Let us defer the execution for a week so that the injured party's case can also be heard and the *beit din* can inspect the ox." That deferral is simply not permitted.

### Plowing First

The *gemara* therefore proposes that the proper order creates a window of opportunity: if the injury case is adjudicated first, the injured party can be paid by using the ox — putting it to work plowing his fields — and only after the debt has been recouped through that use is the *shor haniskal* judgment carried out.

### Postponement Affliction

What makes postponing the execution impermissible? The *gemara* draws a striking parallel to capital cases involving human beings: just as it is considered a form of anguish and affliction to postpone the execution of a person who has already been sentenced to death, so too it is considered affliction to the ox to defer its execution. This is a remarkably formal application of a human legal concept to an animal. The ox presumably has no awareness that such an order has been issued; the *gemara* itself acknowledges the irony. Yet the formalism serves an important purpose: the entire legal apparatus surrounding the *shor haniskal* — including the deliberative process, the witnesses, the court proceedings — mirrors the procedures for capital cases involving human beings. The Torah was radical in insisting that only the ox, and not the owner or his children, is punished, and by treating the process with the full gravity of a capital case, the legal system underscores that this is no trivial matter.

It follows that once the ox is declared a *shor haniskal*, one cannot allow the injured party to use it for plowing during the waiting period — because keeping it alive to plow constitutes the very postponement that is forbidden.

### Owner Absence

Rava himself then offers an alternative explanation that does not depend on Shimon HaTeimani's position at all, making the ruling consistent even with Rabbi Akiva's view. He posits the following scenario: witnesses were accepted to testify that the ox both murdered and injured — and then the owner fled. One cannot adjudicate a case in the owner's absence; the hearing of witnesses must take place with the owner present, and that has already occurred. But the problem now is different: the owner has absconded with all his assets. The only remaining asset from which any recovery is possible is the ox itself.

The *gemara* presses: if the owner has fled, the problem is not the order of adjudication — it is simply that the owner is not present. How does the order of the cases resolve that? The *gemara* clarifies: the witnesses testified and were received, and then the owner fled. The procedural validity of the testimony is not in question. The operative issue is that there are no other assets from which to collect. This forces the question of which case to adjudicate first, because everything turns on what happens to the ox.

### Payment from Ox

If the injury case is adjudicated first, the injured party can be paid by having the ox plow his field until the debt is satisfied — then the *shor haniskal* judgment proceeds. If the *shor haniskal* judgment is entered first, the ox immediately must be executed, and the injured party is left with nothing to collect from.

The *gemara* then raises an apparent objection: if payment via the ox's plowing works for a *shor mu'ad*, why doesn't the same solution apply to a *shor tam*? By a *shor tam*, the *baraita* states that it makes no difference what order the cases are tried — the injured party cannot collect regardless. But seemingly, the same trick should work: let the injured party use the ox to plow before it is stoned, and collect his payment that way, even though a *shor tam*'s liability is limited to the ox's body (*mi-gufo*). After all, he would be getting paid from the ox's body — through the benefit generated by the ox's labor.

## Plowing Benefit Debate

### Plowing Not Body

This is where Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana enters with a crucial analytical point. He derives from the *gemara*'s discussion: *radya alya de-mari hu* — the benefit derived from the ox's plowing is not considered the ox's body. It is considered an asset belonging to the owner. Therefore, collecting payment through the ox's plowing is not equivalent to collecting *mi-gufo*, from the body of the ox itself.

### Shor Tam Exemption

This distinction explains why the solution does not work for a *shor tam*. A *shor tam*'s liability is specifically *mi-gufo* — from the physical body of the ox, meaning the proceeds from its sale. The benefit derived from putting the ox to work does not count as the body of the ox; it counts as the owner's other assets. Since the *shor tam* regime limits recovery strictly to the ox's body, and the owner has no other accessible assets, the injured party simply cannot be paid. No reordering of the cases can solve this.

### Shor Mu'ad Solution

By contrast, a *shor mu'ad*'s owner is liable in cash from his general assets. The benefit derived from the ox's plowing is treated as the owner's asset — and since the *shor mu'ad* owner pays from his assets, using the plowing benefit as the medium of payment is perfectly valid. Accordingly, adjudicating the injury case first, allowing the injured party to work the ox until the debt is covered, and only then proceeding to the *shor haniskal* judgment, is a workable and legally sound arrangement.

## Object Assessment

### Question Formulation

The *gemara* now raises a new question that flows naturally from everything discussed: *yesh omed l'nezikin o ein omed l'nezikin* — when damage is caused, do we assess whether it was reasonable to expect that this damage would occur? In other words, does the same *umdena* — assessment of the capacity of the object — that applies in murder cases also apply in cases of civil damages?

### Murder Standard

The framework for murder is clear. The *pasuk* in Bamidbar says explicitly: *asher yamut bo hika'u yamut* — if he smote him with a wood weapon that could kill him, then he shall be put to death. The Torah itself requires that the weapon have the capacity to kill; this is not a *drash* but close to the *pshat* of the verses. If a person was in a fight and struck another with a stone that would not, under normal circumstances, have been lethal — yet in this instance the victim died — the assailant cannot be executed, because the act is characterized as a freak occurrence rather than a genuine act of murder.

This is striking enough in murder. In order for execution to follow, it is not sufficient that the killer intended to kill and that the victim in fact died. The weapon must have had the capacity. Consider the following scenario: a man tries to kill his victim, takes a rock, strikes him, and the victim dies. If *beit din* determines that the rock should not, under ordinary circumstances, have produced that result, the killer goes free — not because he lacked intent, and not because the victim survived, but because the causal mechanism was, legally speaking, anomalous.

The question posed by the *gemara* is whether this principle extends to *nezikin*, civil damages. Imagine striking someone's valuable object with a stone in a way that, under normal circumstances, should not have damaged it — yet damage results. Does the person escape liability on the grounds that the causation was aberrant? The *gemara* frames the question as potentially factual rather than purely legal: perhaps the very nature of damage is that almost anything can cause it, so there is no meaningful standard of "capacity to cause damage" in the first place. Or perhaps — *lo shana* — it is no different from murder, and we do assess.

### Well Depth Example

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this from the laws of the *bor* — the pit or well. It is established that a well ten *tefachim* deep can kill an animal that falls in, and the owner is liable for the death. If the well is less than ten *tefachim*, the owner is exempt for the death but liable for any injury the animal sustains. The *gemara* initially reads this as teaching that for any depth — even a single *tefach* — there is liability for *nezikin*, suggesting that no assessment of adequacy is performed: *ein omdin l'nezikin*, there is no capacity assessment for damages.

The *gemara* rejects this reading. The proper reading, it says, moves from the higher depth downward. Ten *tefachim* produces liability for death. Just below ten — say, 9.9 *tefachim* — produces liability for injury but not death. This does not imply that any depth, no matter how shallow, produces liability for injury. It may still be that for a very shallow well, one must assess whether that depth was capable of producing the particular injury that resulted. The proof fails to establish *ein omed l'nezikin*.

### Eye Ear Distinction

The *gemara* tries again with a case from the laws of the *eved Kena'ani* — the Canaanite slave. If a master strikes his slave directly in the eye and blinds him, or directly in the ear and deafens him, the slave goes free — for the Torah grants freedom to a slave whose limb is knocked out. The *pasuk* uses the language of *ve-shichatah* — "destroyed it" — which the *gemara* understands to include functional destruction, even where the organ itself remains physically intact.

The interesting case is the following: if the master struck the wall *next* to the slave's eye — without actually touching the slave — and the resulting shock caused the slave to lose his sight; or if he struck next to the slave's ear and the slave lost his hearing — in these cases the slave does not go free. The *gemara* asks: what is the reason? It suggests that it must be because *ba'inan umdena* — we require an assessment, and in this case the act of striking near the body (without contact) was not, under normal circumstances, the kind of thing that should have produced blindness or deafness. Therefore, it counts as a freak occurrence, and there is no legal consequence.

This would seem to prove that *yesh omed l'nezikin* — we do assess in damage cases.

### Direct vs Indirect

The *gemara* rejects this inference as well. The reason the slave does not go free, it explains, is not because of an *umdena* about the object's capacity. It is because *hu d'avise nafshiah* — he frightened himself; he brought it upon himself. When there is no direct physical contact, the legal definition of "causing damage" is simply not satisfied. What happened to the slave was not produced by an act done *to* him; it was his own physical reaction to something done *near* him.

This is a formal legal category, not a factual assessment about likelihood. The *gemara* makes this explicit through a *baraita*: one who frightens his fellow is exempt from human courts but liable in the heavenly court. *Taka be'ozno ve-cheirshah* — if he shouted directly into his ear and caused deafness, he is exempt; *achazo ve-taka be'ozno ve-cheirshah* — if he held the person while shouting into his ear and deaffened him, he is liable. The difference is purely one of physical contact. If there is contact, the act is legally defined as an injury he inflicted. If there is no contact, the act is not legally classified as an injury done to the victim — regardless of how predictably it might cause harm.

This distinction is formally bizarre but halachically consequential. The *gemara* is not saying that blowing out someone's eardrum by yelling at close range is morally innocent; it is saying that without the formal criterion of physical contact, the legal category of *nezikin* does not attach.

### Medical Assessment

The *gemara* makes yet another attempt to resolve the *umdena* question. It cites a ruling that the five heads of damages — *nezek*, *tza'ar*, *ripui*, *sheves*, and *boshet* — are assessed and paid immediately upon the occurrence of the injury. The notable cases are *ripui* and *sheves*: one does not know in advance how long the recuperation period will last or how large the medical bills will be. Nevertheless, *beit din* assesses the expected cost at the time of judgment and pays that amount immediately.

Furthermore: if the assessment predicted a certain recovery period and the victim recovered more slowly — his bad luck, he receives no more than the assessed amount. If he recovered more quickly — his good luck, he pockets the full assessed amount. Rava adds that if someone was assessed to be incapacitated for a full day and recovered in the afternoon and was able to return to work, he still receives payment for the full day's *sheves*, because the injury itself was judged to be worth a day's lost work; the quicker recovery was a gift from heaven, not a revision of that assessment.

The *gemara* considers whether this proves *yesh omed l'nezikin*: we assess what is reasonable and the victim receives only what the injury should have cost. The *gemara* rejects this proof, however, because there are two entirely different kinds of assessment at issue. One kind of assessment — which is never in dispute — is determining *how much* damage was done once liability is established: what are the medical costs, how long is the recovery, what is the loss of income? Everyone agrees that this assessment takes place. The *umdena* question is entirely different: it asks whether we assess the *object* that caused the damage to determine whether it even had the *capacity* to produce the harm. That second question — *le-omed ḥeftza* — is the one that remains unresolved after all these attempted proofs.

## Assessment Conclusion

### Object Inspection Rule

The resolution finally arrives from Shimon HaTeimani's own ruling. The *pasuk* about the stone and the fist — *be-even o be-egrof* — is, as noted at the outset, a *pasuk* about injury, not murder. When Shimon HaTeimani says that the *beit din* must directly inspect the weapon — just as it could inspect the fist — and Rabbi Akiva says reliance on witnesses suffices — both of them are speaking about the injury context. The very debate between Shimon HaTeimani and Rabbi Akiva presupposes that *yesh omed l'nezikin*: all agree that an assessment of the object's capacity must be made in injury cases. The only dispute is whether the *beit din* must make that assessment directly, by physically examining the object, or whether the witnesses' testimony about the object is sufficient.

*Shema mina* — this is the conclusion: *yesh omed l'nezikin*. Everyone agrees that in cases of civil damage, just as in murder, an assessment is made of whether the object that caused the harm had the capacity to do so. The debate between Shimon HaTeimani and Rabbi Akiva is solely about who performs that assessment — the *beit din* itself or the *edim*. According to Shimon HaTeimani, the court must see the weapon directly, which is why the ox must be brought before *beit din* for examination in injury cases. According to Rabbi Akiva, the witnesses' account suffices.

It follows that if someone throws a stone at another's property, causes damage, and *beit din* concludes that under normal circumstances that stone should not have caused that result — the perpetrator goes free. This is genuinely surprising in the context of civil law, especially given the principle of *adam mu'ad l'olam* — that a person is always considered forewarned for his own acts and bears liability regardless of negligence or intent. Evidently, the absence of reasonable capacity in the instrument overrides even that principle and breaks the causal chain entirely.

## Spitting & Shame

### Spit Contact Rule

The *mishnah* states that if someone spat at another person and the spit reached (*higi'a bo ha-rok*) — that is, it physically made contact with the person — the spitter is liable for *boshet*, the *mishnah* specifying a payment of 400 *zuz* or the like. The *gemara* now refines this: *lo shanu ela bo* — this applies only if the spit actually struck the person. But *aval be-vigdo* — if it only hit his garments — there is no *boshet* payment.

### Verbal vs Physical

This raises an important structural question about *boshet*. The *gemara* asks: if spit hitting the clothing rather than the body generates no liability, is that any different from shaming someone with words alone? And indeed, *amri b'ma'arava mishemei de-Rabbi Yossi bar Avin* — they said in the west in the name of Rabbi Yossi bar Avin: this demonstrates that *biyush bidvarim patur mi-klum* — verbal shaming, with no accompanying physical act, carries no legal liability whatsoever.

### Words No Payment

This is a striking feature of *hilchot nezikin*. Shaming someone purely through words — publicly mentioning a private matter, calling someone a name in *reshut ha-rabbim* — may be a severe prohibition (the *gemara* elsewhere likens it to murder), but it is not a tort for which damages are paid. The comparison to *motzi shem ra* — defamation, which in American law generates a cause of action for slander or libel — is instructive: in *halacha*, even serious reputational harm caused by words does not give rise to compensable damages. There may be elements that fall under *garmi* or *grama*, but the basic structure does not provide compensation for verbal shaming and slander.

The logic that emerges is parallel to what we saw with *nezikin* from non-contact acts: just as one is not liable for injury unless there was actual physical contact with the victim's body, one is not liable for *boshet* unless one performed a physical act directed at the person. Removing a woman's head covering, for instance, creates liability even though no skin was touched: the covering was on her body, and removing it is legally treated as doing something to her body. But spitting on her clothes is merely affecting her clothing, not her person — it is categorically closer to verbal shaming, and accordingly carries no liability.

One additional point must be noted: *boshet* is not limited to cases where physical injury also occurred. Spitting on someone, pulling off a head covering — these cause no physical harm whatsoever, yet they constitute independent torts for which full damages are owed. The requirement for *kavanah* — intent — applies here as well: the act must be done with the intention to cause embarrassment or to cause harm. But the point is that *boshet* stands entirely on its own as a cause of action, independent of injury.

## Honor & Payment

### Amounts Min or Max

The *mishnah* provides specific figures for *boshet* payments — 200 *zuz*, 400 *zuz*, and so on — and then adds *ha-kol lefi kevodo*, that all amounts vary according to the honor of the person involved. The *gemara* now asks how to read the relationship between these two elements. Does the *tanna kamma* intend the listed amounts as maximums — meaning that based on a person's lesser honor, one could pay less — or as minimums — meaning that based on a person's greater honor, one would pay more?

The *gemara* resolves this from Rabbi Akiva's formulation. Rabbi Akiva says that even the poor of Israel are to be regarded as if they are free people who have lost their wealth, as sons of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, and are therefore entitled to the full amount. *Shema mina*: since Rabbi Akiva feels compelled to insist on the full payment for the poor, it is clear that the *tanna kamma* had been using the listed amounts as maximums, permitting reductions based on lower social standing. Rabbi Akiva disputes this and rules that everyone receives the maximum.

### Akiva Full Amount

Rabbi Akiva's position reflects a principled egalitarianism in the law of *boshet*: the shame of being spat upon or having one's covering removed is not diminished by poverty. Every person, regardless of station, is heir to a dignity that demands full recompense when violated.

### Hair Covering Story

The *mishnah* concludes with a story illustrating Rabbi Akiva's ruling. A man watched for a woman to appear at the entrance of her courtyard, went and removed her head covering in a public space, and then was instructed by Rabbi Akiva to pay 400 *zuz*. The man asked for time to pay, and time was granted — but he then took advantage of the delay to perform a trick that arguably implicated the woman's own cooperation, apparently attempting to undermine the claim. Rabbi Akiva dismissed the maneuver and imposed full liability.

## Payment Timing Rules

### No Time Injury

This story raises a procedural question. The *gemara* notes that Rabbi Chanina rules: *ein notnin zman l'chavalot* — one does not grant time to pay when the debt is for *chavalah*, physical injury. Why then was time granted in the *boshet* case?

### Financial Loss Logic

The answer lies in the nature of the loss. When someone causes a physical injury, there is an immediate and concrete financial diminishment: medical costs accumulate, income is lost, the body itself loses value. Granting time for payment in such cases means the victim suffers ongoing financial harm while waiting. But *boshet* — shame — does not generate a financial deficit in the same sense. The victim is not out of pocket in any direct way; the 400 *zuz* is a fine for the violation of dignity. Since no ongoing financial loss accrues from the delay, it is appropriate to grant time.

## Honor & Payment (II)

### Time to Pay

Rabbi Akiva's response in the *mishnah* thus concerns the *boshet* case specifically: he confirms that for an act of shaming without physical injury, the court may indeed grant time for payment, since the payment is punitive-compensatory in character rather than a direct reimbursement of quantifiable loss.

## Self-Injury Allowed

### Embarrass Not Wound

The *gemara* now confronts a tension. The *mishnah* states that *ha-chovel b'atzmo af al pi she-eino rashai patur* — one who injures himself, even though it is not permitted, is exempt from paying himself. This implies that self-injury is prohibited. Yet a *baraita* cited earlier quotes Rabbi Akiva as saying *adam rashai l'chavel b'atzmo* — a person is permitted to injure himself. How are these reconciled?

Rava resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya, kan b'chavalah, kan b'boshet* — there is no difficulty; one source speaks of physical wounding, the other of embarrassing oneself. Wounding oneself is not permitted; embarrassing oneself is permitted. The *mishnah* says you may not wound yourself. The *baraita* says you may embarrass yourself if you choose.

The *gemara* presses: but the *mishnah* explicitly addresses *chavalah* — *ha-chovel b'atzmo*. How does that speak to embarrassment? The *gemara* explains: Rabbi Akiva in the *baraita* was making a rhetorical point with a *kal va-chomer* structure. *Lo mibaya boshet* — it goes without saying that one may embarrass oneself. *Ella afilu chavalah* — but even when it comes to physical wounding, which one is not permitted to do to oneself, *acherim she-chavlu bo chayavin* — others who wound that person are still fully liable. The *mishnah*'s point is not that self-inflicted wounding has no consequences for others; it is that self-inflicted wounding carries no personal payment obligation against oneself. The prohibition on self-wounding stands, but it does not generate a compensable claim.

### Oath to Injure

The *gemara* then challenges the prohibition on self-wounding from a different direction. A *baraita* in *hilchot shevuot* teaches: if someone swears to do harm to himself — *le-hara le-atzmo* — and then does not follow through, might he be exempt because the oath was never binding in the first place? An oath to violate a prohibition is non-binding. The *baraita* answers: *talmud lomar le-hara o le-heitiv* — the verse teaches "to do evil or to do good." Just as one has permission to do good to oneself, so one has permission to do harm to oneself — and therefore an oath to do harm to oneself is entirely binding. The oath is not dismissed as an oath on a prohibited act.

This *baraita* seems to state unambiguously that harming oneself is permitted, making such an oath valid. The *baraita* contrasts this with taking an oath to harm someone else — *ekeh ploni ve-eftza mocho* — which is not binding because one has no permission to harm others. The implication is stark: self-harm is in a different legal category from harming others precisely because it is permitted.

### Fasting Interpretation

Shmuel offers a resolution: *be-yoshev be-ta'anit* — the *baraita* about oaths refers to sitting in a fast, not to physical wounding. One may swear to fast, and that oath is binding because one has permission to deprive oneself of food. The *baraita*'s language of "harming oneself" means self-deprivation — fasting or similar acts — not actual physical injury.

The *gemara* challenges this interpretation. The *baraita* draws a parallel: an oath to harm others is not binding, and the case given is *ekeh ploni ve-eftza mocho* — a violent physical assault. If harming others means violent assault, then harming oneself, the counterpart to which the oath *is* binding, must similarly refer to physical injury, not mere fasting. Forced starvation of another — *de-madeik lehu be-androna*, locking them in a room — is the analogous act on the other side. The *gemara* suggests that could work technically, but the parallel is strained: the case of harming another is plainly one of physical violence, and its counterpart of harming oneself should be the same.

### Tannaim Debate

Unable to reconcile the sources through reinterpretation, the *gemara* concludes: *ela tanna'i hi* — it is a dispute among *tannaim*. Some *tannaim* hold that a person is permitted to wound himself; others hold that he is not. As Tosafot points out, the two statements attributed to Rabbi Akiva — one permitting self-injury and one prohibiting it — may themselves represent two different *tannaim* who each report Rabbi Akiva's position differently: *trei tanna'ei aliba de-Rabbi Akiva*. What is clear is that the *Rabbi Akiva* of our *mishnah* holds that self-wounding is not permitted, while the *baraita* reflects a position that it is.

## Self-Injury Sources

### Suicide Verse

Now that the *gemara* has established a *tannaic* dispute on self-injury, it identifies the specific *tanna* whose view underlies the prohibition. The *baraita* cites: *ve-ach es dimchem le-nafshoteichem edrosh* — "and your blood for your souls I will seek." Rabbi Elazar reads this as: I will hold your souls accountable for the spilling of your blood — that is, for suicide. This verse is the basis for the prohibition of taking one's own life.

### Bal Tashchit

The *gemara* presses: is the prohibition of self-wounding really derived from the suicide verse? Suicide is actual killing — *ketala shani* — and surely everyone agrees that is forbidden. The question is physical wounding that falls short of death. For permanent injury — cutting off a limb — the prohibition might rest on *bal tashchit*, the prohibition against wasteful destruction derived from the verse commanding that fruit-bearing trees not be cut down during a siege. Rabbi Elazar states that one who tears his garments excessively in mourning for the dead receives lashes for violating *bal tashchit*. By *kal va-chomer*, if *bal tashchit* applies to property, it certainly applies to one's own body — *kol sheken gufo*.

### Non-Permanent Examples

The *gemara* tests the scope of *bal tashchit* as a basis for prohibiting self-injury. It suggests that *bal tashchit* may apply to garments but not necessarily to the body — because clothes do not heal (*pesida de-lo hadra*), whereas the body does. The example given: Rabbi Yochanan called his garments *mechabduta* — the things that honor him — indicating that he treated his clothing with great care as a vehicle of dignity. Rav Chisda, when walking among thorns and thistles, would lift his cloak to spare it from tearing, even at the cost of scraping his ankles and shins. His reasoning: *ze ma'ale arucha ve-ze eino ma'ale arucha* — the skin heals, the garment does not. The body's capacity to recover distinguishes it from inanimate objects for the purpose of *bal tashchit*. A non-permanent injury to the body, therefore, may not fall under *bal tashchit* at all, leaving the question of its basis unresolved.

### Affliction Sin

The *gemara* then turns to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's teaching. The Torah requires a *nazir* who became *tamei* to bring a *korban* and atone for having sinned against the *nefesh* — the soul. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar reads this broadly: the *nazir* sinned by afflicting himself — by withholding from himself the pleasure of wine. And by *kal va-chomer*: if a *nazir* who deprived himself only of wine is called a sinner, how much more so one who afflicts himself in any other way.

This is a notably weak foundation for a prohibition of self-injury. First, it is not a direct prohibition but rather a characterization — *nikra chotei*, he is *called* a sinner. Second, and more critically, the *kal va-chomer* seems to reach far beyond physical wounding: if skipping wine makes one a sinner, does voluntary fasting also constitute sin? The *gemara* itself seems aware that there is no obvious qualitative line between accepting an unnecessary *ta'anit* and causing oneself some minor physical pain.

### Rambam Wounding

The Rambam, when he codifies the prohibition of self-injury, addresses it specifically in terms of *chavalah* — wounding that draws blood. He rules that a person is forbidden to wound another person, and is similarly forbidden to wound himself. He adds a further prohibition: even striking another person without causing a wound violates a biblical command, derived from the verse *lo yosif lehakoto* — the prohibition against administering excessive lashes. Since even the court-appointed administrator of lashes is restricted by this verse, the principle extends to any person: one may not strike another. What is not fully clear from the Rambam, however, is the specific biblical basis for the self-wounding prohibition in particular — whether it stems from *lo yosif lehakoto*, from the *bal tashchit* principle, from the *nazir* verse, or from some other source.

### Basis Unclear

The *gemara* leaves the precise basis for the prohibition of self-injury unresolved. The suicide prohibition is clear and separately grounded. The prohibition of permanent injury finds support in *bal tashchit*, at least as applied to objects, though the extension to the body is contested. Non-permanent self-injury appears to rest on the *nazir*-based *kal va-chomer* of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, which is itself a less-than-precise foundation. The Rambam appears to absorb the question into the broader prohibition on striking — but that verse is generally understood to apply to others, not oneself. The result is a prohibition that is practically clear in its core applications but theoretically elusive in its precise source — a fitting conclusion to a *sugya* that has navigated between the formal and the intuitive across multiple areas of *hilchot nezikin*.
