The *Gemara* answers: *mipnei takanas hashavin* — because of the ordinance to facilitate repentance, discussed in the following section.

## Takanat Hashavin (III)

### Improvement Example

The ruling that a *gazlan* who improved a stolen object may be compensated for his improvement is, on its face, astonishing. If *shinuy bamkomo omed* — if the object remains the owner's throughout — why should the *gazlan* receive any benefit at all? The answer is *takanas hashavin*: the rabbis recognized a practical obstacle to repentance and restitution. A *gazlan* who has invested significantly in improving a stolen object — fattening an animal, building from lumber, processing raw materials — faces a steep disincentive to return it. If he must surrender the entire enhanced value, he may well choose not to come forward at all.

The *takanah* therefore allows the *gazlan* to be compensated for the *shevach*, the increase in value attributable to his efforts. Consider the concrete example: one steals lumber worth one hundred *zuz* and fashions it into a table worth one thousand *zuz*. Biblically, the owner should receive the full table. The rabbis, however, instituted that the *gazlan* keeps the table and pays the original owner only one hundred *zuz* — the value at the time of the theft, *ki'she'as gezeilah*. The *gazlan* thus retains nine hundred *zuz* of *shevach*. This is a striking arrangement, and it invites the rueful observation that — absent fear of divine punishment or social sanction — the legal structure alone provides remarkably little disincentive to steal. A *gazlan* who is caught need only return the original value, keeping all appreciation. The *takanah*, however, is not designed to benefit the *gazlan* as such; it is designed to bring stolen property back into the legitimate economy and to facilitate the owner's compensation, even if incomplete. In that sense it serves society's interest, not merely the thief's conscience.

## Shinuy Bamkomo Omed (II)

### R. Yishmael Peah

The final member of Abaye's grouping is Rabbi Yishmael, whose case concerns the obligation of *peah* — leaving the corner of a field for the poor. The *braisa* sets out a graduated framework: if one did not separate *peah* from the standing grain, one may do so from the sheaves; if not from the sheaves, from the threshed pile — *kari*; if not from the *kari*, one may still do so up until the *meiruach*.

The *meiruach* — the smoothing of the grain heap — is the halachic trigger for the obligation of *terumos u'maasros*. Its significance for the gifts to the poor is that all such gifts — *peah*, *leket*, *shichcha* — are normally exempt from *terumos u'maasros*, so the poor may receive them without further obligation. Once *meiruach* has occurred, however, the grain becomes obligated in *terumos u'maasros*, which changes the character of what the poor receives. From that point, one must first separate *terumos u'maasros* and then give the net amount to the poor.

Rabbi Yishmael goes further still: *af mafrish min ha'isa v'nosein lo* — even if the grain has been converted into flour and kneaded into dough, one may still separate the *peah* equivalent and give it to the poor. This is striking, because by the stage of dough the object has undergone substantial transformation. Nevertheless, Rabbi Yishmael treats it as the same entity for the purposes of the poor's entitlement — a clear expression of *shinuy bamkomo omed*.

### Rav Pappa Challenge

Rav Pappa challenges Abaye's grouping with a sharp observation: does Abaye mean to say that all of these *Tannaim* hold like Beis Shammai? It seems implausible that such diverse authorities across different areas of *halacha* would all converge on Beis Shammai's position. Abaye responds that his claim is not that they all hold *precisely* like Beis Shammai. Rather, even Beis Hillel — who disputes Beis Shammai's position on *esnan* — would not dispute the principle in all the other cases. The shared orientation of these *Tannaim* is that the threshold for recognizing a genuine *shinuy* is high; in their respective domains, each one insists that the changes under discussion fall below that threshold.

## Rava's Nuanced Reading

### Rava on Dyeing

Rava now offers a sustained counter-reading of Abaye's grouping, arguing that none of these *Tannaim* in fact reflects a blanket principle of *shinuy bamkomo omed*. Each is responding to the specific features of his particular case. Beginning with Rabbi Shimon ben Yehudah: his ruling that dyeing wool is not a *shinuy* is not a general statement about *shinuy bamkomo omed*. It is driven entirely by the fact that dyeing, in the case at hand, is reversible — *yachol lehachziro al yedei tzava*. The dye can be removed. Remove that feature of reversibility, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehudah's ruling disappears with it.

### Rava on Esnan

Beis Shammai's ruling that transformed *esnan* remains forbidden for the *Mizbeach* is similarly explained by specific features of that case. The *esnan* case involves objects designated for the *Mizbeach* — a domain of *gavo'ah*, the sacred. Objects offered to God are subject to heightened scrutiny, and the sense of *mi'us* — revulsion — that attaches to an *esnan* is so strong that it persists through transformation. This is a special *halacha* about sacred offerings, not a universal statement about the persistence of identity through change.

### Rava on Mitzvah

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling, as already discussed, turns on *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* — not on any general principle that *shinuy* leaves identity intact. Rava makes this explicit: it is the *bracha* over stolen food, or more precisely the performance of a *mitzvah* through the fruits of theft, that drives the invalidation. One could, on this reading, hold that *shinuy koneh* as a general matter — that the stolen wheat truly became the thief's own property after the transformation — and still hold that the *mitzvah* of *challah* separation performed with it is invalid, because the avenue to that *mitzvah* was transgression. The analysis thus belongs entirely to the framework of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* and carries no implications for *shinuy* doctrine.

### Rava on Reversibility

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling that a *gazlan* may say *harei shelcha lifanecha* when the animal has weakened is, according to Rava, limited to the specific circumstance of *kachush* — emaciation — which is reversible: *dehadar*. An animal that has grown thin can grow fat again; the change is not permanent. Rava therefore reads Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar not as rejecting *shinuy koneh* across the board, but as recognizing that a reversible deterioration does not trigger *shinuy koneh*. It should also be noted that even without the reversibility argument, a thinner cow is arguably still called a cow by the same name — *shinuy hashem* has not occurred — making it doubtful that such a change would constitute a *shinuy* at all, a point acknowledged by Tosafos.

### Rava on Matanot

Rabbi Yishmael's ruling that *peah* must be given even from dough is explained, according to Rava, by the specific linguistic feature of the biblical text — the extra instance of *ta'azov* (*l'ani ulager ta'azov osam*) written in the *pesukim* governing agricultural gifts to the poor. The word *ta'azov* appears more than once in the relevant passages, and the *yeseira* — the superfluous usage — teaches that the obligation to give gifts to the poor persists even after the grain has undergone transformation. This is a special *derasha* applicable specifically to *matnos aniyim*, not a universal ruling that *shinuy eino koneh*.

## Matanot Aniyim

### Yishmael Position

The question of what actually drives Rabbi Yishmael's ruling is the subject of a formal *ibaya* in the *Gemara*. Rabbi Yonasan asks: *mai ta'ama deRabbi Yishmael?* — what is the underlying rationale? Does Rabbi Yishmael hold as a general principle that *shinuy eino koneh* — that change never transfers ownership — and therefore the poor person's entitlement survives even after the grain becomes dough? Or does Rabbi Yishmael in principle hold *shinuy koneh*, and the ruling here is driven entirely by the extra *ta'azov*, a *limud* specific to *matnos aniyim*?

The question is not merely academic. If Rabbi Yishmael's rationale is the universal principle that *shinuy eino koneh*, then the extra *ta'azov* is superfluous — the *halacha* would follow without it. Conversely, if Rabbi Yishmael holds *shinuy koneh* as a general matter, then the *ta'azov yeseira* is doing real work, supplying an exception specific to gifts to the poor. The *Gemara* notes that for the *Rabanan* — who hold that one need not give *matnos aniyim* from dough — the question arises in the opposite direction: what do they do with the extra *ta'azov*? Since by their view *shinuy* has occurred and the obligation has lapsed, why does the Torah repeat the word?

### Hefker Case

The *Gemara* answers by citing a *braisa* about a vineyard declared *hefker*. If one declares his vineyard *hefker* — ownerless — in the middle of the night when no one is present to take possession, and then rises early in the morning and harvests it himself, he is still obligated in *peret*, *ololos*, *shichcha*, and *peah* — all the gifts to the poor — but is exempt from *maaser*. This is because *hefker* in principle terminates the obligation of *maaser*, and even a brief period of *hefker* status suffices for that purpose. However, the obligation of *matnos aniyim* persists despite the *hefker* interlude. This, says the *Gemara*, is the force of the extra *ta'azov*: even where circumstances would normally extinguish the obligation — here, the vineyard having passed through a state of *hefker* — the gifts to the poor must still be given. This is a distinct application of the *yeseira* unrelated to *shinuy*, which explains why the *Rabanan* require the extra word even as they hold that *shinuy* does terminate the obligation.

### Stringency of Matanot

An important structural distinction emerges from this discussion. The exemption from *maaser* can be triggered by *hefker* even for a brief period; the obligation of *matnos aniyim* is more persistent and cannot be extinguished in the same way. The obligations to the poor — *peah*, *leket*, *shichcha*, and the like — are governed by the language of *ta'azov*, which signals a duty to leave, to relinquish, to let go. That language generates an especially durable claim on behalf of the poor that survives circumstances — a fleeting *hefker*, a transformation of the grain — that would be sufficient to extinguish comparable obligations. It is worth noting that *maaser ani*, which is the *maaser* given to the poor in the third and sixth years of the *shemittah* cycle, is treated as standard *maaser* in this regard — the heightened persistence applies specifically to those gifts defined by the language of *ta'azov* in the relevant *pesukim*, not to *maaser ani* as such.

## Shmuel's Ruling

### Halacha Ruling

The *Gemara* records: *amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel, halacha k'Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. Given the discussion above, this ruling must be understood against the backdrop of the debate between Abaye and Rava as to what Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar actually holds.

### Shamin Contradiction

The *Gemara* immediately raises a contradiction. Shmuel himself stated elsewhere: *ein shamin lo l'ganav v'lo l'gazlan ela l'nezikin* — assessment of the remaining value is done only in cases of damage, not for a *ganav* or *gazlan*. The practical import of this ruling is as follows. In cases of *nezikin*, if a damaging party causes an animal to die or breaks an object, the damaged party retains the carcass or the broken pieces, and the damager pays only the difference between the original value and what remains. But for a *ganav* or *gazlan* who steals an animal and it dies while in his possession, *shinuy koneh* applies — he has acquired it through the change — and therefore he must pay the full original value of the animal. There is no *shamin*, no offset for the residual value of what remains. This clearly presupposes that *shinuy koneh* operates in the case of a *gazlan* whose animal dies — yet Shmuel simultaneously rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who appears to hold *shinuy bamkomo omed*. How are these two rulings reconciled?

### Rava's Resolution

According to Rava, there is no contradiction, because Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling — as Rava has already argued — applies only to reversible deterioration: *b'hachasha d'hadar*. An animal that grows thin can recover. In that case, *shinuy bamkomo omed* applies — the change does not transfer ownership — and the *gazlan* may return the weakened animal. But an animal that dies, or suffers an irreversible injury such as a broken leg that will not heal — *hachasha d'lo hadar* — that is a genuine, permanent change, and *shinuy koneh* applies. When Shmuel rules *halacha k'Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar*, he does so specifically with respect to reversible deterioration. When Shmuel rules *ein shamin l'ganav v'lo l'gazlan*, he is addressing irreversible change. The two rulings are thus perfectly consistent.

### Abaye's Reading

Abaye, however, reads Shmuel differently. In Abaye's view, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that *shinuy* never effects acquisition — a blanket principle with no exception for irreversible change. On that reading, Shmuel's two rulings genuinely conflict, and Abaye resolves the tension by reattributing the ruling: *amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel amru* — Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that *there are those who say* the *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. On Abaye's reading, Shmuel is not himself endorsing that position; he is merely transmitting it as an opinion of others. The dominant read, however — and the one that coheres far more naturally with the overall discussion — is Rava's: the *Tannaim* in Abaye's grouping are not rejecting *shinuy* as a principle but operating with a high threshold for what constitutes a qualifying *shinuy*, and Shmuel's two rulings target different categories of change accordingly.

## Rabbi Yochanan

### Biblical Gezeilah

Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan: *devar Torah, gezeilah hamishtanit chozeret b'einah* — from a biblical perspective, stolen property, even after undergoing change, must be returned as it is. The proof-text is *ve-heshiv et ha-gezeilah asher gazal* — he shall return the stolen object that he stole — read as *mi-kol makom*, regardless of condition or transformation. Strikingly, this same phrase *asher gazal* is read elsewhere to mean *ka-asher gazal* — in the exact state in which it was stolen — implying that if it has changed, one need not return it. Rabbi Yochanan here reads the phrase in the diametrically opposite direction: return the object that you stole, in whatever state it now exists.

The implication runs in two directions simultaneously, and it is worth pausing to appreciate the ambiguity. On the one hand, this is a *chumra*: even if the *gazlan* has transformed the object into something far more valuable, the owner takes title to the enhanced version. On the other hand, it is a *kula*: even if the object has deteriorated drastically or died, the *gazlan* may return it as is and discharge his obligation. The *halacha* of *shinuy*, as elaborated by the *mishnah* and the rabbinic tradition, plainly recognizes change as a relevant factor. Rabbi Yochanan's statement is therefore positioned as a claim about the *Torah* level of the law — what the biblical verse mandates — not about the rabbinic superstructure built atop it.

## Takanat Hashavin (III)

### Purpose of Takanah

Rabbi Yochanan's position thus reframes the entire structure of the *shinuy koneh* doctrine. All of the cases in the *mishnah* and *Gemara* in which *shinuy* is recognized as transferring ownership — the *gazlan* who transformed lumber into furniture, wool into cloth, wheat into flour — are not reflections of a *d'Oraisa* principle that change effects acquisition. On the biblical level, Rabbi Yochanan insists, *gezeilah hamishntanit chozeret b'einah* — the stolen object, transformed or not, must be returned. The rabbinic recognition of *shinuy koneh* is entirely a *de-rabbanan halacha*, enacted as a *takanas hashavin* — an ordinance to clear the path to repentance and restitution.

The *takanah* operates as follows. One who stole lumber worth one hundred *zuz* and built it into a table worth one thousand should, biblically, return the table. The rabbis say: keep the table and pay the original value. The nine hundred *zuz* of *shevach* belongs to the *gazlan*. This is intended not as a reward for theft but as an inducement to come forward. If the *gazlan* must surrender the entire enhancement, the incentive to make restitution collapses. By allowing him to retain the *shevach* while paying the original value, the rabbis create conditions under which a *baal teshuvah* can actually come forward and make the victim whole — at least to the extent of the original loss.

The *takanah* is not, it should be emphasized, a sacrifice of the victim's interests on the altar of the thief's repentance. It is premised on the recognition that a system demanding full restitution of the enhanced object will produce *no* restitution at all. Partial restitution — the original value — is better for society and for the victim than none. And the prospect of *some* meaningful return, rather than complete forfeiture, is the only realistic way to bring *gazlanim* to make good on their obligations.

## Rabbi Yochanan (II)

### Objection to Yochanan

The *Gemara* challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position: Rabbi Yochanan himself holds that *halacha* follows a *stam mishnah*, an unattributed ruling in the *Mishnah*. Yet the *Mishnah* regarding *reishis hageiz* states that if one did not manage to give the first shearing to the *kohen* before dyeing it, he is exempt — *patur*. This is the *mishnah* itself recognizing *shinuy* as a legally operative category, exempting the owner from his obligation to the *kohen* because the wool has been transformed. But this is not a case of a *gazlan* and certainly not a case where *takanas hashavin* is relevant — the wool belongs to the owner himself. If the *Torah* truly never recognizes *shinuy* in the case of *gezeilah*, why does the *Torah* apparently recognize *shinuy* in the context of *reishis hageiz*? Does the recognition of *shinuy* in one context not undermine the claim that it is irrelevant in the other?

### Rabbi Yaakov Explanation

Rabbi Yaakov clarifies that this difficulty was never the intent of Rabbi Yochanan's statement. Rabbi Yochanan never claimed that the *Torah* categorically refuses to recognize *shinuy*. He claimed specifically that *shinuy hachozer l'vriyaso* — a reversible change — would, on the *d'Oraisa* level, still require the return of the *gezeilah*. A change that is genuinely irreversible — transforming raw lumber into a permanent piece of furniture, or weaving wool into a garment — is recognized even by the *Torah* as effecting a transfer of ownership. What the rabbis enacted as *takanas hashavin* is limited to the case of *shinuy hachozer l'vriyaso*: where the change is theoretically reversible, the *Torah* would demand return; the rabbis, for the sake of *teshuvah*, ruled that even here the *gazlan* acquires. The *mishnah* of *reishis hageiz*, which involves true and irreversible transformation — dyeing with *kalla ilan* or similar — is thus not in tension with Rabbi Yochanan's position, because he never denied that the *Torah* recognizes genuinely irreversible change.

## Takanat Hashavin (III)…

### Gazlanim Case

The *Gemara* cites a *braisa*: *hagazlanim u'malvei b'ribbis* — professional thieves and those who lend with *ribbis* — *she-hechiziru* — who have come forward to return what they took — *ein mekablin mehen* — one does not accept it from them. Anyone who does accept it back, *ein ruach chachamim nocha heimenu* — the sages are displeased with him. Notably, Rashi interprets *ruach chachamim* here not as the sages themselves but as *ruach chochmah* — the spirit of wisdom — suggesting that one who accepts from such a person thereby distances himself from wisdom.

### Refusal Doctrine

This ruling is initially puzzling to the point of seeming bizarre. If a *gazlan* has stolen my property and comes to return it, why should I refuse? Tosafos raises the practical objection: *maaseh bechol yom* — every day a *gazlan* comes to return stolen goods and we accept. Tosafos offers two resolutions. First, this ruling applied only to the *dor shel Rabbi* — the generation of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi — and not to earlier or later periods. Second, and more compelling, the ruling applies only to *professionals* — those for whom the return of their stolen goods would effectively require them to liquidate all their assets, as in the story immediately following. For such a person, the awareness that return would be accepted stands as an obstacle to *teshuvah* rather than a facilitator of it. For someone who has stolen one or a few things, the dynamic is entirely different and the normal rules apply.

### Repentance Story

The *Gemara* records the *maaseh* behind this *takanah*. A certain person sought to do *teshuvah*. His wife said to him: *reika* — empty one — *im atah oseh teshuvah, afilu avnetekha shelekha* — if you do *teshuvah*, even your own belt doesn't belong to you; everything in this household has been acquired through theft. And so *venimna velo asah teshuvah* — he was deterred and did not repent.

It was at that moment that the rabbis declared: *hagazlanim u'malvei ribbis she-hechiziru, ein mekablin mehen* — one does not accept from professional *gazlanim* and *malvei b'ribbis* who come to return. The purpose is to lower the stakes sufficiently that such a person can begin the process of *teshuvah* without facing the immediate demand to surrender his entire livelihood.

The *takanah*, read carefully, is directed primarily at the *receiver* rather than the *giver*. The *gazlan* remains obligated to return — *machzirin* — and must make the effort. But the person to whom return is offered is advised not to accept. This creates a dynamic in which the *gazlan*'s obligation is preserved and his *teshuvah* is genuine, but the practical obstacles to beginning the process are reduced. Some people, knowing they have rabbinic guidance to refuse, will decline. Others may choose to accept anyway — and the *Gemara* records that while this is not the preferred course, *ein ruach chachamim nocha heimenu* is a statement of disapproval, not of prohibition. The *gazlan* still discharges his obligation by attempting return. And the fact that some will accept means the victim is not left wholly uncompensated.

## Heirs' Obligations

### Heirs Ribit Money

The *Gemara* raises a new case: *hiniach lahem avihem maot shel ribbis* — if a father left his children money that was collected as *ribbis* — *af al pi she-yodim she-hi ribbis, ein chayavim lehachazir* — even though they know it is interest money, the heirs are not obligated to return it. The *Gemara* clarifies: *in truth, even the father* would not have been obligated to return it — not because there is no underlying moral obligation, but because *takanas hashavin* means that we do not compel return from such persons, and the acceptance by the recipient is likewise discouraged. The reason the *braisa* frames the ruling in terms of the children rather than the father is that the *braisa* wants to introduce its contrasting conclusion in the following clause.

An important structural observation bears noting regarding the nature of *ribbis* obligations. When someone pays *ribbis*, the money paid is arguably the lender's property in a legal sense — there was a contractual obligation to pay it, even though the contract was halachically impermissible. This is unlike outright theft, where the stolen object categorically remains the owner's property. The obligation to return *ribbis* therefore falls specifically on the person who transgressed by taking it; it does not necessarily devolve upon his heirs as a matter of standard property law, which may explain why the heirs are not obligated even where they know the provenance of the money.

### Concrete Objects

The contrasting case: *hiniach lahem avihem parah ve-tallit ve-chol davar mesuyam* — if the father left the children a cow, a *tallit*, or any concrete identifiable object — *chayavim lehachazir mipnei kevod avihem* — the children are obligated to return it, for the sake of their father's honor.

The *kevod avihem* rationale requires attention. The underlying verse — *venasi b'amcha lo sa'or* — prohibits cursing a *nasi* among your people, and the *drasha* reads *b'amcha* as *b'oseh ma'aseh amcha* — one who conducts himself as part of your people. The implication is that if the father behaved improperly — lending with *ribbis*, appropriating others' property — the ordinary duty of filial honor is attenuated. Yet where the father had done *teshuvah* before his death — as the *Gemara* establishes to be the case here — the children's duty to honor him is intact, and the visible presence of a stolen cow or *tallit* in their household constitutes a desecration of that honor. The *Gemara* therefore holds that they must return such concrete, identifiable objects.

### Repentance Case

The *Gemara* clarifies that the requirement of return in the case of concrete objects inherited from a repentant father applies even in a case where the father died before having the opportunity to return the object himself — *shelo hispik lehachazir ad shemes*. The *teshuvah* was genuine; the inability to complete restitution before death does not negate the obligation that devolves on the children with respect to identifiable stolen property. The irony, as noted above, is not lost: if the reason the object remains in the family's possession is precisely that the earlier *takanah* told people not to accept it, then the *takanah* itself has created the very situation it must now address.

## Shepherds/Tax Collectors

### Difficult Repentance

A *baraisa* addresses the specific situation of *roim* and *gabbaim* — shepherds and tax collectors — whose *teshuvah* is described as *kasha*, difficult. The reason is structural: these are people who, in the ordinary course of their occupations, took from many different people in small amounts over long periods. They do not know from whom they took, and even where they do know, the amounts are often too diffuse to reconstruct. The difficulty of their *teshuvah* is therefore not a moral failing but a practical reality arising from the nature of their transgressions.

### Known Victims

With respect to those from whom they know they have taken, they attempt to return. Consistently with the *takanah* discussed throughout this section, however, those approached are instructed not to accept. The *gazlan* thus discharges his obligation of *latzeit yedei shamayim* — fulfilling his duty before Heaven — by making the effort, even where the return is declined.

### Unknown Victims

With respect to those from whom they have taken but cannot identify — the anonymous victims of years of overcharging or improper grazing — the mechanism of return is different. *Ya'aseh bahen tzorchei tzibbur* — they must devote the funds to community needs. Rav Chisda specifies: *borot, shichin u-mearot* — wells, cisterns, and caves for public use. By contributing to communal infrastructure that benefits the broader population from which the victims were drawn, the *baal teshuvah* makes a kind of collective restitution to those he cannot specifically locate.

### Before/After Takanah

The final resolution offered by the *Gemara* is that the apparent contradictions within the earlier sources — some implying that return is accepted, others that it is not — reflect a distinction between *kodem takanah* and *le-achar takanah*: before the *takanah* was enacted, return was accepted and the obligation to return was therefore actively demanding; that is why the *teshuvah* of shepherds and tax collectors was so difficult. After the *takanah*, the receivers are instructed not to accept, which changes the practical dynamic significantly and allows the *baal teshuvah* to proceed with the process even while remaining in a state of ongoing restitution effort. The *Gemara* closes here, noting that the further elaboration of how far this *takanah* reaches will continue in the sugya that follows.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 95

## Rebbi's Takkanah

### Rebbi's Takkanah Intro

The daf opens two lines from the bottom of 94b, three words from the end of the line: *v'hashta d'amar Rav Nachman*. We are in the middle of a discussion about the *takkanah* of Rebbi. Rebbi enacted that when a *gazlan* — or someone who lent money with *ribbis* — comes to do *teshuvah* and wishes to return his ill-gotten gains, we are instructed to refuse to accept the return. The purpose is to lower the barrier to *teshuvah*: we are, in effect, more concerned with the spiritual rehabilitation of the wrongdoer than with the immediate demands of justice. One might find this a striking moral calculus, but it is coherent as a communal policy. If the obstacle to *teshuvah* is the crushing financial burden of making full restitution, then society has an interest in removing that obstacle — we would rather the thief cease stealing and the lender cease charging *ribbis* than demand an accounting that prevents them from ever turning back. That, in any event, is the reasoning behind Rebbi's *takkanah*.

### Rav Nachman's Qualificat…

Now, however, the *takkanah* is qualified. *V'hashta d'amar Rav Nachman b'she'ein gezeilah kayyemes* — now that Rav Nachman has clarified that Rebbi is speaking only about a case where the stolen object is no longer in its original form or is no longer physically present, we must reconsider the scope of Rebbi's ruling. If the stolen object is still exactly as it was — if someone stole my laptop and still has my laptop — then the ownership is vivid and explicit, and there the *takkanah* does not apply. In that case, one must accept the object back. The underlying logic may be that asking the *gazlan* to liquidate his own assets to compensate for past wrongs is the real obstacle to *teshuvah*, whereas returning the tangible stolen object itself may not present the same difficulty. Either way, Rav Nachman's position is that Rebbi's *takkanah* is limited to cases where the *gezeilah* is no longer present.

### Reconciling Baraitot

This qualification allows the *Gemara* to resolve an apparent contradiction between two *baraitot* that were discussed on the previous daf. Yesterday, we encountered two *baraitot* that seemed to contradict one another on the question of whether one accepts returned stolen property. One resolution offered was chronological: one *baraita* predates Rebbi's *takkanah* and the other postdates it, which is why one accepts the return and the other does not. But now, the *Gemara* offers an alternative resolution. *Iidi v'iidi l'achar takkanah* — both *baraitot* may in fact be stated after Rebbi's *takkanah*. *V'lo kashya* — there is no difficulty — *kahn m'gezeilah kayyemes kahn b'she'ein gezeilah kayyemes*. The top of 95a clarifies: one *baraita*, which says you do not accept the return, is dealing with a case where the stolen object is no longer present; the other *baraita*, which says you do accept the return, is dealing with a case where the original stolen object is still intact and available.

The *Gemara*, however, immediately challenges this: *V'ha avneit gezeilah kayyemes hee* — but the very story that motivated Rebbi's *takkanah* seems to involve a *gezeilah* that is still present! The story goes that when someone wanted to do *teshuvah* and return everything, his wife objected: if you start returning everything you stole, you won't be able to keep even your own *avneit*, your own belt — you'll be left with nothing. This implies the *avneit* itself was a stolen object still in hand, which would apparently contradict Rav Nachman's qualification. The *Gemara* answers: *mai avneit d'mei avneit* — the *avneit* is not meant literally. It means the equivalent value of the belt, i.e., we will have to liquidate all our property to pay everyone back. It does not mean the actual stolen item is still at hand. The wife's complaint was about financial ruin, not about a specific identified stolen object.

### Beam in House (Marish)

The *Gemara* presses further with a second challenge. *V'harei marish* — what about the classic case of the stolen beam? This is one of the most well-known examples of *takkanas hashavim*: if someone stole a beam (*marish*) and built it into the structure of a house, the Sages enacted that the owner cannot demand the return of the beam itself and thereby compel the thief to demolish his building. Instead, the owner receives monetary compensation. This is explicitly a *takkanah* enacted to ease *teshuvah* — and yet, the stolen object is clearly still present and identifiable. So how does Rav Nachman's qualification hold?

The *Gemara* responds: *shani hatam d'keivan d'ika psayda d'birah shavyi rabbanan k'd'leisa* — that case is different, because returning the beam would not merely mean returning one object; it would mean destroying the entire structure, causing enormous additional loss beyond the value of the beam itself. The Sages therefore treated it as if the *gezeilah* were no longer present. The general principle is that when the stolen object is still intact, it must be returned — but if doing so would cause catastrophic collateral damage, the situation is treated as equivalent to a case where the *gezeilah* is no longer around.

This also clarifies something about the *marish* case. Rebbi's *takkanah* in its basic form holds that the *gazlan* does not have to pay anything back — which is admittedly a startling position, since the entire point is to ease *teshuvah* by removing all financial barriers. But in the case of the beam, the thief *does* pay the value of the beam. Why? Because since the *gezeilah* is technically still present, he *should* be returning the beam. We do not force him to demolish the house, but since he *should* be returning the object, he is required to pay its value. That concludes the discussion of Rebbi's *takkanah*.

---

## Sheared Sheep/Cow

### Mishna: Return & Compens…

The *Gemara* moves to the next section of the *mishna*: *gazal parah meuberet veyaldah* — one who stole a pregnant cow that subsequently gave birth, or a sheep and sheared it. The *mishna* rules that the thief returns the object as it currently stands — the shorn sheep or the cow that has now given birth — together with monetary compensation for the diminution in value, since at the time of the theft the sheep was worth more (it had its wool) and the cow was worth more (it was pregnant). The shearings and the calf, however, the thief acquires through *shinuy* and does not return. The owner receives the animal in its current state plus the difference in value.

### Baraita: Rebbi Meir's Po…

A *baraita* now presents this as a *tannaic* dispute. *Hagozel rachel vegezezah, parah veyaldah* — one who stole a sheep and sheared it, or a cow and it gave birth: *meshalem otah ve'et gizoteiha ve'et veladoteiha* — according to Rebbi Meir, you pay back the animal together with the shearings and together with the offspring. Rebbi Meir holds that you return everything, even though the animal underwent a *shinuy*. Rebbi Yehudah disagrees: *gezeila chozeret be'eineha* — the stolen object is returned as it is, meaning you return the shorn sheep or the post-partum cow, plus the difference in value, but not the shearings or the calf — which is precisely the ruling of our *mishna*. Rebbi Shimon offers yet another formulation: you assess the value at the moment of the theft and that is what you pay. The difference between Rebbi Yehudah and Rebbi Shimon will be explored tomorrow; for now, the focus is on Rebbi Meir.

### Rebbi Meir's Reasoning

The *Gemara* raises the *ibaya*: *mai ta'ama deRebbi Meir?* — what is the underlying reasoning of Rebbi Meir? Two possibilities are presented. The first: *ei mishum dekasvar shinuy bimkomo omed* — perhaps Rebbi Meir holds that *shinuy* stands in its place, meaning a change to a stolen object is not halachically recognized as an acquisition, and therefore the *gazlan* never becomes the owner of the shearings or the calf, so they still belong to the original owner and must be returned along with the animal. The second possibility: *be'alma shinuy koneh* — in general, Rebbi Meir's principle is that *shinuy* does confer ownership on the *gazlan*, and therefore the *gazlan* should in principle own the shearings and the calf. But *v'hacha knasa hu dekakanis* — in this case, Rebbi Meir is imposing a *knas*, a monetary fine: you stole from this person, so even though technically you acquired the shearings and the calf through *shinuy*, we penalize you and require you to give them back.

The *Gemara* asks: *lemai nafka mina* — what practical difference would it make? The answer: *leheicha dechahasha shemekachash* — consider a case where the stolen animal became worth less over time. If *shinuy koneh* is the underlying principle and the *knas* is imposed on top of it, then in a case where the animal deteriorated (rather than improved), the *shinuy* caused by the deterioration would mean the *gazlan* owns the animal and owes the original value at the time of theft. But there would be no *knas* here, since the animal lost value rather than gained it. Conversely, if *shinuy bimkomo omed* is Rebbi Meir's real view — that *shinuy* is never recognized — then the animal still belongs to the owner and the *gazlan* can simply return it as is, without paying for its original higher value. That is the *nafka mina*.

---

## Aged Animal/Slave

### Aged Animal Case

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve the question from a *baraita*: *gazal behema vehizkina, avadim vehizkinu* — one stole an animal and it aged, or slaves and they aged, so that they are now worth considerably less. The *tanna kama* rules: *meshalem kesha'as gezeila* — you pay as at the time of the theft. You acquired them through *shinuy* and must pay their original value. Rebbi Meir, however, distinguishes: by slaves, you say *harei shelcha lefanecha* — here is yours, take it back. The reason is the principle that *karka einah nigzeles* — land cannot be stolen, and the normal mechanisms of *kinyan* through *gezeilah* do not apply to land. Slaves, Rebbi Meir holds, are *hukshu l'karka'os* — they are treated like land — and therefore the *shinuy* caused by aging does not create any acquisition. The slave was never legally acquired by the *gazlan*, so it remains the owner's property, and if it deteriorated, that deterioration happened to the owner's property. But by the animal — the *behemah* — Rebbi Meir agrees with the *tanna kama*: you are *koneh* the animal through *shinuy* and you pay as at the time of the theft.

### Proof: Shinuy Koneh

This seems to answer the *ibaya*: *v'ilu behemah kesha'as gezeila* — the fact that Rebbi Meir says by the animal you pay as at the time of the theft, and cannot say *harei shelcha lefanecha*, implies that the *gazlan* has acquired the animal. *V'issaka daitach savar Rebbi Meir shinuy bimkomo omed, afilu behemah nami* — if Rebbi Meir held that *shinuy bimkomo omed*, then he should equally allow returning the animal as is, saying *harei shelcha lefanecha*. But he does not. *Ela lav shma mina kasavar Rebbi Meir shinuy koneh* — it must be that Rebbi Meir holds *shinuy koneh*, and therefore by the animal you own it and must pay its original value. *V'hacha* — as for the shearings and the calf — *knasa hu dekakanis* — it is simply a fine. The underlying principle is *shinuy koneh*, but because the person was a *gazlan*, Rebbi Meir penalized him and demanded the return of the gains.

### Alternate Explanation

The *Gemara* deflects this proof. *Omri* — others say — *Rebbi Meir l'divreihem d'rabbanan ka'amar lehu*: Rebbi Meir may simply have been arguing within the framework of the Rabbis' own position, not expressing his own view. His own position, he might say, is *shinuy eino koneh* — *shinuy* does not create ownership at all — and he would say *harei shelcha lefanecha* even by the animal. But since the Rabbis hold *shinuy koneh*, he tells them: at least concede that the slave is like land and cannot be acquired through *gezeilah*, and therefore you should say *harei shelcha lefanecha* by the slave even according to your own view. The Rabbis respond: *lo, avda k'metalteli dami* — we do not agree; we hold that slaves are like chattel, not like land. So Rebbi Meir's stated distinction between the animal and the slave in that *baraita* may be purely rhetorical, and does not necessarily reflect his own *ikkar* position on *shinuy*.

---

## Dyed Wool Case

### Dyer Mistake

A stronger proof is now brought. *L'tzvo lo adom utzva'o shachor, shachor utzva'o adom* — one gives wool to a dyer to dye it red and the dyer mistakenly dyes it black, or vice versa. *Rebbi Meir omer nosin lo d'mei tzemro* — Rebbi Meir rules that the dyer keeps the wool and pays the owner the value of the wool. The dyer acquired the wool through *shinuy* — he transformed it into something different from what the owner wanted — and therefore he pays the owner the value of the raw wool.

### Analysis: Shinuy Koneh

The *Gemara* zeroes in on the precise formulation of Rebbi Meir's ruling: *d'mei tzemro in* — yes, he pays the value of the wool; *d'mei tzemro v'shvacho lo* — but he does not pay the wool together with the added value of the dyeing. This is the decisive point. If *shinuy eino koneh*, the owner should still own the wool. And if the owner still owns the wool, he should receive it back with its newly dyed state — or at minimum, the dyer should pay him not merely the raw value of the wool but the value of the dyed wool, which includes the enhancement. But Rebbi Meir says the dyer pays only the value of the raw wool, *d'mei tzemro*, and retains the improvement. *V'ee salka daitach savar Rebbi Meir shinuy eino koneh, d'mei tzemro v'shvacho ba'ei l'meitav lei* — if Rebbi Meir held *shinuy eino koneh*, he should have to pay for the wool and its improvement and return the dyed wool to the owner.

### Conclusion: Fine Only

*Ela lav shma mina kasavar Rebbi Meir shinuy koneh* — you must conclude that Rebbi Meir holds *shinuy koneh*. The dyer acquired the wool, and therefore he pays the owner for the raw wool and retains the rest. *V'hacha knasa hu dekakanis* — and the reason Rebbi Meir requires a *gazlan* to return the shearings and the calf is purely a *knas*. *Shma mina* — the *Gemara* accepts this as a valid proof.

This also illuminates an important nuance embedded in Rebbi Meir's fine. Why is there no *knas* in the dyer's case? Because the *knas* is a penalty for a *gazlan* who deliberately takes what is not his. A tradesman who makes an honest mistake — who dyes the wool the wrong color through error or even negligence — has not acted as a willful thief. The *knas* is therefore not applied to him. He is *koneh* the wool through *shinuy* and pays only the raw value.

There is also a second version of the question within Rebbi Meir's position. Once it is established that Rebbi Meir holds *shinuy koneh* and that the return of the shearings and calf is a *knas*, the question becomes: does this *knas* apply only in a case of *mezid* — a willful *gazlan* — or does it apply even to *shogeg*, to an unintentional or unknowing actor? That question will be addressed in the following section.

---

## Unencumbered Property

### Liens vs. Unencumbered

The *Gemara* now introduces a new *baraita* that will be used to probe the scope of Rebbi Meir's *knas*. The *baraita* states: *chamisha govi min hamachurarin* — there are five categories of monetary obligations that can be collected only from *b'nei chorin*, unencumbered property, and not from *meshu'abadim*, encumbered property bearing liens.

To understand this, a brief orientation is necessary. When Reuven lends money to Shimon, Reuven acquires a lien on all of Shimon's real estate. Should Shimon later sell that real estate to Levi, Reuven can, under certain conditions, seize that property from Levi to collect his debt — because the lien was in place before Levi's purchase. The rationale for liens on real estate is that land cannot be hidden; it provides lenders with security and confidence that their money can always be recovered. This is the institution of *meshu'abadim*. Unencumbered property, *b'nei chorin*, is property freely held by the debtor — assets in hand, liquid funds, movable possessions — that a creditor can seize directly but that do not carry the same lien-based reach into subsequent purchasers.

There are, however, five types of obligations for which no liens exist. The creditor can collect only from whatever unencumbered assets the debtor currently holds.

### Peiros (Fruits)

The first two categories are *peiros* and *shvach peiros*. Consider the following scenario: Shimon steals Reuven's real estate — or claims title to it — and then sells it to Levi, accepting *achrayus*, a warranty of title. Levi is assured that if the property is seized from him by a third party proving superior title, Shimon will compensate him. The property in this case is an apple orchard, and Levi has been harvesting and selling apples for years. When Reuven eventually proves in court that the land was always his and seizes it back, he also demands that Levi compensate him for all the *peiros* — the fruits and produce — he collected during his years of possession, since that produce came from Reuven's land. Levi then turns to Shimon under the *achrayus* guarantee to recover what Shimon owes him.

When Levi seeks to recover the principal purchase price from Shimon, he has full liens: that was a fixed, known sum at the time of the transaction, and he can collect it even from property Shimon subsequently sold to others. But when Levi seeks to recover the *peiros* — the produce he must now repay to Reuven — he has no liens. He can collect only from Shimon's currently held, unencumbered property. The reason is that the amount of *peiros* was never fixed or predictable at the time of the transaction. How many years would Levi harvest? How productive would the orchard be? A lien must attach to a defined obligation; an obligation whose magnitude is entirely unknown cannot fairly impose a lien on Shimon's property that might prejudice other creditors or subsequent purchasers who had no way of knowing how large this liability might grow.

### Shvach Peiros

*Shvach peiros* is a related but distinct category. Here, Levi did not harvest the produce; instead, he invested heavily in capital improvements to the land — fertilizing, planting trees, building infrastructure. The land, which Shimon sold him for one hundred thousand, is now worth one hundred fifty thousand. When Reuven seizes it back, he takes the land with all its improvements. The first hundred thousand represents the principal Levi paid for the property, and Levi has liens for that: it was a fixed known amount. But the additional fifty thousand in enhanced value — the *shvach* — is in the category of *shvach peiros*. When Levi goes to Shimon to recover that fifty thousand, he has no liens for it. Again, the amount of improvement was not known or fixed at the time of sale; it could have been anything, and therefore no lien can be said to have attached.

These two categories — *peiros* and *shvach peiros* — share a common logic: amounts that are unfixed and unpredictable at the time of the underlying transaction cannot carry liens.

### Stolen Field Case

The *Gemara* spells out the full scenario for *shvach peiros* in the context of this *baraita*: *kegon she'gazal sadeh me'chavero* — Shimon stole a field from Reuven, *u'machra l'acher* — sold it to Levi, *ve'hishpicha* — and Levi made capital improvements, *ve'harei hi yotzei mi'tachas yado* — and then Reuven proved title and seized the field from Levi. *Keshe'hu goveh, goveh es hakeren minichasim meshubadim* — Levi collects the principal from Shimon's encumbered property, because that was a fixed amount with established liens. *V'es hashevach, shevach minichasim b'nei chorin* — the improvement he collects only from Shimon's unencumbered property. *Da'asa ba'al ara v'shakal ara v'shvacha* — Reuven came and took the land and the improvements.

The relevance to the earlier discussion is now coming into focus. Reuven seizes the land and its improvements without compensating Levi for anything. Levi, an apparently honest purchaser, made real investments in property that turned out not to belong to the seller. Yet Reuven walks away with the full value of those improvements. This is structurally parallel to Rebbi Meir's ruling that a *gazlan* must return the shearings and the calf — the original owner takes back not just the stolen object but also the gains that accrued to it. The question will be: was Levi truly innocent, and does this scenario demonstrate that Rebbi Meir's *knas* applies even to a *shogeg*?

---

## Knas & Shogeg

### Problem with Levi

The *Gemara* now asks the pointed question: *mai lav b'am ha'aretz* — are we not dealing here with a case where Levi is an ignorant layman who does not know the law? Specifically, *d'lo yada d'karka nigzeles o einah nigzeles* — he did not know whether land can be halachically stolen or not. Why is this relevant? If Levi assumed that land operates like movable property — that *ye'ush v'shinui reshus* or a similar mechanism would give him full ownership once he purchased it from Shimon — then even if he knew the land was stolen, he might genuinely believe himself to have acquired it legitimately. He was innocent of any wrongdoing, a *shogeg* in the fullest sense. And yet *ka'asi ba'al karka v'shakal ara v'shvacha* — Reuven comes and takes the land and all its improvements without compensating Levi. This would prove that Rebbi Meir's *knas* applies even to a *shogeg*. *Ushma mina b'shogeg nami kanis* — and one should derive from here that even in a case of *shogeg*, Rebbi Meir imposes the *knas*.

### Levi Knew the Law

The *Gemara* rejects this inference. *Ami lo* — no, we need not read the case this way. *Biloke'ach talmid chacham v'yada* — we may assume that Levi was in fact a *talmid chacham*, someone who knew the law. And if he knew the law, he knew the principle of *karka einah nigzeles* — land cannot be stolen. He therefore understood that no matter what, even with *ye'ush* or *shinui reshus*, the land remained Reuven's. If he nonetheless proceeded to buy and improve it, he cannot claim innocence. He is not a *shogeg*; he is a *mezid*. The absence of compensation to Levi therefore tells us nothing about whether Rebbi Meir's *knas* applies to genuine *shogeg* cases — it simply tells us that this Levi was not genuinely innocent.

### Ravad's Question

Before moving forward, a significant question raised by the Ravad deserves attention. Even setting aside the language of *knas* entirely, there is an independent halachic principle at work here. When someone enters another's property without permission and makes improvements — *yored l'toch s'dei chaveiro shelo birshus* — even if the owner never authorized the work and the person had no right to be there, the owner typically owes some compensation for the labor expended in improvements that benefit the property. So even if Rebbi Meir's *knas* were entirely inapplicable, Reuven should at minimum owe Levi something for the labor and investment Levi poured into the improvements. The fact that Reuven pays Levi nothing at all must itself require explanation. The Ravad argues that the only explanation is that this is indeed a *knas* — and the question therefore circles back to whether that *knas* applies in a *shogeg* context. The *Gemara*'s response remains the same: Levi is not a *shogeg*, because he knew the law. That is why he receives nothing — not because the *knas* applies to *shogeg*, but because he was *mezid*.

### Dyed Wool Redux

The *Gemara* returns to the dyed wool case to provide a cleaner resolution. *Vitzvao lo adom vitzvao shachor, shachor vitzvao adom* — one gives wool to a dyer to dye it red and the dyer dyes it black, or vice versa. *Rebbi Meir omer nosin lo d'mei tzemro* — Rebbi Meir rules that the dyer pays the owner the value of the raw wool and keeps the wool. As established earlier, *d'mei tzemro in* — the raw wool value, yes; *d'mei tzemro v'shvacho lo* — the wool with the enhancement of the dye, no.

Now the question is sharpened: if Rebbi Meir's *knas* applied even to *shogeg*, then in this case — which is as clear a *shogeg* as one can imagine, since the dyer made an honest mistake — why does the dyer not give back the dyed wool to the owner? If the *knas* is that you may not retain the improvements, then Rebbi Meir should rule that the dyer must return the wool with the dye, just as the *gazlan* must return the shearings and the calf.

### Knas Only for Mezid

*Ela lav shma mina b'meizid knas b'shogeg lo knas* — you must conclude from this that Rebbi Meir's *knas* applies only in a case of *mezid*, intentional wrongdoing, and not in a case of *shogeg*, unintentional error. The dyer who made an honest mistake is a *shogeg* and is therefore not subject to the *knas*. He is *koneh* the wool through *shinuy* and pays only the value of the raw wool. The *gazlan* who deliberately stole the sheep and sheared it is a *mezid*, and therefore the *knas* applies: he must return the shearings even though he should, in principle, be *koneh* them through *shinuy*. *Shma mina* — the *Gemara* accepts this as a valid and conclusive proof.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 96

## Three Positions

### Rabbi Meir

The daf opens at the top third of 95b, where we are in the middle of a *baraita* presenting three opinions on a case in which someone steals a pregnant *parah* that subsequently gives birth, or a *rachel* laden with wool that is subsequently sheared. Rabbi Meir's position, discussed at the outset, is that the *gazlan* must return both the animal and its offspring, along with the *gizot* and *veladot*. The *gemara* explains that even though Rabbi Meir holds *shinuy koneh* — that a modification in the stolen object effects a legal acquisition — he nevertheless imposes this obligation as a *kenas*: one should not profit from an object stolen from another.

### Rabbi Yehuda

The *gemara* then turns to the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Yehuda states: *gezelah chozeret be'einya* — the stolen object returns in its current state. The *gemara* interprets this to mean that the stolen object is returned as it was at the time of the theft, with the *gazlan* paying the difference if the object is now worth less. Notably, neither Rabbi Yehuda's nor Rabbi Shimon's position makes entirely clear whether the *gazlan* acquires the *gizot* — whether the shearing itself constitutes a sufficient *shinuy* in the sheep — but both positions converge on the principle that the *gazlan* pays the value of the object as it stood at the time of the theft.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon's formulation is: *ro'in otah ke'ilu hi shumah etzlo bekesef* — we assess the value of the stolen object as if it were assessed with him at its monetary value. This similarly points toward payment based on the value at the time of theft (*keshat hag'zeilah*). At first glance, the two positions appear identical, and the *gemara* therefore asks: *mai beinayhu* — what is the practical difference between them?

## Yehuda vs. Shimon

### Zevid Interpretation

Zevid answers that the dispute concerns *shevach she'al gabei gezelah* — the improvement accrued to the stolen object while in the *gazlan*'s possession. In the case where the animal has not yet been sheared but has grown additional wool during the period of theft, who is entitled to that increased value? According to Zevid's reading, Rabbi Yehuda holds that the *shevach* belongs to the *nigzal* — the original owner — since the phrase *chozeret be'einya* implies returning the object along with whatever increase has accrued. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, holds that the *shevach* belongs to the *gazlan*.

This is a striking position. If the wool has simply grown incrementally during the theft, what is the basis for the *gazlan* to retain it? It is not an obvious *shinuy koneh* — the change is gradual and natural, not a deliberate modification. The *gemara* does not immediately resolve this tension.

### Rav Pappa Version

Rav Pappa offers an alternative reading: *dechulei alma shevach she'al gabei gezelah degazlan havei* — all opinions agree that the improvement to the stolen object belongs to the *gazlan*. This is itself a striking assertion, and it begs the question of why the *gazlan* should have any claim to the natural increase of an animal he wrongfully possesses.

## Takkanat Hashavim

### Tosafot Explanation

Tosafot addresses this directly, explaining that the *gazlan*'s entitlement to the *shevach* is not grounded in *shinuy koneh* at all. It makes little conceptual sense to say that because an animal grew a bit more wool while in the possession of a thief, that incremental growth constitutes a *shinuy* sufficient to transfer ownership. Rather, Tosafot explains, this is a *takkanat hashavim* — a rabbinic enactment designed to facilitate the return of stolen property.

### Purpose & Incentive

The purpose of the enactment is to lower the barrier to repentance and return. If a *gazlan* who has increased the value of a stolen object is required to return not only the principal but also every bit of the increase, he may be discouraged from returning it at all. By allowing him to retain the *shevach*, the Rabbis created an incentive to return the *keren* — the principal — even at the cost of the increase. The fact that the *gemara* here describes this benefit as belonging to the *gazlan* without explicit reference to *shinuy* lends support to Tosafot's reading that the underlying principle is institutional rather than legal-theoretical.

## Yehuda vs. Shimon (II)

### Portion Amount

Given that all agree the *gazlan* retains the *shevach*, the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon according to Rav Pappa concerns the *degree* to which he retains it. The *gemara* states: *de-kulei alma shevach gabei de-Gazlan havei, ve-hakha le-machtze le-shlish u-le-revia kamiflegi* — here the dispute is whether the *gazlan* keeps all the increase, a half, a third, or a quarter.

Rabbi Yehuda holds that the *gazlan* keeps the entire *shevach*. His phrase *chozeret be'einya* is now read to mean: you return the object exactly as you took it, and you retain all of the increase over and above that baseline. Rabbi Shimon, whose language is *ro'in otah ke'ilu hi shumah* — we assess its value — implies that the *gazlan* receives only a proportional share of the *shevach*, analogous to the arrangement with a sharecropper who tends animals in exchange for a percentage of their increased value. The precise fraction — half, a third, or a quarter — depends on the local custom for such arrangements.

A *baraita* subsequently confirms this reading of Rabbi Shimon's position: *Rabbi Shimon omer ro'in otah ke'ilu hi shumah etzlo bekesef, ve-lemechtza ve-lishlish ve-lirvia* — the assessment is made, and the *gazlan* takes a portion accordingly. Rav Ashi adds that when he was in the academy of Rav Kahana, a further question was raised: when Rabbi Shimon grants the *gazlan* a share of the *shevach*, does this mean he remains a partner in the animal going forward — entitled to, say, a portion of the calf when it is eventually born — or can the *nigzal* pay him off in cash and thereby dissolve any ongoing partnership? Is the *gazlan* entitled to demand his proportional share of the physical animal itself, or only to receive a monetary payment?

The question is resolved from a ruling of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *shelosha shamin lahen hashevach u-mesalkinan lehu bi-damim* — in three cases, one assesses the *shevach* and pays off the relevant party in cash, without that party remaining a partner. The *gazlan* is presumed to fall into this category as well, meaning he can be paid off and does not retain an ongoing stake in the stolen property.

## Three Separation Cases

### Bechor Case

The three cases enumerated by Shmuel are as follows. The first is *bechor le-pashut* — the firstborn son versus the non-firstborn. When brothers inherit an estate, the *bechor* is entitled to a double share (*pi shnayim*). If, prior to the division of the estate, the *bechor* improves the land through his labor and increases its value, that increase is shared equally among all heirs — since it accrued while the estate remained undivided, it is treated as a collective gain. As a result, when the land is ultimately divided two-thirds and one-third, the *bechor* ends up retaining more of the increase than he is proportionally entitled to, having taken a double share of land that happened to include the full value of his equally-distributed improvement. The siblings cannot demand to remain partners in the land; rather, the *bechor* is entitled to pay them off for the excess and retain his full allotted portion.

### Creditor Case

The second case is *ba'al chov le-lokeach* — a creditor collecting from a purchaser. The scenario is as follows: a debtor sold a field to a purchaser, and that purchaser subsequently improved the field. The creditor now comes to seize the field in satisfaction of the debt, and the field — including the purchaser's improvements — is worth more than the original debt. The creditor is entitled to seize the whole field and pay the purchaser for the value he added, rather than accepting the purchaser as a continuing partner in the land.

### Orphans Case

The third case, *ba'al chov de-yatmei*, follows the same principle: a creditor collecting from orphans who have improved the estate. The improvements made by the orphans are assessed, and the creditor seizes the full property while paying them off for their contribution — they cannot insist on remaining partners.

All three cases share the same structure: someone other than the original owner has increased the value of property to which another party has a prior claim. The party with the prior claim is entitled to seize the whole and pay off the improver, rather than entering into a partnership with them.

## Shmuel Contradiction

### Reimburse Purchaser

Rav Pappa raises a difficulty against this ruling. He asks Rav Ashi: does Shmuel truly hold that a *ba'al chov* must pay the *lokeach* for the *shevach* the *lokeach* created?

### Creditor Collects

There is a second statement attributed to Shmuel: *ba'al chov goveh et ha-shevach* — the creditor collects the *shevach* along with the principal. This appears to say that the creditor takes the full improved value of the land without any obligation to reimburse the purchaser at all. The two statements of Shmuel are directly contradictory.

### Resolution: Ready vs. Na…

The resolution given is: *lo kashya, kan be-shevach ha-magiya li-ktefayim, kan be-shevach she-eino magiya li-ktefayim* — it is not difficult; one ruling applies to *shevach ha-magiya li-ktefayim* and the other to *shevach she-eino magiya li-ktefayim*. Rashi explains *magiya li-ktefayim* as referring to wheat that has grown tall enough to be harvested — crops that are effectively ready to be reaped and are therefore conceptually distinct from the land itself. Since such produce is on the verge of being separable from the land, the creditor must reimburse the purchaser for it. By contrast, if the *shevach* has not yet reached that stage, it is treated as simply an enhancement to the land's value, which the creditor is entitled to seize along with the land.

The *gemara* then raises a further complication: it is known that in practice Shmuel permitted creditors to collect the *shevach* even in cases where crops had reached shoulder height. This seems to undercut the resolution.

## Labor vs. Natural Growth

### Tosafot Alternative

Tosafot offers an alternative reading of *shevach ha-magiya li-ktefayim*. Rather than referring to the physical height of the crops, Tosafot understands the phrase to denote improvement that came about through labor and effort — literally, improvement that required someone's shoulders, their physical exertion. *Shevach she-eino magiya li-ktefayim* is improvement that occurred naturally, without the purchaser's input — for example, an orchard that simply bore fruit over the course of the year as a result of rain alone. For such naturally occurring increase, the creditor need not reimburse the purchaser at all; it is simply an appreciation in the land's value, which the creditor's lien entitles him to take.

For improvement that required the purchaser's labor and effort, however, the purchaser has a legitimate claim to reimbursement. The *gemara* then asks how this squares with Shmuel's known practice of collecting even labor-induced *shevach* without reimbursement.

## Loan Amount Resolution

### Loan Less Than Value

The resolution distinguishes based on the size of the loan relative to the value of the land. If the outstanding loan is smaller than the total current value of the land — including the purchaser's improvements — the creditor is not entitled to take more than the loan amount, and must therefore reimburse the purchaser for the excess created by the purchaser's effort.

### Loan Exceeds Value

If, however, the loan equals or exceeds the total current value of the land, the creditor is entitled to seize the entire property. In such a case, even if the purchaser's labor contributed to bringing the land up to the value of the loan, the creditor takes everything. The purchaser invested in land that he knew was encumbered; and since the debtor has guaranteed the purchaser against loss, the purchaser retains his claim against the original debtor. Tosafot notes explicitly that one reason the creditor can act this way without being considered unfair to the purchaser is precisely because the purchaser has that guarantee of indemnification from the seller.

## Purchaser's Rights

### Purchaser Can Force Paym…

This resolution, however, creates a tension with a separate debate. The *gemara* raises the question: according to the view that if the purchaser has cash on hand, he may pay the creditor off and thereby prevent the creditor from seizing the land — if that is true, then consider the following. The creditor comes to seize the land and pay the purchaser the value of his improvement. The purchaser, who has invested $500 in the land, might argue: had I had the funds, I could have paid you off entirely and kept the whole land. Now that you are seizing the land, you should at least leave me a plot of land corresponding to my $500 share of the improvement.

### Purchaser Cannot Force

The *gemara* addresses the opposing view as well: if the purchaser cannot force the creditor to accept payment and walk away — if the creditor has the right to insist on taking the land — then by the same logic, the creditor can take the full improved land and pay the purchaser the cash value of the improvement. Since the purchaser would not in any case have had the right to force the creditor away, the creditor's right to seize and pay off is unimpeded.

### Apotiki Exception

The *gemara* resolves the tension by invoking a special case: *de-shaviyah nihaleh apotiki* — the debtor designated this specific plot of land as *apotiki*, dedicated collateral. In an *apotiki* arrangement, the creditor's rights are concentrated specifically on that designated property. While this weakens his claims against the debtor's other assets, it correspondingly strengthens his rights to this particular land. Because of this designation, the purchaser has no capacity to pay the creditor off and make him go away — the *apotiki* creates a focused lien that overrides the purchaser's ordinary rights. Therefore, the creditor may seize the land and pay the purchaser off, and the purchaser cannot insist on retaining a share.

The broader point of this entire digression is that when a *gazlan* has increased the stolen object's value, and the time comes for the *nigzal* to reclaim it, the *gazlan* — or his *lokeach* — can be paid off rather than remaining a partner. This principle is consistent across the *bechor*, creditor, and *gazlan* cases.

## Transfer of Shevach Righ…

### Rights Transfer

Returning to the rights of the *gazlan* and subsequent purchasers in stolen property, Rava rules: *gazal ve-hishbiach u-machar* — if one stole, improved the stolen object, and sold it — the *nigzal* comes to reclaim the animal, and the purchaser says: pay me for the increase, since the *gazlan* was permitted to retain the *shevach*, and that right was transferred to me. Rava then raises the question of whether the same applies when the *lokeach* himself was responsible for the improvement. He resolves it: *mah machar rishon le-sheni kol zechut she-ba le-yado* — whatever the first seller transferred to the second buyer encompasses all rights that had accrued to the first seller. Just as the *gazlan* had rights to retain the *shevach*, so too the *lokeach* who purchased from him inherits those rights.

### Non-Jewish Purchaser

Rava then asks: *hishbiach oved kochavim mahu* — what if it is a non-Jew who improved the stolen object? Does a non-Jew benefit from the same entitlement to the *shevach*? Rav Achai of Difti challenges this sharply: *takanta le-ovdei kochavim meiku ve-nabdi* — are we going to institute a rabbinic enactment for the benefit of non-Jews? This formulation is significant, because it is the first time the *gemara* uses the language of *takanta* directly in this context, lending explicit support to Tosafot's position that the entire framework of the *gazlan*'s rights to the *shevach* is grounded in *takkanat hashavim* rather than in any formal *shinuy koneh*.

### Complex Chain

The *gemara* explores the more complex case: a Jewish *gazlan* — Reuven — steals the animal, sells it to a non-Jew (Christopher), who improves it, and then sells it to a Jewish purchaser (Shimon). The question is: *mahu*? Do we say that since the chain began with a Jew and ends with a Jew, the Rabbis' enactment applies and Shimon may retain the *shevach*? Or do we say that since a non-Jew is in the middle — and no enactment was made for non-Jews — the *takanta* is severed and Shimon cannot claim the *shevach*? The *gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teku*.

## Shinuy Koneh Palm Tree

### Chopped Palm Tree

Rav Pappa now opens a systematic analysis of *shinuy koneh* through a series of cases involving progressive transformation of a stolen object. The first: *hai man de-gazal dikla me-chavrei ve-katlei* — one who steals a palm tree from his neighbor by chopping it down and causing it to fall into his own field. Even so, *lo kani* — the thief does not acquire it. The reason: *mei-ikara dikla mikrei ve-hashta nami dikla mikrei* — before, it was called a palm tree; now, it is still called a palm tree — a chopped-down palm tree, but a palm tree nonetheless.

This is a striking ruling on multiple grounds. First, compared to earlier discussions in which even slight physical changes — a cow becoming fatter, a ewe giving birth — were treated as potentially significant, here a dramatic physical act — the felling of an entire tree — is deemed insufficient because it does not produce a *shinuy hashem*. Second, there is an interesting structural issue: normally we assume the theft precedes the *shinuy*. Here, however, since *karka einah nigzelet* — land cannot be the object of *gezelah* — the act of chopping the tree down is simultaneously the act of *gezelah* and whatever potential *shinuy* is involved. The *gemara* implies that had the chopping constituted a true *shinuy*, this would be a case of *gezelah ve-shinuy ba'im ke-echad* — the theft and the modification occurring simultaneously — and the *gazlan* would acquire. But since it does not constitute a *shinuy*, the question does not arise.

### Palm Logs

If one then takes the chopped palm tree and turns it into logs: *hashta mihat guvei de-dikla mikrei* — they are still called "palm logs." Again, *lo kani* — no acquisition.

### Logs to Beams

If, however, one takes those logs and fashions them into beams — *guvei ve-avdinhu kishurei* — then *kani*: the thief acquires. The transformation from raw logs to worked beams is sufficient to constitute *shinuy koneh*. The intuition tracks the lumber industry: felled trees and rough logs retain a natural character; fashioned beams represent something qualitatively different.

### Beam to Smaller Beam

If one stole a beam and reduced it into a smaller beam — *kishurei ve-avdinhu kishurei zutrei* — *lo kani*. Cutting a large beam into smaller ones does not change the category of the object in any meaningful way; they are simply different beams.

### Beams to Planks

If, however, one fashioned beams into planks — *avdinhu kitzutzita* — then *kani*. Planks represent a structurally distinct category from beams, and the transformation is sufficient to effect *shinuy koneh*.

## Shinuy Koneh Lulab

### Lulab to Broom

Rava contributes a parallel series of cases involving a stolen *lulav*. If one stole a *lulav* and fashioned it into a broom (*hutzi*) — detaching the leaves from the spine and binding them to create a sweeping implement — *kani*. *De-mei-ikara lulava mikrei ve-hashta hutzi* — originally it was called a *lulav*, now it is called a broom. The change in name reflects a genuine change in category.

### Broom to Chufya

If one then takes the broom leaves and splits them — *hutzi ve-avdinhu chufya* — again *kani*. A *chufya* is a more worked form of broom, produced by splitting each leaf along its fold to create finer strands for binding. *Me-ikara hutzi ve-hashta chufya* — the name has changed again, and the modification is an irreversible one.

### Reversible Rope

If, however, one takes the *chufya* and weaves the strands into a rope (*sharshura*): *lo kani* — no acquisition. The reason: *dehadar satrah lah* — one could unravel the rope and recover the broom. Since the change is reversible — the material could be restored to its prior form — the *gemara* classifies this as *chozer livriyato* (reversible modification), which does not constitute *shinuy koneh*. Rav Pappa then raises a related question about the *tiyomet* — the central spine of the *lulav* — asking whether its splitting constitutes a *shinuy*. The *gemara* explores this through a ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that a *lulav* whose *tiyomet* has been removed is *pasul*, and reasons by analogy that if it has been split, it should be treated equivalently. Two versions of the ruling are cited; ultimately both point toward the split *tiyomet* being treated as *pasul* and therefore as a *shinuy* that would effect acquisition.

## Reversible Changes

### Dust Reversible

The *gemara* now articulates the general principle of *shinuy hachozer livriyato* through further paired examples. If one stole dirt and fashioned it into a brick — *gazal afra me-chavreih ve-avdeih levinta* — *lo kani*. Despite the apparent radicalness of the transformation, the brick could be crushed and restored to dust, and so it is considered *chozer livriyato*.

### Brick Irreversible

Conversely, if one stole a brick and reduced it to dust — *levinta ve-avdeih afra* — *kani*. One might think: I could simply remold the dust back into a brick. But the *gemara* responds: *hai levinta achriti hi* — that would be a new brick. *Panim chadashos bau lechan* — new form has emerged. The brick one would produce from that dust would not be the same brick that was stolen; it would be a distinct object. The dust itself is treated as continuous with the original material, but the new brick would constitute a transformation into something genuinely novel.

### Metal Reversible

Similarly: if one stole a piece of metal (*naska*) and minted it into a coin, *lo kani* — no acquisition. The reason: one could melt it back down into formless metal, and so the change is reversible.

### Coin Irreversible

If one stole coins and melted them into metal, *kani* — the thief acquires. One might object: I can simply re-mint coins from this metal. But the *gemara* responds: *panim chadashos bau lechan* — those would be new coins, not the same coins that were stolen.

### Polished Reversible

If one stole blackened coins and polished them — *shichimei ve-avdinhu charatei* — *lo kani*. The blackening will return naturally over time, and polishing is therefore *chozer livriyato*. Moreover, the *shinuy hashem* here is questionable — a polished coin and a blackened coin are arguably the same object in different states.

### Blackened Irreversible

Conversely, if one stole polished coins and blackened them — *charatei ve-avdinhu shichimei* — *kani*. One might think this too is reversible, since one can simply polish the coins again. But the *gemara* notes that polishing removes a thin layer of silver each time — the coin that emerges after polishing is not fully restored to its original state. Since it is not entirely *chozer livriyato*, the blackening constitutes an irreversible modification and effects *shinuy koneh*.

## Payment Principle

### Universal Rule

The *gemara* closes this section with the general rule: *zeh ha-klal kol ha-gazlanin meshalmin ke-sha'at ha-gezeilah* — all *gazlanim* pay based on the value of the stolen object at the time of the theft. If the object has since decreased in value, the *gazlan* pays the original value; if it has increased, he pays the original value and retains the increase.

### Natural Development

The *klal* comes to include the case cited by Rav Ila: if one stole a *taleh* (lamb) and it grew into an *ayil* (ram), or a calf that became an ox — *na'aseh shinuy be-yado u-kana'o* — a *shinuy* has occurred in his hands and he acquires it. If he then slaughtered or sold it, it is his — he does not pay four and five (*arba ve-chamisha*). This is a *shinuy* that is *lo bi-yadayim* — it was not actively imposed by the thief but occurred naturally. Yet the *gemara* treats it as *shinuy koneh*. The contrast with the felled palm tree — a far more dramatic physical intervention that nonetheless failed to constitute *shinuy* — is notable and the *gemara* does not directly reconcile the two.

## Stolen Oxen Plowing

### Return Claim

The *gemara* presents the following scenario. A certain person stole a pair of oxen (*padna de-torei*) from his neighbor, plowed his field with them, planted crops, and then returned the oxen to their owner. He claimed he owed nothing further — after all, he had returned the *gezeilah* in its original form.

### Rav Nachman Ruling

The case came before Rav Nachman. This situation is the inverse of what has been discussed: rather than the stolen object itself increasing in value, the *gazlan* used the stolen object as a tool to increase the value of his own land. Rav Nachman ruled: *zil shum shivcha de-ashbach* — go assess how much the land increased in value, and have the *gazlan* reimburse the owner for that increase. This is a striking ruling, essentially requiring the *gazlan* to disgorge the benefit he derived from using the stolen oxen.

## Rava Challenge

### Partial Responsibility
