Rava challenged Rav Nachman on two grounds. First: *torei ashbach, ara lo ashbach?* — the oxen contributed to the increase in the land's value, but the land itself also contributed. If the land is now worth a hundred dollars more, it is not that the oxen alone generated that full increase; the land's own properties contributed to the outcome. Why should the *gazlan* be liable for the full improvement?

### Half Payment

Rav Nachman clarified: *mi kamina neshumei kulei? ela palga kamina* — I did not mean he pays the full increase; I meant he pays half the increase. This accounts for the joint contribution of the oxen and the land.

### Original Form Argument

Rava's second objection was more fundamental: *sof sof gezeilah hi ve-ka hadra be-einah* — ultimately this is a case of *gezeilah*, and the stolen object is being returned in its original form. The *mishnah* itself states: *kol ha-gazlanin meshalmin ke-sha'at ha-gezeilah* — all *gazlanim* pay the value at the time of the theft. If the oxen are returned intact, the *gazlan* has discharged his obligation. The principle of *keshat hag'zeilah* should mean he owes no more. Why should he be required to pay for the increase his land derived from their use?

## Habitual Gazlan Punishme…

### Judicial Authority

Rav Nachman replied with a statement that cuts off further argument: *lav amina lach ki yativna be-dina lo teima li midi?* — have I not told you that when I am sitting in judgment, do not second-guess me? He invoked the testimony of his colleague Huna, who said of Rav Nachman that he and *Shvor Malka* — a name used for Shmuel, reflecting his close relationship with the Persian ruler — are colleagues in *din*. The implication is that Rav Nachman's authority in monetary law is of the highest order.

### Deterrent Punishment

The substantive reason Rav Nachman provided was: *hai inish gazlana atika hu, u-ve'ina de-iknesay* — this man is a habitual, seasoned *gazlan*, and I wish to impose a fine upon him. In other words, Rav Nachman acknowledged that strictly speaking, Rava's analysis was correct — the *gazlan* who returns the oxen intact should owe no more than the value at the time of the theft. But for a recidivist *gazlan*, extra-legal judicial discretion — grounded in *hefker beit din hefker* — permits a court to go beyond the standard rules and impose an additional monetary sanction as a deterrent. This stands in pointed contrast to the many leniencies extended earlier in the *sugya* to encourage repentance; here, at the end, a measure of common sense and proportionality reasserts itself in the opposite direction.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 97

## Shinui & Gezeila Framewo…

### Aged Animals & Slaves

The daf begins mid-*mishna* on 97b, continuing the theme of *kinyanei gezeila*. The *mishna* states: *gazal beheima vehizkinah* — one who steals an animal and it grows old — or similarly *avadim vehizkinu*, slaves who grow old in the thief's possession — *meshalem k'sha'as hagezeila*, he pays according to the value at the time of the theft.

The conceptual difficulty here is worth pausing over. The *mishna* invokes the principle that one pays based on the original value, but it does not explicitly state *which* of two possible legal frameworks underlies this rule. One possibility is *shinui koneh*: the object has changed so fundamentally that the thief has acquired it, and therefore pays its original value as the price of that acquisition. But there is a second, distinct possibility that the *mishna* leaves unexplored — namely, that the animal or slave has changed enough that the thief *cannot* say *harei shelcha lefanecha* ("here is your object, unchanged"), and yet has not changed so drastically that the thief has acquired it outright. In that intermediate case, the object would be returned *and* the thief would pay the difference in value.

This is a logically coherent middle category. When a *mishna* says *meshalem k'sha'as hagezeila*, that formulation could mean either (a) the thief owns the object and pays its original value, or (b) the thief returns the object and pays the difference. The *gemara* has not yet resolved this ambiguity explicitly, and it is worth keeping this conceptual space in mind as the sugya develops.

### Three Response Categories

It helps to lay out the full spectrum of possible responses to theft, as the *mishna* and *gemara* together implicitly define three positions along a continuum.

At one extreme: *harei shelcha lefanecha* — the thief returns the object and owes nothing beyond the return, because the object is effectively the same as when it was stolen. The change, if any, is too minor or too invisible for the owner to demand compensation.

At the other extreme: *nasah shinui b'yado u-kna'o* — the object has transformed so significantly that the thief has acquired it through *shinui*. He no longer returns the object; he pays the owner the original value and keeps what is now, in effect, his own object.

In the middle — and this is the category the *mishna* may be describing — there is a case where the change is real and noticeable enough that the thief cannot simply say *harei shelcha lefanecha*, but is *not* drastic enough to constitute *shinui koneh*. The thief returns the object and pays the difference. The phrase *meshalem k'sha'as hagezeila* in the *mishna* is compatible with this reading: return the object and compensate the owner for the diminution in value.

This threefold structure — *harei shelcha lefanecha*, intermediate payment-plus-return, and full *shinui koneh* — is what the *mishna* cases must be evaluated against. What is clear is that a slave who has grown old, or an animal that has aged, cannot be returned with a breezy *harei shelcha lefanecha*. What is less clear is whether these cases cross the threshold into full *shinui koneh*, or whether they occupy the middle ground.

### Visible Damage Cases

The *mishna* continues with cases that appear far more dramatic: *gazal matbe'a venistak* — a stolen coin that developed a crack; *peiros vehirkivu* — fruit that rotted; *yayin vehechimitz* — wine that turned to vinegar. In all these cases, *meshalem k'sha'as hagezeila*, the thief pays based on the original value at the time of the theft.

These cases seem to involve objects that have changed so thoroughly that the thief surely cannot say *harei shelcha lefanecha*. Cracked coins, rotted fruit, and vinegared wine are categorically different from what was taken. Whether these constitute *shinui koneh* — such that the thief has outright acquired the damaged item — or whether they fall into the intermediate category of return-plus-compensation, is again left implicit. The *mishna*'s language is neutral on that point.

### Non-Visible Damage

The *mishna* then pivots to a strikingly different set of cases: *matbe'a venifsal* — a coin that was not physically cracked but was invalidated by the government; *truma venitmeis* — *teruma* that became *tamei*; *chametz she'avar alav hapesach* — leavened grain that passed through *Pesach* in the thief's possession, rendering it rabbinically worthless; *beheima sheni'avda bah aveira* — an animal used for a sexual transgression, which thereby becomes unfit for the altar; and *shor haniskal* — an ox condemned to stoning. In all these cases, the *mishna* rules *omer lo harei shelcha lefanecha* — the thief simply returns the object and is exempt from further payment.

This is a remarkable ruling. These objects may be worth almost nothing — or in the case of *chametz* after *Pesach*, effectively nothing at all by rabbinic law. And yet, since the damage is not visible, since there is no physical change perceptible to the senses, the thief may return the object and declare, "here is your thing." The owner receives back something essentially worthless, and the thief bears no further obligation. This is a significant *chiddush*.

The unifying principle of this second list is *hezek she'eino nikar* — damage that is not visible. The owner cannot point to any perceptible physical difference in what has been returned. The legal status has changed — the coin is invalid, the *teruma* is *tamei*, the animal is disqualified — but none of these changes manifest in the object's physical appearance.

One might note that a government-invalidated coin still has its raw metal value and could theoretically be melted down, and an animal unfit for the altar is not worth nothing. These are genuinely cases of diminished but nonzero value. The conceptual question of what makes non-visible damage categorically different from visible damage will return later in the sugya.

---

## Permanent Change Criteri…

### Rav Pappa's Weakening

The *gemara* opens this section with Rav Pappa's interpretive move. When the *mishna* says *hizkinah* — that the animal grew old — it does not mean literally that the animal became decrepit and useless. Rather, Rav Pappa says *afilu kichashah* — even if it merely became weaker. The *gemara* immediately pushes back: but our *mishna* says *hizkinah*, old age, which implies a significant degree of change. How can mere weakness trigger the same rule?

Rav Pappa's answer: *kichashah ke'ein hizkinah* — a weakness that resembles old age in the relevant sense, meaning *dilo hadra bari* — that it will not recover. What matters is not the magnitude of the change, but its permanence. A temporary injury or a temporary weakness would perhaps allow the thief to return the object and say *harei shelcha lefanecha* — wait, it will recover. But a permanent change, even a subtle one, crosses the threshold. The thief cannot say the object is effectively the same if it has been permanently diminished, even if that diminishment is modest. This is *dilo hadra bari* as the operative criterion: permanent, non-reversible change.

### Lamb to Ram Example

Mar Keshisha, the son of Rav Chisda, cited to Rav Ashi a teaching in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *afilu ganav taleh ve-na'asah ayil, egel ve-na'asah shor, nasah shinui beyado u-kna'o* — even if one stole a lamb and it became a ram, a calf and it became an ox, this constitutes a *shinui* and the thief acquires it. The consequence: *tevacho u-mechoro, shelo hu tovei'ach shelo hu mocher* — if he subsequently slaughtered or sold it, he is slaughtering and selling his own property, and does not incur the four- and fivefold penalty of *geneivah*.

This is the same teaching we have encountered earlier in the *masechet*, now being introduced here in the context of the *shinui* discussion. It is worth observing that the lamb-to-ram transformation is in some respects more dramatic than aging, in that it involves a categorical change in the animal's identity — the creature now has a different name, *shinui hashem* — and yet it is also more natural, in that no human action caused it. Both features together constitute sufficient *shinui*: a qualitative, categorical change that is permanent, even though it came about through the passage of time rather than through the thief's physical act.

It is also worth noting that a lamb becoming a ram does not make the animal worthless — if anything, it may have become more valuable. This demonstrates that *shinui* for purposes of *koneh* does not require the object to have deteriorated. The category is about qualitative transformation, not about loss of value.

### Source Clarification

Rav Ashi replied to Mar Keshisha: *lav amina lach, lo tachlif gavrei* — have I not told you not to mix up the names? The teaching about the lamb and the ram was not said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, but in the name of Rav Ila. This is a correction of attribution, not of substance.

### Middle Category Debate

Returning to the conceptual question raised by the earlier *mishna* cases: when the *mishna* says *meshalem k'sha'as hagezeila* — whether in the case of an aging animal, a weakened animal, or a cracked coin — does this implicitly mean the thief has *acquired* the object through *shinui*, or does it mean that the object is returned and the difference is paid?

The *gemara* has generally treated *meshalem k'sha'as hagezeila* as implying *shinui koneh*, but this has never been stated explicitly. The case of the lamb becoming a ram *did* explicitly use the language *nasah shinui beyado u-kna'o* — he acquired it. But the cases of aging and weakening simply say to pay based on the original value, without specifying whether the thief retains the object or returns it.

This is precisely the middle ground that remains unclarified: a case where the change is real and permanent enough that the thief cannot say *harei shelcha lefanecha*, but where the *gemara* has not explicitly said the thief is *koneh* the object. The resolution lies somewhere between those two poles. The *mishna*'s *meshalem k'sha'as hagezeila* is consistent with either interpretation — pay the original amount because you own it now, or return it and pay the difference — and the *gemara* has not forced a choice between them.

---

## Slaves as Karka Debate

### Rabbi Meir on Slaves

The *mishna* records Rabbi Meir's position: *ba'avadim omer lo harei shelcha lefanecha* — with respect to slaves, the thief simply returns the slave and owes nothing more. Rabbi Meir's reasoning is that slaves are like *karka*, real property, and the laws of *gezeila* do not apply to land. Since there is no act of *gezeila* with respect to slaves, there is no liability arising from it; the thief simply returns the slave and is done. Whatever has happened to the slave in the interim — including aging — generates no additional obligation.

### Rav's Text Reversal

The *gemara* reports that Rav bar Avdimi said in the name of Rav: *halacha k'Rabbi Meir* — we rule like Rabbi Meir, that slaves are like *karka*. The *gemara* immediately challenges this: does Rav simply abandon the Rabbis and rule with a *da'as yachid*? Rav's reasoning, the *gemara* explains, is that he found a *baraita* in which the positions were reversed — a *baraita* in which it was the Rabbis who said that slaves are like *karka* and Rabbi Meir who said they are not.

The *gemara* presses further: if there is a conflict between the *mishna* and the *baraita*, why follow the *baraita* and adjust the *mishna* rather than follow the *mishna* and adjust the *baraita*? The answer: Rav had not one but two *baraitot* in which the positions were reversed. *Chada mikamei tartei* — one text against two, he reversed the *mishna* in light of two consistent external sources. When Rav says *halacha k'Rabbi Meir*, he is saying: according to your reading of the *mishna*, the position I am endorsing belongs to Rabbi Meir; but in truth, based on my reading, it is actually the Rabbis' position, and we rule that slaves are like *karka*.

### Birth During Sale Case

The second *baraita* that drove Rav to reverse the positions reads as follows: *ha-machlif parah b'chamor ve-yaldah* — one who swaps a cow for a donkey, and the cow gave birth during the process; or similarly *ha-mocher shifchato ve-yaldah* — one who sold his female slave, and she gave birth during the sale. The *baraita* is addressing a situation where possession was transferred through *chalipin* (in the case of the cow) or through money (in the case of the slave), and a birth occurred somewhere in the interval — but it is unclear whether it occurred before or after the transfer took effect.

The *baraita* sets out the legal analysis: if the buyer claims definitively that the birth occurred after he took possession and the seller is uncertain, the buyer wins — *bari ve-shema, bari adif*. If both parties are uncertain, they divide. If both claim definitively, the seller must take an oath: *yishava ha-mocher she-bi-reshuto yaldah* — the seller swears that the birth occurred while it was still in his possession and thereby avoids paying the calf or baby. This is consistent with the rule that in Torah law, oaths get the oath-taker out of payment rather than entitle him to collect.

This is Rabbi Meir's position. The Rabbis, by contrast, say: *ein nishba'in lo al ha-avadim ve-lo al ha-karka'ot* — there is no oath imposed in cases involving slaves or land. Why? Because slaves are like *karka*, and the Torah's oath mechanism does not apply to real property.

The reversal is now plain: in this *baraita*, Rabbi Meir holds that you *can* take an oath about slaves — meaning slaves are *not* like *karka* — while the Rabbis hold that you *cannot* — meaning slaves *are* like *karka*. In our *mishna*, the same positions appear with the names switched. Rav, armed with two *baraitot* presenting the reversed attribution, concluded that the *mishna*'s version of the positions is a scribal error and that the Rabbis are truly the ones who equate slaves with *karka*. Hence his ruling: *halacha k'Rabbi Meir* — meaning, according to the *mishna*'s erroneous labeling, we rule like "Rabbi Meir," but in substance we rule like the Rabbis.

It is worth noting, as one sharp observer pointed out during the discussion, that this reversal of names occurs immediately after Rav Ashi corrected Mar Keshisha for mixing up attributions in the preceding *sugya* — a striking coincidence of theme.

### Kinyan Agreement

Tosafot raises a penetrating question here. The *baraita* uses two different acquisition mechanisms: *chalipin* for the cow and *kesef* for the slave. One might ask why the *baraita* needed to shift from *chalipin* to *kesef* when moving from the animal to the slave case. The answer is that slaves cannot be acquired through *meshicha* (pulling) or *hagbahah* (lifting), as movable chattel typically is. Slaves are acquired through *kesef*, *shtar*, and *chazakah* — the same modes used for *karka*.

This raises a deeper question: if everybody in the *baraita* — both Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis — treats the slave as being acquired through the same modes as *karka*, does that mean there is universal agreement that slaves are like *karka* for purposes of *kinyan*, even while they debate whether slaves are like *karka* for purposes of *gezeila* and *shevua*? Tosafot concludes that the answer is yes, and this is not contradictory. The categorization of slaves as *karka* is not necessarily a single all-or-nothing determination. For *kinyan*, perhaps everyone agrees that slaves follow the rules of real property. For *gezeila* and *shevua*, the exclusion is derived from specific *drashos* — *klal u'ferat u'klal* — which create a more formal, categorical exclusion. When the exclusion is based on formal derivation rather than on logic, we apply it consistently: if slaves fall into the category, they fall in across the board. If they do not, they do not. But this is distinct from the *kinyan* question, where the agreement may be universal regardless of the *gezeila* and *shevua* debate.

---

## Slave Seizure & Use

### Rav's Exemption

The *gemara* now introduces a ruling of Rav cited by Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina: *hatokef b'avdo shel chaveiro v'asa bo melakha patur* — one who seizes his friend's slave and uses him to perform labor is exempt from payment. This ruling sets up the central tension of the entire passage.

### Nigzal vs. Karka

The exemption makes immediate sense if a slave is treated like a stolen animal — that is, if the slave is *nigzal*. In that case, the principle of *kinyanei gezeila* applies: by seizing physical possession of the object, the *gazlan* acquires a kind of de facto quasi-ownership, and as a result, when he returns the object, he owes nothing for its use. This is the counterintuitive consequence of *gezeila* law: the act of theft, paradoxically, generates a form of entitlement to use the stolen object without paying. Yesterday's discussion illustrated this with the case of a stolen cow used to plow a field.

But the question is exactly the opposite of what one might expect. If Rav holds that slaves are like *karka* — as he apparently does — then a slave is *not nigzal*. The person who seizes the slave has not committed an act of *gezeila*. He is simply using someone else's property without permission, much like someone who takes up residence in another's house without authorization. In the house case, the relevant framework is *zeh neheneh v'zeh lo chaser* versus *zeh neheneh v'zeh chaser*. If the house was posted for rental and the unauthorized occupant displaced paying tenants, it is *zeh chaser* and payment is required. If the house was not available for rental, the question is more complex — there may be minimal damage counterbalanced by benefit to the property from being occupied. But the question is: why is the slave-seizer *patur*?

### She'lo B'Shas Melakha

The *gemara* answers: *she'lo b'shas melakha* — the exemption applies specifically when the slave was not being used for labor at the time of the seizure. This is a case of *zeh neheneh v'zeh lo chaser*. If the slave was on his break, not engaged in any productive work for his master, the master has lost nothing — it is a case where the taker benefited but the owner was not harmed. Under *zeh neheneh v'zeh lo chaser*, no payment is owed.

This reframes Rav's ruling significantly. Rav is not making a statement about slaves being like stolen chattel. He is making a statement about when the use of an idle slave causes no loss — which is the same principle that would apply if one lived, without permission, in a friend's house that was not available for rent. The *chiddush* of the ruling is thus not that slaves are like *karka* and the stranger principle somehow applies, but rather that when the slave is not working, the master's loss is zero, and so is the obligation to pay.

### Debtors' Slaves Case

The *gemara* now describes a practice in the household of Rav Yosef bar Chama: they would seize the slaves of people who owed them money — *d'masik behu zuzei* — and have those slaves perform labor for them. This goes beyond the theoretical case. It is a regular practice of taking the slaves of one's debtors and putting them to work.

### Worth Their Bread

Rabba, Rav Yosef bar Chama's son, objected: what is the basis for this practice? Rav Yosef bar Chama replied by citing Rav Nachman's statement: *avda nahom karseh lo shavei* — a slave is not worth the bread in his stomach. The attitude here is stark: slaves are inherently lazy, so any opportunity to put them to work is actually welcome. This is offered as the justification for why seizing and using someone's slave is not a *chaser* — the master presumably *wants* his slaves to be kept busy and productive rather than idle.

### Defense of Use

Rabba pressed further: Rav Nachman said that about a specific slave — Daru, who was *de'markid be'kubeih*, who danced about idly in the tavern. That contemptuous remark was about one particularly worthless slave, not a blanket statement about all slaves. Most slaves do real work. On what basis, then, does one have the right to seize another person's slave?

Rav Yosef bar Chama responded: *ana ke'Rav Daniel sevirah li* — I hold like Rav Daniel. Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina said in the name of Rav: *hatokef b'avdo shel chaveiro v'asa bo melakha, patur*. You are exempt. And the reason you are exempt, if slaves are like *karka*, must be that this is a case of *zeh lo chaser* — the master actually benefits from having his slave kept busy. *Nicha lei d'lo listerei avdei* — it is good for the master that his slave does not become lazy. Therefore, not only is payment not owed after the fact; Rav Yosef bar Chama argued that it is permissible to do this *lechatchilah*.

### Ribbis Concern

The *gemara* objects: even if all of that is true in a normal case — even if using someone's idle slave is *zeh lo chaser* and permissible — it does not apply here. *Keivan d'masik behu zuzei nechzei ke'ribbis* — since these people owe you money, seizing their slaves and enjoying their labor looks like interest. You are extracting benefit from people who owe you money. Even if the benefit would ordinarily be something you are entitled to for free — even if technically there is no *chaser* — the optics of a creditor taking something of value from a debtor create the appearance of usury.

### Debt Exception

This is precisely the principle stated by Rav Yosef bar Minyumi in the name of Rav Nachman: *af al pi she'amru hadar b'chatzer chaveiro shelo mi-da'ato eino tzarich l'haalos lo sachar* — even though we rule that one who lives in a friend's yard without permission owes no rental fee in a standard *zeh lo chaser* case — *halvehu ve-dar b'chatzaro, tzarich l'haalos lo sachar* — if he happened to borrow money from that friend and is now living in the friend's yard, he *does* owe rent. The normal exemption is suspended because the presence of a debt changes the legal and moral character of the arrangement entirely.

Rav Yosef bar Chama accepted this: *hadari bi* — I retract. He acknowledged that the practice, however defensible in the abstract, was impermissible when applied to his own debtors.

The broader conceptual point the *gemara* has now clarified is worth summarizing. By *metaltelin* — movable chattel — if one steals a cow and uses it, one pays nothing for the use because *kinyanei gezeila* create a kind of de facto ownership in the *gazlan*. By *karka* and by slaves (who are like *karka*) — the property is not *nigzal*, and one who occupies or uses it is not a *gazlan*. In such a case, the question is *zeh neheneh v'zeh chaser* or *zeh lo chaser*. If *chaser*, one pays; if *lo chaser*, one does not. For slaves, the *gemara* posits that the standard case is *lo chaser* — the master is taken to prefer his slave remain active — and therefore the slave-user does not pay. But when the user is a creditor of the slave-owner, the entire analysis collapses: even a technically free benefit becomes forbidden because it resembles *ribbis*.

---

## Boat Seizure Case

### Rav: Sechar or Pachis

The *gemara* now turns to a parallel case: *hatokef sefinato shel chaveiro v'asa bah melakha* — seizing a friend's boat, which is *metaltelin*, and using it for labor. Here the person who seized the boat *is* a *gazlan* — it is movable chattel, not *karka*. Rav rules: *rotzeh sechar notel, rotzeh pachas notel* — the owner has a choice, he can collect either the rental fee or the depreciation in the boat's value. The owner would naturally take whichever is higher.

The question is: why should the owner be able to collect a rental fee? If this is a case of *gezeila*, the *gazlan* should have de facto rights to the object — the standard principle should be that the *gazlan* returns the object and owes nothing for use. Why is there an option to collect *sechar*?

### Shmuel: Pachis Only

Shmuel disagrees: *eino notel ela pachas* — the owner collects only the depreciation, not the rental fee. This is consistent with the *gazlan* principle: the *gazlan* is liable for damage to the object but not for its rental value during the period of unauthorized use.

### Rental Status Matters

Rav Pappa resolves the dispute: *lo pligi* — Rav and Shmuel do not actually disagree. Their rulings apply to different cases. *Ha de'avida le-agra, ha de-lo avida le-agra* — one rule applies when the boat is the type that is regularly rented out, the other when it is not. If the boat is normally available for hire, the owner can collect the rental fee; if it is just a private boat sitting in someone's yard, only depreciation is owed.

### Intent & Implicit Terms

The *gemara* refines this further. Even assuming the boat is one that is normally rented out, the framework shifts based on the intent of the person who took it. *Ha de-nachis lah ada'ata de-igra, ha de-nachis lah ada'ata de-gazlanuta* — if the person took the boat with the understanding that he was borrowing it and would return it, not stealing it, then because he is not positioning himself as a *gazlan*, he does not acquire the de facto rights of a *gazlan*. He is, in effect, an unauthorized renter. Since the boat is normally available for rental, he is implicitly agreeing to rental terms, and the owner collects *sechar*.

But if the person took it with the intent of a *gazlan* — genuinely seizing it — then the *kinyan gezeila* analysis applies, and paradoxically the owner collects only depreciation, not rent. The greater the wrongdoing, the less the *gazlan* owes for the use. This is the counterintuitive irony the *gemara* has been tracking throughout: the more culpable the taking, the greater the de facto rights it generates, and therefore the less one owes for the use of the object.

---

## Visible vs. Invisible

### Crack vs. Invalidation

The *gemara* revisits the distinction between a physically cracked coin and a coin that has been invalidated by government decree. Rav Huna states: *nistak nistak mamash* — a crack means a literal physical crack, and in that case the thief cannot return the coin and declare *harei shelcha lefanecha*. But *nifsal* — invalidation — specifically means *psalto malchus*: the government has withdrawn it from circulation. In *that* case, the thief can return the coin.

### Yehuda's Challenge

Rav Yehuda challenges this: is government invalidation really different from a physical crack? If the entire Roman Empire has declared these coins invalid, then functionally, practically, this coin is worthless — just as worthless as one with a physical crack. Anyone who encounters it will treat it as garbage. Should we not say that the status has changed so completely that it is equivalent to visible physical damage, such that the thief cannot return it?

Rav Yehuda therefore proposes a different distinction for what *nifsal* means when the thief *can* say *harei shelcha lefanecha*: it must be a case of *psalto medina* — invalidated in one region only, but still usable in another region of the empire. In that case the coin retains genuine value, even if not locally. But if the entire government has invalidated it everywhere, that is treated like a crack.

### Chisda's Question

Rav Chisda addresses a question to Rav Huna: according to Rav Huna, who says that even full empire-wide invalidation still permits the thief to say *harei shelcha lefanecha*, how is this different from the cases of rotten fruit and vinegared wine, where the *mishna* rules that the thief must pay the original value? After all, rotted fruit and vinegared wine are similarly "invalidated" — they have become something categorically different, something of far diminished or zero practical value. Why should those cases require payment while a government-invalidated coin does not?

### Sense Perception Test

Rav Huna's response: *hasam nishtana ta'amo ve-reicho* — there, with the rotten fruit and the vinegared wine, the taste and smell have changed. These are perceptible, sensory differences. You can taste that the wine is vinegar; you can smell that the fruit is rotten. The physical object itself has transformed in ways detectable by the senses. A government-invalidated coin, by contrast, *lo nishtana* — has not physically changed at all. It looks, feels, weighs, and smells exactly the same. The change is entirely in the legal and social status assigned to it by external decree, not in the coin itself.

### Rava on Teruma

Rava then challenges Rav Yehuda from the opposite direction. According to Rav Yehuda, who says that empire-wide invalidation *is* like a physical crack and the thief cannot return the coin — how does Rav Yehuda distinguish this from *teruma* that became *tamei* or *chametz* that passed through *Pesach*? Those cases also involve complete functional invalidation: *tamei teruma* cannot be eaten, and *chametz* after *Pesach* has no permitted use (at least rabbinically). Yet the *mishna* rules in those cases that the thief says *harei shelcha lefanecha*. Why should an empire-wide coin invalidation be treated differently?

### Minkar Heizika

The answer resolves the entire set of disputes and formulates the governing principle: *hasam lo minkar heizika, hacha minkar heizika* — there, with *tamei teruma* and *chametz*, the damage is not noticeable; here, with empire-wide coin invalidation, the damage *is* noticeable.

This is the key conceptual distinction. The category of damage that triggers the inability to say *harei shelcha lefanecha* is not simply physical change, nor is it simply functional invalidity. It is *minkar heizika* — damage that is perceptible, that registers to observers as a change. Rotten fruit passes the test because taste and smell betray the change. Government-invalidated coins, in Rav Yehuda's view, pass the test because everyone who encounters the coin immediately recognizes it as worthless — even without any physical alteration. The social and legal consensus that this is no longer money is itself a form of perceptible change, even if the physical object is untouched.

*Tamei teruma* and *chametz*, by contrast, are cases of *lo minkar heizika* — the damage is invisible. You cannot look at *tamei teruma* and tell it is *tamei*; you cannot look at *chametz* left over from *Pesach* and distinguish it from ordinary grain. In those cases, the thief may return the object and invoke *harei shelcha lefanecha*, because there is no perceptible difference visible to the observer.

---

## Old Currency Repayment

### Loan Setup

The *gemara* now presents a new case: *ha-malveh chaveiro al ha-matbe'a ve-nifsal ha-matbe'a* — one who lends his friend money (or according to Rashi, enters into a commercial transaction or investment where repayment is owed), and subsequently the coins that were the currency at the time of the transaction are invalidated by the government. When repayment falls due, must the borrower pay with currently valid currency, or may he pay with the old invalidated coins?

### Rav: Current Currency

Rav rules: *nosein lo matbe'a ha-yotzei be-osah sha'ah* — the debtor must give the creditor the currency that is in circulation *now*, at the time of payment. When you owe someone ten thousand, you owe them ten thousand units of real, usable money. If the currency has changed, you must pay in the new currency.

### Shmuel: Old Currency OK

Shmuel rules differently: *yachol lomar lo hotzio be-Meishan* — the debtor may say, "take this money and spend it in Meishan," another region where the old coins are still in circulation. Since the debt was incurred in the old currency and that currency retains genuine value in other locales, tendering the old coins constitutes valid repayment. This is the *psalto medina* scenario — invalidated locally, usable elsewhere.

### Travel Condition

Rav Nachman qualifies Shmuel's ruling significantly: *mistavra milta de-Shmuel de-is lay orcha le-meizal le-Meishan* — Shmuel's position that old coins can be tendered as valid payment makes sense only if the creditor has plans to travel to the place where those coins are usable. If the creditor already has a business trip to Meishan scheduled in the near term, these coins genuinely are money to him — he will be able to spend them. In that case, Shmuel's ruling applies and the old currency constitutes legitimate repayment.

But *aval leis lay orcha* — if the creditor has no plans to travel there — then these coins are effectively useless to him, and one cannot call them valid repayment of a debt. Shmuel's principle holds, but only when the geographic limitation of the currency is a practical inconvenience the creditor can readily address, not when it renders the coins genuinely inaccessible in value.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 98

## Currency Exchange

### Rav vs. Shmuel

We pick up at the top of 98b, in the midst of a *sugya* concerning a case where somebody borrowed money — or sold something, or entered into a business arrangement — at a time when a certain currency was in circulation, and when the time comes to repay, that currency is no longer accepted in this locale. Can the debtor still discharge his obligation by paying with the old currency?

*Rav* holds that he must pay back with the new currency. *Shmuel*, by contrast, maintains that payment with the old currency is still valid, since that currency remains in use elsewhere — go to *Meshan*, he says, and you can use it there. Since the currency has not been rendered entirely *nifsal malchus* — completely invalidated everywhere — it retains legitimacy, and the original terms of the transaction can be honored with it.

### Rav Nachman's Limit

*Rav Nachman*, however, found *Shmuel*'s position somewhat radical and limited it considerably. It is only valid, he said, if the person receiving payment is actually headed to the place where that currency is still in use. If he is traveling to *Meshan*, then paying him back in that currency is acceptable. Otherwise, it is not.

### Rava's Challenge

*Rava* then challenged *Rav Nachman*'s formulation by citing a ruling concerning *maaser sheni*. The *Torah* permits one who is too far away to transfer the sanctity of *maaser sheni* fruit onto money and bring the money to *Yerushalayim* — but only onto money that is currently in circulation. As the text states: *ein mechalelin al ma'os she'einam yotzos* — you cannot transfer the sanctity of *maaser sheni* onto money that is not current.

### Bar Kochba Coins

The *Gemara* illustrates this with a *baraita*: *hayu lo ma'os Kuzbios Yerushalmios* — if one has coins from *Kuzbios*. *Rashi* explains that *Kuzbios* refers to *Ben Kuzbi*, that is, *Bar Kochva*. Indeed, *Bar Kochva* minted his own coins, examples of which can still be seen in museums in *Eretz Yisrael*. The *baraita* continues: *o shel melachim harishonim* — or coins of earlier kings. Such currency, no longer in circulation, cannot serve as the vehicle for *chilul maaser sheni*.

### Current vs. Past Kings

This seems straightforward enough, but the *Gemara* raises a subtle implication. The phrase *shel achronim dumya de-rishonim* — of later, i.e., currently ruling kings, but similar to the earlier ones — suggests that if the currency of a presently reigning government happens not to be in circulation in one's location, it would nevertheless be valid for *chilul maaser sheni*. The inference is that currency from an existing government, even if not locally current, retains legitimacy. This appears to support *Shmuel*'s view.

### Makpido Principle

*Rav Nachman* responds: *hacha be-mai askinan kshe-ein malchuyos makpidos zo al zo* — the permissive case concerns kingdoms that are not *makpid* on one another, meaning that the currency of one circulates or is easily transferable in the other's territory. In such a case, the currency is considered usable and valid even where it is not the primary tender. The lecturer notes some uncertainty about the precise practical meaning of *eino makpidos*: does it mean the currency is actually accepted here, or merely that it is easy enough to exchange or transport across the border? Either way, that is the answer for why the currency would work.

By contrast, when *Shmuel* says one can repay with the old currency — under *Rav Nachman*'s limiting reading — this must refer to a case where the governments *are* mutually *makpid*. The *Gemara* then asks: if they are mutually *makpid*, how can one even bring the currency to the other locale, even if traveling there? The *Gemara* answers: *demati lehu al yedei dachak* — one can get it there with some difficulty. *Delo pacheshi* — they do not search your bags at the border. *Ve-im meshkachi kapdei* — but if they find it, they will confiscate it. So practically, if one acts discreetly, the currency can be transported. That is the scenario where *Shmuel* permits repayment when the creditor is heading to that locale.

---

## Currency Exchange (II)

### Maaser Sheni Cases

The *Gemara* then introduces a further *baraita* in an attempt to resolve the matter. *Ein mechalelin al ma'os shekan vehen be'Bavel* — you cannot transfer *maaser sheni* to *Eretz Yisrael* money if you and that money are located in *Bavel*. This is already an interesting ruling, as we generally assume *maaser sheni* applies only within *Eretz Yisrael* and its immediate environs — yet certain areas including *Bavel* were subject to the *takkanah* of *terumot u'maasrot*.

So: you are in *Bavel*, the money in question is *Eretz Yisrael* currency, and you cannot perform *chilul maaser sheni* onto it. The *Gemara* points out: *afgav desofei lemisik lehatam* — even though you are heading to *Eretz Yisrael* and intend to bring this money there. This seems like a decisive refutation of *Shmuel*: even if one is en route to the very place where the currency is current, it is still not considered valid money in the here and now.

The *Gemara* responds, again, that this *baraita* speaks of a case where the kingdoms are mutually *makpid* — *kshe-malchuyot makpidot zo al zo* — and so the *Eretz Yisrael* currency cannot actually be brought there.

The *Gemara* then challenges from the other case in the *baraita*: *shebe'Bavel vehen be'Bavel mechalelin* — if you are in *Bavel* and the money is Babylonian currency, you may transfer *maaser sheni* onto it. But what use is that? You have to spend the redemption money in *Yerushalayim*, and if the kingdoms are mutually *makpid*, how will you bring Babylonian coins into *Eretz Yisrael*?

### Jerusalem Money Exchange

The *Gemara* answers: *chazu d'zavin behu beheima u'maisye l'Yerushalayim* — you use the Babylonian money to purchase animals and bring them to *Yerushalayim*, and once there you transfer the *maaser sheni* status to something else and consume it. *Tosafot* notes the tension here, since many sources hold that you cannot transfer *maaser sheni* sanctity onto animals — only onto money. *Tosafot* resolves this by acknowledging that in such a scenario there is no other practical option: if the fruit is too much to carry and neither *Eretz Yisrael* currency (unusable in *Bavel*) nor Babylonian currency (unusable in *Eretz Yisrael*) provides a complete solution, this indirect route — redeeming onto Babylonian money and then purchasing animals — becomes the only viable path.

The *Gemara* then raises another question: if the kingdoms are mutually *makpid*, how was any currency universally accepted in *Yerushalayim* at all? Is it not taught *hitkinu sheyihu ma'os yotzos b'Yerushalayim* — that they established that all currencies should be accepted in *Yerushalayim*? *Rabbi Zeira* resolves this: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. When the hand of Israel was strong over the nations, *Yerushalayim* could decree universal currency acceptance. When the nations had power over Israel, they could impose restrictions on which currencies circulated.

### Coin Imagery

The *Gemara* then asks: what does the coin of *Yerushalayim* look like? *David u'Shlomo m'tzad echad, v'Yerushalayim ir hakodesh m'tzad acher* — David and Solomon on one side, and *Yerushalayim* the holy city on the other. Much like modern coins that bear a leader's portrait on one side and a building or symbol on the reverse.

The *Gemara* also describes the coin associated with *Avraham Avinu*: *zaken u'zekeina m'tzad echad, bachur u'vetula m'tzad acher* — an old man and woman on one side (presumably *Avraham* and *Sarah*) and a young man and woman on the other (perhaps *Yitzchak* and *Rivkah*). This description is drawn from a *Bereishis Rabbah* that expounds the phrase *agadel shimcha* — I will make your name great — as referring to a *monitin* (a stamp or coin) that went forth into the world.

*Tosafot* raises the question of whether such coin imagery would violate the prohibition against creating human forms — *assur la'asos tzorat adam*. *Tosafot* therefore suggests, citing *Rashi*, that the coins did not actually bear images of these figures, but rather the words *zaken u'zekeina* were inscribed on one side. *Rashi* applies this same interpretation to the *David u'Shlomo* coin: the names were written, not their portraits. *Tosafot* notes that the harder case is that of *Avraham*, because the *Midrash* language of *monitin* implies an actual image rather than merely a written name, making the purely textual explanation seem less natural there.

---

## Maaser Accessibility

### Bavel-EY Exchange

The *Gemara* continues developing the *maaser sheni* currency discussion, and several of the rulings canvassed here — particularly around whether *Eretz Yisrael* money held in *Bavel* can serve as the vehicle for *chilul maaser sheni*, and vice versa — reflect a broader principle: the currency must be accessible and functional in the place where one seeks to use it, not merely existent somewhere in the world.

### Animal Transfer

As noted in the discussion of the *baraita*, when neither *Eretz Yisrael* currency nor Babylonian currency provides a clean path to *Yerushalayim*, the *Gemara* permits — under duress — the indirect route of purchasing animals with the redeemed Babylonian money and transporting them to *Yerushalayim*. *Tosafot* acknowledges this runs against the general rule that *maaser sheni* sanctity can only be transferred to money, but treats it as an emergency concession when no other avenue exists.

---

## Flattened Coins

### Coin Image Problem

In passing, the *Gemara*'s discussion of coin imagery raises the broader question — taken up by *Tosafot* — of whether images found on coins create problems under the laws of *avoda zara*. The *Gemara* mentions a certain individual praised as *chasid* or *kadosh* because he never looked at the images on coins. This points to an ongoing sensitivity surrounding numismatic imagery and the *issur* of making or benefiting from human forms. The precise scope of that prohibition — whether it applies to two-dimensional representations, to partial forms, or only to fully three-dimensional figures — is a subject of significant *halachic* discussion, though the *Gemara* does not resolve it here. *Tosafot*'s resolution — that the coins of *Avraham*, *David*, and *Solomon* bore only inscribed words and not actual portraits — is offered precisely to sidestep that problem.

---

## Coin Value

### Enlarged Coins

The *Gemara* now poses a new question. *Rava* asked *Rav Chisda*: *ha-malveh es chaveiro al ha-matbe'a ve-hosifu alav mahu* — if someone lent money when a coin was a certain size, and by the time of repayment the coin has been enlarged — what is the law? Does the borrower repay with the same number of coins (now containing more precious metal) or must he account for the discrepancy?

*Rav Chisda* answers: *nosein lo matbe'a ha-yotzei be-osah sha'ah* — he pays back with the currency currently in circulation. Even if the coin is now as large as a sieve — even as large as some great block — the answer remains yes, you pay back in current coin. One simply repays with the same denomination as borrowed.

### Buying Power vs. Metal

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *ve-ha ka zeili peiri* — but produce has become cheaper! If the coin is now larger, one gets more for the same coin, meaning the creditor is receiving back something of greater value. This raises the fundamental question of whether we assess repayment based on the coin's purchasing power or its precious metal content.

### Precious Metal Test

*Rav Ashi* resolves this: *chazinan* — we must assess the situation. *Ei machmas tiv'a zil* — if the reason produce has become cheaper is that the coin now contains more precious metal, then we reduce the number of coins the borrower must repay, since each coin is now intrinsically worth more. *Ve-ei machmas tar'a zil* — but if produce has become cheaper simply because market prices dropped, and the coin's actual purchasing power is the same as before, then *lo mankin lei* — no reduction is made, and the borrower repays in the current enlarged coins.

### Historical Revaluation

The *Gemara* then returns to the question of excess precious metal. Even if the buying power is the same, there is more silver in the coin — and silver has intrinsic value independent of its monetary function. The *Gemara* cites the case of *Rav Papa* and *Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua*, who dealt with a case involving currency lent out to a certain *agardamis* — apparently some sort of monetary official or overseer (Soncino renders it as a title rather than a personal name). The ruling was *ad yahav tamnya* — eight of the new coins were determined to be equivalent to ten of the old ones. This suggests that when coins actually contain more precious metal, one does not simply repay face value for face value; rather, one adjusts for the difference in metallic content. The *Gemara* thus appears to reverse itself: if the coins contain genuinely more precious metal, the precious metal weight — not the face value — controls the repayment calculation.

---

## Mazik: Sea Case

### Sea Coin Case

The *sugya* now turns to a series of striking rulings of *Rava* concerning the *mazik* category. *Rava* states: *hazoreik matbeia shel chaveiro l'yama hagadol* — if someone takes another person's coin and throws it into the Mediterranean Sea — *patur* — he is exempt from payment. The reason: *amar hamunach kamach* — the money is right there, it is accessible to you. Go and retrieve it.

### Visibility Condition

This exemption is qualified: *vehani mili b'tzululin d'kachazei lei* — this applies only if the water is clear and the coin is visible. *Aval achurin d'lo chazei lei, lo* — if the water is murky and the coin cannot be seen, he is not exempt.

### Gezeilah vs. Mazik

There is a further distinction between *gezeilah* and *mazik*. The above ruling — that throwing a coin into the sea is *patur* — applies only *d'adiyaduye* — where one knocked the coin out of the owner's hand so that it flew into the sea, in which case the question is whether a *mazik* act of destruction was committed. If the coin was never in the *mazik*'s possession, whether it is "destroyed" depends on whether it remains retrievable. But *aval shaklei biyadei* — if he physically grabbed the coin and then threw it into the sea, *migu degazlei* — since he already committed an act of *gezeilah* the moment he took it, that act of theft immediately obligated him to make restoration — *hashavah ba'i me'vad*. What happens to the coin after that is irrelevant to his liability.

### Tosafot Position

*Tosafot* challenges the limiting condition of visibility. In *Tosafot*'s view, retrievability — not visibility — is the operative criterion. If one could theoretically hire someone to dive down and recover the coin (even at a cost exceeding the coin's value), the coin is not halachically "destroyed," and therefore no *mazik* liability attaches. On *Tosafot*'s reading, the ruling would remain the same even in murky water, as long as retrieval is physically possible.

The lecturer finds this position genuinely difficult: intuitively, the combination of non-visibility and difficulty of retrieval would seem to constitute destruction. If the coin is invisible and difficult to recover, it seems hard to say it has not been "destroyed" merely because recovery is theoretically possible. Yet *Tosafot* insists that the sole question is in-principle retrievability. This is a striking position — and the underlying conceptual tension is that even if we concede the object is not technically destroyed, the *mazik* has imposed real costs (time, expense, effort) on the owner in order to recover what is rightfully his. According to the framework developing here, that is merely indirect causation of loss — *grama be-nezikin* — and does not rise to the level of chargeable *nezek*, so long as the object remains extant.

---

## Maaser Accessibility (II)

### Inaccessible Money

The *Gemara* now brings a challenge from a *baraita* regarding *maaser sheni*: *ein mechalelin al ma'os she'einam birshuso* — one cannot transfer *maaser sheni* sanctity onto money that is not under one's control. *Hayu lo ma'os be-Kastara* — if your money is in a distant place called *Kastara*, *o be-Har Hamelech* — or in some other remote location, *o she-nafal kiso l'yama hagadol* — or if your wallet has fallen to the bottom of the sea — *ein mechalelin*. You cannot perform *chilul maaser sheni* onto such money.

This seems to establish that money at the bottom of the sea is treated as non-existent. One might ask: does this mean that if someone caused your money to end up in *Kastara* — without technically stealing it — it would be as though they destroyed it? At minimum, the *Gemara* treats such money as if it does not exist for purposes of *maaser sheni*.

### Hand Requirement

*Rabbah* resists this inference. *Shani inyan maaser d'beinan matzui b'yadcha* — the laws of *maaser sheni* are different, because the *Torah* specifically requires that the money be accessible — practically in hand. The verse states *v'tzarta hakesef b'yadcha* — you shall bind the money in your hand — which demands a heightened standard of direct accessibility. This is a special requirement unique to *maaser sheni*, not a general principle of *nezek*. The money at the bottom of the sea is not destroyed — it still exists — but for *maaser sheni* purposes, "existing" is not enough. It must be accessible, and accessibility here is an intermediate category between having the money and having lost it entirely, one that is specifically mandated by the *Torah*'s language for *maaser sheni* but does not apply to the general law of *mazik*.

---

## Flattened Coins (II)

### Flattening Exempt

*Rabbah* continues his series of rulings. *Hashaf matbeia* — if someone takes another's coin and flattens it, smoothing away the minted image — *patur* — he is exempt. He has not removed any silver; the metal is all still there. The coin can no longer circulate as currency, but its precious metal content is intact.

### Material Removal Test

*Mai ta'ama? D'lo avad velo midi* — the reason is that nothing was done, nothing was removed. The parts were merely rearranged. The lecturer notes that this might have made particular sense in the context of coins, where the great bulk of value was the precious metal content; the minting was primarily a guarantee of weight and purity. But the *Gemara* does not limit this principle to coins.

The principle being articulated, it seems, is that an act of *mazik* requires the physical removal of some material from the whole. Merely rearranging an object — flattening it, hammering it — without taking any piece away does not constitute legally cognizable damage. This is, as the lecturer remarks, a genuinely astonishing position. The abstract diminution in value — the loss of the coin's status as currency — does not register as compensable *nezek* because no material substance was removed from the world.

### Filing vs. Hammering

This principle is immediately refined. *V'hani mili d'machyei bekurnasa detarshei* — this rule applies where one struck the coin with a hammer and thereby flattened it. *Aval shapei beshufinei* — but if one used something like a file, which would actually scrape away some of the metal — *chisorei chasrei* — then material was removed, and that constitutes an act of *mazik* for which one is liable. The defining test is whether any physical material was removed. Filing: liable. Hammering to flatten: exempt.

---

## Mazik: Animal Cases

### Slave Deafness

*Rava* now challenges this framework by citing a ruling from a different domain. *Heika'u al eino vesima'ah* — if one strikes a slave on his eye and blinds him, *al ozno vechershah* — or on his ear and causes deafness, *eved yetzei lecheirus* — the slave goes free. But *keneged eino ve'eino ro'eh* — if the blow landed beside the eye and the shock somehow caused blindness, or *keneged ozno ve'eino shomei'a* — near the ear and caused deafness, *ein eved yetzei lecheirus* — the slave does not go free. The implication of the first case is that striking someone's ear — without visibly removing any tissue — is considered a cognizable act of damage. Why, if no material was removed?

### Interior Wound Theory

*Rava leta'amei* — *Rava* resolves this in accordance with his own position. *De'amar Rava chersho le'aviv neherag* — *Rava* had already ruled elsewhere that one who causes his father to become deaf by striking him in the ear is executed. Now, causing a wound that draws blood is a precondition for that liability. How could striking an ear draw blood? *Ee efshar lecharisha belo chavurah* — it is impossible to cause deafness without causing some interior wound. *Detipas dama naflah leih be'ozneih* — a drop of blood must have fallen inside the ear canal; there must have been an internal injury. Therefore, causing deafness by a blow to the ear is categorized as *chisorei chasrei* — something was removed — and that is why it constitutes a cognizable act of *mazik* (and, in the context of the slave, triggers emancipation).

This is a significant move: *Rava* does not abandon the "material removal" test; rather, he argues that the physiology of deafness necessarily entails an interior wound, bringing the case within the principle. The framework is maintained, but the analysis of what physically occurs is refined.

### Pierced Ear Exempt

*Rava* then articulates a case that goes the other way. *Hatzorem ozen parato shel chaveiro* — if one pierces the ear of another's cow — *patur* — he is exempt. *Para kidekaima kaima* — the cow stands as it stood before; its market value is unchanged. *Velo avad velo midi* — nothing was done, nothing of substance was altered. The fact that the cow can no longer be brought as a *korban* is dismissed: *vekulei shovarim lav legabei mizbe'ach kaimi* — not all oxen are destined to be sacrifices. The loss of eligibility for the *mizbe'ach* does not register as a market-value diminution in the context of ordinary commerce.

The lecturer suggests that *Rava*'s real point here may be less about the "material removal" test than about the definition of damage itself. Even granting that something comes out when an ear is pierced (some blood, at minimum), the market value of the cow is unchanged. In an agricultural society, a cow with a hole in its ear is worth exactly the same as one without. The *chidush* may therefore be that when the objective market value does not change, we do not treat the act as *mazik*, even if there was technically some minor physical intrusion. (One might even argue: if there were a premium in the market for unblemished animals — for buyers seeking *korbanot* — some nominal loss of value would perhaps be cognizable. But *Rava* holds that this marginal premium, relevant only to a small subset of buyers, does not constitute a legally actionable change in the cow's value.)

### Red Heifer Work

The *Gemara* then presses the principle. *Maysiv Rava* — a *baraita* is cited: *ha'oseh melacha bemei chatat* — one who performs work using water designated for use in preparing *mei chatat* (water to which the ashes of the *parah adumah* are added) — or *uvifarat chatat* — using the *parah adumah* cow itself — *patur midinei adam vechayav bidinei shamayim*. Such a person is exempt in human courts but liable in the heavenly court.

*Tosafot* anticipates the obvious objection: the entire *parah adumah* context involves sanctified objects destined for sacred use, so of course it is different from ordinary commerce. *Tosafot* therefore focuses the discussion on the water, which at the stage under discussion has not yet acquired any formal sanctified status — the ashes have not yet been added. Even so, the disruption of its intended use generates at least *dinei shamayim* liability.

The *Gemara* then infers: *melacha hu d'lo mincar hezeka* — it is only because performing *melacha* with the *parah adumah* water or cow produces an invisible *hezek* that the result is exemption from *dinei adam*. But *aval tzorem* — had one instead pierced the ear of the cow — *demincair hezeka* — since that *hezek* would be visible, one might be *chayav* in human courts as well. The *Gemara* pushes back: *hu hadin d'afilu tzorem patur* — in fact, even piercing the ear would be exempt. *Veha kamashma lan d'afilu melacha d'lo mincar hezeka chayav bidinei shamayim* — the *chidush* of the *baraita* is that even invisible *hezek*, like performing *melacha* with the water or cow, incurs *dinei shamayim* liability. This is a strange result: one might have expected that piercing the ear of a *parah adumah* — visibly disqualifying it — would clearly be *chayav* even in human courts. *Tosafot* grapples with the difficulty, noting that the whole discussion sits awkwardly, and emphasizes that the focus really should be on the water, where the case for exemption is stronger.

---

## Burned Documents

### Document Burning

*Rava* extends his series of rulings: *hashoref shetarotav shel chaveiro* — if one burns another's loan documents — *patur* — he is exempt. To the creditor's protest that he has lost the ability to collect his loan, *Rava* replies: *nayara kaliti minach* — I burned paper from you. Pay you for paper I will. The loan itself was not destroyed; the debtor still owes the money. The difficulty in collecting it going forward is an indirect consequence — *grama* — not an act of direct *mazik*.

### Witness Rewrite

*Rami bar Chama* challenges this: what exactly is the case? If witnesses are present who know what the document said — that David owed Michael a thousand dollars — *lichtevu lei shitra ma'alya* — let them write a replacement document. In that case, the creditor has suffered no real loss; he can simply reproduce the document. So why would *Rava* even need to declare him exempt? *Ei d'leika sahedi* — and if there are no witnesses who know the contents, then even if the tortfeasor were liable, how would we know for how much? The question of quantum would seem to collapse the claim entirely.

### No Intrinsic Value

*Rava* responds: *tehei bema'amino* — it can be a case where the court accepts the creditor's word as to what the document contained, and the tortfeasor is prepared to pay accordingly — yet *Rava* still holds he is *patur*. The reason is that the document has no intrinsic value. The tortfeasor burned paper; the creditor's loss is entirely abstract and indirect. *Rava* does not even add *chayav bidinei shamayim* here — the loss is seen as so thoroughly indirect as to generate no liability even in the moral realm.

The lecturer finds this genuinely puzzling. One might have thought a loan document functions as an instrument — a *kli*, in some sense — that enables the collection of a debt. Why does it not have intrinsic value? Is it because its value is purely conventional, rooted in social and legal norms rather than any physical functionality? And yet precious metals, whose "intrinsic" value is also largely a social construct, are treated as having such value. The lecturer does not resolve this, but suggests that perhaps the key distinction is marketability: a loan document that is non-transferable, valuable only to its specific holder, may lack the kind of objective market value that defines compensable *nezek*.

---

## Grama Category

### Machloket Source

*Rav Dimi bar Chanina* now offers a unifying observation: *hadar beh Rava* — *Rava* retracted from his various exempt rulings. The positions articulated in *Rava*'s series of cases are not his own final view but rather reflect the debate between *Rabbi Shimon* and the *Rabbanan*.

### Rabbi Shimon

*Rabbi Shimon d'amar davar ha-gorem le-mamon ke-mamon dami* — Rabbi Shimon holds that something whose loss causes a monetary obligation is treated as having monetary value. The classic case: one who steals a *korban* belonging to another person — since the owner now has an obligation to replace it, the loss of the stolen *korban* caused the owner a monetary loss. *Rabbi Shimon* therefore treats the *korban* as if it were the owner's monetary property, and the thief must pay *kefel* accordingly. Under *Rabbi Shimon*'s principle, all of *Rava*'s cases would generate liability, because in each case the tortfeasor's act caused the victim an indirect monetary loss.

### Rabbis Position

The *Rabbanan*, by contrast, hold *davar ha-gorem le-mamon lav ke-mamon dami* — the fact that something's loss causes a monetary obligation does not confer monetary status on the thing itself. Under the *Rabbanan*, all of *Rava*'s cases result in exemption.

### Original Value Limit

*Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua* challenges the equation. When did *Rabbi Shimon* say *davar ha-gorem le-mamon ke-mamon dami*? Only *b'davar she'ikaro mamon* — regarding something that originally had genuine monetary value. In *Rabbi Shimon*'s paradigm case, the stolen object was a cow or similar animal with real market value, which was subsequently sanctified. The debate between *Rabbi Shimon* and the *Rabbanan* concerns whether that original monetary value, transformed by sanctification, retains legal significance. That is entirely different from the cases in *Rava*'s series, where either the object has no intrinsic value to begin with (the loan document), or the harm is purely indirect (the coin at the bottom of the sea). Those cases are simply *grama be-nezikin* — indirect causation — and the *machloket* of *Rabbi Shimon* and the *Rabbanan* does not speak to them.

---

## Burned Documents (II)

### Indirect Loss Debate

The *Gemara* now works through the *chametz* case that most cleanly illustrates the *machloket*. One stole *chametz* before *Pesach*. *Jenna* came along and burned the *chametz* — and notably, everyone is obligated to burn their *chametz*, so she did nothing wrong. Nevertheless, the thief could have returned the *chametz* and discharged his *gezeilah* obligation — *harei shelcha lefanecha* — since no physical change had occurred to the *chametz*. By burning it, *Jenna* deprived the thief of this avenue of discharge. If the thief now holds the *chametz* until after *Pesach* — when it becomes *chametz she-avar alav ha-pesach*, worthless to the world at large — it is still "worth" something to the thief, because he can return it to the owner and say *harei shelcha lefanecha*, thereby discharging his *gezeilah* obligation without paying its original value. *Jenna*'s destruction of the *chametz* thus caused the thief a real monetary loss.

In *this* case — *machlokes Rabbi Shimon ve-Rabbanan*. According to *Rabbi Shimon*, since the *chametz*'s loss will cause the thief a monetary loss, the *chametz* is treated as having monetary value to him, he is considered its owner for these purposes, and *Jenna* must pay him for the *chametz*'s original value. According to the *Rabbanan*, since objectively the *chametz* is worthless, *Jenna* is *patur*.

This case, *Rav Huna* emphasizes, is the genuine terrain of the *machloket*: an object with original intrinsic value that was destroyed by a third party, where the question is whether the subjective, "obligational" value to the thief counts. That is distinct from the cases of *Rava* — loan documents and coins at the bottom of the sea — where the issue is purely indirect causation with no original object of intrinsic value being destroyed.

---

## Grama Category (II)

### Garmi Category

*Meimar* now introduces the category that will fill the gap. *Man de-dan dinei de-garmi* — the one, meaning *Rabbi Meir*, who adjudicates the laws of *garmi*. There is a major *machloket Rishonim* about precisely what *garmi* is — whether it is a *knas*, a *takkanah*, or something else — but its functional role is clear: it bridges the gap between the cases one is technically exempt from under *grama be-nezikin* and the cases one ought practically to be liable for. The *Ramban* wrote an entire treatise — *kuntres de-garmi* — attempting to define its parameters, and even there the lines may not be crisply drawn. But its purpose is to say: all these cases of *grama* from which you are technically *patur*, the ones from which you should not escape liability we will call *garmi*, and you will pay.

### Rav Ashi Case

*Man de-dan dinei de-garmi magbi be-damei shtar ma'alya* — one who adjudicates *garmi* cases collects the full value of the document. Exactly what "full value" means is somewhat unclear: does it mean the face value of the loan (the thousand dollars), or the document's market value (what one could sell it for, discounted for the risk of non-collection)? *U-man de-lo dan dinei de-garmi magbi be-damei niyara be-alma* — one who does not apply *garmi* awards only the value of the paper.

The *Gemara* then relates: *hava uvda de-kafye Rafram le-Rav Ashi* — there was an actual case in which *Rafram* compelled *Rav Ashi* to pay, and *ve-agbi beh ke-khashura le-tsalma* — he assessed against him the full value of the document, like the value of timber used in construction. Here we see *garmi* applied in practice to close the gap.

### Rashi's Question

*Rashi* is troubled by the obvious question: what was *Rav Ashi* doing burning another person's *shtaros*? *Rashi* proposes that *Rav Ashi* did this as a child. This gives rise to an important discussion among the *Rishonim*: if a minor causes damage, does he become obligated to pay upon reaching adulthood? *Rafram*'s compelling *Rav Ashi* to pay — on *Rashi*'s reading of the episode — raises the question of whether there is an obligation, perhaps *bidinei shamayim* even if not fully *bidinei adam*, to make restitution for damage caused in one's youth. The *Gemaras'* larger point, however, is that *garmi* emerges as a vital category precisely because the strict logic of *grama be-nezikin* exemptions, followed to their conclusion, would produce outcomes that cannot stand in any functional legal order — and *garmi* is the mechanism by which the *halacha* draws the line.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 99

## Chometz Post-Pesach

### Intro: Chometz Pesach

We pick up on 98b, approximately ten lines down in the medium-sized text. The opening ruling concerns *chometz she'avar alav ha-Pesach* — leavened bread over which Pesach has passed. If someone stole *chometz* before Pesach and Pesach then passed, rendering it completely worthless, he may nonetheless return the physical object and declare *harei she-lecha lefanecha* — "behold, your object is before you." The primary Biblical obligation is not to pay back the monetary value of a stolen item but to return the object itself: *v'heshiv et ha-gezeilah asher gazal*. The *chiddush* of the *mishnah* is that this obligation is fulfilled even when the object has become worthless, so long as it remains physically identical to what was taken.

### Object vs. Value

The *gemara* asks: *man tana omer be-issurei hana'ah harei she-lecha lefanecha?* — who is the *tanna* who holds that even when an object is forbidden in benefit and entirely worthless, one may still say "behold, your object is before you" and thereby discharge the obligation of return?

### Rabbi Yaakov

Rav Chisda answers: it is Rabbi Yaakov. The source is a *brayta*: *shor she-heimis* — an ox that killed a person. Before a *gmar din*, before the ox has officially acquired the status of a *shor haniskal*, if one sells it the sale is valid, if one consecrates it the consecration takes effect, and if one slaughters it the meat is permitted, as Rashi notes — because these acts prevent the ox from ever attaining the *shor haniskal* status. The *brayta* thus identifies an opportunity to act prior to that status crystallizing.

### Braita Cases

Once *gmar din* has occurred and the ox formally becomes a *shor haniskal*, the situation reverses entirely: any sale is void, any consecration is invalid, and the meat of a slaughtered ox is forbidden even if it was not actually stoned.

### Shor HaNiskal

Crucially for our discussion, the *brayta* rules that if a *shomer* was watching such an ox and the ox attained *shor haniskal* status while in the *shomer*'s care, the *shomer* may return it to its owner before *gmar din* — that is a valid return. But *mi-she-nigmar dino*, once *gmar din* has occurred, if the *shomer* attempts to return the ox to the owner and say "here is your object," that is *not* a valid return. The ox is *asur be-hana'ah* and entirely worthless; returning it does not discharge the obligation. Rabbi Yaakov, however, disagrees and holds that *af mi-she-nigmar dino*, even after *gmar din*, returning the ox counts as a valid return. So it appears that Rabbi Yaakov and the Rabbis are debating the very question of whether one can say *harei she-lecha lefanecha* regarding an object that is *asur be-hana'ah*.

---

## Gmar Din B'Fano

### Rava's Distinction

Rava rejects this framing. He argues that the debate between Rabbi Yaakov and the Rabbis is not about *issurei hana'ah* in general. On the contrary, the principle that one may say *harei she-lecha lefanecha* by *issurei hana'ah* is universally agreed upon — *de-khulei alma amrinan be-issurei hana'ah harei she-lecha lefanecha*. As evidence, Rava notes: if the dispute truly concerned whether one can say *harei she-lecha lefanecha* by *issurei hana'ah*, they should have framed the debate around *chometz ha-Pesach*, the simpler and more straightforward case. The fact that the debate is specifically located in the *shor haniskal* case — which introduces additional complications — demonstrates that the underlying question is something unique to *shor haniskal*.

What is that unique complication? *Hacha be-gomrin dino shel shor she-lo be-fanav kamifligi* — the debate is whether *beis din* can render a *gmar din* on the ox without the ox being physically present.

### Rabbis' Position

The Rabbis hold *ein gomrin dino shel shor she-lo be-fanav* — *beis din* cannot conduct the final judgment unless the ox is present. Consequently, the *gmar din* that gave the ox its forbidden status could only have occurred because the *shomer* allowed the ox to be seen by the court.

### Shomer Cannot Return

The logic of the Rabbis' position is as follows: the owner can now say to the *shomer*, "Had you returned it to me before *gmar din*, I would have hidden it away in the swamps — *mavrikna lei le-agma* — and it never would have become a *shor haniskal*. Now, through your negligence, you have handed it over to an authority — *beis din* — against whom I have no legal recourse." The *shomer*'s negligence in allowing the ox to come before *beis din* is what caused the irreversible harm. That is why the return is invalid.

### Rabbi Yaakov Rebuttal

Rabbi Yaakov counters: *gomrin dino shel shor she-lo be-fanav* — *beis din* can conduct *gmar din* even without the ox present. Therefore the owner cannot blame the *shomer*, because even if the *shomer* had returned the ox beforehand, *beis din* would have proceeded to *gmar din* regardless. The *shomer* did not cause the harm, and the return is therefore valid.

### Negligence Question

This raises an obvious difficulty. Even accepting the Rabbis' position that the *shomer*'s negligence contributed to the outcome — why should negligence matter at all? The principle of *harei she-lecha lefanecha* is precisely that one returns the *same object*, regardless of what has befallen it. The *gazlan* who failed to return the *chometz* before Pesach was also negligent in not returning it in time. The *shomer* was arguably negligent in allowing the ox to gore someone in the first place. Why should negligence disqualify the return when the object is physically the same?

### Tosafot: Visible Status

This question was already treated earlier in Bava Kamma, as both Rashi and Tosafot address it. Tosafot draws an analogy to the earlier principle of *pesulto malkhus* — when something is rendered invalid by governmental or communal decree, that can be treated as a visible damage even if the object has not physically changed. Tosafot applies the same reasoning here: since *beis din* is physically holding the ox, and its being held by *beis din* is a necessary and visible component of its *shor haniskal* status, the status is as though externally visible. Rashi attempts a different explanation — a combination of negligence and non-visible damage that renders return impossible — which is closer to the plain meaning of the *gemara*'s language but harder to fully understand conceptually. Either way, the *gemara* is asserting that the *shor haniskal* presents a unique set of considerations involving the degree of negligence and the visibility conferred by *beis din*'s seizure of the animal — and that this debate would not apply to *chometz she'avar alav ha-Pesach*.

---

## Braita Evidence

### Rav Chisda Asks

Having established Rava's distinction, the *gemara* now records an exchange that tests it empirically. Rav Chisda — who had been the one to suggest that the *shor haniskal* debate reflected a broader dispute about *issurei hana'ah* — encounters Rabba bar Shmuel and asks: *tanisa midi be-issurei hana'ah* — have you taught any *brayta* concerning *issurei hana'ah* that could help us determine whether the debate about *shor haniskal* is purely local, or whether it would extend to *chometz ha-Pesach* as well?

### Torah's Requirement

Rabba bar Shmuel replies that he has. The *brayta* derives from the phrase *v'heshiv et ha-gezeilah asher gazal* — "and he shall return the stolen object that he stole" — that the obligation is to return the item in the state it was at the time of the theft, *k'ein she-gazal*.

### Returnability Examples

From this the *brayta* enumerates cases where the thief can say *harei she-lecha lefanecha* and thereby discharge his obligation, despite the object's worthlessness. These include: *gazal matbe'a ve-nifsal* — he stole a coin and it was invalidated; *peiros ve-hirkivu* (or according to some textual readings, *ve-henitnasakh* — wine that was poured as *yayin nesech*, rendering it *asur be-hana'ah* without any visible change); *yayin ve-hikrim* — wine that turned slightly; *terumah ve-nitme'at* — *terumah* that became *tamei*; *chometz she'avar alav ha-Pesach*; *behemah ve-ne'evda bah aveirah* — an animal used in an act of *aveirah*, which becomes unfit for the altar; and *shor ad she-lo nigmar dino* — an ox before *gmar din*. In all these cases, one may say *harei she-lecha lefanecha*, and this satisfies the Torah's requirement.

### Shor-Only Debate

Critically, the *brayta* permits *harei she-lecha lefanecha* for *chometz* — listed without any qualification — while for the *shor haniskal* it specifies *ad she-lo nigmar dino*: only before *gmar din*, not after. This structure demonstrates precisely what Rava claimed: the restriction in the *shor haniskal* case is particular to *gmar din* and does not reflect a general principle about *issurei hana'ah*. For all other *issurei hana'ah* on the list, including *chometz*, the return is valid unconditionally.

### Rav Chisda Loses

The *gemara* observes: who holds that a *shor haniskal* may be returned only before *gmar din* and not after? The Rabbis — who are the ones who restrict the *shomer*'s return after *gmar din*. And yet even those same Rabbis, as this *brayta* reflects, agree that *chometz she'avar alav ha-Pesach* — listed alongside the other cases — may be returned with *harei she-lecha lefanecha*. This confirms Rava's position and refutes Rav Chisda's original suggestion that they were debating the broader principle of *issurei hana'ah*.

Rav Chisda's response to being proven wrong is memorable: *ei mashkechuhu lehu, lo teimru lehu ve-lo midi* — if you encounter others from the *beis medrash*, tell them nothing. Do not publicize that I was refuted. This raises interesting questions about intellectual honesty, which the *gemara* leaves without comment.

A question arises in passing: is there not something troubling about the very premise of the Rabbis' position — that the owner could have hidden the ox in the swamp to evade *beis din*'s judgment?
