The ox had, after all, killed a person, and the institution of *shor haniskal* is a form of judicial accountability. The *gemara* never voices disapproval of such a strategy. One can note that in human capital cases, *chazal* themselves — Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon — famously declared that had they sat on the Sanhedrin, no one would ever have been executed, for they would always have found a loophole. The case of the *shor* is not a human life, but it raises the same underlying question about the relationship between the individual and the judicial process when the matter is, in some sense, between a person and God rather than a strictly interpersonal claim.

---

## Craftsmen Liability

### Rav Assi's Rule

With the preceding discussion concluded, the *gemara* pivots somewhat from the theme of *gezeilah* — theft and its ramifications — and introduces a set of cases involving craftsmen who damage objects entrusted to them. In some respects this topic belongs more naturally to the first half of Bava Kamma, dealing with *mazik* liability, and indeed the *gemara* will eventually bring us back to the direct *mazik* analysis. For now, the *mishnah* lays the groundwork.

### Two Cases

*Nasan le-ummanin le-taken ve-kilkelu, chayavin le-shalem* — if one gave items to craftsmen to repair and they ruined them, they are liable to pay. *Nasan le-charash shidah teivah u-migdal le-taken ve-kilkel, chayav le-shalem* — if one gave a carpenter a box, chest, or cabinet to fix and he broke it, he must pay. The *mishnah* continues: a builder who was commissioned to knock down a wall and in the process broke the stones or damaged them must pay. But if stones fell on a *different* side of the wall from where he was working — *ha-soser mi-tzad zeh ve-nafal mi-tzad acher* — he is exempt. If, however, those stones fell as a direct result of his striking the wall, *machmas ha-makkah*, he is liable.

Rav Assi refines the liability rule. *Lo shanu ela she-nasan le-charash shidah teivah u-migdal li-no'otz bah masmer ve-na'atz bah masmer ve-shibran* — the case of liability in the *mishnah* is specifically where one gave the craftsman an already-constructed box and asked him to bang a nail into it, and in doing so he shattered it. The craftsman improved nothing; he simply destroyed what was given to him. But: *aval nasan le-charash eitzim la'asot mehem shidah teivah u-migdal, ve-asah mehem shidah teivah u-migdal ve-shibran, patur* — if one gave the carpenter raw wood with instructions to build a box, and the carpenter built a fine box worth many times the wood's value, and then in hammering in the final nail shattered the finished product, the craftsman is *exempt* from paying for the destroyed box.

This is a striking ruling. The owner handed over wood worth twenty dollars; the craftsman built something worth two hundred dollars and then destroyed it. Why does the craftsman not owe for the full value of the box he ruined?

### Uman Koneh B'Shvach

The answer: *uman koneh be-shevach kli* — the craftsman acquires ownership of the improvement in the vessel until the moment he actually returns it to the owner.

### Payment Framework

The conceptual framework underlying this principle is significant. We typically think of a craftsman as someone we hire to work on our property: the wood remains ours throughout, the craftsman adds labor, and we pay for the labor. Under this intuitive model, the finished box is entirely the owner's from the moment it is built, and destroying it would make the craftsman fully liable.

But *uman koneh be-shevach kli* proposes a fundamentally different framing. When you commission someone to build you a box from your raw materials and agree to pay fifty dollars, what you are actually doing — in the *gemara*'s conceptualization — is agreeing to *purchase* from the craftsman the box that he will create. He will build a box, that box belongs to him until delivery, and you have contracted to buy it from him at an agreed price. Payment is not for labor; it is a purchase price for an object the craftsman currently owns. As one might observe, this is conceptually parallel to the earlier discussions in this *perek* about *shinui koneh* — the way transformation confers ownership — though the *gemara* here approaches the question from the angle of commissioned work rather than theft.

A natural question follows: if the craftsman owns the box until delivery and you are buying it from him, and then the box is destroyed before delivery — you owe him nothing for the box he destroyed? Correct, because if the transaction is a sale, you cannot simultaneously demand payment for destroying "your" box. If you wish to claim the box was yours — and therefore the craftsman owes you for a two-hundred-dollar loss — you must first acknowledge that you contracted to pay him for it, in which case you owe the fee. If he does not collect the fee, you owe him for the wood at most. You cannot have it both ways.

---

## Dyer Case Proof

### Wool & Dye Braita

The *gemara* attempts to bring proof for *uman koneh be-shevach kli* from a *brayta* concerning a dyer. *Ha-nosein tzemer le-tzaba ve-hikdicha yora* — one who gives wool to a dyer, and the vat causes it to burn and be destroyed. The ruling: *nosein lo demei tzamro* — the dyer pays the owner for the value of the wool. The *gemara* asks: does he not also pay for the *shevach* — the improvement? If the wool was first dyed, improving in value, and only then destroyed, he apparently pays only the base value of the wool, not the improved dyed value. Does this not prove that *uman koneh be-shevach kli* — the dyer owned that improved value, so he owes you only what you owned (the raw wool)?

### Shmuel's Objection

Shmuel objects. *Hacha be-mai askinan she-hikdicha be-sha'as nefillah* — perhaps we are dealing with a case where the wool was destroyed at the very moment it fell into the vat, before any improvement occurred at all. There was simply no *shevach* to pay for. Shmuel adds: had it been destroyed *after* absorbing the dye and being improved, what would the ruling be? In that case the dyer would pay *demei tzamro ve-shivcho* — for both the wool and its improvement — which would imply that *uman* is *not* *koneh be-shevach kli*. So Shmuel's explanation actually suggests he holds the opposite of *uman koneh be-shevach kli*.

### Dye Provision Effect

But the *gemara* presses further. If Shmuel holds that in the standard case the dyer pays for the full improved value, we would expect the *brayta* to say he pays for the wool *and* the dye. The *brayta* says only the wool. The *gemara* then introduces a qualification: *ke-gon de-tzemer ve-simanim de-ba'al ha-bayit de-tzaba agar yadeih hu de-shakeil* — the case may be one where the owner supplied both the wool and the dye, and the dyer was therefore receiving only the fee for his handiwork, his *schar yadav*. When the owner supplies all the raw materials — including the dye — the dyer is conceived not as a craftsman creating something of his own but as a hired laborer. Under those circumstances, the framework of *uman koneh be-shevach kli* may not apply at all; he is simply a wage-earner.

The intuition behind this distinction is not entirely straightforward. After all, a carpenter might provide only his skill while the owner provides wood and nails, yet we might still think of the result as the carpenter's creation. The *gemara* appears to treat the dye, as the key transformative raw material in dyeing, as the dividing line: if the craftsman brings his own dye, he is creating something new that he then sells; if the owner supplies the dye, the craftsman is merely performing a service. One might further suggest that the provision of all raw materials by the owner positions the craftsman more as an extension of the owner's own activity rather than an independent producer.

The *gemara* pushes back even on this, however: if the owner supplied the dye, we would expect the dyer to owe the owner for the destroyed dye as well — yet that is not what the *brayta* says. So the attempted explanation creates its own difficulties.

### Shmuel Equivocates

In the end, *Shmuel dechuya ka-midachei leh* — Shmuel is simply deflecting. He is not taking a definitive position on *uman koneh be-shevach kli*; he is only demonstrating that the *brayta* cannot serve as proof either way. The dyer case remains inconclusive.

---

## Kiddushin Case

### Garment Pickup

A clearer proof emerges from a ruling about *bal talin*. A *mishnah* teaches: if one gives a cloak to a craftsman to work on, and the craftsman finishes and informs the owner — even if the owner waits ten days (or any extended period) to come and collect it, the owner does not transgress *bal talin*. The owner's obligation to pay does not begin until the moment of physical pickup.

### Bal Talin Rule

The prohibition of *lo salin pe'ulat sachir itcha ad boker* — do not allow the wages of a hired worker to remain unpaid overnight — is triggered by the act of receiving the completed work. *Nasano lo be-chatzi ha-yom, keivan she-shaka ha-chama, over alav mishum bal talin*: if the craftsman delivers the item in the middle of the day, the owner must pay by sunset or transgress the prohibition.

### Bal Talin Problem

Here is where this ruling intersects with our question. If *uman koneh be-shevach kli* — if the craftsman truly owns the improvement and the transaction is conceived as a sale rather than a fee for services — then there should *never* be a violation of *bal talin*. The prohibition applies to *pe'ulat sachir*, the wage of a hired worker. But if the payment is not a wage but a purchase price for an object the craftsman owns, then delaying payment is simply being slow to pay for a sale, not withholding a worker's wages. One does not transgress *bal talin* for being late in paying for a car purchase. Yet the *mishnah* clearly contemplates that *bal talin* can be violated here — it only delays the clock until pickup. This implies that the payment *is* conceptualized as a wage for services rendered, not as a purchase price for an object owned by the craftsman.

This is a striking point — and all the more so because the *mishnah* is speaking of fixing a garment, not creating something from raw materials. Even a modest repair job is, under the *uman koneh be-shevach kli* principle, conceived as the craftsman owning the improvement. Yet *bal talin* still applies, which would seem to undercut the principle.

### Smoothing Wool

The *gemara* addresses this through Rav Mari b'rei de-Rav Kahana. He suggests the case involves *gardi de-sarvala* — someone who smoothed the rough surface of a thick garment — where the improvement is so minor as to be almost negligible. The *gemara* initially entertains the idea that there might be no *shevach* at all, but ultimately rejects this: *le-mai yahavei lei? de-reicha, keivan de-reicha hainu shevach* — whatever the reason you gave it to him, even the softening of the fabric constitutes an improvement, a *shevach*.

### Shvach vs. Kli

This exchange, however, clarifies the precise formulation of the principle. The *gemara* makes clear it is not *uman koneh be-shevach kli* in the sense of owning the entire vessel or object. Rather, it is *uman koneh be-shevach* — the craftsman owns only the *improved value*, not the object itself. The car was worth ten thousand dollars before the repair; now it is worth eleven thousand. The craftsman owns that incremental thousand-dollar value. He does not own the car. Your nine-dollar shirt is now worth ten dollars after softening; the craftsman owns that one-dollar increment. The payment you agreed upon is, in this conceptualization, the price you are paying to *purchase from him* that improvement — at whatever rate you negotiated, which might be less or more than the improvement's market value.

This is an abstract mode of analysis, but it explains why *bal talin* can still apply: even conceding *uman koneh be-shevach*, the craftsman's ownership of a small increment of value does not transform the entire transaction into a commercial sale. The worker is still, in a fundamental sense, working for you, and withholding the agreed payment can still constitute a violation of *bal talin* — even if we simultaneously conceptualize an abstract ownership of the improvement.

---

## Wage vs. Improvement

### Stomping Wages

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty by introducing a cleaner case. *Lo tzricha de-agrei le-vatsha* — what if you hired someone explicitly to stomp on the fabric? *Batsha batsha be-ma'ata* — you agreed to pay a small amount for each act of stomping. That is unambiguously *sechirus* — hourly or per-action wages — with no element of commissioned improvement. Here, the person is clearly a wage-earner, not a contractor producing an end product, and *bal talin* plainly applies. The *gemara* had been seeking a case where *uman koneh be-shevach kli* might operate yet *bal talin* would still apply; the stomping case provides a clean example where *uman koneh be-shevach kli* is irrelevant by construction, since the payment is explicitly per action and not for an end product.

### Rav Sheshet's Question

This case bears on a question posed by Rav Sheshet: does *bal talin* apply to *kablanut* — contracting? If I hire you to complete a defined job, not by the hour but for a fixed fee upon completion, and I delay payment — do I transgress *bal talin*?

### Kablanut Bal Talin

One might think that if *uman koneh be-shevach kli*, then the payment for contracting is a purchase price, not a wage, and *bal talin* does not apply. Rav Sheshet held that one *does* transgress *bal talin* even in *kablanut*, suggesting either that *uman* is not *koneh be-shevach kli* or that *bal talin* applies beyond its most literal domain. The *gemara* raises the question of whether Rav Sheshet's position conflicts with Rav Assi's ruling about the craftsman who built from raw materials.

### Service vs. Improvement

The resolution is offered by Shmuel bar Acha: *be-shlicha de-igarta* — consider a case of someone hired to deliver a letter. Here there is no physical object being improved. The messenger provides a pure service; there is no *shevach kli* whatsoever. And yet this is clearly a form of *kablanut* — you are paying for the completion of a task, not by the hour. In such a case, there is no *uman koneh be-shevach kli* to muddy the analysis, and Rav Sheshet's question about whether *bal talin* applies to *kablanut* stands on its own, entirely independent of the ownership-of-improvement framework. Rav Sheshet held that yes, *bal talin* applies — suggesting the obligation extends to service-based contracting even where no physical improvement is made.

---

## Gold Jewelry Kiddushin

### Jewelry Case

The *gemara* now introduces a *tannaitic* dispute that intersects directly with the question of *uman koneh be-shevach kli*. A woman says to a man: *asei li shirim nezamim ve-taba'ot ve-kadeish li bach* — take my gold, fashion it into necklaces, rings, and nose rings, and with those finished pieces of jewelry, betroth me. The question is whether the betrothal — *kiddushin* — takes effect.

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rabbi Meir rules: *keivan she-asam, mekudeshet* — once the man has fashioned the jewelry, she is betrothed. The implicit reasoning appears to be that the man has given the woman something of value — either the improved jewelry itself, or the improved value he created in her gold, or something equivalent — and that constitutes a valid act of *kiddushin*.

### Rabbis Position

The Rabbis disagree: *einah mekudeshet ad she-yehei mamon mi-yado* — she is not betrothed until actual property passes from his hand into hers. Merely completing the work is insufficient.

### First Reading

The *gemara*'s first reading of this dispute is that Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis are debating whether *uman koneh be-shevach kli*. If the craftsman owns the improved value, then the man has something to give the woman — he owns a portion of her gold in its improved form, and by handing it over he is giving her that owned value. That constitutes *kiddushin*. If *uman* does not own the *shevach*, he has nothing to give her from his own domain; all he has done is discharge a labor obligation, and one cannot betroth a woman with a debt she owes you (*milveh*).

The *gemara* notes a subtlety: even according to Rabbi Meir, the jewelry must apparently be physically handed over — *mamon mi-yado* — which raises a question about why physical transfer is necessary if the man already owns the improvement. One possible answer is that he might have done the work on the object while it remained in her possession — if, for instance, the work was done on her premises without his ever taking custody of the gold. In that case, he could not have acquired the improvement through *kinyan*, and the question of *uman koneh be-shevach kli* may be moot regardless.

### Revised Reading

The *gemara* ultimately revises this first reading. *De-khulei alma ein uman koneh be-shevach kli* — perhaps everyone agrees that the craftsman does *not* own the improvement. The debate is instead about something else entirely: *be-yeshna le-sekhirus mi-techila ve-ad sof kamifligi* — they disagree about whether wages accrue incrementally throughout the work or only become due at the moment of completion.

### Rabbi Meir: Final Wages

Rabbi Meir holds *ein le-sekhirus ela le-vasof* — the wage obligation arises only at the point of completion. Throughout the work, the owner owes the craftsman nothing. When the job is finished and the craftsman says, "I give you my labor as a gift rather than charging you," that gift has value — it is something concrete he is providing at that moment — and it can function as the object of *kiddushin*, worth at least a *perutah*.

### Rabbis: Accruing Wages

The Rabbis hold *yeshna le-sekhirus mi-techila ve-ad sof* — the wage accrues continuously throughout the work. By the time the job is complete, the owner has been accumulating a debt to the craftsman with every passing moment. When the craftsman says at the end, "I am not collecting my fee, accept my labor as a gift," what he is really forgiving is a *milveh* — a debt. And *ha-mekadesh be-milveh einah mekudeshet* — betrothal with a debt owed to you does not create valid *kiddushin*.

---

## Milveh U'Pruta

### Rava's Theory

Rava proposes a unified account that cuts across all three of the previously offered explanations. He holds that certain things are agreed upon by everyone: *de-khulei alma yeshna le-sekhirus mi-techila ve-ad sof* — wages accrue throughout, and by the time the work is done, what exists is an accrued debt. *De-khulei alma mekadesh be-milveh einah mekudeshet* — everyone agrees you cannot betroth a woman with a debt. *De-khulei alma ein uman koneh be-shevach kli* — and everyone agrees the craftsman does not acquire ownership of the improvement. With all three of those propositions agreed upon, what is left to debate?

### Overshadowing Debate

The remaining dispute is about *milveh u-perutah* — the case where a man simultaneously forgives a debt *and* gives the woman something extra, something concrete and personal, as the instrument of *kiddushin*. In our case, the man was commissioned to make jewelry, completed the task, and then added his own personal extra flourish — *nofech mi-shelo* — something beyond what was agreed, a small personal artistic addition that was not part of the contract.

### Rabbi Meir: Extra Matters

Rabbi Meir holds *milveh u-perutah daata a-perutah* — when there is both a debt being forgiven and a concrete item being given, a person's attention and intent focus on the tangible, present gift. The debt being forgiven does not overshadow the concrete *perutah* being given. Accordingly, the woman can be betrothed by that extra personal improvement that the man contributed of his own initiative.

### Rabbis: Debt Overshadows

The Rabbis hold *milveh u-perutah daata a-milveh* — when the debt is the dominant element, the concrete item is psychologically overshadowed. The woman knows that the primary transaction here is the forgiveness of a hundred-dollar debt; the extra little touch cannot transform that dynamic into a valid act of *kiddushin*.

---

## Work Betrothal Dispute

### Past Work

The *gemara* identifies this dispute as parallel to a debate among other *tannaim*. The case: a man says to a woman, *be-sachar she-asiti imach* — "I betroth you in exchange for the work I have already done for you." She is not betrothed. The work was done, the debt accrued, the man is forgiving a *milveh* — and one cannot be *mekadesh* with a *milveh*.

### Future Work

If instead he says *be-sachar she-e'eseh imach* — "in exchange for work I will do for you" — she *is* betrothed. Here the first *tanna* holds that this works.

### Rabbi Natan Rejects Both

Rabbi Natan disagrees: *be-sachar she-e'eseh imach einah mekudeshet ve-khol shekein be-sachar she-asiti imach* — neither the future-work formulation nor the past-work formulation creates valid *kiddushin*.

### Extra Improvement Except…

However, Rabbi Natan concedes: *aval im hosif lah nofech mi-shelo, mekudeshet* — if the craftsman added a personal extra improvement beyond what was contracted, she is betrothed with that addition.

### Wages Accrual Dispute

The *gemara* identifies what divides the first *tanna* from Rabbi Natan: *ika beinaihu sekhirus* — the question of wage accrual. The first *tanna* holds that the obligation to pay arises only at the end — *ein le-sekhirus ela le-vasof* — so "work I will do for you" is a genuine gift of future labor, not a preemptive forgiveness of an accruing debt. Rabbi Natan holds *yeshna le-sekhirus mi-techila ve-ad sof*, so by the time the work is completed, even future-promised work has become an accrued debt. As for the case of adding a personal extra improvement, the dispute between Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is precisely the *milveh u-perutah* question: does the extra concrete personal contribution overshadow the underlying debt, or does the debt overshadow the extra contribution?

---

## Return to Mazik

### Groundwork Complete

At this point a great deal of groundwork has been laid. We have worked through the *shinui* analysis of stolen goods, the conditions under which *harei she-lecha lefanecha* applies even to *issurei hana'ah*, and the *uman koneh be-shevach kli* principle with its implications for *bal talin*, *kablanut*, and *kiddushin*. In one sense, this has been the equivalent of Jughead's lawnmower: the *gemara* needed all of this to get to where it was actually going. The *mishnah* on craftsmen who damage objects is fundamentally a *mazik* issue — under what circumstances is a craftsman who damages something in the course of his work treated as a *mazik* and held to full liability — and that analysis awaits.

### Next: Grama

The *gemara* will now return to that direct *mazik* question and to the cases of *grama* — indirect damage — that were anticipated in the preceding pages. Rav Assi's new ruling, which appears at the top of the next amud, opens: *ha-me'abed kradomo shel chaveiro, amar lei ha kardumach ve-zil* — one who loses his fellow's axe says to him, "Here is your axe, go." The *gemara* immediately asks *ke-man* — like which *tanna* does this ruling accord? *Leima Rabbi Meir hi* — shall we say this is Rabbi Meir's view, who judges cases of *dina de-garmi*, the laws of indirect causation of damage? This exchange will open the final major discussion of the daf.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 100

## Expert Butcher Negligence

### Butcher Slips: Liability

The daf opens on 99b, four or five lines before the wide lines begin, with Shmuel's ruling concerning an expert *shochet* who made a mistake during *shechita*. The case is one of professional malpractice in its most literal sense: a skilled craftsman slaughtered an animal and slipped, rendering it a *neveilah* — not through any question of *treifah*, but through a physical mishap during the act itself. The owner has lost a valuable animal. The question the *mishnah* raised but never fully resolved was whether liability requires negligence, and if so, how we assess it.

The reason the *gemara* emphasizes that the *shochet* is an *uman* — an expert — is precisely because expertise cuts against a finding of negligence. The more accomplished and experienced a practitioner, the more natural it is to assume that any mistake was a freak occurrence rather than the product of carelessness. If anyone should be presumed to have done everything correctly, it is the professional who has performed this procedure hundreds or thousands of times. Yet Shmuel rules that this presumption does not hold.

### Shmuel: Expert Liable

Shmuel states: *tabach uman shekilkel chayav lishalem* — even an expert butcher who ruined the animal is obligated to pay. The reasoning is direct: *mazik hu, poshea hu* — he is a *mazik*, and he was negligent. You cannot claim that a slip of the hand was an act of God, an *ones*. And you cannot deflect responsibility by saying you were simply carrying out the owner's instructions — *anas kamei lo shechat li mikan, ve-shechat li mikan* — you were not authorized to perform the *shechita* incorrectly. The owner commissioned you to slaughter the animal properly; slaughtering it in the wrong way is not an act done on his behalf. So you bear personal liability.

The thrust of Shmuel's position therefore contains two distinct claims: first, that liability in such cases requires negligence (*peshia*), and second, that any slip — even by an expert — should be presumed to constitute negligence. Both claims require examination.

### Mazik vs. Poshe'ah

The *gemara* immediately asks: why did Shmuel need to say both that he is a *mazik* and that he is a *poshea*? Let him just say he is a *mazik* — why add the term *poshea*?

The answer is that each term carries independent legal weight. Had Shmuel said only that the butcher is a *mazik*, one might have thought: fair enough, but that applies only *heicha de-avid besachar* — only when he is being paid. The rationale would be that payment heightens the standard of care imposed on the practitioner. Even without rendering him a more skilled technician, the fact of receiving compensation creates an elevated level of responsibility. It lowers the threshold at which we are willing to say he acted carelessly. One might argue that without payment there is no such heightened responsibility, and since the butcher is an expert, any mishap should be attributed to an unforeseeable event.

To this Shmuel therefore adds: *poshea hu* — I regard any such slip as negligence. Whether or not you are being paid, whether or not you are the greatest expert alive, I will not accept the defense that a slip during the performance of skilled work is an innocent accident. *Ka mashma lan poshea hu.*

A natural question arises: what is the nature of this negligence? Is Shmuel saying that every physical slip in the course of professional work reflects some actual inattention — that the craftsman was distracted or sloppy — or is he making a broader claim that the very context of expertise and professional engagement raises the standard of care so that what would be an innocent accident in an ordinary person becomes negligence in a specialist? Consider the analogy of a surgeon: the threshold of what constitutes malpractice for a surgeon is entirely different from what it would be for someone who picked up a scalpel with no training. A professional dealing with a valuable animal or performing a precision religious act operates under a correspondingly elevated standard. Whether that is Shmuel's reasoning, or whether Shmuel is simply asserting that slips are never truly involuntary, the *gemara* leaves open — but the *halakhic* conclusion is clear.

One point the discussion surfaces but does not resolve: what if the *shochet* had warned the owner in advance of a particular difficulty — a thicker-than-usual neck, an unusual animal, some elevated risk of a mishap? A prior disclosure followed by the owner's agreement to proceed might amount to an assumption of risk, which would presumably exculpate. This is not worked out in the *gemara*, but it is plainly relevant.

### Ramban: Agency Theory

Why does liability require *peshia* at all? This question cuts deeply. After all, the principle *adam mu'ad le'olam* — a person is perpetually liable for damage he causes — appears to apply even in cases of *ones*, genuine accident. The *mishnah* says simply that a craftsman who ruins the object he was given must pay. It does not condition liability on negligence. So why do we need to establish that the *shochet* was *poshea*?

Tosafot, relying in part on the very *sugya* we are reading, argues that the principle *adam mu'ad le'olam* does not truly operate without some minimal degree of negligence. The fact that the *gemara* throughout this discussion scrutinizes whether there was *peshia* — rather than simply imposing liability as a matter of course — proves that you need at least some level of fault.

The Ramban answers differently, and in so doing provides the theoretical foundation for the entire discussion. His ruling is brief and programmatic: *ein be-uman ha-to'eh be-melachto mishum adam ha-mazik* — a craftsman who errs in the performance of his craft is not, in principle, an *adam ha-mazik* at all.

This statement requires unpacking. What defines someone as a *mazik*? The Ramban's answer is that being a *mazik* begins with the absence of a right to be handling the object. When I invade your property or your person without permission — even if a wind pushed me and I had no choice, even if I was completely without fault — I was an uninvited presence, a violator of your domain. That violation is what triggers *adam mu'ad le'olam*. The principle does not demand negligence because the entire legal category of *mazik* is built on the premise that you were where you should not have been.

But a craftsman given an object to repair, or a *shochet* commissioned to slaughter an animal, is in an entirely different posture. He is not an intruder. He is there by invitation, acting within a sanctioned role, handling an object he was specifically authorized to handle. His relationship to that object is not one of violation. Therefore, regardless of what happens to the object, the category of *adam ha-mazik* simply does not apply to him. You might sue him for malpractice — for failing in his professional duties — but you cannot characterize him as a *mazik*. 

The Ramban draws this out with a striking parallel. If someone is a *shomer* — a guardian — who is also permitted, as part of that guardianship, to handle and move the object, and in the course of that handling the object breaks due to genuine *ones*, the *shomer* is exempt. Not because the principle of *adam mu'ad le'olam* is being overridden, but because the *shomer* was never a *mazik* in the first place. He had the right to be handling the object, and so we do not apply *hilchos mazik*. We apply *hilchos shomrim*, and within that framework, *ones* is an exemption.

The same logic applies to an *uman*. As long as the craftsman is acting within his commissioned role, without negligence, we apply *hilchos uman*, not *hilchos mazik*. The moment he is *poshea*, however, he has stepped outside the boundaries of that authorized role. He is no longer acting in conformity with the task he was assigned. That exit from authorized agency — that deviation from the mandate — is what transforms him into a *mazik*. And once he is classified as a *mazik*, then even a minimal act of destruction carries liability. But without *peshia*, the category never attaches.

This creates an illuminating framework. The *Shulchan Aruch* organizes liability in distinct chapters: *hilchos mazik* on the one hand, *hilchos umnim* and *hilchos shomrim* on the other. When a craftsman ruins something, the question of which body of law governs is not merely taxonomic — it is determinative. If we approach him as a destroyer of property, we pull down *hilchos mazik* and ask whether he was acting without permission. If we approach him as a craftsman who made a mistake, we pull down *hilchos uman* and ask whether he was negligent. The Ramban's insight is that the two frameworks are mutually exclusive depending on the nature of the person's relationship to the object.

---

## Rav Chama's Challenge

### Baraita: Expert Exempt

Rav Chama bar Gurya challenges Shmuel from a *baraita*. The *baraita* states: if one gives an animal to a *shochet* and it becomes a *neveilah* — through a slip, not through any question of *treifah* — then *uman patur, hedyot chayav*: an expert is exempt and a non-expert is liable. Moreover, *ve-im nosei sachar, bein uman bein hedyot chayav*: if the *shochet* is being paid, both the expert and the non-expert are liable.

This *baraita* contradicts Shmuel on two counts. First, it holds that an expert is fundamentally exempt — the presumption runs in his favor. Second, it treats payment as the decisive variable: with pay, liability attaches regardless of expertise; without pay, the expert's status protects him. Shmuel had said the opposite: even an unpaid expert is liable, because any slip counts as negligence.

Shmuel's response to both challenges is to dismiss them as obvious — the questioners should have recognized that his ruling was grounded in the position of Rabbi Meir, while the *baraita* reflects the position of the *Rabbanan*. Presenting a source that follows a different authority's view is not a challenge; it is simply the presentation of a different opinion. One might observe that the dismissal is blunt, but the substance is clear: Shmuel was adopting a specific minority position, and the challengers failed to notice.

### Shmuel Adopts R. Meir

Shmuel explains: *ka'amina lachon ana Rabbi Meir* — I was telling you the position of Rabbi Meir. When I said *mazik hu, poshea hu*, and when I said that a slip counts as *peshia*, I was signaling that I adopt the view of Rabbi Meir, who holds that slips are never genuinely accidental. You were then citing me a *baraita* that follows the *Rabbanan*, a different school of thought entirely. *Amai lo daykisu mili* — why were you not paying close attention to my language?

The logic of his complaint is that his very terminology was a marker. By describing the errant *shochet* as both a *mazik* and a *poshea*, and by framing any slip as the latter, Shmuel embedded his source within a specific halakhic framework — the one identified with Rabbi Meir's stringent approach to accidents. *Man is lei hai sevara Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir is the authority who holds that a person has an ongoing responsibility to monitor himself so carefully that slips simply do not occur. For Rabbi Meir, accidents happen because people are not careful enough. Any slip is therefore an instance of *peshia*.

### Rabbi Meir Position

The *gemara* then asks: which teaching of Rabbi Meir is the one Shmuel is adopting? The *gemara* first considers the ruling of Rabbi Meir in the case of an ox that broke free even after its owner had tied it and locked it in properly. Rabbi Meir holds the owner liable regardless. But the *gemara* rejects this as the relevant source: that case turns on a textual debate about what level of *shemirah* the Torah requires for a goring ox, not on any general principle about slips and negligence.

The *gemara* next considers a *mishnah* about a dyer who was asked to dye wool red and dyed it black, or asked to dye it black and dyed it red. Rabbi Meir holds that the dyer pays the owner the full value of his wool. That seems relevant — a craftsman who performs the wrong task and ruins the material. But the *gemara* dismisses this case as well: *hasam beyadayim kalu minei* — there the craftsman destroyed the object directly and entirely with his own hands. It is not a case of a slip in the course of doing the right thing; it is a case of fundamentally doing something else altogether. Rashi adds that Rabbi Meir may be speaking of a case where the dyer *intended* to change the color — *shenitkaven leshanot* — which would render it an intentional deviation rather than a slip. Either way, it is not analogous to an inadvertent physical mishap during *shechita*.

The *gemara* then identifies the correct source in a *mishnah* dealing with a broken pitcher and a fallen camel. If a person's pitcher broke and he did not clear the shards from the street, or his camel fell and he did not lift it, and someone came and was injured, Rabbi Meir holds the owner liable while the *Chachamim* exempt him in human court and hold him liable only before the heavenly court. The *gemara* establishes, drawing on analysis conducted much earlier in the tractate, that the debate between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* in this case is specifically *benitka poshea hu paleig* — whether a slip or trip is considered an act of negligence. Rabbi Meir says yes: you have a responsibility to watch over yourself and your actions, and any slip reflects a failure of that responsibility. The *Chachamim* say no: some things are genuinely beyond one's control.

This, then, is the Rabbi Meir whom Shmuel invokes. Not a Rabbi Meir who applies a special severity to one type of case, but a Rabbi Meir with a systematic position: accidents do not simply happen. Any mishap in the performance of one's activities reflects some measure of inattention, and that inattention is negligence. It is a demanding standard — one that acknowledges degrees of slip (an involuntary twitch differs from walking distracted) but places them all under the same halakhic umbrella — and the *gemara* places it squarely within Rabbi Meir's broader jurisprudential framework.

---

## R. Yochanan: Fee Matters

### Tzipori Shochtim Case

The *gemara* now introduces the position of Rabbi Yochanan. Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan as ruling that an expert *shochet* who ruins an animal is liable — even if he is as accomplished as the *shochtim* of Tzipori, who were renowned for their extraordinary level of expertise. This appears to align with Shmuel: expertise provides no defense.

But the *gemara* immediately confronts this with a story. That same Rabba bar bar Chana reports that a case came before Rabbi Yochanan — apparently at the *beit knesset* of Maon — in which someone complained that a *shochet* had turned his animal into a *neveilah*. Rabbi Yochanan told the *shochet*: go and bring proof that you are a *mumcheh*, that you have genuine expertise in *shechiting* chickens. If you can demonstrate that expertise, I will presume that whatever happened was a freak occurrence and exempt you. So Rabbi Yochanan, in practice, appears to hold that an expert *shochet* is *exempt* — the opposite of what Shmuel holds.

### Free vs. Paid Status

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, kan bechinam kan besachar* — it is not difficult; one case refers to a free service and the other to a paid one. When Rabbi Yochanan said an expert is liable even as accomplished as the *shochtim* of Tzipori, he was speaking of a paid *shochet*. Payment creates an elevated standard of responsibility that precludes any claim of *ones*. But when he exempted the *shochet* who could prove his expertise, he was speaking of a *shochet* performing the service without fee. In that context, genuine expertise supports the inference that any mishap was genuinely accidental.

This resolution is counterintuitive at first glance. One might expect that a higher-paying customer would seek out the finest expert, and that the finest expert should be least prone to negligence. But the *gemara*'s logic runs differently: the level of expertise and the fact of payment are treated as independent variables. Expertise bears on whether we characterize a mishap as negligent; payment bears on the level of responsibility the *shochet* assumed by taking the job. Regardless of how expert you are, if you accepted payment, you accepted the corresponding degree of care. And accepting that degree of care means that a slip — even for the most accomplished practitioner — is your professional responsibility.

Relatedly, one might ask: if the owner gave his animal to an inexpert *shochet*, does the owner's own imprudence operate as *peshia denizak* — negligence on the part of the damaged party? This is a fair question that the *gemara* does not resolve here, but it sits naturally alongside these cases.

### R. Zeira: Payment

Rabbi Zeira draws out the practical implication: *ha-rotzeh sheyitchayav lo tabbach, yakdim lo dinar* — if you want to ensure the *shochet* will be liable for any mistake, make sure to pay him in advance. The phrase *yakdim lo dinar*, pay him a *dinar* beforehand, may emphasize advance payment specifically so that the *shochet* cannot later claim he understood the arrangement to be a free service. Secure the payment, and you secure liability.

A *baraita* is then cited that appears to complicate things: it holds that a miller who ruins your grain, a baker who ruins your dough, or a *shochet* who produces a *neveilah* is liable *mipnei she-hu ke-nosei sachar* — because he is like one who takes a fee. The word *ke-*, "like," suggests that even without explicit payment, the professional status itself creates something equivalent to paid responsibility. If that is so, then Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between paid and unpaid collapses, because even a free *shochet* would be treated as if paid.

The *gemara* resolves this by emending the text: read *eima mipnei she-hu nosei sachar* — remove the *kaf*, the comparative prefix. The *baraita* means he is actually being paid, not that he is *like* one being paid. The distinction between paid and unpaid is maintained.

---

## Magrimussa Case

### Rav's Dual Approach

A case of a *magrumisa* — a problematic *shechita* whose validity is itself disputed in the *gemara* — came before Rav. The owner had two questions: is the meat permitted for consumption, and if it is *treifah*, can I collect from the *shochet*? Rav ruled on both simultaneously: he declared the meat *treifah* and exempted the *shochet* from payment. This strikes many as doing the owner a double disservice — denying him both the meat and compensation.

### Court Ruling Unity

Rav Kahana and Rav Assi encountered the aggrieved owner and told him: Rav did you a *tartei* — a double. The immediate reading is that Rav wronged him twice: first, he should have declared the meat kosher following the opinion of Rabbi Yossi beRabbi Yehuda, and second, even if he was going to rule *treifah* following the *Rabbanan*, he should have made the *shochet* pay.

But the *gemara* rejects this reading. *Umi shari lemeimar ki hai gavna* — is it even permitted to publicly criticize a ruling in that manner? A *baraita* teaches that when a judge leaves the deliberations of a court, he may not approach a litigant and disclose that he voted in the minority. He may not say: I was trying to acquit you, it was only the majority who ruled against you. *Holech rachil megaleh sod* — a talebearing tongue reveals secrets. The court must speak with a unified voice, and the confidentiality of deliberations must be maintained.

There is something jarring about applying this principle here. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi were not formally part of Rav's court; there is no clear indication they participated in deliberations from which a formal ruling emerged. In what sense are they bound by the rules governing a *beis din*? And ordinarily, a *posek* who disagrees with another *posek*'s ruling is entirely free to say so — that is how *halakhic* discourse functions. The *gemara* seems to assume that some form of deliberative process occurred that brought these rules into play, though the details are not spelled out. The application is striking and somewhat difficult to fully account for.

### Dual Benefit Logic

The *gemara* therefore concludes that Rav Kahana and Rav Assi were saying the exact opposite: Rav did you *tartei lema'alyuta* — two good things, not two bad things. You should be grateful for Rav's ruling.

How so? First: *lo achlach sefek issura* — Rav protected you from eating meat that is, according to many authorities, *treifah*. That is a genuine service. Second: *manachach mi-sefek gezeila* — Rav saved you from the prohibition of *gezeila*. Because the *magrumisa* might in fact have been a valid *shechita*, the meat might have been perfectly kosher. If the meat is kosher, then the *shochet* did nothing wrong and owes nothing. Were you to collect from him on the basis of an uncertain ruling, you might be taking money that is not yours. Rav's ruling, by treating the question as one of genuine doubt (*safek*), protected you from inadvertent theft even as it protected you from eating potentially forbidden meat.

This is a remarkable piece of *halakhic* reasoning: a single ruling simultaneously avoided two distinct potential *isurim* — one of *treifah* consumption and one of *gezeila* — without sacrificing the integrity of either concern.

---

## Money Changer Case

### Coin Authenticity

The *gemara* moves from direct malpractice to a case of harmful professional advice. *Ha-marei dinar le-shulchani* — someone shows a coin to a money changer and asks whether it is acceptable currency. The money changer says yes. The coin owner proceeds to use it in a transaction, only to have the coin rejected by a merchant. He has suffered a loss traceable to the money changer's mistaken certification. Can he recover?

This is structurally different from the *shochet* cases. No object was physically damaged or destroyed. The money changer's act was advisory — he gave an opinion, and the coin owner acted on it to his detriment. Whatever loss occurred was the downstream consequence of reliance on bad professional advice. The *gemara* presents two competing *baraitot*: one holds *uman patur, hedyot chayav* — an expert is exempt, a non-expert liable; the other holds that even an *uman* is liable. The debate mirrors the earlier discussion about *shochtim*.

### Expert Exemption Limits

Rav Pappa introduces a crucial refinement. When the *baraita* exempts an *uman*, it is speaking of someone at the very pinnacle of the field — *kegon Danku ve-Issur*, like those two renowned money traders, Danku and Issur, who had nothing further to learn. For a practitioner of that stature, there is genuinely no basis to attribute a mistake to deficiency of knowledge or skill. But what could such a person have gotten wrong? The *gemara* answers: *ta'u be-sikta chadta* — they erred because new coins had just been minted, altering the value of the old ones, and this information had not yet reached them at that very moment. That is the nature of the exemption: only the very best, and only when their error was caused by a genuinely new and unavailable datum. For everyone else, and for every other type of mistake, Rav Pappa's implicit conclusion is that even an *uman* is liable — consistent with Shmuel's position.

### R. Chiya Acts Generously

A woman came to Rabbi Chiyya and showed him a coin, asking whether she could accept it. He told her it was good. The next day she returned, reporting that a storekeeper had rejected it as counterfeit. Rabbi Chiyya told Rav, who was serving as his attendant, to exchange the coin for her — replace the bad one with a good one — and to record the transaction in his personal ledger as a *esek bish*, a bad business deal. Rashi explains the comment: what possessed me to get involved in examining someone's coins? This was a gratuitous involvement that has now cost me. In that formulation, the self-reproach implies that Rabbi Chiyya saw this as the loss of someone who took on an unnecessary obligation.

### Spirit vs. Letter

However, the *gemara* immediately establishes that Rabbi Chiyya was actually an expert in coins — comparable to Danku and Issur in his knowledge of the trade. If he was that expert, why should he pay at all?

The *gemara* answers: *Rabbi Chiyya lifnim mishurat hadin hu de-avid* — Rabbi Chiyya was acting beyond the strict letter of the law. He was technically exempt. But he did not wish to leave the woman with any legitimate complaint against him. He had indirectly caused her loss — however blameless he was in law — and he chose to absorb that loss himself rather than invoke his exemption. The notation *esek bish* was thus not an admission of wrongdoing but a bookkeeping acknowledgment that he was taking a loss he was not required by law to take.

This prompts an extended discussion of *lifnim mishurat hadin*. The phrase is striking: it translates literally as "within the line of the law," yet it refers to conduct that goes *beyond* what the law demands. The conceptual key is to imagine the law as a fence that circumscribes the sphere of permissible human activity. The law defines the outer boundary — what you may do, what you must do, what you may not do. To act *lifnim mishurat hadin* is to voluntarily narrow your own sphere, to decline to exercise permissions the law grants you. You are operating further inside the legal boundary than you are required to. You are not doing something the law forbids; you are refraining from something the law allows.

The *gemara* grounds this concept in the verse from *Shemos* in which Yitro advises Moshe how to organize the people. This advice, given before *Matan Torah* by a non-Jew, is read by the *gemara* as containing a layered map of human obligation — including obligations that lie beyond the formal demands of law:

> *Ve-hodata lahem* — "And you shall inform them": this refers to their livelihood.
> *Et ha-derech* — "the path": this is *gemilut chasadim*, acts of lovingkindness.
> *Yelchu bah* — "they shall walk in it": this is *bikur cholim*, visiting the sick.
> *Ve-et ha-ma'aseh* — "and the act": this is the strict law.
> *Asher ya'asun* — "which they shall do": this is *lifnim mishurat hadin*.

It is remarkable that Yitro's counsel to Moshe, embedded in the Torah itself, is understood to mandate not just legal compliance but the spirit that law alone cannot legislate. Acting with kindness, visiting the sick, burying the dead — these are dimensions of human responsibility that transcend the enforceable norms of *din*.

Tosafot raises a pointed question here. In a famous *sugya* in Bava Metzia, workers who broke something while carrying it were exempt, but their employer refused to pay them their wages and held onto their coats as collateral. When the matter came before a *posek*, the *posek* returned the coats and ordered the employer to pay — invoking the verse *lemaan telech bederech tovim* and *ve-orchos tzaddikim tishmor*, doing what is right and good. Why, Tosafot asks, is the language in that case different from *lifnim mishurat hadin*? One answer Tosafot offers is that there is a distinction between declining an exemption one is technically entitled to — which is *lifnim mishurat hadin* — and performing an act of pure charity or *chessed* entirely outside the framework of legal obligation. Not claiming an exemption that applies specifically to you in your professional capacity is meaningfully different from performing a general act of kindness. Both are admirable; they belong to different categories.

---

## Reliance & Grama

### Express Reliance

Resh Lakish showed a coin to Rabbi Elazar and asked for his assessment. Rabbi Elazar said it was good. Resh Lakish then said explicitly: *chazi de-alach kasamichna* — note that I am relying on you. If this coin turns out to be bad, I will come to you for compensation.

### Reliance Disputed

Rabbi Elazar responded with evident skepticism: *im kasamichat alai, mai lemeimra* — fine, you're relying on me, but what exactly do you think that accomplishes? Do you imagine that by declaring your reliance you have created a legal obligation for me to pay you if the coin is rejected?

### Grama Doctrine Intro

Rabbi Elazar then makes explicit the theoretical challenge that has been lurking beneath the surface of the entire money-changer discussion: *va-atu de-amrit Reb Meir hu de-dan dina degarmi* — and now you're the one who says that the only reason such liability exists is Rabbi Meir's principle of *dina degarmi*. The money changer gave advice. Nothing was physically destroyed. The loss arose because the coin owner acted on that advice and was then stuck with a bad coin. That is *grama* — indirect causation — not a direct act of damage. The conventional rule is that *grama* does not generate enforceable liability in *beis din*.

Rabbi Elazar's implicit argument is: if you think I should pay you, that position only holds according to Rabbi Meir, who goes further than most authorities in imposing liability for indirect causation — *dina degarmi*. Are you really relying on Rabbi Meir for that? And moreover, is that even the *halakha*?

Resh Lakish responds: *lo, Reb Meir u-sevira lan kavateih* — yes, it is Rabbi Meir, and that is indeed how we rule. We do rule in accordance with *dina degarmi*. This is a significant statement. The principle of *dina degarmi* — Rabbi Meir's framework for certain types of indirect causation that rise to the level of actionable liability — is not merely a minority opinion filed away in the name of learning. It is operative *halakha*. This closes a gap that had been left open in earlier discussions on the daf, where Rabbi Meir's position had been invoked in cases of ruining coins or striking a hand holding an object. Here, that position is confirmed as *le-halakha*.

---

## R. Meir: Grama Law

### Dyer Case: Direct Act

Having established that Rabbi Meir's *dina degarmi* is operative, the *gemara* undertakes to identify exactly which teaching of Rabbi Meir is the authoritative source. The first candidate is the *mishnah* about the dyer: wool given to be dyed red that came back black, or vice versa. Rabbi Meir rules *noten lo dmei tzemaro* — the dyer pays the full value of the wool.

This seems like a natural source for *dina degarmi* — a craftsman whose erroneous professional act caused a loss. But the *gemara* rejects it: *hasam beyadayim kalu minei* — there, the dyer destroyed the wool directly with his own hands by performing the wrong act entirely. There is nothing indirect about it. The loss was not a downstream consequence of advice or inaction; it was the immediate product of a direct physical intervention.

### Vine/Wheat: Kilayim

The second candidate is a *mishnah* about *kilayim*: one who extends his vine over his neighbor's wheat thereby causes the wheat to become forbidden as *kilayim*, and Rabbi Meir holds him liable to pay. Tosafot notes that the *hava amina* for treating this as *grama* would be that the wheat does not become prohibited instantaneously — only after the vine and wheat grow together for a period does the prohibition take full effect. One might therefore argue that the damage is not immediate but develops as a natural consequence over time. Yet the *gemara* dismisses this: *hasam nami ka-avid beyadayim* — here too, the person did a direct act, namely, positioning the vine over the wheat. The subsequent natural process is not a meaningful intervention. The direct act was his, and the inevitable consequence follows from it directly enough that it is not characterized as *grama* in any meaningful sense.

### Fallen Wall: Inaction

The *gemara* then identifies the most compelling candidate: a *baraita* about a dividing wall between a vineyard and a wheat field. Even when the two are physically adjacent, a proper partition between them prevents the *kilayim* prohibition from taking effect. If the wall fell, the owner is told to rebuild it; the wall falls again, he is told to rebuild it again. If he finally despairs and says he will not continue to rebuild it, and the plants then grow together into *kilayim*, Rabbi Meir holds that *harei ze kidesh ve-chayav be-achrayuto* — it has become *kilayim* and the vineyard owner is liable.

This is the key case. The owner did not perform any affirmative act. He simply stopped doing something — he ceased rebuilding. His passivity, his inaction, led to the *kilayim* condition and to his neighbor's loss. There is no direct physical act that caused the damage; only a failure to prevent what he had been preventing. And yet Rabbi Meir holds him liable. This is *grama* liability in its most pronounced form — responsibility for indirect causation through inaction.

### Dinei Degarmi Framework

This *baraita* is presented as a *setan mishnah* — an anonymously attributed teaching, which by rabbinic convention is attributed to Rabbi Meir. And it is here that the *gemara* finds the foundation for *dinei degarmi* as a general principle. The framework this establishes is broad: one who causes a loss through sufficiently direct indirect causation — whether by bad professional advice that is relied upon, by damaging a coin's value through deliberate action, by a mistaken legal ruling whose consequences cannot be unwound — is liable to pay. This is not the full sweep of all *grama*, but a subset of it where the causal connection is close enough, and the actor's role in bringing about the loss is clear enough, that Rabbi Meir treats it as actionable.

### Grama vs. Garmi

The *gemara* thus closes its discussion with *dina degarmi* established as operative *halakha*. But a major question is left conspicuously open: what exactly distinguishes *grama* — indirect causation for which one is exempt — from *garmi* — the subset of indirect causation for which Rabbi Meir and, according to the ruling here, the accepted *halakha*, imposes liability?

The two terms are genuinely distinct. *Grama* represents the general category of indirect damage; *garmi* represents those instances within *grama* that carry enforceable liability. Grammatically, the *yod* in *garmi* as against *grama* may signal a stronger or more proximate form of causation — though even that linguistic observation is uncertain. What is clear is that the distinction is real and consequential: it determines whether a money changer, an errant judge, an imprudent *posek*, or a vineyard owner who stops maintaining a wall will be made to pay.

The Rishonim devote extensive discussion to working out the parameters of this distinction, and the *gemara* itself — as the lecturer notes — does not provide a fully explicit resolution. The cases examined here — the dyer who changed colors, the vine placed over wheat, the fallen wall, the judge who ruled incorrectly and whose ruling was irreversible — each illuminate a different aspect of the problem without yielding a clean rule. That open-endedness, far from being a lacuna, reflects the genuine difficulty of drawing lines in a domain where causation shades from the immediate to the attenuated by degrees rather than by sharp breaks. Rabbi Meir's contribution was to insist that the law must grapple with those cases rather than exempting them all. The task of marking precisely where the obligation begins is left to the continuing work of interpretation.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 101

## Worker Negligence

### Intro & Setup

Daf 101 marks a milestone: one hundred daf completed in Bava Kamma. We pick up with the *mishna* on 100b. The preceding *mishna* had addressed workers who damage objects entrusted to them and are liable to pay. That discussion touched on an interesting nuance — whether a person's primary role vis-à-vis an object is that of a workman or a *shomer*, which might place the situation in a different category than ordinary *adam hamazik*, even when damage occurs. That was the backdrop. Now we return to a case involving *shinui*, but *shinui* not in the context of *gezeila*, rather in the context of a craftsman or worker operating on someone else's property.

### Destroyed Wool

The *mishna* opens: *hanotein tzemer latzaba ve-hikdicho yoreh* — someone gave wool to a dyer, and the pot scalded it, destroying the wool. *Noten lo d'mei tzemaro* — he must pay the cost of the wool. Whether the case assumes negligence, and what degree of negligence is required, is not the focus here; the point is simply that the wool was destroyed in the course of the work, and the craftsman must pay. That is the straightforward case.

### Inferior Dye

The *mishna* then turns to a more nuanced scenario: *tzeva'o ka'ur* — the craftsman dyed it with an inferior dye. The word rendered *ka'ur* is written with an *alef* in place of an *ayin*, and means "inferior." The correct color was used, but the quality of the dye was substandard, and the resulting quality of the wool was diminished accordingly. In that case: *im hashevach yoter al hayetzia noten lo et hayetzia; im hayetzia yoter al hashevach noten lo et hashevach* — if the improvement exceeds the expenses, he pays the craftsman only his expenses; if the expenses exceed the improvement, he pays only the improvement.

At the outset, it is worth noting that no one raises the possibility of *shinui* here. The craftsman was told to dye it a certain color and did so — it is therefore not a *shinui* in the sense of taking possession of the object. The question is rather: what recourse does the owner have when the work was done poorly?

### Pshat Expenses

To appreciate the *pshat* of the *mishna*, consider a representative scenario. The owner brings wool worth one hundred dollars, contracts a fee of fifty dollars, and anticipates receiving wool worth two hundred dollars. The craftsman, however, does inferior work, and the end result is wool worth only one hundred fifty dollars. Of the fifty-dollar fee, say twenty-five dollars represented out-of-pocket expenses and twenty-five dollars represented the craftsman's labor. The *mishna* says: pay the lesser of the expenses or the improvement. In this case, pay only the expenses — twenty-five dollars — and forfeit the labor. The owner receives wool worth one hundred fifty dollars and has paid only twenty-five, netting a profit of twenty-five instead of the anticipated fifty.

### Profit Analysis

The same framework applies across different valuation scenarios. If the resulting wool is worth only one hundred twenty dollars, then the improvement — twenty dollars — is less than the expenses — twenty-five dollars — and so only the improvement is paid. The owner breaks even: he neither gains nor loses. The principle is consistent: as long as there is some improvement, however modest, the craftsman is paid the lesser of the two figures, and the owner is guaranteed at minimum to break even. Only in the first half of the *mishna*, where the wool is actually destroyed and rendered worth less than its original value, is the craftsman a *mazik* who must pay full damages.

The mechanism behind this arrangement is worth examining. The craftsman is not a *mazik* — the object is worth more than it was. He is not a *gazlan*, and he has not effected a *shinui* that would make him *koneh* the object. He is a worker who failed to perform as contracted. The response of *chazal* is effectively to re-read the terms of the contract: since you did not perform your labor as required, you are not entitled to be paid for your labor; but since you did incur out-of-pocket expenses, those are recoverable. The result is a form of *peshara* — a reasonable settlement. The owner may not realize the full profit he anticipated, but he will not lose money, and the craftsman loses his labor as the consequence of his inferior work.

A student raised the observation that under secular law, a contractor who completely fails to perform might recover nothing at all — not even expenses. The response is instructive: this is a case of inferior performance, not a complete departure from the contracted work. The craftsman used the right color but an inferior grade of dye. That is not the radical variation addressed in the next section of the *mishna*. The question of exactly what a contractor is owed when work is substandard — as distinct from entirely wrong — is genuinely complex in any legal system.

### Contract Reinterpretation

It bears emphasis that *chazal* are not finding the craftsman liable as a *mazik*, nor are they finding a *kinyan* through *shinui*. They are reinterpreting the contractual arrangement itself. Because the work was below standard, the craftsman loses his labor; because he did have legitimate out-of-pocket costs, those are compensable. This framework ensures the owner does not lose money and the craftsman bears the cost of his poor workmanship in the form of forfeited wages. Whether this is a strict *din* or something *chazal* imposed as a form of equitable adjustment is an interesting question, but that is the structure.

### Tosafot's Reading

*Tosafot* offers an alternative reading, drawing on the *Yerushalmi* as interpreted by the *Ri*, though *Tosafot* acknowledges this is not the *pshat* of the *Yerushalmi*. The conceptual approach is different: rather than simply docking the craftsman's labor, one first determines what profit the owner would have made had everything gone correctly, and that profit is deducted from whatever would otherwise be owed to the craftsman. Any remainder is then paid.

In the scenario described: the owner would have made a fifty-dollar profit had the work been performed properly. So from the value of the dyed wool, fifty dollars is first allocated to the owner as his rightful profit. Only if something remains is the craftsman paid. He does not receive compensation directly for lost profit — the owner does not recover damages for anticipated gains — but the accounting begins with restoring the owner's expected profit before the craftsman sees a penny.

This reading places considerably more pressure on the craftsman. Under the *pshat* reading, the craftsman at least recovers his expenses in most scenarios; under *Tosafot*'s reading, even his expenses might be absorbed by the owner's priority claim to profit. *Tosafot* is starting from the premise that the owner is entitled to the profit he contracted for, and the entire arrangement follows from that premise. Practically speaking, the *pshat* reading is almost certainly the *psak halacha*, and even *Tosafot* acknowledges that this is not the straightforward reading. But the conceptual distinction is meaningful: one approach protects the craftsman's out-of-pocket costs; the other prioritizes the owner's expected return above all else.

---

## Shinui & Possession

### Wrong Color Debate

The *mishna* proceeds to a more radical case: *litzboa lo adom v'tzava'o shachor, shachor v'tzava'o adom* — he was told to dye it red and dyed it black, or told black and dyed it red. Here we are no longer discussing inferior quality — the craftsman produced a different color entirely, in violation of his instructions. *Rabbi Meir omer noten lo d'mei tzemaro* — Rabbi Meir says this is equivalent to a *mazik*: the craftsman is *koneh* through *shinui* and pays for the wool.

### Yehuda's Position

*Rabbi Yehuda*, however, disagrees. *Im hashevach yeter al hayetzia noten lo es hayetzia; v'im hayetzia yeter al hashevach noten lo es hashevach* — the same rule as before applies. Even producing the wrong color is not a *shinui* sufficient to effect *kinyan*. The craftsman simply failed to do the job as instructed; he is treated the same as the inferior-dye case, and the lesser of expenses or improvement is paid.

The debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is a conceptual one: does *shinui* apply in the context of a craftsman who violates his instructions, or is *shinui* a category reserved for the *gazlan*? It is worth noting, as was pointed out in discussion, that it is not necessarily clear which ruling is more favorable to the owner of the wool. If the wrong color happens to be more valuable, Rabbi Meir's ruling — which makes the craftsman *koneh* and requires him to pay only for the raw wool — could actually leave the owner worse off than Rabbi Yehuda's approach. The debate is therefore not about protecting one party over another; it is a purely conceptual question about whether *shinui* is operative here.

### Bench vs Chair

The *gemara* extends the same debate to a more radical scenario. A *baraita* teaches: *hanotein etzim lecharash la'asot mehem kisei v'asa mehem safsal* — one gave wood to a carpenter to make a chair, and he made a bench instead; or gave it to make a bench, and he made a chair. Rabbi Meir says: *noten lo d'mei eitzav* — pay for the wood, the craftsman is *koneh* through *shinui*. This is an even more dramatic departure than wrong color — the very form of the object has changed — yet Rabbi Meir applies the same principle. Rabbi Yehuda again disagrees: *im hashevach yeter al hayetzia noten lo es hayetzia* and so on. The craftsman did not fulfill his commission, but *shinui* does not apply, and the lesser-of-two rule governs.

### Meir's Concession

Importantly, the *baraita* records that Rabbi Meir himself concedes a limitation on his own position. *U'modeh Rabbi Meir im natan etzim lecharash la'asot mehem kisei na'eh v'asa mehem kisei ka'ur* — if one gave wood to make a beautiful, high-quality chair, and the craftsman made a plain, inferior one; or was asked to make a fine bench and made a substandard one — even Rabbi Meir agrees this is not *shinui*. The object is of the same type; it is merely of lesser quality. In that case, *im hashevach yeter al hayetzia noten lo es hayetzia v'im hayetzia yeter al hashevach noten lo es hashevach* — the lesser-of-two rule applies. So the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is confined to cases where the craftsman produces a genuinely different type of object or a genuinely different color: Rabbi Meir says that is *shinui* effecting *kinyan*; Rabbi Yehuda says it is not. Where it is merely inferior work of the same type, everyone agrees it falls under the *mishna*'s lesser-of-two framework.

---

## Dye Presence Theory

### Color Presence

The *gemara* now pivots to a broad conceptual question: *yesh shevach samanim al hatzemer o ein shevach samanim al hatzemer* — is the improvement of the dye still considered to be present in the wool, or not? The *gemara* later reformulates this as *chazuta milta hi o lo* — is the color, the appearance, of a dyed object itself considered a substantive presence of the original material? To put it concretely: when I look at a blue shirt, do I say there is a shirt and there is also blue dye still present within it, or do I say there is simply a blue shirt, with no dye remaining as a discrete entity?

The practical significance of this question — the *nafka mina* — depends on the case, and the *gemara* works through several scenarios to isolate one in which the answer truly makes a difference.

### Stolen Dye Return

The *gemara* initially considers a case where someone steals dye (*samanim*, or more precisely the raw pigment ingredients), processes them — stomping and immersing them to produce liquid dye — and uses the dye to color some wool. The *gemara* notes this is not the right framing: by processing the raw materials, the thief already acquired possession through *shinui* at that earlier stage, before the dye even touched the wool. So the question of whether the dye is present in the wool is irrelevant in that version.

The *gemara* then tries: what if the thief stole already-prepared liquid dye and used it to dye his wool? Even here, the scenario is difficult. If the dye is not considered present, the owner demands payment for his stolen dye. If it is present, the owner could theoretically demand his dye back — but how? The *gemara* notes that any attempt to extract the dye (*tzappan*) would destroy it entirely, so saying "just take it" is not a meaningful remedy. Either way, the thief cannot escape liability.

The *gemara* therefore settles on a case with a genuine *nafka mina*: the thief stole both the wool and the dye from the same person, dyed the wool with the stolen dye, and then has a change of heart and returns the dyed wool. Has he returned everything he stole? If *yesh shevach samanim* — the dye is still considered present in the wool — then yes, by returning the dyed wool he has returned both the wool and the dye, and his obligation is discharged. If *ein shevach samanim* — the dye is no longer present — then he has returned only the wool, and he still owes for the dye separately.

The *gemara* raises a complication: even under *ein shevach samanim*, would the thief not benefit from the rule that a *gazlan* who improves a stolen object and returns it is entitled to compensation for the improvement? If the dye was worth twenty-five dollars and the improvement to the wool is worth fifty dollars, then even if the dye is not present and he owes twenty-five for the dye, he is owed fifty for the improvement, and on net the owner owes him the difference. This is a recurring theme from earlier in the tractate — improving stolen property, whether under *takanas hashavim* or *kinyan gezeila*, entitles the improver to compensation.

The *gemara* therefore refines the scenario further: *d'zil tiva* — the market has fallen. The owner's wool was worth one hundred dollars, his dye was worth twenty-five, and under normal circumstances the dyed product would have been worth one hundred fifty. But the market has since dropped, and the dyed wool is now worth only one hundred ten. If *yesh shevach samanim*, the thief returns the physical object — dye included — and the rule of *harei shelcha lefanecha* applies: he has returned the actual object, regardless of market fluctuation. If *ein shevach samanim*, the dye is no longer present; the improvement to the wool is only ten dollars, but the dye that was destroyed was worth twenty-five, so the thief still owes the owner fifteen dollars after netting the improvement against the stolen dye.

One student astutely noted that this scenario resembles the earlier *gemara* about a building beam incorporated into a structure. Indeed, the conceptual parallel is present. Another student raised the question of whether absorbing the dye into the wool constitutes a *shinui* in its own right — intuitively, dye that has been chemically absorbed into fibers seems to have undergone a real transformation, both in the dye and in the wool. The point is well taken. Dyeing, unlike painting, involves a chemical reaction with the material rather than a surface coating. The dye has arguably ceased to exist independently. Yet the *gemara*'s question presupposes that this may not rise to the level of *shinui* that effects acquisition, and the reason is that dyeing is the natural purpose and destination of dye — it does not live independently; its function is to color something. Whether the visible result of that process constitutes the dye's ongoing "presence" is precisely the question being posed.

### Market Value Drop

As noted above, the market-value-drop scenario is the case the *gemara* identifies as cleanly isolating the *nafka mina*. The thief returns the dyed wool when the market has declined. Under *yesh shevach samanim*, the physical dye is present in the returned wool, the return is complete, and the market loss falls on the owner just as it would had no theft occurred — the thief has returned the object as it stands. Under *ein shevach samanim*, the dye has vanished; only colored wool remains. The thief owes for the dye but can offset only the modest improvement in the wool's value, leaving a net obligation.

The *gemara* then adds a second framing for this same issue: *kegon de-tziva behu kupa* — what if the stolen dye was used not to dye wool but to paint a basket (*kupa*, according to *Tosafot*; *Rashi* reads *kupa* as a monkey, which becomes relevant momentarily). *Tosafot* explains that painting a basket is a suboptimal use of high-quality dye — the painted basket will not command meaningfully more than an unpainted one — and so the end result is an object worth less than the raw materials. This is another version of the question: when the thief returns the painted basket, has he returned the dye?

### Monkey Mixing

*Ravina* introduces an entirely different version of the scenario, one without any theft at all: *kegon de-tzemer de-chad ve-samanim de-chad* — Michael owns wool; David owns dye; *ve-ata kof ve-tzavya lehu tzemer be-hanei samanim* — a monkey came along and, in the manner of curious monkeys, mixed Michael's wool with David's dye, dyeing the wool with it. This is why *Rashi* explains *kupa* as a monkey — the scenario we have just reached involves a monkey (*kof*) as the actor.

There is no *gazlan* here. The monkey is wild; there is no human tortfeasor (setting aside the separate *Bava Kamma* discussion of the owner of an animal that causes damage, which is inapplicable to a wild monkey). The question is therefore purely: *yesh shevach samanim al gabei tzemer* — is Michael's dye still considered present in David's wool, such that Michael can say to David, "Give me back my dye; it's still yours in your wool"? If David cannot extract it physically — which he cannot, since any dye remover would destroy the dye entirely — he would have to compensate Michael for it. Or: *ein shevach samanim al gabei tzemer* — the dye has ceased to exist; David holds nothing belonging to Michael; Michael has no claim.

*Tosafot* raises a pointed question about this scenario: even if the dye is not considered present, David's wool is now worth more. Should David not owe Michael something for the benefit he derived — analogous to the earlier *Bava Kamma* principle that one who benefits from another's property at a loss to the owner owes some compensation, even without fault? *Tosafot* notes the tension but suggests that where neither party nor their agent acted — where it was purely an act of nature, or in this case an act of monkey — perhaps the obligation of *neheneh* (benefiting at another's loss) does not arise. In any event, the *gemara*'s framing is focused on the question of physical presence, not the broader *neheneh* analysis, and the distinction between "the physical dye is present" and "a benefit was derived" is central to the structure of the discussion.

---

## Orlah Proof

### Orlah Must Burn

The *gemara* attempts to resolve the question of *yesh* or *ein shevach samanim* by bringing a *ta shema*: *beged she-tziva'o b'klipei orlah yidalek* — a garment dyed with the shells of *orlah* fruit must be burned. *Orlah* — the fruit of a tree during its first three years — is *assur b'hana'ah*, forbidden for any benefit. The question is whether a garment dyed with *orlah*-derived dye is itself *assur b'hana'ah*. The argument runs as follows: if the *orlah* were no longer present after dyeing, then wearing the garment would not constitute deriving benefit from *orlah* — it would be merely a colored garment, and the original prohibition would have been exhausted in the dyeing process. But if the garment must be burned, this implies the *orlah* is still considered present in the garment, and wearing it continues to constitute *hana'ah* from *orlah*. *Alma chazuta milta hi* — apparently, even mere appearance, mere color, counts as the physical presence of the original material.

The question of requiring destruction is sharper than the mere prohibition on wearing, as was observed in discussion. That the garment must be *burned* — not merely discarded or sold — indicates that the *orlah* is treated as actually present within it, not merely that an aesthetic pleasure is being forbidden. The ruling about destruction is therefore a stronger proof for *yesh shevach samanim* than the *issur hana'ah* alone.

### Special Orlah Rule
