*Rava* responds: *hana'ah ha-nir'eh la'einayim assrah Torah* — the Torah specifically forbade even aesthetic pleasure in the case of *orlah*. He grounds this in the verse *ve-araltem orlato et piryo, arelim lo ye'achel* (Vayikra 19), from which the *gemara* derives through the doubled language — *ve-araltem, orlato, arelim* — that not only eating but also dyeing and using *orlah* as fuel for a lamp are forbidden. The Torah actively extended the prohibition of *orlah* to cover *hana'ah ha-nir'eh la'einayim*, pleasure that is merely visible or aesthetic. This is not, Rava argues, evidence of a general principle that absorbed material remains physically present; it is a special *halacha* specific to *orlah*, established by its own *drasha*, and cannot be generalized to monetary cases or other contexts.

It is worth noting the conceptual layering here. There are in fact two distinct questions: first, whether aesthetic pleasure constitutes *hana'ah* at all (a separate discussion involving *avodah zarah*, where aesthetic pleasure from gazing at an idol is ruled only *derabbanan*); and second, whether the *orlah* remains present after dyeing such that wearing the garment continues to derive benefit from it. Rava's formulation — *hana'ah ha-nir'eh la'einayim assrah Torah* — appears to address both, locating the ruling in a specific Torahic extension to *orlah* rather than in any general rule about presence. The upshot: the *orlah* proof cannot be leveraged to answer the general *yesh* or *ein shevach samanim* question.

The *gemara* then raises a parallel case: *beged she-tziva'o b'klipei shevi'is yidalek* — a garment dyed with shells having *shemittah* status (after the time of *bi'ur*) must also be burned. Again this seems to suggest the dye remains present. The *gemara* answers with a verse: *ve-hayetah shabbat ha-aretz lachem le-ochlah* — *kodesh tihyeh lachem, tihyeh b'havyatah tehei* — it retains its status. This is again a specific *drasha* by *shemittah*, not a general principle. So both the *orlah* case and the *shemittah* case are deflected as exceptions grounded in specific verses, and the underlying question of *yesh* or *ein shevach samanim* remains unresolved by these proofs.

---

## Blood & Tumah

### Blood Contradiction

*Rava* now raises a direct contradiction. The *mishna* on *orlah* implies *chazuta milta hi* — appearance constitutes presence, and the *orlah* is still there. But consider: *revi'is dam she-nivle'ah ba-bayis, ha-bayis tamei* — a *revi'is* of blood (approximately three and a half ounces, the minimum quantity of a corpse's blood that generates *ohel* *tumah*) was absorbed into the floorboards of a house. One *tanna* says the house is *tamei*; another says *tahor*. This appears to be a contradiction about whether absorbed blood is still considered present.

### Blood Resolution

The *gemara* resolves these two positions: they do not actually conflict. *Ha b'keilim de-val mei'ikara* — vessels that were present in the house before the blood was absorbed are *tamei*, because at the moment of absorption, the blood was a real, present quantity of *tumah*, and those vessels were exposed to it. *Ha b'keilim de-atu l'vasof* — vessels brought into the house after the blood was absorbed do not become *tamei*, because at that point the blood is no longer considered physically present. The principle emerging from the *tumah* cases is that absorbed substances are generally not considered present in their new substrate — which would suggest *ein shevach samanim*, cutting against the *orlah* ruling.

### Extractable Test

A *baraita* then addresses blood absorbed into a garment: *im mitkabeset ha-ksut ve-yotzei mimenah revi'is dam, tamei hi* — if you could launder the garment and extract a *revi'is* of blood in the wash water, the garment is *tamei* (and the blood is considered present and capable of extending *tumah* to objects under the same roof). *V'im lav, tehorah* — if the blood is not extractable, the garment is *tahor* on that basis. The principle is one of extractability: if the absorbed substance can be drawn back out, it is still present; if it cannot, it is considered gone. This standard — extractable versus non-extractable — maps onto the dye question in an interesting way, since absorbed dye, like absorbed blood, generally cannot be extracted without destroying it or the substrate.

### Dam Tvuza

*Rav Kahana* offers a resolution to the apparent contradiction between the *orlah* ruling (implying presence) and the *tumah* ruling (implying absence): *mi-kulei revi'yot shanu kan, b'dikei dam tvuza de-rabbanan* — the leniency in the *tumah* case applies specifically to *dam tvuza*, the blood of a dying person. Because it is uncertain whether the full *revi'is* minimum was discharged after death (some may have flowed during life), the *tumah* of *dam tvuza* is only *derabbanan*. Where the *tumah* is only rabbinic, we are lenient and rule that absorbed blood is not considered present. But for ordinary post-mortem blood of a full *revi'is*, absorbed into floorboards, the blood would in fact remain present and continue to cause *tumah*. 

This means the two *amoraim* — the one who said *chazuta milta hi* (appearance constitutes presence, *orlah* is the rule) and the one who said the *orlah* case is the exception — are in a genuine dispute. On 101a the *gemara* had leaned toward *ein shevach samanim* with *orlah* as an exception grounded in a specific verse; now on 101b the argument runs the other way — *chazuta milta hi* is the default rule, and the *tumah* leniency is the exception, limited to *dam tvuza de-rabbanan*. The question of *yesh* or *ein shevach samanim* is left without a definitive resolution, and the conceptual parallel to other contexts — *ta'am k'ikar*, the principle that a flavor can constitute the substance itself — is noted as genuinely related, even if this *sugya* is not the place to pursue it.

---

## Shemittah Dyes

### Woad Safflower

Because the discussion has touched on *shemittah*, the *gemara* turns to a related *mishna* addressing which plants carry *kedushat shemittah*. *Mi-min ha-tzovim* — plants of the dyer's trade — *sefichei satin ve-kotza* — wild growths of woad (which produces a dye chemically identical to indigo) and safflower — *yesh lahem shevi'it u-demeihem shevi'it* — have *shemittah* sanctity, and money received in exchange for them also has that sanctity. Moreover, *yesh lahem bi'ur u-demei bi'ur* — they are subject to the obligation of *bi'ur*, destruction once the corresponding season has passed in the fields, and money received for them carries the same obligation.

The noteworthy feature of this ruling is that these plants are inedible. Unlike *shemittah* grain or fruit, which have sanctity because they are food, these dye plants cannot be eaten. Yet they carry full *kedushat shemittah*. This implies that inedible plants — wood, broadly speaking — have *kedushat shemittah*, which seems to create a problem.

### Grape Leaves

A *baraita* appears to contradict this: *alei kanim ve-alei gefanim* — leaves of reeds and grape leaves — *liktan le-achilah, yesh bahem mishum kedushat shevi'it* — if gathered for eating, they have *shemittah* sanctity; *le-etzim, ein bahem mishum kedushat shevi'it* — if gathered as firewood, they do not. The principle seems clear: non-food use of vegetation does not generate *shemittah* sanctity, which directly contradicts the ruling about dye plants.

### Lesorah Verse

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction through a verse: *ve-hayetah shabbat ha-aretz lachem le-ochlah* — the resting of the land shall be for you to eat. The word *le-ochlah* limits *shemittah* sanctity to things whose benefit is comparable to the experience of eating. This does not mean only literal food; it means any use whose benefit comes *in the manner* of eating.

### Benefit Timing

What characterizes eating as a mode of benefit? *Be-hana'ato u-vi'uro shavim* — the pleasure and the destruction occur simultaneously. When you eat food, you derive your benefit at the very moment the food is being consumed and destroyed. Firewood fails this test: *hana'atan achar bi'uran* — the primary benefit from firewood comes after the wood has been destroyed. When wood burns, the useful heat for cooking comes from the coals — from the part of the wood that has already been consumed — not from the wood that is presently burning. The benefit is displaced from the moment of destruction.

Dye plants, by contrast, pass the test. As the raw plant material is processed — boiled, immersed, broken down — the vegetation is being destroyed at the very moment the dye is being produced. The benefit (obtaining the dye) and the destruction (of the plant) are simultaneous. This is analogous to eating. Therefore, despite being inedible, dye plants have *kedushat shemittah*.

### Rashi Tosafot

*Rashi* and *Tosafot* differ on exactly when the benefit of dyeing occurs, and therefore on precisely how the simultaneity principle is satisfied. *Rashi* says: *be-sha'at retichat ha-yoreh, kalah ha-shoresh ve-koleit ha-tzeva* — at the moment the dyepot boils, the plant material is destroyed and the dye is produced. The benefit is having the dye; the destruction is the dissolution of the raw ingredient; these happen at the same time. The benefit of dye plants is therefore realized during the production of the dye itself, at the moment of processing.

*Tosafot* offers a different explanation: *hana'ato u-vi'uro shaveh* — the benefit and the destruction are simultaneous — *de-hana'ato k'she-lovshan* — because the benefit of the dye comes when one wears the garment. As the garment is worn, the dye is gradually being used up or worn away. Therefore, at the moment of wearing, both the benefit and the gradual destruction are occurring together. *Tosafot*'s position is that the benefit is not the production of the dye but the act of wearing the colored garment.

This last position strikes many as counterintuitive. In practice, dye tends to outlast the garment itself; it is difficult to say that wearing a garment constitutes the simultaneous destruction of the dye within it. *Rashi*'s understanding — that the benefit comes at the moment of processing — aligns more naturally with how dyes are actually produced. But the underlying logic in either case serves to distinguish dye plants from firewood and to bring them within the scope of *le-ochlah*, explaining why they carry *kedushat shemittah* despite being inedible.

# Bava Kamma 102

## Kedushat Shvi'is

### Dyes & Wood

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion, already underway at the bottom of 101b, concerning *kedushat shvi'is* — the sanctity of the sabbatical year's produce. The initial assumption might have been that *shmita* holiness attaches only to food. The question now before the *Gemara* is whether it extends further: does it apply to items used for dyeing, or even to wood itself?

### Benefit & Consumption

The *Gemara*'s conclusion rests on an interpretive principle derived from the verse's use of *le'achla* — "for eating." The verse teaches that *shmita* sanctity applies to things that are *hana'aso u'viuro shaveh*: things from which one derives benefit at the very moment of their consumption. Dyes qualify under this standard. *Rashi* understands the benefit as occurring when the dye is absorbed into the garment; *Tosafot* locates it in the gradual wearing of the dyed garment. Either way, dyes meet the criterion.

Ordinary firewood, by contrast, does not qualify. Even when a branch grows during *shmita*, the benefit from burning wood comes only *after* it has ignited and begun to turn to coal — that is, *hana'as achar biuro*, benefit after consumption. The flame one benefits from is the ember stage, not the moment of burning, and therefore normal wood is excluded from *kedushat shvi'is*.

### Oily Wood Debate

At this point the *Gemara* raises a challenge. The exclusion of wood seems too broad. The verse says *yatzu eitzim* — wood is excluded — *she-hana'as achar biuran*, because its benefit comes after it is consumed. But is that universally true of all wood? The *Gemara* asks: *ve-ika eitzei d'mash'chan di-hana'aso u-viuro shaveh* — is there not oily wood whose benefit and consumption are simultaneous?

*Rashi* understands this as a reference to a particular species of oily wood that burns slowly and is used for light rather than for cooking — the light being produced precisely as the wood burns. *Tosafot* reads the question differently: it is not about a species of wood at all, but about the *manner* of use. If one uses wood to produce immediate heat for a certain kind of cooking — where the benefit comes from the fire itself rather than from the embers — then the benefit and the consumption are indeed simultaneous. On *Tosafot*'s reading, the same piece of wood might or might not carry *kedushat shvi'is* depending on the intended use.

### Rava's Resolution

*Rava* resolves the difficulty with a single principle: *stam eitzim l'hasakah hein omdim* — the default use of wood is for fuel, meaning for the kind of fire from which one benefits at the ember stage. Since that is the presumed purpose of wood, we apply that presumption even where the particular use happens to differ.

This resolution reads more naturally according to *Tosafot* than according to *Rashi*. If the question were about a distinct species of oily wood, it would be strange to say the species is "presumed" to be used in the standard way. But if the question is about intended use, then *Rava*'s answer is precise: the default intention determines the *shmita* status. If the default is that wood is used for ember-producing fires — which is *hana'as achar biuro* — then even wood used in an atypical manner never acquired *kedushat shvi'is* to begin with. The *Gemara* thus leaves open the theoretical possibility that wood whose *stam* use is *hana'aso u'viuro shaveh* might carry *kedushat shvi'is*, but confirms that for ordinary firewood the presumption forecloses this.

---

## Le'Achla Expansion

### Wine & Soaking

Having established the basic framework, the *Gemara* now turns to the underlying *tannaic* debate that informs this entire discussion: *ve-eitzim l'hasakah tannai hi* — the question of whether firewood has *kedushat shvi'is* is itself the subject of a *tannaic* dispute. To understand that dispute, the *Gemara* cites a *braitah*:

One may not soak flax in *shmita* wine, nor use *shmita* wine for laundering. This is the position of the Rabbis. Rabbi Yosei, however, permits both. What drives this disagreement?

The Rabbis derive their position from the word *le'achla* — for eating. The verse's phrase *le'achla* excludes *mishrah* (soaking) and *khivusah* (laundering): *le'ochla velo lemishrah, le'ochla velo lekhivusah*. The reason is that soaking and laundering are *hana'atan achar biuran* — the wine, once absorbed into the flax or garment, only produces its effect after some time has passed. *Rashi* notes that the soaking may continue for several days. The consumption thus precedes the benefit, and therefore these uses fall outside the scope of *le'achla*.

Rabbi Yosei, by contrast, invokes the word *lakhem* — "for you" — which the verse also contains. He reads *lakhem* as *lekhol tsorkheikhem*: you may use *shmita* produce for all your needs, not only for eating. How do the Rabbis respond? They accept that *lakhem* broadens *le'achla*, but insist that the expansion must still be *dumya d'le'ochla* — analogous to eating — meaning that *hana'aso u'viuro shaveh* must still be satisfied. Soaking and laundering fail that test.

### Common Use Standard

At this point the *Gemara* introduces what proves to be a third and broader position — that of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yehuda accepts that *le'achla* alone is not the whole picture. But when the *Gemara* asks how Rabbi Yehuda can be so expansive given the word *le'achla*, his answer is that *le'achla* is needed for a different teaching found in a separate *braitah*: *le'ochla velo lemlugma* — one may not use *shmita* produce for a poultice or medicinal salve. That is what the word *le'achla* limits.

If *le'achla* is used to exclude poultices, how can it simultaneously exclude laundering? It cannot, Rabbi Yehuda would say, once *lakhem* has expanded the scope. The *braitah* then asks explicitly: why does the expansion through *lakhem* include laundering but exclude a poultice? The answer is *shaveh l'chol adam* — laundering is something that every person engages in, while a poultice is used only by those who are ill or have some special need. *Lakhem* expands *le'achla* to whatever is a universal, common human use. This principle will be recognized as parallel to the concept of *davar hashaveh lekhol nefesh* known from the laws of *Yom Tov*.

### Excluded Uses

A *braitah* then catalogs the items excluded even on Rabbi Yehuda's expanded view: *le'ochla velo lemlugma* — not for a poultice; not for heating in some special therapeutic sense; and not for sprinkling wine as a kind of air freshener (*ziluf*); and not for *apiktevizyon* — inducing vomiting, apparently as a form of purging. All of these are excluded because they are not *shaveh lekhol adam*: they serve only the sick, the finicky, or a narrow subset of people, and therefore do not qualify as the kind of common, universal use that *lakhem* was meant to authorize.

The *Gemara* then identifies this *braitah* — *le'ochla velo lemlugma* and its list of exclusions — as going like Rabbi Yosei (*k'Rabbi Yosei*), because if it were going like the Rabbis, it would also have excluded laundering and soaking. That it does not exclude those things shows it operates within Rabbi Yehuda's broader framework, where *shaveh l'chol adam* is the operative criterion.

### Firewood & Tannaim

This clarifies what the *Gemara* means when it frames the question of firewood as *tannai hi* — a *tannaic* dispute. The same verse — *le'achla* and *lakhem* — that governs what *shmita* produce *may be used for* also governs what *types of produce carry kedushat shvi'is* in the first place. As *Tosafot* explains, the two questions are two sides of the same coin.

According to the Rabbis, *shmita* sanctity attaches to anything that is *hana'aso u'viuro shaveh* — benefit simultaneous with consumption. This includes dyes but excludes ordinary firewood. According to Rabbi Yehuda, *shmita* sanctity attaches to anything that is *shaveh l'chol nefesh* — commonly used by all people. Since everyone uses firewood, firewood would carry *kedushat shvi'is* under Rabbi Yehuda's view. Whether firewood has *kedushat shvi'is* thus depends directly on this *tannaic* debate.

---

## Dye Mishna

### Wrong Dye Case

The *Gemara* now returns to the *Mishnah* in our daf. The case: a craftsman receives white wool to be dyed — but dyes it black; or receives black wool and dyes it red. He has applied the wrong dye, contrary to the owner's instructions. How is he liable?

### Shinuy Koneh

Rabbi Meir rules: *shinuy koneh*. The craftsman's unauthorized change in the object effects a transfer of ownership. The craftsman now owns the wool, and must pay the original owner the full value of the wool as it was before the dyeing.

### Yehuda's Position

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees. In his view, a *shinuy* of this kind — where the craftsman was not trying to steal but simply made a mistake — does not transfer ownership. The wool still belongs to its original owner. However, since the craftsman erred and did not produce what was requested, the owner has the upper hand in determining compensation. The craftsman is entitled to the lesser of two amounts: either his material expenses (not his labor), or the amount by which the value of the wool increased due to the dyeing, whichever is smaller.

---

## Rav Huna Ruling

### Huna's Position

Rav Yosef was sitting behind Rav Abba, in front of Rav Huna, at a *shiur* that Rav Huna was delivering. Rav Huna declared two rulings: *halacha k'Rebbi Yehoshua ben Korcha*, we rule like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha in the case we will explain shortly; and *halacha k'Rebbi Yehuda*, we rule like Rabbi Yehuda in the *Mishnah* before us.

### Yosef Challenges

Rav Yosef turned his face away, signaling his disagreement. He accepted the ruling regarding Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha — that case involves a *da'as yachid*, a minority opinion, and it is genuinely necessary for Rav Huna to tell us that we rule even against the majority in that instance. But the ruling like Rabbi Yehuda in our *Mishnah* seemed to Rav Yosef unnecessary, and he challenged it: why state the obvious?

### Yehoshua ben Korcha

The *Gemara* first explains the ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. The relevant *braitah* concerns the prohibition on doing business with idol-worshippers in the three days before their holidays — including the prohibition on collecting repayment of loans. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha draws a distinction: if the loan is documented (*milveh beshtar*), one need not collect it now, as the lender can always prove the debt in court later. But if the loan is only oral (*milveh al peh*) and there is no evidentiary record, then the lender may collect even in those three days, because this is *k'matzil miyadam* — saving one's money from a situation of potential loss. This position is a *da'as yachid*, yet we rule accordingly — hence Rav Huna's declaration is useful there.

---

## Stam vs. Machlokes

### Stam Rule

Rav Yosef's objection to the ruling *k'Rebbi Yehuda* is based on the principle of *machlokes v'achareiha stam halacha k'stam*: when a *Mishnah* contains a named dispute, and that dispute is followed by an anonymous (*stam*) *Mishnah* that resolves the matter without naming the parties, we rule in accordance with the anonymous *Mishnah*. In our case, the *machlokes* between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda appears here in Bava Kamma, and it is followed by a *stam* in Bava Metzia: *kol hamishaneh yado al hatachtona* — whoever deviates from his instructions is in the weaker position. This *stam* reflects Rabbi Yehuda's view. Therefore, the ruling *k'Rebbi Yehuda* is self-evident and required no declaration.

What is the *stam* in Bava Metzia? The *Mishnah* there teaches: *kol hamishaneh yado al hatachtona* — any craftsman or agent who deviates from instructions has the lower hand; *v'khol hachozer bo yado al hatachtona* — and whoever backs out of a contract has the lower hand. The first clause directly applies to our case and reflects Rabbi Yehuda's position. Hence, Rav Yosef argues, the *halacha* was already obvious.

### Order in Masechet

Rav Huna's defense is that one might have thought *ein seder la-Mishnah* — that there is no meaningful order to the *Mishnayos*, and one cannot infer that the *stam* in Bava Metzia was arranged *after* the dispute in Bava Kamma. If the order is not reliable, perhaps the *stam* is actually earlier and the dispute later — which would mean the later position is the dispute, not the anonymous ruling, and we would not apply the principle of *machlokes v'achareiha stam*.

Rav Yosef counters: if you genuinely believed there was no order at all, then the principle of *machlokes v'achareiha stam* could never be applied anywhere, because you could always claim the *stam* came first. The very existence of that rule implies that order is meaningful. The response must therefore be more nuanced.

### Nezikin Unity

Rav Huna refines his position. The principle of *ein seder la-Mishnah* applies only across separate *masechtos*. Within a single *masechet*, the arrangement by the editor — ultimately Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — is treated as deliberate and meaningful, and the principle of *machlokes v'achareiha stam* can be applied within that unit. However, across two different *masechtos*, one cannot assume a meaningful sequence.

Rav Yosef responds: *kula Nezikin chada masechta hi* — all of Nezikin is conceptually one *masechet*. The names Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia, and Bava Basra — "First Gate," "Middle Gate," and "Last Gate" — reflect only a practical division of a single thirty-chapter tractate, just as Masechet Keilim in *Taharos* is similarly divided. The three *Bavas* together form one organic whole, and therefore the ordering principle applies across them. The *stam* in Bava Metzia follows the *machlokes* in Bava Kamma within a single conceptual *masechet*, and *halacha k'stam*.

### Categorical Statements

An alternative justification is offered: even if one does not invoke the *stam* principle, the *Mishnah* in Bava Metzia is formulated as a categorical, universal statement — *kol hamishaneh... kol hachozer bo* — "whoever switches... whoever backs out." Categorical formulations of this type carry particular halachic weight and are treated as more than an ordinary *stam*. They represent accepted principles, not merely one opinion stated anonymously. Therefore, even apart from the question of sequence, the ruling like Rabbi Yehuda was already clear, and Rav Huna's declaration was superfluous.

---

## Wrong Grain Case

### Two Braitot

The *Gemara* now introduces a new case: *ha-nosein ma'os li-shelucho likach lo chitin ve-lakach mehem se'orim* — someone gives money to his agent to purchase wheat for him, and the agent instead purchases barley, or vice versa. The context here is not a personal purchase for household use but an investment transaction — the buyer intends to resell the grain. Two *braitot* are cited that appear to contradict one another.

### First Braitah

The first *braitah* rules: *im pichesu pichesu lo, ve-im hosiru hosiru lo* — if the grain decreased in value, the loss falls on the agent; if it increased in value, the gain belongs to the agent. On this view, the agent's deviation from instructions transfers full ownership to him. He must repay the principal to the one who sent him, but the grain — and all profit or loss from it — is entirely his. This mirrors the *shinuy koneh* principle: by violating his instructions, the agent acquires the purchase as his own.

### Second Braitah

The second *braitah* rules differently: *im pichesu pichesu lo, ve-im hosiru hosiru la-emtza* — if the grain lost value, the agent bears the loss alone; but if the grain gained value, the profit is split between them. This requires background to understand. The original arrangement, the *Gemara* implies, was a partnership of a common type: the sender contributed the capital, the agent contributed the effort, and both were to share profits and losses equally. When the agent violates his instructions, that arrangement is partially disturbed. He cannot make the *ba'al habayis* absorb his mistake, so any loss falls on the agent alone. But since it was ultimately the sender's money and the agent did execute a purchase on his behalf, the original profit-sharing agreement retains some force — any gain is still divided between them.

### Interest Loophole

This arrangement is striking and worth pausing over. The *Tosafot* themselves note that the second *braitah* could be exploited as a workaround for *ribbis* — the prohibition on charging interest. Consider: an investor gives a thousand dollars to an agent with impossibly strict instructions — say, to lend it out only if stored in an extraordinarily secure vault with gold-and-silver collateral. The investor and agent both understand the instructions will not be followed. The agent lends the money out, collects interest, and the investor then claims that since the agent violated the instructions, the result under the second *braitah* is that the investor's principal is guaranteed (any loss falls on the agent) while any profit is split with the investor. The investor thus enjoys a secured principal with participation in upside — effectively a loan with interest, structured through a nominally accidental *shinuy*. The second *braitah*'s ruling thus creates, at least in theory, a vehicle for circumventing the prohibition on interest.

---

## Yochanan Analysis

### Braitot Alignment

Rabbi Yochanan explains the apparent contradiction between the two *braitot* cleanly: *lo kashya — ha Rabbi Meir ve-ha Rabbi Yehuda*. The first *braitah* reflects Rabbi Meir; the second reflects Rabbi Yehuda.

### Meir: Violation

Rabbi Meir holds *shinuy koneh* — when an agent deviates from his instructions, the deviation effects a transfer of ownership. Here the *shinuy* is not a physical change in the object (as in the wool-dyeing case) but a violation of the *ba'al habayis*'s directions. Nevertheless, Rabbi Meir treats it as a *shinuy* sufficient to transfer ownership. The agent must repay the money, but the grain is his: all profit and all loss belong to him.

### Yehuda: No Transfer

Rabbi Yehuda holds that *shinuy eino koneh* — this kind of deviation does not transfer ownership. The grain remains, in some sense, the property of the *ba'al habayis*. Because the agent erred, he cannot impose any loss on the sender. But the grain's identity as the sender's property means the original profit-sharing arrangement persists for any gains.

---

## Personal vs. Trade

### Personal Use Question

The *Gemara* in *Eretz Yisrael* laughed at Rabbi Yochanan's explanation — noteworthy because Rabbi Yochanan himself was from *Eretz Yisrael*, and it is unusual for a scholar's home tradition to mock his own teaching. The challenge is directed specifically at his account of Rabbi Yehuda's position. According to Rabbi Yochanan, for Rabbi Yehuda, the agent's purchase of barley instead of wheat is a genuine *shinuy* — a real violation of the *ba'al habayis*'s will. And yet Rabbi Yehuda still maintains that the wheat or barley belongs to the *ba'al habayis*.

Rav Elazar formulates the objection more precisely: *dilma ad kan lo ka'amar Rabbi Meir ela be-midi de-chazi lei le-gufeh* — perhaps Rabbi Meir's principle of *shinuy koneh* applies only when the item in question is intended for personal use. In the wool case, the owner cared specifically whether the garment would be red or black; the particularity of the item mattered to him personally. In a commercial trade context — *l'schora* — where the sender simply wants product and cares only about profit, maybe Rabbi Meir would not apply *shinuy koneh* at all. If it is all just commodity, the deviation is not weighty enough to transfer ownership.

### Rav Elazar's Fix

If that is correct, then both *braitot* can be explained within Rabbi Meir's framework alone, and no appeal to a Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Meir dispute is necessary. *Ve-lo kashya — kan l'achila, kan l'schora*: the first *braitah* (full transfer) addresses a case where the agent was buying for personal use — the *ba'al habayis* wanted wheat for bread, specificity mattered, and a deviation is a genuine *shinuy* that transfers ownership to the agent. The second *braitah* (split profits) addresses a commercial trade context — the *ba'al habayis* saw it all as product and the deviation is not weighty enough to transfer ownership, so the sender retains ownership and shares in the gain, while the agent bears the loss for his error. Both cases go according to Rabbi Meir; the distinction is purely contextual.

---

## Agent Representation

### Acquisition Problem

At this point a deeper difficulty surfaces regarding the second *braitah* under Rabbi Yochanan's framework. Specifically, the *Gemara* in *Eretz Yisrael* challenges: *ve-chi mi hodi'a l'ba'al chitim she-yakneh chitim l'ba'al ma'ot* — who told the seller of the wheat that his wheat should be acquired by the one who sent the agent? In the second *braitah*, the *ba'al habayis* owns the grain — that is why he gets half the profit. But when the agent buys barley instead of wheat (or wheat instead of barley), he is acting against the explicit wishes of the sender. In what sense does the agent still represent the *ba'al habayis* at the moment of purchase? The seller sees only the agent in front of him and has no intention to transfer ownership to some third party. How then does the *ba'al habayis* come to own the grain?

*Rashi* sharpens the point: the difficulty is particularly acute for Rabbi Yochanan, who identifies this as a case of genuine *shinuy* — a real violation of the sender's will. Once the deviation rises to the level of a true *shinuy*, how can the agent still be viewed as operating in the sender's capacity? And if he is not, how does the wheat come to belong to the sender at all?

### Knowledge Required

Before an answer is offered, Rav Shmuel bar Sasrati raises a preliminary challenge: even when the agent does *exactly* what he was instructed to do, the seller does not know who the *ba'al habayis* is. The seller sees the agent and transacts with the agent. How does the *ba'al habayis* acquire the wheat even in the ordinary, compliant case?

### Zachin Principle

Rabbi Abbahu responds: the straightforward case poses no difficulty. *Shani chitin v'chitin di-shlichusei ka avid ve-chi ba'al habayis dami* — when the agent is performing his agency properly, he is simply an extension of the *ba'al habayis*; he is, as it were, the *ba'al habayis*'s hand. The seller need not know who the principal is. As long as the agent is acting within the scope of his authority, the transaction flows through him directly to the sender.

To demonstrate that an agent can effect acquisition for another party without the seller's explicit awareness, Rabbi Abbahu cites a *Mishnah*: when a person declares *hekdesh* — "all my property is consecrated" — his wife's clothing, his children's clothing, and sandals he has purchased for them are not included in the sanctification, even if not yet delivered. Similarly, if he paid a dyer to dye his wife's garment, that garment is excluded from *hekdesh*, even though the dyer had no idea he was dyeing the wife's garment specifically.

The dyer's ignorance of the intended recipient does not prevent the wife from acquiring the garment. The husband, in commissioning the dyeing, represents his wife by virtue of *zachin* — the principle that one may act to benefit another without that person's explicit appointment, since conferring a benefit on someone requires no formal authorization. The husband is acting as his wife's agent by operation of law. The seller or craftsman need not know. *V'chi yad isha dami* — the husband is like an extension of the wife's own hand. *Hacha nami shlichusei ka avid ve-chi yad ba'al habayis dami* — and so too with a compliant agent: he is an extension of the sender, and the wheat is acquired by the sender without the seller needing to know.

The difficulty, then, is specifically in the deviant case. When the agent's violation is so severe that Rabbi Meir would say *shinuy koneh* — when the agent is no longer acting within his mandate — how does the grain still come to the *ba'al habayis* under Rabbi Yehuda?

---

## Third Party Knowledge

### Abba Objects

Rabbi Abba challenges Rabbi Abbahu's proof. The *zachin* analogy — husband buying sandals for wife — does not demonstrate that the seller's knowledge is irrelevant in the way Rabbi Abbahu claims. Rabbi Abba proposes an alternative explanation of why the wife's clothing and the purchased sandals escape *hekdesh*: *kol hamakdish nechasav ein da'ato al ksus ishto uvanav* — when a person consecrates all his property, he simply does not have his wife's and children's clothing in mind. It is not that his wife owns those sandals through some mechanism of agency; it may be that he has not yet transferred them to her at all. The *hekdesh* does not capture those items merely because the husband did not intend to include them — not because they already belong to her. If that is the correct explanation, then no conclusion can be drawn about whether a seller's ignorance of the principal's identity affects acquisition.

### Tefillin Evidence

Rabbi Zeira challenges Rabbi Abba's proposed explanation. If *hekdesh* excludes the wife's items simply because the husband did not have them in mind, then subjective intention determines what is consecrated. But is that right? *Ve-chi da'ato shel adam al tefillav?* — does a person really intend to consecrate his *tefillin* when he says "all my property"? Presumably not. And yet we learn from a *Mishnah* that when a person consecrates all his property, the *tefillin* are included — the *beit din* assesses their value and requires the owner to redeem them so he may continue wearing them. The consecration of *tefillin* was presumably unintended, yet it stands. This shows that "all my property" is taken literally, regardless of subjective intent. If so, subjective intent cannot be what saves the wife's sandals from *hekdesh* — and therefore Rabbi Abba's explanation fails, and we are back to saying the wife must already own those sandals, which requires the *zachin* principle.

### Abaye Resists

Abaye resists this inference. He accepts that a person does have his *tefillin* in mind when consecrating all his property. The consecration of *tefillin* is intended: the person declaring *hekdesh* thinks, "I am performing a *mitzvah*, and my *tefillin* can go along with everything else." He does not exclude them because there is no social reason to do so. The wife's clothing, however, is different: *mishum eivah* — for fear of domestic conflict. No one wants their wife and children stripping their closets and donating their clothing to the Temple. Therefore, even when saying "all my property," a person specifically and deliberately excludes what belongs to or is destined for his wife and children. The distinction between *tefillin* and the wife's clothing is thus one of rational motivation: the former is consecrated with equanimity, the latter is excluded out of practical concern. Since the husband intends to exclude the wife's items, they need not have been transferred to her already. The *zachin* principle is not established by this case.

### Collateral Evidence

Rav Oshaya presses further with another variant of the *hekdesh* case. There are two scenarios in the *Mishnah*: one where the person himself consecrates his property (*makdish nechasav*), and one where he has incurred an *erech* obligation and the *beit din* seizes collateral (*memashkenin osan*). Rav Oshaya's point targets the second case. In the collateral-seizure scenario, the *beit din* acts against the debtor's will — this is not a voluntary act of dedication where the debtor's intentions matter. It is a compulsory legal proceeding. And yet even there, the wife's clothing and the sandals purchased for her escape seizure. This cannot be explained by the *mishum eivah* rationale — the *beit din* does not care about domestic tranquility. Therefore, the wife must already own those items, which requires the *zachin* principle, and Abaye's solution fails.

### Exception Doctrine

Rabbi Abba offers a final response. He concedes the point about involuntary seizure but reframes the entire category. The ruling that the wife's clothing and sandals escape both voluntary *hekdesh* and involuntary seizure is not a demonstration of a general principle of agency without the seller's knowledge. Rather, it reflects a specific rabbinic institution: *kol hamakdish nechasav na'aseh k'mi she-hikneh lahen ksus ishto uvanav me-ikara* — when a person is about to consecrate property (or, by extension, when *beit din* is about to seize collateral), it is treated *as if* he had already transferred his wife's and children's items to them before the consecration or seizure occurred. This is not a natural legal conclusion but a rabbinic enactment — *na'aseh k'mi*, treated as if — designed to preserve social stability. The *hekdesh* and *arachin* cases are therefore exceptional and cannot be used to prove any general principle about third-party acquisition without the seller's knowledge. As a general rule, the question of whether the seller must know he is transacting with an agent remains unanswered.

---

## Unresolved Issue

### Logical Problem

The *Gemara* has now established the difficulty clearly. According to Rabbi Yochanan, who reads the two *braitot* as a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, there is a genuine *shinuy* in the agent's conduct — he has violated the *ba'al habayis*'s explicit instructions. Yet Rabbi Yehuda maintains the grain belongs to the sender. The question stands: how does the *ba'al habayis* acquire ownership of grain purchased in violation of his instructions, if the agent is no longer acting as his representative and the seller has no intention of transferring the item to the sender?

### Seller Knowledge

The proposed resolution is practical rather than theoretical. If we assume that in such transactions the agent informs the seller that he is purchasing on behalf of a specific principal — "I am buying this for Mr. Jones" — then the seller is aware from the outset that the grain is intended for the *ba'al habayis*. The seller's intent is therefore to transfer the grain to the principal, not merely to the agent standing before him.

### Closure

If that is the case, then the agent's subsequent *shinuy* — his deviation from instructions — does not affect the seller's intent. The seller already directed the transaction toward the *ba'al habayis*. Whether the agent followed instructions or violated them is irrelevant to the question of whom the seller intended to sell to. The *ba'al habayis* acquires the grain because the seller intended him to have it, and that intention was formed at the moment of sale, independent of the agent's compliance or non-compliance with his mandate.

If, however, we assume the seller does not know who the principal is — that the agent transacts anonymously — then the *Gemara* remains unresolved. We understand why the compliant agent effects acquisition for the *ba'al habayis* (he is simply the sender's extension), but we do not understand how a deviant agent does so. The *Gemara* leaves this question open for now.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 103

## Shinui Koneh Review

### Opening

Today's learning is dedicated to the memory of all those who perished in the tragedy of September 11 and those who gave their lives to save others. We pick up on 102b, the second wide line, in the middle of a discussion arising from a *mishna* concerning an agent who was given money to purchase one commodity and instead purchased another — wheat instead of barley, or barley instead of wheat — and the question of what consequences follow from that deviation.

### Shinui Koneh Debate

The *gemara* sought to connect this case to the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir regarding *shinui koneh* — whether a transformation in an object effects an acquisition. The comparison is admittedly strange. The classic case of *shinui koneh* involves a physical object given to someone who changes it: wood given to make a chair, wool given to be dyed. In those cases there is a tangible raw material that the person can be said to acquire through the act of transformation. Here, however, what exactly is being acquired? Money is given for investment, and when the agent invests it contrary to instructions, what is the object of acquisition? The parallel is therefore of an unusual character, but the *gemara* treated it as a meaningful analogy nonetheless.

The logic runs as follows. If one holds *shinui koneh* — as Rabbi Meir does in the case of a craftsman — then by analogy, when an agent acts contrary to his *shlichus*, he is operating outside the scope of his agency and is, in some sense, taking personal possession of the money and what he purchases with it. If, on the other hand, one holds that *shinui* is not *koneh*, then the agent remains within the framework of the agency even when he deviates from the precise instructions, and the consequence of the deviation is not that he takes possession but simply that any resulting loss falls upon him rather than the principal.

### Money Investment

A further nuance was that even according to the opinion that *shinui* is normally *koneh*, this case of monetary investment may be different. The reason: the principal who gave the money to invest does not particularly care what it is invested in — he simply wants a profitable return. Since his real intention is to make money and not to specify the precise investment vehicle, acting outside the stated instructions does not necessarily remove the agent from the scope of his *shlichus* when the investment proves successful. The obligation shifts, however, when the deviation causes a loss: then it is the agent's loss, not the principal's.

### Heter Iska

This structure — in which the principal can only gain and cannot lose — prompted *Tosafos* to observe that such an arrangement closely resembles the mechanics of a *heter iska*, the permitted business arrangement constructed as a workaround for the prohibition of *ribbit*. The background: the *Torah*'s prohibition of lending at interest was rooted in an agricultural society where borrowing was associated with poverty and hardship, and charging interest on such loans was tantamount to exploitation. It is essentially a form of *tzedakah* that the *Torah* mandated. In a commercial context where money is borrowed for investment and profit, the prohibition remains technically in force — *ein dorshin ta'ama dikra* — but the *heter iska* provides a legal restructuring of the arrangement.

The basic mechanics of *heter iska* are as follows. Rather than a lender giving the borrower a thousand dollars at five percent interest, the parties reframe their relationship as a business partnership. The lender "invests" the thousand dollars in the borrower's business, becoming entitled in principle to all gains and losses. The parties then agree that the borrower will pay the investor a fixed fee — say, five percent — in exchange for the investor trusting the borrower's accounting without verification. The fixed payment is thus characterized not as interest on a loan but as a fee within a business arrangement.

*Tosafos* identifies a parallel mechanism arising directly from the *gemara*'s discussion. If one can structure a situation in which all losses fall on the agent and all gains are shared, the same functional result is achieved. *Tosafos* describes a scenario where the principal gives the agent instructions that are practically impossible to fulfill — requiring gold-vessel collateral, maximum-security storage, and so forth — so that the agent is always technically operating outside the instructions. This guarantees that any loss is the agent's, while any profit is shared, effectively recreating the interest relationship within a formally permissible framework.

---

## Field Purchase

### No Condition Case

We turn now to a new *baraita*. The *gemara* cites: *tanu rabbanan* — if someone buys a field in the name of his friend, you do not force him to sell it; but if he stipulated a condition, you do force him to sell. As stated, this is opaque. What precisely is the case, and what is being forced upon whom?

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet explains: the case is one who purchases a field from another person and writes the purchase document in the name of the *Reish Galuta*. The reason for doing so is practical protection against nuisance suits. Once a private individual acquires land, any number of people may come forward claiming prior rights to it and initiating litigation. By writing the document in the name of the *Reish Galuta* — the Exilarch, the head of the Jewish community under the Persian government — potential claimants would be deterred, since challenging a *Reish Galuta* document carried far greater risk and difficulty than challenging a document in a private person's name. The practice is acknowledged as a kind of legal fiction: the buyer was not genuinely acting as the *Reish Galuta*'s agent, and everyone understood this, yet the document served its deterrent function.

The ruling of the first clause is then: if I have purchased the field in the *Reish Galuta*'s name without any prior stipulation, I cannot force the *Reish Galuta* to transfer it to me. The implication is that the *Reish Galuta* has actually acquired it — *michlal demikna kanya lei* — since I bought it nominally on his behalf.

### Bnei Maarava

This leads to a challenge from the position of the *Bnei Maarava*, the Western Rabbis, who held: who informed the seller of the wheat that he was transferring ownership to the owner of the money? Their position, raised in the previous day's discussion, is that for a purchase made on another's behalf to take effect for that other person, the seller must be informed for whom the purchase is being made. If the seller was not so informed, the sale does not vest in the intended beneficiary.

Seemingly, if the *Bnei Maarava* are correct, then merely writing the *Reish Galuta*'s name in the document would not suffice to make him the owner, because the seller — the original owner of the field — was not told that the sale was for the *Reish Galuta*'s benefit.

The *gemara* resolves this: *im mishum ha lo kashya* — the challenge is no difficulty, because the case is one where the buyer did in fact inform the seller (*baal hasadeh*) that he was purchasing on behalf of the *Reish Galuta*. And he also informed the witnesses to that effect. The *gemara* acknowledges that one might have imagined the buyer told only the witnesses — so that the document would be written in the *Reish Galuta*'s name for protective purposes — without informing the seller himself. The answer is that the seller was informed, and therefore even according to the *Bnei Maarava* the acquisition takes effect.

### Abaye's Reading

The *gemara* then turns to the second clause: if I stipulated a condition, you force the *Reish Galuta* to transfer the field to me. The *gemara* objects: why would any court force the *Reish Galuta* to do anything? The *Reish Galuta* could simply say he wants no part of this transaction — neither the honor of having property written in his name nor the imposition of being pressed into executing a transfer document for a private individual's convenience.

Abaye therefore offers an altogether different reading of the *baraita*, one that eliminates the *Reish Galuta* from the central operative role (though Rav Ashi retains him). Abaye's reading: the case is simply one where I purchase a field and wish to have the document written not in my own name — perhaps for tax purposes, to avoid creditors, or for any other reason — but in the name of someone else: a spouse, a business associate, or indeed the *Reish Galuta*. I want two documents: the publicly-facing document in the other person's name, to deter challenges, and a real, operative document in my own name confirming my actual ownership.

The first clause — that you do not force the seller to write a second document — reflects the following situation: I purchased the field without having explicitly conditioned the sale on receiving a document in my name. In such a case the seller can reasonably say: I sold it, I wrote a document as you requested, and I have discharged my obligation. Why should I write you a second document in your own name?

### Stipulated Condition

The *gemara* asks: is that not obvious? Why would anyone think I could compel the seller to write a second document if I never asked for one as a condition?

The answer is that I could have argued: you knew, seller, that I was buying this for myself — *midea yadat d'ana l'nafshei shekilna* — and that the other document was purely protective in character — *panchaya b'alma*, a form of strengthening or securing the transaction. *Rashi* explains *panchaya* as a term for reinforcement or protection. You knew I wasn't going to flush my money buying a field for the *Reish Galuta* — I'm not his agent. You knew the real purchaser was me, and therefore it should be implicit that you owe me a document in my name.

The ruling teaches that the seller can reject this reasoning. He can say: I did not know your arrangement with the person in whose name I sold. Perhaps you had some deal with him. Perhaps there was a reason the property needed to go to him first. It was not my place to inquire. I wrote what you asked me to write; if you want a document in your name, that is your business with the person whose name is on the *shtar*. Therefore you cannot compel me to write a second document.

### Witness Notification

The *gemara* adds one further refinement. Even if I did not explicitly stipulate with the seller that he must write me a second document, I did make an announcement in the seller's presence — addressing the witnesses — saying: take note, I will be asking for another document in my name. The *gemara* asks: does this count as a valid stipulation with the seller?

The *chiddush* is that it does. The seller can still attempt to argue that when I said "I will want another document from him," the word "him" referred to the person in whose name I was buying — meaning I was announcing my intention to obtain a document from that third party, not from the seller. The ruling is that this defense fails: the explicit reason I made the announcement in the seller's presence was precisely so that he should understand it was directed at him. The phrase *l'hachi tarchi v'amri lehu l'kamach* — I took the trouble to say it in your presence for exactly this reason — establishes the stipulation, and the seller can be compelled to write the second document.

One might note, as the lecturer does, that the *gemara* works through all of these details without raising any explicit concern about the legal or ethical status of the fictitious documents themselves. The practice of writing property in another's name for protective purposes appears to have been a recognized convention, even if its precise legal grounding goes unexamined here.

---

## Rav Kahana Flax

### Flax Setup

The *gemara* now presents the case of Rav Kahana, which connects loosely to the preceding discussion through the question of agency and in whose name a transaction is conducted. Rav Kahana gave money to a flax merchant — prepaying for flax at the then-current price. The flax market subsequently rose significantly in value. The merchant sold the flax and came to Rav Kahana with proceeds reflecting the higher price. Rav Kahana then came before Rav with the question: may he accept the additional money, or does the transaction carry the appearance of *ribbit*? After all, he gave four and now he would receive eight.

### Agent Naming

Rav's answer turns on a crucial factual question: when the merchant sold the flax, did he announce that he was selling Rav Kahana's flax — that is, did he identify the principal explicitly? *Amar lei*: if when he sold it he declared *hai kitna deKahana hu* — this is Rav Kahana's flax — then go ahead and collect. It is clear that Rav Kahana owned the flax, the merchant was merely his agent in selling it, and the profit is the natural appreciation of Rav Kahana's own commodity. But if the merchant did not sell it in Rav Kahana's name, then the arrangement looks like a straight monetary transaction: Rav Kahana gave money, and now money comes back at a higher amount — the appearance of *ribbit*.

### Ownership Response

The *gemara* challenges this distinction. Why should it matter whether the flax was sold in Rav Kahana's name or not? Either way, the flax was Rav Kahana's property in the interim — *kitna mimila hu deyakar minefshia*, the flax appreciated on its own. If the merchant sold it in Rav Kahana's name, he was simply Rav Kahana's agent and the profit is legitimate. If the merchant sold it without identifying Rav Kahana, then he effectively stole Rav Kahana's flax and must pay its market value at the time of the theft — and *detnan*, as we have learned, *mikal gazlan meshalem kesha'at hagezeilah*, a thief pays according to the value at the time of the theft. Either as agent or as thief, Rav Kahana is entitled to the eight. So what is the *ribbit* concern?

### Rav's Principle

The *gemara* resolves this: the premise of the question was mistaken. Rav Kahana had not in fact taken physical possession of the flax — *velo mashcha Rav Kahana lekitna*. The transaction was an *amana* — a futures prepurchase — in which Rav Kahana paid the price now with delivery to come later. There was no *meshicha*, no act of taking possession, in the interim.

This is directly relevant to Rav's principle: *osin amana b'peiros v'ein osin amana b'damim* — one may make a futures prepurchase of produce, but not of money. In the permissible case: I pay four now and receive a bundle of flax later, even if by the time of delivery that bundle is worth eight. That is not *ribbit*, because the transaction is a sale of produce and I receive the produce. But if in the end no produce changes hands — if he simply hands me eight in money in place of the flax he owed me — then I gave four and received eight, with no intermediate ownership of any object. That looks like pure *ribbit* and is not permitted.

### Name Mechanism

Given that there was no *meshicha*, the question returns: how does the merchant's selling the flax "in Rav Kahana's name" remedy the *ribbit* problem? If Rav Kahana never took possession, how does the merchant's verbal identification of the flax as Rav Kahana's transform the transaction into something permissible?

The suggestion appears to be that the merchant's act of selling in Rav Kahana's name functions as if Rav Kahana himself had taken possession and then the merchant was simply his agent in making the sale. Whether this works within the framework of *davar shelo ba l'olam* and the precise parameters of what constitutes real versus apparent *ribbit* are large *sugyas* in their own right. The *gemara* also notes the relevance of *heter iska* as an alternative mechanism in such contexts, though its applicability to futures contracts specifically is not straightforward.

---

## Gezel Obligation

### Transition

Having worked through the variations on *shinui koneh* — from the craftsman who transforms an object, to the agent who invests money outside his instructions, to the document written in another's name — the *gemara* now pivots to an entirely different dimension of *gezeilah*: the specific *parsha* in *Vayikra* (perek 5) concerning one who takes possession of another's property, swears falsely that he does not have it, and then confesses. The *pesukim* are: *v'heshiv et hagezeilah asher gazal o et ha'oshek asher ashak o et hapikadon asher hufkad ito* — and he shall return the stolen item, or the withheld wages, or the deposit — *vachamishiso yosef alav* — and add a fifth — *v'ashamo yavi l'Hashem* — and bring his *asham* offering.

Notably, the phrase *v'heshiv et hagezeilah asher gazal* has been cited throughout this *perek* as the foundational source for the general obligation to return a stolen object, and from it the *gemara* derives a great deal, including the principle of *asher gazal k'ein shegazal* — return it as it was when stolen — which underlies much of the *shinui koneh* discussion. However, the context of this *pasuk* is specifically the case of a *shevuat sheker*, a false oath. The implication drawn here is that the heightened *obligation* the *pasuk* expresses — how far one must go to ensure the object reaches its owner — may apply specifically in the oath context, not to every case of *gezeilah*.

### Mishna Gezel

The *mishna* states: if one stole from another an item worth even a single *perutah* — *hagozel et chaveiro shaveh peruta* — and swore falsely about it — *venishba lo* — then: *yolichenu acharav leMadai* — one must follow the victim all the way to Madai (Media/Persia) to return it. The obligation to return the stolen item is so severe, in the context of a false oath, that no distance is too great.

### Maddai Obligation

The practical implication is striking: even if the item is worth a single *perutah* — a coin of minimal value, worth less than a cent in today's reckoning — and the aggrieved party has traveled to Persia, the thief is obligated to travel there personally and return it. Presumably, the travel expense may vastly exceed the value of what is being returned. The obligation is absolute; the economic disproportion is irrelevant.

### To Whom Give

The *mishna* continues: *lo yiten lo livno velo lishlucho* — one may not give it to the victim's son or to a messenger. *Aval noten leshaliach Beit Din* — but one may give it to a court-appointed messenger.

*Rashi* explains: the prohibition on giving to the victim's son or the victim's own messenger means not that doing so is technically prohibited, but rather that the obligation is not thereby discharged. If the money is lost in transit before reaching the victim's hands, the thief remains liable — *delo havei hashava ad demati leidei*, it is not considered a return until it arrives in the victim's possession. Handing money to the victim's messenger does not sever the thief's responsibility if something goes wrong.

This is initially counterintuitive: if the victim sent a messenger, has he not implicitly authorized receipt on his behalf? The *gemara* will address this. The exception — that giving to a *shaliach Beit Din* does discharge the obligation — is explained by *Rashi* as a rabbinic enactment, *takana*, made *mipnei takanat hashavim*, to facilitate repentance. Without such accommodation, the crushing obligation to pursue the victim to the ends of the earth would deter people from even attempting to make amends. By allowing the thief to deliver to the court's agent, the Rabbis created a practical off-ramp.

*Tosafos* takes issue with *Rashi*'s characterization, arguing that the *shaliach Beit Din* mechanism is distinct from the *takana* that will appear later in the *gemara*. According to *Tosafos*, the *shaliach Beit Din* arrangement means the money must still travel to the victim — the court's agent will convey it — but the thief is released from personal liability if the money is subsequently lost. The later *takana*, by contrast, allows the money to be deposited at the *Beit Din* for the victim to retrieve, without any further obligation to ensure delivery.

### Victim Dies

If the victim (*nigzal*) died before the money was returned, the obligation is to return it to his heirs. The *chiddush* here operates specifically in the realm of *kapparah*: one might have thought that since the obligation arose from an interpersonal wrong, returning the money to the heirs rather than to the person wronged would be insufficient to achieve atonement. The *mishna* rules otherwise — returning to the heirs satisfies the obligation, and the *korban* may then be brought.

### Principal Fifth

The *mishna* details several scenarios concerning the *keren* (principal) and the *chomesh* (the additional fifth, which in rabbinic arithmetic equals one-quarter of the principal, since adding a fifth to four yields five, making the added amount a fifth of the total). If the victim forgave the principal but not the *chomesh*, or forgave the *chomesh* but not the principal, these are treated differently. The rule is that the obligation to travel to extraordinary lengths — to *Maddai* — applies specifically to the *keren*, not to the *chomesh*. If what remains outstanding is only the *chomesh*, or only an amount less than a *perutah* of the principal, the thief need not pursue the victim to the ends of the earth, even though the monetary obligation remains.

If, however, even a *perutah*'s worth of the principal remains outstanding — *chutz mishaveh prutah bakeren* — then *tzarich lalechet acharav*, the thief must go after him. It is the nature and character of the remaining obligation, not its dollar amount, that determines the extent of the pursuit required.

### Fifth on Fifth

A further scenario: the thief returns the *keren* but swears falsely regarding the *chomesh*. Now the *chomesh* itself is the subject of a *shevuat sheker*. The *mishna* rules: *harei zeh mosif chomesh al chomesh* — one now adds a fifth upon the fifth. This process can in principle repeat itself, compounding: every false oath generates a new *chomesh* on whatever was falsely sworn, with the obligation continuing *ad sheyismaat hakeren mishaveh prutah* — until the outstanding principal falls below the value of a *perutah*. Each iteration of swearing falsely also requires a separate *asham* offering — a point the *gemara* finds remarkable, since even small amounts trigger the full apparatus of a major *korban*.

### Various Cases

The *mishna* concludes by extending the oath consequence beyond the case of straightforward *gezel*. Citing the *pesukim*: *o pikadon o tishumas yad o gazel o ashak et amito o matza aveidah v'kichash bah* — whether it was a deposit (*pikadon*), a loan (*tishumas yad*, which *Rashi* understands as a denied loan or item taken improperly), an outright theft, withheld wages, or a lost object that was found and denied — *venishba al shaker, harei zeh meshalem keren v'chomesh v'asham*. In all cases, swearing falsely about it triggers the same triad of obligations: return the principal, add the fifth, and bring the *asham*.

The broader principle emerging from this *mishna* is the following. As a baseline rule of *gezeilah*, the obligation is to return what was taken, but the normal rules of *dinin* do not require the thief to exhaust himself in pursuit of the victim. It is specifically in the case of a false oath — where the thief compounded his wrong by swearing falsely before God — that the *pesukim* impose a dramatically heightened standard of return.

---

## Mishna Attribution

### Oath Requirement

The *gemara* opens its analysis with a question arising directly from the *mishna*'s structure: the extraordinary obligation to pursue the victim to *Maddai* is stated in a context that presupposes a false oath — *nishba lo in*, it applies when he swore; *lo nishba lo lo*, it does not apply when he did not swear. This raises the question of which Tanna's opinion the *mishna* represents.

### Not R. Tarfon/Akiva

The *gemara* states that the *mishna* cannot straightforwardly represent either Rabbi Tarfon or Rabbi Akiva, as both appear in a *baraita* that does not distinguish between oath and non-oath cases.

### R. Tarfon v R. Akiva

The *baraita*: if someone stole from one of five people and does not know which one, and each of them claims to be the one who was robbed — *mani'ach gezeilah beineihem umistalek*, Rabbi Tarfon says: place the stolen amount among them and walk away. This satisfies the obligation. Rabbi Akiva says: *lo zu haderech motzi'ah miyedei aveira* — this path does not extricate one from sin. One must pay each person individually the full amount.

*Tosafos* raises a sharp question here. Generally, when one person says "you owe me" (*bari*) and another says "I don't know" (*shema*), the *bari* claim may prevail. Why then must the thief pay all five, rather than waiting for each to prove his individual claim? *Tosafos* answers: the normal rule that *bari adif* applies when there is no contradicting claim. Here, four out of five claimants are lying, and their contradictory claims cancel each other's credibility. Conversely, *Tosafos* notes, even the opinion that normally *shema* prevails over *bari* might concede that here the thief must pay all five — because the thief himself admits he owes someone the money; the uncertainty is only as to whom. These two scenarios are thus analytically distinct on both ends of the usual *bari v'shema* framework.

### Oath Limitation

The *gemara*'s initial attempt to reconcile the *mishna* with the positions of Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva is to propose that Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva are themselves debating only the case of a *shevuat sheker*. On this reading: Rabbi Tarfon holds that even after a false oath, placing the money among the five and walking away is sufficient. Rabbi Akiva holds that a false oath imposes a heightened obligation — one must ensure the money reaches the actual victim — and therefore pays each person individually and, in our *mishna*, pursues the victim to *Maddai*.

According to this reading, the *mishna* aligns with Rabbi Akiva when the condition of false oath is met, and Rabbi Akiva's position is specifically conditioned on the oath: without it, perhaps even Rabbi Akiva would not require such extraordinary measures.

The underlying *pasuk* cited in support: *l'asher hu lo yitnenu b'yom ashmato* — "he shall give it to the one to whom it belongs on the day of his guilt." The word *ashmato* — his guilt — emphasizes that it is specifically in the context of realized guilt, of *shevuat sheker*, that the obligation to ensure the money reaches its rightful owner is at its most absolute.

### R. Elazar Takana

But what of Rabbi Tarfon, who holds that even after a false oath one need only leave the money among the five claimants? The *gemara* explains this through the lens of a *takana* cited by Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Tzadok: *takana gedola hitkinu* — a major enactment was enacted — *she'im hayta hotza'ah yeteirah al hakeren* — if the expenses of retrieval exceed the principal — *meshalem keren v'chomesh l'Beit Din* — the thief pays the principal and the *chomesh* to the court — *umeivi ashamo umitkaper lo* — brings his *asham* and achieves atonement.

*Rashi* holds that this is the same *takana* as the *mishna*'s provision for a *shaliach Beit Din*. *Tosafos* disagrees, distinguishing them: the *shaliach Beit Din* arrangement requires that the money still reach the victim — it merely releases the thief from liability if the money is lost in transit — whereas Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Tzadok's *takana* leaves the money at the *Beit Din* for the victim to collect, with no further obligation of conveyance.

On this reading, Rabbi Tarfon effectively incorporates this *takana*. Even in principle, one should not have to spend more than the amount stolen in order to return what was stolen. Therefore, when the cost of ensuring return to any specific individual would exceed the principal — as in the case of five potential victims, where paying all five would cost four times the original theft — one deposits the money with the *Beit Din* and discharges the obligation.

### R. Akiva Rejects

Rabbi Akiva rejects the application of this *takana* to the five-person case, and his reasoning is pointed. Rabbi Akiva might in principle accept a *takana* when it is known who the victim is — *heicha deyada l'man gazlei*. In such cases, depositing the money with the *Beit Din* still results in the money ultimately reaching the victim, *d'kamahadar mamona l'mareih* — the money finds its way back to the owner. But when one stole from an unknown member of a group of five and gives the money to the *Beit Din*, there is no mechanism guaranteeing the actual victim will ever receive it — *d'lo ahadurei mamona l'mareih*, the money may never be returned to its true owner. Rabbi Akiva holds that no rabbinic *takana* would be enacted in circumstances where the victim is not certain to receive restitution. Therefore, the full obligation stands: pay each person individually.

### R. Shimon Clarifies

At this point Rav Huna bar Yehuda raises an objection from a further *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva did not disagree in the case of an honest *purchaser* who bought from one of five merchants and cannot recall which. In that case — *shelakach echad mechamesh bnei adam veein yodea mimi lakach* — all agree: place the payment among them and walk away. The debate applies specifically to *gezel* — *shegazal echad michamesh bnei adam veein yodea mimi gazal*. Rabbi Tarfon says place the stolen amount and walk away; Rabbi Akiva says there is no remedy but to pay each one.

### Rava Challenge

This *baraita* of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar presents a challenge to the preceding analysis. If the debate between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva is limited to cases of false oath, why would Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguish between an honest purchase and *gezel*? If the critical variable is the oath and not the initial wrong, then once a person swears falsely about either transaction — the honest purchase gone bad or the outright theft — the same heightened obligations should apply, and there should be no reason to distinguish based on how the obligation originally arose. The challenge is then: *mah li lakach mah li gazal* — if it is the false oath that matters, what difference does it make whether the underlying wrong was a legitimate purchase or a theft?

Furthermore, Rava raises a story: *maaseh bechasid echad* — there was an incident involving a *chasid* who had purchased from one of two people and did not know which. He came before Rabbi Tarfon, who ruled: place the money among them and walk away. He then came before Rabbi Akiva, who ruled: you have no remedy but to pay each one. This *chasid* story, cited to illustrate the debate, involves an honest purchase — not a theft at all — directly contradicting Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's claim that the debate does not apply to purchases.

### Chasid Objection

This generates a further problem for the oath-based reading. If the debate between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva applies only when a false oath was taken, then a *chasid* — a person of established righteousness — should never be the protagonist of such a case. *Chasid mi mishtaba beshikra?* Would a righteous person swear falsely?

One might respond: perhaps he swore falsely and subsequently became a *chasid* — it is, after all, precisely the kind of story that fits the spirit of *teshuvah*. However, the *gemara* objects: whenever the phrase *maaseh bechasid echad* appears in the tradition, it invariably refers to either Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava or Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai — *chasidim meikara havu*, people who were righteous from the outset of their careers, not individuals who began with a false oath and later repented.

### Conclusion

The conclusion that emerges is that the debate of Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva cannot be confined to the case of a false oath. They disagree even in the absence of a *shevuat sheker* — and the *chasid* story makes this plain. This, however, now reintroduces the original problem: if Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva debate even without an oath, how does our *mishna* — which limits the extraordinary obligation to the oath context — align with either of them? The *gemara* leaves this question open for the following day's discussion. Having established that the Tannaic debate operates independently of the oath, the task for tomorrow is to identify which opinion the *mishna* reflects and how the oath condition of the *mishna* can be reconciled with the broader scope of the Tannaic disagreement.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 104

## Mishnah Attribution

### Theft & Madai

The *gemara* on 103b had been discussing to what extent the *mishnah* could be attributed to either Rabbi Akiva or Rabbi Tarfon. The *mishnah* states that if one steals from another even a minimal value — *shaveh prutah* — and swore falsely about it, the *gazlan* must pay it back even if he must travel as far as Madai: *yolichenu acharav l'Madai*. Madai, presumably somewhere in Persia, represents an extraordinarily distant journey, and the *mishnah*'s point is that the obligation to return stolen property knows no geographical limit.

### Five People Case

The *gemara* had previously attempted to connect this *mishnah* to the well-known dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon concerning a person who stole from one of five people but did not know which of them was the victim. In that case, Rabbi Tarfon holds that the thief may simply leave the payment with the group and discharge his obligation, while Rabbi Akiva holds that he must actively attempt to repay each of the five. The *gemara* had suggested that our *mishnah* might align with Rabbi Akiva's more stringent position — but that line of reasoning was rejected.

### Tarfon & Oath

Resuming the discussion, the *gemara* now proposes: *ella l'olam Rabbi Tarfon hi* — the *mishnah* should actually be read in accordance with Rabbi Tarfon's view. The proposal is that Rabbi Tarfon would concede a higher level of liability specifically in a case where the thief swore falsely about what he stole. Ordinarily, Rabbi Tarfon would permit the thief to leave a reasonable approximation of the payment and consider the obligation discharged; but having compounded his wrongdoing with a false oath, even Rabbi Tarfon would agree that a heightened standard of personal restitution applies.

### Korban Asham

The *gemara* grounds this reasoning in a *pasuk*: *l'asher hu lo yitnenu b'yom ashmato* — whatever belongs to its rightful owner must be given to him on the day of his guilt. The verse ties the *korban asham*, the guilt offering brought for theft, to the obligation of personal delivery. Whenever a *korban asham* is implicated — that is, when the theft rises to the level of requiring such an offering — the thief bears a correspondingly elevated responsibility not merely to deposit the payment somewhere accessible, but to place it directly in the hands of the person to whom it is owed.

### Akiva's Position

The *gemara* then clarifies the difference between the two Tannaim. Rabbi Akiva — *d'af al gav d'lo ishtava kanis* — holds that this elevated level of obligation applies even without a false oath. Rabbi Tarfon, by contrast, concedes to Rabbi Akiva's position only when a false oath has been sworn; his leniency is reserved for the case where no oath was taken. The *gemara* therefore asks: since Rabbi Tarfon in any event must concede a higher liability when an oath is involved, and Rabbi Akiva extends this even without an oath, why does the *mishnah* need to specify the oath at all? What is the *mishnah* teaching us that was not already clear?

### Admission Case

The *gemara* presses further: *mai irya nishba* — why does it matter whether he swore? Rabbi Akiva's position already mandates the higher standard regardless. A *braita* is then cited: *modeh Rabbi Tarfon b'omer l'shnayim gazalti echad mikem* — Rabbi Tarfon agrees with Rabbi Akiva in a case where the thief said to two people, "I stole a *maneh* from one of you, but I do not know which of you," and therefore must pay both. Crucially, there was no oath in this case. Why does Rabbi Tarfon agree? *Shekvar hoda mipi atzmo* — because he already admitted it of his own accord. Admission, the *braita* teaches, is also a trigger for the higher level of liability, entirely independent of a false oath. Once a person voluntarily confesses, he has so entrenched himself in his liability that a lenient discharge of his obligation is no longer available.

---

## Rava's Shomer

### Rava Rejects

*Ella amar Rava* — the *gemara* now introduces a fundamentally different approach. *Tosafot* notes that there is a textual question about whether the word *ella* appears in the *gemara*; Rashi's reading includes it, making this an outright rejection of the Rabbi Tarfon framework. Rava argues: *shani matnitin* — the *mishnah* is categorically different from the case used for comparison. Stop attempting to read the *mishnah* through the lens of the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon. Those cases involve a thief who does not know whom he stole from; our *mishnah* involves a thief who knows exactly who his victim is, and whose only difficulty is the victim's geographic distance. These are fundamentally different situations and cannot be equated.

### Knows Victim

According to Rava's reading, the *mishnah* presents a scenario in which the *gazlan* knows precisely who he stole from.
