The question is not about resolving ambiguity between potential victims; it is about the *gazlan*'s obligation when the victim is identified but geographically inaccessible. This distinction, Rava insists, changes the entire legal analysis.

### Gazlan to Shomer

Once the thief knows who he stole from and admits it, Rava argues, something remarkable occurs: *keivan deyada leman gazlei ve'odei lei, keivan de'efshar le'ahadoora mamona lemarei, hava lei keman de'amar lei yehei li beyadecha* — because he knows who was wronged and it is possible to return the money to its rightful owner, the *nigzal* is treated as though he had said to the thief, "Hold it in your possession for me." The thief's legal status undergoes a transformation. He is no longer a *gazlan* in the full sense — a person actively resisting restitution — but has been reclassified, as it were, as a *shomer pikadon*, a watchman of a deposit. He holds the money in trust until the owner comes to claim it. This is admittedly a striking legal fiction: the thief becomes a *shomer* without any actual communication from the victim, simply by virtue of his admission and the identifiability of the victim. The Gemara acknowledges the automatic nature of this status change — *keman de'amar lei*, "as though he said" — and it is genuinely unusual that a *shomer* relationship arises without an explicit request from the depositor.

### Shomer Oath

Given this transformation in status, the significance of the false oath becomes clear. *Hilkach nishba* — if the thief, now functioning as a *shomer*, takes a false oath, he has violated the terms of his *shmirah*. *Keivan deba'ei kapara lo sagi ad demati liyadei* — since he requires atonement for this violation, that atonement cannot be achieved until the money actually reaches the hands of its rightful owner. This is why the *mishnah* obligates him to travel even to Madai: the *kapara* is incomplete until personal delivery is effected.

### No Oath Shomer

If, however, the thief took no oath at all, his status as a *shomer* is undisturbed. *Hava gabei pikadon ad de'atei veshakil lei* — the money simply sits with him as a *pikadon* until the owner comes and retrieves it. He has no obligation to pursue the victim; it is the victim who must come and claim what is his. This cleanly accounts for the *mishnah*'s structure: the oath is the dividing line between the obligation to travel to Madai and the mere passive status of a *shomer* waiting for the owner to appear. And because Rava's reading makes the *mishnah* comprehensible without reference to the Akiva–Tarfon dispute, the *mishnah* according to this approach is *lidvrei hakol* — agreed upon by all opinions.

---

## Shaliach & Witnesses

### Shaliach Issue

The *mishnah* had stated *lo yitein lo livno velo lishlucho* — the thief may not give the payment to his own son or his own *shaliach*, and by extension not to the son or *shaliach* of the *nigzal* either. This raises the question of what happens when the *nigzal* appoints a *shaliach* with witnesses — *shaliach she'asao be'eidim*. Normally, appointing a *shaliach* requires no formalities whatsoever; one simply asks another person to act on one's behalf. But does the presence of witnesses at the appointment confer a special legal status on the *shaliach* — enough to make the transfer of funds to him count as payment?

### Rav Chisda

Rav Chisda holds: *havi shaliach* — a *shaliach* appointed with witnesses does count as a proper *shaliach*. His reasoning is straightforward: *le'hachi tarchi ve'ukmei be'eidim deliku bivrushay* — the whole point of going to the trouble of bringing witnesses was so that the *shaliach* should stand in the place of the appointing party. If the thief pays this formally-appointed *shaliach*, the payment is complete, and any subsequent loss is the *nigzal*'s responsibility.

### Rabba's Position

Rabba disagrees: *lo havi shaliach* — even a *shaliach* made with witnesses does not count as a proper *shaliach* for purposes of this *mishnah*. In Rabba's reading, the presence of witnesses at the appointment does not transform the *shaliach* into a legal representative capable of receiving payment on the *nigzal*'s behalf. The witnesses serve only to signal that the appointer regards this person as trustworthy: *inish mehaymna hu* — he is a reliable fellow. But trustworthiness is not the same as legal agency. The *mishnah*'s prohibition on using a *shaliach* remains fully in force, and the obligation is discharged only when the money reaches the *nigzal* himself.

### Bava Metzia Proof

The *gemara* brings a proof from a *mishnah* in Bava Metzia. The *mishnah* there teaches: *ha'shoel et hapara ve'shilcha beyad bno beyad avdo beyad shlucho* — if one borrows a cow and sends it back via his son, his slave, or his *shaliach*, or via the son, slave, or *shaliach* of the borrower, and the cow dies in transit, the borrower is exempt. Normally, a *shoel* bears an extremely high level of liability; yet here, even though the cow was sent with someone acting as his *shaliach*, the borrower is not liable.

The *gemara* then asks: what does "his *shaliach*" mean in this context? If the *shaliach* was not appointed with witnesses, how could we even know he was the *shaliach*? — *mena yadinan*. It must therefore refer to a *shaliach* appointed with witnesses, and yet the *mishnah* rules the borrower exempt. This is a strong proof for Rabba: even with witnesses, the *shaliach* does not effect the legal transfer. *Kashya le'Rav Chisda* — this presents a genuine difficulty for Rav Chisda's position.

### Chisda's Reading

Rav Chisda responds by reinterpreting the *mishnah* in Bava Metzia: *bischiro uvelikito* — the word *shaliach* in that *mishnah* does not refer to a formally-appointed legal representative at all. It refers either to a *sachir*, a hired laborer who simply went and did this task as part of his employment, or to a *lakito*, a sharecropper or tenant who performed the errand informally. Rashi notes that his teachers offered one interpretation of *lakito* while he himself offers another, which gives us an interesting glimpse into Rashi's methodology and the interplay between his own analysis and the tradition he received from his teachers in Germany — a question of broader significance regarding how much of Rashi's commentary represents his own innovative contribution versus the received tradition of the early Ashkenazic authorities.

The same reading is then applied to our *mishnah*: when our *mishnah* prohibits giving the payment to a *shaliach*, it too means only an informal, quasi-representative — *bischira u'likita* — not a properly and formally appointed *shaliach*. A true *shaliach* appointed with witnesses, according to Rav Chisda, would work. So the *gemara* then asks: why does our *mishnah* specifically mention the *shaliach beit din* as the valid exception, without mentioning a formally-appointed *shaliach* with witnesses? If both count equally, the *mishnah* should have stated the case of the private *shaliach* with witnesses explicitly.

### Who Appoints

The *gemara* answers on Rav Chisda's behalf: the *shaliach beit din* is mentioned in the *mishnah* because of its unique generality. *Lo shena asao nigzal lo shena asao gazlan* — whether the *shaliach beit din* was requested by the *nigzal* or by the *gazlan*, it works in either case, because the *beit din*'s appointment renders the *shaliach* an impartial agent. A privately-appointed *shaliach* with witnesses, by contrast, is only effective when it was the *nigzal* who made the appointment — *hu dehavai shaliach* — because in that case the *nigzal* has voluntarily chosen to extend his trust and bear the attendant risk. This is precisely the point raised by one of the students: why would the *nigzal* ever agree to such an arrangement? The answer is that if he does so willingly, he has effectively transferred the risk to himself. But if the *gazlan* unilaterally appointed the *shaliach* with witnesses, *lo havi shaliach* — the *shaliach* does not acquire effective legal status, because the *nigzal* never agreed to modify the terms of the obligation.

The *gemara* also notes that the *mishnah*'s formulation was designed to exclude the position of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that even for a *shaliach beit din* the distinction between whether the *nigzal* or the *gazlan* made the appointment matters. Our *mishnah*, by endorsing the *shaliach beit din* without qualification, rejects Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view. On balance, Rav Chisda's reading of the *mishnah* requires considerable interpretive effort and produces a somewhat convoluted account of the *mishnah*'s language; Rabba's straightforward reading fits the *mishnayot* more naturally.

---

## Yochanan & Elazar

### Agree: Valid

The *gemara* now introduces a parallel Eretz Yisrael tradition: *Rabbi Yochanan v'Rabbi Elazar d'amrei tarvaihu shliach she'asao be'eidim havi shliach* — both Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar agree that a *shliach* appointed with witnesses counts as a valid *shliach* in this context. Their position aligns with that of Rav Chisda rather than Rabba. It is worth noting the geographic pattern: two Babylonian Amoraim — Rav Chisda and Rabba — dispute the question, while two Eretz Yisrael Amoraim both concur on the more permissive view.

### Casual vs Official

How then do Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar explain our *mishnah*, which seemingly prohibits using a *shliach*? Their answer: *be'mamtsi lo shliach* — the *mishnah* refers to a situation of casual, impromptu appointment. The *nigzal* did not formally designate an agent; rather, someone happened to be passing through and was told informally, *ait lei zuzei gabi ploni* — "I have money owed to me by so-and-so; perhaps if you stop by, you can check whether he'll send it with you." That is not an official appointment; it is a casual suggestion. For such an informal arrangement, no legal transfer of responsibility occurs, and the *gazlan* remains liable until the money reaches the *nigzal* directly. A true formal appointment with witnesses, however, is another matter entirely. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar thus read the *mishnah*'s prohibition as restricted to the casual case, leaving intact their ruling that a properly witnessed appointment constitutes valid *shlichut*. Like Rav Chisda, they must therefore also read the *mishnah*'s reference to *shliach* as equivalent to Rav Chisda's *bischiro u'v'likito* — an informal representative rather than a legal *shliach*.

---

## Money via Shaliach

### Shmuel: No Dyuqani

*Amar Rabbi Yehuda amar Shmuel: ein meshalchin ma'ot b'dyuqani* — Shmuel rules that money cannot be sent by means of a *dyuqani*. Rashi explains the term: the owner of a *pikadon* provides a *shliach* with a letter bearing his signature — *chotamo b'igeret* — and instructs him to present it to the designated party and collect the funds. The idea is that the signed authorization serves as proof that the bearer was indeed sent by the rightful owner. Nonetheless, Shmuel rules this is insufficient. *V'afilu eidim chatumim aleha* — even if witnesses have signed the *dyuqani*, it still does not work. The threshold of proof required to transfer liability — to establish that this *shliach* was genuinely dispatched by the owner — is not met by a signed document alone, even a witnessed one.

### Yochanan: Valid

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *im eidim chotmim aleha meshalchin* — if witnesses have signed the authorization, the money may indeed be sent. In Rabbi Yochanan's view, a witnessed document functions like a *shtar*, a formal legal instrument authorizing the *shliach*, and is sufficient to constitute proper *shlichut*. This is consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's broader position that a *shliach* appointed with witnesses acquires genuine legal standing.

### Rabbi Abba Story

The *gemara* then asks: according to Shmuel, what practical mechanism can a debtor use to repay a distant creditor? The answer is provided through a narrative. Rabbi Abba had money owed to him by Rav Yosef bar Chama. He asked Rav Safra, who was traveling to that locale, to collect it on his behalf. When Rav Safra arrived, Rava bar Rav Yosef — the son of Rav Yosef bar Chama — challenged him: *mi katav lach hitkabalti* — did Rabbi Abba write you a document of *hitkabalti*, an acknowledgment stating that receipt of the money by the *shliach* constitutes receipt by the creditor himself? Rav Safra said no. Rava bar Rav Yosef therefore refused to pay, instructing him: *ei hachi, zil bereisha veyichtov lach hitkabalti* — go back first and obtain this *hitkabalti*, and only then will I release the funds. The logic is clear: without such an authorization, handing the money to the *shliach* does not discharge the debt; if the money is then lost or stolen in transit, the debtor remains liable.

### Death Problem

When Rav Safra returned with the *hitkabalti*, Rava bar Rav Yosef confronted him with a second, more penetrating objection: *ei katav lach nami hitkabalti, lav klum hu* — even now that you have the *hitkabalti*, it is still worthless. Why? *D'dilma ad'aitit shakiv Rabbi Abba* — perhaps by the time you return, Rabbi Abba will have died. Since Rabbi Abba was apparently quite elderly at the time, this was a realistic concern. And the *hitkabalti* was issued only in Rabbi Abba's name; it cannot operate as an acknowledgment of receipt for his heirs. If Rabbi Abba dies before the money reaches him, the *yorshim* will have a fresh claim against the debtor, and the *hitkabalti* — which speaks only to Rabbi Abba's receipt — will be legally ineffective against them.

One might ask: ordinarily we do not assume that a person will die in the interim — we send *korbanot*, appoint *shelichim* for *kiddushin* and *gittin*, and transact all manner of legal business across distances without worrying about the other party's death. The *gemara* here seems to treat the risk of Rabbi Abba's death as a genuine concern, perhaps because of his advanced age — which suggests that the general rule operates only where there is no specific indication of particular vulnerability.

### Kinyan Agav

*Amar lei: v'ella mai takanta? Zil nakninhu lach agav arra* — go and effect a *kinyan agav*. The mechanism of *kinyan agav* — acquisition carried on the back of land — allows movable property and money to be transferred together with a land transaction. The debtor could sell Rabbi Abba a tiny parcel of land — even as small as a single *amah* — and include the debt payment as property acquired *agav*, on the back of that land transaction. The transfer of title to both the land and the money would then occur immediately and simultaneously, without the need for a *shliach* to physically transport the funds. Once the *kinyan* is effected, the money belongs to Rabbi Abba — or, crucially, to his estate — regardless of what subsequently happens to anyone involved. This device cuts out the entire problem of the *shliach*: there is no intermediary who might die or lose the money; the transfer is legally instantaneous.

### Rav Papa Example

The practical utility of this solution is illustrated by a story involving Rav Papa. Rav Papa had 13,000 *zuz* owed to him in Bei Chozai — a distant location. He arranged the transfer by way of *kinyan agav*, acquiring the funds through Rav Shmuel bar Abba *agav* — on the back of — even as small a property as *asifa d'beiteih*, the threshold of his house. When the *shliach* finally arrived, Rav Papa went out to greet him as far as the town of Tavach — a sign not merely of personal warmth, but of profound relief and satisfaction that the halakhic puzzle had been solved. The point was not the 13,000 *zuz* per se, but the elegant legal solution that had been devised to navigate all the complications of transferring money through an intermediary.

---

## Chomesh Status

### Mishnah Evidence

The *mishnah* had stated that even after the *gazlan* has paid back the principal — *natan lo et ha-keren* — he remains obligated to pay the *chomesh*, the twenty-five percent additional payment, and must travel even to Madai to do so. The *gemara* draws an inference from this formulation.

### Chomesh Mammon

*Alma chomesh mamona hu* — it is evident from the *mishnah* that *chomesh* is treated as *mamon*, a straightforward monetary obligation, and not as a *kenas*, a punitive fine. This matters significantly for several reasons. First, a *kenas* cannot be collected from the thief's heirs; it is a personal penalty that dies with the person. But our *mishnah* implies that even if the thief dies, the heirs must still pay the *chomesh*, suggesting it is a transferable monetary debt rather than a personal fine. Second, the *gemara* cites a further *mishnah*: *natan et ha-keren v'nishba al ha-chomesh, harei mosif chomesh al ha-chomesh* — if the thief paid the principal and then swore falsely about the *chomesh*, he now owes an additional *chomesh* on the *chomesh* — that is, twenty-five percent of twenty-five percent, amounting to one-sixteenth. *Alma chumsha mamona hu* — only if the *chomesh* is itself a monetary obligation does it make sense for it to compound in this way. A *kenas* does not behave like a monetary debt capable of generating further liability through a false oath. The *chomesh* thus occupies an interesting intermediate space: the Torah has imposed what might technically be characterized as a penalty, yet the halachic system treats it with the full apparatus of ordinary monetary liability — including transmissibility to heirs and the capacity to generate compounded obligations. This parallels the analogous questions raised earlier in Bava Kamma about *chatzi nezek*, where similar tensions between the character of an obligation as *mamon* or *kenas* required careful analysis.

### Heirs Braita

A *braita* confirms and sharpens the point: *hagozel et chaveiro v'nishba lo v'meit, yorshin meshalmin keren v'chomesh u'feturim min ha-asham* — one who steals from another, swears falsely about it, and then dies: his heirs must pay both the principal and the *chomesh*, but they are exempt from bringing the *korban asham*. The exemption from the *korban asham* is obvious — the *korban* is the personal atonement of the wrongdoer and cannot be transferred to his descendants. But the obligation to pay both *keren* and *chomesh* is transmitted, confirming that these are monetary debts in the full sense. *Yorshin b'nei shillumei chomsha d'avuon havu* — the heirs are indeed obligated to pay their father's *chomesh*.

---

## Son's Liability

### Son Pays Chomesh

The *gemara* now encounters a tension with a contradictory *braita*: *adayin ani omer, eimasai eino meshalem chomesh al gezel aviv* — when does a son *not* have to pay *chomesh* for his father's theft? *Bizman shelo nishba lo hu v'lo aviv* — only when neither the father nor the son had sworn about it. The implication is that if at least one of them swore, the son would be obligated to pay the *chomesh*. The *braita* then asks: *hu v'lo aviv, aviv v'lo hu, hu v'aviv, minayin* — how do we know that any of these combinations — the son swore but not the father, the father swore but not the son, or both swore — obligates the son in *chomesh*? The answer is derived from the verse: *talmud lomar asher gazal v'asher asak* — the Torah's language encompasses the full range of the obligation.

### Admission Factor

Rav Nachman resolves the apparent contradiction between the *braita* that obligates the heirs in *chomesh* and the *braita* that seems to condition the obligation on oath-taking: *lo kashya, kan she'hodeh, kan she'lo hodeh* — there is no contradiction. The difference turns on whether an admission was made. When there has been an admission, the analysis differs from a case where there has been none.

### Oath Requirement

Specifically: *ei lo hodeh, keren nami lo meshalem* — if there was no admission, the son does not even pay the principal until witnesses come to establish the claim. The *chomesh* discussion must therefore be set against a backdrop in which the claim has been substantiated in some way, and the question is whether an oath was also taken that would generate the additional *chomesh* liability.

### Principal Always

A parallel *braita* addresses the *keren* separately: *eimasai hu meshalem keren al gezel aviv* — when must the son pay even just the principal of his father's theft? *Bizman she'nishba hu v'aviv, o aviv v'lo hu, hu v'lo aviv* — when either the father or the son or both had sworn about it. But what if neither swore — *lo hu v'lo aviv, minayin* — how do we know the son must still pay the *keren*? The answer: *talmud lomar gezeila v'oshek aveida u'pikadon* — the Torah groups together stolen objects, cheated property, lost objects, and deposits, indicating that the underlying stolen property generates an obligation to return it regardless of whether any oath was taken. The *keren* attaches to the fact of the theft itself; the *chomesh* attaches to the oath.

### Yesh Talmud

The *braita* concludes with the cryptic phrase *yesh talmud* — which prompted the following exchange. Rav Huna was teaching this *braita* in session. His son Rabba challenged him: *yesh talmud ka'amar mar?* — Did you say, literally, "there is a Talmud"? *O yeshtalmu ka'amar mar?* — Or did you say "they shall pay," meaning *yeshtalmu*, which would make obvious syntactic sense as a conclusion to the list? Rav Huna replied: I said *yesh talmud*, precisely as I said. *U'miribbuyya de-krai amrei* — this phrase signals that the obligation is derived through a *midrash halacha*, an inclusion drawn from the grouping of terms in the relevant *pesukim*. The phrase *yesh talmud* is therefore a technical marker indicating that a *derashah* of the text is what extends the obligation to cases of *aveida* and *pikadon* alongside *gezeilah* and *oshek*.

### Rav Huna Clarifies

The *gemara* then works through the remaining logical cases. If the father made no admission — *lo hoda aviv* — but the son admitted — *ve'hoda beno* — the son's own admission generates his liability for *chomesh* based on his own *shvu'a*. But what if the stolen property no longer exists? *Be'she'ein gezela kayyama* — if the physical stolen object is gone, the son cannot pay back even the *keren*, since he did not personally steal anything and has no personal liability for his father's theft absent a surviving object or some form of enforceable claim.

The *gemara* then considers whether an obligation that runs through land — *achrayut* — could fill this gap. But land is generally not subject to the laws of theft — *karka einah nigzelet* — and so *chomesh* would not apply to a claim grounded in real property. This is the explanation offered by Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua: *lefi she'ein meshalmin chomesh al kaparat shibbud karka'ot* — one does not pay *chomesh* for a denial pertaining to the encumbrance of land. Alternatively, the *gemara* considers whether the case involved a loan made without a *shtar* — *milva al peh* — which ordinarily cannot be collected from heirs or from subsequent purchasers of property.

### Saddlebag Case

Rava offers a final, elegant resolution: *hacha be'mai askinan? Ke'gon she'hayta diskiya shel aviv mufkedet beyad acherim* — the case under discussion involves a situation in which the father's *diskiya* — a closed double saddlebag or pouch — was in someone else's possession. The exact contents of the bag were unknown to the son.

*Keren meshalem de'ha itei* — the son pays the *keren* because the physical object still exists and can be identified and returned. *Chomesh lo meshalem* — but he does not pay the *chomesh*, because *dechi ishtaba bekushta, ishtaba de'ha lo hava yada* — when he swore, he swore truthfully, in the sense that he genuinely did not know the contents of the closed bag. The son's oath about the theft was simultaneously true enough — in the sense that his ignorance was genuine — that it does not generate *chomesh* liability, yet false enough in its practical effect — given that a theft claim does attach to the bag — that it does not exempt him from paying the *keren*. This is Rava's proposed scenario: a case in which the son is liable for the principal but not the additional twenty-five percent, because his oath, while ultimately misleading, was not a knowing false oath of the kind that triggers *chomesh*.

The discussion will continue on 105a.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 105

## Hashavah Below Peruta

### Mishnah Overview

The daf opens approximately eight lines from the top, at the phrase *chutz me'hashavat shaveh perutah la'keren* — "except for returning the value of a *perutah* to the principal." The *mishnah* is addressing a specific scenario: a thief who not only stole but swore falsely about it bears a heightened obligation, beyond merely returning the stolen object. He must actively seek out the victim and restore the *gezeilah* wherever that person may be found. The *mishnah* qualifies, however, that this intensified obligation dissolves once the principal has declined to less than a *perutah*. The *gemara* now sets out to probe the contours of this rule: under what circumstances, if any, does an obligation to return stolen property persist even when the remaining value falls below the *perutah* threshold?

### Rav Papa: Gezeilah Gone

Rav Papa addresses the case directly: *lo shanu ela she'ein gezeilah kayyemet* — the rule that no obligation remains applies only when the physical stolen object is no longer present and the entire claim has been reduced to a monetary one. A monetary obligation worth less than a *perutah* has no legal standing. But if the object itself is still physically present — *aval gezeilah kayyemet* — then *tzarich leilech achrav*, one must still pursue the victim and return it.

The reasoning given is *chashinan shema t'yaker* — we are concerned that the object's value may rise in the future. This rationale is admittedly a bit strange: if the concern is only about possible future appreciation, one might wonder why the obligation applies now rather than waiting until the value actually rises. Nevertheless, this is the first position.

### Future Appreciation

The *shema t'yaker* reasoning deserves a moment's attention. Even if the stolen object — say, a paper clip — currently has no *perutah*-worth of value, a court would not hear a claim for it, and the thief has no legal obligation to travel across town to return it. Yet the concern about future appreciation creates at least a possible future obligation, and this is offered as grounds for a present-day duty to return the object while it is still in hand.

One might press the point further: even setting aside future appreciation, the object is fundamentally the victim's property. The thief has no moral right to retain it, regardless of its market value. This dimension — the basic proprietary right to reclaim one's own object — is notably absent from the *gemara*'s explicit reasoning, a lacuna that is at least worth flagging. The related question of whether taking something worth less than a *perutah* even constitutes a transgression of *lo tigzol* is itself unresolved; the *Rambam*'s discussion of wounds worth less than a *perutah* creating *malkus* liability (since there is no monetary compensation, thus removing the principle of *nittan letashlumin*) does not have a parallel ruling in cases of theft below the *perutah* threshold, perhaps because taking something of negligible monetary value is not fully characterized as *gezeilas mamon*.

### Alt View: No Obligation

A second version of Rav Papa's position takes a stronger stance: *lo shna gezeilah kayyemet velo shna she'ein gezeilah kayyemet* — it makes no difference whether the stolen object is still present or not. Even if the thief is holding the actual paper clip, *eino tzarich leilech achrav*, he is not required to chase after the victim. And *leshema t'yaker lo chashinan* — we are not preemptively concerned about future appreciation. If the value rises, the obligation will arise at that point; there is no current duty to act on a merely hypothetical future value.

The practical and moral tension here is real. The thief is holding someone else's object without any right to it. The *gemara* does not resolve this tension directly, though it is clear that *beis din* will not hear the claim, and — according to this second view of Rav Papa — the affirmative legal duty to pursue and return is equally absent.

### Rava: Three Bunches

Rava introduces a more nuanced case: *gazal shalosh agudot beshalosh prutot* — a thief stole three bunches of parsley, each bunch worth one *perutah* at the time of theft. Subsequently the market declined and the three bunches together are now worth only two *perutot*, meaning each bunch is now worth less than a *perutah* on its own.

The rule of *kol hagazlanim meshalmin kishat hagezeilah* establishes that if the stolen objects were lost or destroyed, the thief would owe the full three *perutot* — the value at the time of theft. But if the objects are still present, the question is whether the thief must return them. Rava rules: *im hehzir lo shtayim hayav lehahazir lo aheret* — if the thief returned two of the three bunches, he is still obligated to return the third, even though the third bunch, at current value, is worth less than a *perutah*. The *hayav lehahazir* here implies not merely a moral claim but a genuine legal obligation to return even that sub-*perutah* remainder.

### Hametz Precedent

The basis for this ruling is drawn from a parallel *mishnah*: *gazal hametz ve-avar alav ha-Pesach* — if one stole *chametz* and Passover passed, rendering it entirely worthless, the thief may say *harei shelcha lefanecha* — here is your property before you — return the object and be discharged of the debt. The *chametz* is now worth nothing, yet returning it suffices.

The *gemara* asks how this case illuminates Rava's ruling about the parsley. The answer lies in understanding the structure of the *chametz* case: *ta'ama de-isa be-inei* — the reason returning the worthless *chametz* exempts the thief is precisely because the object is still present. *Ha-leisa be-inei, af al gav de-hashta lav mamona* — if it were not present, even though it is currently worth nothing, the thief would still owe the original hundred-dollar value. Why? *Keivan de-me-ikara mamona hava bai shlumei* — because at the time of the theft it was worth real money, and that original monetary act of *gezeilah* obligates full restitution.

### Original Value Theory

This logic applies symmetrically to Rava's case: *hacha nami af al gav de-hashta lo shaveh perutah, keivan de-me-ikara hava shaveh perutah bai shlumei* — here too, even though the remaining bunch of parsley is currently worth less than a *perutah*, since at the time of theft it was worth a *perutah*, the thief is obligated to make restitution.

The underlying principle can be stated as follows: the original act of *gezeilah*, when it constituted a genuine *gezeilas mamon* worth at least a *perutah*, imposes a permanent obligation. That obligation must be discharged either by returning the original object as it now stands — regardless of its current value — or by paying the original value. Just as with the *chametz*, the ability to say *harei shelcha lefanecha* and discharge a debt by returning a worthless object is available precisely because the debt exists. The *gezeilah* was real, and therefore so is the duty of *hashavah*.

---

## Partial Return Problem

### Rava's Question

Rava now raises a more difficult question: *gazal shtei agudot beperutah* — suppose a thief stole two bunches of carrots that together were worth one *perutah*. Neither bunch alone was ever worth a *perutah*. The thief then returned one bunch. What is the status of the remaining bunch?

This is meaningfully different from the three-bunches case. There, each bunch was originally worth a *perutah* on its own, and the question was only about depreciation. Here, neither bunch was ever individually worth a *perutah*. The entire *gezeilah* was worth a *perutah* only as a combined transaction. The thief has returned half. Does the remaining half — which was never, even at the moment of theft, worth a *perutah* on its own — carry any obligation of return?

### Two Approaches

Two frameworks present themselves. The first focuses on the current status of what remains: *hashta leika gezeilah* — at this point, what the thief holds does not constitute a *gezeilah* in any legally cognizable sense. It was never worth a *perutah* independently, and therefore there is nothing that compels return. The second framework focuses on the original transaction: *ha la hadar degezeilah de hava gabeih* — the thief has not yet fully returned what he stole. He stole two bunches as a single act worth a *perutah* and has returned only one. His *hashavah* is incomplete, regardless of whether what remains would individually qualify as a minimum-value *gezeilah*.

### Gezeilah/Hashavah Gap

Rava resolves the question with a striking formulation: *gezeilah ein kan, hashavah ein kan* — there is no *gezeilah* here, and there is no *hashavah* here. The *gemara* initially parses this in the most natural direction: if there is no *gezeilah* left in the thief's hand — because what remains is sub-*perutah* — then there is nothing outstanding to return, and presumably the *mitzvah* of *hashavah* has been fulfilled to whatever degree possible.

But that reading is rejected. The *gemara* reframes: *af al pi shegezeila ein kan, mitvat hashavah ein kan* — even though what remains is no longer considered a cognizable *gezeilah*, the thief has not fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *hashavah*. *Tosafot* captures the *nafka mina* directly: the thief has no remaining legal compulsion — *beis din* cannot force him — yet he has also not discharged his *mitvat hashavah*, because he never fully returned what he stole.

This creates an interesting intermediate space. The thief is not legally actionable for the sub-*perutah* remainder, yet the *mitzvah* of *hashavah* remains in some sense unfulfilled. What that unfulfillment means in practical terms — and whether, for instance, it blocks bringing a *korban* in a case where a false *shevuah* was involved — is a significant downstream question that emerges from the analysis.

### Nazir Hair Case

Rava draws a parallel from an entirely different domain to illuminate this structure. The *mishnah* establishes that a *nazir* who shaves but leaves two hairs has not fulfilled his *mitzvah* of *giluach* — *lo asa velo klum*. Two hairs constitute a *shiur*, a minimum significant quantity; one hair alone does not.

Rava asks: suppose the *nazir* shaved everything except two hairs, and then one of those two hairs fell out on its own. He then goes back and shaves the remaining one. Has he fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *giluach*? The scenario matters because of the *order* of events. Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina whether Rava's question concerns a case where one shaved one hair at a time — but if so, there would be no question, since shaving each hair individually is obviously valid. Ravina clarifies: the question is specifically where the order is reversed — *kegon shenashra achat ve'achar kach gilach achat* — one hair fell out first, and *then* he went back and shaved one.

### Hair Analysis

The difficulty is this: when the *nazir* finally performs the shaving act, only one hair remains — below the *shiur* of two. The question is whether an act of *giluach* performed on a single hair counts at all. *Mi amrinan hashta miha leika shiur?* — do we say that since there is now no minimum quantity of hair left, the obligation is discharged, as nothing of substance remains? Or do we say — *o dilma hai lav giluach hu dimeikara* — that the *mitzvah* was not originally completed (two hairs were left), and the final act of shaving one hair does not constitute a valid *giluach* because at the moment of that act, there was already less than the required *shiur*?

Rava resolves with the same phrasing as before: *se'ar ein kan, giluach ein kan* — there is no hair, and there is no *giluach*. Again, the *gemara* notes that the natural reading of "there is no hair" would lead one to expect "therefore you are *yotzei*," since nothing remains. But the *gemara* reframes: *af al pi she'se'ar ein kan, mitzvat giluach ein kan* — even though there is nothing left, the *mitzvah* of *giluach* was not properly fulfilled. The original shaving left two hairs and thus was deficient; the subsequent shaving acted on fewer than the requisite *shiur* and thus does not constitute a valid completing act.

*Tosafot* notes that according to some *poskim*, *giluach* is not *me'akev* — it does not block the *nazir* from proceeding — in which case the practical consequence is that he has not fully performed the *mitzvah* but is not entirely barred. If *giluach* is *me'akev*, the *nazir* would have to wait for the hair to regrow and begin again. *Rashi*'s position, according to a discussion in the *shiur*, is that he does not need to wait for regrowth before proceeding to other aspects of completion.

The parallel back to the *gezeilah* case is now clarified: in both domains, the *gemara* is charting a middle territory — there is nothing left that the law can compel one to act upon, yet the core *mitzvah* has not been truly discharged. As one student observed, by tracing the outer limits of legal compulsion so precisely, the *gemara* implicitly identifies what remains in the moral domain: an obligation one cannot be constrained to fulfill, but that nonetheless exists. Whether this has further halakhic consequences — such as whether a *korban* in a *shevuah* case can be brought before full *hashavah* has been effected — is a question that deserves further attention in light of *Tosafot*'s discussion on 103a regarding delivery of payment to an agent of *beis din*.

---

## False Oaths & Monetary D…

### Hametz Oath Question

Rava poses a fascinating question about the intersection of *shevuah* and monetary obligation. The facts: I steal David's *chametz* right before Passover when it is worth a thousand dollars. Once Passover passes, it becomes entirely worthless. Under normal circumstances, if the object is present, I may return it and discharge my obligation with *harei shelcha lefanecha*; if it is gone, I owe the original thousand dollars. Now suppose that when David confronted me, I swore falsely that I did not steal his *chametz* — and then admitted the truth. The question is whether this false *shevuah* carries all the consequences of a *shevuat mamon*: the obligation to bring a *korban*, to pay a *chomesh*, and so on.

The tension is acute. Normally, a false *shevuah* in a monetary dispute obligates these consequences because through the oath one is effectively stealing from the victim — denying him money that is rightfully his. Here, however, my oath only denied David his right to collect a pile of *chametz* that is now *afra be'alma*, dust, entirely without monetary value. Am I really denying him anything of substance? Perhaps: *mamona kachafar lei* — perhaps my oath does deny him a monetary claim, because if the *chametz* were to be stolen or lost, I would owe him the full original value. My false *shevuah* thus prevents him from establishing a claim that could translate into real money under certain future circumstances.

Or perhaps the opposite: since the *chametz* is right there, physically present and worthless — *ha manach, ve'afra be'alma hu, velo kafar lei mamona* — my oath is denying him nothing monetary whatsoever right now. Rava leaves this as a genuine question.

### Rabbah: Possible Liabili…

To Rabbah, the answer is obvious, and the resolution follows from a principle he had already stated. Rabbah's earlier case: David says to me, "You stole my ox." I reply, "I did not steal it — I am merely a *shomer chinam* on it." I take a *shevuah* to that effect, but I am lying. Rabbah rules I am *chayav* — obligated to bring the *korban* and all attendant consequences. The reason: *shepatar atzmo migneiva va'aveida* — through my oath I have exempted myself from a level of liability. A *gazlan* is liable even in cases of *ones* — unavoidable loss. A *shomer chinam* is not. So by falsely claiming to be a *shomer chinam*, I have — for the period between my oath and the animal's return — effectively insulated myself from a class of liability that David had a right to hold me to.

The key principle Rabbah derives is that even a *possible* future monetary liability, if one's false *shevuah* negates it, qualifies as *kafarat mamon* — denying a monetary claim — sufficient to trigger the full *korban* and *chomesh* obligations. Whether the animal actually dies or is stolen during that window is irrelevant; the false oath, at the moment it was taken, stripped the claimant of a genuine monetary right that could have materialized.

Applied to Rava's *chametz* question: even though right now the *chametz* is present and worthless — *afra be'alma* — since if it were stolen I would owe a thousand dollars, *keivan de-mignav bayei shlumei leh, mamona ma'alya, ha nami mamona kachafar* — my false oath denies David that real potential claim. According to Rabbah, this is a fully valid *shevuah* on a monetary matter.

The question of exactly *how much* the *chomesh* would be — a fifth of the original value? a fifth of the current value? — is not resolved in this passage, and the *gemara* does not pursue it. What is established is that the *korban* obligation at minimum attaches.

### Expanded Liability Cases

Rabbah extends the principle through a series of cases. If I claim to be a *shomer sachar* rather than a *gazlan*, I am still *chayav* — *shepatar atzmo mishvuah metah* — because a *gazlan* is liable even for sudden death, whereas a *shomer sachar* is exempt in cases of *ones*. So by falsely claiming *shomer sachar* status, I have exempted myself from a degree of liability, and that suffices.

Even if I claim to be a *shoel* — a borrower, who bears the highest level of liability among *shomrim*, including liability for *ones* — I am still *chayav*: *shepatar atzmo mimita machmat melacha* — because even a *shoel* is exempt if an animal breaks down through normal use in the course of the labor for which it was borrowed. That narrow exemption, which would be unavailable to a *gazlan*, means that by falsely claiming to be a *shoel* I have secured some exemption from liability — and that is enough.

The common thread across all three cases is the same: even a small zone of exemption, obtained through a false *shevuah* conceding that the object is the claimant's but denying the status of *gazlan*, creates full *korban* liability. The monetary claim need not be certain to materialize; the mere existence of a possible future liability that the false oath forecloses is sufficient.

One might ask: in all these cases, I am conceding the object belongs to the claimant and will return it — so what exactly is the monetary claim being denied? The answer is that the claim being denied is not the value of the object itself, but the exposure to liability that attaches to the *gazlan* status. It is worth noting that the *gemara* does not address with precision what the *chomesh* payment would be calculated on in these cases — the full value of the object, or some actuarial fraction representing the incremental liability — and this remains an open question in the analysis.

### Rav Amram's Challenge

Rav Amram raises a challenge against Rabbah's position from a *braita* derived from the *midrash halacha* on the *pesukim* in *Parshat Vayikra* dealing with false oaths: *ve-kichash ba'amito be-pikadon o bi-tesumas yad o ve-gazel...* — and the obligation of *hashavah* and *chomesh* that follows. The *midrash halacha* derives from the phrase *ve-kichash bah* — "he denied it" — *prat le-modeh be-ikar*: this excludes a case where one concedes the underlying claim (*modeh be-ikar*).

The *braita* then enumerates cases where a person concedes the principal: "You sold it to me." "You gave it to me as a gift." "Your father sold it to me." "Your father gave it to me." "It wandered into my yard on its own." "I found it as a lost object." "I am a *shomer chinam* on it." "I am a *shomer sachar* on it." "I am a *shoel* on it." In all these cases, says the *braita*, the person *nishba ve-hoda* — swears and then admits — and the ruling is that one might have thought he is *chayav*, but the Torah says *ve-kichash bah*, excluding the *modeh be-ikar*.

This directly contradicts Rabbah, who held that claiming *shomer chinam* status — one of the very cases listed in this *braita* — does obligate the *korban* and *chomesh*.

### Braita Reconciled

Rava responds — addressing Rav Amram sharply — *tadura*, and proceeds to distinguish the *braita*. The *braita*, he explains, is specifically discussing *de'amar leh heilach* — a case where at the moment of taking the *shevuah*, the respondent says "just take it." In other words, the object is immediately available for collection, the claimant can retrieve it at that very instant, and the oath is therefore not denying him anything at all — not even a potential future claim, because the object is being handed back in the very same breath.

*Ki ka'amina* — when Rabbah's rule applies, Rava clarifies, it is specifically *dekai be'agam* — when the object is out in the swamp, requiring time to go and retrieve. In that interval between the taking of the oath and the actual recovery of the object, the false oath is exposing the claimant to the risk of a period of uncompensated loss should something happen to the animal. It is that window of potential liability, foreclosed by the false oath, which triggers the obligation.

The *braita*'s *modeh be-ikar* exclusion thus applies only in the narrow case of *heilach* — immediate return — where there is genuinely no monetary interest being denied. Rabbah's cases, by contrast, all involve some meaningful gap between the oath and the actual recovery during which the false oath has real monetary consequences. The apparent contradiction is resolved.

### Conceding Principal

The *gemara* then revisits the earlier items in the *braita*'s list — those cases where the respondent claims sale or gift — to ask how those constitute *modeh be-ikar* at all. If I say "you sold it to me," I am claiming ownership, not conceding the claimant's title. How is that a concession of the principal?

The *gemara* answers: *lo natati lecha dameha* — "you sold it to me but I haven't paid you yet, so take it back." By acknowledging that payment was never made, the respondent is effectively conceding that title never fully transferred. *Shkol torech ve-zil* — take your animal and go. In this formulation, the claim of sale becomes a concession that the object is still the claimant's.

Similarly, "your father gave it to me as a gift" — *al mnat de-avadat li niach nafsha*, you gave it to me expecting me to do you a service, *ve-lo avdi lach*, and I didn't do it. So take it back. Again, by acknowledging the conditional nature of the gift and declining to insist on it, the respondent concedes the principal and simultaneously offers immediate return, placing the case squarely within the *heilach* framework of the *braita*.

The case of the wandering found animal — *to'eh baderech metzatziha* — is addressed by Abaye citing Shmuel: the person is saying *shvua aveda matzati ve-lo hayiti yodea she'ishach, she-hakhziranah lach* — "I swear I found it as a lost object and didn't know it was yours; now that you've told me, take it back." This is a classic *aveidah* scenario where the person held the animal pending identification of its owner. Once ownership is established, the willingness to return is immediate, and again no monetary claim is denied.

The *gemara* closes with Ben Azzai beginning to enumerate three types of oaths — a discussion involving false oaths in the context of lost objects — but this topic will be taken up in the subsequent session.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 106

## Shvuat Edut

### Three Scenarios

The *daf* begins on 105b with a *baraita* citing Ben Azzai, who identifies three types of false oaths one might take when asked to testify regarding a lost object. The underlying case is this: a person approaches another and asks whether he has any knowledge of who took or found his lost object, demanding that the witness come and testify. The witness, however, swears he knows nothing of the matter — and the question is whether this false oath of testimony (*shvuat edut*) incurs a *korban*.

Ben Azzai frames the analysis around three scenarios of partial or complete ignorance. In the first, the witness knew the identity of the object — that the wandering animal was indeed his friend's — but did not know who found it (*hikira bah velo bimotzaah*). He nonetheless swore he knew nothing. In the second, he knew that someone had found a lost object, but was not certain it was his friend's (*bimotzaah velo bah*); he too swore he knew nothing. The third scenario, taken at face value, would be that he knew neither the object nor the finder (*lo bah velo bimotzaah*) — but the *Gemara* immediately objects: if he truly knew neither, his oath is truthful. *Lo bah velo bimotzaah kushta ka shava* — he is swearing the truth. The *Gemara* therefore redirects: *eima seifa* — consider instead the concluding case, which is the exact opposite: he knew both the identity of the object and who found it (*bah ubimotzaah*), and swore he knew nothing. This is the paradigmatic false oath of testimony.

### Rav Ammi vs. Shmuel

The question of *lemai hilcheta* — for what practical purpose are these cases enumerated — yields a dispute between Rav Ammi and Shmuel. Rav Ammi, citing Rabbi Chanina, holds that in all these cases the witness is *patur* — exempt from bringing a *korban* for *shvuat edut*. This is a striking position, particularly in the final case where the witness knew everything and still swore falsely. Shmuel, by contrast, holds *lechayev* — the witness is liable. Even if he knew only one piece of the relevant facts, his oath may have indirectly deprived the claimant of a legal remedy: a single witness cannot establish liability directly, but his testimony could have compelled the opposing party to take an oath, and that in itself constitutes a meaningful legal consequence.

---

## One Witness

### Tanaic Debate

The *Gemara* identifies this dispute as rooted in a broader *tannaitic* disagreement. The case in question is *hamashbia ed echad* — one who causes a single witness to swear falsely. The clear case contemplated by the *Torah* involves two witnesses whose combined denial of knowledge definitively deprives the claimant of his case. When only one witness is involved, the analysis becomes more complex: one witness, at best, can only compel the other party to take an oath; he cannot by himself establish any monetary liability. A *baraita* rules: *ed echad patur* — one witness is exempt. But Rabbi Elazar berabbi Shimon holds *mechayiv* — he is liable.

### Indirect Causation

The *Gemara* explains the crux of their dispute. The first opinion holds that *davar hagerum lemamon*, an act that only indirectly causes financial loss, does not carry the weight of direct causation — *lav kemamon dami*. Rabbi Elazar berabbi Shimon disagrees: indirect causation is sufficient to create liability — *kemamon dami*. This parallels a discussion from the prior *daf* regarding an oath about *chametz she-avar alav ha-Pesach*, where the oath does not directly cause a monetary loss but may indirectly do so. The parallel structure underscores the conceptual unity of the principle: where the causal chain to financial harm is attenuated, the *tannaim* disagree as to whether liability attaches.

---

## Denial & Gazlan

### Rav Sheshet

The *Gemara* now transitions to a new subject with the ruling of Rav Sheshet: *ha-kofer be-pikadon* — one who denies that he is holding another's *pikadon* — *na'aseh lo gazlan*, becomes a *gazlan* immediately. Before turning to the oath entirely, the *Gemara* examines the consequences of bare denial, even without any subsequent *shvuah*. The scenario is straightforward: Michael entrusted his phone to Dov, and when Michael asks for it back, Dov says flatly, "You never gave me anything." According to Rav Sheshet, at the moment of that denial, Dov becomes a *gazlan* and is *chayav b'onsin* — liable even for accidents — because his act of denial constitutes an appropriation of the object, even without any physical act.

### Baraita Consequences

A *baraita* is cited to examine this claim through the *pesukim* in *Parshat Vayikra*. The *baraita* works through the stages of the case: *ve-khichesh bah* — he denied having the *pikadon* — and then *v'nishba lashaker* — he swore falsely. The *baraita* first establishes the *onesh* — the punishment — for denial, and then the prohibition — *azhara* — derived from *lo techachashu*. The *Gemara* asks: does the *baraita*'s reference to punishment for the initial denial (*reisha*) mean there is a monetary consequence for mere denial, even without an oath? That would directly support Rav Sheshet. Or does the *baraita* speak exclusively of cases where an oath was also taken, and the two halves of the *baraita* address two different consequences of a false oath — one where the person subsequently admits (*hoda*), and one where witnesses appear (*ba'u edim*)?

The *Gemara* articulates the distinction precisely: *kan shehoda kan sheba'u edim*. If witnesses came, the consequence is that one is *chayav b'onsin* — liable as a *gazlan*. If one admitted on his own, *oduyei odei*, the consequences are more severe in a different dimension: he pays the principal (*keren*), adds a fifth (*chomesh*), and brings a *korban* (*asham*). The surprising feature is that admission, which is normally a path to *kapara*, actually generates greater formal obligations than the mere arrival of witnesses — because admission triggers the *teshuvah* mechanism of the *Torah* with its attendant payments. The *Gemara* ultimately concludes that the *baraita* does not provide proof for Rav Sheshet's position: it may be speaking throughout of cases where a *shvuah* was taken, with the two halves describing post-oath consequences depending on whether one admits or witnesses arrive.

### Mishna Challenge

Rami bar Chama presses the question from a *mishna* in *Shevuot*. The *mishna* discusses a case where a person who is required to take an oath is disqualified from doing so — for instance, because he is already known to be a *gazlan*. The *mishna* specifies that this disqualification applies whether he is suspect of *shvuat edut* or *shvuat ha-pikadon*. The implicit question: if Rav Sheshet is correct that mere denial of a *pikadon* makes one a *gazlan*, then one should be disqualified from oaths from the moment of denial — before any *shvuah* is ever taken. Yet the *mishna* seems to tie the disqualification specifically to having taken a false oath. Why would the *mishna* refer to *shvuat ha-pikadon* as the disqualifying event if simple denial already made him a *gazlan*?

### Possession Requirement

The *Gemara* resolves this by introducing a critical qualification. The ruling of Rav Sheshet — that denial constitutes *gazlanut* — applies only *dekai be-agma*, when the object is directly in the denier's possession at the time of the denial. If the object is elsewhere — say, the cow is grazing in a swamp — then denial alone does not constitute an act of appropriation. In that case, the person denying is merely *ishtamitina*, buying time, intending to retrieve the object and return it. His lie is not an act of seizure because he has no present physical control over the object. It is only when the object is in his possession and he denies it that his denial functions as an act of *kinyan* over someone else's property.

This is further supported by a statement of Rav Idi bar Avin: *ha-kofer be-milveh kasher le-edut* — one who denies a loan is still qualified to testify. But *ha-kofer be-pikadon pasul le-edut* — one who denies holding a *pikadon* is disqualified. The distinction: when denying a loan, the person may simply be buying time, since the money has already been transferred and is no longer the lender's specific property. When denying a *pikadon*, the object remains the owner's specific property, and denial is tantamount to claiming it for oneself — but only, as established, when it is physically in one's possession.

---

## Milveh vs. Pikadon

### Intent Distinction

The *Gemara* now formally articulates the distinction between denial of a *milveh* (loan) and denial of a *pikadon* (deposit). When a borrower denies a loan, his denial can be understood as an attempt to postpone repayment rather than a claim of outright ownership — *ishtamitina*, pushing the creditor off while intending ultimately to pay. The loan itself is an abstract obligation: once the money has been transferred, it belongs to the borrower and his debt is a legal abstraction. Denial of that abstraction, while dishonest, does not carry the same immediate character of misappropriation as denial of a *pikadon*, where the specific object remains the owner's property and any act of claiming it amounts to theft.

### Shvua Konah

At this juncture the *Gemara* invokes the statement of Ilfa — *shvuah konah* — an oath "acquires." In the context of the preceding discussion, this phrase was understood to mean that the oath, rather than the bare denial, is the act that transforms the holder into a *gazlan*. The oath is the moment of formal appropriation. However, the *Gemara* signals that we are about to encounter a radically different interpretation of this same phrase: *ke-de'Rav Huna*, as Rav Huna explains it. The phrase *shvuah konah* is about to be reread not as "the oath creates *gazlanut*" but as something far more counterintuitive.

---

## Rav Huna Position

### Rav Huna's Claim

Rav Huna cites Rav with what the *Gemara* immediately recognizes as a striking and difficult position. The case: *maneh li be-yadcha* — I claim you owe me a *maneh*. The defendant says *ein lecha be-yadi klum* — you have nothing with me. He takes an oath to that effect. Then witnesses come and prove he was lying. The ruling of Rav: *patur* — exempt. He does not have to pay anything.

The source is the *pasuk*: *ve-lakach ba'alav ve-lo yishalem* — "the owners take and he does not pay." Rav reads this not as describing the normal case where the oath is truthful and therefore extinguishes the claim, but as a general principle: once the owners have accepted the defendant's oath against their claim, he is no longer liable to pay, even if it subsequently emerges that the oath was false. *Kivan she-kiblu ha-be'alim shvuah shuv ein meshalem mamon* — once the claimants have received an oath against their claim, the monetary obligation is discharged. This is Rav Huna's reading of *shvuah konah*: the oath "acquires" finality — it constitutes, in effect, a form of payment.

### Rava's Limitation

Rava immediately attempts to limit this position to the case of a loan (*milveh*). His reasoning: *de-le-hotza'ah nitnah* — money that is lent is given to be spent. It becomes the borrower's property and generates an abstract debt. One can at least conceptually speak of an oath cancelling an abstract obligation, in the way that *shemita* cancels debts. But a *pikadon* — a specific object entrusted for safekeeping — never stops belonging to its owner. *Birshutei de-mari kai* — it always remains in the owner's domain. How can taking an oath about a *pikadon* cause it to cease belonging to him? The object is right there in the bailee's possession.

### Rava on Pikadon

However, Rava immediately reverses himself: *afilu be-pikadon* — even a *pikadon* falls under Rav's rule. His basis is textual: the *pasuk* of *ve-lakach ba'alav ve-lo yishalem* is written explicitly in the context of a *pikadon*. If the *Torah* itself says that accepting an oath against a *pikadon* claim extinguishes liability, then this cannot be limited to loans. The *Gemara* does not pause here to supply any further logical justification; it simply takes note of the ruling and turns immediately to testing it against the known cases.

---

## Baraita Challenges

### Avad Case

Rav Acha bar Minyomi challenges Rav Nachman, who has been expounding Rav's position, from a case in what appears to be a *baraita*. The owner asks: where is my *pikadon*? The bailee responds: *avad* — it was lost. The owner demands an oath; the bailee swears. Then witnesses testify that the bailee had in fact consumed it — *she-achalo* — he had appropriated it for himself. In that case, *meshalem es ha-keren* — he pays the principal. If he had admitted on his own, *hodeh me-atzmo*, he would pay principal, *chomesh*, and bring an *asham*. But in any event, he pays. How does this square with Rav's position that a false oath extinguishes liability?

### Beit Din Distinction

Rav Nachman defends Rav by drawing a distinction: *k'gon de-nishba chutz le-veit din* — Rav's rule applies only to an oath taken before the court (*beit din*) in the formal judicial context. An oath taken outside *beit din* does not carry the same halakhic weight as a court-imposed oath and therefore does not constitute "payment." The cases in the *baraita* where one continues to pay after a false oath are cases where the oath was taken outside *beit din*.

### Nignav Case

The questioner immediately presses further by raising the *seifa* — the second case of the same *baraita* or *mishna*. The owner asks: where is my *pikadon*? The bailee responds: *nignav* — it was stolen. He takes an oath to that effect. Witnesses then testify that he himself was the thief — *she-ganavo*. In that case, *meshalem tashlumei kefel* — he pays the double payment (*kefel*). If he admitted before the witnesses came, *hodeh me-atzmo*, he pays principal, *chomesh*, and *asham* — but not *kefel*, since one who admits liability for a penalty (*kenas*) is exempt from the *kenas* itself.

### Kefel Problem

Here the challenge sharpens decisively. The payment of *kefel* for *gneivah* is well established as a penalty that applies only *be-veit din* — in the formal court context. The *pasuk* itself (*ad ha-Elohim yavo dvar shneihem*) implies adjudication before judges. One cannot pay *kefel* for an oath taken outside *beit din*. Therefore, the *nignav* scenario — where *kefel* is paid — must be a case where the oath was taken *in* court. But if it was taken in court, why doesn't Rav's rule apply? Why does the bailee still have to pay *kefel* after taking a court-imposed oath?

---

## Distinctions

### Split Solution

The *Gemara* first considers a simple solution: split the two cases along the *beit din* line. The *reisha* — the *avad* case where one pays the principal — occurred outside *beit din*, so Rav's rule doesn't apply. The *seifa* — the *nignav* case where one pays *kefel* — occurred inside *beit din*, but the *kefel* penalty is itself the exception to Rav's rule. However, the *Gemara* rejects this approach as *shinuya dachika* — a strained resolution — and declines to offer it as a serious answer.

### Kofas/Kafatz

The better answer, the *Gemara* says, is *eidi ve-eidi be-veit din* — both cases took place in *beit din*. The distinction is not about location but about the nature of the oath. In the case where one continues to pay, the oath was *kafatz* — the defendant volunteered it spontaneously, or alternatively (*Rashi*) it was the litigant rather than the court who demanded the oath before the judges had formally imposed it. Rav's rule — that a court-imposed oath constitutes payment — applies only when the court itself (*kofas*) imposed the oath upon the defendant. If the oath was volunteered (*kafatz*), the court's imposition is lacking and the oath does not carry the weight of a formal judicial discharge of the claim.

This answer is acknowledged as formally better than the split approach — at least it keeps both cases within *beit din* — but it is manifestly strained. We are now required to read the *baraita*'s cases as distinguishable on the basis of whether the oath was *kofas* or *kafatz*, which is precisely the difference that Rav would need to be preserved. The *Gemara* does not pretend this is fully satisfying.

---

## Multiple Oaths

### Five Oaths

Rav Hamnuna now challenges Rav from a different direction. The case: I compelled David to take five successive oaths, each time swearing that he does not have my money or object. He takes all five. The ruling is *chayav al kol achas ve-achas* — he is liable for each and every oath, whether the oath was taken before the court or not, *bein bifnei veit din bein shelo bifnei veit din*. The liability in question is bringing a *korban* (*asham*) and adding a *chomesh* for each false oath. The principal (*keren*), of course, is paid only once.

### R. Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon explains why each successive oath generates a new liability: *ho'il ve-yakhol lachazor le-hodo'ot* — since David could have admitted between each oath, every subsequent oath represents a fresh decision to lie. At any moment after the first oath, David might have confessed and paid. His failure to do so, combined with taking another oath, constitutes an independent renewed act of denial. It is therefore a new sin and a new *shvuah* requiring its own *asham*.

### Hamnuna Challenge

This ruling poses a direct challenge to Rav's position. If Rav is right that a court-imposed oath extinguishes liability, then after David's first oath before the court, he should owe Michael nothing. In that case, how does his second oath make him liable for anything? He is not "stealing" anything further — according to Rav, his first oath already settled the matter. Moreover, the *baraita* explicitly specifies *bein bifnei veit din bein shelo bifnei veit din* — "whether before the court or not" — which forecloses the *beit din* distinction, and the language *hishbia alav* — "he was made to swear" — forecloses the *kafatz* distinction, since the oath was clearly imposed by the claimant.

---

## Rava's Limit

### Exclude Admission

Rava attempts to constrain Rav's position by excluding cases of admission. Rava argues that any scenario in which the defendant subsequently admits — *hodeh* — falls outside the scope of Rav's ruling. The *Torah* is explicit: *ve-hitvadda* — and he shall confess — followed by *ve-heishiv es ha-gezelah*, *chamishato*, and an *asham*. Since the *Torah* itself mandates payment of principal and *chomesh* upon admission, Rav cannot have been asserting that an earlier oath eliminates this obligation. *Lo shna ta'anat avad ve-lo shna ta'anat ganav lo amar Rav* — whether the bailee lied that the object was lost or that it was stolen, if he subsequently admits, Rav's exemption does not apply.

### Exclude Gneiva

Similarly, Rava excludes the *nignav* case where witnesses arrive. When a bailee falsely claims the *pikadon* was stolen and witnesses come to disprove this, the *Torah* imposes *kefel* — *yeshalem kefel*. Since the *Torah* explicitly mandates *kefel* in this case, Rav's rule cannot apply. *Nami lo amar Rav de-chsiv yeshalem kefel* — Rav also did not say his ruling in a case of *nignav* with witnesses, because the *Torah* says he pays *kefel*.

### Avad Only

After eliminating every case that the *Torah* explicitly addresses — admission (*hitvadda*), and *nignav* with witnesses (*yeshalem kefel*) — the only scenario remaining is the one where the bailee claimed the object was lost (*ta'anat avud*), took an oath, did not subsequently admit, and witnesses then arrived. This is precisely the case the *Torah* does not address explicitly in terms of a payment obligation following a false oath. Rava concludes: *ki ka'amar Rav ke-gon she-to'en ta'anat avud ve-nishba ve-lo hoda u-ba'u edim* — Rav's rule applies exclusively to this one case: the bailee claimed the object was lost, swore falsely, did not admit, and witnesses arrived.

---

## Hamnuna Objection

### Rav Gamda Report

Rav Gamda came before Rav Ashi and reported Rava's explanation — that Rav's position is limited to the *avad* case with witnesses, and does not apply where the defendant later admitted.

### Rav Ashi Objection

Rav Ashi immediately objects. Rav Hamnuna was Rav's own student — *talmidei de-Rav* — and would have known precisely what Rav meant. When Rav Hamnuna challenged Rav from the *baraita* about multiple oaths, his challenge was explicitly framed around the case where the defendant *could have admitted* between oaths — *yakhol lachazor le-hodo'ot*. If Rav had never applied his ruling to cases of *hodeh*, Rav Hamnuna — who surely knew Rav's position from direct transmission — would never have posed a challenge about admission. Clearly, Rav Hamnuna understood that Rav's ruling extended to cases where the defendant admits. *Ve-yada de-amar Rav hoda* — he knew that Rav stated his ruling even in a case of admission.

### Abaye Defense

Abaye comes to Rava's defense. He addresses Rav Ashi's objection by reframing what Rav Hamnuna was actually asking. It was not about admission at all. The reference to *yakhol lachazor le-hodo'ot* — the ability to admit — was not the substance of the challenge but the mechanism by which multiple oaths each constitute independent sins. The *reason* each oath is a separate sin is that the defendant could have admitted before each one; that is what makes each oath a fresh decision to lie. But the *substance* of the challenge is different.

### Hamnuna's Real Q

What Rav Hamnuna was actually asking, Abaye explains, is this: *ei amarta bishlama nishba ki atu edim mechayiv* — if you say that when witnesses arrive the defendant is liable, then I understand why each oath generates a new *korban shvuah*. Each oath is denying money that witnesses could come and prove is owed. *Amti lehachi mechayvinan lei korban shvuah ba-tras* — that is why we hold him liable for each subsequent oath: because at every moment he is lying about a real debt that witnesses could substantiate. *Ho'il ve-yakhol lachazor le-hodo'ot* is simply the mechanism showing each oath is discrete — because at any moment an admission was available. But the real force is that witnesses could have come and established the debt.

But *ela ei amarta ki atu edim patur* — if, as Rav says, the arrival of witnesses after an oath leaves the defendant exempt, then *mi ika midi* — is there any such thing where witnesses can testify against you and you are off the hook? *Ve-anan nekum ve-nechayvei korban shvuah* — and we should nonetheless hold you liable for a *korban* for each successive oath? *Hashta miha lo odi* — but right now you have not admitted. The logic would collapse: on Rav's view, the oath before the court extinguishes liability even if witnesses come. If so, there is nothing being "stolen" by subsequent oaths — the first oath already discharged the claim. Each subsequent oath cannot be a new act of denial of money owed, because on Rav's own view, no money is owed after the first oath.

The challenge from Rav Hamnuna, properly understood, is thus about witnesses (*edim*), not about admission (*hodah*). This allows Rava's limitation to stand: Rav's ruling applies in the *avad*-with-witnesses case, and Rav Hamnuna's challenge, when correctly read, does not require extending Rav's position to cases of *hodeh*.

---

## Final Summary

### Conclusion

After an extended and multi-layered *sugya*, the *Gemara* emerges with Rav's position radically curtailed. The radical claim of Rav — transmitted through Rav Huna — that a false oath extinguishes all monetary liability, even after witnesses prove the oath was false, cannot be reconciled with the explicit *pesukim* of the *Torah* in the cases of *hodeh* or *ta'anat ganav* with witnesses. The *Torah* is clear in both those scenarios that payment is required. The only surviving domain for Rav's position is the narrow case of *ta'anat avud*: the bailee falsely claimed the object was lost, swore to that effect in court under judicial compulsion, did not subsequently admit, and witnesses then arrived to disprove him. In that one case — and only that case — Rav holds that the prior oath constitutes a form of discharge, and the defendant is exempt from further payment.

This is evidently a very constrained reading of what began as a sweeping and counterintuitive ruling. The *Gemara* makes no secret of the difficulty. As Rami bar Chama observed to Rav Nachman, one need not "mortgage one's soul" for Rav's position; even Rav Nachman himself did not hold by it. The extended discussion serves the purpose of *Torah* learning — understanding what Rav could have meant and what space, if any, the sources leave for his view — even as the practical *halacha* appears to sit very uncomfortably with it.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 107

## Toein Ta'anat Ganav

### Basic Teaching

The *daf* opens with a teaching of R. Chiya bar Abba in the name of R. Yochanan concerning a *shomer* who falsely claims that a *pikadon* entrusted to him was stolen. The case is one of *toein ta'anat ganav b'pikadon*: the watchman denies having the object, swears falsely that it was stolen, and is subsequently exposed. R. Yochanan teaches that such a person pays *tashlumei kefel* — double payment. This follows from the established reading of the Torah's section on *pikadon*, where the verse *asher yarshiun Elohim yeshalem shnayim l'rei'eihu* is understood to encompass not only the genuine *ganav* but also the watchman who falsely invokes *gneivah* as his excuse.

### Ganav vs. Gazlan

One might pause here and ask: why should a *ganav* pay double at all? Why is the *gazlan* — who openly seizes property in broad daylight — exempt from *kefel*, while the *ganav* who steals covertly must pay double? The Gemara offers two distinct rationales. One reason, not stated explicitly in the Gemara but developed by the *mefarshim*, is that the *ganav* who breaks into a home commits a more intimate violation of the victim's space. The second, and the Gemara's own reason, is theological: the *ganav* fears human detection but not divine judgment — a hypocrisy that the Torah singles out for sanction. The *gazlan*, by contrast, acts brazenly in full public view, showing at least a kind of consistency: he demonstrates no greater fear of people than of God. It is this theological distinction that makes the *ganav* more culpable in the Torah's eyes, even though, or perhaps precisely because, the *gazlan* seems more brazen.

Neither of these rationales applies straightforwardly to the *to'ein ta'anat ganav*. He did not break into anyone's home, and he displays no particular hypocrisy between his fear of man and fear of God. Nevertheless, the Torah appears to assign him the status of *kefel* — and R. Yochanan is now taking the next step.

### Double to 4 & 5

R. Yochanan reasons as follows: since the genuine *ganav* pays *kefel*, and the *to'ein ta'anat ganav* also pays *kefel*, we may draw an analogy. Just as the *ganav* who subsequently slaughters or sells the animal — *tavach u'machar* — pays *arba'ah v'chamishah* (four times the value for a sheep, five times for an ox), so too the *to'ein ta'anat ganav* who then slaughters or sells the animal would be liable for four and five. The logic is that *kefel* is the marker of full *ganav* status, and once that status is established, all its consequences follow — including the penalty of *arba'ah v'chamishah* when the animal is subsequently disposed of.

### Gemara Challenge

The Gemara challenges this reasoning. The *ganav* pays *kefel* independently, purely by virtue of the act of theft, without any oath. The *to'ein ta'anat ganav*, by contrast, incurs *kefel* only by virtue of taking a false *shvuah*. This is not a minor distinction: one could argue that the *shvuah* is not merely a procedural trigger but is constitutively part of what generates the liability. If the *shvuah* is what creates the *kefel* — rather than the act of *gneivah* itself — then perhaps the *to'ein ta'anat ganav*'s *kefel* is a consequence of *shvuat sheker*, not of *ganav* status at all. In that case, the analogy to the full *ganav* — who pays four and five for *tavach u'machar* — would not hold. The two situations, while producing the same monetary outcome, may rest on entirely different foundations.

### Hekesh Resolution

The Gemara responds: *lo, hekesha hi*, this is not a mere analogy but a *hekesh* — an explicit textual linkage within the Torah itself — and one does not challenge a *hekesh* on the grounds that the cases are not fully analogous.

The nature of this linkage depends on a dispute about how to read the relevant *pesukim*. One opinion holds that the two verses — *im yimatzei haganav yeshalem shnayim* and *im lo yimatzei haganav venikrav ba'al habayit el ha'Elohim... asher yarshiun Elohim yeshalem shnayim l'rei'eihu* — describe two distinct scenarios within the same *parshah*: the first, an actual *ganav*; the second, one who claims the item was stolen and swears falsely. According to this reading, the *to'ein ta'anat ganav* and the genuine *ganav* are literally juxtaposed in the same Torah passage, constituting a *hekesh* that links their legal statuses fully.

However, according to the opinion that *both* of those verses describe cases of *to'ein ta'anat ganav*, while the actual *ganav*'s obligation of *kefel* derives from an entirely separate *pasuk* — *chayim shnayim yeshalem* — the two categories are not in the same *parshah* at all, and the *hekesh* argument would seem unavailable.

The Gemara resolves this by invoking the word *haganav* — the definite article attached to the word *ganav* in the phrase *im lo yimatzei haganav*. Rather than functioning as a limiting term (excluding all but the classic case), the Gemara reads it as an identification: *you*, the one who claimed the item was stolen, *are* the *ganav*, you are *haganav*. This is less a *hekesh* in the technical sense and more a *ribui* — a derivation from an emphatic or extra-textual element — which equates the *to'ein ta'anat ganav* with the full *ganav* and assigns him complete *ganav* status, including liability for *arba'ah v'chamishah* upon *tavach u'machar*.

---

## Baraita Objection

### Michael Eating Case

Having established that the *to'ein ta'anat ganav* bears the full legal status of a *ganav* — including the penalty of *arba'ah v'chamishah* when he subsequently slaughters or sells the animal — the Gemara now tests this against a *baraita* that appears to contradict it.

R. Chiya bar Abba, who transmitted R. Yochanan's teaching, himself raises this challenge. It is striking that the very *amora* who conveyed the *halakha* was not fully satisfied with it. The *baraita* describes the following case: a person was watching an ox, claimed it had been stolen (*nignav*), was asked to take a *shvuah* and confirmed it — thus becoming a *to'ein ta'anat ganav*. Witnesses then come forward and testify that he had actually been eating the ox. Since he must have *shechted* it in order to eat it, R. Yochanan's principle would seem to demand that he pay four and five. Yet the *baraita* rules that he pays only *kefel*. *Tashlumei arba'ah v'chamishah* — no.

The question is sharp: if *to'ein ta'anat ganav* achieves full *ganav* status, and this person clearly slaughtered and consumed the animal, why does he not pay four and five? The analogy to *tavach u'machar* appears to be precisely realized.
