A *tamei kohen* cannot bring his own *korban*, and therefore the verse *ve-ish et kodashav lo yihyu* does not apply to him. Since he has no right to the *korban*, he likewise has no special claim to the money.

The *gemara* then presses the point: if the entire discussion concerns a *kohen tamei*, how could he have formulated the *davar she-yesh lo chelek bo* argument to begin with? If he is *tamei*, does he even have a claim to the *gezel hager* being brought during his *mishmar*'s week? The *gemara* concedes that the earlier argument assumed he did have such a claim — to the money, if not to the *korban*. But the *gemara* shifts its reasoning: the source that actually establishes that the *kohen* cannot retain the *gezel hager* exclusively is a *gezera shava* from *sdeh achuza* — the case of an ancestral field that has been consecrated and redeemed by a *kohen*.

When the *Yovel* arrives, consecrated fields redeemed from the *Beis Hamikdash* do not revert to their original owners but are distributed among the *kohanim* of the serving *mishmar*. If a *kohen* himself redeemed such a field during the week his *mishmar* serves, one might argue — by the same logic as above — that since it is already under his control and would anyway go to *kohanim*, he should keep it entirely. The *baraita* on *sdeh achuza* rules otherwise: *achuzah shelo v'ein zu shelo* — it is his *achuzah* in the sense that he has a portion, but not entirely his. The word *achuzato* in the verse is read to mean he holds a share in it, not exclusive ownership. Therefore *yotzei mitachat yado u'mit'chalek l'chol ha-Kohanim* — even though the field is under his control, it is divided equally among all the *kohanim*. By *gezera shava* — *l'Kohen* in *gezel hager* is linked to *l'Kohen* in *sdeh achuza* — the same rule applies: the *gezel hager* must be divided equally regardless of the fact that it is in the *kohen*'s possession.

---

## Kohen Korban Rights

### Kohen Bring Anytime

As a digression arising from the previous discussion, the *gemara* now examines in full the *halacha* that a *kohen* may bring his own *korban* at any time. A *baraita* asks: *minayin l'Kohen she'ba makriv korbanotav b'chol eit u'v'chol sha'ah she'yirtzeh* — from where do we know that a *kohen* may come and offer his *korbanot* at any time he wishes?

### Derivation Verses

The source for the right to bring is *u'va b'chol avat nafsho v'shiret* — he comes whenever his soul desires and he serves. The source for the right to benefit from the *korban* — to keep the meat and the hide — is *ve-ish et kodashav lo yihyu*: a person retains his sacred offerings. These two verses together establish the compound right: to perform the *avodah* and to receive its benefits.

### Ba'al Mum Scenario

The *baraita* then addresses the more complex case of a *ba'al mum*: *im haya ba'al mum notnah l'Kohen she'ba'otah mishmar* — if the *kohen* has a disqualifying physical blemish, he cannot perform the *avodah* himself, so he assigns the *avodah* to the *kohen* of the serving *mishmar*. Two distinct questions arise: first, can he designate a specific *kohen* to perform the *avodah*, or must it be assigned generally to the *mishmar*? Second, does he retain the right to the meat and the hide?

On the question of designating who performs the *avodah*: since the *ba'al mum* cannot himself perform it, he cannot assign it to a specific *kohen* of his choosing. The right of designation derives from the right of personal performance, and since he has lost the latter, he loses the former as well. It goes to the *mishmar* generally.

On the question of the meat: here two versions of the *baraita* diverge sharply. According to one version, *ve'avodato ve'oro shelo* — the meat and the hide remain his, since a *kohen ba'al mum* retains the right to eat *kodashim* even though he cannot perform the *avodah*. His right to eat is independent of his right to perform. Rashi, however, has a different *girsa*: *ve'avodato ve'oro l'anshei mishmar* — the meat and the hide go to the *mishmar* equally, because his right to eat the meat is considered derivative of his right to perform the *avodah*, and since he has lost the latter, the meat is distributed equally. These two *girsa'ot* represent a fundamental dispute about whether the right to perform and the right to eat are independent or linked.

The *baraita* then addresses the mirror case: a *kohen* who is elderly or ill — able in principle to perform the *avodah* but unable to eat the meat. Such a *kohen*, since he retains the theoretical capacity to perform the *avodah*, can still assign it to whichever *kohen* he chooses. But because he cannot eat the meat, that right is distributed equally: *v'avodah savrah l'anshei mishmar*.

The *gemara* asks: *hai zaken o choleh heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If he is capable of performing the *avodah*, *avodah savrah nami k'vidi didei* — surely the same should apply to the meat, and he should be able to assign both. And if he is not capable of performing the *avodah*, how can he assign it to anyone else?

Rav Papa resolves this: *sheyachol la'asot al yedei ha'dachak* — he can manage to perform the *avodah* with great effort. When it comes to the *avodah*, *d'chi avid al yedei ha'dachak avodah hi* — struggling through the performance with great difficulty still constitutes valid *avodah*, so he retains the capacity to assign it. But when it comes to eating, *d'chi achil al yedei ha'dachak achila gassa hi* — forcing oneself to eat when one's body resists is categorized as *achila gassa*, which does not constitute a valid act of eating. Tosafos notes that there are gradations of *gassa*: a mild reluctance — as when one pushes through to dessert — differs from genuine bodily resistance that truly prevents meaningful consumption. In this case the level is the latter, and *achila gassa lav klum hu*. Therefore, because the *avodah* is within his capacity (however difficult), he may assign it; because eating is not within his capacity in any halachically meaningful sense, that right falls to the *mishmar* equally.

The broader principle emerging from both cases is that the right to perform the *avodah* and the right to eat the meat are, at least to some degree, independent entitlements.

### Tamei Korban Tzibur

Rav Sheshes addresses the case of a *kohen tamei* bringing a *korban tzibbur*. Rashi explains the scenario: the *mishmar* is impure and it falls to them to bring a *korban tzibbur* for which they are responsible. In such a case, the *halacha* is well-established that *tumah* is overridden for a *korban tzibbur* — the *korban* may be brought even in a state of *tumah* — but it is not eaten in a state of *tumah*. So a *tamei kohen* who has the right to bring the *korban* may assign the *avodah* to whichever *kohen* he chooses — *nosnoh l'chol mi she'yirtzeh*. But since he cannot eat it in his state of *tumah*, he cannot assign the eating, and *ve'avodasav ve'oro l'anshei mishmar*.

The *gemara* challenges: *heichi dami* — what is the precise scenario? If there are *tahor kohanim* present, how does a *tamei kohen* have the right to bring the *korban* in the first place? *Tahor kohanim* should be the ones bringing it. And if everyone is *tamei*, then even though the *kohen tamei* brings it, nobody can eat it — so who exactly are the *anshei mishmar* who are eating?

Rava resolves this: *eima l'ba'alei mumim tehorim sheba'oto mishmar* — all the *kohanim* without blemishes are *tamei*, so the *korban* must be brought by the *tamei kohanim*. The *ba'alei mumim*, however, are *tahor* — and while they cannot bring the *korban*, since they are *tahor* they can eat it. So the *tamei kohen* assigns the *avodah* to another *tamei kohen*, and the eating is done by the *ba'alei mumim tehorim*. The right to perform and the right to eat fall to entirely different groups.

### Kohen Gadol Onen

Rav Ashi addresses the case of a *Kohen Gadol* who is an *onen* — in the period of acute mourning following the death of a close relative. The verse *min ha'Mikdash lo yetzei v'lo yechalel et Mikdash Elokav* establishes that even in a state of *aninus*, the *Kohen Gadol* continues to perform the *avodah* but does not eat the *korbanot*. If such a *Kohen Gadol* brings his own *korban*, he may assign the *avodah* to whichever *kohen* he chooses — *nosno l'chol kohen she'yirtzeh* — but the meat goes to the *mishmar* equally, since he has no right to eat it.

The *gemara* asks: *mai kamashma lan* — what is the novelty here? We already know from a *mishna* that *Kohen Gadol makriv onen v'eino ochel*, and moreover, *v'eino cholek l'echol ba'erev* — he has no right even to a portion of the meat to be eaten later in the evening when his *aninus* ends. Clearly he cannot assign the eating.

The *gemara* answers: *salka da'atach amina ki chas Rachmana aleih d'Kohen Gadol l'kruvei hu* — one might have thought that the Torah's special dispensation allowing the *Kohen Gadol* to bring a *korban* even as an *onen* was a privilege specifically for his own personal performance of the *hakravah*, not a transferable right. If that were so, he could not assign it to another. The novelty of Rav Ashi's ruling is *lo matzi mashvei* — we might have thought he cannot assign it, but in fact he can: once he himself is entitled to perform the *hakravah*, that entitlement is assignable. The right to eat, by contrast, is entirely absent, and so it goes to the *mishmar*.

---

## Gezel Hager Death

### Gazlan Dies

We return now to the case anticipated by the coming *mishna*: *ha'gozel es ha'ger v'nishba lo u'meis* — one who steals from a *ger*, swears falsely, and dies before making restitution. The *mishna* states: *harei zeh meshalem keren v'chomesh* — he pays the principal and the fifth — *l'Kohanim*, and *asham l'mizbe'ach* — the *korban asham* goes to the altar.

The verse providing the basis is *v'im ein la'ish go'el l'hashiv ha'asham eilav, ha'asham ha'mushav la'Hashem la'Kohen, milvad eil ha'kippurim asher yechalel bo alav*: if the *ger* has no redeemer to whom the *asham* — meaning the principal — can be returned, that *asham* which is returned goes to God and then to the *kohen*, in addition to the ram of atonement which is the *korban asham* itself.

### Money to Sons

Now consider what happens when the *gazlan* himself dies while carrying the money and the *korban* to the *Beis Hamikdash*: *hakesef yinasein l'vanav* — the money goes to his sons, not to the *kohanim*. This ruling reflects a fundamental conceptual point about the nature of the money.

### Asham After Death

As for the *korban asham*: *yireh ad she'yista'eiv v'yimacheir v'yiplu damav l'nedava* — the animal grazes until it develops a blemish, is sold, and the proceeds go toward a communal *olah*. This is the standard *halacha* for an *asham* whose owner has died.

### Money as Kaparah

The decisive insight is in understanding why the money goes to the sons. At first one might state the principle this way: the money is treated purely as a *kaparah* obligation rather than a monetary debt, and since there is no *kaparah* to perform for a dead man, the obligation dissolves and the sons keep the money. But this framing needs careful correction.

If the money were simply a monetary obligation — if the *kohanim* stood in the place of the *ger* as his assigned heirs — then even after the *gazlan*'s death, the money should be transferred to the *kohanim*, just as a stolen object would have to be returned to the estate of a deceased *nigzal*. The fact that it is not transferred to the *kohanim* is precisely what reveals that the money is viewed as a type of *korban*, a component of *kaparah*. And since one does not perform *kaparah* for a person after his death, no *korban* is brought, and by the same token, no money is given. The sons keep it.

Rashi makes this explicit: *she'gazlo d'zacha bei meesas ha'ger* — from a monetary standpoint the object already legally belonged to the *gazlan* from the moment the *ger* died without heirs, *ella d'va'ei l'me'evad hashavah ki heichi d'tehavi leih kapara* — but he was required to perform an act of return as part of his *kaparah*. *V'hashta tu leika kapara keivan d'mais leih* — now that he is dead, there is no longer any *kaparah* to be achieved, so the money stays with the sons.

This also raises a question — not explored by the *gemara* here — about the *chomesh* in an ordinary case of *gezeila* (not *gezel hager*). If the *gazlan* dies, the principal must be returned to the *nigzal* because it is a monetary obligation. But is the *chomesh* similarly a monetary obligation, or is it purely a *kaparah* component that would therefore not need to be paid after the *gazlan*'s death? The *gemara* leaves this question open.

### Money Given First

A related case: *nasan ha'kesef l'anshei mishmar u'mais* — the *gazlan* gave the money to the *kohanim* and then died before bringing the *korban*. The heirs claim the money back, arguing that since the *kaparah* was never completed, the transfer should be undone. The ruling is *ein ha'yorshim yecholim lehotzi miyadam* — the heirs cannot recover the money, since the verse *v'ish asher yitein la'kohen lo yihyeh* establishes that once given to a *kohen*, it belongs to him.

### Order of Acts

The *mishna* addresses the question of whether the order in which the money and the *korban* are given matters. The verse *ha'asham ha'mushav la'Hashem la'kohen milvad eil ha'kippurim* suggests money first, then *korban*. The *mishna* confirms: if you gave the money to one *mishmar* (represented by *Yehoyariv*, the first *mishmar*) and the *korban* to the next (represented by *Yedaya*), you are *yotzei*. But if you brought the *korban* first (*asham l'Yehoyariv*) and the money second (*hakesef l'Yedaya*): if the *korban* has not yet been offered, the *mishmar* of *Yedaya* may offer it, and you are *yotzei*. But if the *korban* was already offered before the money was given back, you were not *yotzei*, and you must return the money and bring a new *asham*. The logic is analogous to the general principle that one must obtain forgiveness from the person one has wronged before seeking atonement from God — the return must precede the *korban*.

### Keren Without Chomesh

Finally: *nasan et ha'keren v'lo nasan et ha'chomesh, ein ha'chomesh me'akeiv* — if one gave back the principal without the fifth, the fifth does not prevent the fulfillment of the obligation. One has still achieved *kaparah*, though one remains obligated to give the *chomesh*. What the *mishna* establishes overall is that the money of *gezel hager*, unlike the money owed in an ordinary case of *gezeila*, is a component of *kaparah* and not a monetary debt — and all the consequences that flow from that distinction follow accordingly.

---

## Money as Asham

### Asham = Keren

A *baraita* derives the precise reference of each term in the key verse: *asham zeh keren, ha'mushav zeh chomesh* — the word *asham* in the phrase *ha'asham ha'mushav* refers to the principal, while *ha'mushav* — the returned portion — refers to the fifth. The *korban* is separately designated as the *eil ha'kippurim*. Another interpretation had suggested that *asham* refers to the *korban* itself — the ram — but the subsequent phrase *milvad eil ha'kippurim* rules that out. Similarly, one might read *ha'mushav* as referring to *kefel* — the double payment — making the *pasuk* a case of *geneivah*, not *gezeila*. But the verse *v'heshiv et ashamo b'rosho va'chamishito yosef alav* clarifies: we are speaking of an *asham* that is returned "at the head," meaning the principal, to which a fifth is added — not a doubling.

### Why Call It Asham

The halachic significance of the Torah designating the principal as an *asham* is now developed. Since the principal carries the status of an *asham* — a *korban* — it is subject to the rules governing *korbanot*.

### Cannot Return Night

Rava derives: *gezel hager she'hechziro ba'laila lo yatza* — if one returned the principal of *gezel hager* at night, one has not fulfilled the obligation. Just as a *korban* must be offered during the day, so too the return of this money must take place during daylight hours. Similarly, *hechziro chatziyo lo yatza* — returning only half does not suffice. The operative principle: *asham karya Rachmana* — the Torah called it an *asham*. One might further reason that delivering the money outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, or to a *kohen* outside the context of *avodah*, would also not fulfill the obligation, precisely because of this *korban*-like status.

This raises a natural comparison to the ordinary case of *gezeila* (not involving a *ger*). There too, returning the stolen object is a necessary precondition for *kaparah*. But in the ordinary case, the return is simply a monetary act — the *nigzal* is a private individual, the exchange takes place outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, no *kohen* is involved, and no day-restriction applies. Only in *gezel hager*, where the money is given to the *kohanim* with the structure of a *korban*, does the money itself acquire the full legal character of an *asham*.

### Pruta Requirement

Rava further rules: *gezel hager she'ein bo shaveh pruta l'chol kohen v'kohen lo yatza* — if the amount of *gezel hager* is insufficient to provide a *pruta*'s worth to each individual *kohen* in the serving *mishmar*, the obligation is not fulfilled. This is derived from the *pasuk* *ha'asham ha'mushav* — the *asham* must be returned in a way that constitutes a valid distribution to *each kohen*. Since we have established that the money is divided equally among all members of the *mishmar*, each member must receive at least a *pruta*.

This creates a genuinely difficult practical problem. If someone stole a small amount from a *ger* and the serving *mishmar* is large, he may find it impossible to fulfill his obligation. The *gemara* does not resolve what such a person is to do, and simply notes the *halacha* without offering a remedy.

### Different Mishmar

Rava raises a further question: what if the amount is insufficient for each member of the current *mishmar* (say, *Yehoyariv*'s week) to receive a *pruta*, but the following *mishmar* (*Yedaya*) is smaller and division there would yield a *pruta* per *kohen*? What if the *gazlan* gives the money to a member of *Yedaya* during *Yehoyariv*'s week?

The *gemara* first clarifies the precise scenario. If he waited until *Yedaya*'s week and gave it then, that is straightforward — each *kohen* received a *pruta* and he is clearly *yotzei*. The question is where he gave the money to *Yedaya* during *Yehoyariv*'s week. On one hand, since *Yehoyariv* cannot facilitate a valid distribution (no one would receive a *pruta*), perhaps the right to collect effectively passes to *Yedaya*, and the transfer to *Yedaya* during *Yehoyariv*'s week is a valid *hashavah*. On the other hand, since it is not *Yedaya*'s week, and the money has the status of a *korban*, perhaps giving it to a *mishmar* outside its serving week is not a valid act of return. The *gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teyku*.

---

## Money Fungibility

### Pool All Gezel

Rava poses a further question: *kohanim she'yichalku gezel ha'ger k'neged gezel ha'ger* — suppose many people came this week to return *gezel hager*, each in different amounts. May the *kohanim* pool all the money together and divide the total equally among themselves, so that each *kohen* receives the same total sum regardless of which *gezel hager* contributed to it? In other words, can *gezel hager* be treated as fungible money, allowing a kind of communal pooling?

### Korban Comparison

The comparison is to *korbanot*: one cannot take all the various *korbanot* brought in a given week, pool the meat, and distribute equal portions to each *kohen*. Each *korban* must be divided individually. Does the same apply to *gezel hager*?

### Separate Division

The *gemara* initially presents this as an open question, but then records that Rava concluded — and according to Rav Aha son of Rava, Rava taught it straightforwardly without hesitation: *asham kara Rachmana* — the Torah called it an *asham*. Just as *korbanot* cannot be pooled, each unit of *gezel hager* must be divided separately among the *kohanim*. Money, though fungible in ordinary commercial life, loses that fungibility here by virtue of its *asham* status.

What emerges from the entire sugya is a coherent and demanding legal framework. The money of *gezel hager* is not merely a monetary obligation redirected to the *kohanim* as surrogate heirs of the *ger*. It is an act of *kaparah*, carrying the full formal structure of a *korban*: it must be given during the day; it must yield a *pruta* to each *kohen*; it must be divided individually, not pooled; it must precede the *korban asham*; and if the *gazlan* dies, the obligation dissolves along with any possibility of *kaparah*, leaving the money with his heirs. The *gemara* will continue to explore the further implications of this framework.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 111

## Gezel Hager Status

### Korban Status Setup

The daf picks up on 111b, approximately twenty lines from the top, at the point of a new inquiry by Rava. Before the question itself can be understood, however, it is necessary to recall the broader context established in the preceding sugya. The Gemara has been discussing *gezel hager* — the case where someone steals from a *ger* who subsequently dies without heirs, swears falsely about it, and then wishes to make restitution. In an ordinary case of theft accompanied by a false oath, returning the principal is a prerequisite to bringing the *asham*, but the money itself does not carry any *korban*-like status. It is merely a condition that must be satisfied before the *asham* can be offered.

In *gezel hager*, however, the situation is fundamentally different. The money returned takes on a *korban*-like character in a series of striking ways: it must be returned during the day, it must be returned in full, and when the *kohanim* receive it they cannot pool it with other funds and divide it freely — each unit that was returned must be apportioned equally. The money, in other words, is treated as though it were a *korban* in its own right.

### Heirs vs Gift

Against this backdrop, Rava poses the following question: *kohanim b'gezel hager, yorshim havu o mikablei matanos havu* — when the *kohanim* receive the money returned in a case of *gezel hager*, do they receive it as heirs of the *ger*, or as recipients of a gift? The question is not about the monetary status of the *kohanim* in the abstract. As established in the preceding *mishnah*, if the person requiring *kapara* has died, the *kohanim* have no monetary claim to the money — the *yorshim* keep it, because its only function was to serve as part of *kapara*, and once there is no living person to atone for, that function lapses. The question therefore concerns only the case where the person is alive and actively giving the money to the *kohanim* as part of the *kapara* process: in what capacity do the *kohanim* receive it?

### Chametz Difference

The Gemara asks: *l'mai nafka mina* — what practical difference does it make? The proposed case is one where the *ger* had chametz stolen from him, and that chametz then *avar alav ha-Pesach* — Passover passed over it, rendering it halachically worthless. If we say the *kohanim* are *yorshim* — heirs — then the logic is that you give them exactly what you would have given back to the *ger* himself. Since you would have returned the worthless post-Pesach chametz to the *ger* (as that is what was stolen), you return the same thing to the *kohanim*, even though it has no value. But if we say the *kohanim* are *mikablei matanos* — recipients of a gift — then the Torah is directing you to give them something of real value, not merely the equivalent of what you took. On this reading, handing them the worthless chametz is no gift at all — *afra b'alma hu*, it is mere dust.

### Rav Zeira Resolves

Rav Zeira, however, objects to this proposed *nafka mina*. Even if you say the *kohanim* are gift-recipients, he argues, the question of the worthless chametz is not actually at issue. *Hi matana amar Rachmana d'neisivei lehu* — the gift that the Torah instructs you to give them is precisely what you would have given back to the *ger* himself. If post-Pesach chametz would have discharged your obligation to the *ger*, it likewise discharges your obligation to the *kohanim*. The question of *yorshim* versus *mikablei matanos* does not bear on what you give; it bears only on in what capacity they receive it.

### Maaser Behema

The true *nafka mina*, Rav Zeira explains, involves *ma'aser beheima*. Imagine that through the mechanism of *gezel hager* a *kohen* receives ten sheep. If we say the *kohanim* are *yorshim* — a continuation of the *ger*'s ownership — then their receipt of these animals is analogous to inheriting them. Just as one who inherits animals is a continuation of the original owner and must separate *ma'aser beheima* if the original owner's obligation was still outstanding, so too the *kohen* would be obligated to separate *ma'aser beheima*. But if we say the *kohanim* are recipients of a new gift — *mekablei matanos* — then they are like someone who purchases animals or receives them as a gift, and the *mishnah* teaches explicitly that one who buys or receives animals as a gift is *patur mimaaser beheima*.

The Gemara resolves the question by noting that the *beraita* calls the *kohanim*'s receipt a *matana* — a gift — just as the other priestly gifts are gifts. *Shma mina mekablei matanos havu* — we conclude that the *kohanim* receive the money in the capacity of gift-recipients, not as heirs. This makes sense in light of the broader principle: since the *kohanim* have no monetary claim to the money when *kapara* is unnecessary (as when the obligated party has died and the *yorshim* retain it), the *kohanim*'s right to it is purely functional — it flows from the *korban*-like character of the *kapara* process, not from any inheritance relationship with the *ger*.

---

## 24 Gifts Kehuna

### Klal Perat Structure

The Gemara transitions to a *beraita* enumerating the twenty-four gifts of *kehuna* given to Aharon and his sons: *esrim ve-arba matnos kehuna nitnu le-Aharon u-levanav*. The *beraita* notes that all twenty-four were given through the hermeneutical framework of *klal u-perat u-klal* — a general statement, followed by a list of particulars, followed by another general statement. Rashi cites the relevant verse from Parashat Korach: *lechol kodshei bnei Yisrael lecha netatim lemoshcha* — for all the sanctities of Israel I have given them to you for greatness — followed by an enumeration of the gifts, and concluded with *bechol trumat hakodashim*, another general statement. These twenty-four gifts are included within that comprehensive framework.

The *beraita* adds that this covenant is characterized as *brit melach* — a covenant of salt, eternal and unbreakable. Anyone who fulfills the obligation of giving these gifts is regarded as though he has fulfilled the entire *klal u-perat u-klal* and honored the *brit melach*. Anyone who transgresses and fails to give even one of them is regarded as though he has violated the entire framework.

### Ten Mikdash Gifts

The *beraita* divides the twenty-four gifts into three groups. The first group consists of ten gifts that apply within the *Beis Hamikdash*. These are: (1) *chatas behema* — the animal *chatas* offering, whose meat is eaten by the *kohanim*; (2) *chatas ha-of* — the bird *chatas*; (3) *asham vaday* — the *asham* brought for a definite sin, which includes *asham gezelos* (the case under discussion) as well as *me'ila* and other categories; (4) *asham taluy* — the *asham* brought for a doubtful sin, in cases where if the sin were confirmed one would bring a *chatas*; (5) *zivchei shalmei tzibur* — the communal *shelamim* offerings, most notably the two lambs brought on Shavuot, which unlike ordinary *shelamim* are *kodshei kodashim* and may be eaten only within the *Beis Hamikdash*; (6) *log shemen shel metzora* — the log of oil used in the purification *korban* of a *metzora*, which is likewise consumed only within the *azara*; (7) *mosar ha-omer* — the remainder of the *omer mincha*; (8) *shtei halechem* — the two loaves brought on Shavuot; (9) *lechem hapanim* — the showbread eaten weekly; and (10) *shiyarei menachos* — the portions left over from any *mincha* offering, which are *kodshei kodashim*.

### Four Jerusalem Gifts

The second group consists of four gifts associated with Yerushalayim, accessible to *kohanim* through their *korban*-related functions but not restricted to use within the *Mikdash* itself. These are: (1) *habechor* — the firstborn animal; (2) *bikurim* — the firstfruits; (3) the portions received from a *toda* offering and all *shelamim* — namely the *chazeh* and *shok*, the breast and thigh — which the *beraita* combines with the ram of the *nazir* under a single entry; and (4) *oros kodashim* — the hides of *korbanot*, including those of *kodshei kodashim* such as the *olah*.

The inclusion of the hides in this "Yerushalayim" category warrants attention. Rashi explains that the hides are not listed among the ten gifts that apply *bagevulin* — throughout the land — because they come to the *kohen* through the *korban* process, which takes place in the *Beis Hamikdash*. Yet they are also not listed among the ten gifts restricted to the *Mikdash*, because the definition of that category is items that become invalid if removed from the *kla'im* — the enclosure. The hides, once given to the *kohen*, may be taken anywhere; a *kohen* may fashion them into sandals and walk with them outside of Yerushalayim. Categorizing them as "Yerushalayim gifts" captures this intermediate status: they are given through the *Mikdash* process but are not restricted in use to that space.

### Ten Throughout Land

The third group consists of ten gifts that apply *bagevulin* — throughout the land of Israel. These are: (1) *terumah* — the first portion of grain; (2) *trumas ma'aser* — the tenth of the tithe that a *Levi* receives, which he in turn gives to a *kohen*; (3) *challah* — the portion of dough separated before baking; (4) *reishis hagez* — the first of the fleece-shearings; (5) *hamatanos* — the *zeroah, l'chayayim v'keivah*, the foreleg, cheeks, and maw given to the *kohen* when an animal is slaughtered; (6) *pidyon haben* — the five *shekalim* given to redeem a firstborn son; (7) *pidyon peter chamor* — the sheep given to redeem a firstborn donkey; (8) *sdei achuza* — the ancestral field that is sanctified and not redeemed, which passes to the *kohanim*; (9) *sdei charamim* — a field sanctified through *cherem*; and (10) *gezel hager* — the money returned in the case of *gezel hager*, which goes to the *kohanim*.

### Gezel Location

The inclusion of *gezel hager* in the *bagevulin* category is striking, and Tosafos explicitly flags it as a problem. The *beraita* places *gezel hager* alongside gifts like *terumah* and *challah* that can be given to any *kohen* anywhere in Israel. Yet throughout the preceding discussion, the Gemara has treated the returned money as possessing *korban*-like qualities: it cannot be given at night, it cannot be given in installments, and it must be distributed equally within the *mishmar*. The *mishmar* framework itself implies a connection to the rotating service groups who function in the *Mikdash*. Why then is *gezel hager* categorized as a gift *bagevulin* rather than one requiring delivery in Yerushalayim?

Tosafos poses this question directly, asking why *gezel hager* is counted among the ten *bagevulin* gifts, given Rava's ruling that if the money was returned at night or only in part it is invalid — just as would be the case with an *asham*. By the same logic, if you gave it outside of the *Beis Hamikdash*, should it not likewise be invalid?

Rashi addresses the problem differently. In his view, *gezel hager* is called a *gvulin* gift because you may give it to the *kohen* of the *mishmar* even outside of Yerushalayim — provided, however, that it is given to the *kohen* whose *mishmar* is currently on duty. Rashi adds that if the *kohen* happens to be home rather than serving in Yerushalayim that week, receiving the money outside the city is still valid, because it is his *mishmar* that is serving. The remarkable implication, as Rashi reads it, is that while the money carries all the formal characteristics of a *korban* in terms of timing, wholeness, and equal division, the act of giving it need not occur within Yerushalayim, as long as it is directed to the currently serving *mishmar*. The question of precisely where the act of giving must take place thus remains, in the words of the discussion, unresolved in a fully satisfying way. It is genuinely strange that the money is treated as *korban*-like in all these respects and yet the requirement that characterizes virtually every other *korban* — that it be brought to Yerushalayim — is apparently not applied here.

---

## Abbaye Partial Kapara

### Abbaye Proof

The *mishnah* addresses a case where the *gazlan* gives the money to the *mishmar* and then dies. In light of what has been established — that the *kohanim*'s right to the money exists only when it functions as part of *kapara*, and that if the *gazlan* dies before giving it the *yorshim* retain it — one might think the *yorshim* could demand the money back: their father died, the *kapara* was never completed, and the money was given on the condition that it would serve as *kapara*. The *mishnah* rules that the *yorshim* cannot make this claim. From this ruling, Abbaye derives a significant conclusion: *shma mina kesef mechaper mechtza* — the money achieves partial atonement in its own right.

The logic of Abbaye's proof is as follows. If the money accomplished nothing independently — if *kapara* was achieved solely by the combined force of the money and the *asham*, with neither having effect on its own — then the *yorshim* would have a compelling argument: the money was given under the assumption that *kapara* would be achieved, that assumption proved false, and therefore the *kohanim* should return what was given to them on false pretenses. *Adaata de-hachi lo yahav lei* — had the *gazlan* known that the *kapara* would not be completed, he would not have given the money. The fact that the *mishnah* nonetheless rules against the *yorshim* proves, in Abbaye's view, that the money did accomplish something — it achieved *kapara* in part.

### Future Conditions

The Gemara, however, challenges the premise of Abbaye's argument. Abbaye assumes that when someone acts without explicitly articulating the conditions under which he does so, an unarticulated expectation — one that was never stated but that would have shaped behavior had it been anticipated — can retroactively define the transaction. The Gemara asks: is this really so? Can a person always say, *adaata de-hachi lo yahav lei* — had I known this would happen, I never would have done it — and use that unarticulated assumption to reclaim what was given?

This question has significant implications far beyond the immediate case. The extent to which an unarticulated *da'at* — a privately held assumption that was never expressed — can void a transaction is a question that arises in discussions of *nedarim*, *kiddushin*, and matters touching on *agunah*. The Gemara proceeds to test the proposition through a series of parallel cases.

### Kodashim Parallels

The Gemara first considers the case of *chatas she-mesu be'aleha* — an animal that was sanctified as a *chatas* and then the owner died. The *halacha* is that such an animal must be left to die. Why, the Gemara asks, don't we say that the person never intended to sanctify the animal on the assumption that he would die? Had he anticipated that eventuality, he would never have separated it. If unarticulated conditions can retroactively void acts, the animal should revert to non-sacred status. The Gemara answers that the rule governing a *chatas* whose owner dies — that it goes to its death — is a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, a tradition that overrides the theoretical argument. In principle the argument may have force, but the tradition governs.

The Gemara then raises the parallel case of an *asham* whose owner died. There the *halacha* is that the animal grazes until it becomes blemished, at which point it is redeemed, and the proceeds are used for an *olah*. Why not say there too that the owner never intended to sanctify it assuming he would die? The Gemara answers again: *asham nami hilchisa gemiri la* — this too is a *halacha* transmitted by tradition, rooted in the principle that whatever would require a *chatas* to be left to die requires an *asham* to graze.

### Yevama Case

The Gemara then raises a case outside the realm of *kodashim* where the *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* argument is unavailable. *Yevama she-nafla lifnei mukeh shechin* — a woman whose husband dies and she falls into *yibum* before a brother-in-law who is afflicted with a repulsive physical condition. Ought she be permitted to walk away without even requiring *chalitza*? After all, *adaata de-hachi lo kidshta atzma* — had she known at the time of marriage that her husband would die and leave her bound to this brother-in-law, she never would have agreed to the marriage. If unarticulated assumptions can retroactively undo transactions, her *kiddushin* should be regarded as never having fully taken effect.

The Gemara rejects this argument on a different ground. *Anan sahadei d'minach nicha lah b'chol d'hu* — we know as a matter of fact that even had she been able to foresee the future, she still would have preferred to be married at the time, even knowing what lay ahead. As Reish Lakish states: *tav le-meitav tan du mi-le-meitav armelu* — it is better to dwell as two than to dwell as a widow. The threshold for claiming that a woman would have refused marriage even with full foreknowledge of what might come is very high. Without meeting that threshold, the unarticulated assumption cannot undo the *kiddushin*.

The relevance of this sugya to *agunah* discussions is apparent. The argument that "had I known my husband would withhold the *get* I never would have married him" encounters the same Talmudic response: the presumption is that a woman would still have chosen marriage, so the unarticulated condition cannot retroactively dissolve the *kiddushin*.

### Tosafos Unilateral

Tosafos draws a significant distinction in explaining why the Gemara's cases are not fully parallel to one another. Tosafos observes that the *kodashim* cases — sanctifying an animal as a *chatas* or *asham* — are unilateral acts. There is no other party to the transaction; the sanctification is accomplished by the individual alone. In bilateral transactions, *dvarim she-belev einam dvarim* — what is in one's heart and left unarticulated is legally irrelevant, because the other party to the transaction has rights that cannot be retroactively impaired by the first party's private assumptions. In a unilateral act, however, there may be greater latitude to allow an unarticulated condition to define the scope of the act.

The *yevama* case falls into this category as well, Tosafos explains, because the husband is already dead. The claim that the woman never would have entered the marriage under these circumstances is not impacting a living counterparty; the husband is gone, and the only practical effect is to free her from the *yibum* obligation to the brother-in-law. When there is no living party on the other side of the transaction, the argument from unarticulated assumption carries more weight than it would in a standard bilateral exchange.

### Context vs Condition

This analysis raises a further difficulty with the Gemara's challenge to Abbaye that deserves attention. All the cases the Gemara cites involve a completed transaction — sanctifying an animal as a *chatas*, entering into *kiddushin* — where some subsequent unforeseen development is being invoked to undo what was done. In those cases, the act was precisely what it was defined to be, and it is only some external future event that the party wishes to use to retroactively redefine their intent.

Abbaye's case, however, seems structurally different. The *gazlan* never gave the money as a simple gift. He gave it in the context of *kapara* — as a component of the atonement process. It was not a *stam matana*. If we conceive of it as similar to a down payment in a transaction that was never completed, then the question is not whether some unarticulated future assumption should undo an otherwise completed transaction. Rather, the money was given entirely within the context of *kapara*, and if *kapara* was never achieved, the very purpose for which it was given was never realized. Why the Gemara treats this as parallel to the *kodashim* and *yevama* cases — where the underlying act itself was complete and some external factor is being invoked retroactively — is not fully clear, and the parallel seems difficult to sustain.

---

## Order Money/Korban

### Normal Order

The *mishnah* establishes the basic rule for the order in which the money and the *asham* must be given. The *gazlan* gives the money to one *mishmar* of *kohanim*, and the *asham* is then offered by that same *mishmar*. This is the normal sequence: money first, then *korban*, both to the same group.

### Reversed Order

A *beraita*, however, addresses a case where the order is reversed. The *asham* was given to group one — Yehoyariv, the first *mishmar* — and the money was given to group two, Yedaya. What is to be done?

### Yehudah vs Hachamim

Rabbi Yehudah rules: *yachzir kesef etzel asham* — the money should be returned to follow the *asham*. That is, group two should return the money to group one, so that the money and the *asham* are in the same *mishmar*'s hands. The *chachamim* rule the opposite: *yachzir asham etzel kesef* — the *asham* follows the money. Group one gives the *asham* to group two, and group two brings the *korban*.

### Rava Timing

The *gemara* initially struggles to understand the scenario, since if the respective weeks of the two *mishmarot* have already passed, it is too late to transfer anything meaningfully. Rava clarifies: the case is where the *asham* was given to group one during its week, and the money was given to group two — also during group one's week, in advance of group two's turn. In that setting, the question of who holds what, and whose rights supersede, is still live.

According to Rabbi Yehudah, since it was not yet group two's week when they received the money, they are penalized: *le-Yedaya kensinan lah* — Yedaya must give the money back to group one. Group one will then hold both the money and the *asham*, and can bring the *korban* properly. According to the *rabbanan*, it is group one that acted wrongly: *shelo kedin avad benei Yehoyariv* — Yehoyariv should not have accepted the *asham* before the money was in hand. Because they accepted the *korban* before the money was paid, they are penalized, and the *asham* is given to group two to bring during its week.

### Group One Error

A *beraita* adds detail to Rabbi Yehudah's position. If, while the money is being transferred back to group one, group one jumps ahead and brings the *asham* before receiving the money, the *asham* is invalid and the person must bring another *asham* — this time ensuring the money is paid first. The new *asham* would then be brought by group two, which now holds the money.

### Invalid Korban Leather

One might ask: if the *asham* that group one brought prematurely is invalid, what do they retain? Rava rules: *le'oro* — they receive the hide. The meat of the invalid *asham* may not be eaten, but the leather remains theirs.

This ruling prompts a challenge from Tosafos. Elsewhere the principle appears to be that the leather of a *korban pasul* cannot be used or distributed. Tosafos leaves this as a genuine difficulty. One possible resolution is that the *psul* here is of a qualitatively different kind. A standard *psul* — *pigul*, a blemish, improper *shechita* — is intrinsic to the animal itself. Here, the animal is entirely *kasher*; its only defect is that it was offered before the money was paid. It is a *psul dechutz legufo* — a deficiency external to the animal itself. In that sense it resembles a *korban shelo lishmo*, where the animal is *kasher* but the owners do not receive *kapara*. However, even this parallel is imperfect, since in a *korban shelo lishmo* the *kohanim* do eat the meat, whereas here they apparently do not. The *asham* brought before the money thus occupies an anomalous intermediate status: not invalidated intrinsically, yet not fully valid in its function — and so the *kohanim* receive the leather but not the meat. It is a strange and unresolved issue, as Tosafos acknowledges.

The deeper principle underlying the requirement that money precede *korban* is worth pausing on. It reflects the classic teaching familiar from Masechet Yoma: one cannot seek forgiveness from God before making right what was done to one's fellow. The *korban* to God cannot precede restitution to man.

### Expired Mishmarot

The Gemara then addresses a further complication. What if both groups' weeks have expired and neither group made any demands of the other — group one never demanded the money from group two, and group two never demanded the *asham* from group one?

One might think the parties have been implicitly *mochel* to one another: group two keeps the money, group one keeps the *asham*, and when group one's turn comes around again in the cycle they will bring the *asham* after the money has already been in group two's possession. But the Gemara rules otherwise: *keivan delo tavu lehadadi kam bereisha* — since neither side made demands, the default rule reasserts itself, and the money follows the *korban*. Group two must return the money to group one.

The precise practicalities of how this plays out across the twenty-four week cycle of *mishmarot* are not fully spelled out in the Gemara, and certain logistical questions — such as the age restrictions on *korban* animals and the mechanics of holding a sanctified animal across multiple *mishmar* rotations — are left open.

---

## Scripture Order

### Rava Scripture

The Gemara now turns to the scriptural basis for the rule that the money must precede the *asham*. Rava derives it from the verse in the *parasha* of *gezel hager*: *ha'asham hamushav la-Hashem la-kohen milvad eil ha-kippurim asher yechaper bo alav* — "the *asham* that is returned to God, to the *kohen*, in addition to the ram of atonement with which he shall be atoned." Rava reads *ha'asham* here as referring to the money — the principal that is returned — and the phrase *milvad eil ha-kippurim* ("in addition to the ram of atonement") as establishing that the money comes first, since it is mentioned prior to the ram.

### Objection Order

One of the *rabbanan* challenges this reading. If *milvad* — "in addition to" — means that whatever follows must come second, then the verse describing the *musaf* offering, *milvad olat haboker asher le-olat hatamid* ("in addition to the morning *olah*"), would imply that the *musaf* comes before the morning *tamid*. But we know from a *beraita* that nothing precedes the morning *tamid*: *ve-arach aleha ha-ola* — the *olah* is the thing that inaugurates the altar each morning. The word *milvad* alone, therefore, cannot prove order.

### Future Tense

Rava responds that he does not derive the order from *milvad* alone. The decisive phrase is *asher yechaper bo* — "with which he *will* be atoned," in the future tense. The *korban* has not yet been brought at the time the verse speaks of returning the money. The verse thus presents the money as the present act and the ram as the future act — establishing that the money must come first.

### Learn from Meila

The Gemara then draws a parallel to the laws of *me'ila*. In a case of *me'ila* — misappropriating sanctified property — the offender must likewise return the principal and a *chomesh* and bring an *asham*. How do we know that bringing the *asham* before paying the principal is ineffective? From the verse *be-eil ha-asham ve-nislach lo* — "with the ram of the *asham* he shall be forgiven" — which is read as meaning: the word *asham* in this verse refers to the money (the principal), and only together with the *eil* (the ram) does one achieve forgiveness. But how do we know the word *asham* in the *me'ila* verse means the principal rather than the *korban*? Because in the *gezel hager* verse, the word *asham* is unambiguously the money — the verse says "the *asham*... in addition to the ram," making clear that *asham* and *eil* are distinct. From this the Gemara derives that in the *me'ila* verse as well, *asham* denotes the principal.

### Chomesh Not Required

Finally, the Gemara addresses whether the *chomesh* — the additional fifth — is *me-akev*, meaning whether failure to pay it prevents *kapara*. The *beraita* teaches from the verse *be-eil ha-asham ve-nislach lo* that only the *eil* (the ram) and the *asham* (the principal) are indispensable — not the *chomesh*. While the obligation to pay the *chomesh* exists, its non-payment does not block atonement.

This rule is then extended cross-textually: *ve-yilmed hekdesh me-hedyot ve-hedyot me-hekdesh* — *me'ila* and *gezel hager* illuminate each other. From *gezel hager* we learn how to read the word *asham* in the *me'ila* verse as referring to the principal. And from *me'ila* we learn that in *gezel hager* as well, the *chomesh* is not *me-akev* — the *chomesh*, while obligatory, does not stand between the offender and his *kapara*. Put another way: a monetary penalty (*knas*) is not *me-akev* one's *kapara*.

With this, the daf concludes the chapter *ha-gozel eitzim*, and the Gemara recites *Hadran*.

---

## Final Chapter Intro

### Back to Gezeilah

The final *perek* of Bava Kamma returns us to the foundational territory of the tractate. The preceding chapters explored a specialized corner of the law — the case of *gezel hager* with its unique *korban* and its unusual treatment of the returned money. The new *perek* takes us back to classic *gezeilah*, evoking in particular the beginning of the ninth *perek*, which focused heavily on *shinuy* — the transformation of stolen objects. Whereas the ninth *perek* concentrated on *shinuy ma'aseh*, the physical alteration of an object, this final *perek* will center on *shinuy reshut* — the change of domain or possession — and the circumstances under which a *gazlan* must return the object itself, must pay its value, or is released from obligation entirely.

### Thief Children

The *mishnah* opens with the following case: someone steals and feeds the stolen food to his children, and then dies. The children are *patur* — exempt from paying. This is immediately surprising. If the stolen object still exists (in consumed form, as nourishment to the children), why are they not obligated to make restitution? And the *mishnah* adds a further qualification: *ve-im haya davar sheyeish bo achrayut chayavin lishalem* — if it was something that carries a lien, such as land, they are obligated to pay. Why the distinction? The *mishnah* appears to require unpacking in two very different directions — both why the children are exempt in the ordinary case and why they are liable in the case of *achrayut*. Two distinct readings of the *mishnah* will emerge from the Gemara.

---

## Ye'ush Reshus

### Dual Liability

Rav Chisda states a general principle: if someone stole an object and the owners have not yet despaired of recovering it (*lo nisyashu habealim*), and then a second party comes and consumes the object, the original owner can collect from either party — *ratza mizeh goveh, ratza mizeh goveh*. The original *gazlan* is obviously liable. But so is the person who consumed the object, even though he received it from the *gazlan*. Both are answerable to the victim.

### Not Yet Despaired

The reason, Rav Chisda explains, is that *kol kamma d'lo nisyashu habealim, b'reshusei d'marei kai* — as long as the owners have not despaired, the stolen property remains legally within the owner's domain. When the second party consumed it, he was in effect taking and destroying property that still belonged to Joe. His liability to Joe therefore runs independently of the *gazlan*'s liability.

### Mishnah Resolved

The *gemara* then challenges this principle from the opening *mishnah*: the *gazlan* feeds his children and dies, and the children are exempt. If the property still belongs to the original owner at the moment the children consumed it — because *ye'ush* had not yet occurred — why are they not liable, just as the second party in Rav Chisda's case is liable? Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: *ki tanya hi l'achar ye'ush* — the *mishnah* is speaking about a case that takes place *after ye'ush*. The owner has already despaired of recovering the property by the time the children consume it. That is why they are exempt.

### Weakened Ownership

The distinction between before and after *ye'ush* maps onto a broader principle. Before *ye'ush*, the owner's claim is intact and extends to whoever comes into contact with the stolen property. After *ye'ush*, the owner's legal grip on the object has weakened to the point that those who receive or consume it cannot be held liable as thieves or tortfeasors. The *mishnah* accordingly exempts the children because, by the time they consumed the food, the owner's ownership had already been attenuated through *ye'ush*. The concept of *shinuy reshut* — a change in possession — will be developed further as the *perek* continues, exploring precisely how much the owner's claim diminishes when *ye'ush* and changes of domain combine.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 112

## Rav Chisda & Rami bar Ch…

### Gozel u-Ma'akhil Overview

The daf opens at the bottom of 111b with the phrase *amar mar*, picking up from the discussion of the *mishna* concerning *ha-gozel u-ma'akhil et banav* — one who steals an object and feeds it to his children, or leaves the stolen article for his children to inherit. The *mishna* rules that the children are *patur* — exempt from payment — unless the matter involves *achrayut nechasim*, in which case they are *chayav*. The precise meaning of *achrayut nechasim* in this context is left somewhat open, and the entire ensuing discussion turns on two foundational positions that must be kept clearly in view throughout.

### Rav Chisda: After Ye'ush

The first position is that of Rav Chisda. According to Rav Chisda, if a second party comes and consumes a stolen object before *ye'ush* — before the original owner has despaired of recovering it — that second party is obligated to pay. The principle is stated as follows: *gezel ve-lo nityaeishu ha-be'alim u-va acher ve-akhal* — if an object was stolen and the owner had not yet despaired, and another person came and ate it — then *ratza mi-ze gove ve-ratza mi-ze gove*: the owner may collect from either party. This means that for Rav Chisda, the case in the *mishna* where children who are fed stolen food are *patur* must necessarily be speaking of a situation *after ye'ush*, not before. Before *ye'ush*, the owner retains a claim against whoever consumed the object; only after *ye'ush* does the children's exemption make sense on his account.

### Rami bar Chama Position

The second position is that of Rami bar Chama, who invokes the principle *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach dami* — that a heir's acquisition of property is treated like a purchaser's acquisition, constituting a *shinui reshut*, a change of domain. This principle is relevant to the second clause of the *mishna*, which speaks of *hiniach lifneihem* — the father leaving the stolen article in front of the children — with the *mishna* ruling that the children are *patur*. The straightforward reading of this clause is that the *gezeila* is still *be-ein*, still physically present and extant, and yet the children need not return it. The question is: on what grounds? Rami bar Chama answers that when combined with *ye'ush* — the owner's despair — the *shinui reshut* inherent in the children's inheritance (*reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach*) suffices to exempt them.

### Reconciling Positions

Putting the two positions together: the exemption in the first part of the *mishna*, where the children ate the stolen food, works according to Rav Chisda only *after ye'ush*. The exemption in the second part, where the object is left before them and is still extant, is explained by Rami bar Chama as a case of *ye'ush* combined with *shinui reshut*. If one does not accept either of these explanations — neither that we are speaking after *ye'ush* nor that *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach* — then one would have to say that the reason the children are *patur* in the second case is simply that the *gezeila* was in fact consumed, and the only variable between the two cases of the *mishna* is whether the children consumed it during the father's lifetime or after his death.

---

## Braita of Rabbi Oshaya

### Kayemet vs. Consumed

The *gemara* now turns to the *braita* of Rabbi Oshaya and tests both positions against it. The *braita* states: when the *gezeila* is no longer present — *ein ha-gezeila kayemet* — the children are *patur*. The converse is implied: when the stolen object is still *kayemet*, they are obligated to return it.

### Testing Rav Chisda

This immediately raises the question: does the *braita* constitute a refutation of Rav Chisda? If the exemption when the object has been consumed applies even before *ye'ush*, that would cut against Rav Chisda's position that before *ye'ush* the second party who consumes the object is liable.

### Rav Chisda's Defense

Rav Chisda deflects the challenge: *ki tanya hi le-achar ye'ush* — this *braita* is speaking only of a case after *ye'ush*. Just as the *mishna's* exemption for the children who ate the stolen food is, in Rav Chisda's reading, set after *ye'ush*, so too the *braita* speaks in that same post-*ye'ush* frame.

### Testing Rami bar Chama

The *gemara* then presses the other side. The *braita* states that when the *gezeila* is still present — *gezeila kayemet* — the children are *chayavim le-shalem*, obligated to pay. But this seems to contradict Rami bar Chama, who maintained that *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach* — the children's inheritance constitutes a *shinui reshut* — and the *mishna* seemed to indicate that even when the object is *be-ein*, the children are *patur*. If the *braita* says that when it is *kayemet* they must pay, does this not undermine the principle of *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach*?

### Rami bar Chama's Defense

Rami bar Chama responds in kind: *ki tanya hi lifnei ye'ush* — this *braita* is speaking of a case before *ye'ush*. Before *ye'ush*, of course *reshut yoresh* does not function as *reshut loke'ach*, and the children would have to return the object. It is only after *ye'ush* that *ye'ush* combined with *shinui reshut* exempts them. So both positions survive the challenge from the *braita* by assigning it to the opposite side of the *ye'ush* divide.

---

## Rava on Interest Money

### Interest Money Case Setup

The *gemara* records that Rav Adda bar Ahava taught the principle of Rami bar Chama — *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach* — not in connection with the stolen object cases of the *mishna*, but rather in connection with a *braita* about interest money: *heniach lahem avihem ma'ot shel ribit* — the father left his children money that he had collected through charging interest. Even though the children are aware that this is *ribit* money, *ein chayavim lehachzir* — they are not obligated to return it. From this, Rami bar Chama inferred *zot omeret reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach dami* — the *braita's* exemption can only be explained if the heir's domain is treated like a purchaser's, constituting a genuine change of possession.

The logic being: if the money were still considered to be in the continuity of the father's estate, one would expect an obligation to restore it. The fact that the children are exempt must mean that once it passes to the heirs, it is in a genuinely new domain — and that is the principle of *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach*.

### Rava's Distinction

Rava challenges this inference. *Le-olam eima lecha reshut yoresh lav ke-reshut loke'ach dami* — one can actually maintain that the heir's domain is not like a purchaser's, that there is no fundamental *shinui reshut* when property descends to children. The money remains, in a sense, a continuation of the father's estate. And yet the children are still exempt from returning the *ribit* money — not because of *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach*, but for an entirely different reason.

### Vchi Achicha Imach

Rava points to the *pasuk* that underlies the entire obligation to return *ribit*. The verse says *al tikach me'ito neshech ve-tarbit* — do not take from him interest — and concludes *ve-chai achicha imach*, that your brother should live together with you. From this phrase, the *gemara* derives *ahadreih leih ki heichi de-nichi bahadach* — return it to him so that the two of you may live well together. The obligation to return *ribit* is thus not grounded in the straightforward principle that the money belongs to someone else the way a stolen object does. The person who was charged interest paid it willingly; it is not simply theft. Rather, the Torah issues a special directive aimed at restoring a proper relationship between the lender and borrower.

### Personal Obligation Only

This distinction carries decisive consequences. *Le-didei kamzahar lei rachmana* — it is the individual who charged interest whom the Torah commands to make this restoration. *Livrei lo kamzahar lei rachmana* — the Torah's command does not extend to his son. The obligation to return *ribit* is thus a *personal* obligation incumbent on the one who actually charged it, not a property-based claim against the estate. It follows that the children's exemption has nothing to do with whether *reshut yoresh* is or is not like *reshut loke'ach*. Even if the money is still considered to be in the same domain, the obligation to return it simply does not transfer to the heirs, because the Torah addressed only the one who charged *ribit* and not his children.

---

## Application to Mishna/Br…

### Braita Application

Having established these two understandings of Rami bar Chama's teaching — whether it was said in connection with the *braita* about *ribit* or with the *mishna* about the stolen object — the *gemara* now analyzes the implications of each.

*Man de-masni lah a-baraita kol sheken a-matnitin*: the one who applies the principle of *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach* to the *braita* about *ribit* would certainly apply it to the *mishna* as well. The reasoning, as Rashi explains, is that the *mishna's* plain meaning — that even when the *gezeila* is *be-ein* the children are *patur* — can only be explained by *ye'ush* combined with *shinui reshut*, which is precisely *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach*. The *mishna* therefore provides the stronger case for the principle. If you invoke *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach* in the *braita* — where there is an alternative explanation available — you would certainly apply it to the *mishna*, which demands it.

### Mishna Application

The converse is not symmetric. *Aval a-baraita Rami bar Chama ke-Rava masni lah* — but when it comes to the *braita* about *ribit*, one could well follow Rava's reasoning and say that the exemption for the children has nothing to do with *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach*. The *ribit* money is fundamentally the lender's own property — it was freely paid to him, even if that transaction was forbidden. The reason the children need not return it is simply that the Torah's directive to restore the relationship is a personal obligation on the one who charged *ribit*, and it does not pass to his heirs. This has no bearing on the question of *shinui reshut* at all. So if Rami bar Chama's principle was stated only with respect to the *mishna*, the *braita* about *ribit* can be explained on entirely different grounds.

---

## Mishna: Two Cases

### Case 1: Fed Children

The *gemara* cites a *braita* that tracks the structure of our *mishna*. *Ha-gozel u-ma'akhil et banav peturin li-shalem* — one who steals and feeds it to the children, the children are exempt from payment. This mirrors the first clause of the *mishna* straightforwardly.

### Case 2: Left Before Them

*Hiniach lifneihem* — if he left it in front of them — and here the plain sense, as throughout this discussion, is that the *gezeila* is *be-ein*, the object still exists — *gedolim chayavim li-shalem, ketanim peturim li-shalem*: adult children are obligated to pay, minor children are exempt. The reasons for each of these rulings deserve examination. Adult children must return the object because, whether we are speaking before *ye'ush* or after *ye'ush* under a view that denies *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach*, there is always a framework under which a *be-ein* stolen object must be returned. In neither scenario can the adult heirs retain it.

---

## Gezeilah Be'ein Rule (II)

### Adult Ignorance Claim

The case of the minor children is different — they cannot be sued because requiring them to answer testimony in court is a violation of the principle of *mekabelin eidut she-lo bifnei ba'al din*: one cannot proceed with a case when the opposing party is not capable of defending themselves. A minor does not have full legal standing to face accusers in court, so the proceeding must wait until they reach majority. The stolen object will be retrieved, but not until the children can respond.

The *braita* then introduces a wrinkle: *ve-im amru gedolim einanu yod'in cheshbonot she-chishav avinu imach* — if the adult children declare that they do not know the arrangement their father made with the claimant, perhaps the father paid for the object or was given permission to keep it — in that case, *peturim*, they are exempt. The *gemara* presses: does simply saying "we don't know" actually exempt them? You can see plainly that the object is in their home; the claimant knows what his property looks like. How does a plea of ignorance relieve them of the obligation to return what appears to be a stolen item?

---

## Mishna: Two Cases (II)

### Rava's Reinterpretation

Rava reinterprets the clause entirely. *Hachi ka-amar*: what the *braita* is actually saying is this: *gedolim she-amru yod'in anu cheshbonot she-chishav avinu imach ve-lo pashat lach gabai ve-lo midei peturim* — if the adult children affirmatively state that they *do* know the arrangement, and specifically that their father paid the claimant and nothing further is owed, in that case they are exempt. The reason is *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-rayah* — possession is presumptive and the burden of proof lies with the one seeking to extract property from another's possession. Even if the claimant can demonstrate the object was once his, it is now in the children's possession, and if the children assert their father paid for it, they are believed. The original reading — where "we don't know" creates an exemption — is rejected; it is only an affirmative claim of knowledge of the father's arrangement that suffices.

---

## Alternative Braita

### Consumption Braita

The *gemara* cites a further *braita*: *tanya idach*, there is another teaching. *Ha-gozel u-ma'akhil banav peturin li-shalem* — one who steals and feeds the children, they are exempt — consistent with what we have seen. *Hiniach lifneihem ve-achalum, bein gedolim bein ketanim chayavim* — if the father left the *gezeila* before the children and they consumed it, whether adults or minors, they are obligated.

### Minor Liability Problem

This is a striking formulation. *Ketanim mi-mechayvei?* — how can minors be obligated? In the previous discussion the object was still *be-ein* and the question was whether one can accept testimony against a minor. But here the object has been consumed, so this is not about retrieval. The children would now be obligated to pay from their own resources. But *velo yehei ela de-azik azuki* — even if a minor damages property outright, they incur no monetary liability. There is no mechanism for obligating a minor to pay damages. How then can this *braita* impose liability on minors who consumed a stolen object?

### Rav Papa Solution

Rav Papa resolves the difficulty by correcting the text: *hachi ka-amar, hiniach lifneihem ve-adayin lo achlum* — the word *achalum*, "they ate it," is a misreading. The *braita* is actually saying they have not yet eaten it, the *gezeila* is still around. *Bein gedolim bein ketanim chayavim* then means that both adults and minors are obligated to return it. This *braita* thus differs from the previous one, which exempted minors even when the object was *be-ein*; this *braita* obligates even minors. The disagreement between the two *braitot* reflects the underlying debate — parallel to the dispute between Sumchos and the *rabbanan* — about whether court proceedings may be conducted against a minor who holds property that belongs to another.

---

## Borrowed Cow Case

### Cow Inheritance Setup

The *gemara* now introduces a new case. *Hiniach lahem avihem para she'ula* — their father left them a borrowed cow. The father had borrowed the cow for a fixed period, and upon his death the children inherited his rights in the arrangement — meaning they may use the cow for the duration of the original loan period. One way of conceptualizing *she'ila* is as a *matana le-guf le-feirot li-zman* — a gift of the use of an object for a limited time, analogous to how one can gift property itself or its usufruct for a specified term. The children step into the borrower's shoes and may continue to use the cow during that time.

### Death by Accident

*Meita, ein chayavim be-onsa* — if the cow dies of natural causes, not through any fault of the children, they are not obligated to pay. This requires explanation. A *sho'el* — a borrower — is normally obligated even in cases of *onsin*, accidents beyond one's control; the borrower assumes maximum liability. Why then are the children exempt? The *braita* is operating on the premise that the obligation to pay for *onsin* is a personal obligation assumed by the individual who undertook the *she'ila* — namely, the father. The property rights in the cow — the right to use it — can descend to the children as an inheritance. But the personal obligation of the *sho'el* does not transfer to the heirs. The father took on this obligation; it is his alone.

### Slaughter and Consumption

*Kesvurim shel avihem hi* — if the children did not realize the cow was borrowed and assumed it belonged to their father, and they slaughtered and ate it, *meshalmin demei basar be-zol*: they pay only the discounted value of the meat, approximately two-thirds of the cow's market value, as Rashi specifies.

The reasoning here is layered. We have already established that the children bear no obligation as *sho'el* — they did not personally assume that liability. One might then argue they should pay as *mazik* — as ones who damaged another's property — since they slaughtered someone else's cow. But *adam mu'ad le-olam* applies only when one's relationship to the property is understood from the outset as an encounter with another's object; it is only in that context that even accidental damage generates liability. Here, the children had every reason to believe the cow was their own father's property, located in their home when he died. Their relationship to it was fundamentally one of assumed ownership, not of engagement with another's property. They are therefore not *mazik* in the full sense. The only claim against them is the benefit they received — the value of the meat they consumed — and that benefit is assessed at two-thirds of market value.

### Achrayut Nechasim Releva…

There is a final clause: *heniach lahem avihem achrayut nechasim chayavim le-shalem* — if the father left them real property with liens on it, they are obligated to pay. The *gemara* debates which of the two preceding cases this clause refers to, noting that some teach it against the first case — the cow dying of natural causes — and some teach it against the second case — the slaughter and consumption.

---

## Rav Papa on Obligation T…

### Obligation at Damage

To understand these positions, the *gemara* introduces a teaching of Rav Papa that bears directly on the question. *De-amar Rav Papa*: Rav Papa's view is that the obligation of a *sho'el* — a borrower — arises at the moment the damage occurs, not from the moment the borrowing began.

### Borrowed Before Shabbat

The *gemara* illustrates with the following case: one who stole a cow before *Shabbat* and slaughtered it on *Shabbat* — *chayav*, obligated to pay four or five, the penalty for *geneiva* with *tevicha*. Why? *She-kevar nischayev be-geneiva kodem she-ba li-yedei issur Shabbat* — because the principal obligation and the *kefel* were incurred at the moment of theft on Thursday, before any *chillul Shabbat* took place. The additional payment of four or five is a *kenas* — a rabbinic fine — and a *kenas* incurred prior to a capital offense is not absorbed by the principle of *kim lei be-drabba minei*.

However, if the person had *borrowed* the cow on Thursday and slaughtered it on *Shabbat*, he is *patur* — exempt — because *issur Shabbat ve-issur geneiva ba'im ke-echad*: the prohibition of *Shabbat* and whatever theft-equivalent obligation arises from destroying the borrowed object come simultaneously. There is no prior moment at which a monetary obligation was created and then survives the *chillul Shabbat*. The conclusion is that Rav Papa's position is that the *sho'el's* obligation arises at the moment of the damaging event, not retroactively from the moment the loan was struck.

This also means the borrower owes nothing as *sho'el* for what happened on *Shabbat* — and one might ask whether he owes as *mazik*. The answer is no, because that monetary obligation also arises at the same moment as the *chillul Shabbat*, and is absorbed by *kim lei be-drabba minei*.

### Obligation at Borrowing

The contrasting view holds that when the father borrowed the cow, the owner of the cow immediately acquired a lien on the father's property — because the obligation to return the cow (or its value) attaches from the moment of borrowing. On this view, the moment the father took the cow on loan, the cow's owner became a creditor of the father, with all the normal implications for *achrayut nechasim*. The cow subsequently dying — even during the children's custodianship — simply triggers the collection of an obligation that came into existence when the father was alive and against which his estate was already encumbered.

### Achrayut Application

This debate determines how to read the *achrayut nechasim* clause in our *braita*. If one teaches it against the *first* case — where the cow died of natural causes — one necessarily disagrees with Rav Papa. On Rav Papa's view, the obligation of the *sho'el* did not exist until the cow died, at which point it was already in the hands of the children and the father's estate bore no prior lien. There is therefore nothing to collect from real estate. But if one holds that the obligation began at the moment of borrowing — while the father was alive — then the estate was already encumbered, and the cow's owner may collect from the real property even though the children themselves were not personally obligated as *sho'el*.

If, on the other hand, one teaches the *achrayut nechasim* clause against only the *second* case — the slaughter and consumption — then Rav Papa's position is preserved. In the case where the children slaughtered the cow thinking it was their father's, the question of *achrayut* is distinct: it is not about *sho'el* liability at all, but about whether the children, by consuming the cow, are seen as a continuation of the father's domain. Rashi's formulation suggests that the presence of real estate indicates a degree of continuity between the children and the father — analogous in spirit to *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach* — so that if there is real property, they pay full value rather than the discounted benefit assessment.

---

## Pasuk on Returning Gezei…

### Veheishiv Pasuk

The *gemara* now turns to an explicit *pasuk*. *Ve-heishiv et ha-gezeila asher gazal* — you shall return the stolen object that you stole. The *braita* asks: *mah talmud lomar asher gazal* — what does the added phrase "that you stole" come to teach? *Yachzir ke-ein she-gazal* — one must return it in the form in which it was stolen, i.e., only when the object still exists as it was.

### Children Exempt When Con…

From this the *gemara* derives: *mikan amru, ha-gozel u-ma'akhil et banav peturim li-shalem* — from here they said that one who steals and feeds the stolen object to his children, those children are exempt from payment. Tosafot notes that this *pasuk*-based derivation actually works better *not* according to Rav Chisda. Rav Chisda grounded the children's exemption in the *ye'ush* framework — the obligation of the consuming party depends on whether *ye'ush* has occurred. But this *pasuk* says something broader: the obligation to return a stolen object applies only when it still exists. If it has been consumed — even before *ye'ush* — the children are not obligated, not as *gazlan* and not as *mazik*. The Torah here provides a special teaching: for the children of the thief, the obligation to make restitution applies only when the object is still present.

### Obligation Only If Exists

The logic is carefully bounded. For the *gazlan* himself, destruction of the object does not extinguish his obligation — he must pay the equivalent value. But the *pasuk* teaches that for *his children*, the *she'ila* of restitution is tethered to the physical existence of the object: *yachzir ke-ein she-gazal*. If it no longer exists, the children bear no liability — not as secondary *gazlanim*, not as *mazik*.

---

## Gezeilah Be'ein Rule (II)

### Adults Must Return

Returning to the case where the *gezeila* is *be-ein* — still extant — the *braita* cited earlier rules: *hiniach lifneihem bein gedolim bein ketanim chayavim* — if the father left the stolen object in front of them and it is still present, whether adults or minors they are obligated. The adult children clearly must return it, as there is no framework — whether before or after *ye'ush*, whether or not one accepts *reshut yoresh ke-reshut loke'ach* — under which they may retain another's property when it is plainly before them.

### Minors Cannot Be Sued

The minor children present a different problem. Even if the object is unambiguously identifiable as belonging to the claimant, one cannot bring a court case against a minor to compel its return. This is the principle of *mekabelin eidut she-lo bifnei ba'al din*: court proceedings must be conducted in the presence of the opposing party, and a minor does not have the standing to defend himself. The owner must wait until the children reach majority.

### Sumchos vs. Mainstream
