# Bava Kamma 114

## Previous Topics & Setup

### Prior Discussion Review

The previous daf centered on two major discussions: *dina d'malchuta dina* and *gezel goy*. The key point the *mishna* focused on was the case of someone who has stolen money in their purse — one is not permitted to make change from such a pouch, either because the original owners have not yet despaired of recovering it (*ye'ush*) and one would thereby be directly handling stolen funds, or because even if the owners have despaired, it is nonetheless unseemly to take directly from the very pouch in which stolen goods are stored.

### Tax Collectors & Bandits

The *mishna* continues with the case of tax collectors. *Natlu mochsin es chamoro* — the tax collectors seized your donkey and, out of a kind of *rachmanus*, exchanged it for another. *Natlu listim es kesuso* — bandits took your garment and gave you another in its place. *Harei elu shelo* — what they gave you, you are permitted to keep, even though it was seized from someone else. The reason: *mipnei shekvar nityashu mehem* — we may assume the original owners have already despaired of recovering it, and there is thus *ye'ush v'shinui reshus*.

It is worth noting that *listim* and *mochsin* are treated as the same category — which implicitly acknowledges that the tax collectors here are themselves acting as *ganavim*. Though they operate with a veneer of professionalism, the *halacha* treats them accordingly.

### Ye'ush Resolution

The Rashba reconciles this *mishna* with the earlier prohibition against taking from the stolen-goods pouch by drawing a distinction between *l'chatchila* and *b'diavad*. Although we do presume *ye'ush* once *mochsin* take people's property — since people generally give up hope of recovering what tax collectors seize — taking directly from that pouch *l'chatchila* is nonetheless inappropriate. In the present case, however, there is an element of salvaging something from the situation, and in any case the exchange has already occurred, making it a *b'diavad* scenario in which one may keep what was received.

## Rescue Cases & Ye'ush

### Rescued Items

The *mishna* shifts to a different category of *ye'ush*, one that blends elements of *aveida* and theft: *hamatzil min hanahar, min hagayis, u'min halistim* — one who rescues an object swept away by a river, seized by troops, or taken by bandits. *Im nityashu hab'alim harei elu shelo* — if the owners despaired of recovery, the rescuer may keep it. This is structurally similar to the earlier case: it is after the fact, there is an element of salvaging, and the combination of *ye'ush v'shinui reshus* is operative. One might ask, however, whether by accepting the item the rescuer is himself completing the *shinui reshus* — becoming a party to removing it from the owner's control. Yet the *mishna* permits it, reasoning that since it is after the fact and something is being rescued, the acquisition stands.

### Presume vs. Establish

A subtle but critical distinction emerges from reading the *mishna* as a whole. The first clause, dealing with *listim* and *mochsin*, appears to *presume* *ye'ush* — we assume it occurred. The second clause, dealing with rivers, troops, and bandits, speaks of *ye'ush* in terms of whether it actually occurred. This will be the *gemara*'s central question: when may *ye'ush* be presumed, and when must it be concretely established?

## Swarm of Bees

### Bees & Testimony

The *mishna* continues: *vecheyn nachilo shel devorim* — similarly, a swarm of bees. If bees flee from their keeper's apiary and the owner despairs of recovering them, someone else may acquire them. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka: nemenet isha o katan lomar mikan yatza nachil zeh* — a woman or a minor, whose testimony is ordinarily inadmissible, is believed to say that the swarm emerged from a particular person's property. The obvious difficulty is why their testimony should be accepted at all, and the *gemara* will address this below.

### Field Entry Rights

The *mishna* also addresses pursuit of the swarm: *umehalech betoch sadeh chaveiro lehatzil et nachilo* — one is permitted to enter a neighbor's field in order to retrieve a swarm that has alighted there. *Ve'im hizik, meshaleim mah shehizik* — if one causes damage in the process of pursuit, one must pay for what was damaged. This is permitted because of the urgency of the situation: the bees are in motion and may escape entirely if not pursued immediately.

### Branch Cutting Rule

A more deliberate act is treated differently. *Aval lo yikotz et sacho al menat litein et hadamim* — one may not cut off a branch upon which the swarm has nested, even with the intention of paying for it, without the owner's permission. Cutting the branch is a conscious, deliberate act of *mazik*, qualitatively different from incidental damage caused during hot pursuit.

*Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka* dissents: one may indeed cut the branch and pay for it. The *gemara* will clarify that this is not a general principle permitting deliberate damage to another's property in order to protect one's own — even with the intention to reimburse. Rather, it is a special dispensation for the particular case of a bee swarm. The broader question — whether one may destroy another's lesser-valued property to save one's own more-valuable property — is not resolved by this *mishna*, and the *gemara* treats it as a case-specific ruling.

## Tannaic Ye'ush Debate

### Conflicting Braita

A *braita* appears to contradict the *mishna*: *im natal machzir lib'alim rishonim* — if one took the exchanged donkey, one must return it to the original owners. This seems to say that *ye'ush* alone does not effect acquisition, and that since one was a party to the transition of ownership — accepting the item from the tax collector directly — one has a real obligation to return it.

Rashi explains: *ye'ush kedi shenityashu hab'alim beyad hamoches lo kana hamoches beye'ush lachudo* — the tax collector does not acquire through *ye'ush* alone. And since the recipient's own acceptance was the act that completed the removal of the object from the owner's control, he too bears responsibility.

This seems at odds with everything learned until now — that a third party who receives stolen property after *ye'ush* acquires it fully. The Rashba resolves the tension by reading the *braita* not as a strict legal contradiction but as an expression of *middas chasidus*: the *mishna* states the technical *halacha* — *harei elu shelo*, you legally own it — while the *braita* teaches that the morally appropriate thing to do is to return it to the original owners. This is especially true in the version of the case where the recipient was himself the initiator of the exchange, actively requesting the substitute donkey rather than passively receiving it.

A second version of this teaching (*ve'ika d'amrei*) softens it further: *im ba l'hachzir, yachzir lib'alim harishonim* — if one *wishes* to return it, one should return it to the original owners, not to the tax collector. *Ye'ush kani* — because *ye'ush* alone does effect acquisition, and this is purely a voluntary act. On this reading, the debate within the *braita* may not concern *ye'ush* itself at all, but rather the degree of moral responsibility one bears when one was the direct agent of the *shinui reshus*. One opinion holds that since the recipient completed the transition, there is a genuine moral imperative to return it. The other holds that once *ye'ush* occurred in the hands of the *moches*, one bears no greater responsibility than one who picks up a lost object after the owner has despaired — one may keep it, and returning it is simply an act of piety.

One might ask, as arose in discussion, whether this reflects a broader pattern in the *gemara* whereby the legal standard and the moral sensibility operate on largely independent tracks. That observation is apt: the *gemara* does not routinely derive the legal rule from moral intuition, and the discussion here is a notable example of that divergence.

### Jewish vs. Non-Jewish

With this backdrop established, the *gemara* turns to the narrower question: when may *ye'ush* be presumed, and when must it be proven? *Amar Rav Assi: lo shanu ela listim oved kochavim* — this presumption of *ye'ush* applies only to non-Jewish bandits. *Aval listim Yisrael, lo* — by a Jewish bandit, there is no presumption of *ye'ush*. Why? *Savar l'machar nakitna lei b'dina* — one believes that a Jewish bandit is more subject to *beis din*, that one can pursue the matter legally, and therefore one does not despair.

### Rav Yosef Counter

*Masiv leh Rav Yosef: aderaba, ipcha mistabra* — on the contrary, the opposite makes more sense. Regarding non-Jews: *de-dina be-geisei* — non-Jewish courts are more expansive in their willingness to find defendants liable, accepting even a single witness and relying more readily on circumstantial evidence. Precisely because of this, a victim feels he has a real prospect of winning a case in a non-Jewish court — and therefore does not despair. By contrast, *Yisrael, keivan de-amri meimar miya'esh* — when Jews are involved, since enforcement relies only on words and communal pressure without the backing of governmental force, one is *more* readily *miya'esh*. Rashi offers two explanations of the phrase *de-amri meimar*: first, that a *beis din* ruling cannot be physically enforced and depends entirely on the defendant's voluntary compliance; second, that Jewish courts require higher standards of evidence — *mi yeimar ked-ka'amrat*, "who says you're telling the truth?" — making it harder to prove one's claim.

The irony here is striking. What the *gemara* is effectively saying is that people feel greater confidence in obtaining justice — and actually recovering their property — through the secular legal system. This resonates clearly today. The observation cuts in multiple directions: on one hand, a non-Jewish court may enforce its judgment; on the other, its lower evidentiary standards that the *gemara* associates with greater confidence for the plaintiff are the same standards that a Jewish legal system, rooted in rigorous rules of evidence, deliberately refuses to employ. The *gemara*'s plain sense is that the *niglad* feels more likely to win in secular court — and that itself is a *chillul Hashem* dimension worth noting, as the *gemara* identified just the previous daf.

The *gemara* then repositions Rav Assi's distinction. The statement that *ye'ush* only applies to non-Jewish *listim* was not made about the *reisha* of the *mishna* — where we presume *ye'ush* — but about the *seifa*, where *ye'ush* must be established. *Lo shanu ela Akum* — with non-Jewish bandits, the default is *no* presumption of *ye'ush*; one must know that *ye'ush* actually occurred. *Aval listim Yisrael* — by Jewish bandits, since the victim is more readily *miya'esh*, we do presume it.

## Gannav vs. Gazlan

### Keilim Sources

The *gemara* now probes the underpinnings of these presumptions through a *mishna* in *Keilim*. The case involves a piece of leather being processed: if the homeowner — not a professional tanner — decides the leather is sufficiently processed and intends to use it as a mat, *machshavah metama'atan* — his intention is sufficient to render it a *kli* subject to *tumah*. But if the leather belongs to a professional tanner, *ein machshavah metama'atan* — his intention is irrelevant, because the determination belongs to the customer who commissioned the work. Then: *shel gazlan ein machshavah metama'atan* — if a *gazlan* decides to use the stolen leather in a certain way, his *machshavah* does not render it a *kli*, because we presume the owners have *not* yet despaired. The logic is that a *gazlan* acts openly; the victim knows who robbed him and retains hope of recovering the object through legal recourse. Since *ye'ush* has not occurred, the original owners' claim persists, and the *gazlan*'s *machshavah* is legally irrelevant. By contrast: *aval shel ganav, machshavah metama'atan* — a *ganav* steals covertly, and since the victim has no idea who took the object, he despairs immediately. After *ye'ush*, the *ganav*'s effective de facto control is recognized for purposes of *machshavah*.

### Rabbi Shimon View

*Rabbi Shimon omer chiluf hadavar* — the exact reverse. *Shel gazlan machshavah metama'atan* — by a *gazlan*, the *machshavah* does count, because Rashi explains that the victim, seeing someone so brazen as to rob openly in broad daylight, concludes immediately that there is no hope of recovery and despairs at once. *Aval shel ganav, ein machshavah metama'atan* — by a *ganav*, the victim has not despaired; a burglar, precisely because he operates in secret, can be caught. People tend to feel that a clandestine thief leaves a pattern and can eventually be apprehended, while an open robber seems untouchable.

### Ulla Position

*Amar Ulla: machlokes b'stam* — this dispute between the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Shimon applies only when we do not know the facts. *Aval beyadua* — but when we actually know whether *ye'ush* occurred, *divrei hakol ye'ush koneh* — everyone agrees: established, concrete *ye'ush* effects acquisition. The dispute is purely about the presumptions we make in ambiguous cases.

### Rabbah Disagrees

*Rabbah amar: beyadua nami machlokes* — Rabbah maintains that even when we have concrete knowledge that the owner despaired, the dispute remains. Rabbah's reasoning is almost psychological: one can say one has given up hope, but at some deeper level the owner never truly abandons the wish to recover the object. The person whose car is stolen says "I'll never see it again" while still calling the police monthly. For Rabbah, therefore, even a declared *ye'ush* is subject to the same fundamental debate about whether genuine despair ever occurs for a *ganav* or *gazlan*.

*Abaye* challenged Rabbah, arguing that the *mishna* in *Keilim* itself teaches like Ulla: the language *mishelo nisyashu hab'alim* — "because the owners have not despaired" — implies that the absence of known *ye'ush* is the reason, meaning that *if* the owners did in fact despair, everyone agrees it would count. Rabbah responds: the phrase does not mean "because they have not yet despaired"; it means "because *ye'ush* of the owners is inherently meaningless here" — a significant re-reading that interprets the *mishna* as expressing an objective determination rather than a contingent one.

## Multi-Source Analysis

### Tanna Identification

The *gemara* now attempts to determine which *tanna* the *mishna* on our daf follows. The difficulty is that the *mishna* presumes *ye'ush* in two cases — the tax collector (*mochsin*), who Rashi identifies as a *gazlan*, and the bandits (*listim*), whom Rashi identifies as a *ganav* (since bandits go into hiding after their act, which is the *gemara*'s basis for assigning them *ganav* status). The *mishna* presumes *ye'ush* in both. But that creates a problem: *ee Rabbanan kashya gazlan* — if it follows the *Rabbanan*, why presume *ye'ush* by a *gazlan*, since they hold there is none? *Ee Rabbi Shimon kashya ganav* — if it follows Rabbi Shimon, why presume *ye'ush* by a *ganav*, since he holds there is none? According to Ulla, one could answer: *hacha nami beyadua vedivrei hakol* — perhaps in both cases *ye'ush* was actually known, not merely presumed, and everyone agrees known *ye'ush* is effective. But this is somewhat strained given that the *mishna* speaks in terms of presumption. According to Rava, the problem is even sharper: even known *ye'ush* remains disputed, so one can never have both a *ganav* and a *gazlan* case covered simultaneously by any single *tanna*.

### Armed Bandits

The *gemara* resolves: *delistim m'zuyan veRabbi Shimon hi* — the *mishna* is dealing with armed bandits, *listim m'zuyanin*, who operate openly and without concealment. As such, they are categorized as a type of *gazlan*, not a *ganav*. The *mishna* thus presents two varieties of *gazlan* — the tax collector and the armed bandit — and follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that *ye'ush* is presumed by a *gazlan*. The *gemara* then objects: *ee hachi hainu gazlan* — if the armed bandit is just another *gazlan*, why list him separately? *Trei gavnei gazlan* — because the *mishna* is illustrating two distinct types of *gazlan*: the institutionalized extortion of the *moches* and the violent seizure of the armed bandit. This distinction clarifies the breadth of the rule without introducing a separate legal category.

### Braita Sources

The *gemara* brings a further source: *hagannav vehagazlan veha'anas vehekdesh — hekdesham hekdesh, u'trumasam truma* — whether a *gannav*, a *gazlan*, or an *anas* (one who forces a sale but pays for it), we presume *ye'ush*, and therefore if any of them consecrates the object it is *hekdesh*, and if they designate it *terumah*, that designation takes effect. The pattern repeats: this source presumes *ye'ush* in all cases, which again fits neither the *Rabbanan* alone nor Rabbi Shimon alone. The *gemara*'s answer is once more *delistim m'zuyan veRabbi Shimon hi*. Even though the source explicitly uses the word *gannav*, the *gemara* maintains that it refers to an armed bandit who is halachically a *gazlan*, and the source follows Rabbi Shimon. This is admittedly a forced reading of a source that labels someone as a *gannav* while arguing he is really a *gazlan* — the *gemara* itself acknowledges the strain.

## Rabbi's Position

### Ibbaya Lehu

*Gufah Rabbi omer omer ani: gannav kegazlan* — Rabbi (Judah the Prince) explicitly states that a *gannav* has the same status as a *gazlan*. The question then becomes: like which *gazlan*? *Kegazlan derabbanan kamrat, delo kani* — does Rabbi mean like the *Rabbanan*'s *gazlan*, where there is never *ye'ush*? *O dilma kegazlan deRabbi Shimon kamrat, vekani* — or like Rabbi Shimon's *gazlan*, where *ye'ush* is presumed?

The *gemara* raises the *mishna* on our daf as proof: it presumes *ye'ush* in both the *gazlan* and *gannav* cases. *Ee Rabbanan kashya gazlan, ee Rabbi Shimon kashya gannav* — the same structural problem. *Ee amrat bishlama Rabbi kegazlan deRabbi Shimon kamar, vekani — hamani Rabbi hi* — if Rabbi means that *ye'ush* is always presumed, then the *mishna* is explained: it follows Rabbi, and Rabbi holds *ye'ush* is universal. *Ela ee amrat kegazlan derabbanan kamar, velo kani — hamani* — but if Rabbi means there is never *ye'ush*, then this *mishna* follows no *tanna* — not the *Rabbanan*, not Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi. *Hacha b'mai askinan delistim m'zuyan veRabbi Shimon hi* — once again the *gemara* retreats to the armed bandit answer and attributes the source to Rabbi Shimon. The *gemara* itself signals this is repetitive but necessary to address the question from Rabbi's own position.

### Father's Honor Proof

A cleaner proof emerges from a different *mishna*. Rabbi taught his son, Rabbi Shimon: *lo davar sheyesh bo achrayus mamash* — when the *mishna* earlier in the *perek* said that sons who inherit stolen property must return things that have *achrayus*, this does not literally mean only land. *Ela afilu parah vechoresh bah vechamor acharayiv* — even a cow one is actively plowing with, or a donkey publicly in use and known to be stolen, must be returned — *chayavin l'hachzir mipnei kevod avihem* — because of honor due to their father. The *gemara* draws the inference: *ta'ama mipnei kevod avihem* — the only reason they return it is for the father's honor. *Ha lav kevod avihem, lo* — if not for that consideration, they would not have to return it, meaning they technically *own* it through *ye'ush v'shinui reshus*. And since the opening *mishna* of the *perek* concerns a *gazlan* — *hagezel uma'achil* — this proves that Rabbi holds *ye'ush* is presumed by a *gazlan*, and therefore when he equates *gannav* with *gazlan*, he means like Rabbi Shimon's *gazlan*: *ye'ush* is always presumed. *Shema mina* — this is a solid proof, and the simplest reading of all the *mishna* and *braita* sources is that they follow Rabbi, who presumes *ye'ush* universally by both *gannav* and *gazlan*.

## Bees & Testimony (Detail…

### Bees Status

*Amar Rav Yosef: mai vecheyn* — what does the *mishna* mean when it says "and similarly" regarding the bee swarm? *Afilu nechila shel devorim d'tikun d'rabanan hu* — even a swarm of bees, where the very ownership of bees is only a rabbinic institution, because it is halachically unclear how one can acquire bees through a recognized act of *kinyan* (Tosafot raises this difficulty, noting that picking up the beehive does not obviously transfer possession of the flying bees within). The Rabbis established a form of ownership for bees based on *darkei shalom*, analogous to the Rabbinic ownership of *yonei shovach*, pigeons. Since ownership of bees is only Rabbinic, one might think we simply presume *ye'ush* without requiring it to be established. *Kama shma lan* — the *mishna* teaches us: no. *Meimar tzricha d'ba'ina leh* — even here, one may acquire the swarm only if the owners were actually *miya'esh*; we do not simply presume it.

### Woman Minor Testimony

Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka's ruling — that a woman or minor is believed to say the swarm left from a particular property — immediately raises the question: *isha v'katan bnei edut ninhu?* — since when are a woman or minor competent witnesses? Normally their testimony is inadmissible.

One should note in passing that in medieval Ashkenaz, authorities developed mechanisms for accepting women's testimony in commercial matters, framing it not as formal *edut* but as *ne'emanut* — a form of circumstantial reliability. The *gemara* here, however, is working with the standard rules, and the question is genuine.

### Corroboration & Speech

*Hacha b'mai askinan k'gon shehayu ba'alim mirdafin achareihen* — the *gemara* explains that the case involves corroborating evidence: the owners themselves were visibly pursuing the swarm, which is already strong circumstantial evidence of who owns it. *Ve'isha v'katan mesichin l'fi tuman* — and the woman and child are not formally testifying; they are merely chatting innocently, *mesiach l'fi tumo*, talking without awareness that their words are being used as evidence. The combination of the owners' visible pursuit and the innocent, unconsidered speech of bystanders creates a sufficient basis for the presumption — even without formal *edut*. The *gemara* recognizes that *mesiach l'fi tumo* has a particular credibility precisely because the speaker has no agenda: there is no reason to lie when one is simply gossiping about a neighborhood event.

## Mesiach L'fi Tumo Scope

### Ravina Challenge

*Amar leh Ravina l'Rav Ashi* — Ravina challenges Rav Ashi. If we say that a woman and minor cannot give testimony, and we rely in the bee case only on *mesiach l'fi tumo* combined with corroborating circumstances — are we saying *mesiach l'fi tumo* never works for women and minors beyond that narrow context? *V'harei nachil shel devorim mesiach l'fi tumo hu* — so is the bee swarm case simply a case of *mesiach l'fi tumo*, and does that establish a broader principle?

### Rav Ashi Response

*Amar Rav Ashi: ein mesiach l'fi tumo kasher ela l'edut isha bilvad* — no. *Mesiach l'fi tumo* is valid only for *edut isha* — the specific category of testimony concerning whether a woman's husband has died, where the Sages were particularly lenient because of *agunah* concerns. Outside that category, *mesiach l'fi tumo* does not function as a general principle for women and minors in testimony. The bee case, then, must rest on a different ground.

### Cohen Status Proof

Ravina continues to press: surely *mesiach l'fi tumo* works in other contexts as well. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: ma'aseh b'adam echad shehayah mesiach l'fi tumo* — there was a case of someone who, speaking innocently, said: "I remember when I was a child, being carried on my father's shoulders out of school, and he would strip off my tunic and immerse me so that I could eat *terumah* that evening." *Rav Chanina* adds that this person also recalled his friends keeping their distance from him and calling him "Yochanan who eats *chalot*" — meaning they avoided him lest they become *tamei* by contact. This is *mesiach l'fi tumo* helping oneself, and yet *vehe'alu Rabbi likhunah al piv* — Rabbi used this testimony to establish the man's status as a *kohen*.

This case is striking for a further reason: the testimony concerns something witnessed and experienced as a child, being reported by an adult. As a rule, one cannot testify in court about events witnessed during childhood — yet here the *mesiach l'fi tumo* framework bypasses even that limitation. Furthermore, it is self-serving testimony in a meaningful sense — and yet it is credited.

### Captive Woman Case

*Ki ata Rav Dimi amar Rav Chana Kartigna* — when Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported that a case came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (or, in another version, before Rabbi himself): a child who was chatting innocently said, "My mother and I were taken captive among non-Jews. When I went out to draw water, my mind was on my mother. When I gathered wood, my mind was on my mother." Implicit in this innocent narrative is that the child was constantly attentive to his mother's wellbeing, never leaving her unguarded. The implication — that she was not violated — was drawn from this, and *vehesi'ah Rebbi al piv likhunah* — Rabbi permitted her to marry a *kohen* on the basis of this testimony. Here too, the person speaking is not the woman herself (whose word would not be considered sufficiently *l'fi tumo* in her own case), but a third party whose innocent speech carries no evident self-interest.

### Conclusion

The *gemara* resolves these cases: *bishvuya hikilu* — the Sages were lenient specifically in cases of a captive woman, and *bitrumah derabbanan* — the case of *terumah* and *kohen* status today involves only Rabbinic implications, since *terumah* in the present era is *d'rabanan*. The conclusion is that *mesiach l'fi tumo* is valid only for *rabbinic* concerns — it does not override *de'oraita* prohibitions.

The *gemara*'s conclusion, however, invites closer scrutiny. The cases discussed involved *mesiach l'fi tumo* as a pure, isolated mechanism. Where there is corroborating evidence, where the speaker is a disinterested party, and where the legal stakes are matters of *dinei mamonot* rather than personal status, the picture may be more nuanced. This distinction carries practical implications, including the long-standing *Ashkenazim* and *Sefardim* dispute over whether one may rely on a non-Jew's *mesiach l'fi tumo* testimony to determine whether forbidden food has been mixed into permitted food — a case involving corroborating factors and the question of whether *ta'am* is a *de'oraita* concern. The *gemara*'s rule that *mesiach l'fi tumo* does not work *de'oraita* is the anchor of one position, while the presence of corroboration and the absence of self-interest are the basis for leniency on the other side.

## Property Damage Rules

### Branch Cutting

*Tanya: Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka omer: tenai beis din hu* — it was taught in a *braita* that Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka explains his father's lenient ruling by appealing to a rabbinic court stipulation. It is not that there is a general principle permitting deliberate damage to another's property to save one's own; rather, the court made a specific stipulation: *she'yehei yored letokh sedeh chaveiro vekotzetz sukho shel chaveiro lehatzil nechilato* — one may enter a neighbor's field and cut the branch on which the swarm rests in order to retrieve it. *Venotel demei sukho mitokh nechilato shel chaveiro* — and the field owner is entitled to be reimbursed from the value of the swarm, meaning from the benefit the bee-keeper obtains.

### Extended Cases

The *braita* does not stop there: *tenai beis din hu* — there is a broader category of such court stipulations. *Sheshofekh yeino umatzil devashno shel chaveiro, venotel demei yeino mitokh devashno shel chaveiro* — if someone's honey is spilling and the only available container is another's barrel of wine, one may empty the wine barrel and catch the honey, and the honey's owner must compensate for the wine. *Umefarek etzav veto'en pishtano shel chaveiro, venotel demei etzav mitokh pishtano shel chaveiro* — if one's donkey is carrying wood and another's donkey, carrying the more valuable flax, is collapsing, one may remove the wood and load the flax, and the flax owner must pay for the wood. *Shekach hitnah Yehoshua l'Yisrael et ha'aretz* — these are part of the implicit stipulations that *Yehoshua* established upon entering the land, conditions to which all members of *Klal Yisrael* are treated as having agreed.

### Voluntary vs. Forced

An important distinction must be drawn within these cases. In the honey and flax scenarios, the person saving the property is voluntarily sacrificing his own — he chooses to pour out his wine, he chooses to offload his wood. That is categorically different from compelling someone else to absorb a loss, even with reimbursement. One who willingly sacrifices a lesser asset to save a greater one and then expects to be paid back is acting within a recognizable framework of implicit agreement. That is not a license for a general rule that one may deliberately damage another's property to protect one's own, and then simply pay for it. Whether these stipulations extend beyond the specific cases listed — wine for honey, wood for flax, branches for bees — and what the precise parameters of *who* may act, under *what* circumstances, and with *whose* consent, remain questions the *gemara* leaves with some degree of openness.

# Bava Kamma 115

## Stolen Vessels Framework

### Mishnah Setup

The daf opens with the *mishna* beginning approximately fifteen lines from the bottom of 114b. The *mishna* presents the following case: a person recognizes his vessels or books — at that time, of course, books were scrolls and extraordinarily expensive — in the possession of another. He sees someone walking around with his objects. The *mishna* then adds a critical condition: *veyatza lo shem geneiva ba'ir* — there was a known report in town that he had been burgled. Given that presumption, the *mishna* rules that *yishava lo loke'ach kama natan veyitol* — the purchaser swears how much he paid and collects that sum from the original owner, who then retrieves his object.

The underlying assumption is that this all takes place before *ye'ush* — before the owner has despaired of recovering his property. Prior to *ye'ush*, the stolen object legally remains his, and he retains the right to reclaim it. But here a complication arises: why should the purchaser be entitled to any reimbursement at all? He is in possession of a stolen object. The thief — not the original owner — is the one who wronged him. The owner's obligation to compensate the purchaser flows entirely from *takanat hashuk*, a special enactment designed to facilitate commerce. Without such protection, every buyer would face the specter of having a purchased item claimed as stolen and taken from him, leaving him no recourse but to chase down a thief who has long since absconded. The constraint this would place on commerce was deemed intolerable, and so the Sages enacted that even if an item turns out to have been stolen, the innocent purchaser may recover his payment from the original owner. Once the owner retrieves his object, he in turn may pursue the thief for reimbursement.

The *mishna* closes with the converse: *ve'im lav* — if there was no such report of a burglary — *lav kol heimenu*, the owner is not believed. The reason is *she'ani omer machran le'achar velakan zeh mimenu*: one might simply say the owner sold the object, regretted it, and is now attempting to reclaim it through a fabricated story. Without something to substantiate the claim of theft, the owner cannot compel the purchaser to return the item.

### Takanat Hashuk

Two distinct legal interests are in tension throughout this *mishna*. On one hand, *takanat hashuk* protects the innocent purchaser from suffering a loss through no fault of his own. On the other hand, the *mishna* is also being somewhat lenient toward the original owner: it credits his claim of theft on the basis of a community report, which is a considerably lower evidentiary threshold than one might expect when forcibly retrieving an object from someone else's possession. One way to understand this is that the two considerations reinforce each other: precisely because the purchaser will be compensated, the threshold for crediting the owner's theft claim may be lowered. Since the purchaser is not left empty-handed, there is less injustice in crediting a claim supported merely by community rumor.

### Report Insufficient

The *gemara* immediately challenges the *mishna*'s reliance on the community report. *V'chi yatza lo shem geneiva ba'ir mai havei?* — so what if there is a rumor? Perhaps the owner sold the item, regretted the sale, and is himself the one spreading the rumor to manufacture the appearance of a burglary. The *gemara* presses the point: not only is a mere report not direct evidence, but the same person whose word we would need to trust in order to credit the report is the very person who has a motive to fabricate it. A rumor that can just as easily have been engineered by the claimant offers no genuine evidentiary weight.

### Objective Evidence

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that what is required is objective, independently generated evidence — for example, people who had actually slept in the owner's house that night, and the owner rose in the night screaming *nignevu chelai* — my belongings have been stolen. (The lecturer notes that *hifkin* is the root of the modern Hebrew word *hafganah*, a protest.) The *gemara*, however, dismisses even this: the *gemara* responds *kol sheken ee lo matza* — this is even more reason for suspicion, since all of that could be a performance staged by the owner himself. There is still no truly objective evidence.

Rav Kahana then added in the name of Rav a further element that substantially strengthens the showing: *kegon shehayta machteret chatura betoch beito* — there was a tunnel dug under the house. People had been seen leaving the house with bundles of objects on their shoulders, *tzrorot shel keilim al kitfeihem*, and the entire town was saying that this particular person's belongings had been stolen — *hakol omrim nignevu keilav shel ploni*. This is not evidence the owner could have manufactured: there are eyewitnesses, physical evidence in the form of a tunnel, and a community-wide consensus.

The *gemara* then raises another concern: even granted that the owner was burgled, how do we know that the specific objects now in the purchaser's possession are the very objects stolen? The *mishna* mentions both vessels and books — perhaps only one category was reported stolen. Moreover, how do we match the particular item claimed to the item actually taken? Perhaps the stolen object was old and the owner is now claiming a new one; perhaps it was small and he is claiming a large one.

Rav Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the report must have specifically mentioned books as well. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina added that the report must have identified the specific items. Rav added further that witnesses must directly testify that the items now in the purchaser's hands — *halalu kelim shel ploni, halalu sefarim shel ploni* — are the very ones belonging to the original owner. This is a dramatic escalation of evidentiary requirements far beyond anything the *mishna* itself seemed to demand.

The *gemara* also addresses the *ba bamachteret* ruling of Rav — the principle in Sanhedrin that one who tunnels into a house and steals thereby *acquires* the objects, since by exposing himself to being killed (*masar nafshia likatla*), he is treated as having "paid" for them (*b'damei kaninhu*). The *gemara* distinguishes: that principle applies when the thief tunneled *in*, exposing himself to the homeowner's lethal defense. Here, the intruders merely slept in the house and tunneled *out* — they never assumed the mortal risk entailed by a true *ba bamachteret*, and therefore Rav's acquisition principle does not apply and the objects must be returned.

The *gemara* then records that Rava qualified all the preceding demands: *lo shanu ela bebaal habayis ha'asuy limkor kelav* — these heightened evidentiary requirements apply only when the owner is the sort of person who regularly sells his household items. If he is not someone who typically sells his belongings, the threshold drops considerably, and we return closer to the simple reading of the *mishna*. The *gemara* raises the objection that even someone who normally does not sell might occasionally need money and do so, to which Rav Ashi responds that this is precisely why some substantiating report is needed — but once such a report exists, combined with the low likelihood that this particular owner would sell, that suffices.

### Tosafot Reading

Tosafot raises a difficulty with the final evidentiary requirement as it appears in the *gemara*: if witnesses directly testify that what the purchaser holds is the owner's property, there seems to be no gap at all — it would be direct proof, not a matter of community report and inference. Tosafot therefore reads the statement differently: what the witnesses saw and reported was that the thieves' bags contained a specific item — say, a particular silver *iPhone* — and the purchaser is now holding an item matching that description exactly. There remains a tiny inferential step, but an extraordinarily small one. This reading preserves the *mishna*'s framework of substantiated community report while explaining why the *gemara* required such a close correspondence between the described stolen item and the item actually claimed.

---

## Multiple Parties

### Chanan Bisha

The *gemara* introduces a new scenario: *ganav umachar ve'achar kach hukar haganav* — the thief stole, sold the stolen item to a purchaser, and then was subsequently identified. Unlike the *mishna*'s case, where the thief's identity may be entirely unknown, here all three parties — the original owner, the thief, and the purchaser — are potentially before us. The question is how to structure the legal claims among them.

Before examining that dispute, the *gemara* cites the incident of *Chanan Bisha*, a notorious figure who stole a cloak and sold it. Rav Huna, a student of Rav, ruled that the original owner must pay the purchaser — a classic application of *takanat hashuk* — even though the thief was identified. The *gemara* explains that this case is exceptional: *Chanan Bisha*, despite being known, was effectively untouchable, a sort of mafioso from whom the purchaser could never realistically collect. Since the practical ability to recover from the thief did not exist, even the opinion that holds there is no *takanat hashuk* when the thief is known would concede that in this case the purchaser must be protected and compensated by the owner.

### Rav vs. Yochanan

The core dispute is stated as follows. Rav, in the name of Rabbi Chiyya, says *hadin im harishon* — the owner must deal with the first party. Rabbi Yochanan, in the name of Rabbi Yannai, says *hadin im hasheni* — he deals with the second. The initial assumption is that "first" and "second" refer to the thief and the purchaser respectively: Rav holds the owner must pursue the thief for compensation and cannot bring the purchaser into the dispute, while Rabbi Yochanan holds the owner may go to the purchaser and retrieve his object from him.

### Ye'ush Resolution

Rav Yosef attempts to resolve the apparent contradiction by arguing that the two positions actually do not conflict: *kan lifnei ye'ush hadin im hasheni, kan l'achar ye'ush hadin im harishon*. Before *ye'ush*, the object legally remains the owner's and he may retrieve it from the purchaser — that is Rabbi Yochanan's case. After *ye'ush*, the purchaser has acquired the object and the owner's recourse is only against the thief — that is Rav's case. This appears tidy and uncontroversial.

### Rav Chisda

The *gemara* adds that both positions depend on the principle of Rav Chisda from earlier in the chapter: if a thief steals an item and a third party comes and consumes it, the original owner may collect from *either* the thief *or* the consumer — *ratza mizeh goveh, ratza mizeh goveh*. This principle establishes that even after the stolen object has passed out of the owner's control, his legal claims against subsequent parties remain intact before *ye'ush*. In our case, this principle is what enables the owner to retrieve his object from the purchaser before *ye'ush*: without Rav Chisda's ruling, one might have argued that once the object was stolen and sold, the owner's rights were too attenuated to compel the purchaser — who, after all, had done nothing wrong — to give it up. Rav Chisda establishes that they are not.

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's reconciliation. He contends that the dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan is genuine and that there exists a case analogous to "before *ye'ush*" in which they nonetheless disagree: the case of *matnot kehunah*.

### Matnot Kehunah

The *mishna* governing *matnot kehunah* presents the following scenario: a purchaser tells a butcher, sell me the innards of this cow. The innards include the *keivah* — the stomach — which constitutes one of the priestly gifts that must be given to a *kohen*. The parallel to our case is precise: the butcher is the thief, effectively stealing the *kohen*'s portion; the purchaser is the one who ends up with the stolen item in his possession; and since *matnot kehunah* are owed by religious obligation and there is no specific *kohen* who has yet acquired a personal claim to them, the *gemara* treats this as analogous to a pre-*ye'ush* situation.

If the purchaser bought the innards without explicit weighing, the assumption is that he did not knowingly pay for the *keivah* specifically — he never intended to purchase something he knew was not the butcher's to sell. He therefore gives the *keivah* to the *kohen* without seeking reimbursement. If, however, the purchaser weighed the innards and paid by weight, he has unwittingly paid for the *keivah* as well. In that case he gives the stomach to the *kohen* and recovers its value from the butcher.

### Ye'ush Order

Rav Zvid interprets the dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan differently. He maintains that both agree before *ye'ush* the object is returned from the purchaser, and both agree after *ye'ush* the owner deals with the thief. The dispute, in his reading, concerns a middle case: *ye'ush* occurred after the purchaser took possession — that is, *shinuy reshut* preceded *ye'ush*. One opinion holds that *shinuy reshut she'achar ye'ush* — a change of possession followed by *ye'ush* — does confer ownership; the other holds it does not. If the purchaser acquired the object, the owner must deal with the thief; if not, the owner may retrieve the object from the purchaser.

### Thief Known

Rav Pappa offers yet another reading. He argues that when it comes to the actual physical garment, all authorities agree it is returned to the original owner — *biglima dechulei alma lo pligi dehadar lemarei*. The dispute in the *baraita* is not about *ye'ush* at all, but rather about whether *takanat hashuk* was enacted in a case where the thief has been identified. Rav holds: *dina deloke'ach delishkol zuzei migannav velo asu batakkanat hashuk* — the purchaser's remedy is to collect from the thief, and no *takanat hashuk* was enacted obligating the owner to pay the purchaser when the thief is known and available. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *asu bah takkanat hashuk* — the enactment protects the purchaser even here, because he did nothing wrong by buying in the marketplace, and it would be unfair to force him to run after the thief.

### Well-Known Thief

Rava articulates a principle that moves beyond the *hukar haganav* debate entirely: *im ganav mefursam hu, lo asu bo takkanat hashuk* — if the thief was notorious and well-known as a thief, the Sages did not enact *takanat hashuk* to protect the purchaser. The purpose of the enactment was to enable and protect ordinary commerce, not to subsidize transactions with known criminals. If a buyer purchases from a *ganav mefursam*, he should have known better, and the Sages will not shield him from the consequences.

The *gemara* immediately notes the apparent tension with the *Chanan Bisha* case, in which *takanat hashuk* was applied even though he was notoriously dangerous. Rava distinguishes: *Chanan Bisha* was renowned for his violent character, but was not specifically known as a thief — *lignivusei lo mefursam*. There was no particular reason for the purchaser to suspect he was buying stolen goods. The principle of *ganav mefursam* therefore requires that the person's reputation as a thief specifically — not merely as a bad actor — be publicly established.

---

## Special Circumstance (II)

### Debt Payment

The *gemara* now examines *takanat hashuk* in a series of special transactional configurations. The first: a thief used the stolen object to pay off a pre-existing debt he owed the current possessor. *Ganav ufara bechovo, ganav ufara beheikeifo* — whether he paid an outstanding debt or a running tab, *lo asu bo takkanat hashuk*. The rationale is *lav ada'ata d'hanach yahavit lei midei* — the possessor did not shell out money for the sake of this object. The money he lent was lent earlier, unconnected to this particular item. When the owner retrieves the object, the possessor is simply returned to his prior position — the thief still owes him the original sum — and no special protection is warranted.

### Collateral

The next case involves collateral: the thief gave the stolen object to a lender as security for a loan. Where the collateral is worth 200 and the loan is 100 — *shavi masan be'me'ah* — the lender clearly extended the loan *because of* the collateral, and *takanat hashuk* applies: the lender laid out money on the faith of this object, and the owner must compensate him upon retrieval. Where the collateral and loan are equal in value — *shaveh be'shaveh* — Amemar holds *lo asu bah takkanat hashuk*: since you would not normally lend money against collateral of only equal value, the inference is that the loan rested primarily on personal trust in the borrower rather than on the object itself. Mar Zutra holds that even in this case *takanat hashuk* applies, since money was after all extended on account of the object. The final ruling — *ve'hilchesa bekhlei asu bah takkanat hashuk* — sides with Mar Zutra.

### Pricing Scenarios

Ordinary purchase at fair market value — *zabna shavei be'shavei* — is the paradigm case for *takanat hashuk*, and it applies without question. Two divergent scenarios are then examined. If the purchaser paid substantially *less* than the object's fair value — *shavi me'ah be'ma'san*, worth 200 but bought for 100 — *takanat hashuk* still applies: he shelled out money for the item and is entitled to protection. If, on the other hand, the purchaser grossly *overpaid* — *shavi me'ah be'masayim*, worth 100 but bought for 200 — Rav Sheshet holds *lo asu bah takkanat hashuk*: as Rashi explains, when one so dramatically overpays, it is evident that the excess was essentially a gift to the seller, not a genuine commercial transaction in this object. Rava disagrees and holds *asu bah takkanat hashuk* — and Rashi notes that on Rava's view the owner must reimburse the full 200. The final ruling — *ve'hilchesa bekhlei asu bah takkanat hashuk* — adopts Rava's position, extending protection across all the debated scenarios except the case of payment of a pre-existing debt, where the *gemara* never entertained any doubt.

### Avimi bar Nazi

A real case is then recorded. Avimi bar Nazi, the father-in-law of Ravina, had lent a certain man four *zuz*. That man stole a cloak and gave it to Avimi in payment of the debt. With the debt cleared, Avimi then lent the man another four *zuz*. The thief was subsequently identified. The question: does *takanat hashuk* protect Avimi with respect to either or both loans?

Ravina ruled that the first four *zuz* constitute a clear case of *ganav ufara bechovo* — the cloak paid a pre-existing debt, and no *takanat hashuk* applies to that amount. Regarding the second four *zuz*, however, Ravina argued that Avimi extended this loan precisely because his trust in the borrower had been established by the repayment of the first debt — and that repayment was effectuated through the stolen cloak. The second loan was therefore causally connected to the cloak, and *takanat hashuk* should apply.

### Rabbi Abbahu

Rav Kahana challenged Ravina's reasoning on the second loan: perhaps Avimi lent the second four *zuz* simply out of the same trust that led him to extend the first loan — *ki heichi d'heimanye mei'ikara* — entirely independent of having received the cloak. The matter was deliberated and brought before Rabbi Abbahu, who ruled *hilchasa k'Rav Kahana*: the second loan is treated as independent, and the entire transaction is governed by the rule of *ganav ufara bechovo uve'hekefo*. Avimi must return the cloak and receives no reimbursement from the original owner.

---

## Special Circumstance (II)

### Narsha Sefer

A final case involves multiple purchasers in sequence. A person from Narsha stole a *sefer* and sold it to a man from Papuna for eighty *zuz*. The Papuna man sold it to a man from the city of Mechuza for a hundred and twenty. The thief was then identified. Now there are two purchasers: the man from Papuna, who paid eighty, and the man from Mechuza, who paid a hundred and twenty — the current holder of the book. How should the owner's payment obligations and rights of recovery be structured?

### Abaye Solution

Abaye ruled as follows: the owner goes and pays the man from Mechuza eighty *zuz* — the amount the book originally fetched from the thief — and retrieves his book. The man from Mechuza then recovers the remaining forty *zuz* of what he paid from the Papuna man, who had profited by forty on the transaction. The reasoning is that the original price of eighty is the measure of what was genuinely "shelled out" for the item at the point it left the thief's hands, and that anchors the owner's obligation.

### Rava Counterargument

Rava challenged this analysis on policy grounds: *hashta loke'ach mi'ganav asu bo takkanat hashuk, loke'ach miloke'ach miba'ya* — if we protect a direct purchaser from a thief, certainly we should protect a purchaser who bought from another purchaser, since he had even less reason to suspect anything was amiss. It would be unfair to force the man from Mechuza to chase after two parties; he should be made whole in a single transaction with the owner. Rava therefore ruled: the owner pays the man from Mechuza the full hundred and twenty *zuz* and takes back his book. The owner then recovers forty from the Papuna man — who unjustly profited from stolen goods — and eighty from the Narsha thief. This is the ruling that is adopted.

---

## Unilateral Lifesaving

### Wine Saves Honey

The *mishna* presents a new scenario: two men are walking, one carrying a barrel of wine and the other a barrel of honey. The honey barrel cracks and the honey is about to spill and be lost. The man with the wine pours out his wine and saves the honey by transferring it into his now-empty barrel. *Ein lo ela secharo* — he is entitled only to payment for his service, the market rate for someone hired to perform such a rescue. He may not demand reimbursement for the value of the wine he spilled. No one hired him; no one asked him to sacrifice his wine. Gratitude does not create a legal obligation.

### Stipulated Agreement

If, however, prior to acting, the rescuer said to the honey owner: "I will save your honey if you agree to pay me for the value of my wine," and the owner agreed, then *chayiv litein lo* — the owner is obligated to pay. The explicit stipulation creates a contractual obligation.

### Donkey Wadi

The *mishna* presents a parallel case: a flash flood sweeps through a wadi, carrying away both a man's donkey — worth a hundred — and his neighbor's donkey — worth two hundred. The man can save only one. He abandons his own donkey and saves his neighbor's more valuable animal. Again, *ein lo ela secharo* — he collects only the service fee for saving the donkey, not compensation for the donkey he sacrificed. And again, if he stipulated in advance and the neighbor agreed to compensate him for his lost donkey, *chayiv litein lo* — the neighbor must pay.

### Hefker Question

The *gemara* raises a striking challenge to the *mishna*'s ruling: why is the rescuer of the honey entitled to only a service fee? Granted that the honey owner did not ask him to act, but consider the state of the honey at the moment of rescue — it was entirely about to spill and be destroyed, *holech le'ibbud*. Something in the process of complete destruction and loss should be considered ownerless, *hefker*. If the honey was effectively *hefker* at the moment the rescuer acted, then he should be regarded as having taken possession of ownerless property — in which case he owns all of it, not merely a service fee!

### Terumah Sheni

The *gemara* supports the *hefker* premise by citing a *baraita*: if someone is carrying jugs of wine and oil and sees them breaking, he may not declare that the spilling wine or oil should serve as *terumat ma'aser* on equivalent produce stored in his home. The purpose of such a declaration would be transparent: the wine is doomed, so let it count as the *kohen*'s share — the owner saves himself from having to separate from his good produce, and it costs him nothing since the spilling wine was going to waste anyway. Not only is this not permitted *lechatchila*, but if he made such a declaration, *lo amar klum* — it is legally void. And the reason it is void is precisely because at that moment of complete loss, the produce is considered ownerless. One cannot consecrate or separate *terumah* from *hefker* property.

### Robbery Case

The *gemara* then cites a seemingly contradictory *baraita*: if a person is traveling and a highway robber confronts him to take his money, he should not declare that the produce in his home should be redeemed through this money for purposes of *ma'aser sheni*. Yet if he does make such a declaration, *divrei kayamin* — it takes legal effect. This appears to contradict the previous case: here too the property is about to be completely and irrecoverably lost, yet the declaration is valid.

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: the case of the robber is different because *b'sheyachol lehatzil* — it is possible that the person could save himself, perhaps by running away or otherwise evading the robber. Since recovery of the money is not entirely foreclosed, the property is not treated as *hefker*. The *gemara* refines this further: it is only possible to escape through considerable effort — *al yedei had'chak*. And precisely because escape is difficult but not impossible, the property retains its ownership status for purposes of the declaration, but the Sages nonetheless counseled against making it *lechatchila* — since once you have transferred the *ma'aser sheni* status onto the money, you may have even less motivation to exert yourself to recover it.

### Netting Distinction

Having established the theoretical framework, the *gemara* returns to Rabbi Yirmiyah's distinction. The resolution to why the honey in the *mishna* is not *hefker* is that the barrel was not cracking catastrophically and spilling all at once. Rather, it was encased in a netting — *kesha'aka bisa bar karcha lah* — such that the honey was dripping but not freely pouring out and being entirely destroyed. Since not everything was inevitably lost, since there remained some possibility of partial recovery or containment, the honey did not attain the status of *hefker*. The owner retained his legal ownership, and the rescuer therefore holds the honey subject to returning it upon receipt of a service fee.

### Tafel Cases

The *gemara* then cites another *baraita* to test the boundaries of the *hefker* principle. If a person has ten barrels of *tevel tamei* — produce that is ritually impure and from which *terumah* has not yet been separated — and one of the barrels cracks or becomes exposed, he may declare that broken barrel to be *terumat ma'aser* on the other nine. This seems to permit exactly what was prohibited in the earlier case.

The *gemara* distinguishes on the basis of the *kohen*'s loss. Since the wine is *tamei*, a *kohen* cannot consume it; the only use would be minimal, such as burning it for fragrance. Because the *kohen*'s practical loss from this *terumat ma'aser* declaration is negligible, the Sages permitted it *lechatchila* — or at minimum did not forbid it so severely. However, *uveshemen lo ya'aseh kein mipnei hefsed kohen* — in the case of *tamei* oil, the same declaration should not be made *lechatchila*, because a *kohen* can use *tamei* oil for lighting, and his loss from this declaration would be real and substantial. Yet in both cases, the declaration takes effect *bedi'avad*. This shows that the concern is not that the property is *hefker* — because if it were ownerless, the declaration would be entirely void — but rather a *lechatchila* policy consideration about fairness to the *kohen*.

Rabbi Yirmiyah resolves this as well: in this case too, the barrel is wrapped in the pressing-house netting — *keshehakeivah shel beit habad keruchah aleha* — and the contents are therefore not catastrophically and irreversibly spilling out all at once. The property is not *hefker*, the declaration takes effect, and the only question is one of *lechatchila* policy regarding the *kohen*'s loss. We will continue from here tomorrow.

---

# Bava Kamma 116

*This shiur is dedicated to the *ilui nishmat* of Maoz Morel, who fell defending *Am Yisrael* and *Medinat Yisrael*. *Tehi nishmato tzerurah bitzror hachayim*. *Zecher tzadik livracha*.*

---

## Gilui & Filtering

### Spilled Liquid Question

The daf begins, technically speaking, on 115b, approximately halfway down the page, at the word *bishlema*. The broader discussion concerns a case where a barrel or pitcher breaks and its contents — honey, wine, or oil — are going to waste. A *braita* has been cited holding that such liquid cannot serve as *terumat ma'aser*, because once liquid is flowing out and cannot be recovered, it is effectively *hefker*. The *Gemara* then struggled to reconcile this with several sources that appear to treat such property as still belonging to its owner: a *Mishnah* holding that the honey of a breaking barrel still belongs to the owner; another source permitting the transfer of *kedushah* of *ma'aser sheni* onto money being seized by a robber; and a *braita* permitting *terumat ma'aser* from *tamei* wine or oil that is in the process of spilling, the only limiting factor being whether designating it would cause a loss to the *kohein*.

The *Gemara* resolved all of these cases by explaining that in each instance the liquid is not yet entirely lost — the barrel may have netting that slows the breakage, or the robber's seizure may still be reversible — and therefore none of those cases involves true *hefker*.

### Gilui & Snake Poison

With that framework established, the *Gemara* turns to a new difficulty. The case of *tamei* wine that is spilling has been permitted *lechatchila* — because *tamei terumah* wine, usable only for air freshening (*ziluf*), is of little enough value that designating it as *terumat ma'aser* causes no meaningful loss to the *kohein*. But what about wine that has been left uncovered? The *Gemara* raises the problem of *gilui*: the concern, accepted in the rabbinic period, that a snake may have drunk from uncovered liquid and deposited venom in it, rendering it dangerous. If the wine was *nisgalta* — left exposed — *lemai chazya*? What use is it at all?

One might answer that even after *gilui* the wine retains its value for *ziluf*, since that was the use of *tamei terumah* wine to begin with. But a *braita* closes off this possibility. Uncovered water (*mayim shenitgalu*) is subject to a series of prohibitions: one may not spill it in the public domain lest a barefoot person walk through it and absorb the venom through a wound; one may not use it to mix plaster; one may not sprinkle it to settle dust in a house; one may not give it to one's own animal or another's animal to drink, lest the animal be harmed or lest one later eat the animal's flesh. Given that even vapor contact is prohibited, the wine would seem to have no value whatsoever — and therefore could not become *terumat ma'aser*.

### Sieve Solution

The *Gemara* resolves this by explaining that the wine is passed through a *mistanena* — a sieve or filter, similar in concept to two vessels stacked one atop the other with a screen between them. The *Gemara* specifies that this follows the position of *Rabbi Nechemya*.

A *braita* is cited that discusses this very apparatus: ordinarily, having such a sieve setup does not solve the problem of *gilui*, because the sieve itself does not eliminate the venom. *Rabbi Nechemya* limits this ruling. When is the sieve system still problematic? Only when the bottom vessel is exposed — in which case the snake could drink from that vessel directly. But if the bottom vessel is covered, even though the top vessel is exposed, there is no concern of *gilui*. The reason: *le'fi she'eres shel nachash dome lisfog* — the venom of a snake behaves like a sponge; it floats at the top of the liquid and does not sink through. Therefore, the filter will catch the venom along with the other surface material, and the liquid that passes through is safe. This is why the wine, even after *gilui*, can still have value and can serve as *terumat ma'aser*.

### Pouring Pressure Issue

A complication is immediately raised. It was taught in the name of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*, transmitted by *Rabbi Simon*, that the leniency of the *mistanena* applies only when the liquid was not agitated or poured forcefully — *shelo tarfo*. If it was poured with force (*tarfo*), the velocity of the liquid would drive the venom through the filter even if it would otherwise float at the top. In that case, *assur*.

The *Gemara* resolves that this is not a problem in the case before us. Just as one ordinarily sets up the *mistanena* system in a gradual and gentle manner — letting the liquid seep slowly through the filter rather than pouring it with force — so too here, one can arrange the barrel so that its contents flow out gently across the mouth of the vessel. The answer is thus: *hacha nami d'efshar demaniach midi apuma dechavisa* — one can place something at the mouth of the barrel so that the wine trickles out softly, without the pressure that would push the venom through the screen.

With that, the wine remains usable and the designation as *terumat ma'aser* is valid. The remaining question is why this process — simple enough in principle — disqualifies oil from being designated *lechatchila*. The answer, as we shall see, is that passing the oil through a sieve is genuinely burdensome. Giving the *kohein* oil that he must first strain carefully through such an apparatus is a real imposition, and therefore it constitutes a *hefsed kohein* that forbids the designation *lechatchila*, though it remains valid *bedieved*.

### Demai Exception

Now the *Gemara* notes an internal tension. The solution invoking *Rabbi Nechemya* and the *mistanena* addresses how the wine retains value. But it creates a different problem: according to *Rabbi Nechemya*, one cannot separate *tamei* wine as *terumat ma'aser* on *tamei* grain even in ordinary circumstances, since he holds that even from *tamei* to *tamei*, one must still give the *kohein* *trumah tehorah* wherever possible. The entire *braita* permitting *terumat ma'aser* from *tamei* wine on *tamei* grain — which is what we have here — seems to contradict *Rabbi Nechemya*'s own stated position.

The *braita* on this topic reads: *tormin min hatame al hatame* — one may separate *tamei* terumah on *tamei* grain; *min hatahor al hatahor* — and *tahor* terumah on *tahor* grain; *min hatahor al hatame* — and *tahor* terumah on *tamei* grain. But *lo min hatame al hatahor* — not *tamei* on *tahor*, since that would deprive the *kohein* of something of superior value. *Rabbi Nechemya* goes further: even from *tamei* to *tamei*, separation is not generally permitted — the only exception is *demai*, produce purchased from an *am haaretz* whose tithes are of uncertain status.

The *Gemara* resolves the conflict cleanly: *hacha nami beshel demai* — if one wishes the entire discussion to follow *Rabbi Nechemya*, then read the *braita* as referring specifically to *demai*. *Rabbi Nechemya* agrees that *tamei* may be taken on *tamei* in the case of *demai*, and it is precisely that case that the *braita* addresses. The resolution is consistent and the attribution holds.

---

## Oil vs. Wine Loss

### Comparative Values

With the theoretical framework established, the *Gemara* turns to articulate why the oil case is categorically different from the wine case. The *braita* stated: *uvshemen lo yaaseh kein mipnei hefsed kohein* — regarding oil, one may not do this because it causes a loss to the *kohein*. The *Gemara* asks: *mai shna shemen*? What is distinctive about oil? The answer: *dechazi l'hadlaka* — even *tamei* oil can be used by the *kohein* for illumination, for his oil lamps. That is a genuine and significant use. Therefore, receiving damaged, exposed oil that must be filtered is a real loss.

But this raises an immediate challenge. *Yayin nami chazi l'ziluf* — wine is also usable, as an air freshener. Is that not also a real benefit? One might dismiss this, noting that *ziluf* sounds like a trivial use. But the *Gemara* cites *Shmuel* in the name of *Rabbi Chiyya*: for drinking purposes, one should be prepared to pay one *sela* per *log*; for *ziluf* purposes, one should buy higher-quality wine and pay two *slaim* per *log*. So *ziluf* is not a trivial use — it is actually valued more highly than ordinary drinking wine in terms of the quality one seeks. Why then is there no *hefsed kohein* even in the wine case?

### Takalah Concern

The *Gemara* answers: *hacha bemai askinan bechadash* — we are speaking of new wine. New wine is not yet aromatic enough to serve effectively as *ziluf*, and therefore has minimal value for that purpose. But the *Gemara* immediately presses further: *v'ha chazi l'yashon* — but new wine can become old wine! If the *kohein* simply holds onto it, it will age and become valuable. Surely the *kohein* is being deprived of something of genuine future worth.

The *Gemara* responds: *ati bah lidei takalah* — we would not permit the *kohein* to hold onto *tamei* wine for an extended period, because of the concern that he might eventually forget it is *tamei* and come to drink from it accidentally. Therefore, we would require the *kohein* to use it immediately. A wine that must be used immediately and cannot be stored has very little market value, and so there is no meaningful *hefsed kohein* in the wine case.

### Vessel Distinction

The *Gemara* then asks: *shemen nami ati lidei takalah* — but the same concern of *takalah* should apply to oil as well, should it not? If the *kohein* stores the *tamei* oil for a long time, he might forget and come to eat with it.

The *Gemara* answers: *demanach bichli maus* — oil can be stored in a repulsive vessel. Since *tamei* oil is used only for fuel, the *kohein* would naturally store it in a disgusting container, one that he would never use for eating. The repulsive nature of the vessel itself serves as a constant reminder and removes any concern of accidental consumption.

But could one not do the same with wine — store it in a repulsive vessel and thereby allow it to age? The *Gemara* dismisses this: *hashta l'ziluf kabaei lei bichli maus kamanach lei*? If you want to use the wine for air freshening because of its pleasant aroma, you are simply not going to store it in a disgusting vessel. The very purpose for which the wine is being preserved — its fragrance — makes it impossible to use the solution that works for oil. Therefore, wine cannot be stored safely as *tamei terumah*, must be used immediately, has minimal value, and thus presents no *hefsed kohein*.

---

## Shammai/Hillel Debate

### Three Positions

The *Gemara* observes that the question of *takalah* — the concern of accidental consumption of *tamei terumah* — is itself the subject of a *tannaitic* debate, which takes us to the top of 116a. The *braita*: *chavis shel yayin shel trumah shenitmeis* — a barrel of *terumah* wine that became *tamei*. *Beit Shammai* says *tishafeich hakol*: it must all be spilled out, for we fear the *kohein* will come to drink it. *Beit Hillel* says *taaseh ziluf*: it may be used for *ziluf*, as an air freshener.

*Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yose* then offers a nuanced position, saying *ani achriya* — I will adjudicate. His first version of the ruling: if the wine is in the house, use it for *ziluf*, because it is readily at hand and one will use it right away without risk of forgetting. But if it is out in the field, it must be spilled, because by the time one schleps it to the house, there is a risk of forgetting it is *tamei* along the way. A second version of his ruling, reported as *ika d'amri*, drew the line differently: *beyashan taaseh ziluf, bechadash tishpocheihu hakol* — old wine may be used for *ziluf*, but new wine must be spilled. New wine is too weak as an air freshener and might be left to age; by the time it is old enough to use, the *kohein* may have forgotten its status and come to drink it. Old wine, used immediately, presents no such concern.

### Third Opinion Rule

*Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* respond to *Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yose*: *ein hachra'a shelishit machra'at* — a third opinion does not adjudicate between the original two. This requires explanation, since his position seems to be a reasonable middle path that accounts for real distinctions between cases.

*Rashi* explains that a third opinion carries adjudicatory weight only when it operates within a framework implicitly recognized by both of the original disputants. That is, if *Beit Shammai* had said "spill it in all cases — in the house and in the field, old and new" and *Beit Hillel* had said "use it for *ziluf* in all cases," this would imply that both schools recognized the distinction between house and field, or between old and new, but each chose to rule consistently in one direction regardless. In that scenario, *Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yose* would be selecting from the very categories the disputants had already considered, ruling like *Beit Hillel* in some cases and like *Beit Shammai* in others — and that constitutes a genuine *hachra'a*.

But here, *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* issued categorical rulings without reference to any contextual distinctions. Neither school acknowledged that house versus field, or new versus old, should affect the outcome. *Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yose* is not choosing between their positions in context-sensitive cases — he is introducing an entirely new framework that neither school considered. That is not adjudication between two positions; it is a third independent position, and as such, it cannot serve as the *hachra'a* between them.

---

## Stipulated Payment

### Active Loss Payment

We return now to the *Mishnah*. The case: *im amar lo atzil et shelcha* — if the person explicitly stipulates, "I will save yours if you agree to compensate me for mine," then that agreement is binding, and the owner of the honey must pay for the wine that was spilled.

The *Gemara* asks: *amai*? Why should this be so? Why can the honey owner not respond afterward with *meshahta ani bach* — I was just speaking loosely, making an exaggerated promise under duress? One might simply say: because the agreement was made before the act, and the other party acted in reliance on it. But the *Gemara* frames the question more precisely by comparing it to a *braita*.

The *braita*: a prisoner was escaping from captivity — presumably a just prisoner, not a criminal one would wish returned — and there was a boat at the river's edge. He said to the ferryman: *tol dinar vehaavireni* — take a *dinar* and bring me across. The ferryman did so. The *halacha* is that afterward, when they come before a *beit din*, the prisoner need only pay the standard ferry fare. He can in effect say he was speaking under duress and only owes the market rate.

Why then, in our *Mishnah*, can the honey owner *not* say the same?

The *Gemara* answers: our case is not analogous to the opening clause (*reisha*) of the *braita* but to its concluding clause (*seifa*). The *seifa* states: *v'im amar lo tol dinar zeh besakharkha veha'avirani* — if he said "take this *dinar* as your fee and bring me across," then the full stipulated amount must be paid. The *Gemara* then probes what distinguishes *reisha* from *seifa*, since in both cases the ferryman simply ferried the man.

*Rav Bar Chama* explains the distinction in substantive terms: in the *seifa* case, the ferryman was actually a fisherman who was in the middle of catching fish. He said: *afsadeitani kavari bezzuza* — you caused me to lose my fish for that *zuz*. That is, he was incurring a real opportunity cost or actual financial loss by agreeing to ferry the man. When there is a genuine loss that the party is absorbing in reliance on the agreement, the stipulated price is binding. When there is no actual loss — merely a service that the other party happened to perform — the promise of an inflated payment does not obligate beyond the fair market value of the service.

This is quite a significant *chiddush*. One might have thought the distinction was merely formal — whether the payment was framed as a "reward" versus a "fee." But the *Gemara* roots the obligation in the substance of the transaction: if a real loss was incurred in reliance on the agreement, the stipulated amount is enforceable. If no real loss was incurred, even a formal promise of a large sum does not bind beyond the value of the service rendered. One might add that exposure to genuine risk would similarly support an elevated agreed-upon price — the point being that the law will not permit exploitative windfalls, but it will enforce agreements that reflect real financial sacrifice.

### Passive Loss Rules

The *Gemara* then notes that both the wine-and-honey case and the two-donkey case were necessary to teach. If the *Mishnah* had presented only the wine case, one might have thought: *mishum deveyada kapasidei* — the stipulation is binding because I actively spilled out my wine based on your commitment. The active loss, directly incurred by my own hand at your behest, is what makes the agreement enforceable. But in the donkey case, the loss is passive — I simply refrained from saving my own donkey while I went to save yours. Perhaps in such a case, even with a prior stipulation, you should only owe me the market rate for my service, since you did not instruct me to take any active step that caused me loss. The *Mishnah* therefore teaches that passive loss too, when it is a genuine financial loss that occurred in the context of an agreed-upon arrangement, obligates payment of the stipulated sum.

Conversely, had the *Mishnah* presented only the donkey case, one might have thought: even in the wine case, without a prior stipulation, the person who actively spilled his wine should be compensated in full by the honey owner, since the loss was directly and visibly caused by the act of saving. The *Mishnah* teaches that this too is incorrect — without a stipulation, even actively incurred losses in the course of saving another's property yield only the standard labor fee. Both cases are therefore necessary.

### Lucky Outcome

*Rav Kahana* posed a question to *Rav*: *yarad l'hatzil v'ala shelo me'elav mahu* — what if the person descended to save the other's donkey, succeeded in doing so, and then his own donkey happened to survive on its own? Is the honey owner still obligated to pay the full stipulated amount — including the value of the first person's donkey — even though that donkey was never actually lost?

*Rav* answered: yes. *Mishmaya rachimu alei* — from heaven they had mercy on him, and he simply got lucky. The stipulated price was agreed upon against the background of a foreseeable and genuine risk of loss. The agreement was not conditioned on the donkey actually dying; it was entered into because the risk was real and the sacrifice was undertaken. The honey owner's obligation was created at the moment of the agreement and the act of rescue. The fact that in the end no loss materialized does not retroactively dissolve the binding commitment.

### Rav Safra Story

This principle is illustrated by a story involving *Rav Safra*, who was traveling with a caravan. A trained lion was accompanying and guarding the group, and each night the travelers would take turns providing the lion with a donkey to eat. When *Rav Safra*'s turn arrived, they sent his donkey to the lion — but the lion did not eat it. *Rav Safra* immediately went and re-took possession of his donkey.

*Rav Acha mi-Difti* asked *Ravina*: *lama li l'mizka bei*? Why did *Rav Safra* need to re-take possession? If he only gave the donkey up on the assumption the lion would eat it — *ada'ata d'arya afkrei, ada'ata d'kulei alma lo afkrei* — he had relinquished it with the expectation that the lion would consume it, not as a blanket renunciation of ownership to the world at large. If the lion did not eat it, his conditional relinquishment simply did not take effect. He should still own it automatically.

*Rav Acha* answers: *d'milta hu d'avid* — it was a pragmatic act. Technically, *Rav Safra* remained the owner, since his giving-up of the donkey was conditional on the lion eating it. *Tosafot* notes that it was always understood this was not a certainty. But *Rav Safra* re-took formal possession so that no one else could claim a share or dispute his ownership. The practical act of *zechiyah* — re-acquisition — foreclosed any argument.

*Rashi* connects this back to the *Mishnah*: just as *Rav Safra* retained his ownership because his relinquishment was conditional, and still collected the benefit of his night's obligation being fulfilled even though his donkey survived, so too in the *Mishnah* case — the agreement stands and the stipulated sum is owed even when the anticipated loss did not materialize. It should be noted, however, that there is a complication: the scenario of abandoning one's own donkey to save another's may trigger the principle of *avudah mimenu umikol adam* — a loss so total that the property becomes *hefker* in everyone's eyes. *Rashi* understands the case in the *Mishnah* this way, meaning that the rescuer's donkey does in fact become *hefker*, and if his donkey survives he re-acquires it as ownerless property — while still collecting the stipulated amount for having taken on that risk.
