### Failed Rescue

*Rav* addressed a further question posed to him by *Rebbe*: *yarad l'hatzil v'lo hitzil mahu* — what if the person went to save the other's donkey and failed? Does he still collect the stipulated amount — including the reimbursement for his own lost donkey — in addition to his basic labor fee?

*Rebbe* responded: *vezo she'eilah*? Is this even a question? *Ein lo ela secharo* — he gets only the standard labor fee for the effort expended. The stipulated compensation for the loss of his own donkey was understood to be contingent on actually succeeding in the rescue, not merely on making the attempt. The agreement was: "I will save yours, and in return you will compensate me for mine." If he did not save the other's donkey, he did not fulfill his end of the bargain, and the enhanced compensation does not apply.

---

## Cabbage Plums Case

### Unnecessary Service

A challenge is raised from a *braita*. If someone hired a worker to bring him cabbage and plums for a sick person (*choleh*), at an agreed-upon premium because these ingredients were difficult to obtain, and the worker went and retrieved them — but upon returning found that the patient had died or had already recovered — *noten lo secharo mishalem*: the full stipulated wage must be paid. Here too, the worker's efforts turned out to be unnecessary, just as the failed rescue was unnecessary. Yet full payment is owed. Does this not contradict *Rebbe*'s ruling?

### Success Distinction

The distinction is immediate and clear. *Hatam avad shelichuteih, hacha lo avad shelichuteih* — in the case of the cabbage and plums, the worker did exactly what he was commissioned to do. He brought the cabbage and plums. The fact that the patient subsequently died or recovered is entirely outside the worker's control and entirely unrelated to his performance. He completed his *shlichut* — his assigned task — and is entitled to the full agreed price.

In the case of the failed rescue, the worker did not complete the task he had agreed to. The stipulated sum was not merely compensation for effort or for the risk assumed; it was compensation premised on actually retrieving the other's donkey. Attempting and failing to do so does not fulfill the agreement, and therefore only the standard labor fee applies.

---

## Ransom & Guild Rules

### Ransom Math

The *Gemara* continues with a series of related *beraitot* concerning communal distribution of losses. A caravan traveling through the desert was set upon by troops demanding ransom. *Mechashevin lefi mamon v'ein mechashevin lefi nefashot* — the ransom is divided proportionally according to wealth, not per capita. This is logical: the brigands attacked for money, and in the absence of a ransom they would have taken money proportional to what each person was carrying or owned. The payout should mirror the exposure.

If, however, the caravan had hired a guide or scout to lead them through the desert — protecting them both from getting lost and from attack — then *mechashevin af lefi nefashot*: the cost of the guide is divided both by wealth and by person. The guide is performing a dual service: protecting money and protecting lives. The fee should therefore be split into two components, one allocated by wealth and one allocated equally per capita, since each traveler derives equal benefit from the protection of his life regardless of how much money he carries. The precise arithmetic is left implicit, but the principle is that both factors must enter the calculation.

All of this, the *braita* adds, applies in the absence of an explicit stipulation or an established local custom. *V'lo yeshano miminhag hachamarim* — one does not deviate from the practice of the donkey drivers' guild. If there is a standard practice for how such costs are divided, that governs.

### Donkey Guild

Similarly, *rashaim hachamarim l'hatnot shekol mi sheyovad lo chamor yaamid lo chamor acher* — donkey drivers are permitted to stipulate as a group that if any member loses his donkey in the ordinary course of business, the others will provide him with a replacement. This is a form of mutual insurance, and once the guild has agreed to it, the stipulation is binding on all members.

However, *b'chusia ein maamidim lo* — if the donkey was lost through the negligence (*chusia*) of its owner, the others are not required to replace it. Only non-negligent losses trigger the mutual obligation. *Shelo b'chusia maamidim lo* — where there was no negligence, they must provide the replacement.

### Shared Interest

If the member whose donkey was lost then says: "Don't give me a replacement donkey — just give me the cash value and I will continue watching the herd," the guild need not agree to this. *Pshita*, says the *Gemara* — obvious. But then a subtlety: what if this person already owns another donkey? Perhaps he has skin in the game regardless, and one might think the cash equivalent is sufficient. The *Gemara* rejects this: *shinui netiruta d'chad minetiruta d'bei terei* — the quality of watching one donkey is different from watching two. The more assets a person has at stake, the more diligent he will be. The guild's insistence on providing a replacement donkey — not cash — is specifically designed to maximize each member's personal stake in protecting the herd. Giving cash removes one unit of self-interest and diminishes the collective security of the arrangement.

---

## Boat Jettison

### Weight Division

A parallel *braita* addresses sea travel. A ship was at sea when a large wave threatened to capsize it, and cargo had to be thrown overboard to stabilize the vessel — an echo of the *Yona* narrative. How is the loss distributed among the passengers? *Mechashevin lefi masa v'ein mechashevin lefi mamon* — the jettisoned cargo is allocated by weight (*masa*), not by value (*mamon*). If one person's cargo weighs ten times as much as another's, ten times as much of his cargo should be thrown overboard, regardless of the relative monetary values involved. The reason is straightforward: it is weight, not value, that endangers the vessel. The distribution of sacrifice should correspond to the distribution of the danger created.

### Seafarer Custom

Here too, *v'lo yeshano miminhag hasapanim* — one does not deviate from the established custom of seafarers. If there is a recognized practice for how jettison losses are apportioned, that practice governs.

And just as with the donkey drivers, *rashaim hasapanim l'hatnot shekol mi shetoavad lo sfina yaamid lo sfina acheret* — seafarers may stipulate as a guild that if any member's boat is lost, the others will replace it. The insurance here covers the boat itself, presumably not the cargo.

*Avda lo b'chusia ein maamidin* — if the boat was lost through the negligence of its captain or owner, the guild is not obligated to replace it. *Shelo b'chusia maamidin lo* — if the loss was not due to negligence, they must replace it. An additional exception applies in the maritime context that has no direct parallel in the donkey case: *v'i peirash limakom she'ein sfinos holchos ein maamidin* — if the captain sailed his boat to a location that boats do not normally travel, venturing beyond the standard routes, that deviation is treated as a form of negligence and the guild is similarly not obligated to replace the vessel.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 117

## Ship & Caravan Loss

### Cargo Distribution

The *daf* opens in the middle of a discussion about the practices of sailors and caravan-owners when cargo must be jettisoned to save a ship. The principle established is that when weight must be cast off, the loss is distributed proportionally according to each passenger's share of the cargo. This distribution is subject to one overarching constraint: *u'vilvad shelo yeshanu miminhag hassafanim* — one may not deviate from the established custom among sailors.

### Ship Owner Insurance

The Gemara then addresses a mutual insurance arrangement among ship-owners sailing together as a convoy. The ruling is: *verasha'in hassafanim lehatnot* — the ship-owners are permitted to stipulate among themselves that if any one of them loses his ship, the others will collectively replace it. However, this arrangement carries implicit parameters. If the ship was lost through *kusya* — negligence — it is not replaced. Only when the loss occurred without negligence does the mutual obligation to replace apply.

### Seasonal Routes

The Gemara raises a seemingly obvious point: if a ship owner sailed to a place where ships do not normally travel, he has evidently broken from the group and cannot expect replacement. *Pishita* — this is self-evident, the Gemara objects. The Gemara therefore specifies a more nuanced case: in Nisan, when snowmelt causes river waters to run high, ships sail one unit from the shore; in Tishrei, when water levels are lower, ships sail two units out. The case is one where a ship sailed in Nisan to the position that ships occupy in Tishrei — a normal sailing location, but not for this season. One might have thought that since it is a standard route at other times, the deviation is excusable, perhaps because the ship simply follows its habitual course. The Gemara rules otherwise: in Nisan, the standard is to sail closer to shore, and departing from that constitutes negligence. The ship is therefore not replaced.

### Caravan Rescue

The Gemara proceeds to a *baraita* concerning caravans. A caravan traveling through the wilderness is attacked by troops who plunder it. One member of the caravan stands up and, through some act of bravery, saves the caravan. The ruling: *hitzil le'emtza* — he saved it for everyone. He does not get to appropriate the rescued property simply because his valor preserved it. It still belongs to all the original owners. However, if before acting he declared *ani atzil le'atzmi* — I am rescuing this for myself — then *hitzil le'atzmo*, he keeps it.

### Salvage Rights

The Gemara asks what the underlying logic of this ruling is. It distinguishes two scenarios based on the concept of *hefker*. If the property was *yachol lehatzil* — salvageable through normal collective effort — then the property never became *hefker* to begin with. In that case, no declaration makes a difference; it belongs to the owners regardless of what the rescuer says. Conversely, if it was *eino yachol lehatzil* — not realistically salvageable — then the property is considered *hefker*, and even without a declaration the rescuer might be entitled to keep what he saves.

Rami bar Chama resolves the difficulty by explaining that the *baraita* is dealing with *shutafim* — partners. The logic is that in such circumstances, one partner has the unilateral right to dissolve the partnership — *shutaf cholek shelo l'da'at chaveiro*. If he declares he is acting for himself, he is effectively withdrawing from the partnership, and since the property is *hefker*, whatever he saves is his. If he says nothing, the implicit position is that he continues to act on behalf of the partnership, and what he saves accrues to both partners.

Rava offers a parallel reading: the case involves workers rather than partners. If a worker says nothing, since the property was *hefker* and he was hired to watch it, he is acting on behalf of his employer and saves it for the employer. If he declares he is acting for himself, that declaration constitutes quitting his position on the spot.

### Worker Quits

Rava grounds this in the principle he articulates elsewhere: *po'el yachol lachazor bo afilu b'chatzi hayom* — a worker may quit his job even in the middle of the workday. Employment is not indentured servitude. As long as he has not yet quit — *k'reshutei d'ba'al habayit* — he is operating within his employer's domain and whatever he does is on the employer's behalf. Once he declares he is acting for himself, he has effectively quit. The Torah basis for this right to quit is the verse *ki li b'nei yisrael avadim* — the children of Israel are slaves to God — *v'lo avadim l'avadim* — and not slaves to slaves. The Gemara notes this as a powerful statement against treating employment as a form of enslavement. There may be contractual penalties for quitting, but one cannot be compelled to continue working.

### Rav Ashi Salvage

Rav Ashi offers yet another reading: the case is one where the property is *yachol lehatzil yadei dechaka* — salvageable, but only with effort. Rashi explains this as follows: if the rescuer declares he is saving it for himself and the other owner — Michael in the shiur's illustration — hears this and says nothing, that silence constitutes implicit *ye'ush* and an act of *hefker* on the owner's part, as if to say the property is as good as lost. In that scenario, the rescuer keeps it. If, however, no such declaration is made, the property is still potentially salvageable and is not presumed *hefker*; the owner retains title.

---

## Field Theft

### Mishnah Field

The Gemara moves to the next *mishnah*. *Ha-gozel sadeh me-chavero* — one who steals a field from his fellow. The *mishnah* then addresses what happens when troops subsequently seize that field. If the seizure is a *makas medinah* — a general regional calamity affecting everyone's fields, not just this one — then the thief says to the original owner: *harei shelcha lefanecha*, here is your property, effectively returning it in its diminished state and discharging his liability. The implicit logic is that even had the theft never occurred, the original owner would have lost the field to the same troops. However, if the seizure was *machamas hagazlan* — specifically on account of the thief — then the thief must *l'amid lo sadeh acher*, provide a replacement field.

This *mishnah* raises a difficulty. The ordinary rule is that *karka* — real property — is not subject to the laws of *gezeilah* in the ordinary sense. One who occupies another's land does not incur the standard liabilities of a thief in the way one who takes movable property does. If so, why does this *mishnah* seem to treat the field as stolen? One possible reading is that the *mishnah* is grounded in a concept resembling *garmi* — that even if the technical laws of *gezeilah* do not apply to land, when damage results directly and foreseeably from one's act, liability may still follow on that basis. The distinction between whether the seizure is general or personal could then be understood as turning on whether the owner's situation was made meaningfully worse by the thief's involvement: if everyone's field was seized, the owner is no worse off; if only this field was targeted because of the thief, real damage has been caused.

### Pointing Out

The Gemara reinterprets the phrase *machamas hagazlan* in an unexpected direction. The case is not, the Gemara suggests, one of straightforward theft at all. Rather, it is a case of *d'achvei achveih* — he pointed it out. Troops or authorities came and demanded to know where a certain person's field was, and the man in question disclosed the location. The Gemara uses the term *gazlan* loosely here; the core liability is not for *gezeilah* but for the act of disclosure itself. The *mishnah* becomes a source for the broader principle that one who points out another's property to hostile authorities and causes it to be seized bears liability for the resulting loss.

This case is the gateway into the extended discussion of *moser* — one who informs against or betrays a fellow Jew to non-Jewish authorities. The concern is not merely the immediate financial loss; once hostile governmental power begins to take interest in a person's property, the danger has a way of escalating into a threat against life itself. The Talmudic image is that once the authorities begin seizing a person's assets, they show no compassion — like a trapped bull that is slaughtered without mercy.

### Wheat Case

The Gemara grounds this discussion in a concrete case. A certain person pointed out a stockpile of wheat belonging to the *Reish Galuta* — the Exilarch — to non-Jewish authorities. The case came before Rav Nachman, who was himself related to the Exilarch. Rav Nachman ruled that the man who pointed out the wheat must reimburse the owner. Rav Yosef, sitting two rows behind Rav Huna bar Chiya, observed the proceedings as Rav Huna bar Chiya put a question to Rav Nachman.

### Din vs Knas

Rav Huna bar Chiya asked Rav Nachman: *dina o knasa* — is your ruling substantive law, a *din*, or is it a punitive fine, a *knas*? Rav Nachman replied that it is a *mishnah* — pointing to the ruling derived from our *mishnah* that one who causes another's field to be seized must reimburse. After Rav Nachman left, Rav Yosef asked Rav Huna bar Chiya why the distinction matters. Rav Huna bar Chiya explained: if this is *din* — substantive law grounded in a legal principle — then we may extrapolate from it and apply it to analogous cases. If it is *knas* — a penalty imposed for pragmatic or deterrent reasons — then each ruling stands on its own and one cannot extend it to other cases by logical inference.

### Fine Extrapolation

The question of whether one can extrapolate from a *knas* ruling to similar cases is addressed through a *baraita*. Originally the rabbis said: one who renders another's grain *tamei*, or one who pours another's wine as a libation to *avoda zara*, must pay, despite the fact that the damage is *hezek she'eino nikar* — invisible damage, not perceptible to the eye. The ordinary rule is that invisible damage is not actionable. Subsequently, the rabbis added a further ruling: even one who mixes *terumah* grain into *chulin* grain — causing the entire mixture to have *terumah* status and diminishing its market value — must also pay. The fact that a new ruling was needed in order to include this second case demonstrates that from a *knas* one cannot extrapolate; each application requires its own independent ruling.

### Fine Extrapolation

The Gemara contests this proof. Perhaps the original ruling was in fact *din* — substantive law — and a new ruling was needed not because extrapolation from *knas* is impossible, but because there was a logical reason to distinguish the two cases at the level of *din* itself. Specifically, the original ruling applied to large losses — grain rendered entirely unusable — while the *terumah* case involves a lesser loss, since the grain is not destroyed but merely downgraded in status. Originally the rabbis held that the principle of liability for invisible damage applied only to significant losses, and only later did they extend it to smaller losses as well. In this reading, no extrapolation was made because the cases were genuinely distinguishable on their merits, not merely because extrapolation from *knas* is impermissible.

### Damage Types

A second *baraita* — attributed to the father of Rabbi Avin — presents the cases in reverse order: first the ruling about *metame* and *medam'ea*, and then the subsequent addition of the case of pouring wine to *avoda zara*. Now the second case, pouring wine, involves a *greater* loss than the first; logically it should have been easier to include by extrapolation. Yet a new ruling was still required. This suggests the reason for requiring a new ruling is precisely the principle that from *knas* one cannot extrapolate.

The Gemara deflects this as well. The case of pouring wine to *avoda zara* involves a question of *kim leih bidrabbah minei* — whether the act, which carries a capital penalty, exempts the actor from financial liability simultaneously incurred. This turns on a dispute between Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Yirmiyah. Rabbi Avin held that the entire act of *chillul Shabbos*, including the moment of *akira* (lifting), is subsumed under the capital liability, applying the principle that the greater penalty absorbs the lesser — *kim leih*. Rabbi Yirmiyah disagrees: financial liability for wine attaches at the moment of lifting, while the capital liability for *avoda zara* attaches only at the moment of pouring. These do not coincide, and thus *kim leih* does not apply. The Gemara's resolution is that originally the ruling followed Rabbi Avin and therefore the wine case was excluded on substantive grounds, not merely because extrapolation from *knas* is forbidden. Only later, once the ruling followed Rabbi Yirmiyah, was the wine case added by a new explicit ruling.

The upshot is that the underlying question — whether the liability of one who points out another's property is *din* or *knas* — remains practically significant. As a *din*, grounded in an expansive understanding of *garmi* liability, it can serve as precedent. As a *knas*, it stands alone and cannot be extended. The Gemara's extended discussion of *hezek she'eino nikar* illuminates the structural question: when the rabbis impose liability for a type of damage that would ordinarily be exempt, are they declaring a *din* — that this really is *hezek* — or are they imposing a *knas* to deter harmful conduct?

---

## Forced Disclosure

### Rav Nachman Ruling

Rav Huna bar Yehuda came to a certain place and subsequently appeared before Rava. Rava told him he had recently adjudicated a case in which a Jew was forced by non-Jews to reveal the location of a fellow Jew's property, and he had ruled the man liable to reimburse.

### Baraita Exemption

Rav Huna bar Yehuda challenged Rava's ruling from a *baraita*: *Yisrael she'ansuhu ovdei kochavim l'haros mamon chaveiro patur* — a Jew who was compelled by non-Jews to disclose his fellow's property is exempt. The *baraita* continues: *v'im natal v'nasan b'yad chayav* — but if he physically picked it up and handed it over, he is liable.

### Point vs Hand Over

The *baraita* thus draws a sharp distinction between pointing out (*achvei*) and actively handing over (*natal v'nasan b'yad*). The *Rishonim* debate what this distinction means in practice. Rashi understands it as follows: handing over is more than was required. The person was only compelled to point out the location; when he went further and physically picked up the object and delivered it, that additional act was not coerced. Nobody was holding a weapon to his head at that precise moment, and so he becomes a *mazik* through his voluntary additional participation.

Other *Rishonim*, including the Rif, read the *baraita* differently: even when the gun is literally at his head and he is commanded to physically hand it over, he remains liable. The reasoning these authorities offer is that while no moral culpability attaches — one is not expected to forfeit one's life rather than cause financial damage to another — the fact that the friend's property was destroyed in the course of saving the actor's life does not shift that loss onto the friend. The actor benefited; the actor must reimburse. This reading, while logically consistent, is admittedly difficult. When a person's participation is entirely compelled and the coercing party is genuinely not interested in the actor but only in the victim's property, the degree to which the actor can be said to be an agent of harm is genuinely attenuated.

One might further observe that when it comes to land — *karka* — there can be no *natal v'nasan b'yad* in a literal sense, since land cannot be physically handed over. This arguably makes the case of pointing out land more lenient: with a gun to one's head, one is always exempt, since no physical transfer is possible.

### Rava Voluntary

Rava rules: *im herah me'atzmo kenatfo v'natan b'yad dami* — if the person volunteered the information of his own accord, it is equivalent to handing it over physically. Where there was no compulsion at all, the act of voluntary disclosure is treated as fully active participation, and liability follows.

### Rav Ashi Case

A certain person was compelled by non-Jewish authorities and pointed out the location of wine belonging to Rav Mari, the son of Rav Pinchas, the son of Rav Chisda. The parties came before Rav Ashi, who exempted the man who had disclosed the location. The rabbis challenged: does not the *baraita* say that one who physically hands it over is liable? Rav Ashi replied: *hanei milei dela okmei ileiyei me'ikara* — that ruling applies when the authorities were not already standing directly over the property. But here, once the person pointed out the wine and the troops positioned themselves over it, the wine was as good as destroyed at that very moment — *miklei kalyei*, it was already consumed. His subsequent act of physically loading and transferring it therefore occurred after the property was already considered lost. Since he did not cause the destruction through the physical transfer — the destruction had already occurred at the moment of pointing out — he is not liable for the handing over.

### River Case

Rabbi Abbahu posed a challenge to Rav Ashi from a *baraita*: if a bandit says *hoshit li paki amir zeh* — extend to me this bundle of grain — and the person hands it over, he is liable. This sounds like a case of someone standing directly over the property, yet liability still attaches for the physical transfer. The Gemara resolves this: the case is *kegon d'ka'ei a'avra d'nahara* — the bandit is standing on the opposite bank of a river. He cannot reach the property himself. In that situation, the person who hands it across is genuinely an active agent; the bandit is not in a position to seize it unilaterally. The Gemara notes that the *baraita*'s language is precise: it says *hoshit* — extend to me — not simply *ten* — give. This implies that the bandit is at a distance and needs the item extended toward him, confirming that the case is one where the bandit cannot reach the object himself.

This also helps explain, at a more conceptual level, why active handing-over generates liability even under duress. When the coercing party is not standing directly over the object, the person who physically delivers it retains some degree of agency — he is the one who closes the gap between the victim's property and the thief. Even if his life is threatened, the fact that the transfer would not occur without his active participation lends his role a character distinct from pure passivity.

### Net Dispute

A fishnet was being disputed by two claimants, each asserting *didi hu* — it belongs to me. One of them, unwilling to see the dispute drag on, simply handed the net over to a royal officer — in a gesture reminiscent of the Solomonic principle of preferring the other party's loss to one's own. The other claimant then demanded that the one who surrendered it pay for his share of the net.

### Joint Property

Abaye ruled that the one who surrendered the net could claim: *ana ki mati didi mati* — when I surrendered, I surrendered only my share. He has no claim to have surrendered the other's property. Rava, however, rejected this: why should he simply be believed? The dispute over ownership was unresolved, and his unilateral declaration that he surrendered only his share cannot be accepted on its face. Rava therefore ruled: *meshamtinan lei* — we place him under *cherem* until he retrieves the net from the royal officer and brings the parties back before a proper court. The possibility that the net belongs to the other claimant obligates him to restore it so the case can be properly adjudicated.

### Straw Story

A certain man was prepared to disclose to authorities the location of his fellow's straw — a relatively minor piece of property. The matter came before Rav. Rav warned him emphatically: *lo tachvei v'lo tachvei* — do not point it out, do not point it out. The man replied defiantly: *machvina u'machvina* — I will point it out, I will point it out. At this point, Rav Kahana, who was sitting before Rav, broke the man's neck, killing him to prevent the disclosure.

---

## Rav Kahana Story

### Neck Breaking

Rav responded by reciting a verse: *banecha ulfu shachvu b'rosh kol chutzot k'to michmar* — your children have fainted and lain down at the head of every street like a trapped bull. The Gemara explains: just as a bull that falls into a trap is shown no compassion and is immediately slaughtered, so too once the property of Jews falls into the hands of non-Jewish authorities, *ein merachmin alav* — they show no compassion. Rashi understands this to mean that ultimately the Jew's life itself becomes endangered — which would explain why Rav Kahana viewed the would-be informer as a *rodef*. Tosafot understands the verse as referring to the property, which would make the basis for killing the man more difficult to explain. In any event, the story implies that the man was seen as presenting an existential danger, not merely a financial one, and his act was of sufficient severity that Rav Kahana felt compelled to take his life.

### Persian Greeks

Rav turned to Rav Kahana and said: *ad idna havu Parsai d'lo kafdei ashfikhus damin* — until now we were ruled by Persians who were not particular about bloodshed, and you could have gotten away with it. *V'hashta Yavnai d'kafdei ashfikhus damin* — but now it is the Greeks who are particular about murder, and this will not be overlooked. The Koren edition notes that during Rav's lifetime the Parthian-Persian rulers, who had been culturally Hellenized and exercised loose control over internal Jewish affairs, were replaced by the Sassanid emperors, who were less Hellenized and exercised tighter central authority. Under the earlier, more Hellenized rulers, internal Jewish matters — including a Jew killing another Jew — were largely left to the community's own governance. Under the Sassanids, such actions would not be tolerated by the central government. The authorities would declare *mardin mardin* — murder, murder — and Rav Kahana would face criminal jeopardy.

### Exile Terms

Rav therefore instructed Rav Kahana: *kum sa'ak l'Eretz Yisrael* — arise and go up to the Land of Israel. And he imposed a condition: *kabel alach d'lo tiklei l'Rabbi Yochanan sheva shanim* — accept upon yourself not to challenge Rabbi Yochanan for seven years. The reason for this condition is not explicitly stated in the text. It may be understood as a form of *galus* and *atonement* for the killing, or it may have been intended as a protective measure to conceal Rav Kahana's identity from authorities. In any event, the condition itself — seven years of self-imposed silence in learning — would for someone of Rav Kahana's stature represent a genuine and painful form of exile: not merely geographic, but an exile from the full exercise of his Torah capacity.

### Rav Kahana Arrives

Rav Kahana went to the Land of Israel and found Reish Lakish — Rabbi Yochanan's foremost colleague and student — sitting and delivering the review session of the day's lesson to the assembled rabbis. Rav Kahana asked where Reish Lakish was. When they inquired why he sought him, Rav Kahana enumerated a series of difficult questions — *hai kushya v'hai kushya* — along with the corresponding answers he had worked out. His erudition was immediately apparent. Reish Lakish went and told Rabbi Yochanan: *ari ala mi-Bavel* — a lion has come up from Babylonia. He advised Rabbi Yochanan to review carefully whatever *sugya* he planned to teach the next day, because this new arrival would challenge him strenuously.

### Row Movement

The next day, Rav Kahana was placed in the front row of the *beis medrash*, directly before Rabbi Yochanan — the seat of honor reserved for the most distinguished students. Rabbi Yochanan taught a *sugya*, and Rav Kahana said nothing. He taught another, and Rav Kahana remained silent. Honoring his commitment to seven years of silence, he asked no questions. In response to his silence, the academy progressively moved him back — seven rows to the rear — until he sat in the very last row. Rabbi Yochanan said to Reish Lakish: *ari she-amarta na'asa shual* — the lion you spoke of has turned out to be a fox.

Rav Kahana heard this remark and was deeply offended. He made a declaration: may these seven rows of relegation serve in exchange for the seven years of silence that Rav had imposed upon me. He then rose to his feet and asked Rabbi Yochanan to repeat the first teaching. Rabbi Yochanan obliged, and Rav Kahana challenged it. He challenged every subsequent teaching as well. As the challenges mounted, the academy moved Rav Kahana progressively forward until he was restored to the front row.

### Pillars Removed

Rabbi Yochanan was seated upon seven cushioned pillows — *bastarkei* — a detail that scholars have noted reflects a distinctly Babylonian narrative trope, through which the Babylonian Talmud imagines the great *yeshivos* of the Land of Israel. As Rav Kahana's challenges continued, one cushion was removed from beneath Rabbi Yochanan after each teaching, until all seven were removed and Rabbi Yochanan sat on the ground.

Rabbi Yochanan was very old at this point, and his eyelashes had grown so long that they fell over his eyes. He asked that his eyelids be lifted — they were raised with silver tongs — so that he could see Rav Kahana.

### Death Event

When Rabbi Yochanan's eyelids were lifted, he observed that Rav Kahana's lips were parted — a physical condition Rav Kahana had always had. Rabbi Yochanan misread this as mockery, as if Rav Kahana were laughing at him. *Chalash da'atei* — Rabbi Yochanan was despondent, wounded deeply by what he perceived as contemptuous laughter from his student. As a consequence of Rabbi Yochanan's distress, Rav Kahana died.

The narrative carries a layered tragic irony. Rav Kahana had killed a man and gone into exile as a form of punishment and atonement. The terms of his exile — seven years of silence — were meant to be the instrument of his rehabilitation. By breaking those terms and then challenging Rabbi Yochanan with such force that the master was humiliated, Rav Kahana failed to fulfill the conditions of his exile and suffered its ultimate consequence.

### Revival Condition

Rabbi Yochanan went to the cave where Rav Kahana was buried. He found a snake coiled around the entrance. He addressed it: *achna achna, ptach pumach v'yikaness harav eitzel talmid* — snake, snake, open your mouth and let the master enter to the student. The snake did not open. He tried again: let one colleague enter to greet another. The snake still did not open. Finally he said: let the student enter to greet his master. The snake opened. This detail — that the snake responded only when Rabbi Yochanan positioned himself as the lesser party — underscores the Gemara's implicit sense that Rav Kahana's Torah greatness exceeded even that of Rabbi Yochanan.

Rabbi Yochanan prayed for Rav Kahana's revival, and Rav Kahana was restored to life. Rabbi Yochanan said to him: had I known that the parted lips were simply your natural appearance and not a sign of mockery, *lo chalsha da'ati* — I would not have been despondent. He then invited Rav Kahana to return with him to the *yeshiva*.

### Resolution

Rav Kahana replied: if you can pray that I will not die again at your hands, I will come with you; otherwise I will not. *Chalaf sha'ata chalaf sha'ata* — a miracle occurs once; you cannot guarantee it will occur again. On this condition, Rabbi Yochanan continued. He then posed to Rav Kahana all the questions that had remained unresolved for him — *kol sefeika d'hava lei* — and Rav Kahana answered every one of them.

The Gemara concludes with Rabbi Yochanan's own remark: *Yochana amri*, you the people of the Land of Israel think this Torah is yours — *d'lehon hi* — it is really the Torah of Babylonia. This remarkable conclusion — recorded, of course, in the Babylonian Talmud — brings the entire narrative to a close with a striking acknowledgment that the center of gravity of Torah scholarship had shifted. The story of Rav Kahana, beginning with an act of violent prevention of betrayal in Babylonia and ending with his resurrection and vindication in the *yeshiva* of the Land of Israel, is the Bavli's own testimony to the depth and supremacy of Babylonian Torah learning.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 118

## Damaging Through Words

### Property Pointed to Gov

The daf opens on 117b, approximately ten lines from the top, with the case of *hahu de'achvei amataxa deRav Abba* — a certain individual who pointed out to government officials some silk adornment belonging to Rav Abba. The rabbis sitting together — Rav Abba, Rav Chanina bar Pappa, Rav Yitzchak Naphcha, and Rav Yehuda among them — initially thought the informer should be liable for damages, drawing support from the *mishna* in Sanhedrin: a judge who renders an erroneous verdict, exempting the liable party or condemning the innocent, or who renders a ruling of *tameh* or *tahor* incorrectly, cannot reverse what he has done (*ma she'asa asuy*), yet must compensate from his own pocket (*yeshalem mibeito*). Since the damage was accomplished through words alone and is nonetheless actionable, the same logic would seem to apply here.

### Rav: Nasav Ve-Natan

Rav, however, rejects this parallel. *Vehu shenatal venatan beyad* — the judge's liability obtains only when he physically transferred property from one party to another following his ruling. Mere verbal causation, without a physical act of transfer, is insufficient to impose liability under the judge's malpractice ruling.

### Stolen Field, Gov Seizure

The rabbis therefore direct the aggrieved party to Rav Shimon ben Elyakim and Rav Elazar ben Pedat, who adjudicate cases of *dina d'garmi* — indirect but sufficiently direct causation that imposes liability. These authorities find the informer liable based on the *mishna* stating that if a field was seized because of the *gazlan*, the *gazlan* must replace it (*im machmat hagazlan chayav le'amidi sadeh acheret*). The *gemara* had previously established that this applies even where the *gazlan* did not physically steal the field himself but pointed it out to the authorities (*achvei achvaye*). This conclusion thus confirms that the liability rests squarely on the doctrine of *dina d'garmi*.

---

## Saving Self w/ Other's

### Silver Cup Case

The *gemara* next presents a case: *hahu gavra dahave mufkad leh kasa dekaspa* — a man had been entrusted with a silver goblet. Thieves broke in (*sliku ganvei ilavye*), and he — reading the text carefully — took the goblet himself and handed it over to them (*shakle vehavneih nialei*). This is genuinely a case of *nasav ve-natan beyad*: he physically transferred the object. The matter came before Rabba, who exempted him. The man was protecting his own life with his friend's property — *matzil atzmo bemamon chavero*.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges this exemption: *ha-matzil atzmo bemamon chavero hu* — is it not the case that one who saves himself with another's property is liable? As the *gemara* has established from other contexts, *assur lehatzil atzmo bemamon chavero*. While this phrase cannot literally mean one should allow himself to be killed rather than sacrifice another's property, it means at minimum that the act of self-preservation does not extinguish the legal obligation to compensate the owner.

### Wealthy vs. Non-Wealthy

Rav Ashi introduces a distinction: *ee inish amid hu* — if the man is wealthy, then the thieves came because they knew he had his own money; the fact that he handed over the silver goblet was his own doing and in some sense attributable to the attention he attracted. In that case, presumably he bears liability. *Ve-ilo ada'ata de-kaspa hu* — if he is not wealthy, the thieves came specifically because they knew he was holding that silver goblet. The invasion was, in other words, entirely occasioned by the object itself rather than by the guardian personally. The difficulty, however, remains: even in that scenario, this is a case of *nasav ve-natan beyad*, which in the earlier discussion about pointing out property to the government was cited as the factor that *increases* liability. How then does the object being the thieves' target exempt the guardian?

### Tosafot on Shomer

Tosafot addresses this tension. Even granting that *nasav ve-natan beyad* ordinarily imposes liability, the case of a *shomer* is distinguishable. As Tosafot explains in the name of the Ri: *shelo lada'at ken hifkidu sheyatzil atzmo bo im yavo elav ada'ata de-kaspa* — the implicit terms of the bailment arrangement are such that by entrusting the object to this guardian, the owner effectively caused the guardian to become a target on his behalf. The object's presence in the guardian's home is what drew the danger, and so the entrustor bears some degree of responsibility for placing the guardian in that position. Tosafot acknowledges this is not entirely satisfying given the earlier analysis, and the tension between this ruling and the preceding discussion is not fully resolved.

### Pidyon Shvuyim Case

The *gemara* then presents a parallel case: *hahu gavra de-hava mafkid gabei arneka de-pidyon shvuyim* — a man was entrusted with a wallet filled with money designated for the redemption of captives. Thieves came, and again he took the pouch and handed it over to them. Rabba again exempted him. Abaye again challenges: *ha-matzil atzmo bemamon chavero*. Rabba responds with a striking argument: *ein lecha pidyon shvuyim gadol mizeh* — there is no greater act of redeeming captives than this, for the money was designated to save Jewish lives, and here it was used precisely to save a Jewish life.

One might ask: why could he not have used his own money? Tosafot clarifies: even if the man was wealthy, the thieves came specifically because of the *pidyon shvuyim* money, and in any case, at that moment he did not have his own money available. When a person faces a genuine threat to his life or liberty and has no personal funds at hand, using money designated for *pidyon shvuyim* to save himself is itself regarded as *pidyon shvuyim*. Tosafot is careful to limit this: it applies only if he truly lacked access to his own funds at that moment.

The more fundamental question — why the fact that the thieves came specifically because of that particular object should exempt the holder, as contrasted with the earlier case where someone pointed out another's property to the government and was held liable even though the government came specifically for that property — remains unresolved. The distinction based on the *shomer* relationship and the entrustor's implicit role in placing the guardian at risk is the closest the *gemara* comes to an answer, but the fit is imperfect.

---

## Donkey on Boat

### Donkey Thrown Overboard

The *gemara* presents the classic case: *hahu gavra de-atzin ve-asi chamra le-mavra* — a certain man brought his donkey onto a ferry boat. There is a textual question here about the *girsa*: the standard reading has him bringing the donkey onto the boat before the other passengers boarded (*kamei de-sliku inshi be-mavra*), while other versions simply have him bringing it on along with everyone else. The *gemara* continues: *baei le-atvuei* — the boat was in danger of sinking. A certain bystander came and pushed the donkey overboard (*umalakh lei le-chamra de-hahu gavra va-shadya le-nahr*), and the donkey drowned. The matter came before Rava, who exempted the bystander.

### Rava Exempt, Abaye Objec…

Abaye objects once more: *ve-ha-matzil atzmo be-mamon chavero* — the people on the boat were saving themselves with another's property. Why should the one who pushed the donkey be exempt?

### Rodef Doctrine

Rava responds: *hai me'ikara rodef hava* — this donkey was from the outset a *rodef*, a pursuer threatening the lives of all aboard. Rava then invokes his own principle: *rodef she-haya rodef achar chavero le-horgo*, a pursuer chasing a victim to kill him, who in the course of that pursuit breaks vessels — *bein shel nirdaf bein shel kol adam*, whether those vessels belong to the victim or to any third party — is exempt (*patur*). The reason is *she-harei mitchayev be-nafsho*: since the pursuer may lawfully be killed to stop him, a form of the *kim leh* principle applies. Because during the act of pursuit the *rodef* is subject to being killed, he does not simultaneously incur monetary liabilities.

### Rodef & Nirdaf Rules

The *nirdaf* — the pursued victim — who breaks the *rodef*'s vessels in the course of saving his own life is likewise exempt: *shelo yehei mamono chaviv alav mi-gufo* — the *rodef*'s property is not more precious than the *rodef*'s own life, and if the *rodef* may be killed to save the victim, his property may certainly be destroyed for the same purpose. But if the *nirdaf* breaks the vessels of a third party, he is *chayav*, for *assur le-hatzil atzmo be-mamon chavero*. This is, significantly, Rava's own ruling — and this is the key to understanding the preceding cases. Abaye, Rava's student, was in each of the earlier cases throwing Rava's own principle back at him. When Abaye said *ha-matzil atzmo be-mamon chavero*, he was reminding Rava of Rava's own teaching and asking why Rava was exempting the parties in each case.

### Good Samaritan Law

The *gemara* then discusses a third-party intervener — one who is neither the *rodef* nor the *nirdaf* but steps in to stop the *rodef*, and in the process breaks someone else's vessels. This person is exempt, though the *gemara* acknowledges openly: *lo min ha-din* — strictly speaking, he has no legal basis for exemption. The exemption is a policy ruling: *she-im ata omer kein ein lecha adam she-matzil chaveiro min ha-rodef* — if you impose liability on the intervener, no one will ever step in to save another from a pursuer. This is the *gemara*'s version of good Samaritan law: the one who intervenes to prevent a murder is not required to pay for property damaged in the course of doing so. The *nirdaf* himself needs no such policy exemption, since he will do whatever necessary to save his own life regardless.

The application of the *rodef* framework to the donkey case raises its own difficulties. Who exactly is the *rodef*? If the donkey is the *rodef*, the people on the boat are all victims (*nirdafim*), which should mean they can destroy the donkey without any question. If instead the owner of the donkey is deemed the *rodef* — and the note in our *girsa* that he boarded first and brought extra weight aboard may be relevant, positioning him as having violated the terms of the vessel — then the donkey is treated as the vessels of the *rodef*, and the bystander who pushes it overboard functions as a third-party intervener. The identity of the *rodef* and why the donkey's owner in particular is singled out, when all passengers contribute weight, is not fully unpacked by the *gemara*.

What is clear from the whole section is that in all the prior cases, Rava consistently exempted the party who saved himself with another's money, and Abaye consistently challenged him with Rava's own doctrine. The general answers Rava gives are: where the situation itself constitutes a *rodef* scenario, you are exempt; where the money used was *pidyon shvuyim* funds and the person had no alternative, you are exempt; and where the thieves came specifically because of the entrusted object and the *shomer* relationship is relevant, there may be an exemption — though the last case is the least clearly resolved.

---

## Karka Ein Nigzelet

### Stolen Field Swamped

The *gemara* transitions to the next *mishna*: if someone steals a field and it is subsequently swamped by an overflowing river (*sh'tafa nahar*), the thief may say *harei shelcha lefanecha* — here is your property before you — and walk away without replacing it. This reflects the foundational principle of *karka eina nigzelet*: real property cannot be stolen in the halakhic sense, and therefore the theft of land does not carry the liabilities that accompany theft of movable property.

### R. Elazar vs. Chachamim

A *baraita* records the dispute: *ha-gozel sadeh me-chaveiro ve-shatafa nahara* — one who steals a field and it is swamped. Rabbi Elazar says the thief is obligated to provide a replacement field (*chayav le-ha'amid lo sadeh acheret*). The Sages say he may simply say *harei shelcha lefanecha*. The question is: on what do they disagree?

### Ribui Miut Ribui

Rabbi Elazar employs the hermeneutical method of *ribui u-miut* — a broad formulation, then a narrow one. The verse *ve-chi yechahesh be-amito* (when one denies something of his fellow) is a *ribui*, a broad inclusive statement. *Be-fikadon* (in an entrusted object) is a *miut*, a limiting concrete example. *U-ve-chol asher yishava alav la-sheker* (and anything he swore falsely about) is again a *ribui*, broadening the scope. Applying the rule of *ribui miut ve-ribui*, the result is that everything is included except whatever is most unlike the concrete example. What is the *miut* excluding? *Miet shtarot* — documents, which lack intrinsic value (*ein gufan mamon*). Everything else that has intrinsic value, including land, falls within the scope of *ve-heshiv et ha-gezeilah asher gazal*, the obligation to return what was stolen.

### Rabanan Kelal U'Prat

The Sages, by contrast, apply *kelal u-prat u-chelal* — general, particular, general. Using this hermeneutic, one does not include everything except the most dissimilar; rather, one includes only what resembles the concrete case. *Mah ha-prat davar ha-mitaltel ve-gufo mamon* — the particular case, *pikadon*, is both movable and possessed of intrinsic value. The obligation of *ve-heshiv et ha-gezeilah* therefore extends only to things that are both chattel and intrinsically valuable. *Yatzu karkaot she-einan mitaltelin* — land is excluded because it is not movable. *Yatzu avadim she-hukshu le-karkaot* — slaves are excluded by their analogy to land. *Ve-yatzu shtarot* — documents are excluded because, though movable, they lack intrinsic value. Hence, according to the Sages, *karka eina nigzelet*.

### Cow on Stolen Field

A *baraita* seems to complicate the picture: *ha-gozel sus parah ve-shatafa nahara chayav le-ha'amid lo parah divrei Rabbi Elazar* — Rabbi Elazar says that if one steals a cow and it is swamped, he must replace it, while the Sages again say *harei shelcha lefanecha*. But this appears to be a dispute about an animal, not about land. How does it fit the framework of *karka ein nigzelet*?

### Rav Papa Land Seizure

Rav Papa resolves this: *kegon she-gazal sadeh me-chaveiro u-parah revutza bah* — the case involves one who seized a field from its owner and expelled him, while a cow was resting on that field. The thief never physically picked up the cow; he simply seized the land. The dispute thus turns entirely on whether *karka* is considered *nigzelet*. If, as Rabbi Elazar holds, one can *halakhically* steal land — meaning the act of seizure imposes upon the thief a degree of quasi-ownership — then, since a chattel found on one's land can be acquired through the land itself (*kinyan agav karka*), the thief is considered to have acquired the cow through his seizure of the field, and with that acquisition comes liability. The Sages, who hold *karka eina nigzelet* and therefore deny that any halakhic acquisition occurs through the seizure, deny that the cow was acquired at all, and therefore the thief has no liability for it. *Rabbi Elazar le-ta'ameih ve-rabanan le-ta'ameihu* — each opinion follows its own reasoning consistently.

---

## Return Location Rules

### Mishna Return Limits

The *mishna* addresses the location of return: *ha-gozel et chaveiro o she-hilva heimennu o she-hifkid lo be-yishuv* — one who stole from, borrowed from, or received an object in trust from his fellow in a settled area (*be-yishuv*). *Lo yachzir lo ba-midbar* — he may not return it to him in the wilderness. However, *al menat la-tzet ba-midbar*, if he stipulates at the outset that he intends to travel to the wilderness and may return it there, and the owner agrees, then *yachzir lo ba-midbar* — he may. One cannot of course stipulate when stealing, but this is relevant to the loan and *pikadon* cases.

### Milve vs. Aveidah

The *gemara* raises a contradiction: *milve mi-shtalemet be-chol makom* — a loan can be repaid anywhere; but *aveida u-pikadon ein mishtalmin ella bi-mekomam* — a lost object or an entrusted object can only be returned in their proper place. Does this mean that if a lost object was found in the wilderness and the owner lives in the city, it must be returned in the wilderness? No — the phrase means returned where it properly belongs. But the tension remains: may the *milve* be repaid in the middle of the wilderness?

Abaye clarifies: *milve nitenet li-tava be-chol makom* — a loan can be *demanded* anywhere. The creditor who encounters his debtor in the wilderness may demand payment on the spot. He has the right to ask, even if the debtor has nothing to give. But the debtor cannot *force* the creditor to accept repayment in the wilderness if the creditor prefers to receive it in town and during normal circumstances. An *aveida* or *pikadon*, by contrast, being a concrete object rather than a fungible debt, cannot be demanded in an inappropriate location; *aveida u-pikadon lo nitnu li-tava ella bi-mekomam*. The distinction is between the right to make a demand (*li-tava*) and the right to force acceptance of a return.

### Implicit Stipulation

As for the stipulation allowing wilderness return: the *gemara* observes this would be obvious if the agreement were explicit, and therefore the novelty lies in a subtler case. The owner says: watch this object — *de-le-midbar nafikna* — because I am going out to the wilderness. The guardian replies: *ana nami le-midbar ba'ina le-mifak* — I also may be heading out to the wilderness; *adreina lach* — I will return it to you if I happen to meet you out there. The owner makes no explicit affirmative response, but neither does he object. The *gemara* treats this as a case of implicit stipulation, since the owner's evident reason for the bailment was that he would be in the wilderness and presumably understood the possibility of return there.

---

## Admission of Liability

### Admit but Uncertain

The *mishna* presents the following case: *ha-omer le-chaveiro gezalticha hilvitani hifkadta etzli ve-eini yodeia im hichzarti lach im lo hichzarti lach* — one who says to his fellow: I stole from you, or you lent me money, or you entrusted an object to me, and I do not know whether I ever returned it or paid it back. In such a case he is *chayav le-shalem*: he admits that he incurred liability, but cannot establish that he was ever discharged from it. By contrast, *im amar lo eini yodeia im gezalticha* — if he says he does not know whether he ever stole from the person or incurred the obligation in the first place, he is *patur mi-leshalem*.

### Bari ve-Shema Debate

The *gemara* connects this to the classic dispute: *maneh li be-yadcha ve-halla omer eini yodeia* — Reuven says to Shimon, you owe me a hundred dollars, and Shimon responds, I don't know. Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda rule *chayav* on the principle of *bari ve-shema bari adif*: a definite claim prevails over a doubtful one, even though Shimon is *muchzak* — in possession of the money. Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan rule *patur*: *ve-okei mamona be-chezkat marei* — we leave the money in the possession of its current holder, and a definite claim without evidence is insufficient to extract it.

The *gemara* then asks how to situate our *mishna* within this debate: is a claim being made against the admitting party or not? If no claim is being made (*d'lo katva lei*), then even the first case of the *mishna* — I admit I stole but don't know if I returned it — should be *patur*, since no one is demanding payment. If a claim is being made, then even the second case — I don't know if I was ever liable — should be *chayav* according to the view that *bari adif*.

### Uncertain Liability

The *gemara* resolves this: the *mishna* consistently speaks in a situation where no formal claim is being made. The party is coming forward voluntarily. In the first case — I know I was liable but don't know if I was ever discharged — the ruling of *chayav* is not a legal compulsion but an expression of moral obligation: *reisha le-tzet yedei shamayim*. He wants to do the right thing, and the right thing is to pay. In the second case — I don't even know if I incurred liability — even the moral obligation does not apply, since one cannot be required, even morally, to pay for a debt whose very existence is uncertain.

### Tzeat Yedei Shamayim

This introduces an important distinction between categories. *Patur be-dinei adam ve-chayav be-dinei shamayim* — exempt by human law but obligated by divine law — is a concept the *gemara* invokes at several points throughout Bava Kamma. But *latzet yedei shamayim* is not quite the same as *lifnim mi-shurat ha-din*. *Lifnim mi-shurat ha-din* represents going beyond the letter of the law, an act of exceptional piety or generosity. *Latzet yedei shamayim* is doing what is morally right even when the law does not compel it — occupying the space between legal exemption and ethical obligation. The question of whether one who fails to act *le-tzet yedei shamayim* is actually *chayav bi-dei shamayim* is left open.

This is confirmed by the parallel statement of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ha-omer le-chaveiro maneh li be-yadecha ve-halla omer eini yodeia chayav latzet yedei shamayim* — the same Rabbi Yochanan who holds *patur* in the formal legal dispute (*bari ve-shema, bari lo adif*, the *chazakah* of possession controls) nonetheless rules that the respondent is *chayav latzet yedei shamayim*. If one wants to act ethically, one must pay the person who made a definite claim against him, even though the law would leave the money in his pocket.

---

## Returning Stolen Animal

### Sheep Returned Dies

The *mishna* establishes: *ha-gonav taleh min ha-tzon ve-hechziro* — one who steals a sheep from the flock and secretly returns it, after which it dies or is stolen again — *chayav be-achrayuto*: he has not fulfilled his obligation and remains liable. The owner was not aware of either the theft or the return. However, if *lo yadu ba'alim lo bi-gnevato ve-lo be-hachzirato* — the owners knew of neither the theft nor the return — and *u-manu et ha-tzon* — they counted the sheep and the number was complete — the thief is *patur*.

The simple reading of the *mishna*: if the owner knew he was robbed, the return is effective only when the owner is made explicitly aware. If the owner was oblivious, counting and discovering that the flock is complete suffices — even without knowing that it was stolen and returned.

### Rava: Da'at vs. Minyan

Rava reads the *mishna* straightforwardly: *lada'at tzarich da'at* — if stolen knowingly, the return requires explicit *da'at* of the owner. *Shelo lada'at minyan poter* — if stolen without the owner's awareness, counting (*minyan*) suffices. The phrase *u-manu et ha-tzon* in the *mishna* accordingly belongs to the final clause dealing with the *shelo lada'at* scenario.

### Shmuel: Always Minyan

Shmuel takes a different position: *bein lada'at bein shelo lada'at minyan poter* — counting always suffices. The owner's awareness of the counting exempts the thief regardless of whether the owner knew of the theft. This reading imposes significant strain on the *mishna*, since the *mishna* seems to clearly distinguish cases, but Shmuel's principle is that *minyan* represents adequate knowledge in all circumstances.

### R. Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan shifts the entire framework one step down: *lada'at minyan poter* — when the owner knew of the theft, counting suffices to establish that the animal is back. *Shelo lada'at afilu minyan nami lo tzarich* — if the owner was entirely oblivious, not even counting is required; the thief's quiet return of the animal to where he took it from is sufficient. The *mishna*'s phrase about counting therefore belongs, on this reading, to the first case (*risha*) — the *lada'at* scenario — and in the *shelo lada'at* case, even less is required.

### R. Chisda Reversed

Rav Chisda takes the position that is most counterintuitive: *lada'at minyan poter* — if the owner knew of the theft, counting suffices. *Shelo lada'at tzarich da'at* — if the owner did not know of the theft, explicit *da'at* of the return is required. This inverts the apparent logic: one would expect that the higher the owner's awareness of the wrong, the more demanding the standard for correction. Yet Rav Chisda holds that it is specifically when the owner was unaware of the theft that more is required.

### Animal Neglect Justifi.

The *gemara* explains Rav Chisda's reasoning: *ho'il ve-anketina nagrei baraita* — since the theft itself has encouraged the animal to stray (*chinuch ha-lahal*). A stolen animal that has been removed from the flock once is now more likely to wander off on its own. The owner needs to know that this particular animal was taken away, because if he is unaware, he will not take extra precautions to supervise it. Therefore, the thief is not discharged of responsibility until he informs the owner — not merely as a matter of acknowledging wrongdoing, but to ensure that the owner can now protect the animal properly. When the owner knew of the theft and sees through the counting that his flock is complete, he implicitly draws the conclusion that the missing animal has returned and will naturally be more alert to its welfare. But when he never knew, the mere counting does not trigger this heightened awareness.

---

## Tanaim: Return Metho (II)

### R. Yishmael Location

The *gemara* asks whether the *amora'im*'s debate maps onto an earlier *tanna'im* dispute. *Ha-ganav taleh min ha-eder ve-sela min ha-kis* — one who steals a sheep from the flock or money from a wallet. Rabbi Yishmael rules: *le-makom she-ganav yachzir* — return it to where you took it from, and that suffices.

### R. Akiva: Inform Owner

Rabbi Akiva rules: *tzarich da'at ba'alim* — the owner must be made aware. The *gemara* assumes that all opinions agree with the principle of Rabbi Yitzchak — *adam asui le-mashmesh be-kiso be-chol sha'ah* — a person is constantly checking his wallet. The wallet case is therefore inherently one of *lada'at*: because the owner always monitors his funds, any theft is quickly discovered. The debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva about the wallet is thus a debate about whether *minyan* alone suffices when the theft is *lada'at*, or whether explicit *da'at* of the return is also required. This corresponds to the *amora'im*'s dispute.

---

## Tanaim: Return Metho (II)

### Wallet Case Analysis

The flock case, by contrast, involves a scenario of *shelo lada'at*: owners of large flocks do not immediately notice when an animal goes missing. The debate there — whether simply returning the animal to the flock suffices, or whether the owner must be explicitly informed — corresponds to the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan about the *shelo lada'at* scenario.

### Shomer Took Object

Rav Zavid in the name of Rava introduces a further refinement. If a *shomer* appropriated the object he was entrusted to guard — not by removing it from the owner's premises but by deciding internally to keep it — the question arises of whether his *shmirah* has lapsed. Rabbi Akiva holds *kalu lo shmirato*: the moment he mentally appropriated it and removed it from the agreed storage location, even briefly, he ceased to be a *shomer*. Returning it to the original location is therefore a return *shelo lada'at*, and according to Rabbi Akiva (following the principle of Rav Chisda), explicit *da'at* of the owner is required. Rabbi Yishmael holds *lo kalu lo shmirato*: since the *shomer* never removed it from the owner's purview in any meaningful sense, he is still acting as the owner's representative, and returning the object to the location where he was watching it is considered a return *lada'at* — he is, in effect, returning it to himself in his capacity as guardian.

### Overpaying Repayment

The *gemara* turns to a further case: *ha-gozel et chaveiro ve-hivlio lo be-cheshbon* — one who stole from his fellow and, feeling guilty but unwilling to confess, overpays him when making a purchase, embedding the stolen amount in the payment. One *baraita* says *yatza* — this constitutes valid return. Another *baraita* says *lo yatza* — it does not.

The *gemara* initially assumes that both *baraitot* agree with Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that one always checks one's wallet, and that overpaying would therefore quickly be noticed — analogous to *minyan*. The debate would then be whether *minyan* alone is sufficient to discharge the obligation (*yatza*) or whether explicit *da'at* of the return is required (*lo yatza*). The *gemara* then offers an alternative: perhaps the debate is actually about whether people always check their wallets (*d'Rabbi Yitzchak*). One opinion holds they do — *minyan* is therefore achieved quickly and suffices. The other holds they do not always do so, and therefore there is no reliable *minyan* here.

A final alternative distinguishes by circumstance: *ha d'mani ve-ramayei be-kiseih* — where the repayer counted out the money and placed it directly into the recipient's wallet, the recipient will notice the discrepancy and achieve *minyan*. *Ve-ha d'manyei ve-ramayei be-yadeih* — where the money was counted and placed into the recipient's hand, the recipient will simply pocket it without recounting, and *minyan* will not occur. Thus even under the universally-accepted principle of Rabbi Yitzchak, specific circumstances may prevent the *de facto* *minyan* that the principle assumes.

---

## Buying from Shepherds

### Prohibited Purchases

The *mishna* rules: *ein lokhin min ha-ro'im tzemar ve-chalav u-gediyim* — one may not purchase from shepherds wool, milk, or kids. Similarly, one may not purchase from produce-watchmen (*shomrei peirot*) wood or fruit. These are items the shepherds and watchmen were entrusted to guard on behalf of the owners; purchasing from them creates the presumption of theft and constitutes enabling it.

### Permitted from Women

However, *aval lokhin min ha-nashim klei tzemar bi'Yehudah u-klei pishtan ba-Galil* — from women one may purchase wool garments in Judea and linen garments in the Galilee. This reflects the established local practice: in Judea, women maintained wool-working businesses; in the Galilee, linen was the norm. Though the ordinary presumption might be that a married woman lacks independent authority to sell her husband's property, these were recognized industries conducted by women either on their own account or as their husbands' agents, and there was therefore no suspicion. Similarly, *agalim ba-Sharon* — calves could be purchased in the Sharon region, where this was an accepted trade.

### Transformed Goods

The *baraita* elaborates: one may not purchase from shepherds goats, kids, shorn wool, or plucked wool. However, *aval lokhin mehem tefurim* — woven garments may be purchased, *mipnei she-hen shelahem* — because even if the raw material was stolen, the act of weaving constitutes a *shinui* (transformation), which halakhically transfers ownership to the thief. This is noted as an interesting proposition, since purchasing goods acquired through another's transformation indirectly encourages theft — a separate conversation — but the ruling stands.

### Milk & Cheese Rules

*Ve-lokhin mehem chalav u-gevina ba-midbar ve-lo ba-yishuv* — milk and cheese may be purchased from shepherds in the wilderness but not in the town. The apparent logic: in the wilderness, owners likely give shepherds greater latitude to sell dairy products, since they cannot easily market them directly. Alternatively, in the town the owner himself would be the natural vendor, so a shepherd selling dairy products there raises suspicion. One might add the practical consideration that milk spoils quickly — in the wilderness, the shepherd may have no reasonable alternative.

### Quantity Thresholds

*Ve-lokhin mehem arba tzon arba gizin* — one may purchase four sheep or four bundles of wool. *Aval lo shtei tzon ve-lo shtei gizin* — but not two. The principle is that a large quantity will inevitably be noticed by the owner, and therefore if the shepherd is selling a large amount, he must have received authorization. Two animals, by contrast, could go unnoticed — explained away as a natural loss or a stray.

### House vs. Wilderness

Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes by type of animal: *bayitot lokhin mehem* — house animals may be purchased, *bariot ein lokhin mehem* — wilderness animals may not. House animals are kept close to the owner and their absence is immediately noticed, so a shepherd selling them must have authorization. Animals kept in distant pastures can disappear without the owner's awareness, and their sale by the shepherd is therefore suspect.

### Owner Awareness Rule

The *mishna* states the general principle: *kol she-ha-ro'eh mocher u-va'al ha-bayit margish bo lokhin mehem* — anything whose sale would be noticed by the owner may be purchased from the shepherd, since the owner's implicit awareness guarantees authorization or at least accountability. *Kol she-ein margish bo ein lokhin mehem* — anything the owner would not notice is missing may not be purchased.

### Rav Chisda Numbers

The *gemara* notes an apparent redundancy in the ruling: if four sheep may be purchased, five certainly may be purchased, since the larger the quantity the more conspicuous the transaction. The *gemara* therefore cites Rav Chisda's significant limitation: *arba mitoch hamisha* — four sheep out of a flock of five. The ruling is not a general permission to buy four sheep; it means one may purchase four when that represents eighty percent of the flock, a quantity so conspicuous that authorization is virtually certain. A second version of Rav Chisda's ruling, however, is less restrictive: *arba'a mitoch katan ve-chamisha mitoch gadol* — four from a small flock, five from a large one, without requiring the eighty-percent ratio.

### Healthy vs. Scrawny

The *gemara* resolves the apparent inconsistency between the ruling permitting four and five and the ruling prohibiting two: the threshold is context-dependent. *Ha be-briata ha be-kachishata* — the case permitting purchase refers to healthy, robust animals, whose absence will be immediately noticed. The case prohibiting purchase of even three refers to scrawny animals, whose disappearance might easily go undetected. Whether a given quantity triggers the owner's awareness depends on the animals' condition and visibility. The *masechet* will continue from here tomorrow.

---

---

# Bava Kamma 119

## Purchasing from Shepherds

### Home vs. Wilderness Anim…

The final *daf* of *Bava Kamma* opens with a *mishnah* concerning the permissibility of purchasing goods from shepherds, given the ever-present concern that such goods may be stolen from the flock's owner. The question is whether one may buy sheep, milk, or wool from a shepherd, and *Rabbi Yehuda* weighs in with a distinction based on where the animals are kept.

*Rabbi Yehuda* rules that if the animals are *beisos* — home animals, kept close to town — one may purchase from the shepherd, because the owner will readily notice if animals go missing. By contrast, if the animals are *midbarios* — raised out in the wilderness — one may not purchase from the shepherd, since the owner will have no way of knowing the animals are gone.

### Either Criterion Suffices

This ruling prompts a question in the *Gemara*: is *Rabbi Yehuda* being strict on the first clause — meaning that to permit a purchase, both conditions must be met (a large number *and* home animals) — or is he being lenient on the final clause, meaning that either condition alone suffices to permit the purchase?

The resolution comes from a *braita* that makes the matter explicit: *Rabbi Yehuda* says one may purchase home animals from a shepherd, one may not purchase wilderness animals, and in any location one may purchase four or five animals. The *braita*'s use of the phrase "in any location" (*be-khol makom*) demonstrates that he is commenting on the lenient end of the ruling — and the conclusion is that either criterion alone suffices. Either a large quantity or the status of home animals is enough to permit the purchase.

### Fruit Watchers Exception

The *Gemara* then addresses a related prohibition: one may not purchase wood or fruit from those who watch fruit, since one must be concerned that they took these items from the very garden they were hired to guard.

Yet a question arises from a case involving Rav himself, who purchased a bundle of wood from an *arisa* — a sharecropper. Abaye challenged him, citing the rule that one cannot purchase wood or fruit from those who watch fruit. Rav's reply draws a sharp distinction: that rule applies only to a hired watchman (*shomer*) who receives a flat fee and has no share in the produce itself. An *arisa*, by contrast, receives a portion of the actual produce as his compensation. Therefore, when an *arisa* sells produce, one may presume he is selling his own share rather than the owner's property.

### Public Sales Presumption

A *braita* adds a further avenue of permissibility: one may purchase from fruit watchers when they are openly and obviously conducting a sale — seated at a stand, with baskets of produce arranged before them and large scales displayed. The assumption is that no one would be so brazen as to conduct an outright public operation without the owner's awareness; word would inevitably reach the owner. However, in any of these circumstances, if the seller says "keep this to yourself," the sale is forbidden. Similarly, one may purchase from those who are positioned at the front entrance of a garden, but not from those operating out of the back entrance.

---

## Known Thieves Majority R…

### Rav: Majority of Property

The *Gemara* now turns to a related but distinct scenario: a person who is known to be a *gazlan* — an established thief. Unlike the shepherd, where the question is whether to presume the worst about an otherwise ordinary person, here one knows with certainty that the individual engages in theft. The question is: from what point may one purchase items from such a person?

Rav rules that one may purchase from a *gazlan* as long as the majority of his property (*rov mamono*) is legitimately his own — not stolen. *Rashi* explains this as referring to the majority of his possessions overall. The practical logic, as developed in the *shiur*, is that one must find it more probable than not that the item being purchased is actually the seller's own property.

### Shmuel: Minority Suffices

Shmuel takes a strikingly more permissive position: even if only a *miyut* — a minority — of the *gazlan*'s property is legitimately his, one may still purchase from him. This position is transmitted as a teaching that Rav Yehuda conveyed to his attendant Ada: the law follows the lenient ruling that even a minority of legitimate property suffices.

### Why Majority Rule Works

This raises a genuinely troubling question. In general, one is not permitted to take possession of stolen goods. If one knows that the majority of a person's possessions are stolen, why should it be permissible to purchase anything from him — and why does the *chazaka* that "what is in a person's possession belongs to him" (*chazaka ma she-tachat yad adam harei hu shelo*) override what is effectively a known-majority reality of theft?

One might compare this to the question of *lifnei iver* — the prohibition against enabling another's transgression. In those discussions, the *halacha* tends toward leniency when there remains even a minority possibility that the object will be used for a permitted purpose. But that analysis concerns the future use of an item; here, the question is about the present ownership of an object — a different *cheshbon* entirely. The tension is not resolved cleanly: it is simply striking that the *chazaka* of present possession apparently overrides the majority inference that the goods are stolen, and even more striking that Shmuel permits purchase even when the majority of the *gazlan*'s property is stolen.

This difficulty is compounded by the concern — notably absent from this entire passage — about providing a market for stolen goods. The *Gemara* elsewhere recognizes that thieves are sustained by those who purchase from them ("it is not the rat that steals, it is the hole"), yet here that concern is set aside. The answer implicit in the *Gemara* seems to be that once an object has undergone a *shinui* — a significant alteration — it technically no longer constitutes the stolen object itself, and the market-enabling concern recedes. But the question remains pointed, and the *Gemara* does not address it directly.

---

## Severity of Theft

### Rav Chisda Story

A passage about the *mamon* of an informer (*masur*) provides a brief digression. One who informs against another Jew — even merely handing over that person's property to the government — is considered a *rodef*, since governmental involvement can ultimately endanger the informer's victim. The dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda concerns whether one may actively destroy the informer's property as a form of societal enforcement. One view permits it — if the person can be stopped by greater means, his property certainly can be harmed. The opposing view holds that one may not destroy his property, for perhaps he will have righteous children who should not be punished for their father's sins, as the verse states: *yachin rasha ve-tzaddik yilbash* — the wicked man prepares and the righteous one wears it.

Following this digression, the *Gemara* presents the story of Rav Chisda and his sharecropper. Rav Chisda had an *arisa* who, according to the *Maharsha*'s explanation, was using two different sets of weights — one to measure what he gave and another to measure what he took — effectively cheating Rav Chisda through false measures, an instance of *even va-even*. Rav Chisda dismissed him. Upon doing so, Rav Chisda applied to himself the verse: "treasured away for the righteous person is the wealth of the sinner" — implying that the portion the sharecropper forfeited reverted to Rav Chisda, who deserved it.

### Theft as Taking Life

It is at this point — nearly at the very end of *Bava Kamma*, after 118 *dafim* devoted almost entirely to the financial consequences of theft and damage — that the *Gemara* finally turns to address the moral and spiritual enormity of the act itself. The *Gemara* cites the verse: *ki mah tikvat chanef ki yivatza ki yeshal Eloka nafsho* — "What is the hope of the flatterer who takes ill-gotten gain? God will remove his *nefesh*."

Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute whose *nefesh* is meant. One holds it refers to the *nefesh* of the victim — the person who was stolen from — meaning that the thief, though he imagines he is only taking property, is in truth taking something of the victim's very life. The other holds it refers to the *nefesh* of the *gazlan* himself — God will punish the thief with death.

Each opinion marshals a supporting verse. For the view that it is the victim's soul: *ken orchot kol botzea batza et nefesh ba'alav yikach* — "so are the ways of all who take ill-gotten gains; they take the soul of their owner." For the view that it is the thief's soul: *al tignol dal ki dal hu... ki Hashem yariv rivam ve-kava et koveihem nafesh* — "Do not steal from the poor... for God will fight their cause and take the soul of those who despoil them."
