The *Gemara* then asks: how does each opinion handle the verse cited by the other? The opinion focused on the victim's *nefesh* reads *ba'alav* as referring to the current owner — namely the *gazlan* who now holds the stolen property — so God is taking the soul of the thief, not the original owner. The opinion focused on the *gazlan*'s punishment reads the verse about taking the victim's soul not as a separate claim, but as the *reason* God punishes the thief: God executes the *gazlan* precisely because the *gazlan* effectively took the victim's soul. Both truths are thus present simultaneously — the theft destroys the victim and brings death upon the thief.

### Even a Penny Equals Life

*Rabbi Yochanan* states the principle directly and without exegetical mediation: whoever steals from his fellow even the value of a *pruta* — the smallest coin — it is as though he took his very soul. The verse adduced is the same: *ken orchot kol botzea batza et nefesh ba'alav yikach*.

### Theft Destroys Livelihood

The *Gemara* then chains together several verses to establish a cascading argument, anticipating and closing each potential objection. One might say: granted, it is as though one took the victim's soul — but not as though one destroyed the lives of the victim's children. The verse responds: *ve-achal katzircha ve-lachmecha yochlu banecha u-vnotecha* — "they will eat your harvest and your bread; it will be as though they consumed the flesh of your sons and daughters."

One might then say: that is only when the theft involves no reimbursement whatsoever. But if the thief takes the property and at least pays for it, has he not left the victim with money to feed his family? The verse responds with the case of *chamas* — coercive taking, understood in rabbinic tradition to mean forcing an owner to sell against his will, even at fair market value. Of this the verse says *asher shafchu dam naki be-artzam* — "they have spilled innocent blood in their land." Even compelled sale, even with payment, is likened to bloodshed. The act of stripping a person of property they did not wish to part with is itself a violation tantamount to violence.

### Shaul and Givonim

One might further argue: all of this applies only to direct taking. But indirect harm — *grama* — surely cannot rise to the level of murder. The *Gemara* responds with the verse about Shaul and the Givonim: *El Shaul ve-el beit ha-damim asher hemit et ha-Givonim* — "to Shaul and to the house of blood, because he killed the Givonim." Yet where do we find that Shaul directly killed the Givonim? The *Gemara* explains: he destroyed Nov, the city of *Kohanim*, who had been providing the Givonim with water and food and employing them. By destroying the priestly city, Shaul eliminated the Givonim's entire livelihood. Scripture nonetheless holds him accountable as if he had killed them directly. Preventing a person from earning a living is thus equivalent to murder — even when accomplished indirectly.

The moral weight of all of this at the close of the *masechet* is striking. The entire tractate has been concerned with the technical legal consequences of theft and damage — damages, payments, the *takanat ha-shavim* that allows a thief to simply return the object without bearing the full cost of its use, and the various rules that soften the legal burden on the *gazlan*. Only now, on the final *daf*, does the *Gemara* turn to say: and yet the act itself is among the most grievous a person can commit. The balance between these two realities — the severity of the sin and the pragmatic leniency of the law — reflects a difference between what something is morally and what the best societal response to it is in practice.

---

## Women and Slaves Sales

### Women's Sales Authority

The *Gemara* now shifts to a set of rules about purchasing from members of a household who are not the primary owner of the property: women, slaves, and children. In the legal world of the *Gemara*, a wife's property belonged to her husband, a slave's property to his master, and a child's property to his father. The question is therefore not about outright theft but about whether such persons have the implicit authority of the household to transfer goods.

The *Tanna* rules that one may purchase wool garments from women in Judea and linen garments in the Galilee, since these are standard local trades that women conduct, and the owner (the husband) would be aware of and implicitly sanction such sales. By contrast, one may not purchase wine, oil, or flour from women, nor may one purchase from slaves or children. The concern is that these goods fall outside the understood scope of what such household members have permission to dispose of.

### Pin Money Exception

*Abba Shaul* adds an important qualification: a woman may sell up to four and five *dinarim* worth of goods — this is the *Gemara*'s explicit language, not a vague number of items. The concept is essentially one of *pin money*: there is a presumed general consent from the husband for a wife to make small, ordinary transactions for her personal needs, such as purchasing a small head covering. Whether the threshold applies per transaction or per period is left unresolved in the *shiur*, but in either case, it represents a recognized zone of autonomous economic activity. Any transaction within that threshold is presumed to fall within permitted bounds. As before, all of these permissions are voided if the seller asks the buyer to keep the transaction quiet.

### Charity Collections

The *Gemara* then addresses *gabbai tzedakah* — those who collect charitable donations. The same logic that permits small sales extends to small donations: a *gabbai tzedakah* going door to door may accept a modest donation from a woman, a slave, or a child, without requiring the husband, master, or father to appear and explicitly consent. Just as there is a presumption that the head of household implicitly permits small transactions, there is a parallel presumption of implicit consent for small charitable contributions.

The *Gemara* adds a related ruling: those who press oil (*badadin*) may purchase large quantities of olives and oil from oil-pressers, since large volumes suggest a legitimate commercial arrangement. Small quantities of olives or oil from oil-pressers, however, are suspect, since the fear is that these small amounts were simply pilfered. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* adds a nuance regarding the Upper Galilee: one may purchase even small amounts of olives from women there, because in that region it is socially common for a man who wishes to sell a small amount — but finds it embarrassing to do so himself, since it would advertise his straitened circumstances — to give the goods to his wife to sell on his behalf. Women's sales of small amounts are thus more ordinary there than elsewhere.

### Large as Small Context

Ravina once came to Mechuza, where the wealthy women of the city threw gold necklaces and bracelets before him as charitable donations. He accepted them. When *Rabbah Tosfa'ah* challenged him — citing the rule that *gabbai tzedakah* may accept only small donations, not large ones, from women — Ravina replied that the rule about "small donations" is relative to the community's standard of wealth. In Mechuza, where women are extremely wealthy, such gold ornaments count as a modest donation. The category of "small" is not absolute but contextual.

---

## Craftsmen's Remnants

### Launderer's Rights

With the final *mishnah* of *Bava Kamma*, the *Gemara* turns to a detailed and remarkably precise set of rules about what craftsmen may retain from the materials entrusted to them by clients. These rules carry significant legal weight: retaining something to which one is not entitled constitutes *gezel*, regardless of how trivial the item appears.

The *mishnah* opens with the launderer (*koves*). If a launderer removes stuffing (*muchin*) from a pillow in the course of his work, those pieces are assumed to belong to him — the owner is presumed not to care about such incidental loss. However, if a comber (*sorek*) removes material in the course of combing flax, that material belongs to the owner and must be returned.

A launderer may take up to three threads from the hem of a garment — these are threads he removes in the normal course of his work, such as threads that keep socks together in laundering — and these are his to keep. More than three belongs to the owner. If there are black threads on a white garment, he may take all of them, since they clearly do not belong on the garment. Regarding tailors: if a tailor leaves over a thread long enough to make a stitch, or a patch of cloth of at least three by three fingerbreadths, these belong to the owner. Regarding carpenters: wood chips that come off from planing (*ma'atzad*) belong to the carpenter, while larger pieces from hewing (*kashil*) belong to the owner. If the craftsman is working on the owner's premises, however, even the sawdust belongs to the owner.

### Launderer Instructions

The *braita* elaborates on the launderer's entitlements and adds a remarkable set of instructions about how the launderer must conduct his work in order to protect the client's property — instructions that are notable for shifting from the question of what the craftsman may keep to the question of how he must do his job responsibly.

A launderer may take two of the upper threads from a garment. He may not insert more than three of the special stretching stitches (*chuvin*) into the garment, as adding more may damage it. A contradiction between the *mishnah* (which permits three threads) and the *braita* (which permits two) is resolved by noting that thick threads require a limit of two while thin threads allow three.

When combing the garment, the launderer must comb it in the direction of the warp (*sheti*) and not the woof (*arav*), since combing against the grain damages the fabric. A contradicting *braita* is resolved by distinguishing between types of garments: a cloak (*glima*), which is worn for appearance, is combed in the direction that makes it look nicer; a coat (*sarvla*), worn primarily for warmth, is combed in the direction that makes it last longer.

If the launderer must trim a garment to even it out, he must trim lengthwise, not widthwise, since trimming the width compromises the garment's integrity more than trimming the length. He may trim up to a *tefach* if necessary to achieve an even edge.

*Rav Yehuda* adds that the launderer is called *kitsra* in Aramaic, and the trimmed edge pieces (*kitsra*) are his to keep. He further rules that if the three removable threads at the garment's hem have not been removed by the launderer, they count toward the measurement required for *tzitzit* placement — specifically, they are included in calculating the *melo kesher gudal* (a thumb-width's distance from the edge within which *tzitzit* must be placed). If the threads are still attached, the edge of the garment is measured from their outermost point.

### Comber Prohibition

In contrast to the launderer, one may not purchase stuffing material from a comber (*sorek*), since any such material belongs to the owner. The exception is a locale where local custom (*minhag*) has established that the comber retains such material — in that case, one may purchase it from him. In all places, however, one may purchase pillows that are already filled with stuffing, because even if the stuffing was originally stolen, the act of filling the pillow constitutes a *shinui* — a significant alteration — by which the craftsman has acquired it.

### Weaver's Materials

From a weaver (*gardi*), one may not purchase thread or implements associated with the loom: neither the *irin* nor the *nirin* — the threads associated with the warp and woof around the shuttle — nor the tapestry bobbins (*punkalin*), nor the remnants of thread spools. All of these, even if seemingly trivial, belong to the owner of the material.

However, one may purchase from a weaver a patchwork garment (*beged menumar*), because even if the patches were improperly obtained, the act of creating the garment constitutes a *shinui* by which the weaver has acquired them. Similarly, one may purchase thread that has been spun (*tavui*) or woven. If someone asks whether one may purchase something that has been woven as well as spun — since spinning alone already creates a *shinui* — the *Gemara* clarifies that "woven" in this context does not mean woven after spinning, but rather twisted (*tichi*), a different form of processing that is also a *shinui*.

### Dyer's Samples

One may not purchase from a dyer (*tzaya*) either *otot* or *dugmaot* — samples and test pieces. *Rashi* explains: an *ot* is a small piece of cloth given to the dyer so he may test the dye on it before applying it to the full garment; a *dugma* is an example piece showing the color the owner desires as the final result. These tiny items are presumed to be wanted back by the owner. Similarly, one may not purchase plucked wool (*tluishim*) that comes off garments in the dyeing process.

One may, however, purchase an already-dyed garment (*beged tzavua*) from a dyer, since either the owner has abandoned it or — if it was improperly obtained — the act of dyeing constitutes a *shinui* by which the dyer has acquired it. The question of whether dyeing alone constitutes a *shinui* is worth noting: is this a *shinui ha-shem*, a change of name and identity? The *Gemara* proceeds without resolving this directly.

One may also purchase spun wool (*tavui*) and garments from a dyer. A *Gemara* question notes that if spun wool alone suffices to create a *shinui*, surely a completed garment does as well — and the *Gemara* clarifies that "garments" here refers to felt (*namti*), which is pressed rather than spun, and this too constitutes a *shinui*.

The *braita* then addresses a tanner: pieces trimmed from a hide and hair that comes off in the processing belong to the owner. But material that floats to the surface when the hide is submerged in water belongs to the tanner.

### Tailor's Thresholds

Returning to the tailor (*chayat*): if the tailor leaves over a thread sufficient to make a stitch, it belongs to the owner. How much thread is "sufficient to make a stitch"? *Rav Assi* says: the length of the needle, plus the length that extends outside the needle.

A *she'ila* arises from this formulation: does "the length of the needle plus outside the needle" mean one needle's length *plus* another full needle's length (two needle-lengths total), or does it mean the needle's length *plus* a minimal additional amount sufficient to exit the needle's eye? The resolution comes from a *braita*: if the tailor leaves over a thread *less* than the sufficient stitch-length, or a patch *less* than three by three fingerbreadths, and the owner is *makpid* — particular about these items — then they belong to the owner. If the owner is not *makpid*, they belong to the tailor, which is the default presumption in these cases.

The *Gemara* reasons: if "the length of the needle plus outside" means two full needle-lengths, then the statement that anything less belongs to the tailor makes sense, because a thread just under two needle-lengths can still be used for a specific stitch (*sichsa*). But if "outside" means only a tiny bit, then anything less than that would be too small to serve any purpose at all, and it would be meaningless to say it belongs to the tailor. Therefore, the formulation must mean two full needle-lengths.

### Carpenter's Shavings

As noted in the *mishnah*, wood chips from planing (*ma'atzad*) go to the carpenter, while larger pieces from hewing (*kashil*) go to the owner. A *braita*, however, seems to say that chips from planing go to the owner. Rava resolves the contradiction by noting that in the locale of the *Tanna* of the *mishnah*, there are two types of cutting implements: the large one is called *kashil* and the small one *ma'atzad*. The *mishnah* accordingly assigns the fine shavings of the *ma'atzad* to the carpenter and the larger pieces of the *kashil* to the owner. In the locale of the *braita*'s *Tanna*, there is only one such implement and it happens to be the large version, yet it is called *ma'atzad* — which is why that *braita* assigns its output to the owner.

---

## Custom and Context

### Produce Removers

The *Gemara* then addresses a general category of workers who remove material from an owner's property in the course of their labor: stone carvers, those who prune trees and vines, those who cut thornbushes, those who weed gardens, and those who thin out crowded vegetables. In all these cases, the rule is: if the owner is *makpid* — particular about retaining the removed material — then keeping it constitutes *gezel*. If the owner is not *makpid*, the worker may keep it. What is notably absent here is any declared default: the passage does not specify which presumption governs in the absence of explicit protest, suggesting that in these cases the parties must simply clarify.

### Hops and Grain

*Rav Yehuda* offers a ruling about specific plants: *kashus* (hops) and *chaziz* (green grain, which regrows after being cut) — the worker may keep them without any concern of *gezel*. However, in a locale where the custom is that owners are *makpid* about such things, then keeping them does constitute *gezel*.

### Mata Mechasya

*Ravina* adds a local application: Mata Mechasya — his own city — is a place where owners are habitually *makpid* about such remnants, and therefore what would elsewhere be freely retained by a worker constitutes *gezel* there.

This is the note on which *Bava Kamma* concludes. It is a fittingly precise ending: after exhortations about how even a *pruta*'s worth of theft is like taking a life, the tractate closes by asking whether a worker may keep the weeds he pulls from a garden or the hops he cuts from a vine. The answer depends on where you are and what people expect. Every small thing matters. The *masechet* ends — *hukdran alach ha-gozel batra ve-seika lah Masechet Bava Kamma*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 2

## Intro & Tallis Case

### Masechet Overview

*Bava Metzia* means "middle gate," reflecting its position as the second of the three sections into which *Nezikin* is divided — *Bava Kamma*, *Bava Metzia*, and *Bava Batra*, meaning first section, middle section, and final section. Together these thirty *prakim* comprise the bulk of civil law in the Talmud.

Unlike *Bava Kamma*, which coheres around a single dominant theme — torts, whether damages, robbery, theft, or personal injury — *Bava Metzia* is considerably more varied in its subject matter. The masechet ranges across contested ownership and *metziot* (found objects), through two of the most technically demanding *prakim* in all of *Shas* (*Eizehu Neshech* and *HaZahav*, dealing with *ribbis* and the nature of money), multiple chapters on *shomrim* (the third *perek* and the eighth *perek* both return to this topic), and an extended treatment of workers' rights. One should not expect a single unifying theme; *Bava Metzia* is, in the most direct sense, the middle ten *prakim* of *Nezikin*, covering a broad sweep of civil law.

It is a classic Yeshivish *masechet* with rich treatment by the major *rishonim*, and as will become evident, many of its discussions open onto broader *Shas*-wide questions of principle. Tosafot notes that this *perek* also connects naturally to what immediately precedes it: the final *perek* of *Bava Kamma* dealt with the division of wood shavings and sawdust between a craftsman and his employer — not a question of contested ownership as such, but one of dividing objects between two parties. That may provide the logical transition into our opening *mishnah*.

### Two Holding Tallis

The *mishnah* opens: *shnayim ochazim b'talit* — two people are holding onto a *talit*, a cloak (not a ritual garment with *tzitzit*, but an ordinary cloak). Each one says *ani metzatiha* — I found it. Each one says *kulo sheli* — it is all mine. The ruling is *yachloku*: they divide it. But before simply dividing, each one swears: *she'ein lo pachos mechetzyo* — that he has no less than half of it.

The image of two people clutching opposite ends of a garment is perhaps the defining image of *Bava Metzia*. The situation presents a genuine adjudicative puzzle: both parties have equal claims, both are physically holding the object, and there is no witness or other evidence to privilege one claim over the other. The natural resolution is to split it — not literally with scissors, but by having one party purchase the other's half, or by selling the object and dividing the proceeds. What requires explanation is not the division itself but the accompanying oath and, in particular, the precise formulation of that oath.

### Oath Formulation

One might ask: why does each claimant swear only that he has *no less than half*, rather than swearing outright that the whole garment belongs to him? After all, each party is claiming the whole thing.

The answer lies in the principle that *beit din* must not suborn false oaths. If each party were required to swear *kulo sheli* — it is all mine — then we would be compelling at least one person, and quite possibly both, to swear something false. Equally, if each were required to swear only *chetzi sheli* — half is mine — that formulation would effectively force a claimant to retract his own claim before the oath is even adjudicated. The oath as crafted — *she'ein lo pachos mechetzyo*, that he has no less than half — neither overstates beyond what a truthful claimant could honestly affirm nor undermines the claimant's own position. It is a carefully engineered formulation.

There is an additional elegance to this structure: the oath maps precisely onto the ultimate ruling. Each swears he has no less than half; each receives half. When *beit din* announces its decision, it is calibrated exactly to what each party swore. Justice appears to have been served, and the integrity of the proceedings is preserved.

### Oath Function

The deeper question is: what is the *function* of the oath? Why do we think it will help?

The basic assumption — which will recur throughout the *masechet* — is that a person who might be willing to steal is nonetheless unwilling to take a false oath. I might grab your cloak and claim it as mine, but when confronted with the obligation to swear before *beit din*, I will back down and concede rather than go through with the false declaration. The oath thus serves as a mechanism for drawing out the truth: if I know I am lying, the oath might deter me from proceeding.

### Chashud Amamona

This assumption is crystallized in the principle *chashud amamona lo chashud ashvuasa* — one who is suspect in monetary matters is not necessarily suspect of swearing falsely. The two categories of moral failure are treated as distinct: a person may be the sort who steals but still recoil from the gravity of a false oath. The oath thus operates as a filter that a thief may decline to pass through.

### Rationalization

Yet the more psychologically precise explanation — and one with considerable *mussar* resonance — is the phenomenon of *mori ve-amar*, self-rationalization. Most of the time, a person who takes something that is not fully his is not a brazen thief who knows exactly what he is doing. He is someone who has talked himself into believing it is acceptable. He convinces himself that he saw the object first, or that the other party owes him money, or that he needs it more — and on that basis he acts. In his own mind, he is an honest person.

It is precisely for such a person that the oath is most effective. When he is brought before *beit din* and required to swear, the formal gravity of the moment cuts through the rationalization. He can no longer hide behind his self-justification; he must look squarely at what he is about to affirm before *Heaven*. At that point he may well admit, or at least withdraw his claim. The oath works not because it deters a committed criminal, but because it forces a rationalizer to confront the gap between what he has told himself and what he actually knows to be true.

---

## Variant Claims

### One All, One Half

The *mishnah* proceeds to a variant case: *ze omer kulo sheli ve-ze omer chetzi sheli* — one claims the whole garment and the other claims only half. By saying "half is mine," the second claimant effectively concedes that the other half belongs to his opponent. The dispute is therefore confined to the remaining half. That contested half is divided equally between them, yielding three-quarters to the one who claimed everything and one-quarter to the one who claimed half.

The oaths are calibrated accordingly: the one claiming the whole swears *she'ein lo bo pachos mishlosha chalakim* — he has no less than three-quarters; the one claiming half swears *she'ein lo bo pachos mirvia* — he has no less than a quarter. Each receives precisely what he swore for. The result is not only legally coherent but, as noted above, aesthetically satisfying from the perspective of *beit din*: the ruling tracks the oaths exactly.

### Migo Question

Tosafot raises a pointed question about this ruling. If the half-claimant could have said "it is all mine" — and, had he done so, would have received half — then why does his more modest claim of "half is mine" not earn him that full half via a *migo*? The logic of *migo* is that since a claimant could have made a stronger claim and chose not to, his actual claim deserves credence. Here, the half-claimant voluntarily made the weaker claim; should that not at minimum secure him the half he claims?

### Muchzak Doctrine

Tosafot's answer turns on the concept of *muchzak* — presumptive possession. In *halacha*, the person who is considered in possession of an object has the default status of owner, and the principle *hamotzi mechaveiro alav hara'ayah* applies: whoever seeks to take from another bears the burden of proof. Physical possession, when combined with a claim, establishes *muchzakut*.

In the equal case — each claiming everything — both parties are equally *muchzak* in the entire object, since they are both physically holding it and each asserts full ownership. That equal *muchzakut* is what compels the division. But when one claims all and the other claims half, the analysis shifts: the full-claimant is *muchzak* in the whole; the half-claimant is *muchzak* only in half. The half-claimant's *migo* argument, if accepted, would allow him to use his stronger potential claim to dislodge the other party's *chazakah* over that disputed quarter. That, explains Tosafot, is a *migo le-hotzi* — a *migo* deployed to extract something from another's established possession — and such a *migo* is generally not accepted. The claimed half already has someone else's *chazakah* resting on it, and a *migo* alone cannot overcome that.

It is worth pausing on what this teaches about the underlying logic of the entire *perek*. The division of the contested object is not arbitrary; it is generated by the interplay of physical possession and the claims that frame it. Where neither party has a stronger default claim — because both are equally holding and equally asserting — the only principled resolution is equal division. In a case where one of the parties is not physically holding the object at all (as the *gemara* will discuss regarding a boat in the harbor, where neither party is in possession), the result might be entirely different — not a split, but a standoff, with *beit din* declining to intervene at all.

### Animal Case

The *mishnah* extends the same ruling to animals: *hayu shenayim rochvin al gabi behema* — two people were riding on an animal — *o she-hayah echad rochev ve-echad manhig* — or one was riding and one was leading it. Each claims full ownership, and the ruling is identical: each swears he has no less than half, and they divide.

The novelty of this case, which the *gemara* will explore, is the question of what degree of physical engagement with an object suffices to constitute the kind of possession that generates *muchzakut*. Riding an animal and leading an animal are each forms of control, but they differ from simply gripping a garment. The *mishnah* establishes by example — rather than by articulating a general principle — that both modes of engagement are sufficient.

### Agreement & Witnesses

The *mishnah* concludes with an obvious but important provision: *u-vizman she-shneihem modim*, if both parties agree about the facts, *o she-yesh sham eidim*, or there are witnesses, *cholkin belo shevuah* — they divide without an oath. The oath was introduced precisely because there is no other means of getting at the truth. Where agreement or testimony supplies that function, the oath is unnecessary.

---

## Why Two Cases?

### Double Phrasing

The *gemara* opens with a structural question about the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* states two formulations — *ze omer ani metzatiha ve-ze omer ani metzatiha* ("I found it, I found it") and then *ze omer kulo sheli ve-ze omer kulo sheli* ("it is all mine, it is all mine"). Why are both formulations needed? *Litni chada* — let it state just one of them.

The *gemara*'s first answer is *chada katani* — both phrases constitute a single case. Each claimant is saying: I found it and therefore it is all mine. The compound statement — *ani metzatiha ve-kulo sheli* — is the full claim of each party; the *mishnah* simply presents the two components in sequence.

### Finding = Possession

But if that is the answer, the *gemara* presses further: *ve-litni ani metzatiha ve-ana yadana de-kula sheli* — let the *mishnah* simply have them say "I found it," since the claim of finding already implies full ownership. Why bother adding the phrase *kulo sheli* at all?

The *gemara* answers: *i tana ani metzatiha, hava amina mai metzatiha re'itiha* — had the *mishnah* only said "I found it," one might have understood *metzatiha* to mean merely "I spotted it," and concluded that spotting a *metziah* is sufficient to acquire it. The phrase *kulo sheli* is therefore added to forestall that misunderstanding: the claim of ownership requires actual physical acquisition, not mere sighting.

This is the interpretation associated with Ravina, who in *Bava Kamma* derived from the verse *asher tavad mimenu u-metzatah* that finding means coming into possession — *ata lidei*. The *gemara* here affirms Ravina's exegesis while adding a critical nuance: the biblical text may indeed imply physical acquisition, but ordinary colloquial speech does not. When people say "I found it," they typically mean "I spotted it first." The *mishnah* anticipates this potential misreading of colloquial language and corrects it by appending *kulo sheli*, signaling that mere sighting is insufficient — *re'iya b'alma lo kani*.

The *gemara* then asks the converse: if so, let the *mishnah* say only *kulo sheli* and drop the *metzatiha* entirely. The answer is that the *mishnah* deliberately invokes the scenario of *metziah* — found objects — because it wishes to establish the rule that spotting does not constitute acquisition. Without *metzatiha*, the *mishnah* would simply present two people disputing ownership with no discussion of the *metziah* context, and the teaching about *re'iya* would be lost. Both phrases are therefore necessary: *tana ani metzatiha* to raise the *metziah* scenario, *ve-hadar tana kula sheli* to clarify that spotting alone does not suffice.

### Metzia vs. Purchase

The *gemara* then rejects the *chada katani* reading entirely, on the grounds that the *mishnah*'s phrasing — *ze omer ... ve-ze omer ... ze omer ... ve-ze omer* — presents two clearly distinct cases, not a single case with two phrases. Had the *mishnah* intended to present one case, it would have formulated it as *ze omer ani metzatiha ve-kulo sheli*.

The authoritative answer is given by Rav Pappa (and attributed also to Rav Shimi bar Ashi, or anonymously): *reisha bi-metziah ve-seifa be-mekach u-memkar* — the first case concerns a found object (who picked it up first), and the second case concerns a purchase (who bought the object from a merchant). These are genuinely two distinct scenarios, and the *gemara* now explains why both must be stated — *tzricha*, each is necessary.

### Metzia Rationalization

Had the *mishnah* stated only the *metziah* case, one might have thought: *metziah hu de-ramu rabbanan shevua alei mishum de-mori ve-amar* — it is specifically in the found-object case that the Rabbis imposed an oath, because that is the case most prone to rationalization. The reasoning: my opponent did not own the object a moment ago, he was not looking for it, he was not planning on it — it simply came his way by good fortune. I can easily convince myself that I need it more, that I deserve it more, that he is not truly losing something he had invested in. The rationalization writes itself: *chaverai lav midi chasar bah* — my friend is not really losing anything he had before.

The oath in that case is maximally effective, because the person making the false claim is doing so through self-justification rather than brazen dishonesty. The *shevuah* cuts through the rationalization and forces honesty.

But if only the *metziah* case were taught, one might think: *aval mekach u-memkar* — but in a purchase dispute — *de-leika le-meimar hachi* — you cannot say that. The object was something the other party deliberately sought out, paid for, and clearly wanted. It is much harder to rationalize taking it from him. If one cannot rationalize, one is either a brazen thief who knowingly lies — in which case a *shevuah* is of questionable value — or else genuinely believes his own claim, in which case a *shevuah* will not produce an admission either. *Eima lo* — perhaps in the *mekach u-memkar* case there should be no oath.

### Purchase Rationalization

To counter this, the *gemara* presents the opposite argument. Had only the *mekach u-memkar* case been stated, one might have concluded that it is specifically the purchase case where the oath is necessary and effective, because there too rationalization is very much available. The reasoning runs: *demeika yahiv ve-ana demeika yahiv* — we both paid the merchant. Whoever loses the case will get his money back. So I am not truly taking anything of lasting value from my opponent — he will be reimbursed, he will find another animal, and I need this one more urgently. *Ashkelei ana ve-chaverai leizel litrach ve-lizban* — I'll take it, and he can go to the trouble of buying another one. That entire chain of self-justification constitutes *mori ve-amar*, and the oath is effective precisely at disrupting it.

But in the *metziah* case, there is no such comfortable rationalization available in the other direction: if I claim a lost object that my opponent found, he is not getting it back. He is simply out the value of whatever he found. The loss is real and irreversible. If I claim it anyway, I am either lying outright — knowing I am stealing — or sincerely mistaken. Neither scenario is one where a *shevuah* is the most effective instrument. *Eima lo* — perhaps in the *metziah* case there should be no oath.

### Merchant Case

The *gemara* now turns to a technical feature of the *mekach u-memkar* scenario. If two parties are disputing who purchased an object, why not simply ask the merchant whom he sold it to? *Ve-lechzei zuzei mimi nakat* — let us see whose money he accepted.

The answer is *tzricha* for the specific case of *de-nakat mi-tarveihu* — where the merchant took money from both of them. *Michad mida'ato u-michad ba'al karcho* — one he agreed to accept payment from, and from the other he was compelled to accept it, but he no longer remembers which was which. Both parties pressed money upon him simultaneously; he knows he concluded a sale with one of them, but he cannot say which. In this scenario, the merchant's testimony is unavailing, and the dispute returns to the baseline situation of contested, equally-supported claims — which is precisely where the oath becomes relevant.

---

## Ben Nanas & Sumchus

### Ben Nanas Objection

Having established the ruling of the *mishnah*, the *gemara* asks whether it is consistent with all Tannaic opinions. *Leima matnitin d'lo ke-Ben Nanas* — let us say our *mishnah* does not follow Ben Nanas.

Ben Nanas poses an objection based on a different case. If a person instructs a shopkeeper to extend credit to his workers, and at the end the shopkeeper says the workers took a hundred dinars' worth of goods while the workers say the shopkeeper never gave them anything — both the shopkeeper and the workers swear, and the employer pays both. Ben Nanas objects: *keitzad elu va-elu ba'in lidei shvuat shav* — how can we bring both of them to a false oath? In that case, one of the two groups is definitely lying, and we are causing a *shvuat shav* — a false oath — to be taken.

### Possible Honest Oath

The *gemara* answers by distinguishing the two cases. *Hatam vadai ika shvuat shav* — in Ben Nanas's case, there is definitely a false oath being taken; the shopkeeper and the workers cannot both be telling the truth. *Hacha ika leimeir d'leika shvuat shav* — here, in our *mishnah*, it is possible that there is no false oath at all. *Eima d'tarveihu bahadi hadadi agbeu* — perhaps they both picked it up at the same time, or the merchant agreed to sell it to both simultaneously. In that scenario, each one genuinely owns half, and each one's oath — *she'ein lo pachos mechetzyo* — is entirely true.

The scenario of joint simultaneous acquisition may not be the most likely explanation for most such disputes, but it is a genuine possibility. And because it is possible that both oaths are truthful, the *mishnah*'s procedure does not violate Ben Nanas's principle. Ben Nanas objects only where a false oath is *certain*; where a truthful oath is at least possible, he does not object.

### Sumchus on Doubt

The *gemara* then raises a more pointed challenge. *Leima matnitin d'lo ke-Sumchus* — let us say our *mishnah* does not follow Sumchus.

Sumchus is known from *Bava Kamma* for the ruling: *mamon ha-mutal be-safek cholkin* — money or property whose ownership is in doubt is divided. The classic case involves a cow that was sold, and a calf was found beside it after the sale. The seller claims the calf was born before the sale and therefore belongs to him; the buyer claims it was born after and belongs to him. The *chachamim* say: the seller retains the *chazakah* — he was the owner before the sale — and the burden of proof falls on the buyer. Sumchus says: since there is genuine doubt, we split it.

The *gemara* adds a crucial detail: Sumchus rules *belo shevuah* — without an oath. He requires neither party to swear. The *mishnah*, however, requires an oath. *Leima matnitin d'lo ke-Sumchus* — our *mishnah* seems to be at odds with Sumchus.

The *gemara* asks: and if not Sumchus, is our *mishnah* the position of the *rabbanan* who dispute him? But that creates its own problem — *ha amri*, the *rabbanan* say *hamotzi mechaveiro alav hara'ayah*. They do not say split at all; they say whoever is the default owner retains the object until the other party brings proof. So our *mishnah*, which does split the object, cannot be the *rabbanan* either. *Hai mai* — what kind of question is this?

The *gemara* answers: the *rabbanan*'s position makes perfect sense as applied to the calf case. *Hatam de-lo tafsi tarvaihu* — there, only one party is the *muchzak*, and the other is the *motzi* seeking to extract from that *chazakah*; the *rabbanan* therefore require proof. *Hacha de-tarvaihu tafsi* — here, both are equally holding the garment and equally *muchzak*; the *rabbanan* would agree to split, and given that splitting is necessary but the claims are contested, they would also require a *shevuah* to try to get at the truth.

### Shema vs. Bari

The *gemara* now proposes that Sumchus could still agree with the *mishnah*: *ki amar Sumchus shema va-shema* — Sumchus's ruling of split-without-oath applies specifically when both parties speak in terms of uncertainty (*shema*). In the calf case, neither party actually *knows* when the calf was born; each is expressing what he believes or hopes but cannot assert with certainty. In such a case, what *shevuah* could one even formulate? One cannot swear definitively about something one does not know.

*Aval bari va-bari* — but when both parties make definite (*bari*) claims, as in our *mishnah* where each says flatly "it is mine," Sumchus would concede that an oath is called for. A definite claim can support a definite oath, and the possibility that the oath will induce an admission — or at least stop rationalization — remains live. Sumchus's exception therefore does not extend to the case of two equally definite, competing *bari* claims.

### Drara Demamona

The *gemara* then introduces an additional limiting principle for Sumchus's position. *Ki amar Sumchus heicha de-ika drara demamona* — Sumchus says split without oath only where there is *drara demamona* — an objective monetary stake or objective uncertainty arising from the facts themselves. *Aval heicha de-leika drara demamona lo* — where there is no such objective stake, he would not say so.

The term *drara demamona* is the subject of significant dispute among the *rishonim*, but Tosafot's understanding is that it refers to a situation where, setting aside the parties' claims entirely, the known and agreed-upon facts themselves generate an objective question about ownership. In the calf case: everyone agrees the cow was sold, everyone agrees a calf was born, and the simple passage of time creates an objective factual uncertainty — when exactly did the birth occur? That is *drara demamona*. The doubt is not manufactured by the litigation; it inheres in the facts.

### Sumchus Exception

In our *mishnah*, by contrast, the entire dispute is generated by the parties' claims and their act of grabbing the garment. If one were to set aside the claims and look only at agreed-upon facts, there would be very little — only the bare fact that both are holding opposite ends of a *talit*. The uncertainty arises from the competing assertions, not from any objective factual puzzle that exists independently of those assertions. In Tosafot's formulation: *drara demamona* exists where the doubt would be recognizable to an outside observer examining only agreed-upon facts; it does not exist where the doubt is entirely a product of the parties' claims before *beit din*.

Where there is no *drara demamona*, Sumchus would agree that a *shevuah* is called for — because the mechanism of the oath, which pushes back against rationalization and forces claimants to confront their own honesty, is precisely what is needed when the only source of uncertainty is the claims themselves.

---

## Kal Vachomer

### Kal Vachomer Setup

The *gemara* immediately challenges the *drara demamona* distinction with a *kal vachomer*. If Sumchus rules split-without-oath even in the calf case — where one party is taking from the other's established *chazakah* and the split is therefore, by any reckoning, a significant departure from the default legal position — then why should he require an oath in the garment case, where both parties are equally holding and the split is a far more natural outcome?

### Unfaithful Psak

The force of the *kal vachomer* turns on a pointed observation: in the calf case, the *psak* of splitting is admittedly not *k'fi ha-emet* — not according to the truth. The calf is either entirely the seller's or entirely the buyer's. It cannot genuinely belong to both. Yet Sumchus is willing to issue that ruling without even attempting to use a *shevuah* to get closer to the truth.

### More Truthful Here

In the garment case, by contrast, the *psak* of splitting *could* be *k'fi ha-emet*. As the *gemara* established earlier, it is genuinely possible — *eima d'tarvaihu bahadi hadadi agbeu* — that both parties picked it up simultaneously and each legitimately owns half. The ruling of *yachloku* is not inherently false; it may reflect the actual state of ownership.

The *kal vachomer* therefore runs: if Sumchus is willing to issue a ruling he knows may be wrong, without seeking to refine it through a *shevuah*, then all the more so he should be willing to issue a ruling that may be entirely correct, also without a *shevuah*. The lesser departure from truth (or no departure at all) should require less resort to the oath, not more.

### Unresolved Tension

The *gemara* raises this *kal vachomer* as a genuine challenge and does not resolve it within this *amud*. Why Sumchus might nonetheless agree that the garment case requires a *shevuah* — despite the *kal vachomer* suggesting otherwise — is a question that remains open here and will be taken up in the continuation.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 3

## Oath as Prevention

### Why Shvuah Required

The *gemara* on 3a opens not with a focus on why the disputed *tallis* is split between the two claimants, but rather with the prior question of why a *shvuah* is required at all. The groundwork laid in previous discussion established that a person tends to rationalize his conduct — what the *gemara* calls *moreh heter* — and that the *shvuah* serves to penetrate that rationalization and move the claimant toward truthfulness.

### Rationalizing & Ben Nanas

The *gemara* compared the *tallis* case to the position of Ben Nanas, who objected to any arrangement that would place one of the parties in the position of taking a demonstrably false *shvuah*. The concern operates on two levels: we do not want the individual to commit *shvuas sheker*, and we do not want the *beis din* to preside over a proceeding in which one party is clearly lying. However, Ben Nanas's case involved a situation where *vadai* — certainly — one party was making a false oath. The *gemara* noted that here, by contrast, it is not definitively established that either claimant is lying.

### Sumchos & Claims

The *gemara* then raised the position of Sumchos, who holds that in a case of disputed ownership one splits the disputed amount without requiring a *shvuah* at all. If Sumchos would not require a *shvuah* in his characteristic case — for example, when two parties dispute when a calf was born relative to a transaction — why should a *shvuah* be required here? The *gemara*'s initial answer was that Sumchos's case rests on an objective basis for each party's claim, giving each a legitimate standing that justifies splitting. But this objective basis, the *gemara* countered, explains why we split — it does not explain why we forgo the *shvuah*. If anything, the *shvuah* might be more compelling in Sumchos's case: since one party almost certainly does not deserve the award, the *shvuah* might force that party to admit. So the logic of "objective claim" cannot explain Sumchos's dispensing with a *shvuah*. The conclusion was that if Sumchos forgoes the *shvuah* in his case, he should also forgo it here — which would mean our *mishnah* does not follow Sumchos.

### Rabbinic Takanah

The *gemara* resolves this by introducing a new framework. Five lines from the top of 3a, the *gemara* states: *afilu teima Sumchos* — even Sumchos would agree that a *shvuah* is required in the *tallis* case, and the reason is that this *shvuah* is entirely rabbinic in character. The *gemara* cites Rabbi Yochanan: *shvuah zo takanas chachamim hi* — this oath is a rabbinic enactment. And its purpose is explicitly preventative: *shelo yehei kol echad ve'echad holech ve'tokef be'taliso shel chaveiro ve'omer sheli hi* — so that people will not simply go and seize another's garment and claim it as their own.

Without this *takanah*, a person of sufficient *chutzpah* need only grab hold of another's coat, assert ownership, and walk away with half of it. The system would be trivially exploitable. *Chazal* therefore instituted the *shvuah* not as a truth-finding mechanism — not as part of the *din* — but as a prophylactic social control, a deterrent against opportunistic seizure.

### Shlomo Analogy

This preventative character also explains why Sumchos's case differs. When two parties dispute the timing of a calf's birth relative to a commercial transaction, there is no realistic concern that people will manufacture such disputes for strategic advantage. The scenario cannot be engineered. There, the *shvuah* can only be justified as a tool of *din* — of reaching the truth — and Sumchos, who does not favor that use of the *shvuah*, dispenses with it. But the *tallis* case is different: it is precisely the kind of dispute that can be manufactured with minimal effort. The rabbinic *takanah* targets this vulnerability. Even Sumchos, who generally eschews the *shvuah* as a *din* instrument, would endorse it here as a *takanah* against exploitation — just as one might recall the lesson of *Shlomo Hamelech*: the legal system cannot simply invite such easy manipulation without consequence.

---

## Division vs Escrow

### Rabbi Yosi Problem

The *gemara* now shifts its focus from the *shvuah* to the other half of the *mishnah*'s ruling: the decision to split the *tallis*. Is *yehaloku* — division — really the appropriate resolution? Or should the disputed object be held in escrow? This question is introduced through the position of Rabbi Yosi, who raises a pointed objection to a split: *im kein mah hifsid ha'ramai* — if you simply divide, what does the deceiver lose?

### Deposit Case

The case that frames Rabbi Yosi's concern involves a *shomer* — a trustee — holding deposits from two people. One depositor left one hundred *zuz* and the other left two hundred *zuz*. When both come to retrieve their money, each claims to have deposited the larger amount. The trustee, having failed to keep adequate records, cannot remember who gave what. The *chachamim* rule that each party receives the hundred *zuz* that is certainly his, while the disputed third hundred is placed in escrow — *yehei munach ad she'yavo Eliyahu* — held until Elijah arrives, meaning until the matter can somehow be resolved or one party concedes.

### Escrow Leverage

Rabbi Yosi objects to this arrangement. The liar, in the *chachamim*'s scheme, loses nothing: he walked in claiming two hundred, he walks out with the hundred that was always his, and the disputed hundred sits in escrow. He has no incentive to admit. Rabbi Yosi's counter-proposal is therefore: *hakol yehei munach ad she'yavo Eliyahu* — place all three hundred in escrow, including the hundred that is certainly each party's. By doing so, you impose a real cost on the deceiver. The liar, who is motivated by greed, may crack first and admit the truth in order to retrieve his own money. The innocent party, who is telling the truth, will hold out. The escrow functions not as permanent resolution, but as coercive leverage.

It must be conceded that this strategy is imperfect. Placing undisputed funds in escrow also penalizes the truthful party. And, as with any system of imposed pressure, the guilty party will not always break first. But Rabbi Yosi judges this outcome preferable to one that costs the liar nothing at all.

### Testing Rabbanan

The *gemara* then asks: given that our *mishnah* rules to split the *tallis*, does this mean our *mishnah* cannot be reconciled with Rabbi Yosi? And further, can it even be reconciled with the *rabbanun*, who themselves rule that the disputed third hundred goes into escrow? The *gemara* poses a sharp challenge: the *tallis* is itself the disputed item. Just as the *rabbanun* hold the third hundred — the item in genuine dispute — in escrow, they should by the same logic hold the *tallis* in escrow. *Hani nami ke'shar dami de'sfeka hi* — this *tallis* is equivalent to that disputed hundred; it is the item about which there is genuine uncertainty.

### Split Possible Test

The *gemara* resolves this challenge on behalf of the *rabbanun*: *hai mai* — what kind of question is that? In the case of the three hundred *zuz*, it is certain that the third hundred belongs to exactly one of the two parties — *vadai hai mane de'chad minaihu*. A fifty-fifty split would be a patently false judgment, which is why the *rabbanun* resort to escrow. But in the *tallis* case, it is genuinely possible — *ika le'meimar de'tarvaihu* — that both parties actually picked it up simultaneously. Where the split is possibly true, the *rabbanun* say *yachaloku* with a *shvuah*. Where the split is patently false, the *rabbanun* say *yehei munach*. The distinction is whether the division corresponds to any possible truth on the ground.

This also explains the reasoning behind Rashi's alternative framing: in the version where each claimant says "I wove it" or "I inherited it from my grandfather," one of them is definitively lying in a way that cannot be reconciled with a fifty-fifty ownership split. That formulation would push toward escrow rather than division.

### Yosi & Tallis

The *gemara* now asks whether our *mishnah* can be reconciled with Rabbi Yosi himself. The challenge is powerful. If Rabbi Yosi is prepared to place even *undisputed* money — the hundred *zuz* that is certainly each man's — into escrow as a coercive strategy, then *a fortiori* he should be prepared to place disputed property into escrow. In the *tallis* case, the entire *tallis* is disputed. Rabbi Yosi's logic of *mah hifsid ha'ramai* — what does the liar lose? — applies here with full force. If you simply split the *tallis*, the liar walks away with half of something to which he had no claim whatsoever. He risked nothing and gained something. Under Rabbi Yosi's framework, that is untenable, and he should certainly demand escrow here.

### Not Definite Lying

The *gemara* answers: *afilu teima Rabbi Yosi* — even Rabbi Yosi can be reconciled with our *mishnah*. The reason Rabbi Yosi employs escrow in the deposit case is that there *vadai ika ramai* — it is certain that one party is lying. Someone definitely deposited only one hundred and is claiming two hundred. But in the *tallis* case, *mi yeimar de'ika ramai* — who says there is definitely a deceiver? *Eima tarvaihu bahadi hadadi agbuha* — perhaps both parties genuinely picked it up at the same time. If there is no definite liar, the coercive rationale for escrow does not apply.

### Liar Loses Test

The *gemara* adds a second, and arguably more decisive, answer: *kanis lei Rabbi Yosi le'ramai ki heihi de'lodei* — Rabbi Yosi's escrow strategy works because it imposes a real loss on the deceiver to coerce his admission. In the deposit case, placing all three hundred in escrow means the liar is cut off from the hundred that is genuinely his — he suffers. That deprivation is what creates the incentive to come clean. But in the *tallis* case, the liar has no pre-existing stake in the object. It was found, or it was grabbed. Putting it in escrow takes nothing away from him; there is nothing of his being withheld. *Mai pseda is'lei de'lodei* — what loss would he suffer that would prompt him to admit? The escrow mechanism, stripped of its coercive bite, accomplishes nothing.

Tosafot, it should be noted, understands these as two criteria that must both be met for escrow to be warranted: there must be a definite liar, *and* the escrow must impose a genuine cost on that liar. If either condition is absent, escrow is not the appropriate remedy.

There is a further wrinkle the *gemara* presses: what about the case in the *mishnah* involving a disputed purchase, where both parties handed money to a merchant? There, one might argue, escrow would impose a real cost: each party's payment to the merchant could be frozen along with the item in dispute. The *gemara* responds — *ela mechvarta ke'dishinan me'ikara* — the cleaner answer remains the original: the operative consideration is whether there is definitively a liar. That is the primary criterion.

---

## Shopkeeper Case

### Shopkeeper Setup

The *gemara* now introduces a new case to test these principles further, a case referenced already in the previous day's discussion. A *ba'al habayis* — an employer — instructs a *chanvani*, a shopkeeper who runs a nearby food establishment, to provide meals to his workers as part of their compensation, with the employer to pay the shopkeeper. At the end of the arrangement, the shopkeeper presents his bill and the workers claim they never received any food. The *halacha* in such a case is: *zeh nishba ve'noteil ve'zeh nishba ve'noteil* — each party takes a *shvuah* and collects from the employer. The shopkeeper swears he provided the meals and collects; the workers swear they received nothing and collect. The employer pays both.

### Why Not Escrow

This case demands explanation. As the *gemara* frames it, one of the two claiming parties is definitively lying — *vadai ika ramai*. Moreover, it is not possible for a split to be the correct judgment: either the shopkeeper fed them or he did not. Both conditions that the *gemara* identified as pushing toward escrow are present. Why, then, does the *gemara* not say: take the disputed wages, place them in escrow as *yehei munach ad she'yavo Eliyahu*, and let the parties sort it out?

### Employer's Fault

The *chanvani*'s position is as follows: he says to the employer — *shlichusa didach avdit*, I did exactly what you sent me to do. His dealings are with the employer, not with the workers. When the employer asks why the shopkeeper should be held responsible for a worker's false claim, the shopkeeper responds: *ant heimanteih* — you implicitly trusted him. You never instructed me to pay them in front of witnesses, *de'lo amarta li be'sahadei hav leih*. You set up an arrangement with no evidentiary protections whatsoever. If you wanted to guard against fraudulent claims, you should have required witnesses at the point of payment. By failing to do so, you effectively told me: feed them, I trust your word, and I trust theirs. The consequences of that unprotected system fall on you.

### Worker Defense

The worker makes a parallel argument. He says: *ana avdi avidta gabach* — I did a full day's work for you. You told me to go to this shopkeeper and receive food as part of my wages, and he gave me nothing. *Mai it li gabei chanvani* — what do I have to do with the shopkeeper? My employment relationship is with you. You have no evidence that you paid me. If you wanted to be able to prove payment, you should have structured the arrangement accordingly. His *shvuah* against a person with whom he has no direct dealings means little to him: *af al gav de'mishtatva li lo meheiman li* — even if he takes an oath, I have no reason to trust him; I have no relationship with him.

### Both Collect

The resolution follows directly: *hilchach shneihem nishba'in ve'notlin mi'ba'al habayis* — therefore both swear and collect from the employer. Since the employer structured a system that offered no protection against competing claims, and since neither the shopkeeper nor the worker can reasonably be expected to bear the cost of the employer's poor arrangement, the employer absorbs the loss on both ends. This is not standard escrow logic, nor standard *yehaloku* logic. It is a distinct category: where the party who bears responsibility for having created an unprotected system is the one who suffers the consequences.

---

## Decision Tree

### Muchzak Status

The *gemara*'s extended discussion through these cases makes it possible to articulate a decision framework for how *beis din* adjudicates when neither party's claim is proved and neither holds a clear presumption. Tosafot notes at the outset that our *gemara* deals specifically with cases where both parties enjoy a degree of *muchzak* — physical possession or the equivalent. The *tallis* case involves both parties holding the garment; in the deposit case, the trustee holds the funds on behalf of both parties, which Tosafot treats as a form of shared *muchzak*. Where neither party has any *muchzak* at all — such as a boat sitting in a harbor unclaimed — the *gemara* elsewhere rules *kol de'alim gevar*: let the stronger prevail, which may mean the court simply declines to adjudicate until one party establishes a better claim.

### Possibly True?

Assuming *muchzak* is present, the first question to ask is: is the proposed split *possibly* true? Can we conceive of a factual scenario in which both parties genuinely deserve half?

### Tallis: Possible

In the *tallis* case, the answer is yes. Both parties may have genuinely picked up the garment simultaneously. The split corresponds to a possible truth. In that case, the ruling is *yehaloku* — divide it — with a *shvuah*.

### Deposit: Not Possible

In the disputed deposit case, the answer is no. The third hundred *zuz* belongs, in reality, to exactly one of the two claimants. A fifty-fifty split of that hundred would be a patently false judgment. There is no factual scenario under which each party deserves half of that specific amount. The ruling is therefore *yehei munach* — place it in escrow.

### Equal Claims Test

The principle that emerges is: split only when both parties have an equal, legitimate claim that could conceivably be correct. Where the split would be patently wrong — where there is no possible truth in which it is the just outcome — do not split. Put the disputed property in escrow and wait. The *chanvani* case is sui generis: there, the employer's failure to protect his own interests generates an obligation to pay both parties in full, which is neither a split of the disputed amount nor a straightforward escrow, but rather the employer's self-imposed liability.

---

## Modeh BeHiktzat

### Rabbi Chiya Braita

Having worked through the logic of division and escrow, the *gemara* now shifts gears entirely and examines the *shvuah* from a different angle — not as a *takanah* against grabbing, and not as a preventative measure, but as a biblical *shvuah* of *modeh be'miktzat*, partial admission. Rabbi Chiya, understood to be the editor of the *Tosefta*, taught the following *braita*: if Reuven says to Shimon "you owe me one hundred *zuz*" and Shimon says "I owe you nothing," and then witnesses come and testify that Shimon owes at least fifty, Shimon must pay the fifty and take a *shvuah* on the remaining fifty — *noten lo chamishim ve'yishava al ha'she'ar*.

### Kal Vachomer Logic

Where does the obligation to take a *shvuah* come from in this witnesses case? Rabbi Chiya derives it through a *kal vachomer*: *shelo tehei hoda'as piv gedolah me'ha'adat eidim* — the force of one's own admission should not be greater than the force of witness testimony. The classic *shvuah* of *modeh be'miktzat* is biblical: if I claim you owe me a hundred and you admit to fifty, you take a *shvuah* on the remainder. The reasoning is that partial admission provides an objective basis for believing the rest of the claim may also be true, and the *shvuah* addresses the outstanding dispute. If that logic works when the partial truth is established by the debtor's own mouth, it should work at least as well — and arguably more forcefully — when the partial truth is established by external witnesses, whose testimony is weightier than self-admission in obligating monetary payment.

### Objection to Oath

One might object, however, that the *kal vachomer* is not obvious at all. The standard explanation for why *modeh be'miktzat* generates a *shvuah* obligation is not merely evidentiary — it is psychological. Rabba's principle, which the *gemara* develops at length, holds that a debtor partially admitting is presumed to be a rationalizer, not an outright liar. The *shvuah* is tailored to that psychology: it breaks through the rationalization and forces full admission. If that is the underlying logic, then witnesses who establish partial liability tell us nothing about the debtor's state of mind. He may be a complete *ganav* who never intended to pay anything, and a *shvuah* may be entirely ineffective in his case.

### Tallis & Modeh

The *gemara* adds that Rabbi Chiya's teaching is not unprecedented — our own *mishnah* can itself be read as a case of *modeh be'miktzat*, and thus as a biblical *shvuah*. This is the *gemara*'s basis for having noted earlier that the *shvuah* in our *mishnah* is rabbinic: the *gemara* anticipated that there was a possible framework in which it would be treated as biblical.

### Possession as Witness

The comparison is striking. The *gemara* says: *keivan de'tafsi, anan sa'adei de'mai de'tafsi hai didei hu u'mai de'tafsi hai didei hu* — since each party is physically holding the *tallis*, our collective witness-like observation is that what each one holds is his. Physical possession functions as testimony to partial ownership. Each party is therefore in the position of someone who has just been proven — via something akin to witnesses — to own half. But each party claims the whole. So each party is, in effect, someone against whom there is evidence of partial claim validity who continues to deny the full claim against him. That generates the *shvuah*.

The *gemara* itself acknowledges the bizarreness of this framing. The "testimony" here precedes the claims. The evidence cuts symmetrically in both directions — each party's holding is simultaneously "testimony" for his claim and against the other's. Whether this is truly analogous to *modeh be'miktzat* or is merely a loose structural parallel is a question the *gemara* leaves open. What it establishes is the conceptual path by which our *mishnah* could be read as instantiating a biblical *shvuah*, and Rabbi Chiya's *braita* extends that same logic to the case of actual witnesses.

---

## Rationalizer Psychology

### Rabba's Principle

The *gemara* now develops at length the psychological premise underlying *modeh be'miktzat*, which was already alluded to above. Rabba asks: *mipnei mah amrah Torah modeh be'miktzat ha'tana'ah yishava* — why does the Torah require an oath when one partially admits? The question is sharp. One might have supposed a *migo* argument: since the debtor could have denied everything and walked free, his voluntary partial admission should be credited, not punished with a *shvuah*.

Rabba answers: *chazakah ein adam meiz panav bifnei ba'al chovo* — there is a presumption that a person will not act with brazen shamelessness before someone who has done him the favor of lending him money. The debtor cannot bring himself to look the creditor in the eye and say "I never borrowed a thing from you." That degree of *chutzpah* is beyond him.

### Rashi vs Tosafot

Rashi and Tosafot differ on the precise basis of this inhibition. Rashi attributes it to the *tovah* — the kindness — the creditor extended by lending in the first place. Because the creditor did me a favor, I cannot be so brazen as to deny it entirely. Tosafot disagrees: the inhibition applies even in cases such as *shvuas ha'shomrim*, where the creditor is not doing the debtor a *tovah* — if anything, the *shomer* is doing the owner the favor of watching his property. Tosafot therefore holds that the inhibition is rooted not in gratitude but in a more general reluctance to lie brazenly to someone's face about something that person knows you are liable for, regardless of the underlying relationship.

### Partial Admission

Given this inhibition, why does the debtor not admit to the full amount? Rabba explains: *be'kulei ba'ei di'nichferei* — his better self wants to fully admit. The reason he does not fully admit is *ishtamutei hu de'ka mishtamit minei* — he is simply putting the creditor off. He does not have the cash on hand. He borrowed the money, the creditor has been pressing him, and he says to himself: *ad de'havu li zuzei u'far'ana lei* — let me get the money together and then I'll pay him off. He is not trying to steal; he is trying to buy time. He rationalizes: "I'll eventually pay the full amount, so it's not really lying, I just need a bit longer."

### Oath Breaks Rationalizat…

This is where the *shvuah* becomes decisive. Because the debtor is fundamentally a rationalizer — not a brazen thief — the *shvuah* cuts through his psychological maneuvering. *Ve'amar Rachmana rami shvua aleih ki heihi de'lodei lei be'kulei* — the Torah therefore imposes a *shvuah* on him precisely in order to force full admission. Confronted with the gravity of an oath, the rationalizer can no longer hide behind his excuses. This makes the *shvuah* a remarkably targeted instrument of moral and legal pressure, one whose efficacy depends entirely on the debtor being a rationalizer rather than an outright liar. The *mussar* dimension of this insight is hard to miss: the mechanism by which *halacha* breaks through self-deception is directly analogous to the process of honest *cheshbon ha'nefesh* — taking stock of oneself without the cushion of rationalization.

---

## Witnesses & Oath

### Kal Vachomer Stated

The *gemara* now states the *kal vachomer* of Rabbi Chiya formally. *Umai piv* — when it comes to one's own admission — *she'ein mechayvo mamon* — it does not obligate in monetary payment in all cases — yet *mechayvo shvuah* — it does generate a *shvuah* obligation. *Eidin she'mechayvin oso mamon* — witnesses, who can obligate monetary payment — *eino din she'mechayvin oso shvuah* — how much more so should they generate a *shvuah* obligation?

### Admission vs Kenas

The *gemara* immediately objects: what do you mean self-admission does not obligate monetary payment? *Hoda'as ba'al din ki'me'ah eidin dami* — one's own admission is like the testimony of a hundred witnesses! Of course self-admission obligates payment. The *gemara* clarifies: *mai mamon — kenas*. The reference is not to ordinary monetary obligations but to court-imposed fines — *kenas*. If a person admits to having stolen and would therefore owe the double payment (*kefel*), his self-admission obligates him to pay the principal but not the fine. The additional payment is a punitive sanction, not a debt, and as such it belongs to the category of punishments — like lashes or execution — that can only be imposed on the basis of external witnesses, not self-incrimination.

### Kenas Definition

A *kenas* is thus distinguished from standard *mamon*: it is a court-imposed sanction rather than a restitutive obligation. Because it is punitive in character, it requires external proof. A person cannot, through his own admission alone, obligate himself in a *kenas*, just as no court could execute a defendant on the basis of his own confession alone. Self-admission, for purposes of the *kal vachomer*, is therefore weaker than witness testimony specifically with respect to *kenas* liability.

### Korban Exception

The *gemara* presses further: is it really true that witnesses are always weightier than self-admission? It raises a counterexample. If a person admits that he unknowingly ate *chelev* — forbidden fat — *be'shogeg*, he brings a *korban chatas*. But if witnesses testify that he ate it while he denies it, the consensus view is that he does not bring a *korban*. Here, self-admission generates an obligation — *korban* — that witnesses cannot generate. Self-admission is therefore, in this domain, *more* weighty than witnesses. This would undermine the *kal vachomer*'s foundational premise.

### Rabbi Meir Korban

Rabbi Meir disagrees with the consensus. He argues: *im heviu shnayim li'dei mitah chamurah, lo yaviuhu li'dei korban ha'kal* — if two witnesses can bring a person to the gravest of punishments, capital execution, can they not certainly bring him to the comparatively minor obligation of a *korban*? This *kal vachomer* mirrors the logic of Rabbi Chiya's *kal vachomer* about *shvuah*: witnesses are always weightier, therefore wherever self-admission generates an obligation, witnesses do so as well and to a greater degree.

### Viduy Requirement

The Rabbis reject Rabbi Meir's position. Their argument is that *korban* is categorically different from punishments: it is not imposed on the basis of objective facts alone. Bringing a *korban* presupposes *viduy* — confession and acceptance of guilt. *Ve'hitvadah asher chata aleha* — the verse itself conditions atonement on admission. Without the penitent's own acknowledgment of his act, the *korban* has no foundation. Tosafot sharpens this by noting that the Rabbis' argument is not merely technical. Rather, the *korban* is not about establishing facts; it is about taking responsibility. The entire *korban* process begins with the person's own *viduy*. Witnesses cannot supply what only the person's own moral reckoning can provide. This is in direct contrast to Rabbi Meir, who appears to view the *korban* as an objective metaphysical remedy — a response to the rupture caused by sin, irrespective of whether the sinner has internalized his guilt.

### Chiya & Meir Align

The *gemara* resolves the apparent difficulty for Rabbi Chiya: *Rabbi Chiya ke'Rabbi Meir svira lei* — Rabbi Chiya's position aligns with that of Rabbi Meir. Both maintain that witnesses are always weightier than self-admission across all domains. Just as Rabbi Meir holds that witnesses can obligate a *korban* even without *viduy*, Rabbi Chiya holds that witnesses can generate a *shvuah* obligation through the *kal vachomer*. The two positions are of a piece: a consistent jurisprudential stance that external witness testimony is the weightier form of evidence and always produces at least the legal consequences that self-admission produces. The *gemara* will continue in the next session to develop the further implications of this dispute.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 4

## Witnesses vs. Admission

### Rabbi Chiya's Position

The daf opens by picking up from the bottom of 3b, where the Gemara is examining the position of Rabbi Chiya. Rabbi Chiya maintains that just as a *modeh be-miktzat* — one who admits to part of a monetary claim — is required to take an oath on the remainder, the same obligation applies when witnesses partially substantiate the claim. That is, if the plaintiff claims a hundred and witnesses testify that the defendant owes fifty, the defendant must swear regarding the other fifty, even though he has neither admitted nor fully denied the claim. The Gemara acknowledges upfront that the internal logic driving the *shvua* in the admission case — the defendant's self-interested rationalization — is less present when the testimony comes from external witnesses. Nevertheless, Rabbi Chiya argues that the formal weight of witnesses is sufficient, and that argument rests on a *kal va-chomer*: since the evidentiary strength of witnesses exceeds that of a party's own admission, the oath requirement should apply at least as strongly.

### Power Comparison

The basis for the *kal va-chomer* is a concrete legal asymmetry: witnesses can compel a defendant to pay a *knas* (a penal fine), whereas a party's own admission cannot. The principle *ein adam mesim atzmo rasha* — a person cannot render himself a *rasha* — precludes self-incriminating testimony in the domain of penalties, lashes, and capital punishment. In monetary matters, however, admission is fully operative; indeed, it obligates payment. The relevant question here is not the moral status of the statement but the comparative evidentiary force of witnesses versus admission across legal categories. In the domain of *knas*, witnesses are categorically stronger.

### Ein Adam Mesim

The Gemara complicates this picture by pointing out that a party's admission can trigger the obligation to bring a *korban*, whereas witnesses cannot — since bringing a *korban* is bound up with the acceptance of guilt, and guilt cannot be imposed by external testimony. The Gemara responds that this follows the position of Rabbi Meir, who holds that witnesses carry so sweeping a legal force that they can even impose the obligation to bring a *korban* without any personal acceptance of culpability. Under Rabbi Meir's view, witnesses are stronger than admission across the board.

The Gemara then raises *asham*: a party's admission obligates an *asham*, whereas witnesses do not. The Gemara dismisses this quickly — an *asham* is simply a type of *korban*, and since under Rabbi Meir witnesses can compel a *korban*, they can equally compel an *asham*.

A more potent objection follows: admission obligates payment of a *chomesh* (an added fifth), as in the case of falsely denying a bailment under oath and later confessing — whereas witnesses who expose the lie do not trigger the *chomesh*. Here the Gemara invokes Rabbi Meir's position again: just as Rabbi Meir holds that witnesses can impose the *korban* obligation without personal acceptance of guilt, so too they can impose the *chomesh* obligation via a *kal va-chomer* from the *korban*. The logic is consistent: if the most personal expression of atonement — the *korban* — can be imposed externally by witnesses under Rabbi Meir, then so can the monetarily quantifiable *chomesh*. Thus Rabbi Chiya's position is understood as consistent with that of Rabbi Meir.

### Admission Irreducibility

The Gemara, however, identifies a domain in which witnesses are unambiguously weaker than admission and which cannot be dissolved by appeal to Rabbi Meir. When a party admits to a monetary obligation, that admission is absolutely irreducible: no contrary evidence, no contradictory witnesses, and no proof that the circumstances described never occurred can undo it. The principle *hoda'at ba'al din ki-me'ah eidim dami* — a litigant's admission is equivalent to a hundred witnesses — is not really a statement about the factual weight of testimony. It reflects a deeper point: a monetary admission is not merely an assertion about what happened in the world; it functions as a present act of obligation, independent of the historical facts. If I say I owe David a hundred dollars, I owe David a hundred dollars, even if a thousand witnesses could prove I was elsewhere when the alleged loan was made.

Witnesses, by contrast, are subject to *hachshasha* (contradiction through counter-testimony) and *hazama* (formal refutation by proof that the witnesses were elsewhere). There is therefore at least one dimension in which witnesses are not stronger than admission. This means the *kal va-chomer* cannot operate as a blanket rule, and the obligation to swear in the case of partial witness testimony cannot be derived from it unconditionally.

---

## Kal VaChomer from One Wi…

### One to Two Witnesses

Since the comparison of two witnesses to self-admission is undermined by the irreducibility of admission, the Gemara pivots to a different *kal va-chomer*: from *eid echad* (a single witness) to two witnesses. The structure is as follows: a single witness, whose testimony cannot compel monetary payment, nonetheless obligates the defendant to take an oath to contradict him. If one witness — who cannot make the defendant pay — generates the obligation to swear, then two witnesses — who can make the defendant pay — should certainly generate the obligation to swear on the remainder. Two witnesses are in every respect stronger than one, so there is no basis for the asymmetry that troubled the prior comparison.

### Contradiction Distinction

The Gemara, however, identifies a fundamental structural difference between the two cases. When one witness says the defendant owes a hundred dollars and the defendant denies it, the *shvua* functions as a direct contradiction of the witness's testimony. The defendant swears against precisely what the witness asserts.
