But in the scenario under discussion — where two witnesses testify to fifty dollars and the defendant has already paid that fifty — the *shvua* would be taken on the *remaining* fifty, a claim on which the witnesses say nothing. The defendant is not swearing against the witnesses; he is swearing on something else entirely. The *shvua* in the *eid echad* case and the proposed *shvua* in the two-witness case operate on entirely different logic, and one cannot be used to prove the other.

### Gilgul Shvua

At this point Rav Papa introduces the mechanism of *gilgul shvua* — the "rolling oath." The principle is that once a court compels a party to take an oath in one context, that oath can be extended to cover additional claims by the opposing party. The litigant, having already been placed under oath, is required to swear on any other disputed matter the plaintiff raises. This is why appearing before a court under oath is so consequential: the first oath can cascade into an obligation to swear on unrelated matters.

Rav Papa applies this to the *eid echad* scenario. The single witness generates an initial *shvua*. Once that *shvua* is in place, the plaintiff can use the *gilgul* mechanism to compel the defendant to swear on a separate, unrelated claim. Now compare this to the two-witness case: if two witnesses say the defendant owes fifty, and the defendant — who according to Rabbi Chiya must take an oath on the remainder — is in some sense already "under oath," could that lead, via *gilgul*, to an oath on the other fifty? The argument is that since one witness indirectly generates an oath through the *gilgul* mechanism on claims beyond his testimony, two witnesses — who are stronger — should at least be able to generate an oath on what remains of the very claim at issue.

### Gilgul Inapplicable

The Gemara rejects this reasoning sharply. The *gilgul shvua* in the *eid echad* case works because it piggybacks on an existing *shvua*: one oath drags another in its wake (*shvua goreret shvua*). But in the two-witness case, what is produced initially is not an oath but a monetary payment. The defendant pays fifty dollars. Payment does not function like an oath; it cannot serve as a platform for *gilgul*. The cascade requires an initial *shvua* as its foundation, and absent that, the mechanism does not engage. The Gemara's formulation is precise: *tomar be-eidim de-mamona kam-chaivei* — in the case of witnesses, what is being compelled is money, not an oath, and money cannot roll into further oath-taking the way an oath can.

---

## Three Cases Compared

### Common Denominator

The Gemara now steps back to construct the argument more carefully, using the classical method of *tzad ha-shaveh* — reasoning from a common denominator across two cases to establish a rule applicable to a third. The two established cases where a *shvua* is required are: (1) *eid echad*, where a single witness testifies to the full claim; and (2) *modeh be-miktzat*, where the defendant admits to part. The proposed third case is two witnesses who establish part of the claim. The Gemara sets up this triangular structure explicitly.

Consider the diagram: in the *eid echad* case, the defendant takes a *shvua* to directly contradict the witness's testimony. In the *modeh be-miktzat* case, the defendant takes a *shvua* on what he has not admitted — the rest of the claim. These are two distinct logical structures for how a *shvua* is generated. The defendant in the *eid echad* case swears against what is testified; the defendant in the *modeh be-miktzat* case swears on what he denies despite admitting to part. Each case has a feature the other lacks.

The Gemara proposes that neither case alone can serve as a proof for the two-witness scenario, but that their common denominator can. What is that common denominator? *Shel-ta'anat kefirah hen ba'in* — both cases arise in the context of a claim that has been at least partially substantiated, followed by a counter-claim. In both cases, the opposing party's position has received some evidentiary backing, and in both cases a *shvua* results. By analogy, when two witnesses substantiate part of a claim and the defendant denies the remainder, the same logic should apply: the claim has been substantiated, and the defendant should take an oath. This is Rabbi Chiya's argument.

### Distinguishing Features

The Gemara walks through why neither case can single-handedly establish the rule for the other, and why only the common denominator approach works. The *eid echad* case cannot prove the *modeh be-miktzat* structure, because in *eid echad* the *shvua* targets the testimony itself, not a separate remainder. The *modeh be-miktzat* case cannot prove the *eid echad* structure because admission cannot be contradicted, giving it a strength that testimony lacks. Yet the *eid echad* case has its own advantage over admission: it can be contradicted, and despite that vulnerability it still generates a *shvua*. These asymmetries create a perfect standoff in which neither case is simply superior to the other, which is exactly the condition (*lo rei zeh ke-rei zeh*) that validates the common denominator argument.

The abstraction the Gemara arrives at is clean: whenever there is something that substantiates the claim — whether that is a partial admission or the testimony of a single witness — the opposing party must take an oath. When two witnesses substantiate part of a claim, the same logic applies. The common shape in all these cases is that the plaintiff's claim has been given evidentiary footing, and so a *shvua* is warranted.

### Thief vs. Denier

The Gemara raises a more pointed challenge to the common denominator. In both established cases — *eid echad* and *modeh be-miktzat* — there is no direct evidence that the defendant is a thief or a deliberate liar. The defendant in the admission case has come forward voluntarily; the defendant in the *eid echad* case is contradicting a single, non-dispositive witness. In neither case has the defendant been proven to be dishonest. A *shvua* makes sense precisely because the defendant retains enough credibility to be bound by one.

But in the two-witness scenario under discussion, the defendant declared he owed nothing, and two witnesses established that he owes fifty. The witnesses have, in effect, proven him a liar — *huchzak kafran*. If he is a proven liar, why should we think a *shvua* will accomplish anything? Who are we kidding by imposing an oath on someone who has already demonstrated his willingness to deny what is true?

### Trustworthiness

The Gemara responds by drawing a critical distinction between a *kafran* in monetary matters and one in matters of *pikadon* (bailment of a concrete object). The Gemara cites the ruling of Rabbi Avin in the name of Rav Chisda: one who denies a monetary debt is still *kasher le-edut* — qualified to testify. He has not been disqualified. This is because the denial of a monetary obligation may not reflect an intent to steal; the defendant may simply be delaying payment because he lacks the funds at the moment, intending to pay eventually. He may be dishonest about the present state of the debt without being a *gazlan*. A *gazlan*, who has stolen a concrete object and denies possessing it, is *pasul le-edut* because his denial demonstrates a present intention to appropriate something belonging to another. By contrast, denying a monetary claim is not equivalent to theft in the same direct sense. The defendant who denies owing money and is later shown to owe it remains, technically, a reliable oath-taker. His *shvua* retains legal meaning.

This resolves the concern: the two-witness case does not render the defendant categorically untrustworthy in the way that would make a *shvua* meaningless. The claim has been substantiated, he is not disqualified as a swearer, and the common denominator argument holds. Rabbi Chiya's position is therefore sound: when witnesses partially substantiate a claim, the defendant takes an oath on the remainder.

---

## Tallit vs. Admission

### Asymmetry Problem

Having established the theoretical soundness of Rabbi Chiya's ruling, the Gemara turns to his attempt to ground it in the *mishna* of *shenayim ochazin be-tallit* — two people holding a garment and each claiming it entirely. Rabbi Chiya sought to derive support for his ruling from this *mishna*, but the Gemara identifies a fundamental asymmetry that makes the comparison untenable.

In the classic *modeh be-miktzat* scenario underlying Rabbi Chiya's ruling: the plaintiff claims a hundred, has witnesses to fifty, and the defendant has no witnesses whatsoever. The plaintiff has evidentiary backing; the defendant has none. That asymmetry is precisely why the defendant must swear. But in the *tallit* case, the evidentiary footing is exactly equal on both sides. Each party holds half the garment; each party's possession of his half is just as strong a proof as the other's. Whatever evidence the plaintiff can marshal, the defendant has the mirror image.

### Holding Equals Admission

Rabbi Chiya had attempted to frame the *tallit* case as analogous to *modeh be-miktzat* by treating each party's holding as a kind of implicit admission: since I am holding half, it is as though I am conceding that half and contesting only the other half. That concession-through-possession is structurally similar to handing over the admitted portion, creating a *heilech*-like situation and leaving the remainder in dispute.

### Equal Standing

The Gemara flatly rejects this framing. The fact that I hold half cannot be treated as an admission or concession in my favor, because the same logic applies equally to my counterpart: his holding of half is equally evidence of his claim. *Ki heichi de-anan sahadi be-hai, anan sahadi be-hai* — the same way we have witnesses for this party's entitlement to half, we have witnesses for the other party's entitlement to half. There is no asymmetry, and therefore no *modeh be-miktzat* structure whatsoever.

### Different Teaching

The conclusion is that the *mishna* of *shenayim ochazin* cannot be used to support the teaching about two witnesses and partial oath-taking. However, the Gemara clarifies that the *mishna* does support a different teaching of Rabbi Chiya — namely, the *heilech* ruling. It is to that teaching, and that debate, that the Gemara now turns.

---

## Heilech Question

### Rabbi Chiya on Heilech

Rabbi Chiya's ruling on *heilech* concerns the following case: the plaintiff claims a hundred; the defendant says he owes only fifty and immediately hands over the fifty (*ve-heilech* — "and here it is"). Does this constitute *modeh be-miktzat*, requiring an oath on the remaining fifty? Or does the immediate payment of the admitted amount remove it from the table entirely, leaving the parties in a posture of a simple full-denial case regarding the remainder?

Rabbi Chiya holds that even with *heilech*, it remains *modeh be-miktzat*, and the defendant must take an oath on the rest. The reasoning is that the moment of admission is what counts. The defendant admitted to fifty, and that admission established a partial concession. The fact that he immediately paid does not retroactively dissolve the admission's legal character; *ve-heilech nami ke-modeh be-miktzat ha-ta'ana dami* — *heilech* is also treated as a partial admission.

The Gemara sought to bring support for this from the *tallit* case: in *shenayim ochazin*, each party holds half — which is structurally similar to having already handed over half (*heilech*) — and yet both parties are required to swear. This suggests that even when the "admitted" portion is effectively already transferred, a *shvua* is still required on the remainder. As we have seen, however, this proof was undermined by the equal-and-opposite evidentiary structure of the *tallit* case, which is ultimately a *takkanat chachamim* rather than a biblical *modeh be-miktzat*.

### Rav Sheshet's Objection

Rav Sheshet disagrees categorically. Once the defendant says *heilech* and hands over the fifty, that money is legally as if it already sits in the plaintiff's pocket. The admitted portion is off the table entirely. The only live dispute is now over the remaining fifty, on which the defendant is denying any obligation. That is a case of *kofer ha-kol* regarding fifty dollars, not *modeh be-miktzat* regarding a hundred. And a *kofer ha-kol* does not take a *shvua* under biblical law. Rav Sheshet's formulation is precise: *hanei zuzzei de-ka modeh be-gavaihu ke-man de-nakit lehu malveh dami* — the coins he admits to are as if already in the lender's possession — *ve-inach chamishim, ha lo modeh lei, ve-hava lei kofer ha-kol* — and on the other fifty he is a full denier. *Heilech patur.*

The Gemara then challenges Rav Sheshet from the *mishna* of *shenayim ochazin*: in the *tallit* case, each party's holding is structurally like *heilech* — effectively already in possession — yet both are required to swear. This seems to contradict Rav Sheshet's view.

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic

Rav Sheshet responds that the *tallit* case is not a biblical *modeh be-miktzat* at all. It is a *takkanat chachamim*. The Rabbis enacted the oath requirement in that case either to discourage people from grabbing objects and claiming them as their own, or to create a more accurate evidentiary process. The *tallit* oath is an entirely rabbinic institution with no biblical *modeh be-miktzat* structure underlying it.

The Gemara presses further: if *heilech* is *chayav* biblically, then the rabbinic enactment of the *tallit* oath is modeled on a biblical precedent — the Rabbis made a *shvua* parallel to a *d'Oraita*. But if *heilech* is *patur* biblically, the Rabbis would be instituting a *shvua* for which there is no biblical analogue whatsoever. Would the Sages enact something that has no parallel in Torah law?

### Policy Argument

This is Rabbi Chiya's response to Rav Sheshet: the coherence of the rabbinic enactment in the *tallit* case presupposes that there is a biblical category — *modeh be-miktzat* with *heilech* — that generates an oath. If that biblical category did not exist, the Rabbis could not model the *tallit* oath on anything. The very existence of a rabbinic *shvua* in the *tallit* case argues for the existence of a biblical precedent, which means *heilech* must be *chayav* at the biblical level. Rabbi Chiya thus emerges with his original position intact, at least structurally, even if the *tallit mishna* itself cannot directly prove his case.

---

## Damaged Document Case

### Case Setup

The Gemara now introduces a *baraita* involving a damaged *shtar*. The document records a loan in the currency *dinarim*, but the specific numeral indicating the amount has been obscured or worn away. What the document clearly preserves is the word for a denomination that minimally means two. The plaintiff claims the loan was for five; the defendant claims it was for three. The two-*dinar* minimum is established beyond dispute by the face of the document.

### Rabban Shimon

Rabban Shimon ben Elazar rules that since the defendant admitted to more than the two-*dinar* minimum — that is, since she said three rather than two — she has thereby admitted to part of the plaintiff's claim, and she must take an oath on the rest. The admission to three (one above the undisputed minimum of two) constitutes *modeh be-miktzat*, and the *shvua* follows accordingly.

### Rabbi Akiva

Rabbi Akiva disagrees: one who admits to three is like one who *returns a lost object* (*meshiv aveidah*), and is therefore exempt. The principle of *meshiv aveidah* holds that when a person voluntarily returns something he could have kept without legal consequence, we do not reward that honesty by imposing further obligations on him. The defendant here could have simply said two — the minimum already established by the document — and denied everything beyond it without contradiction. By admitting to three, she volunteered information she could have withheld. To penalize her with an oath would be counterproductive: it would discourage honest admissions.

Whether Rabbi Akiva is making a *takanah* argument (societal policy) or a *migo* argument (since she could have said two, her admission of three should be trusted) is left somewhat open, but the practical outcome is the same: admitting to three is exempt.

### Two vs. Three

The Gemara analyzes the relationship between the two positions. Rabban Shimon ben Elazar's statement says: *since she admitted to part, she must swear* — implying that admitting to three triggers *modeh be-miktzat*. The implicit inference is that had she said two, she would be *patur*. The Gemara asks: why should two be *patur*? Surely if I claim five and she admits to two, that is *modeh be-miktzat*?

The answer is that the two-*dinar* minimum is already established by the *shtar* before any admission is made. Saying two is not an admission of anything beyond what the document already proves. The two *dinarim* are effectively off the table before litigation even begins. Admitting to two is therefore structurally like *heilech* — the money was already effectively allocated — or more precisely, it is not an admission at all, since the *shtar* backs it up entirely. This is why two is *patur*.

---

## Technical Exemptions

### Shiud and Land

Having established that saying two is *patur*, the Gemara offers two distinct technical reasons why. The first, simpler reason is that the *shtar* itself backs up the claim to two *dinarim*, so that the defendant's "admission" of two adds nothing — it merely confirms what the document already establishes. But the Gemara also introduces a more technical ground: *mishum de-havei lei shtar shibud karkaot ve-ein nishba'in al kfirat shibud karkaot* — because the *shtar* creates a lien (*shibud*) on the borrower's land, and one does not take an oath regarding the denial (or admission) of land liens.

The mechanics are as follows: a *shtar* of indebtedness creates a *shibud* on the debtor's land for the amount provable from the document. If the document is damaged and the only legible amount is two *dinarim*, then the *shibud* on land is for two *dinarim*, regardless of what the parties claim the true loan amount was. When the defendant admits to two, what she is admitting is precisely the two-*dinar* *shibud* — an obligation that is, in legal character, tied to land. And the established rule is that there is no *shvua* over matters relating to land: land cannot be stolen (*karka einah nigzelet*), and oaths do not apply to real-property obligations in the same way they apply to movable assets.

Therefore, even if I claim a thousand and the defendant admits only to the two-*dinar* *shibud* provable by the *shtar*, her entire admission consists of a land-lien obligation. That admission does not constitute *modeh be-miktzat* for purposes of triggering a *shvua*, because the admission is entirely in the domain of land. Had she admitted to three, she would be admitting to one additional *dinar* beyond the *shibud* — a cash obligation untethered from land — and that one *dinar* admission, set against the remainder of the claim, would be a genuine *modeh be-miktzat*.

### Shtar's Role

The Gemara elaborates on the *shtar*'s role in this analysis. A *shtar* functions as testimony — it is equivalent to two witnesses for purposes of establishing the debt. When the *shtar* says *dinarim* without a numeral, it establishes the minimum (two) with the force of testimony. Before the parties have exchanged a word in court, the two-*dinar* obligation is already proven. The entire litigation concerns only the disputed amount above two. When the defendant confirms two, she confirms nothing that was not already proven; her "admission" adds no evidentiary weight. And for the *shibud karkaot* analysis, the *shtar*-backed amount creates a land lien of exactly that size, placing the admitted sum squarely within the exempted category.

### Reconciliation

The Gemara notes that there are two versions of the *baraita*: one presented from the perspective of Rabban Shimon ben Elazar, and one from the perspective of Rabbi Akiva. The Gemara reconciles them by showing that both versions, properly understood, agree on one fundamental point: saying two is always *patur*. The debate between Rabban Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Akiva is specifically and only about the case of three. Rabban Shimon ben Elazar says three is *modeh be-miktzat* and requires an oath. Rabbi Akiva says three is *meshiv aveidah* and is exempt.

The Gemara confirms this reading by showing that the alternative interpretation — that Rabban Shimon ben Elazar would say two is also *chayav* — generates an internal contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's position. If two were *chayav*, then a knowing defendant would strategically say three instead to invoke the *meshiv aveidah* exemption. The court would in effect be rewarding deceptive behavior. Since we assume the Rabbis do not construct rules that can be easily gamed in this way, two must be *patur* under both views, and the entire debate is limited to the three case.

### Why Two Is Exempt

The Gemara concludes with a convergence of three independent grounds for the *patur* of two: (1) *heilech* — admitting to two while the *shtar* already establishes two is like handing over money that was already allocated, leaving the remainder as a *kofer ha-kol*; (2) the *shtar* backs up the claim of two with full evidentiary force, so no *shvua* is needed to substantiate it; (3) the admitted two *dinarim* are entirely within the *shibud karkaot* — the land lien — and one does not take an oath on the denial or admission of land-lien obligations. Each of these reasons independently suffices to exempt the defendant who says two from any *shvua* obligation. The daf concludes at this point, with the Gemara having established the convergent technical foundations for this exemption.

---

# Bava Metzia 5

## Heilech & Karka

### Keilim/Karka Mishnah

The daf opens in the middle of an ongoing discussion of *heilech* — the teaching of Rabbi Chiya that when someone admits to part of a claim while denying the rest, that constitutes *modeh be-miktzas* and creates an obligation to take a *shevua* on the denied portion. More specifically, Rabbi Chiya holds that if *edim* testify to fifty of a claimed hundred, that functions like a *modeh be-miktzas* and obligates a *shevua* on the remainder. It is Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman who raises a challenge from a *mishnah*.

The *mishnah* under examination deals with a case where someone was claimed against for both *keilim* and *karka*. The Gemara walks through four permutations. If the defendant admitted to the *keilim* and denied the *karka*, he is exempt (*patur*) from a *shevua*. If he admitted to the *karka* and denied the *keilim*, he is likewise exempt. Even if he admitted to part of the *karka* while denying another part, he remains exempt, because *karka* — whether it appears in the admission (*hoda'ah*) or the denial (*kfirah*) — categorically exempts from *shevua*. The one case of obligation (*chayav*) is *miktzas keilim*: where the defendant denied all of the *karka* and admitted to only some of the *keilim* while denying others. Here, because both the admission and the denial relate entirely to *keilim*, one can treat the *karka* as a separate matter and apply *modeh be-miktzas* to the *keilim* alone.

### Why Karka Example

The Gemara proceeds to analyze the *mishnah*'s structure. The reason one is exempt in the cases involving *karka*, says the Gemara, is stated directly: *de-karka lav bar shevua hi* — *karka* is not subject to a *shevua*, regardless of whether it appears in the admission or the denial. But this raises a pointed question. *Karka* possesses two distinct features: it belongs to a category formally excluded from *shevua*, and it always carries a *heilech* component — since *karka* cannot be hidden or moved, admitting to *karka* is always tantamount to saying "here it is, take it." So why did the *mishnah* choose to illustrate the exemption using *karka* specifically? Perhaps it implies that were you dealing only with the *heilech* aspect — say, *keilim* that functioned like *karka* because they were present and acknowledged — you would still be *chayav*.

The Gemara therefore raises the possibility: *ha keilim ve-keilim dumya de-keilim ve-karka'os chayav* — what about a case of *keilim* and *keilim*, where the *keilim* resemble *karka* because the defendant says *heilech*, "here are the five chairs I admit to, take them," while denying the other five? Would that not imply that *heilech* is *chayav*? The Gemara sees in this formulation a seeming proof in favor of Rabbi Chiya's position on *heilech*.

The Gemara immediately deflects: *le-olam eima lach keilim ve-keilim nami patur* — one might in truth say that even *keilim ve-keilim* where the admitted *keilim* are right there in front of you would be exempt. The *mishnah* did not choose *karka* to signal that *keilim* with a *heilech* quality would be *chayav*. Rather, it chose *karka* to teach a different and important law — that even *karka*, which is categorically exempt from *shevua*, can in certain circumstances be pulled into the *shevua* obligation.

### Gilgul Shevua

The mechanism by which *karka* is drawn into the *shevua* is the principle of *gilgul shevua*, also called *zokekin*. The *mishnah* teaches that if the defendant admitted to some *keilim* while denying others — thereby becoming obligated in a *shevua* on the *keilim* — then once that *shevua* is in place, one can drag along (*zokekin*) the *karka* and require a *shevua* on that as well, notwithstanding the general exemption. This is the operative point: *ha kamashma lan hoda'ah bemiktzas keilim chayav af al ha-karka'os* — the admission of part of the *keilim* obligates him in a *shevua* that encompasses the *karka* as well.

### Shevuos Teaching

But the Gemara observes that this principle of *zokekin* — that property without liens (*metaltelin*) can drag along property with liens (*karka*) into a *shevua* — was already taught in *Kiddushin*: *zokekin ha-nichasim she-ein lahem achrayus es ha-nichasim she-yesh lahem achrayus lishava aleihem*. If so, what does the *mishnah* in *Shevuos* add?

The Gemara answers: *hacha ikkar* — this is the primary place for the teaching. *Masechet Shevuos* is precisely the tractate that deals with the laws of *shevua*, defining when one is obligated and when exempt. *Keilim* — obligated; *karka* — exempt; yet once the *shevua* is triggered by the *keilim*, the *karka* is dragged along. That is the teaching that belongs here. The mention of *zokekin* in *Kiddushin*, by contrast, is incidental — *Kiddushin* is primarily concerned with modes of acquisition, and the *shevua* material appears there only as an aside (*agav grara nasba*).

### Damaged Karka

The Gemara then transitions to a further question. According to the view that *heilech patur* — that handing back the admitted item exempts one from a *shevua* — why did the Torah need to establish a *pasuk*-based exclusion to exempt *karka* from *shevua*? Since *karka* always constitutes *heilech* (it sits immovably before the claimant), the *karka* exemption should follow automatically from the *heilech* exemption. Why invoke a *klal prat u'klal* derivation?

The Gemara offers two answers. First: not every admission of *karka* is in fact *heilech*. If the defendant damaged the land — digging pits, channels, or caves in it — and admits liability, he is not returning the very thing he received. There is an admission, but it is not the clean *heilech* of handing back an intact object. Hence a *pasuk* is still needed for such a case.

Second — and more straightforwardly — *karka* is only *heilech* when one *admits* to the *karka*. When the defendant *denies* the *karka*, there is no *heilech*: the land sits there but is not being acknowledged or tendered. The *pasuk* is necessary to cover precisely that scenario, where *karka* is the subject of the *kfirah* rather than the *hoda'ah*, and there is still an exemption from *shevua*.

---

## Four Shomrim

### Shomrim Obligation

The Gemara continues to probe the *heilech* question. Rami bar Chama's *braisa* is introduced, teaching that the obligation of the four *shomrim* — *shomer chinam*, *sho'el*, *nosei sachar*, and *socher* — to make a *shevuat ha-shomrim* is conditional. Each category of *shomer* carries a defined level of liability: the unpaid watchman is exempt from everything except negligence; the borrower is liable for virtually everything save death in the course of normal use; the paid watchman and the renter are liable for theft and loss but exempt from genuine accident.

The *braisa* teaches that a *shomer* does not simply take a *shevua* when claiming exemption in the ordinary sense. Rather, the *shevua* of the *shomrim* must be embedded within a *modeh be-miktzas* structure. There must be a *kfirah be-miktzas* and a *hoda'ah be-miktzas* — a partial denial and a partial admission — surrounding the *shevuat ha-shomrim* claim.

### Three Cows Case

The Gemara poses the scenario: *heichi dami* — what is the actual case? The initial reading is that the bailor entrusted three cows and the *shomer* admits to one and denies one — a straightforward *modeh be-miktzas* — while the *shevuat ha-shomrim* concerning what happened to the third cow is wrapped within that structure. The Gemara asks whether this might be a case of *heilech*: since these are physical animals being returned, would not the admitted cow constitute *heilech*, and yet the *shevua* still applies?

### Pikadon vs Loan

This distinction is highlighted: a *pikadon*, a deposit of an actual physical object, is by its nature *heilech* when the *shomer* acknowledges it, because the object is right there. A loan, by contrast, is typically not *heilech*, since money can be spent and is not presumed present. Yet even in this scenario, the Gemara holds the *shevua* to be valid.

### Dead Cows Scenario

The Gemara immediately deflects this reading. *Lo* — this is not a *heilech* case. The actual scenario is: the bailor says, "I gave you three cows and all three died due to your negligence — pay me." The *shomer* responds: one cow you fabricated, I never received three, only two (*lo hayu devarim me'olam*); of the remaining two, one died by genuine accident (*ones*), and for that I claim exemption via *shevuat ha-shomrim*; and one died by my negligence (*peshia*), for which I concede I must pay. This is a *modeh be-miktzas* — he admits liability for one, denies one altogether — but not a *heilech*: he is not handing back a live cow, he is admitting that a cow died due to his negligence and that he owes money. *Lav heilech hu* — it is not *heilech*.

---

## Rabbi Chiya II

### Edim Testimony

The Gemara now turns to Rabbi Chiya's first teaching — distinct from the *heilech* principle — which concerns the role of *edim* in creating an obligation equivalent to *modeh be-miktzas*. The *braisa* of Aviha de-Rabbi Aptoriki relates directly to this. The case: Reuven says to Shimon, "You owe me a hundred," and Shimon replies, "I owe you nothing." Witnesses then testify that Shimon is in fact obligated in fifty. The *braisa* raises the question of whether this should obligate Shimon in a *shevua* on the remaining fifty, treating the witnesses' confirmation of fifty as the functional equivalent of a *modeh be-miktzas*.

The *braisa* answers in the negative, citing the *pasuk*: *al kol aveda asher yomar ki hu zeh* — "regarding any lost object that he shall say, 'this is the one.'" From *asher yomar* — "that he shall say" — the *braisa* derives: *al hoda'as piv atah mechayvo ve'ee atah mechayvo al hoda'as edim* — you obligate him based on his own admission, not based on the testimony of witnesses.

### Edim vs Admission

This appears to be a direct contradiction of Rabbi Chiya, who holds that *edim* do create a *modeh be-miktzas* obligation. The Gemara dismisses the contradiction with a foundational point: *Rabbi Chiya tanna hu u'palig* — Rabbi Chiya was himself a *tanna*, among the last of that generation, and possesses the authority to dispute a *braisa*.

But the Gemara presses further: the *braisa* does not merely assert a ruling — it derives it from a *pasuk*. Surely a *pasuk* cannot simply be overridden? The Gemara responds: the *pasuk* of *ki hu zeh* establishes the obligation of *modeh be-miktzas* — it does not necessarily exclude *edim*. Rabbi Chiya reads the *pasuk* as generating the *modeh be-miktzas* obligation and then constructs a *kal va-chomer*: if when you yourself admit to part, you are obligated in a *shevua* on the remainder, then certainly when witnesses — who have no personal stake in the matter and whose testimony carries great weight — oblige you in part, you should be obligated in a *shevua* as well.

Aviha de-Rabbi Aptoriki, by contrast, reads both words *hu* and *zeh* in the *pasuk ki hu zeh* as limiting terms. One limits the application to a genuine *modeh be-miktzas* — partial admission of the very claim being made. The other limits it to cases where the defendant himself speaks (*asher yomar*), excluding cases where *edim* do the obligating.

### Chitim/Se'orim

Rabbi Chiya reads those two limiting terms differently. He agrees that one is needed to establish the basic principle of *modeh be-miktzas*. But he uses the second limiting word to address a different case: *modeh she-lo mimin ha-tana'ah* — an admission that does not correspond to the substance of the claim. The case is illustrated by the *mishnah*: if Reuven claimed that Shimon owes him a measure of wheat, and Shimon admits to owing a measure of barley — which is worth less — is that a *modeh be-miktzas*? The admission is of something less valuable, but it is not the same item being claimed. Rabbi Chiya says this is not a valid *modeh be-miktzas*, using the word *zeh* in the *pasuk* as the exclusion.

Rabban Gamliel disagrees, ruling that such a case is *chayav*: the claimant demanded something worth a hundred and the defendant admitted to something worth fifty — that is partial admission and partial denial, regardless of whether the item itself matches. Aviha de-Rabbi Aptoriki, who uses *zeh* to exclude *edim*, would presumably hold that the *chitim/se'orim* case does not require its own exclusion. Rabbi Chiya, who needs *zeh* for *chitim/se'orim*, derives the *edim* exclusion via *kal va-chomer* — and then, following Rabban Gamliel, rejects the *kal va-chomer* and retains the *edim* obligation.

---

## Shepherd Case

### Theft Evidence

The Gemara now presents an actual case that brings together Rabbi Chiya's teachings. There was a shepherd whom the flock's owners did not trust. Every day, when entrusting him with the animals, they arranged for witnesses to observe the handoff — noting exactly how many sheep he received, much as one marks scratches on a rental car. Tosafos adds that the witnesses were also necessary to confirm that the *pikadon* had in fact been received, lest the shepherd later claim he had already returned the animals.

One day, *chad yoma*, the owners could not find witnesses and handed over the sheep without them. At the end of that day, the shepherd denied everything: *lo hayu devarim me'olam* — you never gave me any sheep. Witnesses then came forward and testified that they had seen him consuming two of the sheep. The owners claimed ten sheep; the shepherd denied everything; witnesses established his liability for two.

### Shevua Question

Rabbi Zeira poses the question: *im isa le-Rabbi Chiya kamaisa* — if we rule in accordance with Rabbi Chiya's first teaching, that *edim* obligating a defendant in part creates the same structure as *modeh be-miktzas*, then the shepherd should be obligated in a *shevua* on the remaining eight sheep. *Mishtava a-shara* — let him swear regarding the others.

### Gazel Invalid

Abaye objects immediately. *Gazlan hu* — the witnesses have proven that he stole. A *gazlan* whose theft is established by testimony is *pasul* to take a *shevua* — his oath cannot be relied upon. So the shepherd is not in a position to swear at all.

### Shekenegdo Nishba

Rabbi Zeira clarifies: *shekenegdo kamina* — that is precisely the point. The shepherd is indeed obligated in a *shevua* as a result of the *modeh be-miktzas* structure created by the witnesses' testimony. But since he cannot take that *shevua* — because he is a proven *gazlan* — the principle of *shekenegdo nishba ve-notel* applies: the opposing party, the owners, take the *shevua* in his stead and collect. The owners swear that there were indeed ten sheep and collect accordingly.

### Takanta vs Torah

The Gemara raises a further point. Even without Rabbi Chiya's ruling, one might argue that the shepherd is obligated in a *shevua* by virtue of Rav Nachman's principle that even a *kofer ha-kol* — one who denies everything — is required to take a *shevuat heiset*, a rabbinic oath. If so, even absent a Torah-level *modeh be-miktzas* obligation, the shepherd would be required to swear, he could not, and the owners could swear and collect.

The Gemara rejects this: *shevuat de-Rav Nachman takanta hi* — the *shevuat heiset* is purely a rabbinic enactment, not a Torah-level obligation. The underlying logic of Rav Nachman's enactment is to pressure the defendant into not making a false denial, by ensuring that at minimum he must back up his denial with an oath. But the principle of *shekenegdo nishba ve-notel* — the opposing party swearing and collecting — applies only where the original obligation to swear is rooted in Torah law. *Ve-takanta le-takanta lo avdinan* — we do not layer one rabbinic enactment upon another. It would be one thing to require the *kofer ha-kol* to take a rabbinic oath; it is another thing entirely to say that because he cannot take that rabbinic oath, his opponent now swears and collects. That second step goes beyond what the rabbinic enactment was designed to accomplish.

The broader principle here is important: a Torah-level *shevua* serves as a genuine mechanism of exemption — the *shomer* or defendant needs the oath to free himself from liability, and if he cannot make it, the logic of shifting the oath to the other side follows naturally. A rabbinic oath, by contrast, is a deterrent tool, and its non-performance does not automatically empower the claimant in the same way.

Tosafos raises an adjacent question: sometimes when a person cannot take a required *shevua*, we say *shekenegdo nishba ve-notel* — the other side swears and collects; yet other times we say *mitech she-eino yachol lishava meshalem* — because you cannot swear, you automatically pay, without the other side swearing at all. What distinguishes these two outcomes? Tosafos offers two answers. First: when someone is categorically *pasul* for *shevua* — as a *gazlan* whose disqualification is permanent — applying the rule that he simply pays whenever he is obligated in a *shevua* would expose him to endless exploitation. Anyone could manufacture a *shevua* obligation against him and he would have to pay without recourse. To protect him, we require the opposing party to themselves take the *shevua* first. Second: where the *gazlan* is willing to take the *shevua* but the court refuses to accept it — because his credibility is disqualified — the opposing party must swear and collect, since the *gazlan* did not choose to forgo his oath. Where, by contrast, someone is simply unwilling or unable to swear due to uncertainty about the facts, the alternative to taking the oath is paying — one who opts out of the *shevua* accepts the financial consequence.

### Ro'eh Status

A further question arises. Why was the shepherd's *shevua* disqualification grounded in the witnessed proof of theft rather than simply in his status as a *ro'eh*? Rav Yehuda teaches: *stam ro'eh pasul* — a generic shepherd, absent information to the contrary, is presumed disqualified, because shepherds routinely graze their flocks on others' land and are thereby presumed to be *gazlanim*. Should not that blanket presumption have sufficed to disqualify him from the outset?

The Gemara resolves the tension: *ha d'didi, ha d'alma* — the presumption of *stam ro'eh pasul* applies when the shepherd grazes his own sheep on others' land, since he directly benefits from the theft. When he is watching someone else's sheep, however, the assumption is reversed: *chazaka ein adam chotei ve-lo lo* — people do not sin when they themselves derive no benefit. A shepherd watching another person's flock will not graze those animals on land that is not his, since he gains nothing from it. Were we to assume otherwise, it would be prohibited to ever entrust one's animals to a *ro'eh*, in violation of *lifnei iver lo titein michshol*. The fact that we routinely do so demonstrates that the working presumption is that a *ro'eh* watching others' flocks is not a *gazlan*.

Accordingly, in the case at hand, the shepherd's disqualification from taking a *shevua* was not automatic from his status as a *ro'eh* watching others' sheep. It required the positive evidence of witnesses testifying that he had consumed two of the flock. Once that proof was established, he became a proven *gazlan*, and Rabbi Chiya's rule — that witnesses obligating in part create a *modeh be-miktzas* structure — meant he was obligated in a *shevua* on the remainder, which, because he could not take it, shifted to the owners.

---

## Tallit Shevua

### No Less Half

The Gemara now returns to the *mishnah* at the opening of the tractate. Two people come before the court each holding a *tallis*, each claiming it is entirely theirs. The *mishnah* rules: divide it, and each one takes a *shevua* with the formulation *she-ein lo vah pachos mi-chetzi* — that he has no less than half.

### Has Something

The Gemara probes the precise meaning of this oath. *Al d'is lei mishtava, o al d'leis lei mishtava?* — is he swearing regarding what he has or what he does not have? This is a subtle but important point. The formulation *ein li vah pachos mi-chetzi* — "what I have in this *tallis* is no less than half" — could technically be true even if he has nothing at all: if one has nothing, then what one has is certainly not less than half, because there is nothing to quantify in that direction. A person who owns zero of the *tallis* could truthfully say "what I have is no less than half" in the same way one might say an empty set has no members below any threshold.

To foreclose this reading, Rav Huna rules that the *shevua* must be formulated as: *shevua she-yeish li vah* — "I swear that I do have an ownership share in this *tallis*" — *ve-ein li vah pachos mi-chetzi* — "and what I have is no less than half." The oath thus consists of two components: an affirmative declaration of ownership, and a quantitative declaration about its scope.

### Beit Din Logic

The Gemara then asks a simpler question: why not just have each person swear to owning all of it, consistent with his actual claim? The answer: *umi yahavinan lei kullah* — the *beit din* is not going to give him all. If the claimant swears he owns the entire *tallis* and the court then awards him only half, the court's own credibility is undermined. It would appear that the court believed his oath — since it made him swear — and then acted contrary to it. The formulation of the *shevua* must be compatible with what the court will actually award.

### Own Claim

The alternative — having each person simply swear that he owns exactly half — is also problematic: *marea lei lediburei* — it forces him to contradict his own claim. He is claiming the entire *tallis*; having him swear that he owns exactly half compels him to take an oath directly at odds with what he genuinely believes and asserts.

### Limited Shevua

The resolution is elegant. The claimant declares: *kullah sheli* — I maintain that this *tallis* is entirely mine. *U-le-divreichem* — but since you, the court, do not accept that and will not award me the full *tallis*, I am prepared to take a *shevua* that I have no less than half. This is not a contradiction of his claim: "no less than half" is fully consistent with owning the whole. He does not concede that he has only half; he swears to a floor, not a ceiling. He refuses, however, to swear that he has exactly half, because that would be an oath that genuinely contradicts what he believes and asserts. The formulation of *she-ein lo vah pachos mi-chetzi* thus threads the needle: it is compatible with the court's award, it does not undermine the claimant's own position, and — per Rav Huna's addition — it affirmatively asserts ownership, eliminating the loophole of swearing truthfully while owning nothing.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 6

## Purpose of Shvuah

### Oath's necessity

The Gemara on 6a, roughly fifteen lines down at the word *pachot*, opens with a striking question: *ve-khi mei'achar she-zeh tofes ve-omed ve-zeh tofes ve-omed, shvuah zu lama?* If this one is grabbing onto the garment and that one is grabbing onto it, each should have a presumption of being a half-owner — why is a *shvuah* needed at all? This question differs from the inquiry at the opening of the *masechet*, which asked why in certain configurations an oath is *absent*. Here the Gemara asks the inverse: what is the purpose of imposing an oath when the facts of the case seem to speak for themselves? Each party is holding on and claiming ownership, and that physical possession should of itself create a *chazakah*. Why must they additionally be made to swear?

### Preventive takkanah

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *shvuah zo takanat chachamim hi shelo yehei kol echad ve-echad holech ve-tokef be-talito shel chaveiro ve-omer sheli hu.* The oath is not primarily an evidentiary device aimed at clarifying what actually occurred; rather, it is a *takkanat chachamim* — a preventive enactment. The Rabbis were concerned that without it, anyone could simply grab another's garment, claim ownership, and thereby obtain at least half. The knowledge that one will be required to make a formal oath is meant either to deter the act in the first place or, once in court, to induce the dishonest claimant to withdraw.

### Thief & oath

This explanation immediately raises a deeper problem, one that was introduced at the beginning of the *masechet* in a different register. The early Gemara had emphasized that a *shvuah* is effective because a person who is rationalizing — telling himself a self-serving story about why he deserves the money — will be forced to confront the falsity of his claim the moment he must state it unequivocally under oath. But here the concern is different: we are afraid not of a rationalizer but of someone who would knowingly and brazenly grab another's property. Will an oath restrain such a person?

## Oath & knowing thief

### Gemara's question

The Gemara now presses this directly: *ve-neima migo de-chashid amamona, chashid nami ashvuata* — if someone is suspect with respect to monetary matters, with respect to theft, should he not equally be suspect for swearing falsely? What good will a *shvuah* do for a person who, in his own mind, knows he is stealing?

### Migo principle

The Gemara answers: *lo amrinan migo de-chashid amamona chashid ashvuata.* We do not say that because one is suspect for monetary wrongdoing he is therefore suspect for false oath-taking. The principle is stated clearly: suspicion of monetary transgression does not carry over into suspicion regarding *shvuah*. The reasoning behind this principle is taken up immediately in the next section.

## Purpose of Shvuah (II)

### Tosafot reasoning

Tosafot explains the rationale for this principle with two distinct arguments. The first is that a false oath is of exceptional gravity. As Tosafot notes with reference to Yoma, when God declared *lo tisa et shem Hashem Elokecha la-shav* and followed it with *ki lo yenakeh Hashem et asher yisa et shemo la-shav* — that God will not cleanse the one who takes His name falsely — the whole world shook. The terror attending a false *shvuah* is of a categorically different order than the discomfort of a monetary transgression. This reflects a broader and, it must be said, somewhat troubling phenomenon: people are often far more scrupulous about ritual matters than about interpersonal and monetary ones. A person might refuse to eat without a reliable *hechsher* and yet feel no compunction about stealing. Tosafot's first answer speaks precisely to this asymmetry — the weight of a *shvuah* reaches people even when monetary prohibitions do not.

Tosafot's second answer is also significant: the *shvuah* can be effective specifically when the person has not yet fully committed to the act. We are dealing with someone who is in the process of making a dishonest claim; the requirement to take a formal oath intervenes at a decision point, before the transgression is complete, and at that stage it may induce him to back down. This is distinct from the case of someone who has already been proven to be a *gazlan* in the past — like the shepherd discussed on the previous *daf* — who is disqualified from taking oaths precisely because there is no longer a decision point at which the oath can intervene. Once a person has fully committed to being a *gazlan*, the oath provides no lever. But when the person is still, so to speak, in motion, the oath may stop him.

So to summarize: a *shvuah* can be effective for a knowing would-be thief either because people generally regard false oaths as far weightier than monetary transgressions, or more specifically because the oath reaches the person before he has fully crossed the line into confirmed *gazlanut*.

## Oath & knowing thief (II)

### Modeh b'miktzat

The Gemara now explores whether the effectiveness of a *shvuah* in cases of potential dishonesty can be demonstrated from established law. It raises the case of *modeh b'miktzat*: the Torah itself (*hai d'amar Rachmana modeh b'miktzas hatana yishava*) mandates an oath when a defendant admits to part of a claim — say, fifty out of a hundred — and denies the rest. If we were to say that someone who lies about money is thereby suspect for false oaths, the entire institution of *modeh b'miktzat* would collapse: why impose an oath on someone who is already lying? The Gemara deflects this, however: the case of *modeh b'miktzat* involves rationalization, not brazen theft. Rabba's famous psychological explanation applies — *ishtamutei ka mishtamit* — the defendant is not really a thief; he is buying time, hoping to gather funds. He wants to pay but cannot, so he denies part of the debt. His *shvuah* is effective precisely because he is rationalizing rather than knowingly stealing, and therefore he will not swear falsely to something he knows to be a lie.

### Loan vs. deposit

The Gemara presses on, noting that Rav Idi bar Avin said in the name of Rav Chisda: one who denies a monetary loan and is proven to be lying remains *kasher* as a witness, while one who denies a *pikadon* (deposit) and is proven to be lying is disqualified — *pasul le-edut*. This distinction is crucial. Denying a loan, even if dishonest, does not constitute a fully realized act of theft in terms of what it does to one's moral character, because the defendant can rationalize that he is only delaying payment and intends to pay eventually. Denying a *pikadon*, by contrast, is a genuine act of *gzel* — there is no analogous rationalization, because the object was entrusted to you and you have no legitimate claim to it.

This raises the question: if a *shvuah* is administered in cases involving a *pikadon* — as Rami bar Chama taught, the four types of *shomrim* require both partial denial and partial admission before an oath is taken — why should that oath be effective if we are potentially dealing with a knowing thief? The Gemara answers that even in a *pikadon* case there can be a rationalization. The *shomer* who denies having the animal may tell himself: *mishtachna leganav ve-atfisna lei* — I will find the thief who stole it and recover it. Or: *inami mishtachna lei ba-agam u-masina lei* — perhaps the animal wandered off into the marsh and I will bring it back. Rather than admit negligence, the *shomer* prefers to say the animal is gone entirely, buying time while he tries to locate it. So even in *pikadon* cases the door to rationalization is not fully closed, and the oath retains its function.

The Gemara then tightens this further: if even in *pikadon* cases there is possible rationalization, why is one who denies a *pikadon* and is proven to lie *pasul le-edut*? The answer is that the disqualification applies specifically when witnesses testify that *at the very moment* the defendant denied possessing the object, *ito pikadon be-veiteh* — it was in his house. There is no room for rationalization if witnesses establish that he knew exactly where the object was and still denied it. In all ordinary cases, however, since we cannot rule out the possibility that the defendant is rationalizing, we impose the oath because it will be effective for the rationalizer even if it would not deter a confirmed knowing thief.

The Gemara proceeds through further cases. Rav Huna rules that when a *shomer* offers payment and claims the object is no longer in his possession, we nonetheless administer an oath — *shvuah she-einah bi-reshuto* — that he is not concealing it. And Rav Nachman rules that a *shomeret* who completely denies a debt must take a *shvuat heset*. In each case the question arises: why not say *migo de-chashid amamona chashid ashvuata*? And in each case the Gemara either finds a rationalization available to the defendant or concludes with the flat ruling that the principle simply does not apply — *lo amrinan migo de-chashid amamona chashid ashvuata* — and that the effectiveness of the *shvuah* is not undermined by the possibility that the person is a knowing wrongdoer.

The case of the two workers and the storeowner (a case introduced earlier in the *masechet*) is also noted here. The employer tells the storeowner to feed his workers; the storeowner says he fed them, the workers say he did not, and both swear and collect. One of them is certainly lying. There is little obvious rationalization available — either the storeowner fed them or he did not — yet both oaths are administered and both are honored. Similarly, Rav Sheshet's ruling that a *shomer* must take three oaths — that he was not negligent, that he did not make personal use of the object, and that it is not in his possession — raises the same issue with the third oath: if it really is in his closet, he is a knowing thief, and why would the oath help? The answer comes in the Gemara's concluding declaration: the principle is that we simply do not say that suspicion of monetary wrongdoing renders a person suspect for false oath-taking.

## Abaye on rationalization

### Old debt claim

Abaye does not dispute the practical conclusion but offers a different theoretical framing. Rather than saying that a *shvuah* can work even for a knowing thief, Abaye argues that in practice people can almost always rationalize. The specific rationalization he invokes is: *chaishinan shema milva yeshana yesh lo alav* — we are concerned that perhaps the person grabbing the garment believes the other party owes him an old debt. A person sees David walking around in a fine coat and thinks: David owes me money from ten years ago; he has forgotten about it, I cannot prove it, so I am entitled to seize this coat as payment. This rationalization is always available. Whatever the context, the would-be thief can construct a story in which he is not really stealing but rather collecting what is owed to him.

### Specificity matters

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *ei hachi, nishkalei belo shvuah* — if you are only rationalizing because you genuinely believe the debt exists, then the oath should be worthless; just let him take it without an oath, since in his mind it is legitimately his. If the rationalization is sufficient to make him think the object is his, he will simply swear that it is his and proceed. The Gemara therefore refines the point: *ela chaishinan shema safek milva yeshana yesh lo alav* — we are not concerned that he is certain of an old debt, but only that he has a vague, uncertain recollection that perhaps he is owed something. The doubt is the key. Because he is not certain, he will not take a firm oath that the object is unambiguously his; the doubt in his own mind restrains him from swearing definitively.

### Rav Sheshet

But the Gemara presses again: *velo amina tafas mamona mi-safek, mishtava nami mi-safek?* If a person will grab property on the basis of a mere doubt — because he might be owed money — why will he not swear on the basis of that same doubt? The answer comes from Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi: *parishi inshi mi-safek shvuah velo parishi mi-safek mamona* — people will refrain from even a doubtful oath but will not refrain from taking doubtful money. The reason: *mamona ita be-chazarah, shvuah leita be-chazarah* — money can be returned. If I later realize I was wrong, I can give the money back and make amends. But a false oath, once spoken, cannot be unsaid or undone. The irreversibility of the spoken word — an insight one student poignantly connected to interpersonal speech as well — is what makes even a potentially false *shvuah* something people are more reluctant to risk.

This is a profound observation about human moral psychology, especially apt before Rosh Hashanah: in the realm of *bein adam la-chavero*, people routinely give themselves latitude, telling themselves that wrongs can be corrected. But when an act is inherently irreversible, people exercise greater caution. Practically speaking, there is not a large gap between the position of the anonymous Gemara and that of Abaye. Both agree that *shvuot* are effective across a very wide range of cases. The difference is theoretical: the earlier view holds that even a person who knows he is a thief will be deterred by a *shvuah*, while Abaye holds that people can nearly always construct some rationalization, making the deterrence possible without needing to posit that a knowing thief fears a false oath. In practice, the coverage is essentially the same.

## Yanking the object

### Rabbi Zeira's question

Having established the purpose and mechanics of the *shvuah* in the standard case of two people holding a garment, the Gemara now introduces a variation. Rabbi Zeira poses the question: *takpah echad befaneinu, mahu?* — if, while both are holding the *tallit* before the court, one party yanks it out of the other's hands, what is the law? Does the person who now holds the entire garment gain a superior presumption, or do we disregard the yanking?

### Silence interpretation

The Gemara initially frames this as a question about how to interpret the behavior of the party whose hands were emptied. *Ei deshatik* — if he said nothing after his companion yanked it away — perhaps *oduyei odei lei*, his silence is an implicit concession that the object is his companion's after all. But *ve-ei dekatzavach* — if he is actively protesting — then what could he have done? He was physically overpowered. The court saw the entire episode. Why should he need to say anything? He might reasonably conclude that the *beit din* witnessed what happened and there is no need to protest. The Gemara complicates this further: *lo tzricha deshatik me-ikara vehadar tzavach* — the real question is where he was initially silent and then began to protest. Does the initial silence indicate concession, with the subsequent protest too late? Or does the fact that he eventually protested make clear retroactively that the silence was not a concession — *savar ha chazu lei rabanan*, he assumed the *beit din* saw exactly what happened and he had no need to shout?

### Rav Nachman braita

Rav Nachman brings a *braita* to address the question. The *braita* states: *she-shneihem adukin bah* — the rule of splitting applies when both are holding onto it with equal grasp. But *aval hayta tallis yotzeit mi-tachat yado shel echad meihem* — if the garment is emerging from under the hand of only one of them, *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* — the other must bring proof. This *braita* seems to be relevant to Rabbi Zeira's question, because the scenario where the garment is under one person's hand must be telling us something about a case where the situation was not so from the outset.

### Braita ambiguity

The Gemara immediately asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case in this *braita*? If it simply means that one person is holding the garment and a stranger walks up claiming it is his, that is obvious — *peshita* — of course the bystander must prove his claim; there is nothing novel there. The *braita* must therefore be addressing the case *she-takaf echad befaneinu* — where they were initially both holding on, but now only one is. This would seem to resolve Rabbi Zeira's question in favor of the one now holding.

### Return with possession

The Gemara deflects this reading. *Hacha b'mai askinan* — the *braita* is not discussing that scenario at all. Rather: both were holding, the court told them to go divide the garment (*zilu palgu*), they left, and when they returned, one was holding it alone. Now each tells a different story: one says the other conceded to him; the other says the first one agreed to buy his half and has not paid. In that situation, *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* — the one not holding must prove his claim. But the Gemara explains why: *ad hashta chashadat lei be-gazlan, ve-hashta mograt lei be-lo sahadi* — until this point you were accusing him of theft, and yet now you are claiming you sold him your half without any witnesses? The inference from that behavior is that the holder came by the garment legitimately. This scenario, therefore, does not speak to the case of yanking in front of *beit din*.

### Edge holding

A further reading is offered: *ve-iba'is eima*, the *braita* addresses a case where from the outset only one person was holding properly while the other was gripping only *be-siruchei* — by the fringes or threads, not the garment itself. *Ve-afilu le-Sumchos de-amar mamon ha-mutal be-safek cholkin belo shvuah* — even Sumchos, who is willing to split any disputed property without an oath, *modeh Sumchos* would agree that *sirkha lav klum hi* — holding by mere threads or fringes counts for nothing. The question of Rabbi Zeira thus remains unresolved.

## Verbal vs. physical

### Dedication question

Rabbi Zeira's unresolved question generates a further inquiry through the *im timtzi lomar* framework. Were one to conclude that yanking the garment in front of *beit din* does not change the presumption — that we treat the parties as still equally *muchzak* — then, by analogy, if Reuven were to declare the *tallit* dedicated to the Temple (*makdish*) while Shimon is still holding it, that declaration should equally be without effect; one cannot consecrate property in which another party holds a *chazakah*. Conversely, were one to conclude that yanking does work — that Reuven who yanks becomes fully *muchzak* — then the question arises whether a verbal declaration of *hekdesh*, without any physical act, could achieve the same result.

### Verbal transfer

The basis for thinking it might is the principle *amirato le-gavo'ah ki-mesirato la-hedyot dami* — a verbal transfer to the Divine is halachically equivalent to physical handing over to a private person. If so, Reuven's declaration of *hekdesh* should be *ke-man de-takfah dami* — equivalent to his having physically seized the garment. And just as physical seizure would make Shimon's silence into a concession, so too his silence in the face of the verbal declaration might constitute a concession.

### Possession requirement

The counterargument is equally compelling. Whatever power words have in the realm of *hekdesh*, the verse teaches otherwise from the case of a house: *ish ki yakdish et beito kodesh, mah beito bi-reshuto, af kol bi-reshuto* — just as a man's house must be in his own possession for him to consecrate it, so too any object must be in his possession. As long as Shimon is physically holding the garment, it is under his control and Reuven's words have no purchase over it. Shimon has no obligation to respond to a verbal declaration that, by law, can have no effect on something he is holding. His silence is therefore meaningless. The question remains unresolved.

## Bathhouse case

### Dedication to Temple

The Gemara now brings a concrete case that directly engages the question of verbal *hekdesh* over disputed property. Two people were disputing ownership of a certain bathhouse. *Hai amar didi hu ve-hai amar didi hu* — each one claimed it as his own. Then one of them, apparently out of frustration at the impasse, got up and declared the entire bathhouse dedicated to the Temple: *kam chad mineihu ve-akdeshah*.

### Sacred concern

Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Oshaya, and all the other Rabbis in the vicinity stopped using the bathhouse, reasoning that it might now be *hekdesh* — sacred property of the Temple — and using it would constitute a misappropriation of consecrated property.

### Rav Chisda query

Rabbi Oshaya said to Rabba: when you go to see Rav Chisda in Kafri, ask him what the *halacha* is with this bathhouse, for we need to know whether we may use it. As Rabba passed through Sura on his way, he encountered Rav Hamnuna and posed the question to him there.

## Safek bechor

### Taharos reference

Rav Hamnuna replied: the answer is already in a *mishnah* — not the *mishnah* of our chapter, but a *mishnah* in Taharos, in the tractate dealing with doubtful firstborn animals.

### Bechor cases

The *mishnah* discusses *safek bechoros* — animals or children whose firstborn status is uncertain. With respect to a human *bechor*: if a woman had a miscarriage and it is unknown whether forty days had passed since conception, the next child's status as *bechor* for *pidyon ha-ben* is in doubt. With respect to animals: if it is unknown whether a cow had previously given birth, the next calf might or might not be a *bechor*. The *mishnah* covers both *tahor* animals (cattle and sheep) and *tamei* animals (donkeys, which require redemption with a sheep). In all such cases, *echad bechor adam ve-echad bechor behemah, bein tehorah bein teme'ah* — the law is the same.

### Hamotzi rule

The *mishnah* rules: *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah*. If the *kohen* claims the animal is a *bechor* and belongs to him, he must prove it. The owner retains the animal by default. Whoever wishes to extract property from another bears the burden of proof.

### Priest grabbing

Now the *mishnah* goes further: even if the *kohen* grabs the animal, it must be taken back from him. The *braita* elaborates: *asurin be-gizah ve-avodah* — the owner who retains the animal may not shear it and may not put it to work. Why not? Because even though the *kohen* cannot prove his claim and therefore cannot take it, the animal might genuinely be a *bechor*, and a *bechor* may not be shorn or worked by its owner. The owner is caught in a paradox: he keeps the animal but cannot fully use it.

### Paradox of ownership

This is a striking halachic configuration: from the perspective of *dinei mamonot*, the owner wins — *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* — and the *kohen* cannot take the animal. But from the perspective of *issurim*, the animal is a *safek bechor* and must be treated accordingly. The owner may wait for a blemish to develop and then slaughter and eat the animal, or bring it as a *korban* if it is unblemished — but he cannot shear it, work it, or otherwise treat it as ordinary livestock. The *mammon* question and the *issur* question are resolved on entirely separate tracks.

## Mammon vs. issur

### Rabba's answer

Rabba addresses the seeming tension. He states clearly that *tokfo kohen motziin oto mi-yado* — if a *kohen* grabs the animal, we take it back from him. The *hamotzi mechavero* principle is a definitive ruling in the owner's favor: the *kohen* cannot grab and keep. This is a full *psak* that the animal belongs to its owner for all *mammon* purposes.

### Sanctity principle

Nevertheless, *kedushah ba'ah me-eleha shani* — the sanctity of a *bechor* is categorically different. It does not derive from the *kohen*'s ownership; it inheres in the animal itself by virtue of being the firstborn. For that reason, even after a clear *psak* that the animal belongs to its owner and even after the *kohen* is turned away, the animal retains its status as a *safek bechor* and the prohibitions on shearing and working remain in force. The *issur* dimension is entirely independent of who wins the monetary dispute.

### Parallel case

This separation of *mammon* and *issur* extends further: if one were to take the animal from one owner and give it to another owner entirely, both the monetary transfer and the *kedushah* question would be resolved on their own terms. The monetary question follows whoever holds it under proper title; the *kedushah* question follows the reality of whether the animal is in fact a *bechor*, regardless of who owns it at any given moment.

## Tokfo kohen

### Ma'aser proof

Rav Chanina now offers a different proof to Rabba in support of the position that *tokfo kohen motziin oto mi-yado* — that the *kohen* cannot grab and keep. The proof comes from the laws of *ma'aser behemah*, the animal tithe. The *mishnah* states: *ha-sfekot nichnasin la-dir le-hit'aser* — doubtful animals enter the pen to be tithed. What are these doubtful animals? They are sheep that were given as redemption for a *safek bechor* donkey. A donkey whose firstborn status is uncertain must be redeemed with a sheep; that sheep then belongs to the *kohen*, unless the donkey was not actually a *bechor*, in which case the sheep belongs to its original owner. The owner has custody by default. These sheep, whose ownership is uncertain, are nonetheless counted together with the owner's other newborn animals for purposes of *ma'aser behemah*.

### Safek animals

The process of *ma'aser behemah* requires the owner to gather all animals born in a given season and have them pass single-file through a gate; every tenth one is set apart as *ma'aser*. The question is whether the *safek* animals — whose status as belonging to the owner or to the *kohen* is unresolved — may be included in this counting.

### Tithe problem

Rav Chanina's argument is: if one were to say that *tokfo kohen ein motziin oto mi-yado* — that if the *kohen* grabs such an animal he is allowed to keep it — then these animals would be genuinely uncertain in their ownership in a way that should prevent them from being included in the *ma'aser* count. If the *kohen* could legitimately seize them at any moment, their inclusion in my *ma'aser* pool means I am potentially using property that might not be mine to fulfill a religious obligation — *nimtza zeh poter mamono be-mamono shel kohen* — I am exempting my animals through another man's property.

### Exactly ten

Abaye refines the argument. He concedes the force of the concern but notes that the proof from *ma'aser* works only in a specific case: *hacha be-mai askinan ke-gon de-leit lei ela tishah ve-hu* — where the owner has exactly nine unambiguous animals plus the one doubtful *safek* animal, making ten in total. In that configuration, *mimanafshach* — either way it works: if the doubtful animal belongs to the owner, he has ten and is obligated in *ma'aser*, and the animal participates normally in the tithe; if the doubtful animal belongs to the *kohen*, the owner has only nine and is not obligated in *ma'aser* at all. There is no case, then, where he is using another's property to exempt his own. But Abaye then retracts this position.

## Jumping sheep

### Interruption case

Abaye withdraws his own defense of the *mimanafshach* argument and declares: *safeka lav bar asura hu* — a doubtful animal cannot be used for *ma'aser* even where a *mimanafshach* analysis would seem to cover all outcomes. He derives this from another *mishnah*: *kafatz echad min ha-menuyim le-tochan, kulam peturim* — if one of the animals that had already been counted jumps back into the pen and becomes mixed in with the uncounted animals, all are exempt from *ma'aser*. The counting process is disrupted because one may not count the same animal twice, and since it is unknown which animal jumped back in, no further counting can proceed.

### Either-way objection

One might object: why not continue counting and apply a *mimanafshach* argument? If the next group of ten does not include the animal that jumped back in, the count is valid and the tenth is *ma'aser*. If it does include the jumped-in animal, then by the principle of *minyan ha-ra'uy* — the animals already counted were part of a valid, fit counting process — those animals are exempt even if the process was cut short. Either way, it would seem that the owner is covered.

### Minyan hara'uy

The principle of *minyan ha-ra'uy* holds that animals which passed through a valid counting process — one that was, at the moment of counting, fit to result in a completed *ma'aser* — are exempt from future counting even if the process was interrupted. Thus, animals counted before the disruption do not need to be re-entered into a future count; they participated in a *minyan ha-ra'uy* and are released from the obligation.

### Definite tenth

The Gemara's answer is decisive: *asiri vadai amar Rachmana, velo asiri safek* — the Torah requires a definite tenth, not a doubtful tenth. Even where a *mimanafshach* analysis would seem to guarantee that the outcome is always either fully valid or fully exempt, the Torah's requirement of *asiri* — definiteness — is not satisfied by doubt. Doubt, even doubt that is covered from all directions, does not produce the definitive tenth that *ma'aser behemah* requires.

### Definitive presumption

The conclusion that flows from this is directly relevant to the *tokfo kohen* question. Since a doubtful animal cannot serve as *ma'aser behemah* under any circumstances, and yet the *mishnah* teaches that these *safek* animals do enter the pen and are tithed, it must be that they are not genuinely doubtful from a *mammon* perspective at all. The ruling of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* is not merely a procedural holding that we stand aside and see who grabs what; it is a definitive *psak* that the animal belongs to its owner. And if the *kohen* grabs it, he does not keep it — *tokfo kohen motziin oto mi-yado*. The owner's presumption is real and complete, and the *ma'aser* process can proceed on the basis of that definitive ownership, not on the basis of doubt.

# Bava Metzia 7

*This shiur is dedicated to the memory of Maoz ben Eitan u-Varda Devora, zecher tzadik livracha, who fell defending Am Yisrael and Medinat Yisrael.*

---

## Hamotzi/Takfo Kohen

### Hamotzi Framework

Yesterday's discussion concluded with an important question about the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav harayah*: does it mean that in a case of doubt we simply throw up our hands as a *beit din* and decline to act — leaving the matter as an unresolved question mark — or does it mean that we are actually rendering a ruling, at least tentatively, that the object belongs to the person currently in possession? The practical difference is significant. If we are merely declining to intervene, then whoever manages to grab the disputed item next would be in the same position as the first holder, and the object could ping-pong back and forth indefinitely. But if we are actually ruling that the current possessor is the owner, then the other party who grabs it away would be required to return it.

### Takfo Kohen Principle

This is the question of *takfo kohen ein motzi'in miyado*. The *Gemara* concluded that we adopt the second position: we are indeed ruling, as a matter of *dinei mamonos*, that the object belongs to the person in whose hands it currently rests. If the other party were to seize it, he would be compelled to return it. This is distinct from the perspective of *issur*, however, where the matter may remain unresolved — which is why, in the relevant cases, the object would still retain *kedushas bechor*.

### Ma'aser Behemah Cases

With that framework established, the *Gemara* turns to the specific scenario that had been under discussion: what is the case of *sfekos* in which one takes *ma'aser behemah* from an animal of doubtful status? *Rav Achai mi-Difti* asks *Ravina*: what exactly is the scenario in which a *Yisrael* who has a doubtfully-firstborn animal in his possession would bring it together with his other animals and take *ma'aser behemah*?

One might suggest the case involves a *safek bechor* — an animal of doubtful firstborn status. But that presents an immediate problem: the Torah says the tenth animal shall be holy, and not something that is already holy. If the animal might already possess *kedushas bechor*, how could it be included among the others for purposes of *ma'aser*?

The answer is rather that the case involves *safek pidyon peter chamor* — a donkey of uncertain firstborn status that was redeemed with a sheep. In such a case, the sheep used for redemption does not carry *kedushas bechor*, even if the donkey was definitively a *peter chamor*; in that case, the sheep would merely be money owed to the *kohen*, without any intrinsic *kedusha*. Since the *Yisrael* is presumed to be the owner, and since either way the sheep carries no *kedusha*, it can be included among his flock and counted toward *ma'aser behemah*.

This is precisely the ruling of *Rav Nachman* in the name of *Rabba bar Avuha*: if a *Yisrael* has ten animals that were used to redeem ten doubtful *peter chamor* cases, he separates ten sheep and redeems each doubtful donkey with a sheep. He then takes *ma'aser behemah* from all ten sheep, and they are all his — the nine that remain after *ma'aser* are his, and the tenth that is designated *ma'aser behemah* also belongs to the owner. The *kohen* may have a monetary claim to some of these sheep, but since *hamotzi mechavero alav harayah* leaves the *Yisrael* as the presumed owner, and since there is no *kedusha* on the sheep at all, the *ma'aser* is valid. Crucially, this only works if we maintain that *takfo kohen ein motzi'in miyado* — that we are ruling the *Yisrael* is the presumed owner, not merely suspending judgment.

---

## Bathhouse Sanctification

### Bathhouse Overview

The *Gemara* now returns to a case that had been introduced earlier in the discussion: the *masuta*, the bathhouse, where one party had sanctified the property while the other remained silent. The question had been whether the act of sanctification functions like physically seizing the object, and whether the other party's silence constitutes an admission that the sanctifying party is the true owner. The *Gemara* now asks: *mai hava ala de-masuta* — what was the final outcome of that bathhouse case?

*Rav Chiya bar Avin* relates that a case of this kind came before *Rav Chisda*, who forwarded the question to *Rav Huna*, and *Rav Huna* resolved it.

### Rav Nachman Principle
