### Techila in Seifa

The *gemara* refines this analysis by zeroing in on the word *techila* — "originally" — which appears in the *seifa*, the latter clause of the *Mishnah*. The *seifa* addresses a case where Shimon picked up the object, already handed it over to Reuven, and then said: *ani zachiti ba techila* — "I originally acquired it for myself." The *gemara* asks: *techila b'seifa l'ma li?* Why does the *Mishnah* need to specify "originally" in this second case? It is self-evident that Shimon is not claiming to take it back *now* — he already gave it to Reuven. Obviously he means to say his *original* intent was to keep it. So why state it at all?

The *gemara* answers: *tana seifa l'gluyei reisha* — the *seifa* is formulated the way it is to illuminate the *reisha*. The word *techila* in the *seifa* signals that the entire legal framework revolves around the question of original intent. Consequently, in the *reisha* — where Shimon still holds the object — the case where Shimon can keep it is specifically where he claims his original intent was to keep it for himself. If his original intent was for Reuven, then Reuven acquired it the moment it was lifted, and Shimon may no longer unilaterally change course.

### Two Positions

This yields two rival readings of the *Mishnah*. The first holds that *magbiya metzia l'chaveiro kanah chaveiro* — the act does work — and the *Mishnah*'s permission for Shimon to keep the object rests entirely on his claim of *techila*, original intent for himself. If he had originally intended it for Reuven, Reuven owns it from the moment of lifting, and no subsequent change of mind by Shimon avails anything.

The second position — *magbiya metzia l'chaveiro lo kanah chaveiro* — holds that the act does not work at all. According to this reading, the *seifa*'s use of *techila* is not definitional for the *reisha*; rather, *tana seifa l'gluyei reisha d'lo amar techila*: the *seifa* spells out the word "originally" to draw a contrast with the *reisha*, where Shimon does *not* need to invoke original intent. Even if Shimon admits he originally lifted the object for Reuven, he may still keep it — because the act never worked in the first place. As long as he hasn't transferred it, nobody owns it yet, and he is free to take it for himself.

This debate also drew a student's observation that is philosophically significant: how can *kavana* — intention — override physical possession of an object that belongs to no one? The answer is that the act of acquisition is never purely physical; it is always a combination of a physical act and intent. Without intent to acquire, mere physical contact does not create *kinyan*. The general rule *chatzero shel adam koneh lo shelo midato* — one's yard acquires on one's behalf even without one's awareness — is itself a *chiddush*, resting on the presumption that a person would want to acquire whatever enters his domain. But that presumption of intent is precisely that — a presumption, which explicit contrary intent can override.

### Rav Nachman Position

The *gemara* now records the explicit ruling of Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda, who both state: *hamagbih metziah l'chaveiro lo kanah chaveiro* — acquiring a lost object on behalf of another does not work. The reason, they explain, is *havay tofes l'baal chov bimkom shechav l'acheirim*: the act is analogous to seizing a debtor's property for one creditor at the expense of others. When a debtor owes money to multiple people and a bystander grabs his property specifically for one of them, the others are injured. Since the act is not for one's own benefit, and since one has no independent right in the matter, the seizure does not take effect.

Rashi raises the question of whether appointing a *shaliach* — a formal agent — would change the analysis. His view is that it would: a properly designated *shaliach* can represent the principal's interests and the act would succeed. Tosafot, however, disagrees; even with formal agency, the problem remains, because one cannot arrogate to oneself the right to interfere with others' opportunities simply by virtue of an appointment. The *Mishnah*'s case — where the man on the horse sends Shimon — sounds like a form of *shlichut*, and yet the *gemara* treats it as raising the same fundamental question, which suggests that even *shlichut* may not be sufficient to overcome the *tofes l'baal chov* problem.

Tosafot further notes that it is logically possible to hold *tofes l'baal chov bimkom shechav l'acheirim lo kanah* while simultaneously holding *magbiya metzia l'chaveiro kanah chaveiro* — because the two cases are not identical. In the debt-seizure case, the person acting has no right to do so on his own behalf at all; he has no claim on the property. But by a *metzia*, he could have kept it for himself. The *gemara* articulates this distinction through the phrase *migo d'ei ba'ei zachi l'nafshei* — since I could have taken it for myself, perhaps that independent entitlement extends to allow me to take it for someone else.

Tosafot also engages a related case involving drawing water from a public well for another person, as it bears on *hilchos eiruvin*. According to Rabbeinu Tam, that case presents no problem of *magbiya metzia l'chaveiro* whatsoever, because there is plentiful water in the well and no identifiable person is being harmed by the act of drawing it — the *chav l'acheirim* concern simply does not materialize when there is no realistic injury to others. Additionally, Tosafot makes the conceptual observation that if the mechanism by which one may acquire for another is the *migo* — because one could have taken it for oneself — then the logical structure is that we view the acquirer as having first taken it for himself and then transferred it to the other person, rather than as having acquired directly on the other's behalf. This has practical consequences for *hilchos eiruvin*: the *techum* of the water would be defined by the person who drew it, not by the person for whom it was drawn.

---

## Po'el Metzia

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges Rav Nachman's position from a *baraita* concerning a *po'el* — a hired day laborer. The rule is *metzi'as po'el l'atzmo*: a laborer who finds a lost object while working keeps it for himself. This seems unproblematic when the laborer is working for himself. But the *baraita* specifies conditions under which the *metzia* belongs to the *ba'al habayis* — the employer — rather than to the laborer. If the employer hired him with the words *asei immi melacha hayom* — "do any work for me today" — then whatever the laborer finds belongs to the employer. This is effectively a case of *magbiya metzia l'chaveiro*: the laborer is acquiring on behalf of his employer. How, then, does this work if *magbiya metzia l'chaveiro lo kanah chaveiro*?

### Task Distinction

The *baraita* itself distinguishes between two formulations of employment. If the employer specified a particular task — *nachish immi hayom* (weed for me today) or *ador immi hayom* (plow for me today) — then at the moment the laborer picks up the diamond, he is not performing that task. His act of picking up the *metzia* lies outside the scope of his employment, and whatever he finds is his own. At most, the employer could claim compensation for the five minutes of work-time lost.

### Po'el Extension

But when the employer says *asei immi melacha hayom* — do any labor for me today — the laborer's entire workday is contracted to the employer. In that case, *yado k'yad ba'al habayis hu* — his hand is treated as the employer's hand. He is, in effect, an extension of the employer, and what he acquires he acquires for the employer. This is why the *metzia* belongs to the *ba'al habayis*. This arrangement is more than mere *shlichut*: there is an actual contractual relationship, a binding engagement, that makes the laborer's acquisitive act an act of the employer.

### Breaking Contract

The *gemara* immediately raises an apparent difficulty with this analysis. Rav states: *po'el yachol lachzor bo afilu bachatzi hayom* — a laborer can quit his job even in the middle of the day. If he can always unilaterally terminate the arrangement, how can he truly be considered an extension of the employer? Does not his retained autonomy demonstrate that he is never really subsumed under the employer's identity?

The *gemara* responds: *kol kamma d'lo hadar bei k'yad ba'al habayis hu* — as long as he has not in fact quit, he is still considered an extension of the employer. The right to exit the arrangement does not negate the arrangement while it subsists. These are two separate issues: *yado k'yad ba'al habayis* describes the status quo during active employment, while the right to break the contract is founded on an entirely independent reason — *ki hadar bei ta'ama achrina hu* — it rests on a different ground altogether.

### Ki Li Bnei Yisrael

That different ground is the verse *ki li bnei Yisrael avadim* — "for to Me the Children of Israel are servants" — which the *gemara* expounds: *avadai hem, velo avadim la'avadim* — they are My servants, not servants of servants. This is a powerful theological and moral statement: Halacha will not allow employment to become a form of servitude. Even while a laborer is fully engaged and is considered *k'yad ba'al habayis*, he retains the inviolable right to exit. This right is not a loophole or a technicality; it is a fundamental safeguard against the degradation of one person's labor being transformed into ownership over another person's will.

Tosafot adds a striking nuance: the laborer not only has the right to break the contract, but he holds the advantaged position in any renegotiation about compensation for the remaining time. This further demonstrates that the laborer is never fully subordinated, even during active employment.

### Rabbi Chiya Position

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yochanan, takes the opposite view on the core principle: *magbiya metzia l'chaveiro kanah chaveiro* — the act does work, and the other person does acquire. Rabbi Chiya must then explain how the *Mishnah* permits Shimon to keep the object. His answer does not require Shimon to have had original intent for himself.

### Delivery vs Possession

The key, says Rabbi Chiya, lies in the specific language used by the man on the horse. He said *tnei li* — "hand it to me" — not *zachei li* — "acquire it on my behalf." The instruction was to *deliver* the object, not to take *possession* of it for him. Acquisition and delivery are distinct acts. When Shimon picks up the object, he does so with the intent to convey it, not to vest title. Since there was no instruction to take possession, no *kinyan* was effected on Reuven's behalf at the moment of lifting. Shimon is therefore free to change his mind before actually handing it over. Once he does hand it over, however, the *kinyan* is complete and irrevocable. But had Reuven explicitly said *zachei li* — acquire it for me — and Shimon had that intention when he lifted it, then Reuven would own it from that moment, and Shimon could not retain it regardless.

This generates three possible scenarios: either *magbiya metzia l'chaveiro lo kanah chaveiro* (Rav Nachman's position, under which Shimon can always keep it before handing it over regardless of his stated intention); or *kanah chaveiro* but Shimon can keep it because he claims original intent for himself (*techila*); or *kanah chaveiro* but Shimon can keep it because the instruction was framed as a request to deliver, not to acquire.

### Tosafot Nuance

Returning to the *ki li bnei Yisrael avadim* discussion, Tosafot draws a careful line. Employment of one person by another is not prohibited; what is prohibited is transforming employment into *avdut* — servitude. The specific case of an *eved Ivri*, a Hebrew indentured servant, who cannot break the contract and cannot leave before the stipulated time without a formal *shtar shichrur* or the arrival of the Jubilee year — *that* is genuine *avdut*. Ordinary employment, even though it creates a relationship in which *yado k'yad ba'al habayis*, remains permissible precisely because the laborer retains the right to exit at any moment. That right is what prevents the quasi-subordination from crossing into morally objectionable territory. Tosafot therefore concludes: *mutar adam l'haskir atzmo* — it is permitted for a person to hire himself out — as long as the right of exit remains intact.

The *Gra*, in a marginal note, cites *Hagahot Maimoni* to the effect that it is forbidden to contract oneself out for more than three years, because even with the theoretical right to exit, a multi-year commitment constitutes a form of quasi-*avdut* that approaches the threshold of genuine servitude. The underlying tension — between the legitimate need for contracted labor and the theological insistence that no Israelite may become a slave to another human being — remains one of the richest moral themes the sugya opens up.

---

## Ra'ah Metzia

### Falling Not Kinyan

The *gemara* turns to another scenario involving a *metzia*. *Ra'ah metziah venafal aleha* — one sees a lost object and throws himself bodily upon it. Another person — smarter and quicker — reaches under him and physically takes the object away. The ruling is *zeh shehechezik bah zachah bah* — the one who physically grasped it acquires it. Falling on an object, however total the bodily contact, does not constitute a *kinyan*. *Kinyan* requires an affirmative act of taking possession — picking up the object, drawing it toward oneself, or the like. Simply placing one's weight on top of something confers nothing.

### Arba Amot Principle

The *gemara* now introduces a statement of Reish Lakish in the name of Abba Kohen Bardela: *arba amot shel adam konot lo bechol makom* — the four *amot* surrounding a person acquire on his behalf wherever he is. The concept rests on the idea of personal space: four *amot* is the halachically defined sphere of one's immediate surroundings, analogous in some ways to one's *chatzer*. If a lost object comes within that radius, the person acquires it without any additional physical act.

The *gemara* notes that this principle is invoked primarily in two contexts: finding lost objects, and *get* (divorce). Both will be elaborated. For lost objects, the intuitive purpose is to reduce conflict: if proximity confers ownership, there is at least a clear rule about who gets priority, reducing the likelihood of physical confrontation over a *metzia*.

### Taknat Rabanan

The *gemara* states explicitly: *takanat rabanan hi d'lo ati l'intzu'ei* — this is a rabbinic enactment to prevent fighting. A student nicely observed that the rule is not merely about who is first to find the object, but about preventing the kind of pile-up that would result if *kinyan* required actually picking it up. If two people are running toward the same object, the requirement of a physical *kinyan* act could generate real physical conflict. The *arba amot* principle cuts off the race earlier and with less danger — possession is established by proximity, making physical scrambling unnecessary.

---

## Arba Amot Challenges

### Pe'ah Challenge

Two challenges are leveled against the *arba amot* principle. Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef challenges from a *Mishnah* about *pe'ah*. The *Mishnah* records: *natal miktzat pe'ah v'zarak al ha-shear* — a person collected some of the *pe'ah* and then threw what he had on top of the remaining grain to claim it. The *Mishnah* rules: *ein lo bah klum* — he has no claim to it. If he fell upon it — *nafal aleha* — or spread his cloak over it — *piras talito aleha* — we remove him from it, and the *pe'ah* remains available for others. Why did *arba amot* not acquire the grain for him? He was standing within four *amot* of it.

### Girsa Question

The *gemara*'s first answer is: *hacha bemai askinan d'lo amar akni* — the case is one where he did not say "I want my *arba amot* to acquire for me." The *gemara* immediately challenges this: if the Rabbis established the *kinyan* of *arba amot*, why should it matter whether one utters any formula? You clearly want to acquire — why require magic words? This response is rejected.

### Gali Da'atei

The *gemara* offers instead: *keivan d'nafal gali da'ateih d'binfilah nicha leh d'nikni* — since he fell upon it, he revealed his intent that he wanted to acquire through the act of falling. And since falling is the *kinyan* he intended to perform, *b'arba amot lo nicha leh d'nikni* — he did not intend to acquire through his *arba amot*, and that *kinyan* therefore does not activate.

### Falling Intent

This is a subtle but important principle. The person clearly wants the object — there is no ambiguity about desire. But the *kinyan* of *arba amot* is not simply an automatic consequence of proximity; it is a legal mechanism that is overridden when the person has demonstrated, through his own actions, that he intended a *different* mechanism of acquisition. His act of falling expressed his chosen mode of *kinyan*. Since *nefilah* — falling — is not a valid *kinyan*, that chosen mode failed. And since he did not intend to rely on *arba amot*, that mechanism is unavailable to rescue him.

An analogy illustrates this: suppose someone intends to perform *hagbahah* — lifting — as the act of *kinyan* for a cup, and lifts it less than three *tefachim* (an insufficiency for *hagbahah*, according to one view). In so doing, he has in fact performed *meshichah* — drawing toward himself — which is a valid *kinyan*. Can we combine his desire to acquire with the physical act of *meshichah* and say he has acquired? Or do we say: he made clear he was performing *hagbahah*, that act failed, and his non-awareness of *meshichah* means the *meshichah* does not take effect for him? The *gemara* here asserts that the act of falling similarly negates the otherwise-available *kinyan* of *arba amot*.

### Moral Not Rasha

Before proceeding, it is worth pausing on a small but striking Tosafot that addresses the moral dimension of these cases. Tosafot notes that even the person who comes and physically takes the object from under the one who fell on it — removing him from the *pe'ah* — is not called a *rasha*. Indeed, *afilla rasha lo mikrei*. This follows from another principle in *Kiddushin*: *ani mehapech b'chararah u-va acher u-netalah lo mikrei rasha* — a poor person turning over a bread roll to examine it, and another person who comes and takes it away, is called a *rasha*. But Tosafot explains: that case involved land, of which there is a finite and identifiable supply. If I am negotiating for a specific plot of land and you swoop in and take it, you are a *rasha* — because there are other plots of land you could have pursued. By contrast, with a *metzia* or *pe'ah* or *hefker*, there is no comparable alternative. One cannot tell the other finder: "go find a similar lost object somewhere else." Each *metzia* is unique, and therefore the competitive acquisition of it, even in a way that denies someone else their opportunity, carries no moral opprobrium. Even if one person pointed out the *metzia* to another who then ran ahead and took it — which seems at least more morally complicated — Tosafot does not address that scenario, though it would presumably warrant further analysis. What is clear is that Tosafot is at least sensitive to the moral dimension of these cases, even if the legal conclusion removes the stigma of *rasha* in the straightforward case.

---

## Context Limits

### Rav Papa Field

Rav Papa offers a contextual limitation on the *arba amot* principle, formulated (according to the *Gra*'s *girsa*) as follows: *ki takinu lei rabanan arba amot besada de'alma* — when did the Rabbis enact that *arba amot* acquires? In a field that belongs to no party with a stronger claim — an ordinary field. But *besada d'ba'al habayis* — in the field of the owner of the grain — the enactment does not apply.

### Owner Override

The concept of *arba amot* is a form of personal space. It is, in effect, a portable *chatzer* — my immediate surroundings function as my domain. But when one is standing in someone else's property, the owner's claim to that space is stronger than any claim the visitor can generate through personal proximity. The *gemara* makes this precise: *ve'af gav d'zacha lei Rachmana lehuluchi bah ulelikutei pe'ah* — even though the Torah grants the *ani* the right to enter the owner's field and collect *pe'ah* — *lemehava chatzeiro lo zacha lei Rachmana* — that right does not extend to treating the owner's field as the *ani*'s own *chatzer*. The Torah gave a right of entry and collection; it did not give a right of territorial claim. And since *arba amot* functions as a personal *chatzer*, it cannot override the owner's actual possession of the land on which the *ani* is standing.

### Rav Sheshes Simta

Rav Sheshes offers a parallel limitation from a different angle. He holds: *ki tikinu Rabbanan be'simta* — the Rabbis enacted *arba amot* specifically for a *simta*, a side street or alleyway. In such a setting, the concept of personal space is coherent: the area is not heavily trafficked, and one can meaningfully speak of a defined radius around oneself as one's own immediate sphere.

### Dachki Rabbim

But *aval be'reshus harabbim d'ka dachki Rabbim* — in the public domain, where crowds are pressing and pushing — *lo tiknu Rabbanan*: the Rabbis did not apply the enactment there. In a crowded *reshus harabbim*, the notion of personal space collapses. People are physically compressed against one another; there is no realistic sense in which four *amot* around any individual constitute his sphere. The term the *gemara* uses is *dachki Rabbim* — the pressing of the multitude — and this physical reality negates the conceptual foundation on which *arba amot* rests. This closely parallels the rule that *meshichah* — the act of drawing an object toward oneself — is also only valid in a *simta* and not in a *reshus harabbim*, where any such act lacks the clarity and definition required to constitute a meaningful *kinyan*.

The *gemara* then notes that the original statement specified *bechol makom* — everywhere — and reconciles this with the limitations articulated by Rav Papa and Rav Sheshes by explaining: *kol makom l'asuyei tziddei reshus harabbim* — the phrase "everywhere" was intended to include the sidewalks and margins of the public domain, not the *reshus harabbim* itself. The principle, then, is considerably more bounded than its initial formulation suggests.

---

## Ketana Chatzer

### Ketana Question

The *gemara* now introduces a further application of Reish Lakish's ruling about *arba amot*, this time in the context of *get*. The background: a man may divorce a minor girl (*ketana*) through delivery of a *get*, because her marriage was itself arranged through her father's *kinyan*. The Torah states *ve'natan beyadah* — he shall place it in her hand — and the *halacha* derives from this that *get* can be delivered not only to her person but also to her *chatzer*. The question now is: can a *ketana* acquire a *get* through her *chatzer*, or through *arba amot*?

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish holds: *ketana ein lah chatzer v'ein lah arba amot* — a minor girl has neither a *chatzer* nor *arba amot* as mechanisms for acquiring. A *get* delivered to her yard or into her four-*amot* radius does not constitute valid receipt.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *yesh lah chatzer v'yesh lah arba amot* — she has both. A *get* may be validly delivered to her *chatzer* or within her *arba amot*.

### Yad vs Shlichut

The dispute turns on a fundamental question about the nature of *chatzer* as a *kinyan* mechanism. There are two competing theoretical frameworks.

### Chatzer as Hand

The first position holds: *chatzer mishum yadah itrabai* — the concept of *chatzer* is derived from, and is an extension of, the concept of *yad* (hand). The *pasuk* says *ve'natan beyadah*, and from this we broaden *yad* to include one's *chatzer* — one's property functions as an extension of one's physical person. Just as the object placed in her hand is on her person, so too an object placed in her *chatzer* is within her sphere. Under this view, *ki heichi d'is lah yad chatzer nami is lah* — the same way she has a hand, she has a *chatzer*. A *ketana* has a hand; therefore she has a *chatzer*. This is Reish Lakish's... wait — actually this is the position that would *support* Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, since a *ketana* obviously has a hand.

### Chatzer Agency

The second position holds: *chatzer mishum shlichut* — the mechanism of *chatzer* is not based on physical extension but on agency. The *chatzer* acts *on behalf* of its owner, analogous to how a *shaliach* acts on behalf of a principal. Under this view, the *chatzer* is not merely an extension of the owner's body but an independent mechanism that operates in a representative capacity. If so, *vechi heichi d'shlichut leit lah chatzer nami leit lah* — just as a *ketana* lacks the legal capacity to appoint a *shaliach* (agency requires *da'at*, and a minor's *da'at* is insufficient for that purpose), her *chatzer* similarly cannot function as an agent on her behalf. This is Reish Lakish's position.

The two positions also account for the parallel question of *arba amot*: if *arba amot* is a form of *chatzer* — a portable personal domain — then it tracks the same dispute. If *chatzer* is an extension of *yad*, *arba amot* also works for a *ketana*. If *chatzer* is a form of *shlichut*, *arba amot* is equally unavailable to her.

---

## Ketana Chatzer (II)

### Chatzer Crime

If *chatzer* is understood as *shlichut* — as acting on the owner's behalf — a striking implication follows: can a *chatzer* commit a *dvar aveirah* for its owner? The principle of *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* holds that agency cannot be invoked to perform an act that constitutes a transgression — if I appoint someone to steal for me, the act of theft is attributed to the agent, not to me, and I bear no liability. But if my *chatzer* is a form of *shlichut*, the same logic should apply: if an animal enters my yard and I lock the gate, using my *chatzer* as the instrument of *gneivah*, shouldn't the principle of *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* negate my liability? This is the problem the *gemara* now confronts.

---

## Agency Crime Limits

### Gneivah Proof

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: the verse *im himatzei timatzei beyado hagneivah* — "if the stolen object is found in his hand" — teaches that liability for *gneivah* attaches to the thief's hand. From where do we know that *gago, chatzero vekarfipo* — his roof, his yard, and his enclosure — also create liability? From the words *himatzei timatzei*, which expand the scope of "being found" to any location under his control. So *chatzer* can serve as the instrument of *gneivah*. But if *chatzer* is *mishum shlichut*, why doesn't *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* protect the owner from liability — just as it would if a human agent stole on his behalf?

### Ravina Answer

Ravina answers: *heichi amrinan ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah? Heicha d'shaliach bar chiyuva hu* — the principle of *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* applies only where the agent himself is bound by the prohibition in question. A *chatzer* is *lo bar chiyuva* — it is not subject to the prohibition *lo tignov*. Since it bears no obligation, the logic of *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* does not apply to it.

### Moral Choice

The rationale underlying *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* is: *divrei haRav v'divrei hatalmid divrei mi shom'im?* — when the words of God and the words of a human master conflict, whose words do you heed? If the agent is commanded by God not to steal but by his principal to steal, the agent should have refused. Having chosen to obey the principal, the agent bears the moral and legal responsibility for his choice. This is why agency is negated — not because it is technically impossible, but because the agent's free moral choice severs the causal and legal link to the principal.

### Chatzer Inanimate

But a *chatzer* is an inanimate object. It cannot be commanded. It cannot choose. The prohibition *lo tignov* does not speak to it. Therefore, *mchayev shalcho* — the sender, the owner, is held liable, because the *chatzer* is simply carrying out the situation created by the owner's act. There is no independent moral agent interposed between the owner and the outcome.

### Woman Slave

The *gemara* presses: what about a woman or a slave? If I tell them to go steal for me, they have no money of their own to pay damages — *leit lehu lishlumei* — so are they also *lo bar chiyuva*, and should I therefore be liable for their theft? The *gemara* rejects this: *ishah ve-eved benei chiyuva ninhu* — a woman and a slave are fully subject to the prohibition against theft. *Ve-hashta miha leit lehu lishlumei* — they simply have no current assets to pay with, but the obligation and liability exist. The proof: *nitgarshah ha-ishah, nishtachrer ha-eved — chayavin lishaleim* — if the woman is later divorced and the slave later freed, they must pay. Their momentary inability to pay does not negate their substantive legal obligation.

### Rava Better

Rava offers what the *gemara* presents as a superior answer. He formulates the distinction not in terms of *bar chiyuva* but in terms of the capacity for free choice: *heichi amrinan ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah? Heicha d'i ba'ei avid, i ba'ei lo avid* — we apply *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* wherever the agent has a genuine choice, where he could have done otherwise. The agent's freedom is what makes him the responsible party. If the agent could have said no and chose not to, it is the agent's act, not the principal's.

### Ba'al Korchah

But a *chatzer* has no such choice. *Aval chatzer de-ba'al korchah* — the *chatzer* does not act voluntarily. It is an inanimate domain that simply is what it is; the animal walks in, the gate is locked, and the result follows mechanically. *Ba'al korchah motvei bah* — it acts, as it were, under compulsion. And therefore *mchayev shalcho* — the one who put it in motion, who created the situation, is the one who bears liability. There is no intervening free agent to absorb the moral or legal responsibility. The owner is fully accountable.

This resolution also illuminates the *shlichut* model of *chatzer* more precisely. Even if we say *chatzer mishum shlichut*, it is not *shlichut* in the same sense as human agency. A human *shaliach* who performs an *aveirah* severs the principal's liability because of his own free choice. A *chatzer* that performs, so to speak, the same act does not sever that liability precisely because there was no choice. The anthropomorphism of treating *chatzer* as a form of agency reaches its natural limit here: it acts on the owner's behalf, but it does so without volition, and therefore it cannot absorb responsibility. *Yesh shaliach l'dvar aveirah* — there is, in this case, agency even for an act of *aveirah* — because the agent is not a free moral actor but an instrument of the owner's will.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 11

## Chatzer: Shliach or Yad?

### Arba Amos & Chatzer

We pick up at the bottom of 10b, in the middle of a discussion that began with the rabbinic *kinyan* of *arba amos* — the rule that an object within one's four *amos*, within one's personal space, is acquired. The Gemara had noted that this *kinyan* is conceptually a type of *chatzer*. That observation, however, opened a broader inquiry: what exactly is the nature of *chatzer*? Why does *kinyan chatzer* work at all?

The question initially arose in the context of a minor girl: if one can place a *get* on her person, can one also place it in her *chatzer*? And if she has a *chatzer*, does she also acquire the *arba amos* around her? These questions drove the Gemara toward a foundational conceptual debate.

### Yad vs. Shliach

The Gemara frames the question as follows: is *chatzer* understood as an extension of the person — a *yad*, literally a "hand" — such that placing something on one's property is tantamount to placing it on one's person? Or is *chatzer* understood as acting in one's behalf, a kind of anthropomorphic agency, holding and possessing objects as one's representative? This second conception is the framework of *shlichus*.

Each understanding carries different implications. If *chatzer* is a *yad*, then it naturally applies to minors, just as their physical hand does. If it is a *shliach*, however, additional complications arise.

### Ein Shaliach Aveirah

One such complication emerges immediately. If *chatzer* functions as a *shliach*, then what happens when an object that was stolen walks into your yard and you close the gate with the intention of taking it? The principle of *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* — that there is no agency for a sinful act — would seem to undermine the entire mechanism: the *chatzer* is apparently acting as your agent to commit theft.

### Two Reasons Explained

The Gemara offers two distinct responses to this challenge, each corresponding to a different understanding of why *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* applies in the first place.

The first reason: *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* applies when a *shaliach* who has been instructed to commit a sin ought to have refused, since he is himself bound by the relevant prohibition. The logic is *divrei harav v'divrei hatalmid, divrei mi shome'im* — when God says do not do something and a human being instructs you to do it, you listen to God. But a *chatzer* carries no obligations. God did not say *lo tignov* to a yard, any more than He addressed such commandments to angels. Since the *chatzer* is not obligated in these *mitzvot*, there is no basis for saying it "should have refused," and therefore the problem of *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* does not apply.

The second reason: *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* applies because the *shaliach* had free choice — he could have declined. A *chatzer*, by contrast, has no choice whatsoever. It does not act on its own agency; it always acts on your behalf because it cannot do otherwise. Therefore, whatever the *chatzer* does is always attributed back to you. If it acquires stolen property for you, you bear responsibility, because the *chatzer* is never seen as acting independently.

These two rationales — the absence of obligation, and the absence of choice — are not identical, and the Gemara will go on to explore where they diverge in practice. What they share, however, is this: under either account, one can invoke the concept of *shlichus* without the problem of *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* blocking it, because neither obstacle that normally triggers that principle is present in the case of a *chatzer*. The discussion of the *chatzer*'s conceptual nature — *shliach* or *yad* — will in fact dominate the rest of this *daf* and the entirety of the next *mishna*'s discussion.

---

## Choice vs. Obligation

### Mai Beinaihu

The Gemara asks: *mai beinaihu* — what is the practical difference between the two reasons? Whether *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* is grounded in the *shaliach*'s being obligated and having violated his own duty, or whether it is grounded in the *shaliach*'s having exercised free choice — what *nafka mina* follows from this distinction?

### Kohen & Grusha

The Gemara's first case: a *kohen* says to a non-*kohen*, "go and betroth a divorced woman for me." The *shaliach* here is not prohibited from marrying a *grusha* — he is neither a *kohen* nor bound by that prohibition — but he may nonetheless run afoul of *lifnei iver lo titen michshol* by facilitating the *kohen*'s transgression. The question is: under which theory of *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* would the *kohen* bear liability?

### Payos Case

The second case is even more pointed. A man instructs a woman to cut the sideburns of a minor boy. A woman is not herself prohibited from performing such cutting, and a minor is not yet obligated in *mitzvot*, so she is not even causing another person to stumble — there is no *lifnei iver* concern at all. Yet if the woman is treated as an extension of the man who sent her, then the man has now, through her, committed the *aveirah* of cutting off the sideburns of a male.

This raises a further, subtle question about the scope of *yesh shaliach l'dvar aveirah*. Normally, *shlichus* operates in a legal domain: your agent's acts of sale, purchase, or betrothal take legal effect for you. But physical acts are different. If I instruct you to take my *lulav*, I have not taken a *lulav*. So when we say *yesh shaliach l'dvar aveirah* — when the *shaliach* is not a *bar chiyuva* — does that mean the man is treated as though he physically performed the act, thereby incurring lashes? Or does it mean only that he bears some degree of moral or heavenly liability, without the full weight of direct physical transgression?

### Extent of Shliach

This question about the extent of *yesh shaliach l'dvar aveirah* sharpens the issue considerably. In ordinary *shlichus*, the question is whether the legal act takes binding effect. Here, the physical reality — the sideburns are cut off — is not in doubt. The question is whether we attribute that physical act to the one who sent the agent. That is a different kind of attribution than the legal effectiveness ordinarily at stake in *shlichus*.

### Resolving Mai Beinaihu

The Gemara resolves the *mai beinaihu* as follows. According to the position that *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* is rooted in free choice — *kol hacha d'baei avid u'baei lo avid* — then even in the *payos* case, since the woman had a free choice whether to carry out the instruction or not, it is she who bears responsibility, not the man. The fact that she herself faced no prohibition is irrelevant: she could have refused, and therefore the act is entirely attributed to her as an independent agent. The man who instructed her is not liable.

According to the alternative position — that *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* applies specifically because the *shaliach* is a *bar chiyuva* who violated his own prohibition — then if the *shaliach* is *not* a *bar chiyuva*, the entire obstacle falls away. *Shlichus* operates normally. The woman, being under no prohibition, is a fully valid *shliach*, and the man who sent her is liable.

### Tosafot Question

Tosafot raises a further question that takes this discussion to a practical level. When we say *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah*, does this mean only that the sender bears no *liability*, while the *shlichus* itself remains legally valid? Or does it mean that the *shlichus* is entirely *batel* — annulled — such that any legal transaction attempted through such agency is void?

This question has direct ramifications. If the *shliach* delivers a *get* on behalf of a husband against the wife's will — thereby violating *cherem Rabbeinu Gershom* — is the *get* valid *b'dieved*? Is *ein shaliach l'dvar aveirah* only about the punishment of the sender, or does it negate the *shlichus* entirely and leave the woman not divorced? The *Noda Biyehuda* addresses precisely this question in a famous responsum, working through this entire *sugya* to determine whether the *shlichus* is merely unenforceable or fundamentally void. Tosafot is the first to raise the question explicitly. The Gemara presents these two *nafka minos* — the punishment question and the validity question — without resolving them definitively.

There remains a residual difficulty worth flagging. Even according to the view that the *shaliach*'s not being a *bar chiyuva* allows *shlichus* to operate, one might still ask: if the *shlichus* is effective and the *kohen* has thereby married a divorced woman, then the woman who served as *shaliach* has helped him commit an *aveirah* — should she not be liable for *lifnei iver*? The matter is somewhat circular: if *shlichus* operates because she is not a *bar chiyuva*, her act enables the *kohen*'s transgression, which would seem to implicate her in *lifnei iver* regardless. This tension is not fully resolved here, and the discussion returns, in any case, to the main subject of *chatzer*.

---

## Chatzer for Minors

### Baraita Get

The Gemara returns to the question of *chatzer* for a minor girl. A *baraita* on the laws of *get* provides the key textual anchor. The Torah says *ve'nasan b'yadah* — he shall place the *get* in her hand. The *baraita* asks: the verse says only her *yad* — how do I know that the *get* can also be delivered via her roof (*gag*), her *chatzer*, or her enclosed yard (*karpif*)? The answer is derived from the formulation of the verb: *talmud lomar ve'nasan mikol makom*, indicating that any placement, even indirectly, satisfies the requirement. Rashi explains that the unusual word order — verb before object — extends the meaning beyond the literal hand. The conceptual point the Gemara draws from this *baraita* is that *chatzer* in the context of *get* is understood as an extension of the *yad*, as the derivation itself is rooted in the term *yad*.

Tosafot adds a further observation: since the *baraita* also permits delivering a *get* to a *ketana* — a minor girl — and the same *pasuk* establishes that her *chatzer* serves as her *yad*, it follows that *chatzer* for a *ketana* is definitively grounded in the concept of *yad*, not *shliach*.

### All Agree: Get

The Gemara states clearly: *le'inyan get, kuli alma lo pligi de'chatzer mishum yad itrabai*. On the question of *get*, there is no dispute. Everyone agrees that *chatzer* functions as a *yad* — that is the foundation of the entire mechanism. The debate that follows pertains to other domains.

### Get vs. Metziah

When it comes to *metziah* — found objects — the positions diverge. One opinion holds that we derive *metziah* from *get*: just as *chatzer* operates as a *yad* for the *get*, so too does it operate as a *yad* across all areas of *kinyan*, including the acquisition of *metziah*. A *ketana* whose *chatzer* contains a found object would therefore acquire it by *kinyan chatzer*, functioning as an extension of her person.

### Only for Get

The opposing view holds that we do not derive *metziah* from *get*. The Torah's ruling that *chatzer* serves as *yad* for *get* purposes is a specific *chiddush* confined to that context; it does not authorize extending the *yad* framework to other domains of acquisition.

### Ketana Works

The first position maintains that once the Torah has established the principle that a *ketana*'s *chatzer* is her *yad* — specifically in the context of *get* — that principle carries over to all *kinyanim*. The *chiddush* reveals a standing feature of the *ketana*'s *chatzer*, not a rule limited to divorce law.

### Katan Question

This leads to a further question: what about a *katan* — a minor boy? Boys are not subject to the *get* framework, so the *pasuk* about *yad* in the context of divorce does not apply to them. Does *chatzer* function as a *yad* for a *katan* in the domain of *metziah*? One opinion holds that we derive *katan* from *ketana*: just as a girl's *chatzer* is her *yad*, so too is a boy's. The opposing opinion holds that no such derivation can be made — it applies only to women and girls, where the *get* framework grounded the concept.

### Reconciliation

The Gemara then suggests a possible reconciliation: *ve'iba'it eima, mar mar chada u'mar chada velo pligi* — perhaps the two views are not actually in conflict. The one who says *chatzer* works as *yad* may be referring to a *ketana*, while the one who says it does not may be referring to a *katan*. Alternatively, one may be speaking of *get* and the other of *metziah*, without any true disagreement between them.

---

## Implications & Transition

### Get vs. Kinyan

Why does the distinction between *get* and *metziah* matter so much? One might expect that once the Torah establishes a principle, it would apply uniformly. But there is a compelling reason to distinguish: *get* may not fundamentally be about *kinyan* at all. The operative requirement for *get* is not necessarily that the woman takes *possession* of the document, but rather that it be *placed on her person*. If that is the correct understanding, then the extension to *chatzer* makes sense as a mode of delivery — something on her property counts as something on her person. But when the domain is *metziah*, where the requirement is genuine *kinyan*, the concept of *yad* as mere placement on one's person may be insufficient. Perhaps *chatzer* in the domain of *kinyan* requires something more than being attributable to one's person — it must actually operate as a mechanism of *kinyan*. This would explain why one might accept *chatzer* as *yad* for *get* while denying it for *metziah*.

This line of analysis also illuminates the unresolved tension in the earlier discussion. The Gemara has established that *chatzer* clearly operates as *yad* under certain circumstances — for a *get*, for a *ketana*. But whether it operates as *yad* in other contexts, or whether it operates instead as *shliach*, remains unclear. And if it operates as *shliach* rather than *yad* in the domain of *kinyan*, further questions follow about its applicability to minors, who cannot appoint agents.

### Open Questions

Several questions remain unresolved as the Gemara transitions to the next *mishna*. First, the general conceptual question: in the domain of *kinyanim*, is *chatzer* a *yad* or a *shliach*? Second, what are the practical *nafka minos* of that distinction — and the next *mishna* will itself provide some answers. Third, the Gemara has not directly addressed the case of transferring ownership *to* a minor — placing an object in a *katan*'s or *ketana*'s *chatzer* for the purpose of their acquiring it. As Tosafot notes, a *katan* generally cannot acquire *metziah* at a biblical level, only rabbinically, because there is no *da'at* directing the object to him. The Gemara's discussion focused on *metziah*, where the absence of *da'at* is precisely the problem. If, by contrast, one were actively placing an object in a minor's *chatzer* with the intention of transferring it — providing the necessary *da'at acheret* — then presumably the *chatzer* should operate even for a *katan* or *ketana*. These questions remain with us as we turn to the next *mishna*.

---

## Metziah Mishna

### Three Cases

The *mishna* presents the following scenario: one sees two people running after a found object — perhaps one sees a rolling object — or running after a deer with a broken leg (*tzvi shavur*), or running after chicks that have not yet learned to fly (*gozalot shelo parchu*). In each case, the object is moving through one's field. One declares: *zachata li sadi* — let my field acquire it on my behalf.

If such a declaration is made under the right conditions, the *mishna* rules: *zachata lo* — one has indeed acquired the object. Despite the fact that others were running after it first, the first valid *kinyan* was performed by virtue of the object being in one's field.

However, the *mishna* qualifies this: if the deer was running normally — not with a broken leg — or if the chicks were already capable of flight, then the declaration *zachata li sadi* is legally ineffective.

### Contained Objects

The logic is clear: *kinyan chatzer* works only when the object can be contained within the *chatzer*. A deer running at full speed or birds in flight are not genuinely "within" the field in any meaningful sense — they will simply leave. A *tzvi shavur* or pre-flight chicks, by contrast, can plausibly be held within the boundaries of the field, and it is that containment that enables the *kinyan*.

---

## Omed B'Tzad Sadehu

### Rav Yehuda/Shmuel

Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel: *vehu she'omed betzad sadehu* — the *mishna*'s ruling applies only when the owner is standing beside his field. This condition is presented as necessary for the *kinyan* to take effect even in the permissible cases — even the *tzvi shavur*, even the pre-flight chicks.

At first glance, this requirement seems to be on the same axis as the *mishna*'s own distinction. The *mishna* says the deer must have a broken leg; Shmuel adds that you must also be standing there. The combined logic appears to be: the *chatzer* acquires only if the object is sufficiently contained — which requires both that the object be unable to escape on its own (*tzvi shavur*) and that the owner be present to prevent escape (*omed betzad sadehu*). Both conditions together establish that the object is genuinely held within the field.

### Teshuvah to Question

One might ask: why is the owner's presence necessary at all? Does not *chatzer* work even without the owner's awareness? Indeed, Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina establishes the principle: *chatzero shel adam konah lo shelo mida'ato* — a person's *chatzer* acquires on his behalf even without his *da'at*. And this would also explain why the *mishna*'s formulation — "one declares *zachata li sadi*" — need not be taken literally as a requirement; as Tosafot notes, the declaration is *lav davka*, the *kinyan* would work even without explicit verbal statement.

So the question stands: if *chatzer* works without the owner's knowledge, why must the owner be standing beside it?

### Protected vs. Unprotected

The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between a *chatzer hamishtameres* — a protected, enclosed field — and a *chatzer she'einah mishtameres* — an unprotected field. For a protected *chatzer*, such as one surrounded by a fence, the objects within it are genuinely contained, and the *chatzer* acquires even without the owner's presence. But for an unprotected field — which is the typical *sadeh*, a large open expanse of grain with no surrounding fence — the *chatzer* acquires only when the owner is standing there. *Ei omed betzad sadehu, ein; ei lo, lo* — if standing there, yes; if not, no.

At this stage, the analysis remains coherent: the owner's physical presence beside an unprotected field serves the same purpose as the fence around a protected one. It renders the field *mishtameret* — capable of containing the object — and thereby activates the mechanism of *kinyan chatzer*.

---

## Shichcha Proof

### Source Question

The Gemara asks: *u'mina teima* — where do we derive the rule that an unprotected field (*chatzer she'einah mishtameret*) requires the owner's presence? The answer comes from a *baraita* about the laws of *shichcha* — the forgotten sheaf that must be left for the poor.

### Sheaf Case

The *baraita* discusses the following scenario: one is in the town and declares, "I know there is a sheaf in my field that the workers will forget." One is standing in town, aware of the sheaf, and wants to prevent it from becoming *shichcha*. The ruling is that such a declaration is ineffective: *lo yehei shichcha* — one cannot prevent it from being forgotten produce from the town.

The *baraita* then brings the verse: *veshachachta omer basadeh* — "you forget a sheaf in the field" — interpreted as *basadeh velo ba'ir*, forgetting in the field is the operative category, not forgetting while in the town.

### Contradiction

This seems internally contradictory. The first clause implies that forgetting in the town would make it *shichcha* — otherwise, why would the person be trying to prevent it? — but the derivation from the verse seems to imply the opposite, that only forgetting in the field counts.

### Resolution

The Gemara resolves: the *baraita* must be read as introducing a distinction between two kinds of forgetting. *Shachuch me'ikara* — something forgotten from the beginning, where no one ever held it in conscious awareness — constitutes *shichcha* when left in the field. *Zachur ulevasof shachu'ach* — something that was known and then forgotten — requires further analysis depending on who remembers and who forgets, and whether the owner is present.

Specifically: if the owner is present in the field and remembers the sheaf even though the workers have forgotten it, there is no *shichcha*. If the owner is in the town remembering while the workers in the field have forgotten, there *is* shichcha.

### Prevents Shichcha

The Gemara explains why the owner's presence prevents *shichcha*: *dekivan dekai gaba, hevei lei chatzero, vezachata lo* — since the owner is standing there in the field, it is as though his *chatzer* has re-acquired the sheaf on his behalf. He is still in possession of it. The workers' forgetting does not constitute *shichcha* because the owner is still there, holding on to it through his presence and his field.

### Critique

It must be said that this is a striking way to explain the ruling. A more intuitive explanation would focus on the question of who is responsible for gathering and whose memory governs: if the owner is present and supervising, his awareness is what matters, not the workers'. The *shichcha* regime depends on the process of gathering having been effectively abandoned, and that abandonment has not occurred while the owner is present and attentive.

The Gemara, however, frames it differently — not in terms of supervision or responsibility, but as a technical matter of possession: the owner being present constitutes his field actively acquiring the sheaf on his behalf, thereby preventing the *shichcha* from taking hold. This implies that *omed betzad sadehu* is not merely a practical criterion for oversight but a formal condition for the *chatzer* to function as a possessive mechanism.

This framing, however, raises its own difficulties. If we say the *chatzer* re-acquires the sheaf and thereby prevents *shichcha*, the implication is that the moment *shichcha* would have applied, the owner's *chatzer* steps in to prevent it. But once something becomes *shichcha*, it belongs to the poor — the owner cannot re-acquire it. The Gemara's answer must therefore mean not that the owner re-acquires after *shichcha*, but that his continued presence prevents *shichcha* from ever taking hold in the first place: he has never truly lost possession.

Consider a telling scenario: the owner steps twenty feet away to knock on a neighbor's door. At that precise moment, the workers forget the sheaf. According to the Gemara's logic, because the owner is not *omed betzad sadehu*, there is *shichcha*, even though he remembers the sheaf and is mere moments away from returning. One might expect that continuous personal awareness and proximity would suffice. But the Gemara insists that the formal condition of standing beside the field is what maintains possession, not the subjective state of remembering. This is a counterintuitive position, and the tension between the formal criterion and the intuitive logic of supervision and memory is worth keeping in mind.

---

## Amoraim Agree

### Ulla & Rabbah

The requirement of *omed betzad sadehu* is not the view of Shmuel alone. Ulla states the same ruling, as does Rabbah bar bar Chana: *vehu she'omed betzad sadehu* — the *kinyan* of the *chatzer* for the *metziah* works only if the owner is standing beside his field. The agreement among these *amoraim* establishes the ruling as broadly accepted.

---

## Rav Abba Challenge

### Ma'aser Story

Rav Abba challenges Ulla's position from a famous *ma'aseh*. There is a story of Rabban Gamliel and the *zekeinim* — Sages — who were traveling together on a ship. Rabban Gamliel declared: "The *ma'aser* that I am going to measure out is hereby given to Yehoshua" — Rabbi Yehoshua, who was a *Levi* present on the boat — "and the space of the *ma'aser* is rented to him." A second *ma'aser* — *ma'aser ani* in this case — he gave to Akiva ben Yosef, who was serving as a *gabbai aniyim*, an agent to collect on behalf of the poor. Similarly, the relevant space was rented to Akiva.

There is a dispute between Rashi and Tosafot about what exactly Rabban Gamliel was doing. Rashi, drawing on a parallel Gemara, suggests that Rabban Gamliel had left his house without separating *terumot u'ma'asrot* and feared his household would eat *tevel*. He was therefore separating the *ma'asrot* from afar. Tosafot questions this reading: the formulation "I am going to measure it out" does not sound like an act of *hafrashah* being performed now, and there would be no need to transfer the *ma'aser* to the *Levi* immediately simply to avoid *tevel*. Tosafot suggests instead that the *ma'aser* had already been separated — this is the end-of-three-years scenario where undistributed *ma'asrot* must be given away — and Rabban Gamliel was now seeking to transfer ownership to the designated recipients.

In either case, the operative question for the Gemara is: was the transfer legally effective? Rabban Gamliel rented a portion of his field to Yehoshua and Akiva; the grain — or the *ma'aser* portion — was acquired via *kinyan chatzer*. But Yehoshua and Akiva were on the ship. They were nowhere near Rabban Gamliel's field.

### The Challenge

This is the challenge: *vechi Rabbi Yehoshua veRabbi Akiva betzad sadehu shel Rabban Gamliel hayu omdim?* — were Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva standing beside Rabban Gamliel's field? Clearly not. They were on a boat, far from the field. Yet the *kinyan* apparently worked. This would seem to be a direct refutation of the requirement of *omed betzad sadehu*.

Tosafot raises an additional dimension: even setting aside the question of proximity, was the field *mishtameres*? If it was grain standing in an open field, it would not be *mishtameres* by default. And even if it were a house, the *ma'aser* inside would not be protected from the family members, who did not know that a specific portion now belonged to Yehoshua or Akiva. How, then, did *kinyan chatzer* operate here at all?

### Ulla Dismisses

Ulla's response to this challenge is dismissive: *dami hai merabbanan dela gmar inshi shmaita* — this sounds to me like someone who has never properly learned the material. This is not an answer; it is a deflection. Rav Abba was not satisfied.

---

## Resolution

### Rav Abba Persists

When Rav Abba came to Sura, he presented the challenge to the scholars of the *yeshiva*: here is what Ulla said, here is the challenge I raised from the case of *ma'aser*, and Ulla gave no real answer. He was looking for a substantive resolution.

### Kinyan Agav

One of the Sages of Sura provided the answer: *Rabban Gamliel mataltlei agav mekarkei hikna lahem* — Rabban Gamliel transferred the movable property (*metaltelin*) to Yehoshua and Akiva by means of *kinyan agav*, not *kinyan chatzer*. The acquisition of the *ma'aser* was therefore never a case of *kinyan chatzer* at all, and the challenge falls away.

### Agav Explained

*Kinyan agav* — incidental acquisition — is a mechanism studied in tractate Kiddushin: when one conveys a piece of landed property to another, any movable property that one wishes to bundle with that transfer can be simultaneously conveyed, even if the movables are not physically located on the land. The act of acquiring the land serves as the act of acquiring the *metaltelin* bundled with it.

This is why Rabban Gamliel arranged for a rental of the space: he was not creating a *chatzer* for purposes of *kinyan chatzer*. He was executing an act of conveying land — a rental being understood, per the Rambam's elegant formulation, as a *kinyan guf le-peiros li-zman*, an ownership of the property's use for a limited period — and bundling the *ma'aser* with it. When Yehoshua acquired the rental, he simultaneously acquired the grain by *agav*, not because his rented field then served as a *chatzer* to acquire what was sitting in it.

### Tovat Hanah

But Rava objects to accepting this answer too quickly: *shapir avid d'la kiblah* — Rav Abba was right not to accept it. If all Rabban Gamliel needed was *kinyan agav*, why did he arrange a land rental at all? There was a simpler option.

The answer lies in the concept of *tovat hana'ah*. Rabban Gamliel did not own the *ma'aser* outright. The *ma'aser* belongs to the *Leviyim*; Rabban Gamliel possessed only a *tovat hana'ah* — the right to designate which *Levi* receives it, without actually owning the *ma'aser* itself. Similarly, *ma'aser ani* belongs to the poor; Rabban Gamliel had only the right to choose the recipient.

The implication is decisive: *tovat hana'ah einah mamon* — this benefit-right is not ownership. Since Rabban Gamliel did not *own* the *ma'aser*, he could not execute a *kinyan* that is grounded in transferring ownership. *Kinyan agav* requires that the one conveying have ownership over the thing being transferred. If you do not own the movable, you cannot bundle it with a land transfer. The same applies to *kinyan chatzer* in the ordinary sense: it works when the owner's *chatzer* acquires something for the owner. But here, Rabban Gamliel was not transferring his property — he was directing an obligation that already belonged to someone else.

What he *could* do is give. The Torah says *venatata* — "you shall give" the *ma'aser* — indicating that the mechanism of transfer for *ma'aser* and *matnot kehunah* is an act of giving, not an act of transferring ownership. And one form of giving is placing something in the recipient's hand. Another form is placing it in the recipient's *chatzer*. That Rabban Gamliel could do, even without being present beside the field, because the mechanism at work is not *kinyan* in the ownership-transfer sense but rather the act of *nesinah*, of giving.

### Why Not Chalifin

The Gemara presses further: even granting that Rabban Gamliel could not do *kinyan agav* because *tovat hana'ah einah mamon*, why could he not simply perform *chalifin*? Let Yehoshua give Rabban Gamliel a handkerchief, and in exchange Rabban Gamliel would convey the *ma'aser*.

The Gemara's answer: *chalifin derech mekach umimkar hu* — *chalifin* is fundamentally an exchange, a form of commercial transaction, not a gift. The Torah requires that *matnot kehunah* be given as a *matanah*, a gift. An act of exchange does not qualify as giving. *Metaltelin agav mekarkei*, by contrast — acquiring movable property incidentally to acquiring land — the Gemara asserts is called *netinah*, it qualifies as an act of giving. Therefore, if one could argue that *kinyan agav* is itself a form of giving, the prohibition against exchange would not disqualify it.

The upshot: the reason Rabban Gamliel could not use *chalifin* is that it is exchange, not gift. The reason he could not use *kinyan agav* in the standard sense is that he had no ownership to convey. The mechanism he *could* use is *kinyan chatzer* — specifically the act of renting space to Yehoshua and Akiva, so that the *ma'aser* sitting in that space would be "placed" in their *chatzer*, constituting an act of giving. And this is indeed a valid form of *kinyan chatzer* that does not require *omed betzad sadehu*, because the question of proximity is a condition that applies when acquiring *metziah* — where the possessive mechanism must be strong enough to ground *kinyan*. But here, where the requirement is merely *nesinah*, a weaker act of placement suffices.

### Rav Pappa

Rav Pappa offers an additional answer: *da'at acheret maknah otan shani* — when another party's *da'at* is actively directing the transfer, a weaker *kinyan* suffices. This principle appeared earlier in the discussion of minors, and its logic is general. Every *kinyan* consists of two elements: the *da'at* — the intention and will — to transfer or acquire, and the physical act that represents the taking of possession. These two elements exist in a relationship of substitutability: where *da'at* is particularly strong, the physical act need not be as robust.

In the case of *metziah*, no one is directing the object toward you. The acquisition depends entirely on the strength of your own possessive act. That is why *chatzer hamishtameres* or *omed betzad sadehu* is required — to establish that your *chatzer* genuinely holds the object. But when Rabban Gamliel is actively and explicitly transferring the *ma'aser* to Yehoshua — when the *da'at* of the giver is entirely directed toward this specific recipient — the requirement for a strong possessive act is reduced. Even a *chatzer* that is not *mishtameret*, and even without *omed betzad sadehu*, suffices. The *da'at acheret maknah* fills in what the physical act lacks. We will continue with more of this tomorrow.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 12

## Standing by Field

### Intro & Background

The present daf is Bava Metzia 12, picking up on 11b approximately fifteen lines from the bottom, beginning with the words *makne osan shani*. The broader context is the *perek*'s sustained discussion of *meziot* — the laws of finding lost objects. Although the *perek* opened with the famous case of two people simultaneously grabbing a found object, the *mishnayot* that follow address a range of scenarios involving the acquisition of lost objects. The particular *mishnah* under discussion earlier concerned a deer running through one's yard: if the deer had a broken leg such that it could effectively be caught, the owner's field could acquire it on his behalf; if the deer was running normally and could not be caught, no acquisition took place.

### Rav Yehuda vs Yose

The *gemara* had already established that Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, requires a person to be standing alongside his field (*omed betzad sadehu*) in order for *kinyan chatzer* to take effect. The *gemara* then challenged this from a ruling of Rabbi Yose bar Chanina, who held that one's *chatzer* can acquire on one's behalf even without one's awareness — which seemingly implies that standing nearby is unnecessary.

### Mishtameret Distinction

The *gemara* resolved this tension by distinguishing between a *chatzer mishtameret* — a protected enclosure where objects placed within it will remain — and a *chatzer lo mishtameret*, where objects are not reliably held. If the *chatzer* is *mishtameret*, no standing is required; if it is not *mishtameret*, one must be standing alongside it for *kinyan chatzer* to operate.

### Yad vs Shlichut

Rashi explains this distinction by noting that when one is standing nearby, one provides the protection oneself, thereby rendering the *chatzer* effectively *mishtameret* through one's own presence. An alternative reading, which the *gemara* will make explicit shortly, flows from the earlier discussion about whether *chatzer* functions as an extension of the person's *yad* or as a form of *shlichut*. If one is standing beside the *chatzer*, it operates as *yad* — a direct physical extension of the person. If one is absent, it can only function as *shlichut*, operating on one's behalf. As *yad*, physical holding suffices; as *shlichut*, one requires a meaningful degree of control — that is, *mishtameret* — for the agency to be coherent.

---

## Rabbis on Boat

### Maaser Transfer

The *gemara* had proceeded to examine a famous case involving Rabban Gamliel and the other rabbis traveling aboard a ship. Rabban Gamliel transferred ownership of *maaser rishon* to the Levite and *maaser ani* to Rabbi Akiva, who served as *gabbai tzedakah*, by renting them the space beneath which the grain in question was located. This appears to be a *kinyan chatzer* — the recipient acquires the grain by virtue of his rented space — yet Rabban Gamliel was clearly not standing alongside any field.

### Challenge to Standing

The *gemara* challenged: does this not demonstrate that one need not be standing beside the field for *kinyan chatzer* to function? Tosafot raises the obvious counter: perhaps the grain was in his house and the *chatzer* was *mishtameret* regardless. However, Tosafot rejects this, reasoning that grain stored within a household is not clearly set apart from the rest of the household's grain — family members would treat it all as undifferentiated, so there is nothing that effectively protects its distinct status. It therefore cannot be considered *mishtameret* in any meaningful sense.

### Two Answers

The *gemara* offered two possible resolutions. The first was to reframe the entire transaction: rather than a *kinyan chatzer*, the transfer may have operated as a *kinyan agav* — whereby ownership of the contents is transferred alongside the transfer of the space itself. The second answer, with which the *gemara* concludes, is introduced by Rav Papa.

### Rav Papa's Resolution

Rav Papa declares: *da'at acheret makneh otah shani* — when another party's intent is what drives the transfer, the case is fundamentally different. The requirement that a *chatzer* be *mishtameret* or that one stand alongside it applies specifically to *metzia*, where the person must exert the full force of his own act of acquisition. When, however, someone else is actively transferring the object — when another's *da'at* is the engine of the *kinyan* — the recipient's own act of possession need not be as robust. A looser form of holding suffices, and therefore neither *mishtameret* nor *omed betzad* is required.

---

## Da'at Acheret

### Source: Chasing Deer

The *gemara* now asks: from where does one derive this principle of *da'at acheret makneh*? The source is the *mishnah* itself, which describes people running after a deer. The *mishnah*'s discussion of a broken-legged deer implies a meaningful condition about what constitutes sufficient holding.

### Deer Seizure Test

Rabbi Yirmeyah, citing Rabbi Yochanan, clarifies that the distinction between a broken-legged and a healthy deer is not the decisive criterion per se. What matters is whether one could run after the animal and seize it before it exits the *chatzer*. If one can, the *chatzer* acquires; if not, it does not. This is the operative test for whether an object is sufficiently "held" within the *chatzer* for *kinyan* purposes.

### Matanah Question

Rabbi Yirmeyah then raises a new question: what is the rule if the deer is being given to you as a *matanah* — a gift — and it is running through your yard? Must you also be able to run after it and seize it before it escapes, or does the act of gift-giving alter the standard? Rabbi Abba bar Kahana understood the intent of Rabbi Yirmeyah's question to point toward a distinction: in the case of *matanah*, the answer is that it works *even if* you cannot run after the deer and seize it before it exits.

### Matanah vs Metzia

What explains the difference? The *gemara* reasons: *lav mishum de-da'at acheret makneh otah shani* — is it not because, when another party is actively transferring the object to you, that is itself the distinguishing factor? When *da'at acheret* is doing the work of the transfer, your own act of taking possession need not meet the ordinary threshold. Thus, a deer running through your yard that you cannot catch suffices for *matanah*, whereas for *metzia* you require either *mishtameret* or *omed betzad sadehu*.

---

## Get Exception

### Rav Shimi Challenge

Rav Shimi poses a challenge to Rav Papa's principle. The case of *get* — a bill of divorce — is itself a paradigmatic instance of *da'at acheret makneh*: the husband is the one transferring it to the wife, and indeed he may do so even against her will. If anything, *da'at acheret* is at its strongest here, since it is exclusively the husband's *da'at* that drives the transaction. On Rav Papa's reasoning, then, even the loosest holding by her *chatzer* should suffice.

### Ulla on Get

Yet Ulla rules precisely the opposite: for a *get* to be received through the wife's *chatzer*, she must be *omedet betzad beita o betzad chatzerah* — standing alongside her house or alongside her courtyard. Even the strong *da'at acheret* of the husband does not relax the requirement; instead, a stricter standard applies.

### Get Forced Transfer

The *gemara* explains: *shani get de-iteih be-al karchah* — a *get* is different because it can be forced upon the woman. Since the *get* is something that can be delivered to her detriment and without her consent, one requires a stronger demonstration of her taking possession. The logic, at least on one reading, is that if the husband can do everything and she plays no active role, her act of possession must correspondingly be more pronounced.

### Kal Vachomer

Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi challenges this reasoning with a *kal vachomer* that runs in precisely the opposite direction. A *get*, which the husband can force upon her — where her participation is not required and the *Torah* itself has empowered the husband to the point of disregarding her role — and yet we still require her to be standing by. Should we not reason: if even in *get*, where she is treated almost as a passive object, we require her standing, then certainly by *matanah*, where her *da'at* and active receipt are relevant, we should require it as well? The *gemara* notes that the argument can indeed go either way with respect to *get*. The matter is clarified definitively by Rav Ashi.

---

## Rav Ashi Framework

### Yad or Shaliach

Rav Ashi provides the definitive framework. He states: *chatzer ishtari beh mishum yad ve-lo gara mi-shlichut* — a *chatzer* functions in two possible modes. When one is standing beside it, it functions as *yad*, a direct extension of the person's own body. Even when one is not standing beside it, it functions no worse than a *shaliach*, an agent acting on one's behalf. These are two distinct mechanisms, and which one applies depends on the circumstances.

### Ein Chavin L'Adam

The critical limiting principle is *ein chavin le-adam ella be-fanav* — one cannot act to another's detriment except in that person's presence. The reason *chatzer* can acquire on someone's behalf even without their knowledge, when it functions as *shaliach*, is rooted in the principle *zachin le-adam she-lo be-fanav*: one may act to another's benefit without that person being present, just as a third party may pick up a *metzia* on someone else's behalf, since doing so only helps that person. But where the act is to the person's detriment, an agent cannot act without explicit designation — and in any case, a *chatzer* is not a real person capable of being formally designated as an agent.

### Get Needs Yad

This is precisely why *get* is categorically different. A *get* is considered to be to the woman's detriment — she loses the rights and protections that inhere in marriage — and therefore *chatzer* cannot function as her *shaliach* in receiving it. The category of *get* is seen as detrimental regardless of whether in a particular case she desires the divorce. Since *chatzer* cannot operate as *shaliach* for something to her detriment, and since she cannot formally appoint her *chatzer* as an agent for this purpose (*chatzer* not being a legal person), the *chatzer* can only function as *yad*. And *yad* requires her to be *omedet betzad beita* — present beside the *chatzer* so that it is a direct extension of her.

### Three Categories

This yields three distinct categories. For *get*, even if the *chatzer* is *mishtameret* — even her own house — she must be standing beside it, because it can only function as *yad*. For *matanah*, which is to the recipient's benefit, *zachin le-adam she-lo be-fanav* applies, and the *chatzer* can function as *shaliach* even without the recipient present or standing nearby; moreover, since *da'at acheret* is transferring it, even the loosest holding suffices. For *metzia*, which falls between these poles, the *chatzer* can function as *shaliach*, but because no one else's *da'at* is actively driving the transfer, the recipient's own act of acquisition must be more robust — requiring either *mishtameret* or *omed betzad sadehu*.

One note that should not be overlooked: the *mishnah* itself states that the person must actually declare, "let my field acquire on my behalf." The *gemara*'s entire subsequent discussion proceeds without engaging this requirement, and Tosafot acknowledges it is puzzling. One might distinguish between *mishtameret*, where perhaps no declaration is needed, and *eina mishtameret* with *omed betzad*, where perhaps a declaration is required — but the *mishnah*'s language has been entirely bracketed in the *gemara*'s analysis, which is itself a striking omission.

---

## Wallet Example

### Flying Wallet

Rava poses a question: if someone throws a wallet (*arneki*) through one opening in a *chatzer* and it is flying toward the other opening such that it will exit without ever landing — is that considered to be within the *chatzer* for purposes of *kinyan*? The question is framed as: *avira she-ein sofo lanu'ach kemanu'ach dami o lo* — does airspace through which an object passes but never comes to rest count as equivalent to the object being stationary within the *chatzer*?

### Flying vs Rolling

Rav Pappa (and according to some versions, Rav Adda bar Matna or Ravina) responds to Rava: is this not addressed by the *mishnah* itself, from which Rabbi Yirmeyah derived that only if one can run after the deer and seize it does the *chatzer* acquire? That ruling implies that something passing through uncontrollably — like a wallet flying through without landing — would not constitute presence in the *chatzer* for the purpose of *metzia*. However, the person throwing the wallet is clearly doing so with intent to transfer — making it a case of *da'at acheret*. And Rabbi Yirmeyah's question about *matanah*, accepted by Rabbi Abba bar Kahana, established that with *da'at acheret* even a deer that cannot be caught suffices. So does not the same reasoning apply here?

The response draws a crucial distinction: *mitgalgel kamarta? shani mitgalgel kemanu'ach dami* — were you speaking of something rolling? Something that rolls through the *chatzer* is treated as if it were stationary. But something flying through the airspace is a different matter entirely. If an object is falling into one's airspace and will land within the *chatzer*, one acquires it at the moment it enters the airspace. But an object flying through the airspace without ever touching the ground cannot be said to be within the *chatzer* at all.

### Presence in Yard

Thus three distinct levels emerge: flying through airspace without landing — possibly not present in the *chatzer* at all; rolling through the ground — treated as stationary, and therefore present; stationary — fully present. For *metzia*, one would need *mishtameret* or *omed betzad* even for a rolling object, since the question of whether it is being "held" remains live. But for *matanah*, with *da'at acheret*, even a rolling or running object (like the deer) suffices, though a merely flying object may not clear even that lower threshold.

---

## Household Metzia

### Mishna Overview

The *gemara* now turns to the next *mishnah*, which addresses several categories of household members whose findings belong to another party: *metziat beno uvito haktanim* — the findings of one's minor son and daughter; *metziat avdo veshifchato hakena'anim* — one's Canaanite slaves; and *metziat ishto* — one's wife. In all these cases, the *mishnah* rules: *harei elu shelo* — they belong to the husband or father.

### Wife Rationale

The rationale for the wife is rooted in the reciprocal structure of obligations that the rabbis established within marriage. The husband bears responsibility for housing, food, clothing, and a range of other provisions; in exchange, whatever the wife earns or finds belongs to him.
