Rather, he figured — *savar achti lo pasuku rabbanan l'dinei* — that since the court had not yet issued a final execution order, perhaps the judges would reconsider and change their ruling. He was buying time, stalling until the court's judgment would be finalized with a *tzei ten lo*. Under this reading, his lie about payment was not genuine theft — it was a tactical deferral, premised on the belief that the case was not yet fully adjudicated.

This rationale is admittedly difficult. The person did lie. He was not planning to steal, perhaps, but he was clearly making a false claim. Why, then, is his subsequent claim of *parati* credited? The *gemara* seems to be drawing a distinction between a moral failing that undermines fundamental credibility and a strategic evasion that, while dishonest, does not rise to the level of *kafran*. One might observe that the court is attempting to account for the realities of human behavior under the pressure of litigation — while still requiring justice to be done. Whether that rationale fully satisfies is, as one may note, a question worth sitting with.

---

## Kafran Applications

### Rabba Case

Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan a case that directly illustrates *huchzak kafran*: "You owe me a hundred dinars." The defendant replies: "I owe you nothing." Witnesses then testify that the debt exists. The defendant, now cornered, says: "Fine — but I have already paid." In this scenario — where the person first made a *fundamental* denial of the entire claim — *huchzak kafran le'oto mamon*: his subsequent claim of *parati* is not believed, even though ordinarily a debtor's claim of payment is credited.

The distinction between this case and the *ishtamutei* scenario is important. The person who said *chayav ata liten lo* and then claimed he had paid was, on one interpretation, not truly trying to escape the obligation — he was misreading the procedural posture of the case. But a person who flatly denies that any debt exists, and is then proven by witnesses to be lying, has made a categorical misrepresentation. When he subsequently claims he has already paid, there is no procedural excuse to explain away the original lie, and so he cannot recover credibility on this particular claim.

### Shabtai Case

The *gemara* illustrates this principle with a concrete case: Shabtai the son of Rav Marinus wrote into his daughter-in-law's *kesubah* an obligation to provide her with a particular silk garment (*itzlita d'milta*), accepting personal responsibility for this obligation. When the *kesubah* was lost (*irkas ksubatah*), he denied that any such obligation had ever existed: *lo hayu devarim me'olam* — "it never happened." Witnesses then testified that he had indeed written the obligation. He then claimed: *l'sof amar lehu parati* — "In the end, I paid her." The matter came before Rabbi Chiya, who ruled: *huchzak kafran l'ota itzlita* — for the obligation regarding this garment, he is established as a denier, and his claim of payment is not credited.

This case differs slightly from the *tzei ten lo* scenario in that it was not a court proceeding but a direct debt dispute. The principle, however, is the same: where a person makes a categorical denial of an obligation, is proven false by witnesses, and then shifts to claiming payment, the *huchzak kafran* doctrine removes his credibility on that specific claim.

### Oath Extension

Rav Avin, citing Rav Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, extends the *huchzak kafran* principle from monetary debts to *shvu'ot*. If a court obligated someone to take a *shvua* in a dispute — as in the classic case of *modeh b'miktzat*, where one admits to part of a claim and is obligated to swear regarding the remainder — and that person then claims: "I have already made the *shvua*, we went to Starbucks together and I swore there," and witnesses then testify that no such *shvua* was made, and the person subsequently says: "Fine, that was a lie, but I made the *shvua* yesterday" — then *huchzak kafran l'ota shvua*: his further claims of having fulfilled the oath are not believed.

This application is noteworthy for a reason beyond the *kafran* doctrine itself. It presupposes that a *shvua* mandated by a court can be validly discharged outside the court setting — that one may, in effect, "pay" the *shvua* to the other party informally, without the court administering it. The *shvua* is treated as a kind of obligation that can be satisfied privately, and the person who owes it is believed to say he has done so — just as he would be believed to say he has paid a money debt. That the *shvua* is treated in this way — as a transferable obligation rather than strictly a judicial instrument — is itself a remarkable premise of the *sugyah*.

### Oath Distinction

Rabbi Abbahu, when presented with this teaching, confirms and clarifies its scope. He says: *mistavera milta d'Rav Avin, shechiyvuh shvua b'beis din* — the rule makes sense precisely because the court obligated him to take the *shvua*. In that case, lying about the *shvua* is analogous to the *tzei ten lo* scenario: the court has issued what amounts to a binding directive, and evading it by falsely claiming it has been fulfilled renders one a *kafran* for that obligation.

But *aval chiyav atzmo shvua* — if the person voluntarily obligated himself to make a *shvua* without any court mandate, and then claimed he had made it, and was proven by witnesses to have lied — he remains believed when he subsequently claims to have fulfilled the oath. The reason is again *ishtamutei ka mishtamit lei*: since the *shvua* was self-imposed and not court-ordered, he did not regard himself as genuinely bound to it, and his initial lie was a casual evasion rather than a deliberate act of defiance of a legal obligation. He therefore does not lose credibility in the way one does when contradicting a *beis din*-mandated commitment.

Rabbi Avin himself later clarifies, when the matter is brought back to him, that this was precisely his intent from the outset: the rule of *huchzak kafran* applies to a *shvua* that the court obligated, but not to one that the person voluntarily assumed.

This is corroborated by a parallel tradition: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav, and some say in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *haya chayav l'chavero shvua b'beis din, ve'amar nishbati, ve'eidim me'idim oso shelo nishba, huchzak kafran l'osa shvua* — if the court obligated him to swear, he claimed to have sworn, and witnesses proved otherwise, he is established as a *kafran* for that oath going forward.

---

## Document Dating

### Same-Day Docs

Rabbi Assi, citing Rabbi Yochanan, addresses a further scenario in the context of returning found debt documents: *hamotzi shtar chov bashuk, v'chasuv bo hanpek, v'chasuv bo zmano bo bayom, yachzir l'ba'alin* — if one finds a validated debt document dated to today, one may return it to the creditor. The reasoning follows the familiar two-part structure. The concern of *kasav lilvos velo lava* is neutralized by the *hanpek* — the court validation demonstrates the money was lent. And *pira bas yoma lo chaishinan* — we are not concerned that a debt would have been borrowed and repaid within the same day. Since the document is dated today, and same-day repayment is exceedingly unlikely, we infer that the debt is still outstanding, and the document may be returned to the *malveh*.

### Reuse Problem

Rabbi Zeira challenges this ruling. He reminds Rabbi Assi of his own reported teaching in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *shtar shelava bo u'para'o eino chozer veloveh bo* — if David borrowed money on a *shtar* and then paid off the debt, he cannot reuse that same document for a subsequent loan. The reason is that *shekvar nimchal shibudo* — the liens created by the document were discharged at the moment of repayment, and a new loan would require a new document with newly created liens. Using the old document for a new loan would be like using a burned match.

Now, Rabbi Zeira notes, when would such reuse even be a concern? If the original document was dated weeks or months ago and the debtor wants to reuse it for a new loan today, there is an independent problem: the document would be *mukdam*, predated, which invalidates it. *Shtarot hamukdamim pesulin* — predated documents are invalid. Therefore, the only scenario in which reuse is genuinely tempting and technically conceivable — the document has not yet become *mukdam* — is when the original loan and its repayment occurred on the same day as the new loan. In other words, the concern of document reuse exists precisely on the same day.

*Alma parei inshi b'yomei* — this shows that people do in fact pay off debts on the same day. Otherwise, there would be no reason to rule that a same-day document cannot be reused. This seems to undercut Rabbi Assi's assumption that same-day repayment is so rare that one need not worry about it when returning a found document.

### Reuse Resolution

Rabbi Assi responds: *mi kamina d'la para* — I never claimed that same-day repayment never happens. *Lo shechiach inshi l'mifrei b'yomei kamina* — I said it is uncommon. It is precisely because it is not the norm that one need not be concerned about it for the purpose of returning a found *shtar*. The ruling that one cannot reuse a document after repaying the loan is a general restriction that applies even to the rare case, and the ruling that one may return a same-day document is a probabilistic assessment that applies despite that rare case. There is no inconsistency: Rabbi Yochanan can simultaneously hold that same-day repayment does technically occur and that it is rare enough not to generate a halakhic concern in the context of returning found documents.

An alternative reading is offered by Rav Kahana: the ruling to return a same-day document applies specifically when the *loveh* himself admits he has not yet paid (*kshe'chayav modeh*). This reading avoids any tension with the reuse problem entirely, but raises its own questions.

### Creditor Cooperation

The *gemara* then addresses the concern that the debtor might be falsely claiming not to have paid — claiming the debt is still outstanding — specifically to engineer the return of the *shtar* so that it can be reused for a subsequent loan, thus saving the cost of engaging a new scribe. This scheme would require the debtor to say "I haven't paid yet" when in fact he has, in order to get the document back into the creditor's hands, after which they would reuse it for a new loan.

The *gemara* dismisses this concern by noting that the creditor would not cooperate: *de'im kein malveh gufei lo shavik* — if this is what the debtor is planning, the creditor himself would refuse to go along with it. Why? *Savar shami bei rabbanan u'mifsidi li* — the creditor would be afraid that the rabbis would find out and he would lose his loan entirely. The creditor knows that reusing a discharged *shtar* is legally impermissible, and he will not jeopardize his investment for the debtor's convenience.

### Early Dating

By contrast, the *gemara* notes that in the parallel case of *mukdam* documents, one might ask the same question: if the *malveh* would refuse to cooperate in any fraudulent scheme, why are we ever concerned about predated documents? The answer is that in the *mukdam* scenario, the creditor actually has a strong incentive to cooperate. An earlier date on the document gives the creditor earlier liens, allowing him to seize properties that were transferred by the debtor between the fabricated date and the actual loan date. The gain from earlier liens outweighs the risk of the document being voided. Therefore, *meinach nicha lei v'lo amar lei v'lo midi* — the creditor is content to accept the risk and say nothing. The concern for *mukdam* documents is therefore legitimate, whereas the concern for same-day reuse is not, because in the same-day scenario the creditor gains nothing from cooperating with the scheme.

The practical conclusion is: a found *shtar chov* bearing today's date and a *hanpek* may be returned to the creditor. The concern of *pira'on* is minimal given same-day repayment's rarity, and the concern of collusive reuse is neutralized because the creditor has no incentive to cooperate.

---

## Ketubah Principles

### Maaseh Beis Din

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yochanan, introduces a further principle: *ha'toein achar maaseh beis din, lo amar klum* — one who asserts a claim against a *maaseh beis din*, his words are nothing. Specifically, in the context of the *kesubah*, which is an obligation that exists by force of rabbinic enactment even without a written document: if a woman's husband claims he has paid her *kesubah*, he is not believed on the basis of his bare assertion. *Kol maaseh beis din k'man d'nakit shtar b'yadei dami* — every *maaseh beis din* is treated as though the claimant is holding a *shtar*, and the burden falls on the one who claims to have discharged it to bring proof.

### Ketubah Proof

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba then asks Rabbi Yochanan whether this principle is not in fact already explicit in a *mishnah* in *Kesubos*: *hotziah get v'ein imah kesubah, govah kesubatah* — if a woman produces a *get* but has no accompanying *kesubah*, she nevertheless collects her *kesubah*. This implies that a woman without a physical *kesubah* document can still collect, meaning that the husband's claim of *parati* is not believed even in the absence of the written instrument. The *kesubah* obligation, being a *maaseh beis din*, stands without documentary proof.

Rabbi Yochanan responds with a statement that is itself an implicit claim to having illuminated the *mishnah* rather than simply derived from it: *had I not lifted the pottery shard, you would not have found the pearl beneath it.* That is, the *mishnah* alone, while consistent with the principle, could have been explained differently; it required Rabbi Yochanan's insight to clarify what it truly teaches.

### Documentation Requirement

Abaye takes up this challenge. He questions whether the *mishnah* truly proves the breadth of Rabbi Yochanan's principle, suggesting an alternative reading: *eima b'makom she'ein kosing kesuvah askinan, de'get hainu kesuvashah* — the *mishnah* may be addressing a place where *kesubot* are not customarily written, and in such a place the *get* itself serves as the functional equivalent of the *kesubah*. When she produces the *get*, she has a document; she is not collecting on the basis of a bare *maaseh beis din* alone.

Under this reading, in a place where *kesubot* are written, the rule would be: *ei nakta kesuvah gavya ve'ei lo lo gavya* — if she holds the *kesubah* she collects, if not she does not. The husband would be believed to claim payment if she produces no documentation. Abaye thus challenges whether the *mishnah* really establishes Rabbi Yochanan's sweeping principle.

### Widow Erusin

Abaye himself, however, immediately retracts this reading. He notes that if one follows his logic to its conclusion — that in a place where *kesubot* are written, a woman always needs a physical document to collect — then the case of an *almanah min ha'eirusin*, a widow from *eirusin*, becomes impossible. Such a woman is entitled to her *kesubah* from the time of the *erusin*, since the fundamental obligation arises then. But the *kesubah* document is typically not written until *nissuim*, and an *almanah* has no *get*. If documentary proof is always required, *b'mai gavya* — how would she ever collect? The heirs of the estate could simply say their father paid, and she would have no recourse.

*Im kein mah ho'ilu chachamim b'takanatam* — if this were the rule, what was the point of the Rabbis' enactment that a woman is entitled to a *kesubah*? The institution would be rendered worthless in precisely the case of the *almanah min ha'eirusin*, because anyone could defeat her claim with a bare assertion of payment.

Abaye therefore concedes that Rabbi Yochanan's principle is correct: the *kesubah* obligation is so firmly grounded as a *maaseh beis din* that the husband — or his heirs — is not believed to claim *parati* without proof. The practical consequence for the husband is that he must ensure he obtains the *kesubah* document itself from the woman upon payment, or a written receipt (*shovar*), and must retain that documentation. *Tosafot* notes that the standard presumption is *kotvin shovar* — the debtor may demand a receipt — and that expectation is the natural corollary of the stringent protection extended to the woman's claim.

### Braita Analysis

The *gemara* then raises a question about the foundational premise of Abaye's argument. Mar Kashisha the son of Rav Chisda asks Rav Ashi: the entire proof rests on the assumption that an *almanah min ha'eirusin* is entitled to a *kesubah* even without a written document. But how do we know this? The basic *kesubah* entitlement might be established only at *nissuim*, with various reciprocal obligations of support and the *tosefet* — the additional amount offered by the husband — all becoming operative only from *nissuim* onward.

The questioner cites a *mishnah*: *nis'es o nisgareshah, bein min ha'eirusin uvein min hanissuim, govah es hakol* — whether she married or was divorced, whether from *eirusin* or from *nissuim*, she collects the full amount. Does this not prove that the *kesubah* obligation exists from *erusin*?

The *gemara* demurs: perhaps this *mishnah* addresses only the case where a *kesubah* was actually written from the time of *erusin*. If so, the novelty of the ruling is not that the obligation exists without a document, but that it exists in full — including the *tosefet* — despite having been written at the stage of *erusin*. And the specific opposition it addresses is the position of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah holds: *shelo chasav lah ela al menas l'chonsah* — when a *kesubah* was written at *erusin*, the husband's intention in writing it, particularly with respect to the *tosefet*, was directed toward the eventual *chuppah*. If she is divorced before *nissuim*, she should not receive the *tosefet*, because that additional sum was contingent upon the marriage being consummated. The *rabbanan* reject this and say that once it is written, she collects everything — *govah es hakol* — even from *erusin*. The *mishnah*'s ruling thus addresses a debate about a case where a document exists, not a case where the obligation arises without any document.

The question of whether Abaye's proof — that an *almanah min ha'eirusin* is entitled to collect her *kesubah* without a written document — can be grounded in this *braita*, or requires some other source, remains open at the close of the *daf*. The full resolution is deferred to the next session.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 18

## Arusah & Ketubah

### Problem Setup

The daf opens in the middle of a broader discussion: can a husband claim *parati* — that he has already paid — against a standing obligation imposed by rabbinic legislation, a *ma'aseh beis din*? Specifically, the question at hand is whether the principle articulated by Rebbi Yochanan — that *ha-to'en achar ma'aseh beis din lo amar klum*, one who claims payment against a court-imposed obligation is not believed — can be proven from the case of a woman who collects her *kesuvah* even without holding a written *kesuvah* document, relying instead on her *get*.

Before returning to that larger argument, the *gemara* works through a subsidiary question: does a woman who was an *arusah* — that is, she had received *kiddushin* but had not yet proceeded to *nisuin*, she had received the ring but had not yet established a shared home or undergone the *chuppah* — have an entitlement to a *kesuvah* if her husband dies?

### Chiya bar Ami

The *gemara* cites a teaching of Rebbi Chiya bar Ami bearing on the status of the *arusah*. The teaching states: *ishto arusah lo onen velo mitameh lah* — if a man's wife is only an *arusah* and she dies, he does not become an *onen* and, if he is a *kohen*, he does not contract *tumah* on her behalf. This is because the verse *ki im lish'ero hakarov eilav* — his flesh that is close to him — implies that the full relationship of *basar echad* does not apply until they actually begin living together in *nisuin*. Similarly, *ve-chein hi* — the same applies in reverse: if he dies, she incurs none of the corresponding obligations. Furthermore, *meisah eino yorshah* — if she dies, he does not inherit her, since all the reciprocal rights of inheritance, support, and housing take effect only from *nisuin*.

Yet the teaching concludes: *meis hu gova kesuvasah* — if he dies, she collects her *kesuvah*. Here, then, is an explicit source that an *arusah* has a right to the *kesuvah*.

### Abyei Rejects

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge: *dilma de-kasav lah* — perhaps the teaching speaks only of a case in which the husband explicitly wrote the *kesuvah* at the time of *erusin*, and without such explicit writing she would have no entitlement until *nisuin*. One might ask why the teaching would bother stating that she collects the *kesuvah* in such an obvious case. The answer is that the primary novelty (*chiddush*) of the passage is the ruling *meisah eino yorshah* — that he does not inherit her — and the *kesuvah* clause came along incidentally. So there is no proof that an *arusah* collects a *kesuvah* by force of rabbinic enactment alone, absent an explicit written document.

This matters greatly for the earlier discussion. Abaye had sought to push aside the proof for Rebbi Yochanan's principle by arguing that the case of the woman collecting based on her *get* — in a locale where a *kesuvah* is not normally written — is not evidence of *ma'aseh beis din* at all. Rather, in such a locale the *get* itself functions as a *kesuvah*. The woman holds a *shtar*, and one is never believed to say *parati* against a *shtar* in the creditor's possession. The *ma'aseh beis din* principle need not be invoked.

### Get as Proof

The *gemara* now sets out to demonstrate why Abaye ultimately abandoned this line of reasoning — not on account of anything external, but *mi-gufei de-masnisin*, from the internal logic of the *mishnah* itself. The *gemara* poses the question: if the *get* is to function as a *kesuvah* in a locale where no *kesuvah* is written, what does it actually prove?

*Atu get maneh masayim kesiv bei?* — Does the *get* state the amount? Does it say whether the husband owed 100 or 200 *zuz*, or whether he had added a *tosefes*? Obviously not. The *get* alone cannot establish the specifics of the debt. The only way the amount can be known is by invoking the standing rabbinic obligation — the *ma'aseh beis din* — which sets the presumptive amounts.

One might respond: *keivan de-takinu rabanan le-migba lei, ke-man de-kasav lah dami* — since the Rabbis enacted that she collects, it is as if the amount were written, and thus the *get* can be treated as a *shtar* attesting to that known amount. If so, the husband should not be believed to say *parati* because he is contradicted by a *shtar* she holds.

But the *gemara* presses further: *ve-leisima lei parati* — why shouldn't he be believed? Ordinarily, when a debtor says he has paid and the creditor still holds the *shtar*, the debtor is not believed because if he had truly paid, he should have insisted on tearing up the *shtar*. But here, the *get* cannot simply be torn, because the woman needs it intact to prove she is divorced and to remarry. As Ravina notes, *linsuvei beih* — she needs the *get* to be whole. So the husband has a ready answer: I paid, but I could not take back or destroy the *get* because she would not permit it.

The *gemara* counters: could he not have torn it and had the *beis din* write on the back that *ketivat dena de-karnuhu* — this *get* was torn not because it is invalid but so that she cannot use it to collect her *kesuvah* a second time? The *gemara* then disposes of this: *atu kol de-migbi be-vei dina migbi* — does every payment of a debt happen in front of a *beis din*? She approaches him, he pays her the 200 *zuz*, there is no *beis din* present, she will not agree to tear it, and there is nothing he can do. He therefore has a perfectly plausible explanation for why she still holds the *get* even after payment.

The upshot is decisive. If the reason the husband is not believed were merely that she holds a *shtar*, there would be a legitimate counter-argument — he could plausibly claim payment despite her holding the *get*. The fact that he is nonetheless not believed forces the conclusion that it is the *ma'aseh beis din* itself — the standing court-imposed obligation of *kesuvah* — that strips him of his credibility. This is the proof for Rebbi Yochanan's principle.

As a practical postscript: while the specific cases discussed above did not yield a proof for the *arusah's* entitlement, the *halacha* is nonetheless that an *arusah* does collect a base *kesuvah*, though she does not receive any *tosefes* unless it was explicitly written.

---

## Parati & Ma'aseh

### Get vs. Shtar

The *gemara* has now established, through the process of elimination described above, that the husband's inability to claim *parati* against the *kesuvah* obligation is rooted in the nature of *ma'aseh beis din* — a court-imposed obligation that cannot be waived by a unilateral claim of payment. The *get*, it turns out, cannot serve as a functional *shtar* for these purposes, because it does not contain the amount and because the husband has a ready excuse for why she still holds it even after payment.

### Tearing Get

The *gemara* had suggested a possible mechanism: have the *get* torn and have the *beis din* write on its back a notation clarifying that the tearing does not render the *get* invalid, but is done solely to prevent its reuse for collection of the *kesuvah*. This would eliminate the husband's excuse and allow the *get* to function as a *shtar* whose continued possession by the wife would preclude his claim of *parati*.

### Practical Issue

This theoretical solution founders on a practical point: *atu kol de-migbi be-vei dina migbi* — not every debt is paid in the presence of a *beis din*. The payment of a *kesuvah* commonly takes place directly between husband and wife. In such a setting, the wife has no obligation to surrender the *get*, the *beis din* is not present to supervise any notation, and the husband has no enforceable recourse. His continued inability to demand the tearing of the *get* therefore constitutes a genuine and plausible excuse. This excuse does not exist in the case of ordinary *shtarot*, where the creditor has no independent reason to retain the document.

### Conclusion

The conclusion that emerges from this entire analysis is that the principle of Rebbi Yochanan stands confirmed: one who owes an obligation imposed by *ma'aseh beis din* and claims to have paid it is not believed, and the inability to claim *parati* in the *get* case is attributable to that principle rather than to the *get's* functioning as a *shtar*. The *get* does not contain the amount owed, and the husband retains a plausible excuse for its non-return — two features that prevent it from operating as a conventional *shtar*. Thus the woman's ability to collect her *kesuvah* even without a written document, and the husband's inability to counter with *parati*, derives from the *ma'aseh beis din* itself.

---

## Found Documents

### Don't Return

The *mishnah* now turns to a different but related set of cases involving found documents. *Motzei gittei nashim ve-shichrurei avadim* — one who finds a *get* for a woman, a writ of manumission freeing a slave, a *diatiki* (a deathbed declaration distributing one's property, akin to a will), a *matanah* (a gift document transferring a parcel of land), or a *shover* (a receipt acknowledging that a debt was paid, issued when the creditor did not have the original *shtar* to return). In all these cases: *harei zeh lo yachzir* — do not return the document to the intended beneficiary. Do not give the *get* to the wife, do not give the manumission to the slave, do not give the gift document to the recipient, do not give the receipt to the debtor.

### Changed Mind

The reason for this rule is: *she-ani omer ketuvin hayu* — perhaps these documents were written but then *venimlach aleihen she-lo litnam* — the writer changed his mind and decided not to deliver them. Because we do not know whether the document fell from the writer before delivery or from the intended recipient after receipt, and because the concern that the writer changed his mind is real, we cannot assume the document was actually given. We therefore hold it rather than completing a delivery that may never have been intended.

### Explicit Consent

The *gemara* draws an inference from the *mishnah*: *ta'ama de-nimlach she-lo litnam* — the stated concern is that the writer changed his mind. This implies *ha amar tenu, nosnin* — that if the writer explicitly says "give it," we do give it, because the only reason we were holding back was the concern about a change of mind, and that concern is now resolved. Moreover, this would apply *va-afilu l'zman merubeh* — even if the document was found long after it was lost, because once the writer affirms his intention, the concern dissipates regardless of the elapsed time.

---

## Lost Get Problem

### Braita Rule

This inference, however, generates a difficulty when compared with another source. A *braita* in *Gittin* states: *ha-meivi get ve-avad heimenu* — a *shaliach* who is conveying a *get* and loses it — *matza'o l'altar kasher ve-im lav pasul* — if he finds it immediately, it is valid; if not, it is invalid. The reason is that if time has passed, we fear that the *get* he found is not the same one he lost but rather belongs to a different couple who happen to share the same names.

### Contradiction

This *braita* stands in apparent contradiction to our *mishnah*. The *mishnah* implies that if the husband says "give it," you give it even after a long time. But the *braita* says that after a significant delay, the *get* is invalid — we are concerned it is a different *get* with the same names. If so, even if the husband affirms he wants to divorce his wife, how can we give this *get* when we cannot be sure it is his?

### Rava's Solution

Rava resolves the contradiction: *kan be-makom she-shayarot metzuyot, kan be-makom she-ein shayarot metzuyot* — the two sources address different situations. When caravans are common in the area — when it is a busy thoroughfare through which travelers from many locales constantly pass — there is a meaningful concern that the found *get* might belong to a different couple from elsewhere who share the same names. The *braita* that invalidates a *get* found after a delay speaks of such a location. The *mishnah*, which implies that you give the *get* upon the husband's say-so even if time has passed, speaks of a location where caravans are not common. In such a place, there is no realistic concern that another couple with identical names happened to leave a *get* in the same area.

The *gemara* then introduces an additional restriction. Even in a place where caravans are common, Rava adds a second criterion: *ve-hu she-huchzeku shnei Yosef ben Shimon be-ir achat* — we are only genuinely concerned that the found *get* is a different one if it is also known that two couples with the same names reside in that same city. A *get* always specifies the city, so if it says Yosef ben Shimon of this city divorces his wife Sarah bas Rachel, the concern that it belongs to a different couple only arises concretely if we know that such a second couple exists in that city. Without that knowledge, the mere fact of a busy thoroughfare does not suffice to disqualify the *get*.

---

## Rava's Criteria

### Rav Huna Story

The two-criterion requirement attributed to Rava emerges from a specific episode. A *get* was found in the *beis din* of Rav Huna. The *get* bore the notation that it was written in the city of Shviri situated on the river Rechis. A *shaliach* came forward claiming it was the *get* he had lost. Rav Huna ruled *chashinan le-shnei Shviri* — we are concerned that there may be another city also called Shviri situated on the same river, with a couple bearing the same names. He therefore declined to return the *get* to the *shaliach*.

### Chisda's Challenge

Rav Chisda instructed Rava to go and research the matter, as Rav Huna would need an answer by evening. In Rav Huna's case, it was known that there were not two couples with the same names within the same city — yet Rav Huna was still concerned, on account of the possibility of an entirely different city by the same name. This suggests that *shayarot metzuyot* — the presence of a busy thoroughfare — alone is sufficient reason not to return, without needing to establish the presence of duplicate names in the same locale.

### Ma'aseh Beis Din

Rava went and researched, and found the following passage in the *mishnah* of this very *perek*: *kol ma'aseh beis din harei zeh yachzir* — anything that has undergone court processing, such as a *shtar chov* whose signatures were validated by the *beis din*, is returned to the *malveh*. Rava understood this *mishnah* as addressing a document found in the courthouse itself. And a courthouse, he reasoned, is precisely the kind of place that qualifies as *makom she-shayarot metzuyot* — a place where people are constantly coming and going from many different locations. Yet the *mishnah* says to return it. This implies that *shayarot metzuyot* alone is not sufficient to withhold the document.

### Two Criteria

From this, Rava concluded that only when both conditions are met — *shayarot metzuyot* and known duplicate names — do we decline to return the document. If only one condition is present, we return it. This explains his ruling in the Rav Huna case as well: Rava told Rav Huna that the *get* should be returned, since it was established that there were not two couples with the same names in that city, and the *ma'aseh beis din* precedent demonstrated that *shayarot metzuyot* alone does not require withholding.

The *gemara* records that Rava acted on this *halacha* in practice in the flax district of Pumbedita. One version of the story holds that *kitna* refers to the marketplace where flax is sold — a busy, high-traffic location — and Rava returned the *get* because there was no known duplication of names. A second version holds that *kitna* refers to the industrial area where flax is soaked, a quiet location where caravans are not common, and Rava returned the *get* because despite a known duplication of names, *shayarot metzuyot* were absent. Both versions confirm the two-criterion framework: the absence of either criterion is sufficient to permit return.

---

## R. Zeira's Q

### Zeira's Framing

Rabbi Zeira raises a parallel question, though he frames it differently from Rava. Rather than contrasting two *mishnayot*, he contrasts a *mishnah* with a *braita*. The *mishnah* in *Gittin* — the same one Rava cited — states that if a *shaliach* loses a *get* and finds it only after a significant delay, the *get* is invalid, because we fear it may be someone else's. Rabbi Zeira then cites a *braita* in *Gittin*: *matza get isha ba-shuk* — if one finds a woman's *get* in the marketplace — *be-zman she-ha-baal modeh yachzir le-isha* — if the husband acknowledges that he had given it, you return it to the wife; *ein ha-baal modeh lo yachzir lo le-zeh ve-lo le-zeh* — if he does not acknowledge it, you give it to neither party.

The *braita* thus states categorically that if the husband acknowledges it, the *get* is returned to the wife — and this is *va-afilu l'zman merubeh*, presumably even after a substantial delay. But this seems to contradict the *mishnah* that says a *get* found after a delay is invalid because we fear it is a different one. Why, then, does the *braita* permit return simply because the husband acknowledges it?

### Zeira's Answer

Rabbi Zeira resolves the tension exactly as Rava did: *kan be-makom she-shayarot metzuyot, kan be-makom she-ein shayarot metzuyot* — the *mishnah* that invalidates the *get* found after a delay addresses a location with heavy caravan traffic, where the concern for duplicate names is realistic. The *braita* that permits return upon the husband's acknowledgment addresses a location without such traffic, where no such concern applies.

### One vs Two

At this point the *gemara* presents an internal dispute regarding Rabbi Zeira's position. One opinion holds that Rabbi Zeira, like Rava, requires both conditions — *shayarot metzuyot* and known duplication of names — before declining to return the *get*: *ve-hu she-huchzaku de-lo nehadar* — it is only when both criteria are present that we do not return it, and this is identical to Rava's view. A second opinion holds that Rabbi Zeira requires only one criterion: the presence of *shayarot metzuyot* alone suffices to withhold the *get*, even without established knowledge of a second couple bearing the same names. On this reading, Rabbi Zeira and Rava disagree: Rava demands both conditions; Rabbi Zeira demands only one.

---

## Rava vs Zeira

### Rava's Evidence

The *gemara* asks: given that Rava and Rabbi Zeira present essentially the same logical difficulty and arrive at the same structural resolution, why did each scholar frame his question the way he did? Rava contrasted two *mishnayot*; Rabbi Zeira contrasted a *mishnah* with a *braita*. The first part of the answer is straightforward: *matnitin alima leh le-akshuyei* — Rava preferred to draw his contradiction from two *mishnayot*, since they carry equal authority and are presumed to reflect a unified *halachic* stance. A contradiction between two *stam mishna* formulations is stronger and more compelling than one between a *mishnah* and a *braita*.

Now the *gemara* asks from the other direction: why did Rabbi Zeira not use the same source Rava did — namely, our *mishnah* here in Bava Metzia, which implies that if the husband says to give the *get*, one would give it? Why did he instead bring the *braita*? The answer is that our *mishnah's* implication is less than ironclad. The *mishnah* says that the reason we do not deliver a found *get* to the intended party is the concern that the writer changed his mind — implying that if he had not changed his mind, we would give it. But this implication does not necessarily extend to a *get* found after a long delay.

### Zeira's Rebuttal

One might think our *mishnah* implies: if the husband says give it, we give it *va-afilu l'zman merubeh*, even after a long time. But Rabbi Zeira would say: *dilma ha-amar tenunu u-le'olam ke-dikayma lan le-altar* — perhaps the *mishnah* only implies that if the husband says give it and the *get* was found immediately, then yes, you give it. But if found after a delay, perhaps even the husband's word is insufficient, and the *mishnah* simply says nothing about the case of late discovery. The *mishnah's* implication is limited to the case before it; it does not affirmatively rule on the delayed-discovery scenario.

### Explicit vs Implied

The *braita*, by contrast, makes an explicit and categorical statement: *be-zman she-ha-baal modeh yachzir le-isha* — if the husband acknowledges it, you give it to the wife, with no qualification regarding timing. If this were only true when the *get* is found immediately, the *braita* would have said so. An unqualified categorical statement implies that the rule holds in all cases, including after a long delay. It is therefore this explicit, unqualified ruling that creates the genuine tension with the *mishnah* in *Gittin*, and that is why Rabbi Zeira preferred to frame his question around the *braita*.

---

## No Return Rule

### R. Yirmeyah

The *gemara* now presents positions that move in the opposite direction entirely. Rather than asking what special circumstances are required before we *withhold* the *get*, these authorities ask what special circumstances are required before we *return* it. Rabbi Yirmeya states that the case in which the *braita* says to return the *get* to the wife — when the husband acknowledges it — is not the rule but the exception. The rule is that we never return it; we are always concerned, even in a location without caravans and even without known duplicate names. The special case that permits return is when the witnesses signed on the *get* testify: *me'olam lo chasamnu ela al get echad she-yatza bein Shimon* — we have never signed a *get* between these parties other than this one. Since the witnesses affirm that only a single such *get* exists in the world, the concern that the found document belongs to someone else is entirely eliminated.

One might ask: if the witnesses say this, it is obvious the *get* should be returned — what *chiddush* does this add? The *gemara* explains: one might have thought to remain concerned that there exists a second couple bearing exactly the same names as the couple named in the *get* and also signed by witnesses bearing exactly the same names. The *gemara* teaches that we do not extend our concern to such a remote possibility. Rabbi Yirmeya's position is thus at the far end of the spectrum: return requires positive affirmative evidence, and absent such evidence the default is not to return.

### R. Ashi

Rav Ashi takes yet another approach to the special case that permits return. He says the case is one where the *shaliach* who lost the *get* provides a *siman* — an identifying mark: *nekev yesh bo be-tzad os pelonis* — there is a hole in the *get* adjacent to a specific letter. He is able to describe precisely where the hole is located, and upon examination, the found *get* matches that description.

### Siman Types

The *gemara* specifies: *davka be-tzad os pelonis* — only if the *shaliach* is specific about which letter the hole is next to. *Aval nekev be-alma lo* — if he merely says there is a hole somewhere in the document, that does not suffice. A generic hole is not meaningful evidence; many *gittin* may have holes, and this does not prove that the found *get* is his.

This reflects the distinction between a *siman muvhak* — an identifying mark so specific and unusual that it effectively constitutes definitive identification — and a *siman she-eino muvhak* — a mark that narrows the field but does not constitute conclusive proof. Why does Rav Ashi require specifically a *siman muvhak*? Because *Rav Ashi mesafeka lei simanin de-Oraisa o de-Rabanan* — Rav Ashi was uncertain whether a non-definitive *siman* carries *de-Oraisa* validity or only *de-Rabanan* authority. If it is only *de-Rabanan*, then while it may suffice for monetary questions such as identifying a lost object (*metziah*) — where rabbinic enactments carry broad latitude — it would not suffice for a *get*, which determines the personal status (*issur ve-hetter*) of the woman and her eligibility to remarry. Since Rav Ashi could not resolve this question, he would only permit return of the *get* on the basis of a *siman muvhak*, which is strong enough to satisfy even a *de-Oraisa* standard.

The positions thus divide into two camps. Rava and Rabbi Zeira hold that the default is to return a found *get* when the husband affirms his intent, and we withhold it only when special circumstances — one or two criteria, depending on the version of Rabbi Zeira's view — create a genuine concern that it may be someone else's *get*. Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Ashi hold the opposite: the default is not to return the found *get*, and return requires positive special evidence — either the testimony of the *eidim* that only one such *get* exists, or a *siman muvhak* from the *shaliach*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 19

## Lost Get - Simanim

### Rabba's Lost Get

The daf opens at the last line of 18b and continues into 19a. Rabba bar Bar Chana lost a *get* in the *beis medrash*. The Aramaic word *ircas* simply means "lost" — it appears elsewhere in the phrase *kesuvah d'ircasa*, the replacement *kesuvah* written when the original has been lost, in which the scribe records that this document is written in place of the one that went missing.

When Rabba bar Bar Chana sought to recover his *get*, he offered two separate grounds for identification: *amar i simana is li b'gavei i tveias eina is li b'gavei* — either he could provide a *siman*, an identifying mark, or, if preferred, he could simply recognize it by sight. He was prepared to satisfy whichever standard would be required of him.

### Simanim vs. Recognition

They returned the *get* to him. Rabba bar Bar Chana then says: *lo yadana im mishum simana ahadrunei nihalei* — I do not know whether they returned it to me on account of the *siman*, *v'kasvari simanim d'Oraisa*, because they hold that *simanim* are Biblically valid, or whether they returned it because of *tveias eina*, personal recognition.

This requires some unpacking. The *siman* he had was not a *siman muvhak* — not an unmistakable, distinctive mark such as a hole immediately beside a specific letter. It was an ordinary *siman*, the kind that could describe other documents as well: perhaps the document was slightly wrinkled at the edges or had an unremarkable perforation. For ordinary lost property, such a *siman* suffices to return the object. But here the question is not merely about returning lost property — it is about whether this is the same *get* that may be used to effect a divorce. For that purpose, greater certainty is required, and a non-distinctive *siman* would only be adequate if *simanim* are valid at the Biblical level, not merely as a Rabbinic accommodation.

The alternative possibility is that they returned it based on *tveias eina* — the capacity to recognize an object by sight without being able to articulate a specific mark. Most people can look at something and say "yes, that is mine," even without explaining why. The concern with relying on this faculty is that one cannot verify it from the outside; a person might claim recognition simply because they want the object. Accordingly, the Gemara notes, *v'davka tzurba m'rabanan* — recognition by sight would only be accepted from a *talmid chacham*, someone whose honesty can be relied upon. It would not be used to return an item to an ordinary person who might be fabricating the claim.

---

## Get Dating Concern

### Braita on Get Return

The Gemara now returns, as a *gufa*, to the *braita* in *Gittin* that was cited earlier. *Matza get isha bashuk* — if one finds a woman's *get* in the marketplace: *bazman shehaba modeh yachzir l'isha* — when the husband admits that it fell from the wife, one returns it to her. *Ein habaal modeh lo yachzir lo lazeh v'lo lazeh* — but if he does not admit this, if he says he had not yet given it to her, one returns it to neither party.

### Nisan-Tishrei Problem

The Gemara now raises a concern about the first case. Even when the husband admits, why do we return it? *V'leichosh shema katav litten b'Nisan v'lo natan ad Tishrei* — let us be concerned that he wrote the *get* in Nisan but did not actually give it until Tishrei. The context here is the husband's rights to the *peirot* — the usufruct, the fruits of the landed property his wife brought into the marriage. As long as they remain married, he retains the right to benefit from that property, though she holds title. Those rights do not expire until the divorce actually takes effect.

### Wife's Claim on Fruit

Between Nisan and Tishrei, suppose the husband sold a harvest — a thousand boxes of cherries, say — which he was fully entitled to sell at the time, since the divorce had not yet occurred. Now the wife possesses a *get* dated Nisan. *U'mapka l'gita d'kativ b'Nisan* — she produces this *get* and claims she has been divorced since Nisan. She then goes to the purchaser of the cherries and argues: my husband sold you produce that was not his to sell, since I was already divorced from Nisan — those cherries were mine. *V'atya l'mitraf lakuchos shelo kadin* — she will attempt to seize property from the purchasers without just cause.

### Loses Rights on Intention

The Gemara notes that this concern is resolved according to one opinion. *Hanei l'man d'amar kivan she'natan einav l'gareshah shuv ein lo baal peirot shapir* — according to the view that from the moment the husband has decided and resolved to divorce his wife, he immediately loses the right to the *peirot* even before the divorce actually takes place. Since he wrote the *get* in Nisan, his intention was clear from that moment, and he therefore had no right to sell the fruit from Nisan onward — so the wife's claim would in fact be legitimate and no injustice would result.

### Rights Until Divorce

*Ella le-man d'amar yesh la-ba'al peiros ad sha'as nesina* — but according to the position that the husband retains rights to the *peirot* until the moment of actual divorce, *mai ika le-meimar* — what can one say? Why are we not concerned that the *get* was written earlier than it was given, and why do we not hesitate to return it to the woman?

### Demand Proof of Receipt

The Gemara resolves this: *amarna ki asya le-mitraf amrinan lah aisi raya eimas mata gitta l'yadech* — when she comes to claim the cherries from the purchaser, we will say to her: bring proof of exactly when you actually received the *get*. The date inscribed says Nisan, but prove that you received it in Nisan and not later. Ordinarily a woman holding a *get* is presumed to have been divorced as of the date written in the document, and no such demand is made. But since this was a *get* that had been found and returned to her, people will remember this — they will recall that the document was not originally in her possession but was recovered and given back to her — and they will know to demand that she establish the actual date of receipt. This assumption is admittedly striking: how exactly everyone is supposed to recall that this particular *get* had been found and returned is unclear, and one might speculate that the *beis din* would place some notation on the document to that effect. Nevertheless, this is how the Gemara frames the solution.

---

## Gittin vs. Debt Docs

### Why Different Rules?

The Gemara now asks: if this is a viable solution — return the document and ensure that any monetary claim will be met with a demand for proof — then why does the same approach not apply to documents of debt? *U-mai shna shtar chov* — why should a *shtar chov* be any different? The Mishna taught, as was studied earlier, *matza shtarei chov im yesh bahen achrayus nechasim lo yachzir* — if one finds debt documents that carry liens on property, one does not return them.

### Debt Doc Concern

This ruling was established even in the case where the debtor himself admits that the document belongs to the creditor. The reason is the concern of *shema kasav lilvos b'Nissan v'lo lova ad Tishrei* — perhaps the document was written in anticipation of a loan in Nisan but the money was not actually lent until Tishrei. If the creditor now uses this document, it will appear as though his liens on property take effect from Nisan, when in reality they can only begin from Tishrei when the loan was actually extended. *V'katraf delo kedin* — he will seize property sold by the debtor between Nisan and Tishrei, to which he has no rightful lien.

### Proof for Debt Docs?

The Gemara raises the question symmetrically: *amri hatam nami l'yahadar* — let us return the *shtar chov* there as well, *v'chi asya l'mitraf amrinan lei aisi raya eimas mata shtar chov l'yadech* — and when the creditor comes to exercise his liens, we will say to him: prove when the money was actually lent. If we can impose this demand in the case of the *get*, we can impose it equally in the case of the debt document. Why should there be any difference?

### Get: Remembered Finding

The Gemara answers: *amri hacha gabei get isha asi lakuach v'sava* — here, in the case of the *get*, the purchaser who bought the cherries will come and make demands. He will remember that the *get* was a document that had been lost and returned, and on the strength of that knowledge he will know to challenge the wife's claim. The *get* was returned to her specifically so she could remarry — not with any view toward the question of who owns the fruit. Therefore, *hashata de'kasya le'mitraf teiteiv ve'teisi raya eimat mata gita leyada* — now that she attempts to use the *get* to establish a date of divorce for the purpose of claiming the fruit, let her sit and bring proof of exactly when she received it. The purchaser, knowing the background, will know to demand this.

### Debt: Assumed Kosher

By contrast, *lo ati lokeach u'tava* — in the case of a *shtar chov*, the purchaser of the debtor's land will not come and challenge. Why? *Mide'ahadru nihaleih rabbanan ve'shtar chov peshita* — because when a debt document was found and the rabbis returned it to the creditor, the purchaser will reason: what other possible purpose could there be for returning a *shtar chov* to a creditor other than to allow him to collect the loan and exercise the liens? *Le'mai hachi ahadru nihaleih le'mitraf hu shma mina kamu rabbanan bemilta* — since the document was clearly returned for the purpose of enforcement, the purchaser concludes that the rabbis must have investigated and determined that everything was in order, that the loan genuinely dates to Nisan, and that the liens are fully valid. *Umikmi didi mata shtra le'yadei* — he assumes the document was verified before being returned. He will not challenge it, and the creditor will unjustly seize property to which he has no rightful lien.

This is why the *shtar chov* cannot be returned, while the *get* can. When a *get* is produced to claim ownership of fruit, people will still remember to challenge the dating because everyone understands the *get* was returned for marital purposes, not for monetary ones. When a *shtar chov* is returned, however, its return carries the implicit message that the liens are valid and the creditor has performed due diligence — and no one will think to question it further.

---

## Manumission Logic

### Master Admits/Denies

The Mishna stated that a *shtar shichrur* — a writ of manumission — found in the marketplace should not be returned to the slave, since perhaps the master wrote it but had not yet given it and may have changed his mind. A *braita* elaborates: *matza shtar shichrur bashuk bizman she'harav modeh yachzir le'eved* — when the master admits that the document fell from the slave, or acknowledges that it should be given to the slave, it is returned to him. *Eino harav modeh lo yachzir lo le'zeh velo le'zeh* — if the master does not admit this, it is returned to neither party.

### Slave's Property Gap

The Gemara raises the same Nisan-Tishrei concern here. Even when the master admits, why do we return the document? *Neichash shema katav litein lo be'Nisan velo natan lo ad Tishrei* — let us be concerned that the document was written in Nisan but not actually given until Tishrei. *Ve'azal avda ve'kanah nechasim mi'Nisan ad Tishrei* — during that interval, the slave went and purchased property. Whatever a slave acquires belongs to his master; the slave has no independent legal personhood in property terms.

### Retroactive Freedom Claim

*Ve'azal harav ve'zabneinhu* — the master, who owns these acquisitions, went ahead and sold the property that the slave had purchased between Nisan and Tishrei. Then the slave receives the manumission document. Though he was actually freed in Tishrei, the document is dated Nisan. *Umapik leih le'shichrura de'kativ be'Nisan ve'taraf lakochei shelo kadin* — the slave now produces this document dated Nisan and approaches those to whom the master sold the property, claiming that he was already free in Nisan, that the purchased goods were therefore his and not the master's, and that the master had no right to sell them.

### Freedom as Benefit

The Gemara notes that this concern dissolves according to one position. *Hani l'man d'amar zchus l'eved sheyotzei mitachas yad rabo l'cheirus* — according to the view that being freed from one's master is an unqualified benefit to the slave, and following the ruling of Abaye that *edei bachasumav zachin lo* — that when witnesses sign a document that confers a pure benefit upon someone, their very act of signing is as though they have delivered the document to him on his behalf — the principle of *zachin l'adam shelo befanav* applies. The slave is freed from the moment the *shtar shichrur* is signed, and there would never be a gap between Nisan and Tishrei to worry about.

### Not Absolute Benefit

*Ella l'man d'amar chov l'eved sheyotzei mitachas yad rabo l'cheirus* — but according to the view that being freed is not an unqualified benefit to the slave — it need not mean it is an absolute detriment, only that it carries some downside: the slave loses his master's household, his board, and certain leniencies in other areas of conduct — then *zachin* cannot be applied, and the slave is not freed until the document is physically delivered to him. In that case, the gap between Nisan and Tishrei is real, and *mai ika l'meimar* — what can one say to justify returning the document?

### Proof of Freedom Date

*Dechi asi l'metraf amrinan lei aisei raya eimas mta shtar shichrur leyadacha* — the Gemara answers precisely as it did with the *get*: when the slave comes to use the writ of manumission to claim property, we will remember that it was a document found and returned to him, and we will know to demand proof of exactly when he was actually freed. The same logic applies: the *shtar shichrur* was returned so that the slave could establish his freedom, not for the purpose of monetary claims. If he then attempts to use its date to reclaim property, he will be required to demonstrate when the document actually reached his hands. And just as with the *shtar chov*, the Gemara would not extend this solution to a debt document, because returning a *shtar chov* carries the implicit endorsement that the liens are valid — an endorsement that a purchaser will not think to question.

---

## Will & Gift Docs

### Basic Rule on Docs

The Mishna and an associated *braita* both address the case of found documents relating to bequests and gifts — *dayatiki*, *apotkiyos*, and *matana* — and establish that they are not returned to the recipient without explicit instruction from the giver.

### What Is Dayatiki

The *braita* asks: *eizeihu dayatiki* — what is a *dayatiki*? *Da tehei l'meikam u'l'mihvei* — it is an acronym for "this shall stand and take effect," meaning it functions as a will. It records the instructions of a *shechiv meira* — a person on his deathbed — directing that upon his death his property should pass to a designated person. The principle underlying it is *divrei shechiv meira k'chusuvin v'chimsurin dami* — the words of a dying person are treated as if they have been written and delivered, meaning that his verbal instruction alone suffices to effect the transfer. It takes effect automatically at death, without requiring a formal act of conveyance.

### What Is Matana

*Matana* — a gift by a healthy person — is defined as any document that says *me-hayom ve-le-achar mita*: the recipient acquires title today, but the right to benefit from the property begins only after the giver's death. The giver of such a document retains the right to the *peirot* throughout his lifetime; ownership, however, vests in the recipient immediately.

### Title/Benefit Split

The Gemara asks why a gift must be phrased in this bifurcated way — title now, benefit after death — and whether it would not be simpler for a healthy person simply to give everything outright. Abaye explains: *eizo hi matnat bari she-hi ke-matnat shchiv me-ra* — the question is, what form does a healthy person's gift take when he wishes it to function like a deathbed bequest, i.e., when he wants the recipient to derive benefit only after his death?

The answer is that a healthy person cannot simply say "you receive this property after I die," because at the moment of his death he is no longer a legal entity capable of effecting a transfer. The conveyance cannot be completed by a person who no longer exists. Therefore, if a healthy person wishes to give something that will only become beneficial to the recipient upon his death, he has two options: he can stipulate that the transfer takes effect a moment before his death, or he can transfer title now while retaining the right to all benefit — *peirot* — until he dies. The formula *me-hayom ve-le-achar mita* accomplishes exactly this: title passes today, benefit passes at death. This is what distinguishes the gift of a healthy person from a standard deathbed bequest, which operates entirely through the Rabbinic mechanism of *divrei shechiv meira*.

### Braita Restriction

A *braita* then states: *matza deitiki apotkiyos u-matanot af al pi she-shneihem modim lo yachazir lo le-ze ve-lo le-ze* — if one finds a *dayatiki*, an *apotiki*, or a gift document, even if both parties admit to its validity, one does not return it to either side.

---

## Deathbed vs. Healthy

### Retractable Nature

The Gemara now reconciles the apparent tension between the Mishna — which implies that if the *shechiv meira* says "give it," one gives it — and the *braita*, which says that even when both parties admit, one does not return these documents. The resolution turns on a fundamental distinction between the two categories of document.

A deathbed bequest — *matnat shchiv mera* — is *bar hadara*, retractable. Until the person actually dies, his most recent expressed wish always supersedes any prior one. This is the nature of a will: each subsequent instruction invalidates what came before. Accordingly, if a *shechiv meira* on his deathbed gives instructions that property should go to Reuven, and then later gives instructions that it should go to Shimon, Shimon receives the property because the later instruction overrides the earlier one. If he then changes his mind yet again in favor of Reuven, Reuven will receive it. Whatever he says last is what governs.

### Later Supersedes Earlier

This principle is stated explicitly: *de-amrinan mai ika le-meimar* — what precisely is the concern? The concern is that perhaps originally he wrote and expressed his deathbed bequest for Reuven in January, then had regrets and never delivered the document to Reuven, then subsequently in February gave his deathbed bequest to Shimon and actually delivered that document. Now he regrets having given it to Shimon and wants it to go to Reuven.

The Gemara answers: whether he gave to Shimon as a deathbed bequest or as a healthy person's gift, Shimon loses nothing — *leis leih pesida de-kama batar batar zachi* — because the later document always prevails, as by giving to Shimon he effectively retracted from Reuven. Therefore, when the *shechiv meira* is alive, we can safely give the found document to Reuven without fear of injustice to Shimon.

### Gift Is Final

A healthy person's gift, by contrast, is final and irrevocable — *dela bar mehadar hu*. It is not superseded by a later gift; rather, the earlier gift takes precedence. If a healthy person gave title to Reuven in January and then purported to give the same property to Shimon in February, Reuven owns it — the January document controls. The later conveyance cannot override the earlier completed transfer.

### Two-Gift Scenario

The concern in the case of a healthy person's gift is therefore as follows. In January, a person wrote a gift document in favor of Reuven but never gave it to him. In February, he gave a gift document to Shimon and actually delivered it. Now he has regrets and wishes he had given it to Reuven instead. The January document, which was written but never given, is now found.

### False Claim Risk

The danger is this: the giver, in collusion with Reuven, claims that he actually did give the January document to Reuven at the time it was written. If the document is returned to Reuven and Reuven produces it bearing a January date, Reuven's document predates Shimon's February document. Since the earlier gift takes precedence for a healthy person's gift, Reuven would win — unjustly depriving Shimon of property he had legitimately received.

### Exploit Risk

*Kasavar ki mafik hai ktava dekadim* — the giver calculates that if Reuven produces this document dated January, it will establish that he received the gift before Shimon did, *zachi beh hu*, and they will split the proceeds. This fraudulent scheme is precisely what the Gemara fears. The Gemara therefore says: we will not give this document to Reuven. If the giver genuinely wants Reuven to have the property and there truly is no Shimon in the picture, let him write a new document now and give it to Reuven today. *Dei yahavtih leinish achrina leika pseida de-kama zachi* — because if there is in fact a Shimon who already received an earlier gift, the earlier document will prevail and Shimon will be protected. This is why, for a healthy person's gift, even if both parties admit, the found document is not returned.

---

## Alive vs. Dead Giver

### Apparent Contradiction

Rav Zvid challenges the foregoing resolution. *Idi ve-idi dayateki katani* — both the Mishna and the *braita* speak of a *dayatiki*, a deathbed bequest. Yet the Mishna implies that when the *shechiv meira* says "give it," one gives it, while the *braita* says that even when both parties admit, one does not give it. The previous answer attributed the Mishna to a *shechiv meira* and the *braita* to a healthy person's gift, but Rav Zvid observes that both sources explicitly discuss the same category of document. How can the contradiction be resolved while keeping both within the domain of deathbed bequests?

### Key Difference

*Ela amar Rav Zvid ha ve-ha be-shchiv mera ve-lo kashya ha beh ve-ha bivrei* — Rav Zvid resolves this by introducing a different distinction: both sources indeed deal with a *shechiv meira*'s bequest, but they differ on whether the *shechiv meira* himself is still alive or has already died and it is now his son who is the relevant party.

### Alive: Later Wins

When the *shechiv meira* is still alive and says "give it," we can safely return the document to Reuven. *De-mahadar hu* — he retains the power to retract. If in fact he never gave the document to Reuven and subsequently gave the property to Shimon, his act of giving it to Shimon constitutes a retraction of his instruction to Reuven. *Leis beh pesida de-kama batar batar zachi* — Shimon will not be harmed, because the later gift will supersede the earlier one, and Shimon will prevail over Reuven regardless of the January date on the found document. There is therefore no risk of injustice, and the document may be returned.

### Dead: Son Can't Override

When the *shechiv meira* has died, however, the situation is fundamentally different. The father died without having retracted his expressed intention to give the property to Reuven. The son inherited the estate. The son then gave the property to Shimon. Now the son says that the document — his father's deathbed bequest to Reuven, found after the father's death — should be returned to Reuven.

Here the crucial asymmetry emerges: a gift made by the son to Shimon does not supersede the father's bequest to Reuven. The father never retracted; it was only the son who conveyed to Shimon. Since a *shechiv meira*'s later instruction overrides an earlier one only when both come from the same person, the son's gift to Shimon carries no superseding power over the father's bequest to Reuven. If the father's document is now given to Reuven with its January date, Reuven will hold a bequest from the father that was never retracted — and that will take the property away from Shimon unjustly.

### Fraud Scenario

The concern is laid out explicitly. The real sequence of events may have been: the father expressed a deathbed bequest to Reuven in January but never gave the document. The father died. The son inherited and gave the property to Shimon. Now the son regrets this. He cannot simply retract his gift to Shimon — *mehadar lo mtzitna hadrina bi* — having made a completed gift, he cannot simply declare he has changed his mind. So instead he conspires with Reuven: he will claim that his father did give the document to Reuven at the time it was written. If the document is returned to Reuven, Reuven can produce it as evidence of the father's bequest, one that was never retracted by the father and that the son's gift to Shimon cannot override. *Veniflog behadeh* — the son and Reuven split the proceeds, while Shimon loses the property he had legitimately received.

### No Return if Dead

*Hilkach amrinan leh anan hai shtara lo yahavinan leh lehai* — therefore we say: we will not give this document to Reuven. *De'dilma michtav katav avuh meihav lo yahav leh* — perhaps your father wrote it for Reuven but never actually handed it over. *Ve'yahavt at l'ne achrini ve'kahadart bach* — and you, the son, gave the property to Shimon and now regret it.

If, however, the son insists that there is no Shimon and that the father truly did intend to give this to Reuven, the Gemara responds: *zil at hashta ktov leh shtara achrina* — then go and write Reuven a new document now and give it to him today. *D'ei nami lo yahiv leh avuch ve'katavt at hashta l'ne achrina leit bei psida* — because if the father never gave it and you are now giving it, dating the document to today creates no injustice.

### Son's Later Doc

If the son's concern is that Reuven will be disadvantaged because the new document is dated later than some hypothetical Shimon's document, the Gemara answers: that is precisely the correct outcome. *De'kama batar kama zachai* — the earlier document wins. If there genuinely is a Shimon who holds an earlier gift, Shimon should prevail, and a new document for Reuven dated today will properly yield to Shimon's earlier claim. If there is no Shimon, then Reuven will receive the property without any competing claim. Either way, the solution of writing a fresh document today is safe — it ensures that Reuven can receive what he is owed without creating the risk of defrauding anyone who may have a legitimate prior claim.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 20

## Receipt/Ketubah Scenario

### Shovar for Ketubah

The daf begins at the bottom of 19b, concluding the discussion of the *mishnah* that enumerated categories of documents one does not return upon finding them — *gittei nashim*, *shichrurei avadim*, and related documents — on the grounds that they may never have been delivered. The final item on that list is a *shovar*, a receipt, and the *baraita* here addresses specifically a receipt for a *kesuva*.

The *baraita* states: *matza shovar* — if one finds a receipt acknowledging that a husband paid his wife's *kesuva* — *bizman shehi moda*, if the wife herself confirms that yes, her husband paid and she issued the receipt, then *yachazir l'ba'al*, one returns the receipt to the husband. *Ein hi moda*, if she does not agree, then *lo yachazir lo lizeh v'lo lizeh* — one returns it to neither party, since she claims she wrote it anticipating payment that never came, while he insists he paid. The operative and interesting clause, then, is the first: when she does acknowledge payment, we return the receipt. The question that immediately arises is why this case differs from an ordinary debt document, where even mutual acknowledgment does not suffice to return the document — given our standard concern that some side arrangement may be at work.

### Nisan-Tishrei Concern

The concern here is classic and familiar: *d'leichush dilma kesavo l'eisein b'Nisan v'lo nasna ad Tishrei* — perhaps she wrote the receipt in Nisan but was not actually paid until Tishrei. One must also assume that she had not even been divorced yet in Nisan; the divorce was anticipated but had not yet occurred. She wrote the receipt in Nisan in preparation, the divorce and payment only materialized months later in Tishrei, and now the receipt bears a date in Nisan. At first glance this seems harmless — the receipt still records that the husband paid. But the question is: who gets hurt by this?

### Cheating Third-Party Buye…

The injured party is a third-party purchaser — call him Michael. *V'azla v'zavanta l'kesuvasa b'tovas hana'ah miNisan ad Tishrei* — the wife, anticipating divorce, sold her *kesuva* to Michael in Nisan at a discount. The *kesuva* is worth ten thousand dollars at collection; she sells it to him for five thousand now. Michael assumes the risk — maybe she will never be divorced, or she will predecease her husband — and in exchange receives the prospect of collecting the full face value when the time comes. The wife then does get divorced, the husband pays her in Tishrei, and she hands him a receipt dated Nisan — before she ever sold the *kesuva* to Michael. When Michael comes to collect, the husband produces the receipt and says: I divorced her and paid her before you ever bought this *kesuva*. Your purchase was of a debt that had already been discharged. Michael is left with nothing.

As *Rashi* explains, if a specific plot of land had been designated as the *kesuva* property, the husband now uses the Nisan-dated receipt to keep that land, defeating Michael's attempt to collect. The concern is thus a predated *shovar* that illegally cheats the third-party purchaser out of his collection rights.

### Rava/Shmuel Ruling

*Amar Rava* — Rava says: *shma mina isa l'diShmuel* — from the fact that the *mishnah* does not voice this concern and simply says to return the receipt when the wife agrees, one can infer that we rule in accordance with Shmuel.

### Shmuel's Principle

What is Shmuel's principle? *D'amar Shmuel hamocher shtar chov l'chaveiro v'chazar u'machalo machul v'afilu yoresh mocheil* — if Reuven sells a debt document to a third party and then forgives the underlying debt owed by Shimon, the forgiveness is effective. And not only that: even Reuven's heir, standing in Reuven's place, can forgive the debt.

### Debt Purchase Logic

The mechanism here requires unpacking. When Reuven sells me a *shtar chov* for five hundred dollars — a debt Shimon owes Reuven of one thousand — the money is still technically owed to Reuven. The purchaser functions, in a sense, as Reuven's designated collection agent or the recipient of Reuven's direct deposit. Shimon's obligation runs to Reuven, not to the purchaser directly. It follows that Reuven retains the legal capacity to be *mocheil* — to forgive — the debt to Shimon. Of course, if Reuven does forgive, he is liable under the laws of *dinei d'garmi* for the loss he caused the purchaser, who can recover the five hundred dollars paid. But the forgiveness itself is legally effective.

This creates a remarkable and admittedly uncomfortable reality for debt purchasers. Once Reuven has sold the *shtar* for five hundred, if Shimon subsequently comes into money, Reuven can approach Shimon and say: instead of paying a thousand to the purchaser, pay me eight hundred, I'll forgive the debt, and I'll reimburse the purchaser his five hundred. The purchaser gets reimbursed but loses the profit he was counting on. This is legally legitimate under Shmuel's principle, though deeply disadvantageous to the purchaser. There are ways to circumvent this — *ma'amad shloshtan*, bringing all three parties together simultaneously, can sever the original creditor's connection to the debt in a manner the halacha recognizes as a direct transfer — but absent such a mechanism, the original creditor retains the power of forgiveness.

How does this address our case? The concern was that the husband could fraudulently cheat Michael by producing a predated receipt. Rava's point is: this is no more harmful to Michael than what the wife could do *legally*, without any fraud at all. She could right now be *mocheil* the *kesuva* debt to her husband — perhaps in exchange for a quiet payment — and under Shmuel's principle that would be effective. Michael would be cheated out of his collection rights entirely through legal means. Since Michael can be legally deprived of the debt, we are not additionally concerned about the illegal mechanism of a predated *shovar*. The category of loss he might suffer is already fully available to the husband and wife through legitimate channels. Hence the *mishnah* does not voice this concern, and from this Rava derives that we hold like Shmuel.

One might ask: does this mean that nobody would ever purchase a *kesuva* or any debt? The answer is that it is a risk the purchaser takes knowingly. There are loss scenarios built into the transaction from the start. The question of whether a purchaser could contractually obligate the original creditor not to forgive the debt is an interesting one — likely a penalty clause could be inserted, making the creditor financially liable for a severe sum if he ever forgives — but the ability to forgive the debt as a legal matter may not itself be contractually waivable. Only through *ma'amad shloshtan* can the creditor be fully cut out.

### Abaye's Three Reasons

*Abaye amar* — Abaye disagrees with the framing and says: *afilu teima leiso l'diShmuel* — even if you do not accept Shmuel's principle, there is no concern about cheating Michael here. Why?

Abaye offers a tripartite answer. First: *hacha b'mai askinan b'shtar kesuva yotza mitachas yadav* — the *mishnah* is speaking of a case where the wife is currently holding the *kesuva* document itself. If the *kesuva* had been sold to Michael, the physical *kesuva* document would have been transferred to Michael at the time of sale. If the wife is the one currently holding the *kesuva*, it is clear she never sold it. There is therefore no Michael to worry about.

Rava challenges this: *im mishum shtar kesuva chashinan l'shtei kesuvos* — the fact that she holds a *kesuva* does not eliminate the concern, since perhaps she has two *kesuvos*. How would that happen? A first *kesuva* was lost and a replacement was written; she sold the replacement and still holds the original. Unlikely, yes, but Rava says we entertain the possibility.

Abaye responds with his second reason: *l'shtei kesuvos lo chashinan* — we are not concerned about such a remote scenario of two *kesuvos* existing simultaneously.

And third: *v'od shover bizmano taref* — even setting aside both of the above, there is a fundamental reason not to fear the predated receipt cheating Michael. This is the third and most conceptually powerful answer, and it rests on Abaye's own well-known principle.

### Edov b'Chosmov Zachin Lo

*Abaye l'taimei d'amar edov b'chosmov zachin lo* — the witnesses by their signatures acquire on behalf of the beneficiary. Abaye's principle, which we have been applying implicitly throughout this *perek*, holds that when a document is signed by witnesses and that document is to the benefit of its recipient, the signature activates the document retroactively from the date of signing — on the condition that the document is ultimately delivered. This is distinct from *shtarei kinyan*, which take effect immediately upon signing without requiring delivery. Here, delivery is still required, but once delivered, the effect is retroactive to the date of the signatures.

Applied to our case: the wife wrote a receipt in Nisan; the husband actually paid only in Tishrei.
