Nevertheless, because of *edov b'chosmov zachin lo*, when the husband pays in Tishrei and receives the receipt, the debt is retroactively considered discharged from Nisan — the date the receipt was signed. This means that when Michael purchased the *kesuva* in, say, Iyar, the debt had already — retroactively — been extinguished as of Nisan. Michael purchased something that no longer existed. He is cheated, yes, but legally. He will be entitled to recover his purchase price, but no illegal fraud is being perpetrated. Hence the *mishnah* has no concern about returning the receipt. Abaye thus provides three independent grounds for not worrying: Shmuel's principle, the absence of a second *kesuva*, and retroactive validity through *edov b'chosmov zachin lo*.

---

## Document Retroactivity

### Witnesses & Delivery

The rule of *edov b'chosmov zachin lo* has been invoked repeatedly throughout this *perek*, but only now does the *gemara* pause to explain its underlying rationale. The practical problem that this principle solves is the following: how can witnesses ever sign a document unless all parties are assembled in the room at the very moment of intended delivery? In the vast majority of cases, a document is signed at one time and delivered at another. If we were to hold that the document takes effect only from the date of delivery, the date written on the document — the date of signing — would systematically misrepresent reality. Worse, all the concerns associated with the gap between signing and delivery — the *Nisan-Tishrei* problem, the possibility of sales to third parties in the interim — would recur perpetually. Abaye resolves all of this: when the document is finally delivered, it is deemed to have been active from the date of signing. The signed document is treated as if the witnesses already acquired on behalf of the recipient from that moment.

### Tosafot on Takanas Chach…

*Tosafot*, commenting at 111a, 117a, and 20b, finally addresses the foundation of Abaye's principle explicitly. *V'nireh shetakanas chachamim hi* — it is a rabbinic enactment. *Shezochin mishas chasima af al pi shelo nimsa lo ad yamim rabim* — the recipients acquire from the moment of signing even if the document was not delivered for many days. The reason for this *takana* is precisely to enable document signing to function practically. *L'olam lo yuchlu edim lachsom ela im yiru hamasira* — witnesses would never be able to sign any document unless they witnessed actual delivery, because the date of signing would otherwise always diverge from the date of effect. *Mishum chashasha d'kozva Nisan v'lo nasan ad Tishrei v'mazbin beinei beinei* — the pervasive fear of the Nisan-Tishrei problem, of sales intervening between signing and delivery, would make the entire institution of legal documents unworkable. Abaye's rule removes all of these difficulties by making the retroactivity operative from the date of signing, once delivery occurs.

### Status Issues & Retroact…

If the principle is rabbinic in origin — a *takanas chachamim* designed to protect monetary interests — a serious question arises regarding its application to personal status matters. We do apply *edov b'chosmov zachin lo* to *shichrurei avadim*, documents of manumission. If a *shtar shichrur* was signed in Nisan and delivered in Tishrei, the slave is retroactively freed from Nisan. But how can a rabbinic ordinance, enacted to protect *lakuchos* — purchasers of property — retroactively alter the personal status of a human being?

*Tosafot* raises the concrete case: *im eved ba al bas Yisroel kodam sheba l'yado get shichrur shepasla* — if a slave had relations with a Jewish woman between the signing and the delivery of his *get shichrur*, did he do so as a slave or as a freed man? If the retroactivity applies to status, she would be *pasul l'kehuna* retroactively from Nisan; if it applies only to monetary matters, his status in the interim remains that of a slave.

*Tosafot* presents two positions. One view: since the entire principle is rabbinic, *ul'inyan issur* — for matters of personal status — the retroactivity does not apply. For money, the document takes effect from signing; for *issur*, only from delivery. The other view: *shema gam gabai issur zochin lo mishas chasima* — perhaps even for status matters the rule applies retroactively from the date of signing, *af al pi d'la shayach ta'ama d'prishas* — even though the original rationale of protecting purchasers does not apply to status issues — because *mikol makom lo plug rabbanan*, the rabbis did not differentiate. Once they enacted the rule, they enacted it uniformly across both domains. The authority for this even in the domain of *issur* rests on the principle of *v'yesh koach b'yad chachamim la'akor davar min haTorah* — the rabbis have the capacity to uproot a Torah law under certain circumstances. By this reasoning, even though the slave is not technically a free man until delivery, the rabbinic retroactivity makes him one from the date of signing. *Tosafot* also raises the question of whether this principle could ever apply to a *get ishah* — a bill of divorce — under circumstances where a *get* might be considered a *z'chus*, a benefit, for the wife. Until now *edov b'chosmov zachin lo* has not been applied to a *get* because a *get* is understood as a *chov* — a burden — on the wife. *V'ein chavin l'adam shelo befanav* — one cannot burden another in their absence. But should a case arise where a *get* functions as a benefit, the question of retroactive validity would re-emerge.

---

## Court Documents/Maaseh B…

### Maaseh Beis Din

The final *mishnah* of the *perek* turns to a new category: documents that one may always return without concern. These are *maasei beis din* — documents issued by a court. The *mishnah* opens: *matza igros shum* — one found assessment letters.

### Court Document Types

Each type listed in the *mishnah* shares two structural features that distinguish it from ordinary debt documents: first, it takes effect immediately upon issuance, so there is no concern about a Nisan-Tishrei gap between writing and activation; second, it does not represent a dischargeable debt in the conventional sense, so there is no concern that the document has been paid off and should no longer exist. The document simply records or authorizes something, and remains as evidence in the hands of the recipient.

*Igros shum* — assessment letters — are documents in which the court has evaluated the debtor's assets and determined that specified property, such as a particular plot of land, is to be levied to satisfy a debt. The document is active the moment it is written, and since it designates real property, it is self-evident from external reality whether the property has already been seized or not.

*O igeret mazon* — a support document. *Rashi* explains this as a husband's written commitment to support his stepdaughter, an ongoing obligation rather than a one-time payment. Since the obligation is continuous and not subject to being "paid off" in a single transaction, there is no concern that the document represents a discharged claim.

*Shtar chalitzah* — a document attesting that *chalitzah* was performed, freeing the *yevamah* from the obligation of *yibbum*. *U'miunim* — a document recording that an underage girl, married by her mother or brothers, exercised her right of *miun*, verbally refusing her husband in a valid manner, thereby dissolving the marriage. Both of these are purely evidentiary: they testify to acts that have already occurred. There is no question of the document having been written in anticipation of an act not yet performed; the act precedes the document.

*V'shtarei beirurin* — we are told to await the *gemara*'s explanation. *V'chol maasei Beis Din harei zeh yachzir* — any document issued by a court is to be returned to the appropriate party.

The *gemara* then asks: *mai shtarei birurin* — what are *shtarei beirurin*? In Babylonia the explanation given is *shtarei ta'anata* — documents recording the claims each party made in court. The court reporter, so to speak, drew up a record: Reuven claimed X, Y, and Z; Shimon counterclaimed A, B, and C. This record was then handed to the parties before judgment.

### Sheteri Beirurin

Rabbi Yirmeyah offers a different explanation: *zeh borer lo echad v'zeh borer lo echad* — this refers to the process by which parties constitute an ad hoc arbitration panel. I choose one *dayan*, you choose another, and those two select a third. A *shtar beirurin* is the court-issued document recording that the parties have agreed to submit their dispute to these three specified judges. The document is active immediately — there is nothing to "pay off" — and it binds the parties to the selected tribunal. It is a clear candidate for the category of *maaseh Beis Din* that one returns without concern.

### Get in Beis Din

The *gemara* then presents a case that sounds familiar: *hahu gita deishtakach be dinei deRav Huna* — a *get* was found in the *beis din* of Rav Huna, bearing the specification that it came from the city of Sheviri, situated on the Rachis river. *Rashi* explains the background: the city of Sheviri on the Rachis is a specific and identifiable location, and presumably there is no one else in that city matching the names written in the *get*. It would seem obvious to return the *get* to the intended party.

### Rav Huna's Concern

Yet *amar Rav Huna bar Rav Yehuda* — even granting all of this, we should be concerned: *chashinan lishnei Sheviri* — perhaps there is another city also named Sheviri, also on the Rachis river. This might seem far-fetched, but rivers pass through many regions, and cities in different areas can independently bear the same name and sit on the same river. As an analogy, along the Mississippi there are many towns sharing names across different states, and there are documented cases of cities in different countries — Stratford-upon-Avon in England and Stratford on the Avon in Ontario, Canada — presenting exactly this kind of coincidence.

### Rabbah's Investigation

*Amar lei Rav Chisda leRabba* — Rav Chisda instructed Rabbah, apparently Rav Huna's legal secretary, to go and investigate: *puk ayen d'le'ursa ba'ei lei Rav Huna minach* — by evening Rav Huna would be asking him whether there is any evidence bearing on whether we need to worry about a second Sheviri. *Nafak dak v'ashkach* — Rabbah went out, investigated, and found: *tnan kol maaseh Beis Din harei zeh yachzir* — the *mishnah* states that any *maaseh Beis Din* is returned. The *mishnah* voices no concern about the possibility of another party with the same name in another city with the same name. The implicit ruling of the *mishnah*, especially given that a *beis din* is a high-traffic location where documents from many parties pass through, is that we do not entertain such concerns. This appears to resolve the question in favor of returning the *get*.

### Rav Ami's Challenge

*Amar lei Rav Ami leRabbah* — Rav Ami challenged Rabbah: *heichi pashit mar issura mi'mamona* — how can you derive a ruling about personal status from a monetary case? In monetary matters, a standard *siman* suffices to return a lost object; for a *get*, one might require a *siman muvhak*, a far more distinctive identifying mark. Here the *mishnah* is dealing with monetary court documents. How do you know the same confidence level extends to personal status, to permitting a woman to be considered divorced?

### Chalitzah/Miun Evidence

*Amar lei tirda* — Rabbah replied: you dullard. *Shtar chalitzah u'miun tnan* — the *mishnah* itself explicitly includes *shtar chalitzah* and *miun* among the court documents that one returns. These are personal status issues. *Chalitzah*, while less severe than a full *get ishah* — the children of subsequent unions are not *mamzerim* and the prohibition involved is lower-level — is nonetheless a status matter. The *mishnah* makes no distinction between monetary court documents and personal status court documents when it says *kol maaseh Beis Din harei zeh yachzir*. So the *mishnah* itself resolves Rav Ami's question. The exchange concludes with the famous detail that the beam of the study hall burst — *paka arza d'bei Rav* — and each of the two disputants attributed the supernatural event to his own vindication.

---

## Multiple Documents/Ident…

### Containers/Siman

The *mishnah* states: *matza b'chafisah o b'diluskama* — if one finds documents in a *chafisah* or a *diluskama*, and the owner can provide a *siman* identifying the container, one returns the documents. Returning to standard *shtarei chov* rather than *maasei Beis Din*, the ordinary concerns about fraud or erroneous return apply, but are overcome when the finder can identify the container. The *gemara* asks: *mai chafisah* — what is a *chafisah*? *Amar Rabbah bar bar Chana*: *chemet ketanah* — a small leather flask, the kind used to carry water or liquids, here apparently repurposed for document storage. *Mai diluskama* — what is a *diluskama*? *Amar Rabbah bar bar Shmuel*: *telika d'savei* — an old person's sack or bag, a container used for storage.

What exactly constitutes the *siman* in these cases is not fully spelled out. *Tosafot* initially considers whether the unusual nature of the container — who keeps documents in a leather flask? — is itself the *siman*, but then notes the difficulty that the second case involves a more ordinary satchel, where the *siman* would presumably be the specific identifying features of that container.

### Wrapped/Bundle Documents

The *mishnah* continues: *o tachrich shel shtaros o agudah shel shtaros* — or a rolling of documents together, or a bundle of documents tied together. Here again one returns the documents to the person who provides the *siman*. The *siman* in these cases relates to how the documents are packaged — something unusual about the manner of their combination serves to identify them.

### Tachrich & Agudah

The *baraita* specifies: *kama hu tachrich shtarot? Shlosha kruchin ze b'ze* — what constitutes a *tachrich*? Three documents wrapped one within the other. *V'kama hi agudah shel shtaros? Shlosha kshurin zeh bezeh* — what constitutes an *agudah*? Three tied together. The *gemara* then makes a careful distinction between the two methods. A *tachrich* is made by rolling one document and then rolling the second around the first, and the third around that — each one layered on top of the previous, *chada chada b'reisha d'chavarta*. An *agudah* is made by laying all the documents flat together in a pile and then rolling or tying them as a unit — *d'ramu ahadadi u'kruchinhu*. The result looks similar but structurally differs: in a *tachrich* the documents are intertwined and inseparable, while in an *agudah* one could, in principle, push out the middle document separately. Either method, when applied to three or more documents, constitutes a meaningful *siman*.

### Bundle Minimum

The *mishnah* specifies *shlosha kshurin zeh bezeh* — three tied together — as the threshold for a bundle. The *gemara* notes that this might imply the number itself is part of the *siman*, and if so, why do we need three rather than two? The answer given invokes a principle that will be developed more fully in the next *perek*: the *gemara* raises the possibility that *kesher siman* — the type of knot serves as a *siman* — but then notes the complications that entails. The resolution draws on what Ravina will state elsewhere: one does not announce the number but merely announces *shtarei* — I found documents — and the claimant must then provide the identifying features, including both the number and the method of bundling.

### Announcing Found Items

*Mai machriz? Minyan* — what does the finder announce? He announces that he found a number of documents, meaning he gives out the number. Then the identifying *siman* comes from the claimant describing the bundling. The *gemara* asks: if the number is given in the announcement, why must there be at least three? Even two documents found together might be claimed by someone describing the manner of their bundling. The answer, following Ravina's approach, is that one does not actually announce the number at all. One simply announces *shtarei* — I found documents — and both the number and the bundling method together constitute the *siman* that the claimant must supply. The minimum of three is required because two documents bundled together might too easily be guessed by someone with no genuine claim. Three, combined with the specific method of bundling, provides sufficient specificity that the *siman* is meaningful. One notes, wryly, that a sufficiently learned claimant who knows the relevant halacha might reason through the possibilities: the finder said *shtarei*, so it can't be two — too obvious to count as a *siman* — so it must be at least three, and since it's being announced at all, the bundling must be unusual rather than a standard individual-roll-with-string. The system is not entirely immune to gaming by the overly learned.

### One Borrower/Three Lende…

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer: echad ha'loveh mishlosha yachzir laloveh* — if one finds three documents each showing that the same borrower took loans from three different lenders, return the documents to the borrower. The reasoning: why would three different lenders' documents, each naming a different creditor but the same debtor, end up together? The most natural explanation is that they all fell from the borrower, who was carrying his own obligations. That implies the debts have been paid and the documents should go to him.

### Validation Scenarios

The *gemara* questions this: perhaps they fell from the various lenders, each of whom happened to have a document naming this borrower. But how did they end up together? *Dilma l'kiyumeinhu azli* — perhaps the borrower had brought them all to *beis din* to be validated simultaneously, sent through a single agent, and they fell from the agent or from the *beis din*. The *gemara* responds: *d'mitkaymi* — but we can assume they are already validated, bearing the court's seal. Once validated, the money has already been lent and the documents should have been delivered to the lenders. No one leaves a validated, active loan document in the hands of a *sofer* or agent once the money has changed hands. Therefore the only plausible explanation remains that all three fell from the borrower.

### Three Borrowers/One Lend…

The reverse case: *shlosha halovim min echad yachzir lamalveh* — if three documents each show a different borrower taking a loan from the same lender, return the documents to the lender. The three borrowers presumably each took their own loan and would each be holding their own obligation; the only party with reason to hold all three together is the common lender. The *gemara* challenges: *dilma l'michtavinhu azli* — perhaps the three borrowers all came together to a single *sofer* to have their documents drawn up, and the documents fell from the *sofer* before the money was lent and before they were delivered. The *gemara* then responds in a way that connects to the next point.

### Scribe Handwriting Evide…

*D'ktivi bitlata yadei safrei* — the three documents are written in three different scribal handwritings. Since each document bears a distinct hand, they cannot have been written by a single *sofer* for multiple clients in one session. Three different sources produced these three documents. The only way they came to be found together is that they were all held by the single party common to all three — the lender — and fell from his possession. Furthermore, even if one considered the possibility that the borrowers had already received their documents and were now bringing them to *beis din* for validation, the *gemara* notes: *malveh mekiyim* — it is the lender, not the borrower, who initiates the validation process. The validation is the lender's proof that the money was lent; the borrower would not take the initiative to get his own obligation validated. Therefore, documents in three different hands, all naming the same lender, with validation already present, must have fallen from that lender.

---

## Receipts vs. Debt Docume…

### Receipt Negates Debt

The *mishnah* states: *im yesh imahem simponos yaaseh mah she'basimponos* — if among one's documents there is found a *simpon*, a receipt or negating document, one acts in accordance with what the *simpon* says and treats the underlying debt as discharged. This is the *mishnah*'s ruling: a receipt found among one's documents is treated as valid.

### Rav Yirmiyah's Rule

The *gemara* presents what appears to be a direct contradiction from an authoritative ruling: *amar Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba amar Rav* — a *simpon hayotzei mitachas yedei malveh*, a receipt found in the possession of the *malveh*, *af al pi she'kasav biksav yado*, even if it is in the *malveh*'s own handwriting, *eino ela k'mesachek u'pasul* — it is nothing but a joke and is invalid. A *malveh* holding his own receipt proves nothing about payment.

### Handwritten Receipt Issu…

The *chiddush* of *af al pi she'kasav biksav yado* — even though it's in his own handwriting — requires explanation, since one might have thought a self-authored receipt is stronger evidence of payment than one written by a *sofer*. The *gemara* explains the logic in reverse. When the *malveh* is not literate and must rely on a *sofer* to write his receipt, there is indeed a concern that the *sofer* was engaged ahead of time because the *malveh* anticipated payment but wasn't sure a *sofer* would be conveniently available at the moment of payment. He pre-writes the receipt so it's ready to hand over the instant the money arrives. This is understandable. But if the *malveh* can write the receipt himself, why would he write it before receiving the money? Surely he would simply write it at the moment of payment. And yet — *savar dilma itrami leh bein hashmashos* — he may have reasoned that the borrower will come to pay right before *shabbos*, or at some inconvenient moment, and if he cannot immediately produce a receipt *d'kaffara li*, the borrower will refuse to pay — *lo yahiv li zuzei*. So he pre-writes the receipt, ready to hand it over the instant payment arrives: *echtov ana d'chi asi li zuzei eiten leh*. Since this is a plausible scenario, even the *malveh*'s own handwritten receipt found in his own possession proves nothing about whether payment was actually received.

### Receipt + Paid Documents

This creates an obvious tension with the *mishnah*, which states that one acts in accordance with a *simpon* found among one's documents. *Amar Rav Safra* — Rav Safra reconciles the two: the *mishnah* is speaking of a case where the *simpon* was found among *shtaros kru'in*, torn-up or paid-up documents. The combination of a receipt and its presence in the drawer where the *malveh* keeps his discharged documents — rather than among his active *shtaros* — creates a meaningful presumption that the debt was indeed paid. On its own, a receipt in the *malveh*'s possession proves nothing. But a receipt filed with documents that are definitively no longer active is a different matter. *Rashi* offers two versions of this: either the specific loan document in question was found among the torn-up documents (though itself not torn), or the receipt itself was found there. Either way, the combination provides the additional evidential weight the *simpon* alone lacks. This is acknowledged not to be the *pshat* of the *mishnah* but the operative halacha.

### Same Name Problem

The *gemara* brings another case to bear: *nimtza l'echad bein shtarosav shtar she'yotzei bein Shimon parua* — among a *malveh*'s documents is found a receipt saying that Yosef ben Shimon has paid his debt, but this *malveh* has two different borrowers both named Yosef ben Shimon, each owing money on separate *shtaros*. The *malveh* knows which *shtar* belongs to which Yosef ben Shimon, but cannot determine which of the two the receipt refers to. The ruling is *shnayim pruim* — both debts are rendered uncollectible. And once again, the fact that the *mishnah* apparently trusts this receipt in the *malveh*'s hands is addressed with the same answer of *Rav Safra*: only when found among paid-up documents does the receipt carry evidentiary weight.

### Orphans' Oath

Another proof text: when orphans seek to collect a debt from other orphans, the halacha requires them to take an oath before collecting. The precise formulation of the oath includes: *shvua she'lo pikadnu abba v'shelo amar lanu abba v'shelo matzanu bein shtarosav shel abba she'shtar zeh parua* — we swear that our father never instructed us about this *shtar*, never told us not to collect it, and that we did not find any documentation among our father's papers indicating this debt was paid. Crucially, had they found such documentation, they would be bound by it. This implies that documentation of payment found among one's papers is treated as valid. Once again, Rav Safra applies: *she'nimtza bein shtaros k'ruim* — only when the documentation is found among the torn-up papers is it treated as conclusive evidence.

### Receipt + Witnesses

*Tashma: simpon she'yesh alav edim yitkayem b'chosmav* — if a *simpon* bears the signatures of witnesses, validate the signatures and it is good. Since stating this of a receipt in the *loveh*'s possession would be obvious, the *gemara* assumes it refers to a *malveh* holding the receipt. This again appears to validate a *malveh*'s receipt. The *gemara* responds: *mai edim edei kiyum* — the *edim* here does not mean simply that the receipt has witnesses on it; it means the receipt was formally validated in *beis din*. A receipt that was brought before the court and had its signatures authenticated will never have been validated unless it was genuinely active and operative. The court does not validate a document that has not yet taken effect. So this case is not evidence that an ordinary receipt in the *malveh*'s hands is trusted; only one that passed through the formal validation process.

This reading is confirmed by the *seifa*: *she'ein alav edim pasul* — without witnesses, invalid. *Mai ein alav edim* — what does "without witnesses" mean? If it means no witnesses at all and it was not even in the *malveh*'s own handwriting, of course it's invalid — obviously a receipt with no attestation of any kind is meaningless. So *ein alav edim* must mean it lacks court validation — *lav edei kiyum*. The two halves of the ruling thus align: a receipt with *edei kiyum* is valid; one without court validation is not.

### Receipt on Document

*Simpon she'yesh alav edim kasher* — the *gemara* returns to consider this ruling in its own right. *O she'yatza le'achar chitum shtaros* — or if the receipt appears written after the signatures on the original loan document itself. Rather than a separate document, below the witnesses' signatures on the *shtar chov* itself, the *malveh* has written that Michael paid his ten thousand dollars, and obtained signatures on that as well. This is obviously valid as proof of payment: *d'i lav d'para lo hava marei leh leshtareih* — if it had not been paid, he would never write on the document itself that it had been, thereby destroying his own *shtar*.

### Third Party Holder

*Ein alav edim v'yotzei mitachas yad shalish* — if there are no witnesses on the receipt but it is found in the possession of a third party who affirms its validity. Why does this make it valid? *Deheymnei malveh leshalish* — the *malveh* trusted the *shalish* by the very act of placing the document with him. Whether the *loveh* deposited the receipt with this trusted third party, or whether the *malveh* himself handed it to the third party with instructions to hold it until the debt was paid, in either case the *malveh*'s act of entrusting the document to the third party constitutes an implicit acceptance of whatever testimony the *shalish* now offers about its status. The third party holds and says: the loan was paid. The *malveh*'s original act of trust makes that claim binding.

With this the *perek* concludes, and we recite *hadran alach shenayim ochazin*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 21

## Intro: Elu Metzios

### Perek Structure

The second *perek* of Bava Metzia, *Elu Metzios*, turns to the foundational questions of *avedah*: when may a finder keep a lost object, and when is he obligated to announce his find so that the owner may come forward and claim it? The first *perek* dealt with interesting disputes over objects already in contention — two people grasping a *tallis*, or questions about returning a *shtar* — but now the *Gemara* arrives at the basic framework governing found objects. Characteristically, the *Gemara* takes its time before laying out the central conceptual issues, beginning instead with secondary matters and working its way toward the heart of the *sugya*.

### Mishna: Keepers

The *mishna* opens: *elu metzios shelo ve'elu chayav l'hachriz* — here are the found objects you may keep, and here are those over which you bear an obligation to announce. The list of objects that may be kept begins with *matza peiros mefuzarin*, scattered fruit — presumably fallen from a cart — and *maos mefuzarim*, scattered money that has fallen from someone's pocket. Two conditions underlie every case on this list. First, the object must be genuinely lost, not merely set down by someone who intends to return for it. Second, there must be no *siman*, no identifying mark; if there is a *siman*, we cannot presume *yeiush* — the owner's giving up of hope — because the owner could come forward, provide the identifying mark, and reclaim the object.

*Yeiush* is the pivotal concept here. It denotes the owner's despair of ever recovering the lost item. The combination of physical detachment — the object is lost and the owner does not know where it is — and psychological detachment — the owner no longer regards the item as his and holds no expectation of its return — together create a state in which anyone who acquires the object bears no obligation to restore it. The first *Rashi* on the *perek* remarks that after *yeiush* the object is *hefker*. Whether this means the object is literally ownerless, such that no one owns it, or merely that anyone may take it while it technically remains the original owner's, is an interesting conceptual question — but the operative point is clear: lost without a *siman* and with *yeiush*, the object is free to be kept.

The *mishna* continues with further cases: *krichot b'reshut harabim*, bundles of wheat left in the public domain; *igulei devela*, rounds of pressed figs with no distinguishing characteristics; *kikarot shel nachtom*, a baker's loaves — generic, unremarkable; *machrozot shel dagim*, a line of fish; *chatichot shel basar*, cuts of meat purchased in the ordinary way. These are all grocery items, so to speak, that have been dropped or forgotten, not intentionally placed with an expectation of return. To these the *mishna* adds *gizei tzemer halekuchim mimdinatan*, raw freshly-sheared wool taken from its source — undyed, uncombed, without particular identifying features — and *anitzei pishtan*, stalks of flax, and *leshonot shel argaman*, strips of purple cloth. All are generic and undistinguished. Rabbi Meir rules: *harei elu shelo* — these are yours to keep.

### R. Meir vs. R. Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda qualifies this list: *kol sheyesh bo shinui chayav lehachriz* — anything on this list that nevertheless has something distinguishing about it must be announced. His examples: if you find one of these rounds of figs and there is a shard of pottery embedded inside — *matza igul uv'tocho cheres* — that is an identifying mark, as is finding a loaf with coins baked into it. The question is whether Rabbi Meir would actually disagree; looking at the cases, it seems Rabbi Yehuda is simply providing a qualification that Rabbi Meir would readily accept. This tension will be addressed in the *Gemara*.

### R. Shimon: Anporya

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds: *klei anporya ein chayav lehachriz* — garments of *anporya* do not require announcement. The *Gemara* will clarify what *anporya* denotes and why such garments, despite appearing to fall into a category that might require announcement, are in fact treated like objects requiring no proclamation.

---

## Kav be'Arba Amot

### Quantity: Kav

The *Gemara* opens on 21a by immediately seeking to quantify the *mishna*'s case of scattered fruit: *v'chama* — how much? Rabbi Yitzchak answers: *kav b'arba amot* — a *kav* (roughly the volume of a large container, somewhere between forty-six and sixty-four ounces) scattered across four *amot*, approximately six feet. Whether this denotes a square area of six by six feet is not specified, but the measure gives a concrete benchmark for what counts as "scattered."

### Quantity vs. Quality

The *Gemara* immediately presses back: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If you can tell simply by looking that the fruit was dropped haphazardly — *derech nefila* — then even a greater density of fruit across those four *amot* would obviously qualify; the visual evidence of an accidental drop renders the quantity irrelevant. And conversely, if the arrangement appears deliberate — *derech hinuach* — then even a sparser distribution still looks like something placed there intentionally. In either case, the quantitative ratio seems beside the point: you make a qualitative visual assessment and the quantity should not change the ruling. The *Gemara* has thus moved from demanding a number to questioning whether any number can do the work. This is a striking *Gemara*: the demand for quantification is introduced and almost immediately undermined.

### Rav Ukva's Explanation

Rav Ukva bar Chama resolves the tension by identifying a third scenario that the quantitative measure is meant to address: *k'vmachnashta d'vei darei askinan* — we are dealing with the situation of clearing out a grain house. A person has been gathering his grain and transporting it away, and when he is done there is a small amount left behind — not accidentally dropped and not deliberately placed for later retrieval, but simply left over from the clearing process. The question is whether he will bother to come back for it.

Here the ratio of *kav b'arba amot* becomes meaningful. A *kav* of grain spread across four *amot* — *nafish tarchaihu* — represents significant effort relative to the modest value of the grain. *Lo tarach inish ve-lo atei ve-shakel lehu* — a person will not exert himself to return and collect it. *Afkurei mafkeir lehu* — he effectively declares it *hefker*, in the manner of *aveida mida'at*: he knows he is leaving it and simply does not care. This is not the case of someone unaware that he has lost something — it is the case of someone who consciously decides the return trip is not worth it.

If, however, the grain is concentrated in a smaller area — *batzir meihachi* — so that a return trip would quickly yield a full *kav*, then *tarach ve-hadar atei ve-shakel lehu* — he would make the effort to come back and gather it, and we therefore do not say he has made it *hefker*. The quantitative measure, then, governs this specific middle scenario of intentionally-left grain, not the simple case of accidentally dropped fruit.

### Variations & Effort

Rabbi Yirmeyah builds on this framework with a series of questions, each designed to probe the relationship between *tarchia* — effort — and *chashivut* — value. The *Gemara* is essentially asking: which factor actually drives the determination of whether the owner will return?

The first question: *chatzi kav bi-shtei amot mahu* — half a *kav* in two *amot*? This is precisely half of the original case in both dimensions. On one hand, *lo nafish tarchaihu* — the effort is less, it is a quicker job, perhaps he will come back. On the other hand, *de-lo chashivi* — but the gain is also less, only half a *kav*, and perhaps even less value makes him less likely to bother. We do not know whether the reduced effort makes return more likely or the reduced gain makes it less so.

Second: *kabaim bi-shmoneh amot* — two *kavim* in eight *amot*? This doubles both the effort and the gain. The effort is now greater than the original case, which is already on the threshold of being too much — *kol sheken denafish tarchia* — so perhaps he definitely will not return. But two *kavim* is worth more — *keivan dechashivi* — and perhaps for a larger sum he would find the effort worthwhile. Again, unresolved.

Third: *kav shumshmin b'arba amot* — a *kav* of sesame seeds in four *amot*. Sesame seeds are far more valuable than grain — *keivan dechashivi lo mafkir lei* — so the monetary gain would seem to justify a return. But they are also far more laborious to gather — *nafish tarchia* — and one might argue that gathering tiny sesame seeds takes far longer than gathering grain of the same volume, making the effort prohibitive. Which dominates?

Fourth: *kav tamrei b'arba amot* and *kav rimonei b'arba amot* — a *kav* of dates or pomegranates in four *amot*. These items are roughly the same monetary value as a *kav* of grain, so by a value calculus one might not return for them, just as for grain. But they are much larger and easier to gather — *lo nafish tarchia* — so perhaps the ease of collection makes return more likely. Or perhaps what matters is only the value, which is the same as grain, and therefore he will not return.

In every case, the *Gemara* leaves the answer as *teiku* — unresolved. Rabbi Yirmeyah is characteristic in his fondness for these edge-case questions. What is illuminating is the framework the *Gemara* has built: the simple *mishna* case of scattered fruit is a matter of visual assessment, but the *Gemara* has introduced a second category — intentionally-left grain — where the quantitative ratio captures a genuine economic calculation, and then probed the limits of that calculation systematically.

---

## Yeiush Shelo Midaat

### Definition

At the top of 21b, the *Gemara* introduces the central conceptual debate of the *perek*: *yeiush shelo mida'at* — *yeiush* without awareness. The scenario is this: a person has lost something but does not yet know it. Someone else comes along and finds the lost object. At the moment of finding, the owner has not consciously despaired of recovering the item — he is entirely unaware of the loss. Yet once he learns of the loss, he will certainly despair, because there is no *siman* by which he could identify the object. May the finder keep it?

### Abaye: Conscious

Abaye rules: *lo havei yeiush* — it is not *yeiush*. *Yeiush* requires active, conscious despair. The owner has not given up hope because he does not even know there is anything to despair of. Therefore when the finder picks up the object, he does so at a time when *yeiush* has not occurred, and he may not keep it.

### Rava: Inevitable

Rava rules: *havei yeiush* — it is *yeiush*. Since we know with certainty that as soon as the owner learns of the loss he will despair — *dechi yada denafal minei meya'esh* — the *yeiush* is effectively operative from now. The object is already so detached from the owner that it may be treated as if *yeiush* has already occurred.

### Agreement Cases

The *Gemara* carefully delineates the cases where Abaye and Rava agree before isolating the case of their dispute. Where there is a *siman* — an identifying mark — everyone agrees that there is no *yeiush*, even if the owner later explicitly despairs. The reasoning is important: *dechi ata liyadei b'issura ata liyadei* — when the finder picked up the object, he did so at a time when it was not permitted for him to keep it. The subsequent *yeiush* of the owner does not retroactively change the status. Furthermore, we should not *impose* *yeiush* on an owner who has not yet declared it in circumstances that do not call for it; a person who loses a wallet with identification inside will naturally say, *yehavna simanin v'shakilna leih* — I will provide the identifying mark and get it back — and we assume he will not despair. If and when he does, that is his *yeiush*, but it cannot be backdated.

The second case of universal agreement is *bezuto shel yam uvshululito shel nahar* — something swept away by the sea at high tide, or carried off by an overflowing river. This represents a case designated by the *Gemara* as *avuda mimenu umikol adam* — lost from the owner and from all mankind. Here, even if the owner insists he has not despaired, his subjective stance is overridden: objectively, the item is so completely beyond human reach that no one has a reasonable claim to it. Even with a *siman*, *Rachmana shar'yei* — the Torah permitted it. So this is the inverse: rather than *yeiush* being blocked by objective circumstances (the siman case), here *yeiush* is imposed by objective circumstances regardless of the owner's stated intention.

### Dispute: No Siman

The debate between Abaye and Rava is thus confined to the intermediate case: an object without an identifying mark, where the owner is not yet aware of the loss. Abaye insists that *yeiush* requires active, conscious giving-up of hope — *deha lo yada denafal minei* — and since the owner does not yet know, there is no *yeiush*. Rava argues that since we know with certainty that upon discovering the loss the owner will have no recourse — *simana leis li bagevei*, he has no identifying mark — his *yeiush* is effective from this moment. *Mehashtah hu demeya'esh*: effectively, he gives up hope now, even if he does not yet know it.

---

## Proofs from Mishna

### Scattered Fruit

The *Gemara* now attempts to bring evidence from the cases of the *mishna* for one side of this debate or the other, working through each item on the list. The *mishna*'s first case — *peiros mefuzarin*, scattered fruit — seems at first glance to support Rava: the owner presumably does not know his fruit has scattered and yet the *mishna* permits keeping it, suggesting that *yeiush shelo mida'at* is operative. But the *Gemara* deflects the proof with the explanation of Rav Ukva bar Chama already developed above: the scattered-fruit case is *aveida mida'at* — the owner knew he was leaving behind the grain that remained after clearing his storehouse, and consciously decided not to bother returning for it. There is no unaware *yeiush* here; it is a deliberate abandonment.

### Scattered Money

The case of *maos mefuzarim* — scattered money — similarly appears to support Rava. But the *Gemara* invokes the principle of Rabbi Yitzchak: *adam asuy l'mashmesh b'kiso b'chol sha'ah* — a person habitually checks his pockets regularly. We therefore assume that within the time between when the owner dropped the money and when the finder came upon it, the owner had already realized the loss, consciously despaired (there being no *siman*), and thereby the *yeiush* that allows the finder to keep the money was in fact active and aware. The case is thus again removed from the domain of *yeiush shelo mida'at*.

### Weighty Items

The cases of *igulei dveilah* — rounds of figs — and *kikarot shel nachtom* — a baker's loaves — present the same apparent challenge. The *Gemara* answers: *agav d'yakiri meida yadei behu* — precisely because these items are physically weighty, the owner will quickly sense that his bag or load is lighter than it should be and will realize something has been lost. Again, rapid awareness means active *yeiush*, not *yeiush shelo mida'at*.

### Valuable Strips

The strips of purple cloth, *leshonot shel argaman*, are neither weighty nor particularly bulky, so the previous answer does not apply. Here the *Gemara* invokes Rabbi Yitzchak's rule directly: *agav d'chashivi mashmesh b'hu* — because these strips are valuable, the owner is regularly checking to make sure they are secure, just as one who carries expensive concert tickets continually confirms they remain in his pocket. Valuable items attract the owner's vigilant attention, producing rapid awareness and thus active *yeiush*.

### Money in Shul

A *braita* is then cited: *hamotzei ma'ot b'vatei k'nesiyot u'v'vatei midrashot u'v'chol makom sheharabbim metzuyin sham* — one who finds money in a synagogue, a study hall, or any place where crowds gather may keep it, because the owners despair. The challenge is the same: perhaps the owner does not yet know he has lost it. Here Rabbi Yitzchak's original statement is positioned: he made this declaration specifically in the context of money found in a *beit midrash* or synagogue, and the principle — that a person regularly checks his pockets — was subsequently extended to the more general *mishna* case of scattered money. In a public space with constant movement, the owner would rapidly discover the loss.

---

## Leket Case

### Leket Permission

A new proof is introduced: *me'ematai kol adam mutarin b'leket* — from when may all people, not only the poor, take *leket*, the gleanings left after the grain harvest? The *mishna* answers: *misheyechlu bah hanimoshot* — once the *nimoshot* have passed through. Rabbi Yochanan explains that *nimoshot* are elderly people who walk with a cane; once even the slowest, most thorough elderly gleaners have gone through the field and gathered every last grain, whatever remains is no longer considered *leket* set aside for the poor and may be taken by anyone. Reish Lakish understands it as a second round of gleaning — gatherers who follow behind the first wave of gleaners.

### Multi-Town Problem

This case is relevant to the debate over *yeiush shelo mida'at* in the following way. Normally one might say that the poor people of this town have consciously despaired — they have gone through the field and gathered what they could — so it is clear *yeiush*. But the *Gemara* presses: the poor people of other towns have not despaired. They are not aware that the local gleaners have already exhausted the field. In principle, *leket* belongs to all the poor everywhere — why should the unawareness of the poor people in surrounding towns not prevent the field from becoming permissible to all? If their lack of awareness forestalls *yeiush*, then the field should remain restricted.

### Preemptive Yeiush

The *Gemara* answers with a striking observation: *keivan deika aniim hacha, hanach meikara yaushi miyashi* — since there are local poor people who will get to the *leket* first, the poor of other towns have effectively despaired from the very beginning of the harvest season. They know they will not be able to compete with the local poor who are present on the scene. Their *yeiush* is preemptive and permanent — they have already conceded that the *leket* in other towns is not for them. Accordingly, when the local poor have finished gleaning, no external claim of unawareness remains to obstruct general permission. There is no *yeiush shelo mida'at* operating here; the non-local poor's despair was conscious from the outset.

---

## Figs vs. Olives

### Braita Rule

The *Gemara* brings a final case from a *braita*: *ketziot baderech* — drying figs on the road, and *teenah hanotah laderech* with figs found fallen under an overhanging fig tree — *mutarot mishum gezel*, there is no prohibition of theft in taking them, and they are also exempt from *terumot umaasrot* because they are ownerless. Conversely, *bezaitim uvecharuvin* — olives under an olive tree or carobs under a carob tree — *assur*, forbidden. The asymmetry between figs and olives or carobs requires explanation.

### Abaye: Known Fall

From Abaye's position — that *yeiush shelo mida'at* is not *yeiush* — the *braita* presents no difficulty. The figs are permissible because either the owner is aware that figs regularly fall and is therefore consciously *mityayesh* when they do, or because fallen figs become disgusting and the owner knows they will be stepped on. Either way, the owner's *yeiush* regarding the figs is a *yeiush mida'at*. Olives and carobs, by contrast, do not regularly fall and remain clean when they do, so the owner has not consciously despaired — it is *yeiush shelo mida'at*, which Abaye holds ineffective.

### Rava's Difficulty

For Rava, however, the *braita* creates a problem. Rava holds that *yeiush shelo mida'at* is operative *yeiush*. If so, why are olives and carobs forbidden? Once the owner learns they have fallen, he will surely despair — there is no *siman* — and by Rava's logic that should already count as *yeiush* from the moment they were found. The *seifa* of the *braita*, prohibiting olives and carobs, seems to contradict Rava's position.

### R. Abahu: Identifiable

Rabbi Abahu resolves Rava's difficulty: *shani zayit hu v'chazuso mochiach alav* — olives are different because their appearance testifies to their origin. Olives found beneath an olive tree are evidently *from that tree*, in that location. People recognize whose olives they are. This means that olives do in fact have a *siman* — their context and appearance identify them — and therefore we cannot presume *yeiush* at all, since an owner with a *siman* would say *yehavna simanin v'shakilna leih*. The case of olives and carobs is thus removed from the domain of *yeiush shelo mida'at* altogether; it belongs to the category of objects with an identifying mark where everyone agrees *yeiush* cannot be assumed.

### R. Papa: Disgust

Rav Papa offers a different and complementary resolution. The reason figs fallen from a tree are permissible is not primarily about awareness or the mechanics of *yeiush*, but about the nature of the object itself: *te'eina im nefilatah nim'eset* — a fig, when it falls, becomes disgusting. It will be trampled, it will rot, nobody wants it. The owner's *yeiush* is therefore essentially guaranteed regardless of awareness, because no owner retains any desire to recover something that has already been rendered revolting by the fall itself. Olives and carobs, by contrast, are hard and durable. An olive before it has been cured is quite hard, and a carob similarly. They do not become disgusting when they fall, and therefore the owner retains an interest in recovering them and will not be *mityayesh* even after becoming aware of the loss. Thus Rava can explain the difference between figs and olives not by invoking *siman* but by noting that the object's post-fall state determines whether *yeiush* — aware or unaware — will ultimately occur at all.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 22

## Yeush Shelo Midaas

### Opening Remarks

The daf begins at the final line of 21b, with the words *ta shema*, "come and hear." We are in the midst of the debate between Abaye and Rava over the principle of *yeush shelo mida'as* — whether an owner's prospective despair, his anticipated abandonment of hope of recovering a lost object, takes effect even before he is consciously aware of his loss.

### Core Dispute

Abaye holds that *yeush shelo mida'as lo havei yeush* — prospective despair does not constitute valid *yeush*. For the transfer of ownership through *yeush* to be effective, the owner must be consciously aware of his loss and must actively despair of recovery. Rava, by contrast, holds that *yeush shelo mida'as havei yeush* — since we can determine with confidence that, upon learning of the loss, the owner would have despaired, we treat that anticipated despair as operative even now, before he has found out.

The *mishna* on the preceding daf appears to support Rava broadly. In the cases discussed there, objects without a *siman* may be kept by the finder, and the assumption is that even if the owner was unaware at the moment of loss, he would eventually despair — and that suffices. Abaye, however, explains each of those *mishna* cases as ones in which there is good reason to assume the owner was already aware that the object had fallen. The *gemara* now proceeds to examine a series of further proofs bearing on this dispute.

---

## Ganav, Gazlan, River

### Mishna Cases

The *gemara* introduces a *ta shema* from the final line of 21b. The *mishna* states: if a *ganav* — a burglar — stole from one person and gave it to another; or if a *gazlan* — an open robber — stole from one person and gave it to another; or if the Jordan River swept away one person's object and deposited it in another person's domain — in all these cases, *ma shenatal natal u'ma shenatan natan*: what was taken was taken, and what was given was given. The acquisition stands.

This is, of course, the well-known principle of *yeush v'shinui reshus*: once the owner has despaired and there has been a change of domain, the recipient acquires the object. The cases of *ganav* and *gazlan* were treated extensively in Bava Kamma. The question the *gemara* now presses is: how do we know in each of these cases that *yeush* has occurred?

### Ganav Case Analysis

The *gemara* reasons as follows. *Bishlama gazlan v'Yarden dechazi lei u'miyash* — I understand the *gazlan* case and the river case: in both, the owner sees what is happening and is aware of it. We can therefore reasonably presume he has despaired. But regarding the *ganav* — a burglar operates covertly — how do we know the owner has even discovered the theft yet? If Reuven's house was burglarized and the stolen item sold to Shimon, we have no certainty that Reuven has learned of the theft. Yet Shimon acquires the object through *yeush v'shinui reshus*. This would seem to vindicate Rava: we apply *yeush shelo mida'as* and say that once Reuven finds out he will certainly despair, and that suffices.

### Rav Pappa Defense

Rav Pappa resolves this by explaining that the *mishna* is not speaking of an ordinary covert burglar but of *listim mezuyan* — armed robbers, who operate openly. Thus the owner does witness the taking, and the case is one of conscious awareness, not prospective despair. The *gemara* then objects: if so, why does the *mishna* need to mention both the *ganav* and the *gazlan* separately? They are essentially the same scenario. The *gemara* answers: *trei gavni gazlan* — the *mishna* wishes to convey two types of open robbery, lest one think the rule differs between them. In any event, the case is not genuinely one of *yeush shelo mida'as*: it is a case where the owner was aware. This is admittedly a very forced reading of the *mishna*, but the *gemara* accepts it.

It is worth noting, as the *gemara* itself recognizes, that the cases of *ganav* and *gazlan* are not cases of *aveidah* at all — they are cases of *geneiva* and *gezeila*. They are brought here because the underlying principle of *yeush v'shinui reshus* is shared, and thus the question of whether *yeush shelo mida'as* is effective applies equally in both contexts.

---

## River Deposits

### Tosefta Text

The *gemara* now brings a *Tosefta*: *shataf nahar korov v'etzav v'avanav* — a river flooded its banks and swept away a person's beams, timber, and stones — an entire building project — and deposited them in his neighbor's field. The *Tosefta* rules: *harei elu shelo mipnei shenityashu hab'alim* — these belong to the finder because the owners have despaired.

### Conscious Yeush

This language is precise and significant. The *Tosefta* does not say that the objects may be kept because we assume the owners *would have* despaired. It says the owners *have* despaired — *nityashu*, past tense, indicating active and conscious *yeush*. The *gemara* draws the inference: *ta'ama denityashu hab'alim* — the reason it is permitted is that the owners actually despaired; *hastama lo* — but by implication, without such active despair it would not be permitted. This appears to be a proof for Abaye.

### Retrieval Scenarios

The *gemara* deflects this reading. *Hacha bemai askinan keshe'yachol lehatzil* — we are dealing here with a case where the owner may actually be able to run after the objects and retrieve them. In such a case, even Rava would not apply *yeush shelo mida'as*, because we cannot confidently predict what the owner would do upon finding out. If recovery is possible, some owners will expend the effort to pursue it. Accordingly, the *Tosefta* is discussing a scenario where the automatic presumption of *yeush* cannot be applied, which is why conscious *yeush* is required.

The *gemara* then says: *ei hachi eima seifa* — if so, let us examine the continuation of the *braita*. The *Tosefta* adds: *im hayu ba'alim mardifim achareihem chayav lehachzir* — if the owners were running after the objects, demonstrating they had not despaired, then one is obligated to return them. The *gemara* presses: if we are dealing with a case where retrieval is physically possible, why does active pursuit matter? Once we cannot presume *yeush* in the first place — because the owner might choose to run after it — even the absence of active pursuit should not suffice for *yeush*. Why does the *Tosefta* specifically require active running as the trigger for the obligation to return?

### Rava Framework

The *gemara* answers: *hacha bemai askinan beyocholim lehatzil al yedei hadechak* — we are speaking of a case where retrieval is possible only with great effort. The logic then runs as follows. Because the owners could theoretically retrieve the objects but only through considerable exertion, we cannot automatically presume what they would do. *Mardifim lo yeiush yiyaish* — if they actively run after the objects, that demonstrates clearly they have not despaired. *Ein mardifim yeiush miyaish* — if they are aware and do not run after the objects, that itself communicates: it is not worth the effort to me. That is *yeush*. The case the *Tosefta* addresses is thus one of conscious awareness throughout — not a case of *yeush shelo mida'as* at all. Because the owners' reaction is genuinely uncertain when they would find out, Rava's principle cannot be applied, and the *Tosefta* accordingly requires active *yeush* or its equivalent. This reading, while strained, neutralizes the *Tosefta* as a proof against Rava.

---

## Terumah Shaliach

### Tosefta Terumah

The *gemara* introduces another *ta shema*, this time from a *Tosefta* in the laws of *terumah*. The *Tosefta* asks: under what circumstances does the rule hold that *hatoram shelo mida'as trumato trumah* — one who separates *terumah* without the owner's awareness has nonetheless effected valid *terumah*?

The scenario: Shimon enters Reuven's field, harvests the grain, and decides to do Reuven a favor by separating *terumah* on his behalf — *shelo birshut*, without having been granted permission. The *Tosefta* states: *im choshesh mishum gezel ein trumaso trumah* — if Reuven, upon learning what happened, would be concerned that Shimon acted improperly with his property — whether by taking too much or by using grain of too high a quality — then the *terumah* is not valid. *V'im lav, trumaso trumah* — but if Reuven has no such concern, and it is clear he is content with what Shimon did, the *terumah* stands.

### Owner Reaction

The *Tosefta* then addresses how we determine whether Reuven approves. If Reuven arrives and finds Shimon in the act of separating *terumah* and says *kolach eitzel yafos* — "you should have taken the higher-quality grain" — this statement may be sincere or sarcastic depending on the facts. *Im nimtzu yafos mehen, trumaso trumah* — if there genuinely is higher-quality grain available, Reuven's comment is sincere: he is glad Shimon separated *terumah* and merely wishes it had been even better quality. This demonstrates approval, and the *terumah* is valid. *V'im lav, ein trumaso trumah* — if the grain Shimon used was already the finest available, then Reuven's remark is sarcastic — "you used my very best grain!" — and that reveals his dissatisfaction. The *terumah* is not valid.

The *Tosefta* continues: if, instead of making any remark, Reuven simply went ahead and harvested additional produce himself and added it to what Shimon had separated as *terumah* — *bein kach u'vein kach trumaso trumah* — in either case, Shimon's *terumah* is valid. Reuven's action demonstrates retroactively that he was fully content with what Shimon had done.

This case appears to be evidence for Rava. At the moment Shimon separated *terumah*, Reuven was unaware — and yet based on Reuven's subsequent reaction we determine retroactively whether Shimon's act was valid. That is precisely the logic of *yeush shelo mida'as*: what the owner would have thought or felt, had he been aware at the time, determines the legal reality even absent actual contemporaneous consciousness.

### Shalichus Defense

Rava comes to Abaye's defense — a striking inversion. The *gemara* states: *amar Rava aliba d'Abaye* — Rava explains how Abaye can answer this proof. The case, Rava argues, must be one in which Reuven had formally appointed Shimon as his *shaliach* to separate *terumah*: *d'shavyu shliach*.

The *gemara* supports this reading. It would make no sense to say that someone who acted on another's behalf entirely without authorization could have effected valid *terumah*, because the very basis for *terumah* by agency is the *pasuk*: *ken tarimu gam atem trumas Hashem* — "you too shall separate the portion of God." From the word *atem*, "you," the Rabbis derive that one's agent can separate *terumah* on one's behalf. But the *gemara* immediately draws the corollary: *mah atem l'da'atchem, af shluchachem l'da'atchem* — just as when *you* separate *terumah* you are consciously aware of the act, so too your *shaliach* must be consciously designated. An unauthorized party stepping in to perform the act on your behalf cannot do so by virtue of *shlichus*, because *shlichus* requires a conscious appointment.

### Gemara Explanation

This is, to be candid, an extremely difficult reading of the *Tosefta*. The *Tosefta* explicitly frames the case as *hatoram shelo mida'as* — separating *terumah* without the owner's awareness — and describes Shimon as acting *shelo birshut*, without permission. To read into this a case of formal *shlichus* strains the plain meaning considerably. One could perhaps argue that *shelo mida'as* and *shelo birshut* refer not to the absence of any agency relationship but to Shimon having exceeded or deviated from the parameters of an appointment that did not specify quality or quantity. But even so, *shelo birshut* is very difficult to reconcile with a formal appointment.

The *gemara* nevertheless proceeds to explain the *Tosefta* along these lines: Reuven appointed Shimon as his *shaliach* and told him *zil trum* — go separate *terumah* — but did not specify from which grain. *V'stamei d'ba'al habayis ki taram m'beinonisa taram* — the reasonable default assumption is that the owner intends *terumah* to be taken from average-quality grain. Shimon, however, went and took from the finest grain — *miyofos*. The *shelo mida'as* and *shelo birshut* thus refer to Shimon's having operated outside the unstated parameters of his appointment: he acted without the *da'as* of the owner in the sense that the owner never contemplated or authorized this particular choice. Whether Reuven is content with what Shimon did — retroactively validating the *terumah* — thus becomes the question the *Tosefta* investigates.

The *gemara* is therefore saying: the whole *Tosefta* is a case of *shlichus*, and what it examines is merely when a *shaliach*'s deviation from implicit parameters is ratified by the owner. This is not a case of *yeush shelo mida'as* — it is a case of agency law and the scope of an agent's authority.

### Applied Case

The *gemara* then records a practical episode. Ameimar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi visited the orchard of Mari bar Isak. Mari bar Isak's sharecropper brought them dates and pomegranates and presented them — clearly from the owner's portion of the crop, not the sharecropper's share. Ameimar and Rav Ashi ate, reasoning that as distinguished rabbis and presumably friends of the owner, Mari bar Isak would obviously be pleased for them to eat. Mar Zutra refused to eat, unwilling to assume the owner's implicit consent.

While they were sitting there, Mari bar Isak arrived. He found them and turned to his sharecropper, saying: *amai lo ayiteis lehu l'rabbanan me'hanech shapirta* — why did you not bring these honored rabbis the better quality fruit? This reaction was parallel to the *Tosefta* case. There was indeed better-quality fruit, suggesting the owner's remark was sincere — he genuinely wanted them to have his best produce. Ameimar and Rav Ashi said to Mar Zutra: surely now you can eat. Is this not precisely the *Tosefta* case — *nimtzu yafos mehen, trumaso trumah* — the owner indicated there was something better, proving his sincerity and his retroactive approval?

### Mar Zutra Refusal

Mar Zutra refused to be moved. He cited Rava's ruling: *lo amru kelapei yafot ela l'inyan terumah bilvad* — the principle that we read the owner's "you should have taken better" as sincere only when the matter concerns *terumah*. Why specifically *terumah*? *Mishum de'mitzvah hu, v'nicha lei* — because *terumah* is a *mitzvah*, and therefore we presuppose that a person wants it done in the best possible way. If better grain exists, we assume the owner would have wanted the *terumah* taken from it; accordingly, his remark is read as sincere.

But in the case of the orchard, a different factor is operative. *Mishum kesifuso hu de'amar hachi* — the owner's remark was driven by embarrassment. What was he to do — berate his sharecropper in front of distinguished guests and say he did not want them eating his fruit? Social pressure and shame compelled him to say "you should have given them something even better," regardless of what he actually felt. In that context we cannot read the remark as sincere approval. Mar Zutra therefore maintained his refusal.

---

## Dew on Produce

### Dew Tosefta

The *gemara* now brings a *ta shema* from the *Tosefta* in *Machshirin*, the tractate dealing with liquids that render produce susceptible to *tumah*. The governing halacha, derived from the *pasuk* *vechi yutan mayim al zera* — "when water is placed upon seed" — is that produce cut from the ground only becomes susceptible to *tumah* upon contact with liquid, specifically when the owner is *nicha lei*, pleased that the liquid came into contact with it. The principle is *dumya d'chi yiten*: the liquid-contact must resemble an active "placing" of liquid, in that it must be something the owner is glad about.

The *Tosefta* states: *hudach tal aleihen vesamach* — if dew condensed on fruit that was drying on the roof, and the owner came up and was happy about it, *harei zeh bechiyutan* — this constitutes valid *hechsher*, rendering the produce susceptible to *tumah*.

### Post-Drying Awareness

A more complex case follows. *Nagvu* — if the dew subsequently dried off — *af al pi shesamach*, even if the owner later expressed happiness that the dew had fallen on the fruit, *eina bechiyutan* — at the top of 22b — it does not constitute *hechsher*. The produce is not susceptible.

This appears to be a direct proof for Abaye. The owner was happy — but only after the fact, once the liquid had already dried. Because he was not actively conscious of and pleased about the situation *at the time* the dew was on the fruit, that later happiness is insufficient. This is precisely Abaye's logic: retrospective or prospective frame of mind does not substitute for actual contemporaneous consciousness.

### Retroactive Happiness

The *gemara* articulates the principle that this *Tosefta* seems to negate. *Lav mishum delo amrinan, kivan de'igla milsa dehasta nicha lei, me'ikara nami nicha lei* — is it not because we do not say: since it is now clear that he is pleased, we treat him as having been pleased from the outset? Here the *gemara* abstracts the conceptual structure of *yeush shelo mida'as* and applies it across categories: just as Rava would say that anticipated despair counts as present despair, one might analogously argue that subsequent pleasure counts as contemporaneous pleasure. The *Tosefta* rejects this — and thus it appears to support Abaye.

### Consciousness Requirement

The *gemara* deflects this as well. *Shani hasam d'chsiv ki yiten, ad she'yiten* — this domain is governed by the special requirement of the *pasuk*: the word *yiten* implies an active, conscious placing of liquid. The obligation of *hechsher* is therefore uniquely demanding: it requires not only *nicha lei* but also *l'da'as* — the owner must be conscious of the liquid's presence at the time it is on the produce. This is derived by *gezeira shava* from *ki yiten*: just as active placing requires full consciousness, so too the passive falling of liquid (*ki yutan*) must be accompanied by awareness and pleasure simultaneously.

Rav Pappa had already noted the apparent tension in the *pasuk* itself: the word is written without the *vav* — *ki yiten* — but is traditionally read as *ki yutan*. The resolution: we need both. Liquid may fall passively (*yutan*), but it must be *dumya d'ki yiten* — analogous to active placing — in two respects: the owner must be *nicha lei*, and the owner must be conscious of it while the liquid is still present. Accordingly, the *Tosefta*'s ruling is not a general refutation of Rava; it reflects a special, heightened *da'as* requirement unique to the law of *hechsher tumah*, which goes beyond even *nicha lei*.

---

## Aveidah River Proof

### Lost Object Teaching

The *gemara* now brings what proves to be the decisive *ta shema*. Rabbi Yochanan taught in the name of Rabbi Yishmael ben Yehotzadak: *minayin l'aveidah sheshatafah nahar shehi muteret* — from where do we know that a lost object swept away by a river is permitted to whoever finds it?

### Lost Object Categories

The source is the *pasuk*: *v'chein ta'aseh lachamoro v'chein ta'aseh l'simlaso v'chein ta'aseh l'chol aveidas achicha asher tovad mimenu umetzasah* — "and so shall you do with his donkey, and so with his garment, and so with any lost object of your brother that is lost from him and you find it." The *gemara* focuses on the phrase *asher tovad mimenu umetzasah* — "which is lost from him and you find it." This describes the paradigmatic case of *aveidah*: *mi she'avudah mimenu umetzuyah eitzel kol adam* — lost to him, but accessible to others. A person lost it in a public place; others can find and return it. In such a case there is an obligation to return.

*Yatzas zu she'avudah mimenu v'eina metzuyah eitzel kol adam* — this excludes the case where an object is lost from him *and* inaccessible to everyone: swept away by a river, out of reach of all people. Such an object is *avudah mimenu umikol adam* — lost to all. This completely severs the owner's connection to it. Even if there is a *siman*, even if the owner has not despaired, the object is free for the finder to keep. The objective inaccessibility itself effects the severance.

### Parallel Logic

The *gemara* then draws a formal analogy. *V'isura dumya d'heteira* — the case where keeping the object is forbidden should be structured analogously to the case where it is permitted. The permitted case — the object swept entirely out of reach — applies regardless of whether there is a *siman* or not. *Bein d'is beih siman bein d'leis beih siman shara* — with or without a *siman*, it is permitted.

By parallel inference, the forbidden case — the ordinary *aveidah* where the object is accessible to others — should similarly apply with or without a *siman*. *Af issura bein d'is beih siman bein d'leis beih siman assura* — whether there is a *siman* or not, the finder is obligated to return it. Where a *siman* exists, the obligation is obvious. But even where there is no *siman*, the obligation stands — and this can only be true if we say, like Abaye, that *yeush shelo mida'as lo havei yeush*. Without conscious *yeush* by the owner, the finder may not keep the object even absent a *siman*, because the absence of a *siman* alone does not suffice to permit taking — we need actual *yeush*, and actual *yeush* requires the owner's conscious awareness.

---

## Halachic Conclusion

### Rava Refuted

The *gemara* declares: *tiyufta d'Rava tiyufta* — an absolute, decisive refutation of Rava. This is striking when one reflects on the full arc of the sugya. The overwhelming weight of the earlier proofs seemed to favor Rava, and each was deflected by the *gemara* through creative — at times quite strained — rereadings. Yet this final argument, which proceeds by analogy from one category of *aveidah* to another, is treated as a *tiyufta*, an irrefutable contradiction.

### Abaye Ruling

The *gemara* accordingly rules: *v'hilchisa k'vosei d'Abaye* — the *halacha* follows Abaye on *yeush shelo mida'as*. The reason the *gemara* presses so hard to arrive at this conclusion is almost certainly because of an established tradition: we follow Rava against Abaye in virtually all disputes between them — *except* for six cases encoded in the mnemonic *ya'al kegam*.

### Mnemonic Exceptions

The mnemonic *ya'al kegam* — יע"ל קג"ם — encodes the six cases in which the *halacha* follows Abaye rather than Rava.

### Exception Details

The *yud* stands for *yeush shelo mida'as*: the case of the present discussion. We rule like Abaye that prospective, unconscious despair does not constitute *yeush*. Conscious *da'as* and active *yeush* are required.

The *ayin* stands for *edim zomemim* — conspiring witnesses. The dispute concerns whether, when witnesses are found to be *zomemim*, they are disqualified retroactively from the moment of their testimony, or only from the point at which they were exposed. We rule like Abaye on this question.

The *lamed* stands for *lechi haomed me'elav* — a post that stands by itself, the question of what constitutes a valid *lechi* to permit carrying in a shared courtyard or alleyway.

The *kuf* stands for *kiddushin shelo nimseru l'biah* — a *kiddushin* that cannot halachically be consummated, whether such a betrothal takes effect at all.

The *gimmel* stands for *gilui da'as b'get* — whether implicit disclosure of intent, such as an attempt to nullify a *get* through gesture or implication, is legally operative in the context of bills of divorce.

The *mem* stands for *mumar ochel neveilos l'tei'avon* — an apostate who violates Torah prohibitions not out of ideological rejection but out of appetite or desire. The question is whether such a person is *pasul l'eidus*, disqualified as a witness. We rule in accordance with Abaye in this case as well.

In all six of these matters — *ya'al kegam* — the accepted *halacha* follows Abaye against Rava. The *gemara*'s conclusion in the present sugya is therefore that *yeush shelo mida'as lo havei yeush*: without the owner's conscious awareness and active despair, no *yeush* has occurred, and the finder acquires nothing.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 23

## Ye'ush Debate & Metzia

### Ye'ush Consciousness

We pick up in the middle of 22b, having just concluded the debate between Abaye and Rava. The Gemara rules like Abaye — and it must be said that if anything, the weight of the textual evidence seemed to favor Rava — establishing that *ye'ush shelo mida'at lo havei ye'ush*: the owner's implicit despair, had he known of the loss, does not constitute legally operative *ye'ush*. According to Rava, *ye'ush shelo mida'at havei ye'ush*: since all of the indications support the conclusion that one may keep a *metzia* lacking a *siman*, the circumstances themselves suffice. But the Gemara chose to rule like Abaye, requiring that *ye'ush* be conscious and deliberate. The owner must actually become aware that he has lost the object and must actively despair of its return. Furthermore, as the Gemara's proofs suggest, this principle extends beyond *ye'ush* alone to other areas of *halacha* where a person's frame of mind is legally relevant.

### Dates from Trees

With this ruling in place, the Gemara poses an immediate practical problem. Rav Aha brei deRava said to Rav Ashi: now that Rava has been definitively contradicted and we rule like Abaye, what of *hani timre de-zikka* — dates blown off palm trees by the wind and found by the roadside? The Gemara had earlier distinguished figs, which owners anticipate will fall and have already despaired of, from other fruits, which the owner does not necessarily anticipate losing. If an owner of dates does not know his dates have fallen, and may not have anticipated it, how can we eat them?

Rav Ashi replied: *keivan de-ika shkatzim u'remasim deka achli lehu, me-ikara ye'ush miya'esh minaihu* — since there are insects and rodents on the ground that will eat or ruin the fallen fruit, the owner despairs from the very outset. This answer bothers Rashi somewhat, because the earlier Gemara seemed to restrict anticipatory *ye'ush* to figs. What the answer must implicitly add is that the owner is aware that some dates will fall from the tree — not necessarily which dates, but some — and further, that whatever falls will be rendered disgusting and not worth recovering. There are thus two components to any valid anticipatory *ye'ush*: that the owner could foresee the loss occurring, and that he would have no realistic expectation of recovering the object even if he learned of it. This case answers the second question — the dates will be fouled — while the first requires the additional assumption that date-fall, at some level, is anticipated.

### Policy & Liberties

One might ask what ultimately drove the Gemara to rule like Abaye when the evidence seemed to cut the other way. The honest answer is that it is not entirely clear from the text itself. But conceptually, Abaye's position reflects an important policy principle. Tosafot, in the preceding discussion, extended the logic to a familiar scenario: even if you are confident your friend would not mind your helping yourself to their property, you cannot act on that assumption without explicit permission. Their hypothetical consent does not constitute actual permission. The fact that they *would* be *meyaiesh* were they to find out does not mean they *are* presently *meyaiesh*, and therefore it is still *shelo mida'at*. This is a significant ruling about not overstepping boundaries to which one is not entitled.

At the same time, ruling like Abaye makes *halacha* practically difficult. How is a finder ever supposed to determine whether the owner is aware of the loss, or could have anticipated it from the outset? These are not easily ascertainable facts. Nonetheless, that is the *psak*.

### Orphans & Fenced Land

The Gemara presses further with additional cases. *Yasmi de-lav benei mechila ninhu* — what about dates found near trees belonging to orphans, that is, minors, whose *da'at* carries no legal weight? Even if the circumstances would otherwise support *ye'ush*, their despair is legally meaningless. The response is practical: *baga be-ara de-yasmi lo machzikinan* — we do not presume that a given valley or plot belongs to orphans, and therefore one need not be concerned.

But what if the land is *muchzak ve-omed*, established as belonging to minors? Then it is *asurin* — forbidden to keep the fallen fruit. And what of land that is *kirchasa*, surrounded by a fence? There the owner clearly anticipates that fallen dates will remain within the protected enclosure, safe from insects. He expects to recover them. If the dates fall outside the fence, the owner would presumably despair — but since his stated expectation is that they remain within, and the land is protected, there is no original *ye'ush*. The answer here too is *asurin*.
