No claim based on a coin's appearance can overcome this presumption of circulation. This is fundamentally different from a *kli*, where one presumes that if a person can correctly identify the *simanim* of a vessel, they have not sold or otherwise transferred it in the interim, and their familiarity with it constitutes a genuine identifying bond.

---

## Birds & Trash Piles

### Tied Birds Rule

The *mishna* now introduces a third category of ruling — distinct from both *harei elu shelo* and *harei elu chayav lehachriz* — with the instruction *lo yigah bahen*, do not touch them. *Matza achar hagafah o achar hageder, gozalot mekusharim* — if one found small birds tied together behind a fence or behind a wall, *o bishvilin shebasadeh* — or in the paths running through a field — *harei zeh lo yigah bahen*. This is a striking ruling. The Torah obligates one not to ignore a lost object — *lo tuchal lehitalem* — yet here the *mishna* instructs the finder to do exactly that: leave them alone.

### Location Siman Reasoning

The *gemara* explains: *mai ta'ama de-amrinan hanei inish atzninehu* — the presumption is that a person went and hid them there. These birds were placed behind the fence or wall deliberately, as a form of storage or concealment, and the location itself is the *siman*. *Ve-ee shakil lehu, leit lehu lemareihu simana begaveihu* — if you take them, you destroy the only *siman* the owner has. Since the birds themselves have no intrinsic *siman* — one tied pigeon looks like any other tied pigeon — the *makom*, the location, is the owner's sole means of identifying and reclaiming them. Removing them from that location eliminates the *siman* and makes return impossible. Therefore, *hilchach leshavkinehu* — leave them in place until the owner comes.

### Knot Challenge

A *gemara* challenge: *ve-amai lehavei kesher simana* — why isn't the knot in the rope binding the birds together a *siman* in itself? Each person might tie their birds differently, and the particular knot could serve as an identifying mark.

### Rav's Explanations

Two answers are offered. *Amar Rabbi Abba bar Zavda amar Rav: bimkusharim bichenfeihem* — the birds are tied by their wings, *dekulei alma hachi mitkasher lehu* — and everyone ties birds by the wings in essentially the same standard way. There is therefore no distinctive knot that could function as a *siman*. The second difficulty then arises: *velehavei makom siman* — very well, but then let the location itself be a *siman* and require the finder to announce. *Amar Rav Ukva bar Chama: bimdadim* — the birds are still able to move and wander slightly, meaning their precise location is not fixed. And if they can wander, one might say they arrived there on their own rather than having been placed there — *ika lemeimar me'alma atu*. At the same time, one cannot rule out that someone placed them there — *ve-ika lemeimar inish atzninehu*. This irreducible uncertainty is *safek hinuach* — doubt as to whether the object was intentionally placed — and *safek makom siman*, uncertainty whether location constitutes a *siman* in this instance.

### Safek Hinuach Ruling

*Ve-amar Rav Abba bar Zavda amar Rav: kol safek hinuach le-chat'chila lo yitol, ve-im natal lo yachzir* — for any case of *safek hinuach*, one should not take the object in the first instance; but if one has already taken it, one does not return it. The latter clause requires explanation. *Rashi* reads *lo yachzir* to mean that the owner cannot compel the finder to return the object, because the owner has no *siman* by which to make a claim — having removed the object, the finder has inadvertently eliminated the owner's sole means of identification, and the owner is now in no better position than any other claimant. The *Rambam* appears to agree with this reading. The *Ra'avad* and *Tosafot*, however, both argue that *lo yachzir* means nearly the opposite: the finder does not get to keep the object for himself, but neither can he give it back to any particular claimant. He is instead obligated to hold it as a *shomer* indefinitely — he has the *mitzvah* to return it but lacks the ability to do so, since no owner can produce a valid *siman* to claim it.

### Vessel in Trash Rule

The *mishna* continues with an analogous case involving vessels in a trash pile. *Matza kli be-ashpah: im mechuseh, lo yigah bo* — if you found a vessel in a trash pile and it was covered, do not touch it. *Im megulah, notel u-machriz* — if it was uncovered, take it and announce. The parallel to the birds case is clear: a covered vessel in a trash pile was presumably placed there deliberately as a hiding spot, so the location (and the act of concealment) is the *siman*; removing it destroys that *siman*. A vessel that is partially exposed, by contrast, appears to have been discarded rather than hidden, and is treated as a normal found object requiring announcement.

### Trash Braita Contradiction

A *braita* is cited as a challenge: *matza kli tamun be-ashpah, notel u-machriz* — if you found a vessel hidden in a trash pile, you take it and announce it — *sheken derech ashpah lifnot* — because the trash pile is regularly cleaned out. This appears to contradict the *mishna*, which said a covered vessel in the trash should not be touched.

### Zevid Vessel Distinction

*Amar Rav Zevid: lo kashya* — Rav Zevid resolves the apparent contradiction through a distinction based on the type of vessel. *Ha bekuba u-khese* — one ruling addresses large containers such as barrels and platters; *ha be-sakinei ve-himnak* — the other addresses small objects such as knives and forks. Large vessels, even if hidden in a trash pile, are unlikely to be accidentally discarded; their size makes deliberate concealment the far more plausible explanation. Small objects, however, might easily have been accidentally mixed into the trash and are presumed lost rather than hidden. Therefore, for small objects, *chayav lehachriz*; for large ones, *lo yigah bo*, since the act of hiding is presumed deliberate and the location is the *siman*.

### Trash Cleaning Distinction

An alternative resolution (*ve-ibeit eima*, here attributed to the *mar bar Rav Pappa* position in the *gemara*): the distinction in both rulings — for large and small vessels alike — depends on the nature of the trash pile. *Kan be-ashpah ha-asuya lifnot* — one case involves a trash pile that is regularly cleared out; *kan be-ashpah she-eina asuya lifnot* — the other involves a pile that is not regularly cleared. If the pile is regularly emptied, hiding anything there makes no practical sense as a long-term storage strategy. The further scenario involves a trash pile not normally cleared that the owner of the courtyard then decided to empty — *ve-nimlach aleha lifnotah* — which accounts for why objects might be found even within a heap that had been used as a hiding place.

### Yeush Mida'at

The *gemara* introduces the category of *aveida mida'at* in this context. If a person hides something in a trash pile that is regularly cleaned out, that itself constitutes a form of *yeush mida'at* — knowing abandonment. The owner effectively forfeited his object by placing it somewhere it was certain to be discarded. In such a case, the finder may take it outright, without any obligation to announce. The cases requiring *chayav lehachriz* or *lo yigah bahen* are precisely those where the trash pile is *not* regularly cleared, so that deliberate concealment there was reasonable, and the owner retains a genuine expectation of recovery. What neither *amora* ultimately invokes is the simple criterion the *mishna* seemed to state — whether the vessel was covered or uncovered by trash — suggesting that both Rav Zevid and the alternative resolution effectively replace that criterion with their own, more analytically precise distinctions.

---

## Objects in Walls

### Wall Ownership Rule

The *mishna* turns to objects found within structures. *Matza be-gal* — if one found something in a pile of rocks — *o be-kotel yashan* — or in an old, crumbling wall — *harei elu shelo*, one may keep it. The reasoning is that such finds are of indeterminate origin; the wall or rockpile is ancient enough that any connection to a current owner has long been severed. By contrast, *matza be-kotel chadash* — if one found something in a new wall — the calculus changes, because new walls were commonly built with deliberate *hidey-holes* (as we know from the *mishna* in *Pesachim* and related sources) into which homeowners would place valuables for safekeeping.

### Midpoint Division

In the case of a new wall, the *mishna* applies a midpoint rule. *Mechetzo lachutz, shelo* — from the midpoint of the wall outward, the object belongs to the finder, because a homeowner would not store valuables in the outer half of his wall. *Mechetzo u-lefanim, shel ba'al habayit* — from the midpoint inward, the object belongs to the householder, because the inner wall is where one would naturally create and use a hiding place.

### Rental Exception

*Im haya maskiro le-acheirim, afilu be-toch habayit, harei elu shelo* — if the property was rented to others, even objects found entirely inside the house belong to the finder. The reason is that in a rental property, the identity of prior occupants is unknown, and any tenant who left something behind has presumably abandoned it, without the ability to return and stake a claim. No current occupant can be presumed to be the owner, unlike in the case of an owner-occupied dwelling where the *ba'al habayit* is the obvious presumptive owner of any hidden item.

### Canaanite Attribution

The *gemara* asks: when we say a find in an old wall or rockpile may be kept because we assume it belongs to the *Emori'im* — the ancient Canaanite inhabitants — is that assumption reasonable? *Atu Emori'im matnyei, Yisrael lo matnyei* — do only Canaanites hide things in walls, and not Israelites? Surely Israelites also hide valuables; why then do we attribute the find to Canaanites and permit it?

### Deep Burial Requirement

*Lo tzericha: de-shaich tfei* — the case must involve a find that is deeply embedded or particularly well concealed, or *halud haluda*, thoroughly encrusted or sealed. Alternatively, it must have been placed inside some container within the wall. The point is that ordinary storage of items in a wall would not result in the kind of burial or containment that characterizes these finds. When an object is found truly embedded within an old wall — sealed inside, corroded into the structure, or held within an ancient container — one can no longer realistically attribute it to any Israelite who might have stored it there in living memory. Only then does the presumption of ancient Canaanite origin become reasonable, and the finder may keep it.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 26

## Objects in Walls

### Rusted Objects

The *mishna* on daf 26a continues its discussion of objects found under rubble or within walls. As established by the *gemara* earlier, when an object is found in an old wall in a state of extreme rust, one may conclude that it was placed there even by the previous inhabitants of the land — the rust itself is evidence of abandonment, and we therefore treat it as a case where *ye'ush* has certainly occurred, allowing the finder to keep it.

The focus now turns to what the *mishna* says about a new wall. If the object is found on the half of the wall facing *reshut harabim*, the finder may keep it, since the object is presumed to have been left there by one of the people from the public domain. If, however, it is found on the half of the wall facing inward toward a person's private domain, it belongs to the homeowner — one must assume it was placed there by the owner, and it may not be kept.

### Hinuach vs. Aveidah

Rashi notes that even where the object faces the *reshut harabim*, it was presumably placed there intentionally — this would make it a case of *hinuach*, something deliberately set down, not an *aveidah* in the classic sense. Because the *gemara* has already established that we are dealing with a rusted object, we may assume that even what began as *hinuach* has since been forgotten and abandoned, and it may therefore be kept. The inner half is a different matter entirely: if the object always belonged to the owner and is found within his own property, it never attains the status of an *aveidah* at all, even if he forgot about it. It remains his, and the finder has no claim.

### Knife & Pouch Rule

The *gemara* introduces a refinement attributed to Rav Ashi. The text states: *sakina batar kata* — for a knife, one follows the handle. Since a person inserting a knife into a wall would naturally hold it by the handle, the location of the handle determines who placed it there. If the handle faces the interior of the property, the owner of that property is presumed to have placed it; if the handle faces outward, it is presumed to have come from the public domain. Similarly, *vechisa batar shinsei* — a pouch or wallet is carried by its straps, so one follows the straps to determine the direction of entry.

The *gemara* then raises an obvious challenge: if this is so, why does the *mishna* speak of the outer and inner halves of the wall as the criterion? Why not simply examine the direction of the handle or the straps? The answer is straightforward: the knife and pouch rule applies only to those two specific objects. The *mishna* is dealing with cases of *udra venaska* — rags or metal strips, objects that give no indication of the direction in which they were inserted. For such items, one falls back on the spatial criterion of which half of the wall the object occupies.

### Full Wall Division

A *braita* addresses the case where an object fills the entire hole in the wall, occupying both the inner and outer halves simultaneously. Which owner is presumed to have placed it? The rule stated is *cholkin* — one divides. The portion on the outer half belongs to the finder, while the portion on the inner half is treated as belonging to the homeowner. This may seem somewhat arbitrary, since the object clearly entered from one side or the other, but when the matter cannot be resolved, the division is made down the middle.

The *gemara* notes *peshita* — this seems obvious — though one might reasonably question whether it is so obvious, given the arbitrary nature of the split. The *gemara* therefore clarifies that the ruling is necessary for a case where the object is situated at an angle, sloping in one direction toward, say, the *reshut harabim*. One might have thought to apply the logic that it all originated on the homeowner's side and simply rolled downward due to the incline — *ishtapuche ishtapach*. The *gemara* therefore teaches that even in this case, one conceptually divides the object at the midpoint. This is indeed a significant *chiddush*: since we cannot determine the origin, we split the object down the middle, with the outer portion available to the finder and the inner portion left as the presumed property of the *ba'al habayit*.

## Rental Properties

### Rental House Case

The *gemara* continues: *im haya maskir l'acheirim afilu b'toch habayis harei eilu shelo* — if the house was regularly rented out to others, then even if you find something inside the house itself, you may keep it. The scenario envisioned is that of a cleaner or similar person sent into the property who finds, for example, coins left behind. Since the property is a rental that turns over regularly, one cannot attribute the object to any specific person. Without a *siman*, and without any particular reason to assume it belongs to the landlord rather than one of the various tenants, the finder may keep it.

### Chatzer Awareness

This ruling prompts an important question: even granting that the object does not belong to an identifiable tenant, should the landlord not acquire it automatically by virtue of owning the property? A person's *chatzer* — their property or domain — can function as an agent of acquisition on their behalf. Why should the landlord not become the owner of whatever is found on his premises?

Tosafos addresses this question. Tosafos draws from this ruling the principle that *chatzer* cannot acquire an object for its owner in a case where the owner would have no awareness of the object's presence — where it is something that might never be found at all. The relevant language from Tosafos is: *ein chatzer koneh b'davar sheyachol lihyos shelo yimtza'enu l'olam k'mo hacha shehu mutman b'ovi hakosel* — a *chatzer* does not acquire ownership of something that one might never find, as is the case when an object is concealed within the thickness of a wall, or, by extension, left behind in a rented property in circumstances that prevent the landlord from knowing it is there. Tosafos also specifies that the context of the ruling involves an object whose character as a lost item — an *aveidah* — is clear; it is not merely some possession of the owner tucked away in a drawer.

## Majority Principle

### Animal Sellers Case

The *gemara* now poses a challenge to the straightforward reading of the rental property case. Given that the property turns over between tenants, should one not apply the principle of *batar basra* — follow the most recent occupant — and attribute the object to the last renter? To address this, the *gemara* invokes a well-known *mishna* about lost money in Jerusalem.

The *mishna* teaches: *maos shenimtzu lifnei socharei beheima* — money found in front of those who sell animals in Jerusalem is always considered *maaser*, i.e., *maaser sheini* money, regardless of the time of year. The rationale is that people would bring their *maaser sheini* funds to Jerusalem throughout the year to spend on food there, and the primary customers of the animal sellers were those purchasing animals with *maaser sheini* money. Therefore, at any point in the year, the majority of money circulating before the animal sellers was sanctified *maaser sheini* funds, and any coins found there are treated accordingly. Tosafos adds a refinement: one might have thought that money dropped after a purchase was completed would no longer be sanctified, since the sanctity transfers to the animal. But Tosafos notes that the sheer numerical majority of buyers over sellers means we presume the money fell from the buyers, not from the sellers, and thus it retains its status as *maaser sheini*.

### Jerusalem Sweeping

The *mishna* continues: *b'shaar yemos hashana chullin* — for the rest of Jerusalem, outside the immediate vicinity of the animal sellers, money found at ordinary times of the year is presumed to be *chullin*, non-sanctified. But *b'shas haregel hakol maaser* — during the pilgrimage festival, everything found is treated as *maaser*, since at that time Jerusalem is flooded with pilgrims all spending their *maaser sheini* funds, and the overwhelming majority of money in circulation is sanctified.

The *gemara* explains the underlying logic through a statement of Rav Shemaya bar Zeira: *ho'il v'shukei Yerushalayim asuyim l'hitkabed b'chol yom* — because the marketplaces of Jerusalem were swept every single day. This daily sweeping is the key. If a coin had been dropped at an earlier time, it would have been picked up when the streets were swept. Therefore, any coin found now must have been dropped recently. This allows one to draw conclusions based on the present time of year: if it is currently the *regel*, the coin was dropped now, during the *regel*, and is therefore *maaser sheini*; if it is an ordinary time of year, the coin was dropped now, at an ordinary time, and is therefore *chullin*.

### Temple Mount Money

The rule is different for the Temple Mount. There, even during the *regel*, one presumes that found money is *chullin*. Rashi explains this by reference to two features of the Temple Mount. First, it was situated on a slope, so the wind would naturally displace items over time, reducing the need for systematic sweeping. Second, one was prohibited from entering the Temple Mount while dusty, which meant foot traffic was more limited and there was less practical need for daily sweeping. As a result, coins on the Temple Mount could have lain there from any prior time — there is no mechanism, analogous to the daily sweeping of the Jerusalem markets, that would have cleared out earlier coins. One therefore cannot say that a coin found there was dropped recently. The relevant temporal frame is the long term, and over the long term, the majority of money in circulation was *chullin*. Therefore, even during the *regel*, found coins on the Temple Mount are presumed *chullin*.

This principle — that daily sweeping enables one to attribute found objects to the most recent period — is precisely what Rashi applies to the rental property case as well. Just as the streets of Jerusalem were swept daily before each new group of visitors, a renter clears out a room upon leaving, checking under the bed and ensuring nothing has been left behind. Any object found by the cleaner after the last tenant departed is therefore attributable to that last tenant — it is analogous to the *shukei Yerushalayim*. This is exactly why the *gemara* pressed the question: if we can attribute found objects to the most recent party, why does the rental property ruling not simply assign the found object to the last renter?

## Last Renter Problem

### Three Renters

Reish Lakish, citing Bar Kappara, answers that the ruling of the *mishna* involves a specific case: *kegon she'asu pundak lishlosha Yisrael* — the lodging was rented out simultaneously to three people. Since three individuals occupied the space at the same time, there is no single "last person" to whom the object can be attributed. Assuming we are dealing with a case without a *siman*, this is a straightforward scenario of an unidentifiable lost object, and the finder may keep it.

However, the *gemara* then suggests that the case might involve an object with a *siman*, and attempts to derive from this ruling that we follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's position — namely, that in a place where many people are present, even an object with a *siman* need not be returned, since the owner despairs of recovery given the crowds. This inference, it must be said, is somewhat puzzling, since Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle was formulated specifically for *makom sheharabbim metzuyim*, a place where masses of people congregate — not a modest rental room shared by a handful of individuals. Nevertheless, the *gemara* pursues this line of reasoning, suggesting that the three renters constitute a sufficient *rabbim* even among Jews. The *gemara* then rejects this inference and instead attributes the ruling to a case of three non-Jewish renters — *lishlosha ovdei kochavim* — since there is no obligation to return a *metziah* to a non-Jew according to the *ikar halacha*. This resolution is itself somewhat awkward, since it makes the ruling hinge on the identity of the renters rather than on the principle of high turnover that seems to animate the *mishna*. The simpler reading remains that the case involves Jewish renters without a *siman*, and since multiple people occupied the space simultaneously, no one person can be identified as the source of the loss.

### Ye'ush No Admission

Rav Nachman, citing Rabba bar Avuha, goes further: *afilu teima lishlosha Yisrael* — even if the three renters were Jews, the finder need not return the object. The reason is that the person who lost it is certainly *miyayeish* — he has despaired of recovery. The argument runs as follows. The loser knows that no one else was in the room aside from his two co-renters. He has asked them, repeatedly, whether they found his wallet, whether they have it — *amri kammaihu kamma zimni lehadru li* — and they denied it. If they were going to return it, they would have done so already. He therefore concludes that one of them has stolen it and will never admit to it, or that it has simply vanished and is unrecoverable. This despair is qualitatively different from losing an object in a public place where many strangers might find it. In a public setting with a *siman*, a person might reasonably hope that an honest stranger will identify the owner and return it. But here, the loser has already confronted the only people who could know, and they have denied any knowledge. He is therefore definitively *miyayeish*, even if the object carries a *siman*. This is Rav Nachman's reasoning, and it is consistent with a broader principle he articulates about the psychology of *ye'ush* in situations involving known associates.

That broader principle is elaborated immediately. Rav Nachman states: *raah sela shenafal mishnayim* — if one saw two people together and one of them dropped a coin, there is an obligation to return it. The reason is that the person who dropped it is not *miyayeish*. Even when he realizes the coin is gone, his reasoning is: there was only one other person with me — *inish achrina lo hava behadai ella hai* — I will confront him and demand to know whether he has my coin. He does not despair because there is a single identifiable party to hold responsible. The object has not dissolved into the anonymity of the crowd; there is someone who almost certainly either saw it or has it, and there is social pressure available to recover it.

The case with three people is the reverse. If one of three people dropped a coin, one does not have to return it, because the person who lost it is definitely *miyayeish*. His reasoning: there are two others with me — *trei havu behadai* — and whichever one I approach will simply say it wasn't him and point to the other. *Ei naktina lehai amar lo shaktilah, ve'ad naktina lehai amar lo shaktilah* — each one will deny it and redirect me to the third. He therefore concludes that he will never recover it; one of them has taken it and will hide behind the other. This despair is certain, and *ye'ush* is complete.

### Partners Exception

Rava challenges the ruling that three people automatically generates *ye'ush*. He accepts the principle that where *ye'ush* applies, there is no obligation to return the object — but he questions when *ye'ush* can actually be presumed. His argument: *eimar shutfei ninhu velo miyayeish* — perhaps the three people were business partners. If they were partners and the money was jointly owned or carried together, the loser would not despair even if confronted by the dynamic Rav Nachman describes. Partners have a relationship of trust; if my partners have my money, I trust they will return it to me rather than lie about it. Therefore, the calculus of *ye'ush* shifts when there is a possibility of partnership, and the finder may have an obligation to return the object.

### Pruta Threshold

Rava therefore qualifies the ruling: *lo amran ella deleis beih shaveh perutah lechol chad vechad* — the principle that one need not return the object applies only when the total value is less than a *perutah* per person. If the object is worth less than three *perutos*, so that each person's share would be under a *perutah*, then there is no obligation even if they are partners, since there is no *chiyuv* to return an *aveidah* worth less than a *perutah* to each owner. But if the object is worth three *perutos* or more — a full *perutah* per person — one must return it, since the possibility of partnership cannot be excluded and *ye'ush* cannot be presumed.

Some authorities (*amri nasha*) report a further refinement by Rava: even if the object is worth only two *perutos*, there remains an obligation to return it. The reasoning: *eima shutfin ninhu, v'chad mineihu achulei achleih l'mansei gabei chavrei* — perhaps all three were partners, and one of them waived his share in favor of the other two. In that scenario, the remaining two partners each retain a stake of a full *perutah*, and there is a *chiyuv* to return it to them. Therefore, the threshold is effectively two *perutos*, not three. Rashi notes the logical possibility that only two of the three were partners and the third was not, though this particular permutation is not developed further by the *gemara*. The operative principle is that wherever a *perutah*-sized stake belonging to a potential partner cannot be ruled out, *ye'ush* is not presumed and the object must be returned.

## Three Intent Scenarios

### Steal Before Ye'ush

Rava now articulates a systematic analysis of the *mitzvos* and prohibitions implicated in the finding of a lost object, depending on the finder's intent and the timing of *ye'ush*. This is a foundational passage for understanding the structure of *hashavas aveidah*.

The first scenario: *raah sela shenafala, natala lifnei ye'ush al m'nas l'gozlah* — one sees a coin drop and picks it up before *ye'ush* with the explicit intent to steal it. In this case, *avar b'chulhu* — one has transgressed all applicable prohibitions. First, *mishum lo sigzol* — one has violated the prohibition against theft, since the object belongs to another and is being deliberately appropriated. Second, *mishum hasheiv teshiveim* — one has failed to fulfill the positive commandment of returning a lost object, *hashavas aveidah*. Third, *mishum lo suchal l'hisalem* — one has transgressed the negative prohibition of turning away from a lost object, the prohibition against abandoning one's obligation to return it.

The *gemara* adds that even if the thief later returns the object after *ye'ush*, *matana b'alma hu d'yahiv leih v'issura d'avad avad* — he is merely giving a gift, and the transgression he committed remains. This line is noted by the *rishonim* as having been appended by the *geonim* rather than being original to Rava's statement, and it raises a genuine difficulty: if one steals an object and later returns it, does that not fulfill the positive commandment of *hashavas gezeilah* and perhaps also *hashavas aveidah*?

Tosafos engages this question directly. The *lav* of *lo sigzol* is connected to the positive commandment of return — it is *nitak l'asei*. If so, why should returning the object after *ye'ush* be regarded as merely a gift, without fulfilling the *mitzvah*? Tosafos answers that the phrase about giving a gift applies specifically to the prohibition of *lo suchal l'hisalem*. The negative prohibition of not turning away — the obligation not to abandon a lost object — was violated at the moment of abandonment, and that transgression is not rectified by the later return. The positive commandment of *hashavas aveidah* and the obligation of *hashavas gezeilah*, however, would indeed be fulfilled by returning the object, even belatedly.

The *Baal HaMaor* takes a different and more creative approach: after *ye'ush*, if we rule that *ye'ush* is *koneh* — that despair transfers ownership — then one cannot fulfill the *mitzvah* of *hashavas aveidah* through the return, since the object now legally belongs to the finder. This is an unconventional position.

The Ramban offers perhaps the most sophisticated analysis. He begins by articulating why *ye'ush* does not normally help after an object has already been picked up with the intent to return it. When a finder lifts an *aveidah* with the intention of returning it, he becomes a *shomer* — a guardian — on behalf of the owner. In this capacity he is, in effect, a *yad be'alim*, an extension of the owner's hand. The object is treated as already within the owner's constructive possession. When the owner then becomes *miyayeish*, the *ye'ush* is ineffective, because the owner does not realize the object is already in sympathetic hands — he is despairing of something he would not despair of if he knew the truth.

But in the case where the object was picked up with the intent to steal, the finder is not operating as a *shomer* for the owner. The object is not in the owner's constructive domain. When the owner becomes *miyayeish*, the *ye'ush* therefore takes full legal effect — even though the object was physically lifted before *ye'ush*, the finder's hostile intent means the owner's subsequent despair is operative, and the finder acquires the object. If the finder then returns it, he is returning something that has already become his own, and the *mitzvah* of *hashavas aveidah* cannot be fulfilled by returning one's own property. The Ramban acknowledges that this is a creative reading, and the *pshat* of the *gemara* is as Tosafos describes: returning the object does fulfill *hashavas aveidah* and *hashavas gezeilah*, and the phrase about "merely giving a gift" is limited to the irremedied transgression of *lo suchal l'hisalem*.

### Change Mind After

The second scenario: *natul lifnei ye'ush al m'nas l'hachzirah, ul'achar ye'ush niskayvein l'gozlah* — one picked up the object before *ye'ush* with the intent to return it, a thoroughly proper act, but subsequently — after *ye'ush* has already occurred — changed one's mind and decided to keep it. In this case, *over mishum hasheiv teshiveim* alone — one transgresses only the failure to fulfill the positive commandment of returning the *aveidah*.

Why does one not also transgress *lo sigzol* and *lo suchal l'hisalem*? Rashi suggests that one cannot steal something already in one's possession. Tosafos challenges this: the principle that one who wrongfully withholds a worker's wages transgresses *lo sigzol* even while holding the money already demonstrates that *lo sigzol* can be violated with respect to objects in one's possession. Tosafos's answer is that the decisive factor here is timing: the decision to steal came only after *ye'ush*. At that post-*ye'ush* moment, the object has become so detached from the original owner's sphere that withholding it does not rise to the level of *lo sigzol*. Similarly, *lo suchal l'hisalem* — the prohibition against turning away — applies to the initial moment of encountering a lost object and failing to pick it up for return. Here, the finder did pick it up to return it. That initial act was proper. The later change of heart does not retroactively constitute *lo suchal l'hisalem*, which addresses the threshold decision of whether to engage with the *aveidah* at all.

### Wait for Ye'ush

The third scenario: *himtin lah ad shenisyayshu habalim* — one saw the object drop, had the opportunity to pick it up and return it before *ye'ush*, but waited deliberately until the owner had despaired, and only then picked it up. Here, *eino over ella mishum lo suchal l'hisalem bilvad* — one transgresses only the prohibition of *lo suchal l'hisalem*.

The analysis is straightforward. One did not transgress *hasheiv teshiveim* — the positive commandment to return — because that commandment is triggered by picking up the object; since one had not yet picked it up, there was no active obligation to return it. One did not transgress *lo sigzol* — after *ye'ush*, one was legally permitted to take the object. But by waiting and watching while the owner stood before one in a state of uncertainty and loss, by doing nothing when one could have intervened to return the object before *ye'ush*, one violated the prohibition of *lo suchal l'hisalem* — the commandment not to turn away, not to abandon one's responsibility in the face of another's loss.

These three scenarios represent a precise mapping of how the prohibitions and positive commandments of *hashavas aveidah* — *hasheiv teshiveim*, *lo suchal l'hisalem*, and *lo sigzol* — interact differently depending on the sequence of intent and *ye'ush*.

## Lost on Beach

### Beach Loss

Rava presents a striking case: *hai man dechazi denafal zuzei mechavrei becholasa* — one who sees his fellow drop coins in the sand, on the beach. He finds them and takes them. *Lo mechayav l'ahadorei lei* — he does not have to return them. The reason is *hu denafal minei mi'ayeish* — the moment the owner dropped the coins in the sand, he despaired. The nature of the beach — shifting sand, the near-impossibility of locating a small object in an undifferentiated expanse — produces immediate *ye'ush* the moment the object is lost.

### Sieve Exception

The real *chiddush* follows. What if, after dropping the coins, the owner returns with a sieve and begins sifting through the sand methodically, clearly in an effort to recover what he lost? Does this active search demonstrate that *ye'ush* never in fact occurred — that the owner retained hope of recovery and therefore never despaired?

Rava rules that even this does not negate the *ye'ush*. The owner's reasoning, when he comes back with the sieve, is not that he expects to find his own lost coins: *ki heichi denafal minai didi hachi nafal me'inash achrina umeshachana midi* — just as I dropped something in the sand, others have dropped things in the sand too. I will come with my sieve and my metal detector, and even if I do not find my own item, I will find someone else's and thereby make up my loss. The very act of returning to sift is not evidence of confidence in recovering one's own object; it is evidence of a general hope to find *something* of value in the sand, using one's own loss as the occasion for a broader search. This reasoning is decisive: the sieve-and-sifting does not demonstrate that *ye'ush* was absent, and the finder therefore acquires the coins.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 27

## Opening Context

### Intro: Safek Chinuch

We take up the *mishnah* at the bottom of 26b, having just completed an important stretch of *gemara* dealing with *safek chinuch* and the various types of *mitzvot* and *aveirot* implicated when one fails to retrieve an *aveidah*, takes it after *yeush*, or takes it with the intention of stealing. With that framework in place, we now turn to the *mishnah* that follows.

---

## Store & Money Changer

### Found in Store

The *mishnah* opens: *matsa b'chanut harei elu shelo* — if one finds a lost object in a store, he may keep it. Rashi explains that this refers to a case without a *siman*, for if there were a *siman* it would open the question discussed in connection with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar regarding a *makom sheharabim metzuyim*. In any case, the point is that the *metziah* in question is something like a coin found on the floor — not an item sitting on a shelf. Since objects in a store are constantly being kicked around and moved, *makom* is not a *siman*, and the finder may keep it.

### Counter vs. Money Changer

The *mishnah* continues: *bein hateivah v'lachanvani* — if money is found between the counter and the storekeeper, one assumes it fell from the storekeeper, from the till. *Lifnei shulchani harei elu shelo* — if found in front of the money changer, loose coins on the floor in front of his table, the finder may keep them.

### Chair & Table

*Bein hakiseh v'lashulchani shel shulchani* — if found between the chair where the money changer sits and the table where he conducts his exchanges, it is presumed to belong to the money changer himself, *harei elu shel shulchani*.

### Money in Fruit

*Halokeach peirot mechavero o sheshalach lo chavero peirot umatsa bahen ma'ot* — if one purchased fruit from another, or was sent fruit as a gift, and found money inside, *harei elu shelo*, he may keep it. This is striking, since one knows precisely who the fruit came from. The *gemara* will address this.

### Bundled Fruit

However, *im hayu tserurim notel umachriz* — if the money was tied in a bundle, then the knot and the count serve as *simanim*, and one must announce it. One might ask: even without a bundle, why not simply return it to the one who sent the fruit, since presumably there has been no *yeush* — the sender did not even know the money was there, making this a case of *yeush shelo mida'at*? The *gemara* will resolve this.

---

## Shulchani Scope

### Rabbi Elazar: Table

The *gemara* opens its analysis with a statement by Rabbi Elazar: *afillu munachim al gabei shulchan* — even if the coins are resting on the table itself, the finder may keep them, provided they are not found in the space directly between the table and the money changer.

### Reisha/Seifa

The *gemara* examines this claim against the *mishnah*. From the *reisha*: *lifnei shulchani harei elu shelo* — "in front of the money changer" you may keep it. The implication is that *al gabei shulchan*, on the table itself, belongs to the money changer — *lashulchani*. But now consider the *seifa*: *bein hakiseh v'lashulchani shel shulchani* — between the chair and the *shulchani*. Here the word *shulchani* in context seems to mean the *shulchan*, the table, not the money changer himself. The implication of the *seifa* would then be the reverse — that money on the table belongs to the finder. The two halves of the *mishnah* thus seem to pull in opposite directions regarding money on the table itself. *Ela meha leka lemishma mina* — from the *mishnah* alone, one cannot infer an answer to that question.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the formulation of the *mishnah* itself is what motivated Rabbi Elazar's ruling. *Matnitin kashya leh* — the *mishnah*'s language is itself the source of the difficulty. Since the *seifa* says *bein hakiseh v'lashulchani* — between the chair and the table — one could ask: why phrase it this way? Simply say *al hashulchan*, "on the table," and it would be self-evident that between the table and the chair also belongs to the money changer. Alternatively, following the structure of the *reisha* which says *matsa b'chanut*, one might have expected the *seifa* to say something like "found in the money-changing area" (*beshulchanot*), and then contrast that with the case between the chair and the table. Instead, the *mishnah* says *lifnei hashulchani* — "in front of the money changer." This phrasing is therefore being read as inclusive of the table itself, which is after all positioned in front of him. *Ela shema mina afillu munachim al gabei shulchan harei elu shelo* — we learn that anything "in front of" the money changer, including what is on the table, the finder may keep.

### Random vs. Merchant

The practical logic underlying this ruling is straightforward: the money changer sits behind his table. Any money lying on the surface of the table in front of him could have been left there by any number of customers coming to exchange money; it is random. Only money found in the space between the table and where the money changer sits is presumed to be his, since that is where he keeps his own funds, behind the table.

### Methodology

This analysis illustrates a broader methodological point worth noting. The *gemara* characteristically does not articulate legal principles in the abstract; it derives them through *diyuk* — close reading of concrete formulations. It would seem more straightforward to simply ask: what does logic dictate in this case? Yet the *gemara* begins from the text and then extracts the principle. This mirrors the *Torah* itself, which speaks concretely — *ki yigach shor et shor reehu vamet* — and from concrete cases the law is derived. One can observe a transitional stage in the *mishnayot*, which often conclude a series of concrete cases with the formula *zeh haklal, kol she-...* — "this is the rule: whatever is..." — moving from the particular toward the general. Having both the concrete cases and the abstracted rule is, of course, more useful than either alone, since an abstract principle without worked examples leaves unclear exactly how it applies.

### Store Privacy

One might ask whether the store itself constitutes private property capable of effecting acquisition on behalf of the owner — after all, *chatzeiro shel adam konah lo*, a person's courtyard acquires objects on his behalf. The answer is that a store open to the public is *einah mishtameret* — it is not a guarded domain. This does not mean the owner cannot lock it at night; rather, it means that at the moment when people are freely entering and moving through it, the owner cannot effectively prevent others from accessing anything found there. A space that functions as a common thoroughfare is not a *makom mishtamer*, and therefore it does not effect acquisition for the owner as a courtyard would. It would, however, be a different question if the owner were *omed betzad chatzeiro* — standing immediately adjacent — but that is a separate matter.

---

## Fruit Money: Merchant

### Reish Lakish Rule

The *gemara* now addresses the *mishnah*'s ruling that money found inside purchased fruit belongs to the finder. Reish Lakish, citing Rabbi Yannai, limits this rule: *lo shanu ela belokeach min hataggar* — it applies only when one bought from a merchant, a middleman who in turn purchases from many wholesalers. *Aval belokeach miba'al habayit chayav lehachazir* — if one bought directly from the farmer who grew the produce, one is obligated to return the money found in it. The reasoning is that in the latter case, the source of the money is known — it came from this specific farmer — and since he is presumably not aware of the loss, this is a case of *yeush shelo mida'at*, which does not constitute valid *yeush*. Furthermore, the farmer knows who bought from him and can reasonably expect to get it back. A *tanna* repeated this same ruling before Rav Nachman: it is only when one buys from the merchant that the finder may keep the money, because the merchant sources from many different wholesalers. Even if the money could be traced to one of those wholesalers, one does not know which wholesaler it was, and each of those wholesalers has already despaired — *miyaesh* — reasoning that once the money entered the merchant's supply, mixed with everyone else's grain or produce, they will never recover it. The situation thus parallels finding a *metziah* in the street, where the loser has no expectation of identifying the finder.

### Rav Nachman

Rav Nachman challenges the other side of the ruling. Even if one buys from the farmer directly, why should the finder be obligated to return it? The farmer himself did not do the threshing — he has workers. *Stam peirot* here seems to refer to grain broadly. Since the farmer employs workers, the money found in the grain could equally have belonged to any one of them. There is no *siman* — none of the workers will know who lost it, and they will despair of recovering it. It would then be a classic case of *lo siman*, and the finder should be entitled to keep it. Accordingly, Rav Nachman presses: should this *braisa* simply be rejected as logically untenable?

### Kena'ani Slaves

The response is *lo* — the *braisa* can be reconciled. *Titarchei matnisin kegon shedashana al yedei avdo veshifchato hakenanit* — the case applies specifically where the farmer's labor force consists entirely of Canaanite slaves. Since Canaanite slaves possess nothing independently — all their property belongs to the master — any money found in the grain is by definition the farmer's money, not theirs. If the farmer had employed free workers, the situation would indeed be as Rav Nachman suggests: one would not know which individual lost the money, and since there is no *siman*, the finder would be entitled to keep it. Notably, the resolution does not suggest returning the money to the farmer on the grounds that he will investigate and figure out who lost it — once there is no *siman* and the precise identity of the loser is unknown, the ruling is *harei elu shelo*.

---

## Garment Paradigm

### Klal U'Prat

We turn now to a *mishnah* that could well have served as the opening of the entire tractate, since it addresses the foundational principles that have been operating throughout: the concept of *siman* and the concept of *yeush*. The *mishnah* reads: *af hasimla hayta baklal* — the garment was already included in the general category. The *pasuk* in *Devarim* states, among other things: *vechein ta'aseh lesimlato vechein ta'aseh lechol aveidat achicha asher tovad mimenu umetzata lo tuchal lehitalem* — you shall do the same for his garment, and for any lost object of your brother that you find; you may not ignore it. Since the *pasuk* already contains the general statement *kol aveidat achicha*, which covers everything, why single out the garment? *Lama yatzat* — *lehakesh lah*, to use the garment as a prototype from which other cases may be derived.

### Simanim & Tov'im

*Ma simla meyuchadet sheyesh bah simanim* — what is distinctive about a garment? Before the era of mass production, a cloak typically had identifying marks — *simanim* — that made it distinguishable. *Veyesh lah tov'im* — and there are claimants: someone who loses a garment is not going to give up on it. It is not *hefker*; the owner will go around asking and searching and will not despair of recovering it. *Af kol davar sheyesh bo simanim veyesh lo tov'im chayav lehachriz* — and so the rule is derived: any lost object that has *simanim* and has claimants actively seeking it must be announced and returned.

This formulation encapsulates the two principles that have run through the entire tractate from its opening. The plain reading of the *Torah* never actually permits keeping a lost object — it says to return everything. The *mishnah*, however, reads *simla* as defining the parameters: the obligation to return applies when both conditions hold. Moreover, there is a meaningful distinction between the two requirements. *Tov'im* — active claimants — points to the principle of *yeush*: you are obligated to return an *aveidah* only so long as the owner has not despaired. *Simanim*, meanwhile, address a distinct question: even granting that the owner has not despaired and is still searching, how does the finder know that the person standing before him is actually the owner? How can *simanim* be sufficient evidence on which to rely?

### Yeiush & Siman

These are two genuinely separate foundations. The *yeush* question concerns the owner's subjective state — whether he has given up hope. The *siman* question concerns the evidentiary basis for the finder's decision to return the object. It is true that the two are often linked: when there is a *siman*, the owner typically does not despair, because he believes he can identify his object and reclaim it. And conversely, when there is no *siman*, the owner may conclude that the finder will have no way of knowing the object is his and will give up hope. But the principles are conceptually independent. We have already encountered cases where a *siman* exists and yet the owner despairs — for instance, in a *makom sheharabim metzuyim* where many people pass through — and cases where there is no *siman* but the owner has not despaired — such as the fruit case, where the identity of the source is known even without a distinguishing mark. The *simla* teaches us both of these principles, and the *gemara* will now explore the extent to which each of them is genuinely derived from the *pasuk*.

---

## Multiple Examples

### Question Setup

The *gemara* asks: *lama li dichtav Rachmana shor chamor seh u-salmah* — why does the *Torah* list all these specific examples — an ox, a donkey, a sheep, and a garment — when the *pasuk* already contains the general clause *kol aveidat achicha*? The answer is *tzrikhi* — each item is necessary, each teaching something that could not be derived from the others alone.

### Direct Simanim

If the *Torah* had written only *simla* and the general *kol aveidat achicha*, one might have read the obligation narrowly: *hani milei be-edim de-gufa ve-simanim de-gufa* — the obligation to return applies only where the identification is direct, either through witnesses who recognize the object itself or through *simanim* on the object itself. It must be noted that the *gemara* hedges here deliberately, because we have not yet resolved whether *simanim* constitute a *d'oraita* basis for return or only a *d'rabbanan* one. The question — which will emerge explicitly shortly — is whether at the *Torah* level, the only valid basis for returning an object is testimony by third-party witnesses who directly identify the object (*tfisat ayin*), or whether a claimant's own description of a *siman* suffices. With this question open, the *gemara* presents both *edim* and *simanim* as possible means of establishing ownership, while noting that both would be understood, under the narrow reading, as requiring identification of the object directly.

### Donkey & Saddle

What, then, does the extra word *chamor* — donkey — teach? *Aval be-chamor be-edim de-ukaf ve-simanim de-ukaf, eima lo mahadrinan leih* — if all one has is testimony or *simanim* pertaining to the saddle, not the donkey itself, one might have thought that is insufficient — perhaps the saddle belongs to a different person than the donkey. *Ktav Rachmana chamor* — the *Torah* writes "donkey" to teach that one may return even the donkey on the basis of *simanim* on the saddle alone. We do not entertain the concern that the saddle found on the animal belongs to someone else; rather, *de-afilu chamor be-simanei ha-ukaf*, one returns the donkey on the strength of identifying marks on its saddle.

### By-Products

*Shor ve-seh ktav Rachmana lama li?* — why are ox and sheep also listed? *Shor de-afilu le-gizat zanavo* — the ox teaches that even the shedding of its tail, which has some material value as hair, must be preserved and returned along with the animal. *Ve-kol she-ken seh le-gizoteiha* — and certainly by extension, a sheep's wool, which accumulates while the animal is in the finder's care and which is far more valuable, must be sheared at the appropriate time, held, and returned to the owner along with the animal.

One might then ask: if we derive from the ox that even the tail sheddings must be returned, do we even need the sheep? Rava himself concedes this point — the sheep might have been derivable from the ox by *kal va-chomer*. He therefore offers a different explanation: *chamor de-vor le-Rabbi Yehuda ve-seh de-aveidah divrei ha-kol* — the word *chamor* by *aveidah* is needed specifically for Rabbi Yehuda's position, and the word *seh* teaches something relevant to *aveidah* according to all opinions. Rabbi Yehuda holds, in the context of *Bava Kamma*, that one is liable for vessels damaged in a pit — *chamor ve-lo kelim* does not serve as an exclusion for him — and so the word *chamor* by lost objects cannot serve the function it would serve according to the *Tanna Kama*. Rabbi Yehuda therefore needs that word for a different purpose. Similarly, the word *seh* must be teaching something that has not yet been covered by the other examples.

### Dung Rejected

What could *seh* be teaching? The *gemara* raises the possibility: *ve-eima le-glalim hu de-ata* — perhaps the word *seh* comes to teach that even the animal's dung must be preserved and returned to the owner, or at least that the finder must sell it and return the proceeds, since dung has value as fertilizer. The *gemara* rejects this: *glalim afkurei mafkir lehu* — people do not expect to reclaim their animal's dung; they effectively renounce ownership of it. This is a striking application of *sevara* — the *gemara* is acknowledging that yes, there is an extra word in the *pasuk* that needs to be accounted for, and technically one could use it to teach an obligation regarding dung. But logic dictates otherwise: no one losing an animal intends to claim back its dung, and the finder who is caring for the animal — and potentially paying costs that will be reimbursed — cannot reasonably be expected to collect and hold the dung. The *Torah*'s words are interpreted in light of what people actually care about, and dung simply does not make the list.

---

## Simanim Authority

### Sheep & Simanim

If the word *seh* is not being used to teach the dung obligation, perhaps it is available to teach something else — specifically, that *simanim* constitute a valid *d'oraita* basis for returning a lost object. After all, *simla* might not be unambiguous on this point, as we will see. Perhaps *seh* is what actually establishes *simanim de-Oraita*, and the *simla* is reserved purely for the *yeush* principle.

### Iba'ya Setup

*Iba'ya lehu* — the question is left open: are *simanim d'oraita* or *d'rabbanan*? This is distinct from the *yeush* question. Whatever conditions lead an owner to despair may sometimes involve *simanim* and sometimes not, but *yeush* is clearly a *d'oraita* principle. The separate question is whether the evidentiary basis for returning an object — namely, a claimant's description of an identifying mark — is itself rooted in *Torah* law or only in rabbinic enactment. The *gemara* is considering using the word *seh* as the source for *simanim d'oraita*, establishing that even by a category of object where direct identification is not self-evident, *simanim* suffice as the return mechanism.

The *gemara* then says: *amri lo — ha detanya u-tana lesimanin gabi simla* — since the *mishnah* itself already teaches *simanim* in the context of *simla*, it is clear that the author of our *mishnah* does not derive *simanim* from *seh*. Either the *mishnah* genuinely holds *simanim* to be *d'oraita* derived from *simla*, or it holds *simanim* to be *d'rabbanan* and is reading the *simla* passage as a mere *asmachta* — but either way, *seh* is being used for some other *drasha* that we have not yet identified. The question of whether *simanim* are *d'oraita* or *d'rabbanan* therefore remains formally unresolved at this stage of the *sugya*. *Shema mina de-seh lav le-simanim hu de-ata* — it is clear the author of our *mishnah* does not use *seh* as the source for *simanim*.

---

## Pesuk Details

### Worth Losing

The *gemara* now turns to a series of *derashot* on the specific language of the *pasuk*. The *braisa* cites the phrase *asher tovad* — "which is lost" — and derives from it that the obligation of return applies only to something substantial enough to be worth losing. This connects to the discussion earlier regarding a lost object worth less than a *shaveh prutah*.

### Shaveh Prutah

Rabbi Yehuda derives the *shaveh prutah* threshold from the word *u-matzata* — "and you found it" — it must be something worth finding. The *Tanna Kama* derives it from *asher tovad* — it must be something worth losing. As Abaye observes: *mashmauta d'krai ika beinaihu* — there is no practical difference between these positions; both conclude that a lost object worth less than a *prutah* carries no return obligation. The disagreement is purely textual — which phrase in the *pasuk* is the vehicle for this *drasha*. But that textual disagreement has downstream consequences, because whichever phrase one uses for this *drasha* is then unavailable to teach something else.

### Ravnai: Jew Only

For the one who derives *shaveh prutah* from *asher tovad*, what does *u-matzata* teach? It goes to the teaching of Ravnai, who derives from *u-matzata d'ata l'yadei mashma* — "and you found it" implies it has already come into your hand — that even after one has picked up a lost object, the obligation to return it applies only to *aveidat achicha*, a fellow Jew's property. One might have thought that even if one is not obligated to pick up a non-Jew's lost item, having picked it up one might be obligated to return it. Ravnai teaches from *u-matzata* that even in that case, the obligation does not apply.

### Yochanan: River Case

For the one who derives *shaveh prutah* from *u-matzata*, what does *asher tovad* teach? It goes to the teaching of Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: *minayin l'aveida she-shatafah nahar she-hi muteret* — how do we know that an object swept away by a river may be kept, even without the owner having despaired? From the phrase *asher tovad mimennu* — "which is lost from him." The complete formula is read as: *ne'evad mimennu u-matzui l'chol adam* — it is lost from him but accessible to others. This defines an *aveidah* subject to the return obligation. *Yatza'ah zu she-avudah heimennu ve-einah metzuyah l'chol adam* — excluded is the case of an object lost from the owner and inaccessible to others as well; that is the river case, where the object is simply gone for everyone. Such an object is not an *aveidah* in the operative sense, and keeping it is permitted.

### Derash Allocation

The *gemara* then addresses the cross-allocation of these *derashot*. For the one who uses *u-matzata* to derive *shaveh prutah*, where does Ravnai's teaching come from? From the extra *vav* — *u-matzata* as distinct from *matzata*. For the one who uses *asher tovad* to derive *shaveh prutah*, where does Rabbi Yochanan's teaching of the river case come from? From *mimennu* specifically — the word *asher tovad* yields *shaveh prutah*, while *mimennu* yields the *aveida she-shatafah nahar* principle: lost from him specifically, yet accessible to others. The remaining position — that *mimennu* does not yield a *drasha* — simply does not accept this reading of the word. The *gemara* concludes that Rava offers yet another distinction between these positions — not merely a difference in textual allocation, but a genuine practical difference — though that analysis opens the next stage of the discussion.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 28

## Pruta Lost or Found

### Pruta Significance

The daf begins by picking up at the bottom of 27a, where the Gemara has been analyzing the various words employed in the *pesukim* dealing with *aveidah*. A prior discussion had noted that the word *שמלה* (*simla*), garment, teaches the principle of *simanim* and of *to'im* — that one returns a lost object when there are claimants and when there is some distinguishing mark. The Gemara had also raised the question of the *pruta* threshold: since an object worth less than a *pruta* need not be returned, from which word in the verse is this derived — from *asher tovad*, "that was lost" (indicating significance at the moment of loss), or from *u-metzata*, "and you found it" (indicating significance at the moment of finding)?

On the face of it, there appears to be no *nafka mina* between the two positions — it is merely a question of which textual emphasis one prefers. Rava, however, argues that a practical difference does exist: *pruta she-huzla ika beinayhu* — the case of an object that was worth a *pruta* at the time of loss but has since depreciated below a *pruta*. According to the view that derives the threshold from *asher tovad*, what matters is its value when it was lost, and since it was worth a *pruta* then, there is an obligation to return it. According to the view that derives it from *u-metzata*, what matters is its value when found — and since it is now worth less, there would be no obligation.

### Both Words Required

The Gemara, however, is not satisfied with this formulation. Even the view that derives the rule primarily from *asher tovad* cannot ignore the word *u-metzata*, which is equally present in the verse. Surely, the Gemara presses, one would need to satisfy both endpoints — and in the depreciation case, the finding-side requirement is not met. Similarly, the reverse case — an object worth less than a *pruta* at loss but more at finding — would fail on the losing-side for the view that derives from *u-metzata*, yet that view cannot simply disregard *asher tovad* either. The Gemara concludes that neither of these simple cases can serve as the *nafka mina*.

### Fluctuating Value

The Gemara therefore proposes a more complex scenario: *pruta she-hokra ve-huzla ve-hazara ve-hokra* — an object that was worth a *pruta* at the time of loss, then dropped below a *pruta* at some intermediate point, and then rose back above a *pruta* by the time it was found. Both endpoints are satisfied. The debate, then, is whether the intermediate dip matters.

The view deriving from *asher tovad* holds that the emphasis is on the moment of loss; the secondary requirement of *u-metzata* is satisfied by the final value, and the transient depreciation in between is irrelevant. The view deriving from *u-metzata*, by contrast, takes a broader reading of "finding": it requires *de'it bei shiur metzia mi-sha'as aveidah v'ad sha'as metzia* — that the object maintain a minimum worth throughout the entire period from loss to finding. The precise logic underlying each position remains somewhat difficult to pin down, but this is at least how Rava frames the possible *nafka mina* between the two readings.

---

## Simanim Source

### Simanim: Torah or Rabbis?

At the very end of 27a, the Gemara raises a fundamental question: *simanim d'Oraisa o d'Rabbanan?* Is the principle that one may return a lost object — or adjudicate ownership — on the basis of distinguishing marks (*simanim*) a Biblical rule, or only Rabbinic?

At the outset it is worth clarifying the taxonomy of *simanim*. There are effectively three categories. First, a description so generic that it does not even qualify as a *siman* at all — for example, identifying an object merely as "black" or "large," something that describes a vast proportion of similar items. Second, a standard *siman*: a mark that narrows the field significantly and renders ownership substantially more probable — something like identifying a garment by its color and style. Third, a *siman muvhak*: a mark so specific and unusual that virtually only the true owner could know it, such as a distinctive tear in a particular location. The universally agreed rule is that a *siman muvhak* has the force of Torah law. The debate about *simanim d'Oraisa o d'Rabbanan* concerns the middle category — the ordinary, reasonable *siman*.

### Simanim Scope

The practical *nafka mina* is stated at the top of 27b: *l'hadurei get isha b'simanim* — whether one may return a *get* to a woman based on her ability to provide *simanim*. In monetary matters, the Rabbis have broad latitude to assign ownership: *hefker beis din hefker*, and in general *Chazal* may regulate property rights. But matters of personal status and *issur* are different. If *simanim* are *d'Oraisa*, they carry evidentiary weight recognized by Torah law and may therefore permit a woman to be classified as divorced. If they are only *d'Rabbanan*, *Chazal* would not have had the authority to apply their enactment to an *issur* question — they could not permit a woman to remarry on the basis of a mechanism that the Torah itself does not recognize as valid evidence.

### Simla & Simanim

The Gemara turns to proof. It quotes the Mishna: *af ha-simla haysa bi-khlal kol eileh* — the garment was already included in the general category of "any lost object." Why then was *simla* singled out by the verse? *L'hakish eleha* — to draw an analogy: just as a garment characteristically has *simanim* and has claimants still demanding it, so too any object with *simanim* and active claimants must be proclaimed and returned. This appears to be a straightforward derivation of *simanim* from a *pasuk*, indicating that *simanim* are *d'Oraisa*.

### Asmachta Theory

The Gemara deflects this proof: *tana tov'in itztericha lei, simanim kedi nasvah* — the real teaching of the *pasuk* was the requirement that claimants still be pressing their claim (i.e., that there has been no *ye'ush*). The mention of *simanim* is incidental — an *asmachta*, a Rabbinic principle attached to the verse rather than directly derived from it. What the Torah actually demands, on this reading, is *edim* — witnesses who can identify the object as belonging to a specific person. The *simanim* principle is a Rabbinic layer built on top of that underlying requirement.

---

## Simanim Testing

### Donkey Saddle

The Gemara continues to probe. A *braisa* cited the previous day had taught that one returns a donkey by providing *simanei ukaf* — identifying marks on the saddle. This too appears to derive from the Torah's mention of *chamor*, suggesting that *simanim* are *d'Oraisa*. Again the Gemara deflects: *eima be'adei ukaf* — perhaps the *braisa* should be understood as requiring witnesses to the saddle, not mere *simanim*.

### Inquiry Principle

Another *braisa* expounds the verse *vehaya imcha ad derosh achicha oso* — "it shall remain with you until your brother seeks it out." The *braisa* asks: would you really give it back before he seeks it? Of course not. So what is the verse teaching? *Darshehu im ramai hu o eino ramai* — you must investigate whether the claimant is telling the truth. The Gemara asks whether this does not indicate that the investigation proceeds by *simanim*. But the answer is equally available: *lo, be'edim* — no, it means he must bring witnesses. The *braisa* never mentions *simanim* at all, and the proof remains weak.

### Husband Identity

The Gemara then pivots from *aveidah* to the personal-status angle directly. A *braisa* teaches: *ein me'idin ela al partzuf panim im ha-chotem* — one may not testify that a woman's husband has died unless the witnesses actually saw the face together with the nose, meaning they had genuine direct recognition of the deceased. Crucially, this is so *af al pi sheyesh simanim begufo u-vicheilav* — even if there are identifying marks on his body and his clothes. On its face, this *braisa* seems to flatly rule that *simanim* do not suffice for a *d'Oraisa* personal-status ruling.

### Face Recognition

The Gemara, however, resists this conclusion. It offers the rejoinder: *amri gufo de'aroch ve-gutz* — the "body marks" the *braisa* dismisses are merely generic descriptions like height and build. These are not really *simanim* in any meaningful sense, as they describe a great many people. So the *braisa* is not categorically excluding *simanim*; it is excluding the weakest, most generic descriptors. This is admittedly a strained reading of the *braisa*, which frames the issue as face recognition versus any bodily marks, but the Gemara works with it.

### Weak Simanim

A further issue presents itself: even regarding the clothes, the Gemara says, one cannot rely on identifying them — *d'chaishinan l'she'ela* — because of concern that the items may have been lent to another person. Even if one could say "I recognize those clothes as Reuven's," the worry that Reuven may have lent them introduces doubt. And so the *braisa*'s dismissal of *simanei keilav* could be explained not as a categorical rejection of *simanim* but as reflecting the weak nature of those particular marks: *bichivrei u-vesumkei* — they amounted to nothing more than "he wore white clothes" or "he wore red clothes," which are entirely generic.

---

## Borrowed Items

### Donkey Lending

This introduces a new thread. If the reason that clothing-based *simanim* fail in the testimony context is the concern about lending (*she'ela*), then one must ask: does the same concern not apply to the donkey saddle case? One would be returning a donkey to whoever can identify the saddle — but what if the saddle was lent to a different donkey's owner?

### Non-Lent Items

The Gemara responds: *ukaf lo sha'ali inshi* — people do not lend out their saddles. The reason is *mishum demiskav* — a saddle is worn in to fit a particular animal, and using it on a different animal would cause irritation and discomfort. It is therefore not the sort of item that gets lent out, and *simanim* on the saddle are reliable. This is the principle: the concern about lending applies to items that are commonly lent, but not to items that by their nature are not passed around. A saddle fits that latter category.

The Gemara then proceeds to examine a *braisa* concerning the *get*: if a *shaliach* who was carrying a *get* lost it and then found it *kashur be-kiso, be'arnaki, u-vetaba'at* — tied up together with his pouch, his wallet, or his ring — or found it among his personal belongings, then even after a prolonged period, the *get* is *kasher*. He can identify it by recognizing the objects it was associated with. This too involves using *simanim* in a personal-status context. Does this not prove *simanim d'Oraisa*?

The Gemara challenges: but if we are worried about lending, why would recognition of the wallet or ring be reliable? The *shaliach* may have lent his wallet to someone, and that person's *get* ended up bundled with it. The Gemara's response identifies three items that are never lent: *kis ve'arnaki* — a pouch and a wallet — because of a concern that lending them away is a bad omen (*menachesh kiso*), a kind of squandering of one's fortune; and *taba'at* — a signet ring — because it could be used to forge one's documents. Since these items are simply not lent out, finding them bundled together with the *get* is meaningful evidence of its identity.

### Get & Items

Having established that these particular items carry reliable identifying weight because they are not lent, the Gemara uses this to explain the *braisa* about the *get* without necessarily proving anything about the general status of *simanim*. The recognition of the wallet or ring may be a case of near-direct identification rather than mere *simanim*, since these items are uniquely associated with their owner and never circulate to others.

### Resolution

The Gemara steps back and acknowledges that the proofs attempted so far — both from *aveidah* texts and from personal-status texts — have not conclusively established whether *simanim* are *d'Oraisa* or *d'Rabbanan*. The *pesukim* appeared to derive *simanim* directly, but each time the Gemara could reinterpret the derivation as concerning *edim* or as an *asmachta*. The *braisa* about testimony for a deceased husband appeared to rule against *simanim*, but the Gemara could explain that as addressing only generic, low-quality marks or items that raise lending concerns. The question remains formally open.

---

## Bodily Marks

### Body Features

A *braisa* is now cited: *ein me'idin al ha-shuma* — one may not testify to identify a deceased person based on a bodily swelling or discoloration of the limbs. Elazar ben Mahabai disagrees: *me'idin al ha-shuma* — such a mark may serve as valid identification. Since this dispute concerns personal status — whether a woman's husband is confirmed as dead — it directly engages the question of what counts as sufficient evidence at a *d'Oraisa* level.

### Multiple Readings

The Gemara asks: should we not read this *tannaitic* dispute as being precisely about whether *simanim* are *d'Oraisa* or *d'Rabbanan* — the first *tanna* holding *d'Rabbanan* (and therefore it does not work for personal status) and Elazar ben Mahabai holding *d'Oraisa* (and therefore it does work)? Rava immediately resists this reading and offers alternative explanations, each of which keeps the underlying question of *simanim d'Oraisa* from being definitively resolved by this text.

### Feature Frequency

The first alternative: *d'kulei alma simanim d'Oraisa*, and the dispute here is about a different question entirely: *be-shuma metzuya b'vnei gilo kamiflagei* — whether this type of bodily characteristic is common among people of that person's demographic cohort. If the mark is prevalent among peers, it is not even a meaningful *siman*; it would be as generic as saying the man was of average height. One *tanna* holds the mark is common enough to disqualify it; Elazar ben Mahabai holds it is rare enough to qualify as a valid middle-level *siman*. Both could agree that *simanim d'Oraisa*.

### Post-Death Changes

The second alternative: *d'kulei alma shuma eina b'vnei gilo* — everyone agrees the mark is uncommon enough to be meaningful. The dispute is instead about *simanim asuyin le-hishtanot le-achar mita* — whether bodily marks of this kind tend to change after death. If they do change, then even if the mark was distinctive during the man's life, it is no longer a reliable identifier once he has died. The *Chachamim* hold that such marks are prone to post-mortem change and therefore cannot be relied upon; Elazar ben Mahabai holds they do not change and remain valid. Both could again agree on the general question of *simanim d'Oraisa*.

### Exceptional Marks

The third alternative: *d'kulei alma shuma eina asuya le-hishtanot le-achar mita* — everyone agrees there is no concern about post-mortem change — and yet everyone also agrees that ordinary *simanim* are only *d'Rabbanan*. The dispute then would be: *be-shuma siman muvhak kamiflagei* — is this particular bodily characteristic exceptional enough to be classified as a *siman muvhak*? A *siman muvhak*, by universal agreement, carries *d'Oraisa* weight. Elazar ben Mahabai holds that the *shuma* rises to the level of *siman muvhak* and therefore works for personal-status testimony; the *Chachamim* hold it is merely an average *siman*, which, if *d'Rabbanan*, would not suffice. All three readings of the dispute leave the underlying question — whether standard *simanim* are *d'Oraisa* or *d'Rabbanan* — unresolved. The debate among the *tannaim* can be fully explained on any of the possible underlying positions.

---

## Loser's Interest

### Finder's Incentive

Rava now poses a broader question: *im timtzi lomar simanim lav d'Oraisa* — if we were to conclude that *simanim* are only Rabbinic, we must explain what motivated *Chazal* to institute the principle at all for *aveidah*. Why would they depart from the Torah's standard of requiring *edim* and allow *simanim* to suffice for returning a lost object? His initial answer is framed from the perspective of the finder: *d'nicha lei l'motzi aveida d'nahadra b'simanim* — it is in the interest of someone who finds a lost object that the system operates on *simanim*, because that same person may someday lose an object himself and want it returned to him via *simanim*.

### Owner's Perspective

Rav Safra challenges this immediately: *ve-chi adam oseh tovah le-atzmo b'mamon she-eino shelo?* How can the finder justify delivering property to Reuven — whose claim is supported only by *simanim* — on the grounds that it benefits his own future interests? The finder has no right to use someone else's property as the currency for securing his own future advantage. Perhaps the item should in fact go to Shimon, who might produce *edim*, and the finder cannot sacrifice that outcome for the sake of a general social policy that happens to benefit himself.

In light of this challenge, Rav Papa reformulates the argument entirely: *nicha lei l'ba'al aveida le-meiyav simanim* — the justification must be grounded in the perspective of the owner who lost the object, not the finder. It is the owner who is the potential loser if the *simanim* principle is misapplied. But remarkably, it is also the owner whose interests are *best served* by the institution of *simanim*.

### Owner's Advantage

The reasoning is as follows. If the Torah requires *edim* to reclaim a lost object, the owner will very often be unable to retrieve it — people rarely have witnesses standing by who can identify their possessions. If, however, the system runs on *simanim*, the owner is actually in a strong position: *kulei alma lo yadi simanim muvhakim didi* — not everyone knows the fine details of my object the way I do. The true owner will be able to give more precise and accurate *simanim* than any impostor. So even though the *simanim* principle theoretically opens the door to a fraudulent claimant walking off with the object, in practice the owner is better positioned than anyone else to give the most specific and convincing marks. The real owner will prevail in the overwhelming majority of cases. Accordingly, even from the owner's perspective, a world with *simanim* is preferable to one requiring *edim*.
