The phrase *simanim muvhakim* here is used somewhat loosely — even if *simanim d'Rabbanan*, the point is that the real owner will know the object better and be able to give more detailed marks than a stranger's guesswork. The principle is not about *siman muvhak* in the technical sense, but about the owner's informational advantage.

### Promissory Notes

This reasoning, however, runs into a serious difficulty. If the *takana* rests on the premise that it is in the owner's interest to have *simanim* available as a retrieval mechanism, there is one category of document where this logic fails entirely: *shtar chov* — a promissory note. The Mishna teaches (*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer*): if one finds three documents and all three name the same person as the borrower (*echad ha-loveh mi-shlosha yachzir la-loveh*) — Reuven borrowed from Shimon, Reuven from Levi, Reuven from Yehuda — the common denominator is the borrower, and one assumes the documents fell from Reuven, who had repaid his debts and retrieved them. Conversely, if the three documents show three different borrowers from a single lender (*shlosha she-lavu min ha-echad yachzir la-malveh*), the common denominator is the lender, and one returns the documents to him.

The difficulty is sharpest regarding the second case, where one returns the documents to the *malveh* on the basis of *simanim*. A *shtar chov* in the hands of the *malveh* is a weapon against the *loveh* — it can be used to collect the debt. It is therefore *never* in the *loveh*'s interest for a *shtar chov* to be easily returned to the *malveh*. The *loveh* would want the barriers to return to be as high as possible. So if the *takana* of *simanim* rests on the principle that all relevant parties benefit from the institution, this is a case where half the parties — the *lovim* — emphatically do not benefit. The justification collapses.

---

## Bundled Documents

### Lender Denominator

The case where three people borrowed from one lender is somewhat easier to explain in terms of *sevara* — pure logic. If one finds documents stating that Reuven lent to Shimon, Reuven lent to Levi, and Reuven lent to Yehuda, the near-certain inference is that these all fell from Reuven the lender, since documents recording one person's loans would naturally be in that person's possession. This is closer to a *siman muvhak* than to an ordinary *siman* — the force of the logic is so compelling that no special *takana* is needed.

### Borrower Denominator

Similarly, when all three documents name the same borrower, the inference that they fell from that borrower is compelling: a single person having borrowed from three different lenders and having retrieved the paid-up documents is the obvious explanation for the cluster. The Gemara frames both cases as *sevara* — the logical evidence is compelling regardless of the *loveh*'s preferences.

### Tied Bundles

But the Gemara then identifies a case that cannot be dismissed so easily. The Mishna teaches: *matza tachrich shel shtarot o aguda shel shtarot, harei ze yachzir* — if one finds a bundle of documents rolled or tied together, one returns them. In what circumstances? Clearly, it is returned to whomever can provide *simanim* identifying the bundle — perhaps by describing the string that tied them, the number of documents, or the like. This is a straightforward case of returning documents based on *simanim*. The person who identifies the bundle might well be the *malveh*, and the *loveh* would have no interest in making that easy. The question *nicha leh la-loveh le-ahadurei lei la-malveh?* is now pointed: on what basis does *Chazal* extend the *simanim* principle to this case?

### Rava's Proof

The Gemara at this point quotes Rava's conclusion: *ella amar Rava simanim d'Oraisa* — Rava declares that he is persuaded. The fact that *Chazal* return a *shtar chov* on the basis of *simanim*, even in a case where the *loveh* would have no interest in it, proves that this is not a Rabbinic *takana* grounded in general social benefit. *Chazal* would not enact a *takana* that operates against the interests of one of the relevant parties. Since the return of a bundled *shtar chov* by *simanim* does operate against the *loveh*'s interests, it must be that *simanim* are *d'Oraisa* — and Torah law does not require justification in terms of whose interests are served.

Rava grounds this in the *pasuk*: *de-ksiv vehaya imcha derosh achicha oso* — "it shall remain with you until your brother seeks it out." As the *braisa* explains, this means you must investigate whether the claimant is truthful. Rava reads this as referring to investigation via *simanim*. The Gemara then interrupts: a moment ago Rava used *im timtzi lomar* — the conditional formulation suggesting he was not certain — yet he now presents *simanim d'Oraisa* as settled? The Gemara resolves this: the *pasuk* alone is not conclusive proof, since it might refer to *edim* rather than *simanim*. So Rava acknowledges that strict proof from the verse is not airtight — *mishum de-ika le-meimar kedei she-nisan simanim kedei she-nisan* — but he proceeds on the working assumption that *simanim d'Oraisa*, and explores its consequences.

---

## Evidence Hierarchy

### Equal Simanim

Even granting that *simanim* are *d'Oraisa*, there remains a hierarchy of evidence when competing claims are made. The first case: *simanim ve-simanim yaniach* — if Reuven provides *simanim* and Shimon provides *simanim* of equivalent weight, they neutralize one another and the object is held until the matter can be clarified further.

### Simanim vs. Witnesses

Even if *simanim* carry *d'Oraisa* force, *edim* are superior: *simanim ve-edim yinasen le-ba'al ha-edim* — you give the object to the party who has witnesses. Direct testimony from people who recognize the object beats out any description of distinguishing marks.

### One Witness

The next variation: *simanim ve-simanim ve-ed echad* — suppose both Reuven and Shimon give equivalent *simanim*, but Shimon also has a single witness who attests the object is his. One might think the single witness tips the balance. The Gemara rules: *ed echad ke-man de-leisa dami* — a single witness has no probative force in this type of dispute, and the result is the same as pure *simanim* versus *simanim*: *veyaniach*, the object is held.

### Weaving vs. Dropping

Suppose Reuven has witnesses that he wove the garment and Shimon has witnesses that Shimon dropped it: *tei-nasen l'edei nefila* — give it to Shimon, the one from whom it fell. The logic is: *zivuni zavneh u-minei d'achrina nefal* — Reuven may have woven it but then sold it on to someone else. The more recent chain of ownership defeats the earlier one. Witnesses to the most recent act of ownership or possession win.

### Dimensions

*Midas arko u-midas rachvo*: if one person testifies to the length of a garment and the other to the width, *tei-nasen l'midas arko* — the testimony regarding length is more probative. The reason: *d'midas rachvo shiurei — kama shayer lah kad mikasei lah mareh* — the width of a garment can be estimated by someone who has seen it being worn. Looking at a person in a cloak, one can approximate their width. But the length is harder to estimate from observation without actually holding or examining the garment. The one who can give the harder-to-estimate dimension is more likely the true owner.

### Precision

*Midas arko u-midas rachvo u-midas gamav*: if one person gives the length and width separately and another gives a combined measurement (like a total perimeter or combined dimensions), *tei-nasen l'midas arko ve-rachvo* — the person who breaks down the measurement precisely wins. Greater precision is more indicative of genuine ownership.

### Weight Wins

*Midas arko u-midas rachvo u-midas mishkelotav*: one person gives length, one width, and one gives the weight of the garment. *Tei-nasen l'midas mishkelotav* — the testimony of weight prevails. Weight is the dimension least amenable to guessing from casual observation; one must have genuinely handled and weighed the object to know it. This is therefore the strongest indicator of true ownership, and the person who gives the weight beats out those who give only the physical dimensions.

---

## Get Simanim

### Recipient Knowledge

The Gemara turns to the application of the *simanim* hierarchy to the *get* case, where the underlying principle has a particular logic of its own. Since the husband is the original owner of the *get* and the wife only gains knowledge of it upon actually receiving it, if both husband and wife provide *simanim* of the *get* and the wife's *simanim* are at least as strong, the object is returned to her: *hu omer simanei ha-get ve-hi omeret simanei ha-get, tei-nasen lah*. The reasoning is that she would not know the *simanim* unless she had actually received it, whereas he naturally knows the *simanim* since it originated with him. Her knowledge is therefore the more probative fact.

### Hole in Letter

The Gemara challenges: what *simanim* are being described? If the claim is based on *midas arko ve-rachvo* — the length and width of the *get* — this is something the wife might have observed while the husband was holding it, without ever having received it herself. The Gemara answers that the relevant case would be something like *nekev yesh lo b'tzad os pelonit* — she says there is a hole next to a particular letter in the fifth line of the document. That is the kind of detail only someone who had actually read or handled the document closely would know.

### String Details

Similarly, if both husband and wife give *simanei ha-chut* — describing the string that tied the *get* — one must ask what exactly they describe. If it is merely the color (*bechivra u-vesumka*), she might have glimpsed the string while he was holding it, so this does not prove receipt. But if she specifies the length of the string — *ela be-midas arka* — that is a detail precise enough that the Gemara assumes she would not have gotten it right without actually having received the *get*.

### Storage Container

The final case: *hu omer be-chafisa ve-hi omeret be-chafisa* — both husband and wife claim the *get* was stored in his carrying case. Here, *yinasen lo* — it is returned to the husband, not the wife. The reason: *meda yad'a de-chol midait lei be-chafisa hu de-manach lei* — she simply knows her husband's habits. She knows that he stores all his important documents in his carrying case. This does not prove she received the *get* at all; it only reflects her familiarity with his organizational customs. Since this knowledge could have been acquired without receipt, it does not carry the evidentiary weight needed to return the *get* to her.

The sugya thus concludes with a rich picture of the *simanim* question: the debate over whether *simanim* are *d'Oraisa* or *d'Rabbanan*; the three tiers of *simanim* — below threshold, standard, and *siman muvhak*; the competing justifications for the Rabbinic *takana* if *simanim* are not Biblical; Rava's ultimate conclusion that the return of *shtarei chov* by *simanim* forces us to regard them as *d'Oraisa*; and finally, the hierarchy governing competing claims — *simanim* versus *simanim*, *simanim* versus *edim*, and the logic of which dimension of identification most closely tracks genuine ownership.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 29

## Duration of Announcement

### Mishnah: Duration

The daf begins on 29a with the *mishnah*'s question: *ad masai chayav l'hachriz* — until when is one obligated to announce that he has found a lost object? The underlying assumption is that after the requisite period of announcement, if no one has come forward to claim the *aveidah*, the finder may keep it. The *mishnah* thus sets the threshold of effort required before that point is reached.

### R. Meir: Neighbors

Rabbi Meir holds that one must announce *ad k'dei sheyeidu bo sh'cheinav* — until one's neighbors know about the found object. The idea is that once knowledge of the find has spread through the neighborhood, anyone who has been searching can be directed to the finder through word of mouth. At that point, further active announcement is unnecessary.

### R. Yehuda: Three Regalim

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and requires a far more extensive process: *shalosh regalim* — three *regalim*, meaning three pilgrimage festivals. The logic is geographic and practical. When all of Israel gathered in Jerusalem for each *regel*, a finder could announce his discovery to an audience drawn from the entire nation. Anyone who had lost something and made the pilgrimage would have the opportunity to hear and respond.

Beyond the three *regalim* themselves, Rabbi Yehuda adds a further seven days after the final *regel*: *k'dei sheyeilech l'veito shlosha v'yachzor shlosha v'yachriz yom echad* — enough time for a person who heard the announcement in Jerusalem to travel home (three days), verify that he indeed lost the object in question, and return (three days), with one final day of announcement to allow the reunion to take place. Rashi understands this final day as the returning owner circulating through Jerusalem asking for the finder, while the Rambam understands it as the finder making one last announcement on the seventh day so that any returnee can find him.

### Gemara: Whose Neighbors?

The *gemara* immediately takes up the ambiguity in Rabbi Meir's formulation. *Mai sh'cheinei aveidah* — whose neighbors must know? The obvious difficulty is that "the neighbors of the owner" seems to require knowing who the owner is, but if you already know the owner's identity, the *gemara* notes *leizei v'lihadrei nihalei* — simply return it to him directly.

### Neighbors of Location

The *gemara* resolves this: *sh'cheinei makom shenimtza bo ha'aveidah* — the neighbors of the location where the object was found. The assumption is that a person who lost something likely lost it in the vicinity of where they live or frequent, and so the people in that area are precisely the ones most likely to know whether their neighbor is missing something. This provides a focused and reasonable coverage without requiring knowledge of the owner's identity. That is Rabbi Meir's approach.

---

## Travel Time Debate

### Three-Day Journey

The *gemara* raises a pointed difficulty against Rabbi Yehuda's framework. The seven-day window after the final *regel* is predicated on a three-day journey home and a three-day return. But a *baraita* elsewhere establishes that one begins reciting *v'sein tal u'matar livracha* on the seventh of Marcheshvan — fifteen days after Sukkot — in order to allow the most distant inhabitants of the Land of Israel to travel home from Jerusalem. If the entire land can be reached in fifteen days but not in three, how can the *mishnah* assume that three days suffice?

### R. Yosef: Population Den…

Rav Yosef answers that the two sources describe different eras: *kan be-Mikdash Rishon, kan be-Mikdash Sheni* — one refers to the First Temple period and the other to the Second. During the First Temple, *d'nifishi Yisrael tuva* — the Jewish population was enormous, as the verse describes: *Yehuda ve-Yisrael rabbim ka-chol asher al ha-yam la-rov*, as numerous as the sand of the sea. With so many people, they were spread to the far reaches of the land, requiring fifteen days to reach the outermost communities. But in the early Second Temple period, *kol ha-kahal ke-echad arba rivo alapim shlosh me'os va-shishim* — the entire community numbered only forty-two thousand, three hundred and sixty. With so small a population, they were presumably concentrated closer to the center, requiring only three days of travel.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye challenges this reasoning sharply. The verse itself states *va-yeshvu ha-kohanim ve-ha-leviyim ve-ha-meshor'rim ve-ha-sho'arim ve-chol Yisrael be-areihem* — all of Israel, even in the Second Temple period, dwelt in their respective cities throughout the land. They may have been fewer in number, but they were just as geographically dispersed. Given that, Abaye argues *ipcha mistabra* — the opposite conclusion would actually be more logical.

In the First Temple period, the vast population produced *mitzvas alma* — constant accompaniment and movement of travelers. Caravans (*shayarsa*) ran continuously, day and night, along well-traveled routes. Under those conditions, *sagi bi-tlata yomei* — three days were sufficient even to reach distant points. But in the Second Temple period, with fewer travelers on the roads and no reliable all-night caravans, the same distances took longer — hence fifteen days. So if anything, the *mishnah*'s three-day assumption fits the First Temple period, and the fifteen-day threshold of the *baraita* fits the Second. Rav Yosef's answer thus inverts. The *gemara* notes the contribution of Tosafot that the scarcity of travelers also meant fewer functioning inns and way-stations, further slowing journeys in the Second Temple period.

### Rava: Limited Duration

Rava cuts through the difficulty with a straightforward resolution: *lo shna Mikdash Rishon ve-lo shna Mikdash Sheni, lo hitrichu Rabbanan b'aveidah yoteir midai* — it does not matter whether we speak of the First or Second Temple period. The rabbis simply did not impose an excessive burden on the finder. He has already announced the *aveidah* across three *regalim*, and now he is being asked to remain in Jerusalem for a further seven days after the final *regel* — time away from his fields, his livelihood, his household. The rabbis declined to demand a full thirty-day window. Seven days captures those who live within practical reach; those who live at the farthest margins of the land had ample opportunity across the first two *regalim* to have acted already.

---

## Announcement Specificity

### Ravina: Specificity Rule

Ravina draws an inference from the *mishnah*'s structure regarding the content of the announcement itself. *Shema mina ki machriz, glima machriz* — one can deduce that when announcing a found object, one announces the specific item: "I found a coat," not merely "I found a lost object." If one were permitted to announce only generically, then a person who heard "I found an *aveidah*" would need to go home and conduct an exhaustive inventory of all his possessions to determine whether anything was missing. That would require an extra day — *be'inan lemitvei chad yoma u-le'ayunei be-manei* — yet the *mishnah* accounts only for three days of travel each way with no such extra allowance. It follows that the announcement must include the type of object, enabling the claimant to identify immediately whether it might be his.

### Rava: Generic Announceme…

Rava pushes back. Even granting that the *mishnah* gives no extra day, one could explain this differently: *lo etrichu Rabbanan b'aveidah yoteir mida'i* — the rabbis did not impose an additional waiting period on the finder even though the generic announcement would require the claimant more search time. The reason one might prefer a generic announcement is to filter out *rama'im* — deceitful claimants. If the finder announces "I found a coat," he hands a would-be fraud the first piece of information they need for a false claim. By announcing only "I found an *aveidah*," the burden of identifying the object falls entirely on the claimant, making fraudulent guessing far more difficult. The tradeoff is that the claimant needs more time to search his belongings — but the rabbis chose not to extend the finder's waiting period to accommodate this. Both the specific and the generic formulations are thus defensible positions, and the *gemara* accepts Rava's counter as a legitimate alternative reading.

---

## Three Regalim Practice

### Original Practice

A *baraita* elaborates on the practice underlying the *mishnah*. In the original period of the Temple, the finder would announce the found object on each of the three *regalim* in Jerusalem, identifying which *regel* in the sequence it was. On the first *regel* he would say, "This is the first *regel* that I am announcing." On the second *regel*, "This is the second *regel*." By the third *regel*, however, he announced without specifying a number at all — *regel shelishi omer stam*.

The *gemara* asks why: let him say "this is the third *regel*." The answer is *delo atei lachlufei be-sheni* — lest people mishear and confuse "third" for "second," leaving a claimant who has one *regel* remaining under the false impression that he still has two. By saying nothing at all on the third occasion, the ambiguity is eliminated; people understand from the omission that this is the final round. The *gemara* notes that a similar confusion on the second *regel* — between "second" and "first" — is less consequential, since even if someone mistakenly thinks they have two remaining chances, they actually still have one more.

### Post-Destruction Adjustm…

Once the Temple was destroyed, the centralized gathering that made the Jerusalem announcement system possible was gone. The rabbis therefore instituted that announcements be made *be-vatei knesiyot u-ve-vatei midrashos* — in synagogues and study halls. These venues, while local rather than national, were the new centers of communal gathering. The *gemara* notes that this shift is emblematic of a broader historical transition: after the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*, the center of religious life and *kedushah* relocated to the *batei midrashos* and *batei knesiyot*.

### Forceful People Problem

A further historical adaptation followed. When *ha-nasim* — forceful individuals — became prevalent, who would insist that any found object be turned over to the king (*aveidata le-malka*), the rabbis adjusted again: rather than making any public announcement at all, the finder was instructed simply to inform his neighbors and acquaintances quietly, and that would suffice. The concern was that a public announcement in a synagogue or study hall might reach these agents of the government who would then seize the object before it could be returned to its rightful owner. Whether these were Jewish collaborators or non-Jewish enforcers is not made explicit in the *gemara*, and this raises broader questions about the principle of *dina de-malchuta dina* — whether the law of the land applies, and whether it applies even to laws that are manifestly unjust, such as confiscating a person's property. The *gemara* clearly regards this law as one the Jewish community should work around, consistent with the *mitzvah* of *hashavat aveidah*.

### Rav Ashi Story

The *gemara* illustrates this situation with a brief narrative. Rav Ashi once found a vessel filled with gold coins (*daisa de-dinrei*) and noticed that a certain bystander — some versions of the text read *bar Roma'ah*, a Roman — observed him with apparent concern, presumably worried that Rav Ashi feared being reported and compelled to surrender the coins to the authorities. The bystander reassured him: *zil shekol le-nafshach, de-lav Parsaya ana de-amri aveidata le-malka* — take it for yourself; I am not a Persian who holds that found objects belong to the king. This anecdote concretizes the social reality behind the legal adjustment: the fear of government confiscation was a genuine concern, not merely theoretical.

### Stone of Claims

A *baraita* records an additional institution from the Temple era: *Even To'en hayta bi-Yerushalayim* — there was a Stone of Claims in Jerusalem. Anyone who had lost an object would go there, and anyone who had found one would go there as well. The finder would make his announcement, and the claimant would provide *simanim* — identifying marks — to establish ownership and receive his property. The *gemara* notes that this institution is referenced in the story of Choni HaMa'agel, who asked whether the stone was submerged in the floodwaters he had inadvertently produced through prayer, the stone serving as a familiar Jerusalem landmark.

---

## Identifying Marks

### Mishnah: Marks & Trust

The next *mishnah* addresses the verification process. If someone claims an *aveidah* but says only the category of the object (*amar aveidah*) without providing identifying marks, do not return it to him. And even one who is known as a *ramai* — a deceptive person — do not return the object even if he does provide *simanim*, until one has investigated sufficiently: *ad she-tidrosh et achicha im ramai hu im eino ramai*.

The *mishnah* thus operates on two tracks simultaneously. For ordinary claimants, *simanim* are required and sufficient. For those known to be deceptive, *simanim* alone do not suffice. Conversely, a *tzurva mei-rabbanan* — a Torah scholar — may not even need to provide *simanim*, since his word alone is trusted.

### Announcement Debate

Here the *gemara* revisits the question of what is announced. Rav Yehuda holds *aveidata machriz* — announce generically that you found a lost object. Rav Nachman holds *gelima machriz* — announce the specific item, e.g., "I found a coat."

Rav Yehuda's reasoning: if you announce "I found a coat," you supply the *ramai* with his opening gambit. He knows what to claim. Better to say nothing about the nature of the object so that a would-be fraudster has no information from which to fabricate. Rav Nachman's reasoning: *le-ramai lo chashinan* — we are not overly worried about deceptive claimants; *simanim* are adequate protection, and an overly generic announcement is practically useless. Moreover, *de-im ken ein la-davar sof* — if you push the concern about fraud too far, there is no end to it. Even a generic "I found an *aveidah*" leaves room for guessing, and you cannot protect against every possible fabrication.

The *mishnah*'s own language becomes a point of contention. *Amar aveidah ve-lo amar simaneha lo yitein lo* — if the claimant identified the object but gave no *simanim*, do not give it back. This phrasing fits naturally with the position that the announcement was generic (*aveidata machriz*): the claimant volunteered that it was a coat, but he still must provide *simanim*. If the finder had announced it was a coat, the *mishnah*'s statement would be trivially obvious — of course identifying it as a coat adds nothing when the finder already said it was a coat.

Rav Safra, however, defends the position that the finder announces *gelima*. The *mishnah*'s phrase *lo amar simaneha* does not mean the claimant failed to name the object; it means he failed to provide *simanim muvhakim* — sufficiently distinguishing identifying marks. He may have said, "Was it a London Fog coat?" but that is not specific enough. The *mishnah* requires genuine *simanim*, not generic category identification. So one can read the *mishnah* as consistent with the announcement of *gelima* — the claimant echoed the category but did not supply the necessary particulars.

### Baraita: Marks to Witnes…

A *baraita* records a historical evolution in the verification standards. Originally, *simanim* were sufficient and any claimant who provided them received the object. Once *ha-ramaim rabu* — deceptive claimants became more prevalent — the rabbis instituted a more demanding requirement: before returning the object, the finder was to tell the claimant, *tze ve-hava eidim de-lav ramai at ve-tol* — go and bring character witnesses who will testify that you are an honest person, and then you may take the object. This represents a more systematic suspicion than the *mishnah*'s baseline, where a known *ramai* is disqualified but an ordinary claimant is trusted on *simanim* alone.

### Rav Papa Story

The *gemara* illustrates this practice with a story about the father of Rav Papa, who had lost a donkey. Someone found it, and the father came before Rabba bar Rav Huna, who instructed him to bring character witnesses attesting to his honesty before the donkey would be returned. He brought the witnesses, and the finder turned to them and asked: *yadeitu beih d'ramai hu?* — do you know him to be a *ramai*? The witnesses, having prepared themselves to affirm his honesty and expecting the question to be phrased accordingly, instinctively answered "yes" — confusing the question's polarity. Rav Papa's father was understandably indignant: *ana ramai ana?* The witnesses quickly clarified that they had misheard the question and intended to testify to his integrity.

The question then arose whether this retraction was acceptable, or whether the principle of *keivan she-higid shuv eino chozer u-magid* — once a witness has testified he cannot retract — should bar them from amending their testimony. Rabba bar Rav Huna ruled that the retraction was credible: *mistabra lo mayiti inish chuvsa le-nafshei* — a person does not ordinarily bring witnesses who will testify against himself. Since the father himself brought these witnesses, it is obvious they intended to vouch for him, and the initial "yes" was plainly a mishearing. The court accepted the clarification.

---

## Use of Found Animals

### Work Animals Permitted

The *mishnah* turns to a practical question that arises once a *shomer aveidah* has taken custody of a found animal. During the period before the owner comes forward, the animal incurs costs. Who bears them? The *mishnah* establishes: *kol davar she-oseh ve-ochel ya'aseh ve-yochel* — anything that performs labor and also eats may be put to work, with the proceeds of that labor used to cover the cost of its feed. If the found animal is a cow, the finder may plow with it. If it is a sheep, he may shear its wool and sell the milk. The net effect is that the owner receives his animal back without incurring a large debt to the finder, which is what the Torah intends when it says *ve-hashevoto lo* — you must see to it that you return something of real value to the owner. Having the finder charge for all upkeep costs would effectively penalize the owner for the loss.

### Sell Non-Work Animals

However, *davar she-ein oseh ve-ochel* — an animal that eats but produces no labor or saleable product — presents a different problem. Keeping it alive generates costs with no offsetting revenue. In such a case, the *mishnah* says *yimmacher* — the finder should sell it and hold the proceeds for the owner. The verse *ve-hashevoto lo* is read as a mandate to find the method of return that preserves the most value: better to hold cash than to accumulate expenses against a living animal whose upkeep the finder cannot recoup.

The *mishnah* then raises the question of what the finder may do with the cash proceeds from that sale while waiting for the owner to claim them. *Rabbi Tarfon omer yishtamesh bahen* — Rabbi Tarfon permits the finder to use the money, treating it as a fund available to him as long as he returns the equivalent amount when the owner appears. *V'lefikach im avdu chayav be-achrayutan* — and precisely because he has the right to use the money, he bears responsibility for it even if it is lost. *Rabbi Akiva omer lo yishtamesh bahen* — Rabbi Akiva forbids use of the money, and *lefikach im avdu ein chayav be-achrayutan* — therefore if it is lost the finder is not liable.

### 12-Month Limit

Even for the case of work animals, the *mishnah*'s permission to continue working them is not indefinite. Rav Nachman citing Shmuel rules: *ad yud-bet chodesh* — for up to twelve months. The owner has a strong interest in recovering the actual animal, and so the finder must make this effort for a full year. After twelve months, even this case transitions to the same solution as non-work animals: appraise the animal at fair market value, sell it, and hold the proceeds.

A *baraita* confirms this ruling and begins to differentiate by animal type.

### Variable Time Limits

For large animals such as cows and donkeys that perform labor, *metapel bahen ad yud-bet chodesh* — twelve months of care, after which they are sold. For calves and foals (*agalim ve-syachim*) — young animals not yet capable of labor and thus generating only expense — the period is three months. For geese and roosters (*avazim ve-tarnegolim*), where the only economic benefit is slaughter and the entire purpose of keeping them alive is to restore them to the owner, thirty days.

A second *baraita*, however, specifies different figures for the latter two categories: calves and foals merit only thirty days, and geese and roosters as few as three days for any animal *she-tipulo merubeh mi-scharo* — whose cost of upkeep exceeds any potential benefit. The *gemara* reconciles the apparent contradiction in the calves-and-foals cases by distinguishing between situations where grazing land is available (low expense, hence three months) and where all feed must be purchased (high expense, hence thirty days). The apparent contradiction in the roosters-and-geese cases is resolved by distinguishing between large birds (high expense, thirty days) and small ones (minimal expense, three days). In all cases, the underlying principle is the same: the finder bears upkeep costs only to the degree that it does not impose an unreasonable burden, always with the goal of returning maximum value to the owner.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds a refinement: a laying hen is classified together with large animals (*ke-vehemah gassa*) for these purposes. Since it produces eggs, it qualifies as *oseh ve-ochel* — the eggs offset the feed, and so the finder may keep the hen working for twelve months before selling.

---

## Use of Proceeds Debate

### Mishnah: Use Rights

The *mishnah*'s dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva regarding the use of proceeds is now examined in the *gemara* at greater depth.

### Guardian Status Debate

The *gemara* frames the dispute in terms of the categories of *shmirah* — guardianship. There are three main types: a *shomer chinam*, who guards without compensation and is liable only for gross negligence but not for loss or theft; a *shomer sachar*, who receives payment and is liable for loss and theft but not for accidents (*ones*); and a *shoel*, a borrower, who is liable even for accidents. The debate of Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva turns on where within this spectrum the *shomer aveidah* falls once money is involved.

### R. Yosef: Paid Guardian

Rav Yosef holds that any *shomer aveidah* — regardless of whether he uses the money or not — has the status of a *shomer sachar*. His reasoning: while watching a lost object, the guardian is engaged in a *mitzvah*, and *osek be-mitzvah patur min ha-mitzvah* — one who is actively fulfilling a commandment is exempt from other commandments simultaneously. Thus, for the duration of his stewardship of the *aveidah*, if a poor person comes to his door soliciting *tzedakah*, he need not stop to give it. This exemption constitutes a form of benefit, and receiving benefit for guardianship makes one a *shomer sachar*.

Rabba disagrees: this benefit is too tenuous and too incidental to constitute the kind of compensation that elevates a guardian's status. In his view, a *shomer aveidah* is a *shomer chinam*.

The *gemara* now considers whether our *mishnah* contradicts Rav Yosef. The *mishnah* appears to say that absent the right to use the money, a *shomer aveidah* would be exempt if the money is lost — which would make him a *shomer chinam*, consistent with Rabba's position. Rav Yosef responds that this is not the correct reading of the *mishnah*.

### Borrower Status

Rav Yosef's reinterpretation is striking. He argues that everyone agrees a *shomer aveidah* is a *shomer sachar*, and so the *mishnah*'s dispute cannot be about the transition from *shomer chinam* to *shomer sachar*. Rather, the debate concerns *onsin d'shoel* — liability for pure accidents, which only a *shoel* bears. According to Rav Yosef: *Rabbi Tarfon savar sharu leh Rabbanan le-ishtamushi be-gavaihu ve-havei lei shoel* — since the rabbis permit the finder to use the money, that permission transforms him into a borrower. A borrower has the highest level of liability, even for accidents — a ship sinking at sea, armed robbery, an act of God. And since Rabbi Tarfon holds that the finder has the right to use the money, *keivan d'sharu Rabbanan le-ishtamush be-gavaihu ke-man d'ishtamesh be-gavaihu dami* — it is as if he has already used it, and he bears the liability of a *shoel*. Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, holds that the finder has no right to use the money. Since he is not a borrower, he retains the status of a *shomer sachar* — liable for ordinary loss and theft but not for accidents.

The *gemara* works through the logical structure of the *mishnah*'s *lefikach* — the "therefore" clauses — to confirm this reading. Rabbi Tarfon's *lefikach*: since you have the right to use the money, I am telling you something not obvious — you are a borrower and liable even for accidents. Rabbi Akiva's *lefikach*: since you do not have the right to use the money, you are not a borrower; you remain a *shomer sachar* and not liable for accidents. The word *lefikach* in each case signals a non-obvious conclusion that requires stating explicitly.

The *mishnah*'s use of the language *im avdu* — "if they were lost" — fits this reading as well. As Rava notes, *geneivah va-aveidah* can sometimes shade into *ones*: theft by armed bandits, loss through shipwreck. When the *mishnah* speaks of liability for *aveidah*, it refers to these extreme cases that are practically indistinguishable from accidents — precisely the zone where *shomer sachar* and *shoel* diverge.

### Halacha: R. Tarfon

Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules: *halacha ke-Rabbi Tarfon* — the ruling follows Rabbi Tarfon. The finder of a lost object may use the proceeds from the sale of the *aveidah*.

The *gemara* applies this ruling immediately to a practical case: Rechava held money belonging to orphans in trust. He came before Rav Yosef to ask whether he was permitted to use those funds — and to be compensated, so to speak, by holding on to equivalent money. Rav Yosef initially indicated that we rule like Rabbi Tarfon and such use is permitted.

### Abaye: Effort Required

Abaye intervened with a critical qualification. He cited a tradition from Rav Kahana in the name of Rav Huna: *lo shanu ela bi-dmei aveidah* — Rabbi Tarfon's permission to use the money applies specifically to the *proceeds of a sold aveidah*, and not to money found directly or entrusted for safekeeping without effort. The reason: *ho'il ve-tarach bah* — the finder exerted effort. He found the object, cared for it for some period, sought an owner, and then undertook the effort of selling it and converting it into cash. In recognition of that effort, the rabbis granted him the right to put the money to use.

But money that comes with no such effort — money found on the ground, or money handed over directly for safekeeping, such as orphans' funds — does not carry that right. *Ve-hanhu ke-me'ot aveidah damu* — such funds are analogous to cash found directly without any transformative effort on the finder's part. There, Rabbi Tarfon's dispensation does not apply.

Rav Yosef accepted Abaye's argument and told Rechava accordingly: *lo shavku li de'ashri lach* — they have not left me the ability to permit you. The permission to use entrusted funds does not follow from the ruling like Rabbi Tarfon; that ruling is limited to proceeds earned through the effort of handling and selling a found object.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 30

## Object Maintenance

### Found Scrolls

The *mishnah* on 29b opens a new topic: the maintenance obligations that apply to found objects beyond animals. The *mishnah* states: *matza sefarim, korei bahen l'echad lishloshim yom* — if one finds scrolls, one should read from them once every thirty days in order to air them out and prevent mold or moth damage. *Ve'im eino yodeiah likros* — and if one does not know how to read, then *golelan*, one simply rolls them from beginning to end, opening them up to expose the parchment to air. Reading is a convenient means of airing them out, and one may derive the incidental benefit of reading along the way, but even someone who cannot read fulfills the obligation by scrolling through them.

*Aval lo yilmad bahem batchilah* — one may not, however, learn something entirely new from them. If one is studying unfamiliar material, one tends to linger too long in a single location, which risks wearing down the parchment in that spot and fails to serve the airing-out purpose. *Velo yikra acher imo* — nor should one read together with another person, as this risks a tugging contest that could tear the scroll.

One might also ask whether *sefarim* here refers exclusively to *sifrei kodesh* or to any type of book — all of which, in the ancient world, were written as scrolls. The question is a genuine one, though the *gemara*'s subsequent discussion, which applies identical parameters to a *sefer Torah*, will bear on how we understand the scope of this *mishnah*.

### Found Garments

*Matza kesus mena'arah echad lishloshim yom* — if one finds a garment, one shakes it out once every thirty days, again to prevent moth damage and the accumulation of dust. *Veshotechah l'tzarchah* — one may spread it out for its own needs, meaning for the purposes of its maintenance, *velo lichvodo* — but not for one's own honor. The example would be someone who thinks: I have guests arriving, this is a fine occasion to display that impressive garment I found. That is prohibited. Notably, with the *sefer*, incidental benefit to oneself was permitted as one scrolled it; with the garment, the *mishnah* appears to draw a distinction. The *gemara* will return to this contrast in detail.

### Silver & Copper

*Klei kesef u'klei nechoshet mishtamesh bahen l'tzarchan velo l'shachkan* — silver and copper vessels may be used to maintain them, but not in a way that wears them out. The *mishnah*'s language — permitting use rather than merely polishing or rinsing — raises an implicit question about whether incidental benefit to oneself is permitted alongside the maintenance purpose. The *mishnah* does not say merely to rinse or shine them; it says to use them. The implication is that modest use keeps them in good condition and that some degree of personal benefit in the process is countenanced, so long as the use is not destructive.

### Gold & Glass

*Klei zahav u'klei zechuchit lo yiga bahen* — gold and glass vessels one should not touch at all, *ad sheyavo Eliyahu* — until Elijah comes, meaning indefinitely. As Rashi explains, gold does not oxidize or rust and therefore requires no use-based maintenance, while glass is too easily broken. In the case of gold, use is simply unnecessary; in the case of glass, it is too dangerous.

### Dignity Principle

*Matza sak o kuppah vechol davar she'ein darko litol, harei zeh lo yitol* — if one finds a sack, a box, or anything not normally taken, one need not take it. One might initially think this refers to *safek hinuach* — objects that may have been intentionally left — but the *gemara* will clarify that this is not the correct reading. *Ein darko litol* does not mean the object is likely to have been placed there intentionally; it means that retrieving it would be beneath one's dignity. This is an important independent principle, and the *gemara* will elaborate on it at length in the closing section of the *daf*.

---

## Found Tefillin

### Shmuel's Ruling

*Amar Shmuel: hamotzei tefillin bashuk, shamin demihen u'manichan l'alter* — Shmuel rules that if one finds *tefillin* in the marketplace, one assesses their value, sets aside the money — effectively purchasing them from the absent owner — and may then put them on immediately. The question the *gemara* will immediately raise is: why can one not simply set them aside and maintain them as one would any other found object?

### Ravina's Challenge

*Metiv Ravina*: the *mishnah* states that if one finds scrolls, one reads from them once every thirty days, and if one cannot read, one rolls them. The implication is that found objects must be maintained and held, not liquidated. Why should *tefillin* be different? Why is one permitted to assess the value, pay it over, and simply use or sell the *tefillin* rather than preserve them for the owner?

### Availability Factor

*Amar Abaye*: *tefillin bar bei bar chavu mishkach shchichi* — *tefillin* are readily available everywhere. *Sefarim lo shchichi* — actual scrolls are not. This reflects a striking historical reality: before the age of printed books, even a modest collection of scrolls represented an enormous and nearly irreplaceable treasure. The Alexandrian library — housing thousands of scrolls of the ancient world — was rightly considered an incalculable loss when destroyed. *Tefillin*, by contrast, were worn by every Jewish male and were produced in large quantities, creating a robust and accessible market.

This raises a further question, though: even granting that *tefillin* are easily replaceable, what is the justification for essentially acquiring them rather than simply setting them aside? One consideration may be that *tefillin* left locked in a box serve no one, potentially for years, if the owner never returns to claim them. Another is that *tefillin* that can be assessed and replaced with cash present an almost interchangeable object — unlike a *sefer Torah* or a broken-in animal, which the owner may have a strong personal attachment to. If one follows the view of Rabbi Tarfon regarding the use of found objects, the money can be set aside and returned if the owner eventually appears, while in the meantime someone actually benefits from the *tefillin*. These considerations together appear to animate Shmuel's ruling, though the precise formal justification remains somewhat elusive.

---

## Sefer Torah Care

### No Re-lending

*Tanu rabbanan: hashoel sefer Torah mechaveiro, harei zeh lo yashilenu l'acher* — if one borrows a *sefer Torah*, one may not lend it to a third party. The *gemara* immediately notes that this seems obvious: *Reish Lakish* elsewhere establishes the general rule that *ein hashoel rashai lehashil* — a borrower may not lend out what he has borrowed — and likewise *ein hasocher rashai lehashkir* — one who rents may not sublet. So why is it necessary to state this rule specifically for a *sefer Torah*?

The answer is that the *sefer Torah* case is actually a *chiddush*. One might have thought that *nicha lei le'inish detei'aved mitzvah bemamonei* — a person is genuinely pleased when others perform a *mitzvah* using their property. If I lend someone my *sefer Torah*, I may well be happy for him to lend it further so that more people can learn *Torah*. Therefore, one might argue that the owner implicitly permits re-lending. *Ka mashma lan* — the ruling teaches us that we do not apply this logic here, because the concern for potential damage overrides the assumption of implicit permission.

This connects to a broader practical reality: books are frequently borrowed and never returned, or are damaged in transit through spilled liquids, torn pages, or broken bindings. Some people therefore inscribe inside their books *mutar lehishtamesh bimkomo* — one may use it in this place — granting permission for in-place use while withholding permission to remove it. The general default, absent such explicit permission, is that *sefarim* may not be used without authorization, even when standing right next to them.

### Reading Restrictions

*Potcho v'korei bo* — one who borrows a *sefer Torah* obviously opens and reads from it, since that is the entire purpose of borrowing it. *U'vilvad shelo yilmad bo batchilah* — but one may not use it to learn material entirely new to oneself. This is noteworthy: it confirms that *sifrei Torah* were in practice used for direct study and learning, not merely for ceremonial or ritual reading. The restriction against learning new material from a borrowed *sefer Torah* parallels the restriction on found scrolls discussed in the *mishnah*, applying the same logic — lingering in one location risks wearing down the parchment. *Velo yikra acher imo* — and a second person may not read together with the borrower.

### Entrusted Care

*Vechen hamaphkid sefer Torah etzel chaveiro, golelo kol shneim asar chodesh* — if one entrusts a *sefer Torah* to another person for safekeeping, the *shomer* must roll it once every twelve months, which is notably less frequent than the once-every-thirty-days standard of the *mishnah* for a found scroll. The *gemara* then states: *potcho v'korei bo* — one may open it and read from it. This seems surprising: the *shomer* is merely watching the scroll; he has not borrowed it for the purpose of reading. Why is reading permitted?

The *gemara* notes the internal tension: the *shomer* is required to roll the scroll every twelve months for its maintenance, but then the *baraita* adds that one may open and read from it — which sounds like permission for personal use. Yet it also states explicitly, *im bishvilo patcho assur* — if one opens it fundamentally for one's own purposes, that is forbidden. *Ha amart poteach v'korei bo* — but you just said one may open and read from it!

The *gemara* resolves this: *hachi ka amar* — what the *baraita* means is that while one is in the process of rolling and caring for the scroll — when the fundamental motivation is the maintenance of the *sefer Torah* — one may incidentally read from it along the way. But if the primary reason for opening the scroll is one's own desire to read from it, that is *assur*. The operative distinction is between incidental benefit derived in the course of fulfilling one's maintenance obligation, and using the *pikadon* as a vehicle for one's own purposes.

### Airing Frequency

*Sumchos omer: bechadash shloshim yom, beyashan shneim asar chodesh* — Sumchos holds that a new *sefer Torah* must be aired every thirty days, while an old one requires airing only every twelve months. *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov omer: echad zeh ve'echad zeh shneim asar chodesh* — Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says twelve months in both cases.

The *gemara* objects: isn't Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov simply repeating the *tanna kamma*, who also said twelve months? The *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov would then be identical, which is halakhically redundant. The *gemara* therefore reframes: *ela eima Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov omer echad zeh ve'echad zeh shloshim yom* — Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov in fact holds thirty days for both new and old scrolls. This revision conveniently identifies Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as the author of our *mishnah*, which prescribed a thirty-day interval without distinguishing between new and old scrolls.

The *gemara* then returns to the *mishnah*'s further restrictions — *aval lo yilmad bo batchilah velo yikra acher imo* — and notes that a *baraita* elaborates: one may not read a *parasha* twice, and one may not read a *parasha* and then translate it, since both practices involve dwelling too long in a single location and serve one's own purposes more than the scroll's maintenance needs. One might note that reading the *parasha* twice and then translating it corresponds to the practice of *shnayim mikra ve'echad targum* — reflecting how ancient this practice is.

### Page Limits

*Velo yiftach bo yoter mi'gimmel dapin* — one should not open more than three parchment sections at once, since a wider opening increases the risk of tearing. The *baraita* also specifies that three people should not read from it simultaneously, while the *mishnah* had already excluded two people reading together. The *gemara* asks whether these rulings are in conflict.

*Amar Abaye lo kashya: kan b'inyan echad, kan b'shnei inyanim* — there is no contradiction: the prohibition applies when multiple readers are focused on the same location, which risks a tugging contest; if readers are positioned at different sections of the scroll, each focused on their own portion, the concern is reduced. As Rashi explains, two readers at different locations — one reading *Nitzavim*, one reading *Vayeilech* — are each focused on their respective passages and are not competing for the same stretch of parchment. But if all readers are looking at the same place, even two creates a dangerous dynamic.

---

## Garment Maintenance

### Over-Shaking Harm

The *mishnah* states that a found garment should be shaken out every thirty days. *L'meimra d'nicha lei* — this seems to imply that shaking is beneficial. Yet *Rabbi Yochanan* offers a pointed, somewhat sardonic observation: *mi she-yesh lo gardi uman b'toch beito, yenachasenu b'chol yom* — if you have a master tailor living in your house, go ahead and shake your garment every single day. His point, of course, is the opposite: excessive shaking damages garments and causes them to tear. There is a parallel in the modern advice of dry cleaners, who may post reminders to clean clothes regularly — though in practice, over-cleaning is itself harmful.

The *gemara* resolves the apparent tension straightforwardly: *b'chol yom kashi lei, achat lishloshim yom ma'alei lei* — every day is harmful, but once a month actually preserves the garment in good condition. These are not contradictory positions but applications to different frequencies.

### Method of Shaking

*Iba'is eima lo kashya: ha b'chad v'ha b'trei* — alternatively, the difference is between one person shaking the garment and two people shaking it. One person shaking is less vigorous and maintains the garment without excessive stress; two people shaking together is more vigorous, which may clean it more effectively but risks damage to its fibers and longevity.

*Iba'is eima lo kashya: ha b'yada v'ha b'chutra* — yet another resolution: shaking with one's hand is less forceful and gentler on the garment, while beating it with a stick — as one sometimes sees with rugs — is more effective for cleaning but obviously more destructive over time. It bears noting that this entire discussion concerns shaking out dust rather than laundering; a garment hanging in storage does not become soiled in the way that would require washing, but it does require periodic airing to remove dust accumulation.

### Fabric Types

*Iba'is eima lo kashya: ha b'damra v'ha d'chitna* — yet another distinction: the material matters. Is it wool or is it flax? Rashi comments that wool, being a fabric that stretches, *she-nimtechet v'nikre'et*, is more susceptible to tearing. Whether or not one agrees with Rashi's assessment of relative durability, the *gemara*'s point is clear: the appropriate frequency and vigor of maintenance depends on the specific fabric's properties.

The *gemara* then appends a series of practical observations attributed to *Rabbi Yochanan*, offered in the same vein of practical wisdom about caring for possessions. *Rabbi Yochanan* observes that he would prefer a cup over which witchcraft had been performed to a cup of lukewarm water sitting in a metal vessel, since lukewarm water in metal may be harmful. This concern does not apply to pottery. Similarly, the problem is mitigated if something — Rashi suggests herbs — has been added to the water, or if it has been brought to a boil. *Rabbi Yochanan* also notes that if a father leaves one a great deal of money and one wishes to dissipate it rapidly, one should wear linen garments — specifically *chitna deromita*, Roman linen — use white glass vessels, and hire many workers without supervising them. The *gemara* specifies that the workers in question are ox-drivers, *betorei*, whose unsupervised work causes disproportionate losses.

---

## Motivation & Benefit

### Dual Purpose Use

The *mishnah* having established that a found garment may be spread out *l'tzarchah* — for its own maintenance needs — but not *lichvodo* — for one's own honor — the *gemara* now poses the question: *l'tzarchah ul'tzarcho mai?* What if one intends the spreading both for the garment's needs and for one's own benefit simultaneously? Is that permitted?

It is worth pausing to note how this question relates to the *sefer Torah* case discussed earlier. There, incidental reading while scrolling through the *sefer Torah* was permitted. Why might the garment case be different? *Tosafot* argues that this is not an absolute formal rule about whether one may ever derive incidental benefit from a maintained object. Rather, it is a practical concern: if one's motivation is partly personal, one may leave the garment out longer than its maintenance requires, rationalizing that it is still "for the garment's needs." With the *sefer Torah*, specific restrictions were already in place — no two readers, no new material, no reading it twice — that constrain the use and prevent overuse. With the garment, no such safeguards exist, and the concern is that mixed motivation leads to misuse. Importantly, one might add that the question is not only whether damage will result, but whether one's initial engagement with the object is fundamentally motivated by personal interest. When one begins from personal motivation, even a use framed as maintenance may really be self-serving — and it is notoriously difficult to disentangle one's actual motivations from post-hoc rationalizations.

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* frames the question through the lens of *shomer* law: the finder is conceptualized as a *shomer*, and the question of whether he may derive incidental benefit while fulfilling his obligation is the operative issue. The *gemara* then attempts to resolve the question from the *mishnah* itself: *l'tzarchah in* — the *mishnah* says "for its needs," implying that this is the only permissible motivation. *Ha l'tzarchah ul'tzarcho lo* — mixed motivation would therefore be excluded.

But *eima seifa* — look at the end of the *mishnah*: *aval lo lichvodo* — but not for one's honor. The implication of the *seifa* is that the prohibition applies when the motivation is exclusively personal. *Lichvodo d'lo* — only that is forbidden, while *l'tzarchah ul'tzarcho shapir dami* — a mixed motivation would be fine. The two halves of the *mishnah* thus appear to contradict each other.

*Ela meha lika l'mishma mina* — the *gemara* concludes that no inference can be drawn from this *mishnah*, because the *mishnah* typically articulates the two extreme cases and leaves the middle ground unaddressed. This is a classic feature of *mishnaic* formulation: the *mishnah* states A and not-B without speaking to the intermediate cases, so one cannot infer the rule for those cases from either half of the *mishnah* alone.

### Guests Arriving

A further *ta shma* presents the relevant rule more directly: one may not spread the garment on a bed or on a frame *letzarcho* — for one's own honor — but one may do so *l'tzarchah* — for the garment's needs. Again, only the two extremes are stated.

The *baraita* then adds: *nizdamnu lo orchin* — if guests happen to arrive, *lo yishtachena lo al gabi mita velo al gabi magod, bein letzarcho bein letzarcha* — one may not spread it out on a bed or on a frame, whether for one's own needs or for the garment's needs. This appears to be precisely the case of mixed motivation — one sincerely believes one is doing it for the garment's sake, yet guests are present, and therefore one may not do it at all. This would seem to establish that mixed motivation — *letzarcho uletzarcha* — is indeed forbidden.

The *gemara* rejects this inference, however: *shani hatam demikla kali lah* — the guest scenario is different, because spreading out the garment when guests are present is effectively destroying it. *Ei mishum eina* — either because the guests may cast an *ayin hara* on it, or *ei mishum ganvei* — from a more prosaic perspective, one is advertising its value and inviting theft. One might add that even setting aside *ayin hara*, a house full of guests increases the practical risk that someone will spill something on it or handle it carelessly. The prohibition in the guest scenario thus rests not on the mixing of motivations but on the specific danger that the circumstances create. Accordingly, nothing can be inferred from this case about the general rule of *letzarcho uletzarcha*.

### Parah Adumah

A final *ta shma* addresses the question through an analogy. If one placed an animal intended for *parah adumah* or *egla arufa* into a barn, and while there it incidentally threshed grain, the animal remains *kshera* — valid — because one did not intend for it to do work. *Bishvil shetinak vetadush* — but if one placed it there specifically so that it should nurse from its mother and also thresh grain while doing so, it is *psula* — invalid. In the latter case, one desired both the animal's own need (nursing) and one's personal interest (threshing), and this dual motivation invalidates it. The *gemara* draws the analogy: here too, a mixed motivation of *letzarcho uletzarcha* would be problematic.

The *gemara* immediately deflects: *shani hatam de-amar kra asher lo uvad bah, mi-kol makom* — the *parah adumah* case is governed by the specific scriptural formulation, which prohibits any work having been done, regardless of motivation or circumstance. The standard there is distinct from the question of care for an *aveida*.

The *gemara* then asks: if the *parah adumah* standard is truly that absolute — excluding even fully incidental work — then why is the case where the animal incidentally threshes while being placed for another reason valid? The *gemara* answers that this is comparable to a *mishnah* about *parah adumah*: *shakhan aleha of, kshera* — if a bird rests on the cow, it is valid; *ala aleha zakhar, psula* — if a male mounted it, it is invalid. In both cases the work occurred without one's direct action. The difference lies in *Rav Pappa*'s principle: the verse is written *avad* (active, "one worked it") but read *uvad* (passive, "it was worked"). The dual formulation yields a combined standard: what invalidates is work that happened by itself — *mi-meila* — but that one would have been *nicha lei*, pleased to have happen.

*Ma avad de-nicha lei, af uvad de-nicha lei* — just as direct work presupposes something desired, so too passive work invalidates only if one would have been pleased by it. One would generally want one's cattle to copulate and produce offspring — so a male mounting the *parah adumah* invalidates even though one did not cause it. But one generally does not particularly care whether one specific animal threshes or not when other animals are threshing anyway, so incidental threshing does not invalidate.

*Tosafot* raises an obvious question: if the animal is being designated as a *parah adumah*, surely one would *not* want it to copulate, since this would destroy its status and its considerable value. How can one say one is *nicha lei*? *Tosafot* answers that we do not measure *nicha lei* based on the animal's specific status as a *parah adumah*; rather, we measure it by whether, under normal circumstances, this would be a desirable outcome. Since copulation is ordinarily desirable for cattle, it is treated as *nicha lei* regardless of the particular circumstances. This parallels discussions in the context of *Shabbat* about *psik reisha de-lo nicha lei* — where something definitely happens as a consequence of one's action but one is not pleased by the result. Some *poskim* have attempted to argue that various *Shabbat* violations fall into the category of *lo nicha lei* on the grounds that one would prefer the violation not occur — but as *Tosafot*'s reasoning here illustrates, the standard is what one would generally prefer under normal conditions, not what one would prefer given the halakhic consequences of the outcome.

---

## Vessel Maintenance

### Wooden Vessels

*Hamotzei klei eitz, mishtamesh bahen kedei shelo yirkavu* — if one finds wooden vessels, one uses them to prevent rotting. As with the *mishnah*'s general approach to vessel maintenance, the prescribed method is actual use rather than merely storing the items or polishing them.

### Copper Vessels

*Klei nechoshet mishtamesh bahen be-chamin aval lo al yedei ha-ur* — copper vessels may be used with hot liquids or food but not placed directly over an open flame, since the direct heat would blacken and oxidize them. The best maintenance for copper is use with hot contents, but not the kind of vigorous, direct-flame use one might employ when cooking.

### Silver Vessels

*Klei kesef mishtamesh bahen be-tzonen, aval lo be-chamin, mipnei she-mashchiran* — silver vessels may only be used with cold water, not hot, since hot liquids cause them to blacken. Both copper and silver tarnish through oxidation under normal exposure to air; polishing removes a small layer of the metal itself, which makes periodic polishing a somewhat destructive form of maintenance. The *gemara*'s prescription of use according to these parameters thus reflects an attempt to keep the vessels functional while minimizing deterioration.

### Tools

*Magrefot ve-kardumos mishtamesh bahen be-rach aval lo be-kasha, mipnei she-pochasan* — shovels and picks may be used for soft tasks, such as shoveling ashes, but not for hard tasks such as breaking up logs, since heavy use damages them. *Tosafot* notes a general question running through all of these cases: why does maintenance require use at all? Why not simply polish or clean the objects? The answer, as *Tosafot* frames it, is that appropriate use actually keeps these objects in serviceable condition — as long as it falls within the parameters specified — whereas improper use or aggressive cleaning might itself cause damage.

The *gemara* then turns back to gold and glass vessels: *klei zahav u'klei zechuchit lo yiga bahen ad she-yavo Eliyahu. Kederech she-amru ba-aveidah kach amru be-pikadon* — the same standards that apply to a found object apply equally to an entrusted object. A question arises: if the owner is present and could use the vessels himself, what business does the *shomer* have using them at all? *Amar Rav Huna bar Chama amar Rav Sheshet*: the rule of *pikadon* applies specifically when the owners have gone overseas — *she-halchu ba'aleihem li-medinas ha-yam* — and are therefore unavailable. In their absence, the *shomer* bears the maintenance obligation.

---

## When to Abandon

### Three Exceptions

Having established that one who finds *matza sak o kuppah she-ein darko litol, harei zeh lo yitol* — a sack or box that it is not customary to take — need not retrieve it, the *gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — from where is this derived? *Detanu rabbanan*: the verse in Deuteronomy asks rhetorically, *ki tireh et shor achicha o et seio nidachim vehitalamta mehem* — when you see your brother's ox or sheep going astray, can you ignore them? — and answers *hashev teshivem le'achicha*, you must return them. But the *gemara* reads the phrase *vehitalamta mehem* non-rhetorically: there are circumstances in which one *may* hide oneself from the obligation, *pe'amim she'ata mitalem* — and circumstances in which one may not. Three such circumstances are identified: *haya kohen ve-hi be-veit hakvarot* — if one is a *kohen* and the object is in a cemetery; *o she-haya zaken ve-eino lefi kevodo* — if one is an elderly or distinguished person and retrieving the object would be beneath one's dignity; and *o she-hayta melachto meruba mi-shel chaveiro* — if the income one would forfeit by retrieving the object exceeds the value of the object itself.

### Cost Consideration

The *gemara* then asks: *lemai itztrich kra* — for which of these three cases did we actually need the verse? The first two, it turns out, can be derived independently, while the verse is needed specifically for the third — or rather, the verse is specifically needed for the *dignity* case.

The loss-of-income exception — *leshelo umishelo shel chaveiro* — is derivable from a *drasha* of *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav* on the verse *effes ki lo yihyeh becha evyon*: the principle is *shelcha kodem leshel kol adam* — your own interests take precedence over those of others. This is a variation of *chayecha kodmin lechayei achicha* — your own life comes first — one of the foundational ethical principles of the Torah. It does not mean that all of one's wants override all of others' needs, but that one's basic welfare takes priority. In the monetary sphere specifically, one is not obligated to sustain a loss that exceeds what the other person would gain. These *mamonot* considerations carry a kind of built-in fungibility — money lost can, in principle, be reimbursed or replaced, in a way that a ritual violation cannot be undone. Therefore the calculus of financial tradeoffs is permitted in ways that it would not be in the ritual sphere.

### Kohen Exemption

The *kohen*-in-cemetery case similarly does not require the verse, because the general rules of *asei docheh lo ta'asei* — a positive commandment overrides a negative prohibition — along with its limits, already resolve it. The *mitzvah* of *hashev teshivem* is an *asei*, but the prohibition against a *kohen* becoming *tamei* is both a *lo ta'asei* and an *asei* of *kedoshim tihyu*. An *asei* does not override a *lo ta'asei* combined with another *asei*. Furthermore, the *lo ta'asei* of *lo tuchal lehis'alem* — one may not ignore a lost object — does not itself serve as a "pushing force" to override the *kohen*'s prohibition; only an *asei* can function that way. Thus the mechanics of the standard rules already exempt the *kohen*, without need of the special verse.

### Kevod Habriyot

What the verse *vehitalamta mehem* is specifically needed for, therefore, is *lezaken ve'eino lefi kevodo* — the case of the person of dignity for whom retrieval is beneath their station. Here, unlike the first two cases, there is no independent derivation. One is not protecting oneself from ritual violation, nor is one protecting one's own money against a greater loss. One is protecting one's dignity against the simple indignity of stooping in the road to retrieve another person's object. And yet the Torah says even *this* consideration — *kevod habriyot* — overrides the positive obligation to return the lost object. That is the *chiddush* that requires the verse.

### Dignity & Ritual

*Tosafot* pursues the implications of *kevod habriyot* further. The principle is not limited to monetary obligations: there are cases where it overrides even ritual obligations. The paradigm case is *meis mitzvah* — an abandoned corpse with no one to bury it. The obligation to bury a *meis mitzvah* can override the obligation to bring a *korban Pesach* or to perform a *bris milah* for one's son. These are ritual *mitzvot*, not merely financial obligations, and yet *kevod habriyot* — specifically the profound affront to human dignity of leaving a body abandoned — takes precedence.

*Tosafot* accounts for this by pointing to degree: the *kevod habriyot* interest in burying an abandoned corpse is of an entirely different magnitude than the *kevod habriyot* interest in not having an important person stoop down in the road. When the dignity interest is sufficiently weighty, it can override even ritual obligations. When it is more modest — the ordinary case of *zaken ve'eino lefi kevodo* — it overrides monetary obligations such as *hashevat aveida*. The principle of *kevod habriyot* thus operates on a scale, and its force depends on how serious the affront to dignity actually is.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 31

## Zaken Ve'eino Lefi Kevodo

### Personal Precedence

Today's *daf* is 30b. We are in the middle of a very important discussion of the principle of *zaken ve'eino lefi kevodo* — the limits of what you are not obligated to do in returning a lost object (*aveidah*). The discussion begins three lines from the top of 30b.

The Gemara has already established that there are times when one need not return a lost object — for instance, if doing so would require entering a cemetery, which the Gemara treats as obvious. But beyond ritual considerations, there is a broader ethical principle at work: a person's own needs take precedence over another's. This does not mean that one places one's desires above another's needs, but rather that one's own needs carry greater moral weight than someone else's needs. Accordingly, before protecting another's property, one must first protect one's own. No special *pasuk* of *ve'hitalamta mehem* was needed to establish that. What we do learn from *ve'hitalamta mehem* — read not rhetorically but as an affirmative statement that one is sometimes permitted to refrain from returning a lost object — is when doing so would violate one's dignity. This is not a case of protecting one's own property over another's, but of protecting one's dignity over another's property.

### Kavod Habriyot

This is the principle of *kavod habriyot*. *Tosafot* discusses at some length how, when there is a significant affront to dignity — a body left in the street, or, as *Tosafot* also mentions, going about naked — the concern for human dignity can override even ritual obligations. Certainly at a lesser degree, it can permit one to forgo financial responsibilities toward another's property.

### Rava: Engagement Obligates

*Amar Rava*: *hishicha chayav bah* — even though you are exempt from returning a lost object when doing so is beneath your dignity, if you have already engaged it, if you struck or drove the animal, you are now obligated and cannot disengage. At first glance this principle might seem to apply generally: once I stop to pick up any *aveidah*, I can no longer claim my exemption.

### Livestock Exception

However, another *gemara* clarifies that this rule applies specifically to livestock. Once you have struck or driven an animal, it will follow you, and you cannot simply restore it to its prior state. Putting it back where you found it will only cause it to stray further. That is why engaging livestock in particular creates an immediate and inescapable obligation. By contrast, if one picks up, say, a wallet that it would be beneath one's dignity to return, another *gemara* indicates — though the present passage does not resolve the point — that one could still put it back where one found it and withdraw. The present *gemara* leaves that case for elsewhere.

### Abaye and the Goats

The Gemara illustrates this with a brief narrative: *Abaye hava yasiv kamei de'Rava* — Abaye was sitting before Rava. He saw some goats standing there, apparently wandering, and he threw a clump of dirt at them — *shakal kala veshada behu*. Whether he intended to shoo them away or to herd them is unclear from the text, but Rava immediately said to him: *ichayavtes behu kum ahadrinhu* — you have now made yourself obligated, go return them. Even an ambiguous act of engagement — not necessarily an attempt to take custody — is sufficient to create the obligation, because by his action Abaye may have caused the animals to stray further and he must now ensure their return to their rightful owner.

---

## Field vs. City Digni (II)

### Unresolved Question

The Gemara now raises a *ibaya*: how does one determine whether a particular act of returning is beneath one's dignity? Consider a case where finding the animal in the field (*basadeh*) presents no indignity — there are few passersby before whom one's standing matters — but bringing the animal into the city (*ba'ir*) would be beneath one's dignity. And yet, the animal was found in the field, where one could not locate anyone who knows the owner, and so the animal will eventually have to be brought into the city and one will need to inquire there.

The question has two sides. On one hand, *mi amrinan hashavah ma'alya be'inan* — perhaps the obligation of returning a lost object must be complete and encompasses all stages, and since the full act of return will involve something beneath one's dignity, the obligation never takes hold. *Ve'ein darko le'hachzir ba'ir lo mechayev* — since it is not within one's dignity to return it in the city, one is simply not obligated at all.

On the other hand, perhaps *besadeh miha ha ichayev lei* — since the obligation attached in the field, where it was fully appropriate for this person to act, the obligation is now live. And once one becomes obligated, *ichayev lei ba'ir* — even the portion of the return that must take place in the city falls within that obligation, and one must see it through entirely.

The Gemara concludes: *teiku* — this question remains unresolved.

One might ask: what does *hachrazah* — the public announcement — look like in practical terms? In the time of the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *Even HaToen* served as the designated site for announcements during the *regalim*. But outside that context, returning a lost object means going to *shuls* and *batei midrash*, posting announcements, doing whatever the local context requires. It is implausible that in ordinary times one would simply wait three months for the *regel*. Local inquiries would naturally have been initiated immediately.

### Rava's Self-Reference Test

*Amar Rava*: *kol she-bishelo machazir be-shel chaveiro nami machazir* — here is a useful way of determining whether an act of return is consistent with one's dignity: would you bother doing this act if it were your own object? If I drop a few pennies in a public square and would not stoop to pick them up, I would not do so for someone else's either. The thought experiment works well when the question is simply whether one would bend down to retrieve something. It is somewhat harder to apply when the question involves the process of returning — going door to door, making inquiries — but the general idea is to ask: if this were my object and these actions were required of me to recover it, would I perform them?

### Context-Dependent Dignity

This criterion, however, is not always a perfect measure. As a student pointed out in discussion, what is appropriate to one's dignity may depend on *context* and *beneficiary*. A wealthy man might not stoop to pick up a coin for himself, yet there is something qualitatively different about doing so in service of another whose needs are genuine. The context — that I am doing it not for myself but for someone else — may itself bear on whether the act is compatible with my dignity. Rava's self-referential thought experiment, while helpful, cannot always resolve the question, and the discussion acknowledged this limitation explicitly.

---

## Field vs. City Digni (II)

### Prika and Te'ina

The same principle extends to the related *mitzvah* of *prika u'te'ina* — unloading and reloading an animal collapsing under its burden. There too, if the act would be beneath one's dignity, one is exempt. The Gemara states: *ve'hakol she-bishelo porek ve'toten uv'shel chaveiro eino porek ve'toten* — if it is not fitting for him to unload and reload his own animal, he is not obligated to do so for another's. And the same diagnostic applies: ask yourself whether you would do it for your own animal. The caveat raised regarding *hashavat aveidah* applies here as well — context and beneficiary may render the self-referential test imperfect, though it remains the starting point for honest self-assessment.

---

## Lifnim Mishurat Hadin

### Bundle of Sticks Story

The Gemara now introduces a famous episode. *Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi hava ka'azil b'orcha* — Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosi was walking along the road when he encountered a certain man carrying a bundle of sticks. The man set them down and asked Rabbi Yishmael to help him reload them. Since Rabbi Yishmael was a distinguished elder, helping with these dirty, cumbersome sticks was clearly beneath his dignity.
