Rather than simply declining, he asked the man the value of the bundle. The man said it was worth half a *zuz*. Rabbi Yishmael purchased the bundle for half a *zuz*, then declared it *hefker* — ownerless. The man immediately reclaimed the bundle, at which point Rabbi Yishmael bought it again for another half a *zuz*, and again declared it *hefker*. When he saw the man was about to reclaim it a third time, he said: *l'chulei alma afkrinehu, lach lo afkrinehu* — it is *hefker* for everyone in the world, but not for you. Someone else may take it.

### Why Not Exempt?

The Gemara immediately raises the obvious question: *v'ha Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi zaken v'eino l'fi k'vodo hava* — Rabbi Yishmael was precisely the sort of elder for whom this act was beneath his dignity. Why did he not simply invoke his exemption and decline to help altogether?

### Rabbi Yishmael's Model

The Gemara answers: *Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosi lifnim mishurat hadin hu d'avad* — he was acting beyond the letter of the law, a principle we have encountered repeatedly in this *perek*. Though he was fully entitled to claim his exemption, he chose not to exercise every exemption available to him. *Tosafot* notes that there are different ways of conceptualizing *lifnim mishurat hadin*: sometimes it means refraining from claiming an exemption one legitimately holds, because the underlying obligation applies to everyone else and the right thing is to act accordingly. Other times, it means performing an act that is genuinely beyond what the law requires of *anyone*, not merely declining to exploit a personal exemption. Here, the former characterization applies: the general obligation to help with another's burden exists for everyone; Rabbi Yishmael had a personal exemption, and *lifnim mishurat hadin* meant not invoking it.

A brief parenthetical: does the *hefker* created in this story even take legal effect? The Gemara raises the question. *Beit Hillel* holds that *hefker* is valid only when it is made available to everyone — rich and poor alike — as with *shmita*. One cannot declare something *hefker* selectively. The Gemara resolves this by saying that Rabbi Yishmael did in fact declare it *hefker* for the entire world: *l'chulei alma afkrinehu*. His statement to the man that it was not *hefker* for him was merely a social deterrent — *uv'milta b'alma hu d'ukmeih* — not a legal limitation on the *hefker*. Technically, the man could have reacquired it; Rabbi Yishmael was simply discouraging him from doing so.

### Rav Yosef's Teaching

The Gemara grounds this discussion in a *baraita* taught by Rav Yosef, which derives a set of life principles from Yisro's advice to Moshe. The verse reads: *v'hodata lahem es haderech yelchu vah v'es hama'aseh asher ya'asun* — "and you shall make known to them the way they should walk in it and the deed that they should do" (Exodus 18:20). *Chazal* understand that Yisro is counseling Moshe not merely to teach *halacha* and *mitzvot*, but to transmit a broader way of living — one that is not fully captured by technical legal obligation. Strikingly, this advice comes from a non-Jew, and before *Matan Torah*, suggesting that it draws on a larger human wisdom about how a life is properly lived.

### Five Life Principles

Rav Yosef's *baraita* derives five distinct principles from this verse. *Zeh beis chayeihem* — "this is the way of their life," referring to *parnassa*, the pursuit of livelihood. Teaching people *halacha* alone is insufficient; they must also learn how to make their way in the world. *Es haderech* — "the way" — *zo g'milus chasadim*: this is the practice of acts of kindness, a way of life that transcends halakhic mandates. *Yelchu* — "they shall walk" — *ze bikkur cholim*: visiting the sick. *Bah* — "in it" — *zu k'vurah*: burying the dead. And *v'es hama'aseh asher ya'asun* — "and the deed that they should do" — *zu lifnim mishurat hadin*: going beyond the letter of the law.

The structure here is instructive. There is a broader morality — *mentshlekhkeyt*, *g'milus chasadim*, building a livelihood — that is not even specifically about the spirit of any particular law. Then there is the law itself. And then there is the spirit of the law, the ideal one should be striving toward: *lifnim mishurat hadin*. Rabbi Yishmael's behavior was an expression of this third category.

---

## Bikkur Cholim & Kevura

### Ben Gilo Obligation

The Gemara now returns to parse the individual elements of Rav Yosef's *baraita*. Regarding *bikkur cholim*: isn't visiting the sick simply a form of *g'milus chasadim*? Why specify it separately? The Gemara answers: *lo nitzrecha ela le'ben gilo* — the *chiddush* is specifically with respect to one's *ben gilo*, a person born under the same constellation or astrological grouping. The Gemara cites a teaching that when one visits one's *ben gilo* who is ill, one actually removes one sixtieth of his illness — but also takes on that portion of the sickness oneself. One might therefore think that the obligation of *bikkur cholim* does not apply in this case, since the visitor will be harmed. The Gemara rules: *ve'afilu hachi mibayei lei lemizal legabeih* — even so, one is obligated to go and visit.

This raises a broader point about *bikkur cholim* and personal risk. Certainly one's primary moral responsibility is to oneself — as the *daf* established earlier — and if there is genuine danger of infection or serious harm, the obligation of *bikkur cholim* does not override that. But in the Gemara's framework, a minor diminishment — one-sixtieth of another's illness — does not rise to that level, and the obligation stands.

### Burial Dignity Question

Regarding *k'vurah*: isn't burying the dead also subsumed under *g'milus chasadim*? The Gemara answers here as well: *lo nitzrecha ela le'zaken ve'eino lefi kevodo* — the *chiddush* is that even one for whom this act would be beneath his dignity is still obligated to attend to burial of the dead.

This is a striking *gemara*. Within a religious society that honors the mitzvot of caring for the dead, how can burying the dead be considered *eino lefi kevodo*? Yet the Gemara acknowledges the reality. The more interesting question is whether the obligation here is a strict *din* or whether it represents *lifnim mishurat hadin*. One could argue that since the dignity of the deceased — *kavod habriyot* — is itself at stake, the competing *kavod habriyot* of the one who would be embarrassed to perform the burial is overridden. It is not merely money versus one person's dignity; it is one person's dignity weighed against another's. This would make it a strict legal obligation. Alternatively, this may be more in the nature of *lifnim mishurat hadin* — an aspirational standard that goes beyond the letter of the law.

Notably, the marginal notes (*hagahot*) in the printed text cite the *halacha* of *bikkur cholim* even in the *ben gilo* case, but there is no corresponding citation bringing down a practical *halacha* for *k'vurah* in a case of *eino lefi kevodo*. This asymmetry invites reflection on whether this case is indeed a binding *din* or something more aspirational. One might also observe — as was raised in discussion — that *Hashem* Himself buried Moshe, suggesting that perhaps the entire framework of *eino lefi kevodo* should not even be acknowledged as a valid consideration when it comes to burial of the dead.

### Jerusalem's Destruction

The Gemara cites a remarkable statement of Rabbi Yochanan: *lo charva Yerushalayim ela she-danu bah din Torah* — Jerusalem was destroyed only because they judged by the law of the Torah. The obvious objection is raised: should they have used some other standard of law? The Gemara clarifies: *ela eima she-he'emidu dineihem al din Torah v'lo avdu lifnim mishurat hadin* — they were destroyed because they insisted on the precise letter of the law in every case and never acted beyond it. "I fulfilled my *halachic* obligation, I am done." There was no broader conversation about what the right thing to do was, no spirit of the law, no *lifnim mishurat hadin*. That orientation — reducing all of Jewish life to technical compliance — is what ultimately brought about the destruction of Jerusalem.

How this connects mechanically to the destruction is a broader discussion; the *Netziv* in his introduction to *Sefer Bereishit* addresses related themes at length.

---

## Defining Aveidah

### Grazing on Path

The Gemara now turns to the next *mishnah*, which asks: *eizo hi aveidah* — what constitutes a lost object? The question might seem strange after all the discussion to this point, but the Gemara (through Rav Yehuda) explains that the *mishnah* is identifying the clearest paradigm: *matza chamor o parah ro'in baderech ein zo aveidah* — if one finds a donkey or a cow grazing on the path, that is not an *aveidah* and one is not obligated to return it.

### Signs of Loss

By contrast, *chamor ve-chelav hafuchin parah ratzah bein hakramim* — a donkey with its saddlebags overturned, or a cow running through the vineyards — *harei zo aveidah*, that is clearly a lost object. These are things no owner would allow to occur, and they indicate that the animal has gone astray without the owner's knowledge. The Gemara distills two criteria: the animal's behavior (grazing versus running) and its location (a normal path versus a vineyard). For an animal to clearly constitute an *aveidah*, both problematic criteria apply; if only one is present, the analysis becomes more complex.

### Three-Day Rule

But what if an animal is simply grazing on the path — normally not an *aveidah* — and one observes this day after day, with no owner in sight? At some point the evidence of abandonment becomes overwhelming. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav: ad shlosha yamim* — after three days without an owner appearing, one treats it as an *aveidah* and is obligated to act.

### Early-Late Observations

The Gemara probes what this means in practice. If the animal is seen grazing at night (*b'leilyusa*), even a single observation suffices — owners do not send animals to graze at night. If one observes it only during daylight hours (*b'yimama*), even many days might not indicate abandonment, since the owner may be collecting the animal at night.

The operative case is the one where one sees the animal before dawn and again into the first hour of night, day after day — *lo tzricha d'havei chazi lei b'kadmusa u'v'chashachta*. Could such early and late grazing simply reflect an unusually diligent or negligent owner? Possibly, for one or two days. But *ad tlosha yomei amrinan ishtrumay ishtrumay lei* — for up to three days we say the owner's schedule might simply account for it. *V'nafak tfei* — beyond three days, it is certainly an *aveidah* and one must take the animal in.

---

## Aveidah Extended

### Flood Protection

The *mishnah* introduces a new case: *ra'ah mayim sheshofin u-va'in harei zeh goder bifneihem* — if one sees water coming to flood a field, one is obligated to build a barrier to stop it. This extends the *mitzvah* of *hashavat aveidah* in two significant directions: to land rather than movable objects, and to *protecting* against an impending loss rather than simply *returning* something already lost.

### Rava's Abstraction

*Amar Rava le-chol aveidat achikha le-rabbot aveidat karka* — Rava derives from the verse "all the loss of your brother" that the *mitzvah* of *hashavat aveidah* encompasses even damage to land. The *mitzvah* is not limited to picking up a lost object and finding its owner; it includes protecting another's property from harm even when the property is immovable and the owner is present.

### Objects vs. Land

Rav Chananya offered a supporting *baraita* from the flood-protection case. Rava, however, was not fully satisfied, noting that the case could be read as protecting the bundles of wheat (*omerin*) in the field rather than the land itself — making it still a case of protecting a movable object. The Gemara engages this suggestion: if there are bundles that are closely associated with the land (*de-tzrikhei le-ar'a*), one might have thought they are treated as part of the land and thus exempt from *hashavat aveidah*; the *baraita* teaches otherwise. Whether the extension to land itself is established remains an open question — the Gemara notes that land (*karka*) is formally excluded from some categories of obligation, as in the laws of theft and robbery. But what is clear in either reading is that protecting a concrete object from imminent destruction — not just returning one already lost — falls within *hashavat aveidah*.

### Pikuach Nefesh

This expanded understanding of *hashavat aveidah* carries a striking implication. One of the sources for the *mitzvah* of *pikuach nefesh* — the obligation to protect a person's life or health when at risk — is precisely this broadened conception of *hashavat aveidah*. If I am obligated to protect your property against an impending loss, then *kal va-chomer* I am obligated to protect you against injury. As the Gemara reasons: if *hashavat aveidah* means protecting against loss and not only recovering what is lost, then it encompasses protecting a person's body as well as a person's property. This is a remarkably broad interpersonal mandate — not merely about lost objects, but about protecting people and their possessions.

---

## Mishna Contradiction

### Contradiction Identified

The Gemara now identifies an internal contradiction within the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* states: *matza chamor o parah ro'in baderech ein zo aveidah* — grazing on the path is not an *aveidah*. The implication is that *ro'in baderech* alone fails the test, but running (*ratzah*) on the path, or grazing in a vineyard (*ro'eh bein hakramim*), would constitute an *aveidah*. Yet later the *mishnah* states that *parah ratzah bein hakramim* — a cow running in the vineyards — is an *aveidah*, implying that only when *both* problematic criteria are present (running *and* in the vineyard) is it clearly an *aveidah*. These two readings appear to conflict.

### Context Resolution

*Amar Abaye*: *yagid alav re'o* — let the context of each clause define what it means. When the *mishnah* says grazing on the path is not an *aveidah*, it implicitly includes all types of grazing — even grazing in a vineyard — since vineyards are mentioned explicitly later, and the contrast being drawn here is purely between grazing and running. Similarly, when the *mishnah* says running in the vineyard is an *aveidah*, path and vineyard are not the operative distinction; it is running versus grazing that determines the outcome. The location (path vs. vineyard) is incidental to the case being described; the *mishnah* is not generating rules about location.

### Direction Matters

Rava, however, is not fully satisfied with Abaye's resolution, and he offers his own: the *mishnah* need not rely on reading location as incidental. Instead, direction of movement is what matters. *Ha de'appa legabei dabra* — if the animal is running *away* from the city, that is an *aveidah*, whether on a path or in a vineyard, because an animal heading away from inhabited areas without an owner is clearly lost. *Ha de'appa legabei mata* — if it is running *toward* the city, that is not an *aveidah*, because perhaps it is heading home of its own accord. The old Chassidic teaching applies: it is not which rung of the ladder you stand on, but which direction you are moving.

### Two Aveidah Types

Regarding the apparent contradiction about grazing in the vineyards — in one place it seems to be an *aveidah*, in another not — Rava offers a resolution that is conceptually significant: *kan be'aveidat gufa kan be'aveidat karka* — in one case we are speaking of *aveidat gufa*, loss of the animal itself, and in the other case of *aveidat karka*, damage to the land. As to the animal: grazing in a vineyard does not necessarily indicate that the animal is lost (*aveidat gufa*), because the owner may simply be allowing it to graze there. As to the vineyard: grazing in a vineyard is absolutely a problem of *aveidat karka*, because the vines are being damaged, and one must intervene to protect the landowner's property even if the animal itself is not technically "lost."

### Running in Vineyards

Why is *running* in a vineyard different? *Deratzah bein hakramim miskiva* — when an animal runs through a vineyard, the thorns and undergrowth injure the animal itself. No owner would voluntarily allow this; it is therefore certain (*aveidat gufa*) that the animal is lost. *Vero'eh bein hakramim lo miskiva* — when the animal merely grazes in a vineyard, it is not injured, so the owner may have permitted it. The obligation to intervene arises not from *aveidat gufa* but from *aveidat karka* — the damage being done to the vineyard.

The Gemara adds: but if the vineyard is not owned by a Jew, there is no *aveidat karka* obligation (according to strict *halacha*, though *lifnim mishurat hadin* might still counsel otherwise). And might not the animal itself be at risk — since the vineyard's owner might kill an animal trespassing on non-Jewish property? The Gemara addresses this: in a locale where the practice is to give warning before taking action against the animal, the first incursion does not yet present a real danger. And if the owner has already been warned and allowed the animal to graze there again, *harei aveida mida'ato* — the owner has implicitly accepted the risk and it is treated as an *aveidah* he has brought upon himself.

---

## Returning Multiple Times

### Doubling Ambiguity

The *mishnah* states that if one returns a lost animal and it runs away again, one must continue returning it — *afilu me'ah pe'amim*, even a hundred times — as the verse states *hashev teshivem*. One of the *rabanan* raised the following challenge to Rava: perhaps *hashev teshivem* means only twice — *hashev* once, *teshivem* a second time. On what basis does the *mishnah* derive a hundred times?

### First Word Indicates Many

Rava's response is elegant and precise: *hashev afilu me'ah pe'amim mashma* — the word *hashev* alone, by its grammatical form, carries the ongoing, iterative sense of "it shall be returned" rather than the simple "you shall return." The doubling is not what generates the obligation to return many times; even the first word alone implies as many times as necessary.

### Teshivem Extension

If so, what does *teshivem* add? The Gemara derives a different *chiddush*: *ein li ela le-veito, ginato u-charto minayin? Talmud lomar teshivem mikol makom* — I might have thought the obligation of return is fulfilled only by placing the animal directly in the owner's house. How do I know that returning it to his garden or his yard also counts? *Teshivem mikol makom* — the double language broadens the forms of valid return, encompassing any protected location belonging to the owner.

The Gemara clarifies: this refers specifically to a *guarded* location. If the garden or yard is not properly enclosed, returning an animal there would not constitute a valid return. The *chiddush* applies only where the alternate location offers real protection — equivalent to the owner's house.

### Return Without Notification

Having established that one may return an animal to the owner's yard rather than his house, the Gemara raises a further question: does a valid return require *da'at ba'alim* — that the owner be informed and aware? Perhaps one must knock on the door and notify the owner directly.

The answer is no: *hashavat aveidah* does not require notifying the owner. This is derived from Rabbi Elazar's ruling: *de'amar hakol tzrichin da'at ba'alim chutz me'hashavat aveidah she'hatorah ribta hashavot harbeh* — virtually all forms of repayment or restoration require the awareness of the recipient, but returning a lost object is an exception, because the Torah's multiple formulations (*ribta hashavot harbeh*) indicate that many forms of return are valid — including return without the owner's active knowledge. One may simply place the animal in the owner's pen and go home.

---

## Double Language Patt (II)

### Shiluach Hakan

The Gemara now traces the same interpretive pattern through several other *mitzvot* that employ double language. *Shale'ach tishalach et ha'em* — the *mitzvah* of sending away the mother bird before taking her young. The *gemara* in *Chulin* teaches that if the mother bird returns, one must send her away again — even a hundred times. Here too, one of the *rabanan* asked Rava: perhaps *shale'ach* means once and *tishalach* means a second time — why assume a hundred?

Rava responds with the same structure: *shale'ach afilu me'ah pe'amim mashma* — the word *shale'ach* alone, in its iterative grammatical sense, implies as many times as the situation requires. What, then, does *tishalach* add? *Ein li ela lidvar hareshut* — I would have known the obligation applies when taking the birds for an ordinary permitted purpose. *Lidvar mitzvah minayin* — how do I know it applies when one is taking the birds for a *mitzvah* purpose, such as the birds used in the purification of a *metzora*? *Tishalach mikol makom* — the doubling extends the obligation across all cases, including those where the taking itself serves a religious purpose.

---

## Double Language Patt (II)

### Hochacha

The same question is posed regarding *hocheach tochiach* — the obligation to rebuke a fellow Jew. Does this mean only twice, or many times? Rava answers: *hocheach afilu me'ah pe'amim mashma* — the first word, *hocheach*, already implies an ongoing obligation, as many times as necessary. *Tochiach* then extends the obligation's scope: *ein li ela rav le-talmid* — I might have thought only a teacher may rebuke a student. *Talmid le-rav minayin* — how do I know a student may, or is even obligated to, remonstrate a teacher? *Hocheach tochiach mikol makom* — the double language extends the obligation regardless of relative standing, provided, of course, that it is done respectfully.

### Prika and Te'ina Revisited

The Gemara applies the same analysis to *azov ta'azov imo* and *hakem takim* — the obligations to unload and reload a collapsing animal. The verse regarding unloading says *azov ta'azov imo* — "you shall surely release with him," implying the owner's participation. *Ein li ela be'alav imo* — I would only know the obligation applies when the owner is present and helping. *She'ein be'alav imo minayin* — how do I know I must unload even when the owner is not present, is unable to help, or it is beneath his dignity? *Talmud lomar azov ta'azov mikol makom* — the double language extends the obligation across all circumstances. Similarly for *hakem takim* — the reloading obligation: the double language teaches that even when the owner cannot assist, the obligation remains. In both cases, the first word alone conveys the iterative, ongoing character of the obligation, and the second word broadens the contexts to which it applies.

---

## Both Mitzvot Needed

### Unloading Rationale

The Gemara now asks a deeper conceptual question: *lamma lei le-michtav prika ve-lamma lei le-michtav te'ina?* Why did the Torah need to specify both the obligation to unload and the obligation to reload? Given that we have already abstracted *hashavat aveidah* to encompass all forms of protecting property from loss, why not derive one from the other?

The answer is *tzrichi* — both are necessary. Had the Torah stated only the obligation to unload, one would have understood it as flowing from two convergent concerns: *mishum tza'ar ba'alei chayim* — because the animal is suffering, and *mishum chissaron kis* — because the owner faces significant financial loss (the animal may die or the goods will not reach their destination). The case is so compelling on both grounds that the obligation is obvious. But *te'ina* — reloading — involves neither animal suffering nor so immediate a financial risk. The animal is fine; the owner can potentially find someone else to reload for him. Without an explicit *pasuk*, one would have thought reloading falls outside the scope of obligation.

### Aveidah Rationale

Conversely, had the Torah stated only the *mitzvah* of *hashavat aveidah*, one would understand it as addressing cases where *the owner is absent* and *detza'ara demarei ita* — the owner's distress is acute. But unloading and reloading (*prika u'te'ina*) occur when *the owner is present*: *de'ita le-marei bahadah*. One might have thought: the owner is right here — why is this my responsibility? Let him handle his own animal. Without an explicit *pasuk* for *prika u'te'ina*, one would not have known that the obligation exists even when the owner is present and capable.

### Reloading Paid

An additional asymmetry between *prika* and *te'ina* further necessitates explicit instruction for each. The Gemara notes that *te'ina* — reloading — may be performed for pay. It is more like the work of a hired laborer assisting in the owner's commercial enterprise than like the emergency intervention of *prika*. Had the Torah told us only about *te'ina*, we might have known it is obligatory (because one can be compensated), but we would not have known that *prika* — which must be done without compensation — is equally obligatory.

### Rabbi Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon goes further, ruling that *af te'ina bechinam* — even reloading must be performed without compensation. From Rabbi Shimon's perspective, there is an even stronger reason why the Torah must specify both: since both unloading and reloading are done without pay, it is not obvious from one that the other is required. And there is a further complication: the verbs used in the *pesukim* — *azov ta'azov* and *hakem takim* — are not so transparently referring to loading or unloading respectively. Had the Torah mentioned only one, it would have been read as referring solely to unloading, and the obligation to reload would have remained entirely unaddressed. Only by specifying both twice does the Torah make clear that there are two distinct obligations, one for unloading and one for reloading.

The broader conceptual takeaway is that *hashavat aveidah* — properly understood — is not merely about recovering a lost object and reuniting it with its owner. It is a *mitzvah* that applies even without *tza'ar ba'alei chayim*, and even when the owner is present. It encompasses protecting people's property against imminent harm, and by *kal va-chomer*, protecting people themselves. This is the sweeping interpersonal mandate that the Gemara, over the course of this *daf*, has carefully elaborated.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 32

## Aveida Parameters

### Three Exceptions

The daf officially begins at the top of 31b, where the Gemara is in the midst of developing the core parameters of *aveida*. The Gemara's *drasha* on the phrase *ve-hisalamta mei-hem* — the verse that commands one to "ignore" the lost object under certain conditions — yields three categories of exception. The first is dignity: just as one may prioritize one's own property over another's, one may prioritize one's own dignity over another's financial loss, and need not return an object when doing so would be beneath one's station. The second is the prohibition against violating another *halacha* in the course of returning a lost object — the paradigmatic case being a *kohen* who would have to enter a cemetery, which will appear explicitly in a later *mishna*. The third exception, which actually appears first in the *braisa* but arose first in the *mishna* as well, is that one need not return a lost object if doing so would cause oneself greater financial loss in the process.

### Aveidat Karka

A conceptually significant extension that emerged in the preceding Gemara is the application of *hashavat aveida* to *aveidat karka* — preventing damage to land. This represents a double abstraction: from movable property to immovable property, and from the act of returning an object to its owner to the more general obligation of preventing loss. That broader framing becomes critical when the Gemara moves to compare *aveida* with *prika u-teina*, since both seem, at the most abstract level, to be expressions of the same principle — protecting another person's property.

### Aveida & Prika U-Teina

This raises an obvious question: if both *aveida* and *prika u-teina* reduce to the same underlying concern of preventing property loss, why does the Torah need to legislate both separately? The Gemara addresses this by pointing out that the two *mitzvot* operate in genuinely distinct ways. In the case of unloading a struggling animal, the elevated obligation is driven partly by *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* — the suffering of the animal — a factor absent in the ordinary *aveida* context. Conversely, in the *aveida* case, one dimension of the obligation is heightened by the fact that the owner is not present and cannot protect the object himself. The various *psukim* are thus teaching the scope of the obligation to protect another's property across a range of distinct scenarios, each with its own configuration of factors.

---

## Doubling Language

### Mos Yumat

The Gemara continues its survey of doubled verbal constructions in the Torah and what each instance comes to teach. The passage *mos yumat ha-makeh* — "the murderer shall surely be put to death" — cannot mean that the execution must be carried out multiple times, since one execution suffices. Instead, the Gemara reads the doubling as teaching: *ein li ela be-misah ha-ksuvah bo* — I know only that the murderer must be executed by the specific mode of execution prescribed for him, such as by the sword. But what if circumstances prevent implementation of that prescribed method — for instance, if the condemned man has escaped and the only way to stop him is by some other means? The double language — *mos yumat mi-kol makom* — authorizes execution by whatever means are available. This applies specifically after a *gmar din* has been issued, not during investigation or in the context of a pursuer trying to commit murder; those are governed by separate *halachot*.

### Hakei Takeh

A parallel case: the verse commanding the smiting of the inhabitants of the *ir hanidachat* prescribes death by the sword. The doubling of *hakei takeh* teaches that if the prescribed mode of execution cannot be carried out, any other form of execution is permitted — *mi-kol makom*, under all circumstances.

### Hashev Tashiv

Returning now to a case directly relevant to *aveida*: the doubled form *hashev tashiv* in the context of returning collateral. The straightforward reading might suggest that the obligation applies only when the lender seized the collateral through a court officer, i.e., *birshut beit din*. The doubling — *hashev tashiv mi-kol makom* — extends the obligation to cover even cases where the collateral was seized through private agreement rather than by court order.

### Chavol Tachbol

The phrase *im chavol tachbol salmat re'akha* — "if you take your neighbor's garment as collateral" — also employs doubled language. One might initially ask why the Torah uses this construction here at all, and then a further question arises: why are there actually two separate *psukim* about collateral, one in Shemot 24 and one in Shemot 25? The answer is that one verse addresses *ksut yom* — a daytime garment that must be returned during the day — and the other addresses *ksut laila* — a nighttime garment that must be returned at night. The doubled language within each verse extends the obligation to cases where the collateral was seized without any authorization whatsoever — not merely without a court officer but even where the lender broke into the debtor's home and seized an item unilaterally. One might have thought that such an illegitimate seizure falls outside the Torah's protective framework, or conversely that the obligation to return might not apply since the original taking was improper. The doubled language — *chavol tachbol mi-kol makom* — establishes the obligation under all circumstances.

### Patoach Tiftach

The phrase *patoach tiftach et yadekha lo* — "you shall surely open your hand to him" — in the context of giving to the poor. The Gemara first reads these *psukim* through the lens of *tzedaka*, noting that the verse also says *dei machsoro* — as much as he lacks. The doubling teaches, first, that the obligation extends beyond the poor of one's own city (*ani irkha*) to the poor of other cities as well. While those of one's own town take precedence, the obligation itself is not geographically limited. The doubling also addresses the question of partial giving: since the verse says to supply what the person lacks, one might think there is no *mitzvah* to give a small amount if one cannot provide everything that is needed. The doubled form *naton titein mi-kol makom* — give regardless — establishes that even a minimal gift fulfills the *mitzvah*.

### Ha'anek Ta'anik

The doubled phrase *ha'aneik ta'anik lo* governs the *mitzvah* of loading up the freed slave with gifts when he goes free in the seventh year. The end of the verse credits the slave's service with bringing divine blessing to the household — *ki mishneh sechar sachir avadcha shesh shanim u-veirach'cha Hashem Elokecha*. One might therefore think that if the household was not in fact blessed — if the master's business suffered during the years of the slave's service — there is no obligation to provide these gifts. The doubled language — *ha'aneik ta'anik mi-kol makom* — establishes the obligation regardless of whether the household was blessed. The comparison to large bonuses paid even in years when a firm loses money is not inapt.

---

## Dibra Torah K'Lishon

### R. Elazar b. Azarya

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, however, holds that the obligation to give the departing slave gifts is indeed contingent on the household having been blessed by his service. If the household was not blessed, there is no obligation. This position must therefore explain what work the doubling of *ha'aneik ta'anik* performs in his reading.

### Doubling as Speech

The Gemara's answer for Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya is that the doubled form here teaches nothing additional: *dibra Torah k'lishon bnei adam* — the Torah sometimes speaks in the ordinary idiom of human language, using emphatic doubling as a stylistic feature rather than as a source of novel law. This principle opens a methodological question that Tosafot addresses directly: how does one determine when a doubled form is *dibra Torah k'lishon bnei adam* and when it carries halakhic content? Tosafot's answer is that the default assumption is that doubling expands the scope of the *mitzvah*, and only when no plausible expansion can be derived from context do we fall back on *dibra Torah k'lishon bnei adam*.

---

## Doubling Language (II)

### Ha'aveit Ta'avitenu

The Gemara returns to the earlier *psukim* about giving to the poor, now focusing specifically on the doubled verb *ha'aveit ta'avitenu* — the root of which connotes collateral and lending — thereby indicating that the *pasuk* is also, or primarily, addressing the obligation to extend a loan. What does the doubling teach here?

The Gemara states: *ein li ela she-ein lo v'eino rotze l'hitparnes* — I know only that the obligation applies when the person has no means of his own and refuses to accept a gift, preferring instead to maintain his dignity by way of a loan. In such a case, the Torah says: give him the loan. This implies, interestingly, that when a person is willing to accept a gift, giving a gift is actually preferable to a loan — a debate addressed more fully in the Gemara in Ketubot 67b for those who wish to pursue it.

But the more pressing question is: what about a person who has money of his own but refuses to use it — *yesh lo v'eino rotze l'hitparnes mishalo ela mishalcha*? Rashi explains the case starkly: the person has assets but refuses to draw on them. One might imagine someone who is, as it were, asset-rich and cash-poor — perhaps unwilling to liquidate a prized possession — and who refuses to accept charity but is willing to accept a loan. Is one obligated to lend money to such a person, or can one say that his refusal to sell his assets is his own affair? The doubled form — *ta'avitenu mi-kol makom* — teaches that one is nonetheless obligated to extend the loan. People have their own particular circumstances and arrangements, and that does not dissolve one's obligation toward them.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *yesh lo v'eino rotze l'hitparnes — ein nizkakin lo*. If a person actually has money, there is no obligation whatsoever. In his view, the doubled form of *ta'avitenu* teaches nothing, and the ruling is again *dibra Torah k'lishon bnei adam*.

---

## Poel Batel Wages

### Poel Batel Definition

The Gemara now turns to the question of reimbursement for returning a lost object. If a person loses time from work in order to return an *aveida*, the owner must compensate him — but not at his full wage rate. The *mishna* states he is paid *ke-schar poel batel* — like the wage of an idle worker. What does this mean?

Abaye explains: *ke-poel batel shel oto melacha de-batel mineih* — like a worker who is taking time off from the specific labor he would otherwise be performing. The key is not what he could earn at that labor, but what he would accept in order to take a break from it.

Rashi elaborates precisely. Consider a quarry worker earning twenty dollars an hour at hard physical labor. If asked how much he would accept in order to take an hour off from that labor and instead do something lighter — such as knocking on doors to find the owner of a lost object — he might well accept five or ten dollars, because the relief from hard labor has its own value. The *poel batel* rate is therefore that reduced figure: the amount a person would willingly accept to stop doing his regular work and do something easier instead. Critically, this rate is not fixed; as Rashi notes, it depends on the nature and difficulty of the original work and the level of compensation it commands.

This produces two asymmetric edge cases. A high-earning professional — say, someone billing at a substantial hourly rate — might find that returning a lost object is actually more demanding or at least no less demanding than his regular work, meaning his *poel batel* rate converges with his ordinary rate. Conversely, a laborer who desperately needs the income might theoretically accept a reduced rate but cannot actually afford to do so. These are the cases in which, as the *mishna* requires, one must stipulate the terms before a *beit din*.

### Beit Din Role

The *mishna* states: *im yesh sham beit din matneh bifneihem* — if there is a court present, the finder stipulates the terms of reimbursement before them. The *beit din* in this context stands in for the interest of the owner of the lost object, approving the terms of compensation when the owner is not available to consent himself. The *beit din*'s precise role — whether it simply provides a formal stamp of approval or actually adjudicates what level of compensation is reasonable relative to the value of the object — is itself a matter for further analysis.

### Issur & Safra

The Gemara introduces an illustrative case. Issur and Safra were business partners who had jointly purchased a stock of goods. Safra, while Issur was absent, unilaterally divided the partnership, taking his half of the merchandise — doing so in front of two witnesses to ensure complete transparency. When the matter came before Rabba bar Rav Huna, he told Safra: two witnesses are insufficient for a unilateral division of partnership assets; you need three, i.e., a *beit din*, or at minimum two witnesses who testify that they were part of a tribunal of three. Safra asked: from where do you derive that a *beit din* is required? Rabba bar Rav Huna replied: from the *mishna* — *im yesh sham beit din matneh bifneihem* — the same logic applies: when one party acts unilaterally in a way that affects another party's interests, a *beit din* must represent the absent party's interests and validate the arrangement.

Safra pushed back: how can you compare the two cases? In the *aveida* case, the finder is extracting money from the owner — creating an obligation the owner did not freely agree to — and therefore a *beit din* is needed to represent the owner. But here, Safra took only what was already his. In a partnership, he owns half; the division is merely a clarification of which specific items correspond to his half. This is *giluya milta b'alma* — a mere disclosure of what was already the case. Two witnesses should therefore suffice.

The Gemara marshals support: a widow selling property from an estate to collect her *ketuva* may do so without a *beit din*, because she has a pre-existing lien on the property. Abaye, however, notes a refinement: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi said in the name of Rav Nachman that the widow does not need a *beit din shel mumchin* — a court of ordained experts — but she does need a *beit din shel hedyotos* — a court of lay members. The implication is that even when one is taking what one fundamentally has a right to, some form of communal oversight is required to protect the interests of others who might be affected, even if it falls short of a full expert tribunal.

---

## Finding Objects

### Matza B'Refet

The *mishna* opens with a straightforward rule: *matza b'refet ein chayav bah* — if one finds an animal in a barn, one is not obligated to return it. In the public domain, *birshut ha-rabim*, one is obligated. An additional exception is introduced: if the animal is in a cemetery and one is a *kohen*, one may not become *tamei* in order to return it — the prohibition against *tum'at kohanim* supersedes the obligation of *hashavat aveida*. This represents the third of the exceptions derived from the *drasha* of *ve-hisalamta mei-hem*, now appearing explicitly in the *mishna*.

---

## Prika U-Teina Intro

### Multiple Times

The *mishna* moves immediately to *prika u-teina* — the obligation to unload and reload a burdened animal — without first describing the general parameters of the *mitzvah*. It opens instead with the question of repetition: if one has unloaded and reloaded the animal, and the animal collapsed again, must one repeat the process? The *mishna* answers: *afilu arba'ah v'chamisha pe'amim chayav* — even four or five times, one remains obligated. The verse *azov ta'azov* — "you shall surely help" — grounds this in the doubled language, which the *mishna* reads as indicating multiple obligatory occurrences. It is worth noting that in the previous *mishna* regarding *hashev teshivem*, Rava had argued that the first word of a doubled form carries the meaning of multiple occurrences, while the second word expands the scope of the obligation. Here the *mishna* again uses the doubling to indicate repetition.

### Owner Present

If the owner is present, able-bodied, and refuses to assist — saying, in effect, since you have a *mitzvah* to help, you go ahead and I will wait — the finder is exempt. The verse states *imo* — "with him" — indicating that the obligation is conditioned on the owner's participation. If the owner is present and capable but unwilling to assist, the obligation lapses.

### Owner Infirm

If, however, the owner is elderly or ill and genuinely unable to assist, one remains obligated even though the owner cannot participate. The *mitzvah* of *prika u-teina* is not voided by the owner's incapacity; it is voided only by the owner's willful refusal to help when capable of doing so.

---

## Reload Obligation

### Mishnah Position

The *mishna* states: *mitzvah min ha-Torah lifrok aval lo litoan* — the Torah obligation is to unload the animal, but not to reload it. The Gemara will press immediately on this formulation.

### R. Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *af litoan* — there is a *mitzvah* to reload as well, and it is an equal Torah obligation. The Gemara will develop the reasoning behind both positions and then use the disagreement as the springboard for examining the principle of *tza'ar ba'alei chayim*.

---

## Finding Objects (II)

### Refet Definition

The Gemara asks what kind of barn the *mishna* has in mind when it exempts the finder from obligation. Rava establishes the parameters: *refet she-amru einah mateh v'einah meshameret* — the barn referred to is one that neither misleads the animal into wandering nor provides it full protection. Each characteristic is inferred from the *mishna* itself.

That the barn is not misleading — not actively encouraging the animal to leave, as a fire or wide-open gates might — is inferred from the fact that the *mishna* exempts the finder. If the barn were the kind of place from which an animal was likely to wander, the situation would constitute *aveidah mi-da'at* on the owner's part: a careless exposure of the animal to likely loss. In that case, one would be obligated to close the gate or take action, since the anticipated departure of the animal is one's responsibility to prevent. Since the *mishna* exempts the finder, the barn must not be creating that kind of situation.

That the barn is nonetheless not fully protective is inferred from the fact that the *mishna* needed to address the case at all. If the barn were completely secure, finding an animal inside it would so obviously not constitute an *aveida* that there would be no need to state the exemption. The *mishna*'s need to specify it tells us the barn provides less than complete protection — perhaps there is a small breach through which the animal might, under unusual circumstances, escape — but the risk is not sufficiently imminent to obligate the passerby.

The practical line the Gemara is drawing is between *anticipated* loss, which creates an obligation to prevent it, and *possible but remote* loss, which does not. One who walks by a barn with a wide-open gate while horses are about to realize they can walk out has an obligation to close the gate. One who walks by a barn with a small breach through which an animal might, in some unlikely circumstance, eventually find its way out does not.

### Two Readings

A further question concerns the relationship between the two conditions mentioned in the *mishna* — the animal being in a barn versus in the public domain — and whether one condition alone suffices to determine obligation. Two readings are presented.

### Yitzchak's View

Yitzchak interprets the *mishna* as follows: *vehu she'omedet toch la-tchum* — the exemption for an animal found in a barn applies only when the barn is within the city boundaries. If the barn is outside the city limits, the combination of reduced protection and distance from the owner creates sufficient risk that one is obligated even though the animal is in a barn.

Under the first reading of Yitzchak's position, the result is an expansive standard of obligation: an animal in the public domain — *birshut ha-rabim* — generates an obligation even within city boundaries, and an animal in a barn generates an obligation if it is outside the city boundaries. Either condition alone may be sufficient.

Under the second reading — attributed to those who place Yitzchak's statement at the *seifa* of the *mishna* rather than the *reisha* — the standard is more restrictive: one is obligated only when both conditions obtain simultaneously: the animal must be in the public domain *and* outside the city limits. A barn outside city limits alone would not suffice; the public domain alone within city limits would not suffice. Both factors together are required.

---

## Aveida Exceptions

### Cemetery Exception

The *mishna* states: *be-veit ha-kevarot lo yitama lah* — a *kohen* should not become *tamei* in order to return a lost animal found in a cemetery. The Gemara moves past this ruling relatively quickly, having addressed the underlying principle earlier: a positive commandment (*aseh*) cannot override a negative commandment combined with a positive commandment (*lo ta'aseh* and *aseh*). The *kohen*'s prohibition against becoming *tamei* — *le-nefesh lo yitama* as the *lo ta'aseh* and *kedoshim tihyu* as the *aseh* — cannot be overridden by the *aseh* of returning a lost object.

### Paternal Commands

The *mishna* then introduces a related case that has nothing to do with *tum'ah*: *im amar lo aviv hitama* — if one's father tells him to become *tamei*, or *al tachzir* — to not return a lost object — *lo yishma lo* — he should not obey. Here, two *mitzvot* are in tension: honoring or fearing one's father on one side, and a Torah prohibition (or obligation) on the other.

### Scripture Basis

The scriptural source for the ruling is: *ish imo ve'aviv tira'u ve'et shabtotai tishmoru, ani Hashem* — fear your mother and father, and observe My Sabbaths; I am God. The verse places both commandments in proximity and concludes with *kulchem chayavin bi-chevodi* — all of you are ultimately answerable to Me. The message is that honoring parents is a genuine obligation, but it operates within a framework in which divine authority is sovereign. When a father commands something that violates a divine obligation, the father's instruction falls outside the scope of legitimate parental authority.

This is a point worth dwelling on. One might have reasoned: returning an *aveida* is a monetary obligation, while honoring one's father is a ritual-spiritual obligation; the latter should therefore take precedence over the former. The *pasuk* forecloses that reasoning — not by saying that monetary obligations are equal in weight to ritual ones, but by establishing that the scope of *kibbud av va'em* does not extend to commanding the violation of divine law.

### Kibbud Av V'Em

A deeper question runs beneath the surface: is obeying one's father actually part of the Torah obligation of *kibbud av va'em* at all? Many *Rishonim* and *Poskim* hold that the core obligations of *kavod* (honor) and *yirah* (fear/awe) toward parents are behavioral rather than volitional — feeding and caring for them, not contradicting them publicly, not occupying their seat, and so on — but that simple obedience to their instructions is not, strictly speaking, a *d'oraita* obligation. Not contradicting parents in a disrespectful manner is different from being required to do whatever they say.

If that is correct, then the *mishna*'s case requires some explanation: why would there even be a question of obeying a father who tells one not to return an *aveida*? Several *Rishonim* therefore read the scenario as one where the father is not simply issuing an arbitrary command but is invoking his *kibbud*-related needs. For example, if the father says: I need you here at home attending to my care — don't go off returning someone else's lost object — then the *mitzvah* of honoring the father by meeting his needs does come into tension with the *mitzvah* of *hashavat aveida*. Similarly, if the father needs something retrieved from the cemetery and asks his *kohen* son to go in.

This reading makes the ruling more striking, not less. The *mishna* is not saying: ignore your father's whims in favor of a Torah obligation. It is saying: even when your father is invoking a legitimate dimension of *kibbud av va'em* — his actual needs — the divine obligation takes precedence and you do not obey. This sits in interesting tension with other cases the Gemara recognizes: one may refrain from returning an *aveida* to protect one's own financial interests, and one may refrain because returning it would compromise one's dignity. Why should protecting one's father's legitimate needs be any different? The question has no simple resolution, and the *Rishonim* are sensitive to it.

---

## Reload Obligation (II)

### Why Both?

The Gemara now returns to the *machloket* between the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Shimon regarding the obligation to reload. The Gemara's question: if both unloading (*prika*) and reloading (*teina*) are Torah obligations — as Rabbi Shimon maintains — why does the Torah mention both? If only reloading were stated, one could derive unloading by *kal va-chomer*; if only unloading were stated, one could derive reloading similarly. The need for two separate *psukim* requires explanation.

The *Rabbanan*'s answer is that the two *psukim* serve to differentiate the two obligations: unloading must be done for free, while reloading may be done for payment. This differentiation cannot be derived by inference alone and requires explicit textual basis. The reasoning is that unloading involves both *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* — the immediate suffering of the overburdened animal — and *chisron kis* — the risk of the animal collapsing and dying, constituting immediate financial loss. These dual factors obligate assistance without any right to compensation. Reloading, by contrast, involves neither the animal's immediate suffering nor the same immediacy of financial loss; it is still a *mitzvah*, but one for which the helper may receive payment.

The practical question this raises is striking. One is obligated to help load a person's animal, yet may request payment for doing so. How does one actually handle that in practice — does one approach the person and negotiate? The answer seems to be that the obligation exists, the right to payment exists alongside it, and the two can be harmonized through a straightforward conversation. More interesting is the question of when exactly the obligation to reload attaches: does one have a *mitzvah* only upon encountering an animal that has already collapsed, or even when one encounters a person in the midst of loading who simply needs assistance? These questions await further *sugya*.

### Rav Huna

Rav Huna takes a position against the majority: *zu va-zu be-chinam* — both unloading and reloading should be performed without payment.

### Rabbis' Reason

The *Rabbanan* respond to Rav Huna's position by articulating why the two obligations must be asymmetric. Their argument is structural: if even reloading — the lesser obligation — carries with it no right to payment, then certainly unloading would carry no right to payment. But the whole point of having two separate *psukim* must be to differentiate the two cases, and therefore the Torah explicitly states the obligation to reload precisely in order to indicate that unloading is the more stringent of the two.

### Kal V'Chomer

The Gemara makes the *kal va-chomer* structure explicit: *uma te'ina de-leit bah tza'ar ba'alei chayim chayav, prika de-it bah tza'ar ba'alei chayim lo kol she-ken?* — if reloading, which does not involve animal suffering, nonetheless carries an obligation, then unloading, which does involve animal suffering, certainly carries one. This *kal va-chomer* is the argument the *Rabbanan* say could have been used to derive unloading from reloading, making it unnecessary for the Torah to have stated both — unless the second *pasuk* is coming to differentiate the two cases in terms of payment.

---

## Tzaar Baalei Chayim

### Both Acknowledge

Rava now derives a broader principle from the *machloket* between the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Shimon: *mi-divrei sheneihem nilmad* — from both positions together we can infer that *tza'ar ba'alei chayim de-oraita* — concern for animal suffering is a Torah principle. The inference runs as follows. The *Rabbanan* explicitly ground the elevated obligation of unloading in *tza'ar ba'alei chayim*. And even Rabbi Shimon's position does not actually reject that principle: he holds that the two *psukim* are of equal obligation only because the *psukim* themselves are ambiguous — *de-lo mesaymi kra'ei* — and it is not clear textually which one addresses unloading and which addresses reloading. But if the *psukim* were explicit — *aval mesaymi kra'ei* — he would agree to the Rabbis' *kal va-chomer* logic, and therefore he implicitly accepts that unloading, involving animal suffering, is a weightier obligation. The agreement in principle between the two positions establishes that *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* is a Torah value, even if the precise halakhic implications of that value are worked out differently.

A caveat is important here: invoking *tza'ar ba'alei chayim de-oraita* in this context does not necessarily mean there is a free-standing independent obligation to alleviate animal suffering whenever one encounters it. What the Gemara is establishing here is that concern for animal suffering is a recognized Torah value that factors into the weight and scope of other obligations — specifically the obligation of *prika*.

### Alternative: Loss

The Gemara does not let the inference stand unchallenged. Perhaps, the Gemara suggests, the difference between unloading and reloading has nothing to do with the animal's suffering at all. Perhaps the relevant factor is purely financial: unloading is more urgent because the animal, if left burdened, might collapse and die — representing a direct property loss to the owner (*chisron kis*) — whereas reloading does not carry the same immediacy of financial loss. On this reading, the entire structure of the *machloket* is about the owner's property interests, not about any concern for the animal per se.

### Refutation

The Gemara refutes this alternative. If the only factor were *chisron kis*, then one could equally describe scenarios in which reloading also involves significant financial loss. A merchant trying to bring goods to market who cannot reload his animal will miss the market entirely — *batil mi-shukei* — losing the commercial opportunity. Or, more dramatically, he will be stranded on the road, exposed to bandits who may rob him of both his goods and the animal — *atu ganvei ve-shakli kol mah de-ika ba-hadeih*. Financial loss is a real risk in the reloading scenario as well.

The counter-argument that unloading involves *immediate* loss while reloading involves only *possible future* loss has some merit, but the Gemara does not find it decisive. Both unloading and reloading can plausibly involve financial loss to the owner of the animal; the genuine asymmetry between them must therefore lie elsewhere — and that elsewhere is *tza'ar ba'alei chayim*. The animal suffers under the burden when it needs to be unloaded; it does not suffer in the same way when it simply needs to be reloaded. That is the real difference.

### R. Yossi H-G

The Gemara cites a further proof from the position of Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili in the *mishna*: *im hayah alav yoter al masa'o ein zakuk lo* — if the animal is overloaded beyond what it can bear, and the overloading was the owner's fault, one has no obligation to help. The verse says *tachat masa'o* — under its burden — which Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili reads as *masa'o ha-raui she-yachol la'amod bo* — a burden it can normally sustain. An animal overloaded beyond that threshold is outside the *pasuk*'s scope.

This position is notable. If the obligation of *prika* were grounded in *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* — concern for the animal's suffering — then Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili's position would be difficult to understand. An overburdened animal is suffering, regardless of who is responsible. Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili's willingness to walk away from the suffering animal strongly suggests that in his view, the obligation is entirely about the owner's property interests, not the animal's welfare. Since the owner caused the problem himself — this is a form of *aveidah mi-da'at* — the owner bears the consequences and the passerby has no obligation.

### Final Question

The Gemara uses the contrast between Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili and the *Tanna Kamma* to sharpen the question. Since Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili holds one may ignore even an overburdened, suffering animal when the owner is at fault, from his ruling alone one cannot prove that *tza'ar ba'alei chayim de-oraita* is the operative principle. But the *Tanna Kamma* — who holds one is *zakuk lo* even in the case of an overburdened animal — seems to demand explanation. If the owner caused the loss himself, one would normally apply the logic of *aveidah mi-da'at* and have no obligation. The only compelling reason to nevertheless require assistance would be concern for the animal's suffering, independent of the owner's culpability. That would suggest that *tza'ar ba'alei chayim de-oraita* is indeed the operative factor for the *Tanna Kamma*.

The Gemara does not close the matter here. It notes the alternative: perhaps the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili are simply in a technical dispute about how to read the word *masa'o* in the *pasuk*, not a substantive dispute about *tza'ar ba'alei chayim*. And even the *Tanna Kamma*'s ruling that one must help in the overloading case may be explicable not as concern for the animal but as concern for the owner — the Torah, one might say, sometimes obligates us to help even those who brought trouble upon themselves, not because we are indifferent to fault but because human beings sometimes do foolish things and deserve assistance nonetheless. Whether *tza'ar ba'alei chayim de-oraita* can be definitively established as a Torah principle from this *sugya* remains the open question with which the daf concludes.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 33

## Tzaar Ba'alei Chayim

### Intro: Tzaar Ba'alei

The daf begins in the middle of a sustained discussion concerning whether *tzaar ba'alei chayim* — the prohibition against causing suffering to animals — is a principle of Torah law (*de'oraita*) or merely rabbinic enactment (*derabbanan*). In other Talmudic contexts, this question bears on whether one may violate a rabbinic prohibition on Shabbat in order to relieve an animal's pain. Here, however, the Gemara frames the question differently: is *tzaar ba'alei chayim* a Torah *value* — operative and weighty enough to shape how we understand the obligations of *prika u'te'inah* (unloading and loading a collapsed animal) and how we interpret the relevant *pesukim*? This is a significant methodological point: sometimes our grasp of the underlying values determines how we *darshan* a verse, rather than the *drasha* being a purely mechanical exercise. The Gemara proceeds to marshal arguments in both directions.

### Proof 1: Mishnah

The Gemara opens with *teda* — "know," or "here is a proof." It cites the Mishnah's ruling that if the owner of the collapsed animal walks away, sits down, and says to the passerby, "You have a *mitzvah* to unload it — go ahead," the passerby is *patur* (exempt) from doing so, as derived from the verse *azov ta'azov imo* — "you shall surely help *with him*," implying the owner must participate.

The Gemara asks: if *tzaar ba'alei chayim* is *de'oraita*, what difference should it make whether the owner is present and helping or not? The animal is suffering regardless. *Mai li itai le'marei bahadei u'mai li leika le'marei bahadei* — why should the presence or absence of the owner affect the obligation? If the concern is genuinely the suffering creature before you, the owner's irresponsibility ought to be irrelevant.

### Response: Paid vs Free

The Gemara responds with a crucial distinction: *mi savrat patur patur legamrei v'dilma patur bechinam ve'chayav besachar* — perhaps "exempt" does not mean fully exempt, but only exempt from doing it *for free*. One may charge for the labor when the owner is being irresponsible. The Gemara then restates the Mishnah accordingly: *itai le'marei bahadei avid gabei bechinam* — if the owner is there helping, you help him at no cost; *leika le'marei bahadei avid gabei besachar* — if the owner abandons his animal, you must still tend to the suffering animal, but you may collect payment. Thus, *tzaar ba'alei chayim* remains *de'oraita*, and the animal must be relieved of its suffering — only the question of compensation shifts based on the owner's conduct.

### Proof 2: Non-Jew's Animal

The Gemara now attempts to *support* the position that *tzaar ba'alei chayim* is *de'oraita* by citing a Baraita: *behemat oved kochavim metapel bah ke'vehemat Yisrael* — one must tend to the animal of a non-Jew just as one would tend to the animal of a Jew. This seems to be a compelling proof. All the brotherly obligations — *tzedakah*, going out of one's way for a neighbor — are generally understood to apply specifically between Jews. If the obligation of *prika u'te'inah* were about protecting the *owner's* property or preventing the owner from being stranded, one would expect it to apply only to Jewish owners. But if it is about the *animal's* suffering — which is the same regardless of who holds the deed — it makes perfect sense that it would apply equally to a non-Jew's animal.

### Resolution: Eivah

The Gemara rejects this proof, however, with the counterproposal: *hatam mishum eivah* — there, the reason one tends to the non-Jew's animal is not because of *tzaar ba'alei chayim* at all, but simply to avoid *eivah* (enmity). Leaving a non-Jew's animal to suffer creates ill-will between Jews and non-Jews, and it is that social concern — not the Torah's animal welfare principle — which motivates the ruling.

The Gemara reinforces this interpretation by noting: *hachi nami mistavra* — and indeed, this reading is more reasonable. For the Baraita continues: *im hayta te'una yayin assur ein zakuk lah* — if the animal was carrying *yayin nesech* (wine used for idolatrous libations), one need not help at all. If the motive were genuinely *tzaar ba'alei chayim*, the nature of the cargo would be irrelevant — the animal is suffering regardless. But if the motive is *eivah*, one can distinguish: concerning wine of *avoda zara*, one may plausibly explain to the non-Jew that religious law forbids handling it, and non-Jews, the Gemara elsewhere assumes, will accept such a religious justification. This cleanly explains why helping would be required in the ordinary case but not when the animal carries forbidden wine. The proof from the non-Jew's animal thus dissolves.

### Proof 3: Non-Jew Animal…

The Gemara introduces a further case: *behemat oved kochavim u'masoy Yisrael* — a non-Jew's animal carrying a Jew's wares. The verse *ve'chadalta* is invoked in the sense of permission to refrain — suggesting that in this configuration, one is not obligated to help. Now the question sharpens considerably: if *tzaar ba'alei chayim* is *de'oraita*, how can one ever refrain from helping a suffering animal? And if the obligation hinges on the wares' owner rather than the animal's owner, what is the underlying logic?

The Gemara responds: *le'olam tza'ar ba'alei chayim de'oraita* — *tzaar ba'alei chayim* remains a Torah principle, but the case here is *te'inah* (reloading), not *prika* (unloading). Reloading is about helping the *person* — getting their cargo to its destination — not about relieving the animal's pain. Thus it is a different category of obligation entirely. Unloading, driven by *tzaar ba'alei chayim*, one would always be obligated to perform. Reloading, which involves assisting the human being standing before you, can legitimately turn on who that person is.

### Loading vs Unloading

The Gemara then tests this reading against the second half of the Baraita: *behemat Yisrael u'masoy oved kochavim* — a Jew's animal carrying a non-Jew's wares — in which case *azov ta'azov* applies and one must help. If this is about reloading, asks the Gemara, why does one focus on who *owns the animal* rather than who *owns the wares*? If reloading is about helping the person who needs to get his goods somewhere, should not the identity of the cargo's owner be decisive?

The Gemara explains: *stama d'milsa inish basar chamrei azil* — ordinarily, the person driving the donkey is the person who owns it. So the owner of the animal is, as a practical matter, the person physically present before you. It is *that* person — the one you face — who is Jewish or non-Jewish, and that is what determines whether the interpersonal obligation of *te'inah* applies. If the driver before you is Jewish (because he owns the donkey), you reload; if he is a non-Jew (because the non-Jew owns the donkey), you are not obligated to reload.

This explains the Baraita's logic when working with the assumption that *tzaar ba'alei chayim* is *de'oraita*: *prika* (unloading) one would always perform, since the animal's suffering is the concern; *te'inah* (reloading) follows the identity of the person present before you. But it is worth pausing to note what the Baraita would have looked like under the contrary assumption — that *tzaar ba'alei chayim* is *not de'oraita*. In that case, *prika* itself would be about protecting *property* — the animal as a possession — and the question would simply be: whose donkey is it? A Jew's donkey, you unload; a non-Jew's, you do not. The distinction between the owner of the animal and the owner of the wares would then be self-explanatory, with no need to recast the Baraita as discussing *te'inah* at all.

### Proof 4: Verse Citations

The Gemara now presses the point further: *v'ha v'chadalta m'azov lo, azov ta'azov b'prika hu d'chtiv* — the trouble is, the verses being cited by the Baraita are the verses about *prika* (unloading), not *te'inah* (reloading). One cannot read this Baraita as discussing reloading when its proof-texts are explicitly about unloading. The Gemara is backed into a corner.

### Rabbi Yosei HaGelili

Faced with a Baraita whose plain meaning cannot be reconciled with the position that *tzaar ba'alei chayim* is *de'oraita*, the Gemara invokes a familiar move: *ella ha mani Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili hi, d'amar tzaar ba'alei chayim lav de'oraita* — this Baraita follows Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili, who holds that *tzaar ba'alei chayim* is not a Torah principle at all.

Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili maintains that if an owner has overloaded his animal, you have no obligation to unload it. This position is coherent: if the operative concern were the animal's suffering, the owner's negligence would be irrelevant — the animal suffers whether or not it was overloaded. But for Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili, whose framework is not about the animal's pain but about assisting the owner in his distress, an owner who has acted irresponsibly forfeits his claim on your assistance. A Baraita that limits the obligation based on whose animal it is, and disregards the suffering of the animal as an independent factor, is therefore consistent with Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili and need not reflect the majority view.

The Gemara then brings a fourth proof: *ohev lifrok ve'sonei liton* — if one encounters two situations simultaneously, the animal of a person one likes being crushed under its load (*prika*), and the animal of a person one dislikes needing to be loaded up (*te'inah*), which takes precedence? The ruling is: *mitzvah b'sonei kedei lachof et yitzro* — the *mitzvah* favors tending first to the enemy's animal in order to subdue one's evil inclination and overcome the enmity.

The Gemara asks: if *tzaar ba'alei chayim* is *de'oraita*, should not the suffering animal — the one requiring *prika* — take precedence, regardless of interpersonal dynamics? The Gemara responds: *afilu hachi kedei lachof et yitzro adif* — even so, overcoming one's evil inclination is itself a Torah value, rooted in *ahavat Yisrael* and *lo tisna et achikha bilvavekha*. Multiple *de'oraita* principles can coexist and compete, and subduing one's *yetzer* may, in this particular configuration, outweigh the animal-suffering concern without disproving it.

A fifth proof is then brought: *sonei she'amru sonei Yisrael velo sonei oved kochavim* — when the verse speaks of an enemy's animal, it means an Israelite enemy, not a non-Jewish one. If the concern were the animal's suffering, the nationality of the owner would again be irrelevant. The Gemara replies: *mi savrat sonei dekra ka'amar* — this is not speaking of the *pasuk*'s case of *chamor soneicha* at all. It refers to the Mishnah's discussion of the interpersonal case we just discussed. And that ruling — favoring the enemy's animal to subdue one's *yetzer* — applies only between Jews, since it is rooted in obligations of mutual Jewish solidarity. No proof against *tzaar ba'alei chayim de'oraita* can be extracted from it.

### Proof 5: Unloading Limits

The Gemara brings yet another proof from a Baraita: *rovetz velo ravtzan* — the animal must be crouching under its load, but not one that habitually crouches; *rovetz velo omed tachat masa'o* — it must be actively crouching, not merely straining while still standing; and *tachat masa'o, masui sheyachol la'amod bo* — only under a burden it is capable of bearing. If the animal was given an excessive load, one is not obligated.

The Gemara's challenge is immediate: *ve'ei amrat tzaar ba'alei chayim de'oraita mah li rovetz mah li ravtzan u'mah li omed* — if the concern is the animal's suffering, why should any of these distinctions matter? A habitually crouching animal still suffers. An animal straining while standing still suffers. An overloaded animal suffers even more. Under a *tzaar ba'alei chayim de'oraita* framework, none of these limitations should exist.

The Gemara again attributes this Baraita to Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili: *ha manni Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili hi de'amar tzaar ba'alei chayim derabbanan* — this entire Baraita reflects his position. The Gemara adds that this attribution is internally confirmed: *dekatani tachat masa'o masui sheyachol la'amod bo* — the clause about "an appropriate burden" is the signature of Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili, for he is the one who holds that the owner's negligence removes your obligation. *Man shamat leh d'it leh hai sevara Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili* — who is it that holds this position? Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili. So the entire Baraita must follow him.

### Charging for Reload

The Gemara raises a complication: the same Baraita also contains the phrase *velo mefurak* — "and not if it is already unloaded" — suggesting no obligation to reload. But surely there *is* a *mitzvah* to reload, as written explicitly: *hakeim takim imo*. The Gemara therefore clarifies that *lo mefurak bechinam ela besachar* — "not unloaded for free, but rather for pay." The obligation to reload exists, but unlike unloading, it may be performed for compensation.

This ruling about charging for reloading reflects the position of the *Rabbanan* in the Mishnah, not Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili specifically. The Gemara resolves the apparent inconsistency: *le'olam Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili hu, u've'ha savar lah ke'Rabbanan* — the Baraita overall follows Rabbi Yosei ha-Gelili, but on this particular point about reloading for pay, he agrees with the *Rabbanan*. These are independent debates, and holding one position does not dictate the other. Even without *tzaar ba'alei chayim* as the operative principle, one can still recognize a meaningful distinction between *prika* — where the urgency of a collapsing animal creates a stronger imperative — and *te'inah*, where the owner simply needs assistance getting his load back on, and for which payment may reasonably be expected.

The evidence across all these proofs weighed, if anything, somewhat in the direction of *tzaar ba'alei chayim* not being the operative principle in *prika u'te'inah* — or at least not the only operative principle. The Gemara elsewhere concludes more definitively that *tzaar ba'alei chayim* is indeed *de'oraita*, but here the debate concludes without explicit resolution.

---

## Distance & Payment

### Distance: One Ris

A new Baraita is introduced that defines the scope of the obligation. The verse *ki tir'eh* — "when you see" — might have implied that the obligation to help a fallen animal applies even at great distance; conversely, *ki tifga* — "when you encounter" — might have suggested only direct physical proximity. The Gemara resolves the tension: one is obligated when one *sees* the animal close enough that it constitutes an *encounter*. The Sages measured this as one out of seven and a half in a *mil* — that is, 2/15ths of a *mil*, which works out to approximately 266 *ammot*, roughly the length of a football field, about 100 yards. This distance is called a *ris*.

### Accompaniment: One Parsah

After unloading and reloading the animal, the obligation does not end there. A Tanna taught: *u'medado imo ad parsah* — one must accompany the owner for a *parsah* (four *mil*, approximately 12,000 feet) after reloading, to ensure the animal does not collapse again under its burden. This is a substantial demand — at the Gemara's standard walking pace of approximately 18 minutes per *mil*, this accompaniment would take around 72 minutes.

### Charge for Parsah

Because of the significant burden of this extended accompaniment, Rabbah bar bar Chanah rules: *u'notel sachar* — for traveling that full *parsah*, one may charge. This is consistent with the broader principle we saw earlier that particularly demanding assistance may be performed for compensation.

---

## Precedence: Self/Father/…

### Your Object First

The Gemara now moves to a celebrated Mishnah addressing *aveida* — the recovery of lost objects — and the question of competing obligations. The general ethical principle in Jewish law is that obligation intensifies with proximity: obligations to those closest to you take precedence. Accordingly: *aveida shelo va'avedat aviv, shelo kodemet* — your own lost object comes before your father's. Even a child is not required to sacrifice his own property for his father's benefit when both are at stake simultaneously.

### Father Over Teacher

By the same logic: *aveida shelo va'avedat rabo, shelo kodemet* — your own lost object also comes before your *rebbi*'s. But now the hierarchy shifts: *avedat aviv va'avedat rabo, shel rabo kodemet* — between your father's lost object and your *rebbi*'s, your *rebbi* takes precedence. The Mishnah provides the rationale: *she'aviv hevi'o la'olam ha-zeh, ve'rabo she'limdo chochma mevi'o le'chayei ha'olam ha'ba* — your father brought you into this world, but your *rebbi* who taught you *chochma* brings you into life in the *olam ha'ba*. One's religious and intellectual formation, the Mishnah holds, constitutes a form of relationship even deeper than biological paternity.

This ruling may seem to serve the interests of the very Sages who authored it, and one might raise that objection. But the underlying logic is not self-serving: it reflects a sincerely held conviction that Torah learning and the religious life it cultivates constitute the deepest and most enduring good one person can confer upon another. The Mishnah is not devaluing the father; it is elevating the significance of Torah to the highest possible station.

### Father Is Sage

There is, however, an important qualification: *ve'im aviv chacham, shel aviv kodemet* — if the father is himself a *chacham*, his lost object takes precedence over the *rebbi*'s. The Mishnah does not require that the father have taught as much as the *rebbi*, or that he specifically be responsible for the son's Torah education. Once the father is in the *parsha* — once he himself represents Torah learning and scholarship — he reasserts his priority. The precise threshold of what it means for a father to be a *chacham* in this context is left somewhat ambiguous in the Mishnah.

### Burdens & Captivity

The same hierarchy applies across analogous cases. *Haya aviv ve'rabo nosim masoy* — if both one's father and one's *rebbi* are carrying burdens and need to be relieved, one relieves the *rebbi* first and then the father. *Haya aviv ve'rabo be'veit ha'shevi* — if both are in captivity, one ransoms the *rebbi* first and then the father.
