Given the Torah's powerful emphasis on *kabeid et avicha ve'et imecha* and the deep bonds of family, the Mishnah's insistence that the *rebbi* consistently precedes the father is striking. Only when the father is a *chacham* does the calculus reverse — and again even then without requiring the father's Torah contribution to equal the *rebbi*'s.

### Verse Source

The Gemara asks: *mena hanei mili* — what is the Scriptural basis for the principle that one's own needs come first? Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav derives it from the verse *efes ki lo yihiyeh becha evyon* — "however there shall be no poor person *in you*." The emphasis on "in you" is read as *shelcha kodem le'shel kol adam* — your own welfare takes precedence over that of everyone else. This is the principle of *chayecha ve'chayei achikha* — your life before your fellow's.

However, Rav Yehuda adds an important caution in the name of Rav: *kol ha'mekayem be'atzmo kach sof ba liyedei kach* — one who always insists on this principle, always ensuring his own needs are met before extending himself for others, will ultimately end up impoverished. The right one has to prioritize oneself is real, but constant self-focus is self-defeating. One must, when possible, transcend this prerogative.

### Who Is a Rabbi?

The Mishnah gave priority to the *rebbi* without defining who qualifies. A Baraita addresses this directly. Rabbi Meir holds: *rabo she'limdo chochma, ve'lo rabo she'limdo mikra u'mishna* — only the teacher who taught you *chochma* counts, meaning deep analytical learning — *gemara* in the broad sense — not mere memorization of *mikra* or *Mishnah*. Rabbi Yehuda holds: *kol she'rov chochmato heimenu* — whoever provided the majority of one's Torah knowledge, regardless of its form. This is more subjective and less elitist than Rabbi Meir's position: if someone has only ever learned *mikra*, the teacher who gave him most of that *mikra* is his *rebbi*; similarly for *Mishnah*. But it also means only one teacher can occupy this role. Rabbi Yosei holds the broadest view: *afilu lo heir einav ela be'mishna achat, zu hi rabo* — even if he illuminated your eyes in only a single *mishnah*, that person is your *rebbi*.

Rava offers a personal illustration of Rabbi Yosei's position: Rav Schora explained to him the meaning of *zuhama listron* in tractate Keilim — a type of ladle used to skim froth from a pot. That single clarification, Rava implies, would suffice to confer the status of *rebbi*. Similarly, Shmuel performed *keriah* (the mourning rending of garments) for a certain rabbinic student — not a major scholar — who had explained to him a particular detail about how the *Kohanim* would open the doors of the *Heichal*, one reaching in to armpit-depth to draw one door open and then pushing the second directly. A single illuminating explanation was enough for Shmuel to regard that person as one of his teachers and respond to his death with the mourning rite appropriate for a *rebbi*.

### Honor vs Precedence

Ulla sharpens an important distinction. He observes that *talmidei chachamim* in Bavel would stand for one another and perform *keriah* for one another — treating each other, in terms of honor, as *rebbeim*. This is the standard of *kavod* owed to Torah scholars as a class.

But *le'inyan aveida bi'mkom aviv*, when it comes to the question of whose lost object takes priority over a father's — that is a different and more demanding standard. For that purpose, only one's *rabo muvhak*, one's primary and singular teacher, suffices. The honors of standing and *keriah* may be extended broadly; but the displacement of parental priority belongs exclusively to the *rabo muvhak*. This sounds like the approach of Rabbi Yehuda.

### Rav Chisda's Question

Rav Chisda posed a question to Rav Huna: *talmid ve'tzarich lo rabo mai* — what is the status of a student whose *rebbi* himself relies on him, perhaps to recall certain memorized material? Would that reciprocal dependence alter the nature of the relationship?

Rav Huna heard the question as a personal affront — as if Rav Chisda were implying that Rav Huna needed *him*, Rav Chisda. He replied pointedly: *Chisda Chisda, la tzerichna lach, at tzerichat li* — "Chisda, Chisda, I don't need you; you need me." From that exchange, the two remained estranged from one another for forty years, *arba'in shanin ikpad ahadadei*, and did not visit one another. Rav Chisda was offended that his purely theoretical question was taken as a personal implication; Rav Huna perhaps felt guilty for having suspected him, yet remained unable to overcome the wound. Rav Chisda sat forty fasts (*arba'in ta'anita*) for having caused Rav Huna distress — even without intent. Rav Huna, in turn, sat forty fasts for having wrongly suspected Rav Chisda of bad faith. The pathos of the episode is not lost: guilt, it seems, did not translate into reconciliation.

### Ruling on Rabbi

The Gemara reports two competing rulings. Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *halacha ke'Rabbi Yehuda* — we follow Rabbi Yehuda, meaning the *rabo muvhak*, the primary teacher from whom one received most of one's Torah. Rav Acha bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav Sheshet: *halacha ke'Rabbi Yosi* — we follow Rabbi Yosei, meaning even one who illuminated a single *mishnah*.

The Gemara then challenges the ruling attributed to Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Yochanan's own general principle is that the *halacha* follows the *stam mishna* — the anonymously stated ruling in the Mishnah — and the Mishnah states *rabo she'limdo chochma*, which sounds more like Rabbi Meir than Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara resolves the tension: *mai chochma rov chochmato* — the word *chochma* in the Mishnah should be read as "the majority of one's learning," not exclusively analytical *gemara*-style study. Read this way, the Mishnah's anonymous ruling aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's position, and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is consistent with his general principle.

---

## Torah Study Hierarchy

### Study Classification

Having discussed what constitutes a *rebbi* — with the debate centering heavily on the distinction between *mikra*, *Mishnah*, and *gemara* — the Gemara now addresses these categories directly. A Baraita lays out an explicit hierarchy: *ha'oskin be'mikra, mida ve'einah mida* — those who engage with *mikra* (Scripture) possess a quality, but it is not of the highest order. *Be'Mishnah, mida ve'notlin aleha sachar* — those who study *Mishnah* have an authentic virtue for which they receive reward, since *Mishnah* leads toward practical *halacha* and the deeper learning of *gemara*. *Gemara ein lach mida gedolah mizu* — but those who study *gemara*, there is no greater level than this.

### Contradiction

The same Baraita then states: *le'olam havei ratz le'Mishnah yoter min ha'gemara* — yet one should always run to study *Mishnah* more than *gemara*. The Gemara immediately notes the internal contradiction: *amarta be'gemara ein lach mida gedolah mizu, ve'hadar amarta le'olam havei ratz le'Mishnah yoter min ha'gemara* — first we are told nothing surpasses *gemara*, and then we are told to prioritize *Mishnah* over *gemara*.

### Rabbi's Reform

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction historically: *bimei Rebbe, nishneit mishnah zu* — this Baraita was composed in the time of Rebbe (Rabbi Yehuda ha-Nasi), during his great editorial project of organizing and codifying the Mishnah. What Rebbe did was gather the tannaitic traditions, adjudicate between contradictory versions, determine which rulings were primary and which secondary, and produce the structured, authoritative *Mishnah* we possess. In doing so, he transformed rote memorization of traditions into genuine understanding.

His conclusion was that *gemara* — analytical engagement — was of supreme importance: *gemara ein lach mida gedolah mizu*. But the unintended consequence was dramatic: *shavku kulei alma matnitin ve'azlu batar gemara* — everyone abandoned *Mishnah* entirely and rushed off to do *gemara*. The problem is that analysis without command of the material is impossible. *Svara* cannot operate in a vacuum; one cannot analyze facts one does not know. Seeing this, Rebbe reversed course and proclaimed: *le'olam havei ratz le'Mishnah yoter min ha'gemara* — go back to *Mishnah*, prioritize acquiring the body of knowledge, because without it the analytical work collapses. The two rulings in the Baraita represent these two different moments in Rebbe's pedagogical campaign, each responding to the distortions of the other.

The underlying logic of *gemara*'s supremacy seems to be its connection to practical *halacha*. Learning *pesukim* alone does not yield legal rulings; *gemara* — the process of working through the law — does. *Gemara* is intellectually demanding and practically consequential. This explains why it ranks above *mikra* in the hierarchy. Of course, the study of *gemara* encompasses tractates like *Kodashim* and *Taharot* that have no immediate practical application, so intellectual intensity and rigor are also part of the calculus. The *Rashbam*, in his introduction to his commentary on the Torah, pushes back: because *Chazal* characterized *mikra* study as *mida ve'einah mida*, Jews became ignorant of *Tanakh*, which is the very foundation of our tradition — and in the medieval period, that ignorance was weaponized against them by those who sought to contest Jewish interpretation. A proper Jewish education, this view holds, requires the full range.

### Gemara: Errors = Sins

The Gemara supplies the *derasha* underlying *gemara*'s supreme status. Rabbi Yehuda bar Ila'i expounded: *hagged le'ammi pish'am u'leveit Yaakov chattatam* — "tell my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sin." *Leammi* — "my people," the favored ones — refers to *talmidei chachamim*, for *pesha* denotes intentional sin. *Elu talmidei chachamim she'shegagot na'asot lahem ke'zedonot* — for Torah scholars, errors are treated as intentional transgressions, because their responsibility is to know the law and rule correctly. Negligence in study that leads to incorrect *psak* is not excused as an innocent mistake; the scholar is held to a higher standard. This is why rigorous *gemara* study is not merely preferable but essential — the consequences of error are of a different category entirely for those who bear the mantle of authority.

This interpretation is corroborated by a Mishnah: *Rabbi Yehuda omer, havei zahir be'talmud, she'shiggas talmud ola le'zadon* — be exceedingly careful in your learning, for an error arising from study rises to the level of intentional sin.

### Learner Categories

Rabbi Yehuda bar Ila'i further expounds another verse: *shim'u devar Hashem ha'charedim el devaro* — "hear the word of God, you who tremble at His word." These tremblers, he says, are the *talmidei chachamim*, who are acutely conscious that their errors carry weighty consequences. Then comes a social portrait embedded in the verse's continuation: *amru achichem* — "your brothers" — refers to *ba'alei mikra*, those who study Scripture. They are your brothers, committed to Torah in their way, but not in the same category as *talmidei chachamim*. *Soneichem* — "those who hate you" — refers to *ba'alei Mishnah*. This startling identification reflects a well-known Talmudic tension: those who know only *Mishnah* believe they possess sufficient knowledge to rule on *halacha*, yet they frequently err, and the Gemara elsewhere calls such people *mavlei olam* — those who destroy the world. The closer a group is to the *talmidei chachamim* in status, the sharper the perceived threat from their partial and potentially misleading knowledge. *Menadeichem* — "those who cast you out" or treat you as *niddui* — are the *ammei ha'aretz*, the unlearned, between whom and *Chazal* there was considerable historical tension as well.

### All Israel Rejoices

Despite these tensions and internal fractures, the Gemara closes on a note of reconciliation. Lest one conclude that the hope of the various groups — *ba'alei mikra*, *ba'alei Mishnah*, *ammei ha'aretz* — is forfeit because of these enmities, the verse continues: *ve'nira be'simchatchem* — you will yet see in their rejoicing. All Israel, despite its divisions, shares in the ultimate joy. And lest one fear that Israel itself will be shamed by these internal conflicts, the verse reassures: *ve'hem yevoshu* — it is the nations, *ovdei kochavim*, who will be put to shame, *ve'Yisrael yismechu* — while Israel rejoices. This closing note perhaps echoes the tension we saw earlier in the daf between the obligations owed to Jews and non-Jews in the context of *prika u'te'inah* — a thread that quietly surfaces here in the final resolution.

*Hadran alach Elu Metzios.* With this, the second chapter of the tractate concludes.

---

## Shomrim: Paid Loss

### Four Watchmen

The Gemara now opens the third chapter of Bava Metzia, turning from lost objects to the laws of *shomrim* — guardians entrusted with another's property. There are four types of *shomrim*: the *shomer chinam* (unpaid watchman), the *shomer sachar* (paid watchman), the *socher* (renter), and the *sho'el* (borrower). Each bears a different level of liability. The chapter opens with the case of the *shomer chinam*.

### Voluntary Payment

The Mishnah addresses a specific scenario: *ha'mapkid etzel chaveiro behema o keilim* — one deposits with a friend an animal or vessels. The friend watches without pay. The objects are stolen or lost. A *shomer chinam* who was not negligent may take an oath asserting this and be fully exempt from payment — *shomer chinam nishba ve'yotzei*. But in the Mishnah's case, the *shomer chinam* does not wish to swear. Perhaps he harbors a general aversion to oaths, a sensibility deeply embedded in Jewish ethical practice over centuries; perhaps he simply feels a residual sense of moral responsibility, however technically unwarranted. Whatever his reason, he chooses to pay rather than swear.

### Thief Found: Kefel

Having voluntarily paid, what happens if the thief is subsequently found? *Nimtza ha'ganav meshalem tashlumei kefel* — the thief pays the double penalty. *Tavach u'machar, meshalem tashlumei arba'ah va'chamisha* — if the theft involved a sheep or ox that was slaughtered or sold, the thief pays four or five times the value. The question is: to whom does this payment go? *L'mi she'ha'pikadon etzlo* — to the one in whose possession the deposited object resided, meaning the *shomer*, not the original owner. The *shomer*, having elected to pay when he was legally exempt, acquires standing to receive any future penalty extracted from the thief.

The incentive structure here is worth noting. The owner's primary interest is in recovering his object, not in receiving the oath of his *shomer*. Granting the *shomer* the benefit of *kefel* or four-and-five creates an inducement for *shomrim* to pay up rather than exempt themselves through a *shevua* — which means the owner is more likely to receive actual restitution if the thief is found, and the *shomer* has something to gain from taking on the liability.

### Swears Not Pays

The Mishnah then presents the contrasting case: the *shomer chinam* takes the oath and does not pay — the standard outcome. If the thief is subsequently found, *meshalem tashlumei kefel, tavach u'machar meshalem tashlumei arba'ah va'chamisha, l'mi meshalem, l'va'al ha'bayit* — the thief's doubled or multiplied payment goes to the owner of the object. This is the ordinary case: the *shomer* who exercised his legal right to swear and exit his liability retains no stake in the object and therefore acquires no claim to whatever the thief eventually pays.

### Animals & Vessels

The Gemara asks a pointed question: *lama li lemitna behema, ve'lama li lemitna keilim* — why does the Mishnah need to specify both *behema* (animal) and *keilim* (vessels)? Both appear in the relevant *pesukim*, but is the Mishnah merely echoing the verses, or does each term add something substantive?

The Gemara answers: both are necessary. Had the Mishnah mentioned only *behema*, one might have thought the *shomer*'s entitlement to *kefel* applies specifically to animals — because watching an animal involves considerable effort (*nafish tircha le'iyula ule'afoka*, taking it out to graze, bringing it in, tending to it), so the bonus of *kefel* is a fitting reward for that labor. Mere vessels, which require almost no effort to watch, might not have generated the same *takanah*. Conversely, had the Mishnah mentioned only *keilim*, one might have thought the *kefel* principle applies specifically there — because *keilim* are typically of modest value, so the *kefel* is not a large sum and the Sages were comfortable granting it. But animals carry the potential of *arba'ah va'chamisha* — four and five times the value — a far more substantial payout, and one might have thought the Sages hesitated to extend the *shomer*'s entitlement that far. Each term is therefore necessary to preclude a different erroneous inference: *tzricha*.

The *Rashbam* adds a structural observation: the Torah itself mentions *keilim* in the context of *shomer chinam* and *behema* in the context of *shomer sachar*, and this is not accidental. *Keilim* are typically watched without pay, since the effort is minimal. *Behema* demands significant effort and so typically generates paid guardianship. The Mishnah's pairing of both reflects the Torah's own awareness of this natural distinction.

### Rami's Challenge

The Gemara closes the daf with a sharp challenge from Rami bar Chama. The entire mechanism by which the *shomer* acquires the *kefel* has been described using the language of *makne* — the owner "conveys" to the *shomer* his right to the *kefel*. But Rami bar Chama objects: *v'ha ein adam makne davar shelo ba la'olam* — one cannot transfer ownership of something that does not yet exist. At the moment the *shomer* agrees to pay, the *kefel* does not exist. There is no thief yet identified, no conviction, no double payment to speak of. How can the owner convey a non-existent entitlement?

Even Rabbi Meir — who is attributed with the position that a person *can* transfer ownership of something not yet in existence — limits this leniency to cases like pre-selling the fruit of a tree that has not yet borne fruit. There, the future fruit is naturally anticipated; it is virtually present, as it were. *Aval hacha* — but here, at the top of 34a — *mi yeimar de'mignava* — who says the item will even be stolen? *Mi yeimar de'mishtakach ganav* — if stolen, who says the thief will be found? *Mi yeimar de'mishalem* — if found, who says he will pay? *Dilma modei u'miftar* — perhaps he will simply confess and thereby be exempted from the doubled payment. The *kefel* is not merely unborn — it is entirely speculative, dependent on a cascade of contingencies none of which is guaranteed. Under these circumstances, how can any form of *kinyan* — transfer of ownership — be operative?

Rava's resolution to Rami bar Chama's challenge awaits us at the beginning of 34a.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 34

## Perek 3: Shomrim Overview

### Perek 3 Structure

We begin the third *perek* at the top of 34a. Just as the first two *perakim* of the *masechet* were devoted to issues of *metzia* — finding lost objects — and yet the first *perek* rather than laying out basic parameters went immediately to special cases, so too this *perek*, rather than laying out the basic parameters of the situations under which *shomrim* are liable, compelled to take a *shevua*, or obligated to pay, begins immediately with special cases. The focus of the *perek* is the complex interplay between a *shomer*'s liability, the oath he might otherwise take, and the consequences when a thief is later apprehended.

### Mishnah: Payment vs. Oath

The *mishnah* that anchors our discussion speaks about a *shomer chinam* — an unpaid watchman — whose object was stolen (*nignav*) and who is entitled to take an oath that he was not negligent and thereby be exempt from liability. Instead of taking that oath, however, he agrees to pay the owner. The *mishnah* then teaches that when the *ganav* is subsequently found, the *ganav* pays the *kefel* — the double payment — or, in the case of an animal that was slaughtered, four or five times the value, to the *shomer* rather than to the owner.

### Two Payment Scenarios

As we will see in the *gemara*, there are two distinct scenarios under which the *shomer* might agree to pay. In the first, he admits that he was negligent, and therefore says: "I will not swear falsely — I was negligent, and paying is my legal obligation." In the second, he maintains that he was not negligent but chooses to make the owner whole anyway: "Even though I am legally exempt, I would rather pay than take oaths — it was in my care and I feel responsible." In both scenarios, the *ganav* is ultimately found, and the question turns on who receives the *kefel*.

---

## Keifel to Shomer Logic

### Keifel Beneficiary

The foundational question is striking: the object belonged to the owner, not to the *shomer*. The *shomer* is liable for the loss, but why should the *ganav* pay the *kefel* — or four and five — to the *shomer*? The most logical framing is that this represents a kind of rabbinic *takana*, undertaken for the benefit of all parties. The owner's primary concern is recovering the value of his object. By incentivizing *shomrim* to simply pay the owner and spare everyone the effort of litigation — rather than standing on their right to take a *shevua* — the system greases the wheels of recovery. If you are willing to pay the owner immediately and make things simple, you might actually receive a benefit from it: in a case of *gneiva*, you could ultimately receive the *kefel*, or even four or five.

### Takanah Purpose

Admittedly, it is not entirely clear how powerful a motive this is, given that it only applies in cases of *gneiva*. But the logic functions on two levels: it benefits the owner, who prefers a bird in hand over four or five in the bush, and it benefits the *beit din* by unclogging the courts — people do not have to drag cases into litigation when the *shomer* simply pays upfront. That framing would render this arrangement a straightforward *takana*.

However, the *stam* of the *gemara* at the beginning of the discussion we covered previously attempts to frame this not as a *takana* but rather as rooted in the psychology of the original owner — the owner himself implicitly wants to transfer the *kefel* to the *shomer* so that he can be paid his principal immediately. By situating the mechanism in the owner's own intent, the *gemara* creates a problem: how can one transfer *kefel* when it does not yet exist at the time of the transfer? If this were purely rabbinic, we might have more latitude. But if it is conceived as an implicit transaction between the two parties, what is the legal mechanism for transferring something that has not yet come into existence?

---

## Rava: Conditional Owners…

### Rava's Mechanism

*Rava* answers this question. Three lines from the top of 34a: *amar Rava* — *na'aseh ke'omer lo*, it is as though the owner is saying to the *shomer*, reflecting either what the owner truly intends or what the rabbis will impute to him in order to make this arrangement work: *lich'shetiganav vetirtzeh veteshalmeni* — if and when it gets stolen and you agree and you pay me — *harei parati knuya lach me'achshav* — this cow that I am giving you to watch is hereby yours as of this moment, contingent on that future event occurring. The condition is implicit: if the object is stolen and the *shomer* agrees to pay for it, then retroactively from the moment the object was entrusted, it will have been the *shomer*'s. This is what the owner truly thinks, or alternatively, this is what we as the rabbis assert the owner must be understood to be thinking, in order to make the mechanism work.

### Rabbi Zeira's Challenge

*Rabbi Zeira* challenges this: *ei hachi* — if that is truly the case, if the *shomer* retroactively owns the animal from the moment it was entrusted to him, then he should also be entitled to any shearings or offspring that accrued during that period. Consider a case where a sheep with wool is given to the *shomer*, or a pregnant cow. The *shomer* shears the sheep or the cow gives birth while in his care, and then the animal is stolen. The wool and the calves remain in the *shomer*'s possession — the *shomer* returns them to the owner along with compensation for the stolen animal. But if a *ganav* is later found, and we now say retroactively the *shomer* owned the animal from the time it was entrusted to him, does the *shomer* not also retroactively own those *gizos* and *velados* — the shearings and the offspring? Why then does a *braita* explicitly state *chutz migizeha vevaladeha* — that those are excluded?

### Zeira's Carve-Out

*Rabbi Zeira* therefore refines *Rava*'s formulation: *na'aseh ke'omer lo* — it is as though the owner says to the *shomer* — *chutz migizeha vevaladeha*. We must insert this exclusion into the implicit condition. The owner is understood to be saying: retroactively you will own it from the moment I gave it to you, except for any shearings or offspring — those remain mine. The ownership is carved out just enough to allow the *shomer* to receive *kefel*, and nothing more.

### External vs. Internal Be…

The *gemara* then asks: *u'mah paska* — what justifies splitting it in that particular way, that retroactive ownership applies for *kefel* purposes but not for *gizos* and *velados*? The answer is *stama d'milsa* — as a general rule: *shivcha d'asi me'alma avid inish d'aknoiyi* — people are willing to transfer an external benefit that comes from outside the animal itself, such as *kefel*, which is an unpredictable windfall that has nothing to do with the animal's intrinsic worth. *Shivcha d'migufah* — benefit that comes from the body of the animal itself — *lo avid inish d'aknoiyi* — people are not willing to transfer. Therefore, the *kefel*, which is not part of the animal itself and may never even materialize, is something the owner is presumed willing to cede to the *shomer*. The *gizos* and *velados*, which are products of the animal itself, are not. The implicit condition is thus carefully scoped to enable *kefel* and nothing else.

---

## Samuch Ligenivas Answer

### Moment-Before Ownership

There is an alternative answer — *ika d'amri amar Rava* — others report that *Rava* gave a different formulation. Here too the owner is understood to say *na'aseh ke'omer lo*, but the moment of ownership transfer is different: *samuch lignevasah knuya lach* — you will own it a moment before it gets stolen. This operates somewhat like a *matnas shechiv mera* — a gift that takes effect a moment before the giver's death. The owner transfers ownership to the *shomer* a moment before the theft occurs. At that instant the *shomer* owns it, the *ganav* then steals it from the *shomer*, and therefore the *shomer* is entitled to *kefel*.

### Avoids Zeira Challenge

The first practical difference between this approach and *Rava*'s first answer is that this formulation entirely sidesteps *Rabbi Zeira*'s challenge about *gizos* and *velados*. Since ownership transfers only the moment before the theft — not retroactively from the time the object was entrusted — all shearings and offspring that accrued during the period of the *shomer*'s watch naturally belong to the owner. No special carve-out is needed.

### Agam Problem

However, this alternative answer has its own difficulty. *Ei nami d'kaima b'agam* — what if the animal is stolen while grazing in a swamp, not from the *shomer*'s property? In that case, even if we want to transfer ownership to the *shomer* at the moment before the theft, there is no mechanism by which he can take possession of it at that instant. He is not holding it, it is not on his property — there is no *ma'aseh kinyan* occurring at that second. He can retroactively own it from the moment it was handed to him two weeks earlier, because then it was in his hand and on his property. But he cannot acquire it the moment before it is stolen somewhere else. The problem with this *samuch ligenivas* answer, elegant as it is, is that it does not cover cases where the object was stolen from a location outside the *shomer*'s possession. Note that *agam* here simply refers to a location where the animal is not on the *shomer*'s property — it does not mean the animal is permanently inaccessible or lost to all. It means only that there is no *kinyan* possible at that moment.

### Tosafos's Tosafos

*Rashi* and *Tosafos* engage this difficulty. The question that arises — and which *Tosafos* explicitly raises — is: why not combine both approaches? Say *na'aseh ke'omer lo* that you will own it *me'achshav* — as of this moment — and the ownership terminates a moment before it is stolen. By adding *me'achshav*, the *kinyan* is grounded in the present moment when the animal is indeed in the *shomer*'s possession, and the ownership simply continues until immediately before the theft. This would obviate the need for any new act of acquisition at the moment before the theft, because the ownership begins now.

*Tosafos* raises this question explicitly — *teima, leneima na'aseh ke'omer lo lich'she'tignav vetishalmeni harei parasi knuyah lach me'achshav samuch lignevasah* — situating the transfer at two points: retroactively as of now, ending a moment before the theft. *Tosafos*'s answer is that even in that formulation, because ownership begins as of now, the *shomer* would be entitled to the *gizos* and *velados* that accrued during the interim, which reintroduces *Rabbi Zeira*'s challenge. So while the question is well posed, that combined approach does not in fact resolve all the difficulties.

---

## Shillem vs. Promise

### Mishnah's Language

With the mechanism of ownership transfer established — however that mechanism is understood — the *gemara* turns to the conditions under which the *shomer* becomes entitled to *kefel*. The *mishnah* says *shilem ve-lo ratzah lishava* — he paid and did not want to take an oath. The language is *shilem* — he actually paid.

### Rabbi Yochanan's Rule

*Amar Rabbi Chiya bar Abba amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *lo shilem shilem mamash* — when the *mishnah* says "paid," it does not mean literal payment. *Ela keivan she'amar hareni meshalem af al pi she'lo shilem* — once he says "I am going to pay," even though he has not yet paid, that suffices. This is a remarkable statement. The *shomer* need not actually transfer money; his verbal commitment is enough to entitle him to *kefel* when the *ganav* is found.

---

## Shillem vs. Promise (II)

### Mishnah Symmetry Problem

Can this be derived from the *mishnah* itself? The *gemara* attempts to reason from the *mishnah*'s structure. The *reisha* says: *shilem ve-lo ratzah lishava* — he paid and didn't want to take an oath, implying: *shilem in, lo shilem lo* — only if he paid, not otherwise. But look at the *seifa*: *nishba ve-lo ratzah lishalem* — he took an oath and didn't want to pay. The *seifa*'s language is *lo ratzah* — he didn't want to pay. If the *seifa* were simply negating the *reisha*, it would say *nishba ve-lo shilem*, he swore and didn't pay. Instead, it says he didn't want to — implying that if he did want to (*ha ratzah*), even if he hadn't yet paid (*af al pi she'lo shilem*), he would get *kefel*. That would support *Rabbi Yochanan*.

### Ambiguity in Coverage

Nevertheless, the *gemara* concludes: *ela mei'ha leika lemishma mina* — from this *mishnah* no inference can be drawn, because the *mishnah* deals with two extremes and does not cover the excluded middle. The *reisha* and *seifa* are indeed symmetrical and elegant, but symmetry does not mean exhaustive coverage. One case states he paid and didn't swear; the other states he swore and didn't pay. The case where he neither swore nor paid but expressed willingness to pay — that is precisely the ambiguous middle ground that the *gemara* must analyze separately.

---

## Socher's Promise

### Socher Braita

The *gemara* brings a *braita* to support *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position. *HaSocher para mechaveiro venigneva* — one who rented a cow and it was stolen. *Ve'amar halah harei ani meshalem ve'eini nishba* — and he says "I will pay and I will not take an oath." Note: he only says he will pay, he does not actually pay. *Ve'achar kach nimtza haganav* — and subsequently the *ganav* is found — *meshalem tashlumei kefel lasocher* — the *ganav* pays the *kefel* to the renter. The *braita* thus explicitly validates the position that agreeing to pay — without yet having paid — is sufficient.

### Socher's Legal Status

There is an additional layer of significance here. Unlike the *shomer chinam* who agreed to pay beyond his legal obligation, the *socher* — the renter — is actually legally obligated to pay in a case of *gneiva*. His only alternative to paying would have been to swear falsely — to claim, for instance, that the loss was an *onus*, an unavoidable accident, when in truth he knows it was stolen. He cannot honestly swear his way out of liability. So in the case of the *socher*, the wonderful thing he is doing is not paying beyond his legal obligation — he is simply doing what he is required to do and not lying under oath. One might think that for such a person no special incentive should be needed and certainly no *kefel* should be transferred. Yet the *braita* teaches that even for the *socher*, agreeing to pay — without yet having paid — entitles him to *kefel*.

### Socher as Proof

This *braita* thus proves two distinct *chiddushim* simultaneously: first, that actually paying is not required — a verbal agreement suffices; second, that even when the *shomer* is merely fulfilling his legal obligation rather than going beyond it, the *kefel* is still transferred to him. Both points emerge from the *socher* case, which serves as a proof for *Rabbi Yochanan*'s principle.

---

## Changed Mind Cases

### Late Agreement

The *gemara* proceeds to analyze a series of cases involving changed intentions and the timing of the *shomer*'s commitment. *Pishita amar eini meshalem vehazar ve'amar hareni meshalem* — a case where the *shomer* initially says he will not pay and will take an oath, and only later agrees to pay. One might have thought that *kefel* should be available only to one who makes everything simple from the beginning, not to someone who has been resisting for weeks and finally agrees after prolonged negotiation. The *gemara* considers this obvious: once he agrees to pay, regardless of the delay or earlier resistance, he is entitled to *kefel* if the *ganav* is subsequently found.

### Retraction Case

The more interesting case is the reverse: *amar hareni meshalem vehazar ve'amar eini meshalem* — he first agreed to pay, and then retracted and said he will not pay. The *gemara* asks: *mai?* What are we to make of this?

### Retraction Analysis

The *gemara* frames the question as a *safek*: *mi amrinan mehadar kahadar beih* — perhaps he has genuinely retracted and is no longer committed, in which case he should lose his entitlement to *kefel*; *o dilma bemilteih ka'ei, vedichuyei hu dekamidchei leih* — or perhaps he is still bound by his original statement and is merely pushing the owner off, saying he will not pay not because he actually intends to retract but because he does not have the funds on hand and is deflecting. This is a familiar dynamic — a debtor who owes money and, rather than admit he cannot pay at the moment, says he no longer intends to pay.

Interestingly, the *gemara* does not seem particularly concerned with the hardship this puts on the owner. Earlier, when the *shomer* first said he would not pay and later agreed, the *gemara* considered that case obvious — once he agrees, he gets *kefel*. Similarly here, if he is ultimately going to pay, it seems he retains his entitlement. The only genuine question is whether he has truly retracted. And if he has truly retracted, the *gemara* appears to imply that he may be entitled to do so — which makes *Rabbi Yochanan*'s rule an even more striking *chiddush*: a verbal agreement that can apparently be revoked still suffices to confer entitlement to *kefel*.

*Tosafos*, however, goes against the plain reading of the *gemara* here. In the *Tosafos* beginning *ve'chazar*, in the passage commencing with the word *gamar*, *Tosafos* argues: *vehacha dekamar mehadar kahadar bei lo sheyuchal lachzor* — it is not that he genuinely has the right to retract; *ela rotzeh hu lachzor af al pi sheino yachol* — he wants to retract even though he cannot. The question then is: if he is legally bound by his commitment, why does he lose *kefel* by attempting to retract? *Tosafos* answers that even though he is bound and cannot actually undo the obligation, his attempt to retract — which will require the owner to drag him to *beis din* to enforce the original commitment — costs him the *kefel*, because *lo makni lei kefela mishum d'ati levei dina* — the owner will not transfer *kefel* to someone who is making him work this hard to get his money back.

### Shomer Dies

The *gemara* continues: *amar hareni meshalem umet* — the *shomer* committed to paying and then died. *Ve'amru banav ein anu meshallmim* — and the children say they will not pay. *Mai?* Is this a genuine retraction on behalf of the children, or are they simply the continuation of their father's commitment and merely delaying? The *gemara* leaves this unresolved.

### Children Pay

A different scenario: the *shomer* died without having said anything, and the children simply paid on their own. *Shillmu banim, mai?* Here the *gemara* raises a new dimension: *matzei amri lehu ki akni kefela lavucha david li naichas ruach* — perhaps the owner can say to the children: I was willing to transfer *kefel* to your father because he did me a favor by watching the object; *ledichu* — but you never did any favor for me. This is not merely a rational business consideration about incentives. The *gemara* here introduces an interpersonal element — a sense of gratitude toward the original *shomer* — as a possible factor in whether the owner is understood to transfer *kefel*. Since we are situating the mechanism in the *da'as* of the owner rather than treating this purely as a *takana*, this kind of sentiment becomes legally relevant.

### Owner Dies

*Shillmu livanim* — what if the owner dies and the *shomer* pays the owner's heirs? From a purely business perspective, one would think the *shomer* deserves *kefel* all the more: the heirs may be unfamiliar with their father's affairs, and having the *shomer* step forward and pay immediately makes their lives considerably easier. Yet the same question arises in reverse: *ki akni kefela lavucha, aval anan ledidon lo yahavinan kefela* — perhaps the heirs of the owner will say: our father would have been willing to give you *kefel* because you did him a personal favor, but you never did anything for us. *O dilma lo shna* — or perhaps it makes no difference?

### Both Parties Dead

*Shamu banim livanim, mai?* Finally: both the original owner and the original *shomer* have died, and the heirs of the *shomer* paid the heirs of the owner. In this scenario, no party presently alive did any favor for any other party presently alive. The question is whether the entitlement to *kefel* is now purely a business matter — a straightforward incentive that runs with the obligation — or whether the absence of any personal relationship between the parties means it lapses entirely.

---

## Partial Payment Cases

### Half Payment

*Shileim mechtzah, mai?* The *gemara* turns to cases of partial or split payment. Since *Rabbi Yochanan* has established that agreeing to pay is sufficient, the scenario here — as *Rashi* explains — must be one where the *shomer* originally declared: *hareni meshalem mechtzah ve'lo yoter* — I will pay half and no more. Because *amar* is generally sufficient, the case of paying half must refer to one who agreed to pay only half, not the full obligation.

### Two Cows

*Sha'al shtei parot ve'shileim achat meihen, mai?* One borrowed two cows, and paid in full for one while remaining uncommitted about the other. Do we treat these as two independent transactions, such that the full payment for the first cow entitles the *shomer* to *kefel* for that one? Or do we view it as a single transaction that has not been fully resolved?

### Partner Payment

*Shamu shutafin ve'shileim le'echad meihen, mai?* One borrowed from partners and paid one partner's full share. The partner was made whole, but the total object has not been fully paid for. Does the *shomer* receive at least half the *kefel*?

### Co-Borrower Pay

*Shutafin she'sha'alu ve'shileim echad meihen, mai?* Two partners borrowed together, and one of the borrowers paid his proportional share of the obligation. His personal liability has been fully discharged. Should he receive *kefel* for his portion?

### Husband-Wife

*Sha'alu min ha'ishah ve'shileim le'ba'alah, mai? O ishah she'sha'alah ve'shileim ba'alah, mai?* The *gemara* presents two scenarios involving a woman and her husband: one borrowed from a woman and paid her husband, and alternatively, a woman borrowed and her husband paid on her behalf. *Rashi* and *Tosafos* debate the precise configuration of these cases — in particular, whether the object involved was *nikhsei melog*, where the principal belongs to the wife and the husband is entitled to the produce — such that the question of who is truly the "owner" for purposes of *kefel* becomes genuinely complex.

### All Teiku

On every single one of these cases — partial payment, two cows, partners, co-borrowers, husband and wife in both configurations — the *gemara* concludes with *teiku*: these questions remain unresolved.

---

## Cases Receiving Keifel

### Pashati Case

*Amar Rav Papa*: *shomer chinam keivan de'amar pashati makne lei kefela* — a *shomer chinam* who says *pashati*, I was negligent, immediately transfers entitlement to *kefel* to himself, even without explicitly saying "I will pay." By admitting negligence, he has effectively declared his legal obligation to pay, and that admission itself functions as the commitment. He could have claimed the object was stolen and been exempt; instead he was honest. That honesty, even though it amounts only to acknowledging what he is obligated to do, suffices.

### Honesty Incentive

Similarly, a *shomer sachar* — a paid watchman — who admits *nigneva*, that it was stolen, acquires entitlement to *kefel*. The *shomer sachar* is liable for theft and loss; his admission of the truth is being rewarded to incentivize honesty over false oath-taking. For if he had wanted to extricate himself, *de'i ba'ei patar nafsheih bishvura u-metah* — he could have fabricated a claim that the animal fell off a cliff and died — an *onus* that would have exempted him. Because he had a way out and chose not to take it, the system rewards him with the possibility of *kefel*.

### Bifnim Question

The *gemara* raises the question of whether these cases are *bifnim* — within the scope of the *shomer*'s possession — or external to it. This question of where the loss occurred relative to the *shomer*'s *reshus* has implications for the mechanism of ownership transfer discussed earlier, but the *gemara* has not yet fully resolved it at this juncture.

### Shoal Exception

The exception to all of this is the *shoel* — the borrower. *Shoel she'amar hareni meshalem lo makne lei kefela* — a borrower who says he will pay does not receive *kefel*. Why? *Be-mai havah lei lemiptar nafsheih?* What option did the *shoel* have for exempting himself? Only *mita machmat melachah* — death of the animal in the normal course of its use. The *shoel* is liable in virtually every case: lightning, disease, attack by predators — all fall on the *shoel*. The sole exception is when the animal dies as a natural consequence of the specific use for which it was borrowed, because the owner implicitly accepted that risk when lending it for that purpose.

### Rare False Claim

The *gemara*'s reasoning for excluding the *shoel* is that *mita machmat melachah* is simply not common enough to generate a meaningful incentive problem. The likelihood that someone will fabricate such a claim when it is false is small. We do not need to create an incentive to prevent the *shoel* from making that lie, because people are unlikely to resort to it. The other *shomrim* and the *socher* have more plausible false claims available to them, and the system therefore needs to incentivize their honesty. The *shoel* does not.

---

## Shoal Gets Keifel?

### Rav Papa Second View

*Ika d'amri amar Rav Papa*: a second formulation attributed to *Rav Papa* holds that even a *shoel* gets *kefel* when he agrees to pay. The reasoning is that even a *shoel* could have made some other claim to extricate himself, and we want to encourage everyone to simply step up and pay as quickly as possible without considering their potential alternative arguments. Under this view, the incentive structure should apply universally.

### Abaye's Distinction

*Amar leh Rav Zvid hachi amar Abaye*: *Rav Zvid* reports *Abaye*'s position. *Shoel ad sheyeshalem* — the *shoel* will indeed receive *kefel*, but only when he actually pays, not merely when he agrees to. The *shoel* must go all the way and pay in full before he becomes entitled to *kefel*.

### Gratitude Factor

*Abaye* frames the reason not in terms of the *shoel*'s limited escape options, but in terms of the owner's disposition: *ho'il ve'chol hana'ah shelo* — since all the benefit of the original transaction ran to the *shoel*, the owner feels no particular gratitude toward him. The dynamic here is a meaningful departure from the purely rational incentive model. The owner agreed to the *shomer chinam* watching his object and feels grateful that the *shomer* bore the burden of safeguarding it, then steps up to pay. That gratitude inclines the owner to transfer *kefel*. By contrast, the *shoel* is the one who received all the benefit: the owner did him a favor by lending the object at no charge. In such a transaction, the owner has no reason to feel warmly predisposed toward the *shoel*, and that absence of gratitude means the owner is not inclined to transfer *kefel* merely on the basis of a promise. Only actual payment — which makes the owner's position immediately whole — is enough to overcome that reluctance.

### Tosafos Nafka Mina

*Tosafos* identifies the practical *nafka mina* between *Rav Papa*'s first formulation (the *shoel* has too few alternatives to warrant incentivizing) and *Abaye*'s formulation (the owner lacks gratitude toward the *shoel*). Suppose the *shoel* made a special stipulation at the outset, negotiating with the owner to limit his liability — for instance, saying he will only be liable for negligence and not for *gneiva* and *aveida*. In such a case, the *shoel* does have meaningful alternative claims available: he can say he was not negligent and thereby avoid paying. Under *Rav Papa*'s first reasoning, this *shoel* with limited liability should therefore receive *kefel* even for a mere promise to pay, because he faces the same incentive problem as other *shomrim*. Under *Abaye*'s reasoning, however, the owner was even more generous to this *shoel* — he not only lent the object but also agreed to reduce the *shoel*'s liability — making the owner even less predisposed to transfer *kefel* on the basis of a promise alone.

---

## Shoal Payment Braita

### Hikdim V'Shillem

A *braita* supports *Rav Zvid*'s report of *Abaye*'s position: *hashoel parah mechaveiro venigneva vehikdim hashoel veshillem ve'achar kach nimtza haganav meshalem tashlumei kefel lashoel* — one who borrowed a cow and it was stolen, and the *shoel* stepped forward and paid, and the *ganav* was subsequently found — the *ganav* pays *kefel* to the *shoel*. The *braita* explicitly says *hikdim veshillem* — he stepped forward and actually paid — before the *shoel* is entitled to *kefel*.

### Socher-Shoal Contrast

This stands in precise contrast to the earlier *braita* about the *socher*, which says *ve'amar* — and he said he would pay. The *socher* need only say; the *shoel* must step forward and pay. The juxtaposition seems deliberate and meaningful: the two *braitot* are applying different standards to the *socher* and the *shoel* respectively.

### Source Analysis

*Rav Papa* resists this conclusion. He argues: *mi alima mimisnisin* — is this *braita* any stronger than our *mishnah*? The *mishnah* says *shilem* — he paid — and yet we established, following *Rabbi Yochanan*, that *shilem* means agreeing to pay. Similarly, *hikdim veshillem* in the *braita* could mean he stepped forward and agreed to pay, not that he literally paid. The *gemara* objects: *hasam lo katani hikdim* — there, in the *mishnah*, it does not say *hikdim*, he stepped forward. Here the *braita* specifically says *hikdim veshillem* — the emphatic language of stepping forward and paying suggests actual payment, not merely a commitment.

*Rav Papa* replies: *mai hikdim hikdim ve'amar* — even *hikdim veshillem* means no more than he stepped forward and declared his intention. The *gemara* then presses: if the *socher braita* says *amar* — he said — and the *shoel braita* says *hikdim veshillem* — he stepped forward and paid — and these two phrases are different, the contrast is legally significant. It appears we have two different standards. But perhaps the two *braitot* come from entirely different collections and were never intended to speak to each other; the language of *hikdim* in the *shoel braita* might be incidental, not contrastive.

### Tanaim Consultation

To resolve this, the *gemara* reports that a query was brought to the *tannaim* — the scholars who preserved the oral tradition of *braitot* — of the schools of *Rabbi Chiyya* and *Rabbi Oshaya*, who organized and systematized the *braitot*, particularly the *Tosefta*. The question put to them was whether these two *braitot* — the one about the *socher* and the one about the *shoel* — were taught side by side as part of the same collection. *Ve'amri gabi hadadi tanya* — and they confirmed: yes, these were taught together. The *braita* reads: *ha-socher she'amar* gets *kefel*; *ha-shoel hikdim veshillem* gets *kefel*. The contrast is explicit and intentional. The *shoel* must actually pay. This is a remarkable moment of textual research within the *gemara* itself — the Amoraim went to the repositories of *braita* tradition to establish the literary context of a ruling, recognizing that *braitot* learned atomistically, as individual units, could be misunderstood without their surrounding context.

---

## Rav Huna's Oath

### Oath Despite Payment

*Amar Rav Huna*: even when a *shomer* agrees to pay — or actually pays — and one would assume this relieves him of any further obligation to take a *shevua*, *Rav Huna* rules: *mashbinan lei shvu'ah she'einah birshuto* — we administer to him an oath that the object is not in his possession. The *shomer* may have believed that by agreeing to pay he was completely dispensing with any oath requirement. *Rav Huna* holds that the *beit din* must still be involved, and the *shomer* must still swear.

### Fraud Concern

The reason is *chashinan shema einav natan bah* — we are concerned that perhaps the *shomer* has set his eyes on the object. He is not being the great *tzaddik* one might imagine. Perhaps he genuinely wants the object for himself, and is fabricating the claim that it was lost or stolen, while agreeing to pay as a strategy to acquire it without taking a false oath about its whereabouts. By paying, he thinks he is getting out cleanly — he avoids swearing falsely about the loss, pays the owner's value, and keeps the object. *Rav Huna* says: this concern is live enough that even a *shomer* who agrees to pay must still swear that he is not in fact holding the object.

### Court Involvement

The implication is that despite all the incentive structure built around getting *shomrim* to pay quickly and spare everyone the litigation, *Rav Huna* insists that court involvement and an oath remain necessary to verify that the claimed loss actually occurred. The entire edifice of *kefel* and the encouragement of prompt payment does not displace the need for basic verification. This ruling thus qualifies the picture considerably: the *shomer* who pays may receive *kefel*, but he does not entirely escape the oversight of *beit din* or the responsibility to swear. We will take up the implications of *Rav Huna*'s position in the continuation.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 35

## Shomer's Oath

### Rav Huna Rule

The daf begins approximately twenty lines down on 34b, at the words *amar Rav Huna*. The context is the *mishna*'s ruling that a *shomer* who agrees to pay — and in doing so obtains the right to collect *kefal* if the thief is later found — has been incentivized to move things along and ensure the owner receives his principal. The *gemara* has been exploring the various dimensions of that arrangement. Now Rav Huna introduces a further requirement: even when the *shomer* agrees to pay, we still administer an oath. As the *gemara* states, *amar Rav Huna mashvinan lei shvua she'eino birshuso* — we make him swear that the object is not in his possession.

### Shomer's Covetousness

The reason is immediate: *chashinan shema einav nasan bah* — we are concerned that he has set his eye upon the object, that he covets it. It is entirely possible, in other words, that the *shomer* is agreeing to pay precisely because he wants to keep the object for himself. By paying, he silences the owner's claim while quietly retaining the deposit. Rav Huna therefore rules that no *shomer* — not even one who volunteers to pay — is ever fully exempt from swearing that the *pikadon* is genuinely not in his *reshus*. This principle will be tested and challenged at length in the sections that follow.

---

## Mashkon Cases

### Mashkon Setup

The *gemara* now pivots to a *braisa* that will serve as a challenge to Rav Huna's position. The case involves a *malveh* — a lender — who holds a *mashkon*, a piece of collateral, against a loan he has extended to a *loveh*. The *mashkon* is then lost. Since the *malveh* functions as a *shomer* over the collateral, its loss falls upon him, and its value is to be deducted from the outstanding loan. The question that arises is: how much of the loan remains after that deduction? And on that question, lender and borrower disagree.

### Four Scenarios

The *braisa* sets out four scenarios, turning on the relative values of the loan and the *mashkon*. In the first sub-case of the opening section: I, the *malveh*, lent a hundred and claim the *mashkon* was worth fifty — so the *loveh* still owes me fifty. The *loveh* says it was worth a hundred, so he owes me nothing. He is *kofer hakol* — denying the entire claim — and is therefore *patur*, exempt from an oath. In the second sub-case: I say it was worth fifty so he owes me fifty; he says it was worth seventy-five so he only owes me twenty-five. That is *modeh b'miktzas* — a partial admission — and he is *chayav*, obligated to take an oath.

The *braisa* then turns to cases where the *mashkon* exceeded the loan. The *loveh* claims the collateral was worth two hundred against a loan of one hundred, so I owe him one hundred. I the *malveh* say it was worth only one hundred — we are even, I owe him nothing. I am *kofer hakol* and exempt. In the parallel case: the *loveh* says it was worth two hundred, I owe him one hundred; I say it was worth one hundred and twenty-five, so I owe him only twenty-five. That is again *modeh b'miktzas* and I am obligated.

The *chiddush* of the *braisa* is its ruling on *who* takes the oath in the *modeh b'miktzas* situations. Ordinarily, it is the party who is making a partial admission — the *loveh* in the first pair, the *malveh* in the second — who swears. The *braisa*, however, rules: *mi shehapikadon etzlo* — the one in whose possession the *pikadon* rested, that is, always the *malveh*, is the one who takes the oath.

### Malveh Swears

Why should the *malveh* always be the one to swear, even in cases where the *loveh* is the *modeh b'miktzas*? The *braisa*'s reasoning: *shema yishba zeh v'yotzi halah et hapikadon* — perhaps the *loveh* will take his oath regarding the value, and then the *malveh* will produce the *mashkon*, rendering that oath either false or moot. If the *loveh* swears that the *mashkon* was worth seventy-five and the *malveh* subsequently produces it and it turns out to be worth only fifty, the *loveh* has now taken a *shvuas sheker*.

Tosfos clarifies that the concern is not primarily for the *loveh*'s personal dishonor — if he swore falsely, one might say he deserves the consequences. The real problem is that it makes the *beis din* look as though it imposed an unnecessary oath: the court compelled the *loveh* to swear about the value of an object the *malveh* had concealed all along. The court process itself is discredited. Therefore, in all such cases, the *malveh* — the party holding the *pikadon* — takes the oath regarding value, because he will not produce the object and prove himself a liar.

### Challenge Rav Huna

The *gemara* now turns to challenge Rav Huna directly. The challenge runs as follows: according to Rav Huna, in every case where the *malveh* claims the *mashkon* was lost, he must swear *she'eino birshuso* — that it is not in his possession — before any further dispute about value proceeds. If that is so, then in all four of the *braisa*'s scenarios, the *malveh* has already sworn he does not have the *mashkon*. Why, then, is there any concern that he will later produce it? Having taken that oath, he cannot produce it without convicting himself of perjury. The entire rationale for taking the oath away from the *loveh* and placing it on the *malveh* collapses. The *braisa*'s distinctive ruling — *mi shehapikadon etzlo* — presupposes that the production of the *mashkon* remains a live threat. But Rav Huna has apparently neutralized that threat.

The *gemara* considers and rejects two intermediate answers. Rava first suggests: perhaps the case is one where witnesses testify the *mashkon* was burned — the *malveh* therefore never had to take Rav Huna's oath in the first place, yet we still worry he might produce something. But the *gemara* pushes back: *meheika meisi lei* — from where would he produce burned goods? Rav Yosef then suggests: witnesses testified it was stolen, so again Rav Huna's oath was not required. But the same objection applies: if witnesses saw it stolen, how will the *malveh* produce it? The *gemara* answers: *de-tirach u-maisi lei* — he could expend effort, investigate who stole it, track down the thief, and retrieve the object. The counterargument is then raised: if so, why isn't the same concern applicable once the *malveh* himself takes the oath? The answer is asymmetric knowledge — *bishlama malveh yodeia man ka'ayil v'nafik b'veitei* — the *malveh* knows who has been in and out of his home and can therefore pursue the recovery of the stolen object. The *loveh*, by contrast, has no such knowledge about the *malveh*'s household and cannot similarly investigate.

One might add — and it is a point the *gemara* itself does not make explicitly — that the *malveh* has a strong financial incentive to find the *mashkon*: having already credited its value against the loan, he would be recovering a real economic loss if he retrieves it.

### Rava's Answer

A cleaner resolution is offered by Rava: *zeh nishba v'zeh nishba* — both parties swear. The *braisa* is not saying that the oath moves entirely from the *loveh* to the *malveh*. Rather, it is describing the sequence: the *malveh* first swears *she'eino b'reshuso*, consistent with Rav Huna's requirement, and only then does the *loveh* proceed to take the classic *shvuas modeh b'miktzas* regarding the value. *Mah nishba techila* — who swears first? — *malveh nishba techila*, the *malveh* swears first that it is not in his possession. Once that has been established and the concern of production has been neutralized, the *loveh* makes his own oath. This is admittedly not the plain reading of the *braisa*, but it preserves Rav Huna's position.

### Defense Rav Huna

Rav Huna bar Tachalifa, citing Rava, then identifies a sharper challenge to Rav Huna from the opening sub-case of the second pair in the *braisa* — the *reisha d'seifa*. There, the *loveh* says the *mashkon* was worth two hundred, the *malveh* says it was worth only one hundred, so the *malveh* is *kofer hakol* and *patur*. According to Rav Huna, however, the *malveh* must always swear *eino birshuso*. Once he is making that oath, the *beis din* may apply *gilgul shvua* — the principle that an existing oath can be extended to cover related matters — and require him to swear as well about the value. That would make him *chayav* on the question of value, not *patur*. Yet the *braisa* simply says *patur*. This is a genuine *tiyufta* — a refutation — of Rav Huna.

### Rav Ashi Explains

Rav Ashi reports that he presented this entire discussion before Rav Kahana, who answered: *tehei b'ma'amino* — the case in the *braisa* is one where the *loveh* declared that he trusts the *malveh*. The *loveh* waived his right to compel the *malveh* to swear *eino birshuso*; he simply believed him and released him from that obligation. Since the *malveh* never takes the initial oath, there is no *gilgul shvua* to attach the value-question onto, and he remains *patur*. This is openly acknowledged as a forced reading — *ukimta* — but it is the available defense of Rav Huna's position.

### Trust Asymmetry

The *gemara* immediately presses the inconsistency: if the *loveh* trusts the *malveh* enough to waive the oath about possession — thereby sacrificing the advantage of *gilgul shvua* — why doesn't the *malveh* reciprocate and trust the *loveh*'s assessment of the *mashkon*'s value? After all, it was the *loveh*'s object; he knows better than the *malveh* what it was worth. Why does the *malveh* refuse to accept the *loveh*'s claim of two hundred? The *gemara* answers: *kim lei b'gavei* — the *loveh* trusts the *malveh* because the *malveh* is the one who actually held and handled the *mashkon* and knows what he received. But regarding value, the *loveh* believes his own knowledge of his object exceeds the *malveh*'s; he is not willing to accept the *malveh*'s lower valuation. The *malveh*, for his part, does not return the trust.

### Wealth Theology

The *gemara* explains the asymmetry with a striking theological aside. The *loveh* applies to the *malveh* the verse *tumat yesharim tanchem* — the integrity of the upright guides them — reasoning that since the *malveh* is prosperous and able to lend money, he must be a righteous man whose word is reliable. The *malveh*, in turn, applies to the *loveh* the verse *ve-selef bogdim yeshaded* — the perverseness of the treacherous destroys them — reasoning that since the *loveh* is in the position of having to borrow, he is presumably less reliable.

This is a genuinely striking *gemara*. The underlying theology — that wealth is evidence of divine favor and therefore of moral trustworthiness, while poverty signals the reverse — is, as one might note, in significant tension with much of the Torah's own treatment of the poor, which accepts economic variation as a social reality and enjoins compassion toward the impoverished. Even the biblical framework of *sechar v'onesh* speaks in aggregate and communal terms rather than translating individual prosperity directly into individual righteousness. That said, there are certainly biblical precedents — Yitzchak's hundredfold return, Avimelech's recognition that God has blessed him — where prosperity is read as divine approbation. The *gemara* here pushes that sensibility to an uncomfortable extreme in service of explaining a legal asymmetry in who trusts whom.

---

## Lost Jewelry Case

### Seizing House

The *gemara* now shifts to a narrative case involving the doctrine of *shuma hadar*. A certain man deposited jewelry with his friend. The friend was asked to return the jewelry and said, *lo yadana heicha otveinhu* — I do not know where I put it. It was not a dramatic loss but a misplacement. The case came before Rav Nachman, who ruled: *kol lo yadana peshiuta hi* — any "I don't know where it is" constitutes negligence. He therefore ordered the *shomer* to pay — *zil shalim*. When the *shomer* failed to do so, Rav Nachman seized his house — *agbei l'apadnei minei* — in payment of the debt.

### Found Item

Subsequently, the jewelry turned up — *ishtakach kifi* — and its value had increased. Rav Nachman then ruled: *hadar kifi l'mareihu v'hadar apadna l'marei* — the jewelry goes back to its owner and the house goes back to its owner.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava reports that he was sitting before Rav Nachman at the time, and they were studying the very *perek* of *Hamafkid*. He raised a challenge from the *mishna*: when a *shomer* pays and thereby acquires the object, he is entitled to any subsequent increase in value — just as he acquires the right to *kefal* if the thief is found. Here, the house was seized as payment; the *shomer* has effectively purchased the jewelry through that payment. The jewelry subsequently increased in value. On what basis do we reverse the transaction and restore both items to their original owners? Rava notes that Rav Nachman did not respond to this challenge — *v'lo hadar li* — and, the *gemara* adds, *shapir avad*, he was right not to respond, because the challenge ultimately fails.

### No Real Debt

The reason: *mai ta'ama hatam lo atrecha l'vei dina hacha atrecha l'vei dina* — in the case of the *mishna*, the *shomer* voluntarily agreed to pay, thereby expediting the process. Here, the *shomer* refused to pay, forcing *beis din* to intervene and seize the property. One who must be compelled by the court does not enjoy the benefit that flows from voluntary payment.

But the deeper answer goes further. The *gemara* distinguishes this case from a standard debt-payment scenario. Here, the seizure of the house rested on a false premise — *shuma b'ta'us hu d'hava kifi mei'ikara* — because the jewelry was never truly lost. The *shomer* never genuinely incurred the debt. The payment was therefore void from the outset, and once the jewelry surfaces there is no obstacle to restoring both items to their rightful owners. In a normal case of seized property in payment of an actual debt, the situation is entirely different — and that distinction opens the broader discussion that follows.

---

## Shuma Hadar

### Intro Shuma

The *gemara* now introduces the doctrine of *shuma hadar* proper. In the standard case: Michael owes a thousand dollars, cannot produce cash, and the court assesses and seizes his property — say, a watch worth a thousand dollars — in payment of the debt. A month later Michael has the cash. Can he buy back the watch? This is the question of *shuma hadar*: when property is assessed and seized in payment of a debt, may the original debtor redeem it by later tendering the monetary amount?

### Nardaei vs Amemar

The scholars of Nardai rule: *shuma hadar treisar yarchei shata* — the debtor may redeem the property for twelve months. Amemar, himself from Nardai, goes further: *ana mi-Narda'ei ana v'sevira li shuma hadar le-olam* — in my opinion, the right of redemption is unlimited. This is, as noted, rather alarming from the creditor's perspective: I seize property in payment of a valid debt and now face the perpetual prospect of having it reclaimed.

### Halakha Shuma

The *halakha* follows Amemar: *ve-hilkhata shuma hadar le-olam* — assessed property can always be redeemed. The justification is explicitly non-legal: *mishum she-ne'emar ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov* — because of the verse commanding us to do what is right and what is good. Strictly speaking, the creditor is owed only money; property was seized only because cash was unavailable at the time. The right and good thing to do, once the debtor can produce the money, is to return the property and accept the payment that was always the true substance of the obligation. What is remarkable here is that an ethical principle — *ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov* — is being translated into a legally enforceable norm. The spirit of the law becomes the letter of the law. One may note that this creates real complications for creditors who cannot freely develop or rely on seized assets, though it is true that any improvements made by the creditor would presumably have to be compensated by the debtor upon redemption.

### Chain Redemption

The *gemara* spells out a significant corollary. If I seized Michael's property and then my own creditor — let us call her Atara — seized it from me in payment of my debt to her, can Michael still redeem it? The answer is yes: *lo adifat mi-gavra de-atit minei* — Atara is no better situated than I was; since I would have had to return it to Michael upon payment, so must she. The reasoning is consistent: Atara, like me, is a creditor who fundamentally sought money. If Michael can produce money, she has no moral claim to retain the land over its original owner's right of redemption.

### Exceptions Property

However, the right of redemption does not travel through all transactions. If I sold the seized property to Atara, gave it to her as a gift, or it passed to someone's heirs through inheritance, the right of redemption is extinguished. In those cases the recipient received the property *as land*, not as a surrogate for money — *ada'ata d'ara nachis v'lav ada'ata d'zuzei nachis* — the transaction was oriented toward the land itself, not toward the monetary claim underlying it. *Ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov* requires the creditor to accept money in lieu of land; it does not require someone who received land as land — as a gift, a sale, or an inheritance — to yield it for money.

It should be noted that one obvious strategy would present itself to a sophisticated creditor: seize the property, immediately sell it to a third party, and then repurchase it from that party. At that stage it would presumably be shielded from redemption. Whether that maneuver would be pierced as a sham is not addressed here.

### Husband Status

A nuanced case is addressed next. Either the property was seized from a woman who then married and died, or the woman was owed the money and seized another's property and then married and died. In either configuration, the husband's status vis-à-vis the property is at issue. The ruling is: *ba'al b'nichsei ishto lokeach havei* — the husband is considered a purchaser with respect to his wife's property, not merely an heir. Therefore, *lo mahadrinan v'lo mahadri lei* — we do not compel the return of the property to him, and he cannot compel return of property to himself.

The source for the husband's status as purchaser is the ruling attributed to Rabbi Yosi berabbi Chanina in the name of the enactment of Usha: if a wife sells her *nichsei milug* — the property whose title she holds but whose usufruct belongs to her husband — during his lifetime, and she subsequently dies, the husband can recover the property from the purchasers. This makes sense only on the theory that the husband is treated as the primary purchaser of his wife's property, so that a subsequent sale by the wife to a third party is subject to the husband's preexisting claim. If he were merely her heir, he would have no stronger claim than any other heir of a vendor, and ordinarily heirs cannot recover property their ancestor sold. The relevance for our context: the husband, being a *lokeach* rather than an heir, stands in the same position as any purchaser, and the right of redemption does not run in his favor or against him.

### Voluntary Seizure

The *gemara* raises one final variable. What if the debtor voluntarily surrendered the property — without court intervention, without a formal seizure process — saying, in effect, "I owe you a thousand dollars, here, take this land"? *Paligi Rav Acha v'Ravina* — Rav Acha and Ravina dispute the matter. One holds that even voluntary transfer allows redemption — *hadra*. The other holds it does not — *lo hadra* — because *hai zvini ma'alya hi*: since there was no coercion, what occurred was a legitimate sale. The debtor of his own free will exchanged his land for the extinguishment of his debt. There is no moral imbalance of the kind that *ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov* is designed to correct.

The view permitting redemption even in the voluntary case responds: *lo zvini ma'alya hu* — it was not truly a sale, because *machmat kisufa d'agbei* — the debtor surrendered out of embarrassment, not out of genuine willingness to sell. He preferred to hand over the property quietly rather than suffer the public indignity of a court-ordered seizure. Since the motivation was social pressure rather than a genuine commercial decision, the transaction is not treated as a true sale, and the right of redemption survives. The irony is pointed: by being cooperative and avoiding the courts, the debtor may actually forfeit a legal protection he would have enjoyed had he forced the creditor to go through official channels.

### Ownership Timing

The *gemara* closes with a further dispute about when, precisely, the creditor acquires ownership of seized property — a question with practical implications for the right to collect the fruits of the property during the interim period. Rabbah holds: *miki mati adrakhta l'yadei* — from the moment the court writ reaches the creditor's hand, he owns the property. Abaye holds: *b'chasimaso* — from the moment the document is signed by the court, even before it is physically delivered. Rava holds: *miki shlimu yemei akhrazta* — only once the full public announcement and auction period has concluded, since during that period a higher bidder might appear, redirect the cash proceeds to the creditor, and take the property. Until that possibility is foreclosed, the creditor's title is not yet perfected. After that period, however — and notwithstanding the doctrine of *shuma hadar* — ownership formally vests.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 36

## Renter & Borrower

### Setup & Oath

The *mishnah* on 35b presents a layered scenario involving a *socher* (renter), a *shoel* (borrower), and the original owner. Reuven rents a cow from Shimon and then lends it to a third party, David. The cow dies of natural causes — *umesa kedarka* — which stands in contrast to *meisah machamas melachah*, death through normal use. The latter exempts all parties, including the *shoel*, on the grounds of assumed risk: when you lend someone an object for use, there is an implicit acceptance that the object may wear out through that use. But *umesa kedarka*, ordinary natural death, is a different matter. Natural death constitutes an *ones* — an unavoidable, uncontrollable accident — yet the *shoel* remains liable even in such cases. The *shoel* bears full liability for everything that befalls the borrowed object, since he receives all the benefit while paying nothing, the sole exceptions being *meisah machamas melachah* and the rule of *ba'alav imo* (the owner working for the borrower at the time).

The *mishnah* therefore rules: the *socher* takes an oath to Shimon — *yishava hasocher shemeisah kedarkah* — attesting that the cow died naturally, and is thereby exempt from liability, since a *socher* is not liable for an *ones*. David the *shoel*, meanwhile, pays the *socher*. The result is striking: the *socher* profits from an oath about someone else's cow.

A preliminary question lurks in the background: by what right did the *socher* lend the cow out in the first place? The *gemara* will address this, and the answer will be either that there is a general presumption permitting such sublending, or — more plausibly — that the original owner explicitly granted permission, much as a lease may or may not include a subletting clause. Either way, the *gemara* assumes that the *socher* did not violate the owner's wishes by lending it out.

### Rabbi Yosei's Objection

It is Rabbi Yosei who gives voice to the moral discomfort embedded in the *mishnah*'s ruling. *Keitzad halaz oseh sechorah beparato shel chaveiro* — how does this person profit from his friend's cow? The *socher* collects payment for the death of a cow that was never truly his. Rabbi Yosei therefore rules: *ela tachzor parah labaalim rishonim* — the cow, or rather its value, must return to the original owners. David the *shoel* is indeed liable, but since he ultimately borrowed Shimon's cow (the *socher* having only temporary use rights), his payment goes directly to Shimon rather than to the *socher*.

This ruling raises a conceptual question worth pausing on. The *Rambam* conceptualizes rental as a *kinyan haguf lizman lapeiros* — a form of ownership of the object for purposes of use, for a defined period. One might grant the *socher* a quasi-ownership for the duration of the rental. And yet even under that framework, the *socher*'s stake in a thousand-dollar cow may be worth only twenty dollars — his one month of use. How, then, does David owe the *socher* the full value of the cow? The *gemara* does not raise this question explicitly, but the logic appears to be that since the *socher* had control over the cow and conveyed it to David, David assumed an obligation to the *socher* commensurate with the object received — namely, the full cow. Whether this is entirely satisfying is another matter; but that is the operative framework.

### Kinyan at Death

Rabidi bar Avin poses a sharp question to Abaye. The *socher*, he says, acquires the cow through his oath (*bishvuah*) — meaning it is the act of swearing to the *maskir* (the owner-lessor) that removes the owner from the picture and entitles the *socher* to collect from the *shoel*. If so, why can't the *maskir* simply say: *dal at u'dal shvuatakh* — set aside yourself and your oath, I will deal directly with the *shoel*? By refusing the oath, the *maskir* would remain a party to the dispute and claim directly against David.

Abaye's response is incisive: *mi savrat sokher bishvuah hu dekakani lah?* Do you really think the *socher* acquires the cow — or more precisely, acquires his position in relation to the cow — only through the oath? No: *misheat mitah hu dekani* — from the very moment of death, the *socher*'s relationship with the *maskir* is severed. The oath serves only to appease the owner — *shvuah kedei lehafis da'ato shel ba'al habayit* — because the owner does not know the facts and deserves some assurance. But as a matter of legal reality, the moment the cow died through no fault of the *socher*, the *socher* had no monetary obligation to the *maskir*, and the *maskir* had no further claim. Even if the *maskir* waives the oath, he remains out of the picture, because his claim evaporated at the moment of death.

### Liability Ends

To be precise about the language: the *gemara* uses the phrase *misheat mitah hu dekani* — "from the moment of death, he acquires it" — which is puzzling. The *socher* does not take possession of the carcass; that returns to Shimon. The language of *kinyan* here seems almost metaphorical.
