What it really means is that from the moment of natural death, any obligation the *socher* might have owed the *maskir* was extinguished. Imagine a *beit din* convened at the instant of death: they would rule immediately that the *socher* owed nothing to the *maskir*, since it was a natural death and he bears no liability for *ones*. That severance is what is meant by the *socher* "acquiring" — it is not a property acquisition, but the termination of the *maskir*'s standing as a claimant. Since the *maskir* has no claim from that moment forward, he cannot re-enter the picture and deal directly with the *shoel*. The *socher*, now the only one with a claim against the *shoel*, collects.

---

## Multiple Liabilities

### Alternating Agreements

Rabbi Zeira opens with a startling proposition: *pe'amim sheba'alim meshalmin kama paros lasocher* — there are circumstances under which the original owner winds up paying the *socher* the value of multiple cows for a single cow. The scenario he constructs involves a rapid alternation of rental and borrowing agreements between the same two parties.

The *socher* rents the cow from Shimon for one hundred days (*agrah minei me'ah yomei*). Shimon then asks to borrow it back for ninety days (*she'ilah minei tishim yomei*), to which the *socher* agrees. The *socher* then re-rents it from Shimon for eighty days (*hadar agrah minei shmonim yomei*). Shimon borrows it back again for seventy days (*vehadar she'ilah minei shivim yomei*). The net result is that the *socher* retains twenty days of rental use: ten from the first rental period (one hundred minus ninety) and ten from the second (eighty minus seventy). But crucially, there are now two distinct rental agreements and two distinct borrowing agreements in play.

Then the cow dies during one of the periods when Shimon holds it. Since Shimon borrowed the cow from the *socher* — even though it was originally his own cow — he is a *shoel* with respect to the *socher*, and as such he bears full liability when the cow dies. But since there were two separate borrowing agreements, each of which independently created its own obligation, Rabbi Zeira argues that each generates a full liability: *dechula she'ilah veshe'ilah mechayev chada parah* — every borrowing agreement obligates a full cow. And since Shimon had two such agreements, he owes the *socher* two cows. Moreover, he must provide two separate cows for the *socher* to use during the remaining twenty days of rental, rather than allowing one cow to satisfy both rental obligations.

The logic, strange as it sounds, is that one should not understand the *shoel*'s obligation as "returning the object" — if it were, one payment would obviously suffice. Rather, embedded within each borrowing transaction is an independent contractual obligation: if such-and-such occurs, I will pay you. Since there were two transactions, there are two obligations. One might compare this to taking out two insurance policies on the same object from the same insurer: the object is the same, but the contractual obligations are independent. The degree to which the *shomer*'s duty is one of object-restoration versus one of contractual liability is precisely what is at stake.

### One Cow Problem

Rav Aha mi-Diphti gives voice to the obvious objection: *chada para hi* — it is one cow! *Ayala v'apka* — he brought it in and took it out, alternating between rental and borrowing, but the object at the center of every transaction is the same animal. All the back-and-forth movement — *apka mis'chirut ve'ayala lish'eilah, apka mishe'eilah ve'ayala lisechirut* — is just reclassification of the same cow. How can one cow generate multiple full liabilities?

The argument operates on two levels. First, if one payment represents giving back the cow, then one payment is sufficient — you cannot claim to have lost multiple cows when only one cow died. Second, each subsequent agreement supplants its predecessor: once the cow was re-rented, the first borrowing agreement became moot; once re-borrowed, the rental became moot. There are no truly independent transactions; each one replaced the last.

### Two Obligations

Mar Bar Rav Ashi provides the resolution. The *gemara* asks: *u'mi ita l'para b'eina?* — is the cow physically present? If the cow were physically available, the objection that there is "one cow" would be decisive — just hand it back once. But the cow is not present; what exists is a *chiyuv*, an obligation, a liability. And liabilities can be multiple even when the underlying object is single, just as multiple insurance contracts on one object create independent claims.

Mar Bar Rav Ashi therefore distinguishes: *chada deshe'eilah* — one cow is owed by virtue of the borrowing obligation, which the *shoel* owes outright; and *chada desechirut* — one cow is owed by virtue of the rental agreement, which requires Shimon to make available to the *socher* the twenty days of rental use he is owed. The *socher* keeps the first cow permanently (as payment for the death of his "loaned" cow) and uses the second cow for his twenty rental days before returning it. The *gemara* also advances the alternative position that all the *she'eilos* are considered one and all the *sechirus* arrangements are considered one — *mishum she'eilah achat hi umishum sechirut achat hi* — yielding a single borrowing obligation and a single rental obligation rather than multiplicative liabilities.

---

## Oaths & Offerings

### Oath Types

Rabbi Yirmiyah now shifts the discussion to a different dimension of the same basic scenario — the *socher* and *shoel* each taking oaths, and what happens when those oaths are false. The organizing principle is as follows. A standard *shevuat sheker* — a false oath made without monetary gain — incurs a *chatat* (sin offering). A false oath that serves to deny a monetary obligation and thereby generate financial benefit — *kefiras mamon* — incurs an *asham* (guilt offering), which carries the additional obligation of a one-fifth surcharge. With this principle in hand, Rabbi Yirmiyah maps out four combinations.

### Both Chattat

The first case: both the *socher* and *shoel* bring a *chatat*. The cow died of natural causes (*umesa kedarka*) but both parties falsely claim it was struck by lightning — some other form of *ones*. The lie concerns the facts, not the underlying liability. For the *socher*, it makes no difference: *bein kach uvein kach patur* — whether the death was natural or from lightning, the *socher* is exempt. His false oath generates no monetary gain. For the *shoel*, whatever the specific form of the *ones*, he remains liable to pay, so his false characterization of the accident likewise changes nothing. Both have lied without profit, and both bring a *chatat*.

### Both Asham

The second case: both bring an *asham*. The cow was stolen (*nignava*), but both claim it died through normal use (*meisah machamas melachah*). This matters because *meisah machamas melachah* exempts even the *shoel* — it is the one *ones*-like circumstance in which the *shoel* is not liable. The actual situation — theft — renders both the *socher* and *shoel* liable. By falsely claiming the cow died through work, both are denying their monetary obligations: *de-tavaihu ka-kafrei mamona*. Both bring an *asham*.

### Mixed: Renter Chattat

The third case: the *socher* brings a *chatat* and the *shoel* brings an *asham*. The cow died naturally, but both claim it died through work. For the *socher*, this makes no difference — he was exempt regardless, so his lie yields no gain: *bein kach uvein kach patur patur*, and he brings a *chatat*. For the *shoel*, however, the lie is consequential: had it truly died naturally (*meisah kedarkah*), he would be liable (*chayav*); by claiming it died through work, he exempts himself. His oath denies a real monetary obligation, and so he brings an *asham*.

### Mixed: Renter Asham

The fourth case: the *socher* brings an *asham* and the *shoel* brings a *chatat*. The cow was stolen (*nignava*), but both claim it died naturally. Theft renders the *socher* liable — a *socher* is liable for theft and loss (*geneivah va'aveidah*). By claiming natural death, he exempts himself from that liability, so his oath constitutes a denial of a monetary obligation: he brings an *asham*. The *shoel*, meanwhile, is liable whether the cow was stolen or died naturally — *bein kach uvein kach havah mechayev* — so his false characterization does not change his actual obligation. He brings a *chatat*.

### Reject Rabbi Ami

One might ask what new information these four cases convey, given that the underlying principles about *chatat* and *asham* were already known. The *gemara* answers: the analysis comes *le'apukei mid'Rabbi Ami* — to exclude the position of Rabbi Ami. Rabbi Ami held that any oath imposed by a court (*shvuah shehadayanim mashbi'in otah*) never gives rise to a *chatat* for *shevuat bituy* (simple false speech). His reasoning was derived from the verse *o nefesh ki tishava levate bisfasayim* — "if a soul swears to enunciate with his lips" — the key word being that the person swears on his own initiative. A court-imposed oath, he argued, falls outside the domain of *shevuat bituy* entirely.

The cases of Rabbi Yirmiyah demonstrate otherwise: court-imposed oaths in this context can indeed generate a *chatat*, and the ruling rejects Rabbi Ami's position outright. *Ka mashma lan d'lo k'Rabbi Ami* — we do not rule like Rabbi Ami.

---

## Watchman to Watchman

### Rav vs. Yochanan

The *gemara* now turns to one of the most conceptually rich disputes in the chapter: *shomer she'masar l'shomer* — a watchman who hands over the object in his care to another watchman. Has he violated his duty to the owner? *Rav amar patur, v'Rabbi Yochanan amar chayav* — Rav holds the watchman is exempt; Rabbi Yochanan holds him liable.

### Rav's Logic

Rav's position is that handing the object to another party does not increase the watchman's liability. Whether the original *shomer* was a *shomer sachar* (paid watchman) or *shomer chinam* (unpaid watchman), giving the object to someone else to watch does not elevate or alter whatever level of liability already applied. The act of delegation, in Rav's view, is neutral with respect to the original custodial obligation.

### Yochanan's Logic

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees sharply: the very act of giving it to someone else constitutes a violation of the watchman's responsibility to the owner. And importantly, this is not merely about diminishing the quality of watchmanship — even if the replacement watcher is superior, the act is still a breach. Rabbi Yochanan's rationale is: *d'amar lei ant lo meimanat li bishvuata* — the owner can say to the original *shomer*, "I trust your oath about what happens to my object; I do not trust the oath of this other person." The owner never agreed to have anyone else hold the object, and it is precisely because he trusted the original *shomer* — and only that person — that the arrangement was made. By placing the object under someone else's care, the original *shomer* has deprived the owner of the ability to receive a credible oath from the person he trusted. That deprivation itself constitutes negligence, making the original *shomer* liable for any subsequent loss that can in any way be attributed to the transfer.

Abaye clarifies the logical structure of both positions. According to Rav: *lo mibaya shomer chinam she'masar l'shomer sachar d'iluyei alyah l'shmirato* — not only does handing off to a paid (and thus presumably more careful) guardian fail to create liability, but even *shomer sachar she'masar l'shomer chinam d'garu'ei gar'ah l'shmirato* — handing off to an unpaid, less-liable guardian also fails to create liability. Why? *Mai ta'ama d'ha masrah l'ven da'at* — because the object was given to a responsible adult (*ben da'at*). The assumption is that every responsible adult, regardless of the financial level of their custodial obligation, will exercise genuine care over someone else's property. Legal liability does not translate into degree of attentiveness; we assume that a *shomer chinam* and a *shomer sachar* alike will do their best to protect what has been entrusted to them.

According to Rabbi Yochanan: not only does lowering the guardian's liability level (*shomer sachar* to *shomer chinam*) render the original *shomer* liable — even raising it (*shomer chinam* to *shomer sachar*) renders the original *shomer* liable, because the owner never consented and can always say: I do not want my deposit in someone else's hands — *ein retzoni she'yehei pikdoni beyad acher*.

### Gardeners Case

The *gemara* notes that Rav's position was not stated explicitly but inferred from a case. *De'hanu ginai* — certain gardeners would deposit their tools each day with a certain older woman (*savta*). One day, they all entrusted their hoes to one of their number who stayed behind while the others attended a celebration. That gardener, hearing the festivities, went and deposited the tools with the same woman they habitually used, then joined the party. The tools were stolen from her. When the case came before Rav, he exempted the gardener.

Observers assumed this meant Rav ruled that *shomer she'masar l'shomer* is *patur*. But the *gemara* corrects this: *shani hatam* — that case was different. Every day the gardeners themselves deposited their tools with that woman. The claim *ein retzoni she'yehei pikdoni beyad acher* — I don't want my object in another's hands — simply could not be made here, because they had implicitly consented to this very arrangement through their daily practice. Even Rabbi Yochanan would agree the gardener is exempt in that case. The case therefore cannot serve as proof of Rav's general position regarding *shomer she'masar l'shomer*.

### Money & Children

A related case is raised: one who deposits money with a watchman, and that watchman either binds it up and throws it behind his back, or gives it to his minor children to watch, or locks it away but not properly — he is *chayav*, because *shelo shamar kederech hashomrim*, he did not watch it in the manner that watchmen are expected to watch. From the fact that the case specifies *minor* children, one can infer that had the watchman given it to his *adult* children, he would be exempt — even though they are, technically, other people. The reason is articulated by Rava: *kol hamaphkid al da'at ishto uvanav hu demaphkid* — anyone who deposits money with someone understands implicitly that that person may rely on his wife and adult children. The owner's consent to the watchman's custody encompasses the watchman's household, much as the daily practice with the older woman constituted implicit consent. The case of strangers, by contrast, is different: whether adult or minor, a stranger falls under the prohibition of *ein retzoni she'yehei pikdoni beyad acher*, and the watchman would be *chayav* regardless. The *Nehardeans* reinforce this by noting that the specification of "children" (as opposed to simply "minors") confirms that only one's own children enjoy this dispensation — others do not.

### Ruling: Liable

Rava issues the *hilcheta*: *shomer she'masar l'shomer chayav*. The original watchman is liable. And the ruling applies regardless of direction: *lo mibaya shomer sachar she'masar l'shomer chinam chayav* — not only is a paid watchman who gives to an unpaid one liable (having diminished the level of protection), but *afilu shomer chinam she'masar l'shomer sachar chayav* — even an unpaid watchman who gives to a paid one is liable, having apparently improved the protection. *Mai ta'ama?* — Rava grounds the ruling not in the language of negligence or diminished care, but in the formulation: *at meheimnat li bishvua, hai lo meheiman li bishvua* — you are trustworthy to me by oath; this other person is not trustworthy to me by oath. By handing over the object, the original *shomer* has placed the owner in the position of being unable to rely on the oath of the one person he chose to trust. That is the essential violation, and it renders the *shomer* liable for any subsequent loss attributable to the transfer.

The *nafka mina* between Rava's reasoning and the prior formulations would emerge in a case where the original *shomer* directly witnessed what happened and can personally deliver the oath to the original owner. In such a case, the concern about oath-reliability would not apply. This question, along with the closely related principle of *techilato bifshi'ah vesofo b'ones* — beginning with negligence and ending with an unavoidable accident — will be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 37

## Shomer Shemasar

### Rav vs. R. Yochanan

Today's daf is 37. We pick up on 36b, approximately ten lines from the top, at the two dots marking a transition in the sugya. The immediately preceding discussion dealt with the question of *shomer shemasar leshomer* — whether the act of transferring a watched object to another *shomer*, even one with greater or lesser liability, itself constitutes an act of *pshia*, negligence. Rav held that it does not; Rabbi Yochanan held that it does — even if a *shomer chinam* transfers to a *shomer sachar*. The first rationale offered by the Gemara is that the original owner may claim, "I never wanted anyone else handling or watching my object, regardless of the level of liability the second *shomer* carries."

### Rava's Reason

In the end, the Gemara rules — in the passage just before the two dots — that Rava holds the transferring *shomer* is *chayav*: the act is *pshia*, negligence. But Rava's reasoning differs from the earlier formulation. In Rava's view, the owner can say, "I never trusted the other person to make an oath to me." As we shall see, this alternative rationale leads to meaningfully different applications and a different scope for when such transfers generate liability.

---

## T'chilato B'pshiya

### Abaye: Swamp Case

The Gemara now introduces a related topic. The text reads: *pasha bo v'yatzah l'agam, umesah kidarkah* — a *shomer* was negligent, the animal went out into the swamp, and it died of a natural death. On the face of it, the question is whether any causal relationship, even a speculative one, exists between the initial act of negligence and the ultimate loss. How does that initial *pshia* bear on the *shomer*'s liability?

Abaye, citing Rabbah, says *chayav*: you must pay, whether you are a *shomer chinam* or a *shomer sachar*, because of that initial act of negligence in leaving the door open. Rava, also citing Rabbah, says *patur*: you are exempt. Both report in the name of the same teacher — Rabbah — and they are disputing what Rabbah actually held.

Abaye's position is stated with striking rhetorical force. He says: *lo mibaya l'man d'amar techilato bipshia vesofo b'ones chayav* — it goes without saying that one who holds that when negligence precedes an unforeseen accident the *shomer* is liable would rule *chayav* here, since this is precisely that structure. But even one who normally rules *patur* in a case of *techilato bipshia vesofo b'ones* would agree that here the *shomer* is *chayav*. Why? *De'amrinan havla d'agma katla* — we say that perhaps the atmosphere of the swamp contributed to the animal's death. The negligence and the death are not cleanly separated; arguably they are all one act of *pshia*.

This raises an important conceptual question about what *techilato bipshia vesofo b'ones* actually means. Does it mean that the very act of negligence immediately creates monetary liability — so that even if the animal later dies of cancer, which clearly has nothing to do with the *pshia*, the *shomer* is nevertheless liable? That is generally not how the principle is understood. Rather, *techilato bipshia vesofo b'ones* operates by shifting the burden of proof: because the *shomer* committed a fundamental violation of his duty of care, there is a presumption of liability for whatever subsequently occurs, as long as some argument can be made connecting the later loss to the initial negligence. Where the loss is completely unconnected — the animal dying of cancer after the door was left open — even the stringent position would concede *patur*.

### Rava: Angel of Death

Rava, equally emphatic, rules *patur*, and likewise declares that any judge who fails to judge accordingly is unworthy of the title. *Lo mibaya l'man d'amar techilato bipshia vesofo b'ones patur* — it goes without saying that one who normally exempts in such cases would exempt here. But even one who holds *chayav* in the standard *techilato bipshia* case must concede *patur* here. Why? *Malach hamaves mah li hacha mah li hasam* — the angel of death will find the animal wherever it is. The death is entirely unrelated to the animal's location; it would have died anywhere. Therefore, despite the initial *pshia*, there is no liability for this death.

### Gray Zone Analysis

The debate between Abaye and Rava can be mapped onto a conceptual spectrum. At one end: I leave the door open and the animal runs away — the loss is immediately and obviously caused by the *pshia*; everyone agrees the *shomer* is *chayav*. At the other end: I leave the door open and the animal dies of cancer — plainly unrelated; everyone agrees *patur*. The entire controversy of *techilato bipshia vesofo b'ones* concerns the gray zone between these poles: cases where the subsequent loss may or may not be connected to the initial negligence.

Abaye's position is that the swamp case falls entirely outside the gray zone, on the side of clear causal connection. The death occurred in a place the animal reached because of the *shomer*'s negligence, and we attribute the death to the conditions of that place. Rava's position is that the swamp case falls entirely outside the gray zone on the opposite side — a natural death is simply a natural death, unrelated to location, and the angel of death finds the animal regardless. Both agree that the genuinely contested cases — those where the connection to the initial *pshia* is uncertain — are what the debate about *techilato bipshia vesofo b'ones* is really about. The disagreement is over how to classify the swamp scenario.

One might observe that this dispute seems to turn on an assessment of fact rather than a disagreement about legal doctrine. The extreme language used by both Abaye and Rava — "any judge who does not rule this way is unworthy" — is typically reserved for clear legal conclusions, not factual judgments. And yet it does seem that the two Amoraim are really arguing about how to characterize the factual circumstances, not about the doctrinal parameters of the rule. It is notable that the Gemara frames the debate in such terms, and it is worth acknowledging that a great deal of what is contested in law — in the Talmud no less than in contemporary jurisprudence — comes down to precisely this kind of assessment.

To illustrate the spectrum further: suppose the animal runs away because the door was left open, and is subsequently struck by lightning. In hindsight, there is a clear causal chain — had it remained in the house, it would not have been struck. But was this outcome something that could have been anticipated from the initial act of *pshia*? Arguably not. That case may still fall in the gray zone, even though post-hoc causation is demonstrable, because the *pshia* cannot be said to have directly embedded this outcome. Rava's position is that a natural death — *mesah kedarkah* — is like the cancer case, entirely disconnected from location. It is categorically not a meteor strike or a lightning bolt; it is simply what happens to animals in the ordinary course of nature.

### Animal Returns Home

Abaye concedes a partial case to Rava's logic. *Umodeh Abaye d'hadrah l'bei marei umesah d'patur* — Abaye agrees that if the animal went to the swamp and then returned home and died there, the *shomer* is exempt. The reason: *leika l'meimar havla d'agma katlah* — one can no longer attribute the death to the atmosphere of the swamp. This is a striking formal rule. A scientist might plausibly argue that the animal inhaled swamp air that contributed to its death even after it returned home. But the Gemara does not entertain that argument. Once the animal is back home, the formal presumption shifts: we attribute the death to natural causes rather than to the conditions of the swamp. This suggests that there are somewhat formalistic parameters operating here. If the death occurs in the swamp, we attribute it to the swamp; if the death occurs at home, we do not — regardless of what a medical examination might reveal. The rule does not rest on a purely objective scientific assessment.

### Theft After Release

Rava in turn concedes a partial case. *Umodeh Rava kol heicha d'ignavah ganav b'agam umesah kedarka bei ganav d'chayav* — Rava agrees that if a thief stole the animal from the swamp and it then died a natural death in the thief's possession, the *shomer* is *chayav*. Why doesn't Rava apply his own reasoning here — that the angel of death would find the animal anywhere, so the death is unrelated to the location?

The Gemara's answer is revealing: *d'ei shavkah malach hamaves, b'vei ganav havei ka'ima* — if the angel of death had passed over the animal, it would still have been in the thief's possession. The *shomer* became liable from the moment the theft occurred. The fact of theft — which is directly connected to the initial *pshia* of leaving the animal unprotected — created the monetary obligation then and there. Even if the animal subsequently died of completely natural causes, that does not dissolve the liability that crystallized at the moment of theft. This clarifies an important conceptual point about when the *shomer*'s obligation to the owner materializes: not at the moment of negligence, and not at the moment of natural death, but at the moment of a concrete loss that is causally traceable to the *pshia*.

---

## Shomer Debate

### Abaye's Challenge

The Gemara now returns to the discussion of *shomer shemasar leshomer*. Abaye poses a challenge to Rava. Recall from the previous discussion: the Mishnah presented a case in which a *shokher* — someone who rents an animal — lends it out to a *sho'el*, and the animal dies in the *sho'el*'s possession. The *sho'el* pays the *shokher* the full value, and the *shokher* takes an oath to the *ba'al habayit* — the original owner — and retains the payment, which seemingly means the *shokher* profits from the transaction. Rabbi Yossi objected to this arrangement on moral grounds, but the Gemara also needed to address a threshold question: isn't the *shokher* lending the animal to the *sho'el* itself an act of *shomer shemasar leshomer*, making the *shokher* liable to the original owner? The answer given was that the owner had granted permission to lend it out.

Abaye now asks: according to Rava, who holds that *malach hamaves mah li hacha mah li hasam* — natural death occurs regardless of where the animal is — why was that answer necessary? Rava should have been able to answer that even if the *shokher* lent out the animal without the owner's consent, even if that constituted an act of *pshia*, the *shokher* is nonetheless not liable to the *ba'al habayit* for a natural death, because a natural death is unconnected to the *shomer*'s location. Why invoke permission at all?

### Rava's Response

Rava's answer is illuminating. *Ledidi de'amina at meheimant li bishvu'ah haich lo meheiman li bishvu'ah* — according to my reasoning, the problem with *shomer shemasar leshomer* is not that handing over the object to another person is itself an act of negligence. Rather, the problem is that the original owner never trusted the second person to take an oath. According to Rava, a *shomer* who transfers the object to a second *shomer* is liable because the owner can say, "I never authorized that person to be in the position of swearing to me."

But in the Mishnah's case — where the *shokher* transfers the animal to a *sho'el* and the *sho'el* pays and the *shokher* himself takes the oath to the *ba'al habayit* — there is no problem of a second person's oath at all. The original *shomer*, the *shokher*, is the one who swears to the *ba'al habayit*. *Leika l'okma klal* — the scenario presents no question to Rava's framework in the first place, because no issue of oath-substitution arises. The Mishnah's case, under Rava's approach, was never a *shomer shemasar leshomer* problem at all.

### Negligence vs. Oath

This exchange clarifies a critical *nafka mina* between the two explanations of *shomer shemasar leshomer*. If the reason the transferring *shomer* is liable is that the very act of handing over the object to an unauthorized party is negligence — the position rooted in "I never wanted my object in anyone else's hands" — then that negligence triggers the full *techilato bipshia* analysis, and every subsequent event must be evaluated in that framework. Under this view, the *shokher*-to-*sho'el* transfer is a case of negligence, and Rabbi Yossi's challenge requires the answer that the owner gave permission.

If, however, the reason is Rava's — that the owner's right to refuse the second person's oath is what generates liability — then the analysis is entirely different. The *shokher* is not liable under *shomer shemasar leshomer* at all in the Mishnah's scenario, because he is the one personally swearing to the *ba'al habayit*. The *ukimta* of "the owner gave permission" was never needed from Rava's perspective, because the question simply did not arise.

---

## Clifftop Negligence

### Baraita: Cliff Case

The Gemara now addresses a *baraita* that seems to challenge Abaye's position on the swamp case. *He'ela lerashei tzukin venafela ein zeh ones, vechayav* — if the *shomer* brought the animal to a clifftop and it fell off, that is not an *ones*; the *shomer* is liable. The clear implication of the *baraita* is that if the animal died naturally at the clifftop — *umesah kedarkah* — that would be an *ones* and the *shomer* would be *patur*.

The question arises for Abaye: if you are willing to say that dying in the swamp should be attributed to the conditions of the swamp, why would you not say — *leima lei avira deharka katlah*, or *uchtza deharka katlah* — that the thinner air at the clifftop, or the physical exertion of the climb, contributed to the natural death? By Abaye's own logic, the death in a different location should be attributed to that location's conditions.

### Good Grazing Defense

The Gemara's answer is that the *baraita* is dealing with a case of *she'he'ela lemira shemen vatov* — the *shomer* brought the animal to the clifftop because that was where the good grazing was. In that case there is no initial *pshia* at all. Taking animals to elevated terrain where the grazing is rich is within the acceptable norms of shepherding practice. Even though it somewhat increases the risk of the animal falling, that increased risk falls within the tolerable range of ordinary care. Without an initial *pshia*, Abaye's presumption that the location contributed to the natural death does not engage.

### Control Issue

The Gemara then asks: *ei hachi, nafela nami* — if there is no initial *pshia* in bringing the animal there, then why is the *shomer* liable when the animal falls off the cliff? If the entire basis for *techilato bipshia* analysis is removed, what grounds the liability for the fall?

The Gemara answers: *shehaya lo letokfa velo tokfa* — because the *shomer* could have grabbed the animal before it fell and failed to do so. The negligence is not in the act of bringing the animal to the clifftop but in failing to prevent the fall. The Gemara then addresses the beginning of the *baraita*, which states that if the animal climbed to the clifftop on its own and fell, that is an *ones* and the *shomer* is exempt. If the operative negligence is failure to grab it, why is the *shomer* not liable in that case too?

The Gemara distinguishes: *lo tzricha shetakfata ve'alta takfata veyerada* — the first case describes an animal that physically broke free from the *shomer*'s grip in climbing up; the same uncontrollable animal then fell off in the same manner. Since the animal escaped the *shomer*'s control on the way up, its fall is likewise an *ones*. In the second case, the *shomer* was leading and controlling the animal up the cliff, and therefore the failure to prevent the fall is attributable to him. This distinction may not be the *peshat* of the *baraita* — the plain reading suggests the issue is simply the initial negligence, not the failure to catch — but this is how the Gemara resolves the apparent difficulty.

The *baraita* thus emerges as supporting Rava: it is only when the outcome clearly results from the initial act of negligence that liability follows. Attributing a natural death merely to a different location — without further grounds — is not sufficient, and the case of dying in the swamp is, according to Rava, precisely that kind of unconnected natural event.

---

## Rabbi Yosi's Ethics

### Kefel Case

The Gemara now returns to the *mishnah*. Rabbi Yossi asks: *keitzad hala oseh sechora beparato shel chaveiro* — how can this person be doing business with his friend's cow? The case he is addressing is the scenario earlier in our *perek* where a *shomer* agrees to pay the owner for an object that was stolen, and then the thief is found, entitling the *shomer* to collect the *kefel* — the double payment imposed on thieves. Rabbi Yossi is morally offended: the *shomer* is profiting from a transaction involving someone else's property.

One could understand Rabbi Yossi as making a technical legal argument — that the *sho'el*'s liability fundamentally runs to the original owner, not to the *shokher*, since it is ultimately the owner's animal. But that does not appear to be his point. His objection sounds more like a moral and policy principle: we cannot tolerate a legal structure that allows a person to profit from another's property, regardless of the technical justifications.

### Both Cases Disputed

Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports to Rav Yehuda that Shmuel said: *chaluk haya Rabbi Yossi af berishona* — Rabbi Yossi disputed even the first *mishnah* of our *perek*. The first case is precisely the *kefel* case: the *shomer* paid the owner and then collected *kefel* from the thief. Rabbi Yossi's objection there is the same — the *shomer* is profiting from another person's property, and Rabbi Yossi regards this as impermissible. This confirms that his position is not a technical legal argument about to whom the *sho'el*'s obligation runs, but a broad moral principle: *ose sachar beparato shel chaveiro* — deriving profit from another's property — is categorically unacceptable. If that is the principle, it applies equally to the *kefel* scenario and to the *shokher*-*sho'el* scenario of our *mishnah*.

Rav Yehuda confirms: we rule like Rabbi Yossi even in the first case. Rabbi Elazar independently corroborates this ruling.

### Ownership Interest

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. In his view, Rabbi Yossi never disputed the first case: *modeh haya Rabbi Yossi berishona* — Rabbi Yossi conceded the first case. Why? *Shekvar shilem* — because the *shomer* already paid the owner. Several considerations operate in the first case that are absent from the second. First, the owner is made whole; he is not disadvantaged. Second, once the *shomer* pays the owner, he can be viewed as having acquired an ownership interest in the object. Third, and perhaps most significantly, there is a broader societal interest at stake: the rule that a *shomer* who pays the owner gets to collect *kefel* creates an incentive for *shomrim* to compensate owners promptly rather than delay, which benefits the entire system. Rabbi Yossi, in Rabbi Yochanan's view, was sensitive enough to these considerations to concede the first case, even as he objected to the second.

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba further refines Rabbi Yochanan's view: the *shomer* need not have literally paid. *Lo shillem shillem mammash* — it is not literal payment that is required. Rather, *kivan she'amar hareni meshallem af al pi she'lo shillem* — once the *shomer* committed to paying, declaring "I will pay," that suffices for Rabbi Yossi to concede the case. The Gemara acknowledges that actual payment is a stronger basis for the concession — it is easier to view the *shomer* as the new owner when he has actually paid — but in order to reconcile Rabbi Yochanan's statements, the rule is read broadly: Rabbi Yossi agrees whenever the owner is assured of receiving his money, whether payment has been made or merely committed to.

### Banking Parallels

The principle of *ose sachar beparato shel chaveiro* has implications that extend well beyond the narrow case of *kefel*. One might observe that the entire contemporary banking system operates on this logic at scale: institutions receive money in bailment, as it were, and invest it for their own profit. The depositor does not have use of the money; the bank does. The critical distinction, as the Gemara's analysis implies, is the nature of the transaction. Borrowing money — a *halva'ah* — is entirely permissible, and the borrower may invest it and profit. The prohibition against profiting from another's property targets a different structure: where the property is not transferred for the recipient's use but is entrusted for safekeeping, and the *shomer* nonetheless extracts profit from it. The legitimacy of the profit depends on whether the legal relationship is one of borrowing or one of guardianship.

---

## Unknown Recipient

### Proactive Admission

The *mishnah* continues with a series of special cases involving *shomrim* and uncertain obligations. The first: *amar lishnayim, gazalti l'echad mikem maneh v'eini yodeia eizeh mikem* — a person says to two others, "I stole one hundred dollars from one of you, and I don't know which." Alternatively: "One of your fathers entrusted me with one hundred dollars and I don't know which one." In both cases, the person is coming forward proactively. The ruling is: *noten lazeh maneh v'lazeh maneh* — he pays each one the full amount.

This is striking. Technically speaking, neither claimant has an actionable claim. *Hamotzi mechavero alav haraaya* — the burden of proof lies with the one seeking to extract money from another's possession, and neither of these two can identify himself as the definite creditor. The person coming forward has no strict legal obligation to pay either of them. Yet the *mishnah* rules that he pays both in full.

### Latzeit Yedei Shamayim

The Gemara explains that the *mishnah* itself signals its rationale: *shehoda mipi atzmo* — he admitted of his own accord. The case is not one of legal compulsion but of a person who voluntarily comes forward seeking to do the right thing. The entire framework of the ruling is *latzeit yedei shamayim* — fulfilling one's obligation before Heaven, beyond what the law strictly requires. If one wants to fully discharge the moral obligation, paying each person the full amount is the only way to ensure that the actual victim is made whole. Splitting the sum and giving each person fifty dollars would leave the actual victim uncompensated, which fails the goal of *latzeit yedei shamayim*. Accordingly, full payment to each person is what conscience demands.

### Reactive Claims

The *mishnah* then shifts to the second scenario: *shnayim shehifkidu eitzel echad, zeh maneh v'zeh matayim* — two people deposited funds with a single custodian; one deposited one hundred dollars and one deposited two hundred dollars. *Zeh omer sheli matayim v'zeh omer sheli matayim* — when it comes time for return, each claims to be the one who deposited the two hundred. This is the inverse of the previous case: it is they who are coming with claims against the custodian, not the custodian proactively admitting uncertainty.

### Escrow Principle

The ruling: *noten lazeh maneh v'lazeh maneh, v'hashar yehei munach ad sheyavo Eliyahu* — give each person the minimum amount they are certainly owed, one hundred dollars each, and the remaining hundred is held in escrow until Eliyahu HaNavi comes — meaning, until further evidence is produced. This ruling reflects the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraaya*: since the custodian is not the one creating the uncertainty, and both claimants are coming with competing demands, the disputed amount remains in the custodian's possession and neither claimant receives it.

The contrast with the previous case is instructive. In the first scenario, the custodian is coming proactively, seeking to fulfill his moral obligation, and the framework is *latzeit yedei shamayim*. In the second, the claimants are pressing him, and the framework is strictly legal: he pays what is certain and holds the rest in escrow.

---

## Two Vessels

### Vessel Solution

A parallel case involving objects rather than money: two people deposit vessels with a custodian. One vessel is worth a hundred dollars; the other is worth a thousand. Each claimant asserts that the more valuable vessel is theirs. The ruling follows the same structure: give one claimant the smaller vessel outright, and from the larger vessel's value give the second claimant the equivalent of the smaller vessel's worth, with the remaining value held in escrow.

### Breaking Vessel

Rashi, in his final comment on the *mishnah*, reads *mitoch hagadol noten d'mei katan l'sheni* in a striking way, apparently based on the subsequent Gemara: *yeshabrenu* — literally, break the larger vessel. One would take the thousand-dollar menorah, break off a portion of it, and hand that fragment to the second claimant. This is, as one might note, a rather extreme measure — reminiscent of the judgment of King Shlomo — and the Gemara will interrogate whether this is indeed the operative ruling.

### Rabbi Yosi Escrow

Here again Rabbi Yossi raises a policy objection: *mah hifsid haramai* — what does the dishonest claimant lose? Under the plain ruling, each person receives at minimum what they are certainly owed, and the disputed portion sits in escrow. The dishonest person who falsely claims the superior item suffers no real consequence: he gets his money back either way, and the disputed remainder, sitting indefinitely in escrow, may eventually be resolved by mutual agreement — perhaps by splitting it. There is no deterrent to dishonesty.

Moreover, the vessel case has a further dimension: if the genuine owner of the thousand-dollar menorah sees it about to be broken or divided, he is highly motivated to capitulate and accept a compromise simply to preserve the object's value. The dishonest claimant, knowing this, faces no risk. Rabbi Yossi therefore rules: *hakol yehei munach ad sheyavo Eliyahu* — everything goes into escrow. The custodian holds all the funds — or both vessels — until the matter is resolved. By putting even the undisputed hundred-dollar amount in escrow, Rabbi Yossi creates a real cost for dishonest claiming: the *ramai* may genuinely need his money and will find it costly to have it tied up indefinitely.

---

## Gemara Analysis

### Doubt Extraction

The Gemara now addresses the theoretical underpinnings of the *mishnah*'s rulings. The first difficulty: why does the *mishnah*'s proactive admission case require paying each person in full? Normally, *mesafeka lo mafkinan mamona* — we do not extract money from a person's possession based on doubt — and *uki mamona b'chezkat marei* — money remains presumed to belong to whoever holds it until the other side proves otherwise. So why in this case do we override that principle and compel payment to both claimants?

### Contradictions

More puzzling still, the *mishnah* seems internally contradictory. The first half — both the theft case and the bailment case involving one of your fathers — rules that the uncertain party pays each person in full. The second half — the two depositors each claiming the higher sum — rules that only the minimum certain amounts are distributed and the disputed remainder is held in escrow. But the second half is also a *pikadon* case. Why does one *pikadon* scenario require full payment to both while the other does not?

### Theft Penalty

The Gemara's first proposed answer draws a distinction between *gezel* and *pikadon*. In the first case, the person committed a transgression — theft. *Gezel d'avid issura, kansu rabanan* — because he sinned, the Rabbis imposed a fine: rather than simply holding the disputed sum, he must pay each person in full. In the *pikadon* case — entrusting without wrongdoing — *lo kansu rabanan*, the Rabbis did not impose a fine; the disputed amount stays in escrow.

But the Gemara rejects this answer. The first half of the *mishnah* includes not only a theft case but also a *pikadon* case: "one of your fathers entrusted me with money and I don't know which one." That case also results in full payment to both. So there is a *pikadon* case where full payment is required, and a *pikadon* case where it is not. The theft/bailment distinction does not resolve the contradiction.

### Rava: Negligence

Rava proposes a different framework. The operative variable is not whether a sin was committed, but whether the custodian was negligent in failing to keep track of to whom he owed the money. When his inability to identify the correct recipient is his own fault, the Rabbis impose liability: he must pay each person in full. When the uncertainty is not traceable to his negligence, the standard rules of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraaya* apply, and the disputed amount stays in escrow.

### Bundle Distinction

Applying this principle requires situating each *mishnah* case. The first case — "one of your fathers gave me money and I do not know which one" — involves a single depositor. There was one transaction, one person. The fact that the custodian cannot identify which of the claimants' fathers deposited the money reflects carelessness on his part. Rava describes this as resembling a case where two separate individuals delivered money on two separate occasions: *reisha na'aseh k'mi shehifkidu lo bishnei krichot* — the *reisha* is treated as if the money arrived in two separate bundles. When money arrives in distinct, sequential transactions, the custodian is obligated to track who gave what; his failure to do so is *pshia*, and he pays in full.

In the second case — two people who each claim the higher deposit — Rava reads the *mishnah* as describing a specific factual scenario: *na'aseh k'mi shehifkidu lo b'krach echad* — they came and deposited together, simultaneously. When both parties were present at the same time and deposited in each other's presence, the custodian's failure to distinguish who gave the larger sum is not negligence. He can reasonably say to them: *attu gufaichu lo kapditu ahadadi* — you yourselves were not suspicious of each other; you were willing to deposit in front of one another. If they trusted each other enough to deposit simultaneously and openly, why should the custodian have been more vigilant than they were?

### Same-Time Deposit

Thus the Gemara's limiting principle for the second case: the ruling of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraaya* — disputed amount in escrow — applies specifically when both depositors came simultaneously. Only then is the custodian free of negligence. This *ukimta*, establishing the factual circumstances, is what resolves the apparent internal contradiction of the *mishnah*: full payment flows from negligence, and escrow follows from its absence.

---

## Five Claimants

### One vs. Two

Having established that the proactive admission case requires paying each person in full, the Gemara raises a further contradiction. Our *mishnah* says that when I come forward and say "I stole from one of two people," I must pay each one a hundred dollars. But a *baraita* discusses someone who stole from one of five people — *gezel echad mechamesha* — and all five are actively pressing claims, each asserting "you stole from me." The ruling there: *maniach gezeila beineihem umistalek* — place the stolen amount in the middle and walk away. That is the position of Rabbi Tarfon. If five active claimants are each pressing demands, and the ruling is merely to put the money in the middle and leave, why does the two-person proactive admission case require full payment to both?

### R. Tarfon Position

Rabbi Tarfon's position, taken at face value, represents a significant application of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraaya*: even in a case of admitted theft, where it is certain that one of the five claimants is owed money, the one who did the stealing need not pay each one in full when they are the ones pressing claims against him. He satisfies his obligation by placing the amount in the middle and stepping back.

### R. Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. In his view, that approach does not suffice to extract the person from his *aveirah* — his transgression of theft is not discharged until the actual victim is fully compensated. Rabbi Akiva would require payment to each of the five. The Gemara therefore asks: perhaps our *mishnah*, which requires paying each person in full in the two-person case, simply reflects the position of Rabbi Akiva and not Rabbi Tarfon?

### Proactive vs. Reactive

The Gemara resolves this by citing a *baraita* in which Rabbi Tarfon himself distinguishes between the two scenarios: *modeh Rabbi Tarfon b'omer lishnayim gazalti l'echad mikem maneh v'eini yodeia eizeh mikem shenosein lazeh maneh v'lazeh maneh* — Rabbi Tarfon concedes that when a person comes forward proactively and says "I stole from one of you and I do not know which," he must pay each one the full amount. It is only when the claimants are pressing demands against him — the reactive scenario of five people each asserting a claim — that Rabbi Tarfon allows placing the money in the middle.

This means the determinative variable is who initiates. When the person comes forward on his own, seeking to fulfill his moral obligation — *ba latzeit yedei shamayim* — full payment to each is required. When they come against him and he is defending against their claims, *hamotzi mechavero alav haraaya* governs, and he need not pay in full.

---

## Gemara Analysis (II)

### Self-Admission Reason

The Gemara confirms this analysis by returning to the text of our *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* states the reason for full payment: *shehoda mipi atzmo* — because he admitted of his own accord. This phrase, the Gemara notes, is not merely a description of the factual circumstances. It is the stated rationale: the person's coming forward voluntarily, without external compulsion, is what places the case in the framework of *latzeit yedei shamayim* rather than in the framework of legal adjudication under *hamotzi mechavero alav haraaya*. *Shma mina* — this is indeed the operative distinction.

---

## Five Claimants (II)

### Silence Analysis

The Gemara now examines the reactive scenario more carefully. When five people each press a claim against me, *v'hala ma to'ein* — what is my response to each of them? Rav Yehuda cites Rav: *halas shotek* — he is silent. Rav Menashya cites Rav differently: *halas tzoveiach* — he protests loudly, denying each claim. The debate concerns the doctrine of *shtika k'hoda'ah* — whether silence constitutes admission.

According to Rav Menashya's reading, the person actively denies each claim: "I did not steal from you, and not from you either." This is the straightforward reactive posture, and Rabbi Tarfon's leniency applies.

According to Rav Yehuda's reading, the person is silent in response to each claim. One might think that silence amounts to admission: if five people each say "you stole from me" and he says nothing, he has in effect admitted to each of them. But the Gemara explains why silence here is not admission. *Shtika dehacha lav k'hoda'ah hi* — in this context, silence is not an admission. The silent person can say: *matzi amar lei hai deshtiki dechol chad v'chad, d'amina dilma hai hu* — my silence when each person came forward with his claim was not an acknowledgment that he was the one; it was because I genuinely did not know. Maybe he was the one who was robbed. I could not say "it was not you" because I could not exclude the possibility. But neither was my silence a positive admission that it was him specifically.

The distinction is precise: silence here constitutes an admission of possibility — I acknowledge I cannot exclude you — but not an admission of fact — I am not confirming that I actually stole from you. *Shtika k'hoda'ah*, as a legal doctrine, operates on actual admissions; it does not convert an expression of uncertainty into a binding acknowledgment of liability.

### Escrow Requirement

Finally, the Gemara interrogates the practical implementation of Rabbi Tarfon's ruling. *Maniach gezeila beineihem umistalek* — he puts the stolen amount in the middle and walks away. Does this mean he literally puts the money down and the five claimants fight over it? Evidently not. *V'ha'amar Rav Adda bar Zavda amar Rav, kol safek hinuach l'chatchila lo yitol* — there is an established principle regarding doubtful *aveidah* cases: an object that may have been intentionally left should not be picked up, because if it was, the finder becomes obligated to return it to its owner and cannot discharge that obligation simply by putting it back and walking away. *V'im natal, lo yachzir* — once he has taken it, he cannot simply replace it, because his obligation to the rightful owner is not discharged by abandonment.

The same logic applies here. The person who stole the money is obligated to return it to the rightful owner. He cannot discharge that obligation by placing the money in a pile and departing. The money must be held in escrow — *y'hei munach* — and preserved until the rightful owner can be identified, not simply abandoned for the claimants to divide as they see fit. Rav Safra makes this explicit: *v'yaniach* — "and he should place it" — means he places it in escrow and steps away from active custody, not that he abandons the money to an unresolved dispute. The word *yaniach* in Rabbi Tarfon's ruling echoes the language of *yihei munach ad sheyavo Eliyahu*, the escrow formula of the *mishnah*, and the two are understood in the same vein.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 38

## Rabbi Akiva & Doubt

### Abaye's Challenge

The daf begins by returning to the debate between *Rabbi Akiva* and *Rabbi Tarfon* regarding a thief who says to five people, "I stole from one of you, but I don't know which one." *Rabbi Tarfon* holds that depositing the money and walking away suffices — which the *Gemara* qualifies to mean placing it in escrow. *Rabbi Akiva*, by contrast, requires paying everyone in full. Having examined *Rabbi Tarfon*'s position, the *Gemara* now turns to scrutinize *Rabbi Akiva*'s.

*Amar Abaye le-Rava*: Did *Rabbi Akiva* really say that this is not the way to be free of transgression — that merely placing the money in escrow is insufficient — and that one must pay every claimant? If so, *alma misfeika mafkinan mamona* — we see that *Rabbi Akiva* maintains that money is extracted even under conditions of doubt, setting aside the ordinary principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya*. The immediate question, of course, is whether *Rabbi Akiva* intends this as a strict legal obligation or merely as a *ba latzet yedei shamayim* — a moral and religious duty beyond the letter of the law. The *Gemara* brackets that question and will circle back to it.

### Bari vs. Shema

The *Gemara* raises a further subtlety. One might think the problem with *Rabbi Akiva*'s position is that it abolishes the principle of *chazaka* entirely — that even in doubtful cases money must be paid out. But as *Tosafot* notes, that would be an absurd reading; the entire system of adjudication rests on *chazaka*. A more careful framing points to the question of *bari ve-shema*: when each of the five claimants says definitively, "You stole from me," and the defendant says, "I don't know," perhaps *Rabbi Akiva*'s rule is specific to that constellation, where a *bari* claim confronts a *shema* response. A definite claim against a doubtful one may well override *chazaka*.

*Tosafot* adds a further distinction. In this case the defendant himself admits he owes money to someone — the only uncertainty is to whom. This is not the standard *chazaka* scenario where the defendant might deny owing anything to anyone. When one admits an obligation but is uncertain of its destination, the dynamics are different from a case where the claimant must simply establish that any debt exists at all.

### House Collapse

The *Gemara* now challenges *Rabbi Akiva*'s position from a case of *nafal habayit alav ve-al immo* — a building that collapsed on a man and his mother, and the order of death is unknown. The son's heirs want the mother to have died first, so the son would have inherited her estate before dying and transmitting it to them. The mother's heirs want the son to have died first, so her estate would pass to her own family. *Yorshei haben omrim ha-em meta rishona; yorshei ha-em omrim haben met rishon.* Since there is no way to determine the order, *elu ve-elu modim sheyachloku* — everyone agrees the estate is divided.

But then *Rabbi Akiva* says *modeh ani bezu* — in this case I agree that *she-hanechasim be-chezkatan*, the assets remain in their *chazaka*. Rather than dividing the estate equally, *Rabbi Akiva* rules that *chazaka* governs and one party retains what they hold. This seems to contradict the theft case directly: why does *Rabbi Akiva* say *chazaka* trumps in the house collapse but require paying everyone in the theft case?

### Bari Wins

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by introducing the *bari ve-shema* distinction. *Hatam shema ve-shema hu* — in the collapsing house case, both sets of heirs have equally doubtful claims. Neither side has a definite position. When all claims are equally uncertain, *chazaka* governs. *Gezel echad mi-chamisha, bari ve-shema hu* — in the theft case, the claimants are making *bari* claims against the defendant's *shema*. Each of them asserts definitively that he is the victim. In that configuration, *Rabbi Akiva* holds that the *bari* claimants prevail.

One might note there are competing considerations: the defendant's admission that he owes someone strengthens the case for paying out, but the fact that each claimant's *bari* contradicts the others — since he certainly did not steal from all of them — complicates matters. Nevertheless, the *Gemara*'s resolution is that *Rabbi Akiva*'s rule is specifically engaged when there is a *bari* claim against a *shema* response, and *chazaka* prevails only when all claims are equally uncertain.

---

## Mishna & Akiva

### Mishna Attribution

The *Gemara* then asks: the *Mishnah* in our tractate, where a person comes forward and says to two people "I stole from one of you but I don't know which," and is told to pay everyone — is that *Mishnah* actually the position of *Rabbi Akiva*? The point seems obvious: *Rabbi Akiva* was the one who argued for paying more generously, so he would naturally be the author. But there is a complication: in that *Mishnah*, the claimants are not demanding — they are silent. Nobody is making a *bari* claim against the defendant. Everyone is in a state of *shema*. So this looks like a *shema ve-shema* case, in which *Rabbi Akiva* himself said *chazaka* governs. How then can this *Mishnah* — which requires paying everyone — be attributed to *Rabbi Akiva*?

### Tarfon Agrees

The *Gemara* answers by pointing to the language of the *Mishnah* itself: *modeh Rabbi Tarfon be-omer lishnayim gezalti le-echad mikem maneh ve-eini yodea eizeh mikem* — even *Rabbi Tarfon*, who in other contexts holds that depositing in escrow suffices, agrees in the case of our *Mishnah* that one pays everyone. The *Mishnah* records *Rabbi Tarfon* agreeing to someone else's position. *Le-mai modeh, le-Rabbi Akiva bar plugtei* — who is he agreeing to if not *Rabbi Akiva*, his disputant? So *Rabbi Akiva* is indeed the author, and *Rabbi Tarfon* endorses the outcome in this particular configuration.

### Moral Obligation

This brings the *Gemara* full circle to the question it bracketed earlier. Why does *Rabbi Akiva* say to pay everyone in our *Mishnah*, where nobody is making a *bari* claim and by his own logic *chazaka* should prevail? The *Gemara*'s answer: *okimna lah be-ba latzet yedei shamayim* — the *Mishnah* speaks of someone who comes forward voluntarily, not because claimants are pressing him. In that case, both *Rabbi Akiva* and *Rabbi Tarfon* agree that he pays everyone — not as a technical legal obligation governed by the *bari ve-shema* calculus, but as a moral-religious duty to go beyond the strict letter of the law. The *Mishnah* is thus entirely consistent with *Rabbi Akiva*'s legal position in the house-collapse case. When a *bari* claim is made, pay everyone legally. When it is purely *shema*, *chazaka* governs — but the person who comes forward on his own initiative must pay everyone as a matter of *ba latzet yedei shamayim*.

---

## Two Deposits

### Rava's Rule

The *Gemara* returns to a point established the previous day. Two people deposit money with a single bailee — one depositing 200 and one depositing 100 — and the bailee cannot recall who gave which amount. The question is whether he must pay each person 100 and place the disputed third hundred in escrow, or whether his failure to keep track renders him negligent and obligates him to pay each person the full amount they claim.

*Rava* distinguished between two scenarios. If the two depositors came together at the same time (*shtei krichot* — two separate bundles presented simultaneously), the bailee was not necessarily negligent; the circumstances did not demand that he carefully track each one's deposit against the other's. But if they came on separate occasions, he should have kept track, and his failure to do so is negligence — in which case he must pay each depositor in full.

### Shepherd Case

The *Gemara* now challenges this rule. *Ve-amar Rava, ve-itayma Rav Pappa, hakol modim bi-shnayim she-hikpidu etzel ro'eh she-mani'ach ro'eh beineihem u-mistaleik* — everyone agrees that if two people deposited animals with a shepherd and the shepherd cannot remember who gave him two sheep and who gave him one, the shepherd simply places the disputed animal in escrow and walks away. He is not obligated to pay each depositor in full.

But this should seemingly be a case of *shtei krichot* — separate deposits on separate occasions — and on *Rava*'s own reasoning, the shepherd should be considered negligent for failing to keep track, and should pay everyone in full. Why is the shepherd excused? The animals are highly visible; surely he should have paid close attention to who gave him what.

### She'lo Mida'ato

*Rashi*'s explanation is that with visible animals one might indeed have expected greater vigilance — so the challenge has real force. The *Gemara* resolves it: *amar lei, hasham ke-she-hikpidu be-edro shel ro'eh she-lo mida'ato* — the case of the shepherd is one where the depositors placed the animals directly into the shepherd's flock without the shepherd's active awareness. They said, in effect, "I dropped my sheep into your flock — I'll collect at the end of the day," without specifying how many. The shepherd never received the deposit as a formal transaction he could monitor. *She-lo mida'ato* means without his having seen it happen; under those circumstances, it is not negligence to have failed to count, and the escrow solution applies.

---

## Vessels & Money

### Two Vessels

The *Mishnah* also discusses a case of two vessels — one worth 200 and one worth 1000 — where each claimant says the more expensive one belongs to him. The ruling is to give one claimant the less valuable vessel, break the second vessel, and handle the remainder accordingly. The *Gemara* reads this "breaking" literally. Although one might have assumed it means to sell the vessel and distribute the proceeds, the *Gemara* takes it at face value.

### Why Both Cases

*U-tzricha* — the *Gemara* explains why both the case of money (two sums of 200 and 100) and the case of vessels are needed. Had the *Mishnah* taught only the money case, one might have thought the Rabbis' solution — pay each person one hundred and place the third hundred in escrow — applies only there, *mishum de-leika pseida*, because it produces no additional loss. But in the case of vessels, if one must break the more expensive vessel, a real loss results. One might then have thought *eima modei lei le-Rabbi Yosi* — the Rabbis might concede to *Rabbi Yosi*'s position in the vessel case and simply place everything in escrow rather than impose a loss.

Conversely, had the *Mishnah* taught only the vessel case, one might have assumed *Rabbi Yosi* confines his position to that case where breaking the vessel creates a practical problem, and would concede to the Rabbis in the money case where no loss is incurred.

### Yosi's Logic

The *Gemara* challenges this framing, however. It notes *ve-tama'ei de-Rabbi Yosi mishum hefsed ha-ramai hu* — *Rabbi Yosi*'s reason for placing everything in escrow is not to avoid loss to the vessel. His concern is to create a disincentive for dishonesty. If a claimant knows he will receive his 100 regardless of what he claims, there is nothing stopping him from claiming 200. *Rabbi Yosi* removes that incentive by putting everything in escrow and giving the liar nothing. That reasoning applies identically whether the subject is money or vessels. The potential loss to the vessel is entirely irrelevant to *Rabbi Yosi*'s logic. He will always say put it in escrow, in every case.

### Vessels Chiddush

If so, the *Gemara* concludes, *ela traveihu le-Rabanan* — the novelty of citing both cases is not to illuminate *Rabbi Yosi*'s position, which is uniform across cases, but to reveal the full scope of the Rabbis' position. *Lo zu af zu katani* — not only do the Rabbis apply their solution (pay each claimant the minimum and escrow the remainder) in the money case where it is costless, but even in the vessel case where this solution requires breaking the vessel and causing a real loss to whoever the true owner is — even there the Rabbis maintain their approach. This is the *chiddush*: that the Rabbis impose their escrow-and-distribute framework even when it inflicts genuine damage on the rightful claimant's property.

---

## Entrusted Fruit

### Don't Touch

The next *Mishnah* addresses a different *pikadon* scenario. *Ha-mafkid peirot etzel chaveiro* — one who entrusts fruit to a friend. *Afilu hein avudin lo yiga bahen* — even if the fruit is deteriorating, the watchman must not touch it. This is counterintuitive. One might have thought that part of the obligation to watch property is to protect its value — that under certain circumstances, especially when a deposit is clearly wasting away, the watchman would be empowered, even obligated, to act. Yet the *Mishnah* says do not touch it.

### Gamliel's Exception

*Rabban Gamliel* disagrees: *mochran bifnei Beit Din* — one sells the fruit in the presence of a court, ensuring the transaction is above board and no one suspects impropriety. The rationale: *mipnei she-hu ke-meishiv aveidah la-ba'alim* — this is analogous to the obligation of returning a lost object, insofar as one is protecting the owner from loss.

### Rav Kahana

The *Gemara* asks what the reasoning of the *Tanna Kamma* is — why does he prohibit touching the fruit even as it rots? *Amar Rav Kahana, adam rotzeh be-kav shelo mi-tishah kavin shel chaveiro* — a person would rather have one measure of his own produce than nine measures of someone else's. There is something irreducible about a person's attachment to his own property. The owner, even knowing he may lose value, would prefer to receive back whatever remains of his own grain rather than receive money representing its market value. For that reason, absent explicit instructions, the watchman has no mandate to convert the owner's property into cash. This argument admittedly loses force if everything is going to be completely destroyed, and presumably there is still some portion that can be salvaged — which is the context the discussion assumes.

### Teruma Concern

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* offers a different reason entirely for the prohibition on selling. The watchman must not sell because there is a concern — *chashinan shema tana ha-mafkid terumos u-ma'asros makom acher* — that the owner may have designated this grain as *terumah* or *ma'aser* on other grain he has elsewhere. If the watchman sells the grain, an unsuspecting buyer receives it, and that buyer — along with everyone in his household — may eat what is in fact *terumah*. The problem is not the watchman's responsibility to the owner's preferences; it is the watchman's responsibility to protect the unwitting public from a serious halachic violation.

The *Gemara* notes a further dimension: it is technically possible to separate *terumah* on grain that is not physically present, as long as it is under one's control. *Tosafot* qualifies that this is only permissible *be-di'avad* and that *le-chatchila* one should not do so — but it can and does happen. The owner, confident that his grain is secure with the watchman, may declare that the terumah on his home produce shall be the grain the watchman is holding. The owner does not know the produce is rotting, particularly before the era of rapid communication.

A *Braita* is then cited: *hamafkid peiros etzel chaveiro harei zeh lo yiga bahen, le-fichach ba'al ha-bayit oseh otan terumos u-ma'asros be-makom acher* — precisely because the watchman does not touch the deposit, the owner may rely on it still being there and may use it as the referent for *terumos u-ma'asros*. The *Gemara* notes that for *Rav Kahana*, the word *le-fichach* means the *terumah* arrangement is a consequence of the no-touching rule. For *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak*, however, the *terumah* concern is the cause of the rule — so how can the *Braita* present it as an effect?

The *Gemara* resolves this by reconstructing the logical sequence in two stages. First, the concern about *terumah* arises as an observed phenomenon — people are sometimes separating *terumos u-ma'asros* on grain that may have already been sold, even though strictly speaking they should not assume it is still in place. In response, the Rabbis legislate that the watchman may not sell. Once that rule is established as *halacha*, owners may now genuinely rely on the grain being present, and the practice of taking *terumos u-ma'asros* on it is fully validated. The *Braita* describes this second stage: now that the Rabbis have prohibited selling, therefore (*le-fichach*) the owner may go ahead and separate *terumos u-ma'asros* with confidence.

---

## Rate of Loss

### Chesronam

*Amar Rabbah bar bar Chana amar Rabbi Yochanan, machlokes be-kedei chesronan* — the debate about whether the watchman may sell deteriorating produce applies only when the produce is depreciating at its normal rate of loss. The *Mishnah* later discusses the standard rates of natural attrition for various types of produce stored over time — some quantity will inevitably be lost to natural deterioration — and it is within those bounds that this dispute operates.

### Exceeds Normal

*Aval yoter mi-kedei chesronan, divrei hakol mocherin be-Beit Din* — but if the produce is depreciating faster than the normal rate, everyone agrees the watchman should sell it in court to protect the owner's investment. Whatever considerations supported not selling at a normal rate of loss — whether rooted in the owner's preference for his own property or in *terumah* concerns — they are overridden when losses are accelerating beyond ordinary expectations.

### Nachman's Issue

However, the *Gemara* immediately observes that this universal ruling creates a serious difficulty for *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak*. His reason for prohibiting sale was not about the owner's preferences but about protecting the public from inadvertently eating *terumah*. If that concern was compelling enough to prohibit selling at a normal rate of loss, how can it be overridden by the magnitude of the owner's financial loss? The risk of someone eating *terumah* remains regardless of how fast the produce is depreciating. *Ad Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak vadai pliga* — the ruling that everyone agrees to sell when losses exceed the normal rate is, it seems, in direct conflict with *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak*'s position.

As for *Rav Kahana*, who rooted the prohibition in the owner's preference for his own property — might he also disagree with the universal rule? The *Gemara* says no. *Ki ka'amar Rav Kahana be-kedei chesronan ka'amar* — *Rav Kahana*'s reasoning about the owner preferring his own property applies only within the range of normal loss. At that rate, the owner is willing to absorb the loss to retain his own produce. But at an accelerated rate, even the owner would prefer to protect his investment. The formulation *adam rotzeh be-kav shelo mi-tishah kavin shel chaveiro* is understood as an approximation: *guzma be-alma* — an exaggeration that captures the general preference, not an absolute principle operative at every level of loss.

### Teruma Risk

The *Gemara* then poses a sharp question: *ve-leichush dilma havu lehu yoter mi-kedei chesronan ve-zavnineihu ve-ka achil tevalim* — now that we have acknowledged exceptions to the no-selling rule, how can we tell owners that they may confidently separate *terumos u-ma'asros* on the entrusted grain? Once the watchman might lawfully have sold the grain, what assurance does the owner have that it still exists?

The *Gemara* first suggests that accelerated depreciation is rare — *yasir mi-kedei chesronam lo shachiach* — and so owners can generally rely on the grain still being present. But the *Gemara* presses: rare as it is, when it does happen, what prevents the combination of (a) the watchman having sold the grain and (b) the owner having designated it as *terumah*? *Ve-leichush shema asaan ba'al ha-bayit terumah u-ma'aser al makom acher* — the question stands.

### Kohanim Solution

The *Gemara* provides its answer: *ki mizabninan nami le-kohanim bi-dmei terumah mizabninan lehu* — in those cases where the watchman is permitted to sell due to accelerated loss, he must treat the grain as if it were *terumah* and sell it exclusively to *kohanim* at *terumah* prices. *Terumah* carries a depressed market value — it may only be purchased by *kohanim*, and they must consume it in a state of ritual purity, making it worth roughly half the price of ordinary untithed grain. But in a case where depreciation is so severe, the owner's interests are better served by receiving even *terumah* prices than by holding deteriorating produce. By treating the grain as *terumah* and transacting accordingly, the watchman satisfies both his obligation to the owner and his responsibility to protect the public.

This carries a poignant consequence: if the grain was not actually *terumah*, the owner suffers a diminished return that he need not have suffered. But it is the only way to balance the watchman's dual obligations. If the grain truly was *terumah*, the *kohen* who buys it is properly situated to eat it. If it was ordinary grain, the *kohen* simply handles it with the care appropriate to *terumah*, and no violation occurs.

---

## Facts Debate

### Takes Time

*Amar Rabbah bar bar Chana amar Rabbi Yochanan* — the position of *Rabbah bar bar Chana* is that accelerated depreciation is not a common or rapidly occurring phenomenon. *Yasir mi-kedei chesronam lo shachiach*, and moreover, *le-kamah hu de-havah* — when it does occur, it only manifests after a prolonged period. Produce does not suddenly begin depreciating at twice the normal rate; it takes considerable time before one can identify that the rate of loss has become anomalous.

This factual claim has a legal consequence. Since accelerated loss takes a long time to develop, if an owner was going to designate this grain as *terumah* or *ma'aser*, he would have done so long before the watchman reaches the point of being permitted to sell. *Mikamei de-havu lehu yasir mi-kedei chesronam avid lehu* — by the time accelerated loss becomes apparent, the owner has already had ample opportunity to separate *terumos u-ma'asros* if that was his intention. The watchman can therefore proceed to sell — treating the grain as *terumah* and transacting with *kohanim* — with reasonable confidence that whatever *terumah* obligations the owner had are already satisfied.

### Happens Quickly

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* disagrees on the facts. *Yasir mi-kedei chesronam mishcha shachiach* — accelerated depreciation is actually not rare, and moreover it tends to appear quickly. *De-ki havi lehu le-altar hu de-havei lehu* — when produce begins deteriorating at a faster-than-normal rate, it typically becomes apparent soon after storage, not after a prolonged period. This directly undermines *Rabbah bar bar Chana*'s claim that owners will have had time to separate *terumos u-ma'asros* before the selling window arrives.

### Early Sell Risk

If accelerated loss appears quickly and is reasonably common, then permitting the watchman to sell early creates a genuine risk. *Zimnin de-kadim mazvin lehu* — the watchman sells early, within the first month, because he immediately observes accelerated loss. *Ve-avid lehu ba'al ha-bayit terumah u-ma'aser mi-makom acher* — and then two or three months into the arrangement, the owner, completely unaware that the grain has been sold, designates it as *terumah* on other grain he has at home. *Lo yada de-zvina* — he does not know it has been sold. *Ve-achal tvelin* — and as a result, he and others eat *tevel*, untithed produce, having performed a *terumah* designation that was legally void.

The concern here is not about the buyer, who can be protected by treating the grain as *terumah* and selling only to *kohanim*. The concern is about the original owner, who acts in good faith based on the assumption that his grain is still under the watchman's care, and who thereby contaminates produce he thought he had properly tithed. No retroactive solution addresses this risk once the harm has occurred. This is why, according to *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak*, the *terumah* concern can never be fully neutralized and the prohibition on selling must remain absolute — regardless of the rate of loss.

---

## Spoiled Produce

### Spoilage Types

A *Braita* now lists several types of spoilage: fruit that rots, wine that turns to vinegar (*yayin she-hechmitz*), oil that spoils (*shemen she-hivish*), and honey that thickens (*devash she-hidvish*). *Rashi* notes regarding the honey that regular bee's honey does not truly spoil — and indeed, a practical point emerges that bee's honey is not subject to *terumah* and *ma'aser* obligations. The *Braita* therefore refers to date honey, a processed product that does deteriorate. *Rashi* also makes a grammatical observation: the root *dalet-bet-shin* can function in both directions, like the English word "shelled," which can mean shells added or shells removed — the form *hidvish* thus means the honey has lost the quality of being honey.

### Meir: Don't Touch
