In all these cases — rotting fruit, soured wine, spoiled oil, deteriorated honey — the *Braita* opens with: *harei zeh lo yiga bahen, divrei Rabbi Meir* — do not touch them, in the words of *Rabbi Meir*. This aligns *Rabbi Meir* with the *Tanna Kamma* of the *Mishnah*: whatever is happening to the produce, leave it alone.

### Sages: Sell

*Va-Chachamim omrim, oseh lahem takkana* — the Sages say one must take remedial action. *Mochran be-Beit Din* — sell the goods in the presence of a court. *Mochran le-acherim ve-lo mochran le-atzmo* — sell to others, not to oneself. This dual requirement ensures both a fair price and clean hands. No one should suspect the watchman of engineering a self-serving transaction, even if he would pay the full market value. The same principle is illustrated in two parallel cases: charity overseers (*gabbai tzedaka*) who hold copper coins that are beginning to oxidize may exchange them for silver — but must do so with others, not with themselves (*porchin le-acherim, ve-ein porchin le-atzman*). Soup kitchen overseers (*gabbai tamchui*) who collect food and find they have more than the poor can receive must sell the excess — but again, to others and not to themselves.

The *Gemara* then asks: do the spoiled goods in the *Braita* represent a case of normal or accelerated depreciation? The apparent answer is that wine turning to vinegar and oil spoiling must surely represent more than the normal rate of loss — and yet *Rabbi Meir* still says do not touch it. Does this not contradict the rule that everyone agrees to sell when depreciation is accelerated?

The *Gemara* resolves the tension: *shani hani kivan de-kam kam* — these cases are different because by the time the *Braita* describes them, the process is complete. The wine has already become vinegar; the oil has already spoiled. At that point there is nothing left to salvage in the original form, and *Rabbi Meir* says it is too late to act. Had the wine been *turning* to vinegar at an accelerated rate, *Rabbi Meir* would agree to sell. But once it *has* turned — *de-kam kam* — intervention can no longer protect the original produce.

### Spoiled Markets

This raises the question: if the goods are completely spoiled, why do the Sages say to sell them? Who would buy them and for what purpose? The *Gemara* explains that spoiled goods retain alternative uses: *shemen chazi le-girdai* — spoiled oil can be used for treating leather. *Ve-dvash le-chtishat gamli* — and spoiled honey can be rubbed into the sores of camels. There are real, if limited, markets for these goods in their degraded state.

### Vessel Protection

But if *Rabbi Meir* is saying it is too late to protect the produce itself, why do the Sages disagree? *Amar Rav Ashi le-kankanim* — *Rav Ashi* explains that what the Sages are actually protecting is the jars. If spoiled wine remains in a jar and is not removed, the jar itself will eventually be damaged. By selling the contents — even at the depressed price appropriate for vinegar — the Sages ensure that the container, which has independent and continuing value, is preserved. This is analogous to the debate about normal versus accelerated loss. Just as *Rabbi Meir* holds that only significant loss justifies taking liberties with the owner's property while the Sages hold that even modest loss justifies action, here too: *Rabbi Meir* does not regard the potential damage to a jar as sufficient reason to sell, while the Sages apply the principle *va-Chachamim savri, ve-afilu le-hefsed muat nami chashoshu* — even a minor prospective loss warrants protective action.

---

## Captive's Fields

### Inference Test

The *Gemara* now draws a broader inference from *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s ruling that deteriorating entrusted produce should be sold to protect the owner's investment. If *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* is willing to take such liberties with an owner's property in service of protecting its value, does it follow that he would similarly permit a close relative to go down and work the fields of someone taken captive (*nechsei shavuy*)? The captive's fields lie fallow while his fate is unknown. His closest relative — the one who stands to inherit — has both the motive and the ability to work the land and protect its productive value. *Mi-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel nishma de-moridin karov le-nichsei shavuy* — from *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s general orientation toward protecting investment, one might infer that he would permit such an arrangement. And conversely, from the Rabbis' position not to touch the produce, one might infer they would prohibit working the fields.

### Different Reasons

*Amar Rav Yehuda* — but the *Gemara* immediately questions whether these two cases are truly governed by the same logic. *Dilma ad kan lo ka'amar Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel hacha ella mishum de-ka kalya karna* — perhaps *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* grants latitude specifically because in the case of produce the principal itself is being destroyed. The fruit is rotting away; the underlying asset is being consumed. By contrast, if a field lies fallow, the principal — the land — remains fully intact. One loses only the profit one might have generated from working it. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* might say: once the principal is at stake, sell; but when only profits are foregone, keep your hands off.

Similarly, the Rabbis' restraint in the produce case may not reflect a general principle against taking liberties with an owner's property, but may be specific to the reasons offered by *Rav Kahana* and *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* — the owner's attachment to his own goods and the *terumah* concerns — neither of which has any application to the case of a captive's fields. The inference does not hold in either direction.

### Rav & Shmuel

*Itmar* — the *Gemara* records the actual dispute: *Rav amar ein moridin karov le-nichsav* — *Rav* holds that the relative may not work the captive's fields. *Shmuel amar moridin karov le-nichsav* — *Shmuel* permits it. The concern *Rav* raises, as *Rashi* explains, is that the relative may not exercise the care of a true long-term owner. He may extract immediate profit at the expense of the land's long-term productivity — strip-mining, in effect — before it becomes clear whether the captive will return.

### Death Reported

*Be-she-shamu bo she-met, kulei alma lo pligi de-moridin* — if reports have come back that the captive is dead, everyone agrees the relative may work the fields. The relative considers himself the owner; he has every incentive to maintain the land's productivity. Even though the reports may not constitute formal testimony sufficient to establish death, once the reports exist, the relative's assumption of ownership is reasonable and his management of the estate uncontroversial.

### Uncertain Death

*Ki pligi be-she-lo shamu bo she-met* — the dispute concerns the case where the captive is known to be held but there are no reports of death. *Rav amar ein moridin, dilma mafsid lehu* — *Rav* rules against permitting the relative to work the land, because the relative knows the owner may return and may be tempted to maximize his own short-term gains before that happens, ultimately damaging the property.

*Va-Shmuel amar moridin, kivan de-amar mar shaiminan lehu ke-aris* — *Shmuel* permits it precisely because even if the captive returns alive, the relative who worked the fields is entitled to compensation like a sharecropper (*aris*), receiving a portion of whatever he produced. Given that arrangement, the relative has no incentive to exploit the land; his long-term financial interest aligns with maintaining its productivity. Whether the captive is alive or dead, the relative benefits from responsible stewardship. *Lo mafsid lehu* — he will not damage the property.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 39

## Captive Property Debate

### Fruit & Captive Parallel

The Gemara on 38b opens in the shadow of the Mishnah's central concern: when fruit entrusted to a bailee begins to rot, may — or must — the bailee sell it to protect the owner's investment, even though no such instruction was given? The Mishnah debated at what stage of deterioration such a sale becomes appropriate. The Gemara now draws a parallel case that is structurally similar but legally distinct: a person is taken captive — lost to war, whereabouts unknown — and his fields lie fallow. May a relative, who stands to inherit and therefore has a stake in the property's preservation, be sent down to work the land? This is the question of *moridin karov l'nichsei shavuy* — whether we deploy a relative to tend the captive's property. The two cases share the same underlying tension: at what point does the imperative to protect someone's investment override the presumption that one should not handle another person's property without explicit authorization?

### Rabbi Eliezer Drasha

The Gemara raises a challenge from a *baraita* citing Rabbi Eliezer, who derives a *drasha* from the verse in the context of divine punishment: *v'charah api v'haragti eschem becharev* — "My anger will be kindled and I will smite you with the sword." The verse then adds that your wives will become *almonos* and your children orphans. Rabbi Eliezer asks: if the husbands have been killed by the sword, it is obvious that their wives will be widows and their sons orphans — why does the verse need to state this explicitly? The answer, he says, is to convey the worst possible situation: *shenisheichem mevakshos lihnasei v'ein manichin osan* — the wives will seek to remarry but *beis din* will not permit them, because the husbands went off to war and their deaths are unconfirmed. And similarly: *beneichem rotzin lereid l'nichsei avihem v'ein manichin osan* — the children wish to take possession of their father's property, believing him to have been killed, but *beis din* does not allow them.

The Gemara reads this *baraita* as an apparent challenge to the position of Shmuel, who holds *moridin* — that we do deploy a relative to work the captive's property. If children cannot take possession of the father's property when his death is unconfirmed, that seems to support the view of Rav, who holds *ein moridin*.

### Possession vs. Working

Rava resolves this difficulty with a careful distinction: *lereid v'limkor tnan* — what the *baraita* prohibits is full possession and the power to sell. The *drasha* on the verse teaches only that the children may not treat their father as definitively dead, seize the property, and sell it off as their own. It says nothing about the more limited act of working the fields — tilling, planting, tending — in a way that preserves the investment without asserting ownership. This reading defuses the challenge to Shmuel entirely.

### Rav Sheshet Ruling

A practical case then arose in Nahardea: a person had been lost to war or captivity, and the question was whether his children could begin working the land. Rav Sheshet applied the same *baraita* from *Avot d'Rabbi Natan* and ruled absolutely: *ein moridin karov l'nichsei shavuy* — a relative may not go down to work the property of someone whose fate is unknown. His ruling was categorical; he read the *baraita* as prohibiting even the limited act of tending the land.

### Rav Amram Challenge

Rav Amram challenged Rav Sheshet: perhaps, as Rava had suggested, the *baraita* means only *lereid v'limkor* — that only full possession and sale are forbidden, but working the land is permitted? Rav Sheshet's response was sharp: *dilma mipumbedisa at? d'mayil pila be-kufa d'machta* — "Perhaps you are from Pumbedisa, who try to squeeze an elephant through the eye of a needle?" Such hairsplitting interpretations, he implied, are not to be entertained. His argument then turned substantive: the *baraita* draws a parallel between the wives' situation and the children's. Just as the wives can do nothing — they cannot remarry, they have no recourse — *klalo* — so too the children can do nothing with the property at all. One might respond that remarriage is more like selling the estate outright — the fullest assumption of the husband's death — whereas working the land falls short of that. But Rav Sheshet rejects this as a strained reading: the parallel is absolute, and so is the prohibition.

---

## Three Categories

### Captive Braita

The Gemara now establishes that the debate over *nichsei shavuy* is in fact a dispute among *Tannaim*, as a *baraita* lays out three distinct categories of abandoned or uncertain property.

The first category is *nichsei shevuyin* — the property of captives. *Hayored l'nichsei shavuy ein motzi'in oso mi-yado* — one who goes down to work the fields of a captive is not removed from possession. More strikingly, *afilu shama she-memashmeshin ba'in* — even if he hears that the original owner is on his way back, if he moves quickly and harvests the produce, *harei zeh zariz v'niskar* — he is praised for his alacrity and keeps what he harvested. The Gemara is evidently amused by this: we are ostensibly working this field to benefit the owner, yet the one who harvests it all before the owner returns is called praiseworthy?

The category of *shevuyin* is further defined: it includes cases where a father, brother, or potential heir went overseas and reports came that he died — *shamu bahen she-meis*. This is crucial to understanding why the worker keeps all the produce. If the worker has reliable reports that the owner is dead, he goes down to the property treating himself as the practical owner. Given that assumption, he invests in the property as an owner would, and therefore he keeps all the profit. If it turns out the owner is alive, the land is returned and the produce is retained — a genuine win-win. The owner's property was maintained, and the worker is compensated for his investment and effort.

### Netushin Retushin

The second category is *netushin* — abandoned property. Here a father, brother, or potential heir has gone overseas but *lo shamu lahem she-meitu* — there are no reports of death. He simply has not returned. In this case, *motzin otam miyado* — what was worked is taken back. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* dissents, saying: *shamati she-netushin kishvuyin* — I have a tradition that the *netushin* case is treated like the *shevuyin* case. Someone who has been overseas with no word for a long time may well be dead; we treat his property accordingly.

The third category is *retushin* — a term that the Gemara carefully distinguishes from *netushin*. Both words translate roughly as "abandoned," and Jastrow renders them similarly, but the Gemara establishes a semantic and legal difference. *Netushin*, as derived from the verse describing *shemita* — *tishmetenna u-netashtah* — carries the connotation of abandonment imposed by external force, an *afkasta de-malka*, an act of God. Going overseas with no return is like that: something may have happened to him beyond his control, his ship may have sunk. *Retushin*, by contrast, is derived from a verse meaning willful abandonment — *eim al banim ruttasha* — as Rashi explains. In the case of *retushin*, the owner is locally present, his whereabouts are simply unknown to others — he told no one where he went. We assume he is a responsible adult who simply failed to arrange for his property, and therefore no one has any license to work it. *Motzin otam miyado* — the worker is removed entirely, and no debate applies.

---

## Aris Sharecropping

### All as Aris

Having established these three categories, the Gemara cites a further teaching: *v'kulan shamnin k'aris* — all of them are treated like an *aris*, a sharecropper, meaning the one who works the property takes a portion of the produce rather than keeping it all. But which of the three categories does this apply to? If it applies to the *shevuyin* category — where the owner is believed dead — this cannot be right, since the *baraita* already says *zariz v'niskar*, the worker keeps everything. If it applies to the *retushin* category — where the owner seems simply irresponsible — the *baraita* already says the worker is removed entirely. It must therefore apply to the middle case, the *netushin* category, where the owner's fate is genuinely uncertain.

But according to whom? If it reflects the opinion of the *Rabbanan*, they hold that even in the *netushin* case the worker has no right and must return everything — so there is no middle category for them at all. If it reflects the opinion of *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, he treats the *netushin* case like *shevuyin*, where the worker keeps everything — leaving again no middle ground. The Gemara resolves this: for *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, *netushin* is *k'shvuyin v'lo shvuyin* — like the *shevuyin* category in that you are not removed from the field, but not identical to it. In the *shevuyin* case you keep all the produce; in the *netushin* case, because you went down knowing the owner's fate was genuinely uncertain, you receive only a portion — the share of an *aris*.

---

## Three Categories (II)

### Captive vs. Overseas

A question arises as to why these two cases are treated differently. Rashi's explanation is precise: in the *shevuyin* case — where there were reports of death — *keivan she-shamu bo she-met, ki nachis ada'ata d'cula peira nachis* — since it was reported that the owner died, the worker went down with the full expectation of owning everything. He treated himself as the actual owner, invested accordingly, and is entitled to the full reward even if the report turned out to be false. But in the *netushin* case — *d'lo shamu she-met* — there was never a report of death. The worker knew from the outset that the owner might still be alive. He therefore went down in a state of uncertainty, and his entitlement reflects that: he gets something for his efforts, but not everything.

---

## Aris Sharecropping (II)

### Psychology of Aris

This raises a further question. The Gemara asks how the *aris* model for the *netushin* case differs from the husband-wife model where a husband works his wife's property — *nichsei milog* — and the rule is *mah she-hotzi hotzi u-mah she-achal achal*: whatever he spent he spent, and whatever he gained he gained. The husband bears all expenses and keeps all profit, with no accounting to the wife. Why is the *netushin* case not structured the same way?

The Gemara clarifies that the *aris* model in the *netushin* case is actually not parallel to the standard husband-wife case at all. Rather, it is parallel to a different case cited in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Rav Chisda: *hamotzi ho-tza'ot al nichsei ishto ketana* — a husband who works the property of his minor wife, a wife married only through the mother and brothers after the father's death, a rabbinic marriage that the minor wife may dissolve at will through *kiddushei mi'un*. In that marriage, the husband does not know whether the property will remain his, since at any moment his wife may walk away. This is precisely the situation of the worker in the *netushin* case: he is working the field knowing the owner may return.

### Minor Wife Case

The Gemara draws out the logic in full: *keivan de-lo samcha date'ih* — since the husband in the minor-wife case is not confident the property will remain his, *takinu lei Rabbanan* — the rabbis established that he receives a portion, like an *aris*, so that he will not simply strip mine the property. The concern, as the Gemara frames it, is *ki heichi de-lo le-fasdinhu* — lest he destroy or exhaust the property. If he knew he would receive everything, he might rush to extract maximum short-term profit — harvest it all as fast as possible before she walks away, before the owner returns. By giving him only a portion, the rabbis created an incentive structure in which he is invested in the property's long-term health. The parallel to the *netushin* case is then explicit: *hacha nami, takinu Rabbanan ki heichi de-lo le-fasdinhu* — here too the rabbis structured the arrangement as an *aris* arrangement precisely to encourage responsible stewardship.

One might wonder: if the worker gets nothing, he simply will not work the field, so there is no destruction — what exactly are we contrasting the *aris* portion to? The answer the Gemara seems to suggest is that the danger is not between getting nothing and getting a portion, but between getting everything and getting a portion. If you think you might get everything, you have incentive to extract the maximum quickly, before your claim evaporates. If you know you get only a portion regardless, you are less tempted to strip mine and more inclined to pace yourself and preserve the property — since a long-term well-maintained property yields more over time even at a third of the produce than a destroyed one would.

The connection back to the Mishnah's core question is now visible. The debate over whether to touch someone else's property when its value is at risk runs through all of these cases. The *Rabbanan* and *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* in the *netushin* context parallel the tannaitic disagreement in the Mishnah about rotting fruit: when does the imperative to protect an owner's investment override the rule that one should not handle property without authorization? *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* is consistently more willing to say that protecting the investment matters enough to act, while the *Rabbanan* insist on a firmer evidentiary basis before touching what is not yours.

---

## Boreach Runaway

### Murder Suspect Case

The Gemara cites Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *shavuy she-nishba moridin karov l'nichsav, yatza lada'at ein moridin karov l'nichsav* — if a person was taken captive against his will, we deploy a relative to work his property; if he simply left on his own accord and his property has lain fallow, we do not. Rav Nachman then adds in his own name: *boreach harei hu ke-shavuy* — a fugitive is treated like a captive. The reasoning is significant: ordinarily, if a person is absent and has not arranged for his property, we say that a responsible adult should have left instructions, and his failure to do so is his own problem. But a *boreach* — someone fleeing for his life — could not leave instructions. His silence is not irresponsibility; it is necessity. Therefore, despite the fact that he is not literally seized and taken captive, his situation is functionally equivalent, and we tend his property accordingly.

---

## Harvest vs. Tilling

### Ready Harvest

This is qualified by a teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel. If a *shavuy* left behind grain already ripe for harvest, grapes ready to be cut, dates ready to be picked, or olives ready to be pressed — *beis din yordin l'nichsav u-ma'amidin apotropus* — the court appoints an *apotropus*, an overseer, and simply arranges for the harvest. *V'achar kach moridin karov l'nichsav* — only after that, when ongoing effort and investment are required to maintain the land, do we bring in the relative and give him his portion. Immediate harvest from already-ripened produce requires minimal effort and yields full reward; that is not the kind of arrangement where an heir-relative should profit. But ongoing stewardship of the land — plowing, planting, tending through seasons — that requires genuine investment and justifies the *aris* arrangement.

---

## Boreach Runaway (II)

### Tax vs. Murder

The case of the *boreach* must be specified further. If someone is running from the government because of unpaid taxes — *machmat karga* — that is not a situation that justifies the same treatment as a *shavuy*. A tax debtor may be in trouble, but he is not in hiding for his life; he has had the opportunity to arrange his affairs and give instructions. His failure to do so falls on him. The case that Rav Nachman means is *boreach machmat mardin* — fleeing on account of murder, the same term that appears in Bava Kama. Whether he committed the act or is merely suspected of it, he is being hunted, he is silent for survival, and therefore *rachmanus* applies: we treat his property as we would a captive's.

---

## Harvest vs. Tilling (II)

### Apotropus Limits

One might ask: why not simply appoint an *apotropus* for the long term and avoid the entire complicated arrangement with relatives and *aris* portions? The Gemara's answer is terse but telling: *apotropa le-diknani lo mukminan* — we do not appoint an *apotropus* for men with beards, meaning for adults. The institution of the court-appointed *apotropus* exists for orphans and minors who cannot manage their own affairs. As Rashi explains, an *apotropus* does his work without compensation, motivated by the honor of a court appointment — it is, in a word, thankless service. That kind of volunteer stewardship works when it is for helpless children whose plight moves people to act without reward. It does not work as a long-term arrangement for an adult male who happened to be taken captive. No one will volunteer to do it indefinitely without compensation. The solution, therefore, is the relative-as-*aris* model: he is invested, he profits from his portion, and he has every reason to maintain the property well.

---

## Minor Workers Banned

### Rav Huna Ban

Rav Huna now introduces a set of restrictions on who may work property in these circumstances. Three prohibitions: *ein moridin katan l'nichsei shavuy* — you do not send a minor to work the property of a captive; *v'lo karov l'nichsei katan* — you do not send a relative to work the property of a minor; and *v'lo karov machmat karov l'nichsei katan* — you do not send a one-degree-removed relative either.

### Brother Exploit Risk

The first rule is straightforward: a minor cannot be trusted to manage property responsibly — *dilma mafsid lehu* — he may simply ruin it.

The more striking rule is the second: why may a relative not work the property of a minor? The case is this: *Reuven* is a minor, and his brother *Shimon* is an adult. *Shimon* begins working *Reuven*'s property — perhaps legitimately, to preserve it until *Reuven* comes of age. Years pass. *Reuven* becomes an adult and demands his property back. *Shimon* says: what do you mean your property? This was always mine, part of what I inherited from our father *Yaakov*. And this claim is dangerous, because *keivan d'lo machi ati l'achzukei beih* — since *Reuven* was a minor and could not effectively protest, *Shimon*'s prolonged possession of the field becomes the basis for a claim of *chazaka*. In Bava Batra, three years of unchallenged possession can establish ownership. A minor's failure to protest is precisely the kind of silence that creates this vulnerability.

The problem, critically, is not that *Shimon* is inherently dishonest. It is that the arrangement creates too much structural opportunity for exploitation — an older brother working a younger brother's property, with the younger brother unable to legally protest, in a context where all parties know the properties derived from the same father. The claim will be believable, and *beis din* cannot easily refute it.

### Chazaka Fails

Rava derives from Rav Huna's ruling a broader principle: *ein machzikin b'nichsei katan* — *chazaka* does not operate against a minor's property. If a total stranger works a minor's field for three years, that stranger cannot later claim that his prolonged possession proves ownership, because the minor's silence is explained by his incapacity — he did not know his father's business dealings and could not protest. And *va'afilu higdil* — even after the minor grew up, if the stranger continued working the field, the initial period of silent possession is tainted by the minority, and no *chazaka* is established. This is why a stranger can theoretically be appointed to work a minor's field without the same fear: the stranger's possession cannot generate a credible ownership claim, because *chazaka* simply does not apply.

### Mother-Side Exception

This explains why the prohibition extends even to the third case — *karov machmat karov*, a one-degree-removed relative. Take *Shimon*'s half-brother on his mother's side, someone with no line of inheritance from *Yaakov*. Could he not work *Reuven*'s property without the same danger? The Gemara answers that even this creates risk. If that half-brother works the field, he can later say: this field was not *Yaakov*'s to begin with — it was always my mother's property, which *Yaakov* had been working as *nichsei milog*, returning to her at his death and thus never passing to *Reuven*. This is a false claim, but it is a claim that the scheme enables. The half-brother and *Shimon* may have some arrangement, and the half-brother effectively launders *Shimon*'s potential claim.

However, *lo amran ela b'achi d'abba, aval b'achi d'ima leit lan bah* — this concern applies only to a brother on the father's side, not to a half-brother on the mother's side alone. A half-brother who shares only a mother with *Shimon* is never in the line of inheritance from *Yaakov* at all, and therefore he cannot himself generate a believable claim, nor launder one for *Shimon*, since *Shimon* himself would not exist in this scenario. If there is no father-side brother whose claim is being enabled, the one-degree-removed relative creates no danger.

### Houses & Documents

Further distinctions are raised: perhaps the concern about brothers working a minor's field applies only to land, not to houses, since houses have neighbors who would know and could challenge any false ownership claim. And perhaps even for land the concern evaporates if there is an *ityada* — a formal document laying out how the estate was divided — since in that case the division is publicly known and the brother cannot credibly claim the land was his.

### Restrictions Absolute

The Gemara rejects all of these distinctions: *lo hi*. *Lo shena achi d'abba v'lo shena achi d'ima, lo shena ara'a v'lo shena b'vatei, lo shana avid ityada v'lo shana d'lo avid ityada* — it makes no difference whether it is a father-side or mother-side brother, land or houses, with or without a document. *Lo machtinan* — we do not allow it under any circumstances. The structural opportunity for exploitation is too great, and the Gemara, as Rashi explains, ultimately envisions even more creative false claims — such as asserting that the property was always the mother's *nichsei milog* and therefore never passed to the minor as an heir of the father at all.

---

## Grandmother Case

### Case Setup

The Gemara presents a complex practical case to illustrate these principles in combination. An old woman — a grandmother — had three daughters. She and one of her daughters were taken captive — *ishtavai hi v'chada barta*. A second daughter died and left behind a minor child — *shchiv chada minaihu v'shavka yinuka*. The third daughter, *Leah*, is the only adult present and accounted for.

We will call the three daughters *Sarah* (captive), *Rivka* (captive alongside the grandmother), and *Rachel* (dead, leaving baby *Binyamin*). *Leah* is the adult sister who remains. The question is: what arrangement do we make for the grandmother's property?

### Abaye First

Abaye frames the dilemma. You cannot simply give *Leah* control over all the property: *dilma shchiv safta* — perhaps the grandmother (*Sarah*, or whichever captive is meant) is dead, in which case part of the property belongs to *Binyamin*, and you cannot have a relative work the property of a minor. You cannot give *Binyamin* the portion that would be his if the grandmother is dead: *dilma lo shchiv safta* — perhaps the grandmother is alive, in which case a minor would be working the property of a *shevuya*, which is also forbidden.

Abaye's solution: *palga yahavinan lah l'achata* — give *Leah* half the property to work. If the grandmother is alive and both captives survive, *Leah* is entitled to work the entire property on their behalf. If both captives are dead, *Leah* is entitled to half — her own portion — while *Binyamin* receives the other half. In either scenario, *Leah* can legitimately work half. *V'idach palga mokminan lah apotropa l'yanuka* — for the other half, appoint an *apotropus* on behalf of *Binyamin*, which is proper regardless of whether the grandmother is alive or dead, since if she is alive it is the captive's property being managed by a court overseer, and if she is dead it is *Binyamin*'s property being managed for him by an *apotropus*.

### Rava Counter

Rava disagrees with giving *Leah* direct control over her half: *migu de-mokminan apotropus le-palga, mokminan leh apotropus le-idach palga* — since we are already appointing an *apotropus* for one portion, let the same *apotropus* manage the entire property, including *Leah*'s half. Once a court-appointed overseer is in place and managing part of the estate, administrative efficiency and propriety dictate that he manage the whole.

### After Death News

Subsequently, news arrives: *lsof shamu de-shachiva savta* — they learned that the grandmother had in fact died. Now the picture clarifies somewhat: *Leah* is alive, *Binyamin* is a minor heir, and *Rivka*'s status remains unknown — she was taken captive and her fate is uncertain.

### Final Thirds

Abaye now recalculates. The property divides into thirds: *Leah* gets a third, *Binyamin* gets a third, and *Rivka* would get a third if alive. What is certain: *Leah* gets at minimum a third — *mima nafshach*, regardless of what happens with *Rivka*. *Binyamin* gets at minimum a third — again, regardless of *Rivka*'s fate. *Tilsa yahavinan le-Leia achasa, v'tilsa yahavinan le-yanuka*.

The uncertain third — *Rivka*'s portion — is divided into two sixths, a *danka* each. If *Rivka* is dead, *Leah* is entitled to this sixth as her full half. So *Leah* gets to work that sixth: *v'idach tilsa yahavinan danka le-achasa*. For the remaining sixth, if *Rivka* is dead, *Binyamin* inherits it; but if *Rivka* is alive, *Binyamin* cannot work it since a minor cannot work the property of a captive adult. So that sixth goes to an *apotropus*: *v'idach danka mokminan apotropus le-yanuka*.

Rava again applies his principle: *migu de-mokmi apotropus le-danka, mokminan apotropus le-idach danka* — since we are appointing an *apotropus* for one sixth, appoint the same *apotropus* for the other doubtful sixth. Unlike his earlier expansion where he extended the *apotropus* to all property including *Leah*'s certain portion, here Rava limits the expansion: the *apotropus* covers the two uncertain sixths, not the portions that are definitively allocated. The certain thirds are left as allocated; only the doubtful portions are consolidated under court oversight.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 40

## Mari bar Isak Case

### Brother's Claim

The daf begins toward the bottom of 39b with the story of Mari bar Isak. A man arrived from Bei Chuzai claiming to be Mari bar Isak's brother and demanding half the estate. Mari bar Isak responded simply: *la yadeina lach* — I don't know who you are.

The case came before Rav Chisda, who said to the claimant that Mari bar Isak's denial was not necessarily dishonest. He cited the *pasuk*: *Vayaker Yosef et echav vehem lo hikiruhu* — Yosef recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him. The Gemara explains: *melamed sheyatza belo chatimat zakan uva bechatimat zakan* — he left without a beard and returned with one. So too here, perhaps Mari bar Isak left when this supposed brother was very young, or perhaps he did not even know his father had a child elsewhere. His denial is therefore not proof of bad faith.

Tosafot notes that this point is not meant to suggest that anyone claiming to be a brother is automatically to be believed. Obviously a stranger cannot collect on a bare assertion of kinship. Rather, the Gemara is clarifying that Mari bar Isak's denial does not itself disprove the claim — it simply means the claimant must bring proof.

### Burden of Proof

Rav Chisda therefore told the claimant: go bring witnesses that you are indeed his brother. This is entirely reasonable — the principle of *hamotzi me-chavero alav ha-rayah* places the burden of proof on the one seeking to extract from another's possession.

### Witness Coercion

The claimant responded: *it li sahedi u-dechali minei* — I have witnesses, but they are afraid of Mari bar Isak, who is *gavra alma hu*, a violent and powerful man. Because of his reputation for intimidation, witnesses will not come forward.

Rav Chisda then turned to Mari bar Isak and said: in that case, *you* bring witnesses that this man is *not* your brother. This is a striking move. Proving a negative is inherently difficult — what witnesses can establish with certainty that this claimant was never known as the son of the same father? One could imagine bringing people from the claimant's place of origin who could establish that he was never known to have this man as his father, or that he never claimed this ancestry, which would at least create a strong presumption against the claim.

Mari bar Isak challenged this ruling: *dina hachi?* — is this really the law? Is not *hamotzi me-chavero alav ha-rayah* the governing principle? Why must he disprove the claim? Rav Chisda answered: *hachi daina lach u-lechol alimei de-chavrach* — yes, this is how I will judge you and all men of violence like you.

### False Testimony

The issue was not simply that witnesses were unavailable — it was that the claimant asserted they existed but were being silenced through intimidation. This gave some credibility to the claim. Rav Chisda was exercising judicial discretion in response to what appeared to be witness suppression. Tosafot emphasizes, however, that this cannot become a general rule permitting anyone to sue a powerful man simply by claiming to have frightened witnesses — the specific circumstances here lent the claim particular weight.

Mari bar Isak then raised a further objection: *sof sof, ati sahadi velo mesahadi* — even if he brings witnesses, what good will it do? If Rav Chisda suspects him of intimidating witnesses into silence, won't those witnesses be equally suspect? Rav Chisda responded: *tarti lo avdi* — witnesses will not do two things. They might be cowed into silence, but witnesses will not actively testify *falsely* out of fear. If witnesses come and testify, their testimony can be trusted.

### Witnesses Confirm

The story resolves itself cleanly: *lesof, asu sahadi de-achuh hu* — in the end, witnesses did come forward and testified that this person was indeed Mari bar Isak's brother. The entire dramatic back-and-forth ended with the brother's identity confirmed through witness testimony.

---

## Property Improvements

### Orchards Claim

Once the brother's identity was established, he pressed a further claim: *liflog li nami mipardisai uvestinai deshatal* — give me half of the orchards and gardens that you planted. Mari bar Isak had invested considerable resources and effort — fertilizer, saplings, labor — into improving the inherited property, believing it to be entirely his. Now this brother claimed half the improvements as well.

### Mishnah Rule

Rav Chisda told Mari bar Isak that this claim was well-founded. He cited the *mishnah*: *hiniach banim gedolim uketanim vehishpichu gedolim et hanechasim, hishpichu le'emtsa* — if a father dies leaving adult and minor children behind, and the adult children improve the property, those improvements are divided equally among all the heirs, including the minors who did no work. And Rava similarly ruled: *hishpichu le'emtsa* — improvements go to the middle, meaning they are shared.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye challenged this comparison: *mi dami?* — how can you compare the two cases? In the case of the *mishnah*, the adult heirs know that minor heirs exist. By choosing to improve the property without stipulating otherwise, they implicitly waive their exclusive claim to the improvements. They are understood to be working on behalf of all the heirs. But here — *hacha mi yadi de'itkha?* — Mari bar Isak had no idea this brother existed. How can his unilateral effort, undertaken in complete ignorance of his co-heir, be said to benefit that co-heir?

### Rabbi Ami's View

The case was brought before Rabbi Ami, who made an argument in the opposite direction. He said: *gedola mizu amru, shamin lahen ke-aris* — they have said something even greater than this. In the case of *karov lenichsei shavuy*, where a relative is permitted to work the fields of an absent person, the relative is compensated as an *aris* — receiving a share of the produce (a half, a third, or a quarter) in exchange for his labor. If someone working another's field entirely is compensated in this way, then certainly when Mari bar Isak worked what he believed to be his own property, he should at least be entitled to compensation like an *aris* for whatever portion of the estate turned out to belong to his brother.

### Rav Chisda Rejects

The case came back to Rav Chisda, who rejected Rabbi Ami's argument on two grounds. First: *hatam birshut nachit, hacha lav birshut nachit* — in the case of *karov lenichsei shavuy*, the relative acts with explicit authorization. The *beit din* permitted him to work the field; there was even a *takana* establishing this arrangement. Therefore he is entitled to the benefits of an *aris*. Mari bar Isak, by contrast, had no such authorization from *beit din*; he simply believed the property was his.

Second, and crucially: *ve-od katan hu* — this brother was a minor. When Mari bar Isak was working the property, the brother was not yet an adult. This makes the situation one of *karov lenichsei katan* — a relative working the estate of a minor — which is a category the Talmud does not sanction. Even though Mari bar Isak did nothing wrong and acted in good faith, the halachic framework under which he was operating was one that would have been disapproved had anyone known about it. On that basis, Rav Chisda ruled that he was not entitled to any compensation for his efforts.

### Concession

The case returned to Rabbi Ami. His response was direct: *lo simu kamei de-katan hu* — when you presented the case to me, you did not tell me that the brother was a minor. Had I known that critical fact, I would have agreed with Rav Chisda that Mari bar Isak is not entitled to compensation for his efforts. The missing detail — that the absent co-heir was a *katan* — changed the entire analysis.

This story thus serves as a practical illustration of several principles discussed earlier in the tractate: the laws of *karov lenichsei shavuy*, the distinction between authorized and unauthorized work on another's property, and the conditions under which *karov lenichsei katan* applies.

---

## Grain Deposits

### Mishnah Deductions

The *sugya* now turns to a new *mishnah*: *hamafkid peirot etzel chaveiro* — if someone deposits produce or grain with a friend to watch. The Gemara will clarify that the operative scenario is one where the depositary mixed the deposited grain with his own. In such a case, the *mishnah* rules that the depositary need not return the full original quantity, because a measurable amount of grain will inevitably have been lost over time — whether consumed by rats, crumbled husks, mold, or other sources of attrition.

### Loss Percentages

The *mishnah* specifies the applicable deductions by grain type. For wheat and rice: nine half-*kabin* per *kor*. Since a *kor* contains thirty *se'ah* and each *se'ah* contains six *kav*, a *kor* equals 180 *kav*. Nine half-*kabin* amounts to 4.5 *kav*, which is 2.5%. For barley and *dochen* (millet): nine *kabin* per *kor*, which is 5%. For *kusmin* (spelt) and flaxseed: three *se'in* per *kor*, which is 10%. The *mishnah* then states *hakol lefi hamidah vehakol lefi hazman* — all amounts are proportional, both to the quantity stored and to the duration of storage. If ten *kor* were deposited, multiply by ten; if stored for three years, multiply by three.

### Fixed Rat Losses

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri disputes this proportional approach: *vechi mah ichpas lahen le'achbarin* — what do the rats care about the size of the deposit? Rats do not eat proportionally to the quantity of available food; they eat a fixed amount regardless. Therefore, he argues, one should deduct only the amount one would deduct for a single *kor* — the fixed quantity the rats will consume — regardless of how large the deposit actually is. Tosafot notes that for a deposit smaller than a *kor*, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri would agree the deduction would be proportionally smaller; his point is that once you reach a *kor*, the rat-consumption figure does not scale upward.

The Gemara then sets out the specific deductions in greater detail. Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the *mishnah*'s figures for rice apply to *orez kaluf* — peeled rice — which loses relatively little. Unpeeled rice, whose husks crumble and fall away, would lose considerably more. Similarly, Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Hiyya that the high 10% figure for flaxseed applies to *zera pishtan begiv'olin* — flaxseed still in the husks, which crumble significantly. A *baraita* confirms: for *kusmin*, flaxseed in husks, and unpeeled rice, the deduction is three *se'in* per *kor* — 10%. The *baraita* thereby clarifies that the *mishnah* addresses peeled rice on the one hand and husked flaxseed on the other, and the *gemara* notes Tosafot's discussion of why the *mishnah* combined these particular cases.

### Multiple Loss Sources

The *chachamim* respond to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri with a *baraita*: *harbeh ovdot mehen, harbeh mitpazrot mehen* — many things are lost from grain, many things scatter. The losses are not solely attributable to rats. Grain crumbles, scatters, and deteriorates through various means, and all of these losses are proportional to the quantity of grain stored. Therefore, the proportional approach of the *chachamim* is correct.

### Rats' Behavior

Tosafot cites an interesting passage from the Yerushalmi that addresses Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's reasoning from a different angle. The *chachamim*'s rationale is explained there as follows: *hanei achbarim rishi'ei ninhu* — these rats are *resha'im*. *Kad chamyan ibur, lo mistaye'u de'achli, ela karun le'chavreihon de'achlin imehon* — when they find grain, it is not enough that they eat it themselves; they call their friends to come and eat with them. The more grain there is, the more widely word spreads, and a greater number of rats arrives to consume it. On this view, rat consumption *is* proportional to the quantity of food — not because each rat eats more, but because more rats are recruited when more food is available. This is a different answer than the one our Gemara gives, and Tosafot notes the distinction.

---

## When Deductions Apply

### Mixing Required

A *baraita* clarifies the conditions under which the *mishnah*'s deductions apply: *bamah devarim amurim, she'eirev mi'peirotav* — when does one apply these percentage deductions? Only when the depositary mixed the deposited grain with his own. In that case, one cannot identify and return the specific grain that was deposited, so the *mishnah*'s fixed rates govern.

### Separate Storage

But if the depositary kept the grain separate — *yichad lo keren zavit*, he designated a particular corner for it — then he simply returns it as it is: *harei shelcha lefanecha*, here is yours, untouched.

### Empirical Measure

This raises an obvious question. Even when the grain is mixed, why not simply measure how much the depositary's own grain shrunk over the period and apply that same proportional loss to the deposited grain? That would provide actual empirical data rather than fixed rabbinic estimates.

### Unknown Usage

The Gemara answers: *be'mistapek mehen* — because the depositary has been eating from the grain himself throughout the period. He cannot isolate how much of the decrease in his stores is due to natural shrinkage and how much he consumed. And when asked why he does not simply track how much he took out — the Gemara responds: *dela yada'ei kamah istapak* — he does not know. He has been drawing from the stores regularly without keeping records of each withdrawal. Since neither the natural shrinkage nor his own usage can be precisely determined, the fixed *mishnah* rates are applied.

---

## Seasonal Expansion

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda adds a further qualification: if grain was deposited in the dry season and returned in the rainy season, the depositary need not deduct anything. Grain expands in the presence of moisture. Returning the same *measure* of grain in the rainy season as was originally deposited already constitutes giving back slightly less grain by weight and density, because the expanded grain takes up more volume. That differential effectively offsets what would otherwise be the required deduction.

### Large Quantities

Rabbi Yehuda's exemption applies only when the deposit was *midah merubah* — a large quantity. Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, and a *baraita* confirms: the threshold is ten *kor*.

### Rashi's Logic

This raises a question: why should the size of the deposit matter for the seasonal expansion argument? Does grain not expand regardless of quantity? Rashi explains by returning to the logic of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. For a very large quantity of grain, rats consume only a small and fixed proportion of it — they cannot eat unlimited amounts. As the deposit grows, the rat-consumption figure becomes a progressively smaller percentage of the total. At ten *kor*, the percentage lost to rats and other attrition is small enough that the volumetric expansion of the grain in the rainy season compensates for it. But for a smaller deposit, the proportional loss to rats is a larger percentage, and the expansion of the grain in the wet season does not fully offset it. Hence Rabbi Yehuda's exemption is limited to large quantities.

### Burst Jug

A *tanna* then taught before Rav Nachman a related point about where the grain is measured. When do the *mishnah*'s deduction figures apply? When grain was measured in the granary and returned at the granary. But if it was measured at the granary and returned in the home, the depositary need not make deductions, because the home measures compensate for the difference.

Rav Nachman objected: *vechi b'shuftani askinan?* — are we dealing with fools? Would anyone give grain in large granary measures and accept it back in small household measures? No sensible person would do that. So the *tanna* clarified: the distinction is not between granary and home as *locations*, but between the *granary season* — *yemot hagoren*, the dry summer — and the *rainy season* — *yemot hageshamim*. When grain is deposited in the dry season and returned in the dry season, deductions apply. But when deposited in the dry season and returned in the rainy season — *ein motzi lo chisaron mipney shemosiros* — no deductions are required, because the expanded grain already compensates.

This prompted Rav Papa to ask Abaye: if grain truly expands in the rainy season, why does a jug filled with grain not burst as the grain expands? Two answers are offered. First: *hava uvda upaka kada* — it has in fact happened; jugs do burst if no space is left for expansion. Second: *mishum itzitza* — when grain is completely compressed with no room to expand, it may not expand at all. The expansion occurs precisely because there *is* room.

---

## Wine & Oil

### Wine Sixth

The *mishnah* now turns to wine and oil deposits. For wine, the depositary deducts a sixth — approximately 16%. This large deduction reflects the fact that pottery jugs absorb wine. If a depositor left wine in a six-unit jug, only five units would remain by the time it is returned, because one sixth would have been absorbed into the porous walls of the vessel. If the original jug can be identified and returned, no calculation is needed. But when the wine was mixed with the depositary's own stores, one deducts a sixth and returns the remainder as the calculated equivalent of what was deposited.

### Wine Fifth

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: the deduction for wine should be a fifth — *chomesh* — not a sixth.

### Oil Measures

For oil, the deduction structure is different. Oil absorbs into pottery at a much lower rate: three *log* per hundred, which is 3%. Of that 3%, one and a half *log* per hundred represents absorption into the jug walls, and one and a half *log* per hundred represents lees — *shemarim* — that settle at the bottom. So when a depositary returns oil from mixed stores, he returns pure oil from the top and deducts 3%: one and a half percent for absorption and one and a half percent for lees.

### Oil Refinements

Two further refinements follow. If the depositor entrusted *shemen mezukak* — oil from which the lees had already been removed — the depositary deducts only one and a half percent, since there are no lees to account for. And if the jugs were *kankanin yeshanim* — old jugs that had already absorbed their capacity of oil — then no deduction for absorption is made, since old, saturated jugs take in nothing further.

### Ongoing Sales

Rabbi Yehuda adds a ruling about ongoing commercial sales: *af hamocher shemen mezukak le'chaveiro kol yemot hashana* — even a merchant who sells purified oil to a customer in regular installments throughout the year must accept upon himself one and a half *log* of lees per hundred. The case is where a customer purchases a barrel of oil and the merchant delivers pure oil from it throughout the year. The customer has bought the barrel with its natural lees included; the merchant delivers refined oil and is therefore entitled to retain one and a half percent as the lees portion.

---

## Regional & Pricing

### Coatings

The Gemara explains that the disagreement between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda over whether the wine deduction is a sixth or a fifth does not necessarily reflect a substantive halachic dispute. Rather, *mar ki atreh umar ki atreh* — each authority speaks according to the practice of his locale. In the region of the *tanna kamma*, barrels were coated with wax (*keri*), which is less absorbent, so only a sixth of the wine was lost. In Rabbi Yehuda's region, barrels were coated with pitch (*chufra*), which is more absorbent, and therefore a fifth was lost. An alternative explanation: *mishum gargishta* — because of the clay used in making the jugs. In some regions the clay itself is more porous than in others, accounting for the different absorption rates.

### Merchant Profits

The Gemara then illustrates the wine deduction in practice with a case drawn from Rav Yehuda's locale. There, 48 units of a particular measure (*kuza*) filled a barrel (*dana*). A full barrel sold for six *zuz*. Rav Yehuda sold the wine from such a barrel at six *kuzei* per *zuz*. Since the barrel held 48 units, dividing by 6 units per *zuz* yields 8 *zuz* as the maximum possible revenue.

The Gemara then works through the arithmetic across the top of 40b. He paid six *zuz* for the barrel. Selling 36 units at six per *zuz* recoups exactly his six *zuz* cost. That leaves 12 units remaining — which at six per *zuz* represents two additional *zuz* of gross revenue. But one must subtract the wine absorbed by the barrel: a sixth of 48 is 8 units. Those 8 units are gone. So he is left with 12 minus 8 = 4 units of actual saleable wine beyond what he paid for, which at the rate of 6 per *zuz* equals two-thirds of a *zuz* in net revenue above his cost.

### Price Control

The Gemara now raises an apparent difficulty. Shmuel ruled that a merchant selling staple goods may not profit by more than one sixth of his purchase price — *hamishtaker al yistaker yoter al shtut*. Rashi emphasizes that this price control applies to staples that the community depends on. Rav Yehuda paid six *zuz* for the barrel, so his maximum permitted profit under Shmuel's ruling would be one *zuz*. But his actual net gain came to only two-thirds of a *zuz* — less than what he was allowed. Why did he not charge more to reach his permitted profit?

### Profit Justification

The Gemara answers: *ika gufa ve'shmarya* — he also received the barrel itself and the lees at the bottom. He did not merely profit from selling wine; he gained the physical barrel (*gufa*) and the settled lees (*shmarya*), both of which have value. So his total gain — two-thirds of a *zuz* from wine sales plus the value of the barrel and lees — may well represent more than a sixth above his cost.

The Gemara immediately raises the opposite concern: if we add in the barrel and the lees, does his total profit not *exceed* one sixth, in violation of Shmuel's ruling? The Gemara responds: *ika tircha ve'dmei barzinayta* — there is also his labor and the cost of the spigot (or, more broadly, the skill and equipment involved in dispensing the wine). Shmuel's one-sixth cap applies to profit *above and beyond* reimbursement for labor and direct expenses. Once one accounts for the merchant's effort and the cost of the *barzinayta*, the remaining profit falls within the permitted sixth. The system is internally coherent: the merchant is compensated for his labor and expenses, and his markup beyond that remains within the halachically sanctioned limit.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 41

## Dross & Lees

### Pure Oil Setup

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion about a *shomer* — one who watches another's property — and the question of what deductions he may legitimately make when returning the item. The Mishnah addresses, among other things, the case of oil: if the owner had entrusted *shemen mezukkak*, pure oil from which the lees had already been removed, the *shomer* may not deduct any quantity of *shmarim* when he returns it, since there were none to begin with.

The Gemara, however, presses a related case: what of the principle that a vessel always absorbs some of whatever is stored in it? The Mishnah states that if the storage vessels were already saturated — having previously absorbed their fill of wine or oil — the *shomer* may not deduct the amount that would normally be absorbed by the walls of the vessel, since the vessel, being already fully laden, cannot take in any more. The Gemara objects: *v'ha i efshar d'lo bala* — is it truly possible that a vessel absorbs nothing whatsoever? Rav Nachman resolves this: *b'mizufafim shanu* — the Mishnah is speaking of vessels that are both aged and plastered on the interior; the combination of those two conditions prevents any further absorption. Abaye offers an alternative: even without interior plastering, once a vessel is genuinely saturated — *keivan d't'on t'on* — it is laden and will not absorb more, and the Mishnah's ruling stands.

### R. Yehuda View

The Mishnah then cites Rabbi Yehuda: if a merchant agreed to sell *shemen mezukkak* to a customer over the course of the year — meaning the buyer would take the oil little by little, drawing against an agreed quantity — the seller is entitled to deduct one and a half *log* per one hundred *log*, representing the *shmarim* that would naturally have settled at the bottom. The reasoning is intuitive: had the buyer taken the entire quantity at once, he would have received the full barrel, lees and all. The pure oil he is receiving piecemeal is slightly less than the nominal agreed amount, but this reflects what the actual net content would have been.

Abaye draws out the underlying logic: *l'divrei Rabbi Yehuda muttar l'arvei shmarim* — according to Rabbi Yehuda, it is permissible for a seller to mix the lees back into the oil when selling in bulk. The seller can therefore say to the buyer: had I wanted, I could have sold you a full hundred units with the lees mixed in; instead I filtered it and gave you ninety-eight and a half units of pure oil with one and a half units of lees on the side. You receive your full entitlement — just in separated form.

### Waiver Objection

A counterargument is raised: why can't the buyer say to the seller — *midelo arvat li acholei achalta li* — since you chose to give it to me pure, you have implicitly waived your right to include the lees? I should read your act of giving me clean oil as an implicit *mechila*, a relinquishing of your entitlement to sell it with the dross. If you had mixed it, I could have resold a full hundred units on the market. By separating it, you have in practice reduced my ability to resell — so your choice of filtering amounts to a concession that I receive the full quantity in pure form.

This is, as the Gemara notes, the position that the Gemara itself briefly entertains. The buyer was a homeowner rather than a reseller, *bevaal habayit askinan*, and he actually preferred the oil clean. But the *mechila* argument remains pressing regardless: if you could have, but chose not to, why doesn't that act of goodwill bind you to deliver the full amount?

### Price Doctrine

The Gemara resolves this by appealing to Rabbi Yehuda's broader jurisprudential principle: *hadamim modiyim* — the price paid reveals the intent of the transaction. Rabbi Yehuda does not hold that we infer *mechila* from generous conduct; rather, we interpret every term of a transaction consistently with the price. This is derived from the case of the *tzemed*: if someone says "sell me your yoke for two hundred *zuz*," it is obvious he meant the two oxen, not the wooden beam, because no one pays two hundred *zuz* for a yoke. *Hadavar yadu'a she'ein hatzemed b'masayim zuz* — the price itself tells you what was transacted. The Rabbis (*chachamim*) disagree, holding that price is not determinative: *ein hadamim ra'ayah*. But Rabbi Yehuda insists that price and contractual terms must be read together, and therefore the transaction is never interpreted as a waiver of the seller's right to account for *shmarim*.

### R. Pappa Counter

Rav Pappa challenges Abaye's presentation with a striking reversal: *ipkha misstabra* — the opposite makes more sense. According to the *chachamim*, he argues, it is permissible to mix the lees into the oil when selling in bulk. And that is precisely why the buyer need not accept the one and a half units of dross: because the seller *could* have sold it to him mixed, but chose to give it pure — *acholei achalta li* — you waived your right. The buyer can legitimately read the seller's act of filtering as an implicit concession to deliver a full hundred units of pure oil.

Conversely, according to Rabbi Yehuda, mixing the lees into oil for sale is *forbidden*. If a seller is prohibited from selling mixed oil, then when the buyer says he wants a hundred units, both parties understand that this means a hundred units of pure oil, since there is no permissible alternative. And yet if the seller must deliver a full hundred pure units with no offset for the natural loss of *shmarim*, there is simply no profit margin: *zavin d'zavin tigra ikri* — a merchant who buys and sells at the same price is not really a merchant.

Tosafot addresses this difficulty. The implication seems to be that the merchant's profit is embedded in the very allowance to deliver ninety-eight and a half units rather than a full hundred — not through a higher sale price, but through the understood convention that a hundred units of oil, given the realities of the trade, means the net content that remains after the natural *shmarim* loss. While this is not fully self-explanatory, the essential point is that the hundred-unit agreement is implicitly premised on the standard of the trade, which already accounts for that residual loss.

### Ptitin Parallel

The Mishnah teaches that the same rule — *echad haloke'ach v'echad hamafkid* — applies both to a purchaser and to one who deposits grain with a *shomer* when it comes to *ptitin*. Rashi understands *ptitin* as the cloudy residue or fine debris that settles out of oil — distinct from the *shmarim*, the lees of the actual seeds. The same deduction that applies in a sale applies when the *shomer* returns the deposit.

The Gemara works out the logic in both directions. On one reading, just as a buyer need not accept *ptitin* as part of his delivery, a depositor need not accept *ptitin* when the *shomer* returns his oil — in other words, the *shomer* must return it clean. On the other reading — which the Gemara appears to favor — just as a *mafkid* understands that the oil will be returned minus the *ptitin*, a buyer must accept that the quantity delivered will similarly reflect the loss of *ptitin*. The two cases track each other: whatever convention governs return of a deposit governs the terms of a sale as well, since in both cases the norm of the trade determines what the agreed-upon quantity actually entails.

### Cloudiness Loss

The Gemara introduces a further distinction regarding *shemen achor*, cloudy oil. Rabbi Yehuda rules that the loss from cloudiness — the fact that freshly pressed oil is murky before the sediment settles — falls entirely on the seller: *lo amru shemen achor ela l'mocher bilvad*. The buyer's acceptance of one and a half *log* per hundred as the *shmarim* deduction already assumes that what he is receiving is clean, settled oil. The seller therefore absorbs the loss from cloudiness; he cannot charge that against the buyer in addition to the *shmarim* deduction. The buyer gets ninety-eight and a half units of pure, settled oil — and the turbidity of the oil at the time of pressing is the seller's problem, not something further deducted from the buyer's allotment.

### Seasonal Pricing

The Gemara resolves an apparent difficulty through the mechanism of seasonal pricing. The ruling on cloudiness is not absolute; it depends on when the price was fixed and when the oil was taken. *Ha d'yahiv lei zuzei b'Tishrei v'kashakil minei b'Nisan* — if the buyer paid *Tishrei* prices and took delivery in *Nisan*, then since *Tishrei* prices reflect the fresh, cloudy, unfiltered state of the oil at harvest time, the seller retains the right to account for that cloudiness. The price paid in *Tishrei* was a *Tishrei* price — one that anticipated receiving unfiltered oil, and from which the *shmarim* and cloudiness loss is legitimately deducted. But if the buyer paid *Nisan* prices and took delivery in *Nisan* — *ki middei d'Nisan* — then by *Nisan* the oil has naturally clarified, prices have adjusted accordingly, and the seller may not deduct further for cloudiness. The price paid in *Nisan* already reflects filtered, settled oil, and a full accounting of pure units is owed.

---

## Barrel Case

### No Designation

The Mishnah turns to a new and more conceptually rich case: *ha-mafkid chavit etzel chaveiro v'lo yichadu lo ba'alim makom* — one who deposits a barrel with his fellow without designating a specific place for it. If the *shomer* subsequently moves the barrel and it breaks, his liability depends on the circumstances.

### Letzorkho Distinction

If the barrel broke while still in his hands — *mitoch yado* — the analysis turns on why he moved it. *Letzorkho chayav*: if he moved it for his own purposes, he is liable. *Letzorkhah patur*: if he moved it for the barrel's sake — to protect it, or simply as part of his duties as *shomer* — he is exempt. Moving it *letzorkhah* is simply fulfilling the role of a guardian; moving it *letzorkho*, for his own benefit, transforms his relationship to the object in a way that creates liability. The precise nature of that transformation — whether it makes him a *gazlan*, a *sholei'ach yad*, or a *sho'el she-lo bi-reshut* — is a question the Gemara will address at length.

### Return & Release

If the barrel broke after he had already set it back down — *mishe-hinichah nishberah* — he is exempt regardless of whether he had moved it *letzorkho* or *letzorkhah*. The act of returning the barrel ends whatever liability had attached to him. This is the rule when no specific place had been designated by the owners.

### Designated Place

When the owners had designated a specific place for the barrel, the analysis shifts. Here, if the *shomer* moved the barrel and it broke — whether while still holding it or after setting it down — *letzorkho chayav, letzorkhah patur*. The rule about return no longer operates as a complete release in the way it did in the first case.

This initially appears puzzling. One would expect the designated-place case to be easier to resolve through return: there is a clear location to restore the barrel to, and returning it there should be at least as effective as returning it to an unspecified location in the first case. The Gemara will ultimately explain that in the *seifa*, the *shomer* did not in fact return the barrel to its designated place — and it is that failure of restoration, not the mere existence of a designation, that sustains the liability.

### R. Yochanan Q

The Gemara raises a striking observation. *Man d'matargem li chavit aliba d'chad tana* — Rabbi Yochanan declared that whoever can explain this Mishnah of the barrel as the coherent opinion of a single *tanna*, he would personally carry that person's clothes to the bathhouse. The difficulty Rabbi Yochanan perceives is this: the *reisha* and the *seifa* appear to operate on contradictory logic regarding what constitutes a valid return. Without a designated place, it is admittedly harder to return the object, and yet the *reisha* treats it as sufficient for exemption. With a designated place, return is easier to execute, and yet the *seifa* treats it as insufficient. This inversion is what Rabbi Yochanan finds inexplicable as a unified ruling.

### R. Yishmael View

The Gemara answers that the entire Mishnah — *v'khula Rabbi Yishmael hi* — follows Rabbi Yishmael's position: *lo ba'inan da'at ba'alim*, there is no requirement that the owners be informed of the return for the *shomer* to be released from liability. Rabbi Yishmael holds that if a thief returns a stolen object to the place from which he took it — *l'makom she-ganav yachazir* — he is exempt, even without the owner's knowledge. Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *tzarich da'at ba'alim*, the owners must be aware.

With this framework, the Gemara reads the *reisha* as a *lo mibaya ka'amar* — a "goes without saying" structure. The *reisha* is not limiting itself to the case where no place was designated; it is saying: not only when a place was designated and you return it there — which would be the easier, more intuitive case for exemption — but even when no place was designated, and the notion of "return" is less clearly defined, once the *shomer* decides to resume his watching and ceases using it for himself, that constitutes return, and he is exempt. The *seifa*, in turn, says he is liable because he did not in fact return it to its designated spot — not because a designated place categorically prolongs liability, but because without restoring it to the right location, no return has occurred.

### Three Categories

Before fully resolving the Mishnah, the Gemara pauses to identify the precise basis for the *shomer*'s liability in each scenario — that is, what type of wrongful taking occurred that created the liability in the first place.

Three categories are laid out. *Gazel* is straightforward: the *shomer* took the object intending to keep it entirely for himself, which constitutes outright theft and requires a *ma'aseh kinyan* — an act of acquisition — such as lifting. *Shlichus yad* is a distinct category applicable specifically to *shomrim*: the *shomer* does not intend to keep the whole object, but does intend to use it in a manner that is *mechaser* it — diminishing it in some way, as when one picks up a barrel of wine with the intent to draw some off. This too requires a *ma'aseh kinyan*. The third category is *sho'el she-lo mida'as*: borrowing the object without the owner's permission, not necessarily with the intent to diminish it, but simply making use of it for one's own purposes — as when one moves a barrel to use as a stepladder. The Gemara's position is that *sho'el she-lo mida'as gazlan havei* — one who borrows without permission is classified as a type of *gazlan* and is liable accordingly.

---

## Shlichus Yad

### Still Holding

The Gemara now focuses on the case where the *shomer* is still holding the barrel — *mitoch yado* — and examines what exactly makes him liable. Two *Amoraim* offer competing interpretations of what the *shomer*'s act was. One says *she-netala al menat ligzola* — he picked it up with the intent to steal it outright. The other says *she-netala al menat lishloach bah yad* — he picked it up with the intent to commit *shlichus yad*, meaning to use it in a way that would diminish it, without necessarily intending to take the whole thing.

The underlying dispute between these two readings, the Gemara clarifies, is the question of *shlichus yad tzericha chisaron* — whether *shlichus yad* requires an actual diminishment of the object. According to the view that *shlichus yad* requires *chisaron*, the Mishnah must be describing a case where the *shomer* intended to steal the whole barrel outright, because mere intent to take some wine — without actually taking it — would not be sufficient to create liability. According to the view that *shlichus yad* does not require *chisaron*, the Mishnah can be describing a case where the *shomer* intended only to draw some wine from the barrel; his very taking of it with that intent is enough to make him liable for the whole.

Rav Nachman addresses the case where the *shomer* simply continues to hold the barrel without doing anything further. One might ask: what exactly did he do that makes him liable? The Gemara's discussion here leads into the detailed analysis of what kind of act generates *shlichus yad* liability in the first place.

### Hitting as Kinyan

Rav Sheshes raises a textual objection to the entire framework: *midei natla katani* — the Mishnah does not say the *shomer* "lifted" the barrel; it says he "moved" it — *tiltela*. Lifting is the classic *ma'aseh kinyan* that would make one a *gazlan* or a *sholei'ach yad*; mere movement (*tiltul*) is not. So what act of *kinyan* occurred?

Rav Sheshes therefore reframes the case: *she-tiltela lehavi aleha gozalot* — the *shomer* moved the barrel in order to stand on it and retrieve something from a high place. He was not committing *gazel* and not committing *shlichus yad* — he performed no act of *kinyan* with intent to take or diminish. Rather, he is a *sho'el she-lo mida'as*, a borrower without permission, and the Gemara establishes that *sho'el she-lo mida'as gazlan havei* — such a person bears the liability of a *gazlan*.

This reframing redirects the discussion. The question of *shlichus yad* requiring *chisaron* does not apply to a *sho'el she-lo mida'as* in the same way; the *sho'el she-lo mida'as* is already treated as having misappropriated the object by the unauthorized use itself.

Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak then offers a different answer in the name of Rav to explain how *shlichus yad* can operate even without the *shomer* having performed a classical lifting *kinyan*: *she-hikisha b'makal v'ratza lefanav* — the shepherd struck the animal with his staff and made it run before him. This act of striking and directing the animal toward himself is treated as a *ma'aseh kinyan* through *meshicha*. The Gemara then asks: but was there any *chisaron*? The animal suffered no diminishment. And the answer, says the Gemara: *shma mina kasavar shlichus yad einah tzericha chisaron* — we may conclude from this that Rav holds *shlichus yad* does not require *chisaron*; the act of taking with the intent to use, even without actual diminishment, is sufficient.

### Rav/Levi Debate

The Gemara now articulates the debate directly. *Chad amar shlichut yad tzericha chisaron, ve-chad amar shlichut yad einah tzericha chisaron* — one holds that *shlichus yad* requires actual diminishment of the object, the other holds that intent and the act of taking alone are sufficient. From the analysis above, the Gemara concludes that Rav is the one who holds *shlichus yad einah tzericha chisaron*, since his resolution of the shepherd case involved a *meshicha* without any actual *chisaron* to the animal.

It is worth noting that *shlichus yad* as a legal category applies specifically in the context of *shomrim*. *Gazel*, *mazik*, and *sho'el she-lo mida'as* can arise with respect to any object, regardless of any prior custodial relationship. *Shlichus yad* is a specific violation of one's responsibilities as a *shomer*, transforming the guardian into something closer to a *gazlan* with respect to the object in his charge.

### No Chisaron

The Gemara turns to the textual basis for each position, examining why the Torah mentions *shlichus yad* in two places — once in the context of a *shomer chinam* and once in the context of a *shomer sachar* — and what the repetition is meant to teach.

Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yose ben Nehorai, argues that *shlichus yad* was not strictly necessary to mention by *shomer sachar*, since one might have derived it from *shomer chinam* by *kal v'chomer*: if a *shomer chinam*, who is exempt from liability for theft and loss, is nevertheless liable when he commits *shlichus yad*, then certainly a *shomer sachar*, whose baseline liability is higher, should be liable for *shlichus yad*. The repetition by *shomer sachar* must therefore be serving a different purpose — namely, to teach that *shlichus yad einah tzericha chisaron*, that intent and act alone are sufficient without actual diminishment.

The counter-view holds that the *kal v'chomer* fails and the repetition is necessary on its own terms, not to add the *ein tzericha chisaron* rule. The challenge to the *kal v'chomer* is: *mah l'shomer chinam she-kein m'shalem kefel b'to'en ta'anas ganav* — a *shomer chinam* has one form of heightened liability that a *shomer sachar* does not: if he falsely claims the object was stolen, swears to that effect, and is later found to have stolen it himself, he pays *kefel*, double. A *shomer sachar* will never be in that position, because a *shomer sachar* who claims theft owes the principal regardless and cannot take an exculpatory oath. Since *shomer chinam* can in some cases bear a more severe consequence than *shomer sachar*, the *kal v'chomer* does not cleanly hold, and the Torah needed to state *shlichus yad* explicitly for *shomer sachar*.

The response to this challenge is also presented: *karna b'lo shvuah adifa mi'kfila b'shvuah* — being obligated to pay the principal without any possibility of oath is a weightier burden than the risk of paying *kefel* for a false oath. The liability of a *shomer sachar* who cannot swear his way out of paying the principal is categorically more severe than the contingent *kefel* exposure of a *shomer chinam*. On this view, the *kal v'chomer* does hold, and the repetition is indeed teaching the *ein tzericha chisaron* rule.

### Rava's Logic

Rava offers a different framework entirely. He argues that one need not even invoke *shomer chinam* as the source: *teisi misho'el* — derive *shlichus yad* liability by analogy from a *sho'el*. A *sho'el* who uses an object with the owner's full permission is *chayav b'ones* — liable for any accident that befalls the object. A *sholei'ach yad* who uses the object without permission — or beyond the scope of his custody — should certainly be no less liable. The *kal v'chomer* is compelling: if authorized use creates full liability, unauthorized misuse surely does as well.

Given that one could derive *shlichus yad* from *sho'el* by analogy, why did the Torah need to state it twice?
