Rava answers: *chad l'meimar lach shlichut yad ein tzericha chisaron* — the first statement teaches that *shlichus yad* does not require *chisaron*; intent and act suffice. And the second statement addresses a different concern: *she-lo tomar dai lo la-vin ha-din l'hiyot k'nidon* — do not say that since we are analogizing to a *sho'el*, we should limit *shlichus yad* to the full scope of *sho'el* liability, including its exemptions. Specifically, a *sho'el b'baalim* — one who borrows an object while its owner is in his employ — is exempt from liability. One might have thought that similarly, a *sholei'ach yad* whose owner is employed by the *shomer* at the time would be exempt. Therefore the Torah states *shlichus yad* explicitly for both *shomer chinam* and *shomer sachar*, to make clear that the *ba'alim* exemption does not apply to *shlichus yad*.

### Oath Requirement

The view that holds *shlichus yad tzericha chisaron* — that actual diminishment is required — must then explain why the Torah states *shlichus yad* twice, since on its terms the extra statement cannot be teaching *ein tzericha chisaron*. The answer: one of the mentions of *shlichus yad* comes in the context of the verse *v'nikrav ba'al habayit el ha'elohim im lo shalach yado b'mlechet re'ehu* — the owner of the house shall come before the judges if he has not cast his hand upon the property of his fellow. This verse establishes not merely that *shlichus yad* carries liability, but that the *shomer* must address the claim through a *shvua*, a formal oath. One might have read the verse as requiring only adjudication — *l'din* — without an oath. The repetition, through a *gezeirah shavah* linking the two mentions of *shlichus yad* in the Torah, teaches that just as one mention clearly involves an oath, so too does the other: *af kan l'shvua*. The oath is not optional; it is an integral part of how *shlichus yad* liability is resolved before the court.

To summarize the essential framework: three categories govern misappropriation of a deposited object. *Gazel* — taking it outright with intent to keep it, requiring a *ma'aseh kinyan*. *Shlichus yad* — performing an act of *kinyan* with the intent to use the object in a way that diminishes it, with the debate turning on whether the diminishment must actually occur or whether intent and act alone suffice. And *sho'el she-lo mida'as* — making use of the object without permission, without necessarily intending to diminish it, treated by the Gemara as a form of *gazel* that generates full liability.

---

## Deposited Money

### Negligent Methods

The daf concludes with a new Mishnah: *ha-mafkid ma'ot etzel chaveiro* — one who deposits money with his fellow. The Mishnah enumerates several methods of guarding that are deemed negligent: the *shomer* bundled the money and slung it behind his back, or handed it to his young child, or locked the door in a manner that was insufficiently secure — and the money was subsequently stolen or lost. In each of these cases the *shomer* is liable, because none of these methods meets the standard expected of a proper guardian of money.

The Gemara's discussion of this Mishnah continues onto the following daf. It is striking, as one reflects on it, that the standard the Mishnah applies is contextual and practical — the benchmark of how money is properly secured. Slinging a bundle behind one's back might today seem oddly specific, but the underlying principle translates directly: a *shomer* is responsible not merely for good intentions but for guarding in a manner that actually provides security.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 42

## Shomrim Overview

### Basic Categories

The daf opens with a *mishna* that marks a transition of sorts within the broader discussion of *shomrim*. The preceding *sugyot* had addressed special cases — most recently, the circumstances under which a *shomer* may liquidate an object he is watching when it faces deterioration, and the related question of *shlichus yad*, taking unauthorized personal use of a watched object and when one's special liability thereby ends. That final topic was somewhat puzzling, because while the *gemara* developed the category of *shlichus yad* extensively, the *mishna* itself did not spell it out directly. A fuller treatment of the four foundational categories — *shomer chinam*, *shomer sachar*, *sho'el*, and *socher*, each with their respective levels of liability — awaits us some four *perakim* hence. But at least here, at the end of this *perek*, we arrive at something approaching a basic discussion of the standard of care, focused specifically on money.

### Mishna Cases

The *mishna* opens: *HaMafkid ma'ot etzel chaveiro* — one who entrusts money to his friend to watch. The *mishna* then enumerates three situations that render the *shomer* liable: (1) *tzaran v'hifshilan l'achorav* — he bundled the money and placed it behind his back, as in a knapsack or back pocket; (2) *o shemasram livno ulevito haktanim* — he gave it to his minor children to watch; (3) *v'na'al bifneihem shelo karauy* — he locked them in the house but not securely. In all these cases, *shebechol elu chayav*, he is liable, because *shelo shamar k'derech hashomrim* — he did not watch it in the manner that *shomrim* normally do. Conversely, *v'im shamar k'derech hashomrim patur* — if he did follow the normal standard, he is exempt.

It is worth noting that the *mishna* does not specify whether the *shomer* in question is a *shomer chinam* or a *shomer sachar*. The default reading of *stam mafkid* — a deposit without further arrangement — is typically a *shomer chinam*, though the point is not entirely free of ambiguity.

### Derech Hashomrim

The *mishna*'s conclusion begs an immediate question: what precisely is *derech hashomrim*? Who defines it, and is it the same standard for a *shomer chinam* as for a *shomer sachar*? The answer, it emerges, is thoroughly contextual — the standard is shaped by prevailing convention, by what is socially and practically reasonable in the given circumstances. There is no single fixed threshold; it is all a function of what responsible people in that situation would do. This contextual nature of *derech hashomrim* will prove crucial as the *gemara* develops the discussion.

---

## Money in Hand

### Challenge to Mishna

The *gemara* probes the *mishna*: *bishlama kulehu shelo shamar k'derech hashomrim* — it is understandable why giving the money to one's minor children, or failing to lock the house properly, constitutes a failure of care. But the first case — bundling the money and putting it behind one's back — raises a pointed question: *mai hava leh l'me'avad?* What else should he have done? What is the affirmative standard that bundling in a knapsack fails to meet?

### In Your Hand

The answer comes from *Rava* citing *Rav Yitzchak* citing a verse: *v'tzarta hakesef b'yadecha* — "and you shall bind the silver in your hand" (Deuteronomy 14:25). This verse, in its original context, addresses *ma'aser sheni* — the second tithe that must be redeemed in money and brought to Jerusalem. Yet *Rav Yitzchak* derives from it a principle applicable to the guardianship of money: *af al pi shetzrurin, b'yadecha* — even if the money is bundled up, it must be *b'yadecha*, literally in your hand. The implication for *shomrim* is that money demands the highest degree of attentiveness — not a back pocket or knapsack, but something more like a front pocket, where it remains immediately within one's grasp and awareness. Money is uniquely attractive to thieves because it concentrates high value in a small package, and the standard of care must reflect that reality.

### Pocket Checking

This ruling of *Rav Yitzchak* resonates with an earlier statement of his from the second *perek* of *Bava Metzia*: *adam asui lemashmesh b'kiso b'chol sha'a* — a person habitually checks his pocket at all times to make sure his money is still there. When that statement appeared earlier, it was offered as a descriptive claim to explain how one can assume *yiush* — that a person knows when money has dropped from his pocket. One might have questioned whether this is truly universal behavior. In light of the present passage, however, it appears that *Rav Yitzchak*'s statement carries a prescriptive dimension as well: if you are responsible for money, constant awareness of its whereabouts is not merely typical behavior but the required standard of care.

---

## Money & Blessing

### Cash Availability

The *gemara* continues with a series of *aggadic* teachings attributed to *Rav Yitzchak*, all touching on money management. The first: *l'olam yehei kaspah shel adam matzui b'yado* — a person should always have cash readily available. The practical connection to the earlier *halacha* is natural: if one is obligated to keep money actively in hand, that presupposes having liquid funds accessible. If you never carry significant amounts of money, the question of where to keep it hardly arises. But if, as sound financial practice demands, one should always have a measure of cash available for unexpected opportunities, then one must correspondingly take greater care about where and how that money is held. The verse is again invoked: *v'tzarta hakesef b'yadecha* — "let it be in your hand," meaning at hand and ready.

### Portfolio Advice

*Rav Yitzchak* continues: *l'olam yashlish adam et ma'otav* — a person should always divide his assets into thirds. *Shlish b'karka* — a third in land, meaning real estate, which retains value over time, appreciates, and cannot be stolen or misplaced. *Ushlish b'prakmatia* — a third in commerce, buying and selling, which represents higher risk but also higher return. *V'shlish tachat yado* — a third in liquid assets, cash readily available. The advice has a strikingly modern ring: diversify, maintain a real estate position, remain active in commerce, and keep liquid reserves.

### Hidden Blessing

*Rav Yitzchak* then states: *ein habracha metzuya ela b'davar hasamui min ha'ayin* — blessing is found only in something hidden from the eye. This is a striking teaching. The idea is that if one constantly monitors an investment — counting today's value and comparing it to yesterday's — it cannot be blessed. Several dimensions of this principle are possible. One reading is metaphysical: God's blessing operates through *nes nistar*, hidden miracle, and constant scrutiny forecloses the space in which that operates. Another, raised by the *Maharsha*, invokes *ayin hara* — when something is publicly known and tallied, others' envious attention affects it adversely. There is also a purely psychological dimension: if one does not check frequently, the aggregate gain discovered upon eventually looking is far more gratifying than the same gain witnessed day by day.

### Hidden Sources

The verse cited in support is: *yetzav Hashem itcha et haberacha be'asamecha* — "God will command the blessing upon you in your storehouses" (Deuteronomy 28:8). *Rav Yitzchak* reads *be'asamecha* as connected to *samui*, hidden. A parallel formulation is brought from the school of *Rabbi Yishmael*: *ein haberacha metzuya ela bedavar she'ein ha'ayin sholetet bo* — blessing is found only in what the eye does not have dominion over, again citing *be'asamecha*, which *Rashi* renders as *lashon genazim*, the language of stored and treasured things. The two formulations subtly differ: *Rav Yitzchak*'s language of *samui* emphasizes hiddenness as enabling divine increase; the *tanna devei Rabbi Yishmael*'s language of *she'ein ha'ayin sholetet bo* more directly invokes the idea of protecting the object from the gaze of an envious eye. The latter reading fits more naturally with *ayin hara* concerns; the former with the idea of leaving room for blessing to accumulate unobserved.

### Measuring Grain

The *gemara* then presents a *baraita* that applies this principle practically. One who goes to measure the grain in his threshing floor should first say: *yehi ratzon milfanecha Hashem eloheinu shetishlach bracha bema'aseh yadeinu* — may it be Thy will, Lord our God, that You send blessing into the work of our hands. This is a *bakashah*, an explicit request before the measuring begins. When the measuring itself commences, one says: *baruch hashole'ach bracha bekari hazeh* — blessed is He who sends blessing into this pile of grain. This formulation uses the classic *matbe'a haberacha* form, framing the request as a blessing.

The relationship between these two formulations is worth exploring. The *yehi ratzon* is future-oriented — one has not yet begun to count, so the request looks forward. The *baruch hashole'ach* is present-tense and is recited as the measuring begins. One way to understand the progression is that the *baraita* moves from future to present: first anticipating God's blessing, then invoking it in the moment of action. The *Rama* suggests that the *bracha* expresses a kind of *bitachon* — confidence that the earlier prayer was heard — though it may simultaneously function as a present-tense petition.

The crucial point comes next: *madad v'achar kach beirach* — if one measured the grain first and only afterward recited *baruch hashole'ach bracha bekari hazeh*, *harei zo tefillat shav* — this is a vain prayer. Once you have counted and established the precise quantity, what are you asking for? That there will somehow be more tomorrow than there is today? That would require a *nes galuy*, a manifest miracle, and God does not do *nes galuy* on demand. The *baraita* concludes with the underlying principle: *ein haberacha metzuya lo bidvar hashakul velo bidvar hamadud velo bidvar hamannuy ela bidvar hasamuy min ha'ayin* — blessing is not found in what is weighed, or measured, or counted, but only in what is hidden from the eye. The verse is again cited: *yetzav Hashem itcha et haberacha be'asamecha*.

---

## Burial in Ground

### Shmuel's Rule

Returning now to the *halachic* question of proper *shmirah* for money, *Shmuel* takes matters considerably further than the *mishna*: *kesafim ein lahem shmirah ela be'karka* — money can only be properly protected by burying it in the ground. The logic is clear: money is uniquely concentrated in value within a tiny, easily concealed package. In a house, no matter how many hiding places one devises — the mattress, the cabinet, behind a painting — a determined thief will eventually search them all. But thieves will not undertake to dig up an entire yard or floor. Burial in the ground is thus, according to *Shmuel*, the *only* adequate protection for money.

*Rashi* makes the implication explicit: *ein lahem shmirah de'im lo shamran v'nignevu peshia hi* — anything short of burial in the ground constitutes *peshia*, negligence. This is a significant ruling, because it means that even a *shomer chinam*, who is ordinarily exempt from liability for theft, would be liable if the money was not buried, since his failure to bury it would be deemed negligence, not mere lack of precaution.

### Shabbat Exception

*Rava* immediately qualifies *Shmuel*'s ruling: *u'modeh Shmuel b'erev Shabbat bein hashemashot* — even *Shmuel* concedes that on *erev Shabbat*, near nightfall, *delo atrachuhu rabanan* — the Rabbis did not burden the *shomer* with the requirement to dig and bury. If someone deposits money with you just before *Shabbat*, and digging a hole at that moment would mean either violating *Shabbat* or requiring you to abandon all *Shabbat* preparations at the last minute, the Rabbis did not demand it. Hiding the money by other means would be acceptable under those circumstances.

The *gemara* extends this: if *Shabbat* has ended and enough time has elapsed for the *shomer* to have buried the money, yet he failed to do so, *mechayav* — he is now liable if it is stolen. Once the constraint disappears, the obligation resumes immediately. There is one exception: if the owner is a *talmid chacham* who is scrupulous about *havdala al hakos*, the *shomer* might reasonably wait a short time, anticipating that the owner may come to retrieve some of the money to purchase wine for *havdala*. In that case, a brief delay is excused.

### Norms Shape Care

This exception illuminates something fundamental about the entire framework of *derech hashomrim*. The standard of care is not purely a function of risk assessment — it is shaped by social norms and reasonable expectations. The risk that thieves will find unburied money is the same on *erev Shabbat* as on any other day. Yet the duty to bury it does not apply on *erev Shabbat* because under those circumstances it is not what reasonable people would demand. This connects to a parallel point from the preceding day's *sugya*: a shepherd who returns to town during his lunch break is arguably exposing the flock to the same dangers as if he had abandoned them entirely — wolves and lions do not observe lunch hours — and yet such a break can fall within *derech hashomrim*. The content of one's duty is partly constituted by prevailing conventions, not solely by objective risk.

### Thief Escalation

The *gemara* then traces an arms race between hiding places and increasingly sophisticated thieves. Initially, burial in the ground was the safest option — *Shmuel*'s ruling. But *v'haidna d'sh'chichi gashushei* — nowadays there are people who bang on the ground and listen for the sound of freshly disturbed earth. Against them, *leit lehu shmira ela b'shmei kora* — the only protection is hiding money in the rafters of the house. But then, *idna d'sh'chichi frumai* — there are those who break through the roof and search the rafters. Against them, *leit lehu shmira ela beini orbei* — one must hide the money within the bricks of the wall.

Yet even this is no longer fully secure: *d'sh'chichi tapuchai* — there are those who knock against walls, listening for the hollow sound of a removed brick. The solution: *leit lehu shmira ela b'tefcha samuch l'karka* — a course of bricks near the base of the wall, or alternatively, *b'tefcha samuch l'shmei kora* — near the ceiling, where the sound test is less reliable.

### Burial Depth

*Rav Acha the son of Rav Yosef* poses a question to *Rav Ashi*: the *mishna* in *Pesachim* rules that *chametz* buried under rubble is considered destroyed (*harei hu k'mevuar*) — *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* specifying that it must be deep enough that a dog cannot dig it out — and a *tanna* teaches that this threshold is three *tefachim*. So when *Shmuel* requires burial in the ground, how deep must the money be buried? Is three *tefachim* required here as well?

The answer is no, and the reasoning is elegant. *Hatam mishum reicha* — there, with *chametz*, the concern is smell: food has an odor, dogs are attracted to it, and one must bury it deep enough that no dog can detect and excavate it. *Hacha mishum iksuyei me-eina* — here, the concern is simply concealment from sight. Money has no odor; one need only ensure it cannot be seen. *Lo ba'inan gimmel tefachim* — three *tefachim* is not required. *V'kama?* How deep then? *Amar Rav Safra: nesicha tefach* — one *tefach* is sufficient.

---

## Tosafot's Question

### Buried & Stolen

*Tosafot* pauses at *Shmuel*'s ruling to raise a question: *tzarich iyun* — it requires examination. We have established that burying money in the ground is the proper *shmirah*, and *Rashi* explicitly states that anything less is *peshia*. The obvious corollary would seem to be that if the money *is* properly buried, and a thief nonetheless manages to find and steal it, that should constitute an *oness* — a genuinely unforeseeable misfortune — for which the *shomer* is exempt. But is that actually the case? Does burying it in the ground represent the floor of one extreme (below which is *peshia*) and the ceiling of the other (above which is *oness*), with no middle ground?

### Liability Conflict

*Tosafot* pursues this question by examining conflicting *gemarot*. A *shomer sachar* is normally liable for theft — *v'nignav* is explicitly among his obligations. But that should mean ordinary theft. If the theft is entirely unpreventable — if it genuinely constitutes an *oness* — should a *shomer sachar* still be liable? *Tosafot* finds *gemarot* that seem to suggest that a *shomer sachar* is liable even for *geneiva be'oness* — theft that occurred despite the *shomer*'s inability to prevent it — which seems deeply counterintuitive. Liability for theft by a *shomer sachar* ought to track negligence, not simply the category label of *geneiva*.

### Armed Robbers

*Tosafot* works toward a resolution: the case of *listim mezuyan*, an armed gang, is clearly an *oness*, and a *shomer sachar* is unquestionably exempt there. That case represents a *geneiva* that is unambiguously beyond the *shomer*'s control. *Tosafot* struggles to explain why other forms of *geneiva be'oness* might be treated differently, finding the distinction difficult to justify. The simplest reading may indeed be the cleanest: burying the money in the ground is *peshia* on one side and *oness* on the other, with no middle ground. Anything less is negligence; once it is properly buried and still stolen, that is a complete *oness* for which the *shomer sachar* is exempt. The tension in the various *gemarot* remains, but this binary reading has considerable force.

---

## Hunting Hut Case

### Duck Blind

The *gemara* presents a case: *hahu gavra de-afkid zuzei gabei chavreih* — a person deposited money with his friend. *Otvinhu b'tzrifa de-urbani* — the *shomer* placed the money in a hunting blind, a small hut out in the fields used for trapping or hunting birds. *Ignuv* — and the money was stolen from there.

### Negligence & Oness

*Rav Yosef* rules: *af al gav de-le-inyan ganavei netiruta hi* — it is true that a remote field hut is actually quite well protected against thieves; no one would ordinarily know to look there. But *le-inyan nura peshiuta hi* — with respect to fire, placing the money in a field hut is negligence. Brush fires can break out; a small wooden hut in a field is obviously vulnerable.

One might object: the money was stolen, not burned. Why should negligence regarding fire render the *shomer* liable for theft, an *oness* he could not have prevented? The answer lies in the principle of *tchilato bifshiya vesofo b'ones* — negligence at the outset followed by an unforeseeable mishap at the end. The key is that a causal argument can be constructed: the money was placed in the wrong location due to negligence. Had it been properly stored, it would not have been in that hut to be stolen. The act of theft, while itself an *oness*, is connected to the initial negligent placement. As long as that argument is available — that the loss would not have occurred but for the earlier negligence — liability follows.

### Opposite View

Some authorities (*ikha d'amri*) formulate it the opposite way: even though the hut is negligent with respect to fire, and protected with respect to theft — *tchilato bifshiya vesofo b'ones patur* — where the negligence is in one domain and the *oness* occurs in a different domain, one is exempt. The logic here is that the negligence with respect to fire is not what caused the theft; the theft was independent. One should not be penalized for a failure in one area when the actual loss came from an entirely different direction.

### Final Ruling

The *gemara* rules definitively: *v'hilcheta tchilato bifshiya vesofo b'ones chayav* — the *halacha* is that negligence at the outset, followed by an *oness* at the end, renders the *shomer* liable. *Tosafot* notes that there was textual uncertainty about whether the *gemara*'s ruling was *chayav* or *patur*, and some versions read *patur*; but *Tosafot* marshals evidence from other passages to confirm that the correct ruling is *chayav*.

---

## Forgotten Money

### Buried & Forgot

The *gemara* brings another case: *hahu gavra d'afkid zuzei gabei chavreih* — someone deposited money with a friend. When the owner later requests his money back, the *shomer* responds: *lo yadana heicha otvinhu* — I don't remember where I put it. He may have followed *Shmuel*'s advice entirely faithfully: he buried it in the ground, covered it carefully so as to leave no trace, and now genuinely cannot locate it.

### Rava's Ruling

*Rabbah* rules without hesitation: *kol lo yadana p'shiyuta hi* — any claim of "I don't know where it is" constitutes negligence. It does not matter that the money may be perfectly preserved underground. The fact that the *shomer* cannot locate an item in his care is itself a failure of custodial responsibility. *Zil shleim* — go pay. If the *shomer* eventually finds the money, it is his to keep, since he will have already compensated the owner. But at the moment of the claim, the loss is attributed to negligence and he must pay.

---

## Son & Mother

### Mother's Box

A new case: *hahu gavra d'afkid zuzei gabei chavreih* — a person deposited money with his friend. *Ashalminhu l'imei* — the *shomer* gave the money to his mother for safekeeping. *V'otvinhu b'kartsilita* — she placed it in a box. *V'ignov* — and it was stolen. She had not buried it in the ground.

*Rava* asks: *heichi nadaynu dayanei l'hai dina* — how should the judges rule? One might say to the son: you are liable; you should have buried this money and instead handed it off to your mother who kept it in a box. But the son has a response.

### Own Money Theory

The son argues: *kol hamafkid al daat ishto uvanav hu mafkid* — whoever deposits something with a *shomer* implicitly understands that the *shomer* may hand it over to his family members to watch, and this is tacitly accepted. Giving money to one's mother (presumably within the framework of one's household) is not a violation of the rules of *shomer she-masar l'shomer*; it falls within normal, accepted practice. So the act of transferring the money to the mother was not itself negligent. The application of *kol hamafkid* extends not only downward to children but also upward to parents, at least in cases of household proximity.

But then why did the mother not bury it? *Lo amar li d'lav deidei ninhu d'akvinhu* — he did not tell me it was not his own money. I assumed my son was handing me his personal funds to keep safe. For my own son's money, I put it in a box — a perfectly reasonable precaution for money I believed belonged to a family member. Had I known it was someone else's money, entrusted to my son with a full duty of care, I would have buried it in the ground.

So was the son negligent for not telling her? He responds: *kol shekein d'ki amina lah d'didi ninhu tfei mizdahara behu* — on the contrary, I deliberately did not tell her it was someone else's money, because I believed that if she thought it was *my* money, she would take even greater care of it. A mother is more protective of her own child's property than a stranger's. The son gambled on this assumption and believed his silence actually *increased* the level of care.

One might reasonably question whether this reasoning exonerates the son. He had a duty of care, and he discharged it based on an assumption rather than by ensuring the facts were communicated. If a reasonable person would not have made the same assumption, the son's reliance on it should be considered negligent. The *gemara* appears to entertain the possibility that nobody was negligent here — that each party acted on reasonable assumptions.

### Both Swear

*Rava* resolves the case: *mishtaba ihu de-hanei zuzei asminhu l'imei* — let the son swear that he indeed handed the money over to his mother; *u-mishtaba imei de-hanei zuzei asvinhu b'kartilya v'ignu* — and let the mother swear that she placed them in the box and they were stolen from there. *U-patur* — and then both are exempt.

The structure of the oaths is noteworthy. Rather than requiring them to swear to the reasoning behind their choices — that the son believed his mother would be more careful if she thought it was his money, or that the mother genuinely believed it was her son's — the *gemara* requires them to swear only to the facts. This likely connects to the broader principle established by *Rav Nachman* that a *shomer* must swear that the item is *eino bireshuso* — no longer in his possession. The son swears he transferred the money to his mother; she swears it was stolen from the box. Given those facts, the legal conclusion is that neither party was negligent — a resolution that may strike one as generous, but that is the *gemara*'s ruling.

### Tosafot Concern

*Tosafot* raises a significant question about the law of *shomer she-masar l'shomer* in this case. *Rabbeinu Tam* explains the ruling of *kol hamafkid al daat ishto uvanav hu mafkid* as follows: the implicit permission to hand the deposit to family members means that the *shomer* does not automatically become liable for the mere act of transfer. Normally, *shomer she-masar l'shomer* without authorization renders the first *shomer* liable for everything that subsequently happens, even *oness*. Here, because the transfer is implicitly authorized, that automatic liability does not apply.

But *Tosafot* insists: *aval im pash'u* — if the second party, the family member, was actually negligent, *afilu ein lahem mah l'shalem* — even if they have no assets from which to collect, *yeshalem hanifkad* — the original *shomer* remains fully liable to the owner. The reasoning is stark: *d'im lo ken, kol mah she-hiphkid etzel baal ha-bayis tavo ishto v'sochal v'tipater* — otherwise one could devise an obvious scheme: accept a deposit, hand it to one's wife, she consumes it, she has no independent assets since *kani isha kanah baalah* applies, and neither party is collectible. Such a result would be absurd. Therefore, even when the transfer to family is authorized, the original *shomer* retains full responsibility for any negligence on the part of whoever he transfers to. The family member may also bear direct liability to the owner, but so does the original *shomer* — he cannot use the permitted transfer as a shield against liability for their failures.

---

## Toothless Cow

### Cow Setup

A new case involving an *apotropos* — an overseer managing the estate of orphans: *hahu apotropos d'yasmi d'zaven lehu tora l'yasmi* — the overseer purchased an ox for the orphans with their funds. *U'mashlei l'bakra* — he gave the ox over to a cowherd to tend. *Lo hava lei kichi v'shinei l'meichal* — it turned out the ox had no incisors or molars and could not eat. *U'meis* — the ox died. The cowherd had been throwing food to a large herd; this particular animal did not eat, was not noticed, and starved.

### Liability Split

*Rami bar Chama* poses the question: how should the judges rule? Tell the *apotropos* to pay the orphans — he was negligent for purchasing a defective animal without inspection. The *apotropos* responds: *ana l'bakra masartei* — I handed it over to the cowherd; the ongoing care was his responsibility. Tell the cowherd to pay: *ana bahadei tori ukmintei v'shadai lehu* — I put him together with all the other cattle and fed them all; *lo yadan d'lo achal* — I had no way of knowing this particular animal wasn't eating.

### Cowherd Liable

The *gemara* cuts through the ambiguity: *michdi bakra shomer sachar d'yasmi hu* — the cowherd is the orphans' *shomer sachar*, being paid for his work. *Itba'ei lei l'iyunei* — a *shomer sachar* cannot discharge his duty merely by performing the mechanical acts of care; he must exercise active attention. Simply throwing food to the herd is not sufficient when one is being paid precisely to ensure the animals are thriving. If this were the complete picture — the orphans suffer a loss because their paid guardian failed to notice the ox was not eating — the cowherd would clearly be liable.

### Mekach Taus

But there is a complicating twist: *d'leka pseda d'yasmi* — the orphans in fact suffered no loss. How? *D'ashkechu l'marei d'tora v'shakal yasmi zuzai minei* — the orphans located the original seller of the ox and demanded a refund on the grounds that the animal lacked molars. The seller conceded — this was a *mekach taus*, a defective sale — and refunded their money. This retroactive *mekach taus* means the ox was, in effect, never the orphans' property; ownership reverted to the original seller. So the ox that died belonged to the original seller. Who is the cowherd liable to?

He was hired by the orphans, not by the original seller. They had no contractual relationship. Yet the cowherd was, in fact, watching the original owner's cow, even if neither party knew it at the time. This generates the question of whether *de facto* possession and care of someone's property creates legal obligations toward that person even without a direct contract — a question *Tosafot* will address explicitly.

### Middleman

A further complication: the *gemara* identifies the seller as a *safsera*, a middleman — *d'zabin me-hacha u-mazbin le-hacha* — he purchased the ox from a farmer and resold it to the orphans for profit, without inspecting it. He did not know about the missing teeth, and the farmer from whom he bought it has presumably disappeared. The *safsera*, acting in good faith, returns the orphans' money because the ox was defective — he acknowledges the *mekach taus* even though it was unwitting on his part. But now he turns to the cowherd: *ibaye leh le-hoduan* — you should have informed me of the problem so I could have retrieved the animal or done something about it.

The *gemara* asks: why does the *safsera* have any claim? He knew he was selling a cow; if it had a defect, he should have known. The answer: because he is a middleman who acquired the animal from someone else without knowing of the defect, his ignorance is genuine and his grievance against the cowherd is real. He would have acted differently had he known.

### Meat Value

The *gemara* rules: *mishtava ihu de-la havah yada* — let the *safsera* swear that he genuinely did not know the animal lacked teeth. Once he swears to his ignorance, *u-mashlim bakra dmei basar bezol* — the cowherd pays him the wholesale value of the meat.

Why the wholesale value of the meat, rather than the full value of the cow? *Rashi* suggests it reflects a kind of sliding scale of partial negligence, which is conceptually difficult — liability normally operates as a binary, either you are liable for the full amount or you are not liable at all. *Tosafot* offers a more analytically satisfying answer: what should the cowherd have done upon noticing the ox was not eating? The responsible action would have been to slaughter it immediately before it died entirely, preserving whatever value could be salvaged. The most that could have been recovered at an off-market slaughter is the wholesale price for the meat. Therefore, the cowherd is liable for exactly what his timely intervention would have saved: *dmei basar bezol*. He failed to take the action that would have protected that much value, so he must compensate for it.

### De Facto Shomer

*Tosafot* then addresses the fundamental question this case raises: why is the cowherd liable to the original owner at all, given that he never contracted with him? *Tosafot* ties this to the *mishna* earlier in the *perek*: when one person rents an animal from another and lends it to a third party, *Rabbi Yosi* objects — *keitzad halah oseh s'chora be-parato shel chaveiro?* How can one make business with another's animal? — and rules that the *sho'el* must pay the original owner.

*Tosafot* reads this not merely as a moral objection but as a legal principle: the *sho'el*'s actual use of the original owner's animal may create a borrower relationship *de facto*, regardless of whether any contract was concluded directly between them. Applied here: the orphans purchased the cow (or so everyone thought), the cowherd was hired by the orphans to watch it, and it turned out to be the original owner's cow. The cowherd's being paid to tend this animal may constitute a *de facto* guardianship relationship with whoever the true owner is — even without any direct agreement. This is a far-reaching principle: legal obligations arising from *shomrim* relationships can be generated by the factual reality of whose property one is caring for, not solely by whose name appears in the contract.

---

## Mixed Hops

### Wrong Pile

A final case: *hahu gavra de'afkid kishuta gabei chavreih* — a person deposited a quantity of hops with his friend. *Hava lei ledidei nami karya dekishuta* — the *shomer* was himself in the beer-making business and had his own pile of hops. *Amar lei lesarsayeih meihai rami* — he instructed his employee to put hops into the brewing vessel, pointing to his own pile. *Azal rami me'idach* — the employee went and took hops from the other pile — the one belonging to the owner of the deposit — and used those instead.

### Negligence Split

*Rav Papa* poses the question: how should the judges rule? Tell the *shomer* to pay the owner: *ana amari lei meihai rami* — I told my attendant to take from this pile (mine), and he took from that one (yours). Tell the attendant to pay: *lo amar li meihai rami meihai rami* — he did not specify *only* this pile and *not* that one; I did not understand there to be a meaningful distinction.

The underlying question is one of reasonable expectation. If the attendant's interpretation — that both piles were interchangeable — was a reasonable one to hold, then the *shomer* should have been more explicit and bears the responsibility for the confusion. If, on the other hand, one should assume that explicit instructions to take from a specific pile exclude all other piles, then the attendant who deviated bears the responsibility. The *gemara* has not yet resolved which assumption governs.

One clarifying factor: *ve'i deshaha shahi lei le'aituyei velo aiti lei* — if the two piles were at different distances, and the attendant was late in returning, the delay itself is evidence that he went to the farther pile. *Gali da'ateih denicha lei* — the *shomer*'s silence upon observing the delay would constitute implicit acquiescence, and the *shomer* would bear the loss. *Bedela shaha* — but in the case where the piles were adjacent and there was no delay, no such inference is available.

### Benefit Principle

The *gemara* cuts through the negligence analysis with a shortcut: *sof sof mai psida ika, ha ka mishtarshi lei* — ultimately, where is the loss? The *shomer*'s beer was improved by the owner's hops. His hops ended up in the *shomer*'s beer. Whatever the question of negligence, the *shomer* benefited from the owner's property without authorization. The remedy is simple: pay back the value of what you benefited from. The technical legal concept here is *mishtarshi lei* — the benefit has taken root in the *shomer*'s property, an idea familiar from *Bava Kamma*'s principle of *meshalem ma she'nehenit*: one who derives benefit from another's property, even absent tortious conduct, must compensate for that benefit.

If the hops improved the *shomer*'s beer, the question of who was negligent becomes largely irrelevant — simply return the value of the hops, and the matter is resolved without needing to adjudicate fault.

### Damage Case

*Rav Sama the son of Rava* introduces a variation: *dehavah shikhra chala* — what if the owner's hops turned the *shomer*'s beer to vinegar? Now there is no benefit to repay; indeed, the *shomer* suffered a loss. The benefit-based shortcut is unavailable. The *shomer* cannot claim compensation from the owner for ruining his beer — that was the result of the employee's actions, for which the *shomer* bears at least some responsibility. But by the same token, the owner cannot invoke *mishtarshi lei* because his hops did not benefit anyone. So we are back to the fundamental question of who was negligent, and the resolution of that question cannot be bypassed.

### Inferior Hops

*Rav Ashi* introduces yet another variation: *bekisi umashlim lei d'mei kisi* — what if the owner's hops were of inferior quality? In that case, the *shomer*'s beer was neither improved nor ruined but perhaps slightly degraded, or the "benefit," such as it is, represents inferior value compared to what the *shomer*'s own hops would have produced. This muddies the *mishtarshi lei* analysis, since the benefit received is not straightforwardly equivalent to the loss suffered.

### Unresolved

The *gemara* ultimately leaves the core negligence question unresolved. It may be suggesting that where *mishtarshi lei* applies — where the *shomer* genuinely benefited from the owner's hops — negligence is irrelevant and repayment is owed regardless. Where there is no benefit — when the hops soured the beer — one must determine who was negligent, and the *gemara* does not deliver a clean ruling. What runs through this case, and indeed through many of the cases on this *amud*, is a recurring pattern: the *gemara* repeatedly imagines situations where multiple parties each acted on reasonable assumptions and neither was clearly negligent. From one perspective, this seems lenient toward *shomrim* — the *gemara* is willing to construct scenarios in which no one bears primary fault. From another perspective, one might argue that the *shomer*, having accepted the fundamental responsibility of custody, ought to bear the consequences when things go wrong even through others' actions, unless a truly clear *oness* is present. That tension between the reasonable-assumptions framework and the *shomer*'s primary responsibility remains alive and unresolved as the *daf* concludes.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 43

## Mapkid & Shulchani

### Mishnah: Tzrurim/Mutarim

The daf opens at a new *mishnah* at the top of 43a. The *mishnah* presents the following case: *hamapkid ma'os eitzel shulchani* — if one deposits money with a *shulchani*, a professional money changer. If the coins are *tzrurim* — bound up together in a leather pouch — then *lo yishtamesh bahem*, the *shulchani* may not use them. Consequently, *im avdu eino chayav be'achrayutam* — if the money is lost, the *shulchani* bears no liability, since he functions as a *shomer chinam*, a free watchman with minimal duties.

If, however, the coins are *mutarim* — unbound, given over as a loose stack — then *yishtamesh bahem*, the *shulchani* may use them. *Lefichach im avdu chayav be'achrayutam* — therefore if they are lost, he bears full liability. The *gemara* will raise the question of whether this liability attaches only from the moment he actually uses the money, or whether it kicks in even before that. This is a persistent question in the laws of *shoel*, since a *shoel* bears liability even in cases of *ones* — unavoidable accident — and the precise moment that liability commences is debated at length by the *rishonim*, including *Tosafot* and the *Ritva*.

By contrast, the *mishnah* continues: *eitzel ba'al habayit* — if the money was given to a private householder — *bein tzrurim bein mutarim*, whether bound or unbound, *lo yishtamesh bahem*, the householder may not use them. Since there is no professional context suggesting any commercial understanding, the deposit is treated as a straightforward *shomer chinam* arrangement in either case. When money is left unbound with the *shulchani*, however, the assumption is that the depositor intended the *shulchani* to operate at a higher level of liability — with the concomitant right to use the funds — since giving unbound coins to a money changer reflects the customary commercial practice of that role. The *mishnah* closes with a dispute: *Rabbi Meir* holds that a shopkeeper (*chanvani*) is like a *ba'al habayit* — no assumed right to use the money. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that a *chanvani* is like a *shulchani*, since shopkeepers, too, routinely require access to deposited funds. The distinction appears to rest on local commercial norms rather than a deep conceptual divide.

### Tzror Hamot Definition

One might wonder what precisely a *tzror* looks like. The *mishnah* in *Kelim* addresses *tzror hamot* — a bound coin-pouch — and rules it *tahor*, not susceptible to *tumah*, because it is not considered a *keli*. The reason is that the flat piece of leather used to wrap coins is continuously opened and closed, like a wallet, so it never conforms to the shape of its contents and does not acquire the status of a vessel. By contrast, a *tzror hamargalit* — a pouch of jewels — is left tied for extended periods and conforms to the shape of the gems inside, and therefore does qualify as a *keli* and is *tamei*. The biblical phrase *vetzarta hakesef* likewise relates to this concept. The *tzror* should be thought of as a wallet: giving one's wallet to the *shulchani* signals an intent merely to have him watch it, while handing over loose coins — like depositing money in a bank — signals an expectation that he will invest or use the funds and bear correspondingly greater liability.

The *gemara* then asks: is it really merely because the coins are bound that the *shulchani* may not use them? *Amar Rabbi Assi amar Rabbi Yehuda*: the *mishnah* must be referring to coins that were not only bound but also sealed — *tzrurim ve'chatumim* — with a signet impression placed on the binding. For even a wallet handed to a *shulchani* might otherwise be presumed usable, since his very trade involves handling coins. Only an explicit seal communicates that the depositor intends the *shulchani* to serve purely as *shomer*. Separately, *Rav Mari* states — or according to an alternative version, inquires — that perhaps a distinctive knot (*kesher meshuneh*) suffices as that signal, analogous to the personal identifying knots discussed earlier in *Eilu Metzios*. The alternative version leaves this as an unresolved *teiku*. There is a *Tosafot* in *Avodah Zarah* (around daf 9) that lists four different opinions regarding the halachic weight of *ika d'amri* formulations.

### When Liability Begins

The *gemara* returns to the case of *mutarim*: if the coins are unbound, the *shulchani* may use them. The question now is what category of *shomer* this makes him — *shomer sachar* or *shoel* — and when precisely his elevated liability commences.

### Huna v. Nachman

*Amar Rav Huna v'afilu ne'ensu* — *Rav Huna* states that the *shulchani* is liable even in a case of *ones*, treating him as a *shoel*, the category bearing the highest level of liability. The *gemara* objects that the *mishnah* uses the language *avdu* — they were lost — which sounds more consistent with *shomer sachar* liability (covering theft but not necessarily *ones*). *Rav Huna* must therefore be reading the *mishnah* according to *Rabba*, who holds that *nignevu b'listim mezuyan* — theft by armed robbers — is the scenario designated by "theft" in such contexts, since even a *shomer sachar* is exempt in cases of armed robbery; and *avdu* — lost — refers not to ordinary loss but to a genuine *ones* such as a shipwreck. On this reading, the *mishnah*'s language is entirely consistent with *shoel*-level liability.

*Rav Nachman* disagrees: *ne'ensu lo* — in a case of *ones*, the *shulchani* is not liable. The *shulchani* is therefore a *shomer sachar*, not a *shoel*. *Rava* challenges *Rav Nachman*: if you say the *shulchani* is not liable in *ones*, then he is not a *shoel*. But if he is not a *shoel*, what makes him a *shomer sachar*? A *shomer sachar* receives payment for watching; what payment does the *shulchani* receive for merely guarding the money if he cannot use it? *Rav Nachman* responds: *be'ha modina lach* — on this point I agree with you — *de'ho'il ve'nehene mimena*, since the *shulchani* does derive a benefit from the money in his possession. Specifically, *de'ee mitrami lei zabina de'is bah ravcha zavin behu* — if a particularly profitable commercial opportunity arises, he is permitted to draw on those funds to purchase at a favorable price and repay them later. That benefit — the standing option to use the money in advantageous circumstances — constitutes the *hana'ah* that qualifies him as a *shomer sachar*.

This reasoning is analogous in structure, though opposite in direction, to the case of *pruta de'Rav Yosef* discussed earlier. The mere ability to use the money in the ordinary course of changing coins of equal value does not itself constitute meaningful *hana'ah* — exchanging a large coin for smaller denominations confers no monetary gain. But the ability to access the funds when an exceptional deal presents itself is a real financial advantage, and that suffices.

### Tosefta: Gizbar Case

*Rav Nachman* now challenges *Rav Huna*'s position. He cites a *Tosefta* from *Masechet Meilah* involving a *gizbar*, a Temple treasury officer, who inadvertently deposited *hekdesh* funds with a *shulchani*. The *Tosefta* mirrors the structure of our *mishnah*: if the coins were bound (*tzuruvin*), the *shulchani* should not use them; if he did take them out (*im hotzi*), the *gizbar* has not committed *me'ilah*, since the wrongdoing belongs entirely to the *shulchani*, while the *gizbar* acted in error. If the coins were unbound, the *shulchani* may use them; if he then takes them out, *ma'al ha-gizbar* — the *gizbar* has committed *me'ilah* — even though his deposit was itself unintentional, as he confused these funds with non-sacred property.

The key point: the *Tosefta* says *im hotzi* — if he took them out — implying the liability is triggered at the moment of removal. *Rav Nachman* presses: if *Rav Huna* holds the *shulchani* is a *shoel*, liable even in *ones*, then the *gizbar*'s *me'ilah* should attach the moment the unbound coins are handed over — *afilu lo hotzi nami*, even if they were never taken out. Why does the *Tosefta* specify *im hotzi*?

*Rav Huna* responds: *hu ha-din af al gav de-lo hotzi* — the same ruling would indeed apply even without the *hotza'ah*; the *Tosefta*'s use of *hotzi* is merely a structural parallel to the preceding clause, not a limiting condition. The *mishnah* formulates both clauses using *hotzi* for stylistic consistency, and one need not read strict legal precision into that parallelism. The broader question of precisely when *shoel*-level liability attaches remains a significant *machloket* among the *rishonim* and is not definitively resolved here.

---

## Shlichut Yad Overview

### Mishnah: B.S./B.H.

The next *mishnah* introduces the topic of *shlichut yad*: *ha-sholeiach yad be-pikadon* — a *shomer* who misappropriates the deposited object. *Beis Shammai omrim yilkeh be-chaser u-ve-yeser* — *Beis Shammai* rules that the *shomer* always suffers the less favorable outcome: if the object depreciated, he pays the higher original value; if it appreciated, he still pays only the lower original value. In either direction, the *shomer* who committed *shlichut yad* bears the maximum burden, since he was *poshea*.

*Beis Hillel omrim ki-sh'as hotza'ah* — *Beis Hillel* says assessment is made at the time of *hotza'ah*, the precise meaning of which the *gemara* will explore. *Rabbi Akiva omer ke-sha'as ha-tviah* — *Rabbi Akiva* rules that assessment goes by the time of the court proceeding. This discussion closely parallels the analysis in *Bava Kamma* in *Perek Merubah*, where similar questions arose about when to assess *kefel* and *arba'ah va-chamishah* — at the time of theft or the time of litigation.

### Rava: Wine Barrel Case

*Rava* presents a foundational case: one who steals a barrel of wine from his fellow. Initially it was worth one *zuz*; afterward the price rose to four *zuz*. If the thief broke the barrel or drank the wine himself — *tavrah o shatyei* — he pays four *zuz*, the value at the time of his action. If the barrel broke on its own — *itbar mimeila* — he pays only one *zuz*, the value at the time of theft.

This is a striking ruling. A *gazlan* is ordinarily liable even in cases of *ones* — so why does an accidental breakage after theft yield only one *zuz* rather than four? The answer lies in the structure of the *gazlan*'s liability: the only action he performed was the theft itself. With no subsequent act of his own to establish a new valuation point, the only moment at which his liability can be calculated is the time of the theft — and at that moment it was worth one *zuz*. But when the *gazlan* breaks or drinks it, he has taken a new action, and that action creates a new moment at which the value must be assessed — at which point it is worth four. *Keivan de'ee ita hadra lemareih be'eina* — so long as the object exists intact, the owner could in principle demand it back *in specie*; but once the *gazlan* destroys or consumes it, the obligation converts into a monetary payment assessed at that moment.

The *gemara* confirms: *kol ha-gazlanim meshalmin ki-sh'at ha-gezeila* — all robbers pay according to the value at the time of theft. Hence the case of accidental breakage: *hashta lo avid velo midi* — since the *gazlan* did nothing at that later moment, there is no basis to calculate a new value, and one returns to the baseline of the theft itself. This *sugya* — examined at length by the *Ketzos* and the *Nesivos* — touches on fundamental questions of ownership, liability, and what it means for a thief to acquire title to stolen property.

### Action Requirement

The *gemara* now turns to the connection between *Rava*'s ruling and the dispute between *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* in our *mishnah* about *shlichut yad*. *Tnan Beis Hillel omrim ki-sh'at hotza'ah* — the *mishnah* says *Beis Hillel* assesses at the time of *hotza'ah*. What does this mean?

One possibility: *hotza'ah min ha-olam* — removal from the world, i.e., consumption. But this creates problems: if the value declined, the principle *kol ha-gazlanim meshalmin ki-sh'at ha-gezeila* would already resolve the matter; and if it increased, that yields the same result as *Beis Shammai*. This reading therefore fails.

The more natural reading: *hotza'ah me-beis be'alim* — removal from the owner's domain, i.e., the moment the *shomer* took it from the owner's house to begin his *shmirah*. But on this reading, *Rava*'s ruling — that the *shomer* pays four when he breaks or drinks it — appears to align with *Beis Shammai*, since *Beis Shammai* also traces liability back to an early moment rather than the time of consumption. Can *Rava* be holding like *Beis Shammai*? The *gemara* deflects: *Rava* must read the *machloket* between *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* as *Rabba* does — *v'yeter kulei alma lo pligi*, that if the object appreciated in value, everyone agrees the *shomer* who committed *shlichut yad* pays the higher value. The *shomer* is always *yada tachtona* — he holds the weakest position — so if the highest claim can be made against him, he has no defense. *Ki pligi be-chaser* — the dispute applies only when the object lost value.

### Chisaron Requirement

With the *machloket* narrowed to cases of depreciation, the *gemara* articulates the underlying conceptual dispute. *Beis Shammai savri shlichut yad einah tzericha chisaron* — *Beis Shammai* holds that *shlichut yad* does not require any actual diminution of the object's value. A *shomer* who appropriates the object — even in a way that causes no physical loss — has already committed *shlichut yad*, and subsequent depreciation occurs *bi-reshutei didei*, in the domain of the one who has already effectively stolen it. *Beis Hillel savri shlichut yad tzericha chisaron* — *Beis Hillel* holds that *shlichut yad* requires an actual loss. The object must be diminished or consumed in some way before the act qualifies as *shlichut yad*; and because the first loss occurs before that threshold is crossed, it takes place *bi-reshut de-marei*, while still legally in the owner's domain.

Under *Beis Hillel*, then, if a *shomer* merely moves a barrel of wine without consuming any, that is not *shlichut yad* — moving the barrel does not depreciate it.

The *gemara* raises the question of *Rabba*'s position. *Rabba* elsewhere states that *shlichut yad einah tzericha chisaron* — seemingly aligning him with *Beis Shammai*. The *gemara* presses: *leima Rabbah de-amar ke-Veit Shammai*? Rather than accept that conclusion, the *gemara* proposes three successive reinterpretations of the *Beis Shammai*/*Beis Hillel* dispute, each of which would allow *Rabba* to remain within the orbit of *Beis Hillel*:

The first attempt reads the *machloket* as concerning a case of *she-tiltela le-havi aleha gozal* — the *shomer* used the barrel as a stepladder to retrieve his doves, causing no damage whatsoever. The *machloket* is then *u-ve-sho'el she-lo mi-da'at kamiphalgi* — whether borrowing an object without the owner's knowledge constitutes *gezeila* or merely *she'ilah*. *Beis Shammai savri sho'el she-lo mi-da'at gazlan havei* — unauthorized borrowing is tantamount to theft, so depreciation thereafter occurs in the *gazlan*'s domain. *Beis Hillel savri sho'el she-lo mi-da'at sho'el havei* — it is merely borrowing, and depreciation falls in the owner's domain. But *Rava* rules that *le-rabbanan*, unauthorized borrowing is like *gezeila* — so does *Rava* then hold like *Beis Shammai*? This attempt also fails.

The fourth and final attempt reads the *machloket* as concerning *shevach shel gezeila* — the natural increase of a stolen object, such as wool that continues to grow on a stolen sheep. *Beis Shammai savri shevach gezeila de-nigzal havei* — the natural growth belongs to the original owner. *Beis Hillel savri shevach gezeila de-gazlan havei* — once stolen, the subsequent growth belongs to the thief. The *gemara* supports this reading by noting that *Beis Shammai*'s language — *yilkeh be-chaser u-ve-yeser* — suggests physical growth and shrinkage of the object itself, not market price fluctuations. This aligns with a parallel *machloket* among *Tannaim*: *Rabbi Meir* holds the thief must pay back the sheep along with its wool and lambs, while *Rabbi Yehuda* holds the thief returns only what was taken, keeping the natural increase. *Dayka nami de-katani* — the precise language of the *mishnah* supports this reading.

The underlying conceptual question — the relationship between *kinyanei gezeila*, the quasi-ownership a thief acquires at the moment of theft, and the subsequent liability for appreciation and depreciation — is what unifies these four attempts and what gives the *sugya* its richness.

---

## Timing of Assessment

### Hotza'ah Definition

The *mishnah*'s phrase *ki-sh'at hotza'ah* continues to require clarification. The initial suggestion — *hotza'ah min ha-olam*, meaning when the object was consumed — has already been set aside. The working assumption is now *hotza'ah me-reshut be'alim*, the moment the object left the owner's domain and came into the *shomer*'s possession. It is this moment, under *Beis Hillel*, at which the value is assessed.

The interplay between *Rava*'s ruling about the wine barrel — *tavrah o shatyei meshalem arba'ah* — and the *Beis Hillel* principle proves subtle. As analyzed above, *Rabba* resolves the apparent tension by restricting the *machloket* to cases of natural growth or depreciation (*chaser* and *yeter*) rather than market fluctuations. If the value increased, all agree the *shomer* pays the higher value; the dispute concerns only whether the first loss occurs in the thief's domain or the owner's domain.

A further question underlies the analysis: is *shlichut yad* by the *shomer* categorized as *gezeila*? The *sugya* confirms this comparison: the *shomer* who commits *shlichut yad* is treated as a *gazlan*, and it is precisely this parallel that makes *Rava*'s case about the wine barrel directly relevant to our *mishnah*. Conversely, what distinguishes *sho'el she-lo mi-da'at* from a *gazlan* is not the external liability structure — both are liable in *ones* — but rather the question of *kinyan*: whether the unauthorized borrower acquires title to the object in the way a *gazlan* does, and what consequences flow from that for appreciation and depreciation of the object's value.

### R. Akiva: Tviah

*Rabbi Akiva* holds that assessment goes by the time of the court proceeding — *ke-sha'as ha-tviah*. This is a coherent position: the court is the institution that formally determines liability, and it is therefore reasonable that the operative moment for valuation should be the moment the court adjudicates.

### Shmuel v. R. Yochanan

*Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: the *halacha* follows *Rabbi Akiva*. Since we generally rule like *Shmuel* in monetary law, this carries significant weight. At the same time, a question is posed from *Rav Assi* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *chaluk hayah Rabbi Akiva afilu bi-makom she-yesh eidim* — *Rabbi Akiva* maintained his position even where there are witnesses who observed the act. This sets up a direct tension between the Babylonian tradition (*Shmuel* via *Rav Yehuda*) and the *Eretz Yisrael* tradition (*Rabbi Yochanan* via *Rav Assi*).

*Rava* ultimately rules: *halacha ke-Veit Hillel* — the *halacha* follows *Beis Hillel*, not *Rabbi Akiva*. This follows the tradition of *Shmuel*, which the *gemara* privileges via the principle *hilkha ke-vatra* — the *halacha* follows the latest *amora* named in a *sugya*. *Rashi* (whose ruling closely parallels that of the *Rif*) writes: *ki-sh'at gezeila ve-anan ke-Rava avinan de-havei lei batra* — we follow *Rava* as the latest opinion, and *Rava* rules like *Beis Hillel*. In *Eretz Yisrael*, the *psak* followed *Rabbi Akiva*; in Babylon, the ruling followed *Beis Hillel*. The interplay of these traditions makes this one of the more instructive windows into *klalei ha-psak* in the *gemara*.

### Witnesses & Ashma

The dispute between *Rav Yehuda*/*Shmuel* and *Rav Assi*/*Rabbi Yochanan* turns on the status of witnesses in this context. *Shmuel*'s position as transmitted by *Rav Yehuda* is: *modeh Rabbi Akiva bi-makom she-yesh eidim* — *Rabbi Akiva* concedes that where there are witnesses, the assessment follows the time they observed the act, not the time of the court proceeding. The source is the verse: *la-asher hu lo yitnenu be-yom ashmato* — "he shall give it to its owner on the day of his guilt." Where witnesses observed the theft, the day of *ashmah* is the day of the act itself.

*Rabbi Yochanan*, however, rules that *Rabbi Akiva* maintains his position even with witnesses: *Beis din hu de-kamachayvei leh ashma* — it is the *beis din* that creates the legal reality of *ashmah*, not the witnesses. This is a profound distinction. Witnesses establish the facts; the court establishes the legal status. Whether a person is *halachically* a criminal — bearing all the attendant consequences — is determined at the moment the court rules, not the moment the act was observed. The consequences for questions such as witness disqualification, monetary liability, and the broader category of personal criminal status make this more than an academic point.

*Rav Ashi* adds: *le-olam* in *Rabbi Yochanan*'s formulation — *halacha ke-Rabbi Akiva le-olam* — comes to exclude the possibility of reading *Rabbi Akiva*'s ruling as limited to cases without witnesses. Furthermore, *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position serves to exclude *Rabbi Yishmael*, who holds that *da'as be'alim* — the owner's awareness — is not required. *Rabbi Akiva*, by tying liability to the court proceeding, ensures that by the time judgment is rendered the owner will necessarily be aware.

### Rava Psak: B.H.

*Rava amar halacha ke-Veit Hillel* — *Rava* rules definitively in favor of *Beis Hillel*. This is presented not as a novel argument but as a ruling grounded in the *Shmuel*-*Rav Yehuda* tradition. As noted, *Rashi* and the *Rif* both confirm that we follow *Rava* here by virtue of the principle *hilkha ke-vatra*. The tension between the *Eretz Yisrael* tradition (following *Rabbi Akiva* via *Rabbi Yochanan*) and the Babylonian tradition (following *Beis Hillel* via *Shmuel* and *Rava*) illustrates the complexity of determining *psak* when authoritative chains of transmission point in different directions. In this case the Babylonian tradition prevails: assessment is made at the time of *hotza'ah* from the owner's domain, consistent with *Beis Hillel*.

---

## Chavita Shomre

### Intent v. Action

The *mishnah* continues with *ha-choshev li-shlo'ach yad be-pikadon* — a *shomer* who merely intends to commit *shlichut yad* but has not yet done so. *Beis Shammai omrim chayav* — from the moment of intent, liability attaches. *Beis Hillel omrim eino chayav ad she-yishlach bo yad* — liability does not attach until the *shomer* physically acts on that intent.

*Beis Shammai*'s position implies a form of mental crime: the instant one resolves to misappropriate the deposit, one has violated the terms of *shmirah* and forfeited the status of *shomer*. *Beis Hillel* grounds their ruling in the verse: *im lo shalach yado bi-mlechet rei'ehu* — "if he did not put his hand to his fellow's property." The verse explicitly conditions guilt on a physical act, not an intention.

*Rashi* is notably uncomfortable with reading *Beis Shammai* as establishing genuine liability from thought alone. He glosses *Beis Shammai*'s position as: *omer lifnei eidim ekachena le-atzmi ve-eshtamesh bah* — that the *shomer* declares his intent before witnesses, thereby concretizing what might otherwise be a purely internal state. This reading removes the full force of the *Beis Shammai* position, but *Rashi* clearly finds the plain reading — that unspoken thought creates criminal liability — untenable in *halacha*. It should be noted, however, that there are other contexts in *halacha* — such as certain aspects of the laws of *get* — where a person's declared intention carries significant legal consequences.

### Braita: Pasha

The *gemara* cites a *braita* exploring the source of this *machloket*. The verse *al kol davar pasha* — "for every manner of crime" — is invoked by *Beis Shammai* to argue that even a mental act of appropriation constitutes *psha*, transgression. *Beis Hillel* counters with the verse *im lo shalach yado*, arguing that actual physical contact is required. *Beis Shammai* rejoins: if so, what is the purpose of *al kol davar pasha*? *Beis Hillel* responds: that phrase extends liability to cases where the *shomer* instructed his slave or agent (*shaliach*) to commit the act on his behalf — *amar le-avdo u-lishlucho minayin? Talmud lomar al kol davar pasha*. This is one of the three exceptions to the general principle of *ein shaliach li-dvar aveirah* — that agency does not apply to sinful acts — alongside *tivicha u-mechira* and *me'ilah*. According to *Beis Hillel*, when a *shomer* instructs another to steal the *pikadon* on his behalf, the *shomer* bears responsibility, invoking *shlichut yad* through an agent.

### Tilting Barrel

The *mishnah* introduces two graduated cases. First: *hita et ha-chavit ve-natal heimena revi'it ve-nishbera* — if the *shomer* tilted the barrel and took out one glass of wine and the barrel then broke, he pays only for the *revi'it*, the single glass he removed. Second: *higbi'ah ve-natal heimena revi'it ve-nishbera* — if he lifted the entire barrel and took one glass and then it broke, *meshalem dmei kullah*, he pays for the entire barrel. The justification for this distinction emerges in the *gemara*.

*Rabba* adds a further nuance: *lo shanu ela nishbera* — this rule (paying only for the *revi'it*) applies only where the barrel broke. *Aval hachmitza meshalem et kullah* — if the wine soured, he pays for the entire contents. *Mai ta'ama*? *Girei didehu de-ahani leh* — his own "arrow" caused the outcome. By removing wine from the barrel, the *shomer* created airspace at the top, allowing oxidation that soured the remaining wine. There is no intervening break between his act and the spoilage. When the barrel breaks on its own, the causal chain is interrupted; when the wine sours due to the air exposure he created, the damage flows directly from his action.

### Shmuel: Basis Theory

*Amar Shmuel*: the word *natal* in the *mishnah*'s second clause — *higbi'ah ve-natal* — does not mean he actually removed the wine; rather, *keivan she-higbi'ah li-tol*, from the moment he lifted the barrel intending to take from it, even if he has not yet removed anything, he is already liable. This is a striking ruling: lifting the barrel alone, with intent to take, suffices.

One might infer from this that *Shmuel* holds *shlichut yad einah tzericha chisaron* — that *shlichut yad* requires no actual loss. The *gemara* rejects this inference: *shani hacha de-nicha lei de-teihavei ha-chavis kulla basis la-revi'it* — the case is distinctive because when the *shomer* lifts the barrel to extract a single glass, he intends the entire barrel to serve as a *basis*, a support-structure, for that one measure of wine. His intention incorporates the whole barrel into the act; the *chisaron* will still occur when he takes the wine, but his relation to the entire barrel is established at the moment of lifting. This does not imply a general ruling that *shlichut yad* requires no *chisaron*.

This leaves an unresolved question: *ibaiya lei le-Rav Ashi, higbi'ah arneki li-tol heimena dinar* — what if one lifts an entire wallet intending to extract only one coin? *Mahu*? Wine in a barrel floats freely and the upper wine is naturally supported by the lower wine, making the *basis* theory applicable. But a coin in a wallet sits discretely; it is secured by the wallet itself, not by the other coins. *O dilma shani netiruta de-arneki mi-netiruta de-dinar* — or perhaps the guardianship of the wallet and the guardianship of an individual coin within it are categorically distinct, such that the other coins do not serve as *basis* for the one being removed. The question is left as *teiku*, unresolved.

With that, *Perek Hamapkid* concludes, and we proceed to *Perek HaZahav*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 44

## Intro: Money vs Object

### Perek Overview

Daf 44 opens the fourth *perek* of Bava Metzia, *Perek Hazahav*, understood to be among the more challenging *perakim* in *Shas*. The *masechet* has been shifting in its thematic focus: after two *perakim* on *Metzia* and one ostensibly about *shomrim* — though notably without ever establishing the basic principles of *shomrim* — the tractate turns to matters of monetary transactions and *kinyanim*. The fifth *perek* will address lending and *ribbis*; this *perek* begins with the exchange of money for money, and more centrally, with the conceptual framework for what constitutes *kinyan* in purchasing transactions.

The topic of *kinyanim* was touched on in *Kiddushin*, where the question was which act — *hagbahah* or *meshichah* — effects acquisition on a given object. Here, however, the question is different: how does *halacha* conceptualize what counts as money and what counts as object within a given transaction?

### Sale Finality Principle

The foundational *halacha* is as follows: when one sells chattel — *metaltelin*, movable property as opposed to *karka* — the sale is finalized when the buyer takes physical possession of the object, whether by *hagbahah* (lifting it) or *meshichah* (drawing it toward oneself). Payment of money, by itself, does not finalize the sale. The rule is thus clear when dealing with an ordinary commercial transaction: we know what cash is, we know what an object is, and the acquisition is effected by taking hold of the object.

### Currency Exchange Problem

The difficulty arises when both items being exchanged are themselves currency. In the modern context, one might think of exchanging dollars for euros or dollars for shekels — but the *Gemara* is not addressing cross-national currency exchange. Rather, it is concerned with exchanges of different types of coins within a single monetary system. If one person holds gold coins and the other holds silver coins, and they are to be exchanged, which one is the *object* and which is the *money* for purposes of *kinyan*? One cannot say they are both money, because then the sale could never be finalized — *kinyan* applies to the object, not to the money. Yet calling them both objects would be anomalous, since at least one of them is functioning as currency. This is the question that opens the *perek*.

---

## Currency Hierarchy

### Gold/Silver Exchange

The first *mishna* states: *hazahav koneh es hakesef* — gold acquires silver. This requires a careful reversal of intuitive thinking. When we hear "gold buys silver," we might instinctively read *gold* as the buyer, i.e., the money. But that is not what the *mishna* means. The *mishna*'s logic is the opposite: the thing that is *koneh* is the object, and the thing it acquires is the money.

### Koneh Terminology

To understand the terminology: when the *mishna* says X is *koneh* Y, it means X is the object and Y is the money. The *kinyan* is effected by taking possession of X, and at that point Y — the money — is owed. So *hazahav koneh es hakesef* means that in an exchange of gold coins for silver coins, the gold is the object and the silver is the money. If one takes possession of the gold, the silver becomes legally owed. The reverse, however, is not true: *hakesef eino koneh es hazahav* — if one takes possession only of the silver, the transaction is not yet finalized.

Later in the same *mishna*, the statement *kol hametaltelin konin es hamatbeah* — all movable objects acquire currency — illustrates the paradigm case: chattel is the object, coins are the money. The phrasing may seem counterintuitive (we might say "coins buy cattle," not "cattle acquires coins"), but the *mishna*'s language consistently identifies the *koneh* as the object. It is also worth noting that when *metaltelin* are said to "acquire" the *matbeah*, this does not mean one literally owns the specific coins in the other party's pocket; rather, it means the transaction is finalized and the money becomes owed.

### Full Hierarchy Listed

The *mishna* then presents a full hierarchy of currency types. Gold coins are the object vis-à-vis silver — *hazahav koneh es hakesef*. Copper coins are the object vis-à-vis silver — *hanechoshet koneh es hakesef* — while silver is currency vis-à-vis copper. Bad money (*maot raot*) is the object vis-à-vis good money (*hayafot*). The term *maot raot* does not refer to counterfeit currency, which would be too obvious a case. Rather, as *Tosafot* explains, it refers to coins that are not universally accepted — perhaps because they are locally limited in circulation, or because the coins themselves are somewhat damaged and therefore rejected in certain transactions. The widely accepted, reliable currency is the money; the less-accepted is the object.

The *mishna* further addresses the *asimon* — an unminted coin, a blank that has not yet been stamped. Its precious metal content may be identical to a minted coin, but the mint's stamp is what certifies purity and weight and thus confers trustworthiness. The *asimon* is therefore the object vis-à-vis the minted *matbeah*: *asimon koneh es hamatbeah*. The minted coin, functioning as recognized currency, is the money.

### Metaltelin vs Matbeah

The general principle is stated explicitly: *hametaltelin konin es hamatbeah* — movable objects effect *kinyan* on coins — and *hamatbeah eino koneh metaltelin* — coins do not effect *kinyan* on movable objects. This is the paradigm: the object is the chattel, the money is the *matbeah*. One cannot have two moneys in a single transaction, for then no *kinyan* could ever be effected.

### Barter Principle

A different rule applies in barter. *Kol hametaltelin konim zeh es zeh* — when two objects are being exchanged for one another, both function as objects and either one can effect the *kinyan*. If one party takes possession of a cow and the other of a donkey, the transaction is finalized for both. In that scenario, we are not talking about a debt being created — one party literally acquires the concrete object the moment the other takes possession.

---

## Fruit Sale Example

### Drawing Without Paying

The *mishna* now turns to the paradigm case illustrating these principles: a sale of fruit. *Mashach himenu peirot velo nasan lo maos* — if the buyer drew the fruit toward himself, performing *meshichah*, but has not yet paid — *eino yachol lachzor bo* — he cannot retract. The *kinyan* is complete. The object has been taken into possession and the sale is final.

### Paying Without Taking

*Nasan lo maos velo mashach himenu peirot* — if the buyer paid the money but has not yet performed *meshichah* on the fruit — *yachol lachzor bo* — either party may retract. The payment of money alone does not finalize the sale of *metaltelin*.

### Mi Shepara Curse

This creates an ethical problem: if the buyer has paid and the seller can still retract, what prevents the seller from simply taking the money and refusing to deliver? The *mishna* addresses this with the institution of the *mi shepara*. The *beit din* pronounces: the One who exacted retribution from the people of the generation of the flood and the generation of the dispersion will exact retribution from one who does not stand by his word — *hu asid lipara mimi she'eino omed bediburo*. The invocation of *dor hamabul* and *dor hapalaga* is striking, and the *Gemara* will explore the connection further. For now, the point is that while there is no binding legal obligation to complete the transaction, withdrawing after payment has been made incurs this rabbinic censure — a form of curse from the *beit din*.

---

## Fruit Sale Example (II)

### Rabbi Shimon's Rule

*Rabbi Shimon* takes a distinct position: *kol hakesef beyado yado al ha'elyona* — whoever holds the money has the upper hand. According to *Rabbi Shimon*, the ability to retract is not symmetric. When money has been paid but the object not yet taken, it is specifically the one holding the money — the seller — who retains the option to reverse the transaction. The buyer, having relinquished the money, has surrendered his position of control. The practical implication is pointed: paying money without taking the object places all power in the other party's hands. The transaction is not finalized, but only the money-holder can dissolve it.

---

## Rebbi's Position Shift

### Youth vs Old Age

A fascinating *sugya* now emerges. The *Gemara* reports that *Rebbi* taught this *mishna* to his son *Rabbi Shimon* (not the *Rabbi Shimon* of the *mishna*, who is *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai*, but *Rebbi*'s own son). His son pointed out a contradiction: in his youth, *Rebbi* had taught *hakesef koneh es hazahav* — that silver is the object and gold is the money — but now in his old age, he was teaching *hazahav koneh es hakesef* — that gold is the object and silver is the money. The *Gemara* interjects to explain what had changed.

### Youth: Gold Standard

*Beyaldusei savar* — in his youth, *Rebbi* held: *dahava de-chashiv havei tiva* — gold, being the most prestigious and valuable, is the standard currency, the *tiva*. Silver, being of lesser standing, is considered *peira* — the fruit, the object. *Vekani lei peira letiva* — the object (*peira*) is what effects *kinyan* on the currency. In this view, everything is defined relative to gold. When the ratio of silver to gold shifts — say, from 25 silver coins per gold to 20 — one articulates this as "the price of silver went up," not "the price of gold went down," because gold is the fixed reference point. The concept is recognizable from the gold standard of monetary history: one defines the value of everything else in terms of gold, and fluctuations are attributed to the other metals.

### Age: Silver Standard
