*Biziknusei savar* — in his old age, *Rebbi* changed his position: *kaspah d'charif havei tiva* — silver, being far more widespread in everyday use, is the true currency. Gold may be more valuable per unit, but very few people possess or transact in gold. The currency that everyone uses, in which prices are quoted and transactions are conducted, is silver. Therefore silver is the *tiva* and gold is the *peira*. *Dahava d'lo charif havei peira veka'rei leh peira* — gold, which is not widespread, is considered the object. On this view, our *mishna* — which says *hazahav koneh es hakesef* — reflects *Rebbi*'s mature opinion: gold is the object, silver is the currency.

It is worth noting that the *Yerushalmi*'s *girsa* of this *mishna* is the opposite: *hakesef koneh es hazahav*, giving this *perek* the name *Hakesef* rather than *Hazahav* — the only known instance in *Shas* where a *perek* carries a different name in the two *Talmuds* because of a variant first word in the *mishna*. Additionally, historical context is pertinent here: within the Roman Empire, silver was apparently the standard metal for coins, which would align with *Rebbi*'s older position.

### Value vs Widespread Use

*Rav Ashi* weighs in: *ki yalduso mistabra* — *Rebbi*'s position in his youth, that gold is the standard, is the more logical one. The proof comes from the end of the *mishna* itself, which states *hanechoshet koneh es hakesef* — copper is the object vis-à-vis silver. Now if the principle were that the more widespread currency is the *tiva*, then copper — which in many localities is used far more frequently than silver — ought to be considered the *tiva* vis-à-vis silver, not the *peira*. If *Rebbi*'s older position held that widespread usage determines the *tiva*, then the hierarchy *zahav, kesef, nechoshet* — with each lower metal being the object vis-à-vis the higher — would not follow logically, since nechoshet is more widely circulated than kesef in many communities.

The *Gemara* responds that nevertheless the *mishna* would need to state the copper-silver rule explicitly, because one might have thought: *salka daitach amina hani priti be-atra de-sagi inu charifi tfei* — in the locale where copper coins circulate, they may actually be more widespread than silver, and therefore one might have thought copper should be the *tiva* there. The *mishna* teaches: *keivan d'ika dukhta d'lo sagi bei, peira havei* — since there are places that do not accept copper at all, and silver always functions as the reference currency even where copper is the daily medium of exchange, copper retains the status of *peira*. The *tiva* is defined not merely by local prevalence but by universal acceptability as the reference standard. Silver meets that criterion; copper does not.

The upshot of *Rav Ashi*'s analysis is that the hierarchy proceeds by metal value, not by circulatory breadth. More valuable metal is the *tiva* vis-à-vis the less valuable, and the *mishna* as we have it — *hazahav koneh es hakesef* — reflects *Rebbi*'s younger position, which is the more coherent one.

---

## Gold Loan Case

### Dinarei Loan

The *Gemara* now cites a case directly bearing on the *tiva*-versus-*peira* question. *Rav* borrowed gold *dinarei* from *Rebbi Chiya*'s daughter — herself evidently a businesswoman of means. *L'sof ikru dinarei* — in the end, the gold coins appreciated in value. At the time of the loan, ten gold coins might have exchanged for 250 silver; now they were worth 300 silver. When it came time to repay, *Rav* was concerned about *ribbis*: would returning ten gold coins constitute paying back something of greater value than he had borrowed?

### Rebbi Chiya Ruling

*Rav* came before *Rebbi Chiya*, who ruled: *zil shlim la tavin v'takilin* — go pay her good, full-weight coins. That is, repay the same number of gold coins, and do so without concern.

### Gold Standard Solution

*Iy amart bishlama dahava tiva havei, shapir* — if gold is the *tiva*, the ruling is perfectly coherent. What has happened, on this view, is not that the gold became worth more, but that silver became worth less. Gold, as the standard currency, always retains the same value by definition — ten gold coins are always worth ten gold coins. The fluctuation is entirely attributed to silver. Therefore, returning ten gold coins to someone who lent ten gold coins is a straightforward repayment with no *ribbis* concern whatsoever.

### Silver Standard Problem

*Ela iy amart peira havei* — but if gold is the *peira*, the object, and silver is the fixed *tiva*, then what one borrowed was an object worth 250 silver, and what one is returning is an object now worth 300 silver. That constitutes repaying more than one borrowed — which is the very definition of *ribbis*.

### Se'ah B'se'ah

This brings into view the principle of *se'ah b'se'ah*, which will be developed more fully in the following *perek* but is essential to introduce here. Even when there is no actual change in price between the time of borrowing and the time of repayment, the rabbis prohibited borrowing an object with the intention of returning an identical object — the paradigmatic case being "lend me two eggs." The concern is that even if prices have not in fact changed, they might have, and therefore returning two eggs for two eggs risks returning something of greater value than what was borrowed. The prohibition is rabbinic and based on potential, not actual, gain. The value of a loan is always measured in monetary terms; one is not borrowing eggs, one is borrowing the money-equivalent of eggs at the time of the transaction.

In *Rav*'s case, the concern is not potential but actual — the gold coins are demonstrably worth more silver now than when he borrowed them. If silver is the *tiva*, he is unambiguously repaying more than he received, which is forbidden *ribbis*. The *Gemara* concludes that *Rebbi Chiya*'s ruling permitting repayment of the same gold coins proves that gold, not silver, is the *tiva* — and therefore no *ribbis* problem arises.

### Home Coins Solution

The *Gemara* offers an alternative explanation to avoid this conclusion. Perhaps gold is in fact the *peira* and silver the *tiva*, yet *Rav*'s case was exceptional: *Rav dinarei hava lei* — *Rav* actually had gold coins of his own at home. The principle is that if a borrower possesses the item at home but simply cannot retrieve it at the moment — analogous to saying *hav li ad she'yavo beni o ad she'emtza mafte'ach*, "lend me this until my son comes home or until I find the key" — the transaction is conceptualized not as a loan over time but as an immediate swap. Since the *se'ah b'se'ah* concern is rabbinic, this conceptual fiction suffices to resolve it: one is treating the coins already at home as immediately transferred, so there is no problematic loan of an object over time. On this reading, *Rebbi Chiya*'s ruling does not prove the gold standard; it merely reflects the special circumstances of *Rav*'s case. The question of which metal is the *tiva* therefore remains open from this episode alone.

---

## Currency Exchange Proofs

### Perutah Definition

The *Gemara* now cites a *baraita* to press the question further. The *baraita* — drawn from *Mishnah Eduyot* — defines the *perutah* mentioned throughout rabbinic literature: *echad mi-shmoneh be-issar ha-italki* — one-eighth of an Italian *issar*. The stated relevance is *le-kiddushei ishah*: kiddushin takes effect with something worth at least a *perutah*, so knowing what a *perutah* is worth is of direct consequence for determining a woman's marital status.

### Issar-Dinar Ratio

The *baraita* continues: one Italian *issar* equals 1/24th of a silver *dinar*. The stated relevance is *le-mekach u-mimkar* — for commercial exchange. *Rashi* understands this as the prevention of fraud in money-changing: knowing the precise ratio of *issars* to silver *dinarim* ensures that neither party in a currency exchange is cheated. Just as there are fixed legal ratios of currency units — one hundred pennies to a dollar — the *issar*-to-*dinar* ratio establishes a standard against which exchange rates are measured.

### Silver-Gold Ratio

The *baraita* then states: one silver *dinar* equals 1/25th of a gold *dinar*. The relevance stated is *le-pidyon haben*: *pidyon haben* requires the equivalent of five *shekalim*, and a *shekel* is four silver *dinarim*, making the total twenty silver *dinarim*. If a gold *dinar* is worth twenty-five silver *dinarim*, then 4/5ths of a gold *dinar* suffices for *pidyon haben*, with the *Kohen* returning the remaining fifth.

### Pidyon Haben Fixed

*Iy amart bishlama tiva havei* — if gold is the standard currency, this all works cleanly. The amount required for *pidyon haben* is defined as a fixed fraction of a gold coin. No matter how the price of silver fluctuates, the *pidyon haben* obligation is stable: it is always 4/5ths of a gold *dinar*. Everything else — silver *dinarim*, *issars*, *perutot* — is defined relative to gold, and gold itself is the fixed reference point. This is coherent precisely because gold is the *tiva*.

### Silver Standard Problem

*Ela iy amart peira havei* — but if gold is the *peira* and its value fluctuates relative to the silver standard, then fixing *pidyon haben* as "4/5ths of a gold coin" becomes meaningless as a stable measure. *Zimnin demahadar lei kahana vezimnin demosif la-hu la-kahana* — sometimes the *Kohen* would have to return more than a fifth of the gold coin's silver-equivalent value, and sometimes less, depending on the current silver price of gold. A fixed *mitzvah*-obligation cannot be expressed in terms of something whose value is in constant flux. The fact that the *baraita* defines *pidyon haben* in terms of a fixed fraction of the gold *dinar* therefore implies that gold is the constant — the *tiva* — and everything else fluctuates around it.

### Ulla's Counter

*Ulla* raises a counterpoint. If gold's status as *tiva* is proven by the *pidyon haben* clause, what about the beginning of the same *baraita*, which defines the *perutah* in terms of the *issar* and the *issar* in terms of the silver *dinar*? The *perutah* is relevant for *kiddushei ishah*. If one wanted to prove that silver — not gold — is the fixed standard, one could equally argue from the fact that the *perutah* is defined relative to silver: it is 1/192nd of a silver *dinar*, and a woman is *mekudeshet* if she receives at least that amount. Does this not suggest that silver is the reference point for determining minimum value?

### Tosafot Resolution

*Tosafot* offers a resolution. The *baraita* presents an ascending chain of definitions: *perutah* → *issar* → silver *dinar* → gold *dinar*. This ascending structure means that everything is ultimately defined in terms of the highest denomination — the gold *dinar*. The *perutah* is not simply 1/192nd of a silver *dinar*; it is ultimately a fixed fraction of a gold *dinar*, mediated through the intermediate steps. Therefore, to determine whether a given *perutah* coin is genuinely worth a *perutah* for purposes of *kiddushin*, one does not simply compare it to silver; one traces the chain all the way up to gold. If the coin is worth at least 1/5000th of a gold *dinar* (approximately — combining the 1/8 issar ratio with the 1/24 silver-dinar ratio and the 1/25 gold-dinar ratio), it is a valid *perutah* and the *kiddushin* is effective. The gold standard is the ultimate reference for all valuations up and down the chain.

### Historical Ratio Change

*Tosafot* appends a historical note from Rabbeinu Tam. The *baraita*'s statement that one gold *dinar* equals 25 silver *dinarim* troubled him in light of contemporary reality: *kashya le-Rabbeinu Tam eich haya beyamav shehaya zahav yakar kol kach* — how could it be that in antiquity, one unit of gold was worth 25 units of silver of the same weight, when in his own medieval time, one unit of gold was worth at most 12 units of silver? A shift from a 1:25 ratio to a 1:12 ratio seemed implausibly dramatic. Rabbeinu Tam's resolution is that the gold *dinar* was not the same size as the silver *dinar* — gold being denser, and the gold coin perhaps also thicker — such that one gold *dinar* actually contained more weight than one silver *dinar*. Therefore the 1:25 ratio in terms of coin-count need not reflect a 1:25 ratio in terms of weight, and the discrepancy with medieval gold-to-silver ratios is smaller than it appears.

---

## Ma'aser Sheni Dispute

### Ma'aser Transfer Q

The *Gemara* now turns to a *mishna* elsewhere that bears directly on the *tiva*-versus-*peira* question: the laws of *ma'aser sheni*. The *halacha* of *ma'aser sheni* permits transferring the *kedushah* of the second tithe from produce to coins (*mechallel* onto money), which allows one to travel to Jerusalem more easily — one brings the coins and purchases food there. The question is whether one may take a further step: transferring *kedushah* already on silver coins onto gold coins, which are even more portable. This is precisely the gold-versus-silver debate of our *perek*.

### Beit Shammai View

*Beit Shammai* says: *lo ya'aseh adam sla'im dinarei zahav* — one may not convert silver *sela'im* into gold *dinarim* for *ma'aser sheni* purposes. Their reasoning, as explained by the *Gemara*, is that silver is the *tiva* and gold is the *peira*. The rule for *ma'aser sheni* is that one may transfer *kedushah* from *peira* (fruit/object) to *tiva* (currency), but not from *tiva* to *peira*. Since silver is the *tiva* and gold is the *peira*, moving *kedushah* from silver to gold would constitute transferring from *tiva* to *peira*, which is forbidden.

### Beit Hillel View

*Beit Hillel* permits it: *matirin*. They hold the opposite: *kaspa peira ve-dahava tiva* — silver is the *peira* and gold is the *tiva*. Moving *kedushah* from silver to gold is therefore moving from *peira* to *tiva*, which is permitted. This is the position of *Rebbi* in his youth and of *Rebbi Chiya*, as established earlier in the *sugya*.

### Kedusha Transfer Rule

The underlying rule is thus: *mechallelin* from *peira* to *tiva*, but not from *tiva* to *peira*. One may always transfer *kedushah* from the object/fruit to the currency, never the reverse. The machlokes between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* is therefore directly and entirely a consequence of which metal each house regards as the *tiva* — and that is precisely the dispute of *Rebbi* in his youth versus his old age.

### Fruit to Coins Fine

On one position of *Rabbi Yochanan* or *Reish Lakish* (they dispute which formulation is correct), the machlokes between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* is specifically about the silver-to-gold transfer. But transferring *kedushah* directly from actual produce (*peirot*) to gold *dinarim* — bypassing silver — would be permitted according to all opinions. *Divrei hakol mechalelin* — there is no dispute that one may go from real fruit to gold, because gold is unquestionably currency relative to actual agricultural produce. *Midi de-hava a-kessef le-Veit Hillel*: just as *Beit Hillel* permits silver to be the object of *challul* from fruit even though silver is considered *peira* vis-à-vis gold, so too *Beit Shammai* would agree that from real *peirot*, even gold coins — despite being *peira* vis-à-vis silver — are nonetheless *tiva* relative to actual produce. The question of which is *tiva* and which is *peira* is always relative and contextual.

### Fruit-Gold Transfer

The second position of *Rabbi Yochanan* or *Reish Lakish*, however, disputes even this. On this reading, the machlokes between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* extends even to whether one may transfer *kedushah* directly from produce to gold *dinarim*. The argument would be that gold is so removed from everyday commerce — more like a commodity or a collectible than a true circulating currency — that even relative to actual *peirot*, gold might not qualify as *tiva*. One might think of the modern analogy of gold Krugerrands: theoretically a currency, but in practice purchased only at specialized dealers and not used in everyday transactions. If that is how gold functions, one could argue that even vis-à-vis produce, gold is the *peira* and the transfer of *kedushah* from produce to gold coins would itself be disputed between the two houses. The *Gemara* leaves this question open, to be resumed in the following *daf*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 45

## Gold vs. Silver Status

### Intro: Silver to Gold

The daf begins, picking up from the bottom of 44b, with a debate concerning the various coinages of precious metals—gold, silver, and copper—and which is understood as the standard by which the others are defined. The immediate context is a dispute between *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* regarding *maaser sheni*: if one has already redeemed *maaser sheni* onto silver coins, may one now transfer those silver coins for gold coins, moving the *kedushah* from silver to gold? *Beit Shammai* held that one may not, and *Beit Hillel* held that one may.

The *Gemara* initially assumes that this debate mirrors the broader question found in two versions of the *mishnah*—whether gold, relative to silver, is classified as a coin (*matbeia*) or as produce (*peirot*). If gold relative to silver is considered a coin, one may transfer *maaser sheni* onto it. If it is considered produce—that is, non-coin—one cannot transfer *maaser sheni* from coin to produce. Under this framing, *Beit Shammai*, who disallows the transfer from silver to gold, must hold that gold is not coin relative to silver, while *Beit Hillel* holds that it is.

### Yochanan vs. Lakish

Within the position of *Beit Shammai*, there is a further debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish. The question is whether *Beit Shammai* would permit a direct transfer from fruit to gold coin—that is, whether *Beit Shammai* regards gold as coin for no purpose whatsoever, even absent a comparison to silver, or whether *Beit Shammai* only objects to gold's status *relative to silver*.

One view (*vachad amar*) holds that the debate would extend even to the case of *hapeiros al dinarim*—transferring directly from fruit to gold coins. On this reading, *Beit Shammai* does not consider gold to be a coin in any context; it is always categorized as produce. The *Gemara* then asks: if that is so, why do *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* debate the case of silver to gold? Why not instead debate the more striking case of fruit to gold, which would demonstrate more clearly that *Beit Shammai* denies gold the status of coin altogether?

The answer is that if only the fruit-to-gold case were debated, one might have thought that *Beit Hillel* objects only there—because at least relative to fruit, gold counts as a coin—but that even *Beit Hillel* would concede that relative to silver, gold is considered produce and the transfer would fail. Therefore, the debate is cast in terms of silver to gold, to teach us the strength of *Beit Hillel*'s position: even relative to silver, *Beit Hillel* considers gold to be a coin, and the transfer is valid.

The question of how *Beit Shammai* would treat gold relative to fruit—as always being non-coin, or only as non-coin relative to silver—remains the crux of the Yochanan-Lakish dispute.

### Borrowing Gold Issue

The *Gemara* now attempts to determine which of the two—Rabbi Yochanan or Resh Lakish—holds which position. It proposes: *tistayem d'Rabbi Yochanan hu d'amar ain michalelin*—let us conclude that it is Rabbi Yochanan who holds that according to *Beit Shammai*, one cannot even transfer from fruit to gold.

The evidence is a teaching of Rabbi Yochanan himself, cited at the top of 45a: *asur lihalvos dinar bidinar*—it is forbidden to borrow a gold *dinar* and pay back a gold *dinar*. This is a striking ruling. The *Gemara* immediately clarifies: surely it cannot refer to silver coins borrowed against silver coins, for no one would argue that silver relative to itself is not currency. The concern is clearly the case of gold *dinarei* borrowed and paid back in gold *dinarei*.

The force of this ruling lies in what was established on the previous daf. When assessing the relative value of currencies, gold is treated as the commodity being purchased, while silver functions as the reference currency. If I borrow a gold *dinar* and the gold has shifted in value relative to silver by the time I repay, the repayment in gold may reflect a different silver equivalent than what was originally borrowed—and this could constitute *ribbis*. The implication of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is therefore that gold, even on its own terms and not merely relative to silver, is always considered produce (*peira*) and never true currency. It is as though one borrowed an egg and returned an egg, where the relative value of that object may have changed.

The *Gemara* then notes that *Tosafot* raises the obvious question: since when does Rabbi Yochanan rule according to *Beit Shammai*? *Tosafot* answers that the ruling should be understood as expressing the view *aliba d'Beit Shammai*, even if the phrasing does not immediately indicate this. *Tosafot* adds—and this is important—that this ultimately connects back to the different versions of the *mishnah*. Our version reads *hazahav koneh et hakesef*: gold is the product, and by taking the gold, the other party becomes obligated to pay the silver. This framing is consistent with the *Beit Shammai* position: gold is product, not currency, perhaps even purely on its own terms.

### Exception Model

The *Gemara* responds to this proof with a qualification: *le'olam eima lach*—one can still maintain that Rabbi Yochanan is the opinion that allows transfer from fruit to gold (i.e., holds gold is coin for *maaser sheni* purposes). The ruling prohibiting gold-for-gold borrowing is different, and the two domains need not be governed by the same logic.

The explanation is as follows: *v'shani halva'ah keivan del'inyan mikach umimkar shav'yuha rabanan kepeirei*—when it comes to commercial exchange, the Rabbis have treated gold as produce relative to silver, meaning that the gold is understood as the fluctuating item whose value is measured in silver terms. Since gold is recognized in the context of commerce as a thing of fluctuating value, this recognition carries over into the law of borrowing as well. One who borrows gold and repays in gold is borrowing something whose silver-equivalent value may have changed, and that creates the potential for *ribbis*. Hence the borrowing is forbidden.

But *maaser sheni* redemption is a distinct matter. There, the act of transferring *kedushah* to money is not a commercial exchange in which silver sets the reference price. It is a one-time act of sanctification onto coin, and perhaps for that purpose gold functions adequately as coin even under the view of Rabbi Yochanan. So the prohibition on gold borrowing does not preclude using gold for *maaser sheni* redemption; rather, *maaser sheni* is the exception.

### Three Scenarios

This creates three distinct scenarios that must be distinguished. The first is the straightforward commercial exchange: a pile of gold is exchanged for silver. In this context, our *mishnah* establishes that gold is treated as produce (*peiros*) and silver as currency. The second scenario is *maaser sheni* redemption: fruit is transferred onto gold coin. In this context, even those who treat gold as produce for commercial purposes may acknowledge that gold functions adequately as coin for the purpose of *kedushah* transfer. The third scenario is a loan: one borrows gold *dinarei* and repays in gold *dinarei*. Here, because commerce has already established gold as a thing of fluctuating value relative to silver, this characterization follows gold into the borrowing context as well.

The *Gemara* supports the conclusion that *maaser sheni* is an exception by citing a tradition: *d'ki ata Ravin amar Rabbi Yochanan*—when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted a teaching in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: even though borrowing a gold *dinar* and repaying in gold is forbidden, *aval mechallelin maaser sheni alav*—one may nonetheless redeem *maaser sheni* onto gold coin. *Shema mina*—this is a clear proof that *maaser sheni* operates as an exception. In commercial settings, gold is produce; for the sanctification of *maaser sheni*, gold retains sufficient coin-status to accept the *kedushah*.

One might ask whether the same prohibition on gold-for-gold borrowing would apply to copper coins. The *Gemara* itself addresses a closely related question in the passage immediately following.

A *baraita* is now introduced: *haporeis sela mema'ot maaser sheni*—one is exchanging a *sela* for *ma'ot* out of *maaser sheni* money. Rashi explains—and *Tosafot* does not disagree—that despite the natural reading of the language, what is actually being described is the reverse: a person who has accumulated *maaser sheni* funds in copper coins (*perutot*) and wishes to avoid carrying heavy sacks of them to Jerusalem. The person therefore wishes to exchange the copper *maaser sheni* coins for silver. *Beit Shammai* says one must exchange the entire amount into silver (*bechol hasela ma'os*—meaning *bechol hama'os sela'im*). *Beit Hillel* says one exchanges half—a *shekel*'s worth of silver and a *shekel*'s worth of copper coins.

The reason for the debate, according to Rashi, is a concern about what happens upon arrival in Jerusalem. If everyone arrives with only silver coins, there will be a run on the copper market as all the pilgrims simultaneously try to exchange their silver for copper to make small purchases, driving down the exchange rate and thereby reducing the purchasing power of *maaser sheni* funds—a loss to *maaser sheni*. To prevent this, *Beit Hillel* requires retaining half the funds in copper for ready use. *Tosafot* offers the alternative explanation for *Beit Shammai*'s position: copper can become damaged over time, and therefore *Beit Shammai* insists on converting everything to silver to avoid that loss.

The *Gemara* now applies this *baraita* to the gold question. *Hashta l'Beit Shammai l'gabe priti mechallelin*—if according to *Beit Shammai* one may transfer *maaser sheni* *kedushah* onto copper coins, then surely there should be no question that gold—a more substantial form of value—should work. The *Gemara* responds: *shani priti*—copper is different. *B'asra d'sagyin charifi*—in the places where copper circulates broadly, it is actually more current and accepted than gold in everyday commerce, even if it carries no status in broader transactions. This is a striking point: the very ubiquity of copper may make it more functional as currency for *maaser sheni* purposes than the rarer gold, even though gold is intrinsically more valuable.

This brings out exactly the asymmetry one might have intuited: it is possible that for *maaser sheni*, gold does not qualify as coin while copper does, precisely because currency status is determined by widespread practical use rather than intrinsic worth.

### Money-to-Money Theory

The *Gemara* now introduces *lishna achrina*—an alternative formulation of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, which reframes the entire debate of *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* along entirely different lines.

On this reading, *Beit Shammai*'s position is not about gold's status as coin or produce at all. Instead, *Beit Shammai* holds *ha-kesef, kesef rishon v'lo kesef sheni*: the verse *v'tzarta ha-kesef b'yadcha* teaches that the money upon which *maaser sheni* resides must be the *first* money—the initial coins onto which the *kedushah* was transferred. Transferring from that first money to any second money, regardless of what it is, is not permitted. *Beit Hillel* counters that the doubled language of the verse—*ha-kesef, kesef*—means to include any money, even a second transfer. And on this reading, the fruit-to-gold case is uncontested: *divrei hakol mechallelin*—everyone agrees one may redeem fruit directly onto gold *dinarei*, since the gold in that scenario constitutes the first money.

Within this *lishna achrina*, the sub-dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish concerns whether the debate extends even to the fruit-to-gold case. One view holds that the debate is purely about coin-to-coin transfers, making the gold-to-silver case the locus of disagreement. The other view holds that even fruit-to-gold can be contested, because if one is concerned about postponement (as will be elaborated shortly), the same concern applies even when starting from fruit.

### Refutation: Copper Case

The *Gemara* challenges the coin-to-coin theory directly. If *Beit Shammai*'s objection is purely about the prohibition of transferring from one *kesef* to a second *kesef*, then *Beit Shammai* should have debated the clearest possible instance of that principle: silver to silver. Why frame the debate around silver to gold, which introduces the gold question as an apparent confound? The *Gemara* responds: had the debate been silver to silver, one might have concluded that *Beit Hillel* objects only there—permitting silver-to-silver—but would agree with *Beit Shammai* that silver to gold is problematic, since gold relative to silver might be considered *peira*. By debating silver to gold, the *mishnah* teaches that *Beit Hillel* accepts the transfer even in that more questionable case.

But the more powerful refutation comes from the *baraita* discussed just above. The *baraita* describes the case of *haporeis sela shel maaser sheni b'Yerushalayim*—breaking a silver coin into copper *perutot* once already inside Jerusalem. *Beit Shammai* allows this, even permitting the full exchange of silver for copper inside Jerusalem. This is manifestly a case of transferring *kedushah* from one coin to another—from silver to copper. If *Beit Shammai* categorically prohibited coin-to-coin transfers, this case should be forbidden.

The *Gemara* reports that Rava defends the coin-to-coin position by distinguishing between these two scenarios: *Yerushalayim ka movat*—you are raising a question about exchanges *within* Jerusalem, which operate under a different framework entirely. Once one is in Jerusalem, the money is no longer in a holding pattern; it is at the stage of active use. The verse *v'nasata ha-kesef b'chol asher te'aveh nafshcha* gives broad license to spend the money on anything. The exchanges that happen within Jerusalem—breaking coins into smaller denominations for immediate purchase—are part of the spending process and not abstract transfers of *kedushah*. They cannot serve as a model for understanding the rules of transfer *outside* Jerusalem.

The *Gemara* then presses further and produces the *baraita* cited earlier regarding the exchange of copper coins for silver *before* arriving in Jerusalem. That *baraita*—*haporeis sela mema'ot maaser sheni*—describes an exchange that takes place outside Jerusalem, and both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* accept that it may be done (they debate only the extent). This conclusively demonstrates that according to *Beit Shammai*, coin-to-coin transfers are not categorically forbidden. *Ella*—the coin-to-coin theory is therefore rejected. *Dechulei alma kesef kesef ribba*—everyone agrees the verse includes even second-generation money.

### Gezeirah Theory

With the coin-to-coin theory rejected, the *Gemara* presents a second *lishna achrina*, an entirely new way of reading the dispute. On this reading, gold is unambiguously a coin from the Torah's perspective. The debate has nothing to do with gold's status as coin or produce. Instead, *Beit Shammai*'s prohibition on transferring silver to gold is a *gezeirah*—a rabbinic safeguard.

The concern *Beit Shammai* anticipates is *shema yish'a aliyotav*—perhaps a person will delay bringing his *maaser sheni* funds to Jerusalem. If the law permits transferring silver coins to gold *dinarei* before making the journey, a person who has accumulated silver but not yet enough to exchange for a full gold coin may say: I will wait until I accumulate the full amount needed before making the transfer. Since gold coins come in large denominations, someone with slightly fewer silver coins than required will postpone the conversion—and consequently postpone the pilgrimage—until he can fill the denomination. *Beit Shammai* therefore enacts a *gezeirah* against allowing such transfers, to prevent this postponement.

*Beit Hillel* responds: *lo gazrinan shema yish'a aliyotav*—we do not enact this safeguard, because even if a person's silver does not fill a full gold *dinar*, he will still bring it to Jerusalem. As Rashi explains: *d'chi lo malu nami b'dinara asukei masik lehu she'ein masan kaved she'ma'akev*—whatever remains after converting the bulk to gold is only a modest weight of silver, easily carried. One will simply take the balance up in silver and convert the rest; the partial remainder creates no real obstacle.

### Fruit Rots Exception

On the *gezeirah* reading, both *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* agree that the fruit-to-gold transfer is permitted according to everyone—*divrei hakol mechallelin*. The question is why the concern about postponement does not apply there as well. If one has only a small amount of *maaser sheni* fruit—not enough to fill the value of a single gold *dinar*—why would one not similarly delay the transfer until enough produce accumulates?

The answer is simple: *d'keivan d'markevi*—because fruit rots. Since *maaser sheni* produce may not be consumed outside Jerusalem, leaving it in a state of *kedushah* means one cannot eat it at home. If a person waits too long, the fruit will decay and the *maaser sheni* will be lost entirely. No one will deliberately allow that to happen. Therefore, *lo mash'ei lehu*—one will not let the fruit sit around; the urgency created by the perishability of produce removes any temptation to postpone, and so there is no need for any *gezeirah* in that case.

The second opinion within this *lishna achrina* argues that even the fruit-to-gold case is contested. If the concern is that insufficient denomination will cause delay, fruit is arguably even more susceptible: if a person waits until accumulating enough fruit to fill the value of a gold coin before doing the transfer, and then the fruit rots in the meantime, the loss would be even more consequential. According to this view, the very severity of the potential loss makes the *gezeirah* more pressing, not less—and therefore even fruit-to-gold is debated.

The *Gemara* closes this section by noting a textual consideration bearing on which version of the debate is correct. *Bishlama lehach lishna*—according to the *gezeirah* reading, where the gold is certainly a valid coin from the Torah and the entire dispute is rabbinic in nature, the language of the *mishnah* fits naturally: *lo ya'ase*—one should not do this. This is the language of a *lechatchila* restriction, which implies that if done it would nonetheless be effective *bedi'avad*. But according to the reading where gold is not genuinely a coin relative to silver and the transfer therefore simply does not work, the *mishnah* should have used the language *ein mechallelin*—it cannot be done—implying that the transfer is ineffective even after the fact. The *Gemara* registers this as a *kashya*—a real difficulty—against the earlier readings.

This concludes the first major *sugya* of *hazahav koneh et hakesef*: the question of whether gold is coin or produce relative to silver, explored through the lens of *maaser sheni*, commercial exchange, and the law of borrowing.

---

## Coins in Chalipin

### Chalipin Concept

The *Gemara* now opens a new and conceptually rich topic, still centering on gold but from a completely different angle. A new teaching is cited: *itmar Rav v'Levi*—there is a dispute between Rav and Levi. *Chad amar matbe'a na'aseh chalipin, v'chad amar ein matbe'a na'aseh chalipin*—one holds that a coin (*matbeia*) may serve as the object of *chalipin*, and the other holds that it may not.

To understand what is at stake, it is necessary to clarify what *chalipin* means as a mode of acquisition. The classic form of *chalipin* is a barter exchange—a cow for a donkey, for instance—in which taking possession of one item finalizes the acquisition of the other. But *chalipin* also operates in a more abstract register: the famous paradigm from the book of Ruth, *shalaf ish naalo v'natan lerei'ahu*, describes handing over one's shoe or sandal to formalize a transaction. This is the basis of *kinyan sudar*—the handkerchief exchange familiar from the *choson's tish* at a wedding, where the groom takes the rabbi's handkerchief and thereby obligates himself to the *kesubah*. In this mode of *chalipin*, the object transferred is not exchanged as equivalent value for something received in return; rather, the physical act of taking an object serves as the formal gesture that expresses *gemirat da'at*—the finalization of intent—and thereby effects the *kinyan*.

The question now is whether a coin—a *matbeia*—may serve as the object handed over in such a transaction. One person wishes to acquire another's cow; rather than paying for it, the parties agree to effect the acquisition through *chalipin*. Instead of handing over a handkerchief, the buyer offers a coin. The recipient takes the coin, and the question is whether this constitutes valid *chalipin* such that the buyer now acquires the cow.

### Rav vs. Levi

Rav and Levi dispute this directly: *chad amar matbe'a na'aseh chalipin*—one holds that a coin may indeed be used for *chalipin*—*v'chad amar ein matbe'a na'aseh chalipin*—and the other holds that it may not.

It is worth noting that there is a separate debate, which the *Gemara* will address, between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet regarding whether *peiros*—produce—may be used for *chalipin*. Those who require a *kli* (a vessel or implement) for *chalipin* would not allow either produce or a coin to serve as the object. But even those who take the broader view and allow *peiros* might still exclude a coin on particular grounds. *Tosafot* suggests that coin might even qualify as a *kli*—since money is an instrument used to accomplish transactions—but in any case the Rav-Levi dispute is specifically about whether the status of coin as currency creates a categorical exclusion from *chalipin*, regardless of one's position on *peiros*.

### Stamp Theory

Rav Pappa offers an explanation for why a coin cannot serve as the object of *chalipin*: *mishum d'da'atei atzurata, v'tzurata avida d'batela*—because one's mindset regarding a coin focuses on its image, its stamp, and that stamp is subject to being nullified.

Rashi explains the underlying logic: a coin is not conceptualized in terms of its intrinsic material—the gold or silver it is made of—but in terms of its purchasing power, which is represented by the governmental stamp it bears. Since that stamp can be invalidated—a government may demonetize a currency—the coin is not a sufficiently stable *object* to anchor a *chalipin* acquisition. The *chalipin* object needs to be conceived as a discrete, usable thing; a coin is conceived instead as an abstraction of value.

One might object that many objects are fragile or easily destroyed, and the probability of governmental demonetization may be lower than the probability of many ordinary objects breaking. But perhaps the deeper point is not about statistical likelihood: a coin's very nature is relational and representational rather than intrinsic. Even a pencil or a piece of fruit is grasped as itself; a coin is always grasped as what it can *obtain*. This abstraction from physical objecthood is what disqualifies it from serving as the object of *chalipin*. By contrast, an unstamped slug of metal—pure gold or silver not yet coined—would presumably qualify for *chalipin*, even under this theory, since it would be treated simply as metal.

### Mishnah Analysis

The *Gemara* now turns to our *mishnah*—*hazahav koneh et hakesef*—and asks whether this teaching can be read as a case of *chalipin* with coins.

*Tenan: hazahav koneh et hakesef*—the *mishnah* states that gold *koneh* (acquires) the silver. The *Gemara* asks: *mai lav d'chalipin*—is this not a case of *chalipin*? On this reading, one party takes the gold and in exchange the other party owns (*koneh*) the pile of silver sitting in the first party's possession. This would constitute a *chalipin* of coin for coin, and would support the view that *matbeia na'aseh chalipin*.

The *Gemara* rejects this reading: *lo, bedamim*—no, the *mishnah* describes a sale with payment, not a swap. The gold is the product being purchased, and the silver is the payment. When the buyer takes the gold, the seller becomes entitled to receive payment—that is, to be paid the silver—not that the seller suddenly *owns* a specific pile of silver coins sitting elsewhere.

### Gold-Silver Asymmetry

The *Gemara* presses further on the *chalipin* reading. If the *mishnah* were indeed describing a *chalipin* transaction with coins, and if coins may in principle be used for *chalipin*, then the mechanism should work symmetrically: whether the gold is taken or the silver is taken, the other party should acquire the remaining pile of coins through the *chalipin* act. Yet the *mishnah* explicitly states that gold acquires the silver—*hazahav koneh et hakesef*—but the silver does not acquire the gold—*hakesef eino koneh et hazahav*. This asymmetry is inexplicable on the *chalipin* reading: if both gold and silver are coins and coins may be used for *chalipin*, there is no reason why taking the silver coin should work any differently than taking the gold coin.

The asymmetry is fully explicable, however, on the sale-with-payment reading. In that model, gold is the product and silver is the currency. Only taking possession of the product finalizes the sale; taking the payment does not. If the buyer takes the gold (the product), the sale is complete. If the buyer instead tries to hand over silver (the payment), that is merely like handing over money, which does not effect the *kinyan*—for it is the *meshichah* on the product, not the tender of payment, that completes the transaction.

### Language of Ownership

A further challenge arises from the language of the *baraita* cited alongside the *mishnah*: *keivan shemashach et hazahav, niknah hakesef b'chol makom shehu*—once the gold is taken, the silver is acquired (*niknah*) wherever it is. This language strongly implies that the silver is actually *owned* by the other party the moment the gold is taken, not merely that payment is now owed. *B'chol makom shehu*—wherever it happens to be sitting—suggests that the silver has changed hands conceptually even before it is physically transferred, as one would expect in a swap arrangement where both piles belong to their respective new owners from the moment of the exchange. This sounds precisely like *chalipin*: you take my gold, I own your silver pile.

### Sale Not Barter

Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty: *le'olam bedamim*—the *mishnah* and *baraita* are indeed describing a sale with payment, not a *chalipin* swap. The phrase *b'chol makom shehu* does not mean that the seller literally owns a specific pile of silver. Rather, *kemot shehu, k'di'amar lei*—it means the buyer is obligated to pay according to whatever was stipulated in the agreement. The phrase is a statement about the terms of the debt, not about proprietary ownership of a pile of coins. For example, if the parties agreed to payment in freshly minted coins (*me'anki chadta yahavina lach*), the buyer cannot discharge the obligation with old coins (*me'anki atika*)—even if those older coins are arguably of higher quality—because the seller specified new coins, presumably intending to hold them in reserve and wanting them in pristine condition. This illustrates that *b'chol makom shehu* is about the precise terms of the obligation rather than about ownership of a specific deposit.

The conclusion of the *Gemara* is therefore that the *mishnah*—*hazahav koneh et hakesef*—describes a straightforward sale in which gold is the product and silver is the means of payment. When the buyer takes the gold, the seller becomes owed the silver. The asymmetry of the *mishnah* is fully explained by the product/payment distinction. The *mishnah* is not evidence that *matbeia na'aseh chalipin*; the discussion of whether a coin may serve as the object of *chalipin* remains unresolved by this *mishnah* and will continue in the *sugya* to follow.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 46

## Chalipin & Coinage

### Chalipin Definition

The sugya on Bava Metzia 46b opens with the institution of *chalipin*, the mechanism of symbolic exchange by which one party transfers ownership to another not through the direct payment of money but through a symbolic act — most classically, the handing over of a *sudar*, a handkerchief or similar article of modest value. The *sudar* itself is not the price being paid; it is merely the instrument that effects the legal transfer. With that framework in place, the Gemara turns to the specific question of coinage and its relationship to *chalipin*.

### Rav Papa's Thesis

Rav Papa opens with a carefully formulated position: even according to the view that a *matbea* — a coin — cannot be used to *enact* a *chalipin* (that is, cannot serve as the instrument of transfer), there remains the separate question of whether money can be *acquired* through *chalipin*. In Rav Papa's formulation: *afilu man de-amar ein matbea na'aseh chalipin, mi'avad hu d'lo avad, chalipin aknu'ei miknu b'chalipin* — even he who holds that a coin cannot function as the operative object of *chalipin* must concede that coins can nonetheless be the *subject* of a *chalipin* transfer, that is, the thing being conveyed from one party to another by means of a *sudar*.

### Rav Nachman Position

The Gemara draws an analogy to Rav Nachman's position on commodities. Rav Nachman holds that any produce or commodity — *peirot* — can be *transferred through chalipin* even though, in his view, *peirot* cannot serve as the operative instrument of the *chalipin* itself. The Gemara reasons that if Rav Nachman allows *peirot* to be the object of transfer through *chalipin* — *af al gav d'inhu lo avdi chalipin, aknu'ei miknu b'chalipin* — then coinage should be no different: *tav'a nami lo shna*. Money, like fruit, is a form of commodity, and what is true of fruit in this regard ought to be true of coins as well.

---

## Maaser Sheni Challenge

### Silo Case Setup

The Gemara immediately raises an objection from a Baraita: *haya omed b'goren v'ein b'yado ma'ot* — a person is standing in his threshing floor or granary and he has no money in hand. He declares to his fellow, "These fruits are hereby given to you as a gift," and then immediately adds, "They are hereby redeemed on the money that I have at home."

### Maaser Sheni Laws

This case operates within the laws of *ma'aser sheni*, the second tithe. Produce designated as *ma'aser sheni* must be consumed in Jerusalem; if it cannot be transported in its current form, it may be "redeemed" — that is, its sanctity may be transferred onto money, which is then brought to Jerusalem and used to purchase food there. However, the Torah imposes a penalty on one who redeems his *own* produce: he must add a *chomesh*, a surcharge of one-quarter of the produce's value (which, when calculated against the total sum paid, amounts to one-fifth — hence the name, which literally means "fifth"). The penalty reflects a concern about cavalier treatment of the sanctity of *ma'aser sheni*.

To avoid this surcharge, a person might transfer the fruit to a friend as a gift — the fruit now legally belonging to the friend — and then have that friend redeem it. Since the redemption is being performed on someone else's produce, the owner is not subject to the *chomesh* penalty. In the Baraita's case, Reuven stands in his granary with his *ma'aser sheni* produce but has no money at hand. He gives the fruit to Shimon as a gift, and then declares that the fruit is redeemed on the money he has at home. This accomplishes the desired result: the fruit technically belongs to Shimon at the moment of redemption, so Reuven does not incur the surcharge. The Gemara explains that the more ideal form of this workaround would have been for Reuven to give Shimon the *money* rather than the fruit — Shimon would then use that money to redeem the fruit, making the transaction resemble a genuine marketplace sale as closely as possible.

### Mishna Inference

The Gemara presses the inference: *ta'ama de-ein b'yado ma'ot* — the only reason the case proceeds by transferring the fruit first is because he lacks money at hand. Had he had money in hand, he would have given the money to Shimon and proceeded from there. This implies that the possibility of using *chalipin* to transfer the money that sits at home — thereby notionally placing that money in Shimon's possession so that Shimon could use it to redeem the fruit — was not considered a viable option. If money could be acquired through *chalipin*, Reuven could have simply used a *sudar* to symbolically transfer the money in his house to Shimon, and Shimon would then redeem the fruit with it. The Baraita's silence on this approach seems to indicate that money cannot be acquired through *chalipin*.

### Gemara Defenses

The Gemara attempts to deflect this inference. Perhaps money could in principle be transferred through *chalipin*, and the reason the Baraita does not suggest it is simply that the man lacked a *sudar* — he had no article to use for the symbolic transfer. The Gemara then considers the possibility of a *kinyan agav*, the mode of acquisition by which movable property is transferred by means of a symbolic conveyance of land — perhaps he could have transferred the money in his house by conveying a corner of his home to Shimon. This too is deflected: perhaps he owned no land. But the Gemara points out that the Baraita describes him as standing in a granary, which would seem to be real property. This in turn is deflected: it was someone else's granary, not his own. The Gemara finally presses the point to its logical limit: *v'chi batna l'ashmi'inan gavra artilai d'leit lei v'lo klum*? Surely the Baraita is not describing a man standing there utterly destitute, without even a piece of clothing he could remove to use as a *sudar*? Even a shirt or a sock would suffice for *kinyan sudar*. It is therefore impossible to maintain that the failure to suggest *chalipin* was merely circumstantial.

### Conclusion

The Gemara concludes: *shma mina ein matbe'a nikneh b'chalipin, shma mina*. The Baraita is to be read as evidence that money cannot be acquired through *chalipin*. This directly contradicts Rav Papa's initial thesis.

---

## Rav Papa Reversal

### Rav Papa Story

The Gemara records that Rav Papa himself ultimately reversed his position. The vehicle for this reversal is a story: Rav Papa had twelve thousand *dinar* deposited at a place called *Bei Chozai*, some distance away. He wished to retrieve them via an agent, Rav Shmuel bar Acha, who would travel there and bring the funds back. The difficulty was that the custodian at *Bei Chozai* would not release the money to someone who was not legally its owner — if Rav Shmuel were merely a messenger rather than an owner, and the money were lost or stolen in transit, Rav Pappa could still hold the custodian liable for having released the funds to an unauthorized party. The solution was to make Rav Shmuel the legal owner of the money for the duration of the transfer. Rav Papa accordingly performed a *kinyan agav*, transferring the threshold of his home to Rav Shmuel along with — *agav*, "by means of" — the money at *Bei Chozai*. In this way the money was legally conveyed to Rav Shmuel, who then assumed full responsibility for it during transport. When Rav Shmuel arrived, Rav Papa went out to meet him at *itztoka*.

The significance of this story is in what Rav Papa chose *not* to do: he did not use a *kinyan sudar* to effect this transfer. *Kinyan sudar* is precisely the classic form of *chalipin*, involving the symbolic handover of a piece of cloth or similar article. Had Rav Papa believed that money could be transferred through *chalipin*, he would presumably have used the simpler and more readily available mechanism of *kinyan sudar* rather than going to the trouble of arranging a *kinyan agav* through real property. His deliberate choice of *kinyan agav* over *kinyan sudar* demonstrates that he no longer held that money could be transferred through *chalipin*.

### Amoraic Consensus

With Rav Papa's reversal in view, the Gemara marshals additional Amoraic support. Ulla, Rabbi Assi, and Rabba bar Bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan all independently state: *ein matbea na'aseh chalipin* — a coin cannot be used to effect *chalipin*. These three parallel statements, all converging on the same ruling, are now introduced in the context of *chalipin* as an instrument — that is, money cannot serve as the operative object that enacts the symbolic transfer.

### Money-Changer Case

Rabbi Abba then challenges Ulla's position from the following case. A donkey-driver and his workers are pressing a man for payment in the marketplace. The man turns to the ever-present money changer and says: *ten li be-dinar ma'ot ve-afarneseim* — give me a *dinar*'s worth of coins so that I may pay my workers. He then adds: *va-ani a'aleh lecha yafeh dinar u-tarsais mi-ma'ot she-yesh li be-veiti* — and I will repay you a *dinar* and a *tarsais* (a small additional sum) from the money I have at home.

The ruling follows: if he in fact has the money at home, it is permitted; if he does not, it is forbidden.

The reason the case might be *asur* is immediately apparent: if the money changer gives the man a *dinar* now and the man promises to repay more later, this has the structure of a loan with a premium — which would constitute *ribbit*, the prohibition on charging interest.

### Ribbit Logic

The Gemara presses this logic. If *chalipin* cannot be effected through money, then what the money changer is doing when he hands over a *dinar* is extending a loan — and the extra amount the man promises to return would then be *ribbit*, forbidden in all circumstances. The permissibility of the transaction when money is available at home must therefore rest on the claim that the money at home is immediately transferred to the money changer through some mechanism, making this a trade — a simultaneous exchange of value — rather than a loan. And if the mechanism is *chalipin* through coinage (the man receiving the *dinar* triggers the transfer of his coins at home to the money changer), the case seems to imply that money *can* in fact function within a *chalipin* transaction. This challenges Ulla's blanket ruling.

### Unstamped Coins

Rabbi Abba himself resolves the challenge. He proposes that both parties in the transaction were dealing not with actual stamped currency but with *prottotat* — pre-minted metal pieces that have not yet received a royal stamp or official designation as currency. Such pieces, though they may be spoken of loosely as having a *dinar*'s worth of value, are not legally coins; they are metal commodities, no different in legal status from produce or any other tradeable good. And as previously established, commodities — *peirot* — can be transferred through *chalipin*. Ulla accordingly accepts this answer. As supporting evidence, the Gemara notes that the text of the case says *yafeh dinar*, "a good dinar's worth," rather than *dinar yafeh*, "a good coin" — implying that what is being referenced is a value equivalent, not a stamped coin. This linguistic observation is taken to support the interpretation that the transaction involved commodity-metal rather than legal currency.

### Rav Ashi Answer

Rav Ashi offers an independent resolution. He maintains that the transaction actually did involve ordinary currency, but that the reason it is not *ribbit* has nothing to do with *chalipin*. Rather, the case falls under a recognized exception to the *ribbit* prohibition: *keivan deit lei na'aseh k'omer halvini ad sheyavo beni o ad she-emtza mafteach* — since the man genuinely has the money available at home, the situation is treated as though he said, "lend me until my son arrives" or "until I find my key." When the funds are readily accessible and the delay is purely logistical rather than reflecting genuine inability to pay, this is not considered a true loan bearing the moral character of *ribbit*. The case in the Baraita is therefore consistent with the position that money cannot be used for *chalipin*; the permissibility of the transaction arises from an entirely separate principle.

---

## Value Transfer Mishna

### Mishna Statement

The Gemara introduces another source, a Mishna from *Kiddushin*: *kol hane'aseh damim be'acher keivan shezacha zeh nitchayev zeh b'chalipin* — whoever effects a transfer of value with another party, once that party acquires the value, the first party incurs the attendant liability through *chalipin*. The practical upshot is that a sale can be considered legally consummated — placing the risk of loss on the buyer — before the buyer has taken physical possession of the item, if some form of value transfer has already occurred.

### Initial Question

One might read the phrase *kol hane'aseh damim* — "whatever constitutes payment" — as a reference to coinage. If so, the Mishna would be saying that money can function within a *chalipin* framework to effect legal transfer, and this would constitute a proof that *ein matbea na'aseh chalipin* is incorrect. The Gemara entertains this reading before subjecting it to scrutiny.

### Rav Yehuda Reinterp

Rav Yehuda rejects this reading. He argues that the Mishna should be understood as: *kol hanishom damim be'acher keivan shezacha zeh nitchayev zeh b'chalipin* — whoever *appraises* value with another, meaning, once a price is agreed upon and a symbolic act of *chalipin* (through a *sudar* or similar instrument) is performed, the legal transfer takes effect. The *damim* in the Mishna refers not to the actual physical transfer of coinage but to the valuation — the act of pricing — that precedes and occasions the *chalipin*. The money itself is never the operative instrument of transfer.

This interpretation is supported by the *seifa* of the Mishna, which asks *keitzad* — how so? — and answers: if one exchanged an ox for a cow or a donkey for an ox. The *seifa* uses examples of commodity-for-commodity exchange, which fits Rav Yehuda's reading that the Mishna is about non-monetary value transfer, not about coins functioning as *chalipin*.

### Rav Nachman View

The Gemara then asks how Rav Nachman would understand this Mishna, given that Rav Nachman holds *peirot* cannot themselves serve as the instrument of *chalipin*. The *seifa* — which the revised reading understood to illustrate *chalipin* through commodities — would then be problematic for Rav Nachman. His answer, according to the Gemara, is that *yesh damim she'hein k'chalipin* — there is a category of value transfer that functions like *chalipin*. Specifically, what the Mishna teaches is that a person may transfer a *debt* — a monetary obligation owed to him by a third party — to another person, and that this transfer of the debt itself, combined with a symbolic act, is sufficient to constitute a legally effective acquisition. The *chiddush* is not that any commodity or coin can be lifted like a *sudar*, but that the conveyance of a legal claim to money can substitute for the physical delivery of money in certain transactional settings. The Mishna therefore has nothing to say about coins functioning as *chalipin*; it addresses the validity of debt-transfer as a mode of commercial exchange.

---

## Rav Nachman Rationale

### Torah & Rabbis

The Gemara now probes the theoretical foundation of Rav Nachman's position. He is said to follow Rabbi Yochanan, who holds: *dvar Torah ma'os konos* — by Torah law, the transfer of money is sufficient to effect acquisition. The Rabbinic rule requiring *meshicha* — physical pulling or taking possession of the object — is not a Torah requirement but a Rabbinic enactment. The reason the Rabbis imposed this requirement is stated as a *gezeirah*: *shema yomar lo nisrefu chitecha b'aliyah* — lest the seller say to the buyer, "Your wheat was burned in the upper story," meaning, lest the seller have already received payment but, before the buyer takes possession, disclaim further responsibility when the goods are destroyed. To prevent such a scenario, the Rabbis required that ownership not transfer until *meshicha* — actual physical taking — has occurred.

### Uncommon Exceptions

However, the Rabbis made their enactment only for common situations: *milta d'shchicha gazru bei Rabbanan, milta d'lo shchicha lo gazru bei Rabbanan*. For uncommon or atypical transactions — such as the transfer of a debt owed by one person to another, which is the mechanism Rav Nachman identifies as operative in the Mishna — the Rabbinic *gezeirah* does not apply. In those cases, the Torah's original rule remains in force: a symbolic act, without *meshicha*, suffices to complete the transfer.

### Resh Lakish

Resh Lakish takes a fundamentally different position: *meshicha meforasha min haTorah* — the requirement of *meshicha* to effect acquisition is derived explicitly from the Torah itself, not merely a Rabbinic enactment. On this view, money alone can never suffice under Torah law, and there is no Rabbinic *gezeirah* to be limited or circumscribed. The Gemara then asks how Resh Lakish would understand the Mishna. If he holds that *peirot* can serve as the instrument of *chalipin* — following the position of Rav Sheshet — then the *seifa*'s examples make sense on those terms. But if he follows Rav Nachman and holds that commodities cannot function as the instrument of *chalipin*, he would face the difficulty that neither money nor produce could explain the Mishna, and debt-transfer — Rav Nachman's solution — itself depends on a Rabbinic limitation that Resh Lakish's framework does not recognize. The Gemara leaves the tension with Resh Lakish's position as a difficulty to be navigated.

---

## Metaltelin Mishna

### Movables Acquire

The Gemara introduces a final Mishna: *kol ha'metaltelin konin zeh et zeh* — any movable objects can acquire one another. That is, a barter transaction involving two physical movables is legally effective: when one party takes possession of the item being offered in exchange, the other party's item is simultaneously acquired by the counterparty.

### Resh Lakish Wallet

On this Mishna, Resh Lakish comments: *va-afilu kis malei ma'ot be-kis malei ma'ot* — even a wallet full of money exchanged for a wallet full of money is encompassed within this rule. The wallets are *metaltelin*, movable objects, and when one party takes hold of the other's wallet, the acquisition is complete.

### Rashi Challenge

Rashi raises a pointed question on this statement. He argues that one is compelled to read Resh Lakish as referring to a *chalipin* transaction rather than a simple barter, because if it were a straightforward value-for-value exchange, money would not effect acquisition — the Rabbis having enacted that *ma'os lo kanu* in the ordinary course. Since an exchange of coins for coins cannot work as a simple monetary purchase, Resh Lakish must mean that one picks up the other's wallet as a *kinyan*, analogous to lifting the *sudar* in a *kinyan sudar*, thereby effecting a *chalipin*. This would imply that money can indeed function as the instrument of *chalipin* — both as the thing being transferred and as the operative object of transfer — a conclusion that seems to contradict everything established in the earlier discussion.

### Demonetization

The Gemara resolves the difficulty. Rav Acha interprets the Mishna as referring to *dinar anaka* and *dinar nigra* — specific coin types — and specifies that in each case the coins had been demonetized: *echad she-paslo malchut ve-echad she-paslo medina* — one case where the sovereign government invalidated the currency, and one where a regional authority did so. Once a governmental authority declares that a coin is no longer legal tender, it ceases to function as money in any legal sense. It may still be minted and bear a royal insignia, but it is now merely a piece of metal — a commodity, like any other form of *metaltelin*. The exchange of two wallets of demonetized coins is therefore simply barter between two commodity-goods, not a transaction involving legal currency. There is consequently no tension with the principle that *ein matbea na'aseh chalipin*: these are no longer coins in the relevant legal sense.

### Two Demonetizations

The Gemara insists that both cases — *paslo malchut* and *paslo medina* — were necessary to include. Had the Gemara taught only the case where the empire (*malchut*) demonetized the currency, one might have thought this works only because the coins truly cannot circulate anywhere — they are universally rejected. But where only a regional authority (*medina*) demonetizes the coins, one might argue that the coins retain monetary status because they remain valid currency in neighboring regions; they can still be used as money elsewhere, and therefore should retain their character as *matbea* rather than becoming mere *metaltelin*, with the result that they should *not* be acquirable through *chalipin*. Conversely, had the Gemara taught only the case of *paslo medina*, one might have thought this works only because within that jurisdiction the coins cannot circulate at all — neither publicly nor privately. But when the empire demonetizes the coins, one might argue that they can still be used informally in private transactions — a kind of black-market currency — and therefore retain enough monetary character to preclude *chalipin*. Teaching both cases establishes that in either scenario — whether the invalidation is total and universal, or merely regional — the demonetized coins lose their status as legal currency and become ordinary movables subject to the standard rules of *metaltelin* acquisition.

---

## Final Synthesis

### Summary

After an extended *shakla ve-tarya*, the Gemara has arrived at a clear and consistent conclusion on two distinct questions. First, money cannot serve as the operative *instrument* of *chalipin* — a coin cannot be used the way a *sudar* is used to enact a symbolic transfer. Second, and more subtly, money also cannot be *acquired* through *chalipin* — it cannot serve as the object of transfer in such a transaction. Sources that appeared to challenge these conclusions — the *ma'aser sheni* Baraita, the money-changer case, the *Kiddushin* Mishna, and Resh Lakish's statement about wallets of coins — have each been reinterpreted. The *ma'aser sheni* case showed that no *chalipin* option was available when money was absent, confirming that money cannot be acquired this way. The money-changer case was resolved either by identifying the coins as unstamped commodity-metal (*prottotat*) or by classifying the transaction as a permissible form of loan under Rav Ashi's principle. The *Kiddushin* Mishna was shown to address the transfer of debt or appraised value through a *sudar*, not a coin functioning as instrument. And Resh Lakish's wallet case was explained as involving demonetized coins that are no longer currency in any legal sense. Throughout, the halakhic lines remain intact: *ein matbea na'aseh chalipin* — coinage has no standard role, whether as instrument or object, in the institution of *chalipin*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 47

## Money vs. Meshicha

### Kinyan Overview

The daf opens in the middle of the celebrated debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding the mechanism of *kinyan* in commercial transactions. Rabbi Yochanan holds that by Torah law it is *kesef* — the payment of money — that effects the *kinyan*, but *Chazal* instituted a *takanah* requiring *meshicha*, the physical act of taking the object into one's possession, in order to finalize the acquisition. Reish Lakish disagrees fundamentally, maintaining that *meshicha* is not a rabbinic override but is itself the Torah's mechanism for *kinyan*. Running alongside this debate is a related set of questions: when is a coin considered money and when is it considered *peiros* (produce or commodity), and whether *chalipin* — the formal act of exchange — can be performed using a coin, or whether a coin can itself be transferred through *chalipin*.

### Handful of Coins

The gemara picks up with a ruling transmitted by Rava in the name of Rav Huna: if Reuven says to Shimon, "*mechor li be'elu*" — "sell me [your cow] with these [coins]," gesturing to whatever handful of coins he holds without specifying the amount — and Shimon agrees, the *kinyan* takes effect, and there is *ona'ah*, the law of overcharging or undercharging, that applies to the transaction.

This formulation raises an immediate tension. On one hand, the applicability of *ona'ah* implies that this is a normal sale for a price — the transaction is understood as a monetary purchase, and the question of whether the price was fair is therefore legally relevant. On the other hand, since no specific amount was named, the money is being treated to some degree as an object rather than a currency, making the transaction function more like *chalipin* — a swap. And if it is like *chalipin*, why was no *meshicha* of the cow required to finalize the deal?

### Ona'ah & Chalipin

The tension in Rav Huna's ruling becomes sharper when contrasted with the analysis that follows. The gemara notes that Reuven used the word *mechor* — "sell" — not "swap." The language of sale is what allows *ona'ah* to apply, because the parties understand the cow is being exchanged for a monetary value. At the same time, the failure to specify the exact amount allows the coins to be treated somewhat like an object, which is why the transaction can function as *chalipin* and does not require physical *meshicha* of the cow. The difficulty is that these two characterizations seem to pull in opposite directions: *ona'ah* belongs to the world of sales, while the dispensation from *meshicha* belongs to the world of swaps.

### Money as Object

A contrasting version of Rav Huna's ruling is cited in the name of Rav Abba: *mechor li be'elu kana ve'ein lo alav ona'ah* — if one says "sell me with these," the *kinyan* takes effect but there is no *ona'ah*. In this reading, the transaction is understood entirely as a swap. The coins function as an object — item number one — Shimon takes possession of them, and Reuven thereby acquires the cow. There is no *ona'ah* because the parties are not conducting a sale at a fixed price but exchanging one object for another, like a cow for a donkey. While this reading is internally more consistent — treating the money purely as an object coheres with the absence of *ona'ah* — it still must contend with the general principle that a coin (*matbe'a*) cannot serve as the instrument of *chalipin*.

The gemara addresses this directly: *lema savar Rav Huna matbe'a na'aseh chalipin* — do we think Rav Huna holds that a coin can effect *chalipin*? The answer is no. Rather, Rav Huna holds like Rabbi Yochanan, who maintains that by Torah law money itself is *koneh*. What is happening in this case is therefore not *chalipin* at all in the technical sense, but a genuine sale effected by money operating on Torah terms. The reason this is permitted — while the usual rabbinic requirement of *meshicha* is set aside — is the principle *milsa dishchicha gazar bah rabanan, milsa delo shchicha lo gazar bah rabanan*: the rabbis enacted their override for common cases, but in unusual or exceptional circumstances they allowed the Torah rule to operate. What makes this case exceptional is the degree to which the money was being treated as an object — the unspecified handful — which takes it out of the standard transaction and allows the Torah's mechanism of *kesef* to function.

This resolves the internal tension in the first version of Rav Huna's ruling as well. It truly is a *mecher* — a sale — which is why *ona'ah* applies. The Torah mechanism of *kesef* is operative, which is why no *meshicha* is required. The quasi-objectlike treatment of the coins is not what effects the *kinyan*, but it is what creates the unusual character of the transaction sufficient to carve it out from the rabbinic *takanah*.

This is confirmed by a subsequent clarification: Mar Huna the son of Rav Nachman told Rav Ashi that in their tradition, Rav Huna had explicitly ruled that a coin cannot effect *chalipin* — *ein matbe'a na'aseh chalipin* — and was counted among the *amoraim* who stated this position unambiguously. The earlier reading of his ruling as possibly endorsing *chalipin* with a coin was thus only a hypothetical. For those who know Rav Huna's position clearly, the only explanation for why the transaction works at all must be the Rabbi Yochanan principle: *min hatorah kesef koneh*.

---

## Chalipin

### Price-Aware Swaps

Before returning to the main debate, the gemara poses an elegant parallel question. We have just seen that when money is treated somewhat like an object — when no exact amount is specified — it can function quasi-like *chalipin* and allow the Torah's mechanism of *kesef* to operate. The reverse question now presents itself: if parties conducting what is formally a *chalipin* swap also take careful account of the value of the objects being exchanged, does that degree of price-consciousness transform the swap into a sale?

### Donkey/Cow Case

Rav Adda bar Ahava brings a *braita* as potential evidence. The case: Reuven stands in the market with his cow. Shimon approaches and asks why he brought the cow; Reuven replies that he is looking to acquire a donkey. Shimon offers his donkey in exchange for the cow, and the two parties then proceed to assess the value of each animal — "*paratcha bekama, bekach vekach; chamorecha bekama, bekach vekach*" — determining what each is worth. Having established the values, Shimon (the owner of the donkey) then takes possession of the cow. Before Reuven can take possession of the donkey, however, the donkey dies. The ruling: *lo kana ba'al hachamor et hapara* — Shimon does not acquire the cow.

The apparent implication is significant. Since the parties set a dollar value on the animals, the transaction was effectively transformed from a swap into a sale. In a sale, one object is the currency and the other is the commodity. If Reuven came to the market to acquire a donkey and offered his cow as payment, then the cow functions as the "money" and the donkey as the "object." Shimon took possession of the cow — analogous to receiving payment — but Reuven had not yet taken possession of the donkey — analogous to *meshicha* of the sold object. Absent *meshicha*, the sale is not final, and Reuven may withdraw. This seems to confirm that price-awareness converts *chalipin* into a sale.

### Rava's Defense

Rava rejects this reading with characteristic sharpness: *atu chalipin beshotni askinan dela kapdi?* — are we really discussing *chalipin* conducted by fools who pay no attention to value? Of course parties to a swap assess whether they are getting equal or fair value; that does not transform the transaction into a sale. People who swap a donkey for a cow are not oblivious to relative worth, and *chalipin* has always contemplated that parties will attend to value. Accordingly, Rava states the affirmative rule: *kol chalipin mikpad kapid vekaney* — in every *chalipin*, one may be careful about value and the *kinyan* is nonetheless valid as a swap.

### Multiple Objects

If value-consciousness does not explain the *braita*'s ruling, what does? Rava reinterprets the case entirely. The scenario being described is one in which the parties discovered, upon assessing values, that the donkey and cow were not of equal worth — say the donkey was worth one hundred and the cow only sixty. To equalize the exchange, Reuven offered not only his cow but also his sheep (worth forty), making the swap a donkey for a cow and a sheep. The *chalipin* remains a genuine swap, not a sale — but now the "package" on Reuven's side consists of two objects. When Shimon takes possession of the cow but not yet the sheep, that is not a complete *meshicha* of Reuven's side of the deal: *delo haveya leh meshicha ma'alya* — it is not a full *meshicha*. Because the entire set of objects Reuven is giving has not been taken into possession, the transaction is not yet finalized, and when the donkey dies Reuven may withdraw.

This reading preserves the integrity of *chalipin* even when value is assessed. The gemara thus determines that price-awareness does not convert a swap into a sale. What the *braita* illustrates is rather that when value-equalization leads to a multi-object package on one side, *meshicha* of that entire package must occur before the *kinyan* is complete.

The gemara notes in passing an interesting open question: what if, rather than adding a sheep, one party said "donkey for cow, and I'll owe you forty"? Would the outstanding monetary obligation assimilate the transaction to a sale? The gemara does not address this case, leaving it as a point requiring further analysis.

---

## Money vs. Meshicha (II)

### Rav Huna's View

The gemara now returns to reconcile the positions that have emerged. The key move is the identification of Rav Huna's ruling with the position of Rabbi Yochanan — *min hatorah kesef koneh* — and the principle that the rabbinic override (*gezeirah*) requiring *meshicha* was enacted for ordinary cases but not extended to exceptional ones.

The reason *Chazal* instituted *meshicha* in place of *kesef* is the well-known *gezeirah*: *shema yomar lo nisrefu chitecha ba'aliyah* — lest the seller say to the buyer, "your grain burned up in my loft." If the payment of money were to finalize the sale, the grain would henceforth belong to the buyer while remaining physically in the seller's domain. The seller, now a *shomer chinam* with no personal stake in the grain's safety, would have little motivation to exert himself to save it in a fire. *Chazal* therefore required that the sale not be final until the buyer took physical possession, ensuring that the person who stands to lose from negligence is also the one in a position to prevent it.

The gemara probes whether this concern can be dismissed: if someone causes the fire, let him pay the buyer for the loss. The response: the *gezeirah* addresses cases of *ones* — an accidental fire, such as one caused by lightning, for which no one is liable. In such a case, absent the *takanah*, the seller would have no incentive to risk himself to save what is already, technically, the buyer's property. With the *takanah* in place — the sale not being final until *meshicha* — the seller knows the grain is still his until possession transfers, and *masser nafshia tarach umatzil*, he will exert himself to save it.

Given this rationale, the principle that *milsa delo shchicha lo gazru bah rabanan* — the rabbis did not extend their decree to unusual cases — becomes intelligible in context.
