What makes the unusual case exceptional is not mere rarity alone; it is that the particular features of the transaction, such as the quasi-objectlike treatment of the coins, remove it from the paradigm the *gezeirah* was designed to address.

This also illuminates what is admittedly still somewhat strange: having one system that operates differently in standard versus exceptional cases. Yet the gemara notes that we already know *meshicha* works in some situations, *hagbahah* in others, *mesira* in others still, so a certain plurality of operative mechanisms is familiar. The philosophical question of why the Torah would have constructed the *kinyan* around *kesef* in the first place — if, in practice, *Chazal* found it necessary to replace it with *meshicha* — is left as a matter for deeper reflection.

---

## Objects in Chalipin

### Rav vs. Levi

Having concluded the discussion of when money can operate as *kesef*, the gemara now addresses the detailed mechanics of *chalipin*: which objects may be used to effect it, and whose object is employed. This is introduced with the question *bameh konin* — with what do we acquire?

Rav rules *b'kelov shel koneh* — with the object belonging to the purchaser. The buyer gives his handkerchief to the seller; the seller takes it, and the buyer thereby acquires whatever is being sold. This follows naturally from the swap model: the buyer gives something and receives something in return. It is also, in fact, the *halakha* as ruled. Levi disagrees: *b'kelov shel makneh* — the object belongs to the one transferring, the seller. Shimon who is selling his cow gives his handkerchief to Reuven; Reuven takes it, and thereby acquires the cow. Everything moves in one direction, which seems counterintuitive.

### Gemurit Da'at

The gemara explains the rationale behind Rav's ruling in terms of *gemurit da'at* — the finalization of intent. In any *kinyan*, the party whose *da'at* is most critical to establish is the *makneh*, the one transferring the object out of his possession. He must reach a point of genuine, settled resolve to part with what he owns. The mechanism of *chalipin*, on this reading, is designed to bring about that finalization of intent in the *makneh*. Therefore, *d'nikha leh l'koneh d'lehavi makneh koneh* — it is in the buyer's interest that the *makneh* be the one who takes possession of the buyer's object, *ki heichi d'ligmar v'likni leh* — so that the seller will reach *gemurit da'at* and transfer the property. The seller receiving something from the buyer is what crystallizes his resolve to give.

### Land & Chattel

A pointed challenge is raised against Levi's position by Rav Huna mi-Diskarta. If *chalipin* operates through the seller giving his own handkerchief to the buyer, and the buyer acquires both the handkerchief and the land being sold, then the buyer is acquiring land by taking possession of a garment. But the established rule runs in precisely the opposite direction: *nechasim she'ein lahem achrayut niknin im nechasim she'yesh lahem achrayut* — chattel can be acquired together with real estate, meaning that taking possession of land brings chattel along with it. The reverse — that chattel drags real estate along with it — is not the rule. Yet on Levi's model, taking the handkerchief would seem to transfer the land, which is exactly that impermissible reversal.

### Benefit Theory

Rava's response on Levi's behalf is striking. He says, with characteristic vigor, that Levi would have been furious at the challenge: *aval maruka lo itzterich* — the question rests on a misunderstanding of the conceptual model. It is not that the buyer acquires the land *through* taking possession of the handkerchief, as if the handkerchief were dragging the land with it. Rather, the mechanism is entirely different: *b'hai hana'ah d'kamakabbel minei gemar v'akni lei* — it is the benefit that the seller (the *makneh*) receives from the fact that the buyer agreed to accept a gift from him. When Reuven accepts Shimon's handkerchief, Shimon experiences a kind of benefit — the honor and goodwill of having one's gift received — and it is that benefit which generates the *gemar da'at* in Shimon, allowing him to finalize his intent and transfer the land. There is no chattel acquiring land; the handkerchief is not a vehicle of acquisition at all. The vehicle is the *benefit* flowing back to the seller from the act of acceptance.

While this formulation avoids the technical objection about *nechasim she'ein lahem achrayut*, it is admittedly a more convoluted mechanism than the simple swap model underlying Rav's position. Why not simply use the natural direction of the buyer giving to the seller? Nevertheless, this remains Levi's position.

### Ruth's Shoe

The debate between Rav and Levi is shown to be rooted in a *tannaitic* dispute about the verse in Ruth: *v'zos l'fanim b'Yisrael al hage'ulah v'al hatemurah l'kayem kol davar, shalaf ish na'alo v'natan l'rei'eihu* — "And this was the custom in Israel concerning redemption and exchange, to confirm every matter: a man drew off his shoe and gave it to his fellow." The gemara identifies *ge'ulah* as referring to sale and *temurah* as referring to exchange — *chalipin* — and notes that *l'kayem kol davar* encompasses anything one wishes to establish, whether a sale, a swap, or an obligation.

The critical question in the verse is *mi natan l'mi* — who gave to whom? The *tanna kamma* says Boaz gave to the redeemer, meaning the *koneh* (Boaz, who was acquiring the right of redemption and Ruth) gave his object to the *makneh* — the position of *kelov shel koneh*, which is Rav's view. Rabbi Yehuda says the redeemer gave to Boaz, meaning the *makneh* gave his object to the *koneh* — the position of *kelov shel makneh*, which is Levi's view.

It is worth noting that the *ketubah* ceremony provides a vivid illustration of *l'kayem kol davar* used not as a swap and not as a sale, but as an act of *hitchayvut* — obligation. The rabbi representing the *kallah* gives the handkerchief to the *chatan*, who accepts it, and through that acceptance obligates himself to the *kallah* in all the terms of the *ketubah*. This usage — establishing an obligation rather than transferring ownership — is arguably a natural reading of *l'kayem kol davar*, though the gemara itself does not develop this point.

---

## Valid Objects

### Any Vessel

A *braita* teaches: *konin bikli af al pi she'ein bo shaveh pruta* — the *kinyan* is effected with a *kli*, a vessel or functional object, even if it is not worth a *perutah*. A handkerchief, a pen, any functional object — regardless of monetary value — suffices. The requirement is that it be a *kli*, an object, not that it have a specific worth.

### Vessels Only

Rav Nachman rules: *lo shanu ella bikli, aval befeirot lo* — only a vessel qualifies; fruit does not. As Tosafot explains and as the context makes clear, this is not a minimum-value requirement but a categorical exclusion: produce and food items, being consumable rather than functional, cannot serve as the instrument of *chalipin* regardless of their worth.

### Produce Allowed

Rav Sheshet disagrees: *afilu befeirot* — even produce can effect *chalipin*. The dispute turns on competing readings of the verse. Rav Nachman derives from *na'alo* — his shoe — that the object must be something like a shoe: a man-made, functional item. Rav Sheshet derives from *l'kayem kol davar* — to establish any matter — that the object used need not be a *kli* specifically; it can be anything, including food, provided it is a complete, discrete item and not half a pomegranate or half a walnut. The word *na'alo*, Rav Sheshet would say, teaches only that the object must be a recognizable whole — a *davar mesuyam* — not that it must be a manufactured vessel.

Each *amora* must also account for the textual element emphasized by the other. For Rav Nachman, *l'kayem kol davar* means one can acquire anything one wishes through *chalipin*, not that one can use anything as the instrument. For Rav Sheshet, *na'alo* teaches that the object must be a complete and discrete thing, not that it must be a *kli*.

### Ketuba Language

The standard formula used in halakhic documents, including the *ketubah*, encodes these disputes: *b'mana d'chasher l'miknya bei* — "with a vessel that is fit to effect *kinyan* with." Each word carries halakhic weight. *B'mana* — "with a vessel" — excludes the position of Rav Sheshet that produce suffices; the formula insists on a *kli*. *D'chasher* — "that is fit" or "appropriate" — excludes the position of Shmuel that *maroka* (a vessel fashioned from dung or date-pits, something considered degraded and inappropriate) may be used. Even if something qualifies technically as a *kli*, it must be fit and seemly. *L'miknya bei* — "to acquire with" — excludes the position of Levi that the *makneh*'s vessel is used; *l'miknya* is the Aramaic for "to take possession," indicating that it is the *koneh* who uses the vessel to acquire, not the *makneh* who uses it to transfer.

### What's Excluded

Three further exclusions emerge from the formula. Rav Pappa derives from the word *bei* — "with it" — that a coin (*matbe'a*) is excluded. A coin, regardless of how it is framed, cannot serve as the *kli* for *chalipin*. Rav Zevid (or, according to some, Rav Ashi) derives from *d'chasher* — "appropriate" — that *issurei hana'ah*, objects from which benefit is prohibited (such as something fashioned from materials of *avodah zarah*), are excluded. Even if such an object is technically a *kli*, it lacks the quality of fitness required. The two exclusions are complementary rather than contradictory: *bei* excludes the coin (on account of its monetary character), and *d'chasher* excludes objects of prohibited benefit (on account of their legal status).

As for *maroka*, the gemara states *lo itzterich* — no special derivation is needed; it is so obviously beneath the dignity of a formal legal act that its exclusion goes without saying. The requirement of *d'chasher* captures not only technical fitness but a standard of appropriateness and dignity.

In summary: the *halakha* follows Rav — *kli shel koneh*; *chalipin* cannot be performed with a *matbe'a*; produce is invalid; and the object used must be fit, seemly, and not one from which benefit is prohibited.

### Rabbeinu Tam

An important qualification to these rules emerges from the position of Rabbeinu Tam, discussed in Tosafot. Rabbeinu Tam draws a sharp distinction between two fundamentally different modes of *chalipin*. The first, which corresponds to *al hage'ulah* (sale) and *l'kayem kol davar* (obligation), is the formal, ritual act of *chalipin* — the handkerchief given as a legal mechanism to seal a sale or create an obligation. It is to this mode that all the formal requirements apply: *kli shel koneh*, only a *kli* and not produce, the requirements of fitness and dignity. The second mode corresponds to *al hatemurah* — an actual exchange, like a donkey for a cow. Here, Rabbeinu Tam maintains, everyone would agree that the restrictions of *kli hara'uy liknot bo* do not apply. In a genuine swap, the parties are exchanging actual items, and the rules of *chalipin* as a formal legal act are simply not operative in the same way. Even produce, Rabbeinu Tam holds, would be valid in the context of an actual exchange — a point on which there would be universal agreement once the two modes are properly distinguished. The question of whether animals fall in the category of *kli* or of produce (since they are not man-made but are also not consumable) remains a point of analysis within this framework.

### Asimon

The gemara introduces the concept of *asimon*, which occupies an intermediate category between money and commodity. The *mishna* states: *asimon koneh et hamatbe'a* — the *asimon* acquires the standard coin. That is, the *asimon* is treated as the object (*peiros*) while the standard coin is the currency; when the buyer takes possession of the *asimon*, that *meshicha* finalizes the *kinyan*.

Rav initially explains *asimon* as coins used as chits at a bathhouse — tokens given to indicate something (perhaps counting patrons, or entitling one to a towel), but not functioning as genuine currency. The gemara challenges this: a *braita* lists both *asimon* and bathhouse chits as separate categories, making them clearly distinct.

Rabbi Yochanan provides the authoritative definition: *asimon* is a *pulsa* — and as Rashi explains, this means an unstamped coin (*mechusar tzurah*), a piece of precious metal that has inherent value by weight but has not yet been impressed with an official image. Such a piece cannot function as ordinary currency — it cannot be exchanged at face value in the market — and is therefore treated as a commodity rather than money.

Rabbi Yochanan adds that his reading of *asimon* is consistent with the position of Rabbi Dosa and Rabbi Yishmael, who apply a broader standard in *ma'aser sheni* redemption. The verse *v'tzarta hakesef b'yadecha* — "you shall bind the money in your hand" — is interpreted by Rabbi Yishmael as including anything that can be bound in one's hand, making unstamped metal eligible for *ma'aser sheni* redemption. Rabbi Akiva restricts this to *davar sheyesh alav tzurah* — only something bearing a stamped image. Rabbi Yochanan sees Rabbi Dosa (who permits *asimon* for *ma'aser sheni*) as sharing the inclusive approach of Rabbi Yishmael, and his own definition of *asimon* as unstamped metal flows directly from that logic.

---

## Yochanan/Reish

### Yochanan: Money

With the conclusion of the *mishnah*'s ruling that *meshicha* finalizes a sale while money alone does not — and that a party who accepted payment but has not yet delivered the object is morally censured but not legally bound — the gemara now presents the original location of the Rabbi Yochanan–Reish Lakish debate. Everything cited earlier was anticipatory; here is the debate as it stands in the text.

Rabbi Yochanan states: *devar Torah ma'ot konot* — by Torah law, it is the payment of money that effects the acquisition. The Torah system is built around *kesef*.

### Gezeirah

Why, then, did the rabbis require *meshicha*? *Gezeirah shema yomar lo nisrefu chitecha ba'aliyah* — lest the seller say to the buyer, "your grain burned in my loft." If money finalizes the sale, the grain is now the buyer's property even while sitting in the seller's domain. The seller, now a *shomer chinam* with no personal stake, has no strong incentive to risk himself to save it. *Chazal* therefore required the buyer to take physical possession before the sale is complete, ensuring that the party with the incentive to protect the property is also the one who controls it.

The gemara tests whether the concern is trivial: if someone causes the fire, let the arsonist pay. The response: the *gezeirah* targets cases of *ones*, where a fire breaks out through no one's fault — lightning, for instance — and no one is legally liable. In such a case, if the grain is already the buyer's by operation of Torah law, *lo masser nafshia tarach u'matzil* — the seller will not exert himself to save it. But if the sale is not final until *meshicha*, the seller knows his own property is at risk, and *masser nafshia tarach u'matzil* — he will go to great lengths to protect it.

This *gezeirah* is a striking feature of halakhic reasoning: *Chazal* overrode a Torah-level mechanism — *kesef* as *kinyan* — in order to produce better incentives and protect the practical interests of buyers. The philosophical question of why the Torah would have established *kesef* as the primary mechanism in the first place, if it produces such problematic incentive structures, is left open.

### Reish: Meshicha

Reish Lakish takes a categorically different position: *meshicha meforashes min hatorah* — *meshicha* is the Torah's own mechanism for *kinyan*, not a rabbinic enactment. The Torah itself establishes that physical acquisition is what transfers ownership, and money plays no direct role in effecting the *kinyan* at the Torah level.

### Textual Proof

Reish Lakish derives this from the verse: *vechi simkeru mimkar la'amisecha o kano miyad amisecha* — "When you sell a sale to your fellow or purchase from the hand of your fellow." The phrase *kano miyad* — "purchase from the hand" — indicates that acquisition occurs specifically through the transfer from one hand to another, i.e., through physical possession changing hands. *Davar hanikneh miyad l'yad* — it is an act that is effected hand to hand, which is the language of *meshicha*.

Rabbi Yochanan reads *miyad* differently: it comes to exclude land (*karka*) from the laws of *ona'ah*. The verse discusses *ona'ah*, and *miyad* serves to limit those laws to chattel — *l'mi'utei karka deleis bei ona'ah* — since the *halakhot* of overcharging do not apply to real estate. This is itself a striking interpretive point: the verse speaks explicitly about land, yet *Chazal* apply its central teachings — *ona'ah* and, on Reish Lakish's reading, *meshicha* — to chattel.

### Ona'ah Dispute

Reish Lakish presses further. If *miyad* is merely coming to exclude land from *ona'ah*, why does the verse need to mention *o kano* — "or purchase" — at all? The verse could simply have said "you shall sell to your fellow from his hand, do not oppress." The inclusion of the purchaser's act (*kano*) must teach something additional. Reish Lakish maintains it teaches two things: first, that the prohibition of *ona'ah* applies to the purchaser (i.e., underpaying is also *ona'ah*, not only overcharging), and second, that *kano miyad* tells us the acquisition occurs only through the hand-to-hand transfer.

Rabbi Yochanan accounts for *o kano* differently: *talmud lomar o kano al tonu* — the verse must say "or if you purchase, do not oppress" in order to teach that the prohibition of *ona'ah* applies whether it is the *lokei'ach* (buyer) who is cheated by being overcharged or the *mocher* (seller) who is cheated by being underpaid. Without this phrase, one might have thought only the buyer's being defrauded triggers the prohibition. *O kano* extends *ona'ah* to the seller's disadvantage as well.

Reish Lakish responds: *tartei shma mina* — one can derive both from the same phrase. *O kano al tonu* teaches that *ona'ah* applies to the seller; *kano miyad* teaches that acquisition is through hand-to-hand transfer — *meshicha*. Both lessons are contained in the same words, and there is no need to choose between them.

---

## Rabbi Shimon

### Upper Hand

The *mishnah* contains a ruling by Rabbi Shimon: *kol shehakesef beyado yado al ha'elyona* — whoever holds the money has the upper hand. This cryptic formulation requires unpacking.

### Back-Out Rights

The *mishnah* goes on to explain: *mocher hu demati hadar bei* — it is the seller, who now holds the buyer's money, who has the right to withdraw from the transaction. *Lokei'ach lo mati hadar bei* — the buyer, who has given his money but has not yet taken possession of the object, cannot back out. The situation, then, is asymmetric: money has changed hands but *meshicha* has not yet occurred. Rabbi Shimon holds that the seller — the one with the money in hand — has the upper hand and retains the right to retract, while the buyer, having given his money, is bound.

### Reish Challenges

This ruling is then deployed as a challenge in the ongoing debate. The gemara asks: *ei amart bishlama ma'ot konot* — if you accept Rabbi Yochanan's position that money effects *kinyan* by Torah law and *meshicha* is only rabbinic, then Rabbi Shimon's position becomes understandable. One can conceive of a system where the rabbinic override of *meshicha* is applied differently to the two parties. But *ela im amart ma'ot einan konot* — if you accept Reish Lakish's position that money is halakhically inert at the Torah level, then nothing has happened at all when money is exchanged without *meshicha*. How could Rabbi Shimon give significance to the money as a basis for distinguishing the rights of seller and buyer?

Reish Lakish responds directly: *aliba deRabbi Shimon lo kamina* — I am not claiming that Rabbi Shimon's view fits with my position. Reish Lakish concedes that Rabbi Shimon, who gives decisive weight to the transfer of money even prior to *meshicha*, must be operating on the assumption that *kesef koneh min hatorah* — money effects *kinyan* by Torah law, a position Reish Lakish himself rejects. Rabbi Shimon's view simply belongs to the opposing camp on that foundational question. *Ki kamina aliba deRabbanan* — Reish Lakish's argument applies to the majority Rabbinic position, not to Rabbi Shimon's. For the Rabbis (who on Reish Lakish's view hold *meshicha* is the Torah-level mechanism), the transfer of money is irrelevant to who may or may not withdraw.

### Rav Chisda

For Rabbi Yochanan, however, a further question remains. Both Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis accept that *kesef* is the Torah mechanism and *meshicha* is rabbinic. What then is the substance of their debate? The gemara answers: *ika beinaihu deRav Chisda* — the dispute between them corresponds to the principle of Rav Chisda. Rav Chisda rules: *keshem shetiknu meshicha bemokhrin kach tiknu meshicha belokkhin* — just as the rabbis established *meshicha* as operative from the seller's side, so too did they establish it as operative from the buyer's side. The override is symmetric and applies equally to both parties: until *meshicha* occurs, neither the seller nor the buyer is bound, regardless of which direction the money has flowed.

### Final Framework

The Rabbis hold of Rav Chisda's principle; Rabbi Shimon does not. For the Rabbis, because the rabbinic enactment of *meshicha* applies equally to seller and buyer, it does not matter who holds the money — until *meshicha* takes place, both parties are free to withdraw. For Rabbi Shimon, who rejects the symmetric application of *meshicha*, the Torah mechanism of *kesef* continues to operate — at least from one direction. The buyer, having given his money, is bound by the Torah-level *kinyan* of *kesef* and cannot withdraw. The seller, however, benefits from the rabbinic protection of *meshicha*: since the object has not yet transferred to the buyer's possession, the seller retains the right to retract.

Rashi's explanation of exactly why the rabbinic enactment would protect the seller but not the buyer is admittedly convoluted, and Tosafot engages in extended analysis of the point, including the question of whether a *mi shepara* curse applies when a party withdraws after money was given but before *meshicha*, particularly in cases where a genuine accident (like a fire) provides a compelling reason for withdrawal. The gemara does not fully resolve the underlying logic of Rabbi Shimon's asymmetric position, but the structural framework — the Rabbis accept Rav Chisda's symmetric application of *meshicha*, Rabbi Shimon does not — remains the operative distinction. This debate of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, and its rippling implications, will continue to be developed in the sugyot ahead.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 48

## Money & Meshicha

### Intro & Distinction

The sugya opens at the bottom of 47b, approximately five lines from the end, with the question: *ella l'Rabbi Yochanan mai ikka bein Rabbi Shimon l'Rabbanan* — according to Rabbi Yochanan, what distinguishes Rabbi Shimon from the Rabbanan? To appreciate the force of this question, one must recall the background *machloket* between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerning *ma'ot konot* — whether money effects a *kinyan* at the *de'oraita* level. Rabbi Yochanan holds *devar Torah ma'ot konot*: the transfer of money is biblically sufficient to complete an acquisition of movable property. Reish Lakish disagrees on both counts: not only does money fail to effect a *kinyan* at the biblical level, but *meshicha* — the physical pulling or taking control of the object being purchased — does work at the biblical level. Against this backdrop, the *Gemara* asks: if Rabbi Yochanan holds that money operates as a full biblical *kinyan*, what exactly was the *machloket* between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbanan in our *Mishnah*? Rabbi Shimon had stated that whoever holds the money has the stronger claim when one party seeks to retract. But if everyone agrees money works, where is the disagreement?

### Rav Chisda's View

The *Gemara* answers: *ikka beina'aihu d'Rav Chisda* — the distinguishing factor is the position of Rav Chisda. Rav Chisda had ruled: *kederech shetiknu meshicha bemochrin kach tiknu meshicha belakuchot* — just as the Rabbanan instituted *meshicha* for sellers (i.e., the seller may do *meshicha* on the money paid to finalize the sale), so too did they institute *meshicha* for buyers (i.e., the purchaser may do *meshicha* on the merchandise to finalize the acquisition). According to the Rabbanan, then, both parties possess the power of *meshicha* — either the seller taking control of the money or the buyer taking control of the goods. Rabbi Shimon, however, does not hold *k'Rav Chisda*: he maintains that it goes only by whoever holds the money, rejecting the parallel *meshicha* mechanism for the purchased object. *Rabbanan it lehu d'Rav Chisda* — the Rabbanan accept Rav Chisda's extension; Rabbi Shimon does not.

### Mi Shepara Curse

The *Mishnah* then introduces the curse invoked against a party who violates the terms of a completed agreement: *mi shepara midor hamabul hu atid lehipara mimi she'eino omed bediburo* — the One who repaid the generation of the flood will repay the one who does not stand by his word. The *Gemara* notes that this formulation fits naturally into Rabbi Yochanan's framework: *im amart bishlama ma'ot konot* — if money effects a *kinyan*, then reneging after payment constitutes a genuine violation, and the curse is well placed. However, if one holds like Reish Lakish that money does not work at the biblical level, why should a party who simply retracted from a monetary exchange receive any form of *aval* — the shorthand the *Gemara* uses for the opening of the curse, *aval amru mi shepara*? The answer offered is *mishum devarim* — because the party violated their word. But the *Gemara* immediately challenges: does violating one's word alone, without any actual *kinyan* having occurred, warrant the *mi shepara* curse?

### Reish Lakish View

A *Baraita* is cited in which Rabbi Shimon articulates an asymmetrical rule: the *tallit* can purchase the gold coin — meaning *meshicha* performed on the *tallit* effects the transfer of the gold coin, since the gold coin functions as currency relative to the *tallit* — but the gold coin cannot purchase the *tallit*, because money does not serve as a *kinyan* mechanism for acquiring goods. Nevertheless, if one violates the agreement, one receives the *mi shepara*. In the *Baraita*'s expanded formulation, four generations are invoked: the generation of the flood (*dor hamabul*), the generation of the tower of Babel (*dor haflagah*), the people of Sodom and Gomorrah (*anshei Sedom va'Amorah*), and the Egyptians at the sea (*uviMitzrayim bayam*).

### Words Alone

The *Baraita* continues: *vehanosei venoten bidvarim lo kanah* — one who conducts an entire transaction by words alone, without any *kinyan*, has not effected an acquisition. *Vehachozer bo ein chachamim nochim heimenu* — if such a person retracts, the Rabbanan are displeased with him, but there is no formal penalty.

### Rava's Rule

Rava draws a precise distinction: *anu ein lanu ella ein chachamim nochim heimenu* — in a case of words alone, the most one incurs is rabbinic disapproval. However, *devarim d'ikka bahadeihu ma'ot kai be'aval* — if there was a verbal agreement accompanied by the actual transfer of money, then the party who retracts receives the *mi shepara* curse. *Devarim velo ka bahadeihu ma'ot lo kai be'aval* — but if it was words alone without any money having changed hands, there is no *mi shepara*. It is worth noting that the *Gemara* consistently refers to the curse by the word *aval*, since the full formulation opens with *aval amru mi shepara* — the word "however, they said: the One who repaid..." This usage can be briefly disorienting on a first read, since *avel* ordinarily denotes mourning.

---

## Reish Lakish Proofs

### Asham Gezeilot

Rava now turns to affirmative support for Reish Lakish's position, declaring *kra u-matnitin mesayeia lei l'Reish Lakish* — a biblical verse and a *mishnah* both lend support to Reish Lakish. The verse in question comes from the *parasha* of *Asham Gezeilot* at the opening of Vayikra perek 5: *ve-chi yechete be-amito be-pikadon u-ve-tsumet yad u-ve-gazel o ashak et amito* — if one sins against one's fellow regarding a deposit (*pikadon*), a *tsumet yad*, theft (*gazel*), or withholding wages (*oshek*). These four cases are the conditions under which one brings a *Korban Asham*, which is distinct from a *Korban Chatat* and applies only in limited circumstances — among the five cases known for *Asham*: *Asham Gezelot*, *Shifcha Charufa*, *Asham Nazir*, *Asham Metzora*, and *me'ila*.

### Tsumat Yad Defined

The *Gemara* asks: what exactly is *tsumet yad*? Rav Chisda explains: *kegon she-yiched lo kli le-halvato* — a case where a specific object has been designated as that from which the loan will be repaid. The borrower, for example, might say: when the loan comes due, you may sell my object and take your repayment from the proceeds. Similarly, for *oshek* — withholding wages — Rav Chisda says: *kegon she-yiched lo kli le-oshko* — one had to have designated a specific object that would serve as the source of the withheld wages. Rashi explains the underlying logic: *ve-ee lo lo mechayev a-kfira't sechar sachir korban shevuah* — without a tangible designated object, comparable to a *pikadon*, there is no liability for a *Korban Asham*. A contractual obligation alone, without some object having been physically set aside, does not suffice.

### Second Pasuk

The *Gemara* then turns to the second verse: *ve-hayah ki yechete ve-ashem ve-heshiv et ha-gezeilah asher gazal o et ha-oshek asher ashak o et ha-pikadon asher hufkad ito* — the verse enumerating what must be returned lists only three of the original four cases: *gazel*, *oshek*, and *pikadon*. *Ve-ilu tsumet yad lo hadar* — but *tsumet yad* is conspicuously absent from the return obligation. The *Gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama lav mishum de-machsara meshichah* — is the reason not that *meshicha* was lacking? That is, the designation of the object for loan repayment (*tsumet yad*) did not involve the lender actually performing *meshicha* on that object, and therefore no completed *kinyan* occurred, and therefore there is nothing to return. This would be a direct proof for Reish Lakish that *meshicha* is the operative moment of acquisition.

### Rav Papa Object

Rav Papa challenges Rava's reading. He proposes: *eima me-oshek hu de-hadar kra* — perhaps we should reread the verse's silence differently. The Torah does require the return of *oshek*, yet *oshek* too involves wages being withheld. So perhaps, Rav Papa argues, the *oshek* case being enumerated for return should be understood as: *hacha b'mai askinan kegon she-netalo mimeno ve-chazar ve-hifkido etzlo* — the object designated for wage repayment had already been taken by the worker (i.e., *meshicha* had already occurred), and the worker then returned it to the employer to hold as a *pikadon* until the wages fell due. That is, the worker already acquired it and is now merely depositing it with the employer.

Rava responds: *hainu pikadon* — but then that is simply another form of *pikadon*, making *trei gavnei pikadon* — two varieties of *pikadon* — appear in the verse. Rav Papa replies: *ei hachi tsumat yad nami le-hadrei* — but if that is so, then *tsumet yad* should similarly be read as a case where the lender had already done *meshicha* on the designated object and then returned it to the borrower, and the verse should also require its return. Why does the verse omit *tsumet yad* from the return obligation if this reading would bring it under the same category?

The *Gemara* ultimately concludes: *kera lo tyuvta ve-lo siyuta* — the verse is neither a definitive refutation nor a definitive support for Reish Lakish. However, there is at least residual support: *hashta zu hadrei kera mesayea lei ve-tsumat yad lo hadrei kera* — insofar as the verse does not require the return of *tsumet yad*, that remains *somewhat* supportive of Reish Lakish's position, even if not probative in the face of Rav Papa's challenge.

A later verse is then adduced: *o mi-kol asher yishava alav le-shaker*, and Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avuha citing Rav explains: *le-rabot tsumat yad le-hishavon* — this verse comes to include *tsumet yad* among those things which must be returned, doing so *be-hedya* — in its concrete, physical form. This means, the *Gemara* concludes, that the earlier verse's silence on *tsumet yad* was intentional — *lo hadrei kra* — and its inclusion requires this later verse, confirming that *tsumet yad* was indeed treated differently from the outset.

### Bathhouse & Hekdesh

The *Gemara* now turns to the *mishnah* that Rava cited as support for Reish Lakish: *natana le-lavlan ma'al* — if one gave coins of *hekdesh* to the bathhouse attendant (*balan*) in exchange for admission to the bathhouse, one has committed *me'ila*. This raises the question of precisely when the *me'ila* is violated — a question on which Rashi and the Ritba disagree, disputing whether payment was made before or after the bathing. But the deeper question is: why is giving a coin to the bathhouse attendant *me'ila* at all?

### Rav on Me'ila

Rav clarifies the scope of this ruling: *davka balan hu delo machsara meshicha* — it is specifically the bathhouse case where no *meshicha* is lacking, because the attendant takes the coin directly and the benefit is immediately experienced. *Aval midi achrita demachsara meshicha lo maal ad demashich* — but in any other case where *meshicha* on the *hekdesh* object has not yet occurred, one does not transgress *me'ila* until *meshicha* is actually performed. This reading of the *mishnah* aligns directly with Reish Lakish's position: *meshicha*, not the transfer of money, is the operative moment of acquisition — and thus of *me'ila*.

### Non-Jew Barber

A complication then arises from another *Baraita*: *vehatanya natna lasapar* — what if one gave *hekdesh* coins to a barber? The *Gemara* notes that a barber finalizes a service agreement by *meshicha* on the scissors — that is, the taking of the scissors by one party was apparently the recognized *kinyan* act for the haircut agreement. If *meshicha* has not occurred, the transaction is not final and *me'ila* should not yet apply. This seems to contradict the bathhouse ruling. The resolution: *hacha b'mai askinan besapar nochri* — the barber case is discussing a non-Jewish barber. *Delav bat meshicha hu* — *meshicha* does not function as a *kinyan* with non-Jews.

Why not? The principle is that certain *kinyanim* operate within a particular legal system. If non-Jews do not recognize *meshicha* as a legally operative act of transfer in their own framework, there is no basis for *meshicha* to function as a *kinyan* between a Jew and a non-Jew in a transaction. This has significant practical implications: one reason the *Mishna Berura* discusses the practice of performing multiple *kinyanim* in the sale of *chametz* before Pesach is precisely this concern. Since various *rishonim* question whether any single *kinyan* — including *meshicha* — is universally operative with a non-Jew, the common practice developed to perform multiple overlapping *kinyanim* (*chalifin*, *kinyan chatzer* by leasing the storage area, *situmta* by handshake, and transfer of money) to ensure that the sale is halachically effective by at least one recognized mechanism.

A second, harmonious *Baraita* confirms: *natna lasapar o lasapan o lechol baal umanut lo maal ad demashach* — if one gave *hekdesh* money to a barber, a boatman, or any craftsman, one does not transgress *me'ila* until *meshicha* on the agreed-upon object occurs. The two *Baraitot* are thus resolved: one speaks of a non-Jewish barber (where *meshicha* does not operate), the other of a Jewish one. *Shema mina* — the lesson stands.

---

## Rav Nachman Agrees

### Money Koneh

At this point, Rav Nachman registers his own position: *devar Torah ma'ot konot* — at the biblical level, money effects a *kinyan* for *metaltelin*. Rav Nachman thereby aligns himself with Rabbi Yochanan against Reish Lakish.

---

## Reish Lakish Proofs (II)

### Levi Grocer

Levi had examined the text of the *Mishnah* in his own version and found: *ashkach natna lesiton ma'al* — in the case where one placed *hekdesh* money on the counter of the *siton* (a large-scale merchant or wholesaler), *me'ila* applies immediately upon transfer of the money, even though the buyer has not yet taken possession of the merchandise. This would support Rabbi Yochanan's position: *me'ila* kicks in at the moment money changes hands, not at the moment of *meshicha*.

---

## Rav Nachman Agrees (II)

### Siton Proof

This version of the *Mishnah* is presented as a challenge to Reish Lakish and a support for Rabbi Yochanan: if *me'ila* applies the moment money is given to the grocer, that implies money is the operative moment of acquisition — consistent with *ma'ot konot* at the biblical level.

### Reish Lakish Reply

Reish Lakish responds: *hamani Rabbi Shimon hi* — that *mishnah* must reflect the opinion of Rabbi Shimon. Since Reish Lakish already knows that Rabbi Shimon's is the minority view and is not followed, he is comfortable attributing that version of the *mishnah* to Rabbi Shimon and maintaining his own position undisturbed. Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan, for their part, regard the *siton* case as legitimate support against Reish Lakish.

A related terminological note arises here: the terms *siton* and *chanvani* are used in the sources — Rashi glosses *siton* simply as *chanvani*, a shopkeeper, though a *siton* is perhaps better understood as a large-scale wholesale merchant. The practical scenario being described is one in which a buyer pays for bulk goods in advance, and the question is whether that payment alone, before taking the goods, constitutes acquisition.

The discussion of *chalifin* also surfaces briefly in this context. Rav Nachman's acceptance of *ma'ot konot* is not contradicted by his earlier ruling (on 45b–46a) that money cannot serve as *chalifin*. These are distinct mechanisms: *kinyan kesef* concerns the purchasing power of money as a medium of exchange, while *chalifin* treats the monetary object itself as a commodity being bartered. Currency attains a distinct halachic status *because* it functions as a formalized medium of exchange, not merely as an object of value — and this is, in many respects, the underlying thematic tension of this entire *perek*.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Abaye Informs

The *Gemara* returns to the nature of the *mi shepara* curse. *Itmar* — there is an *amoraic* dispute. Abaye holds: *odi modinan lei* — the court does not actually curse the party who reneges; it merely informs him of the consequences. Specifically, Rashi explains, the court tells him: *she'im tachzor sofcha l'hipara mimcha* — if you proceed to retract, you will ultimately be repaid in kind. The reason Abaye refrains from calling it an actual curse is the verse *venasi b'amecha lo taor* — one may not curse a member of one's community. The *derashah* on this verse extends the prohibition broadly: *nasi* is not taken literally as referring only to the *nasi*, but as encompassing any person in good communal standing.

### Rava Curses

Rava disagrees: *miliytnin lei* — the court does in fact curse him. The verse says *b'amecha b'oseh ma'aseh amcha* — the prohibition applies only to one who conducts himself as a member of the community, one who keeps the law. Someone who reneges on a completed agreement has forfeited that standing and is no longer protected by the prohibition of *venasi b'amecha lo taor*. He may therefore be formally cursed.

### Rabbi Chiya Story

Rava then adduces his proof: *mana amina lah — deRabbi Chiya bar Yosef havu lei zuzei amalcha* — people came to Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef intending to purchase salt, and they paid him money. Later, the price of salt rose — *aykar malcha* — and Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef sought to retract the deal to obtain a higher price. He brought the matter before Rabbi Yochanan, who told him: *zil hav lehu* — go and give them the salt they purchased. *Ve'ee lo kabil alecha Mi Shepara* — and if you do not, you will receive the *mi shepara*. Now, if Abaye were correct that the court merely informs the party of potential consequences, Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef — as a Torah scholar fully aware of the relevant *halachot* — would hardly need to be informed. *Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef bar oduei hu* — he would already know. The fact that Rabbi Yochanan invoked *mi shepara* as a formal sanction demonstrates that it is an actual curse being administered, in accordance with Rava's position. Indeed, *Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef ata l'kabulei alohi letuta deRabbanan* — Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef ultimately came forward to accept the terms and avoid the rabbinic curse.

---

## Down Payment

### Down Payment Intro

The *Gemara* transitions to the topic of *eravon* — a down payment. This discussion is precipitated by an alternative reading of the story of Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef: *ela Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef eravon hu dehavah lei* — perhaps what they had given him was not full payment but only a down payment. This reframing introduces the pivotal question of how much a down payment acquires.

### Rava vs. Yochanan

Two positions are immediately stated. *Hu savar kenegdo hu koneh* — Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef believed that a down payment acquires only the proportional share of the object corresponding to the amount paid. If the down payment was twenty percent of the purchase price, the buyer has acquired twenty percent of the produce. *Ve'amar lei Rabbi Yochanan keneged kulo hu koneh* — Rabbi Yochanan, however, told him that a down payment acquires the entire object: the full commitment is effected, with the remaining balance becoming an obligation owed to the seller. The down payment, on Rabbi Yochanan's view, is not a partial purchase but a complete acquisition coupled with a debt for the balance. This is also formalized in the *amoraic* statement: *Rava amar kenegdo hu koneh* — Rava holds proportional acquisition — *veRabbi Yochanan amar keneged kulo hu koneh* — and Rabbi Yochanan holds full acquisition.

### Two Formulas

A *meitivei* — a challenge from a *Baraita* — is raised. The *Baraita* describes two types of agreement between parties: *HaNoten eravon lachavero* — one who gives a down payment to his fellow. In the first formulation, the buyer says: *im ani chozer bi ervoni machul lach* — if I default, I forfeit the down payment to you. In the second formulation, the seller says: *im ani chozer bi achpol lach ervonecha* — if I default, I will double the down payment back to you. The *Baraita* rules: *im amar echad me'elu nitkaymu hatna'im* — if either party stated one of these conditions, the stipulation is upheld. *Divrei Rabbi Yosi* — this is the opinion of Rabbi Yosi.

### Asmachta Kanya

The *Gemara* explains: *Rabbi Yosi leta'amei de'amar asmachta kanyah* — Rabbi Yosi holds in accordance with his own broader principle that *asmachta kanya* — an exaggerated or contingent promise does effect a *kinyan*.

### Asmachta Defined

What is *asmachta*? Rashi defines it as *havtacha guzma* — an exaggerated promise. The phenomenon refers to a commitment made contingently, where the promisor does not genuinely intend to fulfill the stated payoff, having made the promise only to incentivize the other party to enter the agreement. The classic example is the kind of exaggerated conditional commitment found in gambling or wagering contexts: one party promises a large payoff under an unlikely condition, not actually expecting to have to pay. Rashi's formulation — *she-adam mavti'ach et chaveiro lismoach alav* — conveys this: a person exaggerates the reliability of the commitment to induce the other party to trust him and proceed.

By extension, the *ketubbah* is sometimes discussed in relation to *asmachta*: it is a guarantee that money will be paid in the event of a future contingency (death or divorce), and in that sense resembles an insurance policy — an obligation that exists only upon a future event and involves no present transfer of value. The same logic applies to financial futures and contingent instruments generally.

In the *eravon* context, the concern is this: the buyer says, "even if I default and you end up keeping the entire down payment, please proceed with the agreement." He is offering the seller a favorable contingency to induce him to sell. But in reality, if the sale does not go through, both parties would ordinarily expect the down payment to be returned — it is a strange economic arrangement to agree in advance to forfeit one's down payment. The economic logic is that the buyer may believe he is receiving a price low enough that the risk is worth accepting, or that the commitment serves to signal seriousness. Either way, *asmachta* captures the sense that the contingent payoff is exaggerated beyond what is genuinely intended. Rabbanan generally hold *asmachta lo kanya* — such a contingent commitment does not effect a *kinyan* — while Rabbi Yosi maintains *asmachta kanya*.

### Rabbi Yehuda View

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with Rabbi Yosi: *dayo sheyikne k'neged eravono* — it is enough that the down payment acquires precisely what it is worth. The buyer acquires only the proportion of the object corresponding to the down payment, nothing more. This is the position of *kenegdo hu koneh*: the down payment is a partial payment, not a lever of full acquisition.

### Rabban Shimon

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel introduces a further distinction: *bameh devarim amurim bizman she'amar lo eravoni yikneh* — the foregoing *machloket* between Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Yehuda applies specifically when the buyer explicitly states, "let my down payment acquire the whole object." That is, when the language of the agreement invokes the *eravon* as a mechanism of full acquisition, that is when the dispute becomes relevant. However, says Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *aval machar lo bayit o sadeh b'elef zuz u'para lo mehen chamesh meot zuz kanah u'machzir lo et hashaar* — if one sold a field or a house for one thousand *zuz* and the buyer paid five hundred, the acquisition is effective for the whole, and the buyer must simply pay back the remainder — even if this takes several years.

### Kesef vs. Maot

The *Gemara* asks: does this rule for land (*karka*) apply equally to movable property (*metaltelin*)? The answer suggested is: *d'bistama lo kani* — by default, a partial payment for *metaltelin* does not acquire. And the language of the sources reflects this distinction: by land, the operative term is *kesef* — a formalized silver-currency transaction — whereas by *metaltelin* the term used is *ma'ot* — coins. This terminological distinction is not merely stylistic. *Kinyan kesef* for land is a formalized transaction in which a partial payment generates a complete obligation to pay the balance, because the legal act of buying land with money is treated as a discrete and binding commitment. With *metaltelin*, however, the concern is that the transfer of money should function more like *chalifin* — a barter of value for value — in which the full value must be exchanged now for the object to pass into the buyer's control. Accordingly, a partial payment for *metaltelin* does not acquire the whole, because *meshicha* or full payment is required.

This yields an important structural point: according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the *machloket* between Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Yehuda may apply only to *metaltelin*, not to *karka*. When it comes to land, even Rabbi Yehuda may agree that a partial payment (*kinyan kesef*) acquires the entirety of the field, leaving only the debt for the balance. The dispute is narrowed to movable property, where Rabbi Yosi holds that the *eravon* acquires the whole even for *metaltelin*, while Rabbi Yehuda holds it acquires only *kenegdo*.

---

## Shemitah Collateral

### Mishna Shevi'it

The *Gemara* now connects this dispute to a *Mishnah* in *Masechet Shevi'it*. The *Mishnah* rules: *Hamalveh et chaveiro al hamashkon* — one who lends money on collateral — does not have the loan cancelled by the *shemitah* year. The basis is that a loan secured by a collateral is treated differently from an unsecured loan under the laws of *shemitah* cancellation.

### Gamliel vs. Yehuda

The *Mishnah* records a dispute: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that even if the *mashkon* is worth only half the loan, the loan is not cancelled — *eino meshamet*. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules: *im haya mashkon keneged halvato eino meshamet ve'im lav meshamet* — if the collateral equals the full value of the loan, it is not cancelled; if not, it is cancelled (at least in part).

### Resolution

The *Gemara* considers whether this is a genuine *machloket* or not. If Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel means the loan is not cancelled in full — *eino meshamet bekulo* — and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi means the uncollateralized half is cancelled — *be'ach palga dela nakit aleh mashkon meshamet* — then in fact the two opinions may not contradict each other at all. They may both agree that the collateralized portion is not cancelled and the uncollateralized portion is.

### Full vs. Proportional

The resolution is that the real *machloket* between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi mirrors the *eravon* dispute. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel savar keneged kulo hu koneh* — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that collateral (or a down payment) acquires the entire object, meaning a partial collateral is treated as if it secures the entire loan, and therefore the entire loan is exempt from *shemitah* cancellation. *Ve'Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi savar kenegdo hu koneh* — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds that collateral acquires only proportionally, and therefore only the portion of the loan matching the value of the collateral is exempt; the remainder is cancelled by *shemitah*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 49

## Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish

### Meshicha vs. Kesef

We pick up from the bottom of 48b, resuming the major debate that has occupied the preceding pages. The question is one that runs to the heart of commercial *kinyan* on *metaltelin*: what is the operative act of acquisition for chattel? As a practical matter, all agree that *meshicha* — taking physical possession — is what effects the transfer. The debate concerns the conceptual and legal basis for this rule. Reish Lakish holds that *meshicha* is the biblically defined mode of acquisition; there is nothing more to say. Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, maintains that biblically the operative act is *kesef* — the payment of money. The rabbis, however, instituted *meshicha* in place of the biblical *kesef* because they wanted the owner of the object to retain responsibility for it until it is physically taken. If money alone completed the sale, a buyer could lose an object still sitting in the seller's domain through no fault of the seller, and that seemed wrong. So the rabbis overrode the biblical mode by requiring physical possession. There is a longstanding question among the *rishonim* as to how we rule between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish — the *Tosafot* discuss this at length without reaching a clean resolution.

### Conceptual Framework

Within Rabbi Yochanan's position, however, there is a further and deeper question about how to conceptualize what the rabbinic institution actually did. Two possibilities emerge. The first: the rabbis completely nullified the effect of *kesef*, so that money payment does nothing at all legally, and only *meshicha* effects the transfer. The second, more nuanced reading: the biblical *kesef* still works — money payment creates a binding sale — but the rabbis gave both parties a right to retract until *meshicha* is performed. On this reading, the sale remains valid and operative unless and until one side exercises the right of retraction. These two readings are not merely theoretical; they have real *nafka mina* implications. Rashi, for instance, raises the case of a man who pays money for an apple but never performs *meshicha* on it, and then uses that apple to effect *kiddushin*. According to the second reading of Rabbi Yochanan — that money creates a binding sale, subject to retraction — the *kiddushin* would take effect, since the man's ownership of the apple is real as long as it has not been reversed.

### Rabbi Shimon's Evidence

This conceptual question is also illuminated by the position of Rabbi Shimon in the *mishnah*, who rules that only the party holding the money — the seller — has the right to retract; the buyer who has not yet taken possession cannot retract. This asymmetry implies that the payment of money does create something binding: the sale is valid, but there is a right on one side to negate it. If the money had done nothing at all, it would be hard to explain why one side's right of retraction should be privileged over the other's. The *mi shepara* — the rabbinic declaration that God will exact payment from one who retracts after money has changed hands — likewise becomes more coherent on this reading. Either the money payment represents a serious and concrete commitment whose reversal is morally weighty, or, on the stronger reading of Rabbi Yochanan, it was actually a binding sale that is now being undone. In either case, the *mi shepara* attaches once money has changed hands, and does not attach to a purely verbal agreement where no money moved at all.

---

## Koneh K'neged Kullo

### Karka Analogy

The conceptual question about the force of *kesef* carries directly into the discussion of partial payment. If I agree to buy a thousand acres of land for a million dollars but pay only a hundred dollars, have I purchased the entire parcel or only a hundred dollars' worth? For *karka* — real property — which is acquired by *kesef* as a matter of biblical law, the *gemara* indicates that you have purchased the whole. The logic is that we treat the initial payment as though the entire price has been paid, with the remainder outstanding as a debt. It is, in effect, a mortgage: the bank pays the seller in full, and the buyer owes the bank. Here, it is as though the buyer paid in full and now owes the balance — but the acquisition of the whole parcel is complete.

### Metaltelin Debate

The more pressing question is what happens with *metaltelin* when only partial payment is made. The *gemara* frames this as a debate between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan, expressed in the language *koneh k'negdo* versus *koneh k'neged kulo*. The language itself is telling: even in the context of *metaltelin*, where *meshicha* is the operative rabbinic act, the *gemara* speaks as though the money is effecting a *kinyan* — fitting naturally with Rabbi Yochanan's position that the biblical *kesef* still operates, subject to retraction.

### Mi Shepara Question

The practical question this debate generates is the *mi shepara*. Suppose I agree to sell a hundred bushels of apples at a dollar a bushel, and the buyer pays me five dollars. Clearly, if the buyer retracts and demands back his five dollars without taking any apples, he gets a *mi shepara* — he paid money and is backing out of that portion. But what if he says: fine, I'll take the five bushels I paid for, but I do not want the other ninety-five. Does he get a *mi shepara* on the remaining ninety-five? That depends entirely on whether his five-dollar payment is understood as having purchased only five bushels (*k'negdo*) or the entire hundred (*k'neged kulo*). Rav says *k'negdo*; Rabbi Yochanan says *k'neged kulo*. One might ask about an indivisible unit — a single cow, for instance — and there it seems even stronger reason to say *k'neged kulo*, since the object cannot be partially transferred. But for divisible quantities, the question is genuinely open between the two positions.

---

## Mashkon & Shemittah

### Mashkon Shemittah Case

The *gemara* asks whether the debate between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on *k'negdo* versus *k'neged kulo* is actually a *tannaitic* dispute — *leima k'tannaei*. The case introduced is: one lends money to a friend and takes a *mashkon* — collateral — and then the *shemittah* year arrives. The rule is that *shemittah* annuls outstanding loans, derived from the verse *lo yigos et re'eihu ve'et achiv* — you shall not press your fellow or your brother — because if you hold the collateral, you are not "pressing" anyone; you already have something in hand. The specific scenario: the loan is for a thousand dollars, but the *mashkon* is worth only two hundred. What does *shemittah* annul?

Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel says: even though the *mashkon* is worth only half (or less) of the loan, *shemittah* does not annul the loan. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — referred to simply as "Rabbi" — says: *shemittah* does not annul only if the *mashkon* is equivalent in value to the entire loan; if not, *shemittah* does annul.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

The *gemara* initially reads this dispute as a direct parallel to *k'negdo* versus *k'neged kulo*. On that reading, when Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel says *shemittah* does not annul, he means it does not annul *any* of the loan — because holding the *mashkon*, even one worth only two hundred dollars, constitutes possession of the entire loan. This is *koneh k'neged kulo*: partial possession represents full possession.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, on this initial reading, holds *k'negdo*: you are in possession only to the extent of what you actually hold. The *mashkon* is worth two hundred, so *shemittah* does not annul two hundred dollars of the loan, but it does annul the remaining eight hundred. Each side holds according to what they actually possess.

### Gemara Resolution

The *gemara* pushes back on this alignment. If that is the debate — whether the two hundred dollars' worth of *mashkon* counts as possession of the full thousand — then according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, even the two hundred dollars would be annulled by *shemittah*. But that is impossible: everyone agrees that if you literally hold something worth two hundred dollars, *shemittah* cannot annul that two hundred. How could it annul what is already in your hand?

The *gemara* therefore retreats to a different resolution: *l'zikron devarim b'alma* — the *mashkon*, when it is worth less than the loan, functions merely as a reminder. Holding an object worth less than the full loan is not really "possessing" the loan in any meaningful sense. It is there so that the lender does not forget, perhaps as a bit of leverage to prompt repayment, but it does not constitute genuine possession of any portion of the loan's value. On this reading, the debate between Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is about whether holding such a symbolic *mashkon* constitutes possession of the loan at all — not a direct parallel to the question of partial payment in a sale. The conceptual analogy is instructive, but the cases are not identical: in the sale context, the question is whether partial money creates a *kinyan* on the whole object; in the *mashkon* context, the question is whether a symbolic token of possession counts as genuine possession of the debt's value. The *rishonim* do not, for the most part, press hard to equate the two, and one can see why: the mechanisms are different even if the underlying logic echoes.

A practical implication is raised: according to Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel on the stronger reading — that holding any *mashkon* prevents *shemittah* from operating on the entire loan — one could solve the problem of *shemittah* annulling loans simply by having every borrower hand over a token *mashkon*, making the institution of *pruzbul* seemingly unnecessary. The *gemara* notes this difficulty; the resolution offered by the reading of *l'zikron devarim* closes the loophole, since on that reading, a sub-value *mashkon* prevents *shemittah* only on the amount one genuinely possesses, which may be nothing at all.

---

## Rav Kahana Flax

### Case Setup

The *gemara* now narrates a concrete case involving Rav Kahana, who had received money for flax. The price of flax subsequently rose, and Rav Kahana wished to back out of the deal — at least partially. The buyers had not paid the full price; they had given only a down payment. Rav Kahana had no interest in retracting on the amount already paid — he understood that doing so would subject him to a *mi shepara* — but he wanted to retract on the remainder, the portion for which no money had yet changed hands.

### Rav's Position

He brought the question to Rav — and notably, he knew whose door to knock on, since Rav is the one who says *k'negdo*. Rav ruled: *b'mai d'nakitat zuzei* — for the amount of money you received, give them the corresponding flax. *Ve-idach devarim ninhu* — the remainder is only a verbal commitment. *U-devarim ein bahem mishum mechusrei amanah* — and a verbal commitment does not implicate the concern of violation of trust.

This is Rav's double position: first, the money paid purchased only that corresponding portion (*k'negdo*, not *k'neged kulo*); second, the unpaid remainder is a purely verbal undertaking, and backing out of a verbal undertaking is not morally wrong. This second point is striking. Legally, there is no question: one cannot be sued for failing to follow through on a verbal agreement. There is no *mi shepara* either, because no money changed hands on that portion. But Rav goes further and says there is not even a moral failing — *ein bahem mishum mechusrei amanah*. It is simply business: prices change, commitments not backed by money are understood by all parties to be subject to revision.

One might object that this renders a down payment essentially meaningless — if the seller can retract on everything beyond what was paid, and doing so carries no moral stigma, then the partial payment accomplishes nothing beyond purchasing that precise portion. Rav apparently accepts this consequence. As long as everyone understands the rules, the buyer who wants protection must pay in full or secure some other form of commitment.

---

## Devarim & Trust

### Rav vs. Yochanan

The *gemara* now formally records the *itmar* — the tradition of this debate as a named dispute. Rav says: *devarim ein bahem mishum mechusrei amanah* — verbal commitments do not implicate violation of trust. Rabbi Yochanan says: *devarim yesh bahem mishum mechusrei amanah* — verbal commitments do implicate violation of trust, and backing out of them is morally wrong. The parallelism between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan here is notable: Rav, who says *k'negdo* and thereby gives the seller more latitude, also says that the verbal portion carries no moral obligation. Rabbi Yochanan, who says *k'neged kulo* and is more protective of the buyer, also maintains that verbal commitments bind morally.

### Hin Tzedek Teaching

The *gemara* challenges Rav's position from a *baraita* citing Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda, who derives from the verse *hin tzedek yihiyeh lach* — "you shall have a just measure" — a principle about verbal integrity. The *hin* is a smaller measure than the *eifah*, and since the verse already obligates a just *eifah*, by *kal v'chomer* the *hin* is obviously included. Why then does the Torah mention the *hin* separately? To teach: *she-hen shelcha tzedek v'lav shelcha tzedek* — your "yes" should be a yes and your "no" should be a no. This is a powerful formulation: when you commit to something, you are bound by that commitment. Some *rishonim* understand Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda as stating a *d'oraita* obligation — not merely an *asmakhta* — to stand behind one's word.

### Abaye's Caveat

Abaye responds on behalf of Rav: the verse is teaching something different. *Shelo yedaber echad ba-peh v'echad ba-lev* — one should not say one thing with the mouth while intending another in the heart. The prohibition is against *duplicity* at the moment of the commitment — making a promise while already planning not to fulfill it. But if one is sincere at the moment of commitment and later changes one's mind, that is a different matter entirely; people change their minds, and that is understood. Abaye's caveat is philosophically important: it distinguishes between bad faith at the moment of promising and a genuine change of mind thereafter. Only the former is prohibited; the latter, according to Rav, carries no moral stain. This is admittedly a troubling conclusion — that there is no moral obligation whatsoever to follow through on a sincere verbal commitment — and the *gemara* notes the discomfort implicitly.

---

## Yochanan ben Matzya

### Worker Hiring Case

The *gemara* attempts to bring a proof against Rav from a *mishnah* involving Rabbi Yochanan ben Matzya (a *tanna*, not to be confused with Rabbi Yochanan the *amora*). Rabbi Yochanan ben Matzya told his son: go hire workers for us today. The son went, hired them, and agreed to pay them a wage plus meals. When the son returned to the father, the father said: my son, even if you made for them a feast like that of Solomon in his glory, you would not have satisfied your obligation to them — for they are descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and their dignity is extraordinary. Therefore, before they begin work, go and tell them: when I said "meals," I meant only bread and legumes — nothing more.

The significance for our sugya is that the father instructed the son to go back and revise the terms *before the workers began their labor*. This implies that revising a verbal commitment is permissible — which seems to support Rav. But doesn't it also imply, against Rav, that once they had begun work it would *not* have been permissible? The *gemara* presses this question.

### Reliance Analysis

The *gemara* deflects: *shani hatam de-poalim gufaihu lo samcha da'atayu* — this case is different because the workers themselves did not fully rely on the commitment. Why? Because the son was clearly acting on behalf of the father, and the workers understood that the arrangement was still pending the father's final approval. They knew the son was not the principal; the father was. So even if they had started working, the workers appreciated that the father's word had not yet been given. This is why the father could still revise the terms even after the son's commitment.

But the *gemara* then asks: if that is the case — that the workers understood the commitment was pending — why does it matter whether they had begun work or not? If the arrangement was contingent throughout, the father could always revise it. The *gemara* answers: *hitchilu b'melacha vadai samcha da'atayu* — once they begin the work, we presume they have relied fully. The reasoning is that by starting work, they are signaling that they assume the father has been informed and has approved. *Meimar amar kamei d'avua v'nicha lei* — they assume the son must have communicated the terms to the father and the father is on board.

### Reliance Principle

The crucial principle that emerges is this: *mechusrei amanah* — violation of trust — is not a categorical rule that applies whenever any verbal commitment is made. It is a function of whether the other side has genuinely relied upon the commitment. This limits Rabbi Yochanan's position significantly: even he acknowledges that not every verbal commitment creates a moral obligation to perform; it depends on the degree and nature of the other party's reliance. What makes Rav's position even more radical in light of this is that Rav apparently holds there is no moral violation *even when the other side is genuinely relying on the commitment*. In cases of real reliance and real opportunity loss, Rav still says: *devarim ein bahem mishum mechusrei amanah*.

---

## Gift Case

### Gift Retraction

The *gemara* questions whether Rabbi Yochanan was entirely consistent. Rabbah bar bar Chana reported in Rabbi Yochanan's name: *ha-omer l'chavero matanah ani noten lach* — one who tells his friend "I am giving you a gift" — *mutar lachzor bo* — is permitted to retract. If Rabbi Yochanan holds that verbal commitments implicate violation of trust, how can he permit retracting a promise to give a gift?

### Reliance Qualification

Rav Papa resolves this: Rabbi Yochanan agrees that when it is a *matanah mu'etet* — a small or modest gift — one may retract, because in that case *samcha da'atayu* — the recipient truly relies on the promise and genuinely trusts that it will happen. Wait — the formulation seems backward. Rav Papa's point is that Rabbi Yochanan's general ruling permitting retraction of a gift promise applies specifically to cases where the other side's reliance is not significant. When it is a small gift promised in passing, the recipient may hope for it but does not deeply rely on it in a way that imposes a moral obligation. But when the promise is one on which the other side truly and deeply relies — *samcha da'atayu* — Rabbi Yochanan agrees there is *mechusrei amanah* even if there is no concrete opportunity loss. The distinction is therefore not only about forgoing other opportunities; it is about the quality of trust and reliance the other party places in the commitment. Even without tangible economic harm from the retraction, the violation of that trust is itself the moral wrong.

---

## Levi Maaser

### Maaser Setup

The *gemara* brings a teaching of Rav Avin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that further illustrates the principle. A *Yisrael* tells a *ben Levi*: I have a *kor* (a large measure) of *maaser* in my threshing floor that I am going to give you. On the basis of this commitment, the *ben Levi* goes home and designates that promised *maaser* — still sitting in the *Yisrael*'s threshing floor, not yet in the *Levi*'s possession — as *trumat maaser* to exempt other *maaser* he already has. This is a remarkable act: he is using produce he does not yet own to perform *hafrashat trumat maaser* on produce he does own.

### Moral Bindingness

The *rishonim* do not extensively discuss the ownership problem here; one *acharon* notes that since the *Yisrael* has promised to give it and we operate on the assumption — per Rabbi Yochanan — that he will keep his promise, the *Levi* can treat the promised *maaser* as effectively his for purposes of designation. It is as though the *Yisrael* has given the *Levi* the right to use his produce in this way. This works only because the *Levi* can be genuinely confident that the *Yisrael* will deliver.

### Tevel Risk

The *gemara* makes the argument explicit: *ei amrat bishlama lo matzu mehadar bei* — if you say the *Yisrael* cannot retract, then it is clear why the *Levi* may perform this *hafrashah* in confidence. But *ela ei amrat matzu mehadar bei* — if you say the *Yisrael* may retract — *amai rashai?* why would the *Levi* be permitted to do it? If the *Yisrael* retracts and gives the *maaser* to a different *Levi*, the first *Levi*'s *hafrashah* was invalid, and *ishtakach d'kachil tavlim* — it will turn out that he has been eating *tevel* — untithed produce whose terumah was never properly separated. The gravity of eating *tevel* makes this an acute concern. The only way to permit the *Levi* to perform this *hafrashah* is if we can say the *Yisrael* is morally bound not to retract — precisely Rabbi Yochanan's position.

The *gemara* then asks how Rav would explain this teaching, since Rav holds that verbal commitments carry no moral obligation. The answer: *k'gon she-natlo heimenu v'chazar v'hipkido etzlo* — the case must be that the *Levi* already physically received the *maaser* from the *Yisrael* and then re-deposited it with him. In that case, the *Yisrael* is merely a *shomer* for the *Levi*, and the produce already belongs to the *Levi* — no promise needs to bind the *Yisrael* at all.

But the *gemara* challenges this from the *seifa*: if the *Yisrael* violated his commitment and gave the *maaser* to a *different* Levi — *ein lo alav ela taromet* — the first *Levi* has only a complaint, no legal claim. If the produce had already been physically transferred to the first *Levi* and re-deposited, it would belong to him, and giving it to someone else would be outright theft. The fact that there is only a *taromet* — a grievance, not a legal claim — shows that the produce was never in the first *Levi*'s physical possession. This dismantles Rav's interpretation and, as the *gemara* notes, *shema mina*: the teaching supports Rabbi Yochanan. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the moral commitment to see the arrangement through is real and the *Levi* can rely on it — but if the *Yisrael* violates it and gives to another *Levi*, the second *Levi*'s acquisition is legally valid, and the first *Levi* is left with only a moral grievance.

---

## Sesame Seeds

### Case Narrative

The *gemara* narrates a new story. A certain person gave money for sesame seeds. Subsequently the price rose, and the sellers wanted to back out. They said to the buyer: we have no sesame seeds for you — take your money back. The buyer refused to take his money back; he insisted on the sesame seeds. The sellers held the money and attempted to return it; he would not accept it. Then the money was stolen from the sellers' possession.

### Shomer Status

The case came before Rava. Rava ruled: since the sellers said to the buyer "take your money" and he refused — *lo miba'ei shomer sachar delo havei* — it goes without saying they are not a *shomer sachar* on the money, since no one is paying them to guard it. *Ela afilu shomer chinam nami lo havei* — they are not even a *shomer chinam*. The analogy is vivid: if a guest at dinner forgets his coat and the host calls after him and says take your coat and the guest refuses, the host does not become a *shomer* on the coat simply because the guest left it there. The host did not consent to be a *shomer*; the object was left against his will. Similarly, the sellers did not consent to hold the buyer's money — they tried to return it and he refused. They bear no *shomer* liability.

### Mi Shepara Acceptance

The Rabbis challenged Rava: *ha ba'ei lekabulei alei mi she-para* — wait, the sellers would have to formally accept a *mi shepara* before the retraction is complete! This introduces a significant new idea: the retraction of a sale after money has changed hands is not simply effected by one side declaring "I am backing out." The reversal requires the retracting party to accept a *mi shepara* upon themselves. Until that acceptance occurs, the sale remains in force. And if the sale remains in force, the sellers hold the buyer's money not as *shomrim* but as parties to a still-valid sale — they are, effectively, *ba'alim* of the money and fully liable for it regardless of what happens.

The concept of "accepting a *mi shepara*" raises interesting questions about mechanism. Does the retracting party stand up and formally declare acceptance of the curse? Does the other party demand it? The *gemara* does not fully spell out the procedure, though the general sense is that the reversal is not complete until the consequences are acknowledged. There is also the question of retroactivity: if acceptance occurs in court after the money was lost, does that mean the sale was retroactively reversed from the moment of declaration, or only from the moment of acceptance? The *gemara* leaves this genuinely unclear.

Rava, upon hearing the Rabbis' challenge, said *hachi nami* — indeed, he agrees they must accept a *mi shepara*. Whether he means they already had accepted it before the theft, or that their accepting it now retroactively resolves the case, is itself uncertain.

### Rav Tuvyumi Account

The *gemara* then records a second version of the story, as told by Rav Papa in the name of Ravina, who heard it from a certain rabbi named Rav Tuvyumi (or, according to another version, Rav Shmuel bar Zutra). This rabbi testified: if someone had offered me all the wealth in the world, I would never have reneged on a commitment I had made — *lo hava kemishani be-diburei*. He was identifying himself as the principal in the story, and he wanted to clarify that it was misreported.

His version: it was a Friday afternoon, close to *shabbat*. A man knocked on his door asking if he had sesame seeds to sell. He said no. The man then said: I have all this money and nowhere safe to put it before *shabbat* — can you keep it for me? The rabbi gestured to his house and said, in effect, my house is here. He did not formally agree to be a *shomer*. The man placed the money in the house, and it was subsequently stolen. When the case came before Rava, Rava ruled: when you say to someone "my house is here" in response to a request to hold money — *lo miba'ei shomer sachar delo havei*, needless to say you are not a *shomer sachar*, *ela afilu shomer chinam nami lo havei* — you are not even a *shomer chinam*. Pointing to your house is not acceptance of *shmirah*.

When the Rabbis' objection about the *mi shepara* was raised — *iba'ei lei lekabulei alei mi she-para* — Rav Tuvyumi said: *lo haya devarim me-olam* — that objection was not applicable. The story the Rabbis were referencing, with the *mi shepara* issue, was a different story entirely — it involved a *pikadon*, a deposit, not a commercial sale retraction. The two stories were confused and conflated; the *mi shepara* element belonged to the other account, not to his.

---

## Money Payment Liability

### Ownership vs. Custody

This brings the *gemara* to a broader question about the legal status of money paid for a sale before *meshicha* is performed. Once money changes hands but before the buyer takes physical possession of the object, what is the relationship of the seller to that money? There is a significant debate among the *rishonim*: is the seller a *shomer* on the money, obligated with whatever level of care a *shomer* carries? Or, alternatively, does the money effectively belong to the seller by virtue of the sale — which, as we have seen, is binding at some level according to Rabbi Yochanan — making the seller not a *shomer* at all but rather a *ba'al*, an owner, who now has a corresponding obligation to either deliver the object or return the money?

### Prevailing View

The prevailing view among the *rishonim* is the latter: money payment creates a binding, if reversible, sale. The seller is not a *shomer* on the money; he is, in effect, an owner of it, and that ownership carries with it the full obligation either to deliver the goods or to return the money — even in a case of *ones*, an unavoidable accident. If the object is lost through *ones* after money was paid but before *meshicha*, the seller still owes the buyer either the object or its value, because he is not merely a custodian but a party to a binding transaction. This accords with the conceptual framework of Rabbi Yochanan: the payment of money creates a real and binding *kinyan*, which can be reversed, but as long as it has not been reversed, the parties are in a full sale relationship with the attendant obligations.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Rule

### Money Holder Rule
