At that point, an unscrupulous person might pass it as a *shekel* when it does not even meet that standard. So long as it retains at least a *shekel*'s worth of metal, its true status is recognizable — it is clearly neither a proper *sela* nor a counterfeit *shekel*, and it can be sold transparently for its weight. Once it drops below that midpoint, the risk of misrepresentation becomes acute.

The same principle governs the *dinar*: *bedinar ad rova* — a *dinar* may be held until it reaches a *rova* of depreciation. As Abaye clarifies — and as Rava's philological observation confirms — the word *rova* here does not mean one-quarter of the *dinar*'s value but rather one-quarter of a *shekel*, which equals half a *dinar*. This makes the threshold identical for both coins: half-value in each case. Rava's proof is linguistic: the Mishnah says *rova* (a quarter of the *shekel*) rather than *revia* (the coin worth one-quarter of a *dinar*). Had the intent been to set the limit at one-quarter of the *dinar*'s value, it would have used the term *revia*. The choice of *rova shekel* signals that the reference point is the *shekel*, not the *dinar* — yielding a half-*dinar* threshold, consistent with the half-*sela* rule.

An additional Gemara observation notes that a *dinar* can in some cases originate from a *shekel* — a *shekel* that has worn down to the size of a *dinar*. Rabbi Ami uses this to distinguish two types of *dinar*-sized coins: a *dinar haba mishekel* — a worn *shekel* now the size of a *dinar* — may still be kept and used at the *dinar* level, since it has only declined to half its original value. A *dinar haba misela* — a *sela* that has worn all the way down to *dinar* size — is forbidden to keep, since it has lost more than half its original value and is susceptible to fraudulent misrepresentation.

---

## Disposal of Bad Coin (II)

### Anti-Fraud Rules

Once a coin has crossed the half-value threshold and can no longer be held or used even for its metal weight, a specific prohibition applies: *harei zeh lo yimkerenu lo letagar velo lecherem velo lehereg* — do not sell it to a merchant, do not use it to pay off a creditor seizing property, and do not use it to ransom one's life from a threatening assailant. (In true life-threatening situations one does what one must, but under ordinary circumstances the prohibition holds.) The reason the Gemara gives is stark: *mipnei shemeramin bah et acherim* — because these parties will use it to deceive others. A coin degraded below half its value but still resembling a higher denomination will be passed on as something it is not. Even an honest person cannot hold such a coin, precisely because it will inevitably pass into hands less scrupulous than his own.

### Destruction Methods

What, then, must be done with such a coin? The *baraita* presents several valid options: *yish'chok* — grind it to powder; *yituch* — melt it down; *yakutz* — cut it into pieces; *yolich l'yam hamelach* — cast it into the sea. The Mishnah had also mentioned making a hole in it and wearing it as a necklace around one's child's neck, and indeed archaeological finds suggest this practice was real. However, a separate *baraita* prohibits this, along with using the coin as a weight among one's standard weights and throwing it into one's scrap metal pile — any arrangement where the coin retains its shape creates the risk that it will be removed and misused.

Rabbi Elazar (cited also in the name of Rav Huna citing Rabbi Elazar) reconciles the two sources: *kan b'emtza kan min hatzad* — the permissible necklace-making involves piercing the coin through its center, which renders it clearly non-functional as currency. The prohibited scenario is piercing at the coin's edge, where the hole could be trimmed away and the coin returned to circulation.

---

## Coin Use Limits (II)

### Abaye vs. Rava

The Gemara re-engages the question of the intermediate range — coins that have depreciated beyond the *ona'ah* threshold but have not yet reached half their value. During this range, the coin cannot circulate as face-value currency but may still be sold for its metal weight. The *baraita* cited earlier had said *yoter al ken mochrah bishviyah* — beyond this point, sell it at its weight value. The question is whether coins in this intermediate range may be freely held or must be destroyed.

Rav Huna holds that both ranges — above and below the half-value threshold — require destruction; the only safe coin is one that has depreciated to exactly half its value (a *sela* now worth exactly a *shekel*, a *dinar* now worth exactly half a *dinar*). Levi disagrees: only below the half-value threshold must a coin be destroyed; in the intermediate range it may be retained and sold at weight. The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from the *baraita*'s language, which appears to permit selling in the intermediate range, and Rav Huna's resolution requires an extremely forced reading of that *baraita* — limiting it to a coin that fell into a fire and depreciated instantaneously, rather than gradually.

### Rova Terminology

The discussion of the *rova* — the threshold below which a *dinar* cannot be retained — required clarification because the same root generates two distinct terms with different meanings. *Rova* in this context means one-quarter of a *shekel*, which equals half a *dinar*. *Revia* refers to the actual coin denomination worth one-quarter of a *dinar*. The Mishnah's use of *rova* rather than *revia* establishes that the threshold is set relative to the *shekel*, not the *dinar*, and therefore represents half the *dinar*'s value — not one-quarter. This ensures the same half-value rule applies uniformly across coin denominations.

### Different Limits

The *baraita*'s phrase *pachat mikan issar assur* — once it goes an *issar* below this, it is forbidden — generates a Talmudic exchange about what exactly is being said. Abaye reads the phrase as a gloss on the *ona'ah* threshold from the earlier Mishnah: what is being said is that the tolerable threshold is four *issurot* per *sela* (one per *dinar*), and once the depreciation exceeds that by even one *issar* — reaching five *issurot* — the coin can no longer pass at face value. Rava objects: if the *ona'ah* threshold is four *issurot*, then anything beyond four *issurot*, however tiny the excess, triggers the prohibition. There is no need or room to speak of one additional *issar*. The phrase *afilu mashehu nami* — even the slightest excess — would logically suffice. Rather, Rava reads the phrase as a restatement of the Mishnah's ruling: *pichas sela issar ledinar assur* — if a *sela* has lost one *issar* per *dinar* of its value (four *issurot* total), it can no longer be used as currency. This is simply the Mishnah's rule restated in the *baraita*, presented as the standard ruling — *ve-stam k'Rabbi Meir* — following Rabbi Meir's position.

---

## Disposal of Bad Coin (II)

### Piercing Method

As noted above, the resolution of the apparent contradiction between the Mishnah's permission to perforate a coin and make it a necklace and the *baraita*'s prohibition on doing so turns entirely on where the hole is made. A hole through the center of the coin permanently disfigures it as currency, rendering it unambiguously ornamental and non-negotiable. A hole at the edge, however, is superficial enough that an unscrupulous person might clip away the perforated section and return the coin to circulation. The prohibition targets precisely that risk.

---

## Taromet vs. Obligation

### Middat Chasidus

The Mishnah's final provision states that if the person who passed the defective coins recognizes them as his own, he should accept them back even after twelve months. The Gemara asks how this can be reconciled with the earlier time limits — in the city, until one can show the coin to a money changer; in a village, until *erev Shabbos*. Once those windows have closed, there is no legal obligation to accept a return. Rav Chisda explains: *middat chasidus shanu kan* — the twelve-month rule describes pious conduct, not legal obligation. The right thing to do, when one recognizes one's own coins, is to take them back and make the recipient whole. But this is a standard of *chasidus*, not a legally enforceable duty.

### Moral vs. Legal

This framing leads to a question about the phrase *ein lo alav ela taromet* — "he has only a complaint, not a legal claim." Who has the complaint, and against whom? If the original passer takes the coins back as an act of *chasidus*, there is nothing for anyone to complain about. If he refuses, the aggrieved party has a moral grievance but no legal recourse. The *taromet* thus describes the standing of the person who received the bad coins: he may be legitimately aggrieved, he may protest and complain, but he has no legal mechanism to compel the return.

### Upset But No Claim

The Gemara works through the precise reading. The case described is one in which the original passer refuses to take the coins back after the legal window has closed. The person who holds the bad coins can genuinely be upset — the conduct is not ideal, and the person who originally gave him bad coins and now refuses to remedy the situation is acting poorly. The language of *taromet* captures exactly this: a well-founded moral complaint, carrying social and perhaps reputational weight, but not a legally actionable grievance. The distinction between what the law demands and what decency requires is one the Talmud marks carefully, and the category of *middat chasidus* is precisely the space between them — where the law ends and the higher standard begins.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 53

## Ona'ah & Deficient C (II)

### Mishna Overview

The daf opens mid-discussion on 52b, continuing the treatment of *ona'ah* — not in the classic sense of overcharging or undercharging for goods, but in the context of coins that are below their proper weight. In the era under discussion, coins carried value roughly equivalent to their metal content, so a coin that was slightly deficient was genuinely worth somewhat less than its face value.

The *mishna* states that such a deficient coin may nonetheless be given for *ma'aser sheni*, and one need not be concerned about this, because anyone who refuses to accept it is simply a *nefesh ra'ah* — a stingy, miserly soul. The question is: precisely what type of deficiency is the *mishna* describing?

### Three Coin Scenarios

There are three possibilities. The coin may be lacking less than the amount of *ona'ah*, exactly the amount of *ona'ah*, or more than the amount of *ona'ah*. The third case is immediately set aside: it would be extreme to permit using such a coin for *ma'aser sheni* at face value. We are therefore left with the first two.

On the most natural reading, the *mishna* is speaking of a coin deficient by less than the threshold of *ona'ah*. In that case, a storekeeper would technically be entitled to refuse it — just as any seller has the right to reject non-standard tender — but someone who actually did so would be considered petty and miserly. Since ordinary people accept such a coin at face value, it may be used at face value for *ma'aser sheni*. This reading is not a great *chiddush*, however, since the coin's loss is genuinely negligible.

The more pointed reading is that the *mishna* permits treating the coin at face value even when it is deficient by a full twenty-fourth — the classic measure of *ona'ah*. Even though the recipient is technically entitled to demand reimbursement for the shortfall, normal practice is that people use such coins without protest. The *chiddush* would then be that despite this technical entitlement, one may use the coin at face value for *ma'aser sheni*. The concern, however, is that when one arrives in Jerusalem to spend the money, merchants there may not honor the face value either — which means *ma'aser sheni* may actually lose out in the transaction.

## Metal vs. Face Value

### Rav Papa's Teaching

Rav Papa derives a practical lesson from the *mishna*: someone who is excessively exacting about what currency he will accept, refusing coins that are slightly off, is called a *nefesh ra'ah*. However, this applies only when the coin genuinely has currency — when it circulates normally and merchants accept it. A storekeeper who refuses a coin that most people would take without hesitation is being unreasonably miserly. But if a coin has genuine difficulty circulating, then refusing it is not stinginess but simple prudence.

## Ona'ah & Deficient C (II)

### Chizkiyahu's Position

The *gemara* notes that the *mishna* appears to support Chizkiyahu's position. Chizkiyahu taught: if you come to exchange a deficient coin into smaller denominations (*ba le-forta*), you will only receive its actual metal value — it is worth less than its face value, and the market will price it accordingly. But if you come to transfer the *kedushah* of *ma'aser sheni* onto it (*ba le-chalela*), you may treat it as though it were a complete, minted coin — that is, you may use it at face value.

This framing suggests that the *mishna* is indeed speaking of a coin deficient by the full amount of *ona'ah*, because only then would the market refuse to give full face value in exchange. The *chiddush* is that even so, you may treat it as face value for purposes of *ma'aser sheni* — even though *ma'aser sheni* ends up losing slightly in the transaction, since the coin you redeem onto is worth less than its stated denomination.

## Metal vs. Face Value (II)

### Chizkiyahu Contradiction

The *gemara* now raises a sharp difficulty: does this position really reflect Chizkiyahu's view? For Chizkiyahu himself stated elsewhere that if one has *ma'aser sheni* worth less than a *pruta*, one should declare: "It and its *chomesh* are hereby transferred to the earlier money" — meaning, transferred onto *ma'aser sheni* money one already possesses. The premise of this ruling is that any sum of money onto which *ma'aser sheni* has been transferred necessarily has some residual value that was not absorbed by the transfer, because it is impossible for a person to assess the exact value of his produce (*lefi she'ei efshar le'adam letzamtzem ma'osav*). The person redeeming always rounds in favor of *ma'aser sheni*, ensuring the money is worth at least as much as the produce. There is always, therefore, some sliver of monetary value left over in the coin beyond what was consecrated.

But this means Chizkiyahu assumes that *ma'aser sheni* is always treated generously — that the money is never fully exhausted by the transfer, always leaving a surplus. This stands in direct tension with what the *mishna* appears to say: namely, that one may transfer *ma'aser sheni* onto a coin at face value even when the coin's metal value is less. In that case, *ma'aser sheni* loses value in the exchange rather than gaining it — precisely the opposite of Chizkiyahu's underlying assumption.

### Reinterpretation

The *gemara* therefore completely reinterprets both Chizkiyahu's statement and the *mishna*. The phrase *mechalelah be-yafeh* — "he redeems it with a fine coin" — does not mean at face value, as it appeared. Rather, following Rashi's reading, it means: treat this deficient coin the same way you would treat any full-value coin when using it for *ma'aser sheni*. And how do you treat a full-value coin? You do not fill it to capacity — you round in favor of *ma'aser sheni*, ensuring that the money retains a small surplus of unconsecrated value. The same applies here: use the deficient coin for *ma'aser sheni*, but transfer only the metal value onto it — not the face value — and leave the standard surplus.

This reading requires a significant stretch of the plain meaning, as Rashi himself acknowledges. What seemed to be a *mishna* telling us we may treat a deficient coin at its full face value for *ma'aser sheni* is now reread as telling us the opposite: we do not treat it at face value; we use only its actual metal value.

### Double Disgrace Principle

The *gemara* explains the underlying logic with the principle of *d'trei zimni lo mezalzalinan beih* — we do not treat *ma'aser sheni* with disrespect twice over. The *drasha* that *ma'aser sheni* must be transferred onto minted coins (*kesef she'yeish bo tzurah*, derived from *v'tzarta ha-kesef be-yadecha*) means that even using a coin that is slightly below its minted value is already one concession — one *zilzul*. We are not going to compound that by additionally pretending the coin is worth more than it actually is. Therefore, even when using such a coin for *ma'aser sheni*, one must calculate by the coin's true metal value, not its face value. The *mishna*'s point about *nefesh ra'ah* is thus reframed: it describes the attitude of a person who would refuse a coin that is nonetheless valid for circulation, not a permission to inflate that coin's worth for purposes of *ma'aser sheni*.

## Less Than Pruta

### Chizkiyahu's Solution

The *gemara* now turns to examine Chizkiyahu's other ruling in its own right. Chizkiyahu taught: *ma'aser sheni* that is worth less than a *pruta* — say, a single olive or two grains of wheat — presents a redemption problem. One might think to simply redeem it onto a *pruta* coin, but this cannot be done: a *pruta* is the minimum unit of monetary significance, and one cannot transfer *kedushah* from something worth less than a *pruta* onto an empty, unconsecrated coin. There is simply not enough value to initiate the transaction.

Chizkiyahu's solution is to say: "It and its *chomesh* are hereby transferred onto the earlier money." The person declares that this sub-*pruta* amount of *ma'aser sheni*, along with the requisite added fifth, is transferred onto money that already bears *kedushat ma'aser sheni* from a previous act of redemption. The logic is, as noted above, that any such money must have a residual sliver of unconsecrated value, because no person is ever able to calibrate the exact value of his produce. He always rounds up in favor of *ma'aser sheni*, so the money is always worth slightly more than what was transferred onto it. That residual — even if it is only a half-*pruta* or less — is enough to absorb the sub-*pruta* olive.

What is the precise mechanism here? It is admittedly somewhat elusive. If the problem is that one cannot initiate a transfer from something worth less than a *pruta*, why should it help that the money already has some *kedushah* on it? And conversely, if there is indeed residual value in the money, why not just transfer the half-*pruta* directly to a fresh coin? The answer Chizkiyahu implies is that the act of transfer works when appended to existing *ma'aser sheni* money — not as a standalone transaction — because the money already has an established *kedushah* identity, and this sub-*pruta* amount is being added to it, not initiating a new consecration from scratch.

### Davar She'yesh Matirim

This discussion of Chizkiyahu's solution brings us to a much broader issue: the principle of *davar she'yesh lo matirim*. Before reaching it, the *gemara* first sets up the relevant *mishna*, which lists the ways in which *terumah* and *bikurim* are treated more stringently than *ma'aser sheni*. Non-*kohanim* who eat *terumah* are liable to *mitat beit din* and must pay back the value plus a *chomesh*; *terumah* is nullified only in a ratio of one hundred and one; one must wash hands before touching it; and a *tamei kohen* must wait until nightfall after immersing before eating it. The *mishna* then says these rules *do not* apply to *ma'aser sheni*.

The most natural reading of the contrast regarding *bitul* is that *terumah* requires one hundred and one for nullification, whereas *ma'aser sheni* is nullified by a simple majority — or at minimum, by a standard amount, without needing the elevated ratio. The *gemara* then asks: if Chizkiyahu is correct that even sub-*pruta* amounts of *ma'aser sheni* can be redeemed, why should *ma'aser sheni* ever be subject to *bitul* at all?

The principle of *davar she'yesh lo matirim* — an item that has an alternative path to permissibility — holds that such an item cannot be nullified even in a thousand times its volume. The classic illustration is new grain (*chadash*) before the *omer* is brought: if it becomes mixed with permitted grain a week before Passover, it cannot be nullified, because in a matter of days it will become permitted on its own. There is no reason to employ *bitul* when a straightforward path to permissibility exists. The governing logic, as Rashi explains, is: since you have another option, use it — we will not let you eat the forbidden item through the legal fiction of *bitul* when you could simply wait.

Now, *ma'aser sheni* is forbidden to eat outside Jerusalem. It has a path to permissibility: either bring it to Jerusalem and eat it, or redeem it. True, *Tosafot* notes that going to Jerusalem when one is far away is not considered a "feasible alternative" in the way the principle envisions. But redemption is always available. So why do we ever permit *ma'aser sheni* to undergo *bitul*? It should always be a *davar she'yesh lo matirim* — just redeem it, and then eat it freely.

The *gemara*'s answer is that the *braisa* identifying *ma'aser sheni* as subject to *bitul* must be speaking specifically of a case where redemption is impossible. That is the only scenario in which *ma'aser sheni* would have *ein lo matirim* — no alternative path — and would therefore be eligible for nullification. And what constitutes an unredeemable *ma'aser sheni*? The *braisa* itself supplies two scenarios: *ma'aser sheni* worth less than a *pruta*, and *ma'aser sheni* that was brought into Jerusalem and taken out. In both cases, no redemption is available, and therefore *bitul* can operate.

But this is precisely what collides with Chizkiyahu: according to his ruling, sub-*pruta* *ma'aser sheni* can indeed be redeemed — transferred onto existing *ma'aser sheni* money — and therefore it should retain the status of *davar she'yesh lo matirim* and never be *batel*. This is the contradiction that drives the next section.

## Braisa & Chizkiyahu

### Terumah vs. Ma'aser

The *mishna* in *Challah* catalogues the various stringencies of *terumah* and *bikurim* vis-à-vis *ma'aser sheni*: liability for death and payment of a *chomesh* for a non-*kohen* who eats *terumah* inadvertently; the prohibition for non-*kohanim*; the status of *terumah* as the *kohen*'s property, which he may transact with at its market value while the receiving party must observe its *kedushah*; the requirement of one hundred and one for *bitul*; the need to wash hands before touching it; and the need to wait for nightfall after immersion before eating it. All of these apply to *terumah* and *bikurim* but not to *ma'aser sheni*.

One might initially wonder whether the contrast regarding *bitul* means that *ma'aser sheni* is actually stricter — not *batel* at all, because it is a *davar she'yesh lo matirim*. The *gemara* rejects this: the *mishna* is cataloguing the *stringencies* of *terumah*, not its leniencies, so the contrast must mean that *ma'aser sheni* requires less than one hundred and one. The *gemara* acknowledges that the *mishna* includes some leniencies of *terumah* (such as the *kohen*'s property status), but this does not save the alternative reading, because we have an explicit *braisa* that settles the matter.

### Braisa on Batul

The *braisa* states — with its key words appearing in Aramaic, which suggests they may be a gloss, though the substance is clear from the continuation — that *ma'aser sheni* is *batel b'rov*. It then immediately qualifies: in what case of *ma'aser sheni* did the Sages apply this rule? Only when it has no path to permissibility (*ein lo matirim*) — specifically, when it is worth less than a *pruta*, or when it was brought into Jerusalem and taken out. Both of these, the *braisa* maintains, are cases of *ma'aser sheni* that cannot be redeemed and therefore lack an alternative path to permissibility, making *bitul* available.

### Contradiction Setup

Here the contradiction with Chizkiyahu is sharpest. If Chizkiyahu's ruling stands — that sub-*pruta* *ma'aser sheni* can be transferred onto existing *ma'aser sheni* money — then the *braisa*'s first scenario falls apart. Sub-*pruta* *ma'aser sheni* does have a path to permissibility according to Chizkiyahu. It should therefore be a *davar she'yesh lo matirim*, never eligible for *bitul*. Yet the *braisa* treats it as *ein lo matirim* and *batel b'rov*.

## Redemption Obstacles

### Combine Options

The *gemara* asks: why not simply apply Chizkiyahu's solution? Transfer the sub-*pruta* amount onto existing *ma'aser sheni* money, and the problem dissolves. The *gemara* answers: suppose he has no such money — no funds onto which *ma'aser sheni* has previously been transferred. Then the *gemara* asks: why not get it? The more basic suggestion is: take other *ma'aser sheni* produce that you have not yet redeemed — say, a full quantity of olives — and combine it with this single olive that is mixed in a vat. Declare the whole lot redeemed onto a coin. Since the total sum is worth more than a *pruta*, there is no *pruta* problem, and Chizkiyahu's issue disappears.

### D'Oraisa/Rabbanan Mix

The *gemara* rejects this on principled grounds: *de'oraisa* and *derabbanan* obligations cannot be combined (*d'Oraisa v'd'Rabbanan lo mitztarfi*). The unredeemed olives sitting in the warehouse are obligated in *ma'aser sheni* at the biblical level. The one olive mixed into the vat, however, is a different matter. Biblically, once produce mixes with non-*ma'aser* produce, it is *batel* — nullified. The entire discussion of whether it should not be *batel* because it is a *davar she'yesh lo matirim* is itself a rabbinic concern. Even if we ultimately say it is not *batel* due to *yesh lo matirim*, that identity is only rabbinic. So at most, the mixed olive has a *derabbanan* identity as *ma'aser sheni*. It therefore cannot be combined with the warehouse olives, which are biblical *ma'aser sheni*, to form a joint unit for redemption. The *d'Oraisa* and *d'Rabbanan* remain separate, and the sub-*pruta* problem reasserts itself for the residual.

### Demai Rejected

One might try to sidestep this by using *demai* — produce purchased from an *am ha'aretz*, which may or may not have had *ma'aser* separated, and is therefore only rabbinically obligated. If the warehouse olives are *demai*, both they and the mixed olive would share the same *derabbanan* status and could in principle be combined. The *gemara* rejects this as well: we will not permit the combination with *demai* because it will lead people to try it with produce that is fully *d'Oraisa* obligated. Since combining *d'Oraisa* with *d'Rabbanan* is invalid, and people will not maintain the distinction, the Sages preemptively prohibit even the technically valid *demai* combination.

### Sequential Transfer

The *gemara* then considers a more elegant solution: instead of combining simultaneously, perform the redemption in two stages. Take two *pruta* coins. Transfer *ma'aser sheni* worth one and a half *prutas* onto them. The first coin absorbs one *pruta*'s worth, and the second coin absorbs the remaining half *pruta*'s worth. Now the second coin has *kedushat ma'aser sheni* on part of it, and its remaining half *pruta* of unconsecrated value is available. At this point, Chizkiyahu's mechanism can operate: the sub-*pruta* olive can be transferred onto that half *pruta* of residual value in the already-consecrated coin.

### Two Prutas Problem

The *gemara* refutes this with a subtle but decisive point: *pruta tafsa pruta, v'chatzi pruta lo tafsa* — a *pruta* coin absorbs a *pruta*'s worth, and a half *pruta* does not absorb anything. The problem is that the two *pruta* coins are not one large coin; they are two separate, discrete vessels for *kedushah*. When one and a half *prutas*' worth of *ma'aser sheni* is to be transferred, the first coin takes exactly one *pruta*, which fills it precisely. The remaining half *pruta* of *ma'aser sheni* value is now left facing a second coin that is completely empty — unconsecrated. And one cannot initiate a transfer of less than a *pruta* onto an empty, unconsecrated coin. That was the entire problem Chizkiyahu was trying to solve in the first place.

This would not be a problem with a single larger coin. If one starts with an *issar* or a *sela* — a coin worth multiple *prutas* — and transfers one and a half *prutas*' worth of *ma'aser sheni* onto it, the coin is not filled; the surplus remains in the coin as a unit, and Chizkiyahu's solution can operate on that surplus. The problem arises specifically when one uses two separate *pruta* coins and treats them as a combined unit: the halakhah does not permit that. Each coin stands alone. The thinking here becomes, as one might note, suddenly very concrete — these are discrete *kedushah* containers, and half a *pruta* simply does not "stick" to an empty one.

### Impracticality Defense

The *gemara* ultimately permits using a single larger coin to accomplish the two-stage transfer — but then withdraws that permission: *dilma ati l'atuyei prutas* — we are concerned that people will come to try it with two separate *pruta* coins, which does not work, and will err. Since the practical details are subtle enough that the average person will not appreciate the distinction between using a single large coin and using two separate *pruta* coins of equivalent total value, the Sages do not permit even the valid method.

The consequence of this refusal is significant: because we are not going to allow Chizkiyahu's solution to be implemented in practice, the sub-*pruta* *ma'aser sheni* effectively has no path to permissibility — *ein lo matirim* — and it therefore may undergo *bitul*. Chizkiyahu's ruling stands in theory; the *braisa*'s ruling stands in practice.

## Jerusalem Entry/Exit

### Return Option

The *braisa* listed a second scenario in which *ma'aser sheni* cannot be redeemed: it was brought into Jerusalem and taken out. The *gemara* asks the obvious question: why not simply walk back into Jerusalem and eat it there? That requires no redemption at all.

### Tamei Exception

The answer is that the produce became *tamei* — ritually impure — and therefore cannot be eaten in its current state even in Jerusalem. But then, the *gemara* says, redeem it: Rabbi Elazar taught that *ma'aser sheni* that became *tamei* may be redeemed even within Jerusalem, despite the general rule that *ma'aser sheni* cannot be redeemed once it has entered Jerusalem. The source is the verse *ki lo tukhal se'eto* — "for you cannot carry it" — understood through the *drasha* that *se'et* refers to eating (as in *vayisa mas'et me'et panav*, where Yosef sends portions of food to his brothers). If you cannot *eat* it because it is *tamei*, the Torah permits redemption even inside Jerusalem — redeem it for money, use the money to purchase *tahor* produce, and eat that.

So we are back to the original question. If the produce is *tahor*, just go back into Jerusalem and eat it. If it became *tamei*, redeem it per Rabbi Elazar. Why is this ever *ein lo matirim*?

### Second Generation

The *gemara* answers: the *braisa* is not speaking of the original *ma'aser sheni* produce itself, but of produce purchased with *ma'aser sheni* money — second-generation *ma'aser sheni*. One had produce in the field, transferred its *kedushah* to money, traveled to Jerusalem, and used that money to purchase food. That purchased food, carrying *kedushat ma'aser sheni*, was subsequently removed from Jerusalem. The assumption here is that second-generation *ma'aser sheni* cannot be redeemed — only the first-generation produce may have its *kedushah* transferred to money; once it has already been transferred once, the resulting food is not subject to a second redemption.

The *gemara* briefly considers whether Rabbi Yehuda's position — that *tamei* second-generation *ma'aser sheni* must be buried rather than redeemed — might resolve matters, but rejects this approach. If Rabbi Yehuda's stringency is the basis for *ein lo matirim*, the *braisa* need not have mentioned that the produce was taken *out* of Jerusalem, since the prohibition on redemption of *tamei* purchased produce would apply regardless of location.

### Walls Principle

Setting aside Rabbi Yehuda, the *gemara* pursues a different resolution. The case is: *tahor* produce, not second-generation, but *ma'aser sheni* that was brought inside Jerusalem's walls — and then the walls fell. The produce did not move; Jerusalem moved, in a sense. With the walls down, the produce can no longer be eaten within Jerusalem, because the *d'Oraisa* obligation is to eat *ma'aser sheni* within the walls. At the same time, it cannot be redeemed, because — and here Rava's principle becomes decisive — the rule that *ma'aser sheni* cannot be redeemed after entering Jerusalem is only *d'Rabbanan*. One might therefore think that once the walls fall, the Sages would not apply their rabbinic prohibition and would permit redemption.

Rava states explicitly: *mechitzah le'echol d'Oraisa, mechitzah liklot d'Rabbanan* — the requirement that Jerusalem's walls be standing in order to *eat* there is biblical; the principle that the walls "absorb" the *ma'aser sheni* and prevent its subsequent redemption is rabbinic.

### No Distinction

But the *gemara* rules: *lo plug Rabbanan* — the Sages did not distinguish. They enacted a categorical rule that *ma'aser sheni* brought within Jerusalem's walls cannot be redeemed, whether those walls currently stand or not. The Sages made no exception for the case in which the walls subsequently fell. Therefore, the produce that entered Jerusalem cannot be redeemed (rabbinic enactment, no exception), and cannot be eaten (walls are gone, *d'Oraisa* requirement unmet), and is thus in a state of genuine *ein lo matirim* — there is no path to permissibility. This is the scenario in which *bitul* operates.

### Reconciliation

The *gemara*'s final answer reconciles everything: the *braisa* is speaking of a single compound case — *ma'aser sheni* that is worth less than a *pruta* and was brought into Jerusalem and taken out (i.e., the walls fell). Both conditions must be present simultaneously. The walls scenario alone might, in principle, raise questions about whether walls really "absorb" a sub-*pruta* amount — one might argue that something without the minimum monetary value was never truly "held" by the *mechitzot* in the first place, and perhaps it could still be redeemed even after entry. The *braisa* therefore teaches us that even in the sub-*pruta* case, the walls did absorb it and the prohibition on redemption applies.

By requiring both conditions, the *braisa* sidesteps the Chizkiyahu objection as well: it is not merely the sub-*pruta* amount alone that generates *ein lo matirim*, but the sub-*pruta* amount combined with the impossibility of redemption due to the walls — circumstances under which even Chizkiyahu's mechanism cannot operate. The resolution is thus not that Chizkiyahu is wrong, but that the *braisa* is describing a scenario in which his solution is inapplicable, leaving the *ma'aser sheni* genuinely without any path to permissibility and therefore eligible for *bitul*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 54

## Ma'aser Below Prutah

### Ona'ah & Coins

The present chapter of the Gemara has been treating questions of *ona'ah* — specifically the degree to which a coin may be physically deficient and still retain its face value for commercial purposes. The Mishnah touched on *ma'aser sheni* in this context, noting that even a somewhat deficient coin may be used to redeem *ma'aser sheni*. This led the Gemara into a sustained discussion of what it means to redeem *ma'aser sheni* whose value is less than a *prutah*.

The background is as follows. When one redeems *ma'aser sheni* outside of Yerushalayim, one transfers the sanctity of the food onto money and then uses that money in Yerushalayim to purchase food eaten in a state of *kedushah*. The minimum meaningful unit of monetary value recognized by halachah is a *prutah*. If the *ma'aser sheni* one wishes to redeem does not reach that threshold, the question arises whether a valid act of *pidyon* — redemption — can be performed at all. Hizkiyah taught that if a coin has already been used in redemption and retains residual value from a previous transaction, one may redeem even *ma'aser sheni* worth less than a *prutah* onto that coin. The question under examination here concerns a fresh coin — one that has not yet been used in any redemption — when the *ma'aser sheni* itself is worth less than a *prutah*.

### Rav vs. Rav Asi

The Gemara now cites the *pasuk*: *Im ga'ol yigal ish mi-ma'asro* — "if a man redeems from his *maaser*" — and derives from the phrase *mi-ma'asro*, "from his *maaser*" and not "from all his *maaser*," that there are circumstances in which redemption is not possible. The teaching states: *prat le-ma'aser sheni she-ein bo shaveh prutah* — this comes to exclude *ma'aser sheni* that is not worth a *prutah*, which lacks the minimum value necessary to constitute a valid redemptive act. Of course, as noted, Hizkiyah's ruling allows redemption even below a *prutah* when the coin already bears the imprint of a prior redemption and carries residual value.

An *amoraic* dispute is then recorded. Rav says the problem is *ein bo* — the *ma'aser sheni* itself does not contain a *prutah*'s worth of value. Rav Asi, by contrast, says *ein be-chomsho* — the difficulty arises even when the *ma'aser sheni* does contain a *prutah*'s worth, but its *chomesh* does not. When one redeems one's own *ma'aser sheni*, one is obligated to add a fifth. This fifth, as the Gemara will explain shortly, is a fifth of the final total rather than of the base — what we might call a quarter of the starting value. If the food is worth four *prutot*, the *chomesh* added is one *prutah*, bringing the total to five, and that one *prutah* constitutes a fifth of the whole. But if the *ma'aser sheni* is worth less than four *prutot*, then the *chomesh* — the increment being added — does not itself amount to a *prutah*, and Rav Asi holds that this too disqualifies the redemption. The addition of the *chomesh* is treated, in some sense, as its own discrete redemptive act, requiring its own minimum value. This same dispute is replicated between Rabbi Yochanan, who holds *ein bo*, and Resh Lakish, who holds *ein be-chomsho*.

### New vs. Used Money

The Gemara challenges these positions from a *baraita*: *ma'aser sheni she-ein bo shaveh prutah, dayo she-yomar hu ve-chomsho mechulalin al ma'ot rishonim* — if the *ma'aser sheni* is not worth a *prutah*, it is sufficient for one to declare that it and its *chomesh* are redeemed upon the original money, i.e., coins previously used in redemption. This is Hizkiyah's ruling applied in practice.

The Gemara then analyzes how this *baraita* bears on the dispute. If one holds like Rav Asi — that the problem arises when the *chomesh* lacks a *prutah* — then the word *dayo*, "it is sufficient," makes good sense. The general rule requires the *chomesh* to be worth a *prutah*, but in the case of money already used in redemption, as long as the *ma'aser* itself is worth a *prutah*, it is enough even if the *chomesh* is not, because something has already been accomplished — the *ma'aser* has crossed the minimum threshold. The *dayo* therefore indicates that one has achieved a partial satisfaction of the requirement.

But if one holds like Rav — that the issue is simply whether the *ma'aser sheni* itself reaches a *prutah* — then the word *dayo* is difficult. The *baraita* should have stated simply that one may redeem *ma'aser sheni* worth less than a *prutah* upon previously used money. The word *dayo*, implying that something short of ideal is being permitted, does not fit naturally. The Gemara acknowledges: *kashya* — this remains difficult for the position of Rav. Nevertheless, the essential halachic conclusion is that once money has already been used in redemption, everyone agrees that redemption may proceed; the dispute concerns only fresh, previously unused money, and whether the threshold requirement applies to the *ma'aser* itself or to the *chomesh* it generates.

---

## Chomesh Mi-Legav/Levar

### How Fifth Calculated

Having established the basic framework of the *chomesh*, the Gemara now asks a foundational question: *chumsha mi-legav o chumsha mi-lebar* — is the fifth calculated from the inside or from the outside? That is, does one take a fifth of the base value — *mi-legav* — or does one add an amount such that after the addition the increment constitutes a fifth of the total — *mi-lebar*? If *mi-legav*, then on something worth twenty one adds four, since four is a fifth of twenty. If *mi-lebar*, then on something worth twenty one adds five, since five is a fifth of the resulting total of twenty-five. The latter formulation means that what the Torah calls a "fifth" is in practical terms a quarter of the starting value.

### Be'alim Redemption

Ravina resolves the question by citing a *baraita* concerning the redemption of *hekdesh*. When a sanctified object is being redeemed and the *be'alim* — the original owners who sanctified it — wish to reclaim it, they enjoy the right of first refusal over other bidders because they are required to add a *chomesh*. The *baraita* presents a series of scenarios: the *be'alim* offer twenty, another person offers twenty. The *be'alim* take precedence because they add a *chomesh*. If a stranger then offers twenty-one, the *be'alim* pay twenty-six — their base of twenty plus five as the *chomesh*, plus the additional one to match the stranger's bid.

What is decisive is that the *chomesh* on a base of twenty is five, not four. That demonstrates conclusively that the fifth is *mi-lebar*: one adds an amount equal to a quarter of the starting value, so that the final result is five parts of which the added increment is one — a fifth of the total. The *baraita* continues through progressive examples: a stranger bids twenty-two and the *be'alim* pay twenty-seven; twenty-three and the *be'alim* pay twenty-eight; twenty-four and the *be'alim* pay twenty-nine; twenty-five and the *be'alim* pay thirty. The owners do not pay a *chomesh* on the stranger's bid — only on their own base of twenty. They pay their *chomesh* of five, and then add whatever premium the competing bid introduced. The Gemara notes a difficulty in the final case — when the stranger bids twenty-five, which equals the *be'alim*'s total of twenty plus five — but refers the reader to the discussion in tractate *Erchin* where that case is addressed.

The conclusion from all this is clear: *shma mina chomesh mi-lebar* — the *chomesh* of the Torah is calculated from the outside, i.e., it is a fifth of the total after addition, which amounts to a quarter of the starting value.

The Gemara confirms that this point was itself a *tannaic* dispute: the verse states *ve-yasaf chamishito alav* — he shall add its fifth upon it. Rabbi Yoshiya reads this as: together with its fifth, the total is five — meaning you start with four, add one, and arrive at five. This is *mi-lebar*. Rabbi Yonatan, however, reads *chamishito* as a fifth of the principal — *mi-legav*. The established halachah, as confirmed by the *baraita* about the *be'alim*, follows Rabbi Yoshiya's reading: the fifth is *mi-lebar*.

---

## Fifth Me'akev?

### Four + One or Four on Fi…

The Gemara now turns to a separate and fundamental question: *chomesh me'akev o ein chomesh me'akev* — does failure to add the fifth invalidate the *pidyon*, the act of redemption? If one redeems *ma'aser sheni* worth twenty outside of Yerushalayim by transferring its sanctity onto twenty coins without adding the requisite five additional coins, has the *ma'aser sheni* in fact been redeemed, such that one may now eat it outside of Yerushalayim?

The conceptual question is framed with precision. One possibility is that the Torah's meaning is: you redeem the four on four — the redemption is transacted at the food's value — and then separately and additionally you add a fifth. Under this reading, the act of redemption and the obligation to add a *chomesh* are distinct. The *pidyon* is complete when you transfer the food's value onto money of equivalent worth; the *chomesh* is an additional financial obligation but does not define or constitute the redemptive act itself. The consequence would be: *alma chomesh lo me'akev* — the fifth does not prevent the redemption from taking effect.

The alternative possibility is that the Torah is telling you to redeem four on five — that is, the proper redemption of an item worth four requires the payment of five. Under this reading, tendering only four is simply not a redemption at the correct value, and the *pidyon* accordingly fails. The *chomesh* is not an add-on but an integral component of the redemptive transaction itself.

### Demai Proof

Ravina offers a proof from the laws of *demai*. *Demai* refers to produce purchased from an *am ha-aretz* whose proper separation of *ma'asrot* is uncertain. At the Torah level, one may assume the separations were performed; rabbinically, one must treat the produce as if they were not and separate again. The Mishnah teaches: *ha-demai ein lo chomesh ve-ein lo bi'ur* — *demai* does not require the addition of a *chomesh* and is not subject to *bi'ur*, the obligation to remove all *ma'aser* from one's home by a certain point in the sabbatical cycle. Yet the *keren* — the principal redemption — does apply. One must still redeem the *ma'aser sheni* of *demai*, even though one omits the *chomesh*.

The Gemara asks: what is the rationale for this distinction? Why would the rabbis require the *keren* but not the *chomesh* for *demai*? The answer is: *keren de-me'akev be-de'oraita ita be-derabbanan; chomesh de-lo me'akev be-de'oraita leita be-derabbanan* — the principal is *me'akev* at the Torah level, and therefore the rabbis preserved its requirement even for *demai*; the *chomesh* is not *me'akev* at the Torah level, and therefore the rabbis did not extend its requirement to *demai*. The logic of the rabbinic extension tracks the Torah-level significance of each component. If one accepts this reasoning, it constitutes a strong proof that the *chomesh* is fundamentally not *me'akev* — its absence does not invalidate the *pidyon* at the Torah level.

### Rabbi Eliezer vs. Yehosh…

The Gemara raises the possibility that this issue is in fact a *tannaic* dispute. A *baraita* states: if one gave the *keren* but not the *chomesh* — *natan et ha-keren ve-lo natan et ha-chomesh* — Rabbi Eliezer says *yochal*, one may eat the *ma'aser sheni*, while Rabbi Yehoshua says *lo yochal*, one may not eat it. Rabbi Yehudah ha-Nasi then offers a split ruling: the position of Rabbi Eliezer appears correct on Shabbat, while the position of Rabbi Yehoshua appears correct on a weekday.

The Gemara reads Rabbi's split ruling as revealing something about the underlying dispute. Since Rabbi says Rabbi Eliezer's view applies on Shabbat and Rabbi Yehoshua's applies on a weekday, this implies that each Tanna holds his position universally — Rabbi Eliezer allows eating regardless of the day, and Rabbi Yehoshua prohibits it regardless of the day — and Rabbi is mediating between them by applying each position to a different context. On the face of it, this appears to reflect a substantive disagreement: Rabbi Eliezer holds the *chomesh* is not *me'akev*, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds that it is.

---

## Fifth Me'akev? (II)

### Rav Pappa Resolves

Rav Pappa, however, rejects the conclusion that this is a dispute about the Torah-level status of the *chomesh*. He proposes: *de-kulei alma chomesh lo me'akev* — everyone agrees that at the Torah level the *chomesh* does not invalidate the *pidyon*. This is clearly the position of Rabbi Eliezer, who permits eating even without the *chomesh*. But even Rabbi Yehoshua, Rav Pappa argues, need not hold that the *chomesh* is *me'akev* at the Torah level. Rather, the dispute is whether we impose a rabbinic deterrent — *chashinan le-fshiyuta* — whether we are concerned that a person will be negligent. If there are no consequences to failing to add the *chomesh* and one can simply eat the *ma'aser sheni* after a *pidyon* without the *chomesh*, one will perpetually defer this obligation and never fulfill it. Rabbi Yehoshua therefore says we do not permit eating until the *chomesh* has been paid, not because the *pidyon* failed *de'oraita*, but as a rabbinic safeguard to ensure compliance.

Rabbi Eliezer, in contrast, holds *lo chashinan le-fshiyuta* — we are not concerned about negligence, and so he allows eating immediately.

This interpretation harmonizes elegantly with Rabbi's mediation. The concern for negligence is not absolute; it is a secondary, utilitarian consideration that can be overridden by competing concerns. On Shabbat, where the need for food is pressing and eating is a *mitzvah* dimension of the day — *u-kerasa le-Shabbat oneg* — Rabbi rules that we do not impose the rabbinic deterrent and the person may eat. On a weekday, where no such countervailing consideration exists, Rabbi endorses the deterrent of Rabbi Yehoshua. This works perfectly if the question is one of rabbinic policy, not *de'oraita* validity.

### Hekdesh & Shabbat

Rabbi Yochanan then introduces an important qualification. He states that everyone agrees — *hakol modim* — that when one has redeemed *hekdesh* and the *gizbarim*, the Temple treasurers, will pursue the unpaid *chomesh* in the marketplace, the *pidyon* is effective even without the *chomesh* having been paid. The rationale is that where there exists an institutional creditor who will enforce collection, the rabbinic concern for negligence does not arise. The person cannot simply forget or defer — the Temple treasury will ensure payment. Consequently, even Rabbi Yehoshua would not impose the deterrent in such a case.

The Gemara challenges this from a different *baraita* where Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim* dispute a case that seems to involve *hekdesh*, and Rabbi again splits the vote — this time ruling that Rabbi Eliezer's permissive view makes sense for *hekdesh* and the *Chachamim*'s restrictive view makes sense for *ma'aser*. The Gemara concludes from Rabbi's split that each disputant actually holds his position across both *hekdesh* and *ma'aser*, and Rabbi is distinguishing between the two for policy reasons — not that everyone agrees by *hekdesh*. The original statement of Rabbi Yochanan must therefore be read more narrowly: it applies specifically to the combined case where *both* the considerations of *hekdesh* (institutional enforcement) *and* Shabbat are present simultaneously. *Hakol modim be-Shabbat be-hekdesh she-chilel* — everyone agrees that if one redeemed *hekdesh* on Shabbat and failed to pay the *chomesh*, the redemption stands: first because there is institutional enforcement, and second because of the honor of Shabbat and the desire to enable one to enjoy food on the holy day.

---

## Ma'aser Below Prutah (II)

### Fifth Not Me'akev

Before closing this topic, a *Tosafot* at the top of 54b raises a subtle question worth noting. The suggestion that the *chomesh* is *me'akev* rests on the premise that the Torah requires redeeming four on five — i.e., the *pidyon* is only valid when transacted at the total amount including the *chomesh*. But *Tosafot* points out that even an undervalued redemption generally works *bedieved* — if one redeems *hekdesh* worth a hundred on a penny, the *pidyon* is valid after the fact. If so, even if the Torah envisions redeeming four on five, why should paying only four invalidate it, given that an underpayment generally suffices *bedieved*?

*Tosafot* resolves this by distinguishing between two types of shortfall. If one explicitly declares, "this item and its *chomesh* are hereby redeemed on this coin" — even if the coin's value is less than the item's value — the *pidyon* works *bedieved* because one has framed the transaction as a deliberate, if undervalued, redemption. But if one says, "I am redeeming this four on four," without mentioning the *chomesh* at all, one is not attempting an undervalued redemption — one is attempting a *full* redemption, but doing so incorrectly, without meeting the Torah's requirement that four be redeemed on five. That formulation does not work even *bedieved*, because the basis of the transaction is wrong. The *chomesh* must be part of the declared redemptive framework.

---

## Chomesh K'Moto

### Fifth Properties

Having established the basic rules of the *chomesh*, the Gemara proceeds to a series of questions about the nature of the *chomesh* obligation and whether it mirrors the properties of the underlying *hekdesh* or *ma'aser*. Rami bar Chama introduces the inquiry by noting an established rule: *hekdesh eino mitchallel al karka* — *hekdesh* cannot be redeemed onto land; the Torah requires payment in money, as derived from the verse *ve-natan ha-kesef ve-kam lo* — one gives money and it is thereby established. The *chomesh* must follow form: *chumsho mahu she-yischalel al karka* — can the *chomesh* be redeemed onto land, or does it too require chattel?

Similarly: *terumah einah mishtalemet ela min ha-chullin* — if a *zar* eats *terumah* inadvertently, he must repay with non-consecrated food that thereupon becomes *terumah*, as derived from the verse *ve-natan la-kohen et ha-kodesh* — one gives the *kohen* something capable of becoming holy. The question is: *chumsho mahu she-yishtalem shelo min ha-chullin* — must the *chomesh* paid alongside that repayment also be food capable of becoming *terumah*, or may it be given in a different form entirely?

And further: *ma'aser ein mitchallel al asimon* — *ma'aser sheni* cannot be redeemed onto an *asimon*, an unmarked metal blank that bears no stamped image, as derived from *ve-tzarta ha-kesef be-yadecha* — you shall bind the money in your hand, which requires a properly minted coin bearing an image. The question again is: *chumsho mahu she-yischalel al asimon* — may the *chomesh* be paid with an *asimon*, or does it require a proper stamped coin just as the principal does?

### Rava's Drasha

These questions were deliberated and eventually reached Rava. He resolved all of them together with a single textual argument. Every *pasuk* in the Torah dealing with the *chomesh* uses the formulation *ve-asaf chamishito alav* — he shall add its fifth upon it. The word *alav*, "upon it," teaches: *le-rabbos chomsho ke-moto* — to include that the *chomesh* must be like the object itself. The *chomesh* must replicate the properties of the principal. If the principal must be redeemed on money, so must the *chomesh*. If the principal must be repaid in food capable of becoming *terumah*, so must the *chomesh*. If the principal must be redeemed on a stamped coin, so must the *chomesh*. The *chomesh* tracks the nature of the original obligation in every respect.

*Tosafot* notes in this connection that this *chomsho ke-moto* principle does not make the *chomesh* strictly *me'akev* — it defines the proper form of the *chomesh*, not a condition for the validity of the *pidyon* itself.

### Terumah Proof

Ravina offers an independent proof for the same principle from a *mishnah* concerning the repayment of *terumah*. The *mishnah* teaches: if someone stole *terumah* but did not eat it, he pays double — *tashlumei kefel* — but the double is calculated at the market value of *terumah*, which is lower than the value of ordinary produce because *terumah* may only be consumed by *kohanim* in a state of *taharah*. If, however, the thief ate the *terumah*, the repayment is more complex: he owes *shenei karnayim ve-chomesh* — two principal amounts and a *chomesh*. Specifically, the *keren* and *chomesh* are paid from *chullin* food that thereby becomes *terumah*, while the *keren* for the *kefel* is paid as a monetary assessment at *terumah* market value.

What is significant here is that the *chomesh* is paid in kind — in food — just as the principal is paid in food. The *chomesh* follows the nature of the original object. This is the proof: *shma mina chomesh ke-moto* — the *chomesh* must be like the original. The proof from *terumah* supports Rava's general principle derived from the word *alav*, and presumably what is true of *terumah* is equally true of the other categories.

---

## Fifth of Fifth

### Gezel Case

The Gemara now turns to the question of whether the obligation to add a *chomesh* applies recursively — that is, whether one may ever owe a *chomesh* on a *chomesh*. Rava introduces the discussion by citing the verse in the context of *gezel*. When one swears falsely that one has not stolen or defrauded someone and then admits the oath was false, one must return the principal and add a fifth: *ve-chamishitav yosef alav* — with his fifths he shall add upon it. The word *chamishitav* is in the plural — "his fifths" — indicating that the obligation of adding a fifth may compound.

The Mishnah cited provides the mechanism: if one gave back the *keren* but then swore falsely regarding the *chomesh* and subsequently admitted it, one now owes a *chomesh* on that *chomesh*. If one then swears falsely on the second *chomesh* and admits it, one owes a *chomesh* on the *chomesh* of the *chomesh*. This process continues — *ad she-yisma'et ha-keren pachos mi-shaveh prutah* — until the amount being sworn upon falls below a *prutah*. As long as each successive amount upon which one takes a false oath exceeds a *prutah*, the cycle of repayment and *chomesh* continues indefinitely. The plural *chamishitav* in the verse explicitly licenses this recursive application of the *chomesh* in the context of *gezel*.

### Terumah Case

In the case of *terumah*, the relevant verse uses the singular: *ve-yasaf chamishito alav* — he shall add its fifth upon it. The plural is absent. One might have thought that the *chomesh* on a *chomesh* therefore does not apply to *terumah*. Nevertheless, the Mishnah teaches explicitly: *ha-ochel terumah be-shogeg meshalem keren ve-chomesh* — one who eats *terumah* inadvertently repays the principal and the fifth. And the Mishnah continues: *va-chumsha de-chumsha* — and a fifth of a fifth. If one then ate the food one was repaying as the *chomesh*, one owes a further fifth on that. Thus, even without a plural form in the verse, the Mishnah teaches that the *chomesh* of a *chomesh* applies in *terumah*.

### Ma'aser No Fifth²

By contrast, with respect to *ma'aser sheni*, neither the verses nor any Mishnah suggests the existence of a *chomesh* on a *chomesh*. The verse says *mi-ma'asro* — from his *maaser* — which led to the conclusion that there are circumstances where redemption cannot occur, but nothing in the text hints at recursive fifths. The Gemara states plainly: *ve-lo ibaya iba'ya lan* — it was never even raised as a question. The silence of both the scriptural sources and the Mishnaic tradition on this point makes clear that no *chomesh* on a *chomesh* applies to *ma'aser sheni*. The recursive obligation arises only from the original food, not from the money onto which it was redeemed. Once the *ma'aser sheni* has been redeemed onto money and the *chomesh* added, there is no further layer of fifths if one subsequently wishes to transfer that money.

### Hekdesh Question

For *hekdesh*, the picture is more complex. The verse reads: *ve-im ha-makdish yigal et beito ve-yasaf chamishit kesef erchecha alav* — if the one who sanctified it redeems his house, he shall add a fifth of the valuation money upon it. The word *chamishit* is in the singular, not the plural. Nor does the Mishnah say *chumsho* and *chumsha de-chumsho* as it does with *terumah*. The Mishnah regarding *hekdesh* says only: *ha-podeh hekdesh mosif chomesh* — one who redeems *hekdesh* adds a fifth. A fifth — singular — with no mention of a fifth of a fifth.

The question therefore arises: what is the basis for saying a *chomesh* on a *chomesh* applies by *terumah*, and does that basis exist by *hekdesh* as well? The Gemara initially considers whether the basis for the recursive *chomesh* in *terumah* might be the word *ve-yasaf* — "and he shall add" — read as indicating an ongoing, cumulative addition. Since the same word *ve-yasaf* appears in the *hekdesh* verse, perhaps the same implication carries over. Alternatively, perhaps the basis for *terumah*'s recursive *chomesh* is a more technical textual maneuver: the extra *vav* of *ve-yasaf* is taken from the root and appended to the end of *chamishato*, transforming it from *chamishato* (singular, "its fifth") to *chamishitav* (plural, "its fifths"). By this reading, it is the *vav* of *ve-yasaf* that generates the plural, and only by *terumah* does the word *chamishato* appear to which this *vav* can be attached. By *hekdesh*, the verse says *chamishit* rather than *chamishato*, and even appending the extra *vav* would produce only *chamishito* — still a singular "its fifth" — not a meaningful plural. Under this reading, the basis for a recursive *chomesh* does not transfer from *terumah* to *hekdesh*.

Before resolving this textual question, the Gemara considers whether there is a separate, threshold reason why the *chomesh* on a *chomesh* might not apply to *hekdesh* — namely, the principle of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the *chomesh* is added only to the original sanctified object, not to transferred *kedushah*. If the *chomesh* itself represents new *kedushah* added to the system, one might argue that it falls into a category of transferred *kedushah* and therefore no additional fifth applies. But Rava addresses this below.

### Hekdesh Resolution

The resolution is provided by Rav Tivumi in the name of Abaye, citing the verse: *ve-yasaf chamishit kesef erchecha* — he shall add a fifth of the money of your valuation. What is striking here is that the verse places the words for "fifth" and "principal" in immediate proximity: *chamishit kesef erchecha* — a fifth alongside the valuation money. The Gemara reads this as a *hekesh* — an analogy: *mah kesef ercho mosif chomesh, af kesef chomsho nami mosif chomesh* — just as one adds a fifth upon the principal valuation, so too one adds a fifth upon the *chomesh* itself. The structural juxtaposition of the fifth and the principal amount in the same phrase indicates that the fifth is to be treated like the principal, and whatever obligation attaches to the principal — including the recursive addition of a fifth — attaches equally to the *chomesh*.

Thus, the *chomesh* of *chomesh* applies to *hekdesh* through this *hekesh*, even though neither the plural form of the word nor the Mishnah explicitly state it. The summary picture is: the recursive *chomesh* applies to *gezel* (derived from the plural *chamishitav*), to *terumah* (derived from the Mishnah's explicit statement, supported by the textual manipulation of *ve-yasaf* and *chamishato*), and to *hekdesh* (derived from the *hekesh* of *chamishit kesef erchecha*). It does not apply to *ma'aser sheni*, where neither verse nor Mishnah hints at it and the question was never even raised.

---

## Original vs. Transferred

### RYBLI Position

The Gemara now formally introduces the teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *al hekdesh rishon mosif chomesh; al hekdesh sheni ein mosif chomesh* — one adds a *chomesh* only upon the original sanctified object; upon transferred *hekdesh* — sanctity that has been conveyed from one object to another — one does not add a *chomesh*. If I sanctify my dresser and it is worth eighty, then redeem it by giving eighty coins to the Temple, those coins have received the *kedushah* by transfer. Were I to then redeem those coins, I would not add a fifth.

### Makdish vs. Metfis

Rava provides the textual basis for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's principle. The verse states: *ve-im ha-makdish yigal et beito* — if the one who sanctified it redeems his house. The Gemara reads this as: *ha-makdish ve-lo ha-matfis* — the one who directly sanctified the object, not the one who created *hekdesh* through the mechanism of transfer. When one transfers *kedushah* from one object to another, the second object's sanctity comes not from the direct act of *hakdashah* but from the process of *hatfasah* — the apprehension or conveyance of *kedushah*. The verse's use of *ha-makdish* in the definite sense teaches that the *chomesh* belongs only to the act of direct sanctification.

### Non-Kosher Animal

A *tanna* taught a *baraita* before Rabbi Elazar presenting a *derasha* connecting the *chomesh* to the case of a *behemah teme'ah* — a non-kosher animal. The verse in the context of *hekdesh* mentions: *ve-im bi-vhemah ha-tme'ah u-fadah ve-erchecha* — and if it is a non-kosher animal and you redeem it at your valuation. The *baraita* draws an analogy: just as a non-kosher animal is characterized by *techilato hekdesh ve-kulo la-shamayim* — its sanctity is original and its entire value goes to heaven, i.e., to the Temple treasury — so too, anything characterized by original *hekdesh* whose entire value belongs to the Temple is subject to the obligation of *me'ilah*.

Rabbi Elazar challenges the *baraita*. He accepts that the phrase *kulo la-shamayim* — all to heaven — is intelligible: it distinguishes the non-kosher animal, whose full value goes to the Temple, from *kodshim kalim* such as *shelamim*, where the owners retain a portion of the meat. Since *kodshim kalim* involve a share for the owners, the leniency regarding *me'ilah* might apply. This is a meaningful distinction.

But the phrase *techilat hekdesh* — original sanctity — is puzzling. Does it mean to say that only things originally sanctified by the owner are subject to *me'ilah*, while things sanctified by transfer are not? But this is incorrect as a matter of halachah: even objects that receive *kedushah* through transfer are subject to *me'ilah*. So what is *techilat hekdesh* coming to exclude?

Rabbi Elazar suggests: *de-ima le-inyan chomesh ka-marta ke-Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* — perhaps when the *baraita* says *me'ilah* it does not really mean the laws of *me'ilah* at all. The word being used is close in sound to *ma'aleh*, meaning to "elevate" or "add upon." What the *baraita* is actually teaching is the principle of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about the *chomesh*: the fifth is added only when the sanctity is original, not when it is transferred. The *tanna* confirms: *in, hachi kamina* — yes, that is precisely what I meant.

### Ha-Article Drasha

The discussion continues with further attempts to locate the precise textual derivation. Rav Ashi asks Ravina: the premise that a non-kosher animal has only *techilat hekdesh* and not transferred *kedushah* is questionable. Surely one can transfer *kedushah* to a non-kosher animal — if I sanctify my dresser and then transfer its sanctity to a donkey, the donkey now has *kedushah* by transfer. So why does the *baraita* use the non-kosher animal as representative of original-only *kedushah*?

The response is: *lefi she-einah be-sof hekdesh* — because a non-kosher animal is not the type of object that features in the ultimate disposition of *hekdesh*. A non-kosher animal cannot be offered as a *korban*; it cannot be used as a Temple building beam. It always ends up being redeemed; it never serves as the final vessel for *hekdesh*. It is not a *sof hekdesh* — an end-stage *hekdesh* object.

Rav Acha mi-Difti presses Ravina further: but if a non-kosher animal can have *kedushah* transferred to it — if it can be a middle stage in the chain of *hekdesh* transfers — does that not suggest that a *chomesh* should apply to it by virtue of being a middle-stage *hekdesh*? The response is: *harei hu ke-sof hekdesh* — even though it can theoretically be a middle stage, in its fundamental character it resembles the end stage, since it is not going to be used directly as *hekdesh*. The end-stage *hekdesh* does not generate a *chomesh*; therefore the middle-stage *hekdesh* analogous to the end stage also does not.

Rav Zutra the son of Rav Mari pushes back: why compare the middle case to the end? Perhaps compare it to the beginning. The beginning case does involve a *chomesh* — something original that is sanctified does get a fifth when redeemed. The middle case, like the beginning, has something further coming after it in the chain. Why not say that the middle case, like the beginning, should have a *chomesh*?

The Gemara initially offers the response that the end-stage comparison is more apt because both the middle and the end share the property of *nitpeset* — having *kedushah* received through transfer — whereas the beginning is unique in representing original *kedushah*. But this line of reasoning is then set aside.

Ultimately the Gemara accepts that the resolution does not lie in reasoning about beginning, middle, and end stages at all. Rather, as Rava teaches, it lies in the *hei* of the definite article. In the verse from *Tzav* — *hi ha-olah al mokdah* — the word *ha-olah* refers to the specific *olah* mentioned earlier in the passage, namely the *olat tamid*, and from this we learn that the *hei* can indicate "the first" or "the original." Similarly, when the verse says *ve-im bi-vhemah ha-tme'ah* — and if with a non-kosher animal — the *hei* of *ha-tme'ah* indicates: the first, the original *behemah tme'ah* that was sanctified, not one to which *kedushah* was subsequently transferred. The verse's use of the definite article thus teaches that the *chomesh* applies only to the originally sanctified object, not to one that received *kedushah* by transfer from another. This is the derivation underlying Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's principle: *al hekdesh rishon mosif chomesh; al hekdesh sheni ein mosif chomesh*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 55

## Hekdesh Transfer Rules

### R. Yehoshua ben Levi

The daf opens in the midst of a discussion about the rules governing the addition of a *chomesh* (a one-fifth surcharge) when redeeming *hekdesh* and *ma'aser sheni*. The Gemara cites a *tanya k'vatei d'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* — a *braita* that corroborates the position of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — establishing the foundational principle that the obligation to add a *chomesh* applies only to a first-generation transfer out of sanctified property, but not to a second-generation transfer. That is, when one redeems the original *hekdesh*, a *chomesh* is added; but when one subsequently redeems the object or money that replaced it, no *chomesh* is required.

### Cow Exchange Rules

The *braita* states: *para zo tachat para shel hekdesh, tallis zo tachat tallis shel hekdesh, hekdesho paduy v'yad hekdesh al ha'elyona* — if one declares "this cow in exchange for this *hekdesh* cow," or "this *tallis* in exchange for this *hekdesh tallis*," the transfer is effective. Significantly, the transfer need not be conducted in money; objects may be exchanged directly for *hekdesh* objects. And *hekdesh* retains the upper hand: if the second object is worth less than the first, one remains obligated to pay *hekdesh* the difference. If the second object is worth more, *hekdesh* receives the full object.

This asymmetry reflects an important principle. As Tosafot notes, there is a famous ruling of Shmuel that even if one transferred *hekdesh* worth a thousand *dinar* onto an object worth a mere *prutah*, the transfer is technically valid *b'dieved* — because one can conceptualize the transfer as moving an abstract status of *kedushah* from one object to another, independent of monetary value. However, that is plainly not the default intent when one uses simple object-for-object language. When one says "this cow for this cow," the language implies an intent to exchange equal value. Accordingly, if the second cow is worth less, the balance is owed to *hekdesh*; if more, *hekdesh* receives the full benefit.

### Explicit Valuation

The *braita* continues with a second case: *para zo b'chamesh sela'im tachat para shel hekdesh* — "this cow, which I know is worth five *sela'im*, in exchange for this *hekdesh* cow." Here the speaker explicitly names the value of the second object. In this scenario, *hekdesho paduy* — the redemption is valid — but the rule of *yad hekdesh al ha'elyona* does not apply. The *braita* concludes by restating the core teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *al hekdesh rishon mosif chomesh, al hekdesh sheni ein mosif chomesh* — the *chomesh* is added when transferring out of the original *hekdesh*, but not when transferring out of the replacement.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot spells out precisely why explicit valuation changes the legal calculus. In the case of *tallis zo b'chamesh sela'im hekdesho paduy*, Tosafot writes: *hacha lo garsinan yad hekdesh al ha'elyona, d'keivan she'nitkavein l'challel hekdesh, afilu shaveh harbeh al davar muat, mechullal* — here we do not apply the rule that *hekdesh* holds the upper hand, because by explicitly stating a value, the speaker has expressed a clear intent to transfer the *kedushah* onto that specific monetary amount, even if the original *hekdesh* was worth considerably more. This parallels Shmuel's ruling, cited by Tosafot as *k'dikmar Shmuel lekaman*.

By contrast, in the first case — where no value is stated and one simply says "this for this" — *aval b'reisha shelo hizkir shum shaveh, lo haya b'daato liknot hekdesh*: the language implies an intent to exchange equivalent value, and therefore if the second object falls short, the shortfall remains owed to *hekdesh*. Tosafot adds that the same logic applies in the upward direction: *ve'im hotir yad hekdesh al ha'elyona, lekach lo eirev leshon sheneihem ke'echad* — in the first case, if the second object is worth more than the first, *hekdesh* receives the full object, whereas when a specific value has been named, the transfer is limited to precisely that stated amount. Thus, the formula *b'chamesh sela'im* fixes the exchange in both directions, at once releasing *hekdesh* from demanding more and releasing the redeemer from offering more.

### Temura Exception

A natural question arises: how can one transfer *hekdesh* by exchanging one object for another directly? Does not the Torah explicitly prohibit *temura* — as stated *ve'haya hu u'tmurato yiheyeh kodesh* — meaning that attempting to substitute one animal for a consecrated one causes *both* to become sanctified, without actually effecting the intended transfer?

Tosafot addresses this directly: *yesh lomar de'hacha be'mai askinan be'kodshei bedek ha'bayit* — the cases in our *braita* concern *kodshei bedek ha'bayit*, donations made to the Temple treasury, as distinct from *korbanot*. The prohibition of *temura* and its extraordinary consequence of dual sanctification apply specifically to the *kedushah* of an animal designated as a *korban* — an offering whose intrinsic sanctity is bound up with its purpose of being brought on the altar. Such an animal cannot simply be transferred onto another object, and even if it bears a *mum* and must be redeemed, the redemption must be onto money rather than another object. But *kodshei bedek ha'bayit* — property consecrated for the Temple's maintenance fund — is treated essentially as a matter of monetary value. Its *kedushah* is not a deep intrinsic sanctity tied to being offered, but rather a sanctity of ownership and value. Therefore, a direct object-for-object exchange is entirely valid for *kodshei bedek ha'bayit*, and the laws of *temura* simply do not apply.

---

## Ona'ah Thresholds

### One-Sixth Rule

The Gemara now transitions to the *mishnah* that opens the discussion of *ona'ah* (overcharging). The *mishnah* states: *ha'ona'ah arba'ah kessef* — the threshold for *ona'ah* is four *kessef* per *sela*, which, since a *sela* equals twenty-four *ma'ah*, works out to exactly one-sixth of the purchase price. This is the familiar rule of *shtus lameikach*. The *mishnah* then states *ve'ha'ta'anah shtei kessef* — that for the law of *modeh bemiktzat* to apply, the original claim must amount to at least *shtei ma'ah*.

### Modeh Bemiktzat

The law of *modeh bemiktzat* requires three elements: a claim of at least *shtei ma'ah*, an admission of at least a *prutah*, and a denial of at least a *prutah*. If one demands payment of *shtei ma'ah* from another, and the defendant admits to part while denying the rest, a *shevuah* is imposed — provided that both the admitted portion and the denied portion each reach the threshold of a *prutah*. The *mishnah* concludes: *ve'ha'hoda'ah shaveh prutah* — the admission must be worth a *prutah*. The *mishnah* then declares *chamesh perutot hen* — there are five areas of law in which the *prutah* serves as the minimum monetary threshold.

The Gemara asks why the *mishnah* needs to teach the *ona'ah* rule at all, since it was already established in an earlier *mishnah* in this same *perek*. The answer is that the *mishnah* needed the *ona'ah* rule as a hook to introduce the two-*ma'ah* threshold for *ta'anah*, which in turn was needed as a hook to introduce the concept of *prutah* in the admission, which finally led to the main purpose: the enumeration of the five *perutot*.

The Gemara similarly asks whether the *ta'anah* of *shtei ma'ah* and the *hoda'ah* of *prutah* needed to be stated here, since they already appear in tractate *Shevuot* in the context of *shevuot hadayanim*. The Gemara explains: *seifa itztricha lei* — each element in the chain was needed to arrive at the final teaching. The first rule brought in the second, the second introduced the *prutah*, and the *prutah* enabled the enumeration of the five categories.

### No Ona'ah Below Isar

The Gemara then raises a pointed question: *velisni nami ha'ona'ah perutah* — why does the *mishnah* not add a sixth category, namely that *ona'ah* also has a minimum threshold of a *prutah*? After all, if one overcharges by less than a *prutah*, that too would seem to qualify as *ona'ah* on a proportional basis.

Rav Kahana's answer is striking: *zot omeret ein ona'ah liprutos* — this omission teaches that there is in fact no *ona'ah* for trivially small amounts. *Ona'ah* requires not only a one-sixth overcharge proportionally, but also a minimum absolute amount. According to Rashi, that minimum is an *isar* — a denomination worth eight *perutot* — since the *isar* represents the lowest denomination still considered silver coinage, while anything below that has entered the realm of copper and is too trivial to sustain a claim of *ona'ah*.

The conceptual point is important. *Ona'ah* is not simply a matter of taking more than one is entitled to in a proportional sense; it involves a meaningful monetary wrong. A few extra pennies, even if they represent a large proportion of the item's value, do not constitute the kind of commercial harm the Torah was addressing. This is in contrast to *gezel*, where stealing even a *prutah* is a formal transgression — because in *gezel* one is taking an object that belongs to another, while in *ona'ah* the buyer did receive what they purchased, merely at a somewhat inflated price.

### Levi Disputes Kahana

Levi disagrees with Rav Kahana and maintains *yeish ona'ah liprutos* — that even an overcharge of a *prutah* constitutes *ona'ah* if it represents one-sixth of the item's value.
