Levi further corroborated this position in his own *baraita*, which offered an alternative version of the five *perutot* list. In Levi's list, *ona'ah* itself appears as one of the five: *ha'ona'ah prutah, v'hoda'ah prutah, v'kiddushi ishah prutah, v'gezel b'prutah*. However, Levi omits *metziah* (found objects) and replaces it with *ha'yeshivas hadayanim prutah* — the rule that a court will convene to adjudicate a claim worth a *prutah*. According to our *mishnah*, which does not include *ona'ah* among the five, Rav Kahana's position prevails: *ona'ah* does not apply below the *isar* threshold.

---

## Five Prutah Categories

### The Five Prutot

The *mishnah* enumerates five domains in which the *prutah* functions as the operative minimum unit of legal monetary recognition: admission in a *modeh bemiktzat* context (*hoda'ah shaveh prutah*); betrothal of a woman (*ha'ishah mitkadeshet bishvei prutah*, in accordance with Beit Hillel); deriving benefit from *hekdesh* (*ha'neheneh bishvei prutah min hahekdesh ma'al*, this constituting *me'ilah*); the obligation to announce a found object (*ha'motzei shaveh prutah chayav lehachriz*); and stealing from another with a false oath (*ha'gozel chaveiro shaveh prutah ve'nishba lo yolichenu acharav afilu leMadai* — one must pursue him to return it even to the farthest regions).

The case of *me'ilah* is worth pausing over. One might ask whether *me'ilah* is properly conceptualized as a form of theft from *hekdesh* — in which case the *prutah* threshold follows naturally as the minimum definition of money — or whether it is better understood as a category of deriving prohibited *hana'ah* from *hekdesh*, in which case the relevant standard might be a *kezayit* rather than a *prutah*. Here the *halacha* is clear that the threshold is a *prutah*, but a related debate does arise among the *acharonim* in analogous contexts — for instance, regarding things that are *assur behana'ah*, such as *basar bechalav* or *avodah zarah*, where there is a dispute whether the minimum for *malkut* is a *kezayit* or a *prutah*'s worth of benefit, depending on whether one frames *hana'ah* as a form of *achilah* or as a form of monetary gain.

### Rav Katina Exception

The Gemara explains why Levi listed *yeshivas hadayanim* — the adjudication threshold — rather than *metziah*, and it does so by revealing that this inclusion is not merely redundant with *gezel*. The *chidush* of *yeshivas hadayanim perutah* is specifically *laapokei mid'Rav Katina* — to exclude the position of Rav Katina. Rav Katina held *beit din nizkakin afilu lefachos mishaveh prutah* — that a court will sit and adjudicate even for a claim worth less than a *prutah*. Levi's enumeration of *yeshivas hadayanim* among the five *perutot* thus serves to establish the opposite: a *beit din* will hear cases starting from a *prutah*, but not for amounts below that threshold.

### Meila Below Prutah

A related question emerges from the *pasuk* in Vayikra 5:16: *ve'et asher chata min ha'kodesh yeshallem v'chamishito yosef alav*. The Gemara reads *ve'et* as a *ribbui* extending the repayment obligation even to benefit from *hekdesh* worth less than a *prutah* — *lerabos pachos mishaveh prutah lehishavon*. How does this square with the *mishnah*'s statement that *me'ilah* requires a *prutah*?

The resolution is that the *prutah* threshold in *me'ilah* applies to the obligation to bring a *korban me'ilah*, not to the obligation of repayment itself. As the Rambam states in *Hilchot Me'ilah* (chapter 7, *halacha* 8): one who derives benefit from *hekdesh* worth less than a *prutah*, whether *b'meizid* or *b'shogeg*, pays back the principal but is not liable for a *chomesh* or a *korban*. Thus, the return obligation extends even below a *prutah* when it comes to *hekdesh*, unlike the analogous case between two private parties — *lekodesh in, aval lehedyot lo* — where no legal obligation to return amounts below a *prutah* exists at all.

### Opening vs. Ending Case

This asymmetry between *hekdesh* and *hedyot* raises a further difficulty: if there is no legal obligation to return less than a *prutah* to a private individual, how can a *beit din* rule on such a claim? The Gemara resolves this with a refined formulation: *amar Rav Katina, huchzeku beit din leshaveh prutah, gomrin afilu pachos mishvei prutah* — a court will open a case only for a claim worth at least a *prutah*, but once the case has been opened on the basis of a *prutah*-valued claim, they will complete it even if the outstanding balance at the end of litigation turns out to be less than a *prutah*. The principle is: *techilas din be'inan prutah, gemar din lo be'inan prutah*. To begin litigation requires a *prutah*; to conclude it does not. This presumably reflects the principle that once a process of adjudication is underway, seeing it through to a conclusion — even for a small residual balance — is required to avoid a perversion of justice, even where no independent legal obligation to pay would have attached.

---

## Five Chomeshim

### Sacred Foods

The *mishnah* now enumerates *chamisha chumshin hen* — five categories in which one is obligated to add a *chomesh*, a one-fifth surcharge, upon repayment or redemption. The first category is *ha'ochel trumah* — one who consumes *terumah* without authorization, *b'shogeg*, and must repay the *kohen* the value plus a fifth. Included within this single category, because they share the same status, are *terumat ma'aser* (the *kohen*'s portion of the Levite's tithe), *terumat ma'aser shel demai*, *challah* (the dough-portion given to the *kohen*), and *bikurim* (first fruits brought to the Temple). All of these are treated as forms of *terumah*, all go to the *kohen*, and consuming any of them *b'shogeg* triggers the same obligation to repay plus a fifth.

### Neta Revai Rules

The second category is *ha'podeh neta revai u'ma'aser sheni shelo* — one who redeems his own *neta revai* (fourth-year fruit, which carries the same sanctity as *ma'aser sheni*) or his own *ma'aser sheni* adds a *chomesh*. The word *shelo* is critical: the *chomesh* applies when the *owner* redeems his own consecrated property. If someone else — a stranger — redeems another's *ma'aser sheni* or *neta revai*, no *chomesh* is added. This parallel structure — owner adds, stranger does not — will recur in the next category.

### Meila & Oath

The fifth category in the *mishnah* is *ha'gozel chaveiro shaveh prutah ve'nishba lo* — one who steals from another and swears falsely about the theft. When the thief eventually confesses and makes restitution, he must return the principal, add a *chomesh*, and bring a *korban asham*. This combines the earlier theme of the five *perutot* (stealing a *prutah* plus a false oath) with the present discussion of *chomesh*.

### Hekdesh Redemption

The fourth category is *ha'podeh hekdesho mosif chomesh* — one who redeems his own *hekdesh* adds a *chomesh*. As with *ma'aser sheni*, this privilege and obligation belongs to the owner: when a stranger redeems *hekdesh*, purchasing it from the Temple treasury, no *chomesh* is added. Only the original owner who redeems his own consecrated property is required to pay the additional fifth. The third category, which completes the list, is *ha'neheneh bishvei prutah min hahekdesh* — deriving benefit worth a *prutah* from *hekdesh*, which constitutes *me'ilah* and obligates payment of the principal plus a *chomesh*; here the minimum threshold of a *prutah* for this obligation cross-references the discussion in the previous *mishnah*.

---

## Terumas Ma'aser Demai

### R. Elazar Question

The Gemara reports that Rava conveyed the following difficulty in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *terumat ma'aser shel demai* — why should consuming *terumat ma'aser* that derives from *demai* produce an obligation to add a *chomesh*? *Ve'chi asu chachamim chizuk l'divreihem k'shel Torah?* — did the Rabbis really strengthen their own enactments to the level of Torah law in this regard? *Demai* is produce purchased from an *am ha'aretz* whose tithing practices are uncertain; the obligation to tithe it and to separate *terumat ma'aser* from it is rabbinic. Would the Rabbis truly go so far as to impose the *chomesh* — a penalty associated specifically with the violation of *terumah* of Torah status — upon one who mistakenly eats *terumat ma'aser* of *demai*?

Tosafot sharpens the question further. While it is common for rabbinic enactments to be treated with great stringency, and sometimes even stricter than Torah law, that is typically when there is a logical reason to build additional safeguards — *heicha d'shayach l'miknos*. But here, the entire concept of adding a *chomesh* is itself a *kenas* (penalty) that the Torah imposes; it is not an intrinsic property of the prohibited act. Why would the Rabbis extend this penalty to a case that is rabbinic in origin? Since the *chomesh* is itself framed as an extrinsic fine, not an organic consequence of the violation, it is difficult to understand why the Rabbis would replicate it in a domain where the underlying prohibition is only of rabbinic force.

### R. Meir Stringency

Rav Nahman, citing Shmuel, answers: *ha mani, Rabbi Meir hi* — this ruling in the *mishnah* follows the opinion of Rabbi Meir, who holds that *asu chachamim chizuk l'divreihem k'shel Torah* — the Rabbis do indeed treat their enactments with the full weight of Torah law, without requiring a case-by-case logical justification for each stringency.

### Get Precedent

The *braita* adduced in support of this characterization concerns the laws of *gittin*. If an agent bringing a *get* from abroad delivers it to the woman without reciting the declaration *bifnai nichtav u'vifnai nechtam* — "it was written and signed in my presence" — Rabbi Meir rules *yotzi ve'ha'valad mamzer* (she must leave the second husband and the children are *mamzerim*), even though the only failure was a rabbinic procedural requirement. The *chachamim* disagree and rule *ein ha'valad mamzer*, although Tosafot notes that the *chachamim*'s formulation — which does not say *lo yotzi* but only *ein ha'valad mamzer* — implies that even they may agree the marriage requires dissolution; they merely decline to declare the children *mamzerim*.

To remedy the defect, the *braita* prescribes that the *shaliach* should *yitlenu himena v'yachzor v'yitnenu lah bifnai shenayim* — take the *get* back from the woman and re-deliver it with the proper declaration in front of two witnesses.

The Gemara identifies this as an expression of *Rabbi Meir l'ta'amei* — his consistent approach across legal domains. As Rav Hamnuna reported in the name of Ulla: *kol ha'meshaneh mi'matbe'a she'tav'u chachamim b'gittin yotzi ve'ha'valad mamzer* — any deviation from the precise formula the Sages established for *gittin* renders the *get* invalid and the children *mamzerim*, according to Rabbi Meir. The underlying principle is that once the Rabbis have established a formal requirement, Rabbi Meir treats any deviation as a complete failure — not as a minor procedural irregularity — regardless of whether the consequence (such as *mamzerut*) seems proportionate to the offense.

Tosafot notes that this extreme position in the *get* case — *Rabbi Meir* declaring children *mamzerim* over a purely procedural rabbinic failure — is the template for his approach here. Even where there is *af al pi she'ein sevara* — no compelling substantive logic — linking the stringency to the concern being addressed, Rabbi Meir imposes the full Torah consequence because, in his view, once a rabbinic enactment is in place, it is treated as if it were Torah law in every respect.

### Rav Sheshet Query

Rav Sheshet now challenges the attribution of the *mishnah*'s stringency to Rabbi Meir. The challenge comes from a *braita* dealing with *ma'aser sheni shel demai*: *mechalelo kesef al kesef, nechoshet al nechoshet, kesef al nechoshet, v'nechoshet al peirot, v'yachzor v'yifdeh et ha'peirot* — one may transfer the sanctity of *ma'aser sheni* of *demai* from silver coins to silver, copper to copper, silver to copper, copper to fruit, and then the fruit may be redeemed back onto coins. This last step — transferring from fruit back to coins — is what Rabbi Meir permits according to the *braita*. The *chachamim*, by contrast, rule *ya'alu peirot v'yei'achlu b'Yerushalayim* — once the sanctity is on fruit, the fruit must be brought to Jerusalem and eaten there; they may not be re-redeemed onto money.

The apparent implication is that Rabbi Meir is actually more *lenient* regarding *ma'aser sheni shel demai* than the *chachamim*. How, then, can the Gemara attribute the *mishnah*'s stringency — adding a *chomesh* to *terumat ma'aser shel demai* — to Rabbi Meir on the grounds that he always treats rabbinic enactments with maximal stringency?

### Mixed Coin Transfer

Before resolving this tension, the Gemara establishes that Rabbi Meir's leniency in the *braita* is not simply a reflection of his general approach to monetary transfers, but is specifically calibrated to the rabbinic status of *demai*. This is demonstrated by contrasting the *demai* rules with the rules for *ma'aser sheni vadai* — ordinary, certain *ma'aser sheni*.

The Gemara cites a *mishnah* dealing with a case where a *sela* of *ma'aser sheni* became mixed with a *sela* of ordinary *chullin* money. To resolve the situation without spending both coins as *ma'aser sheni*, one brings copper coins (*maot*) and declares: wherever the coin of *ma'aser sheni* is, its sanctity is hereby transferred to these copper coins. Then, from the two original silver coins — now both free of *ma'aser sheni* sanctity — one selects the nicer one and transfers the sanctity of the copper coins back onto it. This roundabout procedure is necessary because one cannot redeem silver *ma'aser sheni* directly onto silver of equal denomination: *mipnei she'amru, mechalelin oto kesef al nechoshet midochek* — the Sages permitted going from silver to copper only in a pressing situation (*midochek*), and even then only provisionally, with the expectation that *v'lo she'itkayem ken, ela she'yachzor v'yechalel al kesef* — it should not remain in copper form but should be redeemed back onto silver.

The principle established is: *midochek in, d'lo midochek klal* — redeeming from silver to copper is permitted only under pressing circumstances, and never as a standard practice. This stands in sharp contrast to the *demai* rules in the earlier *braita*, where Rabbi Meir freely permits transfers between silver and copper and from copper to fruit and back — without any requirement of *dochek*. The freer rules for *demai* are thus clearly a function of its rabbinic status, not a reflection of Rabbi Meir's general approach to the *pidyon* process.

### R. Meir Strict/Lenient

This now sharpens Rav Sheshet's challenge. If Rabbi Meir is demonstrably *more lenient* than the *chachamim* when it comes to the *pidyon* of *ma'aser sheni shel demai*, how can one attribute to him a *stringency* regarding *terumat ma'aser shel demai*?

### Eating vs. Pidyon

Rav Yosef resolves the apparent contradiction: *af al pi she'meikel Rabbi Meir b'pidyono, machmir hu b'achilato* — even though Rabbi Meir is lenient regarding the procedural rules of *redeeming* demai *ma'aser sheni*, he is strict when it comes to the act of *eating* improperly. When a non-*kohen* mistakenly eats *terumat ma'aser shel demai*, he has committed a transgression — a violation of the sanctity of *terumah*, even if it is only rabbinic in force. In Rabbi Meir's framework, this transgression is treated with the full severity of its Torah analogue, including the obligation to add a *chomesh*. But when the question is merely one of how to *perform the pidyon* — the technical procedure for redeeming *ma'aser sheni shel demai* — no transgression is involved, and there Rabbi Meir is content to be lenient.

This distinction is further supported by a *braita*: *lo hitiru limkor demai ela l'siton bilvad* — they permitted selling *demai* without first separating *terumos u'ma'asros* only to a wholesaler (*siton*), since everyone understands that a wholesaler is simply reselling without having personally supervised the tithing. A homeowner (*ba'al habayit*), however, must separate *terumos u'ma'asros* before reselling — *bein kach u'vein kach tzarich l'aser, divrei Rabbi Meir*. The *chachamim* are more lenient and permit even a homeowner to resell or give as a gift without separating, when it is clear from the context that no personal supervision of tithing was involved.

The relevance is this: Rabbi Meir's stringency in the *baraita* is directed at preventing people from *eating* improperly — the concern is that buyers will assume that the homeowner, being a *chaver*, has already tithed, and will therefore consume produce that has not properly had its *terumos u'ma'asros* taken. So when the concern is *eating a violation*, Rabbi Meir is strict. When the question is *how to perform the pidyon* of *demai*, Rabbi Meir is lenient.

Thus the *mishnah*'s ruling — that one who eats *terumat ma'aser shel demai* must add a *chomesh* — is entirely consistent with Rabbi Meir's overall approach: strict with respect to violations of eating sanctified produce, even when those violations are only rabbinic in character, but lenient with respect to the procedural mechanics of *pidyon* when no transgression is at stake.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 56

## Terumat Maaser Demai

### Terumat Maaser Mechanism

The daf opens with Ravina's challenge (*masiv Ravina*), picking up approximately ten lines down the page. To understand the question, it is necessary to recall the broader context: our Mishnah had been enumerating the various cases in which a fifth (*chomesh*) is added — among them the case of one who eats *terumat maaser* of *demai*.

The mechanism of *terumat maaser* of *demai* works as follows. When one purchases *demai* — produce bought from an *am ha'aretz* whose tithing status is uncertain — one is obligated to separate *maaser*, but need not give it to a Levi. The reasoning is that since *demai* may already have had *maaser* separated by the original farmer, the Levi cannot prove that the *maaser* belongs to him. The principle of *hamotzi me-chaveiro alav ha-ra'aya* — that the burden of proof falls on the one seeking to extract money from another — means the purchaser retains the separated *maaser* and may consume it himself.

However, one must still separate *terumat maaser* — the tenth of the tenth — because without doing so, the grain retains its *tevel* status and may not be eaten. Even if one could argue with the Kohen on grounds of monetary uncertainty, the concern is not merely financial: the produce might genuinely be *terumah*, and therefore from the standpoint of *issur*, one may not eat it. Crucially, since the *maaser* is not given to the Levi, this *terumat maaser* is separated by the original purchaser himself rather than by the Levi.

### Mishnah Strictness

Given this background, the Mishnah rules that if a non-Kohen eats *terumat maaser* of *demai*, he must repay the principal plus a fifth — exactly as though he had eaten ordinary *terumah* or ordinary *terumat maaser*. The Gemara questions why such stringency is warranted for produce whose very obligation is rabbinic and uncertain.

### Pidyon vs. Eating

The Gemara's answer is that the Mishnah follows the position of Rabbi Meir, who is characteristically stringent in treating rabbinic enactments with the same seriousness as Torah-level obligations — even absent a compelling logical basis to do so. The Gemara then raises a difficulty: we find that Rabbi Meir is actually *lenient* regarding the redemption (*pidyon*) of *maaser sheni* of *demai*, permitting modes of transfer — from silver coin to copper coin to produce and back — that he would not sanction for ordinary *maaser sheni*. This leniency would seem to contradict the claim that Rabbi Meir uniformly applies stringency to *demai*.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between domains. Rabbi Meir may be lenient with respect to the *pidyon* — the act of redemption, which is a matter of procedure — but is strict when it comes to the *aveirah* of actually eating *terumat maaser* of *demai* improperly. These are two distinct categories of concern.

### Nachtom Breads

Ravina now introduces a further challenge from a Mishnah dealing with bread purchased from a *nachtom*, a professional baker. The Mishnah there states that one who buys bread from a *nachtom* may separate *maaser* from bread baked when warm (*cham*) on bread that has grown cold (*tzonenet*) and vice versa — and this applies even when the loaves come from many different molds (*afilu midfusim harbeh*). This is explicitly attributed to Rabbi Meir.

Tosafot notes that the Mishnah is presenting a compound case: the bread is from different days *and* it comes from different molds — two independent grounds to suspect that the loaves originate from different suppliers or even different bakers whom the *nachtom* merely resells. Yet Rabbi Meir permits separating *maaser* from one loaf on the other. The problem is obvious: if the loaves actually derive from different farmers, one set might be genuinely obligated (*chayav*) and the other genuinely exempt (*patur*). Separating from an obligated batch on behalf of an exempt one, or vice versa, would be ineffective — and if the *hafrasha* is invalid, the produce remains in a *tevel*-like state and will be eaten improperly.

The Gemara begins its analysis. It acknowledges that if the only factor were cold bread on warm bread — yesterday's bread on today's — this would not be so troubling. The reason relates to the principle taught by Rabbi Ilai: how do we know that one who separates *terumah* from inferior produce on superior produce has nonetheless effected a valid *terumah*? From the verse (Numbers 18:32): *"ve-lo tis'u alav chet be-harimchem et chelbo mimenu"* — "you shall not bear sin when you raise up its best part from it." The verse implies that one bears sin when separating from inferior on superior — which presupposes that the separation was *effective*, for an ineffective act carries no sin. This teaches that even *terumah* taken from bad produce on good produce is valid *terumah*, albeit done improperly.

Applying this reasoning: if the only issue were that Rabbi Meir permits separating from yesterday's stale bread on today's fresh bread — an act that is performed sub-optimally, like taking from the lesser on the greater — one could accept that Rabbi Meir is lenient about the *lechatchila* of the *hafrasha* in cases of *demai*, so long as the act is effective. Rabbi Meir's leniency in *demai* contexts extends to procedural imperfections; what he will not tolerate is the risk of actually eating something that has not been properly separated.

The real difficulty, then, is the second element of the Mishnah: even when the loaves come from different molds (*midfusim harbeh*) — suggesting they may have been produced by entirely different farmers — Rabbi Meir still permits the separation. Here the concern is no longer procedural imperfection but the genuine risk that the *maaser* will be separated from an obligated batch onto an exempt one, rendering the separation invalid and causing the person to eat untithed produce. Why would Rabbi Meir, who we claimed is strict about eating *demai* improperly, be lenient in a case that carries precisely that risk?

The Gemara at this point does not immediately provide an answer. Instead, Abaye steps back to systematically evaluate the entire chain of questions and responses that has accumulated.

### Abaye's Review

Abaye pronounces a verdict on each prior exchange. First, Rabbi Eliezer's original question — how can our Mishnah be so strict about *terumat maaser* of *demai* as to require payment of a fifth? — was an excellent question (*shapir kakashya leh*). Second, Shmuel's answer — that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who is stringent — was not satisfactory (*lo shapir kameshani leh*). Why? Because Shmuel's proof for Rabbi Meir's stringency was the case of *gittin*, where Rabbi Meir's strict reading of divorce law leads him to consider a child a *mamzer*. But that involves a case of capital punishment by a court (*misas beis din*). Our Mishnah involves *misa bidei Shamayim* — death at Heaven's hands for eating *terumah*. These are not equivalent, and one cannot demonstrate Rabbi Meir's willingness to be strict about *misa bidei Shamayim* by citing his stringency in cases of *misa bidei adam*.

Third, Rav Sheshes's counter-challenge — attempting to prove Rabbi Meir is lenient by citing his leniency regarding *pidyon* of *maaser sheni* of *demai* — was also a poor question (*lo shapir kamosiv leh*). The leniency there involves at most a negative prohibition (*lo suchal le'echol bish'arecha*, that *maaser sheni* must be eaten in Jerusalem), which is categorically less severe than a transgression punishable by death. One cannot use a leniency in a lesser domain to disprove stringency in a capital domain.

Fourth, by contrast, once Rav Sheshes's challenge was accepted as standing, Rav Yosef's resolution was genuinely good (*shapir kameshani leh*): he distinguished between *pidyon* — a matter of *lechatchila*, of doing a procedure optimally — and actually eating something that was improperly separated, which is a true *aveirah*. This distinction pays proper attention to the different weights of the cases.

Finally, Abaye turns to Ravina's challenge from the *nachtom* Mishnah. Here Abaye argues that Ravina chose the wrong proof text. Rather than raising the difficulty from the *nachtom* case — where Rabbi Meir permits separating across different days and different molds — Ravina should have asked from the *palter* case at the end of the same Mishnah, which would have posed the problem more sharply.

### Nachtom vs. Palter

What does the end of the Mishnah say about the *palter* — the wholesale baker? It states: *"ha-lokeach min ha-palter, me'aser mikol dfus ve-dfus divrei Rabbi Meir"* — one who buys from a wholesale baker must separate *maaser* from each differently-molded loaf individually. There, Rabbi Meir is strict. The wholesale baker purchases from multiple suppliers, and Rabbi Meir therefore insists that each type of bread be treated separately, lest one separate from an obligated batch onto an exempt one.

The contrast illuminates everything. Rabbi Meir's leniency by the *nachtom* is not an expression of general leniency toward *demai*; it reflects a factual assumption. A *nachtom* — a small neighborhood baker — typically buys his grain from a single source. Even if his loaves appear in different shapes and were baked on different days, one may reasonably presume they all derive from the same farmer and carry the same *demai* status. A *palter*, by contrast, is a large-scale commercial baker who purchases from two or three different suppliers, and therefore one must treat each batch separately.

Thus, the rule: *palter mitrei tlata gavrei zavin* — a *palter* buys from multiple people, hence stringency; *nachtom nami mi-chad gavra zavin* — a *nachtom* buys from one person, hence the presumption of uniformity holds even across different days and molds. The apparent leniency of Rabbi Meir by the *nachtom* is not leniency about *demai* at all — it is simply an empirical assumption about purchasing patterns.

### Rava's Affirmation

Returning now to Abaye's critique of Shmuel's answer, Rava offers a defense of Shmuel. Abaye had argued that Shmuel's proof from *gittin* was irrelevant because it involved *misa bidei adam* rather than *misa bidei Shamayim*. Rava disagrees: *shmaya misa ba'olam* — both are death. Whether Heaven executes the punishment or a court does, death is death. The equivalence of all death is sufficient to demonstrate that Rabbi Meir's documented stringency in capital matters extends across categories — and therefore Shmuel's answer stands.

The overall conclusion of this section is as follows. The Mishnah's stringency in requiring a fifth for eating *terumat maaser* of *demai* is indeed the position of Rabbi Meir. Apparent leniencies attributed to Rabbi Meir in *demai* contexts are explained in one of two ways: either they are based on specific factual assumptions about the *nachtom* versus the *palter*, or they concern the *lechatchila* of *pidyon* — doing a procedure in a less-than-ideal manner — as opposed to the *aveirah* of eating improperly separated produce. When it comes to the latter, Rabbi Meir is strict, and the *chomesh* applies.

---

## Exclusions from Ona'ah

### Basic Exclusions

The Mishnah now introduces a new topic with the formulation *"elu devarim she'ein lahem ona'ah"* — the following things are not subject to the laws of overcharging. The list comprises four categories: *avadim* (slaves), *shtarot* (debt documents), *karka'ot* (land), and *hekdeshos* (consecrated objects).

One might initially suppose that these exclusions are based in logic — for instance, that some of these items lack a fixed market price and therefore cannot generate a measurable overcharge. Land, in particular, is subject to significant price variability, and establishing a baseline "fair price" for a particular parcel presents genuine difficulties. However, the Gemara will not ground these exclusions in any such logical reasoning. Rather, they rest on a formal derivation from a Scriptural verse, a strictly textual exclusion that stands regardless of whether a logical basis can be articulated.

Before proceeding to the Scriptural derivation, the Mishnah notes that these four categories are also excluded from a range of other laws — not only *ona'ah*. There is no *tashlumai kefel* — no double payment to the victim if these items are stolen. The Mishnah further notes that *shtarot* are excluded from the law of four-and-five-fold payment; Rashi points out that four-and-fivefold applies only to oxen and sheep, so the only case where this additional exclusion is meaningful would be *hekdesh*.

Regarding *shomrim*: a *shomer chinam* who guards these items takes no oath that he was not negligent, and a *nosei sachar* bears no financial liability even when the item was lost or stolen on his watch. This raises a subtle conceptual question, however: even if a *shomer* is exempt from the financial consequences prescribed by the laws of *shomerim*, is he still obligated in the duty of *shemirah* itself? There is a meaningful distinction between exemption from payment and exemption from the underlying responsibility to guard. If a *shomer* is still bound by a *chiyuv shemirah*, then gross negligence — leaving the object in the middle of the street, for instance — might constitute a form of direct damage (*mazik beyadayim*), and liability might attach not through the laws of *shomrim* but through the laws of *nezikin*. This question is noted as a point for further analysis.

### Rabbi Shimon Exception

Rabbi Shimon qualifies the exclusion of *hekdesh* from *ona'ah*. He distinguishes between two types of consecrated property. If one undertook a personal obligation to bring a certain sacrifice — accepting liability upon himself rather than merely designating a specific animal — then if that designated animal is lost or stolen, he must replace it from his own resources. In such a case, the animal is considered, in a meaningful sense, to be his own property, because its loss affects him directly. Accordingly, Rabbi Shimon holds that *kodshim she-hu chayav be-achrayutan* — consecrated items for which one bears responsibility — are subject to *ona'ah*. The verse that excludes *hekdesh* from *ona'ah* reads *lo tonu ish et achiv* — one man shall not wrong his fellow — implying a transaction between two ordinary people, to the exclusion of *hekdesh*. But where one's liability makes the consecrated property effectively "his own," it falls back within the category of *ish et achiv* and the laws of *ona'ah* apply. By contrast, if one consecrated an animal directly — without personal liability for its loss — the animal fully belongs to *hekdesh*, and there is no *ona'ah*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Exception

Rabbi Yehuda introduces a different kind of exception. He holds that one who sells a *sefer Torah*, livestock (*behemah*), or a precious jewel (*margalis*) is not subject to *ona'ah*. The rationale here is plainly not formalistic but practical: these are objects for which no reliable fixed price exists. A *sefer Torah*, a particular animal, or a gemstone — each is assessed differently based on quality, beauty, utility, and other factors that resist standardization. Without a reference price, there is no way to calculate whether a given transaction involved an overcharge of a sixth or more. The Sages respond: *lo amru ela elu* — only the items previously enumerated by the Mishnah are excluded; these items are *not* excluded.

### Mi-Yad L'Yad Source

Where does the Talmud derive the formal exclusions? The Gemara cites the Baraita: *"ve-chi timkeru mimkar la-amitecha o kano mi-yad amitecha"* — when you sell or buy from your fellow *mi-yad*, from the hand. The Gemara reads *mi-yad* as specifying the type of transaction to which *ona'ah* applies: specifically, something transferred from hand to hand — *davar ha-nikneh mi-yad le-yad*.

From this, land (*karka*) is excluded, since it is not *metaltelim* — it does not move from hand to hand but remains fixed in place. Even though there are forms of movable property too large or cumbersome to literally fit in a hand, the halakhic category of *metaltelim* is conceptually opposed to *karka* as a class, not physically dependent on whether the object fits in one's palm. Slaves are excluded because they are formally equated with land (*hukshu le-karka'ot*) through various Scriptural passages. Documents (*shtarot*) are excluded on a different ground: *shegufo machur ve-gufo kanuy* — *ona'ah* applies to something whose very body is what is being bought and sold. A *shtar* is not purchased for the intrinsic value of the piece of paper; the buyer seeks only the debt or right that the document represents. Since the body of the document is neither what is sold nor what is purchased — *she-ein gufan machur ve-ein gufan kanuy* — it is not subject to *ona'ah*. As the Baraita further states, documents exist only as instruments of proof (*ve-einam omdim ela lera'ayah she-bahem*), not as ends in themselves.

Tosafot raises an important technical question in connection with this exclusion. There is a sugya in the Gemara questioning whether the sale of debt (*mechiras shtar*) takes effect at the Torah level or only rabbinically. If the sale of debt operates only by rabbinic enactment, one might wonder why Scriptural exclusion is even needed. Tosafot resolves this by constructing a scenario in which the *shtar* itself — rather than the underlying debt — is what is being sold. For example: if a loan has already been made, the lender might wish to commission a *shtar* as proof of that loan, paying the borrower to write one. Here the *shtar* is purchased not to transfer a debt but purely as an evidentiary instrument. One might analogously imagine paying a landowner to rewrite a deed of land that was already transferred. In this scenario one wonders: if the function of the *shtar* is to serve as proof, and one is purchasing it specifically to serve that function, why is that not considered *gufo mamon* — intrinsic value? The answer, suggested in discussion, is that a *shtar* as an instrument of proof has no objective, transferable value — it is useful only to the specific holder in the specific context of the existing legal relationship.

The Gemara appends a corollary: *"ha-mocher shtarotav lerokcham"* — if one sells documents to a perfumer who will use them to stopper his small perfume bottles, then there *is* *ona'ah*. In that case, the paper is being purchased purely for its physical properties — as a material — and therefore has genuine intrinsic value. Indeed, the Gemara's rhetorical question elsewhere, *"ve-chi la'atzor pi tzluchito hu ba'ei?"* — "does he want it merely to stop up his bottles?" — is actually borrowed from this passage. The Gemara notes that this is not obvious but is needed to counter Rav Kahana's principle that anything worth less than a *perutah* is not subject to *ona'ah*. Here, even though documents sold as scraps of paper may be worth only pennies, there is still *ona'ah* from them since they are being treated as objects of intrinsic value.

Finally, the exclusion of *hekdesh* is derived from the word *achicha* — "your fellow" — which implies a transaction between two private individuals, thereby excluding that which belongs to the Temple treasury.

### Land Exclusion

The formal exclusion of land is subjected to a sharp challenge by Rabbah bar Mari. He observes that if we derive the exclusion from the word *yad* — hand — on the grounds that *ona'ah* applies only to things that can be transferred hand to hand, this depends on reading *yad* literally. But is *yad* always literal? He cites the verse *"va-yikach et kol artzo mi-yado"* — "he took all his land from his hand" — where *yad* clearly cannot mean a physical hand, since land cannot be held in one's hand. It must mean *reshus* — domain, or control.

The Gemara responds with two proof-texts demonstrating that *yad* is indeed presumed to be literal in halachic *midrash*, unless context compels otherwise. The Baraita on theft states: *"im himatzei timatzei be-yado ha-gneivah"* — if the stolen item is found *in his hand*. The Gemara asks: does this mean literally in his hand? How do we know to include one's roof, courtyard, or enclosed field (*gago, chatzeiro, ve-karpifo*)? Only from the doubled language *"himatzei timatzei"*, which extends beyond the literal. The implication is that without that doubling, *yad* would have been read literally. Similarly, by *gittin*, the verse *"ve-natan be-yadah"* — he shall place a *get* in her hand — is expanded to include her courtyard or roof only by the extra word *"ve-natan"*, which signals broader application. In the absence of such expansion, *yad* is literal.

The Gemara therefore concludes: the reading of *yad* as literal hand is the default presumption of halachic interpretation. Only when a verse makes literal reading impossible — as in *"va-yikach et kol artzo mi-yado"*, where land simply cannot fit in a hand — does the word shift to meaning *reshus* or control. Where a literal reading is coherent, as in the verse discussing *ona'ah*, *yad* means *yad mamash* — literal hand — and land is therefore excluded.

This is, as the lecturer notes, a genuinely striking result. The Torah's own discussion of *ona'ah* is embedded in the context of the sale of land — specifically the counting of years until the *Yovel* and the pricing of produce accordingly. And yet the Rabbis deploy a textual argument from the word *mi-yad* to formally exclude the very category of transaction the Torah appears to be discussing. The exemption for land from *ona'ah* is not derived from economic logic — though such logic may be suggested — but from a rigorous and in some ways ironic piece of textual reasoning.

---

## Scope of Ona'ah

### Rentals & Ona'ah

Rabbi Zeira poses a focused question: does *ona'ah* apply to *sechirus* — the renting of property? The specific concern is about renting movable property, since we have already established that land is excluded. If I rent you my car at an inflated price, is that a transgression of *ona'ah*? The initial framing presents the issue as one of category: does the verse's reference to *mimkar* — a sale — encompass only permanent transfers of ownership, or might it also cover transactions that are more temporary in nature?

### Temporary Sale Theory

Abaye answers with a conceptual observation. He notes that the verse does not write *"mimkar le'olam"* — a permanent sale. It says *"mimkar"* simply, without qualification. And a rental, Abaye argues, is a sale for the duration — *be-yomei mechira hu*, it is a sale for that day or period. This reflects a broader halakhic understanding articulated by the Rambam elsewhere: a rental constitutes *kinyan ha-guf le-peiros le-zman* — acquisition of the body of the object for the purpose of its use, for a limited time. The renter does not acquire the right to sell the object, but he does acquire title to its use for the rental period. It is, in conceptual terms, a temporary sale rather than a license or permission. On this analysis, since *ona'ah* governs sales and a rental is a form of sale, *ona'ah* applies.

Tosafot notes a complication: it is not self-evident across all areas of *halacha* that *sechirus* is treated as a temporary sale. The question is whether Abaye's principle here is a general one or is limited to the context of *ona'ah*. The language of the Gemara, however, sounds like a general statement about the nature of rental.

### Seeds in Land

Rava poses a question that sits at the intersection of the preceding discussions: *"chitin u-zra'an be-karka, mahu?"* — what is the law regarding wheat seeds that have been planted in the ground? Are they subject to *ona'ah*? The inquiry is specifically about the status of the seeds themselves — not the land. Before the seeds take root, do they retain the character of *metaltelim* — chattel subject to *ona'ah* — or do they take on the character of land and fall outside it?

### Mekach Taut Issue

Before formulating the precise question, the Gemara considers and eliminates a simpler case. Suppose a laborer contracted to seed a field with six units of grain, but witnesses testify that he planted only five. Is this a case of *ona'ah*? The Gemara rejects this framing: it is not *ona'ah* at all, but *mekach ta'ut* — a flawed transaction based on misrepresentation. Rava had established the principle that *kol davar she-be-midah u-ve-mishkal u-ve-minyan* — anything sold by measure, weight, or count — is subject to reversion even if the discrepancy falls below the threshold of *ona'ah*, because misrepresenting a quantifiable unit is not overcharging but misidentifying what was sold. This applies equally to land: if one claims to sell three acres and delivers 2.9, that is *mekach ta'ut*, not *ona'ah*, and is unaffected by the exclusion of *karka* from *ona'ah*.

### Seeding Adequacy

The Gemara therefore reformulates the question. The case is: the laborer claimed to have seeded the field as required — with the appropriate amount for that plot — and it later emerged that he had not seeded it sufficiently. Here there is no factual misrepresentation of quantity in the simple sense; the dispute concerns whether the work performed met the agreed standard.

Now the conceptual question comes into focus. Tosafot explains why the Gemara does not pose an even simpler case — e.g., I contracted to sell you six units of seeds for ten units of currency, planted them in your land, and it turns out the price was inflated. In that case, Tosafot argues, it would be obvious that *ona'ah* applies, because one is fundamentally paying for the seeds, and the fact that they happen to be in the land is incidental. But in the case of seeding adequacy, the payment is conceptually for what one does *to the land* — for the improvement of the land through appropriate seeding. The question then becomes: is this dispute about the land (in which case there is no *ona'ah*) or about the seeds (in which case *ona'ah* may apply)? One might conceptualize either that the obligation was to improve the land in a certain way and the failure to do so is a land-related issue, or that the shortfall was in the amount of seeds deployed and is therefore a seed-related — i.e., chattel-related — issue. The Gemara leaves the question open.

### Oaths & Batul

The same conceptual tension generates a parallel question regarding oaths. Among the laws excluded from *shtarot*, *avadim*, and *karka* is the obligation of the *shomer* to take an oath; the same exclusion presumably extends to seeds that might be *batel* to land. Rashi's example: I entrusted you with six units of seeds to plant in my land, and you planted only five and a half. I claim you still owe me a full unit; you admit to owing half a unit. This looks like *modeh be-miktzat* — partial admission — which ordinarily obligates the defendant to take a *shevuat modeh be-miktzat*. But the question is whether what we are really disputing is the seeds (in which case there is a *shevuah*) or the planting obligation — which is framed in terms of what was done to the land (in which case the seeds may be *batel* to the *karka*, and no *shevuah* is taken). The question also remains unresolved.

### Omer & Replanted Seeds

The third case raised in this sugya involves the *omer* and seeds that have been replanted. The *omer* offering on the sixteenth of Nisan renders permissible the new grain crop. The Mishnah already rules: *"im hishrishu kodem ha-omer, omer matiran"* — if seeds took root before the *omer* was brought, the *omer* renders the resulting crop permitted; if they had not taken root by then, they must await the following year's *omer*.

But the Gemara identifies a case not covered by that Mishnah. Suppose seeds were cut from last year's harvest — after that year's *omer* had already rendered them permitted — and therefore they could legitimately be eaten. Then the owner planted them in the ground before this year's *omer*. Then the *omer* came and passed, but the seeds had not yet taken root. Now the owner wants to remove the seeds from the ground and eat them. May he?

The question is this: since the seeds were already permitted by last year's *omer*, are they still to be treated as last year's permitted grain — like produce sitting in a bowl that never lost its permitted status? In that case, their brief sojourn in the ground changes nothing, and they may be eaten freely. Or perhaps, by placing them in the ground, they became *batel* to the *karka* and took on the character of this year's crop — new grain that requires the current year's *omer* for its permissibility. Since this year's *omer* passed before they took root, they would need to wait for the following year's *omer*.

The Gemara does not resolve this question either, concluding with *"teiku."*

---

---

# Bava Metzia 57

## Chadash & Omer

### Seeds in Land

Before advancing to the new material on 57a, a brief clarification of the previous day's discussion is in order. The *mishnah* enumerates categories excluded from the laws of *ona'ah* and *shemirah*, and yesterday's focus was on *karka* — land — and its associated *halachos* concerning *ona'ah* and *shevua*. The final case examined involved *chadash* and the *omer*, but it was misread. The correct scenario is as follows.

You cut your harvest before the second day of *Pesach*. Had you left the grain sitting in storage — in your cabinet or jars — the arrival of the second day of *Pesach* would render it permitted through the *omer*. Instead, you placed the grain back into the ground, where it has not yet taken root. The question then is: when the second day of *Pesach* arrives, does the *omer* permit this grain? Is the grain treated simply as grain-in-storage — in which case the *omer* would apply — or has placing it in the ground transformed its status, such that it is now treated as part of the land itself? If the latter, the *omer* would no longer have any bearing on it, and if one were to scoop it out of the ground and eat it immediately after the *omer*, there would be no *heter* for doing so.

To be clear: what grows *afterwards* is obviously a separate matter — that grain has not yet been subject to the *omer* at all. The question is specifically about the grain already in the ground at the time the *omer* arrives. Can one scoop it out and eat it? That was yesterday's case.

---

## Ona'ah vs Bitul Mekach

### Rabbi Ami's Question

Three lines from the top of 57a, the *Gemara* introduces the teaching of Rava in the name of Rav Chasa: *bei'i Rabbi Ami* — Rabbi Ami posed the following question. The *mishnah* established that *ona'ah* does not apply to land, slaves, *shtarot*, and *hekdesh*. But what about *bitul mekach*? Does the voiding of a sale apply to these categories or not?

To appreciate the question, one must recall the structure of *ona'ah*. The *Torah* prohibits overcharging, and the Rabbis determined — drawing on their own judgment, as the *Torah* entrusted such determinations to the Sages — that a one-sixth discrepancy constitutes the threshold for *ona'ah*. Beyond that, the assumption is that so great a disproportion between price and value amounts to a voided transaction. There is, as was noted in an earlier discussion, a certain irony here: the *greater* the overcharge, the more options the seller has, since he too may void the sale. This suggests conceptually that *bitul mekach* may belong to an entirely different legal category.

Thus the question: even if the *Torah*'s specific laws of *ona'ah* do not apply to land, slaves, *shtarot*, and *hekdesh*, perhaps *bitul mekach* — which is less a law of overcharging than a recognition that a grossly disproportionate transaction simply was never a valid sale — does apply. If I sell you the wrong thing, or a fundamentally different thing from what you bargained for, *bitul mekach* would seem to operate regardless of whether the technical *halachos* of *ona'ah* apply. The exemption from *ona'ah* might speak only to moderate overcharges, not to transactions so disproportionate that they were never genuinely agreed to.

Now, the difference between one-sixth and just-over-one-sixth is admittedly not dramatic. But perhaps if the overcharge is double the value — charging 200 for something worth 100 — there is no need to invoke the special *halachos* of *ona'ah* at all. That is simply a voided sale, objectively. The *Gemara* then answers the question: Rabbi Ami himself resolved it. The *Gemara* records that Rav Nachman stated, citing Rav Chasa, that Rabbi Ami concluded — *ona'ah ein lahem, bitul mekach yesh lahem* — the laws of *ona'ah* do not apply to these categories, but *bitul mekach* does. Only the specific *halachos* of overcharging are set aside; an outright voided sale based on gross disproportion remains operative.

### Tosafot on Ona'ah

Before proceeding, it is worth examining Tosafot's reinterpretation of the *Gemara*. Tosafot notes that it *appears* Rav Nachman agrees with Rav Chisda and Rav Pappa that *bitul mekach* applies to *karka*. However, Tosafot raises a difficulty from a later section of Bava Metzia — in the chapter of *ha-mekabbel* — where a case is described of selling for 200 what is worth 100, and Rav Nachman states explicitly: *ein ona'ah le-karka'os*, no *ona'ah* applies to land. The clear implication is that even so extreme an overcharge does not constitute *bitul mekach* with respect to *karka*. This appears to directly contradict the reading that Rav Nachman endorses *bitul mekach* for these categories.

Rabbeinu Tam resolves the difficulty with a significant reinterpretation: when the *Gemara* says *ein ona'ah*, it does not mean merely that a one-sixth overcharge is set aside. It means that the exemption from the laws of *ona'ah* extends all the way up to — and including — double the value. So if something is worth 100, charging up to 200 falls within the scope of *ein ona'ah*. Where does this limit of double come from? From the very case mentioned: *zavin be-reish ve-shavei be-me'ah*, sold for 200 and worth 100 — that is *palga*, half the price, i.e., the full doubling. More than double the value — that is what the *Gemara* means by *bitul mekach yesh lahem*. Only when the overcharge exceeds 100% does *bitul mekach* apply even to these categories.

This is admittedly not the straightforward reading of the *Gemara*, whose plain sense is that *bitul mekach* kicks in as soon as the overcharge exceeds one-sixth, just as with ordinary sales. But one can understand what motivates Rabbeinu Tam. It is hard to see how a one-fifth overcharge is so qualitatively different — so radical a departure from a legitimate transaction — that it would constitute *bitul mekach* applicable even to categories that are otherwise exempt from *ona'ah*. Doubling the price is a different matter; there the objective disproportion speaks for itself.

### Rav Nachman

The *Gemara* states clearly that the conclusion transmitted through Rav Chasa — in the name of Rabbi Ami — is *ona'ah ein lahem, bitul mekach yesh lahem*: these categories are exempt from the laws of *ona'ah*, but the voiding of the sale does apply to them.

### Yona & Yirmiya

The *Gemara* then introduces two parallel transmissions in the name of Rabbi Yochanan. Rav Yona stated this rule with reference to *hekdeshos*, and Rabbi Yirmiyah stated it with reference to *karka'os* — and both transmitted it in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ona'ah ein lahem, bitul mekach yesh lahem*. The plain reading of the *Gemara*, as noted, is that *bitul mekach* applies as soon as the overcharge exceeds one-sixth. According to Tosafot, only when the overcharge exceeds 100%.

---

## Land vs Hekdesh

### Bitul Mekach Scope

Having established that both Rav Yona and Rabbi Yirmiyah said the same thing in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — yet one applied it to *hekdeshos* and the other to *karka'os* — the *Gemara* asks whether this reflects a genuine disagreement. The two categories in the *mishnah* are conceptually quite distinct. One set — *karka*, *avadim*, *shtarot* — is defined by the type of object. The other — *hekdesh* — is not a type of object but a *status* of an object, and it is perhaps better understood as defining the counterparty in the transaction, derived from the verse *achiv o rei'ehu* — one is not doing business with a fellow person but with *hekdesh*.

The *Gemara* resolves the question by noting that the two opinions are not equivalent. The one who said *bitul mekach* applies to *hekdeshos* would certainly agree it applies *kol she-ken* to *karka'os* — the argument for *bitul mekach* is if anything stronger there. But the one who stated the rule only regarding *karka'os* may well hold that *hekdesh* is different — that even gross disproportion does not result in *bitul mekach* by *hekdesh*. Why? Because of Shmuel's teaching: *hekdesh shaveh maneh she-chillelo al shaveh perutah mechullal* — even if *hekdesh* worth a hundred *zuz* is redeemed onto something worth a single *perutah*, the redemption is valid. Since even a grossly disproportionate transfer works by *hekdesh*, there can be no *bitul mekach* — no voiding of the transaction — on grounds of disproportion.

### Rashi on Hekdesh

Rashi explains the rationale behind *hekdesh*'s exemption from *bitul mekach* as follows: no party can truly deceive *hekdesh*, because God is omniscient. When one overcharges a human seller or buyer, the deception operates on a person who could not have agreed had he known the true state of affairs — thus there was no genuine meeting of minds, and the sale is void. But with *hekdesh*, there is no other conscious party to be deceived. God knows what is being done, and therefore the premise that underlies *bitul mekach* — that the other side was misled into a transaction it would never have agreed to — does not apply.

### Kedusha & Pidyon

There is, however, a deeper way to understand why *hekdesh* is different, one that goes beyond Rashi's framing. The key question is whether one thinks of *hekdesh* primarily as an *ownership* entity — like any other institutional property-owner who happens to be the *Beit HaMikdash* — or as a *status*. If *hekdesh* is simply a property-owner, then dealing with its assets is formally similar to dealing with any other party, even if the *Gizbar* (Temple treasurer) rather than a private individual manages the account. If so, the *Gizbar* could theoretically be deceived, or could himself deceive others — which would put pressure on whether *bitul mekach* ought to apply.

But there is a different way to frame *hekdesh*: not as ownership, but as *kedusha* — a sanctified status embedded in the object. Under this view, my car donated to the *Beit HaMikdash* is not simply transferred into an institutional account; it is filled with *kedusha*. Misusing it triggers *me'ilah*. And when I "redeem" it, I am not buying it back from *hekdesh* for a *perutah*. I am *transferring the status of kedusha* from one object to another. That is why Shmuel's teaching makes sense: because I am not buying a thousand-dollar item for a penny, I am relocating *kedusha* from one address to another, and so long as the *kedusha* has a valid destination, the transaction is complete. It is not a *mekach* at all — it is a *pidyon*, a formal transfer of *kedusha* — and therefore the categories of *ona'ah* and *bitul mekach*, which apply to commercial transactions, simply do not engage.

Both framings may in fact be simultaneously true: *hekdesh* is owned by the *Beit HaMikdash* (the *ownership* dimension), and the object possesses *kedusha* (the *status* dimension). The *halacha* may depend on which dimension is operative in a given transaction. When the *Gizbar* picks up a donated car and sells it to a buyer, with the proceeds acquiring *kedusha* and the buyer getting the car — that looks much more like an ordinary *mekach u'memkar*, an ordinary sale. In that case, one might have expected *bitul mekach* to apply. The *Gemara* does not fully unpack all of these distinctions, but establishes the principle that *hekdesh* may well be categorically exempt from *bitul mekach* — whether because there is no party to be deceived (Rashi's framing), or because the transaction can be understood as a *pidyon*, a transfer of *kedusha*, rather than a commercial sale.

---

## Hekdesh Redemption

### Blemished Animals

The *Gemara* now introduces a *mishnah* from *Temurah*: if an animal designated as *hekdesh* has a blemish and is redeemed, it passes to *chulin* — non-sacred status — but *tzarich la'asot lo damim*, an accounting must be done. If the animal used in the redemption is worth more than the original consecrated animal, the extra constitutes an additional donation to the *Beit HaMikdash*. But if the redeeming animal is worth *less*, the difference must be made up. The formula *tzarich la'asot lo damim* demands that equivalent value be provided. The relevant background is that Rashi explains the language involved was not *zu tachat zu* (the language of *temurah*, of exchange) but *zu mechulelet al zu* — "let this be redeemed upon this" — which is the language of *pidyon*, allowing a *blemished* consecrated animal to be redeemed even upon another animal, not only upon money.

### Value Equivalence

Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree about the weight of this accounting requirement. Rabbi Yochanan holds: *yatza le-chulin devar Torah* — the redemption takes full effect at the biblical level as soon as any transfer is made, regardless of whether the values are equivalent. The requirement to supply the difference in value — *tzarich la'asot lo damim* — is only *mi-derabanan*, rabbinic. Reish Lakish disagrees: even *min ha-Torah*, the redemption is not complete until the full equivalent value is provided.

### Gemara Challenge

The *Gemara* now raises a challenge. If the case under dispute involves a discrepancy within the *ona'ah* range — one-sixth or less — one would never say that Reish Lakish requires making up that difference at a biblical level. For the *mishnah* itself establishes *hekdesh ein lo ona'ah* — the laws of *ona'ah* do not apply to *hekdesh*. If that means anything, it means that a discrepancy of up to one-sixth is entirely acceptable and creates no obligation of any kind. It would be absurd for Reish Lakish to demand biblical-level restitution in a case that the *mishnah* tells us doesn't trigger even the standard laws of *ona'ah*. (Tosafot adds parenthetically that if animal one was worth a thousand and animal two worth eight hundred, according to Reish Lakish, eight hundred of the original animal is redeemed on animal two, and the remaining two hundred must be supplemented separately — the redemption is partial, not entirely void.)

Therefore the *Gemara* concludes that the dispute must be about a discrepancy in the range of *bitul mekach* — more than one-sixth (or, according to Tosafot, more than double). The question then becomes: does the concept of *bitul mekach* apply to *hekdesh*, and if so, what are its consequences?

The difficulty now turns back on Rabbi Yochanan. Rav Yona transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that *hekdesh* does have *bitul mekach*. If that is so, how can Rabbi Yochanan also hold that the redemption works at the biblical level even when the disproportion is in the *bitul mekach* range — with only a rabbinic requirement to supply the difference? If there is *bitul mekach*, the transaction should not be fundamentally valid, either in full or in part.

At this stage, Tosafot raises an illuminating point. Normally, *bitul mekach* is designed to protect an aggrieved party from being locked into a grossly unfair transaction — especially once the other side has taken the object and disappeared. But with *hekdesh*, that concern does not arise in the same way. *Hekdesh* is always present; *kedusha* is always operative. If two hundred dollars' worth of the original cow remains unredeemed, the *me'ilah* prohibition remains in place on that portion. *Hekdesh* cannot be cheated and left with no recourse. Therefore, Tosafot suggests, *bitul mekach* by *hekdesh* need not mean the transaction is entirely void and must start from scratch. It can mean instead that the redemption is *incomplete* — it proceeds as far as the value supplied, and the remainder awaits further payment. The protections *bitul mekach* is designed to provide are achieved through the ongoing *me'ilah* liability, without needing to unwind the transaction entirely.

### Positions Reversed

Given this difficulty — that Rabbi Yochanan's position (as transmitted by Rav Yona) implies *bitul mekach* applies to *hekdesh*, yet Rabbi Yochanan apparently holds the redemption is fundamentally valid *de-oraisa* — the *Gemara* resolves the tension by reversing the attributions: *ve-ipoch*, switch the positions. What was attributed to Rabbi Yochanan is actually Reish Lakish's position, and vice versa. Under this reversal, it is Rabbi Yochanan who holds — consistent with Rav Yona's transmission — that *bitul mekach* applies to *hekdesh*, meaning the redemption is not complete until the full equivalent value is provided. And Reish Lakish holds there is no *bitul mekach* by *hekdesh*, so even a grossly disproportionate redemption is fundamentally valid *de-oraisa*.

The *Gemara* identifies the underlying substantive disagreement: *mar is lei de-Shmuel, mar leis lei de-Shmuel* — one authority holds of Shmuel's teaching and the other does not. Shmuel held that *hekdesh* worth a *maneh* that was redeemed on something worth a single *perutah* is validly redeemed. If one holds of this teaching, one holds there is no *bitul mekach* by *hekdesh* — even extreme disproportion does not invalidate the transaction. If one rejects Shmuel's teaching in this context, one holds that *bitul mekach* does apply, and an incomplete redemption remains incomplete until the balance is supplied. The debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish (now in their reversed positions) is thus a debate about whether to accept Shmuel's ruling.

### Intentionality

The *Gemara* then offers a second way of understanding the dispute: *ei ba'is eima*, perhaps both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish accept Shmuel's teaching in principle — that a *perutah* can redeem *hekdesh* worth a *maneh* — and their debate is not about whether Shmuel's rule holds, but about whether it applies *le-chatchila*.

One view holds that while the redemption works *be-di'eved*, it may not be done *le-chatchila*: one is not supposed to redeem a thousand-dollar sanctified object onto an eight-hundred-dollar animal while knowing the values differ. If one did so intending an equivalent exchange, the redemption is not complete until the balance is paid — this is understood as a *de-oraisa* *le-chatchila* obligation. The other view holds that even *le-chatchila*, a disproportionate redemption is permissible.

Tosafot objects to this framing on two grounds. First, there is a moral difficulty: what does it mean to say one may *le-chatchila* shortchange *hekdesh*? Second, the more lenient opinion already holds that *mi-derabanan* one must pay the remaining two hundred — so in what sense is *le-chatchila* being said to be permitted?

Tosafot therefore reinterprets *le-chatchila* not as a question of permission but as a question of *intentionality*. The distinction is between two mental frames: when someone *knowingly* redeems a thousand-dollar object onto a penny — fully aware of the disproportion, deliberately framing the act as a *pidyon*, a transfer of *kedusha* — the redemption works. That is Shmuel's case. But when someone exchanges cow-one for cow-two genuinely *intending* an equivalent exchange, thinking both animals are worth the same, then that person is not performing a *pidyon* — they are attempting a *mekach*, a commercial transaction. And when the transaction is framed as a *mekach*, the rules of equivalent exchange apply, and it is not complete until full value is provided.

This ties back to the fundamental conceptual framework. If one is consciously transferring *kedusha* — aware of the disproportion and choosing to frame the act as a *pidyon* — the *kedusha* transfers because that is all that *pidyon* requires. But if one is genuinely trying to do an equivalent exchange with *hekdesh*, treating it as a commercial counterparty, then *bitul mekach* may apply, and Rabbi Yochanan's position is that the exchange is not fully consummated until true equivalence is achieved. This is what the *Gemara* means, in Tosafot's reading, by the *le-chatchila/be-di'eved* distinction — not a question of what is permitted, but a question of what framework governs based on what the party was consciously trying to accomplish.

---

## Rav Chisda Stringency

### No Limit for Hekdesh

The *Gemara* now introduces yet another way of understanding the *mishnah*'s statement *ein lahem ona'ah* with respect to *hekdesh*, proposed by Rav Chisda. This interpretation is a striking one. Rav Chisda holds that *einam be-torat ona'ah* — they are not governed by the *laws* of *ona'ah*. But this does not mean they enjoy a *leniency*. It means *l'chumra*: that the protections of *ona'ah* do not apply because something far stricter governs. Even an overcharge of *less* than one-sixth must be returned when dealing with *hekdesh*. *De-afilu pachot mi-khdei ona'ah chozer* — even below the usual threshold, the difference must be repaid.

The practical asymmetry is stark. If *you* overcharge *hekdesh* even slightly, you must return the difference. The house always wins — *yad hekdesh al ha-elyona*. This reinterpretation means that the *mishnah*'s inclusion of *hekdesh* in the list of *ein lahem ona'ah* carries the opposite implication from the other items on the list. For *karka*, *avadim*, and *shtarot*, exclusion from *ona'ah* means the ordinary protections don't apply and parties may be overcharged without consequence. For *hekdesh*, exclusion from *ona'ah* means the ordinary ceiling of one-sixth doesn't apply as a *floor* — even a penny of overcharge must be returned. As was noted regarding similar exclusions in *Bava Kamma*, when the *Torah* says a law doesn't apply to *hekdesh*, it sometimes means the ordinary limitation is removed in *hekdesh*'s favor, not that *hekdesh* is disadvantaged.

This is admittedly a very difficult reading of the *mishnah*. The plain sense of *ein lahem ona'ah* as applied to *hekdesh* would suggest the same leniency as for the other categories on the list. But this reading is driven by the desire to protect *hekdesh*'s interests — a motivation that recurs throughout the *Gemara*'s treatment of this topic.

### Braita Comparison

A *braita* is then introduced: *ribbit ve-ona'ah le-hedyot, ve-ein ribbit ve-ona'ah le-hekdesh* — the laws of *ribbit* and *ona'ah* apply to a commoner but not to *hekdesh*. At first glance, this sounds identical to the *mishnah*, and the *Gemara* asks: is this *braita* any stronger a proof against Rav Chisda than the *mishnah* itself? The answer is no — *mi alima mi-matnitin*? — it is no more authoritative. Just as we reinterpreted the *mishnah* to mean not that *hekdesh* is exempt but that the ordinary *thresholds* don't apply (with even small amounts requiring restitution), we can reinterpret the *braita* in the same fashion: *ein ribbit ve-ona'ah* means the ordinary rules of *ribbit* and *ona'ah* — with their specific limitations and exemptions — don't apply to *hekdesh*, because *hekdesh* is governed by stricter rules.

### Obvious Strictness

The *Gemara* raises an objection to this reading. The *braita* concludes: *ve-zeh chomer be-hedyot mi-be-hekdesh* — and this is a stringency of the commoner over *hekdesh*. That phrase makes sense only if there is genuinely a way in which the laws as applied to commoners are *stricter* than those applied to *hekdesh*. Under the reinterpretation, however, *hekdesh* is in fact stricter in the domain of *ona'ah*, which would call for an additional clause: *ve-zeh chomer be-hekdesh mi-be-hedyot* — and this is a stringency of *hekdesh* over the commoner. Why doesn't the *braita* say that?

The *Gemara* responds: *hachi hashta* — this is no difficulty. The *braita*'s purpose is to highlight the one unusual case where the *commoner* is stricter. That *hekdesh* is generally stricter needs no statement — it is self-evident. But the *ribbit* case, where the ordinary laws apply to a commoner but not to *hekdesh*, represents the rare reversal, and that is worth singling out. To add a clause noting that *hekdesh* is stricter by *ona'ah* would be unremarkable — of course *hekdesh* is stricter. The *braita* is teaching us the one surprising exception where the commoner's law is more demanding, not cataloguing all the ways *hekdesh* is the harder standard.

This remains, however, a radical reinterpretation of both the *mishnah* and the *braita*. The plain sense of the text places *hekdesh* in the *leniency* column along with *karka*, *avadim*, and *shtarot*. The reinterpretation restructures the entire passage to protect *hekdesh*'s interests.

---

## Ribbit & Hekdesh

### Lending Scenario

The *Gemara* now asks: *ribbit de-hekdesh heichi dami* — what would be a case of *ribbit* applying or not applying to *hekdesh*? The hypothetical suggested is: what if the *gizbar* lent out a hundred dollars from *hekdesh* funds, to be repaid at a hundred and twenty?

This raises an immediate problem, however. The money in the Temple treasury carries *kedusha*. Using consecrated funds for a loan — placing them in private hands without any sanctified object receiving the *kedusha* in return — constitutes *me'ilah*, the prohibited misuse of consecrated property. There is nothing for the *kedusha* to transfer to in a loan transaction, unlike when *hekdesh* funds are used to purchase building materials (where the *kedusha* transfers to the purchased object) or to pay workers after the fact (where the *kedusha* conceptually transfers to the enhanced value of the work done). A simple cash loan leaves the *kedusha* nowhere to go.

### Gizbar Me'ilah

The *Gemara* therefore states: *ve-keivan de-ma'al gizbar, yatzu ma'osav le-chulin, de-havei lei hedyot* — once the *gizbar* commits *me'ilah* by lending out the funds, the money loses its *kedusha* and passes to *chulin* status. At that point it is effectively treated as ordinary (*hedyot*) money, and the normal laws of *ribbit* would apply to any subsequent loan transaction. The scenario dissolves the *hekdesh* status before any interest question arises.

One might ask: even after *me'ilah* removes the *kedusha*, doesn't the *Beit HaMikdash* still *own* the money? And if *hekdesh* is an ownership entity, might the laws applicable to *hekdesh*-owned property — including the *ribbit* exemption — continue to apply even absent *kedusha*? This is precisely the status-versus-ownership question that has run throughout this discussion. At this stage the *Gemara* assumes that once the money is lent out and taken possession of by the borrower, it simultaneously loses both its *kedusha* and its connection to *hekdesh* ownership. The borrower's act of acquisition severs both dimensions at once, and the remaining transaction is governed by ordinary *ribbit* law.

### Flour Contract

Rav Hoshaya offers a viable scenario for how *ribbit* could implicate *hekdesh* without a *me'ilah* problem. The case involves a supplier who contracts with *hekdesh* to supply flour for *menachos* at the going rate of four *se'ah* per unit of currency. The supplier is paid upfront. When the time comes to deliver, the price of flour has risen, so that the going rate is now three *se'ah* per unit. The supplier, having received payment at the four-per-unit rate, now delivers four thousand *se'ah* — but at current prices, *hekdesh*'s payment would have bought only three thousand. *Hekdesh* effectively receives more flour than its money was worth at the time of delivery. This raises a *ribbit*-like concern: is the supplier's delivery of extra units (relative to current market value) a form of prohibited interest on the advance payment received?

The *braita* cited rules that *yad hekdesh al ha-elyona* — *hekdesh* always gets the better rate. Whether prices rose or fell, the supplier must supply at whichever rate benefits *hekdesh*. This is precisely the context in which the question of *ribbit* applied or not applied to *hekdesh* is relevant — and this scenario involves no *me'ilah*, since the transaction concerned is a supply contract, not a cash loan.

### Building Stones

Rav Pappa offers a second scenario that directly illuminates the status-versus-ownership framework. He describes *avnei binyan ha-mesuros le-gizbar* — building stones that have been handed over to the *gizbar* but which have not yet been formally consecrated. This is precisely the case of *hekdesh* owning something without that thing possessing *kedusha*. As Shmuel taught: *bonin be-chol ve-achar kach makdishin* — one builds in ordinary (*chol*) status and only afterward consecrates the completed structure. This practice exists for good reason: a large stone sitting in a quarry awaiting use is likely to be casually leaned upon or used by passersby; if it already had *kedusha*, every such contact would constitute *me'ilah*. The solution is to donate the stone to the *Beit HaMikdash* without yet making it *kadosh*, allow it to be incorporated into the building, and then consecrate the completed structure.

In such a case, *hekdesh* owns the stones without their having any *kedusha*. The *gizbar* can therefore lend them out — effectively loan five stones and receive six in return — without any *me'ilah* issue, since there is no *kedusha* to be violated. And since the transaction is with *hekdesh*, the laws of *ribbit* may not apply. This neatly separates the two dimensions of *hekdesh*: ownership without sanctity, showing that both can exist independently.

---

## Other Exclusions

### Kefel Exclusions

The *Gemara* now works through a series of additional exclusions, moving at considerable speed. It states that there is no *kefel* — no double payment — for theft of *karka*, *avadim*, *shtarot*, or *hekdesh*. The source is derived hermeneutically. The relevant *pesukim* employ the structure of *klal u-frat u-klal* — a general statement, followed by specifics, followed by a return to the general. The specifics — *shor, chamor, seh, salma* — define the scope: *davar ha-mitaltel ve-gufo mamon*, movable property with intrinsic value. Anything that does not fit this profile is excluded. *Karka'os* are excluded because they are not movable; *avadim* are linked to *karka* by rabbinic tradition; *shtarot*, though physically movable, lack intrinsic value — their worth lies in the debt they evidence, not in the paper itself; and *hekdesh* is excluded by the word *rei'ehu* — "his fellow" — which excludes *hekdesh* as a counterparty.

The *Gemara* further notes that since *hekdesh* is excluded from *kefel*, it is likewise excluded from the four-and-five payment (*tashlumei arba'ah va-chamishah*) applicable to one who steals and slaughters or sells a *shor* or *seh*. The reasoning is straightforward: the four-and-five consists of the base value plus *kefel* plus the additional payment; once *kefel* is removed, only the base value and the additional payment remain — yielding three-and-four — a combination that has no independent *halachic* standing. Exclusion from *kefel* thus entails exclusion from four-and-five.

### Shomer Chinam

The *Gemara* next derives that a *shomer chinam* — an unpaid watchman — takes no *shevua* with respect to these categories. The derivation again proceeds by *klal u-frat u-klal*: the verse *ki yiten ish el rei'ehu* — "when a man gives to his fellow" — is a general; *kesef o kelim* — silver or utensils — is the specific; and a subsequent phrase returns to the general. The *prat* again defines the scope as movable property with intrinsic value. *Karka'os* are excluded as non-movable; *avadim* as linked to *karka*; *shtarot* as lacking intrinsic value; and *hekdesh* by the word *rei'ehu* — one gives to one's fellow, not to *hekdesh*.

### Shomer Sachar

The same analysis is applied to the *shomer sachar* — the paid watchman — who is likewise not obligated to pay for theft or loss of these categories. A third set of *pesukim* employs the same *klal-frat-klal* structure: *ki yiten ish el rei'ehu* as the general, *chamor o shor o seh* as the specific, *ve-chol beheimah lishmor* as the return to the general. The same derivations follow: *karka'os*, *avadim*, *shtarot*, and *hekdesh* are all excluded, each for the same reason as before.

### Negligence Liability

Before concluding, Tosafot on the *shomer chinam* raises a question that was touched upon in the previous day's discussion: if a *shomer chinam* or *shomer sachar* is negligent with respect to these excluded categories — *karka*, *avadim*, *shtarot*, or *hekdesh* — does liability for negligence attach?

Tosafot is inclined to hold that it does not. He argues that if even a *shomer sachar* who is negligent would be exempt, then *a fortiori* a *shomer chinam* would be as well. He cites a *Gemara* in support. However, this position is not without difficulty. The exemptions derived from the *pesukim* concern the specific liabilities of *shomrim* — the oath of the *shomer chinam*, the payment obligations of the *shomer sachar* for theft and loss. These are the formal *halachos* of the watchman relationship. Negligence, however, might be conceived differently: once a party undertakes a duty of care, a failure to exercise that care might constitute not a violation of *shomer* law but an act of *mazzik* — direct damage. If negligence is categorized as *mazzik* rather than as a *shomer* liability, the exclusions derived from the *pesukim* governing *shomrim* would not apply, and liability could still follow.

Tosafot raises this possibility and is inclined to resolve it in favor of exemption, but the question remains genuinely contested. All the *pesukim* establish is that these categories are excluded from *shevua* and from payment for *gneivah va-aveidah*.
