Whether a *shomer* who is negligent — and whose negligence might be analyzed as damage rather than as a watchman's failure — would pay from the category of *mazzik* is a distinct question that the derivations from the *pesukim* do not necessarily resolve.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 58

## Shomer Liability Review

### Mishnah Summary

The daf opens at the bottom of 57b, continuing the discussion of the *mishnah* enumerating categories excluded from various areas of *halacha* — from *ona'ah*, from *shvuah*, and from the laws of *shomrim*. The list includes land, slaves, documents, and *hekdesh*.

### Shomer Exemptions

Two baseline rules are established. A *shomer chinam* — one who watches an object without compensation — is not required to take an oath that he was not negligent. A *shomer sachar* — one who is paid for his watching — is exempt from paying in cases of *gneiva va-aveida*, theft or loss.

### Negligent Admission

One case conspicuously left unaddressed is that of a *shomer* who was actually negligent and admits to his negligence. Negligence may carry a higher level of liability than *gneiva va-aveida*, and there is a view that such conduct rises to the level of *mazid*, intentional wrongdoing, which would carry its own liability. That case remains open. What the *mishnah* has established is that with respect to an oath, a *shomer* is not liable for these things; and with respect to paying for *gneiva va-aveida*, a *shomer* similarly is not liable.

---

## Shekalim & Ownership

### Mishnah Setup

The *gemara* raises a challenge — *u'remi'nei* — from a *mishnah* in *Shekalim*. Each year, the people of a town would pool their obligatory annual *shekel* contribution — the *machatzis ha-shekel* — so that the communal sacrifices (*korban tzibur*) would be purchased from shared funds. They would dispatch a *shaliach* to carry the coins to the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *mishnah* addresses what happens when, along the way, the money is stolen by highway bandits or simply lost.

### Terumat HaLishka

The *mishnah* distinguishes between two scenarios based on whether the theft or loss occurred before or after *terumat ha-lishka* was taken. To understand the significance of this, one must appreciate how the *lishka* functioned. All the *shekalim* contributed from across the land were deposited into a chamber in the *Beit HaMikdash*. Three times a year, the *kohanim* would enter with baskets and scoop out coins, which would then be used to fund the next cycle of communal sacrifices. This act of scooping — separating coins from the chamber — is called *terumat ha-lishka*, analogous to *teruma* as an act of separation.

The crucial legal consequence is that this *teruma* is considered to take effect not only on the coins physically present in the chamber, but also on coins that are still in transit — already collected from the towns but not yet physically deposited. Just as *teruma* can be taken from produce in one location and declared to apply to produce in another location (*bedie'avad*), so too the *terumat ha-lishka* applies conceptually to the coins being carried by the *shaliach*. Once this conceptual application occurs, those coins are treated as if they have already been deposited in the *Beit HaMikdash*. The ownership — or at least the operative control — has transferred.

### Before/After Teruma

The distinction between the two scenarios is therefore as follows. If the money was stolen or lost before *terumat ha-lishka* was taken, the coins conceptually still belong to the townspeople. They never made it to the *Beit HaMikdash* in any operative sense. In that case, *nishba'im livnei ha'ir* — the messengers swear to the townspeople — and *shoklin acheirim tachteichem* — the townspeople must give their *shekel* a second time, since the first never reached the *Beit HaMikdash*. If the money was stolen or lost after *terumat ha-lishka* was taken, however, it is as though it was stolen from the *Beit HaMikdash* itself. In that case, *nishba'im la-gizbarin* — the messengers swear to the Temple treasurers — and the townspeople are not required to contribute again.

It is worth noting the distinction between *kedusha* as a status of an object and *kedusha* in the sense of ownership. Even before *terumat ha-lishka*, the coins may well have been sanctified from the moment they were designated and handed to the *shaliach*. Yet sanctification as a status does not automatically transfer ownership or operational control to the *Beit HaMikdash*. Compare the case of one who vows *harei alai olah* — I obligate myself to bring a burnt-offering — and the animal subsequently dies. The animal's sanctity does not dissolve his personal obligation, because the *Beit HaMikdash* never took effective possession. Similarly here, the coins were *hekdesh* in status, but the ownership dimension — the question of who bears responsibility and who has control — shifts only upon *terumat ha-lishka* or actual delivery.

### Eilu V'Eilu Shekalim

The *mishnah* continues: if the money that was lost is subsequently found, or the thieves are apprehended and the coins recovered, the rule is *eilu v'eilu shekalim* — both the original coins and the replacement coins are consecrated. The original coins remain *shekalim* because nothing ever deconsecrated them. The replacement coins are *shekalim* because they were freshly contributed and there is nothing to prevent their consecration. One might ask: why couldn't the townspeople, at the time they gave the replacement coins, simply declare the original coins — wherever they were — deconsecrated, *mechul*, on the new ones? The answer invokes *Rabbi Yochanan*'s principle that one cannot be *mekadesh* or *mechallel* something not under one's control. Since the original coins were neither physically accessible nor within the townspeople's operative domain, they could not be deconsecrated. Once recovered, there is similarly no mechanism to unravel the double consecration after the fact. The *Beit HaMikdash* therefore receives both. And one more point: *eilu v'eilu shekalim hem v'ein olin lahem l'shanah haba'ah* — they cannot be applied as a prepayment credit toward next year's obligation. The double contribution does not carry forward.

### Shvuah on Hekdesh

All of this is fascinating on its own terms, but the immediate relevance to our *sugya* is the following: in both scenarios — whether the messengers swear to the townspeople or to the *gizbarin* — the coins in question are *hekdesh*, sanctified property. We have just established that one does not make a *shvuah* on *hekdesh*. So what is the *shvuah* being taken on here? The *gemara* therefore asks: what is the basis for these oaths?

---

## Shmuel's Fee Theory

### Fee Collection Purpose

*Shmuel* offers a reading that is admittedly not the straightforward *pshat* of the *mishnah*. He says: *hacha b'netilat sachar askinan* — we are dealing here with the messengers collecting their fee. The messengers are not swearing in order to exempt themselves from liability — they have no such liability, since the object is *hekdesh*. Rather, they want to be paid for their service. Having undertaken to transport the coins and now presenting themselves after a theft or loss, they must take an oath to demonstrate that they were not negligent, not to avoid a payment obligation, but in order to establish their entitlement to receive payment. If they were content to forfeit their fee and simply walk away, no *shvuah* would be required at all.

### Swearing to Gizbarin

The *gemara* immediately challenges this. In the scenario where *terumat ha-lishka* was already taken — when it is the *Beit HaMikdash* that sustains the loss — the *mishnah* says the messengers swear to the *gizbarin*, the Temple treasurers. But according to *Shmuel*'s reading, they are swearing in order to collect their fee from the townspeople who hired them. Why then are they swearing to the *gizbarin*? They should be swearing to the townspeople — *l'vnei ha'ir miba'ei leh*.

### Rabbah's Solution

*Rabbah* resolves this: *nishba'im l'vnei ha'ir b'ma'amad gizbarin k'dei shelo yachshidohu*. They do indeed swear to the townspeople, since the townspeople are their employers and the ones who owe them the fee. But in the first scenario — where the loss falls upon the *Beit HaMikdash* — the *gizbarin* are brought in as witnesses, so that they too can satisfy themselves that the messengers did not steal or misappropriate the funds. Alternatively, so that the *gizbarin* will not accuse the messengers of negligence. Since the messengers are in any case taking an oath to collect their fee, the *gizbarin* are invited to be present so that suspicion is cleared on both fronts — neither theft nor negligence — at least in the eyes of the Temple treasury.

---

## Negligence & Fee

### Negligence Forfeits Pay

The *gemara* is not satisfied with *Shmuel*'s approach and raises a further difficulty. The *mishnah* says the money was stolen or lost. If the messenger was being paid — i.e., he is a *shomer sachar* — then normally a *shomer sachar* is liable for *gneiva va-aveida*. True, the *hekdesh* exemption means he will not actually pay. But the *gemara* argues: *nehi de-shilumei lo meshalmei* — granted he does not pay — *agrai'u mia lifsedu* — at least he should forfeit his fee. If the circumstances were such that a paid *shomer* would normally be liable, that is because his duty of care required him to prevent exactly these outcomes. Even where *hekdesh* relieves him of the payment, it does not mean he fulfilled his duty of care. Since he failed in his *chiyuv shmirah*, he is not entitled to his compensation.

### Duty of Care

This is an important distinction. The question of whether a *shomer* is exempt from *shvuah* and *tashlumin* is separate from the question of whether a *shomer* has any underlying *chiyuv shmirah* at all. Even where there is no formal obligation to pay and no oath to take, the *shomer* presumably still has a responsibility to watch. The *gemara* is pointing out that when a *shomer sachar* fails in that responsibility — when loss occurs under circumstances for which he would normally bear liability — we may conclude that he did not do his job, and consequently he forfeits his fee. An oath cannot change that underlying reality.

### Oath Insufficient

The implication is clear: according to the *gemara*'s objection, a *shvuah* alone is insufficient to entitle the messengers to their fee when the loss is of the type for which a *shomer sachar* would ordinarily bear responsibility. The *gemara* thus rejects *Shmuel*'s rationale as inadequate to explain the *mishnah*.

---

## Rava: Force Majeure

### Unavoidable Disasters

*Rava* rescues *Shmuel*'s basic framework by recharacterizing the facts. He says: *nignevu be-listim mezuyan avdu she-ta'ah sefinato ba-yam* — the cases in the *mishnah* involve not ordinary theft or loss, but armed bandits and a sinking ship. These are *oneis* — situations of absolute unavoidable compulsion, force majeure.

### Oneis Logic

With this clarification, the *gemara*'s objection dissolves. A *shomer sachar*'s liability for *gneiva va-aveida* rests on the premise that he had a heightened duty of care and failed to prevent a preventable loss. But when the loss is an *oneis* — when nothing could have protected the coins against armed robbers or a shipwreck — one cannot say that the messenger shirked his *chiyuv shmirah*. He was not negligent; he was overwhelmed by forces entirely beyond his control. He therefore retains his entitlement to his fee, takes an oath to demonstrate that the loss was indeed an *oneis*, and collects his pay. *Rava* thus preserves *Shmuel*'s reading: the *shvuah* is to collect the fee, the scenarios are ones of *oneis*, and the oath is appropriate.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan View

### Rabbi Shimon Principle

*Rabbi Yochanan* takes a different approach entirely, one grounded in the position of *Rabbi Shimon*. He says the *mishnah* reflects *Rabbi Shimon*'s principle: *kodashim she-chayav be-achrayutan yesh lahem ona'ah ve-nishba'in aleihen* — sanctified property for which a person bears financial responsibility is treated, for purposes of *ona'ah* and *shvuah*, as though it were his own. Since the messengers are carrying coins for which the townspeople remain financially responsible — specifically, before *terumat ha-lishka* was taken, the townspeople must contribute again if the money is lost — it is as though the coins are effectively the townspeople's property. The oath is therefore not on *hekdesh* in the exempting sense, because the liability-nexus makes it *amito*, the property of a private party.

### Principle Limits

The *gemara* immediately identifies the limitation of this approach. It works elegantly for the scenario *before* *terumat ha-lishka* was taken, when the townspeople are still responsible for the loss and must re-contribute. But once *terumat ha-lishka* has been taken, the *mishnah* itself says the townspeople are no longer required to give again — the loss falls on the *Beit HaMikdash*. At that point, the coins are *kodashim she-eino chayav be-achrayutan* — sanctified property for which the townspeople bear no responsibility. *Rabbi Shimon*'s principle would then provide no basis for an oath. Why does the *mishnah* still require one?

### Braita: Teruma Scope

The *gemara* cites a *braita* to address this: *tormin al ha-avud v'al ha-gavuy v'al ha-atid ligvot* — the *teruma* of the *lishka* takes effect upon money that is lost, money that has been collected and is in transit, and money that has not yet been collected at all. *Tosafot* explains the first clause: even if coins were deposited into the *lishka* and subsequently lost before physical use, the *teruma* is treated as having applied to them. The second clause — *al ha-gavuy* — covers the scenario of our *mishnah*: coins collected from a town and being carried by a messenger. The *teruma* applies to those as well, rendering them as though already deposited.

### L'Asid Ligvos

The third clause — *v'al ha-atid ligvot*, on money not yet collected — is the most remarkable. When *terumat ha-lishka* is taken and *korbanot* are purchased, the communal sacrifices are brought on behalf of the entire Jewish people, including towns that have not yet remitted their contribution for that year. The *teruma* conceptually encompasses even those future contributions. This ensures that the *korbanot* are genuinely *tzibur*, communal, even where some contributions come in later. However, this conceptual inclusion does not transfer ownership or discharge liability. The townspeople whose coins have not yet been collected remain responsible for their *shekel*. Only once their coins have been collected, dispatched, and the *hafrasha* has occurred — placing those specific coins within the conceptual orbit of the *lishka*'s *teruma* — are they discharged from responsibility. The distinction between *kedusha* as status and operative ownership remains critical throughout.

---

## Takana on Hekdesh

### Takana Justification

Having pressed *Rabbi Yochanan*'s approach to its limits, the *gemara* ultimately concludes with a different resolution. *Rabbi Elazar* states: *shvua zo takanas chachamim hi shelo yei kol bnei adam mezalzelin be-hekdeshos* — this oath is a rabbinic enactment, instituted so that people would not treat *hekdesh* negligently.

### Policy Rationale

The policy logic is straightforward. If it were publicly known that one who deals with *hekdesh* faces no oath and no payment consequences — neither a *shvuat ha-shomrim* nor *tashlumin* — people would be far less careful with sanctified property. The *takana* imposes an oath requirement as a check on carelessness, even where there is no *ikar din* basis for one. The parallel to the first *perek*'s ruling — that an oath is taken when splitting a disputed *tallis*, explained there too as *shvua zo takanas chachamim* — is apt.

### Scope of Takana

Whether this *takana* is limited to the specific context of *shekalim* — the most financially significant and logistically common category of *hekdesh* transport — or extends as a general principle to all *hekdesh* interactions is left open. What is clear is that the *gemara* is acknowledging a real gap: the Torah formally exempts *hekdesh* from the ordinary *shvuah* framework, yet the practical consequence of that exemption — unchecked carelessness toward sacred property — demands a corrective measure.

---

## Shomer Sachar Cases

### Payment Scenarios

The *gemara* now raises a fresh challenge. *Rav Yosef bar Chama* confronts *Rava* with a contradiction between our *mishnah*'s ruling that a *shomer sachar* is exempt from *gneiva va-aveida* when the object is *hekdesh*, and a *braita* that discusses paid watchmen whose employer is the *Beit HaMikdash* itself. The *braita* discusses three cases: one hired to guard the *parah adumah* — ensuring that no burden is placed upon it that would render it *passul* — one hired to be a babysitter for the children being raised in ritual purity in isolation to assist with the *parah adumah* ceremony, and one hired to guard seeds designated for the *omer* or for produce during *shmitta*.

In each case, the worker is paid by the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *braita* states: *ein notnim lo sechar Shabbat* — if payment is computed on a daily basis, the worker is not paid for *Shabbat*, because one may not pay wages specifically designated for *Shabbat* work. Consequently, *ein achrayut Shabbat alav* — he bears no liability as a *shomer sachar* on *Shabbat*, being at most a *shomer chinam* on that day.

### Havla'ah Concept

The *braita* then presents the countercase: if the worker is paid on a weekly, monthly, annual, or seven-year cycle, the *Shabbat* wages are included — *notnim lo sechar Shabbat* — and correspondingly, *achrayut Shabbat alav* — he bears *shomer sachar* liability on *Shabbat* as well. This is the principle of *havla'ah*: when one is paid for the whole week as a unit rather than day by day, the *Shabbat* component is absorbed into the general wage and is not singled out as payment for *Shabbat*. Crucially, this does not mean we conceptualize the arrangement as paying for six days with the seventh day thrown in free. The worker is genuinely considered paid for *Shabbat* — which is why he bears *shomer sachar* liability on *Shabbat* — but because the payment is not specifically designated for *Shabbat* work, it is halakhically acceptable. The prohibition is against directly paying for *Shabbat*; aggregated weekly pay does not violate that prohibition.

### Liability Problem

The deeper problem this *braita* poses is not about *Shabbat* but about the nature of the *shomer*'s liability altogether. In these cases, the objects being guarded — children, seeds, the *parah adumah* — are not themselves *hekdesh* in the ordinary sense. The exemption from *shomer* liability established by the *mishnah* derives from the verse *re'ehu*, "his neighbor," which the *gemara* reads as excluding *hekdesh* — *re'ehu v'lo hekdesh*. But that exclusion, strictly read, focuses on the nature of the contractual relationship and not exclusively on the sanctity of the object. Here the object may not be *hekdesh*, but the *shomer*'s contract is with the *Beit HaMikdash*. If the exclusion applies to this relationship, the *shomer* bears no liability — yet the *braita* treats him as a *shomer sachar* with standard liability. How?

### Kinyan Sudar

The *gemara* presents the question, and after an initial silence, reports the answer in the name of *Rav Sheshet* and *Rabbi Yochanan*: *be-shekanu miyado* — the arrangement was effected through *kinyan sudar*, a formal act of contractual acquisition. When the *Beit HaMikdash* hired the watchman, both parties knew that the ordinary laws of *shomrim* would exempt him from liability. To create a binding obligation nonetheless, a separate *kinyan sudar* was performed — the watchman grasped a *sudar*, a garment or cloth, and formally accepted liability through this special contractual act. This obligation operates outside the default framework of *dinei shomrim* altogether, or alternatively, within it by the mechanism analogous to *Rabbi Meir*'s principle — *ha-matneh al mah shekatuv ba-Torah b'davar shebe-mamon, tna'o kayam* — that stipulations modifying monetary obligations in Torah law are valid. Either way, the watchman has voluntarily assumed a level of liability beyond what the *halacha* would otherwise impose.

### Kinyan Sudar Effects

This solution, taken together with the *takana* discussed in the previous section, effectively closes the gaps that the Torah's exemptions created. On the one hand, *Rabbi Elazar*'s *takana* ensures that even absent any other arrangement, people will not treat *hekdesh* negligently because an oath is required. On the other hand, *kinyan sudar* enables the *Beit HaMikdash* to contract directly for full *shomer* liability when it hires workers. The result is that one cannot easily escape responsibility when dealing with sacred property — despite the Torah's formal exemptions, the system of rabbinic enactment and private contractual mechanism fills the practical void. There is something striking in this: the Torah exempts *hekdesh* as a formal legal category, and the rabbinic and contractual response says, in effect, that the policy implications of such an exemption are unacceptable, and systematically corrects for them.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Kodashim

### Liability Determines

A *tanna* taught before *Rabbi Yitzchak*: *kodshim she-chayav be-achrayus chayav ve-she-eino chayav be-achrayus patur* — with respect to sanctified property that one bears financial responsibility for, one is liable; with respect to sanctified property for which one bears no responsibility, one is exempt. This reiterates *Rabbi Shimon*'s principle, applying it here to the laws of *shvuah* and *chiyuv* more broadly.

### Braita Analysis

The *gemara* analyzes the *braita* and initially notes that the reasoning seems backwards. *Rabbi Shimon*'s principle, as stated, derives the *chiyuv* from the words *ba-Hashem u-kichesh* — "and he betrayed God and he denied" — and the *patur* from *be-amito u-kichesh* — "and he denied to his neighbor." But one might have expected the logic to run in the opposite direction: when something is more closely associated with *Hashem* (*hekdesh*), it should be *patur*, and when associated with *amito* (a private party), it should be *chayav*. The *tanna* before *Rabbi Yitzchak* initially has no answer, and when asked, reports the following.

### Word Analysis

The *pasuk* in question combines *ba-Hashem v'kichesh* with *be-amito v'kichesh*, effectively bracketing the word *kichesh* — "he denied" — between a reference to God and a reference to one's neighbor. The verse (*Vayikra* 5) lists the wrongs one may commit — *pikadon*, *tesumas yad*, *gazel*, *oshek* — and specifies that one who swears falsely about them is liable for the fifth and the *asham*.

### Amito Principle

The interpretive key is that *ba-Hashem* teaches that there exist categories of *hekdesh* for which one can still be *chayav*, and *be-amito* defines the condition: only when there is an *amito* element — a component of private-party liability and ownership — is one *chayav* even on *hekdesh*. When that *amito* element is entirely absent — when the property is wholly the *Beit HaMikdash*'s responsibility with no private-party dimension — one is *patur*, excluded by the word *amito* itself. The principle therefore runs as follows: if the *hekdesh* item has an *amito* component (i.e., the person bears financial responsibility for it), the *chiyuv* applies — *kodshim she-chayav be-achrayus, chayav*. If there is no *amito* component, *de-itma'atu mi-ba-amito* — the word *amito* excludes it — and one is *patur*.

---

## Rabbi Yehudah Ona'ah

### Sefer Torah Value

*Rabbi Yehudah* offers his own list of items excluded from *ona'ah*, distinct from the formal exemptions of the *mishnah* (land, slaves, documents, *hekdesh*). His list consists of a *sefer Torah*, a *margalit* (precious gem), and *behemah* (large animal). The *gemara* cites a *braita* explaining each. Regarding the *sefer Torah*: *ein ketz li-dameha* — there is no limit to its value. Whether this is an empirical observation about the variability of the market for *sifrei Torah*, or a theological statement that one cannot declare any price excessive for a *Torah* scroll, is a genuine question. Either way, the implication is that no transaction involving a *sefer Torah* can be attacked on the grounds that the buyer paid more than the item is worth.

### Matching Premium

For *margalit* and *behemah*, the reasoning is different: *mishum d'amar rotzeh l'zavgan* — because the buyer may say he wanted to match it. A precious gem that perfectly completes a matched set of jewelry commands a premium far above the ordinary market price for a stone of that size and quality. An ox whose physique and temperament are a precise match for another ox already in one's possession will plow far more efficiently, and one may reasonably pay far above the standard market rate to acquire it. Because these items are routinely purchased for their matching value, one cannot claim *ona'ah* simply because the price exceeded what a standalone item would fetch.

### Matching Question

The *gemara* pushes back: there are many items for which a buyer might seek a precise match and pay a premium accordingly. Fabric for a quilt, thread of a particular color, all manner of goods might attract a matching premium in particular circumstances. What distinguishes the *sefer Torah*, *margalit*, and *behemah* from everything else?

### Particular Value

*Rabbi Yehudah*'s distinction is that these items are *chashivei* — they are particularly and weighty enough in their importance that people regularly pay disproportionately for them. Other goods for which a matching premium sometimes applies are not sufficiently weighty that the market consistently accommodates such extreme departures from ordinary price.

### Doubling Limit

Even for these items, however, there is a threshold. *Amemar* rules: *ad kedei dmeihem* — up to double the standard value. If the buyer pays more than double the ordinary market price, the premium has exceeded what even the matching rationale can justify, and an *ona'ah* claim would lie. This is noteworthy: *Tosafot* had observed that even for the formally excluded categories — land, slaves, documents, *hekdesh* — there is *bitul mekach*, nullification of the sale, if the price is double or more than double. It is precisely this same threshold — double value — that applies here to *Rabbi Yehudah*'s categories, which are excluded not by formal rule but by the logic of the marketplace.

### War Goods Exception

A *tanna* taught before *Rav Nachman*: *Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira* adds another category — one who sells a horse, a sword, or a shield during wartime: *af ha-mocher sus v'sayaf v'taris b'milchama ein lahem ona'ah*. No *ona'ah* claim lies against the seller of war materiel during war.

### Desperate Market

The rationale: *mipnei she-yesh ba-hen chayei nefesh* — because these items are matters of life and death. A soldier facing combat will pay whatever is necessary to equip himself. The market for these goods during wartime is fundamentally different from the peacetime market. The price that prevails under those conditions is the market price for those conditions. One cannot then invoke a peacetime benchmark and cry *ona'ah*. It is worth noting what this ruling does and does not say. The laws of *ona'ah* prohibit selling above the prevailing market rate but do not themselves set that market rate. The *gemara* elsewhere identifies a separate prohibition against price gouging on staple goods — *chayei nefesh* in the ordinary sense, bread and oil — but that is a different *issur* from *ona'ah*. *Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira*'s ruling is simply that the wartime market for combat equipment is its own market, and the seller who charges accordingly has not violated *ona'ah*.

---

## Ona'at Devarim

### Price Without Intent

The *mishnah* now introduces the concept of *ona'at devarim* — the prohibition against afflicting another person with words. The first case: *lo yomar lo b'kama chefetz zeh v'hu eino rotzeh likach* — do not ask a storekeeper the price of an item if you have no intention of buying. This is a serious issue, and not merely a historical one. In the contemporary context, the problem is acute: entering a brick-and-mortar store, trying on merchandise, determining the right size and style, and then purchasing online at a reduced price exploits the physical retailer's services without any intention of patronizing his business. This is categorically *assur* as *ona'at devarim*.

### Modern Application

The prohibition is real and applies broadly. When employees work on commission, the injury is more direct — the salesperson invests time and energy expecting a sale that never comes. But even absent commission, the storekeeper's attention and investment of service are being taken advantage of. One simple mitigation: clearly stating at the outset that one is only browsing and has no present intent to buy, or that one is planning to purchase elsewhere, removes the deception and changes the interaction materially.

### Component Types

This first case sits at the intersection of business and interpersonal harm. The person asking the price leads the merchant to believe a transaction is possible, toys with his expectations and hopes, and then disappoints him — which has both a financial dimension (wasted time, lost opportunity to attend another customer) and a deeply personal emotional dimension. The cases that follow, however, are purely interpersonal, with no business component whatsoever.

### Past Deeds Cases

The *mishnah* continues: *im haya ba'al teshuva, lo yomru lo zechor ma'asecha ha-rishonim* — if someone is a *ba'al teshuva*, do not say to him, "Remember how you used to behave." *Im hu ben gerim, lo yomar lo zechor ma'aseh avotecha* — if he is the descendant of converts, do not say, "Remember what your fathers used to do." You need not even be attacking the person himself — reminding him that his father was a gentile is equally prohibited.

### Torah Source

The *mishnah* cites the verse *veger lo toneh velo tilchatzenu* as a source. It is significant that the *mishnah* shifts to the *ger* case, and that the verse cited speaks of afflicting and oppressing. This brings to the fore the core of *ona'at devarim*: unlike *ona'at mamon*, which is fundamentally about a financial transaction, *ona'at devarim* is about inflicting harm upon a person — injuring their dignity, their feelings, their sense of self. The verse's language of *ona'ah* and *lachatz* (oppression) communicates that we are dealing with something that reaches beyond commercial wrong into the domain of interpersonal injury.

The *gemara* returns to the Torah sources. *Vayikra* 25 contains two verses: verse 14 — *vechi timkru mimkar l'amitecha o kano miyad amitecha al tonu ish et achiv* — and verse 17 — *velo tonu ish et amito*. The first verse occurs in the context of *mimkar*, commerce, and addresses *ona'at mamon*. The second verse, which does not mention commerce, addresses *ona'at devarim*. The doubling of the prohibition is thus not redundant — each verse targets a distinct category of wrong.

### Braita Cases

The *braita* elaborates: *im hayah ba'al teshuva, al yomar lo zechor ma'asecha ha-rishonim* — do not recall a returnee's past. *Im hayah ben gerim, al yomar lo zechor ma'aseh avotecha* — do not recall a convert's ancestry. And perhaps most striking: *im hayah ger u'va lilmod Torah* — if the person is himself a *ger* who has come to study *Torah* — *al yomar lo: peh she'achal neveilot u'treifot shekatzim u'remasim, ba lilmod Torah?* — do not say to him: "This mouth that ate forbidden foods comes to study *Torah*?" The injury here is not the recollection of a factual past but the weaponizing of that past to delegitimize the person's present aspirations and spiritual standing.

### Suffering Cases

The *braita* continues: *im hayu yissurin ba'in alav, o shehayah chola'im ba'in alav, o shehayah mekaber banav* — if afflictions come upon someone, or sickness, or God forbid he is burying his children — *al yomar lo kederech she'amru lo chaveirav le-Iyov* — do not say to him what *Iyov*'s so-called friends said. The friends suggested to *Iyov*: *halo yiratecha kislatecha* — was not your fear your confidence? *Tikvatecha v'tom derachecha* — your hope and the pureness of your ways? Meaning: you thought you were so righteous and upright — yet look what is happening to you. It must be punishment for some hidden sin. This pastoral catastrophe — attributing suffering to secret guilt, compounding a person's pain with accusation — is among the gravest forms of *ona'at devarim*.

### Fool's Errand

Another case from the *braita*: *im hayu chamarin mevakshim tvu'ah mimenu, lo yomar lahem lechu eitzel ploni she-hu mocher tvu'ah, v'yodeia bo shelo machar me'olam* — if donkey drivers come asking where to buy grain, do not send them to someone you know has never sold grain in his life, just to get these unwanted visitors away from you. This case is notable for being a different kind of injury. The person being harmed is not insulted or shamed — he is tricked and sent on a fool's errand. His feelings are not exactly hurt in the way a *ba'al teshuva*'s are hurt. He wastes time, effort, and perhaps money, and eventually feels the sting of having been misled. The scope of *ona'at devarim* is thus broader than shaming or emotional injury in the narrow sense — it encompasses any use of words to cause harm or disadvantage to another person.

### Non-Verbal Ona'ah

*Rabbi Yehudah* extends the prohibition even beyond words: *afilu yitle einav al ha-mekach bi-sha'ah she-ein lo damim* — do not even fix your gaze upon merchandise when you have no money to purchase it, giving the merchant the impression that a sale is imminent. The word *devarim* does not appear in the *pasuk* itself — *lo tonu* alone — which perhaps licenses *Rabbi Yehudah*'s extension to non-verbal conduct. The underlying wrong in all these cases is the same: creating false impressions, manipulating expectations, and thereby injuring another.

### Davar Masur L'Lev

The *gemara* notes: *harei hu davar masur la-lev* — this is a matter given over to the heart, i.e., the inner intention is the determining factor. A person might claim, "I really was thinking of buying," or "I honestly thought that other person sold grain." Since only the individual knows his true intent, and no court can verify it, the *pasuk* appends *ve-yareta me-Elohecha* — you shall fear your God. God knows what was in the heart. It is the awareness that one cannot hide inner intention from the Divine that is meant to restrain behavior in cases where external scrutiny cannot reach.

---

## Ona'ah Severity

### Yochanan's View

*Rabbi Yochanan* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai* states: *gadol ona'at devarim mi-ona'at mamon* — *ona'at devarim* is a graver sin than financial *ona'ah*.

### Yirat Elohim

The proof: *she-ze ne'emar bo ve-yareta me-Elohecha ve-ze lo ne'emar bo ve-yareta me-Elohecha* — the verse addressing *ona'at devarim* includes the phrase *ve-yareta me-Elohecha*, fear your God, whereas the verse addressing *ona'at mamon* does not. As established earlier in the *sugya*, *ve-yareta me-Elohecha* signals not merely that intention is hidden and left to God's knowledge, but that Divine punishment is imminent and deserved. The presence of that phrase by *ona'at devarim* and its absence by *ona'at mamon* thus indicates that *ona'at devarim* carries a more severe Divine response.

### Elazar: Person vs. Pocket

*Rabbi Elazar* articulates the substantive reason behind the severity: *ze be-gufo ve-ze be-mamono* — one injures the person, the other injures the pocket. *Ona'at devarim* strikes at a human being's dignity, sense of self, emotional wellbeing, and inner life. *Ona'at mamon* strikes at one's financial position. The financial injury may feel deeply personal — one who has been cheated feels taken advantage of and violated — but there remains a categorical difference between an injury to the self and an injury to the wallet. When words cut, they wound something that cannot be fully separated from the person who was wounded.

### Nachmani: Irreversibility

*Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani* adds a further dimension: *ze nitan le-hishavon ve-ze lo nitan le-hishavon* — financial loss is correctable; verbal harm is not. Money stolen or overcharged can be returned. The wronged party can be made financially whole. Words, once spoken, cannot be taken back. An apology can be offered, restitution of dignity attempted, but the words remain — people carry them for decades, and no sum of money neutralizes what was said. It is the irreversibility of verbal injury that makes it, in this dimension, categorically more serious than financial wrong.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 59

## Malbin Pnei Chaveiro

### Whitening Face

The *daf* opens in the middle of a discussion about *ona'at devarim* — the prohibition against causing pain through speech. A *tanna* taught before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: *kol hamalbin pnei chaveiro b'rabim ke'ilu shofech damim* — anyone who whitens the face of his friend in public, causing him to blanch from embarrassment, is as though he has spilled blood. This is among the most widely recognized statements of the Gemara.

### Blood Rushing Away

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responded to this teaching: *shapir ka'amart* — that is indeed a well-stated teaching, and here is why. *DeChazeina lei de'azil sumka v'ati chivra* — we can observe that when a person is publicly shamed, the redness drains from his face and is replaced by whiteness. The *malbin pnei chaveiro* thus carries a figurative resonance: you cause the blood to rush out of him, as if you have literally spilled it. The original force of the statement should not be lost, however. Public embarrassment does not merely cause momentary discomfort — it can devastate a person's standing in the community and leave him unsure whether he can ever face the public again. Something deep and destructive is at work. The metaphor of spilled blood reinforces and intensifies that intuition.

### Eretz Yisrael's Caution

Abaye asked Rav Dimi: *b'ma'arava b'mai zahiri* — in *Eretz Yisrael*, what are people particularly scrupulous about? The question is posed in the context of *bein adam l'chaveiro*, and the answer reflects that context. Rav Dimi replied: *b'achvuri appei* — whitening a person's face. The seriousness with which *Eretz Yisrael* regarded this prohibition is itself a significant moral teaching: when people ask what marks a truly *frum* person, the answer is not a stringency in ritual law but rather a sensitivity toward how words and actions affect another human being.

### Three Types to Gehinnom

This is grounded in a teaching of Rabbi Yochanan. The Gemara introduces his statement carefully. One might initially read *hakol yordim l'Gehinnom* as saying that everyone goes to *Gehinnom*, but the Gemara clarifies: the meaning is that all who descend to *Gehinnom* will ultimately ascend — *chutz mishelosha*, except for three. Those three go down and do not come back up. Rabbi Yochanan enumerates them: *haba al eshet ish* — one who commits adultery with a married woman; *hamalbin pnei chaveiro b'rabim* — one who publicly shames his fellow; and *hamachane shem l'chaveiro* — one who gives his friend a derogatory nickname.

### Three Unforgivable Sins

The Gemara raises an apparent redundancy. Is giving a nickname not the same as *malbin pnei chaveiro*? The answer is *af al gav dedash bei bishmei* — even if the nickname has already become so common that everyone uses it, anyone who continues to employ it transgresses, because doing so perpetuates and reinforces a diminished perception of that person in society. The stakes here are striking: it is not only the originator of the nickname who bears culpability, but anyone who perpetuates it.

### Nicknames & Intent

This is admittedly a demanding ruling. A person who uses a name that has become universal — where even the bearer may claim not to mind — is apparently still included. Rashi, sensitive to this difficulty, limits the prohibition to a case where the speaker intends to shame: *mikol makom zeh l'hachlimo nitkaven*. Even if the name is in common usage, if the speaker deploys it with the intention of causing embarrassment, he is culpable. The Maharsha goes further, suggesting that perhaps the concern is akin to *motzi shem ra* — the spreading of a damaging reputation — even where the individual himself is not visibly shamed in the moment. He also notes that the Rambam does not restrict this to degrading nicknames but includes any nickname whatsoever. The range of opinions here reflects a genuine tension between the gravity of the principle and the expansiveness of its application. What remains constant across the authorities is the underlying moral priority: what people in *Eretz Yisrael* are most scrupulous about is not a ritual stringency but the way they speak about and to other human beings.

---

## David & Bathsheba

### Safek Eshet Ish

Rabba bar Bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *noach lo le'adam sheyavo al safek eshet ish v'al yalbin pnei chaveiro b'rabim* — it is preferable for a person to have relations with a woman whose marital status is in doubt than to publicly shame his fellow. This is a remarkable statement: the sin of potential adultery is placed in second position to the sin of *malbin pnei chaveiro*. The *safek eshet ish* referred to here is a case where there is genuine uncertainty — for example, whether the woman's husband has died or is still alive. The basis for this comparison will be explored through the following Scriptural derivation.

### David's Psalm

The Gemara asks: *mena lei* — from where does Rabbi Yochanan derive this? The answer is from what Rava explicated. Rava expounded on the verse in Tehillim: *uvatzali samachu ne'asfu, kar'u v'lo damu* — "in my stumbling they rejoiced and gathered; they tore me and it did not cease." The word *lo damu* is read not as "did not cease" but as *dam* — blood — yielding the meaning "and there was no blood." This reading sets the stage for David's statement to God.

### David Mocked

The Gemara reads the verse as David's address to the Holy One. David says before God: *galui v'yadua lefanecha she'im hayu mekar'im b'sari lo hayah dami shotet la'aretz* — it is known to You that if people were to tear my flesh, my blood would not flow to the ground, because of all the fasting I have done in consequence of my sin involving Batsheva and the child. This personal diminishment is not the end of his suffering. Even when *talmidei chachamim* are engaged in the most demanding areas of *halacha* — *negaim* and *ohalot* — they stop their learning to mock him: *David, haba al eshet ish mitato b'meh* — David, one who commits adultery with a married woman, what is his punishment? They taunt him with his sin of Batsheva.

The Maharsha adds a pointed observation: the association with *negaim* is deliberate, since *tzaraat* is a consequence of *lashon hara*. The implicit message is sharp: these scholars who pride themselves on their *frumkeit*, defending the sanctity of the law, are themselves engaged in shaming another — which is the gravest of sins.

### David's Defense

David's response is striking. He does not deny the sin and does not attempt to deflect the shame entirely. He answers: *mitato b'chenek, v'yesh lo chelek l'olam haba* — yes, the punishment for adultery is strangulation, but the sinner retains a share in the *olam haba*. By contrast, *hamalbin et pnei chaveiro b'rabim ein lo chelek l'olam haba* — one who publicly shames his fellow has no share in the world to come. David essentially turns the mockery back on his tormentors: however terrible my sin, the sin you are committing against me right now is categorically worse.

The earlier teaching about the *safek eshet ish* is also illuminated here. Based on another Gemara, there is a position that David may have arranged for Uriah to die in battle such that Batsheva retroactively was never fully married to him — which is the *safek eshet ish* of that discussion. David's own defense in the Psalm, however, does not even rely on the *safek*: his argument holds even in the case of clear adultery, which he acknowledges carried a real punishment. What he insists is that it did not forfeit his portion in *olam haba*, whereas *malbin pnei chaveiro* does. The parallel between his bloodless flesh and the draining of blood from a shamed face is also worth noting — though the Gemara does not spell it out directly, there is an implicit resonance between his self-description and the mechanism of *malbin pnei chaveiro*.

---

## Furnace Over Shame

### Fire Preference

Mar Zutra bar Tuvya said in the name of Rav — and others attribute the statement to Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida, or to Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: *noach lo le'adam sheyapil atzmo l'kivshan ha'eish v'al yalbin pnei chaveiro b'rabim* — it is better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to publicly shame his fellow. The force of this statement extends beyond intentional shaming: even if one might inadvertently bring about another's public humiliation, one should be prepared to suffer extreme personal harm rather than allow it to occur. The comparison to loss of life recurs here as in earlier statements, underscoring the Gemara's consistent treatment of public embarrassment as tantamount to a mortal offense.

---

## Furnace Over Shame (II)

### Tamar's Discretion

The Gemara derives this principle from the story of Tamar. *Minalan mi-Tamar* — from Tamar, as the verse states: *hi mutzet v'hi shalacha el chamia leimor* — she was being led out to be burned, and she sent a message to her father-in-law Judah with the evidence that he was the father of her child, rather than confronting him directly. She gave Judah the opportunity to recognize his own seal, cord, and staff — and to take responsibility himself — rather than shaming him publicly. She was prepared to be cast into the fire rather than expose him.

It is worth noting that on the level of *pshat*, Tamar's indirect approach may itself have been what made Judah capable of acknowledging the truth: direct confrontation might well have provoked denial. Nevertheless, the Gemara reads her conduct as a moral model — she valued his honor above her own life.

### Fire & Honor

The Maharsha adds a further dimension through wordplay. The word *hi mutzet* — she was being led out — can be read as related to *lehatzit*, to kindle a fire. In this reading, the fire was already being lit upon her, she was already in the face of the flames, and still she would not name him directly. The choice between her own destruction and his shame was made clearly in favor of his honor.

---

## David & Bathsheba (II)

### Tamar's Example

Tamar's precedent is invoked directly in connection with the earlier teaching about preferring to be cast into a furnace over publicly shaming another. Her willingness to be burned alive rather than expose Judah is the paradigmatic demonstration of that principle — the readiness to absorb the full weight of personal destruction rather than transfer shame onto another person.

---

## Ona'ah Conditions

### Torah Commitment

Rabbi Chanina, son of Rav Idi, asks: what is the meaning of the verse *velo tonu ish et amito* — do not afflict a man his fellow? Why does the verse use the word *amito* rather than *chaveiro*? He derives: *im she'itcha b'Torah uvemitzvot al tonehu* — only with one who is with you in Torah and *mitzvot* does this prohibition apply. This is a limiting principle: the prohibition of *ona'at devarim* in its fullest sense applies specifically to one who is committed to a life of Torah and *mitzvot*. By contrast, someone who has openly and defiantly abandoned that way of life — the *rasha* of that era, where such rejection represented a genuine and deliberate break — may appropriately be spoken about critically, in order to maintain distance from his influence and prevent others from following his path. It must be stressed that this limitation does not apply to monetary overreaching, which extends to everyone. The limitation applies specifically to verbal affliction.

### Wife's Sensitivity

Rav teaches: *leolam yehei adam zahir b'ona'at ishto* — a man should always be particularly careful that his words do not cause pain to his wife. Even presumably unintentional words require extra vigilance in this context.

### Women's Tears

The reason given is: *shemitoch shedimaatah metzuyah, ona'atah krova* — because her tears are close to the surface, the likelihood of *ona'ah* is much nearer. The Gemara is drawing on a generalization about emotional sensitivity. While one may set aside the gendered framing, the underlying moral counsel remains sound and practically important: words that would be absorbed without harm in some relationships can cause genuine pain in others, and the closer the relationship, the greater the care required. The particular sensitivity of a spouse — and the ease with which well-intentioned speech can cause harm — demands its own watchfulness.

---

## Gates of Heaven

### Prayer Gates Sealed

Rabbi Elazar teaches: *miyom shenechrav Beit Hamikdash nin'alu sha'arei tefilla* — from the day the *Beit Hamikdash* was destroyed, the gates of prayer were sealed. The *Beit Hamikdash* served as the channel through which prayer ascended — *zeh sha'ar hashamayim* — and its destruction closed that direct access. The verse cited is: *gam ki ezak va'ashavea satam tefillati* — even when I cry out and beseech, my prayer is shut up.

### Tears Gates Open

Yet there is a qualification: *sha'arei dema'ot lo nin'alu* — the gates of tears were not sealed. The verse reads: *shim'ah tefillati Hashem, el dim'ati al techerash* — hear my prayer, God, do not deafen yourself to my tears. Rashi reads this not as a petition but as a declaration: God will not make Himself deaf to tears; He will certainly hear them. The implication for *ona'at devarim* is immediate: if the tears that flow from one who has been verbally afflicted reach God directly through ungated access, then the consequences of causing those tears are correspondingly severe.

---

## Household & Wife

### Husband-Wife Advice

Rav continues on the subject of a man's relationship with his wife, with a statement that at first appears to cut against everything that precedes it. Rav says: *kol haholech be'atzat ishto nofel b'Gehinnom* — anyone who follows his wife's counsel will ultimately fall into *Gehinnom*, invoking the verse: *rak lo hayah ke'Achav* — do not be like Achav, who followed the counsel of his wife Jezebel.

Rav Pappa raises the tension to Abaye: but do not people say — *ittech gutza, gachin vetilchosh lah* — even if your wife is short, bend down and have her whisper in your ear? That is, seek her counsel, value her wisdom. There are indeed precedents in the Gemara for great rabbis consulting their wives on practical matters.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya ha b'meili de'alma v'ha b'meili deveisa* — there is no difficulty; Rav's caution applies to worldly affairs, while the counsel about listening to one's wife refers to domestic matters. In questions of the household, she has direct knowledge and expertise, and her counsel should be followed. In broader worldly affairs, Rav counsels independence.

A second resolution is offered: *lishna acharina, ha b'meili dishmaya v'ha b'meili de'alma* — an alternative version distinguishes between spiritual and religious matters on the one hand, and practical worldly affairs on the other. On this reading, the wife's wisdom extends to all practical matters, including those beyond the household, and Rav's restriction applies only to religious determinations — a considerably narrower limitation, and one that grants women a substantially larger sphere of recognized wisdom.

---

## Gates of Heaven (II)

### Ona'ah Gate Open

Rav Chisda returns to the theme of the gates: *kol hashe'arim nin'alu chutz mishe'arei ona'ah* — all the gates have been locked except for the gates of *ona'ah*. The verse cited is: *hineh Hashem nitzav al chomat anach uveyado anach* — God is standing on a wall of *anach*, holding *anach* in His hand, with *anach* being read as *ona'ah*. God is not behind the wall, inaccessible; He is standing atop it, present and visible, ready to respond directly to those who have been afflicted through *ona'ah*.

### God's Direct Punishment

Rav Elazar sharpens this further: *hakol nifra bidei shaliach chutz me'ona'ah* — all punishment comes through an intermediary except for *ona'ah*, in which case God Himself exacts retribution directly. The same verse provides the support: *uveyado anach* — God is holding the *ona'ah* in His own hand. This is a significant theological statement: not all divine punishment involves direct divine action. Most operates through intermediaries — natural processes, human agents, historical forces. But when a person has been devastated through *ona'ah*, God personally intervenes.

### Three Direct Sins

Rabbi Abbahu adds a related teaching: *gimel ein hapargod ninal bifneihem* — there are three before whom the divine curtain is not locked: those who suffer from *ona'ah*, those victimized by *gezel* — theft — and those afflicted by *avodah zarah*. These three, unlike other transgressions, are direct affronts to God Himself. The *ona'ah* verse is *uveyado anach*; the verse for *gezel* is *chamas vashod yishama bah al panay tamid* — violence and plunder are constantly before My face; and for *avodah zarah*: *ha'am hamachisim oti al panay tamid* — the people who provoke Me to My face continually.

A theological coherence underlies this grouping. *Avodah zarah* is an obvious affront to God's face — the Torah itself says *lo yihiyeh lecha elohim acherim al panai*. *Gezel* desecrates the world that belongs ultimately to God — *laHashem ha'aretz umelo'ah*. And *ona'ah*, one might suggest, attacks the *tzelem Elokim* within the person — to crush the soul of one who bears the divine image is an affront to the face of God Himself.

---

## Household & Wife (II)

### Finances & Peace

Rav Yehuda teaches: *leolam yehei adam zahir bitvuah betoch beito* — a person should always be scrupulous about finances and provisions within his household, because *ein merivah metzuyah betoch beito shel adam ela al iskei tvuah* — the quarrels that arise in a home almost invariably concern matters of sustenance and financial pressure. The verse supports this: *hasam gevulech shalom chelev chitim yasbiech* — He makes your borders peaceful, and sates you with the finest grain. Peace at home is tied directly to material sufficiency.

### Barley Proverb

Rav Papa cites a common saying that captures the same idea: *kemishlam se'arei mikada, nakish va'ati tigra* — when the barley runs out of the jug, contention comes knocking at the door. This folk wisdom confirms the principle: financial strain is one of the most reliable generators of household conflict.

An additional teaching in the same vein: *shelo nikreu Yisrael dalim ela al iskei tvuah* — Israel was never described as truly impoverished except in relation to insufficient grain. The citation is the verse in which Israel is described as very poor in consequence of Midianite raids that depleted their crops.

### Wife's Honor

Rabbi Chelbo teaches: *leolam yehei adam zahir bichvod ishto she'ein bracha metzuyah betoch beito shel adam ela bishvil ishto* — a man should always be careful to give his wife honor, because the blessing in a man's house exists only on her account. The verse is: *ule'Avram heitiv ba'avurah* — and to Abraham it was good for her sake, with the Maharsha reading *heitiv* midrashically as God's goodness to Abraham accruing through Sarah's merit.

Rava accordingly told the residents of his city Mechuza: *okiru le'neshaichu ki heichi d'tisatru* — honor your wives, so that you will become wealthy. After the digression about when and whether to follow a wife's counsel, and after the proverbs about household finances, the Gemara returns emphatically to this note: the blessing of the household flows through her, and her honor is inseparable from its prosperity.

---

## Oven of Achnai

### Oven Purity Dispute

At this point the Gemara introduces one of its most celebrated narratives, cited at this juncture because its conclusion involves *ona'ah* and the power of its consequences. The Gemara opens: *chatcho chulyot v'natan chol bein chulya l'chulya* — if an oven made of pottery sections was broken into segments with sand placed between them, what is its status with respect to *tumah*? A broken pottery vessel no longer has the capacity to become *tamei*. But here, with sand separating the pieces rather than plaster, the question is whether this reconstructed arrangement is considered a complete vessel again. Rabbi Eliezer held it to be *tahor*; the *Chachamim* held it to be *tamei*.

### Achnai Etymology

This is the famous *tannur shel Achnai* — the oven of Achnai. Tosafot suggests that *Achnai* may be the name of a place, but the Gemara prefers a midrashic reading. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *shehikifu devarim k'achna zu* — they surrounded Rabbi Eliezer with arguments like a snake, circling him, and declared the oven *tamei*. The image of a snake encircling its prey captures the relentless argumentative pressure brought against him.

### Miracles Rejected

The Gemara relates what occurred on that day. Rabbi Eliezer brought all the arguments in the world and was not accepted. Frustrated by the refusal of the *Chachamim* to yield to his reasoning, he resorted to miraculous appeals. He said: if the *halacha* is according to me, let this carob tree prove it — and the tree uprooted itself one hundred *amot* from its place, some say four hundred *amot*. The Rabbis responded: *ein mevi'in re'aya min hacharuv* — one does not bring proof from a carob tree. That is a nice miracle, but it does not constitute a logical argument in *halacha*. If you cannot persuade us through reasoning, a supernatural feat proves nothing.

He then said: if the *halacha* is according to me, let this stream of water prove it — and the stream began flowing backwards. Again: *ein mevi'in re'aya me'amat hamayim* — you do not bring proof from a water channel. The Maharsha suggests that the reversal of the stream was symbolically significant: the Gemara compares Torah to water, which always finds the low ground, a metaphor for humility. Rabbi Eliezer may have been suggesting that the *Chachamim*'s arrogance was preventing them from genuinely hearing his arguments. Regardless of the symbolic intent, the response was the same — this is not how *halacha* is determined.

He then said: if the *halacha* is according to me, let the walls of the *beit midrash* prove it — and the walls began to tilt and lean, threatening to fall. Rabbi Yehoshua rebuked the walls: *im talmidei chachamim menatzchim zeh et zeh b'halacha, atem mah tivachem* — if Torah scholars are contending against one another in *halacha*, what business is that of yours, O walls? The walls did not fall out of respect for Rabbi Yehoshua, but they did not return to upright out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer — and they remain inclined to this day.

There is something worth observing here about the character of the dispute. Rabbi Eliezer, finding that logical argument had failed, appealed to supernatural signs. The Gemara's framing suggests he was trying to communicate that the resistance to his arguments was itself unnatural — against the grain of the world. The *Chachamim*, for their part, consistently refused to allow miraculous demonstrations to substitute for the internal reasoning of *halacha*.

### Lo Bashamayim Hi

Rabbi Eliezer then appealed directly to heaven: *im halacha kemoti min hashamayim yochi'chu* — let heaven prove that the *halacha* is according to me. A *bat kol* came forth and declared: *mah lachem eitzel Rabbi Eliezer shehalacha kemoto bechol makom* — why do you argue with Rabbi Eliezer? The *halacha* is always like him.

Rabbi Yehoshua rose to his feet and declared: *lo bashamayim hi* — it is not in heaven. This is the heart of the passage, and among the most audacious statements in all of rabbinic literature. Even a heavenly voice does not determine *halacha*. God gave the Torah at Sinai; the ongoing interpretation and application of that Torah is the province of human beings. Divine revelation has completed its role; human reasoning now governs.

The Gemara explicates: Rabbi Yirmiyah explains — *kvar nitna Torah me-Har Sinai, ein anu mashgichin b'vat kol* — the Torah was already given at Sinai; we do not heed a heavenly voice. The proof text is embedded in the Torah itself: *acharei rabbim le'hatos* — the rule that one follows the majority. God wrote into the Torah the very mechanism that now excludes His own direct intervention. The ruling of the *Chachamim*, arrived at through majority determination, is authoritative precisely because that is what the Torah requires.

### Elijah's Laughter

The Gemara then inserts a passage in Aramaic — marking it as a later addition that confirms and closes the story. Rabbi Natan encountered Elijah the Prophet and asked: *mai avid Kudsha Brich Hu b'hahi sha'ata* — what was God's response at that moment? Elijah answered: *kachayich* — He was laughing, *v'amar: nitzchuni vanai, nitzchuni vanai* — and He said: my children have bested Me, my children have bested Me. The word *nitzchuni* echoes the earlier framing of the dispute: *talmidei chachamim menatzchim zeh et zeh b'halacha* — the scholars competing for victory. But now they have prevailed even over God, and God accepts and even delights in it.

This passage reassures the reader: if there was any doubt whether the ruling of the *Chachamim* was genuinely correct, God Himself confirms it. He wanted it to be resolved by humans, and He accepts that outcome even where it contradicts what a heavenly voice had said.

### Burning & Cherem

The Gemara then describes what followed. That same day, the Rabbis gathered all the foods that Rabbi Eliezer had declared *tahor* in connection with this oven and burned them in fire. This was not merely a quiet halachic correction. It was a public and emphatic statement — they made unmistakably clear where the authority in *halacha* rested. Furthermore, they voted and placed Rabbi Eliezer in a form of *cherem* — excommunication — which echoes the laws of *zaken mamre*, of a scholar who refuses to accept the ruling of the highest court. The authority of the *beit din* requires that those who disagree submit to its procedures. Rabbi Eliezer's refusal to do so — his insistence that his ruling was correct regardless of the procedural outcome — was seen as potentially destabilizing to the entire system of halachic authority, and the *Chachamim* felt they had no alternative.

---

## Eliezer's Suffering

### Akiva's Mourning

The question of who would go and inform Rabbi Eliezer that he had been placed in *cherem* was itself a weighty one. He had to know, because the *cherem* required him to maintain four *amot* of distance from others. But informing him carelessly could trigger catastrophe — *nimtza machriv et kol ha'olam kulo* — as we have seen from his powers. Rabbi Akiva volunteered: *ani eilech* — I will go. His concern was that if an inappropriate person went, Rabbi Eliezer would feel dishonored by the messenger, and the resulting pain could be devastating.

Rabbi Akiva dressed himself entirely in black and sat four *amot* away from Rabbi Eliezer — in an openly visible act of mourning. He communicated the news through implication: *kemidumeh li shechaverim bdilim mimcha* — it appears to me that your colleagues are keeping their distance from you. He never used the word *cherem*. Rabbi Eliezer understood, and himself performed *keriah*, removed his shoes, and sat on the ground in the manner of one observing mourning.

### Tears' Destruction

Then: *vazalgu einav dema'ot* — his eyes flowed with tears. And the consequences were immediate and cosmic. One third of the olives, one third of the wheat, and one third of the barley in the world were destroyed. Some versions add: even dough in a woman's hands would spoil. Rabbi Eliezer's gaze — whether in pain, grief, or anger — burned whatever it fell upon. *Af gadol hayah ba'oto hayom* — there was great wrath on that day.

The connection to the earlier teachings about the gates of tears is now explicit. The Gemara has just taught that *sha'arei dema'ot lo nin'alu* — the gates of tears are never sealed — and that *sha'arei ona'ah* are never locked. Here, the tears of a *talmid chacham* who has been devastated by the actions of the rabbinic court — however justified those actions may have been — produce visible, tangible destruction in the world.

### Gamliel's Prayer

Rabban Gamliel, as *nasi*, had authorized the *cherem*. At that moment he was at sea. A great wave arose, threatening to swallow the ship. He recognized the cause: *kimdumeh li she'ein zeh ela bishvil Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrkanos* — this can be for no other reason than what we have done to Rabbi Eliezer. He stood and addressed God: *galui v'yadua lefanecha she'lo lichvodi asiti v'lo lichvod beit abba asiti* — it is known to You that I did not act for my own honor or for my family's honor, *ela lichvodecha she'lo yirbu machloket b'Yisrael* — but for Your honor, that disagreement not proliferate in Israel. The sea calmed.

This is a nuanced moment. Rabban Gamliel does not recant. He does not say the *cherem* was wrong. He affirms that it was done for the right reasons — for the integrity of halachic authority and the prevention of destructive *machloket* in Israel. And yet the wave arose. The pain of Rabbi Eliezer was real and had consequences even when the decision causing that pain was principled and necessary.

### Ima Shalom Guards

Ima Shalom, the wife of Rabbi Eliezer and the sister of Rabban Gamliel, understood this completely. From the day of the *cherem* onward, she never permitted her husband to perform *nefilat appayim* — the *Tachanun* prayer — because she feared that if he allowed his grief and sense of affliction to pour out in prayer, the consequences would be catastrophic. *Tachanun* begins *tzar li me'od niplah na b'yad Hashem* — I am in great distress, let me fall into God's hand — language of acute suffering, precisely the kind of prayer that, coming from Rabbi Eliezer, could call down destruction.

One day she became confused about whether the preceding month had been a full month of thirty days or a deficient month of twenty-nine, and therefore miscalculated whether it was *Rosh Chodesh* — on which *Tachanun* is not recited. Thinking it was *Rosh Chodesh*, she did not stand guard. In another version, a poor man came to the door seeking *tzedakah*, and while she stepped away to bring him a loaf of bread, Rabbi Eliezer managed to perform *nefilat appayim*.

### Gamliel's Death

When she returned, she found him already prostrate in prayer. She cried out: *kataltia l'achi* — you have killed my brother. And indeed, shortly afterward came the announcement — the *shofar* was sounded from the house of Rabban Gamliel, signaling his death. Rabbi Eliezer asked her: *mina yadat* — how did you know that would happen? She replied: *kach mekublani mibeit avi abba* — this is the tradition I received from my father's household: *kol hashe'arim nin'alu chutz mishe'arei ona'ah* — all the gates are locked except for the gate of *ona'ah*.

This is the conclusion toward which the entire narrative of the *tannur shel Achnai* was driving. The story of the oven, the miraculous signs, *lo bashamayim hi*, the *cherem*, Rabbi Akiva's black garments, the burning crops, the storm at sea — all of it was a vehicle to demonstrate the power of *ona'ah*. The pain of Rabbi Eliezer, however it was caused — whether through words, actions, burning his *taharot*, or formal excommunication — passed through ungated access directly to God, and its consequences could not be contained.

It is worth pausing over what this story is and is not saying. The *Chachamim* made a principled decision. Rabban Gamliel acted for the right reasons. And yet the story does not redeem those actions from their consequences. Sometimes a necessary and correct decision still causes genuine harm to a real person, and that harm does not cease to be harm because the decision was justified. The story insists that we hold both truths simultaneously — the rightness of the ruling and the reality of the suffering it caused. The victory cry of *nitzchuni vanai* does not cancel out *vazalgu einav dema'ot*.

---

## Ona'ah & Converts

### Convert's Protections

The Gemara closes the tractate's treatment of *ona'at devarim* with a focus on the *ger* — the convert. A *baraisa* teaches: *hama'aneh et hager over bishelosha lavin* — one who verbally afflicts a convert transgresses three negative prohibitions. One who monetarily oppresses a convert (*lochatzo*) also transgresses three, correcting an initial version of the text that had read only two.

The three *lavin* for verbal affliction are: *ger lo toneh* (Shemot 22:20), *lo tonu oto* from the verse *ki yagur itcha ger b'artzechem* (Vayikra 19:33), and the general *velo tonu ish et amito* — with the Gemara confirming that a *ger* is included in the category of *amito*, one's neighbor. The three for monetary oppression are *velo tilchatzennu* (Shemot 22:20), *v'ger lo tilchatz* (Shemot 23:9), and *velo tihyeh lo k'nosheh* — do not be upon him as a creditor, which applies to the monetary dimension of affliction.

### Repetition of Ger

Rabbi Eliezer Hagadol asks: why did the Torah repeat the prohibition regarding the *ger* in thirty-six places — some say forty-six, depending on how one counts? His answer is: *mipnei shesoro ra* — because his turning is bad, meaning that a person who has come from outside and joined the community is vulnerable to being made to feel marginal, and there is a real risk that harsh treatment will drive him away. The repeated emphasis serves as a constant reminder that the Torah takes the *ger's* position seriously precisely because of that vulnerability.

This explanation sits alongside the more intuitive one that the Torah itself supplies: *ki gerim hayitem b'eretz mitzrayim* — because you were strangers in the land of Egypt, and you know what it feels like to be treated as outsiders. The call to empathy grounded in historical memory is the *pshat* of the verse. Rabbi Eliezer Hagadol's reading adds a consequentialist dimension: beyond empathy, there is the practical concern that careless treatment of the *ger* will cause him to leave. Both motivations coexist.

### Personal Blemish

Rabbi Natan teaches: *mum she'bach al tomar l'chavercha* — a blemish that is in you, do not point out in your friend. This is a general principle about self-awareness before criticism.

### Glass Houses

The Gemara illustrates with a folk saying: *d'zakif lei zakifa b'dikutei, lo neima lei l'chavrei zakif binassei* — one whose family has had someone hanged should not say to his friend: would you hang up these fish for me? The word *zakif* — to hang — will inevitably call to mind the family disgrace, and what was meant as an innocent request will instead draw attention to a shameful history.

The application to the *ger* is instructive. The verse *ki gerim hayitem b'eretz mitzrayim* — ideally — calls on us to remember our own history of marginalization and to respond with empathy and solidarity. But for those who do not hear that call, Rabbi Natan's principle offers an alternative approach: before you point out that the *ger* comes from a different background, remember your own. The blemish you are about to expose in another may be found in yourself. Sometimes the road to ethical behavior runs through self-interest as much as through moral vision, and the Torah, in its wisdom, provides both paths.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 60

## Onaat Mamon & Devarim

### Opening & Dedication

Our learning today should be in the *zechut* of the protection of the *chayalim* and *chayalot*, the speedy end of the war, the return of the hostages, and a cessation of the horrific antisemitism spreading across college campuses — may this be a true *zman geulatenu* for all of us.

### Previous Topics Review

We pick up with the Mishnah on 59b, having concluded our treatment of *onaat mamon* — overcharging — and *onaat devarim* — causing pain through speech. We now return to the broader subject of honesty in business dealings. The concern is no longer overcharging in the strict sense, but misrepresentation and deception in commerce more generally.

---

## Mixing Produce

### Mishnah: No Mixing

The Mishnah opens: *ein me'arvin perot be-ferot afilu chadashim be-chadashim* — one may not mix fruit from one field into fruit from another field, even if both are of the same vintage, and therefore presumably the same quality. When a buyer purchases a bushel of grain or apples from a given field, he expects to receive produce from that field, and mixing in produce from elsewhere violates that expectation — even if there is no objective difference in quality. Needless to say, *chadashim be-yeshanim* — mixing new produce with old — is certainly prohibited, since old grain is generally superior: it is more ready to be ground into flour and therefore more desirable and more valuable.

### Wine Exception

The Mishnah introduces an exception: *be-emet amru be-yayin hitiru le'arev kasha be-rach mipnei she-mashbicho* — in truth they said that with wine it is permitted to mix harsh wine with soft wine, because the harsh wine actually improves the quality of the soft wine. The Gemara will clarify that *be-emet amru* signals an authoritative *halacha*. Rashi notes that by the same logic, one might add a small quantity of old grain into new grain when the result is genuinely an improvement. The principle is that mixing is forbidden when it deceives, but permitted when it produces a real qualitative enhancement that the buyer benefits from.

### Wine Lees Rules

The Mishnah further states: *ein me'arvin shimrei yayin be-yayin* — one may not mix the *shmarim*, the lees or sediment at the bottom of a wine vessel, into the wine itself. However, the Mishnah adds, *noten lo et shmarav* — one may give the buyer the lees that belong to that very wine. The precise meaning of this clause will be resolved in the Gemara.

---

## Diluted Wine Sales

### Diluted Wine Disclosure

In the time of the Gemara, wine was routinely mixed with water before drinking — sometimes at a ratio of three to one, sometimes six to one. This was not because ancient wine was especially potent, but because pure water was not reliably potable and wine served as the vehicle for producing a safe, palatable drink. In the normal course of commerce, however, wine was sold undiluted. If a seller found himself in possession of wine already mixed with water — whether by accident or for his own intended use — he may not sell it in his store, since buyers reasonably assume they are purchasing undiluted wine, unless he explicitly informs the customer: *mi she-nitarav mayim be-yaino lo yimkarenu be-chanut ela im ken hodio*.

### Middlemen Restriction

The Mishnah adds a sharper restriction: *velo le-tagar af al pi she-hodio* — one may not sell diluted wine even to a *tager*, a wholesaler or middleman, even if one informs him. The concern is that the *tager* will in turn sell it to storekeepers without disclosing its diluted state, or sell it directly to consumers without informing them. By handing him a product that is already diluted, one creates an irresistible temptation: the *tager* now bears the burden of disclosure with every subsequent sale, and he may simply not bother. Although this is not precisely *lifnei iver*, since the *tager* hardly needs one's assistance to add water to wine if he wished to deceive, nonetheless one is placing him in a situation of temptation and easing the path toward deception in a way that one must avoid.

### Standard Practice Except…

There is an important qualification: *makom she-nahagu le-hatil mayim be-yayin yatilu* — in a place where it is the accepted practice to dilute wine before sale, one may do so. When dilution is the norm, every buyer already knows what to expect, and there is no element of misrepresentation. The standard ratio — whether half, a third, or a quarter — should be observed according to local custom.

### Middleman Mixing

Having established the prohibition on mixing, the Mishnah introduces a seemingly contradictory permission: *ha-tagar notel me-chamesh geranot ve-noten le-toch magura achat, me-chamesh gitot ve-noten le-toch pitom echad* — a wholesaler may take grain from five different granaries and consolidate it into one storage facility, or take wine from five different wine presses and combine it into a single vat. This is not a contradiction of the earlier prohibition. When a buyer purchases directly from a farmer, he expects and is entitled to receive produce from that specific field. But when dealing with a *tager*, everyone understands that he aggregates from multiple sources. The buyer purchasing from the *tager* — or from a store that in turn purchased from the *tager* — does not assume he is receiving produce from a single field.

### Intentional Deception

The permission is not unlimited, however: *u-vilvad she-lo yehei mitkaven le'arev* — provided that the *tager* is not intentionally mixing in a deceptive manner. This does not mean that he is literally combining products by accident — obviously he is doing so deliberately. Rather, the prohibition is against mixing in a way designed to mislead. For instance, buying the bulk of one's stock from a single source but blending in a small portion from an inferior source in the hope that buyers will not notice — that is forbidden. When the mixing reflects normal wholesale aggregation that is transparent and understood by all parties, it is permitted.

---

## Grain & Wine Details

### Grain Price Reversal

The Gemara opens with a *baraita* that extends the prohibition on mixing grain. The obvious case is: *ein tzarich lomar chadashot me-arba ve-yeshanot mi-shalosh de-ein me'arvin* — needless to say that if new grain sells at four units for a *dinar* and old grain at three units for a *dinar* (the old being more expensive because it grinds more readily into flour), one may not mix new grain into old and pass it off as all-old. But the *baraita* goes further: *ela afilu chadashot mi-shalosh ve-yeshanot me-arba* — even if this year the new grain is actually more expensive, fetching three for a *dinar* while old grain fetches four for a *dinar*, one still may not mix the new into the old. Why? *Ein me'arvin mipnei she-adam rotzeh le-yashenan* — because a person who is buying old grain wants old grain specifically, even if new grain currently commands a higher market price. As Rashi explains, the reason new grain might sometimes be more expensive is that some buyers wish to purchase the raw new grain and age it themselves, participating in the process of drying and seasoning.
