Where neither of these concerns is present — where the favor is ordinary, voluntary, and privately understood by both parties to be entirely independent of the loan — the prohibition does not apply.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 65

## Slave Seizure & Ribbit

### Mishna Overview

The *mishnah* on this *daf* turns to the question of benefits that a lender receives which were not explicitly stipulated at the time of the loan, and yet — because the lender is receiving some advantage on account of the loan — the arrangement is classified as a form of *ribbit*. The *mishnah* addresses cases such as a lender renting something to the borrower at a discount, or a lender dwelling in the borrower's house without charge. The *Gemara* raises the discussion from Bava Kamma regarding *zeh nehene ve'zeh lo chaser* — one party benefits while the other incurs no loss — and notes that even a benefit with no assignable monetary value, something that would normally cost nothing and could not be collected upon in court, is nonetheless impermissible in the context of a loan relationship.

This prompts *Tosafot* to ask a pointed question: does this mean that a borrower may not do any favor for his lender that he would ordinarily do for others? Surely, if the favor is entirely routine and would have been extended regardless of the loan, it should not suddenly become *ribbit* merely because a loan exists. *Tosafot* answers that such ordinary, habitual favors would indeed remain permissible. The *mishnah*'s prohibition applies in one of two distinct situations: either the favor is highly public, so that even if it is technically unproblematic, observers will perceive it as *ribbit* — or the lender is not receiving an invitation but is rather unilaterally seizing the benefit. If the lender simply arrives and occupies the borrower's house without being asked, he is exercising the coercive power dynamic inherent in a lending relationship, and that assertion of power is precisely what makes the act prohibited, even when no enforceable monetary claim would otherwise exist.

### Slave Work Case

Against this backdrop, the *Gemara* introduces the case of Rav Yosef bar Chama, who seized the slaves of his debtors and put them to work on his behalf. On its face, this seems plainly problematic: the lender is extracting productive labor from the borrower's assets without any corresponding reduction of the debt.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava, Rav Yosef bar Chama's own son, confronted his father directly — addressing him, notably, as "master" — and asked: why does the master act this way?

### Rav Nachman Defense

Rav Yosef bar Chama replied that he was relying on a principle of Rav Nachman: *avda de-umkarsai lo shavei* — a slave is not even worth the cost of feeding him. In other words, the labor extracted from a slave is so minimal that it does not even offset the expense of his upkeep. By this reasoning, Rav Yosef was gaining nothing of real value from working the slave, and there would be no meaningful benefit to qualify as *ribbit*.

### Servants Differ

Rava pushed back: when did Rav Nachman make that statement? He was speaking about his own particular servant, Dari, who was notorious for dancing in taverns and doing no useful work. That kind of slave — utterly indolent — might fairly be said to produce less than his own food costs. But one cannot apply that principle to every slave as a blanket rule. By other slaves, Rav Nachman never said this. Accordingly, Rav Yosef bar Chama's debtors' slaves may well produce meaningful labor, and working them would constitute a real benefit — and therefore *ribbit*.

### Rav Daniel Position

Rav Yosef bar Chama then shifted to a second defense, citing a ruling of Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina in the name of Rav: one who seizes another person's slave and puts him to work is exempt from payment. This ruling seems to establish that using another's slave is not a compensable act.

### Master Benefits Logic

The *Gemara* explains the reasoning: *d'nicha leh d'lo nistaryei avdei* — the slave's master actually prefers that his slave remain occupied rather than idle. A slave left without work risks becoming indolent, and the master would not want that. Thus, paradoxically, working the slave is doing the master a favor, and there is consequently no actionable harm.

### Context Changes Rule

Rava's response, however, is decisive: *hani milei heicha d'lo masik bei zuzei* — that reasoning applies only when the person working the slave is not the slave owner's creditor. In that context, one might invoke the logic of *zeh nehene ve'zeh lo chaser* or simply the master's preference for a working slave. But once money is owed — *keivan d'masik bei zuzei michezi k'ribbit* — the entire situation is recast. Using the debtor's slave now has the unmistakable appearance of *ribbit*, regardless of whatever technical arguments might otherwise apply.

### Living in House Case

In support of this principle, Rava cites a ruling of Rav Yosef bar Minyumi in the name of Rav Nachman, which bears directly on our *mishnah*: even though the general rule is that one who dwells in another's courtyard without permission is not obligated to pay rent — a classic *zeh nehene ve'zeh lo chaser* scenario — if the dwelling party had previously lent the homeowner money, he is obligated to pay. *Halvahu v'dar b'chatzeiro tzarich le'haalos lo sachar*: after lending him money and then residing in his house, he must pay rent, because the arrangement is indistinguishable from *ribbit*.

### Concession

Upon hearing this, Rav Yosef bar Chama conceded: *hadri bi* — I retract. His son had successfully demonstrated that his conduct was improper.

This exchange is instructive on multiple levels. The prohibition here does not rest on a technically actionable monetary benefit — as noted, one could not normally sue for reimbursement in such cases. What makes it forbidden is the combination of context and initiative: the lender is acting on his own initiative, seizing what is not his in a relationship defined by his power over the borrower. *Eved loveh l'ish malveh* — the borrower is servant to the lender — and it is the exercise of that power dynamic, forcefully and publicly, that transforms an otherwise neutral act into *ribbit*.

---

## Ribbit Ketzuza Cases

### Interest Cases Intro

The *Gemara* now turns to a series of cases involving situations where *ribbit* is actually being charged — where parties knowingly enter into interest-bearing loans. It is striking, as it is in other areas of *halacha* such as *shemittah*, that the *Gemara* confronts the phenomenon of widespread violation directly and works through its practical consequences. The central legal backdrop is the question of *ribbit ketzuza yotze b'dayanim*: when interest is made explicit in a loan agreement, creating a Torah-level prohibition, can the borrower subsequently go to court to recover what he paid? The answer, as will be confirmed in the *halachic* rulings at the end of this section, is yes — and it is against that background that the following cases unfold.

### Grain Payment

Abayei presents the following scenario: a lender is owed one *zuz* of interest by a borrower. The market price for grain is four units per *zuz*. Instead of paying one *zuz* in cash, the borrower pays five units of grain — slightly more than the market equivalent of one *zuz*. The borrower now goes to court to reclaim his interest payment. The question: does he recover four units of grain (the exact market equivalent of the interest owed) or five (everything he actually paid)?

### Abayei's Rule

Abayei rules that only four units are returned. His reasoning is that the contractual *ribbit* obligation was for one *zuz* — equivalent to four units of grain at market price. The fifth unit was not part of any interest stipulation; rather, the borrower simply priced his grain favorably to the lender, valuing the five units as if they were worth only one *zuz*. That extra unit was either a voluntary discount on the grain or something resembling a gift — but it was not, in any technical sense, *ribbit ketzuza*. Since the court-ordered recovery (*mafkinan*) applies only to the explicitly stipulated interest, only what was formally required under the loan terms can be reclaimed.

### Rava's Counterargument

Rava disagrees: all five units must be returned. His reasoning is that in the totality of the transaction, the borrower was delivering the grain as an interest payment. Whatever the internal pricing might have been, the grain was handed over *ad'ata d'ribisa* — with the intention and understanding that it constituted the interest payment. Since the entire payment was made in the name of *ribbit*, the entire amount must be returned.

### Cloak Case

Abayei then advances a more extreme case: the borrower owes four *zuz* of interest and, instead of paying four *zuz* in cash, gives the lender a cloak — which is worth considerably more than four *zuz*. Now when the borrower seeks to recover his *ribbit* payment, what does the court order returned?

### Explicit Interest Only

Abayei maintains his position: only four *zuz* are returned in cash. The contractual *ribbit* was four *zuz*, and only that amount was formally stipulated. The excess value of the cloak was beyond any interest obligation; the borrower may have given it willingly as a gift or an overpayment, but the court cannot order its return because it was never part of the explicit *ribbit* term.

### Return All Property

Rava again disagrees, ruling that the entire cloak must be returned.

### Perception Problem

His reasoning here is subtly different from his position in the grain case. Rava acknowledges that the cloak clearly exceeds the value of the contractual *ribbit* — unlike the grain case, where the overpayment was marginal and could be analyzed as a valuation question. Here, there is no pretending that the cloak *is* the four *zuz*. Nonetheless, Rava insists on full return based on a perception concern: *ki heichi d'lo leimru glima d'michasi v'kai glima d'ribisa hu* — so that people not say, "that coat he is wearing is an interest coat." If the lender is seen wearing the cloak while it is known that he lends money with interest, the public perception of *ribbit* is unavoidable. The *Rambam*, it should be noted, appears to rule broadly that whenever a physical object is given as part of an interest payment — even if its value exceeds the amount owed — the entire object must be returned, reflecting Rava's general approach in both cases.

### House Rental Case

Rava himself then presents a third, more complex case. A lender is owed twelve *zuz* of interest by a borrower. The borrower has a rental house that normally commands ten *zuz* a month on the open market. The borrower and lender agree that the lender will rent the house and pay twelve *zuz* per month — the extra two *zuz* above market rate effectively serving as the monthly interest payment. At the end of the arrangement, the borrower goes to court to reclaim his *ribbit*. The question: does the lender return twelve *zuz* — the amount they agreed to attribute to the rent — or ten *zuz*, the actual market value of what he received?

### Lender Agreed

Rav Acha miDifti challenges the ruling, arguing in favor of the lender: when the lender agreed to the twelve-*zuz* valuation, he did so freely, knowing that the excess above market rate was being treated as profit — as his *ribbit* payment — and so he was willing to accept the inflated rate. Now that he is being compelled to surrender his *ribbit*, why should he be held to the inflated rental valuation? From the perspective of a neutral observer, what he actually received was a ten-*zuz* rental. He should only have to return ten.

### Accepted Terms

The response to Rav Acha miDifti is unequivocal: *savart vekibalt* — you understood the terms and you accepted them. The lender entered the arrangement on the understanding that the rental was worth twelve *zuz*. Having accepted that valuation — having treated it as a twelve-*zuz* benefit — he cannot now revalue it at ten when it suits him. He received twelve *zuz* of value by his own reckoning, and he must return twelve *zuz*.

### Borrower Protection

A broader observation emerges from this series of rulings: the analysis consistently tilts in favor of the borrower. While it is true that the borrower also transgresses in entering an interest-bearing arrangement, and there are *poskim* who address that dimension, the *Gemara*'s practical rulings reflect a certain sympathy for the borrower's position. The borrower is often, as the principle *eved loveh l'ish malveh* suggests, operating from a position of economic vulnerability — putting food on the table by whatever means available — while the lender is actively exploiting that need. The rules of recovery are calibrated accordingly, ensuring that the lender cannot retain any portion of what he extracted under the terms of the prohibited arrangement.

---

## Rental vs. Sale

### Mishna Rule

The *mishnah* states: *marbin al hasachar ve'ein marbin al hamekach* — one may increase the rental price for deferred payment, but one may not increase the sale price for deferred payment. Both involve delayed payment, yet the *halacha* treats them differently. The *mishnah* illustrates each case before the *Gemara* explains the underlying distinction.

### Rental Example

In the rental case: if you rent your courtyard to someone and say, "If you pay me now for the full year, it will be ten *sela'im*; if you pay month by month, it will be one *sela* per month" — that is permitted. Even though you are effectively charging twenty percent more for monthly payment, the arrangement is not considered *ribbit*.

### Sale Example

In the sale case: if you sell a field and say, "If you pay me now it is one thousand *zuz*; if you want to wait until the threshing floor when you will have cash from selling the harvest, it will be twelve hundred *zuz*" — that is forbidden. Both situations involve a higher price for later payment, yet only the rental is permissible.

This distinction has obvious resonance with modern financing arrangements. Car payments and mortgages operate on precisely this model: the buyer receives the asset immediately but lacks the full purchase price, so the lender effectively extends the balance as a loan with interest attached. What the *mishnah* is addressing is precisely that structure.

### Baseline Analysis

The *Gemara* asks: *mai shna reisha u'mai shna seifa* — what distinguishes the first case from the second?

### Discount vs. Interest

Rava and Rav Yosef answer jointly: *sechirus eina mishtalemes ela b'sof* — rental payment is not due until the end of the rental period. The tenant acquires the benefit of the rental — the use of the property — in monthly or annual increments, and the payment for each unit falls due only at the conclusion of that unit. Since the natural payment date for rent is the *end* of the period, the baseline rate is what you would pay at that time. When a landlord offers a discounted price for upfront payment, he is not charging extra for late payment — he is giving a *discount* for *early* payment. That is entirely permissible. The critical question is always: relative to the default payment date, are you adding a surcharge for lateness or offering a reduction for earliness? For rent, the default is end-of-period, so early payment merits a discount.

### Sale Baseline

For a sale, the analysis reverses. When you sell a field, payment is due immediately at the moment of purchase. If the seller agrees to accept payment later, he is postponing what is rightfully due now. Any premium attached to that later payment is therefore *agar natar* — compensation for delayed payment — which is *ribbit*, and is forbidden.

### Scriptural Basis

Rava adds that the Rabbis found the principle that rental is payable at the end of the period grounded in a *pasuk*: *kisechir shana b'shana* — like the rental of a year, by year. This was read to mean that the rental for a given year is paid at the beginning of the following year — that is, at the end of the rental period rather than at its start.

### Debt vs. Payable

This raises a question — familiar from the debate of *yeshna l'sechirus mitechila v'ad sof* versus *eina l'sechirus ela b'sof* — about when the rental obligation accrues. Does the tenant incur a debt moment by moment throughout the rental period, or only at its conclusion? *Tosafot* addresses this directly and draws an important distinction: even if one holds that the debt accrues incrementally throughout the period, the obligation to *pay* does not arise until the end of the period. The debt may be running continuously, but it is not yet *due*. Accordingly, a payment made at the beginning of the year is a payment made before the due date — an early payment that warrants a discount, not a late payment that incurs a surcharge.

---

## Tarsha & Pricing

### Rav Nachman Permits

Rav Nachman states: *tarsha shari* — *tarsha* is permitted. This comes immediately after the *mishnah*'s ruling that charging more for deferred payment in a sale is forbidden, which makes the ruling striking on its face.

### Tarsha Definition

*Tarsha* refers to a situation where a seller names a higher price for deferred payment without explicitly contrasting it to a lower price for immediate payment. In the *mishnah*'s forbidden case, the seller states both prices openly: "one thousand now, twelve hundred later." The two prices are placed side by side, making the surcharge for deferred payment explicit — the technical term for this is *katzlei*, meaning the seller has "cut" or articulated the two prices in contrast. *Tarsha* is different: the seller simply names a single price — twelve hundred — for whoever will be paying six months from now. No alternative price is stated. No contrast is drawn. The seller has not framed the higher price as a premium for lateness; it is simply the price.

The practical implication is consequential: if a seller quotes twelve hundred for deferred payment without ever mentioning that today's market price is one thousand, that is *tarsha* — and it is permissible, according to Rav Nachman, because the *ribbit* prohibition requires an explicit statement of the differential.

### Mishna Challenge

The *Gemara* immediately challenges Rav Nachman: but the *mishnah* forbids increasing the price for deferred payment. How can simply quoting a higher price for later payment be permissible?

### Explicit vs. Implicit

Rav Nachman's response is that in the *mishnah*, both prices were made explicit — the seller articulated the lower price for immediate payment and the higher price for deferred payment. In his case of *tarsha*, only one price is ever named. Without the explicit contrast, the transaction does not carry the prohibited structure of *ribbit*.

### Rav Pappa Case

Rav Pappa then advances his own claim: *tarsha didi shari* — my *tarsha* is permissible. He was in the beer business, and his case involves selling beer at the future higher price while allowing the buyer to pay later.

### No Lender Benefit

Rav Pappa's justification runs as follows: the market for beer in *Tishrei* is low — say, one *zuz* a barrel. By *Nisan*, the price will be higher. Rav Pappa sells beer now for the future price of one and a half *zuz* per barrel, payable in six months. Why is this permissible? *Shecharai lo passit* — his beer will not spoil. *Zozei lo tzarichna* — he does not need the money. He could just as easily store his beer, wait six months, and sell it then at the exact same price. The buyer is therefore not doing him any favor by purchasing now; Rav Pappa could achieve the identical financial outcome without the sale. The premium reflects the future market value, not compensation for any sacrifice or delay on the seller's part.

### Borrower Perspective

One might accept that from Rav Pappa's perspective, he loses nothing by waiting — but that is not the whole picture.

### Buyer's Need

Rav Sheshet's son challenges Rav Pappa directly: *mai chazei mar deka azlat batar didach* — why do you look at this only through your own eyes? *Zil batar dideihu* — look at the buyer's situation. If the buyer had cash available, he would be paying today's price — one *zuz* a barrel. Because he lacks ready cash — *deleis lehu zuzei* — he must pay tomorrow's price — one and a half. The buyer's lack of liquidity is what drives the higher price. That is precisely what *ribbit* is: the party in the weaker financial position ends up paying more than he otherwise would, because he needs something — in this case beer — but cannot pay for it today. The definition of *ribbit* cannot be determined solely from the seller's vantage point. Whatever Rav Pappa's financial comfort, the buyer is paying extra because of his own financial constraint — and that is the *neshech* dynamic the Torah prohibits.

---

## Distant Market Case

### Market Arbitrage

Rav Chama introduces a distinct case of *tarsha* that he considers permissible. A buyer takes the seller's merchandise to a distant market where prices are higher, pays for the goods at the higher distant-market price, and remits payment only after completing the sale there.

### Price Differential

The specific structure: goods worth one *zuz* here are worth two *zuz* at the distant market. The buyer takes the goods there, sells them for two *zuz*, and pays the original seller two *zuz* — double what the goods were worth at the point of transfer.

### Permission Granted

Rav Chama rules this *tarsha* permissible, and the *Gemara* explains why in terms of the concrete benefits that flow to all parties. The analysis involves several interlocking considerations.

### Product Insurance

First, the seller insures the product until it is sold at the destination. If something happens to the merchandise en route or before it is sold, the seller absorbs the loss even though the buyer has technically taken possession. This means the transaction is not, in the fullest sense, a completed sale in which the buyer now simply owes money. The seller retains a degree of ongoing interest in the merchandise — it is, to some extent, still effectively his product being carried to market on his behalf. This reframing significantly changes the character of the arrangement.

### Buyer Benefits

Second, the buyer derives concrete advantages from the seller's reputation and standing. Because the merchandise is associated with the seller, the buyer is exempted from import taxes that would otherwise apply — customs officials, knowing the goods belong to the prominent seller, waive the duty. Additionally, the buyer is given the first right to sell upon arriving at the market, ahead of other merchants. These are real, tangible benefits accruing to the buyer on account of the goods being associated with the seller.

### Favor Exchange

*Tosafot* develops the analysis further. Even granting that the seller's insurance of the product until sale means the transaction is effectively structured as the seller sending his own goods to market through an agent, there remains a question: the buyer is doing the seller a favor by transporting the merchandise to a market where it commands a higher price — two *zuz* instead of one. What is the buyer receiving in exchange for providing that service? The answer is that the seller effectively lends the buyer the sale proceeds after the sale is completed, giving the buyer the opportunity to use that capital to purchase cheap goods at the distant market and bring them back for resale at a profit. The buyer's service of carrying the goods to the higher-priced market is counterbalanced by the seller's lending of capital, and that exchange of favors — rather than a simple *ribbit* dynamic — is what makes the arrangement permissible.

---

## Halachic Rulings

### Rav Chama Ruling

The *Gemara* rules: *vehilchasa keRav Chama* — the *halacha* follows Rav Chama's position with respect to the distant market transaction. That case, notwithstanding its surface resemblance to *tarsha* with an explicit price differential, is permissible for the reasons explained.

### Ribbit Ketzuza

*Vehilchasa keRabbi Eliezer* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that *ribbit ketzuza yotze b'dayanin*: explicit interest stipulated in a loan contract constitutes a Torah-level prohibition and can be recovered through the courts. This was the implicit premise of the entire preceding series of cases involving *ribbit ketzuza*, and it is here confirmed as *halacha*.

### Rav Yannai Rule

*Vehilchasa keRav Yannai de'amar malihan mali dameihan* — the *halacha* follows Rav Yannai's ruling, which addresses a case where grain was pre-sold and payment later becomes due. Rather than delivering the grain, the party due to deliver may instead pay its current monetary value. Just as grain can be delivered, money representing its value can be delivered in its place — and this does not constitute *ribbit*.

---

## Tarsha & Pricing (II)

### Reconciliation

*Tosafot* resolves the apparent tension between the rulings of Rav Nachman and Rav Pappa regarding *tarsha*. Rav Nachman permits *tarsha* in the general case — where there is no established, publicly known market price against which the quoted price can be measured as a premium. Rav Pappa's case, by contrast, involved beer with a well-known current market price. Even though Rav Pappa never said the words "one *zuz* now, one and a half *zuz* later," the fact that the current price was universally known made the higher price for deferred payment functionally equivalent to *katzlei* — the explicit articulation of a two-price differential. It is therefore a case of contextually explicit *ribbit*, not genuine *tarsha*. We rule like Rav Nachman — *tarsha* without an established market price serving as implicit contrast is permissible — but not like Rav Pappa, whose situation involved a price comparison that was effectively explicit by virtue of public knowledge.

---

## Land Sale & Fruit

### Partial Payment

The *mishnah* presents a case involving the partial payment for a field with a deferred sale condition. Reuven sells Shimon his field; Shimon pays a portion of the purchase price and Reuven says: whenever you bring me the remaining balance, the sale will be effective — retroactively — as of today.

### Fruit Ambiguity

This creates a serious *ribbit* problem with respect to the produce (*peiros*) of the field during the interim period. If Reuven eats the fruit while waiting for Shimon to pay the balance, and Shimon ultimately pays and the sale goes through retroactively, then Reuven has consumed the fruit of what was retroactively Shimon's field while holding Shimon's partial payment — which looks precisely like *ribbit* on the partial payment Shimon advanced. On the other hand, if Shimon eats the fruit, anticipating that the field will retroactively have been his all along, but then fails to pay the balance — causing the sale to be voided and the partial payment returned — then Shimon has consumed the fruit of what turned out to be Reuven's field while Reuven held his money, again creating a *ribbit* problem. Since it is unknown at the outset which way the transaction will ultimately resolve, it is impossible to say in advance who is the borrower and who is the lender, and therefore neither party can permissibly eat the fruit.

### Third Party Hold

The solution offered is practical: neither party eats the fruit. Instead, the fruit is held by a third party. At the conclusion of the arrangement — once it is determined whether the sale was completed or voided — the fruit is distributed to whoever is retroactively identified as the owner of the field during the interim period. With that mechanism in place, the arrangement is permissible.

### Conditional Pledge

The *mishnah* then addresses a distinct but related case: a lender gives a loan and the borrower pledges his land as collateral, with the explicit agreement that if the loan is not repaid within a set period, the land becomes the lender's.

### Bisos Example

This was the practice of Bisos ben Zonin, conducted with the approval of the Sages: he would lend money, designate the borrower's property as the asset to be forfeited if repayment was not made within a specified grace period, and proceed accordingly. The property pledged might be worth more than the loan amount — which raises the question of why this is not itself a form of *ribbit*. One possible line of reasoning is that since repayment remains an option, there is a *tzad echad* — a possible outcome — under which no *ribbit* occurs at all, which connects to the dispute involving Rabbi Yehuda discussed below.

---

## Fruit Ownership

### Seller Eats

Rav Huna rules that in this case — where a partial payment was received — the seller eats the fruit during the interim period.

### Third Party

The Sages disagree and rule that the fruit is held by a third party until the ultimate status of the transaction is resolved. Rav Huna and the Sages are not in fundamental dispute; the difference lies in the precise terms of the transaction as expressed between the parties. When the seller says "you will own the field *when* you deliver the balance" — that is, ownership transfers only at the moment of final payment, with no retroactive element — then the field belongs unambiguously to the seller throughout the interim, and the seller may eat the fruit without any *ribbit* concern. But when the seller says "you will own it *as of now* when you pay the balance" — implying retroactive ownership — then the outcome is uncertain and the fruit must go to a third party.

---

## Land Sale & Fruit (II)

### Sequential Payment

The *mishnah* endorses a permissible alternative formulation: the sale is structured so that ownership transfers only at the moment of full payment, without retroactivity. Under this arrangement, the seller remains unambiguously the owner throughout the interim and eats the fruit as a matter of right, not as a consequence of any loan dynamic. Since the partial payment is simply a deposit and the sale is not yet complete, there is no loan relationship to speak of, and no *ribbit* issue arises.

---

## Fruit Ownership (II)

### Raba's Framework

Raba undertakes a systematic analysis of the *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Chiyya, which enumerates four possible configurations: both parties permitted to eat, both forbidden, seller permitted and buyer forbidden, and buyer permitted and seller forbidden. Raba supplies the conditions that generate each scenario.

### Proportional Share

Both parties may eat when the seller says to the buyer: "you own a proportional share corresponding to the amount you have paid." Shimon pays one hundred of a one thousand *zuz* purchase price, and Reuven says: you own ten percent of the field right now. Shimon may then eat ten percent of the fruit; Reuven eats the remaining ninety percent. The ownership is clear and proportional from the outset, and no ambiguity exists.

### Retroactive Ambiguity

Both parties are forbidden — the case of the *mishnah* — when the seller conditions full ownership on final payment with retroactive effect: "when you pay, you will own it as of now." Here, neither the outcome nor the ownership status during the interim is determinable in advance, and neither party may eat.

### Sequential Ownership

The seller is permitted and the buyer forbidden when the arrangement is purely sequential: "when you pay, you will own it" — meaning ownership transfers at the moment of payment, with no retroactivity. Until that moment arrives, the field is entirely the seller's, and he eats all the fruit without restriction.

### Immediate Ownership

The buyer is permitted and the seller is forbidden when the seller transfers full ownership immediately: "you own it right now." The remaining nine hundred *zuz* is then simply a loan the buyer owes the seller — a separate financial obligation unconnected to the ownership of the field. Since the buyer unambiguously owns the field from the outset, he eats all the fruit; since the seller now holds the remaining balance as a creditor, he must not eat any fruit that could be construed as interest on the debt.

### Rabbi Yehuda Dispute

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua adds that the rule prohibiting both parties from eating — the case of retroactive ownership — does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

### Tzad Echad Rule

Rabbi Yehuda holds *tzad echad b'ribbit mutar* — a situation that has *one possible outcome* in which no *ribbit* occurs is permissible, even if another possible outcome would involve *ribbit*. Applied to the retroactive sale case: if, at the end of the day, the sale goes through and Shimon eats fruit of what was retroactively his field, there is no *ribbit*. That the arrangement might have resolved otherwise — had Shimon not paid — does not, for Rabbi Yehuda, taint the transaction from the outset. The *mishnah*, which forbids both parties from eating, does not follow Rabbi Yehuda; it follows the Sages, who prohibit even the possibility of a *ribbit* outcome, regardless of whether it ultimately materialized.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 66

## Mishkeno, Asmachta

### Mishkeno Definition

The daf opens at a point roughly mid-page on *amud bet*, at the passage beginning *mishkeno lo bayit*. The word *mishkeno* is vocalized as *mishken*, derived from *mashkon* — collateral. The form is *binyan pi'el*, meaning the act of collateralizing. The broader context of the discussion concerns the practice associated with Baitus ben Zonin, and a major theme running through the entire daf will be the concept of *asmachta* — a conditional verbal undertaking whose legal force is the central question.

### Baitus ben Zonin

The *mishnah* describes a scenario in which a borrower pledges a field worth far more than the loan as collateral — a *mashkon*. The lender, knowing full well that repayment may be difficult, agrees to accept the field. Because the *mashkon* is worth significantly more than the loan, the structure of the transaction raises immediate concern: the borrower is not simply giving security equal to the debt, but potentially surrendering an asset of substantially greater value. The *mishnah* notes that the field should not be acquired except at a fixed price — *ve-lo tehe niknit lo ela bidamim hallalu* — and the discussion turns on what that price is and what legal consequences flow from it.

### Fixed Price, Ribit

The problem the *gemara* identifies is that the price fixed for the field is *less* than the market value of the field — less, in fact, than even the loan amount relative to the field's worth. If the borrower fails to repay and the lender takes the field at a below-market price, the lender effectively gains more than the face value of the loan, which is functionally equivalent to interest. If, on the other hand, the parties agree on the actual market value of the field — say, the field is worth one hundred and fifty and is sold for one hundred and fifty, with one hundred applied toward repayment of the loan and fifty returned to the borrower — then while the transaction may not be entirely at arm's length, it does not generate an *issur* of *ribit*. The rule articulated is: at market value, *mutar*; at a fixed reduced price below market value, *assur*.

The *gemara* asks: *man tana bedamim hallalu assur* — who is the *tanna* that holds that a fixed reduced price is forbidden? Rav Huna bar Yehuda answers in the name of Rav Yehoshua: this ruling is not consistent with Rabbi Yehuda, *de-lo ke-Rabbi Yehuda*, because if it were Rabbi Yehuda's ruling, it would be permitted — since Rabbi Yehuda holds that *tzad echad beribit mutar*.

### Tzad Echad Beribit

*Tzad echad beribit* — literally, one side of *ribit* — refers to a transaction where it is not inevitable that interest will result. There is a *machloket* among the *tanna'im* as to whether such uncertainty saves a transaction from the prohibition. Rabbi Yehuda holds that so long as there is no certainty that the arrangement will result in *ribit*, it is permissible. The rationale here is that the borrower retains the option to repay the loan in full. If he does so, no below-market sale occurs, no field changes hands at a discount, and no benefit accrues to the lender beyond the principal. Since the scenario where *ribit* materializes is only one possible outcome, Rabbi Yehuda would call this *tzad echad beribit* and permit it.

### Likshe'Tirtze Condition

The key phrase introduced at this point is *likshe'tirtze* — "if you decide to sell." The arrangement is not an irrevocable obligation to sell the field at a reduced price; rather, it is structured as: if you ever decide to sell, you will sell only to me, at this price. Since the borrower retains the option not to sell at all — to simply repay the loan and reclaim the field — it is not a foregone conclusion that the below-market arrangement will ever be triggered. This is precisely what makes it *tzad echad beribit* in Rabbi Yehuda's framework. The current ruling, however, which declares it *assur*, reflects the position of the Sages who do not permit even *tzad echad beribit*.

---

## Sale/Repurchase Cases

### Seller Repurchase Clause

The *gemara* turns to a series of cases involving sale with a repurchase arrangement. The *mishnah* presents: *machar lo bayit, machar lo sadeh* — someone sells a house or a field. In the first case, the seller says to the buyer, *kesheyihyu li ma'ot, hahzirem li* — when I have money, return it to me. That is, the seller, having sold the property, explicitly stipulates at the time of the transaction that the buyer must sell it back once the seller has the funds. This case is *assur*.

The key to understanding why this is forbidden is that the transaction looks structurally like a loan masquerading as a sale. The seller parts with the property only because he needs the money now, and the stipulation that the buyer must reverse the transaction once the seller is solvent exposes the arrangement for what it really is. The buyer holds the property for an extended period — perhaps a year or more — enjoys the *peirot* (the produce and use of the land), and then when the seller comes up with the money, returns it at the original price. The seller gets back exactly what he paid; the buyer gets the property and all of its benefits over the intervening period. This is functionally equivalent to interest on the original sum, which is why it is *assur*.

### Buyer Repurchase Offer

The second case reverses the direction of the stipulation: *kesheyihyu lecha ma'ot, achzirem lach* — the buyer says to the seller, "when you have money, I will return it to you." Here, it is the buyer who voluntarily offers a repurchase right to the seller. This case is *mutar*. The contrast is striking, and the *gemara* immediately turns to analyzing what distinguishes the two.

### Peirot Problem

Why is the first case *assur*? The answer is that the seller's stipulation at the time of the sale that the buyer must return it creates what amounts to a loan structure. The buyer holds the property throughout — collecting the *peirot*, the produce and benefits of the land — and then simply hands it back when the seller repays the original sum. The buyer has thus received exactly what a lender receives from interest: use of the property over the loan period, returned to him at the end. This is the *peirot* problem — the buyer's enjoyment of the field's yield during the interval is the equivalent of *ribit*.

The analysis also touches on whether the repurchase price matters — whether it would be worse if the repurchase were at the original price rather than the current market price. If the repurchase price is the same as the original sale price, the arrangement is even more transparently loan-like, since neither party bears any market risk. If the repurchase price is the current market value, the buyer at least in principle absorbs fluctuation in the land's worth. Either way, the problem of *peirot* during the intervening period remains, since the buyer has had the use of the property throughout and returns it at some fixed price.

The Ramban, noted in the commentary, holds that such a transaction does not go through at all — it is void — which is consistent with the ruling that it is *assur* not merely on a rabbinic level but structurally invalid.

### Distinction Analysis

*Mai shna reisha u-mai shna seifa* — what distinguishes the first case from the second? Rabbah formulates the distinction as follows: *reisha de-lo amar lada'atei, aval seifa de-amar lei lada'atei* — in the first case, the buyer did not say the return would be at his discretion (*leda'atei*), while in the second case, the buyer did say it would be at his discretion.

The word *achzirem* — "I will return it to you" — as spoken by the buyer in the second case, carries an implicit qualification of voluntariness. The buyer is not binding himself irrevocably; he is saying, in effect, *likshe'irtze* — if I choose to. This is in contrast to the first case, *hahzirem li* — "return it to me" — which is a demand or stipulation embedded in the sale itself, from which there is no escape. One side is locked in; the other is not. That asymmetry is legally decisive.

### Leda'atei Voluntary

Rabbah clarifies: the permissibility of the second case rests on the word *leda'atei* — at his discretion, if he wants to. *Leda'atei* imports *ratzon*, will or desire. *Achzirem* is understood by the *gemara* to imply this voluntariness: I will return it to you, if I so choose. *Hahziram li*, by contrast, is a stipulation, a condition of the sale itself, that admits no discretion.

The principle being developed here is that where a party is genuinely locked in — where the commitment is binding and inescapable — the arrangement becomes functionally a loan and triggers the *ribit* prohibition. Where the commitment is discretionary, it remains a true sale with an independent and optional future transaction.

---

## No Warranty Sale

### Achrayut Assumption

The *gemara* now introduces a case involving *achrayut* — warranty or guarantee — in the sale of land. As a background principle, *karka* — real property — is normally assumed to carry *achrayut*. There is a concept of *achrayut ta'ut sofer*: if a land deed omits the standard warranty clause, we treat it as a scribal error and read the guarantee in anyway. This is in fact the ruling of Shmuel, and it is the normative *halacha*. Therefore, for the following case to even be legally coherent, it must involve a contract that explicitly stipulates there is no *achrayut* — because otherwise the warranty would be implied by law.

### Seller's Promise

A man sold land to another party *shelo be-achrayut* — explicitly without warranty. This means the seller made clear: if a creditor of mine comes and seizes this land from you, I will not compensate you. Having sold the land on these terms, the seller later saw the buyer looking distressed — *chazayah de-havah ka atziv* — visibly upset about the exposure he had taken on. The seller then approached the buyer and said, in effect: don't worry. *I metzarfu lah minach magvinah lach shufra ve-shivcha u-feirei* — if it is seized from you, I will make you whole: I will compensate you for the enhanced value of the property, for any improvements you made, and for the produce you would have received. He promised to cover everything.

### Pitumei Mili

Ameimar rules on this promise: *pitumei mili be'alma hu* — it is nothing more than empty words. The term *pitumei* means to fatten up, as one fattens livestock; the image is of words that puff someone up without substance. Rashi explains: *ein elu ela divrei tanchumim be'alma lifayeso* — these are merely words of comfort to appease him, without legal effect. The contract already stipulated explicitly that there would be no warranty. The seller's subsequent verbal reassurance cannot override what was written, because it was never intended as a binding commitment.

### Wrong Side Stipulation

Rav Ashi challenges Ameimar: *ta'ama mai* — what is the reason for saying *pitumei mili*? He frames the question analytically: *mishum de-lo'keach ba'ei le-itnuyei* — normally it is the buyer who stipulates the protective conditions in a transaction. The buyer is the one spending money, and the buyer has every incentive to demand guarantees. The seller, by contrast, wants to minimize his post-sale obligations. Therefore, when we see the *seller* making these generous promises, we know something is off — it is not the natural role of the seller to volunteer such guarantees, and that very unnaturalness is evidence that he didn't really mean it.

### Seller's Incentive

Rav Ashi's reasoning sharpens the point: the seller is the *wrong* party to be making these stipulations. A buyer entering a real estate transaction demands title guarantees, freedom from liens, and protection against every contingency — that is the buyer's natural behavior. The seller's natural interest is to shed responsibility as quickly as possible and hand over the property free of ongoing obligation. When the seller spontaneously volunteers expansive guarantees after the sale has already been closed on explicitly warranty-free terms, it is precisely because this is out of character that we can infer he didn't truly mean it. Hence: *ve-hacha mochar ka matni* — here it is the seller making the stipulations — and that is why it is *pitumei mili be'alma*.

### Promise as Leda'atei

The *gemara* ties this back to the principle established earlier. Rabbah's explanation — that the permissible repurchase case works because the buyer said *leda'atei*, at his discretion — is applied here analogously. In the case of Ameimar, the seller made his promise after the sale, not as part of the original contractual terms. Since it was done after the sale, the *gemara* treats it as if the seller had said *likshe'irtze* — "if I choose to." Even though he did not literally use that language, the fact that the promise came after the transaction had already concluded, under terms that specified the contrary, means we read it as though he said "I will consider it." And since it is discretionary and unenforceable, it carries no legal weight. *Na'aseh ke-man de-amar lei leda'atei* — it is treated as if he said it would be at his discretion, and therefore it is indeed *pitumei mili*.

The underlying principle being crystallized is: a commitment made after the fact, particularly when it runs contrary to the written terms of the original agreement, is presumed to be non-binding, because the very timing signals that it was not meant seriously. Had the seller said *leda'atei* at the time of the sale — and had he truly meant it — it would have been a valid, enforceable commitment. But where the promise post-dates the sale and contradicts the written terms, it is structurally equivalent to saying "if I want to" — and is therefore empty.

---

## Get, Pitumei Mili

### Deathbed Get

A *shechiv mera* — a man on his deathbed — gives his wife a *get*. The reason a dying man would give a *get* at this point is to spare his wife from *yibum*: were she to be left a *yevamah*, she would need to undergo *chalitzah* or *yibum* with her husband's brother. To preempt this, he divorces her on his deathbed so that she dies as a divorcée, not as a widow. The man, however, groans — *angid ve-itnach* — and sighs as he hands over the *get*, expressing his reluctance. His wife, moved by his hesitation, says to him: *i kaymet ana didach* — if you live, I will remain your wife. She is offering a kind of comfort: do not be so distressed; if by some miracle you recover, I am yours.

### Wife's Words Insignifica…

Zeiri rules: *pitumei mili de-amrah* — what she said is mere comforting words, legally empty. Just as in the previous cases, the post-hoc verbal declaration carries no binding force.

### Wife Cannot Condition Get

Rav Acha of Difti challenges Zeiri before Ravina: *ve-i lav pitumei mili, mai?* — but even setting aside *pitumei mili*, what would the problem be? The underlying question is: does she even have the legal power to impose conditions on a *get*? A *get* is the husband's instrument to give; it is he who sets its terms and conditions. *Biyada kayma le-mishdei tna'ah be-gitta?* — is it in her power to attach conditions to the *get*? The answer is categorically no. She has no standing to condition the validity of the *get* on anything. If that is true, why invoke *pitumei mili* at all? The *get* is valid on its own terms regardless of what she says; her statement cannot undo it in any case.

### His Da'at Governs

The *gemara* answers: the reason we invoke *pitumei mili* despite the fact that she lacks the power to condition the *get* is as follows. One might have thought: *hu gufeih ada'ata de-didah ka gamar ve-yahiv gitta* — he himself completed the act of giving the *get* with her statement in mind; that is, perhaps his own *da'at* — his intention — was contingent on her declaration, such that he gave the *get* on the assumption that her statement constituted a condition. If his *da'at* were thus contingent, the *get* might be compromised. Therefore, *ka mashma lan* — the ruling teaches us that her statement is *pitumei mili*: since her words carry no legal force, his *da'at* cannot have been genuinely contingent upon them, and the *get* is entirely valid. The operative principle here is not about her capacity but about *his* intention: we rule that he could not have understood her words as a binding condition, and therefore his *da'at* in delivering the *get* was unconditional.

This case thus represents a further step in the development of the concept. Earlier, we saw *pitumei mili* applied to verbal promises that were made after the fact. Here, the ruling applies not even to a verbal promise but to the effect that verbal words might have had on the inner intention of the other party — *da'at* in the most subjective sense. The conclusion is that since the words themselves have no legal substance, they cannot infect the *da'at* of the one who acts.

---

## Baitus Field Case

### Loan Terms

The *gemara* returns to the case of Baitus ben Zonin, now analyzed at greater length. The basic structure is: a lender extends a loan of one hundred and the borrower pledges a field worth three hundred as *mashkon*. The agreement is that if the borrower does not repay within three years, the field becomes the lender's — *im lo natati lecha mikan ve-ad shalosh shanim harei hi sheli*. The lender, under this arrangement, would receive a three-hundred-dollar asset in satisfaction of a one-hundred-dollar loan. This is the core tension: why is this not *ribit*?

### Timing Distinction

Rav Huna introduces a critical distinction based on timing: *be-sha'at mattan ma'ot* versus *achar mattan ma'ot* — whether this condition was established at the time the money changed hands or afterward.

### At Loan Time

If the condition was stipulated *be-sha'at mattan ma'ot* — at the moment the loan was extended — Rav Huna holds that *kanah ha-kol*: the lender acquires everything. The rationale is that a condition made contemporaneously with the transaction is part of the deal itself. The borrower, at that moment, is making a genuine agreement, and the full value of the field is what he has put on the line.

### After Loan Time

If the condition was established *achar mattan ma'ot* — after the money was already lent — then *lo kanah ella ke-neged ma'otav*: the lender acquires only what corresponds to the actual value of the loan, not the full field. A post-hoc verbal condition, as we have seen throughout the daf, carries the character of *pitumei mili* or at least of a non-binding declaration. The borrower, having already received the money, is in no position to make a serious pledge of his entire field; the statement is dismissed as insufficiently grounded.

### Document Torn, Reversal

Rav Nachman, consistent with his own ruling, drafted documents in accordance with the principle that *be-sha'at mattan ma'ot kanah ha-kol*. Rav Yehuda — presumably Rav Yehuda bar Yechezkel — tore up one of these documents. When Reish Galuta heard that his document had been torn, he reported this to Rav Nachman. In one version of the exchange, Rav Nachman asks: *dardaka karaye?* — did a child tear it up? — meaning: can I dismiss the concern? The answer comes back: *gavra rabbah karaye* — a great scholar tore it up. *Chaza bah ta'ama ve-karaye* — he must have seen a reason to do so, and I must reconsider. In the alternate version, Rav Nachman says *dardaka karaye* as a statement, dismissively — a child tore it up and knows nothing — and then proceeds to justify this with the general principle that *halacha ke-Rav Nachman be-dinei*, that in monetary law we rule with Rav Nachman. On this version he adds: *de-kulei alma le-gabei didi be-dinei dardakei ninhu* — compared to me in monetary law, everyone else is a child.

### Rav Nachman Reversal

Regardless of which version one follows for the exchange with Reish Galuta, the *gemara* records that Rav Nachman ultimately reversed his position entirely: *afilu be-sha'at mattan ma'ot lo kanah ve-lo klum* — even when the condition was stipulated at the time the money was lent, the lender acquires nothing. This is a complete *hadar*, a reversal, which at minimum follows from the first version of the story where Rav Nachman acknowledged that Rav Yehuda must have had a compelling reason.

The logic of the reversal is rooted in the concept of *asmachta*. The borrower pledges a three-hundred-dollar field for a hundred-dollar loan and says: if I don't pay, it's yours. The question is whether this verbal commitment — however solemn it sounds — reflects a genuine, serious *da'at* to transfer the field. Rav Nachman concludes that it does not. The borrower says this because he wants the money now and is not thinking realistically about losing his field; he never genuinely intends to forfeit an asset worth three times the loan. Therefore the condition is an *asmachta*, and *asmachta lo kanya* — an *asmachta* does not effect an acquisition. The consideration of *meshichah* — physical taking — as a possible way to validate the acquisition is also noted; the issue of whether an act of *meshichah* could have been used to effectuate the *asmachta* arises in the surrounding discussion.

---

## Asmachta Validity

### Asmachta Lo Kanya

Having arrived at Rav Nachman's final position, the *gemara* now addresses it directly. Rav Nachman holds: *asmachta lo kanya* — an *asmachta* does not effect a valid acquisition under any circumstances. This is a categorical ruling: verbal undertakings predicated on future contingencies, where the obligor does not truly intend to be bound, have no legal force.

### Mishnah Position

But this creates a problem, because our *mishnah* appears to say otherwise. *Matnitin* — the *mishnah* — through the position of Rabbi Yose, states: *asmachta kanya* — such a condition does effect an acquisition. The Baitus ben Zonin practice, which the *mishnah* records approvingly, appears to validate exactly the kind of contingent pledge Rav Nachman is rejecting.

Rav Nachman responds: *ani amar asmachta kanya, u-Minyumi amar asmachta lo kanya* — I used to hold that *asmachta kanya*, and it was Minyumi who convinced me to change my position to *asmachta lo kanya*. So the question about the *mishnah* should be addressed to Minyumi, not to me. And the *gemara* asks accordingly: *Minyumi, kashya mi-mishna* — how does Minyumi answer the *mishnah*?

### Me'achshav Timing

Two answers are offered. The first: *matnitin Rabbi Yose de-amar asmachta kanya* — the *mishnah* follows Rabbi Yose, who holds that *asmachta kanya*, but that is not the accepted ruling. Minyumi does not hold like Rabbi Yose.

The second answer: *iba'it eima amar lei kani me'achshav* — one can say that the *mishnah* involves a case where the borrower said the acquisition takes effect *me'achshav*, from now, in the event that he does not repay. This formulation is different in kind from a standard *asmachta*. When the lender receives the field *me'achshav* — immediately, at the time of the loan — the forfeiture is not a distant, abstract contingency three years in the future. It is a present reality: the field belongs to the lender now, subject to being reclaimed upon repayment. That concreteness makes the borrower's commitment serious; he is not dealing in hypotheticals. The three-year deadline is the window within which he may buy it back, not the moment at which the transfer occurs. This is why *me'achshav* removes the arrangement from the category of *asmachta*: the transfer is immediate and real, not contingent and speculative.

### Neharde'i Rule

The *gemara* records a version of Rav Nachman's ruling attributed to the scholars of Nehardea: *hachi amri Neharde'ei mishmeih de-Rav Nachman: asmachta bizmanei kanya, ve-lo bizmanei lo kanya* — an *asmachta* acquires within its time period, but does not acquire outside its time period. This is understood to mean: if the borrower reaffirms or invokes the condition *within* the period of the loan — before the due date — the *asmachta* takes effect; if he does so after the time has elapsed, it does not.

The sons of Rav Chisda — one called *yanuka* (the younger) and one called *kashisha* (the older) — press on this formulation: *ke-midi bizmanei kanya ve-lo bizmanei kanya* — what does "in its time" even mean? Everything is either at its time or not; the formulation seems to need clarification. The *gemara* explains: *dilma hachi ka-amar lei, ashkacheih be-go zimneih ve-amar lei kani* — perhaps what the Nehardea rule means is that if the lender encounters the borrower *within* the loan period and the borrower at that point says, "go ahead, take it, the field is yours," this declaration is effective and the lender *koneh* the field. The idea is that within the loan's active period, the borrower is still in a posture of voluntarily offering the pledge; the relationship is ongoing, the commitment is still fresh and alive.

### Seriousness Analysis

Rashi explains the Nehardea position with characteristic precision: *de-gemar ve-akni de-i lo amar lei, lema amar lei, halo einecha achshav be-tovah* — he clearly means what he says, for why else would he say it? If the lender is currently holding him to nothing — the loan is not yet due, there is no crisis — and the borrower voluntarily says "take the field," this is a sign of seriousness. He doesn't *have* to say it. There is no pressure on him. The fact that he volunteers this information, when his eyes are currently enjoying a good situation, demonstrates genuine intent. Therefore, within the loan period, the declaration is effective and the *asmachta* acquires.

### Borrower Intent

The *gemara* ultimately rejects even this: *ve-lo hi* — this is not so. *De-afilu be-go zimneih nami lo kani* — even within the loan period, the *asmachta* does not acquire. The reason: *ve-hai de-ka-amar lei kani, kasavar ki mati zimneih lo leite litardeni* — when the borrower says "take it" during the loan period, his motivation is simply to avoid being pestered. He knows the due date is coming; if he does not pay, the lender will appear at his door every day demanding the money. By preemptively saying "if I don't pay, the field is yours," he is buying himself peace of mind until the due date. He doesn't actually intend to forfeit the field — he just doesn't want to be bothered. The moment after the due date arrives and he has not paid, the lender starts coming to collect, and then the embarrassment (*kissufa*) of the post-deadline encounter is what drives any further declarations.

In neither case — neither within the loan period nor after — does the borrower truly, seriously intend to transfer the field. The *asmachta* reflects an aspiration or a social gesture, not a genuine act of *kinyan*. Rav Nachman's final position is therefore unequivocal: *asmachta lo kanya* — categorically, an *asmachta* does not effect an acquisition. The daf ends with this ruling in place, with the full halachic analysis of when it applies and what distinguishes it from valid conditional transfers yet to be developed further.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 67

## Asmachta Mechanics

### Asmachta Conditional

The sugya opens with a statement of Rav Papa on daf 66b, beginning approximately ten lines down: *hai asmachta zimnin kanyia ve-zimnin lo kanyia* — an *asmachta* sometimes effects an acquisition and sometimes does not. By way of background, an *asmachta* refers to a conditional transaction of a futures nature, classically where a borrower stakes a piece of land against a loan, with the lender acquiring the land outright if the loan is not repaid by a fixed date. The fundamental rabbinic concern is that the borrower never fully resolves in his mind to transfer the property, since he fully expects to repay in time, and therefore the conditional sale lacks the definitive mental commitment that a valid *kinyan* requires.

### Bar Drinker Case

Rav Papa illustrates the distinction with a behavioral test case: *ashkechei de-ka shati shakhra, kani* — if one finds the borrower at the tavern drinking, the *asmachta* takes effect. But *de-ka mehapekh a-zuzi lo kani* — if he is out searching for money to repay the loan, the *asmachta* does not take effect. The underlying logic is that a borrower idling at a tavern demonstrates that he has effectively resolved to let the deadline pass, and the conditional sale therefore acquires force. A borrower scrambling to find the funds, by contrast, has not abandoned his intention to repay, and the condition never fully crystallizes into a binding transfer. This reasoning has structural parallels to the *sugyot* in Ketubot dealing with *ones be-gittin*, where a husband who set a deadline for a *get* but was delayed en route faces analogous questions about intent and timing.

Rav Acha mi-Difti challenges Rav Papa's test by raising two alternative readings of the tavern scenario. First, *dilma lefakhukhei pakhdei ka shati* — perhaps the borrower is drinking precisely to dull his anxiety, as Rashi explains, drowning his sorrows rather than acquiescing to the loss. Second, *ei nami inash achrina asmakhyei a-zuzi* — perhaps another person has already promised to lend him the money. Either possibility undermines the inference that sitting in the tavern signals genuine abandonment of the right of redemption, leaving Rav Papa's behavioral test inconclusive even in the paradigm case.

### Precision Doctrine

Ravina proposes an alternative criterion: *ei kappid bidmei, vadai kani* — if the borrower was precise about the monetary amount, the conditional sale definitively takes effect. Rav Acha mi-Difti pushes back here as well, suggesting that the borrower's monetary precision may simply reflect a desire not to let the field depreciate in value — in other words, his precision is about self-interest in the transaction, not a wholehearted commitment to the conditional sale. In response, Rav Papa reformulates: *ei kappid be-ara, vadai kani* — if the borrower is precise and insistent about the land itself, then the *asmachta* takes effect. The underlying conceptual point in both alternatives is that the determination of whether an *asmachta* is valid turns on assessing the seller's subjective mental state — whether his mind was fully settled on the conditional transfer — and that different contextual facts bear on that assessment in different ways.

### Asmachta→Apothiki

Rav Papa then introduces a further principle: *af al gav de-amru rabanan asmachta lo kanyia, apotiki havei le-migba minei* — even though the Sages ruled that an *asmachta* does not effect a sale, the failed *asmachta* can nonetheless function as an *apothiki*. An *apothiki* is the designation of a specific property as the source of repayment for a loan. The lender does not acquire ownership of the field, but the field is earmarked as the asset from which the debt will be collected. Thus, Rav Papa argues, even where the conditional sale is void, the transaction retains legal force as a lien designation.

It is worth pausing here to note the broader taxonomy. *Asmachta*, *mashkon*, and *apothiki* are all distinct forms of collateralized obligation, each with its own *halachic* rules, even though colloquially we might group them together. *Shi'abud* in its general sense is a blanket lien on property, without any particular designation. *Apothiki* is the specific designation of a field as the source of repayment — but as the *gemara* will clarify, there are two gradations even within *apothiki*: the field designated as the primary source, or the field designated as the exclusive source.

Rav Huna the son of Rav Natan challenges Rav Papa: *mi ka'amar lei kani l'migvaya minei* — did the borrower ever actually say that the field was being designated for collection purposes? The language of the *asmachta* was a conditional sale, not a declaration that this field was to be the exclusive means of repayment. The attempted *apothiki* reading therefore lacks explicit textual grounding.

### Mar Zutra Challenge

Mar Zutra, son of Rav Mari, presses the challenge to Ravina: if the borrower explicitly said "acquire this field so that the loan may be collected from it," that would indeed sound like *apothiki* — but *sof sof Asmachta hi* — in the end, that is still an *asmachta*, since the sale remains conditional on non-repayment. The distinction Rav Papa draws between *asmachta* and *apothiki* thus threatens to collapse.

The *gemara* therefore clarifies what Rav Papa's *apothiki* case must actually look like: *lo yehei lach pir'on ela mizo* — the borrower declares that the lender shall have no recourse for repayment other than from this particular field. This is not a primary designation with fallback alternatives; it is an exclusive designation. The exclusivity is precisely what distinguishes the *apothiki* from the *asmachta*. In an *asmachta*, the borrower retains the option to repay in cash and thereby redeem the property — which is why his mind never fully settles on the transfer. In an exclusive *apothiki*, there is no alternative, and therefore the nature of the transaction is categorically different.

---

## Field Designation

### Flood & Fields

The *gemara* presents a case involving a field sold with a quality guarantee (*achrayut*). The seller guaranteed that if a creditor with a prior lien seized the field from the buyer, the seller would compensate from his own best land. The buyer asked: may I collect from your *idei idit* — your finest of the finest field? The seller replied that he wished to retain that field for himself, and offered instead to pay from his next-best field, the *idit*. The parties proceeded on that basis. Subsequently, the creditor did indeed seize the guaranteed field, and the buyer came to collect from the seller's *idit* field. Before he could do so, however, a flood washed away the seller's *idei idit* — the superior field that had been excluded from the guarantee.

### Quality Ranking

Rav Papa initially inclined to rule that the seller must still compensate from the *idit* field, since it physically exists and the guarantee was made against that specific field. Rav Acha mi-Difti challenges this position: *ki amri lach ana magvina lach d'hava idei idit kamai* — the reason the seller agreed to offer the *idit* field was precisely because he still had his *idei idit* field as his personal reserve. Now that the *idei idit* has been destroyed by the flood, the *idit* has effectively moved up in rank to fill that role. *Hashta kaima lei idit bi-mkom idei idit* — at this point the *idit* stands in the place of the *idei idit*, and the seller should therefore only be required to provide from the medium-quality field, since that is now what corresponds to the relative tier that was originally guaranteed. The conclusion the *gemara* leans toward is that the designation of field quality is relative rather than absolute. If the top-tier field is lost, the rankings shift downward by one, and the guarantee adjusts accordingly.

---

## Wine Collateral

### Wine=Currency

The *gemara* presents a case: Rav Bar Bar Shva owed Rav Kahana money, and declared that if he did not repay by a certain date, Rav Kahana could take his wine. This is structurally parallel to the earlier cases involving fields and conditional transfers. Rav Papa sought to argue that the laws of *asmachta* do not apply here: *hani mili be-ara, de-lav le-zavuni kaima* — the Sages' ruling that *asmachta lo kanyia* refers specifically to land, which is not normally in a state of market readiness. *Aval chamra keivan de-le-zavuni kai ke-zuzei dami* — wine, however, since it is essentially a commodity ready for sale, is comparable to currency itself. On this view, pledging wine against a loan is no different from pledging cash, and no *asmachta* problem arises.

### Futures Doctrine

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua counters by citing a tradition in the name of Rabbah: *kol de-ee lo kani* — any transaction structured as a conditional future does not effect an acquisition. The *asmachta* rule applies equally to movables, including wine, and the distinction between land and commodities is insufficient to eliminate the *asmachta* concern. This definitively closes the argument Rav Papa had sought to open.

---

## Asmachta Void

### Land & Produce

Rav Nachman now states: *hashta de-amri rabanan asmachta lo kanyia, hadar ara ve-hadar peiri* — now that the Sages have ruled that an *asmachta* does not effect an acquisition, both the land and all produce harvested during the period of the ostensible acquisition must be returned. The logic is straightforward: if the sale was invalid from the outset, the lender held the field without legal title throughout, and all fruits of the field collected in the interim must be disgorged.

### Mistaken Forgiveness

From this ruling, the *gemara* infers that Rav Nachman must hold *mechilah be-ta'us lo havei mechilah* — a waiver made under mistaken assumptions does not constitute a valid waiver. The reason this inference is necessary is as follows: the borrower and lender had both agreed to the *asmachta* arrangement, and both presumably understood that the lender would enjoy the field's produce during the loan period. One might argue that the borrower's acquiescence amounts to *mechilah* — a voluntary relinquishment of his rights to that produce. Rav Nachman's insistence on returning the produce demonstrates that he rejects this possibility. Since the borrower agreed under the mistaken belief that the *asmachta* sale was legally effective, his apparent *mechilah* was premised on a legal error, and *mechilah be-ta'us* does not stand.

### Date Futures Test

A *baraita* is adduced as a challenge to Rav Nachman's position. The *baraita* discusses the case of one who sells another person the future produce of his date palm: *ad she-lo bau la-olam yachol lachzor bo* — until the dates have actually come into existence, the seller may retract. Rav Nachman is cited as ruling *af misheba'u la-olam yachol lachzor bo* — even after the dates have come into existence, he may retract. This appears to follow from the *asmachta* principle: such a sale of futures is inherently defective, and either party retains the right to withdraw. But if Rav Nachman allows retraction even after the dates exist, then presumably the produce gathered during the period of the agreement cannot all be reclaimed. Does this not contradict his ruling that produce must be returned when *asmachta* fails?

### Consumed Fruits

Rav Nachman defends himself: *modina de-ishmit ve-akhil lo mafkinan minei* — he concedes that if the fruits were actually consumed, they cannot be extracted from the holder. The requirement to return produce applies only where the produce remains identifiable and extractable. If it has been entirely consumed, two compounding considerations converge. First, the *mechilah be-ta'us* analysis: even if the waiver was defective, practically speaking there is nothing to recover. Second, and more technically, there is the principle of *davar shelo ba la-olam* — the sale of something not yet in existence. The fruits of the date palm did not exist at the time of the original transaction, and the sale of such futures is generally unenforceable. These two considerations intersect in the *asmachta* context: the question of when the dates are considered to have "come into the world" — *ba la-olam* — determines the point at which retraction is no longer possible, while the *mechilah be-ta'us* doctrine governs what must be returned when the transaction is unwound. The *gemara* notes that a further distinction applies: in a case of sale (*zevinei*) as opposed to a loan (*halva'ah*), the *asmachta* concern operates differently. In the loan context, the transaction sits much closer to the domain of *ribis*, and this proximity introduces additional stringency, as Rashi notes: *mekhzei ke-ribit she-mitkhila be-halva'ah ba leh, ve-ke-ribit ketzutzah dami* — it resembles interest that arose out of a loan from the outset, and appears similar to explicit prohibited interest.

---

## Ona'ah & Ilonit

### Rava's Challenge

The *gemara* relates that Rava was once sitting before Rav Nachman and wished to challenge him from the laws of *ona'ah*, though he was forestalled when Rav Nachman perceived the question and pre-empted with the answer of *ilonit*. The reconstructed challenge runs as follows: every case of *ona'ah* is by definition a case of *mechilah be-ta'us*. A buyer overcharged in a transaction presumably does not complain if the overcharge is less than a sixth (*shtus*) of the purchase price — and yet that acquiescence operates precisely because the buyer believes he is paying fair market value. The buyer is *mochel* under mistaken assumptions about price. If so, one might argue that *mechilah be-ta'us* here *is* in fact valid *mechilah* — which would contradict Rav Nachman's principle. This presents a potential refutation (*tiyuvta*) of Rav Nachman's position.

### Ilonit Exception

Rav Nachman is understood to have anticipated the *ona'ah* challenge and gestured toward the case of *ilonit* as his response. The *mishnah* rules that an *ilonit* — a woman who does not develop normal secondary sexual characteristics and is typically unable to bear children — forfeits her *ketubbah*, *peiros*, *mezonos*, and *bla'os* in the event of divorce. The situation is one of *mekach ta'us*, a transaction entered under mistaken terms: the husband married on the presumption of normal circumstances, and the marriage is effectively re-evaluated once the wife's condition becomes known. Nonetheless, despite the apparent *mechilah be-ta'us* on the wife's part — since she presumably would have assented to reduced financial protections in order to secure marriage (*denicha lah de-tipuk aleih shma de-ishus*, as Rashi explains, she benefits from acquiring the social standing of a married woman) — the Sages structured the ruling to facilitate her marriage. The *ilonit* exception thus reflects a broader principle: public policy considerations can override the ordinary logic of *mechilah be-ta'us*, allowing the law to treat an apparent waiver as effective even where a strict *mechilah be-ta'us* analysis might not support it.

### Ona'ah Rebuttal

A later *amora* steps in to observe that neither the *ona'ah* challenge nor the *ilonit* answer is actually persuasive. *Lo ona'ah tyuvta velo ilonit mesay'a.* The *ona'ah* case is not a valid challenge because the overcharged buyer was never engaged in a conscious *mechilah* at all. *De-lo yadei de-isye ona'ah de-machil gabeih* — the buyer did not know he was being overcharged and therefore had nothing to waive. He thought he was paying market price. This is categorically different from the *asmachta* case, where both parties entered the arrangement with full awareness that a conditional transfer was being made. In *asmachta*, the borrower actively agreed to a deviant transaction; the only question is whether his *mechilah* of those rights was vitiated by his mistaken legal assumption. In *ona'ah*, there was no conscious *mechilah* of any kind, because the discrepancy in price was entirely unknown to the buyer. The two cases are therefore not analogous, and *ona'ah* fails to serve as a counterexample to Rav Nachman's *mechilah be-ta'us* doctrine.

---

## Redemption Case

### Repurchase Agreement

The *gemara* presents a case: a woman asked an agent to purchase a field on her behalf from one of her relatives. The agent did so. Afterward, the seller asked the agent: *ei havu li zuzei, mahadrat lah nihali?* — if I later obtain money, will she sell it back to me? The agent responded with the expression *at ve-navla achai* — roughly, "you and she are like siblings," implying of course she will accommodate you. There is a dispute in the commentaries over whether *navla* is the woman's name or simply an Aramaic term for sibling; either way, the agent is guaranteeing the seller an informal right of repurchase.

### Buyer's Intent

The *gemara* notes that because of this assurance, *samcha da'tei ve-lo gamar u-makni ara* — the seller's mind was put at ease and he never fully resolved to transfer the field irrevocably. Does this mean the original sale was incomplete? And if the buyer later conveys the field back to him, must she also return the produce (*hadar peiri*) she collected in the interim? These are the animating questions. If the seller's mind was never fully settled on the sale, one might treat the arrangement as an *asmachta*-type transaction, triggering the *mechilah be-ta'us* analysis — and by Rav Nachman's principle, produce would need to be returned along with the land.

### Abaye's Questions

Abaye presses several questions to Raba: how do we categorize the nature of this arrangement? Is the underlying agreement an *asmachta*? Does it raise concerns of *ribis ketzutzah* — explicit prohibited interest that can be remedied in court — or only *avak ribis* — the more attenuated "dust of interest" that is halachically problematic but cannot be extracted by a *beit din*? The *nafka mina* between these two categories is precisely whether a court case lies. Rabbah bar Rav Huna offers his assessment: *mistabra ke-avak ribis havei, ve-ein yotzin be-dayanim* — it appears that this arrangement is *avak ribis*, not actionable in court. Rava is then cited in agreement with that framing.

The broader question Abaye raises about *mashkon* parallels this case: just as the woman's informal repurchase agreement was problematic because *delo katz* — the value was imprecisely defined — similarly a *mashkon* arrangement in which the lender harvests produce of indeterminate value over an indefinite period also suffers from the same lack of precision. Whether it is then categorized as a sale or a loan is a further distinction: in the loan context, the *ribis* concern is even more acute, since *avak ribis* touching a loan more closely resembles the prohibited forms of interest.

### Ravina's Ruling

Rav Papi reports that Ravina actually adjudicated this type of case in practice: *ve-chashiv ve-afik piri* — he calculated the value of the produce and required it to be returned. This was contrary to the ruling of Rabbah bar Rav Huna, who had held that *avak ribis* is not recoverable in court.
