The question becomes whether an *apotropos* making a financial agreement for a minor is acting as the minor's agent, in which case the minor is the one "doing" it, or whether the *apotropos* is the actor. The rule of *ein shaliach l'devar aveira* would typically apply to an agent acting on another's behalf for a prohibited act — but the *beis din* functions differently from an ordinary agent. The underlying rationale for the leniency, according to those who limit it to *d'rabbanan*, is that the rabbinic requirements may be eased for the sake of ensuring the financial welfare of orphans.

### Rav Nachman Objects

Rav Nachman sharply objects: *mishum de'yasmei ninhu safinan lehu issura* — just because they are orphans, are we to feed them something that is *assur*? He invokes the general principle that if a minor is engaged in transgression, *beis din muzarin lo* — the community has an obligation to intervene and stop it, much as we do not simply permit a child to eat *neveilos* on the grounds that the child lacks personal obligation. That principle itself, as a side matter, generates a whole *sugya* in *Yoma* about which categories of *issurim* — *issurei cheftza* and *issurei gavra* — are subject to this requirement.

Rav Nachman goes further: *yatmei d'achlei d'lav did'hu lizlu basar shavkaihu* — orphans who profit from something that is not truly theirs will end up following those who came before them, that is, following their parents to the grave. This is a severe curse. It is not entirely clear whether Rav Nachman is declaring the practice outright *assur* or whether he is condemning it as a harmful practice even if technically permissible.

### Mar Ukva Cauldron

A *she'eilah* arises: given Rav Nachman's objection, what was the actual case that prompted Shmuel's ruling? Rav Anan replies: *hahu duda d'vnei Mar Ukva de'hava bei Mar Shmuel* — there was a large cauldron belonging to the children of Mar Ukva (who was presumably deceased, leaving them orphans) that was kept at the house of Mar Shmuel. Shmuel would rent the cauldron out to others for profit on behalf of the *yetomim*. He would weigh the cauldron when it went out and weigh it again when it came back — *takil v'yahiv lei, takil v'shakil lei*. Why? Because *shakil agra v'shakil pachta* — he collected a rental fee for the use of the cauldron and he also collected the amount corresponding to the decrease in the weight of the pot, that is, the depreciation caused by corrosion or burning off of the metal in use.

The challenge: *ei agra lo pachta, v'ei pachta lo agra* — this is the same objection raised earlier regarding the boat. If you collect a rental fee, you should not be able to collect depreciation, and if you collect depreciation, you should not also be collecting a rental fee, because the combination begins to look like *ribbit*.

One might ask why depreciation in this context raises *ribbit* concerns at all. The intuition behind the question is that *ribbit* is fundamentally a combination of a loan and a sale — I lend you something and charge you for that right, which is the core problem. When you combine a loan-like structure (borrowing the pot and returning it) with an additional charge (for the diminished value of the metal), you create the same structural tension: is this a sale — in which case the borrower effectively purchased the lost metal and should pay for it, but then there is no separate rental fee — or is it a borrowing, in which case the renter simply returns the object as-is? Combining both modes is what generates the *ribbit* issue.

### Measurable Depreciation

Shmuel's response to the challenge in the cauldron case is: *ki ha afilu bididkanani nami shari lemeivad* — this transaction, the dual charge of rental and depreciation, would be permissible even for bearded men, that is, even for fully grown adults to perform, and it is not a special *kula* devised solely for the benefit of orphans.

Why? Because in the case of a copper cauldron used over a fire, *mekablei aleihu chuska denachsha*, there is a real corrosion of the copper: *dechama demeklei nachsha batsir damei* — the more you use a copper vessel over flame, the more the metal corrodes and the more the value of the pot measurably declines. Because the depreciation in this case is entirely quantifiable — you can weigh the pot before and after and see exactly how much metal has been lost — the dual charge is not *ribbit* at all, but rather two genuinely separate and measurable obligations: a fee for use and a charge for the objectively demonstrable reduction in value.

The term *dekanani*, bearded men, is noteworthy. It sets the bar not merely at those who have reached the age of *mitzvot* (twelve or thirteen) but at those who have reached a fuller social maturity. This raises the further question of how the *yetomim* exception operates when the orphans in question are adults. The principle *gadol hasomech al shulchan aviv nikra katan* — an adult child who is still financially dependent on his parents is considered, for certain financial *halachot*, to have the status of a *katan* — may extend the *yetomim* leniencies further than one might initially suppose. There is a charming story of the Vilna Gaon encountering an abbreviation written in someone's *Chumash* next to the *pasuk* *et hamaor hagadol lemshelet hayom ve'et hamaor hakatan lemshelet halaila*, and instantly deciphering it as an allusion to this very principle: the moon, despite its great light, is called *maor hakatan* precisely because it derives its light from the sun — *gadol hasomech al shulchan aviv nikra katan*.

## Orphan Investments

### Risk Profiles

A separate tradition is cited: Rabba bar Shila in the name of Rav Chisda — or in another version, Rabba bar Yosef bar Chama in the name of Rav Sheshet — rules that *ma'ot shel yetomim mutar lehalvosan karov liskhar verakhok lehefsed* — it is permissible to invest orphans' money in arrangements that are close to gain and distant from loss, that is, high-return and low-risk. To understand why this requires a special permission, the *Gemara* cites a *baraita*.

The *baraita* articulates three investment profiles. A case which is *karov liskhar verakhok lehefsed* — easy to profit and low-risk — characterizes a *rasha*: a wicked person. Why? Because in such a business arrangement, one partner carries all the risk while the other enjoys the easy gain, and the disadvantaged partner gets the short end of the deal. Conversely, a case which is *karov lehefsed verakhok liskhar* — high risk and a low payoff — characterizes a *chasid*: a righteous person who goes out of his way to avoid exploiting the other party, taking more risk and less return than strictly necessary to ensure he does not come anywhere near *ribbit*. Finally, a case which is *karov lazeh velazeh rakhok mizeh umizeh* — equitable in both directions, sharing risk and return fairly — represents *midas kol adam*, the standard of ordinary decent people.

The implication is that ordinarily entering into an arrangement that is *karov liskhar verakhok lehefsed* would be exploitative and condemned. For *yetomim*, however, a special permission is granted: precisely because we have a communal responsibility to protect their financial welfare, we allow their guardians to seek out arrangements that would normally characterize a *rasha* — arrangements that favor the orphans' interests at the expense of the other party.

### Rabba's Question

Rabba then poses the practical question to Rav Yosef: *hani zuzei d'yetomim heikhi avdinan lehu?* What are we actually supposed to do with orphans' money? What investment structure would constitute the permitted *karov liskhar verakhok lehefsed*?

### Initial Suggestion

Rav Yosef's initial suggestion is: *motbinan lehu be-vei dina ve'yavinan lehu zuzu zuzu* — we place the money in the custody of the court and pay it out to them coin by coin, like an annuity disbursed over time.

### Principal Concern

Rabba immediately objects: *veha ka-kalya karna* — but the principal itself is being consumed. That is, what Rav Yosef has described is not an investment at all; it is simply placing money in the bank and drawing it down over time. There is no growth, no return — only a steady depletion of the original capital. This is inadequate as a long-term strategy for sustaining the orphans' estate.

### Gold Nugget Investment

Rabba responds with his own proposal: *badkinan gavra de'it lei dehava perikha* — we should identify a person who holds gold nuggets, specifically not gold coins, and *venaktinan dehava minei ve'yavinan lehu nihaleih* — we take the gold from him and pay it back to him, and that arrangement constitutes *karov liskhar verakhok lehefsed*.

Rashi explains the significance of gold nuggets as opposed to coins: *grutot shel zahav devadai shelahen* — gold nuggets can be presumed with confidence to belong outright to the person holding them, since people do not typically deposit unworked gold nuggets as a *pikadon* with someone else. Coins, by contrast, could belong to a third party who deposited them. Furthermore, *bekivan de'ashir hu* — since the person is clearly wealthy, *yesh lo ligabot mimenu im yavdu ma'otav* — if the orphans' investment funds were somehow lost, there would still be sufficient assets from which to collect. This combination of clear ownership and financial stability makes the investment structurally sound, providing the orphans with a high-probability return at minimal risk.

The contrast being drawn is not that the orphans are doing something shady. Rather, they are placing their funds with a reliable, demonstrably solvent investor, someone whose assets are unencumbered and whose capacity to make good on the investment is not in doubt.

### Rav Ashi's Standard

Rav Ashi raises a practical challenge: *teinach, ei mishtakach gavra de'is lei de'hava paricha* — fine, this works if you can find such a person who happens to have gold nuggets. But *ei lo mishtakach gavra de'is lei de'hava paricha, nichlu zuzei de'yasmei?* — if you cannot find such a person, is the orphans' money simply to be consumed and spent down entirely?

Rav Ashi therefore proposes a more general standard: *chazinan gavra de'meshafu nachsei* — we identify a person who is doing well in his business affairs, *u'meheman* — and who is trustworthy, *ve'shama dina de'Oraita* — and who observes the laws of the Torah, *ve'lo mekabbel shamta de'rabbanan* — and has never been placed under rabbinic *shamta*, and *ve'yahavinu lehu nihaleih be'vei dina* — we give the funds to him through the *beis din*. 

The requirement that this be done through *beis din* is itself a matter of discussion among the *Rishonim*. Rashi understands it to invoke the principle of *hefker beis din hefker* — the court's power to reassign property in order to ensure the orphans receive a fair arrangement. Other *Rishonim* suggest that the court's involvement is needed either to formally appoint the *apotropos* for this transaction or simply to provide proper judicial oversight. The broader point is clear: investing the orphans' estate is not merely a practical recommendation but a genuine communal obligation, and the court's involvement lends it both legal force and structural protection.

The underlying economic intuition is sound and the *Gemara* itself takes it seriously: simply holding money in reserve means the orphans' estate will gradually be consumed by living expenses. Finding an investment with a genuine positive return — one that allows the orphans to live off the profits and maintain their estate over time — is the proper and responsible course.

## Tzon Barzel

### Tzon Barzel Definition

The *mishna* at the top of 70b states: *ein mekablin tzon barzel mi'Yisrael mipnei she'hu ribbit* — one may not enter into a *tzon barzel* arrangement with a fellow Jew because it constitutes *ribbit*. Rashi defines *tzon barzel* as an arrangement in which *kol achrayus hanechasim al hamekabel* — the entire responsibility for the assets rests on the one who receives them. One investor provides all the capital, the other partner does all the work, and at the end of the arrangement the initial investment is fully guaranteed to be returned to the investor. Meanwhile, the parties split the profits during the course of the business. The problem with this arrangement between Jews is that the lump-sum payback of the original seed money, on top of the profits already shared, turns all of those accumulated profits into *ribbit*: the investor effectively lent money, enjoyed a share of the profits as though it were interest, and then reclaimed the principal.

### Non-Jew Exception

The *mishna* continues: *aval mekablin tzon barzel min ha'akum* — but one may accept a *tzon barzel*-type investment from a non-Jew. One may borrow from non-Jews and lend to them with *ribbit* — real *ribbit d'oraita*. *Vechen beger toshav* — and the same applies with respect to a *ger toshav*.

The question of who qualifies as a *ger toshav* is a significant *machloket* discussed in Masechet Sanhedrin. Rashi's description seems to suggest that the qualifications are simply that the person does not worship *avodah zarah* but nonetheless eats *neveilos*, non-kosher meat. Most other *Rishonim*, however, understand *ger toshav* to be defined by acceptance of the *mitzvot Bnei Noach*, and the *Gemara* in Bechoros seems to require that the person actually come before *beis din* and formally declare acceptance of *ger toshav* status.

One of the major *sugyot* touching on *ger toshav* involves a person who comes to *beis din lekabel divrei Torah chutz midavar echad* — wishing to accept the laws of the Torah except for one thing. The rule is *ein mekablin oto* — such a person is not accepted. The question is whether this *sugya* is addressing conversion to Judaism, where refusal to accept even one *mitzvah* disqualifies the candidate, or whether it is addressing acceptance as a *ger toshav*, where the one thing not being accepted might be the prohibition against eating *neveilos*. This question has significant implications for understanding conversion *halacha* and the *sugya* in Bechoros, and it is a matter of genuine disagreement.

### Bechoros Contradiction

The *Gemara* identifies a contradiction between our *mishna* and a *mishna* in Bechoros. The *mishna* in our passage implies, from the very fact that *tzon barzel* is characterized as *ribbit*, that the invested assets are considered to have passed into the ownership of the *mekabel*, the Jewish business partner. If the assets still belonged to the investor, there would be no *ribbit* — one cannot charge *ribbit* on something that remains in one's own possession.

However, the *mishna* in Bechoros states: *hamekabel tzon barzel min ha'akum, vlados peturin min habechora* — one who accepts a *tzon barzel* arrangement from a non-Jewish investor, the offspring of the sheep involved are exempt from *bechora*. A firstborn male animal owned by a Jew would normally be subject to the laws of *bechor* and would have to be brought as a *korban*. An animal owned by a non-Jew is exempt. The fact that the offspring are exempt in the *tzon barzel* case implies that the animal remains, in some sense, in the ownership of the non-Jewish investor — not the Jewish partner — which directly contradicts our *mishna*'s implication that the assets transfer to the *mekabel*.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye proposes a resolution. He says: *lo kashya ha demikabel alei onsa uvisola* — there is no contradiction. Rashi adds the word *nochri* to clarify that Abaye is referring to the non-Jewish investor. In one case, the non-Jewish investor accepted upon himself *onsa uzola* — liability for unexpected catastrophic loss (*ones*) and for market depreciation (*zola*). In the other case, the non-Jewish investor did not accept *onsa uzola* upon himself. In the case where the investor bears the risk of loss and price fluctuation, ownership effectively remains with him — and that is the Bechoros case, explaining why the offspring are exempt from *bechora*. In the case where the *mekabel* bears all the liability, ownership is treated as having transferred — and that is our *mishna*, explaining why the arrangement constitutes *ribbit*.

### Rava's Alternative

Rava objects to Abaye's resolution. His first objection: *ei d'kabil alei marei onsa uzola* — if the investor accepted upon himself *onsa uzola*, *tzon barzel karis lei?* Can you still call that *tzon barzel*? The entire point of *tzon barzel* is that the investment is ironclad and fully guaranteed. An investor who accepts responsibility for catastrophic loss and market depreciation has undermined the very essence of the arrangement; it is no longer *tzon barzel* at all.

Rava's second objection: the *seifa* of the *mishna* states that one may accept *tzon barzel* from a non-Jew. If Abaye's resolution were correct, the *mishna* should have distinguished internally — there should be a case within the *mishna* itself where it is and is not called *tzon barzel*, rather than offering the broad permission to accept it from a non-Jew as a separate rule. Rava therefore concludes that any case where the investor accepts *onsa uzola* is simply not *tzon barzel* and would be permissible even with a Jewish investor.

### Rava's Explanation

Rava therefore proposes an alternative resolution that maintains both *mishnayot* as speaking about the standard *tzon barzel* case — where the investor does *not* accept *onsa uzola*, and the *mekabel* bears all liability. *Idi ve'idi delo kabla alei marei onsa vezola* — in both cases, the investor has not accepted *onsa uzola*. 

The question then becomes: why are the offspring exempt from *bechora* in Bechoros if the assets seem to have transferred to the Jewish partner? Rava explains: *keivan de'ilo hai zuzei ati nochri tapis lah lebehema* — if the Jewish partner is ever unable to pay back the *tzon barzel* investment in cash, the non-Jew retains the right to physically seize the sheep themselves. *Ve'ilo meshkach lah lebehema, tapis lah levladot* — and if the original sheep are no longer available, the non-Jew will seize the offspring to satisfy the debt.

### Yad Nochri

Therefore, *vahavei lei yad nochri be'emtza* — the non-Jewish investor retains a residual claim over the partnership, a legal "hand in the pot." And *vechol yad nochri be'emtza patur min habechora* — whenever a non-Jew has such a residual ownership claim over an animal, even a partial one, the animal is exempt from the laws of *bechor*, because it is a case of *shutfus*, joint ownership. Even a partial non-Jewish claim over the animal is sufficient to remove it from the framework of *bechora*.

## Kedusha & Humans

### Taz on Bechor

The *Gemara*'s analysis prompts a broader theological reflection on the nature of *kedusha* and human participation in divine designations. The laws of *bechor* present an interesting internal tension: most of the relevant *halachot*, and even the language of the *Torah* itself, indicate that the *bechor* is *kadosh merachem* — it becomes entirely holy from the moment of birth, even from the moment of conception in a sense. Its *kedusha* is intrinsic, automatic, and divine in origin.

Yet many *mishnayot* and *beraitos* speak of a person actively being *makdish* — formally designating — a *bechor* animal, as though the *kedusha* requires human designation to take effect. The Taz, in his lengthy treatment in *Yoreh De'ah* in *Hilchos Bechor*, addresses this tension at length and offers a genuinely beautiful resolution: even though the *kedusha* is intrinsic, a human being has a certain added role to play in further designating and articulating that *kedusha*. This is why there is no *birkat hamitzvot* recited over the designation of a *bechor* animal — because the *mitzvah* is only partially accomplished by the human actor. Since God already established the *kedusha* and the human being is adding only an additional layer of designation, the person cannot claim to have performed the *mitzvah* in its entirety, and therefore no *bracha* is recited.

### Kiddush Analogy

Rav Soloveitchik, in one of his *Yahrtzeit Shiurim*, connected this to *kiddush* on *Shabbos*. *Shabbos* becomes holy on its own, independently of any human action — God is in charge of *Shabbos* and it arrives whether we participate or not. Yet we have a requirement to recite *kiddush*, to say *mekadesh haShabbat*, and thereby add our own participation to the *kedusha* that God has already established. Our obligation to say *kiddush* represents a human partnership in a *kedusha* that is, at its root, entirely divine. The relationship between the intrinsic *kedusha* of the *bechor* and the human act of designation reflects the same structure.

### Shemita Parallel

A parallel case may be found in the laws of *shemitat kesafim* — the release of loans in the *shemitah* year. The question of how *shemitat kesafim* operates is itself contested: is it an *afka'ata demalka*, an automatic cancellation imposed by the King, operating without any human action? Or is it a *mitzvah* obligating the lender to personally and actively forgive the loan? The Mordechai quotes an opinion that in truth the cancellation occurs automatically, yet there remains a personal *mitzvah* to forgive the loan oneself even though it has already been canceled. This is the same paradigm: something happens automatically by divine decree — the *kedusha* or the cancellation — and yet the human being retains an independent obligation, a *mitzvah*, to do it actively as well. In each of these domains, the interplay between divine automaticity and human agency defines a distinctive structure in *halachic* thinking.

## Tzon Barzel (II)

### Practical Application

Returning from this theological excursus to the *psak halacha*, the principle of *yad nochri be'emtza patur min habechora* has direct and significant practical application. Nowadays, in the absence of the *Beis Hamikdash*, there is no way to bring a *bechor* animal as a *korban*. Yet a *tamim* — unblemished — *bechor* may not be sheared, put to work, or used in any ordinary way; it must be preserved for eventual use as a *korban*, which creates severe practical complications for animal owners. The accepted practice today, therefore, is that when an animal is about to give birth to what may be a *bechor*, a Jewish owner enters into a formal joint ownership — *shutfus* — with a non-Jewish partner. By virtue of the non-Jew's partial ownership, *yad nochri be'emtza*, the animal that emerges is exempt from the laws of *bechor*, the farmer can buy back the non-Jew's share afterward, and the entire practical problem is resolved.

---

# Bava Metzia 71

## Ribbit Overview

### Introduction

With daf 71, we finally turn from the purely technical halakhic discussions — the distinctions between *Torah ribbit* and *d'rabbanan ribbit*, the gradations of *avak ribbit* — toward the broader, practical prohibitions associated with lending at interest. The gemara picks up at the bottom of 71a.

### Mishlei Verse

The gemara opens by quoting a verse from Mishlei (22:16): *marbe hono beneshech uvetarbit, lechonin dallim yikabtzenu* — one who increases his wealth through *neshech* and *tarbit*, through charging interest, will ultimately gather it for one who is gracious to the poor. The meaning is that even if you accumulate wealth through *ribbit*, in the end God will see to it that the money passes on to those who will give it to the poor.

The gemara asks: who exactly is this *chonin dallim*, the one gracious to the poor? Rav answers: like Shvor Malka, the Persian ruler. Rashi explains that the Persian king would tax the Jews and redistribute that wealth to the non-Jewish poor — precisely the irony of amassing wealth through interest. The money does not remain within the Jewish people; it is taxed away and redistributed to outsiders.

### Rav Nachman

Rav Nachman then cites a teaching he received from Rav Huna: this applies not only to *ribbit* charged to Jews, but even to *ribbit* charged to non-Jews — an activity that the Torah seems at minimum to permit, and possibly even to encourage, as the verse states *lanachri tashich*. Nevertheless, the principle of divine redistribution applies even there.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava immediately challenges Rav Nachman: how can you suggest there is a problem with lending to non-Jews at interest when the Torah explicitly says *lanachri tashich* — you shall lend to the non-Jew with interest?

### Tashich Interpretation

At this point the gemara revisits an interpretive move that appeared earlier in the tractate: the word *tashich* is read not as "you shall lend" but as "you shall borrow." The gemara proposes that the verse is not condoning lending to the non-Jew with interest, but permitting borrowing from the non-Jew with interest.

The gemara then asks: if so, why does the Torah need to say this at all? We already know from the explicit prohibition *v'lachicha lo tashich* — do not borrow from your fellow Jew with interest — that borrowing from Jews is forbidden. So why state that you may borrow from a non-Jew? The answer is *la'avor b'lav aseh v'lo ta'aseh*: in order to add a positive commandment into the prohibition, so that one who borrows from a fellow Jew at interest transgresses both the negative prohibition and the positive commandment to borrow at interest only from a non-Jew.

This interpretive move, it must be said, is not the *pshat* of the verse in any straightforward sense. But the gemara is clearly motivated to read the *psukim* in a way that avoids the implication that the Torah openly endorses lending to non-Jews with interest. Why?

### Explicit Permission

The gemara is forced to confront an explicit teaching: *lovin mehen umalvin otan beribbit* — one may borrow from non-Jews and lend to non-Jews with interest. And moreover: *vechen beger toshav* — this applies even to a *ger toshav*, a resident alien who has accepted the seven Noahide commandments. The permission is unambiguous.

### Sustenance Limit

Given this explicit permission, Rav Chiya the son of Rav Huna draws a distinction: the permission is not unlimited. *Lo nitzrecha ella bichdei chayav* — the rabbis permitted it only to the extent of basic sustenance. You may lend to non-Jews with interest to earn a basic *parnassah*, but not to build great wealth through it. Critically, no one is claiming this is a *Torah* prohibition — the distinctions being drawn here are clearly rabbinic in nature.

---

## Rabbinic Concerns

### Rashi's Rationale

Rashi spells out the rabbinic concern. He writes: *bichdei chayav hittiru lo* — only to the extent of his sustenance did the rabbis permit, and *yoter mikan asur miderabbanan* — more than that is rabbinically prohibited. Why? *Dilma ati lemisrach* — perhaps one will become "dragged after" this behavior. There are two possible readings of this concern. One is that once you build a full-fledged business of lending at interest to non-Jews, the psychological and commercial logic of that enterprise will begin to erode the internal barrier against doing the same with Jews. You want to maintain a sense of hesitation, of limits, so that the prohibition against lending to Jews with interest remains felt as a genuine *issur* and not merely a technicality.

### Ravina's View

Ravina offers a different framing: the permission applies specifically to *talmidei chachamim* — Torah scholars. Why?

### Yelmed Mimaaasav

*Taama mai gazaru Rabbanan shema yilmad mimaasav* — the reason the rabbis restricted this practice is the fear of *yelmed mimaasav*, that one will learn from the non-Jew's ways. When a person's entire business consists of lending to non-Jews — where he cannot engage Jews as clients at all — his customer base is exclusively non-Jewish, which draws him socially into the non-Jewish world and risks pulling him away from Jewish observance and ethics. This concern is more specific than simple commerce with non-Jews; it is the situation where the entire orientation of one's livelihood points exclusively outward. Since a *talmid chacham* is grounded enough not to be pulled after those practices, the restriction does not apply to him.

### Tosafot Medieval

This raises a pressing question for the medieval period. The primary economic activity of Jews in Christian Europe — lending money with interest to non-Jews — was not a choice but a necessity. Jews were barred from owning land and excluded from most other professions. The Christian prohibition on lending to fellow Christians (a prohibition the Christians did take seriously, even post-Jesus) left Jews as the only available source of credit. How could the rabbinic restrictions discussed here be squared with the lived reality of European Jewish communities?

### Tosafot First Answer

Tosafot addresses this directly in his comments on *tashich* at the bottom of 71b. He presents several answers. His first answer is that we do not rule in accordance with this restriction at all. The statement of Rav Nachman citing Rav Huna — *afilu ribbit shel oved kochavim* — we will shortly see the gemara reread in an entirely different context. According to the second version (*lishon*) of that teaching that the gemara goes on to present, it was never said in the context of restricting lending to non-Jews with interest. Therefore, that restriction simply does not constitute the operative ruling.

### Tosafot Sustenance

Tosafot's second answer: even accepting the first *lishon* of the gemara, which does apply the restriction, there is still room to permit. *Le-fi she-yesh aleinu mas ha-melech ve-ha-sarim* — we bear heavy taxes from the king and the nobles. *Ve-ha-kol havei kedei chayeinu* — therefore, any money we can earn counts as basic sustenance. Given the crushing fiscal burdens on Jewish communities, even significant earnings are considered *kedei chayav*, the basic minimum needed to sustain the community. Perhaps the logic is that income flowing into any part of the community ultimately circulates and benefits the whole.

### Tosafot Exile

Tosafot's third answer cuts more deeply: *ve-od she-anu sheruyin bein ha-umot ve-ee efshar lanu le-histaker be-shum davar im lo nisa ve-nitan imahem* — we live among the nations and have no way of earning a livelihood through anything other than this commerce with them. The original restriction, Tosafot argues, was aimed at a situation where lending to non-Jews with interest was an active choice among available options — where a Jew could have conducted business within the Jewish community and instead chose to focus exclusively on non-Jews. In that situation, the concern about *yelmed mimaasav* is genuine, because you are choosing to orient yourself outward. But when there are no other options — when the entire structure of medieval society has foreclosed every other avenue — the restriction cannot apply. *Hilkach ein le-asor ribbit* — therefore there is no basis to prohibit it. All three of Tosafot's answers may operate together: we do not rule like the restriction; all income qualifies as basic sustenance; and in any case, the restriction only applied when equivalent alternatives existed.

---

## Lending Priorities

### Rav Yosef Hierarchy

The gemara now introduces a second *lishon* — an alternative reading of where Rav Huna's statement belongs. *Ika de-matni le-ha de-Rav Huna a-ha de-tani Rav Yosef* — some teach the statement of Rav Huna not on the context we just discussed, but on the following teaching of Rav Yosef, which is one of the most important sources in the laws of *tzedakah* and lending priorities.

The verse (Shemot 22:24) states: *im kesef talveh es ami es he'ani imach* — if you lend money to my nation, to the poor among you. Rav Yosef derives from the structure of this verse a hierarchy of obligations.

It is worth pausing here to note something significant about the Torah's approach to charity. Nowhere in the Torah is there an explicit commandment to give money outright to the poor. The Torah's language — *pasoach tiftach* and related verses — is consistently about lending, not giving. This preserves the borrower's dignity: he receives the funds in the framework of a loan, as an equal member of society who intends to repay. The Torah addresses the obvious problems with this structure — that loans create debt and generate interest — by instituting *shemitah* and the prohibition of *ribbit*. After seven years, unpaid loans are cancelled; interest is never charged. It is the ideal system: the dignity of borrowing, without the burdens typically associated with debt. This is why the rabbis interpret the Torah's lending verses as also encompassing obligations of *tzedakah* — the two are deeply intertwined.

### Nation Priority

From the phrase *ami* — my nation — the gemara derives: *ami venochri, ami kodem* — between my nation and the foreigner, my nation comes first.

### Need Priority

From *es he'ani* — the poor among you — the gemara derives: *ani ve'ashir, ani kodem* — between a poor person and a wealthy person, the poor person takes priority.

### Closeness Priority

From *imach* — with you — the gemara derives: *aniyecha ve'aniyei ircha, aniyecha kodmim* — your own poor before the poor of your city; *aniyei ircha ve'aniyei ir acheres, aniyei ircha kodmim* — the poor of your city before the poor of another city.

Two distinct criteria are operating simultaneously. One is degree of closeness — geographic proximity, relational proximity, and shared identity as coreligionists. The other is degree of need — poor versus wealthy. The *poskim* debate extensively how to weigh these two criteria against one another when they point in different directions. If a desperately poor person in another city is competing with a less-needy relative in your own family, which criterion governs? The gemara leaves this genuinely open, and different *poskim* take different positions.

One might also ask: does the priority framework imply any residual obligation to the non-Jew at all, or does *ami kodem* categorically exclude non-Jews from the calculus? The plain language of the *braita* suggests they are lower on the priority list, not entirely excluded. Ha'Meiri takes this seriously and says explicitly that there is some degree of obligation toward non-Jews — or at minimum an ethical obligation — though he qualifies this in different places. Most authorities, however, read the exclusion of non-Jews here as categorical rather than as a mere lower priority, given that the fund of available *tzedakah* resources is never exhausted: there will always be poor Jews whose needs are more pressing before one reaches the level of non-Jewish recipients.

These priorities are better understood as ethical guidelines than as the kind of precisely calibrated *halakha* one finds in, say, the laws of *kashrut*. This is deliberate. In the domain of *bein adam lachaveiro*, an excess of quantification risks converting what should be an exercise of ethical judgment into mere rule-following. The Shulchan Aruch cannot fully specify the obligations of compassion without evacuating them of their moral character.

### Ethics Philosophy

This raises a broader philosophical question: in areas of ethics and interpersonal obligation, the degree of specificity found in *halakhic* literature is markedly lower than in ritual domains. There are two reasons for this. One is simply that the complexity of human circumstances cannot be reduced to a finite set of criteria — context matters in ways that rules cannot anticipate. The other, more fundamental reason is that we want these *mitzvot* to remain genuine ethical acts. If the entirety of *tzedakah* behavior were specified in the Shulchan Aruch and one simply executed the prescribed formula, it would cease to be an exercise of moral judgment. The partial indeterminacy in this domain is not a failure of *halakhic* development but a feature of it.

### Rav Nachman Reinterpreted

The gemara returns to the statement of Rav Nachman citing Rav Huna and now relocates it entirely. *Lo nitzrecha deafilu lenochri beribbit uleyisrael bechinam* — the statement is not saying that lending to a non-Jew with interest is somehow problematic. Rather, it is saying that if one has the choice between lending to a non-Jew with interest — from which one will profit — and lending to a Jew for free, one must lend to the Jew. Even financial gain does not override the priority obligation. This is presumably not a mandate to drain one's entire lending portfolio in favor of interest-free Jewish loans; it addresses the ordinary individual who holds funds and must choose between a profitable deployment to a non-Jew and a free loan to a Jew. The Jew comes first. And this is the context — the *Rav Yosef* hierarchy of lending — in which Tosafot's preferred reading places the Rav Huna statement, removing it entirely from any restriction on lending to non-Jews with interest.

---

## Moral Blindness

### Rabbi Yosi Critique

Rabbi Yosi offers a sharp moral critique: *bo u'rei sumyos eineihem shel malvei b'ribis* — go and see the blindness of those who lend with *ribbit*. If someone were to call another person a *rasha*, the accused would be so outraged he would make the other's life miserable — no one wants that label. Yet the very same person is about to commit a flagrant *aveira* of lending with *ribbit*.

### Public Documentation

And not only is he committing this sin, but he makes a public production of it: he brings witnesses, a scribe, a quill, and ink — *heim mevi'im eidim v'lavlar v'kulmos v'dyo* — and writes and signs a formal document.

### Shtar Declaration

What he does not realize is what he is actually signing. The *shtar* amounts to a declaration: *ploni zeh kafar b'Elohei Yisrael* — this person denies the God of Israel. By publicly documenting his violation of an explicit Torah prohibition, he announces his own *resha'ut* in permanent written form before witnesses. Most sins, when committed, are at least done privately. The *ribbit* lender advertises his.

### Noda B'Yehuda

This calls to mind a story — attributed here to the Noda B'Yehuda, though the exact attribution is uncertain — about a man in a certain town who had lent money with interest to fellow Jews and accumulated great wealth at their expense. When he died, the *chevra kadisha* sought to charge his heirs an exorbitant price for a burial plot, on the theory that the community might at least recover something of what had been taken from them over the years. The heirs brought the matter to secular court, arguing that the standard price should apply. The Noda B'Yehuda was called to testify. His argument: the standard price is appropriate for ordinary Jews because Jews believe in *techiyas hameisim* — resurrection of the dead — and therefore a burial plot is essentially a rental, since the occupant will eventually depart. But, he continued, the gemara teaches that one who lends with *ribbit* has no share in *olam haba*. For this man, it is a permanent sale — and a permanent sale commands a higher price.

---

## Ribbit Consequences

### Rabbi Shimon

A *braita* is cited: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches — whoever has money and lends it without *ribbit*, of him the verse says (Tehillim 15:5): *kaspo lo nasan b'neshech* — he did not give his money with interest, *v'shochad al naki lo lakach* — and did not take a bribe against the innocent. *Oseh eileh lo yimmot l'olam* — one who acts this way will never stumble. The implication runs in the other direction as well: *kol hamalveh b'ribbit, nechasav mismotetin* — the property of one who lends with *ribbit* will ultimately collapse.

### Wealth Failure

The rhetorical purpose of this teaching is clear: if people are lending with *ribbit* because they believe it will make them wealthy, the appropriate response is to demonstrate that it will in fact destroy their wealth.

### Objection Raised

The gemara raises a challenge — interestingly, not the obvious one. One might have expected the gemara to challenge the claim by pointing to *ribbit* lenders who prosper. Perhaps that challenge was too dangerous to put in writing, since admitting the phenomenon openly might undermine the deterrent. Instead, the gemara challenges the converse: *veha chazinan delo mozfi beribis veka mismotetin* — we see people who do not lend with *ribbit* and yet they lose their money. If not lending with *ribbit* guaranteed financial stability, how do we account for innocent people who suffer financial ruin?

### Rabbi Elazar Reply

Rabbi Elazar answers: *halalu mismotetin veolin vehalalu mismotetin veeinan olin* — these cases are not symmetric. Those who do not lend with *ribbit* may experience financial setbacks, but their fortunes recover. Those who lend with *ribbit* suffer declines from which they never recover. The downturns are different in kind.

### Tzaddik Gamur

The gemara then cites a verse: *lama tabit bogdim, tacharish bevala rasha tzaddik mimennu* — why do You look on while the treacherous prosper; why are You silent when the wicked swallows one more righteous than he? Rav Huna comments: *tzaddik mimennu bolea, tzaddik gamur eino bolea* — the wicked can swallow someone who is righteous on a relative scale, but he cannot destroy someone who is entirely and objectively righteous. Rashi reads this as reinforcing the earlier principle: the truly righteous person's wealth may decline temporarily but will always recover. By limiting the guarantee to a *tzaddik gamur*, the teaching becomes both more defensible empirically and more demanding spiritually.

---

## Converts and Aliens

### Tannaitic Statement

A *braita* is now introduced: *Rebbi omer* — when the Torah mentions a *ger tzedek*, a righteous convert, it does so in the context of sale; when it mentions a *ger toshav*, a resident alien, it does so in the context of *ribbit*. Rebbi says he does not know how to read these properly into the relevant verses. The gemara proceeds to unpack this.

### Slave Sale Hierarchy

The verse (Vayikra 25:39) states: *vechi yamuch achicha imach venimkar lach* — when your brother becomes poor and is sold to you. This *parasha* follows immediately after the *parasha* of *shemita*, and the moral teaching the rabbis draw from the juxtaposition is this: if you violate *shemita* in order to get rich through forbidden means, you will ultimately be ruined — you will sell your field, then your house, then eventually yourself. The *parasha* traces an accelerating downward spiral.

Within this context, the verse describes successive stages of to whom a person may be sold: to a fellow Jew, to a *ger tzedek*, to a *ger toshav*, and finally — through the phrase *mishpachat ger* — to an outright non-Jew. And the phrase *o leiker mishpachat ger*, "or to the root of a foreigner's family," is understood by some to refer to being sold into the service of a pagan temple itself — not necessarily to perform idolatrous worship, but to serve in a menial capacity, as one who chops the wood and cleans the floors, as Rashi explains. The escalating stages reflect an escalating spiritual and social alienation.

The gemara now focuses on the stage of being sold to a *ger*: does this mean a *ger tzedek* can actually acquire a Jewish slave? This is the question of Rebbi — he does not know how to understand that.

### Convert Slave

The gemara cites a ruling: *ein hager nikneh beeved Ivri* — a *ger* cannot be sold as a *Hebrew slave* — and *ein isha veger konim eved Ivri* — a woman and a *ger* cannot purchase a Hebrew slave. Why can a *ger* not be sold as a *Hebrew slave*? Because the institution of the *eved Ivri* is bound up with the verse *veshavsata el mishpachto* — and he shall return to his family — meaning, the *eved Ivri* goes free at the *Yovel* and is restored to his ancestral family and ancestral land. The entire structure presupposes a family to which one returns, a sense of belonging that is temporarily suspended but never dissolved.

A *ger*, however, has no such family in the halachic sense. He has left his prior identity, and the Jewish family he now belongs to does not carry the same ancestral continuity that the institution of *eved Ivri* was designed to protect. To sell a *ger* as a Hebrew slave — stripping him further of status, marking him as not fully one of us — compounds an alienation that is already inherent in the convert's situation. The degree of belonging necessary to make the institution bearable and ultimately restorative simply is not present.

### Purchase Principle

Why can a *ger* not purchase a Hebrew slave? *Gemiri* — there is a received tradition: *d'maknei kanei, v'dela maknei lo kanei* — one who can be purchased can purchase; one who cannot be purchased cannot purchase. Since a *ger* himself cannot be sold as an *eved Ivri*, he correspondingly cannot own one.

### Convert Ownership

But this creates a difficulty: the verse clearly implies that a *ger* can acquire a Jewish person in some slave-like capacity. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves it: a *ger* cannot own an *eved Ivri ke-din Yisrael* — in the full legal capacity of a Jewish owner — but *aval koneh ke-din nochri* — he can own one with the legal status of a non-Jew who owns an *eved Ivri*. What is the difference? If sold to a non-Jew (or, by extension, to a *ger* with non-Jewish legal status), the slave does not serve the owner's children after the owner's death — *eino oved lo et haben velo et habat*. This contrasts with a standard six-year Jewish slave, whose contractual obligation continues with the estate if the owner dies. When the ownership is of the more complete variety (*nirtza* or sold to a non-Jew), the relationship is more personal — tied specifically to the original purchaser, not transferable to his heirs. A *ger*, then, can own an *eved Ivri*, but only in this modified form, which is why the verse could mention it.

### Women Converts Purchasing

The gemara then addresses why a woman and a *ger* are grouped together in the ruling that they cannot purchase a *Hebrew slave*. The gemara considers whether this position is at odds with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who rules that a woman *can* purchase male slaves. The resolution: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling applies to non-Jewish male slaves (*eved Kena'ani*), while everyone agrees a woman cannot purchase a Jewish male slave (*eved Ivri*).

### Discretion Distinction

The explanation hinges on an assessment of discretion. *Eved Ivri tznia lah* — a Jewish male slave is discreet. If a woman were to engage in improper behavior with a male Jewish slave, he would keep quiet about it. This very discretion is what makes the situation dangerous: there would be no public indicator that anything had gone wrong, so we are concerned that improprieties might actually occur, or at minimum that appearances of impropriety could arise. By contrast, *eved Kena'ani paritz leh* — a non-Jewish slave will not be discreet. Because the misconduct would become public, the concern is considered less acute; the anticipated consequences serve as a natural deterrent. It is a counterintuitive logic: precisely because the Jewish slave can be trusted to keep a secret, we are more worried about what might happen behind closed doors; the non-Jewish slave's indiscretion paradoxically provides a measure of protection.

---

## Widow Restrictions

### Widow Teaching

Rav Yosef teaches: *armala lo tarbi kalba* — a widow should not raise a dog; *v'lo tishri bar bei rav b'ushpiza* — and she should not host a yeshiva student as a lodger. In both cases, the concern is either actual impropriety or the appearance of it.

### Dog Question

The dog case seems puzzling. If a widow were actually engaging in improper conduct with the animal, the animal would follow her around obsessively — surely people would notice? Why should we be concerned about something that would be so visibly apparent?

### Dog Answer

The gemara resolves this: *keivan d'ki shadya leh umtza misrach bah* — since she is always throwing it juicy pieces of meat, the dog will follow her around regardless. People will simply say the animal is devoted to her because she feeds it so well. The behavior that would otherwise be a visible signal of misconduct is indistinguishable from innocent care for an animal. Therefore, *amri inshi, mishum umtza d'shadya leh hu d'misrach* — people will attribute the dog's attachment to the food, and the appearance of impropriety cannot be dispelled by observing the animal's behavior. The concern is sustained.

---

## Resident Alien Ribbit

### Resident Alien Verse

The gemara returns to Rebbi's statement that he does not understand the role of the *ger toshav* in the context of *ribbit*. The relevant verse (Vayikra 25:35–36) states: *vechi yamuch achicha umata yado imach, vehechezakta bo ger vetoshav vechai imach* — if your brother becomes poor and his means fail with you, you shall sustain him, whether a stranger or a resident alien, that he may live with you. The verse then continues: *al tikach me'ito neshech vetarbit* — do not take *neshech* or *tarbit* from him.

Reading these verses together, one would naturally conclude that lending to a *ger toshav* with interest is prohibited.

### Resident Alien Contradic…

Yet the *braita* cited earlier explicitly states: *lovin mehen umalvin otan beribbit, vechen beger toshav* — you may borrow from non-Jews and lend to non-Jews with interest, and the same applies to a *ger toshav*. How can both be true simultaneously?

### Rav Nachman Resolution

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the apparent contradiction through a careful reading of the verse's pronouns. *Mi ketiv al tikach mei-itam?* — the verse does not say "do not take from *them*." It says *al tikach meito* — do not take from *him*. The "him" does not refer back to the most proximate antecedent, the *ger toshav*. Rather, it refers back to the earlier subject: *achicha*, your fellow Jew. The verse's structure is: sustain both your poor brother and any *ger toshav* living among you; but do not take *ribbit* from *him* — meaning from the Jew who has fallen on hard times. The *ger toshav* is mentioned in the sustaining obligation but not in the prohibition of interest. This reading, admittedly, runs against the natural *pshat* of the verse, but it is necessary to harmonize the *psukim* with the established *halacha*.

---

## Co-Signing Arrangements

### Guarantor Teaching

The gemara cites a further teaching: *al tikach me'ito neshech vetarbit, aval ata na'aseh lo arev* — even though you may not take interest from a non-Jew in certain framings, you may become a guarantor (*arev*) for a non-Jewish loan bearing interest. To illustrate: a non-Jewish borrower takes an interest-bearing loan from a Jewish lender, and a Jew co-signs as guarantor.

### Guarantor Problem

The problem is immediately apparent. Under non-Jewish law, the creditor may proceed directly against the guarantor without first pursuing the primary borrower. If that is the case, then the Jewish guarantor effectively becomes the borrower from the perspective of the transaction: the lender skips the non-Jew entirely and collects from the Jew — including interest. The Jewish guarantor has thus paid *ribbit* to a Jewish lender, which is precisely what is forbidden. As the gemara puts it: *ihu nihu d'kashkil minei ribita* — it is effectively this Jew from whom the *ribbit* is extracted.

### Rav Sheshet Solution

Rav Sheshet provides the solution: *shekibel alav ladun b'dinei Yisrael* — the parties agreed in advance that any dispute arising from this arrangement would be adjudicated in a Jewish court rather than under non-Jewish law.

### Jewish Court Logic

In Jewish law, a creditor must pursue the primary borrower first before turning to the guarantor. Since the lender must go first to the non-Jewish borrower, the Jew's guarantee is only triggered in the event the borrower actually defaults. The relationship between the Jewish lender and the Jewish guarantor therefore never takes the form of a direct loan. At no point did the guarantor borrow a sum and then accumulate a growing debt with interest. Rather, the debt was accumulating entirely within the relationship between the lender and the non-Jewish borrower. Only when that borrower has defaulted and now owes, say, $1,500, does the guarantor's obligation crystallize — and at that moment, the guarantor's debt to the lender begins at $1,500. It is not a case of borrowing $1,000 and paying back $1,500 after interest has accrued; it is a guarantee that has been called in for a pre-existing amount. There is no *ribbit* in the technical sense.

The gemara then asks: if the parties agreed to follow Jewish law, should that not also mean that no interest at all may be collected (since Jewish law would prohibit even the original interest charged to the non-Jewish borrower under the restrictive views discussed earlier)? Rav Sheshet clarifies: they agreed to adjudicate *this particular aspect* — the order of collection — under Jewish law, while the interest arrangement itself was accepted as binding under whatever terms were originally set. The agreement to use Jewish court adjudication was targeted, not global.

---

## Debt Transfer

### Jew Lends Non-Jew

The gemara now extends the analysis to cases where debts are transferred between parties. The opening principle: a Jew may lend out a non-Jew's money on the non-Jew's behalf, with the non-Jew's awareness.

### Transfer Scenario

The scenario: a Jew has borrowed money from a non-Jew at interest and now wishes to repay. As he is carrying the funds — let us say $1,500 (the $1,000 principal plus $500 in interest) — a second Jew encounters him and proposes: give me that $1,500 and I will continue paying the interest to the non-Jew in your place, effectively assuming your debt.

### Forbidden Direct

If the non-Jew is not brought into this arrangement, it is forbidden. The second Jew would be paying interest to the first Jew — Jew to Jew — which is a straightforward prohibition of *ribbit*. The first Jew becomes the effective creditor in the arrangement, and the second Jew becomes the interest-paying borrower.

### Permitted via Non-Jew

However, if they go to the non-Jew and restructure the transaction with his participation — the first Jew transfers the $1,500 to the second Jew in the presence of the non-Jew, and the second Jew now has a direct relationship with the non-Jew as the new borrower — this is permitted. The crucial feature is that the original creditor, the non-Jew, remains the active party in the loan relationship. The money flows through in a way that maintains the non-Jew's position as lender. The first Jew is out of the picture, and the second Jew's obligation runs to the non-Jew, not to the first Jew.

### Reverse Scenario

The gemara then considers the reverse: a non-Jew who borrowed money from a Jew at interest is now coming to repay. A second Jew encounters him and says: give me that money, and I will continue paying interest to the original Jewish lender. In this case, the second Jew's interest payments run to the first Jew — a Jewish lender — but this is permitted, because the second Jew's relationship is with the non-Jew who transferred the funds, and his obligation to the first Jewish lender is construed as continuous with the non-Jew's original obligation.

### Non-Jew Middleman

However — and this is where the gemara points toward a significant structural loophole — if the parties bring the non-Jew in and formally restructure the arrangement so that the non-Jew drops out entirely and the second Jew now owes money directly to the first Jew with interest, this is forbidden. That is *ribbit* between Jews with no permissible intermediary relationship remaining.

The gemara ends here for today, but the shape of what is coming is already visible: the use of a non-Jewish party as an intermediary — a cut-out — to effectuate what is functionally a Jew-to-Jew interest-bearing loan while maintaining the formal appearance of each party transacting only with the non-Jew. This will be the major structural mechanism, the great loophole, that the gemara will continue to analyze in the next session.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 72

## Ribbit via Non-Jew

### Intro: Ribbit Structure

The daf picks up at the bottom of 71b and carries into 72a, addressing a question of enormous practical significance — particularly in the medieval context — namely, whether a non-Jew can serve as an intermediary through whom one Jew effectively lends money to another Jew with interest. The *Tanna'im* and *Amoraim* were acutely aware that the prohibition of *ribbit* could be circumvented by routing a loan through a non-Jewish third party, and the *Gemara* works carefully to identify exactly where the line falls. The discussion builds on the preceding analysis — where Rabbeinu Tam found ways to limit the scope of the Rabbinic restriction on lending to a non-Jew with interest — and now turns to the reverse manipulation: using a non-Jew as a cutout to lend to a Jew with interest.

### Case 1: Jew Borrows

The *Beraita* (*Tanu Rabbanan*) presents two parallel cases. In the first: a Jew — call him Reuven — has borrowed money from a non-Jew, Christopher, with interest. The loan has matured and Reuven wishes to repay the full amount, principal plus accrued interest. Shimon, another Jew, appears and says to Reuven: "Give me the money instead. I will pay you the same interest you were paying Christopher." This is clearly *assur*. Whatever the arrangement between Reuven and Christopher, the operative transaction is now Shimon paying interest to Reuven — a Jew paying a Jew — and that is forbidden *ribbit*.

### Two Scenarios

The *Beraita* then introduces a permitted alternative involving the same parties. Instead of the above arrangement, Reuven and Shimon go together to Christopher's location. Standing in Christopher's presence, Reuven hands the repayment money — rather than to Christopher directly — to Shimon. Shimon then assumes the loan, owing Christopher the money with interest. This, the *Beraita* states, is *mutar*. The underlying logic is that by virtue of occurring in Christopher's presence, the transaction is treated as if Reuven repaid Christopher and Christopher in turn lent the money to Shimon. Shimon thus owes interest to Christopher — a Jew owing interest to a non-Jew — which is permissible.

### Permitted Method

The *heter* in this case turns on the idea that the physical context of the transaction — Reuven handing money to Shimon in Christopher's presence, with Christopher's apparent consent — causes the debt to be reconstituted as a loan from Christopher to Shimon. The *chiddush* is that we do not simply follow the money and say "Reuven gave the money to Shimon, therefore Shimon owes Reuven." Rather, we ask whose money was it originally and through whose act of lending was it placed in circulation. When the full repayment sum is transferred to a new party in the lender's presence and with the lender's assent, the law treats it as if the original loan was repaid and a new loan was made to the new party.

### Case 2: Non-Jew Borrows

The parallel case runs in the opposite direction. Christopher has borrowed money from Reuven with interest. Christopher wishes to repay. Shimon appears and says: "Christopher, give me the money; I will pay back Reuven what you owe him with interest." This is *mutar*, because Shimon is paying interest to Christopher, and that is permissible. However, if instead Reuven, Christopher, and Shimon all go to Reuven's location and Christopher, standing before Reuven, hands the repayment to Shimon, that is *assur* — because we now treat it as if Christopher repaid Reuven and Reuven lent the money to Shimon. Shimon now owes interest to Reuven, a Jew paying a Jew.

### Impermissible Method

The symmetry of the two cases rests on a single operative principle: when the total sum changes hands in the presence of the original lender or creditor, we conceptualize the transaction as if the original debt was discharged and a new loan was made to the new recipient by that creditor. When the creditor is Jewish, this is *assur*; when the creditor is a non-Jew, it is *mutar*. The presence of the original lender is what determines who is deemed to have made the new loan.

### Conceptual Challenge

This raises a genuine conceptual difficulty. At the end of the day, in Case 1 (the *mutar* scenario), it is Reuven who physically gives the money to Shimon — not Christopher. Christopher never handed anything to Shimon. So how does it follow that Shimon's debt and interest obligation run to Christopher rather than to Reuven? Similarly, in Case 2 (the *assur* scenario), it is Christopher who physically gives the money to Shimon — not Reuven. Reuven never gave Shimon anything. Why, then, do we treat it as if Reuven is Shimon's lender?

The *Gemara*'s answer rests on a foundational framing: we do not determine the nature of the loan simply by observing who happens to hand over the cash. We ask, rather, who was the original owner of the funds and through whose act of lending were those funds extended. The physical delivery of cash is merely the mechanism; the legal character of the loan is determined by identifying from whose capacity the money was placed in play. When the entire sum — not just an interest payment but the full principal and interest — is transferred to a new party in the original lender's presence and with that lender's assent, we treat it as if the lender received the repayment and then extended a fresh loan.

### Tosafot's Question

*Tosafot* presses the conceptual question further. One might argue that the simplest test for who owes the *ribbit* is to ask: who is actually handing over the interest payments? In Case 1, Christopher continues to receive his five percent. Why not simply say that since Shimon is delivering the interest to Christopher, Shimon owes interest to Christopher — and since that is Jew-to-non-Jew, it is fine — regardless of how we conceptualize the loan structure? *Tosafot*'s point is that the question of "who pays the interest" and "to whom is the interest owed" are not necessarily the same question.

The response is that we cannot determine the character of the loan merely from the direction of cash flow. Theoretically, Shimon might owe his interest to Reuven, and merely be delivering it to Christopher as a shortcut — since Reuven himself owes Christopher and Shimon's payment to Christopher could simply represent Shimon paying Reuven who in turn pays Christopher. The principle of *shib'uda d'Rabbi Natan* does allow A to pay C directly when A owes B and B owes C, but even that principle does not collapse the intermediate stages — it simply allows the cash to be delivered to the end of the chain. The conceptual debt structure still runs through each link. So the question of whose money Shimon actually took — and therefore to whom his loan obligation runs — must be determined at the outset, not inferred from who ends up holding the interest payments.

---

## Role of Presence

### Gemara's Question

The *Gemara* now turns to its central analytical question: the *Beraita* treats presence — of the original lender at the moment the money changes hands — as the operative legal factor. But why should mere presence accomplish anything? In Case 1, Reuven hands the money to Shimon. Whether or not Christopher is standing in the room, the money went from Reuven to Shimon. How does proximity to Christopher transform the nature of what just happened?

### No Shlichus for Non-Jew

The *Gemara* raises the obvious difficulty with the *mutar* case. *Bishlama seifa lechumra* — the *assur* ruling in Case 2 can be explained by a desire to be strict: even though Christopher gave the money to Shimon and not Reuven, we will treat it as though Reuven lent Shimon the money. But the *reisha*, the *mutar* ruling, is harder. When Reuven hands the money to Shimon in Christopher's presence, the *Gemara* notes: *ein shlichus l'nochri*. A non-Jew cannot serve as a *shaliach*. Therefore Christopher cannot appoint Reuven as his *shaliach* to deliver funds to Shimon on his behalf. When Reuven hands the money to Shimon, he is not acting in Christopher's capacity — there is no legal mechanism for that. He is handing over his own money. So from Shimon's perspective, he has simply received money from Reuven. Christopher never lent Shimon anything. How, then, can we say this is *mutar* on the grounds that Shimon owes his interest to Christopher?

### Rav Huna's Answer

Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Acha son of Rav Ika offers a solution. The *mutar* case does not work by Reuven acting as Christopher's *shaliach*. Rather: Christopher says to Reuven, "Do not bother handing the money to me — put it down on the table, and you are hereby released from your loan." Reuven places the money on the table and walks away, free and clear. Christopher then turns to Shimon and says: "Do you want to borrow this money? Pick it up — you now owe it to me." In this reading, there is no agency involved at all. Reuven completed his repayment to Christopher by placing the money down. Christopher then, in a separate act, lent it to Shimon.

The *Gemara* immediately objects: *ei hachi, mai l'meimra?* If that is the mechanism, what is the *chiddush*? The *Beraita* is telling us something we already know: if Christopher took Reuven's money and lent it to Shimon, then of course Shimon owes Christopher. That is simply a straightforward loan. There is no novelty in stating that fact. The innovation was supposed to be that *presence* of the non-Jew transforms an otherwise impermissible transaction — but under Rav Huna's reading, there is nothing special about the scenario at all. Rav Papa similarly suggests that Christopher took the money from Reuven and handed it directly to Shimon — but the *Gemara* again dismisses this as stating the obvious.

### Full Payment Required

The *Gemara* then offers the *chiddush* it was looking for. One might have thought: when Reuven and Shimon come before Christopher, and Reuven — at Shimon's request and in the context of facilitating Shimon's new loan — hands the money to Shimon, perhaps Christopher in this arrangement is acting merely as Reuven's facilitator. That is, maybe Christopher's role here is just to carry out Reuven's wish that Shimon receive the money, and the underlying structure remains that it is Reuven's money going to Shimon. *Ka mashma lan* — the *Beraita* teaches us this is not so: when conducted properly, the transaction is recognized as Christopher lending Shimon the money, not as Reuven. This is the *chiddush*.

But the *Gemara*'s conclusion, emerging from its rejection of the intermediate answers, is that mere proximity to Christopher is insufficient. The transaction must actually be completed — the money genuinely repaid to Christopher and then re-lent by Christopher — in order for the loan to be reconstituted between Christopher and Shimon. Simply performing the handoff in Christopher's room, without a genuine two-step of repayment and new lending, does not accomplish the legal restructuring.

This conclusion has important practical implications. It means that the permissible structure — a Jew borrowing from a non-Jew and then having a second Jew take over the loan — requires that the full repayment genuinely occur, and then the non-Jew separately lend the funds to the new borrower. The non-Jew need not even be present when the new loan is made; he could send the money via Christopher to the new borrower separately. Conversely, even if everyone is in the same room, if there is no genuine intermediate step of repayment and re-lending, the transaction does not shift the loan relationship to the non-Jew.

### Rav Ashi's Solution

Rav Ashi offers a creative alternative. He proposes: when we say *ein shlichus l'nochri* — that a non-Jew cannot be a *shaliach* — this rule applies only in the context of *terumah*. In all other areas of *halacha*, a non-Jew can in fact serve as an agent. Therefore, in the *mutar* case, when Christopher instructs Reuven to give the money to Shimon, Reuven acts as Christopher's *shaliach* — and that *shlichus* is legally valid. Shimon thereby receives the money from Christopher through his agent, and Shimon's loan runs to Christopher.

### Rejection of Rav Ashi

The *Gemara* dismisses Rav Ashi's proposal bluntly — on one version it says *bruta hi* and on another *bedusa hi* — both expressions indicating that the idea is without merit. The rejection proceeds as follows: the rule that *ein shlichus l'nochri* is derived from the verse regarding *terumah*, *"atem gam atem"* — "you, even you" — which teaches that just as *you* (the one separating *terumah*) are members of the covenant, so too your *shaliach* must be a member of the covenant. But the laws of *shlichus* for the entire *Torah* are derived from *terumah*. Therefore, *ein shlichus l'nochri* is not a rule limited to *terumah* — it is a universal rule derived from *terumah* and applied throughout *halacha*.

Rav Ashi's second formulation — that while a non-Jew cannot be *our* *shaliach*, we can be *their* *shaliach* — is similarly rejected. The derivation from *"atem gam atem"* means that for *shlichus* to operate, the *meshale'ach* (the one appointing the agent) must be a member of the covenant. If Christopher appoints Reuven as his *shaliach*, Christopher is the *meshale'ach*, and Christopher is not a member of the covenant. The verse requires that the *atem* — the party who sends — be Jewish. Since Christopher cannot satisfy that condition, the appointment of Reuven as his *shaliach* is legally void regardless of Reuven's status. The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ela hadar bei Rav Ashi* — Rav Ashi retracted.

### Ravina's Zechiyah

Ravina proposes an alternative that sidesteps *shlichus* altogether. He invokes the principle of *zechiyah* — specifically *zachin l'adam shelo befanav*, the rule that one may acquire something on behalf of another person even without that person's explicit agency. The idea is: Christopher does not need to appoint Reuven as his *shaliach*. Instead, when Reuven hands the money to Shimon, Shimon acquires the money on behalf of Christopher. Shimon is *zocheh* in the money for Christopher. Now Christopher holds the money — through Shimon's act of *zechiyah* — and simultaneously lends it to Shimon. Shimon thus owes the debt to Christopher.

The model for *zechiyah* without *shlichus* is a minor child. A *katan* cannot appoint a *shaliach* — he lacks the legal capacity for *shlichus* — yet one can be *zocheh* in something on behalf of a minor. For example, if someone wishes to give a *Bar Mitzvah* gift to a child who has not yet reached his *Bar Mitzvah*, a third party can take *kinyan* on the child's behalf. The acquisition is valid even though the child could not himself make that person his *shaliach*. *Miderabbanan*, by Rabbinic enactment, *zechiyah* operates independently of *shlichus*. Ravina argues the same should apply to a non-Jew: Shimon can be *zocheh* in the money for Christopher through *zechiyah miderabbanan*, even though Christopher cannot make Shimon his *shaliach*.

### Rejection of Zechiyah

The *Gemara* rejects this as well: *v'lo hi*. The operative principle is: *Yisrael ati l'chlal shlichus, akum lo ati l'chlal shlichus*. The minor child will eventually reach adulthood and will then be capable of *shlichus*. *Zechiyah* is grounded in, or at minimum dependent upon, the eventual potential for *shlichus*. It applies only to someone who will one day enter the framework of *shlichus*. A non-Jew will never be in the *parsha* of *shlichus* — Christopher can never make Shimon a *shaliach* in any context. Therefore, *zechiyah* on behalf of a non-Jew does not function. Shimon cannot be *zocheh* in the money for Christopher.

The conclusion of this entire discussion is that there is no formal legal mechanism — neither *shlichus* nor *zechiyah* — by which Reuven's direct handoff of money to Shimon, however it is framed, can be reconstituted as a loan from Christopher to Shimon. The only genuinely valid structure is the one that actually involves Christopher taking possession of the money and then separately lending it to Shimon. *Tosafot*'s underlying question — whether the direction of interest payments should determine the identity of the loan — is answered by demonstrating that the question of loan ownership must be determined at the level of who actually extended the credit, and the legal tools for reassigning that relationship are narrow and specific.

---

## Conversion & Ribbit

### Reconsolidation Case

The *Gemara* now introduces a new *Beraita* dealing with *ribbit* in the context of conversion. A Jew — Reuven — has lent money to a non-Jew, Christopher, with interest. Over time, the principal and interest together amount to, say, twelve hundred dollars. Reuven and Christopher now agree to consolidate: rather than maintain a loan of one thousand dollars with two hundred dollars of interest outstanding, they write a new *shtar* acknowledging a fresh loan of twelve hundred dollars. The interest is folded into the principal and the debt is reconstituted as a single sum. Christopher then converts to Judaism and becomes Chaim. The question: can Chaim now pay Reuven the full twelve hundred dollars, or does the two hundred dollars that was originally interest remain uncollectible?

### Before Conversion

If the loan was reconsolidated — the twelve hundred dollar *shtar* was written — *before* Christopher converted, then Chaim may pay Reuven the full twelve hundred dollars. At the moment the new *shtar* was written, Christopher was still a non-Jew, and the two hundred dollars was legitimately owed as interest in a Jew-to-non-Jew loan. The new *shtar* of twelve hundred dollars is simply a valid debt instrument, and when Chaim pays Reuven twelve hundred dollars, he is paying a loan — not interest. *Goveh et ha'keren ve'goveh et ha'ribbit*.

### After Conversion

If the reconsolidation occurred *after* Christopher converted — that is, at the moment of conversion he owed Reuven a thousand dollars of principal and two hundred dollars of interest, and only thereafter did they write a new *shtar* of twelve hundred dollars — then Chaim may only pay the principal. He may not pay the two hundred dollars. *Goveh et ha'keren ve'eino goveh et ha'ribbit*.

### Interest Analysis

This ruling has an interesting nuance worth examining. One might point out that the two hundred dollars of interest accrued while Christopher was still a non-Jew — not a single shekel of new interest was generated after his conversion to Chaim. Why, then, should the two hundred dollars be uncollectible? The answer lies in the timing of the reconsolidation. At the moment Chaim stood before Reuven as a Jew, the outstanding balance was framed as "a thousand dollars plus two hundred dollars of interest." It was at that moment — while he was Jewish — that the sum was characterized as interest. Repackaging it into a twelve hundred dollar loan does not undo that characterization. The fact that the interest accrued during his non-Jewish period is part of the *chiddush*: even though the interest never accrued as a Jew, since it was *framed* as interest owed while he was Jewish, it cannot be collected. The reconsolidation cannot launder the character of the obligation.

### Reverse Scenario

The *Gemara* then presents the parallel case in reverse: a non-Jew, Christopher, borrows money from Reuven with interest. The loan similarly reaches a point where a thousand dollars of principal and two hundred dollars of interest are outstanding, and the parties reconsolidate into a twelve hundred dollar *shtar*. Christopher then converts to Chaim. The same two possibilities exist: reconsolidation before conversion, or reconsolidation after conversion. And the same ruling applies symmetrically: if consolidated before conversion, the full twelve hundred is payable; if after, only the principal.

### Rabbi Yossi

Rabbi Yossi dissents with respect to this second case — where the non-Jew was the *borrower* from the Jew. Rabbi Yossi holds that *bein kach u'vein kach goveh et ha'keren ve'goveh et ha'ribbit* — whether the reconsolidation occurred before or after conversion, Chaim always pays the full twelve hundred dollars. This applies regardless of when the new *shtar* was written.

### Rava's Rationale

Rava explains: *Amar Rava amar Rav Chisda amar Rav Huna: halacha ke'Rabbi Yossi*. We rule like Rabbi Yossi. What is Rabbi Yossi's reasoning? *Kedei she'lo yomru bishvil me'otav nitgayer zeh* — so that people should not say that Christopher converted to Judaism in order to avoid paying his debts. If converting to Judaism meant that a non-Jewish borrower could shed his interest obligations, the integrity of *geirut* would be compromised. People would allege that conversions are financially motivated — that Christopher became Chaim not out of sincere religious commitment but to avoid paying Reuven two hundred dollars. To prevent this perception, Rabbi Yossi rules that the non-Jewish borrower who converts must pay the full amount regardless of when the reconsolidation occurred.

One might ask: how is this technically permitted? After all, once Chaim is Jewish, paying interest to a Jew would seem to be *ribbit*. The answer may lie in the point noted earlier: the interest was never accrued as a Jew. No new interest was generated after the conversion. Since the two hundred dollars represents an obligation that arose entirely during Christopher's non-Jewish period, it may be that *me'ikar ha'din* there is no real *ribbit* problem with paying it — and the various rulings in this *sugya* are, at least in part, shaped by considerations of appearances and incentives rather than strict *issur*.

---

## Written Ribbit

### Document Status

The *Gemara* turns to a *Beraita* dealing with a *shtar* that has *ribbit* explicitly written into it — a loan document that specifies both principal and an interest rate. Such a document concretizes the *ribbit* arrangement in written form, and the question is what legal effect that document has. Can it be used in court to collect anything at all?

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rabbi Meir rules: *konesin oto ve'eino goveh lo et ha'keren ve'lo et ha'ribbit*. The lender is penalized (*kenas*), and may collect neither the principal nor the interest. The document is entirely voided. Rabbi Meir's reasoning is that the *shtar* itself is the vehicle of an *aveirah* — the *ribbit* is embedded in the document — and therefore the entire document is torn up. Interestingly, this is not simply that the interest portion is unenforceable; rather, even using the *shtar* as evidence for the principal is forbidden. If the lender had independent witnesses who could testify that a loan was made, those witnesses could in principle be used to collect the principal — but the *shtar* itself, having been used to effect an *aveirah*, is entirely discarded as a legal instrument. This position has a certain compelling integrity: allowing a court to recognize a *ribbit* document for any purpose compromises the court's standing and provides only weak disincentive against the practice.

### Chachamim Position

The *Chachamim* disagree: *goveh et ha'keren ve'eino goveh et ha'ribbit*. The principal is collectible; the interest is not. The *shtar* may be used in court, but only to enforce the portion that represents a legitimate debt.

### Debate Basis
