The *Gemara* identifies the underlying dispute: *Rabbi Meir savar konesin heter mishum issur* — Rabbi Meir holds that we fine a person with respect to the permitted portion (the principal) on account of the forbidden portion (the interest). By lending with *ribbit* and concretizing it in a document, the lender forfeits even his right to collect the principal via that document. *Rabbanan savri lo konesin heter mishum issur* — the *Chachamim* hold we do not extend a penalty into the permitted domain. The principal is owed regardless of how the *shtar* was written, and we can separate the legitimate from the illegitimate.

### Predated Document

The *Gemara* raises a challenge from a ruling taught elsewhere — in Gittin, Rosh Hashanah, and related contexts — that predated documents (*shtarot hamukdamim*) are invalid, while postdated documents are kosher. The problem with a predated *shtar* is that it allows the lender to collect liens from property sold by the borrower between the false date and the actual date of the loan — property that was sold without any actual encumbrance at the time of sale. An innocent purchaser who checked the records and found no outstanding debts against the seller would find his property seized through the fraud of the predated *shtar*.

The *Gemara* asks: why not apply the *Chachamim*'s logic to the predated *shtar* as well? Even under the *Chachamim*, who do not penalize the permitted for the forbidden, one could argue: simply disallow the lender from collecting any liens prior to the true date of the loan, but permit collection from the valid date forward. In other words, split the document — enforce the later portion, void the earlier portion.

### Severability Test

Reish Lakish suggests that the voiding of the entire predated *shtar* is in fact a Tannaic dispute and represents Rabbi Meir's position. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees and says: even the *Rabbanan* — who do not penalize the permitted for the forbidden in the case of the *ribbit* document — would void the entire predated *shtar*. The reason is a *gezeirah*: we fear that if a predated *shtar* is allowed to circulate in any form, the lender may come to use it to collect liens from the earlier, fraudulent date. The predated *shtar* does not reveal on its face that it was predated — it simply states "this loan was made on November 1st" and there is no indication within the document itself that this date is false. A court examining the document cannot tell the difference between a validly dated and fraudulently predated document. Therefore, permitting any use of such a document is too dangerous; the entire *shtar* must be voided.

The case of the *ribbit shtar* is fundamentally different. There, the document itself plainly states the interest terms. The forbidden portion and the permitted portion are clearly delineated within the *shtar* itself. A court can read the document and separate what is enforceable from what is not. That severability makes it possible, under the *Chachamim*'s view, to enforce the principal while ignoring the interest. The predated *shtar*, by contrast, is non-severable in a practical sense — there is no way to know which liens are valid and which are fraudulent without additional testimony, and the document itself would mislead. Hence the two cases diverge.

---

## Property Ruse Case

### Story Setup

The *Gemara* now presents a complex and colorful narrative (*ma'aseh*). A creditor has taken a vineyard as *mashkanta* — collateral — from a debtor. The arrangement is of the *mashkanta de-nachita* type: the creditor takes possession of the vineyard and effectively deducts something nominal from the loan while consuming the produce of the vineyard for the duration. After three years of eating the vineyard's grapes, the creditor approaches the debtor with a threatening proposition: either sell me your vineyard at my price, or I will suppress the evidence that I held the vineyard as *mashkanta* — I will claim instead that I purchased it from you three years ago, have been in possession for three full years, and thereby have a *chazakah* of ownership.

### Transfer to Minor

The debtor, facing this extortion, devises a countermove. Before the creditor can execute his scheme, the debtor transfers title to the vineyard to his minor son. He then — no longer being the owner — sells the vineyard to the creditor. The creditor receives a document of sale and money changes hands. The creditor is now in possession of the vineyard legitimately through purchase, but crucially, the sale comes from the debtor *after* the debtor has already transferred ownership to his son. So the sale is of property the debtor no longer owned.

### Ruse Discovered

When the ruse is discovered, the creditor's original leverage is entirely destroyed. His threat was to claim he purchased the vineyard three years ago. But now a document exists showing he purchased it just recently — from the debtor himself. The predated-purchase theory is impossible to sustain. The ruse has worked perfectly from the debtor's perspective: he has broken the creditor's leverage and sold him property he did not own, thereby recovering money (the purchase price) while undermining any claim of long-standing ownership.

### Liens Question

The creditor has now paid money for a vineyard he will not get to keep — the title was in the minor son, not the seller. The creditor wants his money back. The question becomes: does the *shtar mechirah* — the document of sale — which of course contained the standard clause of *achrayut* (warranty of title, entitling the buyer to reimbursement if the property is lost), give the creditor the power of liens? That is, can he collect not just from the debtor's current assets, but from property the debtor may have sold to third parties in the interim — treating the *shtar* as equivalent to a *shtar chov* with *meshubadim*? Or, since the *shtar* was written for a sale that was fundamentally invalid — the seller did not own the property — is it a meaningless document that creates no liens at all, leaving the creditor only with a claim for reimbursement from the debtor's unencumbered assets?

### Abaye's View

Abaye draws a comparison to a ruling of Rabbi Assi: *modeh b'shtar shektavo eino tzarich l'kaymo ve'goveh minichsei meshubadei*. If David presents a *shtar* against Dov, and the *shtar* has not been externally validated by witnesses, but Dov himself acknowledges the *shtar* is genuine — Dov admits he owes the money — then David can collect from *meshubadim*, from property Dov sold to third parties, even though the validation came only from the borrower himself. This seems analogous: a *shtar* of limited standing can nonetheless create liens. By loose analogy, Abaye suggests the *shtar* of this bogus sale — even though the sale was invalid — might still function to create liens for reimbursement.

### Rava's Objection

Rava rejects the comparison. *Mi dami?* There the *shtar* in Rabbi Assi's case was entirely legitimate as a debt instrument — a genuine loan was made, the *shtar* was properly written, it simply lacked external validation. Nobody questions that it *should* have been written; the only issue is whether Dov's own acknowledgment is sufficient validation. *Nitan likateiv* — it was proper to write such a *shtar*. Here, the *shtar mechirah* purports to sell property the seller did not own. A document of sale for property one does not own is *lo nitan likateiv* — it had no right to exist at all. It was a meaningless document from the moment of its writing. Such a document cannot generate liens.

### Shevach Karka'ot

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge from another *Beraita* dealing with *shevach karka'ot*. If someone steals a field, sells it to Gloria, and Gloria improves it — and then the original owner reclaims the field from Gloria — Gloria seeks reimbursement from the thief for both the purchase price and her improvements. The *Beraita* rules: Gloria can collect the principal purchase price from the thief's *meshubadim* — from property he sold to third parties — but she cannot collect the enhancement value (*shevach*) from those *meshubadim*; she can collect only from the thief's unencumbered (*benei chorin*) property. The reasoning for the distinction is that third parties could anticipate being subject to a lien for the known purchase price when they bought property from the thief, but they could not know how much Gloria would spend on improvements — that is an unspecified and unforeseeable amount, and it would be unfair to extend the lien that far.

The relevance to our case: Gloria collected the purchase price from *meshubadim* based on a *shtar mechirah* of a stolen field — a sale of property the thief did not legitimately own — and yet that *shtar* generated liens. This seems to contradict Rava's position that a *shtar* written for a sale of property one does not own has no legal force. If the *shtar* in Gloria's case generates liens, why can't the *shtar* in our case do the same?

### Legitimate vs. Ruse

Mareimar presents Rava's response, which Ravina then engages with and extends. The key distinction between Gloria's case and our case is *intent*. When the thief sold the field to Gloria, even if he knew or suspected the title might be challenged, he genuinely *wanted* the sale to be valid and legitimate. He did not want Gloria to go around complaining that he had defrauded her. Either because he did not want to be called a *gazlan*, or because he wanted to uphold his reputation and honor his commitments, he had a genuine interest in ensuring that Gloria's purchase was protected and that she would be reimbursed if anything went wrong. His *intent* behind the sale, and behind the *achrayut* clause, was sincere — he wanted the *shtar* to have legal force and for Gloria to have genuine protection. *Mafiyes lei l'marei* — he would even try to pacify the original owner, to buy off the title claim so Gloria could keep the property. Therefore, even though the *shtar* was technically for property he could not transfer, it carries genuine legal weight because the seller *meant* for it to be valid.

In our case, the situation is categorically different. The debtor transferred his vineyard to his minor son and then "sold" the vineyard to the creditor as a deliberate *ruse* — not because he wanted the sale to be valid, but precisely because he wanted it to be exposed as invalid. His entire purpose was to undermine the creditor's leverage, not to create a genuine sale. *Lav revucha minei ka michavein* — he was not intending to benefit the creditor; he was trying to escape the creditor's extortion. The *shtar* was not written with sincere intent to convey rights. It was a tactical maneuver in a dispute. Therefore the *shtar mechirah* in this case is not merely technically deficient — it is a document without *kavana*, without genuine transactional intent — and it creates no liens whatsoever.

The principle that emerges is that the validity of a document of sale for generating liens does not depend solely on whether the seller technically owned the property. It also depends on whether the seller *intended* for the document to carry legal force. A sale of stolen property, made by someone who genuinely wished to honor his obligations to the buyer, can create liens. A sale designed from the outset as a ruse — made precisely because the seller wanted it to be void — cannot.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 73

## Price Fixing & Ownership

### Yatza HaSha'ar Intro

The *mishna* here, toward the end of the chapter, returns to themes introduced earlier: the permissibility of pre-purchasing fruit at the early-season low price for delivery later in the season when prices are higher. The underlying concern is *ribbis* — is such an arrangement effectively interest? The *mishna* establishes that this is permitted, provided two conditions are met. First, a market price must have been set — *yatza hashaar*. Second, the fruit must either be owned by the seller or be available in the marketplace. The logic is that since the buyer could in principle purchase the fruit at that lower price today, there is no real benefit conferred by the later delivery; the higher future value merely reflects market movement, not a lending relationship.

The *mishna* opens: *ein poskin al hapeiros ad she-yatza hashaar* — one may not fix an arrangement for fruits until the market price has been established. Once it has been established, *poskin af al pi she-ein lazeh yesh lazeh* — the arrangement may be made even if the seller himself does not have possession of the fruit, since others do, and the seller can readily acquire it.

### Early Harvesters

The *mishna* continues with a case involving those who harvest early, before a general market price has been set. The rule is *posik immo al hagdish* — one may make an arrangement with such a farmer against the pile of wheat he has already harvested. The same applies to a container of wine (*avit shel anavim*), pressed olives (*maatan shel zeitim*), balls of clay ready to be turned into pottery (*beitzim shel yotzer*), and plaster once it has been placed into the kiln (*sid mishekia b'kivshano*). In each of these cases, the product is substantially ready and in the seller's possession, even if the general market price has not yet been established. What permits the arrangement is that the seller actually holds the product — since he could deliver it now, the arrangement for later delivery does not take on the character of a loan.

This raises a subtle question: does the seller's possession of the goods specifically allow this particular transaction, or does it simply provide enough of the formal features of a sale to eliminate the *ribbis* concern — even if the actual product delivered later need not be the identical product now in hand? This question will surface again in later cases.

### Dung Debate

The *mishna* includes a further rule: *uposik immo al hazavel kol yemot hashana* — one may arrange for the delivery of dung at any time of year, presumably because dung is always available and in unlimited supply. *Rabbi Yosi*, however, dissents: *ein poskin al hazavel ela im ken haytah lo zavel ba-ashpah* — even dung, he holds, requires that the seller actually own the dung himself, located on his property. The debate turns on whether dung falls into the category of *yatza hashaar* — so widely available that no ownership is required — or whether, despite its ubiquity, it remains a case where the seller must have the product in hand. *Vachachamim matirin* — the Sages permit it without requiring personal ownership.

### Sha'ar HaGavoa

The *mishna* introduces the concept of *sha'ar hagavoa*, which despite its literal sound ("high price") actually refers to a favorable rate — that is, more units per dollar. The terminology is counterintuitive: a *sha'ar hagavoa* means a lower price per unit, since more is obtained for the same outlay.

The case is as follows. A buyer gives money now, at a time when prices are low (say, four units per dollar), for later delivery. He and the seller arrange not only that delivery will occur at today's low prices, but also that if prices drop further between now and delivery, the buyer will receive the benefit of that lower price as well. In other words, if prices fall to six units per dollar, the buyer gets six. The buyer is therefore insulated from loss: if prices rise, he benefits from having locked in today's rate; if prices fall, he benefits from the even lower rate at delivery. The Gemara elsewhere characterizes such an arrangement as *karov liskar verachok mehefsed* — near to profit, far from loss. Nevertheless, this is permitted.

### Rabbi Yehuda Opinion

*Rabbi Yehuda* goes a step further. Even if no explicit *sha'ar hagavoa* arrangement was made, he holds that the buyer may still demand the lower price at the time of delivery. His reasoning: since the buyer could at any point say, "forget the delivery, just return my money" — because the sale was never fully final — and then use that money to purchase at the lower prevailing price, he is effectively always entitled to the lower price. *Yachol lomar lo ten li kazeh o ten li ma'osai* — he can say either give me goods at today's rate or return my money.

This ruling highlights the somewhat unusual nature of these transactions. Even though they are structured as sales rather than loans, they carry features that push toward the border of *ribbis*: the buyer gives money now, likely profits from rising prices, and under *Rabbi Yehuda*'s view is also protected from loss.

---

## Market vs Wholesale Price

### Rav Assi Contradiction

The *Gemara* opens with a statement by Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ein poskin ela besha'ar shebashuk* — one may not make such an arrangement except against the price established in the marketplace. This appears to flatly contradict the *mishna*, which permits the arrangement once *yatza hashaar*. The question is whether Rav Assi is drawing a distinction — perhaps between a price established at the wholesale or farm level, which is what the *mishna* addresses, and a retail market price.

### Village vs Major Markets

Rav Zeira presses Rav Assi: would Rabbi Yochanan say this even in the case of a place like *Durmis* — a major, established marketplace whose prices would be widely known and stable? Surely there the price can be relied upon. Rav Assi responds: no — Rabbi Yochanan's restriction was directed only at *shuk shel ayarot*, the small village markets, *delo kvi'i tar'ai hi*, where prices are not fixed and fluctuate from village to village and even within a single village. In such settings, a stated "market price" is not sufficiently stable to serve as the basis for an arrangement. But in a major marketplace with genuinely stable pricing, even Rabbi Yochanan would agree the arrangement is permissible.

### Warehouse Pricing

The *Gemara* then asks: if the *mishna*'s permission is not based on major retail market prices, what sort of price does it contemplate? The answer is *bechitti de'achli v'arfi*, grain that is held in warehouses and on shipping vessels, *demashach tar'eihu tfei* — whose prices are more stable over time. This is essentially a wholesale or storage-level pricing, where large quantities are held and prices do not shift with the daily fluctuations of the retail market. This is the kind of stable, accessible pricing on which a legitimate forward arrangement can be based.

---

## New vs Old Grain

### New-to-Old Problem

The *Gemara* presents a further complication. Suppose new grain is selling at four units per dollar and old grain at three units per dollar. Buyers prefer aged grain because it lasts longer and is better suited to grinding; hence old grain commands a premium. Now, a buyer wishes to pay today's price for new grain and take delivery months later — by which time the grain will have aged and become old grain.

The problem is more than a simple price-appreciation concern. When the *mishna* permits buying now at today's price for later delivery, the underlying rationale is that the buyer could have taken possession of the same product today. But here, what will be delivered later is categorically different from what is available now. The product available today is new grain; the product to be delivered is old grain, which today costs more. One cannot say the buyer could simply have bought it himself today at the agreed price and waited — because buying the aged product today would require paying the higher price. The transaction thus cannot be validated by the standard *yatza hashaar* logic. Accordingly: *ein poskin ad she-yatza hashaar lachadash velayashan* — one may not make this arrangement until the price has been established for both new and old grain alike.

### Rashi's Solution

Rashi explains this tersely stated *Gemara* as follows: the arrangement may only be made for new grain with old-grain delivery if the prices of the two are the same, or alternatively if the buyer is willing to pay today's price for old grain — the more expensive product — in which case there is no concern of receiving something worth more than what was paid. What cannot be done is to pay the current lower price of new grain and then receive aged grain worth more. The mismatch between the product priced and the product delivered is what creates the problem.

---

## Gathered vs Farm Grain

### Gathered Grain Prices

The *Gemara* introduces another distinction. There were individuals who would go from field to field gathering grain — an activity reminiscent of *leket*, gleaning. These gatherers would sometimes collect more than they needed for their own households and sell the surplus. The price of this gathered grain was lower: four units per dollar, versus three units per dollar for grain sold by ordinary householders. The reason for the lower price, as Rashi explains, is quality: grain gathered from the ground tends to be mixed, uneven, and of generally inferior quality compared to grain purchased directly from a farmer.

The question is whether a buyer can make a forward arrangement with a regular householder at the lower price of the gathered grain — reasoning that since he could go buy gathered grain at that rate, the arrangement at four per dollar should be valid. The *Gemara* states: *ein poskin ad she-yatza hashaar lilkot velimocher* — one may not make such an arrangement until the price for gathered grain and farmer's grain are the same.

The reason requires explanation. The *mishna*'s permission to arrange at today's price even without the seller possessing the product rests on the idea that the buyer could purchase that product himself in the market. But which market? The gathered grain market and the householder's grain market are two distinct markets with different price points. If the buyer is contracting with a householder — a person of ordinary standing — the implicit expectation is that he will receive householder-quality grain. He cannot invoke the lower gathered-grain price as though it were interchangeable.

### Rav Nachman Allow

Rav Nachman draws a limited distinction: *poskin le-lakutos keshaar le-lakutos* — if both parties to the arrangement are themselves gatherers, one may make the deal at the gathered-grain price. The reasoning follows the same logic as the *mishna*'s general permission: a gatherer who doesn't currently have grain can turn around and borrow from a fellow gatherer, so the product is effectively accessible. Within that community and market, the arrangement is valid.

### Rava Challenge

Rava challenges Rav Nachman: if that is the rationale — that the seller can obtain the product from others like himself — then why should the same logic not permit a householder-seller to rely on gathered grain prices? Let the householder, who lacks the product, simply turn around and purchase from the gatherers at their lower price and deliver accordingly. *Mai shna lokeit de-ei leis lei yazif milokeit chavrei... baal habayis nami yazif milakutos?* — What is different about the gatherer that if he lacks product he borrows from a fellow gatherer? So too, a householder could borrow from gatherers!

### Quality Expectations

The *Gemara* offers two answers. The first: *baal habayis zila bei milsa lemizaf milakutos* — a householder would find it beneath his dignity to go purchase from gatherers, who occupied a lower social station. This market, while technically open, is functionally off-limits to him; he would not in practice engage in such a transaction. Therefore he cannot be said to have ready access to that product at that price.

The alternative answer, *iba'is eima*: even if the householder could bring himself to purchase from gatherers, the buyer would not accept it. When a person gives money to a householder for grain, the implicit understanding — *man de-yahiv zuzei le-baal habayis apiri shapir yahiv* — is that he will receive quality, farmer-grade grain. To deliver gathered, mixed-quality grain in its place would violate that implicit expectation. Either the seller's reluctance or the buyer's expectation of quality independently explains why the lower gathered-grain price cannot be used in a transaction between ordinary parties.

---

## Borrowing & Fixed Prices

### Rav Sheshet Forbids

Rav Sheshet, citing Rav Huna, states: *ein lovin al hashaar she-bashuk* — one may not borrow against the market price. The precise meaning of this prohibition is not immediately obvious, and Rashi offers two distinct explanations.

### First Explanation

The first explanation connects directly to the permitted arrangement discussed throughout: what is forbidden is calling such a transaction a *loan* rather than a *sale*. If Reuven gives Shimon a hundred dollars and they agree that if Shimon cannot return the hundred dollars in cash he will pay back an equivalent quantity of grain at today's prices, they have structured it explicitly as a loan. But when Shimon repays months later with grain, that grain — measured at today's prices — will be worth more than the hundred dollars originally lent. By naming it a loan and denominating the repayment in kind based on today's rates, the extra value becomes *ribbis*. The same transaction structured as a *sale* — I am pre-purchasing grain at today's price — would be permitted. The prohibition thus concerns not the substance of the deal but its framing.

### Yatza HaSha'ar Logic

The second explanation engages the *se'ah be-se'ah* problem directly. Ordinarily, borrowing a measure of grain and repaying a measure later is forbidden because the price may have risen in the interim; you borrowed something worth ten and repaid something worth twelve. One recognized exception is when the borrower already owns the product — *yesh lo* — in which case he could in theory return it immediately, so the later return at a higher price is not considered a gain.

The question Rav Sheshet addresses is whether *yatza hashaar* — the establishment of a public market price — can serve as an equivalent to *yesh lo*. The reasoning would be: since the product is readily available at a fixed price, it is as though the borrower already possesses it; he can go to the market at any moment and acquire it. If so, borrowing a bag of flour and repaying later ought to be permitted whenever there is a stable, fixed public price for flour.

Rav Sheshet and Rav Huna say no — *yatza hashaar* alone does not create the equivalence of ownership. One cannot borrow on the basis of a fixed market price as though that price confers constructive possession.

This second reading has significant practical implications: it would potentially explain why one may ordinarily borrow a cup of flour from a neighbor. If the stores are open and prices are fixed, perhaps *yatza hashaar* effectively renders the borrower a notional owner of that flour — making repayment permissible even if the price has since risen. Rav Sheshet's ruling pushes back against that reasoning.

### Rav Huna Changes Mind

The *Gemara* then presents a challenge to Rav Huna's position. Rav Yosef bar Chama (others attribute it to Rav Yosei bar Abba) asked Rav Sheshet: did Rav Huna truly say this? For Rav Huna was once asked about *benei bei Rav* — yeshiva students — who would borrow in *Tishrei* and repay in *Tevet*. Rav Huna responded that this was permissible, pointing to the grain readily available in *Hini* and *Shili* — the markets were open and the product was there. That ruling sounds precisely like permitting a loan on the basis of the market price!

The *Gemara* resolves this: *ei ba'u zimni upari'ei lei me-ikara* — if they wanted, they could have repaid immediately. Because the product was so immediately accessible, it was treated as though they already possessed it, and the arrangement was therefore more like a *yesh lo* situation than a pure market-price arrangement. The *Gemara* then reports that Rav Huna originally held the stricter position but changed his mind upon hearing a ruling transmitted in the name of Shmuel that permitted such borrowing — and adopted Shmuel's position. Notably, the *Gemara* does not record that Rav Huna was persuaded by a new argument; the weight of Shmuel's authority was sufficient.

The practical upshot of the second reading of Rashi is particularly instructive for the everyday case of borrowing from a neighbor: one may do so when the stores are open and the price is fixed, because the ready availability of the product at a stable price is sufficient to treat the borrower as a constructive owner.

---

## Market Arbitrage

### Merchant Scenario

The *Gemara* now presents the case of *hamolich chavila mimakom lemakom* — a merchant transporting wares from one location to another, where the price differential is significant. Suppose goods sell for one dollar per unit in Oshkosh but two dollars per unit in Manhattan. I encounter the merchant and say: *tna-li v'ani a-aleh lecha kederech she-ma'alim lecha be-oso makom* — give them to me, and I will pay you at the Manhattan price, i.e., two dollars per unit.

Why would the buyer agree to pay double the current local price? Because by acquiring the goods now, the buyer gains access to funds — he can conduct business in Manhattan, deploy those resources, and pay back the seller at the Manhattan rate later. The seller, meanwhile, is relieved of the labor and risk of transporting the goods himself. The question is how to characterize this arrangement: is it a *purchase* at an agreed price, or is it in substance a *loan* — the seller extending credit (in the form of goods) to the buyer, who pays "interest" in the form of the price premium?

### Liability Analysis

The *Gemara* provides a decisive criterion: *birshus mocher mutar, birshus loke'ach assur* — if the goods remain in the seller's domain and responsibility, the arrangement is permitted; if they pass into the buyer's domain, it is forbidden.

If the seller retains liability — meaning that if the goods are damaged or lost in transit the loss falls on him — then the buyer has not truly purchased them yet. The buyer is in effect serving as the seller's agent, transporting the goods to Manhattan on his behalf, and only upon arrival and sale does the money change hands. At that point the buyer holds two hundred dollars of the seller's money and repays two hundred dollars — no gain, no *ribbis*.

If, however, the buyer takes liability upon himself — meaning he now bears the risk of loss — then he has acquired ownership of goods worth one hundred dollars while agreeing to pay two hundred dollars later. That deferred payment at a higher rate is the paradigm of *ribbis*: he received something worth one hundred, and the additional hundred in the later payment reflects the time value of the seller's money. This is forbidden.

Tosafot raises an immediate difficulty even with the permitted case: even if the buyer never formally acquires the goods, he has done the seller a significant favor by transporting them to the higher-price market. Why would the buyer provide this service for free? Clearly, the seller is compensating him — and that compensation is the buyer's opportunity to use the seller's money while in transit to Manhattan. Does that not itself constitute *ribbis*? The *Gemara* does not address this directly, but Tosafot raises it as a real concern requiring the answer elaborated below.

### Reputation Benefit

Rashi explains the permitted case on the basis of a different logic. The seller pre-commits to a large transaction at the lower local price, which publicly identifies him as a serious merchant with substantial means. When he arrives at the purchasing market flush with committed funds, his creditworthiness and standing are apparent, and sellers are willing to deal with him on favorable terms. This reputational benefit is what the seller provides to the buyer in exchange for the favorable price, and Rashi insists it is not interest in the halakhic sense — because the benefit does not flow from the *delay* in repayment. Even if payment were required immediately, the buyer would still benefit from the public knowledge that he had cash available. *Ribbis* is defined as compensation for waiting; a benefit that accrues independently of the passage of time does not constitute *ribbis*.

This reasoning is admittedly strained. The benefit — having access to the seller's money while traveling — sounds functionally identical to the benefit that interest ordinarily compensates. Nevertheless, this is Rashi's position.

### Tosafot Service Model

Tosafot is unconvinced by Rashi's reasoning and proposes a structurally different reading of the permitted case. On Tosafot's account, the buyer takes the seller's money and goes to the lower-price market — Oshkosh — and purchases the goods *for the seller*, using the seller's funds. From the moment of purchase, the goods belong to the seller; if anything happens to them en route back, the loss falls on the seller. The buyer has effectively provided a purchasing service — acquiring goods in a cheaper market on the seller's behalf — and the seller compensates him for that service by allowing him the use of the funds for the duration of the journey.

This reframes the transaction as a service arrangement rather than a loan: the buyer earns not interest but a fee for labor and logistics. The benefit the buyer receives — temporary access to the funds — is limited and tied to the service rendered, not to an ongoing lending relationship. Tosafot concedes that this reading is not explicit in the *Gemara*, but considers it necessary to avoid the *ribbis* problems that Rashi's account leaves unresolved.

---

## Donkey Drivers Case

### Pre-Selling Model

The *Gemara* describes a practice of *chamorin* — merchant-transporters who owned donkeys and made their livelihood moving goods between markets. In a high-price market (Manhattan, where goods fetch two dollars per unit), these merchants would pre-sell their wares at the lower price (one dollar per unit, as in Oshkosh). They had not yet gone to acquire the goods but were committing to deliver at the lower price. The *Gemara* states *veinam chosheshin* — and they need not be concerned about *ribbis*.

Why is this not a problem? The buyers in Manhattan are giving money now and will receive goods worth more at the local price. If this were framed as a loan, the buyer would be paying "interest" in the form of a favorable price.

### Rav Papa Explanation

Rav Papa explains: *nicha lehu demaglu lehu tara* — it benefits the merchants that their status as active businessmen is publicized. By pre-selling at a stated price, they demonstrate publicly that they are merchants with inventory coming. Rashi elaborates: when they arrive at the purchasing market with known committed sales, their standing is clear, sellers are willing to deal with them, and the whole enterprise is facilitated.

### Rav Acha Variation

Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika offers a variation: *nicha lehu demazpi gabaihu* — it benefits the merchants because sellers will offer them a better price. Specifically, once it is known that a merchant pre-sold at one dollar per unit, sellers in Oshkosh feel some sympathy — they know the merchant's margin is thin — and may offer the goods at slightly below the going rate, say 95 cents. According to Rashi, this modest price advantage in acquisition is the concrete benefit the merchant receives in exchange for the favorable pre-sale price in Manhattan.

The difference between Rav Papa and Rav Acha plays out in the case of a new merchant: does a newcomer stand to gain more from the reputational publicity (since he is unknown and exposure is especially valuable), or less from seller sympathy (since sellers do not know his situation)? The *Gemara* notes this as the practical distinction between the two explanations.

### Rav Conservative

The *Gemara* then records that in Sura goods were priced at four units per dollar, while in Kafri they went at six units per dollar. Rav gave money to the *chamorin* and accepted liability for the journey, and took delivery at five units per dollar — not six, which would have been the full Kafri price. The *Gemara* asks: having accepted all the theoretical justifications for this arrangement, why did Rav not simply take six per dollar? The answer: *adam chashuv shani* — a person of stature sets a more exacting standard for himself. Even where the practice is technically permissible, Rav chose to take less than the full benefit in order to distance himself from any appearance of *ribbis*. The acceptance of liability (*ones*) by Rav is relevant here: Tosafot notes that this element figures into the broader analysis of which party truly bears ownership of the goods.

---

## Secondary Markets Test

### Scrap Metal Question

Rav Assi posed a question to Rabbi Yochanan: *ma la'asot bi-grutaos kan* — can the same arrangement used by the *chamorin* be applied to scrap metal? The underlying question concerns the basis of the permit. Whether one follows Rashi's reputation theory or Tosafot's service model, the permit appears to depend in part on the existence of a stable, large-scale market — one in which the seller can reliably acquire the product and in which the reputational benefits or purchasing advantages are genuine.

Scrap metal markets are different. They are far less regularized: different sellers appear on different days, inventory is unpredictable, and no large stable supplier base exists. Rashi frames the question as whether the benefit to the merchant — whether reputational or in terms of purchase pricing — can operate meaningfully in a hit-or-miss secondhand market without a fixed community of sellers with whom an ongoing relationship can develop.

### Garments Dispute

In the same context, Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose wished to conduct such an arrangement with *klei pishtan* — linen garments — which similarly lack a uniform, stable wholesale market. These are handcrafted goods, not standardized commodities. Rabbi (Rebbi) did not permit him to do so. An alternative version of the tradition reverses the parties: Rebbi wished to make such an arrangement with scrap metal, and Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose refused to permit it. Either way, the point is the same: where the market lacks the stability and scale that makes the merchant's transaction genuinely analogous to a commodity purchase, the arrangement cannot rely on the same justifications and is therefore not permitted.

---

## Vineyard Wine Case

### Grape-to-Wine Problem

The final case on this *daf* involves *pardisa* — a vineyard. A buyer wishes to pre-purchase wine from the vineyard owner at a time when the fruit is still unripe and no fixed price has yet been established. The price agreed upon reflects the current low value of the unripe grapes. The delivery, however, will be in wine — a transformed product worth considerably more.

This presents a compounded problem. First, unlike the standard *yatza hashaar* case, the market price has not yet been set. Second, and more acutely, the product to be delivered is fundamentally different from what exists at the time of the arrangement: unripe grapes become wine only through an extended process, and wine is worth far more than the grapes from which it comes. The transaction thus resembles both the new-grain/old-grain problem and the general concern of receiving something more valuable than what one paid for.

### Rav vs Shmuel

Rav forbids such an arrangement: *keivan de-lichi mati shavi tfei, mitchazi ki agar natar lei* — since when the time of delivery comes it will be worth more, it has the appearance of payment for waiting. The extra value of the wine over the price of the unripe grapes is treated as though the buyer is being compensated for having extended money earlier — which is precisely the definition of *ribbis*.

Shmuel permits it: *keivan de-hava bi'asuta* — because there is an element of genuine risk. This returns to the question raised earlier in the *daf*: is the buyer purchasing a specific, concrete object, or merely a promise of delivery?

### Risk Justification

Shmuel's reasoning is that the buyer is not merely purchasing the future output of the vineyard in the abstract; he is purchasing the wine of this particular vineyard. It remains possible that the entire vineyard will be destroyed — by drought, blight, or other calamity — in which case there will simply be no wine to deliver and the buyer recovers nothing. The transaction therefore carries real commercial risk, which distinguishes it from a lending arrangement. A loan is repaid regardless of what happens in the interim; this transaction is contingent on the survival of a specific agricultural enterprise. That element of risk — the possibility of total loss — makes the arrangement a genuine purchase rather than a disguised loan, and therefore Shmuel permits it.

### Tori High Risk

The *Gemara* records that Rav Shimi bar Ashi said: *u-modei Rav be-tori de-nafish psida hu* — even Rav would concede in the case of *tori*, land that is plowed with oxen, where the risk of crop failure or damage is considerably higher. In such high-risk agricultural settings, even Rav agrees that the element of risk is sufficient to reframe the transaction as a genuine purchase, and the arrangement is therefore permissible. The threshold for Rav appears to be not merely theoretical risk but a meaningfully elevated probability of loss.

### Land Possession Fix

Finally, Shmuel offered practical guidance to those engaged in such pre-purchase arrangements for vineyard wine: *hafukhu be-ara ki heikhi de-tiknu lakhu gufa de-ara* — till the soil a little, so that you take some actual possession of the land itself. By performing a small act of *kinyan* on the land, the buyer acquires a stake — however nominal — in the vineyard itself, rather than merely a contractual entitlement to future wine. This transforms the transaction: instead of what might look like a loan secured by future agricultural output, the buyer is now a partial owner of the underlying land, and the delivery of wine is the yield of his own property. *Ve-i lo havei lakhu ke-halva'ah ve-asir* — without this step, it has the character of a loan and is forbidden.

This concludes the *daf*, which has moved through a wide range of practical applications — from forward arrangements for grain, to quality distinctions between market types, to the *se'ah be-se'ah* problem and borrowed goods, to merchant transport and market arbitrage, and finally to agricultural pre-purchases and the role of risk in validating commercial transactions. The range of cases makes this section of *Bava Metzia* unusual: rather than sustained abstract analysis, the *Gemara* is testing the principles of *ribbis* across the full spectrum of commercial life.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 74

## Deferred Payment Fix

### Watchmen Payment

Today's daf is 74, though we actually pick up near the bottom of 73a with the words *amar lei Rava l'hanei d'mantrei bagi* — Rava said to those who watched the valleys where the wheat was growing. These watchmen were employed to guard the grain fields, but their payment was deferred until after the harvest had been cut, threshed, and brought to market — that is, when the owners actually had money to pay them. In the meantime, the owners would throw in a little extra: instead of the wage that was strictly owed, they would pay somewhat more to compensate for the wait. This creates a problem of *ribbis*: the additional payment functions as interest on the deferred salary.

### Nominal Work Solution

Rava's solution is elegant and practical. He told these watchmen: *puku hafichu b'hadei dari* — go out and turn over the grain at the threshing floor. Continue doing some nominal, trivial work for the owner right up until the moment he is ready to pay you. The operative principle is *d'sechar eino mishtalem ela l'vasof* — payment for service is only discharged at the end of the service. By extending their involvement, even in a perfunctory way, through the threshing period, the watchmen's service is technically not concluded until the moment of payment.

### Service Extension

Once the service formally extends to the point of payment, the extra compensation the owner gives is no longer characterized as interest for waiting. The Gemara expresses this with the phrase *azulei hu d'ka mozil gabaichu* — he is simply selling his grain to you cheaply, or equivalently, being overly generous with you. Once there is no gap between the end of service and the moment of payment, whatever excess he gives you is merely generosity, not deferred *ribbis*. It is only when a worker has already stopped working some time ago, and then receives extra payment later, that the additional amount is cast as compensation for the delay — which constitutes *ribbis*. The practical instruction, then, is clear: keep doing some nominal work until the time of payment, and then if the owner wishes to be generous, that is entirely his prerogative.

### Payment Delay Q&A

This analysis raises a broader question: why can a worker ever agree to defer payment in the first place? The answer is that the prohibition of *halanat sechar sachir* — withholding a worker's wages — can be contractually waived; a worker may arrange in advance to receive payment at a later date. That said, the arrangement carries real risk of abuse. If the employer's market gives him leverage, he might systematically pre-arrange deferred payment and then add extra, effectively charging interest on the wage debt. The further observation that follows naturally from this is that in any commercial society, the prohibition of *ribbis* creates acute difficulties. Purchasing an automobile on installment payments from a Jewish seller, with an interest charge built into the monthly payments, is a paradigm case of *ribbis*. The entire framework of modern consumer credit, and indeed the structure of bank deposits bearing interest, falls within these concerns — hence the reliance in modern Israel and elsewhere on instruments such as the *heter iska*.

---

## Sharecropper Rights

### Rabbis Challenge

The Gemara then records a challenge directed at Rava himself. The Rabbis said to him: *ka-akhil mar ribbis* — it appears that the master is eating *ribbis*. The practice under discussion was land rental: *de-khulei alma shakli arba u-maslaki le-hu be-Nisan* — everyone else who rents out fields to sharecroppers charges four units per measure and removes the sharecroppers in Nisan. Rava, by contrast, waits until Iyar — an additional month — and collects six units. Since he defers collection and collects more, it looks as though the increment is compensation for the delay: a form of *ribbis*.

### Rava's Defense

Rava's response is sharp and unexpected: *attun ka avdatun shelo ke-din* — it is not I who am acting improperly, it is you. The reasoning: *ara le-arisa mishta'abeda* — the land is under the rights and jurisdiction of the sharecropper. The sharecropper has a legal entitlement to remain on the land, and the other landlords who eject their sharecroppers in Nisan are harming them. *Ei attun mesalki le-hu be-Nisan mafsidtu le-hu be-khamma* — when you remove them in Nisan, you cause them to lose profit, because the grain is not yet fully ready for harvest.

### Profit Justification

Rava continues: *ana natarna le-hu ad Iyar u-mavkhana le-hu be-khamma* — I allow them to remain through Iyar, and they therefore reap a larger harvest and earn more money. It is precisely because the sharecropper derives greater benefit from the land under Rava's arrangement that Rava charges more. The higher rental fee is not compensation for a deferral of payment; it is proportionate to the greater profit the sharecropper actually realizes. Rava's arrangement is thus not only free of *ribbis* — it is arguably more equitable than the prevailing practice.

---

## Mashkon House

### Rav Mari Family

The Gemara introduces *Rav Mari bar Rachel*, and Rashi's comment here is fascinating. The name itself is unusual — in a patriarchal society, why identify someone by his mother? Rashi explains: *bat Shmuel havya ve-ishtabai* — this Rachel was Shmuel's daughter, who was taken captive. *U-nesava oved kokhavim* — she was taken by a non-Jew. *Ve-nitgayyer u-shmey Issur Giyyora* — and this non-Jew eventually converted, taking the name Issur Giyyora, an appropriately literal name for a *ger*. Rav Mari's status was therefore: *horato shelo bi-kdusha ve-leidato bi-kdusha* — conceived before his father's conversion, born after it. *U-mekhamat kevodo lo karu leh al shmey de-avuha* — out of respect for Rav Mari, they did not name him after his father, since at the time of conception the father was still a non-Jew; hence he was named after his mother. Rav Mari bar Rachel and his father Issur Giyyora appear in a number of places throughout *Shas*.

### House Collateral

*Rav Mari bar Rachel amshakhne leh hahu nokhri beita* — a certain non-Jew pledged his house to Rav Mari as collateral on a loan. Rav Mari was living in the house — effectively his interest payment, which is permissible when dealing with a non-Jew. *Hadar zabna le-Rava* — the non-Jew then sold the house to Rava while Rav Mari was still residing in it. This raises interesting questions about the transfer of title over property currently occupied by someone with possessory rights; in practice, such transfers do occur, and the Gemara proceeds on that basis.

### Rent-Free Year

*Natar taresar yarkhei sheta* — Rav Mari waited twelve months. *Shakil agar beita amti leh le-Rava* — and then he took rent money and brought it to Rava. He explains his reasoning: *hai de-la amti leh le-mar agar beita ad haidanna — d'stama mashkanta shatta* — the reason he had not paid rent for the entire first year is that, as the Gemara established earlier, a *stama mashkon* — a standard collateral arrangement over a house or field — carries with it a full year during which the creditor cannot be displaced. That year of exclusive possession was effectively his interest payment on the loan with the non-Jew. When the non-Jew sold the house to Rava, Rav Mari's rights for that year were not extinguished. *Ei bei l'salukei lo hava matzi l'salukei* — even had the original owner wished to remove him during that year, he could not have done so. The sale to Rava did not change that.

### Payment After Year

Once the year expired, however, Rav Mari recognized a change in his legal position. *Hashta* — now — if the non-Jew were to pay off the loan, he would have the right to reclaim the house and remove Rav Mari. This means that Rav Mari's rights are no longer absolute; he can be displaced upon repayment of the debt. In the language of the analysis: before the year was up, the non-Jew could not have removed him under any circumstances — his occupation was as secure as ownership. Now, the situation is different: Rav Mari is residing on land that is effectively Rava's, subject to a lien. To continue living there rent-free would resemble receiving a benefit from Rava — and that benefit is connected, however indirectly, to money he has out on loan to the non-Jew. Technically, it is not *ribbis* in the strict sense, because Rava is not the debtor — the non-Jew is. One might recall from an earlier passage in the Gemara the discussion of someone else paying for a loan made to a third party; the same logic applies here. But it does not look right. Accordingly, Rav Mari decides he should begin paying rent.

### Rava Refuses Rent

Rava's response is remarkable. *Ei hava yadana d'hava memashken lei l'mar lo hava zavnina lei* — had I known the house was under your collateral arrangement, I never would have purchased it from the non-Jew; I would not have interfered with your relationship. *Hashta kedineihem avdina lach* — now, I will follow, for these purposes, the terms that would have governed your relationship with the non-Jew: *kol eimas d'lo misalkana lach b'zuzei lo shakilna agar bayta* — as long as the debt has not been repaid, I will not accept rent from you. Rashi clarifies that this means: until the non-Jew pays off the loan and the debt is settled, Rava refuses to take any rent from Rav Mari. The spectacle of each party declining what the other is offering — one insisting on paying rent, the other refusing to accept — reflects the *tzidkut* of both parties. The underlying halachic structure is: Rav Mari is entitled to remain in the house by virtue of his lien on the non-Jew's debt; Rava, recognizing this, refuses to extract rent during the period in which that lien remains in force.

---

## Wine & Grain Ribbis

### Wine Selection Ribbis

*Amar lei Rava miBarnish l'Rav Ashi: chazi mar rabanan d'ka achli ribis* — Rava miBarnish said to Rav Ashi: look at what the rabbis are doing — they appear to be eating *ribbis*. The practice described is: *yahavi zuzei achamra b'Tishrei u'meshachali lei b'Teves* — they give money for wine in Tishrei but only select which wine they will actually take in Teves. In the interval between Tishrei and Teves, some wine turns to vinegar while other wine remains good and clear. Because they are not taking immediate possession, the arrangement functions as a loan to the wine seller — they allow him to hold his wine longer, and in return they receive the right to choose the best wine. That right of selection, obtained in exchange for the delay, is a form of *ribbis*.

### Breira Defense

Rav Ashi's response turns on a conceptual point: *inhu nami achamar kayahavi, achala lo kayahavi* — when they pay for wine, they pay at the rate of wine, not vinegar. They never agreed to purchase vinegar. The underlying claim is: *me'ikara dechamar chamar dechala chala* — what was wine from the beginning was wine, and what was vinegar from the beginning was vinegar. Even at the moment of purchase in Tishrei, the inferior wine already carried within it the quality that would make it turn sour by Teves. The wine that remains good was always good wine; it was not transformed by the passage of time. This is a form of *breira* — a retroactive determination that clarifies what was always the case: the good wine was always the wine they purchased, because they paid for wine, not for vinegar. At the moment of selection in Teves, they are simply identifying which barrels were, all along, the ones they had actually bought.

One might push back: even granting the *breira* argument, a normal purchaser who takes immediate delivery still bears the risk that his wine might turn. By waiting and selecting, these buyers are insulated from that risk entirely — and being freed from commercial risk is itself a benefit. *Hahi sha'ata hu dekamivchari* — it is only at that later moment that the determination is made as to which wine was chosen. Even if the quality differential was latent from the beginning, the buyers are still enjoying a benefit that a standard purchaser, who must accept the goods and bear the risk, would not have. This is what makes the case genuinely difficult, and the *breira* argument — while perhaps technically defensible — does not fully dissolve the intuition that something valuable is being received in exchange for the delay.

### Ravina's Grain

*Ravina hava yahiv zuzei livnei akra deshanvata* — Ravina would give money to the people living by the riverbank plots called Shanvata, pre-purchasing their grain. *Veshafchi lei tefei kufisa* — when it came time to deliver, they would pour a little extra into his bag — a baker's dozen arrangement, as it were. Since the delivery was later than payment, and they gave him extra at the time of delivery, the question arises whether this constitutes *ribbis*. *Azal lekamei deRav Ashi; amar lei: mi sharei? Amar lei: in* — he went before Rav Ashi, who said it was permissible. *Achulei hu deka machli gabach* — they are simply being *mochel*, waiving something in your favor, giving you a gift.

### Rav Ashi Approval

The obvious difficulty is that they are forgiving something in Ravina's favor precisely because he lent them money — or more precisely, because he pre-paid and thus forwarded them funds. One recalls earlier discussions in the Gemara about arrangements where a lender may not live rent-free in the borrower's house, or receive flour with an extra scoop added. The principle in those cases was that even without explicit acknowledgment, the benefit is presumed to flow from the loan relationship. Why is this different?

### Tosafot Conditions

Tosafot addresses this carefully. *Ein zeh ribbis gemurah* — the extra grain does not constitute full *ribbis*. The reasoning proceeds on two grounds. First, *shelo hayu mazkirim shenotnim bishvil me'otav shehayu beteilim etzlam kidefairash bekontres* — they did not say, "here is a little extra because you pre-paid us and your money was tied up with us." The connection to the loan was never made explicit. Second, and more significantly, Tosafot distinguishes this from the case of living rent-free in a borrower's house: *velo dami lehalevehu vadar bechatzeiro shetzarich leha'alot lo sachar* — that case is different because *deshani hasham she'adayan chayav lo* — there the loan is still active, the debt is still outstanding. Here, by the time the extra grain is delivered, the transaction has been completed. The grain has been delivered; there is no longer an outstanding loan.

This generates a precise and important set of conditions. If the debt is concluded and no explicit connection is made to the original loan — "I am grateful for the money you lent me" — then giving a gift or extra measure does not constitute *ribbis*. The counterintuitive *chiddush* is that the gift need not be temporally distant from the delivery; the juxtaposition alone does not render it *ribbis*, so long as the two conditions are met: the loan is over, and the connection is not verbalized. If, on the other hand, one were to say "thank you for waiting the two months" or "thank you for paying up front, here is a little something" — that is *ribbis*. If one simply hands over the grain with a bit extra and says nothing about the earlier arrangement, it is not.

---

## Dina D'Malchusa

### Tax-Seized Land

A new problem emerges. *Amar lei ha'ara lav didhu hi* — suddenly the question arises: how could he even accept delivery of grain from these people? It turns out that the land on which their grain was grown may not have belonged to them at all — they were apparently working land that had been seized from others who had defaulted on their taxes to the government. If that is the case, then the grain itself might be stolen property, making the entire earlier *ribbis* discussion beside the point.

### Government Authority

*Amar lei: ara l'taska meshabda* — the land is subjugated to the tax obligation; by virtue of the tax debt, the government has rights to the land. *U'malka amar: man d'yahiv taska leichol ara* — and the king declares that whoever pays the tax may benefit from the land. The government, through its tax authority, has the power to reassign use of the land to those willing to pay the outstanding taxes. This is a commercially functioning economic system, not arbitrary theft, and it has halachic implications.

### Legal Principle

Why should Jewish law care what the government declares? Because *dina d'malchusa dina* — the law of the kingdom is law. Rashi explicitly invokes this principle here. The government has liens on land for unpaid taxes; it can reassign productive use of that land. That economic and legal reality is recognized within *halacha*. Some *rishonim* and *geonim* observe that *dina d'malchusa dina* applies specifically to public law — areas in which the government has a systemic interest, such as taxation and public land rights — as distinguished from government regulation of purely private relationships between individuals. The case here is paradigmatically a matter of public law: "If you fail to pay your taxes, the government acquires rights over your land." That is precisely the domain where *dina d'malchusa dina* operates.

---

## Poll Tax Slavery

### Enslavement Question

*Amar lei Rav Pappa l'Rava: chazi mar hanei rabbanan d'yahvi zuzei akarga* — Rav Pappa said to Rava: look at this troubling practice. These rabbis of the *yeshiva* — and it is worth noting that it is the anonymous scholars who are apparently engaging in this — are paying the poll tax of individual citizens. *D'akarga d'inish, umeshabbdi behu tfei* — they pay someone else's poll tax to the government, and then they subjugate that person. In practical terms: Charlie owes the government a hundred dollars in poll tax; I pay the government on Charlie's behalf; I then seize Charlie and put him to work as my personal servant until he reimburses me.

### Prepaid Labor

The *ribbis* dimension of this arrangement: Charlie will eventually pay the government his poll tax — or reimburse me — and at that point I will no longer have a claim on his service. So what have I done in the interim? I effectively forwarded Charlie the hundred dollars, and while he owes it, I am working him. My gain for having advanced the money is his labor. Everyone can see why this is structurally a form of *ribbis*: I lend money, and I receive service in return until the loan is repaid.

### Rav Sheshet's

Rava's response is almost theatrical. *Hashta ichu schivna, lo amri lichu hani miltha* — had I died just now, I would have departed this world without teaching you this important *halacha*. What Rav Sheshet taught: *moharkayu de-hani be-tapsa de-malka monach* — the enslavement document of these citizens sits, conceptually, in the king's treasury. Just as the king holds fundamental rights over the land through the tax structure — recalling the story of Pharaoh and Yosef — the king holds fundamental rights over the service of his subjects.

### Public Law

*U-malka amar: man de-lo yaiv karga lishhtabeid le-man de-yaiv karga* — the king declares that whoever fails to pay his poll tax, and someone else pays it on his behalf, that other person acquires rights to the defaulter's service. This is *dina d'malchusa dina*: a public law that governs the relationship between the citizen and the state, and between citizens whose financial obligations to the state are discharged by others. The government's legal framework is recognized as creating enforceable entitlements within *halacha*, just as it does in the case of tax-seized land.

### Ribbis Tension

Yet the problem is not fully dissolved. *Dina d'malchusa dina* may establish my right to Charlie's service in the sense of: what entitles me to seize him at all, given that Jewish law does not ordinarily permit enslaving a debtor? But it does not obviously answer the separate question of why receiving his labor in return for having forwarded his poll tax is not *ribbis*. Saying that the government permits it does not address whether I am gaining something extra for having effectively extended Charlie a loan.

One resolution suggested is a reconceptualization of the transaction: rather than framing it as "I lent Charlie money and I receive his service as interest," one could frame it as "I purchased from the government the rights to Charlie's labor." Under this reading, there is no loan and no debtor-creditor relationship; it is a purchase of a service right. A further resolution — and this may be the cleaner one — is that Charlie is working off his debt through his labor rather than repaying a monetary loan. If the service itself is understood as discharging the obligation, there is no gap between the loan and its repayment; there is simply a sale of labor in satisfaction of a debt. Under this reading, there is no *ribbis* at all, and the sole question is the one *dina d'malchusa dina* answers: what entitles a private person to enslave another for non-payment of taxes? Ordinary *halacha* would not permit this — a *eved ivri* arises only from theft, not from ordinary debt — and so the government's law is doing all the necessary work.

Tosafot, it should be noted, reads this Gemara as a *ribbis* case: *veshafchi lei tefei kufisa... she-levisof hayu machazirim lahem ma'os hakarga she-notnim ba'avoram, v'chol mah shehayu mishtabdin bahen hayu bischar halva'ah* — in the end they would return the poll-tax money to those who had paid it on their behalf, and all the labor they performed during that period was compensation for the loan. Under Tosafot's reading, the *ribbis* problem is real and the answer via *dina d'malchusa dina* is doing even more work — which makes the answer more interesting and more difficult simultaneously.

---

## Rav Sura Seizure

### Criminal Seizure

The Gemara records a related practice. *Rav Sura Ram, achui d'Rava, havay takeish insha d'lo malei* — Rav Sura, Rava's brother, would seize people who were not good — petty thieves or others injurious to society — *u'malyu b'goharka d'Rava* — and put them to work carrying Rava's palanquin. This is distinct from the poll-tax case: here there is no government law, no outstanding tax, and no debtor-creditor relationship. The basis for this seizure is purely communal control.

### Biblical Source

*Amar lei Rava: shappir ka'avidat* — Rava said to him: you did well, this is acceptable. The source is a *braita*: *ra'isa she-eino noheig kashura — minayin she-ata rashai l'hishtabeid bo? Talmud lomar: l'olam bahem ta'avodu* — if you see someone behaving improperly, how do you know you may enslave him as a measure of control? Because the verse says "you may enslave them forever."

### Improper Conduct

The *derasha* reads the verse with a different pause. The full verse continues: *u'v'acheichem b'nei yisrael ish b'achiv lo tirdeh bo b'farech* — but among your brother Israelites, you shall not work one another with harshness. The *derasha* first reads the text as if it includes a Jew who behaves improperly alongside the foreigners who may be enslaved: *l'olam bahem ta'avodu u'v'acheichem* — you may enslave them and your fellow Jew. The *talmud lomar* qualification then restores the verse's actual division, limiting the permission to those who are *not* acting properly. The conclusion: a community has the authority to subject those whose conduct is injurious to society to compelled service as a form of social control — not as permanent enslavement, but as a corrective measure. This is a striking Gemara: prior to this point, the daf had established that enslavement under Jewish law arises only from theft (the *eved ivri* case) or self-sale. Here we find two additional grounds: government authority via *dina d'malchusa dina* in the poll-tax case, and communal authority over those who do not conduct themselves properly.

---

## Negligent Agent

### Wine Purchase

*Amar Rav Chama: hai man d'yahiv zuzei l'chavrei l'mizban lei chamra* — someone gave money to his friend to purchase wine on his behalf. The market timing was right; prices were low. The agent was given the money and a fee for his efforts. *U'pasha v'lo zavin lei* — the agent was negligent and did not make the purchase. The opportunity passed and the prices rose. What does the agent owe?

The preliminary objection is that this seems to be a case of *grama b'nezikin patur* — indirect damage, for which one is ordinarily exempt. No physical property was damaged; there was simply a lost opportunity caused by negligence.

### Compensation Rule

Nevertheless, Rav rules: *meshaleim lei k'ka'azla afarvata d'zushafat* — the agent must pay at the lowest market rate at which wine was available at the best market, the place called Zushafat where wine went cheapest. Despite the absence of direct damage, the negligent agent must make his principal whole at the prices the principal would have secured.

### Standard Wine

*Amar Meimar amritah l'shma'ata kmaih d'Rav Zevid mi-Neharde'a* — when this ruling was reported before Rav Zevid of Nehardea, he qualified it: *hani mili b'yayin stam* — this applies only when the instruction was to buy generic wine. *B'yayin zeh*, however — if the principal specified a particular seller — *lo*: the agent is not liable. Why? *Mi yeimar d'mizabni lei nihalei* — who is to say that seller would have sold to him? Perhaps the specified seller would have declined. Since the success of the mission was not guaranteed even had the agent performed his duty, the causal link between the negligence and the loss is insufficiently certain to impose liability. When the instruction is simply "buy wine" and wine is universally available, there is no such uncertainty; the agent's negligence definitively cost the principal the opportunity. When the instruction specifies a particular source, the outcome was never certain.

### Asmachta Issue

*V'Rav Ashi amar: afillu yayan stam nami* — Rav Ashi goes further and says that even in the case of generic wine, the agent owes nothing. *Mai ta'ama? Asmachta hi* — the reason is that any obligation the agent would have to compensate rests on an implicit penalty clause, and penalty clauses of this type are *asmachta*, which is not legally binding. The agent did not sell anything to the principal, did not rent him anything, did not create a formal exchange. The implicit understanding that "if I fail to do the job I will compensate you for the loss" is a penalty commitment — and penalty commitments, under conditions we will shortly define, are not seriously meant and therefore not legally enforceable.

### Asmachta Definition

*Asmachta* is the concept of a commitment, typically a penalty or forfeiture clause, that one does not expect to have to honor and therefore never truly commits to. Because the obligation arises not from an exchange of property or services but from a contingency the party expects not to occur, it lacks the *gemirat da'at* — the full mental commitment — necessary to create a binding obligation. *V'asmachta lo kanya* — an *asmachta* does not effect acquisition or liability.

Under Rav Ashi's analysis, then, the reason a negligent agent would owe anything at all is not damages in the conventional sense — this is plainly *grama*, and *grama b'nezikin* is ordinarily exempt. The only conceivable basis for liability is an implicit penalty clause, and that penalty clause is *asmachta* and therefore unenforceable.

### Sharecropper Penalty

*V'Rav Ashi mai shna mei'ha d'tnan: im ovir v'lo a'avid ashalem b'meitava* — but what distinguishes the classic sharecropper case, where the contract provides: "if I leave the land fallow and do not work it, I will pay you with the best of the crops" — which is precisely a penalty clause for non-performance, and yet is enforceable? If all penalty clauses were *asmachta*, that clause too should fail.

### Control Factor

*Hatam b'yado, hacha lav b'yado* — the distinction is control. In the sharecropper case, the decision whether to work the land or leave it fallow is entirely within the sharecropper's control. He is choosing to neglect his duty; no external factor prevents him from working. When you fully control whether the penalty-triggering event occurs, the *asmachta* argument collapses: you cannot say you did not seriously commit to the penalty, because you had every ability to avoid it. Here, however — in the agent's case — according to Rashi, the argument is that even with generic wine, there may have been factors outside the agent's control preventing him from securing the exact prices or the exact wine. Since his success was not entirely within his hands, the penalty clause was never fully and seriously meant.

Tosafot presses on this point, noting that it seems odd to classify a case of purchasing freely available generic wine as "not in his hands." Tosafot suggests that perhaps it was not entirely certain that the agent could have obtained the wine at those particular low prices. The deeper question Tosafot raises is whether the *b'yado/lav b'yado* distinction is really the defining factor for *asmachta*, and this opens into a broader discussion: is gambling *asmachta*? What about competitive games? The analysis that emerges is that at the extremes the question is clearer. When something is entirely within one's control — as in the sharecropper case — committing to a penalty is a genuine commitment, and one is held to it. When something is entirely random — as with a roulette wheel — one bets knowing full well that the outcome is beyond control, and the bet is accepted with clear eyes. The more difficult cases are intermediate ones: situations involving both an element of skill or control and an element of chance, where one might genuinely believe one can control the outcome while in fact one cannot fully do so. In those cases, the argument that one never seriously committed to the penalty is most compelling.

---

## Situmta Purchase

### Joint Purchase

*Amar Rava: hani bei tlata d'yahavi zuzei l'chad l'mizban lehu midi* — three people give money to one agent to purchase something on their behalf. *V'zavan l'chad mineihu* — if he ends up buying for one of them — or perhaps, using one person's money — *zavan l'kulu*: since they all gave their money together, he has effectively purchased for all three. He cannot allocate the purchase to only one of the three principals; the collective contribution creates collective ownership.

### Separate Bundles

*V'la amran ela d'la tzar v'chatumi inish inish l'chudei* — this rule applies only if the money was not sealed and individually signed by each person. If each of the three persons handed the agent a separately sealed, signed bundle of money, then clearly there is no collective here — there are three distinct individuals engaging the agent for three separate transactions. In that case, *l'man d'zavan zavan u'l'man d'la zavan la zavan*: whatever he purchased with A's money belongs to A, and B has no claim on it, and vice versa. Here one can see, in embryonic form, something resembling the concept of a corporation — the pooling of capital into a single undifferentiated fund creates collective rights and obligations.

### Situmta Mark

*Amar Rav Pappa mishmei d'Rava: hai situmta* — in the name of Rava, Rav Pappa teaches regarding the *situmta*. According to Rashi, a *situmta* works as follows: I go to a wine merchant and wish to purchase ten barrels, but I cannot take immediate delivery of all of them. I place my mark — my identifying sign — on ten specific barrels. I have not performed *meshicha*, the act of physical pulling or moving that ordinarily effects transfer of movable property. *Hai situmta kanya* — does that mark effect acquisition?

### Full Ownership

*L'mai hilchata? Rav Chaviva amar l'miknei mamash* — for what purpose does it matter? Rav Chaviva holds that the mark effects full, real ownership even without a standard *kinyan*. The moment the mark is placed, those barrels belong to the buyer.

### Commitment Only

*V'rabanan amri l'kabulei alei mi shepara* — the Rabbis disagree. The mark is not a full *kinyan*; it is analogous to the payment of money in a sale, which under rabbinic law does not consummate the transfer of movable goods. It creates a quasi-*kinyan* — a level of commitment such that if either party backs out, the *mi shepara* curse applies. But it is not full ownership.

### Custom Determination

*V'hilchata l'kabulei alei mi shepara* — the ruling follows the Rabbis: the mark alone creates only a commitment, not full ownership. However: *u'v'atra d'nahigi l'miknei mamash kani* — in a place where the accepted practice is that placing one's mark constitutes a final, binding sale, that communal practice is halachically recognized as effecting full transfer of ownership. Where a community or industry operates on the understanding that the mark is the conclusive act of sale, *halacha* honors that understanding.

### Mazal U'Bracha

This is a foundational principle in halachic commercial law, and the most commonly cited contemporary illustration is from the diamond industry, where the declaration *mazal u'vracha* is understood by all parties as the moment the deal is final and irrevocable. In some contexts a handshake functions similarly. Various industries and marketplaces have their own conventional acts that signal binding completion — eBay's formulation that all bids are final binding contracts is a modern parallel. *Halacha* recognizes these conventions. The theoretical underpinning is the concept of *gemirat da'at* — full mental commitment to the transaction. The standard *kinyanim* defined by *halacha* are themselves expressions of *gemirat da'at*, and when a community has developed its own acts that equally express that finality of commitment, *halacha* can recognize those acts as effecting the transfer, even if they fall outside the formally defined *kinyanim*. It is, in a sense, a do-it-yourself *kinyan* — grounded in the same underlying concept but expressed through communally recognized custom rather than formally legislated form.

---

## Early Grain Sales

### Possession Rule

With the foundational rule in view — that one may pre-purchase goods from an early seller only if the seller actually has the goods in some form of possession — the Gemara examines the debate between Rav and Shmuel regarding how far removed from the final product the goods may be.

### Rav Two Stages

*Rav* holds: *mechusar shtayim posek, shalosh eino posek* — if the product is only two processing stages away from its deliverable form, the seller may pre-sell it. If it is three or more stages removed, he may not, because it is considered as though he does not yet have it.

### Shmuel Control

*Shmuel* offers a fundamentally different criterion. *B'yedei adam afilu me'ah posek* — if all the remaining stages are under human control, the seller may pre-sell even if there are a hundred steps remaining. The reasoning ties back to the *asmachta* discussion: when the process is entirely within human hands, the seller genuinely has the product in a meaningful sense, because nothing stands between him and delivery except his own effort.

### Divine Dependency

Conversely: *b'yedei shamayim afilu achat eino posek* — if even one remaining step depends on divine intervention — rain, wind, sun — then even a single step is too much. The seller cannot guarantee delivery; his ownership of the product is too contingent. Rav's quantitative criterion and Shmuel's qualitative criterion thus diverge sharply, and as we shall see, all the cases in the *Mishna* work out better for Shmuel.

---

## Produce Applications

### Wheat Bundle

The *Mishna* permits pre-purchasing on the basis of a *gadish* — a bundle of wheat — even though what will ultimately be delivered is grain. The Gemara notes: *v'ha mechusar misht'cha b'chama l'mevesh u-l'midash u-midra* — the bundle is still lacking: drying in the sun, complete desiccation, threshing, and winnowing. That is four steps. The Gemara resolves this by stipulating: *kegon d'shadya b'chama v'yavesh* — the case in the *Mishna* is where the bundle has already been dried in the sun and desiccated. We are now only two steps removed — threshing and winnowing — which satisfies Rav's criterion.

### Sieve Solution

For Shmuel's criterion, the remaining challenge is winnowing, which appears to depend on wind — a divine factor. *Efshar b'nafavata* — it is possible to accomplish the winnowing with a sieve, without relying on wind at all. The process is thereby entirely within human hands, and Shmuel's condition is satisfied.

### Wine Processing

The *Mishna* also permits pre-purchasing wine on the basis of a *avit* — a barrel of grapes.
