But wine requires: *michmar* — a heating process applied to the grapes, bringing them to the pressing floor, pressing, and having the wine flow into the pit. This is a substantial number of steps. The Gemara resolves the issue by invoking the language of Rav Chiyya's *braita* about olives, which uses the term *komar* — a vessel in which the grapes sit after the heating process has been completed. *Hacha nami al ha-komar shel anavim* — here too, the purchase is made at the stage of the *komar* of grapes, after the heating has occurred.

### Buyer Final Step

Even so, three steps remain: transport to the pressing floor, pressing, and having the wine flow into the pit. *B'atra d'zavin hu d'nagid* — the Gemara explains that in the locale under discussion, the buyer himself performs the final step of causing the wine to flow into the pit. This is admittedly difficult to picture as a standard commercial practice — one imagines a merchant purchasing wine and being informed that he must show up on pressing day to participate in the process. But the Gemara's solution requires it: by having the buyer perform the final step, the number of steps the seller must complete is reduced to two, satisfying Rav.

### Oil Extraction

*V'al ha-ma'atan shel zeitim* — a vessel of olives, where what is being purchased is olive oil. As with the wine, the process is lengthy: the heating, bringing to the pressing floor, pressing, and extracting the oil. The same resolution applies: *tni Rav Chiyya al ha-komar shel zeitim* — Rav Chiyya's formulation positions the purchase at the stage after heating, in the *komar* vessel, reducing the remaining steps. And again, *de'ihu dezavin hu demangid* — the buyer performs the final extraction step himself.

### Potter's Clay

*Ve'al habeytzim shel yotzer* — the "eggs" of the potter, i.e., balls of clay. What is being pre-purchased is not the clay but the finished pottery. The clay in its raw ball form must still be shaped, dried, placed in the kiln, fired, and removed from the kiln. *Kegon demelafefa veyivusha* — the Gemara stipulates that the clay has already been shaped and dried; it now remains only to fire it. This is described as still being called a "ball of clay" even though it is technically an unfired vessel.

### Pottery Removal

Even so, three steps remain for the firing stage: placing in the oven, firing, and removing. *Ve'azdu leta'amei de'ihu dezavin hu demaphik* — the buyer again performs the final step, removing the fired pottery from the kiln. The buyer here receives the honor of the final act of production. Across all these cases, it is striking that the evidence consistently points in Shmuel's direction: the *Mishna* permits pre-purchasing in situations where many steps of processing remain, which works straightforwardly under Shmuel's criterion (all steps are within human control) but requires considerable ingenuity — stipulating that prior stages are already completed and that buyers perform final steps themselves — to fit Rav's two-stage limit.

### Plaster Grinding

*Ve'al hasid misheshika'o bekivshan* — plaster after it has been placed in the kiln. Raw stone is placed in a kiln, fired, and then ground into powder. The Gemara notes three remaining steps: firing, removing, and grinding. *Ve'azdu leta'amei de'ihu dezavin hu dedayyek* — the buyer performs the final grinding step. For Shmuel, the Gemara raises the question: *lama li nishishikao bekivshan?* — why does the *Mishna* specify the stage after placement in the kiln? Under Shmuel's logic, since all steps are under human control, the pre-sale should be permitted even before the stone is placed in the kiln. The answer: *eima mishedaroy leshakao bekivshan* — read the condition as "when it is fit to be placed in the kiln," meaning when the stone has been prepared and is ready for firing, even if it has not yet been put in.

---

## Meir vs. Yosi

### Meir's Rule

A *braita* presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi specifically regarding the potter's clay case. *Ein poskin al habeytzim shel yotzer ad sheye'asu divrei Rabi Meir* — Rabbi Meir holds that one cannot pre-purchase the potter's clay until it has actually been shaped into balls. The underlying principle is that the seller must have the product in his possession in a meaningful sense, and unformed clay does not yet constitute the product being sold.

### Yosi's Rule

*Amar Rabi Yosi: bameh devarim amorim be'afar lavan* — Rabbi Yosi qualifies: when is Rabbi Meir's requirement applicable? When dealing with white clay, which is rarer and not widely available. In that case, the seller must actually own and possess the shaped clay before a pre-sale is valid. *Aval be'afar shachor* — but black clay, of the type produced in the villages of Kefar Chananya and Kefar Shichin and their environs, is different. *Poskin af al pi she'ein lazeh yesh lazeh* — one may pre-purchase it even if the seller does not yet own it, because it is available everywhere, making it equivalent to *yatza hasha'ar* — a commodity with a fixed, publicly known price, which may be pre-sold even without the seller having immediate possession.

### Ameymar Practice

*Ameymar yahiv zuzei miki maytu afra* — Ameymar would pay for the clay from the moment the dirt was brought in to the workshop, before it had even been shaped into balls. The Gemara asks: *keman?* — like whom does this practice accord? It fits neither Rabbi Meir, who requires the shaped balls, nor Rabbi Yosi as usually understood, since Rabbi Yosi's leniency on black clay would seemingly permit payment before possession entirely — not require possession of the raw dirt.

### Compromise Position

*Le'olam keRabi Yosi uv'atra de'Ameymar ashik afra* — the resolution is that this practice does accord with Rabbi Yosi, but reflects a local condition: in Ameymar's locale, dirt of this type was not so freely available as in Kefar Chananya and Kefar Shichin. It was not rare enough to require shaped balls as Rabbi Meir demands, but neither was it so universally available that one could pre-sell it without any possession whatsoever. Once the dirt was brought into the workshop — *v'yahavu zuzei, v'd'lo lo* — that was sufficient possession to permit the pre-sale. The case thus represents an intermediate position: not as stringent as Rabbi Meir (who requires shaped balls) and not as lenient as Rabbi Yosi at his most permissive (who would allow pre-sale with no possession at all when the commodity is widely available), but somewhere in between, calibrated to local conditions of availability.

---

## Dung Availability

### Year-Round Dung

*U'poskin al ha'zevel kol yemot hashana* — the *Mishna* permits pre-purchasing dung throughout the entire year, since dung is always available even if the seller does not have it in hand. Dung is never truly scarce; some owner's animals are always producing it, and one can rely on obtaining it at any time.

### Rainy Season Issue

The Gemara introduces a challenge: during the rainy season, dung is less readily available. Apparently, because of rain and wet conditions, the dung that accumulates becomes less serviceable as a commodity, or its collection is disrupted. This calls into question whether pre-purchasing dung truly can be permitted year-round.

### Three Positions

*Amar Rava yemot hageshamim ika beinyahu* — Rava identifies that the difference between the positions in the *Mishna* turns on the rainy season. Three distinct views emerge. The first position holds that one may pre-purchase dung at any time of year, even during the rainy season when it is less available — because it is sufficiently available even then to permit pre-sale without the seller having possession. The second position holds that pre-purchasing is permissible only during the summer months, when dung is at peak availability; during the rainy season, the seller must actually own it. The third position holds that during the rainy season even ownership is insufficient — the seller must have it physically in hand — while during the summer months, pre-purchasing without possession is freely permitted. The dispute thus mirrors the broader framework of the daf: how available must a commodity be, and what degree of possession is required at various levels of availability, in order to validate a pre-sale transaction?

---

---

# Bava Metzia 75

## Price Protection

### Forward Purchase Rules

The daf opens mid-discussion of the *mishnah*'s ruling on *posek imo k'sha'ar hagavo'ah* — the practice of forward purchasing. When someone pays money upfront for produce to be delivered later in the year, at a time when prices are typically higher, the seller must either own the produce or it must be readily available in the market. The *mishnah* permits the purchaser to stipulate price protection: if, say, a hundred bushels are bought at ten dollars per bushel and the price later drops, delivery can be made at the lower price. This is the position of the *tanna kamma*. Rabbi Yehuda goes further, and Rabbi Yossi holds that even without an explicit stipulation the purchaser retains this right.

### Rav Papa's Decision

The *gemara* opens with a case: a certain man advanced money to purchase jewelry (*nidunya*) on behalf of his father-in-law's household, and by the time delivery was due the price had fallen — meaning he could have received more for his money. The matter came before Rav Papa, who ruled: if you stipulated at the time of payment that you would always receive the benefit of the lowest price, then take delivery at the current lower price. But if you made no such stipulation, you take delivery at the originally agreed price. This follows the *tanna kamma* of the *mishnah*. Critically, throughout this discussion we are dealing with a situation where money was paid but no *meshichah* — no act of formal acquisition — was performed. Since *meshichah* had not been done, the sale is not yet final, which is the entire framework within which these stipulations operate.

### Backing Out Rights

The rabbinical students challenged Rav Papa: if no stipulation was made, why must the purchaser accept the higher price? Since money alone does not finalize a sale (*ma'os lo kanu*), could the purchaser simply back out, demand his money returned, and repurchase at the now-lower price? Rav Papa replied that this question misses the point of his ruling. Of course the purchaser may back out — but doing so without a stipulation exposes him to a *mi shepara*, the formal curse for reneging on an agreement. His ruling was precisely about how to avoid that curse: if the seller stipulated price protection and the seller subsequently wishes to back out, the seller receives the *mi shepara*; if the purchaser made no such stipulation and now wishes to back out because the price has dropped, it is the purchaser who receives the *mi shepara*. The options exist, but they carry consequences.

### Ravina's Position

Ravina then raised a broader theoretical challenge, attempting to reframe the entire structure of the *mishnah*. He argued that the strict position in the *mishnah* — requiring an explicit stipulation — might in fact represent the view of Rabbi Shimon, while the more lenient position of Rabbi Yehuda might actually represent the *chachamim* who disagree with Rabbi Shimon.

To understand this argument, one must grasp the underlying debate. Rabbi Shimon holds that the purchaser generally cannot back out, even to accept a *mi shepara*. The *chachamim* hold that either party may back out and receive a *mi shepara*. Ravina's proposal: the position requiring explicit stipulation is Rabbi Shimon's, since in his view the purchaser normally has no right to back out at all — and therefore the only mechanism by which the purchaser may exit when prices change is through an explicit prior stipulation. For the *chachamim*, however, who routinely permit the purchaser to back out (albeit with a *mi shepara*), a change in market price represents a natural and obvious reason to exit — so obvious, Ravina argues, that the purchaser's intent to have done so should be presumed (*da'atya d'inish a'tara zeila*, people always assume the lesser value). On this reading, the *chachamim* would hold like Rabbi Yehuda of the *mishnah*: when prices change, the purchaser may withdraw without any *mi shepara*, even absent an explicit stipulation. This would make Rabbi Yehuda's position not a lone minority view but the mainstream halachic position of the *chachamim*.

### Rav Papa Responds

Rav Papa rejected this construction. His response: even Rabbi Shimon would permit the purchaser to back out when the market price has changed, though with a *mi shepara*. His proof: the relevant *baraita* articulating Rabbi Shimon's position explicitly invokes the *mi shepara* curse, and the language there — *mikol makom*, nevertheless — includes both seller and purchaser. This can only make sense if Rabbi Shimon envisions a scenario where the purchaser does back out and receives a *mi shepara*. Were Rabbi Shimon's position an absolute bar on the purchaser backing out under any circumstances, there would be no occasion to speak of the purchaser receiving a *mi shepara* at all. The *gemara* attempts to deflect this by suggesting that perhaps for Rabbi Shimon no such scenario ever exists for the purchaser, but Rav Papa insists the *baraita*'s language forecloses that reading.

The conclusion is therefore: Rabbi Shimon allows the purchaser to back out when prices change, but only with a *mi shepara* — and the requirement to stipulate explicitly arises because even in a changed-price scenario, one still incurs a *mi shepara* without such a stipulation. Rav Papa then extends this logic to the *chachamim*: even though they always permit the purchaser to back out, even they would agree that a price change does not automatically exempt the purchaser from a *mi shepara* unless there was an explicit stipulation. He therefore maintains that one must pasken like the *tanna kamma* of the *mishnah*, requiring an explicit stipulation, and does not accept Ravina's attempted reconciliation.

### Shlichut Argument

A final challenge came from Rav Acha the son of Rava, addressed to Rav Ashi. Setting aside the entire *mi shepara* discussion, he raised an agency (*shlichut*) argument: the father-in-law had appointed his son-in-law as his agent (*shaliach*) to make the purchase. Since the son-in-law failed to stipulate price protection — acting imprudently — could the father-in-law simply declare the entire transaction void on the grounds that he appointed an agent to benefit him, not to harm him, and that a *shaliach* who exceeds or betrays his mandate is not acting as a valid agent at all? Rav Ashi replied: the case involves a merchant who buys and sells on his own account (*tagra d'zavin u'mazvin*) — the son-in-law was purchasing from the sellers with his own money and then reselling to his father-in-law, so the *shlichut* framework cannot be invoked to nullify the transaction. The upshot of the entire passage is that we pasken like the *chachamim* of the *mishnah*, requiring explicit stipulation.

---

## Sharecropper Loans

### Seed vs. Grain

The next *mishnah* addresses lending seed to sharecroppers (*malveh arisin*). A landowner may lend his sharecroppers grain for planting (*lezera*) and later receive back an equal quantity at harvest time. However, he may not lend them grain for consumption (*le'echol*) to be repaid in kind later, because that would constitute *se'ah be-se'ah* — lending a measure of food to be returned measure for measure — which is a form of rabbinic *ribbit*. The concern is that by the time of repayment the grain may have risen in value, so the borrower would effectively be returning something worth more than what he received.

### Rabban Gamliel

The *mishnah* notes that Rabban Gamliel would lend his sharecroppers seed for planting, and if the price changed in either direction by the time of repayment, he always accepted the lesser value. If the price rose, he accepted only enough grain to equal the original value; if the price fell, he accepted the lower-value grain even though it represented a loss. The *mishnah* clarifies that this was not because *halacha* required it — lending seed and expecting back equal quantity is in fact permitted — but because Rabban Gamliel chose to be strict upon himself. The point of the *mishnah* is precisely that one should not derive a normative ruling from Rabban Gamliel's personal stringency.

### Before/After Work

A *baraita* introduces a distinction absent from the *mishnah*: lending seed and expecting repayment in kind is permitted only before the sharecropper has gone down and begun working the field (*shelo yarad*), but once he has commenced work (*aval yarad*), it is forbidden. The *gemara* asks: why does the *mishnah* draw no such distinction, while the *baraita* does?

### Renegotiation Logic

Rav Idi explained the discrepancy to Rava as follows. In the locale of the *mishnah*'s author, the practice was for the sharecropper to supply the seed. Since the sharecropper bears responsibility for the seed but lacks it, the landowner retains the right to eject him from the arrangement at any time — whether he has begun working or not — simply on the grounds that the sharecropper has failed to fulfill his obligation. This right of ejection gives the landowner perpetual leverage to renegotiate the terms. When the landowner provides seed under these conditions, it is not a loan but a renegotiated term of the sharecropping agreement: the sharecropper will provide his customary share of the harvest plus one additional measure of seed in lieu of what he owed. This is not *se'ah be-se'ah* because the seed is part of the compensation structure, not a loan.

In the locale of the *baraita*, by contrast, it is the landowner who is obligated to provide the seed. Before work begins, the landowner can still rescind the arrangement and offer revised terms — the provision of extra seed becomes a condition of the new agreement rather than a loan. But once the sharecropper has begun working, the landowner loses the right of ejection. At that point, if the landowner provides additional seed and demands its return at harvest, that is a genuine loan of food repayable in kind, and it does constitute prohibited *se'ah be-se'ah*.

---

## Se'ah Be-Se'ah

### Price Fixing

The *mishnah* teaches that one may say to a friend: lend me a measure of wheat and we will fix the price at the current rate. The mechanism is straightforward: instead of creating an obligation to return grain — which may be worth more at repayment — the obligation is converted into a monetary debt. You lend me a bushel of wheat worth ten dollars; I owe you ten dollars.

### Price Mechanics

The *gemara* raises a difficulty: if the price was fixed and then later falls, why should the borrower be permitted to repay in grain rather than in the fixed monetary amount? Rav Sheshet clarifies that the *baraita* is not addressing the case where a price was fixed. Rather, it addresses the case where no price was fixed at all. If someone says simply "lend me a bag of wheat and I will repay a bag of wheat" — which is technically *se'ah be-se'ah* — how does one avoid the *ribbit* problem at the moment of repayment? The answer: if prices have fallen or remained the same, repaying in kind is permissible because the returned grain is worth no more than what was borrowed; if prices have risen, one must repay the monetary value the grain held at the time of the loan, not a full bag of grain.

### Harvest Return Ban

The *mishnah* further rules that one may not say: lend me a measure of wheat and I will repay you after the threshing season. This too is *se'ah be-se'ah*, since by harvest time the grain may have risen in value. However, the *mishnah* permits one to say: lend me this wheat and as soon as my son returns and opens the storehouse — or as soon as I find the key — I will repay you immediately. This is analogous to the rule on forward purchases: if the item is in one's possession or readily available, the transaction is permissible even if literal repayment occurs slightly later.

### Hillel's Strictness

Hillel, however, would forbid even this. He also extends the concern to the domestic sphere: a woman should not lend her neighbor even a loaf of bread or a small domestic quantity without first fixing a price, lest the price of flour rise and a seemingly neighborly exchange become a form of rabbinic *ribbit*. Hillel's stringency thus operates on two axes: he disallows even deferred repayment when the item is merely accessible but not immediately at hand, and he extends *se'ah be-se'ah* concerns to small domestic loans. It is worth noting the irony that Hillel — normally the lenient authority — adopts the stricter position here, even as he was also the author of the *prosbul*, another institution touching on the law of loans.

### Ownership Requirement

The *mishnah*'s permission to borrow when one already possesses the item raises the question of how much one must own. Rav Huna holds: one may borrow only up to the quantity one possesses. If you have one bag stored away, you may borrow one bag; if you have two, you may borrow two; but you may not borrow more than what you currently own.

Rabbi Yitzchak disagrees: even if you own only a single measure, you may borrow as many large quantities as you wish. His logic is that since *se'ah be-se'ah* is in any case rabbinic (*ribbit derabanan*), the requirement of ownership operates pro forma — a token amount suffices. Conceptually, one can also break the borrowing into serial transactions: you own one measure, you borrow one more (permissible), now you own two, you borrow two more, and so on. Though admittedly a fiction, it provides the halachic basis for the leniency. A *baraita* of Rav Chiya is cited in support of Rabbi Yitzchak: the *baraita* rules that one may not borrow wine if one has not a drop of wine, nor oil if one has not a drop of oil — the implication being that if one possesses even a single drop, one may borrow as much as one wishes.

### Chachamim's Leniency

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules: this is Hillel's position, but the *chachamim* say one may simply borrow and repay without such formalities (*lovin stam u'pormin stam*). In practice, this leniency applies to domestic contexts where the exchanges are not commercial in character, parties are not exacting about precise quantities, and there is an implicit mutual tolerance for slight variations. Because no one is truly *makpid* — strictly insistent — the exchange lacks the character of a commercial loan, and the rabbinic *ribbit* concern does not apply.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel adds a further warning: members of a *chavurah* who take turns hosting one another but are very precise in accounting for every cost and every dish will transgress the prohibitions against measuring on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, and also the prohibition against lending and borrowing on *Yom Tov* — since their exacting accounting turns hospitality into a transaction. From Hillel's perspective, such a group also transgresses *ribbit*, since the precision of their accounting triggers even domestic *se'ah be-se'ah* concerns. Notably, the *gemara* implies that even the *chachamim* might not be concerned about *se'ah be-se'ah* for a group that is *makpid*, which is striking.

---

## Scholar Loans

### Scholar Gifts

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel teaches: *talmidei chachamim* are permitted to lend to one another and to return a little extra. The rationale offered is that they know *ribbit* is forbidden, so any extra given is understood to be a gift rather than interest. This is a striking *gemara*: after so many pages developing protections against *ribbit*, it appears to create a sweeping exemption for scholars. Tosafos is clearly troubled and explains that the permission applies only to a small, token extra that one would have given the person anyway even without the loan — and only among *talmidei chachamim*, where the social context makes the gift's independent character plausible. The difficulty remains: if one knows *ribbit* is forbidden, why does that knowledge transform a payment made in the loan context into something other than *ribbit*?

### Pepper Loan

Shmuel demonstrates the principle in practice, saying to the father of bar Ihi: lend me a hundred peppers and I will return a hundred and twenty — and all will be fine (*v'orach*). Rashi understands this as an illustration of the gift principle discussed above. The most coherent reading is that this operates within an informal domestic register — not a commercial transaction but a personal exchange where a slight overreturn is no different from giving back a full box of cornflake crumbs when only half a box was borrowed, because restoring the exact original quantity would be impractical or socially awkward. The extra is not paid *on account* of the loan; it arises from the natural dynamics of informal exchange.

### Teaching Interest

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that a person is permitted to lend his own children with interest, in order to give them a taste (*ta'am*) of what *ribbit* feels like, so that they will understand the weight of the prohibition. The analogy is to allowing a child to try something harmful so that the experience itself serves as the lesson. The *gemara* immediately rejects this: *v'lav milta hi* — it is not a sound practice — because it may backfire (*d'asi l'misrach*). The child who is made to pay interest may conclude not that *ribbit* is dangerous but that it is profitable. The deeper question — why this pedagogical purpose would suspend an apparent *issur d'oraisa* — is left genuinely open by the *gemara* and is a notable difficulty.

---

## Labor Exchange

### Equal Labor

The *mishnah* teaches that a person may say to his friend: weed with me today and I will weed with you tomorrow (*nakesh immi v'anakesh immach*), or plow for me today and I will plow for you tomorrow (*ador immi v'ador immach*). Such reciprocal exchanges of equal labor are permitted. Agricultural communities routinely coordinated labor this way, pooling workers across fields, and the *mishnah* treats this as an ordinary arrangement. All days of the dry season (*gerid*) are treated as equivalent to one another, and all days of the rainy season (*revi'ah*) are similarly treated as equivalent — so exchanging a day of work in the dry season for another day of work in the same season raises no concern.

### Unequal Labor

However, the *mishnah* prohibits unequal exchanges: one may not say, "You weed for me and I will plow for you" — since weeding and plowing may be valued differently — nor may one exchange labor across seasons, such as: "Plow for me in the dry season and I will plow for you in the rainy season." Work in one season may be harder than in the other. Both of these cases raise a *ribbit*-like concern analogous to *se'ah be-se'ah*: if the service rendered in return is worth more than the service received, it functions as a premium on what was effectively a deferred obligation.

---

## Usury Types

### Prepaid Usury

Rabban Gamliel teaches that there are two additional categories of *ribbit* that operate even without an explicit stipulation in the loan agreement, provided the extra benefit is given on account of the loan. The first is *ribbit mukdemes* — prepaid *ribbit*. If a would-be borrower sends a gift to a potential lender with the explicit statement "in order that you lend me the money," this constitutes rabbinic *ribbit*, even though the loan has not yet occurred. While the classic structure of *ribbit* envisions compensation for the lender's waiting (*natar agar*), even a payment made before the loan — as an inducement — falls within the rabbinic prohibition.

### Delayed Usury

The second category is *ribbit me'ucheres* — delayed or posthumous *ribbit*. If after repaying the loan in full the borrower sends a gift to the lender with the explanation "this is because your money was idle with me," that is *ribbit me'ucheres*. Here the *natar agar* logic applies precisely: the gift is openly described as payment for the lender's forbearance during the loan period. Since it was not stipulated, it is rabbinic rather than biblical *ribbit*, but it is prohibited nonetheless.

### Usury of Words

Rabbi Shimon adds a further category: *ribbit devarim* — *ribbit* of words. A borrower should not say to the lender, "Know that so-and-so has arrived from such-and-such a place," conveying insider information as a form of repayment for the loan. A *baraita* expands this: one who has lent money to another, and the borrower was not in the habit of greeting the lender warmly, should not now go out of his way to do so on account of the loan — for even a greeting, a word of warmth extended because of the debt, constitutes a form of *ribbit*. The source is *neshech kol davar asher yishach* — the word *kol davar* (any matter) includes even speech. This raises interesting practical questions about what constitutes ordinary *menschlichkeit* and what crosses into *ribbit devarim* — questions the later authorities (*poskim*) engage with at length.

---

## Usury Transgressors

### Lender Violations

The final *mishnah* of the chapter enumerates who transgresses and under what prohibitions. Abaye teaches that the lender transgresses all of them: *lo sitten* — the prohibition on giving money at interest — when he hands over the loan; *al tikach* — the prohibition on taking interest — when he receives it back; *lo tihyeh lo kenosheh* — the prohibition on bearing down on the borrower like a creditor — through the entire relationship of demanding repayment; *lo tasimun alav neshech* — the prohibition on placing the bite upon him — through the creation of the debt and its documentation; and *lifnei iver lo sitten michshol* — the prohibition on placing a stumbling block before the blind — by causing the borrower to transgress the borrower's own prohibitions.

### Other Violators

The borrower transgresses *lo sashich le'achicha* — the prohibition on being bitten — and *lifnei iver* against the lender, since the transaction requires two parties and the borrower enables the lender to sin. The guarantor (*arev*) and the witnesses transgress *lo tasimun alav neshech* — by making the loan happen they participate in the imposition of the debt. Tosafos adds that in cases where the loan would not have occurred without the guarantor or witnesses, they additionally transgress *lifnei iver*, since their involvement was a necessary condition of the transgression. If the loan would have occurred without them, their participation is still improper, but the *lifnei iver* analysis does not apply. The *chachamim* add the scribe (*sofer*) to the list of transgressors, for the same reason.

### Financial Loss

Rabbi Shimon closes with a sobering observation: those who lend with *ribbit* lose more than they gain. Ultimately their properties are lost. Beyond the financial consequences, he adds that they implicitly disparage Moshe Rabbeinu and the Torah — since by ignoring the prohibition on *ribbit* they effectively declare that the Torah's law makes no economic sense. The *gemara* gives voice to this implicit attitude: "If Moshe Rabbeinu had known there was profit to be made in this, he would not have written the prohibition." In other words, lending with *ribbit* is an act of defiance against the wisdom of the Torah, particularly pointed in the commercial context where the economic rationale for the prohibition is less intuitively obvious than in the agricultural world for which it was originally articulated.

---

## Loans Without Witnesses

### Avoiding Humiliation

Rav Dimi teaches: how do we know that if one has lent money to someone and knows that person currently lacks the funds to repay, one must not walk past him or allow oneself to be seen by him? From the verse *lo tihyeh lo kenosheh* — do not be over him like a creditor. This prohibition does not require a *ribbit* context; it applies to any loan. The power dynamic of the creditor-debtor relationship, when made visible and felt through the lender's presence, creates a profound and forbidden humiliation. Rav Ami and Rav Asi add: one who does this is as if one has inflicted two punishments upon the borrower, citing the verse *hirkavta enosh leroshinu banu va'eish uvamayim* — You put a person above our heads; we came through fire and water.

### Witness Requirement

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules: if one has money and lends it without witnesses, one transgresses *lifnei iver lo sitten michshol* — placing a stumbling block before the blind. The mechanism is indirect but real: without a record or witnesses, the borrower may forget the loan, or over time convince himself he does not owe it, and will fail to repay — not even necessarily in bad faith. The lender, by creating a situation in which the borrower can easily fall into non-repayment, has caused him to sin. Resh Lakish adds a further consequence: the lender will be cursed, because when he comes to collect and the borrower denies owing, the lender appears as a liar who is making false claims against an upright person — *te'almanah siftei sheker hadovrot al tzaddik atak*.

### Ravina's Example

The Rabbis told Rav Ashi that Ravina was scrupulous in fulfilling every ruling of the Rabbis in this matter. Just before *Erev Shabbos*, someone sent Ravina a message asking to borrow ten *zuz* — a hundred dollars' worth — to purchase a parcel of land, a *metziah* that had just become available. Ravina replied: certainly, but first bring witnesses and we will write a document. The borrower responded: "Even me? You don't trust me? I am a Torah scholar!" Ravina replied: "Precisely you — you are so absorbed in your learning and your *girsa* that you are likely to forget you borrowed the money at all, and then when I come to collect you will deny it in good faith, and since you are such a *tzaddik* people will assume I am lying." This vignette exemplifies the exact harm the rabbis sought to prevent, and Ravina's insistence on witnesses — even with a close colleague, even on *Erev Shabbos*, even with someone who considered the request an affront — illustrates how seriously this teaching was taken.

### Unanswered Prayers

The *gemara* closes the chapter with a *baraita*: three people cry out and are not answered. First, one who has money and lends it without witnesses — he has caused his own loss and has no legitimate claim on heaven's sympathy. Second, one who acquires a master over himself (*hakoneh adon le'atzmo*): some interpret this as one who falsely claims his property belongs to a *nochri* to conceal his wealth, only to find the *nochri* eventually asserting ownership; others interpret it as one who signs over his property to his children while still alive — like King Lear — thereby inverting the natural power dynamic; still others interpret it as one who has a bad reputation in his city and simply does nothing to change it by moving elsewhere. Third, a man who allows his wife to have dominion over him. With this teaching the chapter of *ribbit* concludes.

*Hadran alach eizehu neshech.*

---

---

# Bava Metzia 76

## Intro: Craftsmen/Workers

### Umnin vs. Po'alim

The daf begins a new *perek* at the very bottom of 75b. The opening words are *hasocher et ha'umnin* — one who hires craftsmen. It is worth noting that the following *perek* is called *hasocher et hapo'alim*, and this immediately raises a terminological question. *Umnin* are, technically speaking, craftsmen, while *po'alim* is the more generic term for workers.

### Tosafot: Categories

Tosafot clarifies the distinction: *po'alim* refers more specifically to those paid a daily wage, whereas *umnin* functions as a broader umbrella category that can encompass both daily wage earners and a *kablan* — a contractor paid for completing a job rather than for time worked. This distinction between daily workers and job contractors will bear on the analysis throughout the *perek*.

## Deception/No Recourse

### Taromet Only

The *Mishna* opens: *hasocher et ha'umnin vehitu zeh et zeh, ein lahem zeh al zeh ela tar'omet* — one who hires workers, and they deceive one another, they have only a complaint (*tar'omet*) against one another, but no actual legal recourse for financial compensation. The nature of this deception — who deceived whom, and under what circumstances — is precisely what the *Gemara* will need to unpack. What is already striking is that the *Mishna* immediately proceeds to enumerate cases in which there *are* financial consequences, which raises the question of what the opening case of mere *tar'omet* actually looks like.

### Davar Avad Examples

The *Mishna* gives examples: if one hires a donkey driver or a wagon driver — *chamor* or *kadar* (or perhaps *karar*, as Tosafot notes the textual variant) — to transport materials for a wedding or a funeral, such as *priparin* (a kind of decorative wooden component, which Rashi understands as relating to constructing a *chuppah*, though it may equally refer to the bier used to carry the bride or the deceased) and *chalilim* (flutes, commonly used at funerals as a form of wailing), these are time-sensitive engagements. Similarly, if one hires *po'alim* to remove flax from soaking water at a precise moment — since leaving it too long will ruin it — that constitutes a *davar she'avad*, something that will be irretrievably lost if not attended to immediately.

### Flax Removal

The flax case is the clearest example of tangible loss: if the workers fail to act at the right moment, the flax is ruined and a concrete monetary loss follows. The wedding and funeral cases, however, require additional analysis.

### Tosafot: Davar Avad

Tosafot addresses the wedding and funeral scenarios directly, explaining that *davar ha'avud chashiv lei sha'atah zmano hu la'asot* — it counts as a loss because now is the time to act. If the *chuppah* is not built or the musicians do not arrive, the wedding proceeds without what was needed at the crucial moment. There is no diminution of one's bank account, no measurable net worth reduction — and yet the loss is real. The *davar avad* category, Tosafot makes clear, extends to time-sensitive services even when the harm is not reducible to a simple dollar figure.

## Davar Avad Exception

### Socher Aleihen

The *Mishna* now addresses the *davar avad* scenario where workers back out. If there are no other workers available to replace them — *makom she'ein sham adam* — then one may engage replacement workers even at exorbitant rates, and the original workers bear responsibility for the difference. This is called *socher aleihen*: the employer hires against them, at their expense.

### Deception as Remedy

Alternatively, the *Mishna* permits *mat'an* — deceiving the workers in order to ensure the work is completed. The employer tells the workers he will double their fee; they agree to stay; and after the job is done, he pays only the originally contracted amount. Since they had already reneged on a *davar avad*, the deception used to induce them to complete the work is legally sanctioned. These two remedies — *socher aleihen* and *mat'an* — establish that the opening statement of mere *tar'omet* cannot apply in the *davar avad* context.

## Yad Al HaTachtona

### Workers Back Out

The *Mishna* continues: if workers back out mid-job, *yadam al hatachtona* — they have the lower hand. And conversely, if the *ba'al habayit* backs out, *yado al hatachtona* — he has the lower hand. The expression *yado al hatachtona*, the lower hand as opposed to the upper hand, signals a disadvantaged legal position.

### Rashi on Deduction

Rashi explains the case where workers back out as follows. Suppose the employer contracted for a two-dollar job, the workers completed half, and now the going rate has risen so that finishing the job midday costs a dollar and a half. The workers have earned one dollar for their half, but the employer can withhold from that dollar the additional cost of completing the work, leaving the workers with only fifty cents, so that his total expenditure does not exceed the originally contracted two dollars. This deduction from earned wages is the operative meaning of *yad al hatachtona* when workers are the ones who retract. Of course, this mechanism only functions as long as the amount owed to the workers is sufficient to absorb the additional cost; if the gap exceeds what they have earned, the employer's recourse is more limited.

A natural question arises: if it is not a *davar avad*, must the employer wait until the next morning to hire replacements, or may he hire someone in the middle of the day? The *Mishna* does not make this explicit, and the precise limits of the employer's remedies in non-*davar avad* cases remain somewhat unclear.

### Employer Back Out

When the *ba'al habayit* backs out, the scenario Rashi presents is this: the workers were contracted for three dollars for the whole job, completed half, and then the employer retracted. By the time of the retraction, however, the going rate has fallen to two dollars for the whole job, meaning the workers' half-effort is objectively worth only one dollar at market rates. The ruling is nevertheless that the employer pays them a dollar and a half — the proportional share of the contracted price — rather than the one dollar their work is worth on the open market. The *chiddush* here is not enormous, since a contract was formed and the employer is the one who broke it, but it does illustrate the principle: whoever retracts is in the disadvantaged position.

### General Principle

The *Mishna* concludes by stating the governing principle: *kol hamishaneh yado al hatachtona* — whoever deviates from the agreed terms has the lower hand — and *kol hachozer bo yado al hatachtona* — whoever backs out has the lower hand. The former phrase refers to a broader category (as in the classic *Bava Kamma* case of dyeing wool the wrong color, where one pays the lesser of expenses or improvement to the wool), while the latter appears to be a direct summary of the cases developed in this *Mishna*.

With all of this in view, the original opening of the *Mishna* — the case of *tar'omet* only, with no financial recourse — remains unexplained. The *Gemara* now turns to clarify it.

## Foreman Deception Theory

### Workers Deceive Eachother

The *Gemara* observes: *chazru zeh bazeh lo katani* — the *Mishna* does not say they "backed out," but rather *hitu zeh et zeh*, they "deceived" one another. The *Gemara* takes this as a signal that the opening case is distinct from the subsequent scenarios of retraction. The question then becomes: what constitutes deception that does not involve backing out, and yet yields only *tar'omet*?

The *Gemara*'s initial reading is striking: *de'atu po'alim ahadadi* — the workers deceived one another. That is, *hitu zeh et zeh* does not describe employer deceiving employee, but workers deceiving each other.

### Foreman Pockets Difference

The mechanism the *Gemara* envisions is as follows. The *ba'al habayit* hires one man as a foreman and says to him: *zil ogar li po'alim* — go hire workers for me. The foreman is told to hire them at three dollars a day, but he goes and tells the workers they will receive four dollars a day, pocketing the difference himself. This is the deception: the workers deceive one another in the sense that the foreman, himself a kind of worker, defrauds the other workers he recruits.

One might immediately ask: if the going rate is three and the foreman promised four, why do the workers have any complaint at all? *Savru vekabilu* — they assessed the terms and accepted. Conversely, if the *ba'al habayit* authorized four and the foreman told them three, and then refused to pay more, the foreman has plainly undertaken a contractual obligation toward them.

### Sharchkem Al Ba'al Habayit

The critical case, the *Gemara* explains, is where the foreman tells the workers that their pay is *al ha-ba'al habayit* — the employer is responsible for their wages, not the foreman himself. In this configuration, the foreman has not personally assumed the obligation. He is merely the conduit. The workers' complaint, if any, runs only against the foreman — not against the *ba'al habayit*, who may not have authorized the higher figure, and not as a binding legal claim.

## Promise vs. Misrepresent…

### Foreman Assumes Obligation

A *baraita* clarifies the legal consequence when the foreman changes his posture. If the foreman says *sharchchem alai* — your wages are on me — he personally assumes the obligation. In that case, the workers collect the full promised amount from the foreman directly.

### Foreman Seeks Reimbursement

The foreman can then turn to the *ba'al habayit* and seek reimbursement *mah shenehneh* — for however much the employer actually benefited. This principle is illustrated by a *baraita*: if I hire Michael to mow my lawn and then show him my neighbor Gloria's lawn, telling him it is mine, I must pay Michael his full contracted fee. I may then seek reimbursement from Gloria — but only *mah shenehneh*, only for the benefit she actually received. If the going rate for mowing a lawn is ten dollars and I paid Michael twenty, I can recover ten from Gloria, not twenty.

This draws on the established principle of *yored lesoch sdei chaveiro shelo birshut* — one who enters another's field and improves it without permission. The owner of the field cannot be made to pay the worker's contracted fee, since she never entered into a contractual relationship, but she does owe for the concrete benefit she received. The *da'as* and willingness of the beneficiary matter: if Gloria prefers her lawn overgrown and would not have considered a trimmed lawn a benefit, the calculus becomes more complicated — but that question is set aside here.

Applied to the foreman case: if the foreman said *sharchchem alai*, he owes them four. He may then recover from the *ba'al habayit*, but almost certainly no more than three, assuming three was the authorized rate and presumably the going rate. In that scenario, there is no unresolved complaint — the workers collect from the foreman and the foreman settles with the *ba'al habayit*.

### Foreman Misrepresents Wage

The hard case is where the foreman said *sharchchem al ha-ba'al habayit* — placing the obligation on the employer — but misrepresented the wage. The workers worked for the *ba'al habayit*, trusting that the foreman accurately conveyed what the employer had authorized. Now the *Gemara* considers how much the *ba'al habayit* owes them.

The *Gemara* says: *venichzi po'alim heichi misgarei* — let us see what the going rate for workers actually is. If all workers are going for four, then even though the *ba'al habayit* only authorized three, he may well owe four — because that is the objective value of the labor he received, analogous to the *yored lesoch sdei chaveiro* principle. The *ba'al habayit* clearly needed the work done; the implicit understanding that he required the service may create a quasi-contractual obligation even absent an explicit agreement.

## Complaint Threshold

### Scenario 1: Alt Job Available

The interesting case arises when there is a split market — some workers available at four, some at three. The *Gemara* says: *de'amru lei — ei lav de'amrat lan be'arba, tarchinan u'misgarinan be'arba* — they say to the foreman: had you not told us four, we would have hustled and secured a four-dollar job elsewhere. This is a legitimate complaint. The misrepresentation caused a real opportunity cost. Yet the *ba'al habayit* is not legally liable for more than three, since he only intended to pay three and only received a benefit assessable at three. The foreman's workers cannot extract more than that from the employer, and so their complaint — while genuine — yields only *tar'omet*, a grievance without legal recourse.

This raises a practical question: if the *ba'al habayit* can always instruct his foreman to promise four when he is only willing to pay three, knowing that the workers will end up with three and have no recourse, what protection do the workers have? The honest answer is that, over time, reputation matters, and workers will learn to verify. But it remains a striking vulnerability in the system, and the *Gemara* does not fully resolve it.

### Scenario 2: Own Field

The second scenario is *ba'al habayit askinan* — not generic hired laborers, but someone who owns his own field and would normally have spent the day working his own land. He was induced to leave his own work by the promise of four dollars. His complaint is not that he could have found another four-dollar employer; it is that he would never have left his own work for the standard rate of three. The foreman's misrepresentation specifically caused him to forgo his own productivity. Again, however, since the *ba'al habayit* only intended to pay three and only benefited at the level of three, the worker collects three and registers his complaint.

### Scenario 3: Quality Work

The third scenario is that the workers, believing they were contracted for four, worked extra hard and did superior-quality work. Their complaint is: *kivan de'amrat lan be'arba, tarchinan ve'avidnan lach avidsa shapirta* — because you told us four, we exerted ourselves and did you an exceptional job. If they truly did work worth four dollars, the *ba'al habayit* would in principle owe them four — *mah shenehneh* — since that is the objective benefit he received. But the *Gemara* presents the case where verification is impossible: the job was digging a furrow, and by now it is *demali maya velo yediya* — filled with water, so there is no way to inspect and assess the quality of the work. Since *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* — the burden of proof rests on the claimant — and the workers cannot prove they did a four-dollar job, they collect three and are left with only *tar'omet*.

### Benefit-Based Payment

All three scenarios share a common structure. The workers have a legitimate basis for complaint in each case: they could have waited for a four-dollar job, they would not have left their own land for three dollars, or they performed work of superior quality. These reasons satisfy the threshold for *tar'omet* — a genuine grievance, something like a well-founded complaint to a professional body. But the *ba'al habayit* is not liable beyond what he actually authorized and benefited. If there is no reason to have expected more than three — if, for instance, the entire market was going for three, the worker had no independent work to forgo, and there is no quality premium at issue — then even *tar'omet* falls away, because there is simply no basis for any complaint at all.

The *Gemara* also presents a fourth variation worth noting briefly: *le'olam de'amar lei ba'al habayit be'arba ve'azal ihu ve'amar lehu betlata* — the *ba'al habayit* authorized four and the foreman told the workers three. The workers accepted, saying *nelaseh kemo she'amar ba'al habayit*, "we'll do whatever the *ba'al habayit* says." Their complaint to the foreman rests on the principle *al timna tov mib'alav* — do not withhold good from its rightful owners; the employer was prepared to pay them well and the foreman underpaid them. Yet even here they cannot recover more than three from the *ba'al habayit*, since that is what was agreed.

## Trust/Authority Question

### Whose Word Standard

The *Gemara* now raises a fundamental question about what it means when the workers say *nelaseh kemo she'amar ba'al habayit* — we will act as the *ba'al habayit* has said. Does this mean they trust the foreman's representation, accepting his words as an accurate account of the employer's intent? Or does it mean they reserve judgment and will act according to what the *ba'al habayit* actually said, with his word taking precedence over the foreman's?

This question has real stakes. In the scenario where the *ba'al habayit* authorized four but the foreman told them three, and the workers said *kemo she'amar ba'al habayit*, the *Gemara* observes that it is *pshita* — obvious — that they meant the higher figure, since no one undersells themselves by invoking what the employer said when the employer said more. But the harder question is the reverse: where the *ba'al habayit* authorized three, the foreman told them four, and the workers said *kemo she'amar ba'al habayit* — did they mean "we trust you that this is what the employer said," thereby agreeing to four? Or did they mean "whatever the employer actually said, that is what governs" — thereby, had they known, agreeing to three?

### Gitin Analogy

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve this by analogy to *gittin*. A woman says to a messenger: *hevei li gitti* — go bring me my *get*. She is designating him as a *shliach leholacha*, an agent to deliver the *get* from the husband to her. He goes to the husband and tells him: *ve'ishtecha amra, hitkabel li giti* — your wife told me to be a *shliach lekabbala*, an agent to receive it on her behalf, so that she is divorced the moment he accepts it. He has misrepresented what the wife said, elevating his own role (requiring less travel) instead of what she actually designated. The husband responds: *heilech kemah she'amra* — take it as she said.

The ruling: *afilu higi'a get leyada einah megoresheret* — she is not divorced even when the *get* arrives in her hands. Why not? Because the husband said *kemah she'amra*, trusting the messenger's representation of what the wife said. Since the wife did not designate him as *shliach lekabbala*, the husband's handing over the *get* on that basis accomplished nothing. And since the husband also did not designate him as *shliach leholacha*, delivery to the woman similarly accomplished nothing. The case implies that *kemah she'amra* means "as you represent her as having said" — trusting the messenger, not independently verifying the principal.

### Rav Ashi Distinction

Rav Ashi objects to the application of this case to the employment context. The *get* case, he argues, fails as a proof not because of any ambiguity in the meaning of *kemah she'amra*, but because of a prior structural problem: the messenger rejected his own *shlichus*. When the wife designated him *shliach leholacha* — obligating him to travel and deliver — and he instead declared himself *shliach lekabbala*, taking the easier role, he was in effect saying *shliach leholacha lo havina* — I refuse to serve as the delivery agent. He effectively terminated his *shlichus* before the *get* was even transmitted. The entire transaction therefore failed for a reason independent of whether the husband was relying on the messenger's words or on the wife's actual words.

### Hypothetical Test

Rav Ashi therefore specifies what would have constituted a proper test. Had the wife said *hitkabel li giti* — designating him as *shliach lekabbala* — and he then told the husband *ve'ishtecha amra, havi li giti* — representing her as having designated him *shliach leholacha*, a more onerous role — he would have been *accepting* greater responsibility rather than reducing it. In that scenario, one could ask: if the husband said *heilech kemah she'amra* and the *get* was delivered, is the woman divorced immediately (which would indicate the husband was relying on the wife's actual words, making him *shliach lekabbala*) or only upon delivery (indicating he was trusting the messenger's representation, treating him as *shliach leholacha*)? That would have been a clean test of the question. As reported by Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha citing Rav, in that hypothetical scenario she would be divorced *mishiga'a get leyada* — upon delivery — which would resolve the question in one direction. But since the *Gemara* does not actually have that case before it, the inference remains speculative.

### Unresolved Shlichus

The conclusion is that the *get* analogy does not resolve the employment question. Whether the workers' statement *kemo she'amar ba'al habayit* means they trusted the foreman's representation or reserved their reliance for the employer's actual words remains unanswered. The broader question of whether the foreman functions as a true *shliach* of the *ba'al habayit* — creating binding contractual obligations in the employer's name — is similarly left open. This is partly because *shlichus* in the classical sense typically attaches to concrete transactional acts (buying, selling, delivering a *get*), not to the act of entering into a labor arrangement. Something more like an *adrachta*, a power of attorney, might ordinarily be required for that kind of representational authority. The *da'as* of the *ba'al habayit* and the workers' implicit understanding of whom they are really contracting with may be the operative factors, but the *Gemara* does not resolve this fully.

## Baraita: Specific Cases

### Baraita Agrees

Returning now to the *pshat* of the *Mishna*, the *Gemara* suggests: *ei ba'it eima, hai tanna chazru nami hitu kari lei* — perhaps this *tanna* uses the word *hitu* (deceived) to describe what we would call backing out (*chazru*). The *Mishna* and the subsequent *baraita* may both be about the same employer-employee dynamic, and the word "deceived" is simply this *tanna*'s idiom for reneging on a commitment. A *baraita* is then quoted that opens with language parallel to the *Mishna*: *hasocher et ha'umnin vehitu et ha-ba'al habayit o ha-ba'al habayit hita otan* — the workers deceived the employer, or the employer deceived the workers — *ein lahem zeh al zeh ela tar'omet*, they have only complaints. This makes explicit what the *Mishna* left ambiguous: the deception is between the employer and the employees directly, not among the workers themselves.

### Before Work Begins

Critically, the *baraita* immediately qualifies its ruling: *bameh devarim amurim shelo halchu* — when is this true? When the workers have not yet arrived at the job site. Before the work begins, the arrangement has not yet ripened into a binding contract. It remains a plan, an agreement in principle. If either party backs out at this stage — even at the last moment, even after the other party has made preparations — the consequence is only *tar'omet*. No financial liability attaches. This is a striking rule: even if workers turned down other opportunities or made logistical preparations based on the arrangement, so long as they have not yet physically shown up to begin work, the other party can walk away with only a complaint lodged against them.

### Workers Arrive: Full Pay

Once the workers arrive, however, the calculus changes entirely. The *baraita* gives examples: the donkey drivers went to pick up grain and found none available (*velo matzu tvua*), or workers came to plow a field and found the soil too wet (*vematzu sade kesheehi lach*). In both cases, they showed up — and *noten lahem sechar mishalam*, the employer gives them their full wages. The concept of *poel batel* applies here: the employer does not pay for actual work done, since none was done, but rather the discounted amount a worker would accept to come and sit idle for the day rather than plow. The *Gemara* notes *eino domeh haba ta'un leba reikan* — it is not the same to come bearing a load as to come back with an empty wagon — and *oseh melacha leyoshev ubatel* — it is not the same to do work as to sit and do nothing. So the worker is paid the going rate minus what he would accept to stand idle: less than his full daily wage, but a real obligation nonetheless.

## Work Begun: Proportional Pay…

### Proportional Payment

The *baraita* continues: *elu hitchilu bemilacha, shamin lahem ma sheasu* — if they already began the work, one assesses what they have done and pays them accordingly.

### Grain Cutting Example

The illustration: workers contracted to cut an entire field of grain for two *sela'im*, cut half, and left. Or they contracted to weave a garment for two *sela'im* and completed half. *Shamin lahem et ma sheasu* — you assess what they did. The job is half done; pay them proportionally.

### Tanna Kamma View

What makes the *baraita* significant, however, is the dispute that emerges here. According to the Tanna Kamma, even if completing the remaining half will now cost more than what was originally allocated for it — say, one and a half *sela'im* instead of one — the workers who backed out still receive the full proportional wage for what they completed: one *sela* for the half they did. They are not penalized for the additional cost their departure imposes on the employer. The worker is always protected, even mid-job. This position, the *Gemara* implies, represents the Tanna Kamma view and actually differs from the position of our *Mishna*.

### Rabbi Dosa View

Rabbi Dosa disagrees: *shamin lahem ma she'atid le'hei'asos* — assess not what they did, but what it will cost to complete the remaining work. If finishing the other half will now cost one and a half *sela'im*, and the whole job was contracted for two, then the workers who completed the first half receive only half a *sela* — so that the employer's total outlay remains two. In other words, the additional cost of their departure is borne by the workers, deducted from what they have already earned. The *Gemara* concludes that our *Mishna* follows Rabbi Dosa on this point.

### Cost-Withholding Rule

The rules Rabbi Dosa and the Tanna Kamma give are symmetrical in one direction: if the remaining work is worth exactly one *sela*, then even Rabbi Dosa agrees the workers receive one *sela* — that is simply the proportional payment. The dispute concerns only the case where the remaining work costs *more* than the proportional share. Rabbi Dosa says that excess cost is absorbed by the departing workers; the Tanna Kamma says it is not. An alternative to deducting the extra cost: Rabbi Dosa allows the workers to simply finish the job and collect the full two *sela'im* — *o yigmeru melachtan veyitlu shnay sela'im* — rather than suffer the deduction. The choice between finishing and accepting the reduced payment is theirs to make.

## Davar Avad Remedy

### Replacement Availability

The *baraita* then returns to the *davar avad* situation. Even in a time-critical case, the remedies of *socher aleihen* and *mat'an* are not automatically available. The governing principle is *bameh devarim amurim bizman she'ein sham po'alim liskor* — these stronger remedies apply only when there are no readily available replacement workers in the market.

### Doubled Wage Deception

If *mat'an* is appropriate, the procedure is: *omer lahen, sela katzati lachem, bo'u utelu shtayim* — the employer tells them he will double their wage to keep them working, and then, once the job is complete, pays only the originally contracted amount. Since they had been in the process of abandoning a *davar avad*, the deception is legally sanctioned as a remedy.

### Cost Limit

As for *socher aleihen* — hiring replacements at elevated rates and holding the original workers responsible — the *baraita* says this extends *ad arba'im vechamishim zuz*, up to forty or fifty *zuz* of additional cost, a substantial sum, reflecting how seriously the law treats the harm of abandoning time-critical work.

### Market Availability

However, if there are workers readily available in the market, the employer cannot invoke these remedies even in a *davar avad* case. If the workers who backed out tell him to go hire others — *tze'u sechoru me'eilu* — and replacements are accessible, then *ein lo aleihen ella tar'omet*: the employer has only a complaint against them, no more. The accessibility of alternatives removes the emergency justification for the stronger remedies.

The *baraita* thus both reinforces and qualifies the *Mishna*. It confirms that the *tar'omet*-only rule applies when nothing has yet begun; it establishes that showing up for work converts the arrangement into a binding daily obligation; it records a dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Dosa about worker liability when work has already started; and it carefully circumscribes the *davar avad* remedies by market conditions. Tomorrow's shiur will take up Tosafot's discussion of the questions left open — particularly regarding lost opportunity costs and preparatory expenses incurred before the work begins.

# Bava Metzia 77

## Employment Scenarios

### Baraita Overview

The seventh chapter of Bava Metzia, *Hasokher et Ha-umnin*, is concerned with the consequences that follow when either an employer or employee backs out of a work arrangement. The *baraita* at the center of this discussion covers three broad scenarios. First, if an employer cancels before the workers have arrived in the morning, the workers have a *taro'met* — a grievance — but no financial recourse. Second, if the workers arrive and find no work available, or are told upon arrival that their services are not needed, the employer must pay them for the full day, albeit at the reduced rate appropriate for idleness rather than labor. Third, if workers actually begin work and then leave mid-job, a *tannaitic* dispute governs whether they are paid pro-rated with no further consequence, or whether the employer may dock their wages to cover any additional replacement costs. Finally, in cases of *davar ha-aved* — an irretrievable or unrecoverable loss — the employer may even engage in a degree of deception, promising higher wages to secure replacement workers and then recovering that cost from the departing workers' pay.

### Three Scenarios

These three scenarios map cleanly onto distinct legal regimes. The pre-arrival cancellation, while morally objectionable, generates no monetary liability. The failure to provide work once the workers have arrived imposes full liability on the employer, subject to important qualifications about fault and foreseeability that the *gemara* will shortly develop. The mid-job departure triggers a *tannaitic* debate about whether the worker's right to leave is unconditional or whether it comes at a cost. And the *davar ha-aved* category introduces an exceptional level of employer protection precisely because the stakes of non-completion are so high.

### Tosafot on Garmi

Before the *gemara* proceeds to analyze these scenarios in detail, Tosafot raises a significant question regarding the pre-arrival cancellation. If I have agreed to work for you and, relying on that commitment, turned down other employment opportunities, have I not suffered a real financial loss when you fire me the night before or early in the morning? The case of *garmi* — a heightened form of indirect causation that generates legal liability under the principle attributed to Rabbi Meir — would seem to support a claim for damages. As Tosafot frames it: *im ken, amai lo yiten lahem ke-fo'el batel* — if there is genuine causation, why should the employer not at least pay the workers the value of their lost day, the rate applicable to a worker sitting idle?

Tosafot's answer is that the *baraita* is speaking of a scenario in which workers, even after being told not to come in, can still find alternative employment. *De-mairi keshe-chozer bo od yimtze'u l'histakar* — we are dealing with a situation where, if the employer withdraws before the day begins, the workers can still secure other work. There is therefore no actual loss from which a *garmi* claim could arise. And yet the complaint, the *taro'met*, remains — because *lo yimtze'u ela al yedei torach*, they will only find that replacement work through significantly greater effort and difficulty. Lost ease of opportunity, even without lost income, is sufficient to sustain a moral grievance, though not a legal one. Tosafot's broader principle is striking and important: where there genuinely is a real, concrete loss resulting from the employer's withdrawal, *garmi* liability would apply and recovery would be available. The no-recourse rule of the *baraita* is therefore narrowly construed — it applies only when the workers can realistically find other work in time.

---

## Land Inspection

### Rav Nasan Baraita

The *gemara* records that a *tanna* taught before Rav Nasan: *nosnim lahem s'charan mushlam* — when workers arrive and find no work available, you give them their full wage. Rav Nasan transmitted this in the name of his beloved, *chavivi*, referring to Rabbi Hiyya — the figure traditionally associated with the editing of *baraitot* and the *Tosefta* — and expressed astonishment at the ruling: had I been present, he says, *lo havi yahivna lehu ela ke-fo'el batel* — I would not pay them their full wage but only the lesser rate appropriate for a day of idleness.

### Rashi vs. Rambam

The *gemara* initially presents two explanations for Rav's apparent objection. The first is *lo simua kamei* — the *baraita* was not finished in front of him; he reacted before the clarification was read, not realizing that the *baraita* itself specifies that the payment is for idleness, not for labor. The second account, *ika d'amri*, proposes a more radical version: Rav heard the *baraita* in full and nonetheless insisted that in his view the workers should receive nothing at all — not even the *ke-fo'el batel* rate.

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between the *baraita*'s ruling and Rav's stricter position by introducing a crucial factual distinction: *ha d'sayrei l'ara me-ortya, ha d'lo sayrei l'ara me-ortya* — did the employer inspect the land the night before or not? Here Rashi and Rambam diverge in a significant and consequential way. According to Rambam, the inspection refers to what the *employer* did. If the employer examined the field the prior evening and it appeared ready to be worked, and then an unforeseen event — a flood, for example — rendered it unworkable overnight, the employer has fulfilled his obligation of due diligence. He is blameless, and the workers must absorb the loss. If the employer failed to inspect the field the night before and therefore hired workers without verifying that work would be available, he bears a degree of negligence, and the workers must be compensated at the *ke-fo'el batel* rate.

Rashi, by contrast, reads the inspection as something the workers themselves are expected to perform. If the workers were brought to the field and had an opportunity to examine it but failed to notice that it was unworkable, that negligence is theirs and they walk away with nothing. If, however, they had no such opportunity, they are without fault and must be paid.

The gap between these two positions is significant. Under Rambam, the determining variable is employer negligence. Under Rashi, it is worker negligence. This means there exists a middle case — where neither party is at fault — that each authority would resolve differently. Where Rambam would find for the workers (since the employer did not inspect and is therefore negligent), Rashi might find for the employer (since the workers also had no opportunity to inspect and thus bear no fault either). The underlying principle is consistent across both opinions: liability tracks negligence, and the party whose fault caused the loss must bear it.

### Rava Irrigation

Rava develops the negligence framework through a series of concrete cases involving irrigation work. In the first, *hai man d'agar agirei le-rafka* — one who hires workers to deepen an irrigation ditch — and then rain falls overnight and fills the ditch with water, rendering the work impossible: if the owner inspected the field the night before, *paseida d'po'alim*, the loss falls on the workers. If the owner did not inspect it the night before, *paseida d'va'al ha-bayit*, the employer must pay them the *ke-fo'el batel* rate for the day.

Rava's second case involves workers hired *le-davla*, to irrigate the field, when rain then does the irrigation for them: *paseida d'po'alim* — the loss is the workers' and the employer need not pay. However, if the rain came through the field's own irrigation ditch — *ata nahra* — the loss shifts to the employer. Tosafot explains the logic: a field equipped with an irrigation ditch will be effectively watered by even a modest rainfall. An owner who knows this should have anticipated the possibility that even a small amount of rain would eliminate the need for hired irrigation workers. The decision to hire workers under those conditions carries a degree of foreseeable risk for which the employer is responsible.

The third case of this series involves workers hired to irrigate, where the irrigation ditch dries up halfway through the day. If this is not a recurring occurrence — *lo avid d'fasik* — the employer could not have been expected to anticipate it, and *paseida d'po'alim*, the workers bear the loss for the remainder of the day. But if the ditch commonly dries up mid-day — *avid d'fasik* — the employer should have foreseen it. Even then, if the workers are local residents — *b'nei mata* — they too are presumed aware of this local feature of the irrigation system and thus share the responsibility. In that case, *paseida d'po'alim*: the workers bear the loss. If, however, the workers were brought in from elsewhere and could not have known about this characteristic of the local infrastructure — *lav b'nei mata* — then *paseida d'va'al ha-bayit*, the employer must pay them for the lost portion of the day.

The governing principle throughout is foreseeability and the assignment of fault. The more the employer could have anticipated that work would not be available, the more he bears responsibility for the workers who arrived to find nothing to do.

### Half-Day Completion

Rava adds another scenario: *hai man d'agar agurei le-avidta u-shlim avidta b'palga d'yoma* — one who hires workers for a job that is then completed by midday. If the employer has other work that is equally easy or equivalent in difficulty, *d'nicha minei* or *d'chvatah*, he may assign it to them for the remainder of the day, *yahiv lehu* or *mafkid lehu*. The worker cannot insist that he was hired only for the specific original task and refuse all other assignments, nor can the employer simply discharge him mid-day and pay only for half the work. The arrangement cuts in both directions: the employer has paid for the day and is entitled to direct the worker's labor for its duration, but only to tasks of commensurate difficulty. If the only available remaining work is harder — *d'kashya minei* — the employer may not compel it, and must instead pay the worker the full day's wage, *yahiv lehu s'char mushlam*.

The *gemara* then questions whether that full payment is truly appropriate in such a case — shouldn't the worker receive only the *ke-fo'el batel* rate for the idle portion of the day? — and answers:

### Achlushei Mechuza

The full-pay rule applies specifically in the case of the *achlushei de-Mechuza* — the heavy field laborers of Mechuza. Rambam explains that for this class of worker, *de-i lo avdi chalshi*: if they do not continue working, their muscles atrophy and idleness is actually physically detrimental to them. Because being idle carries no benefit — and may even carry a cost — the ordinary discount applied to *ke-fo'el batel* does not apply. For such workers, the rate for sitting idle and the rate for working are effectively the same, and so they receive their full *s'char mushlam* for the remainder of the day. More broadly, the principle extends to any scenario in which a worker derives no benefit from resting — whether because of physical need, professional preference, or any other reason — in which case *fo'el batel* becomes equivalent to full wages.

---

## Mid-Job Departure

### Tanna Kamma View

The *baraita* now addresses the case in which workers voluntarily leave in the middle of the job. *Amar Mar: shayminan lahem mah she-asu* — we assess what they have done. If they were hired for two *sela'im* for the whole job, and the remaining work would cost a dollar and a half — *hayu yafeh shishah dinarim* — the first opinion, the *Tanna Kamma*, holds that the workers are nonetheless entitled to their pro-rated dollar for the half-job already completed. *Kasavar rabanan yad po'el al ha-elyona* — the *Tanna Kamma* holds that the worker retains the upper hand. Even if his departure causes the employer additional expense because prices have risen since the original hiring, the worker bears no consequence.

The alternative, *o yigmeru melachtam v'yitlu shnei sela'im*, is that they either finish and collect their full two-dollar fee, or they leave and collect only what they have earned. This formulation will be revisited in Rabbi Dosa's name.

### Worker Persuasion

The *gemara* next considers a scenario in which prices rise mid-job and the workers, aware that they could earn more elsewhere, begin to signal that they may leave. *Ve-amru po'alim* — they back off, not yet quitting outright, but creating the impression that they might. The employer, needing them to stay, goes and persuades them — *ve-azal ba'al ha-bayit u-fayasinhu* — without making any explicit promise of higher wages.

### Employer Promise

When the workers agree to remain after being persuaded, the question becomes how to interpret the employer's inducement. One might think — *mahu d'teima* — that the workers can argue: *ki mefaysinan adaita de-tafit lan agra*, we assumed when you convinced us to stay that you were agreeing to raise our wages to the current market rate. The *gemara* teaches, however, that the employer can respond: *adaita de-tarichna lechu be-achilah u-ve-shtiyah* — I meant only that I would treat you better, provide nicer food or drink. I never promised more money. Accordingly, absent an explicit renegotiation of the contract, the workers continue to work under the terms of the original agreement and are not entitled to additional compensation simply because the market rate has risen while they were on the job.

This raises a further question about the case where the workers were hired at above-market rates to begin with. If the going rate for the whole job was a dollar and a half and the employer offered two dollars — *d'zal avida me-ikar v'agran b'trei zuzei* — and the going rate subsequently rises to two dollars, can the workers now demand two and a half, claiming the employer had promised to pay them a premium over market? The *gemara* says no. The employer can respond: *ki amri lach trei zuzei, de-lo hava kim l'chu* — when I promised two dollars, it was because I recognized that your work was genuinely worth two dollars, even though the market had not yet reflected that value. I was not committing to a perpetual half-dollar premium above the going rate; I was paying you what I believed your work was worth. Now that the market has caught up to that valuation, two dollars is exactly what we agreed upon, and that is what you will receive.

### Rabbi Dosa View

Rabbi Dosa's position, which reflects the view of the *Mishna*, takes a more protective stance toward employers. *Shamim lahen mah she-atid la'asos* — we assess what remains to be done. If the workers leave mid-job and the remaining work would now cost a dollar and a half, the workers are entitled only to the difference: fifty cents for the work they have already done, since the employer must expend a dollar and a half to complete the job, and he had agreed to pay only two dollars total. *Kasavar yad po'el al ha-tachtona* — Rabbi Dosa holds that when the worker backs out, the worker bears the consequences.
