Any additional cost the employer incurs to complete the job is deducted from the departing workers' wages.

### Price Decline Case

The *baraita* now introduces the flip side of the price-rise scenario, this time from Rabbi Dosa's more employer-protective perspective. Suppose prices have fallen mid-job, so that the employer could now hire replacements to complete the remaining work for less than the pro-rated contract price. The employer, tempted to let the workers go and hire cheaper replacements, signals that he might dismiss them. The workers, needing the income, come and plead with him to keep them on — *v'azu po'alim le-fayuso*.

When the employer relents, the question is what exactly the workers agreed to when they said they would "make it right" for him. One might think — *mahu d'teima* — that the employer can say: *ada'ata d'vatzirtu li mei-agrei*, I assumed you were agreeing to accept the new, lower market rate. But the workers respond: *ada'ata d'avdinan lakh avida shapira* — we meant only that we would do exceptionally fine work for you. Unless there was an explicit renegotiation, the parties remain bound by the terms of the original contract. The principle is symmetrical: neither side can unilaterally re-read an ambiguous expression of goodwill as a change in the agreed-upon rate. Explicit renegotiation is required, and absent that, the original contract governs.

The scenario also raises, at least implicitly, a question that the *baraita* never directly resolves: under Rabbi Dosa's framework, is the employer permitted to fire workers mid-job without consequence? Until now the *gemara* has been clear that an employer who turns away workers after they have already shown up must pay them for the day. But the structure of this scenario — in which the employer contemplates dismissing workers because prices have fallen — suggests that the answer may be less obvious under Rabbi Dosa's employer-protective approach. The *baraita* leaves this question open.

### Price Decline Case

Where the remaining work is worth the same dollar that it always was — the total job is two dollars, the workers did half, and the remaining half is still worth one dollar — even Rabbi Dosa agrees that the workers are paid their pro-rated dollar. They caused no loss, so there is nothing to dock.

### Rav Huna Case

Rav Huna son of Rav Natan identifies a further sub-case that arises specifically within Rabbi Dosa's framework. Suppose the workers themselves had originally offered a discount: the going rate for the whole job was two and a half, but they needed the work and agreed to do it for two dollars. *De-azulei inhu gabei zuzei me-ikara* — they went to the employer and offered reduced wages. The going rate then falls to two dollars. Can the employer now argue, from Rabbi Dosa's protective stance, that since the workers agreed to charge a half-dollar less than the going rate, they should now do the work for a dollar and a half, maintaining that same discount against the new market price?

The *gemara* says no. The workers can respond: *ki amrinan l'chu b'batzer zuza* — when we agreed to do the job for less, it was because *de-hava kim l'chu*, you were unaware that the work was worth two dollars. We knew the true value, we needed the income, and we agreed to accept two dollars because that was the fair price. We were not agreeing to give you a half-dollar discount in perpetuity. *Hashta kim l'chu* — now that the going rate has confirmed that two dollars is the correct value, that is what we are owed and what we contracted for.

The broader lesson is that protecting one party — worker or employer — does not mean interpreting every ambiguity in that party's favor. Both Rabbi Dosa's employer-protective position and the *Tanna Kamma*'s worker-protective position operate as context-sensitive frameworks, not as blanket rules of construction. The outcome in each case depends on what the parties actually agreed to and what their words, fairly understood, meant at the time.

---

## Mid-Job Departure

### Tanna Kamma View

With the *baraita* analyzed, the *gemara* turns to a striking ruling: *amar Rav halacha ke-Rabbi Dosa* — Rav rules in accordance with Rabbi Dosa, establishing that when workers leave mid-job, their pay may be docked to cover the employer's resulting losses.

---

## Rav's Ruling

### At-Will Employment

The *gemara* immediately challenges this ruling. Rav himself states elsewhere: *poel yachol lachzor bo afilu b'chatzi ha-yom* — a worker may withdraw even in the middle of the day. This principle is grounded in a *pasuk* from the Torah: *ki li bnei Yisrael avadim, avadai hem* — the Jewish people are servants to God, not *avadim la-avadim*, servants to other servants. The Torah's prohibition against reducing a person to slavery means that a worker must retain the freedom to leave employment at any time. If leaving mid-day will result in having one's wages docked or incurring financial liability, that freedom is illusory rather than real. Rav's ruling that workers may withdraw without consequence therefore seems to align with the *Tanna Kamma*, not with Rabbi Dosa.

### Sachir vs. Kablan

One possible resolution is that Rabbi Dosa distinguishes between a *sachir* — a day laborer hired for a fixed period — and a *kablan* — a contractor hired to deliver a completed job. Rashi explains the conceptual distinction elegantly: a *sachir* is hired for a block of time during which he is, in a real sense, under the employer's authority and direction. The power dynamic inherent in that relationship is precisely what the Torah's anti-slavery concern is designed to address, and so the *sachir* must retain the unqualified right to leave. A *kablan*, by contrast, works on his own terms, delivers a completed product, and operates more like a party to an exchange than like a subordinate. He is already, in a meaningful sense, free — not subject to the employer's moment-to-moment control — and so the anti-slavery concern applies with less force. If a *kablan* abandons a job mid-completion, there is no ethical difficulty in holding him responsible for the resulting loss.

Under this reading, Rav could rule like Rabbi Dosa as applied to contractors, while simultaneously holding that day laborers may leave without consequence — and these positions would not be in conflict.

### Emergency Cases

The *gemara* tests this proposed distinction against a *baraita*: *ha-socher et ha-po'el, u'lechatzi ha-yom shama she-met lo met* — one who hires a worker, and at midday the worker hears of a death in the family, *o she-achazato chamah*, or he is seized by fever. *Im sachir hu, noten lo s'charo* — if he is a day laborer, the employer pays him his wages for the work already done. *Im kablan hu, noten lo kablanuto* — and if he is a contractor, the employer similarly pays him his pro-rated fee for the work already completed.

The point is not that the employer pays for work that was never done, but that the worker who leaves mid-job due to an *ones* — an unforeseeable emergency beyond his control — suffers no deduction from his wages. He is paid for what he did, and no more is withheld.

### Emergency Analysis

The *gemara* asks: whose opinion does this *baraita* represent? If it follows the *Tanna Kamma* — who holds that workers may always leave without consequence and that *yad po'el al ha-elyona* — then the specification of death and illness would be superfluous. The *Tanna Kamma* would protect workers who leave for any reason, and there would be no need to single out emergency cases. The fact that the *baraita* specifically invokes cases of *ones* implies that ordinarily there would be consequences for leaving — and thus this must reflect Rabbi Dosa's position. Rabbi Dosa normally docks the pay of workers who leave mid-job, but carves out an exception when the departure is compelled by an unforeseeable emergency.

And since Rabbi Dosa's exception applies equally to the *sachir* and the *kablan*, this seems to demonstrate that Rabbi Dosa himself makes no distinction between the two categories. If he did, there would be no reason to state the rule for both.

This creates the difficulty: Rav rules like Rabbi Dosa, yet Rav also says a *sachir* may leave without consequence. If Rabbi Dosa himself makes no distinction between *sachir* and *kablan*, how can Rav invoke that very distinction to reconcile his two positions?

The *gemara* offers an alternative explanation: *amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, be-davar ha-aved ve-divrei ha-kol* — this *baraita* is not within Rabbi Dosa's opinion at all. It is a case of *davar ha-aved*, an irretrievable loss, and under those circumstances all opinions agree that there would normally be consequences for departure — yet even then, the *ones* of a death in the family or sudden illness suspends those consequences entirely. Rabbi Dosa may well retain his distinction between *sachir* and *kablan* in ordinary cases.

---

## Land Sale

### Retraction Principle

The *gemara* turns to the *Mishna*'s general rule: *kol ha-meshaneh yado al ha-tachtona, ve-chol ha-chozer bo yado al ha-tachtona* — whoever changes the terms of an agreement has the lower hand, and whoever retracts has the lower hand. The first clause — regarding one who changes the terms — follows Rabbi Yehuda's position as discussed in Bava Kamma and need not be elaborated here. The second clause — that whoever retracts has the lower hand — has already been illustrated in the context of workers who leave mid-job and suffer deduction from their wages. Why, then, does the *Mishna* need to state it again as a general principle?

The *gemara* suggests that *kol ha-chozer bo yado al ha-tachtona* is extending the rule to an additional case: the sale of land. A field was sold for a thousand *zuz*, and the purchaser paid two hundred of them. *Bizman she-ha-mocher chozer bo, yad ha-lokeach al ha-elyona* — if the seller retracts, the buyer has the upper hand. And *yad po'el al ha-tachtona* refers here to the fact that the retracting party — in this case the seller — always has the lower hand.

---

## Rav's Ruling (II)

### Rav's Split

Returning to the reconciliation of Rav's positions: the *gemara* ultimately resolves the tension by concluding that *Rav savar lah kavatei be-chada u-falig alei be-chada* — Rav agrees with Rabbi Dosa in one respect and disagrees in another. Rav rules like Rabbi Dosa with respect to the *kablan*: a contractor who abandons a job mid-completion has his pay docked to cover the employer's resulting losses. But Rav disagrees with Rabbi Dosa regarding the *sachir*: a day laborer retains the unconditional right to leave mid-day without having his wages reduced, in keeping with the Torah's principle that the Jewish people are servants of God and not of one another.

Alternatively, the *gemara* proposes *iba'is eima*: perhaps Rabbi Dosa himself does in fact distinguish between *sachir* and *kablan*, and the *Mishna*'s phrase *kol ha-chozer bo yado al ha-tachtona* is not directed at establishing that Rabbi Dosa applies his rule uniformly to both. Rather, it introduces the entirely separate case of the land sale, to which we now return.

---

## Land Sale (II)

### Seller Retraction

When a field is sold for a thousand *zuz* and the buyer has paid two hundred as a partial payment, neither party has yet concluded the transaction fully. Either side may still retract. If the *seller* retracts, *yad ha-lokeach al ha-elyona* — the buyer has the upper hand and the right to choose the form of remedy. *Ratza omer lo: ten li ma'osai* — he may demand his two hundred *zuz* back, or *ten li karka kineged ma'osai* — he may demand two hundred dollars' worth of land instead. Furthermore, when choosing land, *me'heichan magbihu? Min ha-idis* — he takes from the best-quality land, since the wronged party is entitled to the most favorable selection.

### Buyer Retraction

If the *buyer* retracts, *yad ha-mocher al ha-elyona* — the seller has the upper hand. *Ratza omer lo: heilach ma'osecha* — he may return the two hundred *zuz*, effectively throwing the money back, or *heilach karka kineged ma'osecha* — he may offer two hundred dollars' worth of land. In the latter case, *me'heichan magbihu? Min ha-ziborit* — he gives from the poorest-quality land. In both directions, then, the party who was wronged — who kept to the deal while the other retracted — gets to choose both the form of settlement and, if land is involved, the quality of that land. The retracting party has the lower hand in every dimension.

### Rabban Shimon Solution

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers a practical solution to avoid this entire regime of retractions and their attendant complications: *melamdin otan shelo yachzoru* — one should structure transactions in such a way that neither party can retract at all. *Keitzad?* — How? When the two hundred *zuz* are handed over, a *shtar* is written immediately: "I, Ploni ben Ploni, have sold such-and-such a field to Ploni for one thousand *zuz*; he has paid me two hundred of them, *ve-hareini nosheh bo shmoneh me'ot zuz* — and I hold a debt against him for the remaining eight hundred." By treating the remaining eight hundred as a loan owed to the seller, rather than as an unpaid balance that leaves the sale incomplete, the transaction is rendered legally final from the moment of the partial payment. Neither party may thereafter retract. *U-machzir et ha-she'ar afilu achar kamah shanim* — the buyer then repays the eight hundred even if it takes many years, but the sale itself is irrevocable from the moment the *shtar* is executed.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 78

## Retraction & Lower Hand

### Case Overview

The daf opens by picking up from the end of 77b, where the Gemara cites the principle established in the Mishnah: *kol ha-chozer bo yado al ha-tachtona* — whoever retracts from a transaction has the lower hand. The specific context elaborated in the Baraita is not a case involving workers but rather a sale of land. Someone agreed to purchase a plot of land for a thousand *sela*, made a down payment of two hundred, and then one of the parties seeks to retract. The consequence is that the two hundred is returned — the sale is not yet considered final, and neither side may simply forfeit or retain the down payment unilaterally — but the party who did not retract enjoys a privileged position.

### Lower Hand Rights

The operative consequence of *yado al ha-tachtona* is that the non-retracting party has the right to choose the form of compensation. If the seller retracts, the buyer may choose either to receive back his two hundred in cash, or to take two hundred dollars' worth of land — and if he opts for land, he may select from the best portion of the field. Conversely, if the buyer retracts, the seller may choose whether to return the two hundred in cash or in land, and if he returns land, he may choose the worst portion of the field. This asymmetry is not a product of some internal logical mechanism in the law of *kinyanim*; it is more accurately understood as a penalty imposed by *Chazal* on the retracting party — an institution designed to discourage retraction rather than a necessary consequence of the formal structure of the transaction.

### Collection Source

The Gemara raises a pointed question: *me-heichan magbiya* — when the non-retracting party selects land as compensation, from which of the seller's properties may he collect? The Gemara's initial assumption is that *min ha-idit de-nechsav* — he may collect from the best of any of the seller's properties, not merely from within the particular plot that was the subject of the sale.

### Best Property Claim

The logic behind this initial reading is as follows: *kasalka da'atach* — if you were going to collect from the best of all properties, the reasoning would be that a person who needs to assemble a thousand *zuz* to purchase a large plot of land typically sells off his other assets along the way, often at a discount, in order to raise the required sum. Having already incurred losses in preparing to complete this purchase, the buyer suffers real damage when the seller retracts before he can pay the full balance.

### Creditor Comparison

Yet even granting that logic, the Gemara resists the conclusion. *V'lo yehei ela ba'al chov* — the buyer should be no better off than an ordinary creditor. And the rule for creditors, as taught in a Mishnah, is that a *ba'al chov dino be-veinonit* — a creditor collects from middle-grade land. Rashi notes that this rule exists partly to encourage people to lend money, and even so the lender is limited to *beinonit*. Why then should the buyer be able to take the absolute best of all the seller's assets?

Furthermore, the Gemara observes, if this were truly treated like a debt, the seller would retain the option to pay cash — the creditor cannot simply demand land. So neither the analogy to damages nor the analogy to a creditor cleanly justifies giving the buyer unlimited access to the seller's best property. The Gemara acknowledges, incidentally, that even the damage argument is imprecise: at best it is *grama* — indirect causation — and the question of whether *garmi* applies to hold someone liable in such situations is a recurring and complicated issue throughout this tractate.

### Plot Limitation

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak therefore offers a resolution: when the Mishnah speaks of the non-retracting buyer collecting from the *idit*, it does not mean the best of all of the seller's holdings. Rather, *me-idit shebah u-mi-ziborit shebah* — the choice operates entirely within the plot that was the subject of the sale itself. If the seller retracts, the buyer may choose the best portion of that specific field as his two-hundred-dollar portion; if the buyer retracts, the seller may assign him the worst portion of that same field. Conceptually, this framework treats the partial payment as having constituted a partial purchase, with the non-retracting party retaining the right to designate which portion was purchased. To the question of whether this means the buyer gets fewer acres when choosing prime land: yes, precisely — a smaller but higher-quality portion, versus a larger but inferior one, both calibrated to the same monetary value.

### Acha's Position

Rav Acha brei de-Rav Ika, however, maintains the original reading: *afilu teima mi-idit de-nechsav stam* — even so, one may argue that the buyer can indeed collect from the best of all of the seller's properties, not limited to the plot being sold. The rationale is that *stam man de-zavin ar'a be-alfa zuzei* — a person who is trying to put together a thousand *zuz* to buy land typically sells off other assets at a discount to raise the funds. He has incurred real losses in the process. The seller's retraction therefore causes the buyer genuine damage — *shavya ki-nizak* — and for damage, the Mishnah says *nizikin shamin la-hem be-idit*, assessment is made from the finest property. Even so, the Gemara notes the difficulties with this framing: technically it is *grama*, and moreover the seller retains the prerogative to pay in cash rather than land. Nevertheless, Rav Acha's reading is on the table, while the *pshat* of the Gemara, as Rashi confirms, is that collection is limited to within the plot itself.

---

## Partial Payment Sale

### RSBG Method

The Mishnah continues: *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer melamdin oto shelo yachzor bo* — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says we should teach people how to structure transactions so that neither party will wish to retract. The problem underlying all of the above is that a standard partial payment does not yet constitute a full *kinyan* on the land, leaving both sides exposed to the possibility of retraction. His solution is practical: *keitzad* — how does one finalize a sale even when the buyer has only partial funds? The seller takes the partial payment, and a *shtar* is written explicitly stating that the field has been sold in full and that the buyer owes the balance. This converts the remainder into something like a mortgage — the full sale is finalized, the buyer owes the balance as a debt, and the complications of *chozer bo* are avoided entirely.

### Eravon Terms

The Gemara proceeds to a Baraita concerning *eravon* — a form of down payment or surety that carries an explicitly conditional character, distinct from an ordinary partial payment. In this case, the buyer hands over a sum and the two sides articulate mutual penalties: the buyer declares that if he retracts, the seller keeps the *eravon* outright, and the seller declares that if he retracts, he will return the *eravon* and pay an equal additional sum in compensation. The Baraita rules *nitkaymu ha-tena'im* — the conditions are enforceable and binding.

### Asmakhta Kinyan

The Gemara interjects: this is the position of Rebbi Yose — and Rebbi Yose is consistent with his broader ruling that *asmakhta kanya* — a conditional commitment, even one premised on a contingency neither party fully expects to occur, is nonetheless binding. An *asmakhta* is an agreement whose enforceability might be questioned on the grounds that the parties assumed the triggering condition would never arise and therefore never gave their full *gmar da'at*. Rebbi Yose holds that such agreements are valid and fully enforceable.

### Partial Purchase

Rebbi Yehuda offers a middle position: *dayo she-yikne k'neged ervono* — the *eravon* itself constitutes a partial purchase proportional to its amount. The buyer acquires the corresponding fraction of the field, no more. This is precisely the intermediate category mentioned earlier — neither a complete sale nor no sale at all, but a partial purchase reflecting the amount tendered.

### RSBG Stipulation

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes: *bameh devarim amurim* — when does the *eravon* create a partial purchase? Only *bizman she'amar lo ervoni yikne* — when the buyer explicitly declares that his *eravon* should serve as the purchasing act. Rashi explains that even if the buyer intended the *eravon* to purchase the entire field, since it falls short of the full price, he at least acquires a proportional share. The key requirement is explicit stipulation.

### Implied Finalization

By contrast, in the case where a seller agrees to sell a field for a thousand *zuz* and the buyer hands over five hundred without any special declaration — no *eravon* language, no explicit stipulation — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules: *kana u-machzir lo et ha-she'ar afilu l'achar kamah shanim* — the partial payment finalizes the entire purchase and the balance is treated as a loan, recoverable even years later. This raises an immediate tension: earlier, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel appeared to require an explicit *shtar* stipulation for partial payment to operate as a full purchase. Here he seems to rule that partial payment alone suffices, with no written stipulation at all.

A conceptual question underlies this discussion. One might frame it as follows: the buyer paid the full price and received the balance back as a loan, so ownership passed because full payment was made. Alternatively — following a discussion found among the *acharonim* regarding *kinyan kesef* by a woman — perhaps the payment of any sum of value finalizes a sale of land symbolically, the way a minimal *kesef* finalizes certain acquisitions, with the balance remaining as a separate obligation. Either way, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position as stated here appears to be that without any explicit stipulation, a partial payment already finalizes the sale and the remainder becomes a debt.

---

## Seller Intent Contex (II)

### Money-Raising Test

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's rulings with a single principle: *ha d'ka ayil venafik azuzei, ha d'lo ka ayil venafik azuzei* — one ruling applies when the seller is running around trying to raise money, and the other applies when he is not. The key question in any given case is whether the seller clearly needed the cash proceeds of the sale urgently.

### Urgency Evidence

*Ayil venafik azuzei* — literally "going in and going out with coins" — describes a seller who is visibly and urgently scrambling to raise funds. If the seller is demonstrably in this situation, the Gemara reasons that his intent in making the sale was to obtain immediate, full payment. Receiving a partial payment does not satisfy what he actually needed. Accordingly, we do not treat the partial payment as finalizing the sale; both parties remain in a pre-*kinyan* state, and if the buyer fails to produce the remainder, there is no completed transaction. Rashi interprets the phrase somewhat differently — as the seller constantly pressing the buyer for the balance, repeatedly asking "do you have the money yet?" — which similarly manifests the seller's urgent dependence on receiving full payment.

Either way, this standard is a striking one. Establishing in a *beit din* how urgently a seller needed money, how persistently he was pressing for payment, and what this reveals about his subjective intent at the time of the transaction is an extraordinarily difficult evidentiary question. Witnesses might testify to the seller's behavior, but the threshold for "how much running around" constitutes urgency is inherently imprecise. Nevertheless, the Gemara commits to this contextual approach.

### Rava's Rule

Rava codifies the principle: *hai man de-zavin midi le-chavrei veka ayil venafik azuzei lo kani* — if the seller is urgently scrambling to raise funds, the buyer does not acquire through partial payment. *Lo ka ayil venafik azuzei kani* — if the seller is not doing so, the partial payment finalizes the acquisition. At this stage, the discussion has been focused primarily on land, where *kinyan kesef* is operative and the question is whether partial *kesef* suffices.

---

## Chattel Payment Rules

### Donkey Case

A new case now extends and complicates the analysis. Someone sold a donkey to his friend — Rashi makes a point of specifying *chamor*, a donkey, rather than *chamra*, wine — and the buyer paid all but one *zuz* of the purchase price. Meanwhile, the seller has been visibly running around to raise money. The question posed is: does paying ninety-nine out of a hundred *zuz* finalize the sale?

### Full Payment Rule

Rav Ashi was deliberating on this question when Rav Mordechai told him in the name of Avimi of Hagronya in the name of Rava: *zuza ke-zuzei dami, ve-lo kani* — one *zuz* is treated like many *zuz*, and the buyer does not acquire. The logic is clear in principle: if any amount short of full payment can prevent finalization when the seller urgently needs funds, then drawing the line at "only one *zuz* remaining" would be arbitrary. Every partial payment from one *zuz* to nine hundred ninety-nine *zuz* would require its own rule. The Gemara therefore rules categorically: any unpaid balance, however small, precludes finalization when the seller is demonstrably in urgent need.

One might object that this seems inequitably rigid in a context where the Gemara is otherwise so sensitive to context — whether the seller needs money is contextual, but whether one dollar or eight hundred dollars remains unpaid is treated as binary. The Gemara accepts this asymmetry: context governs the question of whether full payment is required at all, but once it is determined that full payment is required, there is no gradation.

### Tosafot Extension

What makes this case particularly striking is that the subject is chattel, not land. For chattel, the standard mode of acquisition is *meshicha* — taking possession — and money alone does not ordinarily complete a sale of movable property. Why then is partial payment relevant at all? Tosafot raises the possibility that the discussion concerns *mi she-para* — whether the partial payer is subject to the rabbinic curse upon one who retracts after payment — but ultimately rejects that reading. Instead, Tosafot understands the Gemara as addressing a case where the buyer has already taken *meshicha*, has already taken possession of the donkey, and the question is whether that *meshicha* finalizes the transaction in a case where the seller was urgently scrambling for funds.

The position Tosafot derives is remarkable: *nira de-ayri afilu mashach ha-mekach* — even if the buyer has taken physical possession of the item, if the sale occurred in a context where the seller was urgently in need of the full payment, and if the buyer did not specify at the time that the *meshicha* itself would be the finalizing act, then possession alone does not complete the sale. The seller's *da'at* — his genuine intent — was not to part with the item until he received full payment in cash.

### Disruption of Rules

This is a genuinely radical implication. Everything learned earlier about *meshicha* finalizing sales of chattel now becomes conditional. A buyer who takes possession of goods sold by a seller visibly running around for funds has not necessarily completed the acquisition until full payment is made. The practical ramifications for *beit din* are vast: virtually every disputed chattel sale would require an investigation into the seller's financial circumstances at the time. The rules of *kinyan* that are supposed to provide clarity and finality are suddenly subject to a sweeping contextual override.

---

## Seller Intent Contex (II)

### Offloading Exception

A counterbalancing factor now enters the picture. Even when the seller is demonstrably running around for money — which would ordinarily prevent finalization with partial payment — a different consideration can override this: *mocher sadeh mipnei ra'asah* — a seller who is effectively trying to unload a piece of property he does not really want. If the circumstances make clear that the seller was happy to be rid of this particular asset regardless of his general financial desperation, then the sale is treated as final even with partial payment, because his intent to divest himself of the property outweighs his need for the specific cash.

### Proof Burden

The Gemara now confronts the full complexity of the evidentiary picture. The default rule is that urgently needing funds prevents finalization with partial payment. But if the seller was offloading an unwanted property, that reverses the presumption and finalizes the sale even with partial payment.

The Gemara offers a straightforward case: a seller needs to raise a hundred dollars, cannot find buyers for his small plot of land, and therefore sells a larger and more valuable plot for two hundred. He urgently needs the money and did not want to part with the larger plot. Here — *lo kani* — partial payment clearly does not finalize the sale. He was not trying to offload that property; he was coerced by circumstance into selling something he regretted selling, and he needs the cash.

The Gemara then poses the harder case: the seller again needs to raise a hundred dollars, again cannot find buyers for his small plot. However, if he had exerted himself more — made more effort, pursued more buyers — he might have found one. Instead, out of laziness, he sold his larger plot for two hundred. He is still visibly scrambling for funds. But is his failure to try harder to sell the smaller plot evidence that he did not really care about the larger one? Does his laziness constitute sufficient proof that he was, in effect, offloading unwanted property? Or do we say that his financial desperation is the dominant fact and his laziness is irrelevant to his intent about the specific property? The Gemara reaches no conclusion: *teyku*.

The overall calculus becomes extraordinarily layered. Whether partial payment finalizes a sale depends on whether the seller urgently needed funds; whether he urgently needed funds can be overridden if he was offloading unwanted property; and whether he was offloading unwanted property is itself a question of degree, subject to contested factual proof. Both parties to any disputed sale will marshal competing narratives — one emphasizing the seller's desperation, the other emphasizing his indifference to the specific property sold — and the court must adjudicate between them.

---

## Worker Breach Rules

### Davar Ha'aved

The Gemara returns now to the first Mishnah. The case: a worker is hired to carry goods or perform labor, and he backs out during a *davar ha'aved* — a task that cannot be interrupted without the work spoiling or causing irreversible loss. The paradigmatic example is a worker engaged with flax or, by extension, something like a band contracted for a wedding that evening, where last-minute cancellation leaves the employer with no practical remedy.

### Employer Options

The Mishnah gives the employer two options. He may deceive the workers by telling them he will pay more than he had originally agreed, induce them to complete the work, and then pay only the original rate — provided there is no binding new commitment. Alternatively, he may hire replacement workers and charge the cost of those replacements to the breaching workers. The question is how far this right to charge for replacements extends.

### Wage Offset

Rav Nachman rules: *ad k'dei secharan* — up to the amount of their wages. Rashi clarifies that this does not mean the employer can spend double the original rate on replacements. Rather, the employer may apply whatever portion of the workers' own earned wages is still in his possession toward the cost of hiring replacements. The breaching workers receive nothing, and whatever he owed them can be redirected to fund the substitute labor.

This is an important structural point. The mechanism *Chazal* provide is not a tort remedy for indirect damage — one might object that the workers' breach is at most *grama*, indirect causation, and *grama* is *patur* from liability in court. Rather, what *Chazal* have authorized is an offset: if the employer already holds the workers' wages, he may apply those wages to cover the cost of replacement labor. This means that if the workers have already been paid in advance, the offset is unavailable — the employer would have no similar action, even if practically this seems harsh given that the workers would appear to owe all the more for accepting pay before completing the job. The principle of *sechirus einah mishtalemes ela be-sofo* — wages are paid at the end — means that prepayment is the unusual case, and when it occurs, the employer loses this remedy.

### Post-Payment Case

Rava challenged Rav Nachman by citing a Baraita that appeared to allow the employer to spend as much as forty or fifty *zuz* on replacements — a sum presumably far exceeding what a half-day's wages would amount to. Rav Nachman responded: that Baraita governs a different case entirely.

### Goods Deposit

The Baraita's rule of forty or fifty *zuz* applies specifically when the workers had already deposited their equipment or goods at the workplace — *sheba chavilo le-yado*. The workers brought their tools or materials to the employer's premises and then cancelled. In that case, the employer effectively holds the workers' equipment, and he may leverage or sell that equipment to fund hiring replacements, potentially up to its full value. The analogy is the band that transported all its equipment to the wedding hall before canceling: the employer may seize that equipment and use its value to secure substitute performers. Without such possession of the workers' goods, the offset is limited to what the employer already owes them in wages.

---

## Rental Breach

### Mountain-Valley Case

The next Mishnah marks a significant conceptual transition. The previous cases concerned *sechirus* in the sense of hiring a person for his service. Now the Mishnah turns to *sechirus* in the sense of renting an object — specifically a donkey — which belongs to a fundamentally different legal category. This is the domain of *shomrim*: a *shomer chinam*, a *shomer sachar*, a *sho'el*, and a *socher* each bear different levels of liability for an object in their possession. Renting a donkey is not a service contract but something closer to a temporary acquisition of its use — the Rambam conceptualizes it as a limited purchase of usage rights for a defined period — and the rules governing it differ accordingly.

The Mishnah's case: a donkey was rented for use on the mountain route, but the renter took it through the valley instead — or vice versa. Even if the two routes were of identical distance and seemingly equivalent effort, if the donkey died, the renter is liable. The question of what the rental terms actually required is worth pausing on: did the owner explicitly stipulate "only on the mountain, not the valley," or was this simply the understood expectation based on the purpose stated at the time of rental? Either way, the donkey was taken to a different location than was contemplated.

### Causation Nexus

The Mishnah's *seifa* complicates the picture considerably, and this is where the Gemara will focus its analysis. If the agreement was to use the donkey on the mountain and it was taken to the valley: *im hichlikah, patur* — if it slipped, the renter is exempt. If it slipped in the valley, the renter is not liable, because mountain terrain is inherently more prone to slipping, and by taking it to the valley he was actually being more cautious with respect to that risk. *Aval im huchmah, chayav* — but if it overheated, he is liable, because valleys are hotter and the heat risk is greater there. The reverse applies if the agreement was for the valley and he took it to the mountain: liability for slipping, exemption for overheating.

This suggests that the *seifa* of the Mishnah requires a demonstrable causal connection between the specific breach of terms and the specific cause of the animal's death. Negligence about risk X does not create liability for harm from risk Y.

### Specific Risks

The logic of the mountain-valley distinction maps onto specific identifiable risks: mountain terrain creates slipping hazards, while valley terrain creates heat hazards. When the renter violated the terms in a direction that reduced exposure to the risk that actually materialized, he is exempt; when he violated the terms in a direction that increased exposure to that specific risk, he is liable.

### Warranty Voiding

But this creates a sharp tension with the *reisha* of the Mishnah, which states simply that if a renter took the donkey to the wrong location and it died — with no specification of why — he is liable. That ruling appears to impose liability regardless of whether a causal connection to the breach of terms can be established. So which principle governs? Is the *reisha* a case of automatic liability upon violation of terms — what might be called voiding the warranty — or does it too require a causal connection that is simply assumed on the facts?

The Gemara offers several answers. The school of Rabbi Yannai suggests that the *reisha* is a case where the donkey died *machmat avir* — as a result of the change of air quality. Since the air quality is genuinely different between mountain and valley, and since it is not a risk that maps cleanly onto "better or worse" terrain, a death attributable to changed air is assumed to be causally connected to the change of location. This is a way of saying: when we cannot clearly attribute the death to a risk that was *less* present at the wrongful location, we assume connection.

Rabbi Yose bar Chanina offers a parallel answer: the *reisha* involves death from *utzna* — weariness or exertion. This again is a cause that can plausibly be linked to either location, and Rashi elaborates that even in the valley, where the terrain is flatter, one can argue that the mountain air would have strengthened the animal and offset the exertion, so the change of location is still causally relevant. Rava adds a third example: the donkey was bitten by a snake — clearly an event whose connection to location is indeterminate, and in such cases, we hold the renter liable because we cannot say the wrong location was irrelevant.

All three of these answers converge on a single framework: the *reisha* represents cases of ambiguous causation, where we cannot clearly exonerate the renter's locational breach. The *seifa*, by contrast, involves causes — slipping, overheating — where the causal connection to the specific location is determinate, and where in a given direction of breach the renter was actually *less* negligent about that specific risk.

### Two-Part Analysis

The apparent resolution is therefore: the *reisha* and *seifa* do not reflect different legal rules. Both require a link between the breach and the harm. But the *reisha* presents circumstances — air quality, snake bites, weariness from exertion — where the causal connection cannot be ruled out, and the renter therefore cannot escape liability. The *seifa* presents circumstances — heat, slipping — where the relationship between location and risk is specific and determinable, enabling precise liability assignments based on which risk the renter's breach increased or decreased.

### Ambiguous Causation

This clarifies an important principle: it is not that the renter is automatically liable for everything once he breaches the rental terms. Rather, where causation is genuinely ambiguous — we don't know why it died, we can't say the location made it more or less safe — the renter bears the loss. He violated the terms and placed the animal in a location not contemplated by the rental agreement; when harm results and the causal picture is murky, the law does not allow him to hide behind that murkiness.

### Rabbi Meir Position

The Gemara then presents an alternative analysis. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan: the *reisha* and *seifa* are not two parts of a unified ruling. They reflect the positions of different *tana'im*. The *reisha* — which holds the renter liable even without a demonstrable connection between his breach and the cause of death — represents the view of Rebbi Meir. The *seifa* — which requires the connection to be established — represents a different opinion.

What is Rebbi Meir's principle? *Kol ha-ma'avir al da'at ba'al ha-bayit nikra gazlan* — one who violates the intent and conditions set by the owner is treated as a *gazlan* with respect to that object. Once the renter places the donkey somewhere he was not authorized to place it, he is no longer using the owner's property legitimately. He has effectively become a robber — a *gazlan* — with full liability for whatever subsequently occurs, regardless of whether the harm flows from his specific breach.

---

## Gazlan Doctrine

### Gazlan Definition

Rebbi Meir's principle — *kol ha-ma'avir al da'at ba'al ha-bayit nikra gazlan* — is a sweeping statement about the consequences of violating an owner's conditions. The moment a person uses another's property in a manner the owner did not authorize, he crosses from the legal category of *socher* or *sho'el* — with their defined liability structures — into the category of *gazlan*, a robber who bears full liability for any harm to the object, regardless of cause.

### Dyer Example

To identify which Rebbi Meir is meant, the Gemara first considers the Rebbi Meir of the dyer case. The Mishnah teaches: if someone gave wool to a dyer to dye it red and the dyer dyed it black — or the reverse — Rebbi Meir rules *nosan lo dmei tzemaro*, the dyer has effectively acquired the wool by his unauthorized act and must pay the owner the value of the wool. Rebbi Yehuda disagrees and holds the owner retains ownership, with only a renegotiation of the fee. The Gemara initially considers whether this is the operative Rebbi Meir — one who holds that acting against an owner's instructions regarding an object causes the agent to take ownership of it.

The Gemara rejects this: *dilma shani hasam dekanya bishinui ma'aseh* — perhaps there is a unique reason the dyer acquires the wool, namely that he physically transformed the object, and transformation can itself constitute a form of *kinyan*. That principle does not necessarily extend to a renter who takes a donkey on the wrong road without physically altering it. The dyer case may turn on the change in the object itself, not on violation of instructions per se.

### Purim Funds

The Gemara then turns to the Rebbi Meir of Purim funds. The Baraita teaches: money collected for Purim must be distributed for Purim — *magbi Purim le-Purim*. Money collected for a specific city's poor must be used for that city's poor. One may not economize — if the funds were raised for *matanos la'evyonim*, they must all be spent for that purpose, even on lavish feasts for the recipients. Whatever remains goes to general *tzedakah*. From the perspective of the *ani* himself, Rebbi Yaakov citing Rebbi Meir rules that a poor person who received money for Purim may not spend even a small fraction of it on anything else — not even to purchase a shoe string — without the explicit consent of the townspeople who contributed. This is stated because the poor person may not *ma'avir al da'at ba'al ha-bayit* — violate the stipulations of those who gave him the funds.

However, the Gemara resists drawing the *gazlan* doctrine from this case as well: *dilma hasam nami ada'ata de-Purim hu de-yahiv lei* — perhaps what this case really reflects is simply that the gift was conditioned on Purim use, and without that condition the donor would not have given at all. That is a specific feature of conditional charitable giving, not a general principle that any violation of terms creates *gazlan* status.

### Shirt-Coat Case

The Gemara therefore turns to a third Rebbi Meir: Rebbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rebbi Meir, who teaches that if one gives a *dinar* to a poor person to buy himself a shirt, the poor person may not use it to buy a coat — and conversely, money given to buy a coat may not be spent on a shirt. The reason stated is *she-ma'avir al da'ato shel ba'al ha-bayit* — he violates the intent and stipulation of the owner of the money. This case has the crucial phrase in full, making it the most natural source for the Rebbi Meir principle under discussion.

### Intent Protection

The Gemara confirms: *shema mina mishum de-shinnui hu ve-chol ha-ma'avir al da'ato shel ba'al ha-bayit nikra gazlan* — this shows that Rebbi Meir is deeply concerned with adherence to the owner's stated intent, and that violating those stipulations is characterized as a form of unauthorized use.

One might try to deflect even this case by arguing the rule is really about protecting the donor's reputation — if the poor person buys something other than what was announced, onlookers will suspect the donor of breaking his promise. But the Gemara rejects this reading: if reputation were the reason, the Baraita would have stated *mipnei ha-chashad* — because of suspicion. Instead it uses the language of violating the owner's intent, which demonstrates that the principle is substantive, not merely reputational.

### Gazlan Implication

This is an important conclusion — but it is worth noting precisely what has and has not been established. The Gemara has demonstrated that Rebbi Meir is strongly committed to the principle that a person must not violate the conditions stipulated by an owner, and that doing so is characterized as *ma'avir al da'ato shel ba'al ha-bayit*. What has not yet been fully demonstrated is whether this characterization automatically confers the legal status of *gazlan* with all that it entails — namely, full liability for any subsequent harm to the object regardless of causation. The *nikra gazlan* formulation points in that direction, and the *reisha* of the Mishnah appears to reflect that consequence, but the precise mechanics of how violation of rental terms translates into unlimited *gazlan*-style liability remains an open question in the Gemara's analysis.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 79

## Donkey Rental Intro

### Previous Context

The daf opens on 78b, approximately five lines before the text widens, with a new *mishnah* that shifts the discussion from workers to rentals. The *mishnah* addresses the case of one who rents a donkey, and its opening concern is liability when the renter uses the animal outside the terms of the agreement.

### Liability Framework

Two distinct frameworks govern this liability. The first is the principle of *techlilato bipshiah vesofo beones*: when a person begins with negligence, he bears responsibility for all that follows, even if the ultimate harm was an *ones* — an unforeseeable accident — since there is a presumption that the accident was an outgrowth of the original negligence. That presumption can, however, be rebutted if the harm was clearly unrelated to the initial negligence, in which case the renter would be exempt. The second framework, associated with Rabbi Meir, is *kol hamavir al daato shel baal habayit nikra gazlan* — one who violates the owner's terms is considered a thief. Under this approach, the renter's liability is not grounded in negligence at all but in the fact that by exceeding the terms of the rental he has effectively assumed full possessory responsibility, making him liable for anything that goes wrong regardless of any causal connection.

### Techlilato Bipshiah

The distinction between these two approaches is significant. Under *techlilato bipshiah vesofo beones*, liability is a consequence of the presumed causal chain from the initial negligence, and a sufficiently remote or unrelated harm could break that chain. Under Rabbi Meir's approach, the liability is total and unconditional from the moment the renter deviates from the agreement. These two frameworks set the conceptual backdrop for the cases that follow.

---

## Minor Defects

### Vehivrika/Avzeket

The *mishnah* continues with a new set of cases concerning defects that arise in the course of the rental. *Vehivrika* — translated in Babylonia as *nahurisa*, a term connoting light or brightness — refers, according to Rashi, to a condition affecting the iris of the eye, a kind of vision impairment. The donkey is not fully functional, but it can still carry burdens. It is, in the language of a familiar analogy, a dented car that remains drivable. Rava adds *avzeket*, which Rashi describes as a type of worm that has invaded the animal's foot or hoof. Again, the donkey remains usable, even if impaired.

### Harei Shelcha

In both of these cases, the *mishnah* rules that the owner need not replace the animal. He may say *harei shelcha lefanecha* — here it is before you, take it as it is. The donkey is still serviceable, and the owner's contractual obligation does not extend to providing a defect-free animal so long as the animal can still perform its function.

### King's Worm Story

A tangential but memorable anecdote is attached to the mention of *avzeket*. The Gemara relates that a certain man warned the royal court: *avzeket bemilsa demalka* — there is a worm eating away at the king's clothing. When asked which garments — *betali dekesaf*, the silver ones (which Rashi explains refers to linen, whose color resembles silver), or *betali dedehav*, the gold ones (wool, dyed a golden shade) — one tradition holds he said the silver ones and was executed, because the worm in question does not in fact eat linen, exposing his claim as a lie that impugned the king's honor. Another tradition holds he said the gold ones and was left alone, since that at least was plausible.

---

## Angarya Cases

### Angarya Hozeret

The *mishnah* then addresses a more dramatic disruption: *angarya* — seizure of the animal by agents of the king for royal use. Here too, the *mishnah* rules that the owner may say *harei shelcha lefanecha*, and need not provide a replacement. This seems surprising, since unlike a visual impairment or a worm, the seized animal is entirely unavailable to the renter.

### Rav's Position

Rav resolves this by drawing a distinction. *Lo shanu ella be'angarya hozeret* — the ruling that no replacement is required applies only to *angarya hozeret*, a temporary seizure after which the animal will be returned. If the seizure is *angarya she'eino hozeret*, a permanent taking with no return, then the owner is obligated to provide a replacement, just as he would if the donkey had died or been incapacitated.

### Shmuel Derech

Shmuel takes a different approach entirely. According to Shmuel, the distinction is not between temporary and permanent seizure, but between the circumstances under which the seizure occurred. *Im be'derech halicha nitla* — if the donkey was seized as it was traveling along the route — the owner may say *harei shelcha lefanecha*, even if the animal will never be returned. *Ve'im lav be'derech halichata nitla* — if it was not seized along its route of travel — the owner must replace it, even if the seizure is only temporary.

Rashi describes the scenario underlying this distinction as one in which royal troops would press a donkey into service for a leg of their journey, release it when they encountered the next available animal, and so move from victim to victim. On this reading, the question of *derech halichata* resolves into whether the seizure occurred in the direction the renter was already heading, since the donkey would eventually be returned once the troops found their next draft animal.

### Tosafot Circumstances

Tosafot offers what appears to be a more intuitive reading. Rather than focusing on the physical direction of travel, the distinction turns on the circumstances under which the seizure occurred. If the royal agents simply came upon the donkey as it was traveling on the road, the renter happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time — something akin to his own ill fortune or *mazal* — and therefore the loss is, in some sense, attributable to him. The owner can say: you happened to be on that road at that time; that is your bad luck, not my responsibility. But if the agents went house to house searching specifically for a suitable animal, the seizure has nothing to do with any choice or circumstance attributable to the renter, and it is a pure *ones*. In that case, even if the animal will never return, the owner must replace it.

This reading produces a striking result in Shmuel's position: if the seizure is entirely the renter's "fault" in this attenuated sense of bad fortune, the owner need not replace the animal even if it is gone permanently. Conversely, if the seizure is a pure *ones* with no connection to any act or circumstance of the renter, the owner must replace it even if the animal will be back in two days. The criterion is not duration but attribution.

---

## Baraita Reconciliation

### Meitivei Challenge

The Gemara now raises a challenge from a *baraita*. The *baraita* states that if the rented donkey died or was seized by the king — *meisa o shenastasa angarya* — the owner is obligated to replace it. This *baraita* flatly contradicts the *mishnah*, which permits the owner to say *harei shelcha lefanecha* in the case of *angarya*.

### Rav Resolution

For Rav, the resolution is straightforward: the *mishnah* speaks of *angarya hozeret* and the *baraita* speaks of *angarya she'eino hozeret*. Each source addresses a different category, and there is no genuine contradiction.

### Shmuel Resolution

For Shmuel, however, the resolution is more complex. Shmuel can propose that the *mishnah* addresses a case where the donkey was seized *be'derech hilucha* — in the course of the renter's own travel, attributable to his circumstances — while the *baraita* addresses a case where it was seized *shelo be'derech hilucha*, a pure *ones* for which the owner bears responsibility. The Gemara objects, however, that the closing clause of the *baraita* itself invokes precisely this distinction, and attributes it specifically to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. If the *baraita*'s conclusion already belongs to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, then the opening clause of the *baraita* — which mandates replacement — must reflect the position of the *Tanna Kamma*, who apparently requires replacement in all cases regardless of circumstances, posing a difficulty for Shmuel.

### Shimon ben Elazar

The Gemara offers Shmuel a response: *lav miklal d'Rabi Shimon ben Elazar d'ka'ei k'vasi* — is Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's opinion not worth having as a source? Shmuel aligns himself with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who he regards as correct. The Gemara then offers a further resolution: *kulah Rabi Shimon ben Elazar hi* — the entire *baraita* is the position of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and the final clause is not a dispute with the earlier ruling but a clarification of it. The *baraita*, properly reconstructed, reads as follows: if the donkey developed an eye condition or went somewhat mad (*nishtata*), the owner says *harei shelcha lefanecha*; if it died or was seized, he must replace it — but this applies only when the seizure occurred *shelo be'derech hilucha*, not through any circumstance of the renter. If it was seized *be'derech hilucha*, the owner may again say *harei shelcha lefanecha*. This is the consistent teaching of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar throughout.

---

## Riding Purpose

### Riding Requirement

The Gemara now raises a further difficulty. Elsewhere, a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states: *hasocher et hachamor lirkov aleha* — if one rents a donkey specifically for riding — *vehivrika o shenishtata*, and it develops the same eye condition or goes somewhat mad, *chayav le'ha'amid lo chamor*, the owner must replace it. But this contradicts the *mishnah*'s ruling that *vehivrika* does not require replacement. How can the whole earlier *baraita* be attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar if his own statement here requires replacement for *vehivrika*?

### Safety Standards

Raba bar Rav Huna resolves the apparent contradiction: *lirkov aleha shani* — riding is different. Rashi explains that when a person intends to ride the donkey, even a mild impairment becomes unacceptable. A donkey with compromised vision or erratic behavior poses a genuine danger to the rider — it might stumble on a bridge or throw the rider into a pit. When the donkey is used only to carry cargo, the worst outcome of a stumble is that the cargo falls and needs to be retrieved. But a rider cannot accept that risk. Therefore, when the rental is specifically for riding, even a defect that would otherwise be tolerated renders the animal unusable, and the owner must replace it.

### Glassware

Rav Pappa extends the logic of this ruling: *uchelei zechochis ke'irchavo alav dami* — transporting glassware is equivalent to riding, in the sense that an impaired or erratic animal creates an unacceptable risk of total loss. Just as a rider cannot tolerate the danger posed by a compromised animal, a shipper of fragile goods cannot accept the risk that a stumble will shatter everything. In both cases, the standard for usability is stricter than for ordinary cargo.

---

## Death Mid-Journey

### Half Payment

The Gemara now introduces a new and consequential category of cases. Raba bar Huna citing Rav states: *hasocher et hachamor lirkov aleha umeisa lo bachatzi haderech* — if one rents a donkey for riding and it dies in the middle of the journey — *noten lo secharo shel chatzi haderech*, the renter pays the owner for half the journey. And *ein lo alav ela teroumes* — the renter's only recourse is a complaint; he cannot demand a replacement.

This ruling is striking. The *mishnah* had established that when a donkey dies, the owner must replace it. Here, the renter pays half and receives only the right to complain — no replacement is forthcoming. The Gemara asks: *heichi dami* — what are the circumstances that make this ruling coherent?

If replacement animals are readily available at the midpoint, the renter has no real complaint: take the remaining payment and rent another animal. If no replacement is available, how can the owner simply collect half the fee and walk away from his obligation to provide a donkey for the full journey?

### Tosafot Reinterpret

Tosafot grapples with this difficulty honestly. The simple reading of the Gemara — that the owner collects half and owes nothing more — is hard to justify when the renter never wanted to stop in the middle. Tosafot therefore reinterprets the case. When the Gemara says that replacement animals are not available *at the same price*, it means they are not available at the original rental rate. But at a slightly higher rate, the renter can find another animal. Since the owner brought him halfway, and the additional cost for the second half of the journey is only marginally higher, the owner is not required to absorb that difference. The renter was brought halfway, he can complete the journey, and the modest extra expense is absorbed as part of the *ones* that neither party caused. Tosafot acknowledges that this interpretation is an imposition on the plain text, but notes that the alternative — demanding nothing from the renter and giving the owner nothing — seems equally untenable when nobody is at fault. The question of who bears the burden of unforeseeable misfortune is at the heart of this case.

### Mid-Route Sales

Tosafot offers an alternative reading as well: the case may involve a renter who is a merchant transporting wares for sale, and the midpoint market — South Carolina, as it were — turns out to be a perfectly viable market for selling those wares. Since the renter can sell his goods where he is and has not in fact suffered a commercially meaningful loss, the owner can say: I brought you to a place where you can do your business, and the claim that you required a specific destination is overstated. On this reading, the *teroumes* — the complaint — is real, but the harm is genuinely limited.

---

## Specified Donkey

### Stam vs. Zeh

The Gemara now introduces a critical distinction that is not explicit in the *mishnah* but proves essential to understanding it: the difference between *chamor stam* — renting an unspecified donkey — and *chamor zeh* — renting this particular donkey. If the owner rented Michael a donkey without specification, and the animal dies mid-journey, the owner owes Michael a replacement, period. He contracted to provide a donkey for the week and must honor that commitment. If, however, he specified *chamor zeh*, the analysis becomes more nuanced.

Even in the case of *chamor zeh*, the renter retains some rights. Rashi notes that the owner may still have an obligation that flows from this donkey, in the sense that if the carcass can be sold and the proceeds used to purchase a replacement animal, that purchase represents a continuation of the original rental relationship — the new donkey stands in for the old one, and the renter is entitled to use it for the remainder of the week. The question then becomes: what if the proceeds are insufficient to buy a replacement outright? Could they at least be used to rent a donkey for the remaining time?

### Rav Principal

The Gemara introduces the debate between Rav and Shmuel in this context. Rav holds *lo mechalinan karna* — we do not consume the principal. Rav's position is that the owner's obligation, when he contracted for *chamor zeh*, is to allow the renter to use his assets, not to actually dissipate those assets. If the donkey dies and its carcass is worth enough to buy a replacement, Rav requires the owner to buy a replacement: the owner reinvests the asset, Michael uses it for the rest of the week, and at the end of the week the owner still has his donkey. The principal is preserved even while its use is extended. But if the money from the carcass is not sufficient to purchase another donkey outright, Rav says it cannot be used to rent one. Renting would mean taking the hundred-dollar carcass value, paying it out in rental fees, and having nothing left — that is consuming the principal. The owner's responsibility to the renter does not extend to an actual diminution of his assets.

Rashi makes this explicit: when the *mishnah* says the owner must replace the animal, this refers to a case where the donkey dies while still at the owner's premises, and the owner digs into his own pocket, adds his own money to the carcass proceeds, and buys a new donkey. This is not cutting into the principal because at the end of the week the owner has a donkey worth its full value. He has lost nothing of his capital base. What he cannot be required to do is take the carcass proceeds and have them evaporate in rental fees, leaving him with nothing.

### Shmuel Rental

Shmuel disagrees: *mechalinan karna*. According to Shmuel, when a renter has a contractual right to the use of an animal for the week, that right is enforceable even at some cost to the owner's principal. If the proceeds of the dead donkey are sufficient to rent a replacement for the remaining days of the rental, that rental is required — even though the money is "consumed" rather than reinvested in a lasting asset. The renter's right to usage for the contracted period is robust enough to justify this. The debate between Rav and Shmuel is therefore not merely about this one case, but about a fundamental question: to what extent does a bailor-type relationship obligate the owner to actively protect the beneficiary's usage rights even at the expense of his own capital?

---

## Tree Seizure

### Yavesh Ilan

The Gemara now draws an analogy to a case involving a *mashkona* — a form of loan collateral — to test the Rav-Shmuel debate in a parallel context. The structure of the *mashkona* arrangement is that Gloria, the creditor, takes possession of a tree on the debtor's property and receives all the fruit — all the profits — from that tree for the duration of the loan, as a mechanism that addresses (in whatever way was addressed in the earlier *perek*) the *ribbis* concern. She owns the tree's yield; he still owns the tree itself. This is structurally identical to the donkey rental: he owns the donkey, Michael has the right to use it for the week. Now, during the loan period, *yavesh ilan v'niktzatz* — the tree dries up and is cut down. Gloria has lost her source of income for the year. What happens?

### Land Purchase

The most obvious resolution would be to sell the wood and give Gloria the proceeds. But *shneichem assurim bo* — neither party can unilaterally do this. The owner cannot sell the wood and hand over the proceeds because Gloria might argue that continued fruit production would have yielded more. Gloria cannot sell the wood against the owner's will because that would terminate his asset. Instead, the Gemara instructs: *yilkach bo karka* — sell the wood and use the proceeds to purchase a plot of land, from which Gloria then eats the fruit, *v'hu ochel peiros*. This preserves the structure of the arrangement: the owner's principal takes a new form (land instead of tree), and Gloria continues to benefit from it. This appears to support Rav's position that we do not consume the principal — we find a way to reinvest it.

### Yovel Impact

The Gemara complicates this picture. If we assume *yovel* — the Jubilee — is in effect, then when the purchased land reaches its *yovel*, it reverts to its original owner, Jenna. The money paid for it is gone, and the owner has lost his investment. So buying land and having it revert at *yovel* does cut into the principal after all. If the *baraita* is nonetheless prepared to mandate this arrangement, it appears that we *are* prepared to consume the principal in service of Gloria's rights — which would support Shmuel.

### Sixty-Year Sale

But the Gemara resolves this: *hacha b'mai askinan d'zavneh l'shishim shani* — the case involves a stipulated sixty-year purchase, which avoids the *yovel* reversion. The basis for this is the ruling of Rav Chisda citing Rav Katina: *minayin l'mocher sadeh l'shishim shana she'eina chozeres b'yovel* — how do we know that land sold for sixty years does not revert at *yovel*? From the verse *ve'ha'aretz lo timacher l'tzmitut* — the land shall not be sold into perpetuity. The *yovel* corrects sales into perpetuity, but a sixty-year sale was never a sale in perpetuity, so the *yovel* mechanism does not apply. The sixty-year purchase therefore preserves the principal — the owner retains a durable asset — and the *baraita* is consistent with Rav's principle of *lo mechalinan karna*.

The Gemara raises the objection that even after sixty years the land reverts to Jenna, so eventually the investment is lost. The Gemara's final resolution is *b'zman she'ein yovel noheig* — a time when *yovel* does not apply, which was in fact the situation during the Second *Beit Hamikdash* period and certainly thereafter. The question of *yovel* turns out to have been somewhat academic. What the *baraita* ultimately demonstrates is that even in this case, the structure chosen — reinvesting proceeds in a new productive asset — reflects the principle that we protect the principal and do not simply let it dissolve into payments. The *baraita* thus aligns with Rav's position.

The Gemara also addresses why the parties cannot simply sell the wood and hand the cash to Gloria rather than going through the inconvenience of buying land. Even in a world where some degree of principal consumption might be tolerated, the arrangement that best preserves the owner's interests is preferred. Buying land, even land that will eventually revert, preserves the possibility that the owner will pay off the loan and recover the land before *yovel*, or that he will derive the land's value himself for the remaining years. Selling the wood outright and handing the cash to Gloria leaves the owner with nothing whatsoever. So even within a framework that is prepared to countenance some erosion of principal, we choose the option that minimizes it.

---

## Boat Sinking

### Boat Payment

The Gemara now transitions from donkeys to boats, presenting a structurally parallel set of cases. The *mishnah*-type scenario is: *hasocher et hasefina vetava lah bachatzi haderech* — one rents a boat and it sinks halfway to the destination. The renter's cargo is lost. The owner's boat is gone. And now the question is: what does the renter owe the owner for the portion of the journey that was completed?

This case differs from the donkey rental in one notable respect. Renting a donkey for the week is a time-based rental; renting a boat for a journey is a task-based engagement — the payment is for completing a delivery, not for a period of usage. This makes the question of partial payment more acute.

### Rav Nosson

Rav Nosson states a principle: *natan lo yitol, ve'im lo natan lo yiten* — if the renter already paid, he cannot recover the payment; if he has not yet paid, he need not pay. This appears to be an application of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraaya*: whoever holds the money has the presumptive claim, and neither party can compel the other to move.

### Specificity Rules

The Gemara immediately asks: *heichi dami* — under what circumstances does this ruling apply? If the boat owner said *sefinah zo* — this boat — and the cargo owner said *yayin stam* — wine generally — then the boat owner is the one who cannot fulfill his end of the agreement, since the specific boat is gone. The cargo owner could in theory provide more wine; he is not bound to *this* wine. The cargo owner could therefore demand: give me another boat and I will supply the wine, and I refuse to pay you since you cannot live up to your terms. Similarly, if it is reversed — the cargo owner specified *yayin zeh*, this wine, while the boat owner said *sefinah stam* — then the cargo owner is the party who cannot fulfill his obligations. The boat owner is in principle able to find another boat. The cargo owner, having specified *this* wine, cannot produce it from the ocean floor. In that case, the cargo owner owes the boat owner, since it is the cargo owner's inability to perform that excuses the remainder of the journey.

### Both Specified

Rav Pappa resolves the most interesting scenarios. If both parties specified — *sefinah zo veyayin zeh* — then each can point to the other's impossibility of performance. Neither can compel the other, and neither can recover from the other. This is a clean application of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraaya*: the money stays where it is, whether paid or unpaid. Each party can deflect the other's claim by pointing to the other's inability to perform.

The case of both *stam* — neither party specified — is equally interesting. In that case, both parties are theoretically capable of continuing: the boat owner can find another boat, the cargo owner can supply more wine. But in practice, neither is likely to want to. Since in principle the agreement could be honored by both sides, the situation resolves to a split: the renter pays for the portion of the journey completed. If the boat owner demands full payment, the cargo owner can say: fine, produce your boat and I will produce my wine. If the cargo owner wants to avoid paying anything, the boat owner can make the same rejoinder. Since neither genuinely wants to reconstitute the arrangement, they split — the cargo owner pays for what was delivered, no more and no less.

---

## Voluntary Abandon

### Mid-Point Unload

A related case: *hasocher et hasefinah uparkah bachatzi haderech* — the renter unloads his cargo midway through the journey voluntarily, without any compelling reason. Again, *noten lo secharo shel chatzi haderech, ve'ein lo alav ela teroumes* — the renter pays for half, and the boat owner's grievance is limited to a complaint.

### Other Customers

Once again the Gemara asks: *heichi dami*? If the boat owner can easily find other customers in the intermediate port, why does he even have a complaint? He simply loads new cargo and continues to Florida. And if he cannot find other customers, should the renter not owe him the full fee for depriving him of the entire journey's earnings?

The Gemara resolves this: the ruling applies where the boat owner can find other customers — and that is precisely why the renter pays only half. The complaint is not about lost income from the remaining journey.

### Shinui Da'at

So what is the complaint? The Gemara offers two answers. First, *mishum rifsata d'sefinata* — wear and tear on the boat. Unloading and reloading causes physical depreciation; switching customers mid-route imposes costs that a continuous journey would not. The Gemara then circles back: if that is so, shouldn't the renter owe actual compensation for the depreciation, not merely suffer a *teroumes*? The Gemara therefore refines the scenario: *parka l'te'unei d'gavei* — the cargo was unloaded in a manner that caused no actual wear and tear. With that ruled out, the complaint is *mishum shinui da'ata* — the disruption of the boat owner's expectations regarding his customer. He contracted with the renter, knew the renter's temperament and requirements, and now must deal with an unknown customer for the second half of the journey — a source of genuine uncertainty and displeasure. Alternatively, *l'ashlei yeteira* — he may need to purchase additional rigging or ropes for a new cargo load, rather than drawing from his home supply, adding an unanticipated expense. Either of these grounds the complaint without rising to the level of enforceable monetary liability.

---

## Cargo Rights

### Food Portions

The Gemara presents a new *baraita* governing what a renter may load onto a donkey hired for riding. *Sokher maniach aleha ksuto v'lignuto u'mezonot shel oto haderech* — the renter may place on the donkey his garment, his water bottle, and provisions for the entire journey. Beyond this, the donkey's owner (*hammar*) can object to any additional loading, since the rental was for riding, not for carrying. The *hammar*, for his part, may load *se'orim v'teven u'mezonotav shel oto hayom* — barley, straw, and one day's worth of food for the donkey. The renter can object to the *hammar* loading more than a day's worth of provisions, since excess weight slows the animal.

The Gemara notes the asymmetry: the renter gets the whole journey's worth of provisions; the *hammar* gets only one day's.

### Employment Status

The Gemara resolves this with a question of circumstances: if food is readily available at each stop along the route, then the *hammar* should be able to resupply at each stop and would have no reason to load a journey's worth. And if food is not readily available at all, why can the renter load the whole journey's worth while the *hammar* cannot? Rav Pappa answers: *lo tzricha d'shchiach l'mitrach u'lmizban me'avna l'avna* — the case is where food can be purchased at stops, but only with effort and hustling. The norm of behavior differs for these two parties. The *hammar* is a worker — *darkei l'mitrach u'lmizban*, it is his way to work hard and hustle. He is expected to manage the logistics. The renter, as the employing party, is not expected to run around acquiring food at every stop. The differential in what each may carry reflects their differential status in the arrangement.

---

## Gender/Pregnancy

### Gender Clause

The *baraita* continues: if one rents a donkey and specifies that *ish* — a man — will ride it, a woman may not ride. The Gemara does not elaborate on the precise reason for this, but it is presumably related either to riding posture or to some differential in how the animal responds, as Rashi and Tosafot do not address the underlying rationale here.

### Female Conditions

Conversely, if the rental specifies that a woman will ride, then the donkey is available for any woman — *bein gedolah bein ketanah*, whether adult or minor, *afilu meuberes va'afilu menika* — even if she is pregnant or nursing. Pregnancy and nursing might be thought to add weight beyond what was contemplated, but the ruling treats all women as within the class contracted for.

### Akarsa Tikla

The Gemara asks: if a nursing woman — who carries a separate infant — is within the permitted class, surely a pregnant woman, whose additional weight is entirely internal to her body, is obvious. Why enumerate pregnant women at all? The Gemara responds: *meuberes vehi menika* — the ruling encompasses even a woman who is simultaneously pregnant and nursing, a condition of compounded weight. Abaye notes a further implication: *shema mina akarsa tikla* — we learn from this that weight is concentrated in the stomach (*tikla* referring to the balance point). The practical application, as Rashi explains, is for commerce: when purchasing fish, one should insist that the fish be gutted before weighing, since the stomach contents add disproportionate weight and can distort the transaction.

### Tosafot Weight

Tosafot reads the Gemara differently and arrives at the opposite conclusion. Tosafot suggests that the Gemara's underlying premise is that a woman carrying a nursing infant actually weighs *less* than a pregnant woman, because the infant bears some of its own weight — the mother supports the child partially, but the child also rests independently. On this reading, *akarsa tikla* means that it is specifically the pregnant woman's belly-weight that is the decisive factor: since a pregnant woman's additional mass is entirely carried by her stomach and cannot be partially self-supported as an infant can, the pregnant woman may weigh more than the same woman nursing her child. This represents an inversion of the plain reading of the Gemara, as the *maggid shiur* acknowledges, and the physiological claim is itself debatable.
