What is clear is that Tosafot is engaged with a different causal logic than Abaye, understanding the comparison between pregnant and nursing riders as a weighting argument rather than a simple accumulation of persons.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 80

## Shinui - Location Change

### Mishnah Setup

The mishnah opens a discussion of cases involving the rental of an animal together with its equipment and workers, building on the previous mishnah's treatment of a renter who deviated from agreed-upon terms. The new case: *hasocher es haparah lachrosh bahar vecharesh babikah* — one who rents a cow to plow on the mountain but instead plows in the valley.

### Kankan & Workers

Rashi explains that the *kankan* is a peg fastened at the back of the plow that creates the furrow. The system involved two workers provided by the owner of the cow along with the animal and equipment as a package arrangement: one worker leads the animal from the front while the other holds the *kankan* firmly from behind, the forward pull of the cow creating the furrow under pressure from the rear. Both workers are rented out by the owner of the cow as part of a single bundled deal with the renter.

### Easier Place - Exempt

If the renter was supposed to plow on the mountain but instead plowed in the valley, and the *kankan* broke — *im nishbar hakankan patur* — the renter is exempt, because plowing in the valley is presumed to be easier than what was contracted for. By making the job easier than agreed, the renter does not bear liability for the breakage.

### Harder Place - Liable

The converse case follows directly: *ubivikah vecharesh bahar* — if the arrangement was to plow in the valley but the renter took the cow to the mountain instead, which is stonier and more hazardous to equipment, then *im nishbar hakankan chayav* — if the *kankan* breaks, the renter is liable. The deviation to a harder location creates the liability.

### Threshing Cases

The mishnah then addresses threshing cases. *Ladush bekitnis vedash betvuah* — if one hired the cow to thresh legumes but instead used it to thresh grain, the renter is *patur*, presumably because grain is easier to crush. The more interesting case runs in the opposite direction: *ladush betvuah vedash bekitnis*, hired to thresh grain but did it on legumes instead — *chayav*, liable, *mishum dekitnis mechalkes*, because legumes are slippery. The issue here is not hardness but slipperiness: legumes are slicker underfoot for the animal, and if the cow slipped, the renter bears liability for having deviated to a more hazardous condition than was agreed.

## Shared Negligence

### Who Pays?

The Gemara now poses the following question: *heich dulo shani baman meshalem* — where the renter did nothing different from the agreed terms and the *kankan* nevertheless broke, who pays? The renter himself has done nothing wrong; he took the animal and workers as arranged and plowed where he was supposed to. The question, then, is between the owner of the cow and his two workers. The owner contends that his workers were irresponsible: one drove the animal and the other held the peg, and the breaking must have resulted from their shared inattentiveness. Rashi's explanation is that the driver must have allowed the animal to veer slightly off course, and had the worker at the back been paying careful attention, he could have adjusted the *kankan* in time to prevent the break. Each one's carelessness may have contributed.

This raises a genuine difficulty: it is not unlike the problem of co-pilots working at cross-purposes, each partly responsible for a single outcome. The assumption in the Gemara is that there was some degree of shared negligence — not an *ones*, an unavoidable accident — and the question is who among the workers bears primary responsibility. The further question, left largely unexplored by the Gemara, is whether the workers are liable as *mazik* — as tortfeasors — or as *shomrim* — as guardians. The framing of the discussion suggests liability as *mazik*.

### Rav Papa

*Amar Rav Papa, deman deparsha meshalem* — Rav Papa holds that the one in front, the driver who leads the animal, pays. In Rashi's reading, this is the worker who initiated the problem by allowing the animal to drift off its straight course. The deviation at the front is what started the chain of events leading to the break.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi disagrees: *denakit mana meshalem* — the one who holds the peg at the back pays. His reasoning is that the break occurred at the *kankan* itself, and the worker holding it was in the most immediate position to have prevented the damage. Whatever the driver did wrong, the rear worker had the last opportunity to adjust and failed to do so.

### Halacha Decision

*Ve-hilchata denakit mana meshalem* — the halacha follows Rav Sheshet: the one holding the peg pays. The Gemara does not spell out the full rationale, but the most compelling way to understand it is in terms of proximate negligence. Both workers may have been negligent to some degree, but the most proximate cause of the actual breakage — the one who was in position to have stopped it at the critical moment and did not — is the worker at the back. Even if the driver's deviation was what set things in motion, the rear worker's failure to respond was the most immediate and direct cause of the loss. This is distinct from *grama* — indirect causation — because these workers are actively handling the owner's property; rather, it is a question of which negligence most directly produced the damage.

### Tosafot Challenge

Tosafot raises a sharp question: *ve-tzarich le-iyun amai lo meshalem* — why, in the case where the renter did make a change — say, he took the cow to the mountain instead of the valley, which is a harder and rockier location — don't we still ask one of the workers to pay? After all, the Gemara has just established that the most proximately negligent party pays. Even if the renter violated the terms of the contract by changing the location, the workers are the ones physically handling the equipment. Being more careful — watching for rocks, adjusting pressure — could theoretically have prevented the break even in the harder location. With three potentially negligent parties — the renter who made the *shinui*, the driver who may have veered, and the rear worker who failed to adjust — why does the Gemara focus exclusively on the renter and not ask whether one of the workers should bear liability?

### Tosafot Resolution

Tosafot resolves this with a principle that is both precise and striking. *De-mara de-na masar et ha-parah hu ve-ha-socher et ha-poalim* — the owner of the cow rented out the workers to go with the cow and perform the renter's work. When the workers agreed to be hired out, they understood the agreed-upon terms: *anan lo hitninu imcha ela lachrosh ba-bik'ah* — we contracted only to plow in the valley. *Ve-lo kibalnu shmirat hakankan ba-har ela ba-bik'ah* — our acceptance of responsibility for the *kankan* extended only to the level of care appropriate for valley conditions, not mountain conditions. The workers can therefore say to the owner: our obligation to you was calibrated to the original contract, and we did not accept liability for the degree of care required in harder terrain.

At the same time — and here Tosafot adds something striking — *u-micol makom schirut shelanu lo nifsad*: the workers can still demand their wages. Their reasoning is that when the renter deviated from the agreement, they listened to him and performed the work as he instructed. They fulfilled their role by following instructions and are therefore entitled to be paid for the labor they performed. There is thus an interesting split: the workers are paid for following the renter's instructions, but their liability to the owner is governed by the original terms of the contract, not by the modified ones.

### Rocky Place Case

The Gemara then presents a further case: *v'dukhta d'machzaka gundrei* — a place known to be rocky and full of stones. If both workers went in knowing that the terrain was particularly treacherous, then *tarvay mshalmin* — they both pay. This is surprising. In the earlier case, only the rear worker paid on the grounds of proximate negligence. Why, in the rocky-place case, do both workers pay, if the rear worker is still the most proximate?

### Mutual Watchfulness

Tosafot addresses this directly. Rashi suggests that in the rocky-place case there is doubt (*safek*) about who caused the damage, since in such terrain the driver may bear equal or greater responsibility. But Tosafot rejects this reasoning, pointing out that we do not rule like Sumchus — who would divide liability under conditions of doubt — but like the Rabbanan, who follow the principle of *hamotzi mechaveiro alav hara'aya*: the burden of proof is on the claimant. If it were merely a doubt, neither worker should pay, since neither can be proven negligent.

Instead, Tosafot argues: *ella nirei le-tosafot d'trvayhu pash'u* — they are both actually negligent. In a place known to be rocky, it is highly likely that the equipment will break easily: *kivun d'machzaka b'gundrei hu nishbar me'od b'kal*. Both workers go in knowing they must exercise extraordinary care. And crucially, *ve-haya l'chol echad litten lev al chaveiro kemo al atzmo u'lehazhiro* — each worker was obligated not only to be maximally careful in his own role but also to watch over his fellow worker and warn him if he saw something going wrong. When the terrain is genuinely dangerous, individual attentiveness is not enough; the situation demands mutual watchfulness. Because the driver failed to watch out for the rear worker as he was obligated to do, he too is negligent — not only for his own actions but for his partner's, having failed to intervene when he should have. The result is shared liability. The principle is powerful: in conditions dangerous enough that collective vigilance is required, a person's negligence extends beyond his own actions to his failure to protect against his co-worker's.

## Defect Disclosure

### Rabbi Yochanan

The Gemara introduces a case from Rabbi Yochanan that at first appears somewhat disconnected from the preceding discussion. *Hamocher para l'chaveiro v'amar lo* — someone sells a cow to his fellow and says: *para zo natchanit hi, nashchanit hi, ba'atnit hi, rabetzanit hi* — this cow is a gorer, a biter, a kicker, and a croucher. He lists four distinct problems. In reality, *vehaya bah mum echad*, only one of those defects was actually present, and *v'sinfo bein hamumim* — he appended the real problem to this list of fictitious ones, concealing it among them.

The seller's intent, as Rashi explains, is to protect himself from future complaints: if he lists every possible problem and the buyer can't see any of them, the buyer assumes the whole list is boilerplate — hollow language designed to foreclose complaints rather than genuine disclosure. The seller is counting on the buyer not taking any of it seriously, while in fact the one real defect is quietly listed among the fabricated ones.

### Mekach Taut

*Harei zeh mekach taut* — this is a mistaken transaction. The halacha is that such a sale constitutes *mekach taut* because the buyer cannot be said to have been genuinely forewarned. The only thing that would prevent *mekach taut* in the case of a serious defect is a real pre-warning that the buyer took seriously and could act upon. A boilerplate list of implausible defects does not constitute such a warning. The buyer looks at the cow, sees no obvious problem, assumes the seller is simply covering himself with standard language, and concludes that the cow is essentially sound. When it turns out the cow has one serious defect that was buried in the list, the buyer can rightly say: you did not warn me in any meaningful sense.

The analogy is instructive. When a seller lists ten problems and the cow visibly has none of them, it is as though the seller said "as is" in the most general and unspecified way imaginable. A general disclaimer of that kind does not put a buyer on notice about a specific, serious defect. The comparison to pharmaceutical advertisements — where a long recitation of side effects may not actually register as meaningful warnings — captures precisely why such a list fails to constitute genuine disclosure.

### Single Defect

The Gemara then draws the critical distinction: *mum zeh umum acher ein zeh mekach taut* — if the seller specifically singled out one defect and mentioned only that one (or that one plus a vague reference to other possible issues), it is not *mekach taut*. When one particular problem is identified clearly and individually, the buyer is put on genuine notice. He should have taken that warning seriously, investigated the specific defect, and made an informed decision. Because he was specifically alerted to the problem, the failure to investigate is on him.

Tosafot adds a further dimension: part of why the boilerplate list fails as pre-warning is that a buyer who checked even one of the listed defects and found it absent could reasonably have concluded that the entire list was fictional. That inference — reasonable in context — is what the seller exploits when he hides the real defect among fake ones. By contrast, when the seller singles out one specific defect, the buyer has no such basis for dismissal and cannot claim he was not genuinely warned.

### Slave Woman

A *baraita* confirms that the same principles apply in the case of selling a female slave. *Tanu rabanan hamocher shifcha lechavero v'amar lo: shifcha zo shota hi, nichpit hi, meshu'amemet hi* — the seller says she is mentally unstable, epileptic, and lethargic or vacant (Rashi and Tosafot offer somewhat different readings of *meshu'amemet*). Again, *vehaya bah mum echad v'snafo bein hamumim* — only one defect was real and it was buried in the list. *Harei zeh mekach taut.* And again: if the seller singled out one specific defect and mentioned others only in passing, *ein zeh mekach taut*, because the buyer was on adequate notice.

### All Defects

Rav Acha son of Rava poses a sharp question to Rav Ashi: *hayu vo kol hamumim halalu mahu* — what if the cow actually had all of those defects? The question is real: perhaps even then the buyer doesn't take the list seriously, because who would believe a single animal could have every one of those problems? Surely the list still looks like boilerplate.

### Verification

Rav Mordechai reports in the name of Rava: *hayu vo kol hamumim halalu ein zeh mekach taut* — even in that case, it is not *mekach taut*. The reasoning Tosafot offers is that if every one of the listed defects was genuine, then the buyer could have checked any one of them and verified it firsthand. Having had the opportunity to confirm at least one item on the list, the buyer cannot claim ignorance. The failure to verify is his own. The framework, then, is essentially one of verification: a specific, checkable warning that the buyer chose to ignore does not support a claim of *mekach taut*, even when a long list is involved — provided the defects were real and verifiable.

## Cargo Overage

### Wheat/Barley

The next mishnah introduces a new set of cases involving deviation from agreed cargo specifications. *Hasocher et hachamor lehavi aleha chitin vehevi aleha seorim* — one who rents a donkey to carry wheat but instead loads it with barley. Barley is lighter than wheat by volume, so if the same weight of barley is loaded, it occupies more space. *Chayav* — the renter is liable. Similarly, *tevuah vehevi aleha teven* — if one said grain but brought straw, which is lighter still — *chayav*. The mishnah states the reason explicitly: *mipnei shehanefach kashe kimasoi* — because increased volume is as problematic as increased weight. The same analysis applies in the reverse direction: if one agreed to bring a volume of barley but substituted grain of the same volume, the weight would be greater and the liability equally clear. The fundamental point is that there are two distinct ways to violate the terms of a cargo agreement — by exceeding the agreed weight, or by exceeding the implied volume — and both create liability.

### Volume = Weight

The principle *shehanefach kashe kimasoi* requires clarification. The question is not merely that volume can be a problem, but whether it is treated as a perfectly equivalent measure to weight or whether it operates differently. The next portion of the mishnah sets up the measurement framework. *Lehavi letach chitim* — if the agreement was to carry a *letach* of wheat, which is fifteen *se'ah*, equivalent to ninety *kav* — and the renter brought instead a *letach* of barley, the renter is *patur*, exempt. Same volume, less weight — no violation. But *ve-im hosif al masao chayav* — if he added weight, he is liable.

To situate the units: a *se'ah* is approximately one and a half liters. A *kav* is one-sixth of a *se'ah*. A *letach* is fifteen *se'ah*, or ninety *kav*. A *kor* is two *letach*, or thirty *se'ah*.

### One-Thirtieth Rule

The mishnah then addresses how much overage is required to trigger liability: *v'chama yosif al masao v'yiyeh chayav* — how much must one add before becoming liable? Sumchus, citing Rabbi Meir, gives the standard: one *se'ah* for a camel, three *kav* for a donkey. Since the *letach* case involves a donkey carrying ninety *kav*, the permissible overage is three *kav* — precisely one-thirtieth of the agreed load. The Gemara generalizes: whatever the acceptable overage for a given carrier, that overage represents one-thirtieth of the normal tolerable load for that carrier. If the overage for a camel is one *se'ah* — six *kav* — then a camel's standard load is one hundred and eighty *kav*. The one-thirtieth rule is thus the universal standard across carriers.

### Abaye vs. Rava

The Gemara records a dispute between Abaye and Rava on the precise application of the volume-weight equivalence. *Abaye amar kasha k'masao tnan* — Abaye reads the mishnah's principle as establishing a full equivalence: increased volume is measured exactly as increased weight. Volume is treated as just as real a burden as weight, and the same one-thirtieth overage rule applies regardless of whether the excess is measured in weight or volume. *V'Rava amar kasha l'masao tnan* — Rava reads the mishnah differently: it says only that increased volume makes the burden more difficult, not that volume is measured the same way as weight.

The practical difference is significant. For Rava, as long as the total weight of the cargo is below the agreed limit, there is no liability even if the volume exceeds what the agreement implied. The volume problem only becomes actionable once the weight has reached the agreed threshold — at which point the increased volume on top of the equivalent weight constitutes a violation. For Abaye, volume is independently measured: even if the weight is less than the agreed amount, exceeding the volume by one-thirtieth creates liability, because volume is treated as its own form of burden equivalent to weight.

### When Volume Violates

The Gemara tests both positions against the mishnah. The mishnah says: brought a *letach* of wheat but brought a *letach* of barley — *patur*; if he added to the load — *chayav*. The immediate reading is that once you have the same number of bags, the standard three-*kav* overage rule applies. This sounds like Abaye: volume is treated the same as weight, and the ordinary one-thirtieth rule governs. But the Gemara says: *lo, se'ah* — no, three *kav* would not suffice; you would need a full *se'ah* of overage. The implication is that only when the additional volume brings the weight up to the equivalent of the original wheat load — which happens at the six-*kav* mark in the barley-wheat case — does the violation occur. That sounds like Rava.

The Gemara further tests the matter with the case: *lehavi letach chitim veheivi sheish esreih se'orim* — one agreed to bring a *letach* of wheat (fifteen *se'ah*) and instead brought sixteen *se'ah* of barley. He is liable. But this is a one-fifteenth increment, not a one-thirtieth increment as the standard rule would require. This leniency — requiring a larger overage before triggering liability — suggests that when the cargo is lighter, the renter is given more latitude, consistent with Rava's position that volume alone, short of reaching the weight threshold, does not immediately create a violation. *Ha shelosha kavin patur* — had the overage been only three *kav*, he would be exempt.

### Lighter Goods

Abaye responds to this challenge with the word *bimechiktsa*. There is a dispute among commentators about what this means: some read it as referring to an exceptionally light variety of barley, in which case Abaye is allowing that when the goods are particularly light he does not apply the full volume-equals-weight equivalence. Others read *bimechiktsa* as a measurement term relating to how precisely the load was measured — a generous measure versus a flush, level measure — which would account for the apparent discrepancy in the overage numbers without conceding the principle. The Gemara's *perush* of Rashi on this word is noted as particularly interesting, though the full analysis is not pursued. The bottom line of the dispute is clear: Abaye treats volume as fully equivalent to weight for purposes of measuring acceptable overage, while Rava holds that volume is only actionable once the weight threshold has been reached.

## Overage by Carrier

### Standards

A *baraita* — *tanu rabbanan* — sets out the acceptable overage standards across different types of carriers. One *kav* for a human porter (*katef*), three *kav* for a donkey, one *se'ah* for a camel, one *letach* overage for a small raft or boat (*adriv* — which Rashi explains is another term for *letach*), one *kor* for a medium-sized boat (*sfinah*), and three *korim* for a large ship (*vurni gedola*). In each case, the acceptable overage represents one-thirtieth of the normal carrying capacity for that carrier. Thus: a human porter's standard load is thirty *kav*, a donkey's is ninety *kav*, a camel's is one hundred and eighty *kav*, a standard boat's capacity is thirty *kor*.

Rav Pappa draws a practical conclusion from this: *amar Rav Pappa shma mina stam sfina bat tlatin korin* — we may infer that the standard carrying capacity of a boat is thirty *kor*. The relevance, as the Gemara explains, is for commercial transactions: if one purchases a boat, the presumed default storage capacity is thirty *kor*, and a deviation from this could give rise to a complaint.

### Porter's Choice

The Gemara raises a sharp question regarding the human porter specifically. When the employer places extra weight on the porter's back — beyond the agreed amount — why can't the porter simply refuse or remove it? Unlike a donkey, a person is an intelligent agent. If he allowed the overage to be placed on him and then suffered injury, one might argue he implicitly accepted the extra load. *Bar da'atu hu, u-shadiye* — he is a rational being; he could have thrown it off. How can he now complain that the overloading caused him harm?

### Abaye

Abaye responds: *beshachavtu l'alter* — if the porter collapsed immediately upon the load being placed on him, there was no opportunity to perceive and reject the overage. The injury was instantaneous, which demonstrates that the load was objectively beyond what he could tolerate and that there was no moment of implicit acceptance.

### Rava

Rava extends the analysis further: *afilu teima v'shelo chavtu l'alter* — even if the injury did not occur immediately, the argument is not that the porter loses his claim entirely. Rather: *lo tzricha ela l'agra yeseira* — what is established by the implicit acceptance of the extra load is not that the employer is absolved of responsibility for harm, but that the porter is owed extra pay. Just as the porter implicitly agreed to carry the excess, the employer implicitly agreed to pay for it. The two implicit agreements mirror each other.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi offers a third position: *hu savar kusha hu denakit leh* — the porter felt that the load was heavy but did not know that the heaviness was because the employer had exceeded the agreed amount. He assumed he was simply not feeling his strongest that day. Because he did not realize the weight was beyond what he had contracted for, he never actually accepted the overage, and there was no implicit agreement. The employer is fully responsible. This raises the interesting empirical question of whether a one-thirtieth increment in weight is actually perceptible to the person bearing it — and the Gemara leaves this as a genuine ambiguity.

### Boats

The one-thirtieth rule for boats is confirmed by Rav Pappa's inference: since one *kor* of overage is the acceptable maximum for a standard boat, and the overage represents one-thirtieth of capacity, a standard boat holds thirty *kor*. This has practical commercial relevance for determining what a buyer of a boat can expect as the default carrying capacity.

## Craftsmen Status

### Mishnah

The mishnah opens with the ruling: *kol umanin shomer sachar hen* — all craftsmen are categorized as *shomer sachar*, a paid bailee. If one gives a craftsman wood to build a box, and while the wood is in the craftsman's possession it is stolen or lost through circumstances that would exempt a *shomer chinam* but not a *shomer sachar*, the craftsman is liable. The question the Gemara will probe is: why? The craftsman is receiving money, but that money is payment for his labor — an equal exchange. What is the additional benefit — the *sachar* — that elevates him to the status of *shomer sachar* rather than *shomer chinam*?

The mishnah adds several related cases. *Vekulan she'amru tol et shelcha vehavei maot shomer chinam* — but if the craftsman tells the owner that the work is done, come take it and bring payment, then the craftsman becomes a *shomer chinam*. However, the Gemara will clarify: if the craftsman says instead "pay me first and then come take it," he is still holding the item in his capacity as an *uman* and retains the status of *shomer sachar*. Only once he has fully relinquished his leverage — by telling the owner to take the item before payment — does he drop to *shomer chinam*.

*Shemor li ve'eshmor lecha shomer sachar* — if two people agree to watch each other's belongings in turn, each is a *shomer sachar* for the other's property during his watch. Though one might characterize this as mutual favors making each a *shomer chinam*, the exchange of watchfulness is treated as a form of payment: each person is compensating the other with *shmirah*, and the reciprocal arrangement creates the status of *shomer sachar* for both.

*Shemor li ve'amar lo hanach lefanai shomer chinam* — if one asks another to watch something and the other says only "put it down," without explicitly accepting the role of watchman, the latter is a *shomer chinam*. The *chiddush* is that even a response as passive as "put it down" creates some degree of *shmirah* obligation, though only at the level of *shomer chinam*.

*Hamalveh al hamashkon shomer sachar* — one who lends money and holds collateral is a *shomer sachar* on the collateral. The nature of the *sachar* here will become a question. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees on similar cases: *hamalveh maot shomer chinam* — a lender of money who holds collateral is a *shomer chinam*, not *shomer sachar*. But *hamalveh peirot shomer sachar* — a lender of fruit is a *shomer sachar*. The reasoning is that when one lends fresh fruit, the borrower actually does the lender a favor by taking it before it spoils; the lender benefits from the transaction in a way that goes beyond the equal exchange, and this incidental benefit constitutes the *sachar* that elevates the obligation.

Abba Shaul adds a related ruling: *rashai adam lehaskir mashkono shel ani* — one who holds collateral from a poor borrower who is unlikely ever to repay the loan may rent out the collateral and apply the proceeds against the loan debt, effectively repaying the borrower's obligation on his behalf, since this is *kemo meshiv aveidah* — like returning a lost object. This grants the lender significant latitude to use another's property, framed as an act of benefit to the debtor.

### Initial Inquiry

The Gemara asks: *leima matnitin dela kerabbi Meir* — does the mishnah's ruling that craftsmen are *shomer sachar* necessarily represent a position in tension with Rabbi Meir? The underlying question is whether the category of *shomer sachar* requires a benefit beyond the equal exchange of money for labor.

### Baraita Dispute

A *baraita* records the dispute directly in the context of a renter (*socher*): *socher keitzad meshalem, Rabbi Meir omer keshomer chinam, Rabbi Yehuda omer keshomer sachar*. Rabbi Meir holds that a renter is a *shomer chinam* on the rented object; Rabbi Yehuda holds he is a *shomer sachar*. The Gemara assumes that a craftsman and a renter are analogous in the relevant respects — money changes hands in exchange for use or labor — and therefore asks whether the mishnah's ruling that craftsmen are *shomer sachar* aligns with Rabbi Yehuda but not Rabbi Meir.

### Employment Benefit

The Gemara proposes that even according to Rabbi Meir, a craftsman might be *shomer sachar* through a distinct benefit not present in a simple rental. *Behahi hana'ah dekashebik kulei alma ve'agar lei ledidi* — the benefit is that out of all the potential employers available, the owner chose specifically this craftsman for the job, giving him employment. The craftsman receives not merely payment for labor but the value of being selected for work in an economy where such work is not guaranteed. This employment-as-benefit is what makes him a *shomer sachar*. The Gemara then asks whether the same logic would apply to a renter: couldn't we say the owner gave the renter a similar benefit by renting to him specifically rather than to others? *Socher nami, behahi hana'ah dekashebik kulei alma umogar lei ledidi* — and therefore the renter should also be *shomer sachar*? This would eliminate the distinction between craftsman and renter and would make Rabbi Meir's position incoherent. The Gemara leaves this version of the answer in difficulty.

### Extra Money

The Gemara tries a second explanation: *behahi hana'ah deka'yahiv lei tefi purta* — the craftsman receives a little extra beyond the precise fair-market value of his labor, since in practice people do not measure compensation with perfect precision and tend to round generously. This small surplus constitutes the *sachar* that makes him *shomer sachar*. But the same objection returns: *socher nami, mi lo askinan dekamashvi lei tefi purta* — perhaps the owner also gave the renter a slight discount on the rental rate, in which case there would be the same extra benefit and the renter would equally be *shomer sachar*, collapsing the distinction. This answer also fails to survive scrutiny.

### Leverage

The Gemara settles on a third and final explanation: *behahi hana'ah detafis lei a'agra* — the craftsman's *sachar* is the benefit of holding the completed item as leverage until he receives payment. The craftsman has given his labor and is owed money. The owner has paid nothing yet. The craftsman's ability to retain the box until payment is a genuine benefit — *dela ba'ei lemizlei ulemifak azuzei*, he does not have to chase after the owner for his money — and this benefit, which exists because the craftsman has possession of the owner's property, is what makes him a *shomer sachar* on that property. This is qualitatively different from the rental case: when someone rents out a donkey, the owner retains no similar leverage over the renter, and the renter holds no comparable advantage that would benefit the owner.

### Uncertainty

Having reached this conclusion, the Gemara then notes a fundamental uncertainty: *tanya ipcha Rabba bar bar Chana* — Rabba bar bar Chana reports that the *baraita* is in fact reversed. According to his version, it is Rabbi Meir who holds that a renter is *shomer sachar* and Rabbi Yehuda who holds he is *shomer chinam* — exactly the opposite of what was stated earlier. Since there is a genuine textual dispute about which sage holds which position regarding a renter, we cannot determine with confidence whether the mishnah's ruling on craftsmen aligns with Rabbi Meir, with Rabbi Yehuda, or with neither — and the question *leima matnitin dela kerabbi Meir* is left unresolved. What does emerge clearly, however, is the Gemara's final and settled reason for the craftsman's status as *shomer sachar*: the leverage afforded by holding the owner's property against payment is a genuine, distinct benefit — one that the Gemara finds uniquely persuasive, and one that does not transfer to the rental context in any obvious way.

# Bava Metzia 81

## Borrowing Return Status

### Mishnah Contradiction

The daf opens at the bottom of 81a, picking up from the *mishnah* that establishes: *kol ha-umanim shomrei sachar hen* — any craftsman who has an object entrusted to him for work becomes a *shomer sachar*, a paid bailee. As a *shomer sachar*, he is liable for *geneivah va-aveidah*, loss and theft, though he is exempt from *onsin*, accidents and damages beyond his control.

The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: *tenan hatam* — a *mishnah* elsewhere appears to contradict this ruling. The *gemara* cites a *mishnah* from 98b dealing with borrowing, which bears directly on the liability of a *sho'el* and the status of objects while in transit.

### Mishnah 98b Citation

The *mishnah* in 98b reads: if a borrower says to the lender, "send it to me by way of my son, my slave, or my agent," or "by your son, your slave, or your agent," and the lender complies and the animal dies in transit — the borrower is *chayav*, liable. The reasoning is that once both parties agreed on the method of transmission, the object effectively entered the borrower's *reshut*, his legal domain, from the moment that agreement was made.

Likewise, the *mishnah* continues: *vechen beshaah shemachzirah* — the same principle governs the moment of return. If there was no prior agreement about how the object would be returned, then the object has not left the borrower's *reshut* until it physically reaches the lender's hands. If it is damaged in transit without such an agreement, the borrower remains liable.

This creates an apparent contradiction with our *mishnah*. In the case of the *uman*, the craftsman, we rule that once he declares the object ready for pickup and demands payment — *tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot*, take your thing and give me the money you owe me — he is immediately downgraded to a *shomer chinam*, an unpaid bailee. Yet the *mishnah* from 98b suggests that a borrower retains liability until the object physically returns to the lender's hands. The two rulings seem to pull in opposite directions.

### Rashi Explanation

Rashi, both in his commentary here and in his notes to 98b, clarifies the mechanism of the *mishnah* from 98b. The rule that the object "enters the borrower's *reshut*" upon an agreed-upon method of transmission means that the borrower has taken on full *sho'el* liability from that point forward. Conversely, when returning the animal, if no agreement was made about the return method, the borrower's *reshut* extends all the way until the object physically arrives back in the lender's hands. The point of tension with our *mishnah* is therefore real: in one case, a declaration by the craftsman terminates his elevated liability immediately; in the other, mere physical possession during transit sustains it.

### Efrayim bar Pappa

The *gemara* resolves this tension through an *okimta* attributed to Efrayim bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda: *lo shanu ela shemachzirah betoch yemei she'elatah* — the *mishnah* from 98b applies only when the borrower is returning the object *within* the agreed borrowing period. If I borrowed Michael's cow for a month and I am returning it on the fifteenth, then during that transit period the object is still in my *reshut* and I remain liable until it reaches Michael's hands.

However, if the borrowing period has already concluded — if it is the first of the following month and I am now returning the cow because I am obligated to — then we say the borrower is *patur* from the moment the return journey is underway. After the term expires, everyone understands the return is necessary, and the object is treated as already partially back in the lender's *reshut*. On this reading, there is no contradiction: the *mishnah* from 98b addresses mid-term returns, while our *mishnah* about the *uman* addresses an analogous situation where the craftsman's completion declaration marks the natural end of the relationship.

### Rav Nachman Challenge

Rav Nachman bar Pappa raises a challenge from a *baraita*: *vechullan she'amru tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot shomer chinam — hagamarti shomer sachar?* The *baraita* implies that saying *tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot* makes the craftsman a *shomer chinam*, but what if he merely said *gamarti*, "I am done with your object"? Does a simple declaration of completion also terminate his status as *shomer sachar* and reduce him to *shomer chinam*?

### Take vs. Completed

The *gemara* draws a distinction. *Tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot* — "take your thing and give me the money" — is a specific formulation that explicitly acknowledges both the completion of the work and the demand for payment. *Gamarti* — "I am finished" — is a simpler statement that leaves the ownership transfer implicit. One might have thought these function differently in law.

The *gemara* then considers a further refinement: what if the *uman* reverses the order and says *havei li ma'ot vetol shelcha* — "give me my money and then take your thing"? Here, the craftsman is explicitly withholding the object pending payment, holding it as a kind of lien. In that case, as we learned in the previous *sugya*, the *uman* retains the status of *shomer sachar*, because he is essentially holding the object on account of his right to payment.

### Formulation Logic

If *gamarti* and *tol shelcha* produce the same legal result — both reducing the craftsman to *shomer chinam* — why does the *mishnah* choose the more elaborate formulation *tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot*? The *gemara* asks: *ei hachi adtane vechullan she'amru tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot shomer chinam nashmi'inan gamarti vechol sheken tol shelcha* — if *gamarti* suffices, teach us *gamarti* and we would know all the more so that *tol shelcha* works as well. Why teach the more complex case?

### Tosefta Versions

One answer the *gemara* entertains involves the parallel *Tosefta*. The *Tosefta* in this context does not use the formulation *tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot* at all. It simply states *tol shelcha* or *gamarti*. In the *Tosefta*, the precise order of the words does not matter — the key is simply that the craftsman communicated completion in some form. The *mishnah*'s specific phrasing, then, is not necessarily presenting a more stringent or different rule; it may simply reflect the version in use in a particular tradition.

### Textual Transmission

Examining the manuscript evidence, there is reason to believe that the formulation *havei li ma'ot vetol shelcha* entered our *mishnah* by a process of textual migration. Chapter five of the *mishnah* contains the phrase *havei li ma'ot vetol shelcha* in a discussion of *ribbit*, where the order of the demand genuinely matters — there, it is the sequence of payment-first and release-second that creates the problematic structure. It appears that this precise phrasing was then absorbed into *mishnah* 6 — perhaps by accident in transmission — and was subsequently reordered in *Bavel* to read *tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot*, either because the order seemed insignificant in this context or because the reversed order was needed to generate the *gemara*'s *diyuk*.

### Explicit Formula Teaching

The *gemara* ultimately explains why the specific formulation *tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot* is necessary as the *mishnah*'s teaching point. One might have thought that in the case of the *uman* who declares both completion and a payment demand, he would not even rise to the level of *shomer chinam* — that is, he would have no *shemirah* obligations whatsoever and could not even be required to take an oath. *Tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot* teaches us that he *does* remain a *shomer chinam*, with the attendant obligations of that status, even after declaring completion. Simple *gamarti* alone does not convey this teaching.

The *ikka de'amri* version of the *sugya* traces the same path through a different entry point: Rav Nachman bar Pappa notes that the *mishnah*'s ruling — all *umanim* who say *tol shelcha vehavei ma'ot* are *shomer chinam* — might seem to imply the same for *gamarti*. The *gemara* rejects the inference: *tol shelcha shani*, "take your thing" is a distinct case, and the *mishnah* is needed to teach it specifically. The operative *halacha*, however, is that *gamarti* does indeed carry the same consequence as *tol shelcha* — both reduce the craftsman to *shomer chinam* — while *havei li ma'ot vetol shelcha*, retaining the object pending payment, keeps him as *shomer sachar*.

---

## Borrower Liability Status

### Exempt Accident Status

A new *sugya* now opens, introduced by the late *amora* Huna Mar bar Amemar, who presents the contradiction between the two *mishnayot* before Ravina and resolves it in precisely the same fashion as above — noting that this very late *amora*, who is himself the student of an *amora*, engages in the same method as the *stam* Talmud: raising a contradiction and deploying an *okimta* from an earlier *amora* to resolve it. There is a certain wry irony in this observation, insofar as it suggests that Huna Mar bar Amemar may himself be part of the *stam* in this passage.

Following this, the *gemara* raises a distinct question through *ibaya lehu*: once a borrower has been declared exempt from liability for accidents — because, say, the borrowing period has ended and the return is underway — what precisely is his status? Is he *patur misho'el* but still *chayav keshomer sachar*, remaining liable for theft and loss but not for accidents? Or is he not even a *shomer sachar*, but rather a *shomer chinam*, such that he could take an oath and be exempt even from theft and loss?

### Amemar Benefit Theory

Amemar addresses this directly: *mistabra patur misho'el vechayav keshomer sachar* — it stands to reason that the borrower loses only his *sho'el* liability for accidents, but retains the elevated status of a *shomer sachar* for theft and loss. The basis for this position is *ho'il veka neheni minei* — because the borrower still derives some benefit from the object, that ongoing *hana'ah* functions as the "payment" that classifies him as a paid bailee. The precise nature of this benefit during the return journey is admittedly puzzling — one might ask what concrete benefit accrues to someone returning a borrowed donkey — but the principle, as Amemar formulates it, is that the *hana'ah* inhering in the very act of borrowing persists even into the return phase.

### Artisan Baraita

A *baraita* is then cited in support of Amemar's position. The case involves someone who goes to an *uman*'s shop to acquire vessels as a gift for his father-in-law, with the arrangement that if the father-in-law accepts them he will pay the full price, and if not, he will pay only *lefi tovat hana'ah*, an amount reflecting the modest benefit he received from his father-in-law's goodwill toward him. The *baraita* rules: *ne'ensu behalicha chayav* — if the vessels are damaged on the way to the father-in-law's house, he is liable as a *sho'el*. But *uvichazira patur mipnei she-hu ke-nosei sachar* — if they are damaged on the return journey, he is exempt from *onsin* because he is classified as a *nosei sachar*, another term for *shomer sachar*.

### Hana'ah Return Phase

This *baraita* thus makes explicit that the return-journey status is *shomer sachar*, not *shomer chinam* — precisely as Amemar ruled from *sevara*. The *hana'ah* on the return leg, though difficult to quantify precisely, is understood as the benefit the father-in-law's increased goodwill generates, and that *hana'ah* is treated as sufficient "payment" to classify the carrier as a paid bailee. The *baraita* confirms that the borrower is neither fully liable as a *sho'el* on the return, nor fully exempt as a *shomer chinam* — he occupies an intermediate position: *patur* from *onsin* but *chayav* for *geneivah va-aveidah*.

---

## Donkey Sale Case

### Donkey Injury Setup

The *gemara* now presents a related case. A certain man was given a donkey by his friend with instructions: take it to such-and-such a place and try to sell it there; if you manage to sell it, you pay me the price; if not, bring it back and I'll take it back from you. He went, failed to sell the donkey, and on the return journey the animal was injured.

### Rav Nachman Liable

The case came before Rav Nachman, who ruled the man *chayav* — liable to pay for the injury despite the fact that it occurred on the return journey, where we might have expected reduced liability.

### Rava Challenge

Rava challenged Rav Nachman: but the *baraita* we just cited teaches *uvichazira patur mipnei she-hu ke-nosei sachar* — on the return journey, the bailee is exempt from damage as a *shomer sachar*, not liable as a *sho'el*. Why, then, does Rav Nachman rule *chayav*?

### Continuous Mission

Rav Nachman clarifies: *chazara de-hai halicha hi* — this return is not a return at all in the relevant sense; it is a continuation of the going. The reason is straightforward: *de-chazara de-hai ilu ashkach lezivunei mi la zavna* — had he encountered a buyer on his way back, would he not have sold the donkey? Of course he would. He had not mentally or legally concluded his sale mission. He remained in the posture of someone trying to sell the animal throughout the entire journey, including the return leg. Therefore, his status is that of a *sho'el* on the outbound journey — fully liable for *onsin* — and this status continues unbroken. The "return" is in a physical sense only; legally, he is still traveling outbound.

### Rental Analogy

This principle can be illuminated by analogy to modern rental arrangements. When you rent a car for thirty days and return it on the thirty-first, you are charged for the additional day — not because the rental company treats the return journey more generously, but because the liability period has simply extended. What the *gemara* is articulating here is a related but distinct idea: when the very purpose of the mission is ongoing — when the seller is still in selling mode — the legal character of his possession does not change merely because he is physically heading home.

### Period Boundaries

The broader principle emerging from this section is that the boundary between *sho'el* liability and *shomer sachar* liability is determined not simply by the direction of travel, but by the legal status of the period. If a borrowing term has expired, the return is treated as the lender's *reshut* drawing the object back, and the borrower's liability is reduced accordingly. If, by contrast, the mission is still active — as in the donkey-sale case where the seller could have concluded the sale at any moment — then the full liability of the outbound status persists throughout. The agreement between the parties, and the continuing purpose of the arrangement, define where one period ends and another begins.

---

## Guard-for-Guard Setup

### Mishnah Reciprocal

The *mishnah* states: *shmor li ve'eshmor lach shomer sachar* — "guard for me and I'll guard for you" creates the status of *shomer sachar* for each party with respect to the other's property. This ruling, however, immediately generates a difficulty.

### Owner Working Problem

The problem is the principle of *shmira biv'alim* — when the owner of an object is in the employ of the bailee at the very moment of the bailment, the bailee's status is reduced to *shomer chinam*. The logic is that the owner's labor for the bailee constitutes a kind of offset or subsidy that eliminates the "payment" element of the *shomer sachar* relationship. If the two parties are simultaneously guarding each other's property, then each is the *ba'al* of his own object while simultaneously laboring for the other party. One might therefore expect each to be no more than a *shomer chinam* — not *shomer sachar*. Why, then, does the *mishnah* call this arrangement *shomer sachar*?

The difficulty is not immediately obvious from the face of the *mishnah*, and working through it is central to understanding the cases that follow. If two people say to each other, "you guard mine, I'll guard yours," right now simultaneously, then at the very moment I am guarding your property, you — the owner of that property — are guarding mine, meaning you are working for me. That is precisely the structure of *shmira biv'alim* that should disqualify the elevated *shomer sachar* status.

### Rav Papa Sequential

Rav Papa resolves the difficulty by giving the *mishnah* a specific reading: *de'amar lei shmor li hayom ve'eshmor lach lemachar* — the arrangement is sequential, not simultaneous. "Guard mine today and I will guard yours tomorrow." At the moment I am guarding your property today, you are not laboring for me at all — you are simply benefiting from the arrangement we made. The "payment" for my guardianship is your guardianship of my property tomorrow, and those two periods of guardianship are non-overlapping. Therefore, the *shmira biv'alim* exemption does not apply, and each party is correctly classified as a *shomer sachar*.

### Baraita Parallels

A *baraita* extends the same logic to mixed arrangements: *shmor li ve'eshmor lach, hash'ileini ve'ash'ilecha, shmor li ve'ash'ilecha, hash'ileini ve'eshmor lach* — guard for me and I'll guard for you; lend to me and I'll lend to you; guard for me and I'll lend to you; lend to me and I'll guard for you. All such combinations, the *baraita* rules, create *shomrei sachar* for one another: *kulan na'asu shomrei sachar zeh lazeh*. The same question arises — *shmira biv'alim hi?* — and Rav Papa's answer applies equally: the arrangements are sequential, so that at no moment is the owner of an object simultaneously laboring for the one guarding it.

One might ask: does this apply even to *hash'ileini ve'ash'ilecha*, a reciprocal lending arrangement? If I borrow your object and you borrow mine, and something happens, am I liable as a *sho'el* — fully liable for *onsin* — or as a *shomer sachar*? The answer, on Rav Papa's reading, is that the sequential structure of the arrangement creates *shomer sachar* status, not *sho'el* status, for each party. The mutual exchange of benefit is treated as the equivalent of payment.

### Non-Overlapping Times

The crucial principle crystallized by Rav Papa is that the *kula* of *shomer chinam* — the exemption from liability for *geneivah va-aveidah* that arises from *shmira biv'alim* — operates only when the owner of the object is *actually working* for the bailee at the precise moment the *shmira* is occurring. It is not enough that the owner has contracted to work for the bailee at some other time, or that there exists a general reciprocal relationship. The exemption requires contemporaneous, simultaneous employment. This point becomes critical in the cases that follow.

---

## Perfume Makers Coat

### First Theft Case

The *gemara* now presents a practical scenario that tests this principle of simultaneity. There was a group of perfume makers (*aloi*) who had a rotating arrangement: each day, one of them would do the baking for the group. On a particular day, they said to one of their number: go do the baking today. He replied: then you all guard my coat (*glimai*) while I am baking. Before he returned with the bread, his coat was stolen. The case came before Rav Papa, who ruled the others *chayav* — they were *shomrei sachar* with respect to the coat, and therefore liable for the theft.

### Rabbis Challenge

The Rabbis challenged Rav Papa: how could he rule *chayav*? This is *pshi'ah biv'alim* — the owner of the coat was working for the guardians at the very moment of the *shmira*. He was baking for them. That should reduce their status to *shomer chinam* and exempt them from liability for theft.

### Drinking Break

Rav Papa was discomfited by the objection. But the situation was resolved when the facts were investigated further: *iglai milta d'hahi sha'ata shichra hava ka shati* — it emerged that at the very moment the coat was stolen, the baker was not in fact baking. He had paused to have a drink and had not yet begun the work. He was therefore not, at that precise moment, in the employ of the other perfume makers. The theft occurred during this interlude, and so *shmira biv'alim* did not apply. The other perfume makers were indeed *shomrei sachar* at the moment of the theft, and Rav Papa's ruling of liability was correct after all.

The *gemara* observes: *hanicha leman d'amar pshi'ah biv'alim patur* — this story only makes sense as a vindication of Rav Papa on the assumption that we hold *pshi'ah biv'alim* exempts from liability. The reason Rav Papa was embarrassed by the Rabbis' objection is precisely that he accepts this principle: if the baker had been baking at the moment of theft, the others would indeed be *patur*. Once it emerged he was on a break, the case shifted, and Rav Papa's original ruling was justified.

### Explicit Condition

The *gemara* then adds a second scenario that sharpens the point. In this version, the day in question was not normally the baker's day to bake — it was an out-of-turn assignment. He agreed to bake, but explicitly conditioned his agreement on reciprocal guarding of his coat: *behai agra d'ka apeina lechu natru glimai* — "in consideration of my baking for you today, you will guard my coat." Here the *shomer sachar* arrangement is explicit and formally articulated. Again the coat was stolen before he returned, again the case came before Rav Papa, and again he ruled *chayav*.

### Break Resolution

Once again the Rabbis objected on grounds of *shmira biv'alim*, and once again the investigation revealed the same resolution: at the moment of the theft, the baker was drinking and had not yet entered into the employ of the other perfume makers. The theft thus occurred outside the window of *shmira biv'alim*, leaving the others fully liable as *shomrei sachar*.

### Simultaneity Principle

The second scenario is necessary, the *gemara* explains, in order to make Rav Papa's ruling defensible according to the opinion that *pshi'ah biv'alim chayav* — that even when the owner is working for the bailee, if the bailee was negligent he is still liable. On that opinion, the first case does not require any *iglai milta*: even if the baker were baking at the moment of theft, the bailee would be *chayav* for negligence. So the story only needs the "drinking break" resolution if we are operating according to the opinion that *pshi'ah biv'alim patur*. The second scenario, with its explicit wage-condition, is constructed to show that Rav Papa's embarrassment and subsequent vindication make sense even according to that stricter opinion.

### Contractor Examples

The operative principle is that *shmira biv'alim* requires not merely that an employment relationship exists, but that the owner of the object be *actually employed* by the bailee at the very moment that the *shmira* occurs. If I am your contractor fixing your house for a week and I ask you to watch my dog, you are a *shomer chinam* for my dog throughout the working hours — because at every moment that you are guarding my dog, I am working for you. But if the theft or loss occurs during my lunch break, at that precise moment I am not in your employ, and the *shmira biv'alim* exemption does not apply. Borderline cases involving breaks, meal times, and pauses in work are governed by whether the owner's labor was actually ongoing at the critical moment.

---

## Tall and Short Travelers

### Exchange Setup

The next case involves two travelers on the road. One was tall (*aricha*) and riding a donkey; he had a linen sheet (*sadina*). The other was short (*gutza*) and walking; he was wearing a heavy woolen coat (*sarbala*).

### Item Exchange Action

When they reached a river, the short traveler removed his woolen coat, placed it on the donkey, and took the tall traveler's linen *sadina* to wrap himself in while crossing. During the crossing, the water carried the *sadina* away — it was lost.

At the moment of the crossing, each traveler was effectively holding something belonging to the other: the short traveler had borrowed the tall traveler's *sadina*, while the tall traveler's donkey was carrying the short traveler's *sarbala*. The short traveler was thus simultaneously the *sho'el* of the *sadina* and in a position where his property was being "guarded" by the tall traveler.

### Rabba Liable

The case came before Rabba, who ruled the tall traveler *chayav* for the loss of the *sadina*. The reasoning was that the short traveler was guarding the tall traveler's *sarbala* while the tall traveler had the *sadina* — the short traveler was, in a sense, "in the employ" of the tall traveler, providing a service by safeguarding his coat in exchange for use of the *sadina*.

### Rabbis Objection

The Rabbis objected: this is a case of *sheila biv'alim* — a borrowing that occurs while the lender is in the employ of the borrower (or, analogously, while the owner of the borrowed object is simultaneously working for the borrower). Under that principle, the tall traveler should be *patur*, not *chayav*, for the loss of the *sadina*.

### Without Consent

Rabba's ruling was vindicated when the facts were clarified: *belo datei shaklei* — the short traveler had placed his *sarbala* on the donkey without asking, without the tall traveler's knowledge or consent. The tall traveler never agreed to guard the *sarbala*. Therefore, the arrangement by which the tall traveler was supposedly "working for" the short traveler — the arrangement that would have created *shmira biv'alim* — never existed from the tall traveler's perspective.

### Unwitting Bailee

This yields an important principle: a *shomer she-lo mi-da'at* — an unwitting bailee, someone whose "guardianship" was imposed without his knowledge — does not acquire the protected status that *shmira biv'alim* would otherwise confer. The tall traveler was never actually in the short traveler's employ in any legally cognizable sense, because he did not know the coat was on his donkey. Consequently, the *sheila biv'alim* analysis cannot apply, and the tall traveler is fully liable as a *sho'el* for the loss of the *sadina*. The *baraita*'s vindication through the *iglai milta* device — the same structure we saw in the perfume makers' case — teaches the rule: guardianship without knowledge creates no *shmira biv'alim* protection.

---

## Wrong Road Case

### Instruction Breach

A man hired a donkey to his friend. The owner instructed the renter explicitly: do not take the road by *nahar Pakod* (*d'ika maya* — because there is water there that will endanger the donkey), and go instead by the road of *Narash* (*d'leika maya* — where there is no water). The renter ignored the instruction and took the road by *nahar Pakod*.

### No Water Claim

The donkey died. When the renter came before the court, he argued: yes, I took the road by *nahar Pakod*, but there was no water there when I traveled it. The donkey did not die because of any water hazard. I essentially followed the spirit of the owner's instruction even if I took the wrong road; I was not exposed to the danger he warned me about.

### Miggo Analysis

Rava initially found this argument compelling on the basis of *miggo*: *mah li l'shaker* — why would the renter lie? If he wanted to fabricate an excuse, he could simply have told the court that he went by the road of *Narash* and the donkey died there for no discernible reason. Instead, he admitted to taking the forbidden road while claiming there was no water. The admission of the route combined with the denial of the hazard creates a *miggo*: since he could have claimed a more convenient lie and didn't, his more costly admission deserves credibility.

### Miggo Refutation

Abaye rejected this reasoning. *Mah li l'shaker b'makom eidim lo amrinan* — we do not apply the *miggo* principle when public knowledge contradicts the claim. The *miggo* argument presupposes that the alternative claim would have been believable. But here, everyone knows that *nahar Pakod* is filled with water. It is publicly established fact — *anan sahadei*.

### Public Knowledge

*Anan sahadei* — "we are all witnesses" — functions as a form of public knowledge so pervasive and certain that it overrides the logical inference of *miggo*. If the renter claims there was no water on the road of *nahar Pakod*, his claim is directly contradicted by common knowledge, and the *miggo* collapses. The Rif is noted to address this passage as well, and the principle articulated here — that *anan sahadei* overrides *miggo* in situations of bailment disputes where the facts are matters of common knowledge — is the operative ruling.

---

## Acceptance Statements

### Mishnah Put Down

A new *mishnah* presents three scenarios involving verbal acceptance or rejection of a guardianship obligation. In the first case, one person says to another, "guard this for me," and the other responds, "put it down in front of me (*hanach lefanai*)." The *mishnah* rules that this response creates the status of *shomer chinam*: the respondent has accepted the object for guarding, but only as an unpaid bailee.

### Rav Huna Rejection

Rav Huna introduces a variant: if instead of *hanach lefanai* the respondent says *hanach lefanecha* — "put it down in front of you" — that is not acceptance of any guardianship obligation at all. *Eino lo shomer chinam v'lo shomer sachar* — he is neither an unpaid bailee nor a paid bailee. The response "put it down in front of yourself" is a rejection, tantamount to saying: I am not taking responsibility for this.

### Unqualified Put

The *gemara* then poses a further question: *ibaya lehu hanach stam mai* — what is the status when someone simply says *hanach*, "put it down," without qualification? He says neither "in front of me" nor "in front of you." Is this an acceptance of guardianship, or is it effectively a rejection? The question is left open — *teiku* — and the *gemara* proceeds to seek resolution from other sources.

### Mishnah Contrast

A resolution is proposed by reading the *mishnah* itself as implicitly contrasting the two cases. Since the *mishnah* uses the specific phrase *hanach lefanai* — "put it in front of me" — and rules that this creates *shomer chinam* status, the implication (*ha stam v'lo klum*) might be that a mere *hanach* without qualification would be no different — or, conversely, from Rav Huna's ruling that *hanach lefanecha* is a rejection, one can infer that *hanach* alone — without the distancing "*lefanecha*" — constitutes acceptance as *shomer chinam*. The *gemara* concludes that *hanach stam* is functionally equivalent to *hanach lefanai*: a qualified acceptance of responsibility as unpaid bailee.

---

## Courtyard Guardianship

### Tannaitic Dispute

The *gemara* now considers a *machloket tannai'm* — a dispute between the Sages — on the related question of what happens when someone brings objects into another's courtyard.

### Rabbanan Position

The Rabbis hold: *im hichnis bireshut chayav* — if someone brings objects into the courtyard of another person with permission, the owner of the courtyard becomes a *shomer chinam* for those objects. *Deki amar lei o'ol v'antar lach* — when the owner of the courtyard says "come in," he is implicitly saying "come in and I will guard your things." Permission to enter the courtyard carries with it implicit acceptance of guardianship responsibility. The *ba'al hachatzer* therefore bears *shomer chinam* obligations for the items stored there, and if they are damaged due to negligence he is liable.

### Rabbi Position

Rabbi disagrees: *eino chayav ad she'yikabel alav ba'al habayit lishmor* — the owner of the house or courtyard incurs no guardianship liability unless he explicitly accepts it with a statement of guardianship. Merely granting permission to enter or to deposit items is not sufficient.

### Guarded Courtyard

The *gemara* explores two ways of explaining this dispute. The first explanation focuses on the nature of the courtyard. A *chatzer de-bat netirah* — a courtyard that is inherently guarded — is a place that is always under the owner's watch. When the owner of such a courtyard grants someone permission to place items there, his granting of permission carries an implicit guarantee of safety: the very act of saying "you may put things here" is understood as saying "and I, who guard this space, will guard your things as well." On this reading, the *rabbanan* and Rabbi agree that what matters is what the owner communicates by his permission; they differ on whether such a courtyard's inherent guardedness makes the implicit guarantee automatic.

### Permission to Enter

The second explanation approaches the dispute from the perspective of the permission itself. A courtyard requires the owner's permission to enter. When the owner grants permission to enter *and* to deposit items, the granting of that permission is itself a statement of assumed responsibility — *tiv venatar lach ka'amar lei*, "sit and I will guard for you." The owner could not have meant merely "enter" without any accompanying commitment, because in a guarded space, permission to enter implies the full range of hosting obligations. Rabbi, however, reads the permission as narrowly as possible: it grants access, nothing more, and explicit acceptance of guardianship must be stated separately.

### Marketplace Contrast

The contrast with a *shuk*, a marketplace or public space, illuminates the logic further. In a public market, there is no permission required to put something down. No one needs Moshe's authorization to place a package on the bench next to him. Therefore, when someone in the *shuk* says to another "put it down (*hanach*)," the words cannot mean merely "you have permission to set it here" — because such permission was never needed. The statement *hanach* in the public context can only mean "put it down and I will guard it." By this reasoning, a simple *hanach* in the *shuk* functions as acceptance of *shomer chinam* status, consistent with the *gemara*'s conclusion in the previous *sugya*.

### Location-Based Rules

The *gemara* thus arrives at a conclusion that turns on the nature of the location and the content of the permission granted. In a courtyard, where permission to enter is necessary and where the space is inherently guarded, granting permission carries an implicit guardianship commitment according to the *rabbanan*; Rabbi requires it to be made explicit. In a marketplace, where no permission is needed, the bare utterance *hanach* already implies acceptance. The *halacha* appears to follow Rabbi's view — that explicit acceptance of guardianship is necessary in the courtyard context — but both explanations offered by the *gemara* converge on the principle that different rules apply depending on whether the location is inherently guarded and whether the act of permission itself communicates a guardianship commitment.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 82

## Creditor & Collateral

### Opening Context

We begin seven lines from the bottom of 81b with the words *hamilveh al hamashkon* — the one who lends on collateral. The daf continues to address cases involving workers handling objects entrusted to them, but the immediate focus shifts to a specific and consequential question: when a creditor holds collateral against a loan and that collateral is lost or damaged, what is the nature of the creditor's liability?

The scenario is straightforward. You ask me for a thousand dollars. I agree to lend it, but I require that you leave your iPhone as a *mashkon* — collateral — until the debt is repaid. Something then happens to the iPhone. What am I responsible for?

### Mishna: Shomer Sachar

The *tanna kamma* of the *mishna* rules that the creditor holding collateral is a *shomer sachar* — a paid watchman. This classification carries meaningful consequences. A *shomer sachar* is exempt only in cases of *ones*, a genuine accident entirely beyond his control. He remains liable for theft and loss (*geneiva va'aveida*). The *mishna*'s baseline, then, is that the creditor-as-collateral-holder bears a heightened responsibility, comparable to someone who receives payment for watching an object.

### R. Yehuda: Money/Fruit

Rabbi Yehuda dissents from this baseline and offers a distinction. When the loan involved money, the creditor receives nothing from the arrangement. He lent money at risk, earns no interest, and derives no material benefit from holding the collateral. In such a case, Rabbi Yehuda holds the creditor to be only a *shomer chinam* — an unpaid watchman — who is exempt upon swearing he was not negligent. However, if the loan involved fruit, the situation changes. If I lend you fresh apples and will receive fresh apples in return, I benefit because I am spared the deterioration I would have suffered had the fruit sat in my possession. In that case, Rabbi Yehuda agrees that the creditor is a *shomer sachar*. This is an eminently reasonable position. The difficulty lies with the *tanna kamma*, who treats all collateral-holding creditors as *shomrei sachar* regardless of the nature of the loan, and the *gemara* will now attempt to clarify why.

---

## R. Eliezer v. R. Akiva

### R. Eliezer: Shomer Chinam

The *gemara* raises the question: is our *mishna* consistent with Rabbi Eliezer? A *baraita* is cited: *hamilveh chaveiro al hamashkon* — one who lends to his friend on collateral, and the collateral is lost. Rabbi Eliezer rules *yishava v'yitol me'otav* — the creditor takes an oath that he was not negligent and still collects his money. In other words, Rabbi Eliezer holds the creditor to be no more than a *shomer chinam*, fully exempt upon taking the requisite oath. This squarely contradicts the *tanna kamma* of our *mishna*, who holds the creditor to be a *shomer sachar*.

### R. Akiva: Debt Collection

Rabbi Akiva disputes Rabbi Eliezer sharply. He frames the creditor's argument from the borrower's perspective: *klum hilvisani ela al hamashkon* — you only agreed to lend me the money because I gave you my collateral. If the collateral is lost, the debt is lost with it. *Avad hamashkon avdu me'otecha* — the collateral is gone, and so is your money. Rabbi Akiva's framing is notably different from the *mishna*'s language. He does not speak in terms of a *shomer sachar* receiving payment for his watchmanship. Rather, he is articulating a structural claim: the collateral was placed as a vehicle through which the debt could be collected. If the creditor can no longer return the collateral, it is as though the debt has been satisfied thereby.

### With Shtar (Document)

The *baraita* then presents an agreed-upon case. If a thousand *zuz* were lent *bishtar* — with a written document bearing witnesses — and collateral was additionally placed, then *divrei hakol*, all agree: *avad hamashkon avdu me'otav*, the loss of the collateral extinguishes the debt. Why does the existence of a *shtar* change things? Because the document itself already serves as the memory record of the loan — both parties can never forget that the debt exists and is documented. Since the *shtar* handles the memory function, the only reason to additionally take a physical *mashkon* must be to secure payment from it. Thus even Rabbi Eliezer concedes that in the case of a *shtar*, the collateral was clearly intended as a source of collection, and its loss therefore cancels the debt.

---

## Rashi: Zichron vs. Colle…

### R. Eliezer: Zichron

According to Rashi, the fundamental disagreement between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva turns on why collateral was taken at all. Rabbi Eliezer understands that in an ordinary loan without a *shtar*, the purpose of the *mashkon* is *zichron devarim* — a memory aid. I take your iPhone so that neither of us forgets the transaction. When you come to repay me, seeing the iPhone in my possession reminds both of us that this loan exists. On this reading, the *mashkon* is essentially an object belonging to you that I happen to be holding. Since I receive no benefit from the arrangement, I am a *shomer chinam* and liable only for negligence. This is entirely coherent and, as Rashi reads it, consistent with the case of a *shtar*: once a document exists, the *zichron* function is redundant, so we must assume the collateral was taken for collection purposes.

### R. Akiva: Payment

Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, holds that collateral is always taken for the purpose of collection — *klum hilvisani ela al hamashkon*. You agreed to lend me money precisely because you held my property as a guarantee that you could be made whole. If the collateral is gone, the loan is gone. This is worth emphasizing: Rabbi Akiva is not invoking the framework of *shomer sachar* per se. He is not saying that the creditor receives a benefit and therefore bears the heightened responsibility of a paid watchman. Rather, the logic is structural: the *mashkon* was designated to stand in for the debt, and when it can no longer be returned, it is deemed to have gone toward satisfying that debt.

The *mishna*, which frames the creditor as a *shomer sachar*, employs a categorically different conceptual framework — and this tension will drive the *gemara*'s analysis. Importantly, there is an additional implication of Rabbi Akiva's position. If the collateral was held as a payment vehicle, then even if the *mashkon* is destroyed by an act entirely beyond the creditor's control — struck by lightning — the logic of *avad hamashkon avdu me'otecha* should apply just as forcefully. It is not that the creditor was a bad watchman; it is that the arrangement itself means the collateral's loss erases the debt, regardless of cause.

---

## Reconcile Mishna

### Timing: At vs. After

The *gemara* now attempts to reconcile the *mishna*'s ruling — that the creditor is a *shomer sachar* — with Rabbi Eliezer's position, which treats the creditor as a *shomer chinam*. The proposed resolution is a temporal distinction: *kan she-mishkeno be-sha'at halva'ato, kan she-mishkeno shelo be-sha'at halva'ato* — in one case the collateral was taken at the time of the loan, and in the other it was taken afterward. Rabbi Eliezer, in the *baraita*, is addressing a case where the *mashkon* was taken at the moment the loan was made. There, one might reasonably understand the collateral as serving a *zichron devarim* purpose, since it was part of the original transaction. But when collateral is taken *after* the loan is already established, the implication is entirely different. At that later stage, the creditor is anxious about repayment and takes the *mashkon* specifically to have something to collect from. In that case, even Rabbi Eliezer would agree the collateral functions as a collection vehicle — and therefore, our *mishna*, which holds the creditor to heightened liability, could be addressing collateral taken after the loan was made.

### Reject Timing

The *gemara* rejects this resolution. *Ve-ha idi ve-idi hilveh al ha-mashkon tanya* — both the *mishna* and the *baraita* use the same language, *hilveh al ha-mashkon*, "he lent on the collateral," which implies that the collateral was given at the time of the loan in both cases. There is no linguistic basis to assign one source to an early-collateral scenario and the other to a late-collateral scenario. The proposed timing distinction therefore cannot be sustained.

### Money vs. Fruit

The *gemara* attempts a second reconciliation. Perhaps the *baraita* of Rabbi Eliezer deals with a monetary loan — where the creditor receives no benefit and is thus a *shomer chinam* — while our *mishna* deals with a loan of fruit, where, as Rabbi Yehuda noted, the creditor does receive a benefit. If so, the *mishna*'s ruling that the creditor is a *shomer sachar* could be reconciled with Rabbi Eliezer, since Rabbi Eliezer might agree that a fruit-loan produces benefit sufficient to create *shomer sachar* status.

### Reject Fruit

The *gemara* promptly dismantles this reading. *Mi-dekattani seifa Rabbi Yehuda omer* — the *mishna* itself contains Rabbi Yehuda's clause, which explicitly distinguishes between a monetary loan (*shomer chinam*) and a fruit loan (*shomer sachar*). If Rabbi Yehuda felt the need to introduce this distinction as a *chiddush*, it follows necessarily — *mi-khlal de-Tanna Kamma lo shani lei* — that the *tanna kamma* did not make this distinction. The *tanna kamma* holds you are a *shomer sachar* whether the loan was of money or fruit. Therefore, one cannot read the *tanna kamma* as restricting itself to fruit loans.

The *gemara* does attempt one further maneuver: perhaps the entire *mishna* is Rabbi Yehuda's view, and the opening ruling represents not an independent *tanna kamma* but rather Rabbi Yehuda himself, with his subsequent clause as a clarification rather than a dispute. This reading would require us to understand the *mishna* as *chisura me-chasra* — missing words — and reconstruct it as: the creditor is a *shomer sachar* when he lent fruit; but if he lent money, he is a *shomer chinam*, as Rabbi Yehuda teaches. The *gemara* notes, however, that this leaves the *mishna* inconsistent with Rabbi Akiva, and a *stam mishna* is attributed to Rabbi Meir — a student of Rabbi Akiva — making it very difficult to accept that the *mishna* runs contrary to Rabbi Akiva's position.

### Conclusion: Not R. Eliez…

The *gemara* concludes: *ela michvarta, matnisin d'lo k'Rabbi Eliezer* — the straightforward conclusion is that our *mishna* is simply not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer. The *mishna* holds the creditor to be a *shomer sachar*; Rabbi Eliezer holds the creditor to be a *shomer chinam*; and no acceptable reading can harmonize the two. This does not mean the *mishna* necessarily follows Rabbi Akiva's exact logic either. As noted, Rabbi Akiva's argument — that loss of the *mashkon* erases the debt — is not the same as saying the creditor is a *shomer sachar* in the technical sense. The *mishna*'s use of the *shomer sachar* framework will require its own explanation.

---

## Shmuel: Disproportionate

### Disproportionate Debate

The *gemara* now explores a different way of understanding the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva. Perhaps their debate is specifically about a case of disproportionate collateral — where the *mashkon* is not worth the full value of the loan. I lend you a thousand dollars and you give me, as collateral, an Apple Watch worth only three hundred dollars. In such a case, the *gemara* suggests, the two opinions may be debating the extent to which disproportionate collateral can be said to represent the loan.

### Shmuel's Position
