Guryon ben Astiyon said in the name of Rav: all that bread was not the bread of the meal itself — it was *la'amilan shel tabachim*, the bread used to clean and absorb the overflow from the cooking pots. Rav Yitzchak adds: all that meat was not the main course — it was *l'tzikei kedeira*, some form of minced meat appetizer. The actual feast itself was something far greater.

### Thousand Wives

Rav Yitzchak further states: *elef nashim hayu li'Shlomo* — Solomon had a thousand wives, *kol achas v'achas asta lo b'veisa kach* — and each one prepared this very feast in her own house. *Zu sevura shema etzli so'ed hayom* — each one thought: perhaps he will dine by me today. So the actual total was a thousand times what was described in the verse.

### Abraham's Angels

By contrast, the feast of Abraham when he received the three angels appears far more modest. The verse says simply: *v'el habakar ratz Avraham vayikach ben bakar rach va'tov* — Abraham ran to the cattle and took a calf, tender and good. It sounds like a single animal.

### Three Calves

Yet Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *ben bakar* — a calf — that is one. *Rach* — soft — that is a second. *Va'tov* — and good — that is a third. Three calves, one for each of the three guests. A possible objection is raised: perhaps *rach va'tov* are simply adjectives describing a single calf — one tender, good animal? The *Gemara* responds: if so, the verse would have simply written *rach tov*. The presence of the *vav* — *va'tov* — signals that it is an independent addition, coming *l'drasha*, to teach a separate animal. And since *va'tov* thus refers to a third calf, *rach nami l'drasha* — the word *rach* must similarly indicate its own separate calf. Three calves for three people. *Hasam tlata torei li'tlata gavrei* — there in the case of Abraham, three calves for three men.

When the verse then says *vayitnehu el ha'na'ar vayimaher la'asot oso* — he gave it to the lad to prepare — the singular *oso* might suggest one animal. But the *Gemara* resolves this: *kol chad v'chad yeiv l'na'ar chad* — each animal was given to a separate youth to prepare simultaneously.

As for the sequence in which it was served — *vayikach chem'a v'chalav u'ven habakar asher asa vayiten lifneihem* — he took butter, milk, and the prepared calf and placed them before the guests — the *Gemara* explains: *dekama dekama dematya ayti l'kama'ihu* — as each dish was ready, he brought it before them in sequence. Like courses at a fine meal: the dairy dishes first, then they were removed, then the meat. Some note that this sequencing is itself suggestive regarding the separation of milk and meat in practice, though this is reading somewhat into the text. And why were three separate calves necessary? *K'dei le'achilan shalosh leshonos b'chardal* — in order to serve three tongues in mustard to each guest, which was considered a great delicacy.

### Endless Obligation

Now the comparison becomes clear. Solomon's feast, enormous as it was, was ultimately a finite quantity — spread across an entire kingdom. Abraham's feast, though appearing modest on its face, was given to three individuals and was truly lavish per person. And since the children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are the descendants of the one who provided such a feast, any explicit commitment to feed them without limit means that you can never fully discharge the obligation. The feast of Solomon himself would not suffice. And that is precisely why Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya instructed his son to go back and clarify the terms of his promise before it became binding.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 87

## Abraham & Angels

### Custom & Minhag

The *aggadeta* of this *daf* continues in the middle of the story of Abraham and the angels, which arose through the *mishna*'s discussion of whether an employer who contracts to feed his workers must provide lavish meals. The reasoning was that since workers are children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, one who contracts to feed them might be obligated to provide near-infinite quantities. This opened the door to the extensive *aggadic* material about Abraham's feast and his generosity toward the angels.

Rav Tanchum bar Chanilai teaches: *le'olam al yeshaneh adam min haminhag* — a person should never deviate from the prevailing custom. This is a striking echo of the *mishna*'s principle of *hakol keminhag hamedina*, though here it carries a more personal, behavioral meaning: when in a particular setting, conduct yourself according to its norms. The illustration is twofold. When Moses ascended to heaven, he did not eat bread, as the verse states: *lechem lo achal umayim lo shata* — bread he did not eat and water he did not drink — conforming to the way of the angels. And when the angels of the divine service descended below, *vayochlu lechem* — and they ate bread — conforming to the way of human beings.

### Angels Eating

The *gemara* immediately raises an objection: *achlu salka da'atcha* — is it conceivable that they actually ate? Angels have no digestive nature. The resolution offered is *nir'u kemi she'achlu veshatu* — they appeared as though they ate and drank. They made it look that way, out of respect for the customs of the place and the dignity of their host.

### Abraham's Merit

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *kol mah she'asa Avraham lemalachei hasharet be'atzmo, asa Hakadosh Baruch Hu levanav be'atzmo* — whatever Abraham personally did for the ministering angels, God personally repaid to Abraham's descendants, the Jewish people. And conversely, whatever Abraham did through an intermediary, God provided for Israel through an intermediary.

### Textual Midrash

The *gemara* now matches the acts of Abraham to God's corresponding acts through a series of textual parallels. Abraham ran to the cattle himself — *el habakar ratz Avraham* — and correspondingly, God sent the wind directly: *veruach nasa me'et Hashem*, gathering the quail for Israel. Abraham took butter and milk — *vayikach chem'a vechalav* — and God directly declared: *hineni mamtir lachem lechem min hashamayim*, I will rain down bread from heaven. The connection seems to be a wordplay: *chem'a* echoes *lechem*, and two of the letters of *chalav* (lamed-chet-mem) recur in *lechem*. Abraham stood and attended to them beneath the tree — *vehu omed aleihem tachat ha'etz* — and God declared: *hineni omed lefanecha sham al hatzur*, I will stand before you at the rock, providing water. Abraham accompanied them on their way — *ve'Avraham holech imam leshalcham* — and God walked before Israel by day: *vaHashem holech lifneihem yomam*.

Now what did Abraham do through an intermediary? He said *yukach na me'at mayim* — let some water be taken — delegating the task. Correspondingly, God provided water to Israel through Moshe striking the rock: *vehikita batzur veyatz'u mayim mimenu veshata ha'am*. God's own standing present for the people corresponds to Abraham's personal attendance; the bringing of the water was through an intermediary, just as Abraham had delegated that task.

### Rabbi Chama Dispute

This set of textual parallels, the *gemara* notes, *upliga deRabbi Chama bar Chanina* — disputes Rabbi Chama bar Chanina. For Rabbi Chama bar Chanina, and so too taught the *tana devei Rabbi Yishmael*, taught a different set of three correspondences: *beschar shlosha zachu lishlosha* — by the merit of three acts, Israel merited three gifts. For the butter and milk (*chem'a vechalav*), they merited the *man* — the manna. Again, this likely turns on the same *lechem*/*chalav* wordplay. For Abraham's standing and attending to them (*vehu omed*), they merited the pillar of cloud (*amud anan*). For the *yukach na me'at mayim*, they merited the well of Miriam. The difference between this list and the previous one is the matching of Abraham's personal attendance: here it is matched to the pillar of cloud, whereas in the earlier list it was matched to God's standing at the rock. The two *amoraim* thus parse the correspondences differently.

---

## Feet Washing

### Yukach Mayim

The *gemara* now proceeds to expound the individual verses of the story *pasuk* by *pasuk*, much of which is familiar from Rashi's commentary on the *parasha*. *Yukach na me'at mayim verachatzu ragleichem* — let some water be taken and wash your feet.

### Arab Practices

Rabbi Yannai the son of Rabbi Yishmael reports that the angels responded: *ve'chi be'aravayin chashadetanu she'hem mishtachavim le'avak ragleihem* — do you think we are Arabs, who prostrate to the dust on their feet? And then, as if to explain why this accusation lands differently here, the *gemara* notes *kevar yatza mimeni Yishmael* — Yishmael has already gone out from me. This exchange is worth pausing over, since the identity of the speaker is itself Rabbi *Yishmael*, and the accusation is pegged to *Yishmael*, his ancestor — a detail the *gemara* seems to find pointed. As for the historical phenomenon itself, a note from the Maharal's second explanation suggests that in Abraham's era, the Arab tribes were nomadic peoples who worshipped a god of the roads, and thus treated the dust on their feet — residue of those roads — as something to bow toward. Whether historically accurate or not, the interpretive thrust is that Abraham's request to wash their feet was misread as though he suspected them of this idolatrous practice. Their protest, and Abraham's tacit acknowledgment via the mention of Yishmael, ends the exchange abruptly without resolution. The story moves on without Abraham offering a counter-explanation, which itself is left somewhat open. Clearly foot-washing as a gesture of hospitality need not have carried any such connotation.

---

## Third Day Healing

### Divine Sensitivity

The *gemara* returns to the beginning of the *parasha*. *Vayera eilav Hashem be'elonei Mamre vehu yoshev petach ha'ohel ke'chom hayom* — God appeared to him in the plains of Mamre, and he was sitting at the entrance of the tent in the heat of the day. Rabbi Chama the son of Rabbi Chanina explains: *oto hayom yom shelishi shel milah shel Avraham hayah* — that day was the third day of Abraham's *brit milah*, which is the day of greatest pain, as we learn from the narrative of Shimon and Levi's attack on Shechem on the third day.

God came to perform *bikkur cholim* — to visit the sick — and in order that Abraham should not be burdened by wayfarers on this painful day, God caused the heat of the day to be extreme, so that no travelers would be on the road. *Hotzi Hakadosh Baruch Hu chamah min nartikah kedei shelo lehatri'ach oto tzaddik be'orchim*. Nevertheless, Abraham, who was desperate to bring in guests, sent his servant *Eliezer* out to find wayfarers. Eliezer went out and found no one. When he returned and reported this, Abraham declared: *lo meheimna lach* — I do not trust you — and went to look for himself. This prompted the *gemara* to cite the popular saying: *leit heimanuta be'avdei* — servants cannot be trusted. One may note an alternative and appealing reading: perhaps Eliezer was complicit in protecting Abraham, not truly searching, so that Abraham would not have to go out himself.

When Abraham went out, he saw God standing at the gate — *dekayei ababa* — and this is why Abraham said *al na ta'avor me'al avdecha*, God please do not pass by your servant. Abraham was, in effect, welcoming God as his guest.

Then *keivan dechaza deka asar veshari*, when God saw that Abraham was untying and retying his bandages from the *milah*, God said it is not appropriate to remain in these circumstances. *Amar lav orach ar'a lemikim hacha.* And at that moment, *vayisa einav vayar vehinei shelosha anashim nitzavim alav* — he lifted his eyes and saw three men standing near him. The angels had initially approached and stood close to him, but when they saw his pain, they stepped back, giving him space. That is why the verse says he *ran* to greet them even though they had been nearby — they had withdrawn out of sensitivity.

This is a remarkable model of *bikkur cholim*. The angels, and indeed God's presence itself, withdrew when they perceived that Abraham was in pain and compromised. Sometimes the right form of visiting the sick is to step back, to not impose one's presence when the person needs space. As has been aptly observed, the principle here is a kind of pastoral sensitivity: you enter the room, but if you see the patient's dignity is compromised, you step back. This is a lesson for all who perform *bikkur cholim*.

The precise relationship between God's own visitation and the angels' arrival is not entirely clear in the *gemara*. One possibility is that God's visit was manifested through the angels' presence. Another possibility, reflected in the *midrash* cited by Tosafot, is that they were distinct: Abraham asked God to wait while he went to welcome the angels and bring them in. Tosafot discusses this: *hashechina hayeta rotza lehistalek me'al Avraham* — the divine presence wished to withdraw — but then the *midrash* suggests that Abraham asked God to wait, *ad sheyachnis otan*, while he attended to the angels. This reading distinguishes the divine visit from the angelic one.

### Angels' Names

The *gemara* asks: *mani hashelosha anashim?* — who were these three men? *Michael veGavriel veRefael.* Michael came to bring the good tidings to Sarah. Refael, whose name evokes *refuah* — healing — came to heal Abraham from his *brit milah*. Gabriel, whose name evokes *gevurah* — strength — went to overturn Sodom.

A textual difficulty is immediately raised: the verse says *vayavo'u shenei hamalakhim Sdoma ba'erev* — only two angels came to Sodom. Why two, if only Gabriel was sent to destroy the city? The answer is that Michael went along to save Lot. This accords with Michael's role as a bearer of good tidings. The proof that only Gabriel destroyed the cities is that the verse says *vayahafoch et he'arim ha'el* in the singular — *he* overturned — not *vayahafechu* in the plural.

Tosafot raises a difficulty here from the principle in *Bereishit Rabbah* that a single angel cannot perform two missions. How then could Michael both announce the good news to Sarah and save Lot? Tosafot offers two answers. First, the missions were sequential, not simultaneous: the first mission ended when he informed Sarah, and only then did a new mission begin — *az hitchil shelichut acheret*. This is permitted; it is performing two tasks simultaneously that is forbidden. Second, Tosafot notes that *Bereishit Rabbah* in some versions assigns the saving of Lot to Refael, not Michael. In that version, healing Abraham and saving Lot are connected types of action — *refuah vehatzalah inyan echad* — and are considered a single category of mission.

### Accept/Refuse

By Abraham, the verse records that when he offered hospitality, they immediately accepted: *ken ta'aseh ka'asher dibarta*. By Lot, by contrast, *vayiftzar bam me'od* — he had to press them greatly before they agreed. Rabbi Elazar derives from this: *mikan she'mesarvin lekatan ve'ein mesarvin legadol* — from here we learn that one may decline an initial offer from someone of lower standing, but one does not refuse a person of distinction. It would be offensive to a *chashuv* person if their hospitality were casually turned down; with someone of lesser standing, a degree of initial reluctance is appropriate social conduct.

---

## Righteous vs Wicked

### Promise & Fulfill

The verse says Abraham promised *pat lechem* — a piece of bread — yet *el habakar ratz Avraham* — he ran to the cattle and prepared a full feast. Rabbi Elazar teaches: *mikan shetzadikim omrim me'at ve'osim harbeh* — from here we learn that the righteous promise little and do much.

### Ephron's Greed

The wicked, by contrast, promise much and do not even deliver a little. The paradigm case is Ephron. He announced grandly that the field was worth four hundred *shekel* of silver — *mah hi beini uveinecha* — essentially suggesting it was a negligible sum. Yet in the end, *vayishkol Avraham le'Efron et hakesef* — Abraham weighed out the full sum — and not merely the standard *shekel*, but coins of the type *over lasocher*, accepted by every merchant. The *gemara* further notes that Ephron ultimately insisted on *kantari* — a coin of greater weight — *de'ika duchta dekaru lei letikla kantari*, in places the *shekel* is called a *kantari*, indicating the payment was even larger than it might first appear. He said he would give it for nothing and in the end demanded a great deal.

### Bread & Purity

The verse says Abraham told Sarah to take *kemach* — flour — yet a moment later the text says *solet* — fine flour. Rather than reading these as a single description, the *gemara* treats them as two distinct things. Rabbi Yitzchak derives: *mikan she'ha'ishah tzarah einah be'orchim yoter min ha'ish* — from here we learn that a woman tends to be more reluctant than a man to give food to guests. The *gemara* seems to suggest that Abraham specified both *kemach* and *solet* precisely because Sarah was inclined to give only the coarser flour. One might note that this generalization could stem from a practical reality: women managing the household provisions know exactly how much food is on hand and must feed the family, while men can more easily make lavish promises.

The bread promised never appears on the table — the verse records that Abraham served the butter, the milk, and the meat, but not the bread. Where did it go? *Efrayim Maksha'ah*, the student of Rabbi Meir, teaches in the name of Rabbi Meir: *Avraham Avinu ochel chullin betaharah hayah* — Abraham maintained a practice of eating even non-sanctified food in a state of purity. And that day, *Sarah Imeinu oto hayom pirsa niddah* — Sarah had her period return, her youth miraculously restored. As a result, her touching of the bread rendered it *tamei*, and since Abraham would not eat something *tamei*, he could not serve it to his guests. This is itself a striking point: even if the guests themselves would not have been troubled by *tumah*, Abraham's personal practice prevented him from serving them something he himself would not eat. There is something profound in that — to treat a guest as less than you would treat yourself is in some sense a diminishment of their dignity.

The question is raised whether Abraham understood his guests to be angels. The *gemara* suggests he did not — or at least was uncertain. One detail offered is that Abraham stood and attended to them while they ate, which may indicate he joined them at table so they should not feel uncomfortable eating while he stood apart. The verse *vehu omed aleihem tachat ha'etz vayochelu* is most naturally read as: he stood over them attending, and they ate.

### Courtesy Duty

The angels then asked: *ayeh Sarah ishtecha* — where is Sarah your wife? The *gemara* says this was to teach: *le'hodi'a she'Sarah Imeinu tzenu'ah hayetah* — that Sarah our matriarch was modest, remaining in the tent. But why would the angels ask something they obviously already knew? Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav (and some attribute it to Rav Yitzchak): *yod'im hayu malachei hasharet she'Sarah Imeinu ba'ohel hayetah* — they certainly knew she was in the tent — but they asked *kedei lechababah al ba'alah* — in order to make her dear to her husband, so that Abraham would be reminded of her modesty. Rabbi Yosei the son of Rabbi Chanina offers a different reason: *kedei leshadar lah kos shel berachah* — in order to include her by sending her the cup of *birkat hamazon*.

This second reason is particularly powerful. In a social setting where men and women eat in entirely separate spaces, a woman is easily made invisible in the proceedings that concern her most. By asking after her, by directing the message to her even in her absence, and by sending her the *kos shel berachah* from the concluding blessing, the angels were finding a way to make Sarah a subject rather than merely an object of the conversation. The good tidings, after all, were addressed to her.

The verse *vayomru eilav* — and they said *to him* — has dots written over the letters *alef*, *yud*, and *vav* in the Torah scroll. A *tanna* in the name of Rabbi Yosei asks: why the dots? *Limdah Torah derech eretz* — the Torah is teaching proper conduct — *sheyish'al adam be'achsanyah shelo* — that when you are hosted, you should ask after your hostess. Tosafot presses further: those three dotted letters spell *ayav* — the masculine form of *where is he* — suggesting the reverse is also implied. Just as a guest should ask the host about his wife, so a guest should ask a hostess about her husband. The Torah is teaching gender-equal courtesy in inquiry.

The *gemara* raises a challenge: doesn't Shmuel teach *ein sho'alin bish'lom isha klal* — one does not inquire about a woman's welfare at all — lest it lead to inappropriate familiarity? The *gemara* resolves: *al yedei ba'alah shani* — asking through her husband is different and entirely permissible. Nobody would impute impropriety to a guest who asks the host: "How is your wife? Please send her my regards." The prohibition is only against direct inquiry to the woman herself, which could lead to excessive personal interaction.

---

## Sarah's Renewal

### Miraculous Nursing

Rav Chisda expounds *acharei beloti hayeta li ednah* — after I have been worn away, shall I have youth? He reads it not as a rhetorical question but as a description of an actual event: *achari she'nisbalah habasar ravu hakmatim nit'adnah habasar venistapshetu hakmatim* — after the flesh had worn away and the wrinkles had multiplied, the flesh became supple and the wrinkles smoothed out. *Vechazar hayofi limkomo* — the beauty returned to its place. (Rashi, in his French gloss, identifies the word *kmatim* — wrinkles — with a French term that, to a modern reader, brings to mind the word "prunes.")

The verse says *va'tedaber Sarah* — Sarah spoke of nursing: *vatomer mi milel le'Avraham heynika vanim Sarah* — who would have declared to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? But why *banim* in the plural — Sarah nursed only one child. Rabbi Levi explains: on the day that Abraham weaned Isaac, he made a great feast. The nations of the world began to mock, saying they had seen this elderly couple produce a foundling from the marketplace, a child they claimed as their own, and were making a grand celebration to legitimize the deception. What did Abraham do? He invited all the great people of that generation and their wives — notably, he invited their wives specifically — and Sarah's milk flowed miraculously: *veniftchu dadeha kishnei ma'ayanot* — her breasts opened like two wellsprings — and she nursed all of the infants who had been brought. That is the meaning of *heynika vanim* — she nursed *children*, in the plural. This was the proof that she had truly given birth.

### Isaac's Features

The skeptics were not satisfied. They continued to mock: even if Sarah gave birth, perhaps Abraham — at one hundred years old — was not the father. Immediately *nehpach klastar panav shel Yitzchak venidmeh le'Avraham* — Isaac's facial features transformed and he resembled Abraham unmistakably. At that, everyone conceded: *Avraham holid et Yitzchak*. This is in fact what the verse in *parashat Toldot* proclaims: *Eleh toldot Yitzchak ben Avraham Avraham holid et Yitzchak* — and this declaration, according to the *midrash*, reflects the universal acknowledgment that followed the transformation of Isaac's face. The phenomenon of an infant's features shifting over time to resemble a parent is itself quite natural, which gives this *midrash* a certain grounding.

---

## Origins of Aging

### Abraham's Prayer

*Ad Avraham lo haya zikna* — until Abraham there was no old age. People aged and died, but the aging was not reflected in their bodily appearance. This created a practical problem: *man dehava ba'i lemishta'ei bahadi Avraham mishta'ei bahadi Yitzchak* — someone who wanted to speak with Abraham would accidentally speak with Isaac, since they looked identical. And vice versa. Father and son were indistinguishable. So *ata Avraham ba'ei rachamei vehava zikna* — Abraham prayed for old age to be visibly present, and there was old age — as the verse states: *ve'Avraham zaken ba bayamim*, which is the first time the Torah explicitly uses *zaken* to describe someone's condition.

One might raise the question: didn't the verse earlier say *adoni zaken* — my master is old — which predates this moment? And indeed the *gemara* does not quote that verse. The *gemara* seems to be working with the idea that the bodily condition of aging was not yet visible, even if people experienced diminished capacities. There is also the consideration that Sarah's own words *acharei beloti* — after I have been worn away — and the *gemara*'s own reading of them, suggest visible physical change did exist. The *gemara* apparently holds that while certain capacities declined with age, the outward appearance of being aged — the kind that would allow you to distinguish a 100-year-old from a 60-year-old — was not present until Abraham prayed for it.

This is a profound mythic idea. Abraham was not asking to look old for honor's sake alone, though in a society that reveres age, that would certainly be a consideration. He was asking that his life experience, his decades, be legible on his face. There is something deeply counter-cultural about this — contemporary culture endlessly seeks to appear younger. Here, the very first prayer for visible aging is an act of claiming one's identity, of saying that one's journey through time should be written on one's body.

### Jacob's Sickness

*Ad Yaakov lo hava chulsha* — until Jacob there was no sickness as a precursor to death. People simply died. Jacob prayed that illness should precede death — *ata Yaakov ba'ei rachamei vehava chulsha* — as the verse records: *vayomer le'Yosef hinei avicha choleh* — and he said to Joseph, your father is ill. This is the first occurrence in the Torah of someone being sick. The purpose is not obscure: illness preceding death gives a person the opportunity to prepare — mentally, spiritually, practically — for what is coming. It is a gift of awareness, of transition, of the ability to put affairs in order and to say what needs to be said.

### Elisha's Illness

*Ad ata Elisha lo hava dechalash ve'itpach* — until Elisha came, no one became ill and then recovered. All illness led directly to death. *Ata Elisha ba'ei rachamei ve'itpach* — Elisha prayed and recovered, introducing the possibility of recovery from illness. The textual proof is *ve'Elisha chala et chalyo asher yamut bo* — the final illness he would die from — which implies *michlal dechali chali achrinei* — that he had been sick from other illnesses before, illnesses from which he had recovered.

The *Talmud* specifies: *tanu rabbanan, shlosha cholayim chala Elisha* — our Rabbis taught that Elisha suffered three illnesses. One for pushing away Gechazi with both hands — for completely rejecting someone where one should push away with the left but draw close with the right. One for inciting the bears against the children who mocked him. And one that brought about his death: *shenemar ve'Elisha chala et chalyo asher yamut bo*.

The introduction of recoverable illness also gives rise to the whole dynamic of *teshuva*, prayer, and healing — the realization that sickness is not automatically terminal opens a space for spiritual response.

---

## Workers' Rights

### Stipulations

The *gemara* now returns to *halakha*, picking up the thread of workers' entitlements and employer stipulations. The case discussed is a father seeking to limit his obligation to feed workers before they begin: *al menat she'ein lachem ela pat vekitnit bilvad* — on condition that I will give you only bread and legumes. Rav Acha the son of Rav Yosef raises a pointed grammatical question: *l'afchuzei — pat kitnit tnan o pat vekitnit tnan* — does the *mishna* mean bread *made of* legumes (a single item: legume-bread), or bread *and* legumes (two separate items)? The answer is that it requires a *vav* — *pat vekitnit* — and indeed that *vav* is essential to the meaning, like the pole used to keep a boat in the middle of the river away from the shore. Without the *vav*, the two items collapse into one.

Rabban Gamliel teaches: even if one stipulates to feed workers, one need not exceed the standard — *hakol keminhag hamedina*. The *gemara* asks what exactly this means. It cites a *mishna*: if an employer hires a worker and says pay him as one of the ordinary workers in town, what does that mean if there is a range of wages? Rabbi Yehoshua says: give him the lower end of the range. The Sages say: *meshamnin beineihem* — calculate the median. The *gemara* implies that the *minhag* is not the minimum; the standard means something closer to the average. The minimum is the floor of the range, not its representative value.

### Mishna Frame

The *mishna* now turns to a different dimension of workers' rights — not stipulated feeding arrangements, but the Torah's own entitlement for workers to eat from the produce they are harvesting. *Ve'elu ochlim min haTorah* — the following workers eat by Torah right. The categories are organized along two axes. For *mechubar lekarka* — produce still connected to the ground — the worker may eat *bish'at gmar melacha* — at the time of the final labor, i.e., the harvest. For *talush min hakarka* — produce already detached from the ground — the worker may eat only *ad shelo nigmra melachto* — before the completion of the process. These two are mirror images of each other.

Additionally, the entitlement applies only to *davar shegidulo min ha'aretz* — something that grows from the ground. The parallel list of those who may *not* eat reverses each of these conditions: one working with produce still connected to the ground but not at the harvest stage may not eat; one working with harvested produce after the final processing is complete may not eat; and one working with something that does not grow from the ground may not eat.

### Biblical Source

*Mena hanei milei?* — what is the biblical source for all this? The verse states: *ki tavo bekerem re'echa ve'achalta anavim* — when you enter your neighbor's vineyard you may eat grapes. From this we know the rule for a vineyard. But how do we extend it to other produce? By analogy: just as a vineyard involves produce that grows from the ground and the worker eats during the final labor, so too for anything with those features.

However, the *gemara* immediately challenges this: perhaps only a vineyard qualifies because it has the special obligation of *olelot* — the incompletely formed grape clusters given to the poor — suggesting a general heightened set of entitlements for vineyard workers. To counter this, the *gemara* invokes a second verse: *ki tavo bekamat re'echa vekatafta melilot beyadecha* — when you enter your neighbor's standing grain, you may pluck kernels by hand — *ve'el chermesh lo tanif al kamat re'echa* — but you may not swing your sickle against your neighbor's standing grain. This establishes the same entitlement for grain. Now we have two paradigms — vineyard and grain — from which to generalize.

### Extending Produce

But perhaps these two categories are still limited in scope, since both have distinctive characteristics: grain (*kamah*) is subject to *challah*, and vineyard (*kerem*) is subject to *olelot*. Each one's special feature could be the reason for the entitlement. The *gemara* applies the standard hermeneutical move of *hatzad hashaveh* — the common denominator: both grow from the ground and in both cases the worker eats during the final labor. From this common denominator we generalize.

A further challenge: both grain and grapes produce offerings for the *mizbe'ach* — flour and wine. Perhaps the entitlement is limited to produce brought to the altar, which would include olives (producing oil for the *mincha*) but not more. To this, Rav Pappa observes that olives are themselves called *kerem* — *kerem zayit* — in the verse *vayav'er migadish ve'ad kamah ve'ad kerem zayit*. So olives are included via *kerem* directly. But *kerem stam*, an unqualified *kerem*, refers to grapes; *kerem zayit* is the olive grove. And beyond olives, how do we extend to all produce, including things not offered on the *mizbe'ach*?

### Sickle & Standing

Shmuel answers: *amar kra ubachermesh* — the verse says "sickle." *Lerabos kol ba'alei chermesh* — to include everything to which one brings a sickle, beyond the categories of altar-offerings. One might object that the verse's mention of *chermesh* is needed for a different *derashah*: *bish'at chermesh tochal, shelo bish'at chermesh lo tochal* — you may eat only at the time of the harvest, not at other times. But the *gemara* rejects this: the timing restriction is already derived from *ve'el kelyecha lo siten* — do not put it into your own vessel — which implies you eat only while delivering into the *owner's* vessel, i.e., during the harvest. So *chermesh* is available to do the broader inclusionary work of extending the entitlement to all produce harvested with a sickle.

But what of produce that is not harvested with a sickle? Rav Yitzchak answers: *amar kra kamah* — the verse says *standing grain*, *lerabos kol ba'alei kamah* — to include everything that stands and grows. One might object that *kamah* was derived via a *gezeirah shavah* to mean specifically grain subject to *challah*. The *gemara* resolves this: that restrictive reading of *kamah* was necessary only *mikamei denaysi chermesh* — before we had *chermesh* to expand the category. Once *chermesh* has already expanded the entitlement to include all produce brought with a sickle, even things not subject to *challah*, the word *kamah* is no longer needed to establish that limitation. *Kamah* is now free to serve its expansive function: *lerabos kol davar kamah* — to include anything that stands and grows, with or without a sickle, provided it grows from the ground. The *gemara* will continue from this point in the next session.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 88

## Worker Eating Rights

### Torah Sources

The topic of today's daf is the right of a worker to eat from the produce he is harvesting as he performs his work. The basic principle is grounded in two *pesukim* in the Torah. The first reads: *ki tavo bekamat re'echa vekatafta melilot beyadecha vechermesh lo tanif al kamat re'echa* — when you enter your friend's standing grain, you may take some kernels by hand, but you may not use a scythe. The second, addressing a vineyard, states that you may eat grapes until you are satisfied but may not place them into your vessel. Although the *pesukim* do not explicitly identify the subject as a hired worker, *Chazal* understood both verses to be speaking about a *po'el*, and in the previous daf the relevant *drashot* were set out in detail.

### All Produce Types

Those *drashot* established that the worker's right to eat is not limited to grain or grapes but extends to all types of growing produce. The word *chermesh* — scythe — implies anything that can be cut by a scythe, and *kama* — standing grain — implies anything growing and upright. Together they expand the right beyond the two examples the Torah provides.

### Growing vs Harvested

The right applies at the moment of *gmar melacha* — here meaning the point at which produce is being cut from the ground, i.e., the harvesting itself. This is a distinct usage of *gmar melacha* from the one that will be introduced shortly in the context of *teruma* and *ma'aser*. In addition to produce that is still attached to the ground (*mechubar*), there is a separate discussion about produce that has already been detached (*talush*), which will be addressed later.

---

## Vineyard Derasha

### Two Verses

The Gemara, at the bottom of 87b, asks: now that we have derived from the words *chermesh* and *kama* that the worker's right applies to all forms of growing produce, why does the Torah also need to state the verse about the vineyard — *ki tavo becharem re'echa*? The verse about grain alone should suffice, and the rest could be derived from it. The Gemara answers, in the name of Rava: *lehilchotav* — the vineyard verse is needed to teach specific parameters of this *halacha*, as the *braita* proceeds to demonstrate through a careful *derasha* of each phrase in that verse.

### Ki Tavo

The *braita* begins with the phrase *ki tavo* — when you come. A *gezeira shava* is drawn from the same root in *lo tavo alav hashemesh*, the verse prohibiting an employer from delaying a worker's wages past sunset. Just as the subject there is a *po'el*, a hired laborer, so too here: the verse is speaking of a *po'el*, not merely someone passing through a vineyard.

### Jewish vs Non-Jewish

The phrase *becherem re'echa* — your friend's vineyard — is interpreted to mean *velo becherem goy*: the rules of the verse do not apply when working in a non-Jew's vineyard. This is a permissive reading: when the worker is employed by a non-Jew, the restrictions that accompany the right to eat do not apply — he is not prohibited, for example, from storing some for later or eating outside the moment of *gmar melacha*.

### Gezel Goy

This raises an immediate difficulty. The Gemara notes: *ha nicha leman d'amar gezel goy asur* — this formulation makes sense if one holds that stealing from a non-Jew is forbidden. In that case, the Torah's specification that the rules apply only in a Jew's vineyard provides a necessary dispensation for the *po'el* — telling him that taking produce in the course of his work is not theft. But *ela leman d'amar gezel goy mutar* — if one holds that stealing from a non-Jew is permitted, why would any special dispensation be required? The worker could simply take whatever he wished anyway.

This is a striking passage. The Gemara treats the view that *gezel goy* is *mutar* as a live option — not to endorse it, but as a methodological counterpoint. Tosafot addresses this directly. Citing *Rashi*'s reference to the *sugya* in Bava Kamma (*Hagozel Umachil*), Tosafot notes that even the lenient opinion in that *sugya* does not permit outright theft; at most it permits *afka'at halva'ato* — evading repayment of a loan — which is itself problematic, but is not straightforward theft. The Gemara there effectively rejects the view that *gezel mamash* from a non-Jew is *mutar*: *aval gezeila mamash modeh kuli alma de'asur*.

Tosafot then adds, in the name of the *Ri*, that there is a voice later in the tractate that does permit outright theft from a non-Jew — so the position is not entirely without a basis in the *sugya*. Nevertheless, Tosafot raises a further difficulty: there is a *pasuk* — *vehishav im koneihu* — from which the Gemara in a later context derives that one must deal honestly and not defraud a non-Jew, which seems to be an explicit prohibition. Tosafot suggests that even according to the view that *gezel goy* is technically *mutar*, that verse may prohibit it on grounds of *chillul Hashem*: the non-Jew trusted him and was conducting business with him, and to take advantage would constitute a desecration of God's name. The practical and dominant position, as reflected in the main *sugya* of Bava Kamma, is that *gezel goy* is *asur*.

The Gemara also derives from the phrase *becherem re'echa* — your friend's — that the allowance does not apply when working for *hekdesh*. Here the direction is reversed: with a Jewish employer the worker has the allowance; with *hekdesh* he does not. One might have thought that just as the Torah permits taking the owner's produce without it constituting theft, it might similarly waive the concern of *me'ila* for produce belonging to *hekdesh*. Tosafot entertains this *hava amina* and notes that it makes more sense if *me'ila* is understood as a species of *gezeila* — taking from *hekdesh* what belongs to it. If *me'ila* instead concerns impinging on the *kedusha* of consecrated property, it is harder to see why the Torah would have waived it. One possible way to construct the *hava amina* is a scenario where something is owned by *hekdesh* but does not possess *kedusha* — for instance, an object that fell into *hekdesh*'s field and was acquired through *kinyan chatzer* without explicit verbal consecration, as the *Ramban* discusses in some contexts.

### Eating Restrictions

Returning to the *derasha* of the vineyard verse: *ve'achalta* — and you shall eat — is interpreted to mean *ve'lo motzetz*: you may eat the grapes but you may not suck out their juice, because that would constitute *shtiya* (drinking) rather than *achila* (eating). The line between the two may seem fine, but the principle appears to be that the worker's right is to eat incidentally as he works — once he begins processing the grape into juice, he has crossed from eating into something different. Similarly, *anavim* — grapes — *ve'lo anavim ve'davar acher*: you may not eat grapes together with something else. *Rashi* explains that this does not mean taking a different fruit from a nearby tree, but rather that you may not add salt or some other enhancer to the grapes to make it easier to consume larger quantities. The right to eat is not a right to strategize one's consumption. *Savecha* — to your fill — excludes *achila gassa*, forced overeating beyond satiety.

---

## Worker vs Owner

### Like Owner

The phrase *kenafshecha* — like yourself — is interpreted in the *braita* as: *k'nefesh shel ba'al habayit kach nafsho shel po'el* — just as the owner is, so is the worker. And the application: *mah nafsho ochel u'patur af nafsho shel po'el ochel u'patur* — just as the owner may eat from his own grapes and is exempt from *teruma u'ma'aser*, so too the worker eats and is exempt.

### Before Gmar Melacha

The reason the owner is exempt is that the produce has not yet reached the stage of *gmar melacha* that creates an obligation in *teruma u'ma'aser* — a different use of the term *gmar melacha* than the one applying to the moment of harvesting. For *terumot u'ma'asrot*, *gmar melacha* refers to the completion of the standard processing: for vegetables, trimming off the leaves and stems; for grain, threshing, winnowing, and heaping into a smoothed mound; for grapes or olives intended for wine or oil, pressing and conversion. Once processing is complete and the produce is ready for market, it becomes obligated. But something additional is also required — a concept called *kovia*, a "fixing" of the produce's status that triggers the obligation. The primary *kovia min haTorah* is *rei'yat pnei habayit* — the produce being brought before the face of the house, i.e., into the home or, as we will see, into the *chatzer*.

### Purchaser Obligation

The *chidush* in the *braita* is that while the owner and the worker are exempt before these conditions are met, a purchaser who acquires the produce out in the field may not eat it without first separating *teruma u'ma'aser*. The purchase itself, it will emerge, functions as a *kovia* — a trigger that creates the obligation. But before working out why, the Gemara must first establish what the nature of that obligation is and on what level it applies.

---

## Vineyard Derasha (II)

### Until Full

The *braita* interprets *savecha* — your fill — to permit eating until genuinely satisfied, while at the same time excluding *achila gassa*, eating beyond one's fill in an artificially forced manner.

### No Own Vessel

*Ve'el kelyecha lo titen* — do not place into your own vessel — is read to delineate the temporal scope of the right: *b'sha'a she'ata noten l'kelyo shel ba'al habayit ata ochel* — at the time when you are placing into the owner's vessel, you may eat; when you are not placing into the owner's vessel, you may not eat. The right attaches specifically while the worker is actively engaged in harvesting, placing produce into the owner's containers. This confirms that the right is tied to the moment of active labor during *gmar melacha* — the harvesting — and not to periods outside that work.

---

## Gmar Melacha & Kovia

### Rei'yat Pnei Bayit

The Gemara cites Rabbi Yannai: *ein hatevel mitchayev b'ma'aser ad sheyeira'eh pnei habayit* — untithed produce does not become obligated in *ma'aser* until it is brought before the face of the house. The source is the verse *bi'arti hakodesh min habayit* — I have removed the holy from the house — which implies that the obligation of *teruma u'ma'aser* pertains to produce once it is situated in the house.

To understand what is actually at stake, it helps to trace the full structure of the obligation. Two conditions must be satisfied before produce becomes obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot*: first, *gmar melacha* — the completion of processing — and second, *kovia* — something that "fixes" the produce's status and renders it fully obligated. The primary *kovia* according to Rabbi Yannai is *rei'yat pnei habayit*. In addition to being brought into the house, other things function as *kovia*: cooking the produce, the onset of *Shabbat*, and — crucially for our *sugya* — *mecher*, a sale. These latter categories are mostly *d'rabbanan*.

### Chatzer Kovia

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees and holds that even bringing the produce into the *chatzer* — the enclosed yard adjacent to the house — constitutes *kovia* at the Torah level. His source is the verse *ve'achlu bish'arecha v'save'u* — they shall eat within your gates and be satisfied — referring to the *ma'aser* given to the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow. Since *sha'arecha* refers to the city gates, and the fields lie outside the city, produce brought within the gates is treated as having been "brought in" and thus becomes obligated.

Rabbi Yannai, for his part, does not dispute that the word *bish'arecha* appears; he reads it differently. For him, it teaches that the produce must be brought in *derech sha'ar* — through the front gate — as opposed to *derech gagot v'karfifot*, i.e., through the roof or through a back enclosure. Only entry through the proper front entrance renders the produce obligated; bringing it in through a back route does not.

### Chatzer Defined

Rabbi Yochanan's position that the *chatzer* is *kovia* comes with an important qualification. His proof-text and his reasoning establish what kind of *chatzer* qualifies: *mah bayit mishtamer, af chatzer mishtamer* — just as a house is protected and enclosed, so too the *chatzer* must be protected, i.e., fenced or walled. An open, unguarded yard to which anyone has access does not have the status of a *chatzer* for these purposes. The *chatzer* must resemble a house in its degree of enclosure.

---

## Field Purchaser

### Field Obligation

Rabbi Chanina raises a challenge from the *braita* itself. The *braita* states *kenafshecha* — just as you are, so is the worker — deriving that just as the owner eats from his grapes and is exempt from *teruma u'ma'aser*, so too the worker eats and is exempt. The Gemara infers from this contrast: *ha-loke'ach chayav* — the implication is that a purchaser out in the field *would* be obligated. But how can a purchaser be obligated for *terumot u'ma'asrot* out in the field, before the produce has been brought to the house or even to the *chatzer*? There is no *rei'yat pnei habayit* and no *rei'yat pnei hachatzer*. This seems to show that *rei'yat pnei habayit* is not an absolute requirement.

### Fig Tree Case

Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty with a specific scenario: *hacha bite'enah ha-omedet begina venofah noteh lechatzer askinan* — the case involves a fig tree standing in the garden (*gina*), whose foliage extends over into the *chatzer*. Crucially, the *gina* is not the *chatzer*: it is a garden plot, analogous to a field, where the produce grows. The *chatzer* is the enclosed yard. For the opinion that the house is the operative location, the scenario is that the foliage extends into the house itself. Either way, the fruit that hangs within the *chatzer* or the house does satisfy the condition of *rei'yat pnei habayit* or *rei'yat pnei hachatzer*.

But then a new question arises: *ba'al habayit nami nichayiv* — if the produce is in the *chatzer*, why isn't the owner also obligated? Why is the *ba'al habayit* still exempt?

### Tree vs Fruit

The Gemara answers: *ba'al habayit einav bite'inato veloke'ach einav benofcho* — the owner's eyes are on the tree, while the purchaser's eyes are on the fruit. *Rashi* explains as follows: the owner's job — and by extension the worker's job — is to harvest the entire tree. Even if some of the fruit physically hangs in the *chatzer*, the owner and worker are conceptually located wherever the tree is, i.e., in the garden, in the field. If asked where the harvesting is taking place, they would answer: out there, where the tree stands. Their relationship is to the tree, not to this particular piece of fruit. Therefore, even though the fruit is physically within the *chatzer*, there is no *rei'yat pnei habayit* for them — conceptually, the harvest is still occurring in the field.

This reading is deeply congruent with a classic type of *Gemara* analysis: when a tree's trunk is in one legal domain and its foliage extends into another — say, the trunk is in *Eretz Yisrael* and the fruit hangs over the border into *Chutz La'aretz* — the question of where the fruit is "located" for legal purposes turns on exactly this kind of conceptual analysis. Here too: the owner says the fruit belongs to the tree and the tree is in the garden.

The purchaser, by contrast, has no interest in the tree. He bought a single apple — or a specific quantity of fruit. He is standing in the *chatzer*, he has his fruit, and he is done. Conceptually, the purchaser is in the *chatzer* with his fruit, and that satisfies *rei'yat pnei habayit*.

### Job Completion

Tosafot offers a different explanation that does not require the tree-in-the-garden setup at all, and suggests that the Gemara's scenario need not be taken literally. According to Tosafot, the real distinction is not about where the tree is located but about whether *gmar melacha* has been completed. *Gmar melacha*, says Tosafot, is not measured fruit by fruit — it is measured by the completion of the job as a whole. Even if the owner or the worker brings one apple into the house, if thousands more remain to be picked, the job is not done. There is no *gmar melacha* yet, and therefore no obligation in *terumot u'ma'asrot* regardless of where the produce physically is. The purchaser who bought only that one apple, however, is done — that is his entire purchase, his *gmar melacha* is complete — and he therefore cannot eat it without separating *terumot u'ma'asrot*.

Tosafot's reading explains why the Gemara constructs a scenario with the tree in the garden: it would seem strange for a fig tree to grow in a front yard, so the Gemara describes it as growing in the garden with the foliage reaching over — but the substantive distinction, says Tosafot, is simply job completion versus job completion.

*Rashi*'s reading is certainly the more natural *pshat* of the Gemara. But in either case, the practical bottom line — as the Gemara will note — is that on a *d'rabbanan* level, purchase itself functions as a *kovia*, substituting for *rei'yat pnei habayit*. The Gemara's elaborate constructions here are attempting to work out the distinction on a *d'oraita* level.

---

## Beis Hino Case

### Torah Level

The Gemara now asks a fundamental question: if we are working on a *d'oraita* level, how can a purchaser ever be obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot* from the Torah at all? A *braita* is cited: *mipnei mah charvu chanuyot shel beit hino* — why were the shops of Beit Hino destroyed three years before Jerusalem? Because they relied exclusively on the letter of Torah law and disregarded rabbinic enactment. Their practice was grounded in two *derashot*: *aser ta'aser* — you shall tithe — is followed by *ve'achalta*, you shall eat — *velo mocher*, but not one who sells. If you are selling your produce rather than eating it yourself, you have no Torah obligation of *ma'aser*. The other *derasha*: *tvuat zar'echa* — the produce of your planting — *velo loke'ach*, not one who purchases it. A buyer who did not grow the produce has no Torah obligation of *teruma u'ma'aser*.

The Gemara does not contest these derivations on a Torah level. The problem with Beit Hino was that they were ignoring the *m'derabbanan* obligation, not that their Torah-level analysis was wrong.

### Not Your Seed

The upshot is stark: *min haTorah*, only a *ba'al habayit* — the original grower — is obligated in *teruma u'ma'aser*. A seller who intends his produce for the market, not for personal consumption, is exempt, and a purchaser is exempt because the produce is not *tvuat zar'echo* — not the product of his own planting. Taken to its logical conclusion, this means that a chain of commercial transactions could, on a Torah level, result in no one ever separating *teruma u'ma'aser*. The Gemara does not contest this conclusion. It only applies to the Torah level, and the rabbis addressed it through the *d'rabbanan* obligation of purchasers and sellers alike.

### Sale Obligation

This also resolves the conceptual difficulty raised earlier: the contrast in the *braita* between the exempt worker and the potentially obligated purchaser cannot be operating at the *d'oraita* level, since a purchaser has no *d'oraita* obligation at all. The Gemara concludes that the entire contrast is *m'derabbanan* — the verse is a mere *asmachta*, a textual support for a rabbinic enactment. On the *d'rabbanan* level, *mecher* — purchase — functions as a *kovia*, and a purchaser becomes obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot* at the moment of acquisition. That is what distinguishes the purchaser from the worker in practice.

Tosafot, troubled by other *sugyot* that seem to assume purchasers are always obligated, introduces a distinction between purchasing before and after *gmar melacha*. One opinion holds that if the buyer acquires the produce before *gmar melacha* and then completes the processing himself, the produce is considered *tvuat zar'echo* — he was the owner at the critical moment — and he is obligated. But if he buys after *gmar melacha*, he is exempt. A second and ultimately more compelling opinion holds the opposite: once the original owner completes *gmar melacha*, an obligation of *terumot u'ma'asrot* inheres in the produce itself as a fixed status. Whoever subsequently holds it remains obligated. The exemption for a purchaser applies only when he acquired the produce before *gmar melacha* was reached — that is, before the critical moment when the obligation was created — and thus the obligation never attached to him as a consequence of someone else's ownership at that moment. This reading is preferable both practically — because it means that almost all commercially sold grain remains obligated, consistent with normative practice — and conceptually, because it parallels the rule that a non-Jew's ownership exempts produce only if he owns it at the moment of *gmar melacha*. The obligation is understood as a status that crystallizes at a specific moment and then inheres in the produce.

---

## Post-Harvest Rights

### Two Domains

Returning to the workers: the Gemara notes that, from the *pesukim* alone, we have established two domains separately — *adam b'mechubar*, a person's right to eat when produce is still attached and being harvested, and *shor b'talush*, an ox's right to eat (or more precisely, the prohibition on muzzling the ox) when produce has already been detached and is being processed in threshing. The question is how to extend each domain to the other case: how do we know a person may eat *b'talush*, and how do we know an ox may eat *b'mechubar*?

### Kal Va-Chomer

The Gemara proposes a *kal va-chomer* for the first extension: *umah shor she'ein ochel b'mechubar ochel b'talush* — an ox, which has no right to eat when produce is *mechubar*, nonetheless may eat when it is *talush*. *Adam she'ochel b'mechubar* — a person who does have the right to eat when produce is *mechubar* — should certainly have the right to eat when it is *talush* as well.

### Muzzling Only Ox

The *kal va-chomer* is rejected. *Mah leshor sheken atah metzuveh chasimato* — an ox is categorically more protected than a worker in one respect: if you muzzle an ox while it is threshing, you transgress a biblical prohibition. If you prevent a worker from eating by muzzling him — or through some equivalent stipulation — you may be violating his monetary rights, but you do not transgress the *lav* of *lo tachsom shor bedisho*. Since the ox's right to eat *b'talush* is bound up with a stricter prohibition, perhaps the ox's right is limited to the ox, and the *kal va-chomer* fails.

The Gemara then turns the logic around: *veyehei adam metzuveh chasimato mikal va-chomer mishor* — perhaps we should derive from this same *kal va-chomer* that one *does* transgress a prohibition when muzzling a worker. After all, *umah shor she'ein atah metzuveh le'hachayoto* — an ox, which you are not commanded to keep alive (you may slaughter it for food) — *atah metzuveh chasimato* — you are nonetheless prohibited from muzzling it. *Adam she'atah metzuveh le'hachayoso* — a human being, whom you are commanded to keep alive — surely you should be prohibited from muzzling him and should transgress the *lav*. The Torah deflects this with the word *kenafshecha*: just as you yourself, if you choose not to eat, do not transgress the prohibition — the prohibition applies only to an ox, not to a person.

### Kama Kama

With the *kal va-chomer* thus exhausted in both directions, the Gemara turns to a textual doubling. The word *kama* — standing grain — appears twice in the *pasuk*: once in *ki tavo bekamat re'echa* and once in *vechermesh lo tanif al kamat re'echa*. Since one occurrence suffices to tell us that a person may eat *b'mechubar*, the redundant second occurrence is redirected: *tineihu inyan le'adam b'talush* — apply it to teach that a person also has the right to eat when the produce is *talush*.

### Ki Tavo Includes

The Gemara adds an alternative source. One need not rely on the doubling at all, because *ki tavo becharme re'echa* — when you come into your friend's vineyard — does not specify what kind of work the worker is hired to do. Perhaps he was hired to carry (*likatef*) the already-harvested grapes rather than to pick them. Since the Torah grants the right to eat in the vineyard without specifying the nature of the work, it encompasses both the picker and the carrier — and the carrier is working with *talush*. This source may be more straightforward and closer to *pshat*.

---

## Ox Rights B'Mechubar

### Ox Attached Rights

Having established that a person has the right to eat *b'talush*, the Gemara now turns to the corresponding question: how do we know an ox has the right to eat *b'mechubar*? The *pasuk* of *lo tachsom* speaks only of threshing, which is a *talush* context.

### Keep Alive Only Humans

A *kal va-chomer* is proposed: *mah adam she'eino ochel b'talush* — a person who does not (explicitly from the *pasuk*) have the right to eat *b'talush* — *ochel b'mechubar* — does have the right to eat *b'mechubar*. *Shor she'ochel b'talush* — an ox that does eat *b'talush* — *eino din she'yochal b'mechubar*? — should certainly be permitted to eat *b'mechubar* as well. This *kal va-chomer* rests on the premise that the person does not have the *talush* right from the *pesukim*, even though we have just established that he does — so the Gemara is working here from the surface reading of the *pesukim* alone, which do not explicitly grant it.

The *kal va-chomer* is challenged: *mah adam sheken atah metzuveh le'hachayoto* — perhaps the person has the right to eat *b'mechubar* specifically because you are commanded to keep him alive. An ox, which you are not commanded to keep alive, might not have that right.

### Reverse Kal Va-Chomer

The Gemara then inverts the *kal va-chomer*: perhaps you *are* obligated to keep an ox alive, derived as follows — *umah adam she'ee atah metzuveh al chasimato* — a human being, whom you are not prohibited from muzzling — *atah metzuveh le'hachayoso* — you are nonetheless commanded to keep alive. *Shor she'atah metzuveh al chasimato* — an ox, which you are prohibited from muzzling — *eino din she'atah metzuveh le'hachayoso*? — should you not certainly be obligated to keep it alive? This would imply a prohibition on slaughtering oxen altogether — a conclusion that would have surprised the many *pesukim* permitting the consumption of meat.

### Fellow Human Only

The Torah deflects this with the verse *v'chei achicha imach* — and your fellow shall live with you: *achicha v'lo shor* — your fellow human being, not an ox. The obligation to sustain life applies only to human beings.

### Re'cha Re'cha

With the *kal va-chomer* neutralized, the Gemara turns again to textual doubling. The word *re'echa* — your friend — appears twice in the *pasuk* about harvesting standing grain: *ki tavo bekamat re'echa* and *vechermesh lo tanif al kamat re'echa*. One occurrence of *re'echa* tells us that the *adam*, the worker, may eat *b'mechubar* — that is explicit. The other occurrence of *re'echa* is likewise not needed to teach the worker's right *b'talush*, which we have already derived. So: *im eino inyan le'adam b'mechubar, teneihu inyan le'shor b'mechubar* — since it is not needed for the person, apply it to teach that an ox too may eat *b'mechubar* when it is engaged in harvesting attached produce.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 89

## Worker Rights & Ox

### Opening

The daf opens in the middle of a cluster of *mitzvot* from the Torah concerning the rights of workers in the field. The Torah states that when one enters a friend's vineyard, the *Chazal* understand this as applying specifically to a worker who has been granted the right to eat from the produce he is harvesting — but not to store it away in his own vessel. In parallel, the Torah commands *lo tachsom shor bedisho*: one may not muzzle an ox while it is threshing. These two *mitzvot* together establish that those who work with produce in the field may eat from what they are handling, subject to carefully delimited conditions regarding the type of produce and the stage of its development.

The Gemara has been working through a fundamental question: how do we know that these *halachot* apply equally to detached produce? The Torah speaks of one who is actively picking grapes — produce still attached to the vine — or, in the parallel case of the ox, of an animal working with produce in that same attached state. Threshing, by contrast, involves grain already cut from the ground. How do we extend these laws from one context to the other?

### Torah Sources

The discussion that has been running through the preceding amud involves deriving these extensions from *pesukim*, and the Gemara has just concluded an argument via *gezeirah shavah*. We now arrive at an alternative position.

### Ravina's Position

*Ravina* asserts that no *gezeirah shavah* is needed at all. *Lo adam betalush velo shor bemechubar tzerichi k'ra* — neither the rule that a human worker may eat from already-detached produce, nor the rule that an ox may not be muzzled while working with still-attached produce, requires a special derivation. The reason: *lo tachsom shor bedisho* already contains both cases implicitly.

The argument unfolds at the top of 89a. Since we learn via *gezeirah shavah* from *Shabbat* — where the verse says *l'ma'an yanuach shorchecha*, "that your ox may rest," and expands this to *kol behemetecha*, all your animals — the prohibition of *lo tachsom shor* is likewise not limited to an ox. It applies to any animal involved in such work. If that is so, why did the Torah specifically write *shor*, ox? The Gemara answers: *leakushei chosem l'nechsam u'nechsam l'chosem* — to create an equation between the muzzler and the muzzled, between the human agent and the animal. Had the Torah simply written *lo tadush bechasimah* — do not thresh in a state of muzzling — it would have spoken only to one party. By writing *lo tachsom shor*, it places both the one who muzzles (the human) and the one being muzzled (the animal) within the same *pasuk*, forging an explicit equivalence.

The consequence is a double inference: just as the human muzzler (*chosem*) may eat from produce that is *mechubar*, attached to the ground, at the moment of its being detached, so too the muzzled animal (*nechsam*) may eat from *mechubar* produce. And just as the ox may eat from *talush*, already-detached produce — so long as *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser* has not yet occurred — so too the human worker may eat from *talush* produce. The word *shor* thus generates this full bilateral equation without any need for an additional *gezeirah shavah*.

---

## Gezerah Shavah

### Shor from Shabbat

The Gemara establishes that the word *shor* in *lo tachsom shor bedisho* cannot be read as limiting the prohibition to oxen alone. Through a *gezeirah shavah* linking the word *shor* here to the word *shor* in the Shabbat verse — *l'ma'an yanuach shorchecha* — where the context immediately expands to all animals (*kol behemetecha*) — we learn that here too, the prohibition and the associated *halachot* apply to any animal engaged in such work.

### Why 'Ox'?

This raises an immediate question: if the *gezeirah shavah* teaches that *shor* here is not meant to limit the law to oxen, then why did the Torah bother writing *shor* at all? The answer, as articulated above, is that the word serves a different structural purpose entirely. *Im ken lichtov Rachmana lo tadush bechasimah* — had the Torah simply stated "do not thresh in a muzzled state," it would have addressed only one dimension of the act. By writing *lo tachsom shor*, the Torah places both the human who does the muzzling and the animal that is muzzled side by side in a single formulation, enabling the equation between their respective rights and obligations.

### Logical Equation

The resulting logical equation operates in both directions. The *chosem*, the human muzzler, may eat from *mechubar* produce — produce still attached to the ground — at the moment of *gmar melacha* when it is being detached. This applies equally to the *nechsam*, the animal. Conversely, the *nechsam*, the animal, may eat from *talush* produce — produce already cut from the ground — until the *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser*; and the same right extends symmetrically to the *chosem*, the human worker. Ravina therefore derives all these extensions from the word *shor* itself, without recourse to any additional hermeneutic device.

---

## Threshing Baraitot

### Growth from Ground

The Gemara now introduces a series of *baraitot* that use the paradigm of *dayish* — threshing — to derive the scope and limits of the worker's right to eat and the prohibition of muzzling. The first *baraita* reasons as follows: *mah dayish meyuchad davar she'gidulei karka u'poel ochel bo* — what makes threshing distinct is that it involves things that grow from the ground, and a worker may eat from such produce. Therefore, *af kol she'gidulei karka poel ochel bo* — the same applies to anything that grows from the ground: a worker may eat from it under the relevant conditions.

The implication is restrictive as well as expansive. *Yatza hacholev vehamachbetz vehamagben* — this excludes the one who milks animals, the one who curdles milk, and the one who makes cheese. All of these are legitimate farm activities, but they do not involve *gidulei karka*, produce grown from the ground. Therefore, *ein poel ochel bo* — a worker engaged in milking or cheese-making does not have the Torah-granted right to consume a portion of what he is handling.

### Exclusions

The exclusion of milking, curdling, and cheese-making rests on a single principle: the Torah's entitlement to eat from one's labor applies only where the work is performed on produce that emerged from the ground. Animal products, even when produced on a farm, do not fall within this category. The worker handling milk or cheese may not invoke the prerogative of *lo tachsom shor bedisho* or the parallel *kerem re'acha* verse to claim the right to consume part of his employer's goods.

### Challenge

The Gemara challenges the necessity of deriving this rule from the paradigm of *dayish*. *Miki tavo bekerem re'acha nafka* — does this not already follow from the verse "when you enter your friend's vineyard"? A vineyard produces grapes; the parallel verse speaks of standing grain (*kama*). Both are explicitly agricultural, clearly *gidulei karka*. Why must we look to *dayish* to establish the ground-growth requirement?

### Response

The Gemara responds: *tzericha* — the repetition is necessary. One might have read the broad language of *kama* — standing grain ready for harvest — so expansively as to include even things that do not literally grow from the ground. Since the word *kama* is used to extend the *halacha* beyond vineyards to all manner of produce being gathered, one might suppose that any "standing" product awaiting collection — even animal products, in theory — could be included. The repetition via *dayish* comes to forestall this: no, the right is limited to what actually grows from the ground.

---

## Gmar Melacha

### Dayish Timing

A second *baraita* addresses a different dimension of *dayish*: its relationship to the concept of *gmar melacha*. The *baraita* reasons: *mah dayish meyuchad davar shebishat gmar melacha poel ochel bo* — what distinguishes *dayish* is that the worker eats from it at the time of *gmar melacha*, the completion of the work. And therefore, *af kol shebishat gmar melacha poel ochel bo* — similarly, for any produce, it is specifically at the time of *gmar melacha* that the worker's right to eat applies.

This formulation is admittedly difficult, since threshing is not itself the moment of *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser*. The full sequence runs: threshing, winnowing, sorting, smoothing the pile — and only that final smoothing (*meruach bakari*) renders grain obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot*. Rashi reads *shebishat gmar melacha* as meaning that the worker is completing the work in this moment — *de'achshav hu gomer melachato* — though the precise meaning remains somewhat elusive. One workable reading is that *dayish* is the paradigm case where grain that is in the process of being brought to completion from its raw harvested state remains available for the worker to eat; it is from this paradigm that we derive the general principle that the worker may eat during the process that leads to *gmar melacha*, but not after.

### Weeding Excluded

The *baraita* applies its principle restrictively: *yatza hamenakesh beshumim ube-vatzalim* — this comes to exclude one who is weeding a field of garlic or onions. *Ho'il ve-ein gmar melacha ein poel ochel bahem* — since this weeding activity does not constitute *gmar melacha* — it is not an act of harvesting the produce from the ground — the worker engaged in this task has no right to eat from the garlic or onions.

### Challenge 2

The Gemara again challenges the derivation from *dayish*: *me'el kelyecha lo titein nafka* — does this not already follow from the verse *el kelyecha lo titein*, "do not put it in your vessel"? That verse, in context, addresses the moment when the worker is actively picking produce and detaching it — the moment of *gmar melacha* in the sense of removal from the ground. From there we already know that the right to eat applies specifically when one is engaged in the act of harvesting, not at preparatory stages. Why invoke *dayish* once more?

### Small Onions Case

The Gemara's response is subtle and striking. *Af al gav d'ka mishlaf kitini mibeini alimi* — even in a case where one is removing small, immature onions from among the larger, developing ones. This is a form of pruning: the small onions will never mature and their presence inhibits the growth of the larger ones. By removing them, the worker is directly handling produce — onions — and physically extracting them from the ground. One might think this resembles the act of harvesting and that the worker could therefore eat from the small onions he is removing.

The *baraita* teaches otherwise. The worker's *gmar melacha* consists in completing the intended work on the crop — harvesting the mature product. When he removes the small onions, his action is aimed at the benefit of the large onions, not at bringing the small onions to their own completion. Since this act is not a *gmar melacha* with respect to the small onions, the worker may not eat them, even though he is in direct physical contact with them and is indeed pulling them from the earth. A simple case of weeding might be excluded on the grounds that the worker is not even directly working on the edible produce itself; but this case — where he is directly handling the small onions — required the additional derivation from *dayish* to clarify that it is nonetheless forbidden.

---

## Ma'aser vs. Challa

### Pre-Ma'aser Stage

A third *baraita* sharpens the picture further. *Mah dayish meyuchad davar shelo nigmar melachto l'ma'aser poel ochel bo* — what is distinctive about *dayish* is that the produce has not yet reached *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser*, and during this time the worker may eat from it. After threshing, the grain must still be winnowed, sorted, and piled before it becomes obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot*. Until that final stage, the worker retains the right to eat.

The affirmative principle: *af kol shelo nigmar melachto l'ma'aser poel ochel bo* — any produce that has not yet reached *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser* may be eaten by the worker. Once it has passed that threshold, the right lapses.

### Pressed Dates/Figs

The *baraita* illustrates the exclusion: *yatza habodeh bitmarim uvegrogros* — this excludes one who is separating pressed dates or pressed figs (*grogros*). Dates and figs that have been compressed together for storage or sale, and are then being separated out, have already undergone their *gmar melacha*. They were picked from the tree and processed; there is nothing further to be done to render them fit. Therefore *ein poel ochel bo* — the worker engaged in separating them may not eat from them.

### Unripe Dates

A contradiction immediately surfaces: a different *baraita* explicitly states that one who separates pressed dates and figs *may* eat from them. *Amar Rav Papa*: the permissive *baraita* deals with a special case — *bituchlani* — dates or figs that were harvested before ripening and stored in baskets designed to allow them to ripen gradually, a process closely analogous to modern controlled-ripening in shipping. In that case, the process is not yet complete at the time of pressing and storage; the final act of separating them, once they have ripened, constitutes the actual completion of the work — *gmar melacha* has not yet occurred — and therefore the worker may eat. The restrictive *baraita*, by contrast, speaks of produce that was already fully ripe when pressed: there, *gmar melacha* preceded the separation, and the worker has no right.

---

## Challa Extension

### Pre-Challa Stage

A fourth *baraita* pushes the boundary still further. *Mah dayish meyuchad davar shelo nigmar melachto lechalla upoel ochel bo* — what distinguishes *dayish* is that the *melacha* for *challa* has not yet been completed, and the worker may therefore eat. The obligation of *challa* arises at a later stage than the obligation of *ma'aser*: *ma'aser* applies once the grain has been piled and smoothed, whereas *challa* applies once flour has been ground, water added, and dough kneaded. The implication of this *baraita* is that even a worker grinding grain into flour — a stage past the *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser* — retains the right to eat, since *gmar melacha* for *challa* has not yet occurred.

### Kneading Onward

The *baraita* defines the exclusion: *yatza halosh vehamikatef vehaofeh shenigmar melachto lechalla* — this excludes one who kneads, one who shapes the dough, and one who bakes, since at those stages *gmar melacha* for *challa* has been reached. From kneading onward, the worker loses the right to eat freely from the dough.

### Contradiction

This fourth *baraita* creates a direct tension with the third. The third *baraita* stated that the worker may eat only until *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser*. The fourth *baraita* implies that even after *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser* — when the grain is already in a stage that triggers *ma'aser* obligation — the worker continues to eat until *gmar melacha* for *challa*. The Gemara flags this: *vehalo nigmara melachto lemaaser* — is it not already at the stage that obligates it in *ma'aser*?

---

## Resolution

### Abaye: Chutz L'aretz

*Abaye* proposes a solution: *lo kashya bechutza laaretz askinan delika maaser* — there is no difficulty, because the fourth *baraita* is speaking of a case in *chutz la'aretz*, outside the Land of Israel, where there is no obligation of *ma'aser*. Without a *ma'aser* obligation to mark *gmar melacha*, the relevant threshold shifts to the obligation of *challa*, which does apply in *chutz la'aretz* — and the worker therefore eats until that later stage.

### Objection

The Gemara rejects this immediately: *ei hachi challa nami lika* — if there is no *ma'aser* in *chutz la'aretz*, the same should apply to *challa*. The obligation of *challa* in *chutz la'aretz* is at most rabbinic in force, and the worker's Torah-level entitlement to eat should not be governed by a rabbinic threshold. The two *baraitot* therefore cannot be distinguished by geography alone.

### Seven Years

The Gemara proposes an alternative: *ela leolam baaretz velo kashya besheva shekavshu uvesheva shechalku* — in fact, both *baraitot* are speaking of the Land of Israel, and there is no contradiction, because there existed a historical period during which *challa* applied but *ma'aser* did not. During the fourteen years of conquest and division of the land — the seven years of conquest (*sheva shekavshu*) and the seven years of division (*sheva shechalku*) — the land had not yet attained the full *kedushah* of *Eretz Yisrael* required for *ma'aser*. Yet the tradition, as cited by the Gemara, is explicit: *sheva shekavshu vesheva shechalku nitchayvu bechalla velo nitchayvu bemaaser* — during those fourteen years, the people were obligated in *challa* but not in *ma'aser*. This is because the verse introducing *challa* (*bevoachem el haaretz*) triggers from the moment of entry into the land, even before full possession, whereas *ma'aser* required the land to be held as a proper inheritance.

That said, the Gemara itself registers some unease about a *baraita* concerning worker rights being framed around a historical situation from the period of initial conquest. But theoretically, in that narrow window, a worker grinding grain would be past no *ma'aser* threshold (since none applied) yet not past the *challa* threshold — and the fourth *baraita* would apply.

The Gemara then offers a decisive reframing: *midi maaser ka garim gemar melacha ka garim* — is it *ma'aser* itself that matters, or is it *gmar melacha*? The point is that *ma'aser* does not create the worker's obligation or the limit on his right; rather, the stages of *ma'aser* liability serve as *indicators* of completion.
