The Torah chose the stages of *ma'aser* to demarcate what counts as the end of the work process. It follows that even in a situation where *ma'aser* does not formally apply — whether in *chutz la'aretz* or in the fourteen years — the underlying concept of *gmar melacha* still governs, because that is what the *ma'aser* stages were measuring all along. The worker's right lapses when the produce has reached a stage of completion, not merely when a formal obligation of *ma'aser* has been triggered.

### Ravina Synthesis

*Ravina* resolves the contradiction between the two *baraitot* directly: *kroch v'sani* — combine them into one. *Mah dayish meyuchad davar shelo nigmar melachto l'ma'aser ul'challah upoel ochel bo* — *dayish* is distinctive in that the *melacha* is not yet complete for either *ma'aser* or *challa*, and the worker may eat. *Af kol shelo nigmar melachto l'ma'aser ul'challah poel ochel bo* — anything not yet at *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser* and for *challa* a worker may eat from. Rather than two competing limits, the *baraitot* together describe a single, composite condition.

### Interpretations

The question then becomes: if we require that *gmar melacha* have not yet occurred for *both* *ma'aser* and *challa*, and *challa* is the later stage, does the worker effectively always eat until *challa*? The *Raavad* reads it differently: once you combine the two *baraitot*, *ma'aser* takes precedence as the operative limit. When two thresholds are stated — A and B, with B later than A — the practical limit is A. The worker may eat until *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser*; the mention of *challa* adds nothing beyond that.

Most *Rishonim* — *Rashi* and *Tosafot* among them — understand it differently. They hold that the relevant threshold depends on the intended use of the produce. If the grain will not be made into dough — for example, produce destined to be eaten as parched grain, or fruit being processed in some other way — then the limit is *gmar melacha* for *ma'aser*. If, however, the grain is in the process of becoming dough and ultimately bread — the normative use of grain — then the worker retains his right to eat until *gmar melacha* for *challa*. The reasoning is that when the entire purpose of the process is the production of bread, one cannot view grain in a pile as "done"; it is conceptually incomplete until it has become dough. The *Ramban* offers additional explanations, but the *Rashi*–*Tosafot* position represents the dominant reading.

---

## Charring Question

### Charring Issue

The Gemara raises a new *she'eilah*: *poel mahu sheyahev ba'or v'yochal* — may a worker go ahead and grill or char the grain in fire before eating it? The issue connects to an earlier ruling that the worker may not eat the produce with *davar acher* — an additional substance — such as salt or bread, which would cause him to eat more than he would otherwise. Grilling is not an additive; there is no foreign substance involved. Yet it renders the grain considerably more palatable and could lead the worker to eat far more than he would in its raw state. Is that permissible or not?

### Wine & Brine

The Gemara seeks an answer from a *baraita*: *rashai baal habayis l'hashkos poalim yayin kedei shelo yochlu anavim harbei* — the owner may provide his workers with wine before they start, so that they will be full and not eat so many grapes while harvesting. *V'rashai poalin litbol pitan batzir kedei sheyochlu anavim harbe* — conversely, workers may dip their bread in brine during their lunch break in order to make themselves thirsty, so that they will be inclined to eat more grapes when they resume. The Gemara infers from this that we are not concerned about actions that make the person more or less inclined to eat, as long as nothing is added to the produce itself. By extension, grilling — which makes no addition — should be permissible.

### Distinction

The Gemara rejects this inference. *Lachshurei gavra lo kamibei lan* — making the person more or less fit to eat is not the question we are asking. The owner can give wine, the workers can eat brine, because all of that affects the person, not the produce. *Ki kamibei lan lachshurei peira mai* — what we are asking is whether one may do something to alter the produce itself, to transform it into a more edible form. The Torah entitles the worker to eat the produce as it comes to him in the field; the question is whether he may perform a further act on the produce — specifically, subjecting it to fire — before eating it.

---

## Head of Rows

### No Charring

The Gemara brings a *baraita* to address this question: *poalin ochlin anavim berashei umaniyot shelahem* — workers may eat grapes at the head of their rows. Rashi explains: in the course of harvesting, there is no opportunity to stop and eat mid-row; only when a worker reaches the end of a row and must pause to turn around does he have a natural moment to eat a few grapes. *U'bilvad shelo yehavvehu ba'or* — but they may not grill them in fire. This appears to resolve the *she'eilah*: charring is prohibited.

### Bitur Melacha

The Gemara, however, deflects this proof. *Hatam mishum bitul melacha* — there, the prohibition is not about the permissibility of altering the produce, but about *bitur melacha*, wasting the owner's time. The workers eat at the head of rows precisely so as not to interrupt the work mid-row and waste the owner's time. The prohibition on grilling is similarly motivated: taking time to grill the grapes would constitute *bitur melacha*, a misuse of the time the owner is paying for, not a violation of any rule about what may be done to the produce itself.

### Wife & Children

This leads the Gemara to refine the question: *ki kamibei lan heicha de'ika ishto uvanav mai* — what we are really asking is the following scenario: what if the worker's wife and children are present, and while he continues harvesting, they prepare the grain or grapes by grilling it, so that when he pauses he can eat it without any loss of time? In that case, *bitur melacha* is not an issue — the worker himself has not stopped working; others have done the preparation. Does the worker then have a right to eat the grilled produce? The Gemara leaves this as an open question.

---

## Prohibited Preps

### Methods Forbidden

A further *baraita* is introduced: *lo yehavvev ba'or v'yochal v'lo yachmor b'adama v'yochal v'lo yafriach al gabei hasela v'yochal* — the worker may not grill the produce in fire and eat it, may not bury it in warm earth to heat it and eat it, and may not break it on a rock and eat it. Three prohibited methods of preparation are enumerated: fire, warm earth, and crushing on a rock.

### Hand Crushing OK

However, *aval mafriach hu al yad al yad v'ochel* — the worker may crush the produce with his hand and eat it. Crushing by hand is permitted because it is essentially part of the act of eating itself, not a distinct preparatory process.

### Question

The Gemara interrogates the rationale of this *baraita*. Are these prohibitions about *davar acher* — about altering the produce to make it more palatable, causing the worker to eat more — or are they about *bitur melacha*, wasting the owner's time?

### Rock Argument

The Gemara pushes on the rock-breaking case specifically: *sela mai mitukei peira ika* — how does breaking produce on a rock sweeten it or make it more edible? If the concern is about improving the produce's palatability, rock-breaking is a difficult fit. *Tosafot* suggests it might refer to a hard-shelled fruit like a walnut, where crushing on a rock releases the interior. The Gemara's response is that this objection does not conclusively prove the rationale is *bitur melacha*; *ei efshar d'lo mimtiki purti* — even rock-breaking might slightly improve the produce's texture or release some of its juices. The question of whether the underlying rationale is *davar acher* or *bitur melacha* remains unresolved from this *baraita* alone.

---

## Comprehensive Rights

### Harvesting Rights

The Gemara now introduces a comprehensive *baraita* summarizing the worker's rights: workers who are harvesting figs, dates, grapes, and olives — the four major agricultural products — may eat from what they are working with and are exempt from *ma'aser* on what they consume. The exemption from *ma'aser* reflects a principle established elsewhere in the Gemara: since the Torah granted the worker the right to eat, his consumption is not considered a form of *mekach*, a purchase, which would otherwise render the produce obligated in *ma'aser*.

### Bread Prohibition

Despite these broad rights, the *baraita* states: *b'pittan lo yochlu ella im ken natlu reshut mi'baal habayit* — workers may not eat the produce together with their bread unless the owner has explicitly given them permission to do so. This is the restriction of *davar acher*: eating with bread enables the worker to consume far more of the produce than he would on its own. Without the owner's permission, this falls outside the Torah's grant.

### Salt Prohibition

Similarly: *v'lo yispot b'melach v'yochal* — they may not dip the produce in salt and eat it. Again, this is the parallel concern: salt, like bread, functions as a *davar acher* that enhances consumption beyond what the Torah permits. Salt is categorized differently from bread — it is absorbed into the produce rather than remaining a distinct substance alongside it — but the Gemara confirms that *melach vadai k'ein davar acher dami*: salt is certainly treated as a form of *davar acher*. If the owner gives permission, both bread and salt are permitted; otherwise, neither is.

---

## Paid vs. Torah Rights

### Non-Harvest

A subsequent *baraita* draws a comparison between workers operating under the Torah-granted entitlement and those operating under a contractual arrangement. A worker hired for non-harvest labor — for example, *l'ader*, tilling the ground, or *lekaskes*, making a circle in the earth around an olive tree — does not have the right to eat. These tasks are performed in preparation for or in service of the harvest, but they do not constitute the act of harvesting itself, and therefore *gmar melacha* in the relevant sense has not occurred. The worker's Torah right to eat does not apply.

### Harvest Work

By contrast, a worker hired for actual harvesting — *livtzor* (grapes), *limsok* (olives), *lilket* (other produce) — may eat and is exempt from *terumah* and *ma'asrot*. These are the conditions under which the Torah grants the right: the worker is engaged in the act of bringing the produce in from the field, at the very moment of *gmar melacha* in the sense of detachment from the ground. *HaTorah zichsa lahen* — the Torah gave them this right — and because it derives from the Torah's grant rather than from a contractual exchange, it does not constitute *mekach* and does not trigger the obligation of *terumah* and *ma'asrot*.

### Paid Deal

The *baraita* then addresses a worker who has made a deal (*katzatz*) with the owner — a contractual arrangement granting the worker the right to eat. In such a case, *achat achat yochal, shtayim shtayim lo yochal* — he may eat one by one, but not two by two. The reason is that when the worker purchased the right to eat from the owner, this transforms his consumption into a form of *mekach*. Since it is now a purchase, the produce becomes subject to *ma'aser* once the worker has acquired it. And the threshold for that acquisition — which the Gemara will elaborate on — is tied to quantity: one fruit at a time does not constitute a *goren*, a granary-stage gathering, but two fruits together does.

### Salt with Deal

The *baraita* adds: *v'sofeit b'melach v'yochal* — in the context of the paid deal, the worker may dip the produce in salt and eat. But again, even so, *achat achat*, one by one — the salt and the deal together do not permit two at a time, since two items dipped in salt, combined with the purchase arrangement, creates *gmar melacha* and obligates the worker in *terumot u'ma'asrot*.

---

## Case Analysis

### Paid Deal Unrestricted

The Gemara now interrogates which case the latter part of the *baraita* is addressing. If the *baraita*'s final clause — permitting salt — is referring to the case of the *katzatz*, the paid deal, then there is no limitation at all: *kivan de'katzatz, kol heicha de'ba'i leichol* — since the worker paid the owner for the right to eat, he may eat however he wishes. The owner's grant is unrestricted, and any mode of consumption is in principle permitted.

### Contradiction

Since that would make the *baraita*'s rulings trivially true and uninteresting, the Gemara concludes: *ela lav a'reisha* — the latter part of the *baraita* must be addressing the first case, that of the worker eating under the Torah's grant rather than a contractual one. And yet, in that case, the *baraita* seems to permit dipping in salt. This is the contradiction: the earlier *baraita* prohibited salt as *davar acher*, and now a later clause appears to allow it under the same Torah-granted right.

### Abaye's Tfisah

*Abaye* proposes a resolution: *kan ba'aretz, kan be'chutz la'aretz* — the cases differ by geography. *Ba'aretz kava sfisa* — in *Eretz Yisrael*, dipping in salt constitutes *tfisat*, a form of acquisition or *gmar melacha*, and therefore obligates in *terumah* and *ma'asrot*. This is why the earlier *baraita* forbids it: not because of *davar acher* per se, but because in *Eretz Yisrael*, dipping renders the produce *tevel*, obligated in *ma'asrot*, and the worker who has not yet separated *terumot u'ma'asrot* would be eating something forbidden. *Be'chutz la'aretz lo kava sfisa* — in *chutz la'aretz*, the dipping does not create this *gmar melacha* effect, and therefore the latter *baraita* — dealing with *chutz la'aretz* — permits salt.

### Rava's Objection

*Rava* rejects *Abaye*'s distinction. *Mi gamidi de'ba'aretz kava sfisa mide'oraysa uv'chutz la'aretz lo kava sfisa umutar lechatchila* — is it really so that in *Eretz Yisrael* dipping creates a Torah-level *gmar melacha* while in *chutz la'aretz* it creates no obligation at all, making it entirely permitted? The *baraita* that permits salt is plainly discussing a context where *terumah* and *ma'asrot* are at stake — that is the entire framework of the passage. Any *chutz la'aretz* that is relevant here must be one where there is at least a rabbinic obligation in *terumot u'ma'asrot*. And if dipping in salt creates *gmar melacha* in *Eretz Yisrael*, the same act must equally create *gmar melacha* in *chutz la'aretz* where *ma'asrot* apply rabbinically. The geographical distinction therefore does not hold.

---

## Rava's Factors

### Quantity Factor

*Rava* offers his own resolution. Two independent factors can generate *tfisah* — the obligating acquisition or *gmar melacha* — that subjects the produce to *terumot u'ma'asrot*. The first is quantity: taking a single fruit does not constitute a *goren*, a gathering sufficient to create obligation, but taking two together does. This applies universally, regardless of geography.

### Purchase Factor

The second factor is the contractual purchase (*katzatz*): if the worker has made a deal with the owner and bought the right to eat, then that acquisition operates independently. It creates *tfisah* regardless of quantity and regardless of whether salt is involved. Once the worker purchased the right, even one fruit at a time triggers the concern of *ma'asrot*, which is why even then he eats one by one.

### Two Scenarios

Putting these together, *Rava* identifies two scenarios that create *tfisah*: a purchase deal with the owner (operative at any quantity), and dipping in salt combined with two fruits. Either one is sufficient on its own to obligate in *terumot u'ma'asrot*.

### Normal Worker

A worker who has neither made a purchase deal nor is dipping in salt — the normal Torah-entitled worker eating as he harvests — *ochel shtayim shtayim*: may eat two at a time, or more. Two items without any further act of acquisition do not constitute a *goren* and do not obligate in *ma'asrot*. The worker's right under the Torah is unconstrained by the quantity issue.

### Worker + Salt

However, if that same normal worker — no purchase deal — proceeds to dip the produce in salt: *achas achas ochel, shtayim shtayim lo yochal* — he may eat one by one but not two by two. Salt functions as a form of *tfisah*, akin to acquiring the produce for consumption; when combined with two items, this creates the *gmar melacha* threshold that triggers obligation in *terumot u'ma'asrot*. With only one item, the salt alone does not suffice to create that threshold.

### Even with Permission

Even if the owner grants the worker permission to dip in salt — which removes the *davar acher* objection — the owner's permission cannot override the *ma'aser* obligation that arises from the combination of salt and two fruits. *De'itvu lehu lema'aser vekava sfisa* — the dipping in salt plus two items renders the produce *tevel* with respect to *ma'aser*, and that obligation cannot be waived by the owner's consent. The permission speaks only to the worker's entitlement vis-à-vis the owner; it cannot alter the produce's status with respect to the obligations of *terumot u'ma'asrot*. This synthesis resolves the apparent contradiction between the *baraitot*: the *baraita* that permits salt is addressing the case of one fruit at a time (where *tfisah* has not occurred), while the *baraita* that prohibits salt is addressing two at a time (where salt plus two creates *gmar melacha*).

---

## Goren Concept

### Sheaf Verse

Having established that two items represent the threshold for *tfisah* while one does not, the Gemara asks for the textual basis. *Rav Matna* provides the source: *ki kavtzam ka-amir gorna* — "for He gathered them like a sheaf into the granary." The concept of *goren*, the granary, represents the stage at which produce becomes obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot*. This verse depicts the *goren* as the result of a gathering — *kavtzam* — an act of collecting multiple items together.

### Goren Stage

The *goren* is not merely a physical location but a conceptual stage: it is the moment at which produce has been sufficiently gathered and prepared to be considered complete and ready for formal disposition, triggering the obligations of *terumah* and *ma'aser*. The verse's imagery — sheaves brought together into the granary — captures the essence of what creates this stage: the act of amassing.

### Two-Item Minimum

Gathering, by its very nature, requires more than one item. A single sheaf cannot be "gathered" in the sense the verse describes; gathering implies plurality. Therefore, *Rav Matna* derives that the minimum threshold for creating a *goren*-level obligation — the minimum number that constitutes a qualifying gathering — is two. One item is insufficient to trigger *tfisah*; two items represent the baseline of what counts as a collection. This scriptural grounding from *ki kavtzam ka-amir gorna* provides the foundation for *Rava*'s entire analysis: the two-item minimum is not a rabbinic fence but a principle rooted in the verse's own conception of what it means to bring produce to the stage of a *goren*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 90

## Terumah/Ma'aser Exemption

### Terumah/Ma'aser Threshing

The sugya opens at the very end of 89b with a *tana rabbanan* and continues into 90a, which forms the primary focus of this shiur. The *braisa* introduces the case of *parot hameraksot batvu'ah* — cows that thresh grain by walking over it — and immediately raises the question of why the prohibition of muzzling would not apply. Rashi and Tosafot explain that the grain in question has already reached the stage of being obligated in *trumot umasrot*, that is, it has achieved *gmar melacha* with respect to the separation obligations. Since the prohibition of muzzling (*lo tachsom*) ceases to apply once the grain is at the *gmar melacha* stage, threshing such grain falls outside the scope of the verse. The Rambam offers a different reading of *meraksot* entirely, understanding it as a case where the animals are not being intentionally used for threshing but happen to be walking over the grain.

The *braisa* then states the central rule for our daf: *hadasot b'truma u'ma'aser* — cows threshing grain that already has the status of *truma* or *ma'aser* — *eino over mishum bal tachsom*, one does not transgress the muzzling prohibition. The background for this is important: it is possible to separate *trumot umasrot* before the grain reaches its formal stage of obligation. Normally, the obligation attaches when the grain has been threshed, winnowed, and piled. However, one can separate *truma* and *ma'aser* at an earlier stage — while the grain is still in the sheaves — and the separation takes effect, even though the grain was not yet obligated. Once that separation has occurred, a cow can thresh the grain that now bears the status of *truma* or *ma'aser*, and the question becomes whether *bal tachsom* applies. The *braisa*'s answer is that it does not.

The underlying rationale, drawn from Tosafot, turns on the word *bedisho* — "in its threshing" — which carries a possessive sense. The verse *lo tachsom shor b'disho* implies that the prohibition applies when the animal is threshing something to which it has access, something that is, in the relevant sense, fit for it to eat from. *Truma* grain does not satisfy that condition. A non-*kohen* cannot feed *truma* grain to his animal at all. Even for a *kohen* who owns the cow, Tosafot specifies that only vetch (*karshinin*), which is animal food by nature, may be fed to one's animal from *truma*, but not wheat, because feeding the wheat to an animal would constitute a loss of *truma*. Thus *truma* grain is not something over which the owner has full license, and it is not properly the *disho* — the threshing domain — of the animal.

### Maris Ayin Solution

Although one does not transgress *bal tachsom* in the *truma* and *ma'aser* case, the *braisa* adds that the owner must nonetheless address the concern of *maris ayin* — the appearance of wrongdoing. Passersby who see the cow threshing grain without being allowed to eat will think that the owner is violating the prohibition, or worse, will conclude from this spectacle that muzzling during threshing is acceptable. The remedy is: *mavi bul me'oto hamin v'tolo lo b'trakselin sheb'fiha* — bring a handful of grain of the same type and hang it in a basket near the animal's mouth, so that it is munching from the basket while it works. The assumption is that the animal will eat from the nearby basket rather than from the grain being threshed, and the appearance of wrongdoing is thus avoided.

Two practical questions arise. First, if the animal is eating from the basket, what is preventing it from also eating from the grain beneath its feet? Presumably the basket is positioned closely enough that the animal prefers it. Second, is it economically sensible for the owner to provide grain from the same batch that bears *truma* or *ma'aser* status? Perhaps the amount provided in the basket is kept limited enough that it remains manageable.

### Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai

Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai offers an alternative to the *maris ayin* remedy: rather than hanging grain of the same type, one should bring vetch (*karshinin*) and hang it for the animal, because *karshinin yafot lah min hakol* — vetch is better for the animal than anything else it could eat. This is a striking formulation. The stated purpose of the remedy is to address *maris ayin*, yet Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai introduces the consideration of what food is healthiest for the animal. If the entire point is to make it visually appear that the cow is eating from what it is threshing, one might expect the remedy to emphasize the visual similarity between what is in the basket and what is on the threshing floor. Why, when addressing a *maris ayin* concern, does Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai pivot to advocating for the optimal diet of the animal? This question will become significant later when the *gemara* uses this very passage to draw conclusions about the operative principle underlying the muzzling prohibition.

### Conflicting Braisas

At this point the *gemara* introduces a *v'reminhi* — a contradiction. The first *braisa* stated that cows threshing *truma* and *ma'aser* are exempt from *bal tachsom*. But a second *braisa* teaches precisely the opposite: *hadasot b'truma u'ma'aser over mishum bal tachsom* — when cows thresh *truma* and *ma'aser*, one does transgress the muzzling prohibition. The *gemara* thus has two explicit *braisas* directly contradicting one another on both *truma* and *ma'aser*.

The *gemara* identifies two separate contradictions: *kashya truma atruma, kashya ma'aser ama'aser*. We have a conflict about *truma* and a conflict about *ma'aser*, and they must be resolved independently.

---

## Reconciling Terumah

### Terumah vs. Gidulei

The *gemara* takes the *truma* contradiction first: *bishlama truma atruma lo kashya* — the contradiction about *truma* is easily resolved. *Kan b'truma, kan b'gidulei truma* — one *braisa* speaks of actual *truma* and the other of *gidulei truma*.

*Gidulei truma* is produce grown from *truma* seeds. If a *kohen* receives *truma* grain and, rather than consuming it, plants it in his field, the grain that grows from those seeds is called *gidulei truma*. From the Torah's standpoint, once the original seed has decomposed and a new stalk has grown from it, the resulting produce is not *truma* at all. The rabbis, however, decreed that *gidulei truma* must be treated like *truma* rabbinically — primarily to prevent the *kohen* from leaving *truma* seed lying around until the planting season, creating conditions for it to become impure or to be treated carelessly. Thus *gidulei truma* carries only a rabbinic status of *truma*.

The resolution follows directly: when the *braisa* says there is no prohibition of *bal tachsom* for *truma*, it means genuine *truma*, which is not *bedisho* because the animal has no claim to it. When the *braisa* says the prohibition does apply, it means *gidulei truma*, which is only rabbinically designated as *truma*. Since from the Torah's perspective this produce is ordinary grain, it *is bedisho*, and therefore the biblical prohibition of *lo tachsom* applies in full. A rabbinic status cannot exempt one from a biblical prohibition.

### Ma'aser Rishon/Sheni

The contradiction about *ma'aser* proves more difficult: *ela ma'aser ama'aser kashya*. The *gemara* considers suggesting a parallel distinction of *gidulei ma'aser*, but immediately rejects it. Unlike *gidulei truma*, which the rabbis treated as having the status of *truma*, produce grown from *ma'aser* seeds — *gidulei ma'aser* — is considered straightforward *chulin*. The rabbis never applied the status of *ma'aser* to such produce. A *mishna* is cited to confirm: *gidulei tevel v'gidulei ma'aser sheini chulin* — produce grown from *tevel* or from *ma'aser sheini* is considered *chulin*. Therefore, no *braisa* could have been referring to *gidulei ma'aser* as if it were *ma'aser*, and the parallel solution does not apply.

The *gemara* resolves the *ma'aser* contradiction differently: *ha b'ma'aser rishon, ha b'ma'aser sheini* — one *braisa* speaks of *ma'aser rishon* and the other of *ma'aser sheini*. *Ma'aser rishon* — the tithe given to a *Levi* — is the Levi's property outright, with no special restrictions on where it must be consumed or how it may be used. It is *bedisho* from the Torah's perspective, and thus the prohibition of *lo tachsom* applies. *Ma'aser sheini*, by contrast, must be brought to Jerusalem and eaten within its walls, and as we shall see, according to some opinions it is considered *mamon gavoha* — property belonging to God. Since the animal has no right to eat it in ordinary circumstances, it is not *bedisho*, and the prohibition does not apply.

### Mammon Gavoh Debate

The *gemara* then proposes an alternative resolution: *v'ibayit eima, ha v'ha b'ma'aser sheini, v'lo kashya — ha Rabbi Meir, ha Rabbi Yehuda*. Both *braisas* may be speaking of *ma'aser sheini*, and the contradiction between them reflects the famous dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda over the status of *ma'aser sheini*.

Rabbi Meir holds that *ma'aser sheini mamon gavoha hu* — *ma'aser sheini* is God's property. The owner has the right of access and consumption, but the property itself belongs to God. Rabbi Yehuda holds that *ma'aser sheini mamon hedyot* — it is ordinary private property of the owner, subject only to the special obligation to consume it in Jerusalem.

What practical difference does this distinction make? One well-known application involves *kiddushin*: if a man betroths a woman using *ma'aser sheini* produce, does the *kiddushin* take effect? The woman can certainly derive value from it — she can bring it to Jerusalem and eat it there. But according to Rabbi Meir, the man has not given her his own money; he has given her access to something that was already God's. The *kiddushin* therefore does not take effect. According to Rabbi Yehuda, it is his property, and the *kiddushin* is valid.

In our context, the same logic applies to *bedisho*: if *ma'aser sheini* is *mamon gavoha*, then even though the owner controls it, it is not truly his to allocate freely, and the animal's eating from it does not constitute the kind of *disha* that the verse has in mind. On Rabbi Meir's view, the prohibition does not apply; on Rabbi Yehuda's view, it does.

### Inside Jerusalem Walls

At this point the *gemara* raises a challenge: *ul'Rabbi Yehuda v'ha ba'ei choma*? Even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who considers *ma'aser sheini* to be private property, the owner is prohibited from consuming it outside Jerusalem's walls. If the animal cannot lawfully eat the *ma'aser sheini* because it is outside Jerusalem, why should it matter whether it is *mamon gavoha* or *mamon hedyot*? Either way, the animal has no right to eat it, and therefore it is not *bedisho* on any view. Rabbi Yehuda would thus also hold that the prohibition does not apply — and both *braisas* would be in agreement, leaving no contradiction to resolve!

The *gemara* answers: *kegon shedash lifnim mechomas Beit Pagi* — the case is where the threshing took place inside the walls of *Beit Pagi*, the outer wall of Jerusalem. In that setting, the *ma'aser sheini* is in the proper location for consumption, and the animal *would* have a right to eat it — if the produce belongs to the owner. Only then does the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda become operative: Rabbi Meir still excludes it from *bedisho* because even in Jerusalem it is *mamon gavoha*, while Rabbi Yehuda includes it because within Jerusalem it is both the owner's property and lawfully available for consumption.

### Demai Status

The *gemara* then offers yet another resolution — one that does not depend on the *ma'aser rishon/sheini* distinction or the *mamon gavoha* debate: *kan b'ma'aser vadai, kan b'ma'aser demai*.

*Demai* refers to produce purchased from an *am ha'aretz* — a person not known to be meticulous about the separation obligations. We assume that even an *am ha'aretz* separates *truma gedola* (the principal priestly portion), since it is a small quantity from the entire granary and even common people generally do so. We are concerned, however, that they did not separate *ma'aser*, which represents a full ten percent — and often twenty percent when both *ma'aser rishon* and *ma'aser sheini* are reckoned. The rabbis therefore decreed that one who purchases grain from an *am ha'aretz* must separate *ma'aser*, treating the produce as if it were *vadai* — certainly untithed. This is called *demai*. The institution of *demai* is attributed to Yochanan Kohen Gadol, who dispatched agents throughout the land of Israel and found that common people were separating only *truma gedola* but not *ma'aser*.

The rabbinic obligation of *demai* cannot override a biblical prohibition. From the Torah's standpoint, we can rely on the *rov* — the majority of *amei ha'aretz* do in fact tithe — and thus the produce is presumptively *chulin*. Therefore, if one treats the *demai* produce as *ma'aser sheini* and refrains from allowing the animal to eat it, that is only a rabbinic *chumra*. From the Torah's perspective, the produce is *chulin*, the animal has a right to eat it, and it is *bedisho*. The *braisa* that says one transgresses *bal tachsom* reflects a case of *ma'aser demai*, where the rabbinic stringency of treating it like *ma'aser sheini* cannot serve as a *kula* to exempt one from the biblical prohibition of *lo tachsom*.

The *gemara* then applies this same logic to *truma*. Having established the *demai* distinction for *ma'aser*, it suggests: *kan b'trumas vadai, kan b'trumas demai*. The *gemara* immediately objects: *trumas demai mi ika?* — there is no such thing as *trumas demai*. An *am ha'aretz* is assumed even by the rabbis to have separated *truma gedola*, so there is no rabbinic obligation to re-separate *truma* from *demai* produce. However, the *gemara* concludes, there is another category that functions analogously: *trumas ma'aser*. After *ma'aser rishon* is given to the *Levi*, the *Levi* must take one-tenth of that tithe and give it to the *kohen* as *trumas ma'aser*. Since an *am ha'aretz* who failed to take *ma'aser rishon* obviously also failed to take *trumas ma'aser*, once one separates the *ma'aser* of *demai*, the resulting *trumas ma'aser* carries only a rabbinic status. That rabbinic status cannot exempt from the biblical prohibition of *lo tachsom*, and thus the *braisa* that says one transgresses refers to this case of *trumas ma'aser* of *demai*.

---

## Animal Benefit Principle

### Eating Causes Harm

The *gemara* now records a question posed to Rav Sheshes: *hayisa ocheles u'merazes mahu?* — what is the law if an animal is of such a constitution that eating while threshing actually causes it distress, specifically diarrhea? Here, allowing the animal to eat is harmful to it, while muzzling it would actually be beneficial. Is one permitted — or perhaps even required — to muzzle the animal under these circumstances?

This is a striking *gemara*. There is no textual peg in the verse to which one can easily attach this case. The question is not about parsing a word or applying a *drasha*; it is a direct inquiry into the underlying rationale of the prohibition. The *gemara* implicitly assumes that if we can identify *why* the Torah prohibits muzzling, we can determine whether that rationale extends to this case or whether it excludes it.

### Benefit vs. Distress

The *gemara* formulates two competing principles. The first: *mishum d'ma'ale leihu* — the reason one may not muzzle the animal is because eating is beneficial to it, and the Torah requires that the animal derive benefit from its labor. If eating is not beneficial in this case — indeed, if it is harmful — then perhaps the prohibition does not apply. The second: *d'chazu mitztara* — the operative concern is not the animal's nutritional benefit but the distress it experiences when it sees grain in front of it and is prevented from eating. An animal does not reason abstractly that eating will cause it harm; it sees the grain, desires it, and suffers when restrained. This distress exists regardless of whether eating would ultimately be good or bad for its health.

### Animal Welfare Principle

Rav Sheshes resolves the question by citing the *braisa* of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: *tanituha* — we have already learned the answer. When addressing the *maris ayin* problem in the case of *truma* and *ma'aser*, Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai said that one should provide vetch for the animal because vetch is the best food for it of all available options. The question is: why, in the context of addressing an appearance concern, does Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai introduce the consideration of the optimal diet for the animal? He could simply have said: hang some grain near its mouth. The fact that he specifies the *best* food indicates that the principle of animal welfare — what is most beneficial for the animal — is not incidental to his ruling but is operative within the framework of the muzzling prohibition itself.

The *gemara* draws the inference: *shema mina mishum d'ma'ale lah hu, shema mina* — we learn from this that the governing principle is indeed what is beneficial for the animal. Since eating causes harm in the case Rav Sheshes was asked about, the rationale of the prohibition does not apply, and one may muzzle the animal.

The depth of this ruling deserves emphasis. Without any explicit textual basis, the *gemara* determines — from a tangential remark of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai in a *maris ayin* context — that the entire prohibition of *lo tachsom* is grounded in animal welfare, specifically in what is beneficial for the animal. And on that basis, a seemingly clear biblical prohibition is set aside.

---

## Non-Jew Worker Issue

### Tell Non-Jew Question

The *gemara* now asks: *mahu she-yomar adam le-nokhri chasom parati v'dosh bah?* — may one instruct a non-Jew to muzzle one's ox and thresh grain with it? This question had already been foreshadowed by the earlier *braisa*, which stated that a non-Jew threshing with a Jew's cow does not cause the Jew to transgress *bal tachsom*. Rashi understood that *braisa* as speaking of the non-Jew threshing his own grain. On Rashi's reading, if the non-Jew were threshing the Jew's grain, a biblical transgression might apply. Tosafot disputes this and reads the *braisa* as speaking of the Jew's grain — since the parallel case involving *amira l'nokhri* on Shabbat concerns an act done for the Jew's benefit. The case before us, per Tosafot, is therefore: the non-Jew is my employee, threshing my grain, and I have instructed him to muzzle my ox. Do I transgress?

### Amira L'Nokhri

The *gemara* formulates the question around *amira l'nokhri*: is the rabbinic prohibition of instructing a non-Jew to perform a forbidden act limited to Shabbat — where the prohibition is particularly severe (*isura d'sekila*) and where there is a broader concern about *melacha* being performed on one's behalf — or does it extend to other prohibitions as well? Perhaps *amira l'nokhri* applies even to a simple negative commandment (*issur lav*) like the muzzling prohibition.

### Non-Jew Using Jew Cow

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this from the earlier *braisa*: *nokhri hadosh b'parato shel Yisrael eino over mishum lo tachsom* — a non-Jew threshing with a Jew's cow does not cause the Jew to transgress. If this is our case — the Jew instructed the non-Jew — and the *braisa* says the Jew does not transgress, perhaps we can infer that instructing a non-Jew is entirely permitted even for non-Shabbat prohibitions.

The *gemara* rejects this inference: *ma'avad hu de-lo avar* — the *braisa* says only that the Jew does not transgress *biblically*. It does not say the practice is permitted. The very fact that it says "he does not transgress" implies that there may remain a *rabbinic* prohibition of *amira l'nokhri*. The *gemara* counters this: *bedin hu de-isura nami leka* — perhaps it is entirely permitted, and the *braisa* merely specifies "he does not transgress" because it follows the contrasting case (*v'adai de-tani seifa*) of a Jew threshing with a non-Jew's cow, who does transgress. The first clause was formulated in parallel to the second, stating only the biblical ruling, but that does not imply a rabbinic prohibition in the first case.

The question therefore remains unresolved: the *braisa* addresses only the biblical dimension, and we do not know whether instructing a non-Jew to muzzle one's animal constitutes a rabbinic prohibition analogous to *amira l'nokhri* on Shabbat, or whether such a prohibition does not apply outside the Shabbat context.

---

## Castration Issue

### Bull Castration Trick

The *gemara* transitions to a related question involving a report sent to the father of Shmuel from the communities of Eretz Yisrael. They described a practice: *halin torei d'ganvin aramaei u'menakhniyan yathon* — non-Jews would "steal" bulls from Jewish farmers in the night, castrate them, and return them. The question was whether this arrangement — which clearly operated with the farmers' knowledge and tacit approval, even if no explicit instruction was given — was permitted.

The background is the biblical prohibition of *sirus* — castration of animals — derived from the verse *u've'artzechem lo ta'asu* ("in your lands you shall not do this"). The practical significance for agricultural communities was substantial: a castrated bull becomes an ox, which in ancient farming was far more valuable as a draft animal. Jewish farmers who needed their bulls castrated devised this workaround precisely to avoid direct transgression, having non-Jews come and perform the castration while maintaining the fiction that the animals were "taken."

The father of Shmuel sent back a clear response: *harama is'avid behu* — they were attempting a *harama*, a legal fiction, and it is not acceptable. *Irimu alaihu v'yizdabun* — act against their scheme and require them to sell the animals. The farmer who had his animals castrated through this scheme cannot continue using them; he must sell them and may not retain the benefit of the castration. This ruling establishes that the arrangement was prohibited. Remarkably, it also implies that even without a direct *amira* — even with merely a wink and a nod — the prohibition applies, at least in the context of *sirus*.

### Rabbi Chidka Position

Rav Pappa immediately qualifies the scope of this ruling: *benei ma'arava savri lah k'Rabbi Chidka*. The communities of Eretz Yisrael who raised this question, and the father of Shmuel who answered it, held like Rabbi Chidka. Rabbi Chidka maintains that *benei Noach metzuvin al ha-sirus* — non-Jews are themselves prohibited from performing castration as part of their seven Noahide obligations, presumably derived from the broader command of *pru u'revu*. On this view, a Jew who facilitates non-Jews in performing *sirus* transgresses *lifnei iver lo titein michshol* — placing a stumbling block before the blind — because the non-Jew himself commits a transgression by performing the act.

The ruling therefore does not necessarily establish anything about *amira l'nokhri* in general. It may have been driven entirely by the concern for *lifnei iver*: the Jew was causing the non-Jew to sin. If Rabbi Chidka is wrong and non-Jews are not prohibited on *sirus*, there might be no *lifnei iver* violation, and then the question of whether the Jew's indirect involvement constitutes a prohibited *amira* returns. The *gemara* thus does not provide a definitive answer on *amira l'nokhri* for prohibitions beyond Shabbat.

Two additional observations are worth noting. First, the fact that this case goes beyond even explicit *amira* — the animals were "stolen" without a direct instruction — and yet was treated as potentially problematic, suggests that for *sirus* there may be something more categorical at work. The verse *u've'artzechem lo ta'asu* applies to the *phenomenon* of castration occurring in one's domain, giving the prohibition a broader reach than a standard negative commandment. Second, the practical implications for our own times are significant: Jews who wish to have pets spayed or neutered must navigate these questions — whether non-Jews are prohibited on *sirus* (which would trigger *lifnei iver*), and whether even if non-Jews are permitted, *amira l'nokhri* applies to prohibitions outside Shabbat.

### Sale Requirement

Returning to the consequences of the *sirus* that has already occurred, Rava initially considered requiring the farmer to sell the castrated animal and to restrict even the sale to uses that would not allow him to benefit from the enhanced value of the animal as an ox. Abaye corrects this: the *knas* — the penalty — is only that the farmer must sell the animal and cannot use it himself. The farmer still retains the monetary benefit of the sale price; the penalty does not extend to stripping him of all financial benefit, only of direct personal use.

The *gemara* then asks: can the farmer sell the animal to his adult son? The answer is yes — an adult son is like any other person (*beno gadol ke-acher dami*), and a sale to him satisfies the requirement. Can he sell it to his minor son? This is disputed: Rav Acha prohibits it, while Rav Ashi permits it.

### Animal Swap Workaround

Mareimar and Mar Zutra — and some say two unnamed *chasidim* — resolved the problem by swapping castrated animals with one another. Each would "sell" his castrated animal to the other, satisfying the technical requirement to sell while ensuring that both parties ended up with functionally equivalent animals. This solution is reminiscent of arrangements made for other occasions, such as swapping *Purim seudot*.

Tosafot observes the difficulty in this entire picture, noting that the *gemara* seems to describe ongoing, structured arrangements among *amoraim* — or even *chasidim* — for managing animals that had been castrated. Tosafot attempts to read these cases as isolated, unanticipated events, but the language *machlifi ahadadi* — they would swap with each other — implies a recurring practice. One way to reconcile this is as follows: if non-Jews are not prohibited on *sirus*, and if there is no *amira l'nokhri* problem when the act is done without a direct instruction (such as when non-Jews came and took the animals without being explicitly told), then the prohibition would not apply, and there would be no *knas* to navigate. But if that were the case, the elaborate swap arrangement would be unnecessary. The internal tension in the passage remains, and the *gemara* ultimately leaves the broader question of *amira l'nokhri* for non-Shabbat prohibitions as unresolved.

---

## Muzzling Impediments

### Various Impediments

The *gemara* now presents a cluster of questions posed by Rami bar Chama: *hoshiv lah kotz b'fiyah mahu* — what if one placed a thorn in the animal's mouth, preventing it from eating? *Hirbitz lah ari mi-bachutz mahu* — what if one positioned a lion outside the field, causing the animal to be too frightened to eat? *Yashav lah kotz b'fiyah mahu* — what if a thorn happened to become lodged in the animal's mouth on its own? *Hirmitz lah ari mi-bachutz mahu* — what if a lion happened to lie down near the field? *He'emid bno mi-bachutz mahu* — what if one placed the animal's calf just outside the field, causing the mother to be so distressed with worry that she cannot eat? *Haysa tzme'a l'mayim mahu* — what if the animal was so thirsty that it had no appetite for food? *Peras lah katavlya al gabei deisha mahu* — what if one spread a leather mat over the grain so that the animal, while threshing, could not see or access it?

These questions form a spectrum. At one end are acts done directly to the animal — a thorn placed in its mouth, a lion positioned to frighten it — that seem clearly analogous to a physical muzzle. At the other end are indirect impediments — a mat over the grain, an animal's thirst — that are further removed from the classical act of muzzling.

### Effective Muzzles

The *gemara* moves quickly to resolve some of these. *Hoshiv lah kotz b'fiyah — chasima ma'alyata hi*: placing a thorn in the animal's mouth is obviously a full-fledged muzzle. The question of Rami bar Chama could not have been asking whether a thorn constitutes a muzzle. Similarly, *hirbitz lah ari mi-bachutz — chasima ma'alyata hi*: positioning a lion to terrify the animal is equally a muzzle. Anything that *effectively* prevents the animal from eating constitutes *lo tachsom* in terms of the active placement of such an impediment.

The *gemara* therefore reframes Rami bar Chama's questions. He was not asking whether these things constitute muzzles; he was asking whether the prohibition requires the owner to *remove* an impediment that already exists — a thorn that accidentally lodged itself, a lion that independently sat down near the field — or whether the prohibition is only violated by the active placement of a muzzle. Does *lo tachsom* prohibit only the act of muzzling, or does it also prohibit allowing the animal to thresh while in a state of being effectively muzzled?

### Hay Over Grain

On one question the *gemara* offers a partial answer. The *braisa* rules: *rashai ba'al habayis lehatir paki'a amir lifnei habehemah kedei shelo tochal min hadeisha* — the owner of the grain may spread straw in front of the threshing animal so that it eats the straw rather than the grain. The farmer who rents out his cow can arrive with a hungry animal — having fed it less the day before — in order to maximize how much it will eat from the grain during threshing. And the farmer using the cow can counter this by spreading straw over the grain.

The *gemara* initially wonders whether spreading straw is comparable to the problematic leather mat case — in both instances something is placed over the grain. The *gemara* rejects this analogy: *shani hatam d'ka'achlah* — there the animal is still eating, merely from straw rather than grain. The prohibition of *lo tachsom* requires that the animal be able to eat; as long as it is eating *something* while it works, there is no violation. Placing hay over the grain ensures the animal eats hay — that is not muzzling. Placing a leather mat that prevents access to any food would be a different matter.

### Timing of Muzzle

Rabbi Yona asked Rabbi Simai a further question: *chasama mibachutz mahu* — what if one muzzled the animal before it began threshing? Is the prohibition violated only by the act of muzzling *while* the animal is threshing — such that muzzling it beforehand and then putting it to work is not a direct transgression — or does the prohibition extend to any threshing done while the animal is in a muzzled state?

### State of Muzzling

Rabbi Simai resolves this with a *kal va-chomer* from the laws of priestly intoxication. The verse states: *yayin v'shechar al tisht ata u'vanecha itcha b'vo'achem* — "do not drink wine or intoxicating drink, you and your sons, when you come into the Tent of Meeting." One might read this literally: the prohibition is the act of *drinking* as you *enter*. But clearly a *kohen* who was already drunk before entering does not thereby avoid the prohibition. The verse *u'lehavdil bein hakodesh u'vein ha-chol* — "to distinguish between holy and ordinary" — indicates that the issue is being in a state of intoxication while serving. The act of drinking preceded the entry, but the state of being drunk is what matters.

The parallel to *lo tachsom* is exact: *mah hatam besha'at bi'ah lo tehe shichrut, hacha nami besha'at disha lo tehe chasima* — just as by the *kohen* the relevant moment is entry into the sanctuary and what matters is whether one is in a state of intoxication at that time, so too by *lo tachsom*, the relevant moment is the act of threshing, and what matters is whether the animal is in a state of being muzzled at that time. The prohibition is not only the act of placing a muzzle during threshing; it is the act of *threshing while the animal is in a muzzled state*. This is a significant broadening of the prohibition's scope.

This restatement of *lo tachsom* as a prohibition on *threshing while muzzled* rather than merely on *the act of muzzling during threshing* has broad implications for many of the cases discussed by Rami bar Chama — the thorn in the mouth, the frightening lion, the leather mat over the grain. If the prohibition is about the state of the animal during threshing, then all of these, to the extent they render the animal effectively muzzled, become relevant. Certain tensions remain — for instance, the earlier ruling that spreading hay *before* threshing begins is permitted, while the present teaching seems to focus on the animal's state *during* threshing regardless of how that state came about. These parameters will require further clarification, as the *gemara* continues with related questions on the following daf.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 91

## Muzzling & Threshing

### Tanu Rabanan Muzzling

The daf begins with a *baraisa*: *hachosem et haparah vehamezaveg bekilayim* — one who muzzles a cow or who yokes together animals of different species for purposes of threshing is exempt from lashes. The lashes fall only upon the one who actually performs the threshing with the muzzled animal, or who leads the mismatched pair. This is a striking point, because the verse reads *lo sachsom shor bedisho* — do not muzzle the ox in its threshing — which one might have read as placing the prohibition on the act of muzzling itself. The *gemara*, however, understands that muzzling in isolation, without threshing, does not constitute the transgression. The violation is consummated at the moment of threshing, and it is therefore the one who performs the threshing with the muzzled ox who receives lashes.

### Act vs. Preparation

This principle — that it is the direct act, not the preparatory act, that triggers liability — runs consistently through both prohibitions. By *kilayim*, the verse reads *lo sachosh beshor uvachamor yachdav* — do not plow with an ox and a donkey together. The prohibition attaches to the act of plowing or threshing itself, not to the prior act of yoking the animals together. The one who yokes them is not the transgressor; the one who actually leads them in the work is.

### Kilayim Principle

The same logic governs both the *chasima* and *kilayim* prohibitions: preparatory actions, even when they make the eventual transgression possible, do not themselves constitute the *issur*. The *gemara* had previously addressed the case of one who muzzled the animal outside, before bringing it in to thresh — and concluded that even in that case, once the animal is used for threshing while muzzled, the one who causes it to thresh is liable. But critically, the liability accrues at the moment of the direct act, not at the prior moment of muzzling.

### Muzzle Outside Issue

The prior *gemara* had asked: *chasmah babachutz mahu* — what if someone muzzled the animal outside and then threshed with it? The resolution was that liability still attaches at the point of threshing. The present discussion clarifies that in any case, the transgressor is the one who does the threshing, not the one who did the muzzling beforehand — even when those are two different people.

---

## Voice as Action

### Yelling & Commands

The *gemara* now turns to a different scenario: *chasmah bekolo vehinhigah bekolo* — what if someone accomplished the muzzling or the leading of the animals not through physical contact but through voice? For instance, suppose the animal was threshing and the person yelled at it, causing it to stop eating out of fear — effectively muzzling it through sound. Or suppose the person drove mismatched animals forward by shouting commands. The *gemara* assumes that such a person has in principle transgressed the prohibition, since the muzzling and the threshing are simultaneous — unlike the case where someone physically muzzled the animal beforehand. The question, however, is whether an act accomplished through voice constitutes a *ma'aseh*, an act sufficient to incur lashes.

### Rabbi Yochanan Position

*Rabbi Yochanan amar chayav* — Rabbi Yochanan holds that the person is liable. His reasoning: *akimat piv havei ma'aseh* — the movement of one's lips is itself a physical act. Why should it matter whether one moved a finger to flick a switch or moved one's lips and produced sound? Both are uses of one's body to bring about a result. There is no principled reason to distinguish between a physical limb and the lips.

### Reish Lakish Position

*Reish Lakish amar patur* — Reish Lakish holds that the person is exempt. *Kala lo havei ma'aseh* — the voice is not the body. What ultimately accomplished the effect was not the person's body but the person's voice — sound waves that traveled through the air. Since the physical work was done by the voice, which is external to the body, it does not constitute a *ma'aseh* sufficient for lashes.

### Temurah Challenge

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the laws of *temurah*: if a person attempts to exchange a sanctified animal for another animal, the act is effective — the second animal becomes *kadosh* — and the person receives lashes, even though the entire act was verbal. Does this not demonstrate that a verbal act is considered a *ma'aseh*?

### Temurah Resolution

Reish Lakish responds: that *mishnah* follows the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that one receives lashes even for a prohibition that involves no act — *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh lokin alav*. This does not prove that speech constitutes an act; it merely proves that Rabbi Yehuda allows lashes without an act.

The *gemara* pushes back: how can we say the *mishnah* follows Rabbi Yehuda? The *mishnah* opens with *hakol memirin* — anyone can perform *temurah* — which the *gemara* elsewhere interprets to include a *yoresh*, an heir who inherited a consecrated animal. But Rabbi Yehuda explicitly holds that a *yoresh* cannot perform *temurah* and cannot perform *semichah*, because he does not consider the heir to be the true owner of the *korban*. Since the *mishnah* includes the *yoresh*, it cannot be authored by Rabbi Yehuda. How then can Reish Lakish invoke Rabbi Yehuda to explain the lashes in *temurah*?

The *gemara* resolves this with the classic principle that a *tanna* may agree with Rabbi Yehuda on one matter and disagree on another. The author of the *mishnah* may reject Rabbi Yehuda's position regarding the *yoresh* while nonetheless agreeing with Rabbi Yehuda that lashes apply to a prohibition without a physical act. The challenge to Reish Lakish is therefore blunted, and the debate remains unresolved by the *gemara*.

### Tosafot Framework

*Tosafot* note a broader tension across the *gemara* regarding when speech is treated as an act, and they propose a governing distinction: whether the speech produces a real-world effect. If someone testifies in court, that speech leads to an execution — it has concrete physical consequences. Similarly, performing *temurah* verbally causes the second animal to become sanctified — another real-world effect. In our case too, yelling at the animal to prevent it from eating has a direct real-world effect: the animal stops eating and is effectively muzzled. Speech acts that produce no such effect — cursing someone, blasphemy, or the like — are less likely to be treated as *ma'aseh*. *Tosafot* thus argue that both *temurah* and *chasima* through voice belong to the category of consequential speech, which is why each raises the question of whether lashes apply.

### Physics vs. Meaning

There is, however, an additional and perhaps more fundamental distinction worth drawing out. When we speak of testimony, blasphemy, or cursing, the speech act is primarily an expression of meaning. It is a vehicle for ideas — the content of the words is what matters. These are not easily reduced to physical phenomena. By contrast, in the case of the person who yells at the ox and startles it into silence, there is no question of meaning at all. The sound waves produced by the voice physically startle the animal. It is a purely physical chain of causation: lips move, air vibrates, the animal reacts. In that sense, this case is far closer to flicking a light switch or creating ripples in water than it is to the act of testifying or cursing. From that perspective, Rabbi Yochanan's position that *akimat piv havei ma'aseh* is especially compelling here, even if one would not extend that reasoning to all speech acts.

This yields three categories: pure sound with a direct physical effect, as in the *chasima* case; speech as pure meaning with no physical effect, as in blasphemy or cursing; and speech that carries meaning but also produces a concrete real-world legal or physical consequence, as in *temurah* or testimony. *Tosafot* focus on the second category as the distinction, while the analysis here suggests the first is genuinely different from both others.

---

## Muzzle Liability

### Lashes & Payment

The *gemara* cites a *baraisa*: one who muzzles his cow and threshes with it receives lashes — and must also pay the owner of the cow for the food the animal was denied: four *kabbin* for a cow, three *kabbin* for a donkey. The animal had a right to eat while working, and by muzzling it, the person effectively stole the animal's food from its owner.

### Double Liability Issue

The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: *ein lokeh u'meshalem* — one cannot receive both lashes and be required to pay money for the same act. These are two independent forms of punishment or liability, and the principle is that the more severe subsumes the lesser. How, then, can this *baraisa* impose both lashes and a monetary obligation?

### Abaye Answer

Abaye answers: *ha mani Rabbi Meir hi d'amar lokeh u'meshalem* — this *baraisa* follows the position of Rabbi Meir, who holds, in the context of *eidim zomemim* — conspiring witnesses who are exposed as false — that the witnesses receive both lashes and are required to pay the monetary penalty they sought to impose on the innocent party. Rabbi Meir allows both sanctions to operate simultaneously. The *baraisa* about *chasima* follows this minority position.

### Rava Answer

Rava offers a different answer, invoking a compact but powerful principle: *esnan isha v'afilu ba'al imo* — the prohibition against bringing a prostitute's fee as a *korban* applies even if the man who paid her committed incest with his own mother. The significance of this is as follows. If a man engages in a capital sexual transgression and later gives payment to the woman, he is technically exempt from paying under the principle of *kim leh b'derabah mineh* — when liable for a capital or corporal punishment, the lesser financial liability is subsumed. Yet the *Torah* tells us that even in such a case, if he does pay, what he gives her is defined as an *esnan*, a prostitute's fee, and cannot be brought as a *korban*. This demonstrates that *kim leh* does not erase the underlying monetary obligation — it merely means the court cannot enforce it.

### Kam Leh Principle

Rashi frames the principle precisely: *kim leh* means the court's hands are tied. If we are prepared to administer lashes, we cannot simultaneously impose a monetary payment. But the debt itself remains. The person genuinely owes the money; we simply cannot act upon it in court. If he chooses to pay — *b'va latzet yedei Shamayim*, in order to discharge his obligation before Heaven — that payment is real and is defined as such. Indeed, the *Bach* cites a version of the *gemara* in which Rava's statement is preceded by precisely that phrase, indicating that the entire discussion is about one who wishes to fulfill his moral obligation even absent court compulsion. *Tosafot* notes that the language of the *baraisa* itself, *u'meshalem*, "and he pays," rather than *yeshalem*, "he must pay," reflects this: it is not that the court imposes payment, but that ideally he should pay.

### Contractual vs. Tort

The principle of *kim leh* most naturally applies when the monetary obligation has the character of a tort or a fine — that is, where the court is imposing one sanction on top of another. But there is reason to distinguish when the monetary obligation arises not from a tort but from a contractual agreement. In the case of the prostitute, the man agreed to pay for services rendered; the obligation is contractual. In the case of the muzzled ox, when the person took another's ox to use for labor, he implicitly agreed to allow the animal to eat — that is part of what it means to use someone's animal. The obligation to compensate the owner for what the animal was denied is therefore grounded in contract, not in a court-imposed penalty. It is far less clear that *kim leh* should extinguish a pre-existing contractual obligation. Both of Rava's applications of the *esnan* principle — the prostitute's fee and the ox's food — may indeed fall into this contractual category, suggesting the principle applies with particular force there.

### Rav Papa Answer

Rav Papa offers yet a third resolution, this one by temporally separating the two liabilities. *Mishas meshicha chayiv lei b'mezonoteha* — from the moment the person took the other's cow by pulling it (*meshicha*), he became liable to feed it. The obligation to provide food arose at the point of acquisition, as an inherent condition of using someone else's animal. The lashes, on the other hand, attach only at the moment of muzzling during the threshing. Since the two liabilities arise at different moments, they do not clash under the rule of *kim leh*, and both can stand.

---

## Dairy Bread & Breeding

### Two Inquiries

Rav Papa then reports: two questions were brought to him from the household of Rav Papa bar Abba — a different Rav Papa — and to both he answered that the matter was forbidden. He then clarifies that in one of the cases his ruling followed the *halakha*, and in the other he was being strict beyond the strict letter of the law: *chada k'hilchasa v'chada lav k'hilchasa*.

### Dairy Bread

The first question was: *mahu l'lush es ha'issa b'chalav* — may one knead dough using milk, producing milk bread?

### Milk Bread Prohibited

Rav Papa ruled that this is forbidden, and this ruling accords with the *halakha*. A *baraisa* states explicitly: *ein lashin es ha'issa b'chalav* — one may not knead dough with milk. And if one did so, *kol hapas kullah asurah* — the entire loaf is forbidden. The reason is *mipnei hergel aveira* — it will lead to transgression, since bread is eaten at every meal, and milk bread will inevitably be consumed together with meat. The same principle applies to smearing the oven with fat from the tail of a kosher animal: any bread baked in such an oven is forbidden until the oven is fired up sufficiently to remove all residue. Milk bread and meat-greased bread are each independently prohibited even to eat on their own, precisely because of this concern. Contemporary questions about whether an external label or packaging notation — rather than a marking on the bread itself — constitutes an adequate *siman* are a matter of ongoing discussion among the *poskim*, but the core prohibition is clear.

### Kilayim Enclosure

The second question concerned the laws of *kilayim*: *mahu lehachnis min vesheno mino ladir* — may one bring two animals of different species into the same enclosure? Not performing the act of cross-breeding directly, but creating the conditions under which it might occur naturally — locking different species in a barn together and allowing events to take their course.

### Breeding Stringency

Rav Papa ruled this forbidden as well, but acknowledged that this ruling does not reflect the strict *halakha* — he was being extra strict. The *halakha*, as Shmuel states, requires direct physical involvement in the act itself before any transgression is committed. Placing animals of different species in an enclosure together, even with the intent that they breed, does not constitute a violation. Rav Papa's prohibition here was a stringency, not a strict ruling.

---

## Kilayim Direct Act

### Shmuel Standards

Shmuel's ruling is that to establish a prohibition or a transgression in contexts requiring witnesses to a forbidden sexual act, the observers must see the actors *kederach hamenafim* — in the manner of adulterers, meaning the physical conduct makes clear what is occurring, though perhaps without seeing the genitals directly.

### Menafim Imagery

The contrast is between *derech menafim* — seeing the actors' behavior in a way that makes intercourse evident — and *kemichol bashfopheres*, like an eyelash applicator being inserted into its tube, which denotes actually witnessing the penetrative act itself.

### Kilayim Insertion

By *kilayim*, however, Shmuel rules that the standard is more stringent: *uvekilayim ad sheyachnis kemichol bashfopheres* — to transgress the prohibition of cross-breeding, one must actually insert, directly handling the genitals. Without direct manipulation of the genitals themselves, the biblical prohibition has not been transgressed. Merely placing animals of different species in proximity, or even holding them at the moment the male mounts the female without directly handling the genitals, does not constitute the act.

### Achiza Challenge

Rav Achdaboi bar Ami raises a challenge from a *baraisa*: had the verse said only *behemtecha lo tarbia* — do not breed your animals — without the word *kilayim*, one might have thought that even holding the female animal while the male mounts her is prohibited. The word *kilayim* comes to teach that the prohibition is specifically *kilayim* — cross-species breeding — and not mere involvement in same-species breeding. But notice: the *baraisa* describes the prohibited act as *achiza*, holding — not as direct genital manipulation. Does this not imply that merely holding the animals constitutes the transgression of *kilayim*?

### Achiza Response

The *gemara* responds: *mai achiza hachnasa* — when the *baraita* says "holding," it means actual insertion. The *baraita* is describing the same act of direct genital manipulation that Shmuel specified. Why then does it use the word *achiza*, holding? *Lishna ma'alya* — the *baraita* is speaking euphemistically. The *halakha* requires direct manipulation of the genitals, yet the text uses softer language. What is perhaps surprising is the consequence: a person who holds the animals at the moment of mating, without directly handling the genitals, does not transgress the biblical prohibition — a result that cuts against intuition but is what the *gemara* establishes.

### Min BeMinoRuling

Rav Yehuda rules: *min bemino mutar lehachnis kemichol bashfopheres* — when breeding animals of the same species, it is permitted to directly facilitate the act, handling the genitals like the eyelash applicator in the tube. *Ve'afilu mishum pritzuta leika* — there is not even a concern of licentiousness. *Mai ta'ama ba'avidtei tarid* — this is the person's work; a farmer engaged in animal husbandry is focused on the task at hand, and the handling of animal genitals in a professional context does not provoke inappropriate thoughts, as Rashi explains.

### Min BeMino Holding

Rav Achdaboi bar Ami then reapplies the *baraita* to the same-species context. The *baraita* states that *kilayim* — and not same-species breeding — is what is forbidden, implying that holding the animal while the male mounts her is permitted when they are the same species. The implication would be that only *achiza*, holding, is permitted for same-species breeding — not direct manipulation.

### Euphemism Response

The *gemara* responds identically: *mai achiza hachnasa* — even here, when the *baraita* says "holding," it means direct insertion. The same euphemistic language applies. Thus, for same-species breeding, direct facilitation including full genital manipulation is permitted; and for different species, no transgression occurs unless there is direct genital manipulation. Both rulings rest on the same reading of the *baraita* as speaking euphemistically.

---

## Mixed Species Barn

### Two & One

Rav Ashi reports a question that was brought to him from the household of Rav Nechemiah of the *Reish Galuta*: *mahu lehachnis min umino veshe'eino mino ledir* — may one bring two animals of one species together with one animal of a different species into the same enclosure? This question assumes that placing a single animal of each of two different species in a barn together would already be problematic — though as established earlier, that is not the strict *halakha*. The question is whether two of one kind alongside one of another is somehow better.

### Animal Preference

The reasoning behind the potential leniency: *keivan de'ika mineih batar mineih garir* — since there is another animal of its own species present, the animal will be drawn to mate with its own kind and will not go to the foreign species. Perhaps the presence of a same-species partner removes the concern entirely.

### Ashi Stringency

Rav Ashi concluded that it is forbidden — *upashat leh le'issura* — but acknowledged this is not the strict *halakha*: *d'lo ke'hilchata*, just as placing one of each species in an enclosure is not the strict *halakha* but is treated as a stringency, so too here.

### Pritzuta Concern

The reason for the stringency: *mishum pritzuta de'avdei* — concerns of licentious behavior. Even if legally no transgression has been committed, bringing different species into proximity in ways that might lead to cross-breeding is considered improper, and for that reason one should not do it even when the technical *halakha* would not prohibit it.

---

## Worker Food Rights

### Body Parts Work

The *mishnah* establishes: *haya oseh beyadav aval lo beraglav* — if a worker was working only with his hands and not his feet, or only with his feet and not his hands, or even only with his shoulder, *harei zeh ochel* — he is entitled to eat. Any form of engagement in the work suffices.

### Both Hands & Feet

Rabbi Yose beRabbi Yehuda disagrees: *ad she'ya'aseh beyadav u'veraglav* — the worker is not entitled to eat unless he is working with both his hands and his feet. One limb alone is insufficient.

### Ox Parallel

The reasoning of the *tanna kamma* is derived from the verse *ki tavo b'kerem rei'echa* — when you come into your friend's vineyard — which implies that any manner of work in the vineyard entitles one to eat. Rabbi Yose beRabbi Yehuda, by contrast, draws an analogy to the ox: just as the ox uses all of its limbs in the act of threshing, so too the human worker must engage both hands and feet. The ox, of course, has no literal hands, but the principle is that the entire body must be engaged in the labor.

### Duck Threshing

Rava bar bar Rav Huna poses a question: *dash be'avazin ve'tarnigolin le'Rabbi Yosi berbi Yehuda mahu* — according to Rabbi Yose beRabbi Yehuda, what is the rule if one uses ducks and chickens to do the threshing? These animals have no hands. Does Rabbi Yose beRabbi Yehuda mean literally hands and feet, or does he mean that the animal must engage its full bodily capacity in the work? If it is the latter, then ducks and chickens that are actively threshing are surely using everything they have.

### Teiku Hands

The *gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teiku*. We do not know whether Rabbi Yose beRabbi Yehuda requires literally hands and feet — in which case ducks and chickens would never be entitled to eat — or whether he requires only that the creature put its full body into the work, in which case they would be entitled.

---

## Grape Stompers

### Stompers Eating

Rav Nachman rules in the name of Rabba bar Avuha: workers who are stomping grapes are permitted to eat. Since grape stomping is the paradigmatic example of working with one's feet, this connects naturally to the earlier discussion. The stompers work simultaneously with grapes and with wine, and the question becomes: from which of the two — grapes or wine — may they eat, and at what point?

### Wine Stages

The *gemara* specifies: until the workers have gone *sheti va'erev* through the vat, they are considered to be working only with the grapes, not yet with the wine. During this stage, *okhlin anavim ve'ein shotim yayin* — they may eat from the grapes but may not drink from the wine, because the wine has not yet begun to flow, or because they are not yet considered to be working with the wine.

### Sheti Va'erev

Once the stomping has proceeded in both directions — *sheti va'erev*, the horizontal and vertical passes across the vat — the workers are then considered to be working with both grapes and wine: *okhlin anavim ve'shotin yayin*. Even though their job is to extract the wine from the grapes, and their direct labor is on the grapes, once the stomping has reached a sufficient degree they are considered to be engaged with the wine as well, and they may drink from it.

---

## Species Restriction

### Figs vs. Grapes

The *mishnah* rules: *haya oseh be'te'enim lo yokhal be'anavim* — if you are working with figs, you may not eat grapes; if working with grapes, you may not eat figs. One is restricted to the type of produce one is working with. Nevertheless, the worker has some discretion: *aval mone'a et atzmo* — even though one is entitled to eat the grapes immediately in front of oneself, one may choose to refrain and wait *ad she'yagi'a limkom yafeh*, until one arrives at the choicer part of the vineyard where the grapes are better, and eat there.

### Time Limitation

*Ve'kulan lo amru ela besha'at melakha* — all of these rights to eat apply only during the time of work itself, the *sha'at melakha*. The moment work ceases, the right to eat lapses.

### Travel Exception

However, *aval mishum hashavat aveidah l'be'alim* — in order to preserve the owner's time, there is a special arrangement: *amru po'alim okhlin behalikhatan me'uman le'uman* — workers may eat as they walk from one row to the next, and *u'vachaziratam min hagat* — as they return from the threshing floor. The logic is practical: if the worker must stop working entirely in order to eat, the owner loses time. It is better for the owner that the worker grab produce and eat while walking to the next row, not pausing the work at all. This is technically outside the *sha'at melakha* — the worker is not actively working at that moment — but the *takana* permits it precisely because it serves the owner's interest.

### Vine Identity

The *gemara* raises a question: *oseh begefen zeh mahu she'yokhal begefen acher* — if a worker is working on vine A, may he eat from vine B, which is adjacent? Both are grapes, both belong to the same employer — but they are different vines. The question is whether the right to eat is tied to the specific physical source one is working on, or merely to the species.

### Extended Vine

Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi, addresses an embedded difficulty: if the rule were that one can only eat from the specific source one is working on — and not merely from the same species — how could an ox ever eat while working on standing grain? The ox's work is done in one place while its mouth reaches elsewhere. Rav Sheshet answers: *besircha* or *beshatcha* — we are dealing with a long vine or extended stalk, where the animal is doing work at one end of the very same object while eating from the other end. The vine or stalk is a single continuous entity, and eating from it while working upon it satisfies even the strictest reading.

---

## Intertwined Vines

### Rashi Handling

Rashi explains the case of *mudeles* — a vine that is wrapped around or intertwined with another plant or vine — as follows: when two vines are physically intertwined, a worker trying to harvest from one vine must physically handle and move the other vine in order to gain access to the grapes he is picking. It is in this context that the *mishnah*'s case of figs and grapes becomes intelligible: if a fig vine and a grape vine are intertwined, and you are harvesting grapes but must physically handle the fig vine to do so, the question arises whether you may eat from the figs as well.

### Dov Question
