# Bava Metzia 94

## T'nai Fundamentals

### T'nai Definition

The *mishnah* on 94a opens with the subject of *t'nai* — conditional statements — and the question of when a given condition is considered halachically valid or invalid. The basic framework is as follows: if a *t'nai* is valid, the action to which one has committed oneself conditionally will take effect only if the condition is fulfilled — the Mishnah uses the language *mekuyam*, fulfilled. If the *t'nai* is somehow invalid, then it is *batel*, nullified, and the action takes effect unconditionally regardless of whether the condition was ever met.

### Shomrim Conditions

The *mishnah* begins with the four *shomrim*, the four categories of guardians, which have been introduced in previous *mishnayot*. The language is: *matneh shomer chinam lihyot patur mishvuah vehashoel lihyot patur milishalem noseh sachar vehasocher lihyot pturim mishvuah umilishalem*. A *shomer chinam* — a free guardian — is obligated only for negligence (*pshia*), and is exempt from payment for any other occurrence — theft, loss, or an act of God — provided he takes an oath. So if this *shomer* conditions his acceptance of the role on being exempt from taking such an oath, the *mishnah* says that condition is valid. At the opposite end of the spectrum, the *sho'el* — the borrower — bears the highest level of responsibility, being liable even for acts of God, and he too may condition his borrowing on being released from these obligations. Between these two extremes, the *noseh sachar* and the *socher* — the paid guardian and the renter — may similarly condition their undertaking on exemption from both the oath and from payment in the cases of *gneivah* and *aveidah*, theft and loss.

### Against Torah

The *mishnah* then states its second rule: *kol hamatneh al mah shekatuv baTorah t'na'o batel* — anyone who makes a condition against something the Torah has commanded, that condition is void, and the person has committed themselves to the act unconditionally. The *gemara* will raise a sharp question about this in light of the first rule, since the obligations of the *shomrim* are themselves rooted in the Torah. The example of such an impermissible condition will be illustrated through the case of *kiddushin*.

### Ma'aseh B'Tchilatov

The third rule of the *mishnah* is: *vechol t'nai sheyesh ma'aseh bitchilato t'na'o batel* — any condition in which the *ma'aseh*, the action, is stated before the conditional clause, is also invalid. Rashi explains: *shehikdim ma'aseh she'alav la'asos l'tnai shehu sho'el mimenu* — the person has stated first the action he is committing to do, and only then articulated the condition he is requesting. For example, saying "This thing is yours, if you do such-and-such" is invalid because the *then* precedes the *if*.

The reason for this rule is that a valid *t'nai* must resemble the model of *bnei Gad u'bnei Reuven*. At the end of *Parshat Matot*, the tribes of Gad and Reuven came before Moshe and asked to remain in the Trans-Jordan. Moshe ultimately agreed, and the structure of his conditional grant was: *im ya'avru u'nesatem* — "if you cross before your brothers and help them conquer the land, then you will be given this land." The conditional statement — the *if* — comes first; the consequent action — the *then* — follows. That is the required form. Rashi cites Yaakov's words to Lavan similarly: *im ta'aseh li hadavar hazeh ashuvah ereh tzonecha* — if you do this thing for me, then I will go and shepherd your flocks. The condition precedes the commitment.

What does it mean for the condition to be *batel*? Rashi explains: *v'havei ma'aseh mikuyam* — the action takes effect regardless. Even though the person has nominally conditioned his act, if the condition was stated improperly, it is as though no condition was made, and the *then* clause is binding whether or not the *if* is ever fulfilled.

### Efshar L'Kaymo

The *mishnah*'s fourth rule: *vechol she'efshar lo l'kaymo b'sofo v'hitnah imo mit'chilato t'na'o kayam* — any condition that is possible to fulfill at the end, and which was stipulated at the outset, is a valid condition. Rashi explains: provided the *t'nai* was stated before the *ma'aseh* — that is, the proper order was observed — then if the condition is possible to fulfill, it is a good *t'nai*. However, if the condition is impossible to fulfill — *ee efshar l'kaymo* — then the *t'nai* is *batel* and the action stands regardless. The *gemara* will supply examples and will clarify the law.

---

## Shomer & Torah

### Initial Problem

The *gemara* opens with an immediate difficulty. The *mishnah*'s first rule permits a *shomer* to condition his guardianship on being released from obligations the Torah itself imposes on him. But the *mishnah*'s second rule declares that any condition made against what is written in the Torah is void. These two rules appear contradictory. The *gemara* frames the question sharply: *amai?* Why is that a valid *t'nai*? *Matneh al mah shekatuv baTorah hu* — it is precisely a condition against what the Torah has written. And the *mishnah* itself says *kol hamatneh al mah shekatuv baTorah t'na'o batel*.

### Rabbi Yehuda

The *gemara* initially suggests: *ha mani? Rabbi Yehuda hi* — this *mishnah* follows the view of Rabbi Yehuda. *De'amar bedavar shebemamon t'na'o kayam* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that while one cannot generally condition against a Torah obligation, in monetary matters such a condition is valid. The *shomer*'s exemption from payment is precisely a monetary matter — he is attempting to be released from a financial obligation — and therefore according to Rabbi Yehuda the condition stands.

### Marriage Case

The *gemara* adduces a *baraita* in support: *amar le'ishah harei at mekudeshet li al menat she'ein li alayich she'er kesut ve'onah harei zu mekudeshet vetna'o batel divrei Rabbi Meir*. A man says to a woman: you are betrothed to me on the condition that you have no claim against me for *she'er*, *kesut*, and *onah* — food, clothing, and conjugal rights. Rabbi Meir rules: she is *mekudeshet*, and the condition is *batel*, because this is a condition against what the Torah has commanded. Then: *Rabbi Yehuda omer bedavar shebemamon t'na'o kayam* — Rabbi Yehuda says that regarding monetary matters, namely *she'er* and *kesut* (food and clothing), the condition is valid.

However, the *gemara* pushes back: can we really attribute the *mishnah*'s first rule to Rabbi Yehuda when the very next clause — *kol hamatneh al mah shekatuv baTorah t'na'o batel* — is an unqualified statement that seems to reflect the position of Rabbi Meir? The *gemara* attempts to resolve this by saying that the latter clause refers only to non-monetary ritual matters, *davar she'eino shel mamon*, and the two clauses can coexist under Rabbi Yehuda. But this resolution is immediately challenged: the clause following that — *kol t'nai sheyesh bo ma'aseh bitchilato t'na'o batel*, the rule about the *ma'aseh* preceding the *t'nai* — is demonstrably the position of Rabbi Meir, as attested by the *baraita* in which Abba Chalafta says in the name of Rabbi Meir: *t'nai kodem l'ma'aseh harei zeh t'nai; ma'aseh kodem l'tnai eino t'nai*. If the latter clause is Rabbi Meir's, the *mishnah* cannot be split between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir in an unstated, inconsistent manner.

### Rabbi Meir View

The *gemara* therefore arrives at a new resolution: *ela kula Rabbi Meir hi* — the entire *mishnah* is the view of Rabbi Meir. And as for the first rule, permitting the *shomer* to condition his guardianship — *shani hacha de'me'ikara lo sha'abed nafshei* — the case of the *shomer* is exceptional because at the very outset he did not obligate himself.

### Rashi Explanation

Rashi's explanation here is illuminating. Even though we might initially think the *shomer chinam* who conditions his exemption from the oath is making a condition against the Torah, that is not so. *Me'ikara lo shavei nafshei* — from the very beginning he did not bind himself. When Reuven asks Shimon to be his *shomer chinam* and Shimon says *ee efshi she'eheyeh shomer shelcha ella b'kach* — I am unwilling to be your guardian except on these terms — he has not yet become a *shomer* at all. *V'shomer lo nachit lishmira ad d'mashach l'vehema* — a person does not become a *shomer* until the act of *meshicha*, the legally valid act of acquisition, takes place, whereby he actually takes hold of the animal. *V'hai ki mashach kvar pirash al menat shelo alav shvua* — and when he did take hold of the animal, he had already preceded that with his condition. Thus he has committed himself only to a partial form of guardianship: *v'lo shavei nafshei l'ayeilei b'torat shomrim ella b'miksas* — he has only obligated himself in a limited sense. He is not accepting the full biblical category of *shomer chinam*; he is saying, in effect, I will watch your animal for free, but without any of the attendant biblical obligations.

The contrast with *kiddushin* is instructive. *Aval hamikadesh et ha'ishah, miki amar lah harei at mekudeshet li, ikadsha lah* — the moment a man pronounces the words of *kiddushin*, she is betrothed. When he then adds that he bears no financial obligations to her, that is *matneh al mah shekatuv baTorah* — a condition against the Torah — because *ein ishut l'chatza'in*, there is no such thing as being partially married. The act of *kiddushin* takes complete effect the moment it occurs. *V'havei matneh al mah shekasuv baTorah*. With the *shomer*, by contrast, he never initially took on the full biblical role; he stepped into a more limited, self-defined form of custodianship before the *kinyan* ever made him a Torah-defined guardian.

---

## Shomer Sachar

### Shomer->Sho'el

A *baraita* now raises a striking case: *umatneh shomer sachar lihyot k'sho'el* — a *shomer sachar* conditions his guardianship such that he accepts the full responsibilities of a *sho'el*, the borrower, who is liable even for acts of God. This might seem puzzling — why would anyone voluntarily accept greater liability? Yet this is precisely the case the *baraita* contemplates.

### Kinyan Required?

The *gemara* records a dispute over whether such an elevation of responsibility requires a formal *kinyan*. *Amar Shmuel beshikanu miyado* — Shmuel says yes, a *kinyan* must be performed. If the owner agrees — and why would he not? — and they perform a *kinyan*, then the *shomer sachar* takes on the full obligations of a *sho'el*.

### Reputation Benefit

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *afilu teima beshelo kanu miyado* — even without a *kinyan*. His reasoning is: *behahi hana'ah d'kanfik leh kala d'inish meheiman hu gamir umeshabed nafshei* — through the benefit (*hana'ah*) that accrues to him from the reputation he gains as a trustworthy person, he fully binds himself to this higher level of responsibility. The relationship between *hana'ah* and responsibility is a direct one: the *sho'el* bears maximum liability because he receives maximum benefit — the free use of an object. But Rabbi Yochanan identifies a different kind of *hana'ah* available to a *shomer sachar* who accepts *sho'el*-level responsibility: his reputation for reliability. The word will spread that he is a person of his word and of exceptional trustworthiness, and that reputational benefit is sufficient, without a formal *kinyan*, to create the binding obligation.

---

## Impossible Conditions

### Possible vs Impossible

The *mishnah*'s rule — that a *t'nai* which is possible to fulfill at the end is valid, while one that is impossible is *batel* — is now taken up by the *gemara* in greater detail. *Amar Rav Tavla amar Rav zo divrei Rabbi Yehuda ben Tema* — this *mishnah* reflects the position of Rabbi Yehuda ben Tema.

### Merely Torment

*Vachachamim omrim af al pi she'ee efshar l'kaymo besofo vehitnah alav mitchilato t'na'o kayam* — the *Chachamim*, however, hold that even if the condition is impossible to fulfill, the *t'nai* is nonetheless valid. Rabbi Yehuda ben Tema's counter-position is that an impossible condition is nothing but *mifliga vekasher* — mere torment — an attempt to make life miserable for the other party. There is no genuine conditional intent; the person making the condition knows it cannot be met.

### Divorce Examples

The *baraita* supplies vivid examples in the context of divorce. *Harei zeh gittech al menat sheta'ali larakia* — this is your bill of divorce, on condition that you ascend to the heavens. *Al menat sheterdi latehom* — on condition that you descend to the depths of the sea. *Al menat shetivli kaneh shel meah amah* — on condition that you swallow a rod one hundred *amot* in length. *Al menat sheta'avri et hayam hagadol beraglayich* — on condition that you cross the Mediterranean Sea on foot. The *baraita* says: if the condition is fulfilled, it is a valid *get*; if not, it is not a *get*. Rabbi Yehuda ben Tema says: in all such cases it is a valid *get*, and frames the matter as a general principle: *kol she'i efshar l'kaymo besofo v'hitnah alav mitechilato eino ela kemifliga* — any such impossible condition is merely the person tormenting the other party, and the *get* is valid regardless.

### Halacha Decision

*Amar Rav Nachman amar Rav: halacha keRabbi Yehuda ben Tema* — Rav Nachman rules that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Tema. An impossible condition does not void the accompanying act. This ruling is then supported by a careful reading of the *mishnah* itself: the *mishnah* says that a condition which is possible to fulfill is valid — the implication, *ha ee efshar*, being that if it is impossible, the condition is *batel* but the act stands. This inference from the *mishnah* corroborates the ruling of Rabbi Yehuda ben Tema.

---

## Ba'alav Imo

### Cow Owner Order

The *mishnah* at this point addresses the principle of *ba'alav imo* — the owner being present with the borrower. The *mishnah* distinguishes between two scenarios. First: *hashoel parah vesha'alah ba'aleha imah* — one borrows a cow and simultaneously borrows or hires the labor of its owner. Second: *sha'al haba'alim o secharan ve'achar kach sha'al et haparah* — one first borrows or hires the owner and only then borrows the cow. In both of these cases, if the cow subsequently dies, the borrower is exempt: *patur*, because the owner was present when the borrowing took effect. By contrast, if one borrowed the cow first and only afterwards engaged the owner, and then the cow dies — *chayav*, he must pay.

### Torah Source

The *mishnah*'s ruling is grounded in the Torah's language. The verse states: *v'chi yish'al ish me'im re'ehu v'nishbar o met ba'alav ein imo shalem yeshalem* — if a person borrows from his fellow and the animal is injured or dies, if the owner was not with him he shall pay in full. *Im ba'alav imo lo yeshalem* — if the owner was with him, he need not pay. The *mishnah* is defining what *ba'alav imo* means: the owner's presence or employment must precede or be concurrent with the borrowing of the animal itself. If the borrowing of the animal preceded the engagement of the owner, it is as though the owner was not present — *ba'alav ein imo* — at the critical moment when the borrowing took effect, and the borrower remains liable.

### Simultaneity Problem

The *gemara* raises a sharp question. The *mishnah*'s first case is understood to describe simultaneous engagement — both the cow and its owner are taken on at once. But *ima mamash mi meshkachat lah para be-meshicha u-baalim be-amira?* — how is that actually possible? Acquiring the *parah* requires a *meshicha*, a formal act of *kinyan* whereby one physically takes hold of the animal. Engaging the owner's labor, however, is accomplished through *amira*, a verbal commitment. These are qualitatively different acts. How can a *meshicha* and a verbal commitment occur simultaneously?

### Simultaneity Solutions

The *gemara* offers two solutions. The first: *ibayit eima kagon de-kaima para be-chatzeiro de-sho'el de-la michtara meshicha* — one may say that the animal was already standing in the *chatzer*, the property, of the borrower. In that case no separate *meshicha* is necessary, since a person's *chatzer* can effect *kinyan* on their behalf. The entire verbal transaction then occurs as one act, and the borrower simultaneously acquires the animal and engages the owner. The second solution: *de-amar lei at gufach lo tishal ad she-at meshichat paratecha* — one can construct the verbal engagement with a conditional clause, saying to the owner: your personal commitment to me does not take effect until the moment I perform *meshicha* on your animal. Even though the verbal statement was made first in time, it takes legal effect only at the precise instant the *meshicha* occurs, creating genuine simultaneity.

---

## Sources Shomrim

### Three Parshiyot

The *gemara* now turns to a more fundamental inquiry: where in the Torah do we find the source for the obligations of the four *shomrim*? A *baraita* is cited: *parsha rishona ne'emra b'shomer chinam, shniya b'shomer sachar, shlishit b'sho'el* — the first Torah passage deals with the *shomer chinam*, the second with the *shomer sachar*, the third with the *sho'el*. The third passage — *pesukim* 13 through 14 of the relevant section — is explicit: *v'chi yish'al ish me'im re'ehu* — if a man borrows from his fellow. That passage is unmistakably about the *sho'el*. The first passage, *pesukim* 6 through 8, describes one person entrusting an object to another for safekeeping, without specifying payment. The second passage, *pesukim* 9 through 12, discusses an animal entrusted for watching, introduces the oath for acts of God, and the obligation to pay if the animal is stolen.

### Attribution Problem

The *gemara* raises the difficulty: *bishlama shlishit b'sho'el meforash* — the third passage is explicitly about a borrower. But as for the first two passages — *ela rishona b'shomer chinam shniya b'shomer sachar ipuch ana?* — perhaps the assignment should be reversed? Perhaps the first *parsha* describes the *shomer sachar* and the second the *shomer chinam*? Neither passage names its subject explicitly. What forces us to read them in the order the *baraita* assigns?

### Kefel Argument

The *gemara* begins to work through the analysis. *Mistavra shniya b'shomer sachar sheken chayav b'gniva v'aveidah* — it makes sense that the second passage belongs to the *shomer sachar* because he is liable for theft and loss, which is the higher level of responsibility mentioned in that passage. But the *gemara* immediately counters: *adderaba, rishona b'shomer sachar* — on the contrary, perhaps the first passage should be assigned to the *shomer sachar*. Why? *Sheken meshalem tashlumei kefel b'toen ta'anat ganav* — because it is specifically in the context of the first passage that we derive the rule of *kefel*, the double payment penalty. The case is this: a *shomer chinam* who swears that the animal was stolen — and thereby exempts himself from payment — and is subsequently found to have stolen it himself, is treated as a *ganav* and must pay double. This rule of *kefel* for *to'en ta'anat ganav* — making a claim of theft to evade liability — applies in the first passage. The *shomer sachar*, who is already obligated to pay if the animal is stolen, cannot swear to exempt himself in that case, and therefore the mechanism that triggers *kefel* does not apply to him. On this reading, the first passage — which contains the *kefel* provision — would be assigned to the *shomer sachar*, who engages in a different kind of legal exposure than the *shomer chinam*.

### Keren vs Kefel

The *gemara* then presents the counter-argument. *Keren belo shvuah adifa mikfela bishvuah* — paying the *keren*, the principal, without any oath, is actually a greater liability than paying *kefel* under circumstances of false swearing. Proof: *teida deha shavek kol hana'ah shelo v'eino meshalem ela keren* — observe that the *sho'el*, who receives the greatest possible benefit from the object, pays only the *keren*, the principal value, when liable. The highest level of *shmira* liability in the system caps at paying the *keren*. That penalty is therefore weightier than the exceptional *kefel* case, which arises only from dishonest dealing outside the normal parameters of guardianship. Accordingly, the first passage, which contains the *kefel* provision, should be assigned to the *shomer chinam* after all.

---

## Sho'el Theft

### Paid Shomer Rules

Returning to the *mishnah* from *Shevuot*: *nosei sachar vehasocher nishba'in al hashvura v'al hashvuyah v'al hameta umeshalmin et ha'aveida v'et hagniva* — the *shomer sachar* and the *socher* swear regarding acts of God — injury, kidnapping, or death of the animal — and pay for loss (*aveidah*) and theft (*gneivah*).

### Theft & Loss

*Minah hani milei?* — where is this derived? The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *im ganov yiganeiv ein li ela gneivah aveidah minayin* — from the *pasuk* "if it is stolen" (*im ganov yiganeiv*), I know only that the *shomer sachar* must pay for theft. How do I know he must also pay for *aveidah*, loss? *Talmud lomar im ganov yiganeiv mikol makom* — the doubled language "if it is stolen, it is stolen" (*ganov yiganeiv*) teaches us: in any case of loss of this kind, including *aveidah*.

### Torah Language

The *gemara* notes that this derivation from the emphatic double language depends on the view that the Torah does not speak the way ordinary people speak — *lo amrinan dibra torah k'lashon b'nei adam*. On that view, the doubled form is intentionally significant and available for *derasha*. But according to those who hold *dibra torah k'lashon b'nei adam* — that the Torah does speak in the manner of ordinary speech — the emphatic form is merely rhetorical intensification and cannot be used as the basis for deriving *aveidah*.

### Kal Vachomer

For those who take the latter position, *amrei d'ma'arava* — the Sages of the west, in Eretz Yisrael, say: the derivation is through a *kal vachomer*. *Uma gneivah shekrova l'ones m'shaleim aveidah shekrova lipshiya lo kol sheken?* — if the *shomer sachar* is required to pay for theft, which is relatively close to an act of God — something largely outside his control — then surely he must pay for *aveidah*, loss, which is closer to negligence and therefore more clearly within the scope of his responsibility. The *kal vachomer* is compelling. The *gemara* then asks: if the *kal vachomer* suffices, why does the Torah bother with the doubled language? The answer: *milta d'ati b'kal v'chomer tarach v'chtav lah kra* — sometimes even when a matter is derivable through *kal vachomer* the Torah writes it out explicitly anyway.

---

## Sho'el Kidnapping

### Shvuyah Derivation

The *mishnah* states that the *sho'el* pays for everything — *vehashoel meshalem et hakol*. The *gemara* examines the sources for this. The verse explicitly covers *shvura* and *metah* — injury and death: *v'chi yish'al ish me'im re'ehu v'nishbar o meis* — and the animal is broken or dies. But what about *shvuyah* — kidnapping? The verse makes no mention of it. How do we know the *sho'el* is liable if the animal is taken captive?

### Comparison Issue

One might propose to derive the *sho'el*'s liability for *shvuyah* by analogy to the *shomer sachar*, who also lists injury, death, and kidnapping in his passage. The *gemara* rejects this: *ika l'mifrach ma lishomer s'char sheken liftor tomar b'sho'el sheken l'chiyuv* — the two cases are not analogous, because in the *shomer sachar*'s passage, *shvura*, *shvuyah*, and *metah* are listed as cases in which he is *exempt*, whereas for the *sho'el* we are trying to establish cases in which he is *obligated*. One cannot draw an analogy between cases of opposite legal effect.

### Rabbi Natan

The *gemara* therefore turns to Rabbi Natan: *ela k'Rabbi Natan. DeTanya Rabbi Natan omer: o l'rabos shvuyah* — the word *o*, "or," in the verse *v'nishbar o meis*, "broken or died," is superfluous in its plain sense and is therefore there to include *shvuyah*.

### Or Necessity

The *gemara* challenges this: *hai o mibay'lei l'chalek* — that word *o* is necessary for another reason. Without it, one might think that the *sho'el* is liable only if both injury *and* death occur together. *D'salka da'atach amina, ad d'mitbra umeisa lo mechayaiv* — one might have thought that unless the animal is both injured and then dies, there is no liability. The word *o* is therefore needed to tell us that injury alone, or death alone, each independently triggers the obligation. If *o* is already needed for that purpose, it is no longer available to include *shvuyah*.

### Logical Inference

The *gemara* then asks: this works according to Rabbi Yonatan — but what does Rabbi Yoshiya say? The *baraita* cited discusses the verse *ish asher yekaleil et aviv v'et imo* — a person who curses his father and his mother. Rabbi Yoshiya holds that the conjunctive language could be read to require both parents to be cursed simultaneously; it is only the closing clause *aviv v'imo kileil* that teaches us that cursing either one individually is sufficient. The implication of Rabbi Yoshiya's hermeneutic is that the word *o* in a verse is necessary to establish disjunction — that the cases are separate, not conjunctive — and therefore the *o* in *v'nishbar o meis* is needed for exactly that purpose and cannot be used to include *shvuyah*. Rabbi Yonatan, by contrast, holds that disjunction is always the default reading unless the Torah specifies *yachdav*, "together," explicitly; therefore for him the word *o* is available for *derasha*.

The *gemara* resolves even Rabbi Yoshiya's difficulty: *afilu teima Rabbi Yoshiya, l'chalek hacha lo tzarich* — even according to Rabbi Yoshiya, in this particular case the word *o* is not needed to establish disjunction, because that conclusion is a matter of pure logic. *Mah liktla kula, mah liktla palga* — what difference does it make whether the animal is killed entirely or only partially? Once the Torah establishes liability for injury, it is self-evident that death is also covered. Therefore the word *o* is not needed to separate the cases — and it is consequently available to teach the inclusion of *shvuyah*, even according to Rabbi Yoshiya.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 95

## Shoel & Ba'alav Imo

### Opening & Context

The daf begins toward the bottom of 94b, picking up a discussion about where we learn certain *p'turim* — exemptions — and how we can derive that a *shoel* (one who borrows an object) is exempt in a case of *ba'alav imo*, where the owner is present and working alongside the borrower. The broader inquiry involves contrasting the liabilities of a *shoel* with those of a *shomer sachar*, someone who is paid to guard an object but does not have permission to use it. Underlying this discussion is a *machloket* between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan in a *braita*, concerning the methodology of certain *drashot* — specifically, whether two criteria mentioned in a *pasuk* must both be fulfilled simultaneously in order to generate liability, or whether each independently suffices.

The *braita* derives its point from the *pasuk* concerning one who curses his parents: *ish asher yekallel et aviv ve'et imo*. One might have thought that liability requires cursing both parents together. Rabbi Yoshiya demonstrates otherwise: since each parent is placed next to the word *killel* at various points, each is independently sufficient to generate liability. Rabbi Yonatan agrees with the *halacha* but arrives there differently. His principle is that unless the Torah explicitly specifies *yachdav* — together, as it does in the prohibition against plowing with an ox and donkey — we assume that two criteria in a *pasuk* apply independently. Rashi notes that the word *yachdav* in the case of *lo yacharosh b'shor vachamor* is precisely what tells us that only the two animals together are forbidden, while without such explicit specification, each criterion stands on its own. The Ritva, citing Rabbi Pinchas Halevi (believed by many to be the author of *Sefer Hachinuch*, the brother of the Ra'ah), adds that this principle of *yachdav* applies only to *mitzvot lo ta'aseh*, since for a *mitzvat asei* such as taking the *daled minim*, it is self-evident that all four species must be taken together — the absence of *yachdav* would not imply that a single species suffices.

With this *machloket* as background, the *gemara* moves to the top of 95a.

### Shoel Liability Review

The *gemara* opens with the question: *gneiva ve'aveida bishoel minalan* — how do we know that a *shoel* is liable in a case of *gneiva ve'aveida*, where the borrowed animal was stolen or lost? The attempt to learn this from *shvura u'meta* — the case where the animal was injured or died — is immediately challenged: *mah lishvura u'meta delo efshar lemitrach vela'atuyei*. If an animal dies or is injured, there is nothing further the *shomer* can do; it is categorically an unpreventable situation. But *gneiva ve'aveida* is different — *de'efshar lemitrach vela'atuyei* — one could exert additional effort to recover a stolen or lost animal, to track it down or reclaim it from the thief. The two categories are thus fundamentally different in character, and one cannot be derived from the other.

Instead, the *gemara* turns to a *braita*: from the explicit *pasuk* we learn only *shvura u'meta*. For *gneiva ve'aveida*, we make a *kal vachomer*: a *shomer sachar*, who is exempt if the animal was injured or died, is nonetheless liable if the animal was stolen or lost. A *shoel*, who is liable even in cases of *shvura u'meta*, should certainly be liable for *gneiva ve'aveida* as well. The *gemara* declares this a *kal vachomer she'ein alav tshuva* — a *kal vachomer* that admits of no refutation. The very fact that this characterization must be stated signals that a potential counter-argument exists and must be addressed.

The potential challenge is as follows: a *shomer sachar* can, in certain circumstances, become liable for *kefel* — double payment. If a *shomer sachar* claims the animal was taken by an armed robber (*listim mezuyyan*) — which ordinarily qualifies as an *ones* and exempts him — and that claim is proven false, he is treated as a thief and becomes liable for *kefel*. A *shoel*, by contrast, can never find himself in such a situation. Since a *shoel* has no exemption to exploit by claiming the animal was stolen — he remains liable regardless — he can never be proven to have made a false exempting claim, and thus can never become liable for *kefel*. One might therefore argue that the *shomer sachar*'s liability structure is qualitatively superior, and the *kal vachomer* would fail.

The *gemara* rejects this: *afilu hachi karna deshoel adifa* — even so, the principal liability of a *shoel* is greater. The capacity to become liable for *kefel* is actually a function of having an exemption available to exploit. The *shomer sachar*'s exposure to *kefel* arises precisely because he has an out — the claim that it was stolen — which, if falsified, generates double liability. The *shoel* pays only one hundred percent, never two hundred percent, but his *karna* — the basic principal obligation — is broader and more demanding, precisely because he has virtually no exemptions. *Karna deshoel adifa*: the *shoel*'s underlying liability exceeds that of the *shomer sachar*, even though he never pays *kefel*. Alternatively, the *gemara* offers a second resolution: *kasavar listim mezuyan gazlan hu* — one might hold that an armed robber (*listim mezuyan*) is not classified as a *ganav* at all but as a *gazlan*, a category that would not generate *kefel* liability in the first place. This is itself a *machloket* debated across multiple places in *Shas*.

### Shoel vs. Shomer Sachar

Having established the *shoel*'s liability for *gneiva ve'aveida*, the *gemara* asks the inverse: *ashkachan lachiyuv* — we have learned what obligates. *Liftor minalan* — how do we learn the exemption? That is, how do we know that when *ba'alav imo* obtains, the *shoel* is exempt even in cases of *shvura u'meta*?

The attempt to derive this from *shvura u'meta* itself is challenged: *mah lishvura u'meta shekein ones* — the case of *shvura u'meta* involves a genuine unpreventable catastrophe, which has its own logic for generating exemption. The *gemara* therefore looks to the *shomer sachar* as the source. But *shomer sachar gufai minalan* — how does the *shomer sachar* himself acquire an exemption for *shvura u'meta*? The answer is: *gemiri chiyuvei deshomer sachar mechiyuvei deshoel* — the liabilities of a *shomer sachar* are derived from the liabilities of a *shoel*. The *gemara* thus proposes a cross-derivation: just as the *shoel* is exempt when the owner is present (*b'baalim patur*), so too the *shomer sachar* is exempt when the owner is present.

At this point, the *gemara* invokes the principle of *dayo*: when something is derived by *kal vachomer* or by *hekesh*, the derived law cannot exceed the source. *Dayo lavo min hadin lihyot k'nidon* — whatever is concluded from the *drasha* can be no more expansive than the original case. Therefore: just as *gneiva ve'aveida* of a *shomer sachar* is exempt *b'baalim*, so too *gneiva ve'aveida* of a *shoel* is exempt *b'baalim*. The *dayo* principle constrains the derivation from expanding beyond what is explicitly present in the source case.

The *gemara* then asks: what of those who do not accept the principle of *dayo*? *Ela l'man d'leit lei dayo* — for that opinion, how is the derivation structured? The answer: *amar kra v'chi yishal* — the Torah uses the letter *vav* at the opening of the section dealing with the *shoel*: *v'chi yishal*. The *vav*, as a conjunction linking the *shoel*'s section to the preceding section on the *shomer sachar*, allows bidirectional learning. *Vav mosif al inyan rishon v'yilamed elyon mi'tachton v'tachton me'elyon*: we can learn the upper case (*shomer sachar*) from the lower case (*shoel*), and the lower case from the upper case. This resolves the need for *dayo* by grounding the derivation in the structure of the *pesukkim* themselves.

## Ba'alav Imo Exemption

### Gezerah Shava Derivation

Having established the *shoel*'s liability for *gneiva ve'aveida* through *kal vachomer*, the *gemara* derives the *shoel*'s exemption when *ba'alav imo* applies by learning from the *shomer sachar* through a *gezerah shava*-style comparison. The *shomer sachar* is exempt for *gneiva ve'aveida* when the owner is present; since the *shoel*'s liability for *gneiva ve'aveida* was itself derived from the *shomer sachar*, the exemption of *ba'alav imo* must travel back along the same path. *Mah gneivah v'aveidah b'shomer sachar b'baalim patur, af gneivah v'aveidah shoel nami b'baalim patur* — just as a *shomer sachar* who is normally liable for *gneiva ve'aveida* is exempt when *ba'alav imo*, so too a *shoel* is exempt for *gneiva ve'aveida* when the owner is present. And by extension, since the *shoel* is exempt for *gneiva ve'aveida ba'alav imo*, he is certainly exempt for the more catastrophic cases of *shvura u'meta* as well, which are greater *ones*.

This leads to a striking result: *ba'alav imo* is a sweeping exemption for the *shoel*. The *shoel* normally bears the highest level of *shmirah* liability — liable even for *ones* — yet the single fact of the owner's presence essentially nullifies all liability. This is one of only two exemptions available to the *shoel* (the other being *metah machmat melacha*, where the animal dies in the normal course of the borrower's work), and it is remarkably broad in its reach.

### Principle of Dayo

The *gemara* raises the concern that the *dayo* principle might constrain the cross-derivation. As noted, *dayo* limits what can be learned through *kal vachomer* or *hekesh* to no more than what was already established in the source case. The question is whether *dayo* applies here in a way that would prevent the *shoel*'s exemption from being derived from the *shomer sachar*'s exemption in *ba'alav imo* cases beyond *gneiva ve'aveida*. An extensive treatment of *dayo* appears in Bava Kamma. *Dayo lavo min hadin lihyot k'nidon* — the derived conclusion must mirror the source.

For those who accept *dayo*, the *ba'alav imo* exemption is learned carefully through the *shomer sachar* case: just as *gneiva ve'aveida* for *shomer sachar* is *b'baalim patur*, so too for *shoel*. The principle does not permit extending the exemption further than what is explicitly established in the source.

### Vav Conjunctions

For those who do not hold of *dayo*, the *vav* of *v'chi yishal* provides an independent basis for bidirectional learning. The conjunction connects the *shoel*'s section to the *shomer sachar*'s section, allowing the Torah's rulings to flow in both directions. *Vav mosif al inyan rishon v'yilamed elyon mi'tachton v'tachton me'elyon* — the *vav* supplements the preceding subject, permitting us to learn the upper case from the lower case and vice versa. This is the mechanism for deriving the *shoel*'s exemption of *ba'alav imo* without relying on *dayo* at all. Both directions of learning — from *shoel* to *shomer sachar* and from *shomer sachar* to *shoel* — are grounded in the structure of the *pesukkim*.

## Peshiah B'Baalim

### Rav Acha vs. Ravina

Having established the scope of *ba'alav imo*, the *gemara* turns to a harder question: *itmar peshiah b'baalim* — what is the *halacha* regarding *peshiah*, outright negligence, when the owner is present? Does *ba'alav imo* exempt a *shoel* even when his loss of the animal resulted from his own gross negligence? On this, *pligi bah Rav Acha u'Ravina* — Rav Acha and Ravina disagree. One holds *chayav*, and one holds *patur*.

### Peshiah Not Exempted

The opinion that holds *chayav* — that the *shoel* remains liable for *peshiah* even when *ba'alav imo* — reasons as follows: *mikra nidrash l'fanav* — a *pasuk* is interpreted to apply to what is directly adjacent, one step removed, but not *l'fne fanav*, two steps removed. The Torah's structure places *shomer chinam* first, *shomer sachar* second, and *shoel* third. The exemption of *ba'alav imo* is written in connection with *shomer sachar* and *shoel* and cannot be extended back to *shomer chinam*. *Peshiah*, however, is the liability of a *shomer chinam* — it is the *shomer chinam*'s baseline obligation, which is then applied to *shomer sachar* and *shoel* by way of *kal vachomer*. Since the *ba'alav imo* exemption does not reach *shomer chinam*, and *peshiah* enters the liability of *shomer sachar* and *shoel* only through a *kal vachomer* from *shomer chinam*, the *ba'alav imo* exemption cannot neutralize a liability that traces its source to a *shomer* category to which *ba'alav imo* does not apply.

More precisely: *hanach chiyuva d'ktiv behu b'hedya hu d'miftar b'hedya* — only those liabilities explicitly written in the Torah with respect to *shoel* and *shomer sachar* fall within the *ba'alav imo* exemption. *Peshiah*, which arrives by way of *kal vachomer* from *shomer chinam*, does not fall within the explicit ambit of *ba'alav imo*. Therefore, the *shoel* who is negligent while the owner is present remains *chayav*.

### Peshiah Exempted

The opposing opinion holds *patur* — *ba'alav imo* does exempt *peshiah*. This position maintains *kasavar mikra nidrash l'fanav u'l'fne fanav* — a *pasuk* can indeed be interpreted two steps removed. The *ba'alav imo* exemption can therefore reach all the way back to *shomer chinam*, and since it applies even to *shomer chinam*, *peshiah ba'alav imo* is fully exempt across all three categories of *shomrim*, including *shoel*. The exemption of *im ba'alav imo lo yishalem* is thus read as applying even to *shomer chinam*, which brings *peshiah* — the *shomer chinam*'s foundational liability — within its scope. This is the *machloket Amoraim* between Rav Acha and Ravina.

## Mishnah Analysis

### Four Mishnah Cases

The *gemara* introduces the *mishnah* directly: *tnan hashoel para v'sha'ala ba'aleha ima* — if one borrows the cow and also asks the owner to work alongside, *hashoel hapara v'sachar ba'aleha ima* — or one borrows the cow and hires the owner, *sha'al ba'aleha o s'charan v'achar kach sha'al hapara* — or one first hired the owner and then borrowed the cow afterward — *v'meta patur*, the borrower is exempt. The *mishnah* thus presents the full matrix: borrowing the cow while the owner works alongside for free, borrowing the cow while hiring the owner, hiring the owner first and then borrowing the cow, and renting the cow while asking the owner to work alongside without pay.

### Explicit vs. Derived

One might notice that the *mishnah* mentions *shoel* and *socher* but omits *shomer chinam*. And it also omits *shomer sachar*. The *gemara* explains: *tana milta d'ktiv b'hedya b'kra katani* — the *tanna* of the *mishnah* includes only those cases that are written explicitly in the Torah. *D'atya midrasha lo katani* — cases derived through *drashot* are not enumerated in the *mishnah*. *Shomer sachar* and *shomer chinam* are categories whose *ba'alav imo* exemptions are derived through *drashot*, and therefore they are not spelled out in the *mishnah*. One might observe that this is not an entirely consistent principle across *Shas* — sometimes *chazal* preferred to include things learned from *Torah she'be'al peh* in the *mishnah*, reasoning that what is already in *Torah shebichtav* need not be repeated. The application here, however, is that only the explicitly textual cases appear.

### Socher Liability

The *gemara* then asks whose opinion the *mishnah* reflects, since it includes a *socher* — a renter. *Svara ha mani Rabbi Yehuda hi* — it sounds like Rabbi Yehuda's position. Rabbi Yehuda holds *socher k'shomer sachar dami* — a renter is treated like a paid guardian. This is somewhat counterintuitive: a *shomer sachar* is paid to watch an object without using it, while a *socher* pays to be permitted to use it. Yet Rabbi Yehuda equates their liability levels. If the *mishnah* reflects Rabbi Yehuda, it includes a liability level derived by *drasha* (since *shomer sachar* itself is derived from the *shoel* through *drasha*), which would undermine the principle just stated.

The *gemara* then suggests the *mishnah* might instead reflect Rabbi Meir's view: *d'amar socher k'shomer chinam dami* — Rabbi Meir holds the *socher* is treated like a *shomer chinam*, with a lower liability threshold, exempt for *gneiva ve'aveida* and liable only for *peshiah*. Under this reading, the *mishnah*'s inclusion of *socher* amounts to inclusion of *shomer chinam*, which itself implies that the *ba'alav imo* exemption extends to *shomer chinam* and that *shomer sachar* follows by *kal vachomer*.

The *gemara* further notes that Rabba bar Avuha transmits the *machloket* in reverse: under his version, Rabbi Meir is the one who equates *socher* to *shomer sachar*, and Rabbi Yehuda equates *socher* to *shomer chinam*. Either way, the *mishnah* can be read consistently with one of these positions, and the *machloket Amoraim* over whether *ba'alav imo* reaches *shomer chinam* (and thus *peshiah*) remains intact.

## Rav Hamnuna Rejected

### Rav Hamnuna's Conditions

Rav Hamnuna restricts the *ba'alav imo* exemption considerably. In his view, a *shoel* is *l'olam chayav* — always liable — unless two very specific conditions are jointly satisfied. First, the *shoel* must be engaged in the precise labor for which the animal was borrowed: *ad she'tehei para v'choresh ba* — the cow must be actively plowing, or *chamor u'mechamer achareha* — the donkey being driven along. Second, the owner must be present and working with the borrower *mishe'as she'ila ad she'as shevura u'meisa* — from the moment of the borrowing all the way through until the moment of the injury or death. *Alma kasavar ba'alav imo akula milta mashma* — Rav Hamnuna reads *ba'alav imo* as requiring the owner's presence throughout the entire episode.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges Rav Hamnuna from the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states: *af al pi she'haba'alim osim melacha b'makom acher u'meisa patur* — even though the owner is doing his work somewhere else, if the animal dies, the *shoel* is exempt. The challenge is direct: *mai lav b'melacha acheres* — does this not mean the owner is doing a different kind of work? Rava reads it as: *lo b'osa melacha* — no, he is doing the same type of work but at a different location. Practically, the image is one of the owner walking slightly ahead of the animal, loosening the earth with a shovel (*d'ka marpei v'azil kama*) while the borrower drives the plow from behind — two feet away, doing the same job, but not standing right next to the animal.

### Reisha & Seifa Analysis

This interpretation creates a tension with the *seifa* of the *mishnah*, which states: if the borrower hired the owner *after* taking the animal, and the owner is plowing right next to the animal (*al gabbah*) when it dies, the *shoel* is *chayav*. The *gemara* resolves this: *amri reisha ve'seifa be'otah melachah* — both the *reisha* and the *seifa* are discussing the same type of labor. *Reisha le'rabuta ka mashma lan* — the *reisha* comes to teach us something novel: even though the owner is not standing right next to the animal but rather working at a different spot (*de'af gav de'lav al gabbah*), as long as it is the same type of labor and the owner was present *bishe'at she'elah* — at the time of the borrowing — the *shoel* is exempt. *Seifa le'rabuta ka mashma lan* — and the *seifa* comes to teach the converse: even though the owner is right there next to the animal (*de'af gav de'al gabbah*), if he was not present at the time the borrowing agreement was made, the *shoel* remains *chayav*. The crucial factor, Rava demonstrates, is not the owner's proximity at the time of the animal's death, but his presence at the moment of *she'elah*.

## Ba'alav Imo Concepts

### Three Explanations

The discussion of Rava's rejection of Rav Hamnuna opens a conceptual question: what is the underlying rationale for *ba'alav imo*? Why should the owner's presence at the time of borrowing exempt a *shoel* who would otherwise bear the highest liability, even when that same owner is entirely absent at the time the animal is harmed?

### Employment Model

One explanation: once you have hired the owner to work alongside you, you cannot simultaneously be understood as a renter of the animal. The agreement to employ the laborer subsumes the transaction regarding the animal — the animal comes along as part of the labor arrangement, not as a standalone rental. In a sense, you hired the person, and the person brought his cow. The animal is incidental to the employment of the worker, not the other way around. This resonates with discussions elsewhere in the tractate (*pirkei* preceding this one) about workers who bring their own tools — in a similar way, if one hires a laborer, the laborer's equipment comes along as part of the package. The fundamental transaction is about the human labor, not about the animal.

### Quasi-Ownership

A third explanation: the reason a *shoel* bears such high liability in the first place is that he acquires a kind of quasi-ownership over the borrowed item by virtue of his permission to use it. His liability is, in a sense, commensurate with his ownership-like status. But when the actual owner is present, the borrower's quasi-ownership is negated — the real owner is there, his dominion is fully in force, and the borrower cannot be treated as a partial owner at all. This explanation works particularly well in combination with the employment model: if the fundamental agreement was about hiring the person rather than renting the animal, then the borrower's quasi-ownership over the animal never fully crystallized, and there is accordingly no *shoel* liability to speak of. These two models reinforce one another — and they also help explain why reversing the order matters: if you borrow the animal first and only afterward hire the worker, the foundational agreement was about the animal, the quasi-ownership has already attached, and no subsequent employment arrangement can undo it.

## Hamnuna Rejected Further

### Second Braitah

Having refuted Rav Hamnuna's first condition through the *mishnah*, Rava brings a second *braita* to reject Rav Hamnuna's second requirement — that the owner's presence must persist from *she'elah* through to *shevura u'meta*. The *braita* states: *mimashma shene'emar im ba'alav imo lo yeshalem* — from the fact that the *pasuk* already says "if the owner is with him, he need not pay," I would already know the converse: if the owner is not with him, he must pay. Why then does the Torah also write *ba'alav ein imo shalem yeshalem*? The *braita* answers: *lomar lach haya imo besha'at she'eilah ein tzarich lihyot imo besha'at shevurah ve'metah* — it comes to teach that if the owner was present at the time of the borrowing, he need not be present at the time of the injury or death in order for the exemption to apply.

### Rava's Conclusion

The *braita* continues with the reverse formulation: from the positive statement (*im ba'alav imo lo yeshalem*) I know the owner's presence exempts; but what if he was only present at the time of injury but not at the time of borrowing? The *braita* teaches: *haya imo besha'at shevurah ve'metah, tzarich lihyot imo besha'at she'eilah* — presence at the time of injury is insufficient; the owner must have been present at the time of *she'eilah*. Presence at *she'elah* alone suffices; presence at the time of the death alone does not. This is Rava's definitive conclusion: *tiyuvta de'Rav Hamnuna tiyuvta* — Rav Hamnuna's position is comprehensively rejected. The *ba'alav imo* exemption hinges entirely on the owner's presence at the inception of the borrowing arrangement. Once that condition is met, the exemption endures regardless of whether the owner is present when the animal is eventually injured or dies.

This conclusion is striking, since it means that in the vast majority of ordinary borrowing situations — where one goes to the owner's home, the owner hands over the animal, and the borrower takes it directly from the owner — the *shoel* would be exempt by virtue of *ba'alav imo*. Rava's reading makes the exemption remarkably broad in practical scope.

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Abaye's Position

The *gemara* now returns to the *machloket* between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan from 94b, which Abaye and Rava respectively adopt as their interpretive frameworks. *Abaye savar lah ke'Rabbi Yoshiya umitaretz likra ke'Rabbi Yoshiya* — Abaye holds like Rabbi Yoshiya and reads the *pesukkim* accordingly. *Rava savar lah ke'Rabbi Yonatan umitaretz likra ke'Rabbi Yonatan* — Rava holds like Rabbi Yonatan and interprets the *pesukkim* in that manner.

### Rava's Position

Rabbi Yoshiya's interpretive method, as Abaye adopts it, requires an explicit textual basis for each distinct criterion — one cannot assume that a single *pasuk* teaches two separate conditions simultaneously. Rabbi Yonatan's method, as Rava adopts it, allows a single *pasuk* to carry multiple implications: unless the Torah specifies *yachdav*, any two criteria apply independently of one another.

### Abaye's Criteria

Abaye reads the two *pesukkim* as follows. The *pasuk ba'alav ein imo shalem yeshalem* — "if the owner is not with him, he must pay" — implies *ta'ama deleita betarvaihu*: the liability arises because the owner is absent at both relevant times, that is, both at the time of *she'elah* and at the time of *shevura u'meta*. One might therefore think that the exemption requires the owner's presence at both times. But the *pasuk im ba'alav imo lo yeshalem* — "if the owner is with him, he need not pay" — implies that the exemption applies when the owner is present at both times. The tension between the two *pesukkim* is resolved as follows: *ha ita bechada veleita bechada mechayev* — if the owner is present at one time and absent at the other, you might be *chayav* according to one reading and *patur* according to the other. Abaye resolves the tension by holding: *lomar lach haya imo besha'at she'eilah ein tzarich lihyot imo besha'at shevurah ve'metah* — if the owner was present at the time of borrowing, he need not be present at the time of injury for the exemption to apply. But crucially — and this is Abaye's distinctive position — the converse also holds: *haya imo besha'at shevurah ve'metah, tzarich lihyot imo besha'at she'eilah* — if the owner was present only at the time of injury and not at the time of borrowing, the *shoel* is still *chayav*. For Abaye, the exemption is triggered only by presence at *she'elah*, but his reading of the *pesukkim* reflects Rabbi Yoshiya's methodology, requiring explicit derivation for each criterion separately.

### Rava's Criteria

Rava reads the same *pesukkim* differently, following Rabbi Yonatan. *Mashma de'ita betarvaihu* — from *im ba'alav imo lo yeshalem*, one might read that the exemption requires the owner's presence at both times. *Mashma nami dechi ita bechada velo ita bechada patur* — and from the same *pasuk*, one could also read that presence at even one of the two times suffices for exemption. These two readings pull in opposite directions. The tension is resolved by *lomar lach* — the Torah is teaching: *haya imo besha'at she'eilah ein tzarich lihyot imo besha'at shevurah ve'metah* — presence at the time of *she'eilah* alone generates the full exemption, and the owner need not be present at the time the animal is harmed. Conversely, *haya imo besha'at shevurah ve'metah tzarich lihyot imo besha'at she'eilah* — presence only at the time of the animal's death, without prior presence at *she'elah*, does not exempt the *shoel*. For Rava, following Rabbi Yonatan's principle that a *pasuk* teaches multiple independent criteria simultaneously, a single *pasuk* suffices to establish both the primacy of *she'elah* and the dispensability of presence at the time of injury. The bottom line is identical to Abaye's in practical outcome — only *she'elah* matters — but the derivational logic differs, rooted in their respective allegiances to Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan.

# Bava Metzia 96

## Ba'alav Imo Timing

### Two Moments Debate

The daf opens approximately ten lines from the top, at the word *aipoch*, within the line beginning *bish'at she'elah*. The Gemara has been analyzing the Torah's principle of *ba'alav imo lo yeshalem* — that if the owner was working for the borrower at the time the object was lent, the borrower is exempt from paying even for an accident. The previous daf established that the *pesukim* indicate one of two possible moments as the relevant point of time: either the moment the object was borrowed, or the moment the accident occurred. The Gemara had tentatively concluded that the relevant moment is the time of borrowing, and now it challenges that assumption.

*Aipoch ana?* — Why not reverse it? Perhaps the moment of the accident is the determinative time. The Gemara first defends the moment of borrowing: *mistavra she'elah adifa mishum dekamaytei lei lirshutei* — it makes more sense that the moment of borrowing is primary, because that is when the object enters the domain of the borrower. The parameters of liability are defined at the moment they are undertaken, and there is a sense — perhaps echoing the language of *imo* — that if the owner is present in some capacity at that defining moment, the object never fully leaves the owner's sphere of responsibility and control.

### Borrowing Precedence

The Gemara pushes back: *aderaba, shvura umesa adifa sheken chayav be'onseha* — to the contrary, the moment of breaking or death should be the more significant moment, because it is then that the actual debt comes into being. The obligation to pay arises when the accident occurs, so should not that moment define whether the borrower is obligated at all?

The Gemara responds that the accident alone does not generate the debt — the underlying liability was assumed at the time of borrowing, and the accident merely triggers it. The critical moment is the one that creates the obligation, not the one that activates it. But the Gemara is unpersuaded: *ve'ilu lav shvura umesa she'elah mai avid?* — without the accident, the underlying liability would produce nothing. The debt ultimately crystallizes at the moment of the accident, so why should the time of borrowing be privileged?

The Gemara's final answer shifts the ground entirely: *afilu hachi she'elah adifa sheken chayav bimzonoteha* — nevertheless, the time of borrowing is more significant, because it is precisely at that moment that the borrower assumes the obligation to feed the animal. This is somewhat surprising — if we are not dealing with an animal at all, there would be no such obligation — but the Gemara appears to be returning to the principle of *reshut*. The obligation to feed the animal signals that at the moment of borrowing, the borrower has taken on full possession and full responsibility over the object. It is that moment of possession that can be curtailed when the owner is simultaneously working for the borrower. The Gemara is satisfied with this answer.

What makes this discussion striking is that there is ultimately no direct textual indication in the *pesukim* as to which moment matters. The Gemara resolves the question through a logical assessment of where the decisive act of undertaking responsibility occurs, rather than from a close reading of the Torah's language.

### Rav Ashi's Proof

Rav Ashi offers an independent demonstration from the *pasuk* itself. The verse states *ve-chi yishal ish me-im re-ehu* — when a man borrows from his fellow. Rav Ashi reads this as implying *v'lo re-ehu imo* — excluding the case where the friend is already working together with the borrower. The very language of borrowing from one's fellow presupposes that the fellow is a separate party at the moment of borrowing, not someone already in the borrower's employ. The key word is *ve-chi yishal* — at the moment of borrowing. If at that moment the owner is already employed by the borrower, the exemption applies.

The Gemara raises an objection: if this exemption is already embedded in the words *ve-chi yishal ish me-im re-ehu*, why did the Torah need to state explicitly the principle of *ba'alav imo lo yeshalem*? Rav Ashi answers: without that explicit statement, one would have dismissed the reading of *ve-chi yishal* as merely the Torah's ordinary manner of expression, conveying nothing beyond the simple act of borrowing. It is only because the Torah separately and explicitly states that the owner's presence with the borrower affects liability that we return to *ve-chi yishal* and recognize what it was communicating all along — that the moment of borrowing, and whether the owner was then already in the borrower's employment, is the legally operative point.

---

## Shoel Parameters

### Forbidden Purpose

Having settled the timing question, the Gemara turns to a series of questions posed by Rami bar Chama concerning the parameters under which a *shoel* incurs liability. The first: *she'ela l'riva mahu* — what is the law if someone borrowed an object for a forbidden purpose? The example given is borrowing an animal for a sexual act with it. Does the law recognize liability arising from such a transaction at all?

Notably, the Gemara does not frame this primarily as a question about whether liability can arise from an *aveira*. Instead, it poses the question in terms of the normal mode of borrowing: *k'dishali inshi ba'inan* — do we require that the borrowing be of the kind that people ordinarily engage in, which this is not? Or, *o dilma ta'ama mai mishum hana'ah* — perhaps the governing principle is simply that the borrower derives benefit without payment, and since there is benefit here, even of this perverse kind, full liability follows? The question remains unresolved.

### Appearance Benefit

The second question: *shala l'raos bah mahu* — what if someone borrowed an object not to use it but merely for appearance's sake? The illustration is borrowing a friend's valuable car and parking it in one's driveway so that passersby will think one owns it, obtaining social benefit — perhaps a promotion, perhaps greater creditworthiness — without ever actually operating the vehicle. Is that the kind of benefit that generates *shoel* liability?

*Mamona be'ina v'ika* — perhaps one only needs to have borrowed an object of value and have done so; or, *o dilma mamona d'it lei hana'ah minei be'ina v'leika* — perhaps one needs specifically to have derived benefit from the use of the object itself. Rashi understands the latter as referring to direct benefit from the object's use. The question probes how narrowly the Torah defines the parameters of *shoel* liability: is it only when one borrows something for normal productive use that the full liability applies?

### Sub-Pruta Benefit

Third: *shala la'asot bah pachot mipruta mahu* — what if the borrower intended to use the object for a purpose worth less than a *pruta*? For example, borrowing a screwdriver momentarily to turn a single screw, where the rental value of that brief use is less than a *pruta*, and the screwdriver then breaks. *Mamona be'ina v'ika* — perhaps all that is required is that one borrowed an object of monetary value; or, *o dilma kol pachot mipruta lav klum hu* — perhaps any benefit amounting to less than a *pruta* is legally insignificant, meaning that when the entire plan was to derive less than a *pruta* of benefit, one was never truly functioning as a *shoel* at all, and full *shoel* liability never attached.

### Multiple Items Benefit

Fourth, building on the previous question: *sha'al shtei paros la'asot bahen pruta mahu* — what if someone borrowed two cows and planned to use them together to perform exactly one *pruta*'s worth of labor? The combined use amounts to a *pruta*, but each cow individually contributes less than a *pruta*.

*Mi amrinan zil batar shoel umash'il v'ika* — do we focus on the transaction between borrower and lender as a whole, in which case the borrowing was indeed for a *pruta*'s worth? Or, *o dilma zil batar paros* — do we look at each cow as a separate entity, *v'chol chada v'chada leika mamona*, in which case neither cow individually was borrowed for a *pruta*'s worth of benefit?

### Multiple Lenders

Fifth: *sha'al mishutfin v'nish'alu echad mehem mahu* — what if someone borrowed jointly-owned property from two partners, Reuven and Shimon, and at the time of borrowing, Reuven was working for the borrower? Is that sufficient for *ba'alav imo*?

The Gemara considers two possibilities: *kula be'alav bein'an ve-ha leika* — perhaps *ba'alav imo* requires that all owners be present in this relationship, and since Shimon was not, the exemption does not apply; or, *o dilma me-hai palga didei mi-pater* — perhaps Reuven's status as a part-owner who was working for the borrower at least exempts the borrower from liability to Reuven specifically. The Gemara does not entertain a third possibility — that one owner's presence might exempt the borrower entirely — and instead frames it as either an all-or-nothing rule or a partial exemption corresponding only to Reuven's share.

This connects to the underlying logic of *ba'alav imo*. If the rationale is that the owner's continued presence means the object remains, at some conceptual level, within the owner's *reshut*, then as long as both owners are not in that relationship with the borrower, the object has at least partially entered the borrower's exclusive control. If, on the other hand, the principle operates on the level of the personal dynamic between owner and borrower, then being employed by only one of two joint owners may not alter that dynamic sufficiently.

### Multiple Borrowers

The sixth question reverses the previous scenario: *shutfin she-sha'alu ve-nish'al le-echad mehem mahu* — Reuven and Shimon jointly borrowed a cow, and the owner was working for Reuven at the time. *Kula sho'el bein'an ve-leika* — does *ba'alav imo* require that the owner be in the employment of the entire borrowing entity, meaning both Reuven and Shimon together, which is not the case here? Or, *o dilma be-hai palga de-sha'il mi-pater* — does the owner's employment by Reuven at minimum exempt Reuven from his share of liability, even while Shimon remains liable?

Again, the question of which logic underlies *ba'alav imo* is directly relevant. If the cow is considered to remain under the owner's aegis by virtue of his working for the borrower, then being employed by one of two joint borrowers may leave the cow at least partially still within the owner's sphere. But if the operative factor is the owner-borrower relationship as a whole, then the absence of that relationship with one of the joint borrowers means the full dynamic of *ba'alav imo* has not been established.

---

## Wife's Property Cases

### Wife as Lender

The Gemara now turns to questions involving marital property. *She'eila min ha-isha ve-nish'al le-va'alah* — what if someone borrowed property belonging to a wife, specifically her *nichsei milog*, the property she brought into the marriage over which she retains title but her husband holds the right of use? Tosafot notes that this cannot mean she lent it unilaterally, since the husband has usage rights; rather, the question concerns a case where both parties agreed to the lending. If the husband was working for the borrower at the time of the loan, is that *ba'alav imo*? The husband does not hold title, but he is the one currently entitled to use the property. Does that make him the relevant "owner" for purposes of *ba'alav imo*?

### Wife as Borrower

The reverse case follows immediately: *isha she-sha'ala ve-nish'al le-va'alah mahu* — what if the wife borrowed a cow from a third party, and at the time, the owner of the cow was working for the husband? Since the husband has *kinyan peiros* over his wife's borrowed property — he is entitled to benefit from whatever she borrows in the same way he benefits from what she owns — is the owner considered to be working for the one who has the rights to the property, thereby triggering *ba'alav imo*?

### Kinyan Peirot Debate

Both of these questions reduce to a single underlying issue: *kinyan peiros ke-kinyan ha-guf dami o lo* — is the ownership right to the produce and benefit of a thing considered equivalent to full ownership of the thing itself?

To illustrate the general principle: one cannot purchase an apple harvest in advance because that would be acquiring something not yet in existence (*davar shelo ba la'olam*). However, one can purchase the tree itself for the sake of its apples — *kinyan guf le-peiros* — acquiring a property right in the tree that entitles one to its produce, analogous to mineral rights. This does not permit one to chop the tree down; it is not *kinyan ha-guf* in the absolute sense. But it is a genuine property right.

In the case of *nichsei milog*, the husband holds exactly this kind of right: *kinyan ha-guf le-peiros*, ownership for the sake of its benefit, for the duration of the marriage, with the possibility that he may eventually inherit it outright. The question is whether, for purposes of *halachot* in which the status of owner is operative, the husband is considered the owner by virtue of this right.

Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute this in the context of *bikurim*. If one sells a field to another for all of its produce — giving the buyer *kinyan peiros* — and the field produces first fruits, may the buyer bring *bikurim* and recite the declaration of *et ha-adamah asher natata li*, "the land which You gave me"? Rabbi Yochanan says yes — *kinyan peiros ke-kinyan ha-guf dami*, the ownership of the produce is tantamount to ownership of the body of the land — and the buyer may both bring and recite. Reish Lakish says *kinyan peiros lav ke-kinyan ha-guf dami* — the buyer must bring the *bikurim* since the fruit is indeed his, but he may not recite the declaration, since the land itself is not his.

This debate is referenced here only briefly; it is developed at much greater length elsewhere in the Gemara. Its resolution governs both of the wife's-property questions above.

---

## Agency Questions

### Messenger Representation

Ravina poses a further question to Rav Ashi: *ha-omer lishlucho tzei ve-hishael li im parasi mahu* — what if the owner, rather than going himself to work for the borrower, sends his agent or messenger to accompany the borrowed cow and assist the borrower? Is that sufficient for *ba'alav imo*?

This question is genuinely puzzling. A *shliach* normally represents his principal in a legal act — purchasing, selling, delivering a *get*, accepting *kiddushin*. The question here is whether the concept of *shlichut* can extend to a non-legal act, namely, physically working for or assisting someone. The owner mowing the borrower's lawn is not itself a legal transaction; it is the fulfillment of an agreement or an act of goodwill. If someone does it in the owner's place, they are not the owner. *Ba'al mamash ba'ina ve-leika* — perhaps we literally require the owner himself, and a representative does not suffice; or, *o dilma shelucho shel adam kemoto* — perhaps the general principle that an agent is like the principal himself applies here as well.

### Related Debates

Rav Acha son of Rav Avya answers Rav Ashi by noting that these two questions — the husband's *kinyan peiros* and the effectiveness of a *shliach* — each corresponds to an established debate among the *Amoraim* and *Tannaim* respectively. The question of the husband's rights as a form of ownership is the debate of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding *kinyan peiros ke-kinyan ha-guf*. The question of whether a *shliach* can serve as the owner's representative for *ba'alav imo* corresponds to the debate of Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya.

### Rabbi Yonatan vs. Yoshiya

A *Baraita* is cited to illuminate the debate between Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya. The case concerns an *apitropus* — a trustee or guardian given full power of attorney over one's affairs — to whom the principal says: annul any vow my wife makes while I am away. The *halacha* is that a husband may annul his wife's vow on the day he hears it. The question is whether this power of annulment can be delegated to an agent, such that the agent's hearing is treated as the husband's hearing and the agent's annulment as the husband's annulment.

Rabbi Yoshiya holds that it cannot: the verse states *ishah yekimenu ve-ishah yeferenu* — the husband establishes it and the husband annuls it — with the word "husband" appearing twice in close juxtaposition, indicating that the actual husband is required, not his representative.

Rabbi Yonatan disagrees: *matzinu be-chol makom she-shelucho shel adam kemoto* — the general principle of *shlichut* applies throughout *halacha*, and an agent is equivalent to the principal.

Tosafot notes that everyone accepts the general principle of *shlichut*; Rabbi Yoshiya's restrictive position must therefore be based on the specific language of the *pasuk*. By analogy, in the case of *ba'alav imo*, Rabbi Yoshiya's position would likely hold that the *pasuk*'s language of *ba'alav* — the owner — means the owner literally, not his representative, just as *ishah* means the husband himself.

One might add a more structural observation: *shlichut* typically operates in the domain of legal acts — buying, selling, giving a *get*, accepting *kiddushin*. These are transactions that can be performed by a representative because their essence is legal. By contrast, the owner physically working for the borrower is not itself a legal act; it is conduct that satisfies an agreement. The act of hearing a wife's vow similarly is not a legal act — the annulment is the legal act, but the hearing is not. If the non-legal act of working or of hearing cannot be delegated through *shlichut* in the same way a legal act can, that is a principled reason for Rabbi Yoshiya's limitation that goes beyond the *pasuk* alone. In any event, the Gemara connects these two debates.

### Slave Extension

A related question is then posed by Rav Ilish to Rava: *ha'omer l'avdo tzei ve-hishayel im parati imahu* — what if the owner sends not a free agent but his non-Jewish slave to accompany the borrowed object and assist the borrower? Does the slave's working for the borrower constitute *ba'alav imo*?

The question, says the Gemara, cuts both ways regardless of how one resolves the debate about a *shliach*. According to the view that a *shliach* does constitute *ba'alav imo* — *shelucho shel adam kemoto* — one might still exclude a slave: *hani mili shliach d'var mitzvah hu* — that principle applies to an agent who shares the principal's obligations, i.e., a Jew equally bound by the *mitzvot*. A non-Jewish slave, *d'lav bar mitzvah hu*, cannot represent the owner in this domain. Rashi elaborates: since a slave has no independent property rights and cannot engage in the legal and social framework of lending, borrowing, and voluntary employment, he is categorically excluded from serving as a representative in these matters.

Conversely, even according to the view that a *shliach* does not constitute *ba'alav imo* — *ein shelucho shel adam kemoto* — there is a distinct and arguably stronger argument for the slave: *aval eved yad eved ke-yad rabbo damya* — a slave's hand is like his master's hand. The slave is not a representative at all; he is an extension of the master's own person and property. Whatever the slave does is an expression of the master himself.

The Gemara concludes: *mistavra yad eved ke-yad rabbo damya* — it stands to reason that the slave is an extension of the master. Whatever one holds about the *shliach* question, the *eved* functions as a physical extension of the master and satisfies *ba'alav imo*.

---

## Husband Liability Type

### Liability Category

The final line of 96a introduces another question of Rami bar Chama: *ba'al b'nichsei ishto, shoel havei o socher havei* — with respect to the wife's *nichsei milog* that the husband uses during the marriage, is the husband's status analogous to that of a *shoel* or that of a *socher*?

This matters for liability. A *shoel* bears full liability even for accidents — *ones*. A *socher* is exempt from *ones*. The husband receives the benefit of his wife's property without paying her for it directly, which suggests a parallel to a *shoel*, who receives benefit without payment. On the other hand, *Chazal* established that in exchange for the husband's rights to the wife's property, he assumes obligations toward her — food, shelter, support. In that framework, the relationship begins to resemble a *socher*, who pays for his use, here in the currency of marital obligations rather than money.

It is worth noting in this context that the Rambam conceptualizes the *shoel*'s relationship to borrowed property as a kind of *kinyan ha-guf le-peiros le-zman* — a property right over the object for the purpose of its benefit, for a limited period. The borrower does not hold title, but has a genuine property interest for the duration of the loan. In that sense, the husband's *kinyan ha-guf le-peiros* for the length of the marriage fits the same conceptual mold — the same structure, simply over a longer and differently-defined period, with the additional possibility that he might eventually inherit the property outright.

### Rental to Marriage

Rava initially points out that Rami bar Chama's question is moot as ordinarily framed: *ממה נפשך*, either way, the husband is *ba'alav imo* with respect to his wife. If he is a *shoel*, it is a *she'ela b'ba'alim* — Rashi explains that the wife is always in the husband's employ in the sense that her labor belongs to him, *bimlachto ve-hi nish'eles lo techila misheniseis*. From the moment of marriage, the wife's labor is effectively borrowed to her husband, making any use of her property an instance of *ba'alav imo*. And if he is a *socher*, the same logic applies — it is *schirus b'ba'alim*. The question therefore dissolves before it can do any work.

The Gemara labors to find a scenario in which the *shoel-socher* distinction genuinely matters. The first attempt: *agrah mina para ve-hadar nasbah* — he first rented the cow from her before she became his wife, and then married her. At the time of the original rental, she was not working for him, so the relationship was not *ba'alav imo*. Upon marriage, his rights to the cow expanded — he now has *kinyan ha-guf le-peiros* for the duration of the marriage, beyond the original thirty-day rental term, and without continued payment. If we consider this to be a new *shoel* relationship, it is *ba'alav imo* from the moment of marriage. If it is continuous with the prior *socher* relationship, it remains not *ba'alav imo* from its inception.

But the Gemara objects: even if he is a *socher* after marriage, the terms of the *schirus* have changed so completely — different duration, different consideration — that it constitutes a new rental agreement in any event. Whether *shoel* or *socher*, the relationship to the cow is redefined upon marriage and assessed afresh. Either way, it is now *ba'alav imo* and the question remains moot.

The Gemara then refines the scenario further: *ela ki kamibaya lei le-Rami bar Chama ki-gon d'agra ihi para me-alma ve-hadar nasba* — what if the wife was the one who first rented the cow from a third party, and then got married? The husband now has rights to the cow she rented, in the same way he has rights to what she owns. The question is whether his relationship to this cow makes him a *shoel* or a *socher* — and critically, this matters *aliba de-Rabbi Yosi*.

The Rabbis hold that if a *socher* lends an object to a *shoel* and an *ones* occurs, the *shoel* pays the *socher*, and the *socher* goes free vis-à-vis the original owner because it was an *ones* for a *socher*. The *shoel*'s obligation runs to the *socher*, not to the original owner. Under that framework, the husband's obligation in this case runs to his wife, and it is *ba'alav imo* in any event — she is in his employ.

But Rabbi Yosi rules *tachzor parah la-ba'alim rishonim* — payment returns to the original owner. If a *shoel* borrows from a *socher*, and the *shoel* is liable for *ones*, his liability runs directly to the original owner, not to the *socher* intermediary. Applied here: the wife rented the cow from Reuven and the husband has the rights of use. The husband is the functional *shoel* of Reuven's cow. According to Rabbi Yosi, if the husband is a *shoel*, he owes Reuven directly, and the question of *ba'alav imo* — was Reuven working for the husband? — is not satisfied. If, however, the husband is only a *socher*, his liability to Reuven is at the level of *socher*, which does not extend to *ones*. That is the genuine *nafka mina* of the question.

### Husband as Owner

Rava cuts through the entire discussion: *ba'al lo shoel havei ve-lo socher havei, ela lokei'ach havei* — the husband is neither a *shoel* nor a *socher*; he is considered a full purchaser, a *lokei'ach*. In the case of the husband and wife, *Chazal* granted the husband rights that go beyond even the general category of *kinyan peiros*, making him effectively the first purchaser of the property.

### Usha Enactment
