The source for this ruling is the statement of Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina: *be-Usha hitkinu* — at Usha they enacted the following. If a wife sells her title to her *nichsei milog* property during the lifetime of her husband and then she dies, the husband may repossess the property from the buyers. Why? Because the husband's *kinyan peiros*, his right to the benefit of the property, predates the buyer's acquisition of the title. When the wife dies and the husband inherits, he is considered a prior *lokei'ach* — a prior purchaser — whose claim precedes that of the later buyer.

This status as *lokei'ach rishon* does not grant the husband unlimited rights; he cannot sell the property out from under the wife, nor make structural changes. But it means that in certain contexts — specifically when competing against a later purchaser of the wife's title — the husband's *kinyan peiros* is treated as tantamount to prior ownership of the property itself. By the same logic, in the context of *basar* liability, the husband is not a *shoel* or *socher* who owes a duty of care to the wife; he is considered the owner, and an owner owes no liability to anyone.

Tosafot, however, notes: *umihu nireh le-Ri d'shomer chinam havei ve-chayav bifshiah* — even given this *takkanah* that treats the husband as effectively the full owner, it seems that he would at minimum be a *shomer chinam*, a gratuitous guardian, and liable for negligence. Making him a *lokei'ach* does not fully relieve him of even basic responsibility. This connects to a broader question treated earlier in the Gemara: whether *pshiah b'va'alim* — negligence in a case of *ba'alav imo* — also earns an exemption, which depends on whether *pshiah* is understood more as a category of damage than as a form of guardianship failure.

---

## Hekdesh Me'ilah

### Me'ilah Issue

Rami bar Chama poses yet another question: *ba'al b'nichsei ishto mi ma'al* — with respect to his wife's property, if among her *nichsei milog* there is money or an animal that was consecrated to the *Beis HaMikdash* — *hekdesh* — and neither she nor the husband is aware of it, who commits *me'ilah*? The husband, upon marriage, acquires *kinyan peiros* over the wife's property and, according to Rava's ruling above, is in some sense treated as a *lokei'ach*. Does the act of marriage — through which the husband's property rights automatically attach — constitute an act of taking possession of *hekdesh*, thereby triggering *me'ilah*?

### Me'ilah Culpability

Rava responds by working through all possible candidates for *me'ilah* and eliminating each. Should the husband be the one who commits *me'ilah*? *D'tafei nicha lei d'likni ve-issura lo nicha lei d'likni* — he would certainly have wanted to acquire her property, but he would never have wanted to acquire something that was forbidden to him. He had no intention of taking possession of *hekdesh*, and the mere fact that his rights automatically attached to all her property upon marriage cannot be said to be a volitional act of taking *hekdesh* into his control.

Should the wife commit *me'ilah* by virtue of transferring the property rights to her husband through marriage? *D'tafei nami lo nicha lah d'likni* — at some level she does not fully welcome his rights over her property even in general; certainly she would not want to be seen as transferring rights over *hekdesh* to him. And in any case, no physical act was performed with the *hekdesh* object.

Should *Beis Din* commit *me'ilah*, since it was their enactment — the *takkanat ha-rabbanan* granting the husband *kinyan peiros* and indeed *lokei'ach* status — that caused *hekdesh* property to flow into the husband's domain? *Ki avud Rabbanan takanta ve-amru ba'al lokei'ach shavei le-heteira le-issura lo avud Rabbanan takanta* — when the Rabbis enacted that the husband is treated as a purchaser, they did so only *le-heteira*, for permissible property; they never intended their enactment to apply to *issur*, to consecrated property that cannot be owned by private individuals. Their enactment simply does not extend to *hekdesh*, and therefore it cannot be said that *Beis Din*'s enactment effectuated any transfer of *hekdesh* into the husband's possession.

### Me'ilah at Spending

Having excluded all three candidates from committing *me'ilah* at the moment of marriage, Rava resolves: *ba'al mo'el lichsheyotzi, midi d'hava amotzi ma'os hekdesh le-chulin* — the husband commits *me'ilah* when he spends the money, by analogy to the general case of one who spends *hekdesh* funds.

The reasoning is as follows. If one has *hekdesh* money in one's home and is unaware of it, simply moving it or placing it in one's pocket does not constitute *me'ilah*, because that act of physical possession is not an act of taking something away from *hekdesh* when one imagines oneself already to be the owner. If one knowingly takes *hekdesh* money and places it in one's pocket to acquire it, that would be *me'ilah* — it is an act of appropriating something from the *Beis HaMikdash*. But in a case where one is unaware of the *hekdesh* status and considers oneself the owner, the act of moving it is not *me'ilah*. The act of *me'ilah* occurs only when one spends the money — at the moment of actual misappropriation of *hekdesh* funds for personal use.

Here too: the husband considers himself the *lokei'ach* of this property. His carrying the bag of coins from one room to another or placing it in his pocket is not an act of taking possession of *hekdesh* as such; he already regards himself as the owner. The *me'ilah* occurs when he actually spends the money or uses the animal, because that is the moment of genuine misappropriation.

---

## Meta Machmat Melacha

### Use Deterioration

The Gemara raises a new question: *kichash basar machmat melacha ma* — if through normal use the animal became thinner, is the *shoel* liable for this diminishment in value? As a *shoel*, one has full liability. Does that extend to ordinary deterioration resulting from the use one borrowed the animal for?

Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua respond with a sharper challenge: the question about the animal getting thinner implies that you believe the *shoel* would be liable if it died from exertion during normal use — *meta machmat melacha*. But why should that be so?

### Implicit Agreement

*Lav le'okmeh be-chilta she'altiah* — the owner did not lend it to be kept locked in a shed. The very act of lending it was an acknowledgment that the borrower had the right to use it. And that right to use it carries with it an implicit acceptance that normal use entails normal wear. If the borrower has the right to use the object in the agreed manner, the owner has implicitly agreed to the consequences of that use. A cow that has a heart attack due to exertion during plowing — where the exertion was perfectly ordinary and within the scope of the loan — is in a sense a case of the owner having lent something that was going to wear down through its intended use. That is not the borrower's responsibility.

This creates a remarkable asymmetry: when a total *ones* occurs — the cow is struck by lightning — the *shoel* is liable, because that has nothing to do with the agreement between them. But when the cow dies precisely from the use the owner agreed to, the borrower is exempt, because the owner implicitly assumed that risk by making the loan. Rava states the rule explicitly: *lo mibaya kichash basar machmat melacha depatur* — it goes without saying that getting thinner does not trigger liability; *ela afilu meta machmat melacha nami patur* — even dying from normal use leaves the borrower exempt. *De'amra lei lav le'okmeh be-chilta she'altiah* — the owner agreed to the use, and therefore agreed to its consequences.

### Hammer Case

The practical application follows: a man borrowed a hammer from his friend, and it broke. He came before Rava. Rava said: *zil ayiti sahadi de-la shanita bah ve'iftar* — go bring witnesses that you used it in an entirely ordinary way, and you will be exempt, because if the hammer broke under normal use, that is *meta machmat melacha* and outside the borrower's liability.

### Proof Burden

The Gemara then asks: what if there are no witnesses? A second incident is cited — the same scenario of a borrowed hammer that broke — and Rava ruled: *zil shalim lei narga ma'alya* — go pay him a full hammer. Rashi explains that in this case the borrower was negligent; this is not the scenario of pure normal use but of *pshiah*. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged Rava: is that really the law? The borrower should not have to pay the full value of a new hammer; he should return the broken pieces and pay only the difference between their value and the value of a whole hammer.

Rava was silent — they were correct — and the *halacha* is established accordingly: *de-mahardar lei tavrei u-mamlei lei dmei mana* — he returns the broken pieces and pays the difference in value between the broken pieces and a whole hammer, as was also established in Bava Kamma.

The broader implication is that while the category of *meta machmat melacha* carves out a significant exemption for the *shoel*, the burden of proof rests on the borrower to demonstrate that the object was used in a normal and unremarkable way. If no witnesses are available to confirm this, the borrower bears liability — and the measure of that liability, even in a case of negligence, is not the replacement cost of the object but the diminishment in value, with the broken item returned to its owner.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 97

## Borrower Exemptions

### Opening & Context

The daf picks up near the top of 97a, continuing the discussion that has been unfolding across the previous pages. We have been transitioning through two distinct exemptions available to a *shoel*, a borrower. The first is *baalav imo* — that the owner of the borrowed object was simultaneously hired or asked to work alongside the borrower, which provides a full exemption from liability. The second is *meita machmat melachah* — that the animal or object died or broke as a direct result of normal, intended use.

### Meita Machmat Melachah

Two explanations are offered for why *meita machmat melachah* exempts the *shoel*. The first is that it actually reflects a degree of *pshia* on the part of the *mashil*, the one who lent the object or animal. If the animal cannot sustain a normal workload, the owner should not have lent it in the first place; the liability therefore reverts to the owner for having effectively guaranteed that the animal or object could withstand that level of use. The second explanation treats it as ordinary wear and tear — something entirely to be expected when one lends an item for use. If it breaks or dies as a result of that expected use, the outcome was foreseeable and the owner implicitly accepted it.

### Rav's Axe Ruling

Turning briefly to the case of Rav's ruling on the broken axe: Rav at first appeared to *pasken lifnim mishurat hadin*, beyond the strict letter of the law. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged this — *dina hachi?* Is that really the law? — and it seems the *halachah* follows them. As Rashi, drawing on Bava Kamma, explains, even where the *shoel* acted negligently and the breakage was not *meita machmat melachah*, he is liable only for the partial loss in value, not the full worth of the axe, because *bealim metaplim bineveilah* — the owner retains the broken object — and that is why Rav's initial ruling seemed difficult.

### Rav Pappa Bucket

The Gemara continues on the third line of 97a. A person borrowed a bucket from his friend; it broke. He came before Rav Pappa. Rav Pappa told him: bring witnesses that you did not misuse it — *ayiti sahadi dlo shinit bah* — and you will be exempt. This extends the principle of *meita machmat melachah* to inanimate objects. What is notable here is that the burden of proof falls squarely on the *shoel*. Given the *shoel*'s elevated level of liability, the default assumption when something breaks is negligence. Only once the *shoel* demonstrates proper use does the exemption apply.

### Shvua & Shoel

One might ask: why must the *shoel* bring witnesses? Could he not simply exempt himself through *shvuat hashomrim* — the oath that *shomrim* typically take, swearing that they were not negligent, did not misappropriate the object, and so on? In most *shomrim* cases, such an oath would suffice. Most *Rishonim* do in fact hold that a *shoel* may take the *shvua*, and the specific cases discussed here simply happen to involve witnesses as the available avenue of proof, with the *shvua* as an alternative where witnesses are unavailable. However, the *Ritva* cites an opinion — ultimately rejected — that a *shoel* differs fundamentally from other categories of *shomrim*. Given the *shoel*'s uniquely high level of liability, perhaps *shvuat hashomrim* is simply not available to him as a vehicle for exemption. While the majority of *Rishonim* do not accept this position, it illuminates the degree to which the *shoel* occupies a distinct and more demanding position within the *shomrim* framework.

---

## Cat Case

### Mice Attack Cat

The Gemara now introduces what is perhaps the most colorful case on the page. *Hahu gavra disha'al shunra michavreih* — a man borrowed a cat from his friend. This requires a brief note: in the world of *Chazal*, a cat is not a pet but a working animal whose job is to catch mice. But here the situation went badly wrong — *chavru aleih achbarei vekatluha* — the mice ganged up on the cat and killed it. The infestation was so severe that the sheer number of mice was able to overpower a single cat.

### Rav Ashi Question

*Yativ Rav Ashi vekamibaia leih ki hai gavna mai* — Rav Ashi sat and posed the question: how should one rule in such a case? Does it qualify as *meita machmat melachah*? After all, the cat was doing precisely what it was borrowed to do — catching mice. Yet one could argue that the *shoel* was a *poshea* in a sense, since the infestation was so extreme that a single cat was clearly insufficient; perhaps he should have arranged for multiple cats. So is this case comparable to *meita machmat melachah* or not?

Rav Mordechai answered on behalf of Rav Ashi, citing a tradition in the name of Avimi from Agronya, who reported in the name of Rava: *gavra denashei katluha, lo dina velo dayana* — a man who was killed by women has no claim and no judge. The saying captures the extreme rarity of the scenario. In an era when violent confrontations were generally determined by brute physical strength, a man overpowered and killed by women would represent something so far outside the ordinary that it would be nearly impossible to convince anyone it had occurred. So too here: mice overpowering and killing a cat is so extraordinary and so far beyond what a borrower could have anticipated or prevented that it falls squarely within the category of *meita machmat melachah*, and the *shoel* is exempt.

### Cat Overstuffed

The Gemara then presents an alternative version of the case. *Ika de-amri hachi achal achbarei tuva vechavil umit* — there are those who say the actual case was different: the cat did not die from the mice attacking it, but rather from overeating — it consumed so many mice that it was overwhelmed and died. Rav Ashi is described as sitting and pondering this version of the case — *yativ Rav Ashi veka maayan bah ki hai gavna mai* — and again asking: how should one rule? Rav Mordechai again cites the same ruling from Avimi in the name of Rava, applying the same phrase: *gavra denashei katluha*.

### Rashi Interpretation

What is striking is that Rashi understands the idiom differently in the context of this second case. Whereas in the first version the phrase evokes an unlikely violent defeat, in the second version — where the cat died from overindulgence — Rashi explains *denashei katluha* as *ba'al be'ilot harbeh umet*: a man who was excessively licentious and was debilitated or died from the consequences of his indulgence. The analogy shifts accordingly: just as such a fate, while self-inflicted, results from the very activity one is engaged in and exceeds all ordinary expectation, so too a cat dying from consuming an excessive quantity of mice is an outcome so unusual and so far outside what the *shoel* could have foreseen that it remains *meita machmat melachah*, and the exemption holds.

---

## Employment Loophole

### Rava's Loophole

The Gemara pivots to a clever but somewhat mischievous scenario introduced by Rava. *Hai man deba'ei lemish'al midi michavreih* — what if someone wants to borrow an object from a friend while avoiding any liability at all? The simplest method, Rava explains, is to invoke *baalav imo* not through a genuine employment arrangement, but through a minimal gesture: *neimei lei ashkayan maya* — just say to the owner, "go get me a glass of water." At the moment of borrowing, the owner is technically performing a service for the borrower and is therefore under his employ — *de'hava she'ila biv'alav* — and the borrowing falls under the exemption of *baalav imo*.

### Closing the Loophole

Rava immediately anticipates the obvious counter-strategy. *I pikeiach hu* — if the lender is shrewd enough to recognize the scheme, he will respond: *neimei lei shtayei bidisha vehadar ashkayan* — finish the threshing first, and only afterward will I go get you the glass of water. That is, the owner insists on completing the actual work — the task for which he is being hired — before the act of lending takes place. By sequencing the labor before the loan, the employment relationship is concluded by the time the borrowing commences, and the *baalav imo* exemption no longer applies. The loophole closes.

It is worth noting that the concept of "hiring" in this context does not require monetary compensation. *Baalav imo* can be established through any form of work, paid or unpaid — even asking someone to perform a small favor constitutes sufficient grounds, which is precisely what makes the loophole so easy to exploit and the counter-strategy so important.

---

## Public Servants

### Service Workers

The Gemara proceeds to a fascinating application of *baalav imo* rooted in the economic realities of the *Chazal* era. Rava rules: *dekari dardekei* — one who reads to children, i.e., a school teacher; *shatla*, a gardener; *tavcha*, a butcher or slaughterer; and *umana*, a bloodletter — *kuleihu be'idan avdeihu keshe'ila biv'alav damu* — all of these, during the time they are engaged in their work, are treated as if one has borrowed something from them in the presence of the owner. If you borrow any object from any of these individuals, it is automatically regarded as *she'ila biv'alav*, and the borrower is exempt from liability. The rationale is that each of these figures works in a service capacity for the general public, and in that sense, the borrower is always already, in some meaningful sense, their employer.

### Communal vs Individual

This ruling generates a significant *machloket Rishonim* about the precise mechanism at work. Rashi understands the exemption to operate on an individual basis: when you have a specific, direct business relationship with one of these professionals — for example, you have engaged the butcher to slaughter and process your animal — then for the duration of that processing work, you have effectively hired him, and *baalav imo* applies. The week of preparation that leads up to the moment you pay for a finished cut of meat means that the butcher was, in a contractual sense, working on your behalf through the entire process, even though your actual transaction lasted only a few minutes.

The Rif takes a broader, more communal view. These professionals are employed, in effect, by the community as a whole. The butcher provides kosher meat for the town; the teacher educates the community's children; the gardener maintains shared spaces. Since the community collectively sustains their livelihood — whether through taxes, communal funds, or simply by being the aggregate customer base — every member of the community is considered to have a share in their employment at all times. The practical difference between the two positions is significant: according to Rashi, the exemption applies only when you have an active, specific engagement with that professional; according to the Rif, the exemption is essentially perpetual for all community members.

---

## Teacher Authority

### Teacher vs Students

This question — who has employed whom — surfaces in a direct and somewhat amusing exchange. The students came before Rava and asked: *shaylan mar akpid* — if we were to borrow something from you, would you be upset? The implicit argument is that they have hired Rava to teach them, so any borrowing from him would automatically fall under *baalav imo*. Rava was not amused. *L'afku'ei mamonai ka ba'itu?* — are you trying to deprive me of my money? And then he turns the claim on its head: *aderaba, atun she'iltun li* — on the contrary, you are hired out to me. It is the students who are in service of the teacher, not the other way around. His proof: *d'ilu ana matzi l'ishtamuti l'chu m'masechta l'masechta, atun lo matzitu l'ishtamuti* — I can switch from one tractate to another as I see fit, but you cannot walk out on me. The teacher's authority to set the curriculum establishes that the teacher is the party in charge and the students are subordinate.

---

## Public Servants (II)

### Modern Cases

These questions about service professionals have obvious modern analogues. One might ask whether an internet service provider, for instance, occupies a similar communal function — employed perpetually by all subscribers in a way that would generate *baalav imo* implications. The same question applies to a *shul* rabbi. If the rabbi is considered a communal public servant in the same way as the school teacher or butcher of the Talmudic era, then borrowing anything from the rabbi would be essentially liability-free — *baalav imo*, always. Whether any of these modern cases actually meets the threshold is a question that would need to be taken to a *posek*, particularly since explicit contractual conditions and communal *minhag* can modify the default halachic rules. In matters of *mamonot*, the general principle *kol tnai she'b'mamon kayam* — that financial conditions stipulated by parties are binding — means that specific agreements can supersede the *Torah*'s default framework, even where *de'oraita* liability would otherwise apply.

---

## Teacher Authority (II)

### Curriculum Choice

The Gemara qualifies Rava's ruling with an *okimta*. Is it really always true that the teacher determines everything and is therefore not the hired party of the students? *V'lo hi* — not exactly.

The distinction hinges on *yomei d'challa*. The *challa* gatherings — the great assemblies held in the weeks before Nisan and Tishrei — involved a fixed curriculum that was set in advance. The topic to be taught was predetermined and could not be deviated from. In that context, it is the students, or more precisely the community that assembled with specific expectations, who have effectively obligated the teacher to a fixed program — and in that case, the students could reasonably claim to have hired the teacher.

### Fixed Curriculum

On regular days, however, when there is no fixed curriculum and the teacher retains the authority to choose which tractate to teach, it is the teacher who is in control. The *okimta* therefore resolves the apparent tension: Rava's claim that students are hired to him applies specifically to regular teaching days, while on *yomei d'challa*, where the curriculum is fixed, the dynamic may well be reversed.

### Daf Yomi Application

This distinction raises an intriguing question about *Daf Yomi* itself. The *Daf Yomi* curriculum is entirely fixed in advance, determined by an external calendar that neither the teacher nor the students can alter. It would seem to fit squarely within the *yomei d'challa* model: the students have, in a real sense, engaged the teacher to deliver a specific predetermined program. Under this analysis, in a *Daf Yomi* framework, the students may well be considered to have hired the teacher — not the reverse — which would have direct implications for the *baalav imo* analysis. The practical details of salary structure — whether a teacher is paid annually, whether a *ba'al koreh* is compensated for his week of preparation in addition to his Shabbat reading, how to classify summer months for a teacher on a ten-month contract — these are all live questions addressed extensively in *shut* literature dealing with public servants and communal employees.

---

## Donkey Loading

### Donkey Dies

The Gemara introduces a case involving Mar bar Rav Chanina. He had hired out donkeys in Bei Chozai. While the donkeys were being loaded, the owner came out — *nafak gaduda'ei* — to adjust the packages being placed on one of the animals. In the course of the loading, someone acted negligently and the donkey died. The case came before Rabba, who ruled that the loaders were *chayav* — liable.

### Supervision Question

The scholars challenged this ruling immediately: *pshia be'ba'alim hi* — this was a case of negligence while the owner was present, which should exempt the *shoel* or the hired party from liability, not impose it. Rabba was taken aback — *ichsif* — he was embarrassed. But then the matter was investigated further, and it emerged that the owner had not actually come out to participate in the loading. *Delmeisar tauna hee denafak* — he came out only to supervise, to watch that the packages were not loaded excessively, not to physically assist with the work. Rashi explains: *lemeisar lirot shelo yarbu be'masao* — to ensure the load was not too heavy. If the owner was present only in a supervisory role and not as an active participant in the labor, then it is not *pshia be'ba'alim*, and the exemption does not apply. This detail makes a profound practical difference: the line between an owner actively helping with the work and an owner standing nearby to watch is legally decisive, and the facts of the case must be established with precision.

### Theft Alternative

The Gemara then shifts to an alternative reading of the case. Perhaps the facts were different from what was initially assumed — not a *pshia* scenario at all, but rather a case where the load or the donkey was stolen: *ignavo u'meita* — it was taken, and then it died while in the thief's possession — *k'darkah be'ganav havai*, as is the way when an animal dies while being led by a thief. Under this reading, the question becomes whether *gneiva be'ba'alim* — theft occurring while the owner is present — generates the same exemption as *pshia be'ba'alim*. The investigators uncovered the same underlying fact: the owner had come out not to assist with the labor but merely to supervise the loading. This resolved why Rabba ruled *chayav*: the owner was not genuinely present as a working participant, and therefore neither *pshia be'ba'alim* nor *gneiva be'ba'alim* could generate the exemption.

As for the underlying *halachah* — whether *pshia be'ba'alim* exempts or obligates — this was itself a *machloket* treated earlier in the sugya, on 95b, derived from the analogy to *shomer chinam*. The prevailing view appears to be that *pshia be'ba'alim* is *patur*. For those who wish to pursue the issue further, the *Rambam* in the opening of *She'ila u'Pikadon* is an excellent place to begin.

---

## Mishnah Cow

### Mixed Days

The Gemara now introduces a new Mishnah, returning to the theme of borrowed and rented animals. *Hashoel et hapara* — one who borrowed a cow. The Mishnah sets up several variants: what if the cow was borrowed for half a day and rented for half a day? What if it was borrowed for one full day and rented for the next? What if one animal was rented and a different one was borrowed? In each scenario, *u'meita* — the animal died.

### Lender's Claim

The first case: the lender claims *she'ula meita be'sha'a she'hayata she'ula meita* — the cow died at the time it was borrowed, not during the rental period. This matters enormously, because a *shoel* bears liability even for unavoidable accidents — *ones* — while a *socher*, a renter, does not. The lender therefore has every incentive to insist the death occurred during the borrowing period, since that would maximize his recovery. The borrower, for his part, says *eini yodea* — I don't know when it died. The Mishnah rules: *chayav* — the borrower is liable. As Rashi notes in his commentary to the Gemara, this is a case of *bari veshema bari adif* — when one party makes a definite claim and the other says "I don't know," the certain claim prevails.

### Renter's Claim

The case then flips. *Hasocher omer sechura metah beyom she'hayata sechura* — the renter says the animal died while it was being rented, not while it was being borrowed. He claims the lower-liability period. The owner responds: *eini yodea* — I don't know. Here too, *bari veshema bari adif* applies, but now in the other direction: the renter's certain claim beats the owner's uncertainty, and the renter is *patur* — exempt.

### Direct Contradiction

When both parties make definite, conflicting claims — *bari vebari* — the Mishnah rules differently. *Yishava hasocher shesechura metah* — the renter must take an oath that the animal died during the rental period. This oath is striking. It is not *shvuat hashomrim* — the standard oath a *shomer* takes to exempt himself — because *shvuat hashomrim* operates as a declaration of non-negligence and non-misappropriation. This oath is about a factual matter: when did the animal die? It resembles in some ways the oath discussed at the opening of Bava Metzia — on 3a — where Rabbi Yochanan explains that such an oath is *takanat chachamim*, a rabbinic enactment to prevent people from casually seizing others' property. The mechanism of this oath and its precise categorization is a major discussion in *Tosafot*.

### Unknown Split

The final case: *zeh omer eini yodea vezeh omer eini yodea* — neither party knows when the animal died. The Mishnah rules *yachloku* — they divide the liability. When both claims are *shema*, neither party has a stronger position, and the equitable resolution is to split the obligation. In practical terms, this means the borrower-renter pays half of what the full liability would have been. This outcome makes intuitive sense: if the arrangement covered, say, two days — one borrowed and one rented — and neither party can establish during which period the death occurred, each scenario is equally plausible, and splitting the loss reflects that symmetry.

---

## Gemara Analysis

### Rav Nachman

The Gemara immediately asks whether the Mishnah contradicts the position of Rav Nachman. The issue is the *bari veshema* case — where the lender makes a definite claim and the borrower says *eini yodea*, and the borrower is ruled *chayav*. The Gemara cites a dispute among the *Amoraim*: *maneh li beyadcha vehalah omer eini yodea* — if someone says "you owe me a hundred dollars" and the other responds "I don't know," Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda say *chayav* — the uncertain party must pay. Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan say *patur* — he is exempt.

Rav Nachman's position, as clarified by the Gemara, is not that uncertainty is irrelevant, but that liability in such a case arises only *kegon sheyesh esek shvua beineihem* — where there is already a *shvua* engagement between the parties, a prior oath obligation that connects them. If no such *shvua* is in play, the uncertain party cannot be compelled to pay and is therefore exempt.

The question is: how then does the Mishnah rule the borrower *chayav* in a *bari veshema* case? According to Rav Nachman, there should be no liability unless some oath obligation already exists between the parties. Is this a *tiyuvta* — a refutation — of Rav Nachman's position?

### Gilgul Shvua

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction. *Hacha nami kegon sheyesh esek shvua beineihem* — here too, the Mishnah must be dealing with a case where there was already a *shvua* obligation between the *socher* and the *mashil*, unrelated to the question of when the animal died. Because such an obligation exists, the mechanism of *gilgul shvua* — the cascading oath obligation — comes into play. Once a party is obligated to take an oath on one matter, the opposing party can require that the oath extend to encompass other related disputes. So the existing oath obligation between these two parties cascades to include the question of when the animal died, obligating the *socher* to swear on that factual matter as well.

### Cannot Swear

The second step of the analysis is equally important. Once the *gilgul shvua* obligation is established — that the *socher* must now take an oath about whether the animal died during the borrowing or the rental period — he finds himself in an impossible position. His own claim is a *shema* claim: he says only "I don't know." A person cannot take a positive oath about something he admits he does not know. Since his claim is uncertain, he cannot truthfully swear to the fact, and therefore the oath cannot be taken.

This brings into play the rule of *mitoch she'eino yachol lehishava yeshalem* — because he cannot swear, he must pay. The inability to take the oath functions as a constructive refusal, and the legal consequence is monetary liability. It is not that *bari veshema* independently forces payment; rather, the *gilgul shvua* creates the oath obligation, the *shema* claim makes it impossible to fulfill, and the impossibility of fulfillment triggers payment.

### Modeh B'Miktzat

The Gemara illustrates this mechanism with a parallel case drawn from the laws of *modeh b'miktzat*. As Rabba articulates it: if someone claims "you owe me a hundred dollars" and the other responds "I only owe you fifty — and as for the other fifty, I don't know," this is a *modeh b'miktzat shema* kind of case. The partial admission of the fifty establishes the *shvua* obligation — a classic *modeh b'miktzat* triggers the requirement to take an oath on the disputed remainder. But since the claimant's position on the remaining fifty is itself a *shema* — he says he doesn't know — he cannot actually take the oath. *Mitoch she'eino yachol lishava meshallem* — because he cannot swear, he must pay the full amount.

This case functions as a precise parallel to the *socher*'s situation in the Mishnah: in both instances, the party is caught between a *gilgul shvua* obligation they cannot escape and an epistemically uncertain claim that prevents them from fulfilling it. The solution in both cases is the same — liability follows from the impossibility of taking the oath.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 98

## Mishnah Overview

### Four Cases

The *mishnah* at the opening of Bava Metzia 98 sits within a broader discussion of the obligations of a *sho'el* — one who borrows an object — but pivots into a distinct and richly complex domain: competing claims of liability when an animal was partly borrowed and partly rented. The scenario involves two parties, an owner and a borrower-renter, who dispute which arrangement was in effect when the animal died or was otherwise damaged in a manner that would render a *sho'el* liable but a *socher* exempt. The *mishnah* presents four cases.

### Case 1: Owner Claims

In the first case, the owner (*mash'il*) asserts definitively that it was the borrowed cow (*she'ula*) that died — meaning the borrower owes compensation — while the borrower responds that he does not know which animal died. The *mishnah* rules that the borrower must pay.

### Case 2: Borrower Claims

In the second case, the roles are reversed: the borrower claims definitively that it was the rented cow (*schura*) that died — freeing him from liability — while the owner says he does not know. The *mishnah* rules that the borrower is exempt.

### Case 3: Opposing Claims

In the third case, both parties make definitive but opposing claims: the owner insists it was the borrowed cow, while the borrower insists it was the rented one. Here the *mishnah* rules that the renter takes an oath (*yishava ha-socher she-schura meta*) that it was the rented cow that died, and he is thereby exempt.

### Case 4: Both Uncertain

In the fourth case, both parties say they do not know. The *mishnah* rules that they divide the liability between them.

---

## Bari ve-Shema

### Initial Inference

The *gemara* opens its analysis on 97b by drawing an inference from the first case of the *mishnah*. If the owner makes a definite claim (*bari*) and the borrower responds with uncertainty (*shema* — "I don't know"), and the *mishnah* rules that the borrower must pay, it would seem to follow that a definite claim overcomes the possession of the one holding the money. The usual rule is *hamotzi mi-chaveiro alav ha-ra'aya* — the burden of proof lies with the claimant. And yet here, without any proof, the mere definiteness of the owner's claim appears sufficient to extract payment from the borrower who has *chezkat mamon*.

### Bari Adif Principle

This is the principle known as *bari adif* — the definite claim is stronger — and it would mean that *bari* prevails even over *chezkat mamon*, the presumption that money remains with whoever currently holds it.

### Amoraic Dispute

The *gemara* immediately identifies a conflict with the view of Rav Nachman. As the *gemara* records: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda hold that in a case where Reuven says "you owe me a hundred" and Shimon says "I don't know," Shimon is *chayav* — he must pay. Rav Nachman and Rav Yochanan, however, rule that he is *patur*, because *chezkat mamon* prevails in the absence of certainty. Our *mishnah*, which rules that the borrower pays in Case 1, seems to be a decisive challenge to Rav Nachman.

### Galgul Shvua

The *gemara* deflects this challenge by invoking a principle Rav Nachman applies in other contexts: the *mishnah* may be speaking of a case where there is already a *shvua* — an oath obligation — in play between the parties. Once a person is independently obligated to take an oath, the doctrine of *galgul shvua* allows additional oaths to be rolled onto that existing obligation. If, for example, the borrower was already a *modeh b'miktzat* — he partially admitted a separate debt — he would be obligated to take an oath about the remainder. The owner could then invoke *galgul shvua* to require him to also swear about which cow died. But since the borrower says he does not know, he cannot take that oath. The result is *mitoch she-eino yachol lehishava meshalem*: because he is unable to swear, he must pay. Thus, the *mishnah* need not be read as endorsing *bari adif* in a pure sense — it may operate entirely through the mechanism of an oath that cannot be taken.

---

## Modeh B'Miktzat

### Rava's Case

At the top of 98a, Rava provides the concrete example that anchors this entire analysis. If a claimant says "you owe me a hundred," and the respondent says "I only owe you fifty — the other fifty I don't know whether I owe you or not," this creates a classic *modeh b'miktzat* situation. The respondent has admitted to half the claim and is uncertain about the other half. Had he flatly denied the second fifty, he would take a *shvua* about it in the standard *modeh b'miktzat* framework. Here, though, he cannot take that oath because he genuinely does not know.

### Chain of Logic

The chain of logic is precise: *modeh b'miktzat* generates an obligation to take a *shvua* on the disputed portion. The respondent is thus *chayav* in a *shvua*. Since he cannot fulfill that obligation — he has no knowledge to swear to — the principle of *mitoch she-eino yachol lehishava meshalem* applies: inability to swear converts into an obligation to pay. This, rather than the raw principle of *bari adif*, is the engine driving the ruling in Case 1 of the *mishnah*.

### Two Cows Case

The *gemara* then works to fold this mechanism directly into the *mishnah*'s own cow-based scenario, rather than importing a separate hundred-dollar debt from outside. For the first case of the *mishnah* (*reisha*), the *gemara* proposes reading it as involving two cows — *reisha b'veiz*. Reuven says to Shimon: "I gave you two cows, half the day borrowed and half the day rented" (or day one borrowed and day two rented). Both cows died. Reuven claims both died during the borrowed period. Shimon the *sho'el* responds: "The first one — I concede, it died when it was borrowed, I owe you for that cow." He has now admitted to one full cow's worth of liability. "The second — I don't know whether it died when borrowed or when rented." He cannot swear about the second cow. Since he is *modeh b'miktzat* — admitting to the first cow — he is obligated to take a *shvua* about the second. Unable to do so, *mitoch she-eino yachol lehishava meshalem*: he pays for the second cow as well.

### Three Cows Case

For the final cases of the *mishnah* (*seifa*), where the scenario involves two cows of different status, the *gemara* adds yet another cow — *seifa b'gimmel*. Reuven says: "I gave you three cows, two borrowed and one rented. Two died, and I say both were the borrowed ones." Shimon responds: "I concede — one of the borrowed cows died, and I owe you for that." That is the *modeh b'miktzat*. "The other — I don't know. Was it the second borrowed cow that died, making the surviving one the rented cow and leaving me liable for both? Or was it the rented cow that died, making the surviving one the borrowed cow, in which case I owe you only for the first?" Again he cannot swear, and *mitoch she-eino yachol lehishava meshalem* compels payment.

### Resolution

The upshot of this entire sugya is that the *mishnah* need not be read as endorsing the position of Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda that *bari adif* suffices to overcome *chezkat mamon*. Rather, the *mishnah* is constructed — in the *gemara*'s reading — so that the payment obligation flows entirely from an inability to swear after having been rendered *chayav* in a *shvua* through *modeh b'miktzat*. This preserves Rav Nachman's position that *bari* alone does not win out over possession.

---

## Rami Bar Chama

### Shomrim Principle

The *gemara* now introduces a further complication. Rami Bar Chama derives from the verse *ki asher yomar ki hu zeh* — "it is this one" — a general principle governing all four categories of *shomrim* (guardians) in the Torah. Each of the four guardians — *shomer chinam* (unpaid guardian), *shomer sachar* (paid guardian), *socher* (renter), and *sho'el* (borrower) — is at times required to take a *shvuat ha-shomrim*, an oath about what befell the entrusted object.

### Hoda'ah + Kfira

Rami Bar Chama holds that *shvuat ha-shomrim* is only operative when the *shomer* is already standing within the framework of *modeh b'miktzat* — but critically, his version of *modeh b'miktzat* requires not only a partial admission (*hoda'ah b'miktzat*) but also a partial denial (*kfira b'miktzat*). The classic *modeh b'miktzat* is: "You claim I owe you a hundred — I admit to fifty and deny the other fifty." The denial is as essential as the admission. If the respondent merely admits to one portion and says he is uncertain about another, that does not satisfy Rami Bar Chama's requirement. He needs an active *kfira* — a genuine denial of one part. Only once both the *hoda'ah* and the *kfira* are in place can *shvuat ha-shomrim* be invoked.

### Three Cows (Rami)

This substantially raises the number of cows required to construct the *mishnah*'s scenario. For the first case (*reisha*), Rami Bar Chama requires three cows — *reisha b'gimmel*. Reuven says: "I gave you three cows, and half the day they were borrowed, half the day rented" (or one day borrowed, the next rented). All three died, and Reuven claims all three died during the borrowed period. Shimon responds: "The first — you're lying, I never borrowed that cow at all (*lo hayu devarim me'olam*)." That is the *kfira b'miktzat* — an outright denial of one unit of the claim. "The second — I concede, it died when it was borrowed, I owe you." That is the *hoda'ah b'miktzat*. Now Rami Bar Chama's conditions are met: there is both a partial denial and a partial admission. With *modeh b'miktzat* properly constituted in his view, *shvuat ha-shomrim* can attach. "The third — I don't know whether it died when borrowed or when rented." He cannot swear, and *mitoch she-eino yachol lehishava meshalem* requires payment.

### Four Cows (Rami)

For the final cases of the *mishnah*, Rami Bar Chama requires four cows — *seifa b'arba*. Reuven says: "I gave you four cows — three borrowed and one rented — and three died, all during the borrowed period." Shimon responds: "The first — I never borrowed that cow (*lo hayu devarim me'olam*)." That is the *kfira*. "The second — I concede, it died when borrowed." That is the *hoda'ah*. Those two extra cows establish the required *modeh b'miktzat* with both its components. "The remaining two — I don't know which is which, whether it was the borrowed or the rented one that died." He cannot swear about those two, which replicate the original two-cow scenario of the *mishnah*, and so he must pay.

### Why Both Required

The reason Rami Bar Chama insists on both *kfira* and *hoda'ah* is that, in his view, *shvuat ha-shomrim* requires the full envelope of *modeh b'miktzat* as its gateway. A partial admission alone, accompanied only by uncertainty rather than denial, does not constitute the complete framework. The *kfira* and the *hoda'ah* together form the protective gate through which *shvuat ha-shomrim* must pass.

---

## Case 3: Opposing Claims

### Galgul Shvua Logic

The *gemara* now turns to the third case of the *mishnah*, in which both parties make definitive opposing claims — the owner says it was definitely the borrowed cow, the borrower says it was definitely the rented cow — and the *mishnah* rules that the *socher* takes an oath and is exempt. This is puzzling. If the *socher* simply denies the owner's claim outright, this is a case of *kofer ha-kol* — a complete denial — and a *kofer ha-kol* normally requires no oath at all; he simply goes free. Why does the *mishnah* impose an oath?

The *gemara* asks this directly: *ve-amai?* What he was claimed from he did not concede, and what he conceded was not what was claimed from him. There is no *modeh b'miktzat* here at all. Ulla answers: *al yedei gilgul* — through *galgul shvua*.

### Renter's Obligation

Unlike the first case, however, where the *gemara* had to introduce external circumstances to generate the base oath obligation, here the *socher* has an inherent, independent *shvua* he must take. The *shvuat ha-shomrim* naturally applies to his situation. Even if we were to accept the *socher*'s version entirely — that it was definitively the rented cow that died — he would still be obligated to take the classic *shvuat ha-shomrim*: an oath that the animal died in an ordinary way (*ke-darkah meta*), without any negligence on his part. This oath is not about which cow died; it is about the manner of death. As a *socher*, he is always subject to this obligation.

### Adding the Oath

Once that underlying *shvua* is in place, *galgul shvua* operates: since he is already taking an oath, the court can add onto it a further oath — that it was in fact the rented cow that died and not the borrowed one. This combined oath covers both the manner of death and the identity of the animal. This is far simpler than the first case, which required constructing *modeh b'miktzat* through additional cows. Here the basis for the oath is already built into the *socher*'s natural situation as a guardian, and *galgul shvua* then extends that oath to encompass the disputed question of which animal it was.

---

## Case 4: Both Uncertain

### Sumchus Principle

The fourth and final case of the *mishnah* — where both parties say *eini yodea*, "I don't know" — leads the *gemara* to identify whose opinion the *mishnah* reflects. The ruling that they divide the payment corresponds to the view of Sumchus, who holds *mammon ha-mutal b'safek cholkin*: when money is in a state of genuine doubt, the parties split it.

### Sumchus Debate

The counterposition is *hamotzi mi-chaveiro alav ha-ra'aya*: even in a situation of total uncertainty, if you wish to extract money from someone else's possession, you must prove your claim; absent proof, the money stays where it is. The *mishnah*'s ruling to divide, rather than leave the money with the current holder, follows Sumchus. The objective structure of the doubt here is concrete — it is known that one cow was borrowed and one was rented, both parties acknowledge they do not know which died — and it is precisely in such circumstances that Sumchus applies his principle of division.

---

## Ba'alim Factor

### Question 1

The *gemara* now opens a new set of questions raised by Rabbi Abba bar Mamal, concerning the interplay between different successive arrangements and the doctrine of *ba'alim* — whether the owner was working for the borrower at the time of the transaction. The rule is that if the owner was working for the borrower (*ba'alim*) at the time of the borrowing, the *sho'el* is exempt from liability even for *ones* (accidents). The question is how this exemption carries across transitions from one arrangement to another.

The first question: if a person borrowed a cow when the owner was working for him (*shala b'va'alim*), and then, in the middle of that period, he converted the arrangement into a rental without the owner being present (*sachar shelo b'va'alim*), what is the law? Two frameworks are possible. Perhaps each transaction — the *she'ila* and the *schirus* — stands independently, such that the rental, having been made without *ba'alim*, carries no exemption. Or perhaps the *schirus* is seen as a continuation of the *she'ila* (*schirus b'she'ila mishach shaichi*), since the liability for *gneiva va'aveida* that began during the *she'ila* continues into the *schirus* period without interruption. If so, the *ba'alim* exemption that protected against *gneiva va'aveida* during the *she'ila* may carry forward into the *schirus* as well.

### Continuity

The question turns on whether *she'ila* and *schirus* are to be treated as discrete transactions or as a single continuous engagement. In favor of continuity: the *socher*'s liability for *gneiva va'aveida* is the same as the *sho'el*'s, making the transition feel seamless. In favor of separation: the payment arrangement and the level of liability for *ones* differ fundamentally between the two.

### Exemption Carry-Over

The specific sub-question is whether the *ba'alim* exemption from *she'ila* — which applied to the full range of *she'ila* liabilities, including *ones* — continues to protect the *socher* against *gneiva va'aveida* during the *schirus* period. If the two arrangements are one continuous thing, it might. If they are separate, the *schirus* period lacks its own *ba'alim* basis and the exemption would not apply.

### Question 2

The second question is the reverse: the person rented the cow with the owner working for him (*sachar b'va'alim*) — exempting him from *gneiva va'aveida* — and then, before the rental ended, converted the arrangement into a borrowing without the owner present (*shala shelo b'va'alim*). Here the question is whether the *ba'alim* exemption from the original *schirus* continues into the *she'ila*.

### New Liabilities

This case is more complex than the first. When a *socher* becomes a *sho'el*, he does not merely continue with existing obligations — he takes on new ones. As a *socher*, he was liable for *gneiva va'aveida* but exempt from *ones*. As a *sho'el*, he becomes liable for *ones* as well. This expansion of liability is arguably a qualitative break. The concern is: since *ones* liability is entirely new and had no *ba'alim* exemption attached to it, perhaps the transition to *she'ila* is so significant a change that even the *gneiva va'aveida* liability is treated anew, without any carryover of the *ba'alim* exemption. Alternatively, one might argue that since the *ba'alim* exemption remains relevant to part of the new arrangement — the *gneiva va'aveida* component — it should be considered relevant to the whole (*keivan d'shaichi b'miktzat keman d'shaichi b'kula dami*), and the *sho'el* would be entirely exempt.

### Question 3

The third question compounds the earlier ones: the person borrowed with *ba'alim*, then rented without *ba'alim*, and then borrowed again — also without *ba'alim* (*shala b'va'alim, sachar shelo b'va'alim, v'chazar v'shala*). The question is whether, when the arrangement cycles back to *she'ila* at the end, the original *ba'alim* status is restored (*hadar ati lei she'ila l'duchtah*).

### Status Return

This question seems to assume, as a premise, that when *she'ila* converted to *schirus*, the *ba'alim* exemption continued into the *schirus* for *gneiva va'aveida* — otherwise the *schirus* interlude would have no relevance to restoring anything. The question then is whether the *schirus* period is a full enough break that the return to *she'ila* does not recapture the original *ba'alim* status, or whether the continuity of the arrangement is such that cycling back to *she'ila* restores all of its original characteristics, including the *ba'alim* exemption even for *ones*.

### Question 4: Teiku

The fourth and final question is the most complex: the person rented with *ba'alim*, then borrowed without *ba'alim*, then rented again (*sachar b'va'alim, sha'al shelo b'va'alim, v'chazar v'sachar*). Here the transition from *schirus* to *she'ila* is, as the *gemara* has suggested throughout, a harder case for continuity — since the *she'ila* introduces genuinely new liabilities, it represents a more substantial break. The question is whether, after that intervening *she'ila*, the final return to *schirus* restores the *ba'alim* exemption that had applied to the original *schirus*, or whether the *she'ila* in the middle definitively severs the chain. The *gemara* leaves this question unresolved: *teiku*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 99

## Borrower & Third Parties

### Mishna Setup

The daf opens with the *mishna* at the bottom of 98b — a *mishna* that appeared earlier in the tractate when the *gemara* brought it in the context of a craftsman who has completed his work. Here we encounter it in its own setting. The *mishna* states: if someone borrows a cow and the owner sends it by way of his son, his slave, or his agent — or by way of the son, slave, or agent of the borrower — and the animal dies in transit, the borrower is exempt.

### Borrower Liability Rules

The background to this ruling requires some orientation. A *sho'el*, a borrower, bears the highest level of liability among the four categories of guardians. Unlike a *shomer chinam* (unpaid guardian), a *socher* (one who rents), or a *shomer sachar* (paid guardian) — all of whom have lower levels of liability — the borrower is obligated even for *onsin*, unavoidable accidents, regardless of whether there was any *peshiah*, any negligence or fault, on his part. Yet in this case the borrower is exempt, because the animal has not yet reached his hand. So long as it remains within the legal *reshut*, the domain, of the owner and has not been formally transferred, the borrower's liability has not yet commenced.

### Requested Delivery

The *mishna* continues with the case where the borrower explicitly requests a particular mode of delivery, or where the lender proposes a method and the borrower consents with the word *shlach* — "send it." In either scenario, where the borrower has either named the agent or ratified the arrangement, the borrower is *chayav*. At that point, the object has entered his legal *reshut* even before it physically arrives.

### Return Rules

The same principles apply in reverse when the object is being returned. If the borrower arranges the return unilaterally, he remains liable until the object reaches the owner's hand. If the return was arranged jointly or at the owner's direction, the borrower's liability concludes when the object leaves his physical possession — even if it is traveling by way of his slave.

---

## Slave as Intermediary

### Yad Eved Question

The *gemara* now homes in on a difficulty with the *mishna*. The *mishna* states that when the owner sends the animal *b'yad avdo* — by way of his slave — and it dies, the borrower is exempt. But this is surprising: is there not a principle of *yad eved k'yad rabo*, that the slave's hand is treated as the master's own hand? If so, how can the animal ever be said to have passed out of the owner's possession while it is being carried by his slave?

### Shmuel's Position

*Shmuel* offers a straightforward resolution: the *mishna* is dealing with an *eved Ivri*, a Hebrew slave, not an *eved Kna'ani*, a Canaanite slave. The principle of *yad eved k'yad rabo* applies in its fullest sense only to the Canaanite slave, whose very body is *kanuy*, entirely owned, by the master. A Hebrew slave involves a much lower level of ownership, and so we do not treat his actions as equivalent to the master's. Hence the *mishna* can consistently say that when the owner sends the animal via his Hebrew slave, the borrower is not yet liable — the animal has genuinely left the owner's domain — and yet when the borrower's side sends it via their agent, the borrower becomes *chayav*.

### Rav's Position

*Rav* disagrees and offers a different answer: even if we grant that the *mishna* is speaking of a Canaanite slave, there is no difficulty. The case of sending an animal by way of a Canaanite slave is treated as equivalent to saying *hakishehu b'makla v'yavo* — "hit the animal with a stick and it will come to you." This is the formal act of *kinyan*, of acquisition, that applies to animals in particular, since one cannot physically drag a living animal the way one performs *meshicha* on an inanimate object. Striking the animal so that it moves toward the recipient constitutes a valid act of *meshicha*. Alternatively, since the Canaanite slave's body is entirely the possession of the master — *gufo kanuy* — the slave's carrying of the animal is treated less like one person transporting something for another and more like an extension of the animal itself moving, such that the borrower's act of acquiring the animal can be complete in this fashion. This is how *Rav* explains that even in the case of a Canaanite slave, the borrower can be *chayav*.

### Braita Challenge

A *braita* is then cited that appears to contradict this framework: *hashoel para v'shilchah lo b'yad bno, b'yad shlucho — chayav; b'yad avdo — patur*. This *braita* states explicitly that when the animal is sent by way of the slave — without distinguishing type of slave — the borrower is *patur*, not liable. This generates an apparent contradiction with the *mishna* which, on *Rav*'s reading, holds the borrower liable even when a Canaanite slave delivers the animal.

---

## Resolving Sources

### Shmuel Reconciles

For *Shmuel*, reconciliation is easy. The *mishna* speaks of a Hebrew slave (*eved Ivri*), and the *braita* speaks of a Canaanite slave (*eved Kna'ani*). Each source is internally consistent, and the two can coexist without difficulty.

### Rav's Difficulty

For *Rav*, however, the contradiction is genuine. Having argued that even a Canaanite slave can serve as the vehicle for a valid *kinyan*, *Rav* is left with one source ruling *chayav* and another ruling *patur* — both apparently referring to the same type of slave.

### Rav's Fix

*Rav*'s resolution is to reinterpret the *mishna*. When the *gemara* originally said *na'aseh k'omeir* — "we treat it as if he said" *hakishehu b'makla v'yavo* — that formulation was imprecise. *Rav* now corrects himself: the *mishna* is not a case of analogy or legal fiction. Rather, *b'amar lei* — the *mishna* must actually be referring to a case where the borrower literally said those words: "hit the animal and send it to me." In that case, and only in that case, is the borrower *chayav* once the animal has left the owner's *reshut*. If the borrower merely said "send it" without specifying *hakishehu b'makla*, then even on *Rav*'s view the borrower would not be *chayav* until it arrives in his hand.

### Hekisha Source

The *gemara* attempts to support *Rav*'s position from a *braita* that describes exactly this scenario: the borrower asks for the cow, the lender asks how it should be sent, and the borrower says *hekishah b'maklo v'hi tavo* — "hit it with your stick and it will come." *Rav Nachman* citing *Rabbah bar Avuha* citing *Rav* teaches that as soon as the animal exits the owner's *reshut*, it is the borrower's *chiyuv* if it dies. The *gemara* then asks whether this *braita* lends support to *Rav*'s position.

### Rav Ashi Objects

*Rav Ashi* objects: that *braita* cannot serve as general support, because it is addressing a very particular case — one in which the borrower's *chatzer* is situated *lifnim michatzer shel mash'il*, within the owner's larger *chatzer*. Only in that topographic arrangement does the *braita*'s ruling make sense.

### Chatzer B'Chatzer

The specific arrangement *Rav Ashi* envisions is a large private courtyard belonging to the owner, within which the borrower holds a smaller domain. In this configuration, when the borrower says "hit the animal and send it to me," the animal need not pass through a *reshut harabim* at all — it travels entirely within enclosed private space. *Rashi* explains that this is crucial: once the animal is struck and set in motion toward the borrower's domain, there is no intermediate public space where it might stray, and so the borrower's assumption that it will arrive is well-founded, sufficient to establish his *chiyuv* from the moment it leaves the owner's possession.

One might then ask what the *braita* adds beyond the obvious. The *gemara* answers: the novelty lies in a case where there are intermediate spaces within the large *chatzer* — gaps or sub-sections within the private domain through which the animal might wander rather than travel directly. The *braita* teaches that even so, the borrower's *da'at*, his reliance that the animal will come, is established and his liability attaches.

The *Ra'avad*, cited in the *Shitta Mekubetzet*, adds a related point: the arrangement must specifically be that the borrower's domain lies within the owner's domain, not the reverse. If the owner's *chatzer* were inside the borrower's *chatzer*, then the owner's ordinary movement of the animal — including moving it out toward the *reshut harabim* — would routinely pass through the borrower's domain, and so the act of sending the animal in that direction would not carry the same unambiguous meaning of a formal transfer to the borrower.

---

## Meshicha & Guardianship

### Huna: Use Required

The discussion now transitions to a related but distinct question. *Huna* states: *hashoel kardom mechaveiro — baka bo, kena'o; lo baka bo, lo kena'o*. If I borrow an axe from my friend, I have not fully "acquired" it for the purposes of the loan until I have actually used it. Merely taking it, performing the formal act of *meshicha*, does not suffice.

### Why Use Needed

*Rashi* explains the underlying principle: *ein meshicha konah b'shomrim* — the standard act of *meshicha* that creates ownership for a purchaser does not create the *chiyuv* of a *shomer*, a guardian. The borrower is a species of *shomer*, and so the same formal act of taking possession that would close a sale does not automatically generate the guardian's obligation. What then does? Actual use. The ruling does not concern liability for *onsin*, which would be the borrower's concern once the loan is effective — rather, it concerns the point at which the loan becomes irrevocable. If the borrower has not yet used the axe, the lender can retract: *lo baka bo, matzi mash'il hadar beih* — the owner may say, I changed my mind, please return it. But once the borrower has used it, the loan is fixed and the lender cannot rescind.

### Me'ila Dispute

This position is then contrasted with that of *Rabbi Ami*. *Rabbi Ami* states: if the lender has a *kardom shel hekdesh* — an axe that is temple property — and lends it out, the lender is *chayav* in *me'ila*, the misappropriation of temple property, *lefi tovat hana'ah shebo* — according to the small benefit he derived from having the axe available to lend. And the borrower, *Rabbi Ami* continues, is permitted to use the axe *l'chatchila*, as a matter of right, because once it has been lent and the lender has already incurred *me'ila*, the axe is no longer *hekdesh* in the borrower's hands.

The question immediately follows: if *meshicha* does not create a *shomer*'s obligation as *Rav Huna* holds, then how does *Rabbi Ami* rule that the lender is *chayav* in *me'ila* the moment he lends the axe, before the borrower has even used it? And why should the borrower be permitted to use it *l'chatchila*? If the *meshicha* accomplished nothing, the axe is still effectively in the lender's *reshut*, the lender was never *over* on *me'ila*, and the borrower should simply return it untouched. The fact that *Rabbi Ami* rules otherwise implies that *meshicha* does create the guardian's obligation, and that the axe legally passed into the borrower's *reshut* at the moment of taking — contradicting *Rav Huna*.

### Rabbi Ami Position

*Rabbi Ami*'s position thus stands in explicit disagreement with *Rav Huna*: *meshicha* is *koneh* for *shomrim*, it creates the borrower's legal acquisition even before use, and this is the case even *mid'oraita* — on a Torah level. The taking of the axe is sufficient to effect the legal transfer, such that the lender is *chayav* in *me'ila* and the borrower is free to use the object.

### Rabbi Elazar View

*Rabbi Elazar* takes a position that navigates between the two. He agrees that *meshicha* works to create the *shomer*'s obligation — *kederech shetiknu meshicha belokochot, kach tiknu meshicha b'shomrim*, just as the Sages enacted that *meshicha* functions as a formal acquisition for buyers, so too did they enact that it functions to create the guardian's legal status. However, for *Rabbi Elazar* this is explicitly *mi'derabbanan*, by rabbinic enactment, not a *d'oraita* rule.

### Baraita Support

A *braita* is then cited in support of this position, stating explicitly: just as *meshicha* was enacted for purchasers, so too was it enacted for guardians. The same *braita* goes on to address *schirus*: just as land is acquired through money, a *shtar* (contract), or *chazaka*, so too a lease (*schirus*) of land is effected through money, a *shtar*, or *chazaka*.

### Land Lease Rules

One might wonder what land leases have to do with the preceding discussion of guardians and *meshicha*. *Rav Chisda* clarifies: *schirus karka* — we are speaking of leasing land, not movable objects. The acquisition methods for real property — payment, written contract, and *chazaka* (physical possession conducted openly in a manner consistent with ownership) — are the operative modes for a land lease as well. Giving someone a set of keys to the property, notably, does not in itself constitute a formal act of *kinyan* in this framework; one must actually pay, document, or be present on the land in the manner of an owner.

---

## Theft: Hedyot vs. Hekdesh

### Date Bulk Rule

*Shmuel* now introduces a case concerning theft and the valuation of damages. If a *gazlan* steals a large barrel of dates — fifty dates packed together — and those fifty dates, sold wholesale as a lot, fetch forty-nine units, while sold individually they would fetch fifty, the question is what the thief must pay back. *Shmuel* rules: *l'hedyot meshalem chamishin naki chada* — when stealing from a normal person, the thief pays back forty-nine, the wholesale price.

### Hekdesh Full Value

The rule for temple property is different. *Lehekdesh meshalem chamishin v'chomsho* — for *hekdesh*, the thief pays back the full fifty units plus the *chomesh*, the additional fifth that *me'ila* requires as a penalty for misappropriating temple property.

### Hekdesh Damage

A further distinction follows: *mah she'ein ken b'mazik d'lo meshalem chomsha* — this *chomesh* does not apply to one who merely damages temple property. The *mazik*, the one who causes damage without misappropriation, does not pay the additional fifth. The textual basis is the verse *ish ki yochal kodesh — prat l'mazik*: the Torah's language of "eating" sacred food (applied by analogy from *trumah* to *hekdesh* via a *gezeira shava*) implies intentional use, which excludes the case of damage. Causing damage to temple property thus incurs regular tort liability but not the *chomesh* of *me'ila*.

### Bulk Discount Q

The question is then raised by *Bibi bar Abaye*: why must the thief pay the wholesale price to the ordinary victim? Couldn't the owner of the dates say, "I sell retail, not wholesale — I would have sold them one by one, and you owe me each date's individual value"?

### Field Damage Rule

*Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua* responds: *bishamin beit se'ah b'oto sadeh t'nan* — we assess damage based on the value of a *beit se'ah* within that field, meaning we evaluate loss against the whole field rather than the individual items destroyed. Just as when an animal enters a field and eats a portion, we do not calculate the precise value of each stalk consumed but rather assess the proportional diminution of the entire field's value — and the field assessed as a whole is always valued at the wholesale rate — so too here. The rule reflects a general principle of damage assessment that looks to aggregate value rather than retail per-unit pricing.

---

## Me'ila Requirements

### Stone Not Me'ila

A *braita* is introduced that details the stages at which *me'ila* occurs for temple property: *natal even o korah mehekdesh — lo maal*. If someone takes a stone or a wooden beam from *hekdesh*, that act alone does not yet constitute *me'ila*.

### Giving to Friend

*Nesanah l'chavero — hu maal, v'chavero lo maal*. If that person gives the stone or beam to a friend, the original taker has now committed *me'ila*, but the friend has not yet.

### Building Me'ila

*Bana b'toch beiso — lo maal ad sheyador tachtea b'shaveh perutah*. If the friend builds the beam into his house, he still has not committed *me'ila* until he has actually lived in the house and derived benefit worth at least a *perutah*, the minimum measurable unit of value. The underlying principle is that *me'ila* requires a tangible, quantifiable *hana'ah* — a benefit that can be assigned a monetary value. Purely symbolic or potential benefit does not suffice.

### Me'ila-Borrowing Link

*Rav Abbahu* reports that he was sitting before *Rabbi Yochanan* and taught in the name of *Shmuel*: *zot omeret* — this *braita* teaches us something about a *hedyot* case as well. Specifically, *Shmuel* infers from the rule about the beam from *hekdesh* — that liability requires actual benefit of a *shaveh perutah* — that one who dwells in another's *chatzer* without the owner's knowledge (*shelo mida'ato*) must pay the owner for that benefit. *Shmuel* thus draws a parallel between *hekdesh shelo mida'at* and *sho'el shelo mida'at*, using the temple property case to illuminate the ordinary borrowing case.

### Mada'at Contradiction

This inference, however, creates a difficulty. *Shmuel* elsewhere distinguishes between *hekdesh* and *hedyot* — he treats them differently with respect to the bulk date discount. And more pointedly, there appears to be a contradiction within *Shmuel*'s own teachings. On one hand, he draws an analogy from *hekdesh shelo mida'at* to *sho'el shelo mida'at*. On the other hand, this analogy implies that the two are governed by the same standard, which conflicts with the intuition — and the explicit logic — that *hekdesh* should be stricter than *hedyot*. The *Almighty*, as the owner of temple property, always knows where that property is — *hekdesh shelo mida'at* from the borrower's perspective is never truly unknown to the "owner." This means *hekdesh shelo mida'at* should more closely resemble *she'ilah mida'at* — borrowing with the owner's full knowledge — not *she'ilah shelo mida'at*.

### Shmuel Retracts

The *gemara* notes: *hadar beh Shmuel* — *Shmuel* retracted one of these teachings. The question then is: which one did he retract? Was it the teaching that drew the analogy between *hekdesh shelo mida'at* and *sho'el shelo mida'at*? Or was it the earlier teaching about the bulk date discount, which distinguished *hekdesh* from *hedyot*? The *gemara* entertains the possibility that *Shmuel* retracted the date-discount distinction and actually held that *hekdesh* and *hedyot* are governed identically.

### Rava Resolves

The *gemara* resolves this by citing *Rava*: *hekdesh shelo mida'at ke-hedyot mida'at dami* — *hekdesh shelo mida'at* is legally equivalent to borrowing from an ordinary person *with* that person's knowledge. This means the analogy *Shmuel* drew — from *hekdesh shelo mida'at* to *sho'el shelo mida'at* — is incorrect. *Rava* explicitly rejects that direction of learning. Since *Rava* articulates this principle clearly, the *gemara* concludes that *Shmuel* must have ultimately agreed with it, meaning the teaching he retracted was the second one: the inference from *hekdesh shelo mida'at* to *sho'el shelo mida'at*. The teaching about the date-discount distinction between *hedyot* and *hekdesh* stands.

*Rashi* explains the logic underlying *Rava*'s position: since the Divine Owner of *hekdesh* always knows where the temple property is, there is no true *shelo mida'at* from the owner's side. This makes *hekdesh shelo mida'at* — misappropriation that the human actor did not realize was *me'ila* — legally comparable to ordinary *she'ilah mida'at*, where the owner is fully aware and has in some sense consented to the use.

---

## Damages & Market Value

### Wine Barrel Case

*Rava* presents a practical case: carriers (*shakulay*) broke a barrel of wine (*chavita de-chamra*) belonging to a wine merchant. On the day of the market (*yoma de-shuka*) the wine sells for five units; on all other days it sells for four. The question is what the carriers owe.

### Market Day Price

The ruling is: *ahadro lei be-yoma de-shuka — ahadro lei chavita de-chamra; she'ar yomey — ahadro lei chamsha*. If the carriers return payment on the market day itself, they return a barrel of equivalent wine. If they return payment on any other day of the week, they must pay five — the market-day value — because that is the price the merchant would have realized had the barrel not been broken at the critical moment.

### Alternate Sale

However, this rule is qualified: *lo amran ela de-lo hava lei chamra le-zivuni* — this higher liability applies only when the merchant had no other wine available to sell. If he had other wine that he could have sold on market day, then his loss from the broken barrel is not the full five units, because he was not actually prevented from selling on that day.

### Labor Deduction

In that case — where the merchant had other wine — the carriers owe less. *U-manchit lei agar tircha u-dmei barzanyata* — one subtracts the amount of labor (*agar tircha*) and the cost of tapping the barrel (*dmei barzanyata*). The *barzanyata* refers to the professional tapping of the barrel, which in the ancient wine trade was a skilled task with its own cost. A second interpretation takes *barzanyata* to refer to a crier who would announce the availability of wine for sale — a form of advertising — though the first reading, rooted in *barza* meaning the spigot or faucet of a wine barrel, appears more linguistically natural. In either interpretation, these ancillary costs are deducted from the carrier's liability, reflecting the principle that damages are assessed net of the expenses the owner would have incurred in any event to bring the wine to market.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 100

## Exchange & Offspring

### Opening & BK Parallel

Today's daf is Bava Metzia 100. The opening of this amud invites a comparison to a parallel *sugya* in Bava Kamma, a connection that will prove illuminating as we proceed. We begin with a new *mishna* that at first seems somewhat out of place within this *perek*, yet it touches on fundamental principles of monetary law — principles far-reaching enough that, as we approach the end of the tractate, we find ourselves circling back to ideas encountered at the very beginning of Bava Metzia.

### Cow-Donkey Exchange

The *mishna* opens with the case of *hamachlif para b'chamor* — two parties engaged in *chalipin*, a barter exchange of a cow for a donkey. Rashi notes that the fact that this is a *chalipin* transaction rather than a standard sale is legally significant, as we shall see. The case turns on the fact that the cow gives birth — *ve'yalda* — and the question arises: did the birth occur before or after the exchange was effected? The seller claims the birth took place while the animal was still in his possession; the buyer claims it occurred after the *kinyan* was completed.

### Slave Birth Dispute

The *mishna* presents a parallel case: someone sold a female slave (*shifchato*), and she gave birth. Here too, one party says the birth occurred before the sale — *ad shelo macharti* — while the other insists it happened after the acquisition — *misheli lachachti*. The same factual uncertainty underlies both disputes: was this offspring born in the seller's domain or the buyer's?

### BK Goring Case

This is precisely why the Bava Kamma parallel comes to mind. There, the case involves a bull that gored a pregnant cow — *shor shenagach hapara ve'nimtza ubar b'tzidda* — and the question is identical in structure: did the cow give birth before or after the goring? The factual uncertainty generating the monetary dispute is the same type of *mamon hamutal b'safek*, a doubtful monetary claim.

### Doubtful Case Split

In both cases, our *mishna* rules *yachloku* — they split the value. The offspring, whether calf or child slave, is divided between the two parties since the matter cannot be resolved. Rashi raises the question of why the *mishna* specifically frames the case as *chalipin*; the *gemara* will need to address this. One reason is that *chalipin* allows a *kinyan* to be effected even when the animal is not physically present before the parties — transferring the donkey effects acquisition of the cow. The *mishna* could alternatively have employed a *kinyan agav*, a transfer of movable property by means of land, but we deal with the case as the *mishna* presents it.

---

## Two Items Claims

### Two Slaves/Fields

The *mishna* continues with a new cluster of cases. Someone possessed two slaves, one adult and one child — *echad gadol ve'echad katan* — or similarly two fields, one large and one small. A sale takes place, and a dispute arises as to which item was sold.

### Bari v. Shema

In the first sub-case, the buyer claims he bought the large slave or field, while the seller says he does not know which he sold. The rule is *zacha bagadol* — the buyer's claim prevails. The principle at work is *bari veshema bari adif*: a certain, firm claim (*bari*) overrides a doubtful one (*shema*).
