Their presence requires explanation, which will be addressed in the following section.

The first: *paritzei zeitim v'ha'anavim, Beit Shammai metamin u-Veit Hillel metaharin* — bad olives and bad grapes. Beit Shammai hold that they are susceptible to *tumah*; Beit Hillel hold that they are not. What are *paritzei zeitim* — bad olives? Rav Huna explains: *risha'ei zeitim* — inferior olives that produce little oil.

The Gemara then asks: how do we know that *paritz* means something bad or inferior? Rav Yosef cites the verse: *u'vnei paritzei amcha yinassu le'ha'amid chazon venichshalu* — the sons of the *paritzim* of your people will try to establish the vision and will stumble. Their failure marks them as *resha'im*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a different verse: *holid ben paritz shofech dam* — he fathers a son, a *paritz*, who is a spiller of blood — likewise a *rasha*. From both verses, *paritz* carries the connotation of wickedness and worthlessness, and by extension *paritzei zeitim* refers to olives that are bad in quality — they do not yield much oil.

How much oil qualifies an olive as *paritz*? Rabbi Elazar says: the olive press produces only four *kabbin* per *kur* of olives. The school of Rabbi Yannai says it produces two *se'ah* — approximately three times the amount. The Gemara resolves this as a non-dispute: *v'lo pligi*. In one locality, the press holds one *kur* of olives; in another, it holds three *kurim*. If you fill a press that holds three *kurim* and get only two *se'ah* of oil, that is the same ratio of poor yield as filling a press that holds one *kur* and getting only four *kabbin*. The two figures correspond to different regional practices for loading the olive press, not to a substantive disagreement about what constitutes a *paritz* olive.

### Weak Trees

The next *tnan hatam*: a pure person and an impure person — a *zav* and a *tahor* — ascend together onto a tree or onto branches whose strength is weak — *ilan she'kocho ra, socha she'kocha ra*. The ruling is *tamei*: the impurity transfers to the pure person. The mechanism, as Rashi explains, is that because the branches are weak, they bend under the combined weight of both individuals — *nichpefet tachteihen*. This bending creates a physical connection between the two, so that the weight of the one above presses upon the one below, allowing the *tumah* to transfer as though the *zav* were pressing directly upon the *tahor*.

What constitutes *ilan she'kocho ra* — a tree whose strength is weak? The school of Rabbi Yannai defines it: *kol she'ein b'ikaro lachok rova* — the root system is so small that there is not enough space within the roots to excavate a *rova*. A tree with such a shallow, narrow root system lacks structural strength, and that is what it means for a tree to be weak.

What constitutes *socha she'kocha ra* — weak upper branches? Reish Lakish defines it: *kol she'nechpeset b'chezyonah* — any branch that you can wrap your hand around and fully cover. A branch so slender that a person's hand encompasses it entirely is one that bends under weight and thus enables the transfer of *tumah*. A large, solid branch, by contrast, physically separates the two individuals on the tree, preventing the contact-based transfer of impurity.

### Beit Hapras

The third *tnan hatam*: one who walks through a *beit hapras* — a field in which a grave has been plowed — upon stones that can be dislodged — *al gabei avanim she'yachol le'hasit*. A *beit hapras* is a field where concern exists that fragments of bone the size of a barley grain — *etzem k'se'orah* — may be scattered throughout. An *etzem k'se'orah* conveys the highest level of *tumat meit* through contact and carrying, though not through *ohel* (overhang). If the stones in such a field shift when one steps on them, and an *etzem k'se'orah* is thereby carried by the force of one's step — *nisa mikocho* — the walker has become impure.

The more difficult case: what if a person is riding atop another person or an animal whose strength is weak — *she'kochan ra* — through a *beit hapras*? The *tumah* transfers to the rider through the weakness of the carrier.

What constitutes a person whose strength is weak in this context? Reish Lakish: *kol she'rchuvav be'arkuvotav nokshot* — one whose knees knock together under the weight of the rider. What constitutes a weak animal? The school of Rabbi Yannai: *kol she'ochma matila gelalim* — an animal so burdened that it excretes droppings while being ridden. That is the sign of an animal whose strength is insufficient, and it is through that weakness that the *tumah* of the *beit hapras* transfers to the rider.

### Prayer/Tefillin

The school of Rabbi Yannai makes one final pronouncement: *litfillah u-litfillin arba'ah kabin* — with respect to prayer and the wearing of *tefillin*, the operative threshold is four *kabbin*. The Gemara unpacks each half of this ruling separately.

With respect to prayer: a *baraita* teaches that if a person is carrying a load on his shoulder and the time for prayer arrives, if the load is less than four *kabbin*, he may shift it to his back and pray in that posture. If it is four *kabbin* or more, he must set it down on the ground before praying.

With respect to *tefillin*: a *baraita* teaches that if a person is carrying a load on his head while wearing *tefillin*, the question is whether the load is pressing on and misshaping the *tefillin*. If it does — *rotzetzot* — it is forbidden. If it does not, it is permitted. The threshold of four *kabbin* is the weight of load under discussion in these rulings.

A further *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Chiyya addresses the case of one who carries *zevel* — refuse or manure — on his head while wearing *tefillin*. He may neither move the *tefillin* to the side of his head, out of the proper position but away from the refuse, nor tie them elsewhere on his body. Both of these are *minhag bizayon* — improper treatment of *tefillin*, since they are placed outside their designated location. Rather, he should move his head *tefillin* to his arm, to the place designated for the arm *tefillin*: that is not considered disrespectful, since it is a proper location for *tefillin*.

A dissenting tradition from the school of Rabbi Sheila holds a stricter position: even the wrapping cloth — *mitpachas* — of the *tefillin* may not be placed on the head on which *tefillin* are being worn. And how small a load triggers this restriction? Abaye says: even a sixteenth of a *kab* or *log* from Pumbedita — an extremely small amount, as Rashi notes.

## Taharot Integration

### Strength Motif

Having worked through the entire sequence of *tnan hatam* passages, it is worth pausing to ask why they appear here at all. Rashi explains that all of them are gathered here because each one is accompanied by an explanatory tradition from *d'vei Rabbi Yannai* — the school of Rabbi Yannai provides the definition or measurement in each case. That is a sufficient reason for the compiler of the *sugya* to bring them together: the thread connecting them is that each mishna arrives with a Yannai-school explanation attached.

There is, however, a more satisfying account of what draws these passages into this context, and it is the one that arises from a careful look at the recurring subject matter. Each of these passages turns on a threshold of strength: the bad olives that are too weak to produce adequate oil; the tree or branch whose structural strength is insufficient to prevent the bending that enables *tumah* transfer; the animal whose strength is so diminished that it betrays itself under load; the person whose knees buckle; the load that is too heavy to carry while praying or wearing *tefillin*. The motif running through all of them is the borderline between adequate and insufficient strength — what is strong enough and what falls short. This is precisely the question that governs the preceding agricultural discussion: how much must a field produce for the lessee to remain obligated? What is the minimum strength, so to speak, of the field's output? The literary structure of the Bavli here follows this thematic coherence, not merely the coincidence of Yannai-school explanations.

David Rozenthal reads this sequence as evidence of something more: he sees in these passages traces of what might be called an incipient *Talmud* on the tractates of Seder Taharot — more formally edited discussions that circulated around those *mishnayot* and found their way into the Bavli when the literary editors (*mesadrei ha-Gemara*) placed them alongside the *mishnayot* they illuminated, sometimes bringing along material that is not strictly relevant to the Bavli's own tractate. On this view, the sequence of *d'vei Rabbi Yannai* passages entered the Bavli already as a set, because those Yannai-school traditions had been transmitted together.

An alternative view is more conservative: perhaps there was no separate Taharot *Talmud* in any formal sense, but simply that the *d'vei Rabbi Yannai* traditions on these *mishnayot* were known and transmitted as a group. When the occasion arose — here, because we were already discussing *d'vei Rabbi Yannai*'s measurement in the context of *kablanut* — they were brought in together. The thematic motif of strength thresholds is the stronger literary explanation for why they appear here; the *d'vei Rabbi Yannai* connection is the more historical one.

## Kdei Nefilah

### Minimum Produce

Returning now to the Mishna's dispute: the *tanna kamma* requires *kedei le'amid kari* — enough to set up a stack — for the lessee to be obligated to continue working the field, a threshold the Gemara established as either two or three *se'ah*. Rabbi Yehuda sets the threshold instead at *kedei nefilah* — the amount of seed needed to replant the field the following year. Below that level, the field's output is so negligible that the lessee is released from his work obligation.

### Land Quality Dispute

The Gemara asks: how much, precisely, is *kedei nefilah*? Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — though the text as emended by the *Hagahot ha-Bach* reads *arba'ah kabbin le-khor* — says four *kabbin* per *kur* of field. Rabbi Ami then offers his own independent view: eight *se'ah* per *kur*, twice the amount attributed to Rabbi Yochanan. An elder explains the discrepancy to Rav Chama son of Rabbah bar Avuha: in the days of Rabbi Yochanan the land was fertile — *shemena ar'a*; in the days of Rabbi Ami the land had become exhausted — *kachsha ar'a*. Weaker land required proportionally more seed to achieve the same result, and so Rabbi Ami's figure reflects the agricultural conditions of his own time.

### Scattered Sheaves

A second *tnan hatam* is now introduced, drawn this time from Seder Zraim — specifically from Masekhet Peah. *Ha'ruach shepizra et ha'omrin* — if the wind scatters someone's sheaves, the Gemara rules that we estimate how much *leket* the field would have produced and that amount is given to the poor. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: we do not estimate, but rather give the poor *kedei nefilah* — the amount sufficient to reseed the field. The Gemara then asks of this second source: how much is *kedei nefilah*?

This passage is brought here because *kedei nefilah* requires definition in both contexts — the *kablanut* context of the preceding Mishna and the *peah*-*leket* context of Seder Zraim. The Bavli, which produced no *gemara* on Seder Zraim any more than on Seder Taharot, handles this by bringing the relevant *mishnayot* together at the point where the shared term requires elucidation in both directions.

### Four Kabin

Rav Dimi, reporting in the name of either Rabbi Elazar or Rabbi Yochanan, gives the answer: *arba'ah kabbin le-khor* — four *kabbin* for a *kur* of field. This is consistent with the figure attributed to Rabbi Yochanan earlier, and it is precisely this consistency that led the Vilna Gaon to emend the earlier text. Where the earlier discussion had *arba'ah se'im le-khor*, the Gra corrected it to *arba'ah kabbin*, since a *se'ah* is three times a *kab*, and the discrepancy between the two formulations was otherwise irreconcilable. Whether this emendation is correct remains a matter of the precise volumetric relationship between these measures.

### Hand vs. Animal

Rabbi Yirmeyah poses two questions about the meaning of *arba'ah kabbin le-khor zera*. The first: is this a *kur* of *zera* — a field large enough to require a *kur* of seed — or a *kur* of *tevuah* — a field that produces a *kur* of grain? These are very different field sizes. A field that requires a *kur* of seed to sow is substantially larger than a field that yields a *kur* of grain as its output. Rashi explains: is it a large field, defined by how much seed it needs, or a small field, defined by how much it produces?

The Gemara attempts to answer this question from the same *tnan hatam* source: *arba'ah kabbin le-khor zera* — the explicit phrase *kur zera* resolves the first question in favor of the larger field, the one requiring a *kur* of seed.

But a second question immediately follows: when we speak of seeding a *kur* of field, do we mean seeding by hand — *mapolet yad* — or by animal-drawn seeding — *mapolet shevarim*? This is not a trivial distinction. Hand seeding allows the farmer to apply seed with discrimination — more here, less there — and tends to use somewhat less seed overall. Animal-drawn seeding is automatic and uniform; the mechanism disperses seed at a constant rate regardless of local conditions, and typically uses more seed per unit area. The two methods would yield a meaningfully different quantity for *arba'ah kabbin le-khor*. The Gemara leaves this question unresolved: *teiku*.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 106

## Tumah & Torah Transmissi…

### Zav & Tumat Midras

Before turning to the new *mishnah*, it is worth clarifying a point from the previous session concerning the transfer of *tumah* when a tree bends under the weight of people climbing it. The relevant figure is not any impure person in general, but *davka* a *zav* — a man or woman who has an abnormal genital discharge and thereby contracts a very high degree of *tumah*. There is a special rule applying to *zavim* and *zavot*: they generate *tumat midras*, the *tumah* produced when they stand or sit upon an object.

Ordinarily, when *tumah* transfers from an *av hatumah* — the primary source of impurity — to a second object, it descends a level: from *av* to *rishon*. The striking feature of *tumat midras* is that the transfer does not descend. The object upon which the *zav* sits or stands itself becomes an *av hatumah*. The question naturally arises: how can *tumah* ever transfer horizontally? *Tumah* should always diminish in potency as it passes from object to object.

The answer, associated with the Brisker analysis, is that no horizontal transfer of *tumah* is occurring at all. The object a *zav* sits upon acquires its own independent identity — it becomes, by definition, "the thing the *zav* sat upon," a halakhic category carrying *av hatumah* status as a matter of biblical law. Rather than the *zav*'s *tumah* somehow flowing into the chair at full strength, the chair is itself constituted as a new *av hatumah* because of the *zav*'s weight bearing down upon it. The weight-bearing object becomes, in a sense, an extension of the *zav* himself. From that new *av hatumah*, subsequent contact produces a *rishon l'tumah*, which is itself still a level of *tumah* of considerable stringency, though the third remove — *shlishi l'tumah* — is likely rabbinic.

### Sussman Theory

A second clarification concerns the discussion of *tirnanim* cited in the previous session. In speaking of those citations as "literary" creations, one must be careful: these traditions were not written down. They were transmitted orally. This is precisely the point argued at length by Yaakov Sussman in his monograph *Torah Shebal Peh Peshuto K'Mashmao: Kocha Shel Kotzo Shel Yod*, in which he demonstrates from evidence throughout both the *Yerushalmi* and *Bavli* that there is no trace of a written *mishnah* in the Amoraic period, and that any contrary impression reflects a misreading of the sources.

The difficulty with Sussman's broader thesis is that he extends this claim to deny the existence of any officially written *Torah Shebal Peh* during the Amoraic period — a position complicated by the fact that the *Bavli* itself repeatedly refers to *Sifra Debei Rav*, meaning either the book associated with Rav, the first-generation Babylonian *Amora*, or the book of the school-house of Rav. This clearly seems to denote some form of written *midrash halakhah* akin to the *Mekhilta*, *Sifra*, and *Sifrei* that we possess today. When confronted with the word "book," Sussman argues that it refers not to a physical written text but to the regimented, formalized interpretation transmitted within a school.

### Literary Transmission

This interpretive move opens onto a broader point about the nature of oral transmission. Even the small-scale exegetical units visible in the *Bavli* — where a *mishnah* is followed by "the school of Rabbi Yannai says that it means such-and-such" — can be understood as part of the intellectual *morasha* of a given school. A school develops characteristic readings of individual passages and transmits them generation after generation, even without committing them to writing. The word "literary," in this context, must be taken in a broad sense that includes any structured, transmissible formulation of meaning — not merely something written down or elaborately composed as a text.

This is not so foreign even in the modern *yeshiva* context. The *Torah* of Rav Soloveitchik, for instance, was transmitted largely orally: students heard his interpretations, repeated them to others, and preserved them in that way. The "literary construction" of a teaching, in this broader sense, is simply its being shaped into a form capable of transmission.

Returning to the *tannan hatam* citations discussed in the previous session: what they share is that each involves a *mishnah* containing a *shi'ur* — a measurement — and each is followed by an explanation from the school of Rabbi Yannai specifying what that *shi'ur* means. They are grouped together on that basis. Moreover, the presence of these citations constitutes evidence that there was indeed a developed *Talmud* — commentary on *mishnayot* — around *Seder Tahorot*, even though that *seder* has no tractates of its own in the *Bavli*. These three *tannan hatam* passages (one of which appears as a *tano rabbanan* but is in fact a *mishnah*) preserve what was effectively Babylonian *Talmud* on *Seder Tahorot*, a body of material that otherwise does not exist in the *Bavli* the way *Seder Nezikin* does.

---

## Makat Medina

### Hamekabel Sadeh

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 105b reads:

> *Ha-mekabel sadeh me-khavero ve-akhala khagav o nishtafa im makat medina hi menakeh lo min khakhuro im einah makat medina ein menakeh lo min khakhuro.*

If someone leases a field from another person — and this is a *chakhirut* lease, meaning the lessee pays a fixed amount rather than a share of the produce — and the entire crop is devoured by locusts or destroyed by blight, then if this disaster constitutes a *makat medina*, a widespread regional catastrophe, the lessor reduces the amount owed under the lease. If it is not a *makat medina*, the lessee must pay the full contracted sum regardless.

### Definition & Rabbi Yehuda

The Tanna *Rabbi Yehuda* adds a further qualification: if the lessee contracted to pay in coin rather than produce, then in either case — *makat medina* or not — there is no reduction.

### Blight on Plain

The *Gemara* asks: what exactly constitutes a *makat medina*? *Rav Yehuda* defines it as a case where most of the *baga* — the plain, the large contiguous agricultural tract — has been blighted. The disaster is thus still geographically contained but covers a substantial and identifiable agricultural area, of which the leased field is part.

*Ulla* offers a somewhat different formulation: a *makat medina* is established when four surrounding fields, one in each direction, have been blighted. This appears to set a more localized threshold than *Rav Yehuda*'s majority-of-the-*baga* standard, though the precise magnitude of a *baga* in the Babylonian context is uncertain. In the land of Israel, where the terrain is broken by hillsides and arable tracts are relatively small, the practical difference between these two definitions may be less dramatic than it initially appears. A contemporary analogy might be the situation of fires in Haifa: a substantial portion of the city is affected, a communal authority declares it a targeted attack, and questions arise about who bears the losses — government or private insurance. The *makat medina* concept is structurally similar.

### Ulla's Questions

*Ulla* further reports that in the West — *Eretz Yisrael* — a series of unresolved questions (*ba'u b'ma'arva*) were posed about the edges of this rule:

If only a single row of plants was damaged across the length of the field — what is the rule? If all but a single row was destroyed — what then? If pits separate the leased field from its neighbors — does that geographic interruption matter? If the surrounding fields are planted with *aspasta* (animal fodder) rather than food crops — is that comparable? If the surrounding fields are planted with a different grain variety — is that treated as a different crop? And specifically: if wheat and barley are involved on different sides, are these treated as *zera acher*, different plantings? Finally, what if the blight that struck the entire world was of one type — *shidafon* — while the blight on this field was of another type, *yerakon*? Or vice versa?

The *Gemara* records a single verdict: *teiku* — these questions remain unresolved. *Ulla* transmits a chain of questions from *Eretz Yisrael* to which neither that tradition nor the Babylonian *Gemara* supplies an answer. A check of the *Yerushalmi* likewise reveals no parallel to these questions there, which suggests this is a tradition preserved in *Bavel* but not recorded in the Palestinian *Talmud*.

---

## Mazal & Divine Providence

### Wrong Crop Case

The *Gemara* now introduces a more intricate set of cases in which the operative question is not simply whether a *makat medina* occurred, but how personal fortune — *mazal* — interacts with contractual obligation and divine providence.

The first case: the *choker* (lessee) contracted to plant wheat but instead planted barley. A blight then struck most of the *baga*, and his barley was destroyed along with it. The *Gemara* poses the question: does the owner argue that had the lessee planted wheat as contracted, the wheat would have been blighted too — and therefore the *makat medina* rule applies and the rent is reduced? Or can the owner argue: had you planted wheat as we agreed, God would have upheld for me the verse *v'tigzar omer v'yakum lach* — that God fulfills the decrees of the righteous — and my crop would have been spared by divine providence?

This is a striking *sugya*. The entire discussion turns on whether metaphysical claims — specifically, claims about how divine providence operates — can be invoked to determine legal obligations. The *Gemara*'s answer (*mistavra*) favors the owner: it is more reasonable to say that had the lessee planted wheat as contracted, God would have protected that crop through the owner's prayers and merit. The owner prayed specifically for wheat, and the lessee disrupted that by planting barley. One might object that the owner should have prayed more generally for a successful harvest rather than specifically for wheat — but the owner's position is that he contracted for wheat, and it was reasonable for him to pray accordingly.

It is important to note that this *sugya* is not simply entertaining metaphysical speculation for its own sake. The metaphysics establish the underlying reality upon which the legal rule is constructed. If divine providence operates in a demonstrable way — protecting certain people's crops under certain conditions — then the legal consequences flow from that factual determination.

### Owner's Fields Destroyed

The second case reverses the direction of the *mazal* argument. All of the landowner's fields throughout the country were blighted. This particular leased field, located in a plain where no other field was blighted, was also destroyed — but the rest of that plain was untouched.

Since most of the *baga* was not blighted, the strict *makat medina* rule does not formally apply. Can the owner therefore demand full payment? Or can the lessee argue: look at your fields — they were all destroyed throughout the country; that is your bad *mazal*, and this field too is a casualty of your bad luck rather than any localized natural disaster?

The *Gemara* resolves this (*mistavra*) in favor of the landowner. The owner can respond to the lessee: had it been solely my bad luck causing this particular field to be blighted, divine providence would have left me something — as the verse says, *ki nisharnu me'at me'harbeh*, "for we have remained a small remnant." Bad luck does not wipe one out entirely; it leaves a small portion. Since the entire field was destroyed with nothing left, the destruction of this field cannot be attributed entirely to the owner's *mazal*. Thus the owner is not responsible, and the lessee still owes the full amount.

### All Fields Blighted

The third case presents the inverse situation. The lessee himself owns many fields in addition to the one he leases. All of his own fields were destroyed by blight. The plain in which the leased field sits was also mostly blighted, and the leased field was destroyed as part of that general catastrophe.

On its face, this is a standard *makat medina* case, and the lessee would expect a reduction. But the owner argues: your fields all over the country were destroyed — that is your bad *mazal*, and that bad luck explains why this field too was blighted. Therefore you owe me the full amount.

The *Gemara* applies the same reasoning in reverse. The lessee can reply: had it been my bad luck causing this particular field's destruction, God would have left me something on it. Since nothing at all remained, the blight on this field cannot be attributed solely to my *mazal*. The broader *makat medina* was the cause, and accordingly the rent is reduced.

This trilogy of cases is analytically elegant: each invokes the principle that bad luck leaves a remnant, and the party whose personal *mazal* cannot account for the total destruction of the field is exonerated from full liability.

---

## Arachin Excursus

### Yovel & Redemption

At this point a challenge is raised from a *mishnah* in *Arachin* (Perek 7), concerning the redemption of land sold during the era when *Yovel* — the Jubilee — is operative. When a person sells ancestral land during such a period, the buyer must hold it for at least two years before the seller may redeem it. The verse states *u've-mispar shenei tevuot yimkor lach* — it is sold to you according to the number of years of produce. The buyer purchases a right to so many years of crops, and the price of redemption is adjusted proportionally based on the years remaining until *Yovel*.

The *mishnah* in *Arachin* teaches that years of *shidafon* or *yerakon* (blight), as well as a *shemitah* year or years like the years of Elijah when no rain fell anywhere, are not counted toward this minimum. Such years are excluded from the reckoning because they were not genuine years of agricultural produce.

### Blight Exclusions

The question arises: the *mishnah* in *Arachin* appears to treat *shidafon* and *yerakon* on analogy with the years of Elijah — that is, years when there were no crops anywhere in the world. How then can our *mishnah* in *Bava Metzia* speak of a localized regional blight as sufficient to trigger the *makat medina* rule? Is it possible that only a worldwide or nationwide agricultural collapse qualifies?

The *Gemara* answers: the cases are not comparable. The rule in *Arachin* is governed by a specific verse — *shenei tevuot*, years of crops. In that context, the only years excluded are years in which there are no crops anywhere in the world. The *makat medina* rule in *Bava Metzia*, by contrast, is not governed by that verse and operates on general principles. A localized regional blight can qualify as a *makat medina* for purposes of lease law without being a global catastrophe.

### Verse Rule

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* makes this explicit: the rule in *Arachin* is different because of the verse *u've-mispar shenei tevuot yimkor lach*, which teaches that only years in which there is *tevuah* in the world count. Years of *shidafon* and *yerakon* qualify for exclusion only when the blight is total — when there is no *tevuah* anywhere, analogous to the years of Elijah when rain ceased everywhere.

### Shevi'it Exception

*Rav Ashi* then poses a sharp question to *Rav Kahana*: if the *Arachin* rule excludes only years in which there is no *tevuah* in the world, why does *Shevi'it* — the Sabbatical Year — also get excluded? In *Eretz Yisrael* no planting occurs during *Shevi'it*, but the rest of the world plants and harvests normally. Crops grow in *chutz la'aretz* during a *Shevi'it* year. It is therefore not a year without *tevuah* in the world.

The answer: *Shevi'it afkata diMalka hi* — the Sabbatical Year is a divine decree of the King. God has declared that *Shevi'it* simply does not exist as an agricultural year in the context of *Eretz Yisrael*. It is categorically excluded from the universe of agriculture as far as the land of Israel is concerned, regardless of what grows elsewhere. This is not a factual judgment about the availability of produce worldwide, but a normative divine pronouncement.

### Hekdesh Paradox

*Mar Zutra*, son of *Rav Mari*, raises a further difficulty to *Ravina*. If *Shevi'it* is excluded from the count of years when redeeming sold land — because it is *afkata diMalka* — why does it count when one is redeeming land consecrated as *hekdesh* (dedicated to the Temple)?

The mechanism of redeeming *hekdesh* land works as follows: when a person consecrates ancestral land to the Temple, the redemption price is assessed at a fixed rate — a *sela* and a *pundyon* per year remaining until *Yovel*. The *mishnah* in *Arachin* teaches this calculation includes all years including *Shevi'it*, yielding a forty-ninth of the total value per year (fifty years in a *Yovel* cycle, minus one for the *Yovel* year itself). If *Shevi'it* is truly excluded as a non-agricultural year, should one not subtract the *Shevi'it* years from the count and pay a forty-second (rather than a forty-ninth) of the total?

### Agricultural Work

The resolution: *shani hatam de-chazya le-mishtach bah peirei* — that case is different because the land can still be used during *Shevi'it* for spreading out fruit to dry. Even though planting does not occur, a form of agricultural use — the spreading and processing of produce — does take place on the land. Therefore, *Shevi'it* counts as a year of agricultural activity for purposes of the *hekdesh* redemption calculation, even though it does not count for purposes of the *Arachin* land-sale redemption calculation, where the verse requires genuine years of *tevuah*.

---

## Planting Requirements

### Shmuel's Caveat

*Shmuel* now introduces a critical limitation on the *mishnah*'s *makat medina* rule. He says *lo shanu* — the *mishnah* only addressed the case where the lessee actually planted the land and the crop grew, and then the locusts or blight destroyed what had grown. But if the lessee did not plant at all, there is no reduction in what he owes. He must pay the full lease amount regardless.

### Divine Verse Argument

The rationale the landowner can invoke: *ilu zar'at hava mekayem bi lo yevoshu beet ra'ah u've-yemei ra'avon yisba'u* — had you planted, God would have fulfilled for me the verse "they will not be ashamed in a time of evil, and in days of famine they shall be satisfied." Since you did not plant, you cannot claim that a *makat medina* struck and you were helpless. You prevented the divine protection from operating in the first place.

### Shepherd & Wolves

*Rav Sheshet* challenges this position. How can such a metaphysical claim be entertained? There is a precedent: a shepherd who left his flock and went into town. While he was away, a wolf came and dragged away a sheep, and a lion came and killed another. The rule is that we do not say: had the shepherd been there, he would have saved the sheep. Rather, we assess the shepherd's capabilities: if he is the kind of person who could have driven off wolves and lions, he is liable; if not, he is exempt. The point is that we do not simply assume that presence guarantees rescue.

By the same logic, *Rav Sheshet* asks: why not argue about the shepherd, that had he been there, God would have fulfilled for him the verse that *David* invoked — "your servant has killed the lion and the bear"? Why is that argument not made on behalf of the shepherd's flock-owner?

The *Gemara* answers: because that would require a *nisa raba* — a great miracle, like the miracle that occurred with *Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa*, whose goat apparently brought a bear on its horns. We do not expect such dramatic miracles. But the counter-argument is pressed: even if we do not expect a *nisa raba*, perhaps we should expect a *nisa zuta* — a minor miracle? The *Gemara* finds this genuinely difficult: *kashya*. The argument is that if God wished to save the sheep, He could have done so whether the shepherd was present or not, and we should not hold the shepherd liable on the basis of what a small miracle might have accomplished. The tension between the metaphysical framework invoked in the earlier cases and the rejection of metaphysical reasoning here is left unresolved.

One also notices that the *Gemara* slips between *ze'ev* (wolf) and *dov* (bear) in narrating this case. This is not accidental: scholars have noted, following Ginzberg's commentary on the *Yerushalmi* in the final portion of Perek 1 of *Berachot*, that in Babylonian sources there is a pattern of interchange between the two, likely because *dov* in Eastern Aramaic phonology is closer in sound to *ze'ev* than one might expect, given that the consonants *dalet* and *zayin* are in fact linguistically proximate.

### Chazakah Disputes

A further dispute emerges from two conflicting *beraitot* on the question of repeated planting failures. One *beraita* says that if the lessee plants once and fails, plants a second time and fails, he does not have to plant a third time — the lease obligation is already reduced. A second *beraita* says that the lessee must plant a third time before he is exempt, and only if a fourth planting would be necessary is he released from the obligation.

### Rabbi vs. R.S.b.G.

The resolution: *lo kashya* — there is no genuine contradiction. These two *beraitot* reflect the well-known *machloket* between *Rabbi* and *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* regarding the threshold for establishing a *chazakah*. *Rabbi* holds that a *chazakah* is established after two occurrences — *be-trei zimnei havya chazakah*. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* holds that three occurrences are required. The first *beraita*, which exempts after two failures, follows *Rabbi*. The second, which requires three before granting exemption, follows *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*.

The underlying conceptual difference between these two positions is worth noting. It is not merely a numerical disagreement. For *Rabbi*, what matters is the occurrence itself — once something has happened twice, it is established as a pattern. For *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, what must be established is the *re-occurrence*; the first instance establishes the thing, and the *chazakah* requires the re-occurrence to have happened twice. On this reading, both agree that two repetitions are needed to establish the presumption, but they disagree about whether the first instance counts as one of those repetitions or merely as the baseline. This *machloket* recurs across many tractates — *Yevamot*, *Eruvin*, *Ketubot*, *Sanhedrin*, and *Niddah* — and applies to contexts as varied as hemophilia and the laws of circumcision.

---

## Planting Calendar

### Resh Lakish

*Resh Lakish* introduces yet another qualification on the *mishnah*. He says *lo shanu ela she-zara* — the *mishnah* speaks only where the lessee planted and the crop *grew*, and then a disaster struck. But if the lessee planted and the crop simply failed to grow — not from a regional blight but from a failed seeding — the owner can instruct him: *kol yemei zera zara ve-azel*, continue to plant for as long as the planting season lasts. The obligation to plant persists through the entire *yemei hazera*.

### End of Planting Season

This immediately raises the question: when does the planting season end? *Rav Pappa* answers: *ad de-atu areisei midabra be-kima* — until the workers come in from the field when the *kima* — the Pleiades star cluster — is directly overhead. *Rashi* works through the entire zodiac to establish when the Pleiades would be visible in this position. There is a *machloket* between *Rashi* and *Tosafot*: according to *Rashi*, we are speaking of sometime in the afternoon, which would place the relevant date in *Adar*; according to *Tosafot*, we are speaking of *tzet ha-kokhavim* — nightfall — when the workers return home, which would place the date earlier, in *Shevat*.

### Seasonal Divisions

A *beraita* in the name of *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* citing *Rabbi Meir*, and affirmed also by *Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya*, divides the agricultural year into six two-month periods:

The second half of *Tishrei*, all of *Marcheshvan*, and the first half of *Kislev* constitute the planting season. The second half of *Kislev*, all of *Tevet*, and the first half of *Shevat* are *choref* — the cold period. The second half of *Shevat*, all of *Adar*, and the first half of *Nisan* are *kor* — the bitter cold. The second half of *Nisan*, all of *Iyar*, and the first half of *Sivan* are *katzir* — the harvest. The second half of *Sivan*, all of *Tammuz*, and the first half of *Av* are *kayitz* — summer. And the second half of *Av*, all of *Elul*, and the first half of *Tishrei* are the hot season.

*Rabbi Yehuda* counts from the beginning of *Tishrei*; *Rabbi Shimon* counts from *Marcheshvan*. The question of who allows the most time for planting: *Rabbi Shimon* is most expansive. Yet *Rav Pappa*'s answer — extending planting into *Shevat* or even *Adar* — goes further than even *Rabbi Shimon*'s outer limit, presenting an apparent conflict.

The resolution: *lo kashya ha de-kabel minei de-charfei ha de-kabel minei de-aflei* — there is no contradiction because they are discussing different types of crops. *Rav Pappa* refers to *aflei*, late-planted crops, which have a longer planting window extending into *Shevat* or *Adar*. The *beraita*'s earlier dates refer to *charfei*, early-planted crops. Different agricultural calendars apply to different crops.

---

## Quality & Contract

### Poor Quality Payment

The *Gemara* then addresses a *guf* from the *mishnah* (*Matnitin*): if someone leases a field with an obligation to pay ten *kor* of wheat per year, and the wheat produced is of low quality, he may pay the owner from that low-quality wheat — he need not purchase standard-quality wheat from the market. However, if the wheat produced was especially fine, he may not say "I will buy wheat from the market and pay you standard quality," pocketing the profit from the superior grain. He must pay the owner from the actual produce of the field.

*Rabbi Yehuda*'s position from the *mishnah* is revisited here: if the lessee contracted to pay in coin, no reduction applies regardless of circumstances. *Rava* had ruled in a practical case — involving a field on the banks of *Nahar Malka* that flooded — that the flood constituted a *makat medina* and the lessee's payment should be reduced, even though the payment was in coin (*bezuzi*). The *Rabbanan* challenged *Rava*: the *mishnah* records *Rabbi Yehuda* as saying that a coin-payment lease is never reduced. *Rava* dismissed this: *leit de-chash la le-d'Rabbi Yehuda* — nobody follows *Rabbi Yehuda* on this point.

### Fodder to Barley

A practical case: a man leased land to plant *aspasta* (animal fodder), with the lease payment denominated in barley. He harvested the fodder, plowed again, and planted barley. His barley crop was then damaged. He claimed that since his payment obligation was in barley, and the barley was harmed, he should be able to pay in low-quality barley under the *mishnah*'s rule.

*Rav Chaviva* of *Sura* on the Euphrates sent an inquiry to *Ravina* on this question. *Ravina*'s answer: this case is not comparable to the *mishnah*. In the *mishnah*'s case, *lo avda ara shelichuta d'marei* — the land did not do what its master directed. The land failed in its assigned task and so the lessee need only pay from what it produced. Here, however, *avda ara shelichuta d'marei* — the land did precisely what it was instructed to do. It grew the *aspasta* as directed. The lessee then chose to plow and plant barley on his own initiative. Since the land fulfilled its mandate, the lessee must purchase standard barley from the market to satisfy his payment obligation.

### Spoiled Wine

A parallel case: a man leased a vineyard (*pardesa d'kerem*) with an obligation to pay ten jugs of wine. The wine that the vineyard produced spoiled. *Rav Kahana* thought this was analogous to the *mishnah*: since the produce was of poor quality, the lessee could pay in that poor-quality wine. *Rav Ashi* disagreed: *mi damei? hatam lo avda ara shelichuta* — in the *mishnah*, the land failed to do what was expected. Here the vineyard did exactly what it was supposed to do: it grew grapes and produced wine. That the wine subsequently spoiled is not a failure of the land's performance. Since the land fulfilled its role — *avda ara shelichuta* — the lessee must go to the market and purchase replacement wine.

*Rav Ashi* himself concedes that his rule does not apply universally. He agrees that the *mishnah*'s principle would govern cases involving wormy grapes (*invei de-kadumi*) or a field where the produce was blighted after being stood up for drying. In those cases, the land can fairly be said to have not fully performed its role, and the lessee pays from what was produced.

---

## Crop Change Rules

### Barley/Wheat Rule

The next *mishnah* addresses what crops a lessee may plant when the lease specifies a particular grain. If the lease specifies that the lessee is to plant barley, he may not plant wheat instead. But if the lease specifies wheat, the lessee may plant barley, because wheat is harder on the soil — it depletes the land more than barley does. Planting barley when wheat was contracted therefore causes the landowner no harm and may even benefit the land. The lessee is permitted to perform an act that is less damaging than what he contracted to perform. This principle illuminates the earlier case in which a lessee contracted to plant wheat but planted barley: the substitution was technically permissible, but as the *Gemara* established, if a *makat medina* then struck, the lessee could not invoke the owner's contractual expectation of wheat to claim protection — his deviation from the contract, even if allowed, voided his ability to make certain claims about divine providence.

### R.S.b.G. Disagrees

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* takes a stricter position. He rules that if the lessee contracted to plant *tevuah* — cereal grain — he may not switch to *kitnit* — legumes — even though legumes are generally considered less taxing on the soil than cereals. But if the lease specified legumes, the lessee may switch to cereals. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* prohibits the cereal-to-legume substitution despite the apparent benefit to the soil because the categories of *tevuah* and *kitnit* are sufficiently distinct that a switch between them represents a meaningful departure from the contracted arrangement, not merely a permissible downgrade within the same category.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 107

## Field Rental & Crops

### Mishna: Crop Changes

The *daf* opens at the bottom of 107b with the *mishna* governing a tenant farmer who has rented a field under an agreed crop arrangement. The *mishna* establishes: if someone received a field to plant barley, he may not substitute wheat, since wheat depletes the soil more heavily than barley. However, if the field was leased for wheat, the tenant may plant barley instead, since barley is less damaging than what was originally specified. On the parallel axis of grain categories: if the field was leased for *tevuah* (cereal grain), he may not plant *kitnit* (legumes), but if it was leased for *kitnit*, he may substitute *tevuah*.

### RSbG: Contract Compliance

In both cases, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissents and forbids any substitution whatsoever. His position is that whatever was stipulated in the contract must be honored — planting something different, even something less harmful to the soil, constitutes a violation of the agreement.

### Chisda's Challenge

The *gemara* opens with Rav Chisda's question: what is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's rationale? On the face of it, if the substitute crop is *less* damaging to the field than what was contracted, the landowner ought to have no complaint — one could even argue the tenant is doing him a favor. The principle *zachi le'adam shelo befanav, aval ein chav leshelo befanav* would suggest that acting in someone's benefit without their presence is permitted, whereas causing harm is not. A less damaging crop should therefore fall on the permissible side of that line.

### No Deception

The answer given is rooted in a verse from the prophets: *She'erit Yisrael lo ya'asu avlah velo yedabru kazav velo yimatze befihem lashon tarmit* — the remnant of Israel shall not commit wrongdoing, shall not speak falsehood, and no deceitful tongue shall be found in their mouth. The principle is that Jews are forbidden to misrepresent what they undertook to do. If a contract specifies one crop, planting a different one — even a superior one for the soil — constitutes a form of deception relative to the agreed terms.

### Purim Collections

This prompts a *meitivi*: a challenge from a *baraita* concerning collections for *Purim*. The *baraita* states that funds collected for *Purim* may only be distributed for *Purim* needs, and a poor person may not even take from those funds so much as a strap for his sandal — unless the town council explicitly permitted it. This represents the opinion of Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Meir. Yet Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel takes a lenient position there, suggesting that one need not be overly strict when no real damage is caused. If Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is lenient in the *Purim* case, why is he strict here about crop substitution? The two positions appear inconsistent. Rashi explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient position in the *Purim* case: when there is truly no loss, people do not insist on strict compliance. Why, then, is he strict with field rental?

### Field Rotation Damage

Abaye resolves the tension by invoking the teaching of his master, Rabbah bar Nachmani: the reason Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel forbids even the "less damaging" substitution is that he is concerned about cumulative damage over multiple seasons. The very statement *hai man de'nicha leih detifshir arei* — one who wants his field to deteriorate — should plant wheat one year and barley the next. The alternation between the two, done carelessly, can in fact harm the field over time. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's concern is therefore not about the single-year effect of the substitution but about the multi-year rotation pattern.

### Plowing & Soil Care

The *gemara* elaborates: planting one year in one direction and the following year perpendicular to that can damage the field. The qualification is added: this concern applies only when the field has *not* been plowed a second time between planting seasons — *dela keriv utnei*. If a full additional plowing cycle is performed after harvest and before the next planting, the damage is mitigated. This connects to a broader agricultural question about whether plowing precedes or follows sowing — a practice that varied between Eretz Yisrael and Bavel, and which is treated differently in contexts such as *hilchot shevi'it* and Shabbat. In any event, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's prohibition is explained: when a landlord specifies a particular crop, it is because he is tracking the rotation of his field across years, and the tenant cannot unilaterally alter that pattern even in a direction that seems beneficial in isolation.

---

## Grain vs. Legumes

### Bavel vs. EY Ruling

The *gemara* records that Rav Yehuda taught Ravin the ruling *tevuah lo yizra'ena kitnit* — but in the opposite formulation from the *mishna*. When the student protests that this contradicts the *mishna*, Rav Yehuda responds: *lo kashya — ha lan ve'ha le'hu* — there is no contradiction, because what I am teaching applies to us in Bavel, and what the *mishna* says applies to them in Eretz Yisrael. Regional variation in *halacha* based on local agricultural conditions is well-attested, and this is simply another instance of it.

### Rain vs. Irrigation

The Nimukei Yosef explains the underlying distinction: the difference between the two rulings turns on whether a region's fields are watered by rainfall or by river irrigation. Eretz Yisrael is predominantly rain-fed (*baal*), while Bavel depends on irrigation from its major river systems. The relative impact of *tevuah* versus *kitnit* on the soil differs depending on the water source, and this is what generates the divergent rulings. The Nimukei Yosef further applies this principle to his own context, addressing whether Spain — where he wrote — falls into the rain-fed or irrigation category.

---

## Tachal in Flax

### Hardened Cress

The *gemara* transitions to a series of teachings framed as Rav Yehuda addressing Ravin bar Rav Nachman with the phrase *Ravin achi* — my brother Ravin. The first concerns *tachal* (garden cress, *Lepidium sativum*), a small-leafed herb also used medicinally, which sometimes grows among *pishtan* (flax). Rav Yehuda teaches that such garden cress growing among flax fields carries no concern of theft — because while it is growing, it actually damages the flax. However, once the cress has hardened and produced its seeds, even cress growing among flax does become subject to theft prohibitions, because by that point it has already done all the damage it will do to the flax. As the *gemara* states: *mai de'afsidei afsidei* — what it damaged, it has already damaged. The cress is now fully grown, the harm to the flax is done, and the cress itself has value that the owner may not be deprived of.

### Cress Damages Flax

Rav Yehuda's baseline ruling rests on Rashi's explanation that the cress, while still growing among the flax, is actively harming it — and therefore the cress lacks independent legal protection during that period.

---

## Border Mound Trees

### Shared Orchard Saying

Rav Yehuda says to Ravin bar Rav Nachman: *hanei diley dilakh u'dilakh diley* — what is mine is yours and what is yours is mine. This is not a generous offer but a description of a practical reality: when two neighboring fields are divided by a *metzar* (a raised boundary mound), and trees have been planted along that mound, it sometimes happens that a tree whose trunk appears on one side actually has its roots drawing nourishment from the other side, and vice versa. The result is that what looks like your tree is nourishing itself from my land, and what looks like my tree draws from yours.

---

## Tachal in Flax (II)

### Border Planting

The exception to the general permissibility of taking garden cress from among flax applies when the cress is found growing specifically on the borders between fields — *agvulei*. In that case it is prohibited to take the cress, since a person who deliberately plants cress on a field boundary has clearly cultivated it intentionally, and it therefore belongs to that owner.

---

## Border Mound Trees (II)

### Rav vs. Shmuel

The *gemara* records a formal dispute: Rav says that a tree standing on the *metzar* is assigned according to which way it leans — *hanoteh le'kan le'kan ve'hanoteh le'kan le'kan* — if the tree leans toward one side, it belongs to that side. Shmuel says *cholkin* — the fruit is split between the two field owners.

### Baraita Support

A *meitivi* is raised: a *baraita* states explicitly that a tree standing on the *metzar* is subject to *yachloku* — the owners divide the fruit. This appears to be a *tiyuvta de'Rav*, a direct refutation of Rav's position. The *gemara* then reports: *tirgeman Shmuel aliba de'Rav* — Shmuel himself provided an interpretation of the *baraita* that would align it with Rav's view.

### Metzer Definition

Before proceeding to the resolution, the *gemara* requires clarity on what a *metzar* actually is. It is not merely an imaginary line; it is a raised mound of earth running between two adjacent fields, serving as a physical border marker. In the agricultural context of this *sugya*, an orchard has been planted along this mound — meaning the trees literally grow on the elevated strip of soil between the two properties.

This is where a significant *machloket* between Rashi and Tosafot emerges regarding what it means for a tree to stand *al ha'metzar*:

### Rashi: Roots & Fruit Spl…

Rashi understands that the *metzar* has real physical width, and the trees planted on it may have their roots extending to one side while the trunk and fruit overhang the other. The *gemara*'s case, according to Rashi, involves trees where the roots are on one side of the imaginary borderline within the mound, while the canopy and fruit are on the other. The principle *diley dilakh u'dilakh diley* describes precisely this situation: a tree whose fruit appears to be entirely on one owner's side is in fact nourished by roots drawing from the adjacent field. Rashi's illustration requires two such trees, leaning in opposite directions, to generate the mutual scenario where each owner has trees whose fruit belongs to the other.

The difficulty for Rashi is then raised: given the principle derived elsewhere in Bava Batra 27a that *shadei nufo batar ikaro* — the canopy of a tree follows its roots, meaning a tree belongs to the property where it is planted — why would a tree whose roots are on one side not simply belong entirely to that side? Rashi's answer lies in the precise configuration: the tree is *mamash al ha'metzar*, directly on the mound, with roots on one side of the border within that mound.

### Tosafot: Shared Space

Tosafot object to Rashi's approach on grounds that their version of the text does not read *al ha'metzar* but rather *al tzad ha'metzar* — beside the *metzar*, not on it. For Tosafot, the principle that a tree's ownership follows its roots renders Rashi's entire construction unnecessary and internally inconsistent. Instead, Tosafot propose that the *metzar* is a boundary line with no spatial width — it is an infinitesimally thin dividing line, not a strip of land. The roots of a tree planted on this line therefore exist in shared space, belonging to neither owner exclusively. Since the roots are in genuinely shared territory, ownership of the fruit cannot be determined by root location. The fruit then falls on one side or the other, and that is what Rav is tracking — which direction the fruit hangs. When Rav says *hanoteh le'kan le'kan*, he is acknowledging that the fruit determines apparent ownership, but the deeper legal reality is shared roots, which is why Shmuel's ruling of *yachloku* ultimately prevails.

### Reconciling Views

The *gemara*'s phrase *tirgeman Shmuel aliba de'Rav* — Shmuel interpreted the case according to Rav — represents an attempt to show that Shmuel's rule of *yachloku* need not flatly contradict Rav's principle. There are cases in which even Rav would agree to split the fruit, and Shmuel is identifying the conditions under which that convergence occurs.

### Rav's Exception

The specific condition under which even Rav would agree to *yachloku* is described as *b'memale kol ha'metzar kulo* — when the roots fill the entire *metzar*. According to Rashi, this means the roots extend equally to both sides of the boundary within the mound. According to Tosafot, it means the roots occupy the full shared space of the boundary line, with the tree's weight and fruit hanging off to one side. In this configuration, even Rav acknowledges that the fruit cannot simply be assigned to the side it physically hangs over, because the root structure that nourishes the tree is equally shared.

The *gemara* then asks: *ei hachi, mai lemimra* — if that is the case, what is the ruling actually teaching us? Surely if the roots are equally on both sides, of course we split the fruit? The answer is: *lo tzricha d'tali t'unei l'chad gisa* — it is necessary to teach us this rule precisely when the fruit load hangs heavily to one side. One might have thought that in such a case, whoever the fruit falls on should receive it, since the physical reality favors them. The ruling teaches that even then, *yachloku*.

### Cutting Method

But *yachloku* raises a practical question: how does one actually divide the fruit equally when the mass of it hangs entirely to one side? The *gemara* addresses this. If one simply cuts the tree along the line of the *metzar* — running the cut in the direction of the boundary — the owner whose side the fruit is on would receive all or most of it, and the distribution would be unequal. Instead, the cut should be made *perpendicularly* — across the line of the *metzar*, slicing through the mass of the tree horizontally, such that each owner receives an equal portion of the fruit even though the whole canopy is displaced to one side. This is the meaning of *mah chazit d'falagat hachi, pelag hachi* — why do you think the division goes *this* way? Divide it *that* way instead. The underlying *svara* is that since the roots are equally shared, the fruit must also be divided equally, and the only way to achieve that when the canopy is asymmetric is to cut perpendicularly to the *metzar* rather than along it.

---

## Proximity Issues

### City Proximity

The *gemara* continues with the series of teachings addressed by Rav Gidal to Rav Nachman in the *Ravin achi* format: do not purchase land adjacent to a city. The concern involves issues of safety and interference — proximity to populated areas creates complications for agricultural property.

### Harvest Field Access

This connects to a ruling of Rav, transmitted through Rav Huna: it is forbidden for a person to stand in his neighbor's field at the time when the grain is standing and ready for harvest. The concern is one of intrusion at a moment of particular vulnerability for the crop.

### Deuteronomy Blessings

The *gemara* then records an encounter in which Rav Abba found students of Rav and asked them: how did Rav interpret the verses in Deuteronomy — *baruch ata ba'ir u'varuch ata ba'sadeh, baruch ata b'vo'echa u'varuch ata b'tzeitecha* — blessed are you in the city, blessed in the field, blessed in your comings and goings?

The students reported Rav's interpretations as follows. *Baruch ata ba'ir* — blessed in the city — means that your house should be near the *beit ha'keneset*. This initially appears to contradict Rav's earlier warning against purchasing land near a city, a tension the *gemara* will resolve. *Baruch ata ba'sadeh* — blessed in the field — means that your property should be near your home. *Baruch ata b'vo'echa* — blessed in your coming — means that you should not find your wife in a state of doubtful *niddah* when you return home from travel. *Baruch ata b'tzeitecha* — blessed in your going — means that your descendants should be like you.

### Alternative Blessing

Rabbi Yochanan offers a competing set of interpretations. *Baruch ata ba'ir* — blessed in the city — means that your bathroom should be near your table. Rabbi Yochanan explicitly rejects the *beit ha'keneset* reading, and the *gemara* explains that this is consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's position elsewhere: *sachar pesi'ot yesh* — there is reward for each step one walks to the *beit ha'keneset*, and therefore proximity to the synagogue is actually undesirable from a spiritual-reward perspective. *Baruch ata ba'sadeh* — blessed in the field — means that your assets should be divided in thirds: a third in grain, a third in olives, and a third in grapes — the Mediterranean agricultural triad. *Baruch ata b'vo'echa u'varuch ata b'tzeitecha* — blessed in your comings and goings — means that your departure from the world should be as pure as your arrival into it, just as you entered without sin, so may you leave without sin.

### Walled City Distinction

The *gemara* returns to the tension in Rav's position — how can Rav say one should live near the *beit ha'keneset* while also warning against buying land adjacent to a city? The resolution: *ha d'mehader lei shura v'ritka, ha d'lo mehader lei shura v'ritka* — the two cases are distinct. When the city has a surrounding wall and moat, the field adjacent to it carries none of the dangers that prompted Rav's warning, and proximity to the *beit ha'keneset* is indeed a blessing. When the city lacks a wall, the adjacent land is exposed to the various problems Rav cautioned against, and one should not purchase it.

---

## Disease Interpretations

### Rav: Evil Eye

The *gemara* now addresses a series of interpretations of the verse from Deuteronomy 7:15: *ve'hesir Hashem mimcha kol choli* — and God will remove from you all illness. What is the *choli* — the illness — that God promises to remove? Rav says: *zo ayin* — this is the evil eye, *ayin ha'ra*. The *gemara* notes that this is *Rav l'taameih* — consistent with Rav's general orientation on such matters. The evidence: Rav would go to the cemetery and perform certain acts — Rashi explains this involved a form of inquiry addressed to those buried there — and Rav determined that 99 out of 100 deaths were caused by the evil eye, with only one attributable to natural causes.

### Shmuel: Wind

Shmuel says the *choli* of the verse refers to wind — *ruach*. This too is *Shmuel l'taameih*, consistent with Shmuel's broader view that *hakol be'ruach* — wind is the underlying cause of most illness. One might object: what about people killed by the Roman government — surely wind does not account for those deaths? The *gemara* responds: even in those cases, were it not for the wind aggravating the situation, a medicinal ointment — *sama* — would have allowed the body to heal and survive. Rashi understands *avdei lehu sama v'chayei* as referring to a healing compound that could have restored the body under better conditions.

### Chanina: Cold

Rabbi Chanina says the *choli* is *tzina* — cold. This is likewise consistent with Rabbi Chanina's position elsewhere: *hakol b'yedei Shamayim chutz mi'tzinim pachim* — everything is in the hands of Heaven except for cold drafts. Rabbi Chanina cites the verse *tzinim pachim b'derech ikesh, shomer nafsho yirchak meihem* — thorns and snares lie in the path of the crooked, one who guards his soul will keep away from them.

### Yosi: Excretions

Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina says the *choli* refers to bodily excretions — *tzoah*. He connects this to a ruling that the discharge of the nose and the discharge of the ear are mostly harmful in large quantities, though small amounts may be beneficial: *ruban kashah u'miutan yafeh*.

### Elazar: Bile

Rabbi Elazar says the *choli* is *marah* — bile, the substance produced by the gallbladder. In the ancient medical framework of the four humors, bile was held responsible for a wide range of physical ailments.

### Bile Diseases

A *baraita* is cited in support of Rabbi Elazar's view: *machalah zo marah* — the word *machalah* (illness) in the verse refers specifically to the gallbladder and its bile. Why is *marah* called *machalah* in general? Because *hi machalah kol gufo shel adam* — it afflicts the entire body of a person. A further explanation: *machalah* is used because there are 83 illnesses that depend upon *marah*, stemming from dysfunction of the bile or gallbladder. And all 83 of these illnesses are counteracted by *pat shacharit b'melach v'kiton shel mayim* — morning bread with salt and a jug of water.

---

## Morning Bread Benefits

### First Benefits

The *baraita* continues with a formal enumeration: thirteen beneficial things are said about *pat shacharit* — eating bread in the morning. It protects from the sun (*chamah*), from cold (*tzina*), from harmful winds (*zikin*), and from demons (*mazikin*). It brings wisdom (*machkimat*), success in legal proceedings (*zocheh ba'din*), enables Torah study (*lilmod Torah*), and enables teaching Torah (*lelamed*).

### More Benefits

The remaining benefits: one's words are heard (*devarav nishma'in*), one's learning is retained (*talmudo mitkayem b'yado*), one's body does not produce fever or excess heat (*ein besaro ma'aleh hevel*), one is drawn only to his wife and not to other women (*nizkak l'ishto v'eino mitaveh l'ishah acheret*), and the bread kills intestinal worms (*horeg kinah she'bivnei me'ayim*).

### Jealousy & Love

An additional opinion adds: *af motziah et ha'kinah u'machnisah et ha'ahavah* — morning bread also removes jealousy and brings love.

### Running Speed

Rabbah cites to Rava bar Mari a popular saying: sixty runners cannot catch up to a man who has eaten his morning bread. The idiom expresses the vigor and alertness that *pat shacharit* confers.

### Seasonal Eating

The rabbinic instruction drawn from this is: *hashkem ve'echol bakayitz mipnei ha'chamah u'vahoref mipnei ha'tzina* — rise early and eat in the summer because of the heat, and in the winter because of the cold. Morning bread protects against both extremes.

### Isaiah Source

When Rava bar Mari asks for a scriptural basis, Rabbah cites Isaiah 49:10: *lo yir'avu velo yitzma'u velo yakeim sharav va'shamesh* — they shall not hunger nor thirst, nor shall heat or sun strike them. The *gemara* explains the verse as a chain: the protection from heat and sun is a consequence of not being hungry or thirsty, and not being hungry or thirsty results from eating morning bread — the elements of the verse are mutually dependent.

### Deuteronomy Source

Rava offers a superior scriptural basis from Deuteronomy: *va'avadtem et Hashem Elokeichem u'verach et lachmecha v'et meimecha* — and you shall serve the Lord your God, and He will bless your bread and your water. The *gemara* interprets: *va'avadtem et Hashem Elokeichem* refers to *keriyat shema* and *tefillah*. *U'verach et lachmecha v'et meimecha* refers to bread dipped in salt and a jug of water. The verse then continues: *va'hasiroti machalah mi'kirbecha* — and I will remove illness from among you. The sequence is complete: prayer, then morning bread with salt and water, and God will remove all illness.

### Bread & Salt

The prescription is thus: *pat be'melach v'kiton shel mayim* — bread dipped in salt accompanied by a jug of water, eaten in the morning after *tefillah*. This practice is attested in later *siddur* traditions as well; the Tunisian liturgical tradition, for instance, includes after *shacharit* a passage on *pat shacharit* explicitly citing this *gemara*.

---

## Land Surveying Rules

### Survey Precision

The *gemara* continues with practical land law. Rav Yehuda instructs Rav Adda the surveyor: *lo tizalzel be'mishchata* — do not be careless in your measurements. Every small piece of land matters, because *kol purta u'purta chazi l'churkama de'rishka* — even a tiny parcel could grow saffron, which was among the most expensive commodities of the ancient world.

### Irrigation Zones

However, Rav Yehuda qualifies: the four *amot* around an irrigation channel — *anigra* — may be measured with somewhat less stringency. Rashi explains that this zone within the field actually belongs collectively to the owners of the surrounding parcels, and since they are co-owners of that strip they can effectively waive precise measurement; the matter of a few inches one way or another does not create a wrongful taking.

### River Banks

Regarding rivers, the rule is different: *de'nahara lo timshach klal* — do not measure the river banks at all. Rav Yehuda states the underlying principle: the four *amot* around the irrigation channel belong to the private co-owners of that field system, but the banks of a public river belong to the entire public — *de'nahara de'chulei alma* — and therefore their precise dimensions cannot be treated as anyone's private property to be measured away.

### Barge Path Clearance

Rabbi Ami made a public announcement: vegetation on both sides of a river must be cleared to the width needed for barge-pullers (*nagdei*) to walk while pulling their ropes — *melo kitfei nagdei bi'trei evrei nahara kutzzu*. Barge-pullers needed to walk along the riverbank while towing vessels with long ropes stretched out behind them, and the cleared path had to be wide enough for that purpose.

### Excessive Clearance

Rav Natan bar Sharya took this ruling and cleared sixteen *amot* on each side. The residents of Mashrunya came and struck him for it. He had reasoned that river banks constitute a *reshut ha'rabbim* — public domain — and the standard width of a *reshut ha'rabbim* is sixteen *amot*.

### Public Domain Distinction

The *gemara* rejects his reasoning: *velo hi* — that is incorrect. In a standard public thoroughfare, sixteen *amot* are required because people need that width to move through freely. On a riverbank, the requirement is functional rather than fixed: *mishum amtuchei ashleihen hu* — the purpose is for barge-pullers to stretch out their towing ropes, and *melo kitfei nagdei sagi* — the width of the barge-pullers' shoulders is sufficient. The principle is that even within the category of public space, different functional needs generate different physical requirements.

### Neighbor Coordination

Rabba bar Rav Huna owned a forest on the side of a river. When told he must clear his portion, he responded: *kutzzu ila'i ve'tata'i va'hadar nikutz ana* — let those above and below me on the river clear their portions first, and then I will clear mine.

### Self-First Principle

This was challenged on the basis of Resh Lakish's principle: *hitkosheshu va'koshu* — the verse says gather yourselves and gather, interpreted as *kshot atzmecha ve'achar kach kshot acherim* — adorn yourself first and then attend to others. One is obligated to fulfill one's own duty without waiting for others to fulfill theirs. If clearing the riverbank is required, Rabba bar Rav Huna cannot condition his compliance on his neighbors' prior compliance.

### Practical Exception

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty: *aba de'vei Parzak Rofila hava* — the land adjacent to Rabba bar Rav Huna's forest belonged to a man named Parzak, who was a military general. Parzak had made clear that he would clear his side only if Rabba bar Rav Huna cleared his first — but in reality, Parzak was not going to do it regardless. In this specific circumstance, Rabba bar Rav Huna's clearing alone would have been pointless: *de'ei mamtu lehu ashleihu masgei lehu* — if there is enough space on the other side for the barge-pullers to stretch their ropes, the path will function. *Ve'ei lo, lo masgei lehu* — and if there is not, the barge-pullers will remain on whichever side of the river has a workable path and will not cross to Rabba bar Rav Huna's side simply because he cleared a portion. Clearing his section in isolation would accomplish nothing for the public benefit the rule is meant to serve — and therefore it was reasonable to withhold compliance under those particular conditions.

This brings the *daf* to 108a.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 108

## Forest & River

### Hitkoshshu Vakoshu

The *daf* opens with a case that actually begins five lines from the bottom of the previous page. Rabba bar Rav Huna owned a forest situated on the bank of a river. The public came to him and said that he ought to cut down the vegetation along the riverbank, since people needed that cleared space to pull their barges along the shore. Rabba bar Rav Huna refused, saying: let the people above me and below me cut first, and then I will follow suit.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this stance: how could he do that? Does not the verse teach *hitkoshshu vakoshu* — gather yourselves and then gather others — and did not Reish Lakish interpret this to mean *kesshot atzmecha ve'achar kach kesshot acheirim*, adorn yourself first and only then concern yourself with others? On this reading, Rabba bar Rav Huna had no business demanding that others act before him.

The *gemara* answers that the situation was exceptional. The other portion of the forest along that stretch of river was owned by a man named Parzak, a Persian military official. The principle of *hitkoshshu vakoshu* presupposes that one's own action will influence or prompt others to do the same. Rabba bar Rav Huna had no leverage over Parzak; he could not expect a Persian general to follow his lead. Furthermore, the opposite bank of the river was already fully cleared, and bargemen were using that side without difficulty. If he cut down his portion on this side, the cleared strip would remain isolated — the bargemen would have no reason to cross to his side for a mere forty feet of cleared bank. His portion, in practical terms, served no public purpose unless the entire stretch was cleared, and since he had no ability to compel Parzak, he was justified in waiting.

### Curse & Consequences

Rabba bar Rav Nachman was traveling by boat when he spotted a forest whose riverbank had not been cleared. He asked whose it was and was told it belonged to Rabba bar Rav Huna. Displeased, he quoted the verse: *yad hasarim vehasganim hayta bamaal haze rishona* — the hand of the officers and the ministers was foremost in this act of unfaithfulness. He then instructed those present: cut it down, cut it down.

When Rabba bar Rav Huna returned and found that the forest had been cut, he was furious. He declared: whoever cut this down — may his branches be cut off. Rashi explains that "branches" here refers to his children. The *gemara* records that throughout the lifetime of Rabba bar Rav Huna, none of the children of Rabba bar Rav Nachman survived.

### Equity & Justice

This is a striking passage. The underlying legal position of Rabba bar Rav Huna was sound — he had genuinely demonstrated why his particular circumstances exempted him from the otherwise applicable obligation to clear the riverbank. Yet the response to having that clearing done against his will was a curse with devastating consequences. The *gemara* does not explain the severity of the reaction. It is worth noting that such extreme outcomes appear in other Talmudic narratives as well, and no clean resolution of the equitable tension is offered. The narrative simply stands.

One question that arises is about the involvement of Rabba bar Rav Nachman himself. He was also a rabbinic leader — a *sar* or *sagan* in the sense invoked by the verse he cited. The verse *yad hasarim vehasganim* was presumably being applied to Rabba bar Rav Huna, yet it was directed at him by another leader. The *gemara* is silent on this tension as well.

There is also a broader point about what is at stake in this passage. The space along the riverbank was not quite a *reshut harabbim* in the classic legal sense — a true *reshut harabbim* is a thoroughfare to which the public has free passage in all directions. The riverbank was something different, more like a zone that functions publicly without technically being *hefker*. Nonetheless, the underlying issue is a communal one: what obligations does private ownership create in spaces that the public depends upon?

## Public Works

### Wall & Gate

This communal theme continues with a statement of Rav Yehuda regarding a city wall and its gate. Rav Yehuda rules that everyone is obligated to participate in repairing the city wall and gate — *ha-kol le-iglei gappa* — including orphans, who are typically exempt from many communal obligations. Rabbis, however, are exempt. The reason given is that *rabbanan lo tzerikhei netiruta*: the rabbis do not require protection. The implication is that divine protection attends Torah scholars, rendering the physical security of the wall irrelevant to them.

This may appear inequitable — the scholars surely benefit from the wall's protection along with everyone else. Within the metaphysical assumptions of the *gemara*, however, the exemption is internally coherent: the obligation to share in the construction of a communal security infrastructure is tied to benefiting from it, and if the rabbis genuinely do not depend on it for their safety, it would be inequitable to require them to contribute. The analogy to other contexts where *talmidei chachamim* enjoy exemptions from marketplace obligations or public levies is instructive: sometimes the reason is their benefit to the community through Torah, sometimes their dignity, and sometimes, as here, the argument that they simply do not require what the obligation is designed to provide.

### Water Sources

Water sources, however, are treated differently. Rav Yehuda rules that for repairing a *ma'ayan* — a spring or water source — even the rabbis must contribute: *va-afilu me-rabbanan*. The qualification is that this applies only when the work is being done by hiring others to perform it. The rabbis are not people who go out themselves as part of a labor force — *rabbanan lav bnei meipak be-akhloza ninhu* — it is beneath their dignity to join a work crew for physical labor. But they do pay their share of the cost of hiring others. This is consistent with a recurring pattern throughout *Nezikin* where rabbinic exemptions pertain to personal participation in labor but not to financial contribution.

The asymmetry between different public works obligations thus maps onto a coherent underlying principle. Physical security through walls and gates: rabbis exempt entirely, because they do not need it. Water infrastructure: rabbis contribute financially, because the water is something they genuinely depend upon.

Rav Yehuda further articulates the asymmetry *within* the water infrastructure itself. When the obligation involves dredging a river or maintaining an irrigation channel — *kharaya denahara* — the *tattai*, those lower on the irrigation chain, must help the *ilai*, those at the upper end. The reverse does not hold: the *ilai* need not help the *tattai* with the portions of the channel that serve only those below. This seems unequal, but the *gemara* balances it with the opposite rule for rainwater drainage: when the concern is getting runoff out of the city, the *ilai* — those higher on the hill — must help the *tattai* at the drainage outlet, because if the exit point at the bottom of the city is blocked, everyone's drainage backs up.
