The people at the very top of the hill, however, are solely responsible for clearing their own portion at the summit, since a blockage there affects only them. The two systems together produce a rough equity: each party bears obligations in one direction that they do not bear in the other.

### Braita on Water

A *braita* confirms this teaching, and it is worth noting that this particular *braita* is unusual for a *tanya nami hachi* passage. Such passages typically introduce a *tannaitic* source whose wording is virtually identical to the Amoraic statement just given — a feature that has made academic scholars suspicious of many such *braitot*, since they often appear only in the Bavli and not in the Tosefta or Yerushalmi. Here, the teaching is the same, but the language of the *braita* differs from Rav Yehuda's formulation.

The *braita* states: five gardens that draw water from a single *ma'ayan* — if the spring is damaged, all five must help repair the portion used by the uppermost field, and the lowermost field must help repair every portion of the channel, but bears sole responsibility for maintaining the final stretch that serves only itself. The analogous rule for drainage runs in reverse: five courtyards that drain into a single channel — if the channel fails, all must help repair the section leading out from the lowermost courtyard, while the uppermost courtyard must help with every section but is alone responsible for its own portion at the top.

## Riverbank Rights

### Shmuel's Rule

Returning to the question of riverbank ownership, Shmuel establishes the following rule: one who takes control — *achzik* — of a riverbank has acted brazenly, *chatsifei havei*, but we do not remove him, *siluki lo mesalkinan lei*. According to the commentators, "taking control" here refers specifically to paying the head tax to the Persian authorities on a piece of land, which confers a degree of legal standing under Persian law even without proper title under Jewish law. The riverbank is a zone the public depends upon, so occupying it is *chutzpadik* — but the rabbis do not forcibly evict the person who has done so.

### Persian Contract

A later development, however, changes this. Once the Persians introduced — or once the Jewish community adopted — a standard contract formulation granting the landowner rights to the riverbank up to the point where a horse is neck-deep in water, the legal landscape shifted. The riverbank is now definitively part of the adjacent landowner's domain. If someone else comes and attempts to occupy or take control of that strip, we do not merely call it brazen — we also remove him. *Siluki nami mesalkinan lei.*

### Brothers & Partners

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav applies a similar structure to land taken from among brothers or among partners. Such a taking is also *chatsifei havei* — it is improper — but Rav holds that we do not remove the person who has done it. Rav Nachman disagrees: we do remove such a person.

### Nahardai & Verse

The *gemara* then introduces the position of the *Nahardai*: even in cases of *dina de-bar metsara* — the neighbor's right of first refusal, which is the subject of the remainder of the *daf* — we remove the interloper. Their basis is the verse *ve'asita hayashar vehatov be'einei Hashem*, "you shall do what is good and upright in the eyes of God." It is this verse that provides the scriptural underpinning for the entire institution of *dina de-bar metsara*.

## Bar Metzra Basics

### Definition & Basis

The *metsara* is literally the border mound that separates two fields. The *bar metsara* — the one who owns the adjacent field — has a privileged claim when the owner of the central field wishes to sell. The basis, as the *Nahardai* cited, is the verse *ve'asita hayashar vehatov*: the *chachamim* interpreted the obligation to do what is good and upright to include giving the neighboring landowner the right of first refusal when one's land comes up for sale. The rule operates with real teeth: if a landowner sells to a third party — a *lokeach* from elsewhere — without offering the land to his neighbor, the neighbor has the right to approach the *lokeach*, pay him what he paid, and take the field. The *lokeach*, in the framework by which this is explained, was acting as the agent of the neighbor when he purchased, which is how the neighbor gains the ability to simply hand over the money and assume ownership.

### Kicking Off

The mechanism by which the neighbor asserts his right is straightforward: he comes to the *lokeach*, pays the price that was paid, and the *lokeach* must leave. The neighbor does not need to go back to the original seller; he takes the land directly from the *lokeach* by reimbursing him.

### Kinyan Required

A question arises when the *lokeach* — before purchasing — approaches the neighboring *bar metsara* and asks whether it is acceptable to proceed. The neighbor says: go ahead and buy. Does this permission eliminate the neighbor's right, or must the neighbor still perform a formal *kinyan* to extinguish his claim?

Ravina holds that no *kinyan* is required — the permission is sufficient. The *Nahardai* hold that a *kinyan* is required. The *gemara* concludes: *ve-hilkheta tzarich lemiknei minei* — the *halacha* follows the *Nahardai*, a formal *kinyan* is needed.

Rashi explains the reasoning: without a *kinyan*, the neighbor can claim *mashti hayiti bach* — I was not being serious. The neighbor retains the right to say his permission was merely casual or even joking, not a legally operative waiver. By contrast, if the *lokeach* has already purchased and the neighbor subsequently signals acceptance without having been asked in advance, no such ambiguity applies — the purchase is done, and the neighbor's acquiescence is unambiguous. As the *Rambam* notes, if one purchased already and the neighbor then concedes, the neighbor's right is extinguished without need for a *kinyan*.

## Bar Metzra Pricing

### Below Market

Once we have established that a *kinyan* is required and that — if it has not been performed — the neighbor can assert his right, we turn to the question of price. If the *lokeach* purchased the field for a hundred *zuz* when it was worth two hundred, we first evaluate whether the below-market price was available to anyone. If the seller was offering the land at half price to the general public — perhaps he needed to leave quickly and was liquidating everything at a discount — then when the neighbor comes to assert his right and displace the *lokeach*, he pays only a hundred: *yehav lei me'ah ve-shakil lei*. He takes the land at the same discounted price the *lokeach* received.

### Above Market

The opposite case: the *lokeach* paid two hundred for a field worth only one hundred. Presumably the seller and the *lokeach* had a special relationship, and part of what the *lokeach* paid was effectively a gift in the guise of an inflated purchase price. When the neighbor now seeks to assert his right and displace the *lokeach*, he must pay two hundred — the full amount the *lokeach* actually paid — since the *lokeach* genuinely parted with that sum and cannot be left worse off.

### No Ona'ah

What is the principled basis for these rules? Mar Kashisha, son of Rav Chisda, cites the position of the *Nahardai* in the name of Rav Nachman: *ein ona'ah le-karka'ot* — the law of *ona'ah*, price fraud or overcharge, does not apply to real estate. Because real estate is not subject to *ona'ah*, the price paid — whatever it is — becomes the operative value of the transaction. The neighbor therefore pays whatever the *lokeach* actually paid, whether above or below the apparent market rate, since that is the legally recognized price of the land.

## Bar Metzra Exceptions

### Strip in Middle

Having established the general contours of *dina de-bar metsara*, the *gemara* turns to the many situations in which it does not apply. The first involves a strip of land sold from the interior of a field. If I sell a narrow strip located in the middle of my holdings — not along the outer edge — we examine whether that strip is distinct in quality from the surrounding land. If it is of particularly high quality (*idit*) or particularly poor quality (*ziburit*), then *zavina zavina* — the sale stands without issue, as the strip is genuinely separate in character from the rest of the field. But if the strip is identical in quality to the surrounding land, the sale is characterized as *ha'aramah* — a circumvention — and is not permitted. The reason: by purchasing an undifferentiated strip in the middle of someone's field, the buyer becomes a *bar metsara* with respect to the land on both sides, and could then use that newly acquired right of first refusal to systematically buy up the entire field in stages, bypassing the original neighbors who should have had priority. When the strip is qualitatively distinct, no such mechanism is available, and the sale is entirely legitimate.

### Gifts

A gift (*matanah*) to a third party is not subject to *dina de-bar metsara*. I may give my land to whomever I choose; the neighbor has no right of first refusal over a gift, because *dina de-bar metsara* is predicated on the framework of sale. However, if the "gift" comes with conditions or is accompanied by a contract that includes *achrayut* — provisions establishing certain ongoing obligations or guarantees about the property — Rashi notes that such a transaction is not truly a *matanah* and may not enjoy this exemption.

### All Properties

If I sell all of my properties at once to a single buyer — *machar kol nekhasav le-echad* — *dina de-bar metsara* does not apply, even if one of those properties happens to be adjacent to a neighbor who would otherwise have the right of first refusal.

Rashi explains: the properties may be located in different places — one in the east, one in the west. If a neighbor of one of them comes and objects, the *chachamim* did not institute *dina de-bar metsara* in a way that would require the *lokeach* to step aside and allow the neighbor to purchase just that one parcel, because doing so would harm the seller. The seller may be unable to sell the bundle without that piece, or he may be leaving and needs to liquidate everything together. The principle of *ve'asita hayashar vehatov* cuts both ways: we must do right by the seller as well as by the neighbor. If honoring the neighbor's right of first refusal causes a genuine loss to the seller — preventing him from completing a package sale — then the *takkanah* of *bar metsara* was never meant to reach that far. Even so, where it is genuinely possible to sell one parcel separately without harming the seller, it may still be preferable to offer the neighbor that opportunity. There is simply no *chiyuv* compelling it.

### Non-Jewish Party

When either party to the transaction is a non-Jew, *dina de-bar metsara* does not apply — but for different reasons depending on the direction of the sale. If a Jew buys land from a non-Jew (*zavan me-akum*), the Jewish buyer can say to the original neighbor: *arya avrakhi lach mimitzerach* — I have driven a lion away from your border. The non-Jewish neighbor was no asset; the incoming Jewish owner is presumably preferable. If a Jew sells to a non-Jew (*zavin le-akum*), the basis for *dina de-bar metsara* is a positive obligation of the Torah — *ve'asita hayashar vehatov* — which does not apply to non-Jews. The non-Jewish buyer is simply not subject to the framework in which *ve'asita hayashar vehatov* operates.

Nevertheless, one who sells to a non-Jew is placed in a form of *cherem* — a communal sanction — until he accepts full responsibility for any harm that comes to his Jewish neighbor as a result of having a non-Jew installed in that adjacent property.

### Mortgaged Property

Mortgaged property (*mashkanta*) is similarly exempt from *dina de-bar metsara*. Rav Ashi cites the elders of Mata Mechasya for a reason embedded in the very word: *mashkanta* derives from the same root as *shachen* — neighbor — because the mortgagee is treated as though he were already the neighbor. The practical implication for *dina de-bar metsara* is that the mortgagee has the status of a *bar metsara* himself.

### Distant or Bad Land

Selling distant land in order to purchase closer land, or selling poor-quality land (*ziburit*) in order to purchase superior land (*idit*), is also exempt from *dina de-bar metsara*. Rashi explains: if the seller is compelled to sell because the land is far away and wishes to consolidate holdings closer to home, the *chachamim* did not institute *bar metsara* in a way that would cause the seller a loss. The entire basis of *dina de-bar metsara* is *ve'asita hayashar vehatov* — doing what is equitable. Equity requires that we not compel the seller to forgo a transaction that genuinely serves his interests. As Rashi formulates it: just as we must do right by the neighbor, so too we must do right by the seller. When the two conflict, neither consideration automatically overrides the other, and in this case the seller's need to improve or consolidate his holdings takes precedence.

### Necessary Costs

Three categories of financial necessity also eliminate the right of first refusal: *l'karga*, *le-mezonei*, *u-likvura* — to pay the head tax, to provide for those one is obligated to support, and to cover burial costs.

These three categories each invoke a different dimension of obligation. *Karga* — the poll tax owed to the ruling authorities — is a personal financial obligation imposed by the external political order. *Mezonei* — food and support for dependents — derives from contractual and rabbinic obligations, falling within the domain of family law. *Kvura* — the burial of the dead — invokes a religious and ritual obligation that operates on a more fundamental level, one that all are bound by to some degree.

The source for all three is the *Nahardai*, who state: for *karga*, *mezonei*, and *kvura* we sell without making a public announcement (*achrazta*). The normal requirement to publicize an impending sale — which gives the neighbor the opportunity to exercise the right of first refusal — is suspended when one of these three pressing needs is the occasion for the sale.

### Woman & Orphans

Selling to a woman, to orphans, or to partners is also exempt from *dina de-bar metsara*, though again the reasons differ. Rashi and the *Rambam* both explain the exemption for a woman by noting that in the social context in which these *takkanot* were formulated, it was not customary (*orach ar'a*) for a woman to venture out and negotiate for the best available land. The presumption is that a woman would simply purchase the first suitable land she found; requiring her to yield to a neighbor's right of first refusal would be unreasonably burdensome in her circumstances. The exemption for orphans rests on a simple principle of *chesed* — it would simply not be kind to deprive orphans of the opportunity to acquire property by requiring them to step aside for a neighbor.

## Priority Rules

### Hierarchy

Stepping back from the specific rules of *bar metsara*, the *gemara* addresses the broader question of priority among competing claimants. A resident of the same city as the seller has priority over someone who lives in a more distant field: *shechina de-mata kodem*. Between a neighbor and a *talmid chacham*, the *talmid chacham* takes priority. Between a relative and a *talmid chacham*, the *talmid chacham* again takes priority.

### Neighbor vs. Relative

The question then arises: what about a neighbor versus a relative, when no *talmid chacham* is involved? The *gemara* brings a verse from Mishlei: *tov shachen karov me-ach rachok* — a near neighbor is better than a distant brother. The neighbor takes priority over the relative.

### Payment Terms

The quality and type of currency offered can also create differentiation among competing claimants. If one person offers coins of superior quality (*tavei*) and another offers heavier or more cumbersome coins (*tekulei*), there is no issue of *dina de-bar metsara* — the seller may accept the better payment and is not compelled to defer to the neighbor. Similarly, if one person offers minted coins and another offers unminted metal, the distinction in payment form can override the neighbor's priority. These distinctions are likely of limited practical relevance today, where currency is standardized, though one might imagine analogous issues arising with payment in different currencies or non-standard instruments.

The *bar metsara* also has no right to request a waiting period in which to gather funds. If the neighbor says *izil ve-aitei zuzei* — let me go and bring the money — we do not wait for him: *lo natrinan lei*. The right of first refusal means the right to purchase *now*, not the right to hold the sale open while one arranges financing. This is not merely a practical constraint; it reflects the structure of the *takkanah* itself. The obligation of *ve'asita hayashar vehatov* was never intended to prevent the seller from completing a timely transaction. Requiring the seller to wait imposes a loss on him, and *bar metsara* was instituted precisely in cases where doing right by the neighbor causes no loss to the seller.

### Capability Test

The *gemara* does, however, recognize a middle case. If the neighbor says not merely that he wants to find money, but specifically *izil, ve-tarach, ve-aitei zuzei* — I am going to go, make an effort, and bring the money — then we look at the circumstances: *chazinan*. If this is a person who is genuinely likely to be able to produce the funds — *gavra de-amid hu* — we wait for him. If he is not such a person, we do not wait. The determination is practical: is this a realistic claim or a stalling tactic? The answer guides whether a brief waiting period is granted.

## Buildings & Trees

### Building on Land

A distinct set of issues concerns the relationship between ownership of land and ownership of structures or plants sitting on that land. It was evidently a common situation in the Talmudic world for buildings to stand on land not owned by the building's occupants. When such a property comes up for sale, the owner of the land can prevent the owner of the building from selling the building to a third party — the landowner has a form of *bar metsara* interest in the building, since ideally his building should sit on his own land. But the owner of the building cannot prevent the landowner from selling the land; the building owner is not the landowner's *bar metsara* and has no recognized interest that overrides the landowner's freedom to convey his property.

### Trees on Land

The same principle applies to trees. The landowner can prevent the tree owner from selling the trees on his land to another party, but the tree owner cannot prevent the landowner from selling the land itself.

### Residential Priority

Finally, if a seller has a choice between conveying land to a buyer who will use it for residential development and one who will use it for agriculture, the residential use takes priority: *yishuv adif*. Furthermore, there is no issue of *dina de-bar metsara* in such a case. Rashi explains: *yishuv de-vattei adif le-didin* — residential settlement is of greater benefit. It is not simply a matter of one good being preferred over another comparable good; it is rather that providing homes for people is a greater contribution to the settlement of the land (*yishuv ha'aretz*) than additional cultivation. When the two goods are genuinely unequal in this way, the framework of *ve'asita hayashar vehatov* does not compel giving the neighbor right of first refusal over the superior outcome.

## Physical Separation

### Natural Fence

With the foundational rules of *dina de-bar metsara* established, the *gemara* closes by addressing when a person qualifies as a *bar metsara* at all. The question arises when there is a physical barrier — a *piska mishnita* (a row of stones) or a *richba de-dikla* (a row of palm trees) — separating the neighbor's field from the field being sold. Does the neighbor still qualify as a *bar metsara*?

The answer depends on whether the barrier can be penetrated for even a single furrow of planting: *chazinan i yachil le-hachnis bah afilu telem echad*. If the neighbor can plant even one row through or past the barrier — establishing that his field is in practical agricultural continuity with the adjacent field — then *dina de-bar metsara* applies. The justification for *bar metsara* is precisely that the neighbor wishes to extend his rows of planting into the adjacent field; if that extension is even minimally possible despite the barrier, his priority right survives. If it is not possible, the barrier creates a genuine agricultural discontinuity, and the neighbor has no right of first refusal.

### Multiple Neighbors

A final case: four neighbors, one on each side of a field being sold. If one of the four arrives first and purchases — *kadim chad minaihu ve-zaven* — the sale stands and he has prevailed. Priority goes to the first to act. If all four arrive simultaneously — *i kulhu atu ba-hadi hadadi* — the field is divided among them diagonally, *palgu lah be-karneizil*, yielding four triangular portions, one for each neighbor. Rashi provides a small diagram in the margin illustrating the diagonal division, which appears in most standard editions of the *gemara*.

With that, the *gemara*'s treatment of *dina de-bar metsara* concludes.

# Bava Metzia 109

## Choker & Shatla Intro

### Kablan vs. Choker

Daf 109 opens by returning from the discussion of *bar metzra* to the laws of *sechirut* — renting land. This daf introduces not only the *choker* but a new figure who will occupy much of the subsequent discussion: the *shatla*, the planter. We have previously encountered the *kablan*, who rents land at a fixed ratio of the produce, and the *choker*, who rents for a fixed sum regardless of yield. The two figures operate under meaningfully different legal frameworks, and that distinction drives the opening *mishnah*. The *shatla*, by contrast, is not a renter in the traditional sense at all — he is hired specifically to plant, receives compensation in a particular form, and if he breaks his contract, distinct rules govern what he owes and what he may claim.

### Flax & Sycamore Restrict…

The *mishnah* begins: *ha-mekabel sadeh me-chavero le-shanim mu'atot* — one who rents land from another *be-chakirut*, at a fixed cost, for a small number of years. Rashi explains, and the *seifa* of the *mishnah* confirms, that *shanim mu'atot* means fewer than seven years. Such a renter *lo yizra bah pishtan* — may not plant flax. The reason, as Rashi explains, is that *pishtan* damages the soil. This restriction also proves, according to Rashi, that the *mishnah* is discussing a *choker* rather than a *kablan*: a *kablan* who rents at a fixed ratio of produce has already agreed with the landowner on what to plant. As we saw in an earlier *mishnah*, a *kablan* may not substitute a crop that is worse for the land than the one contracted — *ha-mekabel sadeh me-chavero lizroa chitin lo yizra'enah se'orin, lizroa se'orin lo yizra'enah chitin* — but may substitute something less harmful. Flax, being harmful to the soil, would be permissible for a *kablan* who expressly contracted for it. Since the *mishnah* prohibits it without qualification, it must be addressing the *choker* who pays a fixed rent.

The *mishnah* further rules: *ve-ein lo be-kurot shikmah* — this short-term *choker* has no rights to the wood produced by the sycamore trees on the property. The particular sycamore common in *Eretz Yisrael* would regularly regenerate after being cut for its wood, but the regrowth cycle takes seven years. That biological fact underlies the entire framework that follows.

### Seven-Year Rental Rules

If the rental is for a full seven-year period, the calculus changes. *Shanah rishonah yizra'enah pishtan* — in the first year, the renter may plant flax, because over a seven-year lease the soil will recover before the land reverts to the owner. *Ve-yesh lo be-kurot shikmah* — and implicitly, in that first year, the renter may also cut the sycamore and use its wood for building, because by the end of his lease the trees will have regenerated to the state they were in at the outset.

---

## Sycamore Overgrowth Deba…

### Abaye: Gets Shevach

The *gemara* opens with Abaye's comment on the *mishnah*: *be-kurot shikmah ein lo* — correct, the short-term renter has no right to the normal wood of the sycamore. *Be-shevach shikmah yesh lo* — but if the sycamore grows beyond the expected amount, that excess growth is his. The *tenai* of the rental, Abaye reasons, was that he would have no rights to the ordinary growth of the sycamore; the excess, however, was not part of that agreement, and he has a claim to compensation for it.

### Rava: No Shevach

Rava disagrees: *afilu be-shevach shikmah ein lo* — even for the excess growth, the renter receives nothing.

### Vegetables Counterargume…

The *gemara* attempts to refute Rava from a *baraita*: *ha-mekabel sadeh me-chavero ve-higi'a zemano latzet, shamin lo* — when a renter's time to leave arrives, an evaluation is made of what is owed to him. The *gemara* asks: does this not mean that we evaluate the excess growth of the sycamore trees, refuting Rava? The *gemara* deflects: *lo, shamin lo yarak u-silka* — no, the evaluation is made for vegetables growing on the property. But this prompts an immediate question: why evaluate vegetables at all? Vegetables can simply be taken and sold — *yarka ve-ashla na'akor venishtakar*. Why is an evaluation (*shimin lo*) necessary?

### Unripe Vegetables

The answer is *d'lo matei yoma d'shuka* — the vegetables are not yet ready for market, either because market day has not arrived or because they are not yet ripe. Since the renter cannot simply take them along, the *beit din* evaluates their worth and the owner compensates him accordingly. The first attempted refutation of Rava thus fails.

### Shvi'it Attempt

A second attempt is made: *ha-mekabel sadeh me-chavero ve-higi'ah Shvi'it, shamin lo* — if the *shemitah* year arrives during a rental, an evaluation is made. This too seems to prove that a renter is owed some assessed value upon having to vacate. But the *gemara* rejects this proof as well: *Shvi'it mi ka mafkat ara'a?* — the sabbatical year does not remove the land from the renter's possession. He still holds the rental; *shemitah* merely prohibits working the land. There is no *din* of *shemitah* that requires the renter to depart, and so this proof cannot establish anything about the evaluation owed to a departing renter.

### Yovel Proof

The *gemara* corrects itself: the *baraita* must actually read *ve-higi'ah Yovel* — the Jubilee year — not *Shvi'it*. When *Yovel* arrives, an evaluation is made for the renter. Now the question becomes: *Yovel mi mafkat kablanu?* — does the Jubilee year actually undo a rental agreement? The *gemara* clarifies: *litzmitut amar Rachmana* — the Torah's rule of *Yovel* applies to land sold *litzmitut*, permanently. The verses describing *Yovel* pertain only to outright sales, not to rentals. Therefore the *baraita* cannot be about a *mekabel* at all — it must be about *halokeach sedei chaveiro ve-higi'ah Yovel* — one who purchased a field, whose ownership *Yovel* does undo. And the evaluation made upon *Yovel* must be for the *shevach shikmah* — the excess growth of the sycamore — not for vegetables, because *silka ve-yarka be-Yovel hefkeira hu* — during *Yovel*, vegetables are *hefker*, ownerless, belonging to all; an evaluation of something that belongs to no one is meaningless. The *baraita* thus appears to require compensating the departing buyer for the excess sycamore growth, directly contradicting Rava's position that *afilu shevach ein lo*.

### Yovel Is Exceptional

Abaye himself resolves the difficulty on behalf of Rava: *shani hatam* — *Yovel* is different. *De-amar kra ve-yatza bi-memkar* — the verse says the land "goes out" from the sale. *Memkar chozer, shevach eino chozer* — the sale itself reverts, but the added value does not revert with it. The Torah establishes a special rule that when *Yovel* undoes a sale, the buyer retains compensation for the *shevach* he caused. This is a particular *din* anchored in explicit verses and in the unique nature of *Yovel* — *afki'ata de-malka hi* — God simply overrides the buyer's ownership — and it is further confined to full sales, *zevina me'alya*.

One might then ask: even if *Yovel* has this particular rule, why can we not derive from it a general principle that applies also to renters? *Ve-nigmar minei* — let us learn from *Yovel* that a renter is also owed *shevach*. The *gemara* rejects this as well: *hatam zevina me'alya hu* — that is a full sale, a fundamentally different transaction. *Yovel* is an exceptional divine decree applicable to a singular category, and one cannot extend its particular rules to the ordinary case of rental. Rava's position — *afilu be-shevach shikmah ein lo* — therefore survives all three attempted refutations.

---

## Rav Pappa Alfalfa Case

### Trees on Alfalfa Field

The *gemara* now shifts to a series of practical cases exploring the boundaries of *shevach* claims. *Rav Pappa kabil ar'a le-asasta* — Rav Pappa once rented land to plant alfalfa, fodder for animals. *Karchu bah talei* — trees sprouted unexpectedly on the land during his tenancy. When his lease ended, *amar lehu havu li shivcha* — he said, give me the excess value for these trees. His argument: he had not contracted for trees, yet they grew during his semi-ownership of the property, and he is entitled to compensation for them.

### Palm Tree Hypothetical

Rav Shisha son of Rav Idi challenged him: *ela me'ata dikla be-alma, hachi nami devayei mar shevcha?* — by that reasoning, if you had rented land to grow palm trees and they grew more than expected, would you also demand *shevach* for the excess growth of the palms?

### Short vs. Long-Term Inte…

Rav Pappa draws a distinction. *Hatam lav ada'ata dehachi nachit ana* — in that case, if I had rented land to grow palms and they grew more than expected, that was never my intent; I rented to get the fruit. *Hacha ada'ata dehachi nachitna* — here, my purpose in renting was to plant things and cultivate growth. The assumption underlying my agreement was that new growth occurring during my tenancy would accrue to me, and these sprouting trees represent exactly that. The *gemara* notes that this position appears consistent with Abaye's, which raises a difficulty — we generally do not rule like Abaye against Rava in matters of *halacha*. The *gemara* deflects: *afilu teima ke-Rava* — one may read Rav Pappa's position as consistent with Rava as well. *Hatam leit leh pseida* — in the original case of the *mishnah*, Rava held that the renter gets no *shevach* because no loss accrued to him from the sycamore's presence; the sycamore was always there. *Hacha ika pseida* — here there is a loss, because land was occupied by these sprouting trees where alfalfa could have been planted.

The *gemara* presses: what exactly is the loss? *Mai pseidatich?* — the land was rented for alfalfa, you planted your alfalfa, what is the damage? *Shkul yada depasti ve-zil* — take whatever alfalfa is on the property now and leave. Alfalfa is apparently planted and harvested monthly; why cannot he simply take what remains?

### Saffron Loss Proof

At this point Rav Pappa reveals: *ana karkuma rishka ravai* — I did not actually grow alfalfa; I grew saffron, a high-value crop. The *gemara* responds: *galeita da'atach d'lemishkal u-leistalukei avadt* — by saying that, you have disclosed that your entire intent was to plant something short-lived, something you would harvest and leave. *Shevach* accrues on the assumption that the renter was planting things with longevity, investments that extend beyond the term of his tenancy and yield value that belongs partly to him. But a crop that is grown and taken within a short cycle — where the renter never intended to leave anything of lasting value in the ground — generates no such entitlement. *Shkul karkuma rishka ve-zil, ein lach ela dmei etzim bilvad* — take your saffron and go; you are owed nothing for these new trees except their value as firewood. The distinction matters: the assessed future value of a growing sapling, including its eventual fruit, would be far greater than its firewood value. But since the renter's entire orientation was toward short-term, annually harvested crops, he forfeits any claim to the long-term appreciation and is limited to *dmei etzim*, the value of the trees as raw wood.

### Rav Bibi Hedge Case

A parallel case: *Rav Bibi bar Abaye kabal ar'a ve-hadar lah mishunita* — Rav Bibi bar Abaye rented land and a hedge or stone border formed around it. *Kadchu bei zaradta* — some small plants grew up among the stones along the border. When his tenancy ended, *amar lehu hav li shvachai* — he claimed the excess value of these border plants. Rav Pappa dismisses the claim sharply. Even Rav Pappa's own ruling — that *shevach* is owed when there is a genuine *pseida* — was limited to cases where the new growth actually caused a loss by occupying space where the renter wanted to plant. *Hacha mai pseida is lach?* — here there is no such loss. The plants grew along the stone border, not within the cultivated field, and caused the renter no damage whatsoever. His claim to *shevach* for those plants therefore fails entirely.

---

## Shatla & Inheritance

### Five Sons-in-Law Problem

The *gemara* presents a case involving Rav Yosef. *Rav Yosef hava lei hahu shatla* — Rav Yosef once employed a *shatla*, a planter. *Shachiv ve-shavik chamsha chatnavata* — the planter died and left behind five sons-in-law as his inheritors. Rav Yosef's reaction captures his practical concern: *ad hashta chad, hashta chamsha* — until now I had one; now I have five. The problem is not merely numerical. *Ad hashta lo havu samchu ahadadi ve-lo masdu li* — with only one worker, that individual relied on himself and a loss to Rav Yosef was unlikely. *Hashta chamsha samchu ahadadi ve-masdu li* — with five sons-in-law, they will rely on one another, no one will take full responsibility, and Rav Yosef anticipates real damage to his property.

### Shevach Offer

Rav Yosef presents them with two options: *ei shaklitu shvacha u-mistalkitu* — if you take the *shevach*, the value that accrued to the land through your father-in-law's work, and leave, *mutav* — that is agreeable to him. *Ve-ei lo, mesalikna lechu bela shvacha* — if not, he claims the right to remove them without paying anything. He frames this as a generous offer: the good option is take the money and go; the bad option, which he claims is also legally available to him, is to evict them empty-handed.

### Rav Yehuda Citation

To support the threat, Rav Yosef invokes an authority: *de-amar Rav Yehuda* — and perhaps it was said in the name of Rav Huna or Rav Nachman — *hai shatla de-shachiv, yorshim dilei mistalkim lehu bela shvacha* — when a planter dies, his heirs are removed without receiving any *shevach*.

### Rav Yehuda Clarified

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *ve-lav milta hi* — that is not actually a correct statement of law. Rav Yehuda apparently never said anything so sweeping. His actual ruling was considerably more limited, and Rav Yosef was extending it beyond its scope in order to intimidate the sons-in-law into accepting the settlement offer. The *rishonim* are explicit: Rivan on 29b explains that Rav Yosef never actually said this as a rule; he said it *le-hafchidan* — to frighten them into accepting the *shevach* and departing quietly. The Rosh in *siman* 37 cites this explanation as well, and the Ramban grounds it in a *tosefta* that circumscribes the scope of Rav Yehuda's actual ruling. Had only one of the five sons-in-law presented himself and asked to continue working, Rav Yosef would have been obligated to accept him; the multiplicity of heirs created a legitimate basis for some form of objection, but not for outright denial of any *shevach*.

---

## Loss Forfeit Conditions

### Damage Forfeiture Clause

The *gemara* turns to a new case. A *shatla* stipulates at the outset: *im afsidehu, mesalkana af afsid* — if I cause a loss, I will leave, having forfeited the *shevach*.

### Yehuda vs. Kahana

Rav Yehuda rules: *mistalek belo shevach* — he leaves without the *shevach* that accrued, but he does receive his base wages. Rav Kahana rules the opposite: *mistalek be-shevach* — he does take the *shevach* despite having caused a loss. Notably, Rav Kahana concedes one narrower case: if the *shatla* explicitly said *im afsidna, mistalakna belo shevach* — if I cause damage, I will leave without *shevach* — then in that case he does indeed leave without the *shevach*. The linguistic precision of the stipulation matters to Rav Kahana.

### Asmachta Unenforceable

Rabba intervenes with a foundational principle: *asmachta hi* — this is an *asmachta*, a verbal condition that goes beyond what the person truly meant to commit to, and *asmachta lo kanyah* — an *asmachta* does not take legal effect. When a worker says "if I cause a loss, it's all on me, I forfeit everything," he cannot genuinely mean to surrender his base wages for labor already performed. Such a declaration is the kind of thing people say loosely — "don't worry, it's all on me" — without a serious legal intention to forfeit their earned compensation. The law therefore does not enforce it as stated.

### Deduction vs. Forfeiture

One might ask: is this not precisely the language used in a well-known *mishnah* — *im ovir ve-lo avid, ashalem be-meitivah* — if I leave the field fallow and fail to work it, I will pay back with the best? Does the *mishnah* not enforce such conditional language? Rabba distinguishes: *hatam mai de-afsid meshallem* — in that *mishnah*, the worker pays only for the damage he actually caused, measure for measure. *Hacha mai de-afsid mankinan leh ve-idach yahvinan leh* — here, the damage caused is deducted from what he is owed, but the remainder of his wages is still paid. The critical difference is between forfeiture of everything and deduction of the actual loss. A condition that amounts to total forfeiture of earned wages is an *asmachta* and is unenforceable; a proportional deduction for actual damage is simply an assessment of net wages owed and requires no special condition to operate.

---

## Runya Firing Case

### Runya Evicted

The *gemara* presents a case involving a planter named Runya who worked for Ravina. *Afsid salki* — he caused some damage and was dismissed. *Ata lekamei de-Rabba* — Runya came before Rabba to complain. *Amar leh chazi mar mai ka-avid li* — look at what he did to me. *Amar leh shapir avid* — Rabba replied: he acted correctly.

### At-Will Employment

Runya protested: *ha lo hitrah bi* — he gave me no warning before dismissing me. Rabba's response is categorical: *lo tsarich le-hatrah* — no warning was required whatsoever. Rabba then articulates a broader principle: certain categories of workers are at-will hires, and no advance notice is necessary before dismissing them. He lists: *makrei dardakei, shatla, tavcha, umana ve-safra mata* — teachers of young children, planters, butchers, bloodletters, and the town scribe.

### Irrecoverable Loss Doctr…

Rava formulates the underlying rationale as a general rule: *kol pseida de-lo hadar* — any loss which is irrecoverable — that worker is treated as an at-will hire who may be dismissed without warning. A teacher who neglects children, a planter who damages crops, a butcher who renders meat *treif* — in each case, the damage cannot be undone. Because the nature of the work is such that a single instance of carelessness causes permanent, unrecoverable harm, the employer's right to terminate immediately without notice is recognized as an overriding consideration. This rule will be elaborated further in *Bava Batra*.

---

## Three-Way Shevach Split

### Early Departure Request

The *gemara* introduces a new case involving a *shatla* who wishes to break his contract early. *D'ba'ina l'meisak l'Eretz Yisrael* — he wants to leave and go to *Eretz Yisrael*, a desire the *gemara* treats sympathetically. He accordingly requests: *havu li shivcha* — give me the *shevach* I am owed for the value I added to the land, and release me from the remainder of the agreement.

### Full Shevach Question

The case comes before Rav Papa bar Shmuel, who rules: *havu lei shivchei* — give him his *shevach*. Rava immediately questions the scope of this ruling: *ihu ashpach ara, lo ashpacha?* — was he alone responsible for all the value added to the land? Surely the land itself contributed to its own improvement. Does the *shatla* receive the entirety of the *shevach*?

### Half Only; Aris Factor

Rav Papa bar Shmuel clarifies: *plaga d'shivcha ka'amina lach* — I meant only half the *shevach*. Half reflects the land's own contribution, which belongs to the owner; the *shatla* is entitled to half. However, a further complication arises: *hashta ba'i l'meitav man talei arisa* — now that the *shatla* is departing early, the owner will need to hire a new *aris*, a tenant farmer, to continue working the land. That new tenant will also require compensation. The owner therefore cannot bear the full loss of that hire while simultaneously paying the *shatla* his full half. Since the *shatla's* early departure forces the owner into an additional expense, his share must be reduced accordingly.

### Quarter Not Half

Rav Papa bar Shmuel revises: *riva d'shivcha ka'amina* — he gets only a quarter of the *shevach*, not half, because part of what would have been the *shatla's* half must now cover the cost of the new *aris*.

Rav Ashi objects that even "a quarter" requires precision: *riva d'hu danka* — the quarter in question is actually a sixth. That is, it is not one quarter of the total *shevach*, but one quarter of the portion remaining after the *aris's* share is accounted for — which, mathematically, equals one sixth of the whole.

### Regional Norms

To understand this, the *gemara* cites Rav Manyumi son of Rav Nachumi, who reports the regional custom: *b'atra d'shakil shatla palga ve-arisa tulta* — in a place where the *shatla* normally takes half and the *aris* normally takes a third. These are the baseline proportions against which the early-departure scenario is measured. The goal throughout the calculation is that *lo nimtei hefsed le-baal habayit* — no loss should be incurred by the owner.

---

## Fraction Calculations

### Reva D'Danka Math

The mathematical question now receives close scrutiny. Rav Ashi's position is that what was called "a quarter" is in fact *riva d'hu danka* — a quarter which is a sixth of the total. The reasoning: because the owner must now hire an *aris* who will receive a full third of the total *shevach*, only two thirds of the pie remains to be divided between owner and departing *shatla*. One quarter of that two-thirds remainder equals one sixth of the whole. Assigning one sixth to the *shatla* and one third to the new *aris* yields a total of one sixth plus two sixths, or three sixths — exactly one half — meaning the owner retains his full half and suffers no loss. This is the *riva d'hu danka* solution: the "quarter" is a quarter of the remainder, which is a sixth of the whole.

### Ari Paid from Planter

Rav Acha son of Rav Yosef proposes an alternative: *ant manta dilach hav lei le-arisa ve-ana manta dili mai de-veina avidna bah* — you give the *aris* from your half, and I will do as I please with my share. In other words, the owner says to the *shatla*: rather than having the *aris's* fee reduce your share from the top, you take your half first, and then you pay the *aris* out of your own half. I keep my half untouched.

### Reva Mamash Solution

This alternative makes *riva mamash* — an actual, literal quarter — workable. Under this approach, the *shatla* receives one quarter of the total *shevach*. The owner takes his full half. The new *aris* is then paid out of the *shatla's* quarter, not from the owner's share. Crucially, the *aris* in this scenario receives not one third of the whole but one third of the remainder after the *shatla* has taken his quarter. Since the *shatla* takes one quarter of the total, three quarters remain; the *aris* then receives one third of that three-quarter remainder, which is one quarter of the total. But this is the *shatla's* quarter — the *shatla* pays the *aris* from his own allocation. The *shatla* thus nets zero from his quarter (he gives it entirely to the *aris*), the owner keeps his half, and the *aris* receives a third of the portion that remained — not a full third of the whole, but a third of the three quarters, which is a quarter of the total.

### Owner Protection

The two solutions can be contrasted directly. In the *riva d'hu danka* approach: the *aris* receives a full third of the whole (two sixths), the *shatla* receives one sixth, and the owner retains one half. In the *riva mamash* approach: the owner again retains one half, the *shatla* receives one quarter and remits it to the *aris*, who consequently receives only one quarter rather than one third of the whole. Both arrangements protect the owner fully. The difference lies in whether the *aris* absorbs the cost of the *shatla's* early departure (in the *riva mamash* solution he receives less than his normal third) or whether the *shatla* alone bears that cost (in the *riva d'hu danka* solution, where his share is reduced from a half to a sixth).

### Rav Ashi Praised

Rav Ashi, upon hearing this resolution, concedes admiringly: *ki mateita li-shchitat kodshim, ta ve-achlah* — when you reach the *masechet* of *Zevachim* in your learning, come and study it with me. Rashi explains this as an expression of praise for the mathematical precision and analytical cleverness that the argument displayed.

---

## Old Vines Split

### Vine Value Rules

Rav Manyumi son of Rav Nachumi adds a further ruling concerning *kufsa saba* — old, withered vines. The one who cultivates them takes half of their value when they wither in the ordinary course. However, *shtefah nahara* — if the vines are destroyed by a river flooding and carrying them away — he takes only one quarter of their value. The distinction apparently reflects the nature and degree of the loss, though the *gemara* does not elaborate further at this point.

---

## Mishkon Dried Trees

### Mortgage Dries Out

The *gemara* transitions to a related question concerning *mashkon* — a mortgage arrangement. The case: *hahu gavra de-mashken pardesa le-chavrei le-eser shanin* — a man mortgages his orchard to a creditor for ten years. The produce of the orchard will serve as repayment of the loan over that period. *Ve-kash le-chamesh shanin* — but the orchard dries out and dies after only five years, halfway through the mortgage term.

### Abaye: Pira Status

Abaye rules: *pirei havei* — the dried trees are considered *pira*, produce. They therefore fall within the creditor's rights as the party entitled to benefit from the field's yield during the mortgage period, and he may take the trees and use their firewood value — *dmei etzim*.

### Rava: Karna Status

Rava disagrees: *karna havei* — the dried trees are classified as *karna*, the principal of the loan, not its produce. The orchard itself was the security for the debt; if it withers, what remains is the underlying asset, not a yield from it. Consequently, neither party may simply consume the firewood value. *Ve-zil ve-lizbon ara ve-hu achil peirot* — the wood should be sold, that money used to purchase new land, and the creditor then eats the produce of that replacement land as his ongoing mortgage payment. The replacement land steps into the shoes of the original orchard as the *keren* of the mortgage.

### Baraita Prohibition

A *baraita* is cited that appears to create difficulty: *yavesh ilan o niktzatz, sheneihem asurim bo* — if a tree withers or is cut down, neither the creditor nor the owner has rights to the wood. *Keitzad yaasu? Yimcheru le-etzim, ve-yilkach bahen karka ve-hu ochel peirot* — what should they do? Sell the wood as timber, use the proceeds to buy land, and the creditor eats the produce of that land. This ruling aligns with Rava's position and seems to contradict Abaye's.

### Normal vs. Abnormal With…

The *gemara* examines the *baraita* closely. The initial reading assumed *yavesh dumya de-niktzatz* — that "withering" is analogous to "being cut," both representing trees that have completed their productive cycle and dried out at their proper time. Under that reading, the *baraita* supports Rava comprehensively. But an alternative reading is pressed: *niktzatz dumya de-yavesh* — no, "cut" should be read as analogous to "withered," and *yavesh belo zemano* — the withering described is premature, abnormal death before the tree's expected productive life has ended. If the trees died before their time, *hazkin bizmano* — aged and dried in the normal course — would be described differently. On this reading, the *baraita* speaks only of trees that died abnormally early, and the dispute between Abaye and Rava comes down to whether the withering in our original case — where the orchard died after five years of a ten-year mortgage — was within the normal expected lifespan of those vines or premature. If it was within normal time, Abaye's ruling that it is *pira* may still stand; if it was abnormally early, the *baraita's* rule of *karna* applies. The daf concludes with this question open, to be taken up in the continuation.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 110

## Dried Vines Dispute

### Vines Drying Out

The *daf* opens by returning to a case introduced at the bottom of 109b, marked by the asterisk approximately twelve lines from the bottom. The case involves a *mashkanta de-Sura* — a mortgage arrangement common in Sura whereby the creditor takes possession of a field or vineyard and consumes its produce for a fixed number of years, after which the loan is considered repaid. In the specific instance before us, someone mortgaged a *pardes* — which Rashi identifies here as a vineyard — for ten years, giving the creditor the right to all produce during that period. The complication is that within five years, some of the vines dried out and died. Since the creditor is entitled to ten years of produce, the question arises: does the wood of the dried-out vines count as a form of produce that the creditor may keep, or must it be treated as principal — as part of the vineyard itself — requiring reinvestment?

### Abaye: Dried Wood as Fru…

*Abaye amar peira havei*: Abaye rules that the dried wood is a form of *peira*, fruit. Since the vines dried out at the expected time — this is when they were naturally meant to cease producing — the drying and its resulting wood should be seen as what those vines produce at the end of their productive life. The creditor accordingly takes the wood as he would take any other fruit of the vineyard.

### Rava: Vines as Principal

*Rava amar karna havei*: Rava disagrees and holds that the dried vines remain part of the principal, the *keren*. They were part of the vineyard when the mortgage was arranged, and their having dried out does not transform them into produce. What must be done, says Rava, is to sell the dried wood and use the proceeds to purchase land — *veyilakach bo karka vehu ochel peiros* — so that the creditor may continue to derive *peiros* from that new asset over the remainder of the mortgage period. He cannot simply pocket the wood as if it were fruit.

### Baraita Proof

The *gemara* cited a *baraita* in support of Rava: *yavesh ha-ilan o niktzas, sheneihem asurin bo* — if a tree dries out or is cut down, both the creditor and the debtor are forbidden to benefit from it. Instead, *yimkru le-eitzim ve-yilakach bahen karka vehu ochel peiros* — it must be sold as wood, land purchased with the proceeds, and the creditor continues to eat the produce of that land. This is precisely Rava's position.

The *gemara* then asks: *mai lav yavesh dumya de-niktzas* — just as "cut down" implies the cutting was planned (i.e., at its natural time), so too "dried out" must refer to drying at its natural time. And the *baraita* rules that even then, it is treated as principal. This seems a strong proof for Rava.

### Abaye's Rebuttal

Abaye, however, pushes back: *niktzas dumya de-yavesh* — read the *baraita* the other way around. Perhaps both cases refer to situations where it was *not* the expected time. In that case the drying out or cutting down was anomalous, and Abaye would himself concede that in such cases the wood is treated as principal — because the vine was never supposed to die during the mortgage period, it remains part of the vineyard in every sense. Abaye's position that the wood counts as *peira* applies only when the vine dries at its natural and anticipated time, since in that scenario the vine is simply completing its normal productive lifecycle and the wood is its final yield.

### Inherited Trees Case

The *gemara* continues with a further attempt to resolve the dispute. The case involves a woman whose husband has usufruct rights over her property — a parallel structure to the *mashkanta de-Sura*, in that one party holds title while another has the right to the *peiros*. The scenario is: *naflu lah gefanim ve-zeisim zekeinim* — she inherited vineyards and olive trees that were already old and dried out. The rule stated is *yimkru le-eitzim ve-yilakach bahen karka vehu ochel peiros* — sell them as wood, buy land, and the husband takes the produce of that land. This again implies that dried vines and olive trees are treated as principal, not as fruit — supporting Rava.

### Abaye's Concession

Abaye offers two responses. First: *eima ve-hizkinu* — perhaps "old" does not mean naturally old at the end of their lifespan, but rather that they became old prematurely. If so, Abaye would concede that this is principal, since he holds that unexpected drying always counts as *keren*. The case therefore does not necessarily speak to naturally aged trees.

Second — *ve-iba'it eima* — Abaye offers an alternative explanation entirely: this case was already established elsewhere as referring to trees that fell to her on land that she does not own. She inherited the trees alone, not the underlying land. In that situation, there can be no question of whether the trees are the "fruit" of the land, because she owns only the trees themselves, and those trees are inherently principal. Under such circumstances, Abaye would agree with Rava. His own view — that naturally dried wood is *peira* — applies only when the owner holds both the land and the trees, so that one can conceptually distinguish the trees' produce from the land's principal value.

---

## Disputed Years Doctrine

### Lost Document Setup

The *gemara* opens a new topic. There was a document of *mashkanta de-Sura* in which the number of years was written simply as *shanin stama* — "years," with no numeral specified. The document was dated and established that the creditor had the right to consume the produce for "years," after which the loan would be considered repaid. The number of years, however, was left unspecified — a significant omission.

### Three vs. Two Years

*Malveh amar shalosh, loveh amar shtayim*: the creditor claims he was entitled to three years of produce; the debtor maintains it was only two. One might initially think this resembles a case of *modeh be-miktzat* — an admission to part of a claim — but the *gemara* develops it differently.

The scenario intensifies: *ve-kadim malveh ve-achlinhu le-peira* — the creditor anticipated the dispute and already consumed the produce of the third year before the case came before *beis din*. Now the debtor seeks to recover the value of that fruit. *Mi ne'eman?* Who is believed?

### Karka Be-Chezkat

*Rav Yehuda amar karka be-chezkat be'aleha kayama*: Rav Yehuda holds that land is always considered to be in the presumptive possession of its owner. This is the principle of *karka be-chezkat be'aleha*. Even though the creditor has already consumed the fruit, the analysis must go back to how the situation stood when the issue first arose. Had the dispute come to *beis din* at the beginning of the third year, the land would have been considered in the debtor's possession, and the creditor — seeking to claim the fruit of that year — would have been the *motzi me-chaveiro*, the one extracting from another, bearing the burden of proof. Rav Yehuda holds that this classification does not change simply because the creditor has now pocketed the money. The burden of proof remains on the creditor, and if he cannot prove his entitlement to three years, he must return the value of the fruit to the debtor.

### Rav Kahana Position

Rav Kahana disagrees: *peiros be-chezkat ochleihen* — the fruit is in the presumptive possession of whoever consumed it. In Rav Kahana's view, the relevant question for *hamotzi me-chaveiro alav ha-ra'ayah* is not the abstract ownership-status of the land as it stood earlier, but the concrete status quo as it exists now, when *beis din* must act. Currently, the creditor has already consumed the fruit. The debtor, seeking to recover that value, is now the *motzi me-chaveiro* and bears the burden of proof. Without proof, the debtor cannot recover anything.

The *gemara* records: *hilchesa ke-vasei de-Rav Kahana* — the law follows Rav Kahana.

### Rav Nachman Contradiction

The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty. We have an established ruling that the law follows Rav Nachman, who stated *karka be-chezkat be'aleha omedet* — the land stands in the presumptive possession of its owner. That ruling emerged from a case involving a rental dispute: a house was rented for twelve months at a rate that also implied a monthly figure, and then it turned out to be a leap year with a thirteenth month. Rav Nachman ruled that the tenant bears the burden of proof. The landlord, as owner of the land, is the *muchzak*, and even if the tenant has already benefited from the extra month, the tenant must pay — because the land's ownership-presumption had already established who bore the burden when the dispute first arose. This appears to mirror Rav Yehuda's position and contradict the ruling in favor of Rav Kahana.

### Evidence Distinction

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction with a principled distinction: *hasam milsa de-lo avida le-igluyei hi, hacha milsa de-avida le-igluyei* — there, the dispute can never be resolved by new evidence, whereas here, it can.

In the rental case, the document said "twelve months" and also implied a monthly rate — a self-contradiction with no way to resolve it. No further witnesses or evidence can emerge. The dispute is inherently unresolvable.

In the mortgage case, the document said only "years" without a number. Witnesses might yet come forward to testify as to what number of years was originally agreed upon. New evidence could surface.

### No Court Reversals

*Ve-atruchei beis dina trei zimni lo matrchinnen* — we do not burden *beis din* with having to reconvene twice. If *beis din* were to rule now — relying on the *karka be-chezkat be'aleha* principle — that the debtor is the *muchzak* and the creditor must return the fruit's value, and then witnesses later emerged proving the arrangement was indeed for three years, *beis din* would have to reverse its ruling and require the debtor to pay back the creditor. To avoid this risk of reversal, the *gemara* applies the *hamotzi me-chaveiro alav ha-ra'ayah* rule in its pragmatic sense: we will not disturb the current state of affairs unless proof is provided. Since the creditor presently holds the consumed fruit's value, the debtor must bring proof to dislodge him.

Where no new evidence can ever emerge — as in the rental case — there is no risk of reversal, and *beis din* can safely apply the conceptual *karka be-chezkat be'aleha* reasoning. In that case, we rule according to Rav Nachman, treating the landlord as the *muchzak* regardless of who currently holds the money.

---

## Lost Document Credibility

### Five vs. Three Years

A related but distinct scenario is now introduced. Here, the *malveh* claims five years of entitlement and the *loveh* claims only three. This time the loan document has been lost before being used in any proceeding. The *loveh* tells the *malveh*: go bring the document and we'll see how many years it specifies. The *malveh* responds: *shtra irkas li* — I lost it.

What makes this case structurally different from the previous one is that the creditor has already been in possession of the land for three years — that much is undisputed. The debtor insists the mortgage period has now concluded; the creditor claims two additional years remain.

### Rav Yehuda Migo

*Amar Rav Yehuda: malveh ne'eman* — Rav Yehuda rules that the creditor is believed. His reasoning is a *migo*: *migo de'ei ba'ei amar lekucha hi be-yadi* — the creditor could have made the stronger claim that he purchased the land outright. The *sugya* in *Bava Batra* establishes that if someone has been in uncontested possession of land for three years without the owner registering a protest, that person may claim he purchased it and be believed — since one does not preserve a bill of sale indefinitely. Since the creditor could have deployed this stronger claim and been believed, he should certainly be believed in the lesser claim of entitlement to two more years under the mortgage.

This *migo* is especially noteworthy given that ordinarily, under *karka be-chezkat be'aleha*, the debtor's ownership-presumption would place the burden of proof on the creditor. The *migo* is doing significant work here to overcome that presumption.

### Rejection of Migo

*Rav Zvid and Rav Avira* reject Rav Yehuda's *migo* entirely. They argue that the premise is flawed: the creditor did not lose the document.

### Careful with Document

*Mai ta'ama? — hai shtra, keivan de-leguvayna kai, mizdehar zahir bei* — this document is used to collect the loan. Unlike a bill of sale, which one might not bother preserving after three years of unchallenged possession, a loan document is kept precisely because it is the instrument of collection. A creditor always knows he may need it to prove the debt if the debtor ever denies it. Therefore, *umichbash hu de-chavshei le-shtarei* — he has not lost it; he has hidden it. The inference is that if the document were produced, it would support the debtor's version of events. The creditor has concealed it to claim two extra years of produce.

Since we suspect the document exists and contradicts him, his claim is not merely unsubstantiated — it is affirmatively undermined. A *migo* does not function when there is such conspicuous counter-evidence against the claimed statement. Moreover, the *migo* here is being deployed *le-hotzi* — to extract from the debtor's possession — making it an even weaker tool. Rav Zvid and Rav Avira accordingly refuse to credit the *migo* in this context.

### Abuse Concern

*Ravina* raises a broader structural concern to *Rav Ashi*. If we accept that a creditor in a *mashkanta de-Sura* could claim *lekucha hi be-yadi* after three years of uncontested possession, the entire institution of the *mashkanta de-Sura* is exposed to systematic abuse. Every creditor, after three years, could simply conceal the document and declare he purchased the property. *Ve-chi matkini rabanan milta de-ati bah lidei pesida* — would the Rabbis have instituted an arrangement susceptible to such exploitation?

### Tax and Trench Test

The response is: *lo — hatam tikinu leh rabanan de-marei ara yaheiv tiska ve-charei charya* — no, the Rabbis structured the *mashkanta de-Sura* so that the owner of the land continues to pay the property tax and to dig the required trenches each year. These acts of public, official ownership make it impossible for the creditor to credibly claim he purchased the land. The ongoing obligations of ownership are visibly performed by the debtor, not the creditor.

### Annual Protest Required

The *gemara* then asks: *ara de-leisa bei charya ve-lo yaheiv taska mai* — what of land that requires neither digging nor property tax? How is the owner protected there? *Amar lei ibei lei lemichuyei* — the owner must register a *machaah*, a formal protest.

One might have thought a *machaah* would be irrelevant here, since the classic *machaah* is a protest against someone who is on your land without authorization — the very outrage of unauthorized presence provokes the owner to object, and silence implies consent. But here the creditor's presence is entirely authorized under the mortgage arrangement, so the owner would have no natural reason to protest. Nevertheless, the *gemara* rules: if the institution of *mashkanta* is to be viable, owners must understand that they must make an annual *machaah* to prevent any future claim of purchase. *Lo imchi, mai? Ihu de-afsid anafshei* — if the owner failed to protest, he has brought the loss upon himself.

---

## Sharecropper Dispute

### Half vs. Third Share

A new dispute: *aris omer le-machetza yaradeti u-va'al ha-bayit omer li-shlish horadeti* — the sharecropper (*aris*) claims the agreement was for him to receive half the produce, and the landowner (*ba'al ha-bayit*) claims the agreement was for one-third. *Mi ne'eman?*

### Rav Yehuda Position

Rav Yehuda rules that the *ba'al ha-bayit* is believed — applying again the principle *karka be-chezkat be'aleha*: the land is in the presumptive possession of its owner, so the *aris*, who is seeking to extract a greater share, is the *hamotzi me-chaveiro* and bears the burden of proof.

### Rav Nachman Custom

Rav Nachman says: *ha-kol ke-minhag ha-medina* — everything depends on local custom. Whatever the prevailing sharecropping arrangement is in that locale is presumed to govern, and that standard operates even against the usual *hamotzi me-chaveiro* calculus.

### Local Variation

The *gemara* initially attempts to reconcile these views by suggesting they are not actually in dispute: where the local custom is for the *aris* to receive half, the *aris* is believed; where the custom is for one-third, the *ba'al ha-bayit* is believed. On this reading, both Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman are simply describing different locales, and the question of *mi ne'eman* is answered in each place by *minhag ha-medina*.

### Abaye Overrides Custom

However, Rav Mari the son of the daughter of Shmuel reports that Abaye rejected this harmonization: *afilu be-asra de-shakeil arisa palga pligi* — even in a place where the local custom is for the *aris* to receive half, they still dispute. Rav Yehuda maintains that *karka be-chezkat be'aleha* overrides even *minhag ha-medina*: the *ba'al ha-bayit* remains the *muchzak* and the *aris* bears the burden of proof regardless of local custom. This reflects how strongly Rav Yehuda holds to the ownership-presumption principle.

### Landowner's Migo

The *gemara* then adds another basis for the *ba'al ha-bayit*'s credibility, apparently independent of the *karka be-chezkat be'aleha* principle. *Rav Yehuda amar ba'al ha-bayit ne'eman de-i ba'ei amar sechiri u-lekiti hu* — the *ba'al ha-bayit* could have claimed that these workers are mere day laborers whom he pays by the day, not sharecroppers at all, and he would owe them only the daily wage. Since he could have made this stronger claim and been believed — particularly given the absence of documentation — the *migo* grants him credibility when he makes the lesser claim of a one-third sharecropping arrangement. One might ask whether this *migo* functions even in cases where the sharecropping relationship is publicly known; that question is left open.

---

## Orphans vs. Creditor

### Improvements Question

The *gemara* now introduces a case involving orphans and a creditor of their late father. The father borrowed money, and a lien was placed on a specific piece of property. After the father's death, the land — now in the hands of the orphans — has been improved. Its value at the time of the loan was, say, a thousand dollars; it is now worth twelve hundred. The question is: who made the improvements? If the father made them before his death, they fall under the creditor's lien and he may collect the improved value. If the orphans made the improvements after inheriting, the lien never attached to those improvements and the creditor has no claim on them.

### Rav Chanina View

*Savar Rav Chanina le-meimar: ara be-chezkat yatmei kayma u-va'al chov alav ra'ayah* — Rav Chanina initially inclined to say that the land is in the presumptive possession of the orphans, and it is therefore the creditor who must bring proof that the improvements were made during the father's lifetime.

### Rabbi Yochanan Position

A certain elder corrected this, citing Rabbi Yochanan: *al ha-yesomim le-havi ra'ayah* — on the contrary, it is the orphans who bear the burden of proof. *Mai ta'ama? Ara, keivan de-leguvayna kaimei, ke-man de-gavya dami* — since this land is subject to a lien and will certainly be collected upon, it is considered as though it has already been collected. The creditor, by virtue of his lien, is regarded as the effective *ba'al*, the possessor, and the orphans must prove that the improvements are theirs.

### Apotiki Lien Status

The *gemara* notes — and Rashi and *Tosafot* introduce this point earlier as well — that this principle applies specifically to a case of *apotiki*, a specific lien: *de-amar lei lo yehei lach pira'on ella mi-zu* — the creditor explicitly designated this single property as the exclusive source of collection for the loan. Because the creditor has no recourse to any other asset, this land is treated as though it already belongs to him in a meaningful sense. It is that heightened degree of lien which shifts the *chazakah* and places the burden of proof on the orphans.

### Tree Analogy

Abaye finds support for this ruling in a *tanna'itic* source: *safek zeh kadam, safek zeh kadam, kotzetz ve-eino nosen damim* — if a tree was planted within seventy-five feet of a city's perimeter and it is uncertain whether the city or the tree came first, the tree is cut down without payment. The reason: *keivan de-lemikatz kai* — since the tree will be cut down regardless of which came first, the only question is whether payment is owed. We therefore do not treat the tree as in the owner's possession such that the city must prove its case and then pay; rather, since cutting is inevitable, the owner must prove his entitlement to payment. *Amina lei: ayisi ra'ayah u-shkol* — bring proof and collect.

So too here: *hai shtra, keivan de-leguvayna kai, ke-man de-gavya dami* — since the document will certainly be used to collect from this property, it is as though already collected, and the orphans must prove the improvements are theirs to avoid the creditor taking them.

---

## Improvements Valuation

### Land Division View

Returning to the case where the orphans have successfully brought proof that they made the improvements: the question now is how the creditor collects. If the land was worth a thousand dollars — the amount of the lien — and the orphans' improvements added two hundred, the creditor is entitled to collect a thousand, not twelve hundred. But how does he do so? *Savar Rabbi Chanina le-meimar: ki mesalkinan lehu be-ara mesalkinan lehu* — Rav Chanina initially thought: the creditor takes his proportional share of the land itself. He is only owed a thousand out of twelve hundred, so he takes five-sixths of the plot and leaves one-sixth — worth two hundred dollars — to the orphans.

### Cash Payment View

*Ve-lo hi* — this is not the *halacha*. *Bi-dmei mesalkinan lehu* — the creditor takes the entire plot of land and pays the orphans two hundred dollars in cash. He is not compelled to divide the land.

### Three Evaluators

This ruling derives from Rav Nachman citing Shmuel: *shelosha shamin lahem et ha-shevach u-ma'alin otam bi-damim* — three appraisers evaluate the improvement and the party who takes the whole land pays for the *shevach* in money. The principle is that we do not compel a litigant to break up a piece of land; instead, whoever holds the superior claim takes the whole and compensates the other party in cash.

### Inheritance Example

Shmuel's ruling enumerated three categories. The first is *bechor le-pashut* — a firstborn son vis-à-vis a regular son. If there are two sons — call them Reuven, the firstborn, and Shimon — Reuven is entitled to two thirds of the estate and Shimon to one third. Suppose that before the estate is divided, Shimon makes capital improvements on the undivided property. When the division occurs, Reuven takes his two thirds, which now includes a portion of Shimon's improvements. Shimon cannot demand that Reuven return a portion of the land corresponding to those improvements; rather, Reuven takes his full two thirds and pays Shimon in cash for the improvement embedded in that share.

### Uniform Treatment

The same rule applies in the second category — *ba'al chov u-ketuvat isha le-yesomim*: a creditor or a wife collecting her *ketubah* from orphans. Even when the orphans have proved their improvements, the creditor or widow takes the entire plot and compensates the orphans in cash. The third category — *ba'al chov le-lakuchos* — covers the case where a creditor exercises a lien against a purchaser who has improved the land. Again, the creditor takes the whole and pays the purchaser for the improvement in cash.

### Valuation Threshold

However, the *gemara* introduces a crucial distinction that governs whether the creditor must pay for the *shevach* at all.

### Improvements Within Loan

*Ha de-masik bei ke-shi'ur ara u-shvacha* — if the loan amount equals the combined value of the land plus the improvements, the creditor collects everything and pays nothing. The purchaser (or orphan) who made improvements took a risk; the creditor's lien covers the full current value, and the improver has no claim against him.

### Improvements Exceed Loan

*Ha de-lo masik bei ke-shi'ur ara u-shvacha* — but when the loan amount equals only the original value of the land, and the improvements push the total value beyond the loan, the creditor takes the whole plot and pays the improver the excess in cash. He has no right to benefit from improvements beyond what his lien entitles him to collect.

### Cash Alternative

The *gemara* then raises a problem with this second scenario. *Ravina* asks *Rav Ashi*: you are saying the creditor takes the whole land and pays the purchaser two hundred dollars in cash. But consider the view that a purchaser who has the money can pay off the creditor and prevent him from seizing the land entirely — *ei it lei zuzei le-lokeiach, lo matzi mesalik lei le-va'al chov* states the opposing view. If the purchaser *could* have tendered the full loan amount and kept all the land, why can he not, when the creditor is collecting and offering him two hundred dollars, say: with that two hundred dollars I want to retain a two-hundred-dollar piece of the land? If cash can stop the creditor from taking everything, a fortiori it should give the purchaser a right to retain a corresponding slice.

### Apotiki Exception

The answer: *hacha be-mai askinan ke-gon de-shavyei nihalei apotiki, de-amar lei lo yehei lach pira'on ella mi-zu* — the case throughout this discussion presupposes a specific *apotiki* lien, in which the creditor designated this single property as the exclusive source of repayment. In such a case, even a purchaser who has the money cannot simply pay off the creditor and hold on to the land — the creditor has a vested right to collect specifically from this property. It is precisely because of the *apotiki* designation that the purchaser cannot leverage the cash payment into a retained slice of land. Rashi and *Tosafot* note that this *apotiki* framing actually underlies and explains the entire discussion of the creditor's enhanced standing from the earlier sections, though the *gemara* makes it explicit only here.

---

## Rental Agreements

### Seven-Year Period

The *mishnah* now introduces rules about the terms of rental agreements. *Ha-mekabel sadeh me-chaveiro le-shavua echad, be-sheva me'ot zuz, ha-shevi'it min ha-minyan* — one who rents a field for *one shavua* — a seven-year period — for seven hundred *zuz*, the *shemitah* year counts within that seven. Since the renter contracted for a *shavua*, a biblical "week" of years, *shemitah* is inherently included.

### Seven Planting Years

*Kibel heimenu sheva shanim be-sheva me'ot zuz, ein ha-shevi'it min ha-minyan* — but if he said he would rent for *seven years* of farming for seven hundred *zuz*, then *shemitah* is not included in the count. In this formulation, "years" plainly refers to productive agricultural years, each of which involves actual planting, and *shemitah* — a year in which the land must lie fallow — does not qualify.

---

## Worker Payment Laws

### Torah Sources

The *mishnah* now shifts to the laws governing the obligation to pay hired workers promptly. The Torah provides two *pesukim* addressing this. One states *lo tavo alav ha-shemesh* — *beyomo titein secharo* — do not let the sun set on his wages, pay him during his day. The other states *lo talin pe'ulat sachir itcha ad boker* — do not let the wages of a hired worker sleep over with you until morning. *Chazal* understand that these two cannot both address the same type of worker, since one cannot simultaneously fulfill both. The first must refer to a worker who labored at night — his payment window is the following day, and one transgresses by letting the sun set without paying. The second must refer to a worker who labored during the day — the following night is his window, and one transgresses by letting his wages remain unpaid until morning.

### Day Workers

*Sechir yom goveh kol ha-laila* — a daytime hired worker can collect throughout the entire following night. If not paid, the employer transgresses *lo talin pe'ulat sachir*.

### Night Workers

*Ve-sechir laila goveh kol ha-yom* — a nighttime hired worker can collect throughout the entire following day. If not paid, the employer transgresses *lo tavo alav ha-shemesh*.

### Hourly Workers

*Sechir sha'ot goveh kol ha-laila ve-kol ha-yom* — an hourly worker, who may have worked spanning both day and night, can collect the entire remainder of the night plus the entire following day. The precise reasoning here is debated further in the *gemara*, but at the *mishnah* level the rule is stated as a compound window.

### Long-Term Workers

The *mishnah* extends the same framework to workers hired for longer periods — *sechir Shabbat, sechir chodesh, sechir shanah, sechir shavua* — weekly, monthly, yearly, or seven-year workers. *Yatza ba-yom, goveh kol ha-yom; yatza ba-laila, goveh kol ha-laila ve-kol ha-yom* — if the engagement concludes during the day, the entire remaining day is the payment window; if it concludes at night, the entire night plus the following day is the window. The same asymmetry applies regardless of the length of the overall engagement. For example, if Yaakov finished his seven years of labor for Lavan at midday, Lavan was obligated to pay before sunset.
