If the term concluded at seven in the evening, payment was due before sunset the following day — a window of nearly twenty-four hours.

Two explanations are given for this asymmetry. One is that *lo talin* is only transgressed if a full night has elapsed since the work was completed without payment; if the work ended partway through the night, no full night has elapsed by daybreak, so the first morning does not trigger *lo talin*, and the operative prohibition is *lo tavo alav ha-shemesh* — sunset of the next day. The other explanation follows the structure that Rashi implies: halachically, the night and its following day form a single unit, so a half-night of uncollected wages extends naturally into the full following day without the worker losing his window.

### One-Time Transgression

The *baraita* makes a striking point: *mamashma she-ne'emar lo talin pe'ulat sachir itcha — eini yode'a she-ad boker?* If the Torah says "do not let it sleep over," of course that means until morning — what does specifying *ad boker* add? *Melamed she-eino over ela ad boker rishon bilvad* — it teaches that the employer transgresses *lo talin* only once — at that first morning. He does not continue to accrue a fresh transgression at each subsequent morning by virtue of having still not paid. This is a striking *din*, since once the initial transgression has occurred, there is no further *lo talin* violation to incentivize payment — leaving the employer without ongoing halachic pressure.

### Bal Teshahe

*Mikan ve-eilach mai?* — what does the employer transgress from that point on? *Amar Rav: over mishum bal teshahe* — he transgresses the prohibition of *bal teshahe*, delaying wages. Rav Yosef asks: where is the *pasuk* for this? The answer is drawn from *Mishlei*: *al tomar le-re'acha lech va-shuv u-machar eten ve-yesh itach* — do not tell your neighbor "go and come back, I'll give it to you tomorrow," when you have the means to pay him now. This constitutes a separate prohibition against delay, apparently of rabbinic character rather than *de-oraita*.

### Money Availability

The critical qualifier is the phrase *ve-yesh itach* — *and you have it with you*. If the employer genuinely does not have the funds on hand — if he himself must collect money to make payment — he has not let wages "sleep over" in his possession and does not transgress *lo talin*. The same caveat applies to *bal teshahe*: one only transgresses by delaying payment when the money is available and one simply chooses not to pay.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 111

## Hiring via Agent

### Opening & Bal Talin

The Gemara on this daf continues the theme of *bal talin* — the prohibition against withholding wages from workers — which was introduced in the previous Mishnah. The discussion ranges from technical loopholes in liability, to the precise timing of wage obligations, to the multiple Torah prohibitions simultaneously violated by a delinquent employer, and ultimately to the scope of these obligations across different categories of workers, animals, and tools.

### Indirect Hiring

The Gemara opens by citing a Baraita: *ha'omer l'chaveiro tzei sechor li po'alim* — if one instructs a friend to go hire workers on his behalf, *shneihem ein ovrim mishum bal talin*, neither of them has violated *bal talin*. The reasoning is twofold: the *ba'al habayit* did not himself hire the workers (*zeh lefi shelo secharan*), and the agent who did hire them is not liable because the work was not performed on his behalf (*vezeh lefi she'ein pe'ulato etzlo*). The hired workers are, so to speak, disconnected from both parties with respect to the formal obligation. The logic is structurally similar to the principle of agency in other areas of Halakha — including *melacha* performed on *Shabbos* through a proxy — where the fragmentation of a transaction between two parties creates a significant loophole.

The Gemara then clarifies what case the Baraita actually addresses. If the agent had said to the workers *scharchem alai* — that he personally would be paying their wages — then the liability would rest on him. This is established from another Baraita: if one hires a worker ostensibly for his own field and then directs them to work in someone else's field, he must pay the worker his full wages (*nosein lo scharo misheleim*) and then go claim reimbursement from the actual *ba'al habayit* for the benefit that person received — *mah shehe'enato*. Notably, this implies a legal claim against that third party even without any prior agreement, which raises the interesting question of whether a person can truly be bound to pay for a benefit conferred on them without their consent — a principle resembling *yored* into another's property.

The Baraita the Gemara actually needs to teach, however, is the case where the agent said explicitly to the workers: *scharchem al ba'al habayit* — your wages are the obligation of the householder. Even in this case, the *aveira* of *bal talin* evaporates, because the person who structured the payment arrangement is not the person who actually owes the wages. One might ask: since *shlucho shel adam kimo'to* — an agent's actions are legally attributed to the principal — why does this loophole work at all? It is a genuine question, and one the Rishonim presumably address in greater depth. The answer lies in the specificity of the verse underlying *bal talin*: *lo talin pe'ulat sachir itcha ad boker* — "you shall not withhold the wages of a hired worker who is with you." The obligation is person-specific, requiring both that one hired the worker and that the work was done for one's benefit.

### Practical Examples

The Gemara records that Yehuda bar Mareimar would instruct his servant (*shamash*) — *zil ager li po'alim* — to go hire workers for him, and would direct the servant to tell the workers that their wages were the liability of the *ba'al habayit*. Similarly, Mareimar and Mar Zutra would hire workers for each other, each acting as the other's agent, thereby using this loophole to avoid personal exposure to the *aveira* of *bal talin*. This is not presented as a problematic evasion — it is straightforwardly a legitimate legal structure employed by major *Amoraim* who wished to be scrupulous in avoiding even potential violations. Of course, none of this eliminates the underlying financial obligation to pay workers promptly and in full; it addresses only the specific religious prohibition of *bal talin*.

---

## Wage Payment Timing

### Marketplace Workers

Rabba bar Rav Huna states that the marketplace workers of Sura (*hanei shokai deSura*) do not violate *bal talin* — *lo avrei mishum bal talin* — because *meyedai de'al yoma deshuka smichei*: the workers understand that payment will only come on market days, Mondays and Thursdays, when their employers actually have cash on hand from selling their wares. Since the workers enter the arrangement with this understanding, the normal timing of the *mitzvah* is adjusted to fit the acknowledged terms of employment. However, Rabba bar Rav Huna adds, *aval mishum bal tishe'ha vadai over* — if the employer then withholds wages beyond what is necessary, he does violate the broader prohibition against prolonged withholding, whether that is understood as a rabbinic enactment or derived from the verse in Mishlei. Concretely, if the worker is paid on Thursday for work done the previous Monday, that is permissible given the understood arrangement; but if the employer had funds on Monday and chose not to pay until Thursday, that would constitute *bal tishe'ha*.

### Rav vs Shmuel

The Mishnah's phrase *sachir sha'ot goveh kol halaila vechol hayom* — an hourly worker may collect all night and all day — generates a dispute between Rav and Shmuel. Rav holds: *sachir sha'ot deyom goveh kol hayom* — a daytime hourly worker's wages are collectable throughout the day, i.e., until sunset; *sachir sha'ot delaila goveh kol halaila* — a nighttime hourly worker's wages are collectable throughout the night, i.e., until sunrise. Shmuel agrees regarding the daytime worker — *sachir sha'ot deyom goveh kol hayom* — but holds that a nighttime hourly worker may collect *kol halaila vechol hayom*, throughout the night and the entire following day, until the next sunset.

The question is pointed: why should a nighttime worker be entitled to a longer window of payment under Shmuel's view? Shmuel's position appears to extend the employer's deadline to pay — which might seem more lenient toward the employer — but the Gemara frames this as an interpretation of the relevant *psukim* and how they are applied, rather than as a straightforwardly intuitive rule. One practical rationale might be that one cannot reasonably be expected to collect wages in the middle of the night, or that an employer cannot be disturbed at that hour, so the window effectively runs until the end of business hours the following day.

### Rav's Defense

The Mishnah's language appears to contradict Rav, since the phrase *goveh kol halaila vechol hayom* suggests that a single worker can collect both all night and all day. Rav responds: *letzdadin katani* — the Mishnah speaks to each case separately. The daytime worker collects throughout the day, and the nighttime worker collects throughout the night; the Mishnah is not saying the same worker collects across both periods.

### Extended Terms

A further Baraita challenges Rav: *haya sachir shabbat, sachir chodesh, sachir shana, sachir shavua* — whether one was hired by the week, month, year, or septennate — *yotze bayom goveh kol hayom, yotze balayla goveh kol halaila*, if the term concluded during the day the employer must pay by sunset, if during the night then by sunrise. Yet the Baraita continues *ve-chol hayom* — "and throughout the day" — which seems to contradict Rav by extending the nighttime worker's window into the following day. Rav responds: *tanai hi* — this is actually a dispute among *Tannaim*, and his disagreement with Shmuel mirrors a pre-existing Tannaitic disagreement. A Baraita confirms this: *sachir sha'ot deyom goveh kol hayom, sachir sha'ot delaila goveh kol halaila* — these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda, whose position matches Rav's; *Rabbi Shimon omer, sachir sha'ot deyom goveh kol hayom, sachir sha'ot delaila goveh kol halaila vechol hayom* — Rabbi Shimon extends the nighttime worker's window, matching Shmuel. The *machlokes* between Rav and Shmuel is thus a reflection of the *machlokes* between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, grounded in competing *drashot* on the relevant *psukim*.

A broader point emerges here: the *mitzvah* of *bal talin* is not coextensive with the ethical and financial obligation to pay workers. There are cases where one can be technically exempt from *bal talin* while still being absolutely obligated to pay — and conversely, the specific rules of timing within *bal talin* sometimes appear almost formal, even arbitrary in their structure. The *shokai deSura* example illustrates that it is the terms of the understood agreement, not a mechanical clock, that determine when the obligation kicks in.

---

## Five Prohibitions

### Chamesh Shemot

The Gemara now draws a broader conclusion from this whole discussion: *kol hakovesh sachar sachir over b-chamisha shemot* — whoever withholds a hired worker's wages violates *chamesh shemot*, five names, meaning five *lo ta'asei* and one *mitzvat asei*, for a total of six prohibitions. These are: *mishum bal ta'ashok et reacha* (do not cheat your friend), *mishum bal tigzol* (do not steal), *mishum bal ta'ashok sachir ani* (do not cheat a poor hired laborer), *mishum bal talin* (do not withhold wages overnight for a day worker), *mishum beyomo titein sacharo* (pay on the same day — the positive commandment), and *mishum lo tavo alav hashemesh* (do not let the sun set on unpaid wages for a nighttime worker). The Gemara notes that *bal talin* and *beyomo titein sacharo* do not apply simultaneously in every case: *hanei de-ika beyomama leika belayla, de-ika belayla leika beyomama* — one applies to day workers and the other to night workers. Rav Chisda therefore clarifies: *shem sechirut be'alma* — the list describes all the prohibitions associated with the general category of hiring workers; not every individual case will trigger all six simultaneously.

### Oshek vs Gezel

This leads to a fundamental question: what is the difference between *oshek* (cheating or oppression) and *gezel* (stealing)? Rav Chisda explains: *lech vashuv lech vashuv* — if one repeatedly tells a worker to come back later and keeps putting him off, that is *oshek*; *yesh lacha biyadi ve'eini noten lacha* — if one openly tells the worker "I have your money and I'm not giving it to you," that is *gezel*.

### Oshek/Gezel Debate

Rav Sheshet challenges Rav Chisda's formulation. Both *oshek* and *gezel* appear in the Torah in the context of the *korban asham* for monetary violations, alongside *pikadon*, and the *halacha* requires that they all share a common structure: the offender must have actively denied the claim (*dekafar lei mamona*), in parallel to the denial involved in a *pikadon* case. Under Rav Chisda's definition, telling someone "come back tomorrow" does not involve a denial — so it cannot be the operative case for the Torah's *oshek*. Rav Sheshet therefore offers a different distinction: *natati lach* — "I already paid you" — is *oshek*; *yesh lacha biyadi ve'eini noten lacha* — "I have it and won't give it" — is *gezel*. In Rav Sheshet's formulation, both involve a denial, but the nature of the denial differs.

Abaye then challenges Rav Sheshet: the same objection applies to *gezel* — *gezel* also requires a denial similar to *pikadon* to trigger the *korban asham* liability. *Be'inan dekafar lei mamona* — you need a denial. Abaye therefore proposes: *lo secharticha me'olam* — "I never hired you in the first place" — is *oshek*, since you are denying the employment relationship itself; *netati lacha* — "I already paid you your wages" — is *gezel*, since you are denying an obligation that you in fact incurred.

The further give-and-take examines why Rav Sheshet only demanded the *pikadon*-style denial for *oshek* and not for *gezel*. His answer is that *gezel* involves a two-stage act: one first takes the object wrongfully (*gezel degazlei*) and then denies it (*vehadar kafrei*) — the act of taking is primary, and the denial is secondary. The Gemara then asks: but isn't *oshek* the same? Rav Sheshet responds by pointing to the linguistic form of the verse: by *gezel* the Torah uses a nominal form (*o begezel*, "the stolen object"), implying prior acknowledgment that the object existed and was taken; by *oshek* the Torah uses an active verbal form (*o ashak*, "he oppressed"), implying that the act of cheating is itself the operative moment. This textual distinction is what allows Rav Sheshet to treat the two differently.

### Rava's Position

Rava cuts through the debate entirely: *zehu oshek zehu gezel* — *oshek* and *gezel* are the same thing. Why then does the Torah mention them twice using different words? *Velama chalkan hakatuv la'avor alav bishnei lavin* — the Torah split them in order to create a double prohibition. One who withholds a worker's wages violates both simultaneously. This is structurally parallel to *bal yera'eh* and *bal yimatze* — the two prohibitions against owning *chametz* on *Pesach*, which overlap entirely in content but create separate *lavin*. According to Rava, there is no meaningful legal distinction between *oshek* and *gezel*: any act of withholding or denying what rightfully belongs to another person constitutes both simultaneously. This means that the distinction Abaye and Rav Sheshet were laboring to construct — which type of denial corresponds to which term — is irrelevant, since both terms cover any denial of liability. Whether the question concerns the *korban asham* specifically is a separate matter; Rava likely would still agree that a *korban asham* requires a *pikadon*-style denial, but holds that as a general matter, the two categories are fungible.

---

## Animals & Tools

### Rental Obligations

The next Mishnah extends the discussion of *bal talin* to additional cases: *echad sachar adam ve-echad sachar behema ve-echad sachar kelim yesh bo mishum beyomo titein sacharo* — whether one hires a person, rents an animal, or rents tools, all of these carry the obligation of *beyomo titein sacharo*. One must pay on time for rental of inanimate objects just as for human labor. Similarly, *veyesh bo mishum lo talin pe'ulat sachir itcha ad boker* — the prohibition against withholding overnight applies equally across all three categories.

### Conditions for Exemption

The Mishnah qualifies this: *eimatai? bizman sheta'avo* — when does the obligation kick in? Only when the worker or owner makes a claim. If the worker never makes a claim for his wages — *lo teva'o* — then the employer has not technically violated the *mitzvah*, since the obligation is triggered by the demand. If the employer arranges credit for the worker with a *chenvani* (shopkeeper) or *shulchani* (money-changer) — *hamamcheihu etzel chenvani ve'etzel shulchani eino over alav* — so that the worker can purchase goods against his anticipated wages, this also exempts the employer from *bal talin*. The arrangement functions like a paycheck advance: as long as the worker has practical access to the value of his wages, the employer is not in violation.

### Worker's Oath

*Sachir bizmano nishba venotel* — a worker claiming wages within the appropriate time period may take a rabbinic oath and collect his wages on that basis. Once the time period has passed — *avar zemano, eino nishba venotel* — the worker can no longer use the oath to collect. However, if there are witnesses that he had already made a claim during the relevant period — *im yesh eidim sheta'avo, harei zeh nishba venotel* — he retains the ability to collect via oath even later. The worker's credibility to take the oath is thus grounded either in the timeliness of his claim or in witnessed prior demand.

---

## Ger Toshav Status

### Ger Toshav

The Mishnah addresses the *ger toshav* — the resident alien, a non-Jew who has accepted certain obligations (presumably the *sheva mitzvot benei Noach*) and thereby acquires a recognized legal status within the Jewish legal system. The Mishnah states: *yesh bo mishum beyomo titein sacharo* — if one hires a *ger toshav*, the positive obligation to pay on time applies; *ve-ein bo mishum lo talin pe'ulat sachir itcha ad boker* — but the negative prohibition of withholding wages overnight does not apply. The reason, as will emerge from the *drashot*, has to do with which *psukim* use the word *re'acha* (your friend) and which do not.

### Attribution Question

The Gemara asks: *mani matnitin?* — whose position does this Mishnah represent? It cannot be the *Tanna Kamma* (*lo tanna kamma de-me'akhikha*) and it cannot be Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda. The *Tanna Kamma* excludes the *ger toshav* entirely from both obligations based on the word *me'achicha* (from your brother), which limits the protections to fellow Jews. If the Mishnah were the *Tanna Kamma*, the inclusion of the *ger toshav* even for *beyomo titein sacharo* would be a contradiction. And if the Mishnah were Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, the inclusion of animals and tools would be a contradiction, since Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds that *behema ve-keilim* are governed only by *bal ta'ashok*, not by the timing-based prohibitions.

### Baraita Sources

A Baraita is cited to lay out the three Tannaitic positions. The *Tanna Kamma* reads: *me'achicha, perat le-acherim* — "from your brother," excluding non-Jews. *Gerkha* — the word "your stranger" — excludes the *ger toshav* specifically, meaning the one who is *okhel nevelot* (permitted to eat non-kosher meat), which is the Talmudic characterization of the *ger toshav*'s status. From where do we know to extend the obligation to animals and tools? *Talmud lomar be'artzakha* — "in your land," meaning anything within the domain of your property or your land is included: *kol she-be'artzakha*. And the Baraita concludes: *vekhulan overim bekhol ha-shemot ha-lalu* — all of these categories, humans, animals, and tools, violate all the relevant prohibitions when withheld without pay. This is the source for the Mishnah's opening ruling.

The parenthetical discussion of the *chenvani* arrangement — where the employer sets up credit at a shopkeeper or money-changer for the worker — naturally raises the question of whether such credit is an adequate substitute for cash wages. The *shulchani* arrangement is simpler, since one can simply go and exchange for cash. The *chenvani* arrangement is more restrictive, since it is limited to purchases at that particular store. The Halakha does not appear to limit what categories of goods the worker may purchase, and the *shulchani* option makes cash available directly.

---

## Tannaim Dispute

### Tanna Kamma

The *Tanna Kamma*'s position is that the *ger toshav* is excluded from *both* obligations — *beyomo titein sacharo* and *lo talin* — by means of a *gezeira shava* of *sachir sachir*. The word *sachir* appears in the context where the verse says *me'achicha*, "from your brother," limiting the scope of the hired worker to whom these laws apply; the *Tanna Kamma* uses the verbal analogy to extend that exclusion across all instances of the word *sachir* in the relevant *psukim*, thereby removing the *ger toshav* from the protections of both the positive and negative commandments.

### Rabbi Yosei Position

Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda does not accept the *gezeira shava* of *sachir sachir* at all. His position is nuanced: a *ger toshav* retains the obligation of *beyomo titein sacharo* (the positive commandment to pay on time), but not *lo talin* (the negative prohibition). Conversely, for *behema ve-keilim*, only *bal ta'ashok* applies — not *beyomo titein sacharo* or *bal talin*. Since he does not employ the *sachir sachir* verbal analogy, his distinctions require separate derivation.

### Rabbi Yishmael School

Rava resolves the attribution question: *amar Rava, hai tanna, tanna de-vei Rebbi Yishmael hee* — the Mishnah follows the school of Rabbi Yishmael. It is worth noting that while most of our Mishnayot reflect the tradition of Rabbi Akiva's students, the school of Rabbi Yishmael developed its own distinct methodology of *drashot* and *halachic* derivation. A *Tanna de-vei Rebbi Yishmael* is often cited anonymously and occupies a somewhat distinctive position within the Tannaitic corpus. The Baraita from Rabbi Yishmael's school states explicitly: humans, animals, and tools all carry *beyomo titein sacharo* and *lo talin*; but a *ger toshav* has *beyomo titein sacharo* and not *lo talin*.

---

## Exclusions Logic

### Ki Ani Hu

The question now is: what is the *Tanna de-vei Rebbi Yishmael*'s source for his two-part position — including *behema ve-keilim* while excluding the *ger toshav* from *bal talin*? The Gemara works through this carefully. The *Tanna de-vei Rebbi Yishmael* does not use the *sachir sachir* verbal analogy. Instead, he derives the basic scope of *bal talin* from the verse *velo talin pe'ulat sachir itcha ad boker* — "do not withhold the work of a hired laborer who is with you until morning." From the phrase *kol she-pe'ulato itcha* — anyone whose work is with you — he derives a broad inclusion: any worker whose labor is performed on your behalf is covered.

### Rabbi Chananya

Rabbi Chananya draws on a different element of the verse: *velo tavo alav hashemesh ki ani hu* — "and the sun shall not set on him, for he is poor." The phrase *ki ani hu* specifies that the prohibition addresses someone capable of experiencing poverty: *mi she-hein ba'in lidei aniyut va-ashirut* — entities that can be poor or rich. Animals and tools cannot become poor; therefore the verse's reasoning excludes them from the literal ambit of *ki ani hu*. Moreover, the owner of an animal available for hire presumably already possesses some assets, giving him a degree of financial stability that the verse's poverty-concern does not obviously reach.

### Priority Principle

The *Tanna Kamma* uses *ki ani hu* differently — not to exclude animals and tools, but to establish a priority rule: if an employer has two workers to pay, one poor and one wealthy, he must pay the poor worker first. This derives from the verse's explicit identification of the worker's poverty as the rationale for the obligation's urgency.

Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, meanwhile, derives this same priority principle from a different verse — *lo ta'ashok sachir ani va-evyon* — "do not oppress a poor and destitute hired worker." He therefore has no need to use *ki ani hu* for the priority rule, freeing the *Tanna Kamma* to use it for that purpose while using *ki ani hu* for the exclusion of animals and tools.

The *Tanna Kamma* also extends the priority principle by reading *ani* and *evyon* as two distinct degrees of poverty. The Gemara then explains why both are needed (*tzricha*): one might have thought the very poor (*evyon*) need not be explicitly protected because they are unashamed to make their wage claims loudly — *de-lo kasif le-mitba* — and therefore already at lower risk of being exploited through delay. The wealthy worker (*ashir*), by contrast, may be embarrassed to press his claim — *kasif le-mitba* — and might therefore need explicit protection. And one might have thought the wealthy worker can be passed over because he does not urgently need the money — *de-lo tzarikh lei*. Each case requires explicit derivation.

### Psychology of Payment

This discussion surfaces a genuine psychological observation embedded in the *halacha*: the worker who most urgently needs the money may in fact be less likely to advocate for himself due to internalized social norms around dignity and deference, while the wealthier worker may actually be more comfortable pressing his claim — yet also less urgently in need. The *Tanna Kamma* addresses both poles. The very poor worker (*evyon*) is unashamed to demand his wages and is urgently in need; the merely poor (*ani*) may have somewhat more dignity to maintain. Each deserves protection on different grounds, making both derivations necessary.

---

## Reconciliation

### Apparent Contradictions

The Gemara now presses on the internal consistency of the *Tanna de-vei Rebbi Yishmael*'s position: *uman nafshakh* — whichever way you look at it, there is a difficulty. If he learns the *gezeira shava sachir sachir*, he should include the *ger toshav* in *bal talin* alongside animals and tools. If he does not learn the *gezeira shava*, then his basis for including animals and tools is unclear. How does he hold both positions simultaneously?

### Peulato Itcha

The Gemara resolves this: *le'olam lo yalif sachir sachir* — the *Tanna de-vei Rebbi Yishmael* never employs the *sachir sachir* verbal analogy. Instead, from *velo talin pe'ulat sachir itcha ad boker*, he derives through the phrase *pe'ulato itcha* — "whose work is with you" — that the obligation extends to any rental or hire arrangement where work or productive use is performed on your behalf, encompassing *behema ve-keilim*.

### Recha Exclusion

Then, from the word *re'acha* that appears in the relevant verse — *re'acha*, your friend, referring to a fellow Jew — he excludes the *ger toshav* from the negative prohibition of *lo talin*. The *ger toshav* is not fully within the category of *re'acha*, and therefore, while many obligations apply to dealings with him, the *lo ta'asei* of *bal talin* is not among them.

### Mamon Recha

Yet *behema ve-keilim*, though inanimate, are included — not because they themselves are *re'acha*, but because they fall under *mamon recha*, the property of one's friend. The rented animal or borrowed tools belong to a fellow Jew, and therefore the obligation to pay promptly for their use falls under the same penumbra of *re'acha* that generates the *bal talin* prohibition. The *ger toshav* himself, by contrast, is not within that penumbra: *eino bikhlal mamon re'acha*. The result is a principled, if subtle, distinction: it is not the entity performing the work that is decisive, but whose property is at stake and whose interests the *pasuk*'s language is designed to protect.

This means that the *lo ta'asei* of *bal talin* does not apply when a *ger toshav* is hired, but the *mitzvat asei* of *beyomo titein sacharo* still does. The practical difference is primarily one of formal category — *asei* versus *lav*, and the accompanying difference in severity — rather than a practical permission to delay payment. The *ger toshav* must still be paid on time; the violation, when it occurs, is assessed differently.

---

## Amaleki Exclusion

### Tanna Kamma Recha

If the *Tanna Kamma* has already excluded the *ger toshav* from *bal talin* through the *gezeira shava* of *sachir sachir* — derived from the word *me'achicha* — what then does he do with the word *re'acha*? He has no need of *re'acha* for the *ger toshav* exclusion, since that is handled elsewhere. So what additional work does *re'acha* perform in his system?

### Amaleki Exclusion

The Gemara answers: *re'acha ve-lo Amaleki* — "your friend, but not an Amalekite." The *Tanna Kamma* uses *re'acha* to teach that an *Amaleki* does not receive the protections of *lo talin*. This is a striking and unusual *drasha*, one that appears rarely if at all elsewhere. The *Amaleki* presents a specific textual problem: because Amalek descended from Esau, he would technically be included in *me'achicha* — "from your brother" — since Esau was Yaakov's brother, making Amalekites genealogical relatives of Israel. Without an additional exclusion, the word *me'achicha* might include them; therefore *re'acha* is used to exclude them specifically.

There is an obvious practical question: is there ever a realistic scenario in which a Jew hires an *Amaleki* as a laborer? The institution of fighting Amalek is a rule of war authorized by the *beit din* and the king, not an individual obligation to harm every person of Amalekite descent on sight. Within the ordinary labor market, however unlikely, the *halacha* addresses the case. The *drasha* thus serves primarily to close a logical gap in the textual analysis rather than to establish a widely applicable rule.

### Oshek/Gezel Drasha

The verse further supplies a double exclusion — *re'acha* used twice, once for *oshek* and once for *gezel* — *chad le-mishra oshko ve-chad le-mishra gozlo*. One application authorizes, in the formal Halakhic sense of the *beit din*'s jurisdiction, the non-application of the *oshek* prohibition regarding an *Amaleki* (or, in broader readings, a non-Jew), and the other authorizes the non-application of the *gezel* prohibition. The Gemara explains why both are needed: one might have thought that while stealing from a non-Jew is tolerated within the *halachic* jurisdictional framework (*de-lo tarach bei* — he didn't work hard to earn it, or *de-ati lidei* — it already came into his possession), cheating him out of wages he earned through labor would still be prohibited, or vice versa. Both cases therefore require explicit derivation.

### Meiri Principle

This is precisely the context in which the *Meiri*'s well-known principle becomes relevant. The *Meiri* holds that the formal permissions — where they exist within the *halachic* system — apply only to members of societies without the rule of law, not to peoples who govern themselves by ethical norms and legal structures. Members of civilized societies committed to law and order (*geder ha-dat*) are entitled to the same protections as Jews within the *halachic* system. This principle significantly softens the practical import of these *drashot*, which may in any case reflect a censored or euphemistic text (often *akum* or *nochri* in other manuscripts, or *Notzri* in some readings), rather than the specific category of Amalek per se. The broader jurisdictional understanding of these passages — that *halacha* governs obligations between Jews before a Jewish court, while non-Jews have recourse to their own legal systems — also serves to contextualize the scope of these rules.

---

## Rabbi Yosei Sources

### Lo Talin Source

The Gemara turns finally to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's derivation. He does not use the *sachir sachir* verbal analogy; he derives his distinctions from the verse *lo talin pe'ulat sachir* directly. From that verse, with its various limiting words and expansions, he derives his particular set of inclusions and exclusions: the *ger toshav* is included in *beyomo titein sacharo* but not *lo talin*, and *behema ve-keilim* are restricted to *bal ta'ashok* alone.

### Rav Assi Principle

But there is one further use Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda makes of the verse *lo talin pe'ulat sachir itcha ad boker*: he uses it as the source for Rav Assi's principle. Rav Assi teaches — *afilu lo sacharo ela livtzor lo eshkol echad shel anavim over mishum bal talin* — even if one hired a worker only to pick a single cluster of grapes, the prohibition of *bal talin* applies in full. The obligation is not proportional to the scope of the task; even the most minimal engagement triggers the same *mitzvah*. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda derives this from the verse, and Rav Assi's formulation preserves that derivation in later Amoraic teaching.

### Work Principle

The conceptual grounding for Rav Assi's principle is expressed in the verse itself: *ve'elav hu nosei et nafsho* — "and to it [the wage] he carries his soul." Any task into which a person invests himself — *davar ha-moser nafsho alav* — any work that one genuinely puts oneself into, however brief, generates the full set of obligations on the employer's side. The investment of one's effort and livelihood into a task, no matter how small, is sufficient to invoke the Torah's full protection of the worker's wages.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 112

## Wage Payment Framework

### Day/Night Workers

The sugya picks up at the bottom of 111b, dealing with the obligations and prohibitions surrounding the timely payment of workers. The Torah formulates this in two distinct verses. One verse states *lo talin pe'ulat sachir itecha ad boker* — do not let the worker's wage remain with you overnight, meaning it must be paid before the following morning. The other states *bayomo titein secharo velo tavo alav hashemesh* — pay him during the day before sunset. The Gemara reconciles these two verses by distinguishing between a night worker, who must be paid by the following day, and a day worker, who must be paid by the following night.

Once the employer has transgressed this prohibition once, he cannot transgress it again — the violation is a single event. However, the rabbis understand that there remains a rabbinic obligation of *lo tisheheh*: even after the initial transgression, the employer still must pay as quickly as possible. That is the basic framework.

### Non-Jews & Vessels

The Gemara then extends the prohibition in two directions that are not explicit in the *pesukim*. First, the verse uses the word *me'achecha* — "your brother" — which would seem to limit the obligation to fellow Jews. Nevertheless, *Chazal* derive from an additional word in the verse that the *mitzvah* of timely payment also applies to a *ger toshav*. This is a genuine *chidush*, given that the plain meaning of *me'achecha* points in the opposite direction. Second, the Gemara extends the obligation beyond hiring a person's labor to renting their vessels or animals.

That second extension invites scrutiny, because the verse concludes with the phrase *ve'elav hu nosei et nafsho* — "he gives his soul for this" — capturing the poignancy of a worker who has toiled all day and returns home empty-handed. That emotional force clearly does not apply with the same sharpness when one has merely rented out a vessel or an animal. And yet the verse extends to those cases as well.

It is also worth noting that the verse in question opens with *lo ta'ashok sechar ani ve'evyon me'achecha o migercha* — "do not oppress the wages of the poor and destitute among your brothers or your strangers" — followed by *bayomo titein secharo vegam ki ani hu ve'elav hu nosei nafsho*. A student might observe that the plain reading seems aimed specifically at the injustice of withholding wages from a poor person, and question whether the Gemara's division into a "day shift" and "night shift" framework compromises that moral thrust. In truth it does not: the division responds to the textual contradiction between the two verses and simply gives the employer a reasonable window within which to pay. Moreover, the prohibition applies even where the worker is not poor — a wealthy employee still has the right to be paid on time. The Gemara's framework reflects a sensitivity to the realities of commercial life without abandoning the Torah's fundamental moral demand.

### Textual Analysis

The Gemara turns to a *machloket* about what is derived from specific words in the verse. Rav Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda asks: what does one do with the word *itecha* in the phrase *lo talin pe'ulat sachir itecha ad boker* — what does one derive from that extra word? The discussion that follows leads directly into the moral dimension of the *sugyah*.

## Moral Imperative

### Single Cluster

The answer is what Rabbi Assi says: *afilu lo secharo ela livtzor lo eshkol echad shel anavim* — even if you only hired the worker to harvest a single cluster of grapes, you transgress *bal talin*. Tosafot links this to an earlier Gemara that established that even a worker hired to harvest one cluster of grapes may eat from that cluster as part of the right of workers to eat from the produce they harvest. If the employer fails to pay him even for that small amount, he transgresses *bayomo titein secharo* and *lo talin pe'ulat sachir itecha ad boker*. The word *itecha* — "with you" — is what teaches this: even a minimal engagement falls within the prohibition.

### Worker Risks Life

The other opinion holds that this ruling can be derived from the phrase *ve'elav hu nosei et nafsho* — "he gives his soul for this" — meaning that anything a person invests effort and life-force into is included. According to that view, the word *itecha* is not needed for that purpose. The question then becomes what the second opinion does with the phrase *ve'elav hu nosei et nafsho*, since if it carries no independent halachic derivation, what is its function in the verse?

The Gemara answers: *miba'ei leh le-chadetanya* — it is needed for what was taught in the *baraita*. The *baraita* reads *ve'elav hu nosei et nafsho* and asks: why would a person climb a high ramp, dangle from a tree, or descend to the depths of the ocean? *Umassar atzmo le-mitah* — because he is willing to risk his life for his wages. And now you are going to withhold those wages? The alternate text that appears in the margin of the Gemara sharpens this further: the focus is not merely that he risked his life, but that he did so because he was relying on you to pay him — *lav she-titein lo secharo*. That is the real poignancy: he put himself in danger on the strength of your commitment to pay, and you are betraying it.

### Huna/Chisda Dispute

The Gemara then offers *davar acher* — another reading of the same phrase: *kol ha-kovesh sechar sachir ke'ilu hu notel nafsho mimenu* — whoever withholds a worker's wages is as if he has taken his very life. This could be read in a moral sense: if the man needs the money to feed his family and you deny it to him, it is as though you have murdered him. Alternatively it can be read as referring to the withholding itself — he gave his life for this work and you gave him nothing in return, which is tantamount to killing him.

Rav Huna and Rav Chisda then dispute the application of this idea. One says *nafsho shel gazlan* — it is the life of the robber himself that is forfeited: this sin is so grave that the perpetrator pays for it with his own life. Note the Gemara's use of the term *gazlan* here, even though the employer may not be refusing to pay outright but merely postponing — the Gemara is deliberately harsh in its characterization. This position is supported by the verse *al tigzol dal ki dal hu* — do not steal from the poor person, and Rashi explains: do not think that because he is poor and powerless no one will defend him. God will defend him — *ki Hashem yariv rivam* — and *kava et koveihem nafesh*, God will despoil the soul of those who despoil the poor.

The other opinion says *nafsho shel nigzal* — it is the life of the victim that is taken. The robber does not merely cost someone money; he takes their sustenance, their very capacity to live. This is supported by *kein orchot kol botzea batza et nefesh be'alav yikach* — this is the way of all who pursue ill-gotten gain: they take the soul of the owner.

### Stealing Soul

The Gemara then asks the obvious question from each position against the other. To the one who says it is the robber's own life that is forfeited: what do you do with the verse that says *et nefesh be'alav yikach*, which seems to say the victim's life is taken? The Gemara responds: *be-va'alav de-hashta* — it refers to the current owner, meaning the robber himself. He has now taken possession of the stolen item, and by doing so it is *his own* soul that is forfeited.

To the one who says it is the victim's life: what do you do with *vekava et koveihem nafesh*, which seems to speak of God taking the perpetrator's soul? The Gemara responds: *mah ta'am kova et koveihem* — why does God punish them? *Mishum de-natlu nafesh* — because they took the victim's life. That verse gives the reason for the divine punishment, not its nature.

Taken together, these two moral arguments address different psychological types. For a person who responds to empathy — one who is moved by the suffering of others — the message that withholding wages is like taking a life is the relevant appeal. For a person unmoved by the plight of others but highly attentive to self-interest — what the Gemara elsewhere associates with the attitude of *sheli sheli ve-shelach shelach* — the warning that this sin will cost you your own life is more compelling. These are not mutually exclusive readings, and neither, strictly speaking, is the *peshat* of the verses. The *peshat* of *ve'elav hu nosei et nafsho* is the first thing the Gemara said: the worker risked his life to earn these wages. The subsequent discussions are the Gemara using the opportunity for *mussar* around this *mitzvah*.

## Conditions & Arrangements

### Upon Demand

The Gemara now turns to the conditions that must be met for the transgression to occur. *Eimatai* — when does one transgress? *Bizman she-teva'o* — only when the worker has made a demand for payment. If the worker has not yet asked to be paid, the employer does not transgress. The Gemara derives this from the word *itecha* — "with you, according to your knowledge" — *le-da'atcha*: only if you are the one consciously holding it back. If the employee has not yet demanded it and has implicitly indicated he is content to wait, the obligation has not yet been triggered.

This is admittedly a striking ruling given the power dynamics involved. It is not difficult to imagine that a worker might refrain from pressing his employer out of fear of losing the job. The fact that silence is treated as acquiescence is therefore counterintuitive from a moral standpoint — and yet that is the *halakha*.

The Gemara also addresses this in the form of a *baraita*: *lo talin pe'ulat sachir* — *yakhol afilu lo teva'o* — perhaps one transgresses even without a demand? *Talmud lomar itecha le-da'atcha*: only when it is you who are choosing to withhold it.

### Available Funds

A further condition is derived from the same word *itecha*. Perhaps one transgresses even if one does not have the money available? *Talmud lomar itecha* — it has to be "with you," meaning *sheyesh itecha*, that you actually have the funds. If the employer is asset-rich but cash-poor and simply does not have liquid money to pay, the prohibition does not attach.

This raises a further question: what does "having the money" mean? Is there an obligation to liquidate investments or convert assets in order to pay on time? This is left open. And of course, if someone knowingly hired workers without the means to pay them, there is a strong moral argument — perhaps *geneivat da'at* or worse — even if the technical prohibition of *bal talin* is not triggered. The *poskim* presumably address this, though it is beyond the scope of the Gemara's discussion here.

### Third-Party Payment

The Gemara continues: *yakhol afilu himchehu eitzel chanvani ve'eitzel shulchani* — perhaps one transgresses even if one directed the worker to a storekeeper or moneychanger to collect payment there, and they delayed? *Talmud lomar itecha* — it must be you who is holding it. *Lo himchehu eitzel chanvani ve'eitzel shulchani* — not when you have arranged for someone else to pay, and that third party has delayed.

Tosafot raises the question of whether the employer may impose such an arrangement unilaterally. The assumption in Tosafot is that the worker must have either requested or agreed to be paid through the third party — whether by asking for it explicitly or by accepting it as a term of employment from the outset. If the employer simply announces mid-day that the storekeeper will be paying instead, that would presumably be impermissible.

This arrangement does raise serious possibilities for circumventing the prohibition. One could in principle arrange in advance for a third party to handle all payments, making it structurally impossible to ever transgress *bal talin*. The Gemara had addressed this earlier, with Tosafot clarifying that such an arrangement is not set up *le-chatchila* in order to evade the *mitzvah* — but perhaps as a safeguard against accidental delay.

### Worker Retraction

The Gemara now poses the question: *chozer o eino chozer* — can the worker retract the arrangement and demand to be paid directly by the employer instead of by the storekeeper?

The very fact that this question is asked makes clear that the arrangement could not be purely the employer's imposition — the worker must have some standing in relation to it, which implies he had a role in establishing it. The practical importance of the right to retract is obvious: if the storekeeper lacks funds, the worker needs to be able to go back to the employer. Tosafot frames the question more precisely: even granting that the worker may retract, does doing so then expose the employer to transgressing *bal talin*? If the original arrangement removed the obligation from the employer, does the worker's retraction reimpose it?

Rav Sheshet says *eino chozer* — the worker cannot retract. Rabbah says *chozer* — he can. Rabbah derives this from the language of the *Mishnah* itself: the *Mishnah* says that when the employer directs the worker to a storekeeper, the employer *does not transgress*. Rabbah reads this as significant: *me'avar hu de-lo avar ha-mahadar hadar* — the point is precisely that the employer does not transgress even though the worker has reverted and now wants direct payment. Were retraction impossible, the *Mishnah* would have nothing interesting to say; the more informative reading is that even when the worker has retracted, the employer is still protected by the original arrangement.

Rav Sheshet counters: *mai eino over eino be-torat lav* — what the *Mishnah* means is simply that there is no way the employer can transgress because the worker has no right to retract in the first place. Since the arrangement cannot be undone, the employer's exemption is structurally guaranteed. The two positions thus disagree about both the procedural question (can the worker retract?) and the reading of the *Mishnah* (does the *Mishnah* presuppose retraction or preclude it?).

## Kablanut

### Bal Talin Applies?

The Gemara proceeds to a question posed to Rav Sheshet: does *bal talin* apply to *kablanut* — contractor work — or only to *sechirut* — standard wage labor?

The moral dimension of the question is worth considering. In a typical employer-employee relationship, the power differential is clear: the worker is dependent, the employer sets the terms. A *kablan* — a contractor — occupies a fundamentally different position. He takes a job, sets his own pace, and functions more like an independent businessperson. The sense of vulnerability that underlies the Torah's concern — the worker who risked his life and goes home empty-handed — applies less sharply in this context.

The Gemara frames the halachic question in terms of *uman koneh be-shvach kli* — does the craftsman acquire ownership of the improvement he produces in the article entrusted to him? This principle has direct bearing on the characterization of the transaction.

### Craftsman Ownership

The Gemara presents the question as follows: if I give you raw materials worth ten dollars and you fashion them into a cabinet worth one thousand dollars, the question is who owns the improvement. If *uman koneh be-shvach kli* — if the craftsman acquires the improvement — then the nine hundred ninety dollars of added value belongs to the craftsman. When you pay him for his work, you are not paying him wages; you are purchasing from him his stake in the improved object. That is more like a sale (*mecher*) than *sechirut*, and the Gemara characterizes the resulting obligation as *halva'ah* — the craftsman has in effect extended you a loan when he delivers the article and you do not immediately pay. In that case, *bal talin* would not apply, because this is not a worker-employer relationship at all.

If, on the other hand, *ein uman koneh be-shvach kli* — the craftsman does not acquire the improvement — then the entire object belongs to the owner from the moment the raw materials were handed over, and the craftsman is simply owed wages for his labor. That is *sechirut*, and *bal talin* would apply.

Rav Sheshet states: *over* — the contractor does transgress, implying *ein uman koneh be-shvach kli*. This appears to be in tension with Rav Sheshet's position elsewhere, as Tosafot discusses.

### Sheshet Reconciliation

The Gemara notes that a *baraita* states *eino over* — one does not transgress — in a case that might appear to be *kablanut*. The Gemara resolves this: *hatam she-himchihu eitzel chanvani ve'eitzel shulchani* — the *baraita*'s exemption is not about *kablanut* at all. It refers to the earlier ruling about directing payment through a third party. The two discussions are entirely separate, and the *baraita* provides no evidence about the *kablanut* question.

### Talit Completion

The Gemara then attempts to bring a proof supporting Rav Sheshet's position that *bal talin* does apply to *kablanut*: *hanoten talit le-uman* — if one gives his *talit* to a craftsman for improvement — *gamrah hodio*, once the craftsman finishes and notifies the owner, *afilu mi-kan ve-ad asara yamim eino over mishum bal talin* — even if the owner waits ten days before picking it up, the employer does not transgress during that period. The clock does not begin ticking when the work is complete; it begins when the article is actually delivered and received.

However — *nasna lo be-chetzi ha-yom mishishka lo ha-chama over mishum bal talin* — once the article is handed over, even if delivered in the middle of the day, the employer transgresses once the sun sets without payment, mirroring the ruling about a *sachir sha'ot* who finishes mid-day. This demonstrates that *kablanut* is treated like ordinary *sechirut* and the same prohibition applies — presumably because *ein uman koneh be-shvach kli*.

The Gemara then presses: *ve'i amarta uman koneh be-shvach kli, amai over* — if the craftsman owns the improvement, why would there be a transgression at all? The answer is that the case in the *baraita* must be one of ordinary *sechirut*, not true *kablanut*. Rav Mari brei de-Rav Kahana specifies: *be-garde de-sarvla* — the case involves a craftsman working on a thick winterweight cloth, and he was hired *le-rukei* — to beat and work the material in order to soften it, paid not for the finished product but at a rate of so many blows per unit of payment. That is *sechirut* by time or by unit of effort, not *kablanut* by the completed job. Therefore, one cannot derive anything from this case about true *kablanut*, and the question of whether *uman koneh be-shvach kli* applies — and whether *bal talin* extends to genuine contractor work — remains unresolved.

## Worker's Oath Takana

### Oath Inversion

The *Mishnah* now introduces an entirely separate but related rabbinic institution. When a worker claims he was never paid and the employer disputes it, what happens in *Beis Din*? Under the normal rules governing monetary claims, this is a case of *kofer be-hakol* — a complete denial. The employer says he paid; the worker says he did not. Ordinarily, the one who makes the claim — the *motzi me-chavero* — bears the burden of proof, and since the worker cannot prove non-payment, he would walk away with nothing.

The rabbis enacted a *takana* inverting this: the worker may take a *shevuah* — an oath that he was not paid — and collect. The Gemara cites this in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, who describes it as *halachot gedolot* — a formulation the Gemara immediately questions, since *halachot gedolot* suggests established law rather than a rabbinic innovation. The Gemara corrects itself: *takanata gedolah* — a great *takana*. But then a further objection: what does "great" mean? Does it imply there are also small *takanot*? Rav Papa finally settles on the formulation *takanata kevua* — an established and fundamental *takana*, one that forms a stable part of the economic order.

The *takana* is described as: *shevuah de-va'al habayit hi* — the oath properly belongs to the employer. He is the one being sued; he denied everything; ordinarily he would take the oath and be exempt. In some configurations, depending on whether there is partial admission (*modeh be-miktzat*), a *shevuah de-Oraita* could apply to the employer. Nevertheless, the rabbis uprooted the oath from the employer — *akruha rabanan li-shevuah me-va'al habayit ve-shadyuha a-sachir* — and transferred it to the worker.

### Economic Balance

The Gemara asks: *mishum kedei chayav de-sachir nafasid lei le-va'al habayit* — just because the worker needs to make a living, we should make the employer lose? That seems to compromise justice in the name of social sympathy. Surely a *takana* cannot simply favor one party because they are more vulnerable.

The Gemara responds with a structural economic argument: *va'al habayit gufei nicha lei de-mishtava sachir ve-shakil ki heichi de-ligru lei po'alim* — the employer himself benefits from this *takana*. If workers cannot be protected by the oath, they will be afraid to hire themselves out, fearing they will be cheated of their wages. The employer needs workers, so from a systemic perspective the *takana* is in his interest as a class, even if in any particular case he finds it uncomfortable.

The Gemara then challenges this symmetrically: *sachir gufei nicha lei de-mishtava va'al habayit ve-ipatar ki heichi de-ligruhu va'al habayit* — one could make the exact same argument in reverse. Workers also benefit from a system in which employers are protected, because if employers feel too exposed, they will stop hiring. So why does the *takana* favor the worker rather than the employer?

The Gemara meets this with a decisive asymmetry: *lo, va'al habayit al korchei agar* — ultimately the employer has no choice but to hire. He has a field that must be plowed, a building that must go up. Protective labor laws will not stop him. So worker protection laws are ultimately not going to suppress hiring to a degree that harms workers. The symmetric argument *sachir al korchei ogar* — that the worker also has no choice but to seek employment — is equally valid, meaning neither side's economic compulsion resolves the question of which direction to tilt. The Gemara therefore sets aside the economic rationale entirely.

### Employer Distraction

The Gemara then pivots to what it presents as the real justification: *va'al habayit tarud be-po'alav hu* — the employer is preoccupied with his workers. An employer managing many workers at the end of a busy day is genuinely distracted. He may have paid dozens of workers in rapid succession and simply cannot recall with certainty whether he paid any particular individual. The worker, by contrast, knows with certainty whether he was paid — it is his own pocket, his own pay.

The *takana* is therefore not simply a welfare measure for workers; it is a probabilistic judgment about where honest error is more likely to occur. We are not assuming employers are dishonest and workers are honest. We are recognizing that an employer can make an *honest* mistake about whether he paid, while the worker cannot honestly be confused about whether he received money.

Given this reasoning, the Gemara asks: *ei hachi nishklei belo shevuah* — if the presumption is that the employer simply forgot, why not let the worker collect without any oath at all? The Gemara gives two answers. First, the obvious one implicit in the discussion: opening unconstrained collection to anyone who claims non-payment is an invitation to dishonesty. The second answer the Gemara offers is more nuanced: *kedei le-hafis da'ato shel va'al habayit* — to settle the mind of the employer. When the worker swears, the employer can conclude that he must have simply misremembered, and the whole situation can be resolved without resentment and without the sense of injustice that would otherwise follow.

The Gemara raises one additional question: why not simply require that the employer always pay in the presence of witnesses, making non-payment provable? The Gemara dismisses this: *tircha de-milta* — it is an unreasonable burden on the employer to bring witnesses every time he pays any of his many workers. The alternative of pre-payment at the start of the day is similarly rejected: *shneihem rotzim be-hakafa* — both parties actually prefer the money to change hands at the end of the workday. The employer wants to delay disbursement, and the worker does not want to carry cash through a day of physical labor.

The Gemara then asks whether this *takana* should also extend to disputes about the *amount* agreed upon — *uman omer shtayim katzatzta li, va'al habayit omer lo katzatzti lecha ela achat*. The *baraita* says no: in a dispute about wages, the normal rule applies — *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-re'aya* — the worker bears the burden of proof and cannot use the oath to collect. The reason is that the entire rationale for the *takana* is the employer's distraction and the risk of honest error. *Katzatz vadai midkar dakar lei inshi* — people remember the salary they agreed upon. Forgetting whether you paid twenty different workers is plausible; forgetting the rate of pay you set is not. Since the rationale for the *takana* does not apply, neither does the *takana* itself.

## Oath Limitations

### Proper Time Period

The *Mishnah* specifies: *sachir bizmano nishba ve-notel* — the worker may swear and collect only when he is still within *bizmano*, the proper time period. A day worker must make his claim during the following night; a night worker must make his claim during the following day. If he waits beyond that window, the oath mechanism is no longer available to him.

The Gemara also asks: if the employer's distraction is the reason for the *takana*, why should not the worker be able to make the oath and collect even after the time period has elapsed? *Afilu avar zmano nami* — even after the period is over, why should he lose this right?

### Post-Period Assumption

The Gemara answers with a *chazakah*: *chazakah ein va'al habayit over mishum bal talin* — we presume that the employer did not transgress *bal talin*. Once the time period has passed, and the employer says he paid, we presume he is telling the truth — because a person who had a *mitzvah* obligation to pay during that window presumably would have focused and paid, rather than allow himself to transgress. During the time period itself, we understand that he may be distracted; once the obligation has crystallized and the threat of transgression is immediate, *rami anafshei u-midkar* — he focuses and remembers.

The Gemara immediately recognizes the tension: but we just said the employer is *tarud*! The Gemara resolves this: *hanei milei mikamei de-limti zman chiyuva* — the distraction is a problem *before* the moment of obligation arrives. Once the clock has run out and transgression is imminent, the employer sharpens his attention and pays. The earlier distraction was at a moment when the obligation had not yet fully pressed; at the final hour it does.

### Witness Requirement

This leads to a new question: if the employee does make his demand during the proper time period but cannot collect immediately and brings the case to *Beis Din* afterward, what is his standing? The Gemara asks: *vechi sachir over mishum bal tigzol* — are we now saying that after the time period has passed and we assume the employer paid, the worker who still claims non-payment is a conscious thief? If the employer is presumed honest, the worker must be lying — and the worker *knows* whether he was paid.

The Gemara resolves this with a two-against-one analysis: *terei chazakei ve-hacha chad chazakah*. Against the worker there are two presumptions: first, that the employer would not have transgressed *bal talin* and therefore paid; and second, that no worker who has truly not been paid would wait so long to press his claim — *ein sachir masheh scharo* — a worker does not sit on unpaid wages. If he had genuinely not been paid, he would have demanded payment urgently. These two presumptions work together against the worker's claim.

In favor of the worker there is only one presumption: that we do not assume he would consciously lie and consciously steal — *bal tigzol*. One presumption against two means the worker cannot use the oath mechanism after the time period has passed. If the employer makes a partial admission (*modeh be-miktzat*), a *shevuah de-Oraita* might apply, but the *takana* allowing the worker to swear and collect does not extend to this situation.

### Delay After Witnesses

The *Mishnah* concludes: *im yesh edim she-teva'o harei ze nishba ve-notel* — if there are witnesses that the demand was made during the proper time period, the worker may still swear and collect even if the court case comes later.

The Gemara asks what the witnesses actually establish. If the worker is demanding in front of *Beis Din* right now, the demand is self-evident; no witnesses are needed. Rav Ashi clarifies: the witnesses testify that the demand was made *during* the proper time period — this is not explicit in the *Mishnah* but is the necessary implication. The *Mishnah* is teaching that timely demand, proven by witnesses, preserves the right to make the oath even if collection is delayed.

The Gemara then raises a further problem: *u-dilma levatar hachi para* — perhaps the employer paid after the demand was made and before the case came to court? The Gemara had established that once the time window closes and the obligation crystallizes, the employer focuses and pays. So between the witnessed demand and the later court appearance, perhaps payment occurred. Abaye answers: *she-teva'u kol zmano* — the witnesses testify that the demand was renewed throughout the entire time period, not just at one moment. The worker kept demanding, right up until the end of the window, so that no gap exists in which unwitnessed payment could have occurred.

But if the demand continued throughout the entire period, there is a final question: *u-le'olam* — can the worker then go indefinitely and make his oath two years later? Rav Chama bar Ukva answers: *kineged oto ha-yom shel tevi'ah* — the worker gets the equivalent of that day of demand. If he made his demand and can prove it with witnesses through the end of the time period, he has one additional day in which to collect via the oath mechanism. Beyond that, the *takana* expires.
