# Bava Metzia 118

## Roof Collapse Rights

### Cliff Structure

The daf opens with a *mishna* at the bottom of 117b that continues the tractate's treatment of divided properties and questions of responsibility when something breaks. The case described is the *beit habad* — a pressing house for olives — built into a cliff, with a garden (*gina*) situated on top of its roof. One can picture the structure: a cliff face with an opening leading into the pressing house, and above it, on the slope of the mountain, someone's orchard or vegetable garden whose soil rests directly atop the roof of the *beit habad* below.

The *mishna* presumably reflects a real-world scenario — such arrangements would not have been invented without precedent. The relevant backdrop is the framework of *socher u'mashkir*, landlord and tenant, which the *gemara* had applied to analogous cases earlier in the tractate, where the party below bears responsibility for the structural integrity of what supports the party above. There is, as *Rashi* and *Tosafot* discuss, some complexity about whether that framework governs here, but that appears to be the operative assumption.

### Planting Remedy

The *mishna* states: if the roof collapsed — *v'nifchas* — the owner of the garden (*ba'al hagina*) may descend and plant below, *ad she'ya'aseh l'veit bado kipin*, until the owner of the *beit habad* constructs arched vaults to restore the roof. In other words, if the person responsible for the roof fails to repair it, the garden owner may come and plant in the space below — within or around the *beit habad* — until the roof is restored. It is a curious remedy, since the *beit habad* is not obviously ideal for planting, but the *mishna* may contemplate adjacent space below, and in any case it functions as a parallel to the earlier rule that a tenant in an *aliya* (upper story) whose floor has collapsed may move into the space below until repairs are made. This is a variation on the same principle: the party who suffers the loss of use has a remedy against the party responsible for the structural failure.

## Collapsed Wall Liabi (II)

### Ones Exemption

The *mishna* introduces a new case: a wall and a tree that fell into *reshut harabim* and caused damage. The ruling is *patur milishalem* — the owner is exempt from paying. The reason is that the collapse is treated as an *ones*, an unavoidable accident. One might note that this raises an interesting *Bava Kamma* question: under which category of *nezikin* would such a case fall? Is it *shor*, *esh*, or something else? But that taxonomic question is set aside; the operative principle is that an unforeseen collapse without prior warning is an *ones*.

### Beit Din Time

The *mishna* then addresses the case where *beit din* had already put the owner on notice: *nasnu lo zman lakotzes et ha'ilan u'lisator et hakotel* — they gave him time to cut down the tree or demolish the wall, and it collapsed anyway. *Betoch hazman patur* — if it fell within the allotted period, he is still exempt, because he has not yet become negligent; he was still acting within the window granted to him and remains in the status of *ones*. *Achar hazman chayav* — after the deadline, he is liable. This is a question of negligence: once the window expires and he has not acted, any resulting damage is no longer treated as *ones*.

Rabbi Yochanan's view is that the standard *zman beit din* — the period ordinarily allotted for such matters — is thirty days. *Tosafot* draws on this *gemara* to establish a general principle: thirty days (*shloshim yom*) is the standard time *beit din* grants for getting things done, whether removing a dangerous structure, repaying a debt, or other obligations. *Tosafot* further notes that *Rabban Gamliel*'s earlier ruling — that a creditor may not sell a debtor's collateral for thirty days — reflects a similar idea: *beit din* puts you on notice, and after thirty days takes action.

At the same time, *Tosafot* qualifies the rule: thirty days is not a universal grace period for anything that might cause damage. Where the hazard is immediate — as in the classic *Bava Kamma* case of a broken jug whose shards have fallen in *reshut harabim* — one must act immediately. The thirty-day standard applies where the risk is not imminently active. Today, *Tosafot* notes, thirty days remains the standard — which, as one might observe, bears more than passing resemblance to the modern thirty-day return policy, though obviously the *halacha* is speaking of something rather different.

### Wall Removal

The *mishna* turns to a further case, one that moves from the domain of *nezikin* into territory more characteristic of *Bava Batra*: someone whose wall collapsed into a neighbor's garden. Here the issue is not active damage but interference — the rubble sits in the neighbor's yard and prevents him from using it. The *mishna* presents the following scenario: the neighbor demands that the wall owner remove the stones, and the wall owner responds *higiu'cha* — "just keep them." The *mishna* rules *ein shom'in lo* — you cannot impose this arrangement on the yard owner. If he does not wish to accept the rubble, the wall owner remains obligated to remove it.

On the other hand, *mishekiblo alav* — if the yard owner agreed to the arrangement and accepted the stones, and then the wall owner returns and says *heilech et yetziat'cha v'ani etol et sheli* — "I will pay your expenses for clearing it and I want my stones back" — *ein shom'in lo*. Once the yard owner has agreed and cleared away the rubble, the arrangement is binding and cannot be reversed. The *gemara* will probe both of these rulings in greater depth.

## Rubble Agreement

### Cannot Force

The principle underlying the first ruling — that the wall owner cannot force the yard owner to accept the rubble — flows naturally from the basic structure of the case. The yard owner has not agreed to anything; the wall owner is attempting to unilaterally resolve his own obligation to remove by imposing something of questionable value on another party. The *mishna* simply refuses to permit this.

### Binding After Work

Once the yard owner agrees and proceeds to clear the rubble, the arrangement crystallizes into a binding agreement. The *gemara* will explain the mechanism: why the agreement becomes final only upon the completion of clearing, and not earlier, raises a significant question that the *gemara* addresses directly.

## Wages in Kind

### Worker Payment

The *mishna* introduces a parallel case: *hasocher et hapoel la'asot imo beteven uvakash* — someone hired a worker to deal with straw and stubble. The worker requests his wages, and the employer offers *tol mah she'asita bischar'cha* — take what you gathered as your pay. Even if the straw is of equivalent or even greater monetary value, *ein shom'in lo* — one cannot force this on the worker. The implicit assumption of a wage arrangement is that payment will be in cash.

### Irrevocable

However, *mishekiblo alav* — if the worker agreed to accept the straw — and then the employer returns and says *heilech schar'cha v'ani etol et sheli* — I found the cash after all, return the straw — *ein shom'in lo*. The agreement, once accepted by the worker, is irrevocable.

### Shaveh Kesef

The obvious question is: why can the employer not pay in straw *lechatchila*? The general principle is *shaveh kesef k'kesef* — something of monetary value is treated as equivalent to cash. *Rashi* explains: the prohibition here is derived from the verse *bal talin scharo* — do not withhold a worker's wages. When one specifies a wage, *mai d'atni bahadei mashma* — what was contracted is implied to mean cash. Saying "I will pay you X" implies an obligation in actual currency, not merely in equivalent goods. Therefore the payment-in-kind does not satisfy the wage obligation, even if its value matches or exceeds the agreed amount.

*Tosafot* in the beginning of *Bava Kamma* elaborates on the broader question of *shaveh kesef k'kesef*, identifying wages and loan repayment as two areas where the principle may not apply in the usual way: if one borrowed cash, one must return cash; if one agreed to pay wages, cash is implicitly required.

## Collapsed Wall Liabi (II)

### Mafkir Defense

Before the *gemara* proceeds to analyze the *mishna*'s cases, *Tosafot* raises an important question about the wall-collapse scenario. One might think that the wall owner could simply declare himself *mafkir* — relinquish ownership of the fallen stones — and thereby escape any obligation to remove them. There is a classical *Bava Kamma* case (*perek hamaniach*) in which a person's glassware falls and shatters in *reshut harabim*, creating a public hazard. If the owner declares the shards *hefker* immediately — before having had an opportunity to clear them — he is exempt from liability: the fall itself was an *ones*, and by declaring *mafkir* before becoming negligent, he avoids the secondary liability for failing to clean up.

Could the same logic apply here? If my wall collapses into your yard and I immediately declare *mafkir*, I was not negligent in the collapse and I have now relinquished ownership before any negligence in failing to remove — so perhaps I owe you nothing?

*Tosafot* concedes the theoretical force of this argument but dismisses it in the present case: *ishamutei kamishtamei v'eino mafkir k'd'amri bigmara* — here the wall owner is not truly making a declaration of *mafkir*, he is merely trying to avoid the inconvenience of removal. When he says *higiu'cha*, he is not sincerely relinquishing ownership; he is deflecting. A genuine, immediate *mafkir* would indeed exempt him, but what the *mishna* describes is not that.

The *halacha* that emerges is significant: if a wall collapses into another's yard and the owner was an *ones*, and he genuinely declares *mafkir* before any negligence, he is exempt even without removing the rubble. The case in the *mishna* is distinguished because the purported *mafkir* is not genuine.

## Roof Collapse Rights (II)

### Rav vs Shmuel

The *gemara* now addresses the threshold for the garden owner's remedy: how much of the roof must have collapsed before he may move his entire planting operation downstairs? *Rav amar beruba* — Rav holds it must be the majority of the roof. *U'shmuel amar bearba* — Shmuel says four is sufficient. Worth noting is that the text here reads *arba* rather than *arba'ah*, which may reflect a difference in the units: earlier in the tractate a parallel dispute used *arba'ah tefachim* (four *tefachim*), while here it appears to mean *arba amot* (four *amot*).

Rav elaborates: even if four *amot* have collapsed, the garden owner is not entitled to move the entire operation below; he plants *chetzvo l'mata v'chetzvo l'ma'ala* — half below and half above. Only when the majority is destroyed does he move the whole operation downstairs. Shmuel counters: *ein adam zorei'ach chetzvo l'mata v'chetzvo l'ma'ala* — one cannot be compelled to split a planting operation between two levels. Even a small opening of four suffices to allow the garden owner to descend entirely.

### Field vs Dwelling

The *gemara* asks: why state both this case and the earlier case involving a domicile? *Utzricha* — both are necessary.

Had the *gemara* only taught the case of a domicile, one might have concluded that Shmuel's leniency — that even a small breach entitles the tenant to move the whole operation downstairs — applies there because *lo avid inish de'dayir portsa hacha portsa hacha*: people do not split their living quarters between two floors. One cannot ask a person to sleep upstairs and keep their belongings downstairs. So in that case, any significant breach justifies full relocation. But one might have thought that for a field or orchard, where it is not unusual for a farmer to work plots in different locations, *avid inish d'shazar hacha portsa vehacha portsa* — one might manage some planting above and some below — and therefore perhaps even Shmuel would agree with Rav that only a majority breach compels full relocation.

Conversely, had only the planting case been taught, one might have concluded that Rav's majority requirement applies there because splitting a field is manageable, but perhaps even Rav would concede that in a domicile any small breach allows full relocation. *Tzricha* — each case is necessary to establish that both Rav and Shmuel maintain their respective positions regardless of whether the space in question is a residence or an agricultural field.

## Rubble Agreement (II)

### Immediate Kinyan

The *gemara* probes the ruling that once the yard owner clears the rubble, the wall owner cannot reverse the agreement. *Michlal d'pinuyei askinan* — it sounds as though the act of clearing is the point at which the yard owner acquires the stones. But *amai* — why? Once the yard owner agrees to keep the stones, they are sitting in his field. *D'tikni lei sadei* — his field should acquire them for him. The principle of *chatzer koneh* should operate: a person's enclosure takes possession on his behalf even of things he has not personally handled.

### Chatzer Koneh

Indeed, *Rabbi Yoshiya bar Rabbi Chanina* states explicitly: *chatzer shel adam koneh lo shelo mida'ato* — a person's yard acquires property for him even without his direct awareness. *Tosafot* notes that the *gemara*'s reference to *shelo mida'ato* is deliberate: it addresses the question of whether *chatzer* operates when the owner is not standing nearby, establishing that it can function even in the owner's absence.

If so, why is the yard owner's clearing of the rubble the operative moment? Why does the *gemara* not say he acquires immediately upon agreement, by virtue of *chatzer*?

### Intent Test

The *gemara* answers: *hani mili heicha d'ka mechavein l'aknoyei lei* — *chatzer* operates when the transferring party genuinely intends to transfer ownership. *Aval hacha achmuyei ashaynach d'ka mishtamit lei* — but here, the wall owner is not genuinely trying to give away his stones. He is simply trying to avoid being pestered to clean them up. His *higiu'cha* is not a serious *matanah* but an evasion. Therefore, since his intent is not sincere transfer, *chatzer koneh* cannot operate on his behalf. Only once the yard owner has actually invested the labor to clear the rubble does it become untenable for the wall owner to claim he was not serious — at that point, the arrangement is treated as genuine and binding.

One might ask: why must the *entire* clearing be completed? Why does not the beginning of the work demonstrate sufficient seriousness to crystallize the agreement? The *gemara* does not address this directly, but its implication is that the completed act is the clearest possible indicator that both parties have treated the arrangement as real.

## Both Cases Needed

### No Debt Relationship

The *gemara* asks: why is it necessary for the *mishna* to teach both the rubble case and the wages case? *Utzricha.* Consider each in turn. In the rubble case, the wall owner has no pre-existing monetary obligation to the yard owner. There is no debt relationship between them. If even there we rule *ein shom'in lo* — that the wall owner cannot force the yard owner to accept the stones — one might think this is only because there is no underlying financial relationship that could make the arrangement compelling. The yard owner owes nothing and is owed nothing; imposing rubble on him is purely gratuitous.

### Debt Obligation

In the wages case, however, the employer *does* owe the worker money — *de'is lei agra gabei*. One might therefore think that because a debt exists, paying it in kind should be acceptable: *d'amri inshi, mimarei reshusach parei efra* — the folk saying goes that when someone owes you money, you should be willing to take whatever you can get, even fodder. There is a *hava amina* that since the employer has a financial obligation and the straw represents equivalent value, the rule of *shaveh kesef k'kesef* should permit him to discharge the debt in goods. The *mishna* must therefore teach that even here, *ein shom'in lo*: you cannot force a worker to accept in-kind payment.

### Forcing Acceptance

Similarly, once the arrangement is accepted, the question of revocability differs between the cases. In the wages case, one might have thought that once the worker agrees to accept the straw, the pre-existing debt structure makes this irrevocable — the employer has discharged his obligation and cannot reassert a claim to the straw. But conversely, one might have thought that without any pre-existing structure, as in the rubble case, the arrangement could always be undone.

The *mishna* teaches both directions: in the rubble case, even without a pre-existing debt, once the rubble is cleared the arrangement cannot be reversed; in the wages case, even though there is a debt that might seem to compel acceptance, the employer still cannot force the worker to take in-kind payment initially. Both rulings are necessary because the *hava amina* in each case runs in a different direction, and without both being explicitly taught, one might err in one case or the other.

## Hefker Field

### Own vs Hefker

The *gemara* returns to the wages case — specifically, the ruling that one cannot force a worker to accept payment in kind — and notes a *brayta* that appears to say *shom'in lo*, that one *can* force it. *Rav Nachman* reconciles the apparent contradiction: *kan b'shelo kan b'shel chaveiro* — it matters whether the worker is laboring in the employer's own field or in someone else's field. In the employer's own field, payment in kind cannot be forced. In another person's field, perhaps different rules apply.

*Rava* challenges this immediately: *b'shelo mai ta'ama* — why can you not force payment when it is your own field? Because *amar lei agrai alach* — the worker can say, "You are the one obligated to pay me." *B'shel chaveiro nami agrai alach* — but equally, when you sent him to work in your friend's field, the obligation to pay still falls on you, as a *brayta* confirms: *hasocher et hapo'el la'asot b'shelo v'her'ahu b'shel chaveiro* — if you hired someone ostensibly to work for you but directed him to your friend's field instead, you must pay him in full, and then you go collect from the property owner for the benefit he received. Rav Nachman's first distinction therefore collapses.

*Rav Nachman* revises: *ella lo kashya kan bishelo kan bishel hefker* — the distinction is between the employer's own field and a *hefker* field, an ownerless field. When the field is the employer's own, he clearly benefits from the work and owes the wages. When the field is *hefker*, the picture becomes more complex.

The analysis turns on the rule of *magbi'ah metzi'ah lachaveiro lo kanah chaveiro* — if a worker lifts found property on behalf of another, the other party does not thereby acquire it. If the employer sent the worker to collect straw in a *hefker* field, and the legal mechanism of *sechirus* requires that the employer actually benefit — that is, actually acquire the collected straw — then it matters enormously whether the employer acquires it at all. If the worker's collection does not vest ownership in the employer, then the employer has not received any real benefit, and the entire wage obligation is called into question.

This yields a striking principle: the structure of *sechirus* (hire) appears to require not merely that an employer ask a worker to do something and agree to pay, but that the activity constitute a genuine service — one from which the employer actually benefits. If the worker collects straw in a *hefker* field and the employer never acquires that straw, perhaps there is no proper *sechirus* at all, and consequently no enforceable wage obligation even if the employer had verbally agreed to pay.

### Rava's Challenge

*Rava* challenges *Rav Nachman* from a ruling about *metzi'as po'el* — a worker's found property. The rule is: *eimasai? bizman she'amar lo ba'al habayis nakesh imi hayom, ador imi hayom* — when does found property belong to the worker himself? When the employer hired him for a specific task such as weeding or hoeing. Then what he finds incidentally is his own, since he was not working as a general agent of the employer.

### Task vs General

However, *aval amar lo asei imi melachah hayom* — if the employer simply said "work for me today" without specifying a task, then *metzi'aso l'ba'al habayis* — what the worker finds belongs to the employer. In that case, the worker functions as an extension of the employer, and whatever he picks up he acquires on the employer's behalf. Therefore, even in a *hefker* field, if the worker is hired generally to work for the employer that day, any straw he collects would vest in the employer — the employer would acquire it and would owe the worker his fee in cash, not in kind. Rav Nachman's *hefker* distinction must therefore account for this.

### Hagbahah Habatah

*Rav Nachman* answers with a final formulation: *lo kashya, kan b'hagbahah kan b'habatah* — the distinction lies not between the employer's field and a *hefker* field as such, but between *hagbahah* (physical lifting) and *habatah* (watching or looking). If the worker was hired to *lift* and collect the straw in the *hefker* field — *hagbahah* — then by lifting it he effects a *kinyan* for the employer, the employer acquires it, a service was rendered, wages are owed, and payment in kind cannot be forced.

But if the worker was hired merely to *watch* the straw — *habatah* — and *habatah* is not a valid *kinyan*, then the employer never acquires the straw, no genuine service was rendered in the *sechirus* sense, and therefore the employer can simply direct the worker to take the straw for himself. *Rashi* elaborates: when hired to collect (*lagbahah*), the worker's lifting effects the acquisition and therefore *secharo alav* — the wage obligation stands. When hired for *habatah* — guarding or moving without lifting, *kegon lishmor o l'hashlich miyad l'yad* — no *kinyan* is effected, the employer has not acquired anything, and therefore *de'amar lei: hashta lo zachi b'hai, ana, zil at zachi beih* — the employer can tell the worker: I have not yet taken possession of this; go take possession of it for yourself.

The difficulty, as the *gemara* itself seems not to fully resolve, is why the employer does not remain obligated to pay the agreed-upon fee regardless. The worker spent the day watching the field. Even if the employer never acquired the straw, the worker performed a service as contracted — or did he? The *gemara*'s implication appears to be that *sechirus* as a legal category requires that the activity constitute a genuine service to the employer in a substantive sense, not merely the execution of an agreed-upon act. If the employer ultimately acquired nothing, the *sechirus* framework may simply not have been activated.

## Habatah Debate

### Temple Watchers

*Rava* observes that the question of whether *habatah b'hefker koneh* — whether watching *hefker* property constitutes a valid act of acquisition — is in fact a *tannaitic* dispute. This connects, remarkably, to the very first *meimra* of *Bava Metzia*, where the *gemara* had asked whether *habatah b'hefker koneh* and concluded it does not. *Rashi* notes that *habatah* in this context is not mere passive observation but active watching and guarding — exerting a form of control — which is why some *tannaim* might regard it as a type of *kinyan*.

The *mishna* cited is: *shomrei sefichi shevi'is notlin secharan mi-terumas ha-lishkah* — those who guard the wild produce of the *shevi'is* year that was intended for the public *korbanot* (*omer* and *shetei ha-lechem*) receive their wages from the Temple treasury.

### Tannaim Disagree

The debate is between the *tanna kamma* and *Rabbi Yose*. *Rabbi Yose* holds that someone who wishes may volunteer to guard the produce without pay. The *chachamim* respond: if the watcher is not paid, then according to our understanding, the *korban* would not be a proper *korban tzibbur*.

### Tanna Kamma

The *gemara*'s first reading is that the *tannaim* disagree about whether *habatah b'hefker* effects acquisition. The *tanna kamma* holds *habatah b'hefker kani* — watching *hefker* produces ownership. Therefore, if the watcher is not paid a fee, he acquires the grain himself through his watching. He would then donate it privately to the *beit hamikdash*, and the *omer* or *shetei ha-lechem* brought from it would be a *korban yachid*, not a *korban tzibbur*. Only by paying him a fee — making him an agent of the *tzibbur* — does the watching accrue to the *tzibbur*'s ownership. *Rabbi Yose* holds *habatah b'hefker lo kani* — watching does not effect acquisition. The watcher owns nothing; when the *tzibbur* comes to harvest, it acquires the grain at that moment, making it a proper *korban tzibbur* regardless of whether the watcher was paid.

### Rava's Resolution

*Rava* rejects this reading. *De-khuli alma habatah b'hefker kani* — everyone agrees that watching *hefker* effects acquisition. The dispute is not about *habatah* as a *kinyan* but about a different concern. According to the *rabbanan*, we pay the watcher a fee so that he is explicitly watching on behalf of the *tzibbur*, thereby ensuring that the acquisition accrues to the *tzibbur* and not to himself. *Ve-ilo* — if we do not pay him — *cheishinan shelo yimsur yafeh yafeh* — we are concerned that even if he intends to donate the grain afterwards, he will not do so wholeheartedly. He has already acquired it as private property and may not genuinely dedicate it.

*Rabbi Yose* holds that a person who volunteers to watch and then donates may be trusted to do so fully and wholeheartedly — *harotzeh minadiv hu* — whoever wishes may volunteer with full dedication, and we are not concerned about half-heartedness.

The *chachamim*'s response to *Rabbi Yose*, according to *Rava*'s reading, is: even within your framework, if we follow your practice of not paying the watcher, then within our framework — where we are concerned about wholehearted donation — the *korban* would not properly be *mishel tzibbur*. *Midvarecha lidvareinu* — granting your premise, applied to our concern, the result is unsatisfactory.

A second version of the *gemara* (*ika d'amri*) holds that *Rav* says *habatah b'hefker lo kani* and therefore the reason to pay the watcher has nothing to do with acquisition. Rather, *de-hashinan l'va'alei zeroa* — we pay him so that forceful people (*ba'alei zeroa*) who hear that the *beit hamikdash* is paying someone to watch this produce know to stay away. The fee is a deterrent, not an instrument of *kinyan*. The *tannaitic* dispute on this reading is whether this institutional deterrent is necessary.

## Public Domain Rules

### Dung Removal

The final *mishna* of the tractate addresses regulations for various activities conducted in *reshut harabim*. The first case: someone who brings out animal dung to sell as fertilizer. The arrangement contemplated is a direct transaction in the public domain: *ha-motzi motzi v'ha-mezabbel mezabbel* — I bring it out and the buyer loads it up immediately. One cannot maintain a standing pile of dung in *reshut harabim*, because if someone slips and is injured, liability follows.

It is worth appreciating the broader context: *reshut harabim* in the Talmudic period was not merely a thoroughfare but a public commercial space — a marketplace, often lined with stalls, where people conducted all manner of business. The *Cardo* and the open plazas along major city streets were venues for trade. The *halacha* therefore does not prohibit all activity in *reshut harabim*, but it imposes limits to prevent public hazard.

### Construction Limits

Similarly, *ein shurin tit b'reshut harabim* — one may not soak clay in *reshut harabim*, and *ein lovnin leveinim* — one may not make bricks there. *Rashi* describes the brick-making process: one lays out a flat expanse of wet cement, scores lines to form the brick shapes, and allows it to harden, producing a batch of bricks. Doing this in *reshut harabim* creates an unattended hazard — people will step on it, slip, or be injured.

However, *aval govlin tit b'reshut harabim* — one may knead clay in *reshut harabim*. Since one is actively present and working, the danger of an unattended hazard is reduced. The distinction seems to be between activities requiring the worker's constant attention and presence versus those that leave an unattended material obstacle.

### Building Setup

*Haboneh b'reshut harabim*: if one is engaged in authorized construction in *reshut harabim* — say, hired by the public to build a wall — one cannot stockpile large quantities of materials on the street. *Hameivi avanim meivi v'haboneh boneh* — the supplier delivers and the builder builds in coordinated fashion, so that materials do not sit idle and unattended as a hazard. *V'im hizik meshalem mah she-hizik* — if someone is damaged, the builder is liable. This is significant: even when operating within the rules, liability for damage is not automatically extinguished. The question of what one is *permitted* to do and whether one is *exempt from liability* are distinct inquiries, a point that becomes central in the *gemara*'s analysis below.

*Rabban Gamliel* adds: *af metaknin et melachtan lifnei shloshim yom* — one may set up the worksite and arrange materials in *reshut harabim* for up to thirty days before commencing construction. Whether this thirty-day allowance also confers exemption from liability, or merely establishes what is permitted *l'chatchila*, is left ambiguous by the *mishna*.

### Rabbi Yehuda

A *brayta* presents *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position: *b'sha'at hotzaat zevelim adam motzi zivlo l'reshut harabim v'tzovro kol shloshim yom* — at the season when people bring out their excrement for use as fertilizer, one may pile it in *reshut harabim* for thirty days, *kedei she-yishof b'raglei adam u-v'raglei beheima* — so that it gets trampled by pedestrians and animals, which improves its quality as fertilizer. *She-al menat kein hinchilu Yehoshua l'Yisrael et ha-aretz* — this right was among the original conditions stipulated when Yehoshua apportioned the land of Israel. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, this is a fully permitted activity, and the thirty days are not a concession but a right.

### Permission vs Liability

This creates an apparent tension with the *mishna*: the *mishna* implies that dung must be removed immediately, not left for thirty days. The *gemara* asks: *leima matnisin dela k'Rabbi Yehuda* — is our *mishna* necessarily not in accordance with *Rabbi Yehuda*?

The *gemara* responds: *afilu teima Rabbi Yehuda* — even *Rabbi Yehuda* could be consistent with the *mishna*. *Modeh Rabbi Yehuda she-im hizik chayav l'shalem* — *Rabbi Yehuda* would concede that if damage results, the person is liable to pay. The *mishna*'s apparent requirement for immediate removal may be read not as a prohibition on leaving the dung for thirty days, but as establishing the liability framework: if you do leave it and someone is hurt, you pay. You are permitted to leave it — but at your financial risk.

The *gemara* then tests whether *Rabbi Yehuda* truly maintains that permission and liability are separable. The case of *ner Chanukah* is invoked: *modeh Rabbi Yehuda b'ner Chanukah she-hu patur mipnei shehu oseh b'reshut* — even *Rabbi Yehuda* concedes that one is exempt from liability for a *Chanukah* lamp placed in the doorway if a camel with flax walks by and is ignited, because the person was acting with legal permission (*b'reshut*). If permission exempts in that case, does it not exempts always?

The *gemara* answers: perhaps *ner Chanukah* is different because it is a *mitzvah* — *rishut d'mitzvah* — and the exemption is specific to the performance of a religious obligation, not to mere legal permission generally.

A *brayta* then addresses the question directly. *Kol elu she'amru mutarin lekalkel b'reshut harabim* — all those whom the *halachah* permits to create a mess in *reshut harabim* (disposing of waste products, rainwater runoff, etc.): the *tanna kamma* holds that *im hizik chayav leshalem* — even if permitted, they are liable for damage. *Rabbi Yehuda poter* — *Rabbi Yehuda* exempts. This is the core dispute: for *Rabbi Yehuda*, permission and liability exemption go together; for the *tanna kamma*, they are entirely independent.

The *gemara* concludes: *mechvarta matnitin d'lo k'Rabbi Yehuda* — the *mishna* is most straightforwardly read as not in accordance with *Rabbi Yehuda*. Our *mishna* — which requires immediate removal (or at minimum imposes liability for delayed removal) — reflects the view that permission does not confer exemption from liability, which is the *tanna kamma*'s position. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s more expansive approach, granting both a thirty-day window and liability exemption within it, does not align with the *mishna*'s framework.

---

---

# Bava Metzia 119

## Public/Private Domain

### Intro & Topic Shift

We arrive today at the final *daf* of *Bava Metzia*, 119. The *perek* in which we now find ourselves represents something of a pivot: we have shifted from the earlier discussions concerning the ground floor and the upper story — who bears responsibility when floors give way or structures fail — toward the broader terrain of neighbor law: walls and trees falling into adjacent properties, and the rights of individuals operating in the *reshus harabim*.

As was observed at the close of the previous session, *reshus harabim* is not a simple, undifferentiated neutral space that everyone shares solely as a thoroughfare. There are *reshuyos harabim* that function as through-streets, and there are those that function more as plazas — spaces where individuals may legitimately conduct their own affairs: preparing plaster, taking delivery of materials, passing goods along. Yet all of this must be done in a manner that respects the public's right of access and does not create hazards for others.

### Two Key Questions

Two distinct questions animate this entire area of law, and they will continue as a dominant theme into the opening of *Bava Batra*. The first is the question of freedom to act: what degree of latitude does a person have when operating in his own domain, or in the public domain, in ways that may cause indirect harm to another? Must I conduct myself so as to prevent all indirect damage to my neighbor, or does he bear the responsibility to protect himself — *al hamazik leharchik et atzmo o al hanizak leharchik et atzmo*? The second question is a *Bava Kamma*-style inquiry: even if I do have the right to act in a certain way, am I *chayav* to pay if someone is actually damaged as a result?

### Operating in Reshus Hara…

These two levels of analysis do not necessarily travel together. One might hold that a person is permitted to empty refuse into the *reshus harabim* because it creates no sufficient hazard — yet still hold him liable if injury results. Conversely, one might hold that such an act is forbidden because of the potential hazard — yet exempt the actor from payment if injury does occur, on the grounds that the harm was indirect. The *Gemara* has presented instances running in both directions: *potchin bevibar birshus harabim*, where even a licensed activity may generate liability. And indeed, this last *perek* of *Bava Metzia*, which really ought to have been the opening *perek* of *Bava Batra*, sits precisely at the intersection of private domain and public domain, exploring both the scope of permitted action and the consequences of damage after the fact.

---

## Abiyi's Position

### Three Tannaim Agree

The *Gemara* at this point on 118b records the following statement: *amar Abaye, Rabbi Yehuda v'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel v'Rabbi Shimon, kulhu sevira lehu: kol makom she'natnu lo chachamim reshus v'hizik, patur.* Abaye — who characteristically gathers disparate *Tannaic* opinions and draws them under a single conceptual umbrella — declares that these three *Tannaim* all share the same fundamental position: wherever the *chachamim* have granted permission to perform a given act, one is exempt from liability if damage results. This is, as Abaye frames it, the coherent and reasonable resolution of the two-level question: if we are permitting you to engage in this activity, that permission carries with it an exemption from liability. Not every *Tanna* holds this, but these three do.

### Rabbi Yehuda

*Rabbi Yehuda had de'amran* — Rabbi Yehuda is the source already cited in a preceding *braita*, which established that one who acts *birshus* — with license — is *patur* from liability. The case of *Chanukah* and other contexts involving Rabbi Yehuda were already adduced.

### Rabban Gamliel

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel de'tnan*: Rabban Gamliel's position is derived from a *mishnah*. The *mishnah* addresses one who has been hired to build a wall in the *reshus harabim*: one may not leave building materials strewn in the street indefinitely, but must take delivery and build promptly. The *mishnah* further states that even if the worker has been authorized and licensed to build in the *reshus harabim*, he would nonetheless be *chayav* if someone is damaged. To this, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel responds: *af metaken hu et melachto lifnei shloshim yom* — one may even spend the entire month preceding construction preparing the site and staging materials there. Rashi notes that Rabban Gamliel does not explicitly state an exemption from liability, but the *Gemara* reads this latitude as implying *patur*: the word *af*, "even," reads almost as an exclamatory rejoinder to the position that one would be *chayav* — if you are going to tell me a person is liable even when acting with full authorization, I am going to tell you that this same person may prepare his worksite for a full month in advance. The generosity of that permission signals an accompanying exemption from liability.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon's position is drawn from a *mishnah* in *Bava Batra* concerning a case where one person occupies the ground floor and another the upper story — a familiar configuration from earlier in the *perek*. The *mishnah* states: *haya maamido ba'aliya, tzarich she'yehei tachtav maaziva shlosha tfachim* — if one places a wood-burning *tanur* on the upper floor, there must be at least three *tefachim* of plaster beneath it, so that the heat does not break through to the floor below. For a *kira*, which burns less intensely, one *tefach* suffices. The *mishnah* then states: *v'im hizik, meshalem mah she-hizik* — even if one has complied with all of these specifications, if a fire nonetheless results and damages the other party's portion of the building, one must pay. Rabbi Shimon dissents: *lo amru kol hashiurim elalu ela she'im hizik patur mi'leshalem* — the entire purpose of these measurements was only to establish that if one adhered to them and damage nonetheless occurred, one is exempt from payment.

### Two Levels Analysis

One might read Rabbi Shimon's formulation extremely literally — as if to say the only purpose of a building code is to ensure that the damaged party will ultimately be compensated, and that if a person deposits the full value of the adjacent property in escrow, he may ignore the specifications entirely. That reading, however, seems unreasonable. The more natural reading is that Rabbi Shimon is making a rhetorical point: obviously one has an obligation to avoid causing harm regardless of one's willingness to pay. But once one has acted within the parameters the *chachamim* established, having conducted oneself in the prescribed manner confers an exemption from payment if something goes wrong despite that compliance. This, then, is the critical two-level structure: the question of what I am *permitted* to do, because my actions may indirectly harm others even when I act within my own domain, is analytically distinct from the question of whether I am *chayav* to pay after the fact. Abaye's contribution is to observe that for these three *Tannaim*, the two questions do track one another: freedom to act entails exemption from liability.

---

## Worker Chain Liability

### Individual Stage Liabili…

The *Gemara* now turns to a *braita* that addresses liability across a chain of workers — and here, I confess, the full analysis resists easy resolution. The *braita* describes a sequence: *hachatzav shemasar lesatat* — the quarrier, who removes the stone from the mountain, hands it to the *satat*, the one who cuts and smooths it to the correct dimensions. *Hasatat chayav*. If the stone then slips from the *satat*'s hand and causes damage, he is *chayav*. This is presumably a case of *adam hamazik*: it does not matter who owns the stone; if I am holding it and it falls and injures someone, I am liable, much as one who is asked to hold a knife and it slips from his hand is liable for any resulting injury.

The chain continues: *satat shemasar lechamar* — the cutter hands the stone to the *chamar*, the donkey driver, who transports it. *Hachamar chayav*. Then: *chamar shemasar lekatef* — the donkey driver hands it to the *katef*, the porter at the worksite. *Hakatef chayav*. Then *katef shemasar lebanai* — the porter hands it to the *banai*, the builder doing the actual construction. *Habanai chayav*. And finally: *banai shemasar leadrichal* — the builder hands it to the *adrichal*, the foreman. *Headrichal chayav*.

This is a remarkably concrete image of an ancient worksite, each stage of the process visible and named. At each stage, the person currently in physical custody of the stone is the one held liable if damage results — though the precise *halachic* category varies depending on the facts. If the stone falls off the *chamar*'s wagon without being dropped from his hand directly, this is no longer straightforwardly *adam hamazik* — one begins to wonder whether it is *eish* or another *av nezikin* altogether, and whose stone it is in the first place. If the stone belongs to the public — if the entire construction project is a communal commission — then individual workers lack ownership, and the question of which *av nezikin* applies becomes genuinely complex.

### Joint Final Stage

The final line of the *braita* is the most striking: *vehiniach even al hadimus v'hizika, kulan chayavin leshalem* — once the stone has been placed upon the building itself, on the top row of stones, if damage results, *all* of the workers are jointly liable. This is surprising. The quarrier who long ago removed the stone from the mountain must now pay? If we are looking for a specific act of negligence — someone who handled the stone badly — the question is who that person is. And if nobody was negligent and it is simply an *ones*, then presumably nobody should be liable at all. Yet the *braita* says all of them pay jointly.

### Kablanut Distinction

The *Gemara* immediately raises a contradiction from another *braita*: *acharon chayav v'kulan pturim* — only the last person in the chain is *chayav*, and all the others are exempt. This resembles the principle from the case of multiple *shomrim* watching a well: when responsibility passes from person to person, it is the last custodian who is *chayav*. The *Gemara* resolves: *lo kashya, kan biskirut, kan bekablanut* — there is no contradiction, because the cases differ in their employment structure. *Biskirut* — hired labor — means each worker has been engaged individually for his specific task. In that configuration, responsibility is personal and sequential: whoever currently holds the stone is the responsible party, and when custody passes, so does liability. The last person before the stone is placed is therefore the one *chayav*. *Bekablanut* — contract work — means that the entire crew has been hired collectively to complete the whole job. In that configuration, the group as a whole is conceptually engaged for the entire project, and so once the stone is placed and no individual can be identified as the responsible party, they all share corporate liability.

### Corporate Responsibility

Rashi makes this explicit: *b'kablanut, kulan chayavin, heicha delo naflu miyad echad mehen, de'al kulan lishmor she'tehei yoshevet yafe* — when the stone did not fall from the hand of any one of them specifically, the duty to ensure it was properly placed rested on all of them jointly. This is, as Rashi frames it, a shared obligation of oversight, not merely individual physical custody. Whether *miyad* is meant literally — if it can be shown to have fallen from someone's hands directly, it reverts to individual *adam hamazik* liability — or whether Rashi means simply that once no single individual's negligence can be isolated, the joint standard applies, is itself a question worth probing.

### Strict Liability Parallel

One way to make sense of this is to view the *kablanut* case not as an ordinary application of the *arba avot nezikin* but as something closer to what modern law would call strict liability: a recognition that certain activities — particularly large-scale construction in a public thoroughfare — are inherently hazardous to the public, and that therefore the ordinary calculus of individual fault gives way to collective responsibility. The public hazard created by a building project in the *reshus harabim* may warrant a different framework, one in which the contractor-entity as a whole assumes the risk regardless of which worker can be pinpointed as the proximate cause. This reading would treat the *braita* as a deliberate carve-out from the standard *Bava Kamma* categories — and it is, as noted, a substantial *chiddush*, since *halacha* does not ordinarily recognize anything resembling a corporate entity or shared *shutafus* of this kind.

---

## Two Gardens

### Case Setup

The *mishnah* now introduces a new scenario: *shtei ginos zo agav zo, v'hayerak baintayim* — two gardens, one above the other, with vegetation growing in the space between them. Reuven owns the upper parcel with its soil; Shimon owns the lower parcel with its airspace directly beneath the overhang. A vegetable is growing — presumably from wild seed — rooted in Reuven's earth but extending into Shimon's airspace. To whom does it belong?

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rabbi Meir rules: *shel elyon* — it belongs to the upper owner, Reuven, from whose ground it grows. Rabbi Meir supports this: *im yirtzeh elyon likach et afaro, ein kan yerak* — Reuven could simply excavate his soil entirely, and the vegetable would cease to exist. This demonstrates that Reuven controls the very substrate from which the vegetable draws its life. The vegetable is his.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda rules: *shel tachton* — it belongs to the lower owner, Shimon, in whose airspace it grows. He counters symmetrically: *im yirtzeh tachton lemalot et ginato, ein kan yerak* — Shimon could fill his airspace with earth, and the vegetable would equally be destroyed. Both parties control the fate of the vegetable.

Rabbi Meir acknowledges this symmetry but draws his conclusion differently: *me'achar she'shneihem yecholim limchot zeh al zeh, ro'im meiheichan yerek zeh chai* — since each has the power to prevent the vegetable's existence, we ask the decisive question: from where does the vegetable actually live? And the answer is: from the ground. The roots draw nutrients from Reuven's earth, and that is what sustains it. Therefore it is Reuven's.

One might note that the case is somewhat misleadingly framed if the vegetation grows above ground — a tomato, for example, on a vine — because in that case the physical presence of the desired produce is entirely in Shimon's airspace, not merely rooted in Reuven's earth. The *mishnah* does not draw this distinction, but the *Gemara* will address it shortly through Rava's intervention.

### Rava's Distinction

Rava clarifies the scope of the dispute: *be'ikaro kulei alma lo pligi de'elyon havei, ki pligi benofo* — regarding what grows below ground, all opinions agree that it belongs to Reuven. If it is a carrot, there is no disagreement; its edible portion is physically located in Reuven's earth and draws from Reuven's earth, and so it is unambiguously his. The dispute is specifically about *nofo* — the foliage, the above-ground portion, which is physically present in Shimon's airspace while drawing its life from Reuven's ground. That is the genuine contested case, and it is to that case that the competing principles of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda apply.

---

## Roots vs. Location

### Nof After Ikar

The *Gemara* now articulates the underlying principles. Rabbi Meir holds *shadi nof batar ikar* — one "throws" the canopy after the roots. Whatever grows from a root system is legally identified with the location of those roots, regardless of where the above-ground growth physically extends. The produce or foliage is deemed to belong to the same domain as the roots from which it springs.

This principle has broad application in the *Gemara*. A classic example: a tree whose roots are in *Chutz LaAretz* but whose trunk and branches extend into *Eretz Yisrael*, bearing fruit in *Eretz Yisrael*'s airspace. Does the fruit belong to *Eretz Yisrael* or to *Chutz LaAretz* for purposes of *ma'asrot* or similar obligations? Do we say *shadi nof batar ikar* and attribute the fruit to the location of the roots in *Chutz LaAretz*? Or do we say the fruit grew in *Eretz Yisrael*'s airspace and is therefore subject to *Eretz Yisrael*'s obligations? Another playful application: a fugitive fleeing to an *ir miklat* jumps into a tree — is he considered to have entered the city of refuge if the trunk is within its boundaries but his body is suspended at a height, or if the roots are within while he hangs in the tree over the border? The answer may well depend on what legal question is being asked.

In our case, the question is ownership. Rabbi Meir applies *shadi nof batar ikar* to conclude that since the roots are in Reuven's ground, the above-ground growth belongs to Reuven as well.

### Yehuda Rejects

Rabbi Yehuda rejects *shadi nof batar ikar* in this context. For Rabbi Yehuda, the above-ground foliage is physically present in Shimon's airspace — and Shimon owns that airspace. The produce grew there; it is his.

### Tree Braita

The *Gemara* then introduces a *braita* that is parallel in some respects, though Tosafot notes it is not an exact analogue. The case: one person owns a tree and another person owns the land in which that tree is planted — the tree-buyer has no land rights whatsoever. New growth sprouts from the tree's root system. *Hayotzei min hageza umin hasharashim, harei elu shel ba'al hakarka, divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir holds that whether the new growth emerges from the trunk or from the roots, it belongs to the owner of the land. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: *min hageza, shel ba'al ha'ilan* — growth from the trunk belongs to the tree-owner, since it resembles the fruit and produce of the tree, which he owns; *min hasharashim, shel ba'al hakarka* — growth from the roots belongs to the land-owner, since the roots are part of the land.

The parallel to our *mishnah* is not perfect, as Tosafot observes: in the *braita*'s case, the tree-buyer has no air rights at all, whereas in our *mishnah*, Shimon does own his airspace. Still, a family resemblance is apparent: Rabbi Meir tends to root everything in the land — defaulting to the land-owner — while Rabbi Yehuda is more attentive to what grows above ground and to rights in the space above the earth.

### Orlah Parallel

A similar debate appears in the context of *orlah*. If a tree produces a new shoot — either from the trunk or from the roots — is it subject to the *orlah* prohibition as a new tree, or is it treated as a branch of the existing tree and therefore exempt? *Ilan hayotzei min hageza umin hasharashim chayav ba'orlah, divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir holds that either way, it is a new tree subject to *orlah*. This reflects the same orientation: growth emerging from below, from the root system or trunk, is treated as a new entity growing from the ground. *Rabbi Yehuda omer: min hageza, patur; umin hasharashim, chayav* — from the trunk, it is like a branch or fruit of the existing tree and is exempt; from the roots, it is a new tree subject to *orlah*.

### Both Cases Needed

The *Gemara* asks: why is it necessary to state both disputes — the *orlah* case and the ownership case? *Tzrichi*. Were only the ownership case taught, one might say Rabbi Yehuda there awards the growth to the tree-owner as a leniency in a monetary matter — he prefers to recognize the tree-owner's rights — but in the realm of *issur*, where *orlah* is a prohibition, perhaps he would agree with Rabbi Meir and treat the growth as a new tree subject to *orlah*. Conversely, were only the *orlah* case taught, one might think Rabbi Meir is strict only because it is an *issur*, but in monetary law he might concede to Rabbi Yehuda. Both cases are therefore necessary, as each ruling might otherwise seem to be the product of its particular legal context rather than a consistent underlying principle.

---

## Access Determines

### Rabbi Shimon Rule

Rabbi Shimon's approach departs from both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's conceptual frameworks and grounds itself in a physical and practical criterion: *kol she'ha'elyon yachol lifshot et yado velitol, harei zeh shelo, vehashe'ar shel tachton* — whatever the upper owner can reach out and take, it is his; the remainder belongs to the lower owner. Ownership is determined not by the abstract question of whether roots or airspace governs, but by the simple, immediate fact of physical access.

### Access Question

The school of Rabbi Yannai immediately qualifies this: access must be possible without endangering oneself — *ubvilvad shelo ye'anes*. One cannot say "if I dangled from a rope I could reach it" and thereby claim ownership. Unaided, reasonable physical access is the standard. A question then arises — attributed in one version to Rabbi Yannai, and in another to Rabbi Yirmiya: *magiya l'nofo v'eino magiya l'ikaro, magiya l'ikaro v'eino magiya l'nofo, mah?* What if Reuven can reach the above-ground foliage but not the underground root, or can reach the root but not the desired produce? What counts as the determinative "access" when the roots and the edible portion are in different locations?

### Teiqu

*Teiku* — the *Gemara* leaves this unresolved.

### Halacha Ruling

Notwithstanding the *teiku*, Efrayim Safra, the student of Reish Lakish, transmits a ruling in his teacher's name: *halacha k'Rabbi Shimon* — the law follows Rabbi Shimon's physical access standard. This is perhaps somewhat surprising: of the three positions, Rabbi Shimon's feels the most pragmatic and the least conceptually grounded. The debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda rests on a genuine and interesting theoretical question — does ownership of foliage follow the roots or the airspace? Rabbi Shimon sidesteps that question entirely in favor of a practical test. Yet Reish Lakish rules like him — perhaps precisely because, given the theoretical deadlock, pragmatism is the most workable resolution.

---

## Shabur Malka Story

### Praise of Shimon

The *Gemara* then reports: *va'amru kamei d'Shavor Malka* — they conveyed this ruling before *Shavor Malka*, and he responded: *Aperion namtei leRabbi Shimon* — words of praise and approbation for Rabbi Shimon.

### Rashi on Identity

Rashi addresses the identity of *Shavor Malka*. He writes: *li nireh Shavor Malka mamash, u'melech Paras haya, u'baki b'dinim* — in Rashi's view, this refers to the actual Persian king, *Shapur*, who was known to take an interest in law and had a close relationship with Shmuel. The *Gemara* elsewhere records conversations between *Shapur* and Shmuel. On Rashi's reading, someone shared Rabbi Shimon's position with this Persian king — not as a *halachic* ruling binding on him, but as an intellectual curiosity, a window into Jewish legal reasoning — and the king responded with admiration. Rashi notes an alternative reading: since Shmuel was so close to the real *Shavor Malka*, he was sometimes himself called by that name in the *Gemara*. But Rashi rejects this: *tmiha li* — it is difficult. If it were Shmuel, what would it mean to say "they told him" about a position in the *mishnah*? Would Shmuel not already know what Rabbi Shimon holds? Even granting that perhaps what they told Shmuel was specifically the ruling of Reish Lakish via Efrayim Safra, Shmuel could have praised Rabbi Shimon on his own merits without waiting to hear that Reish Lakish had ruled accordingly. And notably, it is Rabbi Shimon who is praised, not Reish Lakish. Rashi therefore maintains that *Shavor Malka* here refers to the Persian king himself.

### Afiryon Meaning

The word *aperion* — or in alternate textual traditions, *apria* — admits of several interpretations. Rashi reads the *yod-nun* suffix as possessive — "our" — and understands the phrase as: our favor, our acknowledgment of esteem, should go to Rabbi Shimon; *yikabel chen me'itanu al davar zeh*. The *Aruch*, however, preserves a different *girsa*: *hava lei apria leRabbi Shimon*, reading *apria* as a cognate for something like a bier or litter, and glossing it as a Persian expression equivalent to *yashar kocho* — well done, strength to him. Other versions read it as a term of fruitfulness, from the root of *ben porat Yosef* — may scholars and sages as wise as he flourish and multiply. The *psukim* also offer a suggestive resonance: *aperion asa lo ha'melech Shlomo* — the litter that King Solomon made for himself — though the *Gemara* does not explicitly invoke that verse here.

### Theological Note

There is something arresting about the fact that the final words of the entire tractate of *Bava Metzia* come from the mouth of a non-Jewish Persian king. Is there a message embedded in this editorial choice? *Dinei mamonot* — monetary law — is territory that secular legal systems occupy as well. Unlike prohibitions such as *lo talin pe'ulat sachir* or *ribbit*, which are unambiguously *mitzvot* grounded in *pesukim*, much of the commercial law of *Bava Metzia* and *Bava Batra* finds analogues in every civilized society. *Bava Batra*, which we are about to begin, is notable for having almost no *pasuk* to anchor its vast legal corpus; it is largely the *chachamim* developing a framework for interpersonal and commercial relations — not so much elaborating *mitzvot* as building a jurisprudence. How do we understand such law as *Torah*? Is it the same religious act to study a chapter on *nedunyon* or *shtarot* as it is to study *hilchos shechita* or *Shabbos*?

### Dine Mamon Status

The *Torah* itself seems to anticipate this question. *Rak am chacham v'navon ha'goy ha'gadol hazeh, ki mi goy gadol asher lo chukim umishpatim tzadikim* — the nations of the world will look upon Israel's statutes and judgments and recognize them as just. The endorsement of a foreign king for a *halachic* position is not presented as something embarrassing or incidental; it may be presented as a kind of vindication — that these laws, even when not tied to explicit *mitzvot*, carry an inherent justice recognizable to any thoughtful observer. The ending of *Bava Metzia* with such an endorsement may be a deliberate statement: that *dinei mamon* are not merely pragmatic rabbinic constructions, but laws whose inner logic reflects a genuine and universal *tzedek*.

---

## Conclusion

### Hadran Alach

*Hadran alach HaBayit VeHaAliya, u'salika lach Maseches Bava Metzia.* We conclude *Bava Metzia* and turn, beginning in our next session, to *Bava Batra*.

---

---

# Bava Batra 2

## Intro: Structure & Themes

### Seder Nezikin Overview

We begin *Bava Batra* today, the last of the three *masechtot* that make up *Seder Nezikin* — though what we now call three tractates was originally a single *masechet Nezikin*, thirty *perakim* long, broken into three sections of ten each. *Bava Batra* simply means "the last gate," and there are indeed tractates named *Bava Kamma*, *Bava Metzia*, and *Bava Batra* also within *Kelim* in *Taharos*, which likewise contains thirty *perakim*. The *gemara* debates whether to treat these as one *masechet* or three, but it seems clear that initially the material was conceptualized as a single very long tractate with three distinct parts.

### Three Masechtot Structure

In terms of identity, *Bava Kamma* and *Bava Batra* have a clearer thematic character than *Bava Metzia* — perhaps the inevitable lot of the middle. *Bava Kamma* was entirely about torts: animals that damage, property that causes damage, people who injure other people or destroy property, theft, and burglary. *Bava Batra*, by contrast, fits largely within what the Rambam categorizes as *kinyan* — matters of acquisition — though its opening *perakim* deal with *hilchos shecheinim*, the laws governing neighbors.

### Thematic Organization

The final chapter of *Bava Metzia* served as a lead-in to the themes we now take up: what I may do on my property, how carefully I must ensure that my activities do not impinge on yours, and the distances required to keep certain damaging activities away from a neighbor's domain. The opening *perek* of *Bava Batra*, *HaShutafin*, concerns what happens when parties attempt to divide shared property. The second *perek* continues the theme of neighbors. Then comes the third *perek*, *Chazkat HaBatim* — the one classically studied in *yeshivos* — dealing with the principle that three years of unprotested presence on someone else's property can serve as evidence of a prior purchase, even without documentation. As the Gemara explains, if no one protested for three years, one may plausibly claim that documentation need no longer be preserved. Notably, if one openly admits to having no purchase agreement, three years of presence alone does not confer ownership — a point that is frequently confused.

From there the tractate turns from neighbor-law to questions of ownership and transaction. The fourth, fifth, and sixth *perakim* address the laws of sales: *HaMocher et HaBayit* (what is implicitly included when one sells a house), *HaMocher et HaSefinah* (what is implicit in the sale of a boat), and *HaMocher Peirot* (selling fruit, honest weights and measures, and liability when goods spoil). The final three *perakim* — *Yesh Nochalim*, *Mi she'meit*, and *Get Pashut* — deal with death and the transfer of property: the order of inheritance, deathbed bequests, and wills. Thus the tractate flows from neighbor-law through the laws of buying and selling to the transfer of ownership through death, a coherent arc across all ten *perakim*.

Looking ahead, the next *masechet* is *Sanhedrin*, followed by *Makkot*. One can think of the thirty-*perek* *masechet* of *Nezikin* as laying out the civil law — the rules governing property and interaction between people — while *Sanhedrin* establishes the court system that adjudicates it.

### Pedagogical Challenges

One interesting feature of *Bava Batra* is that almost none of its content can be anchored directly to a *pasuk* in the *Torah*. When we reach *Yesh Nochalim*, there is indeed a scriptural basis for the order of inheritance — though that *perek* is immediately followed by the laws of deathbed bequests that in many ways subvert that order. There is also some connection to *Torah* law in the provisions about honest weights and measures as they arise in the context of *mechirah*. But the bulk of this *masechet* represents *Chazal* legislating the ordering of society entirely on their own authority — not as interpretation of a *mitzvah*, and not merely as a safeguard, but as substantive, original law. For some learners, this is precisely what makes it exciting: it demonstrates the creative legislative power of *Chazal* acting in their own right. For others, the absence of a running conversation with a *pasuk* or *mitzvah* of the *Torah* makes for a less engaging experience.

### Rashi Ends, Rashbam Begi…

The density of *Bava Batra* is also shaped by its unique commentary situation. At the beginning of the third *perek* — specifically at 29a — Rashi's commentary ends and the Rashbam takes over. Right in the middle of the Rashi column one finds the notation *ad kan peirash Rashi zatzal*, and then *mikan ve'eilach peirash Rabbeinu Shmuel bar Meir*, the Rashbam, who was Rashi's grandson. An earlier printed edition, it is noted in the margin, actually read *nidpas kan met Rashi* — "printed here: Rashi died" — though this is not to be taken literally as meaning he died mid-composition of this tractate. There is extensive scholarship on the multiple editions of Rashi's *gemara* commentary, which is why the Rashi found in the Rif does not always match the Rashi on the *gemara* — the former is likely an earlier edition. In other *masechtot*, what appears as Rashi is actually the Rivan or another rishon. In any case, something about the state of Rashi's commentary to *Bava Batra* remains incomplete or unrevised.

The Rashbam is a fascinating and somewhat paradoxical commentator. On the *Torah*, he is even terser than Rashi, deeply oriented toward *pshat*. In the context of the *gemara*, however, he was among the first generation of the *Baalei HaTosafot* — the older brother of Rabbeinu Tam, who became the central driving force of the *tosafot* enterprise. The *tosafot* method is not simply to explain what a line of *gemara* means, smoothing over occasional difficulties, but constantly to compare it with other *sugyot*, working through all the tensions that arise when one looks across the tractates. The Rashbam blends Rashi and *Tosafot* in a way that, while intellectually rich, creates a distinctive pedagogical challenge: one wants a clear *pshat* of the *gemara* before the problematizing begins, but here the *pshat* and the cross-tractate complications arrive simultaneously. The practical effect is also that every page in the latter part of *Bava Batra* carries two major commentaries — *Tosafot* and Rashbam — making the individual *dapim* shorter.

### Word & Daf Analysis

*Bava Batra* is the longest tractate in *dapim*, running to 175 *daf*, yet the number of words per page is relatively low — in part because of the dense, thick *sugyot* that generate large *Tosafot*, in part because of the dual presence of *Tosafot* and Rashbam. There is a well-known story that the Vilna Gaon was asked which tractate contains the most words: he reportedly answered that if one takes everything as printed, it is *Berachos*; if one factors in the variant readings he himself and the Bach would add, it is *Shabbos*; and if one considers what he would add and the Bach would remove, it is *Bava Batra* — encompassing all possibilities across the spectrum of textual variants. A computer search could easily resolve this today, but regardless, while *Bava Batra* is certainly the longest tractate in *dapim*, it is genuinely uncertain whether it is the longest in terms of raw word count. For *daf yomi* study, this means there are somewhat fewer words to cover per sitting — leaving more opportunity, perhaps, to explore depth rather than merely to traverse the surface.
