## Mishnah: Wall Division

### Partners & Shared Yard

The *mishnah* opens: *hashutafim* — partners who jointly own a *chatzer*, a yard. The scenario is that two people each have homes opening onto a shared yard, and they now wish to divide it and, in the course of that division, erect a wall separating their respective portions. The Mishnah's opening word — *sheratzu la'asos mechitza be-chatzer*, "they agreed to make a *mechitza* in the yard" — already raises a question: does *mechitza* here mean a noun (a physical wall) or a concept (a division)? That ambiguity will occupy the *gemara* at length, but for now we continue.

### Wall in Middle

The *mishnah* continues: *bonim et hakotel be'emtza* — they build the wall in the middle. This does not mean they divide the yard geometrically down the center. What *be'emtza* means is that wherever the property line runs between the two parties, the wall's thickness straddles that line equally — half of the wall's footprint on one person's side, half on the other's. The underlying division of the yard may reflect different proportions of ownership, but the wall itself sits symmetrically across whatever that dividing line turns out to be.

### Keminhag Hamedina

The *mishnah* then states: *makom shenahagu livnot gevil gazis kfisim leveinim, bonim* — in a place where the community standard is to build with a particular type of material, one builds accordingly. This principle — *hakol keminhag hamedina*, everything follows the local custom — governs not only the choice of building materials but also the thickness of the wall, and consequently how much of each party's yard is consumed by the wall's footprint. If one agreed to build a wall and the local standard was a particular material, the implicit understanding of the agreement is shaped by that norm, unless explicitly stipulated otherwise.

### Building Materials

The *mishnah* then specifies the materials and their corresponding thicknesses. *Gevil* — unsmoothed, uncarved stone — requires a wall six *tfachim* wide in total, each party contributing three *tfachim* of their yard. *Gazis* — hewn, smoothed stone — requires five *tfachim* total, each contributing two and a half. *Kfisim* — half-bricks, which are bound together with plaster in the middle and therefore wider than whole bricks — require four *tfachim* total, each contributing two. *Leveinim* — whole bricks — require three *tfachim* total, each contributing one and a half. The differing widths matter practically: a party might be willing to pay for materials but unwilling to surrender more of their yard than anticipated, so the standard determines both the type of material and the spatial footprint, unless otherwise agreed.

### Presumption of Equality

From this flows a legal presumption. If a wall has stood between two properties for generations, with no record of how it was originally constructed or who contributed what, the *mishnah* establishes that we assume the standard was followed: each party contributed equally to the materials and equally to the footprint. Therefore: *lefikach im nafal hakotel, hamakom veha'avanim shel sheneihem* — if the wall falls down, both the space beneath and the stones are presumed to belong equally to both parties, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary.

### Gardens vs. Fields

The *mishnah* then extends the discussion: *vechen begina* — similarly in a garden (*gina*). There is an implicit hierarchy of privacy here. A *chatzer* — a private yard adjacent to one's home — is the space where one performs semi-private activities: resting, spending leisure time. A *gina*, a vegetable garden, occupies an intermediate position. A *bikah* — a valley or wheat field — is an open agricultural space where no expectation of privacy obtains.

The *mishnah* states: *makom shenahagu ligdor, mechayivin oto* — in a place where the norm is to build a wall (as is standard between neighboring gardens), you may *compel* the other party to build it. But *aval bivikah, makom shenahagu shelo ligdor, ein mechayivin oto* — in a field, where walls are not the norm, you cannot compel the other party. There may be some demarcating line to mark the property boundary, but there is no wall and no obligation to build one.

### Solo Building & Chazit

However, the *mishnah* continues, if one party wishes to build even in a context where it cannot be compelled — *ela im rotzeh, kones l'toch shelo uvoneh* — one may go ahead, build entirely on one's own land, at one's own expense. This raises a practical problem: the general presumption is that any standing wall is equally owned by both neighbors. How does a party who built entirely alone, at their own cost, on their own land, preserve evidence of that fact decades or generations later? The *mishnah* answers: *ve'oseh chazit mibachutz* — one makes a *chazit*, a marker, on the *outside* of the wall. The *chazit* is placed on the neighbor's side — the side the neighbor faces — so that the building party's side of the wall is finished and polished, while the outer face shows the structural marks of sole construction. This is an interesting inversion of contemporary practice, where convention requires that the finished face of a fence face the neighbor. Here, the rougher or structurally distinctive outer face serves as evidence that the wall was built entirely by the person on whose land it stands. *Lefikach im nafal hakosel, hamakom veha'avanim shelo* — therefore, if the wall falls, both the space and the stones belong entirely to the one who built it.

### Both Agree, Double Chazit

The final clause addresses a different case: *im asu mida'at sheneihem* — if both parties agreed to build a wall in a place where it would not normally be built, such as a *bikah*. In that case, *bonim et hakotel be'emtza ve'osim chazit mikan umikan* — the wall is built in the middle, and a *chazit* is placed on both sides. *Lefikach im nafal hakosel, hamakom veha'avanim shel sheneihem* — if it falls, both the stones and the space belong equally to both.

This raises a natural question: why place a *chazit* on both sides rather than on neither side? In the standard *chatzer* case, no *chazit* is needed because the community norm already establishes equal ownership. Here, in a *bikah* where there is no norm, one might simply say that the absence of a *chazit* on either side signals equality. The *mishnah* nonetheless requires the double *chazit*, a point we will have reason to return to.

---

## Tosafot: Minhag Limits

### Tosafot Question

Before turning to the *gemara*, there is an important *tosafot* that demands attention. The *mishnah* opened with the sweeping principle *hakol keminhag hamedina* — everything is governed by local custom — and then proceeded to enumerate specific building materials and their corresponding widths. *Tosafot* asks the obvious question: if the principle truly is that everything follows local custom, why enumerate the specifics at all? Whatever the norm happens to be, that is simply the norm — why list *gevil*, *gazis*, *kfisim*, and *leveinim* with their respective measurements? One might respond that the list concretizes the abstract principle, but that answer is incomplete, and *Tosafot* presses further.

### Rabbeinu Tam Balance

Rabbeinu Tam's answer, found at the end of the *tosafot* on *gevil*, is that *minhag hamedina* does not govern without limit. *Minhag* operates within a range bounded by objective minimums and maximums. If the local practice were to use *gazis* blocks of eight *tfachim* — far beyond the standard measurement — one could not demand that. The point of specifying the particular measurements is to establish that even where *minhag* rules, it does so only within parameters set by objective norms.

### Minhag Hedyot

Conversely, at the lower end, Rabbeinu Tam writes: *venira leRabbeinu Tam dedavka behutza vedafna* — the minimum legitimate division is something like *hutza vedafna*, thin planks or similar light material. *Aval pachos mikan, afilu nahagu, minhag hedyot hu* — anything thinner than that, even if it were the local practice, is a *minhag hedyot*, a practice beneath the threshold of legitimacy. *Minhag hedyot* is perhaps a more diplomatic formulation than *minhag shtus*, but the point is the same: not every widespread practice rises to the level of a norm that can legally govern an agreement. The conclusion follows: *umuchach mikan deyesh minhagim she'ein lismoch aleihem, afilu heicha ditnan hakol keminhag hamedina* — there exist practices on which one may not rely, even where the general rule is that everything follows local custom.

### Minhag & Standards

This observation opens onto a broader conceptual point. There is an important distinction between two different uses of the word *minhag*. On one hand, *hakol keminhag hamedina* refers to the norms and standards that implicitly govern commercial and social arrangements — the background conventions that shape what parties to an agreement intend unless they explicitly stipulate otherwise. This is not quite "custom" in the sense we usually mean; it is more like the standard practice of a trade or a community that becomes, in effect, an implicit term of every relevant agreement. On the other hand, when we ordinarily speak of *minhagim* — customs like *kapparos* on *Erev Yom Kippur* or eating *milchigs* on *Shavuos* — we mean practices that, once established, carry their own normative weight and create obligations for a community or its descendants. Rabbeinu Tam, famously skeptical of *minhag* as an independent source of obligation (he is said to have noted that the letters of *minhag* are the same as those of *gehinnom*), is making a point that applies across both registers: in monetary matters, *minhag* must be bounded by objective standards, and in the realm of religious practice, *minhagim* that have no rational foundation or that conflict with *halacha* cannot simply entrench themselves by force of repetition. There must be some framework within which *minhag* operates and beyond which it cannot legitimately reach.

---

## Gemara: Compulsion Quest…

### Mechitza: Noun or Verb

The *gemara* opens by noting: *savruah mai mechitza guda* — the initial assumption was that when the *mishnah* said the partners agreed to make a *mechitza*, this referred to a physical wall (*guda*). On this reading, the *mishnah* is saying: they agreed to build a wall, and here is how the wall must be built. The implication would be that building a wall requires agreement — one cannot be compelled to build a wall unilaterally.

But the *gemara* first pauses to confirm that *mechitza* is in fact a noun referring to a physical structure. The word is not so commonly used in *tannaitic* literature as to be self-evident. The *gemara* therefore turns to a *braita* for confirmation.

### Braita: Vineyard Wall

The *braita* cited: *mechitzat hakerem shenifretza* — a wall (*mechitza*) between a vineyard and a wheat field that has been breached. The relevance of this case lies in the laws of *kilayim*: grapevines and wheat planted in close proximity create a prohibited mixture, but a wall between them allows them to stand immediately adjacent without violation. When the wall breaks open, *kilayim* concerns arise. The *braita* states that one says to the vineyard owner *omer lo gdor* — repair the wall — because by the logic of *kilayim*, it is the vineyard that is understood to encroach: the Torah requires four *amos* of clearance for working around vines, so the vines define the spatial need, making the vineyard owner the *mazik*. The *braita* continues: if the wall falls again, you tell him again to repair it; if he despairs and does not bother — *nityaesh mimenu velo gadar* — it immediately becomes *kilayim* and he is liable for damages to the wheat field.

The critical point for our purposes is simply that *mechitza* in this *braita* unambiguously refers to a physical wall. *Tosafot* raises a separate question about whether the resulting damage might be *hezek she'eino nikkar*, but that need not detain us here.

### Agreement Required

Returning to the *mishnah*: on the straightforward reading, *ta'ama deratza* — the reason a wall is built is that the parties agreed to it. *Ha lo ratza, ein mechayvin oso* — had one party not agreed, no wall could be compelled. The consequence is stark: *alma, hezek re'iyah lav shemei hezek* — evidently, damage through sight (*hezek re'iyah*) is not legally recognized as a *hezek*.

### Hezek Re'iyah Defined

It is worth pausing to clarify what *hezek re'iyah* means and does not mean. It does not refer — at least not primarily — to the metaphysical concern of *ayin hara*, the evil eye; that is a separate idea that will arise later. *Hezek re'iyah* refers to what we would call the right to privacy: if I can observe you engaged in activities in your private yard that you would naturally wish to conduct unobserved, is that considered an injury to you?

Notice that the *halachic* framing is deliberate and consequential. The discourse is not cast in terms of "rights" — your right to privacy, my right to gaze — but in terms of injury: am I *damaging* you by observing you in your private space? This framing matters for several reasons. If we say I am causing you *hezek*, then as a potential *mazik* I bear the obligation to prevent that damage; I must contribute to the wall. If we say it is merely your right, one might argue that the obligation falls on you — if you feel exposed, build your own wall. The framework of *hezek* also raises the question of *ha-mazik le-harchik et atzmo* versus *ha-nizak le-harchik et atzmo* — the classic debate from the end of *Bava Metzia* about whether the one causing damage or the one damaged bears the primary responsibility to create distance. By framing *hezek re'iyah* in terms of injury, the *gemara* situates it within this existing conceptual structure.

So: if *hezek re'iyah* is not a recognized *hezek*, then I cannot demand you participate in building a wall, and the *mishnah*'s requirement of agreement makes sense. You looking into my yard is simply not a legal injury to me.

### Alt: Division Reading

The *gemara* then proposes an alternative reading: *ve'eima mechitza pelugta* — perhaps *mechitza* means not a wall but a division, as in *vat'hi mechtzat ha'edah* (the division of the community's spoils of war in the *pasuk*). On this reading, the *mishnah* would be saying: partners who agreed to *divide* their property — once division is agreed upon, you can compel the other party to build a wall. The wall-building would be a consequence of the division, not something requiring separate agreement. This would mean *hezek re'iyah shemei hezek* — once you divide, the visual intrusion becomes a recognized damage that can be legally addressed.

### Mechitza = Wall

The *gemara* rejects this alternative. The *mishnah* uses *mechitza* as the object of *ratzu la'asot* ("they wished to make"), treating it as a noun — a physical thing to be constructed. Moreover, the *mishnah* then says *bonim et hakotel* — "they build the *kotel*" — switching to the word *kotel*. If *mechitza* were the noun (the wall they agreed to build), the subsequent sentence should have said *bonim oto* ("they build it"), referring back to the *mechitza*. The shift to *kotel* suggests the *mechitza* is not the object being built but a conceptual division, and *kotel* is what is separately constructed. Or alternatively: had the *mishnah* used *bonin oto* throughout, we might have thought a mere *mispis* — small pegs marking a boundary line — would suffice. By switching to *kotel*, the *mishnah* emphasizes that the structure must be a proper wall. In either case, *mechitza* most naturally reads as a noun meaning wall (*guda*), and the *gemara* confirms this is the correct interpretation.

### Building Be'emtza

The *gemara* then asks: *pshita* — is it not obvious that if both parties agreed to build the wall, it goes in the middle? Why does the *mishnah* need to state this? The *gemara* answers: *lo tzricha d'kadim chad ve'ratzei l'chavreih* — it is necessary for the case where one party initiated and eventually persuaded the other. In that scenario, the persuaded party might argue: *ki itratzai lach be'avira* — I agreed to the wall in terms of airspace or building costs, but *be'tashmishta lo itratzai lach* — I never agreed to give up part of my property for the wall's footprint; I assumed the whole structure would be built on your land. The *mishnah* therefore establishes *kamashma lan* that without explicit stipulation, once one agrees to build a wall, everything — materials, footprint, ownership — is assumed to go equally down the middle. The persuasion of one party by another does not alter the legal default.

The underlying conclusion remains: *hezek re'iyah lav shemei hezek* — since agreement is required to build a wall, visual intrusion is not a legally recognized injury.

---

## Chatzer vs. Ginah

### Ginah Compulsion

The *gemara* immediately challenges this conclusion: *tashma, vechen begina* — take note of the *mishnah*'s statement that *similarly in a garden* (*gina*), where the norm is to build a wall, one can *compel* the other party. If *hezek re'iyah* is not a recognized *hezek*, on what basis can compulsion be exercised in a *gina*?

### Ayin Hara Damage

The *gemara* proposes: *gina shani* — a garden is different, and the difference lies in a ruling of Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav Huna in the name of Rav: *asur le'adam la'amod bisde chaveiro bisha'ah she'hi omedet bekamoteha* — it is forbidden to stand in another's field and gaze at it while the grain stands tall and full. The concern is *ayin hara*: jealous observation causes real damage to the produce. The harm is not merely psychological or social, it is understood as a tangible injury to the crops themselves. In the case of a *gina*, therefore, one party's ability to observe the other's vegetables constitutes a genuine *hezek*: the gaze can damage the produce through *ayin hara*. That provides a ground for compulsion in the garden context — it is not merely a privacy concern but an actual risk of agricultural harm.

The *gemara*'s reasoning can thus be parsed as follows: *hezek re'iyah* in the sense of someone merely seeing me relaxing in my yard is not a recognized injury. But *hezek re'iyah* in the sense of someone gazing enviously at my thriving vegetable garden — causing *ayin hara* — may be a genuine *hezek*, sufficient to support compulsion.

### Ginah Exception

The *gemara* then attempts to confine *gina* as a special exception on account of *ayin hara*, preserving the general rule that *hezek re'iyah lav shemei hezek* in other contexts. If *gina* can be explained by the specific danger of *ayin hara*, then the apparently compulsory norm of the garden does not undermine the basic principle established by the *chatzer* case. The analogy offered by *Tosafot* is instructive: in a wheat field people do not congregate and observe regularly the way they do around a neighboring garden, so the *ayin hara* concern is not triggered in the same way, and there no compulsion is possible.

### Fallen Chatzer Wall

The *gemara* then cites the next *mishnah*: *kosel chatzer shenafal, mechayivin oto livnot ad arba amos* — if the wall of a *chatzer* falls down, one may compel the other party to rebuild it, up to a height of four *amos*. This appears to be strong evidence that *hezek re'iyah shemei hezek* — one can compel wall-building even in a *chatzer*, not merely in a *gina*.

### Nafal Shani

The *gemara* deflects: *nafal shani* — the case of a fallen wall is different. When a wall pre-existed and then collapsed, the analysis changes. The *mishnah*'s point was not to teach us that *hezek re'iyah* generally supports compulsion; its *chiddush* was the upper limit of four *amos* — one cannot be compelled to rebuild a wall taller than it was or taller than four *amos*, even if it previously stood at ten *amos*. The basic ability to compel rebuilding in the case of a pre-existing wall does not prove anything about compulsion in the absence of a prior wall.

### Habituation & Real Damage

But this raises a further question: *why* is the fallen wall different? One might have thought the answer lies in contract law — there had been an implicit prior agreement, a kind of ongoing arrangement between the neighbors, and rebuilding the wall is simply living up to that earlier understanding. Rashi does appear to lean in this direction. But *Tosafot* offers a more conceptually interesting answer: *she'hurgelu la'asos devar hatznei'ah bechatzer veyilmedu zeh mizeh* — because the parties had been living with that wall, they had grown accustomed to conducting private activities in their yard with an expectation of privacy. Once that habituation is established, the removal of the wall genuinely *does* cause *hezek re'iyah* in a meaningful sense — not because visual intrusion is inherently a *hezek*, but because a level of privacy has been established and the other party has a legitimate claim to maintain it. The damage is real because the expectation is real.

This is a striking formulation. Whether *hezek re'iyah* rises to a legally actionable *hezek* may depend not on any abstract principle but on the actual history of the parties and the degree to which a norm of privacy has been established between them. To be continued.

---

# Bava Batra 3

## Hezek Re'iyah

### Two Mishnah Readings

The daf opens in the middle of a central discussion that has occupied the Gemara on and off: whether *hezek re'iyah* — looking into somebody else's private affairs as they conduct them in their home or yard — constitutes a legally cognizable form of damage. The stakes of this question are significant, because if visual invasion is classified as *hezek*, it would presumably obligate one to prevent it from occurring, including through the construction of a wall.

This question is bound up with a textual dispute about how to read the opening of the Mishnah. The more straightforward reading is that once two partners in a shared courtyard agree to build a wall, they must build one — but there is no independent obligation to build without such agreement. A competing reading holds that the very agreement to divide the courtyard triggers an obligation to build a wall, suggesting that *hezek re'iyah* is itself the operative legal basis. The plain reading favors the former, yet a later Mishnah seems to require wall construction even in the case of a garden (*ginah*), which creates difficulties for either reading.

### Tosafot & Hezek

Tosafot anchors the entire discussion in the framework of *hezek re'iyah*. In explaining a later Mishnah — which states that if a shared wall falls down, neither party can force the other to rebuild it — Rashi suggests a contractual theory: there was an implicit prior agreement to maintain the wall, and the obligation is merely its continuation. Tosafot, however, grounds this ruling explicitly in *hezek re'iyah*: once the parties had grown accustomed to conducting private activities in their yard under the protection of the wall, its collapse now constitutes an invasion of that established privacy. The *hezek* arises precisely because a pre-existing norm of private use has been disrupted.

### Gatehouse Tashma

The Gemara now brings a *tashma* — an attempted proof from a different Mishnah. The case involves a shared courtyard accessed by multiple homes: *kofinoso livnot beit sha'ar vedalet lachatzer* — one may compel one's fellow courtyard members to contribute to the construction of a gatehouse and door for the courtyard. The gatehouse serves to prevent passersby in the public domain (*reshut harabim*) from seeing into the courtyard. Notably, the compulsion here is not directed at the passersby who are causing the visual harm — they cannot practically be forced to do anything — but at the fellow members of the courtyard, who are compelled to collectively protect themselves from this intrusion. The Gemara infers: *shema mina hezek re'iyah shemei hezek* — since the members can be forced to act, visual invasion must be a recognized legal harm.

This is precisely where the framing as *hezek* rather than as a "right to privacy" carries legal weight. One might ask: why does calling it a *right* not achieve the same result? If we speak in the language of rights, it is unclear why the right of one party to privacy entitles him to coerce another party — who is not himself invading that privacy — to fund a gatehouse. But if we speak in the language of damage, the logic follows naturally: the courtyard as a whole is being harmed, and just as members can force one another to build a protective wall against physical intruders, they can equally compel one another to guard against this form of harm.

The Gemara pushes back: *hezeka derabbim shani* — damage caused by the many, by every passerby who glances in, is qualitatively different from the damage caused by a single neighbor's ability to look in. The Gemara is not disputing the principle; it is disputing the scope. The Mishnah may prove only that *hezek re'iyah* applies when the source of the intrusion is the general public, not necessarily when it is a single individual.

### Hezek vs Rights

This distinction matters precisely because the category being invoked is *hezek* — damage — rather than a right. Within the *hezek* framework, the Gemara can ask whether different magnitudes or types of visual intrusion cross the threshold of legal harm. A single neighbor looking in may simply not generate the same kind of damage as the collective gaze of the public street. The framing as *hezek* enables the Gemara to calibrate the scope of the obligation in a way that purely rights-based language would not naturally accommodate.

### Public vs Private Hezek

The Gemara continues to narrow the question. After conceding that *hezek re'iyah* applies when the public can look in (*hezeka derabbim shani*), it asks whether the same applies in the case of a single individual. Another Mishnah is cited: one may not divide a courtyard unless each party receives at least four *amot* — *ein cholkin et hachatzer ad sheyehei bo arba amot lezeh ve'arba amot lazeh*. If there is sufficient space, division can be forced; if not, it cannot. The Gemara asks whether this implies that a forced division would include a forced wall — *mai lav bekosel* — but the answer is no: the Mishnah speaks only of establishing a boundary (*bemistama*), not of compelling wall construction. This again leaves the core question open.

### Windows & Walls

A further *tashma* addresses windows. If a neighbor has windows in his home and one wishes to build a wall or structure on one's own side of the property line, strict limitations apply. The wall must be either more than four *amot* higher than the top window, or more than four *amot* lower than the bottom window, and must be four *amot* removed horizontally — *bein mimalah bein mimatah bein miknegdan arba amot*. The rationale: *kedei shelo yatzitz veyireh* — so that one cannot stand atop one's own wall and look into the neighbor's windows. Even the potential for visual access is regulated; one cannot construct something on one's own property that creates a reasonable opportunity to look in.

This would seem to establish *hezek re'iyah shemei hezek* quite decisively. The Gemara responds: *hezeka dbeita shani* — the privacy of the home is categorically different. One's home is a domain where the expectation of privacy is at its highest, and someone's ability to see inside is recognized as a genuine *hezek*, sufficient to require preventive construction. But this concession still does not resolve whether the same applies to a yard.

### Rooftop vs Yard

A final *tashma* introduces the case of a rooftop adjacent to a neighbor's courtyard, as stated by Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: *gag hasamuch lachatzer chaveiro oseh lo maakeh gavoah arba amot* — a rooftop adjacent to the neighbor's yard requires a parapet four *amot* high, well beyond what is required to prevent falls, specifically to prevent one from looking straight down into the yard below.

This appears to be a case of *hezek re'iyah* applied to a yard — precisely what was in question. The Gemara again distinguishes: *shani hasam deamrei lei bachatzer livaal gag* — there the owner of the yard can say to the rooftop owner: *lididi kevia li tashmishta lididach lo kevia lach tashmishta* — I use my yard regularly and continuously, while you go up to your rooftop only occasionally. And since I do not know when you will choose to ascend, *deitzatna minach* — I cannot take precautions in advance, I cannot know when to adjust my behavior to account for your presence.

Rashi captures this as *divrei hatznei'ah*: in the yard, private activity is a constant and regular occurrence. In the rooftop case, there is an established pattern of private use that is intermittently and unpredictably invaded. The *hezek* lies in the invasion of an existing, established norm. The question that remains unresolved is whether the initial situation — where no wall exists between two yards and people refrain from private activities from the outset — also constitutes a *hezek*. In that scenario, no established private activity is being disrupted; rather, the freedom to engage in such activity is never actualized in the first place. Is the suppression of that freedom itself a *hezek*? The Gemara leaves this open. The weight of the evidence is accumulating strongly in favor of *hezek re'iyah shemei hezek*, yet the plain reading of the Mishnah continues to resist it.

---

## Mishnah Reading

### Lishna Achrina

The Gemara now presents *lishna achrina* — an alternative formulation of the preceding argument that begins from the opposite direction. In this version, the initial assumption is that the Mishnah should be read as obligating a wall once the parties agree to *divide* the courtyard, not merely when they agree to *build* a wall. This reading, if correct, would make *hezek re'iyah shemei hezek* the operative premise — since the obligation to build follows automatically from the act of division.

### Mechitza Definition

The *lishna achrina* turns on the word *mechitza*. Those who read the Mishnah as beginning with division understand *mechitza* to mean *plugta* — division or partition — citing the verse *vatehi mechetza ha'edah* as evidence. On this reading, once the parties agree to divide, the wall follows necessarily. The Gemara then proposes that *mechitza* could just as well mean *guda* — a wall — citing the case of *mechitzat hakerem* from the laws of *kilayim*, where the term clearly refers to a physical wall. If *mechitza* means wall, then the Mishnah requires only that the parties have agreed to build a wall — without such agreement, there is no obligation, which would imply *hezek re'iyah lav shemei hezek*.

The Gemara raises a linguistic objection: if the Mishnah had meant to say that they agreed to build a wall (*mechitza* as wall), it should have said simply *bonin oto* — they build it — rather than *bonin et hakotel*, which introduces the word for wall separately, as if *mechitza* referred to something other than the wall itself. The Gemara then turns this around: if *mechitza* means division, the Mishnah should have used the verb *lachatzot* — to divide — rather than the noun form. The response: *tana avid plugta* — this is simply how people speak, using a nominal form rather than a verbal one.

### Kinyan Devarim

Both readings of the Mishnah raise an acute legal difficulty. If one reading holds that the obligation to build the wall flows from the agreement to divide — and if *hezek re'iyah shemei hezek* — then the Gemara asks: *mai irya sheratzu* — why must they have agreed? If visual invasion is a recognized form of damage, why can't one partner simply compel the other to build a wall regardless of any agreement?

The answer, developed by Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, is that the Mishnah is speaking of a case where the yard is not large enough to compel division (*keshein bah din chalukah*) — each party would not receive the minimum four *amot* required for a forced split. In such a case, one cannot impose division unilaterally. But if the parties agree to divide even a small yard, the division can take effect — and once it takes effect, the wall follows.

This raises an immediate objection: *nahadru behu* — if the yard is too small to compel division, what binds the parties to their agreement? Can they not simply retract? The Gemara notes that even performing a formal *kinyan sudar* — the handkerchief act of acquisition — would not seem to help. *Kinyan devarim be'alma hu* — it is merely a *kinyan* to do what was promised, which the halakha does not recognize as binding.

This is the crucial principle of *kinyan devarim*. The category is not named because the mechanism of *kinyan* was weak — one could use a handkerchief, sign a contract, or make any formal act — but because the underlying commitment is a promise to perform a future action, and the halakha does not treat such a promise as legally binding in the way it treats a transfer of property, the creation of a debt, or the assumption of liability.

### Rashi & Tosafot

Rashi explains the principle directly: *ve'ein chalipin konin ella davar ha-nikneh* — the act of *kinyan* only takes legal effect on something that can be acquired: a sale, a gift, a lien on land (*shibud karkaot*), or a transfer of chattels. Abstract promises to perform an action in the future do not fall within these categories.

Tosafot raises a pointed question: earlier in the sugya, where the Mishnah discussed the obligation to build a wall when parties had agreed to do so, no one asked about *kinyan devarim*. Why not? Tosafot answers that agreeing to contribute to the cost of building a wall is fundamentally different from agreeing to divide a yard. When one agrees to share in the expense of wall construction, one is creating a financial obligation — effectively a monetary liability — and financial obligations can be assumed through *kinyan*. One can create a debt; one can obligate oneself to pay. But agreeing to divide a yard in the future does not create a financial reality, does not transfer property, and does not assume liability. It is simply a promise to do something, and that promise — however formalized — cannot be made legally binding. The contrast Tosafot draws is precise: liability and financial obligation can be undertaken through *kinyan*; performance of a future act cannot.

### Kinyan in Division

The resolution, stated by Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, is *shekanu miyadam beruchot* — they performed a *kinyan* on the directions, meaning on the actual division itself. The act of *kinyan* does not here commit them to divide in the future; it effects the division in the present. As Rashi explains, this may work through *kinyan chazakah* — each party goes to his newly allocated portion and performs some act of physical possession, thereby acquiring actual, present ownership of his half.

The principle, then, is sharp: one cannot commit in a binding way to divide a property in the future, but one *can* divide it now. The *kinyan* operates to create a present legal reality — the transfer of ownership — not to secure a promise of future performance. Once the division has been effected through a proper *kinyan*, the party who now has his own separate yard and is subject to visual invasion by the neighbor can be compelled to build a wall, because *hezek re'iyah shemei hezek*. The obligation emerges after the fact from the legal reality that has been created, not from any prior contractual promise.

---

## Building Materials

### Material Types

The Gemara now turns from the conceptual architecture of *hezek re'iyah* and *kinyan devarim* to the more concrete halakhic discussion of building materials specified in the Mishnah. The Mishnah lists four types: *gevil*, *gazit*, *kfisin*, and *levanim*. The Gemara explains them as follows. *Gevil* are *avnei dela mashpaya* — unsmoothed, rough stones. *Gazit* are *avnei demashpaya* — hewn or smoothed stones, as the verse states, *kol eileh avanim yekarot kemidot gazit*. *Kfisin* are *arichei* — half-bricks. *Levanim* are *livnei* — full bricks.

### Smooth Stones

Rav Acha the son of Rava posed a challenge to Rav Ashi: how do we know that *gevil* means unsmoothed stones? The reasoning behind the question is structural. The Mishnah specifies that a *gevil* wall is one *tefach* wider than a *gazit* wall — six *tefachim* as opposed to five. If *gevil* means unsmoothed stones, this extra *tefach* is explained by the protruding, irregular edges (*morsha dekarnata*) that rough stone requires in the overall measurement. But perhaps *gevil* means smooth stones laid in two halves with plaster (*tina*) between them, and the extra *tefach* is accounted for by that mortar layer — just as *kfisin* (half-bricks kept together with cement) are wider than full bricks because of the binding material.

The Gemara's response: *ela gemara gemiri lah* — we have a received tradition that *gevil* means unsmoothed stones, and that is simply what the term signifies. The same applies to *kfisin*: we know from tradition that they are half-bricks joined by cement, not unsmoothed bricks whose extra width is due to rough edges. These are building terms with fixed meanings transmitted through tradition, not derivable from structural inference alone.

### Half-Bricks

A parallel version of the same exchange is then cited. Some say Rav Acha the son of Rav Avya posed the same question in reverse to Rav Ashi: how do we know *kfisin* are half-bricks whose extra width comes from the cement between them? Perhaps *kfisin* are simply unsmoothed bricks, and their extra *tefach* is due to protruding edges — just as *gevil* are unsmoothed stones with protruding edges. Again the answer is the same: *gemara gemiri lah* — tradition establishes the meaning of each term. The materials mean what they mean; the tradition is the authority.

From this discussion Abaye infers a practical halakhic norm: *kol beinei urbai tefach* — the standard thickness of the cement used to bind two half-bricks is a full *tefach*. As Rashi explains, this has practical consequences: if one contracts to build a wall for another and uses less than a full *tefach* of cement between the half-bricks, the owner can claim the wall has been built below the implied standard, since the Mishnah demonstrates that the accepted measure is a full *tefach* of binding material.

### Width & Height

The Gemara then raises a question about the relationship between wall width and height. The Mishnah specifies widths for each building material, and one might ask why width matters if the concern animating the Mishnah is *hezek re'iyah*, which is fundamentally about height. The answer is that structural stability requires a certain width to support a given height: for a wall of *gazit* (smoothed stones) that is meant to reach the standard four *amot* height, a width of five *tefachim* is sufficient to keep it standing — no more, no less.

The Gemara then raises a remarkable challenge from the *Beit HaMikdash*: the partition wall that separated the *kodesh* from the *kodesh kodashim* in the Temple of Shlomo was thirty *amot* high, yet only one *amah* — six *tefachim* — wide. If a width of five *tefachim* can support only four *amot* of height, how could a single extra *tefach* make it possible to support thirty *amot*? The Gemara offers an initial response: *keyvan de-ika tefach yeseira kai* — one extra *tefach* does make a substantial difference. But a more satisfying answer is forthcoming.

---

## Beit HaMikdash Wall

### First Temple Wall

The wall of partition in the first *Beit HaMikdash* — *ammat traxin* — was thirty *amot* high and one *amah* wide. The wall marked the boundary between the *kodesh* and the *kodesh kodashim*, and its dimensions were fixed accordingly. The structural puzzle, as noted, is how such a narrow base could support such extreme height.

### Extra Tefach

The Gemara's initial response is that one extra *tefach* of width does wonders — moving from five to six *tefachim* dramatically changes what height can be sustained. However, this answer is provisional, and the Gemara will replace it with a structurally more compelling explanation.

### Second Temple Size

The Gemara asks: in the second *Beit HaMikdash*, where the building was taller, why was a similar partition wall not constructed? The Mishnah Gemara cites the verse *gadol yiheyeh kevod habayit ha'acharon min harishon* — the glory of the latter Temple shall be greater than the former. A dispute is recorded between Rav and Shmuel, and similarly between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar: one holds that *gadol* refers to the building itself — the structure of the second Temple was greater, as it indeed was in the Herodian period — while the other holds that it refers to the years of its duration. The Gemara concludes *ve'isa lehai ve'isa lehai* — both are true.

### Ceiling Support

The structurally superior answer now emerges. The Gemara explains that the first Temple's partition wall, while only one *amah* wide, could stand at thirty *amot* because of the support provided by the ceiling: *agav tikrah maziva havei kai* — by virtue of the ceiling holding it at the top, the wall could achieve that height. A free-standing wall of one *amah* width cannot sustain thirty *amot* on its own; it is the ceiling that stabilizes it. Without ceiling support, *lo havei kai* — it simply could not stand.

This reframes the entire structural discussion. The relevant variable is not merely the ratio of width to height in a free-standing wall, but whether the wall is sealed by a ceiling above. A wall that reaches the ceiling and is held by it can achieve heights that a free-standing wall of the same width cannot.

### Curtains vs Wall

One might suggest a compromise: build a wall up to thirty *amot* — the maximum height the wall could achieve with ceiling support — and then use curtains (*parochet*) for whatever additional height was needed in the second Temple. The Gemara rejects this on the basis of a received tradition: *ai kula bevinyan ai kula beparoches* — the separation must be entirely of one type or the other. Either the whole partition is a wall, as in the first *Beit HaMikdash*, or the whole partition is a curtain, as in the *mishkan*. A hybrid of the two is not permitted. Since the second Temple was too tall for the wall to reach the ceiling and be supported by it — *tfei lo kai* — the only option was a curtain for the entire partition, and thus curtains were used throughout.

---

## Building Materials (II)

### Plaster Edges

The Gemara now returns to the Mishnah's wall-width measurements and raises a practical question: when the Mishnah specifies widths — three *tefachim* for full bricks, or six for *gevil* stones — does this figure include the plaster or stucco (*sid*) applied to the outer surface of the wall, or does it refer only to the width of the building material itself?

*Hen vesidan o dilma hen belo sidan.* The Gemara reasons initially that the measurement must include the plaster: if the Mishnah meant to specify the width of the materials alone, it should have also told us separately how much plaster is to be applied. Since it does not, the total figure presumably encompasses both material and finish. *Shema mina hen vesidan.*

The Gemara then pushes back. Perhaps the width refers to the building material alone, and the reason the Mishnah does not specify the plaster thickness separately is that the amount of plaster does not reach even a full *tefach* — *vekivan delo havei tefach lo tanei* — and measurements below a *tefach* are simply not cited.

The Gemara raises a counter-example: when the Mishnah discusses full bricks (*levanim*), it speaks of each party contributing one and a half *tefachim* of yard width — a non-whole-*tefach* figure that is nonetheless mentioned explicitly. This would suggest that fractional measurements are cited when they aggregate to a meaningful total. The Gemara distinguishes: *hasam chazei leitztarovei* — in that case, the two halves of one and a half *tefachim* each combine to make a total of three *tefachim*, which is a full unit. Here, the thin layer of plaster on each side would bring the total to, say, three and a fraction *tefachim* — not a round figure — and that is why it goes unmentioned.

A further *tashma* is introduced from the laws of *eruvin*: the beam (*korah*) placed across an alleyway entrance must be wide enough to support a half-brick (*ariach*). Since this tells us the width of a half-brick is one and a half *tefachim*, and a full brick (*laveina*) is three *tefachim*, this figure is cited without any mention of plaster — suggesting that the three-*tefach* measurement refers to the brick alone, without the stucco finish. The Gemara responds: *hasam beravrevata* — that case concerns large bricks, which are indeed three *tefachim* of solid material without plaster. The bricks in our Mishnah may be slightly smaller, with the three-*tefach* figure including the plaster.

The Gemara infers from the phrasing *shel shlosha tefachim* — a brick *of* three *tefachim* — that there are bricks that are not three *tefachim* wide, confirming the existence of smaller bricks. This supports the possibility that the standard in our Mishnah is a smaller brick for which the three-*tefach* total includes the plaster. The question — whether the Mishnah's wall-width measurements include or exclude the outer plastering — is left without a definitive resolution.

---

## Synagogue Demolition

### Build Before Destroy

The Gemara now turns to a halakhic principle stated by Rav Chisda: *lo listor inish bei knishta ad d'bani bei knishta achrita* — one may not demolish a synagogue until another synagogue has already been built in its place. This ruling applies even when the demolition is for the purpose of reconstruction and improvement; the replacement must be standing before the original is torn down.

### Negligence vs Prayer

Two rationales are offered for this requirement. The first is *mishum pshiyuta* — the concern for negligence: once the original synagogue has been torn down, people will simply fail to get around to rebuilding it in a timely fashion. The second is *mishum tzloyi* — the concern for having a place to pray: even if one assumes the rebuilding will eventually happen, in the interim the community lacks a place for prayer.

The Gemara asks what practical difference there is between these two approaches. The difference, it explains, lies in the case where an alternative place of prayer (*duchta l'tzloyi*) exists elsewhere. If the only concern is having a place to pray, and such a place exists, the demolition should be permissible. If the concern is negligence, the existence of an alternative venue does not guarantee that the new synagogue will actually get built — and so even with another place available, demolition should be prohibited.

### Seasonal Synagogues

The Gemara records the practice of Mareimar and Mar Zutra: *satri u-vani b'kayita u-v'sitva* — they tore down the winter synagogue in the summer and rebuilt it then, and tore down the summer synagogue in the winter and rebuilt it then. Rashi explains that the winter synagogue was constructed with low ceilings, thick walls, and few windows to retain heat, while the summer synagogue had high ceilings and ample ventilation for cooler conditions. Since the community was using one synagogue while rebuilding the other, there was always a place to pray — which suggests this practice accords with the view that the primary concern is having a place to pray. Tosafot, however, attempts to explain how this can work even within the negligence-based approach, though on its face the practice maps most naturally onto the prayer-venue rationale.

### Funds & Materials

The Gemara poses a series of escalating questions to Rav Ashi, asked by Ravina. First: what if the community has already collected sufficient funds (*gavu zuzei u-machatsify*) — can they then tear down the old synagogue, since there is no longer a concern about negligence? The answer is no: *dilma mitrami lehu pidyon shevuyim veyahavi lehu* — it is possible that at the last moment an opportunity to redeem captives will arise, and the community will redirect those funds to *pidyon shevuyim*. Collected money alone is not sufficient assurance.

Next: what if all the building materials have already been delivered — the bricks stacked, the beams ready, the roof tiles assembled (*shavizi livni vehadrei vehadrei umachasei keshura*)? Again the answer is no: *zimnin demitrami lehu pidyon shevuyim mizabni veyahavi lehu* — sometimes a *pidyon shevuyim* emergency arises and the community sells off the materials to fund it. Even a full stockpile of building materials does not eliminate the concern.

The Gemara asks whether even building the new synagogue is sufficient: could one argue that the old synagogue may not be demolished until people have actually begun using the new one? The response: *dirastya de-inshei lo mizabni* — once the new structure is occupied and in use, people will not sell it off. The building itself, once in use, constitutes a sufficiently firm guarantee.

### Decay Exception

The Gemara then carves out an exception: *velo amran ela delo chazi bei tyuva* — all of the above applies only when the existing synagogue shows no signs of serious deterioration. If, however, the building is visibly rotting or cracking (*chazi bei tyuva*), the urgency of the situation overrides the usual requirement: *satrei u-vanai* — one may tear it down and rebuild immediately, without waiting for the replacement to be complete. When the structure is genuinely unsafe, the concern about negligence yields to the more pressing concern about the building's condition.

### Rav Ashi Story

The Gemara closes with an instructive story about Rav Ashi himself. He observed that the synagogue of Mata Machsaya was visibly deteriorating — Rashi reads this as cracking — and that the community was doing nothing about it. Rav Ashi tore it down and then, remarkably, moved his own cot onto the grounds and camped there. He refused to remove it until the community rebuilt the synagogue properly, including the drainage infrastructure (*shefichi*).

The story carries a double message. On one hand, the existence of genuine decay and disrepair is sufficient to permit immediate demolition, even before a replacement is built. On the other hand, Rav Ashi's action makes clear that the concern about *peshiya* does not simply disappear in an urgent case. He recognized that without additional pressure, the community might well address the demolition but then drag its feet on reconstruction. By installing himself on the premises, he created the urgency needed to move the project forward. The *peshiya* concern, in other words, is not merely a theoretical worry that the law addresses through procedural requirements; it is a real behavioral tendency that sometimes requires active countermeasures, even after the halakhic threshold for demolition has been crossed.

Tosafot raises a separate question in this context: whether one is even permitted to sleep in a synagogue — and, further, whether the *kedushah* of the synagogue persists even after its physical structure has been torn down, which would raise additional concerns. These questions are left for further discussion.

---

---

# Bava Batra 4

## Wall Height & Beit HM

### Wall Height Intro

The *gemara* on this *daf* arrives in the middle of a digression. The immediate backdrop is a discussion of the minimum height of a shared wall — whether the obligation to build stems from *hezek re'iya* (visual damage) or from a prior agreement, how high a stone wall must be (four *amot*), and how wide it must be to support that height. From there, the *gemara* raised the case of the *Beit HaMikdash*, whose walls were extraordinarily high yet not proportionally wide — and it is that question that opens the discussion here.

### Teardown Rules

Before arriving at the *Beit HaMikdash* proper, the *gemara* had been exploring a related set of laws: may one tear down a *shul* in order to build a better one in its place? The answer is generally no, for two distinct reasons. First, there would be no place to pray in the interim. Second, and perhaps more practically, there is a concern of *pshia* — negligence — that one might tear down the old building and then simply never get around to rebuilding. The *gemara* had noted some possible exceptions to this rule.

Now the *gemara* uses this framework to set up a striking question: *Bava ben Buta*, a *tanna* who lived during the time of the second *Beit HaMikdash* and who, as we will see, played a role in advising Herod regarding its rebuilding — how could he have given Herod counsel to tear down the *Beit HaMikdash* and build a more magnificent one in its place? As *Rav Chisda* rules: *lo listarei inish beis knishta ad dbanei beis knishta achrita* — one may not tear down a *beis knesset* until another has been built.

Several observations arise here. First, in the case of the *Beit HaMikdash*, the entire premise of the rule becomes complicated: you cannot build on an alternative plot of land — if ever there is a building that must occupy a specific location, it is the *Beit HaMikdash*. Second, there is the historical question of what exactly happened during Herod's reconstruction. It is not immediately obvious whether *korbanot* continued to be offered throughout the construction or whether there was a full cessation. The *gemara* seems to assume significant disruption, though the principle of *makrivim af al pi she-ein bayit* — that offerings may be brought even without a complete structure — might have provided some relief. Third, and perhaps most striking, is the *gemara*'s framing of the *Beit HaMikdash* simply as a type of *beis knesset*. This is a characteristically rabbinic retrojection — applying later institutional categories to an earlier reality — and it reflects a broader rabbinic tendency to present themselves, rather than the *kohanim*, as the dominant religious authority even during the Temple period.

### Herod's Rebuilding Q

The *gemara*'s question is pointed: *heichi aspirei lei eitza leHordus lemisterei leBeis Hamikdash?* — how did *Bava ben Buta* give Herod advice to tear down the *Beit HaMikdash*?

At this point it is worth pausing to consider the historical reality. Herod did not merely renovate the existing structure. He undertook a massive engineering project: leveling the top of *Har HaBayis*, constructing massive retaining walls (the *Kotel* being the most famous), and filling in the space with enormous quantities of earth on three of the four sides to create the vast flat plaza of the *Har HaBayis*. The scale of this project was staggering — a literal uprooting and reshaping of a mountain. This context heightens the *gemara*'s question considerably: this was not a simple reconstruction but a complete destruction and rebuilding of the entire site.

### Possible Answers

The *gemara* offers two answers. The first: *tivya chaza bei* — perhaps they found cracks and structural failures in the existing building, which, as discussed earlier, provides a special license to tear down even a sacred structure. The second: *malchuta shani* — when it is a royal decree or a decision of the king, we do not worry about negligence, because kings have the resources and the will to see their projects through. The *gemara* cites *Shmuel*: *ei amar malchusa akrana turi* — if a king says he will uproot mountains, he will uproot mountains and not retract. Given what we know about Herod's actual feat of reshaping *Har HaBayis*, the phrase *akrana turi* — uprooting mountains — carries more than a little resonance here.

---

## Herod's Story

### Herod's Origins

With the *Beit HaMikdash* as the backdrop, the *gemara* launches into a remarkable aggadic account of Herod's rise. *Hordos avda de'bei Chashmonai hava* — Herod was a slave in the house of the *Chashmonaim*. He cast his eyes upon one of the daughters of the *Chashmonai* family, developing an intense desire for her. One day he heard a *bas kol* — understood here as a heavenly voice, though *Saul Lieberman* has noted that the phrase can sometimes mean simply an echo or rumor — declaring: *kol avda de'marid hashta matzlach* — any slave who rebels today will succeed. Seizing the moment, Herod rose up and killed all of his masters — *kam katlinhu le'khulu marosei* — wiping out the entire house of the *Chashmonaim*, save for the one young woman he desired. Whether his primary motivation was lust or political ambition, the *gemara* presents it as the former: his driving impulse was his desire for the girl, and retaining her would simultaneously satisfy that desire and lend his reign a degree of legitimacy.

### Chashmonai Woman

When the young woman realized that Herod intended to marry her, she went up to the rooftop, raised her voice, and made a public proclamation: *kol man de'ati ve'amar mibeis Chashmonai kasina avda hu* — anyone who hereafter claims descent from the house of the *Chashmonaim* is in fact a slave. She declared herself the sole surviving true descendant of that house, and then threw herself from the roof to her death. Her act was both a declaration of the illegitimacy of Herod's rule and a final, dramatic embodiment of the downfall of her dynasty.

### Body Preservation

Herod preserved her body in honey for seven years. The *gemara* records a dispute about his motivation: *ika de'amri ba'ala* — some say he continued to have intercourse with her even after her death; *ika de'amri lo ba'ala* — others say he did not. According to those who say he did not, he preserved the body either to satisfy his desire in some other manner, or, more politically, to maintain the appearance that he was still married to a *Chashmonai* princess — lending his rule an aura of legitimacy.

### Slave Exclusion

Having seized power, Herod turned to the question of his own legitimacy. He asked: *man darish mikerev achicha tasim aleicha melech* — who are those who expound the verse that one must place over oneself a king "from among your brothers," *veha demi'at lemididi avda* — and who thereby exclude me as a slave? The answer: *rabbanan* — the rabbis. Once again the *gemara* presents the rabbis as the dominant religious authorities of the period, a retrojection of later realities. *Tosafos* raises the obvious question: if it is an explicit verse, why do you need the rabbis to expound it? The answer is that while the verse's plain meaning excludes non-Jews, it is the rabbis who extend the exclusion to include slaves. The rabbis, despite their partial obligation in *mitzvos*, made themselves, in Herod's view, the source of his political vulnerability.

### Slaughter of Rabbis

*Kam katlinu lechulu rabbanan* — Herod went and killed all the rabbis. *Tosafos* notes that this cannot be taken literally, since we know that the *Bnei Beseira* were still present when *Hillel* arrived from *Bavel* shortly thereafter. Rather, it means the vast majority were killed. The one he spared was *Bava ben Buta* — *shavkei leBava ben Buta lemishkal eiza minei* — he kept him alive because he recognized his wisdom and wanted to retain him as an advisor.

### Herod-Bava Encounter

Having blinded *Bava ben Buta* by means of a crown of thorns pressed inward against the eyes, Herod one day came and sat before him without identifying himself. The blind *tanna* could not see who was speaking to him. Herod presented himself as an ordinary person and posed a question: *chazi mar hai avda bisha mai ka avid* — have you seen what this evil slave is doing? — meaning Herod himself, to test how the rabbi would respond.

### Bava's Responses

*Bava ben Buta*'s responses unfold in several stages. First, when Herod suggests cursing this figure, *Bava* declines on halachic grounds: *gam bemada'acha melech al tekalel* — even in your private chamber, do not curse a king. Herod pushes back: but he is not a real king. *Bava* responds: even if he is merely wealthy, *uvechadrei mishkavcha al tekalel ashir* — do not curse a wealthy man. And even if he is simply a *nasi*, a communal leader, *venasi ve'amecha lo ta'or* — do not curse a prince among your people.

Herod then presses further: but the verse says *be'amecha* — "among your people" — implying one who acts as a member of the community, not one who does evil. So perhaps cursing is permitted? *Bava* responds: *mistafina minei* — I am afraid of him. This is a notably different register — no longer a principled halachic argument, but honest self-preservation. Herod continues: there is no one here to carry your words back to him. *Bava* replies: *ki of hashamayim yolich et hakol u'va'al knafayim yagid davar* — the birds of heaven will carry the sound, and a winged creature will tell the matter. I will say nothing.

At this point Herod reveals himself: *ana hu* — I am he. And he says: *i hava yadana de'zehirei rabanan kulei hai, lo hava katilina lehu* — had I known that the rabbis were this careful, this guarded in their speech and conduct, I would not have killed them. It is worth noting that *Bava*'s final motivation was caution rather than loyalty — he was not swearing allegiance to Herod, only expressing that it was imprudent to speak. And yet the point stands: whatever the motivation, the rabbis' behavior toward a ruler, however illegitimate, was circumspect, and Herod regrets not having understood that before.

### Herod's Regret

Herod now asks: *hashta mai takantei de'hu gavra* — what is his remedy? What can he now do to make amends? *Bava ben Buta* responds: *hu kiva oro shel olam* — you extinguished the light of the world, *de'khitiv ki ner mitzvah ve'torah or* — as it is written, a commandment is a candle and Torah is light. The rabbis were the world's source of illumination. Therefore: *yelech ve'ye'asok be'oro shel olam* — go and occupy yourself with the light of the world, a reference to the *Beit HaMikdash*, for *venaharu elav kol hagoyim* — all the nations will stream toward it, and the word *venaharu* echoes the word for light.

### Light & Eyes

A second version is also recorded. Some say *Bava ben Buta* framed it differently: *hu suma eino shel olam* — you blinded the eye of the world. The *gemara* cites the verse *haya me'einei ha'edah* — from the eyes of the community, which the rabbis read as referring to the *Sanhedrin*. Therefore: *yelech v'yitasek be'eino shel olam* — go and occupy yourself with the eye of the world, the *Beit HaMikdash*, for *hineni mechalel et mikdashi ge'on uzchem machmad eineichem* — behold I am desecrating my sanctuary, the glory of your strength, the desire of your eyes.

The imagery here is layered and striking. *Bava ben Buta* himself has been blinded, and the language of light and sight runs through the entire passage. But there is also a historical irony worth noting: in the actual sequence of Jewish history, the *Beit HaMikdash* was the center of religious life and was later replaced, after its destruction, by rabbinic Judaism. Here the *gemara* inverts that relationship — the rabbis are the primary source of light and sanctity, and the *Beit HaMikdash* is offered as a kind of substitute or compensation for their loss.

### Roman Authority

Having decided to rebuild, Herod faces an obstacle: *mistafina mimachusa* — I am afraid of the Roman government. I cannot act without their permission. *Bava ben Buta* advises: *shadar shlicha* — send a messenger, let him take a year traveling there, *v'leakev shata* — spend a year waiting for an audience, *v'leihadar shata* — and take a year to return. That gives you three years. *Adei hachi v'hachi* — by the time he comes back, *sastis lei v'banistas lei* — you will have already torn it down and rebuilt it. Act first; obtain permission after. This reflects a recognizable principle: it is easier to secure forgiveness than permission.

The *gemara* notes that *Rashi* in the last comment on the relevant passage references this story as written in *Yosifon ben Goryon*. It should be noted that *Yosifon ben Goryon* is not the Greek Josephus but a medieval Hebrew work that presented itself as a translation of Josephus — essentially a literary forgery, which explains why many *rishonim* who cite it find parallels to the *gemara*'s accounts but not to Josephus directly.

### Rome's Response

The response eventually came back: *im lo satarta al tistur* — if you have not yet torn it down, do not. *V'im satarta al tivni* — if you have already torn it down, do not rebuild it. *V'im satarta oovanita* — and if you have torn it down and rebuilt it: *avda bisha batar d'avdin mis'malkhin* — a bad slave, who acts first and then asks. The Roman response then turns contemptuous: *im zayanakh alakh* — so you think your weapons give you authority? *Siphrakha kan* — we have your records here in Rome. *Lo racha v'lo bar racha* — not a king and not the son of a king. *Hordis avda kalnya mit'avid* — Herod the slave has made himself into a free man. The *gemara* then clarifies the term *racha*: *dichtiv anochi hayom racha umashuach melech* — I today am young and have been anointed king — indicating *racha* means a king, linguistically cognate with the Latin *Rex*. An alternative derivation is also offered: *v'yakre'u lefanav avrech*, the proclamation before Yosef in Egypt.

---

## Beit HM Construction

### Construction Beauty

Having recounted Herod's rise to power, his slaughter of the rabbis, his encounter with *Bava ben Buta*, and his decision to rebuild, the *gemara* now turns to the construction itself. *Mi shelo ra binyan Hordis, lo ra binyan na'eh miyamav* — whoever did not see Herod's building has never seen a beautiful edifice in their life. With what did he build it? *Raba* says: with stones of *shaisha u'marmara* — according to *Rashi*, a kind of green and white marble. Some say *kuchla shaisha u'marmara* — blue and white marble. *Apheik sapha v'ayeil sapha* — the stones were laid so that the facing protruded and receded in alternating rows, creating a wave-like pattern across the facade. The purpose given is *ki heichi d'nikabel saida* — so that it could receive plaster or some kind of bonding material between the rows. As is now known from archaeology, Herodian masonry is indeed characterized by its distinctive embossed framing, with each stone slightly recessed at the face for stability.

### Wave Pattern

When those supervising the construction considered smoothing over the front entirely with gold — *savar l'mishayei b'dahava* — the rabbis intervened: *shavkei* — leave it as it is. *D'hachi shapir tvei* — it looks better this way. *D'mechzei ki avata d'yama* — it looks like the waves of the sea. The blue and white marble undulating in and out across the facade created a visual effect of ocean waves, and that, the rabbis ruled, was more beautiful than gold plating.

### Bava's Complicity

This brings the *gemara* back to the question that was deferred: *u'Baba Ben Buta heichi avid hachi* — how did *Bava ben Buta* become complicit in advising and cooperating with Herod, an evil king, even for a noble purpose? The *gemara* raises a ruling: *Rava bar Rav Yehuda amar Rav* — and some say it was *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* — asks why Daniel was punished. The answer: *mipnei she'hisi eitza l'Nevuchadnezzar* — because he gave advice to Nebuchadnezzar. When Nebuchadnezzar had his disturbing dream, Daniel counseled him: *lehein malka malchi yishpar alach v'chatayach b'tzidka perok* — your sins should be redeemed through charity, *v'avayasach b'mikan anayin* — and your iniquity through kindness to the poor. This was good advice, intended to benefit others, and it did succeed — the dream's fulfillment was delayed twelve months. And yet Daniel was punished for it.

The lesson the *gemara* draws is that one should not give advice to wicked kings even when the advice itself is beneficial. Merely being complicit in an evil king's enterprise — even in a positive capacity — carries moral risk. The evidence that Daniel was in fact punished: he appears later in the book of Esther as *Hatach*, and *Rav* identifies *Hatach* as Daniel. If the word *Hatach* indicates he had been cut down from his former greatness — *shehatkhuhu migedulato* — then his degraded status as a mere messenger demonstrates he was punished. If instead *Hatach* means he was the one through whose mouth all royal decrees were sealed, then the evidence of his punishment comes from elsewhere: *deshadyuhu leguva de'aryavata* — he was thrown into the lions' den.

---

## Beit HM Construction (II)

### Justifications

Two answers are offered to resolve how *Bava ben Buta* could have done what Daniel was punished for. First: *shani avda dechayev bemitzvot* — it is different because Herod, as a slave, is obligated in *mitzvos*, and therefore we take an interest in helping him fulfill them. This answer is admittedly difficult to understand — surely the concern should be the benefit to the broader population, not the spiritual welfare of a murderous king. Second, and more compelling: *shani beis hamikdash de'i la malkhuta la mivni* — the *Beit HaMikdash* is different, because without royal involvement and resources, it simply could not have been built. This warrants a level of engagement and complicity that other situations would not.

The broader tension running through this entire passage is, as one might put it, the deep ambivalence about how to respond to illegitimate political power. It is dangerous to engage; there is also an ethical and religious imperative to do so in certain circumstances; there may be exceptions; and the danger remains. The *gemara* holds all of these tensions without resolving them neatly.

---

## Wall Ownership Markers

### Custom Rule

Returning from the lengthy digression about Herod and the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *gemara* turns back to the *mishna*'s foundational rule: *hakol keminhag hamedina* — everything follows the local custom. The *gemara* asks what the word *hakol* ("everything") comes to include beyond the basic cases. The answer: *le'atuyei atra denehigi behutza vedafna* — to include a place where the custom is to build walls from branches or wood. Even such a wall, despite not being made of stone or brick, is considered a legitimate fulfillment of the obligation if that is the local norm.

### Ownership Presumption

The *mishna* then addresses what happens when a jointly built wall collapses. The *makom veha'avanim shel shneihem* — the space and the stones belong to both of them equally, since the presumption is that any wall between two properties was built jointly and stands on both parties' land. The *gemara* says this is not obvious: the case where this principle is needed is *denafal lerushuta dechad mineihu* — where all the stones fell into one person's domain, or where one party moved them all to his own side. In that case one might think we should treat it as a *safek* (doubt) and rule that the one in possession has the advantage. The *gemara* rules: *lo tzricha* — no, because the standing presumption is that the wall was always jointly owned, and that presumption overrides the physical fact of where the stones have landed.

### Garden vs Valley

The *mishna* states: *vechein begina makom shenahagu ligdor mechayvin oto* — similarly, in a garden, in a place where it is the practice to build a fence, one is obligated to do so. The simple reading of this would imply that if it is not a place where the practice is to build a fence, one is not obligated. Looking at the *seifa* of the *mishna*: *aval bebika makom shenahagu shelo ligdor ein mechayvin oto* — but in a valley, where it is the practice not to build a wall, one is not obligated. The implication of this *seifa* would be that in a valley without such a practice, one is obligated. But this makes no sense: if in a garden — where there is far more reason for a wall — the default is not to require one, how could the default in an open valley be to require one? The *gemara* declares: *hagufa kashya* — the text itself is difficult.

### Mishnah Reading

*Abaye* offers one reading: *stam gina* — a standard garden carries an obligation, and *uvmakom shenahagu ligdor bebika* — in a valley where there is a practice to build a wall, you are also obligated. This reads the two clauses as addressing two separate cases. *Rava* objects: *im kein mai aval* — if that is so, what is the force of the word "but" in the *seifa*? You would have already addressed the valley case in the first clause. *Rava* therefore proposes his own reading: *stam gina kemakom shenahagu ligdor dami* — a standard garden is treated as a place where the practice is to build a wall, and therefore you are obligated; *aval stam bika kemakom shelo nahagu dami* — but a standard valley is treated as a place where the practice is not to build a wall, and therefore you are not obligated. Rather than reading the *mishna* as conditional ("if there is a practice"), we read it as definitional: a garden simply is the type of place where the norm is to build, and a valley simply is the type of place where it is not.

### Unilateral Construction

After establishing when an obligation to build a wall exists and when it does not, the *mishna* turns to a scenario where one party wants to build but cannot obligate the other: *ela im rotze kones letoch shelo bone ve'ose hazit* — if he wishes, he may recede into his own property, build the wall entirely on his land with his own materials, and create a *chazit* — a marking or facing that signals the wall's exclusive ownership. The concern is that a hundred years hence, when the wall collapses and no one remembers its history, the presumption will be that it was a jointly owned wall. The *chazit* is the mechanism for preserving proof of sole ownership.

### Chazit Methods

The *gemara* explores what exactly constitutes a valid *chazit*. *Rav Huna* says: *kofya lekarna levar* — you turn the corner of the wall outward, so that rather than a flat corner it protrudes on the neighbor's side. The *gemara* asks: why not turn it inward? Because then the neighbor could simply add a corresponding corner on his side and claim joint ownership. And if you turn it outward, can't the neighbor simply cut the corner off? No, *gezuyei meida yedia* — the cutting will be visible.

A second version reverses the positions: *Rav Huna* says turn the corner inward, *miligav*. The *gemara* asks: why not outward? Because the neighbor could cut it off. And inward — won't he just add an inward corner on his side? No, *lifufa meida yedia* — the addition will be visible. The *gemara* notes a tension with the *mishna*, which appears to specify that the *chazit* goes on the outside, *milivar* — and rules: *kashya*.

*Rabbi Yochanan* offers a different method: *meshayaya be'amah milivar* — you plaster over an additional layer on the neighbor's side of the wall. This indicates the wall is yours. Why not plaster on your own side? Because then the neighbor could plaster on his side and claim it is jointly his. If you plaster on his side, can't he just remove it? He could, but *kelifa meida yedia* — the removal of plaster will be visible, though this argument may be harder to sustain over long periods of time.

### Branch Walls

For walls made of branches or wood — *hutza* — the *gemara* considers parallel methods: bending the branches outward so that the points face the neighbor's side, indicating ownership. Similar arguments about tampering and visibility are made. *Abaye* concludes: *hutza leit lei takanta ela beshtara* — for a branch wall, none of these physical markers will be sufficient as a permanent proof. The only adequate protection is a *shtar* — a legal document — signed by the other party, acknowledging sole ownership.

### Joint Markers

The *mishna* then introduces the case where both parties agreed to build a wall together in a place where there would otherwise be no obligation — such as in an open valley. In that case, *simanim* are made on both sides. The *gemara* asks: why not simply make no *simanim* at all? The answer: the provision is needed for a scenario where one party has already gone ahead and made a mark on his side. At that point, the other party must respond by marking his side as well; otherwise, the first party could claim exclusive ownership.

### Anti-Fraud Debate

*Rav Papa mi-Prazika* asks *Rav Ashi*: in the case of the jointly built wall, why not simply make no *simanim* on either side? *Rav Ashi* explains: we are addressing the case where one party has already marked his side, necessitating a response. *Rav Papa* then raises a meta-question: *ve-tani takanta le-ramai?* — is it the *Tanna*'s business to be teaching people how to protect themselves against cheats? Perhaps the *mishna* should only be teaching law, not practical protective measures against fraud.

The *gemara* responds: *bishlama reisha tana dina* — in the *reisha*, the primary teaching is the *halacha* itself: in a valley, one cannot be compelled to build; if one builds unilaterally, it must be entirely on one's own property. Having established that *din*, the *mishna* naturally follows through with how one can protect oneself. *ومشום de-dina tana takanta* — because of the underlying *din*, the protective measure is mentioned as well. But in the *seifa*, where both parties have agreed to build jointly, there is no novel *din* being taught — of course a joint wall may be built jointly. So the *seifa* appears to exist solely in order to teach the protective measure, which seems out of place.

### Extra Clauses

This puzzle — why the *Tanna* includes an apparently redundant or extra clause — reflects a broader method of *mishna* interpretation. Just as the rabbis *dorshen* extra letters or words in a verse to derive halachic lessons, so too an extra clause in a *mishna* is assumed to be teaching something beyond what might be logically derived otherwise.

### Ravina's Explanation

*Ravina* resolves the issue: *hacha be-huzia askinan le-afukei mi-de-Abaye* — the *seifa* is speaking specifically about a branch wall, and it comes to reject *Abaye*'s position. *Abaye* ruled that for a branch wall there is no effective *chazit* and one needs a *shtar*. The *mishna*'s extra clause comes to teach: *de-be-chazi sagia* — a *chazit* suffices even for a branch wall. The *seifa* is not primarily there to advise against fraud; rather, it is there to extend the category of walls for which a physical *chazit* is valid, contrary to *Abaye*'s more restrictive ruling. The extra clause teaches through its very redundancy: since we did not need it to teach the basic *din*, it must be providing new information — namely, that a branch wall can indeed be marked with a *chazit*.

---

## Surrounding Walls

### Three & Fourth Walls

The *gemara* now moves to a new *mishna* on a related but distinct topic: *hamakif et chaveiro mishalosh ruchotav* — one who surrounds his neighbor's field on three sides and builds walls on each of those three sides. This scenario, familiar from *Bava Kamma*, involves a situation where no *hezek re'iya* claim exists and no agreement to build was made. The one who built acted entirely on his own initiative. The *mishna* rules: *ein mechayvin oto* — the neighbor in the middle (the *nikaf*) cannot be compelled to pay for any of it.
