The reasoning is straightforward: he was never obligated to build, and the outer party acted unilaterally. But the *mishna*'s language also invites an inference: when only three walls have been built, there is no obligation. What happens when a fourth wall is added, fully enclosing the neighbor's field? At that point, something qualitatively changes. The surrounded party's field is now genuinely protected — from animals, trespassers, and other intrusions — and this creates a case of *yored letoch sadeh chaveiro*, benefiting someone's property without their request, for which there may be some obligation to reimburse the benefactor.

It should be noted that there is a debate among the *rishonim* — already discussed in *Bava Kamma* — about which walls the *mishna* is referring to: the walls that are literally adjacent to the neighbor's field, or the outer party's own walls which happen to enclose the central field by virtue of their configuration. Either way, once a fourth wall completes the enclosure, the legal situation changes.

### Rabbi Yosi's Rule

*Rabbi Yosi* addresses this directly: *im amad vegadar et harevi'it megalgelin alav et hakol* — if the surrounded party himself rose up and built the fourth wall, then we impose upon him payment for all the walls. By voluntarily building the fourth wall, *Shimon* (the *nikaf*) demonstrates that he genuinely wants and values the enclosure. That demonstration of desire is sufficient to obligate him retroactively for his share of all four walls, not merely the one he built himself.

### Gemara Expansion

The *gemara* significantly broadens *Rabbi Yosi*'s ruling: *lo shena amad nikaf lo shena amad makif* — it does not matter whether it was the *nikaf* (the surrounded party) who built the fourth wall or the *makif* (the one who had built the first three) who built it. Once the enclosure is complete, the *nikaf* benefits from all four walls regardless of who built the last one. Even without the *nikaf*'s personal demonstration of desire, the objective reality of benefit is present, and that is sufficient to obligate him to participate in payment. This, in effect, aligns with the position that might be attributed by implication to the *Tanna Kamma*, who had not directly addressed the fourth wall scenario.

### Cost vs Benefit

A dispute now emerges about how much the *nikaf* must pay. *Rav Huna* says: *hakol lefi mah shegadar* — the payment is calculated based on what was actually built. If the outer party erected a stone wall, the *nikaf* pays his share of a stone wall. *Chiya bar Rav* disagrees: *lo hakol lefi dmei kanim bezol* — no, one calculates based on the cheapest possible wall that would have served the purpose, like a minimal fence of reeds. The reasoning behind *Chiya bar Rav*'s position is that the *nikaf* never agreed to any of this from the outset. He cannot be made to pay for a grand construction he never wanted. His obligation is limited to the benefit he actually derives, and that benefit is measured by the minimum cost of achieving equivalent protection. The *gemara* draws an analogy to a familiar situation: if someone installs an expensive lock on a shared door, a co-tenant who never agreed to it can reasonably say, "I would have bought a cheap lock" — and his obligation is accordingly limited.

### Payment Determination

The *gemara* leaves several questions open for the following session. How precisely is the payment determined in each case? Does it depend on who built the fourth wall — the *nikaf* or the *makif* — and what the *Tanna Kamma*'s position is on that question? These questions will be taken up in the next *daf*.

---

---

# Bava Batra 5

## Payment Amount

### Rav Huna

The daf opens in the middle of interpreting the mishna's case of one who builds walls in a valley where the inner resident cannot be compelled to participate. The mishna established that three walls built without the inner resident's agreement impose no payment obligation on him. Rabbi Yose, however, holds that once a fourth wall is built — thereby completing the enclosure — the inner resident (*nikaf*) can be made to pay. The Gemara has already cited Shmuel to the effect that we rule like Rabbi Yehuda and like Rabbi Yose, and further that this obligation holds even if it was the outer party (*makif*) alone, not the *nikaf*, who built the walls: since the enclosure confers clear benefit, the *nikaf* must pay.

The question that now arises is: how much must he pay? On this point the Gemara records a dispute. *Itmar*: it was stated. Rav Huna holds *hakol lefi mah she-gadar* — the inner resident pays according to the actual building materials used in the wall and his proportional share of their cost. The payment is benchmarked to the real wall as constructed.

### Chiya bar Rav

Chiya bar Rav disagrees. He holds *hakol lefi d'mei kanim be-zol* — the inner resident pays only the equivalent cost of cheap reed or stick fencing, regardless of how expensive the actual wall was. Since the *nikaf* never agreed to any construction, and it is not clear at this stage of the discussion whether he even affirmatively demonstrated desire for the enclosure, he cannot be compelled to pay as though he had commissioned a stone wall. He pays only for the benefit he actually received, and that benefit — having his field protected — could have been achieved even with a cheap wooden fence. So the assessment is pegged to that minimal benchmark.

### Benefit vs. Cost

This debate calls to mind a principle from Bava Kamma: *meshalem mah she-nehenis* — one who indirectly receives benefit from another pays according to the benefit received, not necessarily according to the cost incurred by the other party or the actual market value of the thing. The canonical illustration is a case of *shein* occurring on public ground (*reshus ha-rabbim*): if my sheep wanders and eats your prize produce, I do not pay you the market price of that produce; I pay only what I would have spent to feed my sheep otherwise — the measure of my benefit, assessed at its most minimal level. This is precisely the framework Chiya bar Rav is applying. The wall was not constructed at the *nikaf*'s request, so the benefit is assessed in the most minimal terms possible.

### Reconciling Views

The Gemara now attempts to read this debate into the language of the mishna itself. *Tnan*: the mishna states that once three walls are built, *ein mechayevin oso* — the inner resident pays nothing. The implication of the *Tanna Kamma* is that if the fourth wall is added, *mechayevin oso* — he does owe something. And Rabbi Yose uses the words *megalgelin alav et hakol* — "we roll upon him everything." The Gemara proposes that according to Rav Huna's framework — where payment reflects the actual wall — the debate between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yose can be understood as a dispute about how much is paid: the *Tanna Kamma* implicitly sanctions only minimal payment (*hakol lefi d'mei kanim be-zol*), while Rabbi Yose's emphatic *et hakol* signals payment according to the full cost of the wall as built (*hakol lefi mah she-gadar*). This is a coherent and natural reading of Rabbi Yose's language.

### Wood Fence Cost

But if we adopt Chiya bar Rav's position — that even Rabbi Yose means only the cost of a cheap wooden fence — the Gemara asks: *mai ika bein Tanna Kamma le-Rabbi Yose*? What distinguishes them? Both seem to say the *nikaf* owes something once the fourth wall goes up; if Rabbi Yose's *et hakol* means only cheap sticks, what could the *Tanna Kamma* possibly be saying that is still less? If even the *Tanna Kamma* requires payment of something, and the floor is the cost of a cheap fence, there is no room beneath Rabbi Yose for the *Tanna Kamma* to occupy.

### Watchman Wages

The Gemara answers: *ibayeit eima agar netira ika beinaihu* — there is in fact something less than a cheap wood fence: the wages one would pay a watchman (*agar netira*) to guard the field. Rather than paying for any physical structure at all, the *nikaf* pays only what it would cost to hire someone to watch over the field. In an economy without minimum wage, that might well be less than even rudimentary fencing materials, though the calculation over time obviously raises questions. The point conceptually is that protection of the field is the operative benefit, and that benefit is achievable without any wall at all — through human oversight. So the *Tanna Kamma* holds that the *nikaf* pays only *agar netira*, the cost equivalent of a watchman, and no more; while Rabbi Yose holds he pays at least the cost of a cheap wood fence, a somewhat higher floor. Note too that in a field, the relevant benefit is protection from intruders and animals — not privacy, which is not a concern in an open agricultural setting. So *agar netira* captures that benefit directly and at minimal cost.

## Which Walls Paid

### Tanna Kamma

The Gemara now proposes a third way to distinguish the *Tanna Kamma* from Rabbi Yose, bracketing the question of how much per wall one pays, and instead asking: for which walls does the *nikaf* owe anything? *Ibayeit eima rishona sheniya ve-shlishit ika beinaihu*. Perhaps the dispute is not about the cost metric but about the scope of payment. On this reading, we assume in both positions that the assessment is based on a cheap wood fence — that much is agreed — but the *Tanna Kamma* holds that once the *makif* builds the fourth wall and triggers the payment obligation, the *nikaf* pays only for the fourth wall: *revi'it hu de-yahiv lei aval rishona sheniya ve-shlishit lo yahiv lei*. The first three walls were already built and standing; the *nikaf* is not made to pay retroactively for them. Only the fourth wall, which completed the enclosure and created the triggering condition, is charged to the *nikaf*.

### Rabbi Yose

Rabbi Yose, by contrast, holds *rishona sheniya ve-shlishit nami yahiv lei* — the *nikaf* pays for all four walls, because he benefits from all four. The word *et hakol* in Rabbi Yose's formulation is taken to mean the entirety: all the walls that together constitute the enclosure from which the *nikaf* benefits. Since the enclosure as a whole is what provides the protection, and the *nikaf* benefits from the whole, there is no principled reason to exclude the first three walls from the accounting.

### Rashi Explanation

Why would the *Tanna Kamma* exempt the *nikaf* from the first three walls? Rashi explains it in terms of time and *status quo*. The first three walls were built, and for some period — a month, a year, an indeterminate time — that was simply how things stood. Three walls, one side open: animals and thieves could still enter freely. During that period, the *nikaf* received no real benefit. That was the accepted state of affairs, a historical *status quo*. When the fourth wall was finally built, we treat only that final wall as the one that created the benefit and therefore the obligation. The three prior walls have already been absorbed into the background. Rashi's approach is intuitive, though it raises the question of what length of time is required to establish that *status quo* — a day? a week? a year? — and the Gemara does not specify.

### Tosafot Explanation

Tosafot offers a conceptually different account. *Omer Ri dehainu ta'ama desheni ve-shlishi d'ein lecha adam shelo haya mesaye'a la-revi'it al m'nat sheyigdor me'arba ruchoteha*: in principle, someone who builds without another's agreement or participation cannot compel payment for anything. But every normal person would agree to chip in for a fourth wall if it ensured their property was fully enclosed. There is an implicit presumption that any reasonable person in the *nikaf*'s position would have desired the fourth wall. This is a conceptual shift: the *Tanna Kamma* is not simply exempting the first three walls on historical grounds but is saying that the basis of any obligation at all is implicit consent — and implicit consent extends only to the completing fourth wall, not to the prior three. Rabbi Yose, by contrast, focuses on actual benefit received: if you benefit from four walls, you pay for four walls. Tosafot's approach is somewhat more abstract than Rashi's, though Rashi's is more straightforwardly grounded in the language and facts of the mishna.

## Who Built Wall

### First Reading

The Gemara now turns to a fourth possible way to read the dispute. *Ibayeit eima makif ve-nikaf ika beinaihu* — the debate may turn on who actually built the fourth wall: the *makif* (the outer party who built the first three) or the *nikaf* (the inner resident). The Gemara has been reading the mishna in one particular way throughout, and now introduces an alternative reading that bears directly on the phrase *im amad ve-gadar* in Rabbi Yose's formulation. At this point in the discussion, the Gemara is still treating the question of payment amount and the question of who builds the fourth wall as interconnected, and working through the implications of each combination.

### Second Reading

*Lishna achrina* — an alternative version of the reading: the Gemara presents a cleaner, more textually consistent account of the *makif/nikaf* dimension of the dispute. This second reading is framed as more faithful to the plain sense of the mishna, which opens with the *makif* building walls one through three. The implication of the *Tanna Kamma* in the mishna's own framing is that the *makif* builds wall four as well, and the *nikaf* pays.

### Tanna Kamma View

According to this second reading, the *Tanna Kamma* holds: *im gadar makif et ha-revi'it nami yahiv lei* — if the outer party goes ahead and builds the fourth wall, the inner resident pays. This is the plain reading of the mishna: it is the *makif* who has been building throughout, and once he completes the fourth wall, the obligation kicks in. The *Tanna Kamma* does not require the *nikaf* to have done anything; the *makif*'s completion of the enclosure is sufficient to trigger payment.

### Rabbi Yose View

Rabbi Yose on this reading holds differently: *im amad nikaf ve-gadar et ha-revi'it hu de-yahiv lei — degali da'atei de-nicha lei*. Only if the *nikaf* himself gets up and builds the fourth wall does the full payment obligation arise, because only then has he clearly revealed his preference (*gala da'ato*) for the enclosure. *Aval im gadar makif lo yahiv lei midi* — but if the *makif* builds the fourth wall, the *nikaf* pays nothing at all. On this reading, Rabbi Yose is actually the more lenient position: he requires the *nikaf*'s own affirmative act before any obligation attaches, whereas the *Tanna Kamma* is willing to impose payment even when the *makif* alone built everything.

This is surprising, and the Gemara acknowledges the tension. Rabbi Yose's language — *megalgelin alav et hakol*, "we roll upon him everything" — sounds like the more demanding position. Yet on this reading it is the *Tanna Kamma* who imposes payment when the *makif* builds the wall, while Rabbi Yose actually requires a higher showing before the *nikaf* can be held liable. The Gemara is consistent with its treatment of Rabbi Yose throughout as the one more inclined to impose liability on the *nikaf*, but the second reading of this last alternative creates a real tension with those earlier assumptions. These different dimensions — how much is paid, for which walls, and conditioned on who builds the fourth wall — are all potentially interconnected. One could naturally link them: if the *nikaf* himself builds the fourth wall and thereby signals desire for the entire enclosure, perhaps he pays the higher rate based on the actual cost of the walls; if the *makif* builds it and the *nikaf* never participated, perhaps he pays only a minimal amount, or perhaps nothing at all. These possibilities remain open.

## Ravina-Runya Case

### Case Setup

The Gemara now moves from abstract debate to a concrete legal incident involving two real figures: Ravina and Runya, neighbors with neighboring fields. *Akfei Ravina me'arba ruchotav* — Ravina surrounded Runya's field with walls from all four sides. His own fields surrounded Runya's on all sides, and he built walls throughout. This is thus precisely the scenario of our mishna, with Ravina as the *makif* and Runya as the *nikaf* — except that here the *makif* did everything, all four walls, without the *nikaf*'s participation.

### Payment Dispute

Ravina came to Runya and said: *hav li kamma de-gadrat* — pay me according to the cost of the wall, invoking the position of Rav Huna (*hakol lefi mah she-gadar*). Runya refused — he had never requested a stone wall and would not pay for one.

### Compromise Offers

Ravina then descended to lesser demands. Fine, pay me at least according to the cost of a cheap wood fence — *lefi d'mei kanim be-zol*, in the manner of Chiya bar Rav. *Lo yahiv lei* — Runya still refused. Fine, pay me at least *agar netira*, watchman's wages, the most minimal possible measure of the benefit you received. *Lo yahiv lei* — Runya refused even that.

### Date-Stealing Test

At this point, Ravina took a different approach. One day he noticed Runya was out harvesting dates from his palm trees — the verb *gadar* carrying the sense of gathering or harvesting, not only of building. Ravina told his sharecropper: *zil shkol minei kivura d'ahini* — go and take a cluster of dates from him. The sharecropper went to grab the dates. *Rama bei kala* — Runya immediately cried out: stop, get away from my dates! Ravina responded: *galui ishtachach de-minaich nicha lach* — you have now shown that you want your field protected. You yourself just demonstrated that you care about securing what is inside these walls.

The argument is admittedly somewhat specious — Runya objected because Ravina's own agent was attempting to take the dates, not because of any general risk. The walls would not have prevented Ravina's agent from entering in the first place. But Ravina's point was the general one: any person wants their field to be protected.

### Goat Protection

Ravina pressed further: *lo yehei ela iza b'alma mi lo ba'i netiruta* — even if you are unconcerned about thieves, surely you need protection from goats. Any normal person wants their property secured, if not from human intruders then from stray animals. Your field clearly benefits from these walls.

### Runya's Defense

Runya responded: *iza b'alma lachluyei ba'i* — if all I needed was protection from goats, I could deal with that by simply yelling at them, as I just yelled at your agent. I do not need a wall for that; I would merely have hired someone to shout at any stray animal that wandered near. Ravina came back: *ve-lo gavra ba'it de-machlei lach?* — but you are not in the field every day. If you were serious about that protection, you would have hired a watchman to be there regularly to yell. So at minimum you are getting the benefit of what it would have cost you to employ such a watchman — *agar netira*.

### Rava's Ruling

The case was brought before Rava. Rava told Runya: *zil payisei be-mai de-mifayis* — go and settle with Ravina on whatever he will accept. Ravina had already shown he was willing to take less than the full wall cost — he would accept the wood-fence equivalent or even watchman's wages. So go and pay him something within that range. *Ve-im lo* — and if you refuse to make even that minimal payment, *dayinan lach dina ke-Rav Huna aliba de-Rabbi Yose* — I will rule against you according to Rav Huna's reading of Rabbi Yose, which means payment based on the full cost of the actual stone wall. The implication is that this is the most stringent reading: Rabbi Yose's *et hakol* means full payment, and Rav Huna applies that even in a case where it was the *makif* who built all four walls.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot raises the question of whether Rava's threat was genuine or merely rhetorical — a device to pressure Runya into accepting the compromise. The Gemara elsewhere employs recognizable hyperbolic phrases when rabbis threaten litigants: "I will seize your home," "I will not let you be," and so on. These phrases signal that the actual *halacha* may be less severe and that the threat is persuasive rather than substantive. Here, however, Rava used none of those standard formulas. Tosafot concludes that the absence of hyperbolic language suggests that Rava's ruling was the genuine *psak*: the actual *halacha* is full payment according to the cost of the wall, and because Ravina was willing to accept less, Rava urged Runya to take advantage of that generosity. But if Runya remained intransigent, the full amount would indeed be imposed.

## Bar Metzra Case

### Bar Metzra Claim

The Gemara now introduces a separate incident between the same two parties. *Runia zaven ar'a ametzra de-Ravina* — Runya purchased a field that was on the boundary (*ametzra*) of Ravina's field. *Savar Ravina le-silukei mishum dina de-bar metzra* — Ravina thought he could force Runya off and take possession of the purchased field, invoking the law of *dina de-bar metzra*, the right of first refusal that belongs to an adjacent neighbor. The logic of *dina de-bar metzra* is that contiguous land is worth considerably more to a neighbor than to a stranger: a neighbor who already farms the surrounding land can work a larger, unified plot more efficiently — plowing it all at once, for instance — so the adjacent field has greater value to him than to any outside buyer. The neighbor is therefore entitled to priority when adjacent land comes up for sale.

Importantly, it appears from the Gemara that even after the sale has been completed, the neighbor with first-refusal rights may have the ability to negate the transaction entirely — not merely a claim for compensation against the seller, but a right to step into the buyer's shoes and annul the sale.

Rav Safra, son of Rav Yeiva, said to Ravina: people say — *amri inshi* — *arba letzalla arba letzlalla*. This cryptic phrase requires unpacking, and Rashi offers three readings of its meaning and relevance.

### Principle

The foundation of *dina de-bar metzra* is the verse *ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov* — "and you shall do what is right and good" (Devarim 6:18). One could argue that a property owner has an absolute right to sell to whomever he chooses. The answer of the tradition is: be a *mensch*. If you will receive the same price regardless, why sell to a stranger rather than to your neighbor who will benefit far more? *Ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov* demands that the neighbor be offered first refusal. Crucially, however, this ethical imperative was not left as a moral aspiration — it was codified as *dina*, law. The very term *dina de-bar metzra* signals that this has become a legal obligation enforceable in court.

### Rashi Reading 1

Rashi's first reading of *arba letzalla arba letzlalla* understands it as a contrast between a poor person and a wealthy one — *tzalla* suggesting a poor figure and *tzlalla* a wealthy one. In this reading, Rav Safra is invoking a different dimension of *ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov*: yes, Ravina has a legal right as adjacent neighbor, but Runya is poor and Ravina is rich. The *mensch*-like thing to do is to let the poor man keep his small plot. You, Ravina, would expand from a thousand contiguous acres to a thousand and two; Runya may have no other ready option. The saying — four for the poor man, four for the wealthy man — captures the idea that both need to eat, both need to sustain themselves, and the powerful should not simply use legal entitlement to crowd out the vulnerable.

### Rashi Reading 3

Rashi's third reading is the most analytically compelling. On this reading, Runya himself had a field within or adjacent to the contested area, such that Runya might actually have had his own *bar metzra* claim — perhaps on a different boundary. Ravina could have had a stronger claim as a neighbor on three sides, while Runya was a neighbor on one side only, which might normally give Ravina greater priority. But the phrase *arba letzalla arba letzlalla* is interpreted through an analogy of a poor tanner versus a wealthy tanner. A poor tanner spends four units of expense to process a small piece of leather; a rich tanner spends the same four units to process a large piece. The wealthy tanner already enjoys economy of scale — his fixed costs are distributed across a much larger output, so each unit costs him proportionally less. The poor tanner, with a small operation, bears the full weight of those four units against far less production. Giving the poor tanner the adjacent piece of leather — or the adjacent plot of land — reduces his per-unit cost dramatically; giving it to the rich tanner produces a negligible marginal benefit because he already benefits from scale. On this reading, Runya actually gains more from acquiring the adjacent field than Ravina does, even if Ravina's formal *bar metzra* priority might appear stronger. This third reading has the advantage of remaining within legal rather than purely moral territory.

## Bar Metzra Case (II)

### Tosafot Challenge

Tosafot, following Rabbeinu Tam, challenges Rashi's first reading sharply: *u-ferush ha-kuntres maksha Rabbeinu Tam — hai merachaminan be-din?* How can we say, within a legal ruling, that we simply take pity on the poor man? *Dina de-bar metzra* was elevated from an ethical aspiration into a *din*. Once it is a *din*, you cannot simply override one person's legal right by appeal to the other party's poverty. It is not one *ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov* against another *ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov* — it is a codified *din* versus a moral sentiment, and a *din* should prevail.

This is a striking challenge, and the question deserves to be taken seriously. There are cases in the Talmud — notably in Bava Metzia — where a rabbi rules that a wealthy litigant should forgive a debt or pay workers their wages even when not legally required, invoking *ve-asita ha-yashar ve-ha-tov* or *lema'an telech be-derech tovim*. And the language of the Gemara here — *amri inshi*, "people say" — does not necessarily signal a technical legal holding; it could be read as invoking a norm of decent conduct rather than a strict rule. On that reading, it may well be that Rava Safra was not telling Ravina he had no legal claim, but that the right thing to do — *lifnim mishurat ha-din* — was to stand aside. The tension between these readings is not fully resolved here and will receive fuller treatment when *dina de-bar metzra* is addressed directly later in the tractate.

## Fallen Wall

### Shared Wall Falls

The Gemara now cites the next mishna: *kotel chatzer she-nafal mechayvin oto livnot* — if a shared courtyard wall falls, both parties can be compelled to rebuild it, *ad arba amot* — up to four cubits in height. The rationale, developed earlier in the Gemara, is that even a party who originally did not believe in the claim of *hezek re'iyah* (visual damage) becomes habituated over time to conducting private activities in his yard with the expectation of a wall. Once that wall is gone, real damage results, and both parties share the obligation to rebuild up to the height necessary to restore privacy — four cubits.

### Payment Presumption

The mishna continues: *bechezkat she-natan ad she-yavi re'ayah shelo natan* — once the obligation to rebuild jointly is established, the party who urges rebuilding can compel the other to participate, and the presumption is that the reluctant party *has* paid his share unless the other can bring proof that he has not. Since both are understood to be equally obligated, societal norms create a presumption of payment; and since proving a negative — that payment was never made — is extremely difficult, the burden effectively falls on the one seeking to collect.

### Higher Wall

The mishna adds: *samach lo kotel acher af al pi she-lo natan alav et ha-tikra megalgelin alav et ha-kol* — if one party built the shared wall to a height greater than four cubits, and the neighbor subsequently built a parallel wall on his own side and appears to be preparing to roof the space between them, the Gemara treats this as a demonstration of the neighbor's desire for the greater height. Just as building the fourth enclosing wall reveals that the *nikaf* wanted the enclosure, building a parallel structure reveals that the neighbor desired and took advantage of the higher wall. In that case, *megalgelin alav et ha-kol* — the neighbor is made to pay his proportionate share of the full height, not just the four-cubit minimum.

### Tosafot Benefit

Tosafot raises a question regarding this case that connects back to the foundational principle of *zeh nehene ve-zeh lo chaser* — one benefits while the other loses nothing. If I have already built a tall wall, and my neighbor simply benefits from its greater height at no additional cost to me, why should he have to pay? The principle from Bava Kamma is that when benefit is received at no cost to the provider, no payment is owed. Tosafot answers in two ways. First, once the neighbor reveals through his actions that he desired the height (*gala da'ato de-nicha lei*), that demonstration of preference changes the analysis — the consent-derived obligation arises independently. Second — and Tosafot's preferred answer — there actually *is* a *chaser* here: the neighbor's presence is what caused the original builder to construct a wall higher than four cubits. Had there been no neighboring field, there would have been no need to build beyond the standard privacy height. The additional height was incurred *because* of the neighbor, even if the neighbor did not directly cause a monetary loss in the moment. That causal connection is sufficient to establish that the benefit was not entirely free; it came at an expense the builder would not otherwise have borne.

## Payment Claims

### Reish Lakish

The Gemara now turns to a broader principle triggered by the mishna's presumptions of payment. Reish Lakish states: *ha-kove'a zman le-chavero ve-amar lo paraticha be-toch zmani* — if one explicitly fixes a due date for a loan and the borrower later claims "I paid you before the date arrived," *eino ne'eman* — he is not believed. The reasoning: *delavay she-yifra be-zmano* — it would be enough of an achievement if people simply paid on time. The presumption runs strongly against early payment.

### Abaye/Rava

Abaye and Rava both disagree: *avid inish de-para be-go zamneh* — it does happen that a person pays within the loan period. *De-zimnin de-mitramu lei zuzei amar eizil ve-efreih ki heichi de-lo litridin* — sometimes money becomes available unexpectedly, and the borrower thinks: let me pay now so the creditor won't pester me later. That is a recognizable human motivation, and since it does occur, the borrower is believed to claim early payment.

### Shared Wall Inference

The Gemara attempts to resolve this dispute from the mishna's presumption. The case of the shared courtyard wall — *bechezkat she-natan* — seems to credit the claim of payment. What is the scenario? If the claim is that payment was made after the wall was complete, that is trivial: of course a debtor is believed to say he paid once the debt was due, at least absent a *shtar*. The *chiddush* of the mishna must therefore be that the neighbor is believed to claim payment *during* the construction — before the wall was finished — suggesting that *avid inish de-para be-go zamneh*, in support of Abaye and Rava.

### Ongoing Construction

The Gemara deflects: *shani hacha de-chol shafa ve-shafa zimneh hu* — this case is different, because construction is an ongoing process. Each course of stones laid is its own expense and its own due date. There is no single lump-sum due date that the payment preceded; each installment is payable as incurred. So the mishna's presumption of payment tells us nothing about whether someone is believed to claim early payment on a conventional fixed-term loan.

### Extra Height Case

The Gemara turns to the mishna's second case: *bechezkat she-lo natan ad she-yavi re'ayah she-natan* — the neighbor who built the parallel wall and thereby incurred an obligation for the extra height is presumed *not* to have paid unless he can prove otherwise. The Gemara asks: what is the scenario here? If the claim is that payment was made after the obligation became clear and the debt was fully due, why should the neighbor not be believed — as any debtor is believed to say he paid once the time came?

### Skepticism Argument

The Gemara answers: *shani hacha de-amar mi yeymar de-mechayivei li Rabbanan* — this case is different because the neighbor was genuinely skeptical that *beit din* would impose an obligation on her at all. She built her own parallel wall and did not necessarily accept that she thereby obligated herself for the original builder's extra height. Because she doubted whether the ruling would go against her, she had no motivation to pay preemptively. The presumption is therefore that she did not pay even once the obligation was formally established — and she must prove otherwise. Again, no inference can be drawn from this case about early payment of fixed-term loans.

### Final Halacha

The Gemara concludes by stating the law. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua ruled like Abaye and Rava — a person is believed to say he paid within the loan period. Mar bar Ashi, however, acted like Reish Lakish, holding that early payment claims are not credited. *Ve-hilchata ke-Reish Lakish* — the final ruling follows Reish Lakish. If there was a fixed due date and the borrower claims to have paid before it arrived, he is not believed. *Ve-afilu mi-yasmei* — this applies even when collecting from orphans. Normally, one who seeks to collect from an estate of orphans must take an oath (*shevuah*) that the debt has not been repaid, even if a *shtar* exists, since the orphans cannot know what their father may have arranged. But if the debt is being collected before the due date has arrived, no *shevuah* is required: *chazakah lo avid inish de-para be-go zimneh* — there is an established presumption that people do not pay before the due date, so no realistic possibility of prior payment need be entertained, and the collector proceeds without oath. This presumption is especially strong in a halakhic framework where no interest is charged and where mechanisms like *shemitah* can cancel debts — there is simply no incentive to pay early, making the *chazakah* particularly robust.

# Bava Batra 6

## Migo vs. Chazaka

### Early Payment Claim

The *daf* opens by building on a conclusion established in the preceding discussion: there is a *chazaka* that people do not pay back a loan within the designated loan period — *chazaka lo avid inish deparei bego zimnei*. Ordinarily, the rule of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya* governs debt disputes, placing the burden of proof on the claimant. But when a debtor claims he repaid within the loan period, this *chazaka* overrides his claim and he is not believed.

The *Gemara* now poses a new question: *tava'o achar zman ve'amar lo peraticha betoch zemani mahu?* — what is the *halacha* if the creditor makes his demand after the thirty days have elapsed, but the debtor responds not by saying he paid after the due date, but rather that he had already paid during the loan period, while the loan was not yet due? Had the debtor simply said he paid yesterday — that is, after the due date — he would clearly be believed, since that is a standard case of *kofer hakol* in which the rule of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya* applies and he would at most be required to take a *shevuat hesset*.

### Migo Application

The question, then, is whether a *migo* can operate here. Since the debtor could have made the more advantageous claim — "I paid you after the loan came due" — and would have been believed, does that give him a *migo* to be believed even when he instead claims he paid earlier, during the loan period? In terms of *migo* logic, there is essentially no incentive to lie: it makes no practical difference to the debtor whether he says he paid last week or yesterday. Moreover, he is the one currently *muchzak* in the money. And yet the *Gemara* raises the counter-possibility: when a *migo* collides with a *chazaka* of this strength — the near-certain behavioral presumption that people simply do not repay within the loan period — perhaps even a *migo*, and even *muchzak* status, cannot overcome it.

### Wall Building Case

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve this question by examining the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* teaches *bechezkat shenatan ad sheyavi re'aya shelo natan* — when a wall collapsed and both neighbors share an obligation to rebuild up to *arba amot*, and one party claims he already paid his share, he is presumed to have paid unless the other brings proof that he did not. The *Gemara* asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the scenario?

If the builder demanded payment after the wall was fully built and the debtor said he paid after construction was complete, that would be an obvious case of *kofer hakol* and there is no novelty in the *mishnah* believing him. *Ela lav* — the *mishnah* must therefore be addressing a more striking scenario: that the debtor claims he paid *during* the construction, while the wall was still being built — *de'amar lo peraticha betoch zemani*. And the *mishnah* believes him. If so, the *mishnah* would constitute a proof that *migo* does function even against this *chazaka*: since he could have said he paid after the wall was finished and been believed, that *migo* is enough to credit his claim of earlier payment.

The *Gemara* rejects this proof: *shani hacha dekol shafa veshafa zman hu* — the wall-building case is different, because here every brick laid creates a new obligation. The debt is not a single lump sum due at a fixed endpoint; it accrues continuously throughout construction. Every expenditure of labor and material generates an immediate obligation to reimburse, so there is no true *toch zman* — no period during which repayment would be premature. Since the debt is, in a sense, already owed at every moment, a claim of earlier payment is far more plausible, and the *mishnah*'s ruling does not bear on the question of whether *migo* can override a *chazaka* in the classic loan context.

### Higher Wall Analysis

The *Gemara* then attempts a proof from the second clause of the *mishnah*, which addresses the case of a wall built higher than *arba amot*. Beyond that height, there is no obligation arising from *hezek re'iyah*, so the neighbor cannot be compelled to contribute. However, the *mishnah* states that if the neighbor then builds a parallel wall — *samach lo kotel acher* — he demonstrates that he intends to make use of the additional height, and he becomes obligated to pay for it. In this case, the *mishnah* rules *bechezka shelo natan* — he is presumed not to have paid, and is not believed unless he brings proof.

The *Gemara* applies the same analytical framework: *ilima detav'o le'achar zmano ve'amar lo paraticha bizmani*, if he claimed he paid after the additional wall was complete, why would he not be believed? That would be an obvious *kofer hakol*. So *ela lav* — it must be that the *mishnah* is addressing the case where he claims he paid during construction, *de'amar paraticha betoch zmani*, and that is why he is not believed — *alma bemakom chazaka lo amrinan mah li lishaker* — we do not say *migo* against the *chazaka*.

The *Gemara* rejects this proof as well. The reason the debtor is not believed in the case of the higher wall has nothing to do with the *migo*-versus-*chazaka* question. Rather, *shani hacha de'amar mar mi yeimar demichayvu li rabanan* — the neighbor may simply not know that building a parallel wall obligates him to share the cost of the additional height. Since this is not common knowledge, the presumption is that he assumed he owed nothing and would not pay until a *beit din* ruled him obligated. Even once the obligation arises, he is presumed to be holding out until formally adjudicated. This explains the distinction between the first *arba amot* — where the obligation is well-known — and the higher portion of the wall. The *mishnah*'s ruling in this case therefore proves nothing about the *migo*-versus-*chazaka* problem.

### Baraita Evidence

Rav Acha the son of Rava then presents a *baraita* as a potential proof: *maneh li beyadecha* — if Reuven says to Shimon, "You owe me a hundred dinars," and Shimon admits it, and then the following day Reuven demands repayment — *im amar netativ lach patur*, if Shimon says he already paid, he is exempt. But if Shimon says *ein lacha beyadi*, there is nothing owed to you, he is liable, since this contradicts his own admission of the previous day.

The *Gemara* proposes an interpretation to make this *baraita* relevant: *mai lav netativ lach de'amar lei paraticha bizmani* — "I paid you" means he paid after the debt came due, and *ein lacha beyadi* means not a denial that he ever borrowed, but a claim that the debt never reached maturity because he had already prepaid it — *paraticha betoch zamni*. On this reading, the *baraita* would teach that this claim is not believed — proving that *migo* does not work against the *chazaka*.

### Denial Interpretation

The *Gemara* rejects this interpretation as well: *mai ein lacha beyadi lo hayu devarim me'olam* — the phrase *ein lacha beyadi* means simply a complete denial that there was ever a debt, not a claim of prepayment. And of course, if he is contradicting his own admission of the previous day, it is obvious he is not believed — there is no *chiddush* in that ruling.

The *Gemara* invokes the principle *de'amar mar kol ha'omer lo livisi ke'omer lo parati dami* — one who denies having borrowed at all is treated as if he declared he never repaid. *Tosafos* raises the question of why this principle is even needed here, given that the contradiction with yesterday's admission is self-evident. *Tosafos* explains: the principle is invoked to prevent Shimon from reinterpreting his own words — from claiming that when he said "I never borrowed," he really meant "I had already paid." The *Gemara* forecloses that interpretation; his denial is taken at face value. The *halacha* of *migo* against the *chazaka* of early repayment therefore remains unresolved.

---

## Shared Wall Rights

### Rav Huna Position

Returning now to the *mishnah*, the *Gemara* presents a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman regarding what it means when one neighbor builds a partial parallel wall. Rav Huna states: *samach lepalga samach lekula* — if the neighbor built a parallel wall for only part of the height or only part of the length, we treat it as though he intends to use the entire wall. So if Reuven built a wall ten *amot* high and Shimon built a parallel wall only eight *amot* high, or built it along only half the length, Rav Huna holds Shimon liable for the full height and full length of Reuven's wall. The rationale is that by building any portion of a parallel wall, Shimon signals his intention to use the whole thing.

### Rav Nachman Position

Rav Nachman takes the more intuitive position: *lemai desamach samach lemai delo samach lo samach* — Shimon is obligated only for the portion he actually built parallel to. If he went up eight *amot*, he pays for eight *amot*; if he built along fifty feet, he pays for fifty feet. He does not become liable for anything he did not explicitly parallel.

### Edge Curling Exception

Both *Amoraim* agree on one exception. Rav Huna concedes — *modeh Rav Huna bekarna de-alufta* — that if Shimon curled the edge at the top or the end of his partial construction, this is a clear signal that he is not planning to extend further. As *Tosafos* explains, the curl at the edge demonstrates finality, and in such a case even Rav Huna would not obligate Shimon for the unbuilt portions.

Conversely, Rav Nachman agrees — *u-modeh Rav Nachman be-afriza u-be-kivasa de-kshurei* — that if Shimon took steps clearly indicating that he intends to continue building upward, such as laying a beam across the top in preparation for constructing a second story, then even Rav Nachman would hold him liable for the full height. The *afriza* is the preparatory beam laid across the top of the wall, and the *kivasa de-kshurei* refers to the channel or socket prepared to receive the crossbeams from the adjacent wall. These structural preparations make unmistakably clear that Shimon intends to use the entire height, and Rav Nachman would obligate him accordingly.

---

## Beam Holes Proof

### Holes as Proof

The *Gemara* now takes up a related question. Rav Huna states: *bei kivei lo havei chazaka* — holes made in the wall for crossbeams do not constitute a *chazaka*. Here the term *chazaka* refers not to the three-year *chazaka* of *Perek* 3, which involves a claim of purchase and requires three years of undisturbed possession, but rather to the type of *chazaka* in which a party's silence or acquiescence serves as evidence that rights were granted or a debt was settled. It is a much broader use of the term.

The case is as follows: Shimon built the shared wall to a height of, say, ten *amot*, and within the wall he made holes — and even inserted wooden paddings, *himlei*, within those holes — positioned precisely where Reuven would need to insert crossbeams if he were to build a parallel wall. Reuven argues: the fact that Shimon prepared these holes for me is proof that I had already paid him for my share of the extra height; otherwise, why would Shimon have accommodated me in this way?

### Anticipation Defense

The *Gemara* explains why this argument fails. *De'amar lei amina de-lechi payastei li lo lishat-ei ashitai* — Shimon can respond: "I anticipated that you would eventually build your wall and need to insert your crossbeams, and I made the holes in advance rather than waiting for you to pay me and then having to cut new holes into an already-completed wall, which would damage it." The preparation of the holes was prudent construction practice, not evidence of a prior payment. Reuven's claim that the holes prove he paid is therefore not accepted, and Rav Huna's ruling stands: *bei kivei lo havei chazaka*.

---

## Use Chazaka

### Use Rights Principle

Rav Nachman now turns to a different application of *chazaka* — establishing ongoing use rights through unprotested activity. The scenario is straightforward: Reuven's wall stands entirely within his own property, along the border. Shimon builds his own wall in his field and rests a crossbeam atop Reuven's wall. Reuven says nothing. Does Reuven's silence constitute an acquiescence that gives Shimon established rights to continue using the wall?

This raises a significant question debated among the *Rishonim*: is the silence alone sufficient to establish *chazaka*, or must the silence be backed by an explicit claim on Shimon's part that Reuven had formally granted him the rights — whether through sale, gift, or agreement? This distinction has far-reaching implications for questions involving tenants and neighbors.

### Light/Heavy Beams

Rav Nachman rules: *ahzik l'hurdi lo ahzik l'kshuri* — if Shimon established a *chazaka* by resting thin planks on Reuven's wall, that does not give him the right to rest heavy beams on it. Reuven can say: "I was tolerant of the light planks; I am not granting you permission to impose heavy beams on my wall." The converse, however, is the case: *l'kshuri ahzik l'hurdi* — if Shimon had established a *chazaka* with heavy beams and Reuven acquiesced, then implicitly Shimon also has rights to use the wall for light planks. Reuven's silence in the face of the greater imposition carries with it acceptance of the lesser one.

### Rav Yosef View

Rav Yosef disagrees: *ahzik l'hurdi ahzik l'kshuri* — even establishing a *chazaka* with thin planks gives Shimon rights to heavy beams as well, since the difference in burden on Reuven's wall is not so substantial as to require a separate grant of permission. A second version of the *Gemara* reports that Rav Nachman himself ultimately agreed that the rule operates symmetrically in both directions.

### Drainage Case

An analogous dispute is applied to the case of roof drainage. Rav Nachman states: *ahzik l'nitfi ahzik l'shifchi* — if Shimon established a *chazaka* for rain dripping off his roof in a dispersed pattern onto Reuven's field (*nitfi*), that also gives him the right to channel water through a drainage pipe (*shifchi*), since piped drainage is more concentrated but arguably more controlled. The reverse, however, does not follow: *ahzik l'shifchi lo ahzik l'nitfi* — a *chazaka* established through a drainage pipe does not give him rights to have water run off the roof indiscriminately in all directions across Reuven's field, which is a broader and less predictable form of intrusion.

Rav Nachman adds a further qualification: *aval l'tzrifa d'urbani lo* — even if *nitfi* establishes a *chazaka*, it does not extend to a steeply angled roof that channels rain in heavy concentrated streams, since that represents a significantly more severe incursion than ordinary dripping. Rav Yosef, however, rules: *afilu tzrifa d'urbani* — even the angled roof is included, and he in fact issued a practical ruling to that effect.

---

## Tenant Rights

### Base Extensions

Rav Nachman cites Rabba bar Avuha: *hamaskir bayis l'chavero b'bira gedola* — one who rents a room in a large building — the tenant may use the wall protrusions and the walls that extend beyond the immediate boundaries of his room, up to *arba amot*: *mishtamesh b'zizay u'b'kotlei ad arba amos*. These extensions are considered implicitly included in the rental. Similarly, *u'v'ovi hakosel bimkom shenahagu* — the thickness of the wall, which Rashi understands as the top surface of the wall, is also available for the tenant's use, where local custom supports it.

### Garden/Alley Rights

Beyond these basics, the *Gemara* records a dispute. The base ruling states *aval b'tarbitz apadni lo* — the tenant does not have rights to the garden in front of the building. Rav Nachman himself, however, disagrees: *afilu b'tarbitz apadni* — even the forecourt garden is included in the tenant's rights. As for the back alley behind the buildings — *aval rechova she-achorei ha-batim lo* — the initial ruling excludes this entirely. Rava extends the tenant's rights further still: *afilu rechova she-achorei ha-batim* — even the back alley is included.

---

## Chazaka Time Limit

### Thirty-Day Rule

Ravina now addresses the time threshold required to establish a *chazaka* of use. The case is a beam of a *sukkah* — here meaning a hut or temporary structure, not necessarily a *sukkah* of the *mitzvah* — resting on a neighbor's wall. *Ad taltin yomin lo hovei chazaka* — up to thirty days of unchallenged use does not establish a *chazaka*, since the owner may simply be tolerating it for a short period without intending to cede any rights. *Basar taltin yomin hovei chazaka* — beyond thirty days of silence, however, a *chazaka* is established.

It bears noting that this ruling, coming immediately after the discussions of *chazaka* of a few days and specifying thirty days rather than three years, makes clear that we are not dealing with the *chazaka* of purchase from *Perek* 3. This is an entirely distinct mechanism: the establishment of usage rights through unprotested activity.

### Sukkot Exception

An exception applies during *Sukkot*: if the structure is an actual *sukkah* of the *mitzvah*, the threshold is shortened. *Ad shiva yomin lo hovei chazaka* — up to seven days, the neighbor's silence is expected, since obviously he will tolerate a *sukkah* during the *chag*. *Basar shiva yomin hovei chazaka* — but if after the festival is over the *sukkah* remains and the neighbor still says nothing, a *chazaka* is established, since the normal time to dismantle it has passed. *Tosafos* notes that "seven days" should practically be understood as eight days — or nine for communities that observe *Simchat Torah* as well — since one does not dismantle the *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret*.

### Plastering Rule

A further rule: *v'ei chivreh b'tina l'altar hovei chazaka* — if the crossbeam was plastered into the wall and the neighbor saw this and said nothing, a *chazaka* is established immediately, without waiting for thirty days or seven. The permanence of the plastering and the neighbor's failure to react at that moment constitutes immediate establishment of rights. The *Rishonim* point to the word *la'altar* — "immediately" — as further proof that the thirty-day and seven-day rules discussed here are entirely separate from the three-year *chazaka* of purchase.

---

## Cross-Street Houses

### Property Setup

Abaye introduces a case involving two houses on opposite sides of a *reshut harabbim* — a public thoroughfare. The problem of *hezek re'iyah* arises between them, since each owner can see into the other's property. Since the public street separates the two properties, one cannot simply build a shared wall down the middle and divide the cost. The solution presented is: *zeh oseh makeh l'chatzi gago vezeh oseh makeh l'chatzi gago* — each party builds a parapet along half of his own roof, positioned so that they do not align with each other but rather overlap: *vezeh shelo keneged zeh umadif*. The overlap ensures that there is no angle of sight through the gap between them.

### Public vs. Private

The *Gemara* asks: *mai irya birshut harabbim* — why specify a public thoroughfare? Wouldn't the same problem and solution apply if the two houses were separated by a private street? The answer is that the *reshut harabbim* is the genuine *chiddush*. One might have thought that Reuven could argue: Shimon, you would have built a parapet anyway to shield yourself from the people passing below in the public domain, so my viewing you is irrelevant to your need for a wall — do not make me pay for half. The *Gemara* therefore teaches that this argument fails.

### Visibility Arguments

Shimon has compelling responses. First: *rabbim beyomama chazi li baleila lo chazi li* — the people in the street can see me in the daytime but not at night; I would not bother building for them alone. But Reuven can see me equally by day and by night, so I am building this wall on account of him. Second: *rabbim ki kyamina chazi li ki yasivna lo chazu li* — the public, being below, can only see me when I am standing; when I sit, they cannot see me. But Reuven, at the same height, sees me whether I am standing or sitting. Third: *rabbim ki me'aynu chazu li ki lo me'aynu lo chazu li* — the passersby must make a deliberate effort to look up intently; I would not be especially bothered by that. But Reuven sees me incidentally and without effort. On all three grounds, Shimon demonstrates that his need for a wall is driven specifically by Reuven's *hezek re'iyah*, not by the public's presence, and Reuven is therefore obligated to do his half.

### Half-Wall Method

The ruling itself — *zeh oseh makeh l'chatzi gago vezeh oseh makeh l'chatzi gago vezeh shelo keneged zeh umadif* — might seem obvious, and the *Gemara* acknowledges this: *peshita*. Each party builds half, and the overlap is also self-evidently necessary to prevent diagonal sightlines.

### Full Completion Question

The *Gemara* clarifies that the *chiddush* applies to a case where one of the parties went ahead and already completed his half: *lo tzericha dekadim chad mineihu ve'avid*. One might think that once one party has built his portion, the other can say: take your expenses from me and simply finish building the entire wall yourself — you're already there, just continue.

### Equal Obligation

The *Gemara* rejects this: *ka mashma lan d'amar lei at mai ta'ama lo avadat mishum demitra'e ashitech ana nami mitre'ina ashiti*. The party who has already built can respond: "Why have you not built your half? Because you do not want to impose the weight of a parapet on your own structure. Precisely the same consideration applies to me — I do not want to bear that weight either. The fact that I have already built my half does not change the fundamental principle: you are responsible for your half and I am responsible for mine." Each party must build his own portion on his own side. Prior completion by one party does not shift the obligation to complete the entire wall onto him, and the other party cannot buy his way out of building his own half.

---

---

# Bava Batra 7

## Gag Overlooking Chatzer

### Four Amot Wall

Today's daf picks up in the middle of 6b, where the *gemara* has been discussing who pays for a shared wall. The *mishnah* established that the first four *amot* of wall construction is shared; beyond that, one cannot compel a neighbor to contribute unless that neighbor demonstrates his own desire for the wall by building a parallel structure. But before moving forward, the *gemara* returns to examine some of the foundational questions surrounding *hezek reiyah* — the damage caused by overlooking — and when one can be compelled to build even a basic privacy wall.

Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel: *gag hasamuch lachatzar chaveiro, ose lo maakeh gavoha arba amot* — if one has a roof that overlooks a neighbor's yard, one must erect a wall around the roof four *amot* high. The logic is clear: a wall on the neighbor's side does no good, since the overlooking party can still see in. It is therefore the owner of the roof who must build a *maakeh* for privacy purposes, setting aside entirely the separate *mitzvah* of *maakeh* for safety.

### Adjacent Rooftops

The *gemara* continues: *aval bein gag legag lo* — but between two adjacent rooftops, no such obligation exists. One can imagine the Old City of Jerusalem, where one can walk across the tops of buildings as if traversing a continuous concrete expanse, with the boundary between individual rooftops invisible from below. Even in such a case, no four-*amot* wall is required.

Why the difference? Presumably, Shmuel's position is that rooftops are used only occasionally, and therefore the *hezek reiyah* concern is diminished. Unlike a yard, where one expects the neighbor to emerge from his house at any moment, a rooftop sees far rarer and more irregular use. Whatever private activities one wishes to conduct there, both parties can readily observe whether the other is present. This does not rise to the level of a serious *hezek*.

Rav Nachman himself, however, goes further: *amar eino zakuk l'arba amot aval zakuk limchitzah asarah* — one is not required to build a four-*amot* wall, but one is required to erect a partition of ten *tefachim*, approximately two and a half feet. The *gemara* immediately asks: *lemai* — for what purpose? If the concern is *hezek reiyah*, ten *tefachim* is plainly insufficient; four *amot* would be needed. And if Shmuel maintains there is no *hezek reiyah* concern at all between adjacent rooftops, then even ten *tefachim* seems superfluous.

### Trespass Concern

The *gemara* works through the alternatives. *Iy l'hezek reiyah, arba amot beinan* — if for privacy, four *amot* are required. *Iy lenitzolei alav keganav* — if the concern is preventing trespass, so that no one inadvertently wanders onto a neighbor's rooftop, a simple property marker would suffice. The *gemara* indeed suggests *bemitzra b'alma sagi* — small pegs or boundary markers are enough.

What about *iy legidayim u'rtushin* — to prevent goats and young animals from crossing over? This may seem puzzling in a contemporary context, but if one recalls that rooftops in ancient Mesopotamia and the Land of Israel were regularly used for sleeping, drying fruit, and various agricultural purposes, the presence of animals is not inconceivable. Even so, for that purpose *bechdi shelo yizdaker bevat rosh sagi* — it is sufficient to have a barrier high enough that an animal cannot put its head through, which is only a few *tefachim*, not ten.

The *gemara* concludes: *leolam lo nitfas alav k'ganav* — the function of the ten-*tefachim* partition is indeed trespass prevention. The reason a mere marker is insufficient is that one can evade it with an excuse: *dematzei matzei mishtamit lei* — one could claim to have been pressed against the edge without noticing the small pegs, or as the text puts it, *amrei mitzurei ka mitzureina*, one was simply jostled across. But *mechitzas asarah lo matzei mishtamit lei* — with a genuine partition of ten *tefachim*, no such excuse is available. The partition makes the property boundary undeniable.

This introduces a striking principle: the same way neighbors can compel one another to share in the cost of a wall addressing *hezek reiyah*, one can apparently compel a neighbor to share in building a trespass-prevention barrier. Neighboring relationships and shared spaces generate mutual obligations — not only for the common good, as in the case of a town wall, but also to prevent the specific, interpersonal damage of trespass. The trespass concern is treated as a form of potential damage that both parties share responsibility to prevent.

### Higher Yard Exemption

The *gemara* raises a challenge: *im haya chatzero lemala migago shel chaveiro, ein nizkakin lo* — if one's yard is situated higher than a neighbor's rooftop, no wall is required. Here the person in the yard is constantly and directly overlooking the roof below, which would seem to present a far more serious *hezek reiyah* — the presence is more constant and direct than the adjacent-rooftop case. Yet no wall is demanded.

The explanation is that compromising the use of a *gag* — a rooftop — is simply not treated as a weighty *hezek reiyah* concern. Because the rooftop sees irregular use, the ongoing sight line from above does not constitute the kind of *hezek* that compels remedy. *Ein lo esek imo* — one cannot make any demands.

The *gemara* asks whether this means one cannot demand anything at all, not even the ten-*tefachim* trespass partition. It resolves: *lo ein lo esek imo b'arba amot* — one cannot demand a four-*amot* privacy wall, since the underlying *hezek reiyah* claim regarding a rooftop is insufficient, *aval esek yesh lo b'mechitzah shel asarah* — but one can still demand the ten-*tefachim* trespass barrier.

One might ask why a trespass barrier is needed at all once the two properties are at different elevations. The answer appears to be that if the difference in height is gradual enough, or less than ten *tefachim*, one could still wander from one level to the other without realizing it — particularly if the terrain slopes rather than drops sharply. Only once the step between levels is itself at least ten *tefachim* does the geography itself serve as a sufficient divider. As Rashi notes, without such a barrier, trespass could more plausibly be characterized as intentional, lending it the character of *nitpas alav k'ganav* — being caught as a thief — which is more culpable than mere accident.

## Yards at Different Levels

### Rav Huna Opinion

Having established the framework for rooftop privacy, the *gemara* turns to a related and more complex scenario: *shtei chatzerot zo l'malah mi'zo* — two courtyards, one situated higher than the other. Here *hezek reiyah* is clearly operative: the person at the upper level has a continuous and unobstructed view into the lower yard, which sees regular use. The lower resident has a genuine and serious complaint.

Rav Huna rules: *tachton boneh miknegdo v'oleh, v'elyon boneh miknegdo v'oleh* — the lower party builds up from his own level and the upper party builds up from his. The picture is one of a property line running between the two levels, where the wall that will ultimately block the sight line must be constructed jointly, with each party responsible for the portion corresponding to his own position. Exactly how to visualize this is not immediately obvious. It may be that the slope between the two properties is gradual, with the property line running at some intermediate elevation, and each party is responsible for raising the wall from that line to his own level.

### Rav Chisda Opinion

Rav Chisda disagrees: *elyon mesayeya milimata uboneh* — the upper party must also contribute to the construction of the lower portion of the wall. The reasoning is that in order for the wall to reach the height necessary to protect the upper yard, the foundation of the lower portion must first be built. Since the upper party requires that lower construction to achieve his own protection, he must share in its cost. The *gemara* confirms: *tanyah kevata de-Rav Chisda* — a *braita* is cited in support of Rav Chisda's position. That *braita* also incorporates the earlier rule: *v'im hayetah chatzeir l'malah migago shel chaveiro, eino zakuk lo* — if the yard is higher than a neighbor's roof, there is no obligation to build, consistent with what was established above.

## Shared Housing Structure

### Upper Tenant Refusal

The *gemara* shifts to a scenario involving two tenants sharing a single structure, one occupying the lower level and one the upper. *Chad hava dayar elai v'chad hava dayar tata'ei* — one lived above, one below. Then the lower structure partially collapsed or sank — Rashi explains that the wall sank into the ground, causing the floor of the upper level to drop, and with it the ceiling of the lower space. The upper tenant remains entirely comfortable; the lower tenant now cannot stand upright.

The lower tenant asks the upper one to cooperate in rebuilding. The upper tenant refuses: *ana shappir kadiyerna* — I am fine, why should I rebuild? The lower tenant then offers to pay for the entire reconstruction himself. The upper tenant refuses again: he does not wish to be displaced from his home during construction, even temporarily. The lower tenant offers to rent him alternative accommodations. The upper tenant declines: *lo tarchna* — I do not want the trouble of moving.

At this point the lower tenant resorts to bitter humor: *shufa kreichach v'aeul, v'shufa kreichach v'afok* — squirm in on your belly and squirm out again. That is not my problem.

Rav Chama rules: *b'dina kamiaikeiv* — the upper tenant's refusal is entirely legitimate. One cannot be compelled to vacate one's home in order to accommodate a neighbor's need to rebuild, even at the neighbor's expense.

### Ten Tefachim Threshold

Rav Chama qualifies this ruling: *v'hanei milei d'lo matu kashurei l'mata m'asarah* — this applies only so long as the ceiling beams have not dropped to within ten *tefachim* of the floor. Once the ceiling descends to within ten *tefachim* — approximately thirty to thirty-six inches, the same minimum height that defines a valid *sukkah* — the analysis changes. *Aval matu kashurei l'mata m'asarah, matzi amar lei l'mata m'asarah reshusi didi hu* — the lower tenant can then say: below ten *tefachim* is my domain, and you have no right to encroach upon it.

This is a striking formulation. The *gemara* does not frame the issue merely as uninhabitability — that the space has become too low to live in — but as a genuine property claim. Ten *tefachim* is recognized as the basic airspace belonging to ground level: the height of a *reshut ha-rabim* is ten *tefachim*, and a *reshut ha-yachid* extends upward from there. Within ten *tefachim*, one is, legally speaking, occupying the lower tenant's space. The upper tenant is not merely causing inconvenience; he is effectively residing within his neighbor's domain. What precise share of the reconstruction costs the upper tenant can be compelled to bear in this situation remains an open question.

### Stipulation & Heikhal

All of the above applies when the two tenants — who are presumed to have been brothers dividing an inherited house — made no prior stipulations. *Aval asnu bahadi hadadi, v'ki asnu bahadi hadadi satro u'vanu* — if they stipulated that should the structure ever require rebuilding both parties would cooperate, then rebuilding may proceed. This is not a remarkable *chiddush* on its face.

The more interesting question is: if they stipulated in general terms but did not specify what threshold of deterioration triggers the obligation to rebuild, how far must the ceiling drop before the stipulation is invoked? Scholars reported to Rava in the name of Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman, who cited Rav Nachman: *k'osa sheshaninu, rumo k'chatzi archo v'chatzi rachvo* — like that which we have taught, that the standard height is half the combined length and width. This is derived from the dimensions of the *Mikdash*, which was forty *amot* long, twenty *amot* wide, and thirty *amot* high. Forty plus twenty is sixty; half of sixty is thirty, matching the actual height. On this view, if you have a large space with great width and length, the appropriate ceiling height scales proportionally — a grand hall demands a grand height. This same principle, it was claimed, would apply here: if the height drops below half the combined length and width of the space, the stipulation is triggered.

### Normal Usage Standards

Rava rejected this attribution sharply: *lav amina l'chu lo titlu bei bukei srikei b'Rav Nachman* — did I not tell you not to attribute such empty things to Rav Nachman? He could not believe Rav Nachman would say something so contrived. The attribution came from Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman, citing his own father, which Rava apparently found implausible.

What Rav Nachman actually said, Rava insists, is *k'd'daieri inshi* — as normal people dwell. The relevant standard is not a geometric formula derived from the Temple's proportions but simply the local norm for habitable living space. The *gemara* then asks: and how much is that? Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua answers with a practical image: *k'heichi d'ayeli istura d'machuza v'hadar* — like someone carrying a long bundle of sticks into a house in the city of Machuza and being able to turn around. The image is evocative even if not mathematically precise: the space must be sufficient for ordinary movement while carrying common loads.

An interesting possibility raised in the course of this discussion is that the "turning around" image may itself encode a measurement — take the length of the bundle that allows one to just complete a circle within the space, then stand that dimension upright, and you have the required ceiling height. This would yield something close to half the shorter dimension of the room, a modest variation from the *Mikdash* formula. Regardless, the governing principle is the norm of habitation in that time and place, not an arbitrary geometrical ratio.

## Building Near Windows

### Window Solutions

The *gemara* introduces a vivid dispute: *hahu gavra d'avei banya ashista achorei kivei d'chavrei* — someone began building a structure directly facing his neighbor's windows. The neighbor protested: *ka ma'afeilat alai* — you are darkening my home.

What followed was an extended negotiation, with each proposed solution generating a new objection. The builder first offered to seal the existing windows — now blocked by his construction anyway — and cut new windows higher up in the neighbor's wall, above the height of his own structure. The neighbor objected that cutting new holes would damage the integrity of the existing wall. The builder then offered to demolish the top portion of the neighbor's wall down to where the windows would go and rebuild it with windows already incorporated. The neighbor replied that a wall that is old at the bottom and new at the top is structurally unsound. The builder then offered to demolish the neighbor's wall entirely and rebuild it from scratch, with windows properly placed above the new construction. The neighbor objected that one new wall in an otherwise old house would also be structurally unsound. The builder finally offered to tear down and rebuild the entire house. The neighbor said: then I will have nowhere to live. The builder offered to rent him a place during construction. The neighbor refused: *lo tarachna* — I do not want the trouble of moving my belongings.

### Rav Chama Ruling

Rav Chama again rules: *bedin ka-me'akeiv* — the neighbor is within his rights. The person who built a structure that violated the prohibition against blocking another's light is responsible for fixing the problem; the aggrieved party cannot be compelled to cooperate, absorb inconvenience, or vacate his home to facilitate the remedy. Whatever the cost or complexity, it falls entirely on the one who created the violation.

The *gemara* asks: is this case not essentially identical to the previous one about the upper and lower tenants? *Hainu hach* — is this not the same point? It answers: *mahu d'teima af al gav d'lo mishtamesh ela l'tivna v'tzivei d'alma* — one might have thought that if the building was used only as a storehouse for fodder and straw, not as a residence, the owner could not make such strong demands about light. The second case teaches that even for a storehouse, the claim stands. That is itself a significant *chiddush* — one would not have expected the right to natural light to extend to agricultural storage.

A point worth noting: the word *bedin* used by Rav Chama throughout these rulings is not functioning as a reference to a body of law called *din*, but as an adjective confirming that the claims being made are legally valid. The parties are making demands that might seem extreme, and Rav Chama is confirming that those demands are entirely justified.

### Brothers' Division

The *gemara* introduces a related case. Two brothers divided their father's estate. One received the *asplida* — according to Rashi, a mansion or fine building — and the other received the *tarbitza*, the open yard in front of it. The one who received the yard then began building a wall right in front of the mansion's entrance. The mansion owner complained: *ka mafchat alai* — you are darkening my property.

The builder responded: *bedidi kavenina* — I am building on my own land. And Rav Chama again rules: *bedin ka-amar lei* — that response is legally correct. Rashi explains the underlying reason: at the time of the division, neither brother had yet established a *chezkat orah* — a presumptive right to a particular quality of light. That right crystallizes only after three years of undisturbed use. Since the division just occurred and construction began immediately, no such right has been established, and the builder is acting entirely within his rights to use his own property.

## Estate Division Rights

### Vineyards Precedent

Ravina challenges Rav Chama's ruling from a *braita*: *shnei achim she-chalaku, echad mehem natal sdeh karem v'echad natal sdeh lavan* — two brothers divided an estate, one taking a vineyard and one taking a wheat field. The *braita* rules: *yesh lo l'baal ha-karem arba amot b'sdeh lavan* — the owner of the vineyard retains rights to four *amot* within the wheat field, since that is the standard space required to tend the vines along the border.

The principle embedded here is significant: when an estate is divided, the division is presumed to preserve the normal operational rights associated with each portion. One does not receive a vineyard while simultaneously losing the ability to tend it. So too, one might argue, a person who receives a mansion in a division retains the right to the light the mansion normally enjoys.

Why does this *braita* not refute Rav Chama? The *gemara* explains: *hatam de-alu le-hadadi* — in that case, the parties made up the difference in value with money. Since a vineyard is worth more than an equal acreage of wheat field, the one who received the vineyard paid the other to equalize. Once monetary compensation is exchanged to balance the division, it is reasonable to assume the compensation reflects and preserves all normal usage rights, including the four *amot* for tending the vines.

### Air Space Question

The *gemara* then presses: in the case of the mansion and the yard, surely there was also monetary compensation. One brother took a fine building worth far more than a bare plot of land; clearly money changed hands to equalize. If so, by the same logic, all the mansion's normal usage rights — including light — should be preserved.

The *gemara* responds: *nehi de-alu le-hadadi, d'mivne kishorei v'hudrei* — yes, money was paid, but that money covered the cost of the building materials, the beams, the construction itself. *Da-havu d'mei avira lo halu ah-dadai* — but the payment did not cover the air space. The one who received the yard retained his own right to build on his own plot. When he accepted cash compensation for giving up the mansion, he did not give up the right to use his land. He received the equivalent of the mansion's construction value, but never sold the right to keep his plot of land free of construction. Accordingly, he may build.

One might ask: can the mansion owner not say that by accepting the division he implicitly relied on the assumption that the mansion would continue to be used as it always was, with its light and openness? The *gemara* anticipates this: *matzi amar lei ada'ata d'pag d'diurna beh ka-de-hava hatam* — in an estate division among brothers, one is presumed to intend that what was received continue to be used as it was during the father's lifetime. This is not a straightforward commercial sale of a labeled commodity; it is a joint family settlement with embedded expectations.

### Name & Identity

The *gemara* raises the possibility that the builder could simply insist that a mansion is still a mansion even if it is darkened — *shma b'alma palgei leh*, he gave him what is called a mansion, and it is still called that. A parallel is drawn from a *braita*: *ha-omer beis kor afar ani mocher lach* — if someone says "I am selling you a *kor*-measure plot" and it turns out to hold only half that amount, the sale may still stand if that smaller plot has always carried the name of *kor*. The sale is of the name — *shelo machar lo ela shem* — as long as the buyer receives fair market value for what was actually sold. Similarly: a *pardes* with no pomegranates is still a *pardes*; a *kerem* with no vines remaining is still a *kerem*, provided it still bears that name and the buyer receives his money's worth.

Tosafot flags the peculiarity of this rule sharply: it means one can sell a tiny plot for a fraction of its nominal price, invoke an old place-name, and have the sale stand. Iceland and Greenland, as it were. The one protection the buyer has is monetary: he must receive fair value. But he cannot demand the actual acreage or the actual vines.

The *gemara* distinguishes this from the brothers' case: *hacha matzi amar leh ada'ata d'pag d'diurna beh ka-de-hava hatam* — in a commercial sale, the seller says "I am selling you X" and if it is still called X, the sale stands. But in an estate division, both brothers understood what they were taking. The one receiving the mansion expected to continue living in it as it had always been lived in — with light and normal habitability. It is not about labels; it is about the shared understanding of what was being divided.

### Shmuel Position

Mar Yanuqa and Mar Kashisha, sons of Rav Chisda, explain to Rav Ashi why Rav Chama consistently rules in favor of the builder: *Naharda'ei ta'amayu* — his rulings follow the school of Neharde'a.
