Shmuel is from Neharde'a, and Rav Nachman transmits his position: *ha-achim she-chilku ein lahem lo derech zeh al zeh v'lo chalonot zeh al zeh* — brothers who divided an estate have no rights of passage over each other's portions and no rights to windows or light through each other's property.

The principle is broad and uncompromising. If Shimon took the back portion of a field, he cannot claim a right of way through Reuven's front portion, even if that leaves him with no access to the public thoroughfare. Similarly, if dividing a building leaves one party's windows facing the other's new portion, the other may build freely. *V'lo sulamot zeh al zeh* — no right to lean a ladder; *v'lo amat ha-mayim zeh al zeh* — no right to access an irrigation canal through another's property.

The *gemara* adds: *v'hizharu bahen she-halachot kevu'ot hen* — be careful about these laws, for they are fixed and binding. The word *v'hizharu* likely serves as a practical warning: know these rules before dividing an estate, so that you stipulate explicitly whatever rights you wish to retain. One who accepts a portion without securing those stipulations loses them.

Rava dissents: *yesh lahem* — the divided parties do retain some of those normal usage rights. This is the position Rav Chama opposes. The *gemara* thus frames Rav Chama's repeated rulings as grounded in Shmuel's Neharde'an school, which holds that estate division creates a clean break, with each party limited to exactly what was explicitly allocated.

## Orphans' Receipts

### Keep Original Shtar

The *gemara* presents a final case attributed to Rav Chama. Orphans held a *shtar* — a document establishing that someone owed their late father a sum of money. When they sought to collect, the debtor produced a *tavra* — a receipt indicating the debt had been paid. Rav Chama rules: *agvuyei lo magvinan lei* — we do not collect on the *shtar*, since a receipt has been produced against it. *U'mikra lo karinan lei* — but we also do not tear up the *shtar*.

Why preserve a document that apparently reflects a paid debt? *D'chi gadli yasmi, dilma maisi ra'aya u'marlei* — because when the orphans come of age and are in a position to investigate their father's affairs themselves, they may find evidence that the receipt was forged. Minors cannot adequately represent their own interests; their appointed guardian cannot do so perfectly on their behalf. The *shtar* is preserved so that the orphans, upon reaching adulthood, retain the option to challenge the receipt's authenticity.

### Rav Chama Summary

Looking back over the daf, the *gemara* notes that Rav Chama is the authority behind a series of significant rulings: that the upper tenant cannot be compelled to vacate his home; that a brother who received the yard may build in front of the mansion even though it darkens it; and that the orphans' *shtar* is preserved. Rav Acha son of Rav asks Ravina: *hilchasa mai* — what is the practical ruling?

### Final Psak Decision

The *gemara* rules: *bekulu hilchasa k'Rav Chama, l'bar mi'tafra* — we rule like Rav Chama in all these matters except for the *tavra*, the receipt case. In the other rulings we follow Rav Chama. But regarding the receipt: *d'sahdi b'shikri lo machzinan* — we do not presume that the witnesses who signed the receipt committed perjury. A duly signed and witnessed document cannot simply be treated as suspect on the possibility that orphans might someday disprove it. We tear up the *shtar*.

Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari disagrees: *bahana nami hilchasa k'Rav Chama* — even in the receipt case we rule like Rav Chama and preserve the *shtar*. His reason: *d'im issa d'tavra ma'alya hu, ibayei lei l'afukei b'chayei avuhon* — if the receipt were genuine, it should have been produced while the father was still alive, when he could have contested or responded to it. The fact that it surfaces only after his death, and only when the orphans attempt to collect, is itself grounds for suspicion. *U'med'lo afka, shma mina ziufei zeifin* — since it was not produced earlier, there is reason to conclude that it was forged. On this view, Rav Chama's ruling to preserve the *shtar* is followed even here.

---

---

# Bava Batra 8

## Gates & Walls

### Guard's Gate Obligation

The daf opens by picking up from the *mishna* on 7b, transitioning from the obligation to build a dividing wall within a shared courtyard — motivated by concerns of *hezek re'iyah*, the prohibition against invading a neighbor's visual privacy — toward a broader framework of communal responsibility. The *mishna* establishes that members of a shared *chatzer* bear mutual obligations to protect their common space: *kofin oso livnos beis sha'ar u'deles le'chatzer* — one forces any member of the courtyard to participate in building a guard's gate and a door for the *chatzer*, protecting it both from passersby who might look in and from potential intruders.

### Shimon ben Gamliel

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissents: *lo kol ha-chatzerot re'uyot le-veis sha'ar* — not every courtyard actually requires a guard's gate. As the *Gemara* will clarify, his reasoning appears connected to the *hezek re'iyah* concern: a courtyard that does not open directly onto the main public thoroughfare presents a lesser degree of exposure, and therefore a lesser need for such a structure.

### City Wall Obligations

The *mishna* then moves from the courtyard to the *ir*, the town. Here too the principle of compulsion applies: *kofin oso livnos le'ir chomah u'dlatayim u'vriach* — one forces the members of a town to contribute toward building a wall, doors, and a crossbar to secure the town. The terminology is worth noting: an *ir* is a town, smaller than a *kerach* (a city) and larger than a *kefar* (a village). Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel again limits the obligation — *lo kol ha-ayarot re'uyot le-choma* — not every town requires a wall. In the *braita*, his view is refined: a town near the border (*sefar*) genuinely needs a wall, while one far from the border does not. The Rabbis, characteristically, are more cautious: *zimnin de-mikru ve-atu gaisai* — troops can arrive even in places not on the frontier, and therefore the need for defensive walls may arise anywhere. Notably absent from this discussion is any mention of protection against thieves, robbers, or wild animals — the concern is framed specifically in terms of military threat.

### Residency Duration

The *mishna* then addresses the threshold of belonging: *kama yehei ba-ir v'yehei ke'anshei ha-ir* — how long must one reside in a town before being considered one of its inhabitants and therefore obligated in its communal taxes? The answer is twelve months. An exception applies to one who has purchased a permanent dwelling: *kanah bah beis dirah harei hu ke'anshei ha-ir mi-yad* — purchasing a home makes one an inhabitant immediately, regardless of duration of residence.

This section raises questions that the text itself leaves conspicuously open. The *mishna* identifies certain communal needs — a *beis sha'ar*, a *chomah* — that in some cases can be imposed on all residents by compulsion. But the precise mechanism of communal governance is not spelled out. Who decides when the obligation arises? Is it a majority vote? Elected representatives? The *mishna* gestures toward these questions without resolving them.

---

## Gates & Poor Access

### Pious Sage Story

The *Gemara* opens its analysis with a sharp challenge: *lemeimra de-beis sha'ar maylusa hi?* — is the *mishna* then asserting that a guard's gate is simply a good thing? But there is a famous story that complicates this. A certain *chasid* — a pious sage — was accustomed to regular conversations with *Eliyahu Hanavi*. When this man built a *beis sha'ar* for his courtyard, Elijah ceased speaking with him entirely. Rashi explains: the gate prevented the poor from entering the courtyard to seek *tzedakah*. A structure that serves the residents' privacy and security simultaneously walls out those who depend on their generosity.

### Multiple Resolutions

The *Gemara* offers a series of resolutions to this tension, each carefully distinguishing configurations of the gatehouse that either preserve or eliminate access for the *ani*.

The first resolution: *lo kashya ha mi-gavai ha mi-barai* — there is no contradiction, because the cases differ based on whether the gatehouse is positioned on the inside or outside of the courtyard. Rashi explains that a gatehouse placed on the inside, behind the door, fully blocks the *ani* from entering. A gatehouse on the outside, by contrast, allows the *ani* at minimum to enter the structure itself and make his presence known, even without gaining full access to the courtyard.

The second resolution: *i ba'is eima, ha ve-ha mi-barai* — assume both gatehouses are on the outside; the question then becomes whether there is a door behind the gatehouse. If there is a door, the *ani* is still blocked from the interior. If there is no such door, the *ani* can enter the gatehouse and seek assistance there.

The third resolution: even if both cases have a door behind the gatehouse, the question becomes whether there is an opening (*putcha*) allowing entry into the gatehouse itself. Without such an opening, access is fully denied.

The fourth resolution: even if there is an opening in both cases, the crucial question is whether that opening faces inward or outward — *ha de-putcha didei mi-gavai ha de-putcha didei mi-barai*. If the opening faces inward, only those already inside the courtyard can access the gatehouse; those approaching from the outside cannot enter. If it faces outward, the approaching *ani* at least has a portal through which to make himself known and request help.

The deeper issue this series of resolutions surfaces is the irreducible tension at the heart of communal infrastructure: how does one protect residents — their property, their privacy — without foreclosing access for those who depend on communal generosity? The *Gemara* does not resolve this tension definitively; it maps the range of physical configurations that navigate it.

One question this raises is how Rashi knew the story was specifically about the *ani* being excluded. No explicit explanation is provided in the text itself, and it may reflect either a received tradition or the only available inference from the narrative's logic.

It is also worth clarifying a potential source of confusion: this entire discussion about the *beis sha'ar* and the *ani* concerns the gatehouse of the *chatzer* — the courtyard — not the gatehouse of the town. The town gate is a different structure: a large gate with heavy doors and a crossbar. The *ani* moving through a town goes from courtyard to courtyard seeking *tzedakah*; it is the courtyard gate that blocks or permits his access.

The *braita* then restates Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling about courtyards: *lo kol ha-chatzerot re'uyot le-veis sha'ar; ella chatzer ha-semucha le-reshut ha-rabim re'uya le-veis sha'ar* — only a courtyard adjacent to the public thoroughfare genuinely needs a guard's gate. The Rabbis again push back: even a courtyard set back from the main road may sometimes attract unauthorized visitors — *zimnin de-mishtakchei benei reshut ha-rabim ve-ayilu ve-yasvu* — and therefore all courtyards may reasonably be subject to this obligation.

The *mishna*'s concluding section on city walls is then elaborated in parallel. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that only towns near the border (*sefar*) require walls; towns far from the frontier do not. The Rabbis hold that troops can appear anywhere and that no town is categorically exempt. This raises a broader governance question left unanswered by both *mishna* and *Gemara*: if twenty percent of the residents want a *beis sha'ar* and eighty percent do not — or vice versa — who decides?

---

## Taxation Principles

### Per Person vs. Wealth

With the framework of communal obligation established, the *Gemara* turns to the question of how the costs are to be distributed. *Ba'ei minei Rabbi Elazar mi-Rabbi Yochanan: keshen govin, lefi nefashot govin o dilma lefi shevach mamon govin* — when the town collects for communal needs, does it collect per capita, or proportional to wealth?

To frame the options: a per-capita levy is regressive — every person pays the same absolute amount regardless of means. A proportional levy — everyone paying the same percentage of their wealth — is a flat tax. A truly progressive tax, where rates increase with wealth, is not explicitly discussed. Rabbi Yochanan's answer is clear: *lefi mamon govin* — according to wealth. And he adds, with finality, *de-Elazar beni kava bah masmerot* — my son Elazar has hammered this in with nails; it is not an open question.

### Proximity vs. Income

A second version of the query is then introduced. Here it is already assumed that the tax is not regressive; the question shifts to whether the flat-wealth tax is the correct model, or whether proximity to the wall — and thus degree of benefit derived — is the more relevant factor. *Keshen govin, lefi keruv batim hen govin o dilma lefi mamon govin* — do we assess based on how close one's house is to the city wall, and therefore how much one benefits from it, or purely based on wealth? Rabbi Yochanan rules: *lefi keruv batim hen govin* — based on proximity to the wall. And again: *de-Elazar beni kava bah masmerot*.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot raises the obvious difficulty: if the second ruling is that we follow proximity, what happened to the first ruling that we follow wealth? Are these contradictory? Tosafot, citing Rabbeinu Tam, resolves this by treating the two principles as operating simultaneously. *Nosim aniyim krovim yoter mi-rechokim* — poor residents who live closer to the wall pay more than poor residents who live farther away. *Ve-chen ashirim krovim yoter me-ashirim rechokim* — wealthy residents who live closer pay more than wealthy residents who live farther. But crucially — *aval ashirim rechokim nosim yoter mi-aniyim krovim* — a wealthy resident who lives far from the wall still pays more than a poor resident who lives close to it. Wealth remains the more dominant factor; proximity modulates within each economic stratum, but does not override the primacy of ability to pay.

This produces a nuanced taxation model: both wealth and derived benefit are relevant variables, but they are weighted differently, with wealth carrying greater weight.

Tosafot then introduces a further principle that deepens the analysis considerably. The nature of the communal need may itself determine which factor predominates. *Keivan de-ein sakanat nefashot lo azlinan ela batar mamon* — since the primary purpose of a city wall is to protect property rather than lives (Tosafot understands that troops coming across the border are primarily raiders, not killers), we treat the wall as primarily an economic benefit, and therefore those with more property are the primary beneficiaries and must pay more accordingly. Tosafot cites a parallel ruling in tractate *Hagozel* (the later chapter of Bava Kamma) regarding a caravan that is attacked by troops in the desert: *mechashevin lefi mamon* — costs are allocated according to wealth, precisely because the troops came for money, not lives.

But *aval heicha de-tau ba-midbar* — if people are wandering lost in the desert and their lives are genuinely at risk, Tosafot rules that in that case we calculate *af lefi nefashot* — also per capita — because now every life is equally at stake and the per-person element returns as a meaningful factor, even if wealth still retains some role. Tosafot himself does not fully commit to a pure per-capita rule even in life-threatening situations; he describes a balance.

The deeper question Tosafot is navigating is this: when we say *lefi mamon*, do we mean this because those with more money are better able to pay, or because those with more property benefit more from the protection? Tosafot seems to say: both, and the mix depends on what the communal expenditure is actually for. This is a remarkable early articulation of the distinction between ability-to-pay and benefit-based theories of taxation.

---

## Rabbis & Tax Exemption

### Nesi'ah & Resh Lakish

The *Gemara* now introduces a series of dramatic confrontations over whether *talmidei chachamim* — Torah scholars — are exempt from communal taxes. Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah (the grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, not to be confused with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi himself) imposed a tax for the city wall upon the rabbis. Resh Lakish objected: *rabbanan lo tsrikhei netiruta* — rabbis do not need the protection that the wall provides, because their Torah learning protects them. Since the basis for the tax obligation, as established above, is that one benefits from the protection, those who do not benefit are not obligated.

Resh Lakish's proof is from Psalms: *asaprem mechol yirbuyun* — "I will count them; they will multiply more than the sand." The *Gemara* first raises a difficulty with this reading: if even the entirety of Israel is compared to the sand of the sea, how can the righteous — a subset — be greater than the sand? The resolution: *asaprem le-ma'aseihem shel tsadikim, mechol yirbuyun* — we count not the righteous themselves but their righteous deeds, which are indeed more numerous than the sand. From this the *Gemara* builds a *kal va-chomer*: sand, though less numerous than the deeds of the righteous, nonetheless holds back the sea, functioning as a wall. The deeds of the righteous, which are far more numerous, must surely provide even greater protection. Therefore, *talmidei chachamim* have their own divine protection and require no city wall.

When this argument came before Rabbi Yochanan, he said to Resh Lakish: why did you not use the verse from *Shir HaShirim* — *ani choma ve-shadai ke-migdalot* — I am a wall and my breasts are like towers? *Ani choma zu Torah; ve-shadai ke-migdalot elu talmidei chachamim* — "I am a wall" refers to Torah, and "my breasts are like towers" refers to Torah scholars. This is a more direct image: Torah itself is the wall protecting the city, and the scholars are the towers of that wall. Of course, this protection seemingly applies only to the scholars themselves; the rest of the town still requires a physical wall.

Resh Lakish explains why he did not use this verse: he follows Rava's interpretation of the same passage. *Ani choma zu Knesset Yisrael; ve-shadai ke-migdalot elu batei knesiyot u-vatei midrashot* — "I am a wall" refers to the entire congregation of Israel, and "my breasts are like towers" refers to synagogues and study halls. In Rashi's reading, this interpretation holds that the *chomah* is not about individual scholars being protected, but about the entire Jewish people constituting a unified barrier against assimilation among the nations — *godrin atzman mil-hitame bein ovdei kochavim*. This is a sweeping statement about communal spiritual identity, but in Rava's reading the verse cannot be used to exempt scholars specifically from the wall tax.

### Poll Tax Dispute

The *Gemara* then presents a parallel episode. Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda imposed a *karga* — a poll tax, or head tax — upon the rabbis. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak protested vigorously: *avarta d'Oraita v'd-Nevi'ei v'd-Ktuvai* — you have transgressed obligations rooted in the Torah, in the Prophets, and in the Writings.

### Biblical Proofs

The Toraitic violation derives from Devarim: *af chovev amim kol kedoshav be-yadecha* — even when God shows favor to the other nations, His holy ones remain in His hands. The *Gemara* reads this as Moshe's plea before God: *ribbono shel olam, afilu be-sha'at she-atah mechabev amim, kol kedoshav yiheyu be-yadecha* — even when You empower the nations over Israel, protect Your righteous ones. Rav Yosef adds: *ve-heim tuku le-raglecha* — "they have nestled at Your feet" — refers to *talmidei chachamim* who wear out their legs traveling from city to city and from country to country *lilmod Torah*, in order to engage in *give-and-take* of Torah discourse.

The violation from the Prophets comes from Hoshea: *gam ki yitnu va-goyim ata akabtzem; va-yachelu me'at mi-massa melech ve-sarim*. Ulla offers a creative reading: the word *yitnu* should be read through its Aramaic cognate *tena* — to learn, as in *Mishnah*. The verse then means: *i tanu kulhu* — if all of them are engaged in Torah study, I will gather them now (the *mashiach* will come). And *ve-im me'at meihem* — if only a small number are learning, *va-yachelu me'at mi-massa melech ve-sarim* — those few will be relieved, exempted, from the burden of kings and princes. The word *va-yachelu* is read as related to *lo yachal devaro* — to void, to exempt from an obligation. This is a meaningfully different kind of argument: it is not claiming that scholars are protected and therefore do not benefit from a wall; it is claiming that scholars simply deserve to be freed from taxation as a matter of honor — a point that has broader applicability than protection-based exemptions.

The violation from the Writings comes from Ezra: *minida, belo, ve-halach, lo shalit le-mirma aleihem* — it shall not be lawful to impose various forms of taxation upon the temple servants. Rav Yehuda identifies these three taxes: *minida* is *m'nas hamelech*, the king's portion; *belo* is *kesef gulgalta*, the head tax; and *halach* is the *arnona*. Rashi identifies the *arnona* as an income tax on produce and animals collected annually; other authorities identify it as a levy for provisioning the king's retinue as it passes through. In either reading, the point is clear: communal leaders and religious figures have a recognized exemption from royal taxation.

The distinction between the earlier arguments and these latter two is significant. The earlier proofs — that Torah protects scholars, that divine favor shields them — are specifically relevant to taxes for physical protection. They argue that scholars do not need the benefit and therefore are not obligated. The latter proofs — from the Prophets and the Writings — argue for a more general exemption from taxation as a dignitary matter, not predicated on lack of benefit. A *nafka mina* between these two types of arguments will emerge shortly.

### Tax Categories

The *Gemara* now draws the critical distinction that organizes all the preceding material. *Hakol l'aglei gappa, afilu mi-yatmei* — everybody, even orphans, must contribute to the gates of the city. They are all protected by and benefit from those gates. *Rabbanan lo tsrikhei netiruta* — but the rabbis are exempt, because they do not need the protection.

*Hakol l'karya patya, afilu me-rabbanan* — everybody, including the rabbis, must contribute to the digging of wells. Rabbis drink water too; they derive tangible benefit, and therefore they must pay. The sole qualification: *delo nafik be-achluza* — this applies only to a monetary contribution. If the modality of the communal effort is not a tax but a public muster — *be-achluza*, a public call where everyone physically participates in the digging — then *rabbanan lo bnei mapakei be-achluza ninhu* — it is beneath the dignity of Torah scholars to appear in a public labor gang. They are exempt from personal physical participation, but not from financial contribution.

*Klala de-milta* — the governing principle is this: *kol milta de-it lehu hana'ah mineih, afilu mi-yatmei ve-afilu me-rabbanan* — anything from which they derive benefit, even orphans and even rabbis must contribute. The sole exception is protection-based taxes: because the rabbis' protection comes from their Torah, they are not beneficiaries of physical security measures and therefore bear no obligation to fund them.

This framework has clear contemporary resonance. The claim that *rabbanan lo tsrikhei netiruta* — that Torah protects scholars from physical harm — has historically been invoked in the *Chareidi* community to argue that full-time Torah scholars are exempt from military service in Israel. But this argument is more complicated than it appears. As Rav Aharon Lichtenstein argued in his famous essay *Ve-Zot Torat He-Hesder*, the argument proves far too little if it is applied selectively. If a scholar genuinely lives at a level of *emuna* at which he trusts entirely in divine protection — not locking his door, not worrying about employment, not carrying insurance — then the claim has integrity. But if the same scholar takes every ordinary precaution in daily life and invokes *rabbanan lo tsrikhei netiruta* only when it comes to army service, the argument is not being applied consistently.

More fundamentally, Rav Lichtenstein observed that the *Gemara*'s entire framework concerns tax obligations that arise from being a beneficiary of a service. One pays for the wall if one benefits from the wall. One is exempt if one does not benefit. But military service is categorically different: it is not undertaken to protect oneself. It is undertaken out of an obligation to protect others — framed either as *Milchemet Mitzvah* or as *pikuach nefesh* toward fellow Jews. One cannot say "I don't need to be protected, therefore I need not serve," because the obligation to serve is not premised on one's own need for protection. Just as no one would say "I am a rabbi, therefore I need not drive someone to the hospital on *Shabbat* in a life-threatening situation," the exemption from benefiting from a wall cannot translate into an exemption from an obligation owed to others.

A related argument has been offered within the *Chareidi* community itself: that Torah learning provides protection not merely for the scholar personally but for all of *Am Yisrael*. This is a genuine reframing of the issue — moving away from "I don't need protection" toward "my Torah learning is my contribution to the collective protection of Israel." This is a more substantive argument, though it does not derive from this *Gemara* directly; it reframes the *Gemara*'s logic rather than applying it straightforwardly.

---

## Rabbi's Warehouse Story

### Yonatan's Deception

The *Gemara* now transitions to a celebrated narrative. *Rebbi patach otzaro bi-shnei batzoret* — Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) opened his warehouses during a year of famine to provide food for the public. But he was selective: *yikanesu ba'alei mikra, ba'alei mishnah, ba'alei gemara, ba'alei halachah, ba'alei aggadah* — those who had studied written Torah, *Mishnah*, *Gemara*, legal rulings, or *aggadeta* were welcome. *Aval amei ha-aretz, al yikanesu* — but those who were entirely illiterate in Torah should not enter.

Into this restricted distribution came Yonatan ben Amram, who squeezed through the gate in disguise, presenting himself as an unlearned person. *Rebbi parnaseini* — Rabbi, sustain me. Rabbi asked: *beni karita?* — have you read Torah? *Lo* — no. *Shanita?* — have you learned *Mishnah*? *Lo* — no. *Im kein bameh afarnesecha?* — by what merit should I provide for you? Yonatan replied: *parneseini ke-chelev ve-kha-orev* — feed me as you would feed a dog or a raven. I am a creature; sustain me as one.

Rabbi relented and fed him. After Yonatan left, Rabbi sat in distress: *oy li she-natati pitti le-am ha-aretz* — woe to me, I gave my bread to an illiterate person.

### Yonatan Revealed

Rav Shimon, Rabbi's son, then said to him: *shema Yonatan ben Amram talmidecha hu, she-eino rotzeh leihanot mi-kvod Torah mi-yamav* — perhaps this is your own student Yonatan ben Amram, who has always refused to derive any personal benefit from the honor of Torah. Investigation confirmed this. Upon learning the truth, Rabbi reversed his policy entirely: *yikanesu ha-kol* — let everyone enter.

The interpretive texture here is rich. The *Gemara* follows a reading in which Rabbi was not necessarily wrong to feel troubled — his discomfort was not resolved by discovering that his general policy was mistaken, but specifically by learning that this particular man had deliberately concealed his scholarship, because he refused to benefit from Torah's honor. It was Yonatan's own principled choice to present himself as unlearned that occasioned the situation; Rabbi was not deceived in any morally problematic sense. Once Rabbi understood what had happened, his decision to open the food to everyone followed — though the exact reasoning for this reversal is not fully spelled out. One reading is that the encounter prompted Rabbi to reconsider his categorical policy; another, perhaps more textually accurate, is that the story does not actually establish that the categorical policy was wrong, since Rabbi's relief was specifically tied to discovering that his food had not in fact gone to an *am ha-aretz*.

### Illiteracy & Calamity

The *Gemara* then explains Rabbi's original position more sharply. *Rebbi leta'ameih, de-amar Rebbi: ein pur'anut ba'ah la-olam ella bishvil ammei ha-aretz* — Rabbi goes according to his own reasoning, as he held that calamity comes to the world specifically because of the unlearned. This frames his original reluctance not as a preference for Torah scholars in the allocation of limited charity, but as a genuine conviction that *ammei ha-aretz* are a source of harm to society, and that supporting them is therefore not straightforwardly a benefit to the community.

### King's Crown Tax

A further story illustrates the dynamics of the rabbi-versus-*am ha-aretz* social structure in the context of taxation. A tax for the king's crown (*dmei kelila*) was levied on the town of Tiberias. The townspeople came to Rabbi and asked that the rabbis contribute together with them. Rabbi refused. The townspeople threatened to leave the city rather than bear the entire burden. Rabbi said: leave, what do I care? Half the population departed. The tax authorities reduced the levy by half, asking the remaining residents to pay the remainder. Those residents again came to Rabbi and again asked the rabbis to contribute. Rabbi again refused. Again they threatened to leave. Again he said: leave. The entire remaining population left. Only a single launderer remained, a non-rabbi who was not in a position to leave. The tax collectors placed the entire remaining levy upon him. He too fled. At that point, *paka kelila* — the tax dissolved. The authorities did not impose the levy on the rabbis alone.

This story is striking: it reflects a reality — whether of Roman-era Palestine or of other periods — in which religious scholars were in practice not required to pay royal taxes, at least in certain circumstances. The *Gemara* reads Rabbi's behavior as consistent with his view that the rabbis bear no obligation to contribute to taxes for physical protection, and further that the *ammei ha-aretz* bear the burden of communal taxation in a way that the rabbis do not.

The coda attributed to Rabbi (or according to some, to Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav): *ilmalei ammei ha-aretz, lo hayinu meshalem kol kach* — were it not for the *ammei ha-aretz*, the rabbis would not be made to pay such taxes at all. The irony is pointed: it is precisely the economic activity of the unlearned — they produce the income, grow the food, do the labor — that generates the taxable base from which the crown demands payment.

The question of what happened to the large middle category — those who had learned some *pesukim* or *Mishnah* but were not *rabbanan* proper — is left unaddressed. The *Gemara* shifts between *rabbanan* and *ammei ha-aretz* as if these exhaust the population, when in reality the bulk of the community occupies intermediate positions.

One final observation: the *Rashash* notes that Rabbi's sequential questions — *karita? shanita?* — reveal that in the Talmudic period, one could know *Mishnah* without having properly learned *Tanakh*. The fact that Rabbi asked about *Mishnah* even after Yonatan claimed not to have read *pesukim* shows that the two were not assumed to be sequential prerequisites. The *Rashash* uses this to respond to those in later generations who mocked rabbis for being learned in *Gemara* while ignorant of *Tanakh*: this phenomenon is not novel.

---

## Residency Periods

### Caravan Case

The *Gemara* now revisits the twelve-month threshold of the *mishna* and discovers that the picture is more complex. A *braita* seems to suggest that thirty days, not twelve months, can suffice for some purposes of membership in a community. The case: *ha-chameret ve-hagamelet ha-overet mi-makom le-makom* — a caravan of donkeys or camels passing from one town to another — stopped overnight in a particular city. The next day, that city was condemned as an *ir ha-nidachat* (a city that had gone over to idol worship), and the caravan members had participated in the forbidden worship.

What is their status? Are they individuals guilty of idolatry — in which case they are executed by stoning and their property is preserved — or are they members of the *ir ha-nidachat* — in which case they are executed by the sword and their property is destroyed? The *braita* rules: *hen bi-sekila u-mamonam palat* — if they merely passed through, they are treated as individuals: stoning and property preserved. *Ve-im shehu sham sheloshim yom, hen be-sayif u-mamonam avad* — but if they had been there for thirty days, they are treated as members of the city: execution by the sword and property destroyed.

So thirty days makes one a *yoshev ha-ir* — a dweller in the city — for at least some legal purposes.

### Graduated Timeline

Rava resolves the apparent contradiction between thirty days and twelve months by distinguishing two categories: *livnei masta* — being a person of the city, *anshei ha-ir* — and *li-yishuvei masta* — merely dwelling in the city. The *ir ha-nidachat* text uses the language *yoshvei ha-ir ha-hi* — dwellers of that city — which is satisfied by thirty days. But the *mishna*'s twelve-month threshold is for becoming *anshei ha-ir*, a full civic member who bears the city's tax obligations.

A *braita* then introduces an even more graduated timeline, revealing that communal obligations accrue incrementally based on duration of residence. *Sheloshim yom le-tamchui* — thirty days establishes an obligation to contribute to the *tamchui*, the daily communal food fund for the poor. *Shlosha chodashim le-kuppa* — three months establishes an obligation to the *kuppa*, the weekly charitable distribution. *Shisha le-chesut* — six months, and one must contribute to the communal fund for clothing the poor. *Tisha li-kvura* — nine months, and one must contribute to the fund for providing burial for the poor. *Shneim asar le-passei ha-ir* — and only after twelve months does one bear an obligation to contribute to the city walls.

This is a remarkably detailed and humane structure. The community recognizes not only the *tamchui* and *kuppa* — which are well known — but also organized collections for clothing and burial. These are not acts of individual generosity alone; they are structured communal obligations. And the graduated timeline reflects a principle of progressive inclusion: as one becomes more deeply embedded in a community, more obligations attach, culminating in the most permanent and costly obligation of all — the physical infrastructure of the city wall.

Why is the timeline structured this way? One possibility is that the later obligations are more financially demanding, and it is equitable to wait until residency is more clearly permanent before imposing them. But there may also be a conceptual distinction: the earlier obligations (food, clothing, burial) are about the *ani* — they flow from membership in a community of mutual care. The wall obligation, by contrast, flows from being a *beneficiary* of a physical service. The twelve-month threshold for the wall may reflect a judgment that only after a year does one's stake in the city's physical security justify the levy.

Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan confirms: the twelve months in the *mishna* is specifically about *passei ha-ir* — the city walls. The other obligations follow their own timelines.

### All Contribute to Walls

Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan then states: *hakol le-passei ha-ir, va-afilu mi-yatmei* — everyone must contribute to the city walls, even orphans. They live within the walls; they benefit from the protection; they must pay. *Aval rabbanan lo* — but the rabbis are exempt. The reasoning is, once again, *derabanan lo tsrikhei netiruta*.

Rav Pappa extends this to a list of related items: *le-shura, u-le-parsha'ah, u-le-tarzina, afilu mi-yatmei* — for repairing the wall, for the horsemen-guards who patrol the perimeter, and for the keeper of the armory — all of these require contributions from everyone, including orphans. And once again: *aval rabbanan lo tsrikhei netiruta*.

The governing principle is then stated comprehensively: *kol milta de-it lehu hana'ah mineih, afilu mi-yatmei ve-afilu me-rabbanan* — anything from which they derive benefit, all must contribute, without exception. The only exemption is protection-related taxes, from which rabbis are excluded precisely because they do not, in the *Gemara*'s framework, benefit from physical protection.

---

## Orphans & Charity

### Orphan Charity Tax

Rabba placed a *tzedakah* assessment upon the orphans of the household of Bar Marion. Abaye objected, citing a *baraita*: *ein poskin tzedakah al ha-yetomim afilu li-pidyon shvuyim* — one may not impose a *tzedakah* levy upon orphans, even for *pidyon shvuyim* — the redemption of captives, which is among the weightiest communal obligations. The principle is clear: while orphans can be compelled to pay for things that benefit them, *tzedakah* — by definition directed at benefiting others — cannot be extracted from orphans.

### Status in Society

Rabba justifies his imposition on different grounds: *ana le-achshuvinehu ka aveidna* — I am doing this for the orphans' own benefit. Contributing to *tzedakah* raises their standing in the community. An orphan who gives is perceived as a full and dignified member of society; one who only receives, or who is entirely exempted from communal obligations, occupies a lesser social position.

This argument has a parallel in the *Tosefta*, which teaches that *tzedakah* is collected from gentiles together with Jews *mipnei darchei shalom* — for the sake of social harmony. Even the act of being collected from, of being expected to contribute, confers a form of social dignity and equality. The *Tosefta*'s point is that excluding someone from the obligation to give can itself be a form of marginalizing them.

One might ask: if this reasoning — that contributing to *tzedakah* dignifies the giver — is sound, why does the *baraita* single out *pidyon shvuyim* as something that cannot be imposed on orphans? What makes that case different? The *Gemara* does not resolve this tension directly.

### Ifra's Donation

Ifra Hormiz, the mother of the Persian king Shavor Malka, sent a pouch of dinars to Rav Yosef with a request: *le-havei le-mitzvah rabbah* — use this for a great *mitzvah*. Rav Yosef sat and deliberated: what is the greatest *mitzvah*? Abaye said to him: the answer follows from the *baraita* itself. Since *ein poskin tzedakah al ha-yetomim afilu li-pidyon shvuyim* — we do not impose *tzedakah* on orphans even for *pidyon shvuyim* — *shma mina de-pidyon shvuyim mitzvah rabbah hi* — we may infer that *pidyon shvuyim* is the great *mitzvah* par excellence, the one whose weight alone makes it the subject of an explicit exclusion. Rav Yosef accordingly allocated the funds to *pidyon shvuyim*. The *Gemara* will continue with a broader exploration of *pidyon shvuyim* and *tzedakah* — which will occupy the coming pages.

---

---

# Bava Batra 9

## Pidyon Shevuyim

### Source of Teaching

The Gemara on 8b opens by transitioning into a discussion of *tzedakah* — specifically the obligation of community members to provide for the needs of the poor — building naturally on the earlier discussion of how long one must reside in a town before becoming liable for various communal obligations. Within this context, the Gemara had already introduced a story about the mother of Shvor Malka, who sent a purse full of *dinarei* to Rav Yosef with instructions to use the funds for a *mitzvah rabbah*. Rav Yosef concluded that the supreme *mitzvah* in mind must be *pidyon shevuyim* — the redemption of captives.

The Gemara now opens on 8b with Rava posing a challenge to Rabba bar Mari: *minah ha'milta de'amri rabbanan de'pidyon shevuyim mitzvah rabbah hi?* — where exactly does this teaching come from, that *pidyon shevuyim* is a *mitzvah rabbah*? The answer is drawn from a verse in Yirmiyahu: *ve'haya ki yomru elecha ana netzei ve'amarta aleihem koh amar Hashem asher l'maves l'maves va'asher l'cherev l'cherev va'asher l'ra'av l'ra'av va'asher l'shevi l'shevi* — describing the various fates that will befall the people in the time of the *churban ha'bayis*. Rav Yochanan teaches that each subsequent fate mentioned in this verse is more severe than the one preceding it.

### Hierarchy of Deaths

The Gemara works through the ascending hierarchy with characteristic precision. *Cherev kasheh mi'maves* — death by the sword is worse than natural death. This can be derived either from *sevara* or from a verse. From *sevara*: *hai ka'menuval ve'hai lo ka'menuval* — death by the sword disfigures the body, whereas natural death does not. From a verse: *yakar be'einei Hashem ha'mavesah la'chasidav* — dear to God is the death of His pious ones, meaning that the most precious form of death is natural death, not violent death. Hence the verse lists natural death first and death by the sword second.

Next, *ra'av kasheh mi'cherev* — death by hunger is worse than death by the sword. Again, either from *sevara* — *hai ka'mitztaer ve'hai lo ka'mitztaer* — death by the sword disfigures but is instantaneous, whereas death by hunger involves prolonged suffering — or from an explicit verse: *tovim hayu chalalei cherev me'chalalei ra'av*, better were those who fell by the sword than those who perished by famine.

### Captivity Severity

*Shevi* — captivity — which appears last in the verse, is *kasheh mi'kulam*, more severe than all of them, and no additional verse is needed to establish this: *de'chulhu isnehu bei*, because captivity contains within it all the preceding forms of suffering simultaneously. The captive faces the threat of death by the sword, suffers from hunger, and lives in a state of ongoing fear and degradation. The placement of captivity at the end of the verse thus makes the case for *pidyon shevuyim* as a *mitzvah rabbah* on its own terms.

### Rambam's Teaching

The Rambam's treatment of this topic in *Hilchos Matnos Aniyim*, chapter 8, halacha 10, is characteristically emphatic — unusually so for the Rambam's typically terse style. He writes: *pidyon shevuyim kodem l'parnasas aniyim u'le'chisusan ve'ein lecha mitzvah gedolah ke'pidyon shevuyim* — redeeming captives takes precedence over supporting and clothing the poor, and there is no *mitzvah* as great as *pidyon shevuyim*. The Rambam explains that the captive is simultaneously among the hungry, the thirsty, the naked, and those in mortal danger — precisely the synthesis that the Gemara identified by noting that captivity contains all the preceding forms of suffering. He adds that one who closes his eyes to the obligation of *pidyon shevuyim* violates the prohibitions of *lo te'ametz et levavecha ve'lo tikpotz et yadecha*, along with other transgressions. He concludes: *ve'ein lecha mitzvah rabbah ke'pidyon shevuyim*. The strong rhetorical register here is notable.

This was not merely a theoretical concern. Throughout the medieval period and beyond, *pidyon shevuyim* was a matter of urgent communal practice — entire communities, often including those far removed from the captive's own town, would organize to raise funds. The Gemara in Gittin addresses the inevitable tension between the urgency of immediate redemption and the long-term policy concern that meeting ransom demands incentivizes further captive-taking, a tension illustrated memorably by the case of the Maharam of Rothenburg, whose body was held for ransom.

---

## Charity Collections

### Kuppah & Tamchui

A *baraita* is introduced: *kuppah shel tzedakah nigbeit bishnayim u'mit'chalekes bishloshah* — the communal charity fund is collected by two people and distributed by three. The reason for requiring two collectors is stated explicitly: *ein osim serarah al ha'tzibbur pachot mishnayim* — one may not exercise a position of authority over the community alone; authority must be shared. This is significant because collecting *tzedakah* is not a purely voluntary matter — there is a compulsory dimension to communal charity obligations, and the collectors effectively exercise coercive power over members of the community. The requirement of two is therefore a structural check on that power.

Distribution requires three, *ke'dinei mamonot* — because assessing the relative needs of recipients and allocating funds accordingly is analogous to adjudicating monetary claims, which requires a panel of three.

Tosafot raises the obvious question: if distribution requires three because of the *dinei mamonot* character of the assessment, shouldn't collection also require three, since assessing how much each household must contribute similarly involves evaluative judgment? Rabbeinu Tam answers that when the contribution per household is already established — either as a flat assessment or by prior determination — the act of collection is merely mechanical, not evaluative, and therefore two suffice.

The *tamchui* — the soup kitchen, which operated by collecting food daily from households and distributing it to the poor on the same day — requires three for both collection and distribution: *nigbeit bishloshah u'mit'chalekes bishloshah*. The reason is practical: *she'gviyata ve'chalukata shavim* — since collection and distribution happen in such rapid succession, it would be impractical to assemble a group of two for collection and then reconvene a different group of three for distribution. The same three handle both.

The *tamchui* was distributed daily, while the *kuppah* was distributed every *erev Shabbat*. Furthermore, the *tamchui* served primarily *aniyei olam* — the itinerant poor passing through town — while the *kuppah* served *aniyei ha'ir*, the established poor of the city. The logic is clear: a weekly monetary allowance is appropriate for a resident who must plan for the week; daily food provision suits the transient who needs a meal today. And practically speaking, a week's allowance given to someone passing through places an undue burden on the community's ongoing fund.

### Fund Reassignment

The *baraita* continues: *rashaim benei ha'ir la'asot kuppah tamchui ve'tamchui kuppah* — the townspeople may reassign funds collected for one purpose to the other. If the *kuppah* has a surplus, those funds may be transferred to the *tamchui*, or vice versa. The Gemara goes further: *u'leshanota le'chol mah she'yirtzu* — and they may redirect the funds to whatever purpose they deem fit.

The first comment in Tosafot extends this considerably: Rabbeinu Tam holds that the funds may even be redirected to *devar ha'reshut*, a non-*mitzvah* purpose. And indeed, Tosafot reports that Rabbeinu Tam himself would regularly draw from *kuppah* funds to pay the wages of those guarding the town. He did not feel it necessary to frame this as a *pikuach nefashos* justification — the *kuppah* funds had been collected by the townspeople for the purposes of the town, and in his view, whoever held the relevant authority could redirect them at discretion. The precise question of who constitutes that governing body — and how collective decisions are made — is notably underdeveloped in the Gemara's framework here, a gap that becomes apparent when one asks why Rabbeinu Tam's apparently unilateral decision sufficed.

### Community Authority

The *baraita* continues: *ve'rashaim benei ir le'hatnos al ha'middos ve'al ha'she'arim* — the townspeople may make stipulations about measures and prices. Setting standardized measures addresses the patchwork of different local measurement systems that appear throughout the Talmud. More significantly, *al ha'she'arim* — setting fixed prices or price ceilings — represents a meaningful curtailment of free market dynamics in order to ensure that basic goods remain accessible. As Rashi notes, the intent is a cap, not a mandated floor price. The *baraita* adds *ve'al sechar po'alim* — and regarding workers' wages — which functions here not as a ceiling but as a minimum, a floor below which wages may not fall.

Finally: *u'le'hasia al kitzatan* — and to impose fines on those who violate these edicts. The townspeople not only have the power to make rules; they have the power to enforce them with financial penalties. The theoretical basis for this collective authority — what grants the townspeople this quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial power — is not spelled out directly, but the Gemara implicitly treats the town as a corporate entity capable of its own governance.

### Two Administrators

Returning to the requirement of two for positions of communal authority: *ein osim serarah al ha'tzibbur pachot mishnayim* — the Gemara asks, *minah hanei milei?* Rav Nachman derives it from the verse *ve'hem yikchu et ha'zahav ve'et ha'techelet ve'et ha'argaman* — where multiple individuals are described as acting together in collecting the donations for the *beit ha'mikdash*, a closely parallel case.

A story is cited to support Rav Chanina's related teaching: Rebbe once appointed two brothers to supervise the *kuppah*. As Rashi notes, the significance is that two brothers, from the standpoint of potential collusion, effectively function as one person — they share interests and loyalties. Yet the requirement of two was deemed satisfied. This demonstrates that the requirement of two is not motivated by suspicion of dishonesty; if it were, two brothers would be inadequate. The requirement is rather structural, about the distribution of power and authority, not about preventing embezzlement.

The Gemara then asks what, concretely, is the coercive power that these positions carry: *mai seraruta?* The answer: *lefi shememashkenin al ha'tzedakah va'afilu be'erev Shabbat* — because the collectors may seize collateral from a person who refuses to give, even on *erev Shabbat*. This power — entering a person's home and taking collateral — is substantial, echoing similar issues in Bava Metzia.

---

## Power & Trust

### Coercion Ethics

This immediately raises a difficulty: there is a verse, *u'fakadeti al kol lochatzav* — God will punish all those who oppress the poor. And in the name of Rav, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta teaches that this refers *even to the gabbai tzedakah* — even the charity collector who uses excessive force in collecting is guilty of oppression. So how can the *gabbai* seize collateral?

The resolution: *lo kashya — ha de'amid, ha de'lo amid*. The distinction turns on whether the person has means. If the person is genuinely poor — *de'lo amid* — then using coercive power against them is indeed the oppression the verse warns against. If the person is wealthy and simply unwilling to give — *de'amid* — then the collectors are authorized to compel payment and seize collateral.

The practical illustration is striking: *Rava achpei le'Rav Natan bar Ami u'shakal minei arba me'ah zuzei le'tzedakah* — Rava forcibly compelled Rav Natan bar Ami, a fellow *amora*, and extracted four hundred *zuz* from him for *tzedakah*. That a person of Rav Natan bar Ami's standing was resisting is understandable — the sum was substantial, reflecting what was evidently a progressive assessment system. Yet Rava's authority to compel was clear.

A celebrated Tosafot addresses this episode by raising a fundamental tension. A principle taught in the chapter of *kol ha'basar* states that any positive commandment whose reward is explicitly stated in the Torah — *matan sechara kasuva betzidah* — is one that *beit din* below does not have the authority to compel. And *tzedakah* explicitly states its reward: *ki biglal hadavar hazeh yevarchecha Hashem Elokecha*. So how does *beit din* have the authority to force compliance?

Tosafot's resolution develops the dual character of *tzedakah*. It is simultaneously a *mitzvah* — a religious obligation — and something more: a claim the poor have on the resources of the community, with a *dinei mamonot* dimension. When *beit din* compels someone to give *tzedakah*, it is not acting in the capacity of enforcing ritual compliance (as it might with *tefillin* or *sukkah*). It is acting to vindicate the legitimate financial claim of the poor. The reward stated in the Torah speaks to the *mitzvah* dimension; the *dinei mamonot* dimension provides the independent basis for compulsion, irrespective of the stated reward.

The discussion then moves to the famous verse from Daniel: *ve'hamaskilim yazhiru ke'zohar ha'rakia* — those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the sky. The Gemara identifies these as the *dayan she'dan din emet le'amito* — the judge who penetrates to the genuine truth of a case. Tosafot asks why the verse needs *le'amito* — why not simply say *din emet*? The answer: it is possible to follow all the procedural rules and still arrive at a wrong result because one failed to look beneath the surface. When something seems suspicious, when a claim does not quite add up, a judge who simply processes the evidence as presented without exercising deeper scrutiny is not judging *din emet le'amito*. The *maskil* must be able to read between the lines.

*U'matzdikei harabbim ke'kochavim le'olam va'ed* — those who bring merit to the many will shine like the stars forever. The Gemara identifies these as *gabbei tzedakah* — the charity collectors. The term *matzdikei* resonates on multiple levels: it invokes the language of *tzedakah* (providing justice and charity) and of *lehatzdikim* (causing others to act rightly). The *gabbai tzedakah* causes the many to give; he is not merely a giver himself.

A *baraita* offers an alternative reading: in the *baraita*, the *maskilim* include the *gabbei tzedakah* themselves, and *matzdikei harabbim ke'kochavim le'olam va'ed* refers specifically to teachers of young children — *melamdei tinokot* — who secure the future of the community by educating the next generation. Rav suggests the paradigmatic example of such self-sacrificing dedication: Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, who when found by Rav taking a brief walk in his garden, replied that he had not visited his garden in thirteen years, and that even at that moment his thoughts remained with his students. Ravina adds that the *rabbanan* themselves — those who demonstrate love of God through constant Torah study — attain an even greater level, compared not to stars or sky but to the rising sun: *ve'ohavav ke'tzeit ha'shemesh be'gvurato*.

The Gemara then returns to the conduct of the *gabbei tzedakah* and the practical rules they must observe. *Gabbei tzedakah einan rashaim lifrosh ze mi'ze* — the two collectors may not separate from one another when making their rounds. They cannot divide the neighborhood between them, each visiting different houses alone, because at any given moment one must still be operating with the other present. The qualification: if one goes to a gate and the other to a nearby store and they remain within sight of one another, Rashi explains that this is still acceptable.

The Gemara then addresses a series of scenarios designed to keep the *gabbai tzedakah* above any suspicion of financial impropriety — not because the Gemara suspects them, but because *marit ayin* in monetary dealings involving public trust demands a higher standard of visible integrity. If a collector finds coins on the ground — an *aveida* he is legally entitled to keep — he may not place them in his own pocket while on duty. Instead, he places them into the *tzedakah* pouch and retrieves them only upon returning home. Similarly, if someone repays a personal debt to the collector while the collector is on his rounds, the collector places those funds into the *tzedakah* pouch and retrieves his money only at home. The concern is purely one of appearances: any observer seeing money pass to the collector and disappear into his pocket would reasonably suspect that *tzedakah* funds were being pocketed.

When the collectors have no poor to distribute to and possess copper coins that will rust, they may exchange them for silver coins — but only by making the exchange with others, not with themselves. Similarly, *gabbei tamchui* who have perishable food and no poor to receive it must sell it to others, not to themselves. In all these cases, the structural concern is the same: a transaction in which the *gabbai* is on both sides — buyer and seller, debtor and creditor — cannot be kept free of suspicion.

Finally: *ma'ot shel tzedakah ein monin otam shtayim shtayim ela achat achat* — when counting the *tzedakah* coins, one counts them one at a time, not two at a time. Rashi explains this too as a precaution against suspicion: if someone observes the counting and sees coins being handled in pairs, they might suspect that the counter is counting by ones while taking every second coin for himself.

Abaye reports that his teacher Rabba originally refused to sit on the mats in the synagogue, suspecting they had been purchased with *tzedakah* funds that should have gone to the poor. Once Rabba heard the ruling that *tzedakah* funds may be reassigned to any purpose the community sees fit, he was willing to sit on them.

Abaye further reports that Rabba originally maintained two separate pouches — one for the general poor and one for the poor of the city — in order to keep the collections distinct. Once he heard Shmuel's ruling to Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi — *avid chad kisa ve'atni alah*, maintain one pouch and simply stipulate how it will be distributed — he adopted that practice as well. The *chiddush* here is subtle: even when one explicitly collects for a specific purpose, once the discretion to reassign is established, there is no problem even *lechatchila* mixing the collections. Rav Ashi goes further still: *ana itnuyei nami lo tzerichna* — he holds that no explicit stipulation is even needed, because *de'chol de'ka atei ada'atah didi atei*, anyone who gives money to *tzedakah* and entrusts it to a recognized *tzedakah* collector implicitly accepts that collector's discretion regarding how to distribute it.

---

## Guild Authority

### Butchers' Pact

The Gemara transitions from the *baraita*'s discussion of townspeople imposing fines for violations of communal rules to an illustrative case. Two butchers — *bei terei tavchei* — made an arrangement between them: they divided the working days of the week, each assigned to work on alternating days. Their agreement stipulated that if either worked on the other's day, the offender's animal hide would be torn to shreds — a significant financial penalty. One of them did in fact work on the other's day. The hide was torn. They came before Rava.

### Rava's Ruling

Rava ruled that the one who tore the hide was obligated to pay. Rav Yeimar bar Shelameya challenged Rava: does the *baraita* not state *u'le'hasia al kitzatan* — that communities may fine those who violate their edicts? Did these butchers not do exactly that? Rava did not respond. Rav Papa said that Rava was right not to respond, and explained the underlying rule: *hanei milei heicha de'leika adam chashuv* — this power to make and enforce such rules applies only where there is no *adam chashuv* in the town. *Aval heicha de'ika adam chashuv lav kol ke'minaihu de'matnu* — where there is an *adam chashuv*, the guild or collective cannot make binding rules with enforceable consequences without his authorization.

### Adam Chashuv Role

The *Ri Migash*, cited by many *rishonim*, explains that *adam chashuv* here requires two qualifications simultaneously: the person must be a *talmid chacham* of significance, and he must hold an actual position of civic leadership in the town. Neither qualification alone suffices. The combination of genuine Torah knowledge and recognized communal authority is what constitutes the *adam chashuv* whose approval is required.

The Ramban offers a compelling explanation of why this oversight is necessary. The butchers' arrangement — alternating days and eliminating competition — is not simply an internal matter between two parties. It has substantial consequences for the entire town: less competition means higher prices and reduced consumer protection. Because the arrangement's effects extend beyond the parties themselves to the general public, those parties cannot impose it unilaterally. They require the approval of someone whose role is to weigh both the legitimate interests of the guild and the interests of the townspeople at large. The *adam chashuv*, combining *halachic* knowledge with civic authority, is precisely that person.

The *rishonim* draw an important boundary around this principle. The power to establish binding guild-like arrangements with enforceable penalties is not available to any group of individuals who happen to share a business interest. It applies specifically to a recognized collective — a town, or something analogous to a guild in the sense of comprising *all* practitioners of a given trade in a locale. If the two butchers in the Gemara's case were merely two out of many, they would not have had this power at all; they would have had to rely on ordinary contract law. The shift the Gemara makes — from the *baraita*'s discussion of townspeople to the case of butchers operating as a guild — is a significant conceptual extension, and the *rishonim* are careful to define its limits. Questions of governance within such collectives — decision-making by consensus, the weight of a minority veto — remain largely unresolved in the Gemara's framework.

---

## Power & Trust (II)

### Trust Paradox

The Gemara returns to *tzedakah* and a *baraita* that is striking in its implications: *ein mechashvin be'tzedakah im gabbei tzedakah* — one does not audit the accounts of the *gabbei tzedakah*. Similarly, *ve'lo be'hekdesh im gizbarim* — the treasurers of the *beit ha'mikdash* were not subject to post-hoc accounting of their stewardship. The verse brought as a *zecher* (allusion rather than formal proof) is the verse describing those entrusted with temple funds: *ki ve'emunah hem osim* — they acted faithfully, and faithful agents are not subjected to audit.

Rashi explains why this is only a *zecher* and not a full proof: the temple officials supervised so many concurrent activities that maintaining comprehensive records would have been unreasonable. Tosafot's explanation is more pointed: *raya gemura eina de'shani hatam she'hayu tzaddikim gemurim* — the temple case may have been exceptional because those individuals were of extraordinary personal righteousness, which is not necessarily the default condition of all *gabbei tzedakah*.

The tension this creates is real. The institutional logic — that these positions require absolute trust, and auditing undermines that trust — may have made sense in a community context where appointment was careful and reputations were deeply embedded in social fabric. The practical difficulties of applying this principle without careful attention to character and accountability are significant.

### Preliminary Count

Yet the Gemara does not leave the matter entirely without structure. Rabbi Elazar teaches: even if one has a trusted *gizbar* in one's household, *yitzor veyimneh* — one should bind up the funds and count them out explicitly at the time of handover. The verse cited is *va'yatzuru va'yimnu* — they bound up and counted. There is thus a front-end discipline even where back-end audit is not required. The principle seems to be: establish clarity at the outset, so that both parties know precisely what was entrusted, even if subsequent accounting is left to trust.

---

## Distribution Standards

### Food Investigation

Rav Huna states: *bodkin le'mezonot ve'ein bodkin le'chasut* — one investigates whether a person truly needs food before providing it, but one does not investigate before providing clothing. This can be derived either from *sevara* or from a verse. The *sevara*: *hai ka'meivazeh ve'hai lo ka'meivazeh* — the person who lacks clothing is visibly humiliated in public, while the person who lacks food suffers privately; therefore one acts immediately for the clothing case without delay for investigation. The verse: *halo faros la'ra'ev lachmecha* — where the word *faros* is read as *lifrosh* (to explicate, to investigate), written with a *shin*, meaning: first investigate, then give bread. By contrast, for clothing the verse reads *ki tireh arom ve'chiasito* — as soon as you see the naked person, cover him: *la'altar*, immediately.

### Clothing Check

Rav Yehuda reverses the ruling: *bodkin le'chasut ve'ein bodkin le'mezonot* — one investigates before providing clothing, but not before providing food. The *sevara*: *hai ka'mitztaer ve'hai lo ka'mitztaer* — the person who is hungry is suffering immediately and acutely; delay for investigation is unconscionable. The person lacking clothing is indeed visible and humiliated, but the suffering of hunger is more urgent. The verse is read differently: *halo faros la'ra'ev lachmecha* — *paros*, with the plain reading meaning to break and give bread immediately. And for clothing, the phrasing *ki tireh arom ve'chiasito* is read as: when you see, and then you cover — implying an interval of verification before acting.

The question of whether to investigate at all before giving might seem surprising — the Torah's language of *patoach tiftach et yadecha lo* suggests an immediate response. The *chiddush* is that the Gemara permits, and in some cases requires, some investigation before providing either food or clothing. This reflects the practical reality that resources are limited and genuine need must be distinguished from feigned need, even though investigation introduces delay that can itself be costly.

### Tannaitic Standard

A *tanna* resolves the dispute in accordance with Rav Yehuda: *kesuni — bodkin acharav; parnesuni — ein bodkin, nosnin lo miyad*. If someone says "clothe me," you investigate. If someone says "feed me," you do not investigate — you give immediately.

---

## Traveling Poor

### Transient Support

The Gemara now cites a *mishnah* from elsewhere: *ein pochtin le'ani ha'over mi'makom le'makom mi'kikar be'pundiyon me'arba se'in be'sela* — one does not give a transient poor person less than a loaf of bread worth a *pundiyon* when four *se'ah* of wheat cost a *sela*. The baseline of a full loaf is non-negotiable even for the passing poor.

If the person spends the night: *notnin lo parnasat linah* — one provides him lodging. Rav Pappa explains: *purya u'visadya* — a bed and a pillow. The communal infrastructure thus extends to shelter, not merely food — effectively a formalized system of overnight refuge.

If he remains through *Shabbat*: *notnin lo mazon shalosh se'udot* — one provides him with the three *Shabbat* meals. The principle is clear: a transient poor person is entitled to observe *Shabbat* with its full complement of meals, not to experience a diminished *Shabbat* by virtue of poverty.

### Self-Sufficiency

A related principle: if the person is actively going door-to-door and raising his own funds — *im haya machzir al ha'petachim ein nizkakim lo* — the community is not obligated to provide communal funds for him. He is self-sufficient through his own efforts.

Yet this principle requires careful application. The Gemara relates that a certain poor person who was going door-to-door came before Rav Pappa, who declined to give him anything from the communal funds. Rav Sama the son of Rav Yeiva pointed out the consequence: if people see that Rav Pappa — the overseer of communal funds — refused, no one else will give him either, and the person may starve. The *baraita* says not to give from communal funds, but surely he should not die.

Rav Pappa's resolution: *ein nizkakim lo le'matanah merubah* — one does not give him the full communal allocation; *aval nizkakim lo le'matanah mu'etet* — but one gives him a small, nominal amount. The concern is not primarily halachic but social and humanitarian: publicly turning someone away sends a destructive message that forecloses all other potential giving. Even where the strict rule limits communal obligation, a minimal act of support is required to avoid causing greater harm.

### Minimum Annual

Rav Assi states: *le'olam al yimna adam et atzmo miletet shlishit ha'shekel be'shanah* — a person should never withhold from giving at least a third of a *shekel* per year. The verse cited is *ve'he'emadnu aleinu mitzvot latet aleinu shlishit ha'shekel be'shanah la'avodat beit Elokeinu*. This is the bare minimum annual *tzedakah* obligation — distinct from *ma'aser kesafim*, which is more fully developed in the *rishonim* and certain *midrashei halacha* rather than in the Gemara itself. Even if all other communal collections bypass a person entirely, this baseline remains.

Rav Assi adds: *shkulah tzedakah ke'neged kol ha'mitzvot* — *tzedakah* is equivalent to all the *mitzvot* combined, derived from the same verse, since it uses the plural *mitzvot* rather than *mitzvah*. Tosafot addresses an apparent difficulty: the verse speaks about giving for the *beit ha'mikdash* — *bedek ha'bayis* — not for the poor. Tosafot's response is powerful in its brevity: *kol shekein le'tzedakah* — if anything, *tzedakah* for the poor is *more* important than building the Temple. People who are suffering are present and immediate. This two-word formulation serves as a pointed corrective to the tendency — then and now — to prioritize visible institutional religious giving over direct provision for the poor.

---

## Charity Leadership

### Mobilizers

Rabbi Elazar teaches: *gadol ha'me'aseh yoter min ha'oseh* — the one who causes others to give is greater than the one who gives directly. The verse: *ve'haya ma'aseh ha'tzedakah shalom va'avodat ha'tzedakah hashket vavetach ad olam* — the *ma'aseh ha'tzedakah*, the one who facilitates the *tzedakah* of others, achieves *shalom*, while the direct giver achieves *hashket vavetach* — security and tranquility — which is taken as a lesser reward. This returns to the theme of *matzdikei harabbim* — those who cause the many to give carry the merit of all the giving they have enabled.

### Government Role

The Gemara then addresses the consequences of communal failure to give. The verse *halo faros la'ra'ev lachmecha* is read in light of a condition: *zacha* — if you merit — you fulfill the verse by giving to the poor. *Lo zacha* — if you do not — *ve'aniyim merudim tavi bayit*, you bring the downtrodden into your house. Rashi reads *merudim* as referring to those who complain and press their claims — meaning the government. If the Jewish community does not take care of its own poor, the government will step in to extract the funds and administer the collection, a situation far less desirable than communal self-governance.

Rava instructs the people of Mechuza: *bematuta minaichu, usu ba'hadei hadadei ki heichi de'lehavei lachon shalma de'malchuta* — please, take care of one another, so that there will be peace between you and the government. The government's intervention is not abstract; it is a practical consequence of communal failure to provide internally.

### Forced Charity

Rabbi Elazar draws the comparison to the *beit ha'mikdash*: when the Temple stood, *adam shokel shiklo u'mitkapeir lo* — a person gave his *shekel* for the communal sacrifices and was thereby atoned. Now that the Temple is gone, if one gives *tzedakah*, good; if not, *ba'im ovdei kochavim ve'notlim bi'zroa* — the government comes and takes by force.

Yet even forced *tzedakah* carries credit: *ve'af al pi chein nechshav lahem le'tzedakah* — it is still counted for them as *tzedakah*. The verse: *ve'nogshayich tzedakah* — even those who compel you to give are instruments of *tzedakah*, and the giving that results, however involuntary, retains its character as such. The comparison to the *shekel* and *korbanot* reinforces the importance of *tzedakah* as the functional equivalent of Temple service in the current era — both in its potential for atonement and in the consequences of its neglect.

---

---

# Bava Batra 10

## Tzedakah vs. Korbanot

### Tzedakah Replaces Korban…

The daf opens at the very end of 9b, in the middle of a major *sugya* on *tzedakah*. Rabbi Elazar teaches: *bizman shebeis hamikdash kayam, adam shokeil shiklo umischaper lo* — when the Temple stood, a person would give his shekel and thereby receive atonement. And now that the Temple no longer stands, *im osim tzedakah mutav* — if one gives *tzedakah*, it is good. It is worth noting that we more commonly think of *tefillah* as the replacement for *korbanot*, yet here the *gemara* explicitly draws the parallel to *tzedakah* instead. There have been earlier comparisons as well — the concept of *tzedakah* was learned, in part, from money given to the Temple — but here the identification is direct: the money one gives to the poor serves as a kind of *korban*.

### Gov't Intervention

The passage continues: *v'im lav boin ovdei kochavim umezuyei* — if you do not take care of your own poor, the non-Jewish government will step in and do the job for you, collecting taxes and imposing that burden on you regardless. The *gemara* adds, *v'af al pi kein nechshav lahem l'tzedakah* — and even so, even when they are compelled by outside forces, it still counts as *tzedakah*, as the verse says: *v'nogsaich tzedakah* — those who oppress you will extract *tzedakah* from you, and it will still bear that character. The practical implication is worth considering: one should think carefully about how much one already gives to *tzedakah* — and how much goes to taxes whose proceeds support various social welfare programs.

### Small Gifts Accumulate

The *gemara* then quotes a teaching of Rabbi Elazar: *mai d'chsiv, v'yilbash tzedakah k'shiryon* — what is meant by the verse, "and he clothed himself in righteousness like plate armor"? While the verse speaks of righteousness in its plain sense, the *gemara* reads it through the rabbinic lens of *tzedakah* as charitable giving. The point of the metaphor is *ma shiryon zeh kol klipa u'klipa mitztarefet l'shiryon gadol* — just as every individual piece of metal plate joins together to form a great armor, so too with *tzedakah*: *kol pruta u'pruta mitztarefet l'cheshbon gadol* — every single penny combines into a great sum.

Rabbi Chanina offers a parallel from a different verse: *u'k'veged idim kol tzidkoseinu* — like a worn garment are all our acts of righteousness. The emphasis here falls on the word *beged*, garment. *Ma beged zeh kol nima u'nima mitztarefet l'veged gadol* — just as every individual thread is nothing on its own but together forms a real garment, so too *kol pruta u'pruta mitztarefet l'cheshbon gadol* — every small gift combines into something significant. Interestingly, this point is made from the perspective of the giver's reward: each small amount of *tzedakah* one gives accumulates into a great reckoning of merit.

---

## Rav Sheshet Digression

### Rav Sheshet's Name

The *gemara* introduces a passage attributed to Rav Sheshet in the name of Rabbi Elazar — the very teaching about the *shiryon* we just encountered — but opens with a curious label. The teacher is called *olel meshageish archasei d'imei* — the suckling who perverted the path of his mother. This strange epithet is applied to Rav Sheshet, and the *gemara* explains it through a story.

### Metzora Tumah Questions

Rav Acha bar Adda posed a series of difficult questions to Rav Sheshet: *minayin l'tzipporei yemei tzipporo she'metam'in adam* — from where do we know that a *metzora* during the period of *tzipporo* — after the initial purification process with the birds has been performed and he is awaiting re-entry into the camp — has *tumah* sufficient to render a person *tamei*? For a person to become *tamei* from another person, that person must be an *av hatumah*. What is his *tumah* status during this intermediate period?

Rav Sheshet responded: he is *metamei bgadim* — he renders his garments *tamei* — and therefore, by extension, he renders a person *tamei*. Rav Acha pushed back: perhaps there is a distinction between rendering one's own garments *tamei* while they are worn versus rendering another person or separate garments *tamei*. The case of *heses neveilah* illustrates this: one who lifts or carries a *neveilah* becomes *tamei* along with the garments he is wearing, yet that person does not thereby acquire the capacity to render other people *tamei*. So the fact that something makes one's worn garments *tamei* does not prove it can make other persons *tamei*.

Rav Sheshet then tried a different angle: *ella sheretz d'metamei adam menalan* — how do we know a dead *sheretz* renders a person *tamei*? Is it not inferred from its capacity to render garments *tamei*? Rav Acha replied: *sheretz behedya ksiv bei* — there is an explicit verse, *o ish asher yiga b'chol sheretz* — it is derived from an explicit *pasuk*, not from *bgadim* at all. Rav Sheshet then attempted the case of *shichvas zera* — semen, which renders garments *tamei* and, seemingly by the same logic, renders a person *tamei*. Rav Acha deflected this as well: *shichvas zera nami behedya ksiv bei* — there too, we have an explicit verse, *asher tetzei mimenu shichvas zera*, from which we extend even to one who merely touches it, *l'rabos es hanogea*. In each case, the *gemara* demonstrates that one cannot infer the *metzora*'s capacity to render a person *tamei* from his capacity to render garments *tamei*: either the cases involve garments being worn in different circumstances, or they rest on explicit *pesukim* rather than inference.

### Punishment & Healing

With each answer Rav Sheshet offered, Rav Acha pushed back — and apparently did so with some amusement, laughing at what he may not have intended as mockery. *Chalash datei d'Rav Sheshet* — Rav Sheshet became deeply despondent, feeling that he was being ridiculed. As a result, Rav Acha fell mute and, worse, *ishtakach talmudei* — he forgot all of his learning. A woman then came — Rashi identifies her as Rav Sheshet's mother, while Tosafot identifies her as Rav Acha's mother who had served as Rav Sheshet's nursemaid — and wept before Rav Sheshet, imploring him on behalf of Rav Acha. She cried and cried and he did not respond. She then said: *chazi l'hanei chadi d'matzit mineihu* — look at this breast from which you suckled. Have compassion. In the end, *bei rachamei alei v'itassi* — he prayed for Rav Acha, and he was healed. This is the origin of that curious name — the suckling who perverted his mother's path. How this story connects to the *tzedakah* discussion that precedes it appears to be a genuine digression.

### Explicit Pasuk Solutions

Before returning to the *tzedakah* discussion, the *gemara* resolves the underlying *halachic* question.
