Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai teaches through a *gezeirah shavah*: the Torah speaks of washing garments both during the *metzora*'s period of *sipuro* and during his period of *chaluto* — his full *tumah* status. *Mah lehalan metamei adam, af kan metamei adam* — just as during the period of full *tumah* the *metzora* renders a person *tamei*, so too during the *sipuro* period. The answer came not from logical inference but from an explicit scriptural parallel.

---

## Secret Giving > Moshe

### Greater Than Moshe

Returning now to the main discussion, Rabbi Elazar teaches: *gadol oseh tzedakah b'seser yoser miMoshe Rabbeinu* — one who gives *tzedakah* in private is greater than Moshe Rabbeinu. This is a striking statement. Tosafot clarifies: it does not mean that such a person becomes greater than Moshe Rabbeinu as a person, but rather that the act has greater power to calm divine anger than Moshe's prayers did. *D'ilu b'Moshe Rabbeinu kesiv ki yagorti mipnei ha'af v'hacheimah* — by Moshe it is written, "I was fearful before the anger and the wrath," indicating that Moshe could not counter or stand against God's anger and wrath. *V'ilu b'oseh tzedakah kesiv matan b'seser yichpeh af* — whereas regarding *tzedakah* it is written: a gift in private covers over the anger. And *v'shochad becheik cheimah azah* — giving in the hidden, private realm calms even fierce rage. The act of secret giving thus stands where Moshe's prayer could not.

The *gemara* notes a dissent: *u'pliga d'Rabbi Yitzchak*. Rabbi Yitzchak holds that *af kofeh cheimah eino kofeh* — *tzedakah* can cover *af*, anger, but not *cheimah azah*, the fiercer rage. He reads the verse as split in two: the word *yichpeh*, "covers," applies only to the *af*, while *v'shochad becheik cheimah azah* — despite giving in private, the fierce rage remains beyond what *tzedakah* can address.

There is a second version of Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching: *kol hanosein shochad meivi cheimah azah l'olam* — any judge who takes a bribe brings fierce divine anger upon the world. On this reading the verse speaks of two entirely separate matters: one about *tzedakah* and one about bribery.

### Six vs. Eleven Blessings

Rabbi Yitzchak continues: *kol hanosein prutah l'ani misbarech b'sheish brachos* — one who gives even a penny to a poor person is blessed with six blessings. But *v'hamifayaso bidvarim* — if one uses words to console the poor person, to actually address his spirit and make him feel better — *misbarech b'achas esrei brachos* — he is blessed with eleven blessings. Money is important, but the capacity to speak to a person's *neshamah*, to console and support him emotionally, is worth nearly double.

The six blessings come from the verse: *halo faros lara'ev lachmecha* — is it not to break your bread for the hungry — and the sequence that follows: *v'aniyim merudim tavi bayis, ki sireh arom v'chisiso, az yibaka kashachar orecha, v'halach l'fanecha tzidkecha, v'chvod Hashem ya'asfecha, az tikra v'Hashem ya'aneh, tishava v'yomar hineni* — six blessings. The eleven come from: *v'safek lara'ev nafshecha* — you extend your very soul, not merely your money, to the hungry person — *v'nefesh na'ana tasbia*, you satisfy the soul of the afflicted — and the verses that follow.

Tosafot raises a variant reading: some wish to emend the text so that the eleven blessings apply only to one who both gives *tzedakah* and consoling words together. They base this on the phrase *v'nefesh na'ana tasbia*, arguing it could refer to giving food. But the *gemara* rejects this: *nefesh na'ana tasbia* means *tasbia bidvarim* — you satiate the soul with words, and the verse speaks of pure emotional support without monetary giving. The two tracks — money and words — remain distinct, and pure consolation carries even greater reward than giving alone.

---

## Pursuing Tzedakah

### God Provides Means

Rabbi Elazar raises a question about the verse: *rodeif tzedakah v'chesed yimtza chayim tzedakah v'chavod* — one who pursues *tzedakah* and *chesed* will find life, *tzedakah*, and honor. The difficulty: if *rodeif tzedakah* means you run to give charity, and the reward is *yimtza tzedakah* — you will find *tzedakah* — that means you will need to receive charity from others, which is hardly a blessing. The answer: *ella lomar lach kol harodeif achar tzedakah Hakadosh Baruch Hu mamtzi lo mammon l'asos bahen tzedakah* — if you pursue *tzedakah*, the Holy One will provide you with the financial means to keep giving. The reward for giving is the ability to give more.

### Worthy Recipients

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a different reading: *Hakadosh Baruch Hu mamtzi lo bnei adam hamehuganim l'asos bahen tzedakah* — if you pursue *tzedakah*, God will ensure that the people who come to you asking for it are truly deserving, *kidei lekabel aleihem scharo* — so that you receive proper reward for your giving.

### Unworthy Recipients

This teaching stands *l'apukei* — in contrast to — what Rava expounded from the verse in Yirmiyahu: *v'yiyu michshalim l'fanecha* — let them stumble before You. Yirmiyahu said to God: even when these people overcome their *yetzer* and try to perform *mitzvos*, *hachshilem bivnei adam she'einam mehuganim* — cause them to stumble by sending them undeserving people to give to, so that they receive no reward for their efforts, *kidei shelo yekablu aleihem schar*. Rav Nachman's point is thus the inverse: if you genuinely pursue *tzedakah*, God will help you give it to the right people, and you will receive full reward. It is worth pausing here. The framing of worthy recipients as the means by which one earns reward can make the *ani* feel like an instrument — like a *lulav* one picks up to fulfill a *mitzvah*. This tension is worth keeping in mind as the *sugya* continues.

### Promise of Good Children

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds: *kol haragil la'asot tzedakah zocheh sheyihyu lo banim ba'alei chochmah ba'alei osher ba'alei agadah* — one who makes a regular practice of giving *tzedakah* merits children who are wise, wealthy, and skilled in *aggadah*. This serves an important social function: in a society where rabbinic achievement is the highest form of status, *tzedakah* — accessible to all — is here presented as the path by which even the wealthy philanthropist who is not himself a *talmid chacham* can merit children who are *talmidei chachamim*, as well as children who are themselves wealthy and able to continue the tradition of giving.

The three blessings are sourced from the verse *rodeif tzedakah v'chesed yimtza chayim tzedakah v'chavod*: *chayim* corresponds to Torah wisdom, as Rashi notes from the verse *ki motzai matza chayim* — wisdom is life. *Tzedakah* here corresponds to wealth and the ongoing capacity to give. *Chavod*, honor, corresponds to skill in *aggadah*. Rashi explains this beautifully: *ba'alei agadah mitoch shehem darshanim u'moshchim et halev hakol mechabdim otam* — those who are skilled orators and can draw hearts to them receive wide public recognition and honor. It is a distinct skill from that of the *talmid chacham*, and it brings its own form of *kavod* — still the honor of sages, as the parallel verse states, *kavod chachamim yinchalu*.

---

## Why Poverty Exists

### Pagan Theology Challenge

A *braita* introduces a challenge the Rabbis took seriously: Rabbi Meir teaches that the opposing side — whether an internal skeptic or an external critic — can pose the following: *im elokeichem ohev aniyim hu, mipnei mah eino mefarnesam* — if your God truly loves the poor, why does He not simply provide for them? The existence of poverty, in this view, signals divine disfavor toward the poor. This was indeed a widespread theology in the ancient pagan world: wealth demonstrated divine favor, poverty reflected divine displeasure, and therefore the wealthy were righteous and the poor were sinners. While the Torah's framework of *schar v'onesh* operates at a collective level and never reaches the point of equating an individual's wealth with his righteousness, the critique has force within the pagan framework and must be answered on its own terms.

### Redemption Through Giving

The Talmudic response: *kidei shenitzol anu bahem midina shel geihinnom* — God has created poverty to give us the opportunity to perform the *mitzvah* of *tzedakah*, thereby saving ourselves from *geihinnom*. The tension implicit in this answer — that it treats the *ani* as a means by which the giver earns merit — is real and was noted. Perhaps this response is best read as an answer offered *l'shitasam*, on the terms of the questioner, rather than as a full theological account.

### Turnusrufus Parable

The *gemara* notes that Turnusrufus the wicked, the Roman governor in the time of Rabbi Akiva, posed the same question — *elokeichem ohev aniyim hu, mipnei mah eino mefarnesam* — and received the same initial response. Turnusrufus then pushed back: *zu she'mechayvatan l'geihinnom* — by giving to the poor you are actually sinning. He offered a parable: a human king who was angry at his servant imprisoned him and commanded that no one give him food or drink. One who defied that order and brought him food — would the king not be furious with that person? You are called God's servants, as the verse states, *ki li venei Yisrael avadim avadai hem*. The natural order of the world reflects God's decree; by subverting it through charity, you are violating the divine will.

### Father's Discipline Para…

Rabbi Akiva responded with a counter-parable. It is not a servant the king imprisoned — it is a son. *Keshem she'ka'as al beno, chavsho be'veit ha'asurim v'tzivah alav she'lo le'hakhilo v'lo le'hashkoto* — the king grew angry at his son and imprisoned him, commanding that no one feed or give him drink. But if someone came and fed and cared for the son — *keshe'shama ha'melech lo doron meshagei'r lo* — would the king not send that person a gift in gratitude? Even if a parent must impose a punishment, what the parent truly wants is for the child to be cared for. And we are called God's children: *banim atem la'Hashem Elokeichem*.

### Sons vs. Servants

Turnusrufus pressed the contradiction: we are called both children and servants in different verses. *Bizman she'atem osim retzono shel Makom atem keruyim banim* — when you do God's will you are His children; *bizman she'ein atem osim retzono shel Makom atem keruyim avadim* — when you do not, you are His servants. And now, under Roman subjugation, clearly you are not in God's favor — so you are servants, and the parable of the servant applies.

Rabbi Akiva responded by citing the verse explicitly: *halo faros lara'ev lachmecha v'aniyim merudim tavi bayis* — is it not to break your bread for the hungry and bring the outcast poor into your house? *Eimatai?* When is this commanded? *Ha'idna* — now, precisely in this time of difficulty and subjugation. The command to support the poor addresses us even, or especially, at the moment when we are under oppression. The theological answer is ultimately: we remain God's children, and even within a period of divine displeasure God wants us to respond with compassion to those in need, and through that compassion to merit restoration.

---

## Income & Expenses Decreed

### Sustenance & Loss

Rav Yehuda bar Meramya teaches: *keshem she'mezonotav shel adam ketzuvim lo me'Rosh Hashanah, kach chesronotav shel adam ketzuvim lo me'Rosh Hashanah* — just as a person's income for the year is decreed on *Rosh Hashanah*, so too are his losses. Two figures are set: gross income, and total expenditure. *Zachah, halo faros lara'ev lachmecha* — if one merits, that decreed amount of loss will go to support the poor through *tzedakah*. *Lo zachah, v'aniyim merudim tavi bayit* — if one does not merit, the Roman tax collectors will enter and take that amount regardless. You will lose the money either way. The question is whether you will give it or whether it will be taken from you.

### Nephews' Tzedakah Story

The *gemara* illustrates this with the story of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's nephews. He saw in a dream that they were destined to lose 700 dinars in the coming year. Over the course of the year, without their knowledge of the dream, he made repeated appeals to them, collecting for various causes, until he had taken 683 dinars from them for *tzedakah*. Only 17 remained of the decreed 700. On *Erev Yom Kippur* — Rashi indicates the dream came on *Motza'ei Yom Kippur* the prior year, completing a full annual cycle — agents of the Caesar came and demanded exactly 17 dinars. The full 700 had been expended.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai told his nephews: do not be afraid of further demands. *Shivasar dinarei degavaichu shaklinhu mineichu* — the 17 that were still decreed, they took from you; there will be no more. They asked: how did you know? He told them of the dream. They asked: why did you not tell us at the outset, so that we could have gladly given the full 700? *Amina ki heichi d'ta'avdu mitzvah lishmah* — because I wanted you to give the *mitzvah* for its own sake, not out of the calculated awareness that you were going to lose the money anyway.

### Giving for Its Sake

There is an inherent irony here: by teaching this story, the Rabbis introduce a degree of *shelo lishmah* into our giving. Having internalized the lesson, one is tempted to think, "I should give generously to *tzedakah* because presumably some portion of my income is decreed to be lost this year anyway — might as well give it purposefully." We don't have the dream; we don't know the exact amount. Perhaps this leaves just enough uncertainty — just the right measure of *shelo lishmah* — to encourage more generous giving, without entirely undermining the ideal of *lishmah*.

---

## Ignoring Poor=Avodah Zar…

### Rav Papa's Fall

Rav Papa was ascending some steps when his foot slipped and he nearly fell. He said: I almost died the death of one who violates *Shabbos* or worships *avodah zarah* — i.e., the death of *skilah*, being thrown from a height, which suggested some grave sin. Chiya bar Rav of Diftei said to him: *shema ani ba l'yadcha v'lo parnastato* — perhaps a poor person came to you and you did not provide for him.

### Eyes Hidden = Idolatry

This leads to the *braita* of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: *kol hama'alim einav min hatzedakah ke'ilu oved avodah zarah* — anyone who hides his eyes from *tzedakah*, who ignores the *ani* before him, is as if he has worshiped *avodah zarah*. The derivation: the verse here uses the word *beliyaal* — *hishamer lecha pen yihyeh davar im l'vavcha beliyaal* — and the verse regarding *avodah zarah* also uses the word *beliyaal* — *yatze'u anashim bnei beliyaal*. The Maharsha notes that these are the only two occurrences of *beliyaal* in the five books of Moshe. *Mah halan avodah zarah, af kan avodah zarah* — just as the latter involves *avodah zarah*, so too the former.

Beyond the textual parallel, one can offer a thematic reading as well. Hiding one's eyes from *tzedakah* involves a kind of acceptance of the natural order — a fatalistic theology, the very worldview that Turnusrufus pressed upon Rabbi Akiva. In that sense, it is indeed *ke'ilu oved avodah zarah*: you are worshiping the forces of fate rather than acting on the divine imperative. Alternatively, the refusal to give reflects a worship of money itself — a sense that what you earned is entirely your own, denying God's role in providing your wealth, which is its own form of denying God's sovereignty.

---

## Cosmic Peace via Tzedakah

### Advocates Before God

A *braita* taught by Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yose: *kol tzedakah v'chesed she'Yisrael osim ba'olam hazeh, shalom gadol u'peraklitin gedolim bein Yisrael l'Avihem she'ba'shamayim* — all *tzedakah* and *chesed* that Israel performs in this world creates great peace and great heavenly advocates between Israel and their Father in Heaven. In the rabbinic framework, *tzedakah* refers to the giving of money and *chesed* refers to personal acts of assistance and kindness — and *chesed*, notably, is not limited to the poor.

The source verse is from Yirmiyahu: God says He has taken away His *shalom* — His peace and wellbeing — from the people, removing *et hachesed v'et harachamim*. *Chesed, zu gemilus chasadim; rachamim, zu tzedakah*. That which God withdraws — *chesed* and *rachamim* — is precisely what constitutes His *shalom* between Himself and Israel. Restoring them through acts of *tzedakah* and *chesed* is therefore the means of restoring that relationship. There is sensitivity worth noting in equating *tzedakah* with *rachamim* — compassion: giving must flow from genuine empathy, seeing the other person's full humanity, not merely treating them as an object of pity.

### Brings Redemption Closer

Rabbi Yose teaches: *gedolah tzedakah she'mekarevet et hage'ulah* — *tzedakah* hastens the redemption. *Ko amar Hashem: shimru mishpat va'asu tzedakah ki krovah yeshuati lavo* — thus says God: observe justice and perform *tzedakah*, for My salvation is close to coming.

### Ten Hardest Things

Rabbi Yose further taught that ten hard things were created in the world, each one undone by the next in a chain — a structure reminiscent of *Chad Gadya*. A mountain is hard, iron cuts it. Iron is hard, fire melts it. Fire is hard, water extinguishes it. Water is hard, clouds carry it. Clouds are hard, wind scatters them. Wind is hard, the body contains it. The body is hard, fear humbles it. Fear is hard, wine dissipates it. Wine is hard, sleep dispels it. And *umitah kashah mikulam* — death is the hardest of all. Yet *utzedakah matzela min hamitah* — and *tzedakah* saves from death, as it is written, *utzedakah tatzil mimavet*.

The sequence seems discontinuous: all the prior items follow the *Chad Gadya* pattern, each destroying the previous, but the transition from sleep to death breaks the chain. One suggestion: sleep is described in the *gemara* elsewhere as one-sixtieth of death, which might serve as the conceptual bridge.

---

## Lender to God

### Immediate Divine Reward

Dostai bar Yannai expounds: *bo u'rei shelo kemidat Hakadosh Baruch Hu midat basar vadam* — come and see that God is unlike human beings. When you bring a great gift to a human king, you do not know whether it will be accepted, and even if accepted, you do not know whether you will gain an audience with the king. God is not so. *Adam noten pruta l'ani, zoche umekabel pnei hashchina* — one who gives a penny to a poor person immediately merits an encounter with the divine presence. *Shene'emar: ani betzedek echezeh panecha* — "I, with righteousness, will see Your face."

One can read this verse in a deeper register as well. If we truly saw the *tzelem Elokim* — the divine image — in every human being, how could we fail to give? When we allow ourselves to pass by a person with outstretched hand, it is because we have ceased to see them as fully human, as bearers of the divine image. To give *tzedakah* in response to genuinely seeing that person is itself a *re'iyat pnei HaShem*, an encounter with God's presence. This connects, too, to the earlier equation of ignoring the poor with *avodah zarah*: both involve a failure to see God where God is.

### Tzedakah Before Prayer

Rabbi Elazar made it his practice to give a *pruta* to an *ani* before praying. He would cite the same verse: *ani betzedek echezeh panecha* — first I give *tzedakah*, and then I stand before God. One can also read this as follows: before one feels entitled to stand before God and petition for one's own needs — which is the heart of *Shemoneh Esrei* — one must first demonstrate that one cares about others. If you want God to respond to you with compassion and care, first show that you respond that way to those around you.

### Two Types of Salvation

Rabbi Yochanan then raises a question: why does the verse *utzedakah tatzil mimavet* appear twice — once as *lo yo'il hon b'yom evrah utzedakah tatzil mimavet*, and once as *lo yo'ilu otzros resha utzedakah tatzil mimavet*? If it is the same teaching, why repeat it? The answer: *shtei tzedakos hallalu* — these two mentions correspond to two distinct forms of salvation from death. One saves from *misah meshunah* — a painful or disfiguring death in this world, so that one dies peacefully rather than through suffering. The other saves from *dinat geihinnom* — the punishment worse than death, the judgment of *geihinnom*. Which *tzedakah* saves from *geihinnom*? The one associated with the word *evrah* — anger — since *yom evrah hayom hahu* refers to the day of judgment. Which saves from *misah meshunah* in this world?

### Anonymous Giving

*Nosenah v'eino yodea l'mi nosenah, v'notlah v'eino yodea mimi notlah* — the giver does not know to whom he gives, and the recipient does not know from whom he receives. This is the ideal form of *tzedakah*, the highest level — which the Rambam systematized in his eight stages, though the basis is clearly here in the *gemara*.

### Mar Ukva & Rabbi Abba

The *gemara* clarifies. *Nosenah v'eino yodea l'mi nosenah* — the giver does not know who receives — this stands *l'apukei mi'demar Ukva*, in contrast to Mar Ukva's practice, in which at least the giver did not know who received but the recipient did not know the giver's identity either. *Notlah v'eino yodea mimi notlah* — the recipient does not know who gave — stands *l'apukei m'Rabbi Abba*, in contrast to Rabbi Abba's method. How does one achieve full anonymity on both sides? *Leisiv l'arneki shel tzedakah* — one gives to a communal charity fund administered by a trustworthy person who maintains the privacy of both giver and recipient. Neither party ever learns the other's identity.

---

## Promise of Reward

### Male Children Merit

The *gemara* asks: *mah ya'aseh adam veyihyu lo banim zacharim* — what should a person do to merit male children? Rabbi Eliezer says: *yefazer me'osav le'aniyim* — scatter his money to the poor, give prolifically and without excessive calculation. Rabbi Yehoshua says: *yisammach ishto b'dvar mitzvah* — he should attend to his wife's needs in the context of marital intimacy. These are strikingly different answers; at least Rabbi Yehoshua's connects directly to the question of children being conceived, while the connection between scattering *tzedakah* and male children is less immediately apparent.

### Trustworthy Middlemen

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches within the same *braita*: *lo yitten adam peruta l'ani shel tzedakah ella im ken memunah alav keRebbi Chananya ben Teradyon* — a person should not give a penny to a *tzedakah* collector unless that person is as trustworthy as Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon. At first glance this seems in tension with the earlier recommendation to give through an anonymous middleman. The resolution: *ki kamina demamnu aleih keRebbi Chananya ben Teradyon* — the recommendation to give through a fund presupposes that the fund is run by someone of that caliber. One who gives responsibly should investigate: what is the overhead of the organization, how wisely is the money deployed, how trustworthy are those administering it? This is an important counterbalance to an earlier passage that cautioned against suspecting those actively engaged in *tzedakah* collection. That passage concerned not casting aspersions on those performing their role; this passage concerns the prior decision of where to direct one's giving.

### Moshe's Question

Rabbi Abbahu teaches: Moshe said before the Holy One — *bameh tarum keren Yisrael*, by what means will the glory of Israel be elevated? God answered: *b'Ki Tisa* — by the portion of *Ki Tisa*, the giving of the half-shekel to the Temple. *Ki Tisa* is read here as a template: supporting the sacred causes of one's community is what raises the standing of Israel. Solomon's son and successor is then cited: when asked *ad heichan kocha shel tzedakah* — how far does the power of *tzedakah* extend — he replied, *tze'u ur'u mah peireish David abba* — go and see what my father David wrote: *pizer natan la'evyonim, tzidkato omedet la'ad, karno tarum bechavod* — he scattered his wealth to the poor, his righteousness stands forever, his horn will be raised in honor.

Rabbi Abba adds a verse: *hu meromim yishkon, metzadot sela'im misgavo, lachmo nutan, meimav ne'emanim* — he will dwell on high, in the strongholds of rocks, his bread he has given, his waters are faithful. *Mah ta'am meromim yishkon?* Why does he dwell on high? *Mishum delachmo nutan* — because he gave his bread to the poor.

### Upside-Down Worlds

Rabbi Abbahu reports that Solomon was asked: *eizehu ben Olam Haba* — who merits the world to come? He answered: *kol shekeneged zekenav kavod* — one in whose old age he is honored. Rashi explains: this refers to one who is honored for the wisdom accrued through a life well lived — not for wealth or power, but for the genuine wisdom that commands respect.

The *gemara* then tells the story of Yosef the son of Rabbi Yehoshua, who fell gravely ill and, upon recovering, was asked by his father what he had seen in that state. He replied: *olam hafuch ra'iti* — I saw an inverted world. *Elyonim lemata, vetachtonim lemala* — those who are at the top here were at the bottom there, and those at the bottom here were at the top there. His father replied: *olam barur ra'ita* — that is the true world, the clear world. The one we inhabit is the inverted one.

### Rabbis' Eternal Status

When asked about the *talmidei chachamim* — where do the Rabbis stand? — Yosef replied: *ki heichi dechashvinan hacha, chashvinan hatam* — the same standing we have here, we have there. He did not claim the top. The point is precise: honor earned for money and worldly power will be reversed in the world to come. But honor earned for *Torah* and *chochmah* — that reflects genuine achievement, and it is consistent between the two worlds.

He added: *ashrei mi sheba lechan vetalmudo beyado* — praised is one who arrives in the world to come with his learning in his hand. The Maharsha explains: *beyado* — in his hand — means the learning he truly owns, the material he internalized because he wrote it down. This is a pedagogical point of enduring relevance.

Finally: *harugei malchus ein kol berya yechola la'amod bimchitzatam* — those martyred by the government, who gave their lives *al kiddush Hashem*, no creature can stand at their level. The *gemara* asks: are we speaking of Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues, the great Rabbis of the Roman persecutions? But *pshita delav hachi nami* — they would have been at the highest level in the world to come even without martyrdom. The reference is rather to the *harugei Lod* — those martyred in the story of Lod, where two brothers falsely confessed to a killing they did not commit in order to save an entire city from Roman collective punishment. Their martyrdom was not accompanied by decades of Torah greatness; it was an act of supreme self-sacrifice for the community. And that, the *gemara* suggests, places them at an incomparable level.

---

# Bava Batra 11

## Tzedakah & Chesed

### Opening & Verse

The *sugya* of *tzedakah* continues on 10b, picking up with a *tanya* that opens a remarkable teaching of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai to his students. He poses the question: *banai, mahu she'amar hakatuv* — what is meant by the verse *tzedakah teromem goy ve-chesed le'umim chatat*? Righteousness, or *tzedakah*, will lift up a nation, and *chesed* — acts of kindness — performed by nations is a sin. The verse is genuinely difficult to parse. One approach actually interprets *chesed* not as kindness but as iniquity, in the manner of the verse *ki tikach achoto chesed hi*, where *chesed* carries a negative valence. In any case, the verse is hard, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai invites his students to offer their readings.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer answers first. *Tzedakah teromem goy* — the *goy* referred to here is Israel, as the verse states *umi ke'amcha Yisrael goy echad ba'aretz*. *Ve-chesed le'umim chatat*: any *tzedakah* and *chesed* that the nations of the world perform — *kol tzedakah ve-chesed she-umot ovdei kochavim osim* — is a sin for them. Why? *She'einam osim ela lehitgadel bo*: they do not act *leshaim shamayim*. They give only to aggrandize themselves, to appear as great philanthropists. The supporting verse is drawn from the time of Ezra, when a foreign king contributed to the rebuilding of the *Beit Hamikdash* but appended the condition that offerings be brought and prayers offered for the life of the king and his sons — *umetzalyin l'chayei malka u'venohi*. This reveals that even ostensibly generous acts by non-Jewish kingdoms ultimately serve their own interests.

It is worth pausing here. Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai and his students lived at the moment of the *churban Beit Hamikdash*, with Rome as both their provider of infrastructure and their existential oppressor. The earlier *Gemara* in *Avodah Zarah* captures this tension precisely — some sages acknowledged the genuine benefits Rome bestowed upon its inhabitants through roads, water systems, and civic order, while others insisted those acts were done purely for Rome's own benefit. Here, Rabbi Eliezer's position clearly reflects the latter view.

But then the *Gemara* interjects with an Aramaic question. If someone gives *tzedakah* with a mixed motive — *ha'omer sela zu litzdakah bishvil sheyichye beni uvishvil she'ezkeh lechayei ha'olam haba*, donating a *sela* for charity in the hope that his sick son recovers or that he will merit *olam haba* — the *tanya* declares *harei zeh tzaddik gamur*, he is considered a complete *tzaddik*. How, then, can we condemn the non-Jew's charity as sinful when Jews themselves give with ulterior motives and are still praised?

The *Gemara* resolves: *lo kashya — kan b'Yisrael, kan b'ovdei kochavim*. There is no contradiction, because the cases are categorically different. Rashi explains: when a Jew gives *shelo lishma*, his underlying disposition remains *leshamayim* — *ben yihye ben lo yihye, eino meharher achar midat hadin*. Even if the hoped-for result does not materialize, the Jew does not regret having given the *tzedakah*. The non-Jew, by contrast, gives *ela limnat sheyichye*, exclusively on condition that his desired outcome is achieved, and *im lav mitcharet* — if it is not, he regrets the act entirely. One teacher suggested that the original text may have read *tzedakah gemurah* rather than *tzaddik gamur*, which would flow more naturally from the *Gemara's* earlier language, but the parallel manuscripts consistently read *tzaddik gamur*. In any case, Rashi explains the declaration as applying to this particular act, not necessarily to the person's overall standing.

### Rabbi Yehoshua

Rabbi Yehoshua then offers his reading. The structure is identical — *goy* means Israel — but his explanation of why non-Jewish *chesed* constitutes sin differs subtly: *she'ein osim ela k'dei shetimshach malchutan*, they do it only to extend their kingdoms. His supporting verse is from Daniel's counsel to Nebuchadnezzar: *v'chata'ach b'tzedakah perok ve'avayach b'michan anayin, hen lehavay archa l'shalvatach* — atone for your sin with *tzedakah* to the poor, and your kingdom will be prolonged. The motivation is explicitly the perpetuation of rule, not genuine concern for others.

One might note that the supporting verses in both Rabbi Eliezer's and Rabbi Yehoshua's positions appear to converge on a similar theme — extending the life and glory of the kingdom — even though their stated explanations differ, one emphasizing personal aggrandizement and the other political perpetuation. There is also a meaningful distinction between the two positions regarding scope: Rabbi Eliezer uses the phrase *lehitgadel bo*, which can apply to any individual, while Rabbi Yehoshua speaks of *malchutan*, suggesting his reading applies specifically to rulers and governments rather than to private individuals. This raises the broader question of whether the entire discussion concerns governmental *tzedakah* or includes individual non-Jews who give charity.

### Rabban Gamliel

Rabban Gamliel's reading follows the same structural form — *goy* is Israel — and his explanation is that non-Jewish *tzedakah* and *chesed* are performed *ela l'hityaher bo*, to make oneself appear righteous, which is distinct from both personal glory and political calculation. The *Gemara* appends a serious warning: *ve-chol hamityayer nofel be-Gehinnom*, whoever presents himself as more righteous than he is will fall into *Gehinnom*, for such a person is truly a *letz*, a mocker — *zed yahir letz shemo*.

Rabban Gamliel then says: *adayin anu tzerichim le-Modai* — we still need Rabbi Eleazar HaModai.

### Rav Nechunya

Rabbi Eleazar HaModai provides yet another variant: any *tzedakah* and *chesed* the nations do is a sin for them, and his proof-text suggests the motivation is to make Israel look bad — to use acts of apparent righteousness as a form of implicit accusation against the Jewish people, in the spirit of *Nevuzaradan's* taunt at the time of the *churban*.

Then Rav Nechunya ben HaKanah offers the most sweeping reading. He parses the verse differently by placing the division at a different point: *tzedakah teromem goy ve-chesed le-Yisrael — ule'umim chatat*. Both *tzedakah* and *chesed* accrue to Israel, and the nations have only sin. He manages to bring the word *chesed* from the verse into the column of Israel's merits — not merely acknowledging that Israel gives *tzedakah*, but that Israel also performs *chesed*, an added distinction that the other readings did not emphasize.

### RYZ's Teaching

Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai then declares that Rav Nechunya's words appear better than his own and those of his students — *nirin divrei Rav Nechunya ben HaKanah mi-divrai u-mi-divreichem* — precisely because Rav Nechunya manages to bring *chesed* into the domain of Israel as well. But then the *Gemara* observes: *michlal de-hu nami amar* — his praise of Rav Nechunya implies that he himself had his own reading. What was it? A *baraita* preserves it: *keshem she-ha-chatat mechaperet al Yisrael, kach tzedakah mechaperet al umot ha'olam* — just as the *korban chatat* atones for Israel, so *tzedakah* atones for the nations of the world. This is the one genuinely positive reading in the entire collection — *tzedakah* is itself a form of atonement for non-Jews, analogous to the sacrificial system available to Israel.

This creates a striking paradox. Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's own teaching is the most generous toward non-Jewish *tzedakah*, yet he declares Rav Nechunya's position — perhaps the most restrictive — to be the best. The question of why he would embrace the most negative formulation when his own view is the most positive remains genuinely difficult. One possibility is that his attitude evolved over time, particularly given his famous negotiations with Rome in the wake of the *churban*, which might have shaped a more accommodating posture at an earlier stage and a harsher one later.

---

## Donations & Shalom

### Ifra Hormiz Story

The *Gemara* immediately moves from the theoretical to the practical. Ifra Hormiz, the mother of King Shavor, had appeared earlier in the tractate when she sent money for use in a great *mitzvah* and the discussion turned to *pidyon shvuyim*. Now she sends four hundred *dinarei* directly to Rabbi Ami. The context is pointed: we have just concluded a lengthy discussion about how non-Jewish *tzedakah* is performed for self-interested purposes and constitutes a form of sin. What happens, then, when a non-Jewish benefactress sends money directly to a Jewish communal leader? Do you take it?

Rabbi Ami refused to accept it. Rava, by contrast, accepted it — *mishum shalom malchut*, for the sake of maintaining good relations with the government.

### Ami's Objection

When Rabbi Ami heard that Rava had accepted the money, he was upset. He cited the verse *yavesh k'tzirah tishavarna nashim ba'ot me'irot ota* — when they wither, they shall be broken, and women will come to set them alight — understood through Rabbeinu Gershom as a reference to the non-Jewish nations' eventual downfall when they lose their *zechut*. The concern is precisely that accepting their *tzedakah* grants them *zechut*, spiritual credit, which strengthens them and delays their reckoning.

### Rava's Solution

The *Gemara* then harmonizes the positions. Rava, too, accepted the money with the intent to distribute it to non-Jewish poor — *l'aniyei ovdei kochavim yavinhu*. And why did Rabbi Ami get upset? Because when they informed him that Rava had accepted the money, they did not complete the account by telling him that Rava had directed it to the non-Jewish poor. *Hu d'lo siyemu kamei.*

The logic is striking. By routing the funds to non-Jewish poor rather than to Jewish poor, Rava denies Ifra Hormiz the particular *zechut* of having supported the Jewish community, while still maintaining the *shalom malchut* justification for not having refused outright. The implicit cost of this solution is that Jewish poor do not benefit — a tension the *Gemara* acknowledges but seems to resolve entirely through the *shalom malchut* framework rather than through the humanitarian considerations one might have expected to carry greater weight.

### Rashi Analysis

Rashi raises a pointed question: is this not a problem of *gneivat da'at*? Ifra Hormiz presumably understood her donation to be destined for the Jewish poor. By redirecting it to non-Jewish poor, are we not misrepresenting ourselves to her?

Rashi answers by appealing to established practice. Since it is well-known — as the *Gemara* in *Gittin* states — that Jews customarily support the non-Jewish poor alongside the Jewish poor *mipnei darchei shalom*, there is no misrepresentation. Ifra Hormiz gave the money into the discretion of the Jewish communal leadership, and that discretion is understood to include care for non-Jewish poor as part of standard practice. There is therefore no *gneivat da'at*. Rashi implies, however, that if she had explicitly designated the funds for Jewish poor, the situation would be different: either the money must be refused or the *shalom malchut* concern alone would need to override the designation.

---

## Benjamin & Munbaz

### Benjamin Story

A *baraita* is introduced: Benjamin HaTzaddik, who served as the administrator of the *kuppah shel tzedakah*, the communal charity fund, once had a woman come to him during a famine. She said: *Rebbi, parneseini* — sustain me. He replied with an oath that the fund was empty, all funds having been distributed during the crisis. She answered: if you do not support me, a woman and her seven children face death. He rose and supported her from his own personal resources.

Later, Benjamin HaTzaddik fell gravely ill. The ministering angels then presented the following argument before the Holy One, Blessed be He: You have said that whoever sustains one soul of Israel is as though he sustained an entire world — and Benjamin HaTzaddik sustained a woman and her seven children. Could such a person die so young? Immediately his decree was torn up, and twenty-two years were added to his life.

### Life-Saving Merit

The *baraita* underscores the principle articulated in the angels' petition: *kol ha-mekayeim nefesh achat mi-Yisrael ke-ilu kiyem olam malei*. The act of sustaining even one soul carries cosmological weight. Benjamin HaTzaddik did not merely give charity — he gave from his own pocket when the communal fund had nothing left, and he did so for a woman with seven dependents. The heavenly response was proportionate to the extraordinary nature of the deed.

### Munbaz Teaching

The *Gemara* continues with the story of Munbaz the King. During years of famine, he distributed his own treasuries and those of his ancestors to the poor — *she-bizbez otzrotav ve-otzrot avotav bishnei batzoret*. His brothers and his father's house confronted him: your ancestors added to the family fortune generation after generation, and you are squandering everything they accumulated. Whether Munbaz was a gentile king who converted or, as Rashi suggests, a son of Queen Helena and thus connected to the *Chashmonaim*, his family's complaint carries a different valence depending on his background — if he was a convert, then his biological family is chastising him precisely because he has embraced values that his conversion has instilled in him, which gives the story a particularly poignant dimension.

Munbaz responds with a series of parallel formulations, each structured as: my ancestors stored up *X*, while I have stored up *Y*.

### Metaphors & Rewards

His first response: *avotai ganezu le-mata, va-ani ganazti le-ma'ala* — my ancestors gathered for below, I have gathered for above, as the verse states *emet me-eretz titzmach ve-tzedek mi-shamayim nishkaf*, truth grows from the ground and righteousness looks down from heaven. His second: *avotai ganezu be-makom she-ha-yad sholetet bo, va-ani ganazti be-makom she-ein ha-yad sholetet bo* — they stored in a place vulnerable to seizure or theft; I stored in a place beyond the reach of any hand, as the verse states *tzedek u-mishpat mechon kisecha*, righteousness is the foundation of God's throne, safely beyond earthly reach.

His third formulation: *avotai ganezu davar she-eino oseh peirot, va-ani ganazti davar she-oseh peirot* — my ancestors stored capital without yield; I invested in something that produces fruit, as the verse states *imru tzaddik ki tov ki pri ma'alaleihem yocheilu*. This draws on the well-known principle that *adam ochel peirotehem ba-olam ha-zeh ve-ha-keren kayemet lo le-olam ha-ba* — one enjoys the fruits of such acts in this world while the principal remains intact for *olam haba*.

### Paradox Explained

The fourth formulation captures the deepest paradox: *avotai ganezu otzrot mamon, va-ani ganazti otzrot nefashot* — they stored up monetary treasure; I stored up souls, as the verse states *pri tzaddik etz chayim ve-lokeiach nefashot chacham*.

The fifth and final formulation is the most rhetorically elegant. One would have expected Munbaz's family to argue that he is giving away what is theirs and keeping nothing for himself, while he is the one who is truly wasting the inheritance. He turns it entirely around: *avotai ganezu la-acherim va-ani ganazti li-atzmiy* — my ancestors stored up for others, while I have stored up for myself. They accumulated wealth that they inevitably left behind; he found the only mechanism by which treasure can truly accompany a person, by distributing it in the form of *tzedakah*. As the verse states, *ule-cha tihiyeh tzedakah* — your *tzedakah* will remain yours. And finally: *avotai ganezu le-olam ha-zeh, va-ani ganazti le-olam ha-ba*, as the verse states *ve-halach lefanecha tzidkecha kevod Hashem ya'asfecha*. This concludes the entire major *sugya* of *tzedakah*.

---

## Land Division

### Residency & Purchase

The *Gemara* returns to the last line of the *Mishnah*, which had been the launchpad for the entire *tzedakah* digression. The context is the question of when a person acquires the standing of a town resident for purposes of communal obligations, including contributions to *tzedakah* funds. The *Mishnah* had established the general rule of twelve months, but noted that if one purchases a *beit dirah* — a dwelling — in the town, that residence is conferred immediately.

### Shimon's View

The *Gemara* notes that the *Mishnah* does not follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds in the *baraita* that even purchasing any piece of land (*karka kol shehu*) in the town suffices. A second *baraita* presents a slightly different formulation of his position — it must be land fit for building a residence (*karka hara'uyah le-beit dirah*), not just any land. Even a plot designated for agricultural use at a distance from the settlement might not qualify if it could not plausibly serve as the site of a home. The *Gemara* resolves the two versions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement as a dispute between two *tannaim* who each report his position differently.

### Chatzer Division

A new *Mishnah* begins, returning to the core topic of forced partition of shared property. *Ein cholkin et ha-chatzer ad sheyehei arba amot lazeh ve-arba amot lazeh* — a shared courtyard cannot be divided against one party's will unless each person would receive a minimum of four *amot*. Four *amot* is approximately six feet — a small but functionally meaningful space in front of one's door. The *Mishnah* then addresses fields: *ein cholkin et ha-sadeh ad sheyehei bah tisha kavin lazeh ve-tisha kavin lazeh* — a field for growing grain cannot be divided unless each portion amounts to nine *kavin*, a measure of area reflecting the yield of seed required to make the parcel agriculturally viable.

### Measurements

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, holding that the minimum for a field is nine half-*kavin* per person rather than nine full *kavin*. The *Mishnah* then turns to gardens: *ve-lo et ha-gina ad sheyehei bah chatzi kav lazeh ve-chatzi kav lazeh* — a vegetable garden requires only half a *kav* per person, since intensive vegetable cultivation yields significant value from a much smaller area. Rabbi Akiva reduces the minimum further to a *beit rova*, a quarter-*kav*. A *kav* is a measure of volume, but when applied to land it corresponds to the area that would be sown with that volume of seed, so each measure translates into a meaningful acreage threshold.

### Indivisibles

The *Mishnah* then lists categories of property that cannot be divided even if the mathematical minimum might be satisfied: a *traklin* and a *moran*, which Rashi identifies as two types of large or stately homes; a *shovach* or dovecote; a *tallis* in the sense of a large cloak; a *merchatz* or bathhouse; a *beit ha-bad* or olive press; and a *beit ha-shlachin*, an irrigated field. For these categories, the standard is not a fixed quantitative threshold but rather *kidei lazeh u-kidei lazeh* — enough that each portion remains a meaningful unit of whatever the original thing was.

### Divisibility Test

The *Mishnah* then articulates the governing principle: *zeh ha-klal, kol she-yeichalek u-shemo alav cholkin* — the rule is that forced partition is permissible only when each resulting portion retains the name of the original. If two brothers share a mansion and dividing it would leave each with a room rather than a smaller mansion, the division cannot be forced. One can always voluntarily divide with mutual consent, *aval bizman she-sheneihem rotzim afilu pachos mikan yachaloku*, but a forced partition requires that the divided portions remain recognizable as instances of the same category of thing.

The sole exception is *kitvei ha-kodesh* — sacred scrolls. Even with the consent of both parties, Torah scrolls or other scriptural scrolls may not be divided. The reasoning is not expressed in terms of the divisibility principle but rather the inherent sanctity of the object. One might be tempted to say: I want the first half of *Yeshayahu* for learning, and you take the second half. But the *bizayon* to sacred texts overrides any such arrangement, even when both parties agree.

---

## Four Amot

### Rav Assi

The *Gemara* now addresses a textual difficulty. Rav Assi, citing Rabbi Yochanan, states: *arba amot she-amru, chutz shel pesachim* — the four *amot* referenced in the *Mishnah* are measured exclusive of the space directly in front of the doorways. This means that before any calculation of how to divide the remaining courtyard, each resident first receives a dedicated four *amot* strip opposite his door, and only then is the remaining space assessed to see whether each party can receive an additional four *amot* to justify forced partition.

A *baraita* appears to support this reading by stating that no division may occur unless there are eight *amot* for this one and eight *amot* for that one — a figure twice the *Mishnah's* four. The *Gemara* resolves: this is not a contradiction. The *baraita* counts the four *amot* in front of the doorway plus the four *amot* of courtyard space, yielding eight total per person, while the *Mishnah* references only the four *amot* of courtyard space after the door space has already been allocated. *Shema mina ke-derav Assi, shema mina.*

### Rav Huna

Rav Huna offers a different approach to the question of courtyard division: *chatzer mitchaleket lefi ptacheiha* — a courtyard is divided according to its doorways. If one resident has a house with two doors opening onto the courtyard and another has only one, the first receives twice the share. This has the striking implication that one could substantially improve one's claim to courtyard space simply by adding additional doorways to one's house.

### Rav Chisda

Rav Chisda offers what appears to be a middle position and the most intuitively fair resolution: *notin arba amot le-chol petach u-fetach, ve-ha-sha'ar cholkin be-shava* — each doorway receives its designated four *amot*, and whatever courtyard space remains after all doorways have been allocated is divided equally between the residents. A *baraita* supports Rav Chisda's position explicitly. If one resident has a single door and another has two, the first receives four *amot* opposite his door and the second receives eight *amot* opposite his two doors, and the remainder is divided equally.

The *baraita* introduces a further case: if a doorway is eight *amot* wide, the resident receives eight *amot* in length opposite the door and four *amot* in the courtyard — and Abaye clarifies that this means eight *amot* in the length of the courtyard by four *amot* in the width. In other words, the width of one's allocation in the courtyard corresponds to the width of the doorway itself, with four *amot* as the minimum depth into the courtyard. A doorway that is eight *amot* wide would be exceptionally large — well over twelve feet — and the passage assumes this is an unusual case establishing the principle's outer limit.

Ameimar introduces another application: if there is a *pira de-sufli* — Rashi identifies this as a pit for storing date seeds — in the courtyard, it receives four *amot* of access space on each of its four sides. However, this rule applies only if there is no dedicated door opening directly into it (*delo meyached lei pitzcha*). If there is a door facing it, then only four *amot* directly in front of that door are allocated, because the door provides immediate and sufficient access.

### Special Structures

Rava, citing Rav Huna, states: *achsadra ein la arba amot* — an *achsadra*, a portico or colonnaded structure, does not receive four *amot* in front of it. Tosafot holds that an *achsadra* has three walls; Rashi reads it as having no enclosed walls at all, more like a pavilion. The *Gemara* then brings Rav Sheshet's challenge from a *baraita* stating that the gateways of both houses and *achsadraot* do receive four *amot*. The *Gemara* resolves this by distinguishing the *achsadra de-vei Rav* — an enclosed or semi-enclosed study space — from the *achsadra Rumita*, a Roman-style portico with low partial walls, which is the case Rava was discussing.

A *baraita* is then cited: *beit shaar, achsadra, u-mirpeset yesh lahen arba amot* — a gatehouse, a portico, and an upper landing all receive four *amot*. The *mirpeset* here is the shared external walkway of a multi-unit upper story, like the exterior corridor of a multi-family building, with stairs descending into the courtyard. If five separate homes open onto a shared *mirpeset*, they collectively receive only four *amot* at the point where the stairway descends — not four *amot* per home.

### Rationale

The *Gemara* then makes explicit what has been implicit throughout: *ta'ama mai mishum perik mas'o* — the entire reason for the four *amot* is to allow a person to unload his burden. When you arrive at your door carrying goods on a donkey or with heavy loads, you need a clear space to set down the load, steady the animal, retrieve your key, and enter. That is the functional justification for the minimum clearance.

This explains why an *achsadra* with open access does not require four *amot* — *ha'cha efshar de-ayeil ligavai u-mfarek*, you can simply walk in and unload inside. The same logic governs the question of a house half-covered and half-uncovered: Rav Nachman rules that neither configuration requires four *amot* in front. If the unroofed portion faces outward, you can walk through without difficulty since there is no height clearance issue. If the roofed portion faces outward, you can still pass through and unload in the inner uncovered section. Similarly, the chicken coop gets no four *amot* because chickens hop in and out on their own — they do not need a loading area.

---

## Multi-Unit Dwellings

### Hostels Division

Rav Huna asks Rabbi Ami: when quartering troops in shared accommodation — *achsanya* — and the courtyard space or its resources need to be allocated, does distribution follow the doorways or the number of people? Rabbi Ami answers: *lefi benei adam*, by the number of people. This contrasts with the rule for *zevel* — fertilizer or dung — that accumulates in a shared courtyard from the various households.

### Roofed Spaces

The *baraita* confirms: *zevel she-be-chatzer mitchaleket lefi ptachim* — dung in a courtyard is divided according to doorways, while *achsanya lefi benei adam* — quartered troops are allocated according to the number of individuals. As Tosafot explains, the question underlying the *achsanya* case is precisely whether courtyard resources are apportioned by the number of doorways (on the theory that each door represents one household unit) or by the number of people present (on the theory that consumption and impact scale with population). The *baraita* distinguishes the two cases: *zevel* naturally accumulates from households as units, so doorways are the relevant measure, while the burden of quartering soldiers falls on persons, not on architectural features.

---

## Mavoy Access

### New Doors

Rav Huna asks Rabbi Ami: if one of the residents of a *mavoy* wishes to redirect his doorway to open onto a different *mavoy* — *lehachzir pitcho lemavoy acher* — can the current residents of the *mavoy* prevent him? Rabbi Ami answers: *benei mavoy me'akveina lei*, yes, they can block him.

The next question in the *Gemara* concerns a sealed door — *hayah satum u-bikeish lefotcho*, a door that had previously been open onto the *mavoy* and was then sealed, and now the resident wishes to reopen it. Rabbi holds that in this case *ein benei mavoy me'akveina alav* — the residents of the *mavoy* cannot prevent him from reopening a door he once had. Since his right of access was established when the door originally existed, sealing it did not permanently forfeit that right. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, however, disagrees.

---

## Multi-Unit Dwellings (II)

### Dung Heaps

The *baraita* is revisited in light of the distinction between the *zevel* and *achsanya* cases. *Zevel she-be-chatzer mitchaleket lefi ptachim* — dung in a shared courtyard is apportioned by doorways, because it arises from household waste, the accumulation of animal dung and refuse that each household contributes through its door. *Achsanya lefi benei adam* — quartered troops are apportioned by persons, because what matters there is how many individuals are consuming resources and generating demands on the space. The juxtaposition in the *baraita* clarifies the underlying rationale: the criterion for division in each case follows the nature of what is being divided and what most meaningfully represents each party's claim.

---

## Mavoy Access (II)

### Graduated Rights

The *Gemara* turns to the arrangement of multiple courtyards opening into a single *mavoy*. A *baraita* establishes graduated usage rights: if there are five courtyards opening into a *mavoy*, all of them may use the space in front of the outermost courtyard, since everyone must pass through it to reach the *reshut ha-rabim*. The outermost courtyard, however, may only use its own space — it has no need to traverse any other part of the *mavoy*. Working inward, each courtyard can use the space of all courtyards between it and the exit, but the space directly opposite each courtyard belongs, in the first instance, to that courtyard's residents.

### Innermost Rights

The innermost courtyard has the fullest rights of all — *nim-tzeit ha-pnimit mishtemshet le-atzmah u-mishtemshet im kol achat ve-achat* — because it must traverse the entire length of the *mavoy* to exit, and therefore has a valid claim to the space of every courtyard it must pass through. This has an implication for the sealing question: since the innermost resident has rights to the entire alleyway length, there is a question whether the outermost resident can simply appropriate the far end of the *mavoy* for his own exclusive use.

### Sealed Doors

The *Gemara* frames the question of the sealed door as a *tannaic* dispute. Rabbi holds that a door that was once open and subsequently sealed can be reopened, and the other *mavoy* residents cannot prevent it. Since the right existed originally, sealing the door was a voluntary act that did not forfeit that underlying entitlement. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar disagrees.

### Zoning Issues

The final point in the *sugya* is a *Tosefta* cited by Tosafot: if a person has a store opening onto the *reshut ha-rabim* and wishes to open a rear entrance into a shared courtyard — *l'chatzer ha-shutafin* — the partners in that courtyard can prevent him, *mipnei she-marbe aleihem et ha-derech*. Tosafot understands *et ha-derech* as a reference to increased foot traffic: opening a commercial establishment into the shared courtyard will draw customers and generate substantially more pedestrian activity than the residents bargained for when they entered the shared arrangement. This is a genuine zoning concern — the right to peaceful enjoyment of a shared space includes the right not to have it converted into a commercial thoroughfare without consent.

---

---

# Bava Batra 12

## Courtyard Division & Mav…

### Courtyard Division

The daf begins by picking up from the bottom of 11b, continuing the discussion of how a *chatzer* is divided. The principle established there was division *lefi ptacheha* — according to the doors — meaning that while the overall division follows the number of inhabitants, each doorway nonetheless receives a designated space in front of it. This framework governs how the shared space of a *chatzer* is apportioned among its residents.

### Shift to Mavoy

A *baraita* then enters the discussion and shifts the focus from the *chatzer* itself to the *mavoy* — the private alley into which the courtyards open. The previous amud addressed questions about courtyards that open into a *mavoy*, including whether a back courtyard can assert rights to its own space within it — a claim the *baraita* generally rejected. The present discussion continues with other provisions of that same *baraita*.

## Sealed Door Rights

### Sealed Door Opening

The *baraita* states: *im haya satum uvikesh liftocho, ain bnei mavoy me'akvin alav* — if a back door into the *mavoy* had been sealed and the owner wishes to reopen it, the residents of the *mavoy* cannot prevent him from doing so.

### Paratz Ptzimav

Rava qualifies this ruling: *lo shanu ela shelo paratz ptzimav* — this applies only where the owner has not destroyed the doorframe. The distinction is critical. If one seals a door by filling the opening with wood or other material, the doorframe remains intact, and the essential structure of a functional door is preserved. But if one destroys the frame itself — filling the opening with bricks and dismantling the frame entirely — one has effectively renounced any right to use that space as a door, and in such a case the *bnei mavoy* may indeed prevent the owner from reopening it.

### Four Amot Rule

Abaye offers a *baraita* in support of Rava's distinction: *bayit satum, yesh lo arba amot; paratz ptzimav, ein lo arba amot* — a sealed house retains its four *amot* in the courtyard apportionment, but a house whose doorframe has been destroyed does not. This *chidush* is striking. It is not merely that one retains the right to reopen a sealed door; it goes further and treats even the currently sealed door as a functionally active one, entitling the space before it to its full four *amot* in a division. This makes the principle even more far-reaching than the original ruling about reopening.

### Dead Body Tumah

The *baraita* continues with a parallel application in the realm of *tumah*: *bayit satum, eino metamei kol svivav* — a sealed house containing a dead body does not render everything around it impure. Although the door is closed (and even sealed), since the doorframe has not been destroyed, the house is not treated as a *kever* — a coffin — that would spread *tumah* to its sides and surroundings. The halakhic reasoning is that one assumes a door will be opened and the body removed; accordingly, the house is not viewed as a hermetically sealed coffin.

Rashi and Tosafot engage both relevant principles here — the laws of *kever*, which render the sides and even the surrounding four *amot* impure, and *sof tumah latzet*, the principle concerning the ultimate egress of *tumah*. The practical ruling, however, depends on the same distinction: *paratz ptzimav, metamei kol svivav* — once the doorframe is destroyed, the house acquires the status of a coffin and renders everything around it impure.

## Mevoot Hamefulashos

### Inter-City Alleys

Rabbah bar bar Chana says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: if *mevoot hamefulashot* — alleys open at both ends and connecting to another town — and the residents of the town seek to seal them off, *bnei osah ha'ir me'akvin aleihem* — the residents of that other town can prevent them from doing so.

### Mefulash Definition

To understand this ruling, it is worth clarifying the distinction between a *mavoi satum* and a *mavoi mefulash*. A *mavoi satum* is a dead-end private alley; a *mavoi mefulash* is one open at both ends and functioning almost like a *reshut harabim*, though not precisely so. A typical configuration might be: the *reshut harabim* runs along the main thoroughfare; branching off it are *mevo'ot satumim* (dead-end alleys) into which individual *chatzeirot* open. A *mavoi mefulash*, by contrast, cuts through from one *reshut harabim* to another, or in this case from one town to the next.

The case under discussion involves a *mavoi* that begins in one locality and provides access to another town. The residents of the first locality wish to reassert their rights over this street and seal it off. The *baraita* rules that the residents of the other town can block this. Even if, as the Gemara goes on to say, those residents have an alternative route — *afilu ki ika darcha achrina nami me'akev* — they can still object. The reason is the ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *metzar she'hecheziku vo rabim asur l'kalkelo* — a path over which the public has established use may not be destroyed.

Tosafot clarifies an important limitation: *hainu k'she'hecheziku birshut* — this applies only where the public's use was originally permitted. If the owner had objected from the outset and the public was using the path without permission, the owner retains the full right to exclude them, and the Gemara in Bava Kama confirms this: one may take up a hoe and physically block unauthorized entry. But where the owner initially permitted use and the public established its presence through that permitted access, that right cannot subsequently be revoked.

### Established Access Rights

The contrast with the ordinary law of *chazaka* is worth noting. In the standard case of *chazaka*, one who has been using another's property must produce a claim of purchase — mere use without objection is insufficient to establish a right. Here, with *rabim*, the rule is different. The public does not need to claim that it purchased rights; the very fact of established, permitted use suffices. This is a distinctive type of *chazkat shimush*, one that confers rights simply through the pattern of use.

This principle is striking in its breadth. As the Gemara later underscores, the right of the *rabim* is not limited to use of the alley as a thoroughfare. It extends to any pattern of use the public has established — including simply being present in the space.

### Doors in Public Alleys

Rav Anana says in the name of Shmuel: *mevo'ot ha'mefulashim l'reshut ha'rabim* — alleys that open at both ends onto a *reshut harabim* — if the *bnei mevo'ot* wish to install doors across the entrance to their alley, the *bnei reshut ha'rabim* can prevent them. Here the concern is not that the alley serves as a shortcut — apparently it does not — but rather that the *reshut harabim* has in practice spilled over into the mouth of the alley, and the installation of doors would cut off that use.

One might have thought that the objection was grounded in Rabbi Zeira's ruling in the name of Rav Nachman: *arba amot ha'semuchot la'reshut harabim ke'reshut harabim damyan* — the four *amot* adjacent to the *reshut harabim* are treated as part of the *reshut harabim* itself, functioning as a kind of sidewalk or buffer zone. On that theory, the *nafka mina* would be precise: doors set inward beyond four *amot* would be permitted. But the Gemara rejects this: that four-*amot* principle applies in the context of *tumah* law; here the concern is practical. Since the *reshut harabim* is at times crowded, people spill over into the alley, and that pattern of spillover — however far it extends — is itself the established use that cannot be blocked.

### Four Amot Spillover

The practical upshot is that the question of where doors may be installed depends on the actual extent of the public's established use. If the *rabim* have never practically entered beyond a certain distance inside the alley, a door installed at that point would presumably be permitted. The four-*amot* figure is not the operative boundary here; what matters is the demonstrated pattern of use.

## Forced Land Division

### Nine Kavin Standard

The Gemara now turns to *din chaluka* — the forced division of property — and establishes the governing minimum: one cannot compel a co-owner to divide a field unless each party will receive at least *tisha kavim* (nine *kav*) of land. A *kav* works out to somewhere between 100 and 150 square meters, making nine *kavin* roughly 900 square meters, or the dimensions of a football field — not a vast tract, but meaningful as a threshold of agricultural viability.

The Gemara adds: *v'lo peligi, mar ki atra u'mar ki atra* — the authorities are not in dispute; each speaks according to local conditions. In fertile soil, a smaller plot is genuinely viable; in poor soil, one requires more land to sustain meaningful agricultural activity. The minimum, in other words, is relative to what a plot of that size can realistically produce in its particular context.

### One Day's Plowing

In Babylonia, Rav Yosef translates this standard as *bei radya yoma* — the amount of land one can plow in a day. A full day's plowing establishes the threshold of viability. The practical significance of this measure is tied to the ability to hire workers: a parcel that only provides a fraction of a day's work cannot attract paid laborers, and without that capacity it cannot be farmed in a sustainable way.

### Plowing Seasons

The Gemara probes what exactly constitutes "one day's plowing," since the speed of plowing varies considerably by season. Early plowing, before seeding, is done on harder, unworked ground and takes longer; plowing at seeding time, when the ground has been previously worked and softened, goes faster. The Gemara explores two resolutions. One: take the measure as one day's worth of plowing during plowing season, and during seeding season simply plow twice — the double plowing is agronomically beneficial for the seeds and will constitute a full day's labor. The other: take the measure as one day's worth of plowing at seeding time, and on particularly rocky terrain (*bahadurei*), which offers extra resistance, that same area will in fact require two days during plowing season.

The Gemara acknowledges these as theoretical constructs (*heichi timtzei*). The underlying principle is clear regardless of the precise mechanics: the parcel must be large enough to be genuinely worth cultivating — worth investing labor and hiring workers for. If the specifics of the terrain or the season make it unviable to engage workers for a full day's work, the plot fails the minimum threshold and *din chaluka* cannot be applied.

### Water Division

The Gemara addresses the case of a *davla* — a shared irrigation source, whether a well, a cistern, or a canal — that the partners wish to divide. How one physically divides a shared water source is not entirely clear, and even Rashi's description — whether the reference is to a well or to a shared canal — leaves the mechanics somewhat opaque. It may refer to dividing the resource not physically but temporally: assigning each party exclusive use on alternating days.

Rav Nachman rules: *kedei diluyo yoma* — there must be enough water on each party's "share" to sustain a full day's worth of drawing and irrigation. Rashi explains this in terms of hiring labor: if after the division each party's access to water suffices to keep workers productively occupied for a full day, the division is viable. But if the split would leave one party with only a half-day's worth of water, that portion is too small to sustain a hired workforce, and the division cannot be compelled.

### Orchard Division

Abaye reports in the name of Shmuel: the minimum viable unit for an orchard (*pardisa*) is three *kavin* — not nine. A *baraita* supports this in the context of a sale: if one says to a friend, "I am selling you a *menat b'karem* — a portion of my vineyard," without specifying the size, Sumchus rules that the portion cannot be less than three *kavin*, since that is the minimum that constitutes a meaningful agricultural unit of this type.

Rabbi Yosi responds sharply: *ein elu ela divrei nevi'os* — these are nothing but words of prophecy. As Tosafot clarifies, this is emphatically not a compliment. *Lo l'shavach ka'amar* — he is not praising Sumchus. Rather, he means: *kelomar she-omer belo ta'am* — you are saying something without textual basis or logical argument. The enterprise of *Torah she-ba'al peh* proceeds through text, proof, and reasoned argument, not intuition or arbitrary assertion. To say something without evidence is to speak as though from divine inspiration — and that is no methodology for halakha.

It is worth noting the distinction. When the minimum is applied in the context of *din chaluka* — forced division — it is an assessment of objective viability based on facts about the land, the community, and agricultural practice. That is legitimate halakhic reasoning. But when a document simply says "a portion of my vineyard" and one interprets that to mean the *din chaluka* minimum, that interpretive move — importing the forced-division standard into a contractual context — is what Rabbi Yosi dismisses as *divrei nevi'os*. There are other contextual factors in a sale, including price paid and surrounding circumstances, that make it far from obvious that the bare minimum for forced division is what the parties intended.

In Babylonia, Rava bar Kasna offers the local standard for an orchard: three units of *atzi'ata*, each consisting of twelve vines — thirty-six vines in total.

### Prophecy to Sages

The mention of *divrei nevi'os* occasions a significant digression. But before turning to it, the Gemara provides an additional gloss for context: the minimum viable area for the *pardisa* division in Babylonian terms is also connected to *bei yoma* — the amount of land one person can weed in a day. This is consistent with the general principle that the minimum must correspond to a genuinely productive unit of labor.

On this foundation, Rav Avdimi of Haifa introduces a sweeping statement: *miyom shecharav Beit HaMikdash, nitlah nevuah min ha'nevi'im ve'nitnah la'chachamim* — from the day the *Beit HaMikdash* was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the *nevi'im* and given to the *chachamim*. One might read this as describing a paradigm shift — that the channel through which Israel accesses divine guidance moved from the prophetic institution to the activity of *Torah she-ba'al peh*, to the *chachamim* and their interpretive engagement with text. That is one reading. But the Gemara proceeds to take the statement more literally.

## Chacham vs. Navi

### Chacham Prophecy

Ameimar immediately challenges: *atu chacham lav navi hu?* — what do you mean? Does this imply that *chachamim* did not previously possess *nevuah*? Did they not always have it? He resolves the tension: *af al pi shenitlah min ha'nevi'im, min ha'chachamim lo nitlah* — even though it was taken from the *nevi'im*, it was never taken from the *chachamim*. They always had it, and they still have it. The statement of Rav Avdimi is thus reread as an affirmation of continuity rather than change: the prophetic institution lost its role, but the *chachamim* — who always possessed *nevuah* — carried on without interruption.

This is a remarkable interpretive reversal. A statement that seemed to describe rupture is recast as describing something more like permanence.

### Chacham Superior

Ameimar then adds a further claim: *chacham adif minavi* — a *chacham* is superior to a *navi*. His proof text: *ve'navi levav chochmah* — "and a prophet has a heart of wisdom." If the prophet is described as having wisdom, *mi nitlah bemi* — who is described in terms of whom? *Hevei omer katan nitlah ba'gadol* — the lesser is attached to the greater. Since the prophet is characterized by wisdom, wisdom is the more fundamental quality.

This pulls back toward discontinuity — or at least differentiation. The *chacham* and the *navi* represent distinct modes of religious engagement, and the *chacham*'s mode is superior. This resonates deeply with the Gemara's understanding of how halakha operates: even if Eliyahu HaNavi were to arrive and pronounce a ruling, we would not accept it on the basis of prophetic authority. Halakha proceeds through text and reasoned argument — *Torah she-ba'al peh* — not through prophetic pronouncement. In the domain of *psak*, the *chacham* not only replaces the *navi* but surpasses him, because the method of active human engagement with the divine text is both the proper channel and the superior one.

This also makes *ein elu ela divrei nevi'os* more pointed. Invoking prophecy in a halakhic discussion is not an appeal to a higher authority; it is an abdication of the enterprise. The *navi* may be a conduit for divine will, but the *chacham* — through the rigorous activity of *Torah she-ba'al peh* — is where halakha actually lives.

### Parallel Discoveries

Abaye brings evidence that *chachamim* still possess real *nevuah*: *de-amar gavra rabba milta u-mitamra mi-shmei de-gavra rabba achrina kavateih* — a great scholar articulates an original insight, and it subsequently emerges that another great scholar, independently and at a distance, said the same thing. The phenomenon of two scholars in different places arriving simultaneously at the same original idea, with no contact or shared influence, suggests a form of divine inspiration — something beyond coincidence.

The parallel with the simultaneous independent discovery of calculus by Newton and Leibniz, in entirely different notational systems and without any evident communication, is a striking modern analogue. Historians remain puzzled by it. Abaye would see in it confirmation of his point.

### Mazal Theory

Rava objects: *dilma tarvaihu bnei chad mazla ninhu* — perhaps they are both governed by the same astrological influence, and their shared intellectual output reflects shared *mazal* rather than shared divine inspiration. This, notably, is a naturalistic explanation for what appeared to be a supernatural phenomenon. The concurrence of insight does not require *nevuah*; it can be explained by the mechanics of *mazal* acting on scholars of similar temperament and circumstance.

### Tradition Discovery

Rava therefore proposes a sharper case: a great scholar articulates an insight and it turns out to have been stated *mi-shmei de-Rabbi Akiva bar Yosef* — in the name of Rabbi Akiva, centuries earlier. Here the *mazal* argument cannot apply: no one would suggest that a contemporary scholar shares his astrological configuration with Rabbi Akiva. If independent discovery across that temporal distance is possible, it must reflect some form of genuine divine inspiration.

### Luck vs. Prophecy

Rav Ashi objects even to this: *dilma le-ha milta bar mazlei hu* — perhaps regarding this specific matter, the scholar happens to share a *mazal* with Rabbi Akiva, even if not generally. The *mazal* theory proves difficult to dislodge. Rav Ashi therefore proposes a still stronger case: a scholar articulates an insight and it emerges that it corresponds to a *Halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — a tradition from Moshe at Sinai that was not derivable from any text and that no one would claim could be reached by shared *mazal* with Moshe Rabbeinu. Here, the argument concludes, there must be genuine divine inspiration at work.

The Gemara counters: *dilma ke-suma be-arubba* — perhaps this is like a blind man groping in the darkness. Even a stopped clock is right twice a day. One can arrive at a correct conclusion through sheer luck, without prophecy. To this, the Gemara responds: *v'lav ta'am yahiv?* — but the scholar provides a reasoned explanation for his conclusion! If it were mere luck, a coherent argument could not accompany it.

And yet this very response creates a new tension: if the scholar has a reasoned argument, then why invoke *nevuah* at all? Perhaps the argument itself, rather than divine inspiration, accounts for the correct result. The Gemara leaves suspended the interplay among *nevuah*, *mazal*, and rational argumentation as competing explanations for insight — without resolving which is primary.

### Fools & Children Prophecy

Rabbi Yochanan offers a counterpoint to the entire thesis that *nevuah* now belongs to the *chachamim*: *mi-yom she-charav Beit HaMikdash, nitlah nevuah min ha-nevi'im ve-nitnah le-shotim u-le-tinokot* — from the day the *Beit HaMikdash* was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the *nevi'im* and given to the mentally ill and to children. Rather than the *chachamim*, it is precisely those at the margins of rational society — those unconditioned by systematic thought — who now receive flashes of prophetic insight. The *chacham*, on this reading, operates through a wholly different faculty: rigorous, rational engagement, not prophetic inspiration.

## Prophecy Examples

### Mad Prophecy

The Gemara asks: what is an example of *nevuah* among the *shotim*? The case of Mar bar Rav Ashi. He was standing in the *ristaka* — the marketplace or main boulevard — of Mechuza, when he overheard a certain *shoteh* say: the *reish metivta* — the head of the academy — who will reign in Mata Mechasya signs his name Tivyomei.

Mar bar Rav Ashi took note: among the rabbis, who signs his name Tivyomei? *Ana* — that would be me. *Shema mina le-didi kai le-sha'ata* — if that is what this person is saying, it must be that now is my moment.
