### Self-Fulfilling Rise

Mar bar Rav Ashi rose and set out for the yeshiva. In the meantime, the rabbis had already voted and selected Rav Akha mi-Difti as the next *rosh yeshiva*. But when word reached them that Mar bar Rav Ashi was on his way, they sent two rabbis to consult him about the succession. He detained them. They sent another pair; he detained them too. This continued until ten rabbis had been sent and remained with him. Once there were ten rabbis present, *patach hu ve-tana ve-darash* — he opened and taught and expounded. Since a *kalla* — a formal rabbinic discourse — may not be opened with fewer than ten people, and since only a *rosh yeshiva* opens such a discourse, Mar bar Rav Ashi had effectively installed himself in the position. By the time the situation was clear, the matter was settled.

The interplay between prophecy and human agency here is rich. The *shoteh*'s words were the catalyst: without them, Mar bar Rav Ashi would not have set out for Mechuza, and without his arrival, the rabbis would never have consulted him. Yet what followed was entirely the product of deliberate, strategic choices. The *nevuah* functioned as an inspiration that set events in motion, but the outcome was shaped by the choices of the people involved. This is a form of self-fulfilling prophecy — one hears a prophetic word, acts on it as such, and in so doing brings it about.

### Rav Akha's Lament

Rav Akha mi-Difti, now displaced from the position that had been voted for him, said about himself: *kol de-mari'in lo, lo bimheira metivin lo; ve-khol de-metivin lo, lo bimheira mari'in lo* — one who suffers misfortune will not quickly recover from it, and one who has good fortune will not quickly lose it. For Rav Akha, this meant: this opportunity has slipped away, and there is no reason to expect it to return soon.

Tosafot records a poignant detail. In another source, Rav Akha himself uses stronger language: *le-olam ein metivin lo* — never, not merely not quickly. Tosafot resolves the discrepancy in the most human of ways: *mitechila amar lo bimheira metivin lo she-haya metzapeh she-yachaziru lo gedulato* — initially, Rav Akha still hoped that his prominence might be restored, perhaps after some years. He therefore said: it will not come back quickly. *U'keshera'ah shelo hecheziru, shuv amar l'olam ein metivin lo* — but when years passed and his position was not restored, he gave up hope entirely and said: it will never return. That is very sad.

One might also ask how much of this was truly *divrei nevuah* and how much was Mar bar Rav Ashi's own doing. The *shoteh*'s words were the spark; but Mar bar Rav Ashi was very much an active participant in making the prophecy come true. The *nevuah* opened a door; he walked through it with great deliberateness.

### Child Prophecy

For the *tinokot*, the Gemara cites the daughter of Rav Chisda. She was sitting on her father's lap when both Rava and Rami bar Chama were seated before Rav Chisda learning. Rav Chisda turned to his young daughter and asked: which of these two would you like to marry? She answered: *tarvaihu* — both of them. Rava said: *v'ani batra* — I will be the second. Why would he want to be second? Because the first husband would die. And so it came to pass: she first married Rami bar Chama; after his death, she married Rava.

Here again, the story raises questions about the line between prophecy and the social circumstances that shape outcomes. Rav Chisda's daughter voiced a wish; Rava heard it and oriented his expectations accordingly. The *nevuah* — if it is to be called that — lay somewhere in the young girl's spontaneous expression, which she could not have consciously intended as a prediction.

## Hunger & Wine

### Two Hearts

Rav Dimi of Haifa — having already been cited in connection with prophecy and the sages — is now quoted on an entirely different matter, though it is his name that occasions the transition. *Kodem she-yochal adam ve-yishteh, yesh lo shtei levavot* — before a person eats and drinks, he has two hearts. That is, a hungry person cannot focus: part of his mind is perpetually drawn toward his hunger, leaving him distracted. *Ve-achar she-ochal ve-shoteh, ein lo ela lev echad* — after eating and drinking, he has but one heart, capable of full concentration. The proof text: *ish navov yilavev* — a hollow person will have two hearts, with *navov* parsed as empty, hollow, and *yilavev* read as a doubled *lev*, two hearts. The word *navov* is connected to *nivuv luchot* — the hollow of the tablets — through the Targum's rendering *chalil luchin*, reinforcing the association between hollowness and the doubled heart.

### Wine Opens Heart

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua adds: *ha-ragil be-yayin, afilu libbo atum ke-vetulah, yayin mefakcho* — one who is accustomed to wine: even if his heart is sealed up like a virgin, wine will open it. The proof text: *ve-tirosh yenovev betulot* — new wine will hollow out (or open up) virgins, with *yenovev* again echoing the *navov/nivuv* root, carrying the sense of opening, unlocking, making receptive.

## Bechor Division Rights

### Bechor Adjacent Portions

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua rules: *peshita, chelek bechor ve-chelek pashut yavinan leh achad metzra* — it is obvious that when dividing an ancestral estate, we give the *bechor* his double portion on one shared boundary. The *bechor* receives two portions in the inheritance — his standard portion as a son and the additional portion that is his right as firstborn — and he is entitled to have both portions adjacent to each other, forming one continuous tract of land rather than two separate plots.

### Yavam Status

The question then arises: what of a *yavam* — a man who performs *yibum* with his deceased brother's widow and thereby acquires his brother's share of the inheritance? He now holds two portions: his own original share in the estate and his brother's share that came to him through *yibum*. Can he demand that these two portions be given to him adjacent to each other, as a *bechor* would receive his two portions together?

Abaye rules: *hi hi* — it is the same case. The *yavam* is entitled to the same adjacency right as the *bechor*. His reasoning: the Torah itself calls the child of *yibum* a *bechor* — *ve-hayah ha-bechor asher teled yakum al shem achiv ha-met* — and from this the Gemara derives that the *yavam* who performs *yibum* is himself treated as a *bechor*. Just as the *bechor* receives his extra portion adjacent to his base portion, so too the *yavam* receives his brother's portion adjacent to his own.

Rava disagrees: *amar kra ve-hayah ha-bechor — havayah ke-bechor ve-ein chalukato ke-bechor* — the verse establishes that the *yavam* has the *identity* of a *bechor*, but does not extend to giving him the property-division rights of a *bechor*. The *yavam* is like a *bechor* in name; the entitlement to adjacent portions does not follow.

## Middat Sdom

### Adjacent Plot Request

A further case: a man purchased a plot of land on the boundary of land belonging to his father-in-law's house (*bei nasha* — the household of the women, referring either to his wife's family or specifically to the family estate that will pass through the daughters). When the daughters come to divide the estate, the son-in-law — who stands to inherit his wife's portion — asks that his wife's share be allocated adjacent to the land he himself owns, so that his holdings form one continuous parcel.

### Sdom Accommodation

Rava rules: *kigon zeh, kofin al middat Sdom* — in a case like this, one compels accommodation under the principle of *middat Sdom*. *Middat Sdom* is the posture of *sheli sheli ve-shelcha shelcha* — what is mine is mine and what is yours is yours — an unwillingness to do anything for another even at no cost to oneself. *Kofin al middat Sdom* means that where the accommodation costs the other party nothing — where the plots are of equal value and any arrangement is equivalent — the party who would benefit can compel the other to comply. Since all portions are equivalent, there is no loss to the co-heirs in allocating the wife's portion adjacent to the son-in-law's land, and they cannot simply refuse out of indifference.

### Premium for Service

Rav Yosef objects: the co-heirs — the sisters or other siblings — can say to the son-in-law: *maalinen leh illuya ke-nichsei de-bar Maryon* — we will raise the price on you as if it were the property of Bar Maryon, a byword for enormous wealth. That is, we will charge you a premium for the accommodation. By demanding an adjacent plot, you are effectively asking us to forgo the opportunity to extract payment from you for that convenience. We are not obligated to simply provide it gratis. The fact that it does not cost us anything in terms of the land's value does not mean we have no right to charge for the preference.

The Gemara rules: *hilchasa ke-Rav Yosef* — the halakha follows Rav Yosef. The discussion of how this principle applies in further cases — including scenarios involving two parcels on two boundaries — is left to the following daf.

---

---

# Bava Batra 13

## Bar Metzra & Inheritance

### Two Brothers, Adjacent P…

The daf opens seven lines from the bottom of 12b, at the passage beginning *trai arasa*. The context is a case of two brothers dividing an inherited estate, and the question is whether one brother may demand a preferred plot — specifically, one adjacent to land he already owns outside the estate. Under ordinary commercial law, this right is known as *dina d'bar metzra*, the law of the adjoining plot. Its basis is the principle of *v'asita hayashar v'hatov* — that one must act rightly and justly — combined with the logic of *zeh neheneh v'zeh lo chaser*: when the seller loses nothing by preferring the neighbor, and the neighbor gains considerably more than a random purchaser would, the neighbor holds something close to a right of first refusal.

### Raba's Position

The Gemara reports that *Raba* initially thought this principle would apply even within the context of dividing an inheritance, such that one brother could insist on receiving the plot adjacent to his outside holdings.

### Rav Yosef's Objection

*Rav Yosef* rejected this. His argument, in brief, is that within an inheritance division, the other parties have a legitimate basis to resist: for us, this is worth real money.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

*Rashi* understands Rav Yosef's reasoning as a factual claim — the brothers can argue that the particular plot being sought may well prove to be richer or more productive land, and therefore they are not prepared to simply yield it. *Tosafot* frames the objection differently, and arguably more sharply. In Tosafot's reading, the issue is not really a claim about the land's potential quality, but rather a matter of the claiming brother's audacity in demanding a specific parcel. In a sale, the question is simply to whom the seller directs the transaction; but in a division, to demand a particular portion is to exercise a choice — and the others may say: if you want that choice, compensate us for it. The right to select which side one receives is not a costless entitlement in an inheritance division the way it might be in a sale context.

### Ruling: Rav Yosef

The Gemara rules *v'hilchata k'Rav Yosef* — the *halacha* follows Rav Yosef, and *dina d'bar metzra* does not apply to compel a particular allocation within an inheritance division.

---

## Two Plots, Two Canals

### The Setup

The Gemara now turns to a new case: *trai arasa a-trai nagri* — two plots of land adjacent to two irrigation canals. Imagine a northern plot and a southern plot, with one irrigation canal running along the northern edge of the northern plot and another along the southern edge of the southern plot. Two brothers inherit both plots together. How are they to divide them?

### Raba's Proposal

*Raba* proposes that the division should run north-south — each brother receiving one complete plot, each with its own adjacent canal. His reasoning invokes the principle of *kofin al midat Sedom*: one cannot refuse a division that costs nothing and benefits the other party. If one brother prefers a north-south split, giving each person one unbroken parcel, the other cannot insist on an east-west split simply for the sake of obstruction. Raba's implicit premise is that having one complete, continuous plot is more convenient than two half-plots side by side, and that a north-south division accomplishes that cleanly.

### Rav Yosef's Challenge

*Rav Yosef* challenged this — *maskif lah Rav Yosef*. His argument is practical: *zimnin hai midvi v'hai lo midvi* — sometimes one canal will dry up and the other will not. If you divide the property north-south and assign each brother one plot with one canal, you have eliminated each person's ability to manage risk. A brother whose sole canal runs dry has no recourse. By contrast, if the division runs east-west, each brother holds a strip that includes access to both canals — if one fails, the other remains available. This is a legitimate claim, not mere obstruction, and therefore it overrides Raba's preference for the north-south division.

### Ruling on Division

Importantly, Tosafot notes that Rav Yosef's objection here is structurally different from the *bar metzra* case above. There, the brother was insisting on a specific parcel — choosing north over south — and the others could say: you want to choose, pay for that privilege. Here, neither brother is claiming a preferred side. The argument is purely about the method of division, and the point is that an east-west split offers a genuine risk-management benefit. The other party cannot invoke *kofin al midat Sedom* against a legitimately different interest. The Gemara rules *v'hilchata k'Rav Yosef* — and accordingly, a north-south division cannot be forced when the east-west division provides dual canal access to each party.

---

## Two Plots, One Canal

### Standard Division

The Gemara now takes up *tarti achad nahara* — two plots sharing a single irrigation canal. Here, *Rav Yosef* himself agrees that the standard solution is straightforward: you divide down the center, running along the irrigation canal, so that each brother receives half of the canal. This is *kofin al midat Sedom* in its clearest form — there is no compelling argument against a clean split. Even Rav Yosef raises no objection to this.

A brief clarification on Rashi's understanding of the earlier cases: Rashi actually does say that the cases in the prior segment also involved a neighboring field — one brother had a parcel already abutting the estate on a particular side, and wanted the division to run in a way that would connect his existing field to the adjacent portion of the inheritance. This reading makes the *bar metzra* issue more central to those cases than it might initially appear.

### Abaye's Objection

*Abaye* challenges even this standard arrangement. The Gemara phrases his objection as follows: *matzi amar ba'ina de'afushei arisai* — he says, I want to increase the number of sharecroppers working near my field. Rashi explains the scenario as one where one brother's outside plot borders the estate on one side, and that brother wants the estate divided so that his portion is placed between two separate parcels of the other brother. His reasoning: if the other brother holds parcels on both sides of his field, there will be more sharecroppers working in the vicinity, which provides greater security and activity around his own land. The cost to the other brother — holding two non-contiguous half-parcels instead of one continuous plot — is real. Yet Abaye raises this as a potentially legitimate counter-claim to the standard division.

### Sharecropper Claim Rejec…

The Gemara rejects this. *Afushei arisai lav milsa hi* — seeking more sharecroppers at another party's expense is not a valid legal claim. You cannot demand that the other person's land be fragmented in a way that inconveniences them simply because it incidentally benefits you.

### Comparison & Distinction

This rejection stands in notable contrast to Rav Yosef's accepted argument in the two-canal case. The distinction is this: when a brother insists on an east-west division in the two-canal case, he is not seeking a particular side and is not imposing a cost on the other party for his own incidental gain — he is making a genuine argument about risk management, showing that the proposed division is not symmetrically advantageous. In the sharecropper case, however, the argument reduces to: *I* benefit if *you* are inconvenienced. That is precisely what *kofin al midat Sedom* bars. Tosafot's reading of the single-canal case, it should be noted, differs somewhat from Rashi's. Tosafot sees the case as one where the canal runs through the middle of both plots, and one brother argues for a left-right division — each person taking one full side — while the other prefers a top-bottom division that splits the canal. Tosafot's point is that the preference for a continuous plot along one side of the canal is itself the legitimate basis for the division, and the sharecropper counter-argument cannot overcome it.

---

## Canal & River Division

### Rashi's Approach

The Gemara introduces a final case: *chad gisa nagra v'chad gisa nahara* — one side of the property borders an irrigation canal and the other side borders a river, each offering distinct agricultural benefits. The ruling is *palginan lei bekarna zo* — divide it by the corner, diagonally.

Rashi's treatment of this case is complex. He envisions a situation where the canal and river run perpendicular to one another — one along the eastern edge, the other along the northern edge. In such a configuration, no simple north-south or east-west cut gives each party equal access to both water sources. The result, in Rashi's reading, is an elaborate diagonal division involving multiple triangular sections — something that, while geometrically equitable in terms of access, would be practically very difficult to cultivate given the odd shapes it produces.

### Tosafot's Approach

Tosafot offers a considerably simpler reading. In Tosafot's case, the river and canal are located at opposite corners of the property, and a single diagonal cut gives each brother one triangular half that includes access to one of the water sources. This is a far more workable physical arrangement.

### Complete Unit Requirement

Regardless of which reading one follows, the Gemara establishes a foundational requirement as it transitions to the top of 13a: *b'lo atropklin* — one cannot divide a property like a castle unless each party receives a portion that retains its own independent identity and utility, *shemo alav* — a name upon it, a recognizable complete unit. This requirement governs all of the division cases in the *mishna*: division is only compellable when each party's resulting share constitutes a full, functional thing in its own right.

---

## Gud o Agud Principle

### The Core Question

Having established when division is required, the Gemara now asks the critical follow-up: *ein bahen k'dei l'zeh u'k'dei l'zeh* — what if the inheritance simply cannot be divided into two portions each large enough to qualify as a complete unit? *Mahu* — what is the *halacha*? One party wants to dissolve the partnership; the other is content to remain in it.

### Rav Yehuda's View

*Rav Yehuda* rules: *is dina d'gud o agud* — there is a principle of *gud o agud*. Either you buy me out, or I will buy you out. The claiming party names the objective price and gives the other a genuine choice: pay me that price for my half, or accept that price for your half.

### Rav Nachman's View

*Rav Nachman* disagrees: *leis dina d'gud o agud* — there is no such rule. You cannot force a partner out of a partnership.

### Justification

The logic behind Rav Nachman's position is worth dwelling on. A poor partner may lack the funds to buy the other out. Even if he could scrape together the purchase price, doing so might impoverish him to the point where he can no longer sustain the use of the full property that he has now been forced to acquire. His livelihood may depend precisely on managing a half-share — not a whole one. Moreover, forcing him to surrender his half-ownership in exchange for money does not give him a livelihood; the money is not a substitute for the ongoing revenue stream his partnership interest provides. Rav Yehuda's position is that no one should be compelled to remain in an unwanted partnership. These two considerations are the poles of the dispute.

### Tosafot on Price

Tosafot is careful to note that the entire discussion of *gud o agud* assumes the price is set objectively, at fair market value. One cannot invoke *gud o agud* by naming an inflated price — saying "you buy me out for a million, or I'll buy you out for a million" when the property is worth a fraction of that. That would simply be exploiting the other party's inability to meet an unrealistic number. The *gud o agud* offer is only valid when the price genuinely reflects objective valuation.

---

## Bechor & Pashut Case

### The Problem Setup

*Rava* pressed *Rav Nachman* with a sharp challenge. He invoked the case of a *bechor u-pashut* — a firstborn son who receives a double share, and a non-firstborn son who receives a single share. Suppose their father left them a slave or a non-kosher animal — items that cannot be divided the way a field can be, and cannot be *shechted* and shared the way a kosher animal can. *Keitzad osin* — how are they supposed to divide this? Rava further notes that the case is framed specifically as *bechor u-pashut* rather than simply two equal brothers, because equal brothers could simply alternate days of use. With a two-to-one ownership ratio, alternating days is not a workable solution. Something must give. And if selling and splitting the proceeds is suggested — that too is itself a form of *gud o agud*, dissolving the joint ownership for money. If one brother refuses to sell and insists on retaining his share in kind, is there truly no way out?

### Proof of Gud o Agud

The force of the challenge is this: the situation seems genuinely untenable without some exit mechanism. There must, Rava argues, be a *halacha* of *gud o agud* — otherwise the law provides no resolution to a deadlock over a non-divisible inheritance.

### Rav Nachman's Response

Rav Nachman holds his ground: *shani omer oved le-ze yom echad u-le-ze shnei yamim* — he says the slave works for one brother one day and for the other brother two days, maintaining the two-to-one ratio. Inconvenient as this is, it is not legally untenable, and therefore it does not compel the conclusion that *gud o agud* must exist. Tosafot adds a further layer: the brother who receives two consecutive days of service actually extracts more than double the value of a single day, since continuous labor is more productive than interrupted labor. This makes the arrangement even more lopsided than it first appears — yet Rav Nachman maintains it is the answer, because you cannot force a partner out of their inheritance interest.

---

## Half-Slave Case

### Partnership Problem

The Gemara now cites the classic *mishna* from *Gittin* regarding *mi she-chatzyo eved ve-chatzi ben chorin* — a person who is half-slave and half-free. This situation arises when an *eved Kna'ani* is jointly owned by two partners and one of them frees his half without the other doing the same. The result is a human being who is simultaneously half free and half enslaved, jointly "owned" by his former master (who holds the unfree half) and by himself (who holds the free half). They are, in effect, partners in him.

### Beis Hillel's Solution

*Beis Hillel* offers the initial resolution: *oved et rabbo yom echad ve-et atzmo yom echad* — he works one day for his master and one day for himself, keeping whatever he earns on his free day.

### Beis Shammai's Objection

*Beis Shammai* objects: *tikkantem et rabbo ve-et atzmo lo tikkantem* — you have arranged matters well for the master, who now receives productive labor, but you have not helped the slave's situation at all, at least not in any deeper sense.

### Marriage Impossibility

The crux of Beis Shammai's objection is this: *lissa shifcha eino yachol, lissa bas chorin eino yachol* — he cannot marry a *shifcha Kna'anis*, because the free half of him prohibits it; and he cannot marry a Jewish woman, because the slave half of him prohibits that. He is caught in a legal no-man's-land with respect to marriage.

### Creation Purpose

One might think: let him simply remain unmarried. The Gemara rejects this with force — *lo nivra ha-olam ela le-pirya ve-rivya*, the world was not created for desolation but to be inhabited and populated. To leave this man permanently unable to marry is to deny him the very purpose for which he was created, something no arrangement among humans may impose.

### Forced Manumission

The solution: *kofin et rabbo ve-oseh oto ben chorin ve-chotev shtar al chatzi damav* — we compel the master to free him fully, and the slave writes a document acknowledging that he owes the master half his value. He becomes entirely free, with a monetary debt to his former master.

### Beis Hillel Reverts

*Ve-chazru Beis Hillel le-horot k'divrei Beis Shammai* — Beis Hillel reversed its position and ruled in accordance with Beis Shammai.

---

## Why Gud o Agud Fails Here

### Initial Challenge

The Gemara now uses this *mishna* to probe the scope of *gud o agud*. The question is: why was the elaborate *pirya ve-rivya* reasoning necessary? If *gud o agud* applies, why not simply say — the slave can invoke *gud o agud*, either the master frees him and receives payment, or the slave sells his free half back and becomes fully enslaved again?

### Asymmetric Options

The Gemara answers: *shani hacha d'agud ika, gud leka* — in this case, *agud* exists but *gud* does not.

### Halakhic Impossibility

The *agud* — the slave offering to buy out the master's share, effectively purchasing his own freedom — is legally available. That is, in the end, precisely what the forced manumission accomplishes. But *gud* — the slave offering to sell his free half back to the master, so the master could say "fine, I'll buy you out" and re-enslave the free portion — is halakhically impossible. A Jew cannot be sold as an *eved Kna'ani*. He can only be sold as an *eved Ivri*, which is an entirely different institution. So the *gud* option — "you buy my free half" — is not genuinely available. Because the choice is asymmetric, the standard *gud o agud* mechanism does not apply, and a separate basis — the inability to fulfill *pirya ve-rivya* — was necessary to compel resolution.

### Tosafot Digression

Tosafot takes the opportunity to examine why the Gemara invokes the creation-purpose argument — *lo nivra ha-olam ela le-pirya ve-rivya* — rather than simply citing the positive commandment of *p'ru u'rvu*. Tosafot offers two answers. First, one might have argued that since the man is *ones* — legally compelled by his circumstances — he bears no liability for failing to fulfill the commandment. But the creation-purpose argument transcends the framework of obligation and liability: regardless of whether he is technically exempt as an *ones*, to bar him from fulfilling the very reason for which the world was created is an intolerable wrong in a deeper sense. Second, there is a genuine question whether the commandment of *p'ru u'rvu* applies to him at all. Women are generally exempt from *p'ru u'rvu*, and slaves have the halakhic obligation level of women — so it is debatable whether a male slave is obligated in *p'ru u'rvu*. The Gemara therefore chose an argument that does not depend on resolving that question.

---

## Rich & Poor Brother

### Commercial Use

The Gemara now presents the case of *shnei achim echad ani v'echad ashir* — two brothers, one poor and one rich, whose father left them a bathhouse or an olive press. If these facilities are operated commercially — rented out to the public or run as a business — the solution is straightforward: *hasachar l'emtza*, they share the revenue equally.

### Private Use Problem

The difficulty arises when the facilities are private — not open to the public, not a revenue-generating enterprise. In that case, the rich brother can say to the poor one: *kach l'cha avadim v'yirchatzu ba-merchatz* — take your servants and use the bathhouse. Or: *kach l'cha zeitim u'vo v'aseh b'veit habad* — go get your olives and press them. Come whenever you like. The implication is obvious: the poor brother has no slaves to bring to the bathhouse and no olives to press. The rich brother's offer is formally equal but practically inaccessible to the poor brother.

### Rich Brother's Rights

Nevertheless, the rich brother is, from the Gemara's perspective, not in the wrong. He is making a genuine offer of equal access, structured on the terms by which such facilities are normally used. That the poor brother cannot take advantage of the offer is the poor brother's limitation, not the rich brother's fault.

### Gud Without Agud

The question then becomes: can the poor brother invoke *gud o agud* and demand that the rich brother buy him out? The Gemara answers: *hatam nami gud ika, agud leka* — there also, *gud* exists but *agud* does not.

### Why Agud Fails

The *gud* — the poor brother saying "buy me out" — is in principle available: *he* can make that offer, because a buyer with resources *could* theoretically comply. But *agud* — "or I'll buy you out" — is hollow. The poor brother cannot genuinely offer to purchase the rich brother's half. He lacks the means. And a *gud o agud* offer is only legitimate when both options are genuinely on the table. If the person making the offer can only actually follow through on one of the two alternatives, the choice it purports to extend is illusory. The Gemara implicitly notes an interesting nuance: in a case where the *claiming party* can genuinely present both options but the *recipient* can realistically only pursue one — as seems to be the situation when a solvent party invokes *gud o agud* against a poorer one — the Gemara appears to accept that the offer is valid, since the one extending the choice is legitimately prepared to go in either direction. It is only when the person making the offer cannot genuinely follow through on one of the two alternatives that *gud o agud* fails.

---

## Tannaim Debate

### Accept Less to Exit?

The Gemara now cites a *tanna'ic* dispute that bears directly on the question of how a partner may exit a partnership over a non-divisible item.

### Tanna Kamma's View

Suppose a property is too small to be divided into two fully usable shares — say, six *amot* where four *amot* each would be needed. One party says: *tol ata shiur va'ani pachat* — you take the full four, I'll take two. I simply want out. *Shomin lo* — the *tanna kamma* rules that we accept this. A voluntary acceptance of less is a valid exit mechanism.

### Rabban Shimon's View

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* says *ein shomin lo* — we do not accept this.

### Missing Text Theory

The Gemara asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case, and what is the basis for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's objection? If the property is six *amot* and one brother freely offers to take two while giving the other four, why would Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel object? The Gemara first attempts to resolve this by positing *chasuri mechasra* — that the *braisa* is missing text. On this reading, the *braisa* should be understood as first stating the *tanna kamma's* two positions: both (a) accepting less land is valid, and (b) *gud o agud* is also valid. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then comes to reject specifically *gud o agud*, while the *tanna kamma* permits it. This would make the dispute a debate about *gud o agud* itself, and the *braisa* would constitute a *tanna'ic* proof that the principle is disputed.

### Complete Text Theory

The Gemara then rejects the *chasuri mechasra* approach and reads the *braisa* as complete. *Lo le'olam ki de'katani* — the text is exactly as it stands.

### Poor Person's Refusal

On this reading, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's objection must be understood differently. The brother taking two is, in effect, giving the other brother one extra *amma* as a gift. The recipient can object: *ei bidmei leit li dmei limitan lach* — if you expect me to pay you the difference, I don't have the money. And if the one taking less responds "no, no payment, I give it to you as a gift" — the recipient can still refuse: *lo nicha li*, I do not want it. *Dechtiv sone matanot yichyeh* — as the verse says, one who hates gifts shall live. A person has the right to refuse a gift and decline the attendant sense of obligation. The result is that the *braisa* as written is internally coherent, and the dispute between *tanna kamma* and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is specifically about the validity of an unequal-land exit without payment — not about *gud o agud* at all. The Gemara has thus not derived a *tanna'ic* proof on that question from this *braisa*, though the earlier *braisa* — *malu oto bedamim* — does seem to support *gud o agud* as a concept, and the Gemara treats the dispute as one among *tanna'im*.

---

## Kisvei Kodesh Scroll (II)

### Shmuel's Teaching

*Abaye* connects the *gud o agud* discussion to a teaching of *Shmuel* via the voice of *Rav Yehuda*. Our *mishna* states: *kisvei hakodesh af al pi she-shneihem rotzim lo yachloku* — when it comes to Torah scrolls, even if both parties agree to divide, they may not divide a single scroll, because cutting it would be disrespectful to the sacred text. *Shmuel* explains: *lo shanu ela be-kerach echad aval bi-shnei kerachim cholkin* — this prohibition applies only to a single scroll; if there are two separate scrolls, they may divide them.

### Abaye's Proof

Abaye uses this to demonstrate that *gud o agud* must be a valid principle. The case of two scrolls is not assumed to be two identical scrolls — say, two copies of *Megillas Esther* — where a clean equal split is obvious. The interesting case is where one scroll is *Megillas Esther* and the other is *Megillas Rus*, one more valuable than the other given its greater length. For Shmuel's ruling to be meaningful, the division of two unequal scrolls must be achievable — meaning one party takes the more valuable scroll and pays the other the difference, or vice versa. That is precisely the structure of *gud o agud*: you take the Esther and pay me, or I take the Esther and pay you. If *gud o agud* did not exist, one partner could simply refuse any unequal split and block division altogether, making Shmuel's ruling empty in all but the most trivial cases.

The Gemara responds, however, that Shmuel's ruling is limited to cases where *both parties agree* — *targema k'she-shneihem rotzim*. Shmuel is not authorizing a forced division; he is simply clarifying that when both parties *wish* to divide two separate scrolls, they may do so — and there is nothing halakhically wrong with that arrangement, unlike cutting a single scroll. This means the proof for *gud o agud* from Shmuel's teaching collapses: Shmuel speaks only of consensual division, not forced dissolution of a partnership over an item where the parties disagree.

---

## Ameymar vs. Rav Ashi

### Ameymar's Ruling

The Gemara reports that *Ameymar* issued a definitive ruling: *hilchata is dina d'gud o agud* — the *halacha* is that we do accept the principle of *gud o agud*.

### Rav Ashi's Challenge

*Rav Ashi* immediately challenged him: but what about Rav Nachman, who ruled that *leis dina d'gud o agud*?

### Ameymar's Response

*Ameymar* replied: *lo shamia leh* — I have not heard that ruling. The Gemara clarifies that this is to be understood as *lo sevira leh* — he heard it, but does not hold by it. Ameymar's position is that the *braisa* supporting *gud o agud* is the more compelling authority, and Rav Nachman's view is not accepted as the operative *halacha*.

---

## Two Maidservants Case

### The Setup

The Gemara then raises what appears to be a counterexample. *Rabba bar Chinana* and *Rav Dimi bar Chinana* — brothers sharing the same father's name — were left two maidservants by their father. One maidservant knew how to cook, bake, and prepare food; the other knew how to spin and weave. They came before *Rava* to resolve the dispute over how to divide them.

### Rava's Ruling

Rava ruled: *leit dina d'gud o agud* — there is no *halacha* of *gud o agud* here. One brother cannot tell the other: I'll take the cook and pay you the difference, or you take the cook and pay me.

### Why Difference Matters

This seems to contradict Ameymar's ruling. The Gemara resolves the tension: *shani hasam, de-mar mibayei leh travaihu u-mar mibayei leh travaihu* — the case is different there, because each brother can claim he wants both servants. The cooking-baking servant and the spinning-weaving servant represent complementary skills, and a household genuinely benefits from having both. Each brother can credibly argue that his own share consists not of one servant but of a half-interest in both.

### Whole vs. Partial Split

This reveals an important structural limit on *gud o agud*. The principle functions where the question is who takes the whole and who is bought out — you take everything and pay me, or I take everything and pay you. What *gud o agud* cannot do is force a split of two different items and compel one party to accept a half-split and pay a differential. When each party legitimately wants both things — as each brother could claim with respect to both maidservants — forcing one brother to take only the cooking servant and compensate the other, or vice versa, exceeds what *gud o agud* authorizes. It is like a plot of land that cannot be divided: you can invoke *gud o agud* to force a buy-out of the whole, but you cannot use it to force a cut-and-pay resolution when one party insists the thing is not divisible in that way.

---

## Kisvei Kodesh Scroll (II)

### The Scroll Question

Returning to the scroll case, the Gemara asks whether *gud o agud* could in principle allow one person to take both scrolls — demanding that the other party either take both and pay him, or accept payment and give up both.

### Clarification

The Gemara answers that Shmuel's ruling — *bi-shnei kerachim cholkin* — means only that when both parties agree, they may divide two scrolls between them. Shmuel is not authorizing any forced acquisition. There is no application of *gud o agud* to compel one person to surrender both scrolls and receive a buyout, or to compel a split and differential payment. The *gud o agud* discussion as applied to the scroll case is thus closed: the ruling by mutual consent stands, forced dissolution via *gud o agud* does not apply to this case.

---

## Tanakh Attachment

### Rabbi Meir's View

The Gemara now presents a *braisa* on the separate question of whether one may physically attach all of תנ"ך in one combined scroll. *Rabbi Meir* — himself a *sofer* by trade — permits it: *madbik adam Torah Nevi'im u-Kesuvim ke-echad* — one may affix Torah, Prophets, and Writings together in a single scroll.

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

*Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees: *Torah bifnei atzmah, Nevi'im bifnei atzman, u-Kesuvim bifnei atzman* — Torah must stand alone, Prophets alone, and Writings alone. And even within Nevi'im and Kesuvim, each individual book should have its own separate scroll; *Trei Asar* counts as a single book, but the others must be kept distinct. Each text must retain its own identity.

### Tosafot's Logic

Tosafot notes that one might have thought Rabbi Yehuda's concern was related to the prohibition of placing a scroll of *Nevi'im* on top of a *Sefer Torah* — a mark of disrespect, since the more sacred text should not be beneath the less sacred. Tosafot rejects this as the reasoning here, noting that the prohibition against placement applies only when the scrolls are distinct; when the parchment is physically joined, the issue is different. Instead, Tosafot identifies the operative concern as one of confusion of textual identity: *she-lo yeira hakol k'Torah o hakol k'Nevi'im* — one must not allow the entire combined scroll to be mistaken for a single category of text. If someone sees the scroll opened to *Yechezkel* but knows it also contains *Bereishit*, they might conclude that the Torah passages are merely prophetic literature — downgrading the authority of Torah. Or conversely, seeing *Bereishit* in it, a reader might assume the entirety is Torah and therefore treat later passages from Nevi'im or Kesuvim as if they carried Sinaitic authority. The integrity of each text's distinct status is the concern.

### Section Spacing

The Gemara then specifies the technical spacing requirements when sections are combined. *Bein chomesh le-chomesh shel Torah* — between one book of the Torah and the next — there must be four blank lines, *arba'ah shitin*. This is indeed the practice in our *Sifrei Torah* today. *Ve-chein bein kol navi le-navi* — similarly, between one prophet and the next, if they appear in a combined scroll. *U-ve-navi shel shenaim asar, gimel shitin* — within *Trei Asar*, where a new prophet begins within the same book, only three blank lines are required, since it is a different author but the same *sefer*.

---

## Practical Requirements

### Top Blank Space

The Gemara cites a *braisa* that lays out the physical requirements for constructing a combined scroll of all of תנ"ך. At the top — before *Bereishit* — there must be enough blank *klaf* that the opening can be fully rolled onto the upper pole, the *Etz Chaim*, so that *Bereishit* itself is visible when the scroll is unrolled. This is called *kedei lagol amud* — sufficient to roll over the pole.

### Bottom Blank Space

At the bottom — after the final book — there must be enough blank *klaf* to wrap around the entire circumference of the scroll when it is fully rolled. The Gemara assumes here that the combined scroll is mounted on a single pole rather than two; a *Sefer Torah* is normally wound on two poles, but the combined Tanakh scroll in this discussion uses one. The requirement is *kedei lagol hekeif* — sufficient to cover the full circumference — so that the outermost surface of the rolled scroll consists of blank *klaf* rather than written text, protecting the contents and maintaining proper respect.

### Braita Procedures

These two requirements — the leading blank space and the trailing blank space — frame the *braisa's* account of how such a scroll is to be constructed.

### Column Separation

*U-mesayem milamata u-mas-chil milamala* — one must conclude each book at the bottom of a column and begin the next book at the top of the following column. This requirement of column-level separation between books within the combined scroll is the focus of some discussion. Tosafot understands this requirement as ensuring a clean visual and physical boundary between each book, such that the transition from one to the next is clearly delineated. Rashi suggests an alternative reading — that when a new book begins at the top of a column and the previous one ended at the bottom, the four-line spacing between them is not required. This would imply that the column break itself substitutes for the blank-line separation. However, this does not reflect current practice, where four blank lines are maintained in a *Sefer Torah* regardless of column position, and Tosafot disagrees with Rashi's reading on this point.

### Divisibility Purpose

*Ve-im ba lachtoch, choteich* — and if one wishes to cut the scroll and divide the books, one may do so. The Gemara asks what this adds — after all, it is universally agreed that separate scrolls are permissible. The answer, as Tosafot explains, is that this is precisely the reason for the column-separation requirement stated just before. The rule that each book must end at the bottom of one column and begin at the top of the next is *not* merely aesthetic. It is a functional provision ensuring that if and when the combined scroll needs to be divided — each book separated into its own scroll — it can be done cleanly, with each portion constituting a proper, complete scroll. The practical requirements for the combined scroll are thus designed with its potential future division in mind.

---

---

# Bava Batra 14

## Half-Slave & Pru U'rvu

### Gudo o Agud

Before turning to the new material on *daf* 14, it is worth briefly revisiting several *Tosafot* on 13a that bear directly on yesterday's discussion of *gudo o agud* — the question of whether a court may compel forced division of jointly held property. In that context, the *Gemara* introduced the classic debate of *Beit Hillel u'Beit Shammai* concerning a slave who is half free and half still enslaved, and whether his master may be compelled to free him entirely on account of the *mitzvah* of *pru u'rvu*.

### Slave & Pru U'rvu

The first *Tosafot*, beginning with the words *reish shifcha yachol*, raises a pointed difficulty. *Tosafot* notes — drawing on a *be'aya* in Yevamos — that all opinions agree a slave cannot fulfill *pru u'rvu*, since the children of a slave are legally not considered his children at all; they follow the mother's status. If so, the question sharpens: what precisely is the basis for compelling the master to free him in the name of *pru u'rvu*? Even if one were to argue that the free half of the person retains some capacity to fulfill *pru u'rvu*, *Tosafot* rejects this: were the person a full slave, *pru u'rvu* would not apply to him at all — *kevan she'avad meyuchas achareiha*, since the child's lineage follows the mother. There is thus no obvious mechanism by which *pru u'rvu* drives the obligation to free him.

### Lashevet Yetzarah

*Tosafot* resolves this by invoking the verse *lo tohu bera'ah, lashevet yetzarah* — God did not create the world for chaos, but for habitation. The *Ri* (*Rabbeinu Yitzchak*) rules that we do not compel the master to free the slave merely for the sake of *pru u'rvu* in its technical sense. Yet *mishum d'lashevet yetzarah shayach afilu b'tzad avdus* — the principle of *lashevet yetzarah* applies even on the side of his enslavement, because he is still bringing children into the world. This raises a genuine conceptual question: is *lashevet yetzarah* simply an explication of the weight and scope of *pru u'rvu*, or does it constitute an independent obligation beyond the formal parameters of *pru u'rvu*? *Tosafot* appears to embrace the latter: technically, this person is not fulfilling *pru u'rvu* in the legal sense, yet he is still bringing offspring into the world, which satisfies the thrust of *lashevet yetzarah*. A subsequent *Tosafot* — citing the *Rivam* — similarly holds that *lashevet yetzarah* applies even in his condition of partial servitude, and concludes that it is precisely the weighty, world-purpose-oriented character of *lashevet yetzarah* that gave *Chazal* the impetus to institute the *takkana* compelling the master to free him — not a bare claim of *pru u'rvu* alone.

### Forcing Master to Free

A further *Tosafot* raises a different question: *amay kofin* — why do we need any *takkana* at all? The *mitzvat assei* of *pru u'rvu* should simply override the *lo ta'asseh* of *lo yihiyeh kadesh*. The reason a half-slave cannot marry a freed woman is that doing so would violate *lo yihiyeh kadesh* — a prohibition that normally concerns male prostitution but is applied here to a slave marrying a free woman. The standard rule is that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition. So why not simply invoke *assei docheh lo ta'asseh* and allow him to marry and fulfill *pru u'rvu* without any need for the *takkana* of freeing him?

### Tosafot Answers

*Tosafot* offers two answers. The first, in the name of *Rabbeinu Yitzchak*, is a matter of timing: *mishat ha'araah ka'avir lav* — from the very beginning of the sexual act, one transgresses the *lav*. The *assei* of *pru u'rvu*, however, is not fulfilled until the act is complete — *assei d'Pru U'rvu lo mekayem ad gmar biyah* — since only then does the possibility of conception arise. Since the transgression of the *lav* precedes the fulfillment of the *assei*, the mechanism of *assei docheh lo ta'asseh* cannot operate cleanly here. One might alternatively frame the act of intercourse as a mere *hechsher mitzvah* rather than the *maaseh mitzvah* of *pru u'rvu* itself — which opens broader questions about how to define the operative act of fulfilling *pru u'rvu*, particularly when one holds it is the man's *mitzvah*.

The second answer is that the woman has no *mitzvah* of *pru u'rvu*. The classic rabbinic position is that women are exempt from *pru u'rvu*. Even if the man could be permitted to transgress the *lo ta'asseh* through the mechanism of *assei docheh lo ta'asseh*, the woman has no *assei* of her own — and who permits her to transgress? *Assei docheh lo ta'asseh* would authorize him to act; it says nothing about her.

*Tosafot* then continues into the broader question of whether it is permissible for one person to transgress a prohibition in order to enable another person to fulfill a *mitzvah* — and specifically, whether the master may be permitted to transgress the prohibition against freeing slaves in order to enable the slave to fulfill a *mitzvah*. These are rich questions that *Tosafot* explores at length, and they underscore how much conceptual depth is embedded in what appeared to be a subsidiary discussion from yesterday's *daf*.

---

## Sefer Torah Structure

### Scroll Requirements

We now turn to the *daf* proper, picking up at the top of 14a. The *Gemara* here is concerned not with the ritual *Sefer Torah* used for *Kriat HaTorah* in the synagogue, but with scrolls used functionally — as books for learning — which could contain the entire *Torah*, *Nevi'im*, and *Kesuvim* in a single scroll. Despite their non-ritual character, the *Gemara* establishes certain physical requirements for such scrolls.

### Blank Parchment

One basic requirement is that a blank section of *klaf* be left at the beginning and end of the scroll, to facilitate wrapping around the pole.

### Rolling Direction

*Tosafot*'s understanding of the *Gemara* — which is more functionally intuitive — holds that one rolls from the end toward the beginning. Under this reading, the blank *klaf* left at the end of the scroll (i.e., the end of *Devarim*) provides enough parchment to wrap around the pole, so that the written text does not sit directly against it. The blank section at the beginning similarly allows the opening of the scroll to be fully wrapped after rolling.

*Rashi*, by contrast, reads the rolling direction as beginning to end, which creates the counterintuitive result that one opens the scroll from the back. *Rashi* accordingly reverses the *girsa* of the *Gemara* — holding that the beginning needs enough blank *klaf* to wrap the circumference (*heikef*) and the end needs enough to wrap the pole (*amud*). *Tosafot* maintains the opposite assignment.

### Wrapping Contradiction

The *Gemara* itself registers the tension. The phrase *techilas ha'sefer v'sofo k'dei l'gol* — the beginning and end of the scroll are sufficient to wrap — creates an ambiguity: sufficient to wrap what? If both ends need only enough to wrap a pole (*amud*), the requirement regarding the circumference (*heikef*) is left unaddressed. If both need enough to wrap the full circumference, that contradicts the other requirement. The two ends seem to serve different purposes, and reading the *Gemara* as assigning one to each function creates the apparent contradiction the *Gemara* flags.

### Two Poles

*Rav Ashi* resolves the difficulty: the *Beraita* about the beginning and end is discussing a *Sefer Torah* specifically — and a *Sefer Torah* has two poles, one at each end. The *Gemara* quotes a supporting *Beraita*: *kol hasfarim niglalim mitichilatan l'sofam* — all [other] scrolls are rolled from beginning to end — *v'sefer Torah niglal l'emtzi'ito* — but a *Sefer Torah* is rolled toward its middle. Because a *Sefer Torah* has a pole at each end, one can open it at any point in the middle, which serves the practical need of a large scroll.

With two poles, one end of the scroll wraps around the pole itself (*amud*), and the other end needs enough blank *klaf* to wrap around the full circumference (*heikef*) of the rolled scroll. The contradiction dissolves: the two ends are not parallel requirements; each serves a distinct function.

### Jerusalem Scribes

*Rav Elazar bar Rav Tzadok* confirms that this was actual practice: *kach hayu kotvim sefarim sheb'Yerushalayim osim sifreihem* — this is how the scribes of Jerusalem would make their scrolls.

### Ritual vs. Book

The simple reading of this *Gemara* is that we are not speaking of these scrolls as ritual objects in the technical sense — they are not the *Sefer Torah* used for *Kriat HaTorah*, with all its attendant *halachic* requirements. This raises the question: what is the *Gemara*'s authority here? If these are just books, why not let practical considerations govern? The answer seems to be that even when a *sefer* is not a ritual object in the narrow sense, there remains an obligation of *kavod* — respect — for the text. Rolling an entire *Tanach* on a single pole would require constant unwinding to find one's place, which is simply undignified. Similarly, the prohibition mentioned elsewhere against combining all of *Navi* in one scroll, according to some opinions, reflects a concern for maintaining proper distinction between the different *sefarim*. These are not ritual requirements in the sense that one is or is not *yotze* a *mitzvah*, but they reflect the *Gemara*'s insistence on maintaining appropriate honor for sacred texts.

This distinction between categories is itself worth pausing on. There are effectively three tiers: the *mitzvas ksivas Sefer Torah*, the *Sefer Torah* used for public *Kriat HaTorah*, and an ordinary *sefer* used for learning. We tend to assume that the detailed *halachic* requirements described in the *Gemara* — and codified by the *Rambam* — apply to the middle category. The *Rambam*, however, holds that all those requirements pertain specifically to the *mitzvas ksivas Sefer Torah*, and that for public *Kriat HaTorah* one may technically use a *Chumash*. The question of what language a scroll may be written in — *kol hasefarim nichtavim bechol lashon* — and what script must be used, thus depends entirely on which of these three categories is under discussion.

---

## Torah Proportions

### Length-Width Equality

The *Gemara* now presents a *Beraita* governing the proportions of a *Sefer Torah*: *ein osin Sefer Torah lo orko yoseir al hekefo velo hekefo yoseir al orko* — one does not make a *Sefer Torah* whose length exceeds its circumference, nor whose circumference exceeds its length. The requirement is bidirectional: length and circumference must be equal.

To visualize this: the *orko* is the height of the scroll as it stands — the height of the columns of writing. The *heikef* is the circumference of the fully rolled scroll. The *Gemara* will indicate that the standard measure for each is six *tefachim*. With six *tefachim* as the height and six *tefachim* as the circumference, and using the Talmud's assumption that *pi* equals three, the diameter of the rolled scroll comes to two *tefachim* — approximately six inches — yielding a scroll roughly eighteen inches tall and six inches wide when rolled.

This is a demanding physical specification. One begins with a sheet of *klaf* that is six *tefachim* tall, and the thickness of the *klaf*, the tightness of the script, and the total amount of text must combine so that when fully written and rolled, the circumference is also exactly six *tefachim*. The *Maharsha* notes, and the *Gemara* will make explicit, that the number six derives from the dimensions of the *Luchot* — the Tablets of Stone were six *tefachim* tall, and that measure became the template for the *Sefer Torah*.

### Six Tefachim

When asked *bekama* — what is the proper height — *Rabbi* (Yehudah HaNasi) answers: *b'gevil, shisha* — on *gevil*, the answer is six. The *girsa* and the reasoning will be clarified when the *Gemara* derives six *tefachim* from the dimensions of the *Luchot*.

### Gevil & Klaf

*Gevil* refers to the full-grain leather — the entire thickness of the animal hide used as-is, with writing on the side where the hair grew. The alternative is *klaf*: the hide is split down its thickness, and one writes on the inner face of the outer half — the surface created by the cut. Writing is always on the point of the cut; the difference is which half of the split hide one uses. *Gevil* uses the whole hide; *klaf* uses the outer half; *duchsustus* uses the inner half. For a *Sefer Torah*, one writes on the hair side of *gevil* and on the cut surface of *klaf*.

When asked what the measure would be for *klaf*, *Rabbi* answers: *beklaf bekama eini yodea* — for *klaf*, I do not know. The difficulty with this answer is not immediately obvious: if the requirement is simply that height equal circumference, one need only adjust the size of the script. If *klaf* is thinner than *gevil*, the rolled scroll will have a smaller circumference for the same number of columns, requiring larger script or a different column width to compensate. Why would *Rabbi* not know the answer?

### Scribal Stories

The challenge of achieving the exact proportions in practice is illustrated by two famous stories. *Rav Huna* wrote seventy *Sifrei Torah* and only once — *ela chad* — did a single scroll happen to come out with the height equal to the circumference. *Rav Acha bar Yaakov* wrote one *Sefer Torah* on the skin of a calf — *amshka d'eglei* — and it worked out on the first attempt. The calf skin happened to be precisely the right thickness. *Yavu bei rabanan einaihu* — his colleagues gave him the evil eye — *venach nafshei* — and he died. The conclusion seems to be that either you will never achieve it, or you will achieve it and suffer for it.

### Rabbi Ami's 400

The *Gemara* then reports that *Rabbi Ami* wrote four hundred *Sifrei Torah*. *Rav Hamnuna* is skeptical: *dilma Torah tziva lanu Moshe katav* — perhaps what is meant is not four hundred complete *Sifrei Torah*, but four hundred instances of writing the verse *Torah tziva lanu Moshe*. *Tosafot* supports this reading by citing *Rabbi Yitzchak*, who derives from the *Gemara* in chapter 3 of Sukkah (*perek* 3) that *Torah tziva lanu Moshe* is the distillation of what a father teaches his young child as soon as the child can speak — *mai Torah? Torah tziva lanu Moshe*. The verse thus serves as the condensed embodiment of the concept of *Torah*. A similar reinterpretation is offered when *Rava* tells *Rav Zeira* that *Rabbi Yannai* planted four hundred vineyards: *dilma shtayim keneged shtayim ve'achas yotzei zanav* — perhaps it means the minimum halakhic configuration of a vineyard, two vines parallel to two with one extending between them, which is sufficient to constitute a *kerem* for the relevant *halachic* purposes.

---

## Ark Dimensions

### Ark Size

The *Gemara* now introduces a *baraita* challenging the six-*tefach* standard for *Sefer Torah* proportions: *amatayim vachatzi orko ve'amah vachatzi rochbo ve'amah vachatzi komaso* — the *Aron* that *Moshe* made was, per the *pesukim* in *Shemot*, two and a half *amot* long, one and a half *amot* wide, and one and a half *amot* tall. Taking the standard *amah* as six *tefachim*, these dimensions convert to fifteen *tefachim* in length, nine *tefachim* in width, and nine *tefachim* in height.

### Tablets Placement

The dimensions of the *Luchot* are then given: *vehaluchos arkan shisha verochban shisha ve'ovyan shelosha* — the Tablets were six *tefachim* long, six *tefachim* wide, and three *tefachim* thick. These were rectangular solids, not the arch-shaped form familiar from iconography. They were placed lengthwise within the *Aron* — *munachos keneged orko shel aron* — meaning both *Luchot* were laid end-to-end along the length of the *Aron*.

### Interior Space

*Abaye* proceeds to work out the arithmetic. The two *Luchot* placed lengthwise consume twelve *tefachim* of the *Aron*'s interior. With a total exterior length of fifteen *tefachim*, and subtracting a half-*tefach* for each wall (*chatzi l'kosel zeh v'chatzi l'kosel zeh*), the usable interior length is fourteen *tefachim*. Fourteen minus twelve leaves two *tefachim* of open space at one end. Similarly for the width: the *Luchot* are six *tefachim* wide; the interior width is nine minus one (a half for each wall) equals eight *tefachim*... but the *Gemara* actually works through this in the width direction as well, arriving at two *tefachim* of open space on the width side after accounting for the wall thickness.

### Torah in Ark

That remaining space — two *tefachim* — is where the *Sefer Torah* rested inside the *Aron*, according to *Rabbi Meir*. The *Gemara* knows this from *Devarim*, where *Moshe* instructs the *Levi'im*: *lakioach et sefer hatorah hazeh vesamtem oto b'tzad aron berit Hashem* — take this *Sefer Torah* and place it *b'tzad aron*, at the side of the *Aron*. *Rabbi Meir* reads *b'tzad* as meaning inside the *Aron*, at the wall — not in the middle between the *Luchot*, but pressed against the inner wall.

That the *Sefer Torah* was indeed inside (rather than outside) the *Aron* is derived, remarkably, from the verse *ein ba'aron rak shnei luchos ha'avanim asher hiniach sham Moshe* — there is nothing in the *Aron* except the two stone *Luchot* that *Moshe* placed there. The *Gemara* reads *ein... rak* as a double limitation — *miyut achar miyut* — and applies the rule that a double limitation is actually an expansion: *ein miyut achar miyut ela l'rabot*. Therefore, paradoxically, the verse that says there is nothing there except the *Luchot* is itself the proof that there was something else — namely, the *Sefer Torah*.

### Width Math

The width calculation mirrors the length calculation. The *Luchot* occupy six *tefachim* of width. After subtracting wall thickness, the interior width allows for two *tefachim* of open space. This is exactly the second dimension of the *Sefer Torah*: six *tefachim* in height, two *tefachim* in width. The *Aron*'s interior space thus provides the derivation for the precise proportions of a *Sefer Torah* — six by two — with the six *tefachim* figure then feeding back into the requirement that height equal circumference.

*Tosafot* addresses an obvious question: if accessing the *Aron* required entry into the *Kodesh Kodashim*, which was forbidden except to the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur*, when would anyone ever take out the *Sefer Torah* — and why do we need to specify that it fit without being *dachuk* (overly tight)? *Tosafot* answers that entry into the *Kodesh Kodashim* was permitted when necessary to maintain the *Sefer Torah* — to prevent it from becoming moldy or deteriorating — and cites the *Gemara* in Eruvin to this effect. There are also Talmudic sources (*masechtot ktanot*) which speak of three *Sifrei Torah* found in the *heichal*, used to adjudicate textual variants by majority — an indication that *Sifrei Torah* in the *Beis Hamikdash* served as authoritative reference texts against which other scrolls were compared.

---

## Meir vs. Yehuda

### 5-Tefach Amah

*Rabbi Yehuda* disputes *Rabbi Meir*'s calculation by challenging a foundational premise: when measuring the sacred vessels of the *Beis Hamikdash*, the operative *amah* is five *tefachim*, not six. This is *Rabbi Yehuda*'s general position regarding all the *keilim* of the *Beis Hamikdash*. Accordingly, all the *Aron* dimensions must be recalculated. Two and a half times five is twelve and a half *tefachim* in length; one and a half times five is seven and a half *tefachim* in width.

### Recalculation

The *Luchot* dimensions are not disputed — they remain six by six by three — since that measurement derives from *masorah* rather than from the *amah* used for vessels. But now the arithmetic yields a dramatically tighter fit. The interior length is twelve and a half minus one *tefach* for the two walls, leaving eleven and a half *tefachim*. The *Luchot* together take up twelve *tefachim*. There is simply no room — not even room for a *Sefer Torah*, and barely room for the *Luchot* themselves. The walls of the *Aron* are reduced to a single finger-breadth (*etzba*) on each side, an almost impossibly tight fit.

On the width side: interior width is seven and a half minus a half-*tefach* for the two walls = seven *tefachim*, minus the six occupied by the *Luchot* = one *tefach* of open space. (The *girsa* of the *Gemara* here is somewhat difficult, as *Tosafot* and the commentators note, since the arithmetic of the finger-breadths for the walls does not divide evenly; various readings have been proposed.)

### Decorative Poles

What fills the one *tefach* of open space in the width, according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, is not a *Sefer Torah* but *amudim* — symbolic poles. The *Gemara* derives their presence from the verse in *Shir HaShirim*: *apiryon asa lo hamelech Shlomo me'atzei haLevanon* — *Shlomo* made an *apiryon* (a palanquin or canopied bed) from the cedars of Lebanon — *amudav asa kesef* — its pillars were made of silver. The *Gemara* understands this as a reference to the poles within the *Aron*, made of silver. *Tosafot* in the name of *Rabbeinu Tam* explains: *nireh le'Rabeinu Tam desiman le'ha'amadat Yisrael haya* — these poles were a symbol of the standing and sustenance of the Jewish people. They were not made of gold specifically *shelo lehazkir ma'aseh egel* — so as not to evoke the sin of the Golden Calf.

The arrangement, then, according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, is that the *Luchot* would be slightly shifted toward the center, leaving a half-*tefach* on each side, with a silver pillar in each of those spaces. The visual result is striking: the *Luchot* flanked by silver poles, evoking precisely the image of a *Sefer Torah* on its *atzei chayim*. Even without a physical *Sefer Torah* inside the *Aron*, the symbolic form of a *Sefer Torah* is present.

This is a remarkable observation. The *Luchot* — the most inaccessible sacred object, housed in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, accessible only to the *Kohen Gadol* once a year — are arranged so as to appear as a *Sefer Torah* flanked by its poles. The *Gemara* in *Yevamot* (or wherever the relevant passage appears) teaches that *yekara hi mikohen gadol shenichnas lifnai velifnim* — the *Torah* is more precious than the *Kohen Gadol* who enters the *lifnai velifnim*. What is implicit here is the translation of the supremely hierarchical and inaccessible (*Kodesh Kodashim*, *Kohen Gadol*, *Yom Kippur*) into the universally accessible: the *Sefer Torah*, open to all. The *amudim* inside the *Aron* make that equation visible.

### Philistine Box

Before the *argaz* — the box sent by the *Pelishtim* along with the returned *Aron* containing gold vessels as an *asham* offering — arrived, *Rabbi Yehuda* has a difficulty: where was the *Sefer Torah* kept? According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, there was no room inside the *Aron* for a *Sefer Torah*. The *Gemara* answers: *dappa hava nafik minei* — there was a small shelf extending from the back wall of the *Aron*, and the *Sefer Torah* rested on it.

Once the *argaz* arrived — placed *mitzido*, outside and beside the *Aron*, as the verse states: *ve'et klei hazahav asher hasheivotem lo asham tasimu va'argaz mitzido* — *Rabbi Yehuda* has a place for the *Sefer Torah* as well: *ve'alav Sefer Torah munach* — the *Sefer Torah* rested on top of this box. The verse *lakioach et sefer hatorah hazeh vesamtem oto mitzad aron berit Hashem* is then read as meaning literally outside and beside — not inside the *Aron* at all.

The symbolism compounds. Within the *Beis Hamikdash*'s most sacred chamber, there stood the *Aron* — containing the *Luchot* flanked by silver *amudim* evoking a *Sefer Torah* — and beside it a wooden box with an actual *Sefer Torah* resting on top. An *aron* containing a *Sefer Torah*, standing next to the *Aron HaKodesh*: this is essentially the arrangement every *beit knesset* replicates. The *aron kodesh* in shul, housing a *Sefer Torah*, directly echoes the structure of the *Kodesh Kodashim*.

---

## One Pole Math

### Pi = 3

The *Gemara* now returns to work through the mathematical implications of the *Sefer Torah* dimensions for *Rabbi Meir*'s position. If the circumference is six *tefachim*, then by the Talmudic approximation *pi* = 3, the diameter of the rolled scroll is two *tefachim*. This is geometrically consistent: circumference = pi × diameter = 3 × 2 = 6.

### Two Poles Problem

But a difficulty arises. The *Gemara* has established that a *Sefer Torah* is rolled toward its middle — *niglal l'emtzi'ito* — implying two poles. If there are two poles, each pole takes up some physical space. A scroll with a diameter of exactly two *tefachim* and a two-*tefach* wide space in the *Aron* leaves no room for a second pole. Moreover, if there are two poles, the center of the scroll is exposed when the scroll is open — *kevan de'emtzoito nigleh nafik lei mitrei tefachei* — meaning the total width would exceed two *tefachim* once the additional pole is accounted for. One might ask: why could the second pole not simply be fit into the gap that exists geometrically between the circular cross-section of the rolled scroll and the rectangular corners of the *Aron*? The answer seems to be that once any pole is attached, the combined width exceeds the available space.

### One Pole Solution

*Rav Acha bar Yaakov* resolves the problem directly: *Sefer Azara litchilato hu niglal* — the *Sefer Torah* of the *Azara* had only one pole. It was rolled entirely in one direction, toward the beginning, without a second pole at the other end. (This also answers why the phrase is *litchilato* — toward the beginning — rather than *l'emtzi'ito*.) With only one pole, the diameter is exactly two *tefachim*, fitting perfectly within the two-*tefach* space.

### Slack & Wiggle

*Rav Ashi* adds a further refinement. Even with one pole, placing a two-*tefach* diameter scroll into a two-*tefach* space allows no room to insert or remove it. *Decharich bei purta vecharchayei le'eil* — one leaves the scroll wound slightly less than fully tight, and wraps the tiny excess of parchment on top, creating a small amount of wiggle room. The *Sefer Torah* can thus be eased in and out without being *dachuk* — forced.

---

## Torah Placement

### Back Shelf

*Rabbi Yehuda* is now asked: before the *argaz* of the *Pelishtim* arrived, where did the *Sefer Torah* sit? According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, there was no room inside the *Aron* for the scroll. His answer, as already noted, is that *dappa hava nafik minei* — a small plank or shelf protruded from the back of the *Aron* — and *yasiv alav Sefer Torah*, the *Sefer Torah* rested upon it.

### Meir: Inside Ark

For *Rabbi Meir*, the verse *vesamtem oto mitzad aron berit Hashem* is interpreted as placing the *Sefer Torah* inside the *Aron* but at the inner wall — *hu miba'ei lei demanach lei mitzad velo manach lei beini luchot*. It would not be placed between the *Luchot* in the center of the *Aron*, but pressed against the inner side wall. *Ule'olam begavei de'arona yasiv* — it always sits within the interior of the *Aron*, just toward the edge rather than the middle.

### Poles Outside

Accordingly, for *Rabbi Meir*, the *amudim* — the decorative silver poles derived from *Shir HaShirim* — were on the outside of the *Aron*, not inside it. *Mibara'ei* — from the outside. The debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* thus becomes a matter of inversion: each holds that one of the two elements (the *Sefer Torah* and the *amudim*) was inside the *Aron* and the other was outside; they disagree about which was which.

---

## Ark Contents

### Broken Tablets

*Rabbi Meir* requires a source for the placement of the *shivrei luchot* — the broken Tablets — inside the *Aron*, since for him the verse *ein ba'aron rak* is already fully expended on proving the presence of the *Sefer Torah*. The *Gemara* derives this from *Rav Huna*'s reading of a different verse: *asher nikra sham shem Hashem Tzeva'ot yoshev hakruvim* — it is called there the name of *Hashem Tzeva'ot*. *Rav Huna* notes the doubled word: either *sham sham* (there, there) or *shem shem* (name, name). This doubling teaches that both the *luchot* and the *shivrei luchot* were present — *sheluchot veshivrei luchot munachim ba'aron*.

### Yishmael School

For *Rabbi Yehuda*, who cannot use *ein ba'aron rak* for the *Sefer Torah* (since the *Sefer Torah* was outside the *Aron* according to him), the *shem shem* doubling is instead available to prove the *shivrei luchot*. But then *Rabbi Yehuda* needs his own source. He finds it in the school of *Rabbi Yishmael*: *tani debei Rabbi Yishmael* — *asher shibarta vesamtam ba'aron* — even those *luchot* that you broke, place them in the *Aron*. This is read as a direct divine command to include the broken fragments alongside the whole Tablets.

### Breaking Approved

The other *amora* — for whom *debei Rabbi Yishmael* is needed to answer a different question — must derive the presence of the *shivrei luchot* from *Reish Lakish*'s teaching: *amar lo HaKadosh Baruch Hu le-Moshe, yashar kochacha she-shibarta* — the Holy One said to *Moshe*: well done for having broken them. The breaking of the *Luchot* was not merely forgiven; it was retroactively approved. *God* affirmed that shattering the Tablets was the correct act in that moment.

### Broken Tablets Power

It is worth dwelling on the theological resonance with which this *daf* concludes. The *Gemara* has spent its final pages establishing that the broken *Luchot* remained in the *Aron* alongside the whole ones — not discarded, not hidden, but preserved at the center of *kedushah*. And *Reish Lakish*'s *yashar kochacha* suggests that the breaking was not a tragic necessity but something affirmed. There is a power in the broken *Luchot* that is not despite their brokenness but somehow because of it.

Read alongside the broader discussion of this *daf*, the arc becomes visible. The *Luchot* — direct from *Hakadosh Baruch Hu*, housed in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, accessible only to the *Kohen Gadol* once a year — represent the most hierarchical, protected, inaccessible form of *Torah*. The *Sefer Torah* — present in every *beit knesset*, on every bookshelf, carried by every Jew — represents its most universally accessible form. What the *Gemara* has done across this *daf* is make explicit that these two are not in opposition but in continuity. The broken *Luchot* in the *Aron* sit beside the *Sefer Torah*. The *amudim* flanking the *Luchot* evoke the poles of a *Sefer Torah*. The *argaz* beside the *Aron* holds a *Sefer Torah* on its lid — the original *aron kodesh* of every subsequent *beit knesset*. The move from the inaccessible *Luchot* to the accessible *Sefer Torah* is not a fall from something greater; *yashar kochacha she-shibarta* — it was the right thing.

---

---

# Bava Batra 15

## Order of Nevi'im

### Opening & Context

The daf begins on 14b, transitioning from the physical dimensions and arrangement of the *Sefer Torah* — including its relationship to the *aron* and the *luchot*, and the contrast between the utter inaccessibility of the *luchot* (accessible only to the *Kohen Gadol* on Yom Kippur) and the full accessibility of the *Sefer Torah* — to the broader conceptual questions about the books of *Tanakh*: their canonical order, and their authorship. The *tana'im* address these questions in a *baraita* that opens with the words *Sidran shel nevi'im* — the order of the prophetic books.

### Hoshea's Priority

The *baraita* enumerates the *nevi'im* in the following order: Yehoshua, Shoftim, Shmuel, Melachim — so far, a straightforwardly chronological sequence — then, strikingly, Yirmiyahu, Yechezkel, Yeshayahu, and finally the *Shneim Asar*. The Gemara immediately notices that the sequence of the *nevi'im acharonim* (the Later Prophets) does not match their chronological order and seeks to unpack the underlying logic.

The Gemara's first observation concerns Hoshea. The verse states, *tekhilat dibber Hashem be-Hoshea* — "The beginning of God's speaking was with Hoshea" — which would seem to imply Hoshea was the very first prophet. But surely this cannot mean first among all prophets from Moshe onward, given how many prophets preceded him. Rabbi Yochanan explains: Hoshea is described as first among the four prophets who prophesied during the same historical period — Hoshea, Yeshayahu, Amos, and Micha — and he was chronologically the earliest of those four. So within the *nevi'im acharonim*, Hoshea rightly claims priority.

### Hoshea & Trei Asar

The Gemara then asks: if Hoshea is the earliest of the *nevi'im acharonim*, why not place him first among them as a standalone book? The answer is that his prophecies are written together with those of Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi — who represent the very last of the prophets, at the opening of the *Bayit Sheni* period — and since Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi are at the end, Hoshea is grouped with them. This is because the *Shneim Asar* constitutes a single book; each individual prophetic work within it is too small to stand as a separate scroll without risking being lost. The Gemara reasons very practically here: a separate scroll of small dimensions — a physically tiny book — *mirkas*, gets lost. The concern is explicitly about physical scrolls: if you produce a tiny independent scroll, it will lose its identity and be misplaced. Therefore, Hoshea is embedded within the *Trei Asar*, which in turn is placed at the end because of its association with the final prophets.

### Thematic Ordering

With the *Trei Asar* settled at the end, the Gemara turns to the order among the remaining *nevi'im acharonim*. Chronologically, the sequence should be Yeshayahu, then Yirmiyahu, then Yechezkel — and indeed that is the order familiar from any standard *Tanakh*. So why does the *baraita* list them as Yirmiyahu, Yechezkel, Yeshayahu?

The Gemara's answer is thematic rather than chronological: the book of Melachim concludes with destruction — *Melachim sofei churbana*. Yirmiyahu is entirely about prophesying destruction — *Yirmiyahu kulei churbana*. Yechezkel opens with destruction and closes with consolation — *reisha churbana ve-seifei nechamta*. And Yeshayahu is overwhelmingly oriented toward consolation and the vision of *acharis hayamim* — *Yeshayahu kulei nechamta*. The organizing principle is therefore: *samchinan churbana le-churbana ve-nechamta le-nechamta* — we attach destruction to destruction and consolation to consolation. There is a beautiful narrative arc: Melachim flows into Yirmiyahu, Yirmiyahu into Yechezkel, and Yechezkel — transitioning from *churban* to redemptive vision — into Yeshayahu, who points toward the ultimate *geulah*.

This order, it should be noted, is not the one we follow today, which raises the natural question of why current printed *Tanakhim* depart from it.
