The most likely practical explanation for our current arrangement is that the adoption of standardized chapter divisions — originally a Christian innovation — came along with concordances that made precise cross-referencing possible, including in the context of disputations, and our order shifted accordingly. The Koren *Tanakh* famously attempted to restore a distinctively Jewish chapter division when it was first published, but the effort was not adopted.

---

## Order of Ketuvim

### Ketuvim Order List

The *baraita* continues with the order of the *Ketuvim*: Rus, Sefer Tehillim, Iyov, Mishlei, Koheles, Shir HaShirim, Kinos (i.e., Eicha), Daniel, Megillas Esther, Ezra, and Divrei HaYamim. Unlike our familiar arrangement of *Ketuvim*, which is loosely thematic, this order is largely chronological. Rus comes first — it is set in the period of the Shoftim and is the story of the great-grandmother of David. Tehillim is David's. Iyov's placement will require separate discussion, as will the internal order of Shlomo's books. The three books of Shlomo — Mishlei, Koheles, and Shir HaShirim — follow. Then comes Kinos, which belongs to the period of the *churban*. Daniel is set during the period of exile between the two *Batei Mikdash*. Megillas Esther belongs to the later period of *Galus Bavel*. Ezra is the return. Divrei HaYamim, though its narrative begins far back in history, was composed at the end of this entire period and is placed last accordingly.

### Why Not Begin Badly

The Gemara asks: if Iyov lived in the time of Moshe, why not place his book first — before even Rus — since it would be the earliest? The answer is: *atchulei be-puranusa lo matchilinan* — we do not begin with catastrophe. The book of Iyov is fundamentally a story of devastating suffering.

The Gemara immediately challenges this: does not Rus also begin with suffering — famine, departure from the land, and death? The response distinguishes the two cases: Rus is *puranusa de-is leih achris* — a suffering that has a good end. The arc of Rus is ultimately uplifting; it is the foundation story of David HaMelech. The basic story is not one of calamity. The book of Iyov, by contrast, is suffused with *puranusa* throughout — and even its ending, where God gives Iyov new children to replace those who died, leaves one profoundly disturbed. It does not carry the quality of *geulah* that Rus does. Rabbi Yochanan adds a further dimension: the very name *Rus*, he teaches, alludes to the fact that from her descended David, who *rivahu le-Hakadosh Baruch Hu be-shiros ve-tishbachos* — who satiated the Holy One, blessed be He, with songs and praises. This also explains the natural flow from Rus directly into Tehillim.

### Iyov's Placement

Tosafos raises a pointed question about Iyov's placement between Tehillim and Mishlei. If Iyov was early, one might understand placing him immediately after Rus. But that would interrupt the organic connection between Tehillim (David) and the books of Shlomo (Mishlei, Koheles, Shir HaShirim). Conversely, if Iyov was late — among those who returned in the *Bayit Sheni* period, as one opinion holds — why is he not placed at the end, together with Ezra?

Tosafos answers with a striking observation: Iyov, Tehillim, and Mishlei share a *niggun echad* — a single cantillation system. Their *trop* is not the standard *trop* of the rest of *Tanakh*. The familiar system of *mercha-tipcha-munach-esnachta* gives way to a distinctive system applied only to these three books, reflecting a common poetic genre of short, parallel half-verses (*mikraos ketzarim*) arranged in a particular meter. This is not merely a feature of the written text but was the established manner of public reading going back to antiquity, as the Gemara itself notes in connection with the phrase *meforash be-shum sechel* — *pesukei ta'amei*, the system of cantillation marks. These three books belong together not just generically as poetry but specifically as a single type of poetry with a single system of recitation.

This explains why Iyov must appear between Tehillim and Mishlei: it allows the three books sharing this special *trop* to be grouped together, while also keeping Mishlei, Koheles, and Shir HaShirim — the three books of Shlomo — consecutively together. Placing Iyov here is the only arrangement that achieves both goals simultaneously.

Tosafos adds a further refinement in the name of Rabbeinu Tam: the grouping with Tehillim is also supported by the Gemara's later teaching that David authored Tehillim *al yedei asarah zekenim* — through ten elders — which creates an additional associative link among these books. The result is a placement that is not chronological but is the product of multiple overlapping considerations: genre, cantillation system, compositional grouping, and authorial association.

---

## Authorship Discussio (II)

### Moshe & Yehoshua

Having addressed the *seder* of the *nevi'im* and *Ketuvim*, the *baraita* turns to the question of *mi katvan* — who wrote them. It is important to note at the outset that "writing" here does not necessarily mean who physically took pen to paper; the concept encompasses authorship, compilation, editing, and the process of giving a prophetic composition its final canonical form.

The *baraita* states: *Moshe katav sifro u-farshat Bilam* — Moshe wrote his own book and the portion of Bilam. It is striking that the portion of Bilam is identified separately, distinct from the rest of the Torah. The reason is apparent: the *parshat Bilam* is narrated entirely from an external frame of reference. The omniscient narrator who views events from the perspective of *Bnei Yisrael* is absent; instead, the reader is positioned within the perspective of Bilam and the nations looking at Israel from the outside. This distinctive vantage point explains why *Chazal* felt it warranted separate mention, even though it is entirely part of *Torat Moshe*.

The *baraita* adds: *ve-Iyov* — Moshe also wrote Iyov, under the assumption that Iyov lived in his time. This association is deeply meaningful: Moshe is the *navi* who asks *hodeini na et derachecha* — according to *Chazal*'s understanding, a plea to comprehend why the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper, the same question that lies at the heart of Iyov.

*Yehoshua katav sifro u-shmonah pesukim she-ba-Torah* — Yehoshua wrote his own book and the last eight *pesukim* of the Torah, which describe Moshe's death. The question of those eight *pesukim* is taken up at length in a later section.

### Yirmiyahu's Works

*Yirmiyahu katav sifro ve-Sefer Melachim ve-Kinos* — Yirmiyahu wrote his own book, the book of Melachim, and Kinos (Eicha). The assignment is thematically coherent: Melachim concludes with the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*, Yirmiyahu's prophecy is the voice of that destruction from within, and Eicha is its lamentation. The three form a unified literary and theological response to the *churban*, and they are attributed to the same prophetic voice.

### Chizkiyahu's Role

*Chizkiyahu va-siato kasvu Yeshayahu, Mishlei, Shir HaShirim ve-Koheles* — Chizkiyahu and his group wrote Yeshayahu, Mishlei, Shir HaShirim, and Koheles. This attribution requires unpacking, and Rashi provides the key: Yeshayahu was killed by Menashe and therefore never had the opportunity to commit his prophecies to a final written book. As Rashi explains, prophets would typically compose their books only near the end of their lives, once their prophecies were complete; a violent death deprived Yeshayahu of that opportunity. Chizkiyahu's group therefore took on the task.

For the books of Shlomo, the *baraita* in Mishlei itself supplies the evidence: it states explicitly, *asher he'etiku anshei Chizkiyah* — "which the men of Chizkiyah copied out." Shlomo's wisdom was delivered over a lifetime in separate units — individual *meshalim*, individual poems, individual meditations — and Chizkiyahu's group organized, compiled, and gave these compositions their final form as books. Rashi further notes that Chizkiyahu himself planted the culture that made this possible: he famously drew his sword over the entrance to the *beis midrash* and decreed that anyone who did not study Torah would be penalized, generating a generation of scholars capable of undertaking precisely this kind of literary-religious enterprise.

This raises a profound question about the nature of authorship. *He'etiku* — "they copied out" — suggests something more than transcription. Shlomo did not dictate a book called Mishlei in sequential chapters. The *meshalim* existed as separate oral or written units; Chizkiyahu's people collected, arranged, and edited them into a unified composition. The same almost certainly applies to Koheles and, perhaps more surprisingly, to Shir HaShirim — though Shir HaShirim does appear to consist of discrete poems rather than a single continuous allegory. The attribution of all three to Chizkiyahu's group may reflect a logical extension from the explicit biblical testimony in Mishlei: since they are credited with organizing that book, they are credited with organizing Shlomo's other works as well.

### Great Assembly

*Anshei Knesset HaGedolah kasvu Yechezkel, Shneim Asar, Daniel, u-Megillas Esther* — the members of the Great Assembly wrote Yechezkel, the *Trei Asar*, Daniel, and Megillas Esther. The Great Assembly operated at the beginning of the *Bayit Sheni* period, with Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi among its leading figures.

Why did Yechezkel himself not write his own book? Rashi says plainly that he does not know for certain, but suggests the possibility that prophecies received *be-chutz la-aretz* — outside of *Eretz Yisrael* — could not be given their final canonical form outside the land; the process of a prophecy becoming a book of *Tanakh* in its definitive form was one that required the sanctity of *Eretz Yisrael*. The *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*, upon their return, therefore undertook the task of bringing these works — Yechezkel, Daniel, Megillas Esther — into their final canonical form.

This raises a pointed question about Megillas Esther, whose events took place in *galus*. The answer lies in the Gemara in Maseches Megilla, which preserves a tradition that Esther herself sent a message to the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* saying *kitvuni le-dorot* — "write me down for all generations" — meaning: include me in the canon. The process reflected here involves at least three distinct stages: original authorship or prophetic utterance; the writing down and organization of the material; and the formal act of canonization — the decision that this text belongs to *sifrei Tanakh* and is *metamei es ha-yadayim*, the rabbinic marker of canonical status.

The question of canonization was not fully resolved even by the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*. Debates about whether specific books — Shir HaShirim, Yechezkel, and others — are *metamei es ha-yadayim* continued into the Tannaic period. The discussions recorded among the *Tannaim* about which books convey *tum'as yadayim* are effectively discussions about the boundaries of the canon, addressing books whose status may have remained contested even after the Great Assembly's work. By the time of the *Tannaim*, most of the canon was beyond question; only the peripheral cases remained for deliberation.

The *baraita* concludes: *Ezra katav sifro ve-ha-yachas shel Divrei HaYamim ad lo* — Ezra wrote his book and the genealogical record of Divrei HaYamim up to his own time. The Gemara cites Rav in support: Ezra did not ascend from Bavel until he had fully traced his own genealogy, which reflects the broader enterprise of reestablishing proper lineages for the priestly and levitical families upon the return from exile. The Gemara then asks who completed Sefer Ezra after Ezra himself, and answers: *Nechemiah ben Chakalyah askeih* — Nechemiah finished it.

---

## Authorship Discussio (II)

### Moshe's Death Passage

Having enumerated the authors of the biblical books, the Gemara now returns to unpack several of the more challenging attributions. It begins with the case of Yehoshua and the last eight *pesukim* of the Torah.

The *baraita* had stated that Yehoshua wrote the last eight *pesukim* of the Torah — the passage beginning *va-yamas sham Moshe eved Hashem*, "And Moshe died there, the servant of God." A *tanna* reasons: is it conceivable that Moshe himself wrote *va-yamas sham Moshe* — "Moshe died there"? *Efshar Moshe katav va-yamas sham Moshe*? Therefore, Rabbi Yehuda concludes, *ad kan katav Moshe, mi-kan ve-eilach katav Yehoshua* — up to this point Moshe wrote, from here onward Yehoshua wrote.

Rav Kahana objects in the name of Rabbi Shimon: is it possible that the *Sefer Torah* was missing even a single letter? The verse states *Lakoach es sefer ha-Torah ha-zeh* — Moshe took the Torah and gave it to the *Kohanim Leviyim*, which implies the book was complete and whole in Moshe's lifetime. Therefore, Rabbi Shimon maintains that Moshe himself wrote all eight *pesukim*, including the account of his own death.

How is this possible? The second *tanna* supplies the model: *Hakadosh Baruch Hu omer u-Moshe kosev be-dema* — God dictated and Moshe wrote while crying. The entire Torah, including the passage describing Moshe's death, was written by Moshe himself through direct divine dictation; God spoke each word and Moshe transcribed it, weeping as he wrote those final *pesukim*. The analogy cited is the verse describing Baruch ben Neriyah, Yirmiyahu's scribe: *mipiv yikra eilai es kol ha-devarim ha-eileh va-ani kosev al ha-sefer be-dyo* — "From his mouth he would dictate to me all these words and I would write them in the book with ink." This establishes the model of prophetic dictation, in which the prophet is the amanuensis of divine speech.

### Shmuel's Authorship

The Gemara addresses a parallel problem with Sefer Shmuel. If Shmuel authored his book, how could he have written the account of his own death, which appears already in the middle of the first book — well before the narrative ends? The answer is that *Gad ha-Chozeh ve-Natan ha-Navi askeih* — Gad the Seer and Natan the Prophet completed the book after Shmuel's death. Similarly with Sefer Yehoshua: the text records not only the death of Yehoshua but also the death of Elazar ben Aharon, who presumably wrote the earlier account. *De'askeih Elazar* — Elazar completed the account of Yehoshua's death; and then *de'askeih Pinchas* — Pinchas completed the account of Elazar's own death.

### David & Ten Elders

*David katav sefer Tehillim al yedei asarah zekenim* — David composed Sefer Tehillim through ten elders. These ten are: Adam HaRishon, Malki-Tzedek, Avraham, Moshe, Heiman, Yedutun, Asaf, and the three sons of Korach. The Gemara identifies these figures by connecting the headings of specific *pirkei Tehillim* with these names.

The attribution of *Eitan HaEzrachi* — the figure named in the heading of a *mizmor* — to Avraham is derived through a *gezeira shava*: the term *ezrachi* here is linked to the verse in Yeshayahu that asks *mi he'ir mi-mizrach* — "who aroused from the east" — referring, according to *Chazal*, to Avraham, the one who came from the east with righteousness at his feet. The *af al pi Eitanim* — even the mighty ones — refers to the *Avot*.

A more complex textual problem arises concerning Heiman. Rav had elsewhere said that Heiman in the verse *vayechkam mi-kol ha-adam me-Eitan ha-Ezrachi* — in Melachim — refers to Moshe, based on the parallel between *Heiman* and *ne'eman*, as in *be-chol beisi ne'eman hu* (God's description of Moshe as faithful in all His house). But here in Tehillim, Heiman appears as a separate author alongside Moshe. The Gemara resolves this by saying *trei Heiman havu* — there were two figures named Heiman: the Heiman of Melachim who is an epithet for Moshe, and the Heiman of Tehillim who is a distinct individual.

---

## Last 8 Pesukim

### Dictation Model

The Gemara now focuses at length on the question of the last eight *pesukim* of the Torah. As noted, Rabbi Yehuda holds that Moshe wrote everything *until* the account of his own death, and Yehoshua wrote the final eight *pesukim*. Rabbi Shimon disputes this on the grounds that the *Sefer Torah* could not have been incomplete in Moshe's time — the verse explicitly records Moshe handing over the complete *Sefer Torah* to the *Kohanim Leviyim*.

Rabbi Shimon's position requires an account of how Moshe could have written *va-yamas sham Moshe*. The Gemara's answer is the model of *be-dema* — dictation accompanied by tears. God continued to speak and Moshe continued to write, even as he wept, through those final eight *pesukim*. This is the model of pure, word-for-word dictation: *Hakadosh Baruch Hu omer u-Moshe omer ve-chosev* — for the main body of the Torah, God speaks and Moshe repeats and writes; *Hakadosh Baruch Hu omer u-Moshe kosev be-dema* — for the final eight *pesukim*, God speaks and Moshe writes with tears.

### Moshe's Tears

This model carries enormous theological weight. The second *tanna*'s formulation — that God dictated while Moshe wrote in tears — establishes not only who authored those final *pesukim* but also the precise nature of the relationship between divine speech and prophetic writing throughout the Torah. The analogy to Baruch writing down Yirmiyahu's words *be-dyo* — in ink — makes the point with precision: the *navi* or scribe is the recording instrument; the divine word is the source. Moshe's tears do not alter or mediate the content; they are the human response of a servant faithfully transcribing the words of his own death.

### Torah Authenticity

This passage is the primary locus in *Chazal* for the model of *Torah min ha-shamayim* as verbatim, word-for-word dictation. Other *gemoros* discuss the concept of *Torah mi-Sinai* and state emphatically that anyone who holds that even a single *pasuk* is *Moshe mi-pi atzmo* — from Moshe's own mind — has no share in the *olam ha-ba*. But there is a significant gap between "from Moshe's own mind" and "word-for-word dictation." Between those poles lies a wide range of models: prophecy, divine inspiration, *ruach ha-kodesh*, each of which could theoretically allow the Torah to be authentically divine without being a verbatim transcript. The model of direct dictation — God speaks, Moshe writes — is introduced specifically by the second *tanna* in this Gemara. It is noteworthy that even here, this model is not asserted by the first *tanna*; it is the second *tanna*'s response to the particular problem of the last eight *pesukim*. Nevertheless, this has become the standard model for understanding *Torah min ha-shamayim*, and it is from this Gemara that the model derives its authoritative grounding.

### Gra's Interpretation

The Vilna Gaon offers a striking mystical resolution that attempts to honor both positions simultaneously. The Gemara's formulation uses the word *be-dema* — in tears — while the parallel verse about Baruch uses *be-dyo* — in ink. The Gaon observes that *dema* can also carry the meaning of *dimua*, meaning something mixed or blurred. He suggests that Moshe wrote the letters of the final *pesukim* in a manner that was somehow not yet crystallized — perhaps invisible, perhaps undifferentiated — and that Yehoshua, after Moshe's death, then gave those letters their final, legible form. In this reading, Moshe is genuinely the author of all eight *pesukim* — the divine words passed through him — but the physical crystallization of those words into readable text was completed by Yehoshua. This synthesis allows Moshe to have truly written his own death while also allowing Yehoshua a role in finalizing those *pesukim*, without compromising the integrity of the *Sefer Torah* that Moshe delivered.

### Single Reader Rule

The Gemara cites a related ruling from Rav Gidel in the name of Rav: *shemonah pesukim she-ba-Torah yachid kore otan* — the last eight *pesukim* of the Torah are read by a single person. The Gemara asks whether this ruling reflects the position of Rabbi Yehuda — who holds those *pesukim* have a different authorship — and therefore seems to conflict with Rabbi Shimon, who holds Moshe wrote everything. The Gemara responds: *afilu teima Rabbi Shimon* — even according to Rabbi Shimon, since those eight *pesukim* are distinctive in character — written with tears, describing a death not yet occurred — they retain a special status that warrants treating them as a discrete unit.

Rashi explains *yachid kore otan* as a prohibition against dividing that *aliyah*: the final eight *pesukim* must be read as a single complete unit by one person; they may not be split between multiple *aliyos*. Tosafos, however, raises a difficulty with an alternative interpretation — that *yachid* means the one receiving the *aliyah* reads without a *ba'al korei* — and rejects it on historical grounds: the practice of having a *ba'al korei* read while the *oleh* listens did not yet exist in the period of the Gemara. In the Talmudic period, the person who received the *aliyah* was himself the reader. Therefore *yachid kore otan* cannot be contrasting individual reading with the *ba'al korei* practice, and Rashi's explanation — that the *aliyah* may not be subdivided — remains the operative interpretation.

---

## Iyov Discussion

### Iyov in Moshe's Time

The Gemara now turns to a sustained discussion of the book of Iyov — its historical dating, its authorship, its status as historical narrative or *mashal*, and ultimately its place among the books of the Bible. The statement from the *mi katvan* section that Moshe wrote Iyov is now cited to support Rabbi Levi bar Lachma's view that Iyov lived in the time of Moshe.

The textual evidence for this dating is a *gezeira shava* from the word *eipo*. The verse in Iyov reads *mi yiten eipo ve-yichtevun milai* — "Would that my words were written down" — and concludes with the phrase *mi yiten va-sefer ve-yuchaku*, expressing a longing that his words be engraved. This connects to Moshe, who is called *mechokek* — the engraver, the lawgiver — as in the verse *ki sham chelkas mechokek safun*. The association of engraving with Moshe makes Moshe the natural candidate as the author who fulfilled Iyov's wish.

The Gemara immediately challenges this *gezeira shava*: the word *eipo* appears many times in *Tanakh*. It appears in the context of Yitzchak (*mi eipo hu ha-tzad tzayid*), Yaakov (*im kein eipo zot asu*), and Yosef (*eipo heim ro'im*). How can one particular occurrence of *eipo* be used to anchor a dating to Moshe's time? The Gemara answers: the key is not the word *eipo* alone but the additional phrase at the end of the verse — *mi yiten va-sefer ve-yuchaku* — which specifically invokes the idea of engraving, and it is Moshe who is uniquely designated *mechokek*. That combination clinches the identification.

### Iyov & Meraglim

Rava offers an alternative: *Iyov bi-mei meraglim hayah* — Iyov lived in the time of the spies. This is derived from a different connection: the verse in Iyov describing his homeland as *eretz Utz* is linked to the phrase of the *meraglim*, *ha-yesh bah eitz* — "is there a tree there?" The Gemara challenges this: *Utz* and *eitz* are not the same word. The Gemara responds that the connection is not merely orthographic but substantive: Moshe was saying to Bnei Yisrael, "Is there still alive that man whose years are long as a tree, and who protects his generation like a tree?" — that is, was Iyov still alive and possibly protecting the Canaanites, making the conquest more difficult?

Beyond the textual mechanics, there is a significant conceptual difference between these two datings. If Iyov was in Moshe's time and Moshe authored the book, the text functions as a *sefer chochmah* — a wisdom literature addressing the perennial question of *tzaddik ve-ra lo, rasha ve-tov lo* — through the pen of the greatest *navi*, the one who himself pleaded *hodeini na et derachecha*. If Iyov is associated with the *meraglim*, the historical frame shifts: Iyov becomes associated not with Moshe's authorship but with a particular moment of communal crisis and failure of faith, a moment when divine justice seemed profoundly unclear. The book is thus oriented differently in each case — less toward universal wisdom literature and more toward a specific historical experience of fractured *emunah*.

### Iyov as Mashal

A more radical view is raised anonymously in the Gemara: *Iyov lo hayah ve-lo nivra ela mashal hayah* — Iyov never existed and was never created; he was only a *mashal*. The purpose of the book, on this view, is to dramatize the questions of divine justice and suffering, but it makes no historical claim about an actual individual named Iyov.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani firmly rejects this view. He points to the opening verse: *ish hayah be-eretz Utz Iyov shemo* — "There was a man in the land of Utz, Iyov was his name." How can one claim he never existed when the text gives him a name and a geographic location? The anonymous opinion responds: consider the *mashal* of the poor man and his single lamb told to David by Natan the Prophet — it too employs concrete imagery, a name, and a setting, yet it is obviously a *mashal*. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani replies: that *mashal* does not name the individual or give the name of his city. Iyov is given *both* his personal name *and* the name of his land, which places him as a real historical figure. The *mashal* view is thus rejected by Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, though it is worth noting that the view itself is presented anonymously — the Gemara records it without attributing it to any named *amora*.

### Iyov's Return

Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Eliezer both hold that *Iyov me-olei golah hayah* — Iyov was among those who returned from Babylonian exile to rebuild the *Bayit Sheni*. After his return, his *beis midrash* was located in Tiberias. This dating situates the book of Iyov very differently from the earlier views: rather than a figure of the remote past, Iyov becomes a contemporary of the Second Temple period, someone who lived through the *churban ha-Bayit* and the *galus Bavel* and emerged on the other side. His questioning of divine justice takes on immediate historical resonance — just as Eicha is the voice of lamentation from within the destruction, Iyov could be read as the voice of an individual survivor grappling with the same questions of theodicy that the *churban* raised for the entire nation.

### 210 Years of Iyov

Rav Ashi raises a calculation: *yemei shnosaiv shel Iyov mi-sha'ah she-nichnesu Yisrael le-Mitzrayim ve-ad she-yatzu* — the years of Iyov's life spanned from when Yisrael entered Egypt until they departed. This yields 210 years — the traditional duration of *galus Mitzrayim* — a number that can be derived from the *pesukim* in Iyov itself. The text records that after Iyov's afflictions, God doubled what he had; if Iyov initially had 70 years, doubling produces 140 more, for a total of 210. This figure exactly matches the duration of the Egyptian exile according to *Chazal*.

The implication, taken at face value, is that Iyov actually lived *during* the period of *galus Mitzrayim*. The symbolic resonance is powerful: Iyov's life of suffering, which contains no visible redemption for 210 years, runs precisely parallel to Bnei Yisrael's slavery in Egypt. Both experiences raise with full force the question of where God is and what the logic of divine governance is. And in both cases — though in very different ways — the story ultimately ends with some form of divine response.

This dating connects interestingly with the *midrashic* tradition, not elaborated in this Gemara, that Iyov served as one of Pharaoh's advisors. If Iyov was a figure of the Egyptian period, he was not himself enslaved but was in proximity to the oppressors, which creates its own theological complexity.

### Duration vs. Period

The Gemara recognizes that Rav Ashi's calculation creates a tension with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Eliezer's view that Iyov returned from *galus Bavel*. To resolve this, the Gemara adjusts the interpretation: *eima ki-mi-sha'ah she-nichnesu Yisrael le-Mitzrayim ve-ad she-yatzu* — perhaps the verse means only that the *duration* of Iyov's life was 210 years, matching the length of the Egyptian exile, without necessarily implying that he *lived during* that period. Iyov may have lived 210 years at some other historical moment; the number is what is significant, not the timing.

This resolution allows all views to coexist: Iyov lived 210 years. Those who place him in the time of Moshe, or the *meraglim*, or the *galus Bavel*, are offering different historical locations for those 210 years. Across all these datings, the various rabbinic opinions are unified in their perception that the book of Iyov is always associated with periods of profound national or individual crisis — times when God seems most hidden and the demands on *emunah* are most acute.

### Iyov & Nations

A *baraita* is then cited: *shiva nevi'im nisnab'u le-umos ha-olam* — seven prophets prophesied to the nations of the world: Bilam and his father, Iyov, Elifaz ha-Temani, Bildad ha-Shuchi, Tzofar ha-Na'amati, and Elihu ben Barachel ha-Buzi — that is, Iyov and his four friends from the book itself. This raises an immediate question: if Iyov is among the prophets to the nations, does that not imply he was non-Jewish? Yet the view of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Eliezer placed him among the Jewish returnees from Babylonian exile.

The Gemara challenges the premise: Elihu ben Barachel is identified in the *baraita* as a prophet to the nations, yet Elihu is clearly Jewish. The text itself says he was *mi-mishpachas Ram* — from the family of Ram — which *Chazal* understand as a reference to the lineage of Avraham. So being listed among the prophets to the nations does not in itself determine whether the prophet is Jewish or not; it indicates the direction of the prophecy, not the ethnic identity of the prophet.

### Universal Prophecy

The Gemara then asks a deeper question: all prophets of Israel presumably have relevance for the nations as well — why single out these figures specifically as prophets to the nations? The answer: *hasam ikar nevuasaihu le-Yisrael* — in the case of the prophets of Israel, their prophecy is primarily directed to Israel; the nations can derive insight from it as well, but that is secondary. *Hacha ikar nevuasaihu le-umos ha-olam* — in the case of Iyov and his companions, the primary address of their prophecy is the nations of the world.

This is a remarkable conclusion with which to close the discussion of Iyov. The book of Iyov is unique among the books of *Tanakh* not only in its themes — the suffering of the righteous, the opacity of divine justice, the testing of *emunah* — but in its fundamental orientation. Where the prophets of Israel speak primarily to Israel and only secondarily to humanity, the book of Iyov speaks primarily to all of humanity. It is, in the deepest sense, a universal book. The questions it raises — where is God in suffering? how does one maintain faith in the face of inexplicable evil? — are questions that belong to no single people. The Gemara's conclusion that *ikar nevuasaihu le-umos ha-olam* may thus be understood not as a relegation of Iyov to the periphery of *Tanakh* but as a recognition of its singular character: it is the book within *Tanakh* whose primary address is the human condition as such.

---

---

# Bava Batra 16

## Job's Identity & Dating

### Righteous Gentile

The daf begins mid-passage on 15b, approximately fifteen lines from the top, where the Gemara has been engaged in an extended discussion of the Book of Iyov — who composed it, when it was written, and now, critically, whether Iyov himself was Jewish. The Gemara had already noted the position that Iyov was among those who returned from exile in the time of the Second *Beit HaMikdash*, a position that implies he was Jewish. This now becomes the occasion for a more direct examination of the question.

A *baraita* is cited as a challenge: *Chasid haya b'umot ha'olam v'Iyov shmo* — there was a righteous man among the nations of the world and his name was Iyov. *V'lo ba l'olam ela k'dei l'kabel scharo* — he came into the world solely in order to receive his reward. The *baraita* continues: God brought afflictions upon him, and he began cursing and blaspheming. As a result, God doubled his reward in this world in order to exclude him from the World to Come.

The thrust of the *baraita* is striking. It is not merely placing Iyov among the righteous gentiles but offering a critical reading of his character: he was perhaps a *chasid* in outward behavior, but his righteousness was conditional — performed in expectation of worldly reward. When that reward did not materialize and suffering came instead, he regretted everything and turned to blasphemy. God then settled all accounts in this world, granting him the doubled portion described at the end of the book, while forfeiting his share in the *Olam Haba*. The word *kafal* — doubled — echoes the explicit *pesuk* at the end of Iyov, where God restores twice what had been taken.

It is worth noting that this reading sits in tension with the *pshat* of the book itself, where Iyov does not ultimately blaspheme but maintains his integrity. The Gemara is here offering a critical *midrashic* lens, and as we will see throughout the rest of the daf, this lens will be applied in considerable depth.

The *baraita* clearly indicates that Iyov was not Jewish, which stands in tension with the earlier position that he was among those who returned in the time of the Second Temple. The Gemara therefore declares: *tana'ei hi* — it is a dispute among *Tannaim*.

### Job's Timeline

A *baraita* is then cited presenting several *Tanna'ic* positions on when Iyov lived. Rabbi Eliezer says Iyov lived *bimei shfot ha-shoftim* — in the time of the judges. The proof is from a verse in Iyov: *Hen atem kulchem chazitem, v'lamah zeh hevel tehavalu* — you have all seen, and why are you acting with such foolishness? The word *hevel* connects to a generation described as entirely *hevel*, and Rabbi Eliezer identifies this with the period of the judges, as we will see shortly, a period of profound moral collapse.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says Iyov lived in the time of Achashverosh, deriving this from the verse *v'lo nimtza nashim yafot kibnot Iyov b'chol ha'aretz* — no women as beautiful as the daughters of Iyov were found in all the land. The connection is to the period when beautiful women were sought throughout the entire land — that is, the search conducted for Achashverosh. The Gemara raises an objection: could we not say this refers to the time of David, when a young woman was sought for him in his old age? The Gemara deflects: there it says *b'chol gvul Yisrael* — within the borders of Israel; here it says *b'chol ha'aretz* — the entire land, pointing to a broader and more universal search, consistent with the Purim narrative. These identifications seem more like attempts to anchor a universalist story in a particular historical moment than arguments that carry strong thematic weight.

Rabbi Natan says Iyov lived *bimei malchut Sheva* — in the time of the kingdom of Sheba — drawing directly from the internal evidence of the Iyov narrative itself, where the Shebeans attack his cattle. Whatever the kingdom of Sheba refers to historically, that is when Iyov lived.

The *Chachamim* say he lived *bimei Kasdim* — in the time of the Chaldeans. Rashi identifies this as the Chaldeans of Nebuchadnezzar, thus placing Iyov in the period of the destruction of the First *Beit HaMikdash* — a dating that carries stronger thematic resonance, perhaps connecting him to those who later returned from exile in *golah*. The proof again comes from the story itself, where the Chaldeans form three separate divisions and attack his camels.

Finally, *yesh omrim* — some say — Iyov lived in the time of Yaakov, and indeed married Dinah bat Yaakov after the events involving Shechem. The proof is from a verbal analogy: the word *nevalah* appears in Iyov — *k'davar achat ha-nevalot tedaberi* — and the same word appears in the account of Dinah — *ki nevalah asah b'Yisrael*.

### Post-Mosaic Prophecy

The Gemara now draws a striking conclusion: *v'chulehu Tanna'ei sevira lehu d'Iyov mi'Yisrael havah levar mi'yesh omrim* — all the *Tannaim* implicitly hold that Iyov was Jewish, except for the last opinion that he lived in the time of Yaakov. This requires explanation, because on its face, nothing about these datings implies anything about Iyov's ethnicity. Why should placing Iyov in the time of Achashverosh or the Chaldeans indicate that he was Jewish?

The Gemara explains: *d'ee salka da'atach me'chassidei umot ha'olam havah* — if you were to assume he was a righteous gentile — *basar d'shachiv Moshe mi shari Shchina al ovdei kochavim?* — after Moshe died, does the divine presence come to rest upon gentiles? Assuming that Iyov was a *navi*, as the appearance of God to him at the end of the book suggests, and assuming that all these *Tannaim* place him after the time of Moshe, he could not have been a gentile. After Moshe, *nevuah* was restricted to Israel.

The source for this restriction: *de'amar mar bikesh Moshe shelo tishreh Shchina al ovdei kochavim v'nasan lo* — Moshe requested that the divine presence not rest upon the nations, and this was granted to him, as it says *v'niflinu ani v'amecha* — you and I and your people shall be distinct from all the other nations. That distinctiveness includes the realm of prophecy.

Therefore, any *Tanna* who places Iyov after Moshe must implicitly regard him as Jewish, since a gentile could not have received prophecy in that era. The only exception is the opinion of *yesh omrim*, who places him in the time of Yaakov — well before Moshe's prayer — and thus can consistently hold that Iyov was a righteous gentile. All others must regard him as Jewish.

---

## Job's Licentiousness

### Licentiousness Era

Rabbi Yochanan now offers an observation about the moral character of Iyov's generation: *doro shel Iyov shatuf b'zimah hayah* — his generation was awash with licentiousness. The proof comes from the same verse already cited: *Hen atem kulchem chazitem* — you have all seen. The word *chazitem*, to see, is linked by Rabbi Yochanan to the erotic use of the same root elsewhere — *shuvi shuvi ha-Shulamit shuvi shuvi v'nechezeh bach*, where the gazing is decidedly romantic in character. Here too, says Rashi, the *chazitem* is not a neutral visual act but a lascivious, covetous gaze.

The Gemara raises a challenge: perhaps *chazitem* refers to prophetic vision, *chazon*, as in *chazon Yeshayahu ben Amotz*? The Gemara dismisses this: the verse immediately follows *chazitem* with the rebuke *v'lamah zeh hevel tehavalu* — why are you acting with such foolishness — which would be incongruous if the vision were prophetic. The pairing of gaze with *hevel* reveals the nature of the seeing: something vain, something dissolute.

### Judges & Judges

Rabbi Yochanan adds a further teaching: *mai d'chtiv vayehi bimei shefot ha-shoftim* — what does it mean that in the days when the judges judged? The phrase is homiletically rendered: *dor she-shofet et shofte'av* — a generation that judged its own judges. When a judge would tell someone to remove the splinter from his eye — *tol kisam mibein einecha* — the person could retort: remove the beam from your own eye. The judges had so completely forfeited their moral authority through their own corruption that no rebuke could carry weight.

The Gemara extends the analogy further. If a judge said *caspech haya lesigim* — your silver has become dross — the person could respond *savech mahul bamayim* — your wine is watered down. Moral instruction requires a degree of moral standing in the instructor; when that standing collapses, the entire social order collapses with it. This was the character of the generation associated with Iyov.

---

## Satan's Challenge

### Job vs Abraham

The Gemara now turns to an extended *midrashic* reading of the narrative of Iyov, beginning with the heavenly prologue. The opening verse: *vayehi hayom vayavo'u bnei ha-elohim l'hit'yatzev al Hashem vayavo gam ha-Satan betocham* — it was the day, and the divine beings came to present themselves before God, and the Satan came among them as well.

God asks the Satan where he has come from, and the Satan replies that he has been roaming the earth. The Gemara then adds a *midrashic* expansion of the Satan's report: *shat'ti b'chol ha-olam kulo v'lo matzati ne'eman k'avdecha Avraham* — I have traversed the entire world and I have found no one as faithful as your servant Avraham. The connection to Avraham is established through the verbal echo: the Satan uses the language of *mi-hithalech ba-aretz*, which echoes the divine command to Avraham — *kum hithalech ba-aretz l'orkah u-l'rochbah ki lecha etnenah*. Avraham was promised the land, yet when the time came to bury Sarah, he could find no place of his own and was compelled to purchase a burial plot from Ephron at an exorbitant price. Despite this apparent failure of the divine promise, *lo hirher achar midotecha* — he harbored no thoughts questioning God's justice. No one, says the Satan, comes close to Avraham.

God responds: *ha-samta libcha el avdi Iyov* — have you considered my servant Iyov? *Ki ein kamohu ba-aretz* — there is none like him in the land. Rabbi Yochanan observes that the praise accorded to Iyov is actually greater than that given to Avraham. By Avraham it says: *ki ata yadati ki yerei elohim ata* — now I know that you fear God. By Iyov the verse says: *ish tam v'yashar yerei elohim v'sar me-ra* — pure, upright, fearing God, and turning away from evil. Multiple appellations are applied to Iyov that are absent from the praise of Avraham.

What is the meaning of *v'sar me-ra* — turning away from evil? Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel explains: *Iyov vatran b'mamona hayah* — Iyov was generous with his money, not exacting in financial dealings. The usual way of the world is that if one owes a half a *peruta* to a worker, one might combine it with a purchase to make change. Iyov simply waived what was owed him, forgoing his due.

### Fear for Naught

The Satan responds with his famous challenge: *ha-chinam yerei Iyov elohim* — does Iyov fear God for nothing? *Halo ata sakota ba-ado u-v'ad beito* — you have placed a protective hedge around him and his household. Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak expounds the phrase *maaseh yadav berachta*: anyone who received even a small coin from Iyov was blessed — his giving was like the Rebbe's dollars, carrying a blessing in and of itself. Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Chanina adds that Iyov's flocks had burst beyond the normal bounds of nature — *partzu gidro shel olam* — his sheep were so powerful they would kill the wolves rather than the other way around.

The Satan then issues his challenge: *shelach na yadcha u-ga b'chol asher lo im lo al panecha yevarecheka* — send forth your hand and strike all that he has, and he will surely curse you to your face. *Yevarecheka* here is a familiar Talmudic euphemism, as it is in the biblical text itself. God accepts the challenge, granting the Satan dominion over everything Iyov possesses: *hineh kol asher lo b'yadecha* — all that he has is in your hand. The sole limitation: *rak elav al tishlach yadecha* — do not lay your hand on his person.

### First Afflictions

The narrative then unfolds rapidly. Iyov's children are feasting in the home of the firstborn. The Gemara pauses on the verse describing the cattle plowing and the donkeys grazing nearby: *ha-bakar hayu chorshot v'ha-atonot ro'ot al yadeihem*. Rabbi Yochanan derives from this that God had given Iyov a foretaste of the *Olam Ha-ba* — things were flourishing in a supernatural way, as Rashi explains, with seed sprouting on the very day it was planted.

Messenger after messenger arrives in rapid succession, each arriving before the previous one has finished speaking. The Sabeans attack the oxen and donkeys; fire falls from heaven and destroys the flocks; the Chaldeans form three divisions and take the camels; and finally a great wind strikes the four corners of the house where Iyov's children are gathered, and they perish. Iyov rises, tears his garment, shaves his head, and declares:

> *Arom yatzati mi-beten imi v'arom ashuv shama, Hashem natan v'Hashem lakach yehi shem Hashem mevorach* — Naked I came from my mother's womb and naked shall I return. God has given and God has taken; may the name of God be blessed.

*B'chol zot lo chata Iyov v'lo natan tiflah l'elohim* — with all of this, Iyov did not sin, and did not ascribe any impropriety to God.

### Body Affliction

The heavenly court convenes again. The same exchange takes place: God asks the Satan where he has come from, and the Satan again reports roaming the earth and again places Avraham at the pinnacle of righteousness, recalling the episode of Sarah's burial. God again directs attention to Iyov: *ve-odeinu machazik b'tumaso* — he still holds fast to his integrity. *Va-tesiteni vo levalo chinam* — and you incited me against him for nothing.

Rabbi Yochanan observes here: *ilmalei mikra kasuv ee efshar l'omro* — were it not that the verse itself says this, it would be impossible to say such a thing. The imagery is of God being, as it were, persuaded or provoked — *kaviyachol k'mi she-nistatta* — as if God could be enticed. This is a striking theological problem embedded in the text itself.

The Satan escalates his challenge: *or be-or v'chol asher la-ish yiten be-ad nafsho* — skin for skin, a person will give everything for his own life. Afflict his body and he will curse you. God grants expanded permission: *hinehu b'yadecha ach et nafsho shemor* — he is in your hand, but preserve his life.

### Satan Identified

Rabbi Yitzchak notes that the Satan's predicament was more difficult than Iyov's own: *mashal l'eved she-amar lo rabbo shevor chavit u-shmor yeina* — it is like a servant whose master said: break the barrel but don't spill the wine. The Satan had to afflict Iyov's body while leaving his soul intact.

A *baraita* is cited that broadens the characterization of the Satan beyond the Iyov story: *yoreid u-mat'eh v'olah u-margiz v'notel reshut v'notel neshama* — he descends and leads astray, then ascends and provokes God's anger, receives permission, and takes the person's life. This moves the discussion from the particular narrative of Iyov toward a more general description of the Satan's operating mode — seducing people into sin, then securing divine authorization to take their lives as punishment. The resemblance to the Christian conception of Satan is evident, and this is precisely where Rashi's comment becomes significant.

Rashi adds to his explanation the phrase *mi-kaivan she-nittan reshut, d'chtiv va-tesiteni vo* — since permission was granted, as the verse says "you have incited me against him." Rashi is emphasizing that the entire enterprise — not just the final lethal authorization, but the whole process — operates only within the framework of divine permission. The Satan is not an independent opposing force; everything he does, from the initial seduction onward, is conducted under the authority God has granted him. The verse *va-tesiteni vo* is not simply the moment of authorization for a particular act but the foundational grant that underlies the whole story. This is not the Christian Satan, a power operating with some degree of independence from God; this is a figure who cannot take a single step without divine sanction.

One might press further: if God allowed himself to be incited — *kaviyachol* — does this not mean God can be manipulated, even if the Satan is not acting independently? The Gemara raised this question earlier with the observation *ilmalei mikra kasuv*, and it did not fully resolve it. Rashi's comment can be read as adding another dimension: God's allowing himself to be engaged in this way is itself part of what God is permitting to happen. The Satan is not operating independently, but God's own responsiveness to the process is also, in some sense, something God is choosing.

Resh Lakish then offers a formulation that has generated much discussion: *hu Satan hu yetzer hara hu malach ha-mavet* — the Satan, the evil inclination, and the angel of death are one and the same. This identification pulls in an inward direction: the Satan is not primarily an external metaphysical force but is identical with the *yetzer hara* within the human being. The tendency to read Satan as merely the name for our internal inclination toward evil — as some *acharonim* do in explaining the purpose of blowing the *shofar k'dei l'arvav et ha-Satan* — is at least supported by this identification.

But the equation *hu malach ha-mavet* is harder to fully internalize, as the prooftexts make clear. The verse *rak elav al tishlach yadecha* — do not touch his person — and the corresponding *ach et nafsho shemor* — preserve his life — show that the Satan had the potential to take Iyov's life; therefore he must be the *malach ha-mavet*. This pushes the imagery back toward the external, the literal. The honest reading is that this Gemara holds both simultaneously, and the tension between externalizing these forces and internalizing them is part of what makes the passage so rich.

### Leshem Shamayim

Rabbi Levi teaches: *Satan u-Pninah l'shem shamayim nitkavnu* — both the Satan and Pninah acted with heavenly intent. The Satan saw that God was praising Iyov so lavishly and worried that Avraham's merits were being forgotten — how could it be that this other figure, possibly not even Jewish, was being praised above the greatest of the patriarchs? His challenge, on this reading, was a defense of Avraham's legacy. Similarly, Pninah provoked Channah — *v'ka'astah tzaratah gam ka'as ba'avur har'imah* — in order to prompt Channah to pray, which ultimately led to the birth of Shmuel. Rashi notes that *har'imah* can be read as *l'hartinah* — to provoke her into petitioning God.

Rava bar Yaakov reportedly delivered this teaching in the town of Pappunya. The *aggadah* concludes: the Satan came and kissed him on his feet in gratitude, since it is rare for a *darshan* to advocate on the Satan's behalf.

This teaching is susceptible to two opposing readings. One might see it as tempering the culpability of destructive actors who genuinely believed they were acting for a righteous cause. The other — and arguably more powerful — reading is a warning: even those who are absolutely convinced they are acting *l'shem shamayim* can cause enormous harm and destruction. The path to wrongdoing is often paved with self-righteous intent. The fact that the Satan comes to kiss the preacher's feet does not resolve which lesson is primary, but the very structure of the *aggadah* — linking the Satan's destructive challenge to the same category as Pninah's painful provocations — suggests that the label *l'shem shamayim* does not, by itself, justify the means.

---

## Job's Hidden Heresy

### Against Satan

The narrative now notes that *b'chol zot lo chata Iyov bi-sfatav* — with all of this, Iyov did not sin with his lips. The Gemara emphasizes the qualifier: *bi-sfatav* — with his lips — implying that he may have sinned in his heart. Rava states directly: *bi-sfatav lo chata b'libo chata* — he did not sin with his lips, but in his heart he sinned.

The Gemara then cites a verse from Iyov: *eretz nitnah b'yad rasha pnei shofteha yechaseh im lo efo mi hu* — the land is given over to the wicked; the face of its judges is covered — if not then who is it? Rava explains: *bikeish Iyov la-hafoch k'ara al piha* — Iyov was trying to turn the bowl upside down, to overturn any sense of divine justice. He was denying *hashgacha*, denying that righteousness and wickedness have consequences.

Abaye responds: *lo dibeir Iyov ela k'neged Satan* — he spoke only against the Satan, not against God. His complaint was not that God permits injustice, but that the Satan causes evil in the world. The Gemara then notes that this is in fact a *Tanna'ic* dispute, paralleled by Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that Iyov was trying to overturn everything, and Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that he spoke only against the Satan.

The observation is also made — in line with the reading attributed to the Maharsha — that the text said Iyov did not sin with his lips, and yet immediately proceeds to quote things Iyov actually said out loud. The resolution is that *lo chata bi-sfatav* does not mean he said nothing critical; it means that his explicit words, taken at face value, were not outright heresy. They were, at most, a grappling and a struggle. But the Gemara is now undertaking a close reading that will uncover, beneath the surface of those words, what Iyov was really thinking.

### Causation & Choice

Rava continues the analysis. The verse *al da'at'cha ki lo ersha v'ein mi-yadcha matzil* — on your account I have not done evil, and none can deliver from your hand — yields the following exposition: Iyov was trying to exempt the entire world from judgment. He said: *barata shor parsotav sdukot, barata chamor parsotav klutot* — you created the ox with split hooves, you created the donkey with an uncloven hoof. Everything is simply the product of divine creation. *Barata Gan Eden barata Gehennom, barata tzaddikim barata resha'im* — you created the righteous and you created the wicked. No one truly chooses; everyone is merely what God made them. The phrase *al da'at'cha* — on your account, according to your design — means: it is all predetermined, and judgment is therefore incoherent.

Iyov's friends respond, as quoted by the Gemara: *af ata tifer yira v'tigra sicha lifnei El* — you are dismantling fear of God with your words, you are taking away from the proper attitude before the Almighty. And the response to Iyov's position is: it is true that God created the *yetzer hara*, but *bara lo Torah tavlin* — he also gave the Torah as the remedy. The *yetzer hara* is part of our nature; the Torah gives us the capacity to address it. We make choices. The existence of the evil inclination does not eliminate human agency; it is the context within which human agency is exercised.

### Widow's Blessing

A *derasha* of Rava provides an aside on Iyov's charitable deeds, illuminating the verse *birkat oved alai tavo v'leiv almana arni* — the blessing of the perishing shall come upon me, and the heart of the widow I made sing. The first clause, *birkat oved*, teaches that Iyov had a distinctive way of helping orphans: he would take possession of their field — *gozel sadeh mi-yetomim* — improve it — *u-mashpichah* — and then return it to them. From the orphan's perspective, it looked as though the field had been lost; in the end it was returned improved. The orphan was the *oved* — the one who seemed to have lost — and the experience ultimately became a *berachah*.

The second clause, *leiv almana*, describes how Iyov would assist widows who could not find a husband: he would attach his name to a widow — perhaps creating the impression of his interest in her, or vouching for her family standing — so that others would come forward to marry her, and her heart would sing.

### Equal to God

Rava focuses on the verse *lu yishkol ka'asi va-havati b'moznayim yis'u yachad* — would that my vexation were weighed, and my anguish placed in the scales together. The key word is *yachad* — together — implying that Iyov was placing himself and God on the same side of the scale, demanding that they be weighed as equals. Rava responds: *afra l'fumeih d'Iyov* — dirt in the mouth of Iyov. *Chavruta klapei Shamaya?* — you think you're on equal footing with heaven? This is a different kind of objection from those that preceded it. When Iyov questioned whether God's justice was consistent, or when he denied moral causation, the Gemara did not invoke this level of condemnation. But placing oneself on equal standing with God — that is the crossing of a line.

The distinction the Gemara is drawing is between legitimate theological struggle and an attitude of presumptuous equality. Avraham engaged God in argument over Sodom, but prefaced it with *v'anochi afar va-efer* — I am dust and ashes. The questioning was not from a position of equality but from a position of profound humility. Iyov's *yachad* — let us be weighed together — implies a parity that is theologically impermissible.

The verse continues: *lu yesh beineinu mochiach yashet yado al shneinu* — if only there were an arbiter between us to place his hand upon us both. Again: *shneinu* — the two of us, as equals. Rava repeats: *afra l'fumeih d'Iyov. Klum yesh eved she-mochiach et rabo?* — is there ever a servant who adjudicates against his master? The problem is not the questioning per se; it is the tone, the posture of equivalence.

### Resurrection Denial

Rava identifies one further heresy in Iyov's words: *kalah anan va-yelech ken yored she'ol lo ya'aleh* — as the cloud dissipates and vanishes, so one who descends to the grave shall not rise. Rava says: *mikan she-kafar Iyov bi-tchiyat ha-meitim* — here we see that Iyov denied the resurrection of the dead. Those who descend shall not come back up.

This too is now placed alongside the other items being extracted from beneath the surface of Iyov's words — the denial of moral causation, the presumption of equality with God, and now the denial of *tchiyat ha-meitim*.

---

## God's Answer

### Whirlwind Response

The final section of the book, in which God appears to Iyov in the whirlwind, is now given its *midrashic* treatment. Rava observes: *Iyov bi-se'arah charaf u-vi-se'arah heshivuhu* — Iyov blasphemed with a whirlwind, and was responded to in a whirlwind. The reference to Iyov's blasphemy is the verse *asher bi-se'arah yeshufeni* — who sweeps me away with a whirlwind. The Gemara provides the expanded *midrashic* reading of what Iyov was really saying: *Ribbono shel Olam, shema ruach se'arah avrah lefanecha v'nitchalef lecha bein Iyov le-Oyev* — Master of the Universe, perhaps a stormy wind passed before you and confused you — perhaps you mixed up *Iyov* with *oyev*, you thought I was your enemy and that is why you afflicted me. The wordplay on *Iyov* and *oyev* — Job and enemy — is the vehicle for the blasphemy: you have been mistaken, God; you don't know what you're doing. This is the *chiref* — the blaspheming — referenced by Rava.

God responds in kind, also from within a whirlwind: *va-ya'an Hashem et Iyov min ha-se'arah vayomar, azor na k'gibor chalatzecha, esh'al'cha v'hodi'eni* — gird your loins like a mighty man, I will ask you and you will inform me.

### Hair Follicles

God's response takes the form of demonstrating the depth of divine knowledge and providence through a series of examples from the natural world. The first play on the word *se'arah* — storm — converts it to *sa'ar* — hair. God says: *harbe nimin barati ba-adam* — I have made many hairs on the human being. *V'chol nima v'nima barati lah gumah bifnei atzmah* — every individual hair I created its own follicle, so that no two hairs draw from the same follicle. Why? *She-imale shtayim yonkot mi-gumah achat machshichot me'or einav shel adam* — if two hairs were drawing from a single follicle they would darken a person's eyesight.

*Bein gumah le-gumah lo nitchalef li, bein Iyov le-oyev nitchalef li?* — if I can distinguish between one follicle and the next, do you think I would confuse Iyov with an enemy? The grandeur of the argument is in its very specificity: the God who governs the microscopic logistics of human hair growth certainly knows the difference between the righteous and the wicked.

### Raindrops & Thunder

The same demonstration is extended to the natural phenomena of rain and thunder. *Harbe tipin barati be-avim* — I made many drops in the clouds. *V'chol tipah v'tipah barati lah dfus bifnei atzmah* — every single drop has its own mold, its own form. The Gemara derives the meaning of the word *te'alah* as *dfus* — mold or form — from a verse where *te'alah* appears in the context of a constructed trench or channel. If two drops were to emerge from the same mold, they would completely destroy the land and render it incapable of producing fruit.

*Bein tipah le-tipah lo nitchalef li, bein Iyov le-oyev nitchalef li?*

Similarly with thunder: *harbe kolot barati be-avim* — I made many sounds in the clouds. *V'chol kol v'kol barati lo shvil bifnei atzmo* — every thunderclap has its own path through the sky. If two sounds were to travel the same path they would destroy the world. *Bein kol le-kol lo nitchalef li, bein Iyov le-oyev nitchalef li?*

### Ibex & Eagle

God then turns to the animal kingdom. *Ha-yadeta et ledet ya'alei sela* — do you know the time when the mountain ibex gives birth? The *ya'alah* is described as *achzarit al baneha* — cruel to her offspring. When she crouches to give birth she ascends to the mountaintop, so that the newborn falls from the cliff and would perish. What does God do? *Mazmin lah nesher she-mekablo bi-chanafav u-minicho lefaneha* — I send an eagle that catches the falling newborn in its wings and places it gently before the mother.

*V'ilmale makdim rega echad o me'acher rega echad miyad met* — if the eagle arrives even one minute too early or one minute too late, the newborn dies. *Bein rega le-rega lo nitchalef li, bein Iyov le-oyev nitchalef li?*

### Hind's Birth

The analogy is then given for the hind in childbirth. The hind's womb is narrow. When she crouches to give birth, God sends a snake — *drakon* — that bites her at the womb, causing it to open and allow the birth. *V'ilmale makdim rega echad o me'acher rega echad miyad metah* — if the timing is off by even a minute, she dies in childbirth. *Bein regel le-regel lo nitchalef li, bein Iyov le-oyev nitchalef li?*

### Omniscience

The unified thrust of all these examples is that God manages the universe with a precision that goes down to the individual hair follicle, the individual raindrop, the individual thunderclap, the individual moment of an animal's birth. The one who orchestrates all of this with such perfect particularity cannot be confused about the moral standing of a human being. The challenge of Iyov — that perhaps God confused him with an enemy — is refuted not by a theological argument about divine nature but by the sheer evidence of divine care in the created order.

---

## Friends Arrive

### Spoke Thoughtlessly

After the divine response, the text says: *Iyov lo veda'at yedaber u-vi-dvarav lo ve-haskel* — Iyov spoke without knowledge, and without understanding in his words. Rava derives from here: *mikan she-ein adam nitpas bi-sha'at tza'aro* — a person cannot be held responsible for what he says in his hour of anguish. After all the analysis that has been devoted to excavating the heresies beneath Iyov's words, the divine verdict is not condemnation but an acknowledgment that he was speaking from a place of pain, not of considered theological reflection. God does not say that Iyov sinned grievously; he says that Iyov spoke without knowledge. The tradition therefore establishes that one who speaks out in the midst of acute suffering is not held to the same standard of accountability as one who speaks deliberately.

### Crowns & Trees

The final section of the narrative brings Iyov's three friends onto the scene. *Va-yishme'u sheloshet rei'ei Iyov et kol ha-ra'ah ha-zot ha-ba'ah eilav* — Iyov's three friends heard of all the evil that had befallen him — *Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite* — and they gathered to come to mourn with him and to comfort him.

*Va-yivo'adu yachdav* — they assembled together. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav expounds: *melamed she-nichnasu kulam be-sha'ar echad* — they all entered through the same gate. And a *Tanna* teaches that they each lived 300 *parsaos* apart from one another and yet all managed to arrive at the same moment.

How did they know what was happening? The Gemara offers two traditions. One says that each of them possessed a crown — *klila* — engraved with the faces of the others, and Rashi adds that each face had the person's name inscribed upon it. When one of the companions was suffering, *partzufo mishtane* — the face on the crown would change, signaling distress. The other tradition says they each had a tree that represented the friend, and when the tree withered, they knew.

### Friends & Chavra

Rava cites a popular saying: *o chavra k'chavrei d'Iyov o mituta* — either friends like the friends of Iyov, or death. The point is that the friendship of Iyov's companions was of such extraordinary quality that it becomes the standard by which friendship is measured. They were so attuned to one another that they knew across hundreds of *parsaos* when one of them was suffering, and they traveled immediately to be present. The saying does not romanticize what happened after they arrived — the debates between Iyov and his friends occupy most of the book, and their theology is ultimately rebuked by God — but their act of solidarity, of dropping everything and coming, is held up as the model of true *chavra*.

---

---

# Bava Batra 17

## Daughters & Blessing

### Reviah vs. Merivah

The Gemara opens with the verse from Bereishit describing the proliferation of humanity upon the earth and the birth of daughters: *vayehi ki hechel ha'adam larov al pnei ha'adamah uvanot yuldu lahem*. Two great Amoraim read this verse in starkly contrasting ways. Rabbi Yochanan interprets *ki larov al pnei ha'adamah* as teaching that daughters bring *reviah* — increase — into the world. Daughters grow to become women who give birth, and so their birth is a blessing for the world's fecundity. Reish Lakish, however, reads the phrase as signaling *merivah* — strife — that comes into the world. These are not contradictory positions demanding resolution; they represent a genuine dispute over the valence of daughters' birth.

The dispute comes into focus through a question Reish Lakish presses upon Rabbi Yochanan: if daughters are such a blessing, why, when Iyov was rewarded at the end of the book of Iyov, were his sons doubled in number but not his daughters? If *reviah* is the point, why not twice as many daughters?

### Iyov's Daughters

Rabbi Yochanan's response is that though his daughters were not doubled *bishmot* — in their names, that is, in their numbers — they were doubled *beyofi*, in beauty. The Gemara proceeds to demonstrate this from the very names given to Iyov's three daughters at the end of the book. *Vayikra shem ha'achat Yemima veshem hashniyah Ketziah veshem hashlishit Keren Hapuch* — he called the first Yemima, the second Ketziah, and the third Keren Hapuch.

Yemima, the Gemara explains, was as beautiful as the day — *shehaytah domah leyom*. Ketziah was so fragrant as to recall the *ketziah* herb. As for Keren Hapuch, the school of Rabbi Shila interpreted her name as resembling the horn of a *cheresh*, some manner of antelope. The Sages in Eretz Yisrael, however, ridiculed this interpretation — *karna decheresh lekuta hi*, a horn of that animal is a curse, not a blessing. Rather, Rav Chisda explains: she was like *kurchama derishka*, saffron growing in the garden, which Rashi understands as the most praiseworthy of its kind. The verse *ki tikre'i ba-puch einayich* confirms that *puch* refers to something associated with beauty, much as eye shadow enhances appearance.

This is what draws the entire discussion of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish into the context of the end of the Iyov narrative — a question about whether the restored daughters represent an amplified blessing.

### Tannaitic View

The Gemara reports that when Rabbi Shimon, the son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, had a daughter, he was disappointed. His father consoled him with the principle: *reviah ba'ah le'olam* — increase comes to the world. Yet Bar Kappara dismissed this consolation sharply — *nichumim shel hevel nichmach avuch*, your father comforted you with a consolation that is *hevel*, emptiness. The implication, of course, is that the consolation was hollow.

The Gemara supports this with a *baraita*: *ee efshar la'olam belo zacharim uvelo nekevot* — the world cannot exist without both males and females; both are needed. And yet the *baraita* does not treat them symmetrically: *ashrei lemi shebanav zacharim, oy lo lemi shebanav nekevot* — praised is one whose children are males, woe to one whose children are females. The Gemara offers a parallel: the world cannot exist without perfumers or without tanners, yet one is praised for being a perfumer and bewailed for being a tanner — somebody must do unpleasant but necessary work. This is a striking and difficult passage, and it deserves to be named as such. The tension between the necessity of daughters and the lament attending their birth reflects social realities that are historically attested and that challenge contemporary sensibilities. Rather than explaining away what the Gemara says, it is more honest to acknowledge it directly and allow the reader to grapple with it on their own terms.

This dispute about how to regard the birth of daughters reflects a *machlokes Tannaim*, the Gemara notes — *ketannai*.

### Abraham's Bakol

The Gemara moves from there to the verse *v'Hashem berach et Avraham bakol* — and God blessed Avraham with *bakol*, with everything. What does *bakol* mean? Four Tannaitic opinions are presented.

Rabbi Meir says *shelo haytah lo bat* — he was blessed in that he had no daughters, reflecting the negative valuation of daughters found in the *baraita* above. Rabbi Yehuda says the opposite: *shehaytah lo bat* — the blessing *bakol* means he had a daughter as well, and that itself was the blessing of completeness. *Acherim* — Others — go further and say not only did Avraham have a daughter, her name was actually *Bakol*, so that when God blessed Avraham *bakol*, He was literally blessing him with his daughter whose name was Everything.

Rabbi Eliezer ha-Modai offers an entirely different reading, unrelated to sons or daughters. He says *bakol* refers to the gift of *itztagninus* — astrological knowledge — that was in Avraham's heart, such that all the kings of east and west would come to his door seeking his interpretations.

Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says that Avraham possessed a precious stone hung around his neck — *even tova haytah teluya betzavaro shel Avraham Avinu* — and whoever was ill and looked upon it was immediately healed. When Avraham died, God placed this stone in the sun, which is why people say *idli yoma idli katzira* — as the day grows stronger, the sick gain relief. The healing power of sunlight reflects, in this reading, that Avraham's stone was absorbed into the sun's rays and continues to bring healing to the world.

The Gemara then turns to two additional interpretations of *bakol*, both understood as special gifts Avraham received before he died. One is *davar acher shelo marad Esav b'yamav* — another reading of "everything" is that Avraham was blessed in that Esav, who would become so wicked, waited until after Avraham's death to rebel. He did not have to witness his grandson's *rishus* — that itself was a blessing.

A second *davar acher*: *she'asah Yishmael teshuvah b'yamav* — Yishmael did *teshuvah* during Avraham's lifetime, and Avraham was thus blessed to witness that.

The proof that Esav refrained from his sins during Avraham's lifetime comes from the verse *vayavo Esav min hasadeh v'hu ayef* — that he came from the field exhausted, which the Tanna connects to the day of Avraham's death. Yaakov was making a stew of lentils to comfort Yitzchak — *tavshil shel adashim l'nachem et Yitzchak aviv*. The Gemara asks: why specifically lentils? The Sages in Eretz Yisrael explain in the name of Rabba bar Mari: just as a lentil has no mouth — its surface is smooth with no crevice — so too a mourner should sit in silence rather than challenge or protest. An alternative explanation: lentils are spherical, and *avelut* is similarly spherical — it rolls through the world and returns to all who live. The practical difference between these two readings is whether eggs may be used for mourners' consolation: eggs have no mouth but are not perfectly spherical, so they would fit the first reason but not the second.

The Gemara then notes that Rabbi Yochanan teaches Esav committed five sins on that very day: *ba al na'arah m'orasah* — he had relations with a betrothed young woman; *harag et hanefesh* — he committed murder; *kafar b'ikar* — he denied the fundamental principle of God; *kafar b'tchiyat hametim* — he denied resurrection; and *shat et habechorah* — he despised the birthright, which is the only one made explicit in the text. Each of the first four is derived by *gezeirah shavah* or verbal parallel with other verses. A *Tosafot* notes a conceptual difficulty: according to the Gemara in the chapter of the four death penalties, the legal status of *eirusin* does not apply to the descendants of Noach, since for them betrothal is effected through *chuppah* without *kiddushin*. If so, how can Esav be culpable for relations with a *na'arah m'orasah*? The answer of the *Ri* is that even if it was not legally prohibited, it was morally reprehensible — *micho'ar hadavar* — and just as despising the birthright, though he was not commanded about it, was still counted against him, so too here.

As for Yishmael's *teshuvah*: the Gemara narrates that Ravina and Rav Chama bar Buzi were sitting before Rava, who dozed off. The students were discussing whether the expression *vayigva* — he expired — always signals a righteous death. One objected from the *dor hamabul*: it says *vayigva kol basar* by those who perished in the flood, and they were not righteous. The response was that the tradition applies specifically when the verse says both *vayigva* and *vayei'asef el amav* — he expired and was gathered to his people. Then the other raised a further difficulty: by Yishmael it says *vayigva vayei'asef* — was he righteous? At that moment, Rava woke up and told them: *dardakei* — children — Rabbi Yochanan taught that Yishmael did *teshuvah* in his father's lifetime.

The proof is from the verse *vayikberu oso Yitzchak veYishmael banav* — Yitzchak and Yishmael buried Avraham. Not only did Yishmael come to the burial, but he allowed Yitzchak to go first, thereby accepting Yitzchak's primacy as Avraham's principal heir. One might object that the verse is simply listing them in order of wisdom or importance, not reflecting their actions. But this cannot be the principle, because when Yitzchak was buried, the verse says *vayikberu oso Eisav veYaakov banav* — Esav is listed first. Esav, who did not do *teshuvah*, pressed ahead to be first; Yishmael, who did do *teshuvah*, stepped back and placed Yitzchak before him — *adburei adbreiyei*. From that deferral we derive that *teshuvah avad beyamav* — he did *teshuvah* in his lifetime.

---

## Death & Righteous

### Three Patriarchs

Following the discussion of *bakol*, the Gemara transitions to a series of numerical teachings about categories of righteous individuals and their deaths. The *baraita* teaches: *shlosha hit'iman ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu ba'olam hazeh me'ein ha'olam haba* — three people God gave a foretaste of the World to Come in this world. They are Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. The proof for each is the expression of completeness in the verses: Avraham was blessed *bakol* — with everything; Yitzchak said *va'ochal mikkol* — I ate from everything, before he gave the blessing; and Yaakov said *yesh li kol* — I have everything, when speaking to Esav. To say one has *everything* points to the truest everything, which is the *olam haba*. This is the source for the phrase *bakol mikkol kol* in *bentching*, expressing that Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov were each blessed with this sense of totality.

### No Yetzer Hara

The Gemara continues: *shelosha lo shalat bahen yetzer hara* — over three people the *yetzer hara* had no mastery. Again, the three Patriarchs, proven from *bakol mikkol kol*. One must be careful not to misread this. *Tosafot* clarifies: it cannot mean the *yetzer hara* had no influence whatsoever — for then, how would they have earned reward for their righteousness? Virtue requires the possibility of failure. Rather, *Tosafot* explains based on the principle *raglei chasidav yishmor*: once a person has spent the greater portion of his years without sinning, he is unlikely to sin thereafter. The Patriarchs, having pushed themselves so strenuously to distance themselves from sin from the beginning of their lives, received divine assistance such that from a certain point onward the *yetzer hara* no longer prevailed over them — *siyayam ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu mikan va'eilach shelo shalat bahen yetzer hara*.

There is an additional opinion: *ve'yesh omrim af David* — some add David, on the basis of the verse *v'libi chalal bekirbi* — my heart is empty within me — understood as the absence of the *yetzer hara* from his heart. The other view says David was merely describing the suffering of his afflictions, not a freedom from the *yetzer hara*.

### Six No Malach

The next *baraita*: *shisha lo shalat bahen malach hamavet* — over six, the angel of death had no mastery. This does not mean they did not die, but rather that they did not suffer in their deaths; they died *beneshikah*, with the divine kiss, peacefully, without the torments associated with the *malach hamavet*. The six are Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Moshe, Aharon, and Miriam. For the Patriarchs, the proof is again *bakol mikkol kol* — having all good means no suffering in death. For Moshe, Aharon, and Miriam, the proof is the phrase *al pi Hashem* — they died by the word of God, literally by the divine mouth, alluding to the divine kiss.

Rabbi Elazar adds that Miriam also died *beneshikah*, derived by *gezeirah shavah*: by Moshe it says *vayamot sham*, and by Miriam it says *vatamot sham* — the same language signals the same manner of death. If so, why does the verse not say *al pi Hashem* by Miriam? Because, the Gemara says, *shegnai hadavar lomar* — it would be unseemly to speak of the divine kiss in that way across the male–female divide, as it were. The language is therefore deliberately omitted, though the reality is derived through the verbal parallel.

### Seven Preserved

The *baraita* continues: *shivah lo shaltah bahen rimah vetolei'ah* — seven people were not consumed by worms or maggots after death. The seven are Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Moshe, Aharon, Miriam, and Binyamin ben Yaakov. For the Patriarchs the proof is again *bakol mikkol kol*; for Moshe, Aharon, and Miriam it is *al pi Hashem*. The connection to bodily preservation is explained by Rashi: the *malach hamavet*, in the process of taking the soul, deposits a drop of bile or poison into the body that causes it to decompose. Since these individuals did not die through the *malach hamavet*, their bodies were not subject to that decay.

Binyamin is added from the verse *yedid Hashem yishkon lavetach alav* — the beloved of God will dwell in security — which implies security even in death, meaning the body rests undisturbed.

*Ve'yesh omrim af David* — some add David, from the verse *af besari yishkon lavetach* — my flesh will dwell in security. The other opinion responds that David was praying for this — *rachamei hu dekabei* — it was not a statement of fact but a petition.

### Four Sinless Deaths
