The final *baraita* in this sequence: *arba'ah metu be'etyo shel nachash* — four people died on account of the serpent, meaning they had no personal sin warranting death; they died solely because human mortality entered the world through the nachash's deed in the Garden of Eden. The four are Binyamin ben Yaakov, Amram avi Moshe, Yishai avi David, and Khil'av ben David. These are figures who are almost entirely absent from the active narrative of Tanakh. The implication seems clear: to die without any sin of one's own, one must have essentially withdrawn from active engagement with the world. Those who act, lead, and contend in the world will inevitably, despite their best efforts, accumulate some degree of wrongdoing. A completely blameless death is the province of those who never became protagonists.

For all four, these are matters of tradition — *kulhu gemara* — except for Yishai, whose sinlessness is derived from a verse. The *pasuk* describes Amasa as the son of a man named Yitra *haYisraeli*, *asher ba el Avigayil bat Nachash achot Tzruya em Yoav* — who came to Avigayil the daughter of Nachash, the sister of Tzruya the mother of Yoav. But was Avigayil truly the daughter of Nachash? The verse elsewhere makes clear she was a daughter of Yishai, sister of David. Rather, *bat mi shemet be'etzo shel nachash* — she was the daughter of one who died only on account of the serpent and not due to any sin of his own. The name *Nachash* here is therefore not a proper name but a descriptor applied to Yishai: one who died solely because of the *nachash*'s deed.

This sequence of teachings forms a fitting, if implicit, coda to the entire *aggadeta* of Iyov. The Iyov narrative circles around the question of divine justice and undeserved suffering. The Gemara ends this long excursus with the acknowledgment that some people do in fact die without having sinned in any way that warranted death — they die simply because human beings are mortal, a consequence of events in the *gan eden*. Whether or not that resolves the theological tension, it at least locates the phenomenon honestly within the tradition's framework.

---

## Cistern Distance

### Underground Works

With the conclusion of the *aggadeta*, the Gemara turns to the second *perek* of Bava Batra, which addresses a different set of neighborly obligations — not the forced construction of dividing walls, but the activities one undertakes in one's own property that may cause indirect or direct damage to a neighbor.

The *Mishnah* states: *lo yachpor adam bor samuch l'boro shel chaveiro* — a person may not dig a *bor* adjacent to his neighbor's *bor*. The *bor* — a cistern, that is, an excavated pit that collects rainwater without drawing on an underground spring — is the paradigm case. Nor may one dig a *shiach* (a long narrow ditch), a *me'arah* (a cave-like covered excavation), or an *amat hamayim* (an irrigation canal) too close to the neighbor's cistern, nor a *nifrechet kovsin* (a laundry ditch). All such underground construction projects risk weakening the walls of a neighboring cistern if built too close.

The exception: *ella im kein hirchik mi-kotel shel chaveiro shelosha tefachim* — unless one distances the work three *tefachim* from the neighbor's *kotel*, and also plasters — *v'sad b'sid*. The specification of three *tefachim* from the *kotel* rather than from the *bor* itself is significant, as the Gemara will explain below. Since these underground projects work with water, the liquid seeps through the earth and can damage the neighboring cistern; distancing and plastering together form the required preventive measures.

### Heat-Giving Materials

The *Mishnah* continues with a second category of potential damage: *u-marchikin et ha-geves v'et ha-zevel v'et ha-melach v'et ha-sid v'et ha-sla'im mi-kotel shel chaveiro shelosha tefachim* — one must distance *geves* (remnants from the olive press), *zevel* (excrement), *melach* (salt), *sid* (plaster), and *sla'im* (certain rocks that give off heat) three *tefachim* from the neighbor's wall. All of these materials generate heat, and proximity to the wall may cause structural damage.

A textual question arises regarding the phrase that follows. The first category requires both distancing *and* plastering — *ve-sad be-sid*. But here the language may read *o sad be-sid* — or plaster — making it an either/or requirement: one either distances the materials three *tefachim* or plasters the wall of the cavity containing them. *Tosafot* addresses the variant *girsa* directly, holding that the second category requires only one or the other, whereas the underground works require both.

### Agricultural Activities

The *Mishnah* adds a third category: *marchikin et ha-zra'im v'et ha-macharesha v'et mei raglayim min ha-kotel shelosha tefachim* — one must keep seeds, plowing, and urination three *tefachim* from the neighbor's wall. Seeds and plowing can loosen the soil near a wall and undermine its stability; urine can similarly cause structural harm. These must all be kept at the requisite distance.

### Millstones & Ovens

The *Mishnah* addresses two further cases with slightly more complex distance measurements. For *reichayim* — millstones — the required distance is three *tefachim* from the *shechev*, the lower stationary stone, which translates into four *tefachim* from the *rechev*, the upper moving stone, since the *rechev* sits atop the *shechev* and extends further upward.

Similarly for ovens: three *tefachim* from the *kilya* — which Rashi explains as the lower edge of the plaster cradle in which the pottery-style oven sits — translating into four *tefachim* from the *safa*, the upper rim of that plaster. *Tosafot* understands the oven differently, as a potbelly stove: the *kilya* is the potbelly portion and the *safa* is the base, with three *tefachim* required from the potbelly and four from the base.

---

## Wall Width Standard

### Three Handbreadth Wall

The Gemara now raises a pointed observation: *patach be-vor mesayem be-kotel* — the *Mishnah* opened with the case of a *bor* but concluded by specifying the distance from the *kotel*, the wall. If the concern is proximity to the neighbor's cistern, should not the *Mishnah* have said to distance oneself from the cistern itself, not from its wall?

Abaye — and some say it was Rav Yehuda — resolves this: *mi-kotel boro shananu* — when we say three *tefachim*, we mean from the wall of his cistern. This formulation carries an important implicit teaching: a *bor* by its nature has a surrounding wall, and a standard such wall is three *tefachim* wide. This is not merely a technical point about how to measure distance; it is an independent statement about the normative width of a cistern wall.

One might ask why the *Mishnah* would not simply say to keep three *tefachim* from the *bor* itself. The answer is that by specifying the *kotel*, the *Mishnah* tells us what the standard wall width is — namely three *tefachim*. The practical consequence for measurement is substantial: if I must distance my excavation three *tefachim* from my neighbor's wall, and his wall is itself three *tefachim* wide, then my excavation begins six *tefachim* from the hollow of his cistern.

### Sale Agreement

There is a direct *nafka mina le-makach umimkar* — a practical implication for commercial transactions. A *baraita* teaches: *ha'omer le-chaveiro bor ve-kotlo ani mocher lach* — one who says to his fellow, "I am selling you a cistern and its wall" — *tzarich sheyehei ha-kotel shelosha tefachim* — that wall must be three *tefachim* wide. The standard width of three *tefachim* is thus both a construction norm and a term that carries legal content in a sale. If a seller promises a *bor* and its *kotel*, the buyer is entitled to a wall meeting that standard measure.

---

## Boundary Digging

### Abaye's Position

The Gemara now turns to a fresh question: what if a person wishes to be the first to dig a cistern in a field, and there is no existing cistern on the neighbor's side — may he dig right up to the boundary line itself? This is the *she'elah* of *haba lismoch betzad hametzar* — one who comes to press up against the border.

Abaye's position — *somech* — is that in a field that is not normally suited for cisterns (*sadeh she'einah asuyah le-vorot*), one may dig right up to the boundary line. Since it is not normal practice to build cisterns in such a field, there is no realistic expectation that the neighbor will do the same. Accordingly, there is no imposition upon the neighbor: one is not forcing the other party to absorb the entire required distance within their own property. One simply exercises the right to use one's own land as one chooses, without being obligated to anticipate an unusual use the neighbor is unlikely to make.

### Rava's Position

Rava disagrees: *eino somech* — one may not dig right at the boundary line even in a field not ordinarily used for cisterns. His reasoning is that the neighbor can say: *ki heichi de'at imlacht ve-chafarta*, just as you changed your mind and decided to dig an unusual cistern, *ana nami imlachna ve-chafarna* — I too may change my mind and decide to dig one. The fact that it is not customary does not eliminate the neighbor's right to make a different choice in the future. If I dig at the boundary line, I may be forcing the neighbor — should they later choose to build a cistern — to absorb the entire required distancing within their own property. That is an unfair imposition, and it is therefore prohibited regardless of whether the field is the sort normally used for cisterns.

In a field that *is* normally suited for cisterns (*sadeh ha'asuyah le-vorot*), there is no dispute: everyone agrees the person may not dig right up to the boundary line, since one can readily anticipate that the neighbor will want to do the same, and building at the line forces the full distancing burden onto the neighbor's property.

### Mazik vs. Nizak

The Gemara contextualizes the Abaye-Rava debate within the broader dispute between Rabbi Yose and the *Rabbanan* — a foundational disagreement about who bears primary responsibility for preventing damage in neighboring properties. The *Rabbanan* hold *al ha-mazik le-harchik et atzmo* — the one causing damage must distance himself. Rabbi Yose holds *al ha-nizak le-harchik et atzmo* — the one liable to be damaged must protect himself; the active party is free to do as he wishes within his own domain.

Abaye's leniency aligns with this framework but adds nuance. Even the *Rabbanan*, who require the *mazik* to distance himself, would agree that if there is no existing cistern on the neighbor's side, there is no act of damage being committed at the time of digging. One is not threatening anything present. If no *bor* exists on the other side, one is not the *mazik* in any immediate sense. The *Rabbanan*'s rule applies when there is an existing cistern to protect — *be'idna de-kanta ita le-vor*, at the time of planting the roots have not yet spread, is the comparable principle in the tree-and-well case — but not when there is nothing there yet to be damaged.

### Rabbi Yose Exception

A striking element of Rava's position is that he invokes even Rabbi Yose as support. Rabbi Yose permits planting a tree right up against a neighbor's existing cistern, on the grounds that at the time of planting, the roots have not yet extended into the other's property — *lish'at shav d'maskei lei l'vor*, right now they do nothing — and Rabbi Yose holds that indirect, eventual consequences do not obligate the planter to distance himself. Yet even Rabbi Yose, Rava argues, would prohibit digging a cistern at the boundary line.

Why the distinction? Because in the case of digging, there is an argument that the damage is direct and immediate. *Kol mara u-mara de-kamachis, kamarfis lei l'ara* — every shovel blow weakens the land. Even without an existing cistern on the other side, in a field where cisterns are a normal use of the land, every act of digging diminishes the structural capacity of the adjacent soil. The neighbor can say: right now, as you dig, you are degrading my land's utility for the very type of construction it would naturally support. This is not an eventual future harm like spreading roots — it is a present and ongoing weakening of the ground. Therefore, even Rabbi Yose would concede that in this case the digger cannot press right up to the boundary line.

---

## Mishna Resolution

### Rava's Reading

The Gemara now confronts a challenge to Rava from the *Mishnah* itself. The *Mishnah* states: *lo yachpor adam bor samuch l'boro shel chaveiro* — one may not dig a cistern adjacent to one's neighbor's cistern. The implication of *taama de'ika bor* — the reason is that a cistern is already present — is *ha leika bor, somech*: if there were no cistern on the other side, one could go right up to the boundary line. But this is precisely what Rava denies. If Rava holds that even without an existing cistern on the other side one cannot dig at the boundary, why does the *Mishnah* frame the prohibition in terms of proximity to an existing cistern?

Rava's response draws on the earlier resolution of Abaye and Rav Yehuda: *mi-kotel boro shananu* — the *Mishnah* is talking about distancing from the *wall* of the cistern. And the point is not merely a measurement clarification. The *Mishnah* describes the first party as already having a wall around his cistern. Why does the first party have a wall? Because even the first party — the one who dug before anyone else was there — was not permitted to dig at the boundary line and therefore set his cistern back, leaving room for the wall. The *Mishnah*'s scenario of an existing cistern with a wall is Rava's evidence that the prohibition applies universally: even the first digger could not go to the boundary line. The wall's existence in the *Mishnah* is testimony to that fact.

### Universal Requirement

Building on this, Rava reads the *Mishnah*'s scenario as inherently teaching that the three-*tefach* distancing requirement is not contingent on there being an existing cistern across the border. Whether or not the neighbor has built anything, the requirement to maintain distance applies. The case described — with an existing cistern and wall on the neighbor's side — is simply the vehicle through which the *Mishnah* communicates that even the first actor had to stay back. One should not read the *Mishnah* as implying that without a cistern on the other side, the boundary line would be open for digging. That implication, Rava says, is dissolved once one understands that the wall mentioned in the *Mishnah* represents the constraint already operative on the first party.

### Abaye's Reading

For Abaye, however, this reading creates its own difficulty. If Abaye holds that one *may* dig right up to the boundary line when no cistern exists on the other side, why does the *Mishnah* depict the first party with a wall, implying he pulled back? Abaye's answer is that the *Mishnah* is addressing a scenario in which both parties come to dig simultaneously — *matnitin she-bau lachpor be-vat achat*. When both are digging at the same time, neither can claim priority; neither can press to the boundary line at the expense of the other. Both must therefore share the required distance equidistantly, each pulling back from the boundary line in equal measure. In that scenario, walls naturally appear on both sides, and the required distance between the two cisterns is shared rather than borne entirely by one party.

According to one understanding of Abaye, had a single party come first without any existing cistern on the other side, no wall would have been necessary and the cistern could have been dug at the boundary line. But when both come simultaneously, the equidistant sharing of the required distance is itself the operative principle — and it is this scenario that the *Mishnah* describes.

---

---

# Bava Batra 18

## Cistern Debate

### Perek Overview

The second *perek* of Bava Batra is occupied with a central question: what are you permitted to do within your own property, and how far must you remain from the boundary line in order to avoid indirectly causing damage or disruption to your neighbor's property? The specific focus at the opening of our daf is the *mishna* governing cisterns. When one digs a cistern in one's property, the act can weaken the surrounding ground. Accordingly, if a neighbor already has a cistern, one may not construct a similar pit, ditch, or water-containing structure in a way that will compromise the neighbor's cistern — one must remain *shlosha tefachim* away from the boundary line, and one must also plaster the walls of the excavation.

### Abaye's Position

The plain reading of the *mishna* seems to limit this obligation to situations where the neighbor has already built a cistern. If nothing yet exists on the other side of the boundary line, one would seemingly be permitted to construct right up to that line. This is the position of Abaye: the distancing requirement is triggered only when there is an existing structure that one's project actually threatens.

### Rava's Position

Rava disagrees. In his view, the *mishna* is not to be read as restricted to cases where a cistern already stands on the neighbor's side. Even if nothing has yet been built there, one must still remain *shlosha tefachim* from the boundary line, so as not to compromise the neighbor's future ability to build. The distancing obligation, on Rava's reading, is categorical and anticipatory.

---

## Soft Ground Case

### Soft Ground Setup

The Gemara attempts to resolve this dispute by examining a *braita* regarding what is called *sela haba'ah b'yadayim* — ground so soft that it can essentially be dug by hand. The *braita* states: when two neighbors each wish to dig a cistern, each must remain *shlosha tefachim* from the boundary line and plaster the walls. This appears to support Rava, since the rule is stated without requiring that either party's cistern already exist — each is simply told to stay distant.

### Soft Ground Exception

The Gemara rejects this proof. *HaBa'ah b'yadayim shani* — soft ground is different. Because the ground is so unstable, special precautions are inherently necessary regardless of the general rule. The *braita* may therefore reflect a specific stringency applicable only to that unusual case, and need not indicate anything about ordinary firm ground.

### Three Tefachim Rule

The Gemara then explains what *chiddush* the *braita* actually comes to teach. One might have thought that precisely because the ground is so soft, *shlosha tefachim* would be insufficient — that perhaps a far greater distance, say *asara tefachim* or *arba amot*, would be required. The *braita* therefore teaches that even in the soft-ground case, *shlosha tefachim* of distance with proper plastering is adequate. But the underlying assumption of this *chiddush* — namely, that *shlosha tefachim* is required from the boundary line even absent an existing cistern on the other side — was taken for granted by the Gemara. The *braita* thus does not resolve the Abaye-Rava dispute.

---

## Heat-Based Damages

### Heat Materials Mishna

The Gemara turns to a series of *mishnayot* and attempts to extract a proof from each. The first *mishna* addressed states: one must distance *gefet* (the residue from an olive press), dung, salt, plaster, and certain types of rocks from a neighbor's wall by *shlosha tefachim* — or alternatively, plaster the containing area to prevent damage to the wall. All of these materials generate heat and can damage a wall.

### Boundary Line Reading

The apparent implication of the *mishna* is straightforward: *ta'ama d'ika kotel* — the reason for the distancing requirement is that there is a wall present. *Ha leit ka kotel* — if there were no wall, one could presumably place these materials right up against the boundary line. This would support Abaye's position.

### Heat as Damage

The Gemara rejects this inference. Even without a wall, one cannot bring these materials flush against the boundary line. Rather, the *mishna* is telling us something about the nature of the problem: *d'hani kashu l'kotel* — these materials are damaging to walls. That is the source of the legal concern. Because the underlying problem is their capacity to damage a wall, the obligation to distance applies even when no wall yet stands — so as not to compromise the neighbor's ability to build one. The *mishna* illustrates the concrete mechanism of harm; that mechanism then generates an obligation that applies categorically.

---

## Moisture Damages

### Moisture Mishna

The same pattern repeats with a second *mishna*: seeds, plowing, and urinating must be kept *shlosha tefachim* from a neighbor's wall. Again, the apparent reading is that the obligation is predicated on the presence of a wall.

### Moisture Problem

The Gemara gives the identical response: even without a wall, one cannot position these activities against the boundary line. The *mishna* is teaching that *matunta kashya l'kotel* — moisture is damaging to walls. That is the underlying problem, and it is what generates the distancing obligation in all cases. Once we know that moisture is damaging, we apply the rule even absent a concrete wall on the other side.

---

## Vibration Damages

### Millstone Mishna

The pattern continues with millstones: the lower stone (*shechev*) must be kept three *tefachim* from the wall, and the upper stone (*rechev*) four *tefachim*. The *mishna* phrases this in terms of distance from the neighbor's wall, suggesting again that a wall is a precondition.

### Vibration Source

The Gemara responds identically. Even without a wall, one cannot place a mill against the boundary line. The *mishna* comes to tell us that *tiraya kashya l'kotel* — the trembling and vibrations of the mill are harmful to walls. That is the source of the problem, and it applies regardless of whether a wall currently stands. An additional benefit of identifying the concrete harm in each case — heat, moisture, vibration — is that it allows us to extend these rules to analogous situations not explicitly covered by the *mishna*.

---

## Oven Heat Damage

### Oven Mishna

The same analysis is applied to ovens. An oven must be kept three *tefachim* from the lower part of the plastered area (*kilya*), or four *tefachim* from the narrower upper rim (*safa*) — these measurements following Rashi and Tosafot respectively. The distance is, again, stated in terms of proximity to a neighbor's wall.

### Heat Problem Inference

*Ki leit ka kotel nami lo someich* — even without a wall, one may not place an oven against the boundary line. The *mishna* teaches that *havla kashya l'kotel* — heat is damaging to walls. That is the underlying harm; the distancing obligation follows from it universally.

---

## Dira Exception

### Bakery/Stable Mishna

The Gemara now examines a *mishna* that appears to introduce an important qualification. One may not open a bakery (*chanut shel nechtom*) or a dyer's shop (*tzavaim*) directly beneath a neighbor's storehouse (*otzar*), because the heat (according to Tosafot) or smoke will rise and damage the stored grain and other goods. Similarly, one may not operate a cattle stable (*refet bakar*) beneath a neighbor's storehouse, as the smell will damage what is stored above.

### Dira Exception

Crucially, the Gemara here does not give the same response it has given to every prior *mishna*. In all the earlier cases, the Gemara said: even without a concrete structure on the other side, you cannot go up to the boundary line. Here, however, the Gemara says: *dira shani* — a *dira*, a domicile or basic structure, is different. In this case, if there is no storehouse actually present on the other side, you are permitted to build your bakery or stable right up against the boundary line. The obligation to distance oneself is only triggered when there is an actual, concrete enterprise being directly threatened.

### Rashi on Dira

Rashi explains the principle as follows: *chanut v'refet bakar diratam shel adam hem v'ein lanu l'esor dirato alav ella im ken hizik muchach* — a shop and a cattle stable are basic human domiciles and structures, and we do not restrict a person's ability to build such structures unless there is demonstrated, concrete damage. The category of *dira* functions something like a zoning principle: while one can restrict where a person digs a cistern or places a pile of plaster, basic living and working structures may be erected freely up to the boundary line, so long as no existing structure is being directly harmed. If a neighbor does have a storehouse there, then of course the bakery or stable cannot be built so as to damage it. But in the absence of such a concrete threat, the *dira* category permits full use of one's property up to the line.

### Stable First Rule

The Gemara notes that the *mishna*'s special status as a *dira* case can also be inferred from a *braita* that elaborates upon it: *im hayta refet bakar kodemet l'otzar mutar* — if the stable was built before the storehouse was constructed, it is permitted. This "first in time" rule is mentioned only in connection with the *dira* case and not with respect to cisterns or the other categories discussed earlier. Why? Because the *braita* is emphasizing that in the *dira* case, even building right up to the boundary line was permitted from the outset. In other categories, being "first" might not protect you if you violated the underlying distancing rule — you could have arrived first but still built improperly, and you might still be required to relocate. Here, because the structure was permissible at the boundary line to begin with, arriving first is fully protective.

---

## Vineyard Work Space

### Tree Distance Mishna

The Gemara continues examining *mishnayot*. One may not plant a tree adjacent to a neighbor's grain field unless one has distanced it by *arba amot*. This is a notably larger distance than the *shlosha tefachim* that has appeared throughout the earlier cases.

### Vineyard Labor Space

A *braita* explains: *arba amot she'amru k'dei avodat hakerem* — the four *amot* mentioned is the amount of space needed to perform labor around a vineyard. Tosafot notes that while the tree in the *mishna* is not literally a vineyard, the standard measure of four *amot* derives from vineyard work and applies equally to an orchard. The reason for the distance is practical: one can plow a wheat field by working from the center outward to one's own edge, without needing to enter the neighbor's field. But tending a vineyard or orchard requires working from the outside in — pruning, picking, weeding — and if the trees or vines extend right to the neighbor's field, the orchard owner will inevitably have to step into the neighbor's grain field to perform that work. The four *amot* provides the buffer space needed for *avodat hakerem*.

### Distance Without Field

This again raises the question central to the Abaye-Rava debate: the distancing requirement appears conditioned on a grain field actually existing on the other side. If there is no grain field, it seems the tree could be planted right up to the boundary line. The Gemara observes this implication: *ta'ima mishum k'dei avodat hakerem ha lav mishum k'dei avodat hakerem samuch* — if the reason is the need for working space, then absent that reason, one could apparently go right up to the edge. And strikingly, this seems to mean that even the concern for roots spreading underground into the neighbor's field would not, by itself, mandate distancing. The roots concern is apparently subordinated to the *avodat hakerem* concern.

### Rock Barrier Case

The Gemara resolves this: *hacha b'mai askinan d'mafsik tzunma* — the case here assumes a rock formation running along the boundary line, which extends underground as well. Because the rock prevents roots from spreading, there is no root damage to worry about, and the only remaining concern is the need for working space. That is why, in this particular scenario, proximity to a grain field is what triggers the distancing obligation: it is the *avodat hakerem* concern alone that is operative.

### Wall Between Properties

The Gemara further notes the following scenario: if there is a wall between the two properties, one may place one's vineyard against the wall on one side and the neighbor's grain field against the wall on the other side. The same question arises — what about the roots? The Gemara resolves this the same way: the case involves a rock formation, so root spread is not a concern.

### Root Removal Right

The Gemara then considers the end of the *mishna*: if roots did nevertheless spread into a neighbor's property (*hayu shoreshav yotsim b'tokh shel chaveiro*), the neighbor is entitled to dig three *tefachim* into the ground and sever all roots that might obstruct plowing. The Gemara asks: if we are dealing with a case involving a rock barrier, how could roots have gotten through? The answer: the *mishna* is addressing an alternative scenario. Either there was no rock and roots spread naturally, or the rock was present but the roots somehow traversed it. In either such case, the neighbor may dig three *tefachim* down and remove them.

---

## Long-Distance Roots

### Tree-Cistern Mishna

The Gemara examines a *mishna* requiring that a tree be kept *esrim v'chamesh ama* — twenty-five *amot* — from a neighbor's cistern. The concern is that tree roots can spread that great a distance underground and ultimately crack or undermine the cistern. Twenty-five *amot* is roughly forty feet, a substantial distance.

### Distance Without Cistern

The Gemara raises the question directly relevant to Rava's position: *taama d'ika bor* — the *mishna* frames the obligation around the existence of an actual cistern. If there is no cistern, it sounds as if one could plant a tree even within twenty-five *amot* of the boundary line. But according to Rava, should one not be required to stay twenty-five *amot* from the boundary line even without a cistern, so as not to compromise the neighbor's ability to build one? The Gemara accepts this consequence: *ki leika bor nami lo samikh* — even without a cistern, you cannot plant the tree adjacent to the boundary line. The *mishna* comes to tell us that roots spread up to twenty-five *amot* and can damage a cistern — *that* is the source of the problem — and because that is the underlying harm, the twenty-five *amot* distance applies even in the absence of an existing cistern.

### Purchaser Exception

The Gemara then asks about the end of the *mishna*: *v'im ilan kadam lo yakots* — if the tree was already there first, it need not be cut down. But if Rava holds that even without a cistern one may not plant within twenty-five *amot* of the boundary line, how could a tree ever have been legitimately planted within that zone, such that it could now claim priority? The Gemara resolves this with a principle stated by Rav Pappa in another context: *b'lokayach* — we are speaking of a purchaser. The scenario is one in which the tree was originally planted in the middle of a single undivided field, where it was entirely legitimate. The owner subsequently divided the field and sold part of it to another party. Now, by virtue of the new boundary line, the tree happens to sit within twenty-five *amot* of the division. No violation ever occurred: the tree was planted before the boundary existed. In that case, the new neighbor cannot compel the tree to be cut down. The *lokayach* doctrine thus carves out an exception for trees (or other structures) that were legitimate at the time of planting and became "problematic" only because of a subsequent division of property. If, by contrast, a boundary already existed and the tree was planted within twenty-five *amot* of it, Rava would hold that the planting was a violation from the outset, and the tree would be subject to removal.

---

## Smell & Reciprocal

### Smell Damages

The Gemara examines several additional *mishnayot* in the same vein. One must keep the *misreh* — a place where flax is soaked, which generates powerful and unpleasant odors — away from a vegetable garden. One must keep *krashim* (cress) away from *betzalim* (onions). And one must keep mustard seed away from bees: because bees take nectar from surrounding plants and incorporate it into the honey, mustard in proximity to a beehive will produce undesirable honey, damaging the beekeeper's enterprise.

### Problem Pattern

Following the now-familiar pattern: *ta'ama d'ika yerek* — it sounds as though the flax-soaking restriction applies only when vegetables are actually present. *Ki leika yerek nami lo samikh* — but even without vegetables present, one cannot place the *misreh* against the boundary line. *D'hani kashu ahadadi* — the *mishna* is identifying that these things damage one another, and that underlying relationship generates the distancing obligation regardless of whether the threatened crop currently exists.

### Rabbi Yossi Bees

Rabbi Yossi introduces an exception specifically for mustard and bees: he permits mustard in proximity to bees, because the mustard grower can say to the beekeeper — *ad she'ata omer li harchaik chardalcha midvorai, harchaik dvoraycha michardali* — before you tell me to move my mustard away from your bees, move your bees away from my mustard, because they come and eat (*gilgulei chardali*) the mustard. The logic is one of reciprocal damage: you are damaging me no less than I am damaging you, and therefore I have no greater obligation to distance myself than you do.

This is striking for two reasons. First, Rabbi Yossi is not here invoking his general principle that it is the *nizak*'s responsibility to protect himself. Rather, he is making a specific claim that in the mustard-bee case the damage runs symmetrically in both directions. It is a limited argument confined to this particular case of mutual harm. Second, the question of who arrived first would seem to be highly relevant — if the bees were established first and the mustard grower is the newcomer, it would seem the mustard grower is the one causing disruption. Tosafot notes that enterprises like beehives and mustard crops are perhaps more readily relocated than a planted tree, which might explain why Rabbi Yossi is willing to entertain the argument that even a latecomer need not defer.

### Boundary Existence

This leads to a difficulty: if Rava holds that no one is permitted to establish any enterprise right at the boundary line — because one must always anticipate the neighbor's future use — then how does the mustard-bee scenario ever arise? Who is this mustard grower arguing with? If both parties must remain distant from the boundary line in anticipation of the other, neither would ever be in a position to claim that the other's enterprise is crowding them.

The Gemara works through this carefully. Rav Pappa's answer — *b'lokayach* — again provides the resolution. The scenario involves someone who originally planted or established an enterprise in the middle of a unified field and then divided it, with the result that the enterprise now sits close to the new boundary. The bee enterprise, for instance, was legitimately established; then the field was sold or divided, bringing a new neighbor into proximity. The Rabbanan say: now that the mustard grower is present, the mustard grower must distance himself from the bees. Rabbi Yossi says: no — since my bees damage your mustard as much as your mustard damages my bees, you are no more entitled to demand I move than I am entitled to demand you move.

But this reading, the Gemara notes, makes the Rabbanan's position difficult to understand. If the mustard was already there first — legitimately, by virtue of the *lokayach* scenario in the opposite direction — why would the Rabbanan require the mustard grower to uproot and move? It is at this point that Tosafot offers a fundamentally different reading of the entire sugya.

---

## Tosafot Reframe

### Damager Responsible

Tosafot reads the conclusion of the Gemara — introduced with the word *ella* — as a wholesale revision of how we understood the Abaye-Rava debate. Ravina states: *kasavar Rabbanan al ha-mazik leharchaik et atzmo* — the Rabbanan who dispute Rabbi Yossi hold that it is the *mazik*'s responsibility to distance himself from whatever he is damaging. On Tosafot's reading, this is not just a statement about the mustard-bee case — it retroactively reframes what Rava was saying all along.

### Cistern Direct Damage

Tosafot understands the debate between Abaye and Rava as follows: the *only* case where the distancing obligation applies even without a concrete existing structure on the other side is the case of a cistern. And why there? Because digging a cistern is an act of *direct* damage (*hezek karov*) to the neighboring ground. The very act of excavation weakens the surrounding earth, and that physical effect extends immediately to the neighbor's property — regardless of whether the neighbor has done anything there. In that case, even Rava requires distancing even without an existing cistern on the other side, because the harm is present and direct from the moment of digging.

### Concrete Structure

All other cases are different. In every other scenario examined — heat from plaster or ovens, moisture from seeds or urination, vibration from millstones, smell from flax — the obligation to distance arises only when there is an actual, concrete structure or enterprise on the other side that is being threatened. If nothing is there, one may go right up to the boundary line. The Rabbanan's position is not that one must anticipate the neighbor's future plans; it is simply that one may not be a *mazik* to something that actually exists. Absent any existing target of damage, one is not a *mazik* and there is no obligation to pull back. Rava, on Tosafot's reading, effectively retracts his broader position and is left holding only the narrow rule about cisterns.

---

## Nizak vs Mazik

### Responsibility Debate

The Gemara now addresses the foundational debate explicitly: is the responsibility to prevent harm that of the *mazik* (the one causing damage) or the *nizak* (the one being damaged)? The Rabbanan hold *al ha-mazik leharchaik et atzmo* — the damager must distance himself. Rabbi Yossi holds *al ha-nizak leharchaik et atzmo* — the damaged party must protect himself.

### Rabbi Yossi Nizak

Evidence for Rabbi Yossi's general position comes from elsewhere in the *mishna*: *af al pi she-bor kodemet l'ilan lo yakotz* — even though the cistern preceded the tree, the tree need not be cut down, because *ze chofer b'tokh shelo v'ze noteia b'tokh shelo* — this one digs within his own property and that one plants within his own property. This is a striking ruling. Even if the neighbor's cistern was there first, and even if one is clearly the *mazik* who arrived second and whose tree roots will certainly spread and damage the cistern, Rabbi Yossi says: you are master of your property. If the cistern owner does not want his cistern damaged, it is the cistern owner's responsibility to address that — not the tree planter's. This clearly reflects a categorical position: *al ha-nizak leharchaik et atzmo*.

If that is Rabbi Yossi's general principle, why did he argue the mustard-bee case specifically on the grounds of mutual damage? He should simply have said: even if my mustard damages your bees, it is your responsibility as the *nizak* to move your bees — full stop. Why introduce the mutual-damage argument at all?

### Rabbanan Mazik

The Gemara resolves this: Rabbi Yossi's mustard-bee argument was constructed *l'divreihem d'Rabbanan* — as an argument within the Rabbanan's own framework, accepting their premise. Rabbi Yossi is effectively saying: on my own view, *al ha-nizak leharchaik*, and even the flax grower need not distance himself from the vegetable garden — it is always the damaged party's problem. But I know you do not accept that. So let me argue within your framework. Even granting your position that the *mazik* must distance himself, you must concede that in the mustard-bee case you cannot identify a single *mazik*, because the damage is reciprocal. Therefore, even on your own terms, you cannot require one party alone to move.

### Mutual Damage

Rabbi Yossi's specific claim about the mustard-bee case: *tarvayhu mazkei ahadadi* — they both damage one another. The bees damage the mustard, and the mustard damages the honey. Therefore, even within the Rabbanan's framework of *al ha-mazik leharchaik*, there is no basis to require the mustard grower alone to distance himself, since the beekeeper is equally a *mazik*.

### Damage Threshold

The Rabbanan respond by disputing the factual premise: *devorim b'chardal lo mazkei lei* — the bees do not actually damage the mustard in any meaningful way. *Ei b'zinta lo mishkachat lah* — if the supposed damage is that bees eat the mustard seeds, that does not happen; bees do not eat seeds. *Ei b'tarpa hadri parchi* — if the damage is to the leaves, the leaves grow back. The Rabbanan are therefore denying that the damage to mustard meets the threshold of legally cognizable harm, and thus there is no symmetry. The mustard damages the bees' honey in a real and irreversible way; the bees do not damage the mustard in any equivalent sense. The *tarvayhu mazkei ahadadi* argument therefore fails, and the mustard grower remains the sole *mazik*, who must accordingly distance himself.

---

## Summary & Tensions

### First in Time

One tension that runs throughout the *sugya* and remains incompletely resolved is the question of priority: does it matter who established their enterprise first? The *lokayach* doctrine provides one clean answer — if an enterprise was established before any boundary existed, and a boundary was subsequently created through division or sale, that enterprise has full legitimacy even if it now sits in a position that would otherwise be problematic. And the observation that, on Tosafot's reading, one may in general build up to the boundary line when nothing yet exists on the other side, means that a first-established enterprise is broadly protected: if you planted your mustard before any neighboring beehive existed, you did nothing wrong, and the newcomer with the bees has to find a solution.

### Core Debate

The daf ultimately leaves us with several interlocking tensions. The Abaye-Rava debate — on Tosafot's reading of the *maskanah* — is narrow: it applies only to the cistern, where direct physical damage is caused by the act of digging itself, and Rava requires distancing even without an existing neighboring cistern. In all other cases, the Rabbanan's rule of *al ha-mazik leharchaik* applies, but only when there is a concrete, existing enterprise being threatened. Absent that, one is not yet a *mazik* and may use one's property freely up to the boundary line.

Against this, Rabbi Yossi takes the position that *al ha-nizak leharchaik et atzmo* in virtually all cases — the damaged party, not the damager, bears the responsibility of self-protection — with the exception of direct physical damage to the neighbor's property, where even Rabbi Yossi would concede. His argument against the Rabbanan in the mustard-bee context was purely internal to their framework: even granting their premise of *mazik* responsibility, the symmetry of harm in that specific case removes the basis for singling out the mustard grower.

The balance the Gemara strikes is a nuanced one: strong protection for the freedom to use one's own property; a meaningful but carefully bounded obligation not to damage what actually exists on the other side; and an ongoing conversation about how anticipatory obligations, temporal priority, and the nature of reciprocal harm interact.

---

---

# Bava Batra 19

## Cistern & Plaster

### Mazik vs. Nizak

The daf opens by continuing the discussion of activities that cannot be conducted near a neighbor's structure when doing so would threaten or damage it. By way of orientation, two important points emerge from the preceding Gemara. First, reading the *mishnah* and related sources according to their plain meaning (*p'shat*), one may conduct activities right up to a boundary line so long as nothing on the other side is threatened — the restriction only applies when a neighbor's property stands to be damaged. Second, and more broadly, the daf returns to the ongoing debate between *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Yose regarding who bears the burden of distancing.

The *Rabbanan* maintain *al ha-mazik le-har'chik et atzmo* — it is upon the one causing the damage to distance himself. He must limit his activities in his own yard or field because they may indirectly impact his neighbor. Rabbi Yose, by contrast, grants the occupant wide latitude: one may do as one pleases in one's own domain, and if the neighbor does not wish to sustain damage, it is upon him to move his property — *al ha-nizak le-har'chik et atzmo*. The sole exception Rabbi Yose acknowledges is direct damage, though precisely what falls into that category remains to be worked out as the chapter unfolds.

### Machmetzan & Nadyan

The *mishnah* states: *v'lo ya'aseh et ha-kovsin* — one may not make a laundry pit adjacent to a neighbor's cistern. The seepage of water from such a pit, and the digging involved in its construction, can compromise the neighboring cistern.

Rav Nachman said in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: *lo shanu ela min ha-machmetzan* — the rule stated in the *mishnah* (a distance of three *tefachim*) applies only to the *machmetzan*, the soaking pit. As Rashi explains, this was a vat in which garments were submerged for a day or two in a mixture of water and dog excrement, which served as a kind of detergent to loosen dirt and stains. *Aval min ha-nadyan* — but from the *nadyan*, the rinsing pit where garments were vigorously scrubbed and beaten in relatively clean water, *arba amot*, four *amot* of distance are required.

This is initially counterintuitive: the rinsing pit seems far less noxious than the soaking pit, yet it requires greater distance. Rashi resolves this: *mitokh she-ha-mayim nitazin le-merachok* — because the vigorous scrubbing and beating of garments causes water to splatter far distances. The laundering process was evidently not the gentle hand-washing one might picture; garments were beaten against stone surfaces with force, sending water spraying considerable distances.

### Mishnah vs. Baraita

The Gemara notes a difficulty: *tanya nami hachi* — a *braita* likewise states that the laundry pit must be four *amot* from the cistern, while our *mishnah* says only three *tefachim*. This apparent contradiction is resolved precisely through the distinction between the *machmetzan* and the *nadyan*: the *mishnah*'s three *tefachim* refers to the soaking pit, while the *braita*'s four *amot* refers to the rinsing pit. Some versions of the Gemara open directly with this contradiction and then arrive at Rav Nachman's resolution. Either way, the conclusion is the same. Indeed, Rav Chiya bar Abba and Rav Avia transmit this distinction explicitly in the text of the *mishnah* itself, with the word *machmetzan* appearing there directly.

### And vs. Or Plaster

The *mishnah* states that beyond distancing three *tefachim*, one must also apply plaster — *v'sid b'sid*. The Gemara raises the question: *v'sid b'sid tnan o sid b'sid tnan* — does the *mishnah* require both the distance and the plaster, or does it offer a choice between them?

The Gemara initially suggests this is obvious: the *mishnah* must mean "and" — both are required. The argument runs as follows. Later in the *mishnah*, when discussing damage not to a cistern but to a wall — the *gefet* (residue from the olive press), excrement, salt, and so on — the requirement is either three *tefachim* or plastering, one or the other. If the rule for the cistern were also an "or" formulation, the *mishnah* should have combined all the cases into a single list. The fact that two separate lists appear implies that the legal requirements differ: the first category (cistern) demands both distance and plaster, while the second (wall) demands only one or the other.

The Gemara pushes back: perhaps the two lists are separated not because of different legal requirements but simply because they involve different categories of damage — *reisha heizeika d'matuna*, the first involves seepage and moisture, while *seifa heizeika d'havla*, the second involves heat. Two categories of harm, two separate lists — yet the underlying rule might still be the same.

### Soft Ground Case

The Gemara seeks to resolve the question from a statement of Rabbi Yehuda regarding a case of *sela ha-ba b'yadayim* — ground so soft it can be dug with one's hands. In such a case, if two neighbors each dig a cistern from opposite sides, each must distance three *tefachim* and also plaster — *zeh marchik gimel tefachim v'sid b'sid v'zeh marchik gimel tefachim v'sid b'sid* — so that a total of six *tefachim* separates the two cisterns, with plaster applied on both sides. Here the "and" formulation is unmistakable.

One might infer from this that the "and" requirement applies specifically to soft ground, while hard ground requires only one of the two precautions. The Gemara rejects this: *hu hadin d'af al gav d'lav haba b'yadayim nami sid b'sid* — even with hard, firm ground, both distance and plaster are required. The *chiddush* of Rabbi Yehuda's statement is not that these precautions apply in soft ground; rather, it is that even in soft ground, three *tefachim* suffice. One might have thought that such unstable soil, which allows water to seep more easily, would demand even greater distance. The ruling tells us that three *tefachim* along with plastering is sufficient even there.

The Gemara does not reach a completely clean resolution, but its clear tendency is that the first list — things that damage a cistern — requires both distance and plaster together, while the second list — things that damage a wall — requires only one or the other.

---

## Heat Damage

### Heat-Giving Items

The *mishnah* turns to a second category: *marchikin et ha-gefet v'et ha-zavel v'et ha-melach v'et ha-sela'im* — one must keep at a distance of three *tefachim* from a neighbor's wall the *gefet* (residue from the olive press), excrement, salt, and rocks. The concern here is not moisture but heat: these substances generate heat as they decompose or by their nature, and sustained heat near a wall causes structural damage.

### Two Lists Compared

The Gemara now draws a comparison with a parallel discussion in tractate *Shabbat*, in the laws of *hatmana* — insulating hot foods before *Shabbat*. The relevant *halacha* is as follows. One may insulate hot dishes before *Shabbat* with materials that merely preserve heat. However, one may not insulate with substances that actively add heat. The paradigmatic case is ashes: submerging a pot in hot ashes continues to add heat, and the Rabbis prohibited this lest one come to stir the ashes, which could lead to kindling a fire. This prohibition was extended to all heat-adding substances, even those from which no fire could be created — organic materials that generate heat as they decompose, such as excrement and *gefet*.

The two lists — things that damage a wall and things forbidden for *hatmana* — are nearly identical, but not quite. Each list contains one item absent from the other. The wall list includes rocks; the *Shabbat* list does not. The *Shabbat* list includes sand; the wall list does not. The Gemara asks: *mai shna hacha de-katni sela'im v'lo katni chol, u-mai shna hatam de-katni chol v'lo katni sela'im* — why does each list include precisely the item the other lacks?

### Rocks Explanation

Rav Yosef offers an initial answer: *lefi she-ein darkan shel bnei adam le-hatmin be-sela'im* — it is not the normal practice to insulate food in rocks, and so they were simply not included in the *Shabbat* list.

Abaye challenges this: *ve-chi darkan shel bnei adam le-hatmin be-gizei tzemer u-ve-leshonot shel argaman?* And is it really the normal practice to insulate food in wool shearings or in strands of royal purple thread? A *braita* explicitly lists *gizei tzemer* (wool shearings), *tzipei tzemer* (combed wool), *leshonot shel argaman* (strands of purple thread), and *mochin* (rags) as items permitted for *hatmana*. These are hardly everyday insulation materials, yet they appear in the list. If unusual materials are still listed, "not normally done" cannot explain the omission of rocks.

Abaye therefore proposes a different approach: *yagid alav re'o* — a phrase drawn from the book of Iyov, meaning "his companion will tell about it." The literary device here is that neither list is complete; each informs the other. Whatever appears on one list is implicitly included in the other.

Rava objects to this approach. If the intent were simply to have each list supplement the other, the Gemara should have made one list fully comprehensive and let a single item from the other list cover the remainder. Having two parallel lists of five items each, differing only in the final entry, is a clumsy way to accomplish this — *litninehu le-chulhu be-chada*.

Rava therefore offers a precise explanation for why rocks appear on the wall list but not the *Shabbat* list: *mishum de-mashtchi lah le-kdeira* — rocks damage the pot. Rashi offers two readings of this phrase: either the rocks physically scrape and scratch the pot as it rests among them, or they cause the pot to rust. In either case, rocks are specifically contraindicated for use in insulation because they cause affirmative harm to the vessel, which explains their complete absence from the *Shabbat* discussion.

### Tosafot Practice

Tosafot is not satisfied with Rashi's explanation on its own. Tosafot agrees that *mashtchi le-kdeira* refers to rusting rather than breaking, but notes that this only explains why rocks are an especially poor choice — it does not explain the absence from the list differently from the mere "not normally done" reasoning that Abaye already rejected.

Tosafot offers a further interpretation: *de-lo shechi'cha hi klal, shari le-hatmin bah, u-ve-milta de-lo shechi'cha lo gazru bah Rabanan* — since the practice is not at all common, the Rabbinic prohibition against *hatmana* in heat-adding substances simply never applied to rocks in the first place. Where something is so unusual as to be practically non-existent, the Rabbis never enacted a decree against it.

Tosafot then draws a remarkable practical consequence: *ve-khen minhagenu she-anu nohagim le-hatmin be-sela'im she-korin kilos* — it is the Ashkenazic practice to actually insulate pots in a certain type of rock (referred to as *kilos*, possibly a form of flint or volcanic stone) before *Shabbat*. The reasoning forms an interesting loop: because it was not normally done, no rabbinic prohibition was enacted; because no prohibition was enacted, it is in fact permissible to do it; and therefore they actually do it.

### Sand Explanation

Returning to the second discrepancy, Rava explains why sand does not appear on the wall list: *mishum de-mechameme chame u-mekarere kare* — sand does not generate its own heat. Rather, it functions as a perfect thermal insulator in both directions: it keeps hot things hot and cold things cold. If you embed a hot object in sand, it preserves the heat; if you embed a cold object, it keeps it cold. Sand does not independently produce heat directed at a wall, which is why it poses no concern for wall damage and was therefore omitted from that list.

Rabbi Oshaya does, however, include sand in his version of the wall list — but the Gemara explains that his concern is *de-matuna*, moisture rather than heat. Sand retains and seeps moisture, which can damage a wall's foundation. The Gemara then asks whether sand, if it is a moisture concern, should appear in the earlier list of things to keep away from a neighbor's *bor* (cistern). The Gemara answers that the moisture-related list already includes the irrigation canal (*amat ha-mayim*) and the laundry pit (*nivrechet ha-kovsin*), and each of those needed to be stated independently: had only the irrigation canal been listed, one might have thought the continuously present, fixed canal is uniquely problematic but the intermittent laundry pit is not; had only the laundry pit been stated, one might have thought that only still, standing water is dangerous but not a flowing canal. Each case was necessary, and sand is encompassed within them.

---

## Seeds & Plowing

### Seeds Plowing Rule

The *mishnah* adds: *marchikin et ha-zera'im v'et ha-machresha* — seeds and plowing must likewise be kept three *tefachim* from a neighbor's wall. Here the concern is neither moisture nor heat but damage to the ground structure that supports the wall.

### Redundancy Question

The Gemara questions the apparent redundancy. *Zera'im tipok lei mishum machresha* — why mention seeds separately? If one cannot plow near the wall, one obviously cannot plant seeds there either, since plowing is a prerequisite for seeding. The Gemara answers: *be-mapolet yad* — seeds can be sown by hand, without plowing. A small vegetable garden can be planted by hand-casting seeds without any prior plowing.

Conversely, *machresha tipok lei mishum zera'im* — once we prohibit seeds, why prohibit plowing? Who plows without intending to seed? The Gemara answers: *be-choresh le-ilanot* — one might plow the area near a wall for the benefit of trees already growing there, to loosen and aerate the soil, without any intention of seeding. Each prohibition is therefore independently necessary.

A further question: *v'teipok lei mishum mayim* — since planting a garden implies watering it, and watering near a wall is already prohibited as a moisture concern, why does the *mishnah* need to separately prohibit seeds? The Gemara responds: *tana be-Eretz Yisrael ka'i, dich'tiv limtar ha-shamayim tishteh mayim* — the *mishnah* is written in the context of the Land of Israel, where agriculture depends on rainfall rather than direct irrigation. In Israel one may plant without needing to actively water, relying on rain. Therefore seeds alone, without watering, constitute an independent concern that must be stated.

### Mavrich Vineyard

One might assume the concern with seeds near a wall is that their roots spread laterally, growing outward and eventually undermining the wall's foundation. The Gemara challenges this assumption: vegetable roots do not spread laterally; they grow vertically downward.

Evidence comes from the law of *ha-mavrich et ha-gefen ba-aretz* — the practice of training a vine underground (*mavrich*), where an offshoot is buried and made to emerge at a distance, functioning as a separate vine without being severed. The relevant *halacha* is: if there is not three *tefachim* of soil covering the underground vine, one may not plant seeds directly above it. But one may plant on either side of the underground vine's path. This demonstrates that we do not fear lateral root spread, for if we did, we would prohibit planting to the sides as well. Clearly, seed roots are assumed to go straight down, not outward.

### Ground Damage Theory

If lateral root spread is not the concern, why must seeds be kept from a wall? Rabbi Chaga in the name of Rabbi Yosi explains: *mipnei she-machlidin et ha-karka u-ma'alin afar tichuach* — because seeds cause the ground itself to deteriorate and loosen. The planting process — not the roots spreading sideways — destabilizes the soil directly where the seeds are planted, causes the earth to become soft and crumbly, and in this way undermines the structural integrity of the ground supporting the wall.

---

## Urine & Walls

### Urine Permitted?

The *mishnah* states that *mey raglayim* (urine) must be kept three *tefachim* from a wall. Against this, Rabbah bar bar Channa ruled: *mutar le-adam le-hashtin mayim be-tzad kotlo shel chavero* — a man may urinate against his neighbor's wall without special permission. His proof is a verse from *Melachim*: *ve-hichrati le-Achav mashtin be-kir* — the phrase *mashtin be-kir* (one who urinates against a wall) is used to describe men, and since it describes them in what appears to be a matter-of-fact manner, it reflects an entirely common and accepted practice.

One might ask whether the permissibility here is limited to cases of urgency — the Gemara elsewhere discusses that withholding oneself when one needs to relieve oneself violates *bal teshaktzu*, and grants latitude in public situations on grounds of urgency. What is striking in Rabbah bar bar Channa's ruling is that urgency is not mentioned at all. The formulation sounds like an unqualified permissive ruling, applicable even when there is no urgency.

Why would a man specifically urinate against a wall? Presumably for the sake of privacy — pressing against a wall prevents exposure from a distance in a way that standing in an open field does not.

### Collected vs. Incidental

The apparent conflict with the *mishnah* is resolved as follows: *hatam be-shofchin* — the *mishnah*'s requirement of three *tefachim* distance refers to collected urine, that is, when one gathers and disposes of substantial quantities of urine near a wall. This is qualitatively different from the incidental urination of an individual, which occurs occasionally and in small amounts. Only the collected, accumulated disposal constitutes a sustained moisture threat to the wall.

### Baraita Contradiction

A *braita* poses a more direct challenge: *lo yashtin adam mayim be-tzad kotlo shel chavero ela im ken hirchik mimenu gimel tefachim* — a man should not urinate against his friend's wall unless he distances himself three *tefachim*. This is explicitly about individual urination, not collected disposal.

The *braita* then distinguishes between wall materials. *Bameh devarim amurim be-kotel levenim* — this applies to a brick wall, which the urine will damage. *Aval be-kotel avanim* — but for a stone wall, *kedai she-lo yazik* — one need only stay far enough to avoid causing direct damage, which works out to one *tefach*. Rashi clarifies that the concern with a stone wall is not damage to the stones themselves (which urine would not harm) but rather damage to the ground at the wall's base, which could undermine its stability. If the wall is built directly on rock with no soil at its base, *mutar* — there is no concern at all.

The Gemara concludes: *tyuvta de-Rabba bar bar Channa tyuvta* — this is a decisive refutation of Rabbah bar bar Channa's permissive ruling. He had cited the verse from *Melachim* as proof of universal permissibility. The Gemara reinterprets: *afilu midi de-darkei le-ishtunei be-kir, lo shafkina lei* — even something that naturally urinates against a wall will not be spared from destruction in the context of that verse. *U-mai nihu? Kalba* — the reference is to a dog, not a man. Thus *mashtin be-kir* in the verse refers to dogs, not human beings urinating against walls as a normative practice. Whatever latitude exists in cases of genuine urgency, as discussed elsewhere, the standard rule remains that one may not urinate against a neighbor's wall without maintaining the required distance.

---

## Tumah & Windows

### Wafer in Window

The Gemara now shifts to an apparently unrelated topic — one that will eventually circle back to our *mishnah*, though the connection will only become clear later. The discussion concerns the laws of *tumah* and the spread of ritual impurity through openings.

The governing principle is as follows. When a corpse is present under a roof, the *tumah* spreads throughout the enclosed space beneath that roof. If two adjacent houses share a wall with a window between them, and that window measures at least one *tefach* by one *tefach* (approximately three inches square), the two spaces are considered connected and the *tumah* spreads through the window into the second house as well, rendering everything inside it *tamei*.

The question arises: what if the window opening is partially filled by an object placed within it, reducing the clear opening to less than one *tefach* by one *tefach*? Does this "shrink" the window halachically, preventing the *tumah* from passing through?

Rav Tuvi bar Kisna said in the name of Shmuel: *rakik eino mema'et ba-chalon* — a *rakik* (a thin wafer, a flat piece of baked food) placed in a window does not reduce the effective size of the opening and does not prevent *tumah* from spreading through.

### Wafer Analysis

The Gemara asks: *mai irya rakik* — why specifically discuss a wafer? *Afilu ava nami* — even a thick loaf of bread or substantial piece of food placed in the window clearly would not shrink the opening. Why? *Keivan de-khazei lei, lo mivatel lei* — because it is clearly visible, you will not forget it is there; you will take it out and eat it. It has not been treated as a permanent structural element. Of course it doesn't reduce the window.

The *chiddush* therefore concerns specifically the thin wafer. *De-mais* — a wafer is unappealing; sitting in a window it collects dirt and dust and becomes disgusting. One might have thought: *eima bitulei mevatel lei* — you will simply leave the wafer there permanently, having effectively incorporated it into the structure of the window. And if so, perhaps it does reduce the opening. The ruling of Shmuel tells us this is not the case — the wafer does not reduce the window even when one might have thought it would be left in place permanently.

### Susceptibility Rule

Before even reaching the question of whether something has been permanently incorporated into the window, the Gemara identifies a more fundamental reason why a wafer cannot reduce the opening: *tipok lei d'havei davar she-mekabel tumah* — a wafer is food, and as such it is susceptible to *tumah*. And the principle is: *kol davar she-mekabel tumah eino chotzetz bifnei ha-tumah* — anything that can itself become *tamei* cannot serve as a barrier to the spread of *tumah*.

Even a thick stale loaf of bread, placed intentionally in the window as a permanent seal, would not block *tumah* from passing through — not because you would remove it, but because it is itself *mekabel tumah*.

This leads the Gemara to reframe Shmuel's ruling: *she-nilosh be-mei peirot* — the *rakik* in question was made with fruit juice rather than with one of the seven liquids that render food susceptible to *tumah*. The seven liquids are: *yayin* (wine), *devash* (honey), *shemen* (oil), *chalav* (milk), *tal* (dew), *dam* (blood), and *mayim* (water) — a mnemonic often used to recall them. Fruit juices other than wine and oil do not confer susceptibility. A wafer kneaded exclusively with, say, apple juice, and never subsequently exposed to any of the seven liquids, is not *mekabel tumah* and therefore could in principle serve as a barrier — if properly incorporated into the window structure. It is regarding this wafer that Shmuel rules it still does not reduce the window, because it has not been treated as a permanent fixture.

### Straw & Figs

The Gemara now challenges the emerging principle — that only something permanently left in place can reduce a window opening — from a *braita*: *kupah m'lei'ah teven, v'chavit m'lei'ah grogerot ha-munachim ba-chalon* — a box filled with straw or a barrel filled with pressed figs placed in a window. The rule stated is *ro'in* — one assesses the situation: if the container were removed and the straw or figs could remain in place independently, and they have not been rendered susceptible to *tumah*, then *chotzetzim* — they block the *tumah*. If not, they do not.

The problem is that both straw and pressed figs would normally be taken out and used. Straw is animal fodder; pressed figs are food. If we require intent to leave something permanently in place for it to reduce the window, neither of these should qualify — yet the *braita* seems to say they can.

The Gemara works through each case carefully. Regarding the straw: one might say it can be fed to animals — but it has thorns, making it unsuitable for fodder. One might say it can be used to make plaster or mortar — but it is moist. One might say moist straw can still be added to a large fire — but *hasakah gedolah lo shechi'ach*, maintaining a very large fire is not common. The Gemara thus reinterprets the case as one where the straw is effectively useless and will in fact be left in place.

Regarding the pressed figs, Shmuel himself states — and Rabba bar bar Avuha teaches the same — *be-she-hitrifu*: the figs have become worm-eaten and spoiled. No one intends to eat them; they will remain in the window. Again, the case is reread as one where permanent placement was always the intent or practical reality.

The Gemara's consistent approach is thus confirmed: only something that one plans to leave permanently in place — whether consciously or by virtue of the object's worthlessness — can reduce the effective size of a window opening and thereby prevent *tumah* from passing through.

### Intent to Leave

The Gemara makes explicit what has been implicit throughout: the governing principle is *bitulei mevatel lei* — whether the owner has nullified the object's independent status by treating it as a fixed element of the structure. A *rakik* that is merely set in a window, even if thin and unappealing, has not been treated this way and therefore cannot reduce the opening. Only when the circumstances are such that the object genuinely will remain — because it is spoiled, useless, or otherwise permanently committed to that location — does it acquire the status of a structural fill.

### Metal Barrel

The Gemara returns to the barrel of pressed figs and probes the case more carefully. When the Gemara hears "barrel," it envisions a pottery vessel, not a wooden one. The question becomes: in what configuration is the barrel positioned in the window?

*I de-fumah le-var* — if the opening of the barrel faces away from the house containing the *tumah*, then *hi gufah tachutz* — the barrel itself should block the *tumah* from passing through. The reason: *kli cheres eino mitamei mi-gabo* — a pottery vessel does not become *tamei* through its outer side; *tumah* enters pottery vessels only through their openings. If the opening faces away from the *tumah*, the barrel cannot become *tamei* and therefore itself functions as a valid barrier. There would be no need to look at the food inside.

The Gemara therefore concludes the case must be *ela de-fumah le-gav* — the opening faces toward the house containing the *tumah*. In this configuration, the barrel's opening is exposed to the *tumah*, the barrel becomes *tamei* itself, and therefore cannot serve as a barrier. The blocking function must fall entirely on the pressed figs inside — which, as established, can block *tumah* only if (a) they have not been rendered susceptible to *tumah*, (b) they can stand independently without the container, and (c) they are intended to remain in place permanently.

Alternatively, the Gemara offers a second reading: *le-olam de-fumah le-var* — perhaps the opening does face away from the *tumah*, but the barrel is made of metal rather than pottery. A metal vessel becomes *tamei* regardless of which side faces the *tumah* — metal vessels are *mekabel tumah* from any direction. Therefore the barrel itself cannot block *tumah* regardless of its orientation, and again the burden falls on the food inside.

The full structure of the ruling is thus: the barrel cannot itself serve as a barrier because it is *mekabel tumah*; the food inside can only serve as a barrier if it is not itself *mekabel tumah* and if it can stand independently and if it is treated as permanently in place. All of these conditions must be met, and the Gemara will continue to explore the implications tomorrow — with the promise that this elaborate discussion of *tumah* and windows will eventually connect back to the *mishnah* from which we began.

# Bava Batra 20

## Maysivay to Shmuel

### Shmuel's Wafer Principle

We pick up four lines from the top of 20a with a *maysivay* challenge to a ruling attributed to Shmuel. On the previous *daf*, Rav Tuvi bar Kisna reported in the name of Shmuel that a wafer placed in a window does not reduce the size of that window. The *halachic* context is the laws of *ohel* and *tumah*: when a corpse lies in one room, *tumah* passes into an adjacent room only if the connecting window is at least a *tefach* in height and width. If the window measures exactly a *tefach* but a wafer sitting in it would reduce the effective opening to less than a *tefach*, one might think the window is now too small to transmit *tumah*. Shmuel's ruling is that the wafer does not count toward reducing the window's size, because the wafer is intended to be eaten and will be removed. The principle underlying Shmuel's position is that only something one genuinely intends to leave in place permanently can be considered part of the wall structure; an object one plans to remove does not diminish the window's legal dimensions.

Tosafot notes that this discussion is brought here because it will connect to the broader conversation about vegetation near walls — whether certain growth benefits or damages a wall — which ties into our *mishnah*'s topic of required distancing from walls.

### Tosefta Objects List

The *maysivay* challenge to Shmuel comes from a *Tosefta* in *Ohalos*. The *Tosefta* lists a series of objects that, if placed in a window, *do* diminish its size — meaning they are treated as part of the wall for purposes of measuring the *tefach* threshold. These are:

Grass (*asavim*) that was uprooted and placed in the window, or grass that grew on its own through gaps in the stones. Small rags (*metlanyot*) that lack three by three fingerbreadths in area — it is important to note that the measurement here is *shalosh al shalosh etzbaot*, fingerbreadths, not *tefachim*; we will encounter a four by four *tefachim* standard shortly and the grammatical distinction is critical. A rag smaller than three by three fingerbreadths is not *mekabel tumah*, susceptible to ritual impurity, and that is precisely the qualification at work throughout this list. A hanging limb or flesh (*ha'eiver vehabasar hamedulalin bivheimah uvchayah*) — a limb that has been partially torn from an animal but is still partially attached. A live bird resting in the window (*of sheshachan bechalon*). A non-Jew seated in the window: though a non-Jew is rabbinically a source of *tumah*, he is not *mekabel tumah* on a Torah level. A baby born in the eighth month (*ben shmonah*): the *Gemara* held that such an infant would not survive, and so it has the status of a stone — while still alive it is not classified as a person who is *mekabel tumah*. Salt (*melach*), since salt is not a food in itself and therefore not *mekabel tumah*. A pottery vessel (*kli cheres*) — ordinarily pottery is *mekabel tumah*, but only through its opening, so the case here requires that the opening faces away from the room containing the corpse. And a *Sefer Torah*, which is striking: a *Sefer Torah* is not *mekabel tumah* simply because it is a book, and a book does not meet any of the criteria of a *kli* that renders an object susceptible to impurity.

The *Tosefta* concludes: *kulam mematin bechalon* — all of these diminish the size of the window. Because none of them is *mekabel tumah*, they are treated as part of the wall, and the *tefach* is measured from the top of these objects to the top of the window opening.

## Temporary Objects

### Why They Don't Minimize

The *Tosefta* continues with a contrasting list: *aval hasheleg vehabarad vehagalid vehakefor vehamayim* — snow, hail, frost, and water. For all of these, *kulam ein mematin bechalon*: they do not diminish the size of the window.

The reason is not that these substances are *mekabel tumah* — that consideration would not apply straightforwardly, since random rainwater not set aside for drinking has not been designated as food and therefore lacks that status. Rather, the reason these items do not count is that they will not remain. They melt, flow away, or otherwise naturally dissipate. Even though they are not *mekabel tumah*, they fail the other requirement: physical permanence. An object in a window can only reduce the effective opening if it will stay there.

This now creates the central tension with Shmuel's position. The *Tosefta* seems entirely unconcerned with whether a person *plans* to remove an object — it only asks whether the object is *mekabel tumah* and whether it will physically remain on its own. By contrast, Shmuel's principle was precisely about intent to remove: the wafer does not count because you will take it to eat it. Yet the *Tosefta*'s list includes many objects that one would naturally want to remove, and it rules that they *do* minimize the window. The *Gemara* must now work through this tension, going through the list case by case.

## Maysivay to Shmuel (II)

### Grass through Living Cre…

The *Gemara* takes up each item in the *Tosefta* and asks why, given Shmuel's principle, we would not expect the owner to remove it.

Beginning with grass: *veha'asavim chazu livheimah* — grass is fit to feed to one's animal, so one would presumably want to take it out of the window. The *Gemara* answers: *be'afrazta* — we are speaking of a poisonous variety that cannot be fed to animals. As for grass that grew up on its own through the wall, the *Gemara* notes that since such growth damages the wall — *keivan dekashi lekotel* — the owner would certainly want to remove it. This, incidentally, is why the *Tosefta* is being brought here: the damage that grass causes to walls is the very issue our *mishnah* addresses. Rava answers that we are speaking of a wall in a desolate, ownerless area (*bekotel churva*) where nobody is concerned about maintaining the wall and nobody plans to remove the grass. Rav Pappa goes further and says it applies even to a wall in a settled area (*afilu bekotel yishuv*), because the grass is growing from the ground three *tefachim* away — just as our *mishnah* requires — and is simply bending over and falling into the window from that safe distance, causing no damage, and therefore giving no reason to remove it.

Moving to rags: a rag smaller than three by three fingerbreadths can still serve as a patch for a torn garment, so why would someone leave it in the window? The *Gemara* answers: *b'smichta* — it is a thick, heavy rag that would not work well as a patch. But it could still be used by a blood-letter to wipe away blood after bloodletting. The *Gemara* answers: *b'riska* — it is rough and scratchy material, unsuitable for use on skin. The *Gemara* then raises a further challenge: if we are dealing with sackcloth (*briska*), then the threshold for being *mekabel tumah* is not three by three fingerbreadths but four by four *tefachim* — a much larger standard. So the *Tosefta* cannot be discussing sackcloth. The *Gemara* resolves: *k'ein briska* — not sackcloth itself, but a scratchy material like it, made of ordinary cloth. The upshot is that we have a tiny scrap of rough cloth with no practical use whatsoever, which is why it will be left in the window.
