The *Gemara* then turns to the hanging limb: *v'ha'eiver v'habasar hamiduldalin bivheimah uvchayah* — if a limb is hanging from an animal that is standing in the window, surely the animal itself will wander off. The *Gemara* answers: *bikshurah* — the animal is tied down. But even so, one would eventually slaughter the animal. The *Gemara* answers: *bitmeiah* — it is a non-kosher animal, a mule for instance. But one would sell it to a non-Jew. The *Gemara* answers: *bichshusha* — it is so weak and emaciated that no one would want to buy it. But why not simply cut off the hanging limb and throw it to a dog as food? The *Gemara* answers: *keivan d'ika tza'ar ba'alei chayim lo avid* — since doing so would cause the animal pain, one would not do it. It is worth noting that the *Gemara* does not say it is forbidden; the general ruling of the *poskim*, beginning with the *Trumas Hadeshen*, is that *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* is permitted when it serves a human purpose. Here the point is simply that this would not be one's practical intention. The result is a highly contrived scenario: an emaciated, non-kosher animal tied in a window with a partially dangling limb, where no plan for removal exists.

For the bird: *parach v'azil* — it will fly away. *Bikshur* — it is tied down. *Shachit lei* — but one would slaughter and eat it. *Betame* — it is a non-kosher bird. *Mazbenei lei lenochri* — one would sell it to a non-Jew. *Bekalanisa* — we are dealing with a *kalanisa*, a bird that Rashi identifies as very thin and of no culinary value, so no one would want to buy it. *Yahvei lei lyanuka* — but one might give it to a child as a pet. *Bimsarit* — it is a scratchy, abrasive bird and no one would want it as a pet. The *Gemara* then notes that a *kalanisa* by definition does not scratch — *kalanisa lo masreta* — so the resolution is: *keein kalanisa*, something like a *kalanisa*, a similarly worthless but scratchy bird. One is left with a tied-up, unsellable, uneatable, too-scratchy-to-be-a-pet bird sitting in the window.

The *Gemara* turns to the non-Jew: *kai ve'azil* — he will get up and leave. *Bekafut* — he is bound. *Atei chavreia vesharei lei* — his friend will come and untie him. *Bimetzora* — he has a communicable disease and no one will approach him. *Atei metzora chavreia vesharei lei* — even so, a fellow sufferer might come and free him. *Ela bechavushei malchut* — the final resolution: he is being held prisoner by the government and is chained there under governmental authority, so no one may free him. We have arrived at the scenario of a government prisoner in a window.

### Salt to Sefer Torah

Turning to salt: *chazi lei* — salt is useful, so one would remove it. *Bemarirata* — it is bitter salt with no culinary use. *Chazi le'oros* — one could still use it for tanning leather. *De'it bei kotzei* — it is filled with thistles and therefore unusable for that purpose as well. *Keivan dekashei lekotel shaklei lei* — but salt damages a wall, so one would remove it to protect the wall. *Deyaspa chaspa* — it is sitting on a pottery shard and not in direct contact with the wall, so it does no damage.

The *Gemara* then asks: but the pottery shard itself — *chaspa gufa teichatz* — would also be a partition between the salt and the wall, and so it should independently count as something that diminishes the window size. The *Gemara* answers: *deleis bei shiura* — the pottery shard is so small it has no *halachic* significance. The *Gemara* cites the *mishnah* in *Shabbos*: the minimum significant size of a pottery shard is one large enough to be placed between stacked beams to keep them from warping. This shard is smaller than that. Tosafot raises a difficulty here: we already encountered a rag smaller than three by three fingerbreadths — also not normally significant for *Shabbos* purposes — that nonetheless *does* diminish the window. Why should the pottery shard be any different? Tosafot resolves this by suggesting the pottery shard is so thin in profile that it could not itself reduce the opening to less than a *tefach*, which is why the *Tosefta* does not mention it. The *mishnah* in *Shabbos* is cited only to explain why one would not bother removing the shard — and since neither the shard nor the salt has any use, neither will be removed.

Moving to the pottery vessel (*kli cheres*): *chazi lei* — it is fit for use. *Demitneif* — it has become soiled and is disgusting. *Chazi leumna* — a blood-letter could still use it as a vessel for collecting blood. *Deminkav* — it has a hole in it, rendering it useless even for that purpose.

Finally, the *Sefer Torah*: surely of all things, one would remove it from a window. *Chazi lemikra* — it is fit for reading. *Beviloi* — it is completely worn out. *Veha ba'ei gnizah* — but even a worn-out *Sefer Torah* requires proper burial in a *genizah*; one cannot simply leave it in a window. The *Gemara* answers: *shama gnizaso* — that location in the window is itself its place of resting, effectively its *genizah*. The details of what constitutes a valid *genizah* and whether an open window truly qualifies are questions one could explore at length, but that is the *Gemara*'s resolution.

Stepping back, what is remarkable about the *Gemara*'s treatment of this entire *Tosefta* is that virtually every item on the list would naturally be removed, and in each case the *Gemara* has constructed an elaborate and highly unusual circumstance to explain why removal is not planned. The *pshat* of the *Tosefta* runs squarely against Shmuel's position — intent to remove seems irrelevant to whether something diminishes the window — yet the *Gemara* expends considerable effort constructing these *okimtot* to preserve Shmuel's ruling.

## Salt/Fat Mechitza

### Rav's Mechitza Rule

Rav taught: *bechol osin mechitza chutz memelach verevav* — one may construct a *mechitza* for *Shabbos* purposes from any material, except salt and fat (*revav*). The context here is not the *mechitzos* familiar from *beit knesset* usage but rather *mechitzos* that create a *reshus hayachid* or serve purposes of *eiruv* or *sukkah*. Salt and fat are excluded because they lack permanence: a pile of salt will scatter and fat will dissolve. Even if they currently have a recognizable form, they will not maintain it, and so they cannot function *halachically* as a wall.

### Shmuel vs. Salt Types

Shmuel disagrees: *afilu melach* — even salt may be used for a *mechitza*. Rav Pappa resolves the apparent dispute: *lo peligi* — they do not actually disagree. *Ha b'melach Sedomis ha b'melach Istronknis* — one is speaking of *melach Sedomis*, mineral salt, which is hard and retains its form, especially when cut from the ground; the other is speaking of *melach Istronknis*, sea salt, which is granular and does not hold its shape. Rav's prohibition applies to sea salt, while Shmuel's permission applies to mineral salt.

### Salt Mounds & Beam

The *Gemara* adds a further nuance in the name of Rabbah: *oseh adam shenei tziburei melach umaniyach aleihem korah* — a person may construct two mounds of salt and place a beam across them. The principle at work is mutual reinforcement: the salt supports the beam, and the beam by its weight presses down and keeps the salt in place. In this configuration even sea salt (*melach Istronknis*) can serve as the posts of a *tzuras hapethach* for an *eiruv* or *mavoi*. Thus the final resolution: *ha d'ika korah ha d'leika korah* — the distinction between the positions is simply whether a beam is resting on top of the salt or not.

This discussion of salt and walls flows naturally from the earlier treatment of salt in the window context, which is what prompted the digression.

## Mills & Ovens

### Normal & Donkey Mills

The *mishnah* now turns to objects that must be kept at a distance from a wall: *marchikin es harechayim gimel min hashechev shehein daled min harechev* — one must distance a mill three *tefachim* from the *shechev*, the base of the mill, which translates to four *tefachim* from the *rechev*, the grinding component. The base protrudes more widely than the grinding part, so something three *tefachim* from the wider base is four *tefachim* from the narrower grinding element above it.

Similarly: *v'shel chamor gimel min ha'istrobiel shehein daled min hakelat* — a donkey mill, so called because donkeys were sometimes employed to turn it, though it is a smaller and more portable device, must likewise be kept three *tefachim* from its base (*istrobiel*), which is four *tefachim* from its grinding component (*kelat*). The structural geometry is parallel.

### Vibrations vs. Sound

The *Gemara* asks *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason for distancing a mill from the wall? *Mishum tiraya* — because of the vibrations. When a heavy mill operates close to a wall, the vibrations destabilize it. The *Gemara* then challenges: but by the donkey mill, the same law applies — *mai tiraya ika?* — yet a lighter, more portable mill would not produce significant vibrations. *Ella mishum kala* — rather, the reason for the donkey mill is noise. The sound waves emanating from a mill operating very close to a wall cause damage to the wall. The two rationales — vibration for the large mill, sound for the small one — both lead to the same required distance.

### Tannur & Kirah

*Vechen tannur shalosh min hakalya shehein arba min hasafa* — and similarly, an oven (*tannur*) must be three *tefachim* from its base (*kalya*), which is four *tefachim* from its mouth (*safa*). The *tannur* was shaped roughly like a large pot, wider at the base and narrower at the opening. Rashi understands this as a vessel wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, like an inverted beaker, where the three *tefachim* are measured from the wide base and the four from the narrower mouth. Tosafot suggests a pot-belly shape — narrow at top and bottom, widest in the middle — where the three *tefachim* are from the protruding middle section and the four from the mouth.

### Abaye's Inference

Abaye draws a practical inference: *shema mina kalya de-tannur tefach* — we learn from these measurements that the base (or for Tosafot, the protruding middle section) of a *tannur* extends one *tefach* beyond the mouth. The arithmetic is straightforward: three *tefachim* from one point equals four from another, meaning the difference of one *tefach* represents the protrusion of the base. Abaye notes the practical implication: *nafka mina le-mekkach u-mimkar* — this matters for commercial transactions. If one orders or purchases an oven and it is delivered without the full extent of that base protrusion, the buyer has grounds for complaint.

## Home Oven Safety

### First Story Oven

The *mishnah* now addresses oven safety within a home: *lo ya'amid adam tannur be-toch ha-bayit ella im ken yesh al gabav govah arba amot* — a person may not install an oven inside a house unless there are four *amot* — approximately six feet — between the top of the oven and the ceiling. The concern operates on two levels: fire safety in general, and specifically the damage that rising heat and steam can cause to the ceiling, which is simultaneously the floor of the story above where a neighbor may be living.

### Second Story Oven

*Haya ma'amido be-aliya* — if the oven is being installed on an upper story, *tzarich she-yehei tachtav ma'aziva shelosha tefachim* — there must be three *tefachim* of plaster (*ma'aziva*) in the floor beneath it. This serves to insulate the lower neighbor's ceiling from the heat of the oven above, preventing structural damage or fire. The four-*amot* clearance above the oven remains applicable on the upper story as well.

### Kirah Requirement

*U've-kirah tefach* — for a *kirah*, a smaller oven, it is sufficient to have one *tefach* of plaster beneath it. Rashi explains that because the *kirah* is smaller, it does not produce as large a fire, and the reduced requirement follows accordingly. Though one might ask whether this should also affect the four-*amot* clearance required above — the *mishnah* does not say so explicitly.

### Liability Debate

*Ve-im hizzik meshalem mah she-hizzik* — even if one has complied with all of these specifications, if damage results one remains liable. *Rabbi Shimon omer*: the specifications were given precisely in order to define exemption — *lo amru kol ha-shi'urim ha-elu ella she-im hizzik patur mi-leshalem* — if one followed all the required measures and damage still occurred, one is exempt from payment.

This disagreement touches on a fundamental question in *Bava Kamma*. Normally there is an obligation of *shemirah* — watchfulness — over one's fire, and liability follows from a failure of that watchfulness. Rabbi Shimon's position is natural: compliance with the prescribed standards constitutes adequate *shemirah*, and therefore exempts the owner. The *Tanna Kamma*'s position is more nuanced. One way to understand it is that these specifications, while legally sufficient to permit operating the oven, do not actually constitute full *shemirah* against all possible damage. True *shemirah* might require far greater clearance — twenty feet, or more — but demanding that would make ordinary domestic life impossible. So the *halacha* adopts a middle position: the standards define what is sufficient for the purpose of permitted use, but they do not remove the underlying liability that attaches to fire. A parallel exists in *Bava Kamma* with respect to animals in *reshus harabim*: several *Rishonim* explain that an animal's natural conduct in a public domain does not trigger liability precisely because imposing liability would make ordinary use of public space untenable. Here the tension is similar but unresolved in the permissive direction — we allow the oven but do not eliminate the liability.

## Shops Under Storage

### Bakery & Dye Shop Ban

*Lo yiftach adam chanut shel nachtomim veshel tzeva'im tachas otzaro shel chavero* — a person may not open a bakery or a dyeing shop beneath another's storehouse. The fumes, smoke, and heat rising from these operations will damage whatever the upper neighbor is storing — grain, straw, fruit, and similar goods.

### Cowshed Prohibition

*Velo refet bakar* — nor may one operate a cowshed beneath a storehouse. The odor from cattle is sufficiently penetrating and damaging that it is always forbidden, regardless of what is stored above.

### Wine Exception

*Be'emet beyayin hitiru aval lo refet bakar* — in truth, when the storehouse contains wine, the prohibition on bakeries and dye shops is lifted, because the warmth and fumes from those operations actually improve wine rather than harming it. The cowshed prohibition, however, remains in force even for wine storage, since the smell from cattle spoils the wine.

A *tanna* adds: *beyayin hitiru mipnei she-mashpicho* — the bakery fumes benefit wine. But *velo refes bakar mipnei she-masricho* — the cowshed still ruins it.

### Priority Baraita

A *braita* addresses the question of priority: *im hayta refet kodemet le-otzar muttar* — if the cowshed was there first, and the upper neighbor subsequently decided to use the space as a storehouse, the cowshed owner need not relocate. First occupancy confers rights, and the one who arrived later with the storehouse cannot compel the prior occupant to move.

### Abaye's Questions

Abaye poses a series of questions about the boundary of this priority rule. *Kibbed veribetz le-otzar mahu* — what if the upper-story owner had begun sweeping and preparing the space for use as a storehouse, making his intention clear, but had not yet actually stored anything there, when the lower-story person moved in a cowshed? Is the storehouse considered to have priority because of the preparatory activity? *Reiba be-chalonos mahu* — what if he went further and made structural alterations, opening up additional windows to provide air and light for storage — is that sufficient to establish priority? *Bana aliya gabei bayis mahu* — or what if the upper story itself was built explicitly for storage purposes but has not yet been put to use? The *Gemara* leaves all of these unresolved: *teiku*.

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua poses a further question: *tamrei veriminei mai* — what about a storehouse containing dates or pomegranates, which are presumably less sensitive to the smells from below? Does the same prohibition apply? This too is left as *teiku*.

### Yosef & Sheshes

The discussion of wine generates two further rulings from later Amoraim. Rav Yosef observes: *hai didan afilu kutra de-sharga nami kasha lei* — our wine in Babylonia is particularly sensitive, and even the smoke from a single candle is damaging to it. There is therefore no relaxation of the protective rules for wine; if anything, greater care is required.

Rav Sheshes adds: *aspasta ke-refes bakar damya* — *aspasta*, vetch, a coarse fodder used for animal feed, produces an odor so pungent that storing it below a storehouse is treated exactly like operating a cowshed. The prohibition applies with full force.

---

---

# Bava Batra 21

## Store in Courtyard

### Mishnah: Store in Courty…

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 20b introduces a set of zoning questions that are highly practical and immediately relatable: what commercial activity may one conduct in a shared residential *chatzer*? The *mishnah* opens with the case of *chanut she-be-chatzer* — a store opened within a courtyard shared by multiple households. The ruling is that the other residents may object: *yachol limchot beyado*. The basis for objection, as the *mishnah* phrases it, is "I cannot bear all those coming and going" — the disruption caused not merely by noise, but by the influx of outside foot traffic into what is fundamentally a private residential space.

One might note that the *mishnah*'s language — "I cannot sleep because of those entering and exiting" — seems to limit the objection to hours when sleep is disrupted. It seems likely, however, that this is not the intended limitation. The real concern is the intrusion of outsiders into the *chatzer*, not only the noise generated during nighttime hours.

### Commercial vs. Domestic

The *mishnah* then draws a sharp distinction between a commercial enterprise and domestic craft production. *Aval oseh kelim, yotze u-mocheir ba-shuk* — one may manufacture vessels within one's own home and take them out to sell in the marketplace. The neighbors cannot object on grounds of noise, whether the sound of a hammer, a millstone, or children. *V'eino yachol limchot beyado*.

The underlying principle, familiar to anyone who has lived in an apartment building, is that noise *stam* — incidental noise produced within one's own domain — is generally tolerable and not legally actionable. What crosses the line is opening a commercial enterprise that draws a stream of outside visitors into the shared space. An interesting edge case presents itself: what if one were to host a silent meditation retreat — no noise whatsoever, but heavy foot traffic? The *mishnah* seems to suggest the objection is to the combination of outsiders and noise; yet the two factors may not be fully severable. In any event, the core distinction the *mishnah* draws is clear: outside traffic yes, ambient noise no.

### Gemara Question

The *gemara* immediately asks: *mai shna reisha u-mai shna seifa*? Why is it that in the first clause (*reisha*) one can object to outside traffic, yet in the last clause (*seifa*) one cannot object to the sound of children? The *gemara* initially assumes *tinokot* refers to children coming in to make purchases — which would seem to be exactly the kind of outside foot traffic the *reisha* prohibits. Why then is it permitted?

### Abaye: Neighboring Court…

Abaye resolves the difficulty by reframing the case of the *seifa*: *seifa atiyan l'chatzer acheret* — the store in the *seifa* was opened not in this *chatzer* but in a neighboring one. Imagine two adjacent courtyards opening onto the same *mavoi*. If the residents of the neighboring *chatzer* have no objection to a store operating among them, a resident of the adjacent *chatzer* cannot complain that the resulting foot traffic in the shared alleyway disturbs him. People are not entering his *chatzer* at all. There is a limit to what one may object to: interference must be direct and within one's own space.

### Rava: School Case

Rava, however, offers a superior resolution. He points out that Abaye's reading is strained — if the *seifa* were simply about a neighboring *chatzer*, there would be no reason to specify children. *Ela amar Rava: seifa atan l'tinokos shel beis rabban* — the *seifa* is discussing an entirely different case: a school, a *beis rabban*, being opened in the courtyard. This is the *chidush*. A school generates precisely the kind of bustle and commotion one might expect to object to — children arriving in the morning, departing in the afternoon, noise throughout the day — and yet the residents of the *chatzer* cannot prevent it. The reason, as the *gemara* explains, flows directly from the *takkanah* of Yehoshua ben Gamla.

---

## Education Takkanah

### Yehoshua ben Gamla

*U-me-hiskanat Yehoshua ben Gamla va-eilach* — from the *takkanah* of Yehoshua ben Gamla onward, schools cannot be blocked. The *gemara* records that Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *bram zachor oso ha-ish le-tov, Yehoshua ben Gamla shemo, she-ilmalei hu nishtakach Torah mi-Yisrael* — this man should be remembered for good, for were it not for him, Torah would have been forgotten among the Jewish people. His achievement was the establishment of universal, publicly funded primary education.

### Private Education

What was the situation before his *takkanah*? *She-batchilah mi she-yeish lo av melamdo Torah, mi she-ein lo av lo hayah lomeid Torah* — whoever had a father who could teach him Torah received an education; whoever lacked a father capable of doing so did not learn at all. Education was conceived as a purely personal obligation: *ve-limadetem osam* — you shall teach *them*, understood as the father teaching his own children. The communal dimension was absent entirely.

### Jerusalem Schools

The *gemara* then traces a progression through several stages. In response to the inadequacy of a purely private model, schools were established centrally in Jerusalem: *she-yehu moshivin melamdei tinokos bi-Yerushalayim*. The prooftext was *ki mi-Tzion teitzei Torah* — from Zion Torah shall go forth. The obligation had been shifted from the individual father to a collective institution, but it remained geographically concentrated.

Yet this too proved insufficient. *Ve-adayin*: even with schools in Jerusalem, *mi she-yeish lo av hayah ma-alo u-melamdo* — a child with a capable father who could bring him up to Jerusalem benefited, while *mi she-ein lo av lo hayah oleh ve-lomeid* — a child without such a father still could not make the journey and remained uneducated. Accessibility was formally improved but practically still selective.

A subsequent stage expanded the system to the districts: *hitkinu she-yehu moshivin be-chol pelech u-felech* — in every major region. But even this was insufficiently universal, for the schools remained centralized within each large district, and students were only enrolled from the ages of sixteen and seventeen. By that point, the *gemara* observes, the students were old enough to resent the discipline: *u-mi she-hayah rabo ko'es alav, mavit bo ve-yatze* — if the teacher rebuked him, he would rebel and walk out.

### Universal Education

It was Yehoshua ben Gamla who finally broke through these limitations: *ad she-ba Yehoshua ben Gamla ve-tiken she-yehu moshivin melamdei tinokos be-chol medina u-medina u-ve-chol ir va-ir* — he established that teachers of young children should be appointed in every province and in every town. And he lowered the entry age: *u-machnisin oso ke-ven shesh u-ke-ven sheva* — children were to be enrolled at age six or seven, young enough to form the habits of mind and submission to learning that later schooling cannot instill.

### Schools Protected

The practical consequence of this *takkanah* for our *mishnah* is now clear. Since every town is obligated to maintain a school, anyone who wishes to open a school in his *chatzer* cannot be blocked by the other residents, regardless of the disruption it causes. This remains a striking ruling: one might argue that while the *takkanah* requires a school somewhere in the town, it does not specify that it must be placed in *this particular* courtyard, subjecting its residents to all the attendant noise. The *gemara* nonetheless accepts this consequence as following from the *takkanah*'s force.

### Jerusalem Environment

*Tosafot* adds a dimension of considerable depth here. Quoting the explanation *lefi she-hayah ro'eh kedushah gedolah ve-Kohanim oskin ba-avodah*, *Tosafot* explains that the reason Jerusalem was the site of the first communal schools was not merely logistical centrality. The presence of the *Beis ha-Mikdash*, the sight of *Kohanim* engaged in the *avodah*, and the immersive religious environment of the entire city cultivated *yir'as Shamayim* in students in a way that instruction alone could not. *Haya mechaven libo yoter le-yir'as Shamayim*, the student's heart was drawn more naturally toward reverence. *Tosafot* draws a parallel from *ma'aser sheni*: the very purpose of requiring one to consume the *ma'aser sheni* in Jerusalem was to place the person in an environment where everyone around him was engaged in *melechet Shamayim*, and *haya gam hu mechaven le-yir'as Shamayim ve-osek ba-Torah* — he too would naturally orient himself toward Torah. The point is a powerful one about the irreducible role of environment in religious formation. Instruction transmitted within four walls is one thing; the culture and values modeled by the surrounding world are another, and arguably more powerful, force.

---

## School Administration

### Enrollment & Feeding

The *gemara* records that Rav said to Rav Shmuel bar Shilat: *ad shit lo tekabel* — do not accept students younger than six years old. *Tosafot* notes that six or seven depends on the individual child's readiness to be separated from home. Once enrolled, *askei lehu ke-tora* — feed them like an ox. The imagery is deliberately chosen: not like a camel, which is force-fed with great vigor, but like an ox, which is fed more gently. The *mefarshim* explain the combination: fill the young child with as much Torah and knowledge as possible, but do so *be-nachat* — with gentleness. At this age, the capacity for retention is at its peak, and the educational approach should be to saturate the child with material — *Tanach*, *Mishnah*, by rote — while the analytical faculties are still developing. There may even be a wordplay here, as one participant noted: *safei lei ke-tora*, feed him like an ox — and *tora* sounds remarkably like *Torah* with a different vowel.

### Discipline Standards

When discipline is necessary, Rav advises: *ki machit le-yanuka, lo timchei ela be-arketa de-mesana* — if you must strike a child, do so only with a shoelace, meaning a light, symbolic gesture of correction, not with anything that would cause real physical harm.

### Inclusion Policy

The *gemara* then addresses children who are struggling academically. *Dekari kari* — those who can read, will read. *Delo kari* — if a child cannot yet read, do not expel him from the class. *Havsei le-chavrei* — let him sit next to his peers. *Rashi* elaborates: there is no need to respond to a struggling student with escalating discipline — perhaps the child is simply not yet ready. Do not remove him from your presence; let him sit with others in a communal setting and absorb from the environment. *Ve-sofo latet lev* — in time, he will focus and learn. This reflects a careful balance: taking the educational mission with great seriousness while maintaining a measure of gentleness toward each individual child.

### Baraita Challenge

The *gemara* now raises a challenge from a *baraita*: *echad mi-bnei chatzer she-bikesh la'asot rofe uman ve-gardi u-melamed tinokot, bnei chatzer me'akvin alav* — if one of the courtyard's residents wishes to practice as a doctor (*Rashi* interprets this as *mohel*), a bloodletter, a weaver, or a schoolteacher, the other residents may stop him. This seems to directly contradict the ruling that a Jewish school cannot be blocked.

A second *baraita* makes the same point in the context of two residents: *shnayim she-yoshvim be-chatzer u-vikesh echad mehem la'asot rofe ve-uman ve-gardi u-melamed tinokot, chavero me'akev alav* — his fellow resident may prevent him. And a third *baraita* adds: one who owns a house in a shared *chatzer* may not rent it to a doctor, a bloodletter, or a *sofer*. All three *baraitot* appear to allow blocking the opening of a school.

### Non-Jewish Schools

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: *hacha ba-mai askinan? be-tinokot de-akum* — these *baraitot* are speaking of a school for non-Jewish children. A Jew who wished to open a school for non-Jewish students has no special dispensation overriding the objections of the courtyard's residents. The overriding *takkanah* of Yehoshua ben Gamla applies only to Jewish schools, which serve the communal obligation of Torah education. A school for non-Jewish children carries no such privileged status and is treated like any other business bringing outside traffic.

It is worth noting that the *gemara*'s resolution does not necessarily reflect a historical reality of Jews running schools for non-Jewish children; it may simply be the *gemara*'s legal mechanism for squaring the *baraitot* with the ruling derived from Yehoshua ben Gamla's *takkanah*.

### Multi-Grade Schools

The third *baraita* also prohibits renting to a *sofer*. The *gemara* resolves this too: *hacha ba-mai askinan? be-sofer masa* — we are speaking of a *sofer masa*. *Rashi* explains this to mean not a single-classroom school but a multi-grade schoolhouse — a larger, more disruptive institution than a single class. While the *takkanah* requires every town to have a school, it does not require any particular *chatzer* to absorb the noise and traffic of a full multi-grade institution. Residents may block that.

*Tosafot*, however, offers what is probably the better reading. *Tosafot* notes that there is another version of the *gemara* that reads not *sofer* but *sapar* — a barber — making the case simpler. But more importantly, *Tosafot* argues that *sofer masa* should be understood as the communal scribe, the person who drafts legal documents for the entire town (*koseiv shtaros ha-ir*). A communal scribe brings a constant stream of outside visitors to conduct legal business, and therefore falls under the general prohibition against commercial enterprises that generate outside traffic in a *chatzer*. He has no special dispensation comparable to a school.

One further point arises from *Tosafot*'s treatment of the question of renting to a non-Jew more broadly. *Tosafot* observes that *mashma d'im lo haya sofer, hava shari le-haskir le-armai* — had it not been for the business-traffic objection, it would be permissible to rent a courtyard house to a non-Jew. The concern about non-Jews as a physical threat (*d'amar lei aryei arveisa ametzarai* — you have brought a lion to lie at my border), which appears elsewhere in *Bava Basra*, is addressed by *Tosafot* as applying specifically when a Jewish buyer was available and the seller bypassed him — not as a categorical prohibition against any proximity to non-Jewish neighbors.

---

## Class Sizing

### Class Size Numbers

Rava establishes the class-size standards as follows: *sach mikrei dardekei esrin ve-chamsha yanukei* — the standard number of students per teacher is twenty-five. *Ve-i ika arba'in, mokeiman reish duchna* — if there are forty students, one appoints an assistant teacher. *Ve-i ika chamshin, motvinan trei* — if there are fifty students, one appoints two teachers. This framework raises an immediate logical difficulty: if twenty-five is the standard class size and an assistant is needed at forty, what is the status of classes with twenty-six through thirty-nine students? The *gemara* does not address this directly, and the gap opens the door to significantly different readings among the *rishonim*.

### Rambam Reading

*Rambam* and the *Rishonei Sefarad* read the passage as setting a firm maximum. Up to twenty-five students: one teacher alone suffices. More than twenty-five: an assistant must be added. At forty: the assistant alone no longer suffices; a full second teacher is required. At fifty: two teachers are insufficient; additional support is needed. On this reading, the maximum class size under a single teacher is twenty-five, and any number above that mandates additional staffing.

### Tosafot Reading

*Tosafot* reads the passage differently and, as is noted, probably more naturally with the *gemara*'s own text. On *Tosafot*'s reading, twenty-five is not a maximum but a threshold: a teacher handles up to forty students, and it is only at forty that an assistant becomes necessary. At fifty, two teachers are required. The flexibility between twenty-five and forty is real; one teacher can manage up to forty children. This represents a considerably larger permissible class size.

### Ashkenazi Position

The *Rishonei Ashkenaz* offer a third reading that may reflect practical differences in the educational institutions of their communities. On their view, twenty-five is the minimum number of students below which a town cannot be required to establish a school at all. Fewer than twenty-five children does not trigger the obligation; one may bus those children to a school in the neighboring town. Once there are twenty-five students, the town must open its own school. Between twenty-five and forty, one teacher manages the class; at forty an assistant is needed; at fifty two teachers are required. This reading integrates the immediately preceding *halacha* about busing children between towns, and is likely the most contextually coherent reading of the passage as a whole.

---

## Teacher Quality

### Job Security

Rava rules: *hai makrei yenukei de-garis ve-hai achrina de-garis tefei, lo mesalkinan lei* — if there is a current teacher and another teacher who knows more, we do not fire the existing teacher to hire the better one. The concern is *dilma atei lidei peshiuta* — perhaps the incoming teacher, having secured the position, will become complacent and perform less diligently than the one he displaced.

### Competition Incentive

Rav Dimi of Nehardea disagrees sharply. *Kol sheken de-garis tefei* — to the contrary, competitive pressure is precisely what motivates better performance. *Kinat soferim tarbe chochma* — the competitive zeal among scholars increases wisdom. If a teacher knows that a better-qualified candidate can displace him, he will work harder to remain indispensable. The incoming teacher, knowing the same principle applies to him, will also strive to perform at his best, lest yet another superior candidate come along and take his position.

### Breadth vs. Precision

Rava then addresses a different personnel question: *hanei trei makrei dardekei chad garis ve-chad lo dayek ve-chad dayek ve-lo garis* — two schoolteachers: one covers a great deal of material but is not careful (*dayek*) in following up to ensure students have absorbed it correctly; the other is very attentive and precise but covers less ground. Which is preferable?

Rava's initial position is *masvinan hahu de-garis ve-lo dayek* — prefer the one who covers more material, even though he is less attentive. *Shabeshta mi-meila nafak* — errors will work themselves out over time. The broader base of knowledge is the more valuable asset.

Rav Dimi of Nehardea again disagrees: *masvinan de-dayek ve-lo garis* — prefer the one who is more attentive, even though he covers less. *Shabeshta kivan de-al al* — once an error has entered a student's mind, it stays. The initial formation of knowledge is more critical than its breadth; inaccuracies instilled early are nearly impossible to eradicate.

It is worth clarifying precisely what the contrast between *garis* and *dayek* means here. *Rashi* uses the language *she-lomeid harbe* — who learns much — rather than *she-melameid harbe*, suggesting *garis* refers to the teacher's own breadth of knowledge rather than the pace of classroom instruction. One participant offered the more illuminating reading: both teachers are competent, but one moves through a great deal of material at pace without carefully monitoring student comprehension, while the other moves more slowly, covering less ground but ensuring what is taught is thoroughly grasped. This reading sharpens the practical tension considerably: one teacher is filling students with volume; the other is ensuring that what they receive is accurate and retained. The point of principle cuts in favor of the latter: it is better to teach less and teach it correctly than to teach more and embed errors.

### Joab Story

The *gemara* illustrates this with a striking narrative. The verse reads (*Melachim*): *ki sheishet chodashim yashav sham Yoav ve-chol Yisrael ad hichrit kol zachar be-Edom* — for six months Yoav and all Israel remained there until they had cut down every male in Edom. When Yoav returned before David, David asked him: *mai ta'ama avadt hachi* — why did you do this, killing only the males? Yoav replied: *de-chtiv timche et zachar Amalek* — because the verse says *zachar*, which he had learned to read with a *patach*, meaning "the male." David responded: *ve-hanan zecher karinan* — but we read it *zecher*, with a *tzeireh*, meaning "the memory" of Amalek — the entire people, not only the males. Yoav replied: *ana zachar akreyun* — that is how my teacher read it to me.

They went and asked the teacher. *Heichi akreitan?* — How did you teach him to read it? *Tosafot* makes a critical point here: the teacher answered *zecher* — with the correct vowelization. He did not make an error in what he taught; Yoav simply heard it incorrectly, and the teacher never followed up to verify that the student had received the material accurately. That is the sharper and more instructive read: *Tosafot* emphasizes that the failure was pedagogical, not a mistake in the teacher's own knowledge. The teacher taught correctly but failed in his *dayek*, his attentiveness to whether the student truly understood.

David then drew his sword to execute the teacher, citing *arur oseh melechet Hashem remiyah* — cursed is one who performs God's labor deceitfully, who cuts corners in sacred work. The teacher asked to be spared the death penalty and be left instead with the curse. David then cited the end of that same verse: *ve-arur monea charbo mi-dam* — cursed too is one who withholds his sword from blood. The *gemara* records that opinions differ as to whether the teacher was ultimately executed. The story powerfully illustrates Rav Dimi's point: a mistake in foundational learning, left unverified, had catastrophic consequences. The loss was irreversible.

---

## No-Warning Professions

### Professional List

Rava rules: *makrei yenuka, shatla, tavcha, ve-umana, ve-sofer mata — kulan ke-mutarin ve-omdin daminhu* — a schoolteacher, a sharecropper, a butcher, a bloodletter, and a communal scribe are all considered to stand in a state of perpetual forewarning. They may be dismissed on the spot without the standard procedural warning that an employer must give an employee before termination.

### Irreversible Loss

The unifying principle is *kol psida de-lo hadar* — any loss that cannot be recovered. A schoolteacher who transmits an error creates an intellectual defect in the student that, as we have seen, is nearly impossible to undo. A butcher who slaughters improperly produces a *neveilah* — the loss is complete and unrecoverable. A bloodletter performing a medical procedure that goes wrong may cost a life. A communal scribe who drafts a document incorrectly — writing one hundred where the document should read one thousand, for example — creates a legal instrument that cannot simply be corrected. The sharecropper presents a somewhat harder case to explain on these grounds, but the principle as stated is clear: wherever professional negligence produces an irreversible consequence, the worker is treated as having been perpetually forewarned, and immediate dismissal is legally permissible without prior notice.

---

## Business Competition

### Rav Huna Mill Case

Having addressed the world of schools and teachers, the *gemara* pivots to a broader set of questions about commercial competition. Rav Huna rules: *hai bar mavoi de-oki reicheia, ve-ata bar mavoi chavreih ve-ka moki gavei — dina hu de-me'akev ilei* — if a resident of a *mavoi* has set up a mill, and another resident of the same *mavoi* now seeks to open a competing mill nearby, the original miller may legally prevent him. *Ka paskat lei le-chayuti* — you are cutting off my livelihood.

It is important to note the shift from the earlier discussions. The *chatzer* concerned noise and outside foot traffic in a shared private space. The *mavoi* — larger, encompassing multiple *chatzerot* — concerns something different: the right to protection from economic competition. This is the domain of what would later be conceptualized as *hasagat gevul*, encroaching on another's livelihood, though the *gemara* does not use that phrase explicitly.

### Fish Hunting

The *gemara* seeks to support Rav Huna's position from a *halacha* regarding fish hunting: *marchikin metzudat ha-dag min ha-dag ke-melo ritzat ha-dag* — one must distance one's fish trap from another's by the distance a fish runs. Rabbah bar Rav Huna specifies this as *ad parsa* — up to a *parsa*, which is four *mil*, approximately 8,000 *amah*, or roughly two and a half miles. If a fisherman has staked out a location and is actively drawing fish there — feeding them, setting his nets — all others must stay away from that zone. The one who was there first has a kind of possessory claim on that productive space.

### Fish vs. Customers

The *gemara* pushes back, however: *shani dagim de-yahavi siyara* — fish are different, because the fish are being drawn to a specific location by the fisherman's preparatory work. *Rashi* elaborates: *batuach hu she-yikadenu, havay lei ke-man de-mata le-yadei* — the fisherman is effectively certain to capture those fish; it is as though they are already in his hand. In that sense, the other fisherman who intrudes is causing a concrete, tangible loss — something already nearly possessed is being taken away. *Aval hacha mi she-ba etzli yavo, mi she-ba etzlecha yavo* — but in the case of competing mills, customers are not pre-claimed. My customers may come to me; your customers may come to you. No customer is the equivalent of a fish already in the net. The fish precedent therefore cannot directly support Rav Huna's position.

### Unfair Competition

Ravina then raises a different angle: *leima Rav Huna de-amar ke-Rabbi Yehuda?* — perhaps Rav Huna's position that one cannot open a competing mill is consistent only with Rabbi Yehuda's view in a *mishnah* elsewhere. That *mishnah* records Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that a shopkeeper may not distribute roasted grain and nuts to children as promotional incentives, because it draws customers to his shop unfairly. *Va-chakhamim matirin* — the sages permit it, reasoning that the competitor can do the same thing: if you give out nuts, I can give out nuts too. Rabbi Yehuda restricts unfair competitive practices; the sages allow them. Perhaps Rav Huna's protection of the original miller reflects Rabbi Yehuda's restrictive view, and would not be accepted according to the majority.

### Fair vs. Unfair

The *gemara* responds: *afilu teima Rabbanan* — even if you hold like the *Rabbanan* in that *mishnah*, Rav Huna's ruling could still stand. *Ad kan lo paligi Rabbanan alei de-Rabbi Yehuda hasam ela de-amar lei: ana mapalginan amgozai ve-at palgi kusta* — the sages disagreed with Rabbi Yehuda only in the context where both parties are already in business and the question is whether one may employ a particular promotional tactic, because the competitor can use the same tactic. That is a debate about the rules of fair competition between two existing enterprises. But here — *aval hacha afilu Rabbanan modu, de-amar lei ka paskat lei le-chayuti* — the situation is categorically different: there is already an established business, and someone new wishes to open a competing one and directly undercut the first party's livelihood. Even the sages might agree that this crosses a line.

The underlying tension is a real one. A free-market instinct argues that the consumer benefits from more businesses, more competition, and lower prices, and that no one should be able to hold a monopoly simply by virtue of having arrived first. The protectionist instinct argues that a person who has built a business and a livelihood deserves some security against being immediately undercut. The *gemara* here is at least provisionally following Rav Huna's position that the prior occupant of the economic space deserves protection — a position that will be developed further in the discussion that follows.

---

---

# Bava Batra 22

## Hasagat Gvul Overview

### Hasagat Gvul Definition

Today's daf is 22, and we find ourselves in the midst of a fascinating discussion of a category familiar to many: *hasagat gvul*, encroaching upon another person's territory of *parnassa*. This is at its core an interesting policy question — a tension between protectionism and the free market. On one hand, there is a natural impulse to protect certain individuals from devastating competition; on the other hand, one must ask how such protection ultimately serves the general population. That is the overarching issue the *Gemara* has raised.

### Rav Huna's Mill Rule

The position that opens the discussion is that of Rav Huna, in the name of Rav: if someone already has a *reychayim* — a mill — operating in their *mavoi*, one cannot open up a competing mill in that same *mavoi*. The reasoning is straightforward: the original owner was already there, and the newcomer is unfairly encroaching upon his livelihood.

### Chachamim vs R' Yehuda

The *Gemara* then asks how this ruling fits with the dispute between the *Chachamim* and R' Yehuda recorded elsewhere. The case there involves two merchants: if one of them distributes free candy or nuts to children in order to draw all the business to himself, R' Yehuda holds this to be impermissible, since the merchant is not competing on the genuine merits of his goods but is simply using an enticement. The *Chachamim* disagree, ruling that the other merchant is equally free to adopt the same strategy.

The *Gemara* concludes that the two cases are not directly comparable. According to the *Chachamim*, they may well be prepared to protect a business owner from a competitor who moves in fresh — yet in the case of the candy distribution, both merchants were already present and operating, and either one could freely replicate the other's approach. Conversely, one could argue the other way as well: even R' Yehuda, who seeks to protect against unfair business practices, might permit the opening of a competing store outright, since just as the *Gemara* on the preceding daf observed *kinat sofrim tarbe chochma* — competition among Torah teachers sharpens everyone — so too competition among business owners can improve quality and reduce prices. The *Gemara* is thus indicating that the two issues operate along genuinely different axes.

## Property Rights Framework

### Customers as Property

One illuminating way of understanding the entire *hasagat gvul* framework is through the lens of property rights. When the *Gemara* speaks of *hasagat gvul*, the very term evokes moving a boundary marker — literally encroaching on what belongs to another. The question, then, is: when does one *own* something one expects to receive? If a business owner is sufficiently certain to receive a customer's patronage, that anticipated income can be conceptualized as something already in his possession. To divert it is therefore not merely unfair competition — it is akin to theft; one is taking something that already, in a meaningful sense, belongs to the other person.

This property-rights framing may also explain why the *Gemara* does not extend R' Yehuda's position to cover the case of opening a competing store in the *mavoi*. If R' Yehuda's concern is fundamentally one of theft, then even the candy-distribution case could be framed as a kind of taking — and *kal vachomer*, the problem would apply even more acutely when a competitor has not yet opened at all.

### Fishnet Case

This framework connects naturally to a question the *Gemara* raised earlier: how does the *hasagat gvul* discussion fit with the case of spreading a fishnet near a location another fisherman has already staked out? The *Gemara* noted that the staked-out case may be different precisely because the fisherman has drawn the fish to that spot — the fish are, in a sense, already in his hands. This raises the broader question of how much we treat customers as something already belonging to the business owner. The fish case represents a genuine, tangible property claim: ultimately, the fish will be physically captured. Customers, of course, are not taken home in a net — but the conceptual question of whether we frame the situation as a policy concern or as an already-established ownership claim remains the animating tension throughout the discussion. As for the precise measure of *kimlo ritzas hadag* and the limit of *ad parsa*, the *Gemara* itself does not resolve it with precision.

## Baraita Stores Rule

### Stores Next Door

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge — *meisvi* — from a *baraita*: *oseh adam chanut b'tzad chanuto shel chaveiro* — a person may open a store immediately adjacent to his fellow's store; *u'merchatz betzad merchatzato shel chaveiro* — and similarly a bathhouse immediately next to another's bathhouse. *Ve'eino yachol limchot beyado* — the established owner cannot prevent him. Why? Because one can simply say: *atah oseh betoch shelcha va'ani oseh betoch sheli* — you do as you wish on your property and I do as I wish on mine.

This formulation resonates with earlier discussions about physical damage caused indirectly — the principle that one may do as one wishes on one's own property even when the consequences spill over onto a neighbor's interests. If the result of exercising that freedom happens to be that business is diverted from a competitor, that is not the established owner's concern. On the other hand, there are contexts — such as a *chatzer* whose residents collectively wish to maintain residential rather than commercial character — where zoning-like agreements among co-owners can restrict what is permissible. That scenario represents a communal property interest distinct from the simple neighbor-vs.-neighbor dispute.

### Mavoi vs Property

The distinction between *mavoi* rules and ordinary neighbor conflicts is therefore significant. When the *mavoi* as a whole collectively holds an interest in a space — as a semi-public, collectively owned domain — its residents can exercise certain controls over who operates within it. But where the dispute is simply between two neighbors each acting within their own private property, the default rule is that one cannot prevent the other from opening a competing business.

### Competition Benefits

The economic dimension of this permission deserves attention. It might seem intuitive that having multiple competing businesses in a single location would harm each of them — the lone kosher restaurant on a given block would appear to benefit from having no competitor nearby. Yet economists have found that when competing businesses concentrate in the same location, they can collectively create a destination, driving more overall traffic to the area so that all benefit. The *shuk* of *Machane Yehudah* is a vivid illustration: blocks of sandal vendors, blocks of butchers — all thriving precisely because the concentration makes the entire area a destination. Whether this observation holds depends on circumstances, of course — if the available customer base is too limited to sustain two businesses, opening a competitor may simply ensure that both fail. The size and density of the community, the degree of differentiation between offerings, and the overall market are all relevant parameters that the *Gemara* leaves to practical judgment.

## Tanna'im Debate

### Tannaim Dispute

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between Rav Huna's ruling and the permissive *baraita* by noting that it is in fact a debate among *Tannaim* — *tanai*. The *baraita* elaborates: *kofin benei mavo'ot zeh et zeh shelo lehoshiv beneihem lo chayat velo bursaki velo melamed tinokot* — the residents of a *mavoi* may collectively compel one another not to install among them a tailor, a tanner, or a schoolteacher. The underlying concern, as Rashi explains, is specifically about preventing outsiders from opening businesses within the *mavoi*. The collective ownership of the *mavoi* allows its residents to exclude those who have no inherent right to be there, just as one may exclude strangers from private property. *Ul'shcheno eino kofeh'u* — but one cannot exclude a neighbor who actually resides in the *mavoi* from opening such a business.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: *af lshcheno kofeh'u* — one may indeed compel even a neighbor, a fellow resident of the *mavoi*, to refrain from opening a competing business. The *Gemara* reads this dispute as addressing not the foot-traffic concern of the *Mishnah* but the question of commercial competition: can a *mavoi* resident be stopped from opening a competing enterprise by another resident who shares the same right to be there?

### Outsiders vs Residents

Rav Huna breih de-Rav Yehoshua clarifies what he considers obvious: *bar mata bar mata achrita matzi me'akev* — a resident of one town can certainly prevent a resident of a different town from opening a competing business, since the *mavoi* belongs, collectively, to the townspeople, and an outsider simply has no standing there.

### Same Tax Rule

However, there is an important qualification. *Ve'ei shayich becharga dehacha lo matzi me'akev* — if both parties pay the same tax to the same municipal authority, the outsider is not truly foreign and cannot be excluded on that basis alone. As the *Rishonim* explain, this applies to cases where the outsider is not encroaching on anyone's private courtyard or *mavoi* but is operating from a genuinely public space — a pushcart in the middle of the street, for instance. In that case, since he is effectively a fellow member of the same civic community, he cannot be prevented from conducting business in the public domain.

### Cross-Mavoi Question

A further question remains unresolved. Rav Huna breih de-Rav Yehoshua established that once someone has a right to be in a *mavoi*, they may open a competing business there and cannot be stopped — *bar mavoi l'bar mavoi d'nafsheih lo matzi m'akev*. But what of the case of *bar mavoi l'bar mavoi achrina* — a person who lives in one *mavoi* and wishes to open a competing store in a different *mavoi* within the same town? Both parties pay the same taxes and both belong to the same town. The question becomes: can the residents of this *mavoi* exclude someone from another *mavoi* who wishes to operate here?

The irony is that proximity ordinarily suggests greater competition — the closer one is, the more directly one encroaches. Yet the legal logic runs in the opposite direction: the more one "belongs" to a space, the more one's right to operate there is protected. Can the residents of one *mavoi* assert a quasi-ownership interest strong enough to exclude a fellow townsman from another *mavoi* who wishes to open a shop in their domain? The *Gemara* leaves this without resolution — *teiku*.

## Educational Overrides

### Schools Exception

Rav Yosef now observes that even Rav Huna, who takes the strictest position on protecting existing businesses from competition, agrees in one domain: *b'makrei dardakei d'lo matzi me'akev* — one cannot prevent a competing schoolteacher from opening up even where one would ordinarily be able to block a competing business. Competition in education is not suppressed even by those most committed to protecting commercial incumbents.

### Kinat Sofrim

The reason given is the principle invoked by the *Gemara* itself: *d'amar mar kinat sofrim tarbeh chochmah* — the competitive spirit among Torah scholars increases wisdom. When it comes to Torah education, the value of achieving the highest possible quality of instruction is so paramount that it overrides any concern for protecting the incumbent teacher's livelihood. The same logic that might, in a commercial context, tip the balance toward protecting an established business is decisively outweighed, in the educational sphere, by the overriding communal interest in Torah learning. This is structurally analogous to the *Mishnah*'s ruling that while residents of a *chatzer* may block businesses that generate disruptive foot traffic, they may not block a school — education is simply a value of a different order.

### Ezra's Takkanah

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak similarly observes that Rav Huna concedes a second override: *berochlin hamachzirim ba'ayarot dalo matzi me'akev* — the itinerant merchants known as *rochlin* who travel from town to town cannot be prevented from selling their wares, including fragrances and jewelry, even if local establishments carry similar goods. The reason is that this category of commerce is protected by one of Ezra's foundational *takanot*: *Ezra tiken lahem l'Yisrael sheyehu rochlin machzirim ba'ayarot kedei sheyehu tachshitim metzuyan livnot Yisrael* — Ezra instituted that itinerant merchants should circulate through the towns so that jewelry and adornments would be readily available to Jewish women. The protection of women's access to these goods constitutes the same kind of overriding communal concern as Torah education, and it therefore supersedes the normal protections afforded to local businesses.

### Rochlin Restrictions

Nevertheless, this dispensation has its limits. *Le'ahaduri* — merely passing through and selling as one goes — is permitted. *Aval le'akvei* — but establishing a permanent presence in the town — is not. An itinerant merchant who decides to park in a given town indefinitely and set up shop there has crossed from the protected category of the traveling *rochel* into the category of an outside competitor, and the town's residents can prevent him.

There is, however, an exception. *Ve'ee tzurba me'rabanan hee* — if the merchant is a *talmid chacham* — *afilu le'akvei nami* — he may establish himself permanently even if he comes from outside the town. The *Gemara* cites the ruling of Rava, who permitted Rav Yoshiya and Rav Ovadiah to establish shops in a town where they were not residents, contrary to the standard *halacha*. The reason: *keivan derabanan ninhu atu letirdumei migirsaihu* — since they are Torah scholars, requiring them to travel constantly from town to town would severely curtail their opportunity to learn Torah. The interest in sustaining the quality of their *talmud Torah* is sufficient to grant them this advantage.

### Rava's Exception

This ruling raises a pointed question: does not such an arrangement turn Torah into a *kardom lachpor bo*, a tool for personal financial gain? Rashi addresses this candidly. His comment reads *dalo kehilchata* — this is not strictly according to the law — but *ela lifnim mishurat hadin* — it is rather an application of the principle of *lifnim mishurat hadin*. What makes this a striking application of the principle is that *lifnim mishurat hadin* ordinarily describes a person voluntarily surrendering his own entitlements for the benefit of another. Here, the ruling effectively obligates the townspeople to surrender their legitimate right to exclude outside competitors — they are being asked to act *lifnim mishurat hadin* toward these rabbis, accepting a concession for the sake of Torah. One is, in effect, *paskening lifnim mishurat hadin* for the town.

## Market Day Rules

### Basket Sellers Case

The *Gemara* turns to a related scenario. Outside sellers of wicker baskets — *dikulei* — brought their wares to Babylonia from elsewhere. The townspeople of Mechuza sought to prevent them from selling, on the grounds that they were competing with local businesses. Since everyone agrees — whether following Rav Huna or otherwise — that outsiders can be excluded from encroaching on local commerce, the claim of the townspeople appeared straightforward. Yet Ravina permitted the outside sellers to proceed. The reason lies in the phrase *me'alma atu ule'alma lizbenu* — they came from the general population and therefore they may sell to the general population. The key is that on a day when customers from the surrounding region have gathered, the sellers are not specifically targeting the local townspeople's customer base; they are serving the broader, transient population that has assembled precisely because it is a market day.

### Market Day Limits

The *Gemara* makes the scope of this permission precise. *Vehanei milei beyoma d'shuka* — this applies only on the market day itself, when the town becomes a regional hub and its customer base is no longer exclusively local. *Aval belo yoma d'shuka lo* — on any other day, the outside sellers are genuinely displacing local business, and the townspeople may prevent them.

Even on a market day, the permission is limited in a second way. *Ella lizbonei beshuka* — the outside merchants may sell only in the marketplace itself. *Aval le'ahadurei lo* — they may not go door to door. This is coherent: the market is the space that belongs, in a meaningful sense, to the regional public on that day; the streets and homes of the town remain, in some sense, the private domain of its residents.

### Tosafot Moneylenders

Tosafot applies this principle to a significant practical context. The relevant phrase in the *Gemara* — *me'alma atu ule'alma lizbenu* — implies a permission to serve the broader outside population that comes to the market. Tosafot reasons that on a market day, an outside moneylender may lend money to non-Jews and to non-residents who have come from elsewhere specifically for the market: *lehalvos livne adam habaim mekomos sham leshuk ulenochrim deato mealma*. However, *aval livne makom lo* — he may not lend to the permanent residents of that town. Furthermore, *vedavka beshuka aval adure lo* — his lending activity must be confined to the marketplace; he may not pursue clients door to door, nor operate outside the designated market space.

This is a notably narrow reading of the *Gemara*. Where the plain sense of *le'alma lizbenu* might be taken to mean simply that on a market day one may sell to anyone who comes, Tosafot understands it to mean that the outside seller is limited to those who are themselves outsiders — people who, like the seller, have come from elsewhere. Whether Rashi would read the *Gemara* with equal restrictiveness is less clear from his commentary.

## Wool Merchants Case

### Town's Right

The *Gemara* continues with a parallel case. Outside wool merchants brought their wool to the riverbank — *amlorai de'aisu imra lefum nahara* — and the townspeople sought to block them from selling. Rav Kahana's initial ruling was unequivocal: *dina hu demaakvi alaichu* — the townspeople are legally correct; they have a right to prevent outside merchants from selling and competing with local business.

### Debt Collection Claim

The outside merchants, however, responded: *islan ashrai* — we have outstanding debts to collect here; local buyers have purchased goods from us on credit and have not yet paid. They were not, therefore, simply arriving to undercut local merchants — they had a legitimate prior claim on the town that required their presence.

### Minimal Livelihood Rule

Rav Kahana crafted a balanced response. *Zilu zivnu shir chyusaichu* — you may sell, but only in an amount sufficient to cover your basic living expenses while you are here, nothing more. *Ad deakrisu ashraichu vesilu* — sell only until you have collected your outstanding debts, and then depart. This ruling reflects the principle that the rights of the townspeople, while real, are not absolute. Just as a *talmid chacham* may be granted special access because his Torah learning requires it, so too a merchant with legitimate prior obligations cannot simply be turned away — he must be given a minimum foothold sufficient to discharge those obligations. The right to collect what is owed to you, and to sustain yourself while doing so, limits the exclusionary power of the local community, even if it does not override it entirely.

## Rav Dimi's Figs

### Figs Import

Rav Dimi of Nehardea brought a shipment of pressed dried figs by boat. The Resh Galuta instructed Rava: *puk chazi* — go find out and examine him. *Ee tzorba merabanan hu nakit lei shuka* — if he is a genuine *talmid chacham*, secure for him the right to sell in the market. This invokes exactly the special dispensation discussed above — the privilege extended to Torah scholars to operate commercially even as outsiders. Rashi goes further: *nakeit lei shuka* in his reading means *hachriz she-lo yimkor ish ba-ir grogros ela hu* — an announcement should be made that no one else in the city may sell dried figs, granting Rav Dimi an exclusive monopoly.

Rava delegated the task of examining Rav Dimi to his student Rav Adda bar Ahava, using the expression *puk taamei lei be-kankanei* — go smell his barrel, i.e., taste his wine. The idiom means: go examine his interior, probe the quality of his scholarship.

### Elephant Basket Test

Rav Adda bar Ahava went and posed his question — the most demanding one he could devise. He asked: if an elephant swallows an Egyptian wicker basket (*kfifa mitzrit*) and excretes it through the intestinal tract, what is the *halakhic* status of the object? The underlying issue, as Tosafot explains, is whether the resulting material could be fashioned into a vessel: a vessel made of wicker is susceptible to *tumah*, while a vessel made of excrement is not. What is the status of wicker that has passed through an elephant's digestive system? *Lo hava bideih* — Rav Dimi did not have the answer at hand.

### Rav Adda's Rejection

Having failed the examination, Rav Dimi asked his examiner: *Mar nihu Rava?* — Are you Rava? He was new to the town and did not know that Rav Adda was Rava's student rather than Rava himself. Rav Adda's response was physical: *tapach lei be-sandaleih* — he kicked him on his sandal. Rashi clarifies that this means he kicked Rav Dimi on his foot, not that he struck him with his sandal. He then said: *bein didi le-Rava ika tuva* — between me and Rava there is a very great gap. But the implication was clear: between Rav Dimi and Rav Adda, there was an equally large gap in the other direction. *Ana ravach ve-Rava raba de-ravach* — I am your rebbe, and Rava is your rebbe's rebbe. *Lo nakeitu lei shuka* — Rav Dimi was denied the monopoly right to sell in the market.

### Figs Spoil

The consequences were serious: *psadu grogros dideih* — all of his figs spoiled. Rav Dimi went to Rav Yosef and reported what had been done to him. Rav Yosef responded with a pointed invocation: *man de-la sheya le-unisa de-malka de-Edom lo nish-ha le-unisach* — He who did not withhold avenging the affliction of the king of Edom will not withhold avenging your affliction. The proof-text was from Amos: *koh amar Hashem al shlosha pishei Moav ve-al arbaah lo ashivenu al sarpo atzmot melech Edom la-sid* — thus said God: for three sins of Moab and for four I will not relent — because they burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime. Even the honor of a foreign king, desecrated after his death, was avenged by God. Rav Yosef was invoking the same principle on behalf of Rav Dimi.

## Rav Adda's Death

### Death Aftermath

*Nach nafshei de-Rav Ada bar Abba* — Rav Adda bar Abba died. What follows is a remarkable narrative: multiple leading scholars each stepped forward to claim responsibility for his death, and the *Gemara*'s account of their self-recriminations opens a window into the web of interpersonal tensions, competitive dynamics, and moral scrupulousness that characterized life in the great Babylonian academies.

### Rav Yosef's Blame

Rav Yosef said: *ana nishtei* — I am the one who brought this about, because *d'ana latyei* — I cursed him. The language he had used — invoking God's avenging of honor — was understood as a curse, and he took responsibility for its effect.

### Rav Dimi's Blame

Rav Dimi of Nehardea likewise said: *ana nishtei* — I am to blame, *d'afsi grogaros didi* — because it was through bringing my figs that the entire chain of events was set in motion. This reasoning is poignant: the one who was wronged — who had his figs spoiled, was humiliated in the examination, and was denied his commercial right — felt responsible for the death of the man who had wronged him, on the grounds that the entire episode would never have occurred had he not come with his figs. This reflects a kind of moral accounting that goes beyond simple causation: even the remote cause of a chain of events can weigh upon the conscience, particularly when the chain ends in tragedy.

### Abaye's Blame

Abaye said: *ana nishtei* — I am to blame, because *d'amru lehu l'rabbanan ad d'gamrimitu garmi bei Abaye tu achlu bisra shamna bei Rava* — Rav Adda used to tell Abaye's students: "Rather than chewing bones in Abaye's *yeshiva*, come eat fine, fat meat in Rava's *yeshiva*." He was actively recruiting away from Abaye's study hall, denigrating the quality of Abaye's Torah by contrast with Rava's. Abaye felt that since he was aware of this behavior and had said nothing to Rav Adda about it, he bore responsibility for the consequences — he should have rebuked him, and his failure to do so made him, in some sense, complicit. There may also be a subtler subtext here: several of those claiming responsibility are, in effect, describing ways in which Rav Adda had himself acted improperly — and yet each narrator frames it as his own failing. The moral posture throughout is one of self-examination rather than external attribution.

### Rava's Blame

Rava also said: *ana anishteia* — I brought about his death. The incident he described is this: when Rava's attendant went to the butcher to purchase meat — *lemishkal umtza* — Rav Adda was there and declared to the butchers: *ana shakilna bisra mikamei shamtei de-Rava* — I should receive my meat before Rava's attendant, because *ana adifna minei* — I am more important than he. Even if the claim was only that he outranked the attendant rather than Rava himself, the act of asserting precedence over Rava's representative was implicitly a statement about his own standing relative to Rava. Rava felt that knowing of this incident and failing to speak to Rav Adda about it made him culpable.

### Abaye's Blame

*(See above; Abaye's account has been incorporated in the preceding subsection as it was presented in the transcript.)*

### Rav Nachman's Blame

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: *ana enishteia* — I am to blame. He explained: *de-Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reish kalla hava* — he was the head of the *kalla*, responsible for delivering the major *shiur*. His practice — *kol yoma mikamei deniul le-kalla* — was that before each *shiur* he would review the material with Rav Adda bar Ahava as a preparation partner, *marei badeih Rav Ada bar Ahava leshamta vehadar ayeil le-kalla* — running through the *sugya* together, sharpening his thoughts, before entering to give the *shiur*. Rav Adda was, in effect, his indispensable *chavruta* for this purpose.

### Coffin Wish

On one particular day — *hahu yoma* — Rav Pappa and Rav Huna breih de-Rav Yehoshua detained Rav Adda bar Ahava because they had missed the conclusion of a tractate. Rashi identifies this as the *siyum* of Masechet Bechorot. They asked Rav Adda to relay to them all of Rava's *chidushim* on the final perek: *eima lan hanei shamata de-ma'aser behema heichi amrinhu Rava*. He did so at length — *amar lehu hachi amar Rava vehachi amar Rava* — and the learning extended so that *naga leih le-Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* — it grew late for Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak. His *chavruta* had not appeared and he had not had the opportunity to prepare.

When the assembled students urged Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to rise and begin: *kum denaga lan lama yativ mar* — he replied: *yativna veka mintarna le-arseih de-Rav Ada bar Ahava* — I am sitting here waiting to see the coffin of Rav Adda bar Ahava. The words were heavy with fury: where are you? Come and help me, I need you to have prepared with me before *shiur*.

*Ada-hachi nafak kula denach nafshieh de-Rav Ada bar Ahava* — and at that very moment, word went out that Rav Adda bar Ahava had died. *U-mistabra de-Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak anshieh* — the *Gemara* concludes that it is most plausible that it was Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak who brought about his death, precisely because he had explicitly said that he was waiting for the coffin — a statement far more direct than Rav Yosef's invocation of divine justice — and the temporal sequence was as close as could be imagined.

It is worth noting, in connection with the examination Rav Adda had posed, that Tosafot points out the elephant-basket question is itself one the *Gemara* leaves unresolved elsewhere. One might ask, then, what kind of fair test that was. Tosafot addresses this: *ve'yesh lomar de'mikol makom hava lei le'atuyei hanach re'ayot de'maiti hatam ve'dachi lehu* — even if the question has no definitive answer, Rav Dimi should at least have marshaled the relevant arguments and evidence and engaged with them. Simply saying "I don't know" — without any attempt to reason through the problem — was itself the failing. A *talmid chacham* can be evaluated not only by whether he knows an answer but by how he thinks when confronted with a question he has not seen before.

## Wall Construction

### Wall Distance Rule

The *Gemara* transitions to the new *Mishnah*: *mi she'haya kotlo samuch le'kotel chaveiro lo yismoch lo kotel acher ela im kein hirchik mimenu arba amot* — if one person's wall is situated near another's wall, one may not build a second wall up against it unless one sets it at least four *amot* away. The concern is that if two walls are closer than four *amot* to each other, no passageway remains between them — and as the *Gemara* will explain, that passageway matters.

### Window Privacy

The *Mishnah* continues with *ha'chalonot* — the case of windows on a boundary wall. The rule is: *bein milma'ala bein milmata bein kenegdan arba amot* — whether the neighbor's window is above, below, or directly across, a wall may not be built within four *amot* of it. The concern here is *hezek re'iyah* — the damage caused by being able to see into another's windows. If the new wall is only slightly higher than the window, one could stand on it and look in. If it is only slightly lower, the same problem applies. To fully protect against this, the wall must be four *amot* away in any direction that would permit such a line of sight. The *Mishnah* permits building a wall six feet away even if it substantially reduces the neighbor's access to sunlight — a limitation that seems relatively minimal, particularly if the wall is subsequently built to a great height, though the *Mishnah* accepts this as the operative threshold.

### New Wall Reading

The *Mishnah*'s phrasing, however, presents a difficulty. *Mi she'haya* implies an existing wall — the phrasing seems to describe a situation already in place. How did the wall get there if it was not permitted to be built that close? Rav Yehudah offers a reading: *ha'ba lismoch lo yismoch ela im kein hirchik mimenu arba amot* — read the *Mishnah* as addressing a person who is planning to build: if you want to build a wall next to your neighbor's wall, do not do so unless you leave four *amot* of clearance. The present tense of *mi she'haya* is simply a description of the intended scenario, not of an already-completed wall.

### Wall Fell Reading

Rava objects: *ve'ha mi she'haya kotlo samuch le'kotel chaveiro katani* — but the *Mishnah* says *she'haya*, which grammatically implies that the wall already existed. *Ela amar Rava hachi katani* — Rava therefore offers an alternative reading: *mi she'haya kotlo samuch le'kotel chaveiro berichuk arba amot* — originally the wall was built properly, at a distance of four *amot* from the neighbor's wall, which was permitted. *Ve'nafal* — and then it fell. Now the owner wishes to rebuild it. *Lo yismoch lo kotel acher ela im kein hirchik mimenu arba amot* — when rebuilding, one may not place the new wall within four *amot* of the neighbor's wall; the same distance must be maintained. In either reading, the practical *halacha* is the same: four *amot* of clearance is required.

### Trampling Benefit

*Mai ta'ama?* — what is the reason for this distance requirement, given that these are simply two garden or courtyard walls and no outsiders are obviously affected? The *Gemara* answers: *dechasha dehacha ma'ale lehacha* — the trampling foot traffic on this side is beneficial to that side. If four *amot* of space are maintained between the two walls, a usable passageway is created through which people walk. As people walk alongside a wall, the ground is compressed and hardened, which reinforces the foundation and structural integrity of the wall. Whoever already has a wall therefore acquires a benefit from the passage of foot traffic alongside it. If the neighbor now builds a second wall so close that no one can pass through, that benefit is eliminated. The law therefore protects the existing wall-owner's acquired interest in that passage: you may not build so close to my wall that you deprive me of the foot traffic that is beneficial to it.

# Bava Batra 23

## Kotel Gina vs. Chatzer

### Wall Distance Context

The sugya before us concerns the permissible proximity of one wall to another on neighboring properties. The older *mefarshim* on the *mishnah* — found back on 22a — discuss building a perpendicular wall *l'chatchila*, where walls already exist and one is adding another. But the *gemara*, as we saw with Rabbi Eliezer, is operating under the assumption that this is actually a case where one of the walls has fallen and is now being rebuilt. In that context, when you rebuild, you must leave a certain distance — four *amot* — between your wall and your neighbor's.

### Rav: Gina vs. Chatzer

The *gemara* opens on 22b, eight lines from the top, with *Amar Rav: lo shanu ela kotel gina, aval kotel chatzer, im ba lismoch, somech* — Rav says that the entire rule requiring four *amot* of distance applies only to the wall of a garden, a *gina*. But when it comes to the wall of a courtyard, a *chatzer*, if one wishes to build it somewhat closer, one may do so even within four *amot*.

### Ground Compaction Logic

What is the distinction between a *gina* and a *chatzer*? In a garden where things are grown, no one is walking on one side of the wall; the land there is cultivated rather than traversed.
