The four *amot* distance is therefore required so that people can walk in the space between the two walls. That walking tramples and compacts the ground, which solidifies the foundation of the wall. In a *chatzer*, however, people are constantly moving about within the courtyard itself, compacting the earth around the wall's base on the interior side. With that side already well-packed, we are less concerned about the absence of a passageway on the other side.

One might fairly ask why packing down only one side is sufficient — surely both sides of the wall need support. The question is a reasonable one, and it points directly to the objection that follows.

### Rabbi Oshia Opposes

*Rabbi Oshia omer: echad kotel gina ve-echad kotel chatzer, im ba lismoch, ein somech.* Rabbi Oshia disagrees with Rav's distinction entirely. In his view, there is no difference between the wall of a garden and the wall of a courtyard: in either case, one may not build the new wall closer than the required distance. This is precisely because, as the question above suggested, one side of the wall being well-packed is not sufficient. The other side — the side between the two walls, which belongs to neither party in the usual sense — also needs to be traversed so that the ground there is compacted as well. Therefore, the space must be maintained regardless of what type of enclosure the wall surrounds.

### Old vs. New City

Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina resolves the apparent dispute: *velo pligi* — Rav and Rabbi Oshia do not actually disagree. They are simply addressing two different scenarios. *Ha be-ir yeshana, ha be-ir chadasha* — one is speaking of an old city, and the other of a new city. In an old, established city, the ground has already been compacted over many years of use, and so Rav permits building closer in a *chatzer*. In a newly built city, however, the ground has not yet been packed down, and Rabbi Oshia's stricter requirement applies. There is also a dimension here that resembles the difference between *de facto* urban realities and *l'chatchila* city planning: in old cities the layout has developed organically, with narrow alleyways and dense construction, whereas in a new city one has the opportunity to establish proper infrastructure from the outset.

---

## Window Privacy Rules

### Mishna: Windows

The *mishnah* states: *hachalonot bein milmala bein milmata bein miknegdan arba amot* — with respect to windows, whether above, below, or directly opposite, the required distance is four *amot*. The scenario is that Reuven has a window in his wall, and Shimon now wishes to build a wall that will face that window. The *mishnah* establishes that Shimon's wall must be situated such that its top is at least four *amot* above or four *amot* below Reuven's window, and the wall must stand at least four *amot* away if it is directly across.

### Peeping Prevention

A *braita* elaborates on the reasons: *milmala k'dei shelo yatzitz v'yireh* — the wall must be four *amot* above the window so that someone standing atop the wall cannot lean over and peer in. *Milmata shelo yaamod v'yireh* — it must be four *amot* below so that someone standing on the lower wall cannot look up and see in through the window. In both of these cases, the four *amot* measurement reflects the approximate height of a human being — it is the distance beyond which a person cannot effectively peer in or peer up. This is a fascinating point: we usually think of four *amot* as the horizontal personal space around a person, corresponding roughly to one's arm span. Yet here four *amot* appears in a vertical context, measuring against human height — and it is worth noting that arm span and height are in fact approximately equal for most people, which explains how the same unit serves both contexts.

### Opposite Wall Distance

For the wall built directly *miknegdan* — opposite the window — the reason given by the *braita* is *shelo yaafil*, so as not to cause darkness. This is a different concern entirely: not that someone will peer in, but that a wall built too close will block the natural light that would otherwise enter through the window. If the wall is at least four *amot* away, sunlight can still reach the opening.

### Conflicting Reasons

The *gemara* now raises a difficulty. The *braita* has given a single reason for the four *amot* requirement in the case of the opposite wall — prevention of darkness. But earlier the *gemara* discussed another reason for the distance requirement: the concern about trampling and packing down the earth (*davsha*). These two rationales cannot both be primary without creating a conflict. If the only reason were *davsha*, there would be no need to invoke darkness; if the only reason were darkness, *davsha* would be superfluous.

### Tarpeling Context

The *gemara* resolves this: *hacha b'mai askinan b'va min hatzad* — we are dealing here with a wall being built perpendicular to the wall containing the window, making an L-shape rather than a parallel configuration. In that case, the trampling concern is not directly at issue in the same way — people are not walking through a passage between two parallel walls. The darkness concern, however, is very much applicable: even a perpendicular wall, if built too close to the window, can obstruct the angle of incoming light.

The case involving *davsha*, by contrast, involves walls without windows facing one another, where the passage between them is what matters. The two scenarios — parallel walls facing each other, and a perpendicular wall approaching a windowed wall — each implicate different reasons, and thus different rationales can apply without contradiction.

### Window Width Distance

Once we are in the case of a perpendicular wall, the question becomes: how far must it stand from the window itself? The *gemara* cites an opinion in the name of Rav: *kemlo rochav chalon* — the perpendicular wall must be set back a distance equal to the full width of the window. So if the window is four feet wide, the perpendicular wall must be placed four feet from the edge of the window opening.

### Curved Wall Top

A difficulty immediately presents itself: if the wall is only one window-width away, someone who climbs atop it will still be at an angle from which they can see directly into the window. This seems to undermine the entire privacy rationale. *Amar Rav Zevid bemadrit kotlo* — Rav Zevid answers that the case is one where the top of the wall has been curved or sloped, creating an incline rather than a flat surface. A curved top makes it practically impossible to stand on the wall and look in. This is similar to walls fitted with barbed wire or shards of glass — security features designed to prevent climbing — and here it serves the additional halakhic purpose of eliminating the concern of *hezek re'iyah*, the damage of unwanted visual intrusion.

### One vs. Two Walls

The *gemara* then reconciles the two measurements — four *amot* and window-width — by distinguishing between scenarios. *Lo kashya: kan beruach achat, kan bishtei ruchot* — there is no contradiction. When there is only one wall being built perpendicular to the windowed wall, the window-width distance suffices. When two walls are being constructed — creating something like a passage that funnels directly toward the window — the full four *amot* distance is required, because the combined structural narrowing intensifies the risk of visual intrusion.

---

## Gutter & Ladder Rules

### Trampling vs. Ladder

The *gemara* raises the same analytical question about the next *mishnah* as it did about the window rules: when we require a certain distance between a wall and a neighboring gutter, is the reason the *davsha* concern — that people need space to walk and compact the ground — or is it because of the need to be able to set up a ladder to perform maintenance on the gutter?

### Overhang Solution

The *gemara* resolves this by specifying the case: *b'mazchila meshupaat* — we are dealing with a gutter that extends on an overhang. Because the gutter protrudes overhead, a person can walk beneath it without any obstruction. Therefore, the spacing of the new wall does not affect the trampling of the ground — people can still pass underneath. The reason the four *amot* distance is still required is entirely for the sake of ladder access: the owner of the gutter needs to be able to erect a ladder to repair and maintain it, and the wall being built nearby must leave enough room for that.

### Dovecote & Ladder

The *mishnah* states: *marchikin et hasulam min hashovach arba amot kedei shelo tikpotz hanemiya* — one must keep a ladder at least four *amot* away from a dovecote, so that the *nemiya* — a weasel or mongoose — should not be able to leap from the ladder into the dovecote and attack the doves. If the ladder is placed directly across from the dovecote, the weasel can climb the ladder and jump across. At a distance of four *amot*, that leap is beyond its range.

### Gutter Distance

The *mishnah* continues: *ve-et hakotel min hamazchila arba amot kedei sheyehei zokef et hasulam* — and one must keep a wall at least four *amot* from a neighboring gutter, so that the gutter's owner has sufficient space to erect a ladder for maintenance. This is, as the *gemara* has now clarified, the operative rationale in the case of an overhanging gutter — not ground compaction, but ladder access.

---

## Grama & Bloodletters

### Rabbi Yosi Position

The *gemara* raises the question of whether our *mishnah* — with its various requirements to keep ladders and walls at sensitive distances — is compatible with the position of Rabbi Yosi. Rabbi Yosi held the principle *zeh chofer betoch shelo ve-zeh noteiah betoch shelo*: each person does as he wishes on his own property, and the impact on his neighbor is not his legal concern. Rabbi Yosi's view is essentially a strong property-rights position: what is mine is mine, what is yours is yours, and I am not obligated to limit my activities on my land simply because they may affect yours.

### Direct vs. Indirect

If the *mishnah* is like Rabbi Yosi, why does it impose restrictions on ladder placement and wall distance? The *gemara* answers by citing a statement of Rav Ashi: *ki havina bei Rav Kahana hava amar: modeh Rabbi Yosi begirei dideh* — Rabbi Yosi concedes in the case of one who shoots arrows directly at another's property. Even Rabbi Yosi agrees that direct aggression against a neighbor's domain is prohibited. And in the case of the ladder and the dovecote, the danger is not truly indirect: weasels live in holes and wait for precisely such a ladder to be placed nearby before climbing up and attacking. Placing the ladder directly across from the dovecote is therefore sufficiently direct — close enough to the equivalent of "shooting arrows" — that even Rabbi Yosi would prohibit it.

### Grama is Asur

But then the *gemara* asks: is this not still a case of *grama* — indirect causation? The person erecting the ladder is not himself attacking the doves; it is the weasel that does so. *Amar Rav Tuvi bar Matna: zot omeret grama b'nezikin asur* — this *mishnah* comes to teach us that *grama b'nezikin* is prohibited. Causing damage indirectly is still halakhically forbidden.

### Rav Yosef's Trees

This principle is illustrated by a vivid incident. Rav Yosef had date trees growing on his property. Bloodletters — practitioners of medical bloodletting — had taken to sitting beneath these trees to conduct their work. The blood they left on the ground attracted ravens, which then flew up into the trees and damaged the dates. Rav Yosef told the bloodletters to take their practice elsewhere.

### Abaye Questions

Abaye challenged Rav Yosef: *v'ha grama hu* — is this not merely *grama*? The causal chain here is long: the bloodletters sit and practice their trade, the blood attracts ravens, the ravens fly into the trees, and only then are the dates damaged. The bloodletters are not directly harming the trees at all.

### No Chazaka for Nezikin

The response invokes Rav Tuvi bar Matna's ruling: *grama b'nezikin asur* — indirect damage is still prohibited. A further question then arises: the bloodletters have been coming to this spot for years. Do they not have a *chazaka* — an established usage — that grants them the right to continue? *Amar Rav Nachman amar Rabba bar Avuha: ein chazaka l'nezikin* — no *chazaka* applies when one is causing *nezikin*. The mere passage of time does not legitimize an activity that damages a neighbor.

### Rav Mari Qualification

However, *Rav Mari amar b'kutra, v'Rav Zevid amar b'veit hachisei* — Rav Mari and Rav Zevid each qualify the principle of *ein chazaka l'nezikin*, limiting it to especially severe nuisances: cases involving heavy smoke (*kutra*) or a toilet (*beit hakisei*) placed near one's property. These are situations so offensive that no amount of prior usage can normalize them for the affected neighbor.

Rav Yosef accordingly invokes this framework on his own behalf: *l'didi d'anina da'ati, k'kutra u'veit hachisei damyan li* — for him, with his particular sensitivity, the ravens and the blood are subjectively equivalent to smoke or a toilet placed next door. What is striking here is that the *gemara* appears to honor this subjective claim, treating Rav Yosef's personal threshold of sensibility as halakhically operative. The underlying question — whether the *davsha* causing the dates to spoil is the primary damage, or whether it is Rav Yosef's subjective revulsion at the bloodletting scene — animates the discussion without being fully resolved. Either way, the *gemara* endorses Rav Yosef's demand that the bloodletters leave, and *ein chazaka l'nezikin* remains limited in its application to situations of genuinely severe and ongoing harm.

---

## Dovecote Distances

### 50 Amot Rule

The *mishnah* states: *merachikin et hashovach min ha-ir chamishim ama* — one must keep a dovecote at least fifty *amot* from the city. The doves will inevitably forage in the nearby area, and placing the dovecote too close to inhabited land means they will damage the crops or garden plots of city residents. The fifty *amot* buffer is designed to prevent this.

### Circumference Rules

Furthermore, *velo yaaseh adam shovach betoch shelo ela im ken yesh lo chamishim ama lachol ruach* — a person may not build a dovecote in his own property unless he has fifty *amot* available in every direction around it. The doves' natural ranging area is this fifty *amot* radius, and so the owner must control enough land that the doves' foraging does not encroach upon others' fields.

Rabbi Yehuda offers a different measurement: *beit arba korin melo shegar hayona* — a space of four *kor*, which works out to approximately 273 *amot*, described as the full natural flight distance a dove can cover in one sustained effort. This is a considerably larger area than the fifty *amot* of the first opinion.

### Chazaka Permission

Both opinions agree on one dispensation: *ve-im lekacha, afilu beit rova, harei hu b'chezkato* — if one purchased a property that already had a dovecote in place, even if that dovecote is smaller than required or situated closer to the borders than the rules would allow, it is considered *b'chezkato*, grandfathered in. The assumption is that the previous owner had already arranged some form of understanding with the surrounding neighbors, and the purchaser inherits that established status.

---

## Dove Trapping Rules

### 30 Ris Limit

The *gemara* challenges the fifty *amot* rule by citing a *braita*: *ein porsin nishbin leyona ela im ken haya rachok min hayishuv sheloshim ris* — one may not set out traps for doves unless one is at least thirty *ris* away from an inhabited settlement. If fifty *amot* were the outer limit of a dove's range — beyond which the bird belongs to the finder — why would trapping require staying thirty *ris* away? This seems to imply that doves can travel far greater distances than fifty *amot*.

### Dove Flight Distance

Abaye resolves the apparent contradiction: *mishiti tuva ve-chasheu be-chamishim amata milia* — a dove does eat considerably while traveling, and by the time it has traveled fifty *amot* from the dovecote, it has slowed down substantially from all the foraging along the way. The fifty *amot* limit thus represents the extent to which we consider the bird to be reasonably connected to a nearby dovecote, not the absolute outer limit of how far a dove can physically travel.

### 100 Mil Rule

Yet another *braita* states that within a settled area, one may not set traps even at a distance of a hundred *mil*. This seems far more restrictive than either the fifty *amot* or the thirty *ris* figure.

### Vineyard Context

Rav Yosef resolves this: *b'shuv kramim* — that ruling pertains to a settlement of vineyards. Doves can fly considerably greater distances when vineyards are present, perhaps because the terrain offers different resting and feeding patterns, causing them to continue flying farther than they otherwise would.

### Dovecote Area

Rava adds a further case: *b'shuv shovchin* — a settlement densely populated with dovecotes, where the birds are constantly moving between one dovecote and another. In such an area, a dove may hop from cote to cote across great distances, so one must go much farther afield before setting traps.

### Ownership Determination

The *gemara* then asks why the ruling mentions the concern about *shovchin* at all — could one not simply say that the traps are fine because the doves encountered would be from the trapper's own dovecotes? The *gemara* entertains three possibilities: the additional dovecotes belong to the trapper himself, in which case trapping is unproblematic; or they belong to non-Jews, in which case there is no concern for their ownership; or they are ownerless (*hefker*). The different resolutions determine how far from a settlement one must be before setting traps, and which configuration triggers the full hundred-*mil* restriction.

---

## Dovecote Distances (II)

### Purchaser & Heir Claims

*Amar Rav Papa v'iseyma Rav Zevid: zot omeret, to'anin lalo'ke'ach ve-to'anin layoresh* — Rav Papa, and some say Rav Zevid, infer from the *mishnah*'s statement that a purchaser who acquires a smaller or more closely situated dovecote is nonetheless *b'chezkato*, that the *beit din* is prepared to advance legal claims on behalf of both a purchaser and an heir. That is, if a third party challenges the legitimacy of the dovecote's placement, the *beit din* does not require the purchaser or heir to produce positive proof of prior authorization; the *chazaka* of the previous owner is treated as already having established the right, and the *beit din* builds that presumption into the current possessor's position.

The *gemara* immediately questions whether we need the *mishnah* here to tell us about an heir — do we not already have an explicit *mishnah* elsewhere establishing that one who comes on the basis of inheritance does not need to bring a formal claim? *Haba mishum yerusha eino tzarich ta'ana*. The novelty must therefore lie in the case of the purchaser, *loke'ach*.

But the *gemara* pushes further: do we not also have an explicit *mishnah* about a purchaser? *Lakach chatzer u-va zizin u-guztra'os harei zeh b'chezkato* — one who purchases a courtyard that has protrusions and balconies already extending into the public domain acquires them with their established status. If we already have that precedent, why do we need to derive the rule again from the dovecote case?

The *gemara* answers that each case is necessary — *tzricha*. The case of protrusions over a *reshut harabbim* might have been treated leniently on the theory that the public effectively granted permission, or that the owner appeased the public, or that the public simply forgave the encroachment. One could not necessarily extend that to a private property dispute. Conversely, a case involving only private parties might be explained away by the assumption that the dovecote owner personally negotiated with each affected neighbor. But in the *reshut harabbim* case, there is no identifiable party to negotiate with — *man payis?* Who does one even appease? Each scenario thus teaches something the other cannot, and both rulings are required.

The *gemara* then raises a further challenge: the *mishnah*'s ruling that a purchased dovecote is *b'chezkato* seems to stand in tension with *Rav Nachman's* principle in the name of Rabba bar Avuha — *ein chazaka l'nezikin*. If a dovecote causes damage to neighbors' crops, how can its *chazaka* be honored? The *gemara* resolves this by invoking the qualification of Rav Mari and Rav Zevid: *ein chazaka l'nezikin* applies specifically to severe nuisances such as smoke or a toilet. The harm caused by a dovecote — doves eating from nearby fields — is not of that extreme category, and so the *chazaka* for the dovecote is maintained. Not all sources of *nezek* are treated equally: some are severe enough to override any *chazaka*, while others are tolerated once an established usage has been recognized.

---

## Found Dove Rules

### Nippul Ownership

The *mishnah* turns to the case of a *nippul* — a baby dove that cannot yet fly, a *gozal*, found on the ground. *Nippul hanimtza betoch chamishim ama, harei hu shel ba'al hashovach* — a chick found within fifty *amot* of a dovecote belongs to the owner of that dovecote. Since the chick cannot fly, it could only have gotten there by waddling from the nearby cote.

### Beyond 50 Amot

*Chutz michamishim ama, harei hu shel motza'o* — if found beyond fifty *amot*, the chick belongs to the finder. The assumption is that it could not have walked that far from the dovecote, and so its origin is unknown; the finder acquires it.

This *gemara* raises a broader question that connects to the rules of lost objects in *Bava Metzia*: ordinarily one would expect a found animal to require *simanim* before being claimed. Here, however, proximity to a dovecote serves as an automatic assignment of ownership, without requiring formal identification. One might argue that within fifty *amot* of a known dovecote, the chick is not truly a lost object at all — it simply has not yet flown far enough to sever its connection to the cote.

### Two Dovecotes

*Nimtza bein shtei shovcha'ot, karov lazeh shelo, karov lazeh shelo* — if the chick is found between two dovecotes, each within fifty *amot*, ownership is determined by proximity: whichever dovecote is closer, the chick belongs to its owner. If the chick is found exactly equidistant — *mechtzah al mechtzah* — the two owners split it: *shneihem yachloku*.

---

## Rov vs. Karov

### Rov Challenge

*Amar Rabbi Chanina: rov vekarov holchin achar harov* — Rabbi Chanina raises a pointed challenge. The entire operating principle of the *mishnah* appears to be *karov*, proximity: we assign the chick to the nearest dovecote. But do we not have the competing principle of *rov* — majority? If one dovecote has five thousand doves and another has five, it is statistically far more likely that any given chick came from the larger one. Why does proximity override numerical probability?

### Rov vs. Karov Sources

The *gemara* identifies two distinct *d'Oraita* principles in tension here. On one side is *acharei rabim lehatot* — the Torah's instruction to follow the majority. On the other side is the model of *egla arufa* — the decapitated heifer ritual, where the Torah requires measuring from the discovered corpse to determine which city is closest and must bring the *egla arufa*, without regard for the size of the nearby cities. That procedure clearly operates on *karov*, proximity. *Af al gav d'rov d'Oraita ve-karov d'Oraita afilu hachi rov adif* — Rabbi Chanina maintains that even though both are *d'Oraita* principles, *rov* is the stronger of the two and should prevail.

### Egla Arufa Model

Rabbi Zeira challenges this by citing the *egla arufa* itself: *vehaya ha-ir hakerova el hechalal* — the verse specifies the city closest to the slain person. *Af al gav de'ika achrita denefisha minah* — and this applies even if there are other, larger cities in the vicinity. This seems to be a direct proof that *karov* can and does override *rov* — at least in that context.

### Mountain Area Limit

The *gemara* deflects the proof: the *egla arufa* case is specifically *beyoshevet bein heharim*, situated in isolated mountain terrain. In such a setting, there may not be any significantly larger city available; the nearby towns may all be of comparable size, making *rov* inapplicable. In that narrow context, *karov* governs by default. But in a normal setting where larger cities exist, one might argue that *rov* should prevail, and the *egla arufa* verse would not override it.

This is a striking limitation. Taken at face value, it would seem to confine the *egla arufa*'s *karov* principle to geographically isolated communities alone, which seems difficult to square with the *Torah*'s broader presentation of the *egla arufa* ritual. The *gemara* here appears to be making a theoretical point rather than a comprehensive ruling on the *egla arufa* procedure, but the qualification is notable.

---

## Chick Movement Rules

### Rav Ukva on Waddling

The *gemara* explains the empirical basis for the fifty *amot* limit by citing *Rav Ukva bar Chama: kol hamedadeh ein medadeh yoter mechamishim amah* — any chick that is waddling (*medade*) cannot waddle more than fifty *amot*. This is the physical reality that underlies the *mishnah*'s rule: waddling chicks are simply incapable of traveling farther than fifty *amot* from the nest.

### Rabbi Yirmiya Query

Into this settled framework steps Rabbi Yirmiya with his celebrated question: *raglo achat betoch chamishim amah ve-raglo achat chutz mechamishim amah mahu* — what if the chick has one foot inside the fifty *amot* boundary and one foot outside it? To whom does such a chick belong?

### Rejection

*Afkuh l'Rabbi Yirmiya mibei midrashah* — Rabbi Yirmiya was expelled from the *beit midrash*. The question was deemed so far outside the bounds of serious inquiry as to warrant removal. Yet the condemnation requires explanation, since the *mishnah* itself just addressed the case of a chick found exactly equidistant between two dovecotes — which implies precisely the kind of borderline scenario Rabbi Yirmiya is raising.

*Tosafot* offers the key insight: it was not the form of the question that offended, but its underlying implication. Rav Ukva bar Chama had stated as a matter of established fact that chicks cannot waddle more than fifty *amot*. Rabbi Yirmiya's question presupposes that a chick might take a half-step past the fifty *amot* line — thereby implicitly challenging the factual ruling of the *Chachamim*. It is this subtle questioning of the received scientific determination, rather than any logical absurdity in the question itself, that led to his expulsion. *Rashi* adds simply that Rabbi Yirmiya was being unnecessarily burdensome — *shehayah matriach aleihem* — and the *beit midrash* had already moved on to larger conceptual questions about human mortality, city proximity, and the principles of *rov* and *karov*. Pedantic hypotheticals about the precise placement of a chick's foot were not welcome.

---

## Final Rov Resolution

### Equal Dovecotes

*Nimtza bein shenei shovachot, karov lazeh shelo, karov lazeh shelo, ve-af al gav de-chad mineihu nafish mechavreih* — the chick found between two dovecotes goes to the closer one, even if the other is larger. But if they are equal in size — *sheshneihem shavin* — proximity governs, and the chick belongs to the owner of the nearer dovecote. This resolves Rabbi Chanina's challenge: the *mishnah* is simply not addressing a case where the dovecotes differ in size at all, and so no conflict with *rov* arises.

### Vineyard Exception

But then the *gemara* asks: if the dovecotes are of equal size, why not invoke *rov d'alma* — the majority of all doves in the world? Any given dove is statistically more likely to have originated from some large dovecote elsewhere than from one of two small ones in front of us.

### Vineyard Chick Case

*Hacha bemai askinan b'shvil shel kramim* — we are dealing with a chick waddling along a path through a vineyard. The key point is that any dove coming from "the world at large" would have had to fly, not waddle. And the *gemara* has already established that a waddling chick cannot travel more than fifty *amot*. If we find a *medadeh* chick waddling along a vineyard path, it cannot have come from afar — it must be from one of the local dovecotes. *D'i ita d'me'alma ati, bimdadei lo matzi ati* — if it had come from the broader world, it could not have gotten there by waddling. Therefore, *rov d'alma* is entirely inapplicable, and *karov* — the proximity to one of the two local dovecotes — is the only operative principle. Whichever dovecote the waddling chick is nearest to, that is where it came from.

---

---

# Bava Batra 24

## Rov vs. Karov

### Mishna Overview

The daf continues a discussion that has been unfolding across several pages concerning the tension between two competing principles of attribution: *rov* (majority) and *karov* (proximity). The *mishna* presented a case involving a dove found near a particular dovecote, where the ruling was that the dove is attributed to the owner of that nearby cote — an application of *karov*. This stands in apparent tension with the position of Rabbi Chanina, who holds that one always follows *rov*, the majority, rather than mere proximity. The Gemara has been working systematically to respond to each piece of evidence that might support *karov*, in order to preserve and defend Rabbi Chanina's principle.

### Gemara Defense

With this framework in mind, the Gemara continues its sustained effort to shore up Rabbi Chanina's position, deflecting each apparent counterexample and insisting that under normal circumstances, *rov* governs.

---

## Blood Braita

### Abaye's Proof

The Gemara now records that Abaye offers his own support for Rabbi Chanina. *Af anan nami tanina* — we too have taught a *braita* that corroborates the principle of following *rov*. The *braita* states: *dam she-nimtza ba-prozdor sefeko tamei she-chazakato min ha-makor* — blood found in the *prozdor* (the antechamber or canal) is treated as doubtfully impure, and the reason given is that its presumptive origin is the *makor* (the source, i.e., the uterus). This ruling, Abaye argues, demonstrates that we follow *rov* even when *karov* points elsewhere.

### Anatomy Explained

To understand this *braita*, the Gemara invokes a well-known anatomical metaphor attributed to the Sages: *mashlu mashal chachamim be-isha, ha-cheder ve-ha-prozdor ve-ha-aliya* — the Sages compared the female anatomy to a house consisting of three parts: the *cheder* (inner room), the *prozdor* (antechamber), and the *aliya* (upper story). In halachic terms, the *cheder* represents the uterus; only blood originating there is considered *dam niddah* and renders a woman *tamei*. The *prozdor* is the passage through which such blood would travel. The *aliya* is a third, less clearly identified source, connected to the *prozdor* by a kind of opening or tube (*lul patuach*), from which blood of a different and non-*tamei* character could potentially emerge. The question, then, is this: if blood is found in the *prozdor*, which source do we attribute it to — the *cheder* (which is the *rov*, since the great majority of blood comes from there) or the *aliya* (which, being connected by the *lul*, is *karov*, or more immediately proximate)?

The *braita*'s ruling is that we follow *rov* and assume the blood comes from the uterus. This is Abaye's proof for Rabbi Chanina's principle.

It is worth noting that there is genuine difficulty in identifying what precisely the *aliya* refers to anatomically. One compelling approach — evident in some *acharonim*, though ultimately rejected — draws on a parallel passage in which the Gemara notes that a cow does not have a *prozdor*. What a cow lacks is the external labia. This suggests that the *prozdor* in the human female context might refer not to the inner vaginal canal but to the external space formed by the labia. If that reading is adopted, the *aliya* becomes far more intelligible: it would refer to the urethra, and the concern would be that blood found externally might have come from blood in the urine rather than from the uterus. The *lul patuach* would then describe the urethal opening. This interpretation makes the physiological picture coherent in a way that internal readings struggle to achieve. Nevertheless, other evidence in the sources points toward the *prozdor* being an internal structure, and that reading is generally maintained, leaving the *aliya* as an anatomical puzzle. Either way, the Gemara's underlying point is clear: we go by *rov* and not by *karov*.

### Rov vs. Matzui

Rava responds to Abaye's proof with a pointed objection. *Rov u-matzui ka'amart?* — Are you speaking of a case that is not merely *rov* but also *matzui*, meaning not only quantitatively majority but practically prevalent and established by pattern? These are two distinct concepts. *Rov* in the ordinary sense means simply that more of something comes from one source than another — as when a distant dovecote has five hundred birds while the nearby cote has only a few. *Matzui*, by contrast, reflects a known, observed pattern: not just that there is more blood in the uterus, but that in practice virtually all blood passing through the *prozdor* is known to flow from the *cheder*. It is not merely a numerical majority; it is the established, natural way things work.

Rava's point is that *rov u-matzui leit de-man d'palig* — when you have both majority and established prevalence together, no one disputes that you follow this combined indicator. The woman's case is such an instance: the blood is not just probabilistically more likely from the uterus, but experientially and practically it is the source under normal circumstances. Therefore, Abaye's proof is less than it appears — it is not a proof that *rov* alone defeats *karov*, but rather that *rov* combined with *matzui* does so, and that is uncontroversial.

### Rava's Inferences

Having established that the *braita* of Rabbi Chiya — who rules that blood found in the *prozdor* is treated as certainly *tamei* rather than merely doubtfully so — implies that we follow *rov* and treat the ruling as definitive, Rava proceeds to draw three inferences (*shma mina mid'Rabbi Chiya tlat*). First: when there is a conflict between *rov* and *karov*, the *halacha* follows *rov*. Second: *ruba de'oraita* — the principle of following *rov* and treating the outcome as a *vadai* (certainty) rather than a *safek* (doubt) is a biblical-level rule, as evidenced by the fact that Rabbi Chiya treats the woman as definitively *tamei*, making her liable for *karet* should she enter the *Beit HaMikdash*, and making *terumah* she touches subject to burning — rulings befitting a *vadai* determination. Third: the ruling supports the position of Rabbi Zeira.

### Rabbi Zeira

Rabbi Zeira's position, invoked in the third inference, addresses a classic case: a piece of meat found in the street whose origins are unknown. If there are nine stores in the city selling kosher meat and one selling *treif*, one may rely on the *rov* and eat the meat — even if, as Rabbi Zeira holds, the gates of the city are closed, meaning there is no external *rov* from surrounding communities to add to the equation. Some opinions had required a double *rov* — the *rov* within the city plus the broader *rov* of the surrounding region — in order to permit the meat. Rabbi Zeira maintains that a single *rov* suffices, and the ruling is *vadai* — permissive without qualification. The case of blood in the *prozdor* supports this: the woman is compared to a city with closed gates (*daltot ha-medina ne'ulot*), since no blood is entering from outside her body, and yet we rule with certainty based on the single internal *rov*. This shows that one *rov* is sufficient, that it is treated as *vadai*, and that it overrides *karov*.

### Meat Case

The meat case merits further elaboration, as it raises a number of important questions. One might ask whether the size of the *rov* matters — must the kosher stores vastly outnumber the non-kosher one, or is even a small majority sufficient? The general principle is that *rov* applies even when the majority is not overwhelming; one does not need nine-to-one. What matters more is the nature of the *miut* (minority): is it a *miut ha-matzui* (a prevalent minority) or a *miut she-eino matzui* (a negligible minority)? A *miut she-eino matzui* is generally understood as less than ten percent or perhaps less than five percent. When the *miut* is non-trivial — a *miut ha-matzui* — there is an obligation to investigate further if investigation is possible (*chiyuv levarer*). When the *miut* is negligible, one may rely on the *rov* even if investigation is possible (*efshar levarer*). This is why, for example, after *shechita* one must check the lungs of an animal for *treifos* — because *treifos* in the lungs constitute a *miut ha-matzui* — but need not check every other organ, where *treifos* are a *miut she-eino matzui*. On the question of whether the proximity of the meat to the non-kosher store is relevant: based on everything established about *rov* versus *karov*, even if the meat is found closer to the non-kosher store, the *rov* of kosher stores would in principle prevail, though this is not explicitly stated in the Gemara's discussion here.

---

## Rabba Retracts

### Retraction Question

Having cited Rava's challenge — that the case of blood in the *prozdor* involves not mere *rov* but *rov u-matzui*, and therefore cannot serve as proof for the general principle of *rov* against *karov* — the Gemara notes: *hadar beih Rabbah meihai* — Rabbah retracted. The question is which position Rabbah retracted. Did he retract his earlier characterization of the case as one of *rov u-matzui*, or did he retract the use of Abaye's *braita* as a proof for the general principle?

### Interpretation

The Gemara's language suggests that Rabbah retracted the objection to using Abaye's proof — that is, he accepted that the *braita* does in fact demonstrate the principle of *rov* against *karov*, without requiring the added weight of *matzui*. This is, however, somewhat puzzling. Rava's original point had real force: once a pattern has been empirically established, as it is in the case of blood flowing from the uterus, this constitutes an even stronger basis for attribution than a mere numerical *rov*, and anyone who would argue for *karov* against a simple *rov* would face an even steeper climb against *rov u-matzui*. The conclusion that Rabbah ultimately treated the case as a standard *rov* — assimilating *rov u-matzui* back into the ordinary category — implies that those who would argue for *karov* could theoretically do so even when a practical pattern has been established, though this is very difficult to understand once such a pattern is clear. The Gemara does not elaborate further on this point, leaving it as a somewhat unresolved tension.

---

## Wine Barrel

### Rav's View

The Gemara now presents a new case. *Chavit she-tzafah ba-nahar* — a barrel of wine floating in the river. No one is chasing it, so it may be claimed as *aveidah*. The question is whether it is permitted to drink — i.e., whether it is treated as Jewish wine or as *stam yeinam*. Rav rules: if the barrel is found opposite a city that is majority Jewish, it is permitted, because we attribute it to the nearby city. If it is found opposite a city that is majority non-Jewish, it is forbidden, for the same reason of proximity. Rav's ruling is thus explicitly based on *karov* — he attributes the barrel to whatever city it is nearest.

### Shmuel's View

Shmuel disagrees. Even if the barrel is floating past a city that is majority Jewish, Shmuel rules it is forbidden — because the majority of cities along the river are non-Jewish, and one should follow that broader *rov* rather than the nearby city. Shmuel thus sides with *rov* even against *karov*.

### Reconciliation

The Gemara considers whether Rav and Shmuel debate the principle of Rabbi Chanina itself — whether Shmuel accepts it and Rav rejects it. But consistent with the Gemara's sustained effort to defend Rabbi Chanina, it declines this reading: *de-kulei alma it lehu de-Rabbi Chanina* — in fact, both Rav and Shmuel accept the principle of following *rov*. Their dispute is more specific. Rav reasons that if the barrel had truly come from a distant upstream city, the obstacles of the river — the protrusions (*akulei*) and the still waters (*pshurei*) that Rashi describes — would have stopped or diverted it before it arrived here. Therefore, the distant *rov* is practically inaccessible to this location and should be discounted. Since the access of the distant majority is obstructed, Rav falls back on *karov*. Shmuel responds: *charifa de-nahara nakit ve-atei* — the powerful current of the river carried the barrel past all obstacles. Therefore, the distant *rov* remains relevant and governs.

Both agree that obstacles can in principle reduce the weight of a distant *rov* — just as the Gemara elsewhere, in the context of *eglah arufah*, speaks of physical barriers that limit access from other cities. The question is simply whether the river's current overcomes those obstacles. The Gemara thus reaffirms that everyone holds of Rabbi Chanina; the practical disagreement is only about whether a particular impediment is sufficient to discount the distant *rov*.

---

## Orlah Vineyard

### Ravina Ruling

The Gemara introduces another case. A barrel of wine (*chatzva de-chamra*) was found in a vineyard planted with *orlah* grapes. The circumstances suggest the barrel had been stolen. Ravina ruled the wine permissible — one need not assume it came from the *orlah* grapes in this particular vineyard. This is striking, since the vineyard is *karov* — the barrel is right there in it.

### Evidence Explanation

The Gemara explains that this ruling does not reflect a principled application of *rov* over *karov*. Rather, *shani hatam* — that case is different, because the evidence itself points away from the nearby vineyard. The reason: *demignav minei atsnuyei begaveih lo matsnei* — a thief does not hide stolen goods in the same place from which he stole them. Rashi explains: thieves are afraid that the workers who tread the grapes (*dorchei ha-anavim*) will discover the hidden barrel. Therefore, a stolen barrel found within the vineyard almost certainly came from elsewhere — the thief would not have concealed it in the very location where discovery is most likely. Ravina's leniency is thus not a statement about *rov* triumphing over *karov* in the abstract; it is a specific evidential inference that the very presence of the barrel in this vineyard makes attribution to it less plausible, not more.

### Barrel vs. Grapes

The Gemara qualifies this reasoning. *Ve-hanei milei chamra* — the logic of the thief not hiding the goods at the scene applies only to a barrel of wine, which would be recognized as coming from a particular vineyard and thus discovered. *Aval invei* — if what was found were a bunch of stolen grapes, the Gemara indicates that a thief might indeed hide them within the same vineyard, since loose grapes are less identifiable. The distinction is thus between a recognizable, attributed container (the barrel) and undistinguishable produce (the grapes themselves). The ruling follows accordingly.

---

## Wine Flasks

### Rava's Ruling

A further case: *hanehu zikki de-chamra de-ishtakach bei kufai* — flasks of wine found between the vine rows of a vineyard. Here the relevant question is not *orlah* but *stam yeinam*. The vineyard belongs to Jews. Rava ruled the wine permissible, attributing the flasks to the Jewish owners of the vineyard even though, as the Gemara clarifies, the majority of those who pass through the area are non-Jews.

### Jewish Sellers

The Gemara asks whether Rava's ruling implies he rejects Rabbi Chanina — following *karov* (the Jewish vineyard) over *rov* (the majority non-Jewish passersby). The answer is again: *shani hatam* — no, this is different. *De-ruba de-shafochei Yisrael ninhu* — the majority of those who actually fill and sell wine flasks in this area are Jews. Rashi explains that the Jews operate small wine-filling stations along the road, serving as what one might picture as provisioners for travelers. So although most of the travelers passing through are non-Jews, when it comes to the specific activity of filling wine flasks, the majority of the vendors doing so are Jewish. The non-Jewish travelers are getting their flasks filled with kosher Jewish wine. Thus, Rava's ruling does not rest on *karov* alone but on a *rov* specific to the type of transaction at hand — who fills the flasks.

This raises an interesting question: once a non-Jewish traveler receives a flask of wine and handles it, does the wine remain permitted? The Gemara does not address this directly, but the implication of the case, as presented, is that the flask has not been handled in a way that would render it *stam yeinam* — perhaps because it was sealed or because the evidence indicates it had not been opened.

### Flask Sizes

The Gemara further qualifies the ruling. *Ve-hanei mili be-ravrevi* — this applies only to large flasks. A large flask is the kind one gets filled at a provisioning station, not something carried from home. *Aval be-zutrei* — small personal flasks are presumed to have come from the traveler's own supply (*eima mi-drachei naflu*, they fell from those traveling the road), and those would be suspect as *stam yeinam*. The Gemara adds one more refinement: *ve-i ika ravrevi be-hadayihu* — if a large flask and a small flask are found together, one assumes the small flask was also filled at the Jewish provisioner alongside the large one, for the purpose of balancing the load on the donkey. Rashi notes this practice: when one side of a donkey carries a large, heavy wine container, smaller flasks are loaded on the other side to balance the weight. If found together with a large flask, the small flask is therefore also attributed to the Jewish source.

---

## Trees & Cities

### Mishna Rules

The Gemara now transitions to a new *mishna* on a more classically *Bava Batra* theme: the required distance between trees and a city. *Marchikin et ha-ilan min ha-ir esrim v-chamesh amah* — a fruit-bearing tree must be kept at least twenty-five *amot* from the edge of a city. *U-v'charuv u-v'shikma chamishim amah* — for the *charuv* (carob) and the *shikma* (sycamore), the required distance is fifty *amot*.

### Abba Shaul

Abba Shaul extends the rule: *kol ilan srak chamishim amah* — any non-fruit-bearing tree requires fifty *amot* of distance from the city. Rashi explains this on the grounds that a non-fruit-bearing tree is aesthetically unpleasant near a city (*ilan srak gnai hu la-ir*), and therefore a greater buffer is required. Rashi also explains that the *charuv* and *shikma* specifically require fifty *amot* because of their wide and sprawling branches, which would crowd the space adjacent to the city.

### City Priority

The *mishna* then addresses which party has the prior claim when a conflict arises. *Ve-im ha-ir kadma* — if the city was established first and the tree was planted afterward within the prohibited zone, the city may have the tree cut down *and does not owe payment*, since the planter was in violation from the outset. Notably — and this is a surprising ruling — even if *the tree was there first* (*ve-im ilan kadam*), the city may nonetheless have it cut down; in that case, however, the city *must pay* the owner, since the tree owner was not in violation.

### Doubt Cases

In a case of doubt about which came first (*safek zeh kadam safek zeh kadam*), the *mishna* rules that the tree is cut down and no payment is made. The bias in doubt cases thus favors the city.

---

## Noy Ha'ir Reason

### Ulla's Reason

The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the rationale for requiring trees to be kept distant from a city? Ulla answers: *mishum noy ha-ir* — for the beauty of the city. The open, unplanted space immediately adjacent to a settlement is aesthetically desirable, and this aesthetic interest is a recognized halachic basis for requiring the twenty-five *amot* buffer.

### Migrash Question

The Gemara challenges this: why invoke *noy ha-ir* at all? Let the ruling derive instead from the Torah's principle of *migrash* — the open space surrounding the cities of the Levites. The Torah speaks of a thousand *amot* of green space (*migrash*) that must be maintained outside such cities, which cannot be converted into fields, and conversely, fields cannot be converted into *migrash*. If this is a general principle about maintaining open space near settlements, it would provide a much stronger (and Torah-based) source for the tree-distance rule — though notably at a thousand *amot*, far exceeding our *mishna*'s twenty-five.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

The Gemara responds: the *mishna* is operating according to the position of Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that the laws of *migrash* — maintaining the green belt and not converting it — apply only to the cities of the Levites as specified in the Torah. For ordinary cities, there is no biblical mandate to maintain such open space, and a city may arrange its surroundings as it chooses. Hence the need for a different rationale: *noy ha-ir*.

### Trees in Migrash

The Gemara then addresses the position of the *rabbanan*, who hold that the *migrash* rules do apply more broadly — that one cannot convert a *migrash* into a *sadeh* (field) or vice versa. Even according to them, the *mishna*'s rule is independently necessary, because the prohibition on converting *migrash* applies only to planting it with *zeraim* (seeds, i.e., grain crops). *Aval ilanos avdinan* — trees, however, may be planted within the *migrash*, since trees are consistent with the character of open, habitable green space. A park with trees still functions as a *migrash*; a wheat field does not. Accordingly, even if a city must maintain a thousand-*amah* *migrash* under the *rabbanan*'s view, trees within that *migrash* are permitted — yet our *mishna* still requires that the tree line begin no closer than twenty-five *amot* from the city, for *noy ha-ir*.

---

## Enclosed Spaces

### Karpef Rules

The Gemara supports the distinction between seeds and trees by citing a *braita* from the laws of *eruv*. If one has a *karpef* — an enclosed space — larger than *beis sa'atayim* (fifty *amot* by a hundred *amot*, or five thousand square *amot*) that was enclosed for the purpose of habitation (*hukaf le-dira*), it qualifies as a *reshus ha-yachid* in which one may carry on *Shabbos*.

### Seeds vs. Trees

The *braita* then addresses what happens if the majority of this space is subsequently used for agricultural purposes. If the majority is planted with seeds — converting it effectively into a grain field — it loses its status as a habitable space and carrying within it is prohibited, since a grain field is not the kind of space in which people dwell and conduct their lives. However, if the majority is planted with trees, it retains the character of a courtyard or garden (*harei hu ke-chatzer u-mutar*) — people walk among trees, gather in parks, and use such spaces for living activities. Trees, unlike grain, do not strip a space of its quality as a human habitation. This distinction in *hilchos eruv* provides the conceptual parallel: just as trees are consistent with the *migrash* character of open habitable space, while grain crops are not, so too in the context of a city's green belt, trees are a more acceptable presence — yet the immediate twenty-five *amot* must still remain entirely unplanted for the sake of *noy ha-ir*.

---

## Enclosed Spaces (II)

### City Spacing

Applying this logic back to the city context: even if trees may be planted within the *migrash* under the *rabbanan*'s view without transforming it into a prohibited *sadeh*, the *mishna* still establishes that the tree line cannot begin immediately adjacent to the city. A buffer of twenty-five *amot* of completely unplanted space must be maintained for the aesthetic quality of the city — *noy ha-ir* — regardless of what the broader *migrash* rules permit.

---

## Tree vs. Well

### Well Mishna

The Gemara now directs attention to an upcoming *mishna* on 25b that deals with the required distance between a tree and a *bor* (cistern or well): *marchikin et ha-ilan min ha-bor esrim ve-chamesh amah* — twenty-five *amot*, and fifty for the *charuv* and *shikma*, measured both laterally and downward. The parallel to our *mishna* is explicit, and the Gemara compares the two in detail. The outcomes, however, differ in a revealing way. In the *bor* case: if the well came first (*im ha-bor kadmah*), the tree is cut down and the city pays; if the tree came first (*im ha-ilan kadam*), the tree is not cut down at all; and in a case of doubt (*ve-im safek*), the tree is also not cut down. In the city case, by contrast, the tree is *always* cut down regardless of which came first — the only variable is whether payment is owed.

### Payment Query

This asymmetry prompts the Gemara's question. When the well has priority and the tree owner was in violation, why must the well owner *pay* to have the tree removed, whereas when the city has priority and the tree owner was in violation, the city need *not* pay? Why is the city treated more favorably than a private well owner?

### Committee Pot

Rav Kahana offers one answer: *kidra de-bei shutfei lo chamimei ve-lo kerirei* — a pot under the care of partners is neither hot nor cold. A responsibility shared by many is executed by none. Because the city's obligation to pay would be distributed among many people, no individual would feel the urgency to contribute, and the collective would never get around to reimbursing the tree owner. If payment were required, the practical result would be that the tree would never get cut down. To ensure the city can actually accomplish the removal, the law spares it the payment obligation. There is a certain irony here: the city's collective dysfunction winds up operating to its legal advantage. The Gemara itself notes that this answer, while functional, is not the most satisfying one.

### City Rights

The better answer is simply that the city has greater rights than a private individual. The *hezek de-rabbim* — damage suffered by the many — is treated with greater legal weight than *hezek de-yachid*, harm to an individual. The collective interest of the city in maintaining its proper character and spacing is a more powerful legal interest than that of a single well owner, and it therefore entitles the city to have the tree removed without owing compensation, even when the city is asserting a right that a private party in the same position would have to purchase.

The Gemara then clarifies that Rav Kahana's *kidra de-bei shutfei* reasoning was actually meant to address a different part of the *mishna*: the clause that says when the tree came first, the city cuts it down *and then* pays. One might have expected the tree owner to demand payment upfront before permitting removal. Rav Kahana explains: because it is so difficult to get the collective to pay, and because we want the removal to actually happen, the law allows the city to cut first and pay later. This means the tree owner must wait for his money — a disadvantage — but the alternative, requiring payment in advance, would mean the tree never gets removed. The law therefore prioritizes the outcome the city needs while preserving the tree owner's right to compensation, however delayed.

---

## Tree First Case

### Cut First Issue

The *mishna*'s ruling that when the tree came first, the city cuts it down and pays (*kotzetz ve-noten damim*), raises an immediate procedural question: why should the city be permitted to cut the tree down before paying? The tree owner was not in violation; it seems entirely reasonable that he should demand his money before surrendering his property.

### Logistical Answer

Rav Kahana's answer, as established above, is logistical: *kidra de-bei shutfei* — shared responsibility among the many members of the city means that if payment must precede removal, the city will never actually organize and execute the payment, and the tree will remain standing. Since the city has a legitimate interest in having the tree removed, the law permits them to act first and settle the debt afterward. The tree owner retains his right to be paid, but cannot hold the tree hostage to that right.

---

## Doubt Case

### Burden Shift

The final clause of the *mishna* — that in a case of doubt, the city cuts without payment — stands in stark contrast to the parallel *mishna* on the well, where doubt results in the tree not being cut at all. The Gemara explains the divergence through the principle of *hamotzi me-chavero alav hara'aya* — the burden of proof lies with the one who seeks to extract something from another's possession.

### Presumptive Right

In the *bor* case, if the tree came first with certainty, the tree would not be cut down. Therefore, in a case of doubt, the well owner cannot demand removal: since there is a scenario in which he would have no right to cut the tree, he must prove that scenario does not apply. Absent such proof, the tree remains — the burden falls on him to demonstrate he has the right to cut.

In the city case, however, the tree is cut down regardless of which came first; the only question is whether payment accompanies the removal. Since the city is always entitled to remove the tree, it does so in the doubt case as well. The remaining question — must it pay? — is now governed by *hamotzi me-chavero alav hara'aya* in the opposite direction: the tree owner must prove that his tree preceded the city in order to collect payment. Since he cannot, the city cuts and owes nothing. The city's presumptive right to remove the tree, which exists in all scenarios, anchors the doubt case in its favor — both as to the act of removal and as to the absence of payment.

---

---

# Bava Batra 25

## Threshing Floor

### Fixed vs. Ad Hoc

The *mishna* at the bottom of 24b continues the theme of maintaining appropriate distances between neighbors and begins with the rule: *merachikin et ha-goren ha-kavua min ha-ir chamishim ama* — a fixed, permanent threshing floor must be kept fifty *amot* from the town. The reason is straightforward: the chaff produced during threshing is dispersed by the wind and can blow into people's faces and fields. The requirement of *chamishim ama* creates a buffer large enough to prevent this.

The *mishna* continues: *lo ya'aseh adam goren kavua betoch shelo* — a person may not establish a fixed threshing floor within his own property *ela im ken yesh lo chamishim ama l'chol ruach*, unless he has fifty *amot* clear in every direction, so that chaff cannot drift into a neighboring field. The *mishna* then adds: *umerachik min nitiotav shel chaveiro umin niro k'dei shelo yazik* — one must also keep it sufficiently distant from his neighbor's plantings and from his neighbor's *nir* (a fallow field left to rest or to kill off weeds) so as not to cause damage.

### Abaye's Two Cases

The *gemara* immediately notices a tension: *mai shna reisha u'mai shna seifa* — what distinguishes the opening clause from the closing one? If the rule is fifty *amot* in all directions, why does the *mishna* seem to add a separate requirement about plantings and fallow fields? Abaye resolves this by reading the *mishna* as containing two distinct cases. The opening clause addresses a *goren kavua*, a large, established threshing operation, which requires fifty *amot*. The closing clause, he argues, addresses a *goren she-eino kavua*, a non-fixed, ad hoc threshing floor, for which the required distance is assessed case by case based on what is necessary to avoid actual damage.

### Non-Fixed Operation

This raises a further question: *heichi dami goren she-eino kavua* — what precisely characterizes a non-fixed threshing floor, and why does it create less potential damage? Rav Yosef b'Rebbi Chanina answers: *kol she-eino zoreh b'rachat* — any operation that does not use a large winnowing implement. Without the large-scale vessel that scatters chaff widely, the reach of the dispersed material is more limited, and therefore the required distance is reduced accordingly.

### Rav Ashi's Reading

Rav Ashi reads the *mishna* differently. Rather than two separate cases, he holds that the *mishna* is presenting a single rule and then explicating its rationale. *Mai ta'ama merachikin goren kavua min ha-ir chamishim ama* — why fifty *amot* from the city? *K'dei shelo yazik* — in order not to damage the neighbor's plantings. On this reading, the closing clause of the *mishna* is not adding a new *halacha* but simply explaining the reasoning behind the one already stated.

### Baraita Confirmation

A *braita* is then cited in support: it teaches that just as one keeps the threshing floor fifty *amot* from the city, so too one keeps it fifty *amot* from a neighbor's gourds, cucumbers, plantings, and fallow field — and concludes *k'dei shelo yazik*, in order not to cause damage. This language parallels the *mishna* precisely. *Bishlama l'Rav Ashi nicha* — for Rav Ashi, this fits well: the *braita* treats the reference to plantings and fallow fields as an explication of the same fifty-*amah* rule, not a separate case. *Ela l'Abaye kashya* — but for Abaye, who reads the *mishna* as covering two distinct cases, the *braita* is difficult, since it presents everything as a single unified rule. The *gemara* concedes: *kashya* — it remains a difficulty for Abaye.

### Nir Damage Question

Having established the framework, the *gemara* pauses on a conceptual difficulty. *Bishlama mi-kishu'av u-mi-dilu'av d'azil avka v'ati b'libei u-matzi lei* — the harm to growing crops like gourds and cucumbers is understandable: the wind carries the dusty chaff into the field where it settles and interferes with the growing produce, absorbing nutrients and causing damage. *Ela mi-niro amai* — but if the field is a *nir*, a fallow field with nothing actively growing, why is there any concern? What harm does chaff blown into an unplanted field actually cause?

### Chaff as Manure

Rav Abba bar Zavda (and some attribute this to Rav Abba bar Zutra) resolves the question: if sufficient chaff accumulates, it decomposes and effectively becomes manure. One might think this is actually beneficial, and *Tosafot* addresses this directly: *af al gav she'aso'o galal, af al gav degalal mashbiach hakarka, kesheyesh kullah galal mazik* — while manure in moderation improves soil, if the entire field becomes nothing but decomposed chaff-turned-manure without anything planted, it is actually damaging to the land. This completes the explanation of why the fifty-*amah* requirement applies even with respect to a fallow field.

---

## Odorous Operations

### Nevelot, Kevarot, Burski

The *mishna* at the top of 25a turns to a different category of neighbor damage — not physical harm from dispersed particles, but harm through smell. Three types of operations must be kept fifty *amot* from the city: *nevelot* (carcasses, i.e., operations involving the storage or processing of animal carcasses), *kevarot* (cemeteries), and the *burski* (tannery). These are essentially zoning regulations — not disputes between individual neighbors but categorical restrictions on which kinds of operations may be located within a residential area at all. The concern with *nevelot* is specifically the stench of decomposition rather than any concern about the slaughter itself, which is processed quickly. The concern with the *burski* is similarly olfactory — tanneries generate powerful and persistent odors from the curing process.

### Tannery Eastward

Beyond the general fifty-*amah* requirement, the *mishna* adds a specific directional restriction: *ein osin burski ella l'mizrach ha'ir* — a tannery may only be established to the east of the town. The underlying reason is the prevailing wind pattern. *Rashi* explains that the wind from the east is weak, while *Tosafot* frames it in the reverse: the strong wind blows from the west. Either way, the practical result is the same — the dominant wind current travels from west to east, and by situating the tannery to the east of the city, the wind carries the smell away from the residential area rather than into it. This wind pattern, flowing consistently from west to east, corresponds to well-known meteorological patterns: westerly winds push weather systems eastward, which is also why eastbound flights experience headwinds while westbound flights are assisted by tailwinds.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

*Rabbi Akiva* disagrees with the restriction to the east: *lechol ruach hu oseh chutz mi-ma'arava* — one may establish a tannery in any direction except the west, because placing it to the west would carry the stench directly into the city. North and south, he allows with greater latitude. He also requires the fifty-*amah* distance in all permitted directions.

### Gemara Clarifies Distance

The *gemara* asks how to read *Rabbi Akiva*'s position precisely. One possibility is that when he permits other directions, he permits building even within fifty *amot* — *lechol ruach hu oseh ve-somech, chutz min ha-ma'arav, umarchik chamishim amah* — meaning only the west requires fifty *amot* while other directions require no particular distance. The other reading is that *lechol ruach hu oseh umarchik chamishim amah* — all other directions require fifty *amot* as well, but *chutz min ha-ma'arav, she-eino oseh kelal* — the west is simply prohibited entirely.

A *braita* resolves the question: *Rabbi Akiva omer lechol ruach hu oseh umarchik chamishim amah, chutz min ha-ma'arav, she-eino oseh kol ikar, mipnei shehi tadira* — one may build in any direction as long as it is fifty *amot* away, except the west, where it may not be built at all, because the western wind is constant. The word *tadira* here — spelled with an *alef*, though *Tosafot* notes it is more consistently spelled with a *hei* — means "constant" or "regular." Both the *tanna kamma* and *Rabbi Akiva* thus agree that prohibited directions are absolutely prohibited, and permitted directions require fifty *amot*; they disagree only on how many directions are prohibited: the *tanna kamma* restricts the tannery to the east alone, while *Rabbi Akiva* prohibits only the west.

---

## Wind & Shechina

### Constant Wind Debate

The *gemara* now focuses on the word *tadira* — that the western wind is "constant." *Rava* poses the question to Rav Nachman: *mai tadira* — what does this mean? The obvious reading, the *pshat*, is that the western wind is the most prevalent wind, blowing regularly from west to east and thus most likely to carry odors into the city. But is that actually accurate?

### Four Daily Winds

This reading is challenged from a tradition cited in the name of Rav Chana bar Abba in the name of Rav: *arba ruchot menashvot bechol yom* — four winds blow every single day, and the northern wind is mixed with all of them. *She-ilmalei chen ein ha-olam mitkayem afilu sha'ah achat* — without the northern wind blended into every other wind, the world could not be sustained even for a moment.

### Southern Wind Harsh

Furthermore, *veruach deromit kashah mikullan* — the southern wind is the harshest of all. *Ve-ilmalei Ben Netz she-ma'amida, macharevet et ha-olam* — were it not for *Ben Netz*, the angel (whom *Rashi* identifies as the "son of the hawk," apparently a celestial being whose function is to restrain the southern wind), it would devastate the world entirely. The *gemara* cites a verse from Iyov: *ha-mibinatecha ya'aver netz yifros k'nafav l'teiman* — from your wisdom does the hawk spread its wings toward the south. Notably, this is already at least the second citation from Iyov in this *masechet* since the extended *aggadata* on that subject, a pattern worth tracking. The point of this tradition is that the northern wind, not the western, seems to be the most essential and ubiquitous — so the western wind's claim to being uniquely "constant" is not obviously supported by meteorological observation.

### Constant = Shechina

*Rava* therefore resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting *tadira* entirely. *Ela mai tadira — tadira bi-shechina* — it does not mean that the western wind is the most frequent; it means that the west is the location of the *shechina*, the Divine Presence. The prohibition on placing a tannery to the west is not primarily about wind patterns at all. It is about not situating a malodorous operation in the direction of God's presence.

### Sun Bowing West

This requires justification: why is the west the location of the *shechina*? The *gemara* cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *bo v'nachzik tov l'avotenu, she-hodi'unu makom tefilla* — let us acknowledge the debt we owe our ancestors for having taught us the proper direction of prayer and the location of the Divine Presence. The source is a verse in Nechemya — associated with the *Anshei Knesset Hagedola* — which states: *utzva ha-shamayim lecha mishtachavim* — the hosts of heaven bow down to you. Since the sun is among the hosts of heaven, and since it rises in the east and sets in the west, its arc of movement constitutes a bowing toward the west. The visual image is striking: imagine the sun's daily path as the gesture of prostration — rising in the east, reaching its height, and descending toward the west. The direction toward which it bows is the west, and therefore the *shechina* resides in the west.

This is a remarkable *gemara* for what it does not say. Two straightforward arguments from the *Beit HaMikdash* itself could have been cited: first, the *Kodesh Kodashim* is located to the west within the *Mikdash*; second, for communities in *Bavel* situated to the east of *Eretz Yisrael*, praying westward means praying toward *Yerushalayim*. The *gemara* references neither. Instead, it grounds the westward orientation entirely in a cosmic observation about the sun's movement — and cites a verse from a post-*churban* context, ironically from Nechemya, who was involved in the rebuilding of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *gemara* appears to be articulating a model of *tefilla* and Divine Presence that is deliberately decoupled from the *Mikdash* and from *korbanot*. In a post-*churban* reality, the *shechina* is not to be located by reference to *makom ha-mikdash* but by the movements of the heavens themselves. This is a powerful theological statement, and its near-silence on the *Beit HaMikdash* connection seems intentional.

### Departing Backwards

Rav Akha bar Yaakov challenges Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's proof. *V'dilma ke-eved she-noteil pras me-rabbo ve-chozer le-achorav u-mishtachaveh* — perhaps the imagery should be read differently: a servant who receives something from his master and then backs away, bowing as he retreats. If so, the sun's westward decline could represent departing from the *shechina* in the east while bowing backward as it goes — meaning the Divine Presence would be in the east, not the west. The *gemara* acknowledges: *kashya* — this is a valid difficulty, and the proof from the sun's movement is not airtight.

---

## Post-Churban Theology

### Shechina Bechol Makom

The *gemara* now introduces a position more radical still. Rabbi Oshaya holds that the *shechina* is not concentrated in any particular direction at all: *shechina bechol makom* — the Divine Presence is everywhere.

### Lightning Messengers

Rabbi Oshaya derives this from a verse: *atah hu Hashem levadecha, atah asita et ha-shamayim ve-et ha-aretz* — you alone, God, made heaven and earth. His argument proceeds from a comparison of divine and human messengers. A human king sends a messenger to a distant location; when the messenger completes the task, he must return to the king's location to report. This is because the king is in one place and the messenger must come back to that place to deliver his report. But God's messengers operate differently: *lemakom she-mishtalchim mi-sham machzirim shelichutan* — they deliver their report from wherever they were sent, because God is present everywhere and there is no single location to which they must return. The proof-text is again from Iyov: *ha-tishlach berakim ve-yelechu ve-yomeru lecha hineni* — you send your lightning bolts, they go forth, and they say to you: "here we are." The verse does not say *yavo'u ve-yomeru* — they came back and reported — but *vayelechu ve-yomeru* — they went and reported from there. *Melamed she-shechina bechol makom* — this teaches that the *shechina* is everywhere.

### Opposing Angels

The school of Rabbi Yishmael arrives at the same conclusion through a different route. A verse describes one angel leaving while another angel came *likrato* — to meet him, coming from the opposite direction. If the *shechina* were in a single location and all angels emanate from that place, a second angel following the first would be described as coming *acharav* — after him, from behind. The fact that the second angel came *likrato*, to meet him head-on from the opposite direction, implies that angels can originate from any direction — which in turn implies that the Divine Presence from which they come is present everywhere. *Melamed she-shechina bechol makom.*

### Rav Sheshet Anywhere

Rav Sheshet, who was blind, drew a practical *halachic* conclusion from this position. He instructed his attendant: *lechol ruchah ukman* — orient me in any direction when I stand to pray *Shemoneh Esrei*.

### Heretics Eastward

There was, however, one direction he excluded: *levar mi-mizrach* — do not face me eastward. Crucially, he clarified the reason: *de-lav mishum de-la it beih shechina* — not because the *shechina* is absent in the east; since *shechina* is everywhere, the east is no less valid than any other direction. Rather, *mishum de-mori beih minei* — because that is the practice of the heretics, and he did not want his posture to appear to endorse their custom. The identity of these *minim* who specifically pray eastward is not explained in the *gemara*, and the standard commentaries do not provide a clear answer. The most natural association for *minim* in Talmudic literature is with Jewish Christians, though a specific reason for an eastward prayer orientation in that context is unclear; sun-worshippers praying toward the rising sun is another possibility.

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* makes explicit what the *gemara* has left implicit throughout this entire passage. *Tosafot* notes that all of these *amora'im* — those who hold *shechina bechol makom* and those who hold *shechina b'ma'arav* — appear not to accept the ruling cited in Berachot that one is obligated to pray toward *Yerushalayim*, based on the verse *veyitpallelu eilecha derech artzam*. If the westward orientation had simply been about *Eretz Yisrael* being to the west of *Bavel*, it would not apply universally — someone in America would not pray westward on that logic. But those who say the *shechina* is always in the west mean it universally, regardless of geographic relationship to *Eretz Yisrael*. And those who say *shechina bechol makom* — like Rav Sheshet — hold that one may pray in any direction at all, which straightforwardly contradicts the *Berachot* ruling.

*Tosafot* concludes that these *amora'im* follow the position of Rabbi Yishmael — *shechina bechol makom* — while those who say the *shechina* is specifically in the west align with a reading close to *Rabbi Akiva*'s position that the west is *nefishei hidira*, most regularly associated with divine presence. Only the final opinion to be discussed at the end of the *sugya* — that one in the north of *Eretz Yisrael* should pray southward — follows the *baraita* in Berachot that prayer must be directed toward *Eretz Yisrael*.

This makes the theology of the *sugya* unusually layered. A post-*churban* reality has generated competing responses: one group says God's presence is concentrated in the west, which has nothing to do with the destroyed *Mikdash*; another group says God's presence is everywhere, which similarly has nothing to do with *makom ha-mikdash*; and only the final voice in the *sugya* reasserts *Beit HaMikdash* orientation, though by that point framed around *Eretz Yisrael* rather than the *Mikdash* itself. This is worth pausing over. Just as *Torah* study becomes the universal locus of *kedushah* in the post-*churban* world — *ein laKadosh Baruch Hu b'olamo ella arba amot shel halacha bilvad* — so too the *shechina* is reconceptualized: *shechina bechol makom*, the divine presence accessible anywhere, rather than concentrated in a destroyed sanctuary. The irony that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi grounds this in a verse from Nechemya — written precisely in the context of rebuilding the *Beit HaMikdash* — makes the theological move all the more striking.

---

## Directions & Cosmology

### Directional Etymology

The *gemara*'s discussion of wind directions invites a broader treatment of directional terminology. There are two distinct sets of names for the cardinal directions in *lashon ha-kodesh*, and their etymologies reflect entirely different orientational frameworks.

The first set — *kedem* (east), *achor* (west), *teiman/yamin* (south), and *smol* (north) — derives from the orientation of a person facing the rising sun. A human being naturally orients toward the east, toward the light; hence the very word *orient* in English means "east," from the Latin for rising. With the east as *kedem* — one's front — the west naturally becomes *achor*, one's back. The right hand, when facing east, points south, giving *teiman* from *yamin*; the left hand points north, giving *smol*. *Tosafot* cites several scriptural proofs for this usage: the verse *achor va-kedem tzartani*, interpreted in Chagiga as referring to east and west; and *Aram mi-kedem u-Felishtim me-achor*, where *achor* means west. The word *acharei* in Devarim — *halo heimah b'ever ha-Yarden acharei derech mevo ha-shemesh* — similarly appears to mean simply "westward," toward where the sun sets.

*Tosafot* notes that this set of names can also be derived from the *shechina*'s perspective. If the *shechina* faces east (*p'nei ha-shechina l'mizrach*), then from the *shechina*'s vantage point the west is *achor*, the east is *kedem*, the south is *yamin*, and the north is *smol* — the same map, but oriented from the divine perspective rather than the human one.

### Wind Direction Names
