The second set of directional names — *mizrach*, *ma'arav*, *darom*, *tzafon* — derives from the behavior of the sun. *Mizrach* comes from *zerichah*, the shining or rising of the sun: the east is where the sun shines forth. *Ma'arav* relates to *erev*, evening: the west is where night begins. *Darom* is the south because that is where the sun is at its zenith during daylight hours — rising in the east, reaching its height in the south, setting in the west. *Tzafon* is north because the sun is hidden (*tzafun*) from the north; the sun never travels into the northern hemisphere, so the north is the concealed, unilluminated direction. These two etymological systems thus reflect two different ways of mapping the world — one from the standpoint of a human being facing the sun, the other from the standpoint of the sun's daily movement through the sky.

### Portico Model

The *gemara* now presents two competing cosmological models for understanding how the sun returns from west to east each night. Rabbi Eliezer holds: *olam le-achsadrah hu domeh* — the world resembles a *portico*, a structure with three enclosed walls and one open side. In his model, the northern side of the world is not sealed. *Ve-chivan she-higia chama etzel keren ma'aravit tzafonit, nichsefet ve-olah le-ma'alah min ha-rakia* — when the sun reaches the northwest corner of the sky, it bends around and travels above the *rakia* to return to the east. The open northern side allows the sun to loop back without being enclosed, making the northern wall unnecessary.

### Tent Model

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees: *olam le-kuvah hu domeh* — the world is like a tent, enclosed on all sides. *Ve-ruach tzafonit mesovevet* — the northern side is in fact enclosed. *Ve-chivan she-chama maga'at le-keren ma'aravit tzafonit, mekapelet ve-chozeret achorei kippah* — when the sun reaches the northwest corner, it folds back and travels behind the *kippah*, the dome, to return. The proof-text from Kohelet is: *holech el darom ve-sovev el tzafon* — it goes to the south (by day, traveling the visible arc) and it circuits to the north (by night, traveling behind the enclosed dome). *Holech* refers to the sun's visible daytime movement beneath the dome; *sovev* refers to its hidden nighttime movement behind or around the dome. Since the sun does travel through the north during its hidden return journey, the dome must be sealed there as well to prevent light from coming through at night.

The earlier student question helpfully clarifies the key distinction: in Rabbi Eliezer's model, the sun at night reverses direction and returns through the south, never actually passing through the north — hence no northern seal is needed. In Rabbi Yehoshua's model, the sun continues in the same direction and loops back through the north — hence the northern enclosure is essential to prevent nocturnal illumination.

### Seasonal Variation

The *gemara* adds a further observation about the east-west axis: *elu pnei mizrach u-pnei ma'arav, she-pe'amim mesovevtan u-pe'amim mehalchtan* — with regard to the eastern and western faces of the world, sometimes the sun traverses them visibly (*mehalchtan*) and sometimes it traverses them hidden (*mesovevtan*). This refers to the variation between summer and winter.

### Rashi's Explanation

*Rashi* explains: on a long summer day (*beyom aroch shel tekufat Tammuz*), the sun rises from the northeast corner and sets in the northwest corner, meaning that a substantial portion of its east-west movement occurs visibly during daylight. On a short winter day, the sun rises from the southeast corner and sets in the southwest corner; its arc barely extends northward at all during the day, and *umerachikin balayla gimmel ruchot* — it covers three directions during the night, traversing north, east, and much of the eastern and western approach through the hidden path behind the *kippah*. Thus the same east and west directions are sometimes traversed in the visible daytime arc and sometimes in the hidden nocturnal arc, depending on the season.

---

## Post-Churban Reality

### Southern Wind Loss

Having concluded the cosmological discussions, the *gemara* turns to a series of statements from Rav Chisda (as transmitted by Rafram bar Pappa) that re-engage with the post-*churban* reality. *Mi-yom she-charav Beit HaMikdash, lo hugshama ruach dromit* — from the day the *Beit HaMikdash* was destroyed, the southern wind no longer brings the kind of abundant rainfall it once did. The proof-text: *va-yigzor al yamin va-ra'ev* — he decreed upon the right (i.e., the south) and there was hunger. *Va-yochal al smolo ve-lo save'u* — they ate from the left (the north) and were not sated. The first verse establishes that *yamin* (south) no longer provides abundance; the second demonstrates the equation of *yamin* with south and *smol* with north.

### Exile Consequences

A second statement from the same chain: *mi-yom she-charav Beit HaMikdash, ein ha-geshamim yordim me-otzar tov* — since the destruction, rain no longer falls from the "good storehouse." The verse cited, *yiftach Hashem lecha et otzaro ha-tov*, contains the phrase *lates matar artzecha* — to give rain upon your land. *Rashi* notes that the verse ties the *otzar tov* explicitly to Israel's dwelling upon its land. Thus the loss of rain from the *otzar tov* is not solely about the absence of the *Mikdash* but about exile itself: *bi-zman she-Yisrael shruyim al admasam, geshamim yordim me-otzar tov; bi-zman she-ein Yisrael shruyim al admasam, ein ha-geshamim yordim me-otzar tov*. When Israel dwells on its land in accordance with God's will, rain comes from the good storehouse; in exile, that channel is closed.

### Prayer Directions

Rabbi Yitzchak offers a striking practical teaching that reconnects directionality with *Beit HaMikdash* symbolism: *ha-rotzeh she-yechkam, yadrim; ve-she-ya'ashir, yatzpin* — one who wants wisdom should pray southward; one who wants wealth should pray northward.

### Beit HaMikdash Signs

The mnemonic: *shulchan ba-tzafon, u-menorah ba-darom* — in the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *shulchan* (table, bearing the *lechem ha-panim*) was positioned to the north and the *menorah* to the south. The table represents material sustenance — bread, wealth — and the *menorah* represents light and wisdom. One who prays in the direction of the *menorah* prays for wisdom; one who prays in the direction of the *shulchan* prays for wealth. This is a *Beit HaMikdash*-oriented framework, in marked contrast to the earlier portions of the *sugya* that ignored the *Mikdash* entirely.

### Wisdom to Wealth

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, however, says simply: *le-olam yadrim* — one should always pray southward. His reasoning: *mi-toch she-mis-chakim mis-asher* — wisdom leads to wealth, so if one prays for wisdom, wealth will follow. The verse supports this: *orech yamim bi-minah, u-vi-smolah osher ve-chavod* — in its right hand (*yamin* = south) are long days, and in its left hand (*smol* = north) are wealth and honor. The south thus yields wisdom *and*, through wisdom, wealth as well.

The *gemara* then raises an internal contradiction: *va-ha Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi amar shechina bi-ma'arav* — Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was also the one who said the *shechina* is in the west and that we should pray westward. How can he now be advocating southward prayer? The resolution: *di-metzadei itztidodei* — one angles oneself, orienting somewhat to the west and somewhat to the south simultaneously.

### Eretz Yisrael Orientation

The final ruling of the *sugya* is addressed by Rabbi Chanina to Rav Ashi: *ke-gon attun de-yasvin bi-tzfona de-Eretz Yisrael, adrimu* — you, who sit to the north of *Eretz Yisrael* (in *Bavel*), should pray southward. The source: *mi-tzafon tipasach ha-ra'ah al kol yoshvei ha-aretz* — from the north, evil shall open upon all inhabitants of the land, establishing that *Bavel* lies to the north of *Eretz Yisrael*. Therefore, one in *Bavel* prays southward — toward *Eretz Yisrael*.

The *sugya* thus ends by reasserting the *Eretz Yisrael* orientation that its earlier portions had conspicuously bypassed. *Tosafot*'s observation is borne out by the structure of the *sugya* itself: the early voices — Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's sun-bowing argument, Rabbi Oshaya's and Rabbi Yishmael's omnipresence proofs, and Rav Sheshet's indifference to direction — all operate within a framework that does not depend on *makom ha-mikdash*. Only at the end does the *sugya* explicitly reintegrate *Beit HaMikdash* symbolism through Rabbi Yitzchak's *shulchan* and *menorah* mnemonic, and *Eretz Yisrael* orientation through Rabbi Chanina's ruling. The tension between these two theologies — *shechina bechol makom* and the continued primacy of *Eretz Yisrael* and the *Mikdash* as loci of divine encounter — runs through the entire passage and is left, characteristically, unresolved.

---

## Flax & Vegetables

### Flax Distance

The *mishna* concludes with several additional neighbor-damage rules. *Merachikin et ha-mishrah min ha-yerek* — one must keep the place where flax is soaked away from vegetables. Soaking flax generates significant odor, which damages neighboring produce.

### Rabbi Yosi Mustard

The *mishna* then records a case of mutual harm: *ve-et ha-chardal min ha-devorim* — mustard must be kept away from bees, because bees consume the mustard flowers and the resulting honey is adversely affected. The first opinion — by implication the *tanna kamma* — requires this distance. *Rabbi Yosi*, however, permits the mustard: *sheyachol lomar lecha, ad she-ata omer li harcheik chardalcha mi-dvorai, harcheik dvoracha mi-chardali* — he can respond: before you tell me to keep my mustard away from your bees, I can equally tell you to keep your bees away from my mustard, since they come and consume the flowers of my mustard plant.

### Mutual Harm

The underlying principle invoked by Rabbi Yosi is one of reciprocal harm: since each party is simultaneously *mazik* (the damaging party) and *nizak* (the damaged party) with respect to the other, neither has an unambiguous right to demand that the other relocate. One could theoretically argue the opposite — that each party *does* have the right to demand the other's removal — but Rabbi Yosi holds that mutual harm cancels the respective claims, and neither party can compel the other to move. This reflects a broader position of Rabbi Yosi's that appears in various forms throughout the tractate on the question of *al ha-mazik leharchik o al ha-nizak leharchik*. The *mishna* does not specify a distance for the mustard-and-bees case, and notably, the distance is left open — perhaps to be determined case by case, or perhaps fifty *amot* by analogy, though the text does not say so explicitly.

---

---

# Bava Batra 26

## Trees & Cisterns

### Mishna: Distances

The daf opens by picking up from the *mishnah* of 25b, which continues the general theme of maintaining distances between neighbors' properties — but with a particular focus that brings us to the essential intersection of Bava Batra and Bava Kamma: when does causing indirect harm to a neighbor rise to the level of making one a *mazik*, and how do the *arba avot nezikin* bear on that question?

The *mishnah* states: *marchikin et ha'ilan min habor esrim vechamesh amah* — one must keep a tree at least 25 *amot* from a cistern, because the roots will spread and damage it. For a carob tree or a sycamore, the distance is 50 *amot*, since those roots spread even further. This rule applies anywhere — not just near a town, where distancing requirements have more to do with zoning and the appearance of the city, but even in one's own field. The concern here is entirely about not causing indirect damage to a neighbor's property.

The *mishnah* adds: *bein milmalah bein min hatsad* — it does not matter whether the configuration is on an incline or on level ground. The question of what *milmalah* (above) means — whether it refers to the tree being higher or the cistern — will be addressed in the *Gemara*.

### Compensation Rules

*Im habor kadam kotzetz venoten damim* — if the cistern was dug first, then the person who subsequently planted the tree was in violation of the distancing rule. In that case, he must cut down the tree, but the owner of the cistern must reimburse him for it. This is, notably, less strict than the rule we encountered in the previous *mishnah* concerning trees planted too close to a town: there, the town need not pay anything. A neighbor has fewer rights than the community.

But the question naturally arises: if the tree-planter was in violation, why must the cistern-owner pay at all? Part of the answer is that even though the planting was improper, the actual damage only occurs after many years — the roots take considerable time to spread and reach the cistern. Tosafot makes this point: the delayed nature of the harm creates a kind of balance between the violation and the compensation owed.

### Proof & Uncertainty

*Im ilan kadam lo yikotz* — if the tree was planted first, then of course the cistern-owner has no right to demand its removal. *Safek zeh kadam vesafek zeh kadam lo yikotz* — if the chronological priority is genuinely uncertain, the tree is not cut down. This follows the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah*: since the cistern-owner cannot prove his right to demand the tree's removal, he cannot compel it.

### Rabbi Yosi's View

*Rabbi Yosi omer: af al pi shehabor kodem la'ilan lo yikotz* — Rabbi Yosi takes a radical position: even if the cistern predates the tree, the tree need not be cut down. His reasoning: *shezeh chofer betoch shelo vezeh note'ah betoch shelo* — each party is acting within his own property, and as the *Gemara* frames it elsewhere, *al hanizak leharichik et atzmo* — it is the responsibility of the injured party to distance himself from the source of harm.

This position goes against the entire thrust of the *perek*. Rabbi Yosi is essentially the outlier, the one who seems to reject all the distancing requirements on principle: you are the master of your domain, and indirect damage that befalls a neighbor is not your concern. If a neighbor does not wish to be harmed indirectly, he must take whatever precautions he sees fit.

One might ask how the opening rule of the *mishnah* — the 25-*amah* requirement — fits with Rabbi Yosi's view. The answer is that Rabbi Yosi simply does not hold of that requirement. And practically speaking, if a tree is already 26 *amot* away, everyone agrees: there is no claim against the tree's owner.

### Incline Damage

The *Tanna* clarifies: it does not matter whether the tree is higher on the incline and the cistern is lower, or whether the cistern is higher and the tree is lower. The first case — *bor lematah ve'ilan lemalah* — is intuitive: roots grow downward through the ground and penetrate the cistern directly. The second case — *bor lemalah ve'ilan lematah* — requires explanation.

*Amar Rav Chaga beshem Rabi Yosi*: in that case, the roots *machlidin et hakarka* — they loosen and corrode the ground (the word *machlid* relates to *chaluda*, rust, the sense of structural deterioration) — and ultimately weaken the very foundation of the cistern, even without penetrating it directly. The distance requirement therefore applies in both configurations.

---

## Rabbi Yosi Accepted

### Law Follows Yosi

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: halacha keRabbi Yosi.* This is a striking ruling. We have spent an entire *perek* building up a framework of distancing rules, and Rabbi Yosi is the outlier who rejects them all on principle — and in the end, we embrace him. The *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi.

From a strictly technical perspective, Rabbi Yosi's position is actually quite defensible. The second *perek* of Bava Batra is, in a sense, rabbinic policy: from a Bava Kamma standpoint, there is no direct *mazik* in most of these cases. One plants a tree, and years later roots penetrate a neighbor's cistern — there is nothing immediate, nothing that communicates directly from one person to another. The damage is indirect, deferred, *grama* extended over time. Rabbi Yosi stands on the technical rights and rejects the policy overlay. The Rabbis of the *perek* were creating norms necessary for neighbors to coexist — smoke pollution, structural threats, and the like — but Rabbi Yosi insists that without a technical *chiyuv*, one cannot be compelled to act differently within one's own property.

### Direct Actions

*Amar Rav Ashi: ki havina bei Rav Kahana hava amrinan — modi Rabbi Yosi begirei didei.* Now the *Gemara* begins to limit the ruling: Rabbi Yosi himself would agree that where the harm is a direct product of one's own actions — *girei didei*, literally one's own arrows — one is obligated to keep distance.

The paradigm case of *girei didei* is straightforward: if I shoot an arrow into your property, that is clearly a direct act and a clear Bava Kamma liability. But what of a barbecue whose smoke drifts immediately into a neighbor's crops? Or a fire lit on one's property whose effects occur within minutes? These are far more direct than tree roots spreading over years, but still not a literal arrow. The question is how to define "direct."

### What is Direct?

The category of *girei didei* occupies a continuum. On one end sits a literal arrow — one releases it, it travels, it strikes. On the other end sit tree roots that take perhaps five years to spread and damage a cistern. Somewhere in between is smoke, vibrations, sparks, and loosened chaff. How one positions each case on that continuum determines the extent of Rabbi Yosi's concession.

An instructive example from the *Gemara* involves placing a ladder in one's yard: a weasel immediately uses it as a springboard to jump into the neighbor's property and cause damage. The causal chain here is even more attenuated than smoke — the weasel is acting on its own — yet because it happens almost instantaneously upon the placement of the ladder, there is something in the immediacy that brings it closer to the category of *girei didei*, at least for purposes of the neighbor-law obligation, even if not necessarily from a Bava Kamma liability perspective.

The question of time plays a role in defining *grama* more broadly. As a parallel: when one closes an electrical circuit, it triggers a nearly instantaneous chain of physical events — and it becomes difficult to call that *grama* precisely because it all happens within a split second, even though the sequence of causation is technically mediated. So timing matters, even if it is not the only factor.

There is also the question of how broadly *girei didei* must extend before it swallows Rabbi Yosi's entire concession to the *perek*. Does the smell rising from a barn (*refet bakar*) into a neighbor's warehouse count as one's arrows? Does that operate quickly enough? The boundary is not crisp, and the *Rishonim* will need to work through the cases.

---

## Sesame Case

### Papi Yonah Story

*Papi Yonah ani vehe'ashir havah* — Papi Yonah had once been poor and later became wealthy. He built himself an *apadna*, a fine mansion, on his property. Neighboring him were people who pressed sesame oil — *atzorei* who would pound sesame. When they did so, *havi naydei apadnei* — the mansion would shake from the vibrations.

Papi Yonah came before Rav Ashi. Rav Ashi invoked the principle he had learned in the yeshiva of Rav Kahana: *modi Rabbi Yosi begirei diley* — even Rabbi Yosi concedes when the harm is the direct product of one's actions. And this, Rav Ashi ruled, is precisely such a case. The vibrations travel directly from the sesame-pressing operation; they shake the ground; they shake the mansion. This is as close to one's own arrows as anything short of a literal projectile.

### Vibration Threshold

The *Gemara* then asks: *vekhama* — how much vibration is too much? The measure given is *kadi naydei nakhmata apumei de'khatzva*: if a cover placed on top of a pottery jar would be jostled loose by the tremor, that constitutes a structural threat, and the sesame-pressers must move.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot raises an important question: if we rule that *girei diley* requires distancing even under Rabbi Yosi, what happens when the harmful party was there first? The general rule — stated by Tosafot — is: *af al gav d'samakh beheiter ein tzarikh leharkhik afilu begirei diley* — even in a case of one's own arrows, if you were there first, you need not move. His proof is the case of the barn (*refet bakar*): smells rising directly from the barn into a neighbor's warehouse are treated as a case of *girei diley*, yet the *Baraita* rules that if the barn was established first, it may remain. The same principle applies to the baker's vinegar fumes and the dyer's materials — *ein khilluk bein dira lishar kol hatzrakhin*.

Why, then, were the sesame-pressers required to move? Rabbeinu Tam explains: *delo kevi'a tashmishai kol kakh* — their operation was not sufficiently established or ongoing. They only pressed sesame occasionally, perhaps once a year. Since they lacked the kind of continuous, regularized presence that would constitute "being there first" in a meaningful sense, they could not claim the protection afforded to an established prior occupant. By contrast, if one regularly conducts a smoky barbecue every summer weekend as an ongoing practice, and then a neighbor arrives who finds the smoke objectionable, the established occupant may invoke his priority even in a case of *girei diley*.

Tosafot's analysis here contains several significant *chiddushim*: first, that the barn constitutes *girei diley*; second, that priority in time overrides even *girei diley*; and third, that "being there first" requires an ongoing, regularized presence — not a seasonal or occasional one.

---

## Flax Beating

### Bar Miryon Story

The house of Bar Miryon, son of Ravin — *debei Bar Miryon brei deRavin* — would beat flax: *ki havei nakshei kitna*. The material loosened from the flax — *riksha* — would fly out and strike people nearby, causing injury. On its face, this seems like an unambiguous case of *girei diley*: the beaters put their energy into the flax, the material is propelled by that energy, and it strikes others. It is practically like shooting an arrow.

### Ravina's View

Came before Ravina. *Amar lehu: ki amrina modeh Rabbi Yose begirei diley, hani mili deka azla mikocho* — when we say Rabbi Yosi agrees regarding one's arrows, that is only when the damaging agent travels through the person's own energy. *Hacha zika hu dekamamtila* — here it is the wind that carries the chaff away. The energy of the beaters loosens the material, but it is the wind's force that propels it into people's faces.

This is a remarkably narrow definition of *girei diley*. Under Ravina, almost anything short of direct physical transmission of one's kinetic energy to the damaging object would be excluded. The barbecue: the wind carries the smoke. The roots: they grow through the soil under their own biological process. Even certain cases of vibration might be mediated by the earth rather than direct mechanical force. If *girei diley* is this narrow, Rabbi Yosi's concession becomes very small indeed.

### Winnowing Analogy

Mar bar Rav Ashi challenged: *mai shna mizoreh veruach mesayato?* How is this different from the case of *zoreh* — winnowing? When one throws grain into the air and the wind separates the chaff, one is liable for the *melacha* of winnowing on *Shabbat*, even though it is the wind that does the separating. The principle at work — termed *koach acher me'urav bo* in Bava Kamma — is that one who employs natural forces to accomplish a result is treated as if one acted directly. If that principle makes one *chayav* for *Shabbat*, should it not equally make the flax-beaters liable here, since they are effectively using the wind to carry the chaff away?

The force of this argument is obvious: you would not winnow without wind; you depend on the wind; the wind is, in effect, your instrument. Similarly, the flax-beaters may not "want" the wind in the same deliberate way — but the Gemara will address that distinction.

### Spark Distinction

*Amru kamei deMermer* — they reported this argument to Mermer, who agreed: it is indeed just like *zoreh veruach mesayato*, and the beaters are liable under *girei diley*. But the *Gemara* then asks: and according to Ravina, who said it is different — how does he respond? The *Gemara* does not press the *Shabbat* comparison further, apparently recognizing that *hilchos Shabbat* operates under different principles than *nezikin*. On *Shabbat*, the concept of *melachet machshevet* — intentional, purposive action — can broaden the scope of liability, because the Torah focuses on achieving an end result rather than narrowly defining the precise physical act. This is why cooking by various methods all constitute the same *melacha*, and why *toldot* are liable alongside *avot* — the focus is on the class of result achieved. But that broadened framework may not translate to the domain of damages.

Instead, the *Gemara* poses a challenge from a genuine *nezikin* case: *mai shna migetz hayotzei mitachas hapatish?* When a blacksmith hammers on an anvil, sparks fly and cause damage — and he is *chayav leshalem*. So how is the flying chaff different from flying sparks? In both cases one's action releases something that the wind then carries to cause harm.

The *Gemara* answers: *hasam nicha lei deleizal* — there, with the sparks, one wants them to fly away. A blacksmith does not want the sparks landing on his own property, his own materials, his own body. He benefits from the sparks flying away, and in that sense he is using the wind's dispersal, much like the winnower. *Hacha lo nicha lei deleizal* — here, the flax-beater has no stake in where the loosened material goes. Its dispersal is entirely incidental to the work. That deliberateness — wanting the force to travel away — is what aligns the spark case with the winnowing case and distinguishes both from the flax.

### Tosafot Resolution

Tosafot raises a further difficulty: even granting that *girei diley* does not apply, should the flax-beaters not be liable under the category of *esh* — fire? In the *esh* category, one creates a damaging force and the wind carries it elsewhere. Isn't that precisely what is happening here?

Tosafot's answer draws an important distinction: *esh* requires that the actor create something that is already, in itself, a damaging force — and the wind merely transports it to another location. Fire is inherently destructive; the wind brings the destruction to a new place. But loosened flax chaff is not inherently destructive. It has no intrinsic damaging power. It is the wind itself that transforms the chaff into something capable of injuring people. When the wind is not merely the carrier of a damaging force but is actually what makes the substance dangerous, the actor is not the author of the damage — the wind is. Therefore no liability for *esh* either.

This resolution also illuminates the *Gemara*'s answer about the spark: the blacksmith wants the sparks — which are inherently destructive — to fly away. He is using the wind to transport a damaging force he created. That is *esh*. The flax-beater creates something harmless, and only the wind's intervention makes it harmful. The beater is therefore exempt.

One larger question emerges from this entire *sugya*: what is the relationship between *girei diley* as a Bava Batra obligation to distance oneself and *girei diley* as a Bava Kamma basis for monetary liability? Is it possible that one could be exempt from the obligation to distance yet still be required to pay damages after the fact — as one participant suggested might be the fuller reading of Rabbi Yosi's position? Tosafot appears to assume this is impossible: if we say there is no obligation to distance, then a fortiori there is no liability to pay. But the intersection of the two tractates here is genuinely complex, and the precise scope of Rabbi Yosi's concession remains a matter of debate among the *Rishonim*. Rabbeinu Tam's ruling follows Mar bar Rav Ashi — a broader definition of *girei diley* — which is important practically, since we rule like Rabbi Yosi: one does not want to give that ruling an excessively narrow reading that would leave neighbors essentially without recourse.

---

## Trees & Fields

### Four Amot Rule

The next *mishnah*: *lo yita adam ilan samuch lisedeh chaveiro ela im kein hirchik mimenu arba amot* — one may not plant a tree adjacent to a neighbor's field without maintaining a distance of four *amot*. Unlike the cistern case, roots are not the concern here — we are in open fields, and the roots of various plantings are not threatening one another underground. Rashi understands the *sadeh* to include even a vegetable garden, while Tosafot reads it from the *Gemara* as referring more specifically to a field of trees, vines, or other cultivated plantings — not simply one's front yard. *Echad gefanim ve'echad kol ilan* — the rule applies equally to vines and to other trees.

### Wall Exception

*Haya gader beintayim* — if there is a wall between the two properties, then *zeh someich la'gader mikan vezeh someich la'gader mikan* — each party may plant right up to the wall from his side. The wall removes the practical reason for the buffer: there is no risk of inadvertently crossing into the neighbor's property, so the four-*amah* requirement does not apply.

### Root Cutting Right

*Hayu shorashim yotzim letoch shel chaveiro* — suppose the roots of a tree have in fact spread into the neighbor's field, and that neighbor wishes to plow. His plow will strike the roots and be impeded or damaged. What is he entitled to do?

The *mishnah* rules: *ma'amik shelosha tefachim kedei shelo ye'akeiv et hamachareshah* — he may dig down three *tefachim* deep and cut away any roots he finds within that depth, so as not to impede the plow. This is roughly nine inches below ground level. The tree's owner had every right to plant where he did; the neighbor has every right to plow. The three-*tefachim* depth marks the zone of plow access. If roots are cut in the process and the tree suffers, that is a risk the tree's owner takes when planting near a boundary.

### Deep Digging

*Haya chofer bor siach ume'ara kotzetz veyored veha'etzim shelo* — if the neighbor is not merely plowing but digging a cistern or deep ditch, he may cut away roots to whatever depth is necessary and keep the wood. The *mishnah* says *ha'etzim shelo* — the wood is his — but the *Gemara* will have a dispute about whose "his" refers to: the digger's, or the tree-owner's. We will return to that question.

### Four Amot Purpose

*Tana: arba she'amru kedei avodat hakerem* — the *Gemara* explains that the four *amot* is the standard working space required to cultivate a vineyard or similar planting, providing maneuvering access without needing to encroach on the neighbor's property.

*Amar Shmuel: lo shanu ela be'Eretz Yisrael aval be'Bavel shtei amot* — Shmuel observes a regional variation: the four-*amah* rule applies in the Land of Israel, but in Babylonia, two *amot* suffice, presumably because the plowing implements used there were narrower. A *Baraita* is cited that states the distance as two *amot*, and the *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between the *Baraita* and the *mishnah* precisely on this basis — one reflects Eretz Yisrael practice, the other Babylonian practice.

---

## Birds & Vines

### Rava Case

*Rava bar Rav Chanan havu lei hanhu diklei amitzra d'pardesa d'Rav Yosef* — Rava bar Rav Chanan had palm trees right along the boundary of Rav Yosef's vineyard. *Hava atei tziporei yasvi b'diklei* — birds would come and roost in the palm trees, then launch themselves directly into the vineyard, causing damage to the grapes.

Rav Yosef said: cut down your trees. The owner responded: *ve'ha archiki li* — I have kept the four *amot* required by the *mishnah*. I have done nothing wrong.

### Vine Distance

Rav Yosef replied: *hani mili le'ilanot* — the four-*amah* rule governs the distance between trees. For a vineyard, for vines, *ba'inan tefei* — more is required.

### Tree-to-Vine

But does not the *mishnah* itself say *echad gefanim ve'echad kol ilan* — that the same rule applies to both vines and other trees? Rav Yosef's answer: *hani mili ilan le'ilan, u'gefanim le'gefanim* — that equality applies when you are measuring tree-to-tree or vine-to-vine. But *ilan le'gefanim* — a tree adjacent to a vineyard — presents a qualitatively different problem, precisely because of the birds. Palm trees provide a perch and a launching platform; their proximity to vines creates an access pathway that would not exist if the neighbor were simply another orchard. In that configuration, four *amot* is insufficient and more distance is required.

This ruling also raises the question of what happened to Rabbi Yosi. We appear to have moved from one *mishnah* to the next without reckoning with his position. Tosafot grapples with this: once we broaden the category of *girei diley* to include the bird-pathway scenario — which is even more attenuated than vibrations or smoke — the scope of Rabbi Yosi's concession becomes quite expansive. But where exactly the line falls is not stated explicitly, and the *Rishonim* continue to debate it.

### Moral Hesitation

*Amar lei ana lo katzna* — the tree-owner refused to cut down his trees. Why? *De'amar Rav: hai dikla d'tein kava, asur lemikatzatzei* — Rav rules that any palm tree capable of producing even a *kav* of fruit per year may not be cut down. This invokes the prohibition of *bal tashchit* — the destruction of productive fruit trees — rooted in the *Torah*.

Rav Yosef added a striking personal note: *de'amar Rav Chanina: lo shachiv Shichat beri ella de'katz te'enata belo zimneih* — Rav Chanina said that his son Shichat died young for no other reason than that he cut down a fig tree before its time. The metaphor is vivid: one who cuts down a tree in the prime of its productive life may himself be cut down in the prime of his. The *Gemara* does not frame this as a technical *halachic* prohibition — indeed, the response is *ei nicha lei likotz* — if you wish to cut it down, be my guest. Perhaps technically it is not forbidden in this context. But the moral-religious weight of the act is considerable, and the tree-owner refuses to be the agent of it.

The *Gemara* does not tell us what happened in the end — perhaps the force of the moral argument was enough.

---

## Rav Pappa Story

### Root Cutting Dispute

*Rav Pappa hava lei hanhu diklei amitzra de'Rav Huna berei de'Rav Yehoshua* — Rav Pappa had palm trees right on the boundary of the field belonging to Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua. Rav Pappa went and found that Rav Huna was digging in his field and cutting away the roots — exactly as the *mishnah* permits: *hayu sharshin yotzin letoch shel chaveiro ma'amik shelosha kedei shelo ya'akev hamachareshah*.

Rav Pappa objected. Rav Huna replied: I am doing exactly what the *mishnah* allows. Rav Pappa said: the *mishnah* only permits going down three *tefachim*; you are digging deeper. Rav Huna replied: I am digging cisterns and ditches — *ana borot shichin ume'arot ka'chaferna* — and the *mishnah* explicitly permits cutting roots to full depth when digging cisterns.

### Public Path Analogy

Rav Pappa reported: *amrei lei kulei hai velo yachli lei* — I marshaled every argument I could and was unable to dislodge him, given that the *mishnah* was plainly on his side. Finally, I said to him: consider *ha de'amar Rav Yehuda — meitzar shehechziku bo rabbim assur lekalkelo* — a pathway over which the public has established use may not be damaged or obstructed, even if it crosses private property.

What does that ruling have to do with cutting roots? On Rashi's reading, it is an argument by analogy: just as the public's sustained use of a path through private property gives them enforceable rights in that path, so too the sustained presence of Rav Pappa's roots in Rav Huna's field gives Rav Pappa a form of right in that subsurface space — a right that Rav Huna cannot simply destroy by digging. The roots have been "walking there" just as the public has been walking on the path.

### Rashi & Tosafot

Rashi's analogy is admittedly difficult: the public's right over a pathway is a specific and recognized legal category (*reshut harabbim*), while the spread of roots is something the *mishnah* explicitly permits the field-owner to cut. How does a comparison to the public pathway override a direct *mishnah*? Furthermore, what are the precise parameters of such a "root right" — does it expire? Does it require a minimum time?

Tosafot offers a completely different reading that redirects the entire argument. On Tosafot's account, the path that *Rav Yehuda* speaks of ran directly through Rav Huna's field — the *rabbim* had been using it as a thoroughfare. When Rav Huna decided to dig his cistern, he chose to dig it in that public pathway. Rav Pappa's argument, then, is not about the roots at all; it is that Rav Huna is prohibited from digging in the public pathway. Rav Pappa, having been unable to defend his trees through the *mishnah*, found another grounds entirely to stop the digging. This reading is simpler and more direct, though less immediately connected to the root-cutting question.

### Sixteen Amot

After they left court, Rav Huna reconsidered and said: *amai lo amri lei* — why did I not respond with this: *kan betoch sheish esrei amah kan chutz lesheish esrei amah* — within sixteen *amot* is one rule; beyond sixteen *amot* is another?

On Tosafot's reading, this fits neatly: the standard halachic width of a *reshut harabbim* is sixteen *amot* (as established for *Shabbat*). Even if the public has acquired rights to a pathway, the original property owner retains the right to reclaim portions of it so long as he leaves sixteen *amot* of usable width. If Rav Huna's cistern was being dug in a way that still left sixteen *amot* of path, he was within his rights all along, and Rav Pappa's argument was defeated.

On Rashi's reading, the sixteen *amot* connects to the question of root rights: the *Gemara* going forward will examine whether a tree-owner has a recognized claim to the roots that spread within a certain radius — up to sixteen *amot* — such that the field-owner cannot simply cut them at will within that zone. Beyond sixteen *amot*, different rules may apply. This will be relevant to reconciling the apparent leniency of the *mishnah* with the idea of root-ownership rights. Tosafot engages with this as well and will need to work through how the *mishnah*'s plain permission to cut roots survives if there is a sixteen-*amah* protected zone — a question that carries into the following *Gemara*.

---

## Roots Ownership

### Hekdesh Case

The *Gemara* addresses the question of who owns roots that have grown from a private tree into a neighboring field. Rav Yaakov Hadaiva asked Rav Chisda: *shorshei ilan shel mi* — when roots spread into someone else's field, to whom do they belong — the owner of the tree or the owner of the field in which they now grow?

Rav Chisda replied: we already have a *Baraita* that resolves this. *Shorshei ilan shel hedyot haba'im beshel hekdesh lo nehenin velo mo'alin* — roots of a privately-owned tree that have grown into a field consecrated as *hekdesh*: one may not derive benefit from them (*lo nehenin* — a rabbinic stringency because they are growing in consecrated ground), but if one did derive benefit, there is no violation of *meila* (*lo mo'alin*).

### Meila Inference

The *Gemara* draws the inference: *ei amart bishlama batar ilan azlinan* — if we say we follow the tree, meaning the roots belong to the owner of the tree, then *mishum hachi lo ma'ali* — of course there is no *meila*, because the roots are not actually *hekdesh* property; they belong to a private individual who happens to have his roots in consecrated ground. The Rabbis prohibited deriving benefit as a precautionary measure, but technically they are not sanctified.

*Ela ei amart batar karka azlinan* — but if we say we follow the field, meaning the roots belong to the owner of whatever land they currently occupy, then these roots are growing in *hekdesh* land and are *hekdesh* property — and one who benefits from them should be liable for *meila*. The fact that the *Baraita* says there is no *meila* therefore proves that we follow the tree: the roots belong to the tree's owner, not to the owner of the field in which they happen to grow.

The *Gemara* leaves the matter here for now, noting that the next material will introduce an argument in the opposite direction — and with that, the daf's discussion continues into the following day.

---

---

# Bava Batra 27

## Tree Roots Ownership

### Roots & Excavation

The *mishnah* addresses a case in which someone plants a tree near a boundary line and the roots extend underground into a neighbor's property. If the neighbor subsequently digs a pit, cistern, or cave, he is permitted to cut through any roots he encounters in order to continue digging straight down. The *mishnah* then states that the wood of those cut roots belongs to "him" — but the referent of "him" is ambiguous, and the *gemara* takes up the question directly.

### Ownership Dispute

Yaakov Hadava posed the question to Rav Chisda: to whom does the wood of the roots belong — to the owner of the tree from which they grew, or to the owner of the yard in which they are found? Rav Chisda replied that the matter has already been taught, and he cited a *mishnah* as evidence.

### Hekdesh Baraita

The *mishnah* invoked discusses roots of a tree belonging to a layperson (*hedyot*) that grow underground into property belonging to *hekdesh* (consecrated Temple property). The ruling is: *lo nehenin v'lo mo'alin* — one may not derive benefit from them (even rabbinically), yet there is no biblical prohibition of *me'ilah* (misappropriation of consecrated property). Rav Chisda's argument runs as follows: if ownership follows the tree — that is, if the roots still belong to the *hedyot* tree owner even after entering *hekdesh* land — then the absence of *me'ilah* is perfectly intelligible, since the roots originate from non-sacred property. This would prove that roots remain the property of the tree owner, not the yard owner.

### Me'ilah Problem

The *gemara* rejects this proof by pointing to the *seifa* of the very same *mishnah*. The reverse case is also taught: roots of a *hekdesh* tree that grow into the property of a layperson — and there too the ruling is *lo nehenin v'lo mo'alin*, no *me'ilah*. But this is equally problematic for Rav Chisda's reasoning: if ownership follows the tree, then roots originating from a *hekdesh* tree should be subject to *me'ilah* wherever they go. The fact that *me'ilah* is absent in both cases shows that the ownership rule — whether following the tree or following the land — cannot by itself explain the outcome. The *gemara* thus concludes that neither case proves the point, because the same anomaly appears in both directions.

### Growth Sanctified

The *gemara* resolves both cases together: *bigidulin haba'im le-achar mikan askinan* — we are dealing with growth that occurred after the act of sanctification. The roots in question continued to grow after the tree was already consecrated. Since the additional growth was never explicitly declared *hekdesh*, there is no *me'ilah* by those roots regardless of which property they are located in. Even if the roots of a *hekdesh* tree spread through *hekdesh* land, the subsequently grown portions were never verbally sanctified and therefore fall outside the biblical prohibition of *me'ilah*. The *mishnah* thus cannot serve as proof for either position on the underlying ownership question.

### Sixteen Amot

Rav Papa offers a different resolution of the *mishnah*: the distinction between the two cases is not ownership per se, but proximity. Within sixteen *amot* of the tree, the roots are still functionally connected to the tree and draw their sustenance from it — and within that range, ownership follows the tree. Beyond sixteen *amot*, the roots are no longer considered part of the tree's vital nutrient zone, and at that distance the ownership is governed by the property in which they lie. This is admittedly a difficult reading of the *baraita*, since no such qualification appears in its text, but it anticipates a major topic about to emerge — the significance of sixteen *amot* as the radius within which a tree draws nutrients from the surrounding soil.

---

## Ulla's 16 Amot

### Gazlan Concept

The *gemara* transitions to a teaching of *Ulla* that introduces the principle of sixteen *amot* on its own terms. *Ulla* states: *ilan hasamuch lemeitzar betoch shesh esreh amah gazlan hu* — a tree planted within sixteen *amot* of a neighbor's boundary line is a *gazlan*, a thief, because its roots will grow under the ground and draw nutrients from the neighbor's property within that radius.

### Gazlan Permitted

Strikingly, the language of *gazlan* does not mean that planting such a tree is forbidden. The *mishnah* itself makes clear that the rules of distancing a tree from a boundary are governed by other concerns — specifically, allowing room for plowing (four *amot* from an unenclosed border), or proximity to a well (twenty-five *amot*). Short of those restrictions, one may plant right up to the boundary line. *Tosafot* accordingly notes that the designation *gazlan hu* does not create a prohibition; rather, its practical consequence is the following ruling: *ve'ein meivi mimenu bikurim* — the owner may not bring *bikurim* (first fruits) from such a tree. When bringing *bikurim*, the owner recites the verse *ha'adamah asher natata li* — "the land which You gave to me." If the tree's fruit grew partly off nutrients drawn from a neighbor's soil, that declaration is not entirely accurate, and the obligation of *bikurim* therefore does not apply.

### Saplings Math

The *gemara* asks: from where did *Ulla* derive the sixteen *amot* figure? It initially suggests the *mishnah* discussing ten saplings (*netiot*) distributed across a *beit se'ah*. A *beit se'ah* is the area needed to sow a *se'ah* of grain — it equals twenty-five hundred square *amot*, corresponding to half the courtyard of the *mishkan* (fifty by one hundred *amot* = five thousand square *amot*). The *halacha* (a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*) is that when ten saplings are distributed across a *beit se'ah* in the period before *shemita*, one may plow the entire area up to *rosh hashana* on their behalf, since the whole space is considered necessary for the saplings' sustenance.

### Sapling Calculation

The *gemara* now works through the arithmetic. A *beit se'ah* is twenty-five hundred *amot*. Divide by ten saplings: each sapling claims two hundred and fifty *amot* of surrounding area. *Ulla*'s figure, by contrast, would require a tree to draw from a square of thirty-two by thirty-two *amot* (sixteen in each direction), which is one thousand and twenty-four square *amot*. The *mishnah*'s number — two hundred and fifty per sapling — is far smaller. The *gemara* therefore sets this source aside: that *mishnah* deals with saplings, which require less than mature trees.

### Rounding Question

The *gemara* then tries the *mishnah* about three mature trees: three trees belonging to three different owners in a shared *beit se'ah* may also have their entire area plowed up to *rosh hashana* of *shemita*. Dividing twenty-five hundred by three yields eight hundred and thirty-three *amot* per tree. *Ulla*'s square of thirty-two by thirty-two gives one thousand and twenty-four per tree — still significantly larger. At this point the *gemara* proposes that *Ulla* may simply have been imprecise (*lo dak*). The *gemara* immediately challenges this: one can say a figure is rounded only when rounding is more stringent (*lechumra*). Here, saying sixteen *amot* creates an exemption from *bikurim* over a wider area than is strictly warranted. If the true radius is smaller than sixteen *amot*, then *Ulla*'s figure is rounding in a lenient direction (*lekula*), and we do not say a *tanna* (or *amora*) is imprecise in the lenient direction.

### Square to Circle

At this point the *gemara* corrects its own geometry: *mi savrat b'rivua kamrinan? b'igul kamrinan* — did you think we meant a square? We mean a circle. If a tree draws nutrients sixteen *amot* in every direction, the relevant shape is a circle with a radius of sixteen, not a square with a side of thirty-two. The question then becomes: how much smaller is the inscribed circle than the surrounding square?

### Pi Equals 3

The *gemara* states that a square is larger than its inscribed circle by one quarter. This is the *gemara*'s standard working approximation using *pi* = 3. With a radius of one, the circumscribed square (side = 2) has area four; the circle has area *pi* × 1² = 3. The ratio is thus four to three, meaning the square exceeds the circle by exactly one quarter. Taking a quarter off the square's area of one thousand and twenty-four yields seven hundred and sixty-eight — identically the result of computing the circle directly: 16² × 3 = 256 × 3 = 768.

### 768 Amot Circle

So if *Ulla* is speaking of a circle of radius sixteen, the area in question is seven hundred and sixty-eight square *amot* per tree. But the *mishnah*'s figure is eight hundred and thirty-three. The circle is still smaller than what the *mishnah* requires, meaning the true radius must be somewhat more than sixteen *amot*.

### 16⅔ Amot Exact

The *gemara* resolves this as follows: *lo daku lechumra lo daku* — *Ulla* was indeed imprecise, but imprecise in the stringent direction. He rounded down from the true figure, which means he was more demanding, not more lenient, about the exemption from *bikurim*. The true radius is sixteen and two-thirds *amot*, as *Rashi* and *Tosafot* note that this is the correct *girsa*: (16⅔)² × 3 = approximately 833 square *amot* — matching the *mishnah* precisely. By stating "sixteen *amot*," *Ulla* ensured that anyone within sixteen *amot* of the boundary would certainly fall within the zone of nutrient-drawing, even though the exact cutoff is sixteen and two-thirds. The rounding was toward stringency, making the exemption from *bikurim* apply over the full correct range.

---

## Ulla Challenged

### Buy Tree & Land

Having established *Ulla*'s rule, the *gemara* subjects it to a series of challenges from other *mishnayot*. The first: *hakoneh ilan vekarkao mevi vekoreh* — one who buys a tree together with its land brings *bikurim* and recites the declaration. The *gemara* asks whether *karkao* (its land) implies even the smallest plot of land suffices, which would contradict *Ulla*'s requirement for a full sixteen *amot* radius. The *gemara* deflects: *lo, tes-zayin amos* — no, it means specifically sixteen *amot* of surrounding land. The reply is admittedly forced, since one would have expected the *mishnah* to specify this explicitly.

### Two or Three Trees

The second challenge: *koneh shenei ilanos besoch shel chaveiro mevi ve'eino koreh* — one who buys two trees in a neighbor's field brings *bikurim* but does not recite the declaration; *ha shelosha mevi vekoreh* — but three trees, and one does recite. The implication seems to be that buying three trees automatically includes some surrounding land sufficient for *bikurim* — and the *mishnah* elsewhere clarifies this land is the immediately adjacent area under and between the trees, not a sixteen-*amah* radius. The *gemara* again proposes: no, when three trees are purchased, what is included is the surrounding area up to sixteen *amot* in each direction. *Tosafot* notes that this strains the plain meaning of the *mishnah*, which elsewhere describes the acquired land as whatever lies directly beneath the foliage — but adds that if the foliage extends beyond sixteen *amot*, one would receive that; and if not, one would receive at least sixteen *amot* in each direction.

### Rabbi Akiva Tiny

The third and most direct challenge comes from a statement of Rabbi Akiva: *karka kol shehu chayav bepe'ah uvevikurim* — even the smallest amount of land obligates in *pe'ah*, *bikurim*, and *prosbol*. The *prosbol* connection: a loan was customarily given only when the borrower held land that served as collateral, allowing the creditor to place liens. *Shmita* cancels such loans; *chazal* enacted the *prosbol* by which a creditor hands the debt over to *beit din*, enabling collection after *shemita*. This institution applies only to standard land-secured loans; even a tiny plot of land places the debt within that category. A further principle: *niknin imo nechasim she'ein lahem achrayot* — when real property is transferred, movable property (*chattel*) can be transferred along with it, even chattel not physically located on the land, and this too requires only the smallest parcel of real estate. And critically for our discussion, Rabbi Akiva states that *bikurim* applies even on the smallest amount of land — which seems directly contrary to *Ulla*'s position requiring sixteen *amot*.

### Wheat Not Trees

The *gemara* resolves the challenge by distinguishing the subject matter: *be'chitei* — Rabbi Akiva is speaking about grain crops such as wheat and barley (*eretz chitah u'seorah*), not trees. The obligation of *bikurim* applies to all seven species, and for grain there is no requirement of sixteen *amot*, since grain does not generate the same nutrient-drawing issue as trees. Only for trees does *Ulla*'s requirement apply. The *gemara* reinforces this: the very language *kol shehu* (any amount) indicates we are speaking of grain, since you cannot plant a tree in an infinitesimally small plot of land — that language only makes sense for something like a single stalk of wheat. *Shema mina* — the distinction is textually supported.

---

## Boundary Tree

### Split Tree Fruit

The *gemara* introduces a *mishnah* that presses on the relationship between nutrient-drawing and *halachic* status: *ilan miktzaso ba'aretz u'miktzaso b'chutz la'aretz* — a tree whose trunk straddles the boundary between *Eretz Yisrael* and *chutz la'aretz*. Produce of such a tree raises the question of what is *tevel* (untithed, therefore forbidden) and what is *chulin* (ordinary, exempt from tithing obligations applicable only in *Eretz Yisrael*).

### Nutrient Flow Debate

*Rebbe* (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) holds: *tevel v'chulin me'uravin zeh bazeh* — the produce of the entire tree is considered a mixture of *tevel* and *chulin*. One cannot identify which fruit grew from which side of the tree; the tree is a single organism, and the produce must be treated as a blend. One would therefore set aside half the normal amount of *terumot u'ma'asrot* from the total yield. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* disagrees: *hagadel bechiyuv chayav v'hagadel bip'tur patur* — produce on the *Eretz Yisrael* side of the vertical boundary is obligated; produce on the *chutz la'aretz* side is exempt. Each fruit is assigned to the half of the tree above which it grows.

### Breira Doctrine

The *gemara* initially frames this dispute as one of *breira* — the doctrine of retroactive determination. The question is whether we can retroactively say that the fruit growing on the *Eretz Yisrael* side of the tree was always "the fruit of the *Eretz Yisrael* portion" and vice versa. The *gemara* then clarifies a critical limiting condition: *hacha b'mai askinan d'mafsik tzunma* — the *mishnah* here is dealing with a special case where a rock or boulder runs along the boundary line underground, physically preventing the roots of each side from crossing into the other. Without this qualification, *Ulla*'s principle would require us to say that even the *chutz la'aretz* side of the tree is drawing nutrients from *Eretz Yisrael* soil and should therefore be subject to *terumot u'ma'asrot*. With the rock dividing the roots, this concern is removed, and the debate between *Rebbe* and *Rabban Shimon* can proceed on its own terms.

### Trunk Mixing

The question then shifts: given that the rock physically separates the roots on each side, why does *Rebbe* still treat the produce as mixed? If the nutrients are kept separate by the rock, why not simply say each side feeds its own fruit? The *gemara* answers: *mar savar avira mevalbel* — *Rebbe* holds that even if the roots are divided, the nutrients from both sides ultimately flow into the common trunk, mixing together there and feeding the entire tree indiscriminately. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, by contrast, holds *hai l'chudei ka'ei v'hai l'chudei ka'ei* — each side's nutrients remain in their own channel within the tree, feeding only the fruit on that corresponding side. Because the nutrients do not mix in the trunk according to *Rabban Shimon*, the boundary line can be extended vertically, and the fruit on each side is treated as having grown entirely from the nutrients of that side alone.

---

## 16 vs. 25 Amot

### 25 Amot Well

A further challenge to *Ulla*'s sixteen-*amah* rule arises from a different *mishnah*: *merchikin et ha'ilan min habor esrim v'chamesh amah* — a tree must be kept twenty-five *amot* away from a pit or well. If roots extend their damaging reach only up to sixteen *amot*, why does the *halacha* require a distance of twenty-five?

### Abaye: Weaken

*Abaye* resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between two different effects of roots. Roots will indeed grow far — twenty-five *amot* and beyond — and at that distance they can invade and damage the walls of a well or pit. However, the significant *drawing* of soil nutrients, the weakening of the ground, occurs only up to sixteen *amot*. *Ulla*'s concern for *bikurim* is predicated on where the tree is actually drawing its sustenance from, which is within sixteen *amot*. The rule of twenty-five *amot* by a well addresses physical intrusion and structural damage, which roots can cause at greater distances. The two figures thus measure different phenomena and do not contradict each other.

---

## Reish Lakish & Yochanan

### Gazlan Bikurim

When Rav Dimi came (from *Eretz Yisrael* to Babylonia), he reported a discussion between *Reish Lakish* and *Rabbi Yochanan*. *Reish Lakish* asked: what is the status of a tree situated close to a boundary line — does the *gazlan* designation prevent the owner from bringing *bikurim*?

### Cannot Bring

*Rabbi Yochanan* answered, as reported by Rav Dimi: *gazlan hu ve'ein mevi'in mimenu bikurim* — it is indeed a *gazlan*, and one may not bring *bikurim* from it. This aligns with *Ulla*'s ruling as we have been analyzing it.

### Allows Bikurim

However, a subsequent report by Ravin tells a different story: *Rabbi Yochanan* reversed his position. Whether the tree is close to the boundary or whether its canopy overhangs the neighbor's property, *echad ilan hasamuch lemeitzar ve'echad ilan hanoteh mevi vekoreh* — in either case the owner may bring *bikurim* and recite the declaration. All the evidence brought through the *sugya* had, in a sense, been pushing in this direction, and here we finally have an explicit ruling against *Ulla*'s original formulation.

### Al Menat Ken

The rationale is striking: *al menat kein hinchil Yehoshua le-Yisrael et ha'aretz* — Joshua apportioned the land of *Eretz Yisrael* to the Jewish people with the understanding that this is how things work. Trees near borders draw nutrients from adjacent plots; branches overhang into neighboring fields. These realities are built into the fabric of land ownership in *Eretz Yisrael*, and Joshua's allocation assumed and accommodated them. Because you have a right to these nutrients as part of the normal conditions of land use, it cannot be said that the produce is growing from land that was "given to someone else." You may therefore recite *adamah asher natata li* without qualification. The concept of *al menat ken* effectively transforms what *Ulla* framed as *gezel* (even if permitted) into something entirely within one's rights, thereby removing the obstacle to *bikurim* entirely. The *sugya* thus ends on a note that somewhat undercuts *Ulla*'s framing, while preserving the underlying agronomic observation about root reach.

---

## Branch Cutting

### Plow Clearance

The *mishnah* now addresses a different problem arising from overhanging branches. If a tree's canopy extends over a neighbor's field — a field where grain is grown and plowed — the neighbor may cut back the branches to a height sufficient to allow plowing. The standard of measurement is *melo hamardea al gabei hamachreishah*: the full height of the *mardea* (the goad or prod that the plowman holds over his animals while walking behind the plow) above the *machreishah* (the plow itself). In practical terms, this means enough clearance for the plowman and his equipment to pass through without obstruction.

### Carob Sycamore

An exception applies to carob trees and sycamore trees. These trees produce such dense, heavy foliage that even cutting to plowing height would leave a substantial overhang causing significant shade damage to the field. In these cases, the neighbor may cut the entire overhang — *keneged hamishkolet*, opposite the plumb line. That is, one drops a plumb line straight down from the boundary marker, and any branch extending beyond that vertical plane may be removed entirely, without limit as to height.

### Irrigated Field

The rule is further expanded for *beit hashlachin* — an irrigated field. Irrigation requires maximum sunlight and is especially sensitive to shade. Therefore, in the case of an irrigated field, any tree — not just carob and sycamore — whose branches overhang may be cut back entirely opposite the plumb line.

### Abba Shaul Non-Fruit

*Abba Shaul* adds a further ruling: *kol ilan srak keneged hamishkolet* — any non-fruit-bearing tree may be cut back entirely opposite the plumb line. The significance of his position, and precisely which case of the *mishnah* he is responding to, is the subject of immediate *gemara* discussion.

---

## Abba Shaul Position

### Which Case?

The *gemara* opens with a question: is *Abba Shaul* addressing the *reisha* (the first case of the *mishnah*, concerning a non-irrigated field) or the *seifa* (the second case, concerning an irrigated field)? In the first case, the *Tanna Kamma* limited complete removal to carob and sycamore; in the second, complete removal applied to all trees. *Abba Shaul* is either expanding the first case (adding all non-fruit trees to the list of those that may be fully cut) or restricting the second (limiting the irrigated-field rule to non-fruit trees). Is he being more lenient toward the aggrieved neighbor, or more lenient toward the tree owner?

### Baraita Evidence

A *baraita* resolves part of the question: it explicitly states that for an irrigated field, *Abba Shaul* rules *kol ha'ilan keneged hamishkolet* — any tree may be fully cut back, because the shade is harmful to an irrigated field. Since *Abba Shaul* explicitly allows all trees in the irrigated-field case, he cannot be the one introducing a restriction there. His position on the irrigated field aligns with the *Tanna Kamma*'s ruling in the *mishnah*.

### Non-Irrigated

It follows that *Abba Shaul*'s distinction between fruit and non-fruit trees must address the *reisha*, the non-irrigated field. In that case, the *Tanna Kamma* permitted complete removal only for carob and sycamore. *Abba Shaul* expands this: any non-fruit-bearing tree may be fully cut back even in a non-irrigated field. *Shema mina areisha ka'i* — the *gemara* accepts this conclusion.

### Kol Expansion

Rav Ashi adds a confirmation from the text of the *mishnah* itself. *Abba Shaul*'s language is *kol ilan srak* — "all non-fruit trees." The word *kol* (all/every) signals expansion. If *Abba Shaul* were responding to the irrigated-field case and limiting it to non-fruit trees, the word *kol* would be oddly chosen; one would simply say "non-fruit tree," not "all non-fruit trees." The word *kol* makes sense only if he is broadening the prior category — taking the *Tanna Kamma*'s narrow list of carob and sycamore and expanding it to all non-fruit-bearing trees. This linguistic argument confirms that *Abba Shaul* is arguing on the *reisha*, not the *seifa*. *Shema mina.*

---

## Public Domain Tree

### Camel Clearance

The final *mishnah* of the chapter addresses a tree overhanging *reshut harabbim* — the public thoroughfare. Here the concern is not agricultural damage but physical clearance for those using the public way. The rule is: *kotzetz kedei sheyehei gamal over verokhvo* — the branches must be cut back sufficiently to allow a camel and its rider to pass through without obstruction.

### Flax Measure

*Rabbi Yehuda* refines the standard: *gamal ta'un pishtan o havilei zmorot* — the measure is not the height of a rider on a camel but of a camel laden with flax or bundles of branches. The load sits atop the camel and extends above the rider's head, requiring a higher clearance.

### Plumb Line Tumah

*Rabbi Shimon* takes a more sweeping position: *kol ha'ilan keneged hamishkolet mipnei hatumah* — the entire overhang must be removed, opposite the plumb line, on account of ritual impurity (*tumah*). His concern is for *kohanim* and others who could become *tamei* by passing under branches that form an *ohel* (tent or canopy) over a corpse or part of a corpse. Since corpses or pieces thereof might be found or carried in public areas, and since *tumah* spreads under any covering, any overhanging branch creates a potential corridor of impurity through *reshut harabbim*.

---

## Current vs. Future

### Regrowth Problem

The *gemara* raises a structural difficulty: the *mishnah*'s standard — cut to allow a camel and rider to pass — seems to address only the present situation. Branches grow back. Why does the *mishnah* not require a more permanent solution, such as removing the entire overhang? What principle justifies limiting the remedy to the present clearance need?

### Regular Maintenance

*Reish Lakish* answers: this reflects a deliberate approach, and it follows the position of *Rabbi Eliezer*. The *gemara* cites a *mishnah* in Bava Kamma: the *chachamim* forbid digging cavities beneath *reshut harabbim* — for wells, cisterns, or tunnels — because the roof might eventually collapse. *Rabbi Eliezer* permits it provided the ceiling can currently bear the weight of a wagon laden with stones, attending only to the present structural integrity. The *chachamim* reject this because the ceiling may weaken undetected over time, eventually collapsing without warning. Our *mishnah*, which likewise asks only about the current situation rather than anticipating future growth, accordingly follows *Rabbi Eliezer*.

### Pruning vs. Tunnels

*Rabbi Yochanan* disagrees and holds that even the *rabbanan* can accept the *mishnah*'s approach. The difference is fundamental: *hasam zimnin de-mifchat ve-lav adatei* — in the case of the underground tunnel, the ceiling deteriorates gradually and invisibly; no one knows when it will give way, making the danger essentially impossible to monitor. *Aval hacha kamma kamma ka-kayitz lei* — here, with branches, one can observe regrowth incrementally and prune regularly as needed. Because the hazard is visible and manageable through routine maintenance, there is no structural reason to demand more than the present clearance even according to the *rabbanan*. The *mishnah* can therefore be read as consistent with the majority position.

---

## Flax vs. Person

### Height Comparison

Having recorded the dispute between the *rabbanan* (measuring by camel and rider) and *Rabbi Yehuda* (measuring by a camel laden with flax), the *gemara* raises a threshold question: which is taller — a person seated atop a camel, or a load of flax on a camel?

### Flax Must Be Higher

The *gemara* first establishes that the flax load must be the taller of the two, for the following reason: *de'i salka daitach shiura de-Rabbi Yehuda nafish rabbanan be-shiura de-Rabbi Yehuda heichi avidi* — were the flax load the shorter measure, the *rabbanan* who require clearance for a camel and rider would obviously be requiring even more clearance than *Rabbi Yehuda*, and on the occasions when a camel carrying flax comes through, there would be no protection at all. Since both *rabbanan* and *Rabbi Yehuda* are addressing the realistic hazards of *reshut harabbim* — and camels carrying loads of flax are a foreseeable occurrence — the *rabbanan* could not have permitted a standard that fails to protect against loaded camels. The flax load must therefore be higher than the mounted rider, and *Rabbi Yehuda*'s standard is more demanding in this regard.

### Duck or Cannot

But this immediately raises a reverse question: if the flax load is higher, how does *Rabbi Yehuda* accommodate the *rabbanan*'s case — the person riding on a camel? *Rabbi Yehuda* demands clearance only for the flax height; what about the mounted rider who may be taller than the flax? The *gemara* answers: *efshar de-gachin ve-chalif* — it is possible for a rider simply to duck. A person can lower his head and lean forward when passing under an obstruction. A load of flax cannot duck. Therefore, *Rabbi Yehuda* requires clearance sufficient for the immovable load but does not require it for the rider, who can accommodate himself. The *rabbanan*, by contrast, require sufficient clearance for the rider at full height without ducking — but since the flax load is even taller, the *rabbanan*'s standard by itself does not address the flax case, which is the specific concern that *Rabbi Yehuda* makes explicit.

---

## Tumah Overhang

### Dead Body Tumah

*Rabbi Shimon*'s ruling that the entire overhang must be removed on account of *tumah* is recorded in the *mishnah* with the phrase *mipnei hatumah*. A *baraita* elaborates: *mipnei ohel hatumah* — specifically because of the *ohel* (tent-like covering) created by the overhanging branches. The *ohel* effect means that any *tumah* located beneath the canopy of branches — most critically, a corpse or part of a corpse — spreads its impurity to everyone and everything under that same canopy. Since *kohanim* and others traversing *reshut harabbim* may pass under such overhanging branches, and since there may be a corpse or fragment thereof in the public domain, every overhang creates a potential conduit of *tumah*.

### Ohel Not Dropped

One might ask: is the concern perhaps simpler — that a raven or other bird might drop a piece of *tamei* matter directly onto one of the branches, making those specific branches a source of *tumah* from above? If so, the problem would be contact with *tumah* landing on the branch, not the *ohel* effect of the overhang itself.

### Pruning Insufficient

The *gemara* refutes this interpretation by a process of elimination: *ve-sagi bi-dilulei be-alma* — if the concern were something dropped onto the branches, it would be sufficient to thin the branches (*dilulei*), ensuring no piece of *tamei* material could be supported or lodged there. There would be no need to remove the entire overhang. But *Rabbi Shimon* requires total removal, not merely thinning. This demonstrates that the concern is the *ohel* created by the canopy itself: even a full, intact overhang with nothing resting on it spreads *tumah* from below by forming a tent over a source of impurity in the public domain. Because no amount of pruning eliminates the *ohel* effect — only total removal of the overhang does — *Rabbi Shimon* demands that the branches be cut back entirely opposite the plumb line.

With this we conclude the second *perek* of Bava Batra. *Hadran alach lo yachfor.*

---

---

# Bava Batra 28

## Intro: Chazakah Concept

### Perek Overview

We begin today a new *perek* — the third *perek* of Bava Batra, known as *Chazkat HaBatim*. It is a remarkably long *perek*, extending over thirty *daf*, though if one looks ahead, the actual density of Gemara text on each page is relatively modest — particularly because beginning with tomorrow's *daf* we transition from Rashi's commentary to the Rashbam's, and the Rashbam was considerably wordier.

### Chazakah Definition

The fundamental focus of this *perek* is *chazakah*. The word *chazakah* carries many meanings across different halachic contexts, but here it refers specifically to the following principle: if a person is present on land and makes use of it for three years, that continuous use serves as evidence that he is the legitimate owner. This is not a form of squatter's rights. Mere presence does not, in and of itself, entitle one to ownership. Rather, it functions as evidentiary support for a legitimate claim.

### Kol Chazakah Principle

An important principle that the Gemara introduces at the very outset is *kol chazakah she'eini imah ta'anah einah chazakah* — a *chazakah* that is not accompanied by a *ta'anah*, a legitimate legal claim, is no *chazakah* at all. If one has simply been on land for three years without offering any reason why it is legally his, the *chazakah* is meaningless. But if one can produce a *ta'anah* — "I purchased it from you," or something of that nature — then even absent any other evidence, the fact that one has been openly using the land for three years while the original owner has raised no objection constitutes a presumption, indeed evidence, of ownership. It is, perhaps better stated, a corroboration of a claim of legitimate ownership rather than the creation of ownership *ex nihilo*.

Of course, this immediately raises a host of practical questions. Where were the original owners during those three years? Were they in a position to know that someone else was on their land? Was the use of the land sufficiently provocative as to demand a response? All of these will be addressed as the *perek* unfolds, but this is the foundational principle: three years of open use, backed by a claim of legitimacy, combined with the owner's failure to object, establishes a presumption of ownership.

---

## Mishna: Property Types

### Listed Properties

The opening *mishna* on 28a lists the categories of property subject to *chazakah*: *chazkat habatim vehaborot vehashichin vehame'arot* — houses, cisterns, canals, and other water-holding structures such as caves; *vehashovachot* — pigeon cotes and dove cotes; *vehamerchatzaot* — bathhouses; *uveit habadin* — olive presses; *uveit hashlachin* — irrigated fields; and *ve'avadim* — slaves. All of these are categorized as real property, or are treated halachically as real property — slaves, though not land themselves, carry the same legal status as land in this context.

It is worth noting that the *mishna*, as is typical of rabbinic literary style, does not open with an abstract statement of the governing principle. Rather, it assumes a degree of familiarity and moves directly into categorization, distinguishing different types of property and specifying the applicable duration requirements.

### Continuous Benefit Rule

The *mishna* proceeds: *vechol shehu oseh peirot tadir* — anything that regularly produces benefit, *chazkatan shalosh shanim miyom leyom* — its *chazakah* is three years measured day to day. For something that yields continuous, ongoing benefit — a home being the clearest example, since one lives there on a daily basis — the three years must be continuous, measured from one specific date to the same date three years later. This makes intuitive sense: if the benefit derived from the property is ongoing and uninterrupted, then the use that constitutes *chazakah* must be similarly uninterrupted.

A house, a well, a pigeon cote operating as a business, a bathhouse — all of these involve regular, ongoing use. The *mishna* groups them together precisely because they share this characteristic. This also raises interesting subsidiary questions: does a month-long vacation abroad interrupt one's *chazakah* in an apartment? That is a question the *perek* will explore. But the basic premise is that *miyom leyom* — the continuous three-year period — is the standard for properties that produce benefit on a regular, non-seasonal basis.

### Rashi: Irrigated Fields

Regarding *beit hashlachin*, the irrigated field, Rashi explains: *beit hashlachin mitoch shehama'ayan betocho shemashkin oso mimenu tadir oseh peiros tadir* — because the spring within it allows for constant irrigation, this type of field produces regularly. It is therefore grouped with the properties requiring *miyom leyom* continuity.

There is, however, an important nuance that the *rishonim* tease out. If all one is doing on an irrigated field is irrigating, plowing, and planting — without yet harvesting — an original owner might plausibly say: "I had no reason to object; if someone wants to come onto my field and do all the labor, fine." The question is whether such preliminary acts of working the field count toward establishing *chazakah*. The answer, in context, is that they do count — but only when they form part of a cycle that culminates in harvesting, which is the genuine act of asserting ownership. If one merely irrigates and then walks away without harvesting, that alone cannot constitute *chazakah*. The assumption underlying the *mishna*'s inclusion of *beit hashlachin* in the continuous-benefit category is that the person holding it is deriving the full, ongoing benefit of its yield.

### Tosafot: Seasonality

Tosafot raises an interesting complication regarding the olive press. Elsewhere in the Talmud — in the *perek* of *chomer bakodesh* — there is language suggesting that the time of the wine press and the olive press has a fixed seasonal period: *avru hagittot vehaBaddim*. This implies that olive presses operate seasonally, not year-round. Yet the *mishna* here places them in the category of properties with regular, ongoing use.

Tosafot resolves this by distinguishing between different models of operation. Most people perform the pressing at the time of harvest, during the concentrated seasonal window. However, *yesh bnei adam shematnin kol hashana vedorchin bime'at me'at* — there are those who spread their production throughout the year, pressing in small increments over time. If the press operates as a business catering to the general public, it may function year-round even if the high season is concentrated. The underlying question — how precisely to measure use and benefit in the case of establishments with both high and low seasons — is one of those issues where practical application raises genuine complexity.

---

## Sedeh HaBaal: Three Seas…

### Sedeh HaBaal Definition

The *mishna* continues with a different category: the *sedeh haba'al*, the rain-fed field. Here, *chazkatah shalosh shanim ve'einah mi-yom le-yom* — its *chazakah* is three years, but not measured continuously day to day, because of the seasonal nature of agricultural production. Since such a field lies fallow during portions of the year, one can accumulate three seasons of use without being present for three full consecutive calendar years.

### R. Ishmael's 18-Month Mo…

The question then becomes: how does one measure these three seasons? *Rabbi Ishmael omer*: *gimmel chodashim barishona vegimmel ba'achrona veshneim asar chodesh ba'emtza* — three months at the beginning, twelve months in the middle, and three months at the end, totaling eighteen months.
