# Bava Batra 33

## Migo & Court Integrity

### Opening & Migo Review

Daf 33 continues a series of cases — quite plausibly real disputes rather than mere illustrations — all centered on *chazakah* and its attendant principles, though they frequently illuminate other areas of law, most notably *migo*. Before moving to the new material, it is worth revisiting a case from the previous daf, because it raises a point of enduring importance.

The *gemara* had presented a case involving a forged *shtar*. Everyone in the community believed the document to be genuine, and then the holder himself admitted it was forged. He nonetheless argued: believe me on some underlying claim, because *migo* — had I wished, I could have continued insisting the document was legitimate, and everyone would have accepted it. The *gemara* rejected this *migo* out of hand.

### Forged Doc & Migo

The question is why. If he had the better claim available, why does *migo* not apply? Tosafot articulates what most would intuit: you do not accept a *migo* whose alternative claim would only have existed because the claimant committed wrongdoing in the first place — here, the forgery itself. Even if the lie was universally believed, that is precisely the point. The legal system cannot allow a person to construct a *migo* on the scaffolding of his own fraud.

### Rashba & False Evidence

A responsum of the Rashba engages a scenario strikingly parallel to this case. A litigant approached the Rashba and essentially asked: my underlying claim is true, I lack sufficient legitimate evidence, but I have access to means — perhaps questionable evidence — by which I could prevail in *beis din*. May I use them, on the basis of *ovid inish dina l'nafshei* — the principle that a person may take the law into his own hands to recover what is genuinely his, analogous to breaking into someone's home to retrieve one's own property?

The questioner's very act of asking, of course, suggests he is telling the truth about his underlying claim. The Rashba nevertheless reacts with alarm, and with reference to precisely this *gemara*. The core principle, even if he does not state it in so many words, is that introducing false or fabricated evidence into the proceedings of a *beis din* fatally undermines the integrity of the court system. *Ovid inish dina l'nafshei* operates in the open: you are taking a visible, transparent action to recover what is yours. That is a very different matter from corrupting the internal machinery of a court whose purpose is to arrive at the truth.

### Migo in Modern Courts

This raises a related and genuinely open question about the contemporary *beis din*. In theory, *migo* remains operative in *halacha*, and the call to bring disputes before a *beis din shel Yisrael* rather than secular courts is grounded in the famous *derashah* on *eileh hamishpatim asher tasim lifneihem* — *lifneihem v'lo lifnei hedyotos*, *lifneihem v'lo lifnei batei din shel goyim*. In practice, however, how much of the adjudication in contemporary *batei din* is actually decided through *Choshen Mishpat*? The honest answer is: very little. The overwhelming majority of contemporary *beis din* proceedings function as a combination of *pshara* (equitable compromise), and *dina d'malchusa* — effectively an arbitration panel with occasional recourse to *halachic* sources. What it means, then, for a *beis din shel Yisrael* to fulfill its mandate when it does not adjudicate strictly according to *halacha* is a question worth sitting with.

---

## Rabba bar Sharshom

### Mortgage Explanation

The *gemara* at the bottom of 32b opens the next case. There was a rumor — a *kol* — that Rabba bar Sharshom was unlawfully consuming the property of orphans, *navik alei kala d'ka ochil ar'a d'yasmei*. Abaye, who could not believe the rumor was simply true, pressed him: tell me honestly, *eimli izi gufa d'uvda heichi hava* — what was the real story?

Rabba bar Sharshom explained: I had this land as *mashkanta* — as collateral — from the orphans' father. I had lent him money and held his land as security.

### Mashkanta d'Sura

The arrangement in question is *mashkanta d'Sura*, familiar from our earlier encounter in the chapter of *Perek HaZahav* in Bava Metzia. The structure works as follows: I lend Reuven a sum of money and take possession of his fields. Over, say, ten years, I harvest the produce, and at the end of that term I return the land and the debt is considered discharged. Technically this arrangement carries *ribis* concerns, since ten years of harvest from that land may well exceed the principal of the loan, but it is structured and framed as a kind of sale — I am effectively purchasing the fruit of the land for the term — and on that basis it is permitted. So Rabba bar Sharshom had been legitimately on the land, harvesting its produce, for the duration of the *mashkanta* period.

### Strategy via Migo

By the time we reach the top of 33a, the *mashkanta* term had expired and the land should have reverted to the orphans. The reason Rabba bar Sharshom had remained was that the father had also owed him money on a separate loan, *v'hava lei zuzi achrinei gabei*, and for that second loan he held a *shtar*. The complication: the *halacha* establishes that one who comes to collect a debt from orphans, even with a valid *shtar*, must take a *shevua* — an oath — that the debt has not been repaid. This is a protection for orphans who may be unaware of their father's private arrangements; a *shtar* alone does not suffice.

People — and the *gemara* itself reflects this — are deeply reluctant to take a *shevua*, even one that is truthful, for fear of any inadvertent error that might render it a *shevuat sheker*. So Rabba bar Sharshom reasoned as follows: rather than go through the formal process of producing the *shtar* and taking a *shevua*, I will simply conceal the documentation proving this was a *mashkanta* and remain on the land a further period. Since I have now been on the land for sufficient years, I could claim — even if falsely — that I purchased the land outright and have established *chazakah*. I have a *migo*: since I could have claimed *lekucha hi beyadi* and been believed, I should therefore be believed when I say that the orphans' father owed me additional money, and I should be able to collect that debt through the fruit I am taking — without a *shevua*.

The underlying mechanics deserve attention. A *mashkanta* holder, a sharecropper, and a purchaser all physically occupy someone's land. What prevents a *mashkanta* holder from later claiming he purchased it? Documentation. The same logic that requires a purchaser to retain his *shtar* for the first three years — after which *chazakah* suffices — also means that the landowner who grants a *mashkanta* or employs a sharecropper must retain documentation of that arrangement, so that if the other party later claims *chazakah* and purchase, the arrangement can be demonstrated. Remarkably, in this case the person holding the land — Rabba bar Sharshom — was also the one holding the documentation of its *mashkanta* status. He could simply suppress it, claim *chazakah*, and be believed. That, he reasoned, gave him a *migo* to collect the other debt without a *shevua*.

### Abaye's Rejection

Abaye rejected the strategy. *Lekucha hi beyadi lo masis amrat* — you could not have made that claim. Why? *Deika kala d'ara deyasmi hi* — there was a *kol*, a widespread public perception, that this land belonged to the orphans.

This generates an obvious difficulty. He was on the land for *shnei chazakah*, the requisite years. Why does a public perception that the land belongs to the orphans undermine a *chazakah* claim? If one has truly been on a piece of land for three years, the prior ownership is precisely what *chazakah* is designed to overcome. People may have assumed a field belonged to its previous owner before a sale — no one announces every private transaction. Yet *chazakah* after three years is believed even against the prior owner's claim. Why should the orphans' situation be any different?

The answer lies in understanding precisely what the *kol* communicated. Abaye's point is that the *migo* fails — not necessarily that the *chazakah* itself is legally invalid — and for that we need to understand what the *kol* actually established. Abaye's practical conclusion is clear: return the land to the orphans, *zil ahadar nihalyahu*, and when the orphans come of age, pursue the debt through proper channels — which means producing the *shtar* and taking the *shevua*. No shortcuts.

### Rashbam vs Tosafot

Two distinct explanations are offered for why the *kol* defeats the *migo*, and they reflect a genuine disagreement about the content of the *kol* itself.

The Rashbam reads *kala d'ara deyasmi hi* as meaning that everyone perceived and understood that Rabba bar Sharshom's presence on the land was as a *mashkon* holder — that he was there as collateral-taker, not as owner. The rumor that spread was not merely that the orphans once owned it, but specifically that this man was on it as a *mashkanta* holder whose term had expired and who was now wrongfully remaining. In that context, the claim of *lekucha hi beyadi* — that he purchased it — simply would not have been believed. The *chazakah* mechanism operates on the presumption that three years of open occupation, in the absence of protest, suggests purchase. But that presumption is defeated when there is a concurrent understanding of *why* the person is on the land — namely, as a *mashkanta* holder. A sharecropper cannot establish *chazakah* through his years of work on the land, and similarly a *mashkanta* holder whose status is publicly understood cannot leverage those years into a *chazakah* claim. So the *migo* fails because the alternative claim would not actually have prevailed.

Tosafot reads the case differently — and arguably in a way that makes Rabba bar Sharshom's original reasoning more understandable. According to Tosafot, the *kol* was not that it was known to be a *mashkanta* arrangement. The *kol* was simply that the land had originally belonged to the orphans' father and that they inherited it. That is a perfectly standard scenario for *chazakah* to operate: the prior owner is known, and one claims to have purchased it. Tosafot therefore concedes that had Rabba bar Sharshom actually made the claim *lekucha hi beyadi*, he might well have been believed in court — because witnesses to prior ownership do not contradict a claim of subsequent purchase. The court does not act on public misperception; it adjudicates on evidence.

But that is precisely where Tosafot locates the flaw in the *migo*. A *migo* requires not merely that the alternative claim was *technically* available, but that it was one the claimant would realistically have been prepared to make. *Migo d'ei ba'ei amar lekucha hi beyadi hava ne'eman* — true, he would have been believed — *mikal makom lo havei migo*, yet there is no *migo*, because *delo hayisa yachol leha'iz panecha velomar kein* — he would not have had the brazenness to say it. With the *kol* already established that the orphans inherited the land from their father, for Rabba bar Sharshom to stand up in court and say "actually, the father sold it to me" — when everyone in the community perceived the orphans as the inheritors — would have meant being looked at as someone brazenly trying to rob orphans. People would not have believed him, not because the legal claim was unavailable, but because the social reality of the *kol* would have made the claim appear unconscionably brazen. This is the principle of *migo leha'iz lo amrinan*: we do not apply *migo* when the alternative claim the person did not make would have been more brazen than the one being made.

It is worth noting the distinction between what a *beis din* evaluates and what the public perceives. A court is not and should not be swayed by popular opinion; if a person had genuine evidence, the court would rule on it regardless of communal perception. The *migo* analysis, however, is precisely about what claim the person would *realistically* have made — and there, the social context of the *kol* is directly relevant. Tosafot's point is not that the court would have dismissed the claim, but that Rabba bar Sharshom himself would not have had the nerve to advance it.

---

## Rav Idi Bar Avin

### Inheritance Dispute

The next case: a relative of Rav Idi bar Avin died and left behind what the *gemara* calls a palm tree — presumably an orchard of date palms. Rav Idi bar Avin claimed to be the closer relative and therefore the heir. Another man made the same claim. The factual situation is underspecified, but the Rashbam's reading suggests that neither claimant had documentary evidence establishing their precise position in the line of inheritance. Each was asserting kinship, and there may have been a general social recognition — attending family gatherings, appearing at lifecycle events — that each was *somehow* related to the deceased, but no one could establish who was closer.

What is also unstated but apparently occurred is that the unnamed disputant — more brazen or simply better positioned — squatted on the property and began collecting the fruit. This anticipates the principle of *kol de'alim gevar*, which the *gemara* will address more directly later, but the practical result was that for a period this other party occupied the land and consumed its produce, since no one could adjudicate the competing claims.

### Admission Debate

Eventually, *lesof odei leh d'ihu kariv tefei* — in the end, the disputant admitted or conceded in favor of Rav Idi bar Avin. Rav Idi bar Avin responded: fine, now return the fruit — *leihadar li peirei d'achal mehahu yoma v'ad hashta* — everything you consumed from the moment you squatted until now. This prompted a sharp reaction: is this Rav Idi bar Avin, the one people regard as such a great *talmid chacham*?

Rav Chisda pressed him: *amai ka-samchat mar a'hai d'ka-amar* — on what basis are you relying to claim the fruit? The other party has admitted or conceded, yes — but *ha ka-amar d'ana mikaravna tefei*, he is still asserting that he himself is the closer relative. So the concession, Rav Chisda argues, does not amount to a full legal retraction of his underlying claim of closer kinship; he is merely stepping aside from the contest over the land, not affirming that Rav Idi bar Avin was always the rightful owner. And if he hasn't truly retracted his earlier claim, then his concession with respect to the land is more in the nature of a *matana* — a gift, a non-contested ceding — than an admission of prior wrongdoing. On that reading, Rav Idi bar Avin would have no claim to the fruit already consumed.

Abaye and Rava disagree with Rav Chisda: *keivan de'odi, odi* — once he admitted, he admitted. By conceding the land to Rav Idi bar Avin, he effectively retracted his prior claim to have been the closer relative, and that retraction entitles Rav Idi bar Avin to recover the fruit as well.

### Gift vs Retraction

Much of the complexity here turns on how to read the *gemara*'s phrasing. The Rashbam reads the text with the words *d'ihu karev tefei* — that the disputant explicitly said Rav Idi bar Avin was the closer relative — yet even so, Rav Chisda holds that we do not interpret this as a true retraction, only as a willingness to cede the property without contesting further. Even an explicit statement conceding the other's closer kinship, on this reading, may be interpreted as nothing more than a non-contesting gift. Abaye and Rava, naturally, read the explicit admission as a genuine retraction. The Rashbam's reading makes Abaye and Rava's position more comprehensible; Rav Chisda's position, under the Rashbam, requires some work to understand.

Tosafot resolves this by reading the *gemara* without those words — *d'ihu karev tefei* — in the decisive passage. On Tosafot's *girsa*, the disputant merely conceded the land without saying anything about who was the closer relative. That makes Rav Chisda's position far more understandable: of course a party who simply says "take it" isn't admitting he was wrong about his kinship — he's just done fighting. On the other hand, Tosafot's reading makes Abaye and Rava's position — that *keivan de'odi, odi* — harder to understand, since the concession seems less clearly a retraction. Each reading illuminates one position while making the other require more explanation, and the truth lies somewhere between the two.

### Witnesses & Migo

Tosafot also offers a third explanation that substantially reframes the entire case, though it departs so far from the *girsa* we have as to essentially constitute a rewriting. On this reading, what actually occurred was that Rav Idi bar Avin brought witnesses establishing that he was a relative of the deceased. Not that he was the *closer* relative — the witnesses could not establish the comparative degree of kinship — only that he was indeed in the line of inheritance. The disputant, by contrast, had no witnesses at all; he was simply making an unsubstantiated claim.

Given this, the court ruled in Rav Idi bar Avin's favor on the land — it was a case resembling *bari v'shema*: one party's claim is established by witnesses, the other's is entirely unverified. But when Rav Idi bar Avin then demanded the fruit, the analysis shifts. The witnesses did not testify about the fruit, and they did not establish that Rav Idi bar Avin was the *closer* relative — only that he was a relative. The disputant is still able to claim that he is actually closer in kinship. And here is where *migo* enters: the disputant is admitting that he consumed the fruit, but he is doing so in the context of asserting that he was the rightful heir. Since the witnesses did not contradict this particular claim — they established only that Rav Idi bar Avin is *a* relative, not that he is the *closer* one — there is no *migo b'makom eidim* problem. The *migo* is: he could have denied taking the fruit at all, yet he admits it and offers an explanation. That admission combined with his explanation is believed regarding the fruit, since the witnesses' testimony does not reach this question.

This is on Tosafot's reading what Rav Chisda means when he asks *amai ka-samchat mar* — on what basis do you demand the fruit? You're relying on his concession of the fruit, but his concession is made in the context of claiming closer kinship, which the witnesses don't contradict. And the suggestion of Abaye and Rava — *keivan de'odi, odi* — would then need to be understood as addressing a different dimension of the case, which the *gemara* leaves to be resolved elsewhere.

---

## Ancestral Plot Claim

### Two Claimants

The next case: *zeh moshel avotai v'zeh moshel avotai* — one party says it was my ancestral plot, the other makes the same claim. The language of *avotai* carries significance: not merely that a father once owned it, but that it is ancestral land, inherited and retained within the family, and therefore not subject to having been sold off. One claimant, Reuven, brings witnesses establishing that the land belonged to his father. The other, Shimon, brings witnesses to *shnei chazakah* — that he has been on the land for the years required to establish *chazakah*.

### Rav Chisda Migo

Rav Chisda rules in favor of Shimon, invoking *migo*: *ma li leshaker* — why would he lie? Since Shimon has the *chazakah* years, he could have claimed *i ba'ei amar lei minach zivintei v'achalti shnei chazakah* — "I bought it from you, and I have been here the requisite years" — and been believed. If he could have made that claim and won, then the fact that he instead says it was his ancestral plot should also be believed, even against Reuven's witnesses. Reuven's witnesses establish that at one point the land was in his father's family; they do not preclude the possibility that Shimon subsequently purchased it from Reuven's father. Since the *chazakah* claim would have been believed and would not have been contradicted by those witnesses, the *migo* allows Shimon's alternative claim — ancestral ownership — to be believed as well.

### Abaye & Rava

Abaye and Rava reject Rav Chisda's ruling. The fundamental principle they invoke is *migo b'makom eidim lo amrinan* — we do not apply *migo* in the face of witnesses who contradict the claim. Reuven's witnesses testify to his father's ownership in a manner that directly contradicts Shimon's claim that the land was his ancestral plot. One might ask whether Rav Chisda denies this principle entirely or simply reads the witnesses' testimony more narrowly — as establishing only that the land was once Reuven's family's, not that it remained so and was never sold. On that narrower reading, the witnesses might not directly contradict Shimon's claim; they would simply establish a fact about prior ownership, which is fully compatible with a subsequent purchase by Shimon's family. But the broader and more standard reading — which Abaye and Rava adopt — is that testimony establishing Reuven's family's ancestral ownership is indeed direct testimony against Shimon's claim of ancestral ownership, and *migo* cannot overcome witnesses.

---

## One Witness Case

### Insufficient Proof

The *gemara* now presents a case that begins simply. A man is on someone's land and is asked, *mai ba'it b'hai ar'a* — what are you doing here? He answers: *minach zavni v'achalti shnei chazakah* — I bought it from you and I have been here for the years of *chazakah*. He goes to find witnesses to support his claim, but can only produce witnesses to two of the three required years. Rav Nachman rules: *hadar ar'a v'hadar peirei* — the land reverts to the original owner, and so does all the fruit the claimant consumed. He has not established his case, and both the land and its produce must be returned.

### Sharecropper Claim

Rav Zvid then introduces an important qualification. The Rashbam supplies a critical word that the *gemara* leaves implicit: *if* the claimant had originally framed his claim differently — if he had said not that he purchased the land but that he came down onto it as a sharecropper or had purchased rights to the fruit — *ne'eman*, he would be believed regarding the fruit. Even though the land reverts, he would not have to return the fruit he consumed.

### Brazenness Principle

Why would he be believed about the fruit in that scenario? The *gemara* cites Rav Yehuda's teaching: a person who is walking around with a sickle and a basket and announces publicly that he is going to harvest the palm tree of so-and-so because so-and-so sold him the fruit — *meheiman* — he is believed. The *beis din* does not intervene and treat him as a thief. The underlying principle is stated explicitly: *lo chatzif inish lemeichal piri delav dilei* — a person does not have the brazenness to go ahead and consume, openly, produce that is not his.

This needs careful delimitation. The Rashbam explains that the *gemara* is not saying the *beis din* will preemptively act on this man's behalf against an absent owner. Rather, the *beis din* simply does not step in on the owner's behalf in the absence of the owner's own protest. If the owner were to come forward and say "that man is a *gazlan*," the *beis din* would of course take up the matter. The point is only that without the owner's active claim, we accept at face value that the person openly consuming the fruit has a legitimate basis to do so — because people generally don't act that brazenly with someone else's property in public.

Tosafot questions whether the principle is even limited to public conduct, arguing it would apply even in private. But Tosafot raises a more pointed question: what is the *chidush* here at all? Fruit is *metaltelin* — movable property. If a person has physical possession of movable property, the basic principle of *chazakah mah shetachat yad adam harei hu shelo* — whatever is under a person's control is presumptively his — should already suffice. Why do we need any elaborate reasoning about brazenness and public conduct?

### Land vs Fruit Shtar

The *gemara* addresses the distinction between land and fruit directly. *Arra amina lei achvei shtarcha* — for land, we tell the claimant: show us your *shtar*. The absence of a purchase document for land is telling, because transactions in land are invariably documented. *Ei hachi piri nami* — so why not require a *shtar* for fruit as well? The answer: *shtra l'piri lo avdi inshi* — people do not customarily write documents for fruit. A sharecropping arrangement, an agreement to purchase fruit rights for a season, a simple handshake deal about a harvest — these are not the kinds of transactions that generate formal *shtarot*. Therefore, the absence of a *shtar* does not undermine the claim about fruit the way it would undermine a claim about land.

Tosafot remains unsatisfied, returning to the question of *chazakah* on *metaltelin*. He suggests the case must be read as one where the fruit is not in the claimant's direct physical possession — perhaps it has been harvested and is being held by a third party, or has not yet been formally transferred. Only in that configuration is there a genuine *chidush*: the claimant is not in direct possession and therefore cannot rely on *chazakah mah shetachat yado*, so the believability of his claim must rest on the brazenness principle and the absence of a *shtar* requirement for fruit. Once the fruit has been fully consumed or is under his direct control, the *metaltelin chazakah* would independently suffice.

### Witness Problem

The *gemara* then extends the case in a more interesting direction. The claimant goes looking for witnesses and finds one witness who testifies to *three* years of *chazakah* — the full requisite period, not merely two. Yet he still cannot win the case, because one witness is not two. Now the question becomes pointed: this witness was brought to support the claimant. But given that the claimant has admitted to being on the land and consuming its fruit, and given that he cannot win the *chazakah* claim with only one witness, does this one witness now *turn against* the claimant — establishing that he consumed three years of fruit without right, such that he must return it all? And if he cannot contradict the witness's testimony, must he pay?

### Adverse vs Supportive

The scholars sitting before Abaye initially suggest that this case resembles the famous *naska* case of Rabbi Abba, which the *gemara* proceeds to narrate. However, Abaye ultimately distinguishes the two, and the distinction is illuminating. The *naska* case must first be understood on its own terms.

---

## Silver Ingot Case

### Item Taking Scenario

Someone grabbed a silver ingot — a *naska* — from another party. He was brought before Rabbi Ami, with Rabbi Abba sitting present. One witness testified that the item was grabbed, that Reuven took it from Shimon. Reuven then said: *ein chatafi* — yes, I grabbed it — *vedidi chatafi* — because it was mine. He did not deny the taking; he offered an explanation for it.

### Rabbi Ami's Dilemma

Rabbi Ami articulates the dilemma with precision: *heichi nadaynu dayanei lehai dina* — how should the judges rule on this case? *Lishalem* — should Reuven simply pay? There are not two witnesses to the taking; you cannot impose payment on a defendant based on one witness alone. *Liftreih* — should Reuven simply be exempted? You cannot ignore the testimony of one witness. Normally, when one witness makes a claim against a defendant, the defendant takes a *shevua* contradicting that claim. But here, the defendant *concedes* the factual claim of the witness — that he took the item from Shimon's possession. The only *shevua* available to him would be one that directly contradicts the witness's testimony, and he cannot take that oath because he agrees with what the witness saw.

### Gazlan Principle

*Vekeivan de'amar chatafi havei leih kegazlan* — since he says he grabbed it, he is in the position of a *gazlan*, and this is not a technical designation so much as a functional one: he is not positioned to take the required *shevua* because his own admission forecloses it. The rule that applies here is *mechuyav shevua she'eino yachol lishava meshalem* — one who is obligated to take a *shevua* and cannot do so must pay. Reuven is obligated to take a *shevua* against the single witness, and since he cannot take it — his own admission acknowledging the taking is what prevents him — he must pay.

### Adverse vs Supportive

Now Abaye explains why the *naska* case does *not* apply to the case of the single witness to three years of *chazakah*. The key distinction is the direction of the witness's testimony — not who brought the witness to court, but what the consequence of that testimony would be if there were *two* such witnesses.

*Hatam sahada le'aru'ei ka'ati* — in the *naska* case, the witness comes to damage the defendant's position. Were there two witnesses to Reuven taking the ingot from Shimon's backpack, Reuven would be a *gazlan* and would have to pay, regardless of his explanation. His claim that it was his own property would not be heard against two witnesses to the taking. Two witnesses would be fully adverse to him.

*Hacha lesiyuyei ka'asi* — here, in the *chazakah* case, the witness comes to support the claimant. Were there two witnesses to three years of occupation, the claimant would *win* the case. *Ki asiei achrini mokminan lei behadei* — if a second witness were to come, the claimant's position would be vindicated. A witness whose doubled testimony would result in the claimant's *victory* cannot be treated as an adverse witness against whom the claimant must take a *shevua*. It does not matter that this particular witness was brought by the claimant expecting support and ended up being insufficient; what matters is the nature of the testimony itself. The testimony is supportive in character — there simply is not enough of it. Insufficient supportive testimony does not transform into adverse testimony and does not trigger the *mechuyav shevua she'eino yachol lishava* mechanism.

This is a compelling and clean answer. The *naska* and *chazakah* cases are superficially similar — one witness, defendant cannot contradict — but are structurally opposite: in one, two witnesses would destroy the defendant; in the other, two witnesses would vindicate him. That structural difference determines whether the single witness is adversarial or merely insufficient, and that in turn determines whether the *shevua* mechanism is triggered.

---

---

# Bava Batra 34

## One Witness & Chazaka

### Intro & Setup

The daf opens at the very last lines of 34a with the word *ela idamya*. The case under discussion involves a litigant who possessed a single witness testifying that he had eaten three years' worth of fruit from a given field — the basis for a claim of *chazaka*. The problem is that *chazaka* requires two witnesses; with only one, he cannot establish possessory title over the land. The question then becomes whether that lone witness can at least function as testimony against him — obligating him to pay for the three years of fruit he consumed. After all, the only basis for any claim against him regarding the fruit is that one witness, since without any witnesses at all, the litigant's own admission that he ate the fruit would be neutralized by his simultaneous claim of ownership. That combination would invoke the principle of *peh she'asar peh shehitir* — the same mouth that creates the liability also provides the exemption — and no payment would result. So the lone witness is doing all the work. The question is whether that witness can bear that weight.

### Supporting vs. Damning

The *gemara* draws a crucial distinction between a witness who supports a claim and one who damages it. The lone witness who testifies to three years of fruit consumption is not straightforwardly a damning witness — because if a second witness were to appear and corroborate him, that testimony would actually *help* the litigant establish his *chazaka* and win the land outright. In other words, this witness belongs to the category of supporting evidence for which a second corroborating witness has simply not yet been found. The *gemara* appears to conclude, though without stating it explicitly, that such a witness cannot therefore be used as damning testimony to compel payment for the fruit.

### Naska de-Rabbi Abba

This stands in contrast to the famous case known as *naska de-Rabbi Abba*, which the *gemara* had already invoked as a potential parallel. In that case, a person seized what appeared to be an ingot of silver belonging to someone else, claiming it was his own property. There was one witness who saw him take it. The analysis runs as follows: had there been two witnesses to the taking, he would be classified as a *gazlan* — a robber — and obligated to pay. Had there been no witnesses at all, he would be believed through a *migo*: he could have claimed he always had possession of the object, and since he could have made that stronger claim, his actual claim is similarly credited. With one witness, however, he finds himself in a middle position. That one witness is operating *against* him — it is a damning witness — because if a second were added, he would be liable. Accordingly, Rabbi Abba ruled that the single witness creates an obligation to take an oath contradicting the witness's testimony. Since the man cannot swear that he did not take the object (he openly admits he took it, insisting only that it was rightfully his), he is *chayav* in a *shvu'ah* he cannot fulfill, and therefore must pay.

### Two Years Parallel

The *gemara* now supplies the precise land-based analogue to *naska de-Rabbi Abba*. The equivalent case is not three years of fruit with one witness — which, as established, is a supporting rather than a damning configuration — but rather *two* years of fruit with one witness. If someone claims *chazaka* and a lone witness testifies to two years of fruit consumption, that witness is genuinely damning: two witnesses to two years would establish that the litigant ate the fruit without yet having established ownership, obligating him to pay. One such witness therefore triggers the same mechanism as *naska de-Rabbi Abba* — an obligation to swear against the witness's testimony. Since the litigant admits eating the fruit (claiming only that the land is his), he cannot take that oath, and he must pay. This is the precise structural parallel: just as in *naska de-Rabbi Abba* — "yes, I took it, but it was mine" — so too here, "yes, I ate the fruit, but the land is mine." The *shvu'ah* cannot be made, and payment follows.

---

## Boat & Holding Pattern

### Boat Dispute Setup

The *gemara* at the top of 34b introduces a new case: *hahu arba* — there was a boat. Two people were disputing ownership: *hai amar didi hu v'hai amar didi hu* — this one says it is mine, that one says it is mine. Before reaching the question of ultimate adjudication, the *gemara* first addresses a procedural matter. One of the claimants approaches the court and requests: *tifsuha ad d'maitina sahadei d'didi hu* — seize the boat and hold it while I go and collect my witnesses proving it is mine. The concern is practical: while he is gathering evidence, the other party might sell the boat or otherwise dispose of it, making recovery difficult or impossible. The request, then, is not for a final ruling but for a temporary holding pattern — essentially asking the court to serve as a neutral custodian until proof can be produced.

This case is deeply connected to the opening *sugya* of Bava Metzia, where two people are physically holding a *tallit* and the resolution is *yachloku* — they split it. That case, however, involves *metaltelin* — movable chattels in actual physical possession. Here, by contrast, the disputed objects (plots of land, boats) are not in either party's physical grip, and the resolutions will therefore differ.

### Tafsinan/Lo Tafsinan

The question is *tafsinan o lo tafsinan* — do we seize the disputed object as a holding measure or not? *Rav Huna amar tafsinan* — Rav Huna holds that the court should take possession, serving as a kind of referee to protect the integrity of the eventual adjudication. *Rav Yehuda amar lo tafsinan* — Rav Yehuda refuses. The reason for Rav Yehuda's position becomes clear only once the companion question is posed.

### Mafkinan/Lo Mafkinan

The companion question is *mafkinan o lo mafkinan* — if the court did take possession but the claimant subsequently cannot produce his witnesses, does the court then release the object or continue holding it indefinitely? *Rav Yehuda amar lo mafkinan* — once you take hold of it, you are responsible. You cannot simply release it back into an unresolved situation; you have assumed a judicial responsibility that cannot be walked back. *Rav Pappa amar mafkinan* — Rav Pappa maintains that even after taking possession, the court may release the object if no evidence is forthcoming.

The Rashbam makes an elegant observation: one's position on *mafkinan* directly determines one's position on *tafsinan*. Rav Yehuda, who holds that once you take possession you cannot release it, therefore refuses to take possession in the first place. If the claimant says "hold it while I find my witnesses" and then cannot produce them, Rav Yehuda would be stuck holding an unresolvable dispute indefinitely — a responsibility he has no way to discharge. He therefore declines from the outset. Rav Pappa, who permits releasing possession once no evidence materializes, is correspondingly more amenable to taking possession initially, since he has a viable exit.

The *halacha* follows a combination of both positions: *lo tafsinan* — we do not take possession in a holding pattern, because we do not wish to assume a responsibility we may be unable to fulfill. But *ve-heicha de-tafas lo mafkinan* — if the court did go ahead and take possession contrary to this ruling, it may not then release the object. Having chosen to get involved, it must remain responsible until the matter is resolved.

### Kol D'Alim Gavar

We now arrive at the underlying ruling for cases where neither party has any evidence. If both parties claim — *zeh omer shel avosai ve-zeh omer shel avosai* — this is my ancestral property, that is my ancestral property — and neither can bring proof, *Rav Nachman amar kol d'alim gavar*: whoever is stronger prevails. The Rashbam reads this to mean that the court declines to adjudicate at all. With no evidence, no physical possession, and nothing but unsubstantiated claims, the court simply steps away. The parties are left to resolve it themselves. Other *rishonim* read the phrase more actively — perhaps meaning that whoever can bring stronger circumstantial evidence will be favored — but following the Rashbam's reading, the court's message is: we have nothing to work with; do not bring this matter to us.

---

## Two Deeds Same Day

### Competing Deeds

The *gemara* now raises a comparison: *umai shena mi-shnei shtaros ha-yotzin be-yom echad* — how is the boat case different from the case of two *shtaros* dated on the same day? In this scenario, Reuven writes a deed gifting the same object to Shimon on a given date, and another deed gifting that same object to Levi on that very same date. Both cannot take effect simultaneously. One might suppose that we should determine which deed was written first, but another *gemara* establishes that in the absence of a locale where the hour is recorded in the document — which was not standard practice — deeds take effect at the end of the day, meaning both should have taken effect simultaneously. So what is to be done?

At the top of 35a, *Rav amar yachloku* — Rav says they split the contested object. *U-Shmuel amar shuda d'dayni* — Shmuel says the judges apply their best assessment of the circumstances and make a determination based on what Reuven most plausibly intended, even without definitive proof. Yet in neither option does the court say *kol d'alim gavar* and walk away. Why?

### Full Evidence Required

The *gemara* answers: *hasam leika le-mikam ala de-milsa, hacha ika le-mikam ala de-milsa* — there, there is nothing further to investigate; here, there is. In the case of the two *shtaros*, all available evidence is already before the court. The documents are equally valid, equally dated, addressed to different recipients — there is no additional proof that could ever be produced that would change the halachic picture. Given that this is the totality of the evidence, the court must engage and do the best it can, whether by splitting or by judicial assessment. In the boat case, by contrast, it is presumed that eventually — if the matter is sufficiently important — witnesses or documentation will emerge establishing ownership. The court therefore refuses to render judgment prematurely on the basis of pure claims, holding out for the possibility of real evidence.

---

## Cow/Donkey Birth Case

### Swap Dispute

The *gemara* raises a further comparison: *hamachalif parah ba-chamor v'yaldah* — someone swaps his cow for another person's donkey (via *chalipin*, an exchange that does not require both objects to be physically present), and when the new owner goes to collect the cow, he finds that she has given birth. Did the cow give birth before or after the swap? The calf's ownership turns on this question. Similarly, if someone sells a maidservant and she gives birth before she is physically collected: did it happen before the sale or after? *Zeh omer ad shelo macharti yaldah* — one says she gave birth before the sale; *ve-zeh omer mishekachti yaldah* — the other says it happened after the purchase. The ruling is *yachloku* — split it. Here, too, conceivably further evidence could surface, yet the court does not resort to *kol d'alim gavar* but instead divides the contested property. Why is this different from the boat case?

### Standing Doctrine

The *gemara* answers on 35b: *l'hai is lei drara d'mamona u-l'hai is lei drara d'mamona* — each litigant has *drara d'mamona*, a monetary connection or stake in the matter. Both parties have clear, established standing. We know the sequence of ownership: the cow belonged to one party at one point and passed to the other at a defined moment; the only question is where precisely the calf's birth falls relative to that moment. Each claimant has an objectively grounded basis for his claim — neither is simply making an unfounded assertion.

The boat litigants, by contrast, could be entirely without standing. Either one could be a complete stranger to the property making a baseless claim. The *gemara* captures this with the phrase *hacha ei d'mar lo d'mar v'ei d'mar lo d'mar* — in this case, if it belongs to one, the other has nothing; if it belongs to the other, the first has nothing. This is best read not as a logical observation about mutual exclusivity — which is equally true of the calf — but as a pointed remark about credibility and standing: according to each claimant's own account, the other party is a complete fabricator with zero claim. In the cow/donkey dispute, each party demonstrably had some connection to the cow at some point in time. That concrete monetary connection — *drara d'mamona* — compels the court to adjudicate. Where such standing is absent, the court steps back and declares *kol d'alim gavar*.

---

## Third Party Seizure

### Amri Neharda'a

Having established that the boat dispute defaults to *kol d'alim gavar*, the *gemara* asks what happens if a third party entirely unconnected to the original dispute seizes the boat. *Amri Neharda'a* — the Sages of Nehardea rule — *im ba echad min ha-shuk ve-hichzik bah ein motzi'in otah mi-yado*: if someone from the market came and took hold of it, we do not remove it from his possession. This ruling reinforces the logic of *kol d'alim gavar*: since the original two claimants have no demonstrated standing, a third party who physically seizes the object has no less a claim than they do. The very refusal of the court to adjudicate between Reuven and Shimon reflects the principle that *anyone's* claim is as weak as anyone else's. Why should only those two be considered?

### Gazlan Shel Rabim

This is supported by the teaching of Rabbi Hiyya: *gazlan shel rabim lav shmei gazlan* — one who is a *gazlan* of the masses is not called a *gazlan*. In this context, Rabbi Hiyya's rule applies because the object in question is effectively ownerless — it belongs to the *rabim* not in the sense of public property but in the sense that no individual has any demonstrated title. Taking something that belongs to no identifiable person does not constitute genuine *gezilah*, since there is no established owner from whom one could be stealing.

### Rav Ashi's View

Rav Ashi disagrees: *le'olam shmei gazlan* — this third party is indeed called a *gazlan*. The reasoning appears to be that Rav Ashi's case is somewhat different: the third party is not claiming that the object belongs to his own ancestors or making any affirmative claim of ownership. He is simply seizing it opportunistically, reasoning that since neither of the two disputants can prove ownership, he will take it for himself. That posture — seizure without any claim — stands on even weaker ground than the original two litigants. Rav Ashi therefore rules that even within the *kol d'alim gavar* framework, a claimless third-party seizure is impermissible. The object must be returned to the prior situation, and those with actual claims — however unsubstantiated — must argue it out.

### Gazlan Definition

The *gemara* then clarifies what Rabbi Hiyya's statement *gazlan shel rabim lav shmei gazlan* actually means in its primary sense — which turns out to be different from the boat case entirely. The teaching refers literally to a *gazlan* who has stolen from the general public: someone who overcharged customers systematically, or misappropriated communal resources — water from a shared well, for instance. In such a case, he is a *gazlan shel rabim* in a technical sense: he cannot make restitution, *shelo nitan lehishavon*, because the sheer number of victims makes it impossible to identify and repay each person individually. This is the primary meaning of Rabbi Hiyya's dictum. Its application to the boat case by the Sages of Nehardea is a secondary usage, drawing on the same conceptual structure — that where there is no identifiable owner to whom one owes restitution, the formal category of *gazlan* does not attach in the ordinary sense.

---

---

# Bava Batra 36

## Chazaka Overview

### Opening

We pick up in the top third of 35b, having worked through a series of cases in which one party confronted another with the challenge "what are you doing on my land?" and received in reply the claim "I have been here three years." That extended discussion gave us the opportunity to explore a wide range of conceptual *halachic* issues surrounding the concept of *chazaka*. We now move on to the next phrase of the *mishnah*, working our way through the text now that much of the groundwork has been laid.

### Three Years Day-by-Day

The *mishnah* states: *chazakatan shalosh shanim yom l'yom* — *chazaka* is established by three years of possession from day to day, and applies to something used on an ongoing basis. The best example is a house. The *gemara* has also discussed an irrigated field, and earlier sugyot addressed questions of daytime and nighttime — whether one must testify to nighttime use, and whether one must literally be present every single day.

## Basket of Fruit

### Rav Abba Immediate

Rav Abba states: *idari lei ihu gufei tana d'peirei la'altar havei chazaka* — if the original owner was himself witnessed carrying a basket of fruit from the land alongside the possessor, this creates an immediate presumption of *chazaka* without any requirement of three years. The logic is straightforward: what conceivable reason would I have for helping someone haul a basket of fruit from a field unless he had purchased it from me? Witnesses to such behavior constitute immediate evidence of a completed sale.

### Rav Zevid Exception

Rav Zevid qualifies this: *im ta'an v'amar l'peiros horaditiv* — if the original owner claims that he brought the possessor onto the land specifically for the fruit, meaning the possessor was a sharecropper and not a buyer, then the act of carrying the basket no longer undermines the owner's claim. The owner is believed to say the possessor had rights to the fruit under a sharecropping arrangement without ever having purchased the land. Naturally, this defense requires that the owner advance it from the outset, since reversing course after first denying all knowledge of the possessor's presence would create a problem of *to'en v'chozer v'to'en*.

### Three-Year Cutoff

The *gemara* then establishes: *v'hani milei b'tokh shalosh, aval achar shalosh lo* — the sharecropper defense is available only within the first three years of possession. After three years have elapsed, the owner is no longer believed to say the possessor was merely a sharecropper. The reason is clear: if the sharecropper defense remained available indefinitely, it would hollow out the entire institution of *chazaka*. No matter how many years of uncontested possession a claimant could demonstrate, the original owner could always explain it away as a sharecropping arrangement. Therefore the *halacha* forecloses that defense once three years have passed.

### Mechah Protection

This immediately raises the next question: if the owner is not believed after three years to claim sharecropping, what can a genuine landowner who has legitimately placed a sharecropper on his land do to protect his own interests?

## Mechah Institution

### Sharecropper Problem

Rav Ashi poses the question directly to Rav Kahana: *i l'peira nachit, mai havei lei l'me'evad?* — if the owner genuinely brought someone onto the land only for the fruit, what was he supposed to do? How was he to protect himself?

### Mechah Distinction

The *gemara* answers that the owner can and must make a *mecha'ah*, a formal public protest — but one of a different character than the ordinary *mecha'ah*. The ordinary *mecha'ah* consists of appearing before two witnesses and declaring that the possessor is a *gazlan*, occupying the land without any permission. That formulation is clearly inapplicable to a sharecropper. Instead, the owner must appear before two witnesses and announce: be aware that this person is on my land as a sharecropper, not as a legitimate owner. If the possessor is in fact the legitimate owner, he will hear of this announcement and will know to guard his *shtar* carefully — just as a buyer would protect his deed in response to any *mecha'ah* calling him a thief.

### Mechah Limits

This is a significant *chiddush*: it reveals that *mecha'ah* is not an institution reserved for cases of illegitimate occupation. Any time land is legitimately rented or sharecropped — which must have been exceedingly common — the owner had to make regular *mecha'ot* to protect his interests and prevent the possessor from acquiring a *chazaka* claim. One observes, however, that this places the genuine buyer in a more precarious position. When the *mecha'ah* is of the ordinary kind, calling the possessor a thief, word travels quickly. But an announcement that someone is "merely a sharecropper" does not carry the same social urgency — it is not the kind of thing people necessarily gossip about. This means a legitimate buyer must now keep his ears open not only for a *mecha'ah* declaring him a *gazlan*, but also for a *mecha'ah* declaring him a sharecropper or a renter. Any kind of ruling here will favor one side at the expense of the other, which is why all the more so people must be extremely careful with their *shtaros*.

### Mashkanta Problem

The *gemara* reinforces this conclusion with a compelling case: *hanei mashkanta desura* — the institution of the *mashkanta desura*. In this arrangement, Charlie borrows ten thousand dollars from the lender and transfers his field to the lender for, say, ten years. The lender holds the field, harvests the produce, and applies that produce toward the debt; at the end of ten years, the debt is discharged and the field returns to Charlie. The contract explicitly states: *bemishlam shanya ilein tipok ara bela chaspa* — at the end of these years, the land goes out without payment, meaning the debt is fully settled. This arrangement is structured to avoid a straightforward *ribbit* problem by recasting what happens as a conditional purchase of ten years of fruit rather than an interest-bearing loan.

Now: in a *mashkanta desura*, who holds the document? The lender, because he needs to prove that Charlie owes him money. Charlie has no copy. So if the lender after three years simply chooses to conceal the *shtar* and claim he purchased the field outright, who is going to stop him? He has three years of uncontested possession, no one else holds documentation of the arrangement. This is a gaping avenue for abuse.

### Mechah Conclusion

*Ela ibayei lei lemichuyei* — the answer is that Charlie must make a *mecha'ah*, announcing that the lender is on his land pursuant to a *mashkanta* arrangement and not as a genuine owner. This both protects Charlie and ensures that the lender, if he is acting legitimately, is on notice to preserve his documentation. *Hacha nami ibayei lei lemichuyei* — the same principle applies to the sharecropping case. The possibility of a *mecha'ah* that identifies legitimate use arrangements is what makes the entire rabbinic institution of *mashkanta desura* viable in the first place. Without it, no creditor would be safe from a lender simply claiming ownership after three years.

## Non-Jew Chain

### Non-Jew Blocks

Rav Yehuda rules: *Yisrael haba machmat akum harei hu ke'akum* — a Jew whose chain of title runs through a non-Jew stands in the same position as the non-Jew himself. If Charlie says he bought the field from Christopher, who purchased it from the original Jewish owner, Charlie's *chazaka* claim is only as strong as Christopher's would have been.

### Non-Jew Exception

*Ma akum ein lo chazaka ella beshtar* — a non-Jew cannot acquire land through *chazaka*; he can prove ownership only by producing a *shtar*. *Af Yisrael haba machmat akum ein lo chazaka ella beshtar* — similarly, a Jew who traces his title through a non-Jew cannot rely on *chazaka* and must produce documentary evidence. The reason a non-Jew cannot establish *chazaka* is rooted in the historical reality of power imbalances: non-Jews were frequently in a position of dominance, capable of seizing fields from Jewish owners who dared not protest. The silence of the Jewish owner cannot be taken as *mechila* or acquiescence when the realistic alternative was fear. Since there is a ready explanation for the owner's silence other than acceptance of the transfer, the three years of uncontested possession prove nothing. Charlie, by basing his claim on Christopher's tenure, is building on an unsubstantiated foundation — *chazaka she'eina mitzad ta'ana* — a *chazaka* that lacks a valid underlying claim.

### Rav Yosef Query

Rav Yosef challenges: *lididi amar li akum de-minach zavnah* — what if Charlie says the non-Jew told him directly that he had purchased the field from the original owner? Should that testimony not be sufficient? The *gemara* immediately presses back: *mi ika midi d'ilu akum amar lo meheman, ve'ilu amar Yisrael mishmeih d'akum meheman?* Is there anything where had the non-Jew himself made the claim he would not have been believed, yet a Jew repeating that same claim on the non-Jew's behalf is believed? Charlie's report of what Christopher said does not transform Christopher's legally insufficient claim into a valid one.

### Rava Resolution

Rava clarifies: *ei amar Yisrael kamei didi zavnah minach v'zavnah nihali* — if Charlie says he has direct knowledge that the non-Jew acquired the field legitimately from the original owner — either because he himself witnessed the transaction or because he saw the *shtar* — then *meheman*, he is believed. The key is direct, personal knowledge of the non-Jew's legitimate acquisition, not merely repeating the non-Jew's assertion.

### Miggo Principle

The *gemara* grounds this in a *miggo* argument: *migo d'ei ba'ei amar lei ana zevintah minach* — since Charlie could have simply claimed that he himself purchased the field directly from the original owner, and that claim would have been believed, his alternative claim that he purchased it from the non-Jew who legitimately acquired it from the original owner is equally credible. We believe him not only that he bought from the non-Jew but — given his testimony of direct knowledge of the non-Jew's acquisition — that the non-Jew was a genuine owner.

## Non-Chazaka Cases

### Bold Claim

Rav Yehuda states: *hai man d'nakit migla v'tuvila v'amar eizil egzeiyeh l'dikla d'planya d'zavnteih mineih* — if someone picks up a scythe and a basket and announces that he is going to go harvest dates from a specific palm tree because he purchased it, he is immediately believed. *Lo chatzif inish l'migzar dikla d'lav dileih* — people are not brazen enough to go harvest a palm tree that is not theirs. The act has not yet occurred, so the fruit is still *karka* and not *metaltelin*, but the bold, public declaration of intent constitutes evidence equivalent to a *chazaka*, because no one would make such a claim falsely.

### Buffer Zone

Rav Yehuda also rules: *hai man d'achzik migudi d'arudai l'var lo havei chazaka* — possession of produce from the *gudi d'arudai*, the narrow strip of land outside the fence of a field where seeds fall and animals graze, does not constitute *chazaka*. The reason: *kol d'zarna nami avuda achli lei* — the owner reasons that whatever sprouts in that buffer strip will be eaten by animals regardless. He has no realistic expectation of harvesting that produce himself, so he has no motivation to protest when someone else takes it. The absence of protest therefore proves nothing about ownership.

### Orlah Produce

Rav Yehuda further rules: *achal orla eina chazaka* — eating *orla* fruit does not constitute *chazaka*. Since the owner is forbidden from eating it anyway, he has no reason to protest another's consumption. There is an alternative *girsa* that reads *havei chazaka*, but the accepted version holds it is not. This means that a year in which all the produce is *orla* does not count toward the three-year *chazaka* period.

### Shevi'it Kilayim

A *braita* extends and confirms: *achal orla, shevi'it, v'kilayim — eina chazaka*. Eating *orla* and *kilayim* does not count because the owner has no personal interest in those fruits in any case, and *shevi'it* produce does not count because all have rights to it — the owner cannot meaningfully protest another's access to what is publicly available.

### Sachis Fodder

Rav Yosef rules: *achal shachas lo havei chazaka* — harvesting *shachas*, which is fodder produced by cutting grain before it reaches full growth and then allowing it to regrow, does not constitute *chazaka*. The reasoning: a genuine owner would wait for the crop to reach full maturity and harvest it at its peak value. Someone who harvests only the *shachas* and takes nothing more reveals furtive behavior — he is sneaking in to take what he can quickly, behavior more consistent with a thief than an owner. One might also note that if the person harvested only the *shachas* and the crop nonetheless regrew fully, someone else must have harvested the full growth, which would directly challenge any ownership claim.

### Sachis Exception

Rava qualifies: *ve-i b'tzurei Mechuza ka-amar, havei chazaka* — if this ruling was stated with reference to the valleys of Mechuza, where cultivating fodder was the normal agricultural practice, then harvesting *shachas* does count as *chazaka*, since doing so is consistent with how a genuine owner of such land would behave.

### Tafticha Barren

Rav Nachman rules: *tafticha lo havei chazaka* — possession of *tafticha*, cracked and sun-baked land, does not constitute *chazaka*. Either because the land is so unproductive that virtually nothing grows there, giving the owner no motivation to protest someone else's negligible use of it — or because the cracked surface requires no plowing before planting, so the process of working it is not the normal ongoing agricultural activity that would signal ownership.

### No-Profit Land

Similarly: *apei kura v'ayeil kura lo havei chazaka* — land so infertile that one recovers exactly as much grain as one planted, yielding zero profit, does not support a *chazaka* claim. The owner can credibly say he had no reason to protest because he had no real interest in what the possessor was doing on land of such negligible productivity. One might ask: what if the land was productive in principle but a bad harvest — due to blight, drought, or locusts — happened to yield only a break-even result that year? The *gemara* seems to be speaking specifically about land whose intrinsic quality makes it perpetually unprofitable — what might be called hardscrabble land — as opposed to a temporary circumstantial failure of yield.

## Power Asymmetry

### Resh Galuta

The *gemara* rules: *hanei de-vei reish galuta* — with respect to land involving the household of the *reish galuta* (the exilarch), different rules apply.

### Fear Prevents

*Lo machazikinan behu* — if the *reish galuta*'s household has been occupying one's land, no *chazaka* is established in their favor, because the Jewish minority population might well have been afraid to protest an occupation by those in political power. The absence of *mecha'ah* therefore does not constitute acquiescence.

### Reciprocal

The rule is symmetrical: *ve-lo machazikinan behu* — if Jews have been occupying land belonging to the *reish galuta*'s household, no *chazaka* is established in their favor either.

### Force Override

The Rashbam explains: those in power have no need to make a formal *mecha'ah* — they can simply reclaim by force at any time. Their silence is therefore not evidence of consent. The principle is thus not specifically about Jews versus non-Jews but about power asymmetry in general: whoever is in a position to seize land without legal recourse creates a situation in which neither their occupation of another's land nor another's occupation of their land can produce a valid *chazaka*.

## Animals & Movables

### Animate Property

The *mishnah* includes slaves among the categories for which *chazaka* operates. Unlike ordinary *metaltelin* — where mere physical possession is itself evidence of ownership — slaves are not inanimate objects whose presence in one's domain conclusively proves title. Their status, as the *gemara* will explain, is more complex.

### Roaming Flocks

The *gemara* invokes Reish Lakish's ruling: *ha-godrot ein lahem chazaka* — flocks have no *chazaka*. The word *godrot* refers to *gidrot tzon*, flocks of sheep. By this Reish Lakish does not mean there is no three-year *chazaka*, but rather that immediate physical possession does not constitute *chazaka* the way it does for ordinary *metaltelin*. The reason is that flocks move on their own volition: a lamb wandering into one's field or following someone down the street does not thereby become that person's property. Since animals move independently, the fact that one is currently holding an animal proves nothing about how it came to be there.

### Three Years Needed

Rava clarifies: *ein lahem chazaka le'altar, aval yesh lahem chazaka le'achar gimmel shanim* — immediate possession does not establish ownership, but three years of uncontested possession does. After three years, the silence of the original owner becomes meaningful evidence. Strikingly, this places slaves and flocks in the same legal category as land — not for the formal reason that slaves are *karka*, but because they are living things that move on their own volition, making their physical presence in someone's domain inconclusive as immediate proof of ownership.

### Volition Logic

For slaves, the three-year framework fits well in a second respect as well: slaves are typically sold with a *shtar*, just as land is, and one can apply the same logic of "if you really bought this slave, produce your deed; after three years your inability to do so no longer defeats your claim." For flocks, however, there would normally be no *shtar* accompanying a sale of sheep, which makes the three-year standard feel somewhat less intuitively grounded than it does for land or slaves. Nonetheless, the principle that things moving on their own volition require this extended period appears to operate as a categorical rule. It is worth noting that this creates an apparent gap: between immediate possession — which proves nothing — and three years — which proves ownership. There does not appear to be an intermediate position.

### Infant Exception

Rava adds: *im haya katan mutal ba'arisa, yesh lo chazaka le'altar* — if the slave in question is an infant lying in a cradle, then immediate possession does establish ownership. The *gemara* asks: is this not obvious? An infant in a cradle cannot possibly have walked there on its own — so the concern about independent movement simply does not apply.

### Mother Logic

The *gemara* pushes back: one might have thought we should be concerned that the infant was brought there by its mother, who then left it temporarily — perhaps she stepped away on an errand and the possessor is now falsely claiming ownership. The *gemara* therefore teaches: *ima lo minashya breih* — a mother does not forget her child. A slave mother would not abandon her infant with a stranger, particularly in the context of a slave society where separation from one's child would be a devastating and permanent loss. Therefore, if an infant slave is found in someone's possession, it could not have arrived through the mother's voluntary temporary deposit, and immediate possession proves acquisition.

## Goats Case

### Seize for Claim

The *gemara* presents a practical case from Nehardea. Some goats belonging to Charlie entered a field and ate *chushla* — husk barley — belonging to the field's owner. The owner (the plaintiff) now needs to recover compensation. The difficulty is evidentiary: the plaintiff claims the goats ate a thousand dollars' worth of grain, while Charlie will insist the amount was trivial. Under the rule of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya*, the burden of proof lies on the claimant. To improve his position, the plaintiff seizes Charlie's goats. Now the question becomes how much the plaintiff can claim while holding them.

### Value Limit

The father of Shmuel rules: *yelchu l'itun ad k'dai demeihen* — the plaintiff is believed in his damage claim up to the full value of the goats themselves.

### Miggo Applied

The basis is *miggo*: *migo d'ei ba'ei amar lekuchim heim b'yadi* — since the plaintiff could simply have said "I bought these goats from Charlie," and thereby kept them entirely, he is also believed to say their full value was consumed in damages. The *miggo* supports his claim up to the threshold of the strongest claim he could have made — namely, that the goats are simply his.

### Flocks Paradox

The *gemara* raises an apparent contradiction: did not Reish Lakish rule that flocks have no *chazaka*? If that is so, how does the plaintiff's seizure of the goats give him any standing to claim ownership — even fictively for purposes of a *miggo*?

### Shepherd Supervision

The *gemara* resolves: *shani izzei de'masrinan leroya* — goats are different from sheep because they are handed over to a dedicated shepherd. Goats, apparently, are prone to wandering or running off, and therefore their owners maintain constant active supervision through a shepherd who is specifically in charge of them at all times. Unlike sheep, which might be left to roam somewhat more freely, goats are under a tighter supervisory regime, making their presence in someone's domain more probative of ownership. Accordingly, when someone is holding goats, the logic of independent-volition movement applies with less force.

### Supervision Gaps

The *gemara* qualifies: *v'ika tzipra u'panya* — but there are gaps in the morning and evening when the goats are not under continuous supervision. In the morning, the owner releases them and they make their way out to where the shepherd is waiting in the field, and in the evening the shepherd releases them and they find their way back to their owner independently. During these periods they are unsupervised.

The *gemara* responds that the case concerns Nehardea, where *kayla shechicha* — nomads or bandits were prevalent — and therefore the goats would be handed over directly from owner to shepherd and back again, *mi'yada l'yada meshallmi*, without any gap in supervision. This underscores the broader principle that *chazaka* for animate property is not determined by rigid categories but by the actual circumstances of supervision and movement — exactly as with the infant slave, whose physical immobility places it firmly in the category of property for which immediate possession is conclusive.

## Partial-Year Rules

### Seasonal Cycles

We now turn to the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. The cases we have been discussing involved land used year-round — irrigated fields and homes. But a *sde habaal*, a rain-watered field, follows seasonal agricultural cycles. For such a field, Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva both hold that one need not demonstrate three complete consecutive twelve-month years, but something representative of three years: a full middle year plus partial usage at the end of the first year and the beginning of the third.

### Yishmael Approach

Rabbi Yishmael requires three months at the end of year one, a full middle year, and three months at the beginning of year three.

### Akiva Approach

Rabbi Akiva requires only one month at the end of year one, a full middle year, and one month at the beginning of year three. The *gemara* will clarify what drives this difference.

### Multiple Harvests

The *mishnah* further provides that in certain cases — where a field has multiple distinct harvest cycles within a single year, such as grapes, dates, and figs — three separate harvests within a single calendar year can constitute a three-year *chazaka*, since each harvest represents a distinct cycle of use.

### Nir Debate

One might have thought the difference between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva — three months versus one month for the partial years — hinges on the question of *nir*, plowing or tilling. *Rabbi Yishmael savar nir lo havei chazaka* — Rabbi Yishmael holds plowing alone does not count, so he requires three months to ensure some actual harvest. *Rabbi Akiva savar nir havei chazaka* — Rabbi Akiva holds plowing does count, so one month suffices. But the *gemara* rejects this: if tilling alone were sufficient for Rabbi Akiva, then one month would be far more than necessary — one could tile in a single day. *Ela dechulei alma nir lo havei chazaka* — rather, all agree that plowing alone does not constitute *chazaka*. The difference between them is rather about the minimum harvest required: Rabbi Yishmael requires substantial produce demanding a full three-month growing cycle, while Rabbi Akiva accepts even minimal produce attainable within a single month — perhaps even the kind of *shachas*-level fodder that can be cut quickly.

## Nir Chazaka

### Tannaitic View

The *gemara* now takes up the *nir* question directly. A *braita* states: *nir einu chazaka* — plowing is not *chazaka*. Then immediately: *v'yesh omrim harei zeh chazaka* — and some say it is.

### Pattern Rule

The *braita*'s illustration of when it is *not* *chazaka* is: *neira shana u'zra'ah shtayim* — one tilled for one year and planted for two, or *neira shtayim u'zra'ah shana* — tilled for two years and planted for one. None of these combinations constitute *chazaka*.

### Acha Position

Rav Chisda identifies the *yesh omrim* as Rabbi Acha. According to Tosafot, even Rabbi Acha would not recognize two consecutive years of tilling alone as *chazaka*. What Rabbi Acha does recognize is a pattern such as: till year one, plant year two, till year three. In that context, the years of tilling are set within a framework of genuine agricultural ownership — tilling and planting in alternating years is exactly what a real owner does — and the tilling years are thereby given meaning by the planting year that contextualizes them. This is the *chiddush* of Rabbi Acha: even a single year of actual planting, constituting one-third of the three-year period, provides enough of an ownership context to make the tilling years count.

### Majority View

The *chachamim* disagree. One year of planting is insufficient provocation to compel the original owner to protest the other years of tilling. The *chazaka* must rest on something more substantial than that.

### Authority List

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds to an invocation of "all the *gedolei hador*" — the great scholars of the generation — in favor of *nir* constituting *chazaka*, by countering with his own list of authorities: *ha Rav u-Shmuel be-Vavel, u-Rabbi Yishmael v'Rabbi Akiva be-Eretz Yisrael* — Rav and Shmuel in Babylonia, and Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva in the Land of Israel — all hold that *nir* does not work. The invocation of names is not itself an argument; what matters is who can marshal the stronger analysis.

### Mishnah Proof

That Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva hold *nir* insufficient is demonstrated from the *mishnah* itself. Both require at minimum one month or three months for the partial years flanking the full middle year. If tilling alone were sufficient, neither would need any minimum time at all — a single day of plowing would qualify. The fact that they require a month or three months demonstrates they demand an actual harvest, and therefore both implicitly reject *nir* as a standalone basis for *chazaka*.

### Rav Position

Rav Yehuda citing Rav states: the one-month and three-month approaches belong to Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, but *aval Chachamim omrim, chazaka gimmel shanim mi-yom le-yom* — the *chachamim* require three full years from day to day. The phrase *mi-yom le-yom* serves to exclude *nir*: if three full years are required and tilling counted, then the possessor could spend three years doing nothing but intermittent plowing. But no one would imagine the requirement is to plow continuously for three years — that is not how anyone farms. Three full years must therefore mean three years of genuine agricultural use — planting and harvesting — not merely overturning soil.

### Shmuel Position

Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel similarly identifies the partial-year approaches as belonging to Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. But Shmuel frames the *chachamim*'s standard differently: *ad she-yigdor shalosh gedirot, v'yivtzor gimmel betzirot, v'yimsok gimmel mesikot* — one must complete three full date harvests, three full grape harvests, or three full olive harvests. The partial harvest of a month or three months at the flanking years is not sufficient; three genuinely complete harvest cycles are required. Critically, Shmuel's formulation counts *harvests*, not *calendar years*.

### Young Palm

What is the practical difference between Rav and Shmuel? Rav says three full calendar years; Shmuel says three full harvests. The *gemara* identifies the case where this matters: *dekel na'ara* — a young palm tree that can yield multiple harvests within a single calendar year. According to Shmuel, three full harvests from such a tree, even if all obtained within less than three calendar years, would constitute *chazaka*. According to Rav, three complete calendar years are always required regardless of harvest frequency.

### Mechanics TBD

At this point the question of the precise mechanics of *chazaka* — whether it requires three full calendar years as Rav holds, or three full harvests as Shmuel holds — remains open for further analysis. One thing is clear: both Rav and Shmuel, together with Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, all agree that *nir* alone is insufficient. The discussion of what exactly constitutes the required three-year measure, and how the *chachamim*'s standard operates in practice, will continue in the next session.

# Bava Batra 37

## Chazakah: Years vs. Harv…

### Opening & Previous Summa…

We pick up at the bottom of 36b, having just concluded a discussion about whether *nir* — upturning and tilling the soil — constitutes a valid *chazakah*. More significantly, the *Gemara* there established that the positions of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva in the *Mishnah* — permitting partial years at the beginning and end of the three-year period — represent only those two views. Rav and Shmuel clarified that the *Chachamim* require three full calendar years, while Shmuel adds that three full harvests may suffice, which could in principle be achieved in less than three years, provided the harvests themselves are complete.

### Rashbam's Two Models

Before moving forward, it is worth examining one important passage in the Rashbam that illuminates the conceptual stakes of this dispute. Approximately twenty lines down in the narrow-column commentary, in the entry beginning with the word *shanim*, the Rashbam writes: *zu divrei Rabbi Yishmael ve-Rabbi Akiva*, that this refers to the positions of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva — for whom the *chazakah* of a field is three years but not necessarily day-for-day, being eighteen months according to Rabbi Yishmael and fourteen according to Rabbi Akiva. But the *Chachamim*, in the entry beginning with *chachamim*, require three full years in every matter, measured day-for-day.

The Rashbam then connects this dispute to the two foundational models of *chazakah* introduced at the opening of the *perek*. Recall that one model treats *chazakah* as a status-creating mechanism: doing something three times establishes a presumptive identity or position, analogous to the *shor mu'ad*. On this view, it is the act of doing something three times — three harvests — that generates the legal status, and whether these span full calendar years is secondary. The second model, by contrast, grounds *chazakah* in the practical reality of lost documents: after three years, one has a legitimate claim that one's deed of ownership has been lost or discarded, because a person is not expected to safeguard a *shtar* indefinitely. On this view, the operative measure is calendar time, since the question is how long a person remains vigilant about preserving documents — and that is a function of years, not harvests.

The Rashbam thus proposes a tidy correspondence: those who measure *chazakah* by acts (three harvests, even partial years) align with the status-creation model, while those who require three full calendar years align with the lost-document model. The two conceptual approaches map onto two distinct ways of measuring time.

### Nimukei Yosef's Critique

The Nimukei Yosef pushes back against this framework. He argues that throughout the *Gemara*, both considerations have been operating together and are not independent variables.
