It is not mere calendar time that renders a person less vigilant about preserving a *shtar*; what produces that relaxation is the combination of one's own visible, owner-like conduct over an extended period together with the original owner's unbroken silence in the face of that conduct. The absence of protest is itself evidence that the claim will not be pursued, and that is what gradually diminishes one's motivation to safeguard the deed.

On this reading, the lost-document rationale does not reduce to a fixed quantity of calendar time. It is intertwined with the owner's silence and with the character of one's acts — acts that should have provoked a response but did not. The two conceptual models are therefore not cleanly separable, and the Rashbam's one-to-one correspondence between models and measurement standards does not hold. Whether *chazakah* is measured in harvests or in years is not simply a function of which underlying theory one adopts; it also turns on the nature of the possessor's conduct and the owner's reaction to it.

---

## Thirty Trees Example

### Thirty Trees Case

With this background in place, the *Gemara* on 37a introduces a teaching of Abaye. The *Gemara* had just reviewed Rabbi Yishmael's position that in the case of an orchard, three different harvests within a single year — figs, grapes, and olives, for instance — can each count as one of the three required acts, so that *chazakah* is achieved within a single calendar year. *Amar Abaye*, says Abaye: *miderabbi Yishmael nishma lerabanan* — from Rabbi Yishmael's teaching we can derive something relevant even according to the *Rabbanan*, who reject his leniency and insist on three full years.

The case is as follows: thirty trees are planted across a field at the proper density of ten trees per *beit se'ah* — a plot of fifty by fifty cubits. This ratio is recognized as the standard, non-overcrowded distribution for an orchard. Each year for three consecutive years, the possessor harvests ten of the thirty trees, rotating through different groups of ten, so that over three years all thirty are harvested — but no single year sees a harvest of all of them.

The *Gemara* rules: *harei zo chazakah* — this constitutes a valid *chazakah*. How does Rabbi Yishmael's teaching support this? *Lav mi amar Rabbi Yishmael chad peira havei chazakah l'chulhu peiri* — did not Rabbi Yishmael say that harvesting one type of fruit counts as a *chazakah* for all the fruit of the field? In Rabbi Yishmael's case, the grapes are planted only in one portion of the field, the olives in another, and the figs in a third; yet harvesting the grapes alone represents a *chazakah* for the entire orchard. So too here: even though we do not follow Rabbi Yishmael's leniency regarding the number of years required, we accept his underlying premise that harvesting from a portion of the trees — when they are properly interspersed throughout the field — constitutes a *chazakah* representing the entirety. *Hanei havei chazakah lahanei v'hanei havei chazakah lahanei* — what is done to some counts for the others, and vice versa.

### When Fruits Unavailable

The *Gemara* immediately qualifies this ruling. *V'hanei mili heicha d'lo afiki* — this applies only where the other trees have not yet produced their fruit. The logic is that when the ten trees being harvested are the only ones currently bearing fruit, the possessor's selective harvesting is not a conscious decision to ignore the rest; it simply reflects what is available. *Aval afiki v'lo achlinhu lo havei chazakah* — but if the other trees have already produced their fruit and the possessor is not harvesting them, he is effectively abandoning them, and that abandonment undermines the *chazakah*. The thirty-tree principle functions only when each year's harvest corresponds to what is naturally available that season, mirroring the logic of Rabbi Yishmael's case where each harvest type is in season at its own time.

### Trees Interspersed

The *Gemara* adds a second condition: *vehu debazei bizuyei* — the trees must be genuinely interspersed and scattered across the entire field. The term *bizuyei*, which the Rashbam explains as *lashon beziah*, connoting splitting or dispersal, requires that the ten trees harvested each year be distributed throughout the whole plot rather than clustered in their own section.

The reason is intuitive. If the thirty trees are arranged in three separate clusters — ten in the northern third, ten in the middle, ten in the southern third — then harvesting the northern cluster is a *chazakah* only on that portion of the field. It demonstrates no connection to the rest. But if trees of different ripening cycles are intermingled across the entire area, so that harvesting any ten of them requires ranging across the whole field, then that act of harvesting visibly represents dominion over the entire plot.

The Rashbam notes, somewhat reluctantly, that this interspersed model presupposes that vines, olive trees, and figs are planted among one another throughout the same field — an arrangement that raises concerns of *kilayim* and is in any case highly inefficient from a practical farming standpoint. The *Gemara* is nonetheless committed to this condition, because without it the principle collapses: a harvest confined to one section of a field cannot establish *chazakah* over the rest.

This condition also connects directly to the broader question of when a *chazakah* on trees extends to the land beneath and around them. If the trees are distributed at the proper density across a defined area, that ratio creates what might be called an orchard identity — the land and the trees form an integrated unit, and working the trees represents dominion over the associated land. But if trees are scattered sparsely across a very large space, or densely packed into a small one, the organic connection between tree and land is severed, and the *chazakah* on the trees does not carry over to the ground.

---

## Trees & Land Split

### Rav Zevid Position

The *Gemara* now presents the following scenario. A plot of land with trees — originally owned by a single person — has been in the possession of two different individuals simultaneously for three years: one person, call him David, has been harvesting the fruit of the trees, while another, call her Jenna, has been working the land itself, perhaps cultivating a vegetable garden or otherwise making use of the soil. Each has maintained this conduct for the full three-year period. What does each one's *chazakah* establish?

*Amar Rav Zevid: zeh kanah ilanot v'zeh kanah karka* — David has acquired the trees, and Jenna has acquired the land. Before unpacking the ruling, it is worth noting a significant interpretive dispute between the Rashbam and Tosafot about the very nature of this case. The Rashbam reads it not as a *chazakah* scenario at all but as a straightforward sale or gift: the original owner explicitly gave David the trees and Jenna the land, each performed an act of acquisition, and the question is simply what each transaction included. Tosafot, by contrast, reads the case as a genuine *chazakah* dispute — David and Jenna each maintained possession for three years and now claim ownership — and takes the word *kanah* to mean that each one's *chazakah* establishes the respective ownership. The legal question, however, ultimately converges for both readings: when ownership of an orchard is split between a person who takes the trees and a person who takes the land, what does each party actually receive?

Rav Zevid's position, read through Tosafot's lens, is that the two *chazakot* are entirely severable. David's three years of harvesting the trees establishes ownership of the trees and nothing more — no ownership of the land beneath or around them. Jenna's three years of working the land establishes ownership of the land, with no claim to the trees above it. The two estates are fully separated.

*Matkif lah Rav Pappa* — Rav Pappa challenges this conclusion. *Im ken ein lo lebaal ilanot bakarka klum* — if you are saying that the tree-owner has absolutely no ownership interest in the land, then *leima leh baal karka lebaal ilanot: akor ilnach shekol vezil* — Jenna could simply tell David: uproot your trees, take them, and leave. This is a *reductio ad absurdum*. The Rashbam and Tosafot agree that Rav Pappa is not necessarily claiming that Jenna could evict David from the moment the ruling is made; rather, he is saying that if David has no land rights whatsoever, then as soon as his trees died or were cut down, he would have no right to replant them — he would be left with nothing. This outcome strikes Rav Pappa as untenable: any meaningful ownership of trees must carry with it some ownership of the land that sustains them.

### Rav Pappa Challenge

*Ela amar Rav Pappa: zeh kanah ilanot v'chatzi karka, v'zeh kanah chatzi karka* — rather, says Rav Pappa, David has acquired the trees together with half the plot of land, while Jenna has acquired only the other half. Once we recognize that David's *chazakah* on the trees represents some claim to the land, and Jenna's *chazakah* encompasses the entire plot, the two competing claims on the land are treated as equal, yielding a half-and-half division.

The Rashbam, noting that this seems to swing sharply in the opposite direction, suggests that the figure of half is *lav davka* — not to be taken with strict literalism. David does not necessarily own exactly half of the full acreage; he owns the immediate area beneath and around the trees that is necessary for their survival. The word "half" may be an approximation or a way of saying that his claim on the land is substantial and cannot be reduced to zero, rather than a precise arithmetical division.

### One vs. Two Buyers

Having established the competing positions of Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa in the two-buyer scenario, the *Gemara* now introduces the classic single-seller framework to illuminate why two buyers operates differently. The relevant principles are *mocher b'ayin yafah hu mocher* — a seller sells with a generous eye, the position of Rabbi Akiva — and *mocher b'ayin ra'ah hu mocher* — a seller sells with a narrow, self-interested eye, the position of the *Chachamim*.

These principles come into play when the terms of a sale are ambiguous. If I sell Jenna my land but retain the trees, how much land do I keep for myself around those trees? If I sell David my trees but retain the land, does David receive any of the land that underlies or surrounds the trees? These questions are shaped by whether we presume I sold generously or held back as much as I could for myself.

What makes the two-buyer case categorically different is that when I have fully divested myself of the entire property — giving the trees to one person and the land to another — there is no retained self-interest to invoke. The question is no longer how much I held back for myself; it is how I divided what I gave away entirely. In that setting, the *ein yafah* and *ein ra'ah* framework, which presupposes a seller acting in his own interest versus another's, becomes conceptually inapplicable. The analysis shifts to a different set of interpretive assumptions about how an equal partition between two recipients should be understood, which is why the *Gemara* treats the two-buyer case as governed by distinct principles from the outset.

---

## Seller Keeps Trees

### Trees Retained Case

The *Gemara* now turns to the scenario of a single seller and a single buyer, beginning with the case of *machar karka v'shayar ilanot* — the seller sells the land but retains the trees for himself. The *Gemara* states that this is *pishita* — obvious: *yesh lo karka*, the seller retains possession of some land that goes along with those trees. The Rashbam clarifies that this does not mean he retains the entire plot; he retains the land immediately around and beneath the trees that is necessary for their continued existence. Even if he retained only one or two trees while selling the land, since he is the original owner who has explicitly held back the trees, we presume that a reasonable amount of adjacent land is included in that retention.

### Trees vs. Wells

What makes this case obvious, and why does it differ from the classic case of the well? The *Gemara* explains: *ואפילו l'Rabbi Akiva d'amar mocher b'ayin yafah hu mocher* — even according to Rabbi Akiva, who ordinarily presumes that a seller acts generously and does not hold back more than he explicitly specified. The paradigmatic case for Rabbi Akiva's principle involves a well. If I sell my entire plot to Jenna but retain ownership of the well, and then I wish to walk to my well, Jenna can say: I did not sell you a path, go work that out for yourself. According to Rabbi Akiva, by selling with a generous eye I am assumed to have given Jenna everything right up to the edge of the well, retaining no access easement for myself.

Why does this same reasoning not strip away the land around the retained trees? The *Gemara* answers: *hani mili gabei bor v'dos d'lo machshi b'ara* — this applies specifically to a well or cistern, because a well does not damage or impair the surrounding land. Jenna can plant right up to the edge of the well; the soil is fully usable. Therefore, to grant myself any space around the well would genuinely encroach on what Jenna is entitled to, and since I am selling generously I give her every usable inch.

*Aval ilanos d'kamachshi b'ara* — but trees are different, because the roots of a tree do damage and impair the adjacent land. The soil immediately surrounding a tree, where the roots spread, is not fully available for Jenna's cultivation in any case. There are therefore two reasons why it is assumed that the seller retained the land around his trees: first, that land is not genuinely useful to Jenna since the roots impair it; and second, to give Jenna title to that land would actually undermine the seller's ownership of the trees themselves, since Jenna could then invoke the laws of *nizkei shecheinim* and demand that the encroaching roots be removed. *Shiyurei shiyer* — therefore, even according to Rabbi Akiva, the seller is presumed to have retained the land immediately around the trees. *D'lav hachi leima leh: uki ilnach vezil* — for otherwise Jenna could tell him: raise up your tree and be gone.

---

## Seller Sells Trees

### Buyer Gets Land?

The *Gemara* now addresses the reverse case: *machar ilanot v'shayar karka lefanav* — I sell David the trees and retain the land for myself. Here the outcome is explicitly a *plugta d'Rabbi Akiva v'Rabbanan* — a direct dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim*.

According to Rabbi Akiva, who rules *mocher b'ayin yafah hu mocher*, the sale of trees is read generously: the buyer receives not only the trees themselves but some portion of the land beneath or around them. This aligns with the principle that a sale is construed to include what is reasonably necessary for the meaningful use of what was sold. The Rashbam and Tosafot note that this interacts with the established rule about two versus three trees — three trees sold together normally carry a plot of land; two do not. Here the discussion may concern two trees, where Rabbi Akiva nevertheless grants at least the land directly beneath them.

According to the *Rabbanan*, who rule *mocher b'ayin ra'ah hu mocher*, the sale is read in maximally self-interested terms: the seller gives only what was explicitly named. David receives the trees and nothing more. The seller retains every inch of land, including the ground immediately beneath the trunks.

### Two Buyers Analysis

The *Gemara* then asks: how does Rav Zevid — who ruled that in the two-buyer case David has only trees and no land — coexist with Rabbi Akiva's principle that a seller of trees is presumed to give some land along with them? And conversely, how does Rav Pappa — who ruled that David gets trees plus half the land in the two-buyer case — coexist with the *Rabbanan*'s principle that a seller gives no land with trees?

The answer, as the *Gemara* spells out, is that the one-buyer and two-buyer scenarios operate under entirely different frameworks. *Hanei milei gabei shenei lekuchot* — the ruling of each Amora applies specifically in the two-buyer context, and for different reasons.

In Rav Zevid's case: when there are two buyers, Jenna can say to David: *ki heichi delididi leit li be'ilanot, ledidach nami leit lach be'ara* — just as I received no trees, you received no land. The division was explicit. The original owner gave one item to each party, and to read any land into David's portion is to take from what was given to Jenna. This is not a question of generosity; it is a question of how a clear bilateral division is to be interpreted, and the symmetry of the split controls.

In Rav Pappa's case: David can respond to Jenna by saying, *k'heichi delidach zavin b'ayin yafah, ledidi nami zavin b'ayin yafah* — just as you received something of lasting, permanent value (land, which endures indefinitely), so too should I be assumed to have received something of lasting value. The Rashbam explains that land, unlike movable property, carries an aura of permanence: what you receive in land, you hold forever, and your children after you. Since the seller gave Jenna something of this permanent character, it is reasonable to assume he also gave David something permanent — which means some land to accompany the trees, lest David's trees eventually die and leave him with nothing.

*Aval hacha mocher b'ayin ra'ah mocher* — but if it is simply me selling trees to David and retaining the land myself, then the *Rabbanan* say I retain the maximum for myself. There is no bilateral division to consider; there is only a seller acting in his own interest.

The critical insight is that the *ein yafah* and *ein ra'ah* framework presupposes a seller with retained self-interest. When a seller fully divests himself of a property by splitting it between two buyers, self-interest is no longer operative, and the question becomes instead how a complete division is to be construed equitably. Rav Zevid reads the explicit split as controlling, producing clean separation. Rav Pappa reads the spirit of a complete divestiture as requiring that each recipient receive something of enduring value, producing a partial land grant to the tree-buyer.

---

## Packed Trees Nursery

### Packed Trees Rule

The *Gemara* now shifts to a different problem. *Amri Naharda'ei: achlan retzupin ein lo chazakah* — the sages of Nahardea ruled that if one harvested trees that were packed in — *retzufin*, densely planted beyond the normal ratio — there is no *chazakah* on the land.

The term *retzufin* here does not mean that the harvests were continuous over consecutive years, though the word could carry that connotation. Rather, as the Rashbam explains, it refers to trees planted at a density exceeding ten per *beit se'ah* — more tightly packed than the recognized standard for a functioning orchard. Why should this density prevent *chazakah* on the land?

The Rashbam's explanation is that such a densely packed arrangement is not a permanent orchard setup. When trees are planted in very close proximity to one another, it reflects a nursery situation: saplings are grown tightly together as a temporary holding arrangement, after which they will be uprooted and replanted at proper spacing elsewhere. Because the trees are understood to be temporary occupants of the land rather than its long-term residents, the relationship between trees and land lacks the organic permanence that normally allows a *chazakah* on trees to imply ownership of the associated ground. A *chazakah* on the trees may still exist — the possessor's harvesting is meaningful with respect to the trees themselves — but it does not carry over to establish *chazakah* on the land beneath and around them, because that land is not understood to be the permanent home of those trees.

Rava challenges this ruling: *ela me'ata, hai mishra d'aspasta — be-mai kani lah?* If tightly packed, nursery-style planting prevents *chazakah* on the land, then what about a plot of alfalfa, which is also typically grown densely and replanted? How could one ever establish *chazakah* on such land? Rava therefore reformulates: *ela amar Rava, achlan retzupin ein lo karka* — harvesting packed trees does not establish *chazakah* on the *land*, but the *chazakah* on the trees themselves remains valid. The Rashbam himself notes that the analogy to alfalfa is imperfect: alfalfa naturally grows that way (*darko* to grow densely), whereas trees planted at excessive density are in an abnormal, temporary state. In any event, the bottom line is that the *chazakah* attaches to the trees but not to the land, because the trees' temporary relationship with the ground severs the inferential link between possessing trees and owning the soil.

### Dense Vineyard Debate

*Amar Rav Zeira ke-tannai* — Rav Zeira observes that this dispute is foreshadowed in a *tannaitic* disagreement. The case is *kerem shenitua pachos me'arba amos* — a vineyard in which the rows of vines are spaced less than four *amos* apart, which is the standard minimum spacing for a proper vineyard. *Rabbi Shimon omer: eino kerem* — Rabbi Shimon rules that such a densely planted arrangement does not qualify as a vineyard at all.

The practical stakes of this classification are significant. Tosafot notes two consequences: first, the laws of *kilayim* apply more stringently to a vineyard than to isolated vines; second, the exemption from military service for one who has planted a vineyard and not yet *chillel* it (*asher nata kerem v'lo chilalo*) would not apply if the arrangement does not qualify as a vineyard. Rabbi Shimon's view, like Nahardea's ruling on packed trees, treats a planting that will require uprooting and redistribution as not yet constituting the permanent arrangement it purports to be.

*V'Chachamim omrim: harei zeh kerem* — the *Chachamim* disagree and rule that even an overcrowded vineyard is considered a vineyard. Their reasoning: *ro'im es ha'emtza'im k'ilu einam* — we regard the middle vines, the ones that would need to be removed, as if they do not exist. On this view, because a portion of the vines will remain permanently in place, the vineyard retains its legal identity and its connection to the land. Correspondingly, the *chazakah* on those remaining vines would extend to the land as well.

Rav Zeira's point is that the debate between Nahardea's ruling and an alternative position maps precisely onto this *tannaitic* dispute: Rabbi Shimon's view supports Nahardea's ruling that a temporary, overcrowded arrangement cannot establish *chazakah* on land, while the *Chachamim*'s view — treating the permanent portion of the planting as determinative — would support recognizing *chazakah* on the land even in the dense-planting case.

---

## Palm Tree Sale

### Palm Tree Depths

*Amri Naharda'ei: hai man d'zavin dikla l'chaverei* — the sages of Nahardea further ruled that one who sells a palm tree to another person conveys to the buyer rights extending *mishipulei ad tehoma* — from the surface of the ground down to the very depths of the earth. The buyer acquires not merely the tree that stands above ground but all rights running vertically downward, all the way to the bottom.

### Ownership vs. Rights

This ruling immediately raises the question of how it relates to the broader debate about *ein yafah* and *ein ra'ah*. Does the buyer of a palm tree own the land beneath it, or not? If the *Chachamim* say a seller gives no land with trees, how can Nahardea say the buyer receives rights to the depths?

Two interpretations are offered. The first is that *mishipulei ad tehoma* reflects genuine ownership: the buyer of the palm tree owns the column of earth running directly beneath it, all the way down. On this reading, Nahardea sides with Rabbi Akiva's principle of *mocher b'ayin yafah*, and the ruling is a specific application of that generosity — the sale of a palm tree carries with it ownership of the subterranean earth beneath it.

The second interpretation holds that even if the buyer does not own the land in the full proprietary sense, he possesses rights that prevent the seller from tunneling underneath the tree — even a hundred *amos* underground. As long as the palm tree stands, the buyer's rights of use and enjoyment extend downward without limit, and the seller may not undermine those rights by excavating beneath the tree's root system. On this view, *mishipulei ad tehoma* describes the scope of the buyer's enforceable rights, not necessarily the extent of his title.

The discussion of this ruling will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Bava Batra 38

## Tree Sale & Land Ownersh…

### Intro: Trees & Land

The discussion at the close of 37b builds on a series of questions raised throughout the preceding daf concerning the relationship between trees and the land in which they are planted. When one sells trees, does the sale include any portion of the underlying land? When a plot is sold to two different buyers — one acquiring the trees and the other the land — how do we apportion the rights between them? These questions turn on familiar principles: *mocher be'ayin yafa* (the seller intends generously) versus *mocher be'ayin ra* (the seller intends narrowly), and whether those principles apply differently when there is a single seller and buyer versus when the entire plot is being divided between two buyers simultaneously. The Gemara had also discussed the case of an overcrowded planting, where the trees are understood to be temporary — planted densely with the expectation of being uprooted and replanted — so that no lasting relationship is presumed between the trees and the soil beneath them, and a *chazakah* on the trees therefore carries no implication of ownership of the land.

### Nehardai's View

At the close of 37b, *Amrei Nehardai* — the scholars of Nehardea — offer a ruling: *hai man de'zavin dikla le'chaverei, kanei lei mi-shippulei tehoma* — one who sells a palm tree to his friend acquires the land beneath that tree from the surface all the way down to the depths. The *Rashbam* notes that even according to the view that purchasing a single tree does not ordinarily convey any of the surrounding land, there is reason to hold that the land directly beneath the tree is different. Under the principle of *mocher be'ayin yafa*, a seller who conveys a tree may be understood as conveying at minimum the ground directly underneath it. The Nehardean ruling extends this further, saying that the buyer acquires not just that surface area but the full vertical column of earth below it, all the way down.

### Rava's Challenge

The Gemara at the top of 38a records that Rava challenges this position: *veleima lei kurkema de'rishka zibni lach* — why can't the original owner turn around and say, "I sold you a *kurkema de'rishka*"? The *kurkema de'rishka* is a saffron crocus plant — a crop that is understood to be temporary, sold with rights to use it until it matures, after which the buyer uproots it and leaves. The plant is not conveyed together with its underlying soil. Rava's point is that perhaps the sale of a single palm tree should be understood in the same way: the buyer has rights to the tree and its fruit for as long as the tree lives, but once it dies, there is no ongoing claim to the underlying land, because the land was never truly sold. The analogy to the *kurkema de'rishka* is designed to undercut the assumption that any permanent transfer of land has taken place.

### Mecha'ah Protection

Rava himself then resolves the difficulty: *ba bemachmat ta'ana* — the case under discussion is one where the buyer comes with an explicit claim. He is not relying on a default presumption that the sale of a tree includes the land; rather, he argues that in this specific transaction, the seller explicitly agreed to convey the underlying land as well. He has been working the land for three years, the original owner has said nothing, and he argues that this *chazakah* establishes his ownership of the ground beneath the tree.

The immediate difficulty is obvious: if the default assumption is that a buyer of a single tree does not acquire the underlying land, what exactly is being established by three years of possession? Ordinary use of the land above a purchased tree would be explicable as nothing more than exercising one's rights to the tree itself. How does that silence prove anything about the land?

Mar Kashisha, son of Rav Chisda, presses this question to Rav Ashi: if the seller did in fact sell only the tree — or by analogy, only the *kurkema de'rishka* — with no transfer of underlying land intended, what ought the seller to do to protect himself from a later claim that the buyer acquired the land as well? The Gemara answers: *ibayei lei limchu'ei* — he was obligated to make a *mecha'ah*, a formal protest or declaration.

This is a striking application of the *mecha'ah* concept. The *mecha'ah* here is not a protest against wrongdoing. Nobody is doing anything unlawful. The buyer is legitimately on the land by virtue of owning the tree. Yet the seller is required to go on record — to declare publicly that the buyer is present only as the owner of the tree, not as the owner of the underlying soil. If no such declaration is made within three years, the buyer's claim to the land gains legal traction.

### Mashkanta Precedent

The Gemara anchors this conclusion by citing the case of the *mashkanta d'Sura* — the Suran form of a land pledge. In this arrangement, a creditor lends money and in exchange takes possession of the debtor's land, harvesting its produce for a fixed number of years until the debt is repaid. The document specifies: *b'mishlam shnaya ilu, tipok ara belo chaspa* — when these years have elapsed, the land returns to its original owner and the debt is discharged. The creditor is thus on the land for years, collecting all of the produce himself. Unlike a sharecropper, who returns a portion of the yield to the owner and thereby advertises the nature of the arrangement, the holder of a *mashkanta* keeps everything. An observer watching from the outside would see no visible difference between this creditor and an outright owner.

The Gemara poses the problem starkly: *i kavshi lei l'shtar mashkanta v'amar lekuha hi beyadi* — what if the creditor suppresses the loan document and at the end of the period claims that he purchased the land outright? Would he be believed? The rhetorical answer is: *matkni rabanan milta d'ati bah lidei pseida* — would the Rabbis have established a legal mechanism that opens the door to such loss? They would not. Therefore, the system must include a protection: *ela ibayei lei limchu'ei* — the original owner must make a *mecha'ah*. By publicly declaring that the creditor is on the land by virtue of a *mashkanta* and not as an owner, the original owner protects himself from having the creditor's years of possession ripen into a *chazakah*.

The parallel to the tree sale is then stated explicitly: *hacha nami ibayei lei limchu'ei* — here too, the seller who conveyed only the tree and not the underlying land must make a timely *mecha'ah* to prevent the buyer's three years of presence from being construed as possession with the owner's acquiescence.

One might observe that this system cuts in both directions. The seller who did legitimately convey only the tree must make a *mecha'ah* or risk losing the land. But equally, a seller who already conveyed the land outright might try to exploit the system in reverse — making a quiet *mecha'ah* claiming the arrangement was a *mashkanta* or a sharecrop, hoping the word never reaches the buyer while the buyer, unsuspecting, loses track of his original deed. The *mecha'ah* system is thus not a complete safeguard; it demands vigilance from all parties, and the failure to preserve one's *shtar* remains a serious vulnerability.

### Witness Requirements

The *mecha'ah* system raises a pointed question about what it actually establishes and who bears the burden of proof. In a case of standard adverse possession with no prior transaction between the parties, the original owner has no available witnesses to the underlying facts — there was simply no transaction — and therefore the only tool available to him is the *mecha'ah*. But in the cases under discussion, there *was* an original transaction: a tree was sold under specific terms, or a *mashkanta* was given with specific conditions documented in a *shtar*. Why, in those cases, does the law not require the original owner to maintain witnesses to the specific terms of the transaction, rather than relying on the cruder instrument of a *mecha'ah*?

The witnesses to a *mecha'ah* testify only that the declarant made a certain statement — not that the statement was true. If I tell two witnesses that the man on my land is a sharecropper or a pledgee, those witnesses can report what I said, but they cannot independently verify the terms of the underlying arrangement. It seems, then, that the original owner would be better protected — and the system more resistant to abuse — if witnesses to the actual transaction were required. This is especially pressing in cases, like the *mashkanta*, where the transaction was documented and there was every opportunity to preserve reliable evidence.

One way to frame this is as a question about the allocation of burdens. The *mecha'ah* system places the burden on the original owner to make a timely public declaration. An alternative system would place the burden on the person in possession to ensure that the terms of his legitimate entry onto the land are on record. There is something intuitive in the latter: I never sold you the land, so why must I do something affirmative to protect myself, when all I need is for you not to distort the terms of the arrangement to which you yourself were party? On the other hand, the Talmudic principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ah* — the burden of proof lies with the claimant — might push in the other direction. These tensions are not fully resolved, and the absence of a system of duplicate documents (*shnei shtarot*, as it were, one for each party) is itself a structural gap that the *mecha'ah* mechanism only partially fills.

### System Critique

There is a broader concern about the fairness and reliability of the *mecha'ah* mechanism as a whole. The system depends on the public declaration spreading by word of mouth, reaching the person in possession and thereby putting him on notice that his presence is contested. Yet this is plainly an imperfect mechanism. A protest that the other party is a sharecropper or a *mashkanta* holder is not the kind of news that travels readily or reliably. People are far more likely to gossip about a dramatic act of adverse possession — "Did you hear that Dov is farming Eli's land and acting as if he owns it?" — than about a quiet declaration of legal status: "Did you hear that Eli registered that the arrangement with Dov is a *mashkanta*?" The asymmetry in the gossip value of the two messages creates a structural inequality in how reliably each reaches its intended audience.

Furthermore, the phrase used by the Gemara — *kavshi lei l'shtar mashkanta*, he suppressed the loan document — raises its own questions. The natural reading is that the creditor conceals the document so that at the end of the term he can claim to have purchased the land. But why would he retain it at all, if his plan is to suppress it? One might answer that the prudent schemer keeps his options open: if the fraud fails, the document may still be useful. But whatever the explanation for the word choice, the broader point stands — a system built on oral declarations traveling through informal social networks, with no centralized registry and no requirement that declarations reach their target, is inherently susceptible to manipulation in both directions.

---

## Geography & Chazaka

### Mishna Overview

The Mishnah at 38a opens a new dimension of the *chazakah* discussion: the geographic limitations on when a *chazakah* can take effect. *Shalosh aratzot lachazakah — Yehuda ve'ever haYarden vehaGalil* — there are three lands for the purposes of *chazakah*: Judea, Transjordan, and the Galilee.

The geographic division matters because *chazakah* is not just about the act of possession — it derives its legal force from the absence of protest. If an owner watches someone occupy his land for three years and says nothing, we infer that the possessor's claim must be legitimate. But that inference only holds if we can assume the owner knew about the occupation. News travels within a region; it cannot be assumed to travel between regions. Therefore: *haya biYehuda vehechezik baGalil, baGalil vehechezik biYehuda — eina chazakah* — if the owner was in Judea while the possessor was establishing a *chazakah* in the Galilee, or vice versa, it is not a valid *chazakah*, because we cannot assume the owner was aware. The rule is: *ad sheyehe imo bemedina achat* — until they are in the same region, the *chazakah* does not take effect.

### Rav Yehuda's View

Rav Yehuda offers a strikingly expansive interpretation: *lo amru shalosh aratzot ela kedei sheyehe be'Aspamya veyachazik shana, veyeilchu veyodi'uhu shana, veyavo shana acheret* — the Mishnah's three-land framework was never meant to establish fixed geographic zones. Rather, the principle is that three years suffice for *chazakah* because one year is time enough for the fact of the possession to become known, one year is time enough for a message to travel even as far as Spain — and Spain here represents the most distant imaginable location — and one year is available for the owner to return and protest. The *rishonim* note that even locations further than Spain fall under the same rule by the principle of *lo plug*, once the three-year period is generous enough to accommodate even the most distant case.

Two implications of Rav Yehuda's position are worth noting. First, he significantly expands the reach of *chazakah*, allowing it to operate even when the owner is at a great distance. Second, his formulation — *veyavo shana acheret*, and he must return the following year — implies that for Rav Yehuda, the *mecha'ah* must be made *befanav*, in the person's physical presence. A protest lodged from afar may not suffice; the owner must actually come back and confront the possessor directly. These two rulings together strongly favor the *machzik*, the one in possession: on one hand, the *chazakah* works even at great distance; on the other, the original owner bears the demanding obligation of returning in person to protest.

### Mecha'ah Condition

The Gemara now poses its central analytical question about the Mishnah: *mai kasavar Tanna Kamma?* — what is the *Tanna Kamma*'s reasoning for saying that *chazakah* requires the parties to be in the same region? The Gemara frames the question through the lens of *mecha'ah*:

*Ei kasavar mecha'ah shelo befanav havya mecha'ah* — if the *Tanna Kamma* holds that a *mecha'ah* made at a distance, not in the presence of the possessor, is legally effective, then why should *chazakah* not work even between Judea and the Galilee? The owner in Judea could make a *mecha'ah* that would eventually reach the possessor in the Galilee, and the possessor in the Galilee would have no excuse for not being aware of the protest.

*Ve'ei kasavar mecha'ah shelo befanav lo havya mecha'ah* — but if a *mecha'ah* at a distance is not effective, then it follows that *chazakah* should not work even within the same country if the parties are not face to face. Why, then, does the Mishnah draw the line at the regional boundary between Judea, Transjordan, and the Galilee, rather than requiring direct confrontation in every case?

The Gemara's framing here is notable: why does it ask about *mecha'ah shelo befanav* rather than asking about *chazakah shelo befanav* — the owner's not being present to observe the possession? The reason is that *chazakah* derives its force precisely from the absence of *mecha'ah*. The possessor's three years of undisturbed presence is meaningful only because we interpret the owner's silence as tacit acknowledgment. But that inference is only valid if the owner could have protested and chose not to. If we say that a *mecha'ah* at a distance would not have been effective anyway — because we assume it would not reach the possessor — then the owner had no real option to protest, and his silence means nothing. Conversely, if a *mecha'ah* at a distance *is* effective, then the owner had a viable means of protest, and his failure to use it is significant.

### Tosafot's Logic

*Tosafot* sharpen this analysis with an important observation. One might ask: why not simply say that *chazakah shelo befanav* — the fact of possession when the owner is not present — fails to reach the owner, and therefore no inference can be drawn from his silence? Why focus on the *mecha'ah* side rather than the *chazakah* side?

*Tosafot* answer that the two directions are not equally reliable. The message that someone is occupying your land travels easily and robustly through the community. It is precisely the kind of news people share — "Did you know that Dov is farming Eli's field as if he owns it? Did Eli sell it to him?" — and moreover, it is the kind of news that people will specifically seek out and relay to Eli, knowing he has a stake in it. If Eli has gone away and left fields behind, he will naturally be asking people who travel back and forth: is anything happening with my land? The message of adverse possession is highly likely to reach him.

The *mecha'ah*, by contrast, is a far less compelling piece of gossip. The news that Eli declared Dov to be a sharecropper or that Eli intends to sue Dov is not inherently interesting to anyone else, and nobody has any particular incentive to make sure Dov hears about it. *Tosafot* thus establish an asymmetry: we can take for granted that the *chazakah* message will reach the owner, but we cannot take for granted that the *mecha'ah* message will reach the possessor. The *chazakah* side is not the problem; the *mecha'ah* side is. Therefore, whether *chazakah* works at a distance depends not on whether the owner will hear about the occupation, but on whether we can assume an effective *mecha'ah* could have traveled back to the possessor.

### Abba's Ruling

The Gemara records: *Amar Abba bar Mammel amar Rav — l'olam kasavar mecha'ah shelo befanav havya mecha'ah* — in truth, the *Tanna Kamma* holds that a *mecha'ah* not in the possessor's direct presence is fully effective. A protest need not be delivered face to face; provided it is made before witnesses in circumstances where the word can spread, it is a valid *mecha'ah*. This is the baseline rule. The *Tanna Kamma* of the Mishnah does not disagree with this principle.

### Yehuda-Galil Exception

Why then does the Mishnah treat Judea and the Galilee as separate zones where *chazakah* does not operate across the boundary? *Mishnatenu be-sha'at herum shanu* — the Mishnah was speaking specifically to conditions of *sha'at herum*, a period of regional hostility and restricted travel between the two areas. It is not that Judea and the Galilee are inherently separate; it is that under conditions of antagonism or effective travel bans, we cannot assume that messages are crossing the border in either direction. With travel severely curtailed, neither the news of the *chazakah* reaching the owner nor the *mecha'ah* of the owner reaching the possessor can be taken for granted.

*U-mai shena Yehuda ve-Galil denakat?* — why single out Judea and the Galilee specifically? *Kamashma lan* — the Mishnah is telling us that *stam Yehuda ve-Galil k'sha'at herum damu* — as a matter of practical reality, the relationship between Judea and the Galilee was generally characterized by conditions analogous to *sha'at herum*, whether due to active hostility or simply a lack of regular traffic and communication. This need not necessarily imply ongoing political antagonism; it may simply reflect that people in one region did not regularly travel to the other, so that reliable communication could not be assumed.

The upshot is: *mecha'ah shelo befanav* works. Direct confrontation is not required. The owner in Judea can make a *mecha'ah* that the possessor in Judea will eventually hear about, and that works. But if the regions are effectively cut off — whether by hostility, geography, or simple lack of movement — then the *mecha'ah* cannot be assumed to travel, the possessor's silence loses its evidentiary force, and the *chazakah* does not take effect.

---

## Boreach Case

### Rav: No Chazaka

Rav Yehuda cites Rav: *ein machzikin benichsei boreach* — one cannot establish a *chazakah* on the property of a *boreach*, a person who has fled. If someone has had to leave their home because the government is pursuing them — whether for unpaid debts or, as we will see, for a capital charge — a *chazakah* taken on their abandoned property during their absence is not valid.

The intuitive framing is straightforward: the *boreach* is not simply away from home; his situation may prevent him from doing what an ordinary absent owner could do to protect his property. Whether and how this affects the standard *chazakah* mechanism requires careful analysis, as the subsequent discussion makes clear.

### Shmuel's Objection

When Rav Yehuda related this ruling to Shmuel, Shmuel objected: *vechi limchot befanav hu tzarich?* — does the owner need to show up and protest in person? We have already established that *mecha'ah shelo befanav* — protest at a distance — is fully effective. The *boreach* is absent, not silenced. He can presumably still hear what is happening to his property and make his protest known, just as any other absent owner would. Why, then, should *nichsei boreach* be any different from the ordinary case of *mecha'ah shelo befanav*?

From Shmuel's perspective, then, Rav's ruling is puzzling. If absence alone is not a barrier — and we have established that it is not — the *boreach* is simply an ordinary case of an absent owner, and *chazakah* should either work or not work on the same terms as any other case of *mecha'ah shelo befanav*.

### Alternative: Works

The Gemara presents an alternative version of the tradition: *ika de'amri, amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav machzikin benichsei boreach* — a *chazakah* on the property of a *boreach* does work. When Rav Yehuda reported this to Shmuel, Shmuel responded: *peshita* — of course. Since *mecha'ah shelo befanav* is effective, the *boreach* can protest from wherever he is, and therefore the possessor's three years of undisturbed presence is meaningful: the owner could have protested and did not.

Under this version, the question reverses: what is Rav's *chiddush* in telling us that *chazakah* works on *nichsei boreach*? After all, Rav has already explained the *Tanna Kamma*'s position as resting on the validity of *mecha'ah shelo befanav* — so of course it works. The Gemara responds: *ela ha kamashma lan de'afilu michah bifnei shnayim she'ein yecholim lomar lo havya mecha'ah* — what Rav's ruling teaches is that *mecha'ah* is effective even when made before two witnesses who are themselves physically incapable of traveling to report it to the possessor. This is a more extreme case than ordinary *mecha'ah shelo befanav*. We already know that a protest before traveling witnesses who are not present with the possessor is valid. Rav now extends this to cases where the specific witnesses before whom the protest was made cannot themselves make the journey.

Why would this be valid? The Gemara continues: *chavra chavra isleih ve'chavra de'chavra chavra isleih* — everyone has friends, and everyone's friends have friends. Even if the witnesses themselves cannot travel, word will spread from them to others, and eventually it will reach someone who will carry it back. The network of human communication is assumed to be sufficiently robust that even witnesses who are physically stationary at the point of the protest will initiate a chain of transmission that ultimately delivers the message.

*Rav Anan* adds: Shmuel himself drew a line here. A *mecha'ah* before two people *who can* eventually report to the possessor is valid; a *mecha'ah* before two people *who cannot* report is not valid. From Shmuel's perspective, therefore, the case of *nichsei boreach* — assuming the standard scenario in which witnesses can travel and report — is entirely ordinary and needs no special ruling. From Rav's perspective, the *boreach* case is an opportunity to announce the more expansive ruling: that even witnesses who cannot themselves travel do not disqualify the *mecha'ah*, since the chain of social transmission will carry the message eventually.

It is worth noting what this discussion establishes about the burden of proof. Throughout these *sugyot*, it never appears that the original owner is required to bring direct evidence that the possessor actually heard about the *mecha'ah*. The owner must demonstrate that he made a *mecha'ah* with witnesses, and under the appropriate conditions — whether those witnesses were capable of traveling or simply capable of telling others. The assumption that the message will eventually reach the possessor is built into the legal structure. Whether the possessor actually received it is not a factual question the owner must independently prove.

### Tax vs. Murder

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the two rulings attributed to Rava — that *chazakah* does not work on *nichsei boreach* and that *mecha'ah shelo befanav* is valid — by distinguishing between two types of fugitives: *boreach machmat mamon* and *boreach machmat mardin* — one fleeing because of unpaid taxes or debt owed to the government, and one fleeing because of a charge of murder.

### Location Revelation

In the case of a *boreach machmat mamon*, the practical reality is that a local government will not typically pursue a debtor who flees to another jurisdiction. The fugitive is in no danger from revealing his location; he simply cannot return home. In that circumstance, he is fully capable of making a *mecha'ah* from wherever he is, and the absence of any protest is meaningful. A *chazakah* on his property is therefore valid.

In the case of a *boreach machmat mardin*, however, the situation is fundamentally different. This person is hiding from a capital charge. Revealing his location — even indirectly, by lodging a formal protest about property in his home town — could lead authorities back to him. He is therefore not genuinely free to make a *mecha'ah*: doing so would mean announcing where he is. Since his silence is not voluntary acquiescence but compelled self-preservation, it carries no evidentiary weight. The possessor's three years of undisturbed presence cannot be attributed to the owner's tacit acknowledgment of the possessor's title, because the owner was never in a position to speak. Therefore, *chazakah* on the property of a *boreach machmat mardin* does not work.

This analysis illuminates the precise mechanism of *chazakah*. The inference from undisturbed possession to legitimate ownership depends entirely on the owner's having had a real and uninhibited opportunity to protest. Where that opportunity is structurally foreclosed — not by geographic distance but by the genuine threat of self-incrimination — the foundational assumption of the *chazakah* system collapses.

An interesting practical difficulty arises: what if the possessor had no idea the original owner was a *boreach machmat mardin*? He occupied the land for three years, assumed his *chazakah* was maturing, and discarded his *shtar* accordingly. The owner then returns after the charges are resolved and produces evidence that he had been in hiding all along. The possessor might legitimately argue that he had no basis to suspect the owner's silence was coerced rather than acquiescent. How the law adjudicates between these competing claims in the absence of shared information is a question the Gemara leaves in some tension.

---

## Valid Mecha'ah

### Zutra's Rule

Mar Zutra articulates the minimum required content of a valid *mecha'ah*: if one merely says, "*Planya gazlana hu*" — "so-and-so is a thief" — that is not a *mecha'ah*. The person on the land will hear this and regard it as nothing more than name-calling, a piece of *lashon hara* with no legal dimension. It does not put him on notice that his ownership is formally contested, and it does not give him reason to carefully preserve his *shtar*.

### Three Elements

For a *mecha'ah* to be valid, more is required. The formulation the Gemara endorses is: *Planya gazlana hu, nakit lei le-arai be-gazlanuta, u-le-machar tavna lei le-dina* — so-and-so is a thief, he is taking my land illegitimately, and tomorrow I will bring a legal claim against him. Three distinct elements are present: the characterization of the possessor as acting without right, the explicit identification of the property as belonging to the declarant, and the express statement of intent to pursue a legal remedy.

### Rashbam's Logic

The *Rashbam* offers a careful analysis of what each element contributes, and specifically addresses whether all three are strictly necessary. In a formulation he cites in the name of Rabbi Yaakov bar Yaakov — and which he regards as the primary interpretation — the critical element is not the first phrase but the second: *nakit lei le-arai be-gazlanuta*, he is taking *my* land. Without an explicit reference to the declarant's own property, the protest amounts to nothing more than a statement about some plot of land the declarant has no announced interest in. *She-harei lo micha machmat atzmo* — the declarant is not defending his own claim. *Hu ke-mi she-amar Planya machazik be-karka shel acherim* — it is as if he said merely that so-and-so is occupying someone else's land. *U-le-pigmo mitkavein, ve-lo le-arer* — the intent appears to be to damage the possessor's reputation, not to assert a competing legal claim.

Once the declarant specifies that it is *his* land — *le-arai*, mine — the legal character of the protest is transformed. He is now on record as a claimant asserting a property right. *Ve-hodia she-ha-karka shelo machazik bah be-avla* — he announces that the land is his and that the possessor holds it wrongfully. The third phrase — the stated intent to bring a *din* — then adds emphasis, clarifying that the declaration is not mere grievance but a formal notice of impending litigation. According to the *Rashbam*, however, this third phrase is not independently required; it is implied by the second. If you have said clearly that he is on *your* land unlawfully, the intent to pursue your legal claim is already inherent in the declaration.

What is required, then, is not merely the label *gazlan*, and not merely a reference to land, but the conjunction of the two: a declaration that identifies this specific land as yours, characterizes the possessor's presence as wrongful, and thereby communicates to the world that you are an active claimant who has not abandoned your rights. The possessor who hears this — or who would have heard this had the *mecha'ah*'s chain of transmission run its course — is put on notice that his three years of occupation will not ripen into title undisturbed.

### Secret Mecha'ah

The Gemara closes with a question that will carry into the next session. Rav Zvid introduces a case: *lo teimru lei* — the declarant makes his *mecha'ah* before witnesses and then instructs them not to tell the possessor. This is a striking and troubling move. On one hand, one might imagine a legitimate reason for such an instruction: the declarant does not want the possessor to begin manufacturing false evidence, or to take steps to obscure his fraudulent possession before a court case can be mounted. On the other hand, a *mecha'ah* whose declarant actively suppresses its transmission is a deeply suspicious instrument. It may simply be a scheme to establish a paper record of protest while ensuring the possessor never hears of it, waiting until the possessor has discarded his *shtar* before producing the witnesses to the *mecha'ah*.

Two related questions arise. First, can we assume the message will spread despite the instruction to keep silent? The Gemara has already held that witnesses who cannot travel will nonetheless transmit through intermediaries; but what of witnesses who are capable of transmitting but are actively told not to? Second, even setting aside the practical question of transmission, should we not be suspicious of the purpose of the declaration itself? A *mecha'ah* made in secret is not the spontaneous protest of an aggrieved owner; it looks more like a legal trap. Whether such a *mecha'ah* is valid — and on what grounds it might be invalidated — is the question with which the Gemara will open the following discussion.

---

---

# Bava Batra 39

## Mechah Shelo Befanav

### Mechah & Chazakah

The central concern of the *gemara* on this *daf* is *mechah* — the formal protest an owner must lodge to prevent an adverse possessor from establishing *chazakah* — and in particular the principle of *mechah shelo befanav*: whether a protest made not in the occupant's direct presence constitutes a valid *mechah*. The two institutions are intertwined. If the owner cannot make an effective *mechah* from a distance, the entire system governing *chazakah* shifts accordingly.

### Tosafot's Framework

An important preliminary point, one that clarifies why the *gemara* focuses its scrutiny on the *mechah* rather than on the *chazakah* itself, is a framework offered by Tosafot. The assumption underlying *chazakah shelo befanav* — that is, adverse possession occurring while the original owner is away — is that word of the occupation will reach the original owner. If a stranger is on your land, you want to know what is happening with your property; you will ask questions, and the natural workings of the rumor mill will carry the news to you. This is Tosafot's approach; it is not the position of the Rashbam, but it is a helpful one. We therefore assume the message will reach the absent owner. The live question, then, is not whether the owner learns of the occupation, but rather: once he has learned of it and wishes to protest, can he do so *shelo befanav* — from where he is — and have that protest carry legal weight? Can we assume that his *mechah* will, in turn, reach the occupant?

### Rava's Position

Rava's explanation of the *mishna*'s assumptions is that *mechah shelo befanav* is in principle valid. One obvious advantage of *mechah befanav* — protesting directly in the occupant's presence — is that it creates unambiguous, direct evidence that the message was received. Yet Rava rules that this is not required. The owner may protest from wherever he is, and we assume the message will reach the occupant. Even if, in a given case, the occupant in fact did not hear of it, the halacha does not favor him on that account — a result that may sound counterintuitive, but reflects a considered policy judgment about whose interests the law protects.

### Geographic Limits

There is, however, a geographic limitation. If the owner is in a different country — a jurisdiction where communication cannot be assumed — then *mechah shelo befanav* will not be effective, because in those circumstances we cannot presume that the message will travel there. The consequence of *mechah shelo befanav* being unavailable is significant: if there is no realistic prospect of the message reaching the owner, we cannot treat his silence as meaningful acquiescence, and the occupant's *chazakah* correspondingly loses its evidentiary force.

### Core Principle

The governing principle, then, is this: one need not make a *mechah befanav*, but one must operate in conditions where communication is possible and where we can assume the message will arrive. Absent such conditions, the *chazakah* is not a valid *chazakah*. The point that the owner need only prove that he made the *mechah* properly — and need never demonstrate that the *machzik* actually heard it — is a principle that strongly favors the original owner. The *machzik*, for his part, carries real risk if he has not carefully preserved his *shtar*.

### Squatting Case

This raises an important question: what of someone who squats on land for three years without ever having had a *shtar*? Does the entire framework not break down, since there is no purchase to legitimate? The answer is that the system does work — but precisely as designed. The absence of any protest is probative only when the *machzik* is making a legitimate claim: that he purchased the property and no longer has the *shtar*. After three years of undisturbed possession, the absence of protest is evidence that he owns it — but only in that context. The *machzik* is not required to prove the occupant heard the *mechah*; the owner is not required to prove the *mechah* reached the occupant. What the owner must do is demonstrate that he made the *mechah* under conditions in which it could have reached its destination. Even if the *machzik* could somehow prove he spent the last three years in a silent retreat where no word reached him, it would not matter. The rules must be clear and administrable, and the rule is: make a proper *mechah*, and that suffices.

---

## Restrictions on Mechah

### Lo Temru Leh

The *gemara* now introduces a series of cases in which the protesting owner attempts, in various ways, to restrict the spread of information about his *mechah*. At the top of 39a, the *gemara* presents a case in which the owner says to the witnesses: *lo temru leh* — do not tell him. He issues his *mechah* before witnesses, declaring the occupant a *gazlan* who is unlawfully on his land and whom he intends to sue, but instructs the witnesses to keep the matter to themselves. This is, at minimum, suspicious. Perhaps the owner is acting in bad faith, hoping to prevent the occupant from holding onto his *shtar* so that he can reclaim the land more easily. Alternatively, perhaps the owner simply does not want the *gazlan* to begin shoring up a defense. In any case, the question is whether this instruction — *lo temru leh* — is enough to invalidate the *mechah* entirely. If the witnesses obey, after all, the message will certainly not reach the occupant; it begins to resemble the situation of a different country, where communication is presumed impossible.

### Rav Zvid Strict

Rav Zvid's position is consistent and strict: once you have said *lo temru leh*, the *mechah* is meaningless. If the witnesses comply, the word will not reach the occupant, and the protest has accomplished nothing.

### Rav Pappa Lenient

Rav Pappa disagrees. He reads the instruction narrowly: *ledidi lo temru leh* — don't tell him directly — but *leachrinei emru* — you may tell others. And once you tell others, the principle of *chavrach chavrah it leh vechavrach dechavrah chavrah it leh* — your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend — applies. The witnesses have no obligation in a normal *mechah* to pick up the telephone and notify the occupant directly; they are simply witnesses to a protest that will circulate through ordinary social channels. Saying *lo temru leh* only restricts direct communication, and since direct communication was never the mechanism to begin with, the *mechah* remains valid.

### Lo Tipku Shuta

What if the owner goes further? What if he says *lo tipku shuta* — do not let the word get out at all? This is broader than merely telling the witnesses not to speak to the occupant directly; it is an instruction to suppress the matter entirely. Here, Rav Zvid again rules that the *mechah* is nullified — this is entirely consistent with his position. And notably, Rav Pappa is silent. His silence is taken as implicit agreement: when the instruction is *lo tipku shuta*, even Rav Pappa concedes that the *mechah* fails, because the channels through which the message would have naturally traveled have been explicitly sealed off.

### Offered Silence

The *gemara* now introduces a further variation: what if the witnesses themselves, without being asked, volunteer that they will not tell the occupant — *amru leh lo amrinan leh*? There is a question whether this offer arises in response to the owner's instruction, or whether the witnesses proffer it entirely on their own initiative. The Rashbam suggests that the case may be *davka* where no instruction was given — because when one merely agrees to a restriction imposed by another, one tends to interpret it narrowly, looking for loopholes. If I tell you not to say anything, you might construe that as: I cannot tell *him*, but I can tell others. Whereas if you offer on your own that you will not say anything, the words may carry a broader intent, suggesting you mean to suppress the information entirely.

Rav Zvid is again consistent: if they have offered that they will not tell the occupant, the *mechah* is invalid. Rav Pappa, however, maintains that even here the *mechah* stands — because their offer, just as the owner's instruction, means only that they will not tell the occupant directly, not that the rumor mill will be stopped.

### Voluntary Offers

Now the *gemara* presents the broadest formulation: the witnesses offer, on their own, *lo mapkinan shuta* — we will not let the word get out. This is the equivalent of *lo tipku shuta*, but it comes as a voluntary offer rather than an instruction from the owner. One might suppose this is the same as the case where the owner issued the instruction, and therefore Rav Pappa would again concede the invalidity. And indeed, Rav Pappa does say that when the witnesses have volunteered *lo mapkinan shuta*, the *mechah* is not valid — because once the scope of the undertaking has been expanded from "we won't tell him" to "we won't let the word get out," even Rav Pappa agrees the *mechah* cannot stand.

### Voluntary Offers

But here Rav Huna brei deRav Yehoshua disagrees, and says that even in this last case the *mechah* remains valid. His reasoning is captured in the principle: *kol milta d'lo ramya alei d'inish amar lah v'lav ada'atei* — anything that is not an obligation formally placed upon a person, they will say and not really pay attention to it. When the witnesses volunteer "we won't let the word get out," no one has charged them with that responsibility; they have simply offered it freely. The weight of a freely offered promise is lighter than that of an obligation imposed from without. As a result, people will talk, and they will not even notice that they are violating their own pledge. The word will slip out, the rumor will spread, and the *mechah* will reach its destination.

This last ruling strikes as somewhat counterintuitive. As the cases multiply — don't tell him, don't let the word get out, they offer not to tell anyone — the likelihood that the *machzik* actually learns of the *mechah* diminishes with each step. One might have sympathy for Rav Zvid's consistent position, which tracks that decreasing likelihood honestly. Nevertheless, the trajectory of the *gemara* is toward the broadest possible definition of *mechah*, and the accepted halacha — as the Rashba confirms — follows the most expansive view, consistently favoring the original owner. This has a sobering practical implication: a *machzik* who has relied on three years of undisturbed possession as proof of ownership may be taking a significant legal risk, since all manner of purportedly restricted protests may still turn out to constitute valid *mechah*.

---

## Rava vs Rav Nachman

### Rav Nachman

Rava quotes Rav Nachman as stating: *mechah shelo befanav havya mecha* — a protest not in the occupant's presence constitutes a valid *mechah*. This, of course, is the position around which the entire discussion of *chavrach chavrah it leh* and the various restrictions has revolved. The alternative — that *mechah shelo befanav* does *not* work, that *lo havya mecha* — would mean the owner must appear before the occupant directly, serving him with notice personally or through an agent. The Rashbam adds that if one did hold such a position, *o hu o shlucho* — either he himself or his agent — would suffice, since the essential point is that the occupant receives the message unambiguously. But Rav Nachman's ruling dispenses with that requirement entirely.

### Rava's Question

Rava, however, challenges Rav Nachman from the position of Rabbi Yehuda in the *mishna*. Rabbi Yehuda explains the purpose of the three-year period as follows: *lo amru shalosh shanim ella kidei sheyehei be'Aspamia* — the three years were instituted to allow time for someone in Aspamia (a distant province) to be reached by news that someone is occupying his land, and to return and respond. The breakdown of the three years, as Rabbi Yehuda describes it, is: the occupant takes possession for one year, news travels to the owner for the second year, and the owner returns and protests in the third year — *veyavo leshana achereta*. The word *veyavo*, "he returns," implies that Rabbi Yehuda requires the owner to physically come back and issue the *mechah* directly. If *mechah shelo befanav* were sufficient, why would he need to return? Let him sit in Aspamia and protest from there — *leysev hatam be'duchtei velimchei*.

Tosafot notes a wrinkle in this question: we have already established that when one is in a different country, *mechah shelo befanav* does not work — because we cannot assume the message will travel there. So perhaps Rabbi Yehuda does not require *mechah befanav* at all; he only requires the owner to return to the same country, so that normal communication channels can carry the protest. In that case, the *gemara* should say he must return to the *medina*, not that he must actually appear before the *machzik*. The word *veyavo*, however, implies a more direct return and confrontation. The question thus retains some force at least within Rabbi Yehuda's own position.

### Good Advice

The *gemara* resolves Rava's challenge: *hasam eitzah tovah ka mashma lan* — there, Rabbi Yehuda is not stating a legal requirement; he is offering good advice. The *mishna* is counseling the owner: now that you have learned someone is on your land, go protect your interests. Return and sue the person; reclaim what is yours. It does not mean that you are legally obligated to do so, or that *mechah shelo befanav* is insufficient. Rabbi Yehuda's language describes the practically wise course of action, not a binding legal demand.

### Peiros Issue

The Rashbam makes an additional point that deepens the force of this advice, which bears emphasis: the sooner the owner returns, the sooner he can stop the occupant from consuming the produce — *peiros* — of the land. Produce already consumed is difficult to recover. The occupant may not have assets sufficient to reimburse the owner for fruits already eaten. Every additional year of delay means more consumed produce and a harder road to full recovery. This is why the *mishna* says, in practical terms, come back promptly — not because *mechah shelo befanav* is legally invalid, but because your financial interests demand swift action.

### Rava Accepts

The *gemara* then observes that since Rava himself had challenged Rav Nachman's position, it would appear that Rava did not initially accept that *mechah shelo befanav* is valid — yet we know from all the preceding discussion that Rava was a leading proponent of exactly that principle. The *gemara* resolves this: *basar d'shamei m'Rav Nachman savrah* — after he heard the ruling from Rav Nachman, challenged it, received a satisfying answer, and was persuaded, Rava accepted and adopted the position as his own. It was not his position from the outset; he came to it through this very exchange.

---

## Two vs Three Witness (II)

### Witness Number

The *gemara* now raises a different question about *mechah*: how many people must be present when the *mechah* is issued? We have assumed throughout that witnesses are required, and the cases above all describe the protest as made before multiple people — *lo temru leh* is in the plural. The question is whether the required number is two or three.

### Two Witnesses

Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiya transmits a ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *mechah bifnei shenayim* — a *mechah* requires two people.

### Three Witnesses

A different tradition records Rabbi Yochanan as ruling: *mechah bifnei shalosh* — three people are required.

### Lashon Hara Link

The *gemara* suggests that perhaps the dispute between these two versions tracks a teaching of Rabbah bar Rav Huna in Arachin: *kol milta demis'amra be'appei tlata leit bei mishum lishna bisha* — anything said in the presence of three people is not subject to the prohibition of *lashon hara*. The implication is that once something is said before three, it will become public knowledge; the assumption that it will spread is so strong that repeating it no longer carries the character of private gossip. This principle will require careful unpacking, and the *gemara* will return to it — but the initial suggestion is that the debate between two and three witnesses in *mechah* may reflect a debate about how many people are needed before a matter can be presumed to enter public circulation.

---

## Lashon Hara Issues

### Three & Lashon Hara

The teaching of Rabbah bar Rav Huna — that a matter said before three people is not subject to *lashon hara* — calls to mind what Benjamin Franklin is said to have observed: three people can keep a secret if two of them are dead. The underlying principle is that once three people know something, we presume it will spread. But the full meaning of this teaching requires examination, and there are several distinct interpretations in the *rishonim*.

---

## Two vs Three Witness (II)

### Testimony vs Public

The *gemara* proposes two ways of understanding the dispute between two and three witnesses for *mechah*. The first possibility: perhaps everyone agrees with Rabbah bar Rav Huna that three are needed to make something public, and the debate concerns a prior question. The one who says two holds *mechah shelo befanav lo havya mecha* — you cannot protest from a distance; you must deliver the *mechah* directly to the occupant. In that case, the witnesses need only testify that the protest was directly delivered — two witnesses suffice for testimony, just as in any other legal context. The one who says three holds *mechah shelo befanav havya mecha* — you do protest from a distance, the word must travel and reach the occupant, and for that you need three people to ensure the matter becomes public.

The second possibility is that everyone agrees *mechah shelo befanav* works, and the debate is about what mechanism makes it effective. The one who says two holds *sahadusa ba'inan* — we need testimony, formal witnesses to the act of protest. The one who says three holds *gillui milta ba'inan* — we need the matter to become public. This is a conceptually richer distinction that warrants further exploration.

### Tosafot's View

Tosafot reads the *sahadusa* position differently. Of course, Tosafot says, the message ultimately has to reach the occupant — that is the whole purpose of *mechah*. And in principle, rumors spread even from a single person: *ve'i lav mishum sahadusa hava sagi bechad dechad vechad ve'islei* — if not for the need for testimony, even one person would be enough, since word travels from person to person. But two are required for testimony to the fact that the *mechah* was made. The rumor itself will spread from those two, even without them being formally obligated to carry it. So what, then, is the difference between two and three if the rumor spreads from either number?

Tosafot answers with an important distinction: *ve'af al pi shelishon hara ein nishma, hainu lefi shema'alimin oso mibnei adam* — even though people talk, there is a distinction between whispering something privately and saying it openly. Two people may whisper — they will share the information in private, quietly, among themselves and perhaps one or two others. The rumor travels, but in the shadows. Three people, says Tosafot, makes it *gillui milta* — a public matter, akin to *lashon hara* which, by Rabbah bar Rav Huna's rule, ceases to be a private matter once said before three.

### Private vs Public

This distinction between private rumor and public knowledge is significant. Once something circulates only in whispers, whether it reaches any particular person depends on whether he is plugged into the right network. But when a matter is openly discussed, it enters general circulation and becomes something everyone knows. So the debate between two and three is, at its core, a debate about whether the *mechah* needs to reach the occupant through private rumor or must enter the domain of public knowledge.

### Public Perception

This points toward a deeper question about what *chazakah* is doing and what *mechah* is undoing. One account of *chazakah* focuses on the evidentiary inference from silence: because the owner did not protest, his silence constitutes implicit concession that the occupant is legitimate. On this account, the owner need only ensure that his protest reaches the occupant, breaking the inference of acquiescence and putting the occupant on notice to guard his *shtar*. But there is another account: by occupying the land publicly for three years, the *machzik* has established a kind of public status — in the community's eyes, he presents as the owner. What *mechah* must do, on this account, is not merely reach the occupant privately but recontextualize his public presence. If people are told publicly that this person is a *gazlan*, then his three years on the land no longer look like the occupancy of an owner — his public standing has been altered. Private whispers may not accomplish this. Only when the *mechah* becomes a public matter does it transform how the *machzik*'s presence is perceived by the community.

These two frameworks — the *mechah* as breaking evidentiary inference versus the *mechah* as reshaping public perception — are both operative in the *gemara* and help explain why *gillui milta* might demand more than *sahadusa* alone.

---

## Lashon Hara Issues (II)

### Rashbam's View

Several major *rishonim* offer distinct interpretations of Rabbah bar Rav Huna's teaching that something said before three is not subject to *lashon hara*. The Rashbam's interpretation is precise and narrow. The ruling does not grant license to say negative things about others merely because the statement is made before three people. Rather, it concerns what may be *reported about the speaker*. If I say something disparaging about David in front of three people, those three people are permitted to go to David and inform him of what I said about him — and that act of reporting is not itself *lashon hara* against me. The reasoning is that by making a statement publicly and willingly before three, I have implicitly accepted that the content of what I said, and the fact that I said it, will become known. Since I was willing to say it in a quasi-public setting, I cannot object to others repeating it. The statement becomes fair to report because I have, in effect, authorized its circulation.
