The *mishnah* specifies the acts that constitute this transactional *chazaka*: *na'al* — locking the gate; *gader* — building a fence or wall; *paratz* — opening or creating a necessary breach in a wall, done not destructively but constructively. Even *kol shehu* — even a minimal act of this kind performed on even a small portion of the land — constitutes a valid *chazaka* of possession. This is worth contrasting with the *chazaka* of demonstrating ownership: there, what matters is the *taking* of benefit from the land — harvesting, reaping — since only that sufficiently provokes the original owner to respond. Here, what matters is the *giving* of benefit to the land — improvement, enclosure, construction. The two modes of *chazaka* are thus structurally inverse: the three-year presumption of ownership rests on deriving benefit; the transactional *chazaka* rests on bestowing it.

---

## Shmuel's Position

### Partners Exception

Shmuel's father and Levi taught that a *shutaf* (partner) has no *chazaka* — and that an *uman* (craftsman) certainly has no *chazaka*, a case so obvious it need not even be stated. Shmuel, however, directly disputes his father. Shmuel's version of the *mishnah* includes the *uman* explicitly and excludes the *shutaf*: an *uman* has no *chazaka* (obvious enough to warrant explicit mention), but a *shutaf* does have a *chazaka* under certain circumstances. Shmuel thus removes partners from the categorical exclusion and holds that three years of uncontested possession by one partner against the other can indeed establish ownership.

### Partners as Guardians

Shmuel's broader position on partnership law is laid out in an expansive statement: *ha'shutfin machzikin zeh al zeh u'me'idin zeh al zeh ve'na'asim shomrei sachar zeh la'zeh* — partners can establish *chazaka* against one another, can testify on behalf of one another, and are considered *shomrei sachar* (paid guardians) with respect to one another's share. Each of these three rulings is striking. The *chazaka* point is Shmuel's central thesis here; the testimony point seems to violate the rule against self-interested testimony (*nogei'a b'edut*) and the Gemara flags it as something to be addressed. The *shomer sachar* point has immediate practical consequences: if two partners share a boat and one partner watches it on the other's day off — each taking a turn at supervision, with the "payment" being the reciprocal watch — then the watching partner is a *shomer sachar* on the other's half. If the boat is stolen on his watch, he is liable to compensate his partner's entire half, whereas absent this rule both partners would simply share the loss proportionally.

### Implied Permission

But there is an apparent contradiction within Shmuel's own rulings. On one hand, Shmuel holds that a partner can have a *chazaka* — implying that prolonged sole use of the land by one partner should provoke the other to protest. On the other hand, Shmuel also holds that a *shutaf ke-yored birshut dami* — a partner is always considered to act with implicit permission. If a partner's presence on the land is always deemed permitted, then his presence can never be adverse, and there should be no *chazaka*. The Gemara resolves this tension by distinguishing between the *scope* of the partner's occupation: whether he has descended upon the whole field (*nachas le-kula*) or only upon half (*nachas le-palga*).

### Full vs. Half Field

Here the Gemara records a dispute — *amri lei le-hai gisa ve-amri lei le-hai gisa*, some say it one way and some say the other. One view holds that if Chanan has been working only his half of the field for three years while the other partner is present and working his own half, that *does* constitute a *chazaka*: since both are present and the division of the field's use is visible, the partner working his half exclusively for three years without any rotation or protest provides a genuine basis for claiming that half as his own through purchase. If, on the other hand, Chanan has been working the entire field for three years, that cannot be a *chazaka*, because the other partner can simply say: we have an informal arrangement by which you work it for a few years and I work it for the next few years. The other view inverts the logic: if Chanan is working his half and the partner is visibly working his own half, this simply reflects the ordinary state of a working partnership, and nothing about it should provoke a protest or create a *chazaka*. But if Chanan is working the *entire* field for three years — including the portion that the other partner ought to be cultivating — that *should* provoke the partner to act, and his failure to do so is meaningful silence that supports a *chazaka*.

### Field Divisibility

Ravina offers a further resolution that cuts across the debate differently. Rather than distinguishing between half and whole, Ravina distinguishes based on whether the field is subject to *din chaluka* — whether it is large enough that either partner could compel a division. If the field cannot be divided (*leit bei din chaluka*) because it is too small for each half to be independently viable, then it is entirely expected that one partner will work it alone for a period of time while the other waits for his turn; sole occupation is thus explained by the field's indivisibility and cannot constitute a *chazaka*. If the field is large enough to be divided (*it bei din chaluka*), then joint cultivation of separate halves is practical and normal, and if one partner instead monopolizes the entire field for three years without any participation from the other and without protest, that extended sole use *does* constitute a *chazaka*. Ravina's resolution returns us to the beginning of the tractate and its discussion of *mishpat chaluka* — the law of partition — now deployed here to calibrate when a partner's possession is sufficiently adverse to support a *chazaka* claim.

The upshot of Shmuel's position, taken as a whole, is that the categorical exclusion of partners from the law of *chazaka* stated in the *mishnah* is not absolute. There are circumstances — defined by what portion of the field is at issue and whether that field is subject to division — in which a partner's uncontested possession over three years does ripen into a valid *chazaka*, because the other partner's silence is legally meaningful rather than merely passive acquiescence within the normal latitude of partnership.

---

---

# Bava Batra 43

## Shmuel on Shutaf

### Four Points Preview

The daf opens by situating us within Shmuel's broader statement concerning a *shutaf* — a partner in a jointly owned field. Shmuel makes several distinct pronouncements, and the Gemara spends this daf unpacking each in turn. The first point concerns the principle of *yored bireshut*: a partner who goes and works the jointly owned field is treated as though he has permission from his co-owner. The second point — which, on its face, seems almost impossible to understand — is that partners may testify for one another (*me'idim zeh l'zeh*) regarding each other's portion of the field. The third is that each partner is considered a *shomer sachar* — a paid watchman — with respect to the other's portion. These three points, along with the underlying framework of *yored bireshut* established on the previous amud, form the architecture of the daf.

### Yored Bireshut

By way of review: the Gemara on the previous amud grappled with whether the phrase *shutaf k'yored bireshut dam* — a partner is like one who descends into the field with permission — was introduced solely to teach that a partner cannot establish a *chazakah*, adverse possession, against his co-owner. The Mishnah already establishes that point in some form, so the Gemara pressed: if that were the only intent, why not simply say *shutaf ein lo chazakah*? The answer is that the phrase carries additional legal implications beyond the question of *chazakah*. The Gemara now turns to exploring what those implications are.

---

## Yored Bireshut Explained

### Asuya Lita Analysis

The Gemara cites Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha, who explains that the phrase teaches that a partner who works the field receives *shevach ha-magia le-ktafayim* — the improvement of the field that "reaches the shoulders." It further specifies that this applies both to a field that is *asuyah le-ita* (suited and in need of the work performed) and to a field *she-einah asuyah le-ita ke-sadeh ha-asuyah le-ita* — one that is not ordinarily suited for that kind of work, yet is treated as if it were.

To appreciate this, one must first understand the baseline rules for someone who works another person's field without permission — a *yored l'sdeh chavero shelo bi-reshut*. Halachically, if a person enters a neighbor's field and does work that the field genuinely needed — *asuyah le-ita* — the owner must pay something resembling the standard contracting fee, what Tosafot calls the rate of a *kablan*, a fixed-fee contractor. This is the lower end of compensation. If, however, the work was not something the field normally called for, the owner pays only the lesser of the worker's expenses or the improvement to the field — an even more minimal reimbursement.

Against this backdrop, the *chiddush* of Shmuel's statement emerges. Tosafot understands *shevach ha-magia le-ktafayim* not as a description of produce that has reached shoulder height (though that is Rashi's and Rashbam's reading), but as a description of labor that required genuine effort — putting one's back, one's shoulders, into the work. The force of the ruling is then twofold.

### Sharecropper Rights

First, when the field genuinely needed the work (*asuyah le-ita*), the partner who performed it does not collect at the rate of a *kablan* — the flat-fee contractor rate that a stranger who worked the field without permission would receive. Instead, he collects as an *aris*, a sharecropper, taking a proportionate share of the benefit. The distinction is significant: a *kablan* receives a fixed sum and leaves; an *aris* is given explicit, ongoing authorization and receives a substantially higher percentage of the field's yield. Because the partner, by virtue of his co-ownership, is treated as having been implicitly authorized, he is compensated at the higher *aris* rate for his work on the co-owner's portion of the field — even though no express permission was ever given.

Second — and this is the more striking *chiddush* — even when the field was not suited for the particular work performed, *she-einah asuyah le-ita*, the partner is still compensated as though it were *asuyah le-ita*. In the case of a stranger who plants orange trees in a wheat field, the owner owes little. But in the case of a partner who does the same, the co-owner actually owes compensation at the standard rate.

### Harebrained Ideas

This last point is genuinely surprising. One might have expected that a joint owner would have no right to make unilateral decisions about the use of a shared field — that any such action would require agreement between the partners. Yet the *halacha* as read by Tosafot is that the partner's 50% stake grants him sufficient authority that even eccentric or idiosyncratic agricultural decisions bind the other partner financially. The practical consequence is almost comic: imagine a partner with unconventional ideas who, while the other partner is away, plants orange trees in a wheat field. Upon returning, the other partner finds herself obligated to pay her co-owner as though she had hired him to do precisely that. It seems to grant substantial unilateral authority to a *shutaf* — authority one would not have expected to find in the structure of a joint ownership.

---

## Me'idim Zeh L'Zeh

### Nogei'in B'Eidutan

Now the Gemara turns to Shmuel's second point, the one that seems most difficult to justify: partners may testify for one another — *me'idim zeh l'zeh*. To clarify what is meant: when two people are partners, they do not each own a distinct, physically demarcated portion of the field. They jointly own the entire field together. Neither owns "the north half" while the other owns "the south half." Ownership is undivided.

Now suppose a third party, David, comes forward claiming that the entire field is his and produces evidence to that effect. One partner — call him Dov — cannot testify on his own behalf, since he is a direct litigant. But it seems as though he could testify that the field belongs to his partner Bobby, joining together with another witness to rebuff David's claim. The problem is immediate: testifying to protect Bobby is testifying to protect himself, since every inch of the field is jointly held. If David takes any part of the field, Dov loses as well. As the Rashbam makes explicit, *kol zman she-lo chilku* — as long as the field has not been formally partitioned — any intrusion by David harms both partners equally. This is a textbook case of *nogei'in b'eidusan* — a witness who is personally vested in the very testimony he offers, which renders him halachically invalid.

### Kinyan and Divestment

The Gemara's initial response is to reframe the case: we are dealing with a situation where the testifying partner has already written over his ownership to the other. He forfeits his stake in the field, transfers it to Bobby, and then testifies on her behalf as a disinterested party.

But this raises an immediate technical problem. The Gemara cites a *Baraita*: one who says *din u-devarim ein li al sadeh zo* — I have no claim on this field — and adds *ein li esek bah* and *yadi mesuleket heimena*, has said nothing legally operative. These are declarations of a present state of affairs, and they are false — the speaker actually does own the field. You cannot disclaim ownership; you can only transfer it. Rashbam notes a possible alternative reading: the problem is not the phrasing but the tense — describing a current state (*I have no stake*) accomplishes nothing, whereas an operative declaration of change (*I hereby remove myself*) might be different in principle. Rashbam draws an analogy to *harei at mekudeshet li*, where the word *harei* transforms a descriptive statement into a performative act. Nevertheless, the Rashbam concludes that none of these formulations suffice — whether one says *I have no stake* or *I hereby have no stake*, the effect is the same: zero. Ownership transfers only through actual conveyance.

The Gemara therefore reformulates: we are dealing with a case where a proper *kinyan* was performed. Dov hands Bobby a handkerchief — a formal act of acquisition — and declares that he thereby transfers his ownership of the field to her. Now he no longer owns the field, and it would seem he can testify.

### Creditor Lien Issue

Yet the Gemara immediately objects: *harei ma'amida bifnei ba'al chovo* — by transferring the field to Bobby, Dov has placed it in front of his own creditor. How so? Suppose Dov owes Joe a thousand dollars, and Joe holds a lien on Dov's assets, including his half of the field. Once Dov transfers his half to Bobby, Joe's lien follows that property — he can collect the debt from the half now in Bobby's possession. But consider what would happen if David were to succeed in proving that the field was always his: in that case, the field would never have legitimately belonged to Dov, and Joe could not collect from it, since there would be nothing that meaningfully "went through" Dov. By testifying that the field is Bobby's — and therefore that it was legitimately Dov's before he transferred it — Dov preserves the ability of his creditor to collect from that very property. He remains a beneficiary of the testimony, and therefore *pasul*.

Crucially, this concern arises even when Dov has transferred the field *shelo be-achrayut* — without accepting any warranty obligation to reimburse Bobby if the field is later taken from her. Even without such a guarantee, the fact that the property passed through Dov's hands means that his creditor can still pursue it in Bobby's possession. Dov testifies to benefit himself precisely in that regard.

It is worth noting, parenthetically, that the Gemara is adopting a categorical rule here — we assume a person may have creditors and therefore may benefit from testimony that preserves a field's legal pedigree, even if in a specific case the witness could theoretically prove he has no outstanding debts. The Gemara does not entertain case-by-case demonstrations of this kind; the hypothetical possibility of benefit appears sufficient to disqualify.

### Two Types of Liability

The Gemara proposes a resolution: we are dealing with a case where Dov accepted *achrayut* upon himself when transferring the field to Bobby. But the Gemara immediately asks: *achrayut* for what? *Achrayut d'alma* — liability for an external claimant like David, who argues that the field was never Dov's to begin with — would make things worse, not better. If Dov promised to reimburse Bobby in the event that David takes the field, then Dov has an even stronger financial interest in defeating David's claim. That cannot be the kind of *achrayut* that resolves the problem.

The operative *achrayut* must therefore be *achrayut d'ati leh machmateh* — liability arising from Dov's own debts. Specifically: Dov accepts upon himself that if his creditor Joe were to seize the field from Bobby in order to satisfy a loan Dov owes, Dov will reimburse Bobby for that loss. This changes the calculus entirely. If Joe seizes the field from Bobby, Bobby can recover from Dov. If Dov benefits from Joe collecting the field — because his debt to Joe is now satisfied — he simultaneously incurs an equivalent new debt to Bobby. The net gain is zero. By accepting this form of *achrayut*, Dov has neutralized the financial benefit he would otherwise derive from the testimony, and he is now permitted to testify.

### Achrayut Permits Testimo…

The resulting *halacha* is as follows: Dov may perform a proper *kinyan* transferring his half of the field to Bobby, accept *achrayut* specifically for losses arising from his own debts (*achrayut d'ati leh machmateh*), and thereafter testify on Bobby's behalf against David's claim. Under these conditions, he neither benefits from defeating David (since that protects Bobby against *achrayut d'alma*, for which Dov accepted no liability), nor benefits from preserving the field's legal lineage (since any gain from a creditor collecting from Bobby would be offset by his obligation to reimburse her). The Gemara does not yet directly confront the concern that Dov is simply executing a temporary maneuver — transferring the field, testifying, and then reclaiming his stake from Bobby afterwards. That concern lurks behind the entire discussion and will be addressed through the cases that follow.

---

## Renouncing Stake Debate

### Mistaleik Question

The Gemara now presses the deeper question: even granting that the technical requirements have been met, when a partner removes himself from ownership of the field, is that removal genuine? The Rashbam explains that what the Gemara is probing is precisely the concern of a temporary arrangement — Dov transfers his stake, testifies, and then Bobby quietly transfers it back. The testimony may be entirely truthful, but the divestment is merely instrumental. Can we accept such a procedure, or do we say that *mistaleik nafshia mineih* — his removal of himself — is not a genuine *mistaleik*?

### Sefer Torah Case

The Gemara brings a compelling *Baraita* as evidence. The *Baraita* states: *bnei ir she-ganvu sefer Torah shelahen* — the people of a town whose Sefer Torah was stolen — *ein danin be-dayanei ota ha'ir v'ein mevi'in ra'ayah me'anshei ota ha'ir*. The townspeople cannot serve as judges in the case, and the townspeople cannot serve as witnesses. Every member of the community jointly owns the Sefer Torah and stands to benefit directly from its recovery. They are all *ba'alei din* in the matter.

The practical consequence is startling: the only people who witnessed the theft are the townspeople, and none of them can testify. The thief may well escape accountability. (A similar structural problem arose in the time of the *Rishonim* in *Ashkenaz*, where the only available witnesses to certain commercial transactions were women, who are *pasul* as witnesses under standard *hilchos eidus*. Communal practice eventually developed to treat women's statements not as formal testimony but as credible evidence — a parallel accommodation to the same underlying tension.)

Now, if renunciation of ownership were a reliable mechanism for restoring eligibility to testify, why not simply have two townspeople formally divest themselves of their ownership share in the Sefer Torah and then serve as witnesses or judges, while the remaining community members constitute the other roles? The Gemara raises exactly this: *yisalku be-trei minaihu u-ladun* — let two people step aside and adjudicate. The *Baraita*'s silence on this solution implies it would not work.

### Permanent Beneficiary

The reason it does not work is that ownership of the Sefer Torah is not what constitutes the problem. Even a townsperson who holds no monetary ownership stake in the Sefer Torah is a *beneficiary* of its presence in the community. The Sefer Torah enables *Kriyat HaTorah*, the regular Shabbos leining, the entire fabric of communal Torah life. One might argue that *mitzvot lav le-hanot nitenu* — fulfilling mitzvot is not considered a form of personal benefit. Nonetheless, the Gemara's position is that the ability to maintain regular communal Torah reading constitutes sufficient benefit to render every townsperson a *nogei'a* in the case, regardless of their monetary ownership status. A person cannot renounce a benefit they will continue to receive simply by virtue of living in the town and using its shul.

This is a different and more expansive category of disqualification than mere financial interest. The witness need not own the Sefer Torah or have a monetary stake in its return; the indirect, ongoing, communal benefit of having a functioning Sefer Torah in the town is enough. Renouncing one's property interest cannot cure what is not a property problem to begin with.

### Town Donation Case

The Gemara adduces a further proof. The case: someone declares a donation of a *maneh* — a substantial sum — to the people of his city for general civic purposes, and then denies having made the pledge. The townspeople are the only witnesses. The *Baraita* rules: *ein danin be-dayanei ota ha'ir v'ein mevi'in ra'ayah me'anshei ota ha'ir* — the townspeople may neither serve as judges nor as witnesses. Again, why not have two of them renounce their anticipated share of the donation and testify? The fact that the *Baraita* does not entertain this solution implies that such renunciation is not accepted.

### Public Goods Benefit

The Gemara's analysis of this case becomes more granular. It raises an intermediate puzzle about the version of this case that concerns a donation to the *aniyim* — the poor of the city. If the benefit flows exclusively to the poor, why are the judges of the city disqualified? The judges are not poor; they will not receive the funds. The Gemara therefore revises the formulation: the ruling applies to the *dayanei aniyei ota ha'ir* — the poor of the city cannot be judges, and the poor of the city cannot be witnesses, since they are the direct beneficiaries.

The Gemara then reintroduces the question of why the entire community is disqualified, not merely the poor. The answer: *u-va'aniyei d'ramu aleihu* — it is the responsibility of the entire community to provide for its poor. When a donor pledges a large sum for the poor, he alleviates a burden that falls on every resident. The entire community therefore benefits, which is why no one can testify or adjudicate.

### Fixed Contributions

One might think this concern could be addressed by individuals committing to pay their fixed share regardless of the donation. If Nissan and David declare they will continue contributing their usual amount as though the donation had never been pledged, they no longer benefit from it — can they then testify? The Gemara explores this. If contributions are *katzuv* — fixed in advance — then in principle it might seem that two individuals could formally commit to paying their full fixed share and thereby divest themselves of the benefit of the donation. But the Gemara offers two responses.

First, the immediate case is one where contributions are *lo katzuv* — not fixed in advance. The amount owed is determined dynamically, assessed according to communal need and individual means. When a large donation arrives, it reduces everyone's assessment proportionally. There is no fixed amount any individual can pre-commit to, and so there is no mechanism by which a person can remove themselves from the benefit pool.

Second, even where amounts are fixed, there is an indirect benefit: *keivan de-revach, revach* — once substantial funds have been received for the poor, there is no urgency in collecting from anyone. Even those who will ultimately pay their full share benefit from the breathing room — the immediate pressure is off. This residual benefit, the Gemara concludes, cannot be renounced and therefore disqualifies even those who commit to paying in full.

The conclusion that emerges from all of this is significant. The Gemara's general position — outside the special cases of *Sefer Torah* and communal donations — is that genuine divestment of a financial interest through formal *kinyan* does remove a person from the category of *nogei'a* and permits testimony. We are not categorically afraid that after winning the case the witness will reclaim his stake. It is specifically the Sefer Torah and communal donation cases where the benefit is irreducibly public, cannot be renounced, and therefore permanently disqualifies.

---

## Rishonim Solutions

### Tosafot Approach

Having worked through the Gemara's cases, the *Rishonim* raise a serious structural question. There is a well-established principle: *techilato bi-fsol ve-sofo be-kashrus pasul* — if a witness was disqualified at the time the relevant events occurred, he remains disqualified even if his situation subsequently changes. The classic example: I witness my brother-in-law borrow money. At the time, I am *pasul* as a witness because of our familial relationship. Later, I divorce my wife and the relationship is severed. I cannot testify about what I saw, because *techilato bi-fsol* — at the outset I was invalid.

Why, then, does the Gemara allow a partner who has divested his stake to subsequently testify? At the time he was present and aware of the facts bearing on the case, he was a full owner — clearly disqualified. His later divestment should be no more effective than my later divorce.

Tosafot addresses this by drawing a distinction between two types of disqualification: *beguf* and *be-mamon* — personal status versus financial interest. Being a brother-in-law is a *status* — it attaches to the person as a classificatory label. That label being present at the time of witnessing generates the *techilato bi-fsol* concern. Financial interest, by contrast, is not a status — it is a contingent, situational condition. At any given moment the question is simply: does this person currently stand to gain? If the financial interest has been genuinely eliminated through transfer, there is no residual label of *pasul* that carries forward. The disqualification was never about who the person *is*, only about what benefit he *stands to receive*, and once that benefit is gone, so is the disqualification.

### Ra'avad Framework

A more conceptually elegant approach is attributed to the Ra'avad, who draws a fundamental distinction between two different legal categories: *ba'al din* and *nogei'a be-edut*. A *ba'al din* is the direct litigant — the person whose money or property is immediately at stake in the litigation. A *nogei'a be-edut* (also *nogei'a ba-davar*) is not the litigant himself, but someone who will indirectly benefit from the outcome — a vested interest, but at one remove.

In the partnership cases, before divestment, the partner is a direct *ba'al din*: it is his field, his money on the line. After divestment but before the disqualifying concern about creditor liens is resolved, he is a *nogei'a be-edut*: no longer the direct litigant, but still indirectly benefiting. These are not merely two points on a spectrum — they are categorically different legal statuses.

The Ra'avad argues that *techilato bi-fsol* applies to *nogei'a be-edut*, not to *ba'al din*. The reason is this: a *ba'al din* is not a *pasul eid* — he is a *non-eid*. A litigant and a witness occupy mutually exclusive roles; the litigant is simply not functioning as a witness at all. Since the partner who was a *ba'al din* was never classified as a *pasul eid*, he never acquired the negative label that *techilato bi-fsol* would then perpetuate. Once he divests himself and is no longer a *ba'al din*, he steps into the role of witness for the first time — and at that moment, he is *kasher*.

The irony is striking: the person who had the larger stake — the direct owner, the *ba'al din* — may more readily transition into a valid witness upon divestment than someone who had a lesser, more indirect interest, since the latter was already functioning in the domain of testimony (as a *nogei'a be-edut*) and therefore accumulated a disqualifying history. The Ra'avad's approach is thoroughly formalistic rather than pragmatic, but it illuminates with precision the conceptual boundaries of *techilato bi-fsol* as applied to the testimony of interested parties.

---

## Shomer Sachar Zeh

### Watching Arrangement

The Gemara turns to Shmuel's third point: partners are *shomrei sachar zeh l'zeh* — each serves as a paid watchman for the other's portion of the field. The scenario is as follows: Bobby and Dov jointly own a field. Bobby is watching the field entirely on her own, while Dov is away attending to other matters. Bobby falls asleep, and thieves damage or destroy the field. Bobby obviously bears responsibility for her own half of the loss. But does she bear responsibility for Dov's half as well?

The answer is yes — she is a *shomer sachar* with respect to his portion, and therefore liable. A *shomer sachar* bears liability for negligence (including falling asleep on the job), unlike a *shomer chinam* who has a more limited liability. Since Bobby was watching the entire field, her negligence applies to the whole of it, and she owes Dov for his half of the loss.

The Gemara, however, raises an immediate objection: surely this is a case of *shemirah be-ba'alim* — watching being performed while the owner is simultaneously in the watchman's service. The principle of *shemirah be-ba'alim* exempts a watchman from all liability when the owner is actively working for him at the time the *shemirah* began. If Bobby is watching Dov's portion, and Dov is simultaneously watching Bobby's portion from New Jersey (as partners in a jointly owned field there), then at the very moment Bobby is watching for Dov, Dov is watching for Bobby. The mutual, simultaneous exchange of services should invoke *shemirah be-ba'alim* and exempt Bobby entirely.

### Alternating Watch Days

Rav Papa resolves this: the case is not one of simultaneous watching. Rather, the arrangement is *shemor li hayom ani eshmor lecha le-machar* — watch for me today, and I will watch for you tomorrow. On Bobby's watch day, Dov is genuinely off duty and is not providing any service to Bobby. He is not in her employ today. Tomorrow, when it is his turn to watch, Bobby will be off. The exchange is sequential, not simultaneous, and therefore *shemirah be-ba'alim* does not apply on any given day. Since the partners are compensating each other with their respective service — each paying for the other's watch day with their own watch day — each is classified as a *shomer sachar* when it is their turn to watch. Bobby's liability for Dov's loss on her watch day is therefore intact.

---

## Machar Lo Bayis Case

### Field Sale Problem

The Gemara now introduces a new *Baraita* that picks up the theme of *achrayut* and testimony in the context of sale. The *Baraita* states: if one sells a house or a field to another person (*machar lo bayis*, *machar lo sadeh*), the seller cannot testify on the buyer's behalf regarding that property — *mipnei she-achrayuso alav* — because the seller's liability remains attached to it. The assumption is that when a field is sold, the seller implicitly accepts *achrayut* — warranty liability — such that if the buyer later loses the field to a creditor or a claimant, the seller must reimburse him. This gives the seller a direct financial interest in any litigation that could disturb the buyer's title, and therefore disqualifies him as a witness.

### Movable Goods Contrast

The *Baraita* then offers a contrasting case: if one sells a cow (*machar lo parah*) or a garment (*machar lo tallis*) — movable goods — the seller *can* testify on the buyer's behalf. The reason given: *ein achrayuso alav* — there is no liability on him. At first glance this seems puzzling, because if the movable item turns out to have been stolen, the transaction is a *mekach ta'os* — a mistaken sale — and the seller would owe restitution even without any formal warranty. He cannot simply claim he had no liability; he sold something he didn't legitimately own.

### Difference Question

This generates the natural question with which the daf concludes: *mai shena reisha u-mai shena seifa* — what is the difference between the first case (field) and the latter case (movable goods)? In both cases, the seller stands to benefit from testimony that confirms the buyer's ownership, since in both cases a successful claim by the original owner would expose the seller to liability. Why does the Gemara treat these cases differently? The *Baraita* appears to assert a distinction, but the grounds for it are not yet clear. The Gemara's resolution of this question, which will require some creative interpretation of the underlying principles, is deferred to the following daf.

---

---

# Bava Batra 44

## Initial Baraita & Comple…

### Baraita: No Testimony Po…

The sugya of today's daf opens in the middle of 43b, with the *Tanna* presenting a *baraita* that sets out the fundamental rule governing witness disqualification in cases involving sales. The *baraita* states: *machar lo bayit, machar lo sadeh* — if Reuven sells Shimon a house or a field, *ein me'id lo aleha*, Reuven cannot testify on Shimon's behalf if someone challenges Shimon's ownership of that property. The reason the *baraita* gives is *mipnei she-achrayuto alav* — because the liability rests upon him. The straightforward reading of this phrase is that Reuven has insured the sale: if Shimon loses the property, Reuven will have to reimburse him. This obvious interest in the outcome of any ownership dispute disqualifies Reuven from testifying.

The *baraita* then presents a contrasting case: *machar lo parah, machar lo talit* — if Reuven sold Shimon chattel, a cow or a garment, then *me'id lo aleha*, Reuven may testify on Shimon's behalf. The reason is *mipnei she-ein achrayuto alav* — because he bears no responsibility for it. This distinction between land and chattel is the crux of the *baraita*, and the *Gemara* immediately presses it: since in either case, if the original transaction was tainted — if Reuven never legitimately owned the property — Shimon could return to Reuven and demand his money back, Reuven has an obvious stake in the outcome regardless of whether the sold item is land or chattel. The *Gemara* therefore asks: *mai shna resha u-mai shna seifa* — what distinguishes the opening case from the closing one?

### Theft→Sale→Claim Scenario

To answer this question, Rav Sheshet proposes a highly unusual reading of the *baraita*, one that the *Gemara* will ultimately abandon. The case Rav Sheshet constructs is as follows. Shimon is the rightful owner of a field. Reuven commits *gezeilah* — he steals the field from Shimon — and then sells it to Levi. Now a fourth party, Yehuda, arrives and claims that the field is his.

On this reading, the *baraita*'s language is radically reinterpreted. *Machar lo bayit* — "he sold him a house" — now refers to Reuven's sale of the stolen field to Levi. *Ein me'id alav* — "he cannot testify about it" — refers to Shimon, the original owner, who is prohibited from testifying in the dispute between Levi and Yehuda. And *mipnei she-achrayuto alav* — "because the liability rests upon him" — is twisted to mean not that Reuven must reimburse Shimon, but rather that Shimon somehow has a stake in the field's disposition. This is, as even the *Gemara* will concede, a highly strained reading of the *baraita*'s language, and a needlessly complicated construction of the underlying case. We will not ultimately stay with it, but the *Gemara* works through it in order to expose exactly what is at stake.

The core question is this: why can't Shimon testify in the case between Levi and Yehuda? Shimon is the true owner of the field; Reuven stole it from him and sold it to Levi. Now Yehuda claims it is his. Can Shimon step in and testify against Yehuda's claim, effectively supporting Levi's position in the dispute? The answer is that Shimon has a vested interest — he ultimately wants his field back. The only question is whether that interest is sufficient to disqualify him.

### Why Block Testimony?

One might initially wonder: if Shimon wants his field back, he is going to have to fight for it regardless of whether Levi or Yehuda ends up holding it. So why does it matter to Shimon who wins this case? Why should his interest in the ultimate disposition of the field between Levi and Yehuda be considered a disqualifying stake?

The question becomes sharper when one notes that Shimon, by testifying that the field is not Yehuda's, is effectively saying it belongs to Levi. But in doing so he is also implicitly admitting that the field does not belong to him, since the only way to claim it for Levi in court is to act as a witness on Levi's behalf rather than as a claimant on his own behalf. One might therefore argue that by testifying, Shimon relinquishes his own claim — and a person is surely not going to surrender his own rights without something to gain. This leads the *Gemara* to scrutinize carefully what Shimon does and does not stand to gain.

### Shimon's Self-Interest I…

The *Gemara* raises the following point: *vekivan de-asei lei de-Levi hu, heichi mati mapik lei minei* — once Shimon testifies that the field belongs to Levi, how could he ever subsequently extract the field from Levi's hands? By testifying that it is Levi's, he has made an implicit admission in court that it is not his own. That admission should bind him, and he should not be able to subsequently claim the field for himself.

In response, the *Gemara* clarifies the precise nature of Shimon's potential testimony. Shimon is not testifying affirmatively that the field *is* Levi's. His testimony is *yadana dehai ara delav Yehuda hi* — he is testifying that this field is not Yehuda's. Together with another witness, Shimon can establish a negative fact about Yehuda's claim without making a positive assertion about his own ownership or about Levi's title. This distinction is what allows Shimon theoretically to retain his own claim even after testifying. The *Gemara* then asks: if Shimon testifies that it is not Yehuda's and the field therefore stays with Levi, what has Shimon gained? He still has to prove the field is his in a subsequent proceeding, and he can do that whether his adversary is Levi or Yehuda.

### Opponent Preference Moti…

The *Gemara*'s answer is: *hasheini noach li, harishon kasheh mimenu* — it is easier for Shimon to prevail against Levi than against Yehuda. The two adversaries are not equal in Shimon's estimation. Since Shimon knows he will eventually have to litigate to reclaim his field, it matters to him who his opponent will be. If Yehuda is a more formidable litigant, Shimon has a concrete interest in ensuring the field lands with Levi rather than with Yehuda. Since this interest exists, Shimon is disqualified from testifying in the dispute between Levi and Yehuda.

A second scenario the *Gemara* presents sharpens this further: *kigon de-ika sahadei le-mar ve-ika sahadei le-mar* — suppose Yehuda has two witnesses supporting his claim and there is a contradictory pair of witnesses on the other side. The rule in such a case of equally-matched witnesses contesting ownership of land is *kol dalim gevar* — the party currently in possession retains it, since the court will not intervene when the testimony is evenly balanced. Now consider Shimon's calculation. If he sits out the Levi–Yehuda dispute, and Yehuda wins, then when Shimon later brings his own two witnesses to prove the field is his, he will be met by Yehuda's two witnesses — two against two — and Yehuda, now in possession, will simply retain the field. But if Shimon gets involved now and engineers a Levi victory, then when Shimon subsequently asserts his claim against Levi, his witnesses will establish his title. Levi, now in possession, will be forced to confront Shimon's evidence. The prior ruling against Yehuda removed Yehuda's witnesses from the equation. So Shimon's testimony in the Levi–Yehuda dispute is not neutral — it is strategically valuable to him.

With this, the *Gemara* has worked out the logic of Rav Sheshet's complicated reading of the *baraita*. The basic principle is clear: a person cannot testify in a dispute if the outcome of that dispute will affect his own future litigation over the same property, even indirectly and even through a chain of calculations. The challenge, however, is that this elaborate construction requires a very forced reading of the *baraita*'s language, and the *Gemara* will soon show that the complexity is unnecessary.

The *Gemara* asks: if this complicated multi-party scenario is what the *baraita* intended, why did the *baraita* need to introduce the element of a sale to Levi at all? The underlying logic — that Shimon cannot testify because it affects who he will eventually fight to reclaim the field — would apply equally if Reuven had simply stolen the field from Shimon without selling it. The sale to Levi seems unnecessary for the principle being conveyed. The *Gemara* answers that the sale was necessary in order to generate the distinction between land and chattel that the *baraita* draws in its second half: *d'ba'i l'misni seifa, machar lo parah, machar lo talit* — the *baraita* needed to reach the case of the cow and garment. Why can Shimon testify about chattel?

The answer offered at this stage is that if Reuven stole chattel — say, a cow — and sold it to Levi, then *ye'ush v'shinui reshut* comes into play. Once Shimon despaired of recovering the cow (*ye'ush*) and it then passed into another person's possession (*shinui reshut*), Shimon has lost his legal right to reclaim the physical cow. Levi now owns it regardless of how it got there. Since Shimon will never recover the cow itself, he has no stake in whether it remains with Levi or goes to Yehuda. He can therefore testify freely about the chattel. But by land — since land is not subject to *ye'ush* in the same way, and Shimon retains the ability to eventually reclaim his land — he has a stake in the dispute and cannot testify.

However, the *Gemara* immediately raises a problem with this explanation. Even if Shimon cannot recover the cow itself, can he not recover *compensation*? If the *gazlan* — Reuven — is alive, perhaps Shimon can still collect the value of the cow from him. If so, it matters to Shimon whether the cow is established as originally Yehuda's or originally his own, because that affects whether he can recover payment. The *Gemara* answers: *tzricha d'meis lei gazlan* — the case requires that Reuven has died. If the *gazlan* died without leaving estate assets from which debts can be collected, then Shimon cannot recover compensation either. The *Gemara* cites the *mishnah*: *hagozel u-ma'achil es banav... pturim milishalem* — one who steals and feeds his children, or bequeaths the stolen item, the heirs are not obligated to pay. So with Reuven dead, Shimon has neither the cow nor the prospect of compensation, and therefore no stake in the dispute.

The *Gemara* then asks: *v'lokmah b'yoresh* — if Reuven died, then the cow passed to his heirs, which is itself a *shinui reshut* of sorts. Why did the *baraita* need to introduce the sale to Levi to explain why Shimon cannot reclaim the cow? The death and inheritance by Reuven's son would have been sufficient on its own. The *Gemara* answers that this depends on a dispute: there is an opinion that *reshus yoresh lav k'reshus lokeach dami* — inheritance is not considered a true change of possession equivalent to a sale. On that view, inheriting does not cut off Shimon's right to reclaim the cow, so the sale to Levi remains necessary. But according to the opinion that *reshus yoresh k'reshus lokeach dami* — that inheriting is equivalent to a sale — Levi need not appear in the picture at all. This means the *baraita*'s introduction of a sale to Levi is unnecessary on at least one major opinion, further undermining the entire construction.

Abaye adds another objection. The *baraita* says Shimon cannot testify because of *achrayuto alav* — because of the liability upon him — and in the contrasting case, *ein achrayuto alav* — there is no liability. But on Rav Sheshet's reading, the word *achrayut* is being used in an entirely foreign sense: the real reason Shimon can't testify about land is that he might eventually get the land back, and the reason he can testify about chattel is that he cannot. This has nothing to do with *achrayut* in any recognized sense of the term. The word is simply wrong for the case. This linguistic objection compounds the structural ones, and together they compel the *Gemara* to abandon this entire reading.

---

## Simpler Reading (Liens)

### Abaye's Objections

To summarize the difficulties: the construction requires an improbably complex multi-party scenario, depends on the death of one of the central figures, is unnecessary on one of the two positions regarding inherited possession, and misuses the term *achrayut*. These converging objections leave the *Gemara* no choice but to seek an entirely different reading of the *baraita*.

### Rabin bar Shmuel Explana…

The *Gemara* introduces the resolution with: *ela ki de-Rabin bar Shmuel* — the correct way to read this *baraita* is in light of a teaching reported by Rabin bar Shmuel in the name of Shmuel. That teaching states: *ha-mocher sadeh le-chavero shelo be-achrayut, ein me'id lo aleha mipnei she-maamidah bifnei ba'al chovo* — one who sells a field to another person *shelo be-achrayut*, that is, without warranty, without guaranteeing to reimburse the buyer if the field is taken from him, nonetheless cannot testify on the buyer's behalf if someone challenges the buyer's title. The reason: *mipnei she-maamidah bifnei ba'al chovo* — because by keeping the field in the buyer's hands, the seller is facilitating recovery by his own creditor.

This is a striking principle and worth dwelling on. The simple case is as follows. Reuven sells Shimon a field without warranty. Reuven owes Mordechai a thousand dinars. Now Yehuda comes and claims the field belongs to him. Can Reuven testify that no, the field legitimately belongs to Shimon? If Reuven had *given warranty* — if he had insured the sale — then obviously he cannot testify, because if Yehuda wins and the field is taken from Shimon, Reuven will have to reimburse Shimon. His financial interest is obvious. But what if Reuven gave *no* warranty? One might think that with no obligation to reimburse Shimon, Reuven has no stake in whether Yehuda wins or not — so why not let him testify? The *chiddush* of Rabin bar Shmuel is that Reuven cannot testify even without warranty, because he has a different kind of stake: if the field is established as something that was once Reuven's and was sold to Shimon, then Mordechai can collect his debt from that field even though it is now in Shimon's hands — that is how creditor liens on land work. But if the field is established as always having belonged to Yehuda, then Reuven's sale of it was a nullity, Mordechai's lien never attached to that field, and Mordechai is left without recourse. Reuven therefore has a concrete interest in seeing the field remain in Shimon's hands as a legitimately sold parcel.

### Creditor Liens on Land

On this reading, the *baraita*'s language becomes entirely natural. *Machar lo bayit, machar lo sadeh, ein me'id lo alav mipnei she-achrayuto alav* — *achrayuto alav* now means precisely what it normally means: there is *achrayut*, there are liens, on this property. The seller cannot testify because the existence of those liens gives him a stake in the property's disposition. *Machar lo parah, machar lo talit, me'id lo aleha mipnei she-ein achrayuto alav* — *ein achrayuto alav* now means precisely what it says: there are no liens on chattel. Mordechai has no lien on Bessie the cow. If the field is taken, Mordechai can collect from it; if Bessie is taken, Mordechai has no claim on her. Therefore Reuven has no stake in whether Bessie remains with Shimon or goes to Yehuda, and he can testify freely.

This reading requires no bizarre multi-party scenarios, no fictitious deaths, no dependence on disputed opinions about inheritance, and no distortion of the word *achrayut*. After the elaborate *Gemara* that preceded it, the simplicity of Rabin bar Shmuel's reading is striking — one wonders why the *Gemara* did not arrive here immediately.

The principle that creditors hold liens on land requires some elaboration. When Reuven borrows money from Mordechai, Mordechai does not merely have a claim on Reuven's current cash. He has a *shibud* — a lien — on Reuven's land. If Reuven later sells that land to Shimon, Mordechai can, in certain circumstances, seize that land from Shimon to satisfy the debt, since the lien was created before the sale. This is the mechanism by which a seller maintains a stake in the continued disposition of land even after he has sold it: his creditors' rights travel with the land through the sale.

### Land vs. Chattel Liens

The critical distinction is that this lien mechanism applies to land but not to chattel. *Lo mibaya b'stama* — it goes without saying that in the ordinary case there are no liens on movable property. *Metaltlei ninhu, u-metaltlei l'ba'al chov lo mishtabdei* — they are chattel, and chattel is not encumbered to a creditor. The reasons are practical: a debtor can always conceal his movable property from creditors, and purchasers of chattel have no way to check for outstanding liens the way they might investigate a piece of land. The law therefore does not create liens on chattel in the ordinary case.

---

## Liens & Collateral Rules

### Non-Designated Chattel R…

The *Gemara* now examines the boundaries of this rule more carefully. The general principle is that chattel is not subject to creditor liens. This is true in the standard case where no explicit designation of the chattel as collateral was made. *D'la mishtabdei lei* — the property simply is not encumbered. A creditor who is owed money by Reuven has no claim on Bessie once Bessie has been sold to Shimon. Mordechai's recourse is limited to property that remains in Reuven's hands or, in the case of land, to property that has passed through Reuven's hands via a documented sale.

A creditor does have the right, of course, to seize the shirt off a debtor's back — literally, *niglima d'al katfei*. He can collect from any property currently in the debtor's possession. But *aval leitneihu b'eineihu, lo* — if those items are no longer in the debtor's possession, having been sold or transferred, there is no lien and no right to collect from the new owner. The distinction is between *in personam* collection from the debtor's present property and *in rem* collection from property that was once the debtor's but has since passed to a third party. Only land supports the latter.

### Slave as Collateral

The *Gemara* introduces a partial exception through the opinion of Rava: *asa avdo apotiki, umacharo, ba'al chov goveh heimenu* — if Reuven designated his slave as *apotiki* — designated collateral — and subsequently sold the slave, the creditor can still collect from the slave even in the hands of the buyer. But *shor v'chamor apotiki, umacharo, ein ba'al chov goveh heimenu* — if the designated collateral was an ox or a donkey or any other chattel that is not a slave, the creditor cannot collect from it once it has been sold.

Why the difference between a slave and other chattel? The *Gemara* explains: *hai it lei kala v'hai leit lei kala* — a slave has *kol*, public awareness, while other chattel does not. The *Rashbam* elaborates: when a creditor designates a slave as collateral, this is known — people are aware that this slave has been placed under a lien. A potential buyer of the slave can therefore investigate and discover the encumbrance: *afsidu lokachot anafsheihu* — buyers who proceed despite the public knowledge have only themselves to blame. But when a cow is designated as collateral, this information is not similarly public, and buyers have no way to know. Holding them responsible for a lien they could not have discovered would be unjust and would destabilize commerce in chattel generally.

The connection to real estate is also noted: slaves are in certain respects treated like land in halachic analysis — *eved hokesh l'karka* — and this broader association with the more publicly-documented realm of real property may contribute to the rule's application to slaves.

### Bundling via Shtar

The *Gemara* now raises a complication: what if Reuven, when he borrowed money from Mordechai, explicitly bundled his chattel together with his land in the loan document? *V'leikhush dilma aknei leh metaltalei agav mekarkai* — perhaps we should be concerned that Reuven granted Mordechai a lien on his chattel *agav karka*, by attaching the chattel to the land in a written *shtar*. Rava rules: *yakni leh metaltalei agav mekarkai, kani mekarkai, kani metaltalei* — if one transfers chattel together with land, the transfer of the land effects the transfer — or in this context, the lien on — the chattel as well. If this mechanism was used when Reuven borrowed from Mordechai, then Bessie too might be subject to Mordechai's lien, and Reuven would again have a stake in whether Bessie remains with Shimon.

Rav Chisda adds a condition for this mechanism to be legally effective: the language in the *shtar* must state *de-la ke-as-machtah u-de-la ke-tofshei de-shtarei* — that it is not a mere formality and not boilerplate. The debtor must signal that he genuinely intends to subject his chattel to the lien, not merely repeat standard contractual language.

### Ketubah & Future Property

This leads naturally to a discussion of the language of the *ketubah*, which the *Gemara* introduces because the *ketubah*'s standard formulation addresses precisely these issues. The *nusach* of the *ketubah* includes the phrase *v'kabbilit alai v'al yartai batrai l'hitpara mikol shefar arag nichsin v'kinyanin* — the husband obligates himself and his heirs to pay from all of his possessions, *d'it li t'chot kol shamaya*, everything under the heavens that he owns, *d'kanai v'da'atid ana l'miknei* — what he owns now and what he will acquire in the future. The *ketubah* then explicitly specifies: *nechasin d'it l'hon achrayut u-d'leit l'hon achrayut* — property that has *achrayut*, meaning land, and property that does not, meaning chattel. And it concludes with language to the effect that this is not boilerplate — *de-la ke-asmachta u-de-la ke-tofshei de-shtarei*.

The *ketubah*, then, is an example of a *shtar* that explicitly bundles land and chattel together, subjects both to a lien, and includes the declaration that this is sincerely meant and not merely formulaic. This means that in principle, any married person who sells chattel is selling it subject to the wife's *ketubah* lien — a striking consequence that the *Gemara* does not flinch from acknowledging.

The earlier phrase in the *ketubah*, *v'afilu miglima d'al katfei* — even from the garment on his back — refers only to property currently in the husband's possession. Once that garment has been sold, the lien cannot follow it unless the *agav karka* bundling mechanism was employed. The *ketubah* uses both formulations: the general pledge of all current possessions including chattel, and the *d'kanai v'da'atid ana l'miknei*, which brings us to the next point.

### Future Property Liens

*D'kanai v'da'atid ana l'miknei* — what I own now and what I will acquire in the future. This phrase raises the question of whether one can create a lien on property that does not yet exist — *davar she-lo ba la-olam*. The general rule is that one cannot transfer or obligate something that does not yet exist. Can a *shibud* attach to future acquisitions?

The *Gemara* uses this uncertainty to explain why Reuven can testify about Bessie in the standard case. The argument proceeds: we should perhaps be concerned that when Reuven borrowed money from Mordechai, he used the *de-ikni* language — committing future acquisitions as collateral — and therefore even Bessie, acquired after the loan, is subject to Mordechai's lien. The *Gemara* answers that this concern does not arise here because witnesses testify that *lo hava leh ara me-olam* — Reuven never in his life owned land. Since the *agav karka* mechanism requires land, and Reuven had no land, there was no way to bundle Bessie into a lien even with explicit language. Therefore, Reuven has no stake in Bessie's disposition and can testify.

The *Gemara* then asks whether from this analysis we should derive a general ruling: *shma mina de-ikni kana u-machar, lo mishtaabed* — that the *de-ikni* formulation does not actually create liens on subsequently purchased and sold property. The *Gemara* declines to draw that conclusion definitively, leaving the status of future-property liens unresolved.

---

## False Sale & Reimburseme…

### Mekach Taut Issue

Having established through Rabin bar Shmuel's reading that Reuven can testify about sold chattel because there are no creditor liens on it, the *Gemara* raises a separate and significant problem. The question of creditor liens has been resolved — Mordechai cannot collect from Bessie once she is in Shimon's hands. But there is another reason Reuven might have a stake in the outcome of the dispute between Shimon and Yehuda.

What if Yehuda's claim is correct? What if Bessie always belonged to Yehuda and Reuven had no right to sell her? In that case, the sale from Reuven to Shimon was a *mekach taut* — a mistaken or false sale. And a seller who conveys property that turns out not to have been his is liable to reimburse the buyer regardless of whether he gave warranty. The warranty arrangement — *achrayut* — covers the case where the seller's creditors come and seize the property; a *mekach taut* is a different and more fundamental defect. One does not need warranty language to recover from a seller who sold you something he did not own — the very premise of the transaction was invalid.

Rav Papa expresses this rule explicitly: *ha-mocher sadeh le-chavero shelo be-achrayut, uva ba'al chov u-trafah, eino chozer alav* — if you sold without warranty and a creditor came and seized it, you do not have to reimburse. *Nimtzet she-einah shelo, chozer alav* — but if it turns out the item was never yours to begin with, you do have to reimburse. This means that if Reuven sold Bessie without warranty and Yehuda actually proves that Bessie was always his, Reuven is on the hook for reimbursing Shimon. Reuven therefore has a clear stake in whether Yehuda wins — if Yehuda wins, Reuven pays. How then can Reuven ever testify about Bessie?

### Buyer's Admission

The *Gemara* answers: *hacha be-mai askinan be-makir bah she-hi bat chamoro* — this is a case where Shimon explicitly acknowledged before witnesses that he recognized the animal as having been born from Reuven's own donkey or cow, meaning that Shimon concedes the animal always belonged to Reuven and that the sale was legitimate. Once Shimon has made this admission to Reuven — I know this is genuinely your animal — Shimon has forfeited any future claim for reimbursement even in the event that Yehuda somehow wins in court. Shimon cannot later turn to Reuven and say you sold me something that was not yours, because Shimon himself admitted it was Reuven's. Therefore, Reuven faces no liability toward Shimon regardless of the court's outcome, and his testimony about Bessie is free of any self-interest.

### Rav Zvid: Buyer Beware

Rav Zvid, however, takes a more far-reaching position: *afillu nimtzet she-einah shelo, eino chozer alav* — even if it subsequently turns out that the item was never Reuven's, Shimon still cannot demand reimbursement. Why? *De-amar leh lehachi zevinti lach shelo be-achrayut* — that is precisely what it means to buy something without warranty. When Shimon agreed to purchase without insurance, he accepted all of the risk — including the risk that the property might turn out not to have been the seller's to begin with. Buyer beware is total. Reuven's declaration of no warranty is not merely a hedge against creditor claims; it is a full disclaimer of liability even for a defective title.

This position generates a genuine dispute. The majority view, reflected in Rav Papa's formulation, holds that *shelo be-achrayut* protects the seller only against creditor seizures but not against a fundamental failure of title — when it turns out the item was genuinely not the seller's, the buyer can still recover. On this view, Reuven retains a stake in the Yehuda dispute whenever he sold without the buyer's acknowledgment that the sale was legitimate. Rav Zvid's view holds that *shelo be-achrayut* is a complete disclaimer, and that no reimbursement is ever owed when warranty was explicitly waived — the buyer assumed the totality of the risk. According to Rav Zvid, then, Reuven never has a *mekach taut* liability to Shimon once warranty is disclaimed, and the *mekach taut* problem does not arise as an obstacle to his testimony.

---

---

# Bava Batra 45

## Seller's Benefit

### Sale without Achrayut

The *daf* opens in the middle of a broader discussion about testimonial disqualification — specifically, the circumstances under which a witness stands to benefit from his own testimony and is therefore rendered invalid. The *gemara* resumes with the word *gufa*, signaling a return to a previously cited teaching. Ravina bar Shila transmits in the name of Shmuel: if Reuven sells a field to Shimon *shelo b'achrayut* — without guarantee — he cannot testify on Shimon's behalf to keep the field in his possession.

The case of a sale *with* guarantee (*achrayut*) requires no explanation: if the field is seized, Reuven will be obligated to reimburse Shimon, and his testimony protecting the field is transparently self-serving. One might have thought, however, that a sale *without achrayut* is different — that since Reuven bears no financial exposure if the field is taken, he has no stake in the outcome and should therefore be eligible to testify. The *gemara* rejects this intuition.

### Seller's Indirect Benefit

The reason Reuven is disqualified even without *achrayut* is that the field's continued presence in Shimon's possession still benefits him indirectly: *mipnei she-omedet bifnei ba'al chovo* — because the field stands available for Reuven's creditors to collect from. When Reuven sold the field to Shimon, it passed through Reuven's ownership. If a creditor of Reuven later seeks to collect a debt and Reuven has no available assets, that creditor may seize the field from Shimon, since it once passed through Reuven's hands. Accordingly, Reuven benefits from testimony that establishes the field as legitimately Shimon's: it keeps the field accessible for his creditors. Should the testimony fail and the field be shown never to have belonged to Reuven in the first place, his creditor would have no claim on it — and Reuven would be worse off.

This is not a new principle; the *gemara* notes this is the third occasion on which this reasoning has been cited. And as was discussed on the previous *daf*, the rule is not applied categorically in all conceivable circumstances: there were already cases noted where, if Reuven could be shown to have no connection to creditors, the concern might not apply.

### Creditor Collection Cases

The *gemara* on 45a now asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly are the relevant circumstances? Rather than asking the more elusive question of whether creditors actually exist (a near-impossible negative to prove), the *gemara* focuses on whether Reuven has other assets from which creditors could collect.

The first scenario considered is *d'is lei ara achriti* — if Reuven has other land. In that case, his creditors would collect directly from that other land, and the field that passed to Shimon is irrelevant to their recovery. Reuven gains nothing by keeping it in Shimon's hands, and the concern evaporates.

### Other Land Available

Why does the *gemara* speak specifically of land and not of other forms of wealth, such as money in the bank? The answer is that land is uniquely stable as an asset. Money can be spent, gambled away, or lost in bad investments. Land, by contrast, cannot simply disappear; if sold, the creditor can still collect from the buyer. Because land is the most reliable collateral for creditor collection, the *gemara* focuses on whether Reuven possesses other land as the benchmark for whether creditors will be made whole regardless of this field.

Even granting the *gemara*'s framework, one could still construct cases where having other land does not eliminate the benefit entirely. Suppose Reuven has exactly enough land to cover one of two creditors. If the field now in Shimon's hands is excluded from available assets, the second creditor receives nothing. By keeping it accessible, Reuven effectively ensures both creditors are satisfied — a genuine benefit. Additionally, a larger pool of unencumbered assets improves Reuven's creditworthiness for future borrowing. Nevertheless, the *gemara* is willing to set these more speculative concerns aside: since the entire creditor scenario is hypothetical to begin with, it does not press beyond the basic case.

### No Assets Case

The second scenario is *d'leis lei ara achriti* — Reuven has no other land. Here the *gemara* asks *mai nafka lei minei* — what benefit does Reuven actually derive? If Reuven has no other land (and, extending the reasoning, no other assets at all), then Levi the creditor cannot collect from Reuven under any circumstances. Whether the field remains in Shimon's hands or not, Levi is not being paid. Why, then, should this confer any testimonial benefit on Reuven?

Before recording the *gemara*'s answer, two obvious objections arise that the *gemara* conspicuously does not raise. First, Reuven might acquire assets in the future; if the debt is discharged now through the field, he would be freed of that future liability. Second, the *gemara* restricts its question to land, but Reuven may have other forms of movable property — *mitaltelin* — from which a creditor could collect. The reason the *gemara* does not use movable property as a *nafka mineh*, as becomes clear in context, is that creditors would pursue Reuven's own assets before turning to Shimon; if Reuven had movable property, the creditor would already be collecting from that directly and would never need to reach Shimon in the first place.

### Non-Indebtedness Benefit

The *gemara*'s actual answer is striking: even a person with no assets benefits from not being in a state of indebtedness. *De-amar lo nicha li, lo nicha de-lehevei loveh rasha ve-lo yeshalem* — he says, "It is not acceptable to me to be the type of person who borrows and does not repay." This is a genuinely resonant point. Even when the practical likelihood of ever repaying a debt is negligible, people feel a moral weight in carrying an outstanding obligation. The status of being a *loveh rasha* — a borrower who does not pay — is itself experienced as a burden, independent of any concrete monetary consequence. Reuven, therefore, benefits from testimony that keeps the field in Shimon's hands because it allows his creditor to be paid off, releasing him from that status.

This raises an interesting question about the nature of the benefit that disqualifies a witness. Is non-monetary, reputational, or psychological benefit sufficient? Perhaps it does have a concrete monetary dimension — a person burdened by outstanding debt has diminished creditworthiness and will find future borrowing more difficult or impossible. In that sense, there is a real economic value to clearing one's debt even when current assets are zero.

### Tosafot: Future vs Immed…

*Tosafot* raise a sharp question: the *gemara*'s silence is puzzling. The most obvious benefit of keeping the field in Shimon's hands — that if Reuven later acquires assets, he will never have to pay Levi because the debt would already have been discharged — goes entirely unmentioned by the *gemara*. *Tosafot* articulate this: *nafka minei she-yiftaru im yisasher* — there is a clear practical difference, namely that if Reuven later becomes wealthy, he will be free of the obligation. Why doesn't the *gemara* simply say that?

*Tosafot* then offer a possible resolution: *v'shama bishvil kein ein lefoslo le-eidut kivan de-hashta lo marviach midi* — perhaps the answer is that since there is no immediate, concrete benefit, the future and uncertain benefit is insufficient to disqualify Reuven from testifying. This surfaces a genuinely important methodological question: what kind of benefit triggers testimonial disqualification? An immediate, tangible gain is clearly sufficient. A future gain that is speculative and contingent may not be. The *gemara*'s choice to anchor the disqualification in the immediate non-indebtedness benefit — an intangible but present condition — rather than in the possibility of future asset acquisition, may reflect precisely this distinction.

## Non-Jew Seizure

### Reuven-Shimon-Marduk Case

Rava (and some say Rav Papa) made a public announcement directed at those traveling between *Eretz Yisrael* and *Bavel* in both directions — perhaps because the ruling that follows has relevance under different political conditions, whether under Roman or Persian rule. The case: a Jew sells a donkey to another Jew, and then a non-Jew — call him Marduk — arrives and seizes the donkey from the buyer, claiming it was always his.

This scenario is structurally parallel to the case of a Jew claiming seized land, but with two significant differences. First, the claimant is a non-Jew who may be operating either through his legal system or through sheer force. Second, the animal is *mitaltelin*, movable property, which raises different considerations than land.

Two distinct scenarios are in play. In the first, Marduk wins his claim in a secular court operating under its own legal principles, which may diverge substantially from *halakha*. Under Jewish law, *chazakah* — the presumption that what a person holds is his — would favor Shimon; a secular court might apply different evidentiary standards and rule for Marduk. In the second scenario, there is no legal proceeding at all — Marduk simply takes the donkey by force because he has the power to do so.

### Redemption Obligation

The *gemara* rules that *dina hu de-mafzei lei minei* — Reuven is obligated to assist Shimon in recovering the donkey. The *Rashbam* understands *mafzei* to mean that Reuven must take active steps to retrieve the donkey — bringing evidence in court, advocating on Shimon's behalf, doing what he can to help. The *Rambam*, more stringently, holds that Reuven must actually reimburse Shimon for the loss.

This is a remarkable ruling. Unlike the earlier discussion, which revolved around whether Reuven *may* testify, here Reuven is affirmatively *obligated* to act. The *gemara* even uses the language of *dina* — law, not merely moral suasion. Notably, this obligation seems to operate even in tension with the earlier cases, where Reuven's testimonial disqualification arose from his potential benefit. In the land cases, the technical prohibition against self-interested testimony overrides any moral duty Reuven might feel toward Shimon. Here, where that technical concern is absent, the moral-legal obligation reasserts itself.

### Shimon's Recognition

The *gemara* qualifies the rule: *ve-lo amrin ella she-eino makir be-shivat chamora* — this obligation applies only when Shimon does not recognize the donkey as definitively Reuven's. If Shimon cannot be certain that Marduk's claim is false — perhaps Marduk genuinely believes the donkey is his, or Shimon simply does not know the animal's full history — then from Shimon's perspective there is a real possibility that Reuven sold him something he never legitimately owned. That genuine uncertainty creates Reuven's obligation to come to Shimon's defense.

By contrast, *aval yada lei be-shivat chamora* — if Shimon knows with certainty that the donkey was born from Reuven's own animal, that he witnessed it in Reuven's stable — then Shimon understands perfectly well that Marduk's claim, whatever its legal vehicle, is substantively false. In that case, Reuven bears no obligation, because Shimon knows the seizure has nothing to do with Reuven's ownership and everything to do with power or foreign law.

### Saddle Test

How does one determine whether Marduk is making a genuine ownership claim or simply taking by force? The *gemara* offers a concrete indicator. If Marduk takes the donkey but leaves the saddle behind, this suggests he believes the donkey is genuinely his: he takes what he considers his property and leaves what he knows belongs to Shimon. The saddle is unambiguously Shimon's — no one disputes it — so if Marduk is acting in good faith, he would naturally leave it. In that case, Reuven is obligated to assist Shimon, because the seizure carries the markers of a legitimate (if perhaps mistaken) ownership claim.

If, however, Marduk takes both the donkey and the saddle together, he is plainly acting through force alone. He has no genuine claim to the saddle; he takes everything because he can. In that situation, Reuven bears no obligation to Shimon, because the seizure is transparently an act of *ones* — coercion unconnected to any plausible question about Reuven's original ownership.

### Ameimar's Position

Ameimar takes a sweeping contrary position: *afilu leika kol hani* — even if none of the indicators of forcible seizure are present, even if Marduk left the saddle and Shimon cannot verify the donkey's provenance, Ameimar would still not impose any obligation on Reuven. *Mai ta'ama? Bei yadei de-stama de-akum anuseihu* — because it is simply known that non-Jews as a rule seize property by force. The *gemara* cites a verse in support: *asher pihem diber shav vi-minam yemin shaker* — their mouths speak falsehood and their right hands are hands of deceit.

This is a striking and historically conditioned position. The *gemara*'s announcement that this ruling was directed to those going both to *Eretz Yisrael* and to *Bavel* is significant. The two communities operated under vastly different political regimes. The Roman government, which controlled *Eretz Yisrael* during the period of Hadrianic persecution, was viewed by *chazal* as deeply hostile and illegitimate; its tax collection was considered extortion. The Persian government in *Bavel* was considerably more benign, and the principle of *dina de-malchuta dina* — the law of the land is the law — appears only in the *Bavli* and not in the *Yerushalmi*, reflecting that more favorable assessment of Persian governance.

Against this background, Ameimar's categorical stance is jarring. The preceding discussion had carefully distinguished between cases of genuine legal claims and cases of pure force — distinctions that implicitly acknowledged the possibility of legitimate non-Jewish legal proceedings. To then conclude with a blanket declaration that all non-Jews take by force, overriding those nuanced distinctions, is a formalist position of the most sweeping kind. One can understand it as arising from the cumulative historical experience of Jewish communities living under foreign rule, and many *poskim* have noted that such statements must be read in their historical context and reassessed when circumstances differ.

### Secular Court Authority

*Tosafot* engage directly with the implications of the *gemara*'s earlier analysis — before Ameimar's ruling — for the scope of *dina de-malchuta dina*. The question *Tosafot* raise is pointed: if Marduk wins his case in a secular court, why should that create any obligation on Reuven at all? Reuven could simply say to Shimon: bring me proof that Marduk's seizure was legitimate according to his own court, and if you do, I will reimburse you. Until then, I maintain that I sold you a donkey I legitimately owned, and Marduk simply took it.

*Tosafot* answer that the obligation arises precisely *because* Marduk won in *dayanei oved kochavim* — in a non-Jewish court. The secular ruling provides enough formal validation of Marduk's claim to create a legitimate grievance on Shimon's part: you sold me property, and a court has now determined you may not have owned it. That determination — even from a foreign legal system — is sufficient to hold Reuven accountable.

This is a significant statement about the reach of *dina de-malchuta dina*. The *Ramban* reaches the same conclusion. When *dina de-malchuta* intersects with *dinei Yisrael*, the ruling of the secular court carries enough weight to generate real legal consequences within the Jewish framework — at least at this stage of the *gemara*'s analysis.

### Rambam's Psak

The *Rambam* in *Hilchot Mechira* 19 rules in accordance with Ameimar, and the ruling is unambiguous. He writes that the seller's *achrayut* — his guarantee obligation — applies when the purchase is seized from the buyer *be-veit din shel Yisrael*: in a Jewish court, whether the item was stolen, robbed, or taken by the seller's creditor through the proper *tarfei* process. In all those cases, if the matter was adjudicated in a Jewish court, the seller is liable.

However, the *Rambam* continues: if a non-Jew seized the purchased item from the buyer — *bein be-din ha-melech bein be-arkaot shelahem* — whether through the king's court or through their standard judicial process — the seller bears no liability whatsoever. Even if the non-Jew claims the seller had stolen or robbed the item from him and brings non-Jewish witnesses to that effect, the seller is exempt — *she-ze ones hu*, because this is a case of *ones*, coercion, and the seller is not liable for *ones*.

This ruling is striking on multiple levels.
