The *Rambam* explicitly acknowledges that Marduk may have won his case in a legitimate legal proceeding, brought witnesses, and prevailed entirely within the framework of the secular court — and still rules that the seller owes nothing. This reflects a very narrow conception of *dina de-malchuta dina*, one that limits its applicability to the relationship between the government and the individual (such as tax obligations) but does not extend it to civil disputes between individuals. Several *poskim* understand the *Rambam* to hold this restricted view, and this ruling reinforces it: even a formally correct secular court judgment, adjudicating a dispute between two private parties, does not carry the weight in *halakha* that *Tosafot* and the *Ramban* would assign to it.

## Craftsman's Chazakah

### Uman Principle

The *mishnah* establishes a foundational rule: *uman ein lo chazakah* — a craftsman has no presumptive claim of ownership over objects in his possession. The ordinary rule of *chazakah* holds that whatever is found in a person's hands is presumed to belong to him. A craftsman, however, receives other people's property as a regular matter of his work: the weaver takes in fabric, the blacksmith receives tools, the dry cleaner holds garments. Because possession of another's item is entirely expected and routine in the craftsman's professional context, his holding an object creates no presumption that he owns it. If the craftsman claims he purchased the item from its owner, or received it as a gift, he is not believed on the basis of possession alone.

This rule operates differently from the general testimonial disqualification discussed earlier. There, the question was whether a seller could *testify* on the buyer's behalf. Here, the question is whether the craftsman himself can *claim* ownership based on his current possession, and the answer is that he cannot.

### Rabba's View

Rabba qualifies the *mishnah*: *lo shanu ela she-masro lo be-eidim* — the craftsman has no *chazakah* only when witnesses saw the owner deliver the item to him. If, however, the item was delivered without witnesses — *masro lo shelo be-eidim* — then the craftsman is believed even if he claims he purchased it, because *mitoch she-yachol lomar lo hayu devarim me-olam* — he could simply deny he ever received it. If the craftsman could successfully claim he never received the item at all, then his alternate claim that he received it by purchase is equally plausible and equally credible.

The logic is one of *migo*: since the craftsman could have made a stronger, unassailable claim ("I never had this item"), he is believed when he makes the weaker but still plausible claim ("I purchased it"). Once witnesses establish that he did receive the item in a professional context, however, that *migo* disappears. The receipt is documented; only the nature of the transaction remains in question; and the professional context weighs against him.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rabba's position. If Rabba's reasoning is that delivery with witnesses removes the craftsman's *migo*, then even with witnesses present, the craftsman should still have a fallback claim: *mitoch she-yachol lomar hekhzarti lach* — he could say he already returned the item. If the craftsman is believed to say he returned the item (because no one saw him return it), then he should also be believed to say he purchased it, since in both cases he is making a claim that cannot be directly refuted by the witnesses.

In other words, Abaye presses Rabba: what exactly does the presence of witnesses accomplish? Witnesses establish that the craftsman once received the item. They do not establish that he still has it. If the craftsman can simply deny present possession by saying he returned it, the testimonial weight of the original delivery is undercut — and his alternative ownership claim should be equally credible.

### Return Requirement

Rabba responds sharply: *mi savart?* — do you think that a person who deposits an item with a craftsman with witnesses can retrieve it without witnesses? Rabba holds *hamafkid etzel chaveiro be-eidim tzarich lehakhziro be-eidim* — one who entrusts an item to another in the presence of witnesses must return it with witnesses as well. This eliminates the craftsman's ability to claim an undocumented return. He cannot simply say "I gave it back" if the original deposit was witnessed, because an unwitnessed return would not be credited. Therefore, the *migo* that Abaye proposed — that the craftsman could credibly claim to have returned the item — does not exist according to Rabba. The craftsman is stuck: he cannot deny having it, he cannot claim a quiet return, and since he received it in a professional context, he cannot claim purchase either.

### Garment Test Case

Abaye raises a formal *meitivei* from a *braita*. The case involves a craftsman — a launderer — who is found with a garment. The owner confronts him and asks *mah tivo etzlecha* — what is this doing in your possession? If the craftsman says "you sold it to me" or "you gave it to me as a gift," *lo amar klum* — his claim has no standing. This is straightforwardly the *mishnah*'s rule: the craftsman has no *chazakah*.

The *braita* then states a contrasting case: if a third party says *befanai amarta lo li-mochro v'lisno lo be-matanah* — "in my presence you told him to sell it or give it as a gift" — *devarav kayamin* — that third party is believed. What is the *braita* describing, and why is the third party's testimony effective here when the craftsman's own claim is not?

### Third-Party Testimony

Rava clarifies the *braita*'s second clause: the *seifa* does not involve the craftsman speaking for himself. Rather, it describes a case where the owner encounters a *different* party — not the craftsman — in possession of the item. That second party says: "I heard you instruct the craftsman to transfer this to me." She is believed, the *gemara* explains, because of *migo*: if she wanted to lie, she could have claimed the owner gave the item to her directly, without involving the craftsman at all. Since she instead offers the more complicated story — that she received it via the craftsman on the owner's instruction — her account is treated as more credible than a straightforward fabrication would be.

This is a classic *migo* application: a claimant is believed in a weaker claim because she could have made a stronger, unchallenged claim instead.

### Eidim and Ra'ah

Returning to the *braita*'s first clause, the *gemara* presses the analysis further. The *braita* describes the triggering condition as *ra'ah* — the owner *saw* his item in the craftsman's possession. This language is significant. The *gemara* asks: if the decisive factor is whether witnesses were present at the original delivery, as Rabba maintained, why does the *braita* emphasize *ra'ah* — seeing — rather than *eidim*? If there were witnesses, their testimony should be sufficient regardless of whether anyone currently sees the item in the craftsman's hands. And if there were no witnesses, why would seeing the item in his hands change anything?

The *gemara* pushes further: *ela lav de-leika eidim* — it must be that the *braita* is addressing a case *without* witnesses, and the operative factor is *ra'ah* alone. If so, the *braita* is direct evidence against Rabba's position and in favor of Abaye's: what matters is not witnesses at the original delivery, but whether the item is currently visibly in the craftsman's hands.

### Ra'ah Decisive

Abaye's position crystallizes from this analysis: *ra'ah* is the decisive factor. The *mishnah* denies the craftsman a *chazakah* because the craftsman's professional identity, combined with the visible fact of his holding another's goods, is sufficient to negate the ordinary presumption of ownership. No witnesses to the original delivery are required. If the owner can see that the craftsman currently holds the item — *ra'ah* — the craftsman cannot claim it as his own. If the owner cannot see the item in the craftsman's possession — *lo ra'ah* — the craftsman is believed whatever he says, because he could always deny ever having it.

The logic here is not about witnesses establishing a narrative of professional receipt. It is about the visible, present fact of possession combined with the craftsman's professional identity. That combination alone is enough to rebut the normal *chazakah*.

### Combined Requirements

Rabba is now in difficulty. The *braita* clearly indicates that *ra'ah* — and not witnesses — is the operative criterion. Abaye presses him: but you yourself said that the person who deposits with witnesses must retrieve with witnesses, which means the craftsman cannot claim to have returned the item and therefore the *migo* that would support his ownership claim does not exist. If so, why did you require *eidim* at all?

Rabba concedes: *hadar bi* — I withdraw my position. Pressed by the *braita*, Rabba now accepts that *ra'ah* is necessary. But rather than fully adopting Abaye's view, Rabba arrives at a third position: both *eidim* and *ra'ah* together are required in order to deny the craftsman his *chazakah*. Only when witnesses establish that the item was delivered in a professional context *and* the item is currently visible in the craftsman's possession does the combination conclusively defeat his ownership claim. Without witnesses, the craftsman retains the *migo* of having been able to deny receipt altogether; without *ra'ah*, he can claim to have returned the item. Only when both conditions are present simultaneously — witnessed delivery and current visible possession — is the craftsman's claim to ownership defeated without any remaining avenue of escape.

# Bava Batra 46

## Rava vs. Abaye

### Two Axes

The Gemara on Daf 46 opens in the middle of a debate between Rava and Abaye concerning the rule stated in the Mishnah: *uman ein lo chazakah* — a craftsman does not acquire a *chazakah* (presumption of ownership) over items in his possession. To understand the structure of this debate, two independent axes must be held in mind simultaneously.

The first axis concerns *eidim* — witnesses. Were there witnesses present when the owner gave the item to the craftsman, or not? The second axis concerns *ra'ah* — visual observation. Do we currently see the item in the craftsman's possession, or not? The obvious case in which the craftsman clearly has no *chazakah* is when witnesses saw the owner give it to the craftsman, and the craftsman is currently seen holding it. Conversely, the obvious case in which the craftsman would have a *chazakah* is when there were no witnesses and nobody currently sees the item in his hands — he could plausibly claim he never received it, or that he returned it long ago.

The dispute between Rava and Abaye concerns which of these two axes is the dominant criterion.

### Rava: Witnesses

Rava's position is that *eidim* are the controlling criterion. Once it is established through witnesses that the owner gave the item to the craftsman for a professional purpose — say, for dry cleaning — the craftsman is never believed to claim ownership of it, even if nobody currently sees the item in his hands. This follows from the principle *hamapkid etzel chaveiro be'eidim tzarich lehachziro be'eidim*: one who deposits an item with another in the presence of witnesses must return it in the presence of witnesses. Since the craftsman cannot demonstrate that he returned the item via witnesses, he is not believed to say he returned it, and by extension, not believed to say he purchased it.

A striking implication immediately surfaces: this principle has nothing specifically to do with the craftsman's professional status. The same rule would apply to any person who received any item as a *pikadon* (deposit) in the presence of witnesses. If I deposit something with a neighbor in front of witnesses and the neighbor later claims he bought it from me, he too would be disbelieved. Rava's position, then, does not actually explain why the Mishnah singles out the *uman*. The Gemara will press this point at length, and *Tosafot* addresses how it might nonetheless remain connected to the *uman* context — but the tension is real and acknowledged.

### Abaye: Possession

Abaye's position is far more directly tied to the *uman*'s unique professional role. For Abaye, the controlling criterion is *ra'ah* — whether we currently observe the item in the craftsman's possession. The logic is as follows: a dry cleaner is the type of person to whom one naturally gives one's suit. Therefore, when we see a dry cleaner holding a suit we knew to be someone else's, that very combination — craftsman plus item of the type he handles — strips away his *chazakah*, even without any witnesses to the original handover. Conversely, if we do not see the item in his hands, Abaye holds that the craftsman is believed to claim ownership, because there is no current visual evidence contradicting his claim.

This approach maps cleanly onto the concept of *uman ein lo chazakah*. A normal person seen holding an item we knew was yours would be believed to say he purchased it — *chazakah mah she-tachat yad adam harei hu shelo*, what a person holds is presumed to be his. But a dry cleaner holding your suit, or a leather worker holding your leather goods, cannot avail himself of that presumption. The *uman*'s professional identity transforms the meaning of possession. If a dry cleaner were holding your shoes, however, he would be believed — shoes are not the type of item one gives a dry cleaner. The professional relationship between the craftsman's specialty and the item in question is what triggers *ain lo chazakah*.

### Rava Retracts

A *baraita* was introduced that appeared to demonstrate that the critical variable is indeed *ra'ah* — visual observation — rather than *eidim*. Confronted with this evidence, Rava retracted his broader position and limited himself to a much narrower claim: *ein lo chazakah* applies only when both criteria are simultaneously present — both witnesses to the original transfer and current visible possession. That, of course, is the uncontested case everyone agrees upon from the outset. Rava's retraction thus left him in agreement with the obvious case and added nothing beyond it. This is where the discussion stood at the close of the previous session.

---

## Craft Fee Dispute

### Fee Dispute

The Gemara now introduces a *baraita* as part of Rava's attempt to support the position of *Rabba* — the view that *eidim* are the dominant criterion. The case is as follows: a person gives his *tallis* to a craftsman (*noten taliso le'uman*). The craftsman says they agreed on a fee of two *zuz*, while the owner says they agreed on one. Who is believed? The Mishnah rules: *kol zeman she-tallis beyad uman* — as long as the garment remains in the craftsman's hands, the burden of proof falls on the owner (*al habaal habayis l'havi re'iyah*). The craftsman is believed, because of *migo* — since he could have claimed outright that he purchased the garment, he is believed on the lesser claim of the disputed fee amount.

This is a striking *migo*: the craftsman's credibility on the fee dispute derives from his latent ability to claim ownership of the garment entirely.

### Payment Timing

The Gemara continues with the next clause: if the craftsman has already returned the garment and payment is still owed, the rule changes depending on timing. *Bizmano nishba venotel* — within the normal period of payment, the craftsman may take an oath and collect what he claims is owed him. This is a *takanas chachamim*, a rabbinic enactment, based on the reality that an employer is often too distracted and occupied with paying multiple workers simultaneously to keep careful track; therefore the worker is trusted under oath during this period. *Avar zemano* — once the normal payment window has passed, the craftsman who allowed the deadline to lapse without demanding payment is viewed with greater suspicion; perhaps he was not paid precisely because he was already paid and forgot, or perhaps he waited because he was being cavalier. In that case, *hamotzi mechavero alav hare'iyah* — the one seeking to collect bears the burden of proof.

*Tosafot* raises a pointed difficulty with this entire temporal framework: the classic case in which *bizmano nishba venotel* makes sense is when the parties dispute *whether* payment occurred at all. There, the logic is clean — the employer is distracted at the moment of payment, and if the worker truly had not been paid, he would have pressed his claim immediately. But the case here is a dispute over *what was originally agreed upon* — a conversation that took place at the time of the original commission, not at the time of payment. Neither the distraction of the payment moment nor the significance of delayed demand maps naturally onto this scenario. *Tosafot* raises this problem but does not fully resolve it.

### Scenario Analysis

The Gemara now probes what scenario the Mishnah is actually describing — specifically, which combination of *eidim* and *ra'ah* is at play. The question: in what situation is it interesting and non-trivial to say that the craftsman is believed to claim he could assert ownership of the garment (*lekucha hi beyadi*)?

One possibility: there are witnesses to the original transfer, but nobody currently sees the garment in his hands. This would favor Abaye's opponents — even with *eidim*, and without current *ra'ah*, the craftsman is believed. The Gemara dismisses this: if witnesses were present at the original handover, we could simply ask them what fee was stipulated, and there would be no dispute. So witnesses cannot be present in the Mishnah's case.

The Gemara then reasons: *ela lav deleika edim* — it must be that there are no witnesses. The interesting scenario, then, must be one where there are no witnesses but the garment is seen in the craftsman's possession — and even so, he is believed. This would support the view that the determinative axis is *ra'ah*, not *eidim*: even without witnesses, when we see the item in his hands, the craftsman is still believed because of *migo*.

The Gemara responds: *le'olam deleika edim, vehu delo ra'ah* — in truth the scenario could simply be one without witnesses *and* without current visible possession. That is the uninteresting, uncontested case where of course the craftsman is believed. The Mishnah does not tell us which scenario it is, so it cannot serve as proof for either position. The *migo* argument from the craftsman's ability to claim ownership tells us nothing about which axis dominates.

### Nachman Challenge

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak now mounts the definitive challenge against Rava. The Mishnah states *uman ain lo chazakah* — *the craftsman* does not have a *chazakah*. The implicit contrast is: *uman hu de'ein lo chazakah, ha'acher yesh lo chazakah* — it is specifically the craftsman who lacks *chazakah*, while a non-craftsman in an otherwise similar situation would have one.

Now, on Rava's account, the determinative factor is *eidim* — witnesses to the original deposit. But the principle *hamapkid etzel chaveiro be'eidim tzarich lehachziro be'eidim* applies universally, to any person who received any item via witnessed deposit. If a non-craftsman received an item from me with witnesses and is now holding it without having returned it via witnesses, he too is disbelieved when he claims he returned or purchased it. There would be nothing special about the *uman* at all — the rule would be *hamapkid etzel chaveiro be'eidim ein lo chazakah*, not *uman ein lo chazakah*.

The Gemara presses: if there *are* witnesses, why would a non-craftsman have a *chazakah*? He wouldn't. So the case must be without witnesses. *Ela lav dileika edim, de-tani uman ein lo chazakah* — it must be a case without witnesses, and yet the Mishnah still says the *uman* lacks *chazakah*. This can only be explained by Abaye's position: what distinguishes the *uman* from any other person is that we *see* the item in his hands (*ra'ah*), combined with his professional identity. A normal person seen holding something I once owned would be believed — *chazakah mah she-tachat yad adam harei hu shelo*. But a craftsman holding an item of the type he works on cannot avail himself of that presumption. We assume the item is there because it was given to him for work, not because he purchased it.

*Tiyuvta de-Rava tiyuvta* — this constitutes a decisive refutation of Rava. The *ikar* is *ra'ah*: professional identity combined with visual possession.

---

## Mixed Garments

### Baraita: Accidental Mix-…

The Gemara now introduces a *baraita* from Bava Kamma that, while tangentially related, raises a vivid practical question. *Nitchelfu lo keilim be-keilim be-veit ha'uman* — if garments got mixed up in the craftsman's shop and you came to collect yours but were handed someone else's by mistake, the *baraita* rules: *harei zeh yishtamesh bahen ad she-yavo halaz ve-yitol et shelo* — you may use the other person's garment until the person who accidentally took yours returns it, and then you exchange.

The *baraita* immediately contrasts this with a case of garments mixed up at a gathering — a *shiva* house, a wedding, the coat-room at a synagogue. In that scenario, *lo yishtamesh bahen* — you may not use the other person's garment even while waiting for the mix-up to be untangled. You cannot wear a coat you took home by mistake from the synagogue coat-room even while the other person has yours. The logic is unambiguous: two wrongs do not make a right, and the absence of one wrong does not license another. You have no permission to use something that belongs to another person simply because that person is inadvertently holding yours.

The problem, then, is the first case. Why may you use a garment mistakenly received from the craftsman's shop?

### Craftsman Permission

Rav recounts that he was sitting before his beloved uncle, Rav Chiyya, who offered him the following explanation: *vechi ein adam asui lomar le'uman mechor li taliti?* — is it not entirely normal for a person to say to a craftsman, "sell my garment for me, give me the proceeds"? People leave items with craftsmen on a kind of consignment arrangement.

The reasoning proceeds as follows. Suppose Michael left his coat with the dry cleaner and said "sell it for me." Then David comes to pick up his own coat. The dry cleaner, in confusion, gives David Michael's coat. Even though the dry cleaner did not consciously hand David a loaner or a consignment item, the fact is that Michael's coat *was* legitimately within the dry cleaner's authority to transfer — Michael had given him that right. So David's receipt of Michael's coat, while accidental, falls within the category of a legitimate transfer. David is therefore permitted to use the coat until the situation is clarified and exchanges can be made.

In the synagogue coat-room case, by contrast, no one has given anyone permission to distribute their coat. Whoever holds the garments in that context has no authority to transfer them. So when you take the wrong coat home, there is no possible framework under which you received it legitimately, and you may not use it.

The logic requires that we *hypothesize* a plausible permissive scenario — the craftsman may have had the right to give this item out — and that hypothesis provides enough of a foundation to allow use pending resolution. This is not pure license: as soon as it becomes clear that no such permission existed, the item must be returned.

### Craftsman Only

Rav Papia the son of Rav Nachman adds a limitation: *lo shanu ela hu, aval ishto u'vanav lo* — this permissive rule applies only when the craftsman himself handed you the garment, not when his wife or children did so.

The reason lies in the nature of the authority being invoked. The craftsman has discretion over the items in his shop — he is the one who received consignment rights, who agreed to sell garments for customers, who makes the professional decisions about what to give to whom. His wife and children, working behind the counter, are employees in the relevant sense: they lack the independent discretion to make consignment transfers or loaner arrangements. When they hand out the wrong garment, there is no basis to hypothesize that a legitimate transfer has occurred. We can only assume they made a mistake, and therefore you may not use the item.

This has broader application. When a waiter tells you "it's on the house," or a cashier waives a charge, their authority to do so is not self-evident. Only someone with actual discretionary authority over the item or transaction can make such a determination.

### Grammar Matters

A further limitation is introduced: *hu nami lo amrinan ela d'amar leh tallit stam, aval tallit-cha lo* — even when the craftsman himself hands it over, the permissive rule applies only if he says "here is *a* garment" (*tallit stam*), not "here is *your* garment" (*tallit-cha*).

If the craftsman says "here is your garment" and it turns out not to be yours, it is clear he made a mistake — he thought he was returning yours and was wrong. The intent was a specific return, not a consignment transfer or a loaner arrangement. In that case you must give it back. But if he says "here is *a* garment," the phrasing is open enough to be interpreted as a deliberate offer of a different item — a loaner, a consignment piece, something he had authority to transfer. That interpretive latitude is what permits you to keep using it.

The practical application is somewhat subtle. If you are standing at the counter and know immediately that the garment is not yours, the question of what you are obligated to say on the spot is a genuine *she'eila*. If the craftsman has said *tallit stam* and you have already left, the assumption of a permissive transfer is what you rely on. These distinctions in real-time obligation are worth careful attention.

---

## Pumbedita Scoundrel

### Real-Life Scenario

Abaye, having established the theoretical primacy of *ra'ah*, now turns to a vivid practical illustration of the difficulties that arise when *ra'ah* cannot be cleanly established. He invites Rava: *ta achvei lach rama'ei d'Pumbedita* — come, let me show you the scoundrels of Pumbedita, and how they exploit legal technicalities to cheat people. The Gemara then dramatizes what one such dishonest dry cleaner would do.

A person comes to retrieve his garment. The dry cleaner says: *lav itam me'olam* — I never had it, I don't know what you're talking about.

### Proving Possession

The owner responds: *ha ika sahadei d'chazya gabach* — I have witnesses who saw my garment in your possession. This is not the same as *eidim* who witnessed the original handover. These are witnesses who observed the item — a specific black coat, a distinctive suit — in the craftsman's hands at some point. That constitutes a case of *ra'ah*. And since we have established that *ra'ah* is the operative criterion, this should be sufficient to strip the craftsman of his *chazakah*.

The dry cleaner's counter-move: *ha achreina havai* — that was a different one. You think there is only one coat like yours? The coat my witnesses saw was not yours; it was another customer's, which merely resembled yours. You cannot prove that what they saw was specifically your garment.

The owner says: produce it, let us examine it — *afkinah ve-nechzinah*. The witnesses, if they can see it, may be able to identify it. The dry cleaner refuses: *ibra la mafkinah lah* — I will not produce it. The *Rashbam* explains the dry cleaner's principled-sounding position: in truth (*be'emet*), he is not even claiming that coat as his own — he is saying it belongs to another customer, and he has an obligation to protect the privacy of his clients. He is not going to rummage through his customers' property on the strength of a frivolous claim.

### Rava Concedes

Rava, to the apparent surprise of those listening, sides with the dry cleaner: *shapir ka'amar lei* — he has said correctly. *Ra'ah tanyah* — it is all about *seeing* the specific item. If you cannot establish that what the witnesses saw was definitively *your* garment — if the craftsman can plausibly claim it was a similar garment belonging to a different customer — there is no legally actionable *ra'ah*. Witnesses who saw *a* coat in his possession but cannot identify it as *your specific* coat have provided suspicion, not proof. Suspicion does not override the craftsman's right to withhold. The scoundrel is technically within his legal rights.

This is, as Rava acknowledges, a genuinely frustrating result. Rights are sometimes used to protect wrongdoing. But without the ability to positively identify the specific item, there is no sufficient *ra'ah*, and the claim fails.

### Practical Advice

Rav Ashi offers a clever workaround. If you are dealing with such a craftsman, you can attempt to engineer a *ra'ah* situation that compels him to produce the item. Approach him and say: I understand why you are holding on to my coat — it must be because I owe you back fees. Let us be fair about this. I acknowledge I might owe you something. But you are holding on to a coat worth ten thousand dollars over a debt of perhaps one thousand. Let us bring the item out, have it assessed, you take what is yours and I will take the remainder — *v'shaiminu shkol at didach v'shkol ana didi*. You are not claiming to be a thief; let us resolve this equitably.

If the craftsman agrees and brings out the coat, witnesses will now observe it in his possession and can identify it — a proper *ra'ah* is created, and at that moment the craftsman's *chazakah* collapses.

Rav Acha the son of Rav Avya notes the counter-move available to a sufficiently savvy scoundrel: *lo tzrichna l'shuma didach* — I don't need your assessment. I've already had others appraise it, and I know its value covers your debt. He refuses to produce it and declines the arrangement entirely. One cannot outfox the fox. The practical advice of Rav Ashi works only against a scoundrel who is not quite clever enough.

The episode as a whole reinforces the theoretical conclusion: *uman ein lo chazakah bimkom re'iyah* — but that *re'iyah* must be a positive, specific identification of the item in question. A general sighting that cannot definitively establish identity is legally insufficient.

---

## Sharecropper Cases

### Sharecropper Rule

The Gemara now transitions to the Mishnah's parallel rule: *aris ein lo chazakah* — a sharecropper (*aris*) does not acquire a *chazakah* over the land he works. At first glance this seems puzzling. A *chazakah* of land normally requires three years of uncontested use. If the *aris* worked the land for three years and kept all the produce for himself — whereas previously he gave half to the landowner — that shift should constitute strong prima facie evidence that he is no longer a sharecropper but a legitimate owner. Why then does the Mishnah say he has no *chazakah*?

### Permanent Arrangement

Rabbi Yochanan qualifies the Mishnah: *be'arisei batei avos* — we are dealing with a situation of *batei avos*, a permanent, multigenerational sharecropping arrangement. This family has been working this land for generations as *arisim*. The *ikar* of the difficulty is not merely long duration of possession, but the nature of the institutional relationship.

In a standard yearly arrangement, a landowner would never allow a worker who turns over annually to keep all the produce for three years running and then reverse the arrangement; there is no relationship of trust deep enough to support that kind of flexibility. But in a multigenerational *batei avos* arrangement, the trust is substantial. It is entirely plausible that the landowner and the *aris* family agreed on a rotating arrangement: the family keeps everything for three years, then gives everything for three years. Because that kind of extended trust arrangement is conceivable within a *batei avos* context, the three years of keeping all produce does not constitute anomalous behavior that would signal a change in ownership status. Hence no *chazakah*.

Outside the *batei avos* context, a standard *aris* who harvests everything for himself for three years would indeed have a *chazakah*. This is a significant limitation of the Mishnah's ruling.

### Sub-contractors

Rav Nachman introduces a further refinement: *aris she-horid arisin tachtav yesh lo chazakah* — an *aris* who brought in sub-sharecroppers beneath him, replacing himself with others who do the actual work while he collects his percentage off the top, *does* have a *chazakah* — even within the *batei avos* context.

The reason: *delo avid inish dinachtit arisei le'ar'veih ve-shatik* — a person does not simply bring strangers onto another's land without permission and remain silent about it. The landowner never agreed to have unknown third parties working his land. He trusted the *aris* family precisely because of their long relationship. If the landowner observed strangers working his land and said nothing, the only plausible explanation is that the *aris* had already purchased the land and now had full authority to contract with whomever he chose. Three years of such adverse possession — sub-contractors working the land without the landowner's permission, with the landowner silent — is sufficient to establish *chazakah*.

### Active vs. Passive

Rabbi Yochanan draws a crucial distinction within this scenario. *Aris she-chilek la'arisei ein lo chazakah* — but if instead of removing himself and replacing himself with others, the *aris* actively participates alongside additional workers — dividing up tasks, working the land together with them as a working foreman — he does *not* have a *chazakah*.

The distinction is between *horid tachtav* (he put others in his stead — passive substitution) and *chilek* (he divided the work among others while actively participating himself). In the case of *chilek*, the landowner's silence does not signal anything unusual, because the *aris* is still present and working. The landowner trusts the *aris* personally, and as long as the *aris* is actively supervising and participating, the landowner would naturally be comfortable with additional helpers. This is not adverse possession — it is ordinary *aris* behavior with assistance. The *aris* simply received *harmana* — permission to bring in helpers — either explicitly or by implication. Since the landowner's silence is explained by ordinary permission, it cannot generate *chazakah*.

*Harmana b'alma shavya* — it is mere permission the landowner extended, nothing more.

A brief but notable *Tosafot* digression: whenever the Gemara refers to *Rav Nachman* without further specification, it means *Rav Nachman bar Yaakov*. *Tosafot* proves this by observing that throughout all of *Shas*, the full name *Rav Nachman bar Yaakov* never appears unless there is another *Rav Nachman* in the same sugya — at which point disambiguation is necessary. This implies that *stam Rav Nachman* is always *Rav Nachman bar Yaakov*, making the fuller designation redundant except when contrast is required.

---

## Sharecropper Testimony

### Interest Question

Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda sent a question to Rav Nachman bar Yaakov: *yelamdeinu rabbeinu, aris me'id o eino me'id?* — may a sharecropper testify regarding the ownership of the land he works, or not?

The question seems to answer itself. An *aris* is clearly a *nogea badavar* — a party with a direct interest in the outcome. Who owns the land he works directly affects his terms of employment, his relationship with the landowner, the security of his arrangement, and even the share of produce he is entitled to. If he testifies that the land belongs to Michael rather than Eli, he is simultaneously affirming that Michael is his current employer. The parallel is almost uncomfortably direct: could an employee testify in a lawsuit that determines who his employer is? The potential for bias is obvious.

Rav Yosef, sitting in the room, reported in the name of Shmuel: *aris me'id* — the *aris* can testify. The *Gemara* then challenges this from a *baraita*: *eino me'id* — he cannot. How do we reconcile these?

### No Present Fruit

*Lo kashya* — there is no contradiction. *Ha de'ika peira be'ar'a, ha delika peira be'ar'a* — one ruling applies when there is currently fruit on the land, and the other when there is not.

When fruit is currently growing and ready to be harvested, the *aris* has an immediate, tangible financial stake in the question of ownership. If the land belongs to Michael and the *aris* has an *aris* agreement with Michael, he will collect his full contractual share — half, a third, a quarter, depending on the arrangement. If the land turns out to belong to Eli, and the *aris* had no agreement with Eli, he was working the land without authorization (*yored letoch sdei chaveiro shelo birshut*) and would be entitled only to lower, non-contractual compensation. This is a direct and immediate financial interest, and therefore he cannot testify. He is a *nogea badavar*.

When there is no fruit currently on the land, the question of ownership has no immediate financial consequences for the *aris*. Whatever happened in the past has been resolved; the only question is the future. And for the future, the *aris* has no guaranteed interest: he might work for Michael going forward, or he might work for someone else.

### Future Benefit

*Tosafot* states the reasoning explicitly: *aval leit peira be'ar'a, lo chaishinan shema yesalkennu, dekamah sdot yimtza le'arisut* — when there is no current fruit, we are not concerned that the new owner might dismiss him, because there are plenty of other fields he could find sharecropping work in.

This reasoning is acknowledged to be challenging. The assumption of perfect competition — that the *aris* could find equivalent work with any other landowner without loss — does not obviously hold in reality. The Gemara elsewhere recognizes (*harishon noach li, ha-sheni kasheh heimennu*) that different employers are not fungible, and that a worker may genuinely prefer one employer over another. Why, then, do we dismiss the *aris*'s future interest so readily?

One possibility: when the benefit at issue is entirely prospective, contingent, and non-concrete — not a present entitlement being actively threatened, but a speculative future arrangement — it does not rise to the level of disqualifying *nogea badavar*. The distinction may be between a present interest (fruit currently on the land, money directly at stake) and a future interest (employment that may or may not continue, terms that may or may not be favorable). Future benefit of sufficient uncertainty is not considered enough to disqualify testimony.

The *Rashbam* touches on this distinction, and it provides at least a conceptual framework, even if the practical line is not perfectly sharp.

---

## Other Interested Parties

### Guarantor

The Gemara now catalogs several analogous cases in which a party with a potential financial interest in the outcome is nonetheless permitted to testify, all operating on the same basic logic of attenuated future benefit.

*Areiv me'id l'loveh* — a guarantor (*areiv*) may testify on behalf of the borrower whose loan he guaranteed. *Ve-hu d'is lei ara achriti* — provided the borrower has at least one other plot of land besides the one under dispute.

The relevant dynamic: I am Gloria's guarantor on a loan from Charlie. David now claims that a certain plot of Gloria's land is actually his. I wish to testify that the land belongs to Gloria. My interest in doing so is transparent — the more land Gloria has, the more buffer there is between me and Charlie's collection. If Gloria has no land at all, Charlie comes to me.

Why am I nonetheless believed to testify? Because for my testimony to actually benefit me, an extended chain of circumstances must first materialize. Gloria must have no cash reserves. Gloria's remaining land — the other plot she does retain — must be seized by a different, competing creditor before Charlie can collect it. Only then, once Gloria's assets are fully exhausted and Charlie cannot collect from her directly, does Charlie approach me. Since so many independent and contingent events must occur before I actually benefit from this testimony, the benefit is considered too attenuated to constitute a disqualifying interest.

A subsidiary point arises regarding the mechanics of creditor collection from land: when creditors compete, there is an established priority order, and a creditor who has collected from land through a lien cannot have that land re-taken by a subsequent competing creditor, lest the system dissolve into circularity. The *areiv* is most exposed when Gloria has sold land (in which case Charlie can still follow the lien) but when another creditor has seized remaining land through a competing claim — that is what fully exposes the guarantor. The point stands: the pathway to the guarantor's liability is long, contingent, and uncertain enough to not constitute present *nogea badavar*.

### Lender

A parallel case: *malveh me'id l'loveh, ve-hu d'is lei ara achriti* — a lender may testify on behalf of his borrower, again provided the borrower retains sufficient other land.

The logic is more straightforward. I lent Michael money. Eli is now claiming one of Michael's plots of land is his. I wish to testify that the land is Michael's. My interest: the more land Michael has, the more I can collect from when the time comes to recover my loan. I naturally prefer a wealthier borrower.

But again, the pathway to actual benefit for me is long. For me to collect from Michael's land at all, Michael must have no cash or other liquid assets. And for the one remaining plot to matter, all of Michael's other assets must be exhausted. Since so many preconditions stand between my testimony and any actual gain, the future benefit is not considered enough to disqualify me. *Ve-hu d'is lei ara achriti* — as long as Michael has at least one other plot, my testimony about the disputed plot is not treated as self-interested in the legally disqualifying sense.

The remaining cases in this series — *lokeach* and *kablan* — will be addressed in the following session.

---

---

# Bava Batra 47

## Amalek Siman - Four Cases

### Opening Remarks

The daf we take up today picks up from the bottom of 46, the second-to-last line, returning to the *siman* known as the *Amalek siman*. Some of the *acharonim* on the *Gemara* are interested in why *Chazal* chose specifically these four cases and organized them around a *siman* drawn from the name *Amalek* — a name we are simultaneously commanded to remember and to blot out. But whatever the reason, it serves as an effective mnemonic.

### Four Testimony Cases

The *Gemara* opens with a *tano rabbanan* listing four types of witnesses whose testimony might be suspected as self-interested, and the conditions under which their testimony is nevertheless valid. The organizing principle is the concept of *nogeia badavar* — being personally implicated in the outcome of one's testimony — and the question of when such an interest rises to the level that disqualifies the witness.

### Areiv Testimony

The first case involves an *areiv* — a cosigner on a loan. One might wonder why anyone would agree to cosign a loan, and indeed bankers sometimes refer to such individuals with colorful contempt. Yet in halachic life, serving as an *areiv* can function as a form of *tzedakah*, helping someone obtain a loan they could not otherwise secure.

The concern is that the *areiv* is *nogeia badavar*: if the *loveh* has no attachable property, the *malveh* may come to collect from the *areiv* directly. So if the *areiv* testifies that a particular property belongs to the *loveh*, he appears to be protecting his own interests by increasing the pool of assets available to satisfy the debt. The *tano rabbanan* rules that the *areiv* is not considered *nogeia badavar* to the extent of disqualification — provided that the *loveh* has other properties apart from the one being testified about. If the *loveh* already has *ara'a achriti*, other fields, then the creditor will not so readily turn to the *areiv*, and therefore the *areiv*'s testimony about this specific property carries no particular benefit to himself.

### Malveh Testimony

The second case concerns the *malveh* himself testifying on behalf of the *loveh* — asserting that a particular property belongs to the *loveh* — again *v'hu d'is leh ara'a achriti*, provided the *loveh* has other properties. Although the *malveh* has an even closer financial relationship to the outcome than the *areiv*, since he stands to gain directly from establishing that the *loveh* has assets, the same limiting condition applies: as long as the *loveh* possesses other properties, the *malveh*'s testimony about this particular field does not confer any specific advantage on him.

There is a further nuance worth noting here that the *Rashbam* addresses at the top of 47a: a *ba'al chov* collects from *beinonit*, medium-quality land, and so if a *loveh* holds only *ziburit*, low-quality land, the *malveh* might be especially interested in testifying that a *beinonit* field belongs to the *loveh*, since that would provide a more attractive collection target. This subtlety will become directly relevant in the *kablan* discussion that follows.

### Buyers' Testimony

The third case is the *loka'ach rishon* testifying on behalf of the *loka'ach sheini*. The rule in debt collection from sold properties is that one proceeds against the most recently sold property first. If a seller sold one field to a first buyer and subsequently sold another field to a second buyer, and a creditor now wishes to collect from encumbered property, the second buyer's field is targeted first. Thus the first buyer has an obvious interest in establishing that the second buyer owns the property: he is effectively using the second buyer as a buffer.

Nevertheless, the *Gemara* rules that the first buyer may testify — again *v'hu d'is leh ara'a achriti*, as long as the second buyer has other properties. In such a case, confirming that this particular field belongs to the second buyer does not materially enhance the first buyer's protection of his own purchase.

---

## Kablan Areiv

### Kablan Definition

We now reach the *kuf* of the *Amalek siman* — the *kablan*. The *Rashbam* clarifies that this is not the ordinary *kablan* in the sense of a hired worker, but specifically a *kablan areiv* — a special form of cosigner who has accepted more stringent terms than the ordinary *areiv*. Whereas with a regular *areiv*, the creditor must first attempt to collect from the *loveh* before turning to the *areiv*, the *kablan areiv* has agreed that the creditor may come to him immediately, without first pursuing the *loveh*.

### Kablan Testimony Dispute

Whether this *kablan* may testify is itself a *machloket*. *Amrei lah me'id* — there are those who say he may testify and is not considered *nogeia badavar*. *Ve'amrei lah eino me'id* — and there are those who say he may not.

### Nogeia B'Eidus Issue

The opinion that the *kablan* cannot testify reasons as follows. Since the creditor may collect from the *kablan* immediately, without first exhausting the *loveh*'s assets, the *kablan* has a concrete stake in whether the *loveh* holds *beinonit* or only *ziburit*. A *ba'al chov* is entitled to collect from *beinonit*, so if the *loveh* has no *beinonit* remaining — only *ziburit* — the creditor will be, as it were, pushed toward collecting from the *kablan*. By testifying that this property belongs to the *loveh*, the *kablan* would be increasing the pool of *beinonit* available from the *loveh*, thereby protecting himself. This is the basis for the view that he is *nogeia b'eidus* and may not testify.

### Kablan Can Testify

The opinion permitting the *kablan* to testify holds *k'areiv dami* — that his status is functionally equivalent to that of a regular *areiv*, and the benefit he derives from his testimony is sufficiently minimal that we do not disqualify him on that basis. The reasoning is that since the creditor can come to the *kablan* first regardless, the benefit the *kablan* gains by establishing the *loveh*'s ownership of this particular property is marginal.

### Kablan Benefit Analysis

The underlying *machloket* concerns how one understands the *kablan*'s relationship to the *loveh*'s assets. Does the *kablan*, precisely because he can be collected from immediately, care less about what the *loveh* owns — and is therefore less *nogeia badavar*? Or does he care more, because he wants the *loveh* to appear as an attractive target for collection so that the creditor will go there rather than to him directly? Both perspectives have internal logic, which is why the *Gemara* presents this as a genuine dispute.

### Ba'al Chov Collection

The *Gemara* notes that in both opinions — *tarvayhu* — when the *ba'al chov* comes to collect, *mai d'baei shakil*, he may take whatever he wants. That is the fundamental nature of the *kablan areiv* arrangement: the creditor retains full discretion over how and from whom to collect.

### Ri Megash vs Rashbam

There is a further difference of opinion between the *Ri Megash* and the *Rashbam* regarding the underlying nature of the *kablan* relationship. The question is how this arrangement came to be. Did the *kablan* himself borrow the money from the *malveh* and then lend it on to the *loveh* — in effect functioning as a direct lender in a two-stage transaction? In that case, his relationship to the *loveh* is simply that of a *malveh*. Alternatively, did he enter the arrangement as an *areiv* who simply accepted more demanding terms — agreeing to be collectible immediately? These two framings carry implications for how one analyzes related cases, though in the specific case at hand the practical ruling is agreed upon. There is considerably more to explore here in comparison to the *sugyot* of *Bava Metzia*.

---

## Craftsman & Thief Cases

### Uman & Aris Rule

The *Gemara* now transitions to a teaching of *Rebbi Yochanan*. The *Mishnah* had already established that a craftsman — an *uman* — does not have a *chazakah* on objects in his possession, since we presume that an *uman* holding, say, a pair of shoes is holding them because he is repairing them for someone else. *Rebbi Yochanan* extends and refines this: *uman ein lo chazakah, ben uman yesh lo chazakah*. The craftsman himself has no *chazakah*, but the son of the craftsman does.

The scenario is one in which someone later comes and claims ownership of what is in the craftsman's household. The son — who is not himself a craftsman — can say: just because my father was a repairman does not mean I cannot own these items. Of course, the *chazakah* still requires *chazakah sheyesh imah ta'anah*, a credible accompanying claim, and the *Gemara* will elaborate on what that claim must look like.

Similarly: *aris ein lo chazakah, ben aris yesh lo chazakah*. A sharecropper working on someone else's land for three years does not thereby establish ownership, since the fact of his being an *aris* explains his presence. But his son — who is not himself an *aris* — can create a *chazakah* through three years of uncontested use, provided there is no *mecha'ah*. The principle is clear: it is not a *chazakah* on land generally but specifically on that land, and it applies only to the individual who held the agricultural relationship, not to one who inherited the land or came to use it in his own right.

### Gazlan Hierarchy

The rule extends further — but with a significant distinction. *Gazlan u'ven gazlan* — a thief and the son of a thief — neither of them can establish a *chazakah*. *Aval ben b'no shel gazlan, yesh lo chazakah* — but the grandson of a thief does have the ability to create a *chazakah*.

The immediate question is why the son of a thief is treated more harshly than the son of a craftsman or the son of a sharecropper. After all, the son of a thief is not himself a thief. The *Gemara* will probe this carefully.

### Gemara's Inquiry

The *Gemara* asks: *heichi dami?* What case is *Rebbi Yochanan* describing? If the children come *b'ta'anta d'avuhon* — with the same claim as their fathers — then obviously none of them should have a *chazakah*. If the *ben uman* says "my father received these shoes for repair," that is simply restating the father's relationship, not an independent claim. And *afilu ben gazlan nami* — on the other side, if all three categories of children come without their father's claim, then even the son of a thief should be believed.

So what is the intermediate case? The *Gemara* answers: *tzericha, d'ka'amri edim be-fanenu hodeh lo* — there are witnesses who say that in front of them, the original owner (*mara kamma*) admitted to the father that the property belongs to him. This is the fact pattern: the *mara kamma* acknowledged the father's ownership before witnesses, and now the son has inherited.

### Witness Admission

This should resolve the matter. *Hoda'at ba'al din ke-mea edim* — an admission by the owner is as powerful as a hundred witnesses. Why, then, should the son of a thief not benefit from this admission? The *Gemara* explains the distinction: for the *ben uman* and the *ben aris*, we assume the witnesses are reporting a truthful admission — *kushta kamre*. But for the *ben gazlan* — *afal gav d'odei nami lo meheman* — even if the original owner admitted, we do not trust that admission, because it may have been coerced.

### Coerced Admission

This is the logic of Rav Kahana's statement, which the *Gemara* cites here: *i lav d'odei leh, havei mamti leh u-lechmariya le-shachvar* — "if you don't admit to me," the *gazlan* threatens, "I will hand it over to another strongman" — *shachvar*, a term the *Rashbam* traces to the *Targum* of the verse in *Bamidbar* 16, where Moshe says he took nothing from the people: *ve-lo chamra de-chad minhon shachrit*. The word connotes forcible seizure. So the *gazlan* is essentially extorting a confession: admit in front of witnesses that this property is rightfully mine, or I will make things worse for you. The *hoda'ah* is coerced, and therefore worthless.

This is why even a witnessed admission by the *mara kamma* does not help the *ben gazlan* — we assume the father extracted it under duress.

### RY vs RC Dispute

*Rava* introduces a further refinement: *pe'amim she'afilu ben beno shel gazlan nami ein lo chazakah* — there are even cases where the grandson of a *gazlan* will not have a *chazakah*, namely when he comes with the claim of his grandfather. What kind of *gazlan* are we discussing? *Rebbi Yochanan* says: *ke-gon she-huchzak al sadeh zu be-gazlanuta* — someone who is publicly known to have stolen specifically this field. *Rav Chisda* says: *ke-gon de-bei ploni she-horgin nefashot al iskei mamon* — a family known to kill people over monetary matters, like an organized crime family.

The *nafka mina* between their positions: according to *Rebbi Yochanan*, the *gazlan* is disqualified only with respect to this particular field — for which he is publicly known as a thief — but could establish a *chazakah* on any other field. According to *Rav Chisda*, the entire family is broadly disqualified. It may be relevant, as one might observe, that *Rav Chisda* lived in *Bavel* and *Rebbi Yochanan* in *Eretz Yisrael*, and perhaps the social realities of organized violence differed between those environments.

### Gazlan Teshuvah

The *Tur* in *siman* 139 — a very lengthy passage — quotes a *yesh omrim* to the effect that if a *gazlan* has done *teshuvah* and it is publicly known that his *teshuvah* was complete — *teshuvah gemurah* — then he would be trusted even regarding this field. The *Tur* himself is uncomfortable with this position. The question it raises is a profound one: there is a difference between *teshuvah* between a person and God, and the question of when a community is obligated — or even permitted — to treat a rehabilitated person as fully trustworthy again. Even if the *gazlan* has done *teshuvah* regarding the stolen field itself — presumably returning it or compensating for it — the question of whether the community's *chazakah* of distrust is lifted is a distinct matter. This connects to larger questions about communal treatment of those who have repented.

---

## Chazakah Qualifications

### Quit Profession Rule

The *Gemara* now presents a *baraita* that further specifies conditions under which *chazakah* can be established. *Uman ein lo chazakah* — we know this from the *Mishnah* — but if the *uman* quits his profession, *yarad me'umnato*, then subsequently he can create a *chazakah*. The same applies to the *aris*: while he is a sharecropper he has no *chazakah* on the land he works, but if he quits, *yarad me'arisuto*, he can thereafter create a valid *chazakah*.

### Adult Child Rule

The *baraita* also addresses the case of an adult child who has left home and is financially independent — *ben shechalak*. The halachic principle is that an adult still dependent on his parents, *gadol ha-somech al shulchan aviv nikra katan*, is treated in certain respects as a minor. But a financially independent adult child who has separated from the household has full independent standing, and his use of a field for three years without *mecha'ah* can establish a *chazakah* independent of any relationship to the parents' ownership.

### Divorced Woman

Similarly, *ve'isha shenitgarsha* — a divorced woman — *harei hen ke-shar kol adam*, is treated for purposes of *chazakah* like any other person, with full independent standing. Her ability to establish a *chazakah* is evaluated independently of her former husband.

### Safek Divorce

The *Gemara* notes that the *ben shechalak* case is not surprising — we need the ruling because one might have thought the parents simply forgive use of their property, and so there would be no valid *chazakah*, merely an implied gift. But the divorced woman's case seems obvious — *pshita*! Why state it?

The answer is: *lo tzricha — bim'gureshah v'eina m'gureshah* — the case where it is needed is one of uncertain divorce. In *Masechet Gittin*, there are numerous cases where the status of a woman's divorce is ambiguous — for instance, where the *get* was thrown and landed in a contested location, or other circumstances of uncertainty. In such cases, *Rebbi Zeira* transmits in the name of *Shmuel* via *Rebbi Yirmiyah bar Abba*: *kol makom she'amru chachamim m'gureshah v'eina m'gureshah, ba'al chayav bimzonoteha* — wherever the *chachamim* said the status is uncertain, the husband remains financially obligated to support her.

One might therefore think that if this woman attempts to establish a *chazakah* on her husband's property, the absence of his protest is not meaningful — perhaps he makes no *mecha'ah* simply because he is still financially entangled with her. The *memra* teaches us that this is not so: even a woman in the status of *safek m'gureshah* can establish an independent *chazakah* on property that belonged to her husband. Legally, we emphasize her *m'gureshah* status for purposes of property rights, even while her husband retains the *meizonot* obligation arising from the uncertain status.

### Proof Suffices

*Rav Nachman* quotes *Rav Huna*: *kulan she'hevi'u re'ayah, re'ayatan re'ayah* — for all of these individuals, if they bring actual proof — witnesses or a *shtar* — their proof is accepted and *ma'amidin sadeh b'yadan*, we establish the field as belonging to them.

### Gazlan Proof Rejected

The exception: *gazlan she'hevi re'ayah, ein re'ayato re'ayah* — if the *gazlan* himself brings proof, we do not accept it, and *ein ma'amidin sadeh b'yado*. The reason is that we assume a *gazlan* has strong-armed the witnesses into testifying on his behalf. This applies to the *gazlan* who has not done *teshuvah*; as the *yesh omrim* cited in the *Tur* would hold, a *gazlan* who has fully repented would presumably be believed even with testimony.

---

## Stolen Property Sale

### Sikrikon Scenario

The *Gemara* now connects this discussion to a case drawn from *Masechet Gittin* — the *sikrikon*. A *sikrikon* is a bandit or requisitioner who seizes people's land and then sells it. The *Rashbam* notes that this refers to a non-Jewish robber. The scenario: a *sikrikon* seizes a field from *Reuven* and sells it to *Shimon*. Subsequently, *Shimon*, wanting to secure his claim, goes and purchases the same field from *Reuven* as well. He has now paid twice — once to the *sikrikon* and once to *Reuven*.

The question is whether *Shimon*'s purchase is valid. The concern is that *Reuven*, still the rightful owner, sold the field not out of genuine willingness but because he felt powerless — the field was effectively gone, and he simply tried to make the best of a bad situation. If the sale from *Reuven* to *Shimon* is not genuine, *mekach hu batel* — the sale is cancelled. But which sale is cancelled — the one from the *sikrikon* to *Shimon*, or the one from *Reuven* to *Shimon*? And under what conditions might either sale be valid?

### Rav's Position

*Rav* says: *lo shanu ela de-amar leh lech chazek u-knei* — the *mekach hu batel* ruling applies only in a case where *Reuven* told *Shimon* to go perform a *kinyan chazakah* — to take possession by building a fence, locking a door, digging, and so forth. In that case, *Reuven* is essentially throwing up his hands and waving *Shimon* onto the land without full commitment. *Aval bi-shtar kanah* — but if *Reuven* sold it to *Shimon* by means of a *shtar*, that is a genuine sale and *Shimon* acquires it fully.

### Shmuel's Position

*Shmuel* is more stringent: *af bi-shtar nami lo kanah ad she-yichtov achrayut nechasim* — even a sale by *shtar* is insufficient to establish *Shimon*'s acquisition unless the *shtar* includes *achrayut nechasim*.

### Achrayut Explained

*Achrayut nechasim* is the clause by which the seller accepts liability for any liens that may be extracted from the property after the sale. Ordinarily, if *Reuven* has outstanding debts, a creditor holding a *milveh b'shtar* against him could potentially collect from fields that *Reuven* sold after the loan — including the field *Shimon* bought. If *Reuven* sells to *Shimon* with *achrayut nechasim*, he is committing that if such a lien is ever collected from *Shimon*'s field, *Reuven* will compensate *Shimon*.

This clause benefits *Shimon* and is a disadvantage — a concession — on *Reuven*'s part. *Shmuel*'s reasoning is that the inclusion of this clause demonstrates *Reuven*'s genuine intent to sell: why would *Reuven* voluntarily assume this additional liability unless he truly intended *Shimon* to own the field? A seller acting under duress or out of a sense of hopelessness would not go so far as to take on obligations that benefit the buyer at his own expense. The *achrayut* clause is therefore the decisive indicator of authentic consent.

### Rav Bibi Clarification

*Rav Bibi* then elaborates in the name of *Rav Nachman*, clarifying that this entire dispute concerns *karka* — real estate. But in a case of *maos* — money — *yesh lo*, the right to the money is valid even without these additional conditions.

### Witness Specificity

There is a further qualification regarding testimony. If witnesses say *be-fanenu hodeh lo* — he admitted to him in front of us — without specifying an amount, that is insufficient. But if they say *be-fanenu maneh lo* — he counted out a specific sum to him in front of us — that carries legal weight. The distinction is between a vague, unspecified admission and a precise, quantified one. A general *hoda'ah stam*, without specifying the monetary amount, is too indeterminate to serve as the basis for a claim.

---

## Coerced Sales

### Gazlan Coercion

*Rav Kahana*'s statement, which the *Gemara* cited in the context of the *gazlan* who coerces an admission, reappears here in its original context. The *gazlan* tells the original owner: if you do not admit that this property is rightfully mine in front of witnesses, I will hand it over to another strongman — *shachvar*. This threat explains why a witnessed admission from the *mara kamma* in favor of a *gazlan* is not trusted: it may simply be the product of extortion.

### Threatened Sale Valid

*Rav Huna* now states a broader and striking principle: *talyuhu ve-zavin, zivinei zivina* — if they hung him up and forced him to sell, his sale is nevertheless a valid sale. Coercion of this extreme kind does not invalidate the transaction.

### Ones Reasoning

The reasoning: *kol de-mazbin inish, ei lav de-anis, lo hava mazbin* — any person who sells something would not have done so absent some form of external pressure, some *ones*. This is a foundational halachic principle rooted in the Talmudic understanding that ownership of tangible assets — especially real estate — is always preferable to holding money. One never parts with property unless some external pressure — financial necessity, personal urgency, or even physical coercion — has intervened. Since all sales involve some form of *ones*, the fact of coercion per se does not distinguish a forced sale from any other sale in a way that would render it void.

### Types of Ones

One might raise an objection: is there not a meaningful distinction between *onsa de-nafshei* — pressure arising from one's own circumstances, such as needing money to move to *Eretz Yisrael* — and *onsa de-achrinei* — coercion imposed by another person, including physical threat? The *Gemara* acknowledges the potential distinction but presses forward.

### Forced Korban

The *Gemara* adduces a *braita* concerning the verse *yakriv oso* in *Vayikra* perek 1, regarding the bringing of a *korban olah*. The verse teaches *melamed she-kofin oso* — the *Beis Din* may coerce a person to bring the *korban*. Yet the same verse says *lirtzono* — it must be of his own will. *Ha keitzad?* How can these be reconciled? *Kofin oso ad she-yomar rotzeh ani* — they force him until he says "I want to." Once he says it, it is considered voluntary.

### Forced Get

The *braita* continues: *ve-chein ata omer be-gitei nashim, kofin oso ad she-yomar rotzeh ani* — the same principle applies in the laws of *gittin*. When the *Beis Din* has determined that a husband is required to divorce his wife, they may coerce him until he says that he agrees to give the *get*. This is not considered a forced *get* in the sense that would invalidate it. The principle of *ein ones be-gittin* — which does appear in *Masechet Ketubot* in other contexts — refers to specific *tnai* arrangements, not to this general question of *Beis Din*-compelled divorce.

### Force & Agreement

The *Gemara* considers whether these two cases of *korban* and *get* might be special — in the *korban* case because a person fundamentally wants *kapparah* for his sins, and in the *get* case because listening to *divrei chachamim* is itself a *mitzvah*. But it concludes: *sevara hu, agav onseih gamar u-makni* — it is a fundamental principle of human psychology and halachic reasoning that even under coercion, a person reaches a point where he makes a genuine internal decision to agree. That concluding commitment, however it was arrived at, constitutes a valid act of will. This is the principle underlying *Rav Huna*'s ruling that *talyuhu ve-zavin, zivinei zivina* — a sale concluded under duress is a valid sale.

It is worth noting that the prohibition of *lo tachmod* in the *Aseret ha-Dibrot* is understood to apply precisely to the kind of pressure that compels another person to sell something they do not wish to sell — the coercer may violate *lo tachmod*, yet the sale itself, once concluded with the seller's stated agreement, remains halachically valid.

---

---

# Bava Batra 48

## Taluhu ve-Zavin

### Gezel Background

The *sugya* of Bava Batra 48 is a self-contained and richly layered discussion of *taluhu ve-zavin* — the question of whether a sale conducted under coercion is legally valid. To appreciate the full arc of the argument, we return briefly to the bottom of 47b, where the Gemara had just established that if a *gazlan* produces a signed *shtar* purporting to show that he purchased a field, the document is inadmissible. The reasoning is straightforward: we presume that the original owner agreed to write the *shtar* only out of fear of the consequences of refusing. The coercion underlying the transaction, according to this earlier discussion, strips the document of any legal standing. It is precisely against this backdrop that Rav Huna's general principle must be understood.

### Rav Huna Statement

At the bottom of 47b, Rav Huna states: *taluhu ve-zavin, zevineih zevinei* — if someone was suspended, meaning compelled under duress, and sold his field or some other property, it is nevertheless a legitimate sale. This is a striking position. Rav Huna is not carving out an exception for mild social pressure; he is declaring that coerced sales, as a category, are valid.

### All Sales Forced

The rationale Rav Huna offers is equally striking: *kol demazbin inish, ee lav de-anis lo hava mazbin* — anything that people sell, they would not have sold were they not in some sense forced to do so. This reflects the economic reality of a pre-commercial, agrarian society in which property is not a commodity to be traded for profit. People sell only when circumstances compel them — when they need to raise funds, when a debt presses, when a family must be fed. In such a world, every sale is in some sense an act born of necessity, and the seller, though driven by circumstance, nonetheless makes the decision himself. He weighs his options, determines that selling is the lesser hardship, and proceeds. That decision, however reluctant, is still *his* decision. Therefore, Rav Huna argues, even when an external party is the source of the coercive pressure, if the seller ultimately chooses to go through with the transaction, that choice is real and the sale is binding.

### Self vs External

The Gemara immediately registers the obvious objection, at the bottom of 47b: *v'dilma shani unsa denafshei me-unsa de-achrinei* — perhaps there is a fundamental difference between pressure that originates from within one's own circumstances and coercion imposed by another person. When I decide to sell because my family needs food, I am the author of my decision. I weigh the competing demands on me and I choose. That is very different from a situation in which someone holds a weapon to my head, in which case the decision is not really mine at all — it is simply the coercer's will being executed through my body. This distinction makes enormous intuitive sense, and the Gemara takes it seriously enough to set aside the analogy to ordinary commercial pressure and seek a more direct proof for Rav Huna's principle.

---

## Korban Proof

### Korban & Lirtzono

The Gemara turns to a *baraita* at the top of 48a. The verse concerning the *olah* says *yakriv oto* — "he shall bring it." The *baraita* reads this as implying not only that the individual must bring his vowed *korban*, but that *beis din* may compel him to do so: *melamed shekofin oto*. Yet an adjacent phrase says *lirtzono* — it must be his will, his desire. The *baraita* itself poses the question, *ha katzad*, how can both be true simultaneously?

### Coercion Process

The resolution is: *kofin oto ad sheyomar rotzeh ani* — we compel him until he himself says "I want it." The coercion does not replace his will; it continues until his will is extracted from him, expressed in his own words. At that point, the act is considered genuinely his. The Gemara attempts to derive from this case a proof for Rav Huna's principle: just as external compulsion does not invalidate the *korban* once the individual declares his consent, so too external compulsion should not invalidate a sale once the seller goes along with the transaction.

### Korban Different

The Gemara deflects this proof: *v'dilma shani hasam denichla lei d'teihavei lei kaparah* — perhaps that case is different because the person actually wants the atonement the *korban* provides. There is something he is receiving, something of immense personal value, and that benefit makes it plausible that when he says *rotzeh ani* he genuinely means it. Furthermore, it should be noted — as the *Rashbam* observes — that nobody obligated him to take this vow in the first place. He expressed from the outset his desire for the *kaparah* the *korban* would bring. Compelling him to follow through is not so much imposing something external as reconnecting him to his own prior commitment. For these reasons, the *korban* case may be uniquely suited to genuine reconciliation in a way that a purely secular coerced sale is not. The proof therefore fails.

---

## Get Divorce Case

### Get & Kofin

The Gemara pivots to the second case, introduced with *ve'ela meseifa* — let us try to derive the proof from the following *Mishna*. By *gitei nashim*, the same rule applies: *kofin oto ad sheyomar rotzeh ani*. When a husband is obligated to divorce his wife but refuses, *beis din* can compel him, applying physical pressure until he declares *rotze ani*. Since the husband must be the one to issue the *get* — *beis din* cannot issue it in his stead — and since the *get* must be issued willingly, the mechanism of compelling him until he says *rotze ani* is the operative solution.

### Get Religious Aspect

The Gemara again objects: *v'dilma shani hasam demitzvah lishmoa divrei chachamim* — perhaps this case too is special, because there is a religious dimension to the compulsion. *Chazal* have determined that this man is obligated to divorce his wife. When he is coerced and ultimately says *rotze ani*, we are prepared to accept that declaration as genuine because, at some level, he does want to do the right thing. He wants to align himself with the ruling of the *chachamim*. He wants to fulfil his religious obligation. The coercion is not introducing something wholly alien to his will; it is removing the *yetzer hara* that had been obstructing what his deeper self already wanted. This is qualitatively different from a case where someone is simply being pressured to part with property for purely secular reasons, with no religious obligation in the background. The proof from the *get* therefore likewise fails to establish Rav Huna's principle in the general case.

It is worth pausing here to note a point raised by *Tosafot* that addresses both of these attempted proofs. *Tosafot* cites a resolution by the *Ri*: *de-chol davar she-hu mechuyav la'asos, havei k'mo mecher* — anything one is obligated to do is analogous to a sale. By the *korban*, the person is obligated to bring it; by *gitei nashim*, the husband is obligated to give the *get*. The analogy to a coerced sale thus holds not because both involve getting something in exchange, but because in both situations the compulsion is not purely external — in each case, there is something the person is already bound to do. When one is obligated to act and is then compelled to follow through, we can say, combined with that compulsion, that he has genuinely made his peace with the act. This is structurally analogous to *taluhu ve-zavin*, where what reconciles the seller is the compensation he receives. *Tosafot*'s point is that obligation performs the same reconciling function as money. Nonetheless, the Gemara itself notes that the *korban* and *get* cases may represent an even stronger form of reconciliation — rooted in religious obligation and the mitzvah to heed the *chachamim* — and so they remain distinguishable from the purely monetary case.

### Tosafot Obligation

*Tosafot*'s resolution, then, is that the criterion for a coerced act to be valid is not merely receiving compensation, but more broadly that the actor has some basis — whether financial compensation or pre-existing obligation — upon which to reconcile himself to the transaction. Money provides that basis in the sale context; religious obligation provides it in the *korban* and *get* contexts. The Gemara, while acknowledging the parallel, concludes that the cases of *korban* and *get* cannot serve as direct proofs for our case because their religious dimension makes them categorically stronger. The question of *taluhu ve-zavin* in the purely secular context must therefore rest on independent reasoning.

---

## Rambam Framework

### Rambam Anuss

Before proceeding to that independent reasoning, it is worth examining what the *Rambam* says about the conceptual underpinnings of this entire discussion, particularly in the context of *get*. The *Rambam* in Hilchot Gerushin 2:20 addresses the question directly: why is this *get* not nullified? After all, the husband is plainly *anus* — coerced. The *Rambam*'s answer is definitional: *she-ein omrim anus ela le-mi she-neilchatz ve-nidechak la'asos davar she-eino mechuyav bo min ha-Torah* — we only apply the category of *anus* to someone who is being compelled to do something he is not obligated in from the Torah. In that case, the coercion is wholly external, there is nothing inside the person generating any pull toward the act, and so the act truly is not his. Like someone who was beaten until he sold or gave something — that is a case of genuine *ones*. That is exactly the case of *taluhu ve-zavin*, and the *Rambam* explicitly includes *machar*, selling, as an instance of coercion.

### Yetzer Hara/Tov

But then the *Rambam* introduces a contrasting category: *aval mi she-takfo yitzro ha-ra le-vatel mitzvah o la'asos aveirah ve-huka ad she-asa davar she-chayav la'asoso* — but someone whose *yetzer hara* seized him to violate a commandment or commit a transgression, and he was beaten until he did what he was obligated to do or distanced himself from what he was forbidden to do — *ein zeh anus mimenu*, this is not coercion imposed upon him from outside. Rather, *hu anas atzmo be-da'ato ha-ra'ah* — he himself had been coercing himself through his own corrupt inclination. This is a remarkable psychological and philosophical move. The *Rambam* is saying that the *yetzer hara* is itself a form of self-imposed coercion, an internal tyrant that overrides what the person's deeper, truer will actually wants.

Applied to the husband who refuses to give a *get*: since he wants to be part of the Jewish people, *rotzeh la'asos kol ha-mitzvos u-le-hisrachek min ha-aveiros*, and it is only his *yetzer hara* that has seized him — *ve-yitzro hu she-takfo* — when he is beaten until his *yetzer hara* weakens, *v'amar rotzeh ani*, he is in truth being liberated to do what he genuinely wanted all along. The beating does not impose an alien will upon him; it removes the internal obstruction that had been preventing his true will from expressing itself. It is loosely analogous to the hardening of Pharaoh's heart — there, one might say, the heart was hardened enough to withstand the pressure of the *makkot*, allowing the underlying dynamic to play out; here, in the reverse direction, the *yetzer hara* is weakened so the *yetzer hatov* can emerge.

### Get Lirtzono

The *Rambam*'s framework also illuminates the significance of the term *lirtzono*.
