The woman plainly assumed she had been *machzik* the tree all along, because in the popular understanding, occupying and using a tree for thirteen years ought to demonstrate ownership. Yet the court says that is not what constitutes *chazakah*. Perhaps the phrase is best understood as follows: what makes *chazakah* function as a *kinyan* is that it is an act which demonstrates ownership. And what demonstrates ownership is not taking benefit but taking responsibility — caring for a thing, investing in it. A sharecropper takes fruit. A laborer harvests. An owner is the one who fences, waters, and maintains. The primary *chazakah* of ownership is therefore an act of giving benefit to the land, not extracting it. From this perspective, *kidmachziki inshi* does not mean "whatever people happen to do" but rather "the act by which people demonstrate they are the owner." Harvesting fruit does not demonstrate ownership; it is what non-owners do. Digging at the base of the tree, improving the ground — that is what an owner does.

One might note the apparent irony: a woman who worked this tree for thirteen years is told she has no claim, while a man who turned over a small amount of dirt acquires it entirely. The law here is technically rigorous and practically striking.

## Drawing on Walls

### Tzura on Walls

The Gemara records that Rav said: *hatzad tzura b'nichsei hager kaneh* — one who draws a decorative design (*tzura*) on the wall of a house belonging to a *ger* — here meaning property that has become ownerless, *nichsei hager* — acquires it. By drawing on the wall, one has improved the structure, and this constitutes a valid *kinyan*.

### Rav Huna's Garden

The Gemara specifies: *d'Rav lo kanei l'ginta d'bei Rav ela b'tzurata* — Rav acquired the garden adjacent to his *yeshiva* only by means of its design. The garden was evidently *nichsei hager*, ownerless property, and the act of drawing designs on its walls was considered an improvement and thus a *kinyan*.

It is worth noting the contrast here with the preceding case. A woman who harvested a palm tree for thirteen years acquired nothing; a person who draws a picture on a wall acquires the property. The distinction is technically precise — taking benefit versus giving benefit — but the juxtaposition is arresting.

The Rashbam adds a relevant nuance. Earlier in the Gemara, when discussing plastering and drawing on a wall, the Gemara required that the drawing be at least an *amah* in length and positioned opposite the doorway. Here, no such requirement is mentioned. The Rashbam explains that the earlier rule applied to ordinary decorative work — generic curling designs, flowers, simple patterns (*tziyurin b'alma*, patterns of creatures and flowers). For more significant artistic representations — an actual figure of an animal or bird, something representationally meaningful — the mere act of drawing constitutes a more substantial improvement, and one is not required to meet the criterion of an *amah* opposite the doorway. The quality of the artistry, in other words, affects the legal threshold. A minor decorative flourish must meet stricter locational requirements; a more impressive work does not.

## Field Scope Dispute

### Rav: Whole Field

The Gemara now shifts from discussing the nature of the act that constitutes *chazakah* to asking about the spatial scope of its effect. The question: when one performs a single act of *chazakah* on part of a field, does the entire field thereby become acquired, or only the specific spot on which the act was performed?

*Itmar. Sadeha mesuyemet bemetzareha* — a field that is demarcated and defined, with clear boundary markers establishing exactly where the field begins and ends. Rav Huna said in the name of Rav: *keivan shehikish bah maka achat kanah kulah* — once one has struck it with a single blow, one acquires the entire field. The implicit assumption throughout the preceding discussion has been along these lines: one performs a single act of improvement on a portion of the field and thereby acquires the whole.

### Shmuel: Location Only

Shmuel disagrees: *lo kanah ela mekom makosho bilvad* — one acquires only the precise location where one dug or turned the soil.

### Boundaries & Scope

This immediately raises a difficulty. We have learned that building a fence, locking a gate, or making an opening — the classic *na'al gadar ufaratz* — constitutes a *chazakah* on the entire field. If Shmuel says one acquires only the spot of one's act, how can those acts work for the whole field?

The resolution lies in the nature of the act. A fence or wall surrounds the entire field; building or improving it necessarily touches the whole perimeter that defines the field. Locking a gate or making a breach relates to the wall, which itself defines the entire enclosed area. These acts are, by their nature, acts performed with respect to the whole field. By contrast, turning over a small patch of soil in the middle of a field is an act done to that particular patch. It does not inherently relate to the rest of the field.

This distinction also connects to an important limiting condition: the case of *nichsei hager* — ownerless property — where, unlike in a purchase, there is no money paid and no seller whose intent designates the entire field as a single unit. In a sale, the seller's intention to transfer a defined parcel, or the money that is given in exchange for a defined area, can extend the transaction to encompass the whole field, even fields separated by some distance. When a field comes into one's possession from *hefker*, the act of *chazakah* must itself define the scope of the acquisition, and a single shovelful of dirt does not inherently define the whole.

### No-Boundary Cases

The Gemara then turns to a related question: *veshe'einah mesuyemet bemetzareha* — a field that lacks physical boundary markers. According to Shmuel, we do not know how much one would need to do to acquire the entire field. Even according to Rav, when there are no external markers to define the field's identity as a unit, the question arises: how much of the field must one's act of *chazakah* encompass?

*Ad kamah* — how much? Rav Pappa says: *ki de'azal tayara deshurei vehadar* — like a team of oxen goes in one direction and returns, plowing a furrow the length of the field and back.

The Rashbam and Tosafot disagree about what question Rav Pappa is answering. The Rashbam understands him to be answering: how much must one do in order to acquire the entire unmarked field? The answer is that one must go across one full dimension — back and forth, the width of the field. Even though one has not traversed the length, the dimensions of the field are known from the deed, even if not physically marked. One traversal of one dimension suffices to constitute a *chazakah* on the whole. Tosafot reads the question differently: when one digs a single hole in a field without markers, how much does one thereby acquire? The answer is the area of a single furrow's length and return — the span of one plowing pass. Yet Tosafot essentially agrees with the Rashbam's underlying principle: that to acquire the entire unmarked field, one would need to traverse its full length, without necessarily having to go both length and width.

One might have thought logically that one would need to traverse both the length and the width — to define the entire two-dimensional space. The resonance with *Avraham Avinu* walking the land *le'orchah ulerochbah* — traversing it lengthwise and widthwise — is suggestive: to take possession of land one walks the whole thing. But the *halacha* as articulated here requires at minimum one full dimension to link the act to the totality of the plot.

## Non-Jew Property (III)

### Desert Principle

The Gemara now opens an entirely new and far-reaching discussion. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: nichsei ovdei chochavim harei hen kemidbar* — the property of non-Jews is like the wilderness, like ownerless property. *Kol hamachzik bahen zachah bahen* — anyone who takes possession acquires it. This is a striking statement on its face: can one simply walk over to one's non-Jewish neighbor and perform a *chazakah* on his house? No. As the Gemara will clarify, this applies specifically when property is in the process of being transferred — and there arises a gap between when the non-Jew relinquishes ownership and when the Jew acquires it, during which a third party may seize the property.

### Kesef vs. Shtar

*Mai ta'ama?* What is the reason? *Ovdei chochavim miki matu zuzai lideih istalak leih* — for the non-Jew, the payment of money (*kesef*) is sufficient to complete the transfer; the moment he receives the money, he relinquishes his ownership.

There is a well-known debate in Bava Metzia about whether the standard modes of *kinyan* for Jews and non-Jews are identical or inverse. The Rashbam here assumes that *kesef* is the operative *kinyan* for non-Jews in all domains. Tosafot takes a more nuanced position, suggesting that perhaps for moveable goods the non-Jew's *kinyan* is *meshichah*, but at minimum for real property (*karka*), the *kinyan* is by *kesef* — as demonstrated by the biblical precedent of Efron's sale of the cave of Machpelah to Avraham. Whatever the general rule, it is established that for land, a non-Jew's transfer is effected through money.

So when a Jew pays money to a non-Jew for land, the non-Jew's ownership immediately terminates. However, in a locale where the accepted practice between Jews is to write a *shtar* — and there are many such places, since while *kesef* is theoretically sufficient for Jews acquiring land, the established norm in most places was to insist on a deed to ensure legal certainty — the Jew does not yet take possession until the *shtar* is written. *Yisrael lo kanei ad demati shtar leyadei* — the Jew has not acquired until the deed reaches his hand.

The logic is as follows: since the standard in this locale requires a *shtar* between Jews, and since the Jew's default expectations and customary practice are shaped by that norm, even when purchasing from a non-Jew those same expectations apply. One does not regard the deal as concluded until a *shtar* is written. In the interim — after the non-Jew has received the money and relinquished his ownership, but before the *shtar* has been delivered — the land exists in a kind of legal no-man's land. It is neither owned by the non-Jew nor yet by the Jew. And during that gap, *harei hein kemidbar* — it is ownerless, and *kol hamachzik bahen zachah bahen*, anyone who performs an act of *chazakah* on it acquires it.

The Rashbam notes, though he does not resolve, the moral dimension: the person who swoops in and seizes this land is called a *rasha*. The principle of *ani hamahapech b'chararah* — the poor man who is about to take possession of a found object and is beaten to it by someone else — establishes that such a person is morally condemned even if technically permitted. Here the situation is worse: the Jew had actually paid money to the non-Jew. If a third party seizes the property, the original buyer has lost his money and has no recourse — the non-Jew has no obligation to return the payment, and the Gemara indicates the third party need not compensate him either. The seizure is halachically effective and morally reprehensible simultaneously.

Tosafot raises a substantive challenge. Since *kesef* can in principle work for a Jew acquiring land, and it only fails in this locale because of the customary expectation that a *shtar* will be written, one would think that in a transaction where the non-Jew's ownership ends with *kesef*, the Jew would similarly want his acquisition to take effect with *kesef* — to avoid precisely the dangerous gap being described. Why would any reasonable person maintain the expectation of needing a *shtar* when doing so leaves the property temporarily ownerless, exposing himself to losing everything he paid?

Tosafot's answer: *ve'tzarich lomar d'anan sahadi shelo haya beda'ato ela kemoshehu ragil liknot miYisrael dehainu beshtar* — we attest that the buyer's default assumption is that the transaction works the same way it would if he were buying from a Jew, i.e., not concluded until a *shtar* is written. Even though this leaves a gap, and even though *kesef* could theoretically protect him, the force of habit and customary expectation means the buyer does not fully intend to complete the transaction without a *shtar*. Tosafot acknowledges this answer is less satisfying than the question.

## Dina D'Malchusa (III)

### Abaye's Challenge

Against this entire framework, Abaye poses a powerful objection to Rav Yosef. *Mi amar Shmuel hachi?* — how could Shmuel possibly have held this position? For Shmuel himself is the author of the famous principle *dina d'malchusa dina* — the law of the kingdom is the law. And the king had explicitly ruled that land does not transfer except with a deed — *lo tikni ara ela be'igarta*. If we follow the law of the secular government, then the non-Jew's ownership does not terminate merely upon receiving money; it terminates only when a deed is issued. And correspondingly, the Jew takes possession precisely when the deed is issued. There is no gap, no ownerless interval, no opening for a third party to seize the land. How, then, can the same Shmuel who taught *dina d'malchusa dina* also teach that this land is available for seizure?

## Non-Jew Property (III)

### Dura d'Reusa Case

Rav Yosef replies: I cannot resolve the apparent contradiction between Shmuel's two teachings, but here is how I know Shmuel himself held the position that a third party can seize. *Be'uvda d'hava beDura diReusa* — there was an actual case in Dura diReusa (which the Rashbam explains means either a place name or a village of shepherds, from *raya*, shepherd). A Jew purchased land from a non-Jew. A second Jew came and turned over a small amount of that land — *rafik bepurtah*. The case came before Rav Yehuda, a student of Shmuel, and Rav Yehuda awarded the land to the second Jew who had performed the *chazakah*. Since Rav Yehuda was ruling in keeping with his teacher Shmuel, this demonstrates that Shmuel held the third party can acquire.

## Dina D'Malchusa (III)

### Back Taxes Explanation

Abaye responds: *Dura diReusa kamart?* You want to bring a proof from that case? *Hasam bagei d'mitmari havai* — in that case the lands in question were plots being concealed from the government. The original non-Jewish owners had not been paying their back taxes to the king — *de'inhu gufaiyu lo havai yahavi taska lemalchah*. And following the very principle of *dina d'malchusa dina* — which Abaye himself insists must govern — the king had declared: *man d'yahiv taska lachol ara* — whoever pays the outstanding taxes on a piece of land may claim it. The second Jew, therefore, was not seizing ownerless property in the *halachic* sense described by Shmuel's ruling. Rather, he was entitled to the land under the law of the king because he stepped forward and paid the back taxes that the non-Jew had failed to pay. The case was a distressed-land situation, akin to tax forfeiture. Abaye's reconstruction of the story thus shows that the entire episode was governed by *dina d'malchusa dina*, not by any *halachic* gap of ownership. Rav Yosef's proof collapses: the two statements of Shmuel remain unreconciled.

## Non-Jew Property (III)…

### Rav Huna v. Nachman

A parallel case is then recorded. Rav Huna purchased a plot of land from a non-Jew. A second Jew came and turned over a small amount of it — *rafik bepurtah*. The case came before Rav Nachman, who awarded the property to the second Jew — *okmei b'yadei*. Rav Huna challenged Rav Nachman: on what basis are you ruling this way? If you are relying on Shmuel's teaching that *nichsei ovdei chochavim harei hen kemidbar* and a third party can seize it, then at least be consistent with Shmuel's other ruling: *lo kanah ela mekom makosho bilvad* — the second Jew should acquire only the precise spot where he dug. Let him have his little hole; the rest of the field remains mine.

Here we see the connection back to the earlier discussion in this daf. Shmuel's two teachings — that one acquires only the spot of one's act, and that property of non-Jews in transfer is like ownerless wilderness — are now brought into direct confrontation with each other in a practical case.

Rav Nachman replied: *baha ana kishmai'atich svira li* — on that question, I rule in accordance with your own teaching, i.e., in the name of Rav: *keivan shenikesh bemakom echad kanah kulah* — a single blow acquires the entire defined field. The result: Rav Nachman ruled against Rav Huna on both counts simultaneously. He ruled that a third party can seize — following Shmuel's *kemidbar* principle — and that one act of *chazakah* acquires the entire field — following Rav, as taught by Rav Huna himself. Rav Huna loses the field entirely.

## Dina D'Malchusa (III)…

### Public vs. Civil Law

The Gemara has left unresolved how to reconcile Shmuel's two teachings. The Rashbam offers what he acknowledges to be an unsatisfying answer: the secular law of that locale was simply not the kind that required a *shtar*, and therefore there was in fact no tension with *dina d'malchusa dina*. This amounts to claiming that the disputants were simply mistaken about what the actual secular law required — a resolution that is difficult to accept given the apparent deliberateness of the Talmudic debate.

Assuming the secular law genuinely did require a *shtar*, the question of how to reconcile the two Shmuelian teachings opens into one of the most consequential discussions in halachic literature: what are the limits of *dina d'malchusa dina*? How far does secular law go in overriding *halacha*?

The concern is real and urgent. Obviously we cannot extend *dina d'malchusa dina* to invalidate a *get* because a civil divorce has been obtained. But what about *dinei mamonos*? Consider laws of inheritance. The Rambam is unequivocal that *dina d'malchusa dina* does not apply there: the Torah's laws of inheritance carry the designation of *chok* — they are statutory in a fundamental sense, not merely transactional arrangements between parties. More broadly, the Rashba, in a famous *teshuvah*, takes vehement exception to any suggestion that *dina d'malchusa dina* could wholesale replace *halachic* civil law. His retort: if that were so, why do we need all of *Nezikin*? Why do we need the entire corpus of *Choshen Mishpat*? Who needs all the works of Ravina and Rav Ashi in the domain of *dinei mamonos*? Nearly a quarter of Shas addresses civil law — one cannot simply sweep it aside on the grounds that secular law governs. That this very claim is sometimes implicitly operative in contemporary *batei din* — which frequently resolve cases based on some combination of *dina d'malchusa dina*, compromise, and equitable considerations rather than strict *Choshen Mishpat* — does not alter the theoretical force of the Rashba's position.

So what are the limits? One approach holds that *dina d'malchusa dina* applies only where *halacha* has not addressed a particular area — it fills in the gaps. Intellectual property is a frequently cited example: since *halacha* contains no concept of intellectual property rights, secular law may govern in that domain. A counterargument is that *halacha*'s silence is not a gap but a statement — if *halacha* does not recognize intellectual property, that itself is the *halachic* position. Nevertheless, this approach would potentially harmonize the two statements of Shmuel: the gap of ownership between a non-Jew's transfer and the Jew's acquisition is precisely the kind of legal lacuna that *dina d'malchusa dina* could fill — except that Shmuel himself evidently did not fill it here.

A more satisfying resolution is associated with the *Geonim*. Their position is that *dina d'malchusa dina* applies specifically to what might be called public law — the body of law that governs the relationship between citizens and the government. Taxes, government levies, regulations pertaining to one's obligations to the state: these fall under *dina d'malchusa dina*, as seen from the primary *sugya* in Bava Kamma, where the principle was first applied to taxation. If the government takes wood from one's property to build roads or bridges, one cannot claim the builder of the bridge has stolen from one's neighbor — *dina d'malchusa dina*. But the laws governing relationships between private individuals — classic civil law, the domain of *Choshen Mishpat* — those remain governed by *halacha*.

This division has considerable intuitive force. We have an elaborate body of *halachic* literature governing interpersonal obligations. We have essentially nothing governing the relationship of individual Jews to sovereign governments — no *masechet* dedicated to that question. The reason is historically plain: until modern times, Jews lived under non-Jewish sovereigns, and the laws defining their obligations to those sovereigns were necessarily the laws of those sovereigns themselves. *Dina d'malchusa dina* fills that vacuum. But for the purely interpersonal domain, *halacha* was always present and complete.

Crucially, this resolution works well for our *sugya*. The question of when precisely a land transaction transfers ownership between private parties — a Jew buying from a non-Jew — is a matter of interpersonal civil law, not public law. *Dina d'malchusa dina* does not apply. The *halachic* analysis of *kesef* and *shtar* governs, and the gap of ownerless property remains possible.

### Consent Theory

The Rashbam pauses at the phrase *dina d'malchusa dina* to offer what is in effect a political theory — an explanation of why the law of the government should be binding at all. His account is grounded in the consent of the governed. He writes that *kol bnei hamalchut mekablim aleihem mirtsonam chukei hamelech umishpatav* — all the subjects of the kingdom accept upon themselves, willingly, the laws and statutes of the king. Therefore it constitutes *din gamur*, fully valid law — *ve'ein lemachzik bemamon chaveiro al pi chok hamelech hanehug ba'ir mishum gezel* — and one who retains another's property in accordance with the king's established law is not regarded as committing theft. The basis of governmental authority, on the Rashbam's account, is the implicit consent of those governed. This is a recognizable political theory, and one that appears to predate its most famous later Western formulations by several centuries.

### Feudal vs. Modern

The Ran offers a contrasting political theory, one that reflects a feudal conception of land tenure: the king owns all the land. Because the king is the fundamental proprietor of the territory, he may set the conditions under which subjects occupy and use that land. His authority to make law follows from his status as ultimate landowner. This theory was congruent with the feudal reality of medieval Europe but carries significant implications when extended to *Eretz Yisrael*.

The Ran himself noted that his theory might not apply in *Eretz Yisrael*, because in *Eretz Yisrael* the land belongs to the Jewish people — each family has a Torah-mandated portion. The land is not fundamentally the king's. If the basis of *dina d'malchusa dina* is the king's ownership of the land, that basis is absent in *Eretz Yisrael*.

This observation opens a significant contemporary question. How does one conceptualize, halachically, the authority of the State of Israel? Two broad approaches emerge among the *poskim*. One holds that the State of Israel is simply another secular government, and *dina d'malchusa dina* applies to it just as it applied to the governments of England or France. This is a non-Zionist posture, and it faces the difficulty that if the Ran's theory underlies *dina d'malchusa dina*, it would actually apply *less* to Israel than to other states, since in *Eretz Yisrael* the king-owns-the-land rationale is absent. Some have indeed used this reasoning to argue that the laws of the State of Israel carry less binding force than those of other governments — an argument deployed by those who wish to contest state authority on halachic grounds.

The alternative is to conceptualize the State of Israel not through the lens of *dina d'malchusa dina* at all, but through the category of *melech* in the Torah's framework — a halachically grounded Jewish polity. This is the Zionist aspiration, and it carries its own enormous challenges: the *halacha* of Jewish governance — of a police force, a military, a judicial system, a tax code — was never fully developed precisely because, for two millennia, Jews did not govern themselves. There was no need, and no opportunity. With the founding of the State, many envisioned that a new body of *halacha* would emerge to meet those needs. That project is ongoing, and the theoretical frameworks established in this Gemara and in the *rishonim* who wrestled with them remain directly relevant to it.

---

---

# Bava Batra 55

## Shmuel's Doctrine

### Money vs. Shtar

We begin a few lines into the daf. The discussion picks up from the startling position of Shmuel that when a non-Jew sells land to a Jew, once money changes hands the non-Jew is, from the perspective of non-Jewish law, out of the picture — yet from the perspective of Jewish law, the land has not yet been acquired until a *shtar* is exchanged. There is a whole discussion among the *Rishonim* about what to make of this, given that *karka* can also be acquired by money. The upshot, however, is that this gap creates a zone in which the land is *ke-midbar* — like the wilderness, ownerless — such that whoever seizes it first acquires it. The *Rishonim* debate at length whether such a third party would then be obligated to reimburse the person who had paid the money. The underlying strangeness of the situation is what happens when two legal systems intersect: any internally coherent legal system — whether Jewish or non-Jewish — would naturally hold that when one person's possession ends, the other's begins. It is the collision of two systems that creates this anomalous gap.

### Legal Systems Conflict

The *Gemara* raised a challenge to this ruling based on Shmuel's own principle of *dina de-malkhuta dina* — the law of the government is the law. That principle would seem to close the gap, since it would provide for the fact that such an ownerless interlude cannot arise. The *Gemara* never arrived at a fully satisfying resolution.

### Gemara Response

What the *Gemara* did note was that one of the cases which appeared to underlie Shmuel's ruling was actually consistent with *dina de-malkhuta dina*: it involved land on which taxes had not been paid, so that the government's rule — that whoever is willing to pay the outstanding tax acquires the land — was itself the operative principle. From this it seems that *dina de-malkhuta dina* would override the anomalous ruling Shmuel created. The precise parameters of *dina de-malkhuta dina* and what it does or does not override were explored at length in the previous session.

---

## Third-Party Seizure

### Rav Huna's Ruling

With that background, the *Gemara* now transmits a message sent by Rav Huna bar Avin — apparently addressed either to the scholars of the yeshiva or to an entire community: *Yisrael she-lakakh sade me-oved kokhavim u-va Yisrael akher ve-hekhzik bah, ein motzi'in oto mi-yado* — a Jew who purchases a field from a non-Jew, and another Jew comes and takes possession of it, we do not remove it from the second Jew's hand. This reflects precisely the scenario underlying Shmuel's ruling: money has changed hands but the *shtar* has not, and a third party moves to seize the property and may legitimately do so. The question of whether the seizing party must reimburse the original purchaser remains, as noted, a matter of debate among the *Rishonim*.

### Rabbinic Agreement

The *Gemara* adds: *ve-khen haya Rav Avin ve-Rav Ilai ve-khol raboteinu shavin ba-davar* — Rav Avin, Rav Ilai, and all of our masters agreed on this ruling, which is essentially an endorsement of Shmuel's position.

---

## Three Teachings

### Ukba's Teachings

Rava then introduces a set of teachings: *hani telat milei ishta'ei li Ukba bar Nehemya resh galuta mi-shmei de-Shmuel* — the following three matters were related to me by Ukba bar Nehemya, the *resh galuta* (the secular head of the Jewish community in exile), in the name of Shmuel.

### Dina De-Malkhuta

The first teaching is *dina de-malkhuta dina* itself — the law of the government is the law. How this squares with the previous ruling about *ke-midbar* is not made entirely clear. The *Gemara* is inclined to feel that *dina de-malkhuta dina* would override the anomalous gap, though other possibilities were discussed in the prior session: that *dina de-malkhuta dina* applies only to public law and not to private civil matters, among other limiting principles.

### 40-Year Possession

The second and third teachings are understood as concrete applications of *dina de-malkhuta dina* operative in Persian law. The second teaching is: *ve-arissuta de-Parsaei ad arba'im shanin* — the *arissuta* of the Persians, the *chazaka*, runs for forty years. The literal meaning of *arissuta* is sharecropping, but here it refers to the Persian rule of possession.

### Arissuta Debate

The *Rashbam* explains that this is part of the *dina de-malkhuta* of Persia, and offers two interpretations. The first is a form of squatters' rights — what some people mistakenly understand *chazaka* to be generally — whereby if a person occupies a property for forty years without challenge, even without claiming to have purchased it from the original owner, Persian law considers him the owner. If, operating under this rule, a Jew purchases land from such an occupant, he need not inquire into the basis of the occupant's title, since *dina de-malkhuta* has already established ownership. The second interpretation is that Persian law recognizes a *chazaka* backed by a *ta'ana* — a legal claim — only after forty years, not after three. Underpinning both readings is a claim about sustained, unchallenged possession as the basis of legal title.

### Override Chazaka

If the second interpretation is operative and is to be applied as *dina de-malkhuta dina*, it would mean that Persian law overrides the standard *halacha* of *chazakat gimmel shanim* — the three-year presumption of ownership. The *Rashbam*, for example, states explicitly: *af gav d'bishar makomos havei chazaka l'Yisrael b'gimmel shanim, b'eretz Parsa ein chazaka b'pochos mi-mem shanim d'dina de-malkhuta hu sham* — even though in other places a *chazaka* for a Jew is established in three years, in Persia there is no *chazaka* in less than forty years, because that is the *dina de-malkhuta* there.

This raises a pointed question: if a Jew were bringing another Jew to a *beis din* with a dispute over property, would you tell him that his three years of possession is insufficient because we happen to live in Persia? That does seem like a considerable incursion of secular law into the internal *halacha* governing disputes between Jews. This is precisely the issue the *poskim* grapple with when defining the scope of *dina de-malkhuta dina*. And yet one can understand the other side as well: if a person brings a dispute to a *din Torah* and the question is who owns the property, and one party clearly acquired it according to every operative rule of secular law and is the recognized legal owner, the other party cannot plausibly respond by invoking the rules of *karka* acquisition by *kesef* or *shtar* or *chazaka* as if the wider social context were irrelevant. One might not even need *dina de-malkhuta dina* for this — what the *poskim* call *situmta* and related concepts may already resolve it by treating the prevailing social convention as itself a recognized mode of acquisition. That said, the Persian forty-year rule is somewhat different in character, particularly if it means that in a dispute between two Jews, a three-year possession is treated as legally insufficient. One can argue that we live in a society in which people are expected to preserve their documents for forty years, and that the absence of a document therefore genuinely undermines a claim to the land — but the tension with standard *halacha* remains real.

### Tax Purchasers

The third teaching: *ve-hanei zeharurei d'zavin ara l'tiska, zavinhu zvinah* — wealthy individuals who purchase land to pay the tax, their purchase is a valid purchase. This echoes the case mentioned earlier: if the king's rule is that land on which property taxes have not been paid will be awarded to whoever is willing to pay those taxes, and someone does so and takes possession, that person is considered the legal owner. Presumably this applies not only in transactions involving non-Jews but even when one Jew takes it from another, though here too the question of how broadly *dina de-malkhuta dina* extends to internal Jewish disputes is not fully resolved.

### Tax Distinction

The *Gemara* then qualifies: *ve-hanei milei l'tiska* — this applies specifically to the regular land tax, perhaps specifically property tax. *Aval l'karga, lo* — but for *karga*, the poll tax, it would not be valid. Even if the government were to declare that whoever pays a person's outstanding poll tax may seize his land, that transfer would not be recognized. Why? *Karga akarkafta d'gavra manach* — the poll tax rests on the head of the person; it has nothing to do with any particular piece of land. There is therefore no logical nexus between the tax and the real estate.

This raises a striking point: does *dina de-malkhuta dina* require logical coherence in order to be binding? Can *Chazal* decline to recognize a government rule because it strikes them as lacking internal rationale — not merely as unjust, but as illogical? One possible resolution is that we are not speaking of a formal royal edict at all, but rather a practice of local tax collectors who exercised discretion to allow poll-tax payments to be satisfied by seizing a debtor's land. If so, the rejection is not that the rule is illogical but that it is not *dina de-malkhuta* in the first place — it is a local administrative practice rather than a royal decree. But even that framing leaves some ambiguity, since the *Gemara* phrases its rejection in terms of logical sense rather than formal authority. This is a somewhat unclear *Gemara* on this point.

---

## Poll Tax Lien

### Portable Items

Rav Papa the son of Rav Yehoshua pushes back on the conclusion about *karga*: *afilu sare de-kada mishtabdi le-karga* — even barley sitting in a pot is encumbered by a lien for the poll tax. His argument is that even if the poll tax is not logically tied to real estate specifically, it is a personal obligation of the debtor, and the government has a right to collect it from any of his property whatsoever — including his land. It therefore does make sense that the government would permit someone who pays the outstanding poll tax to seize land equal in value to that tax. The rule is thus coherent, and therefore should qualify as legitimate *dina de-malkhuta dina*.

### Reasonableness

This exchange implies that some *Rishonim* understand *dina de-malkhuta dina* to require not merely that a rule exists but that it be equitable — *dina de-malkhuta* and not *gazlanuta de-malkhuta*, the law of the government and not the brigandage of the government. But what is interesting is that the *Gemara* here seems to go further and require not just equity and fairness but actual rational coherence — a genuine logical connection between the rule and its subject matter. It is at least one reading of this *Gemara* that *dina de-malkhuta dina* demands internal logic, not only general reasonableness.

---

## Amemar's Challenge

### Lien Problem

Rav Ashi reports: Huna bar Natan told him that Amemar raised a difficulty with the ruling that the government has a lien on all of a person's property for an unpaid poll tax, such that even a third party who pays the tax may seize the person's land. *Im kein bitaleta yerushat beno bechor da-havei lei ra'uy* — if so, you have effectively undermined the *halacha* that a firstborn son receives a double portion. Why? Because the *halacha* is that a firstborn receives double only from property that is *muchzak* — actually under the possession of the father at the time of death. Property that is *ra'uy* — fit to come to the estate but not yet in the father's control — does not yield a double portion for the firstborn.

### Muchzak vs Ra'uy

To illustrate: if a father had outstanding debts owed to him, and after his death those debts were collected, the incoming funds are *ra'uy*, not *muchzak*, and the firstborn does not receive double from them. Now, Amemar's concern is this: if the government holds a lien over all of the father's property on account of an unpaid poll tax, then at the moment of the father's death, none of that property is truly and fully in his possession, and all of it would be *ra'uy* — effectively owed to the government — thereby eliminating the firstborn's double portion across the board.

One might object that this is not comparable to an outstanding debt owed to the father. Here the father does own the property; the government merely has a lien on it. After all, if a private individual held a lien on the father's property, we would not say the father is not *muchzak* — the firstborn would still receive double. So why should a government lien be different?

### Two Explanations

The *Rishonim* offer two explanations, both of which may be simultaneously valid. The first is that because it is the government — possessed of sovereign power — holding the lien, the government is in a qualitatively stronger position than a private creditor: it can exercise its right to seize the property at any moment, and therefore the property is not considered to be fully in the father's possession. This explanation is admittedly difficult — one would still need to first fail to pay the tax, and then have the government actually exercise the right of seizure, before the property changes hands. The second explanation, which would have been particularly intuitive to *Rishonim* living in feudal Europe, is the concept that all land ultimately belongs to the king. If sovereignty over the land is understood to reside in the government, then so long as you remain current in your obligations the land is in your possession, but if you fall behind, the land is in a meaningful sense still theirs — it has never fully left their conceptual ownership. It is on this basis that Amemar reasons: if the poll tax creates a government lien over all property, the firstborn is effectively deprived of his double portion.

One might ask whether this is really so troubling. The *halacha* of a firstborn's double portion has not been repealed — it is simply that the circumstances for its application do not exist in this particular social context. In a communist society where no one holds private property, there would similarly be no occasion for *yerushat beno bechor*, but that would not constitute a challenge to the *halacha* itself. Nevertheless, Amemar found the practical elimination of the firstborn's double portion deeply troubling — an outcome he was unwilling to accept.

---

## Gemara Response

### Property Tax Parallel

The *Gemara* responds to Amemar's challenge by turning it back on him: *i hachi afilu tiska nami* — if this is your concern, you should raise the very same objection with respect to the property tax. We already established that the government has rights to seize land for unpaid property taxes, and indeed the *Rashbam* indicates that this too creates a lien. Why doesn't that equally undermine *yerushat beno bechor*?

There is a difference, of course: the property tax lien attaches specifically to the real estate it is levied on, whereas the poll tax — according to Rav Papa — creates a lien on all property including chattels. If the poll-tax lien extends to all of a person's assets, then there is nothing in the estate that would be *muchzak*, and the firstborn's double portion would be completely eliminated. With the property tax lien, at least all the chattel is unencumbered, and the firstborn can still receive double from those assets.

### Tax Timing

But even for real estate under a property tax lien, the *Gemara* answers: *ela mai it lach lemeimar, de-chaiaf tiska u-mit* — the case where the father paid the property tax and then died before the next assessment came due. The language of the *Gemara* makes it sound as if he died immediately after payment, which would make it a very rare case. But Rabbeinu Gershom more sensibly explains: if the father paid at the beginning of the year and the new tax is not due until the following year, then for the remainder of the year his property is entirely unencumbered. He owns it free and clear. In that window, his property is *muchzak* in every sense, and the firstborn receives double. The same logic applies to the poll tax: *hacha nami de-yahiv karga u-mit* — here too, if he paid his poll tax and died before the next poll tax became due, the estate is fully *muchzak* and the firstborn takes double.

### Halacha Report

Rav Ashi then reports that the same Huna bar Natan — who had conveyed Amemar's question — told him: *she'iltinhu le-sifre de-Rava, ve-amru li hilkheta ke-Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua* — I asked the scribes of Rava's yeshiva, and they told me that the ruling follows Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua, namely that there is indeed a recognized lien on all property for the poll tax, and that whoever pays another's outstanding poll tax is considered the legitimate acquirer of that person's property, and that this is the accepted *halacha*.

### Gemara Skepticism

The *Gemara* immediately pushes back: *ve-lav hi* — that does not really prove anything. *Hasam le-ukmei milta hu de-amru* — they said this merely to sustain their practice, meaning these scribes write many documents — evidencing that someone paid a back poll tax and thereby acquired land, and then further documents for the subsequent sale of that land — and so they are motivated to hold that the underlying transaction is valid. Their testimony therefore does not establish the *halacha* independently.

This is a striking objection, and it raises obvious questions. These are *sofrim* connected to Rava's yeshiva; if their practice were illegitimate, presumably Rava would have corrected it. The most reasonable reading of the *Gemara*'s objection is not that these *sofrim* are dishonest, but that they are biased — predisposed to accept as *halacha* what is in fact only a practice — and that the voice of the *Gemara* itself is signaling that the *halacha* should not actually follow this position. The tension, however, remains.

---

## Pardachas Case

### Town vs Collector

Rav Ashi adds a further teaching related to the topic of taxes: *pardachas mesayeia masa* — regarding a *pardachas*, understood by the *Rishonim* as a loafer or layabout who does no work and therefore has no means to pay his share of the communal tax levy. In such a case, if the townspeople persuaded the tax collector not to compel this person to pay and collectively covered his portion on his behalf, he is nevertheless obligated to ultimately contribute his share when he does come to have money. The tax was levied on the whole town, and if others absorbed his share, he owes them.

### Divine Help

However: *ve-hanei milei de-atzluse masa* — this is only where it was the *townspeople* who intervened and protected him, paying his share themselves. *Aval andiski* — but if it was the tax collector himself who, on his own initiative and at his own discretion, decided not to collect from this person and instead drew the full amount from everyone else, then *syata di-shmaya hi* — that is divine intercession, and this person is in fact exempt from paying his share back. The tax collector had the authority to make that determination, and when he chose to exercise it, the person's obligation was genuinely discharged. This connects to the *dina de-malkhuta dina* framework: when the government — through its authorized agent — makes a discretionary determination, that determination carries legal force.

---

## Boundary Markers

### Rav Assi Teaching

Rav Assi, citing Rabbi Yochanan, teaches: *ha-meitzar ve-ha-chatzav mafsikim be-nichsei ha-ger* — a boundary marker and *chatzav* (a particular plant used as a demarcation) serve to divide sections of a *ger*'s property. The *chatzav* is a plant that grows straight down with roots that go deep and do not spread laterally; Joshua reportedly used it to mark the boundaries of the tribes in *Eretz Yisrael*. The context here brings us back from the long digression about taxes and *dina de-malkhuta dina* to the earlier discussion: when a convert (*ger*) dies without heirs and his property becomes *hefker*, whoever establishes a *chazaka* acquires not the whole estate but only the specific plot he took possession of. The boundary markers divide the estate into separate parcels, so that a *chazaka* on one plot does not extend to an adjacent plot separated by a boundary or by *chatzav*.

*Aval le-inyan pe'ah ve-tumah lo* — but for purposes of *pe'ah* and *tumah*, this kind of simple demarcation does not suffice to divide fields. For those purposes, something more substantial is required.

### Mishna Division

The *Gemara* asks what constitutes a sufficient physical break for *pe'ah*. The Mishna teaches: *ha-nachal, ve-ha-shulit, ve-derech ha-rabim, ve-derech ha-yachid* — a *nachal* (here not a river but a dry wadi, like the *nachal eitan* of the *egla arufa*), a *shulit* (a stream of running rainwater that constitutes a real geographical break), a public road, or a private road. The *Rashbam* explains that a road here means something used by vehicles — wagons — a real piece of infrastructure, not merely a line across a field. Any of these, running between two sections of a field owned by one person, requires *pe'ah* to be left separately in each section.

### Path Requirements

A *shvil* — a footpath, whether public or private, even one so narrow as to serve only a single pedestrian — can also divide fields, but with an additional requirement: *ha-kavu'a bein bi-yemot ha-chama bein bi-yemot ha-geshamim* — it must be a fixed path used in both the summer and the rainy season. In the rainy season, people avoid traversing fields because it is muddy and would damage the crops; so a path used even during the rainy season is genuinely embedded in the landscape. Without that criterion, a mere footpath would not constitute a meaningful division. A road, by contrast, does not require this additional criterion.

One might wonder why the Mishna bothers listing both the public road and the private road rather than simply stating the most minimal case of the private footpath. The *Yerushalmi* addresses this: when it comes to trees, even a public road does not divide sections of a field for *pe'ah* purposes. The Mishna therefore wants to establish both extremes: for non-tree fields, the rule applies across the full spectrum from public road down to private footpath (so long as it is used in both seasons); for trees, even the most substantial road is insufficient. The contrast requires both poles to be stated.

---

## Peah & Tumah

### Peah Example

As noted, Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan had said that for *pe'ah* and *tumah*, a simple boundary marker or *chatzav* plant does not divide the field, whereas for the *nichsei ha-ger* it does. The Mishna's list — *nachal*, *shulit*, public road, private road, *shvil* — represents the threshold required for *pe'ah*.

### Logic Difference

The underlying logic of this distinction is worth considering. When the question is one of ownership and acquisition — as in the *nichsei ha-ger* case — any marker that demarcates "I treat this as my property and I am taking possession of this plot as distinct from that one" is conceptually sufficient. Ownership is, to a significant degree, about intentional recognition: this is mine, that is a separate thing. But when the question is *pe'ah* — the obligation to leave a corner of the field from the actual grain growing there — the fact that the owner *considers* two sections of his field to be separate is beside the point. He owns both. The grain in both is his. The question is whether they are physically, geographically, truly distinct fields, and for that you need something real on the landscape. A line someone drew, or a plant someone placed, reflecting his private decision to regard them as separate — that carries no weight when the *halacha* looks at the physical field itself.

---

## Tumah Case

### Eliezer Debate

The Mishna in tractate *Peah* provides the *tumah* parallel: *ha-niknas le-vika bi-yemot ha-geshamim ve-tumah be-sadeh pelonit* — one who enters a valley in the rainy season, and *tumah* is known to exist in one of the fields there. The principle derived from *sotah* is that a *safek tumah* in a *reshut ha-yachid* renders one *tamei*, while a *safek tumah* in a *reshut ha-rabim* leaves one *tahor*. A valley in the rainy season is a *reshut ha-yachid* for *tumah* purposes — it is secluded, no one traverses it in that season, it is muddy, and entering would ruin the crops. If someone entered this valley and there is a grave known to be in one of the fields, and the person says: I went to the valley but I do not know whether I entered the field where the *tumah* is — *Rabbi Eliezer metaher ve-chakhamim metam'in*. Rabbi Eliezer holds the person is *tahor*; the Sages hold the person is *tamei*.

The reason: *shehaya Rabbi Eliezer omer, safek bi'ah tahor, safek maga tumah tamei* — Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes two categories of doubt. A *safek bi'ah* — a doubt as to whether one even entered the relevant space — renders one *tahor*, because the operative principle from *sotah* requires that the person was in the private space in the first place; if you do not know whether you were there, the default is *tahor*. A *safek maga* — a doubt as to whether one made contact with the source of *tumah* — renders one *tamei*, since this is a case where you were in the relevant enclosed space and the question is only whether you touched or walked over the grave. The Sages hold that in either case, since you are in a *reshut ha-yachid* for *tumah*, you are *tamei*.

### Rashbam & Tosfos

The *Rashbam* and *Tosfos* debate the underlying logic of Rabbi Eliezer's position. The *Rashbam* understands Rabbi Eliezer to be working with a principle of *sfeik sfeika* — a double doubt: I do not know if you entered the field, and even if you did, I do not know if you made contact with the *tumah*. Their debate then centers on whether *sfeik sfeika* renders one *tahor* or *tamei* in a *reshut ha-yachid*. *Tosfos* reads Rabbi Eliezer more simply, and closer to the plain language: the *sotah* principle applies specifically to a case of *safek maga* — where one was definitely in the private domain and the question is about contact. Where the doubt is about *bi'ah* itself — whether one ever entered the defined space — the mechanism of *safek tumah be-reshut ha-yachid tamei* simply does not engage, and the default is *tahor*. This reading of Rabbi Eliezer does not require invoking *sfeik sfeika* at all.

---

## Peah & Tumah (II)

### Rabin Update

When Ravin came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he transmitted an updated version of Rabbi Yochanan's position: *afilu le-pe'ah u-le-tumah* — even for *pe'ah* and *tumah*, a simple boundary marker or *chatzav* demarcation suffices to divide the field. This overrides the earlier attribution to Rabbi Yochanan that held otherwise, and collapses the distinction: the same physical marking that divides for the purposes of *nichsei ha-ger* and ownership would also divide for *pe'ah* and *tumah*.

---

## Tumah Case (II)

### Valley Scenario

The scenario for *tumah* is thus: a valley in the rainy season, multiple fields, a grave known to be in one of them, and a person who is uncertain whether he entered the specific field containing the grave. The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages — whether uncertainty about *bi'ah* as opposed to uncertainty about *maga* changes the outcome — turns precisely on how we define and delimit the private domain in question, and what it means to have "entered" the relevant field when the fields may or may not be meaningfully divided.

---

## Shabbat Melacha

### One Obliviousness

*Rava* extends the same underlying logic to *Shabbat*. The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: if someone carried a half-measure of a *grogeret* (dried fig) — that is, half the minimum volume required to be liable for carrying on *Shabbat*, since the *shiur* for most *melakhot* is the volume of a *grogeret* — into *reshut ha-rabim*, set it down, and then carried out another half-measure and set that down as well, do the two half-measures combine to constitute a single prohibited act? The answer is: yes, if they were performed *be-helem achas* — in a single state of obliviousness. The mechanism for combining two half-measures of a *melakha* on *Shabbat* is not time-based (as it is for eating and drinking on *Yom Kippur* or *Tisha B'Av*, where the standard is *kedei achilas pras* or *kedei shetiyas revi'is*), but rather continuity of mental state: as long as the person did not remember in the middle that it was *Shabbat* — and thus experience an intervening moment of awareness — both acts are considered part of one continuous prohibited act, and he is obligated to bring a *korban chatat*. *Bi-shnei helamos patur* — if there were two distinct states of forgetfulness, with an intervening awareness, the acts are separate and he is exempt.

### Same Domain

Rabbi Yosei adds a further condition — at the top of 56a: *be-helem echad be-reshut achas, chayav; bi-shtei reshuyot, patur* — even within a single state of forgetfulness, the two half-measures only combine if they were deposited in the same *reshut ha-rabim*. If one half was placed in one public domain and the second half in a different public domain, they do not combine, and one is exempt. The act of carrying is conceptually complete only when something is brought *to a place*, and if I brought two half-measures to two separate places, I did not bring one thing to one place.

### Separating Domains

This raises the question of how to define one *reshut ha-rabim* versus two. If it is all one continuous road and you deposited one half higher up and one half further down, are they the same *reshut* or different? Rabbah states: *ve-hu she-yesh chiyuv chatat beineihem* — the two sections are considered separate *reshuyot* only if what lies between them would itself impose a *chiyuv chatat* — a Torah-level liability — if crossed, meaning the intervening space must constitute a *reshut ha-yachid*. If you have two stretches of *reshut ha-rabim* separated by a private building or a row of buildings — genuinely *reshut ha-yachid* — then they are two separate domains. *Aval Carmelis lo* — but if the intervening space is merely a *Carmelis* (an intermediate domain, neither fully public nor private), such as a wide expanse of grass or a park, that does not constitute a Torah-level domain separator and therefore does not divide the two stretches into separate *reshuyot* for this purpose.

### Carmelis Debate

Abaye disagrees: *afilu Carmelis* — even a *Carmelis* suffices to divide two stretches of *reshut ha-rabim* into separate domains for this *halacha*. However, Abaye draws his own line: *aval pislo* — a *pislo*, a small platform or minor constructed structure that does not rise to the level of a meaningful domain, is insufficient. Rava goes further still: *afilu pislo* — even a *pislo* divides the two stretches into separate *reshuyot*. This is closely analogous to the position Rava takes on the *meitzar* and *chatzav* for *Shabbat* purposes: just as Rava holds that even a minor constructed boundary can define separate domains in the property context, so too here, even a *pislo* suffices to define two separate *reshuyot ha-rabim* such that two half-measures placed on either side would not combine, and one would be exempt from a *chatat*.

---

---

# Bava Batra 56

## Chazakah & Boundaries

### Field Demarcation Q

The daf opens by returning to a question that had occupied the previous session: what type of boundary marker suffices to demarcate two separate fields for the purposes of *chazakah*? The practical context is *nichsei ha-ger* — property left ownerless when a convert dies without heirs. When someone performs an act of *chazakah* on such a field, the question is how far that acquisition extends. If the field were being sold or transferred, the transaction itself would define the scope of the *chazakah*, even across physically separate parcels. But when the property is *hefker*, the physical reality must do all the definitional work. Accordingly, if there is a boundary line, a mound, trees, or a strip of demarcating grass between two plots, an act of *chazakah* on one does not reach the other.

### Pe'ah & Tum'ah

The previous day's discussion had examined this question through two other areas of *halacha*. The first was *pe'ah*: does one leave a single corner of the field for the poor, or two separate corners — one from each plot? The second was *tum'ah*: when there is doubt whether a person entered a field containing a source of ritual impurity, Rabbi Eliezer's rule that doubt in a private domain resolves to *tamei* applies only if the person definitely entered that field. If the very entry is in doubt, the person is *tahor*. The question then becomes whether a boundary marker causes two plots to be treated as distinct fields for this purpose, or as one. The discussion there reached the conclusion that while such a marker might not create two separate domains for most purposes, Rava held that it would for *Shabbat*.

### Shabbat Domains

The Gemara's last lines on 55b introduce the relevance of Rava's position to *Shabbat*. The general view is that a boundary marker within a continuous field would not create two separate *Shabbat* domains — *aval l'Shabbos lo*. Rava, however, maintains — *afilu l'inyan Shabbos* — that even for *Shabbat* purposes, such a demarcation creates two. The Gemara now proceeds to develop the *Shabbat* question fully.

---

## Reshut Separation

### Half Fig Baraita

The *beraita* cited to frame the *Shabbat* discussion involves a case of carrying half a *grogeres* — half a pressed fig, which is the minimum volume of food whose transfer from a private to a public domain constitutes a biblical violation of *Shabbat*. The case is: one carried half the required measure from a private domain into a public domain, set it down, and then carried another half measure. Do these two acts combine to constitute a single violation?

The operative principle is *he'elam echad* — one uninterrupted state of forgetting. If the person never remembered between the two acts that it was *Shabbat*, those acts collapse into a single continuous episode of inadvertent violation, obligating a *korban chattas*. If the person remembered in between — breaking the continuity of the lapse — then there are two separate acts and no combined liability, even if each act involved only half the minimum measure. The passage of time as such is not what breaks the *he'elam*; one could perform the second act three hours after the first and still be in one uninterrupted state of forgetting. What ruptures the *he'elam* is the moment of awareness in between.

### R. Yosi Requirement

Rabbi Yosi introduces an additional criterion beyond *he'elam echad*. Even granting a single continuous lapse, the two acts combine to form one violation only if both took place *bi-reshut achas* — within one domain. If the person brought half a measure into one public domain and then half a measure into a different public domain, Rabbi Yosi exempts. Tosafot notes that another Gemara implies an even stricter standard — not merely the same domain but the same specific location within that domain — though the *beraita* here is content to speak of the same domain generally.

The natural question that flows from Rabbi Yosi's ruling is: what is the minimum threshold for considering two public domains as distinct, such that carrying into each would yield the exemption?

### Rava Threshold

Rava defines the boundary: for two public domains to be considered separate under Rabbi Yosi's rule, there must be a *reshut ha-yachid* between them — an enclosed private domain. The logic is rooted in biblical categories. For *Shabbat* purposes, the Torah recognizes only two domains that carry biblical force: the enclosed *reshut ha-yachid* and the open *reshut ha-rabim*. Spaces that fall into neither category — neither fully enclosed nor a major thoroughfare — are a *karmelit*, a rabbinic domain. If two public domains are separated only by a *karmelit*, they are not genuinely distinct for these purposes; the carrying of half a measure into each would still combine to create one violation.

### Abaye Karmelit

Abaye disputes this threshold. In his view, even a *karmelit* suffices to separate two public domains under Rabbi Yosi's rule. As long as one public domain ends and something else begins before the next public domain opens, that intermediate zone — even if not a biblical *reshut ha-yachid* — constitutes a genuine separation.

### Rava Pisla

Rava extends his position in the other direction: even a *pisla* — a raised platform set within what is otherwise one continuous public thoroughfare — is sufficient to separate the domains on either side of it. The *pisla* does not transform part of the street into a different *reshut*; it is entirely embedded within the *reshut ha-rabim*. Yet Rava holds that its mere presence as a physical demarcation creates two separate domains for the purposes of Rabbi Yosi's rule.

### Shabbat-Gittin

The Gemara concludes this unit with Rava's programmatic statement: *reshut Shabbat ke-reshut Gittin dami* — the concept of domain for *Shabbat* purposes operates analogously to the concept of domain for *Gittin* purposes. The Rashbam explains the *Gittin* parallel: if a wife is standing in her husband's courtyard and he throws the *get* toward her, but the *get* lands on a small raised platform rather than on the ground beside her, the *get* does not take effect. The husband is presumed to have transferred ownership of one space to her, not two. Even a small platform, though located within the same courtyard, is treated as a distinct space — and it is precisely because of that distinction that the *get* falls outside the space she was *koneh*. Rabbeinu Gershom cites a related *halacha* that the wife and the *get* must occupy the same zone for the ground to function as a *yad*, an extension of the person receiving the *get*; a *get* falling on a platform while she stands on the ground fails this requirement. In either reading, Rava's point is that the same conception of spatial distinctness — in which even minimal physical differentiation creates a separate domain — governs both *Shabbat* and *Gittin*.

---

## Chatzav Plant

### No Marker Case

The Gemara now returns to the original question of field boundaries for *nichsei ha-ger* and asks: *ein sham lo meitzar velo chatzav mai* — what is the law where there is no boundary marker and no *chatzav* plant? If there is no physical demarcation, how does one define the scope of the field within which an act of *chazakah* acquires?

### Community Recognition

The Rashbam understands the question to be asking how much land is acquired when a person performs a single act of *chazakah* on an ownerless estate with no visible boundary. One might have thought that without a marker, everything the deceased owned — however extensive — is acquired in one act; or alternatively, that only the precise area physically worked is acquired. The Gemara resolves this by citing the explanation given in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol shenikreit al shemah* — the defining criterion is community recognition. Whatever extent of land is commonly called by the name of the original owner — "the field of so-and-so," or as Rav Pappa specifies, "the irrigation area of so-and-so" — that constitutes the recognized unit. An act of *chazakah* on any part of it acquires the whole.

### Tosafot Tum'ah

Tosafot reads the question differently. Citing the *Tosefta* in *Taharos*, Tosafot argues that the question of *ein sham lo meitzar velo chatzav* is not a return to the *nichsei ha-ger* problem at all, but a continuation of the *tum'ah* question discussed earlier. When someone enters a valley during the rainy season and there is a source of *tum'ah* in a particular field, the halachic outcome depends on whether the person definitively entered that field. What counts as "that field" when there are no markers? The answer — *kol shenikreit al shemah*, recognized by the community as a distinct unit — provides the definition for *tum'ah* purposes as well.

### Sea Squill ID

The *chatzav* plant, which the Gemara lists alongside the *meitzar* as a recognized field boundary marker, is identified as sea squill. The Rashbam explains the name: *chotzev ba'adamah* — it cuts straight down into the earth. Its roots descend vertically without spreading laterally, and the plant itself grows straight up, making it an ideal boundary marker that does not encroach on either neighboring plot. Sea squill has a large bulb that is typically planted deep in the ground, making it extremely difficult to remove entirely — a property of obvious practical value for a permanent land marker. It produces green leaves in winter, dries out completely in summer, and at the end of the summer grows a tall white-flowered inflorescence. Because of its straight vertical form and annual regrowth, sea squill was used to demarcate field boundaries in ancient times and reportedly continues to serve this function in some Arab villages today. The fact that it is poisonous also discourages people from tampering with it.

### Joshua Boundary

Rav Yehuda cites this identification in the name of Rav: the *chatzuva* is the plant that Joshua used to demarcate the tribal and family land divisions in the land of Israel — *shebo ticham Yehoshua l'Yisrael et ha'aretz*. The choice of plant was deliberate: its straight-down, straight-up growth ensured it would not siphon nutrients from either adjacent plot and would remain precisely where placed, making it a reliable and self-maintaining marker of the divisions between tribe and tribe and between one family's portion and another's.

---

## Eretz Yisrael

### Border Cities

The mention of Joshua's method of demarcation prompts the Gemara to cite a related teaching in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Rav: *lo manah Yehoshua ela ayaros ha'omdos al ha-gvulin* — in Sefer Yehoshua, only the cities situated on the borders are enumerated. The reason is that those cities are the relevant ones for defining the territorial extent of the land. Tosafot, however, objects that this cannot mean the external borders of the land of Israel, since many cities listed in Yehoshua are located in the interior. Tosafot therefore reads the statement as referring to the inter-tribal borders — the cities mentioned are those that served as boundary markers between one tribe's territory and another's, a use of the same principle of marking divisions that motivated Joshua's use of the *chatzav* plant.

### Terumot Ma'aser

Immediately following is a statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel — a separate tradition, though reported by the same Rav Yehuda: *kol she'her'ahu Ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu le-Moshe chayav be-ma'aser* — everything that God showed Moses in his final vision from the heights of Moab is obligated in *ma'aser*. The Torah describes that vision in Devarim: God showed Moses all the land, from Gilead to Dan, all the land of Naftali, the land of Efrayim and Menasheh, and so on. That sweep of land defines what is subject to *terumot u-ma'aser*.

### Extra Nations

The statement's exclusionary force — *le-appukei mai*, what does it come to exclude? — is directed at the lands of *Keini, Kenizi, ve-Kadmoni*. When God makes the covenant with Abraham in the *Brit Bein Ha-Betarim*, He promises ten nations' lands, not the seven Canaanite nations enumerated elsewhere in the Torah. Three nations — *Keini, Kenizi, ve-Kadmoni* — appear in the covenant with Abraham but are conspicuously absent from every subsequent enumeration of the Canaanite nations. The Rabbis understood this discrepancy to mean that these three lands occupy a different status: they were promised to Abraham, but they are not *Eretz Yisrael* proper and their conquest would not subject them to the obligations of *terumot u-ma'aser*.

Tosafot raises a preliminary methodological objection: if the Gemara wants to demarcate *Eretz Yisrael* obligated in *ma'aser*, it would have been more natural to cite the explicit border description in Bamidbar, which specifically draws the boundaries of the land. Tosafot notes this without resolution, simply observing that the two passages are presumably consistent.

### Rashbam Distance

The Rashbam's reading of what it means that *Keini, Kenizi, ve-Kadmoni* are excluded is striking. He maintains that even if Israel were to conquer those lands — even through a proper *kibbush rabbim*, a conquest authorized by the Sanhedrin after the conquest of *Eretz Yisrael* proper — those lands would still never become incorporated into *Eretz Yisrael* and never be obligated in *terumot u-ma'aser*.

This position creates an apparent difficulty from the Gemara's discussion of *Surya* — identified with a Transjordanian region conquered by David — where the question of whether it carries the obligations of *Eretz Yisrael* turns entirely on whether it was *kibbush yachid* or *kibbush rabbim*. That Gemara assumes that had the conquest been a proper *kibbush rabbim*, *Surya* would indeed be obligated in *terumot u-ma'aser*. If so, why would the lands of *Keini, Kenizi, ve-Kadmoni* be treated differently?

The Rashbam's answer appears to be one of geographic distance. *Surya* is immediately contiguous with *Eretz Yisrael* and is the type of land that can be absorbed into it under the right conditions. The lands of *Keini, Kenizi, ve-Kadmoni*, by contrast, are so distant that they can never become *Eretz Yisrael* proper regardless of the manner of their conquest. The Rashbam reads the Gemara in *Bereishit Rabbah* in support: even though the Torah promises these lands to Abraham, and even though we believe we will eventually receive them, they remain permanently outside the framework of *Eretz Yisrael* for purposes of *ma'aser*. The promise of *Keini, Kenizi, ve-Kadmoni* is of a different order — a future, perhaps messianic, addition — whereas the seven Canaanite nations represent the true promised land confirmed by oath.

### Tosafot Conquest

Tosafot substantially moderates the Rashbam's position. In Tosafot's reading, all the Gemara is saying is that the *kedusha rishona* — the sanctification of *Eretz Yisrael* that determines its obligations in *terumot u-ma'aser* — is defined by what was actually conquered in the time of Joshua, not by what was divinely promised to Abraham. The exclusion of *Keini, Kenizi, ve-Kadmoni* is simply the exclusion of what Joshua did not conquer. This is not a surprising statement: those lands were not part of Joshua's conquest, and therefore they are not included in the *kedusha rishona* regardless of the covenant with Abraham.

On this reading, Tosafot is making a conceptual point about the relationship between divine promise and halachic reality: *Eretz Yisrael* for the purpose of agricultural obligations is not determined by the full scope of what God promised Abraham. It is determined by the reality of what was conquered and settled. The boundaries described in Bamidbar function not as a definition of what is *kadosh* but as a directive — this is what you are expected to conquer — and the halachic status follows the actual history of conquest.

The question of *Surya* and David's conquests does not necessarily contradict this, since that discussion may operate under the framework of *kedusha shniya*, the sanctification established in the time of Ezra, which itself runs through the period of the *Chashmonaim* and potentially beyond. According to Tosafot, the conquest of *Keini, Kenizi, ve-Kadmoni* in some future scenario might indeed confer *kedusha* — Tosafot is not closing that door — but the *kedusha rishona* achieved through Joshua's conquest does not automatically extend to those lands.

### Opinions Lands

The Gemara presents three Tannaitic opinions on the geographic identity of *Keini, Kenizi, ve-Kadmoni*. Rabbi Meir identifies them as *Navtiya*, *Arviya*, and *Shalmiya* — nations situated, according to the commentators, in the southern reaches, from the Dead Sea extending toward Eilat and into northern Arabia, encompassing the area of the ancient Nabatean kingdoms. Rabbi Yehuda identifies them as *Har Seir*, *Amon*, and *Moav* — the territories of Esau and Lot, the lands bordering *Eretz Yisrael* immediately to the south and east, which the Torah explicitly instructs Israel not to conquer, for they have been given as a heritage to Esau and to the descendants of Lot. Rabbi Shimon identifies them as *Ardiscus*, *Asya*, and *Aspamya* — lands in Asia Minor and northern Syria.

Rabbi Yehuda's identification is particularly striking. The lands that God promised Abraham beyond the seven Canaanite nations — the lands that went to Abraham's family but not to the Jewish part of that family — turn out to be the territories of Esau and Lot. Abraham was promised ten nations; his descendants received seven. The other three went to his other descendants. It is a remarkable reading of the scriptural record: the covenant with Abraham was fulfilled in full, just not for *Bnei Yisrael* alone.

---

## False Witnesses

### Mishnah Setup

The Gemara now turns to the *Mishnah* at the opening of a new chapter, which deals with *edim zomemim* — witnesses who are exposed as having given false testimony through the *hazamah* process, in which a second set of witnesses testifies that the first set was elsewhere at the time they claimed to have observed the events in question. In the context of *chazakah*, the situation is as follows: a claimant brings witnesses who testify that he occupied and worked a disputed field for three consecutive years, thereby establishing a *chazakah*. If those witnesses are subsequently exposed as *zomemim*, they must compensate the true owner for the value of the field they attempted to steal through testimony. *Meshalmim lo et ha-kol* — they pay him everything.

The Mishnah then complicates the scenario. If the three-year *chazakah* was established not by one pair of witnesses who testified to all three years, but by three separate pairs — the first pair testifying to year one, the second to year two, the third to year three — and all three pairs are subsequently exposed as *zomemim*, then *meshaleshin beineihem*: the obligation is divided equally among the three pairs, each bearing one-third of the liability. They acted together to achieve a single result and share the consequences.

### Brothers Separate

The Mishnah then presents a further case: suppose the three pairs of witnesses were composed of three brothers — Reuven, Shimon, and Levi — each brother pairing with an unrelated fourth witness, Mordechai, who happened to observe all three years. Group one consists of Reuven and Mordechai (year one); group two of Shimon and Mordechai (year two); group three of Levi and Mordechai (year three). The Mishnah rules that these constitute three valid and distinct testimonies — *harei elu shalosh eduyot*. Since each brother testified only to a single year, and each year is a distinct factual matter, there is no problem of two brothers testifying to the same event.

However, for purposes of *hazamah*, the Mishnah rules that it is not one unified testimony — *ve-ein edut achat le-hazamah*. The three testimonies are seen as a combined enterprise, all working toward a single result: awarding the *chazakah* to David. The *hazamah* therefore falls on them collectively, and none of the pairs is penalized as *zomemim* until all three are exposed simultaneously. A related observation is that if the claimant brought all three groups together, they are clearly viewed as one coordinated effort. Tosafot notes the question of why the first two pairs of witnesses cannot claim they were merely testifying that the claimant unlawfully ate the field's produce in those years — which, if true, would mean they were testifying on the original owner's behalf, not against him. Tosafot resolves this by noting that when the claimant himself produces the witnesses and introduces them together, their combined purpose is transparently directed at establishing the *chazakah*, and they are treated as a unified set.

---

## Years Combine

### Davar Question

The Gemara now flags that the *Mishnah* — which assumes that three separate pairs of witnesses, one per year, can collectively establish a *chazakah* — does not follow the view of Rabbi Akiva. A *beraita* records that Abba Chalafta went to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri (or, in the alternate version, Rabbi Yochanan went to Abba Chalafta) to study Torah, and the question was posed: if three different pairs of witnesses testified, respectively, to years one, two, and three of an occupation, do they combine to establish a *chazakah*? The answer offered was: *harei zo chazakah* — yes, they combine. Rabbi Yosi ben Chalafta reports that both parties agreed on this, but notes that Rabbi Akiva dissents.

### Akiva Stringency

Rabbi Akiva's position is grounded in the scriptural requirement of testimony: *al pi shenayim edim yakum davar* — a matter is established on the testimony of two witnesses. Rabbi Akiva infers: *davar*, a full matter — *ve-lo chatzi davar*, not a half-matter. Since any single year of occupation does not by itself constitute a *chazakah* — indeed, one year of another person's presence on one's land proves the opposite of ownership, establishing that the occupier owes a year's produce to the true owner — each pair of witnesses is testifying to only a partial matter. A *chazakah* by definition requires three years; testimony to one year is not testimony to a *chazakah*, it is testimony to *chatzi davar* or less. Rabbi Akiva therefore demands that each pair of witnesses testify to the full three-year *chazakah* — a standard that is practically very difficult to meet.

### Half Matter

The Gemara asks: according to the Rabbis, who hold that these three yearly testimonies do combine, what then does the verse *ve-lo chatzi davar* come to exclude? They must agree that partial testimonies cannot combine in some cases; otherwise the verse teaches nothing. The Gemara proposes: perhaps the verse excludes a case where one witness testifies to seeing a pubic hair from the front (*begava*) and a second witness testifies to seeing a pubic hair from behind (*be-kreisa*), in the context of establishing that a girl has reached halachic adulthood. Could those combine?

The Gemara rejects this formulation.
