# Bava Batra 61

## Intro & Context

### Perek Overview

With today's daf we begin a new *perek*, *Hamocher Et Habayit* — "One Who Sells a House." This chapter represents a notable shift in character from the previous one. Where the preceding *perek* engaged with a range of abstract concepts — *chazaka*, standards of proof, rules of *eidut* — the present chapter is considerably more concrete and practical: when you say you are selling your house, what exactly is included in that sale? When you say you are selling a cow or a horse, what comes along with it, absent any specification to the contrary? This is the animating question of the chapter, and it generates a richly detailed body of law.

### Agadeta Reflection

Before proceeding, it is worth pausing briefly on the *agadeta* at the end of the previous *perek*, which we had to rush through. What emerged from it was, for the most part, a remarkably balanced vision: we are obligated to maintain *aveilus* on the *Beit HaMikdash*, yet we are equally obligated to live our lives fully. The teaching does not demand a life of obsessive mourning — perhaps ninety-nine percent of one's life is lived fully, with a small *zeicher* woven in. The very end of the *agadeta*, however, struck a far more somber and almost nihilistic note, one that is genuinely difficult to reckon with. But before that jarring conclusion, the balance articulated there is, in fact, the one we actually follow in practice.

### Chazka & Churban

There is an interesting thematic resonance worth noting as we transition into this new chapter. The entire previous *perek* was about *chezkas habatim* — establishing a kind of permanence of ownership, asserting that this land is mine, that I have been here three years, that I have a right to it. And yet, as we noted right at the opening of that *perek*, one of the foundational ideas surrounding *chazaka* — including the very question of whether one had a *shtar* — was derived from the *nevua* in *Yirmiyah*: go ahead and write *shtaros* and place them in a *kli cheres*, *lema'an ya'amdu yamim rabbim*, for you are going into *galus*. You are going to be living in *chutz la'aretz*, and who knows when you will return to *Eretz Yisrael*.

There is something worth sitting with there. All of these weighty discussions about proving whose land is whose, about asserting ownership through possession — this is fundamentally a *chutz la'aretz* conversation. This is not where we belong. And so after such an intense *perek* built around the sense of owning property and proving that ownership through a kind of semi-permanence, the *agadeta* at its conclusion reminds us: this is not our permanent place. When you build your house, you leave a *zeicher l'churban*. *Im lo a'aleh es Yerushalayim al rosh simchasenu* — that is the verse the *agadeta* itself quoted. That sense of longing for permanence in the right place is the note on which the previous chapter ends, and it lends a particular resonance to a chapter that is now going to dig deeply into what it means to own, sell, and transfer property in this world.

### Kavod HaMeit

Before beginning, we pause to acknowledge Joe, who is observing his father's *yahrtzeit*. His father's name was *Chanoch ben Hersh Leib*. May his *neshama* have an *aliyah*.

---

## Excluded Items

### Mishnah Text

The *Mishnah* opens: *lo machar yatzia* — one who sells a house does not sell the *yatzia*, the veranda or attached add-on structure, even though it opens into the house. *Ve-lo et hacheder she-liphnim heimenu* — nor does the sale include the inner room located within or behind it. *Ve-lo et hagag bizman she-yesh lo ma'akeh gavoah asara tefachim* — nor does it include the roof, provided the roof has a surrounding wall of ten *tefachim*. Rabbi Yehuda adds: *im yesh tzurat hapetach af al pi she'eina gevoha asara tefachim eino machur* — if the fence around the roof has a *tzurat hapetach*, a doorway-type structure, then even without a wall of ten *tefachim* the roof is not included in the sale.

### Yetzia Definition

What exactly is a *yatzia*? The word seems to denote some kind of structure exterior to the main wall of the house — either an enclosed porch, something resembling a veranda, or an add-on structure of some kind. The parallel usage in the context of *Sukkah* involves a type of balcony, but here the structure appears to be exterior to the wall of the house rather than interior to it.

What is immediately striking about this *Mishnah*, however, is not the definition of *yatzia* so much as the underlying assumption: that one person could own the veranda while another owns the house proper, or that a seller would retain the veranda even while transferring ownership of the house. This is a difficult concept to absorb intuitively. The *yatzia*, after all, may only be accessible through the house itself — and yet, the *Mishnah* treats it as something potentially separable. Perhaps the key is recognizing that the word "house" in a bill of sale cannot be expected to carry more weight than its narrowest, most natural referent, and anything not captured by that referent remains with the seller unless explicitly transferred. Even so, there is something genuinely puzzling about envisioning a division of ownership of this kind.

One might suggest that the difficulty stems from reasoning too much from a modern, New York real estate context. In the ancient world, where structures were built organically — flat roofs with add-on rooms, extensions behind the main living space, separate quarters accessible from a shared courtyard — the division of ownership between different parts of a single complex may have been a far more ordinary social reality than it appears to us. There is something to this point.

### Inner Room

The *Mishnah*'s next exclusion is the *cheder* — the inner room. Here again, one's first instinct is to ask: what does it mean that the bedroom or back room of a house is not included when you sell the house? The more sensible reading, it seems, is that the *cheder* here refers not to an ordinary bedroom but to a separate, self-contained living facility — what we might call a mother-in-law suite or a back unit with its own character as a distinct domicile. We have seen elsewhere the concept that one person owns the ground floor and another owns the upper floor, that one person owns the front and another the back. To the extent that a *cheder* could plausibly belong to a different tenant or function as a separate residential unit, it makes sense that the word "house" in a bill of sale would not automatically encompass it.

The *Rashbam*, however, explains the *cheder* quite differently — as a storage room, essentially an attic or back storeroom where one keeps one's belongings, not as an alternative living space. His language is clear: *de-keivan de-eino asui ela lehatznia sham chafatzav lishmor k'mo betevah*, since it is made only for storing one's possessions like a box, it is therefore not included in the category of *bayit*. This is, to say the least, counterintuitive. The idea that I am selling you my house while retaining the storage room in the back — not because it is a separate dwelling but simply because it is a storage facility — is very difficult to understand. Why should a back storeroom not be considered an integral part of what one is selling? The *Rashbam*'s reading stands, but it is hard to make entirely natural sense of it.

### Roof Conditions

The *Mishnah*'s third exclusion concerns the *gag* — the roof — under certain conditions. If the roof has a surrounding *ma'akeh*, a perimeter wall of ten *tefachim*, then the roof is not included in the sale. The *ma'akeh* in question echoes the *mitzvah* of *asita ma'akeh l'gagecha*, and a roof enclosed by such a wall becomes, in effect, a usable living space in its own right. Anyone familiar with certain neighborhoods in Jerusalem will recognize the phenomenon: what appears to be a flat expanse of concrete turns out to be the rooftops of houses below, functioning as open courtyards or gathering spaces. In densely built urban environments, the roof of one person's house could be effectively the outdoor living space of another. The *Mishnah* treats such a roof as independently functional and therefore not automatically included in the sale.

Rabbi Yehuda holds that even without a full ten-*tefach* wall, if the boundary structure has the form of a *tzurat hapetach* — a post-and-lintel doorway structure — then the roof is similarly understood as its own independent space and is not sold along with the house.

---

## Yetzia Etymology

### Three Terms

The *Gemara* opens its analysis of the *Mishnah* by exploring the semantics of the word *yatzia* itself. *Tani Rav Yosef* — Rav Yosef taught: this structure that the *Mishnah* calls *yatzia* is known by three different names: *yatzia*, *tzeila*, and *ta*. Each of these terms appears in a different classical text, and the *Gemara* proceeds to identify the source of each.

In *Eretz Yisrael*, the Gemara notes, it is translated as *afta* — a low-built structure attached to the side or the back of the house. Rav Yosef identifies it as *bidka chalila*, a latticed or windowed structure, more open to the air, built onto the house. The *Gemara* then draws out the logical relationship between these two readings: if even the fully enclosed *afta* is considered independent of the house and is not sold along with it, then *a fortiori* the open-aired, latticed *bidka chalila* would not be sold with the house. Conversely, according to the view that the *Mishnah* is referring to the *bidka chalila*, the enclosed *afta* would indeed be sold along with the house, since it functions more as an extension of the interior space.

### Tanach Sources

The *Gemara* then traces each of the three terms to its source in *Nach*. *Yatzia dichtiv* — the word *yatzia* appears in the book of Kings in connection with the walls of the *Beit HaMikdash*: *hayatzia hatachtona chamesh ba'ama rachava* — "the lowest *yatzia* was five *amot* wide." This refers to the exterior chambers built onto the outside of the *Beit HaMikdash*'s walls.

*Tzeila dichtiv* — the word *tzeila* appears in *Yechezkel*, in his description of the *Beit HaMikdash*: *vehatzela'ot tzela el tzela shalosh ushloshim pa'amim* — "the *tzela'ot*, *tzela* by *tzela*, thirty-three times." *Yechezkel*'s description differs from that in Kings in various respects, including the number of these exterior chambers — thirty-three rather than three — but structurally the same phenomenon is being described: chambers built exterior to the wall of the *Beit HaMikdash*.

*Ta dichtiv* — the word *ta* appears in *Yechezkel* as well: *vehata kaneh echad orech vekaneh echad rochav uvein hata'im chamesh amot* — describing the dimensions of these exterior chambers and the spaces between them.

### Beit Mikdash Structure

The *Gemara* adds that if one prefers a source from *Mishnah* rather than *Nevi'im*, there is one in *Middot*: *kotel haheichal shesh vehata shesh kotel hata chamesh ama* — "the wall of the *heichal* was six [*amot*], the *ta* was six, and the outer wall of the *ta* was five *amot*." This describes, in architectural terms, the layered structure around the *heichal*: the inner wall, then a six-*amah* chamber built onto its exterior, then a five-*amah* outer wall enclosing that chamber.

The architecture behind this deserves a moment's attention. The wall of the *Beit HaMikdash* was built with a series of stepped indentations along its base, progressively narrowing as it rose. This meant that as the three tiers of exterior chambers were stacked on top of one another going upward, each successive tier was actually wider than the one below — because each could rest on a broader ledge cut into the wall's indented base. This is why the verse in Kings specifies that the *lowest* chamber was five *amot* wide, rather than the widest: counter-intuitively, the upper chambers were wider because of the progressive indentation of the wall below. According to the *Rashbam*, these indentations existed precisely so that the chambers could be supported without the beams being inserted into the sacred walls themselves.

There is something strikingly thematic here. Once again — as was true at the very beginning of the previous *perek* — the textual paradigm for the structures and terms under discussion is the *Beit HaMikdash* itself. The *Mishna* on *chezkas habatim* opened with a *nevua* from *Yirmiyah* about the exile; now, the vocabulary of *yatzia*, *tzeila*, and *ta* — the attached chambers that give legal identity to structures adjacent to a house — is drawn from Kings, *Yechezkel*, and *Middot*, all describing the exterior chambers of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The textual paradigm for ownership and building is the Temple. Whatever legal category we are trying to understand about ordinary houses in exile, it is the *Beit HaMikdash* that teaches us the language.

---

## Four Amot Rule

### Mar Zutra's Rule

The *Gemara* records: *amar Mar Zutra vehu dehazei v'hu d'havei arba amos* — Mar Zutra teaches that the *yatzia* is considered an independent entity, separate from the house and therefore not automatically sold along with it, only if it has minimum dimensions of four *amot* by four *amot*. A *yatzia* smaller than that is simply too trivial a space to carry independent standing; it is functionally an appendage of the house and goes along with it.

### Ravina's Question

Ravina poses a challenge to Mar Zutra: if we require four *amot* as the threshold of independence, does this same standard apply to the case of a well (*bor*) or a cistern (*dos*)? A *Mishnah* later in the chapter will establish that even if one sells a house and specifies in the bill of sale that all rights extend to the full depth below and the full height above — *af al pi she'kasav lo umka v'ruma* — the sale still does not include any well or cistern on the property. Does Mar Zutra hold that a well is only independently excluded if it is four *amot* wide, and that a smaller well would be considered part of the house?

### Tashmishta Distinction

Mar Zutra's response is that the two cases are simply not comparable. By a well and a house, *ha tashmishta l'chud v'ha tashmishta l'chud* — each serves an entirely distinct function. A house is a living space; a well is a water source. Nobody could mistake one for an extension of the other; they are categorically different in their *tashmishta*, their mode of use. The four-*amot* threshold therefore has no relevance there.

The case of the *yatzia* is different: *hacha idi v'idi chad tashmishta hi*. Here, the *yatzia* and the house proper are both enclosed spaces used for habitation. The only meaningful question is whether we are dealing with one living space or two. It is precisely because they share the same *tashmishta* that a size threshold becomes the relevant criterion: below four *amot*, the space is too small to function as an independent habitation and is absorbed into the house; at four *amot* or more, it qualifies as its own living space and is therefore not automatically included in the sale. This distinction is coherent and, once stated, makes considerable sense.

---

## Castle Example

### Castle Setup

Rav Nachman cites a ruling in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: *ha-mocher bayit le-chavero be-birah gedolah* — one who sells a house to his fellow within a large castle (*birah*). The *Rashbam* explains the structure of a *birah* as something resembling a castle in its architectural organization: a large enclosed complex with a shared open space at its center, ringed by individual houses or chambers that each open onto the shared courtyard — separate living units contained within one overarching physical structure, sharing a perimeter wall.

Now imagine: I own one such chamber within this castle complex, and I wish to sell it. I draw up a bill of sale, I call the property a *bayit*, and when I record the dimensions, I give not the dimensions of my individual chamber but the dimensions of the outer wall of the entire castle. The ruling is: *af al pi she-metzar lo metzarim ha-chitzoniyim, metzarim hirchiv lo* — even though I bounded the property with the exterior dimensions of the castle, those dimensions are merely an expansion of the boundaries, not a definition of what was sold. The buyer acquires only my individual chamber; the rest of the castle does not transfer.

### Naming vs. Dimensions

The *Gemara* interrogates this ruling carefully. If the chamber is universally called *bayit* and the whole castle is universally called *birah*, then the answer is obvious — *peshita*, *bayit zavan lei birah lo zavan lei* — I sold you a *bayit*, not a *birah*. Even combined with exterior dimensions, the naming convention conclusively determines what was sold. Conversely, if the word *bayit* can sometimes refer to the whole castle — as occasionally happens in colloquial usage — then combined with the exterior dimensions, one might have thought the entire complex was sold.

The *Gemara* resolves that the ruling is necessary precisely for the intermediate case: the majority of speakers use *bayit* to mean only the individual chamber and *birah* for the whole complex, but there exists a minority who do refer to the whole castle as their *bayit* — much as someone might casually say "come to my little place in Connecticut" when referring to a large estate. In such a case one might have thought that the combination of a word that could apply to the whole and dimensions that match the whole should be read as conveying the whole. The ruling tells us otherwise.

### Shayarti Line

The reason why the narrow reading prevails becomes clear with the key legal principle now introduced: *mi-de-hava lei le-michtav ve-lo shayarti bi-zvinai illeyn klum* — because the seller should have written, and did not write, "I do not retain any ownership in what I am selling." This is the crucial line. The entire subsequent chapter, in a sense, reduces to this: every time the *Mishnah* teaches that selling a house does not include the *yatzia*, the *cheder*, the roof, the well — the practical upshot is that if you want to sell your house and genuinely convey all of these components, you must include in your *shtar* the declaration that you are not retaining any portion of what you are selling. Without that line, the bill of sale will be read as narrowly as possible.

### Narrow Reading

Therefore, when the seller used the word *bayit* and gave the dimensions of the castle, but did not include the *shayarti* declaration, the document must be interpreted in the most restrictive way. The word *bayit* is read at its narrowest, referring only to the individual chamber, and the dimensions are treated as providing nothing more than a locating context — a rough address, as it were — rather than as a definition of what was conveyed. Without the *shayarti* line, the default presumption is that the seller retained anything not unambiguously transferred. *Shema mina shiyurei shiyer* — we infer from the absence of that line that the seller retained ownership of those parts.

---

## Field in Valley

### Valley Setup

A parallel ruling follows, again cited by Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: *ha-mocher sade le-chavero be-vika gedolah* — one who sells a field to his fellow within a large valley. The seller owns many fields within this broad valley, intends to sell one of them, and draws up a *shtar* using the word *sadeh*. When recording the dimensions, however, he gives not the dimensions of the particular field being sold but those of the entire surrounding valley. *Af al pi she-metzar lo metzarim hitzonim, metzarim hirchiv lo* — even so, the dimensions are only an expansion of the boundary context, and the buyer acquires only the one field, not the whole valley.

### Address Theory

The *Rashbam*'s explanation of this case is instructive. Without the kind of precise locational reference systems we take for granted today — no longitude, no latitude, no street addresses — identifying a particular field among many in a large valley could be genuinely difficult. The *Rashbam* describes a situation in which the parties are actually standing in the field at the time of the transaction; the *eidim* and the parties present know exactly which field is being sold. The valley dimensions serve not as a description of what is being sold but as an identifying address — "the valley to the south of town that runs five hundred *amot* by seven hundred *amot*" is something people could locate and recognize, whereas "the third field from the left" would mean nothing to anyone not present. In this reading, the dimensions of the valley function the way we would use a neighborhood name or a zip code: context for identification, not a definition of the property conveyed.

One might then ask: if the document uses valley dimensions as an address, does it not at least create ambiguity about which particular field within the valley is being sold? The *Rashbam*'s answer, it seems, is that the physical context of the transaction — where the parties were standing when the document was written — was itself sufficient identification, and the question the *Gemara* is addressing is not which field but how much of the valley.

### House vs. Field

The *Gemara* then asks why both rulings are necessary — the castle case and the valley case — since they seem to cover the same principle. The answer is that each case independently might have been ruled differently, and only by stating both do we preclude error in either direction.

Had we known only the castle case, one might have argued: of course a single *bayit* within a *birah* does not convey the whole *birah*, because *ha tashmishta l'chud v'ha tashmishta l'chud* — the individual chambers each serve as separate living spaces; no one lives in the entire castle as a single dwelling. People inhabit individual chambers; the castle as a whole is nobody's living unit. Given that naturally differentiated *tashmishta*, it makes perfect sense to read the word *bayit* narrowly and not to be swayed by the castle's exterior dimensions.

But one might have thought the valley case should work differently: *dechula chada tashmishta hi* — the entire valley is, in principle, one unified agricultural unit. It can be plowed and cultivated as a whole; buying the whole valley to farm it as one expanse is a perfectly intelligible transaction. Given that unified *tashmishta*, combined with the broad dimensions recorded, perhaps we should read the *shtar* as conveying the whole valley.

### Could Be Specific

Conversely, had we known only the valley case, one might have thought: of course you don't convey the whole valley, because the seller had no practical way to describe the specific field other than by reference to the valley in which it sat. The use of valley dimensions was effectively forced by the absence of any better descriptive vocabulary; it tells us nothing about intent to convey the whole.

But in the castle case, the seller *could* have been more specific. One could identify a particular chamber within a castle by its location — the one in the northeast corner, the one with the red door, the one beside the well. The failure to be specific when specificity was available, and the use of castle-wide dimensions instead, might seem more deliberate — perhaps indicating that the seller intended to convey the full complex. Therefore, without the ruling of Rav Nachman covering both cases explicitly, one might have erred in different directions for each. *Utzricha* — both statements are necessary.

---

## Shayarti Principle

### Rav Mari

The *Gemara* now draws the thread together with a universal statement: *amar Rav Mari bra debat Shmuel mishmeih de'Abaye* — Rav Mari, the son of Shmuel's daughter, citing Abaye: *hai man demazbin leh midi lechavereih, tzarich lemichtav leh lo shayerit bizvini ilin kadmai klum* — anyone who sells property to another is required to include in the bill of sale the declaration "I do not retain any ownership in what is being sold before me." This is the universal rule, and it follows directly from Rav Nachman's rulings. Both the castle ruling and the valley ruling can only be coherent — that is, the narrow reading of a document that gives broad dimensions can only be legally defensible — if we accept as a background norm that the *shtar* should have contained this line and did not.

### Presumption Logic

The underlying logic is one of burden of proof in the context of documentary ambiguity. This touches on an interesting *halachah* question: even in the presence of a *shtar*, if the terms of that *shtar* are ambiguous, who bears the burden? The *shtar* is, in a sense, a form of *eidut* — testimony that a transaction took place — but the question of *what* the transaction included remains open when the language is unclear. In such circumstances, the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* inclines the resolution toward the seller, who was originally in possession. If the seller had included the *shayarti* declaration, the *shtar* would be interpreted maximally, and the buyer would receive everything. Without that line, the document's ambiguity resolves in the seller's favor: we assume the seller retained ownership of anything not unambiguously conveyed. *Shema mina shiyurei shiyer* — the absence of the line is itself evidence of retention.

---

## Multiple Plots

### Case Setup

The *Gemara* now introduces a specific factual scenario. A seller says to a buyer: *ar'a deRabbi Chiya mezavanna lach* — "I am selling you the land of Rabbi Chiya," referring to parcels he had acquired from Rabbi Chiya. A *shtar* is drawn up accordingly. It then emerges that the seller owned two separate plots of land, both of which were commonly referred to as "the land of Chiya," having been purchased from him at different times and located in different places. The document says "the land" (*ar'a*), in the singular. Which field was sold?

### Singular/Plural Rule

Rav Ashi rules: *chada amar lei tarti lo amar lei* — he said "land" (singular), not "lands"; therefore only one plot was conveyed. Grammatically, *ar'a* is singular and *ar'ata* is the plural form — a point that emerges from the *Gemara*'s own usage, where it describes the seller as having *tarti ar'ata*, "two plots," using the plural. So *ar'a* means one.

But the ruling extends further. If the seller had said *ar'ata*, the plural, this conveys a minimum of two — *mi'ut ar'ata shtayim*. It does not, however, convey all five fields if the seller owned five. To convey all of them, the seller would need to have said *kol ar'ata de'is lei* — "all of the lands that I own" — and even then, this does not include orchards or gardens. The word *ar'a*, even in its plural and even with the universal *kol*, refers to cultivated grain fields; orchards (*bustana*) and gardens (*pardisa*) require a different designation.

If, however, the seller uses the word *zeira* — a more generic Aramaic term for cultivated land — this is broad enough to encompass any form of cultivated property, *afilu bebustana ufardisa*, including orchards and gardens. The one thing it still does not include is houses (*batei*) or Canaanite slaves (*avdei*), since those belong to a categorically different domain than land used for cultivation, even though they are obviously connected to the land in various ways.

### Ambiguity Resolution

Returning to the case of the two plots both called "land of Chiya": since the document says *ar'a* in the singular and only one plot was therefore sold, but neither party can prove which of the two plots was the one intended, the matter resolves according to *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* — the burden of proof falls on the one seeking to extract from the other. The seller retains the right to determine which plot was meant, and the buyer cannot establish a claim to a specific field without proof. This, again, reflects the consistent principle running through this entire section: where a document is ambiguous, the presumption favors the party who was previously in possession.

---

## Property Semantics

### Ar'a Terms

To summarize the terminological distinctions established by Rav Ashi: *ar'a* in the singular conveys one plot of cultivated land; *ar'ata* in the plural conveys a minimum of two; *kol ar'ata*, "all my lands," conveys all grain fields but excludes orchards and gardens.

### Zeira

The term *zeira* is broader in scope, functioning as a generic word for any cultivated land. A sale or transfer denominated using *zeira* therefore includes orchards and gardens in addition to grain fields, since the word does not carry the implicit specialization of *ar'a*. The one category *zeira* does not encompass is houses and Canaanite slaves, which belong to a qualitatively different legal category from cultivated land, regardless of how closely associated with a given piece of land they might be.

### Nichsei

The broadest term is *nichsei* — property in the most general sense. A sale framed in terms of *nichsei* includes all possessions: grain fields, orchards, gardens, houses, and even Canaanite slaves. When the word chosen is *nichsei*, nothing is excluded by virtue of being a different *type* of asset, because *nichsei* does not carry any implicit restriction to one category of holding. This terminological hierarchy — from the narrow *ar'a* through *ar'ata*, *kol ar'ata*, *zeira*, and finally *nichsei* — provides the practical vocabulary for drafting documents that accurately convey the intended scope of a transaction.

---

# Bava Batra 62

## Long & Short Boundary

### Rav: Short Boundary

The daf opens in the context of a broader discussion about boundary language in land sales — specifically the principle of *metzarim hirchiv lo*, whereby a seller may have drawn wider boundaries than the plot he actually intended to convey, perhaps because the most convenient landmarks happened to extend beyond the property in question. Against this background, the Gemara now introduces several scenarios involving irregular or incomplete boundary descriptions and asks what is actually acquired in each case.

The first case concerns a field whose boundaries are described unevenly: *metzar u-metzar echad aroch u-metzar echad katzar* — one boundary drawn long and one boundary drawn short. As pictured in the Rashbam, imagine that the northern and southern edges of the field are fully drawn, but the eastern boundary extends only halfway across the width while the western boundary spans the full width. The question becomes: what shape of plot has the seller actually conveyed?

Rav rules *lo kana ela keneged ha-katzar* — the buyer acquires only as much as corresponds to the shorter boundary. Since the eastern line ran only halfway across, that half-width represents the true extent of the plot. The western boundary, though drawn the full width, should not be read as extending the conveyance; perhaps the seller mentioned a neighbor's plot on the west — a neighbor whose land happened to span the full width — simply as a convenient landmark. This is *metzarim hirchiv lo* applied to the shorter boundary as the controlling measure. Rav takes the more restrictive interpretation.

### Kahana & Assi: Rosh Tor

Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged Rav's position: *veyikne keneged rosh tor* — why not connect the endpoints of both boundaries and include everything in between? By drawing a line from the terminus of the shorter eastern boundary to the far end of the wider western boundary, the result is a trapezoid — described by the Gemara as a *rosh tor*, the head of an ox, an angular, tapered shape. This reading honors both boundary lines as meaningful markers of the plot's extent. It is a reasonable interpretation, and one that tries to give maximum effect to both the long and the short boundary.

Rav was silent — *shatik Rav*. The question of what that silence means is worth pausing on. Does it indicate concession, or merely that Rav declined to press the debate further? The subsequent line suggests that Rav had not actually conceded, since the Gemara goes on to specify a separate case in which he *would* concede — implying that without that special circumstance, he maintained his original position.

### Rav's Concession

There is, however, one configuration in which Rav concedes. If the eastern side is shared between two neighbors — Reuven occupying one half and Shimon the other half — and on the western side the boundary is shared between Levi and Yehuda, and the document listed both Levi and Yehuda as the western boundary, then Rav would agree that the full width on the west is intended. The argument: *mide-hava leh le-michatav leh de-Reuven keneged Levi* — if the seller truly only meant to convey the portion opposite Reuven on the east, which aligns with Levi on the west, he should have written simply "Reuven on the east and Levi on the west." By mentioning Yehuda as well, the seller has added something beyond what was necessary. That surplus language is telling: it demonstrates that the full western width — both Levi's portion and Yehuda's portion — was intentionally included. From this we infer, *shma mina kineged rosh tor hu d'amar lei*, that the acquisition is in fact the trapezoidal *rosh tor* shape, connecting both endpoints. That case Rav concedes.

---

## Perpendicular Boundaries

### Specifying Both Sides

The Gemara shifts to a different scenario. Suppose a seller identifies two different neighbors as the anchoring boundaries: Reuven's land sits to both the east and west, while Shimon's land sits to both the north and south. The Gemara rules that one must not simply say "bounded by Reuven on one side and Shimon on the other." Rather, *tzarich lemichtav lei metzar Reuven ruchin trein u-metzar Shimon ruchin trein* — the document must specify that Reuven's land forms two of the boundaries and Shimon's land forms two of the boundaries. In other words, the language must make explicit that both the east and the west belong to Reuven, and that both the north and south belong to Shimon.

### Ambiguity Risk

Why is this precision necessary? Because without it, the description is dangerously ambiguous. If one merely writes that the field is "between Reuven and Shimon," a diagonal strip running from one corner of Reuven's plot to the opposite corner of Shimon's plot technically satisfies that description. Such a strip would touch the corners of both neighbors' holdings and would be entirely contained within them. One might then ask: why not interpret it as a small square inscribed within the larger field, also entirely contained within Reuven's and Shimon's boundaries? The answer is that the diagonal strip, unlike the inscribed square, actually reaches the edges of both neighbors' plots at its corners — making it a defensible reading of "between" them. The inscribed square would be fully contained but would not abut their borders at any point. To eliminate this ambiguity and make clear that a full rectangular plot is intended — bounded on two sides by Reuven and two sides by Shimon — both pairs of boundaries must be explicitly named.

---

## Kranot & Gamma Marks

### Corner Points Sufficiency

A series of unresolved questions follows. The first: *tzimam lo ha-kranot mahu* — if, instead of specifying entire boundary lines, the seller simply defined the four corner points of the field, is that sufficient to establish acquisition of the full square? One might think so, since four corner points logically define a quadrilateral. But the Gemara entertains the possibility that even this is ambiguous: the four defined corners could equally describe an X-shaped figure, where only the corners themselves are transferred, not the full interior square. The question is left open.

### Gamma Markings

The second question is *kemin gam mahu*: what if, at each of two diagonal corners, the seller drew a small mark indicating a bit of two adjacent boundary lines — like a Greek gamma or the letter *lamed*, gesturing toward both sides of that corner? Does this partial marking of each side convey enough information that the reader should extrapolate the full square? Or might even such marks be interpreted as defining the corners of a smaller, irregular figure — a trapezoid, perhaps — that happens to have those marked segments as its edges? Once again the Gemara does not resolve this question.

---

## Alternating Boundaries

### Partial Edges Question

The final unresolved question in this series concerns the case of *beserugin* — alternating boundaries. Imagine the field is surrounded by eight neighbors: Reuven and Shimon to the east, Levi and Yehuda to the north, Zevulun and Yissachar to the west, and Yosef and Binyamin to the south. The seller specifies, alternating around the field, one neighbor from each side — say Reuven to the east, Levi to the north, Yissachar to the west, and Yosef to the south. Each of the four sides is partially identified, but only one half of each side is named. The question is whether specifying a portion of each side is sufficient to establish that the full square is being conveyed, or whether one should instead try to construct the smallest possible figure consistent with those partial boundary references.

All three of these questions — *kranot*, *kemin gam*, and *beserugin* — remain unresolved. *Teiku.*

---

## Omitted 4th Boundary

### Rav: Except Final Furrow

The Gemara now moves to a case that at first glance appears simple: a seller drew three of the four boundaries — say the northern, eastern, and southern — but did not draw the western boundary at all. Three full sides are defined. What is acquired?

Rav rules *kana hakol chutz mi-metzar revi'i* — the buyer acquires everything except that last boundary. More precisely, since the fourth side was never drawn, the final furrow's width at that western edge is excluded. The buyer gets essentially the full square minus one furrow's depth along the missing fourth side. This is a notable nuance: Rav here takes a position that at first seems more expansive than his earlier ruling in the *rosh tor* case, but may reflect a situation where Rav had already reconsidered his earlier position, or where the difference lies in the structure of what is missing.

### Shmuel: All Included

Shmuel disagrees in the opposite direction: *afilu metzar revi'i* — even the fourth boundary, including that final furrow, is acquired. In Shmuel's view, if three sides are fully specified, no reasonable reading of the document would exclude the last edge. The full square is conveyed.

### Rav Assi: One Furrow

Rav Assi takes the most restrictive position of all: *lo kana ela telem echad al pnei kula* — the buyer acquires nothing more than a single furrow running along each of the three specified boundaries. This is extraordinarily limiting. The logic, as the Gemara explains, combines two principles: Rav Assi holds that the failure to draw the fourth boundary should be read like Rav's principle of *shura shura* — that something has been held back — and then extends this further with the rule *mid-shayar b'metzar shayar nami b'kulah*: if something is withheld at the boundary, one should assume a great deal is withheld throughout. The result is a near-total contraction: the buyer receives only the outermost furrow of each of the three sides, nothing more.

### Rava: Conditional Exclus…

Rava rules as the *halakha*: *kana hakol chutz mi-metzar revi'i* — in line with Rav, the buyer receives everything except the fourth boundary. But Rava immediately introduces a series of conditions that significantly complicate what "except the fourth boundary" means.

### Mivla'ut & Independence

The critical concept is *mivla'ut* — absorption. If the fourth boundary is *mivla*, meaning it is geometrically absorbed within the three boundaries already drawn — in the illustration in the Rashbam, the fourth side's extent is already partially enclosed by the edges of the other three — then the buyer acquires even the fourth boundary. The absorption itself is the decisive factor: when that undescribed edge is caught within the figure you drew, it comes along.

But when the fourth boundary is *lo mivla* — it stands fully outside the three drawn lines, as in the left-hand diagram in the Rashbam — then in principle it is excluded. However, even this exclusion is not absolute. The fourth boundary is only excluded if it also possesses independent significance: either it has a planting of palm trees upon it (*richva de-dikla*) or it is a sufficiently large area, at least nine *kavin* (*tisha kavin*). If the fourth boundary is outside the three lines but has neither of these characteristics — no planting and not large enough — then it is still included.

### Rava Versions Compared

The Gemara presents a second version of Rava's ruling that inverts the structure in a telling way. In this second version, Rava rules *kana hakol v'afilu metzar revi'i* — everything is acquired, including the fourth boundary — and then specifies the conditions under which the fourth boundary is included. It is included *ella de-mivla*: only when it is absorbed. If it is not absorbed, *lo kanei* — it is not acquired at all. The nuance within the absorbed case: even when absorbed, the fourth boundary is acquired *only* if it lacks both *richva de-dikla* and the area of *tisha kavin*. If it is absorbed but has trees planted or is a large enough area, it is not acquired.

The two versions of Rava thus differ in an important structural way. In the first version, the primary case is exclusion of the fourth boundary, with absorption and lack of significance serving as grounds to *include* it. In the second version, the primary case is inclusion of the fourth boundary, with non-absorption serving as grounds to *exclude* it, and within the absorbed case, significance (*richva de-dikla* or *tisha kavin*) serving as a further basis for exclusion.

### Consensus & Dispute

The Gemara maps out which outcomes are agreed upon by both versions of Rava and which are disputed. Both versions agree on two extreme cases. First, when the fourth boundary is absorbed and is also small and insignificant — lacking trees and below *tisha kavin* — both agree it is acquired. Second, when it is not absorbed and has both markers of significance — it is outside the drawn lines and has *richva de-dikla* or *tisha kavin* — both versions agree it is not acquired.

The dispute concerns the middle cases: when the fourth boundary is absorbed but possesses markers of significance, or when it is not absorbed but is also small and without plantings. In those mixed cases, the two readings of Rava's position diverge, one treating the boundary as included and the other as excluded. The *halakha* in such cases is *shuda dedaynei* — it is left to the discretion of the judges, who must assess what the seller most plausibly intended. The Rashbam's explanation of this ruling is unusually long, as is the *Tosafot*, reflecting the complexity of the analysis. Notably, the Gemara does not resort to the ordinary default rules — neither *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* nor *kol dalim gavar* — but assigns the determination to judicial judgment about the seller's intent.

---

## Partnership Language

### Half vs. Half Of

The Gemara now turns to a distinct but related question about the precision of language in the sale of partnership land. Raba identifies a critical linguistic distinction. When Reuven and Shimon are partners in a field and Reuven wishes to sell his interest to Levi, there are two ways he might phrase the transaction. If Reuven says *palga de'is li be'ara* — "the half that I have in this land" — he has sold his entire half-interest. That is, he conveyed the half of the field that he owns. But if Reuven says *palga be'ara de'is li* — "half of the land that I have" — he has sold only half of his share, which is a quarter of the whole field, *riva*. The distinction is subtle: in the first formulation, Reuven identifies his *palga* — the half that is his — as the object of the sale. In the second formulation, he sells *palga* of what he has, which itself is already only a half.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenged Raba directly: *mai shna hai u-mai shna hai* — what is really the difference? Abaye's view was that people do not speak with such precision, and in both phrasings Reuven means to convey his half-share. Abaye further reported that when Raba fell silent in response, he assumed that silence constituted concession: *ana savri mide'ishtik kibulei kibla* — I thought that since Raba was silent, he had accepted my argument. But Abaye was mistaken.

### Documentary Evidence

*Velo hi* — it was not so. The evidence came from Raba's own *beit din*. Documents processed there (*shtarei dinfaku mibei Mar*) demonstrated that Raba consistently maintained the distinction in practice. A document reading *palga de'is li be'ara* was adjudicated as conveying the full half-interest; a document reading *palga be'ara de'is li* was adjudicated as conveying only a quarter. Raba's silence was not concession — he simply did not feel it necessary to press the argument further. The documents from his court prove he never abandoned the distinction.

---

## Portion in Partnership

### My Half vs. My Portion

Raba extends his analysis to a related scenario, this time involving the description of the boundary in a sale where the seller is retaining a portion. Reuven is selling a plot to Shimon and has drawn the northern, eastern, and western boundaries. The southern boundary, however, he is keeping for himself. If Reuven says *metzar ara demina palga* — the boundary on the south is from the half that is mine — then the word *palga* is interpreted precisely: Reuven is retaining a full half of the land for himself. But if Reuven says *metzar ara demina psika* — the boundary on the south is from a portion that is mine — then he is retaining only a small sliver, specifically *tisha kavin*, the minimum area of independent significance we have seen throughout this discussion.

### Abaye Disputes Again

Again, Abaye objects: *mai shena hachi u-mai shena hachi* — what is the difference? Both formulations, he argues, should be understood as meaning a half, or alternatively both as meaning only a portion. Raba did not respond — *ishtik*. And again, Abaye believed the silence to be concession: *savri minei adei ve-adei palga* — he thought Raba meant that in both formulations, the retained piece is a full half.

### Boundaries Language Role

But this too was a misreading of Raba's silence. Rav Yeimar bar Shlimya clarified in Abaye's own name what the true position was: *bein metzar ara demina palga bein metzar ara demina psika* — whether Reuven said the boundary is from the half that is mine or from the portion that is mine — *ei amar lei ilin metzrani nahu palga*: if Reuven added the phrase "and these are the boundaries," then in either case he retains a full half. But *lo amar lei ilin metzrani nahu tisha kavin*: if he did not add that phrase, then in either case he retains only *tisha kavin*.

The Rashbam explains this additional language as *yeter lashon liyafos kocho* — an extra formulation intended to strengthen and clarify the force of the conveyance. When the seller says "and these are the boundaries," he signals that the boundary line he is describing is a fully defined border, and whether he uses the word "half" or "portion" in that context, he means a genuine half. Without that reinforcing phrase, neither the word "half" nor "portion" alone is sufficient to convey a full half-share; the retained piece is interpreted as no more than the minimum significant area of *tisha kavin*. The distinction is subtle in conceptual terms, but the practical consequence — whether one retains a half or merely a small strip — is significant, and the Gemara takes pains to establish which language achieves which result.

---

---

# Bava Batra 63

## Shchiv Mera & Chelek

### Opening

The fourth *perek* of Bava Batra resumes on daf 63 at a somewhat unusual juncture. The *sugya* opens with the word *pshita* — a term that ordinarily functions as an interjection mid-discussion to push an argument forward, not as an opening move. Its precise function here is not entirely clear, but the substance that follows illuminates the context.

### Shchiv Mera Definition

The *Rashbam*, along with other *rishonim*, clarifies that this *sugya* concerns a *shchiv mera* — a person who is gravely ill — dividing up property. There is a conceptual question regarding what exactly defines a *shchiv mera*: is it simply someone so ill as to be confined to bed, or must the person be specifically on their deathbed? The practical stakes of that distinction are significant when dealing with inheritances and end-of-life property arrangements. In reality, one can rarely know at the time of a serious illness whether it will prove fatal — and thus the legal structure of *shchiv mera* transactions is built around conditional gifts or conditional sales. The *shchiv mera* declares, in effect, "I want so-and-so to have this property," and the transaction takes effect upon death.

A further distinctive feature of *shchiv mera* transactions is that they take effect entirely through verbal declaration, without any formal *kinyan*. This stands in contrast to virtually every other mode of acquisition in *halacha*. A major question — to be treated more fully in the ninth *perek* — is whether this power operates *mide'oraita*, perhaps rooted in the laws of inheritance, or whether it is a rabbinic enactment designed to allow people a more equitable and responsive mechanism for end-of-life estate planning.

### Yachlok vs Chelek

The *Gemara* opens with what it presents as obvious: if the *shchiv mera* says *yachlok ploni benichsay* — "so-and-so should split my properties" — then that person receives *palga*, a half. The term *yachlok* implies a precise division into two equal parts. (As the *Gemara* established two days prior, *nichsay* encompasses all manner of real property, including houses and even slaves.)

The difficulty arises when the language shifts. If instead the dying person says *tnu chelek liploni benichsay* — "give a portion of my property to so-and-so" — then *mai*, what does that mean? The word *chelek* (portion) is inherently ambiguous: it could indicate a twelfth, a hundredth, a half, or anything in between. The problem is closely analogous to the ambiguities of gift-giving and sales examined in the preceding discussion, where imprecise language created significant halachic complications.

### Ravina bar Kissi Braita

To address this question, *Ravina bar Kissi* cites a *braita* with the formula *ta shema*. Before examining its content, a critical framing caveat must be noted: this *braita* operates within the position of *Sumchos*, whose general ruling we do not adopt as *halacha*. *Sumchos*, a student of *Rabbi Meir*, holds that in cases of *mamon hamutal besafek* — doubtful monetary disputes — the property should always be split equally. The rabbinic consensus, by contrast, follows the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya*: whoever seeks to extract property from the one currently in possession of it bears the burden of proof, preserving the status quo. The *braita* cited by *Ravina bar Kissi* reflects *Sumchos*'s framework, and its usefulness here is confined to illuminating what *chelek* means as a quantity — not to affirm *Sumchos*'s broader methodology.

---

## Chelek Context & Scale

### Chelek b'Bor

The *braita* opens: *haomer tnu chelek liploni b'vor* — if a person says "give so-and-so a *chelek* in the cistern (*bor*)." *Sumchos omer*: *ein pachot m'revia* — it cannot be less than a quarter.

The reasoning proceeds as follows. The word *chelek* is inherently ambiguous — it could mean the most minimal sliver or it could mean as much as half. The floor of the range is some negligible minimum; both parties agree that at least that tiny amount was intended. The ceiling of the range, for a *bor*, is a full half. The entire span between the minimum and a half is therefore *besafek* — in dispute. Following *Sumchos*'s principle of *yachloku*, one splits that disputed range, yielding a quarter. Adding the undisputed minimal amount produces the result: a quarter plus a little bit. This is what *Sumchos* means by *ein pachot m'revia* — not less than a quarter, with a small addition.

### Chelek L'Chavit

The next case: *l'chavit* — water rights described as a *chelek* to fill a *chavit* (barrel). Here *Sumchos* rules *ein pachot m'shminit* — not less than an eighth (plus a small additional amount). The reasoning is parallel. When the *chelek* is described in terms sufficient to fill a *chavit*, the working assumption is that such an amount constitutes a quarter of the *bor*. That quarter is now the ceiling of the disputed range. Splitting it yields an eighth, plus the undisputed minimum.

### Chelek L'Kdeira & Tafiach

The *braita* continues with progressively smaller vessels. For *l'kdeira* — water rights to fill a cooking pot — *Sumchos* rules *ein pachot mi-yod bet*, not less than 1/12. Here the assumption is that the relevant quantity constitutes a sixth of the *bor*, and splitting that sixth yields 1/12. Finally, for *letafiach* — a drinking glass — the rule is *ein pachot mi-shisha asar*, not less than 1/16, since the relevant quantity is taken to be an eighth of the *bor*, half of which is 1/16.

The *Rashbam* explains that a *tafiach* is a *kli katan lishtot bo bnei adam*, a small vessel used by people for drinking, and notes that it is *v'shiura zuta mikulhu* — the smallest quantity of all.

### Water Usage Context

What emerges from this *braita* is that the meaning of *chelek* is not fixed but contextual — it scales with the frame of reference provided by the surrounding language. The hierarchy moves from large-scale usage (the *bor* itself, potentially for agriculture or animals) down through intermediate quantities (a barrel) to domestic cooking and finally personal drinking. This mirrors a familiar pattern in water allocation: most water consumption in any agricultural society goes not to drinking but to irrigation, livestock, manufacturing, and large-scale use. The *braita*, within *Sumchos*'s framework, captures that intuition formally — the intended portion is understood in light of what the water is actually for.

*Ravina bar Kissi*'s point is thus established: *chelek* can be quite ambiguous, ranging from a minimal amount up to substantially different quantities depending entirely on the context in which it is used.

---

## Ben Levi & Terumah

### Ben Levi Sells Field

A new *braita* is introduced: *tanu rabanan*. The case is that of a *ben Levi* — a Levite — who sells his field to a *Yisrael* and stipulates: *al menat she-ma'aser rishon sheli* — "on condition that the *ma'aser rishon* (first tithe) from this field shall be mine."

A preliminary observation: while the *Torah* envisions the *Levi* as lacking a hereditary ancestral portion in the Land of Israel, a *Levi* can nonetheless own land through purchase or inheritance from a maternal grandfather, and in principle could be a substantial landowner. The *Torah*'s assumption that *Levi'im* would be relatively poor and therefore in need of the social safety net of *ma'aser rishon* does not preclude the possibility of a wealthy *Levi* who happens to own land. The present case takes precisely such a situation as its premise.

### Davar Shelo Ba Olam

The case poses a genuine halachic dilemma with two equally problematic poles. On one extreme: if the *Levi* is understood to have retained outright property rights to one-tenth of the field, that cannot generate valid *ma'aser rishon*. The entire mechanism of *ma'aser rishon* requires that the produce belong to the *Yisrael*, who then separates the tithe and hands it to the *Levi*. A *Levi* who owns the land himself cannot receive *ma'aser rishon* from it, because the produce was never the *Yisrael*'s to separate.

On the other extreme: if the *Levi* is understood to have retained some future claim to the tithe — the produce has not yet grown, the harvest has not occurred, the separation has not taken place — then this appears to be *davar shelo ba l'olam*, a transfer of something that does not yet exist, which *halacha* generally does not permit.

It is worth noting a subtle but important distinction raised in the course of discussion: the initial transaction may not be problematic in the same way. When the *Levi* sells the field and retains a right, he is not selling a *davar shelo ba l'olam* — he is *keeping* something. The halachic complications around *davar shelo ba l'olam* arise most acutely when one attempts to *sell* or *transfer* such a right. This distinction illuminates the later cases in the *braita*.

The parallel case of *kohen hamisayeia b'veit hagranot* — a *kohen* who assists at the threshing floor hoping to be given *terumah* — reflects a related set of concerns: the field owner normally retains the right to designate which *kohen* receives the *terumah*, and any attempt to manipulate that right is halachically fraught.

### Zechut Resolution

The resolution adopted by the *Rashba* and the *Ritva* (with similar reasoning) is that the *Levi* is not retaining a property interest in the land or in any specific fruit. Rather, he is retaining an abstract legal right — a *zechut* — to be the designated recipient of the *ma'aser rishon* when the *Yisrael* separates it in the future. The *Rashbam* articulates this explicitly: *ma'aser rishon shelo va'afilu machra lokeiach l'acher d'zechuto shel levi eino yachol limkor l'acher d'achti birshuto ka'amar* — the *ma'aser rishon* is his, and even if the buyer sells the field to a third party, the *zechut* of the *Levi* cannot be transferred by that sale, because the field remains, in a sense, within the *Levi*'s claim.

The critical halachic weight is placed on the words *al menat* — "on condition." The *Gemara* explains: *keivan d'amar lei al menat shema'aser rishon sheli, shiyurei shayreia limkom ma'aser* — because he used the language of *al menat*, he has "retained the place of the *ma'aser*." This is understood not as ownership of the physical land producing the tenth, but as a retained legal right to the produce that will grow there. The *rishonim* acknowledge that this is not entirely airtight — it is not a fully tangible right, and yet it is treated as legally cognizable precisely because it is articulated through the *al menat* formulation in the contract.

### Variations & Conditions

The *braita* continues with several variations. First: if the *Levi* said *li ulvanai* — "for me and for my sons" — then should he die, the right passes to his descendants (*met yitein livanav*). This is halachically significant: it means that an intangible legal right of this nature — the right to receive *ma'aser rishon* — can be inherited. This might not have been assumed. One might have thought that while property transfers by inheritance, intangible *shibudim* (liens) or abstract legal entitlements to future produce do not. The *braita* indicates otherwise.

Second variation: if the *Levi* specified *kol zman shehasadeh zo biyadecha* — "as long as this field remains in your possession" — then if the buyer sells the field to a third party and subsequently repurchases it, the *Levi*'s right is extinguished. Although the field returned to the original buyer's ownership, it did so under new conditions. The prior stipulation is not revived automatically.

The *Gemara* then presses: *amai? ein adam makneh davar shelo ba l'olam* — why does any of this work? One cannot transfer something that does not yet exist. The answer returns to the *al menat* formulation: the *Levi* did not sell a *davar shelo ba l'olam* — he retained it. The problems arise when a third party subsequently attempts to transfer that right, which is something that cannot be done. This is why when the field is sold to another and returned, the right cannot travel with it: one cannot transfer what one never properly acquired.

What this *sugya* opens up is a remarkably sophisticated conception of ownership — one that moves well beyond tangible real estate into the realm of rights, futures, and intangible entitlements to produce. The legal right to *ma'aser rishon* must be clearly articulated, distinct from property ownership and distinct from a futures arrangement, since most transfers of non-existent things are not recognized in *halacha*. The *rishonim* struggled to define precisely what kind of legal ground this right stands on, and the tension is honestly acknowledged: the answer may not be fully airtight, but the framework is coherent enough to be operative.

---

## Reish Lakish & House

### Diyuta Elyona

*Reish Lakish* draws an inference from the *braita* about the *ben Levi*: *zot omeret hamocher bayit l'chavero v'amar lo al menat shediyuta ha'elyona sheli, diyuta ha'elyona shelo* — this implies that when someone sells a house and stipulates *al menat* that the upper course of bricks (*diyuta elyona*) shall be his, then indeed the upper course remains his.

The *diyuta elyona* refers to the uppermost layer of bricks — a course, in the architectural sense — at the top of the structure. In a one-story house, this corresponds to the air rights above the roof, or more precisely, the right to continue construction from the roofline upward. The question the *Gemara* immediately raises is: what is the *chiddush* here? Why does this need to be said? That question will drive the discussion in the section that follows.

---

## Reish Lakish & House (II)

### Zizin Rights

*Rav Zevid* interprets the force of *Reish Lakish*'s ruling narrowly but concretely: *she'im ratza lehotzi bah zizin motzi* — if the seller wishes to extend small protrusions or ledges (*zizin*) from the upper structure, he may do so. One might have assumed that retaining the *diyuta elyona* meant only retaining it as it stands, with no right to alter or add to it. *Rav Zevid* teaches that the *al menat* language conveys actual construction rights, including the right to extend *zizin*.

### Building Aliyah

*Rav Pappa* goes further: *she'im ratza livnot aliyah al gabah boneh* — if the seller wishes to build an entirely new upper story (*aliyah*) on top of the existing structure, he may. According to *Rav Pappa*, the construction rights conveyed by the *al menat* language are quite expansive, encompassing even major structural additions.

### Rav Pappa Difficulty

The *Gemara* notes an asymmetry. *Rav Zevid*'s position fits naturally within the rhetorical structure of *Reish Lakish*'s statement: *zot omeret* ("this implies") typically introduces a corollary that is analogous and proportionate to the original case. Extending *zizin* is a modest inference from retaining the *diyuta elyona*, and the parallel to the *ben Levi* retaining the *zechut* to *ma'aser rishon* is reasonably apt.

*Rav Pappa*'s position, however, is more difficult. Adding an entire additional story substantially alters the nature of the property sold — the ground-floor buyer's situation is materially affected by the seller constructing a second story above him. Whether this is truly comparable to what *Reish Lakish*'s *zot omeret* implies is questionable. The *Gemara* simply states *kashya* — the difficulty stands; the inference does not sit comfortably with the rhetorical framework *Reish Lakish* employed.

---

## Umka V'Ruma

### Explicit Language

*Rav Dimi of Neharde'a* states: *hai man de-mizban leh beisa le-havreh, af al gav de-chasav leh umka ve-ruma, tzarich le-michatav leh kani lach me-tehom ar'a ve-ad rum reki'a* — when someone sells a house to his neighbor, even if the deed of sale (*shtar*) includes the phrase *umka ve-ruma* (depths and heights), that is insufficient. One must explicitly write that the buyer acquires from the depths of the earth (*tehom ar'a*) to the heights of heaven (*rum reki'a*).

### Umka V'Ruma Logic

The reasoning is that *umka ve-ruma* by itself, written in isolation, conveys nothing beyond what a standard sale of a house already includes. When one sells a house, of course the floor is the floor and the ceiling is the ceiling — those are the natural limits of the structure. Writing *umka ve-ruma* without further elaboration merely restates what is already implied by a plain *stam* sale. To actually convey excavation rights below the house and air rights above it, one must use the more expansive language: *me-tehom ar'a ve-ad rum reki'a*, from the depths of the earth to the heights of heaven. That formula makes explicit what the generic *umka ve-ruma* leaves ambiguous.

### Bor V'Dut Proof

The *Gemara* considers whether this position is supported by the *mishna* that will appear on the following *daf*. That *mishna* states: *velo et habor velo et hadut af al pi shekatav lo umka veruma* — when selling a house, the sale does not include the *bor* (cistern) or the *dut* (water tank) even if the seller wrote *umka ve-ruma* in the deed. A *bor* is a subterranean cistern, a *dut* a water tank, and *michilot* are tunnels beneath the structure. This *mishna* would seem to confirm *Rav Dimi*'s position: writing *umka ve-ruma* alone fails to transfer even the underground features, let alone full excavation and air rights.

### Mishna Reinterpretation

The *Gemara* declines to accept this as a straightforward proof, however. The objection is that if *umka ve-ruma bistama lo kani* — if plain *umka ve-ruma* acquires nothing — then one should expect the *mishna* to say that writing the phrase still fails to transfer the *bor* and *dut*. But by that logic, the *mishna*'s case becomes unremarkable. The *Gemara* therefore proposes a radical reinterpretation — a *hachi ka'amar*: the *mishna* should be read not as "even if you wrote *umka ve-ruma* you do not get the *bor* and *dut*," but rather as "even if you did not write *umka ve-ruma*, it is as though you did." That is, *af al pi shelo katav lo, kimi shekatav dami* — even without explicitly writing the phrase, it functions as though written, thereby conveying the *bor*, *dut*, and *michilot*.

This is a complete reversal of the plain reading. What once appeared to limit the effect of *umka ve-ruma* now becomes evidence that *umka ve-ruma*, even when absent from the text, operates by convention as if present. The legal intuition underlying this is that certain formulaic phrases in contracts carry established semantic content within their legal context, even when not written explicitly — the conventions of contractual drafting supply the meaning. Thus, under this reinterpretation: if one writes *umka ve-ruma*, one acquires; if one does not write it, convention treats it as though written for purposes of the *bor*, *dut*, and *michilot*, though the broader range of *tehom ar'a ve-ad rum reki'a* still requires explicit specification.

---

## Maakaeh & Roof Rights

### Roof Retained

The *mishna* under discussion states: *velo et hagag bizman sheyesh lo ma'akeh gavoha asara tefachim* — when a house is sold, the sale does not include the roof (*gag*) when the roof has a parapet (*ma'akeh*) at least ten *tefachim* high.

### Chashiv Status

The reasoning behind this rule is that a *ma'akeh* ten *tefachim* high renders the roof a distinct and independently usable space — *chashiv*, significant enough to be treated as a separate area. A low parapet, insufficient to be halachically valid, signals that the rooftop is not safely or practically usable and therefore would be transferred along with the house in a plain *stam* sale. But when the *ma'akeh* reaches ten *tefachim*, the roof becomes, functionally, a separate area — comparable in some respects to a parking space in a building that is considered distinct from the apartment above it. In such a case, the seller retains the roof as a separate usable space even though the house below is sold.

### Al Menat Necessity

This *mishna* connects back to *Reish Lakish*'s ruling. *Reish Lakish* taught that the seller must use the language *al menat* — "on condition that" — to retain the *diyuta elyona*, the upper construction rights. The question naturally arises: if a plain *stam* sale already excludes air rights (because the seller retains the roof when it has a ten-*tefachim* *ma'akeh*), why would *Reish Lakish* need the *al menat* formulation at all? The *stam* case would seem to accomplish the same result on its own.

### Ravina-Rav Ashi

This precise challenge is posed by *Ravina* to *Rav Ashi*: *ta shema de-amar Reish Lakish zot omeret hamocher bayit lechavero... v'amrinan lemai hilchata* — and we already discussed *Reish Lakish*'s ruling and asked what it comes to teach. If *bistama lo kani* — if a plain sale without mentioning *umka ve-ruma* does not convey the roof rights — then *lama li al menat*? What work is the *al menat* language doing? The *stam* sale would already exclude the roof in the relevant case (where the *ma'akeh* makes it *chashiv*). Why would the seller need to make an explicit condition?

### Liability Interpretation

The *Gemara*'s resolution is: *ahani lei al menat de-ei nafal hadar banei lei* — the *al menat* formulation accomplishes something distinct from simply retaining the roof. It establishes a condition of ongoing liability: if the upper course (*diyuta*) should collapse, the seller is obligated to rebuild it. In a plain *stam* sale where the seller implicitly retains the roof (by virtue of the *ma'akeh* making it *chashiv*), there is no construction or repair obligation attached. The *al menat* language creates that additional duty. Thus, what distinguishes the *al menat* case from the *stam* case is not the question of who owns the roof, but the question of who bears the liability to maintain and rebuild it.

### Rashbam Caveat

The *Rashbam* is not fully satisfied with any of the interpretations on offer. Relying in part on the commentary of *Rabbeinu Chananel*, he proposes that the ruling of *Rav Pappa* should be understood more narrowly — not as granting the right to build an entirely new second story, but rather as addressing the obligation to rebuild the *diyuta* itself if it collapses. He reads the clause *ahanei de-ei nafla deyuta hadar banei lah* as a limitation, not an expansion, of the seller's construction rights. In his formulation: *le-olam mi-stama lo kani lokeiach ruma*, the buyer in a plain sale simply does not acquire the air rights, and the *al menat* clause functions only to specify the seller's repair obligations regarding the upper course.

The *Rashbam* concludes, however, with a note of honest uncertainty: *ki nira shitat Shmuel zot be-einai ve-yesh shitot acherot ve-ein ba-hen mamash* — this interpretation seems correct to him, but there are other readings, and he is not fully convinced by any of them. The issue, in his view, remains unresolved. That candor is itself instructive: the interplay between *stam* sales, *al menat* conditions, and the scope of construction rights in vertically shared structures is genuinely complex, and the *Gemara* here leaves room for ongoing interpretation.

---

---

# Bava Batra 64

## Umka Veruma Review

### Opening & Dedication

Today's learning of daf 64 is dedicated as a *refuah sheleimah* for Aryeh Menachem ben Raizel Gila, who is undergoing delicate surgery. We pick up at the *mishnah* and continue the broad discussion of what is implicitly included — or not included — when one sells a house or other property.

### Recap: House Sales

The preceding discussion centered on how much a standard sale implicitly conveys: specifically, whether selling a house automatically transfers air rights and rights to the ground beneath it, or whether the seller must use the emphatic phrase *umka veruma* — "its depth and its height" — to convey those rights. The conclusion reached was that *umka veruma* conveys the property rights beneath the ground. However, if one wishes to include things already physically constructed beneath the surface — such as an existing well — even more emphatic language is required: *mitehom ha'ara ad rom rakia*, "from the depths of the earth to the height of the heavens."

### Rights vs. Structures

The critical distinction underlying this discussion is between abstract rights — the right to dig, to use the airspace, to access what lies beneath — and existing physical structures. A sale of the house, even accompanied by the phrase *umka veruma*, conveys the former but not the latter. The ground rights are transferred; the structure is not.

### Well in House Floor

This leads to a striking detail that the *Rashbam* emphasizes throughout: the *bor* (well) and *dus* (cistern) under discussion are not located in a yard adjacent to the house. They are dug directly into the floor of the house itself. This makes the ruling considerably more surprising. One would naturally assume that a well embedded in the floor of a house, used to supply water to that very house, would be included in a sale of the house — especially when the seller explicitly conveys *umka veruma*. Yet the *mishnah* rules otherwise: the well is a separate, independent structure and is not conveyed by the sale. To include it, the seller would need to use the more expansive formula of *mitehom ha'ara ad rom rakia*.

At this point, a terminological difficulty in the *mishnah* prompted brief discussion. The *mishnah* lists both a *bor* and a *dus* as not being sold. *Ravina* was troubled by this: what distinguishes the two? *Rav Tosefa'ah* cited a *braita*: both are dug into the ground, but a *bor* is dug into firm earth whose walls hold on their own, while a *dus* is dug into softer ground and therefore requires a built stone lining to prevent collapse. *Rav Ashi* independently posed the same question, and *Mar Kashisha bereih deRav Chisda* supplied him with the same *braita* in reply.

---

## Access Rights Debate

### Seller Retains Well

Having established that the well is not sold when the house is sold, the *mishnah* raises a practical question of real consequence: if the seller retains ownership of a well embedded in the floor of the house he just sold, how does he get to it? The *mishnah* frames this as a debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim*.

### R. Akiva: Generous Sale

*Vetzarich likach lo derech divrei Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva rules that the seller, having retained the well, must nonetheless purchase access rights from the buyer in order to reach it. In other words, although the seller kept ownership of the well, the sale of the house did not preserve for him a right of passage through that house.

### Chachamim: Seller Retains

The *Chachamim* disagree: *eino tzarich likach lo derech* — the seller need not purchase access. Having retained the well, he implicitly retained the right of passage to reach it. On this view, the buyer of the house acquires the house under the condition that the seller may continue to enter and use his well. This is, as noted, quite a remarkable outcome: the buyer pays for a house and finds that the previous owner retains not only a well in the basement but an ongoing right to enter the premises.

The *mishnah* adds one qualification on which Rabbi Akiva concurs: if, in the deed of sale, the seller explicitly stated "I am selling the house *except for* the well" — *chutz me-ha-bor* — then Rabbi Akiva agrees that the seller does retain access rights. Since retaining the well was already the default rule, the fact that the seller went out of his way to state it explicitly is interpreted by Rabbi Akiva as signaling an intention to retain something beyond the mere ownership of the well — namely, the access rights to it.

### Seller Sells Well

The *mishnah* then presents the inverse case: *machar le-acher* — the seller sells the well but retains the house. Here the positions of Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim* reverse. Rabbi Akiva rules that the buyer of the well does not need to purchase access rights — they come automatically with the purchase. The *Chachamim* rule the opposite: even having bought the well, the buyer must separately acquire a right of passage.

### Generous Seller Principle

What accounts for Rabbi Akiva's position across both cases? The *Gemara* identifies it as the principle of *mocher be-ayin yafah hu mocher* — a seller sells with a generous eye. Crucially, the access rights are not treated as an attribute that automatically accompanies whoever owns the well at any given moment. Rather, Rabbi Akiva's principle concerns the direction of generosity in a transaction: the seller, whoever he is, is assumed to be giving the buyer the fullest possible deal. Abstract rights that are not explicitly reserved — such as rights of access — are presumed to have been granted to the buyer.

This means that in both scenarios — selling the house while retaining the well, and selling the well while retaining the house — the access rights flow to the buyer. When the seller retains the well, he nonetheless gave up his access rights in favor of the buyer of the house. When the seller retains the house, he gave up his access rights in favor of the buyer of the well. The *Chachamim*, by contrast, follow the principle of *mocher be-ayin ra'ah hu mocher* — the seller holds back as much as he can — and therefore the access rights always remain with the seller, regardless of who holds the well.

One participant noted that this is consistent with a broader Talmudic instinct — *ein adam mocher* — the general reluctance attributed to sellers to fully divest themselves of their property. That framing would suggest the default should favor the seller, which aligns with the *Chachamim*. Yet Rabbi Akiva's principle cuts the other way when it comes to abstract access rights specifically. It is worth noting, however, that the debate here concerns *access*, not physical property — a distinction that may explain why the principle can operate differently here than in other contexts.

---

## Competing Claims

### Generous vs. Stingy Sale

The *Gemara* now attempts to characterize the debate of Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim* more precisely. The initial framing is straightforward: Rabbi Akiva holds *mocher be-ayin yafah mocher* — a seller sells generously — while the *Chachamim* hold *mocher be-ayin ra'ah mocher* — a seller holds back. The *Gemara* further notes that wherever in *Shas* Rabbi Akiva's position of *mocher be-ayin yafah mocher* appears, it must ultimately trace back to this *mishnah* as its source.

### Privacy Protection Theory

The *Gemara* then challenges this broad reading. Perhaps the debate of Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim* here is not a general principle about how sellers conduct transactions, but a specific, situational judgment. According to this reading, Rabbi Akiva is sensitive to the psychology of the buyer: *eino rotzeh sheyitein ma'osav veyihyu acherim dorsim* — a person does not pay money for a house and then expect strangers to be trampling through it. Rabbi Akiva's ruling is therefore not a universal principle of generosity but a particular recognition that no buyer would consent to purchasing a house under such conditions.

### Power Position Theory

The *Chachamim*, on this alternative reading, reason from the position of the seller: if the seller is receiving payment and retaining the well, he is in a position of strength and would naturally expect to retain access to his own property.
