# Bava Batra 67

## Oil Press Sale

### Press Sale Basics

The daf opens on 67b with a continuation of the Mishnah's systematic treatment of sales: when one sells a particular piece of property or commercial installation, which components are included by default, and which require an explicit, broader formulation? The governing principle established in prior sugyot is that when selling real property — a home, a field, or a commercial structure — only those items that are physically attached to the ground are transferred as part of the sale. Movable implements, however intimately connected to the operation, do not transfer unless the seller employs an expansive formula such as *hu ve-khol mah she-betocho* ("it and everything in it"). Even that broader phrase captures items that are practically and conceptually bound up with the property's function — not random contents that happen to be on the premises.

With this framework in mind, the Mishnah turns to the *beit ha-bad*, the oil press.

### Press Components

Understanding what the Mishnah includes or excludes requires some reconstruction of the physical layout of an ancient oil press. According to the Rashbam, olive pressing proceeded in three distinct stages. First, the olives underwent an initial crushing — a mortar-and-pestle type operation. Second, they were ground further in a *reichayim*, a millstone arrangement. Third, and most critically, the crushed olives were subjected to sustained pressure from a massive *kora*, a heavy beam, which was lowered onto them and left to press out the remaining oil over time. It is the *kora* that is the defining piece of equipment of the *beit ha-bad*.

### Yam, Mamal, Betulot

The Mishnah states that when one sells a *beit ha-bad*, one sells the *yam*, the *mamal*, and the *betulot*. The Gemara identifies the *yam* — literally "sea" — as the *tlafcha*, a lentil-shaped trough or cistern into which all the pressed olive oil collects. The name apparently refers to its shape. The *mamal*: Rav Abba bar Mamal identifies it with the *mafrachta*, the crusher. The Rashbam explains that this refers to the mortar-like structure fixed to the ground that enables the initial crushing of the olives — the structure itself is attached, even if the pestle-like implement used within it is not. Because it is fixed to the ground, it is sold with the press. The *betulot* — literally "virgins," a somewhat opaque designation — Rabbi Yochanan explains as cedar poles, *konesot shel erez*, that are embedded in the ground and serve to support and stabilize the structure through which the *kora* is raised and lowered. These poles, being fixed to the ground, are included in the sale.

### Avirim, Galgal, Kora

By contrast, the Mishnah lists three items that are *not* sold as part of the default sale: the *avirim*, the *galgal*, and the *kora*. The Rashbam explains the *avirim* as planks — *nisarim* — that are placed on top of the olives beneath the *kora* in order to more effectively distribute the pressure. Because these planks are not fixed to the ground and can be removed and used elsewhere, they are not sold automatically. The *galgal* — literally a wheel — the Gemara explains as a *chumresa*, the mechanism used to raise and lower the *kora*. Whether understood as a pulley system or, more precisely, as a screw-type device (as modern scholarship on ancient oil press technology would suggest), this apparatus is not affixed to the ground and therefore does not transfer. Finally, and most strikingly, the *kora* itself — the enormous beam that is the very heart of the press's operation — is also not sold by default, for it too rests without being fixed to the ground.

### Kol Ma Shebetocho

The Mishnah continues: if the seller said *hu ve-khol mah she-betocho*, "it and everything in it," then *harei kullan mekhurин* — all of these items are sold. Rabbi Eliezer dissents on one point: even without the expansive formula, the seller of a *beit ha-bad* has sold the *kora*. His reasoning is explicit — *she-lo nikra beit ha-bad ela al shem ha-kora*: the very name and identity of an oil press is defined by its beam. The *kora* is so central, so constitutive of what a *beit ha-bad* is, that one cannot plausibly be understood to have sold the press while retaining the beam. Rabbi Eliezer's position is limited to the *kora* alone; he does not extend this logic to the other movable equipment.

### Mamal & Mafrachta

The Gemara's identification of the *mamal* with the *mafrachta* invites a closer look at the three-stage process the Rashbam describes. Stage one is the initial crushing, akin to a mortar and pestle. Stage two is the grinding in a *reichayim*, a millstone. Stage three is the sustained pressing under the *kora*. The *mafrachta* corresponds to the first stage — specifically, the fixed structure (the mortar) into which the crushing implements are applied. The Rashbam considers and rejects the possibility that *mafrachta* refers simply to the striking implement itself, since that would not be attached to the ground and thus its sale with the press would require separate explanation. The fixed mortar structure, however, is clearly *mekhubar le-karka* and thus transfers automatically.

### Betulot Poles

Rabbi Yochanan's identification of the *betulot* as cedar poles supporting the *kora* mechanism is consistent with the visual logic of the press. These poles, planted in the ground, hold the superstructure through which the beam is manipulated. Being fixed in the earth, they are unambiguously part of what transfers in a standard sale — no expansive language is needed. The poetic designation "virgins" for these structural poles remains unexplained by the Gemara, but the functional identification is clear.

### Avirim & Galgal

The *avirim* — which we may render as "pressers" — are planks laid over the olives to distribute the *kora*'s weight. The *galgal*, per the Rashbam, is the raising-and-lowering mechanism: *vin be-la'az*, he writes, *she-megalgalin bah et ha-kora le-ha'alot* — a device by which the beam is wound up or lowered. Whether this is precisely a screw or another mechanical arrangement, the point is that it is removable and therefore not sold. The *kora* itself, as noted, is also movable — massive and weighty, but not sunk into the ground — and it too is excluded from the automatic sale, except according to Rabbi Eliezer.

### Baraita: Equipment

A *baraita* then elaborates on what *is* sold when selling a *beit ha-bad*, presenting a richer list than the Mishnah alone. The *baraita* states: one sells the *nisarim* (planks), the *yekavim* (vats — the same root as *yekev*, used in the Torah for wine and oil collection: *mi-gornekha u-mi-yikvekha*), the *mafrakhot* (the mortar structures), and the *reichayim ha-takhtonim* (the lower millstones). The qualification regarding millstones is significant: *aval lo et ha-elyonah* — the upper millstone is not sold, because the upper stone is movable while the lower is fixed. Here again, *kol mah she-betocho* would include everything; without it, only the fixed lower stone transfers. When the seller does say everything, the *baraita* confirms *harei kullan mekhurін*, all is sold — but even then, the *avirim* are still excluded, because those planks, while certainly used in the press, are the kind of implement one might take elsewhere; they are not seen as sufficiently bound up with the fixed apparatus of the press itself. Similarly, sacks and leather bags (*sakkim* and *martzufim*) remain with the seller — these are purely incidental to the fixed operation.

### Planks Debate

A tension emerges between the Mishnah and the *baraita* regarding planks. In the Mishnah, the *avirim* (planks used to press the olives down) are among the items *not* sold even when *kol mah she-betocho* is said. Yet the *baraita* seems to include *nisarim* among the items that *are* sold. The Rashbam resolves this by distinguishing between two different types of planks. The *avirim* of the Mishnah are the loose pressers placed atop the olives — portable, detachable, and usable elsewhere. The *nisarim* of the *baraita*, by contrast, are planks fixed around the base of the pressing area to prevent the olives from scattering when the *kora* bears down on them — *ke-ein nisarim she-notnim saviv ha-zeitim be-veit ha-bad kedei she-lo yitpazru anah va-anah be-khevid ha-kora aleihem*. The Rashbam adds that these latter planks are affixed to the ground, *me-khubbarim sham*, and thus they transfer automatically. The two categories occupy different positions along the spectrum of attachment, which explains why the Mishnah and *baraita* appear to diverge.

---

## Bathhouse Sale

### Bathhouse Basics

The Mishnah now turns to the *merchatz*, the Roman bathhouse. The Roman bathhouse had a characteristic three-room structure: an outer vestibule where patrons arrived clothed; a middle room serving as the changing area; and an inner room — the steam bath or sauna — in which bathers sat or stood on wooden planks elevated above smoldering coals, with steam rising as water was poured over the heated stone or coals beneath.

### Bathhouse Non-Sales

When one sells a *merchatz*, the Mishnah specifies what is *not* transferred. The *nesarim* — the wooden planks on which bathers stand — are not sold. Counterintuitively, these planks are apparently not nailed down. This makes functional sense: the planks need to be lifted periodically to allow access to the coal pit beneath for stoking and maintenance, and in a facility built primarily of stone, nailing would not be practical in any case. Because they are not fixed, they do not transfer. Similarly excluded are the *sfalim* — either basins or pitchers used for pouring water — and the *balaniyot* (or, in some textual traditions, *vilayot*), which the Mishnah identifies as the towels.

### Bathhouse Inclusivity

If the seller used the formula *hi ve-khol mah she-betochah*, "it and everything in it," then *harei kullan mekhurін* — the planks, the basins, the towels, all are sold.

### Supplies Excluded

However — and this qualification holds regardless of which formula is used — *ubein kakh u-vein kakh*, neither formulation transfers the supplies that feed the bathhouse. The *magorot shel mayim* (the Rashbam reads this as *bereikhot mayim*, pools of water), the water sources or reservoirs that supply the bathhouse, are not sold. Nor are the *otzarot shel etzim*, the wood sheds that store fuel for the coals. The distinction is between equipment and supplies: the planks, the basins, and even the towels are the bathhouse's *kelim*, its functional apparatus, and those transfer when broadly worded language is used. But the consumable inputs — water and wood — and the structures that house them are a separate commercial matter entirely.

### Storage Rooms

A *baraita* elaborates on what the Mishnah left underdeveloped, specifying what *is* sold in the default case. The *baraita* lists: *beit ha-nesarim* (the room where planks are stored at the end of the day), *beit ha-yakmin* (the Rashbam, after considering and rejecting another reading, identifies *yakmin* as head-towels, i.e., the room where head-towels are stored), *beit ha-sfalim* (the room for the basins or benches — and the reading *safsalim*, "benches," which are built into the stone, may be preferable), and *beit ha-vilayot* (the room for the body-towels). The *chiddush* here is substantial: one might have supposed that selling the bathhouse conveyed only the bathhouse itself — its three rooms — while the adjacent storage sheds or closets remained the seller's. The *baraita* teaches otherwise. These storage rooms, built to house the bathhouse's rotating equipment, are so integrally connected to the bathhouse's operation that they are included in the sale even without expansive language. They are *mekhubar le-karka* and serve the *merchatz* directly.

### Rooms vs. Contents

The *baraita* then states with equal clarity what is *not* sold: *aval lo et ha-nesarim atzmam, ve-lo et ha-yakmin atzmam, ve-lo sfalim atzmam, ve-lo et ha-vilayot atzmam* — the rooms transfer, but not the items stored within them. You acquire the storage closet, not the towels and planks inside it. When the seller says *hu ve-khol mah she-betochah*, then everything — rooms and contents alike — is sold. Even then, however, the water sources and wood sheds remain excluded: *im machar et ha-breichot ha-maspekot lo mayim* — the pools that supply the water, *bein bi-ymot ha-chamah bein bi-ymot ha-geshamim*, whether for summer or winter use, are not transferred; nor is *beit kinus ha-etzim*, the woodshed.

### Tashmishim Language

The *baraita* introduces a third, still-broader formula: *im amar lo beit merchatz ve-khol tashmishav ani mokher lakh* — "the bathhouse and all its *tashmishim*," all its appurtenances. With this formulation, *kullan mekhurін* — everything, including all the equipment and storage rooms, is fully transferred. The word *tashmishim* designates the things that serve and attend to the facility, and it is an even more expansive term than *kol mah she-betochah*. This distinction will immediately become significant.

---

## Sesame Seeds Case

### Store & Sesame

The Gemara now presents a case that tests the limits of *kol tashmishav*. A seller said to a buyer: *beit ha-bad ve-khol tashmishav ani mokher lakh* — "the oil press and all its appurtenances." The question is whether two features of this particular *beit ha-bad* complex are included. First, there were shops (*chanvatah*) situated just outside the press complex — perhaps a concession operation serving the workers, selling food and provisions. Second, on the roof of those shops, sesame seeds were being dried, apparently in preparation for pressing them into sesame oil in the same equipment. Does the expanded formula *kol tashmishav* reach these?

The Rashbam is careful to analyze both features independently. The rooftop drying of sesame seeds might seem like a genuine *tashmish* of the *beit ha-bad* — those seeds are destined to be pressed in the same facility. But the store itself sells bread, wine, and provisions to workers: *eila ikkar tashmishan li-mkhor pat ve-yayin hu* — its primary function is an independent commercial enterprise, not the servicing of the press. Even if the press's workers patronize it, a store that generates its own revenue from its own customers is not a *tashmish* of the *beit ha-bad* in any meaningful sense.

### Tashmishim Scope

The parties came before Rav Yosef. He ruled that based on the *baraita* about the bathhouse — *im amar beit ha-merchatz ve-khol tashmishav ani mokher lakh, harei kullan mekhurIn* — the formula *kol tashmishav* is an expansive one, and even ambiguous appendages like this store and its rooftop should be included. The argument, while not fully explicit, seems to be that *tashmishav* is meant to sweep broadly, capturing everything that attends to the press's operation in any connected way.

### Abaye Limits

Abaye challenged Rav Yosef from a *baraita* taught by Rabbi Hiyya: *ein kullan mekhurIn* — not everything is sold even when *tashmishav* is said. This demonstrates that the category of *tashmish* has inherent limits; some things remain outside it even under the broadest formula.

### Boundaries Rule

Rav Ashi offered the resolution: *chazina* — we assess the facts on the ground. If the seller said *beit ha-bad ve-khol tashmishav* and then drew boundaries — *eilein mitzranah* — that explicitly encompassed the shops and the rooftop area, then the buyer acquires them: *kani*. If not, *lo kani*, he does not. One might ask: is it not trivially true that drawing explicit boundaries makes the included items part of the sale? The answer is that earlier discussions in this tractate established that boundary-drawing language is sometimes used merely to identify which property is being sold, not to expand the sale beyond its natural scope — *metzarim hirchiv lo*. Here, however, when the seller has also employed the expansive language *kol tashmishav*, the combination of expansive formula plus explicit boundary-drawing is definitive: those ambiguous adjacent enterprises are sold.

---

## Town Sale

### Town Structures

The Mishnah now presents what is, from a certain vantage point, a striking case: the sale of an entire *ir*, a town. One is reminded that *ir* in rabbinic usage denotes a town rather than a large city (*krach*); a *kfar* is a village below that. But even at the scale of a town, it is conceptually striking that a single individual could own it entirely — though parallels to company towns are not hard to find.

When one sells an *ir*, the Mishnah teaches that one has sold: the houses (*batim*), the wells and cisterns (*borot, shichin u-me'arot*), the bathhouses (*merchatza'ot*), the pigeon coops (*shovakhot*), the oil presses (*batei badim*), and the *beit ha-shlachin* — the irrigated fields. In short, all the land and all the structures — residential, commercial, industrial — transfer. The variety of these categories is notable: the Mishnah does not distinguish between homes and enterprises, between wells and bathhouses.

### Movables & Exception

Nevertheless, *aval lo et ha-metaltalin* — movable property is not included. Even an all-encompassing sale of an entire town does not, by default, sweep up its contents. If the seller said *hi ve-khol mah she-betochah*, however, then all the contents transfer as well — subject, of course, to the seller actually owning those items. Whatever belongs to the townspeople cannot be sold by the town's owner.

### Animals & Slaves

The Mishnah extends the *kol mah she-betochah* formula further: *afilu hayu bah behemah va-avadim, harei kullan mekhurIn* — even animals and slaves are included. This is the *chiddush*. Why would one have thought these might be different? Because animals and slaves can move on their own volition — they are not stationary fixtures of the town the way a building or even a barrel would be. Something that moves independently seems intuitively less "contained in" the town than something that stays put. The Mishnah therefore teaches that even these self-moving entities are sold when the comprehensive formula is used.

The Rashbam notes that once this formula is in play, even food products are included — the formula is fully comprehensive.

---

## Santar Debate

### Santar Included

Rabban Gamliel adds: *ha-mokher et ha-ir machar et ha-santar* — one who sells a town has also sold the *santar*. The meaning of this term is itself the subject of Gemara debate.

### Santar Definition

The Gemara records two interpretive traditions. The first, cited as the local Palestinian interpretation: *bar machvanita* — some type of person, whom the Rashbam identifies as a slave whose function is to know and report the boundary markers and property records of the town: *eved ha-munneh le-haggid u-le-achvuyei techumi ha-sadot*. This slave serves as a living registry of the town's property arrangements — a registrar, embedded in the commercial and civic life of the town, owned by the town's owner, and indispensable to its functioning: *ve-i efshar le-ir be-lo oto*. Shimon ben Aptolmos offers the second interpretation: *bagi* — an irrigated field attached to the town. On this reading, the *santar* is not a person but land.

---

## Town Sale (II)

### Slave Status

Rav Acha bar Rav Avya raised a sharp question to Rav Ashi from the Mishnah's treatment of slaves. The Mishnah teaches that slaves are not automatically sold with the town even though all *karka* (landed property) is sold automatically. May we infer from this that *avda ke-mitaltlei dami* — that slaves are legally classified as chattel rather than land? For if slaves were considered *karka*, they should transfer automatically *agav mata*, as part of the land, just as houses and fields do.

### Movement Logic

The Gemara pushes back. Even granting that the question is well posed, the inference does not follow. The response: *ella mai ait lakh le-meimar* — even if you want to say *avda ke-mitaltlei dami*, why does the Mishnah say *afilu* ("even") slaves are sold when *kol mah she-betochah* is used? The word *afilu* signals that there was reason to think slaves would not be included. But if slaves were simply ordinary chattel, their inclusion would need no special emphasis — ordinary chattel transfers with *kol mah she-betochah* without any drama.

The answer: *shani be-mitaltlei de-nayyadi mi-mitaltlei de-lo nayyadi* — there is a meaningful difference between movable property that moves on its own and movable property that does not. Chattel that sits still is, in some sense, "contained" within the town. A slave who walks around on his own volition is conceptually detached from the town's fixed domain. That conceptual detachment could equally apply whether he is classified as *karka* or *metaltalin* — the self-movement is what creates the intuition that he falls outside *kol mah she-betochah*, not his legal categorization. *Afilu teima de-ke-karka dami* — even if you say slaves are legally land, you might have thought they were excluded from the town sale because their movement makes them conceptually distinct. *Shani bein karka de-nayyadi le-karka de-lo nayyadi* — there is a difference between land that moves and land that does not. The Mishnah's *afilu* therefore proves nothing about the fundamental legal classification of slaves.

---

## Santar Debate (II)

### Santar Scribe

The Gemara now examines the two interpretations of *santar* in detail. The Rashbam understands *bar machvanita* — picking up on the Aramaic root meaning "to tell" or "to speak" — as a slave who serves as the town's living records keeper, articulating (*le-achvuyei*) the boundaries of the various fields and properties. This slave's role is uniquely tied to the town's identity and governance; he is owned by the *sar ha-ir*, the town's master, and his knowledge is, in a sense, what makes orderly civic life possible.

### Santar Guard

Rabbeinu Chananel offers a different reading: *santar hu shomer ha-ir ve-notra de-kharmei* — the *santar* is the town's guard, the sentry who watches over the fields and vineyards. This reading connects *santar* to the Latin *santarius* ("guardsman of fields") or a related Greek form, and *santar* may indeed be a loanword from that root — Rashi too identifies a Greek or Latin etymology. This interpretation has the advantage of linguistic transparency: "sentry" is a recognizable function, and the word *santar* maps cleanly onto it. One might also note that the Aramaic *bar machvanita* (literally "son of the jaw/mouth") could itself be a folk-etymological reading that the Rashbam then builds upon, while the actual word's origin is the Greek/Latin sentry.

### Santar Field

Shimon ben Aptolmos reads *santar* as *bagi* — an irrigated field. On this reading, what Rabban Gamliel is adding to the default town sale is not a person but a tract of land — specifically the irrigated fields lying beyond the town's borders. This interpretation creates a clear hierarchy of difficulty: the irrigated fields adjacent to the town are land, and land normally transfers; the *chiddush* would be that these fields, even lying outside the town proper, are considered appurtenant to it. A human being, by contrast, is not normally sold with real estate at all.

### Field vs. Person

The Gemara observes that the two readings generate opposite hierarchies of *chiddush*. If *santar* means a person (*bar machvanita*), then the *tanna kamma* already includes the irrigated fields (*beit ha-shlachin*) in the town sale, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's addition is that even the sentry — a person — is also sold. The greater novelty is the person. If *santar* means the irrigated field, then the *tanna kamma* refers to orchards (*ginunita*, reading *shlachin* from *shilchayikh pardes rimonim*), and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that even the more distant irrigated fields beyond the orchard are sold. These two readings are shown to be internally consistent with the broader Mishnaic structure, and the Gemara presses each one to see whether the debate's contours make sense.

---

## Remnants & Suburbs

### Yehuda's Terms

Rabbi Yehuda enters the discussion with a different set of positions: *santar eino machur, aval ankolmus machur* — you do not sell the *santar*, but you do sell the *ankolmus*. The Rashbam derives *ankolmus* from *kulmus* (quill), identifying him as the town's scribe. This scribe has a defined role in the town's administrative and commercial life — recording transactions, maintaining documents — and Rabbi Yehuda holds that this figure transfers with the town while the *santar* does not.

### Both Persons

The Gemara initially presses: if the *ankolmus* is a person, surely the *santar* is also a person, and we are simply debating which slave is sold with the town. The Gemara does not accept this inference as determinative — *midi irya?* — and notes that there is no formal requirement that the two terms occupy the same category. It remains possible, on some readings, that *santar* is a field while *ankolmus* is a person, and Rabbi Yehuda is making a claim that you sell a person but not the field. The Gemara, however, finds this difficult to sustain.

### Non-Included Items

The *baraita* appended to Rabbi Yehuda's statement lists what is definitively not included in a town sale: *aval lo shi'areiha* — not its remnants, *ve-lo bnoteiha* — not its daughter towns or suburbs, *ve-lo chorshin ha-muktzin lah* — not the forests designated for the town's use, *ve-lo vivrin shel chayah ve-shel ofot ve-shel dagim* — not the game preserves, whether for wild animals, birds, or fish, even if these are functionally associated with the town.

### Distant Fields

The *shi'areiha* — "its remnants" — requires definition. The Gemara asks: *mai shi'areiha?* What are these remnants? They are called *bizlei*. What is *bizlei*? Rabbi Abba explains: *piskei bagi* — strips of irrigated fields. These are not the contiguous irrigated fields immediately adjacent to the town, but more distant, outlying strips that are separated from the main fields by some natural or artificial break. Even in a town sale, those far strips are not conveyed.

### Partial Agreement

This creates an apparent tension. If Rabbi Yehuda says the *santar* is not sold, and the *santar* (on the "field" reading) means irrigated fields, then Rabbi Yehuda holds that the irrigated fields are not sold. But the *baraita* indicates that the distant *piskei bagi* are not sold — implying that the standard *bagi* are sold. The Gemara resolves this by reversing Rabbi Yehuda's formulation: *afoch* — *santar machur, ankolmus lo machur*. That is, Rabbi Yehuda actually holds that the *santar* (the irrigated fields) is sold, while the *ankolmus* (the scribe) is not. The *baraita* then makes sense: the standard fields transfer; only the outlying strips do not. The Gemara then asks whether Rabbi Yehuda has now been assimilated to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position — and answers that he agrees with Rabban Shimon on the *santar* (the fields) but disagrees regarding the daughter towns. Rabban Shimon holds that selling a town includes its *banot*, its satellite settlements: *mocher ir machar benoteiha*. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the daughter towns are not sold. On that point they diverge. *Rav Yehuda savir lei ke-vatei be-chada u-flig bei be-chada* — he agrees on one point and disagrees on another.

### Final Position

At the end of the discussion, the Gemara has not formally resolved which reading of *santar* is definitive. Both the "sentry" interpretation and the "irrigated field" interpretation remain alive in the sources. That said, the sentry reading has considerably more to recommend it. The standard Mishnaic term for irrigated fields is already *beit ha-shlachin*, which appears at the beginning of this very Mishnah — it would be redundant for *santar* to mean the same thing. Moreover, the comparison to *ankolmus* — clearly a person — makes most natural sense if *santar* is also a person. The etymology connects cleanly to the Greek or Latin word for a guardian or field-warden. The debate in the Mishnah is therefore most naturally read as concerning whether the town's sentry-slave is included in the sale, with Rabban Shimon holding that he is and the *tanna kamma* holding that he is not — while the orchards and irrigated fields transfer in any case as land appurtenant to the town.

---

---

# Bava Batra 69

## Town Sale & Enclosures

### Braita: Town Contents

The daf opens with a *braisa* addressing the sale of a town. The *braisa* states that when someone buys a town, he does not acquire the enclosures containing wild animals, birds, and fish — *v'lo bivrin shel chaya v'shel of v'shel dagim*. These are not mere cages but plots of land functioning as nature preserves.

A contradiction, however, is immediately raised. A second *braisa* states that if a town had outlying daughter-towns, or if the town extended partly over water, or if it possessed enclosures of wild animals and fish, *harei elu nimkarim imah* — they are sold along with it. The two *braisos* appear to flatly contradict one another regarding these enclosures.

### Enclosure Orientation

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya*. The distinction turns on the orientation of the enclosure's opening. If the opening faces inward toward the town, the enclosure is regarded as an extension of the town and is sold with it. If the opening faces outward, it is not considered part of the town and is excluded from the sale.

### Forest Designations

A further question is raised from the *braisa*'s mention of forests. The *braisa* appears to exclude forests that are *muktzin lah* — designated for the town. The *Gemara* corrects the reading: the word should be understood as *muktzin mimena*, meaning forests that are separated or set apart from the town. It is those separated forests that are not sold; forests that are designated and integrated with the town are included in the sale. With this emendation, the *braisa* is rendered consistent.

---

## Field Sale Basics

### Included Items

The *mishnah* now turns to the sale of a field — *hamocher et hasadeh*. One noteworthy feature of this *mishnah* is that certain items are sold with the field even when they are not *mechubar* — physically attached to the ground. This contrasts with the earlier discussion of a bathhouse or similar structures, where even necessary equipment that was not nailed down was generally not sold. Here, items that are functionally necessary to the field are included in the sale regardless of physical attachment.

The *mishnah* lists what is sold with a field: stones that are needed for the field, *shehein ltzorkah*; the sticks in a vineyard that are necessary for it, *shehein ltzorko*; grain that is still attached to the ground, *shehi mechuberes l'karka*; a patch of growing reeds that is smaller than a *beis rova*; and a guard's hut that is not plastered over. Regarding the hut, two textual traditions (*girsaos*) exist. According to one version, a hut that is not plastered over is sold with the field because its impermanence marks it as a mere appendage of the field rather than an independent structure. The other *geirsa* inverts this: a hut that is plastered over is more firmly bonded to the ground and therefore sold with it, while an unplastered hut is more akin to a movable object and is not.

### Young Trees Included

The *mishnah* continues: a carob tree that has not yet been grafted, *she'eino murkav*, and the young growth of a sycamore tree, *pasulat hashikmah*, are also sold with the field. The logic is that when trees are still young — before their branches have been cut and grafted — they have not yet achieved an independent identity. They are simply part of the field. Once a carob or sycamore reaches maturity and begins to be grafted and pruned, it takes on a distinct character and is no longer merely an element of the field in which it stands.

One might ask why the grafting of a carob would be relevant to its status. The grafting referred to here is not necessarily a matter of *kilayim* — the prohibition against mixed species. Rather, it refers to the horticultural practice of grafting a more productive branch onto a younger tree, such as grafting a vigorous carob variety onto an existing one, in order to improve yield. It is this process of cultivation that elevates the tree to the status of a significant and independent entity.

### Excluded Items

The second half of the *mishnah* follows almost mechanically from the first. Not sold with the field are: stones that are not necessary for it; the sticks in the vineyard that are not needed; and grain that has already been harvested and cut from the ground. The *mishnah* notes that if the seller explicitly said "the field and all its contents," everything in the previous list becomes included. However, even with that broader formulation, several items remain excluded regardless: a patch of growing reeds that is the size of a *beis rova* or larger, the guard's hut that is plastered over (according to our *geirsa*), a grafted carob, and the mature sycamore.

### Rashbam's Analysis

The *Rashbam* offers a conceptual framework to explain why these last items are excluded even when the seller says "all its contents." His position is that these items are not merely objects *within* the field — they are themselves independent fields. A patch of reeds of sufficient size, a large plastered hut, a grafted carob of considerable maturity, and above all the great sycamore — these are not seen as things located within the field but as distinct parcels situated alongside or within it.

The *Rashbam* illustrates with an analogy: if a person owns three adjacent plots of land, labeled A, B, and C, and sells "A and C and everything within them," the buyer does not receive B, even though B lies between them. So too, when a field contains a section with its own identity — its own name and independent character — it is not "within" the field being sold; it is its own field, and the language "all its contents" cannot reach it.

This same principle, the *Gemara* makes explicit through Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, extends beyond a patch of reeds. Any sub-plot within a field that possesses its own distinct identity — *yesh lah shem bifnei atzmah* — is not sold with the field even under expansive sale language. Rav Papa illustrates: if a small plot of spices or roses within a field is known as "so-and-so's rose garden" — *varda d'planya* — it carries its own name and therefore its own legal identity. Selling "the field and everything in it" does not convey "the rose garden."

This principle of independent identity also applies to the hut, despite the fact that it is physically attached to the ground. A well-constructed, plastered hut has become its own entity. And the grafted carob or mature sycamore, even if it is not large in the absolute sense, once it has been grafted and cultivated, it is regarded as its own thing — *af al gav d'katini* — even if they are not large, they have acquired an independent identity.

The *Gemara* then raises an unresolved question — *ba'ei Rav Eliezer* — regarding doorframes. If one sells a house, do the doorframes go with it? The *Rashbam* explains that doorframes in that era could be attached after construction was complete, affixed with nails rather than built into the wall itself. The *Gemara* asks: where they are affixed with plaster, they are clearly part of the structure and are sold with it; but where they are held in place with nails alone, and can in principle be removed without structural damage, the question is unresolved — *teiku*. Similarly unresolved is the question of window frames (*malbenot shel chalonot*), which may be purely aesthetic, and the padded frames placed under bed legs to prevent rot — where the question depends on whether they move with the bed or remain fixed in place.

---

## Rabbi Meir Debate

### Weight Stones

The *Gemara* now turns to the *mishnah*'s first item — stones necessary for the field — and asks what type of stones the *mishnah* has in mind. Two explanations are offered. The *Gemara* as interpreted locally in Bavel identifies them as *avnei de'achfa* — weight stones, used to hold down bundled grain so it does not scatter in the wind. The *Rashbam* compares this to placing stones over gathered leaves to prevent them from blowing away.

*Ulla* offers a different explanation: the *mishnah* refers to stones arranged in preparation for building a wall — *avanim hasdurot legader*. These are stones that have been laid out in neat rows, poised to be incorporated into a boundary wall, though the building has not yet commenced. Rabbi Hiyya's *braisa* goes one step further and speaks of *avanim tzevurot legader* — stones piled in an unordered heap, not yet laid in rows, merely gathered in anticipation of wall construction.

The *Gemara* then maps these positions onto the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *Rabbanan*, a debate that properly pervades the entire chapter. Rabbi Meir holds that when a vineyard is sold, the seller conveys *kol tashmisheiha hakarem* — all the accessories of the vineyard; he applies a broader understanding of what "goes with" the sale. The *Rabbanan* take a narrower view.

Applied to weight stones: according to Rabbi Meir, stones that have been designated (*metaknan*) for use in the field are sold with it, even if they have never actually been placed. Designation alone suffices. According to the *Rabbanan*, the stones must have actually been used — placed in position at least once — before they acquire the status of field accessories. Applied to *Ulla*'s explanation: according to Rabbi Meir, stones designated for the wall but not yet laid in rows (*d'lo sidran*) are included; according to the *Rabbanan*, they must actually have been arranged in order.

### Vineyard Sticks

The same analytical structure governs the *mishnah*'s mention of vineyard sticks. The sticks referred to are trellises — supports placed beneath the grapevines to help them grow. The school of Rabbi Yannai explains that these are *kanim hamichulakim*, sticks that have been specially prepared and placed beneath the vines. The *Rashbam* notes that a French gloss in the text sounds cognate to the word "trellis." *Tosafot* reads *michulakim* differently, interpreting it to mean that the sticks were peeled to prevent rot, rather than split or crossed into a lattice.

According to Rabbi Meir, once the sticks have been smoothed and prepared (*mishpayan*), they are considered sold with the vineyard even if they have not yet been erected. According to the *Rabbanan*, the sticks must actually have been put in place — *mokman* — before they are included in the sale.

A student question surfaces the precise nature of the *metaknan* stage: is it a purely verbal designation, or does it require some physical act? The *Rashbam*'s language — *metukanot umezumanot letzorcha* — suggests something more than merely saying "these are for the field." It may require physically moving or setting aside the objects for that purpose, though not necessarily altering them. The *Gemara*'s classic framework of *hazmana milsa hi* versus *hazmana lav milsa hi* — whether designation constitutes a legal act — underlies the entire debate between Rabbi Meir and the *Rabbanan*.

### Unnecessary Items

The parallel structure continues for the items *not* sold with the field. The *mishnah* lists stones not necessary for the field and sticks in the vineyard not needed for it, and one might assume these refer simply to objects with different functions. The *Gemara*, however, reframes the distinction entirely in terms of the stage of preparation. There are not two different categories of stones or sticks — there is simply one category at an earlier stage of designation or use.

For unnecessary stones: according to Rabbi Meir, these are stones that have not yet been designated at all (*d'lo mesaknan*); for the *Rabbanan*, they are stones that were designated but never placed (*d'lo machsan*). For *Ulla*'s version: according to Rabbi Meir, stones not yet designated; according to the *Rabbanan*, stones designated but not yet laid in rows. The logic is perfectly parallel for the sticks: according to Rabbi Meir, sticks not yet smoothed; according to the *Rabbanan*, sticks smoothed but not yet erected.

The *Gemara* also addresses grain that has been harvested. Even grain that has been cut and spread on the ground to dry — which needs and uses the ground to complete the drying process — is not sold with the field once it has been severed. The *mishnah* is clear: the sale of the field conveys only what is physically attached. And regarding the patch of reeds, the formal criterion of size — the *beis rova* — governs absolutely: if smaller than that size it is sold with the field even if the reeds are thick; if it reaches that size it is not sold even if the reeds are thin.

The *Gemara* extends the *Rashbam*'s principle through Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba: the exclusion of patches with independent identity is not limited to a stand of reeds but applies to any sub-plot with its own name. This principle holds even when the seller employs the expansive formula *kol ma shebetocha*. Rav Papa's illustration — "Shimon's rose garden" — conveys that what gives a plot its independent identity is not its size or composition alone, but whether it is understood by the community as a distinct entity with its own name.

---

## Scripture & Boundaries

### Vayikam Pasuk

The *Gemara* now asks for the scriptural source of the rule that trees are generally sold with a field. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav cites the verse from the purchase of the Machpelah cave — *vayakam sdei Efron asher bamachpelah asher lifnei mamre, hasadeh vehamearah asher bo, vechol ha'etz asher basadeh asher bechol gvulov saviv* (Genesis 23:17). The verse states that "all the trees in the field, within all its boundaries all around" were conveyed in the transaction.

From this verse, the *Gemara* derives two things. First, the baseline rule: when you buy a field, you receive *kol etz* — all the trees in it. Second, and more subtly, the verse limits this to trees *asher bechol gvulov saviv* — within all the surrounding boundaries. This limiting phrase implies that some trees are excluded: those that do not require the surrounding boundaries to define them. The *Rashbam* explains this as follows. Ordinary trees in a field require boundaries to establish whose side they fall on — neighbors might dispute whether a small tree stands within one plot or the other. But a tree of exceptional size and prominence — a mature sycamore or grafted carob — is so recognizable and significant that there has never been any question whose land it occupies. Everyone always knew. Such a tree therefore does not "need" the surrounding boundary, and the verse's phrase *asher bechol gvulov saviv* pointedly excludes it from the automatic conveyance.

This is admittedly a *drash* rather than strict *pshat*, and this is acknowledged plainly. Yet as a *halacha l'maaseh* it establishes that trees of independent identity are not simply swept up in the sale of a field.

### Boundary Trees

Rav Mesharsheya draws a further inference from the same verse: *mikan l'meitzarin min hatorah* — from here we see the concept of boundary lines as part of the conveyance. The *Rashbam* explains that when one sells a field, the boundary line of the field is included in the sale, as are any trees planted along that boundary. The verse's formulation — *asher bechol gvulov saviv*, surrounding on all sides — encompasses the trees that form or mark the perimeter of the field.

One might wonder what *chiddush* this introduces, since if the boundary trees belong to the seller they obviously pass to the buyer along with the rest of the field. The possible novelty is that one cannot claim, "I sold you the field but retained the boundary trees for myself as a separate entity." The verse establishes that the boundary trees are part of the field conveyance and cannot be independently reserved. This is analogous to a tenant who has charge of everything within an apartment but has no claim on the walls themselves — one might have thought the seller could argue that the boundary trees, like a wall, belong to a separate category. The verse forecloses that argument.

---

## Deed Language

### Standard Formula

Rav Yehuda now turns to actual documentary practice. When a seller wishes to convey all trees along with a parcel of land, the standard deed formula reads: *kni lach diklin ve'talin ve'hutzin ve'tzitzin* — acquire from me the palm trees, the other trees, the young palms, and the young other trees. The precise meaning of each term is disputed among the *rishonim*. According to the Soncino's interpretation, *diklei* are mature palm trees, *talin* are mature non-palm trees, *hutzin* are immature palm trees, and *tzitzin* are immature non-palm trees. The *Rashbam* understands all four terms as referring to varieties of palm trees.

### Shofra d'Shtara

The *Gemara* immediately notes that this elaborate formula is technically unnecessary. We have just established from the *mishnah* that trees are automatically sold with a field. Yet even so, the formula is used — *afilu hachi shufra d'shtara hu* — it is an embellishment of the deed. *Shofra d'shtara* means making the *shtar* more explicit and elegant, spelling out in formal language what the law would provide by default. The *Rashbam* explains the practical benefit: it ensures that no question arises, and accommodates the possibility that a *beis din* of limited learning might not be aware of the default rule.

There is, however, a risk to verbosity in legal documents. The principle *kol hamosif goreia* — whoever adds, subtracts — means that explicit language can sometimes narrow rather than expand the default scope of a transaction. As the *Gemara* is about to demonstrate, the precise preposition or conjunction used in a deed can significantly alter what is conveyed.

---

## Deed Interpretation

### Ara v'Diklei

The *Gemara* now examines a case in which the deed reads *ara ve'diklei* — "land and palm trees." The conjunction *vav* links two separate items: the land, and palm trees. Since palm trees are already included in the sale of land by default, this phrasing implies that the palm trees referred to are not the ones within the land — those are already conveyed automatically — but rather palm trees located elsewhere. The seller is conveying this plot of land *plus* additional palm trees he owns in some other location.

The *Gemara* then rules: *chazinan* — we look at the circumstances. If the seller owns palm trees elsewhere, he must give the buyer a minimum of two (*t'rei diklei*), and he gets to choose which two. If he owns no palm trees elsewhere, he must go and purchase two palm trees to deliver. If he does own palm trees elsewhere but they are encumbered by a lien, he must pay off the lien so that the buyer can receive unencumbered trees. The entire analysis flows from reading *ara ve'diklei* as promising something beyond the land itself.

### Tosafot Reading

*Tosafot* challenges this reading with a strikingly different *geirsa* and interpretation. According to *Tosafot*, the palm trees in question are in fact growing within the plot of land. Had the seller said nothing, the buyer would have received all the palm trees automatically. But by saying *ara ve'diklei* — "land and palm trees" — the seller may have inadvertently reduced what the buyer receives. The use of the conjunctive *vav*, which treats the palm trees as a separate item alongside the land rather than as an integral part of it, may signal that only some palm trees are being conveyed, not all.

This reading inverts the intuition. Saying more — specifying the palm trees explicitly — actually grants the buyer less than silence would have. *Tosafot* contrasts this with the earlier formula *diklin ve'talin ve'hutzin ve'tzitzin* and suggests the determinative factor may be the use of *vav* rather than *beis*, treating the elements as separate rather than integrated.

### Ara B'Diklei

The *Gemara* then addresses the formula *ara b'diklei* — "land with its palm trees." Here the preposition *beis* indicates that the palm trees are integrated within the land being sold. The *Gemara* rules: *chazinan* — if there are indeed palm trees in the land, the buyer receives them; nothing is added beyond what the default rule would have provided, but the explicit statement confirms it. If, however, there turn out to be no palm trees in the land, this constitutes a *mekach ta'ut* — a defective transaction. The seller represented the land as one that has palm trees, and the buyer received something materially different from what was described.

The *Rashbam* notes that the issue is not one of overcharging, since the principle of *ein ona'ah b'karka'ot* — that the laws of overreaching (*ona'ah*) do not apply to real estate transactions — would normally protect a seller from claims of overpayment. Rather, the claim here is qualitative misrepresentation: the buyer was promised a field *with palm trees* and received a field without them. That is a *mekach ta'ut* regardless of the financial magnitude.

---

## Palm Tree Scenarios

### Scenario One

The first scenario revisits *ara b'diklei* — "land with its palm trees." This is the clearest case of seller representation. The seller has described the land as possessing palm trees, and if palm trees are present, the buyer receives a full conveyance. If they are absent, the transaction is a *mekach ta'ut* and can be voided.

### Scenario Two

The second scenario involves the phrase *atra d'diklei* — "land that is a place fit for palm trees," a location suitable for growing palm trees. Here the seller has made no representation that palm trees actually exist on the property. He has said only that the land is capable of supporting them. Accordingly, *leit diklei* — the buyer has no claim to palm trees. And if there happen to be no palm trees on the land, it is not a *mekach ta'ut*, because the seller never promised palm trees — only suitability. As the *Rashbam* explains, *dechazi lediklei ka'amar lei* — he said it was fit for palm trees, not that there were palm trees. The buyer cannot complain.

### Scenario Three

The third scenario is the most striking. The deed reads: *l'bar midikla planya* — "except for that particular palm tree." The seller explicitly reserves one specific palm tree for himself. The *Gemara* asks: what does this exception tell us?

*Chazinan* — we look at what kind of tree it is. If the reserved tree is a productive, high-quality palm tree (*dikla tava hu*), then *shiurei sheyarei* — we read the language literally, and the seller simply kept that one tree for himself, perhaps out of personal attachment to a productive specimen. The rest of the field, including any other palm trees, passes to the buyer.

But if the reserved tree is a non-productive or inferior palm tree (*dikla bisha hu*), then the *Gemara* draws a remarkable inference: *kol sheken hanei* — if the seller is explicitly reserving even this poor specimen for himself, then certainly he is retaining all the good ones as well. The logic is that no one would go to the trouble of carving out an exception for a worthless tree unless it was intended as the least member of a broader category he is retaining. The explicit exception of the worst tree implies retention of all trees, including the superior ones. This is a substantial *chiddush* in the reading of contractual language.

---

## Exclusion Hierarchy

### Trees Exclusion

The *Gemara* now examines the hierarchy of terms when a seller uses the word *ilani* — trees — as an exception. If the deed states *l'bar me'ilani* — "except for the trees" — the analysis proceeds as follows. If the seller owns trees (*ilani*) in the field, the exception refers straightforwardly to those trees. The buyer receives the field minus the trees, which the seller retains.

### Category Application

But what if the seller has no ordinary trees, only palm trees (*diklei*) or grapevines (*gufnei*)? The *Gemara* establishes a hierarchy of substitution. If there are no ordinary trees but there are palm trees, we apply the word *ilani* to the palm trees — *l'bar midiklei*. If there are neither ordinary trees nor palm trees but there are grapevines, we apply the word to the grapevines — *l'bar migufnei*. The principle is that the word must have some referent, and we apply it progressively down the hierarchy until we find one.

This hierarchy is practically significant. A buyer who knows that a field contains no ordinary trees might assume the word "trees" in the exclusion clause is inoperative — and might be surprised to find the seller retaining the palm trees or even the vines.

### Palm/Vine Ambiguity

The final and most complex case: the seller has no ordinary trees but possesses both palm trees and grapevines, and the deed says *l'bar me'ilani*. To which category does the exception apply? The *Gemara* rules *l'bar migufnei* — the exception applies to the grapevines, not the palm trees. The seller retains the grapevines.

Two rationales are offered. The first is *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya*: the burden of proof rests on the one who seeks to extract from another's possession. The grapevines are presumed to be of greater value, and since the term is equally ambiguous between the two, the principle of possession (*muchzak*) favors treating the more valuable item as what the seller retained. The second rationale the *Rashbam* offers is that the word *ilan* applies more naturally to a *gefen* than to a *dekel* — that is, a grapevine is linguistically closer to the general category of "tree" than a palm tree is, since palm trees have a distinct enough identity that they are not instinctively what one thinks of when one hears *ilan*.

The *Gemara* leaves the matter at this practical ruling without elaborating further on which principle ultimately governs. What is clear is that the resolution is framed in terms of the meaning of the word itself — which referent it most naturally reaches — rather than in terms of the financial consequences or some explicit *din* of *safek*. The formal linguistic question of which term *ilan* more closely approximates thus carries operative legal weight, however formalistic the inquiry may appear.

---

---

# Bava Batra 70

## Trees vs. Saplings

### Rav's Rope Test

The daf opens on the last line of 69b with a ruling from Rav concerning a foundational definitional question that runs through the entire topic of field sales: when a seller says "I am selling you this field except for the trees," which plantings qualify as "trees" subject to the exclusion, and which are merely young saplings that pass to the buyer along with the field?

Rav's answer is formulated in terms of a practical climbing test: *kol she-oleh lo be-chevel hava yishuv* — anything that one must use a rope to climb in order to reach its fruit is considered a tree and is therefore excluded from the sale. *Kol she-eino oleh lo be-chevel lo hava yishuv* — anything that one does not need a rope to climb is not considered a tree in this sense and is not excluded.

### Yoke Bending Test

The *dayanei Gola* — the judges of the exile, identified as Shmuel and Karna — offer a different criterion at the top of 70a. Their test focuses not on the method of climbing but on the tree's structural maturity. When oxen walk through a field bearing a yoke and press up against a tree, if the yoke causes the tree to bend — *kol she-ol kovsho lo hava yishuv* — that tree is still young and pliable and is therefore not a tree subject to exclusion. If, however, the tree does not bend when pressed by the yoke — *kol she-eino ol kovsho hava yishuv* — it is a mature, firm tree and is excluded from the sale.

### No Dispute

The *gemara* resolves any apparent tension between these two positions by noting that *velo pligi* — they do not actually disagree. The two standards apply to different species. The rope test (*Rav's* criterion) applies to palm trees, which are tall and thin, lack climbable branches, and require a rope to ascend; there, the relevant question is whether a rope is needed. The yoke-bending test (the *dayanei Gola's* criterion) applies to other trees, which are not typically climbed by rope, and for those the standard is whether the trunk is firm enough to resist the pressure of a passing yoke. Once the cases are distinguished by species, the two rulings are entirely compatible.

---

## Carob/Sycamore Logic

### Exclude One → Sell Rest?

The *gemara* now turns to a related but distinct question posed by Rav Acha bar Huna to Rav Sheshet. The background is the principle established earlier in the *masechta* that when one sells a field, older carob trees and sycamore trees (*sadan*) are not included in the sale — they are treated, by virtue of their size and independent economic significance, almost as separate entities within the field rather than as ordinary components of it.

Given this, the question is: *chutz mi-charuv ploni chutz mi-sadon ploni mahu* — what is the law if the seller explicitly says "except for that carob tree" or "except for that sycamore tree"? The seller has named a specific tree he is retaining. Does this explicit exclusion of one tree implicitly convey all the other carob and sycamore trees to the buyer? The argument in favor of such a reading is intuitive: the seller went out of his way to carve out one tree, which seems to imply he is selling everything else. Is it possible, then, that the seller's very attempt to protect his interests actually weakens his position and grants the buyer more than he would otherwise have received?

The *Rashbam* notes that there are reasons a seller might name a particular tree even if he does not intend to surrender the others — for instance, he may simply not have known the governing *halakha* — and perhaps the language would even be read generously to preserve his right of access to the named tree. But the dilemma stands: could the explicit exclusion of one thing be read as an implicit inclusion of others?

### Rav Sheshet: No

Rav Sheshet answers directly: *lo kana* — the buyer does not acquire the other trees. The seller's naming of one carob tree does not weaken his position with respect to the others.

### Braita Ambiguity

A *braita* is then cited that seems to address this very case. The *braita* states that if a seller says "except for this carob tree" or "except for this sycamore tree," the buyer *lo kana* — does not acquire. The language of the *braita*, however, is strikingly ambiguous: does *lo kana* mean the buyer does not acquire that one named tree, implying he does acquire the rest? Or does it mean he does not acquire any of the carob or sycamore trees? The text, taken on its face, would seem to support the former reading — after all, the subject of the *braita* is the one named tree, and it says the buyer does not acquire it, leaving the others unaddressed.

Rav Sheshet, however, reads the *braita* as confirming his position: *afilu shar charuvim nami lo kana* — even the other carob trees the buyer does not acquire. He acknowledges that the textual formulation is awkward, but maintains that his reading is correct — and he turns immediately to logic rather than to the text to substantiate the claim.

### Field Analogy

The proof Rav Sheshet offers is elegant. Suppose I own several contiguous fields — call them A, B, C, D, and E — and I am selling you field A. If I say "I am selling you field A, but not field B," would anyone think that this exclusion of field B somehow conveys to the buyer fields C, D, and E, which were never on the table to begin with? Obviously not. The sale concerns field A alone. The other fields are entirely separate and independent entities; explicitly naming one of them as excluded in no way draws the others into the transaction.

The logic translates directly to carob and sycamore trees. The very reason these trees are not included in a standard field sale is that they are conceptualized as entities unto themselves — functionally equivalent to independent fields embedded within the larger parcel. Once we accept that conceptual framework, it follows necessarily that excluding one carob tree cannot implicitly convey the others: they are each separate and are each independently outside the scope of the sale. *Hachi nami lo kana* — here too the buyer acquires nothing.

### Half-Tree Question

The *gemara* then presents an alternative formulation of the question that was posed to Rav Sheshet — one in which the first version (the exclusion of a whole named tree) is taken as already resolved, and the genuinely contested question involves something more subtle.

What if the seller says *chutz mi-chatzi charuv ploni* — "except for half of this carob tree"? Here the intuitive pull toward the buyer's position is considerably stronger. When a seller explicitly retains half of something, it seems natural to infer that he is selling the other half. Does the half-exclusion language implicitly convey the remaining half of that specific tree to the buyer?

Rav Sheshet's answer from the earlier version already makes clear that *she'ar charuvim vadai lo kana* — the other carob trees are entirely out of the picture, separate fields by definition, and nothing the seller says could draw them in. But *ha mah she-shiyer be'oto charuv kani* — what about the remaining half of the one tree he named? Is the buyer acquiring that half?

Or do we say *afilu mah she-shiyer be'oto charuv nami lo kani* — even that remaining half the buyer does not acquire? This would mean that even within the boundaries of the single named tree, the seller's language of "half-exclusion" does not operate as an implicit conveyance of the other half, because the entire tree — in all its parts — is conceptually exterior to the field sale.

### Half-Tree Answer

Rav Sheshet is entirely consistent. *Lo kani* — the buyer does not acquire even the other half of the named tree. The *braita* cited in support of this version states that when a seller says "except for half of this carob tree or this sycamore," the buyer does not acquire any of the other trees — to which Rav Sheshet adds that he does not acquire the remaining half of the named tree either. Once again the *braita*'s language points toward the other conclusion, since it singles out the *other* trees as the ones not acquired, seemingly implying the remaining half of the named tree is acquired. Rav Sheshet again overrides the textual implication with his logical framework.

The confirmatory proof is identical in structure to the earlier one. If I say "I am selling you field A, but not half of field B," does that mean I am selling you the other half of field B? Plainly not. Field B is extraneous to the sale of field A entirely. Saying something — however peculiar — about half of it does not draw any part of it into the transaction. *Hacha nami lo kani* — the same is true of the half-named carob tree. Rav Sheshet's position is that the carob and sycamore trees are so thoroughly exterior to the field sale that no formulation of exclusionary language, whether of a whole tree or half a tree, can serve as an implicit vehicle for conveying any portion of them to the buyer.

---

## Deposit vs. Document

### Deposit Claim

A new case is introduced, brought by Rav Amram who poses a question to Rav Chisda. The connection to what precedes it is the upcoming mention of *dayanei Gola*, which appeared earlier in the daf. The case itself is entirely distinct.

Someone deposits an object with a guardian — a *shomer* — and to prevent any future denial, they draw up a *shtar* documenting that Reuven received a pouch of a hundred gold coins from Dov to watch on such-and-such a date, signed by witnesses, held by the depositor. Now Dov returns to collect his deposit. Reuven does not deny receiving it — he cannot, given the *shtar* — but says: *hechzarti lach* — I already returned it to you.

Can Reuven be believed?

The case for believing him is built on *migo*. A *shomer chinam* who claims that an accident (*ones*) befell the object is believed and is exempt — he need only take the standard *shvuat ha-shomrim*, the oath that accompanies a *shomer*'s claim, to be released from liability. A *shomer sachar* is similarly exempt from events of genuine force majeure. So Reuven could have said *ne'ensu* — an accident occurred — and been believed. Since that alternative claim, which would have been equally exculpatory and equally difficult to disprove, was available to him, the *migo* principle would seem to lend credibility to his actual claim of *hechzarti*.

The counterargument is equally forceful: *shtarcha b'yadi mai ba'ei* — if you really returned the deposit, why am I still holding the *shtar*? When a debt or obligation is discharged, the document evidencing that obligation is returned to the obligor or destroyed. The continued presence of the *shtar* in Dov's hands constitutes what the *Rashbam* characterizes as a *migo be-makom edim* — the *migo* argument runs up against something that functions as affirmative evidence that the return never happened. The depositor's retention of the *shtar* is effectively testimony that nothing was returned.

One might press back: perhaps Reuven did return the deposit but Dov did not yet have the *shtar* readily available, and Reuven accepted the arrangement informally. The *Rashbam* acknowledges this possibility, which is precisely why the question is genuinely difficult. Is the *shtar*'s continued presence in Dov's hands truly the equivalent of *edim* — witnesses — or merely a presumption that can be overcome?

An important distinction must be noted. This case concerns a *pikadon*, not a loan. In a loan case, the *migo* from *ne'ensu* does not exist: *ones* provides no exemption to a borrower, who bears absolute liability for the principal regardless of what happens to it. Since the *ne'ensu* claim would be worthless in a loan context, there is no *migo*, and the borrower cannot be believed to say he repaid it against a held *shtar*. The *pikadon* case is different precisely because *ne'ensu* is a viable and credible claim for the *shomer*, which is what generates the *migo* in the first place.

### Rav Chisda: Migo

Rav Chisda rules that Reuven is believed — *meheman*. The *migo* is operative even against the held *shtar*. The counterargument that it is *migo be-makom edim* is apparently not accepted, at least not as a categorical bar to belief.

The *gemara* presses back: but why should he be believed? The depositor is holding the *shtar* — what is it doing in his hand if the deposit was returned? This seems to restate the original objection. Rav Chisda responds: but consider what happens when someone says *ne'ensu*. In that case too, the depositor is still holding the *shtar*, yet we do not say the *shtar*'s presence disproves the *ne'ensu* claim. The claim of *ne'ensu* is fully believed notwithstanding the *shtar*. By the same token — and this is the *migo* — the claim of *hechzarti* should be equally credible.

*Tosafot* notes that this response is technically non-responsive to the *be-makom edim* objection: a claim of *ne'ensu* is entirely consistent with the depositor still holding the *shtar*, since the object was lost or stolen before any occasion to retrieve the *shtar* arose. But *hechzarti* is different — the very act of return creates an occasion to retrieve the *shtar*, and its non-retrieval seems anomalous. The *gemara* is dancing around this tension, and *Tosafot* acknowledges it.

### Oath Requirement

The *gemara* then adds precision. Even granting Rav Chisda's position, a further objection arises: when someone claims *ne'ensu*, he is believed — but only after taking a *shvua*, the *shvuat ha-shomrim*. So if we are extending that same credibility to a claim of *hechzarti* via *migo*, surely the same oath requirement applies. How can he be believed at all, and certainly without an oath?

The *gemara* clarifies: *hachi nami me'eman bi-shvua* — indeed, Reuven is believed only upon taking a *shvua*, just as he would swear in the *ne'ensu* scenario. When Rav Chisda said "he is believed," he meant believed with an oath. The deposit is considered returned, and Reuven is released from liability, but only after swearing that he did in fact return it. *Tosafot* notes that this was the precise concern that the *gemara*'s earlier objection was driving at — not primarily the *be-makom edim* point, but the apparent circumvention of the oath requirement.

---

## Iska & Orphans

### Iska Mechanics

The *gemara* now transitions to a new case that brings together the themes of *pikadon*, the credibility of the claim of return, and the special evidentiary rules that apply when dealing with orphans. The connecting thread back to the earlier part of the daf is that *dayanei Gola* reappear here in a distinct context.

The case involves a *shtar kis* — literally a "pocket document," a document drawn up in connection with an *iska*, a commercial investment arrangement. The economics of an *iska* require some background.

One party has capital and another has the business acumen or contacts to invest it. They enter an arrangement: the capitalist gives his money to the investor, and they share in the profits. If the capitalist bears all the risk of loss — since the money is his — the arrangement is financially straightforward. But if they wish to share the downside risk as well, a more complex structure is required: half of the money is treated as a loan to the investor, and half is treated as a *pikadon* — a deposit entrusted to the investor to work with. The loan half is the investor's obligation to repay regardless of the investment's performance; the *pikadon* half is invested on behalf of the capitalist, whose money it remains, meaning any loss on that half is borne by the capitalist himself.

To illustrate: the capitalist gives a hundred dollars. Fifty is a loan; fifty is a *pikadon*. If the investment doubles to two hundred dollars, the profit is split: each party gains fifty. If the investment falls to fifty dollars, the loan half has lost twenty-five for the investor (who must still repay the original fifty), and the *pikadon* half has lost twenty-five for the capitalist. The capitalist ends up with seventy-five — recovering the fifty-dollar loan in full from the investor and receiving twenty-five dollars as the residual value of his *pikadon* half.

This structure is the classic *heter iska*, the permissible investment framework. There are also issues of *ribis* — prohibited interest — that arise from this arrangement, since the investor is generating profit from the capitalist's *pikadon* half in exchange, effectively, for having received the loan half. Various technical adjustments are made to address this, as discussed in Bava Metzia, but the essential point here is the split structure: half loan, half *pikadon*. This is the ruling of *Nehardei*, and the *gemara* notes that it is universally accepted: *dikuli alma is lehu di-Nehardei* — everyone accepts the Nehardean position that an *iska* is half loan and half *pikadon*.

### Tannaim Debate

The *shtar kis* case involves this *iska* document being brought against orphans after the father — the investor — has died. The capitalist comes to collect his principal. He holds the *shtar*. The orphans do not know whether their father paid back the *pikadon* half.

A *braita* records a dispute between the *dayanei Gola* — Shmuel and Karna — and the *dayanei Eretz Yisrael*. The *dayanei Gola* say *nishba ve-goveh kulo* — the creditor takes an oath and collects the entire principal, both the loan half and the *pikadon* half. The *dayanei Eretz Yisrael* say *nishba ve-goveh mechtza* — the creditor takes an oath and collects only half, recovering only the loan portion and not the *pikadon* portion.

The *gemara* initially suggests that this dispute might map onto the earlier debate about whether a depositary is believed to say *hechzarti* against a held *shtar*: perhaps *dayanei Gola* hold that a *shomer* would not be believed to claim *hechzarti* even with a *migo*, and therefore the orphans cannot make that claim on their father's behalf; while *dayanei Eretz Yisrael* hold that the father would have been believed, and therefore the claim is made on behalf of the orphans.

### Orphan Exception

The *gemara* rejects this mapping. Everyone — including *dayanei Gola* — actually accepts Rav Chisda's ruling that a *shomer* is believed to claim *hechzarti* with a *migo*. The dispute is not about whether the father, were he alive, would be believed. He would be believed by all. The dispute is specific to the case of orphans.

### Father's Silence

The argument for *dayanei Gola* — that the creditor collects the full amount — rests on the following reasoning: *im ita de-parei meimar hava amar* — if the father had actually returned the *pikadon* half to the creditor, he would certainly have told his children. A father who knows that he returned a substantial sum and that the creditor still holds a *shtar* creating apparent liability would not leave his heirs in ignorance. He would have made a point of informing them so they could defend against any future claim. The fact that the orphans arrive knowing nothing of any such return is therefore itself evidential: the father's silence to them indicates that no return took place. The claim of *hechzarti* cannot be made on the orphans' behalf, because the circumstances that would have prevailed had it truly been returned make the orphans' ignorance essentially impossible.

The *dayanei Eretz Yisrael* — who permit collection of only half — counter with: *amar malach ha-maves hu de-ansei* — perhaps the angel of death is what prevented him. Perhaps the father died suddenly, without opportunity to inform his children. Or perhaps he was preoccupied with his illness and dying and simply did not manage to convey the relevant information in time. In this view, the father's failure to tell the children does not eliminate the possibility that the *pikadon* was returned; we therefore remain willing to make the claim of return on the orphans' behalf, which shields the *pikadon* half from collection.

It is worth noting that the *gemara* does not consider making the alternative claim of *ne'ensu* on behalf of the orphans — arguing that some accident befell the *pikadon* — even though everyone agrees the father would have been believed on such a claim. *Tosafot* explains: we do not make claims on behalf of orphans regarding events that are not *shchiach*, not commonly occurring. An accidental loss of a deposit is sufficiently uncommon that we will not proactively assert it on orphans' behalf as a basis for exempting the creditor.

### Halakha: Half Collection

The *gemara* now draws together the strands and arrives at a halakhic conclusion. Rav Huna bar Avin formulates a summary: in the case of a *pikadon* with a *shtar*, where the depositary claims *hechzarti*, he is believed (*ne'eman*) — understood as believed with a *shvua*, as established above. But in the *iska* case brought against orphans — *shtra ki hai yatmei* — the creditor takes an oath and collects the full amount. The *gemara* challenges this apparent inconsistency: if a depositary is believed against a *shtar* to say he returned it, why can't we make that same claim for the orphans regarding the *pikadon* half, thus blocking the full collection? The *gemara* answers: *shani hasam* — that case is different, precisely for the reason articulated: had the father truly returned the deposit while the creditor held a *shtar*, he would have told his children. Their ignorance defeats the claim.

Rava rules: *hilchesa kidayanei Gola, nishba ve-goveh mechtza* — the *halakha* follows the *dayanei Gola*, and the creditor takes an oath and collects half. Mar Zutra then states: *hilchesa kidayanei Gola* — we rule like the *dayanei Gola*. Ravina challenges Mar Zutra: but Rava explicitly said the creditor collects *mechtza* — half — while the *dayanei Gola* in the *braita* said he collects the full amount! Mar Zutra responds: *anan de-dayanei Gola ipcha masninan lah* — our version of the *braita* has the positions reversed. In our tradition, it is the *dayanei Gola* who say *nishba ve-goveh mechtza*, and the *dayanei Eretz Yisrael* who say he collects the full amount. Everyone is in agreement, then, that the *halakha* is *nishba ve-goveh mechtza* — the creditor takes an oath and collects half.

The *gemara* thus concludes on a harmonious note. The depositary is believed — with a *migo* and a *shvua* — to claim that he returned a *pikadon*, even against a held *shtar*; the continued presence of the *shtar* does not rise to the level of *makom edim*. The orphan case is an exception: because a father who had genuinely returned the *pikadon* would have ensured his children knew of it, their ignorance undercuts the claim of return, and the creditor collects the loan half of the *iska* in full. The *pikadon* half he cannot collect, the claim of return being preempted by the father's silence, and the *halakha* accordingly is that he swears and collects half.

# Bava Batra 71

## Wells & Structures

### Excluded Items

The *daf* opens with a *Mishna* that will sound familiar, as it has been quoted before: when one sells a field, certain items within it are not included in the sale. The *Mishna* enumerates that one does not sell *velo et habor* — the wells in the field — *velo et hagat* — the oil press — and *velo et hashovach* — the pigeon coop — *bein charevin bein yushuvin*, whether these structures are currently in operation or lying desolate and empty. This applies even though such items are, presumably, essential components of a working field. The *bor* is perhaps the most striking example: one can imagine purchasing an entire wheat field and discovering that the wells necessary for irrigation are not included in the transaction.

A further question lurks here: are these excluded items in the same category as the *charuv hamurkav* and *sadan hashikma* — the grafted carob and the trimmed sycamore — which are treated as a conceptually independent field? In other words, does the exclusion of the well and pigeon coop apply only when the seller has not used the language *kol mah shebetochah* ("everything within it"), or does it apply even when such language was explicitly employed? The *Mishna* does not make this fully explicit, and the *Rashbam* will clarify the point below.

### Access Rights Debate

The *Mishna* continues: *vetzarich likach lo derech* — the seller, having retained ownership of the well, must nonetheless acquire separate access rights in order to reach it. He owns the well but has no right of passage through the buyer's field to get to it. This, says the *Mishna*, is the position of Rabbi Akiva — *divrei Rabbi Akiva*. His reasoning, as the *Rashbam* makes clear, is not that generosity (*be'ayin yaffah*) compels one to give the well to the buyer. Rather, it is the opposite application of the same principle: what the seller *did* sell, he sold fully and generously. Having conveyed the field to the buyer, he does not also retain an access path through it to his retained well.
