The Sages, however — *vachachamim omrim einu tzarich* — hold that the seller need not separately acquire access; just as he withheld the well, he implicitly withheld the access path as well. The buyer has the land; the seller retains access.

The *Mishna* adds that Rabbi Akiva concedes one case: *umodeh Rabbi Akiva bizman she'amar lo chutz me'eilu* — if the seller explicitly stated "I am selling you everything *except* for the well," the use of that explicit exclusionary language indicates that he was also retaining access rights. Since he need not have said "except for the well" — the well would not have been sold by default — the fact that he chose to articulate the exclusion signals that he is retaining more than just the physical well; he is retaining the full complex of rights including access.

### Well Sold, Field Retained

The *Mishna* then presents the mirror case: *macharan le'acher* — the seller retains the field and sells the well to someone else. Rabbi Akiva says *einu tzarich likach lo derech*: the buyer of the well does not need to separately acquire access rights, because *be'ayin yaffah hu mocher* — the seller sells generously. This case is necessary to state precisely because one might have supposed that the Sages' position reflected not a *be'ayin yaffah* versus *be'ayin ra'ah* (generous versus narrow eye) framework, but rather a rule that access always travels with the well — whether one keeps the well and keeps access, or sells the well and conveys access. The *Mishna* disabuses us of that reading. The Sages — *vachachamim omrim tzarich likach lo derech* — say that even when the well is sold, the buyer does not automatically receive access rights; he must acquire them separately. The structure, then, is symmetric: Rabbi Akiva consistently favors the buyer and the Sages consistently favor the seller.

### Bein Rah Principle

The *Mishna* then delimits where all of the foregoing applies: *bameh devarim amurim bemocher* — this debate about withholding or granting rights operates in the context of a sale, where the assumption is *be'ayin ra'ah mocher*, the seller acts with a narrow eye, keeping as much as possible. *Aval benoten matanah* — but when one gives a gift, *noten et kullah* — one gives the whole thing, including, according to the Sages, the access rights as well.

### Gift Inclusion

The *Rashbam* broadens this principle considerably. He explains that the *bameh devarim amurim* qualification — that the restrictive rules apply only to a sale — extends beyond the question of access rights to the very question of which physical objects are included. The *Rashbam* identifies three categories of items in relation to a field sale. The first category is items that are routinely included in a sale by default: certain types of stones, wood, and harvested grain already present. The second category consists of items not normally included but that pass if the seller uses the phrase *kol mah shebetochah* — "everything within it." The third category — the most counterintuitive — contains items so conceptually distinct from the field that even the formula *kol mah shebetochah* does not capture them: the grafted carob, the trimmed sycamore, the well, the pigeon coop. These are treated as a virtually independent field and resist transfer even under the broadest conventional language.

And yet the *Rashbam* argues — noting that the point is borne out by the subsequent discussion of *hekdesh* — that even this third category is included when the conveyance takes the form of a *matanah*, a gift. The rationale, as he phrases it, is *denotayn be'ayin yafah notayn yotayr midai* — the giver of a gift gives excessively generously. Although the carob and sycamore are conceptually a separate field, they are nonetheless physically located within the field, and that physical connection is sufficient when the transfer is a gift.

The *Rashbam* adds one limitation: if there happens to be something in the field that has no conceptual connection to the field whatsoever — a dropped wallet, cut grain merely stored there temporarily and drawing nothing from the land — that would not be transferred even in a gift. Likewise, anything so obviously disconnected that the *Tanna* of our *Mishna* had no need to mention it as a case of "not sold" would not be included. The principle of *matanah* generosity, while broad, does not extend to items that are entirely adventitious to the field.

## Inheritance Division

### Complete Separation

The *Mishna* proceeds to the case of *haachin shechileku* — brothers who divide a field inherited from their father. The ruling is *zakhu basadeh zakhu bekulah*: when a brother takes possession of the field, he takes possession of all of it, including the well, the pigeon coop, and every other item that would ordinarily be excluded from a sale.

### Why Different

One might ask why division of an inherited estate differs from a sale between strangers. The *Rashbam* explains: *keivan sheze natul sadeh achat veze achat kenegdo histalek ze mishel ze nistaken lo* — since each brother took one portion against the other's portion, each has fully separated himself from the other. The underlying logic of *chalukah* is not a commercial transaction in which each party carefully calibrates what he is conveying; rather, it is a clean break, a complete mutual withdrawal from the shared estate, so that each brother walks away fully independent of the other. The well falls into one brother's portion not by explicit agreement but as a consequence of the fundamental premise of the division: you take that half entirely, I take this half entirely, and we are done.

This may seem counterintuitive. In a commercial sale between strangers, one expects finality — the seller takes his money and the buyer takes his field and they have nothing further to do with each other, which would seem to argue for full inclusion. And when brothers divide a *yerushah*, one might expect that the bonds of family would leave more room for ongoing shared rights. But the logic runs the other way: a commercial sale is a transaction governed by *be'ayin ra'ah*, the seller holding back as much as possible, whereas an inheritance division is premised on total, clean separation. The *Rashbam* confirms: the point of splitting an estate is precisely that each party should be able to go his own way without any residual entanglement.

A subtler question arises with access. Suppose the well falls on one brother's side of the line while the other brother needs access to the public domain through the same plot. There the *Rashbam* acknowledges that an access right might survive the division, not because the well is jointly owned, but on the separate ground that when their father was alive the entire field had free internal access, and one brother may argue he has not relinquished that inherited right of passage. That, however, is a distinct question of access, not ownership, and it is not the focus of the present *Mishna*.

## Hefker Possession

### Chazaka Possession

The *Mishna* continues: *hamachzik benichsei hager* — one who takes possession of the estate of a convert who died without heirs, whose property becomes *hefker*. The rule is *hechzik basadeh hechzik bechulah*: taking possession of the field through an act of *chazakah* acquires everything in it. This includes the very items — the well, the pigeon coop, the conceptually distinct trees — that are not transferred even by the formula *kol mah shebetochah* in an ordinary sale.

### Chazaka vs. Sales

This result is striking. We have gone to considerable lengths to establish that the carob and sycamore trees, the well, and similar items are so independent from the field that even explicit all-inclusive language fails to convey them in a sale. Yet a simple act of *chazakah* — a man digging with a shovel in one corner of a *hefker* field — acquires all of these things simultaneously. How can that be?

### Rashbam's Explanation

The *Rashbam* resolves this by drawing on a distinction already established elsewhere in the *masechta*. If a *hefker* field has a *metzar* — a boundary line physically dividing it into two portions — then a *chazakah* on one portion does not acquire the other, because the boundary line renders them conceptually separate fields; acquiring one field does not acquire a different field. However, when two fields are conceptually distinct — as with the field and the sycamore tree — but there is no physical *metzar* separating them, an act of *chazakah* on one does extend to the other. The *Rashbam* is walking a carefully calibrated line: these items are distinct enough that a sale, which transfers only what was expressly or conventionally understood to be included, does not transfer them; but they are not separated by a physical boundary, and therefore a *chazakah*, which acquires whatever is physically encompassed by the act, does extend to them. In the case of *hefker* property, the absence of a formal separating line means that a single act of *chazakah* reaches everything.

## Hekdesh & Rav Shimon

### Consecration Scope

The final clause of the *Mishna* states: *hamakdish et hasadeh hikdish et kulah* — one who consecrates his field to *hekdesh* has consecrated all of it. Just as giving a *matanah* draws on the *be'ayin yafah* principle and includes even the third category of conceptually distinct items, so too consecrating a field to the Temple treasury is treated with similar inclusiveness, on the premise that one who gives to *hekdesh* gives generously.

### Rav Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon, however, disputes this. *Hamakdish et hasadeh lo hikdish ela hacharuv hamurkav vesadan hashikma* — one who consecrates a field has consecrated *only* the grafted carob and the trimmed sycamore trees, but not the well, the pigeon coop, or the other items in the analogous category. Rabbi Shimon thus takes an intermediate position: *hekdesh* is not as broad as a *matanah*. The field itself is consecrated, and the trees are included — but the well and similar structures are not.

This immediately raises a question: Rabbi Shimon does not seem to dispute the rule regarding *matanah*. By a *matanah*, everything goes. By *hekdesh*, most of the analogous items do not go — yet the trees specifically do. Why are the trees singled out? What makes them different from the well and the pigeon coop? The *Gemara* will address this question at length below.

## Sale vs. Gift Logic

### Yehuda's Explanation

The *Gemara* now asks *mai shna mecher u'mai shna matanah* — what precisely is the difference between a sale and a gift that accounts for the dramatic difference in what is included? The obvious answer is *be'ayin yafah*, but as the *Rashbam* noted, generosity alone does not fully explain why items that are not even included under *kol mah shebetochah* should suddenly be included in a gift. The *Gemara* reports that *Yehuda bin Nakusa* explained this before *Rebbi* using the formula *zeh peireish vezeh lo peireish* — "this one explicated and this one did not explicate." This is cryptic at best. The *Gemara* immediately challenges it: *zeh lo peireish vezeh lo peireish* — in neither a sale nor a gift does either party actually spell out whether the well or the trees are included. Both cases involve an absence of explicit language. The formula explains nothing.

### Silence Principle

The *Gemara* therefore offers the correct formulation: *ela zeh haya lo lefareish vezeh lo haya lo lefareish* — in one case the party *should have* explicated, and in the other case the party was *not in a position* to explicate. *Rabbeinu Gershom* and *Rabbeinu Chananel* explain as follows. In the case of a sale, the buyer is paying good money for the field. He has every right — indeed, every practical incentive — to turn to the seller and insist on clarity: does the transaction include the well? Does it include the trees? Does it include the pigeon coop? He could have demanded that these items be specified in the *shtar*. The fact that he did not do so is on him. He *haya lo lefareish* — he was in a position to demand explication and failed to do so. We therefore cannot assume he received what he did not ask for.

### Generosity & Silence

The recipient of a gift, however, is in an entirely different position. When someone announces a generous gift, the recipient cannot respond by saying, "Wait — does this include the trees? Does this include the well? I need you to be explicit." Such a demand would be the height of ingratitude. The receiver of a gift is simply not socially or halachically in a position to push back and require the giver to enumerate and specify every component. Since the recipient *lo haya lo lefareish* — was not in a position to demand explication — the absence of explicit language on his side cannot be taken as evidence that those items were not included. When this incapacity to demand clarification is combined with the underlying principle of *be'ayin yafah noten* — that one who gives a gift gives with a generous eye — the result is that we interpret the gift as including even those items that would not pass in a sale under *kol mah shebetochah*. The two principles reinforce each other: generosity of intent on the giver's side, and the impossibility of requesting clarification on the receiver's side, together produce the expansive rule of inclusion in the case of a *matanah*.

## House Gift Case

### Barrel Capacity

The *Gemara* presents a practical application of these principles. A dying man instructed his heirs to give a particular person *beita d'machzik mea garvei* — "my house that holds a hundred barrels." When the heirs examined the one house known to belong to the deceased, they found it held not one hundred but one hundred and twenty barrels. The man apparently did not own a house of precisely one hundred barrels capacity. The question becomes: how do we interpret the instruction? Did he give nothing, since no such house exists? Did he give five-sixths of the house, corresponding to one hundred of the one hundred and twenty barrels? The case has the character of a deathbed gift, the paradigmatic context in which spoken words alone are binding.

### Generous Interpretation

*Mar Zutra* initially observes that the man said one hundred, not one hundred and twenty, seemingly limiting the gift. But *Rav Ashi* responds by citing our *Mishna*: *mi lo tnan bim'deamran bimchar aval b'noten matanah noten et kulan* — did we not learn that in cases of sale the restrictive rules apply, but in the case of a gift one gives all of it? *Alma man deyahiv matanah be'ayin yafah yahiv; hacha nami man deyahiv matanah be'ayin yafah yahiv* — the principle is that whoever gives a gift gives with a generous eye, and so here too the gift should be interpreted generously. The figure of one hundred barrels was, on this reading, approximate — the man was characterizing the house, not specifying a fractional share — and the proper interpretation is that he gave the entire house. Rav Ashi thus establishes a broader hermeneutical principle: whenever a gift can be interpreted either narrowly or generously, we interpret it in the most generous way possible.

## Sale vs. Gift Logic (II)

### Gift Annulment

It is worth noting, however, that the expansive rules governing gifts are not without a counterbalance, though the subject is not fully developed in the *Gemara* here. The principle of *devarim shebelev einam devarim* — that unexpressed conditions or assumptions ordinarily have no legal force — applies quite differently in the context of gifts than in the context of sales.

The *Gemarot* elsewhere discuss cases in which a person gave away all his property believing, for instance, that his son had died, and the gift was subsequently voided when the son turned out to be alive. Some *Rishonim* attempt to explain such rulings by arguing that the assumption in question was *belev kol adam* — obvious to everyone, not merely a private unexpressed thought. But the *Rambam* and the *Tosafot Rid* articulate a more fundamental distinction. They hold that *devarim shebelev einam devarim* is primarily a rule governing commercial transactions: in a *mecher*, where Michael is giving money and receiving something in return, any condition must be made explicit, because one party cannot fairly be bound by unstated assumptions in the other's mind to which he had no access. But a gift is a unilateral act. The recipient contributes nothing; the entire transaction flows from the giver. Because it is entirely the giver's act, his subjective frame of mind — *da'at hanoten* — carries legal weight in a way it does not in a bilateral sale. As the *Rambam* formulates it: *le'olam omdin da'at hanoten* — we always seek to assess the subjective intent of the one who gave the gift.

The result is an interesting duality. On one side, gifts are interpreted expansively and generously in favor of the recipient: more is included, the language is read broadly, and the recipient's inability to demand clarification reinforces the presumption of inclusion. On the other side, because the gift is wholly the giver's act, there are circumstances — false assumptions, conditions that turned out to be unfounded — under which the entire gift can be voided, in ways that would never apply to a completed sale. The receiver gains more, but the gift is also more vulnerable to nullification.

## Hekdesh Trees

### Trees Retained

The *Gemara* now turns to the position of *Rav Huna*, who articulates a principle that lies at the heart of the discussion of *hekdesh* and trees. The principle concerns what happens when a seller retains trees for himself while selling the surrounding land. *Rav Huna* states: *af al gav de'amur rabanan hakoneh shenei ilanot betoch shel chaveiro harei zeh lo kana karka* — even though the Sages ruled that one who *purchases* two trees within his neighbor's field does not acquire the land between or around them. Nevertheless, *machar karka veshayer shenei ilanot lefanav yesh lo karka* — if one sells his land while *retaining* ownership of two trees for himself, he does retain rights in the land. This asymmetry — buying trees does not convey land rights, but retaining trees while selling the surrounding land does — is *Rav Huna*'s core observation.

What is the scope of the land rights retained? Here the *Rashbam* and *Tosafot* diverge. The *Rashbam* understands *yesh lo karka* to mean that the seller retains full ownership of the land beneath the trees, such that if the tree dies he may replant. *Tosafot* reads the case more narrowly: the retained rights do not extend to full replanting rights, but they do include the right to keep the tree in place and to have it continue drawing nutrients from the surrounding soil, as well as rights to that plot that persist as long as the tree is standing — for instance, the right to plant a vegetable garden in the area of soil over which the tree's canopy extends. The analysis that follows in the *Gemara* fits somewhat better with *Tosafot*'s reading, and it will be taken as the operative framework here.

### Nutrients Principle

The critical question is: why should retaining a tree confer land rights, given that under Rabbi Akiva's principle of *be'ayin yafah mocher* — the seller sells generously — the seller should be conveying all rights in the land fully to the buyer, retaining only the bare tree? The answer turns on the physical reality of how a tree exists. *Aval ilanot d'kamachshei b'ara* — trees draw nutrients from the land. Unlike a well or a cistern, which sits in the ground without ongoing interaction with the surrounding soil, a tree is in a perpetual relationship with the land: its roots draw moisture and nutrients continuously. This means that retaining the tree necessarily entails retaining something in the land — namely, the right for the tree to continue drawing from it.

### Wells vs. Trees

The contrast with a well is instructive. *Hani milei gabei bor v'dos* — the rule that Rabbi Akiva's *be'ayin yafah* principle strips the retained well of access rights applies to a well or cistern. The reasoning is that the presence of a well in Michael's field does not damage Michael's field in any ongoing way. The structure is already there; it is not drawing on the land; Michael has no complaint that the retained well is injuring his property. Therefore, by selling generously, the seller conveys everything — including the access path — and retains only the well structure itself, with no access.

But a tree is different. *Im issa d'lo shiyar* — if I retain no rights in the land when I keep the tree, *leima leh akur ilanch v'zil* — Michael could demand that I uproot my tree, because my tree is actively drawing the nutrients from his land. Since ownership of the tree would be illusory without the right to have it remain in the ground and continue drawing nutrients, that right must be retained as well. Once we acknowledge that the seller necessarily retains some land rights when he keeps a tree, *Rav Huna* argues that those rights extend further — even to uses of the land under the tree's canopy, such as a vegetable garden — at least according to the *Rabbanan* who hold *be'ayin ra'ah mocher*. And as the *Gemara* will develop, the scope of those rights has implications for how we understand Rabbi Shimon's position on *hekdesh* as well.

## Rav Shimon Model

### Me'ilah Avoidance

We now return to Rabbi Shimon's ruling: *hamakdish et hasadeh lo hikdish ela hacharuv hamurkav vesadan hashikma* — one who consecrates his field has consecrated only the trees, not the well, the pigeon coop, and similar items. The *braita* cited by the *Gemara* supplies Rabbi Shimon's own reasoning: *ma ta'am — ho'il veyonkim misday hekdesh* — the reason the trees are included in the *hekdesh* is that they draw their nutrients from the *hekdesh* field. This is a decisive consideration. If I consecrate my field to *hekdesh* while retaining personal ownership of the trees, my trees would continue drawing nutrients from *hekdesh* property. That would constitute *me'ilah* — the prohibition against benefiting from *hekdesh* property — since the trees would be using the consecrated field's resources for private gain. To avoid this, we conclude that one who consecrates the field necessarily consecrates the trees along with it. One would not want to keep trees in a *hekdesh* field and thereby be continuously transgressing *me'ilah*.

The *Rashbam* also suggests an alternative formulation: since the trees draw from the *hekdesh* field, their growth is *gidulim* of *hekdesh* — produce of consecrated property — and belongs to *hekdesh*. The difficulty with this reading is that the main tree itself predates the consecration; only subsequent growth would be attributable to the *hekdesh* field. The stronger reading, then, is the first: the trees are included not because of a generosity principle, but as a practical necessity to avoid ongoing *me'ilah*.

### Retaining Tree

The *Gemara* now raises a sharp challenge to Rabbi Shimon's reasoning. If Rabbi Shimon treats *hekdesh* like *mecher* rather than like *matanah*, that means the consecrator retains ownership of things like the well and the pigeon coop. Fine. But why could he not also retain the trees? The *Gemara* proposes: let him retain the tree, and — since retaining a tree, as *Rav Huna* taught, grants him land rights in the surrounding soil — those land rights would include the right of the tree to be *yonek*, to draw nutrients from the field. This is precisely the classic case *Rav Huna* described: the seller retains the tree, therefore the tree retains the right to draw from the land. On that model, there would be no *me'ilah* problem, because the consecrator still legitimately owns the rights for his tree to draw from what is now the *hekdesh* field. Why, then, must the trees be consecrated along with the field?

### Rabbi Akiva Model

The *Gemara* resolves this by establishing that Rabbi Shimon operates according to the model of Rabbi Akiva. *Rabbi Shimon d'amar k'Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Akiva's principle of *be'ayin yafah mocher*. And under Rabbi Akiva's framework, unlike the *Rabbanan*, the seller does *not* retain land rights when he keeps a tree. The well case makes this clear: Rabbi Akiva says that retaining the well does not preserve access rights, because *be'ayin yafah mocher* — whatever was actually sold was sold fully. By the same logic, when one sells the land and retains the tree, Rabbi Akiva would say the seller does not retain rights to the land under or around the tree. The *be'ayin yafah* principle conveys the land completely, and the retained tree is left without any accompanying land rights.

This means that according to Rabbi Akiva, retaining a tree while selling the surrounding field is a somewhat precarious arrangement: the buyer of the field could, it seems, demand that the tree be uprooted, since the tree-owner retains no rights to draw on the sold soil. Rabbi Shimon, working within Rabbi Akiva's framework, therefore concludes that when one consecrates a field, one necessarily consecrates the trees as well — because under Rabbi Akiva's model, there are no retained land rights that would permit the trees to lawfully continue drawing from the now-consecrated field. The trees must go to *hekdesh* in order to avoid the tree-owner being continuously in violation of *me'ilah*.

The result is that Rabbi Shimon's position is a hybrid: like Rabbi Akiva, he holds *be'ayin yafah mocher* (or in this case, *be'ayin yafah makdish*), and unlike the view that *hekdesh* is equivalent to *matanah*, he treats *hekdesh* as equivalent to *mecher*. The field is consecrated with the generosity appropriate to a formal transfer, but without the all-inclusive scope of a *matanah*. The well, the pigeon coop, and similar items are retained — but the trees cannot be, precisely because of the *yonek* problem under Rabbi Akiva's model.

### Land Rights Chiddush

Given this analysis, the *Gemara* revisits *Rav Huna*'s original ruling. *Rav Huna* stated that when one sells the land while retaining the trees, *yesh lo karka* — he retains land rights. The *Gemara* initially notes that this seems obvious according to the *Rabbanan*, who hold *be'ayin ra'ah mocher*: if the seller withholds access to his well and retains other prerogatives, it is no surprise that retaining a tree comes with land rights. *Kerabanan peshita* — it is self-evident under the *Rabbanan*'s framework.

The *Gemara* responds: *nafka mina denafala hadar shatil lehu* — the practical novelty of *Rav Huna*'s ruling is not about the rights that exist while the tree stands, but about what happens *if* the tree falls or is uprooted. On *Tosafot*'s reading, which the *Gemara* appears to favor, the first formulation of *Rav Huna*'s principle — that the retained tree grants rights sufficient for the tree to draw nutrients and perhaps even to use the surrounding plot — may have been obvious. The *chiddush* is that according to the *Rabbanan*, the rights retained are not merely functional rights tied to the existence of that particular tree; they are genuine, lasting rights in that plot of land, such that even if the tree dies the owner retains the right to replant. The seller does not merely have a license that expires with the tree; he holds real property rights in perpetuity over that area. That is *Rav Huna*'s true novelty, and it is what distinguishes his ruling from a straightforward application of *be'ayin ra'ah mocher*.

---

---

# Bava Batra 72

## Rav Huna on Trees

### Rav Huna's Claim

Today's daf is a continuation of 72a, the final daf of the *perek*, picking up from yesterday's discussion. Rav Huna established that even though when one sells trees the land does not accompany them, if one *retains* ownership of trees, one retains ownership of the land beneath them. The precise meaning of this "ownership" is itself disputed. The Rashbam understands it as literal ownership of the underlying plot. Tosafot, by contrast, argues that it means something more limited: not that the seller permanently owns the soil, but that while the tree stands, he possesses sufficient rights over the ground to draw on its nutrients — and even to plant beneath it. Should the tree die, those rights expire.

### Be'ayin Ra'ah vs Yafah

The further question is whether Rav Huna's principle operates according to the Rabbanan, who hold *mocher be'ayin ra'ah* — that a seller transfers with a stingy eye — or even according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds *mocher be'ayin yafah*, that a seller transfers with a generous eye. According to the Rabbanan, the seller keeps as much as possible, so it is straightforward that retaining a tree means retaining the land beneath it, just as retaining a well means retaining the path to it. The more striking claim is that even according to Rabbi Akiva, who in principle would have the seller give away more, the retention of the tree still preserves the underlying land — because the right to draw nutrients from the soil is a practical necessity, and once that right exists by necessity, it crystallizes into full ownership or planting rights in the manner Rabbi Akiva would recognize.

---

## Mishnah Challenge

### Hekdesh & Field

The Gemara then attempts to challenge Rav Huna from a *mishnah*. The case involves one who is *makdish sadeh* — who sanctifies a field. According to Rabbi Shimon, when one sanctifies a field, the *hekdesh* does not receive the pigeon coop or the well, unlike in the case of a *matanah* where those items would transfer. However, *hekdesh* does receive the trees growing in the field.

### R. Shimon Position

Why does *hekdesh* receive the trees? The Gemara explains: since the tree is drawing its nutrients from the field of *hekdesh*, one cannot maintain private ownership of a tree that grows from sanctified land without incurring inappropriate benefit from *hekdesh*. Therefore, once the field is given to *hekdesh*, the tree follows.

The challenge to Rav Huna is now apparent: if retaining a tree means retaining the underlying land, then when the owner sanctifies the field but *retains* the tree for himself, he should retain rights to the ground beneath it — and if he retains the ground, there would be no problem of drawing from *hekdesh* land. Yet Rabbi Shimon rules that the tree *does* become *kodesh*, implying that retaining the tree does not preserve the underlying land.

### Rav Huna Limited

The Gemara resolves this by limiting Rav Huna's statement: it applies only according to the Rabbanan, who hold *be'ayin ra'ah*, and therefore when one retains a tree one retains the ground beneath. But it does not apply according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds *be'ayin yafah*. Since Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Akiva's position — under which even retaining the tree does not preserve the ground — the field passes entirely to *hekdesh*, and the tree, rooted in *hekdesh* land, necessarily becomes *kodesh* as well.

---

## R. Shimon Follow R. Akiva

### Contradiction Posed

At this point the Gemara asks a sharp question: how can one say that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Akiva? Rabbi Akiva was Rabbi Shimon's own *rebbi* — stam "Rabbi Shimon" in the Talmud refers to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, one of the *talmidei Rabbi Akiva*. For a student to follow his teacher is unremarkable and requires no comment. But the Gemara suggests this attribution is actually problematic, and introduces a *baraita* to press the point.

### Baraita on Distribution

The *baraita* states: if one sanctifies three trees that are distributed at the density of ten trees per *beis se'ah* — *hikdish shalosh ilanos mimatu asara l'beis se'ah* — then *hekdesh* receives not only the trees but the land between them and the smaller trees growing among them.

### Distribution Rules

The *beis se'ah* measures fifty *amah* by fifty *amah*, which is twenty-five hundred square *amos*. Ten trees properly distributed across a *beis se'ah* means each tree occupies a space of approximately two hundred and fifty square *amos*. This density is considered the ideal spacing: not so crowded that trees must be uprooted, and not so dispersed that they cannot be regarded as constituting a coherent grove. Three trees that are spaced at this density — meaning each occupies roughly two hundred and fifty square *amos* — together constitute what is treated as a field of trees, and the land between them is implicitly included in the sanctification.

The mention of smaller trees among them (*ilanot shebeineihem*) raises an apparent difficulty: if there are additional trees, does that not disrupt the proper distribution? Tosafot resolve this by explaining that the additional trees are non-fruit-bearing (*ilanot srak*), and since they do not produce fruit they are considered destined for uprooting and are therefore not counted when assessing the spacing of the significant trees.

The upshot is that when three trees of the proper distribution are sanctified, *hekdesh* receives the trees, the land between them, and any small trees growing in between.

### Improper Distribution

If, however, the trees are too condensed or too dispersed — so that they do not fall within the proper density — the field does not accompany them. Similarly, if one sanctified the trees individually, one by one rather than as a unit of three, the land does not transfer. In both such cases, *harei zeh lo hikdish lo et hakarka v'lo et ha'ilanot shebeineihem*: *hekdesh* receives only the three trees themselves, not the land and not the smaller trees between them.

---

## Redemption Values

### Fixed vs Market

The *baraita* continues to address what happens when one comes to redeem the sanctified property. Here the key distinction is between the fixed Torah rate and market rate.

When a *sdeh achuzah* — an ancestral field — is sanctified as a single unit, the Torah sets a fixed redemption price: fifty *shekel kesef* per *chomer beis se'orim* for a field sanctified at the outset of a *yovel* cycle, prorated for the years remaining to *yovel*. This fixed rate applies when the field and its contents are treated as one unit.

When the trees and field are sanctified as separate units — whether because the trees were too condensed or dispersed, or because they were sanctified individually — then redemption proceeds separately: the trees are redeemed at their market value, and the field, if later sanctified independently, is redeemed at the Torah's fixed rate. The *baraita* further adds: even if one first sanctified the trees individually and then went back and sanctified the field — *hikdish et ha'ilanot v'chazar v'hikdish et hakarka* — they remain two conceptually distinct items. The trees are redeemed at market price and the field at the Torah's fixed rate. This is the *chiddush*: even though physically the setup might be identical to a properly sanctified grove, the sequence of sanctification determines the conceptual units, and two separate acts of *hekdesh* produce two separate redemptions.

One might ask: when the whole is redeemed as a unit under the fixed rate, does one pay anything extra for the trees? No — the Torah's fixed rate applies to the field as a whole, and the trees are subsumed within it. It is only when the trees are redeemed separately that their market value is assessed independently, potentially adding to the total cost. Whether the combined total of fixed rate plus market rate is more or less than the fixed rate alone depends on the quality of the land and the condition of the market.

### Who Is the Baraita

The Gemara now asks: whose position does this *baraita* represent? If it is Rabbi Akiva — *hamocher be'ayin yafah mocher, vechol shekein makdish* — then when one sanctifies even a single tree, one would expect some portion of the underlying land to accompany it, since even in a sale, generosity requires giving the buyer access to what he needs. Yet the *baraita*, at least on the Rashbam's reading, seems to assume that when trees are sanctified individually, no land whatsoever accompanies them. That cannot be Rabbi Akiva.

If it is the Rabbanan, a different difficulty arises. The Rabbanan hold that while a seller acts with a stingy eye — *mocher be'ayin ra'ah* — one who gives a *matanah* or who is *makdish* acts with a generous eye. The Rabbanan in the *mishnah* say explicitly that *makdish be'ayin yafah makdish* — *hekdesh* receives everything. But this *baraita* treats *hekdesh* as receiving nothing beyond the trees when they are sanctified individually. That also cannot fit the standard Rabbanan position.

The Gemara concludes: *ela peshita Rabbi Shimon hi* — it must be Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Shimon holds that *makdish* is like *mocher*, not like *matanah* — *hekdesh* receives only what is explicitly given. Now the secondary question arises: Rabbi Shimon's *mocher* — is it *be'ayin yafah* like Rabbi Akiva, or *be'ayin ra'ah* like the Rabbanan? If it were *be'ayin yafah*, then even *hekdesh* would receive some land together with the tree. Since the *baraita* assumes no land accompanies an individually sanctified tree, it must be that this is Rabbi Shimon following the Rabbanan's stingy model: *makdish* is like *mocher*, and *mocher* is *be'ayin ra'ah*.

---

## R. Shimon Stingy

### Proof R. Shimon

Having established that the *baraita* follows Rabbi Shimon operating *aliba de'Rabbanan* — with the stingy eye — the Gemara now draws the implications. According to this model, when one gives *hekdesh* a tree, one gives only the tree: no land accompanies it. Equivalently, when one retains a tree for oneself and gives *hekdesh* the field, one certainly retains the ground beneath the tree, since on the stingy model one never cedes more than explicitly given.

### Contradiction Stated

This creates a new problem. If Rabbi Shimon holds that one retains the land beneath a retained tree — consistent with Rav Huna's principle as applied to the Rabbanan — then when one sanctifies the field and retains the tree, the ground under the tree also remains in private hands. But then why does the Mishnah's Rabbi Shimon say that the tree becomes *kodesh*? The Gemara's earlier explanation was that the tree becomes *kodesh* because it draws nutrients from *hekdesh* land — *yonkim mis'deh hekdesh*. But if the land under the tree still belongs to the owner, the tree is not drawing from *hekdesh* land at all. The problem has apparently come full circle.

There are two distinct sub-questions here that must be kept separate. The first is whether *hekdesh* operates like *matanah* (generous) or like *mecher* (limited in scope). The second is, within the framework of *mecher*, whether it operates *be'ayin yafah* like Rabbi Akiva or *be'ayin ra'ah* like the Rabbanan. Rabbi Shimon says *hekdesh* is like *mecher*, not *matanah* — that is his distinctive position. But within *mecher* we have now shown he must follow the Rabbanan's stingy model. The tension is: if even in that stingy model retaining the tree preserves the land, why does Rabbi Shimon's Mishnah allow the tree to become *kodesh*?

### R. Shimon Resolution

The Gemara resolves the difficulty with a crucial distinction: *Rabbi Shimon l'divreihem de'Rabbanan ka-amar lehu* — Rabbi Shimon in the Mishnah is not stating his own position when he gives the reason about drawing nutrients from *hekdesh* land. He is arguing *within the logic of the Rabbanan*.

Rabbi Shimon's own view is as follows: *l'didi* — as far as I am concerned — just as selling is stingy, *hekdesh* is also stingy. Therefore, when you sanctify the field, you retain rights to the land under the tree, and since you retain the land, the tree remains in your private domain and does not become *kodesh* at all. That is Rabbi Shimon's genuine position: even the tree would not transfer to *hekdesh*.

But then why does the Mishnah present Rabbi Shimon as saying the tree *does* become *kodesh*? Because Rabbi Shimon is addressing the Rabbanan on their own terms: *l'didchu* — according to you, who say that *hekdesh* and *matanah* are generous, you would say that even the well and the pigeon coop transfer to *hekdesh*. Concede to me at least — *odu li mi'at* — that the specifically named items like the *charuva hamurkav* and *sadan hashikma* do not transfer, because those are so distinct as to constitute separate plots of land. And he is willing, in arguing with the Rabbanan, to say that on their generous model the tree would become *kodesh* because of the logic of drawing from *hekdesh* land.

The Rabbanan respond: *lo shna* — we draw no distinction. On our generous model, *hekdesh* receives everything — just as a full *matanah* would include everything in the field.

The ultimate implication for Rav Huna's principle is thus preserved: according to the Rabbanan's model applied to *mecher*, retaining a tree retains the land beneath it. Rabbi Shimon's own view affirms the same. What the Mishnah presents as Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is his dialectical engagement with the Rabbanan's framework, not his personal holding.

---

## Redemption vs Sanctify

### Two-Stage Problem

A further difficulty now emerges against the identification of the *baraita* as Rabbi Shimon. The *baraita* treats the two-stage sanctification — trees first, field second — as producing two separate redemptions, each governed by its own valuation method. But there is a well-known principle associated with Rabbi Shimon: *batar pidyon azil* — he follows the time of redemption, not the time of sanctification. If Rabbi Shimon assesses the status of sanctified property at the moment of *pidyon*, then even when trees and field were sanctified at different times, at the moment of redemption one faces a unified field with trees. That should be treated as one unit and redeemed at the single fixed Torah rate, not as two separate units with two separate redemption schemes.

### Baraita Scenario

To demonstrate that Rabbi Shimon indeed follows the time of redemption, the Gemara cites another *baraita*. The case: Reuven purchases a field from his father Yaakov. He then sanctifies it. After the sanctification, Yaakov dies.

At the time Reuven sanctified the field, it was a *sdeh miknah* — a purchased field. It was not his ancestral field. Had Yaakov been alive when *yovel* arrived, the field would have reverted to Yaakov, since Reuven's purchase only granted him rights for the duration until *yovel*. In technical terms, Reuven held a *kinyan peiros* — usufruct rights — for those years, not full title. One who sanctifies a *sdeh miknah* redeems it at market rate, not at the Torah's fixed rate. Yet after Yaakov dies, Reuven inherits the field — had he not already purchased it, it would have come to him as a *sdeh achuzah*.

### R. Yehuda R. Shimon

Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon rule: since at the time Reuven comes to redeem the field, Yaakov has already died, we treat the field as a *sdeh achuzah* — he redeems it at the Torah's fixed rate, not at market rate. The reasoning rests on the verse: *v'im et sdeh miknato asher lo mi-sdeh achuzato* — "and if it is from his purchased field, which is not from his ancestral field." The phrase *mi-sdeh achuzato* implies a field that does not even belong to the category of things that could be ancestral fields. But this field *could* have been his *sdeh achuzah* — had it not been purchased, at the moment of Yaakov's death it would have been inherited. Therefore it is excluded from the *sdeh miknah* category and treated as a *sdeh achuzah* for redemption purposes.

This is a striking ruling. Even though at the moment of sanctification the field was unambiguously a purchased field — indeed, one that would have returned to Yaakov at *yovel* had Yaakov lived — Rabbi Shimon says that because at the time of *pidyon* the conditions now resemble what would have made it a *sdeh achuzah*, we assess it accordingly.

### Rabbi Meir

Rabbi Meir accepts a version of this logic but draws the line differently. He agrees that if the sequence was: (1) Reuven purchases, (2) Yaakov dies, (3) Reuven sanctifies — then the field is treated as a *sdeh achuzah*, because at the moment of sanctification it genuinely *was* a *sdeh achuzah*: Yaakov had already died, Reuven had already inherited full title, and the field's status had truly changed before the act of *hekdesh*. This, Rabbi Meir says, is not a great *chiddush* — it is simply recognizing that the field's status changed before sanctification.

What Rabbi Meir refuses to accept is the reverse order: (1) purchase, (2) sanctification while Yaakov is still alive, (3) Yaakov's death. In that case, at the moment of sanctification it was a *sdeh miknah*, and Rabbi Meir holds that we assess the field based on its status at the time of *hekdesh*, not at the time of *pidyon*. The subsequent death of the father does not retroactively transform the character of the sanctification.

For Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, the case of father-dies-then-sanctifies requires no verse — it is obvious. The verse is needed for the harder case, where the sanctification preceded the father's death, and yet we still treat the redemption as that of a *sdeh achuzah*.

### Textual Reading

The Gemara probes further: if Rabbi Shimon simply holds as a general principle that we always assess things at the time of *pidyon*, then he did not need a specific verse — his principle would already yield this result. The fact that a verse is required suggests something more limited is happening. The Gemara concludes: in truth, one could have read the verse like Rabbi Meir. What forced Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon into their reading was the specific formulation *asher lo mi-sdeh achuzato* — "which is *not from* his ancestral field." The plain reading would be: a purchased field that simply is not an inherited field. But the phrase *mi-sdeh achuzato* — "not *from* his ancestral field" — implies a field that has no connection whatsoever to the ancestral-field category. This field does have such a connection: it came from the father's holdings and, at the time of *pidyon*, would have been inherited. Therefore it cannot be characterized as a field entirely outside the ancestral-field universe, and it is treated as a *sdeh achuzah* for redemption.

---

## Rav Nachman Clarifies

### General Principle

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak now intervenes to sharpen the point. In general, he states, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon do *not* follow the time of *pidyon* as a standing methodological principle — *l'olam b'alma Rabbi Yehuda v'Rabbi Shimon lo azli batar pidyon*. Their ordinary orientation is to assess sanctified property based on the moment of *hekdesh*. Accordingly, in the *baraita*'s case of two-stage sanctification, they would indeed treat trees and field as two separate units and require two separate redemptions, since that is how the property entered *hekdesh*.

### Text Compels

The exception in the ancestral-field case is not a general principle but a textually compelled result. *V'hacha kra ashkhach v'daresh* — here they found a verse and expounded it. The phrase *asher lo mi-sdeh achuzato* carries the specific implication that we are excluding only a *sdeh miknah* with no connection to the ancestral-field category — thereby including a field that, though purchased, came from a father's holdings and would have been inherited. This is a local textual derivation, not a reflection of a broader commitment to assessing things at the time of *pidyon*.

The Gemara reinforces this: had the Torah simply written *v'im mikanato asher lo achuzato* — without the *mem* introducing *mi-sdeh* — Rabbi Meir's reading would have been natural and unforced. It was the additional *mem* — *mi-sdeh achuzato*, "not from the world of ancestral fields" — that pressed Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon into their alternative reading. Their general inclination remains to follow the time of *hekdesh*, and it is only this specific textual pressure that leads them to classify the field as a *sdeh achuzah* at the time of *pidyon*. One might ask whether this makes the ruling somewhat circular — since the father's having died after the sanctification is a future event that we are reading back into the field's character at the time of sanctification. The Gemara acknowledges this subtlety but maintains that the textual logic of *mi-sdeh achuzato* carries the force, not a general retroactive principle.

---

## Dual Status

### Carob Sycamore

Having concluded the extended analysis of *hekdesh*, trees, and land, the Gemara now turns to a related but distinct set of rulings from Rav Huna concerning objects that carry dual legal status simultaneously.

Rav Huna states: *charov u-murkav de-shikma torat ilan leh ve-torat karka leh* — the grafted carob tree and the sycamore stump possess the legal character of a tree and also the legal character of land. We have already established in the *mishnah* that when one sells a field with everything in it, the sycamore and carob are not included — they are treated not as trees within the field but as independent plots, a separate *karka*. That is their *torat karka*.

But they also carry *torat ilan*: when one sells or sanctifies three trees and one of the three is a carob or sycamore, it counts as one of the three trees for purposes of the rule that three properly distributed trees bring the underlying land along with them. In that context it is treated fully as a tree.

### Large Sheaf

Rav Huna adds a parallel ruling: *omer she-yesh bo sa-atayim torat omer leh ve-torat gadish leh* — a sheaf of wheat that contains two *se'ah* — an unusually large quantity — has simultaneously the legal character of a sheaf (*omer*) and the character of a pile (*gadish*). Ordinarily, a sheaf is a modest bundle; something containing two *se'ah* might seem to cross into the category of a pile, which is qualitatively different.

### Shikhchah Laws

The dual status becomes practically significant in the laws of *shikhchah* — forgotten produce. The Torah commands that if a farmer forgets a sheaf in the field while harvesting, he must leave it for the poor. However, this applies only to one or two forgotten sheaves; if three or more sheaves are forgotten, they are considered too substantial to be the kind of oversight the Torah addresses, and they are not *shikhchah*.

The large two-*se'ah* sheaf generates a ruling in both directions. As *torat gadish* — pile — if it stands alone forgotten in the field, it is not *shikhchah*, because a pile is never treated as forgotten produce. As *torat omer* — sheaf — if two ordinary sheaves are also forgotten alongside it, then together you have what is considered three sheaves, and none of the three constitute *shikhchah*. Had the large bundle been treated purely as a pile, it would not have combined with the two sheaves to create a count of three, and those two sheaves would each have been *shikhchah* independently. But because the large bundle also carries *torat omer*, it is counted as a third sheaf, which removes *shikhchah* status from the two ordinary sheaves as well.

The result is that this large sheaf protects against *shikhchah* in both directions: alone, it is a pile and not *shikhchah*; combined with two other sheaves, it functions as a sheaf and renders all three outside the scope of *shikhchah*.

---

## Rabbi Menachem

### Source Attribution

The Gemara closes the *perek* with a brief but pointed attribution. Rabba bar bar Chana says in the name of Reish Lakish: the debate about the grafted carob and the sycamore stump — whether they transfer when a field is sold or sanctified — comes to expression in the dispute between Rabbi Menachem berabbi Yossi and the Rabbanan. The Gemara immediately asks: why invoke Rabbi Menachem berabbi Yossi and the Rabbanan? Simply say this is the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbanan as recorded in our *mishnah*. The Gemara answers: *ka mashma lan de-Rabbi Menachem berabbi Yossi ke-Rabbi Shimon sevira leih* — the point is to convey that Reish Lakish possessed a tradition that Rabbi Menachem berabbi Yossi holds in accordance with Rabbi Shimon. The Rashbam notes that this must derive from a *mesorah* — an authoritative transmission — rather than from any explicit textual derivation. It is, admittedly, a somewhat unusual note on which to conclude a *perek*, but it serves to ground the anonymous ruling about carob and sycamore in a named tannaitic position.

*Hadran alach HaMocher et HaBayit.* We begin a new *perek* tomorrow.

---

---

# Bava Batra 73

## Boat Sale & Inclusions

### New Perek Intro

With daf 73 we begin a new *perek*, *Hamocher Es Hasfina* — "one who sells a boat." The basic framework of inquiry is the same as the previous *perek*: when one sells something, what is included in the sale? The shift, however, is significant. We are moving away from landed property and into the realm of *metaltelin* — movable property — beginning with a boat, which, though enormous, is itself a *metaltelin*. As will become apparent, this distinction carries important conceptual consequences for what is and is not included in a sale. It is also worth noting at the outset that while this *perek* opens with a legal *mishnah*, the bulk of the next several *dappim* will be dominated by *aggadata* — non-legal narrative material of a markedly fantastical character, the interpretation of which occupied the *rishonim* considerably.

### Mishnah: Boat Sale

The *mishnah* states: *hamocher es hasfina machar es hatoran* — one who sells a boat has also sold the mast; *es hanes*, the sails; *ve'es ha'ugin*, the anchors; and *ve'es kol hamanhiginosah*, all those things that cause it to move — the oars. These items, though not physically fused to the hull, are included in the sale by default.

### Included vs. Excluded

The *mishnah* continues: *aval lo machar lo es ha'avadim* — but one has not sold the slaves who serve as crew. Even though the crew is indispensable to the operation of the vessel, they are excluded. Likewise excluded are *hamartzufim* — the sacks or containers — and *ha'antiki* — the cargo itself. The *chiddush* of the *mishnah* is therefore notable: things that are movable and not physically attached to the boat are nevertheless included in the sale, whereas when land is sold, movables not physically attached are generally excluded. Here, precisely because everything is *metaltelin*, related *metaltelin* may be bundled together in the transaction. What remains excluded are the crew (who move under their own volition and possess a distinct legal identity), the cargo (which is variable and incidental to the vessel itself), and the sacks (which are understood as appurtenant to the cargo rather than to the boat).

### Kol Mah Shebetochah

The *mishnah* concludes with an exception clause: *ubizman she'amar lo hi vechol mah shebetochah* — if the seller said "it and everything in it," then *harei kulan mechorin* — all of it is sold, including the slaves and cargo. A comparison with the earlier *mishnah* on the sale of a city (*hamocher es ha'ir*, 68a) is instructive. There too, the formula *hi vechol mah shebetochah* was required to include *behemah va'avadim*. The conceptual parallel is clear, though the precise texture of what is "in" a boat differs from what is "in" a city, given that the crew are a functional necessity of the vessel in a way that slaves need not be of a town.

---

## Boat Component Terms

### Toran: The Mast

The *gemara* proceeds to define the terms used in the *mishnah*. *Toran* is *iskarya* — the mast. The *Rashbam* explains it as the tall pole over which a sail is spread at the prow of the ship. The *gemara* adduces a biblical source: *erez milevanon lakachu la'asos toran alayich* — "they took cedar from Lebanon to make a mast upon you" (Yechezkel 27:5). The use of cedar — a famously tall and strong tree — makes clear by context that we are speaking of a mast.

### Nes: The Sails

*Nes* is identified as *adra* — the sail. The biblical source is: *sheish berikmah mimitzrayim hayah mafriseich lihyos lach lenes* — "embroidered linen from Egypt was spread over you to be for you as a sail" (Yechezkel 27:7). The image of something woven and spread confirms the identification. One might note the broader semantic range of the word *nes*: a flag, a miracle, something raised high to be seen. The *Ramban* elsewhere discusses this connection — the purpose of a *nisayon* is to raise up and demonstrate, as one raises a banner — and there is a possible conceptual link between the *nes* as ensign or flag and the *nes* as sail, both being things that are unfurled and visible. The *Rashbam*'s reading makes clear that in context this refers to the mainsail.

### Ugin: Anchors

*Tani Rabbi Chiya*: *eilu oginin* — these are the anchors. The *gemara* sources this from the book of Rut: *halehen te'ageina* — "will you be anchored to them?" (Rut 1:13), referring to Naomi's daughters-in-law waiting, bound in place, for husbands who may never come. The word *te'ageina* is cognate with *ugin*, both drawing on the root of *aguna* — a woman who is "anchored," unable to move forward. The *Rashbam* explains that the anchors (*oginin*) are iron implements thrown into the water to hold the ship in place: *umashlichin bamayim l'ha'amid hasafina b'makom echad*. It is striking that the same root yields both the nautical anchor and the *halachic* concept of the *aguna*.

### Manhigin: Oars

*Amar Rabbi Abba*: *eilu hameshotin shelah* — these are the oars. Two biblical sources are offered. The first: *alonim mibashan asu moshotaich* — "oaks of Bashan they made into your oars" (Yechezkel 27:6), again using a large hardwood tree, establishing by context that *mashot* are the instruments of rowing. The second source: *vayerdu me'oniyoteihem kol tofshei mashot* — "all those who hold the oar came down from their ships" (ibid. 27:29), where the *mashot* are clearly the instruments grasped by those who row.

### Additional Items

A *baraita* adds two items not mentioned in the *mishnah* itself. *Hamocher et hasafina machar et ha'iskala* — the sale of a boat includes the gangplank, the ramp used to board and disembark. The *Rashbam* identifies *iskala* as the gangplank. The sale also includes *bor hamayim shebetochah* — the cistern of fresh water kept aboard the vessel. A subtle question arises as to whether this means the cistern together with the water in it, or merely the cistern itself; one might argue that fresh water, being a consumable, is more like cargo and should perhaps be excluded.

---

## Chattel vs. Land Logic

### Movables with Chattel

Before proceeding to the disputes of *Rabbi Natan* and *Sumchus*, it is worth pausing to articulate the conceptual distinction between the rules governing the sale of land and those governing the sale of chattel. When land is sold, movables — *metaltelin* — are generally not included in the sale unless explicitly transferred, even if those movables are necessary for the use of the land. Here, by contrast, we sell the sail, the mast, the oars, and the gangplank together with the boat, even though all of these are independently movable and none are permanently fixed to the hull. The reason is that the boat is itself a *metaltelin*, and as such it is more natural to view the ensemble of related *metaltelin* as a unified package.

### Rashbam's Framework

The *Rashbam* introduces a broader conceptual framework to explain why this *perek* follows immediately after the *mishnah* and *sugya* concerning *hekdesh*. The previous *perek* dealt with what is included when one consecrates or gives as a gift a piece of landed property — and the rule there was expansive: *hekdesh* and *matanah* of land include even items that a regular sale would not convey. The *Rashbam* explains that this *perek* comes to teach the reverse principle for *chattel*: when one is *makdish* a boat, one does not thereby consecrate the cargo, the slaves, or the other excluded items — *lo hikdish et elu* — as is taught further on in this *perek*.

### Rashbam on Gifts

The *Rashbam* elaborates: *vechol hani dechashivna befirkin deleil* — all the items discussed in the previous *perek* (a bathhouse, an olive press, a city, a field) — *culhu mekarkei ninhu* — they are all landed property. Because land is the most fundamental and legally significant form of property, there is a natural tendency to view appurtenant items as secondary extensions of the land itself. Therefore, when land is the subject of a *hekdesh* or *matanah*, additional items become packaged together with it. *Niknin ktzat agav ar'a legabei hekdesh umatanah* — they are acquired, in a sense, as appendages of the land in the contexts of consecration and gift.

By contrast, this *perek* concerns *metaltelin* exclusively — *vechol hani dehai pirka metaltelin ninhu*. And the *Rashbam* states the principle: *lo shena mecher velo shena matanah vehekdesh, culhon shavin behani delo machar* — whether sale, gift, or *hekdesh*, they are equal: what is excluded from a sale is equally excluded from a gift or consecration. There is thus an apparent irony. On one hand, precisely because it is all *metaltelin*, a sale of a boat does include other movable items in a way a sale of land does not. On the other hand, the elevated legal status of land means that gifts and *hekdesh* of land sweep in more than gifts and *hekdesh* of chattel do. The two principles point in opposite directions, and fully reconciling them is not straightforward. Still, the *Rashbam*'s observation is important for understanding why the *mishnah* is placed here, immediately following the *hekdesh* discussion.

---

## Boat Component Terms (II)

### Betzi vs. Dugit

*Rabbi Natan omer*: one who sells a boat also sells the *betzi* — the small auxiliary vessel, essentially a dinghy, towed alongside the main ship and used to transport passengers and goods between the ship and the shore, since large vessels cannot dock directly on land. *Sumchus omer*: one who sells a boat has sold the *dugit*. *Amar Rava*: *betzi haynu dugit* — they are the same thing. If they are identical, why do the two *tanna'im* use different names?

### Regional Terminology

The *gemara* offers a geographically sensitive explanation. *Rabbi Natan bava'ah hava* — Rabbi Natan was from Babylonia, and so he used the Babylonian Aramaic term *butzi*, as in the expression *butzi'atza demayshan* — the little boats of Mayshan, a body of water in the Babylonian region. The word *butzi* is related to *bitza* — mud or marsh — evoking the marshy waterways of that region. *Sumchus devar Eretz Yisrael* — Sumchus, who was from the Land of Israel, used the term *dugit*, as in the verse *acharitchen besirot dugah* (Amos 4:2). The *Rashbam* explains that *dugit* connotes a small fishing vessel. Both terms describe the same object; the difference is entirely regional and linguistic.

---

## Aggadic Waves & Salvation

### Seafarers' Stories

With the legal discussion of boat terminology concluded, the *gemara* transitions into a major section of *aggadata*. *Amar Rabbah*: *ishtau li nechutei yama* — those who go down to the sea have told me these stories. Rabbah is thus reporting what seafarers related to him, not necessarily vouching for their literal truth. These tales belong to the long tradition of maritime travel accounts — a genre always prone to dramatic amplification — and the *gemara* presents them in that spirit.

### Wave & Divine Names

The first account: *hai gala d'mitba l'sefinah* — when a wave comes to submerge a boat, *mitchazi ki tzitzita denura* — one sees at its crest what appears like a fringe of white fire. These are the white caps visible at the top of a cresting wave. *Umachinan lei b'alveta d'chakik aleih* — and one strikes the wave with a rod upon which are carved the words: *Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh, Yah Hashem Tzevaot, Amen Amen Selah* — several divine names. Striking the wave with such a rod causes it to subside — *v'nayach* — and the ship is saved.

### Aggada Interpretation

This account — and the several that follow — raised for the *rishonim* the fundamental question of how to read *aggadata*. The *Rambam*, in the introduction to *Perek Chelek* in his *Perush Hamishnayot*, identifies three categories of readers. The first are those who take all *aggadot* of *Chazal* literally and believe them as stated; the *Rambam* calls these the fools. The second are those who also read them literally but conclude on that basis that *Chazal* were foolish — these are the *reshaim*. The third category — the wise — understands that *Chazal* never intended these as literal accounts but as metaphors. The *Rashba* and others take a somewhat more moderate position, inclining toward accepting *aggadot* as true in principle while acknowledging that certain accounts simply cannot be taken literally. It is largely the *aggadot* of this section of *Bava Batra* that became the primary exhibit in this debate.

### Maharsha: Nations

The *Maharsha* interprets the imagery of the wave according to a political-historical framework. The waves represent the *goyim* — the non-Jewish nations — that have brought devastation upon the Jewish people throughout history. The white caps at the crest, the fringe of fire, evoke the terrifying power of imperial conquest. The divine names carved into the rod represent God's protection of Israel; it is that protection alone which prevents the wave from overwhelming the ship entirely.

### HaGra: Yetzer Hara

The *Vilna Gaon* (the *HaGra*) reads the same passage as a map of internal spiritual struggle. The wave, on this reading, is the *yetzer hara* — the evil inclination. The white fringe at its top is significant: the *yetzer hara* presents itself as pure and appealing, with a bright and innocent appearance, making the danger all the more insidious. The divine names on the rod represent the spiritual resources available to combat the *yetzer hara* from within. This interpretation shifts the entire drama from the external world to the inner life of the human being navigating the turbulent sea of existence.

---

## Massive Wave Sizes

### Wave Measurements

The next account returns to Rabbah reporting from the seafarers: *bein gala l'gala tlas mei'a parsei* — between one wave and the next, a distance of 300 *parsa*. A *parsa* is four *mil*, and a *mil* is roughly a kilometer, making 300 *parsa* approximately 1,200 kilometers. *Verum'yei d'gala tlas mei'a parsa* — and the height of an individual wave, likewise 300 *parsa*. For context, the highest wave ever recorded in modern times was roughly 400 to 500 meters — a small fraction of a *parsa*. The figure of 300 is, throughout *rabbinic* literature, a number of hyperbole; as one might say today "a million people," Chazal use 300 to convey overwhelming magnitude.

### Lifted to Stars

*Zimna chada hava azinan b'orchas* — once we were on a sea journey. *V'dalinan gala ad d'chazinan beei marbeisa d'kochava zuta* — a wave lifted us up until we could see the resting place of a small star, elevated to the very heights of the sky. The *Rashbam* explains that the star was situated in an expanse equivalent in measure to forty *grivyei* of mustard seeds — an extraordinarily large space. *V'ee dalinan tfei havina miklyinan mei'hevlei* — had the wave lifted them any higher, they would have been scorched by the heat of the star, since the seafarers understood the stars to radiate not only light but also intense heat.

### Wave Dialogue

*V'rami lei gala kala l'chaverei* — and this wave, having reached such a height, called out to another wave in a kind of dialogue. It said: *chavartai shavakt midi b'alma d'lo shatfetei* — "my friend, have you left anything in the world that you have not drowned?" Having risen to such an extreme height, the wave presumed that it must have submerged the entire earth. *Emei lian v'navdei* — "tell me, and I will come and destroy it."

### Sand Boundary

The other wave replied: *pook chazi gvurtei d'marach* — "go and see the power of your Master." *Mlo chusa chala v'lo avri* — there is a line of sand, no wider than a hair's breadth, that I cannot cross. Despite all my power and height, I cannot cast myself beyond the shore. The *gemara* cites the verse: *Ha'osi lo tiru neum Hashem im panai lo tachilu asher samti chol gvul layam* — "Will you not fear Me, says Hashem? I have placed sand as the boundary of the sea" (Yirmiyahu 5:22). *Chok olam v'lo ya'avrenhu* — an eternal decree that the sea shall not surpass it. The *Maharsha*'s reading situates this exchange as an allegory of the nations of the world: mighty imperial powers, swollen with self-confidence, imagining they have consumed the entire world, only to be told that God's decree sets limits even on the most fearsome of earthly forces.

---

## Hormin Demon Tale

### Hormin Running

*Amar Rabbah lididi chazi li Hormin bar Lilit* — Rabbah said: I myself saw the demon Hormin, son of Lilit, *ki ka rahit akupa deshura demachuza* — running along the top of the walls surrounding Machuza. *Verahit parsha ki rachiv chayuta mitutei velo yachil lei* — alongside him a horseman riding at full gallop could not keep pace with him. The demon's speed was superhuman.

### Mule Acrobatics

On one occasion, the demon was provided with two mules — *tarti kudenayta* — which were positioned on two separate bridges over the river Rugnag. *Veshavar mehai lehai umehai lehai* — the demon leaped back and forth between the mules spanning the river. *Venakit trei mizgei dechamra bidei* — all the while he held two cups of wine, *umorik mehai lehai umehai lehai* — pouring wine from one cup, leaping, and catching it in the other without spilling a drop. *Velo natfa midi le'ara* — not a drop hit the ground. *Ve'oto hayom ya'alu shamayim yerdu tehomot hava* — this was on a day of violent storms, when even those at sea were being tossed between sky and depths, and he performed this feat without difficulty.

### Half-Demon Status

*Ad desham'u be malkuta vekatlohu* — until the news reached the king's palace, and they killed him. The *Rashbam* offers two explanations of which king this was. His first explanation is the king of the *shedim* — the king of demons — who was displeased that Hormin was displaying his powers before humans. His second explanation invokes Caesar, who feared that so powerful an entity might threaten his own rule. The *Rashbam* explains the mechanism that made Hormin vulnerable: *shehaya oto shed adam haba al hashidah vayador bein hanashim* — this demon was not a pure *shed* but the offspring of a human father and a female demon, a *shidah*, which is why he could ultimately be killed.

### Yetzer Hara Meaning

One reading of this passage frames it as an allegory for the *yetzer hara* and the dangers of self-indulgence. Hormin bar Lilit — the son of Lilit, who in tradition is associated with seduction and temptation — represents the heights of undisciplined self-gratification. His spectacular acrobatic performance on the walls, with wine cups flying between leaps, is a portrait of self-display and indulgence. The mules — sterile animals incapable of reproduction — underscore the ultimate barrenness of a life devoted to self-indulgence. The wall he runs upon represents the *Torah*, which is meant to serve as protection and boundary; instead, Hormin uses it as a stage for his performance. His activities, for all their dazzle, produce nothing.

---

## Antelope Beast Tale

### Antelope Size

*Amar Rabbah lididi chazi li orzila bar yoma* — Rabbah said: I myself saw a *re'em* — a great beast, understood to be some form of antelope or similar large creature — that was only one day old, and yet *dehava kehar Tavor* — it was the size of Mount Tabor. *Har Tavor kama havei? Arba parsei* — Mount Tabor is four *parsa* in extent.

### Antelope Measurements

*Umshacha d'tzavara tlata parsei* — the length of its neck alone was three *parsa*. *Uvei marba'ata d'reisha* — the resting place of its head — *parsa u'palga* — a *parsa* and a half.

### Dung Blocks Jordan

*Rma kufta vsachra l'Yardena* — it relieved itself, and the volume of its excrement was sufficient to block the Jordan River. The *Rashbam* notes that the rushing current of the Jordan eventually forced its way through. This, then, is a creature of almost incomprehensible scale — day-old, and already vast enough to block a major river.

---

## Chain of Creatures

### Creature Chain

*V'amar Rabbah bar bar Chana lididi chazi li hahi akrukashta* — Rabbah bar bar Chana said: I myself saw this *akrukashta*, which the *Rashbam* identifies as a *tzfardei'a* — a frog — *d'havya ki akra d'Hagronya* — that was the size of the town of Hagronya. *V'akra d'Hagronya kama havya? Shitin batei* — that town comprised sixty houses. *Ata tanina uvalah* — a *tanin* came and swallowed it. The word *tanin* has a range of meanings — sea monster, crocodile, serpent — and the *Rashbam* renders it here as a sea monster. Then *ata pushkantza* — a raven came — *uvalah l'tanina* — and swallowed the sea monster. *Vsillik yatib b'ilana* — the raven then flew up and settled on a tree branch.

### Tree's Strength

*Ta chazi kama nafish cheila d'ilana* — consider how powerful that tree must have been to support, on a single branch, the raven that had eaten the sea monster that had eaten the frog the size of sixty houses.

### Maharsha: Scholars

The *Maharsha* develops an allegorical reading of this chain. The *talmidei chachamim* are compared to the frogs — given to speech and to the waters of *Torah*. The successive predators represent the nations of the world, each consuming what came before. What allows everything to be sustained in the end — the tree — is the *Torah* itself, of which it is written that it is a *tree of life to those who hold fast to it* (*Mishlei* 3:18). The *Torah*, on this reading, is the force that sustains the entire chain; the strength of the tree is the strength of *Torah* learning, which supports the world even when all other forces are at work to devour one another.

---

## Massive Fish Narrative

### Fish & Cities

*V'amar Rabbah* — and Rabbah said: *zimna chada hava ka azlinan b'sefinta v'chazinan ha-hu kavra* — once I was traveling on a boat and I saw a certain fish. *V'yatba leh achlatina b'usya* — a parasite of some kind settled itself in the fish's nostrils, *v'adchuhu maya* — and the water cast it ashore, *u'shadyuhu l'guda* — and it was thrown onto the bank. *V'charuv mineh shitin machozei* — and this fish, falling ashore, destroyed sixty cities.

### Fish Utilization

*V'achalu mineh shitin machozei* — sixty other cities ate from its fresh flesh. *U'malchu mineh shitin machozei* — sixty more cities salted its preserved flesh for future consumption. *U'malu mi-chad galgala d'eineh tlat me'ah garbei mishcha* — from a single eye of this fish, three hundred barrels of oil were extracted. *V'chi hadran l'vatar treisar yarchei shata* — when Rabbah bar bar Chana returned to that place a year later, *chazinan d'havu mnasrei migarmei mtalalta* — they were sawing its bones into beams, *v'yatvi l'mivneinhu hanach machozei* — to use in rebuilding the sixty cities the fish had destroyed when it fell.

### Fish as Tzaddik

One interpretive tradition, offered in the *beit midrash*, identifies the fish with a *tzaddik* — a righteous person. God is exacting with the righteous even in small matters; the tiny parasite represents the minor transgression that can prove fatal to one who is otherwise great. The three sets of sixty cities — those destroyed, those that ate fresh, those that preserved — represent three different classes of people and three different responses to the death of a righteous individual: some are devastated, some draw immediate sustenance and meaning from his legacy, and some preserve and transmit that legacy to future generations.

---

## Fish Island Deception

### Island Mistake

*Va'amar Rabbah bar bar Chana* — Rabbah bar bar Chana said: *zimna chada hava ka azlinan b'sefinata v'chazinan ha-hu kavra d'yatba leh chala agabeih* — once I was on a boat, and I saw a fish on whose back sand had accumulated. *V'kadach agma ilaveih* — and reeds and grass were growing from the sand. *Savrinan yaveshta hi* — we concluded that this was a small island in the middle of the sea.

### Fish Overturns

*V'salkinan* — we boarded it. *V'afinan u'vashlinan agabeih* — we baked and cooked upon it, making a camp and a fire. *U'chad cham gabeih* — when the back of the fish began to heat up from our fire, *ithapich* — it overturned. *V'i lav d'hava mkarva sefinata hava tav'inan* — had our boat not been close by, we would have drowned.

### Wicked Nations

On one allegorical reading, the fish that appears as a hospitable island represents the wicked nations, who initially present themselves as friendly and welcoming. One settles in, makes oneself comfortable, builds a fire — and then the surface overturns, betrayal replaces welcome, and one is cast into the sea. The boat that saves the travelers represents divine assistance, the *Shechinah* that remains close even when the surrounding world proves treacherous.

---

## Fish Journey Duration

### Three Days Travel

*Va'amar Rabbah bar bar Chana*: *zimna chada havai azilna b'safinta*, once I was traveling on a boat, *vesagai safinta bein shitsa leshitsa dekivra derabbah* — and the boat was traveling between one fin and the other of a great fish — *tlata yomi vetlata leilvata* — for three days and three nights.

### Wind Dynamics

*Ihu bezikeifa veanan beshipula* — the fish was traveling against the wind, and we were traveling with the wind at our backs, meaning that the fish and the boat were moving in opposite directions, and our effective speed relative to the fish should have been the sum of both velocities. Even so, it took three days and three nights to traverse the length of the fish from fin to fin.

### Boat Speed

*Vechi teima lo masgya safinta tuva* — one might suggest that the boat simply was not very fast, and that is why the journey took so long. The *gemara* rejects this: *dechi ata Rav Dimi amar, kemeicham kumkuma demaya masgya shitin parsei* — when Rav Dimi came up from Bavel he reported that this boat traveled sixty *parsa* in the time it takes to boil a kettle — a matter of minutes. The boat was extraordinarily fast.

### Fish Speed

*Veshadi parasha geira dekadma lei* — and if a horseman were to shoot an arrow, the fish would outpace it. The fish was faster than an arrow shot at full gallop.

### Nations vs. Jews

An allegorical reading situates the fish and the boat as symbols of the nations of the world and the Jewish people respectively. The other nations dwell in their homelands like fish in water, at ease and moving with the current. The Jewish people, in exile, are always traveling against the wind — laboring against the grain of the surrounding world's power and momentum. And yet, supported by *Torah*, they travel with the wind behind them in a spiritual sense. The three days of the journey evoke the three days of fasting and repentance that mark transformative moments in Jewish experience.

### Fish Identity

*Va'amar Rav Ashi*: *hahi gildana de'yama havai* — that fish was identified as a *gildana*, a particular species. *De'it lei tartei shaitsei* — it is characterized by its two distinctive fins, which is why the boat could travel between them for three days.

---

## Giant Bird Vision

### Bird Proportions

*Va'amar Rabbah bar bar Chana*: *zimna chada havai azilna b'safinta vechazina hahi tsipra* — once I was on a boat and I saw a bird — *dekayim ad karsulei bemaya* — standing in the water up to its ankles — *verishei berakia* — with its head reaching up into the heavens.
