### Shallow Assumption

*Ve'amina leika maya* — we concluded that the water must be shallow. This was a natural inference: if the bird was only ankle-deep, surely the water could not be very deep. *Uva'inan lemichat le'akorei nafshin* — and we prepared to go down into the water to cool ourselves off.

### Heavenly Warning

*Venafak bat kala ve'amar lan* — a heavenly voice went out and said to us: *lo teichatu hacha* — do not go down here. *Denafla lei chatsitsa levar nagra ha sheva shanim vlo kamatya ara* — a carpenter's axe fell into this water seven years ago and has not yet reached the bottom.

### Strong Current

*Vlo mishum dnefishi maya ela mishum dradifi maya* — it is not that the water itself is extraordinarily deep, but rather that the current is so powerful and fast-moving that it prevented the axe from sinking to the bottom. The danger is not depth alone but the ferocity of the current.

### Jewish People Symbol

One reading identifies the bird as a symbol of the Jewish people: *raglaim*, feet, planted in the world of physical reality, while the head — the aspiration, the *neshamah*, the intellectual and spiritual dimension — reaches toward the heavens. The warning against descending into the water cautions against going too deep into esoteric disciplines — *kabbalah* and *nistar* — that may appear accessible, like shallow water, but whose currents are in fact dangerous to those not prepared for them. What looks manageable to the masters of those disciplines appears easy only because of their mastery; to others, the current can overwhelm.

### Physical Pleasures Danger

An alternative reading of the same imagery understands the warning differently. The water that looks shallow and inviting represents the pleasures and indulgences of the surrounding nations. The Jewish people, seeing the nations at ease in their environment, may be tempted to think: it looks comfortable, it looks manageable, let us join them. The heavenly voice warns that what appears to be a gentle, shallow pool of tranquility is in fact turbulent and dangerous. The *shalva* — the apparent serenity — of the nations' way of life conceals currents that can sweep away everything.

---

## Fat Geese Story

### Geese Fattiness

*Va'amar Rabbah bar bar Chana*: *zimna chada hava ka azilna b'midbara* — once I was going through the wilderness — *v'chazina hanei avazi dishamti gadpaihu mishamnaihu* — and I saw geese whose feathers were falling off because of their extraordinary fatness. *V'kangadi nachalei d'mishcha mitutaiahu* — and rivers of fat were flowing beneath them, pressed out from their bodies against the ground.

### Future Benefit Query

### Geese Response

*Amina lehu* — I said to these geese: *it lan l'gavaichu chelka l'alma d'ati* — in the world to come, will we have a portion from you? Will we be able to eat you? *Chada dali gadpa* — one lifted its wing. *V'chada dali atma* — another lifted its leg, each apparently indicating that yes, one would be able to eat from it in the future.

### Accountability Statement

*Ki ata l'kamei d'Rabbi Elazar amar li: atidin Yisrael liten aleihem et hadin* — when Rabbah bar bar Chana came before Rabbi Elazar and told him this, Rabbi Elazar said: in the future, Israel will have to give an accounting for these geese.

### Messiah Delay

The *Rashbam* explains: *shebechatatam mitakev mashiach* — because of Israel's sins, the Messiah is being delayed. These geese were created for the Messianic feast, fattening themselves in anticipation of that day. But because the delay is prolonged, *yesh lahem tzaar baalei chayim l'otam avazim machmat shumnan* — the geese suffer greatly from their own corpulence, a form of *tzaar baalei chayim* — animal suffering — caused by their extraordinary fatness. Since Israel's failure to merit the redemption is what prolongs the geese's suffering, Israel will be held accountable for that suffering. The *Rashbam*'s comment brings to mind the contemporary practice of force-feeding geese for foie gras — a practice that causes comparable suffering — and underscores the moral seriousness with which the suffering of animals is treated in *halachic* thought.

---

## Arab Tracker Tale

### Smell Navigation

*Va'amar Rabbah bar bar Chana*: *zimna chada hava ka azilna b'midbara v'itlavai behadan hahu taya* — once I was traveling through the wilderness and a Bedouin traveler joined our company. *D'hava shakil afra v'morach leh* — he would take some sand, smell it, and then say: *ha orcha l'duchta palan v'ha orcha l'duchta palan* — this is the way to such-and-such place, and this is the way to such-and-such other place. He could navigate by smelling the desert sand alone.

### Testing Method

We asked him: *kama marchikan mimaya* — how far are we from water? *Hav li afra* — give me some sand. *Yavina lei* — we gave him sand, and he smelled it.

### Distance Accuracy

*Amar lan: tamni parsei* — he said: eight *parsa* away. We gave him sand again, and this time he said *tlasa parsei* — three *parsa*. *Afichta lei* — we reversed what we gave him, presenting him with sand from a different location to test him. *V'lo yachilna lei* — and we could not disprove him or catch him in error. Whatever test was applied, he met it accurately.

### Tracking Verified

The account concludes with the acknowledgment that trackers of this kind genuinely exist — people with extraordinary sensory attunement to their environment, capable of navigation by means that seem almost impossible to observers. Whatever the metaphorical resonances one might find in this tale, it is also simply a report of remarkable human skill, presented by Rabbah bar bar Chana as something he himself witnessed and could not refute.

---

---

# Bava Batra 74

## Dead Desert & Tzitzit

### Introduction

The daf opens in the middle of a classic section of *aggadata* centered on sea stories and fantastic narratives, picking up at the bottom of 73b. The subject is Rabbah bar Bar Chana, who recounts his encounters with an Arab Bedouin nomad who knew the secrets of the wilderness and offered to show him its hidden wonders.

### Bodies in Wilderness

The nomad said to Rabbah bar Bar Chana: *ta achvei lach mesei midbar* — come, let me show you those who died in the desert, the *Bnei Yisrael* who perished during the forty years of wandering in the wilderness. They went, and Rabbah reports: *vedamu keman demivsemi* — they looked as though they were slightly drunk, with a smile on their faces, as the *Rashbam* explains. They were lying on their backs — the term *aparkid* is debated as to whether it means face-up or face-down, but since Rabbah could see their faces, the implication is clearly that they were lying on their backs.

One remarkable detail: the knees of one of the bodies were raised, and the nomad was able to ride beneath the raised leg on a camel with his spear upright and still clear it without touching. These were clearly giants, reflecting their immense spiritual stature.

### Cutting Tzitzit

Rabbah then reasoned that as long as he was there, he should try to learn something practical. He therefore cut off the corner of one of their *tzitzit* — the *tcheiles* string — in order to bring back evidence of how the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* was originally performed. After all, the *Torah* defines *tzitzit* in only a few words: *ve'asu lahem tzitzit*, *al kanfei bigdeichem*, *knaf pesil tcheiles* — and there are many debates about the precise manner of their construction. What better source than the very people who first received and fulfilled the commandment?

### Curse & Return

After cutting off the corner, Rabbah and the nomad found that they were unable to move forward — *velo hava mistagyei lan*. The nomad asked whether Rabbah had taken anything from the bodies. When Rabbah confirmed that he had, the nomad explained that there is a firm tradition: *deman deshakeil midi mineihu, lo mistagyei lei* — anyone who takes something from the dead of the wilderness will not be able to move. Rabbah returned the *tzitzit* to the corpse, and immediately they were able to travel again.

### Rabbis' Mockery

When Rabbah bar Bar Chana returned to the *beit midrash* and reported what had happened, the rabbis mocked him: *kol Abba chamra, v'kol Bar Bar Chana sachsa* — every Abba is a donkey and every Bar Bar Chana is a fool. The mockery plays on his actual first name, Abba. They then asked: *l'mai hilchasa avdas hachi?* — for what halachic purpose did you do this? To know whether the practice followed *Beis Shammai* or *Beis Hillel* in constructing *tzitzit*? The comparison is apt: when *tefillin* were recovered at Masada, scholars hoped to determine from them whether the order of the *parshiyos* followed Rashi or Rabbeinu Tam — and indeed both types were found. Similarly, Rabbah wanted to see how these ancient figures had made their *tzitzit*. But the rabbis pointed out that even if he had to return the piece he cut, he could at least have counted the strings (*chutin*) and the wraps (*chulyos*) before returning it. He had all or nothing thinking when a middle path was available.

This exchange raises a genuinely interesting question about the relationship between archaeology, history, and *halacha*. How much can physical evidence — whether recovered *tefillin*, the dimensions of *mikvaos* at Masada, or any other ancient artifact — determine *halachic* questions? Does the legal truth of *halacha* develop independently of historical evidence? The *halacha* is rooted in the past — we start with the *mesorah* — but we are not simply frozen there. The development of *Torah she-be'al peh* moves forward from that foundation. Perhaps this is even the deeper metaphor of the story: taking a physical artifact from the dead of the wilderness leaves you stuck, unable to move forward. The *mesorah* handed down from them allows us to move forward, but clinging to a physical relic of the past does not.

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* takes up the *halachic* question raised by this episode. The *Gemara* implies that the dead were buried with their *tzitzit*, but the prevalent *minhag* is actually the opposite — to remove the *tzitzit* from the garment before burial. *Tosafot* addresses why this might be.

One basic answer, alluded to by *Tosafot* here and elaborated elsewhere, is a geographic difference: the practice in *Bavel* was to bury the dead with their *tzitzit*, while in *Eretz Yisrael* it was not. *Ashkenazim* are sometimes influenced by *Eretz Yisrael* practice even when it diverges from the *Bavli*.

Within this *Tosafot*, however, several additional explanations are offered — and notably, many of them describe a historical change over time rather than merely a geographic one. Rabbeinu Tam reports hearing from the elders of Lotharingia that the *gematria* of *tzitzit* is 600, and together with the eight strings and five knots one arrives at 613 — *taryag mitzvot*. The *tzitzit* thus serve as a testimony that the person fulfilled the entire *Torah*. On this view, burying with *tzitzit* was a symbolic declaration: this person was *mekayeim* all the *mitzvot*. Rabbeinu Tam goes on to say that in our time, when people are no longer at that *madreiga*, doing so would constitute something like false testimony — *eidut sheker* — and so the practice changed. A related *midrashic* reading sees the phrase *l'dorotam* as *l'dor tam* — for a generation of the wholehearted.

The *Ri* offers another explanation grounded in the changing nature of daily dress. In ancient times, the standard four-cornered garment was what everyone wore; wearing *tzitzit* was therefore not a matter of putting on a special ritual object but simply of ensuring that one's ordinary clothing fulfilled its *halachic* obligation. On this reading, burying with *tzitzit* was not a statement of piety but simply what you did with a person's clothes — which happened to have *tzitzit* on them, just as you would not bury someone in a garment with *sha'atnez*. Now that four-cornered garments are no longer standard dress, and many people go through their lives without wearing *tzitzit* — not because they violate anything, but because they simply do not wear such garments — even one who did wear *tzitzit* in his lifetime should not be buried with them, *shelo levayesh et mi she'ein lo*, so as not to mark a distinction between the deceased.

This raises a further question: did *Tosafot* mean that people stopped wearing *tzitzit* even during *tefillah*? When exactly did the practice of wearing a *tallit gadol* specifically for prayer develop? And what does *mit'atef b'tallit* in the *Gemara* already assume? At minimum, a *shaliach tzibur* would have worn one. The question of whether one is *yotzei* with a *tallit katan* alone is itself debated, as many *Geonim* hold that only a garment one wraps around oneself qualifies as a full garment for the *mitzvah*.

*Tosafot* also cites Rabbeinu Chaim Kohen, who relies on *Rabbi Yochanan*'s opinion that *mitzvot* will be *betelot le-atid lavo* — *mitzvot* will be nullified in the future. On this view, the *tzitzit* are removed precisely because the deceased will not need them at *techiyat ha-meitim*; they will no longer be obligated. The opposing practice — burying with *tzitzit* — reflects the opinion of Shmuel, who holds that *mitzvot* will not be nullified in the future, and that the *tzaddikim* will rise in their burial garments, so they should be interred with their *tzitzit* intact.

The *Tosafot* also cites *Masekhet Semachot*, where Abba Shaul ben Bitnis instructs his sons to bury him at the feet of his father's grave, and the text mentions removing the *tcheiles* from his garment — the word being readable as *hitiro*, to remove, rather than to affix. *Tosafot* concludes that in *Eretz Ashkenaz* the practice is to place *tzitzit* on the *tallit* of the deceased and then immediately remove them, in order to testify that the person fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit*, but not to leave them in place.

The active removal of *tzitzit*, rather than simple omission, is symbolically powerful. The *Gemara* elsewhere says *keivan shemet adam na'aseh chofshi min hamitzvot* — once a person dies, they are freed from *mitzvot*. Tearing away the *tzitzit* is something like *keriah*, a rupture that marks the separation of the *meit* from the life of *mitzvot* and the world of the living.

## Sinai & Scorpions

### Sinai Scorpions

Continuing with the account of the Arab nomad, he said to Rabbah bar Bar Chana: *ta achvei lach hai Sinai* — come, let me show you Mount Sinai. They went, and Rabbah saw that the mountain was surrounded by scorpions — *de-hadra lei akrava* — scorpions the size of white donkeys. The reference to white donkeys is significant: the *Gemara* records that one does not recover from the bite of a white donkey, making the image of such creatures surrounding the mountain all the more forbidding.

### Heavenly Voice

There, Rabbah heard a heavenly voice — a *bat kol* — saying: *oy li she-nishbati, v'akhshav she-nishbati mi mefer li?* — woe to Me that I took this oath, and now that I have taken it, who can annul it for Me?

### Failed Annulment

When Rabbah returned to the *beit midrash* and reported this, the rabbis again rebuked him: *kol Abba chamra, v'kol Bar Bar Chana sikhla* — every Abba is a donkey, every Bar Bar Chana is a fool. God was effectively inviting someone to be *matir* His *neder* — and Rabbah had missed the opportunity. The *Gemara* explains that Rabbah hesitated because he thought the *shevuah* in question might have been God's oath after the *mabul* never to flood the world again, and he did not want to release that vow lest God destroy the world. The rabbis, however, understood it differently: God would surely not lament an oath that prevented Him from wiping out humanity. Rather, the *shevuah* must have been the oath consigning *Bnei Yisrael* to exile — God suffers alongside the suffering of *Bnei Yisrael*, and that is why He cries out in pain about the oath He has taken.

*Tosafot* raises an interesting technical question here: this *Gemara* seems to assume that even God requires another party to annul a *neder*, yet another *Gemara* suggests that at least in principle God could annul His own *neder*. The question of whether *hatarat nedarim* always requires a third party is thus already implicit in this passage.

Beyond the technical question, there is something striking about the theology embedded in this passage. The *Gemara* uses the word *mefer* — the same term used for a husband annulling his wife's *neder*. A *midrash* reads *Moshe ish ha-Elokim* — Moses the man of God — through the word *ish* as husband, casting God in the role of wife and Moshe as the husband who has the power to annul her *neder*: *ishah yekimenu v'ishah yeferenu*. From this emerges the principle of *tzaddik gozer v'ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu mekayem* — a *tzaddik* can override what God has decreed, in the same way a husband can annul his wife's vow. Rabbah bar Bar Chana, standing at the foot of Sinai — the very site of the giving of the *Torah* — was perhaps uniquely positioned to serve in that role, and he did not act.

One might also ask why the *shevuah* about *galut* would be heard specifically at *Har Sinai*. One might have expected such a lament to be heard at the *Har ha-Bayit*, which more directly represents the *churban*. This remains unexplained in the *Gemara* here.

## Korah & Confession

### Cracks & Wool Test

The nomad then said: *ta achvei lach beluei d'Korach* — come, let me show you where the earth swallowed up Korah's camp. Rabbah saw two cracks in the ground from which smoke was rising. To gauge the heat, he took a clump of wet wool, soaked it in water, attached it to the end of a pole, lowered it into the crack, and when he drew it back up it was singed. The heat below was intense.

### Monthly Return

The nomad then said: *atzit mah shamat* — listen carefully to what is being said. Every thirty days, *kol tlatzin yomin*, the followers of Korah are returned from *Gehinnom* to this place — *mahadu l'Gehinnom l'hacha* — like a piece of meat being turned over in a boiling pot, *k'vasra b'chalachta*, so that both sides are exposed to the heat. This place in the depths of the earth is evidently not *Gehinnom* itself; most of the time they are elsewhere, in *Gehinnom*, but once a month they cycle back to the precise location of their sin.

### Confession

And when they return, they say: *Moshe v'Torato emet v'hen badaya* — Moses and his Torah are true, and we were liars. The imagery is striking, calling to mind the forced confessions of totalitarian regimes, where those condemned are made to acknowledge the justice of their punishment before their execution. Here, those who once challenged the authority of Moshe are condemned to return periodically to the site of their rebellion and, in the very place where they denied his truth, confess it.

## Heaven & Earth

### Mountain Top Window

The nomad continued: *ta achvei lach heicha d'nashki ara v'rakia* — come, let me show you where heaven and earth kiss. He brought Rabbah to a mountain so high that one could actually touch the physical dome of the *rakia* — the firmament understood by the Sages as a tangible covering stretched over the earth. Here at this point, heaven and earth meet one another.

### Basket Disappears

Rabbah placed his bread basket — his knapsack — into a small window or opening in the *rakia*, similar to the *arubbot ha-shamayim* referenced in connection with the *mabul*. He set the basket down there because it was time to *daven* — and what better place than standing at the threshold of heaven? When he finished his prayers and went to retrieve the basket, it was gone. He asked whether there were perhaps thieves even at the mountaintop — or perhaps in heaven itself.

### Spinning Wheel

The nomad explained: *hai galgala d'rakia hu d'hadar* — it is the wheel of the *rakia* that revolves. The entire firmament rotates, and the basket had been carried along with it. *Natar ad le-makhar hakha u-mashkhat lah* — wait until tomorrow and you will find it back here, because the whole revolving structure will have completed its circuit and returned the opening — and thus the basket — to the same position.

The question of how exactly this works — whether the window itself moves with the firmament or remains stationary while an inner mechanism turns — is not fully resolved. One might imagine an arrangement where a fixed outer cover remains in place while the inner moving part rotates beneath it, something like a *Shabbat* lamp with a stationary cover and moving aperture.

One interpretation connects the bread basket to *parnassah*: the Arab nomad — understood in one reading as the *yetzer hara* — is suggesting to Torah scholars that worldly fortune, too, is in the hands of *Hashem*, and that what rises and falls in terms of material wealth does so according to a divine pattern that will eventually return to its place.

## Sea Tales Start

### Moon-eyed Fish

Having concluded the accounts involving the Arab nomad, the *Gemara* transitions to sea tales told by rabbis about their own voyages. The verb used here — *mishtayei* — suggests a storytelling mode rather than a formal legal pronouncement. Rabbi Yochanan told the following: once, while traveling by boat, he saw a sea creature that lifted its head out of the ocean. Its eyes looked like two moons, and water was flowing from its two nostrils like the two rivers of Sura.

### Horned Fish

Rav Saphra likewise told a story: once, while at sea, he saw a creature that stuck its head out of the water and had horns. Inscribed on the horns was the following: *ana birya kala she-ba-yam* — I am merely a small creature of the sea — *ve-havina tlath mea parsei* — and I am three hundred *parsa'ot* long — *ve-azlina le-phuma de-Livyathan* — and I am going into the mouth of the *Livyathan*. If this creature considers itself small and is merely *Livyathan*'s breakfast, one can begin to appreciate the dimensions of the *Livyathan* itself.

### Sea Goat

Rav Ashi commented that the horns identify this creature as the goat of the sea — a *iza de-yama* — which uses its horns to dig in the ocean floor in search of food. Just as sea horses are known, so too were sea goats, and their horns serve a practical foraging function.

### Treasure Chest

Rabbi Yochanan told another story: once at sea, he saw a chest affixed with precious stones and gems (*avanim tovot* and *margaliot*), surrounded by a type of fish called *karsha* — which appears to be the ancient equivalent of sharks. The modern Hebrew word for shark, in fact, derives from this very term. The image is the classic one: a treasure chest guarded by sharks.

### Diver & Vinegar

A *bar Amorei* — a diver, the word apparently deriving from the Latin *mare*, meaning sea — was sent down to retrieve the chest. The shark sensed his approach and moved to tear off his leg, but the diver threw a flask of vinegar (*zika de-hala*), which calmed the creature and allowed him to proceed. The word *bar Amorei* itself is interesting: just as *mare* in Latin refers to the ocean (and in cartography to the seas of the moon), so too the Aramaic term for a professional diver reflects an ancient Mediterranean linguistic influence.

### Heavenly Voice

Before the chest could be retrieved, a *bat kol* — a heavenly voice — declared: *mai isaikhu bahadei kartelita de-dveiteh de-Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa?* — what business do you have with the treasure chest of the wife of Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa? This chest is designated for her in the future. She is described as one who refused to derive benefit in this world from her share in the world to come, and the chest is reserved for her for the *olam ha-ba*. Furthermore, it is said that she will use it to provide *tcheiles* for the *tzaddikim* in the future world. Since *tcheiles* itself comes from the sea, there is a certain poetic logic in the chest being kept there. Some suggest that the *tcheiles* dye, whose source had been lost by the time of the later *Geonim*, will be rediscovered and it is Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's wife who will be the one to provide it.

## Resurrection Stone

### Jewel & Serpent

Rav Yehuda Hindua — Rav Yehuda the Indian, from India — recounted the following: once, while traveling by sea, he saw a beautiful jewel surrounded by a sea serpent (*tanina*). A *bar Amorei*, a diver, was sent to retrieve it. The sea serpent not only tried to swallow the diver but moved to swallow the entire boat.

### Raven & Blood

Then a raven — *pishkantsa* — appeared and cut off the head of the sea serpent. The water in the area then turned to blood. This detail echoes the *makat dam* of Egypt, and indeed there is a resonance with the *pasuk* in *Yechezkel* where *Par'oh* is described as *ha-Tanin ha-Gadol ha-rovetz betoch ye'orav* — the great sea monster crouching in the midst of its rivers, who says *ani ye'ori va'ani asitani* — the river is mine and I made myself. The *tanin* here, cut down and its water turned to blood, may carry echoes of that imagery.

### Revived Monster

A companion sea serpent then came, took what had been severed, and reaffixed it to the body — *v'chaya* — and the sea monster came back to life. The precise detail here — whether the second serpent retrieved the severed head or the stone — would become clearer in the subsequent passage. Having been revived, the monster once again turned to attack the boat.

### Second Decapitation

A second bird came and cut off the creature's head a second time. After this second decapitation, a diver — or perhaps the bird itself — retrieved the precious stone and brought it onto the boat. The moment was opportune, since it appeared from what followed that the stone was what had allowed the sea monster to be revived, and they now had a brief window before anything else could interfere.

### Birds Fly Away

The sailors had stored salted birds aboard the boat for provisions. They placed the stone on the salted birds — and the birds revived, took the stone, and flew away. The stone thus turned out to be a kind of *tachiyat ha-meitim* stone, with the power to restore life to the dead. Its power was demonstrated twice over: first on the sea monster (whose companion used it to revive it), and then on the salted birds. The stone could not ultimately be held — it was taken back by the forces of nature.

The story invites allegorical reading. One might see in it an echo of *Yetziat Mitzrayim*: the ocean, the serpent as an avatar of *Par'oh*, the moment of apparent liberation followed by renewed subjugation, and the stone of ultimate redemption that remains perpetually out of reach until the future time. Each time *Bnei Yisrael* seem to destroy the power that oppresses them, it returns — revived — and the *techiyat ha-meitim* stone remains tantalizingly withheld until the *asid lavo*.

## Leviathan Stories

### Light in Ocean

The *Gemara* presents a *beraitah*: there was an incident involving Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua — both of whom were *rabbeim* of Rabbi Akiva, a generation earlier — who were traveling together on a boat. Rabbi Eliezer was asleep and Rabbi Yehoshua was awake. Rabbi Yehoshua began trembling (*nizda'aze'a*) and his trembling woke Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Eliezer asked him what had alarmed him. Rabbi Yehoshua replied: *ma'or gadol ra'iti ba-yam* — I saw a great luminary in the ocean.

### Leviathan's Eye

Rabbi Eliezer replied: perhaps what you saw was the eye of the *Livyatan*. As it is written: *einav k'afapei shachar* — its eyes are like the eyelids of the morning, like the morning luminary, like the sun. The casual certainty of Rabbi Eliezer's identification — oh, that must have been the eye of the *Livyatan* — is itself a remarkable window into how these *Tannaim* related to the creatures of sacred imagination.

### Self-healing Meat

Huna bar Nasan told Rav Ashi the following: once I was traveling in the wilderness, and we had with us a thigh of meat. We opened it, removed the fat and the *gid ha-nasheh*, and set it down on the grass while we went to gather wood for a fire. When we returned, the leg had healed itself — closed back up as it had been before we cut it. We roasted it and ate it.

When Huna bar Nasan returned a full twelve months later to that same place, he found the coals still smoldering — still whispering, *k'malachshei*. Amemar explained both phenomena: the grass was *samteri*, a species with powerful restorative properties, which had healed the meat. And the coals were from a *retam* tree — broom wood — which is known to burn for extraordinarily long periods. Indeed, there is another *sugya* in *Sukkot* where travelers to *Yerushalayim* would light *retam* wood before their pilgrimage and find it still burning when they returned a year later.

## Leviathan Created

### Male & Female

The *Gemara* now addresses the *pasuk*: *vayivra Elokim et ha-tanninim ha-gedolim* — and God created the great sea monsters. In the *Gemara*'s locale, this was translated as the *arzeilei de-yama*, the great beasts of the sea. Rabbi Yochanan identifies these as the *Livyatan nachash bariach* — the straight serpent — and the *Livyatan nachash akalasson* — the coiled serpent — male and female respectively, as corroborated by the *pasuk* in *Yeshayahu*: *bayom hahu yifkod Hashem b'charbo ha-kasha... et livyatan nachash bariach ve-et livyatan nachash akalasson*.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states the general principle: everything God created in His world He created male and female — *zachar u-nekeivah bera'am* — and so too the *Livyatan*. This is striking, because as the *Gemara* will note, there exist creatures that are not clearly binary in their sex, yet the principle is stated in its fullest generality.

### Procreation Risk

The problem with creating both a male and a female *Livyatan* is that if they were ever to mate, their progeny would destroy the entire world: *ilmalei nizkakkin zeh la-zeh machrivin kol ha-olam kulo*. The same applies to the *Behemoth*, the great land beast — *Behemoth be-harerei alef*, described in *Tehillim* as dwelling on the thousand mountains, which *Chazal* understand as a reference to the immense creature whose flesh will be served at the feast of the righteous in the *olam ha-ba*: those who prefer fish will have *Livyatan*, those who prefer meat will have *Shor ha-Bar*.

### Castration & Death

To prevent the *Livyatan* pair from mating, God castrated the male and killed the female — *siras et ha-zachar ve-harag et ha-nekeivah* — and then salted the female's flesh to preserve it for the righteous in the future: *u-malachah la-tzaddikim le-asid lavo*. This is derived from the *pasuk*: *ve-harag et ha-tannin asher ba-yam* — where the word is singular, indicating that one was killed while the other was left alive.

### Salt Debate

The obvious question is: if the male was castrated, why was it also necessary to kill the female? Why not simply cool her down, as was done with the female *Behemoth*, and keep her alive? The answer is *dagei pritzei* — fish are particularly promiscuous. Even after being cooled, the female *Livyatan* might still mate — perhaps with other fish rather than the castrated male — and that risk could not be tolerated.

Conversely, one might ask why the female *Livyatan* was killed rather than kept alive — why not cool her down as was done with *Behemoth*? Two answers are offered. The first: *nekeivah melicha ma'alei* — salted female fish tastes better than salted male fish, so to provide the best possible meal for the *tzaddikim* in the future, the female was killed and salted. The second: since the *pasuk* says *livyatan zeh yatzarta lesachek bo* — You created this *Livyatan* to play with — and the *Gemara* in *Berakhot* states that God devotes a portion of the day to playing with the *Livyatan* — it would be *lav orech ara*, not proper conduct, for God, who is cast in a male role, to be playing with the female *Livyatan*. Therefore the male was preserved, and the female was killed.

### Behemoth

The same logic applies to the *Behemoth*: God castrated the male and cooled the female rather than killing her — *siras ha-zachar ve-tzinan ha-nekeivah* — and she is kept preserved for the *tzaddikim le-asid lavo*. The *pasuk* is cited: *hineh na kocho be-mosnav* — behold, its strength is in its loins — *zeh zachar*, this refers to the male; *ve-ono be-shirirei vitno* — and its power in its belly — *zeh nekeivah*, referring to the female, evoking the womb.

### Fresh vs Salted

Why was the female *Behemoth* cooled rather than killed and salted, as was done with the *Livyatan*? The answer: *kavara melicha ma'alei* — salted fish is good. *Bisra melicha lo ma'alei* — salted meat is not as good. Fresh meat tastes better than preserved meat. Therefore, for the *Behemoth* — a land animal whose flesh would be eaten as meat — it is preferable to keep the female alive and slaughter her fresh at the time of the feast rather than salt her in advance. The *Livyatan*, being fish, benefits from salting. The practical culinary logic of the eschatological feast thus determines which creature was preserved alive and which was killed and salted.

# Bava Batra 75

## Rahav & Leviathan

### Rahav's Slaying

The *daf* opens with a statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav. At the moment when God sought to create the world, He said to the *sar shel yam* — the angel appointed over the sea — "Open your mouth and swallow all the waters of the world." This appears to be the mechanism behind the verse *yikavu ha-mayim el makom echad*, the gathering of the waters to one place so that the dry land should appear. The angel, however, refused. The Gemara relates: *amar lefanav ribbono shel olam, dai she-amod b-sheli* — Master of the Universe, it is enough for me to stand within what is mine. What exactly his objection was is not entirely clear, since one might think he would have welcomed more water. In any case, God immediately kicked him and killed him — *miyad be-at bo ve-harago*. The proof-text comes from the book of Iyov: *b-kocho raga ha-yam u-vi-tvunato machatz Rahav* — with His strength He stirred up the sea, and in His wisdom He severed *Rahav*.

### Rahav Identity

Rabbi Yitzchak draws the inference: *shema mina sar shel yam Rahav shemo* — we learn from this that the name of the master of the sea is *Rahav*. There is a certain circularity to the proof: we are reading the verse in light of the narrative we just told, and the only basis for reading the verse that way is the narrative itself. Nevertheless, that is how the *pasuk* is being employed.

### Rahav's Stench

*Rahav* has been slain and lies at the bottom of the sea. The Gemara adds: *ve-imalay mayim m-chasim oto, ein kol biryah y-cholah la-amod b-reicho* — were it not that water covers him, no creature could withstand the stench of the corpse. The proof-text is Isaiah 11: *lo ya-re'u ve-lo yash-chitu b-chol har kodshi ki mal'ah ha-aretz de'ah es Hashem ka-mayim la-yam m-chasim*. The verse reads literally that knowledge of God covers the earth *like water covers the sea*, which is linguistically awkward — water does not cover the sea, it *is* the sea. Therefore the Gemara reads it as *al tikrei la-yam m-chasim, ela le-saro shel yam m-chasim*: do not read it as "covers the sea," but rather "covers the master of the sea." The water conceals the corpse of *Rahav* and its stench.

### Creation Myths

This material resonates with a broader cultural context. In ancient Near Eastern mythology, creation accounts frequently involve a primordial battle between the creator-god and a divine power over the sea. The name of that sea-god, *Tiamat*, bears a striking resemblance to the Hebrew *tehomot*. What is remarkable about the Torah's account of creation in Bereshit is that it is entirely non-mythological — not even in the sense of engaging and rejecting these myths, but in simply ignoring them, treating them as though they do not exist. This is perhaps the most powerful form of rejection: to not even dignify the opposing view with a response.

Yet in the book of Iyov, these echoes come more explicitly to the fore. The *pesukim* there about God conquering *Rahav* and the *leviatan* appear to either allude to or actively engage these ancient traditions of divine conquest over the sea as the precondition for creation. The *midrash* here in the Gemara reinforces that connection: it is not a loose *aggadic* reading floating free of its *pesukim*, but rather an interpretation that takes seriously what those *pesukim* in Iyov are actually saying about God's primordial victory over the forces of the sea. The Torah's approach remains non-mythological, but those older traditions did not entirely disappear, and here, in Iyov and in this *aggadata*, their echoes surface.

## Jordan & Leviathan

### Jordan's Path

The Gemara continues with another statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: the Jordan River exits from the cave of *Pamyas* — possibly the Banias — and this is corroborated by a *baraita*. From there it flows through the *yam* of Sibchi, then the *yam* of Tiberias — the *Kinneret* — and then winds its way to the Mediterranean. From there it continues to flow until it reaches the mouth of the *leviatan*, as the verse in Iyov says: *yivtach ki yagiach yarden el pihu* — he will be confident because the Jordan will roar into his mouth. How the Jordan makes its way from the Mediterranean to the *leviatan* is not explained. The geography of these seas is also difficult to reconstruct, though one of them may have been the ancient marsh that once lay near the Banias area, which has since dried up.

### Beasts' Confidence

Rava bar Ulla objects: that verse in Iyov is not talking about the *leviatan* at all — it is written in the context of *behemot beharerei alef*, the great beasts of a thousand mountains. He therefore reinterprets: the verse indeed refers to those beasts — but when are the *behemot beharerei elef* confident, *betuchot*? When the Jordan pours into the *leviatan*'s mouth — that is, when the *leviatan* is well-fed and satisfied, the other great beasts feel secure. The *Rashbam* adds a further dimension: as long as God is actively sustaining the *leviatan*, the *behemot* are confident that they too will be sustained. As long as it lives, they feel confident they will live.

There is also a tradition in *Midrash Vayikra Rabbah* that in the future the *behemot* and the *leviatan* will battle each other as a kind of sport for the righteous — a *milchemet Gog u-Magog* in miniature — which would further explain the *behemot*'s interest in the *leviatan*'s state.

### Seven Seas

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he cited Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of the verse *ki hu al yamim yesada ve-al neharot yechoneneha* — God has established it upon seas and upon rivers. These seas and rivers, says Rabbi Yochanan, are the seven seas and four rivers that surround the Land of Israel. The seven seas are: the *yam* of Tiberias (the *Kinneret*), the *yam* of Sodom (the Dead Sea), the *yam* of Cheilat, the *yam* of Chilta, the *yam* of Sibchi, the *yam* of *Aspamya*, and the *yam hagadol* (the Mediterranean). Of these, three are readily identifiable; the *Yerushalmi* reads *Apamea* in place of *Aspamya*, which appears to refer to a town in Syria with an ancient lake. The four rivers are the *Yarden*, *Yarmokh*, *Kiromon*, and *Pigah*.

## Leviathan's Nature

### Gabriel's Hunt

The Gemara relates that in the future, *Gavriel* will make a *kenigya* — a hunting or sporting expedition — against the *leviatan*. The word *kenigya* appears to be a loan-word, likely Greek, meaning a hunt or chase. The *pasuk* cited is from Iyov: *Hatimshokh Livyatan be-chakkah, u-ve-chevel tashki'a leshono* — will you drag the *leviatan* with a hook and submerge its tongue with a rope? However, even *Gavriel* cannot prevail against the *leviatan* without God's help: *ve-imla Ha-Kadosh Barukh Hu ozro, ein yakhol lo*. The proof-text is: *Ha-oso yiggash charvo* — the one who made it brings the sword against it. That is God Himself.

The same pattern recurs here that we saw earlier with the *sar shel yam*: God's ultimate conquest over the sea monsters. These, too, carry the echo of those ancient creation myths — God slaughtering the female *leviatan*, God conquering the sea monsters. The *aggadata* consistently frames these primordial victories as requiring divine power that transcends what any angel can muster alone.

### Hunger & Steam

When Rav Dimi came, he cited Rabbi Yochanan with another teaching about the *leviatan*: when it is hungry, *motzi hevel mi-piv* — it releases steam from its mouth — *u-marthi'ach kol meimot she-ba-metzulah*, and this boils all the waters in the depths. Whether this is a side effect of its hunger or the mechanism by which it cooks its food is not entirely clear; the image of a dragon whose nostrils emit steam when it is angered is evocative, though cooking fish into soup is equally plausible. The verse cited from Iyov describes it vividly: *Yarti'ach ka-sir metzulah* — it will boil up the deep like a pot. These images are drawn directly from the *pesukim* in Iyov, where the *leviatan* is described in these dramatic, almost fantastical terms — this is not purely the Gemara's creative imagination, but rather an exposition of those remarkable verses.

### Eden Cooling

Were the *leviatan* not to insert its head into *Gan Eden* at such moments — *ve-ilmalei machnis rosho le-Gan Eden* — no creature could withstand the stench or heat that comes from its mouth. *Gan Eden* functions here as a place that sweetens or cools the creature. The verse cited is *yam yasim ke-merkacha* — the sea it will make like a *merkacha*, a sweet-smelling ointment — and the *Rashbam* or *Rashi* understands this as the effect of *Gan Eden* sweetening the *leviatan*'s odor.

### Thirst & Recovery

When the *leviatan* thirsts, it *oseh t'lamim t'lamim ba-yam* — makes furrows in the sea, great wave-like pathways. The verse is *acharayiv ya'ir nativ* — after it the path lights up. Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds: after the *leviatan* has drunk or boiled the waters, the depths do not return to their original strength for seventy years — *ein tehom chozer le-eitano ad shiv'im shanah*. The proof is from the verse *yachshov tehom le-seivah* — the deep will reckon itself old — and since *seivah* refers to old age, which begins at seventy, the restoration takes seventy years.

## Leviathan Feast

### The Feast

Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states: in the future, God will make a *se'udah* for the righteous from the flesh of the *leviatan* — *atid Hakadosh Baruch Hu la'asot se'udah le-tzaddikim mi-besaro shel Livyatan*. This echoes what was mentioned earlier in this *aggadata* — that the female *leviatan* was salted away for the future feast. The verse cited is *yichru alav chaverim* — the friends will feast upon it — and the Gemara establishes that *keriyah* means feasting, as in the verse *vayichreh lahem kera gedolah*, he made for them a great feast.

### Friends & Markets

The "friends" (*chaverim*) in that verse are identified as *talmidei chachamim* — Torah scholars — from the verse in *Shir Hashirim*: *hayoshevet ba-ganim, chaverim makshivim le-koleich, hashmi'ini* — she who dwells in the gardens, the friends who listen to her voice, let me hear it. In *Shir Hashirim*, understood as an allegory of God and Israel, these friends are those who hear and study God's words — the Torah sages.

What remains after the feast is divided and sold in the marketplaces of Jerusalem. The *tzaddikim* appear to profit from the leftovers. The verse *yach'tzuhu bein Kena'anim* — it will be divided among the *Kena'anim* — is read through the Gemara's identification of *Kena'anim* with merchants, as in *Kena'an be-yado moznei mirmah* (Hoshea) and *asher sochareha sarim, kena'aneha nichbedei aretz* (Yeshayahu) — its merchants are princes, its traders the honored of the land. The *leviatan* thus provides both a feast and a commercial opportunity.

The deeper question of why specifically the *leviatan* serves as the meal of the righteous points toward the symbolic dimension of the whole narrative. The *leviatan* represents something large and ancient that only God's power can conquer. Its defeat and consumption by the righteous connects the future victory over evil with the reward of those who conquered their own *yetzer hara* in this world. As a metaphor it is remarkably apt: the greater the *leviatan* you overcame, the larger your portion.

### Merit Levels

Rabbah continues in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: God will make a *sukkah* for the righteous from the *leviatan*'s skin — *atid Hakadosh Baruch Hu la'asot sukkah la-tzaddikim me-oro shel Livyatan*. This resonates with the tradition in *Masechet Sukkah* that in the end all of Israel will dwell in one *sukkah*. The verse is *ha-timaleh be-sukkot oro* — will its skin be filled with huts — and the reading is that its skin will create the *sukkah* in which all dwell.

The reward is then graduated by merit. If the righteous person *zacha* — merits — he receives a full *sukkah*. If he does not fully merit, he receives *tzeltzel*, a shade — as in *u-ve-tzeltzel dagim rosho*, with the shade of fish over his head. If he does not merit even that, he receives *anak* — a necklace — from the bones, as in *va-anakim le-gargerotecha*. And if he does not merit even that, he receives a *kameia*, an amulet — as in *va-tikshreinu le-na'arotecha*. The skin of the *leviatan* thus provides protection, adornment, or at minimum a token of remembrance, each according to what the person achieved in this world.

### Wall Covering

Whatever skin remains after all of this, God will spread over the walls of Jerusalem — *u-vehash'ar, parso ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu al chomot Yerushalayim* — and its radiance will shine from one end of the world to the other. The verse is *ve-halchu goyim le-orech u-melachim le-nogah zarchach* — nations will walk by your light and kings by the brightness of your shining. The verse is often understood as a call to moral example — *or la-goyim*, a light unto the nations — but here its literal meaning is quite material: the luminous skin of the *leviatan* stretched across Jerusalem's walls will illuminate the entire world.

## Jerusalem Walls

### Gate Materials

The Gemara now cites the verse *ve-shamti kadkod shimshosayich* — and I will make your *shimshosayich* (a term interpreted as the walls or windows) like *kadkod*, a precious stone. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports that two angels in heaven debated the meaning of this word: *Gavriel* and *Michael* — though *Tosafot* notes that *Eliyahu* must have been the one who revealed this heavenly debate to us. Alternatively, some say the dispute was between two *amora'im* in the West, namely Yehuda and Chizkiya the sons of Rabbi Chiya. One held that the material is *shoham* (onyx), the other that it is *yashfeh* (jasper, or according to some, carbuncle). God responded: *lehavei kedein ve-kedein* — it will be both. Hence the word *kadkod* encodes *kedein va-kedein*, both this and this. *Tosafot* adds that since both *shoham* and *yashfeh* appear earlier in the surrounding *pesukim*, the resolution of *kedein va-kedein* refers back to those specific stones.

### Block Dimensions

The verse continues: *u-she'arayich le-avnei ekdach* — and your gates like stones of *ekdach*. The word is connected by *derash* to *kodeach*, meaning to carve or pierce. Rabbi Yochanan was sitting and expounding: in the future, God will bring beautiful jewels and pearls of *shoham*, thirty by thirty *amot*, and will carve within them a gate ten *amot* wide and twenty *amot* high. The full block is thirty by thirty, and the gate carved within it is ten wide by twenty tall — meaning the gate occupies the center of the block, with the full block forming the wall through which one passes.

### Student's Mockery

A student mocked this vision: *hashta ke-veiyata de-tzitzela lo mishkachinan* — we cannot even find an onyx stone the size of a small bird's egg — *kulei hai mishkachinan*? You are claiming we will find one thirty by thirty *amot*? Many days later, the student's boat sailed far out to sea. He saw ministering angels sitting and hewing out precious jewels and stones — thirty by thirty — with a gate carved in them ten wide by twenty high. He asked them: for whom are these? They told him: these will stand in the gates of Jerusalem. He came before Rabbi Yochanan and said: Teach further, *Rebbi*, for you it is fitting to expound — *ka-asher amarta, ken ra'iti*, just as you said, so I have seen with my own eyes.

### Divine Punishment

Rabbi Yochanan's response was not warm. He said to him: *reika* — empty one! *Ilmalei ra'ita, lo he'emanta* — had you not seen it yourself, you would not have believed? *Nimtza melagleg al divrei chachamim ata* — you turn out to be a mocker of the words of the sages. He cast his eyes upon him and the student became a pile of bones — *natan einav bo ve-na'asa gal shel atzamot*.

This is a striking conclusion to the *aggadata*. The punishment seems to assert that one must take these teachings seriously — not necessarily that every detail is to be understood with wooden literalism, but that one must be able to believe that it *could* happen. If you genuinely believe in *techiyat ha-meitim* and in God's unlimited power, then the physical impossibility of a thirty-by-thirty *shoham* stone offers no real objection. One might wonder why the student was not punished when he first mocked — when he said there isn't even an egg-sized piece of onyx in the whole world. The story works better dramatically this way: the mockery is silently registered, the evidence is shown, and it is only the student's proud declaration that his belief required empirical confirmation that draws Rabbi Yochanan's rebuke.

## Future Heights

### Two Hundred Cubits

A *meitivei* is raised from the verse *ve-holakhtem komemiyut* — you will walk with upright stature. Rabbi Meir says: in the future, human beings will stand two hundred *amot* tall, *kishtei komot shel adam* — double the stature of *Adam HaRishon*, who was a hundred *amot* tall. The word *komemiyut* is read as a double *komah*, a double stature.

### Temple Height

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: humans in the future will be a hundred *amot* tall, corresponding to the height of the *heikhal* — *kineged heikhal ve-kotlav*. The verse cited is *asher baneinu ki-neti'im megudalim bi-nureihem, benoteinu ke-zaviyot mechutavot tavnit heikhal* — our sons like saplings grown in their youth, our daughters like cornerstones carved in the form of the *heikhal*. Since the *heikhal* was a hundred *amot* tall, the future human stature will match it.

### Height Paradox

A problem immediately surfaces. Whether the future human being will be a hundred or two hundred *amot* tall, how can such a person pass through a gate that is a mere twenty *amot* high? If anything, the problem makes the future vision even grander than it first appeared: a human being two hundred *amot* tall is an even more fantastical image than an onyx stone thirty *amot* square.

### Window Blocks

The Gemara resolves the difficulty: *ki ka'amar Rabbi Yochanan, le-shivei de-bei zika* — when Rabbi Yochanan spoke of the thirty-by-thirty blocks with the ten-by-twenty carving, he was referring not to the gates themselves, but to the windows carved into the gateposts for light and air. The gates themselves are far larger.

## Seven Canopies

### Canopy Merit

Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches: in the future, God will make seven *chupot* for each and every righteous person — *atid Hakadosh Baruch Hu la-asot sheva chupot le-chol tzadik ve-tzadik*. Earlier we saw a *sukkah* from the *leviatan*'s skin; now each *tzadik* receives seven individual canopies of divine glory. The proof-text is Yeshayahu 4: *u-vara Hashem al kol mechon Har Tziyon ve-al mikraeha, anan yomam ve-ashan ve-nogah esh lehava lailah, ki al kol kavod chuppah* — God will create upon every place of Mount Zion and upon those called to it, a cloud by day and smoke and the brightness of flaming fire by night, for over all glory there shall be a *chuppah*.

### Isaiah's Seven

Counting the elements in the verse yields the seven *chupot*: *anan* (cloud) is one, *anan yomam* (cloud by day) could be read as elaborating, *ashan* (smoke) is two, *nogah* (brightness) is three, *esh* (fire) is four, *lehava* (flame) is five, *al kol kavod* is six — though the *Rashbam* notes this phrase is descriptive rather than a discrete *chuppah*, meaning each canopy is calibrated to the person's honor — and seven is the next verse, *ve-sukkah tihyeh le-tzel yomam*, which is also quoted at the opening of *Masechet Sukkah*. Each *tzadik* receives all seven, but just as every person can live in a house while houses vary enormously in grandeur, so each person's *chupot* are calibrated to their individual merit and deeds.

### Burning Jealousy

The Gemara asks: why would *ashan* — smoke — be part of a divine canopy? Rabbi Chanina answers: *she-kol mi she-einav tzarot be-talmidei chachamim ba-olam ha-zeh, mitmal'ot einav ashan le-olam ha-ba* — whoever begrudged the Torah scholars in this world will have his eyes filled with smoke in the world to come. This may represent a different type of *derasha* from the counting of canopies above.

Similarly: why would *esh* — fire — feature in a *chuppah*? Rabbi Chanina teaches the famous dictum: *kol echad ve-echad nichveh me-chuppato shel chaveiro* — every person is burned by the canopy of his companion. Even among the righteous, there are levels; and even having a magnificent *chuppah*, one can see that another's is still more glorious. The resulting feeling — a combination of jealousy, regret, and the painful recognition of what one could have achieved — burns. This is not merely envy in a base sense; it is the anguish of confronting one's own unrealized potential when the alternative stands before you. *Oy la-osa busha, oy la-osa kelimah* — woe to that shame, woe to that embarrassment.

### Moses & Joshua

A parallel is drawn. When God said to Moshe *ve-nasata me-hodcha alav* — put from your glory upon Yehoshua — the word is *me-hodcha*, from your glory, not *kol hodcha*, not all of your glory. The elders of Yehoshua's generation, who had known Moshe, would say: *penei Moshe ke-penei chamah, penei Yehoshua ke-penei levanah* — the face of Moshe was like the sun, the face of Yehoshua was like the moon. The moon, of course, only reflects the sun's light. *Oy la-osa busha, oy la-osa kelimah* — woe to such shame and embarrassment. The *Rashbam* explains this not solely as personal embarrassment for Yehoshua, but as the shame of an entire generation that had so quickly descended from such a level: *bi-zman mu'at nitma'et ha-kavod kol kach* — in such a short time, the honor has diminished so greatly.

## Adam's Canopies

### Eden's Treasures

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina teaches: God made ten *chupot* for *Adam HaRishon* in *Gan Eden* — *eser chupot asah Hakadosh Baruch Hu le-Adam HaRishon be-Gan Eden*. The *tzaddikim* of the future merit seven; the first human being had ten in paradise. The proof is the verse in Yechezkel addressed to *Chiram* the king of Tyre: *be-Eden gan Elohim hayita, kol even yekara* — you were in the Garden of Eden, every precious stone [was your covering]. Counting the ten types of precious things enumerated in that verse — stones and gold together — yields the ten *chupot*.

### Eleven Canopies

Mar Zutra holds that there are eleven *chupot*, not ten, because *kol even yekara* — "every precious stone" — is itself a separate, generalized item beyond the specific ten listed, making it the eleventh. Rabbi Yochanan adds: the least valuable of all these items in *Gan Eden* was gold — *ve-hagarua she-ba-kulam zahav* — because gold is listed last in the verse. The general principle is that the more important items are listed first.

### Chiram's Pride

The verse then asks: *mai melechet tupayecha u-nekevecha bach* — what is the work of your *tupayecha* and your *nekevecha* within you? This is all within Yechezkel's prophecy against *Chiram* of Tyre, who had grown profoundly arrogant. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: God said to *Chiram* — *bach nistakalti u-varati nekavim nekavim be-adam* — it was in anticipation of someone like you that I made human beings full of orifices. From those orifices all bodily waste exits — a reminder that however grand a person's self-image, he is flesh and blood like all others. The *Rashbam* connects *tupayecha* to the word for a grave, *ha-kever she-chalul ke-tof* — hollow like a tambourine — meaning the awareness of mortality is built into human anatomy.

An alternative reading: *nistakalti ve-kanasti mita al ha-adam* — I saw that someone like you would arise, and that is why I decreed mortality upon human beings — not because of *Adam HaRishon*'s sin with the tree alone, but so that human beings would always know themselves to be mortal and not mistake themselves for gods. The whole sequence presents a meditation on humility: the righteous receive magnificent *chupot* but are burned by their companion's greater one; *Adam HaRishon* had ten *chupot* but was mortal; and *Chiram*, who thought himself divine, is reminded through the very structure of the human body that he is not.

## God's Name

### Two Jerusalems

Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan draws the distinction: *lo ke-Yerushalayim shel ha-olam ha-zeh Yerushalayim shel ha-olam ha-ba* — the Jerusalem of the world to come is not like the Jerusalem of this world. In this world, *kol ha-rotzeh la'alot oleh* — anyone who wishes can go up to Jerusalem. But in the world to come, *ein olim ela ha-mezumanim lah* — only those who have been summoned, invited to it, will ascend. Entry into the future Jerusalem requires, as it were, an engraved invitation.

### Three Names

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: three things are called by the name of God — *sheloshah nikra'u shemo shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu*: *tzaddikim*, *Mashiach*, and *Yerushalayim*. The *tzaddikim* are established from the verse already cited: *kol ha-nikra vi-shmi ve-li-chevodi berativ* — all who are called by My name and for My honor I have created. *Mashiach* is established from the verse in Yirmiyahu: *ve-zeh shemo asher yikre'u Hashem tzidkenu* — and this is his name by which he will be called, "God is our righteousness." *Yerushalayim* is established from Yechezkel: *saviv shemonah asar alef, ve-shem ha-ir mi-yom Hashem shamah* — the circumference is eighteen thousand, and the name of the city from that day shall be "God is there." *Al tikrei shamah ela shemah* — do not read it as "there" (*shamah*) but as "her name" (*shemah*): God is its name.

The theological audacity of this teaching is striking. The *tzaddikim* who dwell in Jerusalem are called by God's name; Jerusalem itself is called by God's name; and *Mashiach* bears God's name. If the righteous dwell in Jerusalem, they are dwelling, in a sense, in God — and they themselves bear His name. The image is extraordinary: God dwelling in God, the righteous called God, dwelling in a city named God.

### Called Holy

Rabbi Elazar teaches: in the future, it will be declared *kadosh* — holy — before the righteous, just as the angels declare *kadosh* before God. *Atidim tzaddikim she-omrim lifneihem kadosh.* The proof-text: *ve-hayah ha-nishar be-Tziyon ve-ha-notar bi-Yerushalayim kadosh ye'amer lo* — those who remain in Zion and in Jerusalem, holy will be said of him. The righteous, dwelling in Jerusalem — the extension of the Temple, the place where God's Presence rests — reach a level where the angels address them as they address God. The entire arc of this *aggadata* builds to this point: the conquest of the *leviatan*, the feast, the *sukkot*, the shining walls, the canopies calibrated to merit, and now — the righteous themselves called by God's name, declared holy before them.

## Jerusalem's Future

### Jerusalem's Measure

Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: God will raise Jerusalem three *parsaot* upward — *atid Hakadosh Baruch Hu le-hagbi'ah et Yerushalayim gimel parsa'ot le-maalah*. The proof is *ve-ramah ve-yashvah tachteha* — it will be raised and dwell beneath itself. *Tachteha* is read as *ke-tachteha* — by as much as its current depth below, meaning the elevation from its hilltop base; that same measure will be added upward. Whether this means it will be raised physically into the air — floating, approaching the heavenly Jerusalem — or simply elevated to a far greater height is debated. A floating Jerusalem fits the subsequent imagery of ascending like clouds.

Rabbah relates that a certain elder told him: *ledidi chazi li Yerushalayim kaimaita, ve-tlata parsei havya* — I saw the first Jerusalem, and it was three *parsaot* [high/elevated]. How Rabbah could have seen the first Jerusalem requires clarification — presumably it means before its destruction, or possibly a prophetic vision.

### No Walls

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa teaches: God originally wished to give Jerusalem a fixed measure — *bikesh Hakadosh Baruch Hu latet et Yerushalayim be-mida* — which is a strange idea: why would God wish to limit Jerusalem? Perhaps even a vast but finite size represents a kind of limit on what is, by its nature, unlimited. The measuring angel of Zechariah's vision represents this impulse. But the ministering angels protested: *Ribbono shel Olam, harbeh krachim barata be-olamecha shel umot ha-olam, ve-lo natata midat orchan ve-midat rochban* — You have created many cities in Your world for the nations and gave none of them a fixed size; *Yerushalayim she-shimcha betochah, u-mikdashecha betochah, ve-tzaddikim betochah* — Jerusalem in which Your name rests, in which Your sanctuary stands, in which the righteous dwell — *ata noten bah midah*? You will give it a limit? Immediately: *prazot teshev Yerushalayim* — Jerusalem shall dwell as an unwalled city, spread out without limit, *me-rov adam u-behema betochah* — because of the multitude of people and animals within it.

### Added Structures

Resh Lakish teaches: in the future God will add to Jerusalem a thousand *tapaf* of gardens — the *Rashbam* reads *tapaf* as a *gematria*, yielding approximately 169,000 gardens — along with 210,000 towers, approximately 146,000 castles (*biranyot*), and vast numbers of a structure called *tutafra'ot*, also a type of castle. *Tosafot* takes a different approach, reading the terms as descriptive rather than numerical. In either reading, the multiplication is staggering.

### Building Sizes

Each one of these structures, Resh Lakish continues, will be as large as *Tzippori be-shalvatah* — Tzippori at its greatest height, at its peak of prosperity. A *baraita* provides testimony: Rabbi Yosei said: *ani ra'iti Tzippori be-shalvatah* — I myself saw Tzippori in its prosperity, and it was so abundant that even the remnants scraped from the bottom of the pot were sold in its markets.

### Size Expansion

The Gemara concludes with one final *derasha* on the phrase *ve-tzela el tzela, shalosh ve-sheloshim pa'amim* — side chamber by side chamber, thirty-three times — a reference to the chambers of the *Beit HaMikdash* in Yechezkel. What do thirty-three times mean in this context? In the name of Rav Yehoshua of Sachni: if the future Jerusalem will be three times the size of the current one, then each building will have thirty stories — high-rise Jerusalem. If it will be thirty times the size of the current one, then each building will have three stories. The number thirty-three encodes both possibilities: three Jerusalems each with thirty floors, or thirty Jerusalems each with three floors. With this the *aggadata* of Bava Batra concludes, and the *masechta* returns to *halakhic* discussion.

---

---

# Bava Batra 76

## Boat Acquisition Debate

### Introduction

The sugya on this daf represents a radical shift from the *aggadic* discussions and classic Bava Batra material that had occupied the preceding pages. We now enter a discussion that could have come from many other tractates in *shas* — a careful legal analysis of the mechanics of acquisition. The daf begins approximately fifteen lines from the bottom of 75b, immediately after the double-dot break.

### Rav's Minimal Movement

The opening word is *itmar* — a *sefina*, a boat, is being acquired by *meshicha*. There is something immediately arresting about this. A boat is classified as *metaltelin*, and so in principle the classic modes of acquisition for movable property apply: *meshicha*, *hagbahah*, and as we will see, *mesirah*. One might wonder whether an unusually large vessel should be treated more like land and require a *shtar*, but the *gemara* does not take that path. Instead, the entire focus is a precise technical question: how far must the boat actually be moved?

Rav holds: *kivan shemashach kol shehu kanah* — once the buyer has displaced the boat even a small amount, even a single centimeter, the *kinyan* takes effect.

### Shmuel's Full Displaceme…

Shmuel disagrees: *lo kanah ad sheyimshoch es kulah* — the buyer does not acquire until he has pulled the entire boat completely out of its original position, so that no part of it remains where any part of it had been before.

### Boat Movement Example

To clarify: according to Rav, moving the boat even slightly — displacing it a negligible distance — is sufficient *meshicha*. According to Shmuel, the boat must be moved its full length, so that its new position shares no overlap with its original position. The boat, being an inanimate object, moves as a unified whole; every part of it shifts together whenever it moves at all.

### Animal Movement Tannaim

The *gemara* asks whether this dispute mirrors an earlier Tannaitic debate. A *Tosefta* in Kiddushin enumerates how one performs *mesirah* for large animals: taking hold of its hoof (*achaza b'talphah*), its hair or tail (*besearah*), the saddle (*u'ukaf she'aleha*), the saddlebag (*beshalif she'aleha*), the bit in its mouth (*bafrombaya shebepiha*), or the bell around its neck (*bezog shebetzavara*) — any physical contact with the animal or its appurtenances constitutes *mesirah*. It is worth pausing here on the concept of *mesirah* itself. *Mesirah* — literally "handing over" — cannot be performed on a *hefker* object, because there must be a transferor who hands it over. According to one opinion in *Tosafos*, this requires that the seller or giver literally places the object in the buyer's hand; another opinion holds that it suffices for the transferor to instruct the buyer verbally to take hold, after which the buyer's act of seizing constitutes the *mesirah*. Either way, the critical distinction is that unlike *hagbahah* or *meshicha* — where the physical act in itself demonstrates ownership, as when one lifts something up or pulls it toward oneself — *mesirah* is not self-explanatory as a physical act. Holding a saddle or a hoof does not by itself demonstrate ownership. What gives the act its legal significance is the context of transfer: it is the handing-over that is symbolically meaningful, not merely the physical contact.

Returning to the Tannaitic debate on *meshicha* for animals: the *Tosefta* in Kiddushin asks *keitzad bimeshicha* — how does one perform *meshicha*? One method is calling the animal and having it come (*koreh lah vehia ba'ah*); another is striking it with a stick so it runs forward (*o shehikisha bamakel veratzta lefanav*). The key ruling is: *kivan she'akra yad varegel kena'ah* — once the animal has lifted a foreleg and a hind leg, the *kinyan* is complete. Rabbi Achai (some say Rabbi Acha) disagrees: *ad shetehalech melo komatah* — it must travel its full height, or presumably its full body length. This appears to map directly onto the dispute of Rav and Shmuel.

### Boat vs. Animal Logic

The *gemara* initially suggests that Rav follows the *tanna kamma* and Shmuel follows Rabbi Achai, but then rejects this framing. Each *amora* explains why the boat and the animal are not equivalent, even if they hold different positions regarding one of them.

Rav says: *amar lach Rav ana d'amri afilu l'Rabbi Acha* — I, who require only minimal displacement for a boat, could agree even to Rabbi Achai that an animal must be fully displaced. The reason: when an animal lifts a foreleg and a hind leg, *beduchta kaima* — it is essentially still where it was. The two legs that moved do not mean the body has shifted; the other legs remain planted, and a large portion of the animal's mass has not moved at all. Therefore a more substantial displacement is required. But a boat is different: *kivan denad purta nad kulah* — when a boat moves even a little, every single part of the boat has been displaced from its original position. The boat moves as a rigid whole. Therefore even minimal movement suffices.

Shmuel says the opposite: *ana d'amri afilu k'tanna kamma* — I, who require full displacement for a boat, would agree that for an animal even the lifting of a foreleg and hind leg suffices. Why? *De'keivan d'me'akrai yad varegel, idach me'akrai kai* — once the animal has begun to step, lifting one foreleg and one hind leg, the biological momentum of the living creature means it will continue to move; the step will complete itself. For a living being, beginning the motion is as good as completing it. But a boat is inanimate: *ei mashchei kulah in, ei lo lo* — if you moved the whole thing, yes; if not, no.

The underlying conceptual axis is thus clear: the dispute is about what counts as meaningful displacement for the purpose of *meshicha*, and the answer differs based on the nature of the object. An animal's life-force (*chayut*) means that initiating movement is effectively completing it. An inanimate boat moves uniformly but must be moved completely. These considerations then determine where each *amora* draws the line for each case.

---

## Debt Acquisition Intro

### What Are Otiot?

Having addressed boat acquisition, the *gemara* now pivots to a far more abstract subject, introduced by a *baraita* in Kiddushin. The *baraita* states: *sefina nikneis bimeshicha* — a boat is acquired by *meshicha*. Rabbi Natan then adds: *sefina v'otiot niknot bimeshicha uv'shtar* — a boat and *otiot* are acquired by *meshicha* and *shtar*. The word *otiot*, literally "letters," requires explanation. The *gemara* will understand it to mean a debt — specifically, the legal claim represented by a promissory document. If Reuven holds a *shtar* documenting that Shimon owes him a thousand *zuz*, and Reuven wishes to sell that debt to a third party, the question is how such a transfer is effected.

### Abstract Debt Problem

This is a genuinely difficult conceptual problem. The money is owed personally to Reuven. What exactly is being transferred? One might propose transferring the liens — the encumbrances on Shimon's property that accompany the debt. *Tosafos* in fact raises this question. But the *gemara* does not pursue this avenue, and *Tosafos* offers two reasons why not. First, liens only exist in the context of a personal debt obligation; they cannot be detached and transferred independently, because they exist only as an extension of the underlying obligation. Second, and separately, one does not own enough of the encumbered property to effect a transfer of the lien — one's interest in the property is too abstract a quasi-ownership to be alienated. In any case, a debt can exist without any lien at all, so the mechanism of debt-sale must be conceptualized independently of liens.

There are two ways to conceptualize what is transferred when a debt is sold. One approach holds that the debt remains fundamentally personal — Shimon still technically owes Reuven — but a kind of direct-deposit arrangement is created, such that any payment flows immediately to the purchaser. Under this view, Reuven retains the theoretical ability to forgive the debt even after selling it, leaving the buyer without recourse against Shimon (though potentially with a claim against Reuven in *grama* or *garmi*). This is associated with the position of Shmuel. The second approach treats the debt more abstractly: there is an obligation that exists as a transferable entity, and it can be conveyed outright to a new creditor, who then stands in the original lender's place. This conceptual ambiguity about what a debt *is* underlies the subsequent halakhic debate about how to transfer it.

Because a debt is abstract, the *gemara* refers to it as *otiot* — letters, i.e., what is written in the document. The physical document itself — the parchment and ink — is just a piece of paper. As the *gemara* will note, one could use it as a bottle stopper. The *kinyan* of *meshicha* applied to the document would acquire only the paper. What the purchaser actually wants is not the paper but what it represents: the debt, expressed in its *otiot*. The question, then, is what mode of transfer is adequate to convey not the paper but the obligation it records.

### Physical vs. Symbolic Ac…

The *gemara* returns to the *baraita* and notes that *otiot* seem to appear without introduction — Rabbi Natan is responding to a position the *tanna kamma* never stated. The *gemara* therefore reads the *baraita* as incomplete: *chisuri mechasra vehachi katani* — there are missing words, and the text must be reconstructed. The *tanna kamma* is understood to have stated a position about debts — that a debt is acquired by *mesirah* — and Rabbi Natan then responds to that position. This reading is justified because, as the *gemara* will show, there is another *baraita* that explicitly attributes the *mesirah* position to a Tannaitic authority, and we therefore know the opinion exists to be read into the *tanna kamma* here.

After further consideration, the *gemara* realizes that even Rabbi Natan's position as stated needs re-reading: if the *shtar* element in *meshicha uv'shtar* is attributed to the *sefina*, that makes no sense — one does not use a *shtar* to acquire cattle, and a boat is treated analogously. The *shtar* must therefore pertain to the debt, not the boat. The *gemara* then rereads the *baraita* to yield: both the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Natan agree that a *sefina* is acquired by *meshicha*; they debate only how to transfer a debt, where the *tanna kamma* says *mesirah* and Rabbi Natan says a *shtar* is required.

### Why Mesira Works

This leads to the key conceptual question: why is *mesirah* a better candidate than *meshicha* or *hagbahah* for transferring a debt? The answer lies in what each act signifies. *Meshicha* and *hagbahah* are self-contained physical demonstrations of control: I have pulled this toward me, I have lifted this up — the physical act itself, without any further context, shows that I control the object. That works well for acquiring a lost object or a *hefker* item. But when applied to a *shtar*, *meshicha* or *hagbahah* demonstrates only that I control the piece of paper, not that I have acquired the debt it records.

*Mesirah*, by contrast, is not self-sufficient as a physical act — it derives its significance from the context of transfer. Holding a saddle does not demonstrate ownership by itself; what makes it meaningful is that it occurs within an act of handing over. For the same reason, *mesirah* cannot be performed on a *hefker* item, since there is no transferor to confer context on the act. Applied to a *shtar*, then, *mesirah* says more than *meshicha*: the owner of the document is handing it over, and given what is written in it, that handover can symbolically represent the transfer of the underlying debt, not merely the transfer of the paper.

---

## Rabbi vs. Sages Debate

### Rabbi's Mesira Only

The *gemara* now identifies the debate about debt acquisition with a broader Tannaitic dispute. A *baraita* states: *otiot niknot bimesirah divrei Rabbi* — debts are acquired by *mesirah* alone, this is the position of Rabbi (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi).

### Sages' Mesira + Shtar

The Sages say: *bein katav v'lo masar, bein masar v'lo katav, lo kanah* — whether one wrote a new transfer document without handing over the original, or handed over the original without writing a new document, the buyer does not acquire; *ad sheyichtov veyimsor* — both acts are required together.

### Why Both Acts Needed

The logic of each position is as follows. Rabbi holds that handing over the original *shtar* — the document stating that the debtor owes the money — is symbolically sufficient to convey the debt, since the owner is physically transferring the very instrument that represents the obligation. The Sages hold that this alone is not enough: for *mesirah* of a *shtar* to successfully transfer the debt rather than merely the paper, it must be accompanied by a second document explicitly stating that the creditor is transferring all his rights in the debt and in the debtor's encumbered property to the purchaser. Without this clarifying document, the symbolic act is insufficient.

To be precise about what the Sages require: two documents are involved. The original *shtar* — e.g., "Shimon owes Reuven a thousand *zuz*" — is physically handed over (*mesirah*), and simultaneously a new *shtar* is written stating the terms of the transfer. Rabbi requires only the handing over of the original. The Sages require both the *mesirah* of the original and the *ketivah* of the new one.

### Shtar's Limited Scope

Why does a new *shtar* alone not suffice to transfer the debt, without the accompanying *mesirah*? The technical answer is that a *shtar* as an instrument of *kinyan* has a narrowly defined scope: it operates for land and for acquiring or altering the status of persons (as in *kiddushin* or *gittin*). It does not operate for *metaltelin*, and a fortiori it cannot serve as the instrument to transfer an abstract debt. Therefore, the *shtar* written by the Sages is not functioning as a *shtar kinyan* — it is not the vehicle of transfer. The vehicle of transfer is the *mesirah* of the original document. What the new *shtar* does is serve as a clarifying instrument: it establishes the context that makes the *mesirah* meaningful, declaring explicitly that the handover is intended to convey the debt and not merely the paper. Alternatively, one might frame it symbolically: if the creditor writes a document stating he is transferring the debt but continues to hold onto the original *shtar*, the transfer lacks conviction; the physical handing over of the original, accompanying the written declaration, reinforces and completes the act.

The *gemara* then proceeds to identify which position in the earlier *baraita* (the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Natan) corresponds to which position here (Rabbi and the Sages). If the *tanna kamma* who says *otiot bemesirah* is identified with Rabbi, one immediately faces a difficulty: elsewhere a *baraita* states explicitly that Rabbi holds *sefina nikneis bimesirah* — Rabbi says a boat is acquired by *mesirah*. So if this *tanna kamma* is Rabbi, why does he speak only of *meshicha* for the boat and not mention *mesirah*? And conversely, the Sages in that second *baraita* say a boat requires *meshicha* or *sechirat makom* (renting the space in which the boat sits) — but neither of those, as we will see, works in a *reshut harabim*, which leads to the *gemara*'s next major discussion.

---

## Contexts & Braitot (III)

### Identifying Positions

The *gemara* now undertakes to reconcile the various *braitot* and identify which Tannaitic authorities hold which positions.
