The *baraita* that has the *tanna kamma* saying *sefina bemeshicha* and Rabbi Natan saying *sefina v'otiot bemeshicha uv'shtar* presents an apparent difficulty when mapped onto the second *baraita* featuring Rabbi and the Sages. If the *tanna kamma* of the first *baraita* corresponds to Rabbi, why does he describe the boat as acquired only by *meshicha*, when Rabbi elsewhere says *mesirah* also works for a boat? The *gemara* will resolve this by reference to context.

### Rabbi on Boats

As the *gemara* establishes, Rabbi's position in the second *baraita* is: *sefina nikneis bemesirah divrei Rabbi* — Rabbi says a boat is acquired by *mesirah*. The Sages disagree: *lo kanah ad sheyimshachenah* — one does not acquire until one has dragged it, or alternatively, until one has rented the location where the boat is situated (*sechirat makom*). Rabbi thus accepts *mesirah* as a valid mode for boat acquisition; the Sages do not.

### Context Matters

The resolution is: *kan birshut harabbim, kan besimta* — one *baraita* speaks of a boat in the *reshut harabim* (the public domain), and the other speaks of a boat in a *simta* (a semi-private alley). This distinction is the key to understanding the entire discussion. *Meshicha* works by demonstrating physical control over an object. But in the *reshut harabim* — a busy public thoroughfare — the act of dragging an object toward oneself does not meaningfully demonstrate control. An object left on the ground in a crowded public space is not securely in anyone's domain; dragging it a step or two does not establish dominion in any symbolically convincing sense. *Meshicha* therefore does not effect a *kinyan* in the *reshut harabim*. In a *simta*, by contrast, the semi-private character of the space means that pulling an object toward oneself does carry the significance of establishing control, and *meshicha* is valid there.

*Mesirah*, on the other hand, is not about physical control at all — it is about the symbolic act of transfer. Like *chalifin* (the *kinyan sudar*, where the buyer hands the seller a cloth or utensil and by that act acquires the purchased item), *mesirah* works through the signification of transfer rather than through a demonstration of physical dominion. For the same reason, *chalifin* works in the *reshut harabim* — its efficacy is independent of the location because it is not about controlling the space. Accordingly, *mesirah* functions precisely in the *reshut harabim*, where *meshicha* does not.

The first *baraita* (*tanna kamma*: *sefina bemeshicha*) therefore speaks of a case in the *simta*, where *meshicha* is valid. Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, identified as the *tanna kamma*, is not denying that *mesirah* works — he is simply describing the *simta* context, where *meshicha* is the applicable mode. The second *baraita* (*divrei Rabbi: sefina bemesirah*) speaks of the *reshut harabim*, where *mesirah* is the relevant mode and *meshicha* is not available. There is no contradiction.

One might ask: in the *simta*, if *meshicha* works, why can one not also use *mesirah*? This question generates a fascinating discussion among the *rishonim*. The *Rashbam* and several others hold that when a more robust mode of *kinyan* is available — *meshicha* in a *simta* — only that mode works; the weaker or more symbolic mode (*mesirah*) does not. Rabbeinu Tam sharply rejects this principle: are *kinyanim* like *mitzvot*, where one must do the most preferred form? If *mesirah* works, it works — the availability of *meshicha* does not negate *mesirah*. This debate is left open by the *gemara*, though the basic resolution of the textual contradiction stands.

A further problem emerges: if the second *baraita* is set in the *reshut harabim*, how do the Sages there say that *meshicha* and *sechirat makom* work? *Meshicha* does not function in the *reshut harabim*, as just established, and *sechirat makom* — renting the space in which the boat sits — is impossible in a *reshut harabim*, since one cannot rent out a public thoroughfare that one does not own.

### Sages on Boats

The Sages' position requires a contextual reinterpretation, provided by the next section of the *gemara*.

---

## Kinyanim Principles (III)

### Context & Meaning

The underlying principle at work throughout this discussion is that the meaning and validity of a *kinyan* act is not intrinsic to the act itself but is determined by context. The same physical motion — dragging an object — is a valid *kinyan* in one context and entirely meaningless in another. This is not arbitrary: *kinyan* acts signify ownership and control, and for that signification to be operative, it must be intelligible in the setting where it occurs. Dragging a briefcase across Times Square does not demonstrate meaningful control in the way that pulling an object to oneself in a quiet alley does. *Mesirah*, because it signifies not physical control but the act of transfer, is independent of this spatial dimension and retains its meaning regardless of setting. This is also why *hagbahah* — lifting an object off the ground — works universally: the act of physically lifting something up places it entirely under one's bodily control, and that is unambiguous in any location.

---

## Contexts & Braitot (III)

### Abaye & Rava

Abaye and Rava together articulate the rule precisely: *mesirah konah birshut harabim uvechatzer she'eino shel sheneihem* — *mesirah* effects acquisition in the *reshut harabim* and in a courtyard belonging to neither party. *Meshicha konah besimta uvechatzer shehi shel sheneihem* — *meshicha* effects acquisition in a *simta* or in a courtyard shared by both parties. In the latter settings, the buyer has some degree of right or access to the space, and the act of pulling the object toward himself in that semi-controlled environment carries the meaning of establishing dominion.

---

## Kinyanim Principles (III)

### Hagbaha Universal

*Hagbahah* — lifting — is categorically different from both *meshicha* and *mesirah*: *hagbahah koneh bechol makom*, it effects acquisition everywhere. The act of lifting an object off the ground places it entirely under the lifter's bodily control in a way that is unambiguous regardless of setting. Even if the buyer is standing in the seller's courtyard, lifting the object demonstrates full physical control, and the *kinyan* takes effect. The seller's desire to transfer and the buyer's act of lifting together complete the transaction without any dependence on the character of the surrounding space.

---

## Contexts & Braitot (III)…

### Sages' Solution

Returning to the difficulty about the Sages' position in the *reshut harabim*: *mai ad sheyimshachenah* — what do the Sages mean when they say the buyer must drag it? And *mai ad sheyiskor mekomo* — what do they mean when they say he must rent the space? The *gemara* resolves this: *hachi ka'amar: ad sheyimshachenah mereshut harabim lesimta* — what the Sages mean by *meshicha* is not *meshicha* within the *reshut harabim* (which would be invalid), but dragging it *out of* the *reshut harabim* and *into* the *simta*. Once the boat has been pulled from the public domain into a semi-private alley, the *meshicha* in the *simta* is valid. Similarly, *sechirat makom* applies when the boat is in some privately owned location: the seller rents that space to the buyer, and the boat — now sitting in a space temporarily belonging to the buyer — is acquired through a form of *kinyan chatzer*. The Sages are thus not claiming that *meshicha* works within the *reshut harabim*; they are insisting that the buyer must go to the additional effort of moving the boat to a context where *meshicha* is valid, since they do not accept *mesirah* as sufficient for boat acquisition.

---

## Kinyanim Principles (III)…

### Chalifin Alternative

This leads naturally to a final observation about *chalifin*. If a boat sits in the *reshut harabim* and the Sages hold that neither *mesirah* nor *meshicha* within that domain is valid, what can a buyer do if dragging the boat to a *simta* is not practicable — say, the boat is on the open sea? The answer is *chalifin*: the buyer hands the seller a cloth or utensil, and by that symbolic exchange the boat is acquired. *Chalifin* works universally because, like *mesirah*, its efficacy is not a function of physical control but of symbolic convention — it is, at its core, the legal formalization of the parties' mutual commitment to the transaction. Indeed, this makes *chalifin* conceptually the most abstract of the *kinyanim*: whereas *meshicha* and *hagbahah* are about demonstrating physical mastery over the object, and *mesirah* is about the symbolic handover of the object itself, *chalifin* entirely abstracts away from the object being sold. The buyer hands the seller something unrelated, and by that convention acquires the purchased item. It is, in essence, a formalized handshake. As such, it succeeds precisely where the physically grounded modes of acquisition cannot reach.

---

---

# Bava Batra 77

## Boat Acquisition

### Prior Discussion

Today's *daf* is Bava Batra 77, and we pick up in the middle of 76b, approximately a third from the bottom of the page, at the line beginning with the word *Rava*: *leima Abaye ve-Rava*. We are resuming a discussion that had been underway regarding a very important topic: how one transfers a *shtar chov*, a document of debt, in a case where the goal is not merely to hand over the physical paper but to transfer the underlying loan itself.

The scenario is a familiar one. Shimon owes Reuven a hundred dollars, and Reuven wishes to transfer that debt to Levi. Levi pays Reuven fifty dollars now, and from that point Shimon will owe the money to Levi. The question is how Reuven effects that transfer. Physically handing over the *shtar* is not obviously sufficient. A whole discussion had developed around the concept of *otiyot* — the abstract debt represented by the letters of the document — and whether a *mesira*, a handing over of the *shtar*, suffices to transfer it, or whether one also requires a separately written document, a *shtar* that makes the transfer explicit.

In the middle of that discussion, the *Gemara* had introduced the question of a *sefina*, a boat, and how it is acquired. In one source, Rabbi holds that a boat is acquired through *mesira* — handing over the rope or some attached part of the vessel. In another source, Rabbi appears to say that a boat is acquired through *meshikha*, drawing or pulling it. The *Gemara* reconciles these by distinguishing between domains: in a *reshut harabim*, a public domain, *mesira* works whereas *meshikha* does not; in a *simta*, an alley or side street, *meshikha* works. There is a dispute between the Rashbam and Tosafot as to whether *mesira* also works in a *simta*, but it is clear that in a *reshut harabim* only *mesira* is effective.

### Rabbi vs Chachamim

With that background in place, the *Gemara* now wraps up the boat discussion. The question raised is whether Abaye and Rava, who rule that in a *reshut harabim* only *mesira* works and *meshikha* does not, are thereby aligning themselves with Rabbi — a *da'at yachid*, a minority opinion — against the *Chachamim*, who require *meshikha* into a *simta* and do not allow *mesira* in a *reshut harabim* to suffice.

### Domain-Based Reconciliation

The *Gemara* asks: does this mean Abaye and Rava must follow only Rabbi? The answer is nuanced. Rav Ashi says: *i de-amar lei lekh chazeki u-knei* — if the seller explicitly said "go take possession of it," using the language of *mesira*, then everyone agrees, both Rabbi and the *Chachamim*, that *mesira* in a *reshut harabim* is effective. In such a case, Abaye and Rava's ruling that *mesira* works in a *reshut harabim* would be consistent with the view of all authorities.

### Abaye & Rava Resolution

The question then becomes: what is the specific case in which Rabbi and the *Chachamim* actually disagree? The *Gemara* answers: *de-amar lei lekh mshokh u-knei* — the seller used the language of *meshikha*. He said "go draw it." Now the question is how to interpret that instruction. The *Chachamim* hold *kafida*: the seller was being *makpid*, insisting that the acquisition be effected specifically through *meshikha*, and therefore *mesira* will not work and the buyer must drag the boat into a *simta*. Rabbi, on the other hand, holds *marei makom hu lo*: the seller was merely indicating where the boat is, giving the buyer the option and the freedom to take it home — he was not imposing a condition on the mode of acquisition. Therefore, *mesira* in the *reshut harabim* still works according to Rabbi.

### Intent & Language

This resolution does raise a significant difficulty. If the entire dispute between Rabbi and the *Chachamim* turns only on the narrow question of how to interpret the seller's phrasing — whether it constitutes a binding condition — it is striking that the *baraita* states the disagreement so baldly, without indicating that it hinges entirely on a question of intent. Rabbi says *mesira*, the *Chachamim* say *meshikha*, with no qualification. And yet what the *Gemara* is really saying is that they have no fundamental disagreement about how a *sefina* may be acquired; they agree it can be done by *mesira* in a *reshut harabim*, and they differ only over what the seller meant when he used a particular form of words.

### Seller's Intent

Nevertheless, this is the *Gemara*'s resolution in order to bring Abaye and Rava into agreement with both Rabbi and the *Chachamim* simultaneously. This also occasions a brief aside, noted in the *Rishonim*, about *mesira* itself: there is a dispute among the *Rishonim* whether *mesira* requires a physical handing over, or whether it is sufficient that one verbally conveys it — saying *lekh chazek u-knei*, "go take possession" — without any physical act of transfer.

---

## Debt Transfer

### Rav Pappa's Rule

With the boat discussion concluded, the *Gemara* returns to its major theme: the transfer of a *shtar chov* and the mechanism required to effectuate that transfer. Rav Pappa rules: *hai man de-mazbin lei shtara le-chavrei, tzarich lemichtav lei kni hu ve-chol shibuda de-bei* — one who sells a promissory note to another must write in a document: "acquire this and all the liens attached to it."

To make this concrete: if Shimon owes Reuven a hundred dollars and Reuven transfers the *shtar* to Levi, Levi will now have in his possession the original *shtar* stating that Shimon owes money to Reuven. But what does that alone accomplish for Levi? This is why *mesira* alone is insufficient according to the *Chachamim*: Reuven must write a second document to Levi stating that he, Reuven, is transferring the debt — the obligation Shimon owes him — along with all the liens he holds on Shimon's property, to Levi. Only then, once Levi holds both the original *shtar* and this transfer document, does he fully acquire the debt and the attendant liens.

Rav Pappa's ruling thus accomplishes two things, according to the Rashbam: it specifies what language is required in the accompanying document (*kni hu ve-chol shibuda de-bei*), and it implicitly rules like the *Chachamim* against Rabbi — handing over the original *shtar* alone is not enough.

### Rav Ashi's Challenge

Rav Ashi reports that he presented this analysis before Rav Kahana and raised the following challenge. He reasoned: *ta'ama de-chsav lei hachi, ha lo chsav lei hachi lo kani* — it seems that Rav Pappa is saying the reason Levi acquires the debt is specifically because this additional language was written; had it not been written, Levi would not acquire even though Reuven handed him the *shtar*. But if so, asks Rav Ashi, why? Isn't the very act of Reuven handing the *shtar* to Levi self-evidently an expression of his intent to transfer the debt? *Le-tzoro pi tzluchosav hu tzarich?* — Does Levi need this document to serve as a bottle stopper? What else could he possibly want it for?

### Rav Kahana Response

Rav Kahana's response was direct: *in, letzor u-letzor* — yes, without the additional *shtar*, I will say that all Levi received is a bottle stopper. Unless something makes the transfer of the debt itself — as distinct from the physical paper — explicit in writing, then despite whatever Levi may have intended or expected, the debt itself has not transferred. Levi holds a piece of paper; he does not hold the loan.

### Rashbam Explanation

The Rashbam addresses what might seem like an obvious objection: surely if Levi paid fifty dollars for this hundred-dollar debt, no one imagines he paid for a piece of paper. The Rashbam concedes this point in full — of course Levi's intent was to acquire the debt — but insists that intent is not the operative question. The question is whether a halakhically sufficient act of transfer took place. If it did not, the debt did not transfer, regardless of what either party expected. Were Reuven to change his mind and say he would not go through with the sale, he would be entitled to do so, and would simply return the fifty dollars. The physical piece of paper is not enough; one needs the additional *shtar* to make explicit and to concretize the reality that the debt — not just the paper — is passing from Reuven to Levi.

---

## Otiyot Transfer Rules

### Ameimar's Ruling

We now arrive at the top of 77a. Ameimar rules: *hilchasa, otiyot niknas be-mesira ke-Rabbi* — the *halakha* is that *otiyot* are acquired through *mesira* alone, in accordance with Rabbi's view. This would mean, against what Rav Pappa appeared to be saying, that handing over the original *shtar* is sufficient to transfer a debt.

### Manuscript Variants

However, this ruling is far from settled, and there is a very large Tosafot here — as well as a substantial Tosafot on the preceding *daf* — that complicates matters considerably. The difficulty is a *girsa* question: what did Ameimar actually say? Some manuscripts read the ruling exactly as just stated, *hilchasa otiyot niknas be-mesira ke-Rabbi*. Other manuscripts — and Tosafot prefers this version — read the precise opposite: *hilchasa ein otiyot niknas be-mesira ke-rabbanan*, the *halakha* is that *otiyot* are not acquired through *mesira* alone, and we rule like the *Chachamim*, consistent with Rav Pappa's ruling. Under this *girsa*, one must both hand over the *shtar* and write a second document of transfer. Given that this *halakhic* ruling exists in two diametrically opposed textual versions, the ultimate conclusion about how to transfer a debt is genuinely uncertain from the *Gemara* alone.

### Rav Ashi Inquiry

Proceeding now as Tosafot reads the *Gemara* — i.e., taking the ruling to be that *mesira* alone is insufficient — Rav Ashi asks Ameimar: *gemara u-sevara*? Is the ruling that one needs both *mesira* and a written *shtar* something received as a tradition, or is it a logical conclusion, a *sevara*? Ameimar answers: *gemara* — it is a received tradition.

### Sevara on Abstraction

Rav Ashi then adds: *sevara nami hi* — there is also a compelling *sevara* that supports this conclusion. The reason is: *de-otiyot mili ninhu* — *otiyot*, the abstract debt, are in the final analysis just words. *U-mili be-mili lo miknan* — and words are not transferred merely with more words.

### Sevara Explained

This *sevara* deserves careful unpacking, and Tosafot explains it well. When Reuven hands the original *shtar* to Levi and says, "By my handing this over to you, you now own the debt Shimon owed me" — what exactly is being transferred? The physical piece of paper is a trivial object. What Reuven is really trying to transfer is the debt itself, which is an abstraction. All of the standard modes of *kinyan* — *meshikha*, *hagbahah*, *chazakah* — are grounded in physical acts that concretize the reality of a transfer of ownership. An abstract debt cannot be transferred merely through the words used to frame the handing-over of a document. That is *mili be-mili*, abstractions framed by words, and it is insufficient.

What is required instead is that the transfer itself be concretized. Reuven writes a new *shtar* stating: I, Reuven, am transferring to Levi the debt Shimon owes me, together with all the liens I hold on Shimon's property. Now the abstract debt has been given a concrete written form, and that document — which expresses the new legal reality — is handed over to Levi. Levi takes possession of a physical document that encodes his new status as creditor. The abstraction has been rendered concrete through *ketiva*, and the combination of *mesira* and *ketiva* together effects the transfer.

This reading, following Tosafot, is far more coherent than the alternative. Reading the *Gemara* the other way — that *mesira* alone should suffice because the debt is only words, and therefore a *shtar* cannot do anything further — is extremely difficult to sustain. The *Gemara* reads most naturally in the Tosafot direction: *mesira* alone is not enough precisely because the debt is abstract, and abstraction requires concretization through writing.

---

## Challenge via Agav

### Land & Document Cases

The *Gemara* now challenges this *sevara*. Is it truly the case that something abstract cannot be transferred without a written document to accompany it? The *Gemara* invokes a statement of Rabba bar Yitzchak in the name of Rav, which sets out several scenarios involving the gifting of land together with a written deed.

Rabba bar Yitzchak says: *shnei shtarot hen* — there are two distinct scenarios involving a *shtar* in the context of a land transaction.

### Transfer Then Document

The first scenario: one says *zachu basadeh leploni ve-kitvu lo et ha-shtar* — take possession of this field on behalf of so-and-so, and also write a deed for him. The principle of *zachin le-adam she-lo be-fanav* allows a third party to receive an acquisition on behalf of someone else even in that person's absence. So Reuven and Shimon are summoned, a *kinyan* is performed — perhaps *chazakah*, perhaps *kinyan sudar* — and Levi thereby acquires the field. But the giftor also instructs them to write up a deed memorializing the gift.

The ruling is *chozer ba-shtar ve-eino chozer ba-sadeh*: once the *kinyan* is done, Levi owns the field and that cannot be undone. But since the *shtar* was mentioned as a separate instruction subsequent to the *kinyan*, the giftor retains the right to back out of having the *shtar* written until it is actually delivered to Levi. The deed has been authorized by the giftor, and only he can instruct the scribe to write it, but he may change his mind about that until delivery. Levi owns the field; he may not yet own the proof.

### Conditional Transfer

The second scenario: *al menat she-tichtevu lo et ha-shtar* — "take possession of this field for Levi on the condition that you write him the *shtar*." Here the acquisition of the field is explicitly conditioned on the eventual delivery of the deed. In this case, *chozer bein ba-shtar bein ba-sadeh* — the giftor may reverse course on the *shtar* until it is delivered, and if he does, that reversal also unravels the acquisition of the field itself, since the field was transferred conditionally upon the *shtar* being delivered. The *chiddush* here is not enormous — it is self-evident that a conditional acquisition may be undone if the condition is not met — though the primary novelty is that the giftor has the ability to back out of having the *shtar* written at all.

### Pre-Written Document

Rabbi Chiya bar Avin then says in the name of Rav Huna: *sheloshah shtarot hen* — there is in fact a third scenario. *Im kadam mocher ve-kasav et ha-shtar* — if the seller or giftor went ahead and had the *shtar* written before the transfer took place. This is analogous to what we learned: *kosevin shtar la-mocher af al pi she-ein lokeiach imo* — a deed may be written for the seller even in the absence of the buyer. So the giftor anticipated the transaction, had a *sofer* draw up the deed in advance — essentially a pre-signed document recording that he has given the field to Levi — and carries it with him before the actual transfer is made.

Now when the transfer takes place and Levi (or an agent on his behalf) takes physical possession of the field — through *chazakah* or whatever *kinyan* applies — the ruling is: *keivan she-hechzik zeh ba-karka, niknah shtar be-chol makom she-hu* — as soon as the act of *kinyan* on the land is complete, the pre-written deed automatically passes into Levi's ownership regardless of where it physically is. Even if it is still sitting in the giftor's back pocket, Levi owns it by operation of the land transfer.

### Agav Principle

This is the mechanism of *agav*: *nechasim she-ein lahem achrayut niknin im nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayut be-kesef, be-shtar, u-ve-chazakah*. Property without liens — *metaltelin*, movable chattels — can be acquired along with and by virtue of the acquisition of property that does carry liens, i.e., real estate. This is *kinyan agav*: when one takes possession of real estate, that act of *kinyan* can simultaneously confer ownership of associated chattels, provided the transferor intends them to go together. If I am selling you my plot of land and my dining room chairs, you could separately perform *hagbahah* on each chair and *chazakah* on the land — or you could simply do *chazakah* on the land with the explicit understanding that the chairs are being transferred *agav*, alongside it.

What makes the pre-written-deed case interesting is that in such a case, no explicit bundling statement is even required. The deed is considered to automatically accompany the land, such that the moment Levi acquires the land, the deed passes to him without any additional act.

---

## Agav vs Mesira

### Gemara's Answer

Now the *Gemara* makes its connection. The challenge was: if the *sevara* is that words cannot transfer words and abstraction requires concretization, how can Levi acquire the pre-written *shtar* through the land transfer alone, without any additional document accompanying it? The *shtar* is *mili* — an abstraction — and yet it was transferred without a *shtar* coming with it. Does this not undermine the principle that *mili be-mili lo miknan*?

The *Gemara* answers: *agav shani* — the case of *agav* is different. When the transfer occurs by means of *agav*, through the *kinyan* of land, that is a categorically more powerful mechanism than *mesira*. *Agav* can accomplish what ordinary *mesira* cannot. Therefore, even though *mesira* alone would be insufficient to transfer the abstract debt represented in a *shtar*, *agav* through land can accomplish this. The two cases are not analogous.

### Agav Power

One might ask: how do we know that *agav* is indeed so powerful as to work where other *kinyanim* would not? The *Gemara* demonstrates this from the case of coins. Normally, *chalipin* — the exchange-based *kinyan* such as *kinyan sudar* — works on almost any object. But it does not work on coins, because coins occupy a unique category: they are the medium of exchange, not the things exchanged, and as a result most *kinyanim* cannot be used to acquire them. And yet *agav arba niknei* — coins can be acquired through *kinyan agav* along with land. This demonstrates that *agav* is a uniquely powerful *kinyan*, capable of effecting transfers that other modes of acquisition cannot.

### Rav Pappa Case

The *Gemara* illustrates this with a story. Rav Pappa had twelve thousand *zuz* that were owed to him — or perhaps physically held for him — by the family of Chuzai. *Ve-akni'inhu nihaleh le-Rav Shmuel bar Acha agav asifa de-veitei* — he transferred ownership of this money to Rav Shmuel bar Acha by means of *agav*, using the porch of his house as the piece of land. Rav Shmuel bar Acha was traveling to the location of the Chuzai family and needed to be able to collect the money on Rav Pappa's behalf. But the family would not hand over the money to a mere agent; they needed to be confident that in giving the money to Shmuel bar Acha they were truly and finally paying off their obligation. The only way to achieve that was for Rav Pappa to actually transfer ownership of the money to Shmuel bar Acha, who could then go to the family and say, "Rav Pappa transferred this to me; you now owe it to me, not to him — pay me." And they paid him.

The transfer of the money was accomplished through *kinyan agav*: by Shmuel bar Acha taking possession of the porch, he simultaneously acquired the twelve thousand *zuz* in Chuzai. *Ki ata nafik le-apei ad Tavakh* — when Shmuel bar Acha returned with the money, Rav Pappa went out to greet him all the way to the town of Tavakh, so relieved and grateful was he to have finally recovered the funds.

This story demonstrates that *agav* can transfer even coins, which *chalipin* cannot — proof positive that *agav* is a *kinyan* of exceptional power.

### Final Conclusion

The final conclusion is therefore this: when one wishes to transfer a *shtar chov*, the debt is an abstraction — *otiyot mili ninhu, u-mili be-mili lo miknan* — and *mesira* alone, being itself only a verbal framing of the handing-over of a physical object, cannot transfer what is abstract. To transfer the debt, one needs both *mesira* and *ketiva*: the physical handing over of the document together with a written instrument that explicitly transfers the debt and its liens to the new creditor. *Agav* is powerful enough to overcome this limitation because it is a *kinyan* that operates on a different and higher level — as the case of coins demonstrates — but ordinary *mesira* cannot accomplish the concretization that a written transfer document can. This concludes the discussion of *otiyot niknot be-mesira*, even as the precise *halakhic* conclusion remains subject to the textual uncertainty in the *girsa* of Ameimar's ruling.

---

## Boat Sale Contents

### Mishna Rule

The *Gemara* now moves on to the *Mishnah*'s ruling about what is and is not included in the sale of a boat. *Aval lo machar lo et ha-avadim ve-lo et ha-mirtzufin ve-lo et ha-antiki* — when one sells a boat, the sale does not include the slaves who work on the boat, nor the *mirtzufin*, the containers or pouches (in modern terms, one might think of the cargo containers), nor the *antiki*.

### Antiki Definition

The *Gemara* asks: *mai antiki*? What is *antiki*? Rav Pappa explains: *iska de-veigava* — it is the actual commodities, the wares being transported and stored within those containers. This is unsurprising: it is self-evident that when one sells a ship, one does not thereby sell the cargo stored aboard it, just as one does not sell the containers themselves. The *Mishnah* is simply being thorough in listing what falls outside the scope of the sale.

---

---

# Bava Batra 78

## Wagon & Mules

### Wagon/Mules Trade

The daf begins with a new *Mishnah* on 77b. The *Mishnah* establishes a basic principle regarding the sale of composite items: *machar ha-karon lo machar ha-pardot* — if one sells a wagon, the mules that pull it are not included in the sale. Conversely, *machar ha-pardot lo machar ha-karon* — if one sells the mules, the wagon is not sold with them. These items, despite their obvious practical interdependence, are treated as independent objects for the purposes of commercial transactions. The *Mishnah* continues: *machar ha-tzemed lo machar ha-bakar* — selling the yoke does not include the cattle, and *machar ha-bakar lo machar ha-tzemed* — selling the cattle does not include the yoke.

### Money Indicates Intent

Rabbi Yehuda dissents with what feels, at first glance, like a refreshingly practical position: *ha-damim modiyim* — the money paid reveals the intent of the parties. One need not rely solely on the words used; the price itself is evidence of what the transaction encompassed.

### Price Example

The *Mishnah* illustrates this with a concrete case: *amar lo mechor li tzimdecha be-matayim zuz* — someone says, "Sell me your yoke for 200 *zuz*." Since everyone knows a yoke alone is not worth 200 *zuz*, and the only thing that commands such a price is the cattle yoked together with it, Rabbi Yehuda holds that the money makes clear what was intended: the word "yoke" was being used to refer to the cattle together with the yoke.

### Words Have Fixed Meaning

The *Chachamim* reject this approach: *ein ha-damim re'ayah* — the money cannot serve as evidence to reinterpret the meaning of words. Words mean what they say. If someone overpaid, that is a separate problem to address, but it does not license a court to redefine the terms of a transaction after the fact.

---

## Hadamim Modiyim Debate

### Braitah: Harnessed Items

The *Gemara* opens with a challenge. *Rav Tachlifa bar Arva* taught a *Braita* before *Rav Yafas*: *machar ha-karon machar ha-pardot* — selling a wagon does sell the mules. This directly contradicts our *Mishnah*, which says the opposite. *Rav Yafas* responds: should I simply erase this *Braita* from the corpus? He answers his own question: no. The *Braita* should be understood as applying to a case where the mules are actually strapped and harnessed to the wagon — *adukin bo*. When seller and buyer are standing before a wagon with mules harnessed to it, a sale of "the wagon" naturally encompasses the entire unit as it stands.

### Context & Connection

This resolution presupposes not merely that the mules and wagon were physically connected at some remote location, but that the parties were aware of and referring to them in their combined state. Context matters: are we, as parties to this transaction, looking at a harnessed unit together? That awareness shapes what the words of sale encompass.

### Subset Usage Analysis

The *Gemara* then turns to sharpen the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* by pressing on the underlying scenario. The question is: *heikhi dami* — what exactly is the case?

If we are in a locale where everyone uses *tzemed* exclusively to mean the yoke and *bakar* exclusively to mean the cattle — *peshita*. No one is confused. You said yoke, you get the yoke, regardless of how much you paid. Even Rabbi Yehuda would not suggest that an absurd overpayment can transform the meaning of a word that has no alternative usage.

Conversely, if we are in a locale where *tzemed* is universally understood to mean the cattle together with the yoke — again, *peshita*. There is no question that the cattle are included, and even the *Chachamim* would agree that the money confirms this reading.

The *Gemara* therefore identifies the live dispute: *ba'atar di-kari lei tzimdeh tzimdeh le-bakar bakar, ve-ika nami de-kari le-bakar tzimdeh* — we are in a locale where the standard usage of *tzemed* refers to the yoke alone, and *bakar* refers to the cattle, yet there exists a subset of the population that also uses *tzemed* to refer to the cattle. It is not merely an occasional or idiosyncratic usage, but a recognizable, if minority, practice.

In this situation, Rabbi Yehuda holds *damim modiyim*: if someone uses the word *tzemed* and pays ten thousand *zuz*, it is evident that he is using the word in the manner of that subset of the population — he meant the cattle. The *Chachamim* disagree.

### Burden of Proof

The *Rashbam* explains the *Chachamim*'s position as follows: *keivan de-yesh korin le-bakar bakar ve-lo korin lei tzimdeh, lo amrinan damim modiyim* — since the majority of the population uses *bakar* to mean cattle and would never call it *tzemed*, we do not say the money indicates intent. Why not? Because *dilma hai minaihu hu* — perhaps the buyer is simply of that minority, but we cannot assume so. The operative principle is *yad lokeach al ha-tachtona* — the burden of proof rests on the buyer, and money in the seller's possession is presumed to belong to him. The buyer must prove his claim.

One might frame this slightly differently: a sale requires a meeting of minds. Even if a linguist examining the case would conclude that the buyer "must have meant" the cattle, that is irrelevant if the seller understood the word in its standard sense. The seller used *tzemed* meaning the yoke, as the majority of the population uses it. Are we to reinterpret the seller's words based on the buyer's private or minority usage? The *Chachamim* say no. The question is not merely one of *hamotzi me-chaveiro alav ha-re'aya* — who has the burden of proof — but also the more fundamental point that a transaction depends on the shared meaning of language, not on what one party silently intends. This is closely related to the principle of *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim* — unexpressed intentions have no legal force. One might counter that paying a wildly disproportionate sum is so self-evident that it rises to the level of *devarim she-ba-lev kol adam*, things so obvious that articulation is unnecessary. But the *Chachamim* reject this: we will not hold that money overrides the standard meaning of words.

### Ona'ah Question

The *Gemara* now presses a sharp question. Suppose the *Chachamim* are correct — the sale is of the yoke alone. The buyer paid ten thousand *zuz* for an object worth a fraction of that. Why is the sale not void on grounds of *ona'ah* — the prohibition against overcharging, which can, when sufficiently extreme, invalidate the transaction as a *bitul mekach*? The *Mishnah* implies that the *Chachamim* hold the sale stands. How?

One might respond by arguing that the *Chachamim* simply do not hold that *ona'ah* voids a sale — they may hold that overcharging is a transgression but does not annul the transaction. But the *Gemara* rejects this: there is a *Mishnah* in which the *Chachamim* explicitly dispute Rabbi Yehuda in a context involving the sale of a *sefer Torah*, an animal, or a pearl — *ein lahem ona'ah*, Rabbi Yehuda says, because such items fluctuate in value. The *Chachamim* respond: *lo amru ela elu* — only the formally excluded categories lack *ona'ah*; everything else is subject to it. This proves the *Chachamim* hold that *ona'ah* can void a sale. The problem therefore remains.

### Void Sale Answer

The *Gemara* offers a first resolution: *mai ein damim re'ayah nami de-katani de-havei bitul mekach* — when the *Chachamim* say the money is not evidence, what they mean is that we do not use the money to conclude the cattle were sold. The words meant yoke, so the buyer got a yoke. But the grotesque overpayment for that yoke renders it a *bitul mekach* — the sale is void. This is not the same as saying the cattle were included; it simply means the entire transaction is unwound.

### Gift Interpretation

The *Gemara* then offers a second answer: *ki amar rabanan ona'ah bitul mekach, be-chdei she-ha-da'at to'ah* — the principle that *ona'ah* voids a sale applies when the error is within the range where a reasonable person could be mistaken, that is, where one could genuinely have believed the price was fair. But *aval be-chdei she-ein ha-da'at to'ah* — when no one in the world would believe that a yoke is worth ten thousand *zuz*, there is no *ona'ah* in the relevant sense, because no one was deceived into thinking this was the correct price. In such a case, *eimor matana yahiv lei* — we interpret the excess as a gift. The buyer simply chose, for whatever personal reason, to give the seller a windfall while purchasing his yoke.

### Rashbam Analysis

The *Rashbam* addresses both answers directly. He notes that the first answer is the more logically compelling one: where someone pays slightly more than the market price, we say their mind was mistaken — *savar be-libo she-kach shaveh* — they genuinely believed that was the correct price, and that constitutes *mekach ta'ut*, a mistaken transaction. But in our *Mishnah*'s case, where a yoke worth a *perutah* is sold for a *maneh* or two hundred *zuz*, no such mistake is possible. The *Rashbam* indicates, however, that the second answer is a better fit for the *Mishnah* as written, since the *Mishnah* appears to describe a valid, standing sale — not one that is voided. Yet he acknowledges that the second answer, interpreting an obvious commercial transaction as a gift, is jurisprudentially strained — *ve-chama shinuyei d'chika hu* — it is a difficult reconciliation of the *Mishnah*'s language with the demands of legal logic.

---

## Donkey & Equipment

### Donkey Mishnah

The *Mishnah* turns from mules and wagons to a new case: *ha-mocher et ha-chamor lo machar kelav* — one who sells a donkey has not sold its equipment, *kelav*, the various implements normally associated with it. What exactly *kelav* includes will be clarified by the *Gemara*.

### Nachum HaMadi View

*Nachum HaMadi* disagrees: he holds that selling a donkey does include the equipment. *Nachum HaMadi* appears rarely in the *Mishnah* — he is perhaps best known from *Bameh Madlikin* in the laws of *Shabbos* — yet here he takes a clear and expansive position.

### Yehuda Context View

Rabbi Yehuda, consistent with his broader approach of reading intent from context, says: *pe'amim mechurin u-fe'amim einam mechurin* — sometimes the equipment is sold with the donkey and sometimes not, depending on how the transaction was phrased. If the donkey was standing before the parties with its equipment on it and the buyer said *mechor li chamor zeh* — sell me this donkey — the word *zeh* ("this one") emphasizes the donkey in its present state, equipment and all, and the equipment is included. But if the buyer said simply *chamor hu*, identifying the donkey as the seller's animal without that emphatic *zeh*, then only the donkey is sold, not its equipment.

### Equipment Types

*Ulla* clarifies the scope of the dispute: *machlokes be-sak ve-diska ve-chumni* — the disagreement concerns the sacks, carrying bags, and the *chumni*, which the *Rashbam* explains is a side saddle used by women. These are the items in dispute; the basic riding equipment is a separate question.

### Riding vs. Cargo

The *Tanna Kamma* holds: *stam chamor le-rchov kai* — an ordinary donkey is primarily intended for riding. Therefore, the saddle and its associated riding equipment are naturally part of what one means when selling a donkey, but the sacks and bags used for carrying cargo are not.

### Dual Use Argument

*Nachum HaMadi* counters: *stam chamor le-massa kai* — a donkey is also standardly used as a beast of burden, for carrying loads. Therefore, the carrying equipment is equally part of the donkey's normal complement and should be included in the sale. Importantly, both opinions agree that whatever falls within the animal's primary purpose is included; their disagreement is about how broadly to define that purpose. This stands in some contrast to the sale of land, where equipment used on the land is typically not sold with it, while here by movable property — *metaltelin* — items understood as integral to the object's use are more readily included.

---

## Attached Equipment

### Explicit Kelav

A *Braita* is introduced: *chamor u-chelav ani mocher lach* — "I am selling you the donkey with its equipment." In such a case, one sells the saddle, the saddle blanket, the belly strap, and the breast strap. But one does not sell the sacks, the bags, or the *chumni*. Only if one says *hi ve-chol mah she-aleha* — "it and everything on it" — does everything get transferred.

### Saddle Always Sold

At first glance, the *Braita* implies that the saddle is included only when one explicitly says *kelav*. The *Gemara* rejects this reading. The correct interpretation is: even without saying *kelav*, the saddle is always sold when one sells the donkey — it is sufficiently integral to the riding use of the animal. The *chiddush* of the *Braita* is not that *kelav* is required to include the saddle; rather, it teaches that even when one does explicitly say *kelav*, the sacks and bags are still not included. To obtain those, one must say *ve-chol mah she-aleha*. Thus: *chamor* alone or *chamor u-chelav* both yield the saddle; *kol mah she-aleha* yields everything, including the sacks; but *kelav* alone, even when explicitly invoked, does not reach the cargo equipment.

### On vs. Off Donkey

A question is posed: is the entire dispute between the *Tanna Kamma*, *Nachum HaMadi*, and Rabbi Yehuda taking place when the equipment is actually on the donkey, or when it is not? This parallels the earlier question about the mules and the wagon: does physical attachment at the moment of sale determine what is included?

### Resolution Debate

One answer: the dispute arises only when the equipment is *not* on the donkey. When it is on the donkey, everyone — including the *Rabbanan* — would agree that everything is sold. Evidence is brought from the *Braita*: it says one sells the saddle etc. when one uses the phrase *kelav*, and sells everything when one says *ve-chol mah she-aleha*. Since saying "everything on it" implies the stuff is on it and yet still needs to be explicitly claimed, this would suggest the *Rabbanan* hold that even when the equipment is on the donkey, it is not automatically sold. This would mean the dispute concerns precisely the case when the equipment is on the donkey.

### Ravina Evidence

*Ravina* raises the matter before *Rav Ashi*. He cites evidence from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling within the *Mishnah* itself: Rabbi Yehuda says that when the equipment is visibly on the donkey and the buyer says *chamor zeh* — "this donkey" — the equipment is included, whereas saying only *chamor hu* does not include it. The fact that Rabbi Yehuda addresses the case where the equipment is on the donkey suggests the entire debate is situated in that scenario, not in the case when the equipment is elsewhere.

### Wagon Analogy

A conceptual proof is drawn from the earlier case of the mules and the wagon: when the *Braita* ruled that selling the wagon includes the mules, that was explained as applying when the mules are harnessed — *adukin bo*. The logical corollary is that the *Mishnah*'s default rule — that they are not sold together — applies when they are not connected. By analogy, the same framework governs the donkey and its equipment.

### Case-by-Case

The *Gemara* resists this analogy, however, by introducing a counterexample: when selling a ship, the *Mishnah* earlier established that the cargo and merchandise on board are *not* sold with the ship — even though they are physically on it. This shows that being "on" the object at the time of sale does not uniformly determine whether it is included. The *Gemara* concludes: *tana milei milei katani* — the *Mishnah*'s author treats each case individually, and one cannot mechanically transpose the rule of one case to another. The degree of integral connection varies: mules harnessed to a wagon are more organically part of the wagon's identity than cargo sitting in a ship's hold. Each situation must be assessed on its own terms, and the question of whether the equipment is on the donkey, and what legal weight that carries, remains unresolved.

---

## Tannaim & Context

### All Tannaim View

*Abaye* makes a sweeping observation: *kulhu svira lehu ki mazbin inish midi, ihu ve-chol tashmishav mazbin* — all of the following *Tannaim* share the view that when one sells an object, one sells it together with all of its functional equipment, at least in the relevant context. This does not mean they all say identical things; as both the *Rashbam* and *Tosafot* note, each makes this point in a specific context, and one should not assume any of them would extend the rule automatically to other cases.

### Example Cases

*Rabbi Eliezer*, as taught in a *Mishnah*, holds that selling an olive press includes the beam — *machar beit ha-bad machar ha-korah* — because the entire enterprise of the olive press is defined by and called after the beam. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* holds that selling a city includes the *santar* — the sentry or guardsman — as an integral functionary of the city's operation.

### Vineyard Equipment

*Rabbi Meir* holds, in a *Braita*, that selling a vineyard includes the vineyard's equipment — *tashmishei kerem*. The *Rashbam* here makes a notably academic observation: the *Gemara* attributes this ruling to Rabbi Meir with the formula *de-tanya*, implying a *Braita*, but the *Rashbam* notes that no such *Braita* attributing this to Rabbi Meir is known to him. In the *Tosefta*, this position appears in the name of *Abba Shaul*, not Rabbi Meir. The *Rashbam* thus flags a possible textual problem in the attribution.

### Small Boats

Rabbi Natan and *Sumchus* both hold, as discussed earlier in the tractate, that the small boats — *betzit* and *dugit* — are sold together with the larger ship.

### Yehuda Context

Rabbi Yehuda, as we have seen, takes the contextual approach: whether equipment is included depends on the precise language used. *Pe'amim mechurin pe'amim einam mechurin* — sometimes yes, sometimes no.

### Rava Explanation

*Rava* explains the operative distinction in Rabbi Yehuda's approach. When the buyer says *chamor zeh* — "this donkey" — the use of *zeh* is redundant if one already knows it is the seller's donkey: *yadu'a de-chamara dideih hu*. The only reason to say *zeh* must therefore be to indicate the donkey as it presently stands — *mishum kelim ka-amar lei* — with all its tackle, in its current equipped state. By contrast, saying *chamor hu she-timkarenu li* — "is this your donkey that you can sell it to me?" — the word *hu* identifies ownership but does not indicate the current state of the animal. Rabbi Yehuda's approach, then, is the most internally consistent of all the *Tannaim* discussed: throughout, he reads context and language to determine intent.

---

## Animals & Refuse

### Young Animals

The *Mishnah* continues with a set of rules about what is sold together with what. *Ha-mocher et ha-chamor machar et ha-sayach* — one who sells a donkey has sold its young, the baby donkey. But *mocher et ha-para lo machar et benah* — one who sells a cow has not sold the calf.

### Ground & Manure

*Mocher ashpa machar zivlah* — one who sells a plot of ground used for dumping refuse has sold the manure in it.

### Containers & Contents

*Mocher bor machar meimeiha* — one who sells a cistern has sold the water stored in it. *Mocher kavveret machar devorim* — one who sells a beehive has sold the bees within it. *Mocher shovach machar yonim* — one who sells a pigeon coop has sold the pigeons.

### Rashbam Note

The *Rashbam* points out that these last cases are almost self-evident: of course if I sell you the water in my well, I am not thereby selling you the well itself. The *Mishnah* is therefore not suggesting the reverse — that selling the container sells the contents — is equally automatic. Each direction of the transaction must be examined on its own terms.

---

## Donkey vs. Cow

### Nursing Descriptor

The *Gemara* asks a pointed question: *heikhi dami* — what exactly is the case? If the seller explicitly says "she and her young," then even a cow should be sold with her calf. And if the seller says nothing about the young, then even a donkey should not be sold with its foal. So what is the specific scenario that generates the *Mishnah*'s asymmetric ruling?

### Primary Use

*Rav Pappa* resolves it: *de-amar lei chamor menika u-para menika ani mocher lach* — the seller says "I am selling you a nursing donkey" or "I am selling you a nursing cow." The word "nursing" is a descriptor. *Bishlama para* — when I tell you I am selling a nursing cow, it makes sense: *ikah le-meimar le-chalvah ba'ei* — one might reasonably interpret the descriptor as indicating the cow is currently producing milk, which is the primary reason one acquires a cow. The buyer needs to know the cow provides milk; without that assurance the sale might be a *mekach ta'ut*. There is therefore a plausible reading of "nursing cow" that does not imply the calf comes with her.

### Implication

But when one says "nursing donkey," *mai ka-amar lei?* — what could this possibly mean? Donkey milk has no recognized practical value in this context. The descriptor "nursing" can only mean one thing: the donkey comes together with its young. *Shema mina hi ve-yalda ka-amar lei* — we must infer that "nursing" signals that both mother and offspring are being sold together.

### Etymology: Sayach

The *Gemara* pauses to explain the etymology of *sayach* (the young donkey): *she-mehalech achar sicha na'ah* — it walks after pleasant speech, following when called with a kind word. The term is a play on *siach*, meaning speech or pleasant utterance — the foal follows the voice that calls it gently, as if seduced by agreeable sound. This etymological note serves as the bridge to the remarkable *aggadic* passage that follows.

---

## Cheshbono Shel Olam

### Meshalim Derasha

Rabbi Yochanan expounds the verse: *al kein yomru ha-moshlim bou Cheshbon tibaneh ve-tikonen Ir Sichon* — "Therefore the poets say: Come to Cheshbon, it shall be built and established, the city of Sichon" (Bamidbar 21:27). The *Rashbam* notes the plain context: when *Sichon* went to war against the king of *Moav* and conquered his land, the prophets of the nations — attributed here to *Bilaam* and his companions — foretold this victory. Since *Sichon* had conquered the land from *Moav*, *Bnei Yisrael* were permitted to take it from *Sichon* even though they were otherwise prohibited from warring against *Moav* directly. *Cheshbon* was the capital city of *Moav*. The *Rashbam* presses the question: why does the Torah include this foreign poetry? The fact of *Sichon*'s conquest is stated plainly elsewhere — *ki hu nilcham be-melech Moav ha-rishon*. The verse is evidently here for its *aggadic* interpretation: *le-drasha katbah Moshe Rabbeinu*.

Who are the *moshlim*? Rabbi Yochanan reads the word not as "rulers" or "poets" but as *elu ha-moshlim be-yitzram* — those who exercise dominion over their own desires and inclinations. These are the *tzaddikim*, those who have mastered the *yetzer*.

### Calculation & Restraint

*Bou Cheshbon* — come to Cheshbon — is read as *bou ve-nechashev cheshbono shel olam*: come and let us calculate the accounting of the world. Before allowing the *yetzer hara* to draw one into transgression, one should sit and perform the larger reckoning. *Hefsed mitzvah ke-neged scharah* — weigh the loss incurred by fulfilling a *mitzvah* against the reward. *Ve-schar aveirah ke-neged hefsedah* — and weigh the apparent gain from a transgression against the ultimate loss it entails. This is the *cheshbon ha-nefesh*, the soul's accounting: do not be seduced by the immediate gratification or apparent benefit; calculate the full picture.

### Two Worlds

*Tibaneh ve-tikonen* — you will be built and established: *tibaneh be-olam ha-zeh*, built in this world, *ve-tikonen le-olam ha-ba*, and established in the world to come — if you make this calculation and act accordingly.

### Ayir Seduction

*Ir Sichon* — the city of *Sichon* — is now read through the etymological lens established by the *Mishnah*. *Im mesim adam atzmo ke-ayir zeh she-mehalech achar siyach na'ah* — if a person makes himself like this *ayir*, the young donkey, which follows after pleasant, seductive speech, then one is like the person who is drawn after the *yetzer hara*, seduced by its agreeable-sounding temptations. The wordplay ties together *ayir* (baby donkey), *ir* (city), and *siyach* (pleasant speech / *siach*).

### Fire Imagery

*Ki esh yatzah me-Cheshbon* — fire goes out from *Cheshbon*: *tetzei esh mi-machshavin ve-tochal esh she-einam mechashvin* — fire emanates from those who make the proper accounting and consumes those who are led entirely by their appetites and do not reckon the full consequences. The *Rashbam* notes a connection here to the earlier *aggadic* teaching in the tractate that a person is burned by a friend's *chuppah* — *adam nichveh me-chupato shel chaveiro* — that in the world to come one will be seared by the achievements of those who were more righteous. Here the fire of the *tzaddikim*'s reckoning is what destroys those who abandoned calculation in favor of appetite.

*Ve-lehava mi-kiryat Sichon* — the flame from the city of *Sichon*: here *Sichon* is read not as the seduced donkey-follower but as a *siyach*, a plant or tree — the *tzaddikim* who are compared to a cedar of *Levanon* growing tall. The fire goes out from the righteous and destroys the city of *Moav*, meaning those who go after their *yetzer* like the *ayir* following pleasant speech.

### Arrogance & Judgment

*Ba'alei bamot Arnon* — the masters of the high places of *Arnon* — are read as *elu gasei ha-ruach*, the arrogant ones. The *Gemara* cites the principle: *kol adam she-yesh bo gasut ha-ruach nofel be-Gehinnom* — anyone possessed of arrogance falls into *Gehinnom*. This represents a second category of sin, distinct from the weakness of will illustrated by the *ayir*: here the transgressor is driven not by passive seduction but by the active conviction of entitlement and self-importance.

*Ve-niram* — the word is read as *ein ram*, "there is no God," the declaration of one who in his arrogance denies divine sovereignty. *Avad Cheshbon* — one who loses the *cheshbon*, the accounting of the world: *avad cheshbono shel olam* — has forfeited the great moral ledger. *Ad Divon* — until *Dibon* — is read as *ad din*, "until judgment arrives." *Va-nashim ad Nofach* — "until Nofach" — is read as *ad she-tavo esh she-einah tzericha nipuach*, until the fire comes that needs no fanning, the self-sustaining fire of *Gehinnom*. *Ad Medva* — until *Medva* — is read as *ad she-tadviv nishmatan*, until their souls are in anguish. An alternative reading: *ad mah de-ba'i* — until God does what God needs to do; the verse hints that divine justice, though deferred, will inevitably arrive.

---

## Leaving Torah

### Fire Consumption

*Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav*: *kol ha-poreish mi-divrei Torah, esh ochlato* — whoever abandons the words of Torah will be consumed by fire. The proof text: *ve-natati et panai bahem, me-ha-esh yatza'u, ve-ha-esh tochlem* — "I will set My face against them; from the fire they went out and the fire will consume them." Since Torah itself is fire — *halo kho devarai ka-esh, ne'um Hashem* — one who departs from the fire of Torah is consumed by a different fire.

### Gehinnom Fall

*Rav Dimi* in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds a parallel teaching: *kol ha-poreish atzmo mi-divrei Torah, nofel le-Gehinnom* — whoever separates himself from Torah falls into *Gehinnom*.

### Refaim Gehinnom

The proof: *Adam to'eh mi-derech ha-sekhel, bi-kehal Refa'im yanuach* — "A man who strays from the way of knowledge will rest in the congregation of the *Refa'im*" (Mishlei 21:16). And *ein Refa'im ela Gehinnom* — the *Refa'im* are none other than *Gehinnom* itself, as another verse states: *ve-lo yada ki Refa'im sham, be-imkei She'ol keru'eha* — "He does not know that the *Refa'im* are there, in the depths of *She'ol* are those called to it." *She'ol* is *Gehinnom*. Whoever abandons the way of knowledge finds his resting place in the depths of the netherworld.

---

---

# Bava Batra 79

## Two Sets of Terms

### Selling Chatzer & Zivlah

The daf begins approximately ten lines down, with the *mishnah*'s ruling on the sale of a *chatzer* — a dung heap or refuse area. When one sells such a space, the sale includes not only the ground or the pit itself but also the manure and garbage contained within, which can carry significant monetary value. Similarly, the *mishnah* rules that when one sells a cistern, the water inside it is included in the sale.

The *gemara* then invokes a *baraita* from tractate *Me'ilah*: *kol harauy lamizbe'ach velo libedek habayis* — anything fit to be placed upon the *mizbe'ach* but not fit for *bedek habayis*, the construction and maintenance of the *Beis Hamikdash*, is subject to the laws of *me'ilah*, as is anything it contains.

An unblemished animal is the paradigmatic example of something fit for the *mizbe'ach*. Such an animal is not fit for *bedek habayis* — not because one could not theoretically put a sheep into the walls of the *Beis Hamikdash*, but because an unblemished animal that one wishes to sanctify for monetary proceeds of the Temple would constitute a violation of a positive commandment: an unblemished animal, once sanctified, must be dedicated to the *mizbe'ach* itself.

### Four Categories

Before proceeding further, it is important to identify two distinct sets of terms that are often conflated but must be kept separate.

The first set is *kedushat haguf* versus *kedushat damim*. *Kedushat haguf* means that the thing itself will be used for a *Beis Hamikdash* purpose — it will physically serve in the Temple's service. *Kedushat damim* means the object is valuable only for its monetary proceeds: it will be sold and the money put to use. The object itself is of no direct ritual interest; only its value matters.

The second set is *kedushat mizbe'ach* versus *kedushat bedek habayis*. *Kedushat mizbe'ach* refers to sanctification for use on the altar — sacrificial animals, flour, wine, and the like. *Kedushat bedek habayis* refers to sanctification for the upkeep and maintenance of the Temple. The natural assumption is that *kedushat mizbe'ach* corresponds to *kedushat haguf* (the object itself goes on the altar) and that *kedushat bedek habayis* corresponds to *kedushat damim* (the object will be sold and the proceeds used). But this alignment is not exact.

There are in fact two types of *kedushat bedek habayis*. One type involves the object itself being used directly — construction beams, gold plating, marble for the floor, materials built into the structure of the *Beis Hamikdash*. These would constitute *kedushat haguf* within the framework of *kedushat bedek habayis*. The other type, however, involves objects whose value is the point — a plow donated to work the fields of *hekdesh*, for example. The Temple does not need the plow as a plow for sacred ritual; it needs the income the plow generates. This is *kedushat damim*: the object is interesting only for its worth. As a formulation: *kedushat damim* is like the cynic who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing — *hekdesh* cares only about the monetary return, not the thing in itself.

Thus the four categories are not perfectly mirrored pairs. *Kedushat mizbe'ach* will typically be *kedushat haguf*; but *kedushat bedek habayis* can be either, depending on whether the object itself is incorporated into the Temple structure or merely sold for proceeds.

### Examples & Me'ilah

The *baraita* illustrates the principle by cycling through examples in each category, noting that in every case *me'ilah* applies both to the sanctified item and to whatever it contains. The three operative categories are: things fit for the *mizbe'ach* but not *bedek habayis*; things fit for *bedek habayis* but not the *mizbe'ach*; and things fit for neither — meaning their sanctity is purely *kedushat damim*, their value alone being what is consecrated.

The *baraita* asks: how can there be *me'ilah* on something fit for neither the *mizbe'ach* nor *bedek habayis* directly? The answer is that *kedushat damim* is precisely this third category. If one consecrates one's car to the *Beis Hamikdash*, the car cannot be placed on the altar and cannot be built into the Temple walls; yet the *Beis Hamikdash* will sell it and use the proceeds. That car has *kedushat bedek habayis* in the sense that its ultimate destination is the upkeep of the Temple, even though the car itself is not *rauy libedek habayis* — it will not literally be incorporated into the structure. Accordingly, *velo rauy lo lamizbe'ach velo libedek habayis* is the *baraita*'s way of describing *kedushat damim*.

The specific examples given are: a cistern filled with water (*bor malei mayim*) — water collected in a cistern is not considered fit for the *mizbe'ach* (unlike, say, water from a spring, which might qualify for *nisuch hamayim*); the *Rashbam* notes it is usable for *bedek habayis*, since water can be used to mix cement for construction. Dung heaps (*ashpos mele'os zevel*) are fit for neither the altar nor Temple construction and fall into the *kedushat damim* category. A pigeon coop filled with pigeons (*shovach malei yonim*) is an example of something that can actually be used *lamizbe'ach*, since pigeons are valid sacrifices. A field covered with grass (*sadeh malei asavim*) is fit for neither altar nor structure. A fruit-bearing tree (*ilan oseh peiros*) — the fruit itself cannot go on the altar and is not *bedek habayis*; while *bikurim* are brought in a ceremony at the *Beis Hamikdash*, they go to the *kohen* rather than being offered on the *mizbe'ach*. In all of these cases, regardless of which category they fall into, *me'ilah* applies to the consecrated item and to its contents.

One interesting discussion among the *rishonim* arises from the cases of the cistern and the field. There is a general principle that *me'ilah* does not apply to *karka* — real property, land, or things attached to the ground. The *Rashbam* appears here to hold that there is indeed *me'ilah* by *karka*, a position that other *rishonim* find difficult. One solution offered by *Tosafot* is that *me'ilah* would apply if one uprooted a clump of earth from within the cistern and thereby derived benefit — though at that point the dirt is no longer *mechubar lakarka*, no longer attached to the ground. The *Ramban* offers a more creative answer: if one built a brick wall inside the cistern, that constitutes *talush ulevasof chibro* — something detached that was subsequently attached. If one then derived benefit from that wall — leaning against it, cooling off, scratching one's back — one has derived benefit from something that is arguably no longer *mechubar lakarka*, depending on one's position in the earlier dispute. This remains a genuine open question, but it is worth flagging that the entire discussion proceeds against the backdrop of the general exemption of *karka* from *me'ilah*.

It is also important to clarify what is meant when we say *yesh bo me'ilah* or *ein bo me'ilah*. The question is not only whether one transgresses the prohibition against benefiting from *hekdesh*, but whether one incurs the full consequences of *me'ilah*: the obligation to add a fifth, and the requirement to bring a *korban*. These are the operative stakes in the discussions that follow.

---

## Gidulei Hekdesh

### Empty vs. Full

The *baraita* that drives the subsequent discussion introduces a distinction: what is the law when one sanctifies an empty vessel or property, and it subsequently becomes filled? The items mentioned are a cistern, a dung pit, a pigeon coop, a tree, and a field — the same objects discussed in the *mishnah*, but now considered in the scenario where they were empty at the time of sanctification and became full only afterward. The case of the tree that subsequently bears fruit is particularly significant, as is the cistern that is later filled by rain.

### R. Yehuda's View

*Rabbi Yehuda* rules: *me'ilin bahen ve'ein me'ilin bema shebeisochan* — *me'ilah* applies to the sanctified object itself, but not to what fills it afterward. Since one sanctified only the cistern, the tree, the field, or the pigeon coop, but did not sanctify the water, the fruit, the grass, or the pigeons that came later, those subsequent contents carry no *me'ilah*.

### R. Yosi's View

*Rabbi Yosi* disagrees in one specific category: *hamakdish hasadeh veha'ilan me'ilin bahen uvigiduleihen mipnei shehen gidulei hekdesh* — one who consecrates a field or a tree generates *me'ilah* not only on the field and the tree but on whatever grows from them, because those are *gidulei hekdesh*, growth produced by a sanctified object. Notably, *Rabbi Yosi* does not extend this position to the cistern and the water, or to the pigeon coop and the pigeons. His reasoning is specific to produce generated by the consecrated entity itself.

---

## Two Sets of Terms (II)

### Ownership vs. Sanctity

The question that all the *rishonim* struggle with is this: if one owns a well and it rains, one acquires the rainwater through *kinyan chatzer* — the principle that objects entering one's domain are automatically acquired. If *hekdesh* owns the well, why does *hekdesh* not similarly acquire the water through *kinyan chatzer*? And if *hekdesh* owns the water, why is there no *me'ilah*?

Two important answers are given. The *Rashbam* and *Tosafot* hold that *hekdesh* does not have *kinyan chatzer* at all. *Kinyan chatzer* is a legal fiction specific to human property law; there is no *pasuk* establishing that *hekdesh* acquires objects that enter its domain. Therefore, when rain falls into a consecrated cistern, *hekdesh* does not own the water. Even though in some cosmic sense everything belongs to God — *ki li ha'aretz*, as the Torah says — the legal institution of *hekdesh* as a property-owning entity does not have *kinyan chatzer*.

The *Ramban*, however, offers a more analytically compelling distinction. He insists that we must separate two entirely different concepts that the word *hekdesh* bundles together. On one hand, *hekdesh* is an institution that owns property — like a corporation with a bank account, able to own, sell, and transact. On the other hand, *hekdesh* describes a status of sanctity that attaches to an object when it is verbally consecrated. These are two different things.

According to the *Ramban*, when rain falls into a consecrated cistern, *hekdesh* does indeed own that water — it entered *hekdesh*'s domain and *hekdesh* can sell it, use it, and no one has the right to take it. But the water is not *kadosh*. It has not been sanctified. It was never the subject of *kedushat peh* — a verbal act of consecration. And *me'ilah* requires that the object itself have the status of *kedushah*. Ownership by *hekdesh* and sanctity of the object are independent questions, and it is only the latter that triggers *me'ilah*.

This is a brilliant distinction because it forces a recognition that *hekdesh* plays two distinct roles simultaneously. Sometimes an object has *kedushah* without being owned by the *Beis Hamikdash* — the paradigmatic case being *kodashim kalim*, which according to *Rabbi Yossi HaGlili* are *mammon ba'alim*, remaining the property of their owner even while possessing sanctity. A *korban Pesach* is eaten by its owners; it is theirs, yet it is holy. Conversely, rainwater that falls into a consecrated cistern is owned by *hekdesh* yet lacks the sanctity that triggers *me'ilah*.

This framework illuminates the debate over *gidulei hekdesh* as well. *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Yosi* debate whether the fruit of a sanctified tree is subject to *me'ilah*. The *Rashbam* and *Tosafot* are notably silent on the *kinyan chatzer* argument in this context, because it is hard to argue that *hekdesh* does not own the fruit of its own tree. For the *Ramban*, however, the framework works elegantly: of course *hekdesh* owns the fruit. The question is whether the fruit was sanctified. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that no verbal act of sanctification was directed at the fruit — only at the tree — so the fruit lacks *kedushat peh* and there is no *me'ilah*. *Rabbi Yosi* holds that the sanctity of the tree extends to its produce, since the fruit is *gidulei hekdesh*, growth generated by the sanctified entity, and therefore the fruit shares the tree's sanctity.

One participant raised the pointed question of a *bechor behemah* — a firstborn animal that is sacred from birth, *kadosh merachem*, without any verbal act of sanctification. What would the *Ramban* say about that case? The answer offered is that situations in which the Torah itself automatically assigns sanctity — such as a firstborn animal designated directly for the *mizbe'ach* — may operate under a different principle than cases of human consecration. The *Ramban*'s framework focuses on cases where sanctity derives entirely from human ownership and natural processes of acquisition, and where no independent *Torah*-mandated sanctity intervenes. But the question is acknowledged as genuinely sharp.

---

## Gidulei Hekdesh (II)

### Clarifying Scope

A *baraita* then reports that *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position appears correct regarding the cistern and the pigeon coop, and *Rabbi Yosi*'s position appears correct regarding the field and the tree. The *gemara* challenges this formulation: the first part makes sense — *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Yosi* do debate the case of the tree, so one can say that *Rabbi* agrees with *Rabbi Yehuda* only in the case of the cistern and pigeon coop while rejecting him in the case of the tree. But the second part is strange. *Rabbi Yosi* only explicitly addressed the case of the field and tree — he never claimed *me'ilah* applies to pigeon coop pigeons or cistern water. What does it mean to say *Rabbi* agrees with *Rabbi Yosi* "in the case of the field and tree"? That sounds as though *Rabbi Yosi* had a broader position from which *Rabbi* selectively endorses part.

The *gemara* considers the possibility that *Rabbi Yosi* was addressing *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position dialectically — arguing that even if one accepts *Rabbi Yehuda* elsewhere, at minimum the case of the tree should generate *me'ilah*. But this reading cannot be sustained, because a separate *baraita* makes *Rabbi Yosi*'s own scope entirely clear: *ein ani ro'eh divrei Rabbi Yehuda basadeh veilan* — I do not agree with *Rabbi Yehuda* regarding the field and the tree. By implication, regarding everything else — cistern and pigeon coop — *Rabbi Yosi* fully agrees with *Rabbi Yehuda* that there is no *me'ilah* on subsequent contents.

The *gemara* therefore rereads *Rabbi*'s statement. *Rabbi* is not endorsing *Rabbi Yehuda* against *Rabbi Yosi* in one domain while endorsing *Rabbi Yosi* against *Rabbi Yehuda* in another. Rather, *Rabbi* is saying: *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position is correct — and even *Rabbi Yosi* agrees with *Rabbi Yehuda* — in the case of the cistern and pigeon coop, since the sole dispute between them is the field and the tree. *Rabbi*'s statement is simply a way of saying he *paskens* like *Rabbi Yosi*: both agree there is no *me'ilah* on cistern water or coop pigeons, and *Rabbi Yosi* additionally holds that *me'ilah* does apply to the produce of a consecrated tree or field.

---

## Well Filling with Water

### Dispute Framework

The *gemara* now presents a new *baraita*: *hikdishan rekanim ve'achar kach nitmal'u* — one sanctified these items empty and they subsequently became filled. The ruling: *me'ilin bahen ve'ein me'ilin bema shebeisochan* — *me'ilah* applies to the items but not to what filled them. *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon* dissents: *af me'ilin bema shebeisochan* — *me'ilah* applies even to the contents.

On first reading, this *baraita* seems to map cleanly onto the earlier debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Yosi* about a tree that subsequently bears fruit. The *tanna kamma* parallels *Rabbi Yehuda*; *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon* parallels *Rabbi Yosi*. And Abaye reports a companion ruling: *hikdishan mele'im me'ilin bahen uvema shebeisochan* — one who sanctified them already filled has *me'ilah* on both the item and its contents — and *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon machalif*, reverses.

This reversal is striking — indeed perplexing. *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon* appears to hold that if one sanctifies an empty cistern and it later fills with water, the water is subject to *me'ilah*; but if one sanctifies a cistern already full of water, the water is not subject to *me'ilah*. This seems exactly backwards: surely water present at the moment of sanctification should more readily be included than water that does not yet exist at that moment.

The *gemara* first attempts to locate the dispute in the case of the field and tree — the earlier debate about *gidulei hekdesh*. But the *gemara* immediately rejects this: if one sanctifies an empty tree and then fruit grows, versus sanctifying a tree already bearing fruit — what conceivable logic would exclude the already-present fruit while including future fruit? The reversal makes no sense in the context of a tree.

*Rava* therefore reassigns the debate: *machloket bevo'r veshovach* — the entire dispute concerns the cistern and the pigeon coop, not the field and tree. In this reading, the debate about the tree is settled: *divrei hakol me'ilin bahen uvema shebeisochan* — everyone agrees that *gidulei hekdesh* carry *me'ilah*, following *Rabbi Yosi*, and this is not in dispute. The open question is the cistern that fills with water and the coop that fills with pigeons — and it is there that the reversal must be explained.

### Tanna Kamma View

The *gemara* now explains the structure of the debate. *Rikkanim peligi bifluggeta deRabbi Meir veRabbanan* — the dispute about sanctifying these items empty, and what happens when they subsequently fill, is the same dispute between *Rabbi Meir* and the *Rabbanan* on the principle of *adam makneh davar she'lo ba l'olam* — whether one can effect a legal transfer of something not yet in existence.

The *tanna kamma* holds like the *Rabbanan*: *ein adam makneh davar she'lo ba l'olam* — one cannot sanctify future water or future pigeons because one does not yet own them. When one says "I hereby consecrate this cistern," one consecrates only the cistern. When rain later falls into it, the water becomes owned by *hekdesh* because it entered *hekdesh*'s domain — but it was never verbally sanctified. Following the *Ramban*'s framework: the water is owned by *hekdesh* but is not *kadosh*, having never been the subject of *kedushat peh*. Therefore there is no *me'ilah* on the water.

It is worth noting that the *gemara* here applies the principle of *amira legavoha kimesiraso lehedyot* — that a verbal declaration of consecration has the legal force of a formal act of transfer. This equation means that the rules governing what one *can* transfer to an ordinary party also govern what one *can* consecrate, making the *adam makneh davar she'lo ba l'olam* debate directly applicable.

### R. Elazar Position

*Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon*, by contrast, holds like *Rabbi Meir*: *adam makneh davar she'lo ba l'olam* — one can effect a legal transfer of something not yet in existence. When one sanctifies the cistern, there is an implicit — or according to the *Ramban*, an explicit — declaration consecrating the cistern and any future water that will fill it. Similarly for the pigeon coop and future pigeons. Since *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon* holds that such a forward-looking declaration is effective, those future contents are subject to *kedushat peh* and there is *me'ilah*.

One might object: *Rabbi Meir*'s principle about *davar she'lo ba l'olam* was stated in contexts where the future item is virtually certain to materialize — like fruit from a palm tree. Who can guarantee that water will ever fall into this particular cistern, or that pigeons will ever enter this coop? Is that really comparable to the near-certainty of fruit growing on a tree?

### Water via Courtyard

*Rava* addresses this: *mishtacha lah bimayim arba'im derech chatzeiro labor, veyonim ba'im derech shovcho leshovach* — the case is one where we know with certainty that water will reach the well because it flows through the owner's courtyard on its way there, and pigeons are coming through the owner's pigeon coop before nesting in the consecrated one.
