The reason one's own courtyard is specified is not merely to establish probability. *Tosafot* and the *Ramban* point out that this answers a different and deeper question: even if *adam makneh davar she'lo ba l'olam* works, it works only for something that one will own in the future. If I sanctify a palm tree and consecrate its future fruit, the mechanism is that had I not consecrated the fruit, the fruit would have been mine — I have the standing to consecrate what will be mine. But once I have consecrated the cistern, the cistern belongs to *hekdesh*. When rain subsequently falls into *hekdesh*'s cistern, that water belongs to *hekdesh* — not to me. So how can I have standing to consecrate it? I will never own that water; it goes directly into property I have already given away.

The answer is that the water first flows through *my* courtyard — my personal property, not yet *hekdesh*. I take possession of it there. Then it flows into the consecrated cistern. Since at the moment it enters my domain it briefly becomes *mine*, I do have the standing to consecrate it in advance, because it will indeed at some point be mine before it becomes *hekdesh*'s. The same logic applies to pigeons nesting briefly in my personal pigeon coop before moving to the consecrated one.

### Tosafot Critique

*Tosafot* (and the *Ramban* in parallel) press a more fundamental critique. They observe that the *gemara*'s reference to *Rabbi Meir* is puzzling in a different way. *Rabbi Meir*'s principle of *adam makneh davar she'lo ba l'olam* was not originally stated in the context of trees and fruit at all. The *gemara* links the principle to *Rabbi Meir* via cases involving conditional *kiddushin* — a man who says to a woman that he betroths her on condition that he converts, or that she is freed from slavery, or that her husband dies. The extension from those cases to the case of a palm tree and its fruit involves a chain of associations in the *gemara*, and *Tosafot* and the *Ramban* argue that this chain obscures the fact that *Rabbi Meir*'s original cases are quite different. In those cases, there is no assumption that the condition will be fulfilled — the master might never free the slave, the husband might not die. The requirement that the future item be *avida de'asi* — naturally bound to materialize — is a criterion applied later in the discussion, not part of *Rabbi Meir*'s original position.

Both *Tosafot* and the *Ramban* conclude that the *gemara*'s attribution of the palm-tree case to *Rabbi Meir* is somewhat imprecise; it is actually a formulation developed by a later *amora* — perhaps *Rav Huna* — and then retroactively associated with *Rabbi Meir*'s principle. The parameters that govern *Rabbi Meir*'s actual ruling and those that govern the palm-tree case operate with different criteria, and the *gemara* does not resolve this cleanly.

---

## Already-Filled Well

### Filled When Sanctified

The companion case is the reverse: *hikdishan mele'im* — one sanctified the cistern when it was already full of water. Here, intuitively, there should be no difficulty establishing *me'ilah* on the water: the water was present at the moment of consecration, there is no issue of *davar she'lo ba l'olam*, and one might expect *me'ilah* to apply straightforwardly. Yet this is precisely where *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon* holds there is *no* *me'ilah* on the water.

### Hekdesh = Hedyot

The *gemara* explains that *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon* holds like his father — *Rabbi Shimon* — who maintained *danin din gavoah midin hedyot*: the laws governing *hekdesh* are derived from the laws governing ordinary transactions. Whatever is included when a layperson sells something is what is included when one consecrates it; *hekdesh* does not receive more than an ordinary purchaser would receive.

### Well Includes Water?

This generates the central question: in an ordinary sale, does selling a cistern include the water inside it? If yes, then when one consecrates a filled cistern, the water is consecrated along with it, and there is *me'ilah* on the water. If no — if in an ordinary sale the water is excluded unless explicitly specified — then consecrating the cistern similarly excludes the water, since *hekdesh* is no different from an ordinary buyer. *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon*, following his father's principle, adopts the latter position: selling a cistern does *not* include the water, and therefore consecrating a cistern does not include the water.

### Mishna Status

The *gemara* immediately challenges: but our own *mishnah* rules that *machar bor machar meimav* — selling a cistern *does* include the water! If even in an ordinary transaction the water is included, then *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon*'s position collapses, because even granting that *hekdesh* equals *hedyot*, the *hedyot* case already includes the water.

*Rava* responds: *matnistin yichidaah hi* — our *mishnah* does not represent the unanimous opinion. A *baraita* preserves the debate explicitly: the first *tanna* holds *machar bor lo machar meimav* — selling a cistern does *not* include the water; *Rabbi Natan* holds it does. Our *mishnah*, which rules that the water is included, reflects the position of *Rabbi Natan* alone. *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon* follows the *tanna kamma* of that *baraita*: selling a cistern does not include the water, and accordingly consecrating a cistern does not include the water.

### Reconciliation

With this in place, the apparent paradox of *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon*'s reversal resolves into a coherent and consistent position.

Case one: one consecrates an empty cistern, explicitly declaring, "I consecrate this cistern and all water that will fill it." There is no water at the moment of consecration, so the *tanna kamma* — holding *ein adam makdish davar she'lo ba l'olam* — says no *me'ilah* on the water when it arrives. *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon*, following *Rabbi Meir*, holds the explicit forward-looking declaration is effective, and since the water will eventually pass through the owner's courtyard, the owner will briefly hold title to it before it enters *hekdesh*'s cistern. The declaration therefore has legal force, and *me'ilah* applies to the future water.

Case two: one consecrates a filled cistern, saying only "I hereby consecrate this cistern" — without mentioning the water. The *tanna kamma* says: either *machar bor machar meimav* applies, so even without explicit mention the water is included; or even if it is not automatically included under ordinary sales law, *hekdesh* receives the benefit of the doubt and is presumed to include more than an ordinary sale. Either way, there is *me'ilah* on the water. *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon*, however, holds both that *hekdesh* is no greater than *hedyot*, and that even in an ordinary *hedyot* sale, a cistern does not include its water unless explicitly stated. Since the consecration mentioned only the cistern and not the water, the water was never consecrated. There is no *kedushat peh* on the water, and therefore no *me'ilah*.

The reversal is thus not truly paradoxical. In case one, *Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon* finds *me'ilah* because there was an explicit forward-looking declaration of *kedushat peh* covering the future water, valid under the principle of *adam makneh davar she'lo ba l'olam*. In case two, he finds no *me'ilah* because the verbal declaration covered only the cistern, not the water; since *hekdesh* follows the same rules as *hedyot*, and *hedyot* sales do not automatically include the water, the water was simply never consecrated.

The key insight to carry away — the *Ramban*'s central contribution — is that *hekdesh* operates simultaneously as a property-owning institution and as a framework of sanctity attaching to specific objects. Ownership by *hekdesh* and sanctity of an object are distinct. An object can be owned by *hekdesh* without being *kadosh*, and it is only sanctity — produced by *kedushat peh*, a verbal act of consecration — that triggers the laws of *me'ilah*. This distinction between the question of ownership and the question of the intrinsic status of *kedushah* is the conceptual spine around which the entire discussion of *Bava Batra* 79 turns.

---

---

# Bava Batra 80

## Dovecote & First Brood

### Mishna Overview

The *mishna* at the top of 80a opens a new subject: *halokeach peiros shovach mechaveiro* — one who purchases the fruit, meaning the offspring, of a dovecote from his fellow. The buyer acquires all the young doves born from the dovecote. This marks a shift from the earlier *mishnayot*, which asked whether the purchase of one item includes associated items — does buying a house include the well, does buying a ship include the cargo containers, and so on. Here the question is not what is included in the sale but rather what must nonetheless be left behind despite being technically included.

### First Brood Rule

The *mishna* rules *mafriach berecha rishona* — the buyer must cause to fly away, that is, must leave with the seller, the first brood. According to the *Rashbam*, doves give birth once a month for most of the year, producing each time a male and a female. The first pair of offspring must be left behind with the mother. The reason is straightforward: if all the young are removed, the mother will have no reason to remain in the dovecote and will fly away. Since the seller intends to maintain his dovecote for the future — whether to sell next year's offspring or keep them for himself — he needs the mother to stay. Leaving the first brood behind serves as the anchor that keeps her there.

### Beehive Swarms

The *mishna* turns next to *peiros kaveret* — the offspring of a beehive. If one purchases the bees born from a hive, the ruling is *notel gimel nechilin umesares*: the buyer takes the first three *nechilin*, three swarms, and then the owner is *mesares*. Bees reproduce in groups, and each such cluster of newborns constitutes a swarm that can be removed to start a new hive. The buyer receives the first three. As for *mesares*, the *gemara* will debate its precise meaning, but reading it provisionally as sterilization: once the buyer has taken his three swarms, the seller retains the right to sterilize the remaining bees so that they return to producing honey. The *Rashbam* explains that as long as bees are reproducing, they are not producing honey; sterilizing them redirects their activity toward honey production, which is what the seller wants to preserve.

### Honey Loaves

A related case: if one purchases the honey from a beehive rather than the bees themselves, the *mishna* rules *maniach shtei chalot* — one must leave behind two *chalot*, two loaves of honey still embedded in the wax. Honey is the food of the bees, and the seller, while willing to sell the honey, is not trying to destroy his beehive. Leaving two loaves sustains the remaining bees. Those two loaves are therefore not included in the honey the buyer purchased.

### Olive Branches

Similarly, *zeisim lilkot meniach shtei gurofiyot* — if one purchases olive trees in order to cut down their branches, he must leave behind two *gurofiyot*, two branches, so the tree can grow back. The word *likkot* here denotes cutting the branches entirely, not merely picking individual olives. Even so, the seller is not understood to have forfeited his tree's future productivity, and the two remaining branches ensure the tree's regeneration.

---

## Generations Theory

### Brood Discrepancy

The *gemara* raises an apparent contradiction. The *mishna* states that the buyer must leave behind the first brood — *berecha rishona* — while a *baraita* says the first and second brood — *berecha rishona ushniya*. How are these reconciled?

### Rav Kahana Resolution

Rav Kahana answers: *lo kashya — ha lah ha le'imah* — this is no difficulty; one teaching speaks about her, and one about the mother. The *Rashbam* acknowledges that there are many unsatisfactory explanations of this passage in the literature, and he offers one that more or less works. What Rav Kahana means is the following: yes, the first brood is left behind to keep the mother anchored in the dovecote. But that first brood will itself grow up, and when it does, what prevents it from flying away? If it leaves, the mother loses her offspring and will also fly away. So the first brood must itself be given a reason to stay.

### Multi-Gen Anchoring

Using generational labels for clarity: call the mother Generation A. A gives birth, and the buyer takes all the offspring — except the first brood, which is Generation B, left behind for A. Now B grows up. B begins giving birth, and the buyer is entitled to those offspring as well — except for B's first brood, which is Generation C, left behind for B. So when the *baraita* says one leaves behind *rishona ushniya*, the first and the second, it does not mean the first two consecutive broods born from A. It means the first and second *generations*: B, the first generation left for A, and C, the second generation left for B.

### Why Offspring?

The *gemara* challenges this. When we are dealing with the mother, A, she stays because *demitztatfa abarta ve'azuga* — she has an attachment, a bond of connection, to her daughter B and to her mate, who are both left behind for her. Very well. But then why does B need C in order to stay? B also has its mother, A, and its own mate still present. *Ee nami titztatef ima ve'azuga deshavkinan lah* — let B find its anchoring from its mother and its mate, just as A found anchoring from its daughter and mate. Why must we leave C behind for B?

### Mother vs. Daughter

The *gemara* answers: *ima abarta mitztatfa; abarta ima lo mitztatfa* — a mother is anchored by her daughter; a daughter is not anchored by her mother. A parent stays because her child is there. But a child does not stay simply because her parent is there — that is not how offspring behave. They grow up, and they leave. So if you want B to remain in the dovecote, you cannot rely on the fact that A is present. You must give B her own child, C, who will keep B there. And if B is there because of C, then A will stay because of B.

---

## Mesares Debate

### Mustard Method

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: when one purchases the offspring of a hive, *notel gimel nechilin umesares* — one takes three swarms and then *mesares*. The *gemara* asks: how exactly does one perform this *mesares*, this sterilization? Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *bechardal* — through mustard. The bees consume mustard and as a result are sterilized, redirecting their activity to honey production.

### Honey Consumption

The *amri bamaarava* — the sages of *Eretz Yisroel* — said in the name of Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina: it is not precisely that the mustard sterilizes the bees. Rather, *mitokh shepihen chad* — because the mustard leaves their mouths with a sharp, pungent taste, they then seek something sweet to neutralize it, *ve'okhlo et dovshan* — and they go and eat their honey. Once they are consuming honey and spending their time on that activity, they are not reproducing. According to the *Rashbam*, this is the mechanism: occupying the bees with eating honey rather than reproducing achieves the intended effect.

### Alternation Theory

Rabbi Yochanan offers a fundamentally different reading of the word. He says *mesares* does not derive from *sirus*, sterilization, but from *serugin*, alternation — the same root as *kippot serugin*, knitted caps, implying an interwoven pattern. Under Rabbi Yochanan's reading, *notel shlosha nechilin besirus* means the buyer takes three swarms *in alternation* — that is, swarm one, swarm three, and swarm five, while the seller retains swarms two, four, and six. The earlier swarms are presumably stronger and more valuable, so rather than the buyer taking all three of the first and best swarms, the arrangement alternates so that the benefit is shared.

### Three Then Alternate

A *baraita* then clarifies and provides the most satisfying reading of the *mishna*: *notel gimel nechilin zeh achar zeh* — the buyer takes the first three consecutive swarms, one after the other. *Mikan ve'eilach, notel achas umaniach achas* — from that point on, alternation begins: the buyer takes one, the seller keeps one, the buyer takes one, and so forth. So the word *mesares* in the *mishna* does mean alternation in the sense of Rabbi Yochanan, but it does not mean three swarms taken alternately from the start. The buyer first receives three straight, and the alternating pattern governs only subsequent swarms. This is, as noted, a considerably better reading of the *mishna*.

---

## Honey Status

### Rav Kahana Position

The *mishna*'s mention of the two honey loaves left for the bees prompts a broader *halakhic* discussion about the status of honey in the hive. Rav Kahana states: *devash bekiveret eino yotzei midei maakhal le'olam* — honey that is still in the beehive, still embedded in the wax, never loses its status as food. This carries two implications. First, the honey automatically has the status of *ochel*, food, even before it has been removed from the hive and extracted from the wax — which is somewhat surprising, since it is not yet in the form people would ordinarily eat. Second, it is not a liquid but a solid, and this distinction matters for *tumah* purposes, since the *halakhic* rules for food and liquid differ. The *gemara* adds that this means Rav Kahana holds *lo ba'ei machshava* — no conscious intent is required to confer food status. Just as one need not think "I intend to eat this apple" in order for an apple to carry the *halakhic* status of food, so too honey in the hive is automatically food.

### In Wax vs. Extracted

*Tosafos* notes that *halakhically*, honey is normally classified among the seven liquids. However, *Tosafos* draws a careful distinction: that classification applies to honey once it has been extracted from the wax. When honey is still inside the beehive in its wax state, it begins its existence as food, and while in that state it cannot be considered a liquid.

### Neither Status

The *gemara* challenges Rav Kahana's position. A *baraita* teaches: *devash bekiveret eino lo ochel ve-lo mashkeh* — honey while still in the beehive has neither the status of food nor the status of liquid. This stands in apparent contradiction to Rav Kahana's ruling that honey in the hive is automatically and irrevocably food. The question is how to reconcile these sources.

### Two Loaves Exception

Abaye resolves the tension: *lo tzricha ella le'otan shtei chalot* — that *baraita* is speaking specifically about the two loaves left behind for the bees. This is entirely reasonable. The totality of honey in a beehive exists for the purpose of human consumption — that is the nature of the enterprise — and therefore it automatically carries food status without any special intent. But the two loaves set aside expressly for the bees to eat are a different category: their default purpose is bee sustenance, not human consumption. Those two loaves, accordingly, do not automatically have food status; only if one specifically intends to remove them for human use will they acquire the *halakhic* status of food or liquid depending on how one intends to treat them.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

Rava offers a different resolution. He says: *Rabbi Eliezer hi* — that *baraita* which says honey in the hive is neither food nor liquid reflects the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer. The reference is to a *mishna* from 83b that was treated earlier in the tractate.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Honey

### Ground Attachment

The *mishna* in question states that Rabbi Eliezer holds: *kiveret devorim — harei hi ke-karka* — a beehive of bees is treated as land. *Tosafos* clarifies that we are speaking here about the honey within the hive. Rabbi Eliezer's position is that honey within a hive is treated *halakhically* as though it were fruit still attached to a tree — it is considered part of the land, still connected to the ground. This is Rabbi Eliezer's *chiddush*: one might argue that honey does not grow in the hive the way an apple grows from a tree; rather, the bees manufacture it there. You could compare it to placing a basket of apples in a tree — that would not be *karka*. But Rabbi Eliezer rules that nonetheless, since the honey is a product of the hive and remains within it, it is treated as though still attached to the ground.

### Pruzbul & Tamei

Several *halachic* consequences flow from this position. *Ve-kotvin aleha pruzbul* — one may write a *pruzbul* using the honey in the hive as the debtor's landed property, since a *pruzbul* can only be written when the debtor possesses land, and Rabbi Eliezer treats this honey as land. Furthermore, *ve'eina mekabeles tumah bimkomah* — just as an apple attached to a tree cannot become *tamei* until it is detached, the honey in the hive, while still there and still considered attached to the ground, cannot become *tamei*.

### Shabbat Violation

Perhaps the most striking ruling is: *ve-ha-rodeh mimena be-shabbat chayav chatat* — one who removes honey from the hive on *Shabbat* is liable for a *chatat* offering, having violated *Shabbat*. One is liable on *Shabbat* for *kotzer*, harvesting — plucking something from where it grows. If one had a basket of apples hanging from a tree, taking apples from it would not constitute *kotzer*. But Rabbi Eliezer holds that since the honey is *halakhically* treated as growing from the ground, removing it is equivalent to picking an apple from a tree, and thus one has performed a prohibited *melacha* on *Shabbat*.

### Verse Proof

Rabbi Elazar the *Amora* asks: *mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Eliezer* — what is the scriptural basis for Rabbi Eliezer's position? *Dichtiv vayitbol otah be-yaarot devash* — the verse describes someone dipping into *yaarot devash*, literally "forests of honey." *Ve-chi ma inyan yaar etzel devash* — what does a forest have to do with honey? The juxtaposition teaches: *mah yaar ha-toleish mimenu be-shabbat chayav chatat* — just as with a forest, plucking from a tree constitutes a *Shabbat* violation, *af devash ha-rodeh mimenu be-shabbat chayav chatat* — so too with honey: removing it from the hive on *Shabbat* constitutes a violation. The *halakha* treats the honey as though it had grown in and from the hive, as attached to the ground, and therefore all of these *halachot* apply.

This is precisely relevant to Rava's explanation of the *baraita*. If honey in the hive is treated as *karka* by Rabbi Eliezer — as attached to the ground like fruit on a tree — then it cannot become *tamei* while in that state, and therefore it has neither food nor liquid status for *tumah* purposes. That is what the *baraita* reflects.

---

## Separation Intent

### Separated Status

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita* that poses a fresh challenge: *devash she-zav mi-kavarto eino lo ochel ve-lo mashkeh* — honey that has flowed out from the hive has neither food nor liquid status. This is striking because at this point the honey has already separated from the hive — it is no longer embedded in the wax and no longer inside the hive itself — and yet the *baraita* says it is still neither food nor liquid.

### Intent Determines

The *baraita* continues: if one had intent *le'achila*, to eat the honey, it becomes *metamei tumat ochlim* — it acquires the *tumah* status of food and is subject to the laws governing solid foodstuffs, with the relevant *shiur* of *ke-beitza*. If one had intent to treat it as a liquid — perhaps to use it as a dripping substance, or to drink it, or to produce mead — it becomes *metamei tumat mashkin*, a liquid for *tumah* purposes, with the different *shiur* of a *revi'is*. So the *baraita* posits that even after the honey has separated from the hive and the wax, it has no *halakhic* status until one consciously decides how to use it.

### Abaye Consistency

For Abaye this poses no difficulty. Under his reading, Rav Kahana's position is that normal honey in the hive is automatically food. The earlier *baraita* that said honey in the hive is neither food nor liquid was referring to the two loaves set aside for the bees. Now this *baraita* about honey that has flowed out is also consistent: the honey that flows out is still the honey of those two loaves — it began its existence set aside for bee consumption, not human consumption. Because it started without food status, it retains that statusless quality even after separation from the wax and hive. Only specific *machshava*, conscious intent, transforms it into food or liquid for *tumah* purposes. The entire picture — Rav Kahana's automatic-food ruling for normal honey, and the two *baraitas* — coheres into a clean package under Abaye's reading.

### Rava Reading

For Rava, however, there is a difficulty. Under Rava's reading, the *baraita* that describes honey in the hive as neither food nor liquid is following Rabbi Eliezer, who treats the honey as attached to the ground. The problem is the end of this same *baraita*, which says that once the honey has flowed out, *machshava* — intent — can confer food or liquid status. But under Rabbi Eliezer's framework, the operative factor is ground-attachment. Once the honey has separated from the hive and is no longer attached to the ground, it should simply revert automatically to its natural status as food. *Machshava* should not be required. So how does Rava account for this *baraita*?

Rava would respond: *taretz hachi* — read the end of the *baraita* with the word *eino* inserted. *Chishav alav le'achila eino metameh tumat ochlim; le-mashkeh eino metameh tumat mashkeh* — if one thought to eat it, it does **not** thereby become *tamei* as food; if one thought to drink it, it does **not** thereby become *tamei* as liquid. The *baraita* is not saying intent makes it food; it is saying intent does not suffice to make it *tamei* — because while it remains in its ground-attached state, nothing can make it *tamei*.

### Disgusting Vessel

The *gemara* then challenges Rava's position from another *baraita*: *devash she-zav mi-kavarto eino lo ochel ve-lo mashkeh* — honey that flowed from the hive is neither food nor liquid — followed again by the clause that intent to eat makes it food and intent to use as liquid makes it liquid. Rava faces the same problem: once it has flowed out, it should automatically be food; why does intent matter?

Rav Zevid offers a solution: the *baraita* is speaking *ke-gon she-zav agav keli ma'us* — of a case where the honey flowed into or over a disgusting vessel. Rav Acha bar Yaakov says: *ke-gon she-zav agav kaskasin* — it flowed over wood chips and was absorbed into them, making it unretrievable in any normal sense. The significance of these scenarios is as follows. Under Abaye's reading of Rav Kahana, once something acquires food status, it retains that status even if it falls into a disgusting vessel — as long as it is still edible by a dog, it remains *halakhically* food for *tumah* purposes. But Rava's reading follows Rabbi Eliezer, according to whom the honey started its existence as ground-attached and thus not yet food. When it then flows out into a disgusting vessel or onto wood chips, it is not edible by normal humans. Since its pre-existing status was "not food," and its current condition is "not normally edible by humans," it still does not automatically acquire food status. Only explicit *machshava* — a conscious decision to eat it or treat it as a liquid — will confer *halakhic* status. That is how Rava accounts for the *baraita*.

---

## Consensus & Baraita

### Rav Kahana Consensus

The *gemara* concludes: *tanya kevata de-Rav Kahana* — there is a *baraita* that has been taught in accordance with Rav Kahana's position. *Devash bekiveret metameh tumat ochlim she-lo be-machshava* — honey in the hive conveys the *tumah* of food without requiring any *machshava* at all. This establishes that the *halakha* follows Rav Kahana: honey in the hive is automatically food.

### Full Reconciliation

The full picture is now clear. Rav Kahana's ruling — honey in the hive is automatically food, requiring no intent — is the accepted position. Abaye explains the apparent contradictory *baraita* as referring exclusively to the two loaves left for the bees: since those are set aside for bee consumption by default, they do not automatically bear food status, and intent is required to reassign them for human use. Rava's explanation — that the *baraita* reflects Rabbi Eliezer's view of honey as ground-attached, such that no *machshava* can make it *tamei* while in that state — stands as a minority reading tied to Rabbi Eliezer's specific position.

---

## Trees Cutting

### Standard Cutting

The *mishna*'s ruling about olive branches is fleshed out by a *baraita*: *halokeach ilan mechaveiro lilkot magbi'ah min hakarka tefach vekotzetz* — one who buys a tree from his fellow to cut it down must cut from a height of one *tefach* above the ground, approximately three to four inches, in order to leave enough of the trunk that the tree can grow back. The buyer purchased the wood, not the right to uproot the tree entirely.

### Sycamore Heights

For a *bisculas hashikmah* — a virgin sycamore, one that has never previously been cut — one must leave *gimel tefachim*, three *tefachim*, near the ground. For a *sdan hashikmah* — a sycamore that has been cut before and has already grown back — *shtei tefachim* suffice, since a once-cut sycamore is sturdier and will regenerate with less trunk remaining.

### Other Trees

For reeds and grapevines, the buyer must cut *min hapkak ulema'alah* — above the knot in the reed or vine. For date palms and cedar trees, however, *chofer umesharesh* — one may dig down and uproot them entirely — because *she'ein gizmo machalif*, their trunk does not regenerate once cut. Since no regrowth is possible, there is nothing to preserve for the seller, and the buyer may remove them entirely.

---

## Sycamore Shevi'is

### Shevi'is Ban

The *gemara* challenges the requirement of three *tefachim* for a virgin sycamore from a *baraita* concerning *shevi'is*: *ein kotzetzin be-visculas hashikmah beshevi'is mipnei shehi avodah* — one may not cut a virgin sycamore on *shevi'is* because doing so constitutes *avodah*, a prohibited act that promotes growth. *Shevi'is* prohibits not only planting and sowing but any agricultural labor that encourages crops or trees to grow: *sadcha lo tizra, ve-charmecha lo tizmor*. Cutting a virgin sycamore causes it to regenerate, which the Rabbis understood as a prohibited form of agricultural enhancement.

This seems consistent with what we have been learning — cutting the sycamore encourages new growth. But the question from the *baraita* about *shevi'is* is: if cutting it at all causes growth, the cut should be forbidden. And indeed it seems that even cutting at one *tefach* would stimulate regrowth. So why does the buyer's case require three *tefachim* — what difference does the height make?

### Yehuda Exception

Rabbi Yehuda says: *kidarko asur* — cutting in the normal manner that allows regrowth is forbidden on *shevi'is*. However, two alternatives are permitted if one simply wants the wood without encouraging growth. First, *magbi'ah yud tefachim vekotzetz* — one may cut starting from ten *tefachim* above the ground; at that height, the cut will not stimulate regrowth. Second, *ugomem me'im ha'aretz* — one may cut the tree flush against the ground, leveling it completely; that too will not promote regrowth.

### Range Theory

This raises the question: the *baraita* about the sale requires three *tefachim*; Rabbi Yehuda says for *shevi'is* you must either go very high or cut completely flush. The implication seems to be that only cutting flush against the ground prevents regrowth — so why does the buyer in a normal sale need to leave three *tefachim* for the tree to grow back? Would leaving even one *tefach* not be sufficient?

Abaye explains that there is a range. *Gimel tefachim ma'ali lei* — cutting at three *tefachim* is optimal; the stump left behind is robust and the tree will regenerate vigorously. *Me'im ha'aretz vadai kashi lei* — cutting completely flush with the ground is certainly harmful to the tree and it will definitely not grow back. *Mikan ve'eilach lo makshe kashi lei, ve-lo ma'ale ma'ali lei* — anywhere between zero and three *tefachim*, the cut is neither clearly harmful to the tree nor truly beneficial; the tree will grow back, but not as well as it should.

### Shevi'is vs Sale

These two distinct legal contexts therefore require different standards. *Gabei shevi'is avdinan midi d'vadai kashi lei* — on *shevi'is*, since the goal is to permit cutting for the wood without in any way encouraging growth, one must ensure the cutting definitively impedes regrowth. Any height above ground, even one *tefach*, provides some encouragement to regrowth, so the only permissible option is cutting completely flush. *Gabei mekach umimkar avdinan midi d'vadai ma'ali lei* — in the context of a commercial sale, the seller must be left with something genuinely adequate for the tree to regenerate properly, so the buyer must cut at three *tefachim* to ensure robust regrowth. The different requirements are thus not contradictory but reflect the different purposes each rule serves.

---

## Cedar Regrowth

### Contradiction

The *baraita* stated that for date palms and cedar trees, the buyer may uproot them entirely *she'ein gizmo machalif* — because their trunk does not grow back. The *gemara* challenges this with respect to cedar: *ve'erez ein gizmo machalif* — is it really true that a cedar tree does not grow back once cut?

### Righteous Drash

Rabbi Chiya bar Lulina's *drash* demonstrates precisely the opposite. He asks: *mai dichtiv tzadik katamar yifrach ke'erez balvanon yisgeh* — what is meant by the verse that a righteous person will blossom like a palm tree and increase like a cedar of Lebanon? If both images are being used to describe the *tzadik*, what does each one contribute that the other does not?

*Im ne'emar erez velo ne'emar tamar* — had the verse mentioned only the cedar, I would have thought: just as a cedar does not bear fruit, so too a *tzadik* produces no spiritual fruit, no reward, no consequence from his good deeds. That would be a deeply discouraging message. *Lekach ne'emar tamar* — therefore the verse also compares the righteous person to a palm tree, which does bear fruit, to teach that the *tzadik*'s deeds do bear fruit and yield reward.

Conversely, *im ne'emar tamar velo ne'emar erez, hayisi omer mah tamar ein gizmo machalif af tzadik ein gizmo machalif* — had the verse mentioned only the palm tree, I would have thought: just as a palm tree does not regenerate when cut, so too if a *tzadik* stumbles and falls he cannot rise again. *Lekach ne'emar erez* — therefore the verse also compares him to a cedar, teaching that even if a *tzadik* stumbles, he will ultimately rise again. The *gemara* observes that this is notably being demonstrated from a textual source rather than from direct observation — which is, of course, the natural mode of reasoning in the *beis medrash*. The implication is unmistakable: cedar trees do in fact regenerate when cut.

### Arz Variety

How then does one reconcile this with the *baraita* that says cedar trees do not grow back? The *gemara* answers: *ela hacha bemai askinan — bishe'ar minei arazim* — when the *baraita* says that *arzim* do not regrow, it is referring to other species that are called *erez* but are not in fact the cedar tree. Those non-cedar varieties of *erez* do not regenerate; the true cedar does.

### Ten Types

This resolution draws on a teaching of Rabba bar Rav Huna: *asarah minei arazim hem* — there are ten species called *erez*. This is derived from a verse: *eten bamidbar erez* — I will place in the wilderness an *erez* — followed by a list of different tree species. The *gemara* identifies each in turn. *Erez* itself is *arza*, the cedar. *Shita* is *turnisa*, the acacia. *Hadas* is *asa*, the myrtle. *Etz shemen* is *afarsema*, which is the balsam tree. *Berosh* is *barti*, the juniper. *Tidhar* is *shaga*, identified by the Koren as teak. *Te'ashur* is *shurbina*, the cypress. That accounts for seven species from the verse.

### Additional Types

Since ten species were declared but only seven appear in that verse, the *gemara* notes that when Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisroel*, he transmitted that three additional species are also called *erez*. According to the first version, these are *alonim*, *almonim*, and *almugim*. *Alonim* is *butni*, the pistachio. *Almonim* is *baluti*, the oak. *Almugim* is *kasita*, the coral tree. A second version — *ika d'amri* — substitutes *aronim*, *armonim*, and *almugim*: *aronim* is *arei*, the laurel; *armonim* is *dulvi*, the plane tree; and *almugim* is again *kasita*, the coral tree.

The precise botanical identification of many of these species remains uncertain, and whether most of them truly resemble cedar in any meaningful way is an open question. The *halakhic* point, however, is clear: of all these species called *erez*, only the true cedar regrows when cut; the others do not. One *baraita* addresses the true cedar, which does regrow and which may therefore not be uprooted by a buyer; the other *baraita* addresses the remaining varieties called *erez*, which do not regrow and may be uprooted entirely.

---

---

# Bava Batra 81

## Mishnah: Trees & Land

### Two Trees Case

The *daf* opens with a *mishnah* several lines from the top of 81a: *hakoneh shne ilanot betoch sdei chaveiro* — one who purchases two trees situated within his friend's field. This case was already referenced earlier in the tractate, but it is now presented in full. The ruling is *harei zeh lo kanah karka*: the buyer acquires only the trees themselves, not the ground. This means not merely that he fails to acquire the land between the two trees, but that he does not even acquire the soil directly beneath each tree. He has the right to have the trees standing there — the landowner cannot demand that he remove them — but, as the *mishnah* will make clear, that right is tied entirely to the trees themselves. Rabbi Meir dissents: *Rabbi Meir omer kanah karka* — in his view, purchasing two trees implies the acquisition of a plot of land as well, and the *gemara* will later examine precisely how much land that entails.

### Branch Rights

Returning to the position of the *chachamim* — or equivalently, to the case where the buyer does not own the land — the *mishnah* addresses what happens when the branches grow and spread: *higdilu, lo yishpeh*. The landowner may not trim the canopy, nor may he compel the tree-owner to do so. The reason is straightforward: the landowner cannot tell the tree-owner to confine his tree to his own property, because the tree-owner has no property of his own. Implicitly, the right to have the tree growing there entails the right to draw nutrients from the soil, to shade the surrounding land, and to allow the branches to spread wherever they reach — even if this inconveniences the landowner's farming. This is, paradoxically, an upside of not owning land: the absence of a defined plot means the tree's needs take precedence across the entire surrounding field.

### Trunk & Roots

The *mishnah* then draws a precise distinction regarding what grows from the tree itself. *V'ha-oleh min ha-geza shelo* — whatever sprouts from the trunk belongs to the tree-owner, since he clearly owns the tree. But *u-min ha-shorashim she-ba-karka* — whatever grows from the roots belongs to the landowner. Because the roots are underground and the buyer did not acquire the ground, the roots themselves are considered to remain part of the landowner's domain, and anything that emerges from them follows accordingly. This is a counterintuitive consequence: one might have assumed that roots, being part of the tree, belong to whoever owns the tree, but the *mishnah* treats roots as inseparable from the land in which they are embedded.

### Tree Death

The *mishnah* concludes the two-tree case with *v'im mesu ein lo karka*: if the trees die, the buyer has no remaining claim. He cannot argue that he should be permitted to plant replacement trees. His purchase was of those specific trees and the right to have them there — nothing more. Since he owns no land, there is nothing for him to retain once the trees are gone.

### Three Trees Case

By contrast, *kanah shlosha kanah karka* — if one purchases three trees (in the view of the *chachamim*), land is indeed acquired, and the *gemara* will specify how much. This land ownership, however, comes with a corresponding limitation: *higdilu yishpeh* — if the branches spread beyond the bounds of that owned plot, the landowner now has the right to trim them, because he can legitimately say that the tree-owner has rights only within his defined parcel. On the other hand, *v'ha-oleh min ha-geza u-min ha-shorashim shelo* — whatever grows from both the trunk and the roots belongs to the tree-owner, since he owns the full tree and the ground beneath it. And *v'im mesu yesh lo karka* — if the trees die, he retains the land and may plant new trees in their place.

---

## Bikkurim Obligation

### No Recitation

The *gemara* now cites a *mishnah* from tractate Bikkurim: *hakoneh shne ilanot betoch sdei chaveiro mevi v'eino korei* — one who purchases two trees in his friend's field brings *bikkurim* from the fruit, but does not recite the accompanying *pesukim*. The recitation includes the phrase *ha-adamah asher natata li* — thanking God for the land He has given — and since this buyer owns no land, that declaration would be false. The fruit itself may qualify as *bikkurim*, so the physical act of bringing is performed, but the verbal declaration is omitted.

### Rabbi Meir View

Rabbi Meir's position in that same *mishnah* is *mevi v'korei*: with two trees, he holds, the buyer does acquire land, as established in our *mishnah* in Bava Batra, and therefore the full *bikkurim* obligation — including the recitation of *ha-adamah asher natata li* — applies. This appears to be a straightforward application of his position on land acquisition, but the *gemara* finds the repetition curious.

### Extreme Position

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, advances a more radical reading of Rabbi Meir's view. Rabbi Meir, he claims, would obligate *bikkurim* with recitation even for one who purchases fruit in the marketplace — *lokeiach peiros min ha-shuk* — having bought neither trees nor land at all. On this reading, Rabbi Meir's position is not simply about deriving land acquisition from the purchase of two trees; it extends the *bikkurim* obligation far beyond any conventional understanding of land ownership.

### Extra Mishnah

The basis for this extreme reading is textual: *mimai midkatni mishnah yateirah* — why was an additional *mishnah* needed in Bikkurim? Given that the dispute in Bava Batra already establishes whether two trees carry land acquisition, the *bikkurim* implications follow automatically. According to the *chachamim*, two trees means no land, which means *mevi v'eino korei*. According to Rabbi Meir, two trees means land, which means *mevi v'korei*. All of this is directly derivable from our *mishnah*. Perhaps the *chidush* in the Bikkurim *mishnah* lies in clarifying that even according to the *chachamim*, the buyer of two trees must still *bring* — lest one think that without land there is no *bikkurim* obligation at all. But then why does the Bikkurim *mishnah* need to tell us Rabbi Meir's position? For Rabbi Meir, *mevi v'korei* is self-evident from Bava Batra. The *gemara* therefore concludes that the extra *mishnah* must be teaching something more: Rabbi Meir really holds that even without any tree ownership, even with fruit purchased in the marketplace, one would bring and recite.

This is a striking *gemara*. Beyond the substantive oddity of the ruling — what makes marketplace fruit *bikkurim* in any recognizable sense? — the derivation itself is puzzling. Bikkurim predates Bava Batra in the ordering of tractates, so the more natural reading is that Rabbi Meir's teaching originated in the context of Bikkurim and was extracted therefrom when Bava Batra addressed questions of sale. To infer from a "doubling" of sources that the earlier source must contain a novel ruling beyond what the later source teaches is methodologically unusual. The *gemara* itself will challenge this position.

The *gemara* first tries to defend the extreme reading against apparent scriptural objections. *Ve-hachtiv asher tavi me'artzecha* — doesn't the verse say "from your land"? The response is that this phrase excludes *chutz la-aretz*, not that it requires personal land ownership. *Ve-hachtiv admasecha* — "your ground"? That excludes fruit grown on a non-Jew's land (*admat akum*), but does not require the individual to own the land personally. And when the declaration says *asher natata li* — "which You gave me" — the *gemara* suggests this can be read broadly: God gave me the money, I bought the fruit, all of it ultimately comes from God. The *gemara* pushes this reasoning quite far before the challenge arrives.

---

## Refutation

### One Tree Braita

*Masiv Rabba* — Rabba raises an objection from a *braisa*: *hakoneh ilan echad betoch shel chaveiro mevi v'eino korei lefi shelo kana karka divrei Rabbi Meir* — one who purchases a single tree in his friend's field brings *bikkurim* but does not recite, because he has not acquired land — and this is the ruling of Rabbi Meir. This *braisa* provides precisely the test case needed. One tree, no land ownership — and Rabbi Meir says *mevi v'eino korei*, not *mevi v'korei*. For Rabbi Meir, what one tree achieves is what two trees achieve for the *chachamim*: you bring without reciting. The *braisa* thus demonstrates that Rabbi Meir does require land ownership for the recitation — he merely draws the threshold differently.

### Tiyuvta Proof

The *gemara* declares *tiyuvta* — a conclusive refutation. The extreme reading advanced by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, that Rabbi Meir would obligate *bikkurim* with full recitation even for marketplace fruit, cannot be sustained. It is clear from the *braisa* that even Rabbi Meir conditions the recitation on land ownership; he simply holds that one tree, not two, is sufficient to establish that ownership.

---

## Central Question

### Elazar's Response

With the extreme position refuted, a fundamental question remains: why does one who owns a single tree (according to Rabbi Meir) or two trees (according to the *chachamim*) bring *bikkurim* at all? If the declaration *ha-adamah asher natata li* cannot be made because there is no land ownership, why is the act of bringing required? *Amar lei Rav Shimon ben Yakim le-Rabbi Elazar* — at the opening of 81b, Rav Shimon ben Yakim poses exactly this question to Rabbi Elazar: what is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir in the one-tree case, and what is the reasoning of the *rabbanan* in the two-tree case?

Rabbi Elazar's response is remarkable: *davar she-rishonim lo amru lo bo ta'am tishaleni be-veit ha-midrash kedei le-vaysheni* — "You are asking me in public about something for which earlier authorities gave no reason, as if to embarrass me." The earlier generations who transmitted these rulings from Rabbi Meir and the *rabbanan* did not supply an explanation, and the question was well known precisely because no satisfactory answer had been offered. It is a candid and disarming response — and, it must be said, one that sits in some tension with the principle that a person who is ashamed to ask will never learn. But clearly Rabbi Elazar felt that this was a question whose difficulty was notorious and whose public airing without a ready answer was genuinely embarrassing.

### Rava's Solution

The *gemara*, undeterred, offers its own resolution through Rava. *Dilma Rabbi Meir be-ilan echad sfukei mesafke leih, rabbanan bi-shnei ilanos sfukei mesafke lehu* — perhaps Rabbi Meir in the one-tree case, and the *rabbanan* in the two-tree case, each hold that it is *possible* — not certain — that land is acquired in those circumstances. The question of land ownership in those borderline cases is genuinely uncertain.

When it comes to property law — *dinei mamonot* — the principle of *hamotzi me-chavero alav ha-ra'ayah* applies: the one seeking to extract money or property from another bears the burden of proof. Since the tree-buyer cannot prove he owns the land, the presumption favors the original landowner, and the buyer acquires nothing for purposes of civil law. But because the matter is doubtful, and because in the realm of ritual obligation doubt demands stringency, the buyer must bring *bikkurim* — perhaps the land really is his, and if so, the obligation would apply. He does not recite, however, because the declaration might be false — he cannot confidently say *ha-adamah asher natata li* when it is uncertain whether God gave him the land.

This is an elegant but not simple solution. It treats the obligation to bring and the obligation to recite as resting on different thresholds: bringing requires only the possibility of land ownership, while reciting requires its certainty. When the *gemara* is pressed on whether the language of the *braisa* — *lefi shelo kana karka*, "because he did not acquire land" — implies definitive non-ownership rather than mere doubt, it answers that the phrase means *shema lo kana*, "perhaps he did not acquire" — a tentative formulation, not a conclusive one.

---

## Safek & Sanctification

### Chulin ba-Azarah

The *gemara* presses further: *ve-leihush she-dilma lav Bikkurim ninhu ve-ka ma'ail chulin la-azarah* — if these fruits are only doubtfully *bikkurim*, perhaps they are not *bikkurim* at all, in which case one would be bringing *chulin* — non-sanctified produce — into the *azarah*, the Temple courtyard, which is prohibited.

What exactly is the prohibition of *chulin ba-azarah*? The classic case is slaughtering a non-sacrificial animal within the Temple precincts, treating the *azarah* as an ordinary abattoir. Whether this prohibition is *d'oraisa* or *d'rabbanan* is itself a matter of discussion, but it is well established as a serious concern. The Rashbam explains that it creates confusion — people will observe treatment of meat inconsistent with how *kodshim* are handled — or, more fundamentally, it blurs the essential boundary between *chulin* and *kodshim*, between what belongs inside the *beit hamikdash* and what belongs outside it.

One might wonder: does bringing a piece of fruit into the *azarah* really implicate *chulin ba-azarah*? Is it not comparable simply to carrying one's food through the Temple grounds? Tosafot addresses this directly. The concern is not merely physical presence in the *azarah*, but performing an act *ke'ein hakravah* — one analogous to the ritual acts of sacrifice. The *gemara* will specify that *bikkurim* involves *hagashah* or *tenufa* — bringing the fruit near the *mizbe'ach* or waving it — acts that parallel the ritual of *korbanot*. It is this ritual treatment of the fruit, performed with something that may not be *bikkurim* at all, that raises the problem of *chulin ba-azarah*.

### Sanctification

The *gemara*'s solution is *demakdish lehu* — one sanctifies the fruit to the *beit hamikdash* before bringing it. The declaration is conditional: if this fruit qualifies as *bikkurim*, it is being treated as such; if not, it is being sanctified as Temple property. In either case, the fruit is no longer *chulin*, and the concern of *chulin ba-azarah* is resolved. One might ask whether sanctifying fruit to the Temple really permits performing *bikkurim*-like ritual acts with it, given that ordinary sanctified property — a chair, for instance, dedicated to the Temple — would never be subject to waving. The *gemara*'s implicit response seems to be that as long as the object is not *chulin*, the integrity of the Temple's space is preserved, even if the ritual acts remain somewhat awkward.

### Redemption

A further complication arises: *bikkurim* are ultimately consumed by the *kohen*. If the fruit has been sanctified to the *beit hamikdash*, how can the *kohen* eat property belonging to the Temple? The *gemara* answers *deparkinehu* — the fruit is redeemed. After the ritual is performed, the sanctity is transferred onto a monetary substitute — say, twenty dinars — which is given to the Temple treasury, and the fruit itself reverts to ordinary status and may be eaten by the *kohen*. The *gemara* continues from here to work through additional implications of this *safek* framework, but the essential resolution has been reached: the doubtful *bikkurim* are brought, sanctified, the ritual is performed without recitation, and the fruit is then redeemed and given to the *kohen* for eating.

---

## Conceptual Analysis

### Bikkurim Status

Before concluding, two important Tosafot from the previous *amud* deserve attention. The first addresses a question that arises from the *gemara*'s discussion: why does the verse *asher tavi me'artzecha* need to exclude *chutz la-aretz* from the *bikkurim* obligation? Is not *bikkurim* a *mitzvah hatluya ba-aretz* — a commandment dependent on the Land — and therefore automatically inapplicable outside it, just as *terumot* and *ma'aser* do not apply to produce grown abroad?

Tosafot, citing the Rashbam, answers that *bikkurim* is in fact *not* a *mitzvah hatluya ba-aretz* in the classic sense, because it is not analogous to *terumah*, *ma'aser*, or *challah*. The key distinction lies in the nature of the obligation. With *terumah* and *ma'aser*, the obligation begins with the object — the food itself. Grain grown in *Eretz Yisrael* acquires the status of *tevel*, untithed produce, which is forbidden to eat and which demands separation. The *kedushah* — the sanctity demanding action — inheres in the food and derives from the fact that it grew from the holy soil of *Eretz Yisrael*. This is why these commandments are genuinely *tluya ba-aretz*: they start with the ground and flow to the food.

### Personal Obligation

*Bikkurim*, by contrast, works differently. If one fails to bring *bikkurim*, the fruit is not forbidden. There is no status of *tevel*, no prohibition on eating the fruit. The obligation does not inhere in the food as a *cheftza* — as an object with a legal status — but rather in the *adam*, the person. It is a *chovas haguf*, a personal obligation: the person who owns this fruit must bring it to the Temple. The food's own status is not altered by the failure to bring it.

### Early Sanctification

This distinction is further reinforced by an additional difference. *Terumot* and *ma'asrot* become obligatory only when the produce reaches a certain stage of completion — specifically, when the grain pile is smoothed over after winnowing (*mismareiach bakeri*). The obligation is tethered to the food reaching its final processed state, confirming that it is the food's status that drives the obligation. *Bikkurim*, however, work in the opposite direction: the obligation begins *be-odan ba-ilan*, while the fruit is still on the tree. When one sees the first ripening fruits, one ties a ribbon designating them as *bikkurim* — before they are even harvested. The obligation is thus triggered by the person's recognition and dedication, not by the food reaching any stage of completion. These two features together — the absence of a *tevel*-like status and the early onset of the obligation while fruit is still on the tree — confirm that *bikkurim* is a *chovas haguf*, a personal obligation, and not a *kedushah* emanating from the ground in the manner of classic *mitzvot hatluya ba-aretz*. A scriptural exclusion is therefore necessary to establish that *bikkurim* does not apply to produce from *chutz la-aretz*.

---

## Gerim & Bikkurim

### Ger Exclusion

The second Tosafot addresses a variant reading that the Rashbam had before him: that the phrase *lema'utei admat akum* — excluding land owned by a non-Jew — also extends to land owned by a *ger*, a convert. This leads Tosafot into a broader discussion of whether a *ger* brings *bikkurim* with or without the recitation.

### Rabbeinu Tam

The starting point is an explicit *mishnah* in tractate Bikkurim: *ha-ger mevi v'eino korei* — a convert brings *bikkurim* but does not recite. The reason given is *lefi she-eino yachol lomar asher nishba la-avoseinu lases lanu* — because he cannot say "which [God] swore to our forefathers to give us," since the covenant with the patriarchs was not made with his ancestors.

Rabbeinu Tam drew a practical ruling from this *mishnah*: a *ger* should not lead *birkat ha-zimun* — the communal blessing after meals — because the text includes the phrase *she-nachalata la-avoseinu eretz tova u-richava*, "which You gave as an inheritance to our forefathers, a good and spacious land," language that a *ger* cannot truthfully utter. The *mishnah* in Bikkurim further specifies that when a *ger* prays privately, he should say *Elohei avos Yisrael* — "God of the fathers of Israel" — rather than *Eloheinu v'Elohei avoseinu*, always marking his distinct status. And when serving as *shliach tzibbur*, he says *Elohei avoseichem* — "God of your forefathers." The ruling is consistent but carries a striking human cost: a person who has fully embraced the Torah and the Jewish people is perpetually reminded, even in his private prayer, that he is other than native-born. This sits in sharp tension with the principle of *kager ka-ezrach* and the Torah's repeated admonition *v'lo sonu*.

### Yerushalmi View

The *Ri* — a later Tosafist — disagrees. He holds that a *ger* may indeed say *la-avoseinu*, citing a different authority: Rabbi Yehudah, whose position is recorded in the Yerushalmi. Rabbi Yehudah rules that a *ger* brings *bikkurim* and recites the full declaration — *ger atzmo mevi v'korei*. The reasoning is drawn from a verse: *ki av hamon goyim netaticha* — "I have made you the father of many nations." Abraham was not merely the father of Aram; from that moment forward he was designated as the father of all nations. A *ger* who accepts the covenant is counted among the spiritual descendants of Abraham, and Abraham's patriarchal relationship extends to him.

### Halacha Ruling

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi affirms: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yehudah* — the law follows Rabbi Yehudah. A *ger* is considered a descendant of Abraham in every spiritually meaningful sense, may say *Eloheinu v'Elohei avoseinu*, and need not maintain a formal linguistic distinction marking his origins. This ruling coheres with the broader practice of identifying converts as *ben Avraham* or *bat Sarah*, acknowledging Abraham as their spiritual progenitor.

### Rambam Letter

The Rambam addressed this question directly in his famous letter to Ovadia HaGer, who inquired how his prayer should reflect his status as a convert. The Rambam ruled in full accordance with the position of the *Ri*: Ovadia HaGer is the spiritual heir of Abraham and may say *Eloheinu v'Elohei avoseinu* with complete integrity. The Rambam's ruling is grounded not only in the legal tradition traced through Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi but in the moral imperatives of *lo tonu* and *kager ka-ezrach* — the Torah's insistence that the convert be treated as fully equivalent to the native-born Israelite. The *daf* concludes here, leaving us with this profound question about the nature of belonging and spiritual inheritance that the *halacha* of *bikkurim* brings to the surface.

---

---

# Bava Batra 82

## Bikkurim without Land

### Review & Ger Status

Today's daf picks up in the middle of 81b, in the midst of a discussion about whether one brings *bikkurim* when one owns the tree but not the land. The position shared by Rabbi Yanai and the *Chachamim* is that they debate the cases of owning the land — when you have two trees or three trees — but agree that when one owns the tree without the land, one brings *bikkurim* but does not make the declaration.

Two important *Tosafos* from the previous daf bear reviewing. The first concerns why a special *pasuk* is needed to exclude *bikkurim* brought from *Chutz La'aretz*. *Tosafos* draws a crucial distinction between *mitzvos hateluyos ba'aretz* — agricultural commandments tied to the land — and *bikkurim*. The former, such as *tevel* and *terumos u'ma'asros*, concern the status of the fruit themselves: the land has *kedusha* and that *kedusha* affects the produce. But *bikkurim*, though it involves produce that grows from the land, is not about the status of the produce; it is a personal obligation — a *gavra* obligation, not a *cheftza* one. Therefore a special *pasuk* was required to confine that personal obligation to the Land of Israel.

The second *Tosafos* addresses the *ger* and whether he may bring *bikkurim* and make the declaration. Two problems confront the *ger*: the first is the ability to recite *ha'adamah asher nasata li* — "the land which You gave me" — when he has no ancestral portion in the land. The second, more general problem is his ability to pronounce the *Arami oved avi* declaration. *Tosafos* cites the well-known *Yerushalmi* discussion of whether a *ger* may say *Elokeinu v'Elokei avoseinu* — whether he participates in the national narrative of the Jewish people. The *Mishnah* in *Bikkurim* appears to deny him this, but the *Yerushalmi* sides with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the *ger* does share in that national identity. This is consistent with the approach of Pesach, where a *ger* brings a *Korban Pesach* and enters the narrative of the nation — themes that figured prominently in Rambam's famous letter to *Ovadia HaGer*.

### Core Problem

This brings us to the core difficulty: if one cannot make the declaration because one cannot say *ha'adamah asher nasata li* — why bring *bikkurim* at all? What is the justification for bringing them?

### Safek Framework

The *Gemara*'s answer, though it reads the sources with some effort, is that the case involves genuine doubt (*safek*) as to whether one owns the land. Rabbi Meir is uncertain whether owning one tree confers land ownership; the *Rabbanan* are uncertain whether two trees do. Since there is a *safek* as to whether one is obligated to bring *bikkurim*, the *halacha* is that one brings — lest one be obligated — but does not make the declaration, which might be false.

### Chullin Ba'azarah

This generates an immediate difficulty: if there is doubt whether you own land and are obligated in *bikkurim*, how may you bring them at all? Perhaps you are not obligated, in which case you are bringing unsanctified produce into the *Beis Hamikdash* as though it were a *korban* — the problem of *chullin ba'azarah*. As *Tosafos* notes, *chullin ba'azarah* is not merely the presence of an ordinary item in the Temple precincts, like having food in one's pocket; it is the act of presenting unsanctified produce as though it were a sacred offering.

The *Gemara*'s answer is that one first sanctifies the produce for *bedek habayis*. *Tosafos* notes that this resolves the presentation issue — sanctified property dedicated to *bedek habayis* would indeed be brought into the *Beis Hamikdash* and presented in a manner similar to *bikkurim*. But this creates a further problem: if it has been dedicated to *bedek habayis*, how may the *kohen* eat from it? The *Gemara* therefore says: one sanctifies it and then redeems it, and gives it to the *kohen* thereafter. A remarkable number of legal mechanisms are being deployed here — sanctification, redemption, and presentation — all to manage the underlying *safek*.

### Trumot & Ma'asrot

The *Gemara* then raises the *terumos u'ma'asros* problem. *Bikkurim* is not obligated in *terumos u'ma'asros*. But if the produce is only doubtfully *bikkurim*, then on the possibility that it is not *bikkurim* at all, it remains ordinary produce — *tevel* — and the *kohen* who receives it would be eating untithed produce.

The *Gemara*'s answer is that one separates *terumos u'ma'asros* before bringing. But this requires working through each component. *Trumah gedolah* goes to the *kohen* — that is straightforward. *Ma'aser sheni* presents no difficulty either, since *ma'aser sheni* is eaten in Yerushalayim, which is precisely where the *bikkurim* are being brought, so it can be given to the *kohen* there. *Ma'aser ani*, for the years in which it applies, can similarly be given to the *kohen* if he is poor. What of *ma'aser rishon*, which belongs to a *Levi*? The *Gemara* resolves this by citing the position of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah: *ma'aser rishon* may also be given to a *kohen*. The *Gemara* grounds this in the ten places in the Torah where *kohanim* are called *Hakohanim HaLeviim*, demonstrating that *kohanim*, who are themselves members of the tribe of Levi, may receive *ma'aser rishon* according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah — and indeed *Tosafos* notes that this may be the Torah-level reading of the entitlement. Alternatively, this may reflect the post-*Ezra* rabbinic enactment: when the *Leviim* remained in Bavel rather than returning to Eretz Yisrael with Ezra, *Ezra* imposed a *knas* upon them, redirecting the *ma'aser* from the *Leviim* to the *kohanim*. Whether one reads it as the *d'oraisa* position of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah or as a rabbinic enactment, the practical result is that the entire basket may be given to the *kohen*.

### Kriha Problem

With the *chullin ba'azarah* and *terumos u'ma'asros* concerns resolved, the *Gemara* raises the next question: *v'dilma bikkurim ninhu u'va'i keriah* — perhaps they actually are *bikkurim*, in which case they require the declaration. And if you do not make the declaration, have you fulfilled the *mitzvah*? The *Gemara* initially says that *keriah* is not *me'akev* — one is *yotzei* without making the declaration. But the *Gemara* then challenges this.

### Bilah Principle

The challenge comes from a well-known principle cited by Rabbi Zeira: *kol hara'uy l'bilah ein bilah me'akeves bo, v'she'eino ra'uy l'bilah bilah me'akeves bo* — whatever is fit to be mixed, the absence of actual mixing does not invalidate it; but whatever is not fit to be mixed, the absence of mixing does invalidate it. The context is a *minchah* offering. Up to sixty *esronim* of flour may be brought in a single vessel, since it is theoretically possible to mix that quantity with oil. But sixty-one *esronim* cannot be properly mixed in a single vessel — the *Rabbanan* understood that so large a quantity cannot achieve *blilah* — and therefore must be divided among multiple vessels. If it was brought undivided, it is invalid.

The underlying principle is fundamental: sometimes the law does not require that an action actually be performed — it requires only that the item possess the *capacity* for that action. The question *Tosafos* presses is: how does one ever know whether the law demands actual performance or mere capacity? The *Rashbam* provides an answer at least within the domain of *korbanot*: where the Torah states a requirement only once, the rule is that it is not *me'akev*, meaning only the capacity is needed; where the Torah repeats the requirement, actual performance is mandated — *ela im kein shana alav hakatuv le'akev*. If stated once, the Torah is describing a quality the object must have. If stated twice, it is prescribing an act that must be performed.

Applying this to *bikkurim*: if one is *fit* to make the *keriah*, not actually making it does not prevent *yetziah*. But if one is *not fit* to make the *keriah* — lacking the capacity — then the *keriah* is *me'akev*. In our case of doubtful *bikkurim*, the *Gemara* says one lacks the capacity: if they truly are *bikkurim*, the person is fully obligated in *keriah*, yet cannot say it. Therefore *keriah* is *me'akev* and one has not been *yotzei*.

This is complicated by the *Rashbam*'s observation that there are cases in *bikkurim* — such as the *ger* — where the *halacha* establishes from the outset that one brings without the declaration. The *ger* belongs to the category of *mevi v'eino korei* — a defined category of bringing without declaration. Our case is different: if one truly owns the land, one is fully obligated in *keriah*; if not, it is not *bikkurim* at all. There is no defined intermediate category where *bikkurim* applies but *keriah* does not. Thus if these produce items fall into the *bikkurim* category, they carry a full *keriah* obligation, and the inability to fulfill it renders *keriah me'akev*.

### Two-Person Solution

The *Gemara* therefore resolves the problem by invoking the ruling of Rabbi Yose bar Chanina: one arranges matters such that two separate people are involved in the stages of harvesting and bringing. The relevant verse — *velakachta uva'ta* — requires that the same person who takes (or harvests) also brings, for the *keriah* obligation to apply. If the act is split between two people, the obligation to make the declaration never attaches to the *bikkurim* from the outset, placing them in a category that is simply not *ra'uy l'keriah* at all.

The *Rashbam* understands this as covering two scenarios: either one harvests and sends the produce with an agent, or an agent harvests and dies en route so that someone else finishes the bringing. *Tosafos* reads it as one unified scenario: the *shaliach* takes the produce from the house (which constitutes the *lekichah*), but dies before completing the journey, and another person completes the bringing — thereby ensuring that no single person performed the entire act. There is also a separate debate between *Rashi* and *Tosafos* as to whether, if the *shaliach* is alive and you catch up with him and take the produce for the final stretch, that would suffice. In any event, the practical mechanism is that the bringing is divided between two parties, so the *keriah* obligation never applies.

### False Declaration

Having established all this elaborate machinery, the *Gemara* entertains one final suggestion: given that the declaration consists of *pesukim*, why not simply recite them? After all, one reads those same *pesukim* in a Torah reading — what harm is there in saying them here?

The *Gemara* rejects this on two grounds. The first is *michzi k'shikra* — it appears as a falsehood. The *Rashbam* notes that in the *Beis Hamikdash*, one is making a formal declaration to God: *"You gave me this land"* — and if the land is not truly one's own, this is a false statement before God. The *Rashbam* cites the verse *dover shkarim lo yikon l'neged einai* — one who speaks falsehood cannot stand before God. The distinction from simply reading those verses as Torah is precise: *k'korei baTorah* — reading them as part of a Torah portion — is no problem. But making them as a formal declaration in the *Beis Hamikdash*, where they may be false, is entirely different.

The second reason, offered by Rav Mesharsheya the son of Rav Chiya, is that making the full declaration will lead observers to conclude that these are fully-fledged *bikkurim* with no *safek*, and they will therefore fail to separate *terumos u'ma'asros* from similar produce. The one who brought them with the full declaration effectively signals to others that no *safek* exists, and the next person in the same situation will eat *tevel*. It is worth noting that both of these reasons — whether *michzi k'shikra* or the concern for *terumos u'ma'asros* — appear to be rabbinic in character, yet the *Gemara* earlier treated the inability to make the declaration as rendering the produce *eino ra'uy l'keriah* and thereby making *keriah me'akev*. That tension is somewhat pointed: the rabbinic prohibition on making the declaration should not, strictly speaking, render the produce ontologically unfit for *keriah* from the Torah's perspective. But that is where the *Gemara* leaves it.

To summarize the *bikkurim* discussion: the *Gemara* explains the ruling that one brings without a declaration not by positing a genuine intermediate status — *bikkurim* without *keriah* — but by framing the entire case as a *safek* of land ownership. The mechanisms required to bring under *safek* include sanctification and redemption to address *chullin ba'azarah*, separation of *terumos u'ma'asros* under the position of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah to handle the *tevel* concern, and a two-person division of the harvest-and-bring process to ensure the *keriah* obligation never attaches. It is a remarkable and intricate construction.

---

## Land Ownership Thresholds

### One Tree Rule

Turning back to the *halacha* of buying a single or small number of trees: when one sells Michael one or two trees, he owns the trees but not the land. What he does have, however, is the right to maintain his trees in someone else's land. The irony is that precisely because he has no land of his own, he has no property line that his tree can violate. When one owns land alongside one's tree, the seller can demand that overgrowth beyond the property line be trimmed — that is *yishveh*. But when one has no land, the entire tree sits on the seller's property by right, and the buyer is entitled to have it there — roots drawing nutrients from that land, branches shading it. Accordingly, the rule is *higdil lo yishveh*: even if the tree grows very large, the land-owner cannot compel its trimming.

### Trunk vs. Roots

Now the *Gemara* addresses what happens to things that grow off of that tree. What belongs to the tree-buyer and what reverts to the land-owner? The distinction drawn is between growth from the *geza* (trunk) and growth from the *shorashim* (roots). Anything growing from the trunk belongs to the tree-owner — he owns the tree, and this is an extension of it above ground. Anything that sprouts from the roots belongs to the land-owner, since those are underground extensions of the seller's property.

How exactly do we define *geza* versus *shorashim*? Rabbi Yochanan states: *kol she-ro'eh pnei chama* — anything that sees the face of the sun, that is, anything growing above ground, is considered part of the trunk and belongs to the buyer. *V'kol she-eino ro'eh pnei chama* — whatever does not see the sun, whatever is below ground, is from the roots and belongs to the land-owner. The criterion is not the anatomical distinction between trunk and root per se, but rather whether the growth is above or below ground. This addresses the reality that trunks can dip underground and roots can emerge above it.

### Land Shift Problem

The *Gemara* then raises a concern: *dilma mati ara sirton* — what if the land level shifts? If growth has been springing from the roots and peeking above ground, and then silt or earth deposits raise the ground level, what was once visibly connected to the original tree now appears to be a cluster of separate trees. The buyer, who has been tending these shoots, might then claim: *tlata zevinta li* — you sold me three trees; *v'is li ara* — and therefore I own the land between them. After all, the rule is that purchasing three trees conveys the land. If the ground level shifts so that what are actually root-shoots look like three independent trees, the buyer could fraudulently assert a land claim that was never part of the transaction.

### Pruning Solution

Rav Nachman provides the answer: *yikotz* — prune. The tree-owner is not permitted to allow root-shoots to grow to the point where they begin to resemble independent trees. When they reach a size at which they could be mistaken for separate trees, they must be cut back. Rabbi Yochanan agrees: *yikotz*. The mechanism of mandatory pruning prevents the root-growth from ever generating a false land claim.

---

## Palm Tree Exception

### Palm No Trunk

Rav Nachman introduces a further ruling: *naktinan dekel ein lo geza* — we hold that a palm tree does not convey trunk-growth rights to the buyer. Whatever might sprout from the side of a palm trunk does not belong to the person who purchased the palm tree.

### Total Loss Risk

The first explanation proposed — attributed to Rav Zevid in the *Gemara*'s initial formulation — is as follows: a palm tree, unlike other fruit trees, does not regrow if it is cut down. Other trees, even if the trunk is severed, will send up new growth from the stump. A palm tree, once destroyed, is gone entirely. Because of this, the buyer of a palm tree knows from the outset that his investment is existentially at risk; a calamity to the tree means total and irreversible loss. This awareness causes the buyer to mentally give up on long-term planning — *asuchei aschei datei* — he does not think of his ownership as a long-term investment. Since he does not project long-term, he is not mentally accounting for whatever might grow from the trunk over time; he is focused only on the dates the tree produces from the top. Therefore, when he acquires the palm tree, there is no implicit understanding that he acquires trunk-growth rights.

This is an unusual idea: the very risk of total loss, rather than simply the likelihood of it, causes the buyer to abandon any long-term expectation. Yet this is how the *Rashbam* reads the *Gemara* here.

### Two Trees Challenge

Rav Pappa challenges this reasoning from our *Mishnah*: when one purchases two trees, one does not acquire rights to replant after the trees die — ownership is only for the life of the tree. So the buyer of two trees is in a position not unlike the buyer of a palm: he too knows that when the tree dies, that is it, he cannot replant. And yet the *Mishnah* says that the buyer of two trees *does* receive whatever grows from the trunk. If the prospect of a total, irreversible loss causes *asichut da'at* — an abandonment of long-term expectation — for the palm buyer, why does it not do the same for the buyer of two trees, who similarly cannot replant?

### Five-Year Insurance

Rav Pappa answers his own challenge. The two-trees case in the *Mishnah* is where one buys the trees for a defined period — five years. This seemingly less permanent form of ownership is paradoxically more protective. If the trees die within the five-year term, the buyer has the right to replant, because the contract guaranteed him trees on that land for five years, not merely the life of those particular trees. The explicit duration in the contract thus functions as an insurance policy: the buyer knows with certainty that for five years he will have a productive tree there, whether it is the original or a replacement. This confidence in the long-term viability of the investment restores his long-term planning mindset, and therefore he does receive the trunk-growth rights.

The *Rashbam*'s explanation here is striking: if you own the trees outright without a fixed term, your ownership is actually more precarious — if the tree dies tomorrow, it is a total loss. But if you purchase for five years, even though you own the trees for less time in absolute terms, you know your rights are guaranteed for that period regardless of what happens to the individual trees. Therefore the five-year buyer thinks long-term and receives trunk-growth rights; the open-ended palm-buyer does not.

### Practical Botanics

The *Gemara* then presents what it calls the final and decisive answer — one already foreshadowed at the outset of the discussion: *lephi she'ein motzi geza* — palm trees practically do not produce lateral trunk-growth. The botanical reality of palms is that they grow from the crown, not the sides.
