Other trees regularly produce shoots and offshoots from their trunk and root zone, and so when one buys such a tree, the expectation that one will receive whatever grows from the trunk is built into the transaction. A palm tree, by contrast, simply does not grow that way. There is never any trunk-growth to speak of, and therefore the category never arises. In the rare and unexpected event that something does sprout from a palm's trunk, it was never part of the transaction because neither party anticipated it.

This final answer is distinct from Rav Zevid's psychological argument about risk and long-term planning. The first explanation turned on the buyer's mental state given the risk of total loss. The final answer turns on practical botanical reality: trunk-growth is not a feature of the palm, and therefore the sale of a palm never implicitly included it.

---

## Three Trees & Land

### Three Trees Scope

When one buys three trees, one acquires land. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states: the buyer acquires *tachteihen u'veineihen u'chutza lahen kemelo ora vesalo* — the land beneath them, the land between them, and outside of them to the extent of the space needed for a picker with his basket.

*Tachteihen* — beneath the trees — means the footprint of the trees themselves, so that if a tree dies the owner may replant it on that spot, and indeed use that plot for any agricultural purpose. *Beineihen* — between them — refers to the area enclosed by the three trees: three trees define a copse, a bounded area, and the entire interior space including the area under the canopy belongs to the buyer. *Chutza lahen* — outside of them — extends, as the *Rashbam* explains, beyond even the canopy line: one needs space for a worker to stand outside the tree and reach up to pick. *Ora vesalo* — the picker with his basket — is the unit of measure for this outer strip: enough room for a person holding a basket to stand at the edge of the foliage and harvest.

### Access Challenge

Rav Elazar raises a sharp challenge. The grant of outer space rests on the claim that the buyer needs it to pick from the trees. But, asks Rav Elazar: *hashta derech ein lo* — right now, the buyer does not even have a path to the trees. The debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim* concerns whether a seller conveys access when selling trees: Rabbi Akiva rules that the seller sells *b'ayin yafa* — generously — and therefore access is implicitly included; the *Chachamim* rule that the seller sells *b'ayin ra'ah* — restrictively — and access is not included. If we follow the *Chachamim*, the buyer has no path to his trees.

Rav Elazar therefore argues: the outer picking-space is far less essential than access. If the buyer does not receive even the right to reach his trees — which is a bare necessity — why should we assume he receives the right to stand outside them and pick? *Over v'salo yesh lo?* — he gets space for a picker and basket? *Derech ein lo* — he has no path.

### Two vs. Three Trees

Rabbi Zeira draws a significant inference from Rav Elazar's challenge: if Rav Elazar finds it problematic that the three-tree buyer lacks access, he must believe that the two-tree buyer *does* have access. And this is not paradoxical — it reflects the same logic we saw with the trimming rule. When one owns land alongside trees, there is a property line, and trees that cross it must be trimmed. When one has no land and merely owns trees embedded in another's property, there is no property line to violate. The buyer can say to the seller: *ba'ara didach qaymani* — my tree is in your land anyway; by selling me this tree, you implicitly gave me the right to be here, and being here includes the right of access. The irony is that having fewer rights in one domain — no land ownership — translates into broader rights in another: since the seller committed to letting my tree reside in his land, he committed to letting me access it. But once one owns three trees and thereby owns the land, one is confined to one's own property, and the seller has not implicitly granted a path through the remaining portions of his land.

### Rabbi Akiva Rule

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then asks Rava whether Rav Elazar's reasoning implies that he does not hold like his own *rebbe* Shmuel, who ruled *halacha k'Rabbi Akiva* — that the law follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a seller sells *b'ayin yafa*. If the *halacha* follows Rabbi Akiva, then the buyer does have access even when he owns three trees and therefore owns land — and if he has access, there is no difficulty with granting him the outer picking-space as well. Rav Elazar's challenge only works if he assumes the buyer lacks access, which would mean rejecting Rabbi Akiva.

### Overhang Rights

The response is that Rav Elazar could in principle hold like Shmuel and like Rabbi Akiva, since his challenge is directed at explaining the *Mishnah*, and the *Mishnah* itself need not reflect Rabbi Akiva's position. The evidence is internal to the *Mishnah*: the *Mishnah* states that if the trees grow beyond the property line, the land-owner may demand trimming — *higdilu yeshafeh*. If this were a Rabbi Akiva *Mishnah*, where the seller sells *b'ayin yafa*, one might have expected that Rabbi Akiva's generosity would extend to permitting the canopy to overhang the seller's field. The *Gemara* then refines this: Rabbi Akiva's principle of *b'ayin yafa* does not mean unlimited generosity. By a *bor* — a cistern or well — granting access causes no harm to the land, and so Rabbi Akiva would be generous. But by trees, the overhang does real damage: it shades the land below and interferes with cultivation. Even Rabbi Akiva concedes — as is explicitly stated elsewhere — that a tree which extends over a neighbor's field may be cut: *ha'ilan hanoteh l'toch s'deh chaveiro shekotzetz melo hamardei* — one may trim the overhang to the width of a plow-beam. Generosity in granting access does not entail tolerating damage. Therefore our *Mishnah* could still reflect Rabbi Akiva's position: access yes, overhang no.

The practical upshot, as the *Rashbam* presents it, is that the question of the outer picking-space hinges on the debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim*: according to Rabbi Akiva, the buyer has access and the outer space; according to the *Chachamim*, he has neither. This is supported by a *baraita* of Rabbi Chiyya that explicitly grants the buyer the space beneath, between, and outside the trees — consistent with the Rabbi Akiva position.

### Outer Space Rights

A final question is raised by Abaye to Rav Yosef: *chutza lahen kemelo oreh v'salo — mi zara?* — the space outside the trees to the width of a picker and his basket — who may plant it?

Even granting that the buyer has the right to stand there and harvest, the land itself may still belong to the seller. The right of access, on the Rabbi Akiva model, is a right of ingress and use — the seller grants the buyer the right to pass through or stand on his land for the purpose of reaching and harvesting the trees. But that right of use does not necessarily convey ownership of the soil, any more than a path through someone's field becomes the walker's land. Just as access is a right to use another's land without owning it, the right to station a picker in that outer strip might be merely a right to use that strip — not to plant it.

The *Gemara*'s response is: *hachizon zoreya et haderech* — the outer party, the seller, plants the path. This establishes that the land remains the seller's to cultivate. The buyer's right is one of use, not ownership. We will take up the full analysis of this conclusion in the next shiur.

---

---

# Bava Batra 83

## Land Between Trees

### Three Trees Setup

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion on 82b concerning the purchase of three trees. As established, when one buys three trees from a seller's field, the buyer acquires not only the land directly beneath the trees and the land between them — measured according to the extent of the canopy's overhang — but also an additional strip of space extending beyond the canopy sufficient for a picker to stand and harvest. This additional strip is expressed by the Talmudic phrase *kimlo oreh v'salo*, "the full space of a picker and his basket."

The Gemara had previously compared this right of access to the position of Rabbi Akiva, who held that one who purchases trees acquires not merely the trees themselves but also a right of ingress to reach them. The structural parallel is precise: just as the buyer of trees under Rabbi Akiva's ruling does not technically own the access path but holds a legal right of passage over it, so too here the buyer may not own the surrounding strip of land but possesses a right to stand there and pick. The question that follows is therefore sharpened: who retains the right to plant that outer strip — the one who owns the trees or the one who owns the field?

### Oreh v'Salo

The Rashbam explains the phrase *oreh v'salo* with care: *oreh* is the specific verb used for harvesting from a fig tree, and *salo* is his basket. The language thus designates a very concrete image — the picker standing outside the canopy's edge, basket in hand, gathering fruit.

### Who Plants Space

Abaye raises the question directly with Rav Yosef: *osan oreh v'salo mi zor'an* — as for that strip outside the overhang, who has the right to plant it? Rav Yosef responds that the answer may be inferred from a *mishnah* already taught: *hachitzon zorea es haderech* — the owner of the outer garden may plant the path.

### Two Gardens

The analogy invoked is the case of two adjacent gardens, one nested within the other: an inner garden (*p'nimi*) and an outer garden (*chitzon*), with a path running through the outer garden that grants the inner owner access. The ruling there is that the owner of the outer garden retains the right to plant that path. The buyer of the trees, it is argued, is analogously situated — he has a right of access, but the underlying land remains the *ba'al hasadeh*'s to cultivate.

### Falling Fruit Problem

The Gemara rejects this analogy, however. Abaye responds: *mi dami* — are the cases comparable? In the garden case, the planting of the path causes no real loss to the person with access rights. One might trample the plantings in passing, but the planting itself does not compromise the right of ingress. Here, however, if the field owner plants that outer strip and the buyer's figs or apples fall from the tree onto those plantings, the fallen fruit will damage what is growing there. This is the stated concern: *kamitanfi peiri* — my fruit becomes ruined or dirtied.

What is striking about this argument is its logic. The fundamental justification for granting the buyer that outer strip in the first place is to allow him to stand and pick. One might have expected the challenge to be that planting there physically prevents the picker from standing. Instead, the Gemara shifts the concern to the falling fruit damaging the field owner's crops. This is a somewhat different axis of argument, yet it is sufficient to distinguish the two-gardens case.

### Neither Plants Space

Having distinguished the inner-garden analogy at its first stage, the Gemara draws the comparison to the end of that *mishnah* instead: *be'zeh u've'zeh einam resha'im lizroa* — where a specific path has been agreed upon between the parties, neither side may plant it. The reasoning is that once both parties have, as it were, designated that strip, the buyer's rights in it are more explicitly recognized. By analogy — or more precisely, because planting there would compromise the buyer's right — neither the field owner nor the buyer may plant that outer strip. The conclusion is that both are precluded. This, the Gemara acknowledges, is not entirely straightforward in its fairness to the *ba'al hasadeh*, but that is the ruling.

---

## Distance 4-16 Amot

### Distance Question

Having resolved the question of access rights outside the trees, the Gemara turns to a new and central question: *ve-kamma yehei beineihem* — how much distance must there be between the three trees in order for the purchase to confer ownership of the land between them? There is both a minimum and a maximum. If the trees are too close together they resemble a grove rather than individually tended fruit trees; if they are too far apart they are not considered a coherent unit. What are these thresholds?

### 4-8 Amot Opinion

Rav Yosef cites a tradition in the name of Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel: the range is *me-arba ve-ad shemonah* — from four *amot* to eight *amot*. Trees spaced within this range are considered properly connected and their purchase conveys the land between them.

### 8-16 Amot Ruling

Rava, however, cites a tradition in the name of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: the range is from eight *amot* to sixteen *amot*. Abaye then says to Rav Yosef: do not argue with Rav Nachman. The Rashbam notes that this phrasing is unusual given that Abaye was Rav Yosef's student, and suggests that Rav Yosef had at some point suffered memory loss, and Abaye may be gently reminding him not to stand against a ruling he ought to remember. Rava's position — the wider range of eight to sixteen — is supported, says Abaye, by a *mishnah*.

### Kilayim Support

The *mishnah* in question comes from tractate Kilayim. The laws of *kilayim* provide that a vineyard planted with rows spaced sixteen *amot* by sixteen *amot* apart — *shesh esrei amma al shesh esrei amma* — is considered a properly formed *kerem* (vineyard) in which the full *kerem* restrictions apply. A *kerem* requires its adjacent area to be kept free of foreign seeds to a substantial distance, whereas a single isolated row requires only a minimal clearance. Whether one is dealing with a *kerem* or merely isolated rows turns on how close the rows are to one another.

The *mishnah* rules: if the rows are a full sixteen *amot* apart, *mutar lehavi zerah lesham* — one is permitted to plant seed right up to that row, because at that distance the rows are not considered connected into a single *kerem*. They are separate rows. This demonstrates that up to sixteen *amot* the rows remain a cohesive unit; at sixteen *amot* or beyond, they are considered disconnected. The upper limit of sixteen *amot* is thereby established.

### Tzalmon Story

At the end of that *mishnah*, Rav Yehudah relates a story: there was a case in the village of Tzalmon where a man had planted his vineyard with rows sixteen *amot* apart. His practice was to take the hanging tendrils of two rows — the overhang that extended inward on each side — and in alternating years fold them back over toward the same direction, thereby leaving a full open gap of sixteen *amot* in the middle with no vines hanging into it. Because this gap was fully open, those rows were regarded as disconnected, and he was therefore permitted to plant that middle strip with another crop. The following year he would reverse the process, folding the tendrils back the other way and opening the previously planted strip. This case came before the Sages and they permitted it. The point for our purposes is that once there were sixteen *amot* completely clear between the rows, they were considered separate, confirming sixteen as the threshold.

### Four Amot Case

Rav Yosef responds that he does not have any comment on that *mishnah*, but he does have a story of his own. In the village of Dura de'Re'uta — apparently a village of shepherds — a case came before Rav Yehudah, and Rav Yehudah ruled: *zil havu leh mlo bakar vechelov* — give the buyer the equivalent of "the fill of an ox and its implements," which turns out to equal four *amot*. The Rashbam understands this as a case where the distance between the trees was between four and eight *amot*, and Rav Yehudah ruled that the buyer receives the land — thereby establishing four *amot* as the lower bound.

Rav Yosef then relates that he did not initially know how much *mlo bakar vechelov* was, until he heard a different *mishnah*: one may not plant a tree near the boundary of a neighbor's field unless one maintains a distance of four *amot*, and a *baraita* explains that four *amot* is the space needed for *avodat hakerem* — to work the vineyard with an ox. He therefore concluded that *mlo bakar vechelov* equals four *amot*. So from this story, the lower limit of four *amot* is supported.

### Story vs. Opinion

The Gemara then asks: why did Rav Yosef respond to Abaye's citation of the sixteen-*amot* *mishnah* with a story, rather than citing the opinion of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon in that same *mishnah* in Kilayim, who maintain that the threshold is eight *amot* rather than sixteen — thereby showing that his position of a smaller range was consistent with a *tanna'ic* view? The Gemara answers: *afillu hachi maaseh adif* — even so, a story is preferable, because a story reflects an actual practical ruling, a *psak lema'aseh*. Citing an opinion among other opinions does not resolve which view to follow; citing a story from practice gives the position real weight.

The Rashbam reads the passage slightly differently: the question is not only why Rav Yosef cited the story rather than the minority opinion, but also what made Abaye's original challenge from the sixteen-*amot* mishnah so forceful. The answer, on the Rashbam's reading, is that Abaye's position was strengthened precisely because the majority view in the Kilayim *mishnah* was bolstered by the story of Tzalmon. And Rav Yosef correspondingly wanted to answer with a story of his own, rather than merely citing a competing theoretical opinion. The interplay between these two modes of argument — theoretical opinion versus practical precedent — is itself significant.

### Kilayim Inference

The Gemara now considers how each of the two positions — the four-to-eight range of Rav Yosef and the eight-to-sixteen range of Rava — derives both its upper and lower limits from the laws of *kilayim*. For Rav Yosef, whose position aligns with Rabbi Shimon in *kilayim*: Rabbi Shimon holds that vines more than eight *amot* apart are *mefuzarin* — considered separate — and vines less than four *amot* apart do not form a proper *kerem*, as stated explicitly in the *mishnah*: *kerem ha-natu'a pachot me-arba amot eino kerem divrei Rabbi Shimon*. Both the upper and lower limits thus emerge directly from Rabbi Shimon's rulings. The Rabbanan there disagree and say that even tightly packed vines can form a *kerem* — the extra vines are simply to be uprooted — but this does not undercut Rabbi Shimon's coherent framework.

For Rav Nachman, whose position aligns with the Rabbanan, the upper limit of sixteen *amot* is established by that same *mishnah*, but where does one infer that his lower limit is eight? The Gemara answers: *svara hu* — it follows by logical inference. Since for Rabbi Shimon the lower limit is exactly half the upper limit (four is half of eight), we apply the same proportion for the Rabbanan: half of sixteen is eight. The lower limit for the Rabbanan's range is therefore eight *amot*.

### Final Ruling

Rava then states the *halacha*: *hilchosa me-arba amot ve-ad shesh esrei* — the law follows neither of the ranges in isolation but rather combines them. The lower limit of four *amot* appears to be universally agreed upon — all opinions seem to accept that trees closer than four *amot* are too compressed to constitute a meaningful planting arrangement. The dispute is over the upper limit, and Rava rules like the Rabbanan that sixteen *amot* is the upper threshold. A *baraita* is then cited that confirms this ruling directly: trees must be at least four *amot* apart and no more than sixteen *amot* apart for the purchase to convey the land; within that range, the buyer acquires both the land and the minor trees growing between the main trees.

One should note that this ruling rests on two applications of *kilayim* to the laws of tree purchase: first, that the conceptual framework of a connected planting unit applies equally to vines and to trees; and second, that the minimum required spacing — which in *kilayim* reflects how compressed vines can be before they lose their agricultural character — may similarly define the minimum viable spacing of trees. While the upper limit question seems more conceptual (at what point are the trees simply two unrelated units?), the lower limit question is arguably more agricultural in character. The direct application of vine-spacing standards to trees of other types is thus a noteworthy interpretive step.

---

## Land Ownership Rules

### Mishnah Statement

The Gemara now presents the *mishnah* that encapsulates the rules governing land ownership through tree purchase. If the three trees are spaced between four and sixteen *amot* apart, the buyer acquires not only the trees but the land between them.

### Minor Trees

Additionally, any small or minor trees growing between the three main trees also belong to the buyer. One might wonder how there can be minor trees in between if the spacing requirements remain in effect — the answer is that these are young shoots or insubstantial growths that do not redefine the spacing between the primary trees.

### Ownership After Death

The ownership of the land is robust: *yavesh ha-ilan o nikta, yesh lo karka* — if the tree dries up or is cut down, the buyer retains ownership of the land. Once the land was conveyed, that conveyance is permanent and does not depend on the continued existence of the trees.

### Distance Limits

If the trees are closer than four *amot* or farther than sixteen *amot* apart, the buyer acquires neither the land nor the minor trees between them. In such cases, if a tree subsequently dies, the buyer has no land rights whatsoever.

### Sequential Purchase

Equally, if the buyer purchased the three trees one at a time rather than as a single unit, no land is conveyed. It is specifically the purchase of three trees as a coherent unit that creates the legal basis for the land grant. Purchasing them sequentially means each transaction is an isolated purchase of a tree, not the purchase of a planting unit.

---

## Measuring Distance

### Measuring Point

Rabbi Yirmiyah raises a concrete question: *keshe-hu moded, mi-makom katzar hu moded o mi-makom rachav hu moded* — when measuring the distance between the trees to determine whether it falls within the four-to-sixteen range, does one measure from the narrow part of the trunk or from the wide part? The Rashbam notes that this is not necessarily a *chumra* or *kula* question, since it depends on which end of the range one is working with. The Rashbam also entertains the possibility that *makom rachav* refers to the canopy rather than the trunk, but he rejects this, reasoning that we are interested in where the tree is planted, and the canopy also presents practical measurement difficulties. He therefore assumes the question is about the base versus the upper part of the trunk.

### Vine Knee Case

Rav Geviha of Bei Katil brings a proof from a *mishnah*: *ha-rekuva she-ba-gefen, eino moded ela me-ikar ha-sheni*. The term *rekuva* refers to a vine that has been bent at the knee — *arkuva*, as Tosafot explain, drawing on the word *berech* (knee). The practice described is that of bending a mature vine downward, burying the bent section underground, and allowing it to come back up and grow as what appears to be a separate vine. This technique (*mavriach*) causes the vine to root at the underground bend and send up a new shoot. The *mishnah* rules that when measuring the relevant distance, one measures from the *ikar ha-sheni* — the second root or the point from which the vine re-emerges.

### Root Measurement

Tosafot understand *ikar ha-sheni* to mean "the second root" in the sense of the base of the new growth — the point at which the bent vine comes back up from the ground. The key word for Tosafot is *ikar*, which they take to mean root or base. The implication is that one measures from the base of the trunk, i.e., the *makom rachav*, the wide point. This resolves Rabbi Yirmiyah's question in favor of measuring from the wide base.

### Middle Knob

The Rashbam reads *ikar ha-sheni* differently. Vines have characteristic knobs along their length, and the Rashbam understands *ikar ha-sheni* to mean the second knob — not the first and not the tip, but the middle point. On this reading, the Gemara resolves Rabbi Yirmiyah's question by ruling that one measures from neither the widest nor the narrowest point but from the middle of the trunk. The two rishonim thus arrive at different practical conclusions from the same source, and the dispute between them turns on the meaning of *ikar ha-sheni*.

---

## Connected Trees

### Three Branches

Rabbi Yirmiyah raises a further question, more in his characteristic style of pushing cases to their limits: *machar lo shlosha badei ilan mahu* — if someone sold another person three branches of a single tree, does this qualify as "three trees" for the purpose of land acquisition? The case is as follows: a single tree sends out a branch that bends down to the ground and comes back up, appearing to be a separate tree, and this process repeats, yielding what look like three distinct trees but are all still physically connected to and continuous with the original trunk.

### Batei Ilan

The answer comes from a *mishnah*: *ha-mavrich gimel gefanim ve-ikreihen nir'in* — if one has bent three vines (using the same *mavriach* technique) and their roots are visible, Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Tzadok says: if there is between them from four *amot* to eight *amot*, they are considered to join together as a unit; if not, they do not join. The key phrase is *ve-ikreihen nir'in* — and their roots are visible, which the Rashbam explains means they have actually taken root underground. Once the bent section has taken root beneath the ground, these are considered separate entities — *batei ilan* — distinct trees or vines, even though they remain physically connected to the original.

### Distinct Roots

The ruling thus follows: even when branches or vines are physically continuous with one another, if they have independently taken root underground, each is treated as a separate tree. The underground connection does not negate the distinctness conferred by independent rooting. This principle determines that three such branches can indeed qualify as three separate trees for the purpose of the land-acquisition laws — provided the spacing requirements are met.

---

## Special Cases

### Boundary Trees

Rav Pappa raises a question: *machar lo shnayim betoch sadehu ve-echad al ha-metzar mahu* — what if someone sold two trees located within the interior of the field and one tree standing right at the boundary line (*metzar*)? Does the tree at the edge of the field, by virtue of its position at the border, not combine with the other two to form the required unit? Perhaps a tree standing at the very edge is visually and conceptually distinct from the group, and fails to create the impression of a cohesive planting. The question is left unresolved.

### Cross-Property Trees

A related and more striking question: *shnayim betoch shelo ve-echad betoch shel chaveiro mai* — what if two trees are within the seller's own field and the third tree is located within the field of a different person, yet the seller owns that third tree as well? If one were to connect them, the necessary range might be satisfied, but the fact that the third tree is physically situated within someone else's property may undermine the notion that they form a single continuous plot. Does the intervening ownership of the surrounding land sever the connection? The Gemara concludes with *teiku* — this question remains unresolved.

### Interruptions

Rav Ashi then raises a series of questions about physical interruptions between the trees. If a well (*bor*) sits in the middle of the space between the three trees, does it break the unit? One might argue that a well actually enhances the desirability of the plot, but one could also note that in a working agricultural field a well is typically situated at the edge rather than in the center of a planting area, and its presence in the middle may therefore conceptually sever the space. Similarly: does an aqueduct (*amat ha-mayim*) that physically cuts through the space between the trees interrupt the unit? A public thoroughfare (*reshut ha-rabbim*) passing between them? A grove of palm trees (*richba di-dikla*)? All of these are posed as *mahu shetefsik* — does it constitute an interruption? — and all remain with *teiku*.

### Cedar Tree

Hillel asks of Rebbi: *ala erez beineihen mahu* — if a cedar tree grew up between the three purchased trees, does it break the unit? The Gemara quickly notes that this formulation is odd: if the land already belongs to the buyer by virtue of the three-tree purchase, and a cedar tree then grows in that land, it has grown in the buyer's own property — *ala bireshusa didei nafik*. The question is therefore reformulated: *haya erez beineihem mahu* — what if a cedar tree was already standing between the three trees at the time of purchase? Does its presence interrupt the unit?

Several factors make the cedar a candidate for breaking the unit: it is large, it is typically a non-fruit-bearing tree, and *ilan* (the standard word for tree in this context) usually refers to fruit trees. The cedar, being categorically distinct from a fruit tree, may render the space between the three purchased trees not a coherent planting unit. Rebbi answers: *karnei ve-karnei* — the buyer gets the land regardless; the cedar does not break the unit.

One further observation is worth noting: the interlocutors here are Hillel and Rebbi — apparently *tannaim* — appearing after a long series of *amoraic* discussions. This is striking, and one of the participants in the shiur observed that it is unusual to have a *tanna* posing questions that are then answered, in what looks like the format of later *amoraic* exchange.

---

## Row vs. Triangle

### Line or Triangle

The Gemara now turns to the question of the physical configuration of the three trees: *keitzad hein omdin* — how must the trees be arranged? Rav says *ke-shura* — they may stand in a straight line. Shmuel says *ke-chatzuva* — they must be arranged like a tripod, i.e., in a triangle formation.

### Land Depends on Form

The Gemara derives that these two positions are not simply parallel alternatives but stand in logical relation to one another. Whoever holds that trees in a row (*shura*) convey the land would certainly hold that a triangle (*chatzuva*) does — the triangle more obviously defines an enclosed space. But whoever holds that only a triangle conveys the land would not extend this to trees in a row.

### Plantability Factor

The reasoning behind the restrictive view is: *mishum de-mistara beintayhu* — because the space between trees in a row is still accessible and plantable by the seller. If the seller can still run a plow between the trees and cultivate that strip, it is reasonable to assume he would not intend to sell it. The space is still functionally his to use. By contrast, when the trees are arranged in a triangle, the land enclosed between them cannot be efficiently planted by the seller — the configuration makes agricultural use of the interior impractical. In that case, the seller has no strong reason to retain the interior land, and we assume it passes to the buyer along with the trees.

### Thorny Bush

Rav Hamnuna challenges the triangle-based reasoning: if the operative principle is that the seller cannot plant the enclosed space, then consider a case where someone sold three large thorny bushes (*higei u-maisai*) arranged in a triangle. Between them, the seller certainly cannot plant — thorns make the space inaccessible. Would we say the buyer therefore receives the land between the thornbushes?

### Trees Plus Space

The response is decisive: *lo hanech lo chashivi, hanech chashivi* — thornbushes are not significant enough, not *chashiv* enough, to convey land. Both conditions must be met simultaneously. The items sold must be trees — which by virtue of their importance can serve as a basis for a land transaction — *and* the enclosed space must be one that the seller cannot efficiently plant. In the case of a triangle of trees, both conditions are satisfied. In the case of trees in a row, the trees meet the first condition but the space between them remains plantable, so the second condition fails. In the case of thornbushes in a triangle, the second condition is met but the first is not. Only when both are present does the buyer acquire the land.

---

## Animal Parts

### Large Animal Head

A new *mishnah* begins here, addressing a different domain of commercial law: the sale of animal parts. *Ha-mocher rosh behema gassa lo machar et ha-raglayim* — one who sells the head of a large animal (such as a cow) has not sold the legs. The word "head" (*rosh*) might in other contexts function as a synecdoche for the whole animal — we commonly speak of "heads of cattle" — but the *mishnah* establishes that here it means literally the head, and even the legs are not included.

### Organs and Parts

The *mishnah* then covers the reverse: *machar et ha-raglayim lo machar et ha-rosh* — selling the legs does not include the head. Similarly: *machar et ha-kane lo machar et ha-kaved* — selling the *kane* (the trachea, here representing the trachea and lungs together) does not include the liver; and *machar et ha-kaved lo machar et ha-kane* — selling the liver does not include the lungs and trachea. Each organ complex is treated as a distinct item; purchase of one does not entail the other.

### Small Animal Rules

For a small animal (*dakka*), such as a sheep or goat, the rules differ somewhat. *Machar et ha-rosh machar et ha-raglayim* — if one sells the head, the legs are included, presumably because the head of a small animal has relatively little meat and the legs are naturally assumed to come along with it. However, selling the legs does not include the head. As for organs: *machar et ha-kane machar et ha-kaved* — selling the trachea and lungs of a small animal includes the liver, perhaps again because the trachea-and-lungs unit is the less substantial portion. But *machar ha-kaved lo* — selling the liver does not include the lungs and trachea.

---

## Four Categories

### Good to Bad

The *mishnah* introduces a new and conceptually rich section: *arba midot be-mocheim* — four categories of transactions. Despite the formulation (literally "four categories among sellers"), the intent is to classify four types of transactions and the legal rights each generates. The first: *machar lo chitin yafot ve-nimtze'u ra'ot* — he sold him high-quality wheat and it turned out to be low quality. In this case, *ha-loke'ach yachol lachzor bo* — the buyer may retract.

### Bad to Good

The second category is the reverse: *ra'ot ve-nimtze'u yafot* — he sold low-quality and it turned out to be high quality. Here, *ha-mocher yachol lachzor bo* — the seller may retract. This might seem counterintuitive — the buyer received something better than he paid for — but the seller can claim that the transaction was not what he intended.

### As Promised

The third category is where delivery matches the agreement: *yafot ve-nimtze'u yafot, ra'ot ve-nimtze'u ra'ot* — whether the transaction was for high or low quality and the delivery matched, *ein echad meihem yachol lachzor bo* — neither party may retract. This is not a great novelty but is necessary to complete the structure of the four cases.

What requires further reflection is the precise mechanism of the first two categories. One might assume that any discrepancy between what was promised and what was delivered constitutes a *mekach ta'ut* — a fundamentally mistaken transaction — rendering the sale void from the outset, with both parties free to retract. The *mishnah* reveals that this is not so. When the discrepancy is one of degree within the same category — better or worse quality of the same item — the transaction remains binding unless and until the aggrieved party chooses to retract. Only the party who received less than promised has the right to retract; the other party may not. A practical consequence: if the buyer receives lower quality wheat than promised but uses it to effect another transaction — say, betrothing a woman or purchasing a *lulav* and *etrog* — those transactions remain legally valid until he actually retracts the original sale.

### Different Type

The fourth category is the most conceptually distinct: *shachamtit ve-nimtze'u levana, levana ve-nimtze'u shachamtit* — sold as red and turned out to be white, or sold as white and turned out to be red. More broadly, the *mishnah* includes: sold as olive wood and turned out to be sycamore; sold as sycamore and turned out to be olive wood; sold as wine and turned out to be vinegar; sold as vinegar and turned out to be wine. In all of these cases, the discrepancy is not one of better versus worse but of different kind or color, where preferences among buyers and sellers may vary. *Sheneihem yecholim lachzor bo* — both parties may retract.

The reasoning is that when the item delivered is of a different type than what was agreed upon — even if not clearly inferior — each party can legitimately claim the transaction was not as intended. Some people specifically require vinegar; others specifically need wine. Some need sycamore; others need olive wood. Because neither item is straightforwardly better or worse, both parties stand on equal footing to declare the transaction not what they had in mind.

### Mekach Ta'ut

The *mishnah* thus carves out a subtle distinction within what might loosely be called *mekach ta'ut*. A truly radical discrepancy — say, agreeing to sell wheat and delivering a donkey — would presumably void the sale entirely from the outset, with no transaction to speak of. But the cases in this *mishnah* involve discrepancies that are real but not so extreme as to make the sale simply nonexistent. Within this range, the *mishnah* distinguishes: a quality discrepancy gives the disadvantaged party (and only that party) the right to retract; a type discrepancy gives both parties that right.

This is conceptually distinct from the laws of *ona'ah* — overcharging or undercharging — which apply when the item is exactly as described but the price is wrong. *Ona'ah* addresses price distortion; the four categories of this *mishnah* address discrepancies in the nature of the item itself. These two frameworks — while related and sometimes overlapping at their margins — are analytically separate, and the discussion will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Bava Batra 84

## Taʿut & Ona'ah Intro

### Four Types Taʿut

The *gemara* on today's daf picks up immediately after the *mishna* at the close of 83b, which concluded its discussion of what is included or excluded when purchasing different parts of an animal, and pivoted to a new category: four types of *ta'ut* — mistake — that can arise in a commercial transaction when the item received turns out to be different from what was agreed upon.

The *mishna* establishes the following basic framework. If the seller represented the grain as good quality and it turned out to be inferior, the buyer has been wronged and may demand his money back or nullify the sale — but the seller may not. Conversely, if the grain was represented as inferior and turned out to be of good quality, it is the buyer who has received something other than what he bargained for, and he may reverse the sale — but again, not the seller. In both of these cases, one side has been hurt and only that side holds the right of reversal. In a third category, where the item is not merely better or worse but is an entirely different thing — red wine versus white wine, wine versus vinegar — the error is bilateral, neither side can be said to have obtained what was agreed upon, and accordingly both sides may back out.

### Taʿut vs Ona'ah

The *mishna* itself makes no reference to *ona'ah* — the laws of overcharging or undercharging. *Ona'ah* is a distinct body of law governing cases where the item sold is exactly what was described, but the price paid was more than one-sixth above or below the market value. That gives rise to a right to demand the price differential back or, in cases of gross *ona'ah*, to nullify the sale. This is categorically different from the *mishna*'s concern, which is not with price at all but with whether the item delivered matched the item described.

The distinction carries practical implications. For instance, if the difference between good and bad wheat was less than a sixth, would the *mishna* still apply? And what is the time window within which a party may act? In *ona'ah*, the accepted rule is that the wronged party has until he has had the opportunity to show the item to relatives or to a merchant who can assess whether he was cheated. Is that same window applicable to *ta'ut*? It appears to be a fundamentally different legal category. Nevertheless, the *gemara* proceeds to draw an analogy between the two — though, as will become clear, this does not collapse them into a single *halacha*.

## Rav Chisda Ona'ah

### Overcharging Case

The *gemara* begins at two lines from the bottom of 83b with a teaching of Rav Chisda. The case: someone sold an item worth five *zuzim* for six — a classic instance of *ona'ah*, since the excess of one constitutes one-sixth of the price paid. (The precise method of calculating the sixth — whether relative to the value of the object or to the sum paid — is the subject of an extended discussion in Bava Metzia and need not detain us here.) For present purposes, the buyer has been overcharged and therefore holds the right either to recover the overcharge or to nullify the sale entirely.

Now Rav Chisda introduces a complication. After the sale, and still within the time window during which the buyer retains his right to act — that is, before he has had the opportunity to verify the price with relatives or a market expert — the price of the item rises sharply, so that what was worth five at the time of sale is now worth eight. The seller, who originally overcharged his buyer by one *zuz*, would now very much like to undo the transaction, since he gave away something worth eight for only six.

### Wronged Party Right

Rav Chisda rules: *mi nitaneh* — who was wronged? The buyer. *Lokayach yachol lachzor bo velo mocher* — the buyer may reverse the sale, not the seller. The reasoning, stated at the top of 84a, is that the seller can be told: had you not cheated me, we would not be having this conversation, and you would clearly have no right to reverse the sale. The fact that you overcharged me gives rise to a right of reversal — but that right belongs to me, the party who was wronged, not to you. Your wrongdoing does not generate a privilege for yourself.

This ruling requires a *hava amina* to justify its being stated at all. One might have thought that the window in which the buyer may demand his money back should be conceptualized not as a one-sided right accruing to the wronged party, but rather as a period during which the sale is simply not yet final — a period of verification during which neither side is fully bound. Under that framing, both parties should be free to withdraw during that window. Rav Chisda's ruling rejects this: the proper frame is not that the sale is suspended, but that the wronged party holds a specific right, and that right does not extend to the other side.

Rav Chisda then notes that the *tanna* of our *mishna* teaches the same principle: *yafos v'nimtzu ra'os lokayach yachol lachzor bo velo mocher* — if the grain was represented as good and found to be bad, the buyer may reverse and the seller may not. Now, if the going price had not changed, the seller would have had no reason to want the sale reversed, and the *mishna* would be stating something obvious. The *chidush* of the *mishna* must therefore be addressing precisely the scenario where conditions have shifted — where the grain that was bad has since become worth considerably more — and yet the seller still cannot reverse. This confirms Rav Chisda's principle: the right of reversal is one-sided, belonging to the wronged party alone.

### Undercharging Case

Rav Chisda then presents the mirror image. Suppose something worth six was sold for five — the seller was undercharged, a case of *ona'ah* in the reverse direction. Subsequently, *v'huzlu v'amdu al gimmel* — the market collapses and what was sold for five is now worth only three. The buyer, who originally got a bargain, now finds himself holding an asset worth less than he paid, and would gladly reverse the transaction. Who may reverse?

*Mi nitaneh? Mocher* — the seller was wronged. *Mocher yachol lachzor bo velo lokayach* — only the seller may reverse, not the buyer. The logic is the same: the seller can say to the buyer, had you not underpaid me, the sale would have been final from the moment of the exchange and you would have had no right to reverse. The fact that you cheated me generates a right of reversal — my right, not yours. Again, the *mishna* teaches correspondingly: *ra'os v'nimtze'u yafos mocher yachol lachzor bo velo loke'ach* — if the grain was described as bad and found to be good, only the seller may reverse, not the buyer, even in a case where the buyer might now prefer to undo the sale.

## Gemara Challenge

### Apparent Circularity

Having laid out Rav Chisda's two cases together with the parallel passages from the *mishna*, the *gemara* objects: *mai kamashma lan masnisin hi* — what is Rav Chisda adding? His ruling seems to be nothing more than a restatement of the *mishna*'s own principle. The *mishna* already makes clear that the wronged party has the right to reverse and the other side does not. Why, then, did Rav Chisda need to teach this?

### Ona'ah vs Taʿut Distinct…

The *gemara* resolves this by pointing to the circumstantial difference between *ona'ah* and *ta'ut*, even if the underlying *halacha* turns out to be the same. Without Rav Chisda's ruling, one might have thought: in a case of *ona'ah*, where the price paid was objectively wrong relative to the going rate, perhaps both sides should be able to reverse during the verification window — precisely because the price was objectively out of line, which throws the entire transaction into question. One could argue that when the monetary terms of a sale are demonstrably improper, both parties should be released from it.

And conversely, one might have thought that our *mishna*'s case — where the item was misdescribed — should allow *only* the wronged side to reverse. Why? Because in the world of commercial negotiation, the seller always overclaims the quality of his goods and the buyer always underclaims.

### Overclaiming Logic

This is the crux of the *gemara*'s point. When a seller says "good wheat" and the buyer receives bad wheat, the buyer can legitimately claim *mekach ta'ut* — this was not what I agreed to. But if the seller then says, "since the item was not as described, I too should have a right to reverse," the buyer might reasonably respond: when you said "good," I never fully believed you anyway — sellers always overclaim. So it is not clear that anything objectively different from what was agreed upon actually occurred, because the buyer may have factored in the seller's habitual overstatement. Similarly, when the buyer declared the grain "bad" as a negotiating posture, the seller might argue that the buyer's language was equally strategic and that the item was not objectively misrepresented.

Under this reasoning, one might have distinguished: in *ta'ut*, where the objective deviation from the agreed description is uncertain due to the overclaiming conventions of commerce, perhaps both sides can reverse — precisely because it is unclear whether there truly was a misrepresentation. And in *ona'ah*, where the deviation from market price is an objective fact, only the wronged side should be able to reverse.

Rav Chisda teaches that this distinction does not hold. In both contexts, the principle is the same: the wronged party has the right to reverse and the other side does not. The *gemara* emphasizes that this is so in both directions — neither the formulation about *ona'ah* nor the formulation about *ta'ut* carries an exception. In every case, it is the side that was hurt that holds the right, and no amount of changed circumstances transfers that right to the other party.

## Red vs White Grain

### Sun Is Red

The *mishna* had listed among the cases of *ta'ut* a scenario where grain was described as *shachamtis* — red — and turned out to be white. The term *shachamtis* is related to *chamah*, the sun, signifying a reddish-solar hue. Rav Papa observes: *midkatni levanah* — since the *mishna* frames the contrast as "red versus white," and since the word chosen for red is *shachamtis*, derived from the sun, we may infer from this that the sun is intrinsically red in color. *Shema minah: hai shimsha sumakta hi* — learn from this that the sun is red.

### Sun Color Explanation

One might then ask: if the sun is red, why does it not appear red throughout the day? The *gemara* answers: *dekasmi tzafra ufanya* — because at dawn and at dusk, the sky is indeed red, and this is consistent with the sun's true color being red. As for why it does not appear red during the full brightness of the day: *nehorin hu delo bari* — our eyesight is simply not capable of perceiving the true color when the sun shines at full intensity. It is only when the sun is lower on the horizon and its light is less overwhelming — at dawn and at dusk — that we are able to see the redness that is always there. This is somewhat analogous to a solar eclipse, when the reduced intensity of light allows one to perceive aspects of the sun not normally visible.

The *gemara* then raises an objection from the laws of *tzara'at*. The verse in the context of *tzara'at* states that the appearance of the affliction is *amok min ha'or* — deeper than the skin — and the comparison given is *ke'mareh chamah amukah min hatzel*, analogous to the way sunlight appears deeper than shade. Since *tzara'at* is white, and the comparison is drawn to sunlight, this would seem to imply that sunlight is white. The *gemara* answers: the verse means something more nuanced — that the *tzara'at* resembles sunlight in the specific quality of appearing deeper than its surroundings (as sunlight appears deeper than shade), but the comparison does not extend to color. *Ke'mareh chamah* — in the sense of that quality of apparent depth — but *velo ke'mareh chamah* in the sense of color, *de'ilu hatam lavan vehacha adom* — for by *tzara'at* we deal with white, while the sun is red.

### Reflection Theory

The *gemara* then entertains the view it was originally countering — that the sun's true color is white — and asks: if that is so, how do we explain the redness at dawn and dusk? The *gemara* offers a striking answer: *be'tzafra de'chalfa a'varda de'Gan Eden* — in the morning, as the sun rises in the East, it passes by the rose garden of *Gan Eden*, which is located in the East (*Gan be'Eden mi'kedem*), and the reflection of that rose garden imparts the red color. And *u've'panya de'chalfa a'pitcha de'Gehinnom* — in the evening, the sun passes by the entrance of *Gehinnom*, which is in the West, and the fires of *Gehinnom* give the sky its red color at dusk. *Ve'ika de'amri ipcha* — some say the opposite: *Gan Eden* is in the West and *Gehinnom* in the East, but the interpretive logic about the sun reflecting what is opposite it rather than what is alongside it remains the same.

## Wine vs Vinegar

### Wine Vinegar Different

The *mishna* includes among its cases: wine was sold and vinegar was received — or vice versa. Since one person might specifically want wine and another vinegar, with neither being simply better or worse than the other, this constitutes a bilateral error: the item delivered was categorically different from the item agreed upon, and both sides may reverse.

### Rabbi vs Rabbanan

The *gemara* raises a pointed question: *leima masnisin Rabbi hi velo Rabbanan* — perhaps our *mishna* follows specifically the position of Rabbi (Rebbi) and not the *Rabbanan*, based on the following *baraita* at the top of 84b. The *baraita* records a dispute: wine and vinegar constitute one type — *min echad* — and Rabbi says they are two distinct types — *shnei minim*. This dispute arises in the context of *terumah*: when separating *terumah*, one must take from the same *min* as that for which the *terumah* is being designated. If wine and vinegar are one *min*, one may take *terumah* from wine on vinegar and vice versa; if they are two distinct *minim*, one may not. The *Rabbanan* hold they are one *min*; Rabbi holds they are two. Since our *mishna* treats the substitution of wine for vinegar as a grounds for both parties to reverse — treating them as categorically distinct — it would seem to align with Rabbi's position.

### Consumer Preference

The *gemara* rejects this inference: *afilu teima Rabbanan* — the *mishna* can be explained even according to the *Rabbanan*. The *Rabbanan* dispute Rabbi's ruling *only* with respect to *terumah* and *ma'aser*, in the specific context analyzed through the teaching of Rabbi Ilai. Rabbi Ilai derives from the verse *velo tisu alav cheit be'harimchem et chelbo mimenu* — "you shall not bear sin when you take the choicest from it" — that when one takes *terumah* from inferior produce on behalf of superior produce, the *terumah* is nonetheless valid, though a sin has been committed. The logic: if such a separation were entirely ineffective, there would be no sin to declare. Rabbi Ilai's derivation demonstrates that taking *terumah* from bad on good is *chal* — legally effective — even if improper, and the *Rabbanan* build their lenient classification of wine and vinegar as one *min* on the basis of this principle, which relaxes the requirement of strict categorical identity in the domain of *terumah*.

But this tells us nothing about the laws of commerce. *Aval l'inyan mekach u'memkar* — when it comes to transactions, says the *gemara*, *de'chulei alma ika denichlei bechamra velo nichlei bechala ve'ika denichlei bechala velo nichlei bechamra* — everyone agrees that some people specifically want wine and not vinegar, and others specifically want vinegar and not wine. This is not merely a question of quality or price; it is a question of what the buyer actually wanted. When someone goes to purchase wine and receives vinegar, he has not received an inferior version of what he ordered — he has received something he may not want at all. The same applies in reverse.

The *gemara*'s point is elegant: objective taxonomic classification — whether two things belong to the same *min* for purposes of *terumah* — need not govern commercial law, where the operative question is consumer preference. Even if wine and vinegar are taxonomically one species, since there are people who want one and not the other, delivering the wrong one is not simply a matter of better or worse quality but a matter of category from the buyer's perspective. Therefore, even the *Rabbanan*, who classify wine and vinegar as one *min* for *terumah*, would agree that in commerce they are distinct enough to allow both sides to reverse.

## Finality of Sale

### Meshicha Rule

The next *mishna* opens: *hamocher peros lachaveiro* — one who sells produce — meaning grain or any agricultural commodity — to his fellow. The *mishna* establishes the rules for when such a sale becomes final. The *Rashbam* notes that in all of these cases, the price per unit has already been agreed upon; what remains undetermined is the total quantity. That caveat is important: the openness as to total amount does not prevent the sale from being final once the proper act of *kinyan* is performed.

*Mashach velo madad kana* — if the buyer performed *meshicha*, pulling or drawing the grain toward himself, the sale is final even if the grain has not yet been measured. *Madad velo mashach lo kana* — if the grain was measured out but the buyer has not yet performed *meshicha* or any other formal act of *kinyan*, the sale is not final and either side may withdraw.

### Flax Hagbaha

The *mishna* then addresses flax, a lighter commodity: *halokeach pishtan mechaveiro harei zeh lo kana ad sheitaltelnu mimakom lemakom* — the buyer does not acquire it merely by *meshicha*; because flax is light enough to be lifted, the *Rashbam* explains that the *mishna* requires *hagbahah*, actual lifting, to effect the *kinyan*. *Meshicha* alone is insufficient for flax precisely because the buyer is capable of and expected to perform the stronger act of *hagbahah*.

### Attached Items

If the buyer is purchasing something still attached to the ground — an apple on a tree, for instance — then *im hayah mechubar lakarka vesalash kol shehu kana*: as soon as the buyer plucks even the smallest amount from the ground, the *kinyan* is complete. This *ma'aseh kinyan* through detachment is itself an effective mode of acquisition in this context.

Finally, the *mishna* notes: *im hayah pikeach socher es mekomon* — if the buyer was astute and wished to lock in the sale before performing *meshicha* or *hagbahah*, he could rent the space on which the grain rests. As the *gemara* will clarify, the location matters for determining which *kinyan* is available and from whom the space can be rented; the *mishna* here anticipates a scenario where the transaction is taking place in a space that can be rented to establish *kinyan chatzer*.

## Rav Assi Simta

### Rav Assi Position

The *gemara* now introduces a teaching of Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *madad vehiniach al gabei simta kana* — if the seller measured out the grain and placed it in a *simta*, the buyer acquires it. A *simta* is an alleyway or semi-private passage — not a fully public thoroughfare (*reshus harabbim*), but not a privately owned domain either. It is a space in which buyers and sellers have temporary, quasi-private access. This is the location where *meshicha* is effective: in the seller's private domain, *meshicha* does not express the buyer's ownership; in *reshus harabbim*, the transience of the space prevents *meshicha* from conferring stable ownership. But in a *simta*, where both parties have a kind of shared, semi-private right of use, the buyer's *meshicha* is a meaningful assertion of ownership.

Rav Assi's teaching goes further: even without *meshicha*, the seller's act of measuring the grain out and placing it before the buyer in a *simta* is sufficient to finalize the sale. The logic seems to be that when the seller places the grain in the *simta* with intent to transfer ownership, the buyer thereby takes possession of the *simta*'s space as his domain for that grain, without needing to perform any additional act. This is a bold position, since it invokes no classical *kinyan*.

### Rav Zeira Challenge

Rav Zeira challenges Rav Assi: *shema lo shamar Rebbi ella be-moded le-tokh kupato* — perhaps what Rabbi Yochanan actually said was limited to a case where the seller measured the grain into the buyer's own vessels. In that case, the *kinyan* would be explained straightforwardly as *kinyan kli* — acquisition through the buyer's vessel. The buyer's personal vessel, even when located in a *simta*, functions as an extension of the buyer's domain, and placing the grain inside it constitutes a recognized mode of acquisition. Rav Zeira is suggesting that Rabbi Yochanan's teaching is not the bold innovation Rav Assi understood it to be, but simply a well-established application of *kinyan kli* in a *simta* context.

### Rav Assi Rebuttal

Rav Assi responds sharply: *damya lee rabbana ke-lo gamar inish shema'ta* — it seems to me as if this rabbi never properly learned a *daf* of *gemara*. If Rabbi Yochanan were speaking of a case where the seller poured the grain into the buyer's vessels, that would not be a *chidush* worth transmitting at all — it would be the standard *halacha*, since *kinyan kli* in a *simta* is uncontroversial. Rabbi Yochanan's teaching is clearly being cited as a novel ruling; therefore it must address the more challenging scenario, namely, the grain placed directly on the ground of the *simta* without any vessel. Of course Rabbi Yochanan was making a broader statement than Rav Zeira assumed.

## Rabbi Yochanan Contradic…

### Rav Assi Version

Rav Assi's position, then, is that Rabbi Yochanan taught: measuring and placing grain in a *simta* — even directly on the ground, without the buyer's vessels — constitutes a complete *kinyan*. This is the bold reading that Rav Assi was defending with his dismissive reply to Rav Zeira.

### Rav Yaakov Version

The *gemara* now introduces a direct contradiction. Rav Yaakov quotes Rabbi Yochanan to say: *madad v'heniach agabi simta lo kana* — if the seller measured out and placed the grain in a *simta*, the buyer does not acquire. This is the exact opposite ruling, attributed to the exact same authority. *Kashyan ahadadi* — these two statements directly contradict one another. The same scenario — seller measuring grain and placing it in a *simta* — yields acquisition according to Rav Assi's version of Rabbi Yochanan, and no acquisition according to Rav Yaakov's version.

### Resolution Vessels

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: *kan b'moded letoch kuppato kan b'moded al gabi karka* — one statement refers to measuring the grain into the buyer's vessels, and the other to placing it directly on the ground. *Shema minah.* The version that says the buyer acquires — Rav Assi's version — must be speaking of grain poured into the buyer's vessels, where *kinyan kli* applies. The version that says the buyer does not acquire — Rav Yaakov's version — speaks of grain placed directly on the ground, where there is no *kinyan*. This resolution means, importantly, that the *gemara* sides with Rav Zeira's original challenge after all. Despite Rav Assi's confident and dismissive rebuke, measuring grain into a *simta* on the ground does not effect a *kinyan*; Rabbi Yochanan himself taught both sides of the distinction. The *chidush* of Rabbi Yochanan was nothing more than the application of *kinyan kli* to a *simta* setting — precisely what Rav Zeira had proposed.

## Mishna Reinterpretation

### Meshicha Domain Transfer

The *gemara* now turns back to the *mishna* itself to see whether it supports or contradicts the conclusion just reached. The *mishna* states *madad velo mashach lo kana* — measuring without *meshicha* does not finalize the sale. The *gemara* asks: is this *mishna* speaking of a *simta*? If so, it supports the conclusion that measuring alone in a *simta* is insufficient. But the *gemara* initially resists this reading, because if we are in a *simta*, the first clause of the *mishna* — *mashach velo madad kana*, *meshicha* without measuring finalizes the sale — would be unproblematic. The difficulty is that if the *mishna* were set in *reshus harabbim*, *meshicha* would not work there either, which would render the first clause incoherent.

The *gemara* then proposes a reinterpretation: *mai mashach nami d'kasani mereshus harabbim l'simta* — when the *mishna* says *meshicha* works, it means *meshicha* from the *reshus harabbim* into a *simta*. The transaction begins in the public domain; the buyer drags the grain from there into the *simta*, and that transfer of location constitutes the effective *meshicha*. Measuring alone in the *reshus harabbim*, without bringing it into the *simta*, does not work — which is what the *mishna*'s second clause teaches.

### Rental in Private Domain

The *gemara* then addresses the *mishna*'s final case: *im hayah pikeach socher mekomo* — the smart buyer rents the space. If the *mishna* were set in the *reshus harabbim*, the *gemara* objects, there would be nobody to rent from — a public thoroughfare has no owner from whom one could lease a private corner. The very option of rental implies that the space has an identifiable owner. Therefore, the *gemara* reinterprets: *ve'im bi-reshut bealim hi* — this final clause addresses an entirely different scenario, where the goods are located in the private domain of the seller. In that setting, if the buyer wishes to effect a *kinyan* without performing *meshicha* or *hagbahah*, he can rent that space from the owner — the seller — for a moment, thereby converting it into his own domain, and acquire the goods through *kinyan chatzer*.

The upshot is that the straightforward reading of the *mishna* places the entire transaction in a *simta*: *meshicha* works there; measuring alone does not; and the smart buyer may rent the *simta* from those who own it, effecting acquisition through *kinyan chatzer*. This natural reading provides clear support for the *gemara*'s conclusion that measuring grain directly on the ground of a *simta* is insufficient. To avoid treating this as a definitive proof — since the *gemara* wishes to preserve the alternate reading — it offers the strained but possible interpretation that *meshicha* in the *mishna* refers to dragging from *reshus harabbim* into *simta*, and that the rental clause speaks of a separate, *reshus bealim* scenario. The shiur will continue from this point tomorrow.
