# Bava Batra 85

## Kinyan Kli Overview

### Kli as Chatzer

The sugya on daf 85a opens by continuing a discussion carried over from the final lines of 84b concerning *kinyan kli* — the act of acquisition effected by placing an object into the buyer's vessel. The underlying conceptual basis of this *kinyan* is not that the *kli* constitutes an independent mode of transfer, but rather that the buyer's vessel functions as a miniaturized *chatzer*: just as placing an object in someone's domain can effect acquisition, so too does placing it in his vessel, which stands as a surrogate for his personal domain. In the same way that placing goods on a buyer's donkey might effect acquisition, filling the buyer's bag or basket operates on an analogous principle.

### Kli in Reshut Hamocher

This framework immediately generates a sharp question. If the vessel functions as the buyer's *chatzer*, the mechanism depends on the vessel being meaningfully "his" domain at the relevant moment. This works cleanly when the vessel is located in a *simta* — a side alley — or in a *chatzer shel shneihem*, a space belonging to neither party exclusively, since in those settings the buyer has an uncontested right to have his vessel present. The problem intensifies when the vessel sits in the seller's own domain. The seller has, of course, permitted the buyer to set down his bag in the store while the goods are being loaded into it — so the buyer has some right to have the vessel there. Yet the store remains fundamentally the seller's domain, and the goods have not yet left the seller's sphere of control. Has a genuine transfer of possession occurred? This is the central question the *gemara* now pursues: does *kinyan kli* operate when the buyer's vessel is in *reshut hamocher*, the seller's domain?

## Kli in Reshut Harabim

### Rav and Shmuel

The *gemara* opens the formal discussion at the top of 85a with a paired ruling attributed to Rav and Shmuel, who state together: *kelo shel adam koneh lo b'chol makom* — a person's vessel acquires on his behalf anywhere — *chutz mirshut harabim*, except in the public domain. The reason for this exclusion is that in *reshut harabim* one has no right to leave one's vessels on the ground; absent that entitlement, the vessel cannot function as a surrogate domain. Importantly, this formulation of Rav and Shmuel implies that *kinyan kli* would work even in *reshut hamocher*, since the seller does permit the buyer to place his bags in the store — a question the *gemara* will press later.

### Rabbi Yochanan EY Positi…

Against this, Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish — the preeminent *Eretz Yisrael* authorities — state that *kinyan kli* works *afilu birshut harabim*, even in the public domain. On its face, this creates a direct dispute: Rav and Shmuel say it fails in *reshut harabim*; Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish say it succeeds even there. One might speculate whether this *Bavel*–*Eretz Yisrael* divergence reflects genuine differences in how *reshut harabim* functioned practically in those respective societies, though the *gemara* itself does not pursue that line.

### Rav Papa Reconciles

Rav Papa attempts to dissolve the apparent conflict. He proposes that the two schools are not actually arguing: when Rav and Shmuel say *kinyan kli* does not work in *reshut harabim*, they mean a literal, full public thoroughfare. When Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish say it does work in *reshut harabim*, they do not mean it literally — they mean a *simta*, a semi-public alley, and they call it *reshut harabim* only in the loose sense of "not a private domain." On Rav Papa's reading, everyone agrees that in a true *reshut harabim* it does not work, and everyone agrees that in a *simta* it does.

### Gemara's Counter-Proof

The *gemara* questions whether this harmonization can be sustained. A *baraita* is cited in which Rabbi Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kelo shel adam koneh lo b'chol makom sheyesh lo reshut lehanicho* — a person's vessel acquires for him wherever he has the right to place it. The *gemara* reasons from this formulation: if *kinyan kli* operates precisely where one has the *right* to leave one's vessel, then it should fail where one lacks that right — i.e., in *reshut harabim* — and this principle, stated in Rabbi Yochanan's own name, supports the Babylonian reading of his position rather than undermining it.

### No Kli in True RH

The *gemara* therefore concludes — *shema mina* — that *kinyan kli* does not work in a true *reshut harabim* because one lacks the right to deposit vessels there. The question of *hagbahah* is briefly noted as a separate matter: if a person is actually holding or carrying the bag rather than resting it on the ground, that operates as *hagbahah* — lifting — or perhaps as something the *acharonim* would call *kinyan yad*, since the object is directly on one's person. But a bag sitting on the ground in the public domain, unconnected to the buyer's body, cannot effect acquisition.

## Four Categories

### Measure Filling Rule

The *gemara* now introduces a *Tosefta* — introduced with the formula *ta shema* — that enumerates four categories (*arba middos*) relevant to commercial transactions. The first category concerns the measuring process itself. Imagine a buyer purchasing three cups of flour from a seller, who fills a measuring vessel to the three-cup mark. The *Tosefta* states: *ad shelo nismaila hamiddah lamocher* — before the measure is filled to the purchased amount, the goods belong to the seller; *mishenismaila hamiddah lalokeach* — once the measure is filled to that amount, they belong to the buyer.

### Third Party Vessel

The *Tosefta* immediately qualifies this rule: *bameh devarim amurim bemiddah she'einah shel shneihem* — in what circumstances does this apply? When the measuring vessel belongs to neither party, i.e., it was borrowed from a third party. The *gemara* supplies the logic. Since neither the seller nor the buyer owns the vessel, the third party's loan operates sequentially: until the seller completes measuring out the purchased quantity, he is the current user of the borrowed vessel and it functions as his *kli*; once the measure is full, the buyer becomes the current user, and at that moment he acquires the goods by *kinyan kli*. This explains why the transfer occurs precisely at the moment the measure is filled.

### Rishon Rishon Kanah

The *Tosefta* continues: *aval im hayetah middah shel echad mehem — rishon rishon kanah*. But if the measuring vessel belongs to one of the parties, then *rishon rishon kanah* — each successive portion acquires immediately as it is poured in. The Rashbam clarifies the meaning of *kanah* here: it does not signal the completion of a transaction but describes the state of possession. If the vessel belongs to the seller, each increment poured remains in his possession — *kanah* means it stays his — and no *kinyan* has been effected on behalf of the buyer even once the measure is full, since the vessel throughout has been the seller's. If the vessel belongs to the buyer, then each successive portion poured in is immediately acquired by the buyer, since it is entering his vessel. Thus *rishon rishon kanah* captures the buyer's continuous, incremental acquisition as the goods flow in.

This generates a curious question: what is the practical difference if the vessel belongs to the seller versus a third party? If the vessel is the seller's, nothing transfers until the buyer physically removes the goods or performs *hagbahah*. If borrowed from a third party, the transfer occurs automatically at the moment the measure is filled, by *kinyan kli*. This discussion is all preliminary to the central spatial question: where exactly is this transaction taking place?

### Tosefta Domains

The *Tosefta* now becomes directly relevant to the *gemara*'s central inquiry. It specifies the domains in which the above rules operate: *bameh devarim amurim — birshut harabim uvechatzer she'einah shel shneihem*. In what circumstances do these rules apply? In a *reshut harabim* and in a *chatzer* belonging to neither party. *Aval birshut mocher lo kanah* — but in the seller's domain, the buyer does not acquire — *ad she'yagbihennah*, until he lifts it, *o ad she'yotzienu mereshuto*, or takes it out of the seller's domain.

This is a striking *gemara*. The *Tosefta* takes a position that is almost the precise inverse of what the Babylonian *gemara* has been assuming. The Babylonian *gemara* treats *reshut harabim* as the paradigm case where *kinyan kli* fails — precisely because one has no right to leave vessels there. Yet the *Tosefta* says *kinyan kli* works in *reshut harabim*, while it is *reshut hamocher* where it fails. The *Tosefta*'s reasoning can be understood on its own terms: perhaps what matters is not the buyer's formal right to deposit the vessel but whether the goods have left the seller's sphere of control. Once the goods are in the buyer's vessel and no longer under the seller's hand, they are the buyer's — even if the buyer's vessel is technically sitting somewhere it should not be. Conversely, even if the buyer has permission to set his bag down in the seller's store, as long as they remain in the seller's domain they remain fundamentally under the seller's control.

### Reshut Lokeach

The *Tosefta* then addresses *reshut lokeach* — the buyer's own domain. Here, *keivan she'kibel alav mocher — kanah loke'ach*: once the seller has accepted the terms of the sale, the buyer acquires immediately. This is because the goods are already in the buyer's domain and *kinyan chatzer* operates automatically. One might find this somewhat counterintuitive: the usual value of a formal *kinyan* is to identify a concrete, unambiguous moment of transfer, and a simple statement of agreement seems less concrete than a physical act. Yet when the goods are already in the buyer's house — whether because the seller is a traveling merchant who has come to the buyer, or for some other reason — the act of agreement itself, *kibel alav*, is sufficient to trigger *kinyan chatzer*. The *chatzer* of the buyer is already in place; it only awaits the finalization of terms.

A related question arises whether this changes if the goods remain in the seller's own vessels within the buyer's domain. The *gemara* treats the two configurations — buyer's vessel in seller's domain, and seller's vessel in buyer's domain — as parallel and symmetrical. Whatever principle determines acquisition in one case must apply in the other.

### Third Party Domain

The fourth domain addressed in the *Tosefta* is that of a third party — for example, the seller's goods are being stored in David's warehouse, and the buyer wishes to acquire them while they remain there. The *Tosefta* rules: *lo kanah* — the buyer does not acquire — *ad she'kibel alav*, until David accepts upon himself to hold the goods on behalf of the buyer, *o ad she'yischar mekoman* — or until the buyer rents the space from David.

The underlying principle here is essential. If the goods are in the seller's own domain, the seller cannot simply declare "I will now hold these on your behalf" and thereby effect a transfer: one cannot simultaneously be the party relinquishing possession and the party receiving it on behalf of the other side. But if a neutral third party is holding the goods, David can declare that he now holds them for the buyer. This functions on the principle of *zachin l'adam shelo befanav* — one may act to confer benefit on another in his absence. David, as an independent third party, can use his *chatzer* or his *yad* to be *zocheh* on the buyer's behalf, effecting acquisition. This is precisely why *kibel alav* by a third party works, whereas the same declaration by the seller would be meaningless.

The question is raised whether David could, at the outset, make a blanket agreement to hold goods for whichever buyer the seller designates at the time of sale, without needing to know the buyer's identity in advance. This would resemble a form of *breira*, though not quite, since the *kinyan* would not operate retroactively — David would become the buyer's representative only at the moment the seller makes the designation. Such an arrangement might well be valid.

Tosafos and the Rashbam disagree about how exactly to count the "four categories" (*arba middos*). The Rashbam objects that the rules applicable in the seller's domain and in the third party's domain are in practice the same — *hagbahah* and removal work in both — and so they do not constitute genuinely distinct categories. Tosafos responds that there is indeed a difference: in the third party's domain, *kibel alav* by the third party suffices to effect acquisition without any rental or physical act, whereas in the seller's domain no such declaration by the seller can work. It is this difference that justifies treating them as four distinct categories.

The *gemara* returns to the *Tosefta*'s most significant ruling for the current discussion: *kinyan kli* works in *reshut harabim* and in a *chatzer she'einah shel shneihem*, but not in *reshut hamocher*. The *gemara* attempts to reread *reshut harabim* here as meaning merely "not a fully private domain," i.e., a *simta* shared by both parties — *she'einah shel echad mehem ella shel shneihem* — rather than a literal public thoroughfare. Similarly, *chatzer she'einah shel shneihem* is reread to mean *chatzer shel shneihem*, a jointly held space. This is a frankly forced reading. The *Tosefta* compares *reshut harabim* and *chatzer she'einah shel shneihem* in a way that implies they share the quality of not being either party's private domain — which would suggest a true *reshut harabim* is meant. Nevertheless, the Babylonian *gemara* insists on the reread, maintaining its position that *kinyan kli* does not work in a genuine *reshut harabim*. The *Eretz Yisrael* tradition — represented by Rabbi Yochanan, Reish Lakish, and apparently this *Tosefta* — seems to hold the opposite view, that once goods are in the buyer's vessel and outside the seller's control, the buyer acquires them regardless of whether he had a formal right to leave his vessel in that location. The Babylonian *gemara* rejects this position and rereads all the supporting evidence to conform to its own view.

## Gittin Case Analysis

### Get in Basket

Having set aside the *Tosefta* evidence, the *gemara* turns to a case from *Gittin* as a potential proof for the question of *kinyan kli* in *reshut hamocher*. The case: a husband throws a *get* into his wife's *cheikah* — her lap — or into her *kaltah* (basket; the word appears to be of Greek origin), while she is standing in his house. The ruling is *harei zu megureshset* — she is validly divorced. The implicit logic is that if the *get* lands in the wife's basket and takes effect as a valid delivery, then the wife's vessel must be considered her domain — her *reshut* — even while it sits in the husband's house. And if *kinyan kli* works in this way for *gittin*, it should likewise work for commercial transactions: the buyer's vessel in the seller's domain should be considered the buyer's domain, and the goods placed into it should be acquired.

The connection between *gittin* and *kinyanim* rests on a shared underlying question: whose domain is the object considered to be in? The *pasuk* instructs *venatan beyadah* — he shall place it in her hand — and the *gemara* on *gittin* extends this to include her *chatzer*, her roof, her enclosure, and her basket. The mechanism in both *gittin* and commercial *kinyanim* thus reduces to the same inquiry: does the wife's basket in the husband's house constitute *her* domain for these purposes?

### Suspension and Tie

Rav Nachman immediately deflates this proof, noting that this question was raised and thoroughly addressed in the tractate of *Gittin* itself — so thoroughly that the expression *demachla me'ah*, "they knocked it down a hundred times," is used. Several answers were proposed there, each of which explains the *gittin* ruling on grounds that do not extend to the general case of *kinyan kli* in *reshut hamocher*.

The first explanation, attributed to Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *pashita kaltah teluyah bah* — the case is obvious if the basket is suspended from her body. If the basket hangs from her person rather than resting on the ground, it is effectively an extension of her body, analogous to *hagbahah* or to *kinyan yad*. In that circumstance it is not a case of *kinyan kli* in the ordinary sense at all — it is more like the object being placed directly on her person. Reish Lakish adds: *keshurah* — even if the basket is merely tied to her body without being lifted off the ground, it is considered sufficiently connected to her person to effect the transfer. The question of whether being tied to a person while resting on the ground constitutes *hagbahah* or a distinct form of *kinyan yad* is left open, but either way these cases are distinguishable from the general question of a free-standing *kli* in someone else's domain.

### Mekom Cheika Kanuy

Rabbi Yochanan offers his own formulation: *mekom cheika kanuy lah, mekom kaltah kanuy lah* — the place of her lap is acquired by her, the place of her basket is acquired by her. This is a more expansive principle, going beyond the technical question of suspension or attachment.

### Rava's Explanation

Rava explains the rationale behind Rabbi Yochanan's principle: *ein adam makpid lo al mekom cheikah velo al mekom kaltah* — a husband is simply not particular about where his wife sits or where she places her basket. This non-particularity amounts to an ongoing, de facto grant of rights to that space. The wife therefore has a genuine, continuous entitlement to the space her lap and basket occupy within the household — not a momentary permission like that extended to a customer in a store, but something more like an enduring proprietary right.

This distinction is critical for understanding why the *gittin* case cannot simply be transplanted into the commercial setting. In a store, a seller permits a customer to set down a bag for the brief duration of a transaction, but this is a purely temporary and instrumental accommodation. The seller remains fundamentally in control of the space and the goods; the customer's bag is there for a moment. By contrast, a wife in her husband's home has an ongoing, ambient right to the space she occupies, so much so that the husband is not *makpid* — not even mildly asserting his ownership over that particular patch of floor. Because of this ongoing entitlement, her basket can be considered to be in her domain in a substantive sense.

### Gittin Distinction

The *gemara* therefore concludes that the *gittin* case cannot prove *kinyan kli* in *reshut hamocher* for commercial transactions. The circumstances are categorically different: either the basket in *gittin* is suspended or tied to her body (making it effectively *hagbahah* or *kinyan yad*), or she has an ongoing proprietary right to the space (not merely a customer's transient permission), or both. None of these conditions obtain in the typical commercial scenario, so no proof can be drawn.

## Tosefta Evidence

### Tosefta Simple Read

The *gemara* returns to what seems the most straightforward source: the *Tosefta* itself, which states explicitly — *birshut mocher lo kanah ad she'yagbihenu o ad she'yotzienu mereshuto* — that in the seller's domain the buyer does not acquire until the goods are lifted or removed from that domain. The simple reading of this *Tosefta* is transparent: it does not matter that the goods may be sitting in the buyer's vessel; as long as they remain in the seller's domain, the buyer has not acquired them. Only *hagbahah* or physical removal from the seller's domain suffices to complete the transaction. This apparently settles the question of *kinyan kli* in *reshut hamocher* — it simply does not work.

### Gemara Challenge

But the *gemara* resists this conclusion and probes the *Tosefta* for internal consistency. The challenge arises from the *Tosefta*'s ruling on *reshut lokeach*: in the buyer's domain, once the seller accepts the terms (*kibel alav mocher*), the buyer acquires. If the *Tosefta* is uniformly discussing cases where the goods are in the seller's vessels, then why does *kinyan chatzer* of the buyer work in his domain — after all, the goods are still in the seller's bags? If the reasoning is that it is the seller's *kli* that matters and not the domain, then the buyer's *chatzer* should be irrelevant. If the reasoning is that the domain determines acquisition, then being in the seller's *kli* within the buyer's domain should not undermine *kinyan chatzer*. The *gemara* is pressing the point that the two principles — domain-based acquisition and vessel-based acquisition — cannot both be operative simultaneously without contradiction.

### Goes by Reshut

The *gemara* resolves this by stepping back and concluding that the *Tosefta* is in fact entirely domain-based (*reshut*), not *kli*-based. The reason the *Tosefta* produces consistent results across all four cases is not that we are tracking whose *kli* the goods are in, but simply whose domain they are in. The *Tosefta* simply assumes, as a matter of practical reality, that goods in the seller's store are typically in the seller's vessels, and goods in the buyer's home are typically in the buyer's vessels — *stama demilta, bei mocher mani democher shechichei, bei loke'ach mani delokeach shechichei* — in the seller's premises, the available containers are the seller's; in the buyer's premises, the available containers are the buyer's. The whole rule goes by *reshut*, and the mention of *kelim* is incidental to the typical circumstance in each location. This is a notably forced reading, since the *Tosefta* nowhere says anything about whose *kli* it is — but the *gemara* maintains that the *Tosefta*'s principle is domain-based, and that the question of *kinyan kli* independent of domain remains open.

## Donkey Proof

### Pirkan Setup

Rava introduces a new attempt to resolve the question, drawing on a *baraita* concerning a seller's donkeys loaded with goods. The case: the buyer leads the seller's donkey-drivers and their donkeys — laden with bags of apples — into the buyer's house. On its face, this might seem to constitute *meshichah* — the pulling or drawing that effects *kinyan* on movable goods — but the *gemara* notes that the buyer did not perform *meshichah* directly on the apples; he pulled the donkeys, not the apples themselves, and perhaps only guided the donkey-drivers rather than the donkeys. Moreover, even if one argued for *meshichah* on the donkeys, the goods on the donkeys' backs may not be affected. Similarly, while the goods have now entered the buyer's domain, they remain on the backs of the seller's donkeys — not resting in the buyer's space independently — and so *kinyan chatzer* may not apply either. The *baraita* then addresses the case of *pirkan* — where the donkeys have been unloaded and the bags now sit in the buyer's house.

### Pesak and Madad

The *baraita* introduces a distinction based on *gemirut da'at* — finality of intent. If the price has been established (*pasak*) but the goods have not yet been measured (*madad*), or if the goods have been measured but no price established, then even after the donkeys are unloaded into the buyer's house, *shneihem yecholim lachzor bahen* — either party may retract, because there is no *gemirut da'at*. However, if both a price has been agreed upon and the goods have been brought into the buyer's domain via *pirkan*, then *ein shneihem yecholim lachzor bahen* — neither party may retract. The *kinyan chatzer* is complete once there is both *gemirut da'at* (established price) and physical entry into the buyer's domain. The measurement need not be complete for the *kinyan* to take effect; what matters is that both parties have committed to the transaction with sufficient finality.

### Chatzer Proof

The crucial implication of the *pirkan* case is that once the goods have been unloaded into the buyer's house — even though they remain in the seller's bags — the sale becomes final. This appears to be a direct proof that *kinyan chatzer* operates according to the domain, not the vessel: the goods are in the seller's bags (*kelav delokeach* in the buyer's *reshut*), and yet the buyer acquires. If *kinyan kli* in the buyer's domain could be undermined by the fact that the goods remain in the seller's vessel, then the *baraita* would not rule that the buyer acquires at *pirkan*. The case thus appears to demonstrate symmetrically that it is the domain that controls, not the *kli*.

### Gemara Defenses

The *gemara* refuses to accept this proof and offers two defensive readings. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes that *pirkan* — "he unloaded" — means the seller literally poured out the apples, emptying them directly onto the floor of the buyer's house, so there are no seller's bags involved at all. Rava objects sharply: the *baraita* uses the word *pirkan*, not *shafchan* — it says he unloaded, not that he dumped or poured out. *Pirkan* implies removing the bags from the donkeys while the goods remain inside them; the bags are still present. The *gemara* then offers a second defense, attributed to Mar bar Rav Ashi: the case involves *matachli detuma* — strings or braids of garlic, which were typically not packed in bags at all but carried loosely or braided together directly on the donkey's back. Since garlic was sold and transported in this form without bags, *pirkan* in this context means simply unloading the garlic strands onto the buyer's floor — and since there were never any bags, the proof says nothing about what happens when the seller's vessels are present. The question of *kinyan kli* in *reshut hamocher* thus remains unresolved, and the *gemara* leaves it open for the continuation of the sugya.

# Bava Batra 86

## Vessels & Price

### Intro & Baraita

Daf 86 opens eight lines into the page, completing a discussion carried over from the previous daf. The *baraita* under examination deals with donkey drivers or workers carrying loads into the buyer's house: at what point does the buyer acquire the merchandise? The broader question, which occupied the preceding discussion, concerns *keilo shel lokei'ach birshut mocher* — whether the buyer's vessels effect a *kinyan* while still in the seller's domain. The present *baraita* adds a further condition, one that at first glance seems puzzling: the sale is only final once the price has been set.

### Price & Kinyan

Huna bar Rav Sheshes poses this difficulty to Ravina. The *baraita* specifies that once the merchandise has been unloaded — *pirkan katani* — the goods are in the buyer's domain. Given that, why should it matter whether the price has been set? If the *kinyan* is taking effect, and the goods are no longer on the worker but in the buyer's possession, what difference does *psak* — price-setting — make?

Ravina's response is crisp: *pasak, samcha daatei; lo pasak, lo samcha daatei.* Once the price is fixed, the buyer's mind is settled and his intent to purchase is final. Without a set price, the seller might yet demand more, or the buyer might offer less — neither party has truly committed to the transaction. Even if the physical act of *kinyan* is underway, the absence of a settled price means the transaction lacks the mental finality required for *kinyan* to take hold.

### Rav & Shmuel

Ravina then turns to Rav Ashi and invites him to consider a related source. Rav and Shmuel both say: *keilo shel adam koneh lo b'chol makom* — a person's vessel acquires for him in any location. The phrase *b'chol makom* seems to resolve the question directly: does it not come to include even the seller's domain? If so, *keilo shel lokei'ach* works even *birshut mocher* without any additional condition.

### Seller Permission

The *Gemara* rejects this reading. The phrase *b'chol makom* applies, but only where the seller has explicitly said *zil kani* — "go, take possession." This is a significant ruling. The reason the buyer's vessel does not automatically acquire in the seller's domain is that the merchandise is still perceived as being under the seller's control, effectively within his sphere. If, however, the seller actively relinquishes that control by telling the buyer to take possession now, the vessel of the buyer will work. The seller's utterance of *zil kani* is what removes the impediment. This is the *Gemara*'s conclusion regarding *keilo shel lokei'ach birshut mocher*: the buyer's vessel does not acquire in the seller's domain unless the seller grants explicit permission through the declaration *zil kani*.

---

## Meshicha Debate

### Chattels via Meshicha

The *Gemara* now pivots to a new topic, introduced by the phrase *tnan hatam* — "we learned elsewhere." The *Mishnah* in Kiddushin establishes that real property — *nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayut* — is acquired through money, document, or *chazaka*, while *metaltelin*, chattel, is acquired only through *meshicha*, dragging. The *Mishnah*'s formulation seems to make *meshicha* the sole *kinyan* for all chattels.

### Hagbaha vs Meshicha

This universal rule, however, was significantly qualified by a teaching transmitted in the academies. In Sura it was taught in the name of Rav Chisda; in Pumbedita, in the name of Rav Kahana, with some attributing it to Rava. The teaching limits the applicability of *meshicha*: *lo shanu ela devarim she-ein darkan lehagbiya* — *meshicha* is effective only for objects not normally lifted, objects heavy enough that dragging is their natural mode of handling. For such objects, the act of dragging is the meaningful expression of taking possession. But *aval devarim she-darkan lehagbiya behagbahah in bemeshikhah lo* — for objects normally lifted, only *hagbahah*, lifting, constitutes a valid *kinyan*; *meshicha* does not suffice. The reasoning is that for a light, easily portable object, picking it up is the genuine demonstration of ownership. Dragging such an object carries none of that significance.

### Wallet Theft

Abaye was in the midst of teaching this ruling when Rav Adda bar Matna raised an objection from a *baraita* concerning the principle of *kam lei bid'raba minei*. That principle holds that when a single act simultaneously incurs both a monetary liability and a criminal penalty — such as lashes or death — the heavier penalty overrides the monetary obligation, and the offender is exempt from financial restitution.

The *baraita* applies this principle to a case of stealing a wallet on *Shabbat*. If someone steals a wallet and carries it out into *reshut ha-rabim*, he is nevertheless *chayav* to pay for the theft, because the two liabilities do not coincide in time: *she-kvar nit-chayev bi-gneivah kodem she-ba lidei issur Shabbat*. The act of *gneivah* is defined by the moment of *kinyan*, which occurs when he lifts the wallet — *hagbahah* — while still inside the owner's house. The *chiyuv Shabbat*, the Shabbat violation, is only triggered when he crosses the threshold from the private domain into *reshut ha-rabim*. Since the two occur at different moments, *kam lei bid'raba minei* does not apply, and the thief must pay.

However, if the thief was dragging the wallet — *haya mgarer ve-yotze* — sliding it along the ground from inside the house until it crossed into *reshut ha-rabim*, then he is *patur* from paying: *she-harei issur Shabbat u-gneivah ba'in ke-echad*, the Shabbat violation and the act of *gneivah* coincide. He has not performed *hagbahah* at any earlier point; it is only when the wallet crosses from the *reshut ha-yachid* into *reshut ha-rabim* that both the *meshicha* (completing the acquisition for *gneivah*) and the Shabbat violation occur simultaneously.

One might wonder how *meshicha* is possible in *reshut ha-rabim*, since *meshicha* requires a domain suitable for *kinyan*. The *Gemara* addresses this: the dragging occurred in the *simta*, the alleyway alongside the public thoroughfare, which is treated as *reshut ha-rabim* for Shabbat purposes but as a valid domain for *kinyan* purposes.

The challenge this presents to Abaye's teaching is pointed: *ve-ha kis de-bar hagbahah hu* — a wallet is precisely the kind of object that one normally lifts up, yet the *baraita* treats *meshicha* as an effective *kinyan* for it. Abaye responds: *be-mista* — he was speaking of a case involving a rope. Rav Adda counters that a rope changes nothing if the wallet itself is the kind of object normally lifted. Abaye then clarifies: *be-midi de-ba'ei mista* — he means a bag so large and heavy that it requires a rope to drag, not a simple wallet at all. This is admittedly a forced *okimta*; the plain reading of the *baraita* is clearly a wallet. But Abaye's position is that *meshicha* is effective only for things not naturally lifted, and the case must be read accordingly.

### Different Objects

A second challenge comes from a different direction. The *baraita* dealing with acquisition in the seller's domain states: *birshut mocher lo kana ad sheyigbihena o ad sheyotziena meirshuto* — the buyer does not acquire until he either lifts the item or removes it from the seller's domain. This seems to present a single object that can be acquired through either *hagbahah* or *meshicha* — two *kinyanim* applicable to the same item — which would undermine the distinction between naturally-lifted objects (only *hagbahah*) and naturally-dragged objects (only *meshicha*).

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this: *letzitadin katani* — the *baraita* is not presenting two options for the same object. It is speaking in a bifurcated fashion: *meidi debar hagbaha behagbaha, meidi debar meshicha bemeshicha* — things naturally lifted are acquired by *hagbahah*, and things naturally dragged are acquired by *meshicha*. The two clauses of the *baraita* address two different kinds of objects.

The *Rashbam* notes that one might have resolved the difficulty differently: perhaps the *baraita* speaks of a naturally-dragged object, and the teaching is that even such an object can be acquired through *hagbahah*, since lifting is always a meaningful expression of ownership. The *Gemara* does not pursue this reading, but the *Rashbam* acknowledges its theoretical plausibility — particularly given the assumption that *hagbahah* always works. Regardless, the *Gemara*'s chosen answer stands: different objects, not different options for the same object.

### Produce Cases

The *Gemara* continues to test this framework. The *Mishnah* discusses *hamocher perot lechavero* — one who sells produce to a friend — and states that *meshicha* effects the *kinyan* even before measuring. The *Gemara* observes that produce is the sort of thing one normally lifts, and yet the *Mishnah* says *meshicha* works. How does this square with the teaching that objects normally lifted require *hagbahah*?

The *Gemara* resolves this with a contextual qualification: *hacha bemai askinan beshlifi ravrevi* — the *Mishnah* is dealing with large sacks, quantities so heavy that lifting is impractical. When it is a matter of a massive sack of produce, *meshicha* is the natural act, and therefore *meshicha* effects the *kinyan*.

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge from the *seifa*, the latter clause of the *Mishnah*, which distinguishes produce from flax: *halokeach pishtan mechavero lo kana ad sheyitaltlenu mimmakom zeh lemmakom acher* — one who purchases flax does not acquire until he moves it from one place to another. If both the produce case and the flax case involve large sacks — as the *Gemara* just established for produce — the contrast is difficult to explain. The *Gemara* asks: *atu pishta bi-shifa rabba mi lo avdi?* Can one not make large bundles of flax as well?

The *Gemara* answers: *shani pishta de-mishtamet* — flax is different in character; it frays or slips apart and cannot be gathered into large, consolidated sacks the way grain can. Therefore flax comes only in small bundles that are natural to pick up. The *Rashbam* explains that because flax only comes in small quantities, it is necessarily of the kind that one normally lifts — and therefore *meshicha* does not apply. The phrase *motzi mi-makom zeh le-makom acher* in the *Mishnah*, which one might have read as describing a more complete form of *meshicha*, is here reinterpreted: it means *hagbahah*, lifting and relocating. The two clauses of the *Mishnah* are thus distinguishing not between simple *meshicha* and complete displacement, but between large bags of produce (acquired by *meshicha*) and small bundles of flax (which require *hagbahah*).

### Animal Acquisition

Ravina raises one further challenge to Rav Ashi. A *Mishnah* in Kiddushin states: *behema gassa nikneit bi-mesira ve-ha-dakka be-hagbah divrei Rabbi Meir* — a large animal such as a cow or horse is acquired through *mesira*, handing over the reins, while a small animal is acquired through *hagbahah*, lifting, according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. The *Chachamim*, however, say: *behema dakka bi-meshicha* — a small animal may be acquired through *meshicha*, dragging.

The challenge is clear: a small animal is something one can lift, yet according to the *Chachamim* it may be acquired through *meshicha*. The *Gemara* defends the framework: *shani behema de-sarcha* — an animal is different, because it clings to the ground. The rule that naturally-lifted objects require *hagbahah* and not *meshicha* applies to objects where lifting is the most natural and easy act. An animal that resists, braces, and is difficult to lift is not in that category — leading or dragging it is the more natural act. This may in fact be the very point of the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim*: Rabbi Meir holds that even for a small animal, where *hagbahah* is possible, it is required; the *Chachamim* hold that since an animal naturally resists being lifted, *meshicha* suffices.

---

## Sale Finality

### Kor Lump Sum

The *Gemara* turns to a new ruling of Rav and Shmuel, who both say: *kor bi-shloshim ani mocher lach* — if a seller says "I am selling you a *kor* for thirty dollars," stated as a lump sum, then *yachol lachzor bo afilu ba-se'ah achrona* — either party may retract even when twenty-nine of the thirty *se'ah* have been measured. A *kor* contains thirty *se'ah*. When the sale is framed as a single unit — a *kor* for thirty dollars — the unit of sale is the entire *kor*, and until the full thirty *se'ah* have been delivered, the object of the sale has not yet been fully transferred. The *kinyan* is not complete on any partial amount. This is analogous to selling an apple and a pear together for a dollar: acquiring the apple alone does not complete the purchase, since the deal was structured as a combined unit. As the *Rashbam* notes, this differs from a case where the object is fully identified but unmeasured — there, if the buyer knows what he is purchasing, measurement is merely administrative, and the sale stands. Here, the delivery of the full *kor* is itself constitutive of the transaction.

### Per-Unit Pricing

The contrast case follows. If the seller instead says *kor bishloshim se'ah besela ani mocher lecha* — "I am selling you a *kor*, thirty *se'ah* for a *sela* each" — then *rishon rishon kanah*: each *se'ah* as it is measured becomes a separate completed sale. By identifying the price per *se'ah*, the seller has made each *se'ah* a discrete unit of transaction. As each *se'ah* is measured into the buyer's vessel, it is acquired independently and the sale on that unit is final.

### Vessel Ownership

The *Gemara* now draws on a *baraita* that was introduced earlier in the tractate, dealing with *arba midot bemochrin* — four cases of sellers — and the role of the measuring vessel. The *baraita* established that when the measuring cup belongs to a third party, acquisition depends on the vessel being fully filled. But if the measuring cup belongs to the buyer, *im hayetah midah shel echad meihem rishon rishon kanah* — the buyer acquires each portion as it enters the vessel, even before the vessel is filled.

The *Gemara* then notes: *ve'af al gav dela nitmala hamidah* — it works even before the measuring vessel is full. This might seem to contradict the rule of Rav and Shmuel, which holds that a lump-sum *kor* sale is not final until the last *se'ah*. The *Gemara* resolves the apparent tension.

### Sub-Unit Pricing

The *Gemara* explains that the *baraita* is dealing with a specific formulation: *kegon de'amar leh hin bishneim asar log besela ani mocher lecha* — where the seller said "I am selling you a *hin* for twelve *sela*, one *sela* per *log*." In this framing, each *log* has been priced as an independent unit. Therefore, as each *log* of the *hin* flows into the measuring cup and reaches each gradation mark, the buyer acquires that unit. The *Gemara* concludes by invoking a statement of Rav Kahana: just as Rav Kahana noted in a related context that measuring vessels had gradation marks — *shenatot hayu bahen* — so too here the measuring cup has marked lines. When the price has been specified per sub-unit, and the vessel bears gradations corresponding to those units, each level reached constitutes a separate completed sale. It is the combination of per-unit pricing and identifiable sub-units that transforms what would otherwise be a single reversible transaction into a series of individually finalized ones.

---

---

# Bava Batra 87

## Rav & Shmuel: Sale Compl…

### When Sale Finalized

The daf opens by picking up a statement of Rav and Shmuel introduced at the end of 86b. Their ruling distinguishes between two ways of framing a grain sale. If a seller says, "I am selling you a *kor* for thirty dollars," the transaction is treated as a single unit, and the sale is not final until the entire *kor* has been measured out. But if the seller says, "I am selling you a *kor* for thirty dollars — one dollar per *se'ah*" — explicitly naming both the aggregate and the sub-unit — then each *se'ah* constitutes an implicit separate sale, and the sale of each *se'ah* becomes final as it is measured out. This distinction was already challenged at the end of the previous day's learning and resolved: a formulation that highlights the sub-unit treats each piece individually, while a formulation focused on the whole *kor* treats it as a single undivided transaction.

### Worker Hiring Braita

The *gemara* now introduces a *braita* that appears to cut in the opposite direction — suggesting that a transaction is always viewed as a unified whole rather than as a series of sub-units. The *braita* discusses the hiring of workers before the harvest season. At harvest time, demand for labor is extremely high; a worker can command a *sela* per day, which equals four *dinar*. Months before the harvest, however, a worker who needs money now might agree to work during the upcoming harvest for only a *dinar* a day — a quarter of the standard wage — in exchange for being paid in advance. The *braita* rules that such an arrangement is *assur l'hanot mimenu*: the employer may not derive benefit from it, meaning the deal is not valid. The concern is a form of *ribbit*: money is given now, and repayment — in the form of labor — comes later, at a time when that labor is worth significantly more. Even though this is not a formal loan, *rabanan* recognized that analogous quasi-*ribbit* arrangements, sometimes called *avak ribbit*, can be prohibited at a rabbinic level.

The *braita* then permits a different scenario: if the employer hires the worker today, one month before the harvest, and the work begins immediately — paying him a *dinar* per day for a two-month period covering both pre-harvest and harvest labor — this is permissible. Because work commences right away, the payment and the labor begin simultaneously; there is no gap between money given and work rendered.

The *gemara* then presses: but if we follow Rav and Shmuel's principle that when a price per sub-unit is specified, each sub-unit is a separate transaction, then each day of labor should be its own separate deal. In that case, the employer is paying the worker now for harvest-season days that the worker will only "repay" through labor later, when that labor is worth four times as much. This should be *agar natar lei* — giving money now in exchange for something returned later at greater value, the classic structure of usurious lending. How, then, can the *braita* permit it merely because work starts immediately?

### Agar Natar: Work Timing

The *gemara* articulates the concern precisely: *ve-ha agar natar lei hu* — this is payment now for a deferred and more valuable return. If each day is a separate unit of hire, then the thirty days of harvest-season labor are being paid for in advance at well below their going rate, and this looks structurally identical to a usurious loan.

### Rava: No Fixed Labor Val…

Rava intervenes with a fundamental reframing. He asks: *zilzulei bi-sechirut mi asar?* — who ever said that a person is forbidden from renting themselves out cheaply? There is no *halacha* that fixes a market rate for labor, and therefore there is no objective sense in which the worker is returning something "worth more" than what he received. This is the crucial distinction between labor and goods. With goods, *halachot* of *ona'ah* — overcharging — establish that there is an objectively recognized fair market price. Deviating significantly from that price has *halachic* consequences. But with hired labor, *halacha* makes no such claim. A worker is entirely free to rent himself out at whatever price he chooses, and an employer is free to hire at whatever rate the worker accepts.

The Rashbam explains Rava's position accordingly: because *halacha* does not recognize any fixed objective value for labor, there is no formal *agar natar* problem. The worker is not returning something objectively worth more; the market rate may be higher, but *halacha* takes no notice of it in the context of labor. Therefore, even if each day were treated as a separate unit, there is no real usury problem.

If so, however, why does the *braita* forbid the first case at all? The *gemara* answers: *reisha dela ka'avid be-hedeih — mehashtah michzei ke-agar natar lei*. In the first scenario, where the work does not begin until the harvest season — months after the money was paid — the transaction *looks* like a loan with *ribbit*: money now, a significant pause, then repayment later when the going rate for that repayment is much higher. Even though there is no objective *agar natar* problem given that labor has no fixed *halachic* value, it has the *appearance* of one. By contrast, in the second scenario — *seifa de-ka'avid behedeya — mehashtah lo mechzi ke-agar natar lei* — when work begins immediately, even though each day may technically be a distinct unit, the optics are completely different. Money and labor flow together from the start, and there is no visual break that makes it resemble a usurious loan.

The operative distinction, then, is entirely about *appearance* rather than objective legal reality. Rava concedes that there is no true *agar natar* either way, because labor has no fixed *halachic* value. What the *braita* is prohibiting and permitting is not based on objective economic analysis but on how the transaction presents itself. When the break in time is stark — money now, work only later — it looks too much like *ribbit* even if technically it is not. When work begins immediately, that appearance dissolves.

---

## Flax & Chazakah

### Pulling Flax: Full Acqui…

The final clause of the *mishna* states: *ve-im hayah mechubar la-karka ve-talash kol she-hu kanah* — if the flax being sold was still attached to the ground, then as soon as the buyer rips up even a tiny amount, he acquires all of the flax he is purchasing. This is striking: pulling up a small piece of flax that is still rooted in the earth somehow effects acquisition of all the remaining flax, which is also still rooted in the earth. What *kinyan* has the buyer performed on the flax he has not yet touched?

### Rav Sheshet: Kinyan Chaz…

Rav Sheshet explains: *hacha be-mai askinan de-amar lei leich yafei lach karka kol she-hu u-knei kol mah she-aleha* — the owner says to the buyer: "Go, improve the land slightly, and thereby take possession of everything growing from it." The pulling up of the flax is not being conceptualized as *hagbahah* — lifting — on the flax itself. Rather, it is conceptualized as an act of improvement performed on the land. Plucking flax advances the preparation of the ground, whether for threshing or for the next stage of cultivation. That act of improvement constitutes a *kinyan chazakah* on the land — the recognized mode of acquiring real property by performing a beneficial act upon it — and through that *chazakah* the buyer acquires all the flax growing from it.

### Rashbam vs. Tosafot

The Rashbam and Tosafot offer two distinct explanations of precisely how this works. The Rashbam holds that flax attached to the ground has the *halachic* status of *karka* — land itself. Just as one can acquire land through *chazakah*, one can acquire the flax through *chazakah* because the flax is treated as an extension of the land. The buyer performs a *kinyan* that works on *karka*, and since the flax is *karka*, the *kinyan* takes effect on all of it.

Tosafot raises a difficulty with this: the *chazakah* is being performed on the dirt, not on the individual stalks of flax, and each stalk is arguably a distinct unit. How does a *chazakah* on the soil extend to the flax? Tosafot therefore proposes a different mechanism: by performing the act of improvement, the buyer acquires a degree of rights over the land underneath the flax — not a full *kinyan*, but sufficient to constitute the land as his *reshus*, his domain. Once the land qualifies as his *reshus*, it effects acquisition of the flax growing from it through the mechanism of *kinyan chatzer* — acquisition through one's domain. The buyer's ownership of the land then ceases, but the flax has already been acquired.

---

## Wine & Oil: Possessi (II)

### Filled Vessel = Possessi…

The next *mishna* addresses the sale of wine and oil — liquids that are viscous and adhere to the sides of vessels — and asks when the sale becomes final. The *mishna* rules: *im ad shelo nismala hamida lamoicher, mishenismala hamida lalokeiach* — as long as the measuring vessel has not been completely filled, the wine or oil belongs to the seller; once it is full, it passes to the buyer.

This ruling, as the *gemara* will explain, corresponds to a *braita* taught earlier and presupposes that the vessel belongs to neither buyer nor seller but to a third party. The seller retains ownership or rights of use while the vessel is being filled; once full, those rights transfer to the buyer, who then effects *kinyan* through the vessel.

### Middleman: Purchase or C…

The *mishna* adds: *ve-im haya sarsur beineihem, nishbera hachavis nishbera lasarsur* — if there was a middleman between seller and buyer, and the barrel broke, the loss falls on the middleman.

The Rashbam and Tosafot dispute the underlying model. The Rashbam understands the middleman to be a buyer in the full sense: he purchases from the original producer and then sells to the end consumer. He is not acting on consignment. The *mishna*'s statement that the barrel's loss falls on him follows directly — he owns it, so he bears the risk.

Tosafot objects: if the *mishna* were simply establishing that the middleman buys outright, why would it choose the specific case of a broken barrel rather than addressing far more consequential questions, such as whether the middleman is exposed to price fluctuations or when payment is due? These would seem to be far more significant implications of outright ownership. Tosafot therefore argues the opposite: the standard arrangement described by the *mishna* is consignment. If so, why does the barrel's loss fall on the middleman? Because Tosafot reads the *mishna* as holding the middleman liable for negligence — he is responsible for ensuring that the barrel is sound, and if it breaks, that reflects his failure of care. The framework is not about ownership at all, but about responsibility. As Tosafot frames it, the middleman does not own the goods; he is entrusted with them, and his liability arises from his duty of care, not from title.

---

## Oil Measures & Drops

### Three Drops Rule

Continuing with matters of accurate measurement, the *mishna* states: *ve-chayav lehatif lo shalosh tipin* — when measuring out oil for a buyer, the seller is obligated to add three extra drops. This compensates for the oil's viscosity: after what appears to be a full measure has been poured out, oil continues to cling to the interior walls of the measuring vessel. Waiting for three drops to drip off after the main flow ceases — or adding three drops directly to the buyer's vessel — is the recognized way of ensuring the buyer receives his full measure, given the practical impossibility of capturing every last trace of oil.

### Inclined Vessel: Seller…

The *mishna* further rules: *harchina u-mitzetz harei shel mocher* — if the seller inclines the measuring vessel and oil still remains adhering to the inner walls, that residual oil belongs to the seller. Even though a full measured quantity was poured, the fraction left clinging to the vessel walls is not required to be delivered. The practical reasoning is that waiting for every last drop to be extracted would be excessively time-consuming, and *halacha* does not impose that burden. The seller keeps what remains on the walls.

The *mishna* adds two further qualifications. A storekeeper — *chanvani* — is not obligated to provide even the three drops, given the volume of transactions he conducts; we do not demand that level of precision from him under those conditions. Rabbi Yehuda rules that on *Erev Shabbos* as darkness approaches, the storekeeper is exempt — a point the *gemara* will return to in order to determine whether Rabbi Yehuda is relaxing the standard for ordinary sellers (disagreeing with the *tanna kamma* who requires three drops) or restricting the storekeeper's blanket exemption (disagreeing with the majority who exempt the storekeeper entirely).

---

## Wine & Oil: Possessi (II)

### Vessel Ownership Question

The *gemara* probes the rationale behind the *mishna*'s rule that the sale of wine or oil becomes final only upon the vessel being filled. It asks: *hamida d'man* — whose vessel is this? If it belongs to the buyer, then everything poured into it should belong to the buyer from the first drop — why should the seller retain ownership until the vessel is full? And if it belongs to the seller, then even after it is full the seller should retain ownership — why does the *mishna* say the buyer takes possession upon filling?

### Rabbi Elazar: Middleman'…

Rabbi Elazar resolves this: *b'midas sirsur* — the vessel belongs to the middleman, who is lending its use to both parties. As in the *braita* cited earlier, there is an implicit understanding governing the use of this third-party vessel: the seller holds rights to it and its contents while it is being filled, and those rights transfer to the buyer once it is full.

The *gemara* then raises a difficulty from the *mishna* itself: the *mishna*'s next clause (*ve-im haya sirsur beineihem*) introduces the middleman as a new case — implying that the first case does not involve a middleman at all. How, then, can Rabbi Elazar say the first case involves the middleman's vessel? The *gemara* resolves this: in the first case the middleman is present only as the owner of the vessel, lending it passively without playing any active role in the transaction. In the second case the middleman is actively involved — functioning either, according to the Rashbam, as the actual purchaser who resells to the end buyer, or, according to Tosafot, as a consignee responsible for the goods' safety. It is only when the middleman plays this active role that the *mishna* addresses his liability for the barrel's loss.

---

## Oil Measures & Drops (II)

### Rabbi Elazar's Inquiry

When Rabbi Elazar traveled to *Eretz Yisroel*, he encountered Zeiri and asked him: *mikun tana d'asniyei Rav midos?* — is there a *tanna* who either received or transmitted Rav's teachings on the laws of measurement? He was directed to Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi, the authority on these matters, who was either Rav's teacher or student in this area. Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi immediately perceived that something was troubling Rabbi Elazar and asked him to articulate it.

### Sales vs. Trumah: Yeush

The difficulty Rabbi Elazar was grappling with is a contradiction between two *mishnayot*. One *mishna* states that after inclining the measuring vessel and allowing the oil to drip out, whatever remains adhering to the inner walls belongs to the seller. A second *mishna*, in the laws of *truma*, rules that if a *kohen*'s portion is being measured out and the oil is poured into the *kohen*'s vessel, whatever remains on the inner walls of the measuring vessel still has the status of *truma*.

These two rulings appear to conflict. In the sales context, the residual oil reverts to the seller — the person who originally owned it. Why, then, in the *truma* context, does the residual oil not revert to the original owner but instead retains its *truma* status, belonging to the *kohen*?

The resolution is attributed to Rav Abba: *mishum yeush ba'alim nangu bah* — the distinction turns on *yeush*, the owner's waiver of his claim. Technically, when oil is measured out for a buyer, every last drop — including what clings to the walls — belongs to the buyer. The seller is obligated to provide the full measure. However, when the oil is poured and the buyer sees that thin film of residue clinging to the walls, he simply does not have the patience or inclination to wait while the seller coaxes out every remaining drop. He waives his right to it — he is *miya'esh*, he foregoes that portion. It is this implicit *yeush* on the part of the buyer that permits the seller to retain the residue. In the *truma* context, no such *yeush* applies. Once oil has been designated as *truma* and declared *kodesh*, it is entirely sanctified — even the portion that clings to the walls — and there is no basis for the original owner to waive his sanctification of it. The *truma* remains *truma*, including the residue.

### Storekeeper & Erev Shabb…

The *gemara* then resolves the ambiguity about Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on *Erev Shabbos*. A *braita* clarifies: *Rabbi Yehuda omer erev shabbos im chashecha chanvani patur mipnei she-chanvani tarud* — Rabbi Yehuda says that on Friday afternoon as darkness falls, the storekeeper is exempt from the three drops because he is under extreme pressure. The implication is that at all other times, Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with the *chachamim* and holds that even a storekeeper is obligated to provide the three drops. Rabbi Yehuda's ruling is therefore a restriction relative to the majority position, not a leniency: the *chachamim* exempt storekeepers entirely, while Rabbi Yehuda limits that exemption to *Erev Shabbos* alone, when the pressure is genuinely acute.

---

## Child to Storekeeper

### Father Sends Child

The final *mishna* of the daf introduces a new scenario: a father sends his young son to the storekeeper with a *pundyon* — worth two *issar* — to purchase one *issar*'s worth of oil. The storekeeper measures out the oil, gives it to the child, and hands back the *issar* in change. On the way home, the child breaks the jug and the oil spills. Who is liable?

### Tanna Kamma vs. R. Yehuda

The *tanna kamma* rules that the storekeeper is liable. The reasoning is straightforward: a minor cannot perform a *kinyan*. The child cannot legally take possession of anything, and therefore neither the oil nor the change has ever left the storekeeper's legal domain. The father gave the storekeeper a *pundyon*; the storekeeper now holds the father's money and has given him nothing in return that *halacha* recognizes as delivered. The storekeeper must make good.

Rabbi Yehuda exempts the storekeeper: *she'al menas ken shalacho* — the father sent the child precisely for this purpose. Rabbi Yehuda reasons that if the *tanna kamma*'s view were correct, no storekeeper would ever sell anything to a child, since no transaction could ever be completed. Moreover, the father obviously wants his child to bring home the oil and the change — that is the entire point of sending him. Rabbi Yehuda therefore holds that by sending the child, the father implicitly communicates to the storekeeper: give the oil and the change to my child, and you will have fulfilled your obligation to me. You may keep the *pundyon* once you have done so. Even though the child cannot technically perform a *kinyan*, the father's act of sending him constitutes an implicit waiver of the storekeeper's liability.

### Child Holding Jug Except…

The *mishna* then adds that the *chachamim* agree with Rabbi Yehuda in one specific case: *bizman she-hatzluchit be-yad hatinok u-madad chanvani l'tocha, ha-chanvani patur* — if the child is holding the jug and the storekeeper measures oil directly into it, the storekeeper is exempt.

The Rashbam immediately notes an important qualification: this exemption applies only to the jug itself, not to the oil or the change. According to the *chachamim*, the oil and the money remain the storekeeper's responsibility until they reach the father — consistent with their view that the child cannot effect a *kinyan*. But the jug is a separate question.

The *mishna* distinguishes between two situations: if the storekeeper takes the jug from the child to fill it, he bears some degree of liability; if the jug remains in the child's hands throughout, he does not. The natural reading of the *mishna* is that the jug belongs to the father, who sent it along with his child. The question then becomes: why should the storekeeper ever be liable for a jug that was never his and that he simply filled and returned?

### Storekeeper Liability: I…

The difficulty is acute. The father already handed the jug to the child — someone *halachically* incapable of guarding it — before anything else happened. One might therefore argue that the father has already placed the jug in a vulnerable situation, and no subsequent handling by the storekeeper should create liability. How does the storekeeper's act of taking the jug generate responsibility?

### Shmuel: Inspection = Sho…

One answer is offered by invoking a ruling of Shmuel: *de-amar Shmuel hanotel kli min ha'uman al menat levakro, ve-ne'enas beyado, chayav* — one who takes a vessel from a craftsman to inspect it, and even if a complete accident occurs while he holds it, is liable. The theory is that the inspector is considered a *shoel*, a borrower, during the period of inspection: he is the only one currently deriving any benefit from the exchange — the craftsman is not receiving anything while his vessel is being examined — and therefore all risk of loss falls on him, just as a borrower bears full liability.

Applied to the *mishna*: the *gemara* proposes that the father also sells jugs, and sent the jug with his child as an opportunity for the storekeeper to inspect it. When the storekeeper takes the jug to inspect it, he becomes a *shoel* and assumes liability. If the jug then breaks after being returned to the child, the liability he assumed during the inspection period attaches to him. If the jug was never taken from the child — never inspected — no *shoel* status arises and there is no liability.

### Beyond Inspection Theory

This *okimta* is, however, quite forced. It requires positing that the father happens to be a jug-seller and sent the jug along for the storekeeper's commercial consideration — a contrived reading of an otherwise straightforward *mishna*. Moreover, accepting it would mean that Shmuel's ruling about inspection creating *shoel* status is precisely the point of debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim*, which would make Shmuel's position a *tannaitic* dispute — something the *gemara* prefers to avoid.

The *gemara* therefore rejects this approach and turns to a different explanation offered by Rabba and Rav Yosef: *hacha b'chanvani mocher tzluchi'ot askinan* — it is the storekeeper who sells jugs. In other words, when the child arrives, he is purchasing both the oil and the jug from the storekeeper with the father's *pundyon*. This is at least more intuitive than the reverse scenario. The debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim* then remains exactly what it was before: do the *chachamim* hold that the father only sent the child to inform the storekeeper of his wishes, without implicitly waiving the storekeeper's liability? And does Rabbi Yehuda hold that sending the child constitutes such an implicit waiver for all the goods — jug, oil, and change alike? On this reading, the jug is not categorically different from anything else; the storekeeper owns it just as he owns the oil and the change, and the same debate applies.

### Reconciling Positions

Yet this explanation immediately runs into the *mishna*'s final clause. The *mishna* states that even the *chachamim* agree the storekeeper is exempt when the child is holding the jug and the storekeeper measures into it. But if we follow Rabba and Rav Yosef — that the storekeeper owns the jug — and the *chachamim* hold that sending the child only informs the storekeeper of the father's wishes without waiving liability, then who is holding the jug should not matter at all. The jug is the storekeeper's regardless; the *chachamim* should hold him responsible whether the child holds it or not, just as they hold him responsible for the oil and the change. Why does the *chachamim*'s position change based on who is physically holding the jug?

The *gemara* ends the daf without fully resolving this problem. What seems clear from the *mishna*'s structure is that the simplest reading remains that the jug was sent by the father — that is precisely why the *mishna* singles out the question of who is holding it. If the storekeeper never removes the jug from the child's hands, he presumably has no liability, since the jug was always the father's and was never in the storekeeper's possession. The outstanding question — to be addressed on the next daf — is what precisely happens when the storekeeper does take the jug from the child. By what mechanism does that act generate liability, if the inspection theory (*shoel* through *levakro*) has been set aside?

---

---

# Bava Batra 88

## Storekeeper Jug Liability

### Mishnah: Child Purchase

The daf opens by resuming from the final line of 87b, which sets up the *mishnah*'s central debate. When a father sends his minor son to a storekeeper to purchase oil, the storekeeper sends back the oil in a jug along with change — and then everything is lost or broken. According to the *Chachamim*, liability falls on the storekeeper. Since the child lacks the legal capacity to effect a *kinyan*, the transaction was never completed from the storekeeper's perspective; sending the child should be understood merely as placing an order, leaving the storekeeper responsible for ensuring safe delivery to the father. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: the father's act of sending the child implicitly authorized that mode of delivery, and the father thereby assumed the risk.

### Jug Ownership Problem

This framework works cleanly for the oil and the change, but raises a pointed difficulty regarding the jug. If the jug belonged to the father, why should the storekeeper bear liability for it at all? The *Chachamim*'s reasoning — that the *kinyan* never transferred — does not obviously extend to an object the storekeeper never owned.

### Rav Yosef: Storekeeper's…

The best answer offered thus far is that of Rav and Rav Yosef, who maintain that the jug too belonged to the storekeeper. On this reading, the jug, oil, and change are all the storekeeper's property, and the child was simply the vehicle of delivery. The *mishnah*'s concluding clause — that if the jug is in the child's hand the storekeeper is exempt — would then be read simply as: if it is the father's jug, the storekeeper is exempt on that jug.

### Gemara Rejects Simple Re…

The *Gemara*, however, declines this straightforward reading of the *mishnah*'s conclusion, preferring instead to maintain that the jug remains the storekeeper's throughout, which creates a different interpretive challenge: if the jug always belongs to the storekeeper, why should the *mishnah*'s emphasis on whether the jug was in the child's hands matter at all? The *Gemara* may simply be exploring alternative frameworks rather than responding to a strictly logical compulsion — and it is worth acknowledging that the simple reading favored by Rav and Rav Yosef remains the more intuitive one.

---

## Shoel Shelo Midat Model

### Storekeeper Borrows Jug

The *Gemara* therefore introduces a third approach, attributed to Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin, who both say: *hacha b'mai askinan kegon de-natla limod bah* — the case concerns a storekeeper who took the jug without permission in order to use it for measuring out oil, not for the customer in question, but for other customers. The child arrives with the father's jug, and the storekeeper, before filling the order, appropriates the jug for his own commercial purposes. This renders the storekeeper a *shoel shelo midat* — a borrower without permission — and that status creates his liability.

On this reading, the *mishnah*'s final clause becomes coherent: if the storekeeper never removed the jug from the child's hands — never borrowing it for his own use — he is exempt on the jug. But if he took it from the child for his own purposes, he becomes liable as a *shoel shelo midat*.

### Rava: Animal Analogy

The *Gemara* introduces a parallel from Rava: *hikeishah ve-chayav bah* — if a person who has no obligation of *hashavat aveidah* (because returning a lost animal would be beneath his dignity) nevertheless strikes the animal to set it moving, he thereby assumes liability for it. The *Gemara* initially suggests that this principle might apply to the storekeeper as well: even if he takes the jug at the owner's behest — using it to measure oil for the very child who brought it — the mere act of taking it into his hands makes him responsible.

The *Gemara* then rejects this application. The logic of Rava's animal case rests on a specific mechanism: *deha ankiteihu nigra brayta* — once the animal has been set in motion, it will no longer remain grazing in the meadow where it was safe. Having disturbed its natural resting place, the person who struck it has created a new vulnerability, and negligence now attaches if he fails to follow through. That is why liability arises even absent a positive obligation of *hashavat aveidah*. But where the storekeeper takes the jug purely to serve the owner's own order — using it for the very customer who brought it — there is no analogous negligence. The *Gemara* therefore asks: *ki hai gavna mi amar* — would Rava's principle really apply in such a case?

### Refining Animal Case

This leads the *Gemara* to distinguish: Rava's principle generating liability without a prior obligation applies specifically because the actor's intervention destabilizes a previously stable situation. Taking an object at the owner's direction, for the owner's benefit, creates no such destabilization and thus no independent liability.

### Rava's Position: Unautho…

Rava accordingly clarifies — noting that he and Rav Zeira had already worked through this together: *hacha b'mai askinan kegon shentalo limod bo l'acherim* — the storekeeper took the jug without permission to measure out for *other* customers entirely. And the underlying dispute between the *Tanna'im* is precisely *u'v'sho'el shelo mida'at kamifligi* — whether one who borrows without permission is classified as a *shoel* or a *gazlan*.

---

## Borrower vs. Thief Debate

### Shoel vs. Gazlan

The question now becomes: what practical difference does it make whether the unauthorized borrower is classified as a *shoel* or a *gazlan*? In either case he is liable — a *shoel* bears liability even for *ones* (unavoidable accident). The jug is returned to the child; if it breaks, the storekeeper is liable regardless. So what turns on the classification?

### Return Obligations Differ

The answer lies in the nature of the return obligation. A *shoel* discharges his responsibility by restoring the object to the state from which he took it. He took the jug from the child's hands; returning it to the child's hands is therefore a complete return, even though the child's hands constitute an unprotected place. The *shoel*'s liability is a liability framework — it is not that the object has been alienated from the owner; it is simply that the borrower bears risk. Once the object is returned to the point of departure, the liability ends.

A *gazlan*, by contrast, has effectively dispossessed the owner. The object is no longer in the owner's domain; something has been taken away. Restoration therefore requires more than returning to the point of departure — it requires restoring the object to a genuinely protected state, placing it back under the owner's actual control. Returning to the child, an unprotected intermediary, does not accomplish this.

### Tosafot: Protected Return

Tosafot raises a complication: we have a general principle that *gazlan shelo midat* — someone who stole without the owner's knowledge — may effect return without the owner's knowledge. If I pickpocket someone and later slip the wallet back without their noticing, I have discharged my obligation of return. But — and this is the critical point — that principle applies only when the return is to a *protected* place. The child's hands are not a protected place. Even though the jug was initially taken from an unprotected situation, restoring it to an unprotected situation does not make the *gazlan* whole. That, then, is the operative dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* regarding the jug — not a question about who owns it, but about what standard of return the storekeeper must meet after having borrowed it without permission.

---

## Shmuel: Inspection Model

### Shmuel: Inspection Liabi…

Having resolved the *mishnah*'s framework, the *Gemara* turns *gufa* — to examine on its own terms the earlier statement of Shmuel: *hanotel keli min hauman levakaro* — one who takes a vessel from an artisan in order to inspect it becomes liable if an accident befalls it in his hands. The *Gemara*'s interest is in what legal category this creates. Is the inspector a *shoel* — a borrower — who has temporarily assumed the object under his control for his own benefit (assessing whether he wants it)? Or is he already something more like a *lokeach*, a purchaser, whose acquisition is merely conditional on the inspection's outcome?

### Price Question: Lokeach…

This question has practical stakes beyond the *ones* liability they share. Tosafot and the Rashbam both engage the question, and the *Gemara* itself supplies a clue: *ve-hani mili dekaitzi dameha* — this liability obtains only where the price is fixed. This condition is telling. If the inspector were simply a *shoel* — borrowing the object to determine whether he wishes to buy it — it would be puzzling why a fixed price should be required. The price is irrelevant to a borrower's liability. The need for a fixed price suggests instead that the inspector functions as a *lokeach*: he has effectively purchased the item subject to a right of return if unsatisfied. The fixed price is necessary precisely because a purchase, even a conditional one, requires a determinate price to be operative.

### Butcher's Meat Case

A concrete illustration follows. A man entered a butcher's shop, lifted a side of meat (*atma de-visra*) to inspect it — checking freshness, fat content, and quality — and while he was holding it up, a horseman came and snatched it away. Rav Yeimar made the inspector liable to pay for it, applying Shmuel's principle directly. The man was doing nothing more than inspecting; he was not test-driving the meat or using it in any meaningful way. Yet the liability attached. And, as the *Gemara* reiterates, this is specifically *dekaitzi dameha* — where the price was already fixed.

---

## Gourds: Kedush Case

### Gourds at Market

A further case: a man brought gourds to *Pum Nahara* — the mouth of the river, a marketplace — and the entire crowd descended on his stock, each person grabbing a gourd to inspect it. The owner, overwhelmed and unable to reassert control, feared he would never recover his merchandise. In desperation he announced: *harei hen mukdashim la-shamayim* — these are hereby consecrated to Heaven, to the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Rav Kahana: No Kedush

When the matter came before Rav Kahana, he ruled: *ein adam makdish davar she-eino shelo* — one cannot consecrate something that does not belong to him. The implication is striking: the gourds were no longer his to consecrate, because the crowd of inspectors had already acquired them in some fashion.

### Tosafot: Konayim Model

Tosafot draws an important inference from Rav Kahana's ruling. If the liability of inspection arose from *shoel* status, the owner could certainly have consecrated the gourds, because one may consecrate an object one owns even while someone else has borrowed it — the *shoel*'s status does not divest the owner of ownership. But Rav Kahana said he could not consecrate. This proves that the inspectors are not *shoelim* but *konim* — they are deemed to have acquired the gourds, however temporarily. The inspection model, at least when a price is fixed, places the inspector in the position of a conditional purchaser, not a borrower.

### Tentative Purchase Logic

This conclusion raises a puzzling logical problem. If the inspectors are temporary *konim* who may nonetheless choose to return the goods, can the owner equally choose to void the transaction on his side? A *kinyan* normally requires the full assent of both parties — a fixed price, an act of acquisition, and *da'as* on both sides. Is the mere act of a stranger lifting a gourd sufficient to constitute the owner's *da'as* to sell? And if both parties retain a right to back out, why could the owner not simply treat his declaration of *hekdesh* as an exercise of that right — backing out of the tentative sale and consecrating the item? The *Gemara* provides a partial resolution: *aval lo kaitzi dameihu birshus mareihu kaimei* — if the price was not fixed, the gourds remain in the owner's domain and his *hekdesh* is valid. But where the price was fixed, Rav Kahana's ruling stands, and the full logic of why the owner cannot simultaneously back out and consecrate remains, as acknowledged, not entirely transparent.

---

## Chavér Demai Problem

### Mishnah: No Purchase, No…

The *Gemara* now presents a *baraita* that introduces the question of *terumot u-ma'asrot* into the inspection model. A *chavér* — an observant Jew scrupulous in the separation of tithes — purchases vegetables from an *am ha-aretz*, a seller not trusted to have separated properly.
