If one buys from such a seller and brings the produce home, one must separate *demai* — the rabbinic tier of uncertain tithes — because the *am ha-aretz* may have failed to do so. The *baraita* states: *ha-lokeach yarak min ha-shuk u-viyeir ve-heniach afilu kol ha-yom kulo lo kanah ve-lo nitchayev be-ma'aser* — one who picks up vegetables in the market, inspects them, and sets them down has not acquired them and incurs no obligation of *ma'aser*, even if he spent the entire day doing this.

### Intent Creates Liability

Immediately, however, the *baraita* introduces a contrasting rule: *gamar be-libo liknoso, kanah ve-nitchayev be-ma'aser* — if, at the moment of picking it up, he had formed the definitive intention to purchase it, then he has acquired it and is immediately obligated in *ma'aser*. This is a striking development. The inspector has not yet paid; the seller has not yet accepted; no formal *kinyan* has been completed. Yet intention alone — *g'mar da'as* to purchase — creates both acquisition and its attendant obligations.

The *baraita* then confronts the consequences directly: *le-hachziro ee efshar, shekvar nitchayev be-ma'aser* — he cannot simply hand it back, because he is already obligated to tithe it. *Ve-le'asro ee efshar, shekvar mafchis be-damim* — nor can he tithe it in place and return the diminished produce, because he would be reducing the value of what he returns. The resolution: *maasro ve-noten lo d'mei ma'aser* — he separates the *ma'aser* and pays the seller for that portion he has taken.

Tosafot notes that this is not as complex as it sounds with respect to most tithes. For *demai*, once *ma'aser rishon* is separated, it may be eaten even by a non-*Levi*, since the underlying obligation is uncertain; the *Levi* who wants to claim it must prove it was not already taken — *ha-motzi me-chaveiro alav ha-ra'ayah*. Similarly with *ma'aser ani*. The genuinely difficult cases are *ma'aser sheni* — which is *kadosh* and must be eaten in Jerusalem or redeemed — and *terumas ma'aser* within the *ma'aser rishon*, which may only be consumed by a *Kohen*. For those portions, separation and compensation are the only path.

### Rav Hoshaya: Yarei Shama…

At this point the *Gemara* raises a sharp objection: *atu mishum de-gamar be-libo liknoso kanah ve-nitchayev be-ma'aser?* — does the mere fact that he made up his mind to buy it mean he has acquired it? This seems to contradict everything the *Gemara* has labored to establish about the requirements of a *kinyan*. The *Gemara* answers with Rav Hoshaya: *hacha be-yarei shamayim askinan* — the *baraita* is speaking specifically about a *yarei shamayim*, a person of exceptional scrupulousness, one who holds himself to a higher standard than strict law requires.

### Rav Safra Story

The paradigm of such a person is Rav Safra, cited immediately: *kegon Rav Safra de-kayem be-nafsheih ve-doveir emes be-levavo* — he upheld in his own conduct the verse "who speaks truth in his heart." The well-known story: Rav Safra was reciting *Shema* when a merchant approached wishing to sell him something. The merchant, receiving no response, kept raising his price. When Rav Safra finished *Shema*, he said: I had already agreed in my heart to buy it at the original price — I could not interrupt my prayer to say so — and therefore I will pay only that original price. A *yarei shamayim* honors the intent formed in his heart as though it were a completed transaction.

### Rash'bam: Intent as Purc…

The Rashbam articulates the principle directly: *ve-hachi nami gabei mekach, keivan de-yarei shamayim hu, keivan she-gamar be-libo zacha ba-mekach ve-nitchayev ba-mechir, ve-chi machzir ke-chozer u-mocher lo dami* — since this person is a *yarei shamayim*, once he formed his intention to buy, he treats himself as though he has acquired the produce and incurred the price. If he subsequently returns it, he treats this as a resale back to the original seller, and compensates accordingly.

This resolution, however, produces a certain tension with the earlier cases. In those cases — the butcher's meat, the gourds — the *Gemara* appeared to treat inspection-with-intent as acquisition for everyone, not merely for the especially pious. The *Gemara* here seems to be saying that, in principle, a tentative inspection does not constitute acquisition, and one who changes his mind was never truly *koneh*. The liability in cases of *ones* arises specifically when the inspector cannot restore the object to its original state — at that point his conditional purchase is locked in. But if he simply puts it down undamaged, he was retroactively never the owner. The *yarei shamayim* holds himself to a stricter standard: even when he could legally walk away, he honors the intention he formed. It is for such a person that the *baraita*'s *ma'aser* obligation applies.

---

## Weights & Measures

### Mishnah: Cleaning Standa…

The *Gemara* now turns to a new *mishnah*, continuing the theme of commercial integrity but shifting from the act of purchasing to the instruments of commerce themselves: weights, measures, and scales. The *mishnah* introduces three categories of seller, each with different cleaning obligations for their measuring vessels.

The *siton* — a wholesaler, as the Rashbam explains, *hu chanvani gadol she-koneh harbeh yachad u-mocher le-chanvanim ketanim*, one who buys in bulk from producers and sells to smaller retailers (the word itself, as Steinsaltz notes, derives from the Greek *sitones*, a commissary for grain) — must clean his measuring vessels once every thirty days. The *ba'al habayit* — the homeowner who sells only occasionally from domestic stock — must clean only once a year. The underlying logic of the *tanna kamma* is that heavier use produces more residue: if I am constantly filling and emptying my liter vessel, residue will accumulate faster and must be cleaned more often. If I barely use it, residue builds up slowly.

The practical stakes are significant: residue lining a measuring vessel reduces its effective capacity. Even without any intent to deceive, the buyer will not receive the full amount purchased. This is the *halakhic* analogue to *eifa va-eifa* — using different standards for buying and selling — but produced by negligence rather than malice.

### Rabban Shimon: Inverse R…

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reverses the reasoning entirely: *chiluf ha-devarim* — it is the opposite. Where a vessel is used rarely, whatever residue adheres to it clings and hardens, demanding more frequent cleaning. Heavy use, paradoxically, keeps vessels cleaner through the constant flow of material. On this view, the *ba'al habayit* whose vessel sits idle must clean more often, not less.

### Storekeeper Obligations

The *mishnah* then addresses the *chanvani* — the regular storekeeper — who occupies the middle position: he must clean his measuring vessels twice a week, reflecting their constant daily use. He must also wipe down his weights once a week. This is less frequent than the vessel cleaning because the concern with weights is different: not internal residue from repeated filling, but external accumulation — dust, dirt, or debris adhering to the surface that incrementally alters the weight. 

It is worth noting that this works asymmetrically: if the dirt makes a selling weight slightly heavier, the buyer actually benefits, receiving slightly more than purchased. But if it afflicts the purchasing weights, the seller benefits at the supplier's expense. Someone, in either scenario, is being shortchanged, and so regular cleaning is required.

Beyond the weights themselves, the *mishnah* adds: *u-mekaniach moznayim al kol mishkal u-mishkal* — he must wipe down the balance pans between every single weighing. The balance pan is the surface on which the goods themselves are placed. With adhesive substances — meat, wine, oil — material clings to the pan and adds to the apparent weight of subsequent goods, systematically cheating buyers. This must be addressed after every transaction.

### Liquid vs. Dry Measures

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies this last requirement: *bameh devarim amurim, be-lach* — this applies specifically to *lach*, to wet or liquid-adjacent goods, which adhere. *Aval be-yavesh eino tzarich* — for dry goods, the pan need not be wiped between each weighing, since dry material does not stick. The Rashbam clarifies: *lach* encompasses meat, wine, and oil — goods that carry moisture and leave residue on the pan. Apples, for instance, would generally not raise this concern; fine flour might approach the *lach* category depending on how it adheres.

### Tefach & Geirumin

Beyond the question of accurate measurement lies a further obligation: *ve-chayav le-hachria lo tefach* — the storekeeper is obligated to tip the scale in the buyer's favor by a *tefach*. That is, after placing the purchased goods on one side and the weights on the other, one must add enough additional goods to cause the buyer's side of the scale to descend by a full *tefach* — approximately three to four finger-breadths. This is a remarkably large margin. The Rashbam specifies that this is the standard for a *litra* (a pound-weight). For such a small unit, a full *tefach* depression of the scale seems substantial, and the requirement is genuinely surprising even if a highly sensitive scale might require less actual material to achieve that deflection.

The *mishnah* then addresses a different commercial custom: *ha-shokel ayin be-ayin, notnin lo geirumin* — where the local practice is to weigh precisely, eye to eye, with an exactly even balance, the storekeeper gives the buyer *geirumin*. The Rashbam connects the word *geirumin* to *hagramah* as in *shechitah* — a tipping or deflection — which is a linguistically interesting suggestion. Functionally, *geirumin* refers to a small extra measure thrown in after the weighing: not tipping the scale during measurement, but tossing in something additional afterward, like a baker's dozen.

The *mishnah* specifies the amount as *echad le-asarah be-lach ve-echad le-esrim be-yavesh* — one in ten for liquid, one in twenty for dry. The *Gemara* will significantly reinterpret these numbers, reducing them from what appears to be ten percent and five percent to something far smaller.

### Custom Determines Method

The *mishnah* concludes with the principle that local custom governs commercial practice: where it is the custom to measure with small vessels, one may not switch to large ones; where large vessels are the norm, small ones are prohibited. The reason is that the practice of small measures customarily involves giving a small additional amount with each unit, benefiting the buyer incrementally; switching to a single large measure removes that accumulated benefit. Someone is disadvantaged whenever the established practice changes, whether seller or buyer, and therefore custom must be respected.

Similarly: *limchok o ligdosh, ligdosh lo yimchok* — if the custom is to smooth the top of the measuring vessel (giving a level, flat measure), one may not heap it up; if the custom is to heap (*ligdosh* — to pile), one may not smooth it down. Changing in either direction disrupts the equilibrium of local commercial expectations.

---

## Source of Extra Measures

### Reish Lakish: Even Shele…

The *Gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — what is the scriptural source for the requirement to give extra? Reish Lakish answers from the verse: *even sheleima va-tzedek* — a complete and just stone — which he expounds as *tzedek mi-shelcha ve-ten lo*: be righteous from your own — give something of your own to ensure the buyer receives everything owed. This establishes the general principle that one must give a small increment beyond the precise weight.

### Tipping vs. Adding

The *Gemara* then notices a tension. If *even sheleima* establishes a requirement to give extra *in the act of weighing* — by tipping the scale — then the *mishnah*'s practice of *ayin be-ayin* (precise weighing followed by a separate *geirumin*) seems to violate a *d'Oraita* obligation. How can precise, exactly-even weighing ever be permitted?

The *Gemara* resolves this: *ela reisha be-makom she-nahagu* — the *mishnah* is describing local customs. The *d'Oraita* principle requires giving something extra, but does not mandate the specific form — whether by tipping the scale during weighing or by adding afterward. Both methods satisfy the underlying requirement; local convention determines which form is used.

Accordingly, Reish Lakish's derivation is relocated: *ve-chi itmar d'Reish Lakish, a-seifa itmar* — his teaching applies to the latter clause, where one weighs precisely and then gives *geirumin* afterward. The verse *ve-tzedek, tzedek mi-shelcha ve-ten lo* supports adding something from one's own stock *after* the precise measurement, not necessarily during it. The general obligation to give something extra — in one form or another — is thus grounded in scripture.

### Rav Abba: One of Ten

The *Gemara* turns to quantification. The *mishnah* stated *echad le-asarah be-lach* — one in ten for liquids — which, read literally, would mean ten percent. This seems far too large. Rav Abba bar Mamal citing Rav introduces a creative re-reading: *echad me-asarah be-litra be-lach le-asarah litrin* — one tenth of a single unit when purchasing ten units. That is, the extra measure is one tenth of one unit given when buying ten units — which is one percent, not ten percent. The *mishnah* is read as compressing two layered fractions.

### Dry Measures: Percentage…

The corresponding figure for dry measures — *echad le-esrim be-yavesh* — is then subjected to the same question. The *Gemara* poses a *be-ayah*: does it mean one twentieth of a unit for every twenty units of dry measure (*echad me-esrim be-yavesh le-esrim de-yavesh*), yielding one four-hundredth of a percent — a quarter of a percent? Or does it mean one twentieth of a unit for every ten units, as in the liquid case (*echad me-asarah le-asarah de-lach, u-le-esrim be-yavesh*), yielding one two-hundredth — a half of a percent? The *Gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teku*. As for why dry measures should require a smaller *geirumin* than liquid measures, the *Gemara* does not explain, and the question remains open.

---

## Severity of Fraud

### Rav Levi: Measure Fraud…

The *Gemara* now steps back from technical analysis to deliver a striking moral statement. Rav Levi says: *kasheh onsham shel middos yoter me-onsham shel arayos* — the punishment for weights-and-measures fraud is more severe than the punishment for *arayos*, the gravest sexual prohibitions. This is a deliberately provocative formulation, precisely because it inverts the intuitive hierarchy: we tend to regard *arayos* as among the most serious of all transgressions. The *Gemara* supports the comparison with a textual argument: the verse concerning *arayos* uses the formulation *eil* (singular), while the verse concerning measures uses *eileh* (the fuller form), which connotes greater gravity.

The *Gemara* then challenges its own reading: does the *arayos* passage not also contain the word *eileh* — *ki kol asher ya'aseh mi-kol ha-to'eivos ha-eileh ve-nichretu*? Yes — and that is precisely the point. The *eileh* in the *arayos* passage specifies that *karet* applies *only* to *arayos*, not to measure fraud. So while measures are described in graver terms, the concrete punishment of *karet* is reserved for *arayos* alone.

### Impossible Restitution

The *Gemara* then asks: in what sense, then, is the punishment for measure fraud more severe? *De-hasam efshar bi-teshuvah ve-hacha lo efshar bi-teshuvah* — because in the case of *arayos*, repentance is possible, while for measure fraud, full repentance is structurally impossible. The merchant who has systematically shortchanged customers has stolen fractionally from every person who ever entered his shop. To do *teshuvah* properly for theft requires returning what was stolen — *ve-hashiv et ha-gezeila* — but he cannot identify all his victims. He does not know who they are, how many there were, or how much each lost. Even if he contributes to communal needs — *tzorchei rabbim* — that is not complete *teshuvah*. The case of Crazy Eddie's was raised as a contemporary illustration: one of those involved spent the remainder of his life lecturing students on business ethics, but acknowledged he could never locate all those he had defrauded.

### Theft Comparison: Order

Rav Levi extends this theme with a second statement: *kasha gezel hedyot yoter mi-gezel gavoha* — stealing from an ordinary person is worse than stealing from God (i.e., *me'ila*, misappropriating consecrated property). The proof is structural: when the Torah describes stealing from a person, it says first *ve-chata u-ma'ala ma'al ba-Hashem* — "he has sinned and committed a *ma'al* against God" — and only then describes the human theft. The *chet* against the person comes first in the sequence, suggesting its primacy. By contrast, when the Torah describes *me'ila* with consecrated property, it says *ki timol ma'al mi-kodshei Hashem* — the *me'ila* is named first, the *chet* only later. 

The Rashbam's reading is that *ma'al* in the theft context means *deriving benefit* — so in the human-theft case, the sin itself (*chet*) precedes the benefit derived, suggesting a more immediate transgression. In the *me'ila* case, benefit from the sacred comes first; the formal *chet* designation follows. This sequencing — the *chet* arriving earlier in the theft-from-person case — indicates that stealing from a person carries a more urgent moral charge. This point reinforces the broader *mussar* lesson that the hierarchy of *bein adam la-Makom* and *bein adam la-chaveiro* is not what the intuitive religious sensibility typically assumes.

Tosafot addresses the obvious objection: can one really say that *teshuvah* is possible for *arayos* but not for measure fraud? Many *arayos* violations produce lasting, irreparable damage — children who are *mamzerim*, devastated marriages, profound psychological harm. Tosafot answers by distinguishing: where *mamzerus* does not result and the harm is less concrete, *teshuvah* to God remains achievable even if the human damage is hard to reverse. Rav Chaim adds a further clarification: between the sinner and God, *teshuvah* is always available for any *aveirah* — God commanded repentance precisely because it is possible. But for theft, the *teshuvah* process is defined by *hashavat gezeila*, the physical return of stolen property. Where that return is structurally impossible because the victims cannot be identified, the *teshuvah* process itself is incomplete.

### Blessings vs. Curses

Rav Levi closes with a reflection on the asymmetry between divine and human communication: *shelo ke-middat HaKadosh Baruch Hu middat basar va-dam* — God's ways are not the ways of flesh and blood. God blessed Israel with twenty-two letters — from *alef* to *taf*, encompassing the whole alphabet — and cursed them with only eight. The *berachot* in *Vayikra* begin with *Im be-chukotai telechu* (opening letter *alef*) and end with *komemiyut* (closing letter *taf*); the *kelalot* begin with *im be-chukotai tim'asu* (opening letter *vav*) and end at *mem* — only a third of the alphabet.

Moshe Rabbeinu, a human being, reversed this proportion: he blessed Israel with only eight letters — from *vav* to *mem* (*Ve-haya im shamo'a tishme'u* through *la-avdam*) — and cursed them with twenty-two, from *vav* in *Ve-haya im lo tishme'u* all the way around to *hei* in *ve-ein koneh*. This observation connects to the well-known *Gemara* in other contexts that the *kelalot* of *Devarim* are longer and more intense than those of *Vayikra*, since Moshe spoke them in the first person without the softening of divine mediation.

---

## Parshiyot Timing

### Vayeilech & Nitzavim

Tosafot takes note of the *Gemara*'s derivation — that the *kelalot* of *Devarim* span from *Ve-haya im lo tishme'u* through *ve-ein koneh* — and uses it to address a practical question of the annual Torah reading cycle: why do we sometimes separate *Nitzavim* and *Vayeilech* into two distinct *parshiyot*, even though *Vayeilech* is exceptionally short and would more naturally be combined with *Nitzavim*, while we routinely combine the much longer double *parasha* of *Matot-Masei*?

The common explanation is that we need *Nitzavim* to fall before *Rosh Hashanah*, ensuring a *parasha* of relative comfort and gathering (*atem nitzavim* — "you stand together") immediately before the new year, and that separating *Nitzavim* from *Vayeilech* creates enough additional weeks to achieve this. Implicit in this is a desire not to read the *tochacha* — the curses — immediately before the new year.

### Rabbeinu Nissim: Buffer

Tosafot cites Rabbeinu Nissim for a refined version: *le-fi peirush Rabbeinu Nissim*. He explains that we always read *Nitzavim* before *Rosh Hashanah* in order to insert a *parasha* as a buffer between the *kelalot* of *Ki Tavo* and the beginning of the new year — *k'dei le-hafsik be-parsha bein klalos d'shana she-avra de-Ki Tavo le-shana ha-ba'ah*. We want the *kelalot* to belong entirely to the expiring year, and we want a neutral intervening *parasha* to mark the separation. Simply finishing *Ki Tavo* and beginning the new year the very next week would feel too abrupt; *Nitzavim* provides the necessary pause.

Tosafot then engages the current *Gemara*'s implication: since the *Gemara* here derives that the *kelalot* of Moshe's *tochacha* span from *Ve-haya im lo tishme'u* through *ve-ein koneh*, the *kelalot* effectively conclude at the end of *Ki Tavo*, not within *Nitzavim*. On this reading, *Nitzavim* itself is not truly a *parasha* of *kelalot* — so there would be no textual reason from this *Gemara* to require it before *Rosh Hashanah* on account of the curses. Rabbeinu Nissim's point is therefore not that *Nitzavim* itself contains unacceptable *kelalot*, but rather that it functions as a buffer between *Ki Tavo*'s curses and the new year — a clean structural separation between the old year's judgment and the new one's beginning.

### Bamidbar Before Shavuot

The same logic applies, Tosafot continues, to the *parasha* of *Bamidbar*: *le-olam anu korim Bamidbar lifnei Atzeret* — we always read *Bamidbar* immediately before *Shavuot*. *Shavuot* is *Rosh Hashanah le-peirot ha-ilan* — the day of judgment for tree fruits — and is therefore a form of *yom ha-din* for the new fruit of the year. Just as we separate the *kelalot* from the new year of *Rosh Hashanah*, so too we insert *Bamidbar* — a *parasha* of census and tribal order, without *tochacha* — as a buffer between the *kelalot* at the end of *Vayikra* (*Im be-chukotai*) and the new year of fruits. *Bamidbar* thus functions as a structural pause, ensuring that the curses of *Vayikra* do not flow directly into the judgment of *Shavuot*.

Tosafot cites in support the *Gemara* in Megilla, which records that Ezra established the reading of the *kelalot she-be-Mishneh Torah* — the curses of *Devarim* — before *Shavuot/Atzeret*, for this same reason of temporal separation between curse and judgment.

---

---

# Bava Batra 89

## Measures & Custom

### Mishna Overview

The *mishna* at the center of today's daf addresses a deceptively broad topic: what it means to deal honestly with weights and measures. Honesty in this domain is not limited to ensuring that one's measuring vessels are physically accurate. It also encompasses a set of related obligations — cleaning out the measuring containers and wiping down the scales, and attending carefully to the very act of weighing or filling: whether one adds a small amount extra in the buyer's favor, whether the scale tips slightly toward the buyer, and whether a volume measure is filled level or heaped. All of these practices bear on the question of whether a buyer receives a fair measure.

### Large vs Small

The *mishna* establishes: *makom shenahagu lamod begasa al yimod bedaka* — in a place where the custom is to use a large measure when selling, one may not switch to using a small measure, and vice versa. The reasoning behind this rule is instructive. Since perfect precision is essentially unattainable in any act of measurement, there will always be some slight margin of error. The expectation, and the norm of honest dealing, is that this margin should consistently favor the buyer. When multiple small measures are used, that slight error occurs repeatedly — each individual measuring carries a small surplus — and the cumulative effect benefits the buyer more than a single large measurement would. This is why switching to a large measure in a place where small measures are the norm would disadvantage the buyer.

Equally striking, however, is the *mishna*'s concern in the reverse direction: one may not switch to small measures in a place where large measures are standard, even if this would benefit the buyer. The *mishna* clearly protects the seller's legitimate interests as well, not merely the buyer's.

### Lifnim Mishurat

Even in a place where the measuring practice is a level, flat fill, and even if the norms of that place are strictly followed, there remains a separate obligation to give something extra beyond the precise measure — a *lifnim mishurat hadin* consideration. This is distinct from the question of how the measuring itself is conducted. The question of whether the act of measuring is done in a balanced or slightly generous manner is one issue; the question of throwing in an additional unit as a gesture of honest generosity is a separate matter entirely.

### Smooth vs Heap

A *baraita* is then cited: *minayin she'ein mokechin bemakom shegodshin ve'ein godshin bemakom shemokechin* — how do we know that one may not smooth the top of a volume measure in a place where the custom is to heap, and may not heap in a place where the custom is to smooth? The source is the *pasuk*: *eifah shleimah vetzedek yihyeh lach* — "a complete and just measure shall be yours." "Complete," the *baraita* understands, means complete in accordance with the norms of the place. A heaped measure in a smoothing locale is not a complete measure; it exceeds the norm. A smoothed measure in a heaping locale falls short of it.

Why should this be a problem when both parties agree to it? The *Rashbam* explains that the concern is a social one. Even if buyer and seller privately arrange to deviate from the local norm, other people see the transaction visually but do not know its terms. They observe the flat measure and assume it is the going practice — and this disrupts the established norms of the marketplace, ultimately harming either buyers or sellers who thereafter expect the wrong standard.

### Eifah Shleima

The *baraita* continues: *uminayin she'im amar hareni mokech bemakom shegodshin ulephachot lo min hadamim* — how do we know that even if the seller says "I will smooth it rather than heap it, but I will charge a reduced price to compensate," one may not follow this approach? The *Rashbam* explains that the additional word in the *pasuk* — *vetzedek*, "and just" — prohibits even this arrangement. The reason is the same: *de'ika dechazi bimdidah velo yada lo bifchas velo betosefes* — observers see the manner of measuring but have no way of knowing whether a corresponding price adjustment was made. This visual discrepancy leads to disruption of honest practice throughout the marketplace. One student added a sharper formulation: this amounts to *rama'ut* — it actively invites deception, since other sellers, seeing the deviation, may adopt it without the compensating price adjustment. The *Rashbam* includes this concern implicitly, but the full force of the point is that the visual impression creates the opening for fraud.

*Tosafot* offers a somewhat different explanation of the underlying prohibition, which we will return to below.

A note from the *mishna* suggests that the difference between a heaped and a level measure is substantial — as much as a third more for the heap. This is a striking figure. If the deviation is that large, it would obviously need to be reflected in pricing; one cannot simply pretend the difference is negligible. Similarly, the *mishna* mentions later that the scale should tip a full *tefach* in the buyer's favor when weighing — which also seems like an enormous amount, one that would necessarily affect the pricing structure. These details suggest that whatever these measures mean in practice, they were understood as embedded in a larger system of pricing conventions, not as isolated acts of generosity.

### Even Shleima

The *baraita* then extends the identical analysis to weight measures. *Minayin she'ein me'aynin bimkom shemachri'in* — how do we know that one may not weigh to the exact balance (*me'aynin*, literally, "eye-level") in a place where the norm is to tip the scale (*machri'in*) in the buyer's favor? And the reverse: one may not tip the scale where the norm is to weigh precisely. The source is *even shleimah vatzedek yihyeh lach* — "a complete and just weight shall be yours." The word *even* (weight measure) parallels *eifah* (volume measure) exactly, and the same analysis applies. Exact balance, in a tipping-custom locale, defrauds the buyer. Tipping, in an exact-balance locale, defrauds the seller. And the same prohibition against compensating through adjusted pricing applies here as well, with *even shleimah vatzedek* as its source.

It is worth pausing on the linguistic observation that *machri'ah* — "to tip the scales" — is the same word used in halachic discourse for "to decide between competing opinions," because tipping in one direction is itself the act of deciding. The metaphor is built into the vocabulary.

---

## Midrash & Officials

### Rav Yehuda

The *gemara* then presents a remarkable *midrashic* reading of the *pesukim* in Devarim 25, attributed to Rav Yehuda Mi-Sura. The verse *lo yihyeh lecha b'veitecha eifah va'eifah* — "you shall not have in your house two measures" — is read as a prediction of poverty: *lo yihyeh lecha b'veitecha*, "you will have nothing in your house." Why will this person end up with nothing? *Mishum eifah va'eifah* — because he maintains two sets of measures in his house: the larger measure with which he buys and the smaller measure with which he sells. This is the classic "two sets of books" — one for acquisition and one for sale, each manipulated in the seller's favor.

The reading extends further: *lo yihyeh lecha b'chisecha* — "you will have nothing in your pocket" — because of *even va'even*, maintaining two sets of weights. But by contrast, *even shleimah vatzedek yihyeh lach* — if you maintain a just weight, *yihyeh lach*, you will have wealth. *Eifah shleimah vatzedek yihyeh lach* — and if you maintain a just volume measure, you too will be rewarded with prosperity.

This is a powerful *midrashic* inversion: the very phrase the deceiver hopes will describe his gains — *yihyeh lach* — becomes the description of the honest dealer's reward, while the cheater ends up with *lo yihyeh lach* precisely because of the deception he practiced.

The *gemara* then takes the final *pasuk*, *eifah shleimah vatzedek yihyeh lach*, and notes that the use of the singular pronoun *lach* (rather than *lachem*) is instructive in a surprising direction. Normally one might think the singular *lach* addresses the individual and the plural *lachem* addresses the community. But the *midrash halacha* often reads the singular as a communal address — the nation as a unified entity — while the plural distributes obligation to each individual. The parallel from *Sefirat HaOmer* is instructive: *u'sefartem lachem* imposes an individual obligation on each person to count, while *v'safarta lecha* regarding *yovel* is a communal obligation fulfilled through the *Beit Din*. So too here: *eifah shleimah vatzedek yihyeh lach* addresses the community as a whole, teaching that the community bears collective responsibility to ensure the integrity of weights and measures.

### Agardomin

This communal reading leads directly to the practical ruling: *melamed she'ma'amidim agardemin l'middot* — the community must appoint *agardomin* (market inspectors, from a Greek term meaning officer in charge of the market) to oversee weights and measures. These officials go from stall to stall, testing whether the measures are accurate — the ancient equivalent of the government inspectors who once visited butcher shops incognito to weigh a pound of meat after purchase.

However, *v'ein ma'amidim agardemin l'sha'arim* — one does not appoint such officials to regulate prices. The *Rashbam* explains: free-market competition is sufficient to bring prices to their natural level. If one vendor overcharges, a competitor will undercut him and attract the business. This principle implicitly assumes a competitive marketplace without collusion, but it is a strikingly early articulation of the idea that market prices regulate themselves while the integrity of the measuring instruments does not.

### Nasi Disagreement

The house of the *Nasi* in Bavel, however, took a different position: *debe Nesia ukmi agordemi bein le-middot bein le-shearim* — they appointed officials for both weights and measures *and* for prices. Shmuel, upon learning of this, sent a pointed message through his colleague Karna: *puk tani le-hu ma'amidin agordemi le-middot ve-ein ma'amidim agordemi le-shearim* — go teach the house of the *Nasi* that the *halacha* is that officials are appointed for measures but not for prices.

That Shmuel dispatched Karna to deliver this correction to the *Nasi*'s household is itself noteworthy. The *gemara* then reports that when Karna arrived, he instead taught *ma'amidin agordemi bein le-middot bein le-shearim* — the position of the *Nasi*'s house, which he had been sent to correct. Shmuel's response was sharp: *ma shimcha?* — "What is your name?" *Karna* — "Horn?" *Tepuk lei karna bein einai* — "A horn should sprout between your eyes." And, the *gemara* notes, *nafka lei karna bein einai* — it did. The *Rashbam* mentions a parallel account in *Gemara Shabbat* in which Shmuel was angered at Karna for a different reason; perhaps both incidents contributed to the result.

### Rav Yitzchak

The *gemara* then asks: when Karna taught the position of the *Nasi*'s house, whose opinion was he relying on? It would be unthinkable that he would teach an entirely unsupported view even under social pressure. The answer: *ki ha de'amar Rami bar Chama amar Rav Yitzchak ma'amidin agordemi bein le-middot bein le-shearim mipnei ha-ramaim* — there is indeed a tradition that officials are appointed even for prices, because of the *ramaim*, the deceivers. The *Rashbam* explains that this is not merely about setting prices, but about broader forms of market deception — selling lower-grade goods as higher-grade, misrepresenting quality, and similar frauds that a simple price check would not catch. More straightforwardly, collusion among sellers to fix prices artificially is a classic form of *ramaim* that free-market competition alone cannot remedy. It is worth noting that the *Rambam* rules in accordance with Rav Yitzchak's position — officials are appointed for both measures and prices.

### Price Gouging

This discussion of *ramaim* opens into a broader theme: the historical phenomenon of price gouging tied to religious observance. When a community is known to *need* certain goods — fish for *Shabbos*, *matzah* for *Pesach*, or whatever the religious occasion demands — unscrupulous vendors exploit that need to charge inflated prices. The *gemara* itself records cases of this kind, and the communal response was often dramatic: Rabbis and community leaders would issue a prohibition on purchasing the gouged item until the price came down. This was a form of organized communal pressure — effectively a boycott — to counteract the leverage that religious necessity created for dishonest sellers. Similar dynamics appear in later *teshuvot* regarding funeral expenses, where communities adopted the principle of maintaining minimal expenditures rather than allowing funeral homes to exploit the grief and guilt of mourners. The appointment of *agardomin* for prices, in Rav Yitzchak's view, is precisely the institutional response to such structural vulnerabilities.

---

## Weighing Procedure

### Standard Units

A *baraita* teaches: *hayah mevakesh mimenu litra shokel lo litra, chatzi litra shokel lo chatzi litra, revia litra shokel lo revia litra* — if someone wants to buy a pound, weigh it with a one-pound weight; half a pound, with a half-pound weight; a quarter pound, with a quarter-pound weight. The *gemara* asks: *mai kamashmalan* — what does this add? The answer is that the *baraita* establishes which specific weight denominations must be available and used: a full pound, a half, and a quarter. The reason for mandating these specific units is twofold. First, if only large weights are available, buyers may be forced to overbuy. Second, and more significantly, the differences between these denominations — half, quarter — are large enough that the weights cannot easily be confused or swapped. Weight units that are too close in size to one another create the risk that a slightly lighter weight will be substituted undetected.

### Three-Quarter Measure

The case of a three-quarter pound purchase presents an interesting problem. The *baraita* rules: *lo yomar lo shokel li shlosha reviei litra achat achat* — one should not make three separate quarter-pound weighings. Instead: *shokel litra umeiniach revia litra im habasar* — one places a one-pound weight on one side of the scale and adds a quarter-pound weight *together with* the meat on the other side, so that they balance. Why not simply use a half-pound weight and a quarter-pound weight on the counterbalancing side? The *Rashbam* explains the objection to three separate weighings: even in a locale where exact-balance (*me'aynin*) weighing is the norm, the honest dealer will always err ever so slightly in the buyer's favor, because perfect precision is unattainable. Three separate weighings would give the buyer three such tips in his favor, which is more than the norm provides for. Hence the single combined weighing.

### Ten Pounds

The same principle governs larger quantities. *Hayah mevakesh mimenu eser litrin* — if someone wants to buy ten pounds — *lo yomar lo shkol li achat achat v'yachria* — one should not make ten separate one-pound weighings, each with its own slight tip in the buyer's favor. Instead, *shoklan kulan b'vat achat v'noten hechra echad l'kulan* — weigh all ten pounds at once, with a single tip for the entire transaction.

### Scale Mechanics

A *baraita* now turns to the physical specifications of the scale itself, referring throughout to the *nefesh moznayim* — the entire scale assembly. For scales used to weigh the heaviest goods — the *gemara* will clarify these are the scales of smiths dealing in brass and iron — the following specifications apply: *tluya ba'avir gimmel tefachim v'gvoha min ha'aretz gimmel tefachim* — the suspended scale must be at least three *tefachim* below the ceiling point from which it hangs, and at least three *tefachim* above the ground. *V'hakaneh v'hamachta shela yod-bet tefachim* — the bar (*kaneh*) and the ropes (*machta*, or *masna*) together measure twelve *tefachim*.

The *Rashbam* explains this as follows: the bar is four *tefachim* in length, and the ropes on each side are four *tefachim* each, yielding four plus four plus four equals twelve. The practical reasoning behind the ceiling and floor clearances is that heavy goods, when placed on one side of an unloaded scale, will cause a dramatic drop; if the pan swings too close to the ceiling at the top or the ground at the bottom, it will be obstructed, distorting the reading. There is also a physical principle at work — the longer the ropes, the more sensitive the scale, since any slight imbalance causes a larger visible arc of movement.

### Scale Sizes

For sellers of lighter goods — specifically wool merchants and glass sellers (it is notable that glass was sold by weight) — the specifications are reduced. The scale hangs two *tefachim* from the ceiling, stands two *tefachim* from the ground, and the combined bar and ropes measure nine *tefachim* (bar of three *tefachim* plus ropes of three *tefachim* on each side). For a retail storekeeper or private householder selling still lighter quantities, the scale need only be one *tefach* from ceiling and ground, with a combined bar and rope measure of six *tefachim* (bar of two *tefachim* plus ropes of two *tefachim* on each side).

### Metal Scales

For the *turtani* — the seller of precious metals, essentially a smith or jeweler — the scale need only be three *etzba'ot* (fingers) from the ceiling and three *etzba'ot* from the ground, roughly half a *tefach*. For this scale, however, the *baraita* states: *vekaneh u'masna shelo eini yodea* — the dimensions of the bar and ropes are unknown. This is a striking admission. Why, having specified every other scale precisely, does the author not know this one? One might have expected that for precious metals — where the stakes of imprecision are highest — the specifications would be the most carefully defined. Indeed, one might reason that precisely because of the value involved, the ropes should be *longer*, not shorter, to maximize sensitivity. The *gemara* leaves this unresolved.

---

## Equipment Materials

### Pan Materials

A *baraita* rules: *ein osin mishkalos lo shel ba'atz v'lo shel avar v'lo shel gisteron v'lo shel shear minei matachos* — the pans of the scale (the *mishkalos*, and here the word refers to the pans, not the weights themselves) may not be made of tin, lead, mixed alloy (*gisteron*, per the *Rashbam*), or other metals. Instead, *ela oseh hu shel tsunma v'shel zechuchis* — one should make the pans of rock or glass.

Why not metal pans? *Tosafot* cites Rabbeinu Tam's explanation: the concern is specifically for scales used to weigh meat, fat, and other moist goods — *shelachluchis midabek bahen u'misyabesh* — because the residue from such goods adheres to the metal pan and dries there, creating a buildup that affects subsequent weighings. This concern parallels the earlier *mishna*-level obligation to wipe and clean measuring vessels; even the pan itself must be constructed of material that does not retain residue. It is not, as Rashi suggested, a concern about the metal wearing away — these are hard metals and will not abrade — but a concern about the *accumulation* of material on them.

### Leather Linings

An exception exists: *aval mishkalos sheshoklim bahen kesef v'zahav mutar la'asosan shel mataches ela shetzarich lachaposo or* — for scales used to weigh gold and silver, metal pans are permitted, because precious metal transactions do not involve moist goods and therefore carry no residue concern. However, these pans must be lined with leather, for a different reason: without a protective lining, the gold or silver being weighed might scrape against the metal pan and lose minute quantities in the process. The leather lining protects the integrity of the metal being weighed — much as precious gems and metals are presented today in velvet-lined cases to protect their surface.

### Cleaning Tools

The *baraita* next addresses the *machak* — the tool used to clean out a measuring container (such as a one-liter vessel used to measure wine or grain). *Ein osim hamachak shel dala'at* — one may not make it of a gourd, *mipnei shehu kal* — because it is too light and will not do a thorough job. *Velo shel matechet* — nor may it be made of metal, *mipnei shehu machbid* — because it is too heavy and may scrape away at the walls of the measuring vessel itself, enlarging its interior volume and thereby disadvantaging the seller in future transactions.

### Uniform Cleaning

The *baraita* further specifies: *ein osim et hamachak tziddo echad av vetziddo echad katzar* — one may not make the *machak* with one side wide and one side narrow. The *Rashbam* explains that a narrower edge can get into the nooks and crevices of the vessel more thoroughly, while a wider edge will clean less completely. If the tool has one of each, both buyer and seller have an interest in which end is used: the buyer will want the narrow end used to ensure the full volume is available, while the seller will prefer the wide end. This would reintroduce the very asymmetry the halacha seeks to prevent. The *machak* must be uniform, so that the manner of cleaning is consistent and neither party can manipulate it to their advantage.

### Cleaning Technique

Beyond the tool's construction, the *baraita* governs the speed of its application. *V'lo yimchok bevat achat shehamochek bevat achat ra lamocher* — one may not clean in a single rapid swipe, because a quick clean is disadvantageous to the seller. Nor, in the opposite direction, *v'lo yimchok me'at me'at she'ra lalokeach veyofeh lamocher* — may one clean very slowly and repeatedly, which disadvantages the buyer. The text here presents some difficulty: intuitively, one might have expected the directionality to run the other way — a quick clean that leaves residue would seem to harm the buyer by leaving less volume available, while an overly thorough clean would harm the seller. The *Rashbam*'s explanation of this passage is puzzling, and several attempts to re-read the passage as referring to the pans or the weights themselves (rather than the measuring container) do not resolve the difficulty cleanly.

### Rabban Yochanan

On all of these practices — each of which describes a method by which one party could subtly cheat the other — *Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* made a famous remark, preserved in a *mishna* in *Keilim*: *oy li im omer, oy li im lo omer* — "Woe to me if I say it, and woe to me if I do not say it." The dilemma: *im omer, shema yilmedu ha-rama'in* — if he publicizes these methods of cheating, he risks teaching the cheaters new tricks they had not thought of. But *v'im lo omer, shema yomru ha-rama'in ein talmidei chachamim beki'in b'ma'asei yadeinu* — if he stays silent, the cheaters will say that the *talmidei chachamim* have no idea how they operate, and they will continue with impunity.

The *gemara* records a dispute about what Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai ultimately decided. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak rules: *amrah* — he did say it, and he based his decision on the *pasuk*, *ki yesharim darchei Hashem, tzaddikim yelchu vam u'fosha'im yikashlu vam* — "the paths of God are straight; the righteous walk in them and the wicked stumble upon them." Torah knowledge is meant to guide the righteous, and that purpose cannot be abandoned because the wicked might misuse it. The disclosure of cheating methods is necessary for honest people to protect themselves, and the responsibility for its misuse lies with the one who misuses it.

---

## Scripture Derivations

### Land Measurement

The *baraita* now turns to the verse *lo sa'asu avel bamishpat bamiddah bamishkal u'vamsurah* — "you shall not do injustice in judgment, in measure, in weight, or in liquid measure." The *baraita* expounds each term. *B'middah* — in measure — refers to land measurement: *shelo yimdod l'echad biyemos hachamah v'la'echad biyemos hageshamim* — one may not measure land for one party in the summer and for another in the rainy season. The reason is that measuring ropes absorb moisture in the rainy season and stretch, so the same rope will give a different reading in winter than in summer. Using different seasonal conditions for different parties is a form of deception, even if the physical instrument — the rope — is the same object.

### Weight Storage

*B'mishkal* — in weights — teaches: *shelo yatmin mishklosav bamelach* — one may not store the weights in salt. *Rashi* interprets this as a concern that salt makes the weights heavier, which would benefit the buyer at the seller's expense. *Tosafot*, however, cites Rabbeinu Tam's objection: the context, by analogy to the subsequent liquid-measure case, is clearly speaking about the seller's conduct. Rabbeinu Tam therefore explains that salt actually makes the weights *lighter* — it draws out moisture from the material, reducing their mass — which benefits the seller at the buyer's expense.

### Liquid Measures

*U'vamsurah* — in liquid measures — the *baraita* teaches: *shelo yartiah* — one may not pour with froth. Pouring frothy liquid into a measure means that part of what is being sold is foam rather than substance; the buyer is receiving less than the full volume he paid for. Notably, it is not the measuring vessel itself that is false, but the manner of using it — and the transgression is still prohibited by this *pasuk*.

### Tosafot Question

*Tosafot* raises the question that applies to all of these cases: *pshita d'gezel gamur hu* — obviously, each of these practices constitutes outright theft. Why does the Torah need a special *pasuk* to prohibit them? Does *lo tigzol* not already cover every case? *Tosafot*'s answer is precise: *d'asa kra l'chayeiv m'shaat hartichah af al pi she'adayin lo madad* — the *pasuk* creates liability from the *moment of the improper act* even before the actual theft is consummated. In the case of pouring with froth, the transgression begins the moment one pours with froth, even before one has collected payment or completed the transaction. A parallel formulation appears in the discussion in *Eizehu Neshech*: *lav d'chsiv b'mishkalos lama li litmon mishkalos even u'melach hagzeilah mealyei hi* — if you are maintaining fraudulent weights, that is already full-fledged *gezeilah*, so why the extra *lav*? The answer there too is: *laavor lav m'shaat asiyah* — you transgress the prohibition at the moment you *create* the fraudulent weights, before you have used them in any transaction at all.

### Kal Vachomer

The *baraita* closes with a *kal vachomer*: *v'kal vachomer mah mesurah she'hi echad mishloshim v'shishah b'log hikpid alav Torah* — the *mesurah* is one of the smallest liquid measures, one thirty-sixth of a *log*, an amount whose monetary value is negligible in absolute terms. Yet the Torah is exacting about even this tiny measure. *Kal vachomer* — how much more so with the larger measures listed in the *baraita* — the *hin*, the half-*hin*, the third-*hin*, the quarter-*hin*, the *log*, the half-*log*, the quarter-*log*, the half-*tuman*, the *uchla* — each of which represents a more substantial volume, and correspondingly greater potential for harm when used dishonestly. The daf ends here, and the exposition of these various measures will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Bava Batra 90

## Inaccurate Measures

### Assur L'Adam Measures

The *daf* opens at the bottom of 89b, where Rav Yehuda cites Rav: *assur l'adam she'yish'heh midah chasera o yesera betoch beito* — it is forbidden for a person to keep in his home a measure that is either too small or too large. As Tosafot notes, the biblical prohibition of *lo yihiyeh lecha be'veitcha even va'aven* applies even before one actively uses the inaccurate measure to defraud; the mere act of keeping it with the intention to use it for that purpose already constitutes a biblical violation. However, if one has no intention of using it as a measure — for instance, one discovered it was inaccurate and intends to repurpose it as a storage bin — there is no biblical prohibition. Nevertheless, Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that even then it is *assur lish'ha betoch beito* — forbidden to keep it around at all.

This prohibition extends even to the most mundane repurposing: *v'afilu la'asot b'hein mei raglayim* — even if one intends to use it as a bedpan. One might reason that a vessel pressed into service as a receptacle for urine would never be returned to commercial use. The Gemara rejects this: we are always concerned that in a moment of forgetfulness or urgency, one might repurpose it back for measuring, and thereby come to use an inaccurate measure inadvertently.

### Raba: Gov't Stamps

Raba qualifies this ruling: *lo aman ela b'asrah d'lo chasimi* — this prohibition applies only in a locale where the government does not require official stamps on weights and measures. Where no stamps are required, any container might be pressed into service as a measure, and the concern is genuine. However, *aval b'asrah d'chasimi* — in a place where governmental authorities require that all merchant measures bear an official approval stamp — *ei lo chazi chasima lo shakil*: if a buyer sees no stamp, he will simply refuse to use it. Under those circumstances, there is no realistic concern that an unstamped vessel will be used fraudulently, and the prohibition does not apply with the same force.

This reflects a historically fascinating reality: governmental stamp systems for weights and measures already existed in the Talmudic period, paralleling the development of minted coinage, where the act of minting was itself the governmental guarantee of accurate weight in the precious metal.

The Gemara adds a further qualification: *b'asrah d'lo chasimi nami lo amin ela d'lo mehandesi* — even in a place that lacks stamping, the concern is further limited to locales where government inspectors (*mehandesi*) do not circulate and conduct spot inspections. If inspectors do make rounds, one presumably would not risk using an unauthorized measure. This raises an internal question: how would the presence of circulating inspectors prevent *accidental* misuse, as opposed to merely deterring intentional fraud? The Gemara's answer seems to address primarily intentional misuse.

### Bein Hashmashot

In any case, the Gemara concludes — *v'lo hi* — that relying on circulating inspectors is ultimately insufficient. The reason: *zimnin d'mikri bein hashmashot d'mishkei v'shakil* — there are times when *bein hashmashot* of *Erev Shabbat* arrives, and in the rush of those final moments before Shabbat, the merchant, the buyer, and any Jewish government inspector will all be preoccupied. Under such conditions, an inaccurate measure may be grabbed and used without the usual care. Therefore, even the presence of governmental oversight does not justify keeping an inaccurate measure in one's home.

### Sefer Torah Analogy

A parallel principle applies in other domains: one may not keep a *sefer Torah* in one's home that contains uncorrected errors, for *lo yishkon be-oholecha avla* — one may not allow something that is in a state of perversion to reside in one's tent. The underlying concern is the same: whether the object is a defective measure or a defective *sefer Torah*, keeping it in one's environment creates the conditions for its misuse, whether intentional or inadvertent.

### Modern Scales Q&A

This discussion raises a natural contemporary question: what is the *halacha* in practice today regarding scales in Jewish-owned stores? Digital scales in modern markets are far more precise than the manual balance-and-weight systems of antiquity, but the question of whether a store owner may systematically offset a digital scale slightly in the customer's favor — in order to give a bit more than the exact reading — touches on these very issues. Indeed, one notable kosher establishment apparently calibrates its scale to begin slightly below zero, effectively ensuring the customer always receives a bit extra. As for which type of scale is inherently more accurate, it is worth noting that a traditional balance scale using physical weights has several advantages over a modern spring-loaded scale: springs lose tension over time and are affected by temperature fluctuations, whereas physical weights remain constant. Moreover, a balance scale is unaffected by gravitational variation with elevation. These are not merely theoretical points — they bear on the practical reliability of commercial weighing instruments.

---

## Permitted Measures

### Baraita Se'ah List

A *baraita* reinforces and extends Rav Yehuda's ruling: *lo yisha adam mida chaseira yoter betoch beiso v'afilu hu yavi otam mei raglayim* — one may not keep an inaccurate measure in one's home even as a bedpan. However, the *baraita* then enumerates which measures one *may* produce and keep: *aval asu se'ah, tarkav, chatzi tarkav...* and so on through a list of standard units. The underlying principle governing this list is not merely that these units are legitimate measures — obviously one may keep legitimate measures — but that we are not concerned any of these measures will be confused with one another and thereby used deceptively. The specific question that will emerge is whether any two measures on the list are so close in size that an unscrupulous merchant might substitute one for the other without a buyer's detection.

### Dry Measures

Beginning with dry measures: a *se'ah* is a large unit equal to six *kavs*. A *tarkav* — the name itself being a contraction of *trei va-kav*, meaning "two plus a *kav*" — equals three *kavs*, i.e., half a *se'ah*. Below that comes *chatzi tarkav*, half of a *tarkav*, which is one and a half *kavs*. Then a single *kav*. Then *chatzi kav*. Then *rova*, a quarter *kav*. The pattern is one of successive halving throughout most of the list.

### Log & Ounces

A *rova ha-kav* — the quarter-*kav* dry measure — corresponds in volume to a *log* in liquid measure. A *log* is approximately 14 to 16 ounces. Working upward from a *log*: two *log* equal a *tuman*, four *log* equal roughly a half-gallon equivalent, and six *kavs* (a *se'ah*) works out to something in the range of three gallons in liquid terms, with all the usual caveats about cross-applying dry and liquid volume equivalences. A *revi'it* — one quarter of a *log* — is approximately 3.5 ounces, the well-known minimum for a *kiddush* cup.

### Hin & Liquid

For liquid measures, the *baraita* introduces the *hin*, a biblical unit equal to 12 *log* (equivalent in volume to a *tarkav* in dry measure). The Rashbam's equation of these two terms — *hin* and *tarkav* — reflects not a shared name but a shared volume, and explains why the two lists begin to re-synchronize at this point.

The *baraita* permits: a *hin*, a half *hin*, a third of a *hin*, a quarter of a *hin*, and then a *log*, a half *log*, a *revi'it* (quarter *log*), and an eighth of a *log*. Because liquid measures serve more varied purposes than dry — wine is measured out in small quantities for liturgical use, recipes, and daily consumption — the liquid list descends to much smaller increments than the dry list does. Below the *revi'it*, the *baraita* permits an eighth of a *log* and even an eighth of an eighth, which works out to roughly a tenth of an ounce, known as a *kortav*. The *kortav* appears famously in the context of *mikvah*: if a *mikvah* of forty *se'ah* is missing even a *kortav* — a mere smidgen — it is *pasul*.

### Kav Problem

The Gemara raises a pointed question about one apparent gap in the list: why is a measure of two *kavs* not included? After all, the list permits both one *kav* and one-and-a-half *kavs*, and separately permits three *kavs* (*tarkav*). If the gap between one and one-and-a-half is acceptable, shouldn't the gap between one-and-a-half and two also be acceptable, since both pairs share the same ratio?

The Gemara initially suggests that two *kavs* might be confused with three *kavs* (the *tarkav*), but immediately objects to that answer: *alma tau inshi tilsa?* — are we saying people make errors of a full third? If that were the threshold, then a *kav* should also be prohibited, since the difference between one and one-and-a-half is also a third of the larger figure. The Gemara therefore reframes the answer: two *kavs* is excluded not because it would be confused with three, but because it falls too close to *chatzi tarkav*, which is one-and-a-half *kavs*. The difference between two and one-and-a-half is a quarter of the larger number — and we are apparently concerned that people will not reliably discern a difference of a quarter.

### Quarter & Fifth

This conclusion — that a discernment threshold of a quarter is too close — sets up the next question: if so, why does the *baraita* permit both a *chatzi tuman* (a quarter *log*) and an *uchla* (a fifth of a *log*)? The difference between these two measures is smaller than a quarter. Specifically, if one considers the relative gap between four and five equal parts, the difference amounts to a fifth of the larger — even less than the quarter that was just ruled insufficient. How can these two measures both appear on the permitted list?

### Small Discernable

Rav Pappa answers: *midot katanot beki'ei behu inshi* — with small measures, people are highly discerning. When the measures themselves are tiny objects, users who work with them regularly develop a practiced eye and can readily detect the difference between, say, a quarter *log* and a fifth of a *log*. This is at least the Gemara's claim, even if it runs somewhat counter to intuition: one might think larger measures are easier to distinguish because the absolute difference is greater, while smaller measures might seem harder to differentiate. The Gemara's position appears to be that familiarity and daily handling of small measures sharpens one's ability to detect differences, even when the absolute quantities involved are minute.

### Mikdash Measures

A final question remains: the *baraita* permits both a third of a *hin* and a quarter of a *hin*. A third of a *hin* is four *log*, and a quarter of a *hin* is three *log*. This is the same ratio as four to three — precisely the ratio of two *kavs* to one-and-a-half *kavs* — which we just established is close enough to cause confusion. How, then, can a third and a quarter of a *hin* both be permitted?

The Gemara answers: *keivan de-havu be-Mikdash lo gazru behu Rabbanan* — since these measures are found in the Torah in the context of the *Mikdash*, the Rabbis did not wish to prohibit their use. To prohibit a third and a quarter of a *hin* would effectively outlaw biblical measures. The concern would otherwise be that an unscrupulous merchant could substitute one for the other without a buyer's awareness; but we do not legislate away biblically mandated measures.

Tosafot asks a pointed follow-up: even granting that one cannot simply abolish these measures, why not require that they always be measured out in *log* units rather than as fractional *hin* — e.g., three *log* rather than a quarter *hin*? The Gemara's answer is directed specifically at the *Mikdash* context: *Kohanim zerizim heim* — the *kohanim* are careful and meticulous in their service, and there is no realistic concern that a *kohen* performing the *avodah* will confuse a third of a *hin* with a quarter of a *hin*. Outside the *Mikdash*, for ordinary commerce, the Rabbis were rightly concerned about substitution. Within the *Mikdash*, that concern does not apply with the same force.

---

## Shmuel's Sixth Rule

### Ein Mosifin Shtut

Shmuel states a broader and more conceptually significant rule: *ein mosifin al ha-middot yoter mi-shtut, v'lo al ha-matbeia yoter mi-shtut* — one may not increase measures by more than a sixth, and one may not alter coinage by more than a sixth. This statement addresses a specific but consequential practice: the governmental or communal redefinition of weights, measures, or currency so that the old name now refers to a larger (or different) quantity. The example is vivid: if what was once called a gallon contained 100 units, and authorities now mandate that a "gallon" contain 150, that is a 50% increase — far beyond what Shmuel permits. Even if the intent is to standardize or modernize the system, the increase cannot exceed a sixth of the new, larger measure.

The coinage parallel is equally direct. Rather than a fixed-weight precious metal simply being recoined at a different weight, the concern is that the name of the unit — the *shekel*, the *maneh* — might be reassigned to refer to a different quantity of silver or gold. Shmuel rules that any such redefinition is capped at a sixth.

The *shtut* — the sixth — immediately recalls the threshold in *ona'ah*, and the Gemara will shortly engage with whether this rule is indeed grounded in concerns similar to *ona'ah* or something distinct.

### Price Spike Concern

The Gemara raises the first candidate rationale: *ilima mishum afkuei tara* — perhaps the concern is that a large increase in measure size will cause a spike in prices. The reasoning: if what was sold as a "gallon" now contains fifty percent more, the nominal price of a gallon must rise proportionally. Once a merchant has occasion to raise prices significantly, he may pad the increase beyond what is justified. A small change can be managed cleanly; a large change invites abuse.

But the Gemara immediately challenges this reasoning: *shtut nami hava* — even a sixth can give rise to a price spike. If a merchant is inclined to use the legitimate occasion of measure-adjustment to pad his prices beyond what is warranted, a sixth increase is just as much an opportunity as a larger increase. There is no principled reason why the price-spike concern would draw the line precisely at a sixth rather than at some other figure. This explanation for the rule therefore fails.

### Rava: Bitul Mekach

The Gemara pivots to a second candidate rationale: *ella mishum ona'ah — de-lo le-havei bitul mekach* — the concern is *ona'ah*, specifically that a large change in measures will lead to widespread cancellation of sales. The scenario: a merchant travels between towns selling oil. He is unaware that the destination town has redefined its standard measure to be substantially larger. He sells what he believes is a standard gallon but is actually receiving, from the buyer's perspective, significantly less than a gallon's worth. When the discrepancy is discovered, the sale must be unwound. If this happens on a large scale, commercial life is severely disrupted.

The Gemara then invokes Rava's significant principle — *kol davar she-be-midah u-she-be-mishkal u-she-be-minyan afilu pachot mi-kedi ona'ah chozer* — any transaction involving a mistake in measure, weight, or count may be unwound even if the discrepancy is smaller than the threshold of *ona'ah*. This is a critical distinction: *ona'ah* concerns a mismatch between the agreed price and the market price for a known object. A mistake in *midah* or *mishkal* is categorically different — it is not that the price was wrong, but that the *object* delivered was not the object purchased. You ordered a pound and received ten ounces; the mismatch is in the *res*, not merely in the pricing. Such a transaction is a *bitul mekach* — a nullification of the sale — and even a tiny discrepancy triggers this result.

This principle, established by Rava and endorsed by the Gemara's citation of it, undermines the second candidate rationale: if *any* mistake in measure — however small — leads to *bitul mekach*, then capping the measure change at a sixth accomplishes nothing with respect to this concern. A sixth is still a mistake in measure, and the sale would be voidable regardless. The *bitul mekach* rationale thus cannot explain why a sixth was chosen as the threshold.

### Merchant Loss

The Gemara therefore settles on a third rationale: *ella de-lo le-hevei psida le-tagra* — so that the merchant not suffer a loss. This explanation operates in conjunction with Shmuel's other ruling — stated later in the same passage — that a merchant may not profit by more than a sixth. Suppose a merchant buys produce in one town and travels to another to sell it. Following Shmuel's dictate, he adds one-sixth to his cost and sets his price accordingly. Now he arrives in a town that has, unbeknownst to him, enlarged its standard measure by more than a sixth. When he fills the buyer's measure, he is dispensing more produce than his price accounts for. If the increase in the local measure is exactly a sixth, the merchant breaks even — his one-sixth markup is precisely absorbed by the one-sixth excess he dispenses. If the increase were greater than a sixth, he would actually lose money on the transaction.

The Gemara presses the point: is it sufficient that the merchant merely not suffer a loss? *Revacha lo ba'ei* — does he not also deserve to make a profit? He invested capital, bore risk, and transported goods. *Zavin ve-zavin tagra ikri* — someone who buys and sells at cost is not a merchant in any meaningful sense. The Gemara's answer to this objection is that the principle is grounded in a scriptural source, not purely in economic logic, and the source determines its limits. The goal of protecting merchants from outright loss is what the rule achieves; the guarantee of profit is not what the rule promises.

### Yechezkel Source

Rav Chisda states that Shmuel *kra ashkach ve-darash* — found and expounded a biblical verse as the source for this rule. The verse is from Yechezkel: *ve-ha-shekel esrim gerah; esrim shekalim, chamesh ve-esrim shekalim, asarah va-chamishah shekel — ha-maneh yihiyeh lachem*. That is, twenty *gerah* to the *shekel*, and the *maneh* consists of twenty, twenty-five, and fifteen *shekalim*, totaling sixty *shekalim* to the *maneh*.

### Maneh 50 to 60

The difficulty is immediate: a *maneh* is standardly 50 *shekalim*, not 60. How can Yechezkel say it is 60?

The Gemara resolves this by drawing three simultaneous inferences — *shema mina tlat*:

First, *shema mina maneh shel kodesh kaful hayah* — the *maneh* of the *Mikdash* was double the standard *maneh*. A standard *maneh* is 25 *shekalim* (which, at four *dinar* per *shekel*, yields 100 *dinar* — the familiar *maneh* of 100 *zuz*). In the context of the *Mikdash*, the *maneh* was double: 50 *shekalim*.

Second, *shema mina mosifin al ha-middot* — it is permissible to increase the value of measures. We see that what was once 50 is now being described as 60. The old *maneh* has been redefined to contain more.

Third, *shema mina shtuta milbar* — the sixth is measured from the outside, i.e., from the larger number, after the addition has been made. From 50 to 60 is an increase of 10. Measured against the new, larger figure of 60, that increase is one-sixth. Measured against the old figure of 50, it would be one-fifth. The rule requires that the sixth be computed from the new, larger total — *milbar*, from the outside. Therefore: the maximum increase permissible is one-sixth of the final, enlarged measure, which corresponds to one-fifth of the original.

### Tosafot Gerah

Tosafot raises an alternative reading of how the *maneh*'s redefinition actually worked. The opening of the verse in Yechezkel states *ve-ha-shekel esrim gerah* — the *shekel* is twenty *gerah*. But Tosafot observes from other sources that a *shekel* is actually twenty-four *gerah*, not twenty. Tosafot therefore proposes that what changed was not the number of *shekalim* in a *maneh*, but rather the number of *gerah* in a *shekel*. If a *shekel* was originally twenty *gerah* and was enlarged to twenty-four *gerah*, that is an increase of four out of twenty-four — exactly one-sixth, measured from the larger final figure. And a *maneh* containing fifty of these enlarged *shekalim* would contain the same quantity of metal as sixty of the old *shekalim*. The mathematical identity is preserved; only the mechanism differs.

### Birchat Kohanim

Tosafot cites the view of Rabbeinu Meshullam of Antioch, who asks: if Yechezkel intended simply to state that a *maneh* equals sixty *shekalim*, why did he not say sixty directly? Why specify twenty, twenty-five, and fifteen as separate components?

Rabbeinu Meshullam answers that these three numbers — fifteen, twenty, and twenty-five — correspond to the three verses of *Birchat Kohanim*. *Yevarechecha Hashem ve-yishmerecha* contains fifteen letters; *ya'er Hashem panav eilecha vi-chuneka* contains twenty letters; *yissa Hashem panav eilecha ve-yasem lecha shalom* contains twenty-five letters. Yechezkel expressed the *maneh* in terms of these three numbers because Israel is blessed through the giving of *shekalim* to the *Mikdash*, and so the measure of the *maneh* was encoded in the very letters of the priestly blessing.

---

## Applications

### Rav Pappa Cheila

Rav Pappa bar Shmuel created a new container — a *cheila* — of a certain size (the Rashbam understands it as nine *log*, built from three *kafizei*). He was immediately challenged: *ve-ha-amar Shmuel ein mosifin al ha-middot yoter mi-shtut* — has not Shmuel ruled that one may not increase measures by more than a sixth? If this *cheila* was being positioned as a replacement for an established six-*log* measure, moving from six to nine is an increase of fifty percent — far exceeding the permitted sixth.

Rav Pappa replied: *ana cheila chadta takkini* — I did not enlarge an old measure; I created an entirely new one. Shmuel's prohibition applies to the renaming of existing measures: if a unit that previously contained X is now being declared to contain more than one-sixth above X under the same name, that is forbidden. But introducing a brand-new measure with a new name falls outside the prohibition entirely. The concern that motivated Shmuel's rule — that merchants traveling between towns might be caught unaware by a changed measure — simply does not arise when the new measure is genuinely novel and is not displacing an existing standard.

### Pumbedita & Papunia

Rav Pappa's new measure was then disseminated to two communities with opposite results. It was sent to Pumbedita — *v'lo kibluhu* — and they refused to adopt it. It was sent to Papunia — *ve-kibluhu* — and they accepted it, calling it by the name *Roz Papa*, apparently a vernacular designation for Rav Pappa's measure. The episode illustrates that even when the halakhic legitimacy of a new measure is established, its practical adoption depends on community reception — and different communities may respond differently to the same innovation.

---

## Hoarding Fruit

### Otzrei Peirot

A *baraita* catalogues several categories of economic wrongdoers: *otzrei peirot* — those who hoard produce to drive up prices; *malvei be-ribbit* — those who lend at interest; *maktinei eifah* — those who use undersized measures; and *mafkiei she'arim* — those who manipulate market prices. These are not presented as independent transgressions but as a coherent portrait of those who exploit markets and the vulnerable people who depend on them.

### Amos Example

The *baraita* draws its conceptual vocabulary directly from the prophet Amos, citing the verse *leimor matai ya'avor ha-chodesh ve-nashbirah shever, ve-ha-Shabbat ve-niftachah bar* — "saying: when will the month be over so that we may sell grain, and the Shabbat so that we may open the grain store?" These are people who hold their produce off the market while awaiting optimal prices — waiting for the end of the month or the end of *shemita* — and then flood the market at elevated prices. The verse continues with references to *lehaktin eifah* — making the measure small — and *lehagdil shekel* — demanding that payment be measured in heavier weights — as well as *le'avvet moznei mirmah* — perverting the scales of deceit. The *baraita* quotes the divine oath: *nishba Hashem bi-gaon Yaakov im eshkach la-netzach kol ma'aseihem* — God swears by the pride of Yaakov that He will never forget their deeds.

When the Gemara asks for a concrete example of a *otzar peirot*, Rav Yochanan answers: someone like Shabtai the fruit hoarder — a figure apparently known by reputation for cornering the market.

### Abua Dishmuel

Shmuel's father employed a specific strategy to counteract market manipulation: *mazbin lehu la-peirei be-tara charfa ke-tara charfa* — he would sell his produce at the early-season price, even as the season progressed. When produce was first harvested, prices were at their lowest. Rather than allowing prices to drift upward as supply was absorbed and demand continued, he maintained the early-season low price throughout, preventing the gradual escalation that would otherwise occur.

### Shmuel Bereih

Shmuel's own son employed a different approach: *mashhei la-peirei* — he would withhold some of his produce from early-season sale. Rather than selling everything at the outset when prices were already low, he held reserves. Later in the season, when everyone else's prices had risen, he would bring his stored fruit to market — *u-mazbin lehu be-tara afla ke-tara charfa* — selling at what was now the going high-season rate, but at the old early-season low price. The effect was to drive prices back down at precisely the moment when the market had elevated them, using supply to counteract price inflation.

### Father Better

Both strategies were aimed at keeping prices affordable. The question of which was superior was resolved by a ruling sent from Eretz Yisrael: *tava de-abba mi-dereih* — the father's approach is better than the son's. The reason: *tara de-ravach ravach* — once prices have been eased from the start, they remain low. If the early-season price is kept at a low baseline, the market tends to hold there. By contrast, if prices are allowed to rise and then one attempts to bring them back down by releasing stored supply at lower prices, one is fighting an established higher price point. Once a higher price becomes the going rate in people's minds and market practice, it is far harder to dislodge. It is better never to allow prices to escalate than to intervene after they have already risen.

---

---

# Bava Batra 91

## Hoarding & Prices

### Personal Storage

The Gemara opens on 91b, in the midst of a broader discussion concerning the manipulation of produce prices and the prohibition against hoarding. *Amar Rav*: *oseh adam et kavo otzar* — a person may make his *kav*, his personal measure of produce, into a storehouse. The Gemara carves out a clear distinction between two kinds of holding back produce from the market. On one hand, cornering the market — buying up all available supply in order to drive prices up — is forbidden. On the other hand, retaining one's own grain, the produce of one's own fields, while waiting for a more favorable time to sell, is entirely permissible. One is simply maximizing returns on one's own produce, not engineering artificial scarcity. A parallel reading permits even purchasing produce from the marketplace, provided it is done to meet one's own household needs rather than to speculate.

A *tanya nami hachi* — a parallel *baraita* — supports Rav's ruling: *ein otzrin peirot devarim sheyesh bahem chayei nefesh*, one may not hoard produce that constitutes basic sustenance needs. The *baraita* then draws the limiting principle: *bameh devarim amurim bilokeach min hashuk* — this restriction applies when one is buying from the marketplace, effectively cornering available supply. But *b'machnis mishelo mutar* — holding onto one's own produce is permitted. This confirms Rav's ruling.

### Necessities vs. Luxuries

The *baraita* specifies which categories of produce fall under the prohibition: *kegon yeinot shemanim veslatot* — wine, oils, and flour. It is worth noting that wine is classified here as a basic necessity, which reflects its ubiquity as a beverage in the ancient world. By contrast, *tavlin* — spices such as *kamon* (cumin) and *pilpelin* (peppers) — are considered luxury items, and hoarding them is *mutar*.
