---

## Garden Access Rights

### Garden Hours

A parallel *mishnah* addresses the case of *mi sheyesh lo ginah lifnim miginato shel chavero* — one who has a garden situated behind another person's garden, with access rights through that outer garden. The same time restriction applies: *nichnas besha'ah shebnei adam nichnasin, veyotzei besha'ah shebnei adam yotzin* — entry and exit are restricted to normal hours when people ordinarily come and go.

### No Commercial Use

The *mishnah* adds: *ve'eino machnis letochah tagrin* — he may not bring merchants through the outer garden to conduct business in his own. His access right is personal. If, for example, he wishes to sell the produce of his inner garden, he cannot bring a buyer through the outer garden for that purpose. The right of passage was granted for his own use, not as a commercial thoroughfare.

### No Shortcuts

Nor may he use the path as a shortcut to other destinations: *velo yikanes mitochah letoch sadeh acheret* — he may not pass through the outer garden and continue on to a third property. The access right exists solely for the purpose of reaching his own garden. One could theoretically disguise such a shortcut by pretending to visit the garden before moving on, but the *mishnah* is addressing honest conduct: the right is bounded by its purpose.

### Planting Rights

The *mishnah* then rules: *vehachitzon zorei'a et haderech* — the outer garden owner may plant along the path. Because the path running through the outer garden has not been transferred to the inner garden owner — he merely has access rights, not ownership — the outer garden owner retains full ownership of that strip of land and may plant it. The inner garden owner can walk through the planted area, perhaps trampling what grows there, but he cannot prevent the planting.

### Side Path Agreement

A different arrangement is addressed next: *natnu lo derech min hatzad mida'at sheneihem* — where by mutual agreement, a side path was designated rather than a straight cut through the middle of the garden. In this case, since both parties agreed and the access was not simply imposed, the inner garden owner acquires a stronger sense of right in that path. Consequently, *nichnas besha'ah shehu rotzeh, veyotzei besha'ah shehu rotzeh* — he may enter and exit at whatever time he wishes, including in the middle of the night, since he is using the side path and not cutting through the outer garden.

He may also bring merchants through this path: *umachnis letochah tagrin*. His greater degree of right, born from the bilateral nature of the agreement, extends his entitlements in this respect. However, one restriction remains unchanged: *velo yikanes mitochah letoch sadeh acheret* — he still may not use the path as a shortcut to other properties. The path was agreed upon for his garden's sake, and its purpose remains bounded accordingly.

As for planting: *vezeh vezeh einam resha'im lezor'ah* — in the case of a side path established by agreement, neither party may plant it. The inner garden owner cannot plant it because it is still not his; the outer garden owner cannot plant it because the inner garden owner has a sufficiently firm right of access that planting would interfere with it. The side path sits in a middle category — more stable than a mere imposed access right, but still not full ownership.

---

## Irrigation Canal Rights

### Canal Allotments

The *gemara* now introduces a series of related cases taught by Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel, continuing the theme of access rights. The first case: *amah bat hashlachin* — an irrigation canal, so called because it is approximately one *amah* deep and is used for irrigating a *beis hashlachim*, a field requiring intensive watering. When one sells another the right to such a canal, the seller gives: *noten lo beis amos letocha, ve'ama mikan ve'ama mikan le'agaseha* — a grant of two *amot* and an *amah* on each side for the *agafim*, the banks.

There is a question of how to parse this formulation. One reading takes it as listing two separate grants: the two *amot* are for potential expansion of the canal, and the additional *amah* on each side is for access — standing space to allow the buyer to dig or maintain it. A second reading, preferred by the *Rashbam*, takes the phrase as a single statement: two *amot* total, meaning one *amah* on each side, designated for access, parallel to the garden case. Under this reading, the emphasis is on access rather than expansion. Either way, these grants do not necessarily constitute a transfer of ownership; they represent rights.

### Non-Irrigation Use

The case changes when the sale is *amah beis hakillon* — a channel used not for field irrigation but for other purposes, such as watering animals or washing clothes. (Some texts read *beis hasillon*, from a Greek word related to a type of pump or conduit.) For this lesser use, the allotment is reduced: *noten lo amah achas letocha, vechatzi amah mikan vechatzi amah mikan le'agaseha* — one *amah* for the channel itself, and half an *amah* on each side for the banks. The precise correlation between the intended use of the water and the required standing space alongside it may not be immediately obvious, but presumably the scale of the enterprise — the equipment used, the volume drawn — corresponds to the lateral space needed for maintenance and access.

### Edge Planting Dispute

The *gemara* then asks about the banks themselves: *otzon agaseha nizra'im* — may these *agafim* be planted? The question recalls the garden case, where the outer owner could plant the path because it remained his property. Here, the situation is somewhat different because the *agafim* are directly contiguous with the canal and were specifically allocated in connection with the sale.

Two opinions are reported, both in the name of Shmuel, attributed to Rav Yehudah and Rav Nachman respectively. One says *baal hasadeh zoraam* — the field owner may plant seeds, i.e., vegetables, there. The other says *baal hasadeh notaam* — the field owner may plant trees. The relationship between these two opinions is not simply a matter of one permitting more than the other. In fact, the *gemara* treats planting vegetables as the more striking ruling, because while planting trees (*nota*) obviously implies planting seeds (*zore'a*) is permitted as well, the reverse is not true.

The reason is *chalchulei mechalchali* — vegetables planted at the edge of a canal undermine and loosen the banks. The root systems and moisture-drawing behavior of vegetables destabilizes the soil at the canal's edge, potentially causing the banks to collapse into the canal. This would harm both the canal's integrity and the buyer's standing space alongside it. Trees, by contrast, are held to send their roots downward rather than horizontally through the bank in the same destabilizing fashion. Therefore, the opinion that permits only trees — not vegetables — is the more protective one for the canal buyer, while the opinion permitting vegetables is the more expansive grant to the field owner.

### Bank Collapse Repair

A further *halakha* of Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel: *amat hamayim shekalu agapeha* — if the banks of a water channel have actually collapsed, *metaknah me'osah sadeh* — he repairs them using dirt from that same field. The rationale offered is *beyadua shelo kalu agapeha ela be'osah sadeh* — it is known that the banks did not collapse except into that field; the dirt that formed the banks found its way into the field owner's land when they fell.

Rav Pappa challenged this: *veleima lei maya'ach ashpluha le'ara'ai* — let the field owner say, "Your water caused them to collapse into your canal; the dirt is at the bottom of the canal, not in my field." Rav Pappa therefore reformulates the basis for the ruling: *she'al menat kein kibeil alav baal hasadeh* — the field owner accepted this arrangement implicitly when the original transaction was made. Just as certain access rights are implied by the nature of the transaction even when not explicitly stated, so too is the right to draw upon the surrounding field for dirt to rebuild collapsed banks understood to be part of what the field owner took on when he sold or granted the canal rights.

---

## Public Road Transfer

### Road Relocation Case

The *gemara* now turns to a *mishnah* that introduces a new but thematically related scenario: *mi she'hayetah derech harabbim overet betochah* — one who has a public road running through his field. Imagine a large agricultural field bisected by a public thoroughfare, making efficient farming difficult. The field owner decides to relocate the road: *natal venasan lahem min hatzad* — he takes back the middle portion and assigns the public a path along the edge of his field instead.

The *mishnah*'s ruling is stark: *mah shenasan nasan, veshello lo higi'a* — what he gave them, he gave; and what was his did not come back to him. The field owner loses on all counts. He does not recover the original road through the middle, and the public retains the new road he offered along the edge. This outcome is clearly not the one the field owner intended, and it demands explanation. Either the transaction was legitimate — in which case, why can't he reclaim the old road he was supposedly taking back? — or it was illegitimate — in which case, why does the public keep the new road?

An important preliminary question is who, in fact, has the authority to enter into such an arrangement on behalf of the *rabbim*. The *Rashbam* notes that the *gemara* initially considers this to be permissible on the basis of *kofin al midas Sedom* — the principle that where one party gains and the other suffers no loss, one can compel cooperation. Since the field owner would argue that the public is not harmed by receiving one equivalent road in place of another, perhaps the transaction can be conducted unilaterally, without formal representation of the other side. However, this analogy to *midas Sedom* is imperfect, as a classic case of *zeh neheneh vezeh lo chaser* involves no exchange at all — here something is given and something is taken.

### Path Width Standards

Before turning to the analysis of the *mishnah*, the *gemara* records several standard measurements. *Derech hayachid arba amot* — a private path must be four *amot* wide, enough to accommodate a wagon and allow individual passage. *Derech harabbim shesh esrei amah* — a public road requires sixteen *amot*. *Derech hamelech ein lah shiur* — the King's Highway has no defined limit. If the king and his forces are passing through, they may proceed by whatever route is most direct and convenient for them, and no private claim of property stands as an obstacle.

### Burial Road Rights

*Derech hakever ein lah shiur* — similarly, a burial road has no fixed limit. The *Rashbam* offers two interpretations of this rule. The first is that when a funeral procession must pass through a town or a field on the way to a grave, they have the right to proceed along whatever route is necessary, analogous to the King's Highway — though unlike the king's forces, they could not knock down a structure; they could only traverse open ground such as fields or grass. The second interpretation is more specific: this is the case of someone who has sold another the right of a *derech hakever* — a burial road — to access a family cave or family burial plot. In that case, once the right is sold, there is no limit on how many people may use the path simultaneously, or on its effective width when the entire family processes through.

### Mourning Space

The *mishnah* adds a ruling from *dayanei Tzipori* — the judges of Tzipori — regarding a related matter: *beit arba kavin*. Since a *se'ah* is six *kavin* and a *beit se'ah* is fifty by fifty *amot*, four *kavin* represents two-thirds of that area. The judges of Tzipori specified this as the required standing space for those who come to greet the mourners after a burial — the area needed to accommodate the crowd gathering to offer condolences and pay their respects.

---

## Road Transfer Analysis

### Illegitimate Transaction

The *gemara* now addresses the core analysis of the *mishnah*'s ruling. Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav asks: if the original transaction gave the field owner rights to reclaim the old road, why can't he simply take a pitchfork, station himself at the entrance to the old path, and prevent people from using it? After all, *lo avid inish dina lenafshei* — one may not take the law into one's own hands — but that principle typically yields when a person is protecting his own property from active loss. A property owner defending what is his from ongoing trespass should be entitled to enforce his right. The fact that this is apparently not possible suggests something more fundamental: the transaction itself was not valid.

### Gezeirah: Twisted Roads

Rav Zevid in the name of Rava explains that the transaction is indeed illegitimate, and the reason is a *gezeirah* — a rabbinic enactment: *gezeirah shema yitein lahem derech akalton* — lest one give the public a twisted, roundabout road. Because there is no one to represent the *rabbim* in negotiating this exchange, the field owner's claim that the new road is equivalent to the old one cannot be verified or challenged. A unilateral arrangement could easily be abused: the field owner offers a path that is technically a road but is in practice inconvenient, circuitous, or poorly situated. To prevent this abuse, the rabbis invalidated all such transactions categorically.

Rav Mesharshiya also in the name of Rava offers a superficially similar formulation but with a meaningfully different position: he is actually describing a case where the owner *did* give a twisted road. Under his reading, a genuinely equivalent road could be validly exchanged — the *mishnah* is simply discussing a case where the road offered was not in fact equivalent, and therefore the transaction fails. This position is more permissive than Rav Zevid's across the board invalidation.

### Rav Ashi: Any Change Har…

Rav Ashi states a more sweeping principle: *kol min hatzad derech akalton hi* — any side road is, by definition, a twisted road for someone. *Kerova lizeh verachoka lizeh* — what is close for one person is far for another. Any change in the routing of a public road inevitably benefits certain travelers and inconveniences others. The people who used to live along the original road now have a longer walk; the people who happen to live near the new road benefit. Since no change can ever be neutral for all members of the public, and since the public has no formal representative in the negotiation, any such unilateral transaction must be considered illegitimate. The field owner simply lacks the authority to impose a road change on a community of diverse interests.

### Rabbi Eliezer: Path Sele…

Given that the transaction was not valid, the *gemara* asks: the field owner should be able to recover his old road — *shaklu didchu vehavu li didi*, take back yours and give me mine. Why does the *mishnah* rule that he does not get it back?

The *gemara* answers with a *tannaitic* source: *hamani Rabbi Eliezer hi* — this follows the position of Rabbi Eliezer. As taught in a *beraita*, Rabbi Yehudah says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: *rabbim shebereru lahem derech le'atzmam, mah shebereru bereru* — if the public selects a path for themselves, whatever they have selected is selected and is theirs. The *gemara* immediately asks: *rabbim gazlanin ninhu* — are the *rabbim* simply thieves, empowered to appropriate whatever path they walk through? Rav Gidel in the name of Rav clarifies: this applies specifically to a case where the *rabbim* had a path through a field that was lost — perhaps washed away by rain or otherwise obliterated — and they now need to reconstitute it. Since they have an underlying right to *some* path through that field, whichever route they now choose becomes their path. The word *bereru* — they selected — makes sense in this context: they already had a right; they are now exercising that right by selecting among the available options.

### Unresolved Question

The *gemara* then applies this to our case: since the field owner offered the side road, even though the original transaction was invalid, the act of offering is treated as analogous to the *rabbim* reconstituting a lost path, or at least as triggering their right to select a path. But this analogy is strained. In Rabbi Eliezer's case, the *rabbim* had an existing underlying right and simply needed to select among available routes. In our case, the original road still exists — it has not been lost — and the field owner is trying to reclaim it. Why should the offer of a substitute road, made in the context of an illegitimate transaction, confer upon the *rabbim* rights to both roads?

The *gemara* leaves this question open, and the daf concludes with this unresolved tension: the transaction was invalid, the field owner logically should recover his original road, and yet the ruling of the *mishnah* — that he does not — remains in need of a fully satisfying justification.

---

---

# Bava Batra 100

## Road Swap & Proximity

### Landowner's Swap

The daf opens two lines from the top of 100a, picking up the case of a landowner through whose field a major thoroughfare passed. Wishing to reclaim that road for himself, he offered the public a different route. The *mishna* rules that the *rabbim* retain both roads — the original and the one he offered. The situation is reminiscent of *tmura*, the exchange of sanctified animals, where one attempts to substitute one animal for another and the result is that the first remains *kadosh* and the second becomes *kadosh* as well: the landowner loses on both counts. The obvious difficulty is that this seems internally inconsistent. Either the swap was valid, in which case the *rabbim* should accept the new road and surrender the old one, or it was invalid, in which case they should keep only the old one. Why should they have both?

The *gemara*'s answer is that the swap was fundamentally invalid from the outset, because it was made unilaterally, with no one representing the *rabbim*. Since no authorized party agreed on their behalf, there is reason to fear that whatever road the landowner provides will be less convenient, more circuitous, or simply out of the way.

### Rav Ashi's Principle

Rav Ashi sharpens this point with a sweeping principle: *kol min hatzad derech akalkalot hi* — any road that is off to the side, even a perfectly straight one, is by definition an indirect, out-of-the-way path. The reason is *karov lezeh verachok lezeh*: any shift in a road's location benefits those living on one side and disadvantages those living on the other. Since the swap was unilateral and no one represented all the affected parties, it is inherently invalid, regardless of how geometrically straight the new road may be.

### Why Both Roads?

This explanation accounts for why the *rabbim* retain their original road, but it raises a further question. Once we establish that the swap was invalid, why should the *rabbim* also keep the new road that the landowner offered them? The *gemara* poses this precisely: *lema lehu shkulu didchu vehavvei didi* — why cannot the landowner now tell the *rabbim* to keep their old road and return his field to him, since the entire exchange was void? This question drives the discussion forward.

## Rabbi Eliezer Lost Path

### Rabbi Eliezer Cited

The *gemara* answers: *ha meni Rabbi Eliezer hi* — our *mishna*, which awards the *rabbim* both roads, follows the position of Rabbi Eliezer. A *braita* is cited: Rabbi Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that *rabbim sheberu derech leatzmam* — if the masses simply chose a path for themselves through someone's field, *ma sheberu beru*, their selection stands and they may take possession of it. On its face this is a striking position. Does a community simply begin walking through someone's property and thereby acquire it?

### Communities as Robbers?

The *gemara* is immediately troubled: *Rabbi Eliezer rabbanan gazlanim ninhu?* — according to Rabbi Eliezer, are the masses simply robbers? On what basis could a community seize a path through private property, and on what basis would such a seizure be legitimated?

### Rav Gidel's Lost Path

Rav Gidel said in the name of Rav that the case must be understood carefully — and his reading illuminates the precise language *beru* (selected). The scenario is not that the *rabbim* arbitrarily began cutting through someone's yard. Rather, the community had always possessed an established path through that field. At some point the path became lost — for instance, a rainy season rendered the ground muddy and swampy, and no one could any longer identify where the original road had been. Since the community retains a legal entitlement to *a* path through the property, they are now entitled to *select* a new one. The word *beru* thus means exactly what it says: you have a right to one path, and you are choosing among the available options. This is not seizure but selection among legitimate alternatives.

This reading also explains why the rule might apply differently to a *yachid* than to the *rabbim*. For an individual, one might invoke *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya*: the burden of proof falls on the claimant, and perhaps the landowner would get to designate which path the individual may use, rather than the individual choosing for himself. But the authority of the *rabbim* suffices to give them the prerogative of selection.

### Two Versions of Rav

However, this resolution creates a difficulty. If Rav himself explains Rabbi Eliezer as referring to a lost path and a lawful selection, then Rabbi Eliezer's position is entirely reasonable. Why, then, does another tradition record Rav bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav as ruling *ein halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer* — that we do not rule in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer?

The *gemara* resolves this by noting that there are two independent versions of Rav's position: *ma'an d'masni ha lo masni ha*. One version of Rav is precisely the reading of Rav Gidel — Rabbi Eliezer is addressing only the intelligible case of a lost path from which the community selects a replacement, and according to this version Rav rules in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer. The other version of Rav takes Rabbi Eliezer's statement at face value: that the *rabbim* can begin using any path through private property and thereby acquire it with no prior entitlement — a radical position. According to this second reading, Rav rules against Rabbi Eliezer. The two traditions are thus not in conflict; they simply reflect two different understandings of what Rabbi Eliezer said.

## Rav Yehuda Chazaka

### Better Explanation Needed

Having worked through the discussion of Rabbi Eliezer, the *gemara* circles back to ask: *v'ta'ama mai* — what is actually the underlying rationale of our *mishna*? The *mishna* deals with a case where the *rabbim* already have their original road intact; it is not a lost-path scenario. Tosafos notes that this is precisely why the *gemara* now asks for a better explanation: once it becomes clear that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling only makes sense in the lost-path scenario, it is no longer applicable to our *mishna*. The *gemara* therefore seeks a different basis for the ruling.

### Rav Yehuda's Seizure

The *gemara* answers: *mishum d'Rav Yehuda* — the rationale derives from the principle stated by Rav Yehuda: *meitzar she'hecheziku bo rabbim asur l'kalkelo* — a path in which the *rabbim* have established *chazaka*, taken possession, may no longer be destroyed. The *rabbim*, by having de facto seized rights to it, have made it theirs. Strikingly, this sounds very close to exactly what the *gemara* rejected when it objected to Rabbi Eliezer — *rabbim gazlanin ninhu?* If the *rabbim* simply start using a path and that suffices to make it theirs, are they not simply acting as robbers?

### Rashbam Tones Down

The Rashbam, without explicitly addressing this tension, attempts to mitigate it. In his commentary to the phrase *she'hecheziku bo rabbim*, the Rashbam explains: *she'hishvuhu v'tiknuhu l'hiluch* — the community did not merely walk through the property; they actively went in and improved the path, clearing debris, leveling the way. This is the classic form of *chazaka* — an act of improvement that manifests ownership. Furthermore, he adds: *v'haba'alim yadu v'shatku* — the owners saw what was being done and remained silent. When townspeople send workers to clear a path through your field, and you see them working and say nothing, that silence constitutes an implicit *mechila*, a waiver of your rights. The Rashbam then extends this point: *devadei lerabbim mechila* — even silent acquiescence that would not rise to the level of *mechila* vis-à-vis a single individual does constitute *mechila* when the party acting is the *rabbim*. The public nature of the act, combined with the owner's silence, is sufficient.

The Rashbam then applies this — though with some difficulty — to our *mishna*: *vechol sheken* — and certainly when the landowner actively handed over the road with his own hands, even though he did so under a misapprehension that a valid swap was occurring, that voluntary conveyance to the *rabbim* is interpreted in the *rabbim*'s favor as having been intended regardless. He concludes, however, that even under this analysis the *rabbim* would only keep the new road *ukegon shehechiziku* — where they actually took physical possession of it. A mere declaration or a failed swap would not suffice; there must be some act of de facto possession, whether actively improving the path or, as the *gemara* will now discuss, walking upon it.

There is something genuinely surprising about this conclusion. The *gemara* was offended by the idea that the *rabbim* could acquire a path simply by using it, yet ends up affirming something remarkably similar, now framed under Rav Yehuda's statement. The Rashbam's effort to tone it down — by introducing active improvement and owner complicity — softens the edge somewhat, but the basic structure remains: because it is the *rabbim*, we interpret the owner's conduct in their favor. Notably, this differs from the situation of an individual who acts under a misapprehension; here, because the owner did not explicitly articulate his assumptions, we do not treat the invalidity of those assumptions as sufficient to undo what he conveyed.

There is a real-world parallel here. Just as in certain legal systems a landowner who consistently allows others to use a path through his property may find that an easement arises — which is precisely why property owners post signs warning that trespassers will be prosecuted, making clear that any use is not consented to — so too the *gemara* is tracking the idea that unchallenged use, especially by a community, can ripen into legal entitlement. The *gemara* does not, however, fully specify the precise threshold: how long, how openly, how actively must the *rabbim* act before we assume the owner's acquiescence? That is left without complete resolution.

## Walking as Chazaka

### Walking Acquires

The *gemara* now turns to Rabbi Eliezer's underlying mechanism: once the *rabbim* have the right to select a new path in a lost-path case, how exactly do they take possession of it? The *gemara* answers: *behilucha* — by walking on it. The very act of walking through a space constitutes *chazaka* for a path. A *braita* is cited in support: *halach bah le'orka u'lerochba kana mekom hilucho divrei Rebbi Eliezer* — one who walked a field its length and its width acquires the place he walked. This is the same Rabbi Eliezer, now in a completely separate context: not the *rabbim* and not a lost path, but a straightforward case of one person buying a field from another, where the buyer walks the perimeter. Rabbi Eliezer holds that even though walking the perimeter is not a *kinyan* on the entire field, it is a *kinyan* on the area walked, because walking is itself an act of *chazaka*. The *chachamim*, by contrast, maintain that *ein hiluch mo'il klum ad she'yachazik* — walking alone accomplishes nothing; one must perform a classic act of improvement to effect *chazaka*.

The Rashbam notes that in the context of the *rabbim* seizing a path, he understands *chazaka* to mean they fixed it, as classic *chazaka* requires. But where Rabbi Eliezer uses only the language of selection (*beru*), the *gemara* infers that for Rabbi Eliezer even mere walking suffices.

### Abraham's Walking

Rav Elazar — the *amora*, not Rabbi Eliezer — is asked: *mai ta'ama deRebbi Eliezer* — what is Rabbi Eliezer's source? He answers from a verse: *kum hishalech ba'aretz le'orka u'lerochba ki lecha etnenah* — the command to Abraham to walk the land its length and its width, for it would be given to him. The implication is that Abraham's act of walking through the land was itself a form of taking possession. If so, walking is indeed a recognized act of *chazaka*.

The broader theme this invokes is *ma'aseh avot siman labanim*: the deeds of the patriarchs prefigure and, more than merely foreshadow, help bring about what will happen to their descendants. Abraham walks through the land, and that act lays some form of metaphysical groundwork making the eventual conquest more achievable for his children. In the case of a path, the principle applies with even greater directness: if walking the length and width of an entire field as a *chazaka* is derived from Abraham, then walking a path — whose very function is to be walked — is certainly an act of *chazaka*.

### Sages' Objection

The Sages respond to this proof: *hasam mishum chavivusa deAvraham hu* — there, God told Abraham to do this *kedei she'yei noach lichvosh lifnei banav*, so that the land should be easy for his descendants to conquer. In other words, Abraham's walking was not a standard legal act of *chazaka*; it was a special divine command motivated by God's love for Abraham and was directed toward facilitating the future conquest, not toward establishing a legal precedent for *hiluch* as *chazaka*. Therefore, one cannot derive a general rule from that episode.

The Rashbam's reading of this passage is particularly interesting. He explains the *chavivusa* dimension not merely in metaphysical terms — though the classic formulation of *ma'aseh avot siman labanim* would apply — but in terms of legal standing: *dehavu lehu kiyorshim velo kegazlanim, velo yehei reshus leSatan lekatreg, velo pis'chon peh leba'al middas hadin* — so that the Jewish people would relate to the land as heirs and not as robbers, giving no foothold to the Adversary to bring charges, and closing the mouth of the attribute of strict judgment. This reading carries considerable weight in contemporary political context: it is not simply that Abraham's walking made the conquest easier in some instrumental sense, but that it established the character of the relationship to the land — as rightful inheritance rather than seizure. The irony the Rashbam himself implicitly acknowledges is that if Abraham's walking was not a legally cognizable act of *chazaka*, it is somewhat paradoxical to describe it as conferring the status of *yorshim*. But the point seems to be that it functions symbolically and spiritually to create that status, even if not through the formal mechanism of *chazaka*.

### Vineyard Path Exception

Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina introduces a mediating position: *modim chachamim l'Rabbi Eliezer b'shvil shel kramim* — the *chachamim* concede to Rabbi Eliezer that walking is a form of *chazaka* specifically for a narrow vineyard path. The reason is *ho'il v'na'aseh l'hiluch nikneh b'hiluch*: since the path's entire function is to be walked, the act of walking upon it is the appropriate and natural form of taking possession. The Rashbam notes that this connects to an earlier *gemara* principle: when something cannot be subjected to the classic forms of *chazaka* — just as the *gemara* earlier discussed hard rock, where planting and plowing are impossible — then using the thing in the way it is meant to be used constitutes *chazaka*. A path through a vineyard has no purpose other than to be walked; therefore, walking it is the definitive act of possession, even according to the *chachamim*. The implication is that for a path through a wheat field, since the field's primary character is agricultural and the path is secondary, walking alone would still not suffice for the *chachamim*. But for something that is unambiguously and exclusively a path, the concession holds.

## Path Width Standards

### Vineyard Path Width

When people came before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ami with a dispute over a vineyard path, he ruled: *havu lei k'heicha d'dari tuna d'shavishta v'hadar* — give him the width of a person carrying a bundle of sticks on his back, with enough room to turn around. The Rashbam explains that this case concerns a vineyard path specifically, which may be narrower than the standard private path in the *mishna*. This ruling is then qualified: *lo amran ela d'mesaymi mechitza* — this width applies only where there are walls or defined enclosures on both sides. When there are tall walls, the width of the path must be sufficient for a person carrying a wide bundle to pass through; if the walls are too close, the person simply cannot get through despite the bundle extending beyond him. But if there are no walls — *ela d'shakil kara u'manach kara* — then an even narrower path suffices, just enough to place one foot in front of the other in single file, since the load protruding to the sides is unobstructed.

### Path Measurements

The *mishna* itself states: *derech hayachid arba amot* — a private path, sold by one individual to another, has a minimum width of four *amot*, approximately six to eight feet. A *baraita* records a dissenting view: *acheirim omrim k'dei sheyavor chamor b'masa'o* — others say it is the width sufficient for a donkey to pass with its load. Rav Huna rules: *halacha k'acheirim*. The *dayyanei gola* — the judges of the diaspora — give a measurement of two and a half *gmadim*, which appears to be a variant unit roughly equivalent to the *amah*, though the Rashbam notes uncertainty as to whether it represents a slightly larger or slightly smaller *amah*; the Rambam simply rules in standard *amot*. In any event, Rav Huna rules *halacha k'dayyanei gola* as well, and the *gemara* observes that the two rulings are consistent: *hai v'hai shiura chad hu* — two and a half *amot* is the width a donkey with its load requires.

For a *derech me'ir l'ir* — a road connecting two towns, used only by residents of those two towns to pass between them — the *baraita* prescribes eight *amot*. For a *derech harabim*, a true public road that will be used by anyone passing through the region, the standard is *shesh esrei ama* — sixteen *amot*, roughly twenty-four feet. One begins to appreciate why such roads cut through agricultural fields: towns were surrounded by farmland, and there was no other terrain through which to build them.

For roads leading to the *arei miklat*, the cities of refuge, the *pasuk* states *tachin lecha haderech* — you shall prepare the way — conveying a special obligation of accessibility. Accordingly, the prescribed width is *shloshim ushtayim amot* — thirty-two *amot*, approximately fifty feet, twice the standard public road. Rav Huna asks *mai kra* — what is the textual derivation? He reads it from the doubling: *derech haderech*, the extra *heh* of *haderech* being interpreted to indicate that this road requires double the standard measure. This width is comparable to a modern four-lane highway with a shoulder.

### King & Grave Roads

*Derech hamelech ein lo shiur* — a king's road has no limit. *Shehamelech poretz geder la'asot lo derech ve'ein mochin beyado* — the king may break through any fence or wall to make his road, and no one may prevent him. Reading this in the context of the *mishna* — which is discussing sales of paths — the Rambam understands this as addressing someone who has sold a path to the king. Since the king's road has no fixed measure, the sale cannot be specified, and this creates a problem of indeterminate subject matter. The Rambam does not himself state the conclusion, but the *nosei keilim* note that he would apparently rule the king gets nothing, since when a sale's subject matter cannot be identified there is nothing to convey — a somewhat extraordinary result. The Ra'avad, by contrast, understands it to mean the king himself sets the measure, which practically means one should never make such a deal without spelling out the terms precisely.

*Derech hakever ein lah shiur* — a grave path also has no limit. The Rambam and Ra'avad again read this in the context of a sale. Alternatively, it simply states a standalone *halacha*: people carrying a body have the right to cut through private property to reach the burial place, without limit, *mishum yikara deshichvi* — out of honor to the dead. The larger entourage, the greater the honor. Rabbeinu Gershom adds a further dimension: *zivluta deshichva v'ikara* — the path must also be wide enough so that those surrounding the body are not overwhelmed by its odor as it decomposes, a matter of basic dignity that requires additional space.

## Grave Rights & Ma'amad

### Grave Revocation

The *mishna* states: *hamocher kivro derech kivro mekom ma'amado beis hespedo* — one who sold his grave, or the path leading to it, or the place designated for *ma'amadot*, or the location set aside for *hespedim*. All of this property might be owned and maintained by a family in anticipation of eventual burial, and a person in financial straits might sell it. The *halacha* is that *bain bnei mishpacha vekovrin oso al korcho* — the family members come and bury their relative there by force, against the will of the buyer. The reason is *mishum pgam mishpacha* — because it would be a disgrace to the family for their member to have no proper burial place. The buyer is compensated, but the family's right takes precedence.

This ruling makes intuitive sense when the grave site is part of a larger family burial compound, where the whole extended family has been interred over generations. If one family member has sold his designated plot within the compound to a stranger, so that a stranger now occupies the space while the family member has no place among his kin, the *pgam mishpacha* is vivid and concrete. If the grave were simply an isolated plot with no family context, the reasoning would be less obvious — the family could take the proceeds and purchase a different grave. The *pgam mishpacha* logic is most powerful precisely because of the collective nature of the family burial site.

The *mishna* also introduces the space designated for *ma'amadot*, described as *sadeh beit peras hi beit arba kavin* — an area of four *kavin*. Since a standard *beit se'ah* is a space of fifty by fifty *amot* (2,500 square *amot*) and equals six *kavin*, four *kavin* represents two-thirds of a *beit se'ah*, approximately 1,666 square *amot* — something like forty by forty *amot*, or roughly sixty feet by sixty feet. That is a substantial area.

### Ma'amad Ritual

A *braita* defines the core ritual: *ein pochtin mishiva ma'amadot umoshavot lames* — one must not perform fewer than seven *ma'amadot* and *moshavot* for the deceased. The number seven is derived from *hevel havalim amar Kohelet hevel havalim hakol havel*: the word *hevel* appears five times in that verse from Kohelet, but two appearances are in the plural *havalim*, yielding a total count of seven. The ritual thus numbers seven standings and sittings.

The Rashbam describes the practice: *b'chazirasam min hakever holchin me'at v'yoshvin lenachem ha'avel* — upon returning from the grave, those performing the ritual would walk a short distance and then sit to console the mourner, then rise and walk again, and repeat this seven times. This has an obvious parallel in contemporary practice, where funeral processions pause seven times on the way to burial, though the *gemara* here clearly frames it as occurring on the return from the cemetery. David notes that Rashi in *Megillah* records a version where the practice was performed on the way to the burial rather than on the return, and the Rambam also situates it on the return; both are thus attested in the sources.

### Ma'amad Purposes

Three explanations are offered for this ritual. First, the Rashbam suggests it was a form of *nichum aveilim*, consoling the mourners. Second, it was meant *le-harbos tzar le-meis she-meis u-le-harbos be-vechi* — to multiply grief for the deceased and to multiply weeping, functioning as a form of ritualized lamentation, closer to the *hesped* tradition of wailing than to polite condolence. The *hesped* in classical form — *spod al yerech*, slapping the thigh and wailing — is a visceral, communal act of grief, not a celebration of life. Third, the Rashbam says: *v'nasna isha el libah el libah lashuv be-teshuva, ki chayei adam hevel* — it was meant to move those present to *teshuva*, recognizing the vanity of human life. The standing and sitting, repeated against the words of Kohelet, impresses upon participants that human life is fleeting and that repentance is called for.

The connection to *hevel havalim* could be read in a consoling direction — this world is not where ultimate meaning resides, and the deceased has passed to their true reward. The Rashbam, however, does not emphasize that register. As for the explanation involving *shedim*, demons that cling to those returning from a cemetery and for whom the repeated standing and sitting would provide an opportunity to depart: the Rashbam himself dismisses this: *v'lo nehira* — it is not convincing. If the purpose were to dislodge demons, the practice would be universal, whereas the *gemara* makes clear that it was only observed where there was an established *minhag* to do so.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Account

Rabbi Yehuda describes the actual conduct of the ritual in Judea: *be-rishona lo hayu pochtim mi-shiva ma'amados u-moshavos* — they never performed fewer than seven standings and sittings. The participants would be directed: *amdu yekarim, amdu — shivu yekarim, shevu* — honored ones, stand; honored ones, sit. This gave the signal for each movement, though it says nothing about what was said or done while in place. The *chachamim* pointed out that if the ritual consisted entirely of standing and sitting — nothing more — then it could equally well be performed on *Shabbat*, since standing and sitting involves no prohibited labor. The challenge for Rabbi Yehuda is to explain why *ma'amad u'moshav* is prohibited on *Shabbat*. Presumably the answer is that the ritual necessarily included wailing and formal lamentation, which are not appropriate on *Shabbat*, even though technical *nichum aveilim* would be permissible.

The *gemara* further addresses how the *Shabbat* scenario even arises, given that burial on *Shabbat* is prohibited. The answer is: *be-ir ha-smucha le-veis hakvaros de-mitu bein ha-shmashos* — the town was adjacent to the cemetery, the burial took place just before *Shabbat* began, and those returning found themselves in the cemetery context as *Shabbat* commenced. This also reinforces the understanding that the ritual occurred on the return from the cemetery, not on the way there.

### Rav Avya's Mistakes

The sister of Rami bar Papa was married to Rav Avya. When she died, Rav Avya performed a *ma'amad u'moshav* for her. Rav Yosef said: *ta ba-tartei* — he made two mistakes. First, *she-ein osim ela bi-krovim* — the *ma'amad u'moshav* is performed only by relatives of the deceased, and Rav Avya included non-family members, apparently friends who participated in the arrangements. Second, *she-ein osim ela be-yom rishon* — the practice is only for the day of burial itself, and Rav Avya performed it on the second day, the day after the burial. Abaye added a third mistake: *she-ein osim ela be-veis hakvaros* — it must be done in the context of the cemetery, and Rav Avya conducted it in the town itself, having waited until everyone had already returned. Rava added a fourth: *she-ein osim ela be-makom she-nahagu* — it is only practiced where there is an established local custom, and in that community there was no such custom. Rav Avya apparently attempted to institute the practice without understanding that all four conditions — relatives only, first day only, at the cemetery, and only where it is an established *minhag* — must be satisfied.

## Cave Burial Specs

### Cave Dimensions

The closing *mishna* of the daf addresses the physical specifications of a family burial cave. Whether one has sold a plot for use as such a cave or taken a contracting job to construct one, the standard dimensions are: *arba amot al shesh* — four *amot* by six *amot* — with eight niches (*kuchin*) opening into it: three along one wall, three along the opposite wall, and two facing the entrance. These burial caves were a feature of wealthy families; the archaeological record has preserved impressive examples with grand facades, columns, and elaborate entranceways, though such structures represent only a small fraction of those who died in antiquity. Ordinary burial was in the ground.

The Rashbam works out the geometry: each niche is one *amah* wide, with half an *amah* at each edge and one *amah* between adjacent niches. Along the six-*amah* wall accommodating three niches: three *amot* for the niches themselves, two for the spaces between them, and half at each edge accounts for the full six. Along the four-*amah* wall with two niches: the same logic applies, fitting neatly within four *amot*. The interior space of four by six *amot* is thus fully accounted for.

### Niche Measurements

The niches themselves are specified as follows: *orchan arba amot* — four *amot* in length, corresponding to the full height of a human body, approximately six feet. *Veruman shivah* — seven *tefachim* in height, which is one *amah* and one *tefach*, or roughly twenty-one inches. *Verachban shishah* — six *tefachim* wide, which is exactly one *amah*, or approximately eighteen inches.

These dimensions are the dimensions of a body. Four *amot* at six feet accommodates the average stature of the ancient world, somewhat shorter than today. Seven *tefachim* at roughly twenty-one inches reflects the height — or perhaps the depth — of the body as placed. The six-*tefachim* width of eighteen inches raises an immediate question: how does a body fit into a niche only eighteen inches wide, given that the average shoulder width is close to that or wider? One possibility is that the body was placed on its side. The fuller answer, however, emerges from understanding the actual burial practice: the body was initially laid in the cave on a shelf and allowed to decompose. Once decomposition was complete, the bones were gathered and transferred to the niches for longer-term storage. At the stage of secondary burial — with bones rather than a full body — the six-*tefachim* width would be adequate, particularly if the bones were arranged rather than left in skeletal alignment. This two-stage process of primary deposition followed by ossuary interment is consistent with what has been found archaeologically in the region, and it is the most coherent explanation of how the niche dimensions correspond to a human body. The question of the exact arrangement of the bones within the niche remains open, and whether they were placed in skeletal form or more compactly gathered is a matter that warrants further investigation.

---

---

# Bava Batra 101

## Crypt Dimensions

### Cave 4×6, 8 Niches

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 100b opens a detailed discussion of burial crypt construction, addressing both the seller of a burial plot and the contractor hired to excavate one. In either case, there are presumed minimum dimensions that define what a proper burial cave must include. The *mishnah* states: *oseh tocho shel me'arah arba amot al shesh* — the interior floor of the cave must be four *amot* by six *amot*. Into this space, eight niches (*kochin*) are cut: three along one long wall, three along the opposite long wall, and two facing the entrance. The spacing follows a consistent scheme described by the Rashbam: along the six-*amah* wall, each niche occupies one *amah*, with one *amah* of space between adjacent niches, yielding five *amot*, and a half *amah* at each end — totaling six. Along the four-*amah* wall, the same logic produces three niches: one, one, one, with spacing and corner allowances adding up to four.

### Niche Specs

The dimensions of each individual niche are specified as follows: *orkan arba amot* — the depth is four *amot*, approximately six feet, sufficient for the length of a body. The height is *shiva tefachim*, seven *tefachim*, slightly more than one *amah*, or roughly twenty-one inches — enough for the thickness of a body. The width is *shisha tefachim*, six *tefachim*, approximately eighteen inches, which accounts for the width of the body at its broadest point.

These dimensions raise an interesting question. Eighteen inches of width and twenty-one inches of height are workable for many bodies, but clearly not for everyone. The Rashbam and Tosafot discuss these measurements in terms of the actual dimensions of a human body and a coffin, which implies that the niche was intended for the burial of a whole, recently deceased body rather than for the secondary deposit of bones following decomposition. And yet, from what we know historically, the common practice was to allow the body to decompose and then collect the bones in a process known as *likut atzamot*, the gathering of bones. If that were the case here, the precise dimensional requirements would be far less pressing — one could simply compact or arrange the bones as needed. The fact that the *mishnah* specifies these dimensions so carefully suggests we are dealing with the initial burial of the body in its full form, though the exact relationship between these two practices remains somewhat unclear.

### Rabbi Shimon 6×8

Rabbi Shimon takes a more expansive view. He requires the interior of the cave to be six *amot* by eight *amot* — *oseh tocho shel me'arah shesh amot al shmona* — and specifies thirteen niches: four along each of the two long walls, three facing the entrance, and one each to the right and left of the entrance opening — *arba'ah mikan ve'arba'ah mikan ushlosha miknegdan ve'echad miyemin hapetach ve'echad mismol*. The arithmetic is straightforward for the long and facing walls: four plus four plus three is eleven. The remaining two are placed at the sides of the doorway itself. As the *gemara* will explore, the precise placement of these two additional niches is not simple, since they appear to run beneath the courtyard rather than into the body of the cave.

### Courtyard Layout

Each cave opens onto a courtyard. The *mishnah* specifies that the courtyard (*chatzer*) at the mouth of the cave must be six *amot* by six *amot* — roughly nine feet by nine feet. The rationale given is *ki-mlo ha-mitah ve-kovre'ha*, the length of the bier and those who carry it. The coffin itself is four *amot* long, and one needs additional room for the pallbearers to maneuver, hence the larger six-by-six space.

Into this courtyard open two caves, one on each side. Rabbi Shimon, characteristically maximizing the design, requires four caves, one on each of the four sides of the courtyard — *arba le-arba ruchote'ha*. This raises a natural question: how does one produce such a geometrically regular complex from naturally occurring rock? The answer seems to be that it would require substantial excavation. Perhaps one begins with a large natural cave, collapses part of the interior to create a central courtyard, and carves the surrounding burial chambers from there. The Rashbam illustrates both a simpler configuration with two caves and the more elaborate four-cave complex.

### Rock Type Rule

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel introduces a significant qualification: *hakol lefi hasela*, all of these dimensions depend on the type of rock. He is noting that you cannot apply fixed dimensional standards regardless of the geological conditions. If the rock is particularly hard and sturdy, it may safely support more niches; if it is soft or crumbly, fewer may be safe. This has direct practical implications in the context of a dispute between a contractor and a client. If a contractor was hired to produce eight niches and produced only six, claiming the rock could not safely hold more, who determines the truth of that claim? Conversely, if the client argues that a stronger wall could have supported additional niches, on what basis do we adjudicate? The *mishnah*'s final word effectively acknowledges that rigid standards have their limits when geology intervenes.

---

## Diagonal Niches

### Placement Query

The *gemara* opens by asking a pointed question about Rabbi Shimon's two additional niches — the ones to the right and left of the entrance: *hanei terei l'heicha shadi lehu?* Where exactly are these to be placed?

### Purity Issue

The *gemara* immediately identifies the problem with placing them outside the cave, in the wall of the entrance opening extending beneath the courtyard: *haka midashi lehu* — they would be subject to the constant foot traffic of the courtyard above, which could compromise the structural integrity of the ceiling above the niches. But more significantly, the *gemara* raises the issue of ritual purity. We have a rule: one who stands in the *chatzer hakever*, the courtyard of a burial complex, is *tahor* — ritually pure — because all the graves are located within the enclosed cave chambers, and an open, roofless courtyard does not convey *tumah* the way a covered space does. But if there are niches directly beneath the courtyard floor, then a person standing there is standing above a grave, and *tumah* travels upward. The person would in fact be *tamei*. How then can the *mishnah*'s premise that one standing in the courtyard is *tahor* hold? Clearly, these niches cannot extend beneath the courtyard.

### Vertical Bolts

Rabbi Yosei the son of Rabbi Chanina proposes a creative solution: *de'avid lehu kemin nagar* — one makes them like a bolt, specifically like a vertical doorbolt. The image is of a niche cut straight into the wall at the entrance itself, with the body placed vertically upright rather than lying horizontally. This would situate the niche within the cave wall at the opening, rather than running beneath the courtyard, thereby avoiding both the structural and the *tumah* concerns.

### Disrespect Objection

Rabbi Yochanan objects forcefully: *kevurat chamorim hi zo* — this is the burial of donkeys, not of human beings. The Rashbam explains: when a donkey carcass is disposed of, it is thrown into a pit and lands upright. A human being, by contrast, is laid out horizontally. The very language of the Torah reflects this: *v'shachavti im avotei* — "I will lie with my fathers." To bury a person standing is to treat the human body with contempt. Rabbi Yochanan therefore rules that bodies may not be interred in a vertical posture, rejecting the nagar solution entirely.

### Corner Placement

According to Rabbi Yochanan's view, the resolution is: *d'avid lehu b'keren zavit* — one places the two additional niches in the corners. The simplest reading, reflected in the first diagram of the Rashbam, is that these niches are not placed at the entrance wall at all, but rather at the opposite end of the cave, one to the right and one to the left of the wall facing the entrance. In this way the body lies horizontally, the niche is within the cave, and the courtyard above is not affected.

### Intersection Problem

The *gemara*, however, immediately raises a geometric objection: *v'ha nogei kukin l'hadadi* — but then these niches in the corners will intersect with one another! The problem arises from the half-*amah* margin at each corner. The diagonal of a half-by-half right triangle — using the *gemara*'s standard approximation that the diagonal of a one-by-one square is 1.4 *amot* — is 0.7 of an *amah*. But a niche must be one *amah* wide. If the available wall space at the corner, measured diagonally, is only 0.7 of an *amah*, then to carve out a full *amah*-wide niche from that corner, one would inevitably cut into the openings of the adjacent niches on the neighboring walls. The niches would literally intersect, which is structurally and halachically untenable.

### Height Staggering

Rav Ashi resolves the problem elegantly: *b'mamek* — one simply does not place the corner niches at the same vertical level as the others. If the two diagonal niches are dug either higher or lower than the surrounding niches, there is no intersection. Each niche occupies its own plane, and the physical conflict disappears entirely. The *gemara* then generalizes this principle: in the four-cave complex of Rabbi Shimon, where four caves open off a central courtyard, niches on perpendicular walls would also necessarily intersect if all were at the same depth. The answer there too is *b'mamek* — some caves are set at a lower level, others at a higher level, so that perpendicular niches running toward each other pass at different elevations and do not meet.

---

## Palm-Branch Theory

### Palm-Branch Idea

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua proposes an entirely different approach to avoiding intersection among the four caves of Rabbi Shimon's complex, one that does not require different elevations at all: *de'avid lehu ki charuza* — one arranges the caves like a palm branch. A *lulav*, once its fronds begin to spread, presents a series of diagonal projections fanning out from a central spine. Rav Huna proposes that instead of digging the caves perpendicularly into the walls of the courtyard, one digs them all at angles, like the fronds of a palm branch, so that they splay outward and never meet. It is a geometrically appealing idea.

### Geometry Refutation

The *gemara* dismisses this proposal: *baduta hi* — it is a fabrication, an impossibility. The refutation is geometric. The *gemara* invokes the standard principle: *kol amta be-ribu'a amta ve-trei chumshai be-alchasona* — any square of one *amah* by one *amah* has a diagonal of one and two-fifths *amot*, that is, 1.4 *amot*, representing the rabbinic approximation of the square root of two.

### Diagonal Math

The *gemara* now applies this to the eight-*amah* side of Rabbi Shimon's six-by-eight cave. The diagonal of the eight-by-eight square formed at the corner is eight times 1.4, which equals 11.2 *amot* — *chad sari ve-chumsha*, eleven and a fifth. There are eight niches along those walls. Each niche, projected conceptually onto the diagonal of the cave, occupies one *amah* of diagonal space. Eight niches account for eight *amot* of that diagonal. That leaves only 3.2 *amot* for all the gaps between niches — far too little, given that each gap must also be at least one *amah*. The *gemara* thus concludes that the wall space simply cannot accommodate angled niches of the required width. Cutting a niche at an angle into a wall demands more wall surface than cutting it perpendicularly: if the niche is one *amah* wide but is being carved at a diagonal, the opening it creates in the wall is significantly larger than one *amah* — potentially the full 1.4 — and there is simply not enough wall space to fit all eight. Rav Huna's palm-branch arrangement is therefore rejected as geometrically incoherent.

### Infant Niches

The *gemara* offers a second resolution to the intersection problem, introduced as an alternative: *binpili* — fetuses or very small infants. The intersection points created by niches in adjacent walls, or by corner niches overlapping with the main array, need not be wasted or avoided; they can serve as burial niches for *nefili*, miscarried or newborn infants who do not require a full-sized niche. This is a striking suggestion. If we accept that the intersection zones are used in this way, it follows that in Rabbi Shimon's thirteen-niche cave, approximately three out of every thirteen niches would be allocated to infant burials. That is roughly twenty percent — a figure that, however sobering, aligns with what we know of mortality rates in the ancient world.

---

## Disinterring Bodies

### 1–2 Bodies Rule

The *gemara* now turns to a *baraita* (*tnan hatam*) dealing with a different but related scenario: a person digging in a field who uncovers a buried body. The *baraita* states: *hamotzi met mushkav kedarko* — one who finds a deceased person lying in the natural manner of burial, accompanied by the *tfusah*, the soil immediately beneath and around the body, may disinter both the body and that surrounding earth and reinter them in a proper cemetery. The qualification *mushkav kedarko*, lying in the natural position, is deliberate: a body found in an unnatural posture — upright, contorted, or otherwise abnormally positioned — suggests a violent or improper burial rather than a deliberate one, which carries different implications. The same rule applies if two bodies are found: one may disinter and reinter both, along with their respective *tfusat*, since finding one or two bodies does not in itself suggest that this location was a designated burial ground.

### 3 Bodies = Cemetery

Once three bodies are discovered, however, the situation changes fundamentally. If the three bodies are found with a spacing of between four and eight *amot* from one another — *im yesh beinehem me'arba ve'ad shmona* — the *baraita* declares: *harei ze shchunat kvarot* — this is a burial neighborhood, a recognized cemetery. The spacing parameters reflect what we would expect of a deliberately planned burial ground: too close together might suggest a mass or emergency burial; a consistent spacing of four to eight *amot* is characteristic of an organized cemetery. Once this threshold is met, the bodies may no longer be disinterred. The finder has effectively discovered that the land beneath his field was a cemetery, and the bodies must remain in place.

### 20-Cubit Search

Having established that the area contains a cemetery, the *baraita* requires that the extent of the cemetery be determined. One must probe in all directions from the initial three bodies, extending the search twenty *amot* in every direction: *uvodek himenu ulehalan esrim amah*.

### Iterative Search

If a body is found at the edge of that twenty-*amah* perimeter, that body itself becomes a new reference point, and the search must extend another twenty *amot* from there: *bodek himenu ulehalan esrim amah*. The process iterates outward until no further bodies are found at the edge of the probed zone.

### Context Principle

The *baraita* states the underlying principle explicitly: *she'raglayim ladavar* — once three bodies establish the presumption of a cemetery, there is substantial contextual evidence (*raglayim ladavar*) that any body found within the explored radius is part of that cemetery rather than an isolated burial. Therefore, even a body found alone at the twenty-*amah* boundary — which, had it been discovered first, would have been classified as a single isolated burial and could have been disinterred — is now treated as part of the cemetery and must be left in place. Context determines status. A body found in isolation is treated one way; the very same body, found in the course of exploring a confirmed cemetery, is treated entirely differently.

---

## Cave Application

### Reinterpretation

The *gemara* reads this *baraita* not purely in terms of ordinary ground burial but through the geometric framework established in the earlier discussion of cave-niche complexes.

### Ground vs. Cave

It is worth noting that the *baraita* almost certainly originated in the context of ground burial rather than cave niches. Someone digging in a field and hitting buried bodies is plowing through soil, not breaking into the wall of a carved crypt. Ground burial, as we know from historical sources, was far more common than the elaborate multi-chamber cave complexes described in the *mishnah* — those were the domain of the wealthy. Yet the *gemara* presses the *baraita*'s specific numbers into service as explanations of the cave system.

### Spacing Rationale

The *gemara*'s reinterpretive move asks why the *baraita* specifies four to eight *amot* between bodies, and why twenty *amot* as the search radius. The answers, read through the lens of the cave system: the spacing of four to eight *amot* maps onto the spacing between niches and between cave walls in the configurations described by the *mishnah*. Three bodies found within that range would correspond to three niches from the same cave complex being encountered. The twenty-*amah* search radius corresponds to the overall dimensions of the courtyard and surrounding cave layout — the outer boundary within which one would expect to find all members of the same burial complex. If the field above which one is digging turns out to overlie such a cave system, the geometric parameters of the *baraita* make sense as a way of delineating the extent of the underground complex below.

---

---

# Bava Batra 102

## Finding Bodies

### Intro & 1-2 Bodies

The *gemara* on today's daf picks up from a *braita* at the bottom of 101b, which quotes a *mishna* from *Oholot*. The *mishna* opens with the case of *hamotzei meit mushkav kedarko* — one who finds in a field a body that has been laid down in the manner consistent with intentional burial, as opposed to a body that has fallen in battle or been murdered and placed in some irregular position. The distinction is significant: the proper positioning of the body indicates deliberate burial rather than accidental or hasty disposal.

The *mishna* then addresses what one may do with such a body. If only one or two bodies are found, the ruling is *notlo ve'et tefusato* — one removes the body together with the soil directly beneath it, the *tefusah*, into which bodily fluids may have seeped and which is buried together with the body. This right of relocation exists because the landowner has an interest in removing the source of *tumah* from his field — a practical concern given that *tumah* restricts *kohanim* from the area and complicates agricultural activities. It bears mention that this removal of the surrounding soil applies only when the body was buried; if the deceased fell in battle and was not interred, the halakha does not require taking the soil beneath, a distinction that the *gemara* leaves somewhat unexplained. The rule for two bodies is the same: *notlan ve'et tefusan*, one removes them together with their respective soil.

The primary concern driving this entire discussion is *tumah*. It should be clarified that walking on top of ground beneath which bodies lie buried deep below does not necessarily carry a prohibition for the landowner; there is no *issur* in using the land above such caves. The concern is rather one of practical consequence — the *tumah* that permeates the area.

### 3 Bodies = Graveyard

The *mishna* then addresses the case of *matza sheloshah* — finding three bodies. One might argue that even three bodies in a field could reflect a tragic incident, such as a caravan attacked by bandits whose members were hastily buried at the site before the group moved on. The *mishna* therefore specifies two conditions that together warrant an assumption of a graveyard: the bodies must be laid out in a manner consistent with proper burial, and they must be spaced at the intervals one would expect in a genuine burial site. When three bodies satisfy both conditions, one must assume the existence of an established graveyard beneath the field.

Once a graveyard is assumed, one may not relocate the bodies. The rationale has two dimensions. First, the bodies may already be in an established public burial ground, which the individual landowner has no right to disturb. Second, if there is a graveyard here, there may well be additional graves extending outward in multiple directions, and a broader investigation is required to determine the full extent of the *tumah*.

A question naturally arises about *kavod ha-met* — the honor owed to the dead — in a case where a buried *beit ha-kevarot* lies beneath what is functionally a wheat field. The distinction seems to lie in whether the nature of the space is visibly that of a graveyard. A field with a *beit ha-kevarot* buried below it does not present itself as a graveyard in any perceptible sense, and the obligations that flow from the sanctity of a cemetery may not attach in the same way to ground that simply happens to have graves beneath it.

### 4-8 Amot Spacing

The *mishna* specifies that if there are between four and eight *amot* encompassing the three bodies — *im yesh beinehen me'arba ve'ad shmoneh* — then *harei zu shechunat kvarot*, this constitutes a neighborhood or district of graves. Reading the language carefully, *yesh beinehen* might seem to indicate spacing between individual bodies, but it is being understood as the total distance that encompasses all three — the outer edges of the first and third bodies span between four and eight *amot*.

The language *shechunat kvarot* is notable: it designates not quite a full *beit ha-kevarot* but a recognized area of burial, which then triggers the investigation described next.

### 20 Amah Search

Once three bodies are found within the qualifying range, the *mishna* requires: *ubodek mimeno ulehalan esrim amah* — one must search outward from there in twenty *amot*, presumably in multiple directions, as will be discussed. The logic is that if a graveyard has been established, there may be additional graves extending beyond the three discovered.

If a body is found at the end of twenty *amot* — *matza echad besof esrim amah* — the search does not terminate there. Rather, *bodek mimeno ulehalan esrim amah*, one continues checking another twenty *amot* from that newly found body, and so on, until twenty *amot* are cleared with no additional findings.

The reason one cannot simply stop upon finding a body at the outer edge of the first twenty *amot* is grounded in a principle of *sheraglayim ladavar* — substantiation. Ordinarily, a single grave standing alone would be treated as an isolated burial and could be relocated. But once that grave is found in the context of an established graveyard, it must be presumed part of that graveyard. And since it is part of the graveyard, one cannot declare the graveyard to have ended at that point; perhaps it continues further. The *mishna* itself notes this: *she'ilu*, had this single body been discovered in isolation, *notlo ubitfusato*, it would have been relocated. But found after establishing that a graveyard exists in the area, it must be treated as part of that graveyard, and the search must continue.

---

## Cave Dimensions

### Rashbam: 4-8 Amot

The *gemara*'s treatment of this *mishna* is somewhat surprising: it reads the case through the lens of cave burial, not through the more common model of straight burial in the ground. This requires explanation, because the *mishna* does not mention caves, and historically, burial in caves with niches — *kokhim* — was largely a practice of the wealthy. Ordinary people were generally buried directly in the ground. Nevertheless, the *gemara* insists on interpreting this *mishna* through the framework of cave burials, and the discussion of four-to-eight *amot* flows from that interpretive choice.

Where does the four-to-eight range come from? According to the *Rashbam*, the minimum of four *amot* is achieved by assuming that the spacing between the individual niches is less than a full *amah* — perhaps half an *amah* or even less. With compressed spacing, three graves can fit within four *amot*.

### Tosafot Corner

*Tosafot* offers a more elegant explanation. The minimum of four *amot* can be understood if the three bodies are arranged around a corner of the cave. In the earlier *gemara*, a small margin was assumed at the corner — about half an *amah*. With three bodies, two along one wall and one turning the corner, the total linear distance measured along the outer edge can fall within four *amot*. This accounts for the minimum without requiring any unusual compression of spacing.

### R. Shimon: 6×8

The maximum of eight *amot* is explained by reference to Rabbi Shimon's dimensions for a burial cave: six *amot* by eight *amot*. According to Rabbi Shimon, a cave wall could be as long as eight *amot*. If a wall is eight *amot* long and accommodates four niches, a cave with only three occupied niches would have three bodies within eight *amot*. The fact that one niche is unoccupied is not extraordinary; the *mishna* is describing a scenario in which not every available space has been filled.

### Why Not Beyond 8

The upper limit of eight is therefore tied directly to Rabbi Shimon's understanding of cave dimensions: since no wall exceeds eight *amot* according to the standard, finding three bodies spread across more than eight *amot* would not warrant an assumption of graveyard — the spacing would be too wide to reflect a normal cave configuration. Although the *mishna* is setting a standard and not a maximum for the size of any individual's burial plot, the practical assumption is that beyond eight *amot*, the natural inference of a unified graveyard no longer applies. Either they are not all affiliated or they are simply not close enough to one another to compel that conclusion.

Thus: four *amot* as the minimum because any more compressed would suggest accidental or emergency placement rather than an organized graveyard; eight *amot* as the maximum because that corresponds to Rabbi Shimon's longest cave wall and the standard spacing that a legitimate burial arrangement would produce.

---

## 20 Amah Analysis

### Multi-Directional

The *gemara* now turns to the question of why the search must extend twenty *amot* and in what directions. Consider a typical cave complex under Rabbi Shimon's dimensions: a cave six *amot* wide and eight *amot* long, with niches along the walls. When three bodies are found, one does not know which wall they occupied or which part of the complex they represent. The three discovered might be along the longer wall, or they might be along one of the shorter walls, or they might represent bodies from different walls.

If the three bodies were on one of the longer walls, then on the opposite longer wall — eight *amot* away — there could be additional bodies. Beyond the far wall there may be another cave complex. In all, the total distance to check along the main axis could reach the length of the first cave plus the width of the courtyard plus the length of a second cave — a significant span. Similarly, one does not know if the three bodies found are at the near end or the far end of the cave, which means the search must also proceed in the opposite direction.

Because the exact configuration is unknown, the search must be conducted in multiple directions — not just along the axis of the wall where the bodies were found, but laterally as well — since the discovered bodies might have been on a transverse wall.

### Rashbam Diagonal

The *Rashbam* explains why the twenty-*amah* search protocol requires checking at an angle — *be-alakhsona* — in addition to a straight-line search. Since not only is the cave six *amot* wide, but each niche runs four *amot* deep into the wall, the searcher must account for bodies buried at varying depths. A straight-line search directly down the cave's axis might miss a body buried at a different depth. By checking at an angle, one covers more ground relative to depth, increasing the likelihood of intersecting a burial regardless of how far into the niche it lies. According to the *Rashbam*, one would make this diagonal check on both sides. The intuition is that if all burials are at the same depth but that depth is unknown, a diagonal pass will intersect the burial plane at some point regardless of its exact position.

### Configuration

The deeper problem is that the searcher cannot know the configuration of the cave complex. The direction of the search — and how far one needs to go — depends on which wall the discovered bodies were on and which direction the remaining cave extends. Since one does not know which of the bodies found is at the head or foot of the grave, and since the *mishna* does not require that this be determined, the search must account for all plausible configurations. This means going twenty *amot* in multiple directions even though a precise knowledge of the cave's orientation might reduce the required scope.

The *Rashbam*'s explanation of the twenty *amot* as deriving from one cave complex does not fully resolve why one would have to search in all directions equally. If the bodies are pointing in one direction, that should indicate which wall they are on and thus which direction is relevant. The *gemara* nevertheless proceeds on the assumption that the twenty-*amah* search is required in multiple directions since the orientation cannot be determined with certainty.

One further point: the *mishna*'s rule that finding a single body at the end of twenty *amot* requires continuing the search can be understood, under the cave-complex reading, as follows. If the cave complex extends from one group of bodies to another, finding a body at the end of twenty *amot* might seem to mark the boundary of a single cave complex — one could argue the complex has been fully identified and no further search is needed. But the *mishna* rejects this: once one cave complex has been established, finding another body nearby does not allow one to say the graveyard ends there. That body might be the beginning of an entirely separate cave complex. Only when twenty *amot* are cleared with no findings can the search end.

---

## 22 to 20 Resolution

### Problem Stated

The *gemara* now raises a sharp problem. *Amar Mar*: the *mishna* specifies a range of four to eight *amot* and a search radius of twenty *amot*. *Me'arba ve'ad shmona mani* — whose opinion does this reflect? *I Rabbanan* — if it is the *rabbanan*, who hold that a cave wall is four *amot* by six *amot*, one would not find three bodies in a wall of eight *amot*, since eight exceeds the *rabbanan*'s maximum wall length. *I Rabbi Shimon* — if it is Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the cave is six *amot* by eight *amot*, then you could have three bodies within eight *amot* with one niche empty. That accounts for the maximum of eight.

The *gemara* then turns to the twenty *amot*. *Eima seifa: bodek heimenu ulehalan esrim amah. Mani?* — whose opinion does this reflect? *I Rabbi Shimon esrim ve-tarten havyan* — according to Rabbi Shimon with his six-by-eight cave, the total distance to check should be twenty-two *amot*, not twenty: eight for the first wall, six for the width, and eight for the opposite wall. *I Rabbanan tmoneh esrei havyan* — according to the *rabbanan* with a four-by-six cave, the total would be eighteen: six plus six plus six. Neither figure matches twenty.
