At this stage it should also be noted that the *Rashbam* observes a difficulty in his own reading: if we are going to now argue that the cave is six *amot* wide (to fit the *rabbanan*'s dimensions) as a way of approaching the twenty-*amah* number, we cannot simultaneously claim that three bodies can fall within eight *amot*, since under the *rabbanan* the wall is only six *amot* long. The *gemara* is aware of the tension but proceeds.

### Rabbanan & Diagonal

The *gemara*'s first answer: *le-olam Rabbanan hee* — the *mishna* follows the *rabbanan*, whose cave is six *amot* by four *amot* (or rather, whose wall length is six *amot*). Under the *rabbanan*, the straight-line calculation yields eighteen *amot*, not twenty. But the *mishna*'s protocol calls for checking *be-alakhsona* — at a diagonal — and by going at a diagonal rather than straight, the effective distance covered is longer. Specifically, the *gemara* argues that a diagonal across a six-by-four rectangle is eight *amot*, producing eight plus six plus six equals twenty.

The *Rashbam* explains the rationale for the diagonal check: because the searcher is uncertain of his exact position within the cave complex, and because the niches run four *amot* deep, going at an angle covers more ground and reduces the risk of missing a buried body.

### Tosafot Math

*Tosafot* challenges the *Rashbam*'s mathematics. The *gemara*'s claim is that the diagonal of a six-by-four rectangle is eight *amot*. This is what the *Rashbam* accepts. But *Tosafot* demonstrates that this cannot be correct. The *gemara* elsewhere operates with the principle that the diagonal of any square is approximately 1.4 times the side — this is the rabbinic approximation of the square root of two. A four-by-four square therefore has a diagonal of approximately 5.6 *amot*. A six-by-four rectangle can be divided into a four-by-four square and a two-by-four remainder. The diagonal of the four-by-four portion is 5.6, and adding the remaining two *amot* gives 7.6 — not eight. *Tosafot* thus proves geometrically, without recourse to any formula, that the *Rashbam*'s claim that the diagonal of a six-by-four equals eight is incorrect.

For those who prefer the precise calculation: by the Pythagorean theorem, the square root of six squared plus four squared equals the square root of thirty-six plus sixteen equals the square root of fifty-two, which is approximately 7.2 *amot*. In either approach — *Tosafot*'s rabbinic method or the Pythagorean formula — the diagonal falls short of eight. *Tosafot*'s proof is impressive precisely because it is made without a formula, relying instead on the *gemara*'s own approximation method.

The *gemara* itself anticipates part of this problem. *U-midde-ha be-alakhsona hai nami be-alakhsona esrim ve-tartei havyan* — if one is going to do a diagonal check at one end, consistency would require doing a diagonal at the other end too, which would bring the total back to twenty-two rather than twenty. The *gemara* responds: *chada be-alakhsona amrinan tartei be-alakhsona lo amrinan* — we require a diagonal check in one direction but not in both. The rationale is that the diagonal check, which demands greater care and coverage, is required closer to where the original bodies were found, but not necessarily at the far end of the search. This is first answer to the problem of twenty versus twenty-two.

### Infant Graves

The *gemara* then offers a second answer through Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi: *le-olam Rabbi Shimon hi* — the *mishna* actually follows Rabbi Shimon, with his eight-*amah* wall. *Ve-hacha be-mai askinan bi-nefili* — the case involves infant graves (*nefili*). If the original three bodies discovered were infants, one might assume the entire cave complex was dedicated to infant burials. Infants' bodies are smaller, so the niches and the overall cave would be proportionally smaller — perhaps only six *amot* rather than eight. This brings the math from twenty-two back toward twenty.

The *gemara* then asks: *u-midehava bi-nefili ha nami bi-nefili?* — if we have established that the first set of graves involved infants, why not assume that the graves found at the far end of the search are also infant graves, and therefore shrink that end as well? The answer is: *chada bi-nefili amrinan tartei bi-nefili lo amrinan* — we apply the infant-grave assumption once, to the first set, but we do not extend it to both ends of the search. This parallels the logic of the diagonal answer: leniency in one direction, not both.

All of this analysis rests on the *gemara*'s unusual insistence on reading the *mishna* through the framework of cave burial rather than straightforward ground burial — an interpretive choice that the *gemara* does not explicitly justify, and which generates considerable difficulty throughout.

---

## Extra Bodies Logic

### Compressed Burials

The final portion of the *mishna* addresses a case of *retzufim* — bodies buried with more compression than normal, so that four bodies fall within less than four *amot*. The *tana kamma* rules that such compactly arranged bodies do not constitute a graveyard: they are not laid out with the standard spacing, and therefore the presumption of an established burial ground does not apply. The three or four bodies found together may nonetheless be removed and reinterred elsewhere, along with the soil beneath them.

Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon: *ro'in et ha-emtza'in ke'ilu einam* — one looks at the middle bodies as if they are not there. That is, if four bodies are buried within, say, five *amot* — too condensed to qualify as a graveyard under normal rules — Rabbi Shimon instructs us to disregard one of the middle bodies. The remaining three would then fall within four to eight *amot* and the site would qualify as a *shechunat kvarot*.

### Vineyard Parallel

The *gemara* notes that precisely this type of reasoning — whether to ignore extra or intermediate items when determining whether a legal threshold has been met — appears in a parallel dispute involving vineyard spacing, and that Rabbi Shimon and the *rabbanan* take the opposite positions there. A vineyard planted with fewer than four *amot* between the vines — *kerem hanatu'a pachot me'arba amot* — is not a proper vineyard, and the laws of *kil'ayim* do not apply to it in the same way. Rabbi Shimon says: *eino kerem* — it is not a vineyard, period; the compressed spacing disqualifies it. The *chachamim* say: *harei zeh kerem ve-ro'in et ha-emtza'iyim ke'ilu einam* — it is a vineyard, and we look at the intermediate vines as if they are not there. So in the vineyard case, the *chachamim* apply the principle of ignoring extras to establish a legal classification, while Rabbi Shimon refuses; whereas in the grave case, Rabbi Shimon applies that principle and the *tana kamma* refuses.

### Emergency vs Intent

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *kashya de-Rabbanan a-de-Rabbanan kashya de-Rabbi Shimon a-de-Rabbi Shimon* — both the apparent self-contradiction of the *rabbanan* and the apparent self-contradiction of Rabbi Shimon are not difficult. *De-Rabbi Shimon a-de-Rabbi Shimon la kashya* — Rabbi Shimon's positions are in fact consistent. In the vineyard case, Rabbi Shimon refuses to ignore the extra vine because *lo nata inish ada'ata le-me'ekar* — one does not plant a vine with the intention of uprooting it. The act of planting was intentional and deliberate; it cannot be treated as an accident or a temporary measure. Therefore the vine is counted, the spacing is too tight, and it is not a vineyard.

By contrast, in the grave case, *zimnin de-mishtarmi lei bein hashmashot* — sometimes it happens that someone has to bury a body on *erev Shabbos*, rushed and unable to prepare the proper spacing, *u-mikrei u-manach lei* — and he simply places it wherever he can. The implied understanding is that he intended to return after *Shabbos* and reinter the body in its proper place. Because the extra burial was not meant to be permanent, one can treat it as though it is not really part of the graveyard, ignore it for purposes of determining spacing, and conclude that the remaining three bodies do constitute a *shechunat kvarot*.

For the *rabbanan* the logic is the inverse. In the grave case, *de-minaval* — because it is deeply disrespectful to bury a body with such compressed spacing — *lo mikrei kever*, it does not constitute a proper grave. The disrespectful treatment itself disqualifies the site from being recognized as an established graveyard, regardless of the emergency circumstances. But in the vineyard case, one can easily imagine planting an extra vine with the intention of keeping only the best ones — *d'shapir shapir, de-la shapir lihevei le-tzivei*, a good vine remains and a weak vine will become firewood. Since that extra vine was always a candidate for removal, the *chachamim* are willing to look past it and treat the remaining vines as a proper vineyard.

### Respect Argument

The *Rashbam* presses a counter-argument against the *gemara*'s explanation of Rabbi Shimon's position in the grave case. The *gemara* had said that the extra body was placed there under emergency conditions — *erev Shabbos* — with the intent to relocate it afterward. The *Rashbam* argues that this logic fails: even in an emergency, no one would bury a body in a manner that is so disrespectful of the deceased. *Kavod ha-met* is a serious obligation, and the very fact that the body ended up compressed into this space shows that its placement was not an emergency measure — it was simply done incorrectly, by someone who did not understand the proper way to establish a burial site. The placement was therefore entirely intentional, not a temporary accommodation, and there is no basis to treat it as though the body is not really there. On the *Rashbam*'s reading, Rabbi Shimon's ruling — that we ignore the extra body and recognize the site as a graveyard — must rest on some other logic than the emergency-intent rationale the *gemara* offers.

---

## Land Measurement

### Beis Kor Measure

With *hadran lach ha-mocher et ha-peiros*, the *gemara* transitions to an entirely new *mishna*. The new perek opens with a case of land sale. *Ha-omer la-chaveiro: beis kor afar ani mocher lach* — one says to his fellow: I am selling you a *beis kor* of land. The *beis kor* is a measure of area derived from volume: a *kor* is a volumetric measure for grain, and a *beis kor* denotes the area of land required to sow one *kor* of seed. More concretely, a *beis se'ah* — fifty by fifty *amot* — is a standard unit. There are six *kavim* in a *se'ah*, and a *kor* equals thirty *se'ahs*, making a *beis kor* equal to thirty *beis se'ahs*. This is an enormous area — approximately 150,000 square feet — and the halakhic rules governing its sale are the subject of the new *mishna*.

### Boulder Exclusion

The *mishna* addresses a scenario in which the sold parcel contains obstructions: *hayu sham neka'im amukim asarah tefachim* — deep crevices of ten *tefachim* in depth — *o sla'im gevohim asarah tefachim* — or boulders protruding ten *tefachim* in height. The *Rashbam* understands these obstructions to be four *amot* by four *amot* in their horizontal dimensions as well, approximating the area of an independent domain. When such a feature — a crevice or boulder that is ten *tefachim* deep or tall — sits within the parcel, the ruling is *ein nimdadin imah*: it is not included in the measured area. The seller cannot count the space occupied by this boulder or crevice as part of the *beis kor* being sold; he must make up that space elsewhere in the parcel or adjust accordingly.

If the obstruction is *pachos mikan* — less than ten *tefachim* in height or depth — the ruling is *nimdadin imah*: it is included in the measured area, and the buyer receives no additional land to compensate.

### Precise vs Approx

The *mishna* distinguishes between a precise sale and an approximate one. If the seller said not *beis kor* but *ki-beis kor* — *like* a *beis kor*, approximately a *beis kor*'s worth — the word *ki* introduces an element of approximation. Under this formulation, *afilu hayu sham neka'im amukim yoser me'asarah tefachim o sla'im gevohim yoter me'asarah tefachim, harei elu nimdadin imah* — even if there are crevices deeper than ten *tefachim* or boulders taller than ten *tefachim*, they are all included in the measured area. The approximate formulation signals that the buyer is acquiring the land as it stands, with all its features, and the stated measure is a rough approximation rather than a precise guarantee. The lack of precision does not mean the buyer receives less than a full *beis kor*; it means the full area including all obstructions counts toward the promised measure.

---

---

# Bava Batra 103

## Masechta Structure

### Daf 103 Opening

Today's daf is 103. We pick up immediately after the *mishnah* on 102b, beginning the seventh *perek* of the *masechta*.

### Perek Structure

To appreciate the position of *perek* seven within the larger structure of *Bava Batra*, it is worth stepping back for a bird's-eye view. The first two *perakim* form a natural unit centered on the laws of neighbors — building walls, questions of privacy, and activities in one's own domain that might encroach upon another's rights. The third *perek* addresses *chazaka*: the principle that three years of uncontested presence on land substantiates one's claim to it. *Perakim* four, five, and six then turn to matters of buying and selling — what is included in a sale of various objects, how acts of *kinyan* are performed, and questions of *mekach ta'us* when a seller delivers something other than what was promised. *Perek* seven, our present subject, is the concluding chapter of this group, the last of the *perakim* concerned with acts of commercial transaction.

### Future Sections

A meaningfully different section of the *masechta* begins with *perek* eight and runs through *perek* ten. Those chapters address death, inheritance, bequests, and the rabbinic forms of wills — material quite distinct in character from everything that precedes it. Within a few days, then, we will find ourselves in a significantly different part of *Bava Batra*.

---

## Beit Kor Dimensions

### Beit Kor Conversions

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 102b opens with the case of a *beit kor*, defined as thirty *se'ah*. To give a sense of scale: a single *beit se'ah* is approximately 5,000 square feet, or roughly 500-plus square yards. Thirty *beit se'ah* therefore amounts to approximately 18,000 square yards — somewhere in the vicinity of three and a half American football fields, or approximately four acres. That is the expanse of land under discussion.

### Se'ah & Mishkan

A helpful point of reference is the *chatzer* of the *mishkan*, which measured 50 by 100 *amot*, yielding 5,000 square *amot*. That corresponds to two *beit se'ah*, meaning a single *beit se'ah* is half the area of the *mishkan* courtyard. With that frame of reference in mind, the scale of a *beit kor* — thirty *beit se'ah* — becomes easier to appreciate.

---

## Rocks & Crevices

### Mishnah Setup

The *mishnah* establishes that when land is sold, certain features within that land are not counted toward its measured area. Specifically, rocks that rise ten *tfachim* or higher, and crevices that descend ten *tfachim* or deeper, are excluded from the calculation of the field's area. Ten *tfachim* is approximately two and a half to three feet. If such features are present, the seller must compensate by providing additional tillable land to make up the difference.

### Rashbam 4x4

The *Rashbam* adds a further requirement not made explicit in the *mishnah* itself: beyond the height or depth of ten *tfachim*, the feature must also measure at least four *tfachim* by four *tfachim* in its horizontal dimensions. The *Rashbam* grounds this requirement in the laws of *reshut hayachid* for *Shabbat*. A private domain for purposes of *Shabbat* is defined as a space four *tfachim* by four *tfachim* in area and ten *tfachim* in height — approximately a foot by a foot by three feet. A rock meeting those dimensions would constitute its own *reshut hayachid* at its summit; a crevice of those dimensions would form a *reshut hayachid* at its base, naturally walled by its own sides.

### Domain Separation

The conceptual logic follows directly: if such a space is recognized by *halacha* as a separate domain for *Shabbat*, it is coherent to regard it as a separate unit within the field for purposes of a land sale as well. The field and the rock or crevice are, in the relevant sense, different places.

### Rock Ownership Q&A

This raises a question that the *mishnah* leaves unresolved: who owns the rock or the crevice? When we say it is not counted in the land area and the seller must make it up with other land, does that mean the rock was excluded from the sale altogether — in which case it remains the seller's property — or does the buyer receive the rock while simply being entitled to additional compensatory land? Logically, if the rock constitutes a separate unit and that is precisely why additional land must be provided, then the rock was never part of what was sold. It would remain the seller's. The practical stakes are not trivial: if oil were ever to be found beneath such a rock, the question of ownership would matter considerably.

---

## Hekdesh Redemption

### Tannaim Source

The *Gemara* now adduces a parallel case from an entirely different domain — the laws of *hekdesh* — and uses it to probe the logic of the *mishnah*. The *Gemara* opens with the phrase *tnan hatam*, "we have taught elsewhere," referring to the laws of one who sanctifies a field to the *Beit Hamikdash*. The *Torah* establishes that when a person sanctifies a *sadeh achuza* — a hereditary field of inheritance — and wishes to redeem it, the rate is fixed: fifty *shekel* of silver per *beit kor* of plantable land. This redemption rate is not market-dependent; it is a *Torah*-mandated fixed price, prorated based on how many years remain until the *yovel*.

### Rashbam Girsa

The *Gemara*'s source text reads *bishnat hayovel*, "in the year of the *yovel*." The *Rashbam*, however, emends the reading to *bishat hayovel*, "at the time of the *yovel*" — meaning during the historical period when *yovel* was operative, roughly the era of the First Temple and, debatably, part of the Second Temple period. His reason is straightforward: one cannot meaningfully sanctify a field during the actual *yovel* year itself, since the field reverts to its original owner at that moment and would not remain in the possession of the *hekdesh*. *Tosafot*, by contrast, defends the standard reading *bishnat hayovel* on the grounds that it can refer to the period immediately following the *yovel* year rather than within it.

### Logic of Separation

The *Gemara* now raises its challenge. The *mishnah* in the context of *hekdesh* states — precisely as our *mishnah* does about sales — that rocks ten *tfachim* high and crevices ten *tfachim* deep are not measured together with the field. The *Gemara* asks: *v'amai?* Why not? If one sanctifies one's entire field and it contains a rock or crevice that constitutes a distinct unit, let both be sanctified — the field at its rate and the rock at its own. The mere fact that they are separate units does not mean the rock escapes sanctity; it was included in the declaration of sanctification.

The *Gemara* then entertains the possibility that perhaps, since the rock does not itself constitute a *beit kor*, it does not fall under the *Torah*'s special redemption rate and must therefore go by market value. But the *Rashbam* is careful to clarify: the *Gemara* is not suggesting the rock would fail to become *hekdesh* at all. Rather, the point is that the fixed redemption rate of fifty *shekel* per *beit kor* applies specifically to a *sadeh achuza* — an actual cultivable field. Something that is not a field, such as a courtyard or a purchased field rather than an inherited one, is redeemed at market value. So the question is whether the rock, treated as a separate unit, would follow the *Torah*'s fixed rate or the market rate.

The *Gemara* then quotes a *baraita* that seems to resolve this: the *Torah* says "a field," and derives from the word *sadeh* that the fixed rate applies to fields of all sizes — not only those as large as a full *beit kor*, but even to a *lesech*, half a *lesech*, a *se'ah*, a *tarkav*, half a *tarkav*. Any proportional piece of a *sadeh achuza* follows the same rate. Thus even a small separate rock, if it constitutes a *sadeh achuza*, should follow the fixed rate. The question then reasserts itself: if both the main field and the rock are redeemed at the same rate, what difference does it make whether we treat them as one unit or two?

### Rav Ukva Untillable

Rav Ukva bar Chama resolves the difficulty: *hacha binkaim mele'im mayim askinan* — we are speaking here specifically of crevices filled with water, which are not tillable land. The *Torah*'s fixed redemption rate applies to a *sadeh achuza*, which means cultivable land. Non-tillable land — such as a rocky crevice filled with water — does not fall under that category and must be redeemed at market value instead.

The force of this answer is considerable. When a person sanctifies his field, the tillable portion — say, twenty-nine *se'ah* out of thirty — is redeemed at the rate of fifty *shekel* per *beit kor*, prorated accordingly. But the crevice, constituting a separate unit of non-tillable land, is redeemed at market rate. The *Gemara* adds that this reading is consistent with the *mishnah*'s language, since the case of rocks — which are paradigmatically non-tillable — is mentioned alongside that of crevices, supporting the interpretation that we are dealing with untillable spaces throughout.

The *Gemara* immediately follows with a question: if the reason crevices are excluded is that they are untillable, then even a small crevice — below the ten-*tfachim* threshold — should also be excluded, since it too is not tillable. The *Gemara* answers: *hani nigni d'ara mikru, shadrei d'ara mikru* — small bumps and minor dips are called simply "the unevenness of the land." They are absorbed into the overall character of the field and do not stand as independent units. A small imperfection is simply part of what it means to have a field. Only once a space is large enough and defined enough to constitute its own distinct unit does it cease to be *batel* to the larger field.

---

## Tillable vs. Untillable

### Bumps in Field

Having established the logic for *hekdesh*, the *Gemara* turns to apply the same framework to the case of an ordinary sale. The principle derived from the *hekdesh* discussion is that small bumps (*negligim*) and shallow dips (*shadrei d'area*) are simply part of the land and are subsumed within it. They do not stand as separate units and do not reduce the measured area of the field.

### Buyer Expectations

The question then becomes: in the context of a sale, does the same reasoning apply only when the rock or crevice is untillable, or does it apply even when it is tillable? In the *hekdesh* case, the distinction mattered because the redemption rate differed for untillable land. But when someone buys a field, the concern is different — the buyer wants flat, usable, contiguous land. Even a tillable mound may be objectionable if it disrupts the continuity of the field.

### Permafrost Discussion

This raises a broader question: what if a large portion of the land is not rocky or elevated, but simply of very poor quality — hard, untillable soil, like permafrost — across a wide expanse? Does the buyer have a grievance even if no individual feature reaches the ten-*tfachim* threshold? The answer, which the *Gemara* will address, is that once enough land is genuinely untillable and the area is large enough to stand on its own rather than being *batel* to the rest, the buyer does indeed have a claim. The critical distinction is not framed in terms of quality gradations but in terms of what can be called a *field*: a space defined as its own unit is not a field; a bump integrated into a larger field still is. As the *Rashbam* puts it, the seller's words were *beit kor afar* — a *kor* of tillable land — and if a substantial portion is not tillable, those words have not been fulfilled.

### Rav Papa Flat Land

Rav Papa articulates the principle for sales explicitly: *af al pi she'ein mele'im mayim* — even if the crevice is not filled with water, even if it is in principle tillable, it is still not included in the sold land. The reason he gives is: *einenu rotzeh sheyiten me'otav bemakom echad veyihyu lo kishnayim ulishlosha mekomot* — the buyer does not want to pay for one place and receive what amounts to two or three places. The buyer's expectation in purchasing a *beit kor* is a single, contiguous, flat parcel. A mound that must be climbed or a crevice that must be descended into violates that expectation, regardless of its agricultural usability. A feature defined enough by its height or depth to constitute its own space is therefore excluded from the sale and must be compensated for, whether or not one could theoretically plant there.

---

## Four Kav Rule

### Rav Yitzchak 4 Kav

Rav Yitzchak now introduces a quantitative limit on the tolerance for untillable or irregular spaces within a field. The rule articulated earlier — that small bumps and dips are simply part of the land — applies only up to a point. Rav Yitzchak states: *terashim she'amru beit arba'at kabin* — the rocky or untillable areas tolerated without complaint must not exceed four *kav* for each *beit kor*.

### Math of 4 Kav

The mathematics are worth spelling out. There are six *kav* to a *se'ah* and thirty *se'ah* to a *beit kor*, yielding 180 *kav* per *beit kor*. Four *kav* out of 180 is approximately one forty-fifth of the total area, or just over two percent. Up to that threshold, minor untillable patches are considered absorbed into the larger field and are not grounds for complaint. Beyond it, the buyer has a legitimate grievance.

### Concentration Rule

Rav Ukva bar Chama refines this principle: the four *kav* of untillable area is only problematic — and only counts toward this threshold — if it is concentrated within a space of five *kav*. That is, if the untillable patches are scattered throughout the entire field, they may individually be negligible, each absorbed into its surroundings. But if they are all clustered together so that within a defined space of five *kav*, four *kav* of it is untillable, that constitutes a distinct, identifiable problem-area that the buyer cannot be expected to absorb.

### Majority Distribution

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan offers a different formulation: the four *kav* is tolerable if it is spread throughout the majority — more than sixty percent — of the field. The framing here is one of distribution relative to the field as a whole. If the minor imperfections are spread across the majority of the field's expanse, they are part of the texture of the land and the buyer must accept them. But if the concentration of untillable space exceeds four *kav*, or if that four *kav* falls in less than the majority of the field — meaning its density within the area it occupies is too great — then the buyer has a valid claim.

---

## Unresolved Questions

### Density Question

Rabbi Chiya poses a case that the *Gemara* leaves unresolved. According to Rabbi Yochanan's principle, four *kav* distributed across the majority of the field is acceptable. But what if most of the untillable space — say, three *kav* — is compressed into a small portion of the field, while only a little remains scattered across the larger part? The majority of the problematic area is, paradoxically, in the minority of the field's space. Is that still acceptable because the overall quantity remains within the four-*kav* threshold, or is the high local density itself disqualifying? The *Gemara* answers: *teiku*.

### Shape Scenarios

Rabbi Yirmiah, characteristically drawn to edge cases that probe the conceptual boundaries of a principle, poses a series of further unresolved questions concerning the geometric configuration of untillable patches. If they are arranged in a circle (*ke-shir*), the enclosed form makes navigation around them especially difficult — is that configuration more objectionable even within the acceptable threshold? If arranged in a straight line (*ke-shura*), tilling becomes harder in one direction — the *Rashbam* notes that fields were plowed in both directions, making a linear obstacle disruptive in a way that scattered patches are not. If shaped like the horns of an ox (*itztadin*), curved and branching outward, or arranged in a zigzag (*derech akalton*), are any of these configurations inherently more problematic than an even distribution? On all of these questions, the *Gemara* answers *teiku*.

---

## Boundary Edge Cases

### Edge & Solo Rocks

A *tanna* teaches: a *sela yechidi* — a solitary rock — is not measured with the field, even if it is quite small, *afilu kol shehu*. Similarly, a rock *samuch lemeitzar* — adjacent to the boundary of the field — is not measured with the field, again regardless of size.

### Rashbam Edge

The *Rashbam* explains: a rock at the edge of the field, even one too small to ordinarily constitute a separate unit, is not *batel* to the field as a whole. When a feature sits at the periphery, it does not become incorporated into the field in the way that a small bump in the interior would. It stands apart rather than being absorbed into the surrounding land. The *Rashbam* also addresses the case of the *sela yechidi* — a rock outside the formal boundary of the field but adjacent to it — as essentially the same principle: it is not organically part of the field and therefore not counted with it.

### Tosafot Named Rock

*Tosafot* reads the term *yechidi* differently. Rather than referring to physical isolation at the edge, *Tosafot* understands it to mean a rock with its own name — a recognized landmark in the community, known to everyone as a distinct place. Such a rock has a separate identity independent of the field it sits within, and that independent identity is what causes it to be excluded from the field's measurement. The two interpretations — edge-placement for the *Rashbam*, named identity for *Tosafot* — represent meaningfully different understandings of what constitutes separateness.

### Dirt Gap Question

Rav Pappa poses the following question: *mushech afar beintayim mahu?* What if there is a small amount of dirt between the rock and the boundary line? The rock is not right up against the edge; there is a thin strip of earth separating it from the *meitzar*. Does that small gap suffice to integrate the rock into the field, so that it is treated like any interior feature subject to the ordinary thresholds? Or is its proximity to the boundary still sufficient to exclude it? The *Gemara* answers: *teiku*.

### Subterranean Shape

Rav Ashi poses a further question about cases where the rock's relationship to the boundary varies depending on depth. Suppose that at ground level the rock appears to sit exactly at the boundary — a case where we would ordinarily say it is not measured with the field — but underground the rock narrows away from the boundary, leaving dirt between the base of the rock and the border. Or conversely: at the surface there is a visible gap of dirt between the rock and the boundary, but below ground the rock widens until it is flush with or extends past the border. In which direction do we assess the rock's position? The *Gemara* entertains both scenarios — *afar milmata vetsunma milmala*, dirt below and rock above, and *afar milmala vetsunma milmata*, rock below and dirt above — and concludes on both: *teiku*.

---

## Measured Sale

### Precision Promise

The *mishnah* now introduces a distinct category of sale. Rather than a general transaction in which the seller describes the land approximately, the seller here uses the formula *beit kor ani mocher lecha mida bechevel* — "I am selling you a *beit kor*, measured by the rope." The phrase *mida bechevel* signals a commitment to precision: this is not an approximate description but a warranted measurement. The buyer is purchasing a specific, exactly-measured quantity of land.

### Deficit & Overage

The consequences of that precision commitment are rigorous. *Pichat kol shehu yinakeh* — if the actual measurement falls short by any amount whatsoever, even the smallest deficit, the seller must reduce the price proportionally. Similarly, *hotir kol shehu yachzir* — if it turns out the field is even slightly larger than stated, the buyer must return the value of the overage, either in money or, as we will see, in land.

### Approximate Sale

By contrast, when the seller uses the formula *hen chaser hen yeter* — "whether it is less or more" — he signals that the sale is approximate. He is explicitly acknowledging that the stated size is not guaranteed. In that case, the *mishnah* rules that discrepancies of up to a *rova* — one quarter of a *kav* — per *se'ah* are within the tolerable range. Neither party can make a claim against the other on account of such a variance.

### 7.5 Kav Tolerance

The arithmetic of this tolerance for a full *beit kor* is as follows. One quarter of a *kav* per *se'ah*, multiplied by thirty *se'ah* per *beit kor*, yields seven and a half *kav* of permissible variance for the entire parcel. Within that margin, the sale stands as stated. Beyond it, an adjustment must be made.

---

## Overpayment Remedy

### Return Remedy

The *mishnah* now asks: when the field proves to be larger than warranted and the buyer must return the overage, what form does that return take? Does the buyer return money (*ma'ot*) or land (*karka*)?

### Money Default

The *mishnah* answers: the default is that the buyer returns money. The *Rashbam* explains the rationale: if the overage is small, the seller cannot realistically make use of a tiny sliver of land returned to him. A seller whose field has been slightly over-measured would be left with an unusable strip of land if the buyer returned it physically. In order to protect the seller's practical interests — *liyafot kocho shel mocher* — the *halacha* defaults to monetary restitution.

### 9 Kav Threshold

However, if the seller *wishes* to reclaim the land rather than money, and the overage is large enough, the *mishnah* allows for that. The threshold is nine *kav*: if the overage amounts to *beit tishah kavin* — the area of nine *kav* — the seller can insist on receiving the land back rather than money, because nine *kav* constitutes a functionally usable plot of land.

### Usable Minimums

The *mishnah* sets out the minimum sizes that define usable land for these purposes. For a field (*sadeh*), the minimum is nine *kav*. For a vegetable garden (*gina*), it is half a *kav*. Rabbi Akiva holds that even a quarter of a *kav* suffices as a usable minimum. These thresholds determine at what point a returned parcel of land is considered a genuine, functional piece of property rather than a useless fragment.

### Total Return

A further principle concludes the *mishnah*: when the seller is entitled to a return because the overage exceeds the tolerable threshold, the buyer does not return only the portion above the threshold. He returns the entire overage. If the field was off by, say, two and a half percent when one and three-quarters percent would have been acceptable, the buyer does not return only the excess three-quarters of a percent — he returns the full two and a half percent.

To situate this within the *beit kor* framework: the tolerance in an approximate sale is seven and a half *kav*. If the overage is within that amount, no return is required. If it exceeds seven and a half *kav* but has not yet reached nine *kav*, the seller can demand money but cannot force the return of land. Once the overage reaches nine *kav*, the seller may demand the land itself — and when he does, he receives back not just the portion above seven and a half *kav* but the entire overage from the first *kav* onward.

---

---

# Bava Batra 104

## Land Sale & Ona'ah

### Beit Kor Measurement

The Mishnah at the bottom of 103b introduces the case of someone selling a plot of land described as a *beit kor* — a unit of approximately thirty *se'ah* — and the consequences that follow depending on how the sale was characterized. If the seller declares that the sale is *mida bechevel*, measured precisely by the yardstick, then any discrepancy, however small, must be corrected: if the buyer received too little, he receives a price reduction, and if he received too much, he returns the excess, whether land or money. If, however, the seller qualified the sale as *hen chaser hen yeter* — more or less — then a tolerance of one *rova* per *se'ah* is permitted. Since there are six *kav* to a *se'ah* and four *reva'im* to a *kav*, this tolerance works out to 1/24 of the total. So long as the discrepancy falls within that 1/24, both buyer and seller must absorb it without adjustment. Once the discrepancy exceeds that threshold, however, the entire overage — not merely the portion beyond the tolerance — must be made good. The mechanics of how this correction is made, and who bears what prerogative, are taken up in the *gemara* and will be addressed in due course.

### Ona'ah & Bitul Mekach

Before turning to the *gemara*, it is worth pausing on a foundational question: why do the rules of *ona'ah* not simply dispose of this entire discussion? *Ein ona'ah bekarka'ot* — the principle that overcharging does not apply to real property — would seem to immunize land sales from any financial correction. But this principle is not quite what is at stake here. *Ona'ah* is the remedy when you receive exactly what you bargained for in terms of quantity, but the price paid was above the fair market rate. Here, by contrast, the quantity itself is off — the buyer received more or less land than the stated amount. That is not a question of pricing but of delivery, and *ona'ah* does not govern it.

The more pressing question is *bitul mekach* — the voiding of a mistaken transaction. Normally, when you receive something materially different from what you contracted for, the sale is null. Why then does the Mishnah not say that the entire sale is void when the measurement is off? The *Rashbam* explains that by landed property, people do not generally wish to unwind the transaction entirely. They understand that a field may not come out to an exact figure and they remain attached to the underlying object — the field itself — rather than to the precise quantity. Accordingly, the remedy is adjustment, not nullification.

### Tosafot: Measured vs. Un…

*Tosafot* takes a different and arguably more precise approach. At the top of 104a, in the *tosafot* beginning *pachot kolshehu yenakeh*, the *Ri* draws a critical distinction between two fundamentally different types of discrepancy. The first is where the seller claimed to have actually measured the land and represented a specific figure, which then turned out to be false — whether through deception or error. In that case, the *Ri* says, we have a genuine *mekach ta'ut*: the buyer was led to believe a precise measurement had been conducted and relied upon it, so when the measurement proves wrong, the transaction is vitiated.

The second case — which is the case of our Mishnah — is where no precise measurement has yet been conducted. The parties are standing in the field or dealing with a known parcel, and the seller says, "I am selling you this field, which is a *beit kor*," or "approximately a *beit kor*." Here, *Tosafot* explains, everyone understands from the outset that the figure has not been rigorously established. The seller is not representing that the land has been surveyed to the inch; he is giving an estimate of a known object. Because imprecision is implicitly acknowledged, the discrepancy does not constitute a *mekach ta'ut*.

This distinction also clarifies what it means when a seller says he is selling *mida bechevel*, precisely. According to *Tosafot*, this does not mean he is asserting that the land has already been measured and found to be exactly a *beit kor*. If he were asserting that and it proved wrong, there would be a *mekach ta'ut*. Rather, *mida bechevel* means: whatever the field turns out to measure, I commit to making it exactly right — any deviation, however slight, will be corrected. The precision is a commitment, not a factual claim about a completed measurement.

A further *Tosafot*, in the *tosafot* beginning *pachas kol shehu yenake*, addresses the question of why the buyer cannot simply demand his money back when the land falls short. The buyer might argue: I wanted a full *beit kor*, not a discounted price for less land. *Tosafot* answers that since the parties were dealing with a specific, known field from the start, and everyone understood that measurement might yield slightly more or less than anticipated, the buyer is not in a position to claim total surprise. The object of the sale was always this particular field; the size was an attribute of it, not the independent subject of the transaction. Because of that, *bitul mekach* does not operate to unwind the sale.

This understanding — that the case presupposes a known, identified field with understood boundaries — is central to the entire sugya and becomes essential when the *gemara* turns to the *stam* case.

---

## Stam Land Sale

### Stam Case Question

The *gemara* opens with a classic *iba'ya lehu*: what is the *halacha* in a *stam* land sale — that is, where neither *mida bechevel* nor *hen chaser hen yeter* was specified? The seller said simply, "I am selling you a *beit kor*," with no modifier whatsoever. Does the absence of any qualifier mean that the slightest discrepancy must be corrected, as if he had said *mida bechevel*? Or does silence carry the more lenient implication of *hen chaser hen yeter*, allowing the 1/24 tolerance?

### 1/24 Tolerance Proof

The *gemara* first attempts to resolve the question from the Mishnah itself. The Mishnah states that if the seller says *mida bechevel*, precision is required; the inference is that had he said nothing — *stam* — it would be treated as *hen chaser hen yeter*. The *gemara* then tests the reverse inference from the second clause: the Mishnah also says that if the seller says *hen chaser hen yeter*, the 1/24 tolerance applies; from which one could infer that *stam* would be treated as *mida bechevel*. Since both inferences are possible, the Mishnah itself yields no definitive answer. The *gemara* therefore says: *ella meha leika lemishma mina* — from this Mishnah we cannot draw a conclusion.

A *braita* is then cited: "A *beit kor* of soil I am selling you; like a *beit kor* of soil I am selling you; more or less I am selling you." The *braita* states that in any of these three formulations, a tolerance of a *rova* per *se'ah* — 1/24 — applies, and if the discrepancy stays within that tolerance, the sale stands as is. This appears to settle the matter: the first formulation, *beit kor afar ani mocher lach*, is the pure *stam* case with no modifier, and it is treated identically to the explicit *hen chaser hen yeter* formulation.

### Stam = Tolerance

The *gemara* attempts to resist this reading by suggesting that perhaps the *braita* is not presenting three separate cases but rather one case described cumulatively: "a *beit kor* — that is, like a *beit kor* — that is, more or less." Under this reading, only the combined formulation with all three phrases would carry the *hen chaser hen yeter* tolerance. The *stam* case alone would remain unresolved. Rav Ashi rejects this interpretation forcefully: if the *braita* intended a single combined case, it would not have repeated *ani mocher lach* after each separate phrase. The repetition of the full sale declaration after each formulation demonstrates that each is a standalone case with independent legal force. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *alma stam nami ke-hen chaser hen yeter dami* — even without any modifier, a *stam* land sale carries the 1/24 tolerance. *Shema mina*.

### Field-Specific Context

*Tosafot* adds a qualification that prevents a misreading of this ruling. One might think that because a *stam* sale allows a 1/24 tolerance, a seller could deliberately measure out slightly less than the full *beit kor* and invoke this rule. That is not the case. The entire framework of this Mishnah, as *Tosafot* explains in two places, assumes that the parties are dealing with a specific, known field with established boundaries. The subject of the transaction is the field itself; the stated acreage is a description of it. The tolerance exists because when dealing with a concrete, identified piece of land, everyone understands that measurement will be approximate. It is not a license for the seller to intentionally short-deliver a quantity of land.

If, by contrast, the seller simply said he would sell the buyer some land to be measured out from a larger holding — without a specific identified parcel as the object — then even a *stam* statement of quantity would obligate him to deliver the full amount precisely. In that case, the quantity is not an attribute of a known object but is itself the subject of the transaction, and full delivery is required.

---

## Seller's Prerogative

### Excess Land Handling

The Mishnah addresses not only the case of the buyer receiving too little, but also the case where he received too much. When the buyer receives less than expected and the discrepancy exceeds the tolerable amount, the remedy is straightforward: the buyer receives a price reduction proportional to the shortfall. *Tosafot* has already explained why the buyer cannot demand full rescission — because the sale was always of this specific field, and the parties understood that measurement might vary.

The more interesting case is when the buyer receives too much. Here the Mishnah grants the *mocher* — the seller — a prerogative: he may choose either to recover the extra land or to demand the monetary equivalent of that extra land from the buyer. This makes intuitive sense when the excess is a small strip that would be difficult to use independently. What use is a tiny sliver of land? The seller may prefer to be compensated in money rather than take back a strip too small to farm on its own. However, the Mishnah qualifies this: once the excess land is objectively large enough to be a usable plot in its own right — the Mishnah specifies nine *kav* for a wheat field — the seller loses his prerogative. At that point, only land is returned; the seller cannot force the buyer to pay money for an independently usable parcel.

### Mishna vs. Baraita

A *braita* appears to contradict the Mishnah's allocation of prerogative entirely to the seller. The *braita* states: if the discrepancy is within 1/24, the sale stands. If it exceeds seven and a half *kav* per *kor* — the 1/24 threshold for a full *kor* — then *kofin et hamocher limkor ve'et halokeach likach*: we force the seller to sell and the buyer to buy. This language seems to grant both sides an independent right to demand that the excess land be incorporated into the buyer's purchase. The seller can be forced to sell even if he wants the land back, and the buyer can be forced to buy even if he would rather return the land. This stands in apparent tension with our Mishnah, which places the choice entirely with the seller.

### Price Adjustment

The *gemara* resolves the tension by explaining that the *braita* is addressing a specific economic scenario: the land was worth more at the time of the original sale and has since declined in value. In this context, "forcing the seller to sell" does not mean overriding his fundamental prerogative — the seller always retains the choice of whether to demand the land or demand money. Rather, it means that *if* the seller chooses to sell the extra land to the buyer rather than taking it back, he is forced to sell it at the current lower market rate, not at the price prevailing when the original transaction was made.

The logic is that the baseline position is that the buyer should return the extra land, since he should never have had it. The extra land becomes the subject of a new transaction only if the seller elects to sell it. Since that transaction takes place now, it is governed by current prices. The seller cannot insist on selling at the original rate merely because that was the context of the initial sale.

The *gemara* then cites a further *braita* which states that when the seller does convey the extra land, it is priced at the rate at which the buyer originally acquired. The *gemara* explains this as the converse situation: the land was cheap at the time of the original sale and has since appreciated. Now the buyer, who must purchase the extra sliver, can legitimately argue that his entire involvement with this land was premised on the lower price, and he cannot be forced to pay today's inflated rate for the overage. In both scenarios — whether land has declined or appreciated — the buyer is entitled to the benefit of the lower price: the original price if land has gone up, and the current price if land has gone down. The Mishnah's principle that the seller holds the prerogative is fully preserved; what the *braita* governs is the price at which any forced sale occurs.

---

## Prerogative Limits

### Rav Huna: Absolute Amount

With the basic framework established, the *gemara* turns to a dispute about the precise point at which the seller loses his prerogative — that is, the threshold at which the excess land is considered independently usable and must be returned rather than monetized. The Mishnah states that for a *sadeh* — a wheat field — this threshold is nine *kav*, and for a *ginah* — a vegetable garden — it is a half *kav*.

Rav Huna holds that these figures represent absolute amounts, not proportional ones. Once the excess reaches nine *kav* in absolute terms, the seller loses his prerogative, regardless of the total size of the field being sold. Even if one is selling an enormous tract — a large *bik'ah gedolah* — the seller cannot argue that because the total acreage is vast, nine *kav* is a proportionally negligible amount that should still fall within his range of discretion. Nine *kav* is nine *kav*: it is an objectively usable plot of land, and the seller can farm it, so he must take it back.

### Rav Nachman: Proportional

Rav Nachman disagrees. He holds that the nine *kav* threshold — and by extension all the thresholds in the Mishnah — applies proportionally, *per kor* of land sold. So if a seller sold two *kor*, the relevant threshold for losing his prerogative doubles to eighteen *kav*. The seller does not lose his prerogative until the per-*kor* equivalent of the excess exceeds nine *kav*. Rav Nachman's formula is *nosei shiva kabin u'mechtza lechol kor ve'kor* — seven and a half *kav* per *kor* as the tolerable overage, and nine *kav* per *kor* as the point at which the prerogative is lost.

This is, frankly, a counterintuitive position. The debate between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman is not merely technical: it reflects a fundamental disagreement about whether the usability standard is absolute or relative. Rav Huna's position has considerable intuitive force — nine *kav* is nine *kav*, usable by any standard. Nevertheless, the *halacha* follows Rav Nachman.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges Rav Nachman directly from the language of the Mishnah. The Mishnah states: *im shayer basadeh beit tisha kabin* — if nine *kav* were left over in a field — the seller must return it. Does the Mishnah not seem to be stating an absolute rule, applicable regardless of whether one *kor* or two *kor* was sold? Rava presses: *lav d'zavin lei kora'im?* — is the Mishnah not speaking of a case where two *kor* were sold, yet nine *kav* still triggers the mandatory return?

Similarly, the Mishnah states *u'vigenah beit chatzi kav* — in a vegetable garden, a half *kav* triggers mandatory return. Does this not apply even if two *se'ah* of garden were sold, so that the threshold remains a half *kav* in absolute terms rather than doubling?

### Case-Specific Sizes

The *gemara* deflects each of Rava's challenges in turn. For the first: *lo d'zavin lei kor* — the Mishnah is speaking of the case where exactly one *kor* was sold, and that is why nine *kav* is the threshold. Had two *kor* been sold, the threshold would be eighteen *kav*. For the second: *lo d'zavin lei se'ah* — the Mishnah's half-*kav* threshold for a *ginah* applies to the case where one *se'ah* of garden was sold. Had two *se'ah* been sold, the threshold would be one *kav*.

The *gemara* proceeds similarly with the ruling attributed to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva holds that a *ginah* is usable even at the size of a *rova kav* — a quarter of a *kav* — so that the seller loses his prerogative when the excess reaches that size. Rava's challenge here parallels the earlier ones: *mai lav d'zavin lei se'ah?* — does this not apply even for a *se'ah*-sized garden sale, meaning the quarter-*kav* is absolute? The *gemara* answers: *lo d'zavin lei chatzi se'ah* — Rabbi Akiva's ruling applies to a sale of half a *se'ah*, scaled accordingly.

This pattern of responses is somewhat strained, and as the lecturer candidly notes, the *gemara* is reading the Mishnah's examples as each applying only to a specific total sale size rather than as absolute thresholds — a reading that serves Rav Nachman's proportional framework but does not emerge naturally from the Mishnah's language.

---

## Unresolved Cases

### Field-to-Garden Conversi…

Rav Ashi poses a question left unresolved: *sadeh ve-na'aset ginah, ginah ve-na'aset sadeh mai?* — what if a field became a garden, or a garden became a field, in the interim between the sale and the measurement?

The question arises as follows. Suppose the seller sold what is classified as a *sadeh*, and the excess land was eight *kav* — below the nine-*kav* threshold, so the seller retains his prerogative under the *sadeh* standard. Before the parties got around to formally measuring and resolving the discrepancy, that excess plot underwent a change: a stream began flowing through it, or the buyer planted vegetables, and it became usable as a *ginah*. The threshold for a *ginah* is only a half *kav*, and eight *kav* obviously exceeds that. The buyer can now argue: as a garden, this plot is independently usable at any size, so you no longer have a prerogative — you must take it back.

Does the classification follow the nature of the land at the time of the sale, which would preserve the seller's prerogative? Or does it follow the current state of the land, which would eliminate it? The *gemara* leaves this question standing: *teiku*.

### Contiguous Property

A separate ruling, introduced by a *tanna*, addresses the case where the excess land is contiguous to the seller's own remaining property: *im haya samuch lesadehu afilu kol shehu machzir lo karka* — if the extra land is adjacent to the seller's field, even if it is a tiny amount, the buyer always returns the land and the seller can never claim a money payment instead.

The rationale is transparent. The entire basis for the seller's prerogative to demand money rather than land was the uselessness of a small strip to someone who has no adjacent property to integrate it into. But if the excess is contiguous to the seller's own field, it is trivially easy for him to incorporate it — he simply adjusts the boundary line. There is no hardship in taking the land back, and therefore no justification for forcing the buyer to purchase what should never have been included in the sale.

### Physical Obstacles

Rav Ashi then raises a series of related questions, all *teiku*, about what counts as "contiguous" for this purpose. If a *bor* — a well — separates the seller's remaining field from the excess strip, does the well constitute enough of a physical break to defeat the *samuch lesadehu* principle, restoring the seller's prerogative? What about *ammas hamayim* — an irrigation canal running between the plots? Or *derech harabbim* — a public path cutting across? Or *richpa de-dikla* — a copse of palm trees standing in between?

In each of these cases, one could argue that the physical feature makes it impractical to simply fold the excess into the seller's adjacent field, thereby reviving the original rationale for giving the seller a choice. On the other hand, one could argue that the adjacency is still effectively there and the physical feature does not eliminate it. All of these remain unresolved: *teiku*.

---

## Return of Excess

### Entire Amount Returned

The Mishnah's language at this point states: *velo et harova bilvad machzir lo ela et kol hamotar* — and not only the *rova* does he return, but the entire excess. The *gemara* flags this as stated backwards. If the Mishnah means to say that once the discrepancy crosses the tolerance threshold, the entire amount — not merely the excess over the threshold — is returned, it should say: not only the extra beyond the *rova*, but all of it, including the *rova* itself. Saying "not only the *rova*" implies the *rova* is the baseline and something additional beyond it is also returned — which reverses the actual rule.

Ravin bar Rav Nachman therefore emends the reading: *ro'eh hamotar bilvad machzir lo, ela et kol hareva'im kulam* — he does not return only the excess beyond the tolerance; he returns the full amount including that which falls within the tolerance. Once the threshold is crossed, the entire discrepancy is corrected, not merely the marginal amount above the *rova*.

---

## Contradictory Language

### Second Clause Wins

The daf concludes with the beginning of a new Mishnah that addresses a scenario not yet covered: what happens when the seller uses contradictory language in a single statement?

The first Mishnah established three cases: *mida bechevel* (precise), *hen chaser hen yeter* (approximate), and *stam* (unmodified, treated like approximate). The new Mishnah takes up what happens when both formulations appear together. If the seller said *mida bechevel ani mocher lach, hen chaser hen yeter* — I am selling you this precisely, more or less — the two clauses directly contradict each other. Likewise if he said *hen chaser hen yeter ani mocher lach, mida bechevel* — more or less, precisely.

Ben Nanas rules that in both cases, the second clause controls: *batel hen chaser hen yeter, mida bechevel* — when "more or less" comes second, it nullifies the "precisely" that preceded it, and the sale is governed as *hen chaser hen yeter*. Conversely, when *mida bechevel* comes second, it nullifies the *hen chaser hen yeter*, and the sale is treated as precise. The principle is that the second, later statement reflects the speaker's final intent, overriding what came before.

The Mishnah presents this as the view of Ben Nanas alone — *divrei Ben Nanas* — without stating a dissenting opinion within the Mishnah itself, though the *gemara* will introduce one. The broader question of how contradictory contractual language is resolved, and whether Ben Nanas's principle generalizes beyond land sales, will be addressed in the discussion that follows.

---

---

# Bava Batra 105

## Mishna: Mida vs. Chaseir…

### Mishna Setup

The *mishna* at the bottom of 104b introduces a case that will animate the entire discussion on our daf: a seller uses contradictory language in describing a land transaction. He says, "I am selling you a *beit kor* — an acre — by the measuring stick, more or less." On its face, the phrase *mida bechevel* ("by the measuring stick") suggests precision, while *hen chaseir hen yeter* ("more or less") suggests approximation. Both appear in the same contractual statement. How does the law treat this conflict?

### Chaseir Yeter Negates Mi…

The *mishna* rules that one goes by the last phrase stated. In the first scenario, the seller says *mida bechevel ani mocher lach, hen chaseir hen yeter* — he begins with the precise language and concludes with the approximate. The result: *batel mida bechevel* — the earlier phrase, "by the measuring stick," is nullified by the closing phrase, "more or less." The sale therefore follows the rules of approximation, as elaborated in the preceding *mishna*, meaning the measurement may vary by as much as a *rova* per *beit sa'ah*.

### Mida Negates Chaseir Yet…

In the second scenario the order is reversed: *hen chaseir hen yeter, mida bechevel* — he begins with the approximate language and concludes with the precise. Here too the *mishna* rules by the final phrase: *batel hen chaseir hen yeter* — the "more or less" opening is nullified by the closing "by the measuring stick," and the sale must conform to the rules of precision.

### Ben Nanas Attribution

The *mishna* attributes this ruling — that the last language stated always governs — to Ben Nanas: *divrei Ben Nanas*. What is striking is that the *mishna* presents only this single opinion, without recording any dissent. It is unusual for a *mishna* to stand alone with one named view and no counterposition. The *gemara* will supply the missing voice.

---

## Gemara: Rental Proof

### Chachamim Disagree

The *gemara* opens by noting, in the name of Rav Abba bar Mamal citing Rav, that *vecholkin alav chaverav al Ben Nanas* — Ben Nanas's colleagues in fact disagreed with him. The *mishna* therefore does not represent a consensus, even if it presents no alternative.

### Tzipori Bathhouse Case

The *gemara* then asks: is this information new? We might already know from another *mishna* that *tannaim* disputed Ben Nanas's position. The *gemara* points to a case in Tzipori: *maaseh beTzipori be'echad shesachar merchatz mechaveiro bishneim asar zehuvim leshanah* — a man rented a bathhouse from his fellow for twelve gold *dinarim* per year, followed by the phrase "one *dinar* of gold per month." At first glance these seem equivalent, but they are not. In a leap year containing thirteen months, the annual figure of twelve *dinarim* and the monthly rate of one *dinar* per month produce different totals. Which phrase controls? The case is structurally similar to ours: an opening formula and a closing formula with different legal implications.

### Split Difference Ruling

The *mishna* there records that the case came before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yossi, who ruled *yachloku et chodesh ha'ibur* — split the leap month. Unable to determine whether the first or the second phrase should govern, they treated the dispute as a *safek* and divided the ambiguous month between landlord and tenant.

### Mammon Hamutal Besafek

This ruling reflects the principle of *mammon hamutal besafek*: when there is a genuine doubt over money, and one cannot resolve it through *muchzak* — the party currently in possession — one option is to divide it. The *gemara* cites this *mishna* to demonstrate that at least some *tannaim* did not follow Ben Nanas's rule of going by the last language; instead they held both phrases in tension and split the difference.

---

## Clarification vs. Revers…

### Reversal/Explication

The *gemara* presses further: can we really derive from the rental case that the debate applies equally to our *mishna* about land sales? Not necessarily. *Hava amina hatam hu de'ika leimar mehadar ka hadar beih ve'ika leimar peirushei ka mefaraish* — in that case, the second phrase could be understood either as a reversal of the first, or as an explication of it. The distinction initially seems unclear. If it is a reversal, one goes by the second phrase — the landlord declared one *dinar* per month, overriding his earlier statement. If it is an explication, it would also seem to favor the second phrase: what did he mean by "twelve *dinarim* per year"? He was simply clarifying that he assumed a normal twelve-month year, meaning one *dinar* per month. Whether characterized as reversal or explication, the outcome appears identical — the second phrase wins.

### Rashbam Explication

The Rashbam resolves this difficulty by explaining that "explication" here does not mean a reinterpretation of the total price. Rather, the second phrase — one *dinar* per month — may have been intended to clarify the *structure* of the rental arrangement, not its total cost. The tenant was saying: I intend this to be a monthly lease rather than an annual lease, governing questions of when payment is due and when either party may exit the arrangement. Under this reading, the twelve-*dinar* annual total stands, and the second phrase addresses only the periodicity of payment, not the question of the leap month. Since the second phrase may therefore be read as consistent with the first rather than contradicting it, the two phrases do not stand in outright opposition, and the doubt is genuine — hence the ruling to split the difference.

### Clear Contradiction

Given that ambiguity, one might have thought the *tannaitic* debate over splitting applies only where the second phrase can be read as mere explication — leaving open the possibility that where phrases are in clear contradiction, all would agree to go by the last phrase, as Ben Nanas holds. It is to forestall this inference that Rav Abba bar Mamal's statement is necessary: even in cases of clear, unambiguous contradiction — where approximation and precision cannot be harmonized — there are those who maintain that the phrases remain in tension, the matter is a *safek*, and one does not simply defer to the last language stated.

---

## Shmuel: Pachot Shebalesh…

### Ben Nanas vs. Chachamim

A parallel tradition is then introduced: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says, *zu divrei Ben Nanas* — this is Ben Nanas's view — *vechachamim omrim halach achar pachot shebilshono* — but the Sages say: go by the minimum of the two formulations.

### Pachot Shebaleshonot

The principle of *pachot shebaleshonot* — follow the lesser of the stated terms — is here articulated as the position of the *Chachamim* against Ben Nanas. The minimum in question, as the Rashbam explains, is minimum from the perspective of the buyer: one goes by the formulation that gives the purchaser the least, and thus favors the seller, who remains in possession of his property.

### Muchzak Principle

The reason for this disposition, as the *gemara* makes clear, is the principle of *muchzak*: the owner of the land is currently in possession, and when two contractual formulations stand in contradiction, the party seeking to wrest assets from the *muchzak* must make his case unambiguously. Since the buyer cannot point to a clear, uncontested formulation supporting his claim to the larger quantity, he receives only the minimum the language unambiguously supports. This is distinct from splitting the difference — rather than halving the disputed amount, the law simply leaves the seller holding what the language cannot definitively transfer.

---

## Kor Beshloshim Case

### Kor for 30 / Se'ah per S…

When Shmuel says "these are the words of Ben Nanas" without explicitly endorsing them, the *gemara* infers that Shmuel rejects Ben Nanas and holds instead like the *Chachamim* — that contradictory language creates a *safek* resolved by *muchzak*. But this inference is immediately challenged. The *gemara* notes: *veha Rav u'Shmuel d'amri tarvaihu* — Rav and Shmuel both said — *kor bishloshim ani mocher lach yachol lachzor bo afilu bese'ah achronah* — "I am selling you a *kor* for thirty": until the very last *se'ah* is transferred, either party may retract, because the entire *kor* is treated as a single unit. However, if one says *kor bishloshim, se'ah besela ani mocher lach* — "a *kor* for thirty, each *se'ah* for one *sela*" — then the second formulation governs: the transaction is structured as thirty separate unit sales, and *rishon rishon kana* — each *se'ah* as it is measured out becomes a completed, irrevocable sale.

### Last Language Wins

The *chiddush* of this ruling is not merely that a *kor* for thirty differs structurally from a *se'ah* per *sela*. The novelty is that when both formulations are stated together, the second determines the structure of the transaction — the bulk pricing of the *kor* gives way to the unit pricing of the *se'ah per sela*. The later language wins.

### Shmuel & Ben Nanas

This appears to place Shmuel squarely in Ben Nanas's camp: when two phrases conflict, go by the second. Why, then, did Shmuel seem to dismiss Ben Nanas in favor of *pachot shebaleshonot*?

---

## Resolution: Muchzak Rules

### Consistent Muchzak

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *ela le'olam zu velo sevira lei* — in truth, Shmuel does reject Ben Nanas. When Shmuel says "these are the words of Ben Nanas," he consistently means he does not hold that way. Shmuel's own position is that contradictory formulations are held in tension, the matter becomes a *safek*, and one goes by the *muchzak*. This is coherent with *pachot shebaleshonot*: the *chachamim's* rule of taking the minimum is simply the application of *muchzak* to the specific context of a land sale.

### Rental Case Timing

The *gemara* then revisits the rental case to confirm this consistency. Shmuel himself explained the *mishna* in Tzipori as a case where the dispute arrived before the court in the middle of the leap month — *beva be'emtza chodesh askinan*. In that scenario the ruling to split the month follows directly from *muchzak*.

### Middle/Beginning/End

Three distinct scenarios emerge depending on when the case comes to court. If the dispute arises in the middle of the leap month (*Adar Sheni*), the tenant has already lived there for half the month without paying, so he is in possession of that half; the landlord, meanwhile, retains possession of the remaining half of the month's rental value. Each holds the *muchzak* in half, and therefore they split it. If the case arises at the *beginning* of the leap month — before the tenant has dwelled there at all — then the landlord is fully *muchzak* in the month's rent, and *kula lemashkir*: the tenant must pay the full *dinar* for that month if he wishes to remain. If the case arises at the *end* of the month — after the tenant has already lived out the entire month — then the tenant is *muchzak*: he has already resided there and has not yet been made to pay, and so *kula lesocher*, the landlord cannot compel payment for that month. In every scenario, the outcome tracks who is in possession at the moment of adjudication. This is entirely consistent with Shmuel's principle, and not with Ben Nanas's rule of automatically following the later language.

### Kor Muchzak Logic

But if Shmuel consistently applies *muchzak*, what of the *kor* case, where Shmuel appeared to rule by the second language and not by *muchzak*? The *gemara* answers: *de-hatam taama mai? mishum de-tafis, hacha nami ha-tafis* — the reason there is precisely *muchzak*, and the same logic applies here. When both formulations appear together, the two understandings of the transaction stand in contradiction — is this a single bulk sale or thirty unit sales? Since the language does not clearly resolve the question, the law defaults to *muchzak*. As each *se'ah* is measured out and transferred, the buyer takes physical possession of it. At that moment he is *muchzak* in that unit, and *rishon rishon kana* — each *se'ah* is a finalized sale. The *gemara* acknowledges a certain complexity here: if the buyer is simultaneously *muchzak* in the object and in his money, he could arguably claim both that the sale is final (because he holds the *se'ah*) and that it is not (because he intended the whole *kor* as a unit). The *gemara* does not pursue this further, but the principle it invokes is consistent throughout: Shmuel's ruling on the *kor* case is not an endorsement of Ben Nanas but another application of *muchzak* to a case of genuinely ambiguous contractual language.

---

## Istira Case

### Istira Definition

The *gemara* then turns to a new teaching attributed to Rav Huna in the name of Rav. The case involves the *istira*, a coin whose nominal name suggests a round figure but whose actual value is ninety-six *ma'im*, not one hundred. So if a seller says *istira, me'ah ma'ei* — "an *istira*, one hundred *ma'im*" — he has combined an approximate term (the *istira*, which implies ninety-six) with a precise figure (one hundred). The situation mirrors our *mishna*: approximate and precise language appear together.

### Rav: Last Language

Rav rules: *tfos lashon acharon* — go by the last language stated. If he said *istira, me'ah ma'ei*, the buyer owes one hundred *ma'im*, because that is the final formulation. If he said *me'ah ma'ei, istira*, the buyer owes ninety-six, the value of an *istira*. This is the Ben Nanas position applied to a monetary transaction.

### Apparent Repetition

The *gemara* immediately challenges: did Rav not already say this? *Ha amrah Rav chada zimna* — Rav said it once before. In the context of the bathhouse rental, the *gemara* records Rav as saying: *ee havei hatam havei yahivna kula lemashkir* — had he been present at the rental adjudication, he would have awarded the entire disputed month to the landlord. Since "one *dinar* per month" is the final phrase, and that formulation favors the landlord, Rav would have ruled entirely in his favor. That too reflects the principle of *tfos lashon acharon*. Why, then, does the *gemara* need Rav to state it again in the *istira* case?

---

## Explication Caveat

### Explication vs. Contradi…

The answer lies in the potential to distinguish the rental case. One might have concluded that Rav's ruling in the rental context rested not on the general principle that the second language always wins, but on the specific feature that in the rental the two formulations could plausibly be read as consistent — twelve per year, meaning a normal year, meaning one per month. Under that reading, the second phrase does not override the first but rather explicates it, clarifying what the speaker intended all along. If so, Rav's ruling there would apply only when explication is possible — when the second phrase can be understood as commentary on the first rather than as a contradiction of it. In a case of genuine contradiction, like nine-ninety-five versus ten dollars, where no harmonization is available, perhaps even Rav would treat it as a *safek*.

### Second Language Wins

The *istira* case forecloses this interpretation. *Ma'u detema perusha kimefaresh kamashmalan* — one might have thought that in the rental Rav was merely ruling based on possible explication. The *istira* case makes clear that Rav's principle operates even where the two formulations flatly contradict one another and no harmonization is possible. In that setting too, the second language wins outright.

### Rav Consistent

This confirms that Rav holds consistently with Ben Nanas across all cases: whether the language can be explicated or whether it is a true contradiction, the final formulation stated is the one that governs the transaction.

---

## Three Positions Summary

### Ben Nanas/Rav Camp

Three distinct positions now emerge from the *sugya*. The first is that of Ben Nanas, endorsed by Rav: *tfos lashon acharon* — in all cases of contradictory contractual language, one follows the last phrase stated. Applied to the land sale, whichever term appears at the end of the formulation — whether precise or approximate — is the operative one. Applied to the rental, Rav would give the entire disputed month to the landlord because "one *dinar* per month" was the closing phrase. Applied to the *istira* case, the final stated price is the one binding on buyer and seller alike.

### Tannaim: Split

The second position is that of the *tannaim* in Bava Metzia, reflected in the ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yossi in the Tzipori case: the two formulations remain in genuine tension, creating a state of *mammon hamutal besafek*, and one therefore *cholkin* — divides the disputed amount between the parties.

### Shmuel: Muchzak

The third position is Shmuel's: the formulations are likewise held in contradiction and create a *safek*, but rather than splitting the difference, one resolves the doubt by identifying the *muchzak* — the party currently in possession — and ruling in his favor.

### Apply to Cases

Each position yields distinct outcomes across the cases examined on this daf. In the land sale, Ben Nanas and Rav follow whichever phrase came last; the *tannaim* would split the disputed portion of land; and Shmuel would apply *pachot shebaleshonot*, awarding the seller — the *muchzak* in the land — the benefit of the contradiction, leaving the buyer with only the minimum the language unambiguously supports. In the rental, Ben Nanas and Rav award the leap month entirely to whichever party is favored by the final phrase; the *tannaim* split the month; and Shmuel goes by *muchzak*, producing the three-way split depending on whether the case comes to court at the beginning, middle, or end of the disputed month. In the *kor bishloshim* case, what appears to be a ruling by the final language is, under Shmuel's analysis, actually an application of *muchzak* as well — each *se'ah* transferred finalizes as a completed sale at the moment the buyer takes possession of it.

---

---

# Bava Batra 106

## Boundaries & Sixth

### Boundaries vs. Estimate

The 106th daf opens a new *mishnah* dealing with a familiar theme: the sale of land described as a *beis kor* — but now with an important variation. Where the earlier *mishnayos* discussed a sale framed primarily in terms of acreage ("a *beis kor* more or less," "a *beis kor* exactly"), this *mishnah* introduces the case of *besimanav uvemetzarav* — a sale defined by explicit boundary markers. The paradigm here is the purchase of *sadeh Ephron* by Avraham, where the Torah enumerates the field's borders, its cave, and every tree within its boundaries with meticulous precision. When a seller specifies the northern, southern, eastern, and western borders with that same exactitude, the description of acreage becomes a secondary element: the true object of the sale is the bounded plot itself, whatever it contains.

This shift in emphasis has a direct *halachic* consequence. Because the boundaries are so clearly defined, the parties are presumed to understand precisely what is being conveyed, and therefore a greater tolerance for measurement error is permitted before any adjustment is required. Unlike the case of *beis kor* sold by estimate — where the tolerable margin is only one twenty-fourth — here the *mishnah* permits a discrepancy of up to one sixth. As the Rashbam notes, that is exactly *kiflei kiflayim* — fourfold more tolerant — than in the estimate case. The logic is straightforward: the claim of acreage is less weighty than the claim of explicit boundaries, because anyone can go measure the plot themselves.

A further point concerns the mechanism of adjustment. When the sale was purely by acreage estimate and the discrepancy exceeded the tolerable threshold, the Gemara previously considered the possibility that the seller could offer to return money in lieu of land.
