A son represents the continuation of the person into the next generation, stands in his father's stead for a range of *halachot*, and is self-evidently the primary heir. *Karov karov kodem* — the closer relative comes first — places sons unambiguously at the head of the line.

### Father vs. Daughter

The more interesting question is whether the father might be inserted between sons and daughters — that is, before daughters. Might we say that in a patriarchal system, when there are no sons, the estate should revert to the father as the closest surviving male rather than pass to a daughter?

### Daughter Continuation

Here the *Gemara* makes a striking move. The rule that a brother performs *yibbum* only when the deceased left no son is stated in the *Torah* as *uven ein lo* — he has no son. *Chazal* rule, however, that even if the deceased left only a daughter, the obligation of *yibbum* does not apply, because the daughter is considered a continuation of her father. This ruling is itself a *chiddush* — the plain sense of the *pasuk* speaks of a son, and one might have thought that only a son satisfies the condition. Yet *Chazal* extended it to daughters as well, treating them as genuine continuations of the person.

### Family Structure

This *chiddush* has direct consequences for the inheritance hierarchy. The *Gemara* reasons: since for purposes of *yibbum* both a son and a daughter are treated equivalently — both are considered to be the person's continuation — so too for purposes of inheritance, a son and a daughter are treated equivalently. Neither creates an opening for *yibbum*, and neither yields to the father. The daughter is considered a more direct continuation of the deceased than his father is, even though she may marry into another tribe and leave her father's household entirely. It is not purely a matter of biological proximity. It is about how family structure is defined: a daughter is still *this man's child*, and that relationship — as the continuation of his family unit — outweighs even the closeness of the father. In contrast, a maternal half-sibling may be biologically close but is entirely irrelevant to *halachic* inheritance, because the family structure is defined through the paternal line. Closeness here is not a genetic calculation; it is a structural one.

---

## Father Before Uncle

### Placement Objection

Even granting that the father cannot displace daughters, one might still object: why not simply insert the father in the slot that logic obviously dictates — before the uncles, but after the brothers? The *pesukim* list brothers before uncles; the father is clearly closer than his own brothers; so let the order be sons, daughters, brothers, father, uncles. Why does the *Gemara* insist on moving the father all the way up to before the brothers?

### Logical Derivation

The *Gemara's* response is elegant. *Achei ha-av lo tzrichi kra* — you do not need a special *pasuk* to tell you that the father comes before his own brothers. That is obvious. The *father's* brothers receive the inheritance only *mikoach av* — through their relationship to the father. Could one possibly imagine that the father's brothers would inherit while the father himself is still alive? Of course not. If the father is alive, he takes before his brothers — that requires no derivation whatsoever.

### No Indicator Needed

And precisely because it is so obvious that the father precedes his brothers, no *pasuk* would be needed to establish that point. The placement of father before uncles would be self-evident from first principles. No special indicator in the *Torah* would be required to communicate it.

### Textual Indicator

But the *Torah* does use a special indicator — *she'ero ha-karov elav* — to insert the father into the hierarchy. Since that indicator is doing real work, it must be communicating something that would *not* have been obvious without it. The only placement that qualifies — the one that genuinely requires a *pasuk* to establish — is the father's precedence over the *brothers*, not merely over the uncles. The *pasuk* is therefore teaching us that the father comes before the brothers, even though one might logically have expected the brother to come first. That is the *chiddush* the *pasuk* is communicating.

---

## Ve'avarta Derivation

### Ve'avarta Drasha

A second *tanna* derives the same conclusion — that the father precedes the brothers — from a different *pasuk*. *Rabbi Yishmael berabi Yosei* focuses on the word *ve'ha'avartem* in the verse *ish ki yamut uven ein lo ve'ha'avartem et nachalato le-vito*. The word *ve'ha'avartem* — you shall transfer — implies that the inheritance is being taken away from someone who would otherwise have been entitled to it and redirected to the daughter. The *Torah* is saying: instead of giving it to the person who logically comes next, transfer it away from him and give it to the daughter.

### Away From Father

Who is that person who would otherwise have been next in line, from whom the inheritance is being taken away and redirected to the daughter? *Rabbi Yishmael berabi Yosei* reads the *pasuk* as follows: *bi-makom bat atah ma'avir nachala min ha-av* — when there is a daughter, you take the inheritance away from the father and give it to the daughter. *Ve-ei atah ma'avir nachala min ha-av bi-makom achim* — but when there are brothers, you do not take the inheritance away from the father in their favor. In other words, the father comes before the brothers, but the daughter comes before the father.

### Daughters From Brother

The *Gemara* presses the point: could one not read the *pasuk* differently? Perhaps the word *ve'ha'avartem* means that when there is a daughter, you take the inheritance away from the *brothers* — not from the father — and give it to the daughter. In that reading, the father would not be placed here at all; his position would be determined separately. The brothers would follow the sons, and the daughter would intervene between sons and brothers, with the father inserted before the brothers but after the daughters by a different principle.

### Father Before Daughter

A second, bolder alternative: perhaps *ve'ha'avartem* should be read to mean that even the father loses out to the daughter — meaning we should insert the father even *before* the daughters, and the *Torah* is saying that when there is a daughter, you take the inheritance away even from the father and give it to her. This would place the father between sons and daughters.

### Ve'avarta Necessity

The *Gemara* rejects this reading: *im ken lo nichtav rachmana ve'ha'avartem* — if that were the correct reading, the *Torah* would not have needed the word *ve'ha'avartem* at all. It should simply have said *u-netatem* — you shall give it to the daughter — the same formulation used for all other heirs. The very fact that the *Torah* switches to the language of transferring signals that something notable is happening.

### Patriarchy Disruption

And what is that notable thing? The inheritance is being taken away from a *male* heir who would otherwise have been next in line, and redirected to a female. That is the *chiddush* — the disruption of the expected patriarchal order. If the father came *before* the daughters, then after the sons the next in line would be a male heir — the father — and giving it to him would involve no disruption to patriarchal continuity whatsoever. The word *ve'ha'avartem* would be superfluous; *u-netatem* would have sufficed. The word *ve'ha'avartem* is therefore necessary only because the inheritance is going to a daughter *instead of* a male heir who would otherwise come next. That male heir is the father, and therefore the father must come *after* the daughters. The *pasuk* of *ve'ha'avartem* thus establishes the same result as the first *tanna's* derivation: sons and daughters first, then the father, then the brothers.

---

## Wife as She'ero

### Husband Inherits Wife

We have seen that the first *tanna* uses *she'ero ha-karov elav* to insert the father into the inheritance hierarchy. The *Gemara* now raises a second reading of *she'ero*: perhaps it refers not to the father, but to the man's wife, and the *pasuk* is teaching that a husband inherits from his wife.

The *Gemara* reads *u-netatem et nachalato li-she'eiro* not as "give the inheritance to his *she'er*" — which would suggest bequeathing to the wife — but as "give what belongs to his *she'er* to him," meaning: a man inherits his wife's estate. It bears noting that whether a husband's inheritance of his wife is *de-Oraita* or *de-rabbanan* is a debate among the *rishonim*. The *Rambam* holds that it is only *de-rabbanan* and that this *drasha* is an *asmachta*, since inheritance, in his view, requires a blood relationship. Most *rishonim*, however, understand it to be *de-Oraita*, reading *she'ero ha-karov elav* as genuinely applying to a wife through the principle of *basar echad*, which we will return to shortly.

### Closest Flesh

Why should a wife be considered *she'er* — flesh? The concept has a parallel in an entirely different domain. This week's *parsha* discusses the circumstances under which a *kohen* may become *tamei*. The *pasuk* states: *ki im li-she'eiro ha-karov elav* — only for his closest flesh relative may he defile himself — and then enumerates mother, father, son, daughter, brother, and unmarried sister. A wife is not explicitly listed. Yet *Chazal* read *she'eiro ha-karov elav* as including a wife, on the grounds that she is his closest *she'er*. The following *pasuk*, *lo yitama ba'al be'amav le-hechalo*, may even suggest in its *pshat* the opposite — that a husband should not defile himself for his wife — but *Chazal* read *she'eiro* as encompassing her. The *Rambam*, consistent with his position on inheritance, holds that a *kohen's* permission to become *tamei* for his wife is also *de-rabbanan*, with the Rabbis treating her as a *meit mitzvah* for whom the *kohen* is obligated. Most *rishonim* disagree.

### Onah & Flesh

A further dimension of the concept of wife as *she'er* emerges from a different context altogether. The verse *she'eirah kesutah ve-onatah* — her flesh, her clothing, and her conjugal rights — lists among a husband's obligations to his wife the provision of *she'eirah*, which plainly means "her flesh." One reading understands this as the obligation to provide sustenance — food that puts flesh on her body. But the *Ramban* offers a deeper interpretation.

### Ramban Sustenance

The *Ramban* notes that while some understand *she'eirah* as referring to food and material provision — *she'er* as sustenance, the meat on one's bones — he himself reads it as a reference to conjugal relations and the obligation of *onah*. The *Ramban* sees different aspects of the husband's intimate obligations reflected in the word *she'eirah*.

### One Flesh

This reading connects to the foundational verse of marriage: *ve-hayu le-basar echad* — and they shall become one flesh. Once husband and wife are *basar echad*, one flesh, the wife becomes his *she'er* — the flesh closest to him. And this, *Chazal* argue, is what entitles the reading that *she'eiro ha-karov elav* refers to his wife: there is no blood relationship between them, no biological connection, but through the union of marriage and the becoming of one flesh, she is considered closer to him than any other relative. Indeed, one could argue she is closer than any of them — he is *basar echad* with his wife in a way that he is not *basar echad* with his father, mother, son, or daughter. It is a powerful and far-reaching reading by *Chazal*, grounding both the *kohen's* right to become *tamei* for his wife and the husband's right to inherit her estate in the same concept of marital union as the ultimate closeness of flesh.

---

## Rebbi's Ve'avarta

### Transfer Vs. Give

*Rebbi* offers a distinct *drasha* on the word *ve'ha'avartem* that illuminates the same inheritance structure from a different angle. He observes: *be-kulah ne'emar bahen netina* — throughout the entire passage, the Torah uses the language of *giving* when speaking of all other heirs. It is only with regard to daughters that the *Torah* uses the language of *ha'avara* — transferring or passing over.

### Tribe Transfer Reason

Why the distinction? Because with daughters, the inheritance does not simply pass to the next heir within the family — it may leave the tribe entirely. A daughter who marries a man from another tribe creates the conditions for the estate to migrate: *ho-il u-vinah u-va'alah yorshin otah* — because her son and her husband inherit from her. Her son, who belongs to his father's tribe, and her husband, who is from a different tribe, will both be positioned to inherit her estate. So what was the land of one tribe can find itself, a generation or two later, in the possession of members of an entirely different tribe. The word *ve'ha'avartem* — you shall transfer — signals precisely this: that giving to a daughter is a transfer not only of property but of tribal affiliation.

### Husband Inheritance

*Rebbi's* formulation carries an implicit derivation that the *Rashbam* highlights. By noting that the inheritance reaches another tribe because the daughter's husband and son inherit from her, *Rebbi* is also affirming — from within the plain sense of the *pesukim* — that a husband inherits his wife. Indeed, this is arguably the *pshat* of the complaint raised by the uncles of *benot Tzelofchad*: they said that if these daughters marry men from other tribes, the inheritance will leave. The implicit assumption in that complaint is precisely that a wife's husband inherits her estate. *Rebbi's* *drasha* on *ve'ha'avartem* makes that assumption explicit.

---

## She'ero Contexts

### Dual Meaning

A question now arises: if *she'ero* is used by the first *tanna* to insert the father into the inheritance hierarchy, how can a second *tanna* use the same word *she'ero* to teach that a husband inherits his wife? The two readings would seem to be in tension.

### Levitical Reference

The *Gemara* notes that *she'er* in the sense of a marital connection does appear explicitly in the *Torah*, since the verse says *she'er avicha hi* — your father's wife is his *she'er*. This demonstrates that *she'er* can be applied to a marital relationship, providing a basis for reading it as "wife" in the inheritance context.

### Different Sources

The resolution is that these are two different *tannaim* deriving two different *halachot* from the same term, each reading it according to a different context.

### Father Insertion

The first *tanna* reads *she'ero ha-karov elav* as a reference to the father, using it to insert the father into the inheritance hierarchy — specifically before the brothers, as we have established.

### Wife Reference

The second *tanna* reads *she'ero* as a reference to the wife, deriving from the same passage that a husband inherits his wife's estate. The two *tannaim* are not contradicting one another; they are each extracting a different teaching from the same word, drawing on different contextual associations.

---

## Patriarchy Principle

### Mother vs. Daughter

Having established that daughters can inherit — an acknowledged disruption of the purely patriarchal model — the *Gemara* raises a natural follow-up question: if daughters can be included in the inheritance hierarchy despite not carrying on the patrilineal family name, why not extend the same logic to mothers? If a man dies leaving no children and no father, why shouldn't the estate pass to his mother, who is certainly a close relative? After all, both a daughter and a mother represent relationships that cut across the strictly patrilineal structure.

### Father's Family Only

The *Gemara* responds with a foundational principle: *mishpachat av keruyah mishpacha, mishpachat em einah keruyah mishpacha*. The father's family is called a family; the mother's family is not called a family. This is the *halachic* articulation of what patriarchy means as a descriptive term: family structure is defined through the father. Two people who share only a mother but have different fathers belong to two entirely different families. Their biological relationship is real, but they are not part of the same *mishpacha*. The family unit is constituted by the paternal line, not the maternal one.

### Father-Defined Family

This principle has direct implications for inheritance. *Nachala* — inheritance — flows within the *mishpacha*, and since *mishpacha* is defined exclusively through the father, only relatives on the father's side can inherit. A mother, however close she may be emotionally and biologically, belongs to a different *mishpacha*. She cannot inherit from her son, because her son's *mishpacha* is his father's, not hers.

### Household Evidence

The *Gemara* grounds this principle in a *pasuk: le-mishpachtam le-veit avotam* — according to their families, their father's household. The explicit linkage of *mishpacha* to *beit avotam* — the father's house — confirms that family identity is constituted through the paternal line. This is not merely a social convention; it is the *Torah's* own definition of what a family is.

---

## Levi From Judah

### Apparent Contradiction

With the principle of patrilineal family identity established, the *Gemara* confronts a textual challenge. The story of *Pesel Micha* includes the following description of the Levite who became *Micha's* priest: *va-yehi na'ar mi-Beit Lechem Yehuda, mi-mishpachat Yehuda, ve-hu Levi* — there was a youth from Beit Lechem Yehuda, from the family of Yehuda, and he was a Levi. This seems internally contradictory. If he was from the family of Yehuda, how could he also be a Levi? And conversely, if he was a Levi, how can the *pasuk* describe him as being from the family of Yehuda?

### Paternal Tribe

The straightforward resolution is that his father was a Levi and his mother was from the tribe of Yehuda. His tribal identity — Levi — follows his father, as the principle of *mishpachat av* demands. Yet the *pasuk* still describes him as *mi-mishpachat Yehuda*, from the family of Yehuda, because his mother's family, while not his primary family, is not entirely invisible either. This would seem to support the view that a mother's family can serve as at least a secondary form of family identification.

### True Identity

But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this reading. A different voice in the *Gemara* points out that the man's name was not simply "Levi" — that was not his name at all. His name was *Yehonatan ben Gershom ben Menashe*, as revealed later in the narrative when the Danites adopt him and his descendants as priests. And *Gershom* — as the *Gemara* knows — was the son of *Moshe Rabbeinu*. This Yehonatan was, in fact, the grandson of *Moshe* himself.

### Menashe Association

If he was the grandson of *Moshe Rabbeinu*, why does the *pasuk* call him *ben Gershom ben Menashe* rather than *ben Gershom ben Moshe*? The *Gemara* explains: *mitoch she-asa ma'aseh Menashe* — because he acted in the manner of *Menashe*, the later king notorious for his idolatry, the *pasuk* attributed him to *Menashe*, making it as if that idolatrous king were his grandfather. This is admittedly anachronistic — *Menashe* lived many generations after the period of the Judges — but the point is homiletical: the *Katuv* associated him with the most notorious idolater in Israel's history because his behavior paralleled that legacy.

### Idolater Association

With this in mind, *Rabbi Yochanan* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai* proposes the same solution for the phrase *mi-mishpachat Yehuda*: just as *ben Menashe* does not mean he was literally descended from *Menashe* but rather that he acted like *Menashe*, so too *mi-mishpachat Yehuda* does not mean he was literally from the family of Yehuda through his mother. It means he acted like the idolatrous members of *Yehuda*. The description is comparative and moral, not genealogical. The *Gemara* thereby rescues the principle that *mishpachat em einah keruyah mishpacha*: even in this *pasuk*, family identity through the mother is not genuinely being invoked. The reference is to character and conduct, not lineage.

It must be acknowledged that this resolution is somewhat strained — the *pshat* of the *pesukim* does seem to be describing actual family connections, and the reading that "from the family of Yehuda" means "he behaved like Judahite idolaters" is clearly secondary. Yet the *Gemara* insists on it, because the alternative — recognizing the mother's family as a legitimate, if secondary, form of family grouping — is precisely what the principle of patrilineal *mishpacha* cannot accommodate.

---

## Chiddush & Patriarchy

### Daughters Only

We are left with an important clarifying principle. The inclusion of daughters in the inheritance hierarchy is a genuine *chiddush* — a departure from what a purely patriarchal system would have dictated. And yet it does not open the door to including mothers.

### Daughter vs. Mother

Why does the *chiddush* extend to daughters but not to mothers? The answer lies in the nature of the relationship. A daughter is still *this man's child*. She belongs to his family unit — she is a product of his household, a continuation of him, even if she will eventually join another household upon marriage. The inheritance passing to a daughter is still in some sense passing within the father's family, even if it will eventually leave the tribe. A mother, by contrast, is not part of the father's family at all. She is a member of a different *mishpacha* — her own father's family. The man's *mishpacha* is his father's; his mother belongs to her father's *mishpacha*, not to his.

### Exclusive Patrilineality

Therefore, the *Gemara* will not permit even a secondary role for the mother's family. One might have proposed a tiered model: primary family through the father, secondary family through the mother, with maternal relatives inheriting only after all paternal relatives have been exhausted. The *Gemara* rejects even this. A man belongs to *one* family: his father's. His mother's family is simply not his family at all, in any halachic sense. The *chiddush* of daughters thus finds its precise limit here: daughters expand the family's reach slightly beyond the strictly male-to-male chain, but the family itself remains exclusively defined by the paternal line. That boundary is absolute.

---

---

# Bava Batra 110

## Family Structure

### Inheritance Order

The daf begins at the bottom of 109b, picking up from the previous session's discussion of the order of inheritance. The Gemara had worked through various *drashot* to establish that the sequence runs: son, then daughter, then father, then brother. It had also introduced the important principle that a man inherits from his wife, derived from the phrase *she'er hakarev elav* — "his close relative" — where one reading identifies *she'er* as the wife, and another as the father, with the latter insertion placing the father ahead of the brothers.

The Gemara then raises the question: from where do we know that *she'er* refers to the father? It quotes *she'er avicha* — "the flesh of your father" — though as noted, that is not really the *pshat* of those *psukim* either. This leads to the central principle that anchors the entire discussion: *mishpachat ha'av kruya mishpacha, mishpachat ha'em einah kruya mishpacha* — the father's family is called a family; the mother's family is not called a family.

### Patriarchal Principle

This statement is, in effect, the Talmud's articulation of patriarchal family structure. All children of the same father — even if born of different mothers, like Rachel and Leah — are of one family. Children of the same mother but different fathers are of different families entirely. The family is defined by the father. This is why when a person dies without children, the inheritance does not pass to the mother: doing so would mean leaving the family, since he belongs to his father's family, not his mother's. The daughter, at least until she marries out, remains part of her father's family, and so the inheritance still stays, conceptually, within that family unit.

### Bnot Tzelofchad

This principle makes the ruling of *Bnot Tzelofchad* all the more striking. What the daughters of Tzelofchad accomplished was not merely a matter of girls receiving a portion — it was a radical disruption of the entire patriarchal and tribal structure that kept ancestral land within the family estate.

Consider the following scenario: a man dies without sons, leaving only a married daughter whose husband is from a different tribe. The daughter herself inherits — but now suppose she subsequently dies, leaving behind a son. That son, a member of a different tribe entirely, directly receives the inheritance. So the land passes not gradually but immediately to a member of another tribe. The *chiddush* of *Bnot Tzelofchad* was truly disruptive in this sense.

### Practical Consequences

The Gemara notes, of course, that practically speaking such cross-tribal inheritance would have been rare, since people generally remained within their tribal territories — much as, before the age of modern travel, one simply did not frequently encounter someone from a distant region. But in principle, the possibility was entirely open.

This was precisely what the uncles of *Bnot Tzelofchad* argued: if these daughters marry men from other tribes, sections of our tribal inheritance will pass to strangers. Moshe's response — that they must marry within their tribe — was acknowledged by the Gemara to apply only to that generation. In subsequent generations, there was no technical restriction preventing the land of Yehudah, for instance, from having portions belonging to Shimon, or Yissachar, or Zevulun. Yet the Gemara insists that the fundamental patriarchal structure remains intact: the inheritance does not travel up to the mother, because the deceased belongs to his father's family, not his mother's.

---

## Micha Idol Story

### Tolin Kalkala

The Gemara transitions to a striking aggadic principle arising from the narrative of the *pesel shel Micha*. It had been established in the preceding discussion that the Levite priest of Micha's idol was identified as a grandson of Moshe — and yet the text also associates him with the tribe of Yehudah and (through the Gemara's *drasha*) with the name Menashe rather than Moshe, so as to link him to the later idolater Menashe. Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: *mikan she-tolin et ha-kalkala ba-mekulkal* — from here we learn that one associates corruption with the corrupt. Even when the association is not technically accurate, the Torah goes out of its way to make the thematic link, because such people share a moral character.

### Adoniyah Case

Rabbi Yossi be-Rabbi Chanina offers a parallel example from the story of Adoniyah, of whom the verse says: *vegam hu tov to'ar me'od ve'oto yaldah acharei Avshalom* — "he too was very handsome, and she bore him after Avshalom." The Gemara asks the obvious question: was Adoniyah not the son of Chagit, while Avshalom was the son of Maachah? What does it mean that she bore him after Avshalom? The Gemara answers: *mitoch she-asa ma'aseh Avshalom de-marad be-malchut* — since Adoniyah acted like Avshalom in rebelling against his father David and against the monarchy, the verse deliberately associates him with Avshalom. The text forges a connection that is morally apt even if genealogically inapposite. This is the principle of *tolin kalkala ba-mekulkal* in operation.

### Cleave to Good

Rabbi Elazar draws the positive corollary: *le'olam yidbak adam be-tovim* — a person should always cleave to good people. The proof is that Moshe married the daughter of Yitro, and from that union descended Yehonatan, who became a priest to the *pesel shel Micha*. Aharon, by contrast, married the daughter of Aminadav, and from him descended Pinchas. The implication, taken at face value, carries an irony worth noting: Aharon himself made the Golden Calf, yet because he married into a worthy family, his grandson came out righteous. Moshe Rabbeinu, who spoke *panim el panim* with God, yet married into a family associated with *avodah zarah*, and his grandson became a priest to an idol. The lesson is presented without softening.

---

## Moshe's Grandson

### Pinchas & Yitro

The Gemara immediately notes a complication: if the principle is that Moshe's lineage was compromised because Yitro was an idolater — for Yitro, whatever his later recognition of God, was a *kohen Midyan* and presumably served foreign gods — then what about Pinchas? The verse in Shemot states: *Elazar ben Aharon lakach lo mi-bnot Putiel le-isha* — Elazar married from the daughters of Putiel. The classic *drasha* identifies Putiel as Yitro, *she-pitem agalim la-avodah zarah* — who fattened calves for idol worship. So Pinchas was also a descendant of an idolater on his mother's side. How then can we contrast Moshe's descendant unfavorably with Aharon's?

### Women Invisible

This is where the discussion takes a revealing turn. The Gemara's entire framing — *Moshe who married the daughter of Yitro* and *Aharon who married the daughter of Aminadav* — places the women almost entirely out of the picture. The interest is in the men: whose daughter did he marry? What kind of man was her father? What kind of man was her brother? And then: what will your grandson turn out to be? The women function as conduits between male lineages; the men on each side of the marriage are the primary subjects of scrutiny. This is, in a sense, a striking reinstatement of the patriarchal logic after *Bnot Tzelofchad* had disrupted it — women become nearly invisible in the transmission of character and family standing, while the focus falls entirely on fathers and brothers.

### Putiel Descent

The Gemara resolves the Pinchas difficulty as follows. Rather than read *Putiel* as referring solely to Yitro, the Gemara proposes a different *drasha*: *lo de-asi mi-Yosef she-pitpeit be-yitzro* — Putiel refers to Yosef, who combated his *yetzer ha-ra* when tempted by Potiphar's wife. Elazar thus married a woman who descended from Yosef, not Yitro. But the Gemara does not want to abandon the well-known *midrash* that the tribes mocked Pinchas on account of his Yitro connection: *re'isem ben Puti ze she-pitem avi imo agalim le-avodah zarah yahrog nasi shevet mi-Yisrael* — "Have you seen this son of Puti, whose mother's father fattened calves for idolatry, and he goes and kills a prince of Israel?" This *midrash* is too important to set aside.

The resolution offered is therefore: *avuah de-imei mi-Yosef, imei de-imei mi-Yitro* — either the father of his mother was from Yosef and the mother of his mother was from Yitro, or vice versa. Either arrangement is possible. The word *Putiel* itself, notably written in a form that can be read as dual, hints at this double descent: *tarti* — two lineages, one from Yosef and one from Yitro.

Tosafot and the Rashbam both acknowledge that this resolution is not entirely clean: Pinchas also had an idolatrous grandfather, and yet he turned out righteous, while Moshe's grandson — despite Moshe's own greatness — did not. Perhaps the Yosef lineage counterbalances; perhaps the degree of removal over generations matters. The argument is not as tidy as it first appears. Nevertheless, the overall thrust — that *yidbak adam be-tovim*, that one must deliberately align oneself and one's family with good people — is maintained.

---

## Marriage & Brothers

### Check Brothers

Rava introduces a related but distinct principle: *ha-nosei ishah tzarich she-yivdok be-acheiha* — when a man marries a woman, he must investigate her brothers. The proof-text is the verse describing Aharon's marriage: *vayikach Aharon et Elisheva bat Aminadav achot Nachshon* — Aharon took Elisheva the daughter of Aminadav, the sister of Nachshon. The Gemara asks: if she is the daughter of Aminadav, is it not obvious that she is the sister of Nachshon? Why does the verse add the detail? From here we learn that one should check the brothers when marrying a woman.

### Rov Banim Domim

The reason is stated explicitly: *rov banim domim le-achei ha-em* — most sons resemble their mother's brothers. If you want to know what kind of sons you will have, look at your wife's brothers. The logic may be genetic or it may be environmental — one could argue that a woman raises her sons the way her mother raised her brothers, so the brothers serve as a preview of the type of boys likely to emerge. Either way, the practical advice is to attend to the brothers.

### Patriarchal Focus

And yet here too the patriarchal framing is striking. The woman one is marrying — her own qualities, her own *middos*, her own upbringing — might seem the most natural source of information about the children she will raise. But the Gemara's focus falls on the men in her life: her father and her brothers. The concern is specifically about sons and how they will turn out, not daughters. The girls, it seems, do not feature in this calculus. One is marrying a woman, but the inquiry is directed toward the male relatives — father and brothers — and the outcome of interest is the male offspring.

This connects directly to the earlier structural principle: the family is defined by the father and the men. The women, including the wife herself, become almost invisible in this framework of looking forward to the next generation. Counterexamples, of course, exist — Ruth, whose father's family were *ovdei avodah zarah*, and whose great-grandchild was David HaMelech; Devorah; the pairs of siblings throughout Bereishit who did not resemble one another. The Gemara does not address these, but they hang in the background as complicating data.

---

## Self-Sufficiency Teaching

### Danites Question

The Gemara returns to the narrative of *pesel Micha*. When the Danites came to Micha's house and found the Levite — who, according to the *midrash*, was Moshe's grandson Yehonatan — they questioned him. The verse reads: *vayasuru sham vayomeru mi hevi'acha halom* — "they turned aside and said, who brought you here? What are you doing? What business do you have here?" The Gemara reads these phrases as echoing language associated with Moshe himself — *al tikrav halom*, *ma zeh be-yadecha*, *ve-ata poh amod imadi* — so as to heighten the irony and confrontation. They were essentially saying: are you not a descendant of Moshe, of whom God said "do not draw near" at the *sneh*? And you are here serving as a priest to *avodah zarah*?

### Yaskir Adam

His response is extraordinary. He said to them: *kach mekubalni mi-beit avi aba* — this is the tradition I received from my grandfather's house, meaning from Moshe: *le'olam yaskir adam atzmo le-avodah zarah ve-al yitztarech la-briyot* — a person should sooner hire himself out to *avodah zarah* than need to depend on others.

The principle itself is entirely sound as a teaching about self-sufficiency and the dignity of earning one's own living. It is better to take any work, even work that feels foreign or beneath you, than to become a dependent on other people's charity. The verse in the narrative makes clear that Micha attracted Yehonatan with a salary — it was indeed a matter of earning a living.

One might also note that *yaskir adam atzmo le-avodah zarah* need not even imply actual *avodah zarah*: hiring yourself out to work in such a place — chopping wood, maintaining the grounds — is categorically different from serving as a *kohen* in that place. The phrase, taken carefully, need not have led to the conclusion he drew.

### David Intervenes

The Gemara delivers the punchline: *v'hu savar le-avodah zarah mamash* — he understood it to mean literally idolatry. *V'lo hi* — but that is not what was meant. *Ela avodah zarah* means *avodah she-zarah lo* — work that is strange or foreign to him, completely outside his natural sphere, but not literally idol worship. It is a pointed observation — and a cautionary one — about how a teaching can be profoundly misunderstood when taken literally rather than figuratively. There is also, as one participant noted, a lesson about what one says around children or descendants: if a teaching can be heard in a dangerous literal sense, one must be careful in how it is transmitted, especially in a home already adjacent to *avodah zarah*.

### Rav's Teaching

The Gemara brings a parallel teaching. Rav said to Rav Kahana: *nitosh nevielta be-shuka u-shkol agra ve-lo teima gavra raba ana ve-zeila bei milta* — go and flay a carcass in the marketplace and take your pay, and do not say "I am an important person and this is beneath my dignity." It is more self-respecting to work and earn one's keep, even in repulsive or demeaning labor, than to depend on others.

Some have the variant reading *ve-lo teima kahana ana* — do not say "I am a *kohen*." This connects to the story directly, since Yehonatan was a *levi* serving as a *kohen*. Tosafot raises the objection that Rav Kahana may not actually have been a *kohen*, and suggests that just as the Gemara earlier noted that the Levite's name was "Levi" rather than actually being from that tribe, so too here the statement may refer to the *name* Kahana rather than to priestly status.

The Rashbam elaborates: there is no *chillul Hashem* in a *talmid chacham* doing hard physical labor to earn a living. The *chillul Hashem* condemned elsewhere — as in the teaching from Masechet Shabbat that a *talmid chacham* who wears stained clothing causes people to degrade the Torah — applies to one's presentation. But performing *melacha le-hitparnes*, working to support oneself, carries no shame whatsoever. The distinction between a one-time crisis requiring temporary support and a permanent condition of dependence on others is also important here: the Gemara's concern is with the latter, the general posture of self-sufficiency rather than any specific emergency.

### Shevuel Repents

The Gemara closes this narrative thread. David saw that Moshe's grandson — referred to here as Shevuel ben Gershom ben Moshe, with the Gemara noting that this is the same individual previously called Menashe (Moshe) — was extremely devoted to money. Rather than condemning him outright, David appointed him *nagid al ha-otzarot*, supervisor over the royal storehouses. It is, admittedly, a somewhat surprising appointment given that his money-hunger was what led him to the *avodah zarah* in the first place.

Rabbi Yochanan explains: *sheshav le-El be-chol libo* — he returned to God wholeheartedly. Hence the name *Shevuel*, from *shuv* — return. The Rashbam notes a difficulty: the *psukim* in Shmuel indicate that his descendants continued to serve as priests to the *pesel Micha* until the exile. He resolves it via the Yerushalmi: when Shlomo HaMelech came to power, he dismissed the entire royal staff and appointed a new one — at which point Shevuel returned to Micha's temple. His *teshuvah*, apparently, did not survive the regime change.

---

## Sons vs. Daughters

### Sons Inherit

The Gemara now returns to the *mishna* and the formal derivation of the inheritance order. The *mishna* teaches: *ve-ha-banim et ha-av* — sons inherit from father. This seems obvious, and yet the Gemara asks: *minalan* — from where do we derive it? The verse states: *ish ki yamut u-ven ein lo ve-ha'avartem et nachalato le-vito* — if a man dies and has no son, you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter. The implication is clear: *ta'ama de-ein lo ben* — the reason the daughter gets it is that there is no son. If there is a son, the son comes first.

### Rav Pappa's Reading

Rav Pappa challenges Abaye with an alternative reading. Perhaps the verse is saying something more nuanced: if there is a son and no daughter, the son inherits; if there is a daughter and no son, the daughter inherits. But when there is both a son and a daughter, perhaps *lo hai leyaras ve-lo hai leyaras* — neither inherits exclusively — meaning perhaps the son and daughter share equally. On this reading, the verse would not establish that sons precede daughters when both are present; it would only tell us what happens when only one type of heir exists.

The Gemara dispatches the absurdist version of this reading immediately — the suggestion that if neither inherits it goes to the *moshel ha-ir*, some civic authority, is obviously not a reasonable reading of the *pasuk*. So Rav Pappa clarifies: what he means is that perhaps sons and daughters inherit equally when both are present.

### Abaye's Response

Abaye responds: if sons and daughters are fundamentally equal heirs, the verse would not need to say anything special. *Ve-itzrecha kra le-ashmiunan* — why would the verse need to tell me separately what happens when there is only a son or only a daughter? If they are equal, the general rule would cover all cases without requiring the specific statement that in the absence of a son the daughter gets it.

But the Gemara then asks: perhaps the verse *does* need to tell us explicitly about daughters — because without it, one might have assumed that *banim* means only sons, and daughters do not inherit at all. On that reading, the verse's mention of the daughter is necessary simply to establish that daughters can inherit, and once that is established, maybe they are equal to sons.

### Bnot Tzelofchad Claim

The Gemara responds: that information — that daughters can inherit — is already derived from the separate verse *kol bat yoreshes nachalah* — every daughter who receives an inheritance. Once that verse has introduced the principle of female inheritance following the *Bnot Tzelofchad* episode, the verse at hand (*im ein lo ben ve-ha'avartem nachalato le-vito*) no longer needs to do that work. Its only function is therefore to establish priority: only in the *absence* of sons does the daughter receive it. The verse's formulation is fully explicit in this structure.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov proposes yet another approach: we can derive the same point from the *claim* of *Bnot Tzelofchad* themselves. They said: *lama yigara shem avinu mi-toch mishpachto ki ein lo ben* — why should our father's name be diminished because he has no son? Give us a *nachalah* among our father's brothers. The very framing of their plea presupposes that if there had been a son, the son would have gotten it and they would not be making any claim. They were explicitly accepting the subordination of daughters to sons; they were only asking to fill the vacuum left by the absence of sons.

### HaKarov Eilav

The Gemara objects: one cannot prove from what *Bnot Tzelofchad* asked what the law actually is. Perhaps God responded to their request more expansively than they had asked — *nitnah Torah ve-nis'chadshah halachah* — the Torah was given and a new ruling emerged, one that placed sons and daughters on equal footing when both are present. The daughters were willing to accept the secondary position, but God may have granted more than they sought. Therefore one cannot use their *claim* to derive the *psak*.

The Gemara concludes: *ela michvarta ki-deshanin me-ikara* — the clearest proof remains the one stated earlier, from the verse itself, which plainly says *im ein lo ben* — only in the absence of a son does the daughter inherit.

Ravina then adds a separate proof. The verse says *uve-nesatem et nachalato li-sh'eiro ha-karov eilav mi-mishpachto* — you shall give his inheritance to his close relative from his family. The principle is *ha-karov karov kodem* — the closest relative comes first. From this one might infer that sons precede daughters on the grounds that sons are closer relatives to the father than daughters are.

---

## Son's Closeness

### Son Closer Logic

The question is immediately raised: *u-mai kurva de-ven mi-bas* — on what basis do we actually know that a son is closer to the father than a daughter? This is not as self-evident as it might appear. The inquiry is not merely reaffirming the known *halacha* but probing whether there is an independent source in *halacha* or Scripture that reflects this structural closeness — a source from which we could then derive the inheritance order through *ha-karov karov kodem*.

### Failed Proofs

The Gemara suggests two areas where a son is treated as an extension of the father while a daughter is not. First: *ben kam tachas aviv le-ye'adah* — a son can step into his father's role with respect to the *yi'ud* (betrothal) of a Hebrew maidservant whom the father acquired but did not himself marry. Second: with regard to *sedei achuzah* — a sanctified ancestral field — if the son redeems it, it is treated as if the father redeemed it, and therefore does not pass to the *kohanim* at *yovel*; but if a daughter redeems it, this benefit does not apply.

Both proofs fail, however. With respect to *yi'ud*: a daughter is simply not eligible to perform *yi'ud* at all — the institution applies only to a male master. The inapplicability of the rule to the daughter does not show that she is a more distant relative; it shows only that the institution is sex-specific. With respect to *sedei achuzah*: we know the daughter cannot redeem it with the same effect as the father only because we already assume from elsewhere that she is a more distant heir. The proof is circular — it presupposes the very hierarchy it is trying to establish.

### Closeness by Default

The Gemara concludes: *ela michvarta ki-deshanin me-ikara* — there is no independent source establishing that a son is closer than a daughter. The only place we actually derive this is from the verse *im ein lo ven ve-ha'avartem nachalato le-vito* itself. The son's superior position in the family hierarchy is established by the inheritance order, not the other way around. One cannot use *ha-karov karov kodem* as an independent proof that sons precede daughters, because the very fact that sons are considered "closer" is derived from that same inheritance order. The argument from Ravina's verse is therefore not an independent proof.

### Banim Definition

The Gemara then examines another potential source: *ve-hisnachaltem otam li-vneichem achareichem* — you shall bequeath them (slaves) to your sons after you. Does *livneichem* here mean sons specifically, to the exclusion of daughters? The Gemara asks: *bneichem ve-lo bnoseichem* — sons and not daughters?

But this cannot be the implication in all contexts. The verse *le-ma'an yirbu yemeichem vi-mei vneichem* — so that your days and the days of your children be increased — surely extends the blessing to daughters as well. *Bracha shani* — the context of a blessing is different; there, the inclusive meaning is obviously intended.

This raises a genuine question about the default interpretation of *banim* and *bneichem*. The Gemara's apparent position is that the default is *sons* unless context pushes toward the more inclusive meaning of *children*. This is directly relevant to the *mitzvah* of *talmud Torah* as well: *ve-limadetem otam et bneichem ledaber bam* — *bneichem ve-lo bnoseichem* — and there the exclusion of daughters from the paternal obligation of *talmud Torah* is derived from the same default reading. The modern instinct may run the other way — to read *bneichem* as *children* by default — but the Gemara's interpretive assumption appears to run in the direction of *sons* as the baseline meaning, requiring an affirmative reason to extend the term.

---

## Paternal Brothers

### Paternal Brothers Only

The *mishna* states: *ve-achei min ha-av nochalin u-manchilim* — brothers of the same father inherit from one another and transmit inheritance to one another. The restriction to paternal brothers — *achi min ha-av* — needs derivation. The *mishna* specifies that only brothers through a common father are in the inheritance relationship; maternal half-brothers, who share a mother but not a father, are not.

### Yaakov Sons Proof

Rava derives this from the sons of Yaakov. The verse in Bereishit records them saying: *shneim asar avadecha achim anachnu bnei ish echad* — "we your servants are twelve brothers, sons of one man." They call themselves *achim* — brothers — and immediately qualify it as *bnei ish echad*, sons of one man. This is the biblical paradigm of brotherhood: defined by a shared father. *Ma le-halan min ha-av ve-lo min ha-em, af kan min ha-av ve-lo min ha-em* — just as in that paradigm brotherhood is defined through the father and not through the mother, so too throughout the laws of inheritance, brothers are those who share a father, not merely a mother.

### Family via Father

The Gemara then notes that one need not go all the way to the sons of Yaakov for this derivation. The general rule already tells us everything we need: *uve-nesatem nachalato le-mishpachto, mishpachat ha-av kruya mishpacha, mishpachat ha-em einah kruya mishpacha* — the family is defined by the father. If family is patrilineally defined, then obviously brothers — as members of the same family — are brothers through the father, not through the mother alone.

Why, then, did Rava need to go to the sons of Yaakov? The answer is: Rava's derivation was actually stated in the context of *yibum*, not inheritance. For *yibum* — where the obligation falls on a *brother* of the deceased — the patrilineal definition of brotherhood is equally essential, but there the verse (*ki yeshvu achim yachdav*) does not occur in the explicit context of the patriarchal family structure, so an independent derivation from the precedent of the sons of Yaakov is needed. For inheritance, by contrast, the principle of *mishpachat av kruya mishpacha* suffices on its own. The family is the father's family, and brotherhood within that family is necessarily paternal brotherhood. This closing rule thus returns us to the foundational axiom with which the daf began.

---

---

# Bava Batra 111

## Inheritance Hierarchy

### Prior Coverage

Today's daf is 111. We pick up on the last line of 110b, continuing through the roster of people who inherit from one another. The previous daf covered several key relationships. A father inheriting from his children is not derived from the plain sense of the *psukim* but is learned through a *drasha* — specifically, the phrase *she'ero hakaro elav*, "his flesh who is close to him," which inserts the father into the order of inheritance between the children and the brother. The plain meaning of the *psukim* establishes that when someone dies, the estate first passes to sons, then to daughters. The father is then inserted by derivation, and the brothers follow. The brother is explicit in the *psukim*: *ve'im ein lo bat unetatem et nachalato le'achiv*, "and if he has no daughter, you shall give his inheritance to his brother" — though the Gemara's critical point there was that "brother" is defined as a paternal half-brother, governed by the principle that *mishpachat av kriya mishpacha, mishpachat em eina kriya mishpacha* — the patriarchal family is called a family, the maternal family is not. So the full sequence from the previous daf is: son, daughter, father, brother, and father's brother. That covers essentially the entire Mishnah, aside from two figures who are not derived from the plain sense of the *psukim*: a wife and a mother.

### New Topics Intro

We now turn to those two remaining cases — a man inheriting from his wife, and a man inheriting from his mother. The word *she'ero*, used in various contexts, is related to flesh — *ki achinu vesarenu hu*, "for he is our brother, our flesh." The *Ramban* elaborates on this in connection with the *pasuk* *vayihyu levasar echad*, which is relevant to husband and wife — and there is of course the usage in *she'er kesuta ve'onata* as well. The Gemara now asks how we know that a man inherits from his mother, and separately, how we know that a man inherits from his wife.

## Son Inherits Mother

### Tosafot Question

The Gemara asks: *mena hanei milei* — where do we know this from? Before proceeding to the Gemara's answer, Tosafot raises a pointed question: why do we need a special derivation at all? We have already established the general order of inheritance. If that order applies when a man dies, it should apply equally when a woman dies. When a woman dies, her son should obviously inherit her, just as when a man dies, his son inherits him. What requires a *pasuk*?

### Tribal Disruption

Tosafot answers with a distinction that cuts to the heart of what this entire sugya is about. For other cases involving women who die — a man's daughter or sister, for example — it is self-evident that her father or brother would inherit her, because the property remains entirely within the patriarchal family. There is no disruption, and so no *chiddush* is needed. Men and women are treated identically in this regard: *bein lirash bein lehorish*, whether inheriting or bequeathing.

But the case of a son inheriting from his mother is genuinely different. Tosafot explains: *lefi shenisvet nachala lah mimateh aviha al yedei haben* — because the inheritance that came to her from her father's tribe now passes, through her son, potentially out of that tribe entirely. If a woman born to *shevet HaDan* marries a man from *shevet Reuven*, the property she received from her Danite family — her ancestral portion in the territory of Dan — will now pass to her son, who is a Reuvenite. Geographically and tribally, a patch of Danite land ends up held by someone from Reuven.

This is profoundly disruptive because even *yovel* does not undo it. When the Jubilee year arrives and *ish el nachalato yashuvu* — each person returns to his ancestral holding — this son retains that land. It was his *nachala* that came through his mother. It does not revert to the tribe of Dan. Every tribe could end up with scattered patches belonging to people from entirely different tribes. So this is the reason a *pasuk* is needed specifically for a son inheriting from his mother: we are permitting the *nachala* to leave the *mishpachat av* through the maternal line, and that requires an explicit textual basis.

This is also why the uncles of the *Bnot Tzelafchad* complained. When a woman inherits and then passes that inheritance on — whether to her husband or to her son — the property leaves the ancestral tribe. That is precisely what their complaint was about. And this, Tosafot explains, is why the Torah requires a *chiddush* for the case of the mother: it is not simply restating the general inheritance rules; it is authorizing a transfer of *nachala* that goes outside the patriarchal household.

### Braita Derivation

The Gemara answers with a *braita*. The *pasuk* states: *vechol bat yoreshet nachala mimatot bnei Yisrael* — any daughter who inherits an inheritance from the tribes of Israel. The Gemara asks: *heich bat yoreshet shnei matot?* — how can a daughter inherit from two tribes? The answer: this is a case where her father is from one tribe and her mother is from another tribe, both die, and she inherits from both. With no sons surviving, she inherits from two separate tribes.

From this the *braita* derives: *ve'ein li ela bat* — I know only that a daughter inherits from her mother. *Ben minayin?* — how do I know a son does?

### Qal Va-Chomer

The *braita* answers with a *kal va-chomer*: a daughter, whose legal standing regarding the father's estate is weaker — she inherits only in the absence of sons — nevertheless clearly inherits from her mother. A son, whose standing by the father's estate is stronger — he is first in the order of inheritance — surely inherits from his mother as well. *Eino din she-yafe kocho b'nichsei ha-em?*

One might pause here to appreciate the *hava amina*. As Tosafot noted, the effect of a woman dying and passing her estate to her son is that the property immediately leaves the tribe. If she passes to her daughter instead, the disruption is at least not immediate: the daughter might marry within the mother's original tribe, or might not, but the transfer is one step further removed. If she passes to her son, the property crosses tribal lines without delay. So there is a genuine reason one might have thought the derivation applies only to daughters and not to sons.

The *braita* then continues: *u-mimakom she-bata* — from the same source from which you derived the son's right to inherit, apply the same logic. Just as by the father the son precedes the daughter, so too by the mother the son precedes the daughter: *ben kodem le-bat*.

Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yossi then cite a ruling in the name of Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav, which takes a fundamentally different position.

### Rabbi Zechariah Equal

Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav rules: *echad ha-ben ve-echad ha-bat shavin be-nichsei ha-em* — sons and daughters inherit equally from the mother's estate.

His reasoning is the principle of *dayo*: when a law is derived through a *kal va-chomer*, the derived rule cannot exceed the source from which it was learned. The son was brought in by learning from the daughter — since the daughter inherits, certainly the son does. But this logic only establishes that the son inherits; it does not prove that he inherits more than the daughter. *Dayo la-ba min ha-din lihyot ke-nadon*: it is sufficient for the derived case to equal the source case. Therefore, son and daughter divide equally.

The Gemara asks: does the *Tanna Kamma* — who rules that the son comes first — not accept the principle of *dayo*? After all, *dayo* is a biblical rule embedded in the framework of *kal va-chomer* itself. The source text is the episode of Miriam, where God says: if her father had spit in her face, she would be embarrassed for seven days. By *kal va-chomer*, if God Himself is angered, she should be shut out for more than seven days — perhaps fourteen. Yet the *pasuk* says seven days. Why? *Dayo la-ba min ha-din lihyot ke-nadon*: the derived case cannot exceed its source. (Tosafot notes that the logic would in principle yield more than seven, but since periods of exclusion come in seven-day units, and we cannot know precisely how much more, the *dayo* principle limits it to the original seven.)

So why does the *Tanna Kamma* rule that the son comes before the daughter from the mother's estate, apparently exceeding the *dayo* limitation? The Gemara answers: *d'l'rabbanan be'alma darsha* — of course the *Tanna Kamma* accepts *dayo* in general. But this case is different, because the *pasuk* itself provides an additional basis. The phrase *mimatot bnei Yisrael* contains the word *matot*, tribes — in the plural. This creates an *hekesh*, a juxtaposition: inheriting from the mother's tribe and inheriting from the father's tribe are placed side by side in that single word. Just as by the father's tribe the son precedes the daughter, so too by the mother's tribe the son precedes the daughter. This is not purely a *kal va-chomer* subject to *dayo*; it is an *hekesh* that transfers the rule directly. Hence the *Tanna Kamma* can rule that the son comes first without violating *dayo*.

## Mother's Estate Debate

### Rav Nisa'i Rebuke

The debate over this question — whether sons and daughters inherit equally from the mother, or whether sons retain their priority — generated intense controversy among the Amoraim. Rav Nisa'i wished to rule in practice like Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav and divide the mother's estate equally between sons and daughters. Shmuel rebuked him sharply: *ke-man? ke-Zechariah? efes Zechariah* — who are you ruling like? Zechariah is a zero; forget him entirely.

### Rabbi Tavla Rav Nachman

Rabbi Tavla actually issued a ruling in practice following Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav, dividing the mother's estate equally. Rav Nachman confronted him: *mai hai?* — what is this? Rabbi Tavla defended himself by citing a tradition in the name of Rav — through Rabbi Chinana bar Shmaya — that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav. Rav Nachman was unmoved. He told Rabbi Tavla: *zil la-hadar bakh* — go and reverse yourself. He demanded not merely a change of position, but reversal of the actual ruling in the case at hand — taking the property back from the daughters and giving it to the sons. *Ve'ei lo, mafki-na lakh Rabbi Chinana bar Shmaya me-unakh* — and if you do not, I will pull Rabbi Chinana bar Shmaya right out of your ears. The *Rashbam* explains this as a threat to place Rabbi Chinana bar Shmaya in *cherem*, which would invalidate him as a source and prevent Rabbi Tavla from relying on him. *Rabbeinu Gershom* interprets it differently: Rav Nachman is threatening to compel Rabbi Tavla to compensate the sons from his own assets for having improperly awarded property to the daughters.

### Rav Huna Bar Chiya

Rav Huna bar Chiya similarly wished to rule like Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav. Rav Nachman again confronted him: *mai hai?* Rav Huna bar Chiya cited a tradition from Rav Huna in the name of Rav — not merely through Rabbi Chinana bar Shmaya, but through the great authority Rav Huna himself — that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav. Rav Nachman responded: *eshlach lei?* — shall I send to Rav Huna and ask him directly whether he really holds this position? At that, Rav Huna bar Chiya was embarrassed — *ichsif* — and backed down. The *Rashbam* explains that he had honestly transmitted the tradition from Rav Huna, but feared that under Rav Nachman's relentless pressure, Rav Huna himself might reverse his position if directly confronted. Rav Nachman pressed further: *hashta delav dachna apeih de-Rav Huna* — now that Rav Huna is still alive and I can go check your claim, you concede; had he not been available, you would have stood your ground against me unjustifiably.

It is worth noting which authorities line up on each side. Rav Nachman — Shmuel's foremost student in Babylonia — is fiercely opposed to the equal-division position, and he invokes Shmuel himself on this. Those who favor equal division appeal to traditions in the name of Rav. Rav himself came originally from *Eretz Yisrael*, where women had considerably stronger legal standing than in Babylonia — and Rav Nachman is a thoroughgoing Babylonian. Whether that geographic and cultural divide contributes to this dispute is worth considering, though it cannot be stated with certainty.

### Rav Nachman Traditions

Rav Nachman's own position rests on a different tradition from Rav — one that explicitly contradicts what the other authorities cited: *ki ha de-Rav u-Shmuel, de'amri tarveihu ein halacha ke-Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav* — both Rav and Shmuel said: the *halacha* does not follow Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav. So we have a genuine dispute about what Rav himself ruled, with Rav Nachman holding that Rav and Shmuel both rejected equal division.

## Patriarchal Logic

### Tribes Analogy

The Gemara now introduces a narrative that brings the conceptual stakes into sharp focus. Rabbi Yannai, elderly and infirm, was being carried on the shoulders of his attendant Rav Simlai. His attendant described a man approaching them — a striking individual with a beautiful cloak. When they drew close, Rabbi Yannai felt the garment and remarked: *dein shirei tasak* — this is an inferior material, the dimensions of which would qualify as sackcloth for *tumah* purposes. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, then asked Rabbi Yannai: *minayin le-ven she-kodem le-vat be-nichsei ha-em* — what is the source that a son precedes a daughter in inheriting from the mother?

Rabbi Yannai answered from the *hekesh* we have already discussed: the *pasuk* says *matot* — tribes — placing the mother's tribe and the father's tribe in one word. Just as by the father's tribe the son comes before the daughter, so too by the mother's tribe.

### Bechor Double Portion

Rabbi Yehuda Nesia pressed further: *ei ma mateh ha-av bechor notel pi shnayim, af mateh ha-em bechor notel pi shnayim* — if you are drawing a complete parallel between the mother's tribe and the father's tribe, then just as the firstborn son takes a double portion from the father, the firstborn son should take a double portion from the mother as well. Once you adopt the non-egalitarian position and rule that sons take priority, why not go all the way and apply the full law of *bechora* — double portion — to the mother's estate?

Rabbi Yannai told his attendant: *gud* — let's go. This person, he said, does not really want to learn — *leit dein tzevi lemilaf* — he just wants to be contentious. The question may have felt like retaliation for the remark about the cloak. But the Gemara is unwilling to let it drop. The question is entirely legitimate: if we are applying the *hekesh* fully, what is the basis for excluding *pi shnayim*?

## Bechor Mother Estate

### Abaye Lo Pronoun

Abaye answers from the *pasuk* governing the *bechor*: *bechol asher yimatzei lo* — the firstborn receives double from everything found belonging to *him*. The *lo* — "to him" — refers to the father. The firstborn gets double from the father's estate, not from the mother's.

The Gemara challenges: perhaps this *pasuk* is limited to a case of a *bachur* — a man on his first marriage — who married an *almanah*, a widow. In that case the child is a *bechor* for the father but not for the mother, since she already had children. Perhaps it is only in that configuration — firstborn to the father, not firstborn to the mother — that the child does not receive double from the mother's estate. But if the child is both the father's firstborn and the mother's firstborn, perhaps he would receive double from her estate as well.

This raises an important underlying distinction. The *bechor* for *nachalah* purposes is defined by the father — *reshit ono*, his first strength — not by the mother. For *pidyon haben*, the relevant status is *peter rechem*, the first issue of the womb, and thus defined by the mother. The two can come apart: if a man previously had a son from another woman and now has a son with a new wife, that new son is a *peter rechem* for his mother and obligates *pidyon haben*, but does not receive the double portion of *bechora* for *nachalah*, since the father's firstborn is elsewhere. Conversely, a man's firstborn son by his first wife is the *bechor le-nachalah* regardless of whether his mother previously had children.

The Gemara further notes that *reshit ono* also teaches that the *bechor le-nachalah* must be a viable birth — a child whose death would cause the father grief, *mi she-libo davah alav*. If a woman had a prior miscarriage or non-viable birth, that does not affect who qualifies as *peter rechem* only if it occurs before the threshold of forty days; but for *nachalah*, what matters is the first viable son born to the father.

The Gemara then pushes back: perhaps the *pasuk* ראשית אונו — *reshit ono* — is needed entirely for this latter purpose, to teach about the viability requirement, and cannot do double duty as a proof that the double portion comes only from the father's estate.

The Gemara responds: *im ken leima kra ki hu reshit on* — if the only purpose were to establish viability, the *pasuk* could simply have said "his first strength" without the personal pronoun *ono*, "his." The presence of *ono* — the possessive — teaches something additional: *shema mina tartei* — derive two things from it. Both that it must be the father's firstborn viable son, and that the double portion applies only to the father's estate and not the mother's.

### Rava Father Only

A final challenge: perhaps the *pasuk* ראשית אונו applies only to a case of an *almon* — a man on his second marriage — who married a *betulah*. In that case the son is a *bechor* to his mother but not to his father. Maybe in that limited configuration — where the firstborn status derives only from the mother and not from the father — the son does not receive double from his mother's estate, since his *bechora* status lacks the father's stamp. But if the son is a full *bechor* to his father and simultaneously the mother's firstborn, perhaps he should receive a double portion from her estate.

Rava resolves this definitively. The *pasuk* says *mishpat ha-bechora lo* — "the law of firstborn is to him." Rava reads *lo* not as referring to the son, but as referring to a male parent: *mishpat ha-bechora le-ish ve-lo mishpat ha-bechora le-ishah* — the law of firstborn applies to a man's estate, not to a woman's estate. The double portion of *bechora* is a rule governing what flows from a father, not from a mother. Full stop.

The irony, as the Gemara itself makes apparent, is that Rabbi Yannai's dismissal — *this man doesn't want to learn* — was wrong. It took the Gemara considerable effort, through Abaye's preliminary answer and Rava's final resolution, to establish that the son coming first by the mother's estate does not entail the firstborn receiving a double portion. This confirms that once the property passes through a woman, the full patriarchal structure — with its hierarchy of priority and its double portion for the firstborn — no longer applies intact. The son retains his priority, but the special law of *bechora*, which is the signature institution of the patriarchal inheritance system, applies only when inheriting from a father.

## Husband Inherits Wife

### Rava Sharp Knife

The Gemara now turns to a husband inheriting from his wife. One Tanna derives this from the words *she'ero zo ishto* — "his flesh, that is his wife" — reading the phrase *ve-nataten et nachalato li-she'ero* as giving the estate to the wife. From there, the Gemara derives by implication — *hu yoresh otah ve-ein hi yoreshet oto* — that he inherits from her, but she does not inherit from him. Abaye proposes a rereading of the *pasuk* to extract this: *ve-nataten et nachalat she'ero lo*, rearranging the words to mean "you shall give the inheritance of his wife to him." Rava objects: *sakina charifa mafseka kra'ei?* — is a sharp knife going to cut the *pasuk* like that? You cannot dismember the verse so drastically. Instead, Rava proposes a minimal rearrangement — transposing two letters (*vav* and *lamed*) between *nachalato* and *li-she'ero*, yielding *nachalat she'ero lo*, "the inheritance of his wife to him" — operating on the principle of *gore'in, mosifin, ve-dorshin*: you may subtract a letter, add it elsewhere, and derive your law.

### Rambam Oraita Status

Because these *drashot* are so strained — involving substantial rereading of the *pasuk* — the Rambam holds that a husband's inheritance from his wife is only *derabbanan*, not a biblical law. Nearly all other Rishonim disagree and treat it as a *de'oraita* derivation. The Rambam's position has further implications: he also holds that a *kohen* becoming *tameh* to his wife is permitted only *derabbanan*, on the grounds that the Rabbis treated her as a *meit mitzvah* — an unattended corpse — obligating her husband to bury her. The other Rishonim assume the full *de'oraita* reading throughout.

### She'ero Drasha

The *braita* states: *she'ero zo ishto* — "his flesh, that is his wife." The *pasuk* *ki im li-she'ero ha-karov elav* — in the context of the laws of *tumah* for a *kohen* — refers to blood relatives: *le-imo, le-aviv, le-vno, le-vito, le-achiv, u-le-achoto ha-betulah*. The wife is not mentioned there. So the *pshat* of *she'ero* would normally mean blood relative, not wife. Once we read *she'ero* as the wife in the inheritance context, the *pshat* would suggest that the wife inherits from the husband. The Gemara then has to rework the verse to derive the opposite — that the husband inherits from the wife. This creates a double difficulty: first, the word *she'ero* probably means blood relative; second, once we extend it to wife, the plain reading implies she inherits from him, and we have to strain further to reverse that.

One might ask: if the *halacha* were simply that a husband does not inherit from his wife, who would inherit her? Her father, her brother — the property would return to her ancestral family. It is specifically the rule that the husband inherits that ensures the *nachala* will leave her tribe, passing to a man from a different tribal affiliation. This is exactly what the uncles of *Bnot Tzelafchad* feared — that once women inherit, the property could transfer to another tribe, whether through the wife's sons or through her husband.

### Abaye Hermeneutics

As noted above, Abaye proposes to read the *pasuk* as *ve-nataten et nachalato li-karov elav she'ero, ve-yarash otah* — taking *she'ero* as a separate clause that addresses the wife specifically: as for his *she'ero*, his wife, *ve-yarash otah*, he shall inherit from her. Rava rejects this as too violent a restructuring of the verse — hence the "sharp knife" objection — and instead proposes the minimal two-letter transposition yielding *nachalat she'ero lo*, supported by the hermeneutic principle of *gore'in u-mosifin ve-dorshin*.

### Akiva Yishmael Debate

A different *tanna* takes a simpler approach. Rabbi Akiva derives the rule directly from the words *ve-yarash otah* — he shall inherit from her — reading those two words in isolation as a standalone statement: the husband inherits from his wife. Rabbi Yishmael says this is unnecessary: *eino tzarich* — the rule can be derived from elsewhere.

### Yishmael Five Proofs

Rabbi Yishmael marshals a series of *psukim* to demonstrate that a husband inherits from his wife, drawing from the context of *Bnot Tzelafchad*. The *pasuk* states *ve-chol bat yoreshet nachala mi-matot Bnei Yisrael le-echad mi-mishpachat mateh aviha tihyeh le-ish le-ishah* — any daughter who inherits shall marry within her tribe — *ve-al esek ha-ba'al ha-katuv medaber*, and it is the matter of the husband that the *pasuk* is addressing. If a woman with an inheritance marries, the property goes to a different tribe — which implies the husband inherits it.

The *pasuk ve-lo tisov nachala li-vnei Yisrael mi-mateh el mateh acher* — the inheritance shall not transfer from tribe to tribe — and a nearly identical *pasuk* that follows both point to the same conclusion: this prohibition is necessary only because a husband inheriting from his wife is the mechanism by which the transfer occurs.

Rabbi Yishmael also cites two narrative proofs. First: *ve-Elazar ben Aharon met va-yikberu oto be-givat Pinchas bno* — Elazar died and was buried in the plot of his son Pinchas. Where did Pinchas get a plot that had not come from his father Elazar? *Ela melamed she-nasa Pinchas isha u-meta ve-yarsha* — it must be that Pinchas married a woman, she died, and he inherited from her. Second: *u-Segev holid et Yair va-yihyu lo esrim ve-shalosh arim be-eretz ha-Gilad* — Segev fathered Yair, who had twenty-three cities in Gilead. Where did Yair get cities that his father Segev did not have? *Melamed she-nasa Yair isha u-meta ve-yarsha* — he must have married a woman and inherited from her.

The Gemara notes that each of these proofs is inconclusive on its own — Pinchas might have purchased the land, or received it through his mother; Yair's cities might similarly have come through his mother rather than a wife. The question of whether any of these *psukim* conclusively establishes that it is specifically the *husband* who inherits the wife, rather than the wife's property passing to her *sons*, remains to be resolved — and that discussion will continue.

---

---

# Bava Batra 112

## Husband Inherits Wife

### Intro: Husband Rights

The daf opens two lines from the top with the words *mah v'omer*, situating us in the middle of a discussion carried over from the previous day: from where do we know that a husband inherits from his wife? The operative principle is that if a wife dies, her estate passes first to her husband, and only in the absence of a husband does it descend to her children. The *gemara* attempts to derive this rule from various *pesukim*, but the textual basis turns out to be deeply problematic.

### Sheiro Zo Ishto

One candidate *pasuk* reads: *v'natan et hanachala l'sheiro hakarov eilav mimishpachto v'yarash otah* — "you shall give his inheritance to his flesh that is closest to him from his family, and he shall inherit it." The difficulty is that this language sounds like a blood relationship, describing a man passing his estate to his nearest kin. To the extent that we apply the principle *sheiro zu ishto* — that the word *she'er*, meaning flesh, also refers to one's wife on account of the concept of *basar echad*, that husband and wife become one flesh — the *pasuk* would seem to indicate that the *wife* inherits the *husband*, not the reverse. The *gemara* therefore attempted to work with this *pasuk*, in particular seizing on the two words *v'yarash otah* — "he shall inherit *her*" — to derive, somewhat out of context, that the husband inherits the wife. That reading was attributed to Rebbi Akiva.

### Rebbi Yishmael Pesukimim

Rebbi Yishmael took a different approach, marshalling a chain of *pesukim* centered on the concern that a woman's inherited property would pass out of her *shevet*. The straightforward reading of these *pesukim* is that a woman who inherits from her father must marry within her *shevet* so that the land does not pass to a different tribe through her son — since the son follows his father's *shevet*, and if the husband belongs to a different *shevet*, so will the son. This was the central issue with Bnot Tzelofchad and the requirement that they marry from within their tribe. Rebbi Yishmael, however, argues that those *pesukim* collectively demonstrate that if a woman were to die, her estate would pass to her husband — meaning the concern about tribal diversion is animated by the husband's inheritance right, not only by the son's. He further adduced two *pesukim* from *Nach* in which a son appears to hold property that his father never possessed, from which Rebbi Yishmael infers that the son must have inherited through his mother — that is, the father inherited the mother's property upon her death and then passed it to the son.

### Rambam Sofrim

It is worth pausing here to note that the very weakness and non-*pshat* character of all these *pesukim* led the Rambam to a striking conclusion: the husband's right to inherit from his wife is *d'vrai sofrim* — rabbinic in nature — and is not a *d'raita* law at all. A parallel example the Rambam cites is the rule that a *kohen* husband may become *tamei* for his deceased wife, even though the plain reading of the *pasuk* *lo yitama ba'al b'amav l'heichalo* — which can be read as prohibiting a *kohen* from defiling himself — would cut against this. Nevertheless, *Chazal* read *l'sheiro, sheiro zu ishto*, and permitted the *kohen* to become *tamei* for his wife. The Rambam holds that this too is rabbinic, grounded in the category of *meis mitzvah*: since the husband alone bears the obligation to bury his wife, he is treated like a *meis mitzvah* case and permitted to become *tamei*. Throughout, the *gemara* here speaks in the register of *d'raita*, but the force of the Rambam's observation should be kept in mind as we watch the *gemara* struggle to sustain any of these derivations.

---

## Pesukimim Challenge

### Mah V'omer

The *gemara* now turns to scrutinize Rebbi Yishmael's entire chain of *pesukim* by asking *mah v'omer*: why were multiple *pesukim* needed at all?
