Beginning with the *pasuk* cited by Rebbi Yishmael — *v'chol bat yoreshet nachala mimatot bnei Yisrael* — the *gemara* notes that the *Torah*'s instruction that the generation of Bnot Tzelofchad marry within the *shevet* so that land not be diverted, while suggestive, is not a clean proof that the husband inherits. The concern about tribal diversion could be explained entirely by the son's inheritance: the son follows his father's *shevet*, and if the husband is from a different *shevet*, so is the son. The husband's own inheritance right would not be necessary to explain this concern.

### B'sibat Haven

The *gemara* therefore raises the objection directly: *v'chi teima b'sibat haben ko kapid kra, aval ba'al lo yarit* — perhaps the entire concern of this *pasuk* is that the inheritance will be diverted through the son, and the husband simply does not inherit at all. That objection forces the *gemara* to seek a different *pasuk*.

### Lo Tisov Nachala

The *gemara* brings *ta shma*: the *pasuk* *v'lo tisov nachala livnei Yisrael mimateh el mateh* — that the inheritance shall not be diverted from one tribe to another. The argument is that since we already knew the concern about tribal diversion from the previous *pasuk*, this additional *pasuk* must come to teach a new mode of diversion — not through the son but through the husband, who actually takes precedence over the son as an heir. The *gemara*, however, deflects: *v'chi teima la'avor alav b'lav v'asei* — perhaps this *pasuk* is not introducing a new halachic mechanism at all, but is simply adding a negative prohibition to the positive commandment already established. The generation of Bnot Tzelofchad was warned: if a woman who inherited land marries out of her tribe, she will transgress the positive command — *v'chol bat yoreshet nachala mimatot avoteiha tihyeh le'ishah* — and she will transgress the negative prohibition — *velo tisov* — because she will have caused the inheritance to be diverted. The *pesukim* thus may be about layering prohibitions, not about establishing the husband's inheritance right. Accordingly, the *gemara* introduces yet another *pasuk: velo tisov nachalah mimateh lemateh acher* — that the inheritance shall not go to a different tribe. Once again the inference is that this additional language must be teaching a new mode of diversion.

The *gemara* pushes back yet again: *v'chi teima lav velav bishnei lavin v'aseh* — perhaps this is still only about the son, and we are merely establishing that this single concern — diversion through the son — now carries the weight of two negative prohibitions and a positive commandment, not just one.

### Tosafot Extra Pesuk

Tosafot register a pointed observation here: normally, when a *pasuk* appears to be duplicating something already stated, we prefer to read the extra *pasuk* as teaching something substantively new rather than as simply stacking additional *lavin*. The expectation would therefore be that the doubled language of *lo tisov nachala* is coming to introduce a new case — namely, diversion through the husband — rather than to merely multiply the prohibitions surrounding diversion through the son. It is therefore somewhat surprising that the *gemara* does not deploy this logic here and instead continues to entertain the possibility that both *pesukim* address only the son. The resolution to this difficulty will come later, on *amud bet*, where the *gemara* does in fact insist that the doubling teaches two separate cases: one concerning the son and one concerning the husband.

---

## Elazar & Pinchas

### Elazar Pinchas

Since the *pesukim* from Bnot Tzelofchad have proven insufficient to cleanly establish the husband's inheritance right, the *gemara* turns to *Nach*. The *pasuk* reports: *Ve'Elazar ben Aharon met* — Elazar the son of Aharon died — and states that he was buried in a valley belonging to Pinchas his son. The *gemara* is puzzled: how did Pinchas come to possess this property? If he did not inherit it from his father Elazar, and yet the valley bears his name, the inference is that he must have acquired it through his wife — that is, Pinchas's wife died and Pinchas inherited her estate.

### Wife vs Mother

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *v'chi teima Elazar hu denasiv iteta umeta veyartah Pinchas* — perhaps it was not Pinchas who married and inherited from his wife, but rather Elazar who married a woman, she died, and *she* passed the property to *her son* Pinchas. In other words, the property in question may have come to Pinchas through his mother rather than through his own wife. The *gemara* therefore looks for a second proof.

### Segov & Yair

The *gemara* brings *ta shma*: the *pasuk* tells us that Segov fathered Yair, and that Yair possessed extensive property in the land of Gilad. The question is the same: how did Yair come to hold property his father Segov apparently did not have? By the same reasoning, he must have inherited it from his wife. The *gemara* argues that the existence of two parallel cases — Pinchas and Yair — eliminates the possibility that either is simply an incidental story about property acquisition. Since both situations describe a son possessing what his father did not, and they cannot both be explained away, the *gemara* concludes that the *Torah* is teaching a *halacha*: one can acquire property through a deceased wife.

One might ask why two cases are needed. The *gemara*'s logic is *im ken terei karai lamah li* — if both are just incidental stories, there would be no reason for the *Torah* to mention both. The duplication implies that the *Torah* is establishing a rule. As the Rashbam notes, however, this reasoning is strained: there is no inherent reason to assume these narratives are halachic rather than historiographical. The stories of Pinchas and Yair and Segov are simply telling us what happened. Nothing in the text compels us to read them as conveying a legal principle, and the mere fact that the *Torah* tells two such stories does not automatically transform them into a redundancy that must be teaching a *halacha*.

### Rav Pappa Objection

Rav Pappa poses this challenge directly to Abaye. *Mimay* — who says Yair inherited through his wife? *Dilma le'olam eima lach ba'al lo yarit* — perhaps a husband never inherits at all — *v'karai besibat haben k'deshninan* — and the earlier *pesukim* about Bnot Tzelofchad are entirely about diversion through the son. As for Yair: *Yair d'zavin mazbin* — perhaps he simply purchased the property. And similarly for Pinchas: *uPinchas nami d'zavin mazbin* — perhaps Pinchas too merely purchased his holdings. There is no need to invoke inheritance from a wife at all. The Rashbam adds further that in both cases one could equally have said the sons received the property from their mothers — no *halacha* need be inferred; the *pesukim* may simply be recording facts about individual circumstances.

### Abaye Defense

Abaye responds to Rav Pappa's objection. He acknowledges that it is a strong challenge to Rebbi Yishmael's position, but argues that at least in the case of Pinchas, the purchase theory cannot stand: *Pinchas d'zavin mazbin lo matzit amrat*.

### Yovel Property

The reason Abaye gives is rooted in the law of *yovel*: *ve'im ken nimtza sadeh chozeret biyovel venimtza kover b'kever she'eno shelo*. If Pinchas purchased the field from someone else and then buried his father Elazar in that land, the field would revert to its original owner at the *yovel*, and Elazar HaKohen would be interred in a burial site belonging to another person — a valley that would no longer belong to the family of Pinchas. That is untenable. Accordingly, the field cannot have been a purchase. Yet this still does not establish that Pinchas inherited from his wife; it remains possible that he received the land from his mother.

### Cherem Alternative

Rav Pappa returns with a third alternative. Even granting that the field was not purchased, Pinchas could have acquired it through *cherem*: when a person dedicates a field as *cherem* and fails to redeem it, the field passes to the *kohanim* at the *yovel* — and crucially, property received through *cherem* would not itself revert in a subsequent *yovel*. So Pinchas, as a *kohen*, could have received the field through this mechanism, and the valley would remain his without reverting. The *gemara* thus leaves unresolved the question of how precisely one demonstrates from these narratives that the husband inherits from his wife according to Rebbi Yishmael. The discussion about the *pesukim* from *Nach* has effectively been neutralized, and the *gemara* signals that it will return to the doubling of *lo tisov nachala* on *amud bet* for the real resolution.

---

## Abaye: Two Shevat

### Two Shevatim Problem

Before arriving at that resolution, the *gemara* introduces a self-contained sugya built around a statement of Abaye — one the lecturer notes may seem somewhat wordy and repetitive on first encounter, but which the Rashbam reads as addressing a distinct question about the *pesukim* of *lo tisov nachala* rather than about the proof of the husband's inheritance. The scenario Abaye contemplates is one where a woman has inherited from *two* tribes: she has received property from her father, who belongs to, say, the tribe of Reuven, and also from her mother, who belongs to, say, the tribe of Shimon.

### Sof Sof Diverted

Abaye's concern is expressed in the phrase *sof sof ha ka mitakra nachala misheivta d'ima l'sheivta d'abba*: ultimately, the inheritance will be diverted from her mother's tribe to her father's tribe. The Torah commands this woman to marry within her father's tribe — within Reuven — so that the land she received from her Reuvenite father not be diverted away from Reuven. But what about the Shimon property she inherited from her mother? If she marries a man from Reuven, the Shimon property passes with her into Reuven hands. The Shimon inheritance has been diverted from Shimon to Reuven. Why is the Torah not equally troubled by this?

### Already Diverted

The *gemara* attempts an answer: *umimai v'dilma shani hatam shek'var husevah* — perhaps the Torah is not concerned about the Shimon property because, at the moment she inherited it from her mother, it was already diverted. She, the inheriting woman, belongs to the tribe of Reuven — that is her tribal identity — and when the Shimon property fell into her possession, it immediately moved into Reuven's sphere of control. The further diversion that will occur when she marries a Reuvenite man is not a new crossing of a tribal line; the diversion already happened the moment she received the inheritance. Accordingly, the Torah is focused exclusively on preserving the Reuven property, which is at risk of being diverted, and says nothing more about the Shimon property, which has already crossed tribal lines.

### Abaye Rejects

Abaye rejects this reasoning: *shek'var huspah lo amrinan*. He is not satisfied that the property's having been somewhat diverted already is sufficient to relieve the Torah of concern about its further diversion. It still troubles him that the Torah instructs her to marry from Reuven — which will result in the Shimon property becoming fully and definitively embedded in Reuven — without offering any remedy for the diversion of the mother's tribal inheritance.

### Same Mixed Heritage

Rav Yeimar then addresses Rav Ashi, and the *gemara* articulates what Abaye's implicit concern was pointing toward: if the approach of *shek'var husevah* — that already-diverted property no longer concerns the Torah — is rejected, then what possible solution could there be for a woman who has inherited from two tribes? If she marries someone from Reuven, the Shimon property is diverted; if she marries someone from Shimon, the Reuven property is diverted. There is no clean answer unless we posit a third option.

The *gemara* provides precisely that: *dimenasvinan lah legavra de-avuh mishevetah de-avuh ve-imeih mishevetah de-imeih* — perhaps she must marry a man who mirrors her exact dual lineage. She holds property from a Reuven father and a Shimon mother; she should marry a man whose own father is from Reuven and whose own mother is from Shimon. In such a marriage, she brings her dual inheritance to a husband who reflects the same composite identity.

### Property Preservation

The logic of this solution is intricate. When the Reuven property was in her hands, it was held by someone from the tribe of Reuven. After she dies and her husband inherits, the Reuven property remains in the hands of someone from the tribe of Reuven — his father is from Reuven. No diversion has occurred. As for the Shimon property: when it was in her hands, it was held by someone whose father was Reuven but whose mother was Shimon. After her husband inherits, the situation is exactly the same — the property is now held by someone whose father is Reuven and whose mother is Shimon. The Shimon property has not moved; it remains at precisely the same remove from its tribal origin as it was before. This is what Abaye was suggesting the Torah may have had in mind: that the requirement to marry within one's father's tribe carried with it, implicitly, a further refinement that the mother's tribe should also be matched — ensuring that each inherited property tracks back through the same composite lineage.

### Husband Inherits Proof

There is also a relevance here to our overarching discussion about whether the husband inherits. If we posit that the Torah is concerned about the Shimon property maintaining its level of connection to Shimon even after it passes to the husband — and if that concern makes sense — this works only on the assumption that the husband inherits. If only the son inherited, the son's father would be from Reuven and his mother would also be from Reuven (since she is the woman who inherited from her Reuven father), and the Shimon connection would be entirely lost. The fact that the Torah might be articulating a solution in which the property stays at the same Reuven-Shimon level thus implicitly assumes that the husband is the one inheriting, not the son.

### Father's Tribe Core

The *gemara* on *amud bet* raises an immediate objection to the proposed solution: if the Torah truly intended that the woman marry someone who mirrors both her father's and mother's tribal origins, why does the *pasuk* say only *mimateh aviha* — only from her father's tribe? Why is the mother not mentioned? The *gemara* answers: *ichtiv hachi hava amina afilu ipecha* — had the Torah written "from her father's and her mother's tribe," one might have supposed that the direction of the match does not matter. It would not matter whether the man's father is from Reuven and his mother from Shimon, or his father from Shimon and his mother from Reuven. But tribal identity is determined patrilineally. The core concern is that the father's tribe be the same, because that is what ultimately defines one's *shevet*. The Reuven property she holds, held as she is a member of the tribe of Reuven, must pass to someone who is also tribally Reuven — and that is determined by the father's line. The Torah therefore emphasizes *mimateh aviha*: the father's tribe is the essential anchor. That the mother's tribe should also match is an additional refinement, parenthetically serving the Shimon property — but since the primary obligation concerns the father's tribal identity, and since specifying only the father's tribe captures the essential rule, the Torah's formulation is appropriate. With this, Abaye's extended discussion concludes.

---

## Lo Tisov Doubled

### Two Beraitot

The *gemara* now returns to the central derivation of Rebbi Yishmael and resolves the impasse that had been left hanging throughout *amud alef*. The resolution, signaled earlier in passing, is that the doubled language of *lo tisov nachala* is not redundant and is not merely adding an additional *lav*. Rather, the two *pesukim* are addressing two distinct modes of tribal diversion — one through the son and one through the husband. The *gemara* presents two *beraitot*, each making the same fundamental point but starting from opposite directions.

### Son: Mimatteh Lematteh

The first *baraita* begins with the *pasuk* *v'lo tisov nachala livnei Yisrael mimateh el mateh* — it should not be diverted from one tribe to another. The *baraita* states: *besivah haben hakasuv medaber* — this *pasuk* is speaking about diversion through the son. One might ask whether this *pasuk* in fact concerns diversion through the son or diversion through the husband.

### Husband: Matteh Acher

The *baraita* resolves the question by invoking the companion *pasuk*: *keshehu omer v'lo tisov nachala mimateh el mateh acher* — when the *Torah* says it should not be diverted to a *different* tribe, *harei besivah habaal emur* — that one is clearly referring to diversion through the husband. The term *mateh acher* — a different tribe — captures the husband's situation precisely: he is from a tribe that is genuinely *other* relative to the wife's tribe. Once she has married him and he has become part of her world, her son does not come from a genuinely *acher* tribe in the same sense — the son is born into the merged reality of the household. The husband, however, comes from outside, from a tribe that was *acher* from the start. The first *pasuk*, without *acher*, therefore speaks of the son's inheritance, while the second, with *acher*, speaks of the husband's. Since the first *pasuk* has thus been assigned to the son, the *baraita* concludes that the second *pasuk* — which says *mateh acher* — is entirely about the husband: *harei besivah habaal emur*.

### Second Baraita

The second *baraita* covers the identical ground but reverses the order of presentation, opening with the *pasuk* that includes *acher*.

### Matteh Lematteh Son

Having assigned the *acher* formulation to the husband, the second *baraita* then turns to the *pasuk* without *acher* — *v'lo tisov nachala livnei Yisrael mimateh el mateh* — and confirms: *harei simas haben emur* — that is the one speaking about diversion through the son.

### Both Diversions

The conclusion is clear and symmetric: the two *pesukim* of *lo tisov nachala* together establish both modes of tribal diversion. The *pasuk* without *acher* — from one tribe to another — teaches that a woman's inheritance can be diverted through her son, who follows his father's tribe. The *pasuk* with *acher* — to a *different* tribe — teaches that her inheritance can be diverted through her husband, who is genuinely from another tribe. Together, they are what Rebbi Yishmael had been building toward all along: a *d'raita* basis for the principle that the husband inherits from his wife. The *gemara* will continue on 113a.

---

---

# Bava Batra 113

## Braisas: Husband/Son

### Problem Setup

The Gemara on this daf continues a discussion that has occupied the preceding pages: what is the textual source for the rule that a husband inherits from his wife? The classical *drasha* is the verse *uvenasatem et nachalaso lish'eiro hakarov eilav* — "you shall give his inheritance to his flesh, the one close to him" — with *she'eiro* being read as a reference to his wife. The grammatical difficulty, however, is glaring: the plain meaning of the verse would suggest that the property goes *to* the wife, not *from* her to her husband. This drove the Gemara to seek other textual anchors, and the discussion focused in particular on the verses in Parashat Masei concerning the daughters of Tzelafchad.

The context is this: the *bnos Tzelafchad* were instructed not to marry men from a different tribe, lest the inheritance be transferred from the mother's tribe to another. The Gemara asked whether those verses — *velo sishov nachala* ("do not let the inheritance pass away") — are evidence that a husband inherits from his wife, or whether they might all be referring exclusively to the son inheriting from his mother. After all, when a woman dies, her property does pass to her son, and her son belongs to his father's tribe, not hers. So perhaps the prohibition against inter-tribal marriage is entirely about preventing the inheritance from passing through a son to a different tribe, and nothing in these verses establishes that the husband inherits at all.

### Two Braisas Text

The Gemara now presents two *braisos* that appear to address precisely this question. The two *psukim* in question are nearly identical. The first reads: *velo sishov nachala livnei Yisrael mimatteh el matteh* — do not let the inheritance pass from one tribe to another. The second reads: *velo sishov nachala mimatteh el matteh achair* — do not let the inheritance pass from one tribe to a different, or "other," tribe. Each *braisa* takes up these two verses and asks whether a given instance of inheritance passing refers to the son or the husband.

### Rashbam Reading

According to the *Rashbam*, both *braisos* are substantively identical — they present the same argument and reach the same conclusion, linking one verse to the son and the other to the husband. The only difference between them is which verse each *braisa* leads with. The first *braisa* opens with the verse about the son: *tanya besibas haben* — it teaches with respect to the turning that happens through the son. It then asks: perhaps this verse is about the husband? It resolves the question by pointing to the second verse — the one containing the word *achair* — as the verse that speaks about the husband. Once we have a verse for the husband, the first verse must be about the son. The second *braisa* simply reverses the order of presentation: it opens with the *achair* verse and identifies that as referring to the husband, then resolves that the other verse must be about the son.

In the *Rashbam*'s reading, therefore, the Gemara is not recording a dispute between *braisos*. They are structurally parallel, each confirming the same result through the same pair of verses, simply beginning from different ends of the analysis.

### Tosafos Reading

*Tosafos* finds this unsatisfying. If both *braisos* say the same thing and reach the same conclusion, presented in different order alone, there would be no reason for the Gemara to distinguish them as two separate *braisos*. *Tosafos* therefore maintains that the two *braisos* reflect a genuine textual disagreement and proposes a different *girsa*.

According to *Tosafos*, the *achair* verse is agreed upon by all — everyone accepts that this verse speaks about the *baal*, the husband, as we will see below. The dispute between the *braisos* concerns the other verse, *velo sishov nachala livnei Yisrael mimatteh el matteh*. One *braisa* maintains that this second verse speaks about the son — the words *livnei Yisrael* connecting to inheritance passing through children. The other *braisa* in *Tosafos*'s *girsa* reads differently: it says *benachalas habaal hakasuv omer* — the verse is speaking about the inheritance of the husband. According to that *braisa*, both verses refer to the husband, and the *achair* verse then serves to confirm this reading rather than to distinguish the two. So in *Tosafos*'s account, one *braisa* holds that one verse is about the husband and the other about the son, while the second *braisa* holds that both are about the husband.

This reading has the advantage of explaining why the Gemara proceeds the way it does. The Gemara's subsequent analysis focuses entirely on why everyone agrees that the *achair* verse refers to the husband. From the *Rashbam*'s perspective, the Gemara could just as well have asked the symmetrical question about the son — what signals that the other verse speaks about the son? *Tosafos*'s reading renders the focus on the *achair* verse natural: it is the one verse about which there is no disagreement between the *braisos*, and so the Gemara asks what marks it as specifically referring to the husband.

## Markers: Ish/Yidbeku

### Consensus: Acher

The Gemara states plainly: *d'kulei alma miha* — in any event, everyone agrees that the verse *mimatteh lemateh achair* speaks about the passing of inheritance through the husband, *besibas habaal hakasuv medaber*. Having established this consensus, the Gemara then presses the question: *mai mashma*? What in the text of that verse signals that it concerns the husband rather than the son?

### Ish Signal Rejected

The Gemara's first answer is offered in the name of Rabba bar Rav Shila: *amar kra ish* — the verse uses the word *ish*. The full verse reads *ki ish benachalato yidbeku matos Bnei Yisrael*, and the word *ish* is taken as a signal that we are speaking about a husband, on the model of *ish Naomi* — where *ish* denotes a husband. The *Rashbam* cites this usage. Although it is not the plain meaning of *ish* in this context, the term carries a connotation of marital relationship.

The Gemara immediately objects: *tarveihu ish kesiv behu* — the other verse also uses the word *ish*. Looking at the parallel verse, *ki ish benachalas mateh avosav yidbeku Bnei Yisrael*, it too contains *ish*. If the word *ish* marked the *achair* verse as referring to the husband, it would equally mark the other verse the same way. The signal therefore cannot be *ish* alone.

### Veyidbeku Rejected

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative: *amar kra yidbeku* — the word *yidbeku* (they shall cleave) signals the husband, evoking the verse *veyidbak be'ishto*, the cleaving of a husband to his wife. This is the marital union described in *Bereishis*; the use of the same root *dalet-beit-kuf* in the inheritance verse links it to the husband.

The Gemara once again objects: *tarvaiyu veyidbeku ketivu* — both verses use *yidbeku*. The root appears in the parallel verse as well, so it cannot serve as the distinguishing marker.

### Acher Signals Other

Rava then offers the resolution: *amar kra veyidbeku matot* — the verse uses the plural *matot* (tribes), not the singular *mateh*. When two tribes are bound together through *deveika*, it signals that the person to whom the inheritance passes belongs to a different tribe entirely — and that is the husband, who cleaves to his wife across tribal lines. The singular *mateh*, by contrast, suggests a connection within one tribal line, pointing toward a son who belongs to the mother's tribe through his father.

### Acher Signals Other

The Gemara finally arrives at the resolution of Rav Ashi: *amar kra mimmateh lemateh achair* — the distinguishing word is *achair*, "other." This word appears in the *achair* verse and not in the parallel verse. It signals that the inheritance is passing to someone who is, in some sense, an *other*. A child is biologically connected to the family in a way that cannot be severed — even after death, the child remains the grandchild, the nephew, the heir in the biological chain. A husband, however, is in a different category: the relationship was created by marriage, and marriage can end through death or divorce. However deep the *deveika* of husband and wife, the husband remains, in some structural sense, an *achair* — an other — in a way the son does not. This, says Rav Ashi, is why that verse refers to the husband.

### Matot vs. Mateh

An important observation: *Tosafos* raises a striking point about the earlier attempts involving *ish* and *yidbeku*. The Gemara rejected each because the same word appears in both verses. But surely the *amoraim* who proposed these signals knew that both verses contained the same word? *Tosafos* suggests, almost startlingly, that *pe'amim shelo hayu beki'in bipesukim* — sometimes the Sages were not fully expert in the exact wording of particular verses. He cites a parallel case where one *amora* was asked why the word *tov* does not appear in the second *Dibrot*, and responded that he did not even know whether it appeared in the first *Dibrot* or not.

*Tosafos* himself, however, is uncomfortable with this explanation in the present context. The continuation of the Gemara — in which the objection *tarveihu ish kesiv behu* is raised precisely because both verses contain *ish* — suggests that the Sages knew the texts perfectly well. The *Rashbam* offers a more refined reading: the *amoraim* were not claiming that the word *ish* or *yidbeku* was absent from the other verse. Rather, they were pointing to these words as sufficient grounds to identify the *achair* verse as referring to the husband. The Gemara's response was not "you are wrong about what this word means" but rather "given that the same word appears in both verses, you have not explained why you begin with this verse and allow the other to refer to something else." The final answer — the word *achair* — works because it appears in one verse only, providing an asymmetric signal that anchors one verse to the husband and leaves the other for the son.

## Husband: Ra'uy Exclu (II)

### Ra'uy vs. Muchzak

The Gemara introduces a tradition in the name of Rabbi Yannai, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: *minayin l'baal she'eino notel b'rauy k'vemuchzak* — from where do we know that a husband does not inherit *rauy* in the same way he inherits *muchzak*? This is a significant and somewhat counterintuitive *halacha* that requires careful unpacking.

*Muchzak* refers to property that a woman already possesses at the moment of her death. *Rauy* refers to property that she was in line to receive — property to which she had an expectation of entitlement — but which had not yet come into her possession when she died. The rule being articulated is that while the husband inherits the former, he does not inherit the latter. This parallels the rule concerning a *bechor*: a firstborn receives a double portion of the estate only from property the father actually possessed, not from *rauy* — property the father was entitled to but had not yet received.

### Grandson/Husband Logic

Consider a concrete case. A woman's father is still alive and owns property. The woman has both a husband and a son. If the sequence of deaths is: father dies first, then woman, then her property passes to her husband in the normal course — her husband inherits her *muchzak*, the property she actually possessed when she died, before it goes to her son. But suppose the sequence is reversed: the woman dies first, then her father dies afterward. At the moment of her death, the father's property had not yet come to her — it was *rauy*, expected but not possessed. When the father subsequently dies, where does his property go?

The ruling is that in this case the property bypasses the husband entirely and descends to the woman's son — or, if the son is also deceased, to any surviving descendant in her line. The husband does not receive it. The logic, as *Tosafos* will explain, is rooted in the nature of the marital bond: once the woman has died, the connection between the husband and her family of origin has been severed. The grandfather has no relationship with his son-in-law. His biological heirs are his grandchildren. The property therefore flows downward through the biological line, not sideways to the former husband.

This reasoning clarifies why *muchzak* and *rauy* are treated differently. When a woman dies with property she already possesses, the inheritance takes effect at the moment of death — and at that moment she is still, legally and halakhically, his wife. The property transfers to him. But property held by her father at the moment of her death cannot transfer to the husband, because after her death there is no remaining legal or familial nexus between the husband and the grandfather's estate.

## Ya'ir & Pinchas Cases

### Ya'ir Proof

The Gemara brings two prooftexts from Chronicles and the book of Yehoshua to establish that a son does indeed inherit *rauy* — property that was expected to come to his mother but had not yet arrived before she died. The first involves the genealogy of *Chevron* in Divrei HaYamim: *veSeguv holid et Ya'ir vayehi lo esrim veshalosh arim b'eretz haGil'ad* — Seguv fathered Ya'ir, and he had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilad. The puzzle is that Ya'ir had cities that his father Seguv did not have. Earlier in the Gemara's discussion, this was explained by saying that Ya'ir married a woman who brought property with her, and she died, leaving Ya'ir with cities that Seguv never possessed.

But now the Gemara offers a different reading of the same case. The explanation proposed here is that *shenasa Seguv ishah umetah bechayei morisheha* — Seguv married a woman who died while her own father was still alive. She was in line to inherit from her father — the property was *rauy* to her — but she died before that inheritance materialized. Subsequently, her father died, and the property descended not to Seguv the husband, but directly to Ya'ir the son. This is why Ya'ir had cities that Seguv never had: the property bypassed Seguv entirely, going to the grandson as the closest biological heir.

### Pinchas Proof

A parallel case is derived from the book of Yehoshua: *veElazar ben Aharon met vayikberu oto* — Elazar son of Aharon died and they buried him, and a detail in the text implies that Pinchas possessed property that Elazar did not. The same structure applies: *shenasa Elazar ishah* — Elazar married a woman, Pinchas's mother — *umetah bechayei morisheha* — she died while her own father was still alive — *umetu morisheha veyirshah Pinchas* — and when her father subsequently died, that inheritance descended directly to Pinchas rather than to Elazar. Again the husband was bypassed because she died before her father, and once she was dead the connection between Elazar and her father's estate was severed.

### Two Cases Needed

The Gemara asks why both cases are necessary — could we not have learned the rule from Ya'ir alone? It answers that without the Pinchas case, one might have thought the peculiar distribution in Ya'ir's case was because his cities came through his wife's own direct property, not through a grandfather's estate descending after her death. The Pinchas case rules out that alternative reading. Similarly, one might have thought the Pinchas case involved property consecrated to *hekdesh* and released under unusual circumstances — *sedeh charamim* — rather than through the ordinary *rauy* mechanism. The verse in the Pinchas case uses the word *bno* — "his son" — and the Gemara reads this as emphatic: it is the property that Elazar might have been entitled to, yet it went to *bno*, his son, and not to him. Together the two cases close off alternative explanations and establish firmly that *rauy* passes to the biological heir, not to the husband.

## Husband: Ra'uy Exclu (II)

### Tosafos: Connection Seve…

*Tosafos* addresses a question that arises naturally from this whole discussion: if a son inherits *rauy* from his mother — property she was in line to receive but did not yet possess — and the husband does not, what is the theoretical basis for this asymmetry? The answer *Tosafos* articulates is that once the wife has died, the connection between the husband and her family is severed. There is no biological relationship between him and her father. His entitlement was derived entirely from the marital bond, and that bond no longer exists. By contrast, the son remains the grandfather's biological grandson regardless of the mother's death. The biological chain is not broken by death; only the marital one is.

### Basar Echad vs. Korvah

This leads *Tosafos* to articulate an important conceptual distinction. There are two different categories relevant to the husband's inheritance: *she'erut* — the marital connection described as *basar echad*, one flesh — and *korvah* — biological relation. The husband inherits from his wife on the basis of *basar echad*, not *korvah*. *Tosafos* frames this as follows: *keivan she-habaal eino yoresh machamat kurva ela machamat she'erut* — since the husband inherits not by virtue of biological relation but by virtue of marital union.

The practical implication of this distinction is significant. When asking whether the husband takes priority over the son in inheriting from the wife, the answer is yes — but for a reason that illuminates the *rauy* rule as well. Consider: if there were no husband and no son, the woman's property would pass to her father, or her brother, or some other biological relative. We see clearly that the marital bond takes precedence over these biological relationships for purposes of inheritance. Why? Because the *basar echad* relationship is treated as primary — the two are considered as one, and this oneness takes priority before we begin to look at other relatives.

### Final Rule

But this same logic explains why *rauy* does not follow the same path. The *basar echad* relationship is operative at the moment of death — property the wife possesses at that moment flows to her husband before her son, because at the instant of her death they are still one. But property that comes into the estate *after* her death — property that was *rauy* but not yet *muchzak* — cannot flow to a husband who is no longer connected to that family at all. At that later moment there is no marriage, no *basar echad*, and therefore no basis for his claim. The property instead descends through the biological line to the son, who remains tied to the grandfather's estate regardless of when his mother died.

The rule that emerges is thus: a husband inherits from property his wife already possessed at the moment of her death; he does not inherit from property she was in line to receive but had not yet come into her hands. That latter category — *rauy* — goes to the biological heir, the son, through the continuing biological nexus that is not severed by her death.

## Son Before Daughter

### Bnei Achot Rule

The Gemara now introduces a rule about what happens when inheritance passes through a collateral relative — specifically a sister. If a man dies without children and without a father, the estate passes to his siblings. If he has a living brother, the brother inherits. If his only sibling is a sister, and that sister has predeceased him, the estate passes to her children. The question addressed here is whether it passes to all of her children equally or whether sons take priority over daughters.

The rule taught is *bnei achot velo bnot achot* — the sons of sisters inherit, but not the daughters of sisters, meaning that when there are sons available in that generation, they take priority over the daughters. As Rav Sheshet explains, this is a matter of *likadem* — of establishing which among the eligible heirs comes first, not of categorically excluding the daughters. If there are no male descendants in that line, the daughters will ultimately inherit. And of course, if a son in that line has died but left children, his descendants take his place and come before any living daughter at that level. The principle is the familiar one: *ben kodem l'bat* — son before daughter — applied not only at the level of direct inheritance but at every tier of the inheritance hierarchy.

### Makish Yerusha

The Gemara then provides the textual basis for this rule through a *midrash halachah*. The passage in *Parashat Pinchas* enumerates the order of heirs: if a man dies and has no son, the inheritance passes to his daughter; if no daughter, to his brothers; if no brothers, to his father's brothers; and if there are none, *lish'eiro hakarov eilav veyarash otah* — to his nearest relative, and he shall inherit it. The Gemara reads the concluding phrase *veyarash otah* as establishing a link — *makish yerusha shniya liyerusha rishona* — the secondary inheritance is *hukash* to, bound by the same rules as, the primary inheritance. Just as in the primary inheritance son comes before daughter (*mah yerusha rishona ben kodem l'bat*), so too in the secondary inheritance — at any subsequent level in the chart — son comes before daughter (*af yerusha shniya ben kodem l'bat*).

### Yerusha Shniya Scope

The *Rashbam* and *Tosafos* disagree about the scope of *yerusha shniya*. According to the *Rashbam*, *yerusha rishona* refers to the first level of inheritance — the man's own sons and daughters — and *yerusha shniya* refers to the subsequent levels enumerated in the verse: the man's siblings, uncles, and so forth. At each of these collateral levels, the rule of son before daughter applies just as it does at the direct level. The *drasha* links all of these tiers to the primary tier.

*Tosafos* reads *yerusha shniya* more expansively: it encompasses not merely the lateral tiers but also the generational descent through any heir. If a nephew inherits and that nephew has descendants, the rule of son before daughter applies within his line no matter how many generations down one goes. The *drasha* covers any level of inheritance, including cases far removed from those explicitly enumerated in the *psukim*. Either way, the principle is the same: wherever one is on the inheritance chart — whether inheriting directly, through a sibling, through an uncle, or through a nephew's descendants — sons precede daughters at the same generational level, and a descendant of a son, however many generations removed, will come before the living daughter of that son's sibling.

## Din: Daytime Rule

### V'haya B'yom Pasuk

The Gemara shifts to a different aspect of inheritance law: the procedural status of inheritance adjudication. A *braisa* is cited in the name of Rabba bar Chinnana, brother of Rav Nachman: *v'haya b'yom hanchilo et banav* — "it shall be on the day that he bequeaths to his sons." The *braisa* derives from this verse: *b'yom atah mapil nachalot v'ee atah mapil nachalot balayla* — in the daytime you distribute inheritances, and you do not distribute inheritances at night.

Abaye immediately challenges this reading: is the verse really saying that a man has to die during the day for his sons to inherit? *D'shachiv biyomama hu d'yarsi lei bnei, v'dah d'shachiv balayla lo yarsi lei bnei?* — If he dies during the day his sons inherit, and if he dies at night they don't? That is obviously not the meaning of the verse. The Gemara responds: *dilma din nachalot kamashma lan* — perhaps the verse is teaching us about the adjudication of inheritance cases, not the timing of the death itself.

### Dinei Mamonos Status

The *halacha* that emerges is grounded in a second verse: *v'hayata livnei Yisrael lechukat mishpat* — "it shall be for the children of Israel as a statute of judgment." This phrase appears at the conclusion of the passage concerning the daughters of Tzelafchad. Because the Torah characterizes the laws of inheritance with the term *mishpat* — judgment — the Gemara concludes that the entire *parasha* has the status of *din*. And since it is a *din*, it is subject to the procedural rules that govern *dinei mamonos*: the adjudication must begin during the day, though it may continue into the night.

### Chidush Debate

The *Rashbam* and *Tosafos* disagree about what the *chidush* of this ruling actually is. According to the *Rashbam*, one might have thought that determining inheritance is merely a *birur* — a fact-finding exercise. If a man dies, we simply research who his closest surviving relatives are. There is no plaintiff and no defendant in the conventional sense; we are just clarifying a genealogical fact. The *chidush* is that the Torah characterizes this as a genuine *din*, with all the procedural requirements of *dinei mamonos* — including the requirement that proceedings begin during the day.

*Tosafos* finds this *chidush* too modest. It is obvious, *Tosafos* argues, that inheritance adjudication is *dinei mamonos* — of course it requires *beit din* and of course it must begin by day. The real *chidush*, according to *Tosafos*, lies elsewhere: because inheritance law is a *din*, a *beit din* that was present at the moment of death — for example, three witnesses attending a deathbed distribution — can impose its ruling on the parties. The heirs cannot simply reject that *beit din* and demand a different venue of their choosing. In a normal monetary dispute, both parties must agree on a venue; but because *nachalah* is a *din* in the full sense — not merely a transaction between consenting parties but a *Torah*-imposed transfer — a *beit din* present at the relevant moment has the authority to adjudicate without the consent of the heirs.

### Chukat Mishpat Weight

The phrase *chukat mishpat* carries additional weight beyond the procedural rules discussed here. The *Rambam* and other *rishonim* use it to establish that inheritance law is not subject to *dina d'malchuta dina* — the principle by which secular law governs monetary transactions between parties. In ordinary monetary matters, the law of the kingdom shapes the implicit terms of transactions, and *dina d'malchuta dina* can displace *Torah* law. Inheritance, however, is not a transaction between parties. It is the *Torah*'s dictation of who receives property when a person dies. The word *chok* — statute — signals that this is a Divine enactment, not a contractual arrangement that can be governed by the norms of the surrounding legal system. Some *rishonim* therefore rule that *nachalah* is categorically exempt from *dina d'malchuta dina*, and the *chukat mishpat* formulation is their textual basis. In the present context, the Gemara uses the same language more narrowly — to establish the procedural status of inheritance as *dinei mamonos* requiring daytime commencement — but the language carries this broader resonance as well.

## Night Exception

### Asukin B'Oso Inyan

Having established that inheritance cases must begin during the day, the Gemara immediately introduces an exception: *v'im hayu asukin b'oso inyan mutar* — if the court was already occupied with that case, it is permitted to continue and conclude at night. This is the standard rule for *dinei mamonos* generally: the requirement is that proceedings *begin* by day, not that they must be completed before nightfall. Once a *beit din* has commenced its adjudication during daylight hours and becomes *asukin* — engrossed in the case — it may carry the proceedings through into the night without interruption.

### B'Chol Eis Source

The Gemara asks: *mana hanei mili* — what is the source for permitting nighttime continuation? Rav Chisda answers by citing the verse *v'shaftu es ha'am b'chol eis* — "and they shall judge the people at all times." The phrase *b'chol eis*, at all times, is read as encompassing the night: once a court has lawfully begun a case during the day, it may judge *b'chol eis* — at any time, including after dark. The rule of daytime commencement is thus not absolute; it governs when proceedings must open, not when they must close. A court already *asukin b'oso inyan* — occupied with that very matter — may see it through to resolution regardless of the hour.

---

---

# Bava Batra 114

## Inheritance as Din

### Overview & Context

Daf 114 is a relatively brief daf, and it picks up from the bottom of 113b. We have shifted gears momentarily from the detailed tree of inheritance to some fundamental *halachot* about the concept of *nachalot* as a form of *din* and *mishpat*. The daf also contains a notable digression that has nothing directly to do with inheritance at all. Both threads are worth following carefully, as they illuminate the broader legal framework within which the laws of inheritance operate.

### Day vs Night Rule

A *baraita* is taught before Rav Nachman: the verse *ve-hayah be-yom hanchilo et banav* — "and it shall be on the day he bequeaths to his sons" — is read to mean that the distribution of an estate takes place in the daytime and not at night.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye immediately exposes the absurdity of taking this statement too literally: does it mean that only if a person dies during the daytime do his children inherit? And if he dies at night, they do not? Clearly that cannot be the intent.

### Clarification: Din Nacha…

Abaye therefore redirects: perhaps what was meant is *din nachalot* — the adjudication of inheritance law. It is the legal proceeding, not the biological fact of death, that must take place during the daytime.

### Chukkat Mishpat

The *baraita* then supplies the textual basis. At the conclusion of the entire *parasha* of *Bnot Zelophehad*, the Torah states: *ve-hayetah li-venei Yisrael le-chukkat mishpat* — "this shall be for the children of Israel as an edict of judgment." The verse designates the entire *parasha* as *mishpat*, thereby establishing that *nachalot* constitutes a form of *din*.

### Rashbam's Chiddush

According to the Rashbam, the *chiddush* is simply that *nachalot* is classified as *dinei mamonot* — monetary adjudication. And since it is *dinei mamonot*, it follows the rule that all monetary adjudication must be initiated in the daytime. One might ask: what else could it possibly be? The Rashbam acknowledges the difficulty. Perhaps one might have imagined that the laws of inheritance are more a matter of clarifying facts — identifying the closest surviving heir — rather than a true legal dispute. But whenever there is a genuine contest, whether over the terms of a will or the fair distribution of assets among competing parties, it rises to the level of formal *din*. That, for the Rashbam, is the *chiddush*.

### Rishonim: Chok Status

Many *Rishonim*, however, go considerably further. The Rambam, the Rashba, and others focus not just on the word *mishpat* but on the full formulation: *chukkat mishpat*. The word *chok* evokes something closer to ritual law — a fixed, immutable ordinance that cannot be tampered with. This has immediate practical implications. A question that arises in every generation is whether secular inheritance law can govern the division of an estate, particularly in cases of intestacy, on the grounds of *dina d'malchuta dina* — the principle that the law of the sovereign governs monetary matters. The Rambam and Rashba answer emphatically: *chas ve-shalom*. Because *nachalot* is *chukkat mishpat*, it carries the weight of a *chok*, and *dina d'malchuta* has no purchase here.

The deeper reason they offer is structural. In ordinary *dinei mamonot*, two parties enter into a transaction with mutual intent; there is a meeting of minds, and that element of consent makes the legal framework somewhat malleable. Inheritance, by contrast, happens automatically at the moment of death. The deceased does not choose to transfer property — the transfer simply occurs by operation of Torah law. Since there is no underlying agreement between living parties, there is nothing subject to renegotiation by reference to secular convention. It is, in this sense, more like ritual law than like ordinary monetary law — and for that reason *dina d'malchuta dina* cannot override it.

---

## Rav Yehuda & Din Rul (II)

### Dinei Mamonot Timing

The *Gemara* now connects the principle of daytime adjudication to a more general rule articulated by Rav Yehuda. Any form of *din* must be initiated during the daytime. *Dinei mamonot* is the most lenient category: the proceedings must begin in the day but may continue and conclude at night. *Dinei nefashos* is the most stringent: both the opening and the conclusion of the case must take place during the day. The laws of inheritance, as *dinei mamonot*, therefore require at minimum that adjudication begin in the daytime.

### Three Visitors Case

As an illustration of how this plays out in practice, Rav Yehuda introduces the following case: three men entered to visit a sick person — a *shochiv mera*, one who is on his deathbed — and in the course of that visit, the dying man gave some form of verbal distribution of his property. After his death, those three visitors must now somehow give legal effect to what they heard. The question is what role they may play.

---

## Matnat Shechiv Mera

### Rabbi Yochanan Position

Before continuing with Rav Yehuda's case, it is worth setting out the legal landscape governing deathbed transfers, which will occupy later *perakim* more fully. Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka takes the position that a dying person retains the power to redistribute his property among his heirs — though not to non-heirs. While the Torah's default rules dictate who inherits and in what proportions, Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka holds that the dying person has some latitude to reallocate shares among those who are already in the line of succession. Interesting questions flow from this: can he favor a daughter over a son? A brother over a child? How broadly is "heirs" to be defined?

### Shechiv Mera Definition

Setting aside Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka's position — which represents a minority view — the Rabbis developed their own institution of the *matnat shechiv mera*: a verbal bequest made on the deathbed. The conditions are specific: the person must be genuinely dying and anticipating death; he must give away his property by speech alone, without any formal *kinyan*; the bequest must cover all of his property; and he must not retract before he dies. If all conditions are met, the Rabbis declared this verbal instruction binding — *divrei shechiv mera ke-khtuvim u-kmesurim dami*, the words of a dying person are treated as if they have been written and delivered. This is an entirely rabbinic institution, but a robust one. The particular *chiddush* is that it takes effect not at the moment of speech but at the moment of death, and it applies even to property acquired between the time of the declaration and the time of death.

### Kinyan Bemiktzat

The third mechanism is not a rabbinic institution at all but rather the application of an existing legal tool — *kinyan* — to the deathbed context. The dying person performs a standard *kinyan sudar*, taking or giving a handkerchief (or similar object), thereby transferring a designated piece of property to the recipient. Crucially, the transfer can be structured to take effect at the moment before death. This is a classic *kinyan bemiktzat* — it operates only on property already in the person's possession at the time of the *kinyan*, not on property he might acquire afterward. And unlike *matnat shechiv mera*, it does not require giving away everything.

### Three Methods Summary

To summarize, there are three distinct mechanisms by which a person can control the distribution of his estate beyond the Torah's default rules: first, the redistribution among heirs according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, which is *de-oraita* in character and limited to those already in the line of inheritance; second, the *matnat shechiv mera*, which is a rabbinic institution based on verbal declaration and effective across all property including future acquisitions; and third, the *kinyan bemiktzat*, which uses the classic legal mechanism of *kinyan* and is effective only on existing property at the time of acquisition. In the case of the three visitors, it is not immediately clear which of these mechanisms the dying man employed. Most likely he gave a verbal *matnat shechiv mera*, though the possibility of a formal *maaseh kinyan* is also raised by the *Rishonim*.

---

## Rav Yehuda & Din Rul (II)

### Witnesses vs Beit Din

Returning to the case of the three visitors: after the dying man makes his distribution, those present must decide what role they are playing. The *Gemara* states that if they choose, they may function as witnesses — *ratzu kotvin* — writing up a *shtar* that records what they heard the man say. That *shtar* is then presented to a *Beit Din*, which adjudicates on the basis of it. Alternatively, if there are three of them, they may function directly as a *Beit Din* — *ratzu osim din* — and adjudicate the case themselves without requiring separate testimony, relying on the principle of *lo tehei shemia gedolah mire'iyah*: the direct perception of a *Beit Din* is no weaker than testimony presented through witnesses. If only two visitors were present, they may only serve as witnesses, and the case must be brought before a separate *Beit Din*.

### Daytime Requirement

Rav Chisda now introduces the critical qualification. The option of functioning as a *Beit Din* is available only if the visit took place during the daytime. *Lo shanu ela be-yom* — this was only taught with respect to daytime. If all three were there and it was daytime, they may choose to adjudicate directly.

### Night Visit Restriction

If the visit took place at night, then even if there were three of them, they may only serve as witnesses — *kotvin ve-ein osim din*. They cannot retroactively constitute themselves as a *Beit Din* that sat in judgment, because a *Beit Din* cannot open a case at night.

### Ein Ed Na'aseh Dayan

The reason is twofold. First, the case cannot be opened at nighttime — all *din* must begin in the day. Second, and relatedly, *ein ed na'aseh dayan* — one who has functioned as a witness cannot turn around and serve as a judge. If a person heard the dying man's declaration at night, his legal status at that moment was that of a witness; a *Beit Din* cannot be constituted from witnesses to whom the case has already been presented in their capacity as *edim*. This demonstrates concretely that *nachalot* is *din* — we have witnesses, we have a *Beit Din*, we care about whether there are two or three present, and we require that adjudication begin in the day.

This passage raises several important questions among the *Rishonim*. One concerns what actually designates someone as a witness. The Rashbam cites his grandfather Rashi, from a *teshuva*, who holds that if the dying man explicitly called the visitors in as witnesses — if he summoned them in that capacity — then they are labeled as witnesses, and *ein ed na'aseh dayan* applies even if there were three of them and they came in the daytime. Tosafot disagrees. For Rashi, the very act of designation as a witness is sufficient to preclude the role of judge; for Tosafot, the designation alone does not carry that legal consequence unless they have actually testified.

---

## Tosafot: Chok Nature

### No Forum Selection

Tosafot offers a different reading of the *chiddush* of *chukkat mishpat* — one that connects directly to Michael's question about whether the heirs can simply select their own *Beit Din*. Tosafot argues that the *chiddush* is not merely that *nachalot* is *dinei mamonot*, but that the heirs do not have the ordinary right of forum selection. In a standard *dinei mamonot* case, litigants may contest which *Beit Din* hears the matter, and there is established *halacha* about which venue governs. Here, there is room to argue that one heir might say, "I don't want those three men as my *Beit Din*; let's take the case to a different court."

### Imposed Jurisdiction

According to Tosafot, *chukkat mishpat* establishes that once a *Beit Din* has directly witnessed the bequest — once these three men were present and heard the declaration — they may judge the case even against the will of the heirs, even without the heirs' consent. The jurisdiction, in effect, is imposed. This is tied to the broader point that inheritance is not a classic transaction between identifiable litigants. When there is genuine uncertainty about who qualifies as an heir, who received a valid bequest, and what the dying man intended, the "parties" to the dispute cannot be neatly defined in advance. A *Beit Din* that witnessed the relevant facts may therefore step in and adjudicate regardless of the preferences of those who later assert claims.

### Rashi: Witness Label

Rashi's position, as cited by the Rashbam, is that the dying man's explicit designation of the visitors as witnesses — his having called them in to serve in that capacity — gives them the label of *ed*, witness, and from that point forward *ein ed na'aseh dayan* applies. Tosafot disagrees, and distinguishes between designation and actual testimony.

### Ed Types Discussion

This leads to a broader distinction among the *Rishonim* between two different applications of *ein ed na'aseh dayan*. The first is the case of *ed hame'id* — one who has actively come before a *Beit Din* and testified. Such a person cannot subsequently serve as a *dayan* in that same case; once testimony has been formally given, the roles of witness and judge are incompatible. The second is the case of *ed haro'eh* — one who merely witnessed the relevant facts but has not testified. This person may still serve as a *dayan*, since what the rule prevents is not his sitting in judgment, but his treating his mere observation as equivalent to the *Beit Din* having had the case formally presented. An *ed haro'eh* who witnessed a transfer at night is not prevented the following morning from sitting as a *dayan* if other *edim* come to testify before him. The key distinction is between having witnessed something and having functioned formally as a witness in a legal proceeding — and between whether the witnessing constitutes the opening of a case before a *Beit Din*.

---

## Kinyan Chalipin

### Retraction Window

The *Gemara* now introduces a discussion that appears at first glance entirely unrelated to inheritance. Because one of the mechanisms for a deathbed transfer is the *kinyan bemiktzat* — which employs *kinyan chalipin*, the exchange of a *sudar* or similar object — the *Gemara* takes the opportunity to explore a question about *kinyan chalipin* more broadly: *ad ematai chozer* — how long after performing the *kinyan* may a party retract?

The scenario is straightforward: two parties have agreed on the sale of a car, say, and instead of performing *meshikha*, they do *kinyan chalipin* — one party takes a pen from the other, sealing the deal, in the presence of witnesses. The question is whether there is any window after this act during which a party may back out.

### Rabba's View

Rabba holds that one may retract *kol zman she-yoshvin* — as long as both parties remain seated together in the same room. Once they have risen and dispersed, the *kinyan* is final and irrevocable.

### Rav Yosef's View

Rav Yosef holds a more restrictive position: one may retract only *kol zman she-asukin be-oto inyan* — as long as the parties are still engaged in discussion of the same subject matter. Even if they remain seated in the same room, if they have moved on to other topics — discussing the weather, the ball scores — the *kinyan* is final and no retraction is possible.

### Gmirot Da'at Basis

The underlying principle that makes this question intelligible is the unique nature of *kinyan chalipin* among all the modes of *kinyan*. In all other forms of *kinyan* — *meshikha*, *hagbaha*, *chatzer* — the physical act itself carries symbolic weight: it demonstrates ownership, it reflects the reality of possession. There is a physical correlate to the legal transfer. In *kinyan chalipin*, by contrast, there is nothing demonstrated. The taking of a pen or a handkerchief does not show ownership of anything. The act is purely a signal — a signal that both parties have reached complete *gmirot da'at*, full finality of intent. The *kinyan* is valid not because of what the act symbolizes physically, but because the exchange is understood as an agreed-upon mechanism for expressing unconditional commitment to the deal.

This means that *kinyan chalipin* operates entirely in the domain of mental commitment. And if it operates entirely in the domain of intent, then the question of whether that intent is truly complete becomes live in a way that it is not with other forms of *kinyan*. With *hagbaha*, once the object is lifted, the physical reality has changed and the legal change follows necessarily. With *chalipin*, everything depends on the inner state of the parties — and it is therefore conceivable that for a brief moment after the act, the commitment has not fully crystallized. That window is what Rabba and Rav Yosef are debating.

### Application & Reconcilia…

The *Gemara* now ties this dispute back to the case of the three visitors. Rav Yosef himself argues that the *halacha* of the three visitors — namely, that they may function as a *Beit Din* and adjudicate the case right then and there — is actually evidence for his position over Rabba's. If, as Rabba holds, one may retract as long as the parties are still sitting in the same room, then why would the visitors be able to adjudicate immediately? The dying man performed his *kinyan* and is still in the same room — according to Rabba, he could retract at any moment. It would be premature and futile to open the case when he might still undo everything he just did.

Rav Yosef, however, can explain the case cleanly: once the dying man completes the *kinyan* and the conversation moves on to other matters — once they are no longer *asukin be-oto inyan* — the transfer is final. At that point the *Beit Din* can convene and adjudicate without any concern that the man will retract.

Rav Ashi reports that he presented this argument to Rav Kahana, who immediately challenged: does Rav Yosef really do better here? Even according to Rav Yosef, if they are sitting in judgment while still discussing the very same matter, the man could theoretically retract — they are still *asukin be-oto inyan*. Rav Kahana resolves this by saying that in the case of the visitors, the judgment takes place after the topic has shifted — *d'asliku me-inyana le-inyana* — so by the time they convene as a *Beit Din*, the *kinyan* is already irrevocable. And he offers a parallel resolution for Rabba: one can construct the case so that the visitors left the room — *kamu ve-hadar yasivu* — before reconvening to adjudicate. Once they have all risen and dispersed, even Rabba concedes that retraction is no longer possible, and the *Beit Din* can then sit to execute what was already finalized.

### Halakha Rules Rav Yosef

The *Gemara* rules *ve-hilkhata ke-vosei de-Rav Yosef* — the *halacha* follows Rav Yosef. And it specifies that this ruling applies in three cases within *Bava Batra*, remembered by the mnemonic *sadeh, inyan, u-mechtza*: the case of the division of a field from an earlier passage; our case of *asukin be-oto inyan*; and a later case of *mechtza*, where a person instructs that his property be given to his wife and his son, and the ruling is that this means half to each. Tosafot notes that the phrase "we rule like Rav Yosef in these three cases" does not necessarily imply that we rule like Rabba in all other disputes between them. The formulation might simply be identifying three specific cases within this *masechta* where Rav Yosef's position prevails — not establishing a general preference for Rabba.

---

## Chain of Inheritance

### Mishna Structure

With the various digressions concluded, the *Gemara* returns to the chain of inheritance and addresses what appears to be a redundancy in the *Mishna*. The *Mishna* on 108a stated: *ha-ish et imo ve-ha-ish et ishto nochalim ve-lo manchilim* — a man inherits from his mother and from his wife, but they do not inherit from him. His son inherits, his brother inherits, his father inherits — not his mother, not his wife. The *Mishna* then continued: *ha-ishah et benah ve-ha-ishah et ba'alah manchilim ve-lo nochalim* — a woman and her son, a woman and her husband, they cause the inheritance to pass on, but they themselves do not inherit in return.

### Redundancy Question

The *Gemara* asks: why state the second clause at all? It is the exact mirror image of the first. The first clause says these parties inherit going one direction but not the other; the second clause simply reverses the perspective and says the same thing from the other side. Why is this not mere redundancy?

### Bakever Analogy

The *Gemara* answers: the second clause is not mere repetition. It comes to teach us that *ha-ishah et benah* — the relationship of a woman and her son — is analogous to *ha-ishah et ba'alah* — the relationship of a woman and her husband, with respect to the law of *bakever*, inheritance through the dead.

### Bakever Principle

What is the *bakever* principle? The husband does not inherit from his wife if he is dead — *ein ha-ba'al yoresh et ishto ba-kever*. That is, if the husband has already died and then his wife dies, we do not say: "Let us trace the estate as though it first passed to the husband and then from him to his heirs." Once the husband is dead, the marital relationship no longer exists. He was never a blood relative; the connection was created entirely through the institution of marriage. Death severs that bond. He and his wife are, in legal terms, as divorced — and if she died after a divorce, her estate would not pass to his family. So too, once he is dead, her estate does not pass through him to his relatives. He does not inherit *ba-kever*.

The practical consequence is this: suppose a woman has property and her husband has already died. He had a son from a previous wife. Should we say that the woman's estate notionally passes to the deceased husband, and from him to that son? No. *Ein ha-ba'al yoresh et ishto ba-kever*. The connection is severed. Her estate goes to her own family — her father, her brother, her son if she has one.

### Blood vs Marital Kinship

The contrast with blood relationships is instructive. If a man died leaving a son and a daughter, and the son subsequently died before the grandfather — so that the inheritance now passes from the grandfather to the grandchildren's generation — the deceased son's child would take priority over the surviving daughter. We apply *yoresh ba-kever* in that case: we trace the inheritance as though the son had lived to receive it and then ask who would succeed him. This is because the bond of blood (*korva*) persists; lineage is not severed by death. The son's child is the son's child regardless of whether the son is alive.

But the bond of marriage (*she'arut*) — the *basar echad* unity created by the marital relationship — exists only while the marriage endures. Death dissolves it entirely. And the *Gemara* now says: the same principle applies to the relationship of a woman and her son. If the son has died before the mother, we do not say that her estate passes notionally through the dead son to his paternal brothers — brothers who share a father with him but who are in no way related to her. He does not inherit *ba-kever* to take the property away from her family and deliver it to people she has no relationship with at all. *Yerushat ba-kever* operates where *korva* persists; it does not operate where the effect would be to transfer property entirely outside the relevant family.

---

## Mother Inherits (Radical)

### Rav Yochanan's View

Having established the *bakever* principle, the *Gemara* now presents a position that is genuinely striking. Rav Yochanan, in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon, states: *dvar Torah ha-av yoresh et bno ve-ha-ishah yoreshes et bnah* — by Torah law, both a father and a mother inherit from a deceased son. This is a direct challenge to the ruling of the *Mishna*, which places the mother outside the line of inheritance entirely.

### Daughters of Z. Source

The source is the *parasha* of *Bnot Zelophehad*. The verse states *kol bat yoreshes nachala mi-matot* — every daughter who inherits an estate does so from the *matot*, the tribes. The *Gemara* reads this as establishing a parallel between the *mateh* of the father and the *mateh* of the mother: *mah mateh av yoresh et bno, af mateh em hi yoreshes et bnah* — just as the father's tribe inherits from a son, so too the mother's tribe inherits from a son. The *Bnot Zelophehad* precedent, which established that daughters could inherit in the absence of sons, is now extended upward: the same logic that recognizes female claimants in the descending generation is applied to the ascending generation as well, recognizing the mother as an heir to her son.

### Rashbam's Limitation

The Rashbam immediately limits the scope of this ruling. It cannot mean that the mother always inherits from her son — that would completely overturn the established structure. The Rashbam therefore reads it as applying only when the father is not alive. If the father is alive, the entire estate goes to him; only in the father's absence does the mother enter the picture as an heir.

### Tosafot's Objection

Tosafot is deeply troubled by the ruling even in its limited form, and articulates why. If a mother can inherit from a son whenever the father is deceased, the implications for the patriarchal structure of inheritance are severe. Consider: the entire system of inheritance is built around *mishpachat av* — family is defined through the father's line, and the estate is meant to circulate within the father's *shevet*. If the mother inherits, the estate passes into her family, her *shevet*, and it may never return to the father's brothers and paternal relatives who would otherwise be the next in line. The Torah itself was concerned about property passing from *shevet* to *shevet* — that was the entire reason the daughters of Zelophehad were told to marry within their tribe. And yet this ruling would allow property to migrate out of the patriarchal family with extraordinary ease: a man marries a woman from a different tribe, he dies, his property passes to the son, the son dies, and the property goes to the mother — to the other tribe — without any of the safeguards the Torah put in place. Tosafot notes that the concern about tribal transfer would apply at every generation and for men and women alike, making the concern over *Bnot Zelophehad* seem almost unnecessary if this principle were broadly operative.

### Tosafot: Ger Exception

So disturbed is Tosafot by this position that he — or rather Rabbeinu Tam and Ri — radically reinterprets it. They argue that Rav Yochanan's ruling applies only in the case of a *giyoret* — a female convert — who has a son. The convert has no halakhic relatives on her side; her family connections before conversion are severed. If her son dies, his estate would normally become *hefker* — ownerless — since a *ger* who dies without heirs leaves property that no one can claim. But since he does have one halakhic relative — his mother, the *giyoret* — the ruling is that she inherits. The *chiddush*, on this reading, is not a general principle that mothers inherit from sons, but a narrow rule that prevents the estate of a *ger* from becoming *hefker* when the only surviving relative is his converted mother. This interpretation is admittedly not *pshat* — it does not follow naturally from the text — but it shows how disruptive Tosafot considers the straightforward reading to be.

### Assessment of Radicality

Whatever one makes of Tosafot's reinterpretation, the position attributed to Rav Yochanan is genuinely radical. The reasoning from *Bnot Zelophehad* is applied not only downward — establishing that daughters can inherit in the absence of sons — but upward, establishing that a mother stands in a parallel position to a father in the ascending generation. This cuts against the foundational principle that *mishpachat av kruyah mishpachah, mishpachat em einah kruyah mishpachah* — family identity is traced through the father, and the mother's lineage does not define one's tribal or familial belonging. Rav Yochanan's view essentially challenges that asymmetry, insisting that the same equality extended to daughters by *Bnot Zelophehad* must be extended to mothers as well. How the *Gemara* will reckon with this position, and how it interacts with the *Mishna*'s explicit ruling to the contrary, will be the subject of the continuation.

---

---

# Bava Batra 115

## Mother Inherits Son

### Radical Position Stated

The daf opens with one of the most disruptive positions in the laws of inheritance: the teaching of Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon, transmitted by Rabbi Yochanan, that a mother inherits from her deceased son. This opinion stands in direct conflict with the *mishna*, and its implications are sweeping. As *Tosafot* notes, the innovation of *Bnos Tzelofchad* already introduced the possibility of property passing down to daughters rather than remaining along the patrilineal line; the position of Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon effectively squares that innovation, allowing property to pass not only downward to daughters but upward to mothers as well, with all the attendant consequences for property leaving the father's family and tribe.

### Source & Mishna Conflict

The *gemara* opens by recording that Rabbi Yochanan transmitted this ruling in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon. Yet Rabbi Yochanan himself immediately confronts the teaching with our *mishna*, which states explicitly: *ish es benav, isha es ba'alah, v'achei ha'eim, manchilin v'lo nochlin* — a man bequeaths to his children, a woman bequeaths to her husband, and the mother's brothers may bequeath but do not inherit. The *mishna* thus explicitly excludes both a wife from inheriting her husband and a mother from inheriting her son. To this challenge, Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon responds: *mishnasenu eini yodeia mi shenasnah* — I do not know who taught that *mishna*; it does not reflect my view. In other words, he dismisses the *mishna* as representing some minority position without binding authority, acknowledging the conflict but declining to be governed by it.

### Rabbi Zechariah Challenge

The *gemara* presses further: granted that you wish to treat the *mishna* as a *da'as yachid* — the isolated opinion of a single *tanna* rather than a consensus ruling — why not identify who that *tanna* is? The *gemara* suggests: why not say the *mishna* represents the position of Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav, who does not expound the *drasha* of *matot*?

### Matot Drasha Explained

To appreciate this suggestion, it is necessary to recall the *drasha* of *matot* developed on earlier *dapim*. The *pasuk* reads: *v'chol bat yoreshet nachala mi'matot* — every daughter who inherits a portion from the tribes. The use of *matot* in the plural signals a case in which the daughter's father belongs to one tribe and her mother to another, and the verse equates the two — *mateh ha'eim* equals *mateh ha'av*. The tribe of the mother is rendered equivalent to the tribe of the father.

### Twin Implications

This equation carries two distinct implications. The first concerns what happens when the *mother* dies: just as when the father dies the sons inherit before the daughters, so too when the mother dies the sons take priority over the daughters, because the mother's tribe is equated to the father's tribe in the transmission of property downward. The second implication runs in the opposite direction: just as when a son dies his *father* inherits from him, so too — if the two tribes are truly equated — his *mother* should inherit from him alongside the father. These two implications point in different directions from the perspective of any simple analysis of whose interests are served: the first preserves the patriarchal ordering of sons over daughters even in a matrilineal transmission, while the second opens the door to property departing the father's tribal line entirely if the father has predeceased the son and the inheritance passes to the mother.

### Zechariah Rejects Equati…

Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav rejects this equation altogether. He holds that *mateh ha'em* is not equated to *mateh ha'av*, and therefore when the mother dies, the sons and daughters inherit her property equally — there is no basis to impose the prioritization of sons over daughters when it is the mother's property at stake.
