By the same logic, when a son dies, the property passes only to his father, not to his mother, since the two parental lines are not equated.

### Nephews Before Nieces

The *gemara* now explains why the *mishna* cannot be attributed to Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav. The *mishna* includes in its discussion the inheritance of nephews — specifically the sons of a sister — and a *baraita* clarifies that the *mishna*'s intent is *bnei achot v'lo bnos achot*: nephews inherit before nieces. Rav Sheshet explains that this is not to exclude nieces entirely, but to establish that nephews take priority. Now consider the scenario: if a brother is dying and his estate passes to his sister's children, that means the sister herself has already died. The inheritance is thus flowing through a deceased woman to her children — structurally equivalent to the case of a mother dying. The *mishna*, by specifying that nephews precede nieces in this scenario, implicitly establishes that even when property passes through a woman, sons take priority over daughters. This is inconsistent with Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav's view that sons and daughters inherit equally from their mother. Therefore, the *mishna* cannot represent his position.

### Yoreshet Resolution

This creates an acute difficulty. Our *mishna* appears to maintain both rulings simultaneously — that when the mother dies, the sons get first (inferred from the nephews-before-nieces ruling), and that when the son dies, only the father inherits, not the mother. But these two positions seem to pull in opposite directions with respect to the *matot* equation. As the *gemara* frames it: *mi manafshach* — whichever way you turn, there is a problem. If the *mishna* does expound the *drasha* of *matot* and equates mother and father, then the mother should inherit from her son just as the father does. If the *mishna* does not expound *matot*, then how does it know to give priority to sons over daughters when the mother dies?

The *gemara* resolves this by pointing out that the *drasha* has two components, and the questioner had only considered one. The *gemara* says: *le-olam darish matot* — the *mishna* does indeed expound the *matot* equation, and that is how it establishes that sons precede daughters in the mother's estate. But the same *pasuk* contains another word: *yoreshet*. The full phrase is *v'chol bat yoreshet nachala mi'matot* — the *bat yoreshet*, the daughter who inherits. The *drasha* on *yoreshet* teaches: *yoreshet v'eina moreshet* — she inherits but she does not cause others to inherit. The equation of *matot* — mother's tribe to father's tribe — applies only in the downward direction, when property is passing down from parent to child and we are ordering among the heirs. In that context, mother and father are equated and sons take priority. But the equation does not apply upward, when a child dies and we ask who inherits from him. In that case, the property rises only to the father, not to the mother. The word *yoreshet* restricts the scope of the *matot* equation to the downward transmission.

### Two-Part Drasha

The structure of the resolution, then, is that the full *drasha* has two parts. *Matot* equates the mother's tribe to the father's tribe, ensuring that the patrilineal ordering of sons before daughters governs even when property descends through the mother. *Yoreshet* limits that equation to the case of descent, preventing it from operating in the upward direction when a son predeceases both parents. The *mishna* thus upholds both principles in a coherent framework, and cannot be attributed to Rabbi Zechariah ben HaKatzav, who rejects the *matot* equation entirely.

---

## Seder Nachalos

### Intro to Order

Having addressed the opening controversy of the *daf*, the *gemara* turns to the *mishna*'s systematic exposition of *seder nachalos* — the ordered hierarchy of inheritance. The opening *mishna* of this *perek* established who can give and receive inheritance in terms of the categories of relatives involved, but did not lay out a priority order. The present *mishna* supplies that structure. It is worth noting that this is an unusually well-organized *perek*: it opens with a conceptual framework — *nochlin u-manchilin* — and now moves to elaborate the hierarchy from *pesukim*. The *perek* itself is quite substantial, extending to thirty *dapim* and eventually reaching the topic of rabbinic instruments for transferring property that function analogously to wills.

### Descendants Priority

The *mishna* begins with the foundational *pasuk*: *ish ki yamut u-ven ein lo v'ha'avartem et nachalato le-vito* — if a man dies and has no son, his estate passes to his daughter. From this the *mishna* derives: *ben kodem le-vas* — the son precedes the daughter. But the *mishna* immediately adds the critical refinement: *kol yotzei yerecho shel ben kodmin le-vas* — all the issue of the loins of the son precede the daughter. The phrase *yotzei yerecho* is precise and intentional: it does not refer to relatives generally but to direct lineal descendants. Every direct descendant of the son — however many generations removed — is treated as standing in the son's place and takes priority over the daughter.

### Replacement Principle

The animating principle here is that a child or grandchild is understood as a generational replacement for the person who died. When a son predeceases the deceased, all of that son's descendants — sons, daughters, grandchildren, great-grandchildren — step into his place in the inheritance hierarchy. Before the estate moves to the next category on the list, one must first exhaust every possible descendant of the prior category. *Tosafot* raises the question of whether this rests on the general principle of *bnei banim harei hem ke-vanim* — that grandchildren are treated as children — noting that this principle may be more firmly established when the *pesukim* use the word *zera*, which can connote any descendant, than when they use *ben*, which might suggest only the immediate first generation. But regardless of the precise derivation, the operative rule is clear: no matter how many generations removed, a descendant counts as a replacement.

### Gender Blindness Query

This raises a genuinely interesting question about how gender-blind the replacement principle is. The basic rule is that when a son has predeceased the testator, all of that son's descendants take his place — and the *mishna* states this without qualification, so even a great-great-granddaughter through that son comes before the testator's own daughter. Superficially this seems ironic: a daughter of the testator is closer in degree than a many-generations-removed female descendant through a son, yet the latter takes priority.

The deeper question is what happens when multiple descendants of the predeceased son are alive simultaneously. If the predeceased son had both a son and a daughter, does the grandson take priority over the granddaughter, or are they treated equally since we are already in a gender-blind "replacement" mode? The answer appears to be that if they are both alive, the grandson does take priority — we are not fully gender-blind within the replacement generation, and the male descendant would inherit before the female descendant. The question becomes more complex when asking whether, if the grandson himself predeceases his sisters, one should prefer a line through him over a line through a female sibling. This requires further verification, but the basic framework of the replacement principle is clear.

The seemingly paradoxical result — that a granddaughter through a son comes before a daughter — also raises a structural puzzle. The preference of sons over daughters was originally grounded in the goal of keeping property within the patrilineal tribe. Yet once a daughter of a predeceased son is inheriting, the property may well pass out of the tribe through her marriage. As *Tosafot* observes in connection with the earlier discussion, the introduction of female inheritance through *Bnos Tzelofchad* set in motion a logic that plays out in many directions — the "joint account" has complex downstream consequences.

### Full Hierarchy Listed

The *mishna* then continues down the list. After the daughter and all her descendants come the brothers — the deceased's siblings. The *mishna* then specifies *achei ha'av* — the father's brothers, i.e., the deceased's uncles — as coming after brothers. Notably, the *mishna* does not insert the father into this explicit sequence; the *gemara* supplies that omission. The full hierarchy, once the father is incorporated, is: children (and all their descendants), then the father, then brothers (and their descendants), then the father's brothers.

### Father's Position

The *mishna*'s closing rule states: *ha'av kodem l'chol yotzei yerecho* — the father precedes all of his own issue. This places the father before the deceased's brothers, since the deceased's brothers are precisely the father's children. The logic is that a sibling relationship is mediated through the father: the deceased is connected to his brother only through their common father. Therefore, the father — as the direct ancestor — takes priority over his own descendants.

This resolves what might initially seem like an omission. The *mishna* lists the order as: son, daughter, brothers, father's brothers — and the father seems to be missing. In fact, the father enters between the daughter and the brothers, based on the rule that he precedes all his own issue. So the operative order is: children (all descendants), then father, then siblings (and their descendants), then grandfather, then uncles, and so on.

### Recursive Pattern

Once this structure is grasped, the full order of inheritance follows a recursive pattern. The estate passes downward as far as possible through direct descendants; when that line is exhausted, it rises one generation; from there it again passes downward through all descendants of that generation before rising again. The movement is always: down as far as possible, then up one step, then down again. Children of the deceased first — exhausting every descendant; then the father; then the father's children (siblings), exhausting their descendants; then the grandfather; then the grandfather's children (uncles), exhausting their descendants; and so on back through the generations. The *gemara* notes that ultimately this chain leads all the way back to *Reuven ben Yaakov*, because the entire Jewish people share a common ancestry.

### Two-Rule Summary

Underlying this entire hierarchical structure are really only two rules. The first is the ordering of son before daughter — with the accompanying principle that all descendants of a son precede a daughter, and all descendants of a daughter precede the next category. The second is the rule that the father precedes all his own issue. With just these two rules, the complete *seder nachalos* follows automatically: go down through sons and daughters and all their descendants; rise to the father; go down through the father's sons and daughters and all their descendants; rise to the grandfather; repeat. Everything else is a consequence of applying these two rules recursively. The *Rashbam* notes that the formulation *kodem l'chol yotzei yerecho* in the *mishna* is slightly imprecise in the context of the father's rule, but the intent is clear.

---

## Descent Drasha

### Baraita on Descent

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *tanu rabbanan*, the Sages taught — *ben u-ven ein lo*: the son, and if there is no son. The *baraita* asks: I know only that we go to the son; how do I know to continue down through the son's son, the son's son's son, and so forth, through all subsequent generations?

### Ayin Alav Drasha

The *drasha* is derived from the phrase *ein lo* — the *gemara* reads this as *ayen alav*, "investigate concerning him": investigate whether there are any descendants in his line before moving on to the next category. The word *ein*, which in its simple meaning signals absence ("there is no"), is read as an instruction to scrutinize (*ayen*) the line for any surviving descendants, however remote. This is admittedly a striking *drasha*, but it establishes the textual basis for the unlimited downward extension of each category in the inheritance hierarchy.

### Female Line Extension

The same logic extends to the daughter's line. The *pasuk* reads: *v'ha'avartem et nachalato le-vito* — if he has no son, his estate passes to his daughter. Here too, the verse includes *ein lo* — "if he has no daughter" — and the same *drasha* applies: *ayen aleha*, investigate the daughter's line. Thus the granddaughter through a daughter, and the great-granddaughter, and so on, all continue the daughter's place in the hierarchy before the estate moves to the next category.

### Nachala Metaphor

The *baraita* captures this dynamic with a vivid image: *nachala memashmeshet ve-holechet* — the inheritance flows and travels, moving continuously down the generations and then back up through the families. The estate descends through the son's line, through the daughter's line, up to the father, through the father's children and their descendants, up to the grandfather, and so on, traveling through the entire network of relatives until an heir is found.

### Tribal Safeguard

The *baraita* says this chain extends *ad Reuven* — all the way back to Reuven son of Yaakov. But the *gemara* immediately asks: why stop at Reuven? Why not go all the way back to Yaakov himself, and then down through all the other tribes?

### No Tribe Extinction

Abaye answers with a fundamental principle: *gmiri de-lo kalya shivta* — it is a received tradition that no tribe of Israel disappears entirely. If the inheritance were to rise above Reuven to Yaakov and then descend through another tribe, that would necessarily imply that the entire tribe of Reuven had ceased to exist — every last descendant of Reuven had died without heirs. Since we hold as a matter of received tradition that this will not occur, we do not extend the chain beyond the tribe. As long as any descendant of Reuven exists anywhere, that person is related to the deceased and will be found somewhere in the chain. Crossing over to another tribe would only become necessary if an entire tribe were extinguished, which we presume cannot happen.

### No Heirs Found

This raises a practical modern question: what happens when no heirs can actually be located? After exhaustive searching, if no heir is found, what becomes of the property? Is it *hefker*? Does it revert to some communal authority? The *gemara* does not address this directly, and it remains an interesting unresolved question, with analogues in civil law systems — where courts have grappled with similar problems involving institutions such as churches whose last surviving member dies before the property's disposition is legally settled.

---

## Sadducean Heresy

### Equal Inheritance Condem…

Rav Huna citing Rav states: *kol ha-omer tirash bat im bat ha-ben* — whoever says that a daughter should inherit together with a granddaughter through a son has articulated a position that is utterly rejected. To appreciate the force of this, recall the hierarchy established above: when a son predeceases the testator, his daughter — the testator's granddaughter — takes the son's place in the inheritance order, and therefore comes before the testator's own daughter. The position being condemned here is the suggestion that once a granddaughter is receiving inheritance, the daughter ought to receive alongside her, dividing the estate between them.

### Nasi Authority Limited

Rav Huna adds: *afilu nasi she-be-Yisrael, ein shom'in lo* — even if the *Nasi*, the supreme communal authority in Israel, were to rule this way, one does not listen to him. The *Rashbam* understands this as referring to a *nasi* who convenes a great *beis din* and issues a ruling. *Tosafot* goes further: even a *nasi* who is not claiming this is genuine *halacha* but is instead seeking to institute a *takkanah* — a rabbinic ordinance — for communal purposes, even one framed as a temporary measure responding to particular social circumstances, is not to be heeded. The principle of *hefker beis din hefker* — that a *beis din* has the power to render property ownerless and redirect it — would ordinarily permit a rabbinic body to accomplish something like this. Yet even that avenue is blocked here. The ruling is so completely off the table that it cannot serve even as the basis for a temporary institutional arrangement.

### Sadducean Attribution

The reason for this extraordinary exclusion is that the position is identified as *mi-Tzedukim* — it is a Sadducean doctrine. Because of this historical association, the ruling is not merely a legitimate minority opinion that lost; it is placed entirely outside the range of permissible positions. This is a noteworthy phenomenon: sometimes a position that might otherwise have been treated as a *da'at yachid* — a minority view worthy of consideration — is rendered categorically illegitimate because of its historical association with a heterodox movement. One might observe that the very persuasiveness of the Sadducean argument — if a granddaughter inherits, why should a daughter not share in that inheritance? — may itself be part of why the Sages felt it necessary to place it so firmly beyond discussion.

### Megillat Taanit

The *gemara* cites the source for this historical attribution: *de-tanya, be-esrim ve-arba be-Tevet, tavna le-dinana* — as the *baraita* teaches, on the twenty-fourth of *Tevet*, we returned to our ruling. This text is drawn from *Megillat Ta'anit*, the ancient document from the period of the Second Temple that records minor holidays on which fasting is prohibited. The document itself was written in Aramaic — an unusual feature, since typically the original authoritative text is in Hebrew and Aramaic serves as the *gemara*'s gloss, but here the situation is reversed, with the *tanna*'s elaboration serving as a commentary on an originally Aramaic source. *Megillat Ta'anit* is of great historical interest as one of the earliest pieces of non-scriptural Jewish writing, and the discussion brought here is drawn from its *skolion* — the explanatory commentary that accompanies the list of dates.

The *baraita* continues: *she-hayu Tzedukim omrim, tirash ha-bat im bat ha-ben* — the Sadducees used to say that a daughter should inherit together with a granddaughter through a son. *Nitpal lahem Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* — Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was dispatched to deal with them. The verb *nitpal* carries something of a dismissive tone — "go take care of them," as if the matter were being handed off as a nuisance to be managed.

### Old Man's Logic

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai opened by challenging them: *shotim, minayin lachem?* — Fools, where do you derive this? And *lo haya adam she-hechiziro davar* — no one was willing to articulate a defense. *Chutz mi-zaken echad she-haya mefatpet knegdo* — except for one old man who was chattering away against him, the word *mefatpet* again carrying a dismissive tone. This old man put forward the following argument: *u-mah bat bno ha-ba'ah mi-koch bno tirashenu* — a granddaughter, who comes to inherit only through the medium of her father, will inherit the testator. *Bito ha-ba'ah mi-kocho, lo kol she-ken?* — His own daughter, who comes directly from him, surely all the more so should she inherit. This is, as the *gemara* implicitly acknowledges, a genuinely strong argument. The granddaughter's claim depends on an intermediary — her father — and yet she inherits. The daughter's claim is direct and unmediated. The logical inference from the lesser to the greater seems compelling.

### Anah Derasha

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's response was to cite a *pasuk*: *eleh bnei Se'ir ha-Chori yoshvei ha'aretz, Lotan v'Shoval v'Tzivon v'Anah* — these are the sons of Se'ir the Chori, dwellers of the land: Lotan, Shoval, Tzivon, and Anah. And a second *pasuk* states: *v'eleh bnei Tzivon, v'Ayah v'Anah* — these are the sons of Tzivon: Ayah and Anah. The difficulty is immediate: in the first verse, Anah appears as a sibling of Tzivon, both being children of Se'ir; in the second verse, Anah appears as a child of Tzivon.

### Anah Identity

The *gemara* addresses the apparent contradiction: *ela melamed she-ba Tzivon al imo v'holid Anah* — the *baraita* teaches that Tzivon committed incest with his mother and thereby produced Anah, who is thus both his child and his sibling. The *gemara* anticipates the objection — *u-dilma terei Anah havu*, perhaps there are simply two different people named Anah? — and dismisses it on the basis of the phrase *hu Anah*, "he is Anah," which appears in a third verse: *hu Anah asher matza et ha-yemim ba-midbar bi-r'oto et ha-chamorim l'Tzivon aviv* — he is the Anah who found the *yemim* in the desert while tending the donkeys of Tzivon his father. The word *hu*, "he is," signals that this is the same Anah referenced in both earlier verses. Rava (some say Rav Papa citing Rava) introduces the explanation with the remark that he is offering a reading even the great authorities of *dinei mamonot* had not articulated — a rhetorical flourish underscoring the subtlety of the interpretation.

*Tosafot* adds an important point: Anah is in fact a woman, not a man, as can be shown from various *pesukim*. With this in mind, the *drasha* becomes more meaningful. Anah is listed as an inheritor together with her siblings in the context of *yoshvei ha'aretz* — inheritance of the land. Although her father is Tzivon, she is recorded as a child of Se'ir in the inheritance context, because Tzivon is no longer alive and she stands in his place. Yet she is listed as a *daughter* of Se'ir's household, inheriting equally alongside the remaining siblings — not as if she had independent status as a child of Se'ir, but as a descendant of Tzivon taking his place. Crucially, if Tzivon had daughters — sisters at the same generation — those sisters would not be inheriting. Anah, a granddaughter, inherits while hypothetical daughters of Se'ir at that level do not. This is precisely the rule being debated: a granddaughter through a son takes the son's place and inherits in the presence of the surviving brothers, while a daughter who lacks that connection to a son's line does not share.

### Torah Superiority

The old man responded: *Rebbi, be-chach atah potreni?* — Master, is that your answer? That *drasha* is your proof? Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai replied: *shoteh, v'lo tehei torah sheileimah shelanu ke-sichah bateilah shelachem* — Fool. Our complete *Torah* should not even be put in conversation with your nonsense. The dismissal is sharp: the *drasha* from *Anah* was offered not as the substantive proof but as a rhetorical move, demonstrating that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai could engage on their terms while treating their position with contempt.

### Granddaughter Equivalence

The actual argument — the substantive *halacha* — is then stated: *mah le-vas beno, shekein yafeh koachah be-makom ha'achim* — what distinguishes a son's daughter? The fact that her position is strengthened in the presence of brothers. A son's daughter is treated as equivalent to the brothers in the inheritance hierarchy: she takes her father's place and stands alongside the brothers as an heir at the same level, displacing those below. *Ta'omar be-vito, she-hora'ah koachah bi-makom achim* — but can you say the same of the daughter? The daughter's position is weaker in the presence of brothers; she does not take a place equivalent to a brother. The *Rashbam* explains that the actual proof for this distinction comes from *Bnos Tzelofchad*: the daughters of Tzelofchad inherited in the presence of brothers — specifically, in the presence of their uncles, the brothers of their father Tzelofchad. Conceptually, since Tzelofchad had predeceased the entry into the land, the relevant inheritance is from Chefer, Tzelofchad's father. The daughters of Tzelofchad stood in Tzelofchad's place and inherited together with Tzelofchad's brothers — his siblings — even though at that level there were no surviving daughters of Chefer receiving a share. This establishes the principle: a son's daughters, standing in the son's place, inherit in the presence of brothers; the testator's own daughters do not share when the estate has already been assigned to the son's line.

### Victory Established

*Oso ha-yom nitzchum va'asa'uhu yom tov* — on that day they prevailed over the Sadducees, and it was made into a holiday. However the Sadducees were positioned politically, on that day the rabbinic position became established as authoritative *halacha* — and the twenty-fourth of *Tevet* was commemorated as a minor holiday recorded in *Megillat Ta'anit*, a day on which fasting was prohibited.

### Tzelofchad Proof

The proof from *Bnos Tzelofchad*, as the *Rashbam* explains, is the cornerstone of the substantive *halacha*. Tzelofchad had died, leaving daughters but no sons. His father Chefer was the conceptual owner of the ancestral portion in *Eretz Yisrael*. When Chefer's estate was distributed, Tzelofchad's daughters — granddaughters of Chefer — inherited Tzelofchad's share, doing so in the presence of their uncles, who were Chefer's other surviving sons. At that same level, any daughters of Chefer who lacked a son's line standing behind them received nothing. The granddaughters through Tzelofchad displaced the testator's own daughters because they stood in the place of a son. This is the case that established the rule and refuted the Sadducean claim: a daughter inheriting in the presence of uncles, because she is occupying a son's place, is proof that the son's descendants have a strengthened position that the testator's own daughters do not share.

---

---

# Bava Batra 116

## Bnot Tzelofchad & Binyam…

### Yerushah & Binyamin

The daf opens with a *pasuk* from *Shoftim*: *vayomeru yerushat pleitah l'Vinyamin v'lo yimacheh shevet miYisrael* — "And they said: an inheritance for the remnant of Binyamin, so that a tribe shall not be wiped out from Israel." The historical backdrop is the aftermath of *Pilegesh b'Givah*, when only six hundred men remained of the tribe of Binyamin. The other tribes arranged for their daughters to be taken by the men of Binyamin so that the tribe could repopulate. This episode also echoes the principle stated on the previous *daf* — *d'lo khalah shivta* — that no tribe will ever be completely destroyed. Here it nearly happened, and the *pasuk* records their determination to prevent it.

The word *yerushah* — inheritance — is striking given the tractate's subject matter. What does it mean to speak of an "inheritance" for the remnant of Binyamin?

### Takanah: Daughters & Sons

Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami explains: *melamed she-hitnu al shevet Binyamin she-lo tirash bat haben im ha'ahim* — this teaches that they enacted a *takanah* for the tribe of Binyamin that a son's daughter would not inherit together with his brothers.

To appreciate the force of this enactment, it is necessary to recall the general rule of inheritance: if a son has died, his children — even daughters — step into his place and inherit together with the surviving brothers. That is the case of *Bnot Tzelofchad*, which the Gemara has already established. The *takanah* for Binyamin was a suspension of that principle. Since only six hundred men survived, any portion of tribal land that passed to a woman risked leaving the tribe's holdings, as a woman who married outside the tribe would take her inheritance with her. Rather than allowing a son's daughter to inherit alongside her uncles, the *takanah* directed that only sons — not daughters — would step into a deceased father's place.

This was not a permanent abolition of daughters' rights, but a temporary measure to slow the potential outflow of property from the tribe until it could repopulate. Even so, the *takanah* is of limited effectiveness, since property could pass to a son who then dies leaving only a daughter, at which point the same problem recurs a generation later. The Gemara acknowledges this and treats the enactment as more modest in scope: it did not say that property would *never* pass to a female heir in any circumstances, but only that, where brothers exist to receive it, a son's daughter would not displace them.

### Tzelofchad's Daughters

The general rule, against which this *takanah* stands in contrast, is the inheritance of the daughters of Tzelofchad. Tzelofchad was a son of Chefer, and Chefer had other sons as well. When Tzelofchad died without male heirs, one might have thought his portion would go only to his surviving brothers — after all, they are alive and at the same generational level. One might further suppose that descending a generation to find an heir is appropriate only when there is *no one* remaining at the current level.

The Gemara rejects this. Even in the presence of the brothers, Tzelofchad's daughters step into their father's place and inherit alongside their uncles. His daughters are not competing with the brothers as daughters; they are representing their father. They inherit *as* Tzelofchad, taking the portion that would have been his had he lived.

### Sons' Descendants Priori…

This leads to a broader principle: a son's descendants — even daughters — take priority over a daughter. The reason is that before passing to a daughter in the inheritance chart, one must first exhaust all descendants of the sons. The male line is followed as far down as necessary, and it is only when there are truly no descendants to be found anywhere in that line that the inheritance moves to a daughter.

Furthermore, the *takanah* of Binyamin also sheds light on the reverse concern. Normally, even if those descendants are female, they precede the daughters of the original owner. The Binyamin *takanah* temporarily overrode this to prevent property from leaving the tribe — but in doing so, it implicitly confirmed that under ordinary law, daughters-replacing-sons would indeed inherit even in the presence of uncles. That is the ordinary rule; the Binyamin enactment was an acknowledged departure from it, sensitive to the reality that when property passes to a woman it is liable to leave the patrilineal tribe.

---

## No Son = God's Anger

### Kol she'eino maniach ben

Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: *kol she'eino maniach ben leyoresho, HaKadosh Baruch Hu malei alav evrah* — whoever does not leave behind a son to inherit him, the Holy One, Blessed be He, is filled with wrath against that person. The Gemara derives this from the language of the *pesukim*: the word *havartem* — "you shall transfer" the *nachala* to his daughter — is read as *evrah*, wrath. And a further verse reinforces this: *asher ein chalifot lamo* — there is no substitute or exchange for him — meaning he has left no son who serves as his continuation, *velo yiru Elohim* — and they will not see God.

This is a striking statement. There is an obvious tension: the person who died without a son presumably did not choose that fate. And if one views dying without a son as a mark of divine anger, it creates a troubling implication for those who mourn. Yet the Gemara's tone is not simply punitive; the language of *evrah* seems to be expressing how deeply disruptive — how contrary to the proper order of things — it is when there is no continuation of the person. In a profoundly patriarchal context, the absence of a son meant that the name, the property, and the identity of the father came to an end.

### Son vs. Student Dispute

The Gemara records a dispute between Rav Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about the precise meaning of this teaching. *Chad amar*: it refers to one who does not leave behind a son — a biological heir. *Vechad amar*: it refers to one who does not leave behind a *talmid* — a student, a spiritual heir. The concept of the *talmid* as a form of son is well-established: *velimadetem et beneichem* — *beneichem elu talmideichem* — "your sons" refers to your students. A *rav* functions as a father and a student as a son, and there are practical *halachot* that reflect this, such as the principle that returning a lost object to one's *rav* takes precedence over returning it to one's father.

The Gemara then attempts to determine which sage held which position: *tistayeim* — let us conclude — that Rav Yochanan is the one who says the teaching refers to a *talmid*.

### Resolution & Rav Yochanan

The proof is from a well-known story in *Berachot*: Rav Yochanan would carry with him a small bone — the *Rashbam* identifies it as a tooth, since a detached tooth does not convey *tumah*, which would have been a concern for *kohanim* — and would use it to console those who had lost a child. He would say: know how much I myself have suffered — this is the bone of my tenth son who died. All ten of Rav Yochanan's sons predeceased him.

Now, Rav Yochanan did not leave any surviving sons. If he were the one who taught that God is filled with wrath toward one who does not leave a son, he would hardly use that teaching to comfort mourners — it would compound their grief rather than console them. The *Rashbam* explains that the proof lies not just in the fact that it happened to him, but that he specifically employed this as a source of comfort. Therefore, *tistayeim de-amar talmid* — Rav Yochanan is the one who says the teaching is about failing to leave behind a *talmid*. God's wrath is directed at one who has not transmitted Torah to a spiritual heir. Dying without a biological son, by contrast, is a tragedy — but not necessarily a mark of divine anger.

This then reverses the attribution: it is Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi who says the teaching refers to a biological son. And indeed, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would visit a *shiva* house only when a person had died leaving no sons — *ela lebei ma deshachiv bela benei* — because he considered that the true tragedy warranting special mourning. The verse he cites: *becho vacho leholech* — weep for the one who goes — and Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *leholech bela ben zachar* — for the one who departs without leaving a male son.

Here is where the reasoning becomes subtle. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi frames dying without a son as a tragedy, not as something that invites blame. Precisely because he views it this way, he would *not* say that God is angry at such a person — anger implies fault, and he does not see fault here. Therefore it is he who says God's anger is reserved for one who leaves no *talmid*, where there may be an element of personal failing. Rav Yochanan, then, is the one who says God is angry at the one who leaves no son, since his formulation — transmitted in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai — ties the phrase *ben leyoresho* to the language of *evrah*.

This creates an apparent contradiction within Rav Yochanan himself: he both teaches this statement in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and comforts mourners using his own experience of having no sons. The Gemara resolves it: *lo kashya — ha didei, ha d'rabbih* — there is no contradiction. His own view (*didei*) accords with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that God is angry only at one who leaves no *talmid*. What he transmitted in the name of his teacher, Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, is a different, stricter position — that God's wrath applies to one who leaves no son. It remains striking that Rav Yochanan would transmit in his teacher's name a ruling of such personal poignancy, yet that is the nature of faithfully reporting received tradition.

The conclusion is that Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai held that God is angry at one who does not leave a son; later *amoraim* — both Rav Yochanan in his own view and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — somewhat softened the emphasis, directing the concept of divine anger toward one who leaves no spiritual heir.

---

## Midrash: David & Yoav

### David & Yoav Drasha

The Gemara turns from *halacha* to *aggadata*, though still within the thematic orbit of leaving behind an heir. Rabbi Pinchas ben Chama expounded the verse from *Melachim*: *V'Hadad shama b'Mitzrayim ki shakhav David im avotav* — Hadad heard in Egypt that David had lain with his fathers — *v'ki met Yoav sar hatzava* — and that Yoav the general had died. The *drasha* notes an asymmetry in language: regarding David it says *shakhav* — he lay down — a softer, more euphemistic expression; regarding Yoav it says *met* — he died, plainly. Why the difference?

*David she'heni'ach ben ne'emar bo shkhivah* — David left behind a son, so the text uses the language of lying down; he is not truly gone, his line and name continue. *Yoav shelo heni'ach ben ne'emar bo mitah* — Yoav left no son, so the text says he died; in a real sense, that name died with him.

The Gemara immediately challenges this: did Yoav not leave a son? Is it not written that there were *bnei Yoav*? The answer leads to a refinement of the *drasha*.

### Ben Kamoso Concept

The resolution is: *ela David she'hini'ach ben kamoso ne'emar bo shkhivah* — it is not merely leaving a biological son, but leaving *a son like oneself* — *ben kamoso* — a son who embodies one's values and continues one's spiritual legacy. David left a son who was in some meaningful sense a continuation of what David stood for. Yoav had biological descendants but not a *ben kamoso*, and so the text uses the language of death.

This formulation elegantly synthesizes the two sides of the earlier dispute. A *ben kamoso* is simultaneously a biological heir and a spiritual one — the one who continues the name, the values, and the path of the father. The earlier discussion about *talmid* as heir and the concept of *ולימדתם את בניכם — בניכם אלו תלמידיכם* both converge here. It is not enough to have sired a son, and it is not enough to have taught a student; the ideal is a son who is truly like you in what matters, who will carry forward both your identity and your substance.

### Poverty & Wisdom

Rabbi Pinchas bar Chama continues with additional *drashos*. He taught: *kashe aniyut b'soch beiso shel adam p'amim yoter mikhamishim makah* — poverty in a person's home is more difficult than fifty plagues. The derivation follows the method familiar from the *Haggadah*: the verse in *Iyov* says *ki yad Eloh nig'ah bi* — the hand of God has struck me — and since a hand is equivalent to five times what a finger (*etzba*) represents, and *etzba* equals ten plagues, therefore a *yad* equals fifty. His companions then say to him: *ki al zeh bacharta mei'oni* — this is preferable to poverty — meaning even all that Job suffered was considered preferable to destitution.

Rabbi Pinchas bar Chama also taught: if there is a sick person in one's house who may be dying, one should go to a wise man and ask him to pray for mercy on that person's behalf — *ish chacham yikhaprena* — a wise man will atone for it or intercede. The verse is from *Mishlei*: *chamat melech malakhei mavet* — the king's wrath brings angels of death — but a wise man can avert it. It is notable that the text here specifies a *chacham* — a wise person — rather than a *chasid* or a particularly righteous individual, suggesting that wisdom itself, in the Talmudic conception, confers a special proximity to divine favor.

---

## General Inheritance Rules

### Son, Daughter, Father

The Gemara now returns to the substance of the *mishnah* and its general formulation of inheritance order. The *klal* stated is: *kol hakodem benachala, yotzei yerecho kodmin, v'av kodem lechol yotzei yerecho* — whoever takes precedence in inheritance, his descendants take precedence before him; and the father takes precedence over all of his descendants.

At the most basic level, the order is: sons first, then daughters, then the father. That is the structure of the entire chart, and everything else derives from it.

### Heir Depth Question

A natural question arises: how far down a generational line must one search before concluding that there are no descendants and moving to the next category? One might have thought that the rule of replacing a deceased heir with his own children applies only within the first generation. But the *Rambam* and the *Shulchan Aruch* treat the principle as extending without limit, and the *Rashbam* in his comprehensive summary at the end of the *daf* confirms this explicitly, taking it as an established rule that one always follows the male line downward before moving laterally or upward in the chart.

### Males Over Females

At every level, males are preferred over females. The Gemara establishes this through the principle of *maki yerusha shniya liyerusha rishona* — the second inheritance is compared to the first. Just as at the primary level men inherit before women, so too at any subsequent level where descendants are standing in for their parent, male descendants are preferred over female descendants.

The concrete case is *bnei achot velo bnot achot* — nephews inherit before nieces. One might have thought that since they are all standing in the same position — children of the deceased's sister, for instance — sex would not be a differentiating factor. But the Gemara says no: the preference for males applies at every level of descent, by analogy to the primary level.

This means that, in a case where a man dies and the inheritance passes through multiple generations, a great-great-granddaughter in the male line may inherit together with a surviving daughter of the deceased — or even before other women who are closer in generation — because she is taking her male ancestor's place, and that place carries priority over the female line at the same or even higher generational level. The *Rashbam* states this explicitly: *kach seder nachala* — this is the order of inheritance. The rule that males precede females is applied at every node in the descent, not only at the top.

---

## Grandfather vs. Uncle

### Avi ha'av Question

Rami bar Chama posed a question: *avi ha'av ve'achei ha'av* — the grandfather versus the paternal uncles. He framed it using the biblical cast: *Avraham veYishmael benichsei Eisav* — Avraham and Yishmael with respect to the property of Eisav. Eisav is dead, Yitzchak is dead, Yaakov is dead. Who inherits? Does it go to Avraham, Eisav's grandfather, or to Yishmael, Eisav's uncle?

The question presupposes that Eisav had no children and no direct descendants, so the inheritance must move elsewhere on the chart. Once we are past the direct descendants of the deceased, does the principle *av kodem lechol yotzei yerecho* — the father takes precedence over all of his descendants — mean that the grandfather takes precedence even over the uncle?

### Rava vs. Rami Answer

Rava initially answered: *ta shma — ha'av kodem lechol yotzei yerecho* — the father takes precedence over all his descendants. He read this phrase to mean that Avraham, as grandfather, would come before Yishmael. On a literal reading, *av* who is higher in the chart should precede any of his own descendants — and Yishmael is after all a descendant of Avraham.

Rami bar Chama then refined the question: *Avraham veYaakov benichsei Eisav* — replacing Yishmael with Yaakov. Now the question becomes whether the grandfather Avraham takes precedence over his grandchild Yaakov. Rava's answer of *av kodem lechol yotzei yerecho* would, taken literally, give it to Avraham. But the Gemara comments: *Rami bar Chama agav churpei lo ayin bah* — because of Rami bar Chama's characteristic sharpness, he posed a speculative question without noticing that it was already essentially answered by the *mishnah*. And indeed, once the Gemara presses on the meaning of the phrase, a problem emerges.

If *av kodem lechol yotzei yerecho* means the father precedes *all* descendants at every remove, it would produce an absurd result: Eisav's own children could never inherit before Yitzchak, since Yitzchak — as father — would always come first. But clearly the children of the deceased are the *first* heirs. The phrase cannot be read that absolutely.

### Direct Descendants First

Rami bar Chama therefore explains: *yotzei yerecho shelo velo yotzei yerecho shel beno* — *yotzei yerecho* means only the father's own first-generation descendants, not the descendants of his son. The father comes before his own children — that is the content of *av kodem lechol yotzei yerecho*. But the father does not come before his son's descendants.

The Gemara confirms that this reading is the more sensible one: *hachi nami mistavra*. The *klal* in the *mishnah* says: *kol hakodem benachala yotzei yerecho kodmin* — whoever takes precedence, his descendants take precedence. If Yitzchak were alive, he would precede Yaakov. Since Yitzchak is not alive, the rule kicks in: before moving elsewhere on the chart, look for Yitzchak's descendants. Yaakov is Yitzchak's descendant, so Yaakov inherits — taking Yitzchak's place — before the chart moves up to Avraham.

The governing logic is now clear: before you move from one position on the chart to another, you must first exhaust all direct descendants of the person currently at that position. So if Yitzchak would have inherited but is not alive, you look for Yitzchak's children, then Yitzchak's grandchildren, and so forth, before ever moving up to Avraham. Only when Yitzchak has no descendants at all does the inheritance rise to Avraham; and then, if Avraham is not alive, one looks for Avraham's descendants before moving further.

Interestingly, the underlying structure here parallels the logic of *yibum*: there is an idea of a person standing in for another, of continuity and replacement, of a living individual taking the place of one who is gone so that the name and portion are not lost. The *drasha* that the daughters of Tzelofchad inherit because they replace their father — derived from the phrase *va'avatem et nachalato levito* — uses similar interpretive moves.

---

## Rules Summary & Examples

### Three Essential Rules

The Gemara's extended discussion collapses into a compact set of rules. The first and most fundamental is the chart itself: *ben, bat, av* — son, daughter, father. Those three positions and that order are all one needs to know; everything else is derived. If a man dies, his estate goes to his sons. If there are no sons, it goes to his daughters. If there are no daughters, it goes to his father. If the father is gone, the process iterates: it goes to the father's sons (brothers of the deceased), then daughters of the father (sisters of the deceased), then the father's father, and so on up.

The second rule is that before moving from any position on the chart to the next, one must look for direct descendants of the person who holds that position. If a son would have inherited but is dead, his children — not the daughter of the deceased — take his place. And that process continues: if those children are dead, their children substitute, and so on without limit.

The third rule is that males are always preferred over females at any given level of descent, by the principle of *maki yerusha shniya liyerusha rishona*.

Together, these three rules generate the entire inheritance system.

### Edge Cases & Exceptions

Several unusual cases are worth noting. First, the mother never inherits. She is simply absent from the chart entirely. In a case where a man dies leaving no children and no known or halachically cognizable father — for instance, where the father is a gentile, or where paternity is unknown — one might expect the estate to pass to the mother. The *Rama* rules otherwise: in such a case, the property becomes *hefker*, ownerless, as in the death of a *ger* without heirs. This is a striking result: the biological mother is passed over entirely, and the estate becomes ownerless rather than devolve to her.

Second, one cannot waive inheritance rights. The *poskim* address a case where a son had a bitter dispute with his mother and, before communal witnesses, performed a *kinyan* and formally declared that he renounced any claim to her estate. When the mother later died, he sought to inherit. The *poskim* held that the renunciation was void: the laws of inheritance are not *dinei mamonot* in the ordinary sense of a bilateral arrangement between parties, but a *chukat mishpat*, a fixed legal rule that operates automatically. One cannot contract out of it any more than one can contract out of secular inheritance law by private oath. The correct way to disinherit an heir is to write a will transferring property to another party before death; absent such a will, inheritance follows the fixed rules regardless of prior declarations.

In this particular case, however, because the community had imposed the renunciation as a form of fine or communal sanction, it was enforceable for that distinct reason — not because one can generally waive inheritance rights, but because communal authority to impose penalties is independent of the ordinary inheritance rules.

---

## Tzelofchad's Three Porti…

### Yotzei Mitzrayim Division

The *mishnah* states: *Bnot Tzelofchad natlu gimel chalakim benachala* — the daughters of Tzelofchad received three portions in the inheritance. To understand why, the *mishnah* invokes the first of several key principles: *leyotzei mitzrayim nechlekah ha'aretz* — the land of Israel was divided according to those who left Egypt, not according to those who entered the land.

The plain meaning of the verse *le'eileh techalek ha'aretz benachala* — "to these shall the land be apportioned as an inheritance" — might suggest that the division is determined by the generation that actually entered *Eretz Yisrael*. But the *halacha* as the Gemara presents it is that conceptually the division was structured around those who left Egypt. Every adult male who left Egypt received, as it were, a foundational share; those shares then passed through the rules of inheritance to whoever survived to enter the land and to their descendants.

The practical implication is significant. Two men leave Egypt, one with no children and one with many. In the *midbar*, the first man sires ten children and the second only one. When *Eretz Yisrael* is divided, the ten children share one portion between them and the one child receives an equal single portion — because the entitlement was fixed at the moment of the Exodus, not at the moment of entry. It is a retroactive conceptual inheritance: those who left Egypt are treated as having already acquired the land, and the physical division at the time of Yehoshua merely realizes that prior entitlement.

### Tzelofchad's Portions

Applying this principle: both Chefer and Tzelofchad were among *yotzei Mitzrayim* and therefore each received one foundational portion in the land. Tzelofchad's own portion — the one share he was entitled to as one who left Egypt — is the first of the three portions his daughters ultimately received.

When Chefer died, his estate — including his own *yotzei Mitzrayim* share — was divided among his sons. Tzelofchad was a *bechor*, a firstborn, and therefore received *pishnayim* — a double portion — from his father Chefer's estate. That means Tzelofchad received two portions of Chefer's land, while the remaining brothers divided the rest. These two portions constitute the second and third of the three portions that the daughters of Tzelofchad inherited.

### Daughters Get Bechor

This analysis contains an important *chidush*: the daughters of Tzelofchad inherited not only their father's personal *yotzei Mitzrayim* share but also his double portion as *bechor*. One might have thought that the right of *bekorah* — the double portion of the firstborn — would not pass through daughters, or that it would be lost when the firstborn dies before the division occurs. The *mishnah* teaches otherwise: since the daughters step into their father's place entirely, they receive everything he would have received, including the double portion of the firstborn.

This is the *chidush* on the law of *bekorah* specifically: even when the firstborn is no longer alive at the time of the division, his heirs — here, his daughters — receive the double portion that would have been his. The right of *bekorah* vests in the firstborn and passes through his estate to his heirs.

### Muchzekim Principle

This in turn requires the resolution of a further difficulty. The law states that a *bechor* does not take a double portion in property that is *ra'uy* — expected but not yet in the father's possession — only in property that is *muchzak* — already in the father's possession. *Eretz Yisrael* was never physically in Chefer's possession; he left Egypt and died in the desert. How then could Tzelofchad, as *bechor*, receive a double portion from Chefer's share of *Eretz Yisrael*?

The answer the Gemara asserts is: *Eretz Yisrael muchzeket hi* — the land of Israel is considered as already in possession. The entire framework of *yotzei Mitzrayim* implies not merely that the generation of the Exodus was *entitled* to the land, but that they are treated as having already acquired it, as already being *muchzak* in it. Chefer's portion in *Eretz Yisrael* was therefore considered to be in his possession from the moment of the Exodus conceptually, even though he died before physical entry. As a result, the laws of *bekorah* apply: Tzelofchad received a double portion, and that double portion passed to his daughters, giving them in total three portions — his own share, and a double share from his father Chefer's estate.

# Bava Batra 117

## Bnot Tzelofchad Setup

### Nachala Concept

The *mishna* on this *daf* concerns *bnot Tzelofchad*, and it affords us a rich opportunity to examine how the *nachala* — the inheritance of the Land of Israel — was conceptually structured for the generation that entered *Eretz Yisrael*. The central question animating the entire sugya is deceptively simple: when the land was divided, was it distributed to *yotzei Mitzrayim* — those who left Egypt — or to *ba'ei ha'aretz* — those who actually entered the land? The practical stakes of this question are considerable, and the *mishna* itself implicitly takes a position.

### Three Portions

The *mishna* teaches that the daughters of Tzelofchad received three portions of land, and to understand why, one must reconstruct the family tree. Chefer was Tzelofchad's father. Chefer had Tzelofchad and several brothers. Tzelofchad died in the *midbar*, and his daughters then petitioned for his share. According to the *mishna*'s underlying assumption — namely, that portions were assigned to those who left Egypt, who then passed them on to their descendants — Chefer himself received a portion as one who left Egypt, plus an additional portion as a *bechor*, for a total of two portions derived from Chefer's own father. Tzelofchad, as Chefer's firstborn son, inherited both of these portions. His daughters therefore stood to receive not just the ordinary portion Tzelofchad would have taken as one of Chefer's sons, but also the *bechor* portion. This accounts for the three portions the *mishna* credits to them.

The *mishna* thereby teaches several distinct *chiddushim*. First, that the land was distributed conceptually to *yotzei Mitzrayim*. Second, as the *Rashbam* explains, that daughters may replace their father and receive together with the father's brothers, even though brothers are present in that generation. Third, it is not self-evident that heirs of a deceased *bechor* are entitled to the *bechor* portion at all, since the father himself never lived to hold it — yet the *mishna* affirms they do. Fourth, the ordinary rule is that a *bechor* does not receive a double portion unless the asset was already in the father's possession before death — the requirement of *muchzak* — yet here the father never actually held land in *Eretz Yisrael*, and the *mishna* rules nevertheless that the portion passes as though he had been entitled to it.

## Yotzei vs. Ba'ei

### Yotzei Mitzrayim

The *Gemara* opens by observing that the *mishna* proceeds according to the opinion that the land was divided to *yotzei Mitzrayim*: *tnan Gemara keman de'amar leyotzei Mitzrayim nitchalkah ha'aretz*. The practical significance of this choice cannot be overstated. Imagine two brothers, both *yotzei Mitzrayim*. One has a single child entering the land; the other has ten. If distribution is pegged to the *yotzei Mitzrayim* generation, each brother receives an equal share, which then descends to his children. The brother with one child passes down one full share; the brother with ten children passes down one share divided among ten. The ten cousins each receive one-tenth of what their single cousin receives. By contrast, if the land is distributed directly to *ba'ei ha'aretz*, then portions are sized according to the number of people actually entering, and all eleven children receive equal portions relative to one another. The stakes of the debate are therefore not abstract but bear directly on the relative allocation of land among families.

A *baraita* is then cited: *Rabbi Yoshia says the land was divided to yotzei Mitzrayim*, as derived from the verse *lishmot matot avotam yinchalu* — they shall inherit according to the names of their fathers' tribes. The straightforward reading of *lematot avotam* would be merely that the land is divided by tribe. Rabbi Yoshia, however, reads the verse as indicating that the inheritance is conceived as flowing *from* the fathers — meaning the *yotzei Mitzrayim* generation received it notionally and transmitted it downward.

### Ka'eleh Exclusion

The *Gemara* then asks how Rabbi Yoshia handles the verse *la'eleh techalek ha'aretz benachala* — "to these shall the land be divided as an inheritance" — which plainly speaks to the generation standing on the cusp of entry. He answers: *le'eleh ka'eleh* — "to these as these" — meaning the people actually entering the land must resemble the *yotzei Mitzrayim* in one critical respect, specifically to the exclusion of *tefelim*, the underaged. The *Rashbam* explains *tefelim* as derived from *taf*, young children. This creates a striking consequence: a man who left Egypt at age nineteen would not himself receive a portion, because the *yotzei Mitzrayim* entitlement applied only to those counted in the census, which required being twenty years of age or older. Not only does that man fail to receive a portion, but his own children entering the land also receive nothing — because distribution goes to the *yotzei Mitzrayim* generation, not to *ba'ei ha'aretz*, and he was not eligible as one of the former. It is theoretically possible, then, for an entire family line to have no portion in *Eretz Yisrael* — specifically if a man left Egypt under the age of twenty and his father had already died. As the *Rashbam* states, without a *morish* who left Egypt with sons, *az lo natlu chelek ba'aretz*. The one saving circumstance is that if the underage person's father was alive and had left Egypt above the required age, the portion would still descend through the father.

### Metim Yorshim

Rabbi Yonatan disagrees. He holds that the land was given to *ba'ei ha'aretz*, which represents the simpler reading of *la'eleh techalek ha'aretz*. When confronted with the verse about fathers' tribes, he does not dissolve it but rather draws a sweeping conceptual distinction: *meshunah nachala zo mikol nachalos sheba'olam* — this inheritance is unlike all other inheritances in the world. In all other inheritances, *chaim yorshin es hameisim* — the living inherit from the dead. Here, *meisim yorshin es hachaim* — the dead inherit from the living. The verse about the fathers' tribes thus reflects a genuine inversion: the generation that entered the land passed their portions back up to the *yotzei Mitzrayim* fathers who had already died in the *midbar*, and those fathers' estates then redistributed downward to their heirs.

### Two Brothers Parable

To illustrate this remarkable mechanism, the *Gemara* offers a *mashal*. Two brothers, both *kohanim*, live in the same city. One has a single son; the other has two sons. When the time comes to collect *terumah* from the threshing floor, the brothers reason that rather than going themselves — and receiving one portion each, for a total of two — they should send their children. The *ba'al habayis* gives one equal portion to each *kohen* who comes, so three children going yields three portions. The children collect the three portions and return them to their fathers. The fathers then divide equally: each receives one and a half portions. The children have effectively acted as agents on behalf of their fathers, the dead collecting through the living.

### Family Fairness

The *mashal* raises an obvious question: if the three portions are ultimately divided equally between the two brothers, why does it matter whether the scheme runs through the children or directly between the fathers? The answer emerges when one considers not just these two brothers but their relationship to other families. If the land had been distributed directly to *yotzei Mitzrayim*, each *yotzei Mitzrayim* individual would have received one equal share, which would then descend to his children. Relative to another family — say, one with a single *ba'ei ha'aretz* member — each family's patriarch would have received an identical share. But under the *ba'ei ha'aretz* framework as Rabbi Yonatan describes it, the children go in, collect portions proportional to their number, and pass those up to their fathers. A family with nine children entering the land and a family with one child both had fathers who were *yotzei Mitzrayim*, but the nine-child family now sends nine portions back to its father, giving that family five times as much as the one-child family once the fathers divide the pooled resources among themselves. The mechanism therefore produces significantly different outcomes across families, with larger *ba'ei ha'aretz* families commanding far greater inherited wealth than smaller ones, even if the *yotzei Mitzrayim* ancestors were originally equal. The verse *lishmot matot avotam yinchalu* is thus not a mere formality but an operative inheritance mechanism with real distributional consequences.

## Third Opinion

### Both Get It

Rav Shimon ben Elazar offers a third position: *la'elu u'le'elu nitchalkah ha'aretz* — the land was divided to both generations simultaneously, so as to fulfill both verses. There is no need to force a choice between *yotzei Mitzrayim* and *ba'ei ha'aretz*; each generation receives its own portion in parallel. Practically, this means tallying the entire population of *yotzei Mitzrayim* — some 600,000 — alongside the entire population of *ba'ei ha'aretz* — also approximately 600,000 — and creating a total pool of roughly 1.2 million portions, divided tribe by tribe. Those eligible as *yotzei Mitzrayim* receive from that pool and then, having died in the *midbar*, pass their portions down to their children. Those entering the land receive their own portions as *ba'ei ha'aretz* directly. The result is that a child entering the land might receive both: his own portion as *ba'ei ha'aretz* and, through inheritance, his father's portion as *yotzei Mitzrayim*.

### Yehoshua Calev

The most striking potential beneficiaries of this dual system are Yehoshua and Calev — the only two men who were both *yotzei Mitzrayim* and *ba'ei ha'aretz*. They would seemingly be entitled to a portion from each pool. *Tosafot* raises the complication that both men were over sixty years old when they entered the land, and there is a question whether the *ba'ei ha'aretz* entitlement was capped at those under sixty, consistent with the census counts. The *Rashbam* and *Tosafot* suggest that even if Yehoshua and Calev cannot serve as the paradigm case, the *mikan umikan* principle still operates for others: a man who was a *yotzei Mitzrayim* has his father's portion descend to him, and he also receives his own portion as *ba'ei ha'aretz*, yielding two portions through two distinct legal channels. The dual system also helps address the problem created by the age-twenty requirement: even if a man entered the land too young to qualify as *yotzei Mitzrayim*, he at least receives as *ba'ei ha'aretz*; and if a man was ineligible as *ba'ei ha'aretz* for some reason, he might still receive through descent from a *yotzei Mitzrayim* father.

## Wicked Groups

### Meraglim Lost

The *Gemara* now takes up the question of those whose wickedness affected their inheritance rights. Beginning with the *meraglim* — the spies — the *Gemara* establishes that Yehoshua and Calev received the portions of the *meraglim*: *lo b'shel Meraglim Yehoshua v'Calev natlu chelkam*. The source is a *drashah* from the verse *chayyu min ha'anashim ha'eleh* — they survived from these men — which is read to mean that Yehoshua and Calev were enriched from the *meraglim*, inheriting what had been assigned to the spies. The *meraglim* had been *yotzei Mitzrayim* and therefore had been assigned portions; those assigned portions were then transferred to Yehoshua and Calev rather than descending to the *meraglim*'s own children. An additional source from the *Sifrei* derives from *ka'eleh* that those who were *reshaim* were excluded from receiving portions. This means that even under Rav Shimon ben Elazar's dual approach — where having been a *ba'ei ha'aretz* might have allowed the *meraglim*'s children to receive on their own merit — the specific legal transfer of the *meraglim*'s assigned portions to Yehoshua and Calev was an affirmative redistribution, not merely a lapse.

### Korach's Children

The *mitlonenim* — the complainers — are identified by the *Gemara* as the members of *adat Korach*, specifically the 250 men who joined Korach's rebellion. Unlike the *meraglim*, these men *lo hayah lahem chelek ba'aretz* — they had no portion in the land at all. Yet the *Gemara* teaches that their children received portions — *bizchut avi avihem* — by virtue of their grandfathers. The verse from *bnot Tzelofchad*'s own petition is cited in support: *avinu meit bamidbar v'hu lo hayah b'toch ha'eida hano'adim al Hashem ba'adat Korach* — our father died in the *midbar* but he was not among the congregation that gathered against God in *adat Korach*. The implicit logic is that had Tzelofchad been part of *adat Korach*, he would indeed have had no portion, confirming that *adat Korach* was entirely excluded. The grandchildren's salvation comes through the grandfather: if a grandfather was a *yotzei Mitzrayim* in good standing, and his son was a member of *adat Korach* and thus forfeited any entitlement, the grandson could still receive through the grandfather's portion descending past the disqualified middle generation. It is possible for a father and son both to have been over twenty when they left Egypt, so the grandfather's eligibility as *yotzei Mitzrayim* remains intact even if the father is struck from the list.

The *Gemara* also notes an additional dimension: *habanim natlu bizchut avi avihen u'vizchut avi imoteihen* — the children received by virtue of both their paternal and maternal grandfathers. Women would not receive portions on their own merit as *yotzei Mitzrayim*, but once the innovation of *bnot Tzelofchad*'s ruling was established, inheritance could flow through a maternal grandfather as well. Thus even grandchildren whose mothers were the sole link to a *yotzei Mitzrayim* grandfather could receive through him.

### Assigned vs. Unassigned

There is a meaningful distinction between the *meraglim* and *adat Korach* with respect to what they lost. The *meraglim* had been assigned specific portions as *yotzei Mitzrayim*, and those assigned portions were affirmatively transferred to Yehoshua and Calev. *Adat Korach*, by contrast, were never assigned portions at all — they were, so to speak, struck from the distribution list entirely, and their would-be shares were absorbed back into the general pool, effectively redistributed proportionally among everyone else. This distinction matters for how we conceptualize the forfeiture: the *meraglim* had something concrete taken from them and given to specific individuals, while *adat Korach* were simply excluded from receiving anything, with no specific successor to their shares.

## God's Promise

### Yerusha Promise

The *Gemara* then challenges the assumption embedded in the *lishmot matot avotam* derivation, asking whether that verse simply means the land is divided by the twelve tribal groupings descending from the sons of Yaakov — the natural reading of *matot* as *shevatim* — rather than specifically evoking the *yotzei Mitzrayim* generation. The *Gemara*'s response is striking: it cites the verse *venasati osah lachem morashah ani Hashem* — I shall give it to you as a heritage — which Moshe declares to *bnei Yisrael* at the outset of the Exodus. The *Gemara* then cites the related phrase *yerushah hi lachem me-avoseichem* — it is an inheritance for you from your fathers. This was said directly to *yotzei Mitzrayim*, as the *Gemara* states: *le-yotzei Mitzrayim ka'amar*. God's promise was made specifically to that generation. All three opinions in the *Gemara* therefore share the premise that *yotzei Mitzrayim* must receive some portion of the land, because God explicitly promised it to them. The debate is only about whether *ba'ei ha'aretz* also receive portions, not about whether *yotzei Mitzrayim* do.

### All via Fathers

The verse carries an additional layer of meaning. The promise was not framed as a direct grant but as a *yerushah* — an inheritance — *me-avoseichem*, from their forefathers. This means that even the *yotzei Mitzrayim*, who received God's explicit promise, did not receive the land as conquerors earning it by right of valor alone. They received it as an inheritance from the *Avot*. And this principle cascades: those who enter as *ba'ei ha'aretz* receive it as a *yerushah* from *yotzei Mitzrayim*, who themselves received it as a *yerushah* from the *Avot*. In this way, every generation's relationship to *Eretz Yisrael* is mediated by *yerushah* — inheritance — never by pure independent entitlement. Even the generation that physically conquered the land cannot regard its acquisition as *kochi ve-otzem yadi*. The *Gemara*'s insistence that *ba'ei ha'aretz* receive their portions through *yotzei Mitzrayim* rather than directly is therefore not merely a technical legal mechanism but a theological statement about the nature of every generation's claim to the land.

## Growth Verses

### Larov Tarbeh

Rav Papa then mounts a challenge from the verse *larov tarbeh nachalaso ve-lama'at tam'it nachalaso* — for the many you shall increase the inheritance and for the few you shall diminish it. He argues that this verse works more naturally if the land was distributed to *yotzei Mitzrayim*. His challenge to the *ba'ei ha'aretz* position is formulated as *kashya*: if distribution is to those entering the land, the verse is simply saying give more land to a large group and less to a small group — which is unremarkable and requires no special formulation. But why, under that reading, does the verse use the language of *tarbeh* and *tam'it* — increase and diminish — language that implies changing something from what it otherwise would have been?

### Changing Shares

The *yotzei Mitzrayim* reading makes better sense of this language. Under that approach, the verse is directing that the portions going to *ba'ei ha'aretz* should be adjusted based on the *preceding* generation — the *yotzei Mitzrayim*. If the *yotzei Mitzrayim* family was large, then even if the *ba'ei ha'aretz* generation is relatively small, their inherited share should be increased — *tarbeh* — beyond what their own numbers alone would warrant. Conversely, if the *yotzei Mitzrayim* family was small, the *ba'ei ha'aretz* descendants receive a diminished — *tam'it* — share, even if they are numerically many. The active language of changing reflects the fact that the size of the inheritance is being adjusted relative to the incoming generation's own headcount. The *Gemara* itself acknowledges the difficulty with *kashya*, implying that the point is subtle.

### Tosafot Girsa

*Tosafot* preserves a different *girsa* of the *Gemara* — a variant textual reading. Rather than the verse *larov tarbeh nachalaso*, the operative text in *Tosafot*'s version is *bein rav lama'at*, drawn from the verse *la'eleh techalek ha'aretz bein rav lama'at* — "to these shall the land be divided, whether many or few." Under this *girsa*, the *Gemara*'s argument is more direct: the phrase *bein rav lama'at* — "whether many or few" — makes sense only if the distribution is keyed to *yotzei Mitzrayim*, because it instructs the apportioners to disregard the size of the incoming *ba'ei ha'aretz* generation entirely and look instead to the previous generation. This directly contradicts the *ba'ei ha'aretz* reading, under which the size of the entering group is precisely what drives the allocation. The *Rashbam* on the corresponding page notes that he does not have the *bein rav lama'at* reading in his text, suggesting that manuscript traditions diverge here, and that the *girsa* known to *Tosafot* clarifies the *Gemara*'s intent more sharply.

## Daughters' Complaint

### Complaint Logic

Rav Papa presses a final challenge directly from the narrative of *bnot Tzelofchad* themselves. If the land was given to *ba'ei ha'aretz*, he asks, *amai tzavachan* — why were the daughters complaining? *Halo leitnehu delishkalu* — they themselves could simply receive portions as *ba'ei ha'aretz*! The daughters' complaint, as recorded in the Torah, was not that they deserved portions on their own independent merit. They argued specifically that their father was being left without a portion — that they should be permitted to step into their father's place. That argument presupposes a framework in which the land was initially distributed to *yotzei Mitzrayim*, leaving a portion notionally belonging to Tzelofchad which, upon his death, risked passing away from his family. Under a pure *ba'ei ha'aretz* system, there would be no such prior paternal entitlement to claim. The daughters would have had to argue for an entirely different right — a direct personal entitlement — and that is not the argument they made.

### Uncles' Portion

The *Gemara* does not leave this unanswered. Even under the *ba'ei ha'aretz* framework, it turns out that the daughters had a coherent and forceful argument — though a somewhat different one from what is initially intuited. The *Gemara* states: *ella lachazara u-litol be-nichsei Chefer* — rather, they were seeking to reclaim through Chefer's estate. The *Rashbam* confirms this reading explicitly: *she-hem achei avinu nachalu lehachzir oto lachevel avihem* — the brothers of our father inherited in order to return it to the ancestral portion.

The argument works as follows. Under the *ba'ei ha'aretz* system, the uncles of Tzelofchad — Chefer's other sons — were themselves *ba'ei ha'aretz* and would receive portions. According to Rabbi Yonatan's mechanism, those entering the land pass their portions back up to the *yotzei Mitzrayim* fathers, and Chefer then divides the pooled family inheritance among all his sons, including the portion that would have been Tzelofchad's share. The daughters are thus arguing: our uncles are *ba'ei ha'aretz* and are entitled to portions; those portions would flow through Chefer and be divided among all of Chefer's sons, including our father; our father's share in that redistribution would then descend to us. By being daughters rather than sons, are we to be told that our father forfeits the portion he would have received through his brothers? That argument is entirely within the *ba'ei ha'aretz* framework and does not require invoking any direct *yotzei Mitzrayim* entitlement.

This reading makes the daughters' complaint stronger and more precise than the first impression suggests. They are not claiming a direct personal right. They are not even claiming, in the primary instance, that had they been sons they themselves would have entered and generated a portion for their father. They are pointing to an existing mechanism — their uncles' *ba'ei ha'aretz* portions flowing upward through Chefer — and asking only that they not be cut off from the share of that flow that would have been their father's. It is, in the end, still an argument grounded in their father's entitlement, which is why the *Gemara*'s initial intuition — that the complaint only makes sense under *yotzei Mitzrayim* — required refinement rather than outright rejection. And it is precisely because our *mishna* ultimately awards them three portions rather than this more limited claim that the *mishna* is understood to proceed according to the *yotzei Mitzrayim* framework throughout.

---

---

# Bava Batra 118

## Three Division Approaches

### Yotzei Mitzrayim vs Ba'ei

The daf continues in the middle of a debate over the basis on which *Eretz Yisrael* was divided among the tribes. Two principal approaches were introduced previously: *yotzei Mitzrayim* and *ba'ei ha'aretz*. To illustrate the difference, consider two brothers — one with one child and one with ten. Under the *yotzei mitzrayim* approach, the number of plots is reckoned according to those who left Egypt. Those who left received virtual allotments that were never actualized in their lifetimes but were passed down to their children. The result is that the first family receives one unit and the second family divides one unit among ten children — a potentially dramatic disproportion between the size of a family and its share of the land.

The *ba'ei ha'aretz* approach is more nuanced than a simple per-capita division of the generation that entered. There remains a sense that the land is an inheritance, not merely a reward for personal achievement. Under this view, the number of plots is reckoned based on those who entered the land, but those portions are then passed virtually upward to the parents' generation and reinherited back downward. The division is thus proportional to the entering generation but retains the character of *nachalah*.

### Combined Approach

A third approach combines both *yotzei mitzrayim* and *ba'ei ha'aretz*: the total number of those who left Egypt and the total number of those who entered are both counted, portions are allocated accordingly, and each individual receives directly what he earns through *ba'ei ha'aretz* as well as what he inherits through *yotzei mitzrayim*. These are the three positions the Gemara works through as it examines various biblical narratives.

---

## Bnei Yosef Complaint

### B'shlama Yotzei Mitzrayim

The Gemara now tests these approaches against textual evidence from *Tanakh*, picking up several lines from the top of 118. The Gemara states: *b'shlama le-man d'amar le-yotzei mitzrayim* — it works out well according to the view that the land was divided among those who left Egypt, *haynu d'katzivchan B'nei Yosef*, that is why we understand why *Bnei Yosef* came and complained to Yehoshua. The verse states *vayidabru B'nei Yosef* — the sons of Yosef spoke to Yehoshua, declaring that they were a numerous people and their allotted territory was insufficient.

The Gemara's reasoning is this: if the division was based on *yotzei mitzrayim*, the allotments were fixed according to the population that left Egypt.
