The tribe of *Menashe* and *Ephraim* may have been small at the time of the Exodus but grew disproportionately large by the time they entered the land. A significant skewing could therefore arise between the size of their allotted territory — fixed by the earlier, smaller headcount — and their actual population at the time of settlement. Their complaint to Yehoshua thus makes perfect sense.

### Ba'ei Ha'aretz Challenge

The Gemara then turns to the challenge: *ella le-man d'amar le-ba'ei ha'aretz* — but according to the view that the land was divided among those who entered, what is the complaint? The allotment was calibrated precisely to the population at the moment of entry, with no time having passed for that population to change. *Mai katzivchu? Kulhu shaklu* — why are they complaining? Everyone received a share proportional to their numbers.

### Tfelim Explanation

The Gemara answers: *mishum tfelim* — because of *tfelim*, a term the *Rashbam* explains as referring to those under the age of twenty. The situation envisioned is that *Bnei Yosef* had a very large population of young people under twenty whose parents had died in the *midbar* and who therefore had no parent among the entering generation through whom to inherit. Since everyone over twenty would bequeath their portion to their own children, these orphaned young people under twenty had no one to bequeath to them. The complaint was that a substantial population segment would receive nothing proportional to their numbers. One may note that this would need to represent a significant demographic crisis to motivate the formal complaint, though this is the Gemara's resolution.

### Equal Tribal Lands

A different, and in some ways simpler, resolution is available: if one assumes that each tribe received an equal-sized territorial allotment regardless of its population — that is, that tribal lands were uniform in size rather than proportional to headcount — then *Bnei Yosef*'s complaint needs no special explanation and is independent of whether the division followed *yotzei mitzrayim* or *ba'ei ha'aretz*. They would simply be saying: our tribal land is the same size as every other tribe's land, but our population is far greater, and therefore each individual in our tribe receives far less than individuals in smaller tribes. This approach requires no reference to *tfelim* or demographic asymmetries.

However, this resolution is in tension with the historical record. The map of *Sefer Yehoshua* makes clear that tribal territories were not uniform — *Menashe* alone received a vast area spanning both sides of the Jordan, representing a substantial portion of the entire land. The Gemara at this point assumes equal individual portions (calibrated per person), while later the Gemara will shift to assuming equal tribal allotments, which will seem puzzling in light of the evident historical disproportion.

---

## Abaye's Inference

### Nobody Excluded Logic

Abaye now draws a broader inference from the narratives of *Bnot Tzelofchad* and *Bnei Yosef*: *shema mina lo havi chad dlo shakil* — we can learn from these stories that there was not a single person who failed to receive a portion in *Eretz Yisrael*.

One might imagine circumstances under which someone would be left without any share. Under *yotzei mitzrayim*, a child born in the *midbar* to a father who had left Egypt under the age of twenty would receive nothing — neither by virtue of entering the land himself nor by virtue of *yotzei mitzrayim*. Under *ba'ei ha'aretz*, a young person under twenty who entered the land without a living parent and without any surviving relative through whom to inherit in the manner of *Bnot Tzelofchad* could similarly find himself landless. Yet Abaye asserts this never occurred.

His reasoning: *d'ai salka daitach hava chad dlo shakil, ibaye leh limzvach* — if there had been even one person excluded from the land, he would surely have complained. *Bnot Tzelofchad* complained; *Bnei Yosef* complained. The cultural pattern of formal complaint was clearly operative and recorded. It follows that anyone who lacked a portion would have stepped forward. And since no additional complaints are recorded, no additional person was excluded.

### Bnei Yosef Counterpoint

The Gemara challenges this inference. Perhaps some people did complain, and their complaint simply went unheeded — and the Torah does not record every complaint that failed. The implied principle the Gemara tests is: *d'tzvach v'hani, kasvi kra; d'tzvach v'lo hani, lo kasvi kra* — that which was complained and succeeded was recorded; that which was complained and failed was not recorded. If so, Abaye's argument collapses, since we cannot infer from silence that no one complained.

Abaye responds by pointing to *Bnei Yosef* themselves: their complaint was recorded even though it ultimately did not succeed. The straightforward reading of *Sefer Yehoshua* seems to suggest their complaint did succeed — Yehoshua told them to go conquer the forests — but the Gemara cannot accept this *k'pshuto*. If the forests were already within *Bnei Yosef*'s tribal allotment, Yehoshua was telling them nothing new. If the forests belonged to another tribe, Yehoshua had no authority to reassign them. Therefore, the Gemara understands the complaint as having not actually been granted. Yet the Torah recorded it. This demonstrates that the Torah does record complaints that led nowhere, and therefore Abaye's argument is reinstated: since no other complaints are recorded, no one else was excluded.

### Ayin Hara Lesson

The Gemara then offers a different resolution to the *Bnei Yosef* episode, one that renders Abaye's inference moot regardless. The Gemara says: *eitza tova k'mashma lan* — the Torah recorded this narrative not as a halachic precedent regarding land distribution, but to convey a moral lesson. *D'ba'i l'inish l'izdaharu mei'ayna bisha* — a person must be vigilant against the *ayin hara*.

This, the Gemara explains, is what Yehoshua was actually telling *Bnei Yosef*: *im am rav ata alei l'cha hayara* — if you are a great nation, go into the forest. Not to conquer additional territory, but *lechu v'hachavu atzmechem b'yaarim shelo tishlot bachem ayina bisha* — go and conceal yourselves in the forests so that the *ayin hara* will not dominate you. Do not publicize your great numbers; remain hidden as fish are hidden in the sea.

*Bnei Yosef* replied: *anan m'zara d'Yosef, d'lo shalta bei ayina bisha* — we are the descendants of Yosef, over whom the *ayin hara* has no dominion. The verse states *ben porat Yosef, ben porat alei ayin* — a fruitful son is Yosef, fruitful by the wellspring. Rabbi Abbahu reads *alei ayin* as *olei ayin*, meaning that Yosef's descendants transcend the *ayin hara* rather than succumb to it. Rabbi Yosei the son of Rabbi Chanina derives the same from the verse *vayidgu larov b'kerev ha'aretz* — they shall multiply like fish within the land: just as fish are covered by water and unseen, and therefore free from the *ayin hara*, so too the descendants of Yosef are immune.

The Gemara thus establishes that the *Bnei Yosef* narrative was preserved for this moral lesson about *ayin hara*, not as evidence of a systematic pattern of recording all complaints. Once the narrative's purpose is reassigned, Abaye's inference from it — that all excluded persons would have been recorded — is undermined.

---

## Excluded Groups

### Meraglim & Spies

The Gemara now resumes working through the *braita* that catalogs which groups of sinners from the *midbar* did not receive a portion and what became of their shares. Regarding the *meraglim* — the spies who scouted the land and returned with a faithless report — the *braita* states: *Yehoshua bin Nun v'Calev ben Yefuneh natlu chelkam* — Yehoshua and Caleb took their portion.

### Chayu Derasha

The Gemara asks: *mena hani mili* — how do we know this? We know from another verse that Yehoshua and Calev were the sole survivors of that generation; that verse is redundant. The Gemara therefore derives the point from the verse *chayu min ha'anashim ha-hem* — they lived from among those men. Since the simple meaning of "they lived" is already known, the Gemara interprets *chayu* as *shechayu b'chelkam* — they were enriched through their portions, that is, they inherited the portions of the fallen spies.

### Mitlonenim Debate

The *braita* then states that the *mitlonenim* — the complainers — and *adat Korach* did not receive a portion in *Eretz Yisrael*. The Gemara notes a second *braita* that states these groups' portions went to Yehoshua and Calev as well, and resolves the contradiction as a *machloket*: one authority links the *mitlonenim* and *adat Korach* to the *meraglim* by analogy, concluding that just as Yehoshua and Calev inherited from the *meraglim*, so too from the *mitlonenim* and *adat Korach*; the other authority does not draw this analogy and holds that those portions were distributed among all of *Klal Yisrael*.

A further question arises: if the *mitlonenim* refers to all who ever complained against Moshe, then Yehoshua and Calev would have inherited an absurdly large share of the land, encompassing virtually all of *Klal Yisrael* at one point or another. The Gemara clarifies: *mitlonenim she-ba-adat Korach kamina* — the *mitlonenim* in question are specifically the complainers within *adat Korach*, not every instance of *vayilonu*.

### Bnot Tzelofchad Arg

The source from which we know that these three groups — *meraglim*, *mitlonenim*, and *adat Korach* — forfeited their portions is the argument of *Bnot Tzelofchad* themselves. The *braita* cites their declaration: *avinu met ba-midbar* — our father died in the wilderness, *ze Tzelofchad*. He was not among *adat ha-meraglim* — as derived from the verse *ad matai la-eda ha-ra'ah ha-zot*, from which we learn the *meraglim* constituted a formal *edah*. He was not among *ha-noadim al Hashem b'adat Korach* — derived from the verse *ve-chol adatcha ha-noadim al Hashem*. And the *mitlonenim* are equated with that same group.

By arguing that their father belonged to none of these categories, *Bnot Tzelofchad* implicitly confirmed that membership in any of these groups would have disqualified him from an inheritance. Their argument thus serves as the *braita*'s proof that the *meraglim*, *mitlonenim*, and *adat Korach* did not receive portions. The *machloket* that follows concerns not whether they were disqualified but rather to whom their notional shares were assigned.

A brief digression: a famous responsum of Rav Moshe Feinstein observes that *adat Korach*, from which we derive the minimum *minyan* of ten, included individuals who were in effect *apikorsim* — they denied God's ability to bring them to *Eretz Yisrael*. Since they nonetheless count toward the quorum from which we derive the *minyan*, this supports the position that even a *rasha* may be counted.

---

## Menashe's Ten Portions

### Why Ten Portions?

Rav Papa poses a question to Abaye: *v'amar lei Rav Pappa l'Abaye*. Under *yotzei mitzrayim*, the verse in *Sefer Yehoshua* that says *vayiplu chevlei Menashe asarah* — the portions of *Menashe* fell to ten — makes sense. *Menashe* had six sons who served as the heads of the *batei avot* of the tribe. One of them was *Chefer*, and *Tzelofchad* was *Chefer*'s son. The verse mentions *Tzelofchad* and *Bnot Tzelofchad* and then says the total came to ten portions.

### Yotzei Mitzrayim Count

Under *yotzei mitzrayim*, the portions attributed to *Bnot Tzelofchad* can be enumerated as follows. *Tzelofchad* himself, as one who left Egypt, receives his own individual portion: that is the first. As *Chefer*'s *bechor*, *Tzelofchad* receives a double portion from *Chefer*'s share: that accounts for two more. And if one or more of *Chefer*'s other sons died without male heirs, their portions would revert upward to *Chefer* and be redistributed among his surviving sons, including *Tzelofchad*. With one dead uncle, one arrives at three portions for *Tzelofchad*'s line — which matches the *mishnah*'s count of three. Adding this to six for the *batei avot* yields nine; to reach ten, a second dead uncle is posited, a conclusion the Gemara supports from the superfluous language *achuzat nachalah*.

### Ba'ei Ha'aretz Count

Under *ba'ei ha'aretz*, the picture changes significantly. Since the focus is on the generation that entered the land, *Tzelofchad* himself does not receive a personal portion — he was not among those who entered. All inheritance flows upward through *Chefer* and back down. *Tzelofchad*'s line thus receives only the double *bechor* portion from *Chefer* — two portions — plus whatever accrues from dead uncles. Six plus two yields only eight, leaving the verse's figure of ten unaccounted for without positing two dead uncles. The Gemara points out the asymmetry: *tamniya hu dahavu* — there would only be eight.

### Batei Avot & Bnot

The Gemara resolves the difficulty for *ba'ei ha'aretz* by the same device applied to *yotzei mitzrayim*: positing two dead brothers of *Tzelofchad*'s father rather than one. *Hacha nami trei achi d'abba hava lehu* — here too we say there were two brothers of the father who died, and their portions, redistributed through *Chefer* and back down to the surviving sons including *Tzelofchad*'s line, yield four portions for *Bnot Tzelofchad*, bringing the total to ten.

One must then ask: in what sense does the verse's figure of ten combine six major *batei avot* portions with four relatively minor *Bnot Tzelofchad* portions? These are portions of vastly different magnitude. The Gemara's answer, anticipated by Rav Papa's question, is addressed in the following segment.

---

## Naton Titein Braita

### Yotzei Mitzrayim Braita

The Gemara cites a *braita* that articulates the *yotzei mitzrayim* position through close reading of the relevant verse. *Naton titein lahem nachalah* — give, give them an inheritance. *Titein lahem* — this refers to *nachalat avihen*, the direct inheritance of their own father *Tzelofchad*, who himself left Egypt and is entitled as a *yotzei mitzrayim*. *Betoch achei avihen* — in the midst of their father's brothers, meaning what they receive through *Chefer* in parallel with their uncles. *Zu nachalat avi avihen* — this is the portion of their father's father, that is, the portion flowing through *Chefer*. And *ve-ha'avarta nachalat avihen lahem* — the additional transfer of their father's inheritance — yields the *chelek bechorah*, the double portion, since *Tzelofchad* was a *bechor*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Addition

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds a further element: *af chelek achei avihen natlu* — they also received the portion of their father's brothers, that is, the dead uncle or uncles whose shares were redistributed. This is derived from *naton titein* — the doubled language implying an additional grant beyond the straightforwardly inherited portions.

### Dead Brothers Logic

For the view that requires two dead brothers — which the Gemara needs to reach the figure of ten under *yotzei mitzrayim* — the additional exegetical basis comes from the phrase *achuzat nachalah*. The verse could have said either *nachalah* alone or *achuzah* alone; the combination signals yet another portion, providing the textual hook for a second dead brother's redistributed share.

### Rav Papa Question

Rav Papa's question, now addressed directly, is: *kra mai kachashiv* — what category of portions does the verse enumerate when it says ten? If it is counting *tfelim*, the subdivided portions of later generations, there would be far more than ten by the time of *Bnot Tzelofchad*. If it is counting *batei avot*, the major tribal divisions, there are six.

### Batei Avot Resolution

The Gemara resolves: *le'olam batei avot kachashiv* — the verse is always counting the major *batei avot* divisions. *Ve-ha kamashma lan d'Bnot Tzelofchad natlu chelek bechorah* — the reason the verse reaches ten, incorporating *Bnot Tzelofchad*'s portions alongside the six *batei avot*, is to teach that *Bnot Tzelofchad* received the *bechor* portion. The numerical exercise is thus an exegetical device to highlight the legal significance of their inheritance, and as noted, it simultaneously elevates their claim to a prominence comparable to the foundational tribal divisions themselves.

---

## Muchzeket Principle

### Bechor Paradox

A fundamental difficulty now surfaces. The Gemara has established that *Tzelofchad* received a *chelek bechorah* from *Chefer*. But the rule governing a *bechor*'s double portion — derived from *Devarim* — is that it applies only to property that was in the father's actual possession at the time of his death: *muchzak*, held and possessed. Property to which the father was merely *ra'uy* — entitled but not yet in hand — does not carry the double portion. *Eretz Yisrael* was never actually in *Chefer*'s possession; it was allocated to him only retroactively and conceptually. How, then, can *Tzelofchad* claim a *chelek bechorah*?

### Muchzeket Answer

The Gemara's answer is striking: *alma Eretz Yisrael muchzeket hi* — we see from this that *Eretz Yisrael* is regarded as *muchzeket*, as fully and actually possessed, not merely *ra'uy*. The entire enterprise of the allocation of *Eretz Yisrael* — passing portions up to the *yotzei mitzrayim* and back down — is treated not as a fictional entitlement but as genuine possession. The land of Israel carries a *chazakah* of ownership rooted in the divine promise and the ancestral inheritance, such that even retroactive conceptual assignment suffices to constitute *muchzak* for purposes of the *bechor*'s double portion.

---

## Children's Inheritance

### Braita Both Sides

A final *braita* addresses the children of those groups who forfeited their portions — the *meraglim*, *mitlonenim*, and *adat Korach*. The *braita* states: *ve-habanim natlu bizchut avi avihem u-vizchut avi imoteihem* — the children inherited through the merit of their paternal grandfathers and through the merit of their maternal grandfathers. The scenario is that the father, belonging to one of the disqualified groups, did not himself receive a portion, and yet his children were not left landless — they could receive through a grandfather on either the paternal or maternal side who was *yotzei mitzrayim* or *ba'ei ha'aretz* and thus did hold a valid portion.

### Contradiction Resolved

Against this, a second *braita* states that the children received *bizchut atzman* — by virtue of themselves. The apparent contradiction between inheriting through grandparents and receiving by one's own merit is resolved simply: *lo kashya, ha k'man d'amar l'yotzei mitzrayim, ha k'man d'amar l'ba'ei ha'aretz*. Under *yotzei mitzrayim*, a child of a disqualified father has no personal claim to the land and must rely on grandparents through whom to inherit; under *ba'ei ha'aretz*, the child who himself entered the land acquires a portion in his own right.

### Age Distinction

The Gemara offers an alternative resolution that keeps both *braitot* within the *ba'ei ha'aretz* framework: *ha d'havu ben esrim* — for those who were twenty years of age and entered the land, they received *bizchut atzman*, by their own standing as *ba'ei ha'aretz*; *ha d'lo havu ben esrim* — for those who were under twenty at the time of entry, they did not qualify on their own and therefore received only through their grandparents. On this reading, both *braitot* assume *ba'ei ha'aretz*, and the operative distinction is simply one of age at the time of entry into the land.

---

---

# Bava Batra 119

## Tzelofchad's Portions

### Three Portions

The *mishna* on 119a establishes that *benot Tzelofchad* received three portions of the Land. The reasoning runs as follows: Tzelofchad himself was entitled to one portion as one of the *yotzei Mitzrayim*, the generation that left Egypt, and he passed that portion down to his daughters once they prevailed in their case before Moshe. In addition, Tzelofchad's father Chefer was also among the *yotzei Mitzrayim*, and since Chefer had predeceased him, Tzelofchad — as a *bechor* — received a double share of Chefer's portion. Chefer's portion was itself subdivided among all the brothers of that family, so the two shares Tzelofchad received from that subdivision were smaller than his own personal portion; nevertheless, he held two of them by virtue of being the firstborn. All three portions — his own and the two from his father's share — passed to his daughters, and this is what the *mishna* records.

### Ra'ui vs. Muchzak

The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: why was Tzelofchad entitled to a double portion at all? The principle is that *ein ha-bechor notel be-ra'ui ke-vi-muchzak* — a firstborn does not receive a double portion in property that was merely *ra'ui*, coming to the father, rather than *muchzak*, already in the father's actual possession at the time of death. If a business owned by the father generated profits only after the father's death, those profits are *ra'ui* and the *bechor* receives no double share in them. Since Chefer never actually took possession of his portion of *Eretz Yisrael* — it was something he stood to receive, not something he held — why should Tzelofchad receive a double portion of it?

### Movables, Not Land

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel offers one resolution: the double portion was not taken from the land at all, but rather from other movable property — *be-yishuv olam* — whatever Chefer actually owned in his possession. The *mishna* speaks of the double portion in that context. This answer is acknowledged to be far from the plain meaning (*pshat*) of the text, since the entire discussion in both the *mishna* and the surrounding *pesukim* is self-evidently about portions of land.

## Eretz Yisrael Muchzaket

### Rabba's Challenge

Rabba challenges Rav Yehuda's answer directly. He cites a *braita* in which Rabbi Yehuda holds that *benot Tzelofchad* actually received four portions, not three, as the verse states: *vayipplu chavlei Menashe asara* — the portions of Menashe were ten. Six of those went to the main families of Menashe, and four, of varying sizes, went to Tzelofchad's daughters. The point is that the discussion is unmistakably about portions of land. Telling us that the double portion was in "ten pegs" misses the entire point of the *mishna*.

### Already Possessed

Rabba therefore offers a different resolution: *Eretz Yisrael muchzeket hi* — the Land of Israel is already considered to be in the possession of those who left Egypt. This is a principle introduced earlier in the *masechta*: because the *yotzei Mitzrayim* already hold the land in a legal sense, it is not merely *ra'ui* but *muchzak*, and the laws of a *bechor*'s double portion therefore apply.

### Ve-natati Interpretation

The *Rashbam* explains this principle by citing the verse *ve-natati otah lachem morasha* — "I have given it to you as an inheritance." The verb is in the past tense: not "I will give," but "I have given." The land is already treated as received, already in the possession of those who left Egypt. What is notable is that this possession is attributed not to the *avot*, the patriarchs, nor to the generation that actually entered the land, but specifically to the *yotzei Mitzrayim* — the generation of the desert. They are considered to hold the land even before they set foot in it.

## Moshe's Knowledge

### What Moshe Knew

The *gemara* now cites a *braita* in which Rabbi Hidka relates a teaching in the name of Shimon HaShikmoni, a colleague who was among the students of Rabbi Akiva. The teaching addresses a potentially troubling implication of the story: did Moshe not know the law of daughters' inheritance? Shimon HaShikmoni insists: *yodea hayah Moshe Rabbeinu she-benot Tzelofchad yorshos hen* — Moshe certainly knew that daughters inherit in the absence of sons. What he did not know was whether they were entitled to the *chelek bechora*, the firstborn's double portion — specifically, whether they could stand in for Tzelofchad vis-à-vis his brothers and receive two shares of Chefer's portion. That narrow question — touching on whether *Eretz Yisrael* is considered *muchzak* for the *yotzei Mitzrayim* — was what Moshe lacked. All the broader *halachot* he already possessed; it was one precise point of clarification that he needed.

### Merit and Attribution

Because Moshe already knew essentially all of this, Shimon HaShikmoni continues, the *parsha* of inheritance *ra'uya hayta lehikashev al yedei Moshe* — it was fitting to have been communicated through Moshe, as all other Torah law was. It need not have been prompted by the daughters' petition; God could have simply transmitted it through Moshe in the ordinary fashion. Yet: *ela shezaku benot Tzelofchad venichteva al yadan* — the daughters merited, through their initiative and their love of *Eretz Yisrael* and their righteousness as *tzidkaniyot*, that the *parsha* was written attributed to their prompting. The purpose of this framing is to prevent any impression that Moshe had a serious blind spot, or that without the daughters this *halacha* would never have been taught.

### Gatherer of Wood

A parallel case is offered: Moshe also knew that the man who gathered wood on Shabbat was deserving of death — *mechaleleha mot yumat*, the Torah had already stated this — but he did not know the specific mode of execution. Yet the *parsha* of the wood-gatherer (who, according to some opinions, was Tzelofchad himself) need not have waited for that event to be taught. It would have been written regardless. *Ela shenitchayav mikoshesh venichteva al yado* — it happened that the event provided the occasion, but the law was not contingent on it.

### Megalgelin Zechut

The principle that emerges is: *megalgelin zechut al yedei zakai ve-chov al yedei chayav* — merit is brought about through the meritorious, and liability through the guilty. Because *benot Tzelofchad* were righteous, the *parsha* of inheritance was written in connection with their case even though it would have been written anyway. Because the wood-gatherer was deserving of punishment, the *parsha* of that execution was connected to his act. In each case, the underlying law existed independently; the virtuous or the culpable person simply became the vehicle through which it was expressed.

## Moshe's Doubt

### Exact Doubt

Having established what Moshe did and did not know, the *gemara* sharpens the analysis. One might ask: if *Eretz Yisrael* is considered *muchzeket* in the possession of the *yotzei Mitzrayim*, then there is no *halachic* question — the *bechor* plainly gets his double portion. And if it is *not* considered *muchzeket*, then equally there is no question — the *bechor* plainly does not. So what exactly was Moshe's doubt? The *gemara* answers: *hi gufa kamistapka lei* — that very question, whether *Eretz Yisrael* is *muchzeket* in the hands of the *yotzei Mitzrayim*, was what Moshe was uncertain about. He knew all the surrounding *halachot* perfectly; the one open question was the status of the land itself.

### Morasha Ambiguity

The uncertainty traces back to the verse: *ve-natati otah lachem morasha ani Hashem* — "I have given it to you as an inheritance, I am God." Moshe did not know how to read the word *morasha*. Does it mean *yerushah lachem me-avoteichem* — a patrimony, an inheritance already received from your ancestors, meaning you are already in possession? Or does it mean *morishin* — something you will pass on, a bequest to your children, meaning you yourselves have not yet inherited it?

### Dual Meaning

The resolution, *u-fashtu lei tarvaihu*, is that both readings are correct simultaneously. The land is both a *yerushah* already received — meaning the *yotzei Mitzrayim* are already considered to hold it — and something that they will transmit as *morishin* to the next generation.

### The Irony

This creates a striking irony: *einam yorshin* does not mean they will not be considered to possess it for legal purposes. Rather, it means they will not physically enter and inherit it. They are considered *muchzak* in the land for the purposes of the *bechor*'s double portion, enabling Tzelofchad's firstborn status to generate two shares. Yet at the same time, they themselves will pass through the desert and die without entering *Eretz Yisrael*. They hold it in a legal sense sufficient to transmit it, yet they will never actually come into physical possession of it.

### Prophecy Unknowing

The *gemara* finds this irony embedded in *Shirat HaYam* itself. At the sea, the verse reads *tavi'eimo ve-tita'eimo be-har nachalatecha* — "You will bring *them* and plant *them* in Your holy mountain." Crucially: *tavi'einu lo ne'emar, ela tavi'eimo* — it does not say "You will bring *us*," but "You will bring *them*." Moshe and *Bnei Yisrael* sang a prophecy they did not fully understand: *melamed she-mitnab'im ve-einam yod'im mah mitnab'im* — they prophesied without knowing what they were prophesying. In their moment of triumph at the sea they were already foretelling that it would be a future generation, not themselves, who would enter the land. And yet — by the same logic — they were already considered to hold it.

## Daughters' Approach

### Before All

The Torah recounts that the daughters stood before Moshe, before Elazar the *kohen*, before the *nesi'im*, and before the entire congregation. The *gemara* examines this progression closely.

### Sequential or Simultaneo…

Is this a sequential account — did the daughters approach each authority one after another — or did they approach all of them at once? If it was sequential, then the verse lists Moshe first but he was actually approached last. If it was simultaneous, the verse accurately reflects that all these figures were present together.

### Yoshiyah's View

Rabbi Yoshiyah holds that they went to each authority in turn, working their way upward. They approached the entire congregation, then the *nesi'im*, then Elazar, and only finally Moshe — yet the verse, out of deference to Moshe's honor, mentions him first while implying through context that the others preceded him. The reason the other figures appear in the verse at all is precisely because the approach was sequential; each received the petition and evidently lacked the authority or knowledge to resolve it.

### Abba Chanan's View

Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer disagrees. He holds that Moshe was sitting in the *beit midrash* together with everyone — Elazar, the *nesi'im*, and the whole *eidah* — and the daughters approached the entire assembled group at once. The approach was not sequential but a single presentation before all authorities gathered together.

### Student vs. Master

The underlying dispute, the *gemara* explains, is whether *cholkin kavod le-talmid bi-mekom ha-rav* — whether one shows honor to a student in the presence of the master. If one does, then when all were gathered together, there was no impropriety in the verse's acknowledging the *nesi'im* and Elazar alongside Moshe; their mention alongside the supreme authority does not diminish him. This is Abba Chanan's position. Rabbi Yoshiyah holds the opposite: *ein cholkin* — one does not acknowledge students or lesser figures in the master's presence. Therefore, had they all been together, the verse would have mentioned only Moshe. Since the verse does mention the others, it must be because they were approached separately, before Moshe.

### Master's Signal

The *gemara* rules that both positions contain truth: *hilchasa cholkin ve-hilchasa ein cholkin*. The resolution is that the determining factor is whether the master himself has signaled recognition of his student — *ha d'palig lei rabeih yikara*. If the *rav* has indicated, through word or gesture, that he wishes his *talmid* to be acknowledged in his presence, then one does acknowledge the *talmid*, mentioning both master and student. If the *rav* has given no such signal, one does not. The protocol follows the cues the master provides.

## Their Virtues

### Wisdom

A *braita* praises *benot Tzelofchad* with three distinct qualities: they were *chachmaniyot* — wise; *darshaniyot* — skilled explicators of Torah; and *tzidkaniyot* — righteous. Their wisdom, *she-le-fi sha'ah dibru*, consisted of keen awareness of timing — of reading circumstances and waiting for precisely the right moment to present their case.

### Yibum Argument

Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak teaches that the daughters did not simply walk up to Moshe with their petition. Rather, they waited until Moshe was expounding the *parsha* of *yibbum* — levirate marriage — before they approached. The verse in that context reads: *ki yeshvu achim yachdav*, when brothers dwell together and one dies childless, the brother-in-law is obligated in *yibbum*.

### If Sons Then Inherit

The daughters seized on this moment. They asked Moshe: if we are considered like a son — such that we exempt our mother from *yibbum* (which is in fact the operative *halacha*: a daughter exempts the widow just as a son would) — then grant us an inheritance as a son would receive. *Im ke-ven anu chashuvot, t'nah lanu nachalah ke-ven.* And if not — if we are not considered equivalent to a son — then let our mother be subject to *yibbum*. Since it was manifestly clear that their mother was not obligated in *yibbum*, they were essentially demonstrating through reductio: since we are already treated as equivalent to sons in the law of *yibbum*, we should be treated as equivalent to sons in the law of inheritance. Furthermore, *yibbum* and inheritance are conceptually intertwined: the institution of *yibbum* operates on the principle of *yakum al shem achiv ha-met*, that the brother-in-law continues the line and acquires the dead brother's estate. If the daughters are considered a continuation of their father sufficient to obviate the need for *yibbum*, the inheritance should naturally flow through them as well. *Miyad vayakrev Moshe et mishpatan lifnei Hashem* — Moshe recognized immediately that they had raised a compelling argument and brought it before God.

### Darshaniyot

Their quality as *darshaniyot* — skilled explicators — is demonstrated by the precision of their legal reasoning. They stated: *ilu haya la ben lo dibarnu* — had our father had a son, we would not have spoken. This formulation reveals sophisticated legal literacy: they were not asserting that daughters are in all circumstances equal to sons, but rather that in the specific absence of sons, daughters step into that role.

### Legal Acumen

One might ask: what text precisely were they expounding, and how did they know the rules of inheritance clearly enough to formulate this argument? The *Rashbam* suggests they were expounding the *pesukim* of *nachala* — specifically *im ben ein lo*. *Tosafot* raises a difficulty: that *parsha* had not yet been transmitted; indeed it was transmitted only in response to their very petition. *Tosafot* therefore suggests they derived their position either from the verse *ve-hitnachaltem otam li-vneichem* — "you shall give it as inheritance to your children" — which could have been read as excluding daughters (*li-vneichem ve-lo li-vnoteichem*), or from the broader understood principle that daughters' inheritance could cause property to pass out of the tribe. They understood the legal landscape sufficiently to know that in the presence of sons they had no claim, and said so directly. It is this combination of textual fluency and principled restraint that earns them the designation *darshaniyot*.

## Righteousness

### Proper Marriage

The third quality — *tzidkaniyot* — is illustrated by their conduct in marriage. They did not marry hastily or indiscriminately; they married only those who were genuinely *hagun la-hen*, suitable for them. This is derived from the verse *la-tov be-eineihen tihyena le-nashim* — "they shall be wives to whoever is good in their eyes" — which *chazal* understand not as a license to marry freely, but as a directive and indeed a commendation to exercise patience and discernment in finding an appropriate husband.

### Waiting Till 40

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches in a *braita* that even the youngest of the daughters did not marry until she was forty years old. She waited to find someone truly worthy. *Tosafot* notes that this may also reflect the chronology of events: Tzelofchad died near the beginning of the forty years in the desert, and the story of the daughters takes place near the end, which accounts for some of the elapsed time.

### Fertility Problem

This raises an obvious question. Rav Chisda states: a woman who marries before twenty can give birth until sixty; one who waits until her twenties can give birth until her forties; one who waits until her forties — *shuv einah yoledet* — can no longer give birth. If the daughters waited until forty to marry, would they not forfeit the ability to have children? Was this truly wise?

### Miraculous Fertility

The *gemara* answers: *mitoch she-tzidkaniyot hen, na'asa la-hen nes* — because they were righteous, a miracle was performed for them, as it was for Yocheved. Their righteousness in waiting for the right partner was itself the source of their merit, and that merit enabled them to conceive beyond the ordinary boundaries of fertility.

### Yocheved's Age

The parallel to Yocheved is developed at length. The verse in *Shemot* reads: *vayeilech ish mi-beit Levi vayikach et bat Levi* — a man from the house of Levi went and took the daughter of Levi. The *gemara* notes the strange usage: she is called *bat Levi* as though she were young, yet she was 130 years old when Moshe was conceived. How do we know? Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains: Yocheved was *shehorasah ba-derech ve-nolda bein ha-chomot* — conceived on the journey to Egypt and born between the walls, at the very moment of entry. This resolves the famous numerical discrepancy: when Yaakov's family descended to Egypt, 69 descendants are enumerated; the Torah states that 70 came to Egypt. The missing seventieth is Yocheved, who was born precisely as they arrived. Since *Bnei Yisrael* were in Egypt 210 years, and Moshe was 80 at the time of the Exodus, Yocheved was 130 when she conceived him.

### Youth Restored

Why then is she called *bat* — a daughter, a young woman? Rav Yehuda bar Zvida explains: *melamed she-noldu lah simanei na'arut* — when Amram retook Yocheved as his wife (as we shall see, this was a renewed marriage ceremony), the signs of youth returned to her. *Nisaden ha-basar* — the flesh became supple again. *Nispashtu ha-k'matim* — the wrinkles smoothed out. *Ve-chazar ha-yofi li-mkomo* — her beauty was restored to what it had been. This is the sense in which she is called *bat*: not that she was chronologically young, but that her youth was miraculously restored to her.

### Remarriage Ceremony

The verse says *vayikach* — he took her — as though for the first time. But the *gemara* asks: should it not have said *vayachzir* — he took her back — since she had already borne him Miriam and Aharon? Rav Yehuda bar Zvida explains: *melamed she-asah bah ma'aseh likuchin* — he performed a full act of betrothal and marriage with her anew. He seated her in a bridal carriage, *hoshivah be-apiryon*, and made a proper wedding ceremony. *Ve-Aharon u-Miriam meshorerin le-faneha* — Aharon and Miriam rejoiced and sang before her. And the *mal'achei ha-shareit* — the ministering angels — proclaimed: *eim ha-banim semeichah* — "the mother of children rejoices," she who was already mother to two and would soon give birth to Moshe.

### Miriam's Prophecy

This *midrash* is embedded in the broader narrative of Amram's separation from Yocheved. When Pharaoh decreed *kol ha-ben ha-yilod ha-ye'ora tashlichuhu* — that every newborn son be cast into the Nile — Amram separated from Yocheved, and the entire people followed his example. Miriam challenged her father: Pharaoh's decree applies only to sons, but your separation means no children will be born at all — your decree is harsher than Pharaoh's. Moreover, Miriam had already prophesied that the redeemer would be born through her mother — this is the force of *Miriam ha-nevi'ah achos Aharon*, that she is called the sister of Aharon (not yet the sister of Moshe), because her prophecy preceded Moshe's birth. It was Amram who listened to his daughter's wisdom and prophecy, took back Yocheved, and through that reunion Moshe was conceived. The story thus closes with an echo of the larger themes of the *daf*: the wisdom and righteousness of women — Miriam, Yocheved, *benot Tzelofchad* — operating alongside and at times correcting the hesitations of the men around them, including Moshe himself.

---

---

# Bava Batra 120

## Bnot Tzelofchad Aggada

### Yocheved Birth Story

The daf opens in the middle of an *aggadic* section discussing the manner in which *Bnot Tzelofchad* approached Moshe and Aharon, and it includes a digression touching on the famous *aggadata* concerning Yocheved. The tradition records that Yocheved was born at the precise moment that the sons of Yaakov entered Mitzrayim, and that she was 130 years old when she gave birth to Moshe. The Gemara recalls the well-known episode of Amram separating from her and then, through the prophecy of Miriam, remarrying her — Miriam's prophetic insight leading ultimately to Moshe's birth.

### Women's Wisdom

The reason the Gemara introduced this *aggadata* in the first place was a discussion of the age of *Bnot Tzelofchad* and questions of childbearing. But there is an additional thematic layer worth noting: once again, a woman — Miriam — through her prophetic wisdom, knows more than her father Amram about the correct course of action. The parallel with *Bnot Tzelofchad* is striking: just as Miriam knew better than Amram, so too did *Bnot Tzelofchad* know better than Moshe in the sense of pressing their claim. The interplay of female wisdom and prophetic agency runs through both stories.

---

## Wisdom vs. Age

### Different Orders

The Gemara now turns to a textual question: *Bnot Tzelofchad* are listed in different orders in different contexts in the Torah. Later in Bemidbar, in the epilogue to the story where the uncles come to complain and the daughters ultimately marry their cousins, the names are given in the order of their birth — *derech gedulatan*, in accordance with their age. By contrast, when they approached Moshe with their legal claim, the names appear in a different sequence. The Gemara resolves this by explaining that the second context follows *derech chachmatan* — the order of their wisdom. Since the Gemara earlier declared that *chachmaniyot hen*, that they were women of great wisdom, it stands to reason that when they are coming forward with an intellectual claim, the wisest among them is listed first. When the epilogue records their marriages, however — where older daughters would naturally wed before younger ones — the order reverts to age.

### Yeshiva/Mesiba Rule

This distinction is then taken as support for a ruling of Rabbi Ammi: *mesayei lei l'Rabbi Ammi*, it lends support to what Rabbi Ammi said. Rabbi Ammi taught that *b'yeshiva halach achar chachma* — when people are gathered for an intellectual discourse or deliberation (here *yeshiva* does not mean a study hall in the modern sense, but rather a formal sitting for discussion), one gives precedence and a place of honor to the wisest participant. But *b'mesiba halach achar zikna* — at a meal, where the gathering is more social in character, one follows age. This is also consonant with the episode in Bereishit where Yosef seats his brothers at the meal in precise birth order: *habechor kevichorato vehatzair ketzeirato*.

### Significant Gap Req.

The Gemara then adds an important qualification from Rav Ashi: *vehu d'maflig b'chachma vehu d'maflig b'zikna* — this rule of giving precedence to the wiser or older person applies only where there is a *significant* gap. If two siblings are both highly capable and one is merely somewhat sharper than the other, that marginal difference does not justify honoring the younger over the older. One might ask: if the context is fundamentally intellectual, why should the size of the gap matter? The answer is that wisdom is not as objectively measurable as age. Unless the difference is obvious and dramatic — unless one person is unmistakably on a different level entirely — it is not an appropriate basis on which to set aside the clearer, more quantifiable standard of age.

There is a further reason as well. Being told that one's younger sibling is being honored because he is smarter carries a sting that is fundamentally different from the convention of respecting an older sibling. Age is something neither party controls; it reflects no personal judgment. To say, however, that we are honoring your younger brother because he is more intelligent reads as a direct critique. Consequently, only a truly overwhelming difference in wisdom justifies overriding the ordinary convention.

### Rashbam Logic

The *Rashbam* makes this point explicit and also addresses the reverse scenario — why is there a *significant gap* requirement even when honoring the older person at a meal? His analysis proceeds as follows. If the younger sibling is so dramatically more gifted — a genius of the highest order — then even at a meal, where the default is to follow age, if the age gap is minimal, one might honor the younger prodigy. It is only if the elder is *significantly* older that the convention of honoring age holds firmly even in the presence of outstanding intellectual distinction.

The *Rashbam* then addresses the case where neither party has a significant advantage in wisdom and neither is significantly older. He writes: *nir'eh b'einai de-v'chol makom holech achar ziknah* — it appears to him that by default one always follows age. The reasoning, as he articulates it, is that honoring someone who is only somewhat smarter causes embarrassment: *ein lanu l'vayesh et ha-zaken*. We should not embarrass the elder by suggesting, even implicitly, that he is less intelligent. By contrast, the person of somewhat greater wisdom is not embarrassed when the elder receives precedence: *v'he-chacham eino bosh b'kach*, because everyone understands that the societal convention is to honor the older. It is only when the age gap or the wisdom gap becomes large enough to be unmistakable that the relevant criterion shifts from its default.

One interesting question raised during the discussion was what precisely *chochmah* means in this context — whether it refers to raw intelligence, erudition in learning, or something closer to wisdom in the broader sense. The observation was made that *Bnot Tzelofchad* were praised as *chachmaniyot* not because of book knowledge but because of judgment and insight. The conclusion reached was that *chochmah* here is probably closer to wisdom than to mere intelligence or accumulated information.

---

## Tzelofchad Equal/Tribe

### Shkulot Hayu

The Gemara now introduces a teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *Bnot Tzelofchad shkulot hayu* — the daughters of Tzelofchad were all of equal worth. The different orderings of their names in different contexts are not actually indicating hierarchy; rather, they are employed precisely to demonstrate that no one daughter was superior to the others. The Gemara invokes the same interpretive move used for Moshe and Aharon, where the Torah alternates between *Moshe v'Aharon* and *Aharon u'Moshe* to convey that neither was greater than the other. The verse *vatihyenah bnot Tzelofchad* lists them all together, and the Gemara derives: *havayah achat l'chulan* — they shared a single, equal standing.

### Marriage Permission

Rav Yehuda then teaches in the name of Shmuel: *Bnot Tzelofchad huteru linasei l'chol hashvatim* — the daughters of Tzelofchad were permitted to marry from any tribe. This is a striking statement, since throughout this chapter the impression has been that the *p'sukim* in Bemidbar explicitly require daughters who inherit to marry within their tribe so that the *nachalah* does not pass to another tribe. Rav Yehuda appears to be saying the direct opposite of the straightforward reading.

### Advice vs. Restriction

The source Rav Yehuda cites is *latov b'eineihen tihyenah l'nashim* — let them marry whomever seems good to them. He reads this as granting permission to marry freely, setting aside the subsequent phrase *ach l'mishpachat mateh avihem* — only within the family of their father's tribe. That trailing clause, the Gemara explains, is not a legal restriction but *eitza tovah* — good counsel. The Torah is advising them that it is in their best interest to marry within the tribe, not commanding it. The formulation *ha-hagun lahem* — that which is fitting for them — frames tribal endogamy as prudent and beneficial rather than obligatory. Whether *hagun* here refers to the preservation of the *nachalah*, or more broadly to the likelihood of finding a compatible partner within one's own family and background, is a question the discussion leaves suggestively open. There is also a resonance with the observation that they were praised as *tzidkaniyot* — righteous women — and that by following this divine counsel they fulfilled exactly what was expected of women of such character.

---

## Rava's Challenge

### Dor Sinai/Future

Rava raises a challenge from a *baraita*. The *baraita* exposits the verse *emor aleihem ledoroteichem kol ish asher yikrav...* in the context of *tumah* and *kodashim*. It derives that *emor aleihem* refers to the people standing at Har Sinai in the moment of the giving of the Torah, while *ledoroteichem* — for your generations — extends the law to all future generations. The *baraita* then asks: if you state it for the fathers, why state it for the children, and vice versa? The answer is *mipnei sheyesh ba'avot ma she'ein babanim v'yesh babanim ma she'ein ba'avot* — because there are *mitzvot* that applied to the generation of the wilderness but not to future generations, and there are *mitzvot* that apply to future generations but not to that original generation. Since each category exists, one cannot simply infer one from the other; the paradigmatic verse must therefore state both explicitly.

The *baraita* then illustrates a *mitzvah* that applied to the fathers but not the children: *v'chol bat yoreshet nachala mimishpachat mateh aviha tihyeh l'isha* — every daughter who inherits must marry within her father's tribe. The Gemara reads this as applying only to that generation of *dor Sinai*, not to future generations. This is precisely what has been maintained throughout the chapter — that the restriction of marrying within the tribe was a *mitzvah* limited in its scope to the generation of the wilderness. The *Rashbam* likewise notes that *mitzvot* tied to the land of Israel, such as *bikurim* and *terumot uma'asrot*, would represent the opposite case: obligations that apply to later generations but not to the generation of the *midbar*.

### One Gen. Restriction

With this *baraita* in hand, Rava's challenge to Shmuel's statement becomes clear. The *baraita* states explicitly that *v'chol bat yoreshet nachala* was a real legal obligation — not merely advice — for the generation of the *midbar*. This seems to contradict Shmuel's position that *Bnot Tzelofchad* were permitted to marry freely. The Gemara resolves this — *hu motiv lah v'hu mefarek lah*, he raised the difficulty and he answered it — by drawing a careful distinction: *levar miVnot Tzelofchad*, the restriction applied to *other* women of that generation who were in similar circumstances, that is, daughters who inherited on account of the initiative of *Bnot Tzelofchad* and found themselves holding a *nachalah*. Those women were obligated to marry within their tribe. But *Bnot Tzelofchad* themselves, by virtue of their being *tzidkaniyot v'chachmaniyot*, were accorded a kind of exceptional permission. Future generations entirely are free to marry whomever they wish, *Bnot Tzelofchad* are free to marry whomever they wish, and for all of them the counsel is to marry within the tribe. The only ones legally bound are the other women of that specific generation who piggybacked on *Bnot Tzelofchad*'s legal claim. This represents a strikingly narrow reading of what seemed to be a broad prohibition in the *p'sukim*.

---

## Gen. Limitation Rule

### Shchutei Chutz

The Gemara now investigates from where exactly the Gemara derives that the obligation to marry within the tribe was limited to the generation of the *midbar*. Rava states: *amar kra, zeh hadavar asher tziva Hashem* — the verse says "this is the matter which Hashem commanded," and *davar zeh* carries a limiting force: *lo yehei noheg ela b'dor zeh* — this applies only to this generation. But a challenge immediately arises: the passage dealing with *shchutei chutz* — one who slaughters a consecrated animal outside the *Mikdash* — also opens with the formula *zeh hadavar asher tziva Hashem*. Does that mean the prohibition of *shchutei chutz* also applied only to the generation of the wilderness? Clearly not. The Gemara answers: *shani hatam d'chtiv ledorotam* — that case is different, because the verse there explicitly states *ledorotam*, for their generations, establishing unambiguously that the law extends to all time.

The same question is then raised regarding the *parasha* of *nedarim*: *zeh hadavar asher tziva Hashem ish ki yidor neder...* — does the *zeh hadavar* there mean the entire *parasha* of vows and *hatarat nedarim* was only for the generation of the *midbar*? *Hachi nami delo yehei noheg ela b'dor zeh?* The Gemara answers that the *zeh hadavar* in the *nedarim* passage is linked by *gezeira shava* to the *zeh hadavar* in *shchutei chutz*, and since the *shchutei chutz* passage contains *ledorotam*, this establishes that the *nedarim* passage too applies to all generations.

### No Gezeira Shava

One might then try the same move for *Bnot Tzelofchad*: since both the *nedarim* passage and the passage regarding daughters who inherit contain the phrase *zeh hadavar*, why not link them by *gezeira shava* and say that daughters who inherit are also not limited to one generation? The Gemara rejects this: *bishlama hatam itrich gezeira shava* — there, a *gezeira shava* was genuinely needed, because the word *zeh* would otherwise have been superfluous. Its presence is not meant to limit the law to one generation; rather, it serves as the vehicle for the *gezeira shava* itself, creating the link to *shchutei chutz* and its explicit *ledorotam*. Here, by contrast, if the Torah had wanted to indicate that the restriction applies to all generations, it would simply have said nothing — silence would have sufficed and the default rule would apply. *Lishtok kra minei v'ana yadana d'ledoros hu.* The only reason to write *zeh* here, where there is no *gezeira shava* to be made and no surplus purpose for the word, is precisely to limit the law to that moment. This is the textual basis for the ruling that the restriction on daughters who inherit marrying within the tribe was confined to the generation of the *midbar*.

---

## Gezeira Shava

### Zeh Hadavar

The Gemara now turns to elaborating the *gezeira shava* itself between *shchutei chutz* and *nedarim*. The *baraita* teaches: *ne'emar kan zeh hadavar* — it says *zeh hadavar* in the *nedarim* passage — *v'ne'emar l'halan zeh hadavar* — and it says *zeh hadavar* in the *shchutei chutz* passage. The *parasha* of *shchutei chutz* is addressed to Aharon, his sons, and all of Israel: *dabeir el Aharon v'el banav v'el kol bnei Yisrael*. The *parasha* of *nedarim* is addressed to *rashei hamatos livnei Yisrael* — the heads of the tribes. The *gezeira shava* teaches that each passage imports something from the other: just as *shchutei chutz* was directed to Aharon, his sons, and all Israel, so too does the law of *nedarim* apply in a context that includes all Israel; and just as *nedarim* was given to *rashei hamatos*, so too is the concept of *rashei hamatos* relevant to *shchutei chutz*.

### Three Hedyotot

What is the practical *halachic* import of bringing *Aharon uvanav v'chol Yisrael* into the context of *nedarim*? Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains: *lomar she'hafarat nedarim b'shloshah hedyotos* — to teach that *hatarat nedarim* may be performed by three ordinary laypeople who are not *talmidei chachamim*. The background is as follows. The *parasha* of *nedarim* is addressed to *rashei hamatos* — the heads of the tribes — and from the phrase *lo yachel devaro* the Gemara derives that while the one who made the vow cannot nullify his own words, *aval acheirim matirin umeichalin lo* — others can release him. Those "others" are the *rashei hamatos*, which implies a sage or authority figure. The *gezeira shava* therefore comes to expand this: since the *shchutei chutz* passage involves all of Israel — not only the distinguished leadership — the capacity for *hatarat nedarim* is not confined to established authorities. Three ordinary individuals, *shloshah hedyotos*, may together constitute a *beis din* for this purpose. As the Gemara notes, following Tosafos, once we know the number must be greater than one, the halachically significant grouping is three. The role of *rashei hamatos* in the *nedarim* passage is, in turn, read through the teaching of Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *b'yachid mumche* — a single authoritative expert may perform *hatarat nedarim* alone. The *rashei hamatos* thus teaches the sufficiency of a single *mumche*, while *kol Yisrael* teaches the sufficiency of three *hedyotos*.

---

## Hatara for Hekdesh

### Rav Sheshet

Returning to the *gezeira shava*, the Gemara asks: what does importing *rashei hamatos* into the context of *shchutei chutz* teach? Rav Sheshet answers: *lomar she'yesh she'eilah b'hekdesh* — to teach that one may perform *she'eilah*, the act of retroactively releasing a vow before a sage, with respect to *hekdesh* — items consecrated to the *Mikdash*. The underlying question is whether *hatarat nedarim* extends beyond its most obvious domain of personal prohibitions to encompass acts of *hafla'ah* more broadly. *Hafla'ah* is the category of verbal acts that change the status of a person or object — *ish ki yafli lindor neder nazir*, and similarly the verbal sanctification of *hekdesh*. Since consecrating an animal to the *Mikdash* is structurally analogous to making a *neder*, one might have thought that the same mechanism of *she'eilah* before a *chacham* could undo it.

### Hafla'ah Concept

This brings into focus the broader category of *hafla'ah*. When one makes a *neder*, the speech act transforms the status of an object: these fruits become forbidden to me as if they were *hekdesh*. The term *konam*, commonly used in *nedarim*, is indeed a linguistic surrogate for *korban*: just as one's words can sanctify an animal to the *Mikdash*, they can impose an analogous forbidden status on ordinary objects. The same logic applies to *nezirut*: declaring oneself a *nazir* is an act of *hafla'ah* that transforms one's personal status through speech. The question then becomes: does *hatarat nedarim* extend across all instances of *hafla'ah*, including *hekdesh* proper?

The question has real stakes. If one consecrates an animal to *bedek ha-bayit* — for the maintenance of the *Mikdash* — and subsequently regrets it, can one go to a *chacham* and have the *hekdesh* undone? The act of consecration is weighty, and there is reason to think that once something truly belongs to the *Mikdash*, it is beyond the reach of retroactive dissolution. Furthermore, once *terumah*, for example, has actually been given to a *kohen*, it is out of one's hands in a way that is qualitatively different from a personal prohibition. The Gemara's interest is in whether the link established by the *gezeira shava* extends the reach of *she'eilah* into the domain of *hekdesh*.

One additional dimension is worth noting. Consecrating an animal and then slaughtering it outside the *Mikdash*, so as to be liable for *karet*, raises the theoretical possibility that one could retroactively undo the *hekdesh* through *she'eilah* — *had I known I would be liable for karet, I never would have sanctified that animal* — and thereby escape liability. This underscores why the question of whether *she'eilah* applies to *hekdesh* has significant practical and conceptual ramifications.

A related question arose regarding *kiddushin*: could the speech act of *harei at mekudeshes li* be understood as an act of *hafla'ah*? This seems partially correct. Rashi emphasizes that the language of *kiddushin* does more than express intent; it effects a status change, and it appears to be borrowed from the conceptual world of *hekdesh* and *hafla'ah*. The view that *kiddushin* involves a speech act that effects a *kinyan* of status — beyond merely transferring property — finds resonance in this world. By contrast, *divrei shchiv meira*, the bequest of one on his deathbed, which operates *kesuvim u'mesurim dami*, is distinct: it is fundamentally about transferring ownership, not about changing the status of an object, and so belongs to a different analytical category.

### Shammai/Hillel

The Gemara then reveals that the question of *she'eilah b'hekdesh* is itself the subject of a fundamental dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Beit Hillel holds that *she'eilah b'hekdesh* is valid — one can approach a *chacham* and have a mistaken or regretted consecration retroactively undone. Beit Shammai holds there is no such thing: *ein she'eilah b'hekdesh* — *hekdesh* cannot be dissolved through *hatarat nedarim*.

---

## Hekdesh Taus

### Piv v'Libo

The source for Beit Shammai's position is a *Mishnah*: *Beit Shammai omrim hekdesh taus hekdesh* — if one consecrates something in error, it is nevertheless *hekdesh*. Beit Hillel disagrees: *eino hekdesh*. The principle underlying Beit Hillel's position is *neder piv v'libo shavim* — what one says must be in alignment with what one intends. When one sanctifies an item while mistaken about what that item is, the speech act is not in sync with the speaker's actual intent, and the *hekdesh* therefore does not take effect. Beit Shammai, by contrast, holds that *hekdesh* is of such gravity that the speech act alone is binding, independent of whether it reflects one's true intention.

### Temura Example

Beit Shammai's position finds support in the laws of *temura*. By *temura*, one attempts to transfer the *kedushah* from one animal to another — designating animal B as a substitute for the originally consecrated animal A. The *halacha* is that animal B acquires *kedushah* but animal A does not lose it: both become *hekdesh*. Since the entire point of the *temura* was to remove the *kedushah* from animal A, the outcome — that animal A remains *hekdesh* — was entirely contrary to what the person intended. Had he known this would be the result, he never would have performed the exchange. And yet animal B still becomes *hekdesh*. This demonstrates, according to Beit Shammai, that *hekdesh b'taus hekdesh*: even when the act of consecration is demonstrably an error, even when the error is obvious at the moment of the act, the *hekdesh* takes effect. If a patent, contemporaneous error cannot undo *hekdesh*, then surely retroactive regret cannot dissolve it either. Beit Shammai thus concludes that there is no *she'eilah b'hekdesh*.

---

## Shammai Gezeira Shava

### No Hatara Hekdesh

For Beit Hillel, the *gezeira shava* of *zeh zeh* between *shchutei chutz* and *nedarim* teaches the possibility of *she'eilah b'hekdesh*. The question arises: for Beit Shammai, who rejects *she'eilah b'hekdesh*, what does the *zeh hadavar* of *shchutei chutz* come to teach? It cannot be used for the same *gezeira shava* that Beit Hillel employs.

### Shechita Not Meliga

For Beit Shammai, the *zeh hadavar* by *shchutei chutz* is not available for a *gezeira shava* and instead teaches something internal to the laws of *shchutei chutz* itself: *al hashochait hu chayav, v'eino chayav al hamalik* — one is liable only for *shechita* performed outside the *Mikdash*, not for *melikah* performed outside. *Melikah* is the form of slaughter performed on bird offerings — using the fingernail at the back of the neck — and it is performed exclusively by *kohanim* within the *Mikdash*. If a bird offering is slaughtered outside the *Mikdash* by *shechita*, one is liable for *shchutei chutz*; if *melikah* is performed outside, one is not liable. The word *zeh*, in Beit Shammai's reading, serves to define and limit the scope of the prohibition in precisely this way, rather than to create a *gezeira shava* with the *nedarim* passage.

Similarly, for Beit Shammai, *zeh hadavar* by *rashei hamatos* teaches the distinction between the *chacham*'s mode and the husband's mode of addressing vows — that the *chacham* releases (*matir*) while the husband annuls (*meifer*), each operating exclusively in his own domain. This is the *halacha* that Beit Shammai derives from the *zeh* of the *nedarim* passage in place of the *gezeira shava*.

---

## Hatara/Hafara

### Hafara Husband

The distinction between *hatara* and *hafara* — between the sage's release and the husband's annulment — is a fundamental one that deserves careful attention. The husband's *hafara* operates by virtue of the verse *ki hefer osam b'yom shamo*: upon hearing his wife's vow, the husband has until the end of that day to exercise his power of *hifara*. What he does is void the vow — not retroactively, but going forward. The vow was fully binding at the moment it was made. If the wife violated it before the husband voided it, she has transgressed and bears responsibility for that transgression. The husband's power is prospective: from the moment he exercises *hafara*, the vow no longer binds her.

### Hatara Sage

The *chacham*'s *hatara* is entirely different in nature. The sage does not merely override the vow; he undoes it retroactively. The process is one in which the person who made the vow articulates that had he foreseen a particular circumstance or consequence, he never would have made it. On that basis, the *chacham* releases the vow — *matir*, as one unties a knot — and the vow is treated as if it had never existed. There is no time limit analogous to that day's hearing; and if the person violated the vow, the retroactive dissolution means that no violation occurred.

### Language Matters

These two modes are strictly separate and the language used must correspond to the correct mode. If a *chacham* performing *hatarat nedarim* employs the language of *hafara* — saying *mufar lach* rather than *mutar lach* — the *hatara* is ineffective. Conversely, if a husband employs the language of *hatara* rather than *hafara*, his act has no effect. The modes are not interchangeable, and using the wrong terminology for the wrong actor voids the act entirely. In practice, the formulation *hakol mutarim lach* is the language appropriate for the *chacham*, while *heifer* language is reserved for the husband.

---

## Moados/Nedarim

### Shabbat Exclusion

The Gemara now turns to a *baraita* that addresses the final verse in *Parshat Emor*: *vayedaber Moshe et moadei Hashem el bnei Yisrael*. The *parasha* had opened with *eileh moadei Hashem asher tikre'u otam mikra'ei kodesh eileh heim moadai sheishes yamim te'aseh melacha*, with *Shabbat* listed at the beginning. But the concluding verse — *vayedaber Moshe et moadei Hashem* — seems to refer back to only part of what was taught. Rabbi Yossi HaGlili teaches: *moadei Hashem ne'emru, Shabbat Bereishit lo ne'emra* — the *moadim* were stated, but *Shabbat Bereishit* was not included in this final summary. Ben Azzai adds: *moadei Hashem ne'emru, hafarat nedarim lo ne'emra* — the *moadim* were stated but *hafarat nedarim* was not included.

A sage named Rabbi Yossi bar Nasan had received a tradition of this *baraita* but could not explain it. So troubled was he that he traveled first to Narda'ah and then to Mechuza in pursuit of Rav Sheshet to obtain the explanation.

### Mumchinim

Rav Sheshet explained both teachings. Regarding Rabbi Yossi HaGlili's exclusion of *Shabbat Bereishit*: the verse *asher tikre'u otam mikra'ei kodesh* — you shall declare them holy — implies that these occasions require *kiddush beis din* to take effect. One might have thought, since *Shabbat* is mentioned alongside the *moadim* and the same formula of declaration appears, that *Shabbat* too requires a formal declaration by a *beis din* each week. The final verse, *vayedaber Moshe et moadei Hashem*, clarifies that only the *moadim* are included in this requirement; *Shabbat Bereishit* does not require *kiddush beis din*. Its sanctity is inherent and does not depend on human proclamation.

Regarding Ben Azzai's exclusion of *hafarat nedarim*: Rav Sheshet explained that *moadei Hashem tzerichin mumchin* — the *moadim* require a *beis din* of *mumchin*, of expert authorities, for the purpose of *kiddush ha-chodesh* and the determination of the calendar. *Hafarat nedarim lo ne'emra mumchin* — *hatarat nedarim* does not require *mumchin*. This is the source that Beit Shammai uses to derive that *hatarat nedarim b'shloshah hedyotos* is valid — a point that Beit Hillel derived from the *gezeira shava*, but which Beit Shammai, rejecting that *gezeira shava*, must learn from elsewhere.

### Resolved

The role of *rashei hamatos* in the *nedarim* passage is then accounted for by the teaching of Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *b'yachid mumche* — *rashei hamatos* teaches that a single individual who is a *mumche* may perform *hatarat nedarim* alone. The distinction is thus: *kiddush ha-chodesh* requires a *beis din* of expert *mumchin*; *hatarat nedarim* does not require *mumchin* at all and may be performed by three *hedyotos* — and if there is a single *mumche*, he suffices alone.

---

## Shabbat Sanctity

### Inherent Kedusha

The Gemara's teaching that *Shabbat Bereishit* does not require *kiddush beis din* points to a fundamental theological distinction. The *moadim* — Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot, and the other festival days — acquire their sanctity through human action: the *beis din* sanctifies the new month, which determines when the festivals fall, and in this sense *mekadesh Yisrael v'ha-zmanim* — Israel sanctifies the appointed times. Remove that human act, and there is no festival. *Shabbat*, by contrast, possesses an intrinsic *kedushah* rooted in creation itself. It is holy whether or not any human authority declares it so.

### Tosefet Shabbat

And yet the making of *kiddush* on *Shabbat* is not therefore meaningless. Rav Soloveitchik developed this point in several writings, arguing that the *kiddush* we make on Friday night — drawn from *zachor et yom ha-Shabbat le-kadsho* — adds a layer of human sanctity upon an already-sanctified day. *Shabbat* will be *Shabbat* regardless, but our *kiddush* brings our own consecration to it. This is reflected in the concept of *tosefet Shabbat*: by accepting *Shabbat* early, before nightfall, we extend its sanctity in a way that reflects human agency. The *moadim* exist only because of human sanctification; *Shabbat* exists independently of it. But just as human beings can add sanctity to the *moadim* through the declaration of *kiddush ha-chodesh*, so too can the individual add a personal dimension of sanctity to *Shabbat* through *kiddush* and *tosefet Shabbat* — not creating what was not there, but joining one's own act of sanctification to what God has already sanctified from the beginning of creation.

---

---

# Bava Batra 121

## Bnot Tzelofchad & Tu B'Av

### Bnot Tzelofchad Setup

The daf opens mid-page — the line begins with the word *mumche* — with the Gemara continuing its treatment of *Bnot Tzelofchad*. By way of background: the Gemara has just established that the restriction on intertribal marriage applied only to that particular generation, specifically to women who, like *Bnot Tzelofchad*, inherited a share of the land through their father. Future generations were free to marry whomever they wished. Moreover, even *Bnot Tzelofchad* themselves were not strictly prohibited from marrying outside the tribe — they were advised against it, but chose to follow that advice. With that background in place, the Gemara proceeds to quote a famous *Mishna* in Taanit, because it intersects directly with what has just been discussed.

### Mishna: Tu B'Av & Yom Ki…

The Gemara introduces the passage with the formula *tnan hatam* — "we learned over there," in Taanit. Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel declares: *lo hayu yamim tovim leYisrael kechamisha asar b'Av ukYom HaKippurim* — there were never days as joyous for Israel as the fifteenth of *Av* and *Yom Kippur*. The *Mishna* explains that on these days the young women of Israel would go out wearing borrowed white garments — *chelei lavan she'ulin* — so that anyone who needed to borrow would not be embarrassed. Even those who owned their own clothes would borrow, so that the practice became universal. The Gemara elsewhere describes that the daughter of the *Cohen Gadol* would borrow from a princess, and people would borrow from friends of similar station. The young women would then go out and dance, and the day served as an occasion for courtship.

### Women's Sayings: Beauty…

A *Braita* preserves what the young women would call out to the young men watching. The beautiful ones said: young man, look toward beauty, for a woman is prized for her appearance. Those from distinguished families said: look toward *yichus*, for a woman is for her children. And those who were neither beautiful nor well-born said: choose a wife *leshem Shamayim* — for the sake of Heaven. The *Brisker Rav* is said to have quipped: and what did those who were both beautiful and *meyuchasot* say? They were already married.

---

## Reasons for Tu B'Av Joy

### Yom Kippur Joy & Tablets

The Gemara now asks: what made these days so joyous? Regarding *Yom Kippur* the answer is relatively straightforward — *bishlama Yom HaKippurim*, one can understand it. It was *yom slicha umechila*, a day of forgiveness, and historically it was the day Moshe came down with the second set of *luchot*. The arithmetic works out as follows: *matan Torah* was on *Shavuot*, the sixth of *Sivan*. Forty days later is the seventeenth of *Tammuz*, when Moshe descended and broke the tablets. Although the narrative in Shemot and the account in Devarim each seem to describe only one subsequent forty-day period, *Chazal* harmonize the two accounts and posit three distinct forty-day periods. From the seventeenth of *Tammuz* plus forty days arrives at approximately the twenty-eighth of *Av*, and then another forty days brings one to *Yom Kippur*. On that day Moshe descended with the second *luchot*, which is why *Yom Kippur* carries the designation *yom slicha umechila* — it marked a new beginning, as if starting over.

### Husband-Wife Metaphor

What *Yom Kippur* has to do with courtship and the dancing of young women is not made explicit by the Gemara itself, but a suggestive parallel may be drawn. The *Nevi'im* employ the metaphor of husband and wife to describe the relationship between God and *Bnei Yisrael*, and *Chazal* apply a version of this metaphor to the breaking and restoration of the *luchot*. The breaking of the tablets was, as it were, the tearing up of the marriage contract; the giving of the second *luchot* on *Yom Kippur* represented the reconciliation and reunion. There is an added dimension: in the *Nevi'im*, it is often the woman — here, *Bnei Yisrael* — who takes the initiative in seeking the reconciliation, just as in the episode of the Golden Calf it was Moshe's prayers that moved God to agree to restore the relationship. Something of that dynamic may be reflected in the women taking the initiative on these days of courtship. The Gemara in Taanit also touches on this theme of reunion, though the connection between *Yom Kippur* and the specific custom of courtship remains more implicit than explicit.

### Rav Yehuda: Tribes Permi…

The question now turns to *Tu B'Av*: *u'v'chamisha asar b'Av mai hi* — what is the significance of the fifteenth of *Av*? Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers: *yom she'hutru shevatim lavo zeh ba'zeh* — the day that the tribes were permitted to intermarry with one another. This is precisely the context that brings the *Mishna* from Taanit into the discussion of *Bnot Tzelofchad*. The restriction that a woman who inherited a share of the land could not marry outside her tribe was limited to that generation. When that generation died out — perhaps fifty years or so after the entry into *Eretz Yisrael* — the restriction lapsed entirely, and all were free to marry whom they chose. That day of freedom is identified with the fifteenth of *Av*.

This answer connects elegantly to the courtship theme of the *Mishna*. The women going out and calling *bachur sa na einecha* — lift your eyes, young man — mirrors the verse from our passage, *hatov b'eineihem tihyena l'nashim*. The initiative of women in selecting their own husbands also resonates with the story of *Bnot Tzelofchad* throughout. No specific *pasuk* identifies the fifteenth of *Av* as the date; rather, it reflects a received tradition that this generation had by then fully died out. The *drasha* that grounds the ruling itself is *zeh hadavar* — *davar zeh lo yehe noheg ela b'dor hazeh*, the matter shall apply only to that generation.

### Binyamin Rejoins via Mar…

Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan offers a second answer: *yom she'hutru shevet Binyamin lavo b'kahal* — the day that the tribe of Binyamin was permitted to rejoin in marriage with the rest of Israel. After the affair of *Pilegesh b'Givah*, the other tribes had sworn at Mitzpah: *ish mimenu lo yiten bito l'Binyamin l'isha* — no man from among us shall give his daughter to Binyamin as a wife. This led to the extraordinary episode in which the men of Binyamin seized women for themselves, since no one would give voluntarily.

What *drasha* indicates that this oath had an expiration date? *Mimenu v'lo mibaneinu* — from *us*, but not from *our sons*. The oath was binding on that generation alone; the next generation was free to give their daughters to Binyamin. Binyamin survived that one difficult generation, and from that point the restriction dissolved. Here too the theme of freedom of marriage and the restoration of inter-tribal bonds is directly connected to the courtship customs of *Tu B'Av*.

### Dor Hamidbar Deaths End

Rav Dimi bar Yosef in the name of Rav Nachman offers a third answer: *yom she'kalu vo metei midbar* — the day on which the deaths of the wilderness generation finally came to an end, before the entry into *Eretz Yisrael*. The reason this constitutes a day of joy is that after the dying stopped, a new generation could begin fresh.

The Gemara cites a striking teaching: *ad she'lo kalu metei midbar, lo haya dibur im Moshe* — until the wilderness generation had finished dying out, God did not speak directly to Moshe. The proof-text juxtaposes the verse describing the completion of the deaths — *vayehi ka'asher tamu kol anshei hamilchama lamut mikerev ha'am* — with the very next verse: *vay'dabber Hashem elai lemor*, God spoke to me. The immediate juxtaposition implies that the divine speech to Moshe was conditional on the death of that generation.
