This is a striking teaching. After all, the Torah records God speaking to Moshe extensively during those thirty-eight years — *vayomer Hashem el Moshe* appears throughout. The Rashbam resolves this by drawing a distinction between *dibur* and *amira*. The term *vay'dabber*, with its connotation of directness and intimacy — the kind of speech described as *peh el peh adabber bo*, face to face — was suspended during this period. God spoke only when necessary, but the full, intimate, restored relationship was not resumed until the generation had passed.

The deeper message is powerful, and in some ways counterintuitive. The episode of the *Meraglim* seems to portray Moshe's relationship with God as something entirely independent of the people — God even says He would destroy them all and make Moshe into a great nation. Yet *Chazal* here communicate precisely the opposite: Moshe's special access to God was a function of his role as leader of *Bnei Yisrael*. While that people was in a state of divine disfavor — described in Taanit as *menudeh lashamayim*, placed under a kind of ban — Moshe's intimacy with God was correspondingly diminished. Only when the next generation stood ready to enter the land was the relationship fully restored. The connection between this answer and the courtship theme of *Tu B'Av* is, admittedly, less direct than the preceding answers, though one can point to themes of intimacy and the restoration of relationship.

### Midrash: Grave-Digging S…

The Rashbam cites a *Midrash* from *Midrash Eichah* that attempts to connect the answer of *kalu metei midbar* specifically to the date of the fifteenth of *Av*. The *Midrash*, brought in the name of Rabbi Levi, describes the following scene: every year on the eve of *Tisha B'Av*, a proclamation would go out — *hakol yetzu lachpor chafirim*, everyone go out and dig graves — and the people would go and lie down in the graves they had dug. In the morning, another proclamation: *yibadlu hachayim min hameitim*, let the living separate themselves from the dead. Each year approximately fifteen thousand people would remain in their graves — since forty times fifteen thousand equals six hundred thousand, roughly the number counted — and the rest would rise and go on. This continued for forty years.

In the final year, they all went into their graves on the ninth of *Av* — and in the morning, no one was dead. Uncertain whether they had miscounted the date, they tried again the following night, and the night after that, repeating this through the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth of *Av*, until the full moon appeared on the fifteenth. At that point they understood: *bitel HaKadosh Baruch Hu osah gezeira kasha me'aleinu* — the Holy One had annulled the harsh decree against them. And they made a feast and a celebration and a *yom tov*.

### Tosafot Rejects Midrash

Tosafot objects to this *Midrash* sharply, and in particular to the way the Rashbam reads it. The *pesukim* are unambiguous: *lo notar mehem ish ki im Kalev ben Yefuneh* — none of them remained except Calev ben Yefuneh. According to the Rashbam's reading of the *Midrash*, some fifteen thousand people from the wilderness generation had their decree waived and actually entered *Eretz Yisrael* — a reading that directly contradicts the plain meaning of the verses.

Moreover, Tosafot notes that even on its own terms, the *Midrash* does not actually support the Gemara's statement that this was the day *kalu* — that they finished dying. To the contrary, it is the day they discovered they were *not* dying — the day the decree was lifted for the survivors, not the day the generation concluded. The *Midrash* thus does not fit what the Gemara is saying. Tosafot's own reading, without the *Midrash*, is simpler: *Tu B'Av* was simply the day the last member of the wilderness generation died out, and that is all.

---

## Further Tu B'Av Reasons

### Hoshea: Removes Guard Po…

Ulla offers yet another answer: *yom she'bitel bo Hoshea ben Elah pardesa'os she'hoshib Yeravam al hadrachim shelo ya'alu Yisrael leregel* — the day that Hoshea ben Elah removed the guard posts that Yeravam ben Nevat had placed on the roads to prevent the northern kingdom from making the *aliya laregel* to Yerushalayim.

The background is as follows: when the kingdom split and Yeravam established the golden calves in Dan as an alternative center of worship, he feared that if his subjects continued to make pilgrimage to Yerushalayim, their political and religious loyalties would remain with the Davidic kingdom in the south. He therefore stationed guards on the highways to physically block travel to Yerushalayim during the pilgrimage festivals. Every subsequent king of Israel is described in the formula *vayelech b'derech Yeravam ben Nevat uvachat'aso asher hichti et Yisrael* — he walked in the ways of Yeravam and in his sin by which he caused Israel to sin. But of Hoshea ben Elah the verse says only *rak lo kemalchei Yisrael asher hayu lefanav* — only, he was not like the kings of Israel who preceded him. The Rashbam, citing *Seder Olam*, explains that what distinguished Hoshea was precisely this act: upon seeing that the golden calves had been carried off by the enemy, he removed these roadblocks and allowed free movement to Yerushalayim for the festivals.

One might ask: with the golden calves gone, would there not be even more reason to block access to Yerushalayim, lest the northerners fully return to its orbit? Nevertheless, the tradition identifies Hoshea's removal of these barriers as occurring on the fifteenth of *Av*. The connection to the courtship theme here is perhaps the weakest of all the answers — one might suggest it is about removing barriers between people, allowing the two kingdoms to draw closer, though the Gemara does not make this connection explicitly.

### Beitar Burial & Bracha

Rav Masna offers still another answer: *yom she'nisnu harugei Beitar likvura* — the day that permission was granted to bury those slain at Beitar in the aftermath of the destruction of the second *Beis HaMikdash*. The bodies had lain unburied, and when they were finally permitted to be interred, the rabbis at Yavneh instituted a new *bracha* — *HaTov veHaMeitiv* — the fourth blessing of *Birkas Hamazon*.

### Hatov Vehameitiv Bracha

This fourth *bracha* is in some ways structurally distinct from the first three. The first three *brachos* of *Birkas Hamazon* function as a unit — one ordinarily does not answer *amen* to one's own *bracha*, and the absence of an intervening *amen* after the third *bracha* signals their unity. *HaTov veHaMeitiv* then begins as a separate, later addition, opening with its own *baruch ata*.

What does *HaTov veHaMeitiv* mean in this context? *Hatov shelo hisrichu* — it was good that God caused the bodies not to decompose or stench; *veHaMeitiv she'nisnu likvura* — and He did good in that they were permitted to be buried. The standard understanding of *veHaMeitiv* — that the good extends beyond the immediate beneficiaries to others as well — applies here in that the entire people was able to feel that these dead had been properly treated and honored.

The broader architecture of *Birkas Hamazon* is worth pausing on in this context. The first *bracha*, *Hazan es Hakol*, concerns food in a universal sense. The second, *Al Ha'aretz ve'Al Hamazon*, reflects the *pasuk* in the Torah — *uveirachta et Hashem Elokecha al ha'aretz hatovah asher natan lach* — situating gratitude for food within the larger context of living in, farming, and harvesting the land of Israel; it is not merely thanks for sustenance but acknowledgment of divine gift of the land itself, reminiscent of the bringing of *bikkurim*. The third *bracha*, *Boneh Yerushalayim*, naturally follows once the theme of *Eretz Yisrael* has been introduced — though it strikes an elegiac note, looking back toward a Yerushalayim that is destroyed and forward toward its restoration. Then *HaTov veHaMeitiv*, linked to the tragedy of Beitar — an episode in which people arguably pressed too hard, *dachaku et haketz*, for national restoration before its time — closes the sequence. The question of what all this is doing in the framework of a blessing over food is itself a rich one, but the thematic thread running from food, to land, to Yerushalayim, to Beitar, has its own internal logic.

### Wood-Cutting Ends

Rava and Rav Yosef both say: *yom shepaskin bo milichot etzim l'ma'arakha* — the day on which the cutting of wood for the altar fires ceased for the season. Throughout the summer, wood was cut and dried for the *ma'arakha*, the arrangement of wood atop the altar. Dry wood was necessary to minimize smoke and prevent worm infestation, which moisture would encourage. After *Tu B'Av*, with the summer waning and conditions becoming less favorable, the wood-cutting season ended.

Why was the completion of this task a cause of celebration? The Rashbam explains simply that they had been engaged in this significant *mitzvah* throughout the summer, and its completion was marked with joy. As for the connection to the broader courtship theme of *Tu B'Av*, this answer is the most difficult to connect directly, though the association of harvest-time celebrations with communal dancing and courtship is attested in the ancient world more broadly. One might note that the verse describing the fourth year's produce — *kodesh hillulim l'Hashem* — is understood by some as *hillulim* deriving from *chalulim*, circular dances, suggesting a connection between harvest and the kind of festive dancing described in the *Mishna*.

### Breaking of the Hatchet

Rabbi Eliezer the Great states: *kivan she'higi'a chamisha asar b'Av, tashash kocha shel chamah* — from the fifteenth of *Av* onward, the strength of the sun wanes. And Rav Menashe adds: *karu lei yom tavar magal* — they called it the day of the breaking of the hatchet, because the hatchet used for the summer's wood-cutting was put away.

### Increase Torah Study

From this point, the Gemara states: *de'mosif yosif, she'eino mosif ye'asef* — one who adds will be added to, and one who does not add will be gathered in. The Rashbam explains: as the nights lengthen after *Tu B'Av*, one must add time for Torah study in the evening hours to compensate for the shorter days. The one who takes advantage of this opportunity will be blessed; the one who fails to do so — *tikberei imei*, as the expression goes, his mother should bury him. A rather discordant coda to a discussion of a joyous day, but characteristic of the Gemara's tonal range.

### Seven Lifespans Span His…

The Gemara then introduces a seemingly unrelated teaching: *shiva kiflu et kol ha'olam kulo* — seven people whose combined lifespans encompass the entire history of the world. The Rashbam suggests the connection may lie in the preceding saying about *de'mosif yosif*: these individuals lived to such extraordinary ages because they added to their Torah study, and their days were therefore added to them. The connection is admittedly tenuous, but the tradition is introduced here.

---

## Witnesses & Desert Decree

### Chain: Adam to Elijah

The seven individuals whose overlapping lives span all of world history are presented as follows. Metushelach saw Adam — their lifespans overlap, as the reader of Bereishit can verify by calculating the years. Shem saw Metushelach. Yaakov saw Shem — again, the mathematics of the genealogies in the Torah bear this out. Amram saw Yaakov. Achiyah HaShiloni saw Amram. And Eliyahu saw Achiyah HaShiloni — this is attested in the *pesukim* themselves. And Eliyahu, of course, is still alive.

Regarding Amram and Yaakov: this overlap is not stated explicitly in the Torah, but the Rashbam derives it by inference. Yaakov descended to Mitzrayim together with Kehat, and lived there for seventeen years before his death. Amram was Kehat's eldest son. If Kehat was alive when Yaakov died and was at least seventeen or eighteen years old by that point, it is reasonable to assume he had already fathered his firstborn son Amram. Thus Amram could have seen Yaakov, even if the Torah does not say so explicitly.

### Achiyah & Amram Problem

The more difficult link is between Achiyah HaShiloni and Amram. Achiyah HaShiloni was a prophet in the time of Yeravam ben Nevat — considerably later in history. For him to have seen Amram, who died in Mitzrayim, Achiyah would have had to be present in Mitzrayim while Amram was alive, then left with the Exodus — presumably at an advanced age — then traversed the wilderness, entered *Eretz Yisrael*, and lived for hundreds of years thereafter until the time of Yeravam. Moreover, if Amram died at 137, and the people were in Mitzrayim for approximately 210 years, then anyone who could have seen Amram alive would have been roughly seventy years old at the time of the Exodus. This compounds the difficulty: not only must we posit an extraordinary lifespan for Achiyah, but also that he survived the period of the *midbar* — when, after all, the verse says *lo notar mehem ish ki im Kalev ben Yefuneh v'Yehoshua bin Nun*.

### Levi Tribe Exempted

The Gemara answers the second difficulty first, through Rav Hamnuna: *lo nigzera gezeira al shivto shel Levi* — the decree of dying in the wilderness did not apply to the tribe of Levi. Achiyah HaShiloni was a Levi, and therefore not subject to the decree.

### Levi Counted at Thirty

The basis for this exemption is derived from the language of the verses themselves. The decree is formulated: *bamidbar hazeh yiflu figreichem v'chol pkudeichem l'chol misparchem miben esrim shanah vama'alah* — in this wilderness your corpses shall fall, all of your counting, to all your numbers, from twenty years and upward. The phrase *mi she'pkudav miben esrim* — those who are counted from age twenty — excludes Levi, *she'pkudav miben shloshim* — for the Levites are counted from the age of thirty, as the verse states *yavo litzvo tzava ba'avodas Ohel Moed*. The Rashbam observes that even this formulation borrows the language of military service — *tzava* — parallel to *kol haba latzava* used for the general census, but for the Levites the threshold is thirty rather than twenty. Since the decree was framed in terms of those counted from twenty, and Levi was counted from thirty, Levi falls outside the decree's scope. Thus the entire tribe of Levi — not merely Yehoshua and Kalev — could have survived the desert period and entered *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Yair & Machir Survive

Having opened this door, the Gemara immediately asks: *u'mishar shvatim lo hayu* — were there really no exceptions from the other tribes? The *Braita* is cited: Ya'ir ben Menashe and Machir ben Menashe were born in the days of Yaakov — *noldu bi'mei Yaakov* — yet they did not die until *Bnei Yisrael* entered the land — *v'lo meisu ad she'nichnesu Yisrael la'aretz*.

The proof that Ya'ir ben Menashe made it into *Eretz Yisrael* comes from the battle of Ha'Ai. The verse says *vayaku mehem anshei ha'Ai kishloshim v'shisha ish* — and the men of Ha'Ai struck down approximately thirty-six of them. A *Braita* records the debate: Rabbi Yehuda says it means literally thirty-six. Rabbi Nechemia objects: the verse says *kishloshim v'shisha*, *like* thirty-six, not exactly thirty-six. Rather, says Rabbi Nechemia, this refers to Ya'ir ben Menashe, who was *shakul k'rubah shel Sanhedrin* — equivalent in weight to the majority of the Sanhedrin. The Sanhedrin consists of seventy-one members; a majority requires thirty-six votes. The verse's formulation of "like thirty-six" is thus a reference to Ya'ir's singular importance. The assertion is that Ya'ir survived from the time of Yaakov all the way through the desert and into *Eretz Yisrael* — raising the same question as with Achiyah HaShiloni: how did he survive the desert decree?

One sharper question arises here as well: Tzelofchad — whose daughters are central to this entire sugya — was himself from the tribe of Menashe. If Ya'ir ben Menashe survived the desert, the question of how Tzelofchad did not, and why his daughters inherited from him, becomes more intricate.

### Ages 20-60 Decree Only

Rav Acha bar Yaakov provides the resolution: *lo nigzera gezeira lo al pachot miben esrim v'lo al yeser miben shishim* — the decree was not issued against those under twenty years old, and not against those over sixty years old. It applied only to the range of twenty to sixty.

### Over Sixty: Exempt

The textual basis for the lower bound is clear: the verse itself says *miben esrim shanah vama'alah*. The upper bound is derived through a *gezeira shava*: the word *ma'alah* appears both in the desert decree and in *Erchin*, where the Talmud treats those over sixty as a separate category, distinct from the twenty-to-sixty range. *Mah lehallan yeser miben shishim kepachot miben chaf* — just as in *Erchin* a person over sixty is treated differently from one in the twenty-to-sixty range, so too here, a person over sixty falls outside the scope of the decree. The Rashbam clarifies that this does not mean the over-sixty and under-twenty categories are identical to one another — they are not — but only that both stand outside the category against which the decree was directed.

This resolution now makes sense of both Achiyah HaShiloni and Ya'ir ben Menashe. If Amram died at 137, and the descent to Mitzrayim was roughly 210 years before the Exodus, then someone who could have seen Amram alive would have been approximately seventy at the Exodus — over sixty, and therefore exempt from the desert decree. Achiyah HaShiloni could thus have entered *Eretz Yisrael* and lived the additional centuries needed to reach the time of Yeravam. Similarly, Ya'ir ben Menashe, born in Yaakov's time, would have been well over sixty at the Exodus and likewise exempt.

As Rashi notes in the *Chumash*, this resolution considerably qualifies the apparent meaning of the verse that *only* Kalev and Yehoshua survived. In addition to the exemption of the entire tribe of Levi, and possibly the fifteen thousand whose decree was waived according to the Rashbam's reading of the *Midrash* — a reading Tosafot rejects — anyone over sixty was also exempt from the decree and could enter *Eretz Yisrael*. The categorical statement of the *pesukim* thus applies strictly to those in the twenty-to-sixty range who were counted in the original census.

---

## Division of Eretz Yisrael

### Equal vs. Proportional

The Gemara now transitions to a new question concerning the division of *Eretz Yisrael* among the tribes: *Eretz Yisrael lishvatim iplog o dilma lekarkaf gavrei iplog* — was the land divided into twelve equal sections, with the size of each individual's portion depending on whether his tribe was numerous or small? Or was each tribe's section proportional to its population, so that all individuals received equal per-capita portions regardless of their tribe?

### Territory Map Evidence

The intuitive answer — and the one strongly supported by visual evidence — is the second option. The map of tribal territories in Yehoshua shows sections of clearly varying sizes, suggesting that the division was proportional to population. The evidence from the geography of *Eretz Yisrael* itself seems to favor this reading decisively.

### Torah Verses on Division

Yet the Gemara brings two apparently contradictory *pesukim* and uses them to reach the opposite conclusion. One verse states *larav tarbeh nachalato velamaat tamit nachalato* — to the many you shall increase their portion and to the few you shall decrease their portion. Another verse states *bein rav lemaat* — whether many or few. How are these reconciled?

### Interpretation: Equal La…

The Gemara's resolution is that *bein rav lemaat* means each tribe receives the same amount of land regardless of its size. The former verse, which speaks of increasing and decreasing portions, refers to the distribution within each tribe — individuals within a more numerous tribe receive smaller personal allotments, while individuals within a smaller tribe receive larger ones. But the tribal sections themselves were of equal size.

### Division by Value Not Ar…

The *Braita* adds a further layer: *v'lo nitchalkah ela b'kesef* — it was divided not simply by area but by value. Rav Yehuda illustrates: *seah biYehudah shaveh chamesh sein baGalil* — one *seah* of land in Judah equals five *seah* in the Galilee in value. The land in Judah was far more valuable than equivalent acreage in the Galilee. The division thus aimed at equalization of value rather than equalization of area. Two mechanisms could achieve this: giving people different sizes of land but of equal worth, or giving everyone the same size and then compensating the difference financially.

### Urim v'Tummim & Lots

The *Braita* further states: *v'lo nitchalkah ela b'goral* — it was divided by lot, as the verse says *ach b'goral techalek ha'aretz*; and *v'lo nitchalkah ela b'Urim v'Tummim* — it was also conducted through the *Urim v'Tummim*, as the verse says *al pi hagoral*, by the mouth of the lot. The word *pi* — mouth — implies that there was speech, an oracle, emerging from the *Urim v'Tummim*, not merely a silent drawing.

### Drawing Lots Procedure

How could the division have been accomplished by both lot and prophetic oracle simultaneously? The *Braita* describes the procedure in detail. Elazar the High Priest stood dressed in the *Urim v'Tummim*, with Yehoshua and all of Israel assembled before him. Two boxes were placed before him: one containing placards bearing the names of the twelve tribes, the other containing lots bearing the names of the territorial sections of *Eretz Yisrael*. Before reaching into either box, Elazar would first prophesy through the *Urim v'Tummim*, declaring what he was about to draw. He would say, for example: *Zevulun oleh, tchum Akko oleh imo* — Zevulun is going to come up, and the boundary of Akko will come up with it. He would then mix the lots in the tribal box and draw — and Zevulun would emerge. He would then mix the lots in the territorial box and draw — and the boundary of Akko would emerge. And so on for each tribe in turn.

The Rashbam explains the purpose of this dual procedure: so that the people would recognize that the outcome was divinely ordained and not the product of chance. If lots alone were drawn without prophecy, an unhappy tribe might attribute its portion to bad luck. But when the outcome was declared in advance and then confirmed by the draw, all could see that God Himself had assigned each tribe its inheritance. One might note the inverse concern as well: if the draw always matched the prophecy, a skeptic could suspect the process was rigged. But the combination of public prophecy, witnessed drawing, and consistent confirmation served to establish the divine character of the division.

The Gemara illustrates with another example: *Naftali oleh, tchum Ginosar oleh imo* — Naftali comes up, and the boundary of Ginosar — the Kinneret region — comes up with it. And so it was for each tribe.

### Future Division: 13 Sect…

The *Braita* contrasts this with the division that will take place in the future, at the time of *Olam HaBa*. It is worth noting that *Olam HaBa* in Talmudic usage typically refers not to some post-mortem spiritual realm but to the future messianic era, when all of Israel will be living in *Eretz Yisrael* on this physical earth. That future division will differ from the present one in several respects.

First, it will encompass thirteen portions rather than twelve — the tribe of Levi will receive its own section along with the others. Second, the inequities of the present world will be remedied: *adam yesh lo sadeh lavan ein lo sadeh pardes* — in this world one might have a wheat field but no orchard, or an orchard but no wheat field. *B'Olam HaBa ein lecha kol echad v'echad she'ein lo bahar u'vashefeilah u'va'emek* — in the world to come, every individual will have a portion that includes mountain, lowland, and valley. Third, the division will be performed by God directly: *veHaKadosh Baruch Hu m'chalek lahen b'atzmo* — the Holy One will distribute it Himself, as the verse says *ve'eleh machlekotam neum Hashem*.

### Conclusion: 12 Equal Por…

The Gemara concludes from the *Braita*: *katani mi-ha she'b'tchilla lo nitchalkah ela lishneim asar shevatim* — the tradition states explicitly that originally it was divided into twelve. The Gemara reads this as establishing that the division was into twelve equal sections, thereby proving *lishvatim iplog* — that the tribal sections themselves were of equal size. Individuals in a numerous tribe therefore received smaller personal portions than individuals in a small tribe.

This conclusion is in some tension with the visual evidence of the territorial map, where the sections clearly vary in size. Yet the Gemara consistently returns to the principle of *bein rav lemaat* — whether many or few, each tribe received an equal share — and the conclusion the Gemara draws is that equality operated at the tribal level. Each of the twelve tribes received a section of equal value, and within that section, the size of each individual's personal allotment was inversely proportional to the tribe's population.

---

---

# Bava Batra 122

## 13th Tribe & Nasi

### Atida Eretz Yisrael

The *gemara* opens with a striking statement from one of the *amoraim*: *atida Eretz Yisrael she-techalek l'shlosha asar shevatim* — in the future, the Land of Israel will be divided not among twelve tribes but among thirteen. The immediate question is: *l'man* — for whom is the thirteenth portion? Rav Chisda answers: *l'nasi* — it is for the *nasi*.

The *nasi* described in Yechezkel is a figure who functions somewhat like a king but is conspicuously not called one. Yechezkel depicts the *nasi* as having special *korbanot* to bring, a designated place in the *beit hamikdash*, and a particular gate through which he enters. Much of this appears in the *haftarot* as well — notably the *haftarah* for Parshat HaChodesh, which dwells at length on the *nasi*'s role in preparation for Pesach.

A central question surrounds whether Yechezkel's *nevuot* about the *beit hamikdash* were intended for *bayit sheni* or *bayit shlishi*. The conclusion reached in the Tannaitic period was that they cannot have been intended for *bayit sheni* — the Sages of that era saw *bayit sheni* with their own eyes and built it differently, closer to *bayit rishon* in structure. Therefore, Yechezkel's *nevuah* must be pointing toward *bayit shlishi*, and the *nasi* he describes must correspond in some way to *melech hamoshiach*. Yet this raises a genuine difficulty: why would a *navi* prophesying during the first *galus*, before *bayit sheni* had even arisen, be speaking about *bayit shlishi*? The general principle that *nevuah* can only be understood after the fact offers some comfort, though the full tension here is not easily resolved.

The broad consensus is that *bayit shlishi* and *yemei hamoshiach* are effectively coextensive. The underlying difficulty is that many components of the ideal *halachic* society are interdependent: you need *kohanim* who are *tahor*, a functioning *beit hamikdash*, a king, and a *sanhedrin* — and each presupposes the others in ways that create something of a logical loop. The solution is that *mashiach* will come, and a *navi* will be needed to identify the *kohanim meyuchasim*, to establish who descends from *Dovid HaMelech*, and to determine where the *mizbeach* belongs. The *nasi* of Yechezkel is, on this reading, the precursor or embodiment of the restoration of *malchus beit Dovid* — and his ancestral portion is to be a separate *nachala* from those of the twelve *shevatim*, with the inherited land of *Yerushalayim* itself remaining, as always, beyond the domain of any single tribe.

The question of which twelve tribes form the base count is itself non-trivial: do we count Yosef as a single tribe with Levi receiving no territorial portion, or do we count Ephraim and Menashe separately while Levi again goes without? Either arrangement yields twelve. In the Messianic context, the question of whether the *leviim* will receive a full *nachala* like the other tribes rather than being confined to designated cities is left open, though the closing chapters of Yechezkel address this at length.

It is worth noting that *chazal* were already acutely aware of internal tensions within Sefer Yechezkel — to the point that there were voices in the Tannaitic period calling for the book to be *gonez*, to be set aside as canonical. Various *drashot* were marshalled to defend its place, but that discussion belongs elsewhere.

### Nasi's Proof

Rav Chisda's proof that the *nasi* receives a distinct territorial portion derives from the verse: *ve-ha-oved ha-ir ya'avduhu mikol shivtei Yisrael* — the city that serves him shall be worked by all the tribes of Israel. The force of the proof lies in the phrase *mikol shivtei Yisrael*: the area subject to the *nasi*'s authority is drawn from all the other tribes, implying it constitutes a reallocated portion carved out of the collective holdings. It is worth noting that other passages in Yechezkel might seem to offer more direct proof of the *nasi*'s special *nachala* — including passages read in the *haftarah* of Parshat HaChodesh — which makes the *gemara*'s choice of this particular verse somewhat surprising.

### Workers vs Inheritance

Rav Pappa challenges the inference by raising an alternative reading: *eima rungar be-alma* — perhaps the verse is speaking of nothing more than hired laborers. The *Rashbam* explains *rungar* as *schirim be-alma la-avod bo ke-talmidim le-rav* — ordinary hired workers, akin to students who serve their teacher. On this reading, the verse describes workers from various tribes laboring in fields the *nasi* happens to own, without implying that he possesses a distinct ancestral *nachala* carved from the other tribes' portions. The *gemara* rejects this interpretation based on another verse in Yechezkel: *ve-hanosar l'nasi mizeh umizeh litrumat hakodesh v'la'achuzat ha'ir* — the remainder goes to the *nasi* from this side and that side, as a dedication to the *kodesh* and for control of the city.

This verse creates its own complexity, since it appears to give the *nasi* property rights over the *kodesh* and the city of *Yerushalayim*, which we would normally say was not apportioned to any tribe: *Yerushalayim lo nitchalka lishvatim*. The resolution seems to be that the *nasi*'s control does not violate the principle that *Yerushalayim* belongs to all the tribes collectively, but precisely how those two claims are reconciled remains a genuine difficulty in parsing Yechezkel.

### Yechezkel's Nasi

The broader picture that emerges is as follows: there are twelve tribal portions plus a thirteenth for the *nasi* and his family. The *nasi*'s holding is distinct from *shevet Yehudah*'s allocation and is not the same as *Yerushalayim* itself, which belongs to *kol hashevatim*. Whatever the *nasi*'s summer estate or seat of governance turns out to be, it is somewhere separate from the capital. These questions cannot be resolved fully from the *gemara*'s discussion alone.

### Land Valuation

The *gemara* then turns to the question of how compensation was managed when the land was divided — this now referring to the original division under Yehoshua. The principle stated is *velo nitchaleka ela bechasafim* — it was divided according to cash value. The question raised is: *lemai* — what precisely does this mean?

The *gemara* first considers whether the cash-value adjustment was meant to account for the superior or inferior quality of the land itself — better arable soil versus worse. But it dismisses this: *atu beshuftani askinan* — are we really dealing with people so foolish that they wouldn't automatically account for agricultural productivity when sizing portions? Of course the physical quality of the land factors in.

The real issue, the *gemara* concludes, is *lekurva velirchoka* — proximity to or distance from the city. A field located near an urban center commands a premium because of market access and ease of commerce. A more remote parcel of equivalent arable quality is simply worth less. It is this locational differential that requires some form of cash-value equalization. In modern terms: location, location, location.

The question then becomes what form the compensation takes — does the equalization happen in cash paid into some communal fund, or is the land itself simply re-partitioned until each person receives an equivalent value? The *gemara* poses this directly: *velo nitchaleka ela bechasafim* suggests it was denominated in cash terms rather than purely re-divided in land. This itself creates a tension, since land is regarded as intrinsically more valuable than cash — it is productive, permanent, and in the context of *nachalot* will belong to a family essentially forever. The best use of any cash compensation would be to reinvest it in land, yet land purchased in this era would revert at the *yovel*. These considerations suggest that the all-cash model leaves the compensated party with the short end of the deal.

## Goral & Exceptions

### Eliezer vs Yehoshua

The *gemara* notes that the dispute among the *amoraim* over cash versus land compensation mirrors a Tannaitic *machlokes*: *Rabbi Eliezer omer bechasafim he'aluha* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that equalization was effected through cash payments; *Rabbi Yehoshua omer becharka he'aluha* — Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the equalization was done through land itself, i.e., the parcels were re-subdivided until each was of equivalent value. Both agree, however, on the fundamental point: *velo nitchaleka ela begoral* — the division was ultimately determined by lottery.

### Ach Begoral

The *gemara* derives this from the verse: *ach begoral*. The word *ach* characteristically signals an exclusion. Who, then, is excluded from the *goral*? *Yatzu Yehoshua veCalev* — Yehoshua and Calev did not participate in the lottery. These were the only men who had been over the age of twenty at the time of the Exodus and were permitted to enter the land. All other men of that generation had died in the wilderness.

The *gemara* then asks: *l'mai* — what precisely does the exclusion mean? One possibility: they simply did not receive any portion at all — *d'lo shakil klal*. But the *gemara* dismisses this: *hashta d'lav didhu shakol didhu mibaya* — if even properties belonging to others were acquired for them, surely their own personal *chelekei meraglim* would be theirs. The earlier discussion in this chapter established that Yehoshua and Calev received the portions that would otherwise have gone to the ten *meraglim* who failed — a kind of providential reassignment. Just as the *bnot Tzelafchad* had to contend to receive their father's portion, here the two faithful *meraglim* received what the unfaithful ones forfeited.

The correct interpretation of *ach begoral* is therefore: *shelo natlu begoral* — they received their inheritances, but those inheritances were not assigned by random lottery. Rather, they were designated directly: *ela al pi Hashem* — by divine instruction.

### Joshua's City

For Yehoshua, the *gemara* cites the verse: *al pi Hashem natnu lo et ha'ir asher sha'al et Timnat Serach b'har Ephraim* — God designated for Yehoshua the city of Timnat Serach in the hill country of Ephraim. This places Yehoshua's city within the tribal territory of Ephraim, in the Shomron region, where he would live and where his descendants after him would inherit.

The *gemara* then notes a textual problem: the city is called *Serach* in one place and *Cheres* in Sefer Shoftim. *Cheres* means pottery. How is the same city referred to by two different names?

Rabbi Elazar explains that the two names are anagrams of each other — the same letters, reversed. What the name-shift signals about the city's character is the subject of a further dispute. One view: *batchila peroteha k'cheres* — originally the fruits of the city were dry and inedible like pottery, *u'l'basof peroteha masrichin* — and eventually they rotted and spoiled. The other view reverses the order: initially the fruits were putrid, and ultimately they became dry like pottery.

There is a suggestion that *k'cheres* might actually be positive — fruit that is hard and dry-textured can be stored for a long time without spoiling — but this reads as somewhat apologetic. The more natural reading of both descriptions is that the fruits of Timnat Serach were consistently poor. This may carry a thematic resonance: the ten faithless *meraglim* brought back a negative report about the land, focusing precisely on its fruits. Yehoshua, who could see beyond the surface, inherited a city whose fruit was objectively unimpressive — yet he valued the *nachala* for what it was. The *gemara* in Berachot describes the fruits of Ginosar near the *Kineret* as so extraordinarily sweet that one had to eat bread afterward to neutralize the sweetness. The contrast with Yehoshua's city is striking.

### Caleb's Hebron

For Calev, the verse states: *vayitnu leCalev et Hevron ka'asher diber Moshe vayoresh misham et shlosha bnei ha-anak* — they gave Calev the city of Hevron as Moshe had promised, and he drove out the three giants remaining there. It was called *Kiryat Arba* because four giants had once inhabited it; by the time Calev arrived, three remained, and he conquered them himself.

The *gemara* raises an apparent difficulty: *Hevron ir miklat havei* — was Hevron not a city of refuge? The six *arei miklat* were part of the forty-two or forty-eight cities assigned to the *leviim*. How, then, could Calev receive Hevron as his personal *nachala*?

The resolution, attributed to Abaye, is: *parvar ha* — it is the suburbs. The verse specifies: *ve-es sdei ha-ir ve-es chatzereha nasnu leCalev ben Yefuneh be-achuzaso* — the fields of the city and its environs were given to Calev as his holding. The city proper, including the *migrash* surrounding it as defined by *halacha*, belonged to the *leviim*. What Calev received was the broader suburban and agricultural zone surrounding those boundaries. This arrangement also has the elegant consequence that Calev, like Yehoshua, received his *nachala* within the tribal territory he would naturally have been assigned — Calev is of *shevet Yehudah*, and Hevron lies within *Yehudah*. Yehoshua's city of Timnat Serach is in *Ephraim*, which is his own tribe. Both men receive *nachalot* that are simultaneously exceptional — not assigned by *goral* — and fitting within the natural tribal geography.

Calev's connection to Hevron also carries midrashic resonance: the tradition holds that during the journey of the *meraglim*, Calev separated himself and went to pray at *Me'arat HaMachpelah* in Hevron, which became a source for the practice of visiting *kever avot*. His inheritance of that very city is a fitting reward.

## Son & Daughter Equal

### Contradiction Setup

The next *mishna* opens with the statement: *echad ha-ben ve-echad ha-bat be-nachala* — a son and a daughter are equivalent in *nachala*. The *gemara* immediately identifies an apparent contradiction: have we not already learned in an earlier *mishna* that a son inherits before a daughter, and that *kol yotzei yerech shel ben kodmin labat* — every descendant of a son takes precedence over a daughter? How, then, can the *mishna* here declare them equivalent?

The *gemara* then embarks on a four-part *sugya*, signaled by the mnemonic *nafsham* — *nun* for Rav Nachman, *peh* for Rav Pappa, *shin* for Rav Ashi, and *mem* for Mar bar Rav Ashi. Each *amora* proposes an interpretation of the opening clause of the *mishna*, and each attempt is blocked by the *ela* clause that follows. The structure is unusual — a four-part *sugya* of this kind is not common.

### Nachman's Resolution

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: *echad haben ve'echad habat notlin biraui kivemuchzak* — a son and a daughter inherit equivalently with respect to both *raui* and *muchzak* property. *Muchzak* property is what the father currently holds and controls. *Raui* property is what is due to him — property that would flow to him under standard inheritance rules from some other relative, even if not yet in his possession.

The *Rashbam* formulates it precisely: when the father is himself an heir to a more distant relative and that inheritance passes through him to his children, a son or daughter will receive it on equivalent terms. The concern the *mishna* addresses is that one might think a daughter's inheritance rights are a special exemption applicable only to ancestral land — to *nachala* in the narrow sense — but not to the full breadth of the father's estate. The *mishna* therefore establishes: *echad haben ve'echad habat* — they are equivalent across the board, whether the property is *raui* or *muchzak*.

This is supported by a *baraita*: *benot Tzelofchad natlu shloshah chalakim banachalah* — the daughters of Tzelofchad received three distinct portions: their father's share as one who left Egypt, his portion among his brothers in the inheritance from their grandfather Chefer, and a further portion from Tzelofchad himself. Three portions in total, demonstrating that daughters can inherit across the full range of *nachala* circumstances.

### Pappa's Bechorah

Rav Pappa then proposes an alternative reading: *echad haben ve'echad habat notlin chelek bibechorah* — a son and a daughter can each receive a share of the firstborn's portion. A supporting *baraita* already states that the *bechor* takes a double portion. The implication here is that a daughter who inherits from her father can also participate in whatever the *bechor*'s double portion generates. But again the question arises: if a *baraita* already establishes this, why does our *mishna* need to say it? And the *ela* clause still has not been adequately accounted for.

### Ashi's Context

Rav Ashi proposes: *echad ben bein habanim ve'echad bat bein habanot* — a single son among other sons receives one portion, a single daughter among other daughters receives one portion, and in those respective contexts they are equivalent. If someone declares in a form of living will that a particular heir should receive all of his property — *im amar yerash kol nechasai devarav kayamin* — his words are upheld. The *gemara* identifies this position as that of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, as stated in a later *mishna*: if one designates someone *she-raui le-yorsho* — who is already a fitting heir — to inherit the entirety, his words stand; but if the designated person would not otherwise be a fitting heir — *she-eino raui le-yorsho* — the designation is ineffective.

The *gemara* then raises a difficulty with Rav Ashi's reading: does this mean our *mishna* is a *stam mishna* that follows the minority position of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka? The principle of *stam ve'achar kach machlokes* — an unattributed *mishna* followed later by a dispute — generally tells us that the position of the *stam* is the rejected one, since the *machlokes* that follows reveals it to be a contested view. The rule is that *ein halakha ke-stam* in such a case, and one must instead adjudicate by the rules of *klalei hafsak*. Normally we say *halakha ke-stam mishna*, but when a later *machlokes* bears on the same topic, the *stam* cannot be taken as definitive.

### Mar's Synthesis

The final and accepted explanation comes from Mar bar Rav Ashi: *echad ha-ben ve'echad ha-bat shavin be-nichsei ha-em u-ve-nichsei ha-av* — a son and a daughter are equivalent in inheritance from their mother and from their father alike. The *ela* clause of the *mishna* then fits precisely: *ella she-ha-ben notel pi shnayim be-nichsei ha-av ve-eino notel pi shnayim be-nichsei ha-em* — the sole exception is that a *bechor* son collects a double portion from the father's estate but not from the mother's. The equivalence between son and daughter is the general rule; the *bechor*'s double portion from the father is the specific, named exception. This reading makes the *ela* clause integral and necessary rather than redundant, and it is Mar bar Rav Ashi's formulation that resolves the *sugya*.

## Pi Shnayim Debate

### Two Models

The *gemara* turns to a *baraita* analyzing the phrase *latet lo pi shnayim* from Parashat Ki Teitzei. The context is the passage forbidding a father from displacing his firstborn son in favor of a son born of a more beloved wife: *et ben ha-snu'ah yakir latet lo pi shnayim* — he must recognize the son of the less favored wife and give him the double portion. The question posed is: what exactly does *pi shnayim* mean?

Two interpretations are presented. The first is *pi shnayim ke'echad*: the *bechor* receives twice the share of any single one of his brothers. The second is *pi shnayim bechol hanechasim*: the *bechor* receives a double share of the total estate — meaning two-thirds of the entire inheritance, with the remainder split among all other heirs.

### Double Proportion

Under the *pi shnayim ke'echad* model, the inheritance is divided into one more share than the number of sons. With five sons, the estate is divided into six portions: the *bechor* takes two and each of the other four takes one. The *bechor*'s share is thus one-third of the total, and each other brother receives one-sixth. The *bechor* receives exactly double what any other single son receives.

### Two-Thirds Model

Under the *pi shnayim bechol hanechasim* model, the *bechor* always receives two-thirds of the total estate, regardless of how many brothers he has. With five sons, the four remaining brothers divide the remaining one-third among themselves, each receiving one-twelfth. His portion is double the combined sum of all the other heirs put together.

The *gemara* notes that both models agree in the simplest case — two brothers. With two sons, the *bechor* receives two-thirds and the other receives one-third under either interpretation: two times one-third is two-thirds, and two-thirds of the whole is also two-thirds. The case of two brothers therefore cannot distinguish between the models, making it impossible to derive one from the other by simple analogy.

### Hanchilo Resolution

The *gemara* resolves the ambiguity from the continuation of the verse: *vehaya beyom hanchilo et banav* — on the day he apportions to his sons. *HaTorah rivtah nachala etzel achim* — the Torah increases the *nachala* to be distributed among the brothers. The word *hanchilo et banav* implies that each son receives a meaningful *nachala* in his own right.

The *Rashbam* formulates this directly: *rivtah nachala shelo yitol pi shnayim bechol hanechasim heikha de'ika shnayim ushlosha achim milvado* — the Torah amplifies inheritance precisely so that the *bechor* does not take two-thirds of the whole when there are two or three other brothers. Under the two-thirds model, as the number of heirs grows, each non-*bechor* son is left with so small a portion that it barely constitutes a real *nachala* at all. The *pi shnayim ke'echad* model, by contrast, ensures that each son retains a proportionally fair share. The *halachah* therefore follows the first interpretation: the *bechor* receives double a single portion, not two-thirds of everything.

---

# Bava Batra 123

## Pi Shnayim Definition

### One vs. All Sons

The daf opens with a *baraisa* addressing a fundamental definitional question regarding the *bechor*'s double portion: what precisely does *pi shnayim* mean? Two interpretations are possible. The first holds that the *bechor* receives double the share of any individual brother — *pi shnayim ke'echad*. The second, far more radical interpretation would grant the *bechor* double whatever all of the other sons receive in aggregate — *pi shnayim bechol hanechasim*. The practical difference is enormous. If there are five other sons, the first interpretation produces six equal units, with the *bechor* receiving two; the second would produce fifteen units, with the *bechor* receiving ten and each remaining son receiving only one. The *baraisa* takes up both possibilities seriously.

### Logical Comparison

The *baraisa* attempts a logical resolution through analogy. Consider the simplest case: one *bechor* and one other son. The *bechor* receives double. Under either interpretation, that result is identical — he receives two parts and his brother one. One could therefore read *pi shnayim* in that scenario as "double what one individual receives," or equally as "double what all the others combined receive," since in that case the two formulations coincide. The *baraisa* tries to extend this to the case of five additional sons, but the argument is reversible in both directions, and neither inference is conclusive on its own. The *baraisa* therefore turns to a *pasuk* for resolution.

The verse *vehayah beyom hanchilo et banav* — "it shall be on the day he bequeaths to his sons" — is read as placing all of the sons front and center in the inheritance. The word *banav*, "his sons," signals that the other brothers have a substantial stake in the estate. The *gemara* therefore concludes that we cannot adopt the second interpretation, which would render the remaining brothers' collective share trivial compared to the *bechor*'s. The correct reading is *pi shnayim ke'echad*: double any individual brother's portion.

### Yosef Proof

The *baraisa* then adduces further evidence by linking the word *bechorah* as it appears in the laws of inheritance to the *bechorah* as it applied historically to Yosef. Two verses from *Divrei HaYamim* are cited. The first: *uvnei Reuven bechor Yisrael ki hu habechor uvechalelo yetzuei aviv nitnah bechorato livnei Yosef ben Yisrael* — the sons of Reuven, the firstborn of Israel, for he was the firstborn, but because he desecrated his father's bed, his firstborn rights were given to the sons of Yosef son of Israel. The verse is careful to add *velo lehityaches labechorah* — the personal title of firstborn remains with Reuven; only the *privileges* were transferred to Yosef. The second verse: *vehabechorah l'Yosef* — the *bechorah* belongs to Yosef. The *gemara* notes that the word *bechorah* appears in both this context and in the Mosaic law governing inheritance, thereby establishing an analogy: just as Yosef's *bechorah* meant a double portion relative to any individual brother, so too does the legal *bechorah* mean double any individual brother.

But this raises an immediate sub-question: where do we see that Yosef's double portion was specifically double that of one individual brother, as opposed to double all the brothers combined? The *gemara* cites the verse *va'ani natati lecha Shechem echad al achecha* — I have given you one *Shechem* above your brothers. Whether *Shechem* refers to the city or to an additional portion, the word *echad* — "one" — establishes that Yosef received one extra share over his brothers, not double their combined total.

The verse continues: *asher lakachti miyad ha'Emori becharbi uvekashti* — which I took from the Emorite with my sword and my bow. This is textually puzzling: Yaakov was not a warrior. The *Rashbam* addresses this by noting that Yaakov's "sword" and "bow" are understood as *tefillah* — prayer. The term *charbi* alludes to prayer, and *kashti* is a play on *bakashah*, beseeching. The *Rashbam* reads this as a reference to Yaakov's prayers on behalf of his sons and his efforts to acquire Eisav's *bechorah* — and it is this, the fruit of his prayers and strivings, that he now bequeaths to Yosef.

### Rav Pappa Challenge

Rav Pappa challenges the proof from *Shechem echad*. Even if Yaakov says he gave Yosef "one *Shechem*," perhaps *Shechem* denotes something minor — a palm tree, a small additional gift — rather than a full tribal portion equal in size to any other brother's territory. On that reading, the verse would not establish that Yosef received a full double portion commensurate with each individual brother.

### Ephraim Menashe

Abaye responds simply: look at the explicit verse, *Ephraim u'Menashe k'Reuven v'Shimon yihiyu li* — Ephraim and Menashe shall be to me like Reuven and Shimon. Yaakov granted Yosef's two sons the status of independent tribes equal to full brothers. That means Yosef received precisely two full tribal portions — exactly double the one portion of any individual brother. This is *pi shnayim ke'echad*, and this is the *halacha* of the *bechor*.

---

## Reuven to Yosef

### Initial Question

Having established the halachic point using the narrative of Yaakov and Yosef, the *gemara* transitions into a sustained *aggadic* passage. Rav Chelbo poses a question to Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani: *ma ra'ah Yaakov she'natal bechorah mi'Reuven u'netanah l'Yosef* — what motivated Yaakov to take the *bechorah* from Reuven and give it to Yosef?

### Simple Answer

The *gemara* dismisses the first half of the question almost immediately. Why did Yaakov take it from Reuven? The verses in *Divrei HaYamim* say it plainly: *uvechalelo yetzuei aviv* — because Reuven desecrated his father's bed. That requires no further explanation.

### Parable

The real question is the second half: why was it given specifically to Yosef? Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani offers a parable. A homeowner raised an orphan in his house. The orphan later became wealthy and said: let me now benefit this man from my wealth, in gratitude for having raised me. The *bechor* and the homeowner in the parable are Yosef and Yaakov respectively — Yaakov came down to Egypt dispossessed and without means, and Yosef sustained him. At the end of his life, Yaakov had something of value to give back: the *bechorah*. He gave it to Yosef as a return of the favor.

### Counter-Objection

An objection is raised: if Yaakov was obligated to return the favor regardless, then even had Reuven not sinned, Yaakov would still have been compelled to give something to Yosef. Why then did the *bechorah* specifically have to be taken from Reuven to accomplish this? Yaakov could have returned the favor with his own property. The *Rashbam* makes this point explicit: you do not return a favor at a third party's expense. There must be a deeper explanation for why the *bechorah* in particular went to Yosef.

### Intended Firstborn

Rabbi Yonatan's formulation, as transmitted by his student, provides that deeper explanation. *Re'uya hayta bechorah latzet mei'Rachel* — the *bechorah* was properly destined to emerge from Rachel all along. The verse *elleh toldot Yaakov Yosef* — "these are the generations of Yaakov: Yosef" — places Yosef in the position of Yaakov's primary son, as if he were the firstborn. Had Yaakov married Rachel first, as he intended, Yosef would have been the literal firstborn. It was Leah who, through her prayers, *kidmatah l'Leah be'rachamim* — preceded Rachel by means of supplication — and thereby became the first wife and bore the first son. The *bechorah* was therefore not arbitrarily reassigned; it was returned to where it had always naturally belonged.

### Primogeniture Narrative

This leads the *gemara* into a broader reflection on what might be called the narrative of primogeniture running through *Bereishit*. The inversion of the firstborn's rights is not an isolated anomaly — it is a recurring pattern. Kayin and Hevel, Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Yosef: in every generation the expected right of the firstborn is displaced in favor of the more worthy. The irony is pointed: in *Devarim*, the Torah explicitly prohibits a father from giving the firstborn's portion to the son of the beloved wife over the son of the less-favored wife — *lo yuchal levaker et ben ha'ahuva al penei ben haSenu'ah habechor* — and yet that is precisely what Yaakov did, giving the rights to Yosef, the firstborn of his beloved Rachel, over Reuven, the firstborn of the less-favored Leah.

The *gemara*'s move here is subtle. It does not frame the *bechorah*'s transfer as merely a reward for virtue or a personal favor repaid. It frames it as the restoration of a destiny that was always rightfully Yosef's — rooted in the fact that Rachel was the wife Yaakov had always intended to marry first. This also reflects the broader dual narrative of the Torah: the structural norms of society demand that the firstborn maintain his position, but the deeper logic of the Torah is that the *bechorah* follows the deserving, not the merely chronologically prior. As God says of Israel: *beni bechori Yisrael* — my son, my firstborn, Israel — not because Israel was the first nation, but because Israel is the worthy one, elevated to the status of *bechor*.

---

## Rachel & Leah Merit

### Leah's Eyes

The *gemara* now elaborates on precisely how Leah preceded Rachel through prayer, and what merited Rachel's son the restoration of the *bechorah*. The starting point is the verse *ve'einei Leah rakot* — Leah's eyes were *rakot*, soft or weak. The *gemara* asks: what does *rakot* mean here? The straightforward reading — that her eyes were literally soft or weak — seems problematic. The Torah goes so far as to avoid saying the word *teme'ah* (impure) about a non-kosher animal, preferring the circumlocution "the animal that is not *tehorah*." If the Torah exercises such care about its language even regarding animals, would it speak disparagingly about the righteous Leah?

Rabbi Elazar offers a reading that turns the apparent slight into a compliment: *matnoteha aruchos* — her gifts are long, meaning her descendants will receive great gifts. The tribe of Levi will receive the priestly gifts — *matnot kehunah* — and the tribe of Yehudah will receive the kingship. The term *einei* may suggest a wellspring of blessing.

Rava, however, maintains the plain meaning — *rakot mamash*, literally weak — but reframes it as praise rather than criticism. Leah used to sit at the crossroads and ask passersby about the two sons of Rivkah and the two daughters of Lavan. People assumed the elder daughter would marry the elder son and the younger the younger. Travelers would tell her: the older son, Eisav? *Ish ra hu, melastem briyot* — an evil man, a bandit who attacks people. What of the younger? *Ish tam yoshev ohalim* — a wholesome man who sits in tents. And Leah wept until her eyelashes fell out — *ad she'nashru riseha* — so pained was she at the prospect of being assigned to Eisav. Her eyes' appearance, then, was the physical trace of her deep and sustained prayer to be spared from marrying a wicked man and to be joined instead with a righteous one.

### Leah's Prayer

The verse *vayar Hashem ki senu'ah Leah* — God saw that Leah was hated — raises a parallel difficulty. The *gemara* asks: *mai senu'ah*? Does it mean Yaakov literally hated her? Once again, the principle applies: if the Torah does not speak disparagingly of unclean animals, would it say something disparaging of righteous people? The answer reframes the word entirely. *Ra'ah Hakadosh Baruch Hu she'snu'in ma'aseh Eisav befaneha* — God saw that the actions of Eisav were hateful in her eyes. *Senu'ah* describes not how others regarded Leah but what Leah herself despised: the ways of Eisav.

### Eyelashes

Returning to the physical manifestation of her prayer: the description of Leah's eyes as *rakot*, according to Rava, is a *shevach* — a mark of distinction, not a blemish. The eyes that looked diminished were the eyes of a woman who had cried out of her commitment to righteousness and her longing to marry a *tzaddik*. The unusual physical appearance was the outward sign of an inner spiritual seriousness.

### Hated Eisav's Ways

It was precisely because of this — because she hated the ways of Eisav and prayed fervently to avoid them — that *vayiftach et rachmah*: God opened her womb. Leah merited to bear Yaakov's firstborn son not arbitrarily but because of this personal righteousness. Her prayers and her love of goodness preceded Rachel's; and so, her son Reuven was the actual firstborn.

### Rachel Warns

The *gemara* now turns to Rachel's *tzni'ut* — the modesty that merited the return of the *bechorah* to her son. The verse reads: *vayaged Yaakov l'Rachel ki achi aviha hu* — Yaakov told Rachel that he was her father's brother. The *gemara* notes the inaccuracy: Yaakov was not Lavan's brother but his nephew, the son of Lavan's sister. The *gemara* explains that what this verse really records is the following exchange. Yaakov asked Rachel to marry him. She agreed, but immediately warned him: *abba rama'ah hu* — my father is a deceiver, and *lo yachlat leh* — you will not be able to handle him.

### Deception Strategy

Yaakov asked her: in what way will he try to deceive me? She explained that Lavan would not allow her to marry before her older sister. This was not simply a refusal — it was a warning that Lavan would agree and then substitute Leah. Yaakov replied: *achiv ani b'rama'ut* — I am his equal in deception. Rachel then asked a pointed question: *u'mi sharei l'tzaddiki l'saguyei b'rama'uta* — is it permitted for righteous people to engage in deception? Yaakov answered with the verse *im navar titbar v'im ikesh titapal* — with the pure, act in a pure way; with the devious, act deceptively. If that is the adversary one faces, that is how one must respond.

This exchange carries weight well beyond the immediate narrative. The figure of Yaakov navigating Lavan's household became a template for the Jew in *galut* — the disempowered party who must exercise a different kind of resourcefulness when faced with an adversary who operates by different rules. The tension between integrity and strategic accommodation in conditions of powerlessness runs through many of the narratives of *Tanakh*.

Yaakov then gave Rachel secret signs — a kind of private code — so that if Lavan substituted Leah on the wedding night, Yaakov would know he was not with Rachel, because Leah would not know the signs.

### Secret Signs

When the time came, Lavan brought Leah into the tent. Rachel, at that moment, considered: *hashta michsafah achtai* — now my sister will be humiliated, publicly rejected. And so Rachel gave the secret signs to Leah. This is why the verse says: *vayehi vaboker vehineh hi Leah* — it was in the morning and behold, it was Leah. The *gemara* presses: does this imply that until that moment Yaakov did not know it was Leah? The answer: yes — *mitoch hasimanim shemasar l'Yaakov l'Rachel u'masartan l'Leah*, because of the signs that Yaakov had entrusted to Rachel, and that Rachel transmitted to Leah, Yaakov could not tell the difference.

### Sister's Honor

It is this act — Rachel's willingness to sacrifice her own marriage and her own position as Yaakov's first wife in order to spare her sister from public humiliation — that constitutes her *tzni'ut*. The word *tzni'ut* here does not refer to modesty in the narrow sense of dress or demeanor, but to a profound self-effacement in the service of another's dignity. Because of this act, her son Yosef ultimately merited the restoration of the *bechorah* that was, as Rabbi Yonatan said, always properly destined to come from her.

---

## Yocheved Birth

### Counting Problem

The *gemara* now turns to a separate question that arises from the same family narrative. Aba Chalifa Karuya posed the question to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba: when you look at the total number given for those who descended to Egypt with Yaakov's household, the Torah states *shivim* — seventy souls. But if you actually enumerate the names listed, you arrive at only sixty-nine.

### Leah's Count

The problem is already visible within the count of Leah's children specifically. The Torah states that Leah's descendants numbered thirty-three, yet an actual tally of the names yields only thirty-two. One cannot dismiss this as rounding, because the Torah itself gives a precise internal count for Leah that is off by one. The missing person must therefore be found among Leah's descendants.

### Dina Twin

One proposed solution is that Dina had a twin sister. The verse *v'et Dinah bito* — "and Dinah his daughter" — contains the word *v'et*, which some read as implying a twin. The *gemara*, however, challenges this: if *v'et* signals a twin, then by the same reasoning Binyamin should also have had a twin, since the verse reads *v'et Binyamin achiv*. The proponent of the Dina-twin theory responds: *margalit tovah haytah b'yadi* — I had a precious pearl in my hand, and you are trying to make me lose it. In other words, now that you are forcing me to give my real answer by showing that the Dina-twin reading leads to unwanted consequences, I must disclose the true solution, which I had preferred to keep as my own. The *Rashbam* explains: he was not truly upset about sharing the answer; he was dramatizing how fine the explanation was. The remark raises, in passing, the interesting question of intellectual ownership of *chiddushim* — a question that resonates differently in an age when private scholarship easily becomes public property.

### Yocheved Solution

The resolution, as stated by Rabbi Chama bar Hanina, is that the missing person is Yocheved — the daughter of Levi and the future mother of Moshe. *She'haratah baderech v'ladata bein hachomot* — she was conceived during the journey and born once they passed through the walls of Egypt. The verse *asher yaldah otah l'Levi b'Mitzrayim* is read carefully: her birth was in Egypt, *ladata b'Mitzrayim*, but her conception was not, *v'ein haratah b'Mitzrayim*. When the family set out from Canaan, there were sixty-nine souls. By the time they arrived within the walls of Egypt, Yocheved had been born, bringing the number to seventy. The count of thirty-three for Leah's descendants thus includes Yocheved, born in transit, and is exactly correct.

---

## Yosef Born

### Timing Question

A new question is posed by Rabbi Chelbo to Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani: the verse states *vayehi ka'asher yaldah Rachel et Yosef* — it was when Rachel gave birth to Yosef that Yaakov turned to Lavan and demanded to be released to return to his father's house. Why specifically at that moment? What was it about Yosef's birth that made Yaakov ready to leave?

### Yosef Defeats Eisav

The *gemara* explains: *ra'ah Yaakov Avinu she'ein zaro shel Eisav nimsar ela b'yad zaro shel Yosef* — Yaakov perceived prophetically that the descendants of Eisav would only be delivered into the hands of the descendants of Yosef. Yaakov knew that when he turned back toward Canaan he would immediately face Eisav, who was coming with four hundred men. He could not be ready to face that encounter — and, more broadly, could not be prepared for the long historical confrontation with Eisav's descendants — until Yosef had been born.

### Fire & Flame

The proof text is the verse from Ovadiah: *vehaya veit Yaakov eish uveit Yosef lehava uveit Eisav l'kash* — the house of Yaakov shall be fire, the house of Yosef a flame, and the house of Eisav shall be stubble. Fire does not ignite stubble without a flame as intermediary. The house of Yaakov alone — the other tribes — cannot bring Eisav down. It is the house of Yosef, the flame, that is the essential catalyst. Yaakov therefore waited until that catalytic force was present before he could contemplate the return journey.

### David Challenge

A challenge is raised: was there not a case where Eisav's descendants — specifically Amalek — were defeated without the involvement of Yosef's tribe? The verse in *Shmuel* records: *vayakem David mei'haneshef ve'ad ha'erev* — David smote them from dawn until the following day. David was from the tribe of Yehudah, not Yosef.

### Menashe Help

The response: *d'akrayach Nevi'ei lo akrayach Kesuvei* — whoever taught you *Nevi'im* did not teach you *Kesuvim*. In *Divrei HaYamim* it is written: *uvlecho Tziklag naflu alav mi'Menashe* — when David went to Tziklag, members of the tribe of Menashe joined him. The verse then lists them by name: Adnah, Yozavad, Yediael, Micha'el, Yozavad, Elihu, and Zilsai — *rashei ha'alafim asher l'Menashe*, captains of thousands from Menashe. David did not defeat Amalek alone; he had with him the tribe of Menashe, which is the tribe of Yosef. The principle stands.

### Shimon Challenge

Rav Yosef raises a second challenge. The verse in *Divrei HaYamim* records: *umeihem b'nei Shimon halchu l'Har Se'ir* — from the sons of Shimon, five hundred men went to Har Se'ir, the territory of Eisav. They are listed as going under the leadership of *b'nei Yish'i*, and the verse concludes *vayaku et she'erit hapeleita l'Amalek* — they struck down the remnant of Amalek. This was entirely under the banner of Shimon, with no apparent involvement of Yosef's descendants.

### Yish'ei Resolution

Rabba bar Shila resolves this: *Yish'i mibnei Menashe asi* — Yish'i, despite appearing in the context of Shimon, was in fact a descendant of Menashe. The textual support is a verse which lists Eifer and Yish'i among the descendants of Menashe: *v'eileh rashei beit avosam v'Eifer v'Yish'i*. Though the name appears in the context of Shimon's campaign, the leader Yish'i was from Menashe — from Yosef's tribe. The principle is thereby preserved: in every case where Eisav's descendants fell, the descendants of Yosef were present.

---

## Double Portion Categories

### Five Categories

The *gemara* returns to the halachic discussion with a new *baraisa*. The *bechor* takes a double portion in five categories: *zro'a, lechayim*, and *keivah* — the gifts given to a *kohen* from slaughtered animals; *mukdashin* — sanctified animals; and *shevach* — the appreciation in value of the estate after the father's death.

### Unguarded Property

The *baraisa* illustrates the rule of *shevach* with a case involving a cow. If the father left a cow that was leased out to a third party under a profit-sharing arrangement (*muchkeres*), or rented out outright (*muskeres*), or was simply grazing in the field — and it then gave birth after the father's death — the *bechor* takes a double portion of the newborn animal.

### Improvement Rule

By contrast, if the heirs actively built houses on the land or planted vineyards after the father's death, the *bechor* does not receive a double portion of the value of those improvements. The principle governing both rules will be analyzed further, but the distinction in outline is clear: passive appreciation that flows from assets already in the father's possession benefits the *bechor* doubly; active improvements generated by the heirs' own labor do not.

### Kohen Gifts

The *baraisa*'s inclusion of *zro'a, lechayim*, and *keivah* — the arm, cheeks, and maw given as priestly gifts when a non-sacred animal is slaughtered — is immediately puzzling. These gifts do not belong to the father; they must be given to a *kohen*. How can the *bechor* receive a double portion of something that was never the father's property?

---

## Mechari Kehunah

### Double in Ra'uy

The *gemara* sharpens the difficulty. If these priestly gifts had already been given to the father-*kohen* during his lifetime, then they are simply part of the estate and the *bechor*'s double portion is obvious — it falls within the ordinary rules of inheritance. But if the father died before receiving them, then they are *ra'uy* — something that was fit to come to him but had not yet arrived. And the rule of *bechorah* is explicitly that *ein habechor notal b'ra'uy k'vmuchzak* — the *bechor* does not receive a double portion in *ra'uy* as he does in property the father already held. So how can the *bechor* receive double in these gifts?

### Mechari Definition

The *gemara* answers: *hacha b'makirei kehunah askinan* — the case involves *makirei kehunah*, an established practice whereby particular families of householders always gave their priestly gifts to a specific *kohen* or *kohen* family. Under this arrangement, the gifts were not simply unclaimed goods awaiting assignment to any available *kohen*; they were as good as designated for this particular *kohen*. The relationship was sufficiently entrenched — and in some cases institutionalized across families — that the specific *kohen* effectively had a presumptive claim to them before they were formally handed over.

### Already Separated

Beyond the question of *makirei kehunah*, there is a further condition: *d'ishtachit b'chayei d'avuhon* — the animal must have been slaughtered during the father's lifetime. Only once the animal is slaughtered does the obligation to give the priestly portions take effect.

The underlying principle is then stated: *d'kasavar matnot shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu damu* — the priestly gifts, even before they have been physically separated and handed over, are regarded as if they have already been separated. This is a significant legal presumption: although the gifts still reside physically within the carcass of the animal, the obligation to separate them is treated as having already been fulfilled in a juristic sense.

### Gifts Presumption

The double *chiddush* operates as follows. The animal has been slaughtered, the obligation to separate the priestly portions has arisen, and because of the practice of *makirei kehunah* this *kohen* was the designated recipient. The combination of *matnot shelo hurmu k'mi shehurmu damu* — gifts treated as if already separated — and the established designation to this particular *kohen* means that, juristically, the father-*kohen* is treated as having already received these portions before his death. They are therefore *muchzak*, not merely *ra'uy*, and the *bechor* takes a double share.

*Tosafot* raises the question of whether this constitutes genuine ownership. Could the *kohen*, for instance, betroth a woman with these gifts before physically receiving them? The answer is probably not — the *kohen* is not yet technically the owner. But there is a middle category: not yet owned, yet already quasi-possessed by virtue of designation and legal presumption. It is this intermediate status that is sufficient to allow the *bechor* to take a double portion upon the father's death.

---

## Kodashim Kalim

### Kodashim Problem

The *baraisa* also lists *mukdashin* — sanctified animals — as a category in which the *bechor* takes double. This is at first glance even more difficult than the priestly gifts. Sanctified animals are not the father's property at all; they belong to the *Beit HaMikdash*. A *chatat*, for instance, is entirely *hekdesh*; the father has no proprietary interest in it whatsoever. How could the *bechor* receive double of something his father never owned?

### Shelamim Solution

The *gemara* resolves this by specifying: the case involves *kodashim kalim* — lesser-sanctified offerings — and specifically *shelamim*, peace offerings. In a *shelamim*, the owner eats virtually all of the meat; only the entrails are placed on the altar and a small portion goes to the *kohen*. The bulk of the animal remains, in a meaningful sense, the owner's.

### Mammon Ba'alim

According to Rabbi Yosi HaGelili, *shelamim* are considered *mammon ba'alim* — the financial property of the owner — even after they have been sanctified. This position allows the owner to betroth a woman with a *shelamim* animal, since he is giving her something of real value that he owns. The *gemara* uses this principle to resolve the *baraisa*: if a *kohen* — or indeed any person — sanctified a *shelamim* and then died before the offering was brought, his children bring it to the Temple, and upon eating the *bechor*'s portion of the meat, the *bechor* is entitled to double — because under Rabbi Yosi HaGelili's principle, the meat was and remains the owner's property, and the *bechorah* applies to it.

### Ma'ala Ma'al

The *gemara* cites a *baraisa* in support of Rabbi Yosi HaGelili's position. The verse dealing with a bailment reads: *uma'ala ma'al b'Hashem* — and he trespasses against God — in a case where one denies holding another's deposit and swears falsely. The plain meaning is that the false oath constitutes a trespass against God. Rabbi Yosi HaGelili reads it differently: the object itself has a dimension of belonging to God. An ordinary object held in trust does not belong to God. What object could simultaneously be denied to the human owner and constitute a trespass against God? A *shelamim* animal. If someone entrusted me with his *shelamim* before it was offered, and I deny it, I have robbed both him of his property *and* denied something that is also consecrated to God. The verse thereby implies that *shelamim* retain the character of *mammon ba'alim* — the owner's property — even while sanctified.

### Non-Kohen Shelamim

The implication extends beyond the case of a *kohen*-father. If any person sanctified a *shelamim* and died, his heirs bring the offering and the *bechor* among those heirs takes double of the meat. This is so because, according to Rabbi Yosi HaGelili, the meat of the *shelamim* is the owner's property — *mammon ba'alim* — and is therefore subject to the laws of inheritance and the *bechor*'s double portion, in contrast to other categories of *korbanos* where the concept of *mishulchan gavoah kazchu* applies: those who eat them eat from God's table, and the meat is not regarded as the personal estate of the owner.

---

---

# Bava Batra 124

## Bechor & Property Value

### Bechor Double Portion

The daf picks up at the bottom of 123b, in the middle of a discussion about whether a *bechor* receives a double portion in property that has increased in value after the father's death. The general rule is that a *bechor* does not collect *k'rauy k'muchzak* — he does not receive double in assets that were merely destined to come to the father, in the way that he receives double in assets already in the father's possession. Nevertheless, a *baraita* had stated that when property increases in value naturally, the *bechor* does receive the double portion. The Gemara will reveal that this is a disputed principle, attributed specifically to Rabbi and contested by the *rabbanan*.

### Stake vs. Estate Frame

One conceptual approach to the *bechor*'s double portion in post-mortem appreciation is to reframe the question entirely: perhaps the *bechor* is not receiving double in new value at all, but is simply receiving the natural yield on his already-established double stake in the principal. If a bank account earns interest after the father's death, each heir's share of that interest flows proportionally from his ownership of the principal — the *bechor*, holding two-thirds, simply earns interest on two-thirds. On this reading, no special *halacha* about *rauy* or *muchzak* is needed; the *bechor* earns the increase because he already owns more of the underlying asset.

### Tosafot Division Theory

Tosafot, however, draws a critical distinction: this logic applies only after the estate has been divided. Once each heir has taken possession of his specific portion, any subsequent appreciation belongs to him as owner of that portion. But prior to division, one cannot say that the *bechor* already holds two-thirds of the principal — the estate remains undivided, and any increase accrues to the estate as a whole, not to the *bechor*'s as-yet-unclaimed share. The question then becomes whether the *bechor* is entitled to double in the estate's post-mortem increase, and that is precisely where the dispute between Rabbi and the *rabbanan* lies.

To illustrate: if the estate is worth one million dollars and has not yet been divided, and it subsequently appreciates by ten thousand dollars, the *bechor* cannot claim that his portion of the estate grew by a proportional amount.
