He has not yet received his portion. When he comes to collect his double share, the *halacha* limits him to double of what the father possessed at the time of death. The ten thousand dollars that accrued afterward would, absent Rabbi's principle, be divided equally among all the heirs. What Rabbi says is that natural appreciation — appreciation requiring no investment by the heirs — is treated as though it had already existed in the father's possession, and therefore the *bechor* takes double of it as well.

---

## Rented Cow & Growth

### Baraita Sources

The Gemara presents a *baraita* addressing the case of a cow the father left behind, either rented out to others (*muchkeres*) or put out for profit-sharing (*mushkeres*), or alternatively left to graze freely in the wild (*ro'ah ba'eifer*). In all these cases, if the cow gave birth after the father's death, the *bechor* takes double of the offspring.

### Rented vs. Grazing

The Gemara immediately questions the *baraita*: if we already know from the case of a cow grazing freely that the *bechor* gets double — since the birth is entirely spontaneous and requires no effort — why do we need to be told the case of a rented or profit-sharing cow? Intuitively, one might have thought that a rented cow is more difficult: it is not even on the estate's premises, and to call the calf "already in the father's possession" seems like a greater stretch.

### Auto Growth Principle

The Gemara answers: the two cases illuminate each other. The emphasis in *ro'ah ba'eifer* — grazing literally in the dust, in the wild — highlights that the essential criterion is *shivcha di-meimeila*, an increase that comes about by itself, without requiring any expenditure from the heirs. The case of the rented or profit-sharing cow is then shown to satisfy the same criterion: from the perspective of the estate, the birth happens without any investment on the heirs' part. The fact that the person who rented the cow may have to feed it or that the profit-sharing partner has to exert effort is irrelevant — the heirs themselves invest nothing. Since from the heirs' vantage point the increase is entirely automatic, it is treated as *shivcha di-meimeila*, and the *bechor* gets double.

### Rashbam on Orphans

The Rashbam articulates this reasoning precisely. His concern is that one might have thought the rented cow does not qualify as automatic increase — after all, other people are exerting effort in connection with the animal. He answers: since the *yetomim* themselves do not plow, toil, or bear any costs in connection with it, and crucially since they do not pay for its feed (*d'ein ma'alin li-mezonot*), the increase is reckoned as *shivcha di-meimeila* from their perspective. It is this absence of investment on the part of the heirs that determines whether an increase qualifies, and wherever that criterion is met, the *bechor* takes double.

---

## Rabbi vs. Rabbanan

### Attribution to Rabbi

The Gemara now asks: whose position does this *baraita* represent? The answer is *Rabbi hi* — it is Rabbi's position. A further *baraita* makes the dispute explicit.

### Natural = Possessed

The *baraita* reads: the *bechor* does not receive double in appreciation that occurred in the estate after the father's death — this is the view of the *rabbanan*. Rabbi says: I maintain that the *bechor* does receive double in appreciation that occurred after the father's death, provided the appreciation came about naturally and not through the effort and investment of the heirs (*shivchu yetomim*). For Rabbi, natural increase is deemed as though it was already under the father's dominion, and the *bechor* therefore receives double of it. The *rabbanan* hold that only what was fully and actually in the father's possession at the time of death transfers with the double portion.

---

## Debts & Liens

### Debt Owed In

Among the cases listed is the following: if the heirs inherited a *shtar chov* — a debt instrument, money owed to the estate — the *bechor* takes double. This is presented as a case alongside the natural appreciation cases, and it invites examination of which authority it follows and what the underlying conceptual framework is.

### Accounts Receivable

The conceptual question is whether a debt owed to the estate is considered *muchzak* — already in the father's possession — or *rauy*, merely destined to come. On one reading, money that the father lent out is entirely out of his control at the time of death: the borrower holds it, and repayment is contingent on future events. On this reading, it seems squarely *rauy*. On another reading, however, since the father extended credit and holds a legal claim — he shipped goods, he performed services, he made a loan memorialized in a document — the receivable is very much a part of his estate. The principle *shtar chov ha-omed ligbot k'gavuy dami*, that a debt standing ready for collection is treated as though already collected, intersects directly with this question, even though the Gemara does not invoke it explicitly at this stage.

Rabbi's position, as will emerge, is that the debt — including interest owed by a non-Jew — is treated as part of the estate because it accrues automatically. The *rabbanan* dispute this, though with some internal nuance that will be addressed below.

### Debt Owed Out

The *baraita* also addresses the inverse: if the estate owes a debt, the *bechor* pays double his proportional share of that creditor's claim. The creditor holds a lien against the real estate, and since the *bechor* receives two-thirds of the real estate, two-thirds of the creditor's claim falls on him and one-third on the other brother. Whether the creditor chooses to collect the full amount from one heir or distributes his collection across both, the proportional liability is structurally tied to the proportional inheritance, and the *bechor*'s larger share carries a correspondingly larger burden.

### Waiving Double

Here the Gemara introduces an important *chiddush*: if the *bechor* says *eini noten ve-eini notel* — I will neither pay the extra portion nor receive it — he is permitted to do so. This option is unique to the double portion. A person cannot waive his basic share of an inheritance: *yerusha* descends automatically, and no *kinyan* or declaration, whether before or after the parent's death, can prevent an heir from receiving his statutory portion. Once received, he may give it away, but he cannot block himself from receiving it. The double portion of the *bechor* is different, because the verse says *latet lo pi shnayim* — "to give him double" — which the Gemara reads as conferring a *matana*, a gift. Just as one cannot be compelled to accept a gift against one's will, the *bechor* can decline his extra portion.

What would motivate a *bechor* to waive a benefit? The most obvious case is when the estate's debts equal or exceed its value. If the creditor is going to take everything anyway, the *bechor* gains nothing from accepting the double portion and immediately surrendering it to satisfy the lien. One might ask: since the creditor will pursue all the heirs regardless, what practical difference does the waiver make? Tosafot addresses this: if, for example, the other brothers are minors against whom the creditor cannot presently collect, the *bechor*'s waiver rolls his additional portion back into the general estate and effectively places it behind the shield of his minor siblings' legal protection. The creditor can still pursue the adult *bechor* for his basic share, but the extra amount, now absorbed into the general estate, cannot immediately be seized. Eventually the creditor may collect it when the minors come of age, but there is always the chance that circumstances change in the interim.

### Rabbeinu Tam View

Rabbeinu Tam offers an alternative reading of this case. He suggests that the *bechor*'s waiver is not directed at a debt against the estate but at a personal debt the *bechor* himself owes to a third party. Suppose the *bechor* personally owes a large sum. He knows that upon receiving his double portion, his creditor will immediately seize it. By declaring *eini notel*, he declines the extra inheritance so that it flows instead to his brothers — beyond the reach of his creditor. He still owes the money personally, but since he never received the extra portion, his creditor may never be able to collect. It is, as Rabbeinu Tam's reading implies, an early form of asset protection.

---

## Rabbi vs. Rabbanan (II)

### Rabbanan Limit

The Gemara now articulates the *rabbanan*'s principle directly. Their position is that only what was fully in the father's actual possession transfers with the double portion. The post-mortem increase, however natural, has not been in the father's domain.

### Verse Interpretations

The *machloket* turns on competing readings of the Torah's language. The *rabbanan* read *latet lo pi shnayim* — the double portion is described as something "given" — and derive from this that it functions like a *matana*. Just as one cannot give a gift of something one does not yet possess, the father cannot transmit a double portion in something that had not come into his hands before his death. Whatever increases after death is new, and the *bechor* has no prior claim to double of it.

Rabbi reads the verse differently. The Torah equates the *chelek bechorah* — the firstborn's extra portion — with the *chelek pashut*, the normal portion. Just as all heirs receive increases in the estate even if those increases only materialized after the father's death (since no one argues that the other sons lose the benefit of natural appreciation), so too the *bechor* continues to receive double of natural appreciation. The extra portion tracks the normal portion in this regard.

The Gemara anticipates an objection: do not the *rabbanan* also see the verse comparing the extra portion to the normal one? They do, but they interpret that comparison more narrowly — it teaches only that the *bechor*'s two portions must be physically contiguous: he receives one larger, unified plot rather than one portion in the north of a field and another in the south, with his brother's portion in between.

Conversely, does not Rabbi also contend with *latet lo*, the language of gift? He does, but he reads that phrase as establishing only the rule that the *bechor* may waive his extra portion, since gifts cannot be forced on an unwilling recipient. The comparison to a *matana* does not, for Rabbi, carry the implication that the property must have been fully possessed by the father. Everyone agrees that the *bechor* can waive the extra portion, and everyone agrees that the two portions must be adjacent. The sole dispute is whether natural increase qualifies as already possessed.

---

## Rav Pappa Refinement

### Agreed Natural Cases

Rav Pappa seeks to narrow the scope of the dispute by identifying cases where all opinions agree. If a palm tree grew thicker, or if land became enriched through natural flooding or soil improvement, all agree that the *bechor* takes double. The object is recognizably the same thing — only larger, only richer. This is considered so closely continuous with what the father possessed that even the *rabbanan* treat it as part of the original estate.

### Object Transformation

The dispute, Rav Pappa explains, arises in cases of genuine transformation: *shachas* — young shoots just emerging from the ground — that have become stalks of grain, or small saplings that have grown into full date palms. Physically, the growth is entirely natural and required no human intervention. But the entity has changed its essential character: it is now called something different and functions as something different.

### Transform Dispute

On this point Rabbi and the *rabbanan* divide. Rabbi maintains that even transformation is natural growth — *shivcha di-meimeila* — and since it happened without any investment by the heirs, it is treated as though the father had already possessed the resultant object. The *rabbanan* hold that because the object has genuinely changed its identity, what now exists is in effect a new object, not merely an improved version of the old one. The father never possessed this new object, and therefore the *bechor* cannot take double of it.

---

## Psak Halacha Authori (II)

### Both Legitimate

Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Chiyya: *asa k'divrei Rabbi asa, k'divrei chachamim asa* — if a judge ruled like Rabbi, he has acted legitimately; if he ruled like the sages, he has also acted legitimately. There is no established *psak* that definitively resolves the dispute, and a *dayan* is free to adjudicate either way. This freedom is meaningful precisely because there is a threshold beyond which a position is considered settled *halacha*, and a judge who departs from it would be *to'eh bi-dvar mishna*, rendering a reversible error. Here, both positions remain within the range of legitimate adjudication.

### Halacha Ke-Rabbi Rules

This prompts the Gemara to note a broader unresolved question: is it uncertain whether the general principle is *halacha ke-Rabbi mechaveiro velo mechaveirav* — we rule like Rabbi when he disagrees with a single colleague, but not when he disagrees with many — or whether the rule is that we follow Rabbi even against multiple colleagues. Since this general principle is itself unresolved, it is unclear whether the majority position of the *rabbanan* in this dispute carries decisive weight against Rabbi, and therefore both rulings remain viable.

### Rav Nachman Rejects

Rav Nachman citing Rav goes further: *assur la'asot k'divrei Rabbi* — one is not permitted to rule like Rabbi. The Rashbam explains that this is stronger than merely saying the *halacha* follows the *chachamim*; it implies that Rabbi's position is actually rejected. Accordingly, if a judge did rule that way, the judgment would potentially need to be reversed. This reflects the view that *halacha ke-Rabbi mechaveiro velo mechaveirav* — Rabbi's ruling authority holds only against a single disputant, not against the majority.

### Rav Nachman Permits

Rav Nachman in his own name, however, states: *mutar la'asot k'divrei Rabbi* — one is permitted to rule like Rabbi. The Gemara interprets this as equivalent to saying one is obligated to follow Rabbi's position, understanding *mutar* in its strong sense: the *halacha* follows Rabbi even against multiple colleagues, and ruling like the *chachamim* would be the error. This is a striking reading of the word *mutar*, and the Gemara acknowledges the interpretive tension it creates.

---

## Books of Beit Rav

### Midrashei Halacha ID

At this juncture the Gemara notes that Rav Nachman taught from *sh'ar sifrei d'vei Rav* — the other books of the house of Rav. The occasion to explain this phrase arises naturally, since the upcoming *baraita* will be a *drash* on a *pasuk* in Devarim and thus derives from the *Sifrei*.

The *midrashei halacha* are the halakhic midrashim on the four books of the Torah following Bereishit. The *Mechilta* — meaning "collection" — covers Shemos. The *Sifra*, meaning "the book," covers Vayikra and is the earliest and most extensively developed of the *midrashei halacha*; indeed, there is a scholarly argument that it was the first *Torah she-be'al peh* ever committed to writing. The *Sifrei* covers Bamidbar and Devarim, and editions of the *Sifrei* itself sometimes carry the label *Sifrei d'vei Rav* on their title pages. The *Mechilta* is also included in *sh'ar sifrei d'vei Rav* — the remaining books — while the *Sifra* is *the* book, the primary reference, and the others are secondary.

---

## Psak Halacha Authori (II)

### Rava: Prohibited

Rava stakes out a position between the extremes: *assur la'asot k'divrei Rabbi* — it is prohibited to rule like Rabbi — *aval im asa, asuy* — but if one did so rule, the judgment stands. The ruling is not the preferred *psak*, but it is not so far outside the range of legitimate positions that we would overturn it. The Gemara explains that this reflects the view that we incline toward the *chachamim* as a default, but we do not entirely reject Rabbi's position. One might say that this represents a middle path: not the open-ended latitude of Rabba bar bar Chana, not the full endorsement of Rav Nachman in his own name, but a nuanced ruling that treats the *chachamim* as the preferred authority while leaving Rabbi's ruling within the bounds of non-reversible adjudication.

---

## Books of Beit Rav (II)

### Rashbam Sources

The Rashbam provides a precise bibliographical note. *Sifrei d'vei Rav* refers to the *Torat Kohanim* — the *Sifra*, the *baraita* of Vayikra. *Sh'ar sifrei d'vei Rav* refers to the *midrash* on Bamidbar from *Va-yehi bi-nso'a ha-machaneh* through the end of that book, the *midrash* on Devarim (*Ve-eileh ha-devarim* through the end), and the *Mechilta* covering Shemos from *Ha-chodesh ha-zeh lachem* through the end. All three of these are called *sh'ar sifrei d'vei Rav*.

The Rashbam then adds the famous principle: the anonymous voice in the *Mishna* (*stam Matnitin*) is Rabbi Meir; the anonymous voice in the *Sifra* is Rabbi Yehuda; the anonymous voice in the *Sifrei* is Rabbi Shimon — that is, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai; the anonymous voice in *Seder Olam* is Rabbi Yose; and the anonymous voice in the *Tosefta* is Rabbi Nechemia. All of them follow the line of Rabbi Akiva, as all these sages were students of Rabbi Akiva.

### Debei Rav Meaning

As for the meaning of *d'vei Rav* in this context, early authorities disagree. The Rambam, in the *Mishneh Torah*, understands it as referring to the school of Rav the *amora*, who was responsible for the final editing of these volumes — meaning that even though the content derives from *tannaim*, the compilation as we have it was redacted under Rav's supervision. Rashi in Chullin interprets it differently: *d'vei Rav* means "the study hall," and the expression denotes the *midrash* that was universally familiar in the great academies.

---

## Debt Owed Analysis

### Debt Braita

The Gemara cites a *baraita* taught by Rami bar Chama from the *Sifrei* on the verse *be-chol asher yimatzei lo* — "with everything that is found belonging to him." The verse is read to exclude an increase in value that occurred after the father's death: the *bechor* takes double only in what was found in the father's possession at the time of death. This exclusion applies *a fortiori* to increases caused by the heirs' own efforts and investment, in which the *bechor* certainly does not receive double. The Gemara identifies this *baraita* as reflecting the position of the *rabbanan*, not Rabbi.

### No Double Position

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states: *ein bechor notel pi shnayim bi-milveh* — the *bechor* does not take double of a loan. The Gemara immediately asks: according to whom? If this is according to the *rabbanan*, the statement is so obvious as to need no teaching — the *rabbanan* already deny the *bechor* double even in natural appreciation of property that was physically within the estate's domain. How much more obviously would they deny double in a loan, where the money was completely outside the estate's control? The statement must therefore be directed at Rabbi's position — it comes to tell us that even according to Rabbi, a loan does not qualify as *shivcha di-meimeila*.

### Attribution Resolved

But the Gemara immediately challenges this: we have a *baraita* stating that if the heirs inherit a *shtar chov*, the *bechor* takes double — both of the principal (*milveh*) and of the interest (*ribis*). This *baraita* clearly contemplates that a debt owed to the estate, including interest accrued on a loan to a non-Jew, is fully subject to the double portion. That *baraita* must be Rabbi's view. So now the statement of Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name — that the *bechor* does not take double of a loan — cannot be according to Rabbi after all, since Rabbi appears to say the opposite. The Gemara resolves: the *baraita* allowing double on the loan is indeed Rabbi's view; the statement of Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name is *l'olam rabbanan* — in fact it does represent the *rabbanan*, and it is not as obvious as the Gemara initially supposed.

### Rabbi on Loans

The explanation is that Rabbi treats money owed to the estate — both principal and interest from a non-Jewish borrower — exactly as he treats rental income or the natural birth of a calf: it accrues automatically, without any effort by the heirs, and therefore it is treated as *shivcha di-meimeila*, as though it were already in the father's domain. The double portion applies. Interest on a loan to a non-Jew, which accumulates without requiring any action from the estate, is on the same footing as money from a rental property and is included in the *bechor*'s double.

### Middle Position

A report from Eretz Yisrael — *shalchu mi-tam* — introduces a middle position: *bechor notel pi shnayim bi-milveh aval lo bi-ribis* — the *bechor* takes double of the loan principal but not of the interest. The Gemara again asks: according to whom? If this is the *rabbanan*, we just established that the *rabbanan* deny double even on the principal. If it is Rabbi, we just said Rabbi grants double on both principal and interest.

### Rabbanan Split

The Gemara resolves: this is in fact the *rabbanan*'s position — but it reflects one version of what the *rabbanan* hold. There is an internal dispute within the *rabbanan* about the status of the principal of a loan memorialized in a document. One view — the position of *shalchu mi-tam* — holds that since the creditor possesses the *shtar* and holds liens on the debtor's property, the debt is sufficiently concrete and already-claimed that it counts as part of the estate: *milveh keivan d'nakit shetara k'man d'gavya dami*, once you hold the document it is as though you have already collected. On this view the *rabbanan* grant double of the principal. The interest, however, is genuinely new money that accrued after the father's death with no analogous anchor in a document, and the *rabbanan* deny double of it. The other version of the *rabbanan* — the position stated by Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name — holds that even the document is not enough, and neither the principal nor the interest is considered part of the estate for purposes of the *bechor*'s double.

The structure is thus: Rabbi holds that both principal and interest are part of the estate. The *rabbanan* divide — one view grants the principal alone, treating the *shtar* and its attendant liens as sufficient to make the debt already-possessed; another view denies double even of the principal, holding that money outside the father's physical control is simply not part of his estate.

---

---

# Bava Batra 125

## Bechor & Natural Growth

### Muchzak vs Ra'uy

The daf opens by returning to a question that has occupied the preceding discussion: does a *bechor* receive his double portion only in property that was already in the father's possession — *muchzak* — or also in property that was merely *ra'uy*, coming to the estate but not yet received at the time of death? The governing principle is that the *bechor* takes double only in *muchzak*, not in *ra'uy*.

### Rabbi vs Chachamim

Within this framework, *Rebbi* stakes out an expansive position. Where assets grew naturally — on their own, without any investment or effort on the part of the heirs — *Rebbi* maintains that the *bechor* does receive the double portion. The *chachamim* disagree. The Gemara refines the contours of this dispute: where a cow has simply grown fatter or a tree has grown larger, no one need ask how the animal or tree appeared at the moment of the father's death — that is uncontroversial incremental growth. The real debate concerns genuinely new income: rental proceeds that arrived after death, interest earned, or a cow that gave birth. When natural growth produces something substantively new, without any act of the heirs, does the *bechor* take double? *Rebbi* says yes; the *chachamim* say no.

---

## Loans & Debts

### Amemar on Loans

The Gemara then pivots to an analogous question involving loans and debts owed to the estate. *Rebbi*, consistent with his permissive stance on natural growth, would hold that both the principal and any interest from a loan made to a non-Jew are considered as having been in the father's possession, entitling the *bechor* to double. Among the *rabbanan*, two traditions emerge. *Shalchu mitam* — the ruling sent from Eretz Yisrael — holds that at minimum the principal of a debt is considered part of the estate, and the *bechor* receives double on it. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, by contrast, maintains that even collecting the principal is *ra'uy*: the father did not truly possess it at death, and the *bechor* therefore gets nothing.

Against this background, Rav Acha bar Rav asks Ravina about a teaching he had heard: *Amemar* arrived in their locale and expounded that a *bechor* receives his double portion in the principal of a loan (*milveh*) but not in the interest (*ribbit*). This position aligns with the *shalchu mitam* version of the *rabbanan*: the principal is sufficiently in the estate's possession to entitle the *bechor* to double, while the interest, being genuinely new income never possessed by the father, is excluded.

### Nehardea View

Ravina's response to hearing Amemar's ruling is pointed: *Nehardei l'ta'maihu* — Amemar is a Nehardean, and he rules consistently with the Nehardean school. The Nehardeans hold that at least under some circumstances debts owed to the estate are considered part of the estate, entitling the *bechor* to double.

### Rabba vs Rav Nachman

Ravina then invokes Rabba's formulation to illustrate what the Nehardean position entails. Rabba stated: *gavu karka yesh lo, gavu ma'ot ein lo* — if the heirs collected the debt in the form of land, the *bechor* receives double; if they collected cash, he does not. Rav Nachman states precisely the mirror image: *gavu ma'ot yesh lo, gavu karka ein lo* — cash gives the *bechor* double, land does not. Both Rabba and Rav Nachman are thus working within the shared premise that under at least some circumstances the principal of a debt is part of the estate. The dispute concerns the form in which it is collected.

A further observation: Rav Nachman is himself from Nehardea, and Rabba, though not a Nehardean, also takes a position within this framework. Amemar, for his part, made no distinction based on form of repayment — he simply said the *bechor* gets double in the principal. So the Nehardean connection is real but imprecise, and we will return to that below.

### Liens & Possession

What is the conceptual basis for distinguishing cash from land in this context? Rabba's position — that land counts but cash does not — is initially the easier one to understand. When a father lends money, he acquires a lien on the debtor's land. That lien constitutes a genuine monetary right in the land that was already in the father's possession at death. The *bechor* therefore inherits that right as part of the estate.

Rav Nachman's opposite ruling requires more explanation. He holds that land is *not* considered part of the estate — because, he reasons, even though liens exist, the debtor can always prevent their exercise by paying with other assets. The creditor has no guarantee of ever receiving that specific land. But why should cash be considered as having been in the *muchzak* of the father? The Gemara is about to challenge this, but it is worth articulating the prima facie logic: one might say that since the father lent cash and cash came back, conceptually it is as though the debtor returned what was always the father's. The loan is not the paper of the *shtar* — it is the money. The returned cash represents what was always owed, and so it can be viewed as if it was already part of the estate.

### Tosafot on Cash

That is indeed the explanation offered by the Rashbam: *ma'ot yahiv uma'ot shakil* — he gave money and he received money back, so it is as though the estate is simply reclaiming what it had. Tosafot, however, objects. The Gemara elsewhere treats damages owed to the estate — money owed not because of a loan but because someone harmed the estate's property — identically to a loan. There, the father never "gave" any cash; the debt arose from an act of damage. If the Rashbam's reasoning were correct, that case should be treated differently. Since it is not, the reasoning must be reexamined.

Tosafot therefore proposes an alternative: the reason Rav Nachman says that collecting cash entitles the *bechor* to double is that the ordinary expectation when a debt is owed — whether from a loan or from damages — is repayment in cash. *Derech ba'al chov lifroa b'chovo ma'ot v'lo karka* — it is the way of a creditor to be paid in money, not in land. Since cash is the natural expected mode of repayment, the father mentally relied on receiving it. That reliance renders it sufficiently like something already in his possession. Land, by contrast, is collected only when the debtor cannot pay otherwise; since the debtor can always satisfy the debt differently and prevent the creditor from reaching the land, the land cannot be considered *muchzak* — there is no assurance it will ever be received. The cash, by contrast, because it is conceptually what the debt *is*, is treated as if it were already in the estate.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye now challenges both positions. He addresses Rava first: *mai shna ma'ot d'lo* — why do you say that when the heirs collect cash it is not considered as having always been part of the estate? After all, it is not the same cash the father once held; it is entirely new bills. And the land they might collect — *lav hai karka shavak avuhon* — the father did not leave behind this specific land either. So the asymmetry is puzzling in both directions.

Abaye then turns a second challenge on Rava himself: you yourself have said that the position of *Bnei Ma'arava* — the sages of Eretz Yisrael — makes sense in the case of the grandmother. And in that case, he will argue, the logic of *Bnei Ma'arava* actually undermines Rava's distinction between cash and land. This takes us to the grandmother case, which the Gemara is about to develop.

### Creditor Collection

But first, Abaye raises a deeper problem for Rav Nachman's position specifically. He cites a ruling attributed to Rabbah bar Avuha — reported in the name of Rav Nachman himself — which states: *yetomim she-gavu karka b'chovot avihen, ba'al chov chozer v'goveh mehen* — if heirs collect land in satisfaction of a debt owed to their father's estate, a creditor of the father can then come and collect from that land.

Consider the structure of this case: the father died owing money to Reuven. He was himself owed money by Shimon. After the father's death, the heirs go and collect from Shimon, taking a parcel of land. Then Reuven arrives and says: now that the estate has assets, I will collect my debt from this land the heirs received. This only makes sense if that land is conceptualized as having *always been part of the estate* — as if it were property the father had possessed. If collecting the land were seen as the heirs acquiring entirely new property, Reuven would have no claim whatsoever; it would be their personal property, not subject to the father's debts.

But if collecting land is treated as though it was already part of the estate — which is what allows Reuven to collect — then Rav Nachman has a serious internal contradiction. He rules that when the heirs collect land, the *bechor* does not get double, precisely because it is not considered as having been part of the estate. Yet here, Rav Nachman himself apparently endorses a ruling that treats collected land as if it *were* part of the estate. This is a powerful challenge.

### Shibuda Mechanism

Rava responds to both challenges together: *lo l'didi kashya v'lo l'Rav Nachman kashya* — neither difficulty applies to me, nor to Rav Nachman. The reason: *ta'ama d'Bnei Ma'arava kamina, v'li lo sevira lan* — we were articulating distinctions *within* the position of *Bnei Ma'arava*, not expressing our own personal views.

This response, however, raises a further question: if neither Rava nor Rav Nachman actually hold the cash-vs.-land distinction, what are their own positions? The Rashbam explains that both hold the entirely restrictive view: nothing collected after the father's death — neither cash nor land — is considered part of the estate, and the *bechor* receives double in none of it. This is consistent with the practical *halacha* as we will rule it. As for the seeming contradiction in Rav Nachman's ruling — that a creditor can collect from land the heirs received — the Rashbam says this operates through an entirely different mechanism: *shibuda d'Rav Nosson*. If A owes B and B owes C, we can eliminate the middle step, treating it as if A owes C directly. Reuven therefore had a direct lien on Shimon's land already, independent of whether the inherited property was "part of the estate." The creditor's ability to collect from that land requires no assumption that the debt was *muchzak*; it flows from Rav Nosson's principle of direct cross-lien liability.

### Tosafot Position

Tosafot sharply disagrees with the Rashbam's reading and presents a strikingly different account of what Rava and Rav Nachman personally hold. According to Tosafot, the cash-vs.-land and land-vs.-cash distinctions are indeed the positions of *Bnei Ma'arava* — and Rava and Rav Nachman were merely articulating and subdividing that framework for reasons rooted in other *sugyot*, not expressing their own views. But when it comes to their personal positions, Rava and Rav Nachman hold precisely *opposite* to one another. Rava holds that nothing collected after the father's death — no debt, in any form — is ever considered part of the estate; the *bechor* receives nothing in any of it. Rav Nachman, by contrast, holds that it is *always* considered part of the estate, regardless of whether cash or land was collected — and accordingly the *bechor* always takes double in the principal. This, says Tosafot, is why Amemar's ruling — the *bechor* takes double in the *milveh* without any qualification based on form of repayment — was immediately identified as a Nehardean position: Amemar holds like Rav Nachman, who says simply that the principal is always *muchzak*, always part of the estate.

This raises the natural question of *pesika*: we generally rule like Rav Nachman in monetary matters. Does that mean the *bechor* takes double in the principal? We will address this when the Gemara renders its summary ruling.

---

## Grandmother Case

### Property Condition

The Gemara now turns to the grandmother case, which Abaye had invoked in his challenge to Rava. A person declared: *nichsai l'savta uvasra l'yarsai* — my property should go to my grandmother (or, depending on the relationship, his mother), and after her to my heirs. He had a daughter, who was married. The daughter died while her husband was still alive and while the grandmother was still alive. Then the grandmother died. The husband came forward claiming the property, arguing that his wife had been next in line, that right passed to her, and therefore it now passes to him.

### Rav Huna vs Anan

Rav Huna and Rav Anan initially frame the debate as a question of how to parse the word *yorshai* — my heirs. Does it mean immediate heirs only, or does it extend to the heirs of heirs? Rav Huna says *yorshai* includes even *yorshai yorshai* — the heirs' heirs. Since the husband (when the gift was constituted) would have stood as the heir of the daughter, he presents himself as satisfying that clause and claims the property. Rav Anan says *yorshai* means immediate heirs and not the heirs of heirs, so the husband does not qualify.

### Parsing Heirs

The Gemara reports that *shalchu mitam* — they sent from Eretz Yisrael — that we rule like the *rabbanan* but not for their stated reason. The *rabbanan* held that *yorshai* excludes second-degree heirs, meaning even a biological grandchild of the daughter would be excluded. But the Gemara rejects this: if the daughter had a son, that son would certainly inherit. The language of *yorshai* does not restrict us to first-degree heirs; biological heirs-of-heirs are included.

### Husband Status

The real reason the husband does not inherit, says *shalchu mitam*, is entirely different: *mishum d'hava lei ra'uy v'ein ha-ba'al notel b'ra'uy k'v'muchzak* — because what was coming to the wife was *ra'uy*, and a husband does not take *ra'uy* as he takes *muchzak*. A son inherits even *ra'uy* — new property arriving into the mother's estate after her death still passes to her blood relatives, because the blood relationship persists through death. But the marital bond is severed at death, so the husband has no claim on anything that was merely *ra'uy* to his wife.

Why is this property considered *ra'uy* and not *muchzak*? Because the grandmother could have sold the property at any point. Had she done so, the chain would have been broken and the daughter would have received nothing. The daughter's entitlement was therefore never a sure possession; it was entirely contingent on the grandmother dying with the property intact. That contingency renders it *ra'uy*. Since it was only *ra'uy* to the daughter, the husband cannot collect it.

### Shachid Mitam

The ruling of *shalchu mitam* thus introduces a sharp but important distinction: the son of a deceased heir would collect because blood heirs take *ra'uy*, while the husband does not collect because he takes only *muchzak*. The entire debate about parsing the words of the gift — does *yorshai* include second-degree heirs — turns out to be the wrong question. The question is halachic: what is the nature of the deceased's claim, and who may inherit something that was merely *ra'uy* to her?

### Rav Elazar's Rule

In response to these positions, Rav Elazar offers a formulation that reorients the analysis entirely: *kol ha-omer acharecha ke-omer me-achshav dami* — whoever says "after you" is as if saying "from now." When the giver declared that first the grandmother, and after her, his heirs should receive the property, the legal effect, according to this principle, is as if he immediately transferred the property to the ultimate recipient — here, the daughter. The grandmother is not the owner; she is, as it were, the custodian with rights of use during her lifetime. The actual ownership vests immediately in the daughter. If so, it is not *ra'uy* to the daughter at all — she already owns it. And if she fully owned it, upon her death that ownership passes to her husband. This is the position that explains Rav Huna's ruling that the husband does collect.

The logical corollary of this principle is striking: if the daughter is the true owner from the moment of the gift, the grandmother should not be able to sell the property outright. She may transfer her own right of use, but the underlying ownership belongs to the daughter and cannot be alienated. This is precisely what distinguishes the two camps in this case.

### Rava's Argument

Rava now closes the loop with Abaye's earlier challenge. Rava says: *mistabra ta'ama d'Bnei Ma'arava* — the position of *Bnei Ma'arava* is well-reasoned, specifically their ruling that the husband does not collect. Why? *D'kadim savta v'zabna, zvinei zvinei* — because the grandmother could preemptively sell the property, and the sale would be valid. If the sale is valid, then the daughter was never in actual possession; she never truly owned it; the grandmother retained the power to divest her at will. Therefore what the daughter stood to receive was *ra'uy*, and the husband, taking only *muchzak*, cannot collect.

One should note that this is a consistency argument rather than a proof. The person who holds that the daughter is the full owner from the moment of the gift (*ke-omer me-achshav dami*) will say that the grandmother *cannot* validly sell it, so the premise is disputed. What Rava is showing is that the two positions are each internally coherent: if you assume the grandmother can sell, then the daughter's interest is *ra'uy*, and the husband is excluded; if you assume she cannot sell, then the daughter is *muchzak*, and the husband collects. Neither side is arguing from neutral ground — each is articulating what is consistent with its own assumptions.

### Rav Papa Ruling

The Gemara concludes with Rav Papa's definitive ruling: *ein ha-ba'al notel b'ra'uy k'vi-muchzak* — the husband does not take *ra'uy* as he takes *muchzak*. The Rashbam explains that this ruling implicitly endorses the position of *Bnei Ma'arava* and of Rav Anan: the grandmother retains the power to sell; the daughter's entitlement is therefore *ra'uy*; and the husband does not collect.

---

## Bechor Summary

### No Double in Ra'uy

The Gemara now draws together all the threads of the discussion into a series of definitive rulings. *Ein ha-bechor notel b'ra'uy k'vi-muchzak* — the *bechor* does not take double in *ra'uy* as he takes in *muchzak*. This principle is of course foundational and undisputed, but the ruling here is understood to resolve all the contested applications we have been examining. In all the gray areas — natural growth, new rental income, interest from a non-Jewish borrower, a cow giving birth — the *halacha* takes the restrictive view. Since none of these were fully in the father's possession at the time of death, the *bechor* receives no extra portion. By contrast, things like a cow simply growing fatter or a tree growing thicker, where nothing new has been created, present no question — everyone agrees those increments belong to the estate. What the ruling settles is the disputed middle ground: anything that constitutes genuinely new income, however naturally it arises, does not count as *muchzak*, and the *bechor* does not receive double.

### No Double in Debts

Furthermore, *ein ha-bechor notel pi shenayim b'milveh* — the *bechor* does not receive double in any debt owed to the estate. This applies *bein she-gavu karka bein she-gavu ma'ot* — whether the heirs collected the debt in the form of land or in the form of cash. The ruling thus cuts across both positions in the Rabba-Rav Nachman debate and adopts the most restrictive outcome: nothing collected after the father's death in satisfaction of a debt is treated as *muchzak*. Notwithstanding that we ordinarily rule like Rav Nachman in monetary matters, the practical *halacha* here does not follow his expansive personal view.

### Bechor's Own Debt

The Gemara adds one final and rather elegant case: *u-milveh she-imo palgi* — where the *bechor* himself owed money to his father, we split. The case is as follows: the *bechor* owed the father a thousand dollars. After the father dies, the *bechor* pays the debt into the estate, and now that money must be divided among the heirs. Does he receive double his share of it — treating the money as *muchzak* that was always essentially his — or only a single share, since the money arrived after the father's death and is *ra'uy*? The answer is: we split. He receives not a full double portion and not a single equal share, but half of the additional portion he would have received had the money been treated as *muchzak*.

The logic of splitting rests on genuine uncertainty. Since the *bechor* owed the money to his own father — not to some arm's-length creditor — there is reason to think he would have wanted to settle the debt before the father's death, and the father might have considered it as good as paid. On that reasoning, the money could be viewed as already effectively in the estate. But we cannot be certain. Faced with this *safek*, we do not know whether the money should be treated as *muchzak* — entitling the *bechor* to double — or as *ra'uy* — giving him only an equal share. We therefore split the difference, with the *bechor* receiving half of the extra portion.

### Ketubah & Geonim

Tosafot, in a discussion carried over onto 126a, notes that the rules for what counts as *muchzak* are not uniform across all contexts. By *ketubah*, the widow operates with a broader definition of *muchzak*, ensuring that she is protected to a greater degree than the *bechor*'s entitlements might suggest.

More consequentially for practical law, Tosafot observes that the landscape shifted fundamentally in the *geonic* period: *u-vezman hazeh de-takinu geonim de-gavya isha ba'al chov mi-mitaltelei de-yatmei* — in our times, the *geonim* enacted a *takana* permitting creditors — and a widow with her *ketubah* — to collect even from the movable property (*metaltelin*) left by the deceased, not only from land. The background is straightforwardly commercial: in a less landed, more mercantile society, restricting creditor collection to real estate would severely chill lending. The *geonim* therefore expanded the scope of collectible assets, allowing creditors to recover from *metaltelin* of the orphans just as they could previously recover from land. This *takana* substantially reshapes the practical application of the principles discussed throughout the daf.

---

---

# Bava Batra 126

## Bechor Micha & Muchzak

### Muchzak vs. Ra'uy

The daf opens with a ruling transmitted by Rav Huna in the name of Rav Assi. The discussion continues the theme that has occupied the preceding pages: the *bechor*'s entitlement to a double portion (*pi shnayim*) applies only to what is *muchzak* — property already in the father's possession at the time of death — and not to *ra'uy*, property that was merely "coming his way" but had not yet been received. The parameters of this distinction are applied narrowly: even a loan the father had extended, with the repayment still outstanding, is treated as *ra'uy* and therefore excluded from the *bechor*'s enhanced share.

### Bechor's Objection

Against this backdrop, Rav Huna in the name of Rav Assi introduces the principle of *bechor she-micha micha* — if a *bechor* formally objects, his objection is legally significant. The context, as the Rashbam explains it, is as follows. Suppose a father died leaving, say, four fields to three sons. The *bechor* is entitled to two of those fields while his brothers share the remaining two. Before the estate has been formally divided, the *bechor* might fear that if the brothers work the undivided fields and improve them, any increase in value will be treated as *ra'uy* — as something that arose after the father's death and before division — and will therefore be split equally rather than double. He therefore protests: do not work the fields. I want the division done now, and I will then work my own portion. His objection, says Rav Assi, is legally effective. If the brothers proceed to work the fields in defiance of his protest, the improvement is treated as having been made to his portion, not to the undivided estate, and he retains his double share in it.

### Shevach Di-Mimmela

Rabba qualifies this ruling significantly. Even granting the force of the *bechor*'s protest, Rabba refuses to accept it in full. His concern is conceptual: since the estate has not yet been divided, the *bechor* does not yet know which specific fields are his. When he protests, there is no identified portion to which his protest can attach; everything still belongs generically to the estate. If the brothers proceed to harvest the grapes or the olives (*batzira* and *maskika* respectively), Rabba will concede that the *bechor* retains his double portion in the harvested produce — but only because harvesting, in the Talmud's framework, does not constitute a major transformation of the object. Even absent any protest, the rabbis treat a *shevach di-mimmela*, a natural or minimal enhancement that does not substantially alter the object's character, as *muchzak* rather than *ra'uy*. In such a case, the *bechor*'s protest reinforces what would already follow from the underlying rule.

However, if the brothers went further and *darchum* — pressed the grapes into wine or the olives into oil — that is a fundamental transformation. At that point, Rabba holds that even after the *bechor*'s protest, since the specific fields have not been demarcated as his, the newly created wine or oil remains part of the undivided estate and is therefore *ra'uy*. The *bechor* cannot claim a double share in it. Rav Yosef disagrees and rules *afilu darchum* — even if they pressed — the *bechor* retains his double portion, apparently accepting that the fact of the protest is enough to treat the *bechor*'s share as already crystallized.

### Damage Compensation

The *gemara*, however, refuses to accept either reading at face value. The transformation from grapes to wine (*meikara invi ve-hashta chamra*) is so substantial that the *gemara* insists: there is no way to say the *bechor* gets a double portion in the wine. It is simply *ra'uy*, full stop. The *gemara* therefore reinterprets the entire sugya — including the ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, which stated that even after pressing the *bechor* takes *pi shnayim* — on the basis of a principle stated by Rav Ukva bar Chama: *leiten lo d'mei hezek anavav*, we are not talking about the *bechor* receiving a double share of the improved value. Rather, the discussion is about *damage compensation*. If the brothers worked the estate over the *bechor*'s explicit objection, and in the process something went wrong — the grapes were ruined, the produce diminished in value — then the *bechor* is not required to absorb a proportional share of that loss. He protested; they proceeded anyway. Had they left well enough alone, his double portion in the original grapes would have been protected. Since they acted against his objection and caused harm, they bear responsibility for the damage to his share.

To illustrate: if the entire estate's grapes were worth four hundred dollars, the *bechor* stood to receive two hundred dollars' worth as his double portion. The brothers work the grapes, press them carelessly, and the whole batch is now worth only two hundred dollars. The natural instinct would be to divide the two hundred proportionally — one hundred to the *bechor*, fifty each to the other two brothers. But because the *bechor* protested, he is entitled to the full two hundred he would have received had they left his portion untouched. The brothers must absorb the loss.

The Rashbam frames this in terms of *gezel*: by proceeding against his explicit objection, the brothers effectively appropriated his share and are liable as a *kegazlan*. That framing is admittedly strained, since the *gemara* itself has not yet treated the *bechor*'s share as formally his before *chalukah*. But the operative principle is clear: his objection insulates him from losses the brothers cause. This is, as the lecturer notes, a genuinely unsatisfying *gemara*. The scenario of *hezek* is left vague, the precise mechanism of *micha* is unclear, and the ruling about pressing is entirely recharacterized. Nevertheless, within the Rashbam's reading, the underlying principle is coherent: formal *chalukah* is the only event that concretizes the *bechor*'s claim to specific property. Short of that, his protest cannot turn *ra'uy* into *muchzak*, but it can prevent him from suffering at the hands of brothers who acted in defiance of his expressed wishes.

---

## Waiving Bechor Rights

### Implicit Waiver

The *gemara* introduces a new ruling from Rav Assi: *bechor she-natal chelek k'pashut, viter* — if a *bechor* accepted a portion equal to that of a regular son, he has waived his rights. The underlying conceptual foundation here is the principle, encountered earlier in the *gemara*, that the *chelek bechorah* — the extra portion — is characterized by the Torah almost as a *matanah*, a gift given to the *bechor*, rather than as a standard inheritance that accrues automatically. Because it has the character of a gift, it is, in principle, refusable. One who does not insist on his *bechor* portion during the division of the estate has implicitly declined that gift. The question the *gemara* proceeds to debate is: how far does that waiver extend?

### Rights Kodem Chalukah

Two opinions are transmitted by different Amoraim, both ostensibly in the name of Rava. Rav Papa says: *viter b'ota sadeh* — he has waived only in that specific field. He has not waived his *bechor* portion for the rest of the estate. Rav Pappi says: *viter b'chol ha-nechasim kulam* — by waiving his portion in one item, he has waived his double share across the entire estate.

The conceptual basis of each position rests on a deeper dispute: *yesh lo la-bechor kodem chalukah* or *ein lo la-bechor kodem chalukah* — does the *bechor* have an existing, actionable claim to his double portion before the estate has been formally divided?

Rav Papa holds *ein lo la-bechor kodem chalukah*: until the division actually occurs, the *bechor* does not yet possess his extra portion in any legally meaningful sense. Because a waiver can only relinquish something one currently holds, a *bechor* can only waive at the moment the division is taking place and specifically with respect to the item being divided at that moment. When they are dividing the field and he agrees to take a third, he waives in that field. But he cannot be said to have waived his claim to the stocks, the cash, or the other real estate — those divisions have not yet happened, and at this moment he holds no claim to them that could be surrendered. When those subsequent divisions occur, he remains free to assert his *bechor* right, or even to reverse what he seemed to concede earlier.

Rav Pappi holds *yesh lo la-bechor kodem chalukah*: even before formal division, the *bechor* already holds a 50 percent stake in the estate — 25 percent as a regular heir and 25 percent as *bechor*. That 25 percent *bechor* claim is real and present, even if not yet localized to specific assets. Because he already holds it, he can waive it. And if we are prepared to read his acceptance of an equal share in one item as an implicit global waiver — meaning he intended to relinquish his entire *bechor* claim — then that waiver is binding immediately and applies to everything.

The Rashbam notes that the earlier *gemara* about the *bechor*'s right to protest and prevent his brothers from working the estate before division appears to presuppose the position of Rav Pappi — that the *bechor* already has an existing claim *kodem chalukah*, which is why his protest carries legal weight.

The *gemara* adds that these positions of Rav Papa and Rav Pappi were not stated explicitly (*lo b'ferush itmar*), but were inferred (*michlala itmar*) from a practical ruling each gave in the following case.

### Sale Before Division

There was a certain *bechor* who went and sold not only his own portion but also that of his brother — both the *bechor* portion and the *pashut* portion he was treating as his to dispose of. The children of the *pashut* (referred to for clarity as the children of Shimon) had been accustomed to eating dates from the palm trees in that field. Now that the field had been sold to purchasers, the purchasers drove them off. The relatives of Shimon's children complained: it is not enough that you have taken our property — now you beat them as well? The matter came before Rava, who said: the sale was invalid. Reuven had no right to sell Shimon's portion — that is straightforward.

The dispute between Rav Pappi and Rav Papa, inferred from their positions in this case, concerns Reuven's own portion. According to Tosafot's reading: Rav Pappi held that the sale was invalid only with respect to Shimon's one-third, but it was valid for Reuven's own two-thirds — both his *pashut* portion and his *bechor* portion. The other position held that it was valid only for his *pashut* portion, not for his *bechor* portion, since the *bechor* portion before *chalukah* is not yet his to sell. The Rashbam reads the case differently and more complexly, but the debate is difficult to reconcile precisely with the language of the *gemara* as it stands.

The *gemara* then cites a ruling transmitted from Eretz Yisrael: *bechor she-machar kodem chalukah lo asa klum* — a *bechor* who sold his *bechor* portion before division accomplished nothing. This seemingly settles the matter in favor of the position that the *bechor* has no rights before *chalukah*. Yet the *gemara* immediately records the *halacha*: *yesh la-bechor kodem chalukah* — the *bechor* does have a claim before division, and therefore his sale or waiver is meaningful from that moment. The debate between Tosafot and the Rashbam concerns whether the same principle extends to his *pashut* portion or only to the *bechor* portion, which carries the character of a *matanah*.

### Pepper Basket & Total Wa…

Mar Zutra from Rishba divided a basket of peppers equally with his brothers, even though he was a *bechor*, implicitly waiving his *bechor* portion in that one transaction. The matter came before Rav Ashi, who ruled: *hovil u-vitarta be-miktzat, vitarta b'chol ha-nechasim kulam* — since you waived your rights in part, you have waived your rights in the entire estate.

This ruling flows directly from the position that a *bechor* has *yesh lo kodem chalukah*: because his *bechor* claim is already an existing right across the whole estate, waiving it in one place is read as a global forfeiture. Yet the conclusion is striking. Whatever the legal architecture, it is difficult to understand why agreeing to an equal division over a basket of peppers should be read as surrendering one's double share in lands, liquid assets, and an entire multi-million dollar estate. One might say that *Chazal* were themselves somewhat uneasy with the rigidity of the *pi shnayim* right, and this pattern — characterizing the *chelek bechorah* as a *matanah*, treating minimal waivers as sweeping forfeitures, and enabling broad workarounds through the language of gifts — reflects a broader tendency to soften the Torah's strict allocation. This theme will continue immediately in the next *mishnah*.

---

## Gifts vs. Inheritance

### Direct Stipulations Void

The *mishnah* presents two cases of explicit paternal intervention. If a father says *ish ploni bni bechor lo yitol pi shnayim* — "this person is my firstborn son but shall not receive a double portion" — or *ish ploni bni lo yirash im echav* — "this is my son but shall not inherit alongside his brothers" — *lo amar klum*, his words are legally void. One cannot directly countermand the Torah's structure of inheritance. The father's attempt to override *din Torah* through explicit declaration is simply ineffective, because *heistna al ma she-katuv ba-Torah* — he has stipulated against what is written in the Torah.

### Matana Workaround

The *mishnah* then introduces the workaround. If a father is *mechalek nechasav al piv* — distributing his estate by verbal instruction — and he increases one heir's share, decreases another's, and equalizes the *bechor* with the other sons, this is *divrav kayamim* — his words stand — provided it is framed as a gift (*matanah*) rather than as an inheritance. This is the operative mechanism of the rabbinic will and of *matnat shechiv mera*, the deathbed bequest: rather than reassigning inheritance, the father converts his entire estate into gifts, which he then distributes as he sees fit. The Torah's rules of inheritance apply to what remains as *yerushah*; if everything has been designated as gifts, nothing is left to which the inheritance laws apply.

There is a practical implication: if the father wants the *bechor* to receive no more than any other son, he cannot leave anything undistributed. As long as any property remains undistributed, the *bechor* will receive a double portion of that remainder by operation of Torah law. Complete equalization therefore requires converting the entire estate into gifts.

The *mishnah* adds a nuance: *katav bein be-techilah bein be-emtza bein be-sof mishum matanah divrav kayamim* — whether the language of *matanah* appears at the beginning, middle, or end of the document, his instructions are valid. A person who writes "let so-and-so inherit (*yirash*) twenty percent of my estate, and have it as a gift (*matanah*), and be his inheritance" has satisfied the requirement by including the word *matanah* somewhere in the document. The courts will treat the disposition as operating through the mechanism of gift, even though it is surrounded by the language of *yerushah* and clearly designed to reassign the inheritance. As long as somewhere the word *matanah* appears, the operative legal category is gift, and the distribution is valid.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Principle

The *gemara* challenges the *mishnah*. Perhaps it represents only the view of Rabbi Meir, not of Rabbi Yehuda — and therefore cannot be assumed to be authoritative. The underlying question is Rabbi Yehuda's principle: *bidvar she-be-mamon, tna'o kayam* — in monetary matters, a stipulation against a Torah-assigned obligation is valid.

The principle is illustrated through a *beraita* concerning *kiddushin*. If a man betroths a woman *al menat she-ein li alayich she'er kesut ve-onah* — on the condition that he will have no obligations of food, clothing (*kesut*), and conjugal relations (*onah*) toward her — Rabbi Meir holds that the *kiddushin* takes effect but the stipulation is void: one cannot contract out of Torah-mandated marital obligations. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *bidvar she-be-mamon tna'o kayam* — the monetary components of the obligation, food and clothing, can be stipulated away. What cannot be stipulated away is the personal obligation of *onah*, because that is a fundamental personal dimension of the marital relationship, not merely a financial one.

Rabbi Yehuda's broader position is that wherever the Torah imposes financial obligations as the default terms of a two-sided transaction, those are precisely that — defaults. Because both parties can agree, and because monetary obligations are always in principle waivable (*mechilah* is always available), the Torah's assignment of financial responsibilities in bilateral relationships does not preclude the parties from structuring those responsibilities differently. The same logic, one might think, would apply to the laws of inheritance: these too are monetary matters, and if the Torah assigns them as defaults, perhaps the parties — including the heirs — can stipulate otherwise.

The *gemara* therefore raises the possibility: perhaps our *mishnah*, which says one cannot stipulate against Torah-defined inheritance, is specifically the view of Rabbi Meir, not Rabbi Yehuda. According to Rabbi Yehuda, perhaps even direct stipulations against the *bechor*'s double portion would be valid.

### Not Two-Sided

The *gemara* deflects this challenge: *afilu teima Rabbi Yehuda* — even according to Rabbi Yehuda, our *mishnah*'s ruling is valid. The key distinction is: *hatam yada ve-kamachla* — in the cases where Rabbi Yehuda validates stipulations, there is a party who knows what they are giving up and consciously waives it. A woman entering *kiddushin* knows the default obligations and can agree to forgo the monetary ones. A *shomer* entering a bailment arrangement knows the default liability rules and can agree to different terms. Both cases involve two active parties who knowingly restructure a bilateral transaction.

Inheritance is fundamentally different. It is not a transaction. The heir does not enter into a deal; property transfers automatically upon death by operation of Torah law. There is no act of "bequeathing" by the deceased — he simply dies, and the Torah moves the property. The heir did not agree to anything, and one cannot say *kamachla* — that the heir waived — because the heir was never in a position of choosing to receive or not receive. Even if the heir were to say explicitly "I waive my inheritance," the Rashbam notes, we cannot fully trust it, since he may be saying so only to please his father. But more fundamentally, the absence of a bilateral transaction means there is no two-sided framework within which stipulations can operate. The conclusion of the *gemara* is that Rabbi Yehuda's principle has no foothold here: *hachi lo kamachla* — in the context of inheritance, there is no *mechilah* structure in place that could validate a stipulation against the Torah's rules.

---

## Proving Bechor Status

### Father-Firstborn Required

Rav Yosef establishes an important evidentiary distinction. If a father says *ish ploni bni bechori* — "so-and-so is my son, my firstborn" — the son receives the double portion, as the *mishnah* teaches. But if the father says only *ish ploni bechor hu* — "this person is a *bechor*" — that is insufficient to entitle the son to *pi shnayim*, even if those present understood him to be referring to his son. The reason: *dilma bechor de-imma ka'amar* — perhaps he meant that this person is firstborn to his mother (*bechor de-imma*), not firstborn to his father. The *bechor* entitled to a double portion under Torah law is specifically the firstborn male of the father, *peter rechem ha-av*. A person who is the first male child of a mother but not of his father (*bechor de-imma*) has the status of *peter rechem* for certain purposes — such as *pidyon ha-ben* — but does not receive the patrimonial double portion. The father's ambiguous statement cannot be read as a definitive declaration of paternal firstborn status, since another plausible interpretation is available.

### Buchra Sikhla Nickname

A case came before Rabba bar bar Chana (with the Rashbam noting that there were two witnesses, as required). A witness claimed to know that a certain individual was the *bechor* of his deceased father. When asked the basis for this knowledge, the witness replied: *da-hava kari lei avuh buchra sichla* — his father used to call him "foolish firstborn." The nickname "foolish firstborn," the witness reasoned, demonstrates that the father himself viewed this son as his *bechor*.

### Rabba's Skepticism

Rabba bar bar Chana rejected this evidence. *Dilma bukhra de-imma hu* — perhaps this person is the firstborn of his mother but not of his father. *De-chol bukhra de-imma nami bukhra sichla karu lei* — any person who is a *bechor de-imma* but not a *bechor de-abba* might be called a "foolish firstborn," since he is, as it were, a near-miss: he has the firstborn status that pertains to *peter rechem* of the mother, but lacks the more consequential paternal firstborn status. The term *sichla* ("foolish" or "unfortunate") might itself be a commentary on this incomplete status — a *bechor* in name only, not in the fullest legal sense. Because this alternative reading of the nickname is plausible, the evidence is insufficient to establish paternal *bechor* status.

### Spittle Healing Proof

A similar case came before Rav Chanina. Again witnesses appeared, claiming to know that a certain individual was a *bechor*. When asked how they knew, they reported: *de-ki havu atu gabbei avuha, amar lehu: zilu le-gabbei Shichchas beri, de-bechor hu, u-masi rokei* — when people would come to his father for treatment, the father would direct them: go to Shichchas my son, he is a *bechor*, and his spittle has healing properties. The Rashbam explains that there was a widespread belief that the spittle of a firstborn son had medicinal efficacy for eye ailments.

The *gemara* anticipates the obvious objection: *dilma bechor de-imma hu* — perhaps he is only firstborn of his mother? This time, however, the objection fails. *Gemiri: bechor de-abba masi rokei, bechor de-imma lo masi rokei* — it is a received tradition that only the spittle of a *bechor de-abba* has these healing properties, not that of a *bechor de-imma*. Whatever one thinks of the medical belief itself, the decisive point is that the father was sending patients specifically to this son for a treatment whose efficacy depends entirely on the son being a *bechor de-abba*. Had the son been only a *bechor de-imma*, the father — who presumably knew which type of firstborn his son was — would not have recommended this treatment. The father's own conduct therefore constitutes reliable evidence that he considered this son his paternal firstborn.

---

## Tumtum Status Issues

### Tumtum No Double

Rabbi Ami rules: *tumtum she-nikra ve-nimtza zachar, eino notel pi shnayim* — a *tumtum* whose skin covering tears and who is thereby discovered to be male does not receive the double portion of a *bechor*. A *tumtum* is a person born with genitalia that is covered or indeterminate, such that it cannot be established whether the individual is male or female. Halachically, such a person is treated as a *safek* — a case of genuine uncertainty — though it is presumed that the person is definitively one or the other, and our ignorance is about fact rather than about status. Here, however, Rabbi Ami introduces a principle that goes beyond the typical *safek* analysis: even once the ambiguity is resolved and the person is confirmed to be male, certain halachic statuses that depend on recognition at the moment of birth cannot retroactively attach. Specifically, the *bechor*'s double portion is lost.

### Recognition at Birth

The scriptural source is the verse: *ve-haya ha-ben ha-bechor la-seni'ah* — "the firstborn son shall belong to the hated wife" (Devarim 21:17). The *gemara* derives: *ad she-yehei ben mi-sha'at havaya* — he must be recognized as a *ben*, a son, from the moment of his coming into being, i.e., at birth. The *tumtum*, at the moment of birth, was not recognizable as a son. Since his maleness was not apparent, the legal status of *bechor* did not crystallize at that moment, and it cannot be imposed retroactively once the covering is torn and his male status is discovered.

### Sorer U-Moreh

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak extends this principle to the laws of *ben sorer u-moreh*, the wayward and rebellious son (Devarim 21:18). Even though the status of *ben sorer u-moreh* is a matter of conduct that occurs years after birth — during adolescence — the scriptural description begins with *ki yihyeh le-ish ben* — "when a man has a son." The *gemara* applies the same interpretive principle: *ad she-yehei ben mi-sha'at havaya* — he must have been a recognized *ben* at the moment of birth. Since the *tumtum* was not recognized as a son at birth, he falls outside the category of *ben sorer u-moreh* entirely, even after his male status is established.

### Portion Calculation

Amemar adds a further ruling at the top of 27a: the *tumtum* does not diminish (*lo mema'et*) the size of the *bechor*'s portion in the estate. To understand this, consider the arithmetic. If a father left an estate worth four hundred dollars and had three sons, the *bechor*'s double portion is calculated as follows: the estate is notionally divided into four shares (one extra for the *bechor*), so each share is one hundred dollars. The *bechor* receives two hundred; each *pashut* receives one hundred. Now suppose one of those three sons was born as a *tumtum* and only later discovered to be male. Since the *tumtum*, as established by Rabbi Ami, is not counted as a *ben* for *bechor*-related purposes, he is excluded from the initial calculation that determines the size of the *bechor*'s double portion. The calculation proceeds as if there were only two sons: the estate of four hundred is divided into three parts, making each part approximately 133 dollars, and the *bechor* receives 266 while the remaining 133 belongs to the second *pashut* son. The 266 is then split among all three actual sons for their *pashut* shares. The *tumtum*'s presence does not compress the *bechor*'s enhanced portion.

The scriptural basis: *ve-yaldu lo banim* — "and they bore him sons" — followed by the *bechor* law. Since the *tumtum* was not *ben be-sha'at leidah* — recognized as a son at the moment of birth — he is excluded from the count of "sons" that determines the *bechor*'s entitlement.

### Brit Milah Exception

Rav Shizbi adds: the *tumtum* who is later discovered to be male does not have his *brit milah* performed on the eighth day in a manner that overrides *Shabbat*. The verse states: *ishah ki tazria ve-yaldah zachar u-va-yom ha-shmini yimol* — when a woman gives birth to a male, he shall be circumcised on the eighth day. The *gemara* applies the consistent principle: *ad she-yehei zachar mi-sha'at leidah* — he must have been recognized as male from the moment of birth. The *tumtum* was not. Accordingly, even after his male status is confirmed, his *milah* does not carry the special status that overrides *Shabbat*.

A broader reflection emerges from the accumulation of these rulings. In ordinary halachic analysis, the *tumtum* is treated as a *safek* whose status, once clarified, is simply established going forward. Here, however, we see that for several specific *halachot* — the *bechor*'s double portion, the *ben sorer u-moreh* category, the calculation of the *bechor*'s share, and the *brit milah* on *Shabbat* — the moment of birth is not merely one data point but the decisive moment, and ignorance at that moment permanently forecloses certain statuses. What is notable, and somewhat challenging, is the inclusion of *ben sorer u-moreh* in this list: unlike the others, that status depends on behavior during adolescence, yet the *gemara* still traces its precondition back to recognizable male identity at birth. The scope of this principle — how broadly it applies to other *halachot* that define status at a particular life stage — is a question the *gemara* leaves with open edges.

---

---

# Bava Batra 127

## Tumtum Birth Status

### Rav Ami: Tumtum

The *mishna* on 127a shifts from the laws of the double portion itself to the question of identifying who qualifies as the firstborn son, and it is this question that drives the *gemara*'s ensuing discussion. Rav Ami opens with the ruling that a *tumtum* — a child whose genitalia have not descended or whose genitalia are concealed by a membrane at birth, such that gender cannot be determined — does not receive the double portion of the firstborn even if, after birth, the child is revealed to be male. The reason is that the verse states *vehaya haben habechor* — "and it shall be that the firstborn son" — meaning that the child must be recognizable as a *ben* from the very moment of birth. Since this child was not identifiable as a son at birth, the *halacha* of *bechor* does not attach. The *gemara* applies this same principle to the case of *ben sorer umoreh* and similarly rules that a second boy born in such a state would not affect the size of the firstborn's double portion.

### Rav Shizvi: Brit Milah

The *gemara* then records a parallel ruling by Rav Shizvi. Reading from the top of 127a: *Rav Shizvi amar — af eino nimal lishmona* — even if a baby is born in the state of a *tumtum* and is subsequently identified as male before the eighth day, the *brit milah* is not performed on the eighth day in a manner that overrides *Shabbat*. The source is the verse *isha ki tazria veyalda zachar… uvayom hashmini yimol besar orlato* — "if a woman gives forth seed and gives birth to a male… on the eighth day you shall circumcise the flesh of his foreskin." The phrase *yalda zachar* requires, as the *gemara* phrases it, *ad sheyehe zachar mishat leida* — the child must be male from the moment of birth. Since this condition was not met for the *tumtum*, the special weight of the eighth day — the weight that ordinarily overrides *Shabbat* — does not apply.

### Rav Sharvia: Tumat Leida

Rav Sharvia then draws from the same verse and the same *drasha* — *ad sheyehe zachar mishat leida* — but with a different halachic consequence: *af ein imo tme'a leida* — the mother of such a child has no *tumat leida*, the impurity that accompanies childbirth. The verse *isha ki tazria veyalda zachar vetame'a shivat yamim* — "if a woman gives birth to a male she is impure for seven days" — appears even before the laws of *brit milah* and applies only when the child is identifiable as male from the moment of birth. Here, since neither male nor female status was apparent at birth, the mother does not fall into either *parasha* of *tumah* — neither the *parasha* of a male child nor that of a female child. She would presumably remain subject to *derabbanan* obligations, and there is a point worth noting: this ruling is in some respects an even greater *chidush* than the case of an *androgynos*, since here the child may have been fully male in a biological sense — simply unknown.

---

## Childbirth Impurity Doubt

### Meseivei Challenge

At this point the *gemara* raises a challenge. *Meseivei* — the *gemara* asks from a *baraita*: *hamapelet tumtum ve'androgynos* — if a woman gives birth to a *tumtum* or an *androgynos*, since it is unknown whether the child is male or female, the *halacha* is *teshvei lezachar ulenekeiva* — she must observe the stringencies of both. This stands in apparent contradiction to Rav Sharvia's ruling, since the *baraita* presupposes that even where gender is indeterminate the mother is indeed subject to *tumat leida* — she is not excluded from the category entirely. The *gemara* therefore declares *tiyufta d'Rav Shavya tiyufta* — a complete refutation of Rav Sharvia's position.

### Seven & Forty Days

The content of the stringency *teshvei lezachar ulenekeiva* is as follows. For a male child, the mother is *tme'ah* for the first seven days, and thereafter — through day forty — any bleeding she experiences has the status of *dam tohar* and does not render her impure. For a female child, she is *tme'ah* for the first fourteen days, and thereafter — through day eighty — any bleeding is likewise *dam tohar*. When the child's gender is unknown, both stringencies apply simultaneously. Practically: she is treated as having given birth to a female for purposes of the initial period of *tumah*, meaning she is *tme'ah* for fourteen days; and she is treated as having given birth to a male for purposes of *dam tohar*, meaning the special dispensation expires at day forty rather than day eighty. There is no *halacha*, the *baraita* implies, that renders her entirely exempt from *tumat leida* on account of the ambiguity.

### Both Stringencies

The *gemara* then asks: *leima teihavei tiyufta d'Rav Shizvi* — should this same *baraita* also refute Rav Shizvi? Rav Shizvi had applied the very same *drasha* from *yalda zachar* — only now to the context of *brit milah* and its capacity to override *Shabbat*. Once it is established that the verse does not exclude a *tumtum* from *tumat leida*, it would seem that the verse similarly cannot exclude a *tumtum* from the laws of *brit milah*, and the *brit milah* of such a child should override *Shabbat* once he is identified as male before the eighth day.

The *gemara* responds: *tanna sapokei mesapka leih* — the *tanna* who authored the *baraita* was himself uncertain how to read the verse. Does *yalda zachar* exclude a child who was a *tumtum* at birth, or does it not? The *tanna* resolves his uncertainty through stringency in each domain. Regarding *tumah*, since the uncertainty exists, he does not exclude the *tumtum* from *tumat leida*, and the mother must observe both stringencies — fourteen days and the end of forty days — because perhaps the verse does not exclude such a child.
