Each thought Yonatan ben Uziel generated in his learning was immediately overtaken and consumed by an even higher thought, which in turn yielded to yet another. His mind was in a state of perpetual ascent, each level of insight dissolving into the next.

---

## Son Identification

### Son Declaration

The *gemara* now moves to a topic previewed at the very opening of the *daf*: *ha'omer zeh beni ne'eman* — if a person says "this is my son," he is believed. This is the converse of the *bechor* cases, which concerned identifying which of one's known sons held the status of firstborn. Here the question is about recognizing as a son someone who is not publicly known to be one's child at all.

### Brother vs. Son

By contrast, *zeh achi eino ne'eman* — if a person says "this is my brother," he is not believed. If Reuven declares that Levi is a long-lost brother, Shimon — the other known heir — need not accept that claim. Reuven is, however, bound by his own declaration: *veyitol imo bechelko* — Levi receives from Reuven's portion. In practical terms: if the estate consists of three fields, Reuven and Shimon would each ordinarily receive one and a half. If Reuven declares Levi a brother, Levi should in theory receive one field, with half coming from each brother. But Shimon refuses to accept the claim, invoking *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'ayah* — the burden of proof rests on the one making the claim. Reuven, however, having made the claim, must honor it from his own portion.

### Property Reversion

If Levi subsequently dies, *yachziru nechasim lemekoman* — the property returns to its source. Even if Shimon never accepted that Levi was a brother, he does not now benefit from Levi's death by claiming a share of whatever Reuven had already conceded to Levi. The half-field Levi received from Reuven reverts to Reuven; Shimon cannot suddenly assert brotherhood now that it would benefit him.

### Selective Heir

The reverse scenario, however, works differently. If Levi comes into great wealth from an external source, Shimon may now reverse his earlier position and affirm that yes, Levi is indeed a brother. This may seem unfair, but it follows from the structure of the claims: Reuven has always maintained that Levi is a brother, and on that basis, Shimon is in any event entitled to half of whatever Levi inherits. If Shimon also confirms the fraternal relationship, that changes nothing with respect to what he receives from the estate — and he stands to gain from Levi's new wealth.

### Paternity Functions

The *mishna* having established that a father is believed to say "this is my son," the *gemara* asks: *lemai hilcheta* — for what halachic purpose is he believed? This is not a trivial question. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *leyorsho* — the son inherits from him. And second: *ulifetur ishto min hayibum* — to exempt the father's wife from *yibum*. If the father had no publicly known children and declares "this is my son" before his death, his wife is thereby exempt from *yibum* with the father's brother.

### Property Control

The first ruling — that the son inherits — is intuitive, and the *gemara* declares it *peshita*, obvious. Both the Rashbam and Tosafos explain that the reason the father is believed is that he could have given the property to this person as a *matanah* even without invoking the claim of paternity. Since he could effect the same result through a gift, he is believed to do it through a declaration of kinship. But this also defines the *limit* of the belief: just as a gift can only convey property currently in the donor's possession, the father's declaration of "this is my son" is credited only with respect to property he presently controls. Property acquired after the declaration would not automatically pass to the declared son; a renewed declaration would be necessary to bring such subsequently acquired property within the son's inheritance.

### Brother/Son Distinction

That the father is believed about a son for purposes of *yibum* exemption is *not* obvious, since the ability to gift property does not obviously translate into the ability to affect one's wife's *yibum* status. The *gemara* therefore notes that this ruling required specific articulation: *itztricha leh*.

The *gemara* also contrasts this ruling with a parallel case. If a person says at the moment of death *yesh li banim* — I have sons — he is believed and his wife is exempt from *yibum*. But if he says *yesh li achim* — I have brothers — he is *not* believed to thereby obligate his wife in *yibum*. The reason is asymmetrical: in the default state, where no brothers are known, the wife is presumed exempt from *yibum*. A declaration of sons reaffirms the exemption from another angle; a declaration of brothers seeks to impose a burden that contradicts the default. The *gemara* cannot accept the latter on mere say-so.

Our *mishna* concerns a different situation: one where the brother is *known* — *af al gav de-muchzak lan be-ach* — and the wife is therefore already presumed *chayevet be-yibum*. In that case, can the dying man's declaration of "this is my son" override the presumption of *yibum* obligation?

### Divorce Power

Rav Yosef initially cites Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: the husband is believed to say "this is my son" — and by analogy, also believed to say "I divorced my wife" — because *ho'il uva'al she'amar gerashti et ishti ne'eman*, a husband who says he divorced his wife is believed. But this immediately meets with Rav Yosef's own sharp objection: *tali tanya bedelo tanya* — you are grounding an explicit ruling in something that has never itself been stated! We have not yet established anywhere that a husband is believed to say he divorced his wife; you cannot use that as the premise for explaining why he is believed to declare his son.

The corrected formulation is therefore: *mipnei mah amru zeh beni ne'eman? Ho'il u'veyado lgareshah* — why is a father believed to say "this is my son"? Because it is *within his power to divorce her*. If the husband wished to exempt his wife from *yibum*, he could do so directly by divorcing her before he dies. Because he has this power over her *yibum* status, he is believed when he makes a declaration that achieves the same result — namely, that he has a son.

This is not precisely a *migo* in the classic sense. A *migo* argues: believe me because if I wanted to lie I could have done so more effectively through another available claim. Here there may well be reasons the husband would not wish to divorce his wife — it would render her *asurah* to a *kohen*, he might still expect to recover his health and live longer, and so forth. Rather, the principle is one of *beyado lgareshah*: because he has power over this domain, he is believed regarding it. Control over a legal status generates credibility in that domain.

This principle, the *gemara* notes, then extends: *hashta d'amart amrinan ho'il u-ba'al she'amar gerashti et ishti* — once we have established that a man is believed because it is *beyado lgareshah*, we can now also say that a husband who declares he divorced his wife is likewise believed, for the same reason. He could have divorced her; therefore he is believed to say that he did. Both rulings — belief in "this is my son" and belief in "I divorced my wife" — rest on the same foundation of *beyado lgareshah*. That discussion will be taken up on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Bava Batra 135

## Biyado Legarsha

### Paternity Claims

The *mishnah* on our daf continues the discussion begun earlier regarding the scope of a father's credibility in establishing paternity. A previous *mishnah* had established that a man is believed to identify someone as his *bechor*, his firstborn, on the basis of a *pasuk*. Here the *mishnah* addresses a broader claim: a man is believed to say that a certain person is his son — meaning that person receives a share in this man's estate. One might think this is obvious, since he could simply gift the property to him. The *gemara* therefore clarifies that the genuine *chiddush* lies elsewhere.

Even regarding property, there is an important limitation: a person is not believed about paternity in any absolute sense. His credibility rests entirely on the principle that he could have gifted the property to this person anyway. Consequently, his declaration of paternity covers only the property he currently holds — not property he will acquire later. If one wishes to ensure the child receives a full and proper share of the estate going forward, he must periodically renew the declaration so that it covers property accumulated since the last statement. But when a child is already *muchzak* — known and recognized in the community as his son or daughter — no declaration is needed at all.

The *gemara* identifies the real *chiddush* as the credibility of this declaration for purposes of *yibum*. If a man has known brothers and it is not known that he has children — a category that includes daughters as well — he is believed to claim that a certain person is his son or daughter, thereby exempting his wife from *yibum*. This is remarkable because it runs directly against the *chazaka* that his wife is obligated in *yibum*.

### Yibum Credibility

The *gemara* explains this credibility through the principle of *biyado l'garsha*: since he has the power to divorce his wife and thereby free her from *yibum* on his own initiative, he is believed to assert that she is already exempt. This might superficially resemble a standard *migo* — why would he lie when he could accomplish the same result through divorce? But that framing is not entirely satisfying, since there may be many reasons a man would not want to divorce his wife, making the lie potentially more attractive than the act. A better reading is that *biyado l'garsha* functions as a principle of authority: because he has control over this area of *halacha* — because it is within his power to free his wife from *yibum* — that very position of power confers upon him a degree of credibility within this domain. He is, in effect, a recognized actor in this legal sphere, and that standing gives his claims believability.

### Divorce Claim

Once this principle is established, Rav Yosef extends it significantly. *Hashta d'amarta amrinan ho'il* — now that we say we invoke the principle of *ho'il*, since he could have divorced his wife to achieve the same result, a husband who simply declares *gerashti et ishti*, "I divorced my wife," is believed — *ho'il u'biyado l'garsha* — even without producing any documentation. The *nafka mina* is substantial: upon his death, his wife could remarry freely, and any children born thereafter would not be *mamzeirim*, all on the basis of his say-so alone.

One might ask whether this applies even when the wife herself denies having received a *get*. While there are parallel cases — such as a seller who is believed to say to whom he sold something, since he was in a position to decide — counterclaims would presumably complicate matters. The principle of *biyado* here cannot be read as a simple *migo*, since it is always easier to claim one did something than to actually do it. The *biyado* principle must therefore be understood as something distinct: a kind of domain-authority that confers credibility, not merely a strategic inference from available alternatives.

---

## Divorce Retroactivity

### Yitzchak's Rejection

However, this extension of *ho'il biyado l'garsha* is immediately contested. When Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef came from Eretz Yisrael, he cited a ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that is the direct opposite: *ba'al she'amar gerashti ishti eino ne'eman* — a husband who claims he divorced his wife is not believed. Upon hearing this, Rav Sheshes dismissed Rav Yosef's reasoning with an expressive wave of his hand — pfft — as if to say: there goes Rav Yosef's *ho'il*. Goodbye to that principle.

But a wholesale rejection of *biyado l'garsha* is impossible, since the very *mishnah* we are explaining relies on it to explain why a husband is believed to identify his child for *yibum* purposes. The principle must therefore survive in some form.

### Limited Application

Both the Rashbam and Tosafos explain that what is being rejected is not the principle itself but its application to the divorce claim specifically. The question is: what distinguishes the case of *yibum* — where *biyado l'garsha* works — from the case of a divorce claim, where it does not?

The answer, drawn from another *gemara*, returns to a point about counter-evidence. A claim that one has children is inherently plausible: a man can father children in circumstances that remain entirely private, with no public knowledge and no communal record. But a divorce is a different matter entirely. The absence of a *get*, the absence of any knowledge in the community, the absence of any *kol* — these are not merely neutral silences. The absence of evidence here functions as meaningful evidence against the claim. If a man had truly divorced his wife, there would be a *get*, a *beis din* record, some trace in the community. The very invisibility of the divorce undercuts the claim's believability, even granting the principle of *biyado l'garsha*.

One might add that the weight of what is at stake also differs: exempting a woman from *yibum* avoids an *issur lav*, whereas believing a false divorce claim would expose a woman to the *issur* of *eishes ish*, with the children potentially being *mamzeirim*. The Rashbam and Tosafos, however, focus specifically on the evidentiary asymmetry — the conspicuous absence of documentation — rather than on the relative severity of the consequences.

So the principle of *biyado l'garsha* stands, but it operates only where the claim itself is inherently plausible. The divorce claim is not sufficiently plausible, given the complete absence of supporting evidence, and therefore fails.

### Lemafrea Lehaba

The *gemara* then resolves the apparent contradiction between the two traditions in the name of Rabbi Yochanan. *Lo kashya: kan l'mafre'a, kan l'haba.* The tradition that a husband is not believed refers to a retroactive claim — *l'mafre'a* — as when a man, faced with his wife's suspected adultery, suddenly announces that he had divorced her a year ago. In that scenario, there is no *biyado l'garsha* at the operative moment: the power to divorce applies going forward, not backward. He cannot now, from where he stands, divorce his wife a year ago. So his claim about the past carries no credibility.

But going forward — *l'haba* — a husband is believed to say he has divorced his wife, because from this moment onward he retains the power to do so, and that power confers credibility from this point in time.

---

## Splitting Words

### Last Week Claim

This resolution immediately generates a new question. If a husband announces *gerashti et ishti* last week — a claim we cannot credit retroactively — can we at least accept the statement as effective going forward? The practical stakes are significant: does the wife become free to remarry from today? If the husband dies, is she subject to *yibum*? If she does remarry and the retroactive claim cannot be believed, then children born in the interim could be *mamzeirim* — a serious *nafka mina*.

The structure of the question is: must we treat his statement as a single indivisible unit, rejecting it entirely because part of it is beyond credibility, or can we accept it as effective prospectively even though we cannot accept it retrospectively?

### Split Application

This is the question of *mi palginan dibura o lo palginan dibura* — do we split his words or not? Notably, "splitting" need not be taken literally, as though we excise the words "last week" from his sentence. The deeper question is whether we can apply his statement selectively — crediting it for some legal purposes while disallowing it for others — regardless of exactly how it was phrased.

The *gemara* records a debate between Rav Mari and Rav Zvid: one says we split his words and one says we do not. The *gemara* then raises a challenge: does not Rava's ruling in a classic case already demonstrate that we do split testimony? Rava rules that if a man says that Reuven committed adultery with his wife, this testimony is accepted against Reuven — with whom the witness has no disqualifying relationship — but rejected regarding his own wife, against whom he is a *karov*. The testimony is thus accepted for one party and rejected for another. Why, then, should we not similarly accept this husband's claim going forward while rejecting it for the past?

### Adultery Parallel

The *gemara* answers: *bitrei gufai palginan, b'chad gufa lo palginan.* When we split testimony across two different persons — two separate defendants — we do so because the testimony stands complete and unchallenged as applied to each individual in their own right. The witness is not disqualified from testifying against Reuven; the question of whether to credit him against the wife is a separate legal question about a separate person. In each individual case, the testimony either stands fully or falls fully; we are not dividing the testimony itself in half.

But in the case of the husband's divorce claim, we are being asked to apply a single statement to a single person — his wife — crediting it for the present while discrediting it for the past. That is a different kind of division. There, we are not choosing between two defendants; we are fragmenting the application of a single claim to a single subject. That is what the *gemara* means by *chad gufa*, and it is there that the split may not be permissible.

It is worth noting that, intuitively, one might have expected the analysis to run in the opposite direction. In the adultery testimony case, the witness has a clear personal stake that should, arguably, taint the entire enterprise. In the divorce claim, the concern is simply that *biyado l'garsha* applies only prospectively, not that anything inherently corrupts the claim. Yet the *gemara* permits the split in the adultery case and questions it in the divorce case — operating, it seems, on formal structural grounds rather than intuitive ones.

Given this unresolved question, the Rashbam concludes that even according to the opinion that a husband is believed to say he divorced his wife, this credibility clearly operates only when he either says "I divorced her today" or gives no timeframe at all. The moment he specifies a past moment — even yesterday, even moments ago — the statement becomes retroactive and the entire claim becomes questionable.

---

## Dying Man Case

### Wife Status

The *gemara* now transitions to a related narrative. A man was dying. Those around him asked about the status of his wife — was she subject to *yibum*, or was she free to marry whomever she wished? Had he divorced her, or did he have children? His response was: *chazya l'kahana rabba* — my wife is fit to marry even the *kohen gadol*. Since she will become a widow, she cannot marry the *kohen gadol* on that basis, so the implication of his statement is that she is completely free — no *yibum* obligation stands in her way.

### Vague Statement

Rava initially rules: *mai nichush lah* — what is there to worry about? He should be believed. But the question is how to interpret this vague statement. Is he claiming he divorced her, or is he claiming he has children? The Rashbam explains that since we have a *chazaka* that this man has no sons, we should not read this ambiguous statement as a claim that contradicts that *chazaka*. We would rather interpret his words as a claim of divorce — something he always retained the power to do — rather than a claim of children, which would run against our standing presumption. Under this reading, his statement is treated as *gerashti et ishti*, and since he gave no specific timeframe, it is credited going forward.

### Abbaye Challenge

Abbaye challenges this. He points out that there is a conflicting tradition in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — that a husband who says *gerashti et ishti* is *not* believed. If that tradition is correct, then reading this vague statement as a divorce claim actually makes things worse, not better, since it invokes a claim that won't be credited. Why should we choose the interpretation that ends in disbelief?

In response, the earlier resolution is invoked: the two traditions in Rabbi Yochanan's name were already reconciled — one refers to retroactive claims, the other to prospective ones. Since this dying man gave no specific timeframe, his statement can be read as a present-moment divorce declaration and therefore should be believed going forward.

Abbaye, however, pushes back: should we really stake a practical ruling on what amounts to a reconciliation of conflicting *amora'im* traditions? Perhaps the contradiction was never truly resolved, and represents a genuine dispute about Rabbi Yochanan's position. If so, according to the stricter tradition, this woman would not be exempt and would require *chalitza*. Rava responds to Rav Natan bar Ami: *chushla* — we must be concerned. The ruling seesaws back. Rather than being confident the woman is exempt, we must entertain the possibility that she is not and that *chalitza* is required.

This brings out a striking irony that deepens the difficulty. Given the ambiguity of the dying man's statement, why not read it as a claim of children rather than divorce? If he claimed children, *all* opinions would agree he is believed, since that falls squarely within the *mishnah*'s ruling. The answer is that since our *chazaka* is that he has no children, we will not read his vague statement as a direct claim against that *chazaka* unless he states it explicitly. We therefore default to reading it as a divorce claim — but that is precisely the claim that is now in doubt. The result is that interpreting his statement in the way that does not challenge our presumptions leads to a claim that may not be believed, while the interpretation that would have been unambiguously believed — children — requires him to have directly said so.

---

## No Brothers Case

### Dying Claim

A parallel case is now presented. A man was *muchzak* in the community as having no brothers — that was the longstanding perception, based on years of communal life in which no brother ever appeared. As he lay dying, he reinforced this: he explicitly declared that he has no brothers. His wife is thus doubly exempt from *yibum*: first by communal presumption, and second by his own credible dying declaration. The Rashbam adds, notably, that even if the man had been *muchzak* to have brothers — a widespread perception, though not definitive knowledge — he would still be believed to say he does not, for the same reason that he is believed to say he has children: *biyado l'garsha* is not defeated by mere perception, only by actual established fact.

Rav Yosef asks: *mai leichosh lah* — what is there to worry about? We have the *chazaka* that he has no brothers, and we have his explicit dying declaration reinforcing it. Two independent grounds for permitting his wife to remarry without *chalitza*.

### Distant Witnesses

Abbaye interjects with a complication. People are saying — *amri* — that there are witnesses in distant lands who have concrete knowledge that this man does have a brother. Not that we have established testimony; not that anyone has come before *beis din* with evidence. But there is a rumor that somewhere, witnesses exist who know of a brother. Should this rumor require us to delay, to investigate, before permitting the wife to remarry?

### No Rumors

The *gemara* responds: *hashta meihacha leis ninhu kamman* — right now, those witnesses are not here. We have no obligation to be paralyzed by rumors of potential future evidence. The principle is *ein ladayan ela mah she'einav ro'os*: a judge rules based on what stands before him, not on rumors about what might someday appear.

This is compared to the ruling of Rabbi Chanina in the case of Shmuel's daughter, who was taken captive and testified that she was *tehorah ani* — untouched by her captors. When it was rumored that witnesses in a distant city knew otherwise, Rabbi Chanina ruled: *eidim be-tzad Etztan vete'aser* — should she be forbidden because witnesses sit in some far city? They are not here; we do not wait for them.

### Concrete Concern

Abbaye draws a distinction, however. The case of the *shvuyah* — the captive woman — involves at most a rabbinic prohibition, since even if she had been violated, her status as *eishes ish* is not in question, and her defilement would only rabbinically disqualify her from a *kohen*. The principle *in hikalnu bishvuyah, neikul b'eishes ish?* — just because we are lenient about the captive, should we be equally lenient in matters of *eishes ish*? The *yibum* question, while not identical to an adultery case, is still a weightier matter than the *shvuyah* scenario.

Rava concludes — again in a message to Rav Natan bar Ami — *chush lah*: we must be concerned. Where there is a concrete hint of hard evidence about a weighty matter, we cannot simply proceed. We must take some measure of concern seriously, even if the precise parameters — how widespread must the rumor be, how much investigation is required, what happens if inquiries yield nothing — remain undefined by the *gemara*.

---

## Brother Dispute

### Levi Claim

The *gemara* now turns to the second part of the *mishnah*, which introduces a three-brother scenario. Reuven and Shimon were the only known brothers and each received one and a half fields from their father's estate. Reuven now claims that Levi is also their brother and should have received a share. Shimon says he has no such knowledge.

### Inheritance Split

The *mishnah* rules: Reuven's claim is not believed as against Shimon, so Shimon is not compelled to give Levi any portion of his inheritance. Reuven, however, is bound by his own claim, and so Levi takes a share from Reuven's portion. Moreover, if Levi later dies, Reuven and Shimon split his estate equally as his presumptive brothers.

### Eini Yodeia

The *gemara* asks: what exactly is Shimon's position? If Shimon were conceding that Levi is a brother, the question would be why Levi receives only from Reuven and not from Shimon as well. So Shimon must be denying it. But if Shimon is denying that Levi is a brother, why would Shimon be entitled to inherit from Levi when Levi dies?

The answer: *lo tzricha deka amri einu yodim* — Shimon takes the strategically sound position of *I don't know*. He does not affirmatively deny the brotherhood, and he does not affirm it. Because he does not know, and because *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* — the burden of proof lies on the claimant — Shimon need not give Levi anything from his own share. But when Levi dies, Reuven's claim is now in Shimon's favor: Reuven is already asserting that all three are brothers. As long as Shimon does not contradict that claim — since he says only *eini yodeia* — he stands to benefit from it. The estate of Levi is therefore split between them.

### Bari Veshema

Rava draws a broader principle from this case. Reuven is essentially saying to Shimon: you owe Levi a half field. Shimon says: I don't know. Is this not a classic case of *bari veshema* — a certain claim versus a doubtful one — and does *bari* not ordinarily prevail? Rava concludes: *zos omeres mane li beyadecha vehala omer eini yodeia patur* — this teaches that where someone says you owe me a hundred *maneh* and the other says he doesn't know, the respondent is exempt.

Abbaye disagrees. He argues that ordinarily, a *bari* claim does override a *shema* — it is only here that Shimon is exempt, for a specific reason: *deka maneh le'acher beyadcha dami* — this resembles a case where Reuven says "you owe the other person a hundred *maneh*." Reuven is not making a claim for himself; he is making a claim on behalf of Levi. And crucially, Levi himself cannot come with a *bari* claim — Levi does not know with certainty who his father was. The only *bari* voice in this entire proceeding is Reuven's, and Reuven is asserting a claim on someone else's behalf. A *bari* claim can overcome a *chazaka* when the claimant is asserting his own interest directly. It is not powerful enough to extract property from another person's possession on behalf of a third party who cannot himself assert certainty. Therefore, whatever one holds in general about *bari veshema*, Shimon is exempt here — not because *bari* is categorically insufficient, but because the *bari* here belongs to Reuven rather than to Levi.

### Return Property

When Levi dies without issue, having earned his own money independently, Reuven and Shimon divide his estate equally — since Shimon said *eini yodeia* and Reuven claims brotherhood, and that claim now works in both brothers' favor. But the half field that Reuven had given Levi — the portion Reuven himself transferred to him — returns to Reuven. The logic is that Shimon retained the half field he should, according to Reuven's claim, have given Levi long ago. Now that Levi is dead, Shimon inherits what he was always holding. Reuven, correspondingly, reclaims what he himself had given. Any independently earned money of Levi's is divided equally between the two brothers, since both stand as equal heirs.

### Shevach Value

Rava then poses an unresolved question: *shevach she-shivchu nechasim me'alehem mahu* — what about an increase in the value of Reuven's half field that occurred naturally, without anyone's effort? If the real estate value rose, or a palm tree grew thicker, or the land became more fertile due to flooding — none of it through Levi's investment — does that natural appreciation simply return to Reuven along with the field, or must it be split?

The *gemara* clarifies that appreciation which is the result of visible, active effort — *shevach hamagi'a liktefayim*, meaning either that the crop has visibly grown tall or that it required putting one's shoulder into the work — clearly constitutes new property and would be divided equally. That is not in question. The unresolved *sha'aleh* concerns passive appreciation: a change in value that no one caused, that simply happened by itself. Does Reuven recover the field in its current enhanced state, or must Shimon receive half of the natural appreciation as a co-inheritor of Levi? The *gemara* concludes: *teiku* — this remains unresolved.

---

## Will Doctrine

### Diatiki Defined

With this the *gemara* transitions fully into the institution of *matnat shchiv meira* — the deathbed bequest — though in a form that has been mentioned in passing throughout the tractate and is now addressed directly. The instrument under discussion is the *diatiki*, a Greek word meaning "will" — a written testament. In the conceptual framework of *chazal*, the primary legal instrument is the verbal deathbed bequest: a dying person declares orally what he wishes done with his property, and that declaration is binding by rabbinic enactment. The *diatiki* is a variation: instead of the oral declaration, or alongside it, the person writes out his wishes. This seems like the prudent course — put it in writing, have a record — but the *halacha* treats it differently from a standard *shtar kinyan*.

The *diatiki* does not function as a *shtar kinyan*. It is not a formal deed of acquisition in which witnesses attest to a transaction. It is a written expression of the person's desires and intentions regarding his estate — a will in the fullest sense of the word. As such, it is subject to different rules. A person can revise his will repeatedly, just as a person on his deathbed can retract a verbal bequest and issue a new one. The prime model in *halacha* remains the oral declaration, with the written will as a derivative form.

### No Effect

The *mishnah* states: if a person died and a *diatiki* — a written will — was found bound to his thigh, it has no legal effect whatsoever. The binding to his thigh removes any question about authorship; this is clearly his will. Yet *harei zeh einah klum* — it accomplishes nothing — because it was never handed over. The act of handing over is the required act of legal execution for a written will.

### Handed Over

If, however, he performed *zichah bah l'acher* — he caused someone else to take hold of the will on his behalf — whether that person is among his heirs or not among his heirs, *devarav kayamim* — his words stand and the will is binding. The Rashbam notes that the will need not name specific beneficiaries. If the will makes bequests without naming the recipient, the person who receives the document is presumed to be the beneficiary, like a blank check that becomes payable to its holder. As long as someone has received the document in this act of *zicha*, the will takes legal effect.

### Execution Required

This leads to a pointed question: why should a written document be ineffective when all other *shtarot* serve as evidence or instruments of transfer? The answer lies in the fundamental nature of the document. A normal *shtar* bears the signatures of witnesses who are testifying to a fact or transaction. This *diatiki* is not that. It is a written expression of the person's wishes — a declaration of intent, not a witnessed transaction. Anyone could theoretically have composed such a document; the question of authorship may be resolved, but the question of legal execution remains. Without the act of handing over, there is no legally recognized execution of the will.

More fundamentally, the *halacha* requires a recognized legal instrument to transfer property. The fact that someone wishes to give his property to another person, however well-documented, does not by itself effect a transfer. What makes a deathbed bequest legally operative is either the verbal oral declaration — which is heard by another person and thus communicated — or the written will that is handed over. Both require that the intent be communicated and actualized through some recognized act. A document sitting tied to a man's thigh, however clearly his own work, lacks *gmirat daat* — the finalization of intent as manifested through a completed legal act. The document has not yet been communicated to anyone.

Indeed, there is something counterintuitive here: an oral statement is more immediately binding than a written document that has not been handed over. The reason, however, is clear: the oral deathbed bequest is spoken to someone else, it is received, it is communicated. Even a verbal declaration made to oneself in private would not qualify. The *gmirat daat* requires that the act of giving be, in some real sense, completed — and handing over the will is the written equivalent of the verbal declaration heard by another. Until that act occurs, the will remains, legally, a private expression of intention with no binding force.

---

---

# Bava Batra 136

## Matnat Shchiv Mei'ra Bas…

### Opening & Orientation

The daf under discussion is 136, though the material opens on 135b, at the *mishnah* that transitions the tractate into the terrain of *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra* — the deathbed bequest — and its written counterpart.

### Oral Deathbed Bequest

*Matnat sh'chiv mei'ra* is the oral deathbed bequest, a special *takana* established by the Rabbis whereby a dying person's verbal declaration of his wishes takes effect at death. Because it is oral, it requires witnesses to establish that it was actually said — but no formal document or act of acquisition is necessary for its validity.

### Diatiki & Meshichah

The *mishnah* shifts focus to the written form of the deathbed bequest, known as a *diatiki* — a Greek term for a written will. The critical distinction is that whereas an oral *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra* takes effect the moment the declaration is made (subject to proof), a written will has no binding force until it is physically handed over — until *meshichah*, delivery to the recipient.

### Mishnah: Binding Rules

The *mishnah* illustrates this with a striking case: if a person dies and the written will is found bound to his thigh — a gesture redolent of the ancient Near Eastern oath (recall *sim na yadecha tachat yireichi* in the context of Avraham) — the will is nonetheless not yet legally binding. There is no question that he wrote it; the binding to the thigh establishes authorship beyond doubt. Yet legal force only attaches once the document has been handed over. Once he has transferred it to another person — whether that recipient is an heir or not an heir — *devarav kayamim*, it is valid and binding. The *gemara* will add that this holds even if no specific name appears in the document: a blank-check-style will transferred to the recipient is effective.

### Diatiki vs. Shtar

The *diatiki* must not be confused with a *shtar matana*, an ordinary gift document. A *shtar matana* takes effect immediately upon delivery and operates through the standard mechanisms of property transfer — the document itself effects the *kinyan* of the land by containing language such as *sadi netuna lecha* or *sadi mechura lecha*, which expresses the donor's present intent to convey. The *diatiki*, by contrast, is an expression of the person's last will and testament; it takes effect only at death. The *gemara* makes this distinction precise: a *shtar matana* says *me-hayom u-le'achar misa* — from today and completed at death — whereas the *diatiki*'s defining language is, as the *beraita* will explain, *da tehei lemeikam ulehayos*, "this shall be established and stand" — the classic formula of a last will and testament.

---

## Diatiki Definition & Mat…

### Diatiki Definition

The *tana rabbanan* offers a formal definition: what is a *diatiki*? Any document in which the language *da tehei lemeikam ulehayos* — "this shall stand and be established" — appears. This is the *gemara*'s characteristic etymological derivation of the Greek legal term through Aramaic phrasing. It is, in essence, the declaration: this is my last will and testament.

### Matnat Bari Structure

The *gemara* then raises the obvious question: what is a gift document? How do we distinguish a *shtar* that is a will from one that is a *shtar matana*? The *gemara* notes that land is acquired through *kesef*, *shtar*, or *chazakah*. For *shtar*, all that is required is that the document contain the operative words — *sadi netuna lecha* or *sadi mechura lecha* — specifying the field, together with delivery of the document. That is a *matana*. The *gemara* then asks: is it exclusively a document that says *me-hayom u-le'achar misa* that qualifies as a *matana*? What about a simple present-tense declaration, *me'achshav*? Of course that is also a gift. The formulation *me-hayom u-le'achar misa* therefore cannot be the general definition of a *matana*.

### Abaye's Explanation

*Ela amar Abaye*: here is what the *beraita* actually means. *Eizehu matnas bari she-hi ke-matnas sh'chiv mei'ra* — what is a gift given by a healthy person (*matnas bari*) that operates not through the special *takana* of *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra* but nonetheless approximates its effect? The answer is a gift structured as *me-hayom u-le'achar misa*. Not everyone has the luxury of waiting until they are on their deathbed to arrange their affairs; people who are young and healthy may wish to set up testamentary-like arrangements in advance. The mechanism of *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra* is unavailable to them. So they employ a *matnas bari* that achieves a similar result.

### Me-hayom Structure

How does *me-hayom u-le'achar misa* approximate *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra*? The full phrase means: the title (*gufa*) is transferred today, but the *peiros* — the income, the usufruct, the benefit — passes to the recipient only after the donor's death. The next *mishnah* will spell out the practical consequences: since the title passes today, the donor cannot sell the principal; since the donor retains the *peiros* for his lifetime, the recipient cannot yet fully benefit from the property. The donor effectively says: I want you to own this land, but I want to continue drawing the income from it until I die. This is structurally similar to *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra*, where the recipient really only gets full benefit after the donor's death. The choice to transfer title now — thereby surrendering the ability to sell the principal — is admittedly an unusual one. One might ask: why not simply arrange for the acquisition to take effect a moment before death? That would preserve full flexibility in the interim. Yet the *gemara* treats the *me-hayom u-le'achar misa* structure as the classic vehicle, and the following *mishnah* will explore why.

### Retraction Rights

*Tosafos* addresses whether a *matnas bari* structured as *me-hayom u-le'achar misa* can be retracted. The *Rashbam* holds that since the gift is made while healthy, and the *me-hayom* transfers title at the moment of writing, the donor cannot subsequently retract it — this is unlike a *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra*, which can always be superseded by a later will. The *Rashbam* acknowledges, however, that certain other *gemaras* imply that such a gift *can* be retracted, and *Tosafos* raises this tension explicitly.

*Rabbeinu Tam* resolves the tension differently. He argues that when the *gemara* speaks of a *matnas bari she-hi ke-matnas sh'chiv mei'ra*, it refers to a case where the donor explicitly wrote: *me-hayom im lo achzor bi ad le'achar misa* — "from today, provided I do not retract it until after my death." The donor expressly reserves the right of retraction. According to *Rabbeinu Tam*, this explicit reservation is what makes the *matnas bari* truly approximate a *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra*, since wills by their nature are always revocable until death. Without such an explicit clause, a simple *me-hayom u-le'achar misa* would, per the *Rashbam*, be irrevocable. The *Rashbam*'s position and *Rabbeinu Tam*'s position thus represent two distinct readings: the *Rashbam* understands the *matnas bari* as irrevocable absent a specific retraction clause, while *Rabbeinu Tam* holds that the cases under discussion in the *gemara* are specifically those in which retraction was explicitly built in. It is also reasonable to suppose that if the document itself were headed with the notation *matnas bari she-hi ke-matnas sh'chiv mei'ra*, that context alone might suffice to import the right of retraction.

---

## Writing & Delivery Rule

### Shichiv Mei'ra Order

Rava bar Rav Huna was sitting in the portico (*achsadra*) of the academy of Rav, and taught in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *shchiv mei'ra she-amar kitvu u-tnu mana le-ploni u-met, ein kotvin ve-nosnin* — if a person on his deathbed said "write a document and give a hundred *maneh* to so-and-so," and then died before the document could be written and delivered, one does not write the document and deliver it after his death.

The practical issue is this: a verbal declaration of *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra* — simply saying "give my property to Reuven" — would be fully effective. But this dying man did not simply make a verbal bequest. He said *write it and give it*. Does this instruction transform the bequest into a verbal *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra* — effective immediately upon utterance — or does it constitute a directive that the *written* document shall be the vehicle of the gift, in which case delivery of the document is required? If the document is the vehicle, and the man died before it could be written and delivered, the bequest fails entirely: there is no *shtar achar misa*.

### Verbal vs. Written

The concern is captured in the phrase *shema lo gamar le-haknoto ela bi-shtar* — perhaps he only intended to effect the transfer through the written document, not through the verbal declaration alone. And since a *shtar* cannot take effect after death (*ein shtar achar misa*), if that is indeed what he intended, the recipient gets nothing. The case is thus a *safek*: did the verbal instruction constitute a present-tense effective bequest, or was the *shtar* meant to be the sole vehicle? Because of this doubt, and because the doubt favors non-transfer, we do not write and deliver the document posthumously.

### Rebbi Eliezer Warning

Upon hearing this teaching of Rava bar Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, Rebbi Eliezer turned to those present and said *izdaharu bah* — be careful about this *halacha*, pay close attention to it. One might instinctively assume that since the dying man already declared his wishes verbally, the verbal bequest is effective and the *shtar* is merely supplementary documentation. Rebbi Eliezer warns that this is not the case: when the instruction is specifically to write a *shtar*, we must entertain the possibility that the *shtar* was intended as the sole operative mechanism.

There is a dispute about the attribution of this exchange. One version has Rava bar Rav Huna teaching in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, with Rebbi Eliezer urging attention to the ruling. Rav Shizbi offers an alternative version: it was Rebbi Eliezer who originated the ruling, and Rabbi Yochanan who said *izdaharu bah* — affirming the teaching of his student.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rules that Rav Shizbi's version is more plausible. The logic: if Rebbi Eliezer was the one who formulated the ruling and Rabbi Yochanan endorsed it by saying *izdaharu bah*, that is entirely natural — a master lending the weight of his authority to his student's teaching. But if Rabbi Yochanan was the author of the ruling, what need would there be for Rebbi Eliezer to say *izdaharu bah* in relation to his own master? A student affirming his teacher's position in a manner implying the teacher needed endorsement is itself problematic — it carries an echo of the *kibbud av va'eim* concern that you do not publicly second your father's opinion in a way that implies he required your validation.

The attribution is further clinched by a transmission from Ravin, who reported in the name of Rebbi Abbahu that Rebbi Eliezer sent the following ruling to the diaspora (*le-golah*, to Bavel) in the name of *rabbeinu* — which in this context refers to Rav. Rebbi Eliezer was a student of both Rabbi Yochanan and Rav, and sent the ruling to Bavel in Rav's name: *shchiv mei'ra she-amar kitvu u-tnu mana le-ploni u-met, ein kotvin ve-nosnin, shema lo gamar lehaknoso ela be-shtar, ve-ein shtar achar misa*. Rabbi Yochanan then added *tibadek* — one must examine the circumstances.

### Rav Yochanan Qualification

What does *tibadek* mean? Rabbi Yochanan is not disagreeing with the ruling but qualifying it: the outcome depends on context. When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael he explained the qualification.

### Later Will Override

Rav Dimi delivered two teachings. The first, while relevant to the broader topic of wills, is not directly about the *kitvu u-tnu* case: *deyateki mevateles deyateki* — a later will overrides an earlier one. This is the standard rule of testamentary succession. The *gemara* will later discuss whether a will executed with a formal *kinyan* can nonetheless be overridden by a later will; *Shmuel* rules that even in such a case the later will prevails, since the entire context of *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra* preserves the right of revision until death.

### Roiin Assessment

Rav Dimi then addresses the *kitvu u-tnu* case directly. *Roiin* — one assesses the circumstances. *Im ke-miyafes es kocho* — if from the context it is clear that the man wanted the document written as additional strength (*miyafes es kocho*), meaning he obviously intended his verbal declaration as the operative bequest and wanted the document merely as corroborating evidence, then *kotvin* — one may write the document even after death. *Ve-im lav* — if it is not clear that this was his intent, and the ambiguity remains whether he intended the *shtar* to be the sole vehicle, *ein kotvin* — one may not write it.

The challenge with this framework is that it offers no objective test; every case requires judgment. The *gemara* therefore seeks clearer criteria. Rebbi Abba bar Memel raises an apparent contradiction from a *beraita* about a *bari* — a healthy person — who says "write and give a hundred *maneh* to so-and-so" and then dies: one does not write it. The implication (*ha*) is that by contrast, in the case of a *shchiv mei'ra*, one always *would* write it — suggesting that by a *shchiv mei'ra* we invariably assume the verbal bequest was operative. However, Rebbi Abba bar Memel himself resolves this: the implication only applies *be-miyafes es kocho*, when there are contextual indicators that the document was intended as supplementary. The *beraita* does not collapse the distinction entirely; it merely suggests that for a *shchiv mei'ra* the presumption more readily tilts toward *miyafes es kocho* than for a *bari*.

### Rav Chisda Kinyan

The *gemara* then asks: *heichi dami miyafes es kocho* — what specific language in the document indicates that the document was intended as *miyafes es kocho*? The answer is the formulation articulated by Rav Chisda: *u-kanina minei mosif a-matanata da* — "and we effected a *kinyan* on him in addition to this gift." When the *shtar* contains language explicitly framing the *kinyan* or the document as an addition (*mosif*) to the underlying bequest, this demonstrates that the verbal declaration was the primary vehicle and the document is supplementary. This is analogous to a case where the dying man said *af kitvu ve-chatumu ve-havu lei* — "and also write and sign and give it to him." The word *af* — "also," "in addition" — is the marker that the written document is secondary.

Conversely, if the *shtar* or the *kinyan* is framed as the primary mechanism rather than as supplementary, there is a risk that it displaces the *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra* mechanism entirely and subjects the transfer to the ordinary rules of *kinyanim*, with all their attendant limitations. A *kinyan sudar* may seem like "more is better," but if it signals that the donor wanted the *kinyan* to be the operative vehicle rather than his verbal declaration, then its failure before death means the transfer fails. The key question in every case is therefore: did the donor want the *shtar* or *kinyan* in *addition to* the verbal bequest, or *instead of* it?

### Final Ruling

The *gemara* concludes with the ruling: *itmar, Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: halacha, kotvin ve-nosnin* — in the relevant case (where it is *miyafes es kocho*), one does indeed write and deliver the document after death. So too Rabba amar Rav Nachman: *halacha, kotvin*. The *Rashbam* cautions against reading this as a wholesale abandonment of the *miyafes es kocho* framework developed above. Rather, the ruling applies specifically in the case where the context clearly indicates that the written document was intended as supplementary evidence to the operative verbal *matnat sh'chiv mei'ra*.

---

## Father-to-Son Transfer

### Mishnah Text

The *mishnah* states: *ha-kosev nechasav le-vanav tzarich she-yichtov me-hayom u-le'achar misa* — one who writes his property over to his sons must write the formula *me-hayom u-le'achar misa*, "from today and after my death." This is the position of Rebbi Yehuda.

### Rashbam Context

The *Rashbam* situates this *mishnah* not necessarily in the context of a will, but in a common practical scenario: a healthy man (*bari*) who is about to remarry and wishes to protect his existing assets for the children of his first marriage. If he remarries, the children from a potential second marriage would share in the inheritance of his current property. Moreover, his new wife would have *sheibud* — a lien — on his property for her *kesubah*. To forestall this, he transfers title to his current children now, retaining only the *peiros* for his lifetime. The transfer protects the principal from future heirs and from the new wife's claims, while still allowing him the benefit of the property during his life.

### Rebbi Yossi

Rebbi Yossi disagrees with Rebbi Yehuda: *eino tzarich* — the explicit words *me-hayom* are not required. If the document says *le-achar misa*, that suffices. We will see shortly that this is because Rebbi Yossi holds that *zmano shel shtar mochi'ach alav* — the date in the document itself testifies that the transfer is meant to take effect as of the date of writing.

### Rights Restrictions

The *mishnah* then lays out the rights and restrictions that follow from this structure. The father cannot sell the principal because the property is *kesuvim le-ven* — the title is already written to the son. The son equally cannot sell, because the property is *be-reshus ha-av* — under the father's control and benefit. Note the asymmetry in the *mishnah*'s language: the father's inability is framed in terms of ownership (*kesuvim le-ven*), while the son's inability is framed in terms of control (*birshus ha-av*). The father has the *peiros*; the son has the title. Neither can alienate what belongs to the other.

### Father Selling

If the father sells: what he is selling is only his right to the *peiros*, which is all he owns. He can sell the income stream — the right to benefit from the land until his death — and such a sale is valid. A buyer acquires the *peiros* for the duration of the father's life: *mechurin ad she-yamut* — sold until he dies. Once the father dies, the buyer's right to the income ceases, and full ownership consolidates in the son.

### Son Selling

If the son sells his interest — the title — the buyer acquires nothing he can immediately use. *Ein la-lokei'ach bahem klum ad she-yamut ha-av* — the buyer has no benefit in the property until the father dies. Once the father dies, the buyer acquires full ownership along with the right to the *peiros*. The son has sold everything he had: a present title with deferred access, which becomes fully operational upon the father's death. Whether the buyer can further alienate this deferred interest will be addressed in the *gemara*.

---

## Me-hayom Effectiveness

### Formula Mechanics

The *gemara* opens with the question: *v'chi kasav me-hayom u-le'achar misa, mai havay?* — when one writes *me-hayom u-le'achar misa*, how does this formula actually function? What makes it effective?

### Get Comparison

The *gemara* raises a challenge from *Gittin*: the *mishnah* there rules that a *get* given with the formula *me-hayom u-le'achar misa* is a *get ve-eino get* — it is uncertain whether it is a valid bill of divorce or not. If the husband dies, the wife performs *chalitza* (since perhaps she was not divorced and is therefore obligated), but cannot perform *yibum* (since perhaps she was divorced and remarriage with the brother would be *arayos*). She is a *safek megureshes*. If the formula is ambiguous in the case of a *get*, why is it unambiguous — and fully effective — in the case of a property transfer?

The *gemara* answers: *hasam mesapka lan ei tenai havi ei chazara havi* — there, in the case of a *get*, we are genuinely uncertain how to read the formula. Does it mean: "it should take effect today in the event that I die" (*tenai* — a condition)? Or does it mean: "it takes effect today" but then the husband is retracting himself by saying "no, only after I die"? Either reading is grammatically possible, and the second reading would be problematic since a *get* cannot take partial effect today and complete itself after death — a *get* must be fully valid at the moment of delivery or not at all.

In the case of a monetary transfer, however, *hacha hachi ka-amar lei* — the formula yields a perfectly coherent and direct reading: *gufa kani me-hayom* — the title you acquire today; *peira le-achar misa* — the income-right transfers after death. Title and *peiros* are two distinct property interests that can be allocated across time. This parsing works cleanly in *dinei mammonos* in a way it cannot in *dinei gittin*.

### Rav Yosef Position

Rav Yosef now takes up Rebbi Yossi's position and declares: *ein tzarich* — the explicit words *me-hayom* are not even necessary. Even if the document merely says *le-achar misa*, we interpret it as though it said *me-hayom u-le'achar misa*. The date in the *shtar* renders *me-hayom* implicit.

### Rabba Anecdote

At this point the *gemara* relates an anecdote that both contextualizes and confirms the ruling. Rabba bar Avuha fell ill. Rav Huna and Rav Nachman came to visit him. Rav Huna said to Rav Nachman: go ask him whether we rule like Rav Yosef or not. The context of deathbed visits and the topic of wills and bequests lends the scene an added resonance — one that may not be entirely coincidental. Rav Nachman replied: I do not even understand the reasoning behind Rav Yosef's position; how can I ask him how we rule? Rav Huna responded: you ask about the ruling; I will tell you the reasoning. Rav Nachman asked Rabba bar Avuha, who replied: *hachi amar Rav* — this is what Rav taught: *halacha ke-Rav Yosef* — we rule like Rav Yosef. They departed, and Rav Huna proceeded to explain the reasoning.

### Rav Yosef's Reason

*De-amar zmano shel shtar mochi'ach alav* — because the date of the document testifies on its own behalf. If the document's entire operative effect was meant to be *le-achar misa*, there would be no reason to date it; the date would be superfluous. The very fact that the document bears a date implies that something is meant to take effect as of that date. The date is therefore an implicit declaration of *me-hayom*. This reasoning applies specifically in the context of property transfers: the date carries this implication because property documents are routinely dated to reflect when rights begin to accrue.

A parallel application arises by *get*: Rebbi Yossi holds that if a *get* contains the phrase *im masi* ("if I die") and the *get* is dated, the date functions as an implicit *me-hayom*, making the *get* effective from the date of writing in the event of the husband's death. Whether we rule the same way for *get* as for property documents involves additional considerations, but the present *gemara* establishes clearly that for property transfers, *halacha ke-Rav Yosef*.

### Beraita Support

The *gemara* notes that a *beraita* independently supports this position: *Rebbi Yossi omer eino tzarich mipnei she-zmano shel shtar mochi'ach alav* — Rebbi Yossi says it is not necessary to write *me-hayom*, because the date of the document testifies on its own behalf. The *beraita* thus gives the explicit rationale, confirming both the ruling and its underlying logic. The *halacha* follows Rav Yosef, and consequently follows Rebbi Yossi.

---

## Kinyan in Shtar

### Hakna Question

Having established that we rule like Rebbi Yossi — that a dated document saying *le-achar misa* is treated as though it said *me-hayom u-le'achar misa* — Rava poses a further question to Rav Nachman: *be-hakna mahu?* What is the law when the *shtar* contains a *kinyan* — when the document records that a formal act of acquisition (*kinyan sudar*) was performed? Does the presence of the *kinyan* in the *shtar* itself supply the equivalent of *me-hayom*, even without the explicit phrase and without reliance on the date?

The question is significant. Rebbi Yossi and Rebbi Yehuda disagree about whether a bare dated *shtar* saying *le-achar misa* is treated as *me-hayom*. But perhaps even Rebbi Yehuda would concede that a *shtar* recording an explicit *kinyan* necessarily implies *me-hayom*: if you did a *kinyan* today, you must have intended the transfer to be operative today.

### Kinyan Not Required

Rav Nachman's initial response: *be-hakna ein tzarich* — when there is a *kinyan* recorded in the *shtar*, one does not need the explicit phrase *me-hayom*. The *kinyan* itself implies present-tense intent to transfer.

### Pappa's Distinction

Rav Pappa, however, introduces a nuance: *ika akna'ata de-tzarich ve-ika akna'ata de-lo tzarich* — there is a formulation of *kinyan* language that requires the explicit *me-hayom* declaration and a formulation that does not.

### Order of Language

The distinction turns on the order of the *kinyan* language in the document. If the *shtar* says *akneiyei ve-kanina minei* — "he instructed us to effect a *kinyan* for [the recipient], and we effected a *kinyan*" — then *lo tzarich*, no explicit *me-hayom* is needed. If however it says *kanina minei ve-akneiyei* — "we effected a *kinyan*, and he had instructed us to" — then *tzarich*, the explicit declaration is still required.

### Rashbam: Language Order

The *Rashbam* explains the distinction as follows. When the *shtar* begins with *akneiyei* — he told us to effect a *kinyan* — and then adds *kanina minei* — and we did — the second clause appears somewhat redundant, since the witnesses' signatures already attest to the *kinyan* having been done. This redundancy is read as carrying extra weight: it signals that the *kinyan* was done with an intent to take effect immediately, *me-hayom*. The double language represents an extra degree of conviction. Conversely, when the *shtar* begins with *kanina minei* — we did a *kinyan* — and then explains *akneiyei* — because he instructed us — the second clause is explanatory rather than emphatic. It answers *why* the *kinyan* was done, not adding any additional commitment. This formulation therefore does not carry the extra implication of *me-hayom*.

### Rav Chanina Challenge

Rav Chanina miSura challenges this analysis sharply: *mi ika midi de-anan lo yadeinan ve-safra yadi?* — is there really a distinction that we here in the *beis medrash* are unaware of, which the scribes understand? The implication of the distinction is that scribes consciously chose one formulation over the other to signal different legal intents. Can it be that this craft-level knowledge resided with the scribes but was unknown to the sages?

### Scribal Confirmation

The *gemara* reports that messengers were sent to the scribes of Abaye and to the scribes of Rava to ask whether there was any meaningful distinction between the two formulations or whether it was purely stylistic. Both sets of scribes confirmed: *yadi* — yes, they knew the difference. The formulations were not interchangeable; each carried a distinct legal implication. This is a striking moment: the *gemara* acknowledges that there is specialized craft knowledge belonging to professional scribes that is not necessarily possessed by the scholars of the *beis medrash*. Just as a patent judge need not be a technical expert in the underlying field, the *amora'im* do not always know the precise conventions of the scribal profession. The scribes' confirmation vindicates Rav Pappa's distinction.

### Huna's Synthesis

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua offers a synthesis: *bein akneiyei ve-kanina minei bein kanina minei ve-akneiyei, lo tzarich* — in fact, either order of the *kinyan* language renders explicit *me-hayom* unnecessary. Whenever a *kinyan* is recorded in the *shtar*, in whatever formulation, the *shtar* is treated as *me-hayom*, and there is no debate.

### Debate Scope

If so, where does the debate of Rebbi Yehuda and Rebbi Yossi actually apply? *U-veduchran pisgamei de-havi be-anpana pligi* — their debate applies to a *shtar* that is framed as *beduchran pisgamei*, a record of things the witnesses have seen and heard. In this mode, the witnesses are not recording that they themselves performed a *kinyan* on behalf of the recipient; they are simply testifying that they witnessed Reuven transferring his field to Shimon *le-achar misa*. When no *kinyan* by the witnesses is recorded in the document, only their testimony to an event, the debate applies: Rebbi Yehuda requires explicit *me-hayom*; Rebbi Yossi holds that the date suffices.

### Final Clarification

Rav Kahana reports that he presented this analysis before Rav Zevid miNehardea, and that there were variant traditions about exactly how the teaching was formulated. The version that Rav Kahana's academy taught runs as follows, in the name of Rava citing Rav Nachman: *be-aknoi, ein tzarich* — whenever there is a *kinyan* recorded in the *shtar*, regardless of formulation, explicit *me-hayom* is unnecessary and the document is always treated as conveying *me-hayom*. *Be-duchran pisgamei de-havu be-anpana* — in the case of a bare witness-record without an explicit *kinyan* performed by the witnesses themselves — *pligi*: that is where Rebbi Yehuda and Rebbi Yossi debate, and where the question of whether the document's date suffices as an implicit *me-hayom* determines the outcome.

# Bava Batra 136b

## Son's Sale After Death

### Intro: Father's Transfer

The Mishnah concludes with the case of *hakosav nechasav livno le'achar moso* — one who writes the title of his property to his son while retaining the *peirot* (fruits, i.e., usufruct) for himself during his lifetime. As the Rashbam notes, the motivation may be to shield assets from a second wife and her children, or any number of similar concerns. Whatever the underlying purpose, the legal structure is clear: the father transfers title but continues to enjoy the benefits of the property. The Mishnah teaches that no one can sell more than he possesses. If the father sells the property, he has sold only his right to the *peirot* for the duration of his life — the underlying title is no longer his to convey. If the son sells the property, the purchaser acquires nothing until the father dies, since the father's right to the *peirot* remains intact in the interim.

### Central Question

The *gemara* now raises a sharper question: suppose the son sold the property while the father was alive — transferring to Reuven whatever title he possessed — and then the son predeceased the father. When the father subsequently dies, does Reuven acquire the property?

On first reflection, the answer seems obvious. The son sold Reuven his title to the property, subject to the father's right to *peirot* until death. Reuven accepted that limitation and took the risk that the chain of events would unfold favorably. Even if the son is no longer alive, Reuven already acquired the title, and once the father's *peirot* rights terminate at death, Reuven's ownership should fully actualize. But the *gemara* is not so certain.

### R. Yochanan Opinion

Rabbi Yochanan says: *lo kanah lokeach* — Reuven acquires nothing.

### Reish Lakish Opinion

Reish Lakish says: *kanah lokeach* — Reuven does acquire and gains full ownership of the property.

### R. Yochanan Explains

Rabbi Yochanan's position rests on the principle of *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf dami* — the right to the fruits of a property is considered equivalent to ownership of the body of the property itself. Here is the structure: the father transferred the *kinyan haguf* (title) to the son but retained the *kinyan peirot* (the right to all practical benefit). If we say that *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf*, then it is the father who is effectively perceived as the real-world owner, even though the son holds technical title. The father is not the registered owner, but he is the functional owner — the one with actual control and benefit.

From this perspective, the son, though technically holding title, has no actualized ownership. What he possesses is a future interest — a right that will materialize only when the father dies and the *peirot* rights extinguish. When the son purports to sell to Reuven, he is not transferring actual ownership of property; he is, at most, transferring his contingent stake — essentially saying: "You will receive this through me, when I receive it." If the son dies before that moment arrives, he never receives it, and there is nothing to pass through to Reuven. The sale therefore cannot take effect.

It is worth pausing to note, as the Rashba makes explicit, that the son's technical title does carry some real consequences. A second wife the father marries would have no lien on the property, since it is no longer legally registered in the father's name. And if the son were to die without having sold the property, it would pass to the son's own heirs — because it *is* registered in the son's name. The distinction that *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf* draws is more nuanced: the son has title in the registered sense, but he lacks the powers and status of an *owner* in the functional sense. He cannot exercise dominion over it, cannot transfer it as a true owner would. One might frame it this way: under whose name is the property registered? The son's. But who holds the owner's practical power and role? The father. Since the son lacks the owner's role, his purported sale transfers only his contingent future interest — and if he predeceases the father, that interest evaporates.

### Reish Lakish Explains

Reish Lakish holds *kinyan peirot lav k'kinyan haguf dami* — the right to *peirot* is not equivalent to ownership of the body of the property. On this view, the father's retention of the *peirot* does not elevate him to the status of owner; the son is the genuine owner. When the son sold Reuven the property, he conveyed actual title. Reuven takes subject to the father's *peirot* rights, which will terminate at the father's death. At that point, Reuven's ownership — already fully acquired — is no longer encumbered, and he possesses the property outright. The son's death is irrelevant: he had already transferred ownership, and ownership once transferred does not revert simply because the seller is no longer alive.

## Kinyan Peirot Debate

### Case: Field for Fruit

The *gemara* questions why Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish needed to articulate their dispute here. This is, after all, a well-known debate between them — *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf* or not — that was already stated in another context. Specifically, the prior formulation of the debate involves the case of *hamocher sadeh l'peirot*: one who sells his field not outright but for the sake of its fruits. The seller retains the title (*kinyan haguf*) while the buyer, call him Michael, acquires the right to all benefit from the land — its usufruct. That prior case sufficiently establishes the general dispute. Why restate it in the context of the father-son transfer?

### Bikkurim: R. Yochanan

In the *hamocher sadeh l'peirot* case, the *gemara* had recorded that Rabbi Yochanan says Michael *meivi v'korei* — he must bring his first fruits (*bikkurim*) to the Temple and recite the declaration of *mikra bikkurim*, including the phrase *al ha'adama she'nasata li*, "the land which You gave me." Even though Michael does not hold title, since *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf dami*, Michael's ownership of the *peirot* is tantamount to ownership of the land itself. He is therefore treated as the owner of the land for purposes of *bikkurim* and can truthfully declare it as his land.

### Bikkurim: Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish, who holds *kinyan peirot lav k'kinyan haguf dami*, says Michael *meivi v'eino korei* — he brings the *bikkurim* but does not recite the declaration. Since the *kinyan peirot* does not make him the owner of the land, he cannot say *al ha'adama she'nasata li*. The Rashbam and Tosafot debate the basis for the obligation to bring at all under Reish Lakish's view: the Rashbam suggests there is an intermediate level at which Michael's connection to the land suffices to require bringing, though not to permit the declaration; Tosafot holds that the obligation to bring in this case is only rabbinic, since without *kinyan haguf* there is no biblical basis to treat it as his land.

### R. Yochanan Clarifies

Despite this prior statement of the dispute, Rabbi Yochanan explains why he needed to restate his position in the father-son case. Even granting that he generally holds *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf*, one might have thought that in the specific context of a father giving property to his son, the father would be *mochel* — would willingly relinquish — his status as effective owner, deferring to his son. The logic would be: since the son will ultimately receive everything when the father dies anyway, perhaps the father does not insist on retaining the functional title of owner. He is willing to let the son step into that role even while the father still holds the *kinyan peirot*.

This is a genuinely difficult point to articulate. The father's *kinyan peirot* is a real legal right — not a mere social preference — so it is not obvious what exactly he would be relinquishing by being *mochel*. One cannot simply confer the "title of owner" as though it were a separate transferable thing; it would seem to be a natural outgrowth of legal ownership, not something independently conferred. Nevertheless, the concern was real: perhaps when it is one's own son, the father's willingness to be *mochel* effectively means he no longer insists on being perceived as the functional owner, and therefore the son's ownership would be more substantial. Rabbi Yochanan therefore needs to state that even in the father-son case, the *kinyan peirot* is *k'kinyan haguf*, and this does not change merely because the relationship is familial. The father retains his functional status as owner regardless.

### Reish Lakish Clarifies

Reish Lakish similarly explains why he needed to restate his position. Even granting that he holds *kinyan peirot lav k'kinyan haguf* in general, one might have thought that a distinct principle applies when the original owner divests himself partially: whichever element of ownership the original owner retains, he remains considered the owner. Since the original owner started with everything, any portion he keeps should keep him identified as the owner. In the *bikkurim* case, where I sell the *kinyan peirot* to Michael and retain title, I should still be considered the owner — not because of the general rule that *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf*, but simply because I started with full ownership and never completely divested myself. On this reasoning, Michael is not the owner precisely because the original owner retained something.

But one might then think the reverse also follows: when the father retains the *kinyan peirot* and gives the son the *kinyan haguf*, perhaps the father should still be considered the owner, again because whoever retains any element of original ownership remains the owner. Reish Lakish therefore needs to clarify that the identity of "owner" follows the person who holds the *kinyan haguf* — full stop. It does not depend on who held everything originally. If I sell you the *kinyan peirot* and retain the *guf*, I am the owner. If I give over the *guf* and retain only the *peirot*, the one who holds the *guf* is the owner. The principle is consistent and directional: ownership is identified with the *guf*, regardless of the original starting position. Together, the two cases establish that Reish Lakish's view is a general principle and not an artifact of the seller-retains-something scenario.

## Conditional Inheritance

### Gift Sequence Formula

The *gemara* now introduces the formula *nechasai lecha ve'acharecha yirash ploni ve'acharav yirash ploni* — "my property is yours, and after you, so-and-so shall inherit, and after him, so-and-so shall inherit." This formula creates a cascading chain of ownership. If everyone dies in the proper sequence — if the first recipient dies, the second acquires; if the second dies, the third acquires — the arrangement works neatly. The *gemara* notes this explicitly: *meis rishon kana sheni, meis sheni kana shlishi*.

Understanding the mechanism of such a chain requires some care. How does the original giver control the disposition of property after he himself is dead? Once property is transferred to Reuven, it is Reuven's property — ordinarily, the giver cannot dictate where it goes after Reuven's death. One might think of this as some form of *kinyan le-zman* (a time-limited acquisition) or a *tenai* (conditional gift), but both of those frameworks raise their own difficulties. The most intuitive conceptualization, prior to the *gemara*'s clarification, would be that the *guf* was actually transferred to the final recipient — Levi — while the intermediate parties received only *kinyan peirot* for the duration of their lives. On this model, Reuven and Shimon have the usufruct and Levi has the title, and the whole dispute about *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf* becomes directly relevant to this chain.

### Chain Breaking Question

A problem arises: what if Shimon, the second in line, dies before Reuven, the first? Shimon never received the property from Reuven, so Levi cannot receive it through Shimon. The chain breaks. To whom does the property now belong?

If we operated on the initial conceptualization — where Levi holds the *kinyan haguf* and Reuven holds only the *kinyan peirot* — then under Rabbi Yochanan's view (*kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf*), Reuven functions as the virtual owner of the *guf*, and since the chain cannot continue to Levi, the virtual title would revert and effectively consolidate in Reuven. It would then pass to Reuven's heirs upon his death. Under Reish Lakish's view (*kinyan peirot lav k'kinyan haguf*), Reuven's *peirot* right is not *kinyan haguf*, so Reuven is never the owner; Levi, as the holder of the *kinyan haguf*, is the owner, and the property should go to Levi even when the chain breaks. But if the conditions under which Levi was to receive it cannot be met, one could argue instead that the property should revert to the original giver.

The *gemara* raises this latter possibility as a challenge: the *gemara* notes *leyorshei noten mibaei lei* — if Reuven is not an owner (under Reish Lakish's view), and the proper recipient cannot receive, should the property not revert to the original giver's heirs rather than Reuven's?

### Acharecha Mechanism

The response, transmitted in the name of Rav Oshaya in Bavel and confirmed by Rami bar Chama before Rava, is: *acharecha shani* — the word *acharecha* is categorically different. The use of the word *acharecha* ("after you"), particularly in conjunction with *yirash* ("shall inherit"), fundamentally reconceives the nature of the transfer. It is not a case of *guf* to Levi and *peirot* to Reuven and Shimon. Rather, the word *acharecha* means that each party receives full and complete ownership — *guf* and *peirot* together — for the duration of his life, and only thereafter does the full ownership transfer completely to the next person.

This is, as the Rashbam emphasizes, the force of the word *yirash*: the next party *inherits* — receives complete ownership — at the moment the prior party's ownership ends. Whatever the precise legal mechanism by which the original giver can structure this chain (and the *gemara* does not fully articulate it), the outcome is that the formula *acharecha* confers genuine, complete ownership on each person in sequence. Reuven holds the property fully. Shimon is to hold it fully after Reuven. Levi is to hold it fully after Shimon.

With this understanding, the question of what happens when Shimon predeceases Reuven resolves differently. Reuven had full ownership. Shimon, who would have been the next full owner, died without receiving. Since the chain cannot continue through Shimon to Levi, the property simply remains in the full ownership of Reuven and passes, upon Reuven's death, to Reuven's heirs. There is no reversion to the original giver, because Reuven was a genuine owner — not a mere usufructuary — and full owners pass their property to their heirs.
