The *gemara* acknowledges that not everyone accepts *acharecha shani*, and this is indeed a dispute among *tannaim*, as the subsequent *baraita* will demonstrate.

## First Heir's Power

### Baraita: Sale Effect

A *baraita* is cited: in a case of *nechasai lach ve'acharecha l'ploni* — the property is given to Rachel with the instruction that after her, it goes to Sarah — the first recipient sold the property. What is the legal effect? Does the second heir, Sarah, reclaim the property from the purchaser, or is Sarah left with nothing?

The *gemara* notes that a second *baraita* appears to state the direct opposite ruling, creating an apparent contradiction: *kashya deRabbi aDeRabbi u'deRabban Shimon ben Gamliel aDeRabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. Both Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel seem to contradict themselves across the two *baraitot*.

### Tannaic Debate

In the first *baraita*, Rabbi says *hasheni motzi miyad halakochot* — Sarah can reclaim the property from the purchaser. Rachel was not a full owner with the power to sell the underlying property away from Sarah; her sale of the *guf* is therefore void with respect to Sarah's entitlement. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says *ein lashen ela ma sheshiyer rishon* — Sarah receives only what Rachel chose to leave over for her. If Rachel sold the property, the sale is valid and Sarah receives nothing.

In the second *baraita*, the positions appear reversed: Rabbi permits the first recipient to sell and benefit, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel restricts the first recipient to nothing more than the *achilas peirot* — the right to consume the fruit.

### Resolution: Fruit vs. La…

The *gemara* resolves the internal contradiction for each sage. For Rabbi: the two statements are not contradictory — *ha begufa, ha bepeiros*. When Rabbi ruled that Rachel could sell freely, he meant she could sell the *peirot*, the fruits of her entitlement, which she genuinely owns. When Rabbi ruled that Sarah could reclaim the property from purchasers, that was a case where Rachel had attempted to sell the *guf* itself, the underlying property — which Rachel, under Rabbi's view, lacked the power to convey away from Sarah.

### Rabban Shimon View

For Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the *gemara* resolves the contradiction as follows: *ha l'chatchila, ha di'eved* — one ruling addresses the permissible norm, the other the post-facto outcome. *L'chatchila*, Rachel should not sell the underlying *guf*; that would contravene the intention of the original giver who wanted Sarah to receive it. But if Rachel went ahead and sold it *di'eved* — after the fact — the sale takes effect and Sarah is left with nothing. How can this be? Because *acharecha shani*: the word *acharecha* transferred genuine, full ownership to Rachel. Sarah's entitlement exists, but it has not yet actualized — the original giver divested himself of the property entirely, and no one is currently standing as its owner in a way that blocks Rachel's power. Since Rachel holds the full *guf* by virtue of *acharecha shani*, and since there is no explicit stipulation in the gift that would invalidate a sale, Rachel's sale — though contravening the giver's wishes — is legally operative. It was not the most upright thing to do. No one would award Rachel a gold star. But there was no explicit condition that would render the transaction void.

The distinction from the father-son case discussed at the outset is instructive. There, the father *retained* the property and transferred only the title; since he had not fully divested himself, no one could step in and claim uncontested ownership. Here, the giver divested himself entirely, Sarah's ownership has not yet actualized, and Rachel holds what amounts to the only fully actualized title. This creates the space for Rachel to exercise full ownership rights — including the ability to sell.

## Ethics & Wickedness

### Advisor is Rasha

The *gemara* now turns to the ethical dimension of this arrangement. Abaye asks: *eizehu rasha arum* — who is the scheming wicked person? It is *ze hamashi eitza limkor benechasim k'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — the one who advises Rachel to sell the property, invoking the ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel to enable her to break the chain and prevent Sarah from ever receiving the property.

### First Heir's Motivation

Remarkably, Rachel herself is not deemed the *rasha*. Even though she is the one who actually carries out the sale that deprives Sarah of her entitlement, the *gemara* declines to apply that designation to her. The reason is that Rachel acts out of self-interest: she is protecting her own family, benefiting her own children, doing what people naturally do when they look after their own. She has a legal right to do it. It may not reflect the highest standard of *yoshrus* (ethical rectitude), and we would not commend it, but acting within one's legal rights out of self-interest does not make one a *rasha*.

### Advisor's Pure Harm

The *rasha* is the external advisor — the one who has no personal stake in the transaction and whose only contribution is to walk up to Rachel and say: "Did you know that according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, you can sell this property a moment before you die, break the chain, and leave Sarah with nothing?" This person stands to gain nothing. The only effect of his counsel is to harm Sarah. It is this quality — intervening in a dispute that is not one's own, causing harm to another party with no benefit to oneself — that the *gemara* identifies as the hallmark of the *rasha arum*. The *gemara* elsewhere captures a related idea with the phrase *over al riv lo lo* — one who inserts himself into a quarrel that does not belong to him. There is something deeply troubling about deploying one's knowledge of Torah law not to protect a right one holds, but to arm someone else against a third party whom one has no reason to harm. Paradoxically, it is precisely *because* the advisor acts without personal self-interest that he is more culpable, not less: he cannot even claim the partial justification of looking after his own needs.

### Halachic Ruling

The *gemara* records that Rav Yochanan rules *halacha k'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*: the first heir may indeed sell the underlying property and thereby break the chain. The Rashbam notes that this ruling simultaneously reflects the position that *kinyan peirot lav k'kinyan haguf dami* — and that the operative mechanism enabling Rachel to sell is *acharecha shani*, the word *acharecha* having conferred upon her genuine and complete ownership of the *guf*.

## Matnat Shachiv Mera

### Competing Claims

The *gemara* now introduces a closely related scenario that carries significant practical implications. In the same *acharecha* framework, rather than selling the property to an outside purchaser during her lifetime, Rachel makes a *matnat shachiv mera* — a deathbed gift — conveying the property to a third party, Devorah. The question is: when Rachel dies, does the property go to Devorah by virtue of the *matnat shachiv mera*, or does it go to Sarah by virtue of the *acharecha* formula?

Both claims purport to take effect at or upon Rachel's death. This is the tension.

### Timing Distinction

Abaye rules: *matnat shachiv mera lo kanah ela l'achar mita, v'kodam acharecha* — the *matnat shachiv mera* takes effect only after death, and the *acharecha* transfer has already preceded it. The property goes to Sarah. Devorah's *matnat shachiv mera* does not override the *acharecha*.

### Moment vs. After

This ruling requires an important conceptual distinction. Did both transfers not take effect "after Rachel's death"? How can one precede the other? Abaye draws the line between *im gmar mita* — at the very moment of death — and *l'achar mita* — after death. The *acharecha* formula takes effect *im gmar mita*, at the precise moment Rachel ceases to be alive. The *matnat shachiv mera*, by contrast, takes effect *l'achar mita*, after that moment has passed.

Why should *acharecha* be read as occurring at the moment of death rather than after? Because *acharecha* means "after you" — after you are no longer among the living. At the instant of death, Rachel is no longer the subject "you"; the moment the living state ends, *after you* has arrived. By contrast, *l'achar mita* — the framework for both *matnat shachiv mera* and ordinary *yerusha* — refers to after the death has already occurred, a beat later. One can visualize it as: here is Rachel alive, here is the moment of death, and here is the moment after death. *Acharecha* occupies the threshold moment itself — the transition from alive to dead. *L'achar mita* occupies the moment after that threshold has been crossed. Sarah's entitlement under *acharecha* attaches at the threshold; Devorah's *matnat shachiv mera* attaches only once the threshold has been passed. Sarah therefore takes priority.

### Deathbed Gift Timing

The *gemara* immediately questions whether Abaye himself actually held this position consistently. A *baraita* records a dispute: *matnat shachiv mera — aimasai kanah?* — when does a deathbed gift take effect? Abaye says *im gmar mita* — at the moment of death. Rava says *l'achar gmar mita* — after the moment of death.

This internal tension within Abaye's position creates a difficulty. If Abaye holds that *matnat shachiv mera* takes effect *im gmar mita* — at the very moment of death — then Devorah's claim through the *matnat shachiv mera* and Sarah's claim through *acharecha* would be simultaneous, arising at precisely the same moment. The earlier ruling, in which Abaye seemed to say the *acharecha* precedes the *matnat shachiv mera*, would be undermined. Whether Abaye can reconcile these two positions, and what the practical *nafka mina* between *im gmar mita* and *l'achar gmar mita* would be in other cases — whether, for instance, a *matnat shachiv mera* takes effect at the same moment as an ordinary *yerusha* or a beat after it — is where the *gemara* will continue.

---

---

# Bava Batra 137

## Achareicha Ownership

### Sarah & Rachel Setup

The sugya opens by revisiting the debate between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel concerning the mechanics of an *achareicha* transfer. The case runs as follows: a donor gives property to Sarah with the stipulation *achareicha* — that after Sarah it should pass to Rachel. The question is what precisely Sarah receives. Does the *achareicha* language mean that everything is conveyed to Sarah, including the underlying land, and Rachel merely stands to inherit after Sarah's death? Or does *achareicha* preserve the *karka* for Rachel from the outset, leaving Sarah with only *kinyan peirot* — the rights to the produce and usufruct?

### Rabbi's Position

Both authorities agree that *lechatchila* Sarah should not attempt to sell the *karka* outright. But the disagreement surfaces when she actually does so. Rabbi holds that *kinyan peirot lav k'kinyan haguf* — the right to the produce does not constitute ownership of the body of the property — and therefore Sarah lacks the power to alienate the land.

### RSG's Position

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that she can sell it. His reasoning is either that *kinyan peirot k'kinyan haguf* — the usufruct right is tantamount to full ownership — or, alternatively, that *achareicha shani*: the *achareicha* formulation itself is distinctive and actually conveys the *guf* of the property to Sarah, with Rachel receiving it only thereafter. Under Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view, Sarah holds genuine title and can therefore convey it to another.

### Rasha Arum Question

The *gemara* then raises a related question: what if Sarah, rather than attempting an outright sale, were advised to convey the property to a third party as a gift, thereby severing the chain and cutting Rachel out entirely? Anyone who counsels such a strategy is characterized as a *rasha arum* — a wickedly shrewd person — because they are engineering harm to Rachel without any benefit to Sarah herself. Sarah *lechatchila* should not pursue this course; and while if she actually did so we might not invoke the harshest terminology for her conduct, the advisor who orchestrated it bears that designation.

---

## Death Timing Stages

### Three Death Stages

A more sophisticated question then arises: what if Sarah, instead of making an outright gift, attempts to convey the property through a *matnat shchiv mera* — a deathbed gift — to a third party, thereby breaking the chain before it reaches Rachel? To analyze this, the *gemara* conceptualizes three distinct temporal stages. First, there is the period while Sarah is still alive. Second, there is the moment of death itself — *gmar misa*. Third, there is the period after death has already concluded.

### Achareicha vs. Matna

The *gemara* reasons as follows. The *achareicha* transfer to Rachel takes effect at the moment of death — the instant Sarah is no longer alive. The classic formulation of a *matnat shchiv mera*, by contrast, is *mehayom ule'achar mita* — operative after death. Accordingly, if Sarah attempted a *matnat shchiv mera* to a third party, Rachel would prevail: the *achareicha* chain to Rachel kicks in at the moment of death, while the *matnat shchiv mera* to the third party would only take effect after death. The attempted conveyance does not succeed in breaking the chain.

### Bein Hashmashot

This analysis invites a conceptual observation that is worth pausing over. The framework requires us to distinguish not merely between "alive" and "dead" but to treat the moment of death as its own discrete category — almost like a *bein hashmashot*, a twilight zone that is neither the prior state nor the subsequent one. Death, of course, is experienced practically as a process rather than a binary switch. Yet the *gemara* conceptualizes it as two stages: the moment of death and what comes after. Whether the *gemara* means to posit a literally instantaneous sliver of time or is simply working with a conceptual distinction between two phases is not entirely clear, but the analytical framework depends on maintaining that distinction.

---

## Matna Timing Debate

### Abaye's Position

The *gemara* quotes Abaye as the authority for the ruling that *matnat shchiv mera* takes effect *l'achar misa* — after death — and that therefore the *achareicha* to Rachel beats it out. But the *gemara* immediately challenges this: was that really Abaye's position? For it was taught elsewhere that Abaye and Rava disputed precisely this question. Abaye had said: *matnat shchiv mera lo kani ela im gmar misa* — it takes effect at the moment of death, not after. Rava had said: *l'achar gmar misa* — only after death has concluded.

What might have motivated Abaye's original position of *im gmar misa*? The underlying tension in *matnat shchiv mera* is that it is a rabbinic institution attempting to combine two incompatible legal mechanisms. On one hand, it seeks to function like an inheritance — something that passes upon death. On the other hand, it operates through the power of a living person to make a gift; one cannot give a gift to take effect after one's own death, since at that point one no longer has the legal capacity to convey anything. The compromise Abaye may have been reaching toward is to locate the operative moment as close to death as possible without crossing entirely into the post-death period — *im gmar misa*, at that threshold moment when death is completing.

### Rava's Position

Rava, by contrast, places the operative moment squarely after death — *l'achar gmar misa*. For Rava, the *matnat shchiv mera* fully approximates a *yerusha*, a natural inheritance, in its timing.

### Abaye Reverses

The *gemara* reports that Abaye ultimately reversed himself — *hadar beih Abaye* — and came to agree with Rava that *matnat shchiv mera* takes effect *l'achar gmar misa*. The question the *gemara* then poses is: from which position exactly did Abaye retract? Perhaps, the *gemara* suggests, Abaye did not retract from his position of *im gmar misa* at all. Perhaps instead he retracted from his ruling in the *achareicha* case — and his revised view would be that both the *achareicha* and the *matnat shchiv mera* operate *im gmar misa*, splitting simultaneously at the moment of death. On that reading, the chain to Rachel and the deathbed gift to the third party would arrive at the same instant, and the question of which prevails would remain open.

### Get Proof

The *gemara* rejects this reading. *Lo salka datach* — it is inconceivable, the *gemara* argues, that *matnat shchiv mera* operates *im gmar misa*. The proof is from the laws of *get*. The *mishnah* presents three formulations a dying man might use when giving his wife a *get*: *ze gitecha im mati* — this is your *get* if I die; *ze gitecha mecholi ze* — this is your *get* of this illness; and *ze gitecha le'achar mita* — this is your *get* after my death. The last formulation, *le'achar mita*, renders the *get* entirely invalid — *velo amar klum*. From this the *gemara* infers that a deathbed *get* takes effect after death, and therefore that the equivalent mechanism for a *matnat shchiv mera* likewise operates after death. Accordingly, Abaye must have retracted from his *im gmar misa* position and now agrees with Rava that *matnat shchiv mera* is *l'achar gmar misa* — and thus Rachel's *achareicha* claim at the moment of death precedes it.

### Proof Analysis

This is a striking piece of reasoning that warrants careful scrutiny, because the *gemara* is making at least two significant assumptions that are not self-evident.

The first assumption is that the timing of a deathbed *get* is the same as the timing of a *matnat shchiv mera*. These are genuinely different legal instruments. A *matnat shchiv mera* is a special rabbinic institution with its own mechanics; it need not operate on the same clock as a conditional *get*. The *gemara* assumes they are equivalent in this respect, but the reason for that assumption is not made explicit.

The second, more fundamental question concerns how the *get* case actually demonstrates that the operative moment is *l'achar gmar misa* rather than *im gmar misa*. The *mishnah* tells us that *ze gitecha le'achar mita* is definitively invalid. But why does that prove that *im gmar misa* would also be invalid — and thus that the *get* must be operating *l'achar misa*? Two possibilities present themselves. One is that if the operative moment were *im gmar misa*, we would expect the *get* to be at least a *safek* — doubtfully valid — rather than definitively invalid. The *gemara* apparently assumes the *get* is *vadai* not effective, which means *im gmar misa* cannot be the operative moment either. The alternative possibility — which is worth taking seriously — is that the phrase *im gmar misa* does not in fact refer to a gray transitional instant at all. Perhaps *im gmar misa* simply means "a moment before death" — the instant just before the transition is complete, while the person is still halachically alive. If so, a *get* given *im gmar misa* would be perfectly valid, and the contrast the *gemara* is drawing is between the moment-before-death formulation (where the *get* works) and the after-death formulation (where it does not). The *gemara*, on this reading, is demonstrating that since *le'achar mita* fails, the operative moment must be placed earlier — and whatever label we apply to that earlier moment, it is the functional equivalent of what Rava calls *l'achar gmar misa* for *matnat shchiv mera*.

The upshot is that the *gemara* concludes both Abaye and Rava agree: *matnat shchiv mera* operates *l'achar gmar misa*. Consequently, in the original case, Rachel's *achareicha* claim ripens at the moment of death and Sarah's attempted *matnat shchiv mera* to the third party takes effect only afterwards — the chain remains unbroken and Rachel receives the property.

---

## RSG Halacha

### Slaves & Shrouds

The *gemara* now returns to the ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and extends it to a series of cases. Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Yochanan states: *halacha k'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — we rule like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that in an *achareicha* transfer the first recipient has genuine title and may convey the property. *V'afilu hayu bahen avadim v'hotzian lecheirus* — and this applies even if the gifted property included slaves and she freed them. Freeing the slaves would break the chain, since Rachel would have expected to receive them.

The *gemara* objects: *pshita* — is this not obvious? If she owns the property, of course she can free the slaves. The *gemara* responds: *mahu detaima* — one might have thought the original donor could argue that while he accepted she might redirect the property, he never contemplated she would commit an *issur* with it. According to the *gemara*, there is a prohibition against freeing a Canaanite slave — a position that requires acknowledging the conceptual difficulty of reading the Torah's extensive concern with ethical treatment of slaves and liberation from bondage as establishing such a prohibition. Regardless, the *gemara* rules: *ka mashma lan* — we are nonetheless taught she may do even this.

Similarly, Rabbi Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan rules *halacha k'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*, and extends it to a case where the gifted property was cloth and the recipient turned it into *tachrichim* — burial shrouds. By becoming *assur b'hana'ah*, the shrouds are removed from Rachel's ability to benefit from them, effectively breaking the chain. Again the *gemara* raises a *hava amina* that the donor could protest: *leshabbinei issurei hana'ah lo yahavi lach* — I did not give it to you to transform into something from which benefit is forbidden. And again the *gemara* rules: *ka mashma lan*, she may do so.

These rulings might superficially seem strange. Once a gift is given, how can the original donor dictate subsequent use? The answer lies in a principle discussed earlier in the *gemara* that in unilateral gift transactions we are more attentive to the mindset of the giver — *da'at hanosein* — because the recipient risked nothing. In some circumstances, *devarim she'b'lev* — unstated intentions — carry halachic weight in the gift context. Nonetheless, in these cases the *gemara* concludes that such implicit restrictions do not override the recipient's full ownership rights. Had the donor wished to impose such restrictions, he would have needed to do so through explicit conditions.

### Esrog Yotzei

The *gemara* now introduces a celebrated case. Rava bar Rav Chisda teaches: *esrog zeh nassun lach b'matanah v'acharecha li-ploni* — this *esrog* is given to you as a gift and after you it should go to so-and-so. Sarah received the *esrog* with an *achareicha* to Rachel. Sarah took the *esrog* and sought to fulfill the *mitzvah* of the Four Species. Was she *yotzei*?

At first glance this would simply replicate the debate between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, *achareicha shani* — she has genuine ownership — and she can certainly be *yotzei* with her own *esrog*. According to Rabbi, she has only *kinyan peirot*, not *kinyan haguf*. Since being *yotzei* with an *esrog* requires full ownership — *lachem mishelachem*, the *esrog* must be yours — it would seem she cannot fulfill the *mitzvah*.

The *gemara*, however, challenges this conclusion even with respect to Rabbi's position.

### Intent Presumption

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak raises the following objection. The debate between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel concerned whether *kinyan peirot* is equivalent to *kinyan haguf* for purposes of commercial transactions — can she sell the land? But here, with an *esrog*, what possible use does *kinyan peirot* afford her? *Im mafik lo nafik bei, lemai yahavis nihaleh* — if she cannot use it to be *yotzei* the *mitzvah*, why did the donor give it to her at all? With a field, *kinyan peirot* means she benefits from the produce. With a table, *kinyan peirot* means she can use the table. But with a single *esrog*, no natural use presents itself that would constitute *kinyan peirot* — she cannot eat it in any meaningful quantity, she cannot sell it. The only conceivable purpose for which the *esrog* was transferred to her was to enable her to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *netilas lulav*. Therefore, the *gemara* concludes, even Rabbi must agree that the conveyance was designed to enable her to be *yotzei* — and the *gemara* rules: *ela mafik, d'chulei alma modu denafik* — regarding fulfilling the *mitzvah*, everyone agrees she is *yotzei*.

### Everyone Agrees

The ruling is thus that on the question of being *yotzei* the *mitzvah*, Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel do not disagree. Both hold that she may fulfill her obligation with this *esrog*. The *gemara* grounds this not in an objective determination that *kinyan peirot* satisfies the ownership requirement of *lachem*, but rather in an assessment of the donor's intent: since there was no other conceivable purpose for this gift, we read the transfer as specifically designed to give her whatever title is necessary to be *yotzei*.

### Sale vs. Eat

The dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel remains operative in the other direction. *Machrah achlah — banu lemachlokes Rabbi v'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — if Sarah sold the *esrog* or ate it, thereby breaking the chain to Rachel, that is precisely where the classical debate resurfaces. According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, she had *kinyan haguf* and was entitled to do so. According to Rabbi, she had only *kinyan peirot* and by consuming or selling it she violated the terms of the conveyance and Rachel is entitled to redress.

The *Rashbam*'s explanation of why being *yotzei* counts as a form of *kinyan peirot* deserves attention. He writes that being *yotzei* the *mitzvah* is the *peri* — the fruit — of this *esrog*, and that is what was granted to her. This framing is difficult to accept straightforwardly. The Torah's requirement of *lachem* demands ownership, not merely the benefit of use. Lending someone an *esrog* does not enable them to be *yotzei* — only genuine transfer of ownership does. If Sarah truly lacks *kinyan haguf*, then simply designating the fulfillment of the *mitzvah* as a form of *peri* does not resolve the underlying ownership deficiency.

A more satisfying account would be that the conveyance in this context actually does grant Sarah full *kinyan haguf* — but only for the limited domain of *hilchos esrog*. In other words, the transfer is not a global *kinyan peirot* that somehow extends to ritual purposes; rather, the donor's expressed intent creates a genuine, if circumscribed, ownership right in Sarah for precisely this purpose: she has title to the *esrog* for the *mitzvah*, and for that purpose alone. This is not unlike other cases in the *gemara* where an entity is considered an owner within one legal domain but not another. Just as ownership of a slave can be notionally transferred to a second party for limited purposes — such as determining liability if the slave is gored — so too here Sarah may be treated as the owner within the narrow compass of *mitzvah* fulfillment.

---

## Estate vs. Partners

### Estate Entity

The *gemara* introduces a related and analytically rich case. Rabba bar Huna states: *ha'achim shekanu esrog b'tfusas habayis* — brothers who jointly inherited an estate used estate funds to purchase an *esrog*. This *esrog* is thus collectively owned — but through the distinctive mechanism of *tufsat habayis*, estate ownership, rather than ordinary partnership.

The legal significance of *tufsat habayis* lies in the fact that it functions similarly to a corporate entity. In ordinary *shutfus*, partnership, each partner owns a defined fractional share — half mine, half yours. In an undivided estate, by contrast, no individual brother owns any specific fraction. The estate itself is the owner, and the brothers are beneficiaries or shareholders in that abstract entity until a formal division takes place. This makes *tufsat habayis* a remarkable precedent in halachic thinking for something approaching the modern concept of a legal person distinct from its human members.

The problem with using a jointly-owned *esrog* in ordinary *shutfus* is well established: one cannot be *yotzei* with a *lulav* and *esrog* belonging to partners, because *lachem* demands that the object be fully yours, and half-ownership is insufficient.

### Brother Yotzei

The question, then, is whether *tufsat habayis* is different. The *gemara* rules: *natlo echad meihem v'yatza bah* — if one of the brothers took it and sought to be *yotzei* — *im yachol lochlo yatza, v'im lav lo yatza* — if he could have eaten it without the other brother objecting, he was *yotzei*; if not, he was not.

The eating criterion invites analysis. One reading is that eating functions as a mere indicator of effective ownership: the fact that the brother could have consumed it without objection shows that the others implicitly ceded their interest to him — effectively allowing him to treat it as if he had extracted it from the estate for his own use. On this reading, the *esrog* has been constructively removed from the estate and he is effectively its sole owner at the moment he takes it, and the eating test is simply a diagnostic tool.

A deeper reading draws on a principle in *Sukkah* regarding the *esrog*: the *esrog* must be *rauy l'achilah* — fit for eating — in order to satisfy the requirement of *lachem*. The Rambam, in *Peirush Mishnayos*, explains that the Torah specifies *pri eitz hadar* — a fruit — and something that cannot be eaten does not fully qualify as such. Inability to eat might arise because the produce is *tevel* and hence halachically inaccessible, or because one's rights over it are incomplete. If the brother's interest in the estate is such that he cannot freely consume the *esrog* without objection, his claim on it is insufficiently robust to constitute the ownership the *mitzvah* demands.

The further question is whether the estate structure genuinely does something legally that plain partnership does not, or whether the operative principle is simply that wherever — whether in an estate or a partnership — the other party would not object to consumption, that is sufficient to treat the consumer as the functional owner. The *gemara*'s specification that the ruling applies *davka d'ika esrog l'chol chad u'chad* — only when each of the other brothers had his own *esrog* — suggests that the absence of objection is itself the operative fact: when Michael has his own *esrog*, his willingness to let his brother take the estate *esrog* without protest functions as an implicit concession, bringing the case within a framework similar to the conditional gift discussed below.

### Community Esrog

The *Rashbam* records an illuminating historical practice from his own community. The custom in his time was for the entire congregation to share a single *esrog*, since *esrogim* were difficult to obtain. The *Rashbam* explains the halachic basis: since the *esrog* is communally owned — which would be a form of *shutfus* and thus ordinarily problematic — the community operates on the understanding that whenever any individual's turn comes to take the *esrog* and make the *bracha*, every other member of the community implicitly grants that person, as a gift, their respective portion in the *esrog* at that moment. Thus the person holding the *esrog* owns it fully at the instant of the *mitzvah* — *kol echad ad she-yivareich alav*.

The *Rashbam* grounds this in the principle that even an unexpressed but universally understood intent is legally operative: *af al gav de-lo parish k'man de-parish dami* — even where it was not explicitly stated, it is treated as if it were. He connects this to the framework of *matanah al menat l'hachzir* — a gift on condition it be returned — since each member effectively transfers the *esrog* to the current holder for the duration of his use and it then reverts to the communal pool.

---

## Conditional Return

### Return Condition

The *gemara* now takes up the paradigmatic case of *matanah al menat l'hachzir* — a gift on condition that it be returned. Rava states: *esrog zeh nassun lach b'matanah al menat she-tachzireihu li* — this *esrog* is given to you as a gift on condition that you return it to me. Michael took it and was *yotzei*, and then returned it. He was *yotzei*. If Michael took it but did not return it — *lo yatza* — he did not fulfill his obligation, and moreover he now holds a stolen *esrog*, since the original transfer to him was conditional and the condition was never satisfied, meaning retroactively the *esrog* was never validly his.

A series of nuanced questions arise from this framework. First, what exactly constitutes *hachzarah* — returning? Does it require a formal act of *kinyan* transferring ownership back, or merely physically placing the object back in the original owner's hands? If the *beis din* compels Michael to return the *esrog* after he refused to do so voluntarily, has the condition been retroactively satisfied? Intuitively, *al menat she-tachzireihu li* implies a volitional act of return — and involuntary restitution would not seem to qualify. Intermediate cases — where Michael neither intended to keep it nor actively returned it, simply leaving it in the room for the original owner to retrieve — present their own difficulties regarding what constitutes fulfillment of the condition.

A separate question concerns giving the *esrog* to a minor child *al menat she-tachzireihu li*. A *katan* can acquire property *al yedei acher* but cannot himself transfer title back. If the condition requires a formal act of *makneh* by the child, it cannot be fulfilled. But if *she-tachzireihu* means only physical return rather than a formal legal act of transfer, a *katan* might be able to satisfy it.

### Valid Conditional Gift

The *gemara* derives from this case a significant conceptual ruling: *matanah al menat l'hachzir shma matanah* — a gift conditioned on return is nonetheless a legally valid gift. This is not self-evident. One might naturally reason that any gift destined to be returned is a mere fiction — the recipient was never truly the owner, only a temporary possessor. The *chiddush* of Rava is that the conditional gift confers genuine ownership during the period of possession, with a stipulation governing what must subsequently occur. The recipient is a full owner; the condition does not negate the *kinyan* but rather creates an obligation that runs alongside it.

---

## Palm Tree Case

### Tree Transfer

The *gemara* presents a case involving a woman who held a palm tree situated within the property of Rabibi bar Abaye. Whenever she wished to go and harvest the tree, Rabibi bar Abaye would object and impede her access — insisting the timing was inconvenient, that she was disturbing his land, and so forth. Eventually she transferred ownership of the tree to him for the duration of his lifetime, apparently calculating that after his death the ownership would revert to her and she could then access the tree without conflict.

### Transfer to Son

Rabibi bar Abaye, however, proceeded to transfer the tree to his minor son. The choice of a minor son was deliberate: a *katan* can acquire property — *koneh* — but cannot himself transfer it — *eino yachol l'haknos*. By placing the tree in his minor son's hands, Rabibi bar Abaye ensured that no one could subsequently acquire it from the son, insulating it from alienation.

The question is whether this maneuver broke the chain. The woman was the *achareicha* — she was the one who had stipulated that ownership should revert to her upon his death. According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, a recipient in an *achareicha* arrangement can sell or convey the property to another, thereby breaking the chain. If that is so, did Rabibi bar Abaye's transfer to his son sever the woman's reversion rights?

### RSG Allows

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua addressed Rabibi bar Abaye dismissively, saying — in a colorful idiom — that because he came from the place of Mamula, he offered Mamula-style arguments, an expression the *Rashbam* explains as meaning either crude, cut-down reasoning or perversely twisted logic; in any case, it was not intended as a compliment. The substance of Rav Huna's critique: even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who permits the first recipient to convey the property and thereby break the chain, *lo ka'amar ela l'acher* — said so only when the conveyance is to a genuinely independent third party. Conveying the property to one's own son does not constitute a chain-breaking transfer. The son remains within the domain of his father; after the father's death, the reversion to the woman remains operative, and the transfer to the son does not interrupt it.

---

## Ox & Hekdesh

### Hekdesh Return

The *gemara* concludes with a case that illuminates the boundaries of *matanah al menat l'hachzir*. Rava citing Rav Nachman states: *shor zeh natun lach b'matanah al menat she-tachzireihu li* — here is an ox as a gift, on condition that you return it to me. The recipient declared the ox *hekdesh* — consecrated to the Temple — and then returned it. The *gemara* initially suggests: *harei zeh mukdash umuchzar* — the ox is *hekdesh* and the condition has been satisfied. This would follow from the principle that *matanah al menat l'hachzir shma matanah*: the recipient was a genuine owner during his period of possession and therefore had the capacity to declare *hekdesh* with binding effect.

Rava, however, challenges Rav Nachman: *mai ahadrei* — what did he actually return? He returned an ox that the original owner cannot use, since it is now *hekdesh* and *assur b'hana'ah*. That does not satisfy the condition. Rav Nachman responds: *umai chasrei* — and what did the owner lose? The ox is physically intact. This exchange is bracketed by Rav Ashi, who resolves the matter through a linguistic distinction.

### L'Hachzir Variants

Rav Ashi distinguishes between two formulations of the condition. If the donor said *al menat she-tachzirehu* — on condition that you return it — then so long as the object is physically returned, the condition is fulfilled, regardless of its subsequent usability. On that formulation, declaring it *hekdesh* and then returning it satisfies the condition. But if the donor said *al menat she-tachzirehu li* — on condition that you return it *to me* — the condition requires that what is returned be *midi d'chazi li* — something fit for the donor's use. Returning an ox that is *hekdesh* and from which the donor may derive no benefit fails this standard.

### Circular Logic

On the formulation *she-tachzirehu li*, a striking circularity emerges. The recipient declares the ox *hekdesh* and then returns it. But because the returned ox is *assur b'hana'ah* and thus unfit for the donor, the condition *li* is not satisfied. If the condition is not satisfied, the gift was never valid — the recipient never received genuine ownership. If he never owned it, he lacked the capacity to declare *hekdesh* in the first place. And if the *hekdesh* declaration is void, then the ox is not actually *hekdesh* — in which case one might think the return is valid, which would mean the gift was valid, which would mean the *hekdesh* was valid after all. The *gemara* does not continue this cycle. The conclusion stands: where the donor stipulated *li*, the *hekdesh* declaration fails, the condition is unmet, and the ox reverts to the donor's unencumbered ownership. Where the donor stipulated without *li*, the condition is satisfied and the *hekdesh* is operative.

---

---

# Bava Batra 138

## Matana al Mnat Lehachzir

### Topic Introduction

The sugya on daf 138 emerges from a discussion that had occupied the preceding amud — the concept of *matana al mnat lehachzir*, a conditional gift given with the requirement that it be returned. This topic was loosely connected to the broader principles of *kinyan perot* and *kinyan haguf*, and the question of what constitutes genuine ownership of an object. The classic case of *lulav* and *esrog* comes to mind, but here it is Rava who introduces the principle into the Talmudic discussion. The Gemara even entertains the question of whether the recipient of such a conditional gift might have the capacity to be *maktish* the object — and whether that depends on the nature of the return condition: whether one must return the object in a usable state or merely return the thing itself.

### Hakoteiv Nechasav

With this context in place, the Gemara pivots — loosely but naturally — to a teaching four lines from the bottom of 137b. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states: *hakoteiv nechasav leachair* — one who writes over his property to another person. Whether this is a *matnat shchiv meira* or an ordinary *matnat bari* is not entirely clear from the context, though the Gemara seems to be describing a standard transfer. The giver executes a *kinyan agav* — conveying all his property via a deed linked to a parcel of land — and hands the *shtar* to the recipient. The recipient, upon receiving the *shtar*, declares: *iy afshi bahen* — I want no part of this. The ruling: *kana*. He has acquired. The transfer is complete.

This is, at first glance, deeply counterintuitive. How can a person acquire property without his *ratzon*? The Gemara continues: *v'afilu omeid v'tzoveiach* — even if he stands and shouts that he does not want it, the acquisition holds. Rabbi Yochanan, however, disagrees: *lo kana* — he has not acquired.

## Tzavach vs. Shatek

### Rav vs. Rabbi Yochanan

The apparent dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan — one holding the acquisition valid even over protest, the other holding it invalid — demands resolution. At first reading, the position of *kana* seems almost coercive: property is forced upon a person against his expressed will. The principle that one cannot be compelled to receive a benefit against his wishes — *ein mazkin l'adam ba'al karcho* — seems to cut directly against this result.

### Rav Abba bar Memel

Rav Abba bar Memel steps in at the opening of 138a to clarify that the two positions do not actually conflict. The key is the timing of the objection: *kan b'tzoveiach meikara* — one case concerns someone who protests from the very outset, and *kan b'shoteik meikara u'lesof tzoveiach* — the other concerns someone who is initially silent and only protests afterward. If the recipient objected immediately upon being handed the *shtar*, from the very first moment, everyone agrees he has not acquired anything. But if he initially accepted it — or at least remained silent in a way that could be interpreted as acceptance — and only later began to protest, then the acquisition is complete, and his subsequent objection is merely a change of mind.

The practical question of what counts as *meikara* is not trivial. If it took him ten seconds to react, perhaps he was momentarily stunned — is a brief pause still within the window of *achar k'dei dibur*? What exactly is the *shiur*? But the operative principle is clear: if there was a meaningful pause before the protest, during which he held the *shtar* and could be understood to have accepted it, then the acquisition stands. His later yelling does not undo it.

### Giluy Milta

One might argue that the subsequent protest functions as *giluy milta* — a retroactive revelation that the person never truly wanted the acquisition. Perhaps his initial silence was nothing more than cognitive processing of the information, not genuine consent. The Gemara's *chiddush* is precisely that we do not interpret the later *tzoveiach* as revealing that he never wanted it. Once sufficient time has passed in silence, the acquisition has taken root, and the subsequent protest is merely an attempt to divest — one that may succeed going forward but cannot retroactively undo what has already occurred.

### Rashbam's Moral View

The Rashbam, in his first comment on this passage, frames the case of *tzoveiach meikara* with a moral dimension. He notes that when the recipient protests immediately, the acquisition fails because *ein mazkin l'adam ba'al karcho* — one cannot bestow a benefit on someone against his will. The Rashbam then cites the verse *sonei matanot yichyeh* — he who hates gifts shall live — suggesting that a person's refusal of a gift may itself be principled and morally admirable. Beyond the verse, there are practical concerns as well: *marbeh nechasim marbeh da'aga* — greater wealth brings greater anxiety. A person might well not want the obligations, the exposure, or the responsibilities that come with owning more property.

This brings the Rashbam to note the principle of *zachin l'adam shelo b'fanav*, which operates in the background here. Normally, Halacha presumes that acquiring property on someone's behalf is a benefit to them — and thus it can be done without their knowledge or presence. If the recipient is not present and a third party acquires on his behalf, the acquisition is valid on the assumption of benefit. But this is only a presumption; it can be defeated.

## Zachin Shelo B'Fanav

### Principle of Zachin

The principle of *zachin l'adam shelo b'fanav* holds that one may acquire property on behalf of another person even without that person's presence or knowledge. The underlying logic is straightforward: we presume that it is to a person's benefit to receive property, and therefore a third party may act on that presumption without being formally appointed as a *shaliach*.

### Eruvin Applications

This principle has direct practical applications in areas of *eruvin*. When establishing a *chatzeirot* eruv that requires joint ownership of a food item — bread or *matzah*, for instance — one person can acquire a share on behalf of all the residents of a courtyard or town without their explicit knowledge or authorization. The same presumption of benefit animates that acquisition: it is taken for granted that participation in an eruv is beneficial to each resident.

### Exception: Objection

However, because the entire mechanism rests on a presumption rather than on actual expressed consent, it follows that once the beneficiary learns of the acquisition and objects, the presumption is defeated. If I acquired my car for Michael through a third party's act of *kinyan*, and Michael upon learning of it declares that he cannot afford the insurance payments, or invokes *sonei matanot yichyeh*, or offers any other grounds for refusal, then retroactively he never acquired it. The acquisition was premised on the assumption that it served his interest; his protest demonstrates that it did not, and so nothing took hold.

The scenario of *shatek meikara u'lesof tzoveiach* — initially silent, later protesting — could also arise in this context of third-party acquisition. If Michael was present when Gloria performed the *kinyan* on his behalf and said nothing, and only protested afterward, is that initial silence meaningful acceptance? One could imagine a case where it was done in another room, after which Michael is informed — in which case the moment of informing him is analogous to the moment of the *kinyan* itself, and his reaction from that point is determinative.

### Geirus Katan

This framework plays out with striking significance in the laws of *geirus*. A *ger katan* — a minor being converted — lacks the *da'at* of an adult. Who authorizes the *beit din* to convert him? The Gemara answers: *zachin l'adam shelo b'fanav*. The minor is not present in the relevant legal sense, and the *beit din* acts on the presumption that it is better to be Jewish than not. (The Gemara itself challenges this presumption, but leaves the principle intact for the purposes of the ruling.) Where a biological father who is Jewish is present, one can argue that paternal *da'at* supplies the necessary will. But in the case of a foundling or adopted child, it is the *beit din* acting on the *zachin* principle that authorizes the conversion.

### Shatek in Geirus

The corollary, however, is that when the child reaches adulthood — *bar mitzvah* or *bat mitzvah* — and acquires independent legal will, he or she has the right to be *mocheh*: to reject the conversion on the grounds that it was done only on the presumption of benefit, and that now, being capable of making the decision for oneself, the benefit is denied. The *geirus* unravels. It is therefore common practice for rabbis to meet with converts who underwent conversion as children — particularly those who were adopted — before their *bar* or *bat mitzvah*, and to confirm their continued commitment to Jewish identity. Ideally, a proper upbringing has resolved the question in advance.

The application of *shatek meikara u'lesof tzoveiach* here is similarly interesting. Some authorities hold that if the young convert continues to practice Jewishly after reaching *bar* or *bat mitzvah* — observing *Shabbat*, keeping *kashrus*, participating in the community — that ongoing practice constitutes an implicit acceptance. In that case, a subsequent attempt to reject the conversion would be too late: the silence, in the form of continued observance, has already spoken.

## Slaves in Bequest

### Slaves Scenario

With the discussion of *zachin* and third-party acquisition in place, the Gemara now cites a *Braisa* that sharpens the analysis. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak frames the question: if the acquisition was done through a third party — *ziku lo al yedei acher* — and the recipient was initially silent but then protested, we arrive at a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbanan.

The *Braisa*: *hakoteiv nechasav leachair* — one who writes all his property over to another. *V'hayu bahen avadim* — and among the property were slaves. The recipient initially accepts the *shtar*, then upon reviewing the details realizes he is also acquiring slaves — with all the attendant responsibilities of housing and feeding them — and declares *iy afshi bahen*, I want no part of them. The question posed is exactly the one raised above about *matnat bari*: can he now back out?

The scenario has an additional complication. Perhaps the recipient was initially happy to take the estate in the abstract but did not realize the specifics. This is reminiscent of the *go'el* in Megillat Ruth, who enthusiastically agreed to redeem the land until he learned that the obligation also included marrying Ruth — at which point he withdrew. The initial acceptance may have been genuine, but it was made without full information.

### Tanna Kamma Position

The Tanna Kamma rules: once the *shtar* was taken, the acquisition is complete. As a dramatic illustration of the halachic consequence, the Gemara specifies: if the recipient is a *kohen*, the slaves he has now acquired may eat *terumah* — because they are now the slaves of a *kohen*. The acquisition is fully operative in the ritual domain, not only the monetary domain, and there is no way to undo it retroactively.

### Rabban Shimon Position

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees. Once the recipient says *iy afshi bahen* — I do not want them — *kvar zachu bahen yorshim*: the heirs of the original owner have already acquired them. The *kinyan* did not take hold. The moment of protest undoes the acquisition — or more precisely, reveals that it never fully materialized.

A possible intermediate position is raised by Tosafos and the Rashbam: that upon rejection, the property becomes *hefker* — ownerless, belonging to neither party. The Rashbam entertains this possibility but Tosafos argues strenuously against it. The logic of rejection is that I divested myself of the property for the purpose of Michael owning it. If that purpose was not fulfilled, nothing happened — the property reverts. I was not declaring it ownerless and inviting Michael to scoop it up from *hefker*; I was giving it to him directly. If the gift failed, the status quo ante is restored.

### Gemara's Distinction

The Gemara then asks a pointed question: does the Tanna Kamma really hold that even if Michael was *tzoveiach meikara* — yelling from the very moment he found out — he still acquires? That seems untenable. So Rava (or, some say, Rabbi Yochanan) clarifies: *b'tzoveiach me'ikaro d'kulei alma lo pligi d'lo kani* — if the recipient protested from the outset, everyone agrees he has not acquired. And if he was silent and only protested afterward — *shatek u'levasof tzoveiach* — *d'kulei alma lo pligi d'kani* — everyone agrees he has acquired and his later protest is irrelevant.

The actual dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applies specifically to the case where the acquisition was made through a third party and the recipient was initially silent, then protested: *she-zikah lo al yedei acher v'shasok u'levasof tzovach*. The Tanna Kamma holds: *mi-deshashok kannehu* — his initial silence was acceptance, and the subsequent yelling is merely a *hadar*, a change of mind, which does not undo the *kinyan*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds: *hochich sofo al techilaso* — the end proves the beginning. The fact that he protests now reveals that he never truly wanted it; his initial silence was not meaningful consent but rather an absence of any occasion to protest, since he had not yet internalized that the *kinyan* had been performed on his behalf.

The reason the Tanna Kamma's and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's positions are not applicable to the case of direct acquisition — where the recipient himself receives the *shtar* in person — is that in the third-party scenario, the recipient's silence is more ambiguous. He sees Gloria and Dov performing some transaction with a handkerchief and does not immediately grasp that it relates to him. It is only when he is directly informed, or when the reality sinks in, that he begins to react. That moment of dawning awareness, and what he does in response to it, is what the dispute is about.

The Rashbam's reading places the recipient in Michael's presence during the third-party acquisition — he sees it happen but does not fully register it as applying to him. This is the gray zone: not absent, not fully engaged. The first moment of genuine awareness becomes the operative one, and whether silence at that moment constitutes acceptance or merely continued obliviousness is the crux of the debate.

## Shchiv Mera Bequests

### Asset Distribution

The Gemara now shifts to a series of rulings about a *shchiv mera* — a person on his deathbed — who distributes his estate among multiple recipients. The *Braisa* taught: *shachiv meira she'amar tenu matayim zuz leploni, v'shalosh me'ot leploni, v'arba me'ot leploni* — a *shchiv mera* who said, give 200 to Shimon, 300 to Rivka, and 400 to Leah. The total allocation is 900 *zuz*, but suppose he only had 700. How should the estate be distributed?

The Gemara rules: *ein omrim kol hakodem b'shtar zocheh* — we do not say that the first person named in the document takes priority. The order in which recipients are named is not legally significant: one must list names in some sequence, but the sequence does not reflect the testator's preferences or his order of priorities. Similarly, the amount allocated to each person does not confer priority — one might think the person who received the largest bequest was most beloved and therefore most deserving, but this too is rejected. Rather, the assets are divided proportionally. If he had 700 instead of 900, each recipient receives a proportional share of what was promised: instead of 200, 300, and 400, they would receive amounts in those ratios.

Now what happens when a creditor emerges? *Lefikach yatza alav shtar chov* — a creditor comes forward and his claim consumes part of the estate. The Gemara rules that the creditor collects proportionally from all the recipients: *goveh mikulam*. No single beneficiary bears the full loss; it is spread across all of them in proportion to their shares.

### Distribution Order

But this proportional rule applies only in the absence of language indicating a priority sequence. If the testator explicitly stated an order — saying "give 400 to Leah, and after her give 300 to Rivka, and after her give 200 to Shimon" — then the word *acharav* signals that the subsequent bequests are contingent: they are to be paid only from whatever remains in the estate after the prior recipient has been satisfied. In that case, when a creditor claims against the estate, the losses fall on the last recipient first. The rule becomes *goveh min ha'acharon* — collect from the last person listed. If that is insufficient, *ein lo goveh mishelifanav* — proceed to the second-to-last. Only if both of those prove inadequate does the creditor reach the first person on the list. This is a last-in, first-out principle driven by the explicit sequential language of the bequest.

### Creditor Liens

A technical complication arises: if the bequests were in cash (*zuz*), a creditor who comes to collect after the testator's death would normally have no right to take that cash — post-mortem, creditor collection is limited to land. So either the Gemara is describing a scenario in which the creditor came before death, seizing cash while the testator was still alive, or the amounts referred to as *zuz* are not literally cash but rather represent parcels of land of corresponding value, against which the creditor can exercise his liens after death.

Both readings are defensible, but they cannot both be correct simultaneously. After the *gaonim takana* — the enactment of the Geonim extending creditor rights to movable assets including cash in the estate — the straightforward reading becomes more viable: a creditor could collect from cash held in the estate, and so the *pshat* of the Gemara can be taken at face value.

## Karaui Lo Language

### Firstborn Bequest

The Gemara now introduces a series of cases governed by the phrase *karaui lo* — "as is fit for him." The first: *shachiv meira she'amar tenu matayim zuz leploni beni bechori karaui lo* — a *shchiv mera* who says, give 200 *zuz* to my firstborn son, as is fit for him. The question is how to read this. Does specifying *bechori* — my firstborn — and adding *karaui lo* suggest that the 200 *zuz* is being assigned as payment of his *chelek bechora*, the double portion that the firstborn is biblically entitled to? The Torah prohibits disinheriting a firstborn: *lo yuchal levaker* — you may not override the *bechora*. So the father cannot strip the firstborn of his extra portion in any case.

The ruling: *notlan venotel bechorato* — he takes the 200 *zuz* and also takes his *bechora* inheritance. The *karaui lo* language does not function as a substitution but as an addition. The 200 *zuz* is a gift, and the *chelek bechora* remains intact.

However, there is a *chiddush*: *im amar bevechorato* — if the father explicitly says "take 200 *zuz* as his *bechora*" — then *yado al ha'elyona*, the son has his choice. He may take the 200 *zuz* in lieu of his normal double portion, or he may forgo the 200 *zuz* and claim his full *chelek bechora* instead. The father cannot strip the *bechora* outright, but he can present the son with an option: if you prefer 200 *zuz* in cash over your share of the estate, you may waive your *bechora* in favor of the fixed sum. The son decides which serves him better.

### Wife's Bequest

An analogous structure applies to the wife. *Shachiv mera she'amar tenu matayim zuz leplonit ishti karaui lah* — a *shchiv mera* who says, give 200 *zuz* to my wife Sarah, as is fit for her. Two hundred *zuz* is the standard *ketubah* payment. One might reasonably read this as the husband ensuring that his wife receives her *ketubah*. But the ruling is: *notlam venotelet ketubatah* — she takes the 200 *zuz* and also receives her *ketubah*. The *karaui lah* language does not convert the gift into *ketubah* payment; it is a gift in addition to what she is owed.

Again, the *chiddush* runs in the opposite direction: *im amar biketubatah* — if he explicitly says "take these 200 *zuz* as your *ketubah* payment" — *yadah al ha'elyona*, she has the upper hand. She may take the 200 *zuz* in satisfaction of her *ketubah*, or she may decline and collect her *ketubah* as it stands.

Why would a widow ever prefer the *ketubah* to a sum that might be identical in nominal amount? Several considerations arise. The *ketubah* typically includes not only the base amount (*ikar*) but also the *tosefet* — the additional amount the husband undertook — and the *nichsei tzon barzel*, the fixed-value property she brought into the marriage, the value of which is guaranteed by the husband in the *ketubah*. If she forgoes the *ketubah* in favor of a cash payment, she may lose those components. Whether the word *biketubatah* here refers specifically to the base *ketubah* amount or to the entire package she collects under the *ketubah* is not resolved with complete clarity, but the practical stakes are real.

### Creditor Bequest

The third case: *shachiv mera she'amar tenu matayim zuz leploni baal chovi karaui lo* — give 200 *zuz* to Reuven my creditor, as is fit for him. The ruling parallels the prior cases: *notlan venotel hovo* — he takes the 200 *zuz* and also collects his debt. The *karaui lo* means the gift is in addition to the debt. And if the testator explicitly said *behovo* — in payment of the debt — then the creditor receives it in satisfaction of the loan.

This case, however, provokes genuine resistance. It is one thing to give a gift to your son or wife in addition to what they are owed — the relationship invites generosity. But a creditor? This is someone whom the testator has identified purely by his financial role. The Gemara itself raises the objection: *mishum de'amar karaui lo notlan venotel hovo?* — just because he said the words *karaui lo*, he gets it on top of the debt? Perhaps *karaui lo* itself means "as is fitting given the debt" — *karaui behovo kaamar* — in payment of what he is owed.

### Rabbi Akiva Principle

The Gemara's answer draws on a principle attributed to Rabbi Akiva: *dedayek lishna yetira* — he infers from extra language. The source is the Mishnah from earlier in Bava Batra dealing with the sale of a house. The rule is that a seller who sells his house does not include the cistern or pit within it. Even if the seller wrote a deed granting *umka ve'ruma* — height and depth — all vertical dimensions of the property, the underground cistern is excluded. This is the ruling of the Mishnah. Rabbi Akiva adds: *v'tzarich likach lo derech* — and the seller must therefore purchase a right of way from the buyer in order to access his retained cistern. The Chachamim disagree: just as the seller retained the cistern, so too does he retain access to it.

The Gemara explains the framing: according to Rabbi Akiva, *mocher be'ayin yafah mocher* — a seller transfers generously, giving the buyer maximum benefit of what falls within the category of "house." The cistern is outside that category, so the seller keeps it. But he gave away everything called "house," including access rights, and must therefore repurchase the right of way if he wants it. The Chachamim hold *mocher be'ayin ra'ah mocher* — a seller retains as much as possible, including access.

Then comes the critical ruling: *u'modeh Rabbi Akiva bizman she'amar lo chutz me'eilu* — Rabbi Akiva concedes that if the seller explicitly said "I am not selling you the cistern and the pit," thereby using words he did not need to use (since the cistern was already excluded), the extra language signals an intention to hold on to even more. *She'ein tzarich likach lo derech* — in that case he retains the right of access and does not need to purchase it from the buyer. The principle: *keivan d'lo tzarich ve'ka'amar, le'tifuyei milta ka'ata* — since he said words he did not need to say, he is understood to be adding to what he is already retaining.

### Karaui Lo Override

This principle is now applied to the creditor case. Had the testator merely said "give 200 *zuz* to my creditor," without any additional language, the natural reading would be payment of the debt. But the testator went out of his way to add *karaui lo* — words that were unnecessary if all he intended was to pay the debt. Those extra words, by Rabbi Akiva's principle, carry interpretive weight. They signal that the testator intended to give something beyond what was already owed: *le'tifuyei milta ka'ata* — the extra language comes to add. Therefore, the 200 *zuz* is a gift on top of the debt.

The Rashbam extends this logic to the cases of the *bechor* and the wife. If the testator said "give 200 *zuz* to my firstborn son" without *karaui lo* and without explicitly saying *bevechorato*, the Rashbam reads this as placing the son in a position of *yado al ha'elyona*: he can take the 200 *zuz* as his inheritance share, or he can take his *chelek bechora*. Similarly for the wife, if no *karaui* language is used: the bequest would be interpreted as an inheritance share, not an unconditional gift.

This is a striking conclusion. One might expect that a *shchiv mera* who says "give my son the stamp collection" or "give my wife the Corvette" is simply leaving them a gift, with the bulk of the estate to be divided by the normal rules of inheritance. But according to the Rashbam, absent the *karaui* language, such a bequest is read as the recipient's inheritance portion — and taking it means taking it in lieu of a share in the remaining estate. The Gemara itself only reacted to the creditor case, not to the wife and *bechor* cases — which suggests that for those relationships, the Gemara was less inclined to assume the bequest was a substitute for the legal entitlement rather than a gift. The Rashbam, seeking to render the three cases parallel, extends the logic; but the Gemara's literary choice to single out the *baal chov* for explicit questioning suggests that the default presumption differs depending on the nature of the relationship.

## Debts Owed to Shchiv Mera

### Witnesses Recording Claim

The final section of the daf takes up a different kind of deathbed declaration. The *Braisa*: *shachiv meira she'amar maneh yesh li etzel ploni* — a *shchiv mera* who says, I have a claim of one *maneh* against so-and-so. He is not paying a debt — he is making a claim. He is telling those assembled that a third party owes him money, and he wants this fact recorded. The question: *ha'eidim kotvim* — may the witnesses write this down?

The witnesses know what he said. They do not know whether it is true. They may have no idea who the alleged debtor is. The Mishnah says they may write it down — *af al pi she'ein makirin* — even without knowing the other party's identity, and even without knowing whether the claim is accurate. But the question is what this document actually attests to.

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak transmits that the names are reversed from how they first appeared in the *Braisa*. The version he received has Rabbi Meir saying: *ein kotvin* — the witnesses may not write it down. Why? Because when they do write it, the concern is that a *beit din* will see the document and treat it as testimony to the truth of the claim, ordering collection without requiring additional evidence. Since the witnesses themselves do not know whether the claim is true, writing it in the form of a witnessed document is dangerous.

### Chachamim Position

The Chachamim hold: *kotvin* — write it. The witnesses are testifying to what they heard, not to the veracity of the claim. A document saying "we heard so-and-so state on his deathbed that Ploni owes him a *maneh*" is not the same as a document saying "Ploni owes a *maneh*." The content of the attestation and the attestation itself are distinct. And therefore the heirs, armed with this document, still must bring additional evidence if they wish to collect — as the ruling states, *tzarich lehavi ra'aya* — they need to produce proof.

### Erring Courts Concern

The reason Rabbi Meir objects — in this version of the tradition — is not that the witnesses are overstepping by writing what they heard, but that *beit din to'in*, erring courts, may misread the document. A sloppy *beit din* might see a signed, witnessed *shtar* and assume that the signatures attest to the underlying facts rather than merely to the testimony of what the *shchiv mera* said. On this reading, everyone agrees in principle that a properly functioning *beit din* would understand the document correctly. The concern is practical and institutional, not conceptual.

### Rav Dimi Ruling

Rav Dimi mi-Nehardea rules: *hilchata ein chosheshin le-beit din to'in* — the Halachic practice does not worry about erring courts. The witnesses may write the *shtar*, and a competent *beit din* will read it for what it is: testimony to a deathbed statement, not testimony to the truth of the claim itself.

### Beit Din Review Rules

But then the Gemara raises a tension. Rava ruled that a *beit din* may not perform *chalitzah* unless they know the identities of the parties — that this man is indeed the *yavam*, the brother-in-law. Similarly, *miun* — a minor bride's rejection of her rabbinic marriage — cannot be performed without the *beit din* knowing the parties. *Aval af al pi she'ein makirin* — and yet, *get chalitzah* and *get miun* may be written down even without independent knowledge of the parties' identities by the witnessing scribes, because the *beit din* itself would never have acted without certainty.

Why is the *beit din* constrained? Why not allow a *beit din* to perform *chalitzah* even without knowing the parties, and let the next *beit din* investigate? The answer: *beit din batar beit din lo dayki* — a court does not scrutinize the actions of another court. If *beit din aleph* performed a *chalitzah*, *beit din bet* will assume it was valid and will not reopen the question of whether the *yavam* was properly identified. This is an expression of institutional deference — courts do not second-guess each other. And precisely because that deference exists, a *beit din* cannot offload the problem to the next court by performing a *chalitzah* of uncertain validity. The next court will not investigate; it will assume validity. Therefore, the first *beit din* must itself be certain.

By contrast, *beit din batar eidim dayki* — a court does scrutinize the testimony of witnesses. If witnesses wrote a *shtar* attesting to what a *shchiv mera* said, the *beit din* that receives that document is expected to ask: does this attest to the underlying facts, or only to the statement itself? The *beit din* will investigate the content of the testimony and not simply accept it at face value. Therefore, allowing witnesses to write down what a *shchiv mera* said does not create the danger of automatic, unexamined collection. The court will do its due diligence with respect to witness testimony in a way that it would not with respect to another court's formal act.

The distinction carries a subtle but important moral implication. The institutional deference that one *beit din* extends to another is a form of respect for rabbinic courts as institutions — something conspicuously absent, it must be said, in contemporary disputes over *agunah* and related matters, where courts routinely second-guess each other's rulings. The Talmud's vision is one in which judicial acts, once taken by a legitimate *beit din*, are presumed valid and not subject to collateral attack. Witnesses, by contrast, are individuals whose testimony is always subject to examination and whose records may always be probed. That difference in institutional standing is what resolves the apparent contradiction between Rav Dimi's ruling and Rava's requirement of *makirin* for *chalitzah* and *miun*.

# Bava Batra 139

## Guf & Peirot Transfer

### Father's Harvested vs. U…

The daf opens with a *mishnah* at the very bottom of 138b concerning a father who wishes to transfer property to his son while retaining personal benefit from it during his lifetime. The mechanism employed is *guf me-hayom u-peirot le-achar mita*: the son receives title (*guf*) immediately — thereby avoiding the problem of a gift that takes effect only after death — but the father retains the right to all produce (*peirot*) from the field until he dies.

The *mishnah* specifies: *ha-av tolesh u-ma'achil le-chol mi she-yirtzeh* — as long as the father is alive, he may harvest the fruit and distribute it to whomever he pleases; the son has no claim on it. Furthermore, *u-ma she-hiniach talush* — if the father harvested fruit and then died, that already-harvested fruit belongs to *harei hu shel yorshim*, all the heirs collectively, not to this particular son who received the field. The *gemara* draws the implication sharply: *talush* — yes, the father retains what he harvested; *mechubar* — no, fruit still attached to the tree at the time of the father's death passes specifically to this son, not to the general heirs.

This is not entirely intuitive. Since the father holds the rights to *peirot*, one might have expected that even unharvested fruit growing on the tree belongs to him, and only upon his death would it pass — together with everything else — to the general heirs. Yet the *mishnah* implies otherwise.

### Ulla: Son vs. Third Party

A *baraita* at the top of 138a appears to contradict this ruling. The *baraita* addresses a case where the son, while the father is still alive, sells his interest to a third party, and then the father dies. In that scenario, *shamin et ha-mechubarim la-lokeach*: one assesses the value of the fruit still on the tree, and this purchaser — who now steps into the son's position with respect to both title and fruit rights — must pay the heirs for that fruit. This implies that the unharvested fruit belongs to the father (and thus passes to all heirs), in direct tension with our *mishnah*.

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction through Ulla: *lo kashya kan be-veno kan be-acher* — there is no difficulty. The two cases differ based on whether the recipient is the son or a stranger. *Da'ato shel adam kerova etzel beno* — a father's disposition (*da'at*) is naturally inclined toward his son.

### Da'ato Kerova: Intent Ma…

Although technically the father retains the fruit rights and the unharvested fruit logically belongs to him, when dealing with his own son, the father's intent is that the son should benefit even from fruit still on the tree. Therefore, in the case of our *mishnah* — where the recipient is the son — the father's rights extend only to fruit he has actually harvested. Unharvested fruit at the time of death passes to the son. When, however, the son sold his interest to a third party, no such paternal closeness (*da'ato kerova*) operates, and the *baraita* applies: the unharvested fruit belongs to the father and passes to all the heirs.

---

## Sons: Clothes vs. Food

### Mishnah Rule

The next *mishnah*, at the top of 139a, addresses an entirely different situation: a father dies leaving behind both adult sons (*banim gedolim*) and minor sons (*banim ketanim*). The estate is jointly owned by all of them in equal shares, and division has not yet taken place. The practical question is whether ongoing expenses — clothing and food — can simply be drawn from the estate as a whole, or whether each heir must bear his own costs from his individual portion once division occurs.

The problem is that these two categories of expense fall unevenly across age groups. Minor children generally incur higher food costs relative to their share, while adult sons incur substantially higher clothing costs. If clothing expenses were paid equally from the undivided estate, the younger heirs would effectively subsidize the older sons' wardrobes; if food expenses were paid equally from the estate, the older heirs would be unfairly burdened with the younger children's higher food bills.

The *mishnah* therefore rules: *ein ha-gedolim mitparnasim al yedei ha-ketanim* — the older sons cannot have their clothing costs (*mitparnes* referring here specifically to clothing) paid from the estate at the expense of the younger children — *ve-lo ha-ketanim nizonim al ha-gedolim* — and the younger children cannot have their food costs (*nizonim*) paid from the estate at the expense of the older sons. *Ella cholkim be-shava* — instead, the estate is divided equally and each heir bears his own costs from his portion.

The *mishnah* then turns to wedding expenses: *nasu gedolim yisu ketanim* — if the older sons were married after the father's death and wedding costs were drawn from the estate, then when the younger sons come to marry, they are likewise entitled to draw equivalent wedding costs from the estate. However: *ve-im amru ketanim harei anu nosim ke-derech she-nasatem atem, ein shomin lahem* — if the younger sons say, "we wish to marry just as you did," they are not heeded.

This last clause appears contradictory, and the *gemara* will resolve it. The *mishnah* is addressing a different scenario: the older sons were married while the father was still alive, and the father personally paid for their weddings as a gift. After the father died, the younger sons demand that equivalent amounts be drawn from the estate. The *mishnah* rules they cannot: *ella mah she-natan lahem avihem natan* — what the father gave the older sons was a personal gift from the father, and the estate — now equally owned by all — cannot be tapped to replicate it.

### Rava: Eldest Exception

The *gemara* records a ruling by Rava that qualifies the *mishnah*'s general prohibition: *hai gadol achi de-lavash ve-ichasi mi-beisa, mai de-avid avid* — if the eldest brother who represents the household — the one who appears in court, conducts business on behalf of the estate, and represents the family in public — uses estate funds for his clothing, what he has done stands. His clothing costs are legitimately for the benefit of the entire estate, since his public role requires a certain appearance, and may therefore be borne by the estate rather than his personal share.

However, Rava's formulation — *mai de-avid avid*, "what he did stands" — suggests that even this is only *be-dieved* acceptable. The potential for abuse is obvious: one might claim an extravagant wardrobe is necessary to represent the family's honor. Accordingly, Rava's ruling is not a blanket license but a post-facto validation, and *beis din* may scrutinize whether the expenditure genuinely served the estate's interests.

The *gemara* then raises an objection: but our *mishnah* explicitly prohibits the older sons from having their clothing paid from the estate! Rava answers: *masnisin be-sircha* — the *mishnah* addresses a ne'er-do-well, someone who is simply lounging about and not representing anyone. The *gemara* presses further: *sircha peshita* — isn't that obvious? Of course such a person cannot claim estate funds for his wardrobe. The *gemara* responds: one might have thought that even then it is to the family's benefit that older sons maintain their appearance, and the ruling is therefore necessary to clarify that it is not. It is worth noting the slightly unusual framing: the *gemara* appears to treat Rava's case as the norm and the *mishnah* as the exception, when intuitively it is the opposite — the default is that clothing costs come from one's own share, and Rava's case of the family representative is the narrow exception.

### Wedding Costs Context
