The *gemara* (Rav Yehuda) clarifies the *mishnah*'s apparently contradictory lines about wedding expenses. *Nasu gedolim achar misat avihem* — if the older sons married after the father's death and took wedding costs from the estate, *yisu ketanim achar misat avihem* — the younger sons may do the same. *Aval nasu gedolim be-chayei avihem* — but if the older sons married during the father's lifetime and the father paid, then when the younger sons seek to claim equivalent sums from the estate after the father's death, *ein shomin lahem* — they are not heeded. What the father gave was the father's gift; it cannot be replicated from what is now a jointly-owned estate.

---

## Daughters: Same Rules

### Parallel Halacha

The *mishnah* then addresses *hiniach banot gedolot u-ketanot* — a father who died leaving older and younger daughters. The identical rules apply: older daughters may not take clothing costs from the estate at the younger daughters' expense; younger daughters may not take food costs from the estate at the older daughters' expense; the estate is divided equally and each daughter bears her own costs. The wedding expense rules parallel those of the sons as well.

### Daughters Supported

The reason the *mishnah* repeats these rules for daughters rather than simply cross-referencing the sons is to introduce the concluding distinction: *ze chomer be-banim mi-be-banot* — here is one way in which the case of sons is more stringent than that of daughters. *She-ha-banot nizonot al ha-banim ve-ein nizonot al ha-banot* — when an estate is inherited by sons, daughters have a right to be supported from it (a condition of the *ketubbah* written by the father to the mother, extending maintenance rights to daughters until they marry or reach maturity). But when daughters are the sole heirs and there are no sons, younger daughters cannot claim their food support from the estate against the older daughters — all divide equally. This heightens the stringency for minor daughters in a daughters-only estate relative to their position in a mixed estate where sons inherit.

---

## Ba'al: Lokeach or Yoresh?

### Avuha bar Geniva Question

Avuha bar Geniva sent a question to Rava: *lavta ve-achla ve-amda ve-nisat, ba'al lokeach havei o yoresh havei?* — a woman borrowed money, incurred debt, then married, bringing property into the marriage. The husband now holds rights to this property as *nichsei milog*: she retains title while he enjoys the usufruct (*peirot*). Her creditors wish to exercise their liens against this property now that it is in the husband's hands. The question is: how do we classify the husband's relationship to *nichsei milog* — is he like a *lokeach* (purchaser) or a *yoresh* (heir)?

The practical stakes are clear. A creditor holding only a *milveh al peh* (oral loan, without a formal *shtar*) cannot exercise liens against a purchaser — we protect innocent buyers who had no notice of the debt. But such a creditor *can* collect from heirs, even without a *shtar*, since an heir received the property without paying for it and cannot claim to be an innocent purchaser. If the husband is treated as a *lokeach*, the wife's pre-marital creditors cannot touch the property. If he is treated as a *yoresh*, they can.

One might note that the question makes more natural sense after the wife's death, when the husband fully inherits — at which point you could ask whether his prior usufruct right transforms his inheritance into something resembling a purchase. While the wife is alive, the husband does not yet hold title, which makes the framing somewhat unusual, as *Tosafot* addresses. But the *gemara* proceeds with the question as posed.

### Raba: Daughters' Marriag…

Rava replies: *tenina* — the answer is already contained in our *mishnah*. He invokes the rule about daughters' wedding expenses: if the older daughters were married after the father's death using estate funds, the younger daughters may claim equal wedding costs from the estate. Now consider what this actually means. Suppose four daughters — call them Sarah, Rivka, Rachel, and Leah — share the estate. Sarah and Rivka marry, drawing $20,000 each from the estate. They bring their respective shares into their marriages. When Rachel and Leah come to marry, they too are entitled to $20,000 from the estate — meaning they can recover part of that sum from the property Sarah and Rivka brought into *their* marriages, property now in the hands of Sarah's and Rivka's husbands. This is precisely our question: the younger daughters had a lien-like claim against the estate, the older daughters took estate property into their marriages with their husbands, and now the younger daughters exercise that claim against property in the husbands' hands. The fact that they may do so implies the husband is treated as a *yoresh*, against whom liens are enforceable.

### Gemara Disputes Reading

The *gemara* pushes back: *lo* — perhaps the *mishnah* is not describing such a complicated scenario at all. Perhaps Sarah and Rivka married without the estate having been divided yet, so their husbands never received any estate property. The wedding costs come from the still-undivided estate itself, and the younger daughters' subsequent claims are likewise drawn from those same undivided funds — with no lien being exercised against any husband. In that reading, the *mishnah* teaches nothing about our question. The *gemara* acknowledges the ambiguity and presses on.

*Rabbi Hiyya* then teaches in a *baraita*: *nisat gedola le-ba'al yasia ketana mi-ba'al* — explicitly, when the younger daughters come to collect their wedding costs, they collect from the husbands of the older daughters. This resolves the textual ambiguity and appears to establish decisively that the husband is a *yoresh* against whom liens may be enforced. But the *gemara* deflects again: *dilma shani parnasa de-it lah kala* — perhaps wedding costs (*parnasa* here referring to the marriage expenses) are publicly known. Everyone is aware that Sarah and Rivka's marriages cost $20,000, and therefore everyone — including the husbands — knows that Rachel and Leah hold a corresponding lien. Since the husbands had constructive notice, we allow the lien to be enforced in this case. But the general rule for a creditor whose lien is not equally well-known might be different, and one cannot generalize from the wedding case to ordinary *milveh al peh* debt collection.

### Ravin: Widow Support

Rav Pappa puts to Rava: is this not precisely what Ravin sent in a letter from Eretz Yisrael? The case Ravin described is: a man died leaving a widow (*almanah*) and a daughter, with no sons. The daughter inherits the estate. The widow (*almanah*) has a right — a condition of the *ketubbah* — to be supported from the estate until she remarries or collects her lump-sum *ketubbah*. *Almanato nizonet mi-nechasav* — the widow draws support from the estate now in the daughter's possession. *Niset ha-bat, almanato nizonet mi-nechasav* — even when the daughter marries and brings the estate property into her own marriage, the widow continues to draw support. *Meta ha-bat* — and if the daughter then dies, transferring the property to the daughter's husband?

Rav Yehuda the nephew of Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina reported: *le-didi hava uvda* — this very case came before me, and the ruling was *almanato nizonet mi-nechasav* — the widow continues to be supported even from the property now in the hands of the son-in-law. The *gemara* draws the inference: *ei amrat bishlama yoresh havei, hainu de-almanato nizonet mi-nechasav* — if the husband is treated as a *yoresh*, it makes perfect sense that the widow's lien persists, just as a creditor can collect from an heir even without a *shtar*. *Ela ei amrat lokeach havei, amai nizonet mi-nechasav?* — but if he is a *lokeach*, why should the widow be able to collect? A *milveh al peh* cannot be enforced against a purchaser. This seems to be a compelling proof that the husband is a *yoresh*.

### Yovel & Terminology

Abaye interjects that the proof from Ravin's case was not even necessary. The *mishnah* explicitly lists what does not revert to its original owner at *yovel*: *ha-bechorahshah* — the firstborn's double portion is not considered a purchase and therefore does not revert, and turning to 139b: *ve-ha-yoresh et ishto* — "one who inherits his wife." The *mishnah* itself employs the language of *yerushah* to describe the husband's acquisition of his wife's property upon her death. This is a direct terminological proof that the husband is a *yoresh*.

### Usha Enactment

At this point, having assembled substantial evidence that the husband is a *yoresh*, Rava complicates the picture. Rabbi Yossi berabi Chanina taught: *be-Usha hitkinu* — at Usha they enacted the following: if a woman sells her *nichsei milog* during her husband's lifetime — she holds title and can technically sell it — and then she dies before her husband, *ha-ba'al motzi mi-yad ha-lakochot* — the husband may reclaim the property from the buyers.

Why is this significant? If the husband were purely a *yoresh*, he could only inherit what remained in the wife's hands at her death. Since she sold the property before dying, he would have nothing to claim — just as an heir cannot recover assets a decedent sold during his lifetime. The only way the husband can reclaim property the wife sold is if his relationship to it is that of a *lokeach* — someone who "purchased" his interest when he married, and whose claim therefore antedates and can override a later sale. The *takana* of Usha thus seems to treat him as a *lokeach*, in tension with all the evidence pointing to *yoresh*.

### Rav Ashi: Context Determ…

Rav Ashi resolves the apparent contradiction by rejecting the premise that there is one uniform answer: *ba'al shaviyuh rabanan ke-yoresh u-shaviyuh rabanan ke-lokeiach* — the Sages treated the husband as a *yoresh* in some contexts and as a *lokeach* in others. The governing principle: *ve-heicha de-tava lei avdu lei* — they applied whichever classification served to prevent undue loss.

Working through the cases: regarding *yovel*, *shaviyuh rabanan ke-yoresh mishum pesida didei* — they classified him as a *yoresh* for his benefit, so that property he received through his wife's estate would not revert at *yovel*, sparing him a highly disruptive loss. Regarding the *takana* of Usha (*gabei de-Rabbi Yossi berabi Chanina*), *shaviyuh rabanan ke-lokeiach mishum pesida didei* — they classified him as a *lokeach* for his benefit, enabling him to reclaim property his wife sold out from under him if she predeceased him. Regarding the case of Ravin — the widow drawing support even after the property passed through the daughter to the son-in-law — *shaviyuh rabanan ke-yoresh mishum pesidat almanah* — they classified him as a *yoresh*, this time for the benefit of the *almanah*, ensuring her support rights remain enforceable and she suffers no loss.

As for the buyers who lose out when the husband reclaims property under the Usha enactment — the *gemara* says *hatam inhu afseidu anafshaihu*: they assumed the risk themselves. *Keivan de-ika ba'al lo iba'i lei le-mizban mi-iteta* — knowing that she was married, they should have understood that if she died before her husband, he would have a claim to the property. They purchased with eyes open and did not pay full price. Their loss is self-inflicted.

The *Rashbam* concludes from this analysis that in the original case posed by Avuha bar Geniva — a wife's pre-marital creditors seeking to enforce their liens against property she brought into the marriage — the husband is treated as a *yoresh* and the creditors may collect, paralleling the widow's right to continued support. The true exception to the *yoresh* classification, motivated by protecting the husband's interests, is the Usha enactment alone.

---

## Daughters' Support Thres…

### Large Estate Rule

With the conclusion of *Yesh Nochalin*, the *gemara* opens the next *perek*, whose central subject is the support of daughters from an estate that sons inherit. The *mishnah* states: *mi she-met ve-hiniach banim u-vanot* — someone died leaving sons and daughters. *Bi-zman she-nechasim merubim, ha-banim yirshu ve-ha-banot yizonu* — when the estate is large (*nechasim merubim*), the sons inherit and the daughters receive maintenance (*mezonot*) from the estate. This reflects a standard condition of the *ketubbah*: a husband undertakes that upon his death, his daughters will be maintained from his estate until they marry or reach *bagrut* (maturity).

### Small Estate Rule

*Nechasim muatim* — when the estate is small, the daughters receive their maintenance and the sons must go begging. Admon expresses outrage: just because I am male I am left with nothing? Rabban Gamliel acknowledges the force of Admon's argument, but the normative ruling follows neither of them in any practically operative sense; the *halacha* remains that when the estate suffices only for the daughters' maintenance, the sons receive nothing.

The *mishnah* will be explained to mean not that the girls receive more than their maintenance — they do not — but rather that an estate below the threshold is conceptually under the daughters' control as a fund designated for support, not under the sons' control as inherited property.

### Rav Yehuda Definition

*Ve-chama merubim* — how much constitutes a "large" estate? Rav Yehuda citing Rav defines it as: *kedei she-yizonu mi-hen elu va-elu shenayim asar chodesh* — enough to support boys and girls alike for twelve months. Even if the girls are years away from reaching *bagrut*, once the estate suffices to cover everyone's expenses for a year, it is considered *nechasim merubim* and passes under the sons' control, with the daughters retaining a lien for their support until maturity.

When Rav Yehuda reported this ruling before Shmuel, Shmuel responded: *zo divrei Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi* — that may be Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi's position. *Aval chakhamim omrim kedei she-yizonu mi-hen elu va-elu ad she-yivgaru* — but the Sages hold that the estate must be sufficient to support everyone — boys and girls — until all the girls reach maturity. Only then is it truly *nechasim merubim*. Anything short of that threshold, even if the estate is quite substantial in absolute terms, is *nechasim muatim*, and the money is treated as a fund designated for support rather than as an inherited estate.

This position is corroborated by the tradition of Ravin (and alternatively attributed to Rabbah bar bar Chana) citing Rabbi Yochanan: *kol she-yizonu mi-hen elu va-elu ad she-yivgaru, hen merubim; pachot mi-kan, harei elu muatim* — if there is enough to support both boys and girls until the girls reach maturity, that is a large estate; anything less is a small estate.

### Raba: Before Threshold

The *gemara* then presses on the language *elu va-elu* — both groups. If there is $15,000 and the girls need $10,000 until *bagrut* while the boys would need another $10,000, is it really the case, as the *mishnah* seems to say about *nechasim muatim*, that the girls receive everything? *Shakli lehu banot le-chulhu?* — do the girls take all $15,000? That is clearly not right. Rava clarifies: *motzi'in lahen mezonot le-vanot ad she-yivgaru* — you cordon off the $10,000 needed for the girls' support until *bagrut*, *ve-ha-sha'ar le-vanim* — and the remainder, the $5,000, goes to the sons. They need more than that and will have to go begging for the rest, as the *mishnah* stated — but no one ever suggested the girls receive funds beyond their entitlement.

### After Threshold

The conceptual point Rava is drawing out is this. Below the threshold — when the total estate does not exceed what is needed to support everyone until the girls reach maturity — the money is not a *yerushah* in any meaningful sense. It is a designated fund for maintenance. Within that fund, the daughters' claims are prior: their full support is guaranteed first; any residual amount then goes to the sons for whatever portion of their support it covers. No one has "inherited" an estate; everyone is merely receiving subsistence.

Only once the estate exceeds that threshold — when there is more than enough to cover every child's maintenance until the girls mature — do the sons truly inherit. At that point, the daughters hold a lien against the sons' estate for their support until *bagrut*, and the sons control the remainder as legitimate heirs. The distinction, then, is not merely quantitative but conceptual: it determines whether the property is characterized as a maintenance fund (under the daughters' prior claim) or as an inherited estate (under the sons' ownership, subject to the daughters' lien).

---

---

# Bava Batra 140

## Estate Division Basics

### Perek Mi Shemeit Intro

Today's daf is 140, and we are in *Perek Mi Shemeit*, the penultimate chapter of the tractate. This *perek* deals with the legal framework governing inheritance when a man dies leaving behind both sons and daughters. The fundamental rule is that males inherit while females, if they are minors — that is, below the age of *bagrut*, maturity, which the *Gemara* sets at twelve and a half — are supported by the estate until they either marry or reach that age of maturity.

### Daughters as Creditors

The conceptual model underlying this framework is that the daughters are, in effect, creditors of the estate. There is an obligation that the estate bears toward them, analogous to a lien or a debt. This framing will prove crucial as we follow the *Gemara*'s analysis, because how one characterizes the daughters' claim — as a true creditor's debt, or as something more nuanced — determines the outcome across a range of practical scenarios.

### Merubim Definition

Against this backdrop, the *mishna* introduces the distinction between *nechasim merubim* and *nechasim muatim*, a large estate and a small estate. *Merubim* means the estate contains at least one additional unit of value beyond what is needed to support all the daughters through *bagrut*. To illustrate: if there are five daughters of varying ages, and the total remaining years until each reaches *bagrut* amounts to twenty girl-years, and it costs one thousand dollars per year to support a person, then the required support is twenty thousand dollars. Any estate worth more than twenty thousand dollars — even by a single *sela* — is classified as *nechasim merubim*, because something remains for the sons to inherit. If the estate is worth exactly twenty thousand or less, it is *nechasim muatim*, and the sons inherit nothing; the entire estate goes toward supporting the daughters.

---

## Merubim Shrinks

### Pshita: Heirs Protected

The *Gemara* opens by noting that one case is *pshita* — self-evident. *Merubin venismatu*: what happens when a large estate subsequently shrinks? Suppose at the moment of the father's death the estate was worth twenty-five thousand dollars — twenty thousand designated for the daughters' support, five thousand for the sons to inherit. Then the value declines. The *Gemara* rules: *kvar zachu bahen yorshim* — the sons have already acquired their portion. Their share is protected.

### Two Shrinkage Scenarios

This ruling, though stated as obvious by the *Gemara*, actually encompasses two quite different scenarios, each with its own internal logic. The first is a decline in the value of the assets themselves — say the estate was invested in property or stocks that lost value, so that what had been worth twenty-five thousand is now worth twelve thousand five hundred. In that case, everyone loses proportionally. The sons had an asset worth five thousand; if the entire estate has fallen by half, their portion is now worth two thousand five hundred, and the daughters' portion has similarly declined. One does not reallocate everything to the daughters on the grounds that they still need twenty thousand for support; rather, all parties absorb the loss proportionally.

The second scenario is different: the assets themselves have not lost value, but the cost of food has risen dramatically. What the court estimated would cost twenty thousand dollars to provide support until *bagrut* now will cost forty thousand. Here the sons clearly retain their five thousand, because the estate was definitively partitioned at the moment of death — twenty thousand for the daughters, five thousand for the sons — and subsequent inflation in food costs cannot retroactively strip the sons of what they had already been allocated.

### Creditor vs. Lien Model

This raises a sharper conceptual question. If the daughters are genuine creditors — if the estate owes them a debt — then in a case where the asset values have dropped and the twenty thousand dollars no longer suffices, why should the daughters not continue pressing their claim against the remaining estate until the full debt is paid? The answer could go either way depending on a further question: has any formal assignment of property actually taken place? If the sons had sat down, done the accounting, and transferred specific assets to the daughters — signed over stock certificates, conveyed title to real estate — then one can say the debt was paid. Whatever happens to those assets afterward is the daughters' problem, not the estate's. But what if the father died and nothing had yet been formally distributed? If two days later the stock collapses, why is the daughters' debt considered satisfied? They were never paid.

### Nachala DeOraisa

The answer that emerges, made explicit by *Tosafot* even if not spelled out verbatim in the *Gemara*'s text, is grounded in a different consideration: *nachala d'oraita*. There is a religious and legal value to the existence of a Torah-mandated inheritance. It is not ideal when an entire estate is consumed by the daughters' support obligation, even if that result is sometimes unavoidable when the estate is genuinely small. The institution of inheritance carries intrinsic weight. Therefore, even in a case where at the moment of death the estate would have produced a surplus for the sons and nothing has yet been formally divided, the *Gemara* protects that notional surplus. The sons retain their share as computed at the time of death, even if subsequent changes in value would, under a strict creditor model, have entitled the daughters to claim the entire estate. This is a prioritization of *nachala d'oraita* even at some cost to the daughters' support.

---

## Muatim Grows

### Muatim Growth Question

Having established that *merubin venismatu* is *pshita* — the sons retain their portion — the *Gemara* poses the harder question: *muatim venisrabu mai?* What if the estate was initially small — insufficient to fully support the daughters — and then grew in value? Say the estate was worth fifteen thousand dollars when the father died, in a situation where twenty thousand dollars was needed to support the daughters. The entire estate is effectively absorbed into the daughters' support obligation. Then, a day later, the assets surge in value to twenty-five thousand. Do the daughters keep the full twenty-five thousand? Or does the surplus of five thousand revert to the sons?

---

## Merubim Shrinks (II)

### Formal Assignment Impact

The *Gemara* does not distinguish between scenarios based on whether property was formally assigned before or after the change in value. Even if nothing was placed in a specific account for the daughters, even if the change occurred the moment after the father died, the ruling of *kvar zachu bahem yorshim* applies as of the moment of death. The *Gemara* does not require that an actual *kinyan* or formal transfer have occurred; the classification made at the moment of death is determinative. The question of formal assignment becomes significant in a different direction — in the debate between *Tosafot* and the *Rashbam* regarding *geviya*, which we will reach shortly.

---

## Muatim Grows (II)

### Two Property Models

The *Gemara* frames the *muatim venisrabu* question in terms of two competing models. On one view — *birshut yorshim kaime* — even in a case of *nechasim muatim*, the property remains fundamentally under the control and ownership of the sons. The daughters are creditors: the estate owes them a debt, and they are entitled to collect up to the amount of that debt, but no more. If the property increases in value, the benefit of that appreciation belongs to the sons, who own the underlying asset. The daughters collect twenty thousand dollars and nothing beyond that.

On the other view — *siluki mesalki yorshim mehacha* — in a case of *muatim*, we do not treat the sons as having inherited anything at all. The entire estate passes to the daughters outright. If the value subsequently rises, that increase accrues to them as the owners of property that has grown in their hands.

The *Gemara* brings a proof from a ruling of Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *yetomim shekadmu umachru benechasim muatim, mah shemachru machru* — if the heirs went ahead and sold property in a case of *nechasim muatim*, the sale is valid. This is decisive evidence for the first model. A sale is valid only if the sellers have ownership. If the sons can sell the property even in a *muatim* situation, it means the property is fundamentally theirs; the daughters hold a lien against it, not title to it. Accordingly, if the value rises, the daughters have a twenty-thousand-dollar claim against an asset now worth twenty-five thousand — they collect their debt, and the five-thousand-dollar surplus remains with the sons.

### Support vs. Debt

*Tosafot* raises a sharper objection here, one that cuts to the heart of why the daughters' claim is not really like an ordinary creditor's debt. An ordinary creditor is owed a fixed sum: the estate owes him twenty thousand dollars, he collects twenty thousand dollars and walks away. The daughters' situation is fundamentally different. Their entitlement is not a fixed lump sum; it is an ongoing obligation of support — two dollars today, two dollars tomorrow, day after day, until they marry or reach *bagrut*. In that sense, even if property is formally set aside for them, it was never truly given to them as a lump sum payment. It was placed in reserve to ensure that ongoing support would be funded, but the daily support obligation continues to generate new entitlement in real time.

### Sons Can Sell

The validity of the sons' sale, as established by Rav Assi and Rabbi Yochanan, demonstrates that the daughters hold a lien rather than ownership. Crucially, that lien does not follow the property into the hands of a buyer. The daughters cannot collect their support from someone who purchased the property from the sons, because *mezon ha'isha vehabanot* — support of the wife and daughters — does not attach to buyers. The rationale is straightforward: the amount owed to the daughters is indeterminate, fluctuating with time and circumstance, and it would be grossly unfair to encumber a buyer with an open-ended and indefinite lien. The daughters may collect their support from the estate while it remains under the sons' control, but once sold, their claim against that property ends. Whatever proceeds the sons received from the sale, however, remain available to satisfy the daughters' support.

### Geviya & Ownership

There is an important dispute between the *Rashbam* and *Tosafot* regarding the moment at which the daughters' claim crystallizes into something more than a lien. The *Rashbam* holds that once *beit din* formally adjudicated the matter and collected (*gavya*) the property on the daughters' behalf — awarding specific assets to them through a court proceeding — the sons may no longer sell it. At that point the daughters have true ownership, and any subsequent changes in value, up or down, are theirs to bear.

*Tosafot*, however, disagrees. Even after *beit din* has formally allocated property to the daughters, the sons retain the ability to sell. The reason returns to the conceptual point above: what *beit din* did was not transfer ownership of a fixed debt that has now been discharged. Rather, it set aside property to fund an ongoing support obligation. Because the support is ongoing and never resolves into a single completed payment, the property is always, in a sense, still under the sons' control. The daughters have security and a guarantee of their support, but they do not hold title. According to *Tosafot*, therefore, there is no moment at which the daughters ever acquire full ownership of the designated amount; according to the *Rashbam*, formal court adjudication creates that moment.

---

## Widow & Creditors

### Widow's Impact

The *Gemara* now addresses a more complex configuration. Rabbi Yirmiya, seated before Rabbi Abbahu, asks: *almana mahu shetam'it benechasim?* — does a widow reduce the estate for purposes of the *merubim/muatim* classification? Suppose the deceased left an estate of twenty-five thousand dollars, and the daughters' support will cost twenty thousand dollars. At first glance this is *merubim* and the sons inherit five thousand. But the deceased also left a widow, whose ongoing support (*mezonot*) must be paid from the estate. If we estimate her support at ten thousand dollars, then taking her claim into account, there is nothing left for the sons at all. The question is: do we factor in the widow's entitlement at the outset, making this a *muatim* estate from the start? Or do we classify the estate without regard to the widow's claim, treat it as *merubim*, and then address her claim as a subsequent deduction — in which case the principle of *kvar zachu bahem yorshim* protects the sons' five thousand?

### Widow Uncertainty

The *Gemara* reasons as follows: the widow's support is inherently uncertain. She may remarry, at which point her entitlement to *mezonot* from this estate ceases entirely. Because her claim is contingent — *ilu minsava, leit lah*, were she to remarry she receives nothing — we do not factor it into the initial classification of the estate. The estate is assessed as *merubim* without deducting her potential entitlement. Her claim then arrives as a stage-two consideration, and the principle of *kvar zachu bahem yorshim* comes into play, protecting the sons' portion to some degree. *Tosafot* notes the difficulty: the daughters' entitlement is similarly uncertain in certain respects — they too may marry early, reducing the cost of their support — yet the daughters' claim is factored in from the outset. The *Gemara* does not fully resolve this tension; the distinction appears to rest on the widow's unique susceptibility to remarriage as a decisive event that terminates her claim entirely.

### Stepdaughter Obligation

The *Gemara* then asks the parallel question about a *bat ishto*, a stepdaughter from the wife's prior marriage. It was common practice for a man marrying a woman with children from a previous relationship to undertake in the *ketubah* a specific obligation to support her daughter for a fixed period — typically five years — after his death, regardless of whether the stepdaughter subsequently marries or reaches *bagrut*. This is a more definite obligation than either the widow's ongoing support or the daughters' ordinary entitlement, because the stepdaughter's support runs for the fixed contractual term without regard to marriage. The question is therefore: does her definite, marriage-proof entitlement reduce the estate from the outset?

The *Gemara* presents the argument in both directions. On one hand, *kivan d'chi minsava nami it lah* — even were she to marry she still receives her support — making this a virtually certain expenditure from the estate, which should reduce it from the outset. On the other hand, *kivan d'ei metah leit lah* — were she to die, she would not receive anything — so there remains some contingency, and perhaps we do not deduct her share initially either.

### External Creditor

The *Gemara* then asks the analogous question about a plain *ba'al chov*, an ordinary external creditor to whom the estate owes a fixed debt of, say, five thousand dollars. Does this debt reduce the estate for *merubim/muatim* purposes? The *Gemara* presents the argument for automatic deduction: *kivan d'chi mayet nami it leh* — even if the creditor himself dies, his heirs can collect the debt, making this an essentially certain expenditure. The counterargument: *kivan d'mechassar govayna* — since the debt has not yet been collected, it does not yet reduce the estate. The practical consequence of *not* reducing the estate initially is the same as in the previous cases: we classify the estate as *merubim*, the sons get their portion, and then the creditor's claim arrives as a secondary consideration governed by *kvar zachu bahem yorshim*.

### Reversal Framing

Strikingly, the *Gemara* presents the entire sequence of questions a second time in reverse order: starting from the *ba'al chov* and working up through the stepdaughter to the widow. This is not mere stylistic repetition. The direction of the questioning signals where the conclusion is being pushed. When the *Gemara* starts with the widow and escalates to the creditor, it seems to be reaching toward the conclusion that *none* of these reduce the estate — even the *ba'al chov* perhaps does not. When the *Gemara* starts with the creditor and escalates to the widow, it seems to be reaching toward the conclusion that *all* of these reduce the estate — even the widow perhaps does. The framing of the question reveals the direction of the intended *psak*, and the fact that both framings appear reflects the *Gemara*'s unresolved state on these questions.

Underlying all of this, as *Tosafot* emphasizes, is the principle of *nachala d'oraita*. The consistent thrust of refusing to deduct these various creditors from the initial estate assessment has the systematic effect of classifying more estates as *merubim* and triggering *kvar zachu bahem yorshim*, thereby ensuring that the sons retain some inheritance. This is not merely protecting the sons' financial interest; it is preserving the institution of Torah-mandated inheritance.

### Widow Priority

Rabbi Yirmiya had also posed a final question: as between the widow and the daughters in a *nechasim muatim* situation where the estate cannot fully support both, which claim takes precedence? Rabbi Abbahu said he had no immediate answer and asked Rabbi Yirmiya to return the following day. When Rabbi Yirmiya returned, Rabbi Abbahu reported that he had at least one clear ruling, citing Rabbi Abba citing Rabbi Assi: *asu almana etzel habat k'bat etzel ha'achin benechasim mu'atin* — they made the widow vis-à-vis the daughter as the daughter is vis-à-vis the sons in a small estate. Just as in a *muatim* estate the daughters are supported and the sons go begging, so too the widow is supported and the daughters go begging. The widow's claim takes priority over the daughters'.

The reasoning follows from the posture of the man at the time of marriage. When he undertakes obligations in the *ketubah*, he is committing to this woman standing before him. The daughters are as yet unborn; his present commitment is to his wife. It also reflects the practical reality that daughters are young and have a longer horizon for marriage and eventual self-sufficiency, while a widow — particularly an older one — may have fewer such prospects. Whatever the underlying rationale, the ruling is clear: the widow is fed first, and if nothing remains, the daughters must seek support elsewhere.

---

## Admon's Argument

### Admon's Torah Plea

The *mishna* records Admon's complaint: *bishvil she'ani zachar hifsadeti?* — just because I am male I lose out? In the *nechasim muatim* scenario, the daughters are supported and the sons receive nothing. Admon objects on the grounds that this result is unjust. The *Gemara* asks: what exactly is Admon's argument? Abaye initially explains it as follows: *bishvil she'ani zachar vera'ui ani la'asok baTorah hifsadeti?* — because I am male and suited for Torah study, I should lose out? The claim is that a male's spiritual superiority — his capacity for *talmud Torah* — entitles him to equal support even in a small estate.

### Rava Rejects Spirit

Rava immediately dismisses this reading. *Man de'asik baTorah hu deyaris, udela asik baTorah lo yaris?* — do you think inheritance rights depend on who is actually engaged in Torah learning? If so, one might argue that among three sons, only the one who studies in *yeshiva* should inherit while his brothers receive nothing. Spiritual attainment does not determine property rights. The *Gemara* emphatically rejects any conflation of religious virtue with legal entitlement in *yerusha*. Whatever Torah learning confers in terms of religious standing, it has no operative force in the law of inheritance.

### Privilege Argument

Rava then offers what he considers Admon's real argument: *bishvil she'ani zachar vera'ui ani lirash benechasim merubim, hifsadeti benechasim mu'atim?* — because I am male and therefore privileged to inherit the bulk of a large estate, should I lose out entirely in a small estate? This is a strictly legal argument, not a spiritual one. The system of inheritance explicitly favors males. In a large estate, the sons inherit the substantial surplus while daughters receive only their fixed support entitlement. The system is designed to advantage males. Given that the law privileges males in the large-estate scenario, Admon finds it incongruous that males receive no protection whatsoever in the small-estate scenario.

### Counter: Different Rights

The response to Admon is that having different rights in different contexts is not inherently contradictory. Males are privileged in large estates, but females have protected support in small estates. The asymmetry is explicable: males have greater capacity to earn a living, to go out into the marketplace, to knock on doors and find means of sustenance. Females in that society were not expected to do so and therefore required a protected legal entitlement to support. The two scenarios present different considerations that yield different results — not a logical inconsistency, but a coherent system in which distinct interests receive distinct protections depending on circumstances. That males sometimes win greatly and sometimes receive nothing does not make the system unfair on its own terms.

### Tosafot vs. Rashbam

There remains a dispute as to what Admon's precise standing is in *halacha*. The *Rashbam* rules that the *halacha* follows Admon, meaning that in a *muatim* scenario the sons do receive some support alongside the daughters. *Tosafot* disagrees, arguing that the *Gemara* consistently ignores Admon's position when analyzing the various *muatim* scenarios, and therefore we do not rule like him. In *Tosafot*'s reading, Admon is not making a binding *halachic* claim at all; he is simply drawing attention to the irony — pointing out that the privileged party in one context becomes the disadvantaged party in another — without asserting that the law should be otherwise.

---

## Tumtum & Gifts

### Tumtum Definition

The *mishna* now introduces cases involving a *tumtum* and an *androgynous*. These are distinct categories. An *androgynous* has both male and female genitalia and presents an irreducible legal ambiguity. A *tumtum* is different: the genitalia have either not descended or are obscured, so that sex is presently indeterminate, but the presumption is that only one set exists — we simply do not yet know which. Both create legal complexity in the context of inheritance.

### Tumtum Strategy

In a large estate — *nechasim merubim* — a *tumtum* finds himself caught between adversarial classifications. The sons want to classify him as female, in which case he gets only the daughters' limited support entitlement and does not inherit alongside them. The daughters want to classify him as male, in which case he is grouped with the sons and his claim comes from the sons' portion rather than from their support allotment. The *tumtum*'s maximum recovery in either case is bounded by *mima nafshach* reasoning: whatever he might be, his claim against the estate cannot exceed the lesser of what a daughter or a son would receive.

### Tumtum vs. Support

In a *nechasim muatim* situation, the *tumtum* fares worse. He cannot prove he is female, and the daughters reject his claim for support: *hanekeiva docha oto etzel zcharim* — the females push him toward the males. Since he cannot establish female status, he has no support entitlement and ends up in the unenviable position of the sons — receiving nothing and having to seek support elsewhere.

### Conditional Gifts

The *mishna* then takes up the case of conditional gifts to an unborn child. A father declares: if my wife gives birth to a boy, let him receive one hundred *maneh*; if a girl, two hundred *maneh*. The *mishna* establishes that if a boy is born, he receives one hundred, and if a girl, she receives two hundred. The substantive novelty here is that such gifts are effective at all — that a *kinyan* can be effected on behalf of an *ubar*, an unborn child. The asymmetry — more money designated for a daughter than a son — is also notable, appearing immediately after Admon's argument and implicitly reflecting the view that a daughter may need greater protection.

### Twins Disagreement

The *mishna* further provides: *im zachar maneh im nekeiva masayim, veyalda zachar unekeiva* — if the declaration covers both possibilities, and the wife delivers both a boy and a girl, then both conditions are met and each child collects the designated amount. The *Rashbam*, however, disagrees with this reading. In his view, if a man says "if a boy, a hundred; if a girl, two hundred," he is assuming a single child. The birth of twins was unforeseen, and since his conditional gift was predicated on a single birth, neither condition was met and neither child collects anything. The *Rashbam* reads the *vov* in the phrase *zachar unekeiva* as disjunctive — meaning "or" rather than "and" — rendering the *mishna* as simply saying that whichever sex the single child turns out to be, that child takes the designated amount.

### Tumtum Own Category

Finally, the *mishna* asks: what if a *tumtum* is born? One might reason that the child should at least receive the lesser of the two amounts — the hundred designated for a boy — on the principle of *mima nafshach*. The *mishna* rules otherwise: *eino notel* — the *tumtum* receives nothing. This ruling reflects the position that a *tumtum* is *beriya bifnei atzmo* — its own independent category of being, not a *safek* oscillating between male and female. If the *tumtum* were merely a factual uncertainty — we do not know whether this person is male or female — then logically the child should at minimum receive the lesser amount. But if the *tumtum* is treated as a distinct category altogether, then neither condition set by the father has been satisfied: the condition "if male" was not met, and the condition "if female" was not met. The child is something else entirely, and both gifts fail. This is a striking position — one that, as the *Gemara* will continue to explore, resonates in unexpected ways with contemporary thinking about biological sex as non-binary — and we will pick up with its further ramifications tomorrow.

---

---

# Bava Batra 141

## Tumtum/Androgynous Heirs

### Gender Categories

The ninth *perek* of Bava Batra, *Perek Mi Shemet*, opens with a *mishnah* addressing the inheritance rights of heirs of ambiguous gender. Because the halakhic system operates within a rigid gender binary, and because external sexual characteristics do not always conform to that binary, the tradition developed distinct legal categories for such cases. Two such categories appear here: *tumtum* and *androgynos*.

### Tumtum vs Androgynous

The *tumtum* generally refers to a person with what we might describe as ambiguous genitalia, while *androgynos* refers to a person who presents with both types of sexual characteristics. Both are classified as *safek zachar safek nekevah* — of doubtful male or female status — yet the nature of that *safek* differs in an important way. The *tumtum* is understood to be a *safek bechesron yedia*: a doubt arising from lack of information, potentially resolvable through some later event, and therefore assessed case by case. The *androgynos*, by contrast, represents a class *safek* — every individual falling into that category is by definition of doubtful gender, and that status cannot be resolved. The *sugyot* in the *gemara* and the elaborations of the *rishonim* work extensively to flesh out the practical ramifications of this distinction.

### Large Estate Case

The *mishnah* states: *hini'ach banim uvanot ve-tumtum* — if someone leaves both sons and daughters and a *tumtum* child. The first case concerns *nechasim merubin*, a large estate: when there is sufficient property both to provide *mizonot* for the daughters and to leave an inheritance for the sons, *ha-zekarim dochin oto etzel nekevot* — the sons may push the *tumtum* off toward the daughters.

### Small Estate Case

Conversely, *nechasim muatin hanekevot dochot oto etzel zekarim* — when there is a small estate, such that the property will be consumed providing *mizonot* for the daughters with nothing left for the sons, the daughters push the *tumtum* off toward the sons.

### Safek Dynamics

The logic underlying both cases is the same: because the *tumtum* is a *safek*, neither the sons nor the daughters wish the *tumtum* to be counted among their number, as doing so would reduce their own respective shares. The ambiguous gender status of the *tumtum* thus creates a situation where the child is caught between two groups, each of which seeks to exclude it — a direct consequence of the rules governing *mamon ha-mutal be-safek*, money in a situation of doubt.

### Eino Notel Rule

The second half of the *mishnah* turns to a different case: *ha-omer*, where a father declares that if his wife gives birth to a son, a certain sum should be paid, and if to a daughter, a different sum. Here the *mishnah* states that if a *tumtum* is born, *eino notel* — the child cannot claim anything — because *tumtum* is *safek zachar safek nekevah* and cannot make a positive claim to be either male or female.

---

## Abaye vs Rava

### Abaye Position

The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: if the sons can push the *tumtum* off toward the daughters in the *reisha*, why does the *seifa* say the *tumtum* receives nothing? Abaye resolves this by explaining that *dochin oto ve-ein lo* — the sons push him off, and he receives nothing even from the daughters. The sons say he is not male; the daughters say he is not female; and so he collects nothing from either group.

### Rava Position

Rava disagrees: *dochin oto ve-yeish lo* — even when pushed off, the *tumtum* should have some claim. Being pushed from one group to another does not mean receiving nothing at all.

### Mamah Nafshach

Rava's reasoning is *mamah nafshach*: one way or another, the *tumtum* should receive something, since either as a son or as a daughter he would be entitled to some portion. A doubtful case should still yield some claim, not a complete forfeiture.

### Doubtful Claim Problem

Abaye's rejoinder is that a doubtful claim can never obligate us to hand over money that belongs to another party. The rules of *mamon ha-mutal be-safek* cannot operate here to award property to someone who cannot establish a positive status.

### Priority Question

The deeper issue underlying this dispute is the question of sequence: does child status get determined first — is this person a son or a daughter — with the inheritance flowing from that determination? Or is the child's status as heir primary, with the gender classification coming second? If Abaye holds that gender determination must precede any inheritance claim, then a *tumtum* who cannot establish a clear gender simply cannot make any claim at all. Rava, by contrast, allows the *safek* itself to generate a claim, however limited.

---

## Rabban Shimon

### Kedusha Rule

The *gemara* suggests that the *seifa* of the *mishnah* accords with the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *ein kedusha chala aleihem* — no designation of sanctity takes effect on a *tumtum* or *androgynos*.

### Korban Analogy

The context is one of *korbanot*. Suppose a person has a pregnant animal and declares: if the offspring is male, I will bring it as a *korban olah*, and if female, as a *korban shelamim*. If the offspring turns out to be a *tumtum* or *androgynos*, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that no *kedusha* takes effect at all.

### Gender First Principle

The reasoning is that the determination of male or female must come first; only after that determination can the specific type of offering be designated. If the animal cannot be identified as either male or female, the conditional designation never attaches, and no *kedusha* operates.

### Alignment Analysis

This position fits naturally with Abaye — who holds that gender must be established before any claim can arise — but not with Rava, who allows the *safek* itself to generate entitlement. The *seifa* of the *mishnah*, supported by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling on *korbanot*, thus provides implicit support for Abaye's framework.

---

## Tumtum Baraita

### Contradictory Source

The *gemara* now raises a challenge from a *baraita*: *meitivei*, *tumtum yoreish ke-ven ve-nizon ke-bat* — a *tumtum* inherits like a son and receives *mezonot* like a daughter. This *baraita* appears to grant the *tumtum* both forms of entitlement simultaneously, which seems to contradict the *mishnah*'s position that the *tumtum* receives nothing at all.

### Rava's Solution

The *gemara* explains that this *baraita* fits well with Rava's position. Rava reads *yoreish ke-ven be-nechasim muatin*: the *tumtum* inherits as a son in the case of a small estate — where the male inheritance share is minimal or nonexistent. And *nizon ke-bat be-nechasim merubin*: he receives *mezonot* as a daughter in the case of a large estate, where he would otherwise stand to receive a substantial male share. In each scenario, the *tumtum* receives the lesser of the two possible claims — a kind of applied *mamah nafshach*.

### Reconciliation

This reading allows Rava to reconcile the *baraita* with the *mishnah*, by understanding the *baraita* as awarding the *tumtum* only the weaker entitlement in each situation. The approach also reflects a broader halakhic preference: we generally rule like Rava, and we generally follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and the goal here is to fit those authoritative positions together with both the *mishnah* and this *baraita*.

### Abaye Problem

For Abaye, however, the *baraita* presents a serious problem. Abaye holds *dochin oto ve-ein lo* — the *tumtum* gets nothing. How, then, can the *baraita* say he inherits as a son and receives *mezonot* as a daughter?

### Abaye Reframe

Abaye reinterprets the *baraita* to mean *ra'ui* — suitable, in principle, but not actually receiving. *Ra'ui liresh ve-ein lo*: he is conceptually placed in the son's category — to push him out of the daughter's category — yet cannot actually inherit with the sons. Likewise, *ra'ui lazon ve-ein lo*: he is conceptually placed in the daughter's category for *mezonot* purposes, yet does not actually receive *mezonot* either. The *baraita*'s language of inheriting as a son and receiving sustenance as a daughter thus describes not actual entitlement but rather the legal mechanism by which the *tumtum* is pushed between categories — and receives nothing from either. This interpretation reads the *baraita* in a direction opposite to its plain sense, which the *gemara* acknowledges. Such re-readings of *baraitot* are a recognized mechanism: when an *amora*'s position cannot accommodate a *baraita* directly, the *baraita* may be reinterpreted rather than treated as a straightforward refutation.

---

## Son vs Daughter

### Lemara Question

Having discussed a *mishnah* that awards a larger gift for the birth of a daughter than for a son, the *gemara* raises a pointed question: does this imply that a daughter is preferable? This seems to contradict a well-known statement attributed to Rabbi Yochanan.

### God's Anger

Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, taught: *kol she-eino mani'ach ben le-yorsho ha-kadosh baruch hu malei alav evrah* — whoever does not leave a son to inherit his property, God fills him with anger. The proof-text is *ve-ha'avartem et nachalato le-vito* — and you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter — where *ha'avara* (transferring) is read as evoking *evrah* (anger), as in the verse *yom evrah ha-yom ha-hu* from the book of Tzefanya. There is thus an apparent tension between the *mishnah*'s seemingly greater valuation of daughters and this tradition's implicit preference for sons.

### Inheritance vs Gains

The *gemara* resolves this tension by distinguishing between two different contexts. *Ben adif le-inyan yerusha* — a son is preferable when it comes to inheritance, since the son fills the role of the father in a qualitative sense, not merely receiving property but continuing the father's presence in the world. *Bat adifa le-inyan harvacha* — a daughter is preferable when it comes to *harvacha*, some form of provision or gain. Rashbam explains this in terms of *mezonot*: the daughter's claims on the estate are a different kind of entitlement, though the precise mechanism is not entirely clear from his explanation.

### First Child Sign

Shmuel offers a different resolution: our *mishnah* is dealing specifically with a *mivakeret*, a woman giving birth to her first child. In this context, the reference is to the teaching of Rav Chisda: *bat techila simanya yafeh la-banim* — a daughter born first is a good omen for the sons who will follow.

### Omen Explanations

Two explanations are offered for why a firstborn daughter is considered a good sign. One tradition holds *de-marbei le-achaha* — that an eldest daughter will be able to help raise her younger brothers, assisting the mother in bringing up the children. Another tradition holds *de-lo shaletah bah eina bisha* — that there is less *ayin hara* when a daughter is born first, whether because the arrival of a girl draws less jealous attention or because it avoids whatever concerns surround the *brit milah* procedure.

### Rav Chisda

Rav Chisda himself applied this principle personally: *binatai adifan li mi-banai* — my daughters are preferable to me over my sons. One explanation offered is that if a man had two wives and one gave birth to a son first, this could stir jealousy between the wives; if a daughter was born first, the lesser social premium attached to the birth would reduce such tensions. Another explanation, offered by Tosafot, is that without a clear *bechor*, there would be no subsequent quarreling among sons over the double inheritance share, making the household more peaceful overall.

---

## Meir vs Yehuda

### Bakol Beriyah

The *gemara* now considers who is the *tanna* of our *mishnah* — specifically, which *tanna* would hold that having a daughter is in some respect preferable. The candidate proposed is Rabbi Yehuda, whose position is known in connection with the verse *va-donai berach et Avraham ba-kol* — and God blessed Avraham with everything. This verse provides the basis for a *machloket* among the *tannaim*.

### Meir Position

Rabbi Meir interprets the blessing of *bakol* as the fact that Avraham did not have a daughter. On this reading, the absence of a daughter was itself the divine gift.

### Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: the blessing was that Avraham did have a daughter, and her name was *Bakol* — an unusual name, but one that explains the verse. This *machloket* maps onto a broader question of whether having a daughter is beneficial or detrimental. However, the *gemara* immediately notes that one cannot extrapolate from Rabbi Yehuda's position that having a daughter is *better* than having a son. He may regard daughters as a genuine blessing without ranking them above sons, and so Rabbi Yehuda's view on *bakol* does not directly support the *mishnah*'s apparent preference for daughters.

### Feeding Obligation

A different *baraita* is then invoked to demonstrate Rabbi Yehuda's actual position more precisely. The *baraita* records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on the obligation of financial support for children. Rabbi Meir says: *mitzvah lizon et ha-banot ve-kal va-homer la-banim de-askei be-Torah* — there is a *mitzvah* to support one's daughters, and *kal va-homer* for sons who are engaged in Torah study. Since sons were the ones studying Torah, their claim to support is, on Rabbi Meir's account, even stronger.

### Yehuda Kal Vachomer

Rabbi Yehuda reverses the *kal va-homer*: *mitzvah lizon et ha-banim ve-kal va-homer la-banot de-lo litzalan* — there is a *mitzvah* to support the sons, and *kal va-homer* for the daughters, so that they should not become degraded by having to support themselves in ways unsuitable to their station. This Aramaic phrase *de-lo litzalan* is likely a gloss appended to the *baraita* to explain the reasoning, as such Aramaic interpolations within the Hebrew text of a *baraita* are a recognized phenomenon. Rabbi Yehuda's *kal va-homer* thus gives daughters a stronger claim to support, and it is this position — not the *bakol* *derasha* — that identifies him as the likely *tanna* behind our *mishnah*'s preference for daughters.

A *baraita* recording the same basic case as the *mishnah*, but with the son receiving six *dinarim* and the daughter only two, suggests that its *tanna* considered sons preferential. This illustrates that the *tannaim* themselves were divided on the question, with different versions of the case reflecting the underlying *machloket*.

---

## Birth Gift Case

### Conditional Gift

The *mishnah* presents the case of *ha-omer im teled ishti zachar yitol maneh* — if someone declares that if his wife gives birth to a son, that son should receive 100, and if a daughter, 200. The initial reading of the *mishnah* understands the gift as going directly to the child born.

### Child as Recipient

On this reading, the *mishnah* is a case in which the father designates property for the benefit of the child, contingent on whether that child is a son or a daughter. The larger gift for the daughter — double that for the son — is what prompted the earlier discussion about whether the father prefers to have a daughter. The complication that arises is a case of twins: if a boy and girl are born together and it is unknown which was born first, the son can claim 100 *zuz* in any case — either because he was born first and is entitled to 200, or because he was born second and is entitled to 100. The disputed 100 *zuz* may then be divided as *mamon ha-mutal be-safek*.

### Messenger Recipient

Ravina offers a fundamentally different reading of the *mishnah*: the gift does not go to the child at all, but to whoever brings the father the news of the birth — the messenger. The *mishnah* is then not a case of transferring property to a fetus or newborn, but a straightforward conditional gift to an adult who brings tidings.

### Baraita Support

A *baraita* is cited in support of Ravina's reading: *ha-mevasrani be-mah niftarah rechem shel ishti* — whoever informs me of the first birth from my wife's womb, *im zachar yitol maneh* — if it is a son, he receives 100; *yalda zachar notel maneh* — and if a son was born, he gets 100. The *baraita* thus explicitly frames the recipient as the messenger, *ha-mevasrani*, whoever brings the news.

### Twins & Nefel

The *baraita* further specifies that if the wife gives birth to twins, a boy and a girl, the messenger receives only 100 — not 200. Although the father did not explicitly address the twins case, it is explained that he had indeed stated that even in the case of twins, a boy and a girl, the messenger would receive only 100. The exclusion this provision accomplishes is the case of a *nefel* — a miscarriage or non-viable birth. In such a case, the messenger would receive nothing. While a *nefel* counts as *pitrat rechem*, opening the womb for purposes of birth order, it does not qualify the messenger for the conditional payment, as there is no viable birth to celebrate.

---

## Shchiv Mera & Ubar

### Designation Case

The *gemara* turns to a related case: *ha-hu de-amar lehu le-diviteih nechasai le-hai de-mi'avrat* — a dying man who declares to his wife that all his property shall go to the one with whom she is currently pregnant. This is a *shechiv mera* case, a dying declaration, in which the husband seeks to designate the inheritance before his death, while the child is still in utero.

### Rav Huna Position

Rav Huna rules: *havei mezakeh le-ubar ve-ha-mezakeh le-ubar lo kana* — this constitutes an attempt to transfer ownership to a fetus, and such a transfer does not take effect. An *ubar* cannot acquire property.

### No Yad Problem

The conceptual basis for Rav Huna's ruling is the absence of *yad*: there is no hand, no agent, no legal presence through which a *kinyan* can be effected on behalf of a non-existent legal person. Without someone present to receive the transfer, the *kinyan* is a nullity, regardless of the sincere intent of the dying father. One might ask whether the mother could serve as proxy — through the principle of *ubar yerech imo* or otherwise — but the *gemara* does not resolve this in Rav Huna's favor, and he maintains his position directly.

### Rav Nachman

Rav Nachman challenges Rav Huna from our *mishnah*: *ha-omer im yalda ishti zachar yitol maneh* — if my wife gives birth to a son, he shall receive 100. When a son was born, he received 100. This *mishnah*, on its plain reading, presupposes that the fetal son was the beneficiary of the conditional gift at the time the declaration was made — which would mean the *mishnah* assumes that *mezakeh le-ubar* works.

### Rav Huna Defense

Rav Huna defends himself: *mishnateinu eini yodea mi shan'ah* — I do not know who taught our *mishnah*. This is a recognized halakhic move: if the authorship of a *mishnah* can be identified with a rejected or minority *tanna*ic opinion, the *mishnah* loses its claim to authority as a proof. Since, as will emerge, there was already a dispute about which *tanna* authored this *mishnah* — with implications touching the disputes of Abaye and Rava, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and others — Rav Huna can plausibly claim that the *mishnah* reflects a *da'at yachid* that he does not follow.

---

## Mishnah Author

### Rabbi Meir Option

The *gemara* now works through the possible *tanna*ic authors of the *mishnah* in order to determine whether any of them can support the position that *mezakeh le-ubar* is valid. The first candidate is Rabbi Meir, whose position across *Shas* is *makneh davar shelo ba la-olam* — a person can transfer ownership of something that does not yet exist.

### Meir Limitation

The *gemara* immediately rejects this: one must distinguish between *ledavar she-yeshno ba-olam* — transferring something that exists to a recipient — and *ledavar she-eino ba-olam* — transferring something to a party that does not yet exist. Rabbi Meir's principle addresses the former: he allows the transfer of future property, of something not yet in existence, to a person who does exist. But it does not follow that Rabbi Meir permits transferring existing property to a person — the *ubar* — who does not yet legally exist. There is no *yad*, no legal agent, on behalf of whom the *kinyan* can operate. Rabbi Meir's *chiddush* is about the object of the transfer, not the recipient.

### Rabbi Yose Option

The next candidate is Rabbi Yose, who states *ubar posel ve-eino ma'achil* — a fetus disqualifies but does not enable. The context is a *kohen*ic family and the laws of *terumah*. If a *bat kohen* married to a *Yisrael* becomes widowed while pregnant with his child, the fetal *zar* prevents her from returning to eat *terumah* at her father's house — *ubar posel*. But a *bat Yisrael* married to a *kohen*, who becomes widowed while pregnant with his *kohen* fetus, cannot eat *terumah* either — *eino ma'achil*. Rabbi Yose's position is thus characterized as *ubar kani* — the fetus has sufficient legal presence to generate halakhic consequences, specifically the disqualification from *terumah*.

### Yerusha Distinction

The *gemara* rejects Rabbi Yose as a basis for our *mishnah*: *shani yerusha ha-ba'ah me-eleiha* — inheritance is different because it is automatic. The implication, however, cuts in either direction: perhaps an *ubar* has even more standing in the context of *yerusha* precisely because inheritance operates automatically, without the *ubar* needing to perform any act of acquisition. Or perhaps the very automaticity of *yerusha* means the *ubar*'s passive presence is not enough to trigger it. Either way, the *gemara* concludes that Rabbi Yose's principle in the context of *terumah* cannot be straightforwardly applied to *yerusha*, and so he cannot serve as the author of our *mishnah*.

### R. Yochanan b. Beroka

The next candidate is Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds *lo shna yerusha ve-lo shna matana* — there is no distinction between inheritance and a gift. On his view, a *shechiv mera* who designates his estate to someone who would in any case inherit it is effectively making a conditional gift, and *divrav kayamin* — his words stand. Because he treats *yerusha* as fundamentally a subspecies of *matana*, the bequeathing father retains greater control: he can set conditions, modify the distribution, and, one might argue, transfer property to a fetus, since he is the master of the giving process.

### Beroka Limitation

The *gemara* limits Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka in the same way it limited Rabbi Meir: *eimor di-shamat leih le-Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka le-davar she-yeshno ba-olam* — his principle may apply only to giving a gift of something that actually exists. *Le-davar she-eino ba-olam mi amar* — but who ever heard of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka permitting a gift to a fetus? His ruling addresses a living recipient; it says nothing about transferring property to one not yet born.

### Combined Option Rejected

One further attempt is made: perhaps the *mishnah* reflects the combined position of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka operating within Rabbi Yose's framework — *ve-savar lah ke-Rabbi Yose*. The *gemara* dismisses this as unattested: there is no tradition that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka held like Rabbi Yose in this matter, and one cannot simply compound two independent opinions into a synthetic position without evidence.

### Ravina Escapes

At this point the *gemara* returns to Ravina's reading of the *mishnah*: *bi-mevasreni* — the gift goes to the messenger, not to the child. On this reading, none of the difficulties about *mezakeh le-ubar* arise at all, since the recipient of the gift is an adult who is already present. Ravina's interpretation thus escapes the entire problem Rav Nachman raised against Rav Huna.

### Seifa Problem

However, the *gemara* immediately identifies a difficulty with Ravina's reading from the *seifa* of the *mishnah*: *ve-im ein sham yoresh ela hu, yoreish ha-kol* — if there is no other *yoresh*, this child inherits everything. If the *mishnah* were talking about a messenger receiving a reward for bringing news, what does it mean to speak of the messenger as a *yoresh*? The messenger is not an heir, and *yerusha* has no relevance to his entitlement. The *seifa* thus appears to be speaking of the child as the direct recipient, which pulls the reading back toward the problem of *mezakeh le-ubar* — and leaves the question open for continuation on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Bava Batra 142

## Tumtum & Gender

### Tumtum Background

Today's *daf* is 142. We pick up at the bottom of 141b, in the context of the *Mishna* presenting scenarios where a man declares: "If my wife gives birth to a male child, let him receive a hundred dollars; if to a female child, two hundred," and so on — with the *Gemara* then drawing out the implications that spin off from this. One issue that arose was the case of a *tumtum*, a child of indeterminate sex. The *Gemara* had a rich discussion about whether a *tumtum* is a *biryah bifnei atzmo* — an entirely independent category — and therefore falls into neither the male nor the female designation and receives nothing, a position that, as noted, touches on broader questions about the gender binary.

The alternative view is that a *tumtum* represents a *safek*, a genuine case of doubt. Even so, one position holds that this *safek* status does not entitle the *tumtum* to receive even the lower common denominator of the two amounts.

### Abaye's Tumtum

This is where Abaye's position enters: *v'yeiti v'lo yahavinan lei* — the *tumtum* comes forward but receives neither the male nor the female portion. One way to understand this is as treating the *tumtum* as a categorically distinct creature (*biryah*). But another way to understand it is rooted in the *da'at* of the donor — the subjective intent behind the declaration. When a person says "if it's a boy" or "if it's a girl," he likely means someone who is unambiguously identifiable as one or the other, not someone who may objectively belong to one category but cannot be clearly identified as such. The ambiguity in the recipient's identity defeats the mechanism of the gift.

### Daughter Preference Joke

The *Gemara* also raised the question of why the father in our *Mishna* gives more money to his daughter than to his son, running against the general cultural assumption that sons are preferred. One answer offered is that everyone wants a daughter to be the eldest child, since she helps raise the younger siblings. The *Gemara* then cites a tradition that a certain Sage preferred daughters because his sons-in-law turned out to be greater *talmidei chachamim* than his sons.

In the midst of this discussion, the *Gemara* raises the verse that God blessed Avraham *bakol* — "with everything" — and a tradition that Avraham had a daughter whose name was *Bakol*. Does this not prove that daughters are superior? Tosafot seizes on this with a pointed question: if Avraham had a daughter named *Bakol*, why did he go to such lengths to find a wife for Yitzchak from far away? Since a *ben Noach* is permitted to marry his half-sister on his father's side, why did Yitzchak not simply marry his half-sister *Bakol*? Tosafot provides its own answers — though one suggestion, offered more lightly, is that Yitzchak wanted to marry a real woman, not a *Midrash*.

---

## Transfer to Ubar

### Rav Huna's Position

The *Gemara* now turns to what is the central question animating the rest of today's discussion: how does the mechanism of the *Mishna* actually function? When the father declares that his unborn son or daughter shall receive this gift, he is attempting to transfer ownership to a fetus — to an *ubar*. But we have a principle: *hamezakeh l'ubar lo kanah* — one who attempts to transfer property to a fetus, even through a third party acting on the fetus's behalf (invoking the principle of *zachin l'adam shelo b'fanav*), has effected no transfer, because the fetus is not yet a legal person who can take possession. This is the position of Rav Huna.

The *Gemara* notes that Rav Huna therefore cannot identify who authored the *Mishna*, since he is unaware of any position that would permit transferring ownership to a fetus. The *Gemara* attempts to rescue the *Mishna* by suggesting it reflects Rav Meir's view that *adam makneh davar shelo ba l'olam* — a person can transfer an object not yet in existence. But the *Gemara* pushes back: in Rav Meir's case, the recipient at least exists; here, even the recipient is not yet a legal person. Another possible rescue — that we have evidence a fetus can inherit — is also deflected: natural inheritance (*yerusha*) that occurs automatically is different from actively conferring possession on a fetus.

### Reinterpretation Attempt

The *Gemara* proposes a creative reinterpretation: perhaps the *Mishna* is not describing a case where the father is attempting to transfer property to a still-unborn *ubar* at all. Perhaps the father is in a distant location, his wife has already given birth, and he simply does not know the sex of the child. His declaration — "if it's a boy, give him a hundred; if it's a girl, give her two hundred" — would then be a gift to a child already born, just one whose sex is as yet unknown to him. This would sidestep the *ubar* problem entirely, since the transfer would be to a child already in existence.

The *Gemara*, however, rejects this reading from the language of the *Mishna* itself. The closing clause of the *Mishna* uses the future tense — *kol mah sheteiled ishti*, "whomever my wife will give birth to" — rather than the past tense *kol mah sheyalda*, "whomever my wife gave birth to." The future tense makes clear that the child is not yet born at the time of the declaration, and so the *ubar* problem cannot be avoided.

### Rav Huna Rejects

The *Gemara* then raises another possible workaround: *v'leima lei d'amar liksheteiled* — what if the declaration is structured so that the *kinyan* takes effect not while the child is still a fetus, but at the moment of birth? The act of transfer would be performed now, but would only take legal effect once the child enters the world.

This is a conceptually interesting mechanism. If a third party is acting to acquire property on behalf of the *ubar* — representing him — the difficulty is that a fetus is not a legal entity that can be represented. But there is arguably a distinction between representing someone who does not yet exist as a legal person, on the one hand, and performing an act now that is designed to take effect for a person once they do exist, on the other. Perhaps a person can initiate a *kinyan* now, with the effect suspended until the recipient becomes a cognizable legal entity.

Rav Huna rejects this as well. His position is *d'amar Rav Huna af liksheteiled lo kanah* — even if the intent is that the *kinyan* should take effect only upon birth, it still does not work. Since the fetus is *ubar yerech imo* — legally regarded as a limb of the mother, not an independent entity — no act performed now can be grounded in the fetus's eventual legal personality. The act has no one to latch on to. Rav Huna therefore maintains that the *Mishna* cannot be reconciled with any known position, and so the question of its authorship remains open for him.

### Rav Nachman's Compromise

Against Rav Huna's sweeping rejection, Rav Nachman offers a more calibrated position: *hamezakeh l'ubar lo kanah, liksheteiled kanah* — a fetus cannot take possession while still a fetus, but one may perform an act that takes effect for the fetus once the fetus is born. The *Mishna* can therefore be explained: the transfer takes legal effect at the moment of birth, not during gestation. Rav Nachman thus accepts the first part of Rav Huna's position — *hamazakeh l'ubar lo kanah* — while rejecting the second. *Liksheteiled*, he holds, works.

### Rav Sheshet Permits

Rav Sheshet goes further still: *echad zeh ve'echad zeh kanah* — both work. A fetus can take possession even while still a fetus, and certainly when born. This is the most expansive position, and it rejects Rav Huna's foundational premise entirely.

It is worth pausing to appreciate why Rav Sheshet's position has some intuitive force. The *Gemara* earlier analogized the *ubar* problem to Rav Meir's principle that one can transfer something not yet in existence. But one might actually argue that the fetus is in a better position than Rav Meir's case, not a worse one. When transferring fruit that has not yet grown, there is no object whatsoever to point to. When a woman is already pregnant, the fetus is at least partially present in the world. So Rav Sheshet's view — that *mezakeh l'ubar kanah* — is quite coherent, at least within the framework of Rav Meir, and perhaps even more defensible.

---

## Ger Case Study

### Ger Dies & Looting

Rav Sheshet now provides his source. *Detanya*: a *ger* — a convert from a non-Jewish background — dies. Because a *ger* who has converted carries no halachic family relationships with his biological relatives, he has no natural heirs unless he sired children after converting. If he dies without such children, his estate becomes *hefker* — ownerless — available to whoever takes possession first. And so, the Baraita relates, Israelites swooped in and looted his property — *vizbezu Yisrael nechasav* — the verb carrying the full weight of wholesale plunder.

Then they heard: *she-yesh lo ben* — he actually has a son, a biological son born after his conversion. Or — since a wife does not inherit her husband even in the case of a *ger* — perhaps his wife was pregnant: *o she-hayetah ishto me'uberet*. The relevance of the wife's pregnancy is that if she gives birth to a viable child, that child is an heir and the estate is not *hefker*. Upon hearing this, the Baraita rules *chayavim lehachzir* — they are obligated to return everything. The looting must be undone; the estate must be restored and held for the potential heir.

### Return & Miscarriage

They restore everything. And then — *ve'achar kach shamu she-met beno o she-hipilah ishto* — they subsequently hear that the son died, or that the wife miscarried. So the sequence, reconstructed, runs as follows: the *ger* dies; the Israelites loot his property; they hear there is a son or a pregnant wife; they return everything; they then hear the son died or the wife miscarried.

In that case, the Baraita rules: *chayavin haleh shehechazir karka vechazar vehechezik basheniyah kanah* — whoever returned the property and then re-took possession in this second round has acquired it. *Uvarishonah lo kanah* — but the original taking of possession was not valid.

### Why First Kinyan Fails

This Baraita is what Rav Sheshet uses as his proof. The striking feature is the case of the pregnant wife. If the *ubar* cannot take possession of anything — cannot even inherit — then from the moment the *ger* died, the estate was pure *hefker*. There was no heir. Why, then, did the first round of possession-taking not work? If the fetus was never going to be a valid heir (either because it died or because a fetus cannot inherit), then the property was already ownerless at that first moment, and whoever grabbed it first should have acquired it legitimately.

The fact that the first *chazaka* did not work, and a second *chazaka* was required after the miscarriage, implies that during the pregnancy the fetus did have some proprietary claim over the estate. This, Rav Sheshet argues, demonstrates that *mezakeh l'ubar kanah* — a fetus can take possession.

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye responds: *yerushah me'eleha shani* — natural inheritance operates by its own rules and is categorically different. A fetus may be able to inherit automatically through the operation of halachic succession, without any active acquisition being performed on its behalf. That natural capacity tells us nothing about whether one can affirmatively *mezakeh* — actively transfer — property to a fetus.
