The Baraita therefore provides no proof for Rav Sheshet's expansive position.

### Rava's Rifyon Answer

Rava takes a different approach. He does not concede that a fetus can inherit at all. Rather, he explains the Baraita's ruling differently: *shani hasam derafui mirafya biyadei me'ikara* — the situation there is different because even the original act of taking possession was weak, *rifyon*, from the outset.

What does this mean? At the moment the Israelites first grabbed the property, they had already heard — or at a minimum, had reason to suspect — that the wife was pregnant. Even if the fetus cannot technically inherit and the estate was therefore technically *hefker*, the subjective state of the person taking possession was not one of complete certainty. He knew, or strongly suspected, that there was a possibility he would have to give it back. That awareness — that background doubt — undermined the completeness of his *da'at*, his intent, at the moment of the *chazaka*. A *kinyan* requires full and settled intent; a *kinyan* performed while the person already anticipates having to relinquish the property is weakened, *rifyon*, from the start.

This distinction between the two approaches — Abaye's and Rava's — is significant. For Abaye, the *ubar* actually owns the property during gestation through the mechanism of natural inheritance; the first *chazaka* failed because the property was not truly *hefker*. For Rava, the *ubar* owns nothing; the first *chazaka* failed because the possessor's own subjective intent was incomplete.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Nafka Mina Scenario

The *Gemara* probes the practical difference between Abaye and Rava with a *nafka mina* scenario: *deshama bo shemet velo met ve'achar kach met* — a person heard that the son (or that the fetus) had died; in fact it had not died at that point; and only subsequently did it actually die.

In this scenario, someone goes to take possession of the *ger*'s estate. At the moment he takes possession, he has heard — and sincerely believes — that the heir is dead. He is not proceeding with any background awareness that he might have to give the property back. His *da'at* is full and confident. But as a matter of objective fact, at that moment, the heir had not yet died. Only afterward did the heir die.

### Abaye: Subjective

According to Abaye, the fetus actually did own the property at the time of the first *chazaka*. The possessor's sincere but mistaken belief that the heir was dead does not change the objective reality that the property had an owner. His confident *da'at* is irrelevant — the property was not *hefker* at that moment, so his act of possession did not acquire anything. Only once the heir actually died did the property become *hefker*, and a new *chazaka* would be required to acquire it at that point.

### Rava: Objective

According to Rava, the problem with the original *chazaka* was never that the fetus owned the property — Rava holds the fetus cannot inherit at all. The problem was the possessor's subjective uncertainty. But in this *nafka mina* case, his subjective mindset was one of complete certainty: he had heard and believed the heir was dead. There was no *rifyon* — no weakening of his intent. He proceeded with total confidence. Rava would therefore say this *chazaka* worked. The property was genuinely *hefker*, he had complete *da'at*, and the acquisition was valid, even though his belief about what had happened to the heir was factually incorrect. His sincere but erroneous certainty was sufficient.

The two positions thus hinge on whether the impediment to *kinyan* is objective — the fetus actually holds the property and so it is not truly *hefker* (Abaye) — or subjective — the possessor's own internal state of doubt or certainty (Rava). In the *nafka mina* scenario where the person had mistaken but sincere confidence, Abaye says the *kinyan* fails (objectively, property was not *hefker*), while Rava says it succeeds (subjectively, his *da'at* was complete).

---

## Fetus Inheritance

### Mishna: One Day Old

The *Gemara* now turns to a famous *Mishna* in *Niddah* that catalogs the halachic statuses of children at various ages. The *Mishna* states: *tinok ben yom echad nochal u'manchil* — a one-day-old infant can inherit and can bequeath. *Ben yom echad in, ubaro lo* — only a one-day-old infant qualifies; a fetus does not.

This *Mishna* appears to prove once again that a fetus cannot inherit, seemingly contradicting Rav Sheshet's position. Rav Sheshet, recall, is the one who holds not only that a fetus can take possession when directly transferred property, but that a fetus can inherit through natural succession as well.

### Why It Matters

Before engaging with whether a fetus inherits, the *Gemara* pauses to ask why it matters that the *Mishna* says a one-day-old infant inherits and bequeaths. After all, if a one-day-old infant inherits from his father and then dies, his estate passes to his brothers. But had he never been born, the father's property would have gone directly to those same brothers. Either way, the brothers receive the property — so what is the practical significance of this rule?

### Rav Sheshet's Read

Rav Sheshet answers: the *Mishna* is not speaking about the infant inheriting from his father. It is speaking about *nochal b'nichsei ha'em l'hanchil l'achin min ha'av* — the infant inheriting from his mother, so as to then bequeath to his paternal brothers.

Consider the following scenario: the mother has property of her own. She dies. If the infant is alive at the time of her death, the property passes to him as her son. When he then dies, it passes to his brothers on his father's side — the paternal brothers. But if the infant had not been halachically capable of inheriting at that moment, the mother's property would pass to her own family — her father, her brothers — and would never reach the paternal brothers at all. The *Mishna*'s ruling that *nochal u'manchil* therefore has real consequences: it determines whether property crosses from the mother's family line to the father's family line through the child.

Now, the *Mishna* specifies one day old, not a fetus. Rav Sheshet explains: he would have been perfectly willing to say that a fetus can inherit, but the scenario envisioned by the *Mishna* involves the mother dying. If the mother died, a fetus that was in her womb at the time cannot inherit from her, because the fetus does not survive the mother's natural death — *d'hu mayis b'reisha*, the fetus dies first.

### Fetus Dies First

And since the fetus dies before the mother in such a case, we cannot apply the principle of having the fetus inherit and then bequeath, because *ein haben yoresh et imo b'kever l'hanchil l'achin min ha'av* — a son does not inherit from his mother while in the grave in order to bequeath to his paternal brothers. Once the fetus has died first, and then the mother dies, we do not fictionally pass the estate through the already-dead fetus to his paternal heirs. The estate goes instead to the mother's own heirs. Therefore the *Mishna* correctly limits the ruling to a *ben yom echad*, a live-born infant, not because a fetus categorically cannot inherit, but because in this specific scenario a fetus would have already died when the mother did.

The *Gemara* then challenges this: is it really true that the fetus always dies first? The *Gemara* cites an incident where, after a woman died, the fetus was observed quivering in the womb three times. Mar bar Rav Ashi dismisses this as analogous to the tail of a lizard that continues to twitch after being severed — the movements are post-mortem reflexes, not signs of life.

Tosafot, however, points out that this cannot be categorically correct. Other Talmudic sources make clear that a fetus can survive the mother's death in certain circumstances — specifically when the mother suffers a violent, sudden death, as opposed to a slow natural death. In a slow natural dying process, the fetus's vitality ebbs along with the mother's and it dies first. But in the case of sudden trauma — an accident or a violent act — the fetus can survive. Tosafot additionally notes a second scenario: if the child was already *ne'ekar*, already in the process of being born such that it had begun to detach from the mother biologically, it may survive even if the mother does not, since at that point its life is no longer fully dependent on hers.

This does leave the *Mishna* somewhat imprecise, since there are cases where a fetus could in theory inherit from a dying mother — and Tosafot acknowledges this without providing a fully resolved answer.

---

## Chelek Bechora

### Initial Question

Having established the relevance of the *Mishna*'s ruling in the context of inheriting from the mother, the *Gemara* now raises a further question. Even setting aside the mother-to-paternal-brothers scenario offered by Rav Sheshet, why tell us that the one-day-old infant inherits and bequeaths at all? If the infant inherits from his father, and then when he dies his estate passes to his brothers, the brothers ultimately get what they would have gotten anyway had the infant never existed. What halachic difference does it make that the property passed through the infant?

### Double Portion Math

Mar bereih deRav Yosef in the name of Rava provides the answer: *lomar shemema'et b'chelek bechorah* — the infant's existence and legal status as an heir at the moment of the father's death affects the calculation of the *bechor*'s double portion.

The *bechor* — the firstborn son — is entitled to a double share of the estate. The size of that double share is calculated by treating the *bechor* as receiving two ordinary shares. The calculation thus depends on how many heirs there are in total: the more heirs, the smaller each ordinary share, and therefore the smaller the *bechor*'s double portion as well.

If the infant is recognized as an heir at the moment of the father's death, he increases the number of heirs by one. This means the estate is divided into more units, each unit is smaller, and the *bechor*'s double portion — pegged to the size of two such units — is correspondingly reduced.

### Math Example

To illustrate: suppose there are four units of property and, at the father's death, three sons are already born. The *bechor* receives two shares; each of the other two receives one. Under this calculation, each ordinary share is one unit, and the *bechor* takes two units.

Now suppose the father also had a fourth son who was born after the father's death — or who was a fetus at the time of death. If this fourth child is counted among the heirs for purposes of calculating the *bechor*'s double portion, the estate would be divided into five ordinary shares (since the *bechor* takes two and the remaining three brothers each take one, for five total). Each ordinary share would then be four-fifths of a unit, and the *bechor*'s double portion would be four-fifths of a unit as well — smaller than the full unit he would have received with only three heirs.

The infant's existence at the moment of death thus directly diminishes the *bechor*'s portion, even though the infant's own share will eventually be redistributed to the brothers when he dies.

### Only Born Count

However — and this is Rava's ruling — only children already born at the time of the father's death factor into this calculation. *Aval ubar lo*: a fetus does not diminish the *bechor*'s double portion, even if the fetus will go on to inherit. The reason is derived from the verse *yaldu lo banim* — the Torah's language concerning the *bechor*'s calculation refers to children who have been born, not to fetuses.

### Born After Father

The same principle governs whether a *bechor* himself receives a double portion. *Mar bereih deRav Yosef mishmeih deRava*: *bechor shenolad le'achar mitat ha'av eino notel pi shnayim* — a firstborn son born after the father's death does not receive the double portion of the *bechor*. This scenario can arise, for instance, if the father had multiple wives and died leaving behind pregnant wives, and the firstborn of one wife is born after the father's death. Despite being the *bechor* by order of birth, he does not receive the double portion.

The reason: *yakir amar Rachmana* — the Torah says the father must "recognize" the firstborn, which requires the *bechor* to already be born and recognizable at the time of the father's death. As the *Rashbam* clarifies, this does not mean the father must have literally laid eyes on the child — a father who was in a distant country and died without ever meeting his son certainly does not forfeit his son's status as *bechor*. What is required is that the child be born, and thus capable of being recognized, even if only in principle.

---

## Final Rulings

### Rule Like Rava

The *Gemara* now delivers the decisive rulings. *Vehilcheta kechol hanei shema'ateta de'amar Mar bereih deRav Yosef mishmeih deRava* — we rule in accordance with all the positions stated by Mar bereih deRav Yosef in the name of Rava. This means: to calculate the *bechor*'s double portion, we count only children already born at the time of the father's death; and a *bechor* himself must be born before the father's death in order to receive the double portion.

### Rav Yochanan Rule

With respect to the core question of *mezakeh l'ubar*, the *Gemara* records: *Amar Rav Yitzchak amar Rav Yochanan: hamezakeh l'ubar lo kanah* — actively transferring property to a fetus does not work. This is the operative halachic ruling.

### Own Child Exception

However, Tosafot notes that the *Gemara* appears to carve out an exception for one's own child. *Vehilcheta dehamezakeh l'ubar lo kanah* — the ruling stands as a general matter; but in the case of our *Mishna*, where a father is gifting property to his own unborn son or daughter, *hava da'ateh de'adam krova etzel beno* — a person's *da'at* is uniquely close when it comes to his own child. Because the father feels such powerful subjective connection and intent toward his own unborn child, the mechanism of transfer may function even though it ordinarily would not. The subjective barrier that defeats *mezakeh l'ubar* in the general case is overcome by the intensity of paternal intent.

This is admittedly a striking result. It might seem that if the fetus is not a legal person capable of taking possession, the sincerity of the giver's intent cannot conjure that capacity into existence. Yet the *Gemara* appears to locate at least part of the problem of *mezakeh l'ubar* in the giver's subjective orientation — in how fully and genuinely the giver relates to the fetus as a recipient — rather than purely in an objective determination about the fetus's legal status. When that subjective barrier is removed by the closeness of the father-child bond, the *kinyan* can take effect.

### Shmuel's Minority

Finally, the *Gemara* records that Shmuel had at one point sought to publicize the opposite ruling. He told Rav Chanana bar Bagta'a — the epithet apparently referring to Baghdad — *puk aytei li bei asara*: go and gather ten people for me, so that I may declare before them publicly that *hamezakeh l'ubar kanah*, that transferring to a fetus works. Shmuel wanted to issue this as a practical ruling, not merely a theoretical position.

But the *Gemara* closes with the definitive word: *vehilchata hamezakeh l'ubar lo kanah* — the halacha is that it does not work. Shmuel's view does not prevail. The exceptions remain: possibly *yerusha haba'ah me'eleha*, natural inheritance, where Rav Yosef's formulation in the name of Rava leaves open that an *ubar* may inherit; and the case of one's own child, where paternal *da'at* appears to be a sufficient foundation for the transfer. But as a general operative rule, *mezakeh l'ubar lo kanah*.

# Bava Batra 143

## Zachin Le'ubar

### Intro & Fetus Rules

The daf opens by revisiting the conclusion of the previous sugya: *v'hilchasa hamizakeh le'ubar lo kanah* — one cannot actively transfer property to a fetus. Two subsidiary questions had been left hovering at the edges of that ruling. First, can a fetus inherit through the ordinary mechanism of *yerushah*? The thrust of the sugya, as understood by both the Rashbam and Tosafos, is that yes, a fetus can inherit. Second, what if the transfer is structured to take effect only at birth — can that work? That question was the subject of a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman and was not cleanly resolved. With those threads still open, the Gemara now proceeds to a new case.

### Future Children Gift

The Gemara introduces its case with the words *hahu d'amar lidvasaihu* — a certain man who said to his wife. This man had children from a first marriage and was now entering a second marriage. By way of *kinyan* — or possibly as a *matnas sh'chiv mei'ra* — he declared: *nechasai livni dehavu li minach*, all of my property should go to the children I will have from you. The complication is that those children do not yet exist; she is not even pregnant. We are not dealing with a *ubar* in the narrow sense — someone already conceived — but with children not yet conceived at all. The Rashbam is explicit that before there is even a *ubar*, everyone agrees that no transfer can take effect. So there is no question that those future children acquire nothing.

### Son's Equal Portion

Upon hearing of this arrangement, the older son from the first marriage came forward and protested: *hahu gavra mai tavei alei* — what will become of me? Am I to be disinherited in favor of half-brothers who do not yet exist? The father responded: *zil kani kechad mibra* — go perform a *kinyan* and you shall receive a portion equal to what each of those future children will receive. A *kinyan* was performed — presumably a *kinyan sudar* — and the son received, at least nominally, an equal stake in the estate alongside the future children.

This raises the central question of the passage. Those future children, *hanach vadai lo kanu* — they certainly acquired nothing, as there was no *ubar* to acquire. But what of the older son, *l'talya*, this young man who did perform a valid *kinyan*? *Hai ishtachach lei bemakom b'neya o la ishtachach lei bemakom b'neya* — does he have a portion alongside those children or not?

To make the stakes concrete: suppose the father dies leaving four hundred dollars and three sons from the second wife. Had the father's original arrangement been effective, each son would have received one hundred dollars, and the older son, having been given an equal portion, would also have received one hundred dollars. But since the future children's acquisition failed, does the older son's *kinyan* still entitle him to his one hundred dollars — after which the remaining three hundred are divided among the three inheriting sons — or does his *kinyan* collapse entirely because it was keyed to a portion that no one ever received?

## Abin vs. Abbahu

The Gemara presents this as a debate of three against three. Rabbi Abin, Rabbi Meisha, and Rabbi Yirmiyah hold that the older son does retain his portion: *hai chulka d'talya bemakom b'neya*. His *kinyan* stands even though the future children acquired nothing. Opposed to them, Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha hold that he does not: *lai chulka d'talya bemakom b'neya*. His *kinyan* fails along with the failed acquisition of the others.

Rabbi Abbahu then turns to Rabbi Yirmiyah and asks, somewhat playfully, *hilcheta kevatanu hilcheta kevataichu* — is the ruling like us or like you? He immediately supplies his own answer: *pshita de-hilcheta kevatanu* — it is obvious the ruling follows us. Why? *De-kashishna minaichu* — we are older than you. He adds, pointedly, *velav hilcheta kevataichu de-dardakei atun* — it is certainly not like you, you are merely children.

## Reasoning > Age

Rabbi Yirmiyah's response is direct and memorable: *midi bekashishuta talya milta? Beta'ama talya milta* — is it truly about age? It is about who has the more compelling reason. This phrase — that halakhic authority flows from the force of reasoning rather than from seniority — resonates beyond this particular dispute. But then Rabbi Yirmiyah goes further. He tells Rabbi Abbahu: *zil legabei Rabbi Avin, de'afreshah nihaleih, vekarkash beih reisheih bei midrasha* — go to Rabbi Avin; I explained my reasoning to him and he nodded his head in concession in the *beis medrash*.

This requires a moment of attention, because an important detail had initially been easy to miss. Rabbi Avin is not a neutral party — he belongs to the camp of Rabbi Abbahu, that is, he holds that the older son does *not* receive a portion. Rabbi Yirmiyah is saying that even a member of the opposing camp, a senior authority who had originally held the opposite view, conceded when confronted with the stronger argument. This dramatically reinforces his point: it is not age or camp affiliation that determines the *halachah* — it is the reasoning. And so Rabbi Yirmiyah went to Rabbi Avin, and Rabbi Avin, *amar lei ilu amar lei*, confirmed his concession and explained why he had changed his position.

## You & Donkey Principle

Rabbi Avin's explanation, which Rabbi Yirmiyah now presents, is built around the principle of *at vachamor* — you and a donkey. The logic works as follows: the father did not say to the older son, "I give you one hundred dollars." He said, "take a portion equal to what the other children receive." The gift was not denominated independently; it was defined entirely in relation to what those future children would get. And what did they get? Nothing. Therefore the older son receives a portion equal to nothing, which is nothing.

Rabbi Avin frames this as a case of *kni kachamor* — take possession as a donkey would. If someone says to another person, "acquire this just as a donkey would acquire it," the acquisition fails, because a donkey cannot perform a *kinyan*. The older son's *kinyan* was structurally equivalent: its content was defined as what the future children acquired, and since they acquired nothing, his *kinyan* has no content.

This then transitions into a broader discussion of the *at vachamor* principle itself — what happens when a transfer is directed jointly to a person and an entity incapable of acquiring? Three Amoraic positions are presented. *Rav Nachman amar kanah mechtza*: since he said "to you and to your donkey," the person gets half — the human half works even if the donkey's half does not. *Rav Hamnuna amar lo amar klum*: the transfer was conceived as a unit; since one element of the unit cannot acquire, the whole thing fails. *Rav Sheshet amar kanah hakol*: the person acquires everything, because it is obvious that when the donkey cannot receive its share, the intent of the full gift falls on the person alone.

It is worth noting that Rav Sheshet appears here, as elsewhere in this sugya, as the voice most willing to uphold acquisitions: he had previously favored the position that an *ubar* is *koneh*, and here he says *kanah hakol*, the remaining human party acquires the whole. The Rashbam explains Rav Sheshet's position psychologically — the donor obviously intended to give it all to the human recipient — though one might also frame it structurally: even if the transfer was conceived as a joint unit, since only one member of the corporate entity is left standing, that member acquires the full interest.

## At Vachamor Cases

### The Terumah Parallel

The Gemara now brings the case of *terumah* from a spoiled gourd to test the limits of the *at vachamor* principle. Rabbi Yosei teaches: *ein lacha mar bekishut ela penimi shebo* — the only part of a certain type of gourd that is truly bitter and inedible is its inner portion; the outer portion remains edible. In the scenario presented (following Tosafos's reading based on the Yerushalmi): one had fifty such gourds and separated one gourd as *terumah*. Upon opening it, the inner portion is found to be sour and spoiled. Rabbi Yosei rules that one need only add a small amount from another gourd to supplement the outer portion — since the outer part is still edible, the bulk of the *terumah* stands.

The Gemara immediately asks: but is this not a case of *at vachamor*? When one set aside this gourd as *terumah* for the entire batch, the intent was that the whole gourd — inner and outer portions together — should function as a unit of *terumah*. Since the inner part is inedible and thus cannot properly serve as *terumah*, should not the whole designation collapse? If *at vachamor* means nothing works, then even the outer portion should not be valid *terumah*.

The Gemara answers: *shani hatam demide'oraisa terumah ma'alyasa hi* — the inner portion is in fact valid *terumah* by Torah law. How so? The Gemara cites Rabbi Ila's derivation: *minayin latoram min hara al hayafa sheterumaso terumah* — we know that one who separates from the inferior produce on behalf of the superior that the *terumah* is still *terumah*. The verse says: *velo sisu alav cheit beharimchem et chelbo mimenu* — you shall not bear sin by taking the choice portion from it. The implication is that if one takes the inferior rather than the choice, one does bear sin — meaning the designation is legally effective, even if improper. If the designation were entirely null, there would be no sin. So even the inner bitter portion is technically valid *terumah de'oraita*, though we require one to supplement it. The *at vachamor* problem therefore does not arise, because there is no element that fails to qualify — both portions are *terumah*, and we only require adding a supplement as a practical matter.

### The Five Women Case

The Gemara proceeds to a far more striking case. *Ma'aseh bechamesh nashim* — a story of five women, *uvehen shtei achayos* — among them two sisters. A man entered the shared orchard of these five women, picked a basket of figs, and declared: *harei kulchem mekudashos li bekalkalah zo* — all five of you are hereby betrothed to me with this basket. One of the women accepted on behalf of all. The further complication: the figs were *shevi'is* produce, sabbatical-year fruit.

The sages ruled: *ein ha'achayos mekudashos* — the sisters are not betrothed, but the three unrelated women are.

Several principles are at work simultaneously. First, the *shevi'is* produce: one might have thought that *kedushas shevi'is* restricts such fruit from being used as *kiddushin* money, since the produce carries sanctity that limits its use. The Gemara establishes from this case that *shevi'is* produce can in fact be used for *kiddushin*. Second, the fact that he picked fruit from their own trees: this would ordinarily be theft, and stolen property cannot effect *kiddushin*. The reason it is not theft here is that *shevi'is* produce does not truly belong to the owners in the usual sense — anyone may take it. So we learn simultaneously that stolen property does not work for *kiddushin* and that *shevi'is* produce does.

Third, and most directly relevant to the *at vachamor* discussion: why is neither sister betrothed, even as an unknown one of the two? The answer lies in the principle of *kiddushin she'einah mesurah levi'ah* — a betrothal that can never be consummated halachically is not a valid *kiddushin*. For each sister, there is no way to identify which one he might be married to. If he were to consummate the marriage, he might be doing so with the sister he is not married to, thereby violating the Torah prohibition against relations with a wife's sister, an *issur kares*. Since neither sister's *kiddushin* could ever be permissibly consummated, *kiddushin she'einah mesurah levi'ah* applies to both, and neither is betrothed.

The Gemara then asks: but this man attempted to betroth all five simultaneously — should this not be *at vachamor*? Since the sisters cannot be betrothed, should not the entire act collapse, leaving none of the five women betrothed? The Gemara's answer is that the case demonstrates the opposite: the *at vachamor* principle does not necessarily void the remainder. The three unrelated women *are* betrothed. The failure of the betrothal for the two sisters does not contaminate the valid *kiddushin* of the other three.

This constitutes a significant proof that *at vachamor* does work — at minimum, it works for the elements of a joint transaction that are themselves capable of taking effect. Whether the remainder receives half (Rav Nachman), nothing (Rav Hamnuna), or everything (Rav Sheshet) may remain debated, but the five-women case establishes that at least partial effectiveness is real.

The response to this proof is remarkable: *hainu d'chazai Rav Huna bar Avia b'chalma* — that is why I saw Rav Avia in my dream last night. The speaker now understands that the dream was a message that Rav Avia had posed a challenge to the position that *at vachamor* never works. Dreams aside, the legal answer is then supplied: *lav mi oukimna d'amar hareuyos mikem l'via yiskadeshu li* — no, the Gemara in Kiddushin explains that the man said something more qualified than it appears. He said: those of you for whom it is possible to consummate the marriage should be betrothed to me. He explicitly conditioned the *kiddushin* on its being consummable, which is why neither sister is included. According to Shmuel, who maintains that *kiddushin she'einah mesurah levi'ah* is valid *kiddushin*, two sisters betrothed simultaneously would result in one of them being validly betrothed — we simply would not know which. The reason the *mishnah* rules otherwise is that the man's phrasing explicitly excluded women for whom consummation would be impossible. And once one recognizes that the man was *not* making a single indivisible five-way proposal but rather qualifying it from the outset, the *at vachamor* problem dissolves — he was never saying "all five as one unit," but rather "whichever of you qualifies." The proof for *at vachamor* working partially thus remains intact on the surface, even if the *mishnah* is ultimately explained otherwise.

## Wife & Children Gift

A new case is introduced: *hahu d'amar la l'devithu, nechasai lichi u'l'vnaich* — a man on his deathbed who said to his wife, "my property is to you and to my sons." The question immediately arises: how much does the wife receive? Does the formulation "you and my sons" mean she receives fifty percent while the sons divide the other fifty percent among themselves? Or does it mean she is included as equal to one son, receiving whatever each individual son would receive?

## Wife Share Dispute

Rav Yosef rules: *kansa palga* — she acquires half. He derives this from the verse governing the distribution of the *lechem hapanim*, the showbread: *vehaitah le-Aharon u-le-vanav*, and Rabbi, the editor of the Mishnah, rules that Aharon receives half and his sons — many kohanim — receive the other half collectively. When one says "A and B," even if B is a large group, the formulation creates two equal halves.

Abaye objects. *Bishlama hatam, Aharon bar chaluka hu* — in that case it makes sense: even had the Torah not specified Aharon's share, he would have received some portion of the bread as a *kohen*. By singling him out explicitly, the Torah is granting him additional weight — specifically, half. *Ishah lav bat yerushah hi* — a wife, however, does not ordinarily inherit at all. Since she has no baseline entitlement, when the husband says "you and my sons," the most natural reading is simply that he is including her in something she would otherwise have been excluded from. *Dayo*, it is sufficient, says Abaye, to read this as granting her an equal share to one son — *shetitnol ke-echad min ha-banim*. She has been brought into the inheritance, but not elevated to the position of an equal partner with all the sons as a collective.

The Gemara challenges Abaye's position with actual precedent: *veha uvda hava bi-Nahardea, ve-adbeih Shmuel palga* — there was a case of this nature in Nehardea and Shmuel awarded the wife half. *Vahava uvda bi-Tverya, ve-adbeih Rabbi Yochanan palga* — there was a parallel case in Tiberias and Rabbi Yochanan also awarded her half. These are not merely theoretical positions; leading Amoraim actually ruled in practice that the wife receives fifty percent.

An additional source is brought: the case of a royal levy imposed on *avulei* and *istrugei* — the ultra-wealthy and the officer class — for the cost of a crown. Rabbi ruled that the *avulei* pay half and the *istrugei* pay half. When a decree says "A and B," it creates two equal halves. The Gemara, however, pushes back on the relevance of this comparison: *hatam me-ikara ki havo katvei a-avulei havo katvei* — originally, the obligation had been written solely upon the ultra-wealthy; the officers were merely assisting voluntarily. When the king discovered this and formalized both groups' obligations, the explicit singling out of the officers — who were previously voluntary participants — elevated them to equal status, just as Rabbi Abbahu's group argued about Aharon. But in the wife-and-sons case, the wife had no prior connection to the inheritance at all. Abaye's argument thus survives the analogy.

The Gemara also tests the question through the case of a *mincha* vow of a hundred *isaron* to be brought in two vessels. The rule is that no single vessel may hold more than sixty *isaron*, because the *bila* — the mixing of flour with oil — cannot be performed effectively beyond that volume. So one brings sixty in one vessel and forty in the other. If "A and B" always means fifty-fifty, why does the *halacha* not require — or at least allow *lechatchila* — an equal split of fifty and fifty? The Gemara replies: this is not a comparable case. When someone vowed a hundred *isaron* in two vessels, his underlying intent was always a single large *korban*; the two-vessel arrangement was only a concession to halachic necessity. Therefore, one fills the first vessel to its maximum capacity — sixty — and places only the overage in the second. The structure of the vow was never "two equal halves"; it was "one unit, divided only as required."

The *hilcheta* is then stated: *veHilcheta kevatei d'Rav Yosef* — the ruling follows Rav Yosef. When a man says "to you and to my sons," the wife receives half. The discussion of Shmuel's position on *kiddushin she'einah mesurah levi'ah* is also woven through this section, illustrating how the qualification of a transaction's terms can determine whether it operates as a single indivisible unit or as a series of independent designations.

## Ambiguous Designations

### Silk to the House

The Gemara turns to a case where a man sent a consignment of silk — *piska d'shira'i* — to his household. No explicit instructions accompanied it. Rav Ami rules: *hara'uyim l'vanim l'vanim, hara'uyim l'vanos l'vanos* — whatever is suitable for the sons goes to the sons, whatever is suitable for the daughters goes to the daughters. The difficulty the Rashbam notes is that this works neatly only if the silk was already fashioned into garments; if it is raw bolts of fabric, it is not obvious how one determines what is "suitable" for which child.

The Gemara then introduces a limiting principle: *v'lo amran ela d'leis lei kalla* — this ruling applies only when the man has no daughter-in-law. If he does have a daughter-in-law, *l'kallateih shadar* — we presume he was sending it to her. However, *v'ei b'noseih lo nesivan* — if his own daughters are not yet married, he would not bypass his unmarried daughters to send silk to a daughter-in-law, since providing daughters with attractive clothing serves the pressing concern of enabling them to marry.

## Singular 'Sons'

A more complex question follows. A man declared: *nechasai l'vanai* — my property should go to my sons. He had one son and one daughter. *Mi kari inish l'v'ra banai* — would a person refer to a single son as "my sons"? And if the word is read as genuinely plural, might it be intended to include the daughter, treating *banim* as "children" rather than strictly "sons"?

One reason the man might have used this formulation even with a single son in mind is *l'saluki barta me'ishur nechasai* — to exclude his daughter from the *ishur nechasim*, the provision in the *kesubah* entitling daughters to one-tenth of the estate. By transferring the property as a gift rather than allowing it to pass by ordinary inheritance, he can circumvent *tnai kesubah* obligations — gifts fall outside the estate from which those obligations are calculated. Tosafos offers a related but distinct explanation.

Abaye attempts to resolve the question from a biblical source: *u-vnei Dan Chushim* — "the sons of Dan were Chushim." Since *Chushim* appears to be a single individual's name, and yet the verse uses the plural *bnei*, we see that one can use the plural "sons" when referring to a single son. Rava objects: perhaps *d'vei Chizkiya* taught that this verse means something altogether different — that the children of Dan were as numerous as reeds (*chushim shel kanei*), making Chushim a description rather than a proper name. Rava then offers a cleaner prooftext: *u-vnei Pallu Eliav* — the sons of Pallu were Eliav — where Eliav is clearly a single person. Rav Yosef adds: *u-vnei Esan Azarya* — similarly. The conclusion is that one does use the word *banim* in reference to a single son.

The consequence is poignant: since *banim* can refer to a single son, and since Hebrew lacks a gender-neutral word for "children" that would naturally distinguish sons from daughters — the word *banim* carries a grammatical male-gender default — the declaration *nechasai l'vanai* is interpreted as referring to sons. Even if there is only a single son, the property goes to him, and the daughter is excluded. The practical effect, depending on how one reads the relationship between a gift and *tnai kesubah* obligations, may be that the daughter loses even the tenth-of-the-estate entitlement.

## Grandson Question

The final question in this series: a man declared *nechasai livnai*, and he had a son and a grandson. *Kare inshi l'var bra bra o lo* — does ordinary usage extend the word "son" to include a grandson?

*Rav Chaviva amar: kare inshi l'var bra bra* — yes, it is common usage to call a grandson a son. *Mar bar Rav Ashi amar: lo kare inshi l'var bra bra* — no, it is not common usage. A *braita* supports Mar bar Rav Ashi: *ha-mudar hana'ah m'banim, mutar bivnei banim* — one who is forbidden to derive benefit from "sons" is permitted to derive benefit from grandchildren. This establishes that in ordinary halakhic usage, *banim* does not include *bnei banim*.

The Rashbam notes, however, that this does not mean grandchildren are never treated as children for halakhic purposes — *aval le-inyan piryah ve-rivyah chashivei k'vanim*, for the obligations of *piryah ve-rivyah* they may count, and in contexts like *yibum*, even grandchildren or great-grandchildren can satisfy the requirement of having offspring. But when someone uses the word *banim* in an act of transfer or declaration, the ordinary linguistic meaning controls, and grandchildren are not included. Thus the grandson receives nothing from the declaration *nechasai livnai*, while the single son receives everything.

## Estate Improvements

A new *mishnah* opens: *hiniach banim gedolim u-ketanim* — a man died and left behind both older and younger sons. *Ve-hishpichu gedolim et ha-nechasim* — the older sons proceeded to make capital improvements to the undivided estate: planting, tending, harvesting.

*Hishpichu la-emtza* — those improvements are divided equally among all the heirs. This might seem counterintuitive. If one partner improves jointly-held property without prior agreement, the other partners ordinarily owe at least compensation for expenses. Why should the older sons simply absorb all the cost and labor while the younger sons share equally in the benefit?

Tosafos explains: in an ordinary partnership, one does not implicitly waive the right to reimbursement for expenses. But in the context of a shared inherited estate — where the heirs are in a family relationship and the estate has not yet been formally divided — a person who goes ahead and works the land without any declaration is presumed to be doing so on behalf of the estate as a whole. Out-of-pocket expenses could perhaps be recouped by submitting receipts, but labor and effort are not separately compensable when the person never announced any intent to profit individually.

*Ve-im amru re'u mah she-hiniach abba, harei anu osim ve-ochlim* — but if the older sons stood up and declared: look at what our father left; we intend to work it and to keep what we earn — *hishpichu le-atzmam*, they keep the improvement for themselves. Their declaration, met with silence from the younger sons or their representatives, functions as consent to a separate arrangement. The silence of those who could have objected is treated as acquiescence.

The *mishnah* adds a parallel: *ve-chen ha-isha she-hishpichah et ha-nechasim hishpichah la-emtza* — the same rule applies to a woman who was somehow a co-heir and made improvements without any declaration; the improvement is shared. *Im amrah re'u mah she-hiniach li ba'ali, harei ani osah ve-ochelet* — if she declared her intent to work it and keep the benefit, *hishpichah le-atzmah*, she retains it for herself. Notably, the *gemara* will need to explain how a woman comes to be in the position of co-heir at all, a question taken up in the continuation.

---

# Bava Batra 144

## Brothers' Estate Investm…

### Minors & Estate Protecti…

The daf opens by continuing the discussion begun at the bottom of 143b concerning an estate left to both older and younger children. Tosafot reads the scenario as one in which the younger children are *ketanim* — minors — and this distinction carries significant halachic weight throughout the sugya.

The basic rule established by the *mishnah* is that if the older brothers invest estate funds, plant fields, or otherwise work the property without making any explicit declaration, we assume they are acting on behalf of the entire estate — even though ordinarily, if one *shutaf* were to work the land of another, he would be entitled to compensation for his efforts. Here, because they are brothers, the default assumption is that everything goes *l'emtza*, to the common estate.

If, however, the older brothers make a declaration — stating, as the Rashbam frames it, that they are acting for their own benefit and are prepared to divide if the others are ready — then whatever appreciation they generate accrues to themselves alone. The question immediately arises: why should such a declaration entitle them to profit from the portion of the estate that belongs to their younger brothers? Tosafot answers that the premise is precisely that the others are *ketanim*, minors who are incapable of investing the money themselves. The older brothers can therefore say: we are not depriving you of anything — without our intervention, your share would simply lie idle. Since the minors have no independent capacity to generate any return, they are not genuinely harmed when the older brothers declare and retain the profit.

Tosafot further cites a *Tosefta* requiring that this declaration be made before a *beit din*. The reason, Tosafot suggests, is that even granting the above logic, there is still something not entirely equitable about the arrangement. The *beit din*, before approving the declaration, would consider whether it is appropriate to appoint an *apotropos* — a guardian — to represent the minors' interests in the investment. By mandating that the declaration pass through *beit din*, the process gains legitimacy: the *beit din* has assessed the situation and concluded that the minors cannot meaningfully participate, and so the older brothers may proceed. This procedure makes the outcome more palatable, even if it cannot be characterized as fully fair in every scenario.

### Rava's Shevach Rule

The Gemara now introduces a qualification attributed to Rava, transmitted through Rabbi Chanina son of Rav Yosef son of Rava: *lo shanu ela shevach nechasim machmat nechasim* — the rule that without a declaration everything goes to the estate applies only when the appreciation of the property came from the property's own resources. That is, if the brothers used estate funds to hire workers, plant the fields, or invest in the market — even though they expended some minimal effort — this is considered *shevach nechasim machmat nechasim*, appreciation generated by the assets themselves, and the default is that it belongs to the entire estate.

But *aval shevach nechasim machmat atzman* — if the appreciation came from the brothers themselves, meaning they personally invested their own money or exerted significant personal effort, working the fields daily in the manner of Boaz supervising his workers, then even without any declaration, the assumption is that they are doing it for themselves. The logic is that a serious personal financial or physical investment constitutes an implicit declaration. In that case, *hishbichu le'atzmam* — they enhanced it for themselves — and of course they could choose to dedicate their efforts to the estate, but absent any such commitment, the assumption runs the other way.

### Udayni Exception

The Gemara then challenges this with a statement of Rabbi Yochanan: even if the father left the brothers nothing but an *udayni* — a cistern — the income is *hashachar la'emtza*, shared by the entire estate. But an *udayni* requires someone to stand there, manage the transactions, protect the water — is that not *machmat atzman*, effort from the brothers themselves? Especially since, the Gemara notes, if the entire estate consists of nothing but this cistern, there are no estate funds to hire an operator. The only way the cistern generates income is through the personal effort of one of the brothers.

The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing the *udayni* as a special case: *shani udayni delentiruta hu de'avida* — it requires nothing more than watching, *de'afillu ketanim nami mantru lei* — and even the minors can do that. Here Tosafot's framework becomes decisive. The entire basis for allowing the older brothers to retain the profit — with a declaration or through implicit declaration by investing their own funds — is that the minors are not being deprived of anything, because they could not have done it themselves anyway. But when even children can operate the asset, that justification collapses. The minors can say: we are capable of doing this ourselves; you are actively displacing us from income we could have earned. In such a case the income must be shared, and it remains *la'emtza* regardless.

### Rav Safra Case

The Gemara introduces the case of Rav Safra. His father died and left him an inheritance — estate money. Rav Safra took that money and did business with it, *avad behu iska*. On its face this is *shevach nechasim machmat nechasim*: he used the estate's own funds, not his personal money. He made a profit, and the question is whether his brothers are entitled to share in it. The brothers came before Rava and demanded their portion.

Rava ruled in Rav Safra's favor: *Rav Safra gavra raba hu* — Rav Safra is a great personage — *velo shavik girseih vetarach leachrinei* — he does not abandon his learning to exert himself on behalf of others. Every moment taken away from his Torah study is precious; he works only to support himself. The Rashbam explains that this is considered *shevach nechasim machmat nechasim*, because what Rav Safra did was essentially buy and sell — *liknot velimkor* — which does not require, as the Rashbam puts it, an enormous amount of *torech*, of effortful exertion. The case is analogous to making a stock investment: the intellectual discernment to identify a good opportunity is real, but the physical effort is minimal.

At the same time, Rava's reasoning introduces something conceptually distinct: because it is well known that Rav Safra would never divert time from his learning to do work for others, any effort he invests carries an implicit declaration that he is acting for himself. He does not need to say so explicitly; his entire character and conduct broadcast the message. The Rashbam generalizes from this, stating: *ushma'inan meihacha dechol heicha deman dehu kemo Rav Safra* — we learn from here that anyone who resembles Rav Safra in this respect, even without explicitly saying "I am doing this for myself," is treated as though he made that declaration, and the appreciation belongs to him.

This raises a pointed question: is this standard limited to *talmidei chachamim* who never take time from learning except for their own sustenance, or does it extend to any individual who demonstrably never acts for the benefit of his brothers? If a brother is known to be completely indifferent to his siblings' welfare, acting always for his own gain, should that track record constitute the same implicit declaration? The text does not resolve this. And one might also note the tension in the ruling: the older brothers are using estate funds — funds that belong in part to their siblings — to enrich themselves. It is not merely that they fail to give *tzedakah*; they are leveraging communal assets for personal profit.

### Rashbam on Rav Safra

The Rashbam's analysis establishes that what functions as an implicit declaration is not merely the investment of personal funds but any circumstance that makes it apparent the person could not plausibly be acting on behalf of others. For Rav Safra, it is the standing reality that a scholar of his stature would not sacrifice Torah study for anyone else's financial benefit. The Rashbam codifies this as a general principle: *af al gav delo amar le'atzmi ani osek keman de'amar lehu vehishbiach le'atzmo* — even without saying "I am doing this for myself," such a person is treated as though he said it, and the appreciation is his.

The sugya thus presents a continuum. At one end is the *udayni*, which requires so little effort that even minors can operate it, and the income must always be shared. Somewhere in the middle is the ordinary business investment using estate funds, where the default is sharing unless a declaration is made or personal funds are invested. At the other end is a figure like Rav Safra, whose personal profile itself constitutes the declaration.

### Woman Heir

The Gemara now extends these rules to the case of a woman among the heirs. The case reads: *hahi isha d'ashbacha nechasim ashbacha l'emtza* — a woman who enhanced the estate property, the enhancement goes to the middle, to the estate. If she declares that she is acting for herself, she keeps it. But the Gemara asks: *isha b'nichsei yatmi mah avidta* — what is a woman doing as an heir among orphans? Rabbi Yirmiya answers: *b'isha yoreshet* — she is a *yoreshet*, an heir.

The Rashbam identifies two possible scenarios. The simpler case is that the deceased wrote a will through the instrument of *matnat shechiv mera*, a deathbed gift, designating his wife as an equal co-inheritor together with his children. This was discussed in the preceding daf. She thus becomes a full participant in the estate alongside the sons, and all the same rules apply to her as apply to the older brothers vis-à-vis the younger ones.

The more complex scenario involves inheritance by operation of law. Consider: Reuven marries his niece — the daughter of his brother Shimon. Their father Yaakov dies, leaving his estate jointly to Reuven and Shimon. The estate is never divided. Then Shimon dies, and his daughter inherits his share. Then Reuven dies, leaving his sons. Now Reuven's sons and the woman — their mother, who inherited from her father Shimon — are co-heirs in the same estate of Yaakov. They find themselves as joint inheritors through entirely distinct lines of succession, yet participating together in what is structurally a single estate.

This scenario also provokes a broader question: the concept of *tfisat habayit*, the estate as a corporate entity, has been the animating framework throughout this section. Does that entity arise only from standard *yerusha*, from ordinary inheritance by legal heirs? Or can it also arise from *matnat shechiv mera*? If a man distributes his estate by deathbed gift to a group of people who are not natural heirs — even complete strangers — can they constitute a *tfisat habayit* in the same sense? The answer would seem to depend on how the gift is framed. If specific assets are assigned individually to specific people, there is no shared estate — each person simply owns a parcel. But if the dying man designates a group of people collectively as inheritors of the whole estate, then a corporate entity seems to arise, perhaps even among strangers. The Gemara's framing of the woman as a *yoreshet* alongside the children is consistent with this reading.

Tosafot offers a variant of the second scenario that the lecturer acknowledges is difficult to reconstruct fully, but the principle is the same: the woman is a *yoreshet* together with brothers or other male heirs, and the rules of the estate apply to her equally.

### Woman's Unusual Effort

The Gemara entertains a possible distinction between the woman and the male heirs. One might have thought — *mahu d'teima, keivan delav darchah lemitrach* — since it is not typical for a woman to go out and engage in business activity, if she does go to that unusual effort, we should treat it analogously to Rav Safra: just as Rav Safra's deviation from his norm of Torah study signals that he is acting for himself, a woman's deviation from the norm of not engaging in commerce should signal that she is acting for herself. On this theory, even without a declaration, her effort would generate profit for herself alone.

The Gemara rejects this: *kama mashma lan* — the law teaches us that without a declaration, her *shevach* still goes to the estate, just as with the brothers. Her unusual effort does not by itself constitute an implicit declaration.

The Gemara further considers the converse: if she does make an explicit declaration — *re'u mah she-hiniach li ba'ali ha-reini osah ve-ochelet* — does she nonetheless keep it? One might argue that since a woman who goes out and does business on behalf of orphans earns significant public admiration — people will say, look how this woman sacrifices herself for the heirs — she may actually want to be seen as doing it for them, and her earlier declaration is therefore overridden by her subsequent desire for that acclaim. The Gemara rejects this as well: *kama mashma lan* — an explicit declaration stands, and we do not presume that public praise retroactively dissolves it. She made her declaration; she keeps the profit.

---

## Father's House Gift

### House Gift Presumption

Rabbi Chanina states: *hamasi isha livno hagadol bevayit kna'o* — one who marries off his oldest son and holds the wedding in a house has acquired it for the son, meaning we presume the father has gifted the house to the son. The Gemara adds a series of conditions: this presumption operates only for the oldest son (*davka gadol*), only when the bride is a virgin (*davka besulah*), only when it is the son's first marriage (*davka isha rishona*), and only when the father is marrying off this son first. The rationale is that the combination of all these firsts — oldest son, first wedding for both — makes this such a significant occasion that we interpret the father's gesture as a genuine gift. A further limitation not explicit in this passage is that the father must have another house in the same town, so that the gift does not leave him without a residence.

### Limitations & Rooms

The Gemara begins qualifying the scope of the gift. If the father designated a house with an upper story and held the wedding in the lower story, *bayit kanah aliyah lo kanah* — the son acquires the lower story but not the upper. The gift extends only to the space in which the wedding took place. The Gemara raises further cases: if there was a house and a portico (*achsandra*), and the wedding was held in the house proper, does the son also acquire the portico? What if there were two houses, one accessible only through the other — does the son acquire both? These cases are left as *teiku*, unresolved.

### Dishes vs House

A *beraita* is then cited that appears to contradict the basic presumption. The *beraita* says: if the father designated a house and household dishes for the wedding — *bayit u-chlei bayit* — the son acquires the dishes (*klei bayis kana*) but not the house (*bayis lo kana*). This is precisely the reverse of the earlier ruling, which assumed the house is gifted.

### Father's Storage Rule

Rabbi Yirmiya resolves the contradiction: *kegon dehayu otzaros shel aviv munachim sham* — the *beraita* refers to a case where the father's storage remained in the house. The continued presence of the father's belongings in the house signals that he has retained possession; he has not relinquished it. By contrast, the dishes designated for the wedding belong to the son because there is no such countervailing signal regarding them.

### Small Item Negates Gift

The Gemara then dramatically limits what constitutes "the father's storage." It need not be a warehouse of grain filling the entire house. The Nardeans taught: *afilu shuvcha deyonei* — even if the father left only a pigeon coop there, that suffices to negate the presumption of a gift. Rav Yehuda bar Pappa extended this further: *afilu atzitza d'harsana* — even a small bowl of fish hash left behind is enough. The Amoraim drew the practical conclusion immediately. Mar Zutra, when marrying off his son, simply left a sandal hanging on a peg in the house — *v'tala lei sandala*. Rav Ashi, when marrying off his son, left a small pot of oil — *v'tala lei ashisha d'mishcha*. Both thereby retained ownership of the house. What began as a sweeping presumption of generosity has been qualified almost to the point of nullification: the father need leave almost nothing in the house to demonstrate that the gift was never made.

### Arbitrary Laws

Mar Zutra comments: *hanei tlat mili shavinhu rabanan k'hilchasa b'lo tama* — the following three laws the Rabbis established as halacha that seem arbitrary, lacking obvious derivation. Tosafot qualifies this by noting that the laws are not entirely without reason — they only appear somewhat arbitrary. The first is the presumption we just discussed, that the father who makes a wedding for his oldest son in a house is presumed to have gifted it. The second is the ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *hakosev kol nechasav l'ishto lo asaa ela apitropah* — one who writes over all his property to his wife has merely made her an executor of the estate, not an outright beneficiary, because we presume he would not entirely disinherit his children. The third is the rule of *ma'amad sheloshtan*: if Reuven says to Shimon, "That hundred zuz you owe me — give it to Levi," and all three are present, Levi acquires the debt. This is a mechanism for transferring an abstract monetary obligation through words alone — without a formal *kinyan* — by virtue of all three parties being present together.

---

## Estate Partnership Jobs

### Job Profit Sharing

The *mishnah* now turns to brothers who are partners in an estate — *achim hashotfin* — the shared estate functioning as a kind of corporate entity, as close as halacha comes to the concept of a corporation, with all brothers as equal shareholders. The *mishnah* states: *shenafal echad mehem l'umanut* — if one of them is appointed to a position or gets a job, *nafal l'emtza* — the income goes to the estate. The intuition here seems counterintuitive: this brother is earning his own money; why should his income from outside employment be shared simply because the brothers have not yet divided the estate?

The Gemara will limit this: the rule applies only when he obtained the position because of the family connection. If he would not have been hired but for being a member of this particular family, the income belongs to the estate.

### King's Service Position

A *baraita* teaches that the relevant case is *umanut hamelech* — service in the king's employ. The Rashbam explains that certain families held rotating positions of service to the king — appointed on a family rotation, one member serving in the family's turn. Because the appointment came to any member of the family by virtue of the family's standing, whoever happened to serve in that rotation was in effect working on the family's behalf. The result is shared income, even though only one brother physically performed the service. It is true that this brother could not lie on the beach during his term of service; one might expect some compensation for his lost time and opportunity. But the Gemara does not address this nuance, and the basic rule is that because the appointment derived from the family connection, the income belongs to the estate.

### Personal vs Family Job

The *baraita* draws the governing distinction clearly: *im machmat ha'achim — la'achim* — if the appointment came because of the brothers' family standing, the income is shared. *Im machmat atzmo — le'atzmo* — if the appointment came because of the individual's own demonstrated qualities, the income is his alone. If the king's court appointed this brother because it recognized his personal brilliance, his character, or his independently established reputation — not merely because he is a member of family X — then the income belongs to him personally.

### Ambiguous Job Cases

The *baraita* anticipates an ambiguous case. Suppose the family would ordinarily have had a candidate appointed, but this particular brother is also *charif* — unusually sharp and capable. The Gemara asks: *mahu d'teima churfeh garam leh* — perhaps one should say it was his personal sharpness that caused the appointment? The Gemara answers that we do not say this: if the family connection was itself a sufficient basis for the appointment, we attribute the appointment to the family and the income goes to the estate. The Gemara's default is to assume that connections, rather than individual talent, drove the outcome — a presumption, the lecturer notes, that reflects how the world often works. Of course, when both factors are genuinely intertwined and neither would have sufficed alone, the categorization remains difficult, and the sugya does not offer a definitive resolution for that scenario.

---

## Brother Leaves Estate

### Support Location

The *mishnah* and accompanying *baraita* address a case in which one brother leaves the shared estate to go learn a trade or study: *echad min ha'achim shenatal matayim zuz lamasher v'lilmod amnut* — one of the brothers took two hundred *zuz* to go engage in commerce or learn a craft. The brothers may say to him: *im attah etzlenu yesh lecha mezonot* — as long as you are living with us, you receive your food from the estate; *ve'im ein attah etzlenu ein lecha mezonot* — if you are not living here, you do not. This ruling reflects the presumption that the estate's obligation of *mezonot* is tied to communal residence on the estate property. In the pre-modern world presupposed by the Gemara, the brothers are all living together on the father's property after his death, sharing food, clothing, and expenses from the common estate. The one who leaves that framework exits the support structure.

Several questions surrounding this case remain unaddressed by the Gemara: Was it the departing brother's own initiative to leave, or did the other brothers send him? Is the two hundred *zuz* he took relevant to the support question — did receiving startup funds waive his right to ongoing *mezonot*? What if he took nothing? The sugya does not resolve these questions.

### Rav Huna Blessing

The Gemara asks: since the estate is obligated to support this brother regardless, why not simply pay his food costs wherever he happens to be? The Gemara answers that this supports a principle of Rav Huna: *birchas habayis berovah* — the blessing of a house depends on its population. The more people living in a household, the greater the prosperity of that household. The brother's absence therefore genuinely costs the estate something; his presence would have increased the household's fortune. Since his departure causes a loss to the remaining brothers, they are not required to support him away from home.

The Gemara then asks: if that is so, why not simply pay him according to the proportional *birchas habayis* he would have contributed — deducting that amount from his support? The Gemara accepts this: *hachi nami* — indeed, that is how it is calculated.

### Tosafot Cost Correction

Tosafot objects to the entire framework of *birchas habayis* as a basis for calculating the support reduction. How does one quantify the blessing a single person adds to a household? If the household income happened to rise in his absence and fall in his presence, does that mean his presence was a curse? Tosafot therefore proposes a different and more straightforward economic explanation. Supporting a large family is cheaper per capita than supporting an individual separately. If you are already feeding nine people and you add a tenth, you simply add a piece of chicken to the pot — the marginal cost is low. But to support that person entirely independently, in a separate household, is far more expensive. The estate's obligation is therefore measured by what it actually costs to add this person to the existing household, not by what it costs him to live on his own. The Gemara's resolution — pay his proportional share — is then understood as: pay the additional cost his presence in the house would have incurred, which is lower than independent living costs. This is a more tractable and reasonable calculation.

---

## Medical Expenses

### Negligence vs Accident

The *mishnah* states: *chala venitrapa nitrapa mishel atzmo* — if a brother falls ill and recovers, the medical expenses come from his own funds, not from the estate. This is surprising given that the estate covers food and clothing for all the brothers. If the brothers are all living off the estate as a corporate unit, why should illness be treated differently?

The Gemara cites Ravin in the name of Rabbi Ila'i from Eretz Yisrael, who qualifies the *mishnah*: *lo shanu ela she-chala bifshia* — the ruling that the brother pays his own medical expenses applies only when the illness was caused by his own *peshiah* — his own negligence. But *be-ones* — if the illness came upon him through no fault of his own, through circumstances entirely beyond his control — then *venitrapa min ha-emtza*, the medical expenses are paid by the estate.

### Heaven Principle

What constitutes *peshiah*? The Gemara defines it by invoking a famous teaching of Rabbi Chanina: *hakol biyedei shamayim chutz mitzinim u-pachim* — everything is in the hands of heaven except *tzinim u-pachim*. Everything that befalls a person is ultimately *bashert*, divinely ordained — except for cold and *pachim*. *Pachim* can mean pits: falling into a pit because one was not watching where one walked. It can also mean heat, as Tosafot suggests, linking *pachim* to *pecham*, coal or burning. Regardless, the pasuk states: *tzinim pachim be-derech ikesh* — cold and *pachim* are in the path of the crooked; *shomer nafsho yirchak me-hem* — one who guards himself keeps away from them. These are the paradigm of self-inflicted harm: going out into the cold without a coat, walking without watching where one steps. These result from negligence, not from divine decree, and the person is therefore responsible for the resulting medical expenses.

A normal illness — an ordinary cold contracted under normal circumstances — would be an *ones*, and the estate would cover it. By contrast, if someone went out in a snowstorm without a coat and fell ill, that is *peshiah*. The line between *ones* and *peshiah* is not always sharp; one might ski carefully and still be struck by another skier, so that even a dangerous recreational choice is not automatically negligent in every moment of its execution.

### Chronic vs Acute

An important Tosafot limits the scope of this distinction significantly. The *Tosefta* teaches: *bameh devarim amurim bi-refuah she-yesh lah kitzvah* — when is it that we apply the *peshiah/ones* distinction? Only when the illness requires a finite course of treatment — a discrete medical expense with a beginning and an end. *Aval bi-refuah she-ein lah kitzvah* — but if the illness is ongoing, requiring indefinite treatment, *harei hi bikhlal mezonot viyisrefu min ha-emtza* — it is treated as part of the brother's ongoing sustenance and is paid from the estate, just as food is. Chronic illness, in this framework, is not categorically different from food: just as every person requires nourishment as an ongoing condition of life, a person with a chronic condition requires ongoing treatment. The estate covers both.

Tosafot then anticipates an objection from earlier in the *masechta*: we were told that brothers cannot claim higher food allocations on the basis of greater appetite or need — each receives an equal share. How then can one brother's chronic illness generate disproportionate expenses covered by the estate? Tosafot answers that the equality principle applies only to ordinary *mezonot*, food costs that are discretionary in some sense. Ongoing medical necessity is different in kind and is always covered.

This raises a further difficulty that the Gemara itself creates. The Gemara limits estate liability to cases of *ones*; *peshiah* is the individual's own responsibility. But Tosafot's rule adds: if the condition is chronic, it is covered regardless. Does that mean that if someone was negligent — *peshiah* — but the resulting condition became chronic, the estate must pay? That conclusion seems counterintuitive: if the person's own negligence is what generates the liability, why should chronicity change the analysis? Tosafot's position here is not entirely resolved, and the sugya leaves this tension without a full answer.

---

## Reciprocal Gifts

### Formal Wedding Gifts

The final *mishnah* of the daf introduces the laws of *shoshvinut* — the formal system of reciprocal wedding gifts. When one family sends representatives to another family's wedding bearing gifts, there exists a recognized social and legal obligation to reciprocate in kind when the occasion arises. The *mishnah* poses the following case: some of the brothers, while the father was still alive, went and represented the family at a neighbor's or friend's wedding, bringing *shoshvinut* gifts. The father has since died. Now that same family is sending *shoshvinut* back to the estate, on the occasion of one of the brothers' weddings. Does this reciprocal gift belong to that particular son whose wedding it is, or does it belong to the estate?

The answer is that *chazar shoshbinut chazar la'emtza* — the returned *shoshvinut* goes to the estate. The reasoning is that *shoshbinut nigvis b'veit din* — *shoshvinut* is a formal legal obligation, collectible through *beit din*. The gift brought in the father's time was brought on behalf of the family as a whole; the obligation to reciprocate is therefore owed to the estate, and the estate is the proper recipient. The fact that the occasion for repayment happens to be this particular son's wedding does not transform the gift into his personal property. It is the discharge of a debt owed to the estate, and it flows back to the estate accordingly.

### Informal Gifts

The *mishnah* draws a sharp contrast with informal acts of generosity. *Aval hashaleach l'chavero kad yayin v'chad shemen ein nigvin b'veit din mipnei shehen gemilus chasadim* — but one who sent a neighbor a jug of wine and a jug of oil, which were not sent as formal *shoshvinut* at a *chuppah* but simply as a gift — such an act of *gemilus chasadim* is not collectible through *beit din*, and its reciprocation is treated as a personal gift to the recipient, not as a payment to the estate.

The distinction tracks the difference between legal obligation and social kindness. *Shoshvinut* at a *chuppah* is a formal, legally enforceable commitment; it creates a debt. When someone sends wine and oil as a *Chanukah* gift, there is no legal obligation to reciprocate, even if the social expectation is that one will. When the recipient of that earlier kindness later sends a reciprocal gift back — addressed to the specific person who had shown him that generosity — it is a personal gift to that individual, not to the estate. The estate has no claim on it, because no debt was created in the first instance.

---

---

# Bava Batra 145

## Shushbinut Overview

### Mishna Setup

The Mishna on 144b introduced the institution of *shushbinut* — the gifts brought by close friends of the groom to a wedding, together with the reciprocal obligation those gifts create. The scenario the Mishna describes is as follows: one family sends a son as representative to a neighbor's son's wedding, bearing a gift on behalf of the entire family. The father of that son subsequently dies. When the representative son himself later marries, and the other family sends a gift in return, the question arises: to whom does that return gift belong? Is it the personal property of the son who originally represented the family, or does it belong to the family estate and get divided among all the heirs?

The Mishna rules that the gift belongs to the entire family — *chazra l'emtza*, it returns to the middle — because the son was acting only as a representative of the family, not in his own capacity. The Mishna further contrasts this with a case where a son brings a purely personal gift to a friend's wedding. In that case, the return gift is not collectible in *beis din* at all (there is no legally enforceable obligation of reciprocity the way there is with *shushbinut* proper), and the implication is that whatever does come back would belong to the son personally rather than to the family estate.

### Gift Reciprocity

The institution of *shushbinut* is built on a mechanism of community-wide gift reciprocity: when you receive a *shushbinot* gift at your wedding, you are legally obligated to reciprocate when the giver's family makes a wedding. This is not merely a social expectation but an enforceable legal debt. One might think of it as analogous to a communal cost-sharing arrangement in which the expense of the wedding is distributed across a network of families, each bearing the cost in turn. The gifts given by the *shushbinin* to the groom are understood to carry this reciprocal obligation, and it is precisely because of that legal structure that when the son brought the gift on behalf of the family, he was seen as acting for the family — and therefore, the return gift flows back to the family, not to him individually.

---

## Braita Reconciliation

### Braita's Rule

The Gemara now raises a tension from a *braita*. The *braita* states: *shalach lo aviv shushbinut, keshe'hi chozeret chozeret lo* — if a father sent his son as *shushbin* to the wedding of another, when the gift is repaid, it comes back specifically to that son. This appears to contradict the Mishna, which holds that the return gift goes to the entire family.

Before the Gemara resolves the contradiction, it presents an intermediate case: if a son received the *shushbinut* gift on behalf of his family while his father was still alive, and the father then died before the obligation was reciprocated, when the obligation to reciprocate falls due, it falls upon the entire estate. The rationale is symmetric: the gift was received as a gift to the family; therefore the obligation to return it is borne by the family. The Gemara notes, however, that the *braita*'s framework is actually directionally asymmetric — the gift flows from the entire family to the individual groom, and the reciprocal obligation flows from that individual groom back. This creates the tension with the Mishna, which seemed to assume a family-to-family dynamic.

### Rabbi Assi's Rewrite

Rabbi Assi citing Rabbi Yochanan attempts to resolve the conflict by rewriting the Mishna to match the *braita*. His argument runs as follows: rather than reading the Mishna as a case where the son went and gave a gift on behalf of the family, read it instead as the opposite — the son was the *recipient* of the *shushbinut*, and the Mishna is telling us that when the obligation to reciprocate arises, it falls upon the entire family (*min ha'emtza*). In this reading, the Mishna and *braita* would describe the same basic rule — the gift goes specifically to the groom who received it — but the Mishna would be addressing the separate question of who bears the repayment obligation.

The Gemara immediately pushes back. The text of the Mishna is explicit: *ha'achim she'asu miktzatan shushbinut* — the brothers who performed the *shushbinut*, which clearly indicates that they were the givers, not the recipients. Rabbi Assi's attempt to rewrite the Mishna as a case where they were the recipients cannot be sustained without fundamentally altering the text. *Hachi katani* — the Gemara tries to reparse the language to make it fit, but ultimately the rewrite is recognized as untenable. As the Gemara notes with uncharacteristic directness: this reading requires one to erase and rewrite the Mishna wholesale.

### Rav Ashi's Resolution

Rav Ashi offers a far more elegant resolution: *lo kashya — kan bistam, kan bimfaresh*. There is no real contradiction, because the two sources describe two different factual contexts. When the father *designated* a specific son to go and serve as *shushbin* — *shalach lo aviv shushbinut* — that act of designation focuses the gift on the son personally, and therefore when the gift is returned, it returns to that son. When the father sent a son as a generic, unnamed representative of the family — *shelach aviv shushvinut stam*, simply sending the *shushbinut* without specifying a particular child — then the son is understood as a mere conduit for the family's obligation, and the return gift goes to the whole family.

### Rashbam's Distinction

The Rashbam unpacks Rav Ashi's distinction in precise terms. When the father gives the son money and specifically dispatches *him* to serve as *shushbin* — *natan lo aviv ma'ot v'shalcho la'asot shoshvinut* — the son's personal involvement is highlighted, and the reciprocal gift accordingly returns to him alone (*chozeret lo levado*). By contrast, when the father sends the *shushbinut* generically, without designating one son in particular — *af al pi she'al yedei echad mi'banav shelach* — even though it ultimately happens to be carried out by one of the sons, he is acting as an anonymous family representative. The return gift therefore goes back to the entire family estate. This parallels the principle established in the preceding Mishna: when a son is hired for labor, whether his wages belong to him or to the family depends on whether the employer engaged him personally or simply hired whomever the family sent.

### Samuel's Yibum Case

Samuel offers a different reading of the Mishna altogether. He maintains that the fundamental rule is as the *braita* states — the *shushbinut* always returns to the specific groom.
