The case in the Mishna where it returns to the entire family (*chazra l'emtza*) is a special scenario involving *yibum* (levirate marriage). As the Rashbam explains: *u'matnitin diktani chozeret le'emtza — hani mili she'met haben*. The case in the Mishna is one where the son who originally received the *shushbinut* gift died, and his brother has now performed *yibum* with the son's widow. The *yavam* claims that as part of his acquisition of the deceased brother's estate through *yibum*, he is entitled to the *shushbinut* that is owed to that estate. Samuel rules that this claim fails, because the *yavam* cannot take *b'ra'uy k'vemuchzak* — he does not receive anticipated assets as though they were already in hand. The *shushbinut* that has not yet been paid back is *ra'uy*, not *muchzak*, and therefore it does not pass to the *yavam* but is distributed among all the heirs.

---

## Yibum & Rav'ui

### Yabam Exclusion

Samuel's *yibum* case raises a further question. If the *yavam* cannot collect the *shushbinut* gift because it is merely *ra'uy* — an anticipated but not yet possessed asset — one might accept that he cannot claim it exclusively. But the Gemara presses further: why is *anyone* obligated to send the gift back at all? The *shushbinut* system is built on the expectation of a wedding celebration, of spending the seven days of *sheva brachot* together with the groom. The groom is dead. No wedding is taking place. Why should the opposing family feel obligated to send a gift to the estate of a man who has died before *nisuin*?

The Gemara frames this in parallel to a separate case being introduced: *leima tnu li shushvini ve'esmakh immo* — let the obligated party say, "Give me back my friend who is getting married and I will rejoice with him, and then I will bring the gift." Just as a bride can make the claim *tnu li ba'ali ve'esmakh immo* — "give me my husband and I'll celebrate with him" — to avoid having to return *kesef kiddushin* when the husband dies, so too here the gift-giver might argue that his obligation has not ripened because the wedding never truly concluded.

### Obligation Trigger

The Gemara resolves this through Rav Yosef: *kegon she'samach immo shiva yemei mishteh v'lo hispik lifro'o ad shemeis* — the Mishna's *yibum* case is specifically one where the groom lived through the full seven days of wedding celebration, the *sheva brachot* were completed, and only then did he die before the opposing family had the chance to repay. Once both parties have gone through the full week of celebration together, the legal obligation to repay the *shushbinut* has fully crystallized. The *tnu li shushvini* argument no longer applies, because he did in fact get to rejoice at the wedding. The obligation is thus fully enforceable — only the question of *who* collects it (the *yavam* alone or the whole family) remains, and the answer is that since the gift had not yet been received before death, it is *ra'uy* and therefore goes to the whole family rather than exclusively to the *yavam*.

---

## Kiddushin Returns

### Woman Dies Scenario

The Gemara's exploration of the *tnu li ba'ali ve'esmakh immo* argument leads into an extended discussion of the rules governing the return of *kesef kiddushin* when the betrothal is disrupted before *nisuin*. A *braita* is cited: in a place where the custom (*minhag*) is to return *kiddushin* money, it is returned; in a place where the custom is not to return it, it is not returned. Rav Yosef bar Abba citing Mar Ukva citing Samuel adds a crucial qualification: *lo shanu ela shemeisa hi* — this rule (that it depends on *minhag*) applies only when *she* dies. *Aval meis hu* — if *he* dies, the bride's family need not return the *kiddushin*, because she can say *tnu li ba'ali ve'esmakh immo*: I am willing to proceed with the marriage; it is not my fault he died.

### Le-Tibu'in Debate

The Gemara now identifies this as a point of dispute among *Tannaim*. The underlying question is whether *kiddushin* money is *le-tibu'in nitnu* — given to be "done with," in the sense that once transferred, it belongs to the woman absolutely and is not subject to recovery under any circumstances — or whether it retains some conditional character. The Rashbam explains *le-tibu'in nitnu*: if the woman dies and he never merits marrying her, the money is nonetheless gone; it does not return to him. The opposing view holds that the money is not simply consumed upon transfer and may, under certain circumstances, need to be returned.

### Rabbi Yehuda vs. Noson

The *braita* records a dispute between Rabbi Noson and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. Rabbi Noson holds that whether *kiddushin* is returned depends on local custom (*minhag*), which seems identical to the opening of the *braita*. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi states: *be'emes amru* — "in fact they said" — *makom she'nahagu lehachzir machzirin*, which also seems merely to echo the same rule. The Gemara therefore presses: *hainu Tanna Kama* — isn't Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi simply repeating the *Tanna Kama*?

The Gemara resolves this by arguing that the two statements address different scenarios, and that the *braita* must be read as missing some words (*chasurei mechasra*). The first part of the *braita* addresses the case where *he* dies — in which case the base *kesubah* payment (two hundred *zuz* for a virgin, one hundred for a widow) falls due. It is in this context that Rabbi Noson states the *minhag*-based rule for returning *kiddushin*. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi then comes and says: *bein mes hu uvein mesah hi* — whether he dies or she dies, whether one must return the ring is a function of local custom. In other words, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi explicitly rejects the *tnu li ba'ali* argument even in the case where he dies, insisting that even then it is purely a question of *minhag*.

### Gemara Reconciliation

The Gemara then reverses itself. It proposes that in fact, *kuli alma* — everyone agrees — that if he dies, she can invoke *tnu li ba'ali ve'esmakh immo* and never has to return the ring. The disagreement between Rabbi Noson and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is therefore not about the case where he dies, but about the case where *she* dies. This requires rereading the *braita* with an internal gap: the first clause (two hundred or one hundred *zuz* payment) concerns the case of his death; then there is an implicit shift to the case of her death; and it is in the context of her death that the *minhag* debate about return of *kiddushin* is situated. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, on this reading, is saying that even when she dies, whether the ring must be returned depends on *minhag* — and *v'lo masi amrah tnu li ba'ali ve'esmakh immo*, she cannot invoke the *tnu li ba'ali* argument in that case, since she is the one who has died.

### Core Debate

With this restructuring established, the Gemara identifies the root of the disagreement: *b'kiddushin le-tibu'in nitnu kamiplegi* — the debate turns on whether *kiddushin* money is given to be simply consumed. Rabbi Noson holds that it is *not le-tibu'in nitnu*, and therefore in the case where she dies, whether the groom recovers the money is a function of *minhag*. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds that it *is le-tibu'in nitnu*, meaning the ring is hers absolutely once given, and it never returns — even when she dies.

The Gemara then asks: but Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi himself says *makom she'nahagu lehachzir machzirin* — he explicitly allows for return in places where that is the custom. This seems to contradict the claim that *kiddushin* is *le-tibu'in nitnu*. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between *kiddushin* proper and *savlonot*. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's concession to *minhag* applies only to the *savlonot* — the gifts sent by the groom to the bride or her family during the *eirusin* period. Those gifts, which are tied to the anticipation of *nisuin*, are not *le-tibu'in nitnu* and do go back depending on *minhag*. The *kesef kiddushin* itself, the ring or its equivalent, is *le-tibu'in nitnu* on Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view, and never returns.

The Gemara then introduces a further *braita* to illustrate this with a dispute among *Tannaim*: if a man betrothed a woman with a loaf of bread (*kikar*), and then he died, the question is whether she collects the full *kesubah* and keeps the bread, or must deduct the bread's value from her *kesubah* payment. Rabbi Meir says the woman collects two hundred *zuz* (or one hundred for a widow) outright — the *kiddushin* gift is *le-tibu'in nitnu* and she keeps it. Rabbi Yehuda says she collects her *kesubah* but returns the remainder — the *kikar* comes back. Rabbi Yosi splits the difference, as will be discussed below.

### Rape Exception

The Gemara asks about the framing of this *braita*: the scenario where she collects her *kesubah* but must return the *kiddushin* seems to require simultaneously that (a) the *kesubah* is paid out (implying he died or she was divorced) and (b) the *kiddushin* is being returned. If he died, she should be able to invoke *tnu li ba'ali* and never return anything. If she committed adultery willingly, she forfeits her *kesubah* entirely. The Gemara resolves that the case must involve a woman who was raped (*ones*) after *kiddushin*. However, if the woman is an ordinary Israelite woman who was raped, she is not forbidden to her husband and the marriage can continue — so *tnu li ba'ali* would still apply. The case must therefore be that of a *kohen*'s wife who was raped (*eishet kohen she'ne'ensa*): she becomes forbidden to her husband by force of law, he must divorce her, she collects her *kesubah*, but since the situation is not one where she can say *tnu li ba'ali ve'esmakh immo* — the marriage cannot proceed through any action of hers or anyone else's — she cannot invoke that argument, and the *kiddushin* question is purely whether it is *le-tibu'in nitnu*.

### Deduction Dispute

In this case of the *kohen*'s wife who was raped: Rabbi Meir holds that *kiddushin le-tibu'in nitnu* — the bread is hers, and she collects the full *kesubah* without any deduction. Rabbi Yehuda holds *lav le-tibu'in nitnu* — the *kiddushin* gift is not simply consumed, and she must return its value, deducting it from what she receives. Both agree she collects the *kesubah*; they disagree on whether the *kesef kiddushin* (here, the value of the loaf of bread) comes back out of what she receives.

### Rabbi Yosi Split

Rabbi Yosi is uncertain which position is correct — *mesafeka lei ei le-tibu'in nitnu ei lav* — and therefore splits the difference. His ruling is expressed through two parallel cases. If the man betrothed her with twenty *shekalim* (worth eighty *zuz*): Rabbi Yosi awards her thirty "halves" (*shloshim chatza'in*), meaning thirty half-*shekalim*, which equals sixty *zuz*. The logic is that she is conceptually treated as having half of the *kiddushin* returned, so she is left with forty *zuz* worth of *kiddushin*, and the *kesubah* balance owed to her is correspondingly sixty *zuz*. Conversely, if he betrothed her with thirty *shekalim* (worth one hundred and twenty *zuz*): she is awarded twenty half-*shekalim* (forty *zuz*), on the same logic of splitting the uncertainty down the middle.

### Rav Yosef Ruling

Rav Yosef bar Minyumi citing Rav Nachman rules: *bechol makom she'nahagu l'hachzir machzirin* — wherever the *minhag* is to return, one returns. The Gemara qualifies that this ruling applies specifically to *Nehardea* and communities like it, where the practice was indeed to return *kiddushin* in cases of the woman's death, and therefore the operative rule is not *le-tibu'in nitnu* but rather follows local custom.

### Babylonian Practice

Rabbah and Rav Yosef both say, with respect to the rest of *Bavel* outside those communities: *ma'ori hadri, kiddushei lo hadri* — the *savlonot* (here called *ma'ori*, a term the Rashbam explains as related to *mohar*, a gift sent by the groom during the *eirusin* period and noted in the *kesubah*) are returned, but *kiddushin* is not. The Rashbam observes the interesting semantic evolution: the biblical *mohar* was *kesef kiddushin*; here the word has shifted to denote the *savlonot*-type gifts, reflecting a transition in which the *kesubah* absorbed and reframed the original *mohar* obligation, while the term migrated to describe the betrothal-period gifts.

### Rav Pappa Final

Rav Pappa states the *halacha*: *bein shemet hu bein shemetah hi v'hadri behu* — whether he dies, whether she dies, or whether either party calls off the engagement, the *ma'ori* (the *savlonot* gifts) are returned, and *kiddushin* is not. The *kesef kiddushin* is *le-tibu'in nitnu* and belongs to the woman under all circumstances — unless she is the one actively initiating the cancellation, in which case Rav Pappa suggests that even the *kiddushin* itself would have to be returned.

### Amimar Dissent

Amimar disagrees with Rav Pappa's exception. Even if she is the initiating party, *kiddushei lo hadri* — the *kiddushin* ring does not go back. The reason is a *gzeira: shema yomru kiddushin tofsin b'achotah* — lest people say that *kiddushin* takes effect with her sister. The concern is that if the ring is visibly returned, onlookers will conclude that the *kiddushin* never took place or was fully undone, and the man might proceed to betroth the woman's sister without realizing that a *get* is required first. Once he has given a *get*, he would ordinarily be forbidden to her sister only as long as she is a *gerusha* — but absent a *get*, if people believe there was no binding *kiddushin*, he might believe himself free to marry the sister outright. To prevent this confusion, the ring must never be returned, regardless of who initiates the cancellation.

Rav Ashi initially disagreed with this *gzeira*, arguing that *gita mochiach alah* — the existence of the *get* makes it self-evident that *kiddushin* had taken place. But the Gemara reports that Rav Ashi retracted (*vehadar Rav Ashi bediburei*), because *d'ika desham'a beha v'lo sham'a beha* — not everyone hears everything; one person may have seen the ring returned but not heard about the *get*, and the confusion Amimar feared is entirely realistic. Amimar's protective *gzeira* is therefore the accepted position.

---

## Shushbinut Properties

### Collectible Nature

Having completed the extended digression through *kiddushin* and *savlonot*, the Gemara returns to *shushbinut* and enumerates its distinctive legal characteristics. *Shushbinos nigbis b'veit din* — *shushbinut* is collectible in *beis din*. This is a striking ruling: unlike an ordinary gift, which carries no legal obligation of reciprocity, *shushbinut* functions as an enforceable debt. The irony, as the Gemara immediately makes clear, is that while it is collectible like a loan, it is simultaneously a debt with no fixed amount and no fixed payment schedule.

### Five Characteristics

*Tanu Rabbanan*: the Rabbis taught that five things were said about *shushbinut*. First, *nigbis b'veit din* — it is collectible in court. Second, *chozeres b'onasah* — it is returned specifically at its proper time: when the gift-giver himself makes a wedding, and not before; one may not prepay the obligation. Third, *ein bah mishum ribis* — there is no prohibition of *ribis* (prohibited interest), even if the amount returned differs from the amount originally given. Fourth, *eina shevi'is m'shamatata* — the *shemitta* year does not annul it. Fifth, *ein habechor notel bah pi shenayim* — the firstborn son does not receive a double portion of *shushbinut* assets in an inheritance.

### Collectibility Explained

The Gemara explains each ruling. *Nigbis b'veit din mai ta'ama? K'milveh damya* — why is it collectible in court? Because it functions like a loan. This analogy to a loan is what places it within the jurisdiction of *beis din*, even though the social dynamics of the relationship are not those of a creditor and debtor.

### No Interest Rationale

There is no *ribis* because *d'lav ada'ata d'hachi yahav lei* — it was not given with the understanding that an exact equivalent amount would be returned. The parties understood from the outset that the repayment amount might differ. Since the original gift was not extended as a commercial loan with a fixed repayment expectation, returning a larger or smaller amount does not violate the prohibition of *ribis*.

### Shmita Exemption

*Shemitta* does not annul it. The Rashbam explains this on technical grounds: *she'eino yachol l'dachko b'veitin b'shvi'is she-harei lo higia zmano* — if the recipient has not yet married and hosted his own wedding, the time for repayment has not yet arrived at all. *Shemitta* can only cancel a debt whose due date has passed; a debt whose due date has not yet arrived at the onset of *shemitta* remains in force. There is also a deeper structural point, which *Tosafot* notes in anticipation of the Gemara's own language: *d'lo kari bei lo yigos* — the verse prohibiting creditor pressure (*lo yigos et re'eihu v'et achiv*) does not apply here, because the power dynamic of borrower and lender is absent from *shushbinut*. The obligation exists between friends and equals, not between those in the coercive relationship of creditor and debtor.

### Bechor Exclusion

Finally, the firstborn does not receive a double portion of *shushbinut* assets — *d'hava lei ra'uy, v'ein habechor notel b'ra'uy k'v'muchzak*. In the case where the return gift flows to the entire family estate (as in the *yibum* case discussed earlier, or in the case of a generic family representative), the *shushbinut* owed back to that estate has not yet been paid; it is money anticipated but not yet in hand. The *bechor* receives a double portion only of assets that are *muchzak* — already in the possession of the estate at the time of inheritance — not of assets that are merely *ra'uy*, awaiting collection. Since the reciprocal *shushbinut* gift had not yet been paid at the time the estate came into being, it is *ra'uy*, and the *bechor* receives only his single proportional share along with the rest of the heirs.

---

---

# Bava Batra 146

## Shoshbinut & Reciprocity

### Shoshbinut Definition

The daf opens, picking up on 145b approximately eight lines down, with a discussion of the institution of *shoshbinut* — the practice whereby designated groomsmen bring gifts to a wedding and, in turn, are owed a reciprocal gift when their own weddings take place. This is not merely a social custom but a genuine legal obligation: the recipient of a *shoshbin* gift incurs a real debt to repay it when the roles are reversed.

### Havi be-mata Rules

Rav Kahana states the general rule — *klal de-shoshbinuta* — governing what happens when a person who once received a *shoshbin* gift was, for some reason, absent from the giver's wedding. The underlying assumption had been that one would be invited to the other's wedding and repay the gift in that context, but Rav Kahana addresses the complications that arise when this does not occur.

If one was *havi be-mata* — present in the town at the time of the wedding — then *iba-ei lei lemeisei*: one should have come. The wedding was a known community event, and absence is one's own fault. The obligation to repay the *shoshbin* gift therefore stands in full. Similarly, if one was not in town but heard the wedding drum — *shama kol tavla* — the public announcement that a wedding was taking place, the same rule applies: *iba-ei lei lemeisei*, one had sufficient notice and should have attended. Failure to do so does not exempt one from the reciprocal obligation.

### Lo Shama Kol Tavla

The real question arises in the case of *lo shama kol tavla*: one was out of town and received no notification whatsoever. Here, one might reasonably argue: "You didn't invite me, you didn't inform me — why should I be obligated to repay a gift in the context of a wedding from which I was effectively excluded?" The claim seems compelling, rooted in the very logic of friendship and conviviality that underlies *shoshbinut* in the first place.

Surprisingly, however, this is not the *halacha*. The Gemara acknowledges that yes, *iba-ei lei lo-odeiyei* — the groom should have informed him, and *tarumas it lei* — the uninvited groomsman has a legitimate complaint. Yet despite this valid grievance, *shalumei meshalem*: he is still obligated to repay the gift. The fact that he had a right to be informed, and was not, gives him grounds for complaint but does not dissolve the underlying debt.

### Zuza Deduction Rule

The Gemara then raises a practical refinement. When one was not at the wedding and had a good reason — specifically in the case where one was not informed — must one repay the full value of the original gift? After all, had one attended, one would have enjoyed a meal and *smorg* at the groom's expense. The host provides food for the guest, and that value was already factored into the original gift's social context.

Abaye teaches: *nahagu benei ganuna* — the practice among wedding participants was as follows. If the *shoshbin* gift was worth up to one *zuza*, the principle *aisei be-kapei, achlei be-charsei* applies — what you bring with your hands, you eat with your stomach — meaning the food one would have received is presumed to be worth at least as much as the gift, and therefore nothing need be repaid. If the gift was worth up to four *zuza*, half is repaid, on the assumption that roughly half the gift's value would have been offset by the meal one would have enjoyed. Beyond four *zuza*, the *Rashbam* indicates the calculation proceeds according to the individual's status and the presumed quality of the feast — *inish inish k'chashivusei* — each person according to their standing.

This framework strikes a deliberately commercial tone. An institution rooted in friendship and communal celebration is here subjected to precise monetary accounting — yet that, it seems, is the nature of what this legal institution ultimately became.

### Equivalence Requirements

A *Tanna de-Bei* teaching elaborates on a further dimension of *shoshbinut* obligations: the requirement of equivalence between the two weddings. If one threw a grand public wedding — *bifumbi*, with hundreds of guests and a lavish feast — and the other now wishes to hold a small, private affair, the first may say: *bifumbi esseh imach kederach she'asita imi* — I will fulfill my *shoshbin* obligation at a wedding comparable to the one you gave for me. If the other's wedding does not rise to that level, there is no legal obligation to serve as *shoshbin* or to give the equivalent gift.

Similarly, if one's wedding was for a *betulah* — a first marriage — and the other now marries a widow, one may say: *bivtulah esseh imach kederach she'asita imi* — my obligation applies to a first wedding, not a second. The reverse situation also generates an asymmetry: if one's own wedding was a second marriage and the other's is a first, one may say: *lichshe'tissa ishah acheret esseh imach* — when you have your second marriage, then I will fulfill my obligation, not now. And if one married one woman and the other now seeks to marry two women simultaneously — the plain reading of *asa imo be'achat ubikesh la'asot imo bishtayim* — one may declare the obligation inapplicable to that scenario as well.

It is worth noting the practical context of these rulings. They are not predicated on the assumption that people would routinely refuse to participate in a friend's wedding under such circumstances. Rather, when the matter arrives before a court and becomes a question of legal liability — of actually suing to recover or compel a gift — the technical obligation applies only where there is genuine equivalence. That is the narrower claim these teachings are making.

---

## Scholars & Wealth Metaph…

### Otzar Nechasim Case

At this point the Gemara transitions, somewhat unexpectedly, into an extended *aggadic* passage employing metaphors of wealth to characterize different types of Torah scholars. The connection to the preceding discussion of *shoshbinut* and its varying levels of obligation may be thematic — different types of celebration, different levels of social standing, different magnitudes of wealth — but the passage stands largely on its own terms as a celebrated *aggadic* teaching.

*Tanu Rabbanan*: *otzar nechasim otzar pumbi* — one who is wealthy in property and whose wealth is publicly known, visible to all in the form of land and flocks and assets that everyone can observe. The *Rashbam* reads this as referring to landed property and livestock. This describes, the Gemara teaches, *zehu baal aggadot* — the scholar who excels at *aggadah*, at popular preaching and inspiring public discourse. His Torah is as visible and accessible as publicly displayed wealth: hundreds or thousands come to hear his beautifully crafted sermons, and the full richness of his knowledge is on open display for all.

### Atir Sela'im Case

*Atir sela'im atir takua* — wealthy in coins, and *takua*, a term the *Rashbam* explains with some uncertainty, possibly referring to houses or, given that *Takua* was a town known for its oil, to oil. But setting aside the precise meaning of *takua*, the emphasis here falls on the coins: liquid wealth that is not publicly visible, that reveals itself only when someone comes to the money changer and transacts with him. This is *ze baal pilpul* — the scholar of profound analytic ability. *Pilpul* today carries a sometimes pejorative connotation, but in the Gemara's idiom it refers to genuine analytical depth and incisiveness. This scholar does not deliver crowd-pleasing homilies; he is not the one whose Torah is on public display. But sit down with him in learning, and the full depth of what he possesses becomes immediately apparent — like the coin changer who reveals his resources only when the moment of exchange arrives.

### Atir Mashach Case

*Atir mashach atir kamas* — wealthy in stored goods. *Mashach*, the *Rashbam* suggests, may refer to things that are measured out, and he reads it as something akin to grain stored in a storehouse; *kamas* more clearly means stockpiled goods. Together the image is of someone with vast reserves that are not circulating, not generating new wealth, but available to draw upon when needed. This is *zehu baal shmuot* — the scholar of wide factual knowledge, a walking encyclopedia of traditions and received teachings. Unlike the *ba'al pilpul*, this scholar is not generating new analytical insight; unlike the *ba'al aggadah*, this scholar's wares are not on public display. But his stored knowledge is indispensable.

Here the Gemara interpolates what appears to be a parallel teaching from elsewhere: *hakol tzrichim lemarei chittaya* — everybody needs the master of the wheat. This echoes the famous Talmudic question of which scholar type is preferable, the *oker harim* — the one who uproots mountains with analytical prowess — or the *Sinai*, the one who received the Torah at Sinai, as it were, possessing the comprehensive factual knowledge of traditions. The Gemara's answer: *hakol tzrichim lemarei chittaya*, everyone needs the one who has the wheat. The image is apt: *agirsa ligros*, grinding grain, is the analytic work of breaking down knowledge, crushing and developing it into something usable — but none of that can happen without the raw grain to begin with. Facts and received traditions are the necessary foundation before any analysis can proceed. The *ba'al shmuot* may not be generating new wealth, his knowledge may not be growing or producing, but it is the most essential starting point.

### Poor Days Verse

Rav Zeira says in the name of Rav: what is meant by the verse in Mishlei, *kol yimei ani ra'im* — "all the days of a poor person are evil"? This refers to *ze ba'al Gemara* — the scholar who dedicates himself to Talmudic analysis. He is constantly struggling, banging his head against the wall of a difficult passage, wrestling with the analytical demands of *gemara* study. And *v'tov lev mishteh tamid* — "and the good-hearted is always at a feast" — that refers to *ze ba'al Mishnah*, the scholar who occupies himself only with memorizing the received traditions without the burden of analysis. His life is comparatively easy: he learns what the teachings are, he has no need to think too hard, and so his heart is always at ease, his learning always like a pleasant feast.

### Rava's Reversal

Rava reverses this entirely: *amar Rava ipcha* — it is precisely the opposite. The *ba'al Gemara*, who labors through the analysis, ultimately arrives at the *halacha* — he knows what to do, and the satisfaction of reaching a conclusion, of knowing how to act, makes his life *v'tov lev mishteh tamid*. The *ba'al Mishnah*, on the other hand, for all his stored knowledge, cannot reliably arrive at the proper *halacha* on his own, and so *kol yimei ani ra'im* — all his days are troubled. He carries the weight of accumulated knowledge without the analytical tools to render it actionable.

### Stone & Wood Metaphor

This position, Rava adds, underlies the teaching of Rav Mesharshaya in Rava's name, drawing on another verse. *Massa avanim ye'atzev bahem* — "one who carries stones will be anguished by them" — these are *ba'alei Mishnah*. They carry vast weight, all this accumulated knowledge, but it causes anguish because ultimately it does not lead them to knowing the correct *halacha*. And *bokei'a etzim yissachen bam* — "one who chops wood will be warmed by it" — these are *ba'alei Gemara*. Chopping, grinding, breaking down: the analytic act generates energy, warmth, and ultimately illuminates the *halacha*. The contrast is clean and unambiguous in Rava's reading.

### Alternative Readings

The Gemara then offers several alternative interpretations of the same verse from Mishlei that have nothing to do with Torah study typologies at all, exploring instead various dimensions of human experience and disposition.

Rabbi Chanina reads *kol yimei ani ra'im* as referring to a man with a bad wife — *ze she'yesh lo isha ra'ah* — and *v'tov lev mishteh tamid* as the man blessed with a good wife. Rabbi Yannai reads the "poor person" as an *istenis* — an extremely finicky individual for whom nothing is ever quite right, who is always disturbed by some small imperfection, who finds nothing in life quite satisfactory. The *v'tov lev mishteh tamid* is correspondingly the *she'da'ato yaffa* — the easygoing soul, the person of broad and relaxed temperament for whom minor disorder causes no distress. Rabbi Yochanan offers the striking, almost ironic, reading that *kol yimei ani ra'im* refers to the *rachman* — the excessively compassionate person, someone too empathic and too open, who lacks the self-protective filter needed to get through life without being overwhelmed by the pain of others. And *v'tov lev mishteh tamid* is, in this reading, *ze achzari* — the cruel person, or at least the emotionally insulated one, who goes through life unbothered by others' suffering. The point is not an endorsement of cruelty but a recognition that the unguarded heart pays a price — while still acknowledging the need for a balance that allows one to genuinely help and empathize.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads the verse in terms of *da'ato ketzarah* versus *da'ato rechavah* — the narrow versus the broad spirit. The narrow-spirited person, always measuring, always chafing at what others have that they lack, lives in constant resentment and perceived injustice. The broad-spirited person, generous in outlook, genuinely happy for others' good fortune, lives in a kind of permanent contentment. The distinction maps broadly onto the contrast between the pessimist and the optimist, each going through life with a fundamentally different orientation.

### Poor Man's Misery

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, however, raises an objection against the original formulation: *kol yimei ani ra'im* — surely not *all* the days? What about *Shabbasos* and *Yomim Tovim*, when even the poor person receives food from the charitable community and enjoys something of a respite? He answers this with a teaching from Shmuel: *shinui vest techilas choli* — a change in one's dietary routine is itself the beginning of illness. Even the comparative richness of a Shabbos meal, for someone accustomed to deprivation, may cause physical distress through the disruption of bodily norms. So even those days offer no true relief.

The Gemara closes this digression by quoting from *Sefer Ben Sira* — one of the *Sefarim Chitzonim*, yet occasionally cited by the Gemara — which extends the verse further. Not only are the poor person's days evil, but *af leilos* — even the nights are evil. Why? *Bishfal gagin gago*: the poor person's roof is lower than those of his neighbors, and so *mimatar gagin l'gago* — all the rainwater from the surrounding rooftops runs down onto his and creates perpetual leaks. And *b'rum harim karmo me'afar karmo l'charamim* — his vineyard sits at the top of the mountain, so whatever good topsoil he has trickles down to the vineyards below him. Even his nighttime sleep brings no reprieve, while the wealthy rest peacefully. It is a vivid and affecting close to what was, structurally, an unexpected digression from the legal sugyot on either side of it.

---

## Sabalonot Gifts

### Meal Finalizes Gift

The Gemara now moves to the Mishnah governing *sabalonot* — the traditional gifts sent from the groom to the bride and her family after *kiddushin* (betrothal) but before *nissu'in* (marriage). The Mishnah teaches: *ha'shole'ach savlonot l'veit chamiv* — one who sends gifts to his father-in-law's house, worth as much as one hundred *maneh*, and then goes there and participates in a *seudat chatan*, a celebratory meal at the father-in-law's house — even if that meal cost only one *dinar* — then *afillu b'dinar ein nigbin*: even so, if the marriage subsequently does not reach *nissu'in* — whether through death, divorce, or some other rupture — the gifts cannot be reclaimed. The participation in a celebratory meal, however modest, is treated as an act of finalization: the groom has, in effect, committed to the gift unconditionally, and it passes fully to the bride and her family.

### No Meal, Gift Recovers

If, however, *lo achal seudat chatan* — they did not hold that meal — then *harei elu nigbin*: in the event the *nissu'in* does not take place, the gifts may be recovered. Without that moment of celebratory consummation, the *sabalonot* retain a provisional character; the *kiddushin* has occurred, but the incompleteness of the relationship means the gifts have not yet passed irrevocably.

### Large vs Small Gifts

The Mishnah then draws a further distinction regarding large versus small *sabalonot*. *Shalach savlonot merubim she'yachzeru ima l'veit ba'ala* — if the gifts sent were substantial, understood by their nature to be brought back with the bride when she moves to the husband's house at *nissu'in*, then *harei elu nigbin* — they may be recovered if *nissu'in* does not occur. *Savlonot muatim she'tishtamesh bahen b'veit aviha* — but if the gifts were small, of the sort understood to be used up while the bride is still in her father's house before *nissu'in*, then *einam nigbin* — they are not recovered.

Much remains ambiguous at this point in the Mishnah's formulation. Do the large versus small distinctions apply only when there was no *seudat chatan*, or do they operate independently? Is the Mishnah speaking of explicit stated intentions, or of implied presumptions based on quantity? What of intermediate amounts? The Gemara will attempt to resolve these ambiguities.

### Dinar Threshold

Rava rules: *davka dinar* — the Mishnah's ruling that the gifts are finalized applies specifically to a meal worth a full *dinar*; *aval pachot mi'dinar lo* — anything less than a *dinar*, even if a *seudat chatan* of sorts took place, does not finalize the gifts, and they may still be recovered if *nissu'in* does not occur.

The Gemara challenges this: *pshita dinar tnan* — the Mishnah explicitly said *dinar*, so this seems obvious. The Gemara responds that one might have thought the Mishnah used *dinar* only as a conventional way of speaking to contrast with the enormous sum of one hundred *maneh*, and that even less than a *dinar* would suffice. Rava therefore teaches that *davka* — the *dinar* threshold is precise and not merely illustrative.

### Eating vs Drinking

The Gemara then examines the Mishnah's language more closely. The Mishnah says *achal* — he ate. What if he only drank — *shata mai*? Does drinking alone at the father-in-law's house constitute sufficient participation to finalize the gifts? Furthermore: the Mishnah seems to presume that the groom himself ate — but what if a representative, a *shlucho*, ate on his behalf? And: the Mishnah says he ate *sham*, there at the father-in-law's house — what if food was sent to him and he ate it at his own house, a kind of *shagar lo*? None of these questions are resolved directly; the Gemara turns instead to a narrative that sheds light on at least some of them.

### Hot Water Story

Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel: there was a man who sent to his father-in-law's house one hundred flasks of wine and of oil, silver and gold vessels, silk garments — an extraordinarily lavish array of *sabalonot* — and then rode joyfully toward the house. He arrived and stood at the doorway of his father-in-law's house, and before entering, they brought him a cup of hot water (*kos shel chamin*), which he drank — and he died right there on the threshold.

This case — the *halacha* of which was brought by Rav Acha Sarbiya before the sages in Usha, the seat of the Sanhedrin — prompted the following ruling: *savlonot ha'asuyot livlot ein nigbin* — *sabalonot* that are of the type normally consumed or worn out are not recovered; *she'einan asuyot livlot nigbin* — those that are not of that type are recovered.

This is a crucial reconceptualization. The distinction shifts from simple quantity (large or small) to the inherent nature of the gift: will it naturally be consumed before *nissu'in*, or was it always intended to last and return with the bride at *nissu'in*? Food, clothing that would be worn out, even money that would be spent — these are *asuyot livlot*, made to be used up, and once the gift is finalized (as it apparently was here through the cup of hot water), they do not return. A pearl necklace or gold vessels — *einan asuyot livlot* — those were always expected to come back into the marriage at *nissu'in*, and so even when gifts are otherwise finalized, these always remain subject to return if *nissu'in* does not occur.

### Eshuyot Livlot

This ruling also clarifies the end of the Mishnah, reconceptualizing it from a distinction between large and small into a distinction between *asuyot livlot* and *einan asuyot livlot*. And crucially, it applies this distinction even when the gift has been finalized by a meal: even after the *seudat chatan*, the items that were expected to return — the *einan asuyot livlot* — still revert to the groom's family if *nissu'in* does not take place. The finalization accomplished by the meal applies only to those gifts that were always destined to remain in the bride's father's house.

The story of the cup of hot water also seems to indicate that even *drinking* — not eating a full meal — can constitute sufficient participation to finalize the *asuyot livlot* category of gifts. And the question of whether the finalization requires eating at the father-in-law's house specifically is at least partially addressed: the man died *at the doorway*, and the ruling treated this as sufficient, though the Gemara notes — *dilma kol petach beit chamich kebeit chamich dami* — perhaps the immediate doorway of one's father-in-law's house is halachically equivalent to being inside, without resolving the question of what would apply further afield.

The Gemara draws inferences: *shma mina afilu shata* — we can infer that even drinking (not eating) suffices to finalize the gifts. And apparently *shma mina afilu pachot mi'dinar* — this seems to contradict Rava's requirement of a full *dinar*, since the cup of hot water was presumably worth far less than a *dinar*.

### Pearl Objection

Rav Ashi deflects this challenge: *man leima lan dela shachki lei marganita deshvya alfa zuzei ve'ashkeih* — who says they did not grind a pearl worth a thousand *zuza* into the drink? Perhaps what he consumed was worth far more than a *dinar*. The *Rashbam* suggests this might reflect a belief that ground pearl had medicinal properties. The argument strikes one as intentionally far-fetched — the grinding of an enormously valuable pearl into a cup of water seems absurd — yet Rav Ashi's point may be precisely that the *dinar* requirement, if insisted upon, can never be conclusively disproven, since one can never know exactly what went into the drink. The practical upshot is that the Gemara appears unable to cleanly maintain the *dinar* requirement in the face of this narrative, though it does not formally abandon it.

The Gemara similarly considers whether *shgar lo* — sending him food from the house for him to eat elsewhere — would be sufficient, and tentatively suggests that the doorway of the father-in-law's house may be treated as equivalent to the interior, leaving the more distant case unresolved.

### Gift Appreciation

A further set of questions now confronts the Gemara. *Ibaya lehu: mahu sheyisholash* — what is the rule if a full *dinar*'s worth was not consumed, say only half a *dinar*? Do the gifts become proportionally finalized — half finalized, half recoverable? This is a strange implication of the *dinar* requirement and the Gemara leaves it unresolved.

*Shevach savlonot mahu* — what is the *din* if the *sabalonot* appreciated in value during the period between *kiddushin* and *nissu'in*, in a case where the gifts are ultimately to be returned? Who owns the increase in value?

The Gemara frames this as a conceptual question about the underlying nature of the transaction. *Keivan de'inhu ledidei hadri birshutei shevach* — since these gifts ultimately revert to the groom, does that mean they were always effectively his property, and therefore the appreciation belongs to him? Or, *keivan de'i avdu o ignavu ba'ei shalumei lei* — since if the gifts were lost or stolen during this period, the bride's family would have had to compensate the groom for them, does that indicate that the gifts were in fact in the bride's *reshut* (legal domain), and therefore the appreciation belongs to her? The Gemara answers: *teiku* — the question is left unresolved.

This is a genuinely pivotal conceptual question, and closely parallels a discussion treated on the previous daf regarding the *kesef kiddushin* — the betrothal gift — and its status if the wedding does not proceed. There, too, the underlying question is whether these gifts constitute an absolute transfer of ownership with a contingent obligation of repayment, or something more like a conditional gift, a *matana betnai*. The Gemara there — *letivuyei nitnu*, "they were given to beautify her" — seemed to indicate that the *kiddushin* gifts are absolute gifts, with the repayment obligation existing alongside the transfer rather than negating it. The same conceptual tension applies here to *sabalonot*, and the *teiku* leaves it unresolved.

Rava then raises yet another question: *savlonot ha'asuyin livalot velo balu mahu* — what if the gifts belonged to the *asuyot livlot* category — food, wearable clothing, consumables — but in fact were not consumed? They are still intact. Do they now revert to the groom's family, since they are actually present and recoverable?

The Gemara attempts to resolve this from the earlier ruling of Usha, which spoke of gifts that are *ha'asuyot livlot* — made to be consumed — without specifying that they were actually consumed. This seems to support the view that the category designation, not the actual fact of consumption, is determinative. But the Gemara pushes back: perhaps *d'balu* is what was meant — that they are things that have in fact been consumed. The Mishnah's language — *savlonot muatim she'tishtamesh bahen b'veit aviha* — items used up in the father's house — also does not clearly resolve it. Rava interprets the Mishnah narrowly: *targama Rava beivei v'savchei* — the Mishnah was speaking only of trivial items like a kerchief or scarf, and for more substantial items that happen still to be intact, the matter may be different. This reading is admittedly far from the plain meaning of the Mishnah, but it is at least what the Gemara offers.

### Atzeret Story

Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: there was a man who sent to his father-in-law's house new wine, new oil, and new flax garments on *Atzeres* (Shavuos). The Gemara asks: *mai kamashma lan* — what is this story meant to teach us? Two possible answers are offered. One is simply a point of praise for the Land of Israel: *chashivus d'Eretz Yisrael kamashma lan* — in Eretz Yisrael, the agricultural bounty is so abundant that new wine, oil, and fine linen are already available and ready to send as gifts even at the early date of *Atzeres*, far sooner than in the Diaspora. Alternatively, the story establishes evidentiary credibility: if someone claims in court that he sent wine, oil, and linen as *sabalonot* at *Shavuos* time, one should not automatically dismiss this as implausible — the story proves it actually happened and is therefore not inherently a false claim, even if it raises questions of burden of proof.

### Impaired Smell

Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: there was a man who was told *ishto tutranis hi* — his wife's sense of smell is impaired. Following the *Rashbam* and *Tosafot*, this is understood to refer to a situation after *kiddushin* but before *nissu'in*; the impaired sense of smell would constitute a *mum* — a blemish — with potential legal consequences regarding *get*, *ketubbah*, and the validity of the marriage, questions elaborated in Kesubos and Kiddushin.

To investigate the claim, the man followed his wife into a deserted area — *nichnas achareiha l'churba l'vodkah*. He said to her: *rei'ach tzonan ani meri'ach baGalil* — I can smell radishes from the Galilee, apparently either concealing a radish or a date beneath his garment and gauging her response. She replied that if only she could have the pressed dates of Jericho to eat — the city known for its dates — she would delight in them together with the radishes. According to the *Rashbam*, it was apparent from her response that she knew what he was about.

Whatever the result of this informal investigation, what followed was that the ruin collapsed upon her and she died — *nafal aleiha churba umesa*. The husband sought to inherit her estate, which as a general principle a husband can do only after *nissu'in*, not after *kiddushin* alone. He argued that he had brought her onto his property and that she had entered it for the purpose of *nissu'in*, which under halachic principles can constitute *chuppah* and thus effect *nissu'in*.

The sages, however, ruled against him: *ho'il v'lo nichnas achareiha ella l'vodkah* — since his entire purpose in bringing her there was to test her and to investigate whether to proceed with the marriage, this entry could not possibly be characterized as entry onto his property for the purpose of *nissu'in*. It was, if anything, an act of doubt and scrutiny, the very opposite of a consummating intention. Therefore, no *nissu'in* had taken place, and he could not inherit her.

---

## Conditional Return

### Ravin's Rule

Ravin the Elder, sitting before Rav Pappa, teaches the following comprehensive rule governing when *sabalonot* are returned. In all cases where the gifts are to be returned — whether because they are *einan asuyot livlot* or because no *seudat chatan* took place — the return applies across all scenarios of the marriage's dissolution: *bein shemesa hi ubein shemes hu* — whether she died or he died, and *hadar hu* — or he was the one who called off the *nissu'in*. In all of these cases: *savlonot hadrei* — the *sabalonot* that are returnable are returned; *ma'achal umishteh lo hadrei* — food and drink are not returned.

To be precise about the scope of this rule: it describes the situation where the groom did eat *b'veit chamiv* — at the father-in-law's house. In that case, the *asuyot livlot* category — the best example being food consumed — is finalized and does not return. The *einan asuyot livlot* — items expected to come back with the bride at *nissu'in* — always return, regardless of who died or who called off the wedding, so long as the items are still present.

### Woman Backs Out

The *chidush* comes now. *Hadra ba ee hi* — if she is the one who calls off the *nissu'in*, who backs out on her own initiative, then the equation changes dramatically. In that case, *hadra afilu kishara d'yarka* — even a bundle of vegetables must be returned. Even food that was consumed at the *seudat chatan*, even items entirely within the *asuyot livlot* category — everything must be repaid, because it was her decision to walk away. The finalization ordinarily accomplished by the *seudat chatan* is effectively nullified when the cancellation is her unilateral choice.

### Cheap Meat Valuation

However, Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: even in this case — where she bears responsibility and must repay even consumed food — *shamin lahen d'mei basar b'zol*, the repayment is calculated not at the price the groom paid for the food but at the price of inexpensive meat. *Ad kama — ad tilsa*: figure it at approximately one-third below what was actually paid.

This reflects a general halachic principle: when someone consumes another's food without having stolen it, under a reasonable assumption that they were entitled to it, and it subsequently turns out the entitlement was absent, the measure of unjust enrichment is calculated not at the market price of what was consumed but at what the consumer would themselves have spent on equivalent food. The luxury steaks provided at the celebration are not necessarily what the bride's family would have purchased for themselves, and so when computing what they owe back, we assess at the standard of inexpensive rather than premium food. That is the final *chidush* of the sugya: even when she is fully obligated to repay everything, the valuation is adjusted downward in keeping with this general principle of benefit calculation.

---

---

# Bava Batra 147

## Shechiv Mera Principles

### Institution Overview

After a brief excursion into the world of *shushbinot* and *sovlonot* — which arose in the context of determining how reciprocal gifts are handled when a father dies and the question of which brother receives them — the sugya returns to the fundamental issue of inheritance and finally arrives at the *mishnah* that directly introduces *matnat shechiv mera*, the deathbed bequest that functions as the rabbinic institution designed to play the role of a will. This represents the culmination of a long progression: the Torah's laws of inheritance, the modifications permitted to a dying man under the framework of Yochanan ben Broka, the role of inter vivos gifts, and now the full institution of *matnat shechiv mera* as a vehicle for bequeathing property outside the ordinary channels of *yerusha*.

### Words Create Kinyan

The first foundational principle of *matnat shechiv mera* is captured in the phrase *divrei shchiv mera k'chtuvim u'chemesurim dami* — the words of a deathbed declaration are considered as if written in a document and physically handed over. Whether the subject is movable property (*metaltelin*) or real estate, the spoken words of the *shechiv mera* function as a complete *kinyan*. No formal act of acquisition is required. That is the *chiddush* of the institution: the mere verbal expression, under the appropriate circumstances, creates a legally binding transfer.

### Void Upon Recovery

The second foundational principle — which follows almost as a corollary from the nature of the institution — is that the gift takes effect at death. Since the entire premise of the *matnat shechiv mera* is that the person believes he is about to die and is disposing of his property on that assumption, the *gemara* establishes the rule of *im amad chozer*: if he recovers from the illness, the gift is automatically voided. This is not merely a right to revoke; it is automatic nullification. The property reverts without any further act, because the condition underlying the entire transaction — the expectation of imminent death — has been rendered false by the recovery itself.

### Kol vs. Miktzat

A critical distinction governs how these two principles apply, and it turns on whether the *shechiv mera* is giving away all of his property (*kol nechasav*) or only a portion of it (*miktzat nechasav*). If he is dividing all of his property, the implication is unambiguous: he is doing so because he believes he is about to die. The totality of the disposition signals that this is genuinely a deathbed bequest.

But if he is dividing only part of his property, a problem arises. If he truly expects to die, why is he not dividing everything? One could answer that he intends the remainder to pass by ordinary *yerusha* to his children — and indeed we will see that the explicit designation of the remainder for the heirs may well bring such a case under the rubric of *kol nechasav*. But where it is truly *miktzat nechasav* with no such designation, the partiality of the disposition suggests that he does not view this as a final deathbed act, and accordingly the full force of the institution does not apply.

### Kinyan Requirements

The practical consequence of this distinction is as follows. When giving away all his property (*kol nechasav*), no *kinyan* is required — his words alone suffice. When giving away only part (*miktzat nechasav*), a *kinyan* is required, because the rabbinic dispensation that allows words alone to function as a transfer applies only where the context unmistakably signals a genuine deathbed disposition.

### Partial Gift Recovery

The distinction between *kol nechasav* and *miktzat nechasav* also bears on the question of *amad v'chozer*. For a gift of all one's property, recovery automatically voids the gift. For a gift of only part of one's property — where a *kinyan* was in any case required — recovery does not void the gift. Since the partial gift was treated essentially as an ordinary *kinyan* made while the person happened to be ill, it is governed by the normal rules of *kinyanim*: *amad v'eino chozer*, he recovered and the gift stands. The institution of *shechiv mera* in its full force — words without *kinyan* and automatic revocation upon recovery — applies only to *kol nechasav*.

---

## Mishnah: Shiyer Karka

### Mishnah Text

The *mishnah* addresses the case of a *shechiv mera* who writes away all of his property to others — *shechiv mera she-kasav kol nechasav l'acherim* — but leaves over a small parcel of land, *v'shiyer karka kol shehu*. The reservation of even a minimal piece of land is the operative act. The *mishnah* then pronounces: *matanaso kayemes* — his gift is valid. And crucially, as the *gemara* reads it, this validity holds even if he subsequently recovers (*amad*).

One might ask: why should leaving over a piece of land make any difference to the validity of the gift upon recovery? The answer lies in understanding precisely what issue the *mishnah* is addressing.

### Gift Valid with Land

The *gemara* reads the *mishnah*'s declaration that the gift is valid as speaking to the *amad* scenario — the case where the *shechiv mera* recovers. If he left over a piece of land, the gift remains valid even though he got better. The Rashbam notes explicitly (*v'hu hadin chilek al piv belo kesivah*) that the *mishnah*'s use of the word *she-kasav* does not restrict the case to one where a document was written — the same rule applies when he made his disposition orally. However, since the *mishnah* is discussing *shiyer karka kol shehu* — a case of *miktzat nechasav* — some formal act of *kinyan* is required, and the *kasav* reflects that some such act was performed.

### Invalid Without Land

Conversely, if he did not leave over any land — *aval lo shiyer karka kol shehu* — the gift is not valid in the event of recovery. This is the natural counterpart: a gift of *kol nechasav* with no reservation is subject to *im amad chozer*, and recovery automatically voids it.

### Amad vs. Kinyan

It is important to clarify that the *mishnah* here is addressing the *amad* question — what happens if he recovers — not the *kinyan* question. The *mishnah* is not saying that without *shiyer karka* the gift is categorically invalid; rather, it is saying that without *shiyer karka* the gift does not survive recovery. The two issues are analytically distinct, and the *mishnah* is speaking to the former.

### Inheritance Portion

A natural question arises from an earlier discussion: we had seen that one should not completely disinherit one's heirs, and that there is a principle discouraging the total diversion of one's estate away from the natural inheritors. If that principle is in force, it would seem that one would always retain at least something, and therefore pure *kol nechasav* cases would be rare. The *gemara* will address the precise definition of *kol nechasav* in the coming discussion, and it may well be that an explicit statement that the remainder goes to one's children can itself qualify as a form of *kol nechasav*. The relationship between *shiyer karka kol shehu* and these broader inheritance concerns will become clearer as the sugya unfolds.

---

## Umdana & Intent

### Who Holds Umdana?

The rule that recovery automatically voids the gift of *kol nechasav* rests on a particular legal principle: *azlinan batar umdana*, we assess the presumed intent of the giver. The rationale for voiding the gift upon recovery is not that the Rabbis simply decreed it as an arbitrary feature of the institution, but rather that we evaluate the *shechiv mera*'s frame of mind — he gave the gift because he thought he was going to die, and had he known he would recover, he never would have given it. The *gemara* now asks: which *tana* holds that we operate on the principle of *azlinan batar umdana*?

### Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya

Rav Nachman attributes this principle to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, citing a *braita*. The case: a man's son traveled overseas, and the father then heard that his son had died. Subsequently, the father gifted all his property to others. Afterward, the son returned alive. The *tana kama* holds that the gift is valid — *matnaso matana*. The sequence of events establishes no explicit condition; since the father never said his gift was contingent on the son's death, the principle of *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim* applies: unstated mental conditions are not legally operative, and the gift stands.

### Tana Kama vs. RSbM

Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya disagrees: *ein matnaso matana* — the gift is not valid. His reasoning: *she-ilu haya yodei she-b'no kayam, lo haya kosvan* — had the father known his son was alive, he would never have written the gift. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya is willing to void the transaction based on a reconstruction of the giver's presumed state of mind, notwithstanding the absence of an explicit condition. This is *azlinan batar umdana* in its purest form.

### Execution & Anticipation

Rav Sheshet offers an alternative attribution, locating the principle of *azlinan batar umdana* in a different *tana* entirely: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri. The *braita* cited involves the case of *hayotzei b'kolar* — a person being led out in chains to be executed by the Roman government — who says *kitvu get l'ishti*, write a *get* for my wife. The halachically precise formulation should have been *kitvu u'snu get l'ishti* — write and give — since a *get* takes effect only upon delivery, not mere writing. Yet because the context makes the intent self-evident, the word *kitvu* is read to include *u'snu*. This was then expanded to cover one who is departing on an overseas voyage or joining a caravan, and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri extends it further: even *af hamiskukan* — one who is critically ill — falls within this rule. Tosafot notes that even the earlier authorities in the *mishnah* agree to the basic principle of reading into the word *kitvu* the word *tnu*; Rabbi Shimon Shezuri simply extends the principle to a broader range of cases.

### Umdana & Devarim

This raises a fundamental tension: how does *azlinan batar umdana* — assessing presumed intent to override or modify a transaction — coexist with the principle of *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*, which holds that unstated mental conditions are legally inoperative? If we need everything to be explicit for a transaction to be binding, how can we void or condition a transaction based on what we presume was in someone's mind?

### Tosafot's Question

Tosafot raises precisely this question: *tzarich iyun l'shavecha hachamirosta b'devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim* — it requires analysis how the principle of *azlinan batar umdana* squares with the stringency of *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*. Tosafot refers the reader to the second chapter of Kiddushin, where the question is treated at length. One approach offered there is that the reconciliation depends on how self-evident the presumed intent is — where it is evident to all, it need not be stated; where it is not so evident, explicit statement is required.

### One-Sided Transactions

The best answer, attributed to the Rambam and the Tosafot Rid, is that *azlinan batar umdana* applies specifically to one-sided transactions — a *matana* or a *get*. In both cases, the other party is not giving up anything of their own; they are simply receiving. In a bilateral transaction, the other party cannot be bound by unstated conditions swimming in the mind of the first party — that is precisely why *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim* applies with full force. But where the transaction is essentially one-directional, where it is only the giver's or the husband's intent that is at stake, we can legitimately assess and reconstruct that intent. This distinction is reflected in the Rambam's formulations: in *Hilchos Mechira*, governing sales, *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim*; in *Hilchos Zechiya U'Matana*, governing gifts, *l'olam omdin da'as hanosein* — we always assess the intent of the one who gives.

### RN's Preference

The *gemara* then asks: why did Rav Nachman prefer Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya over Rabbi Shimon Shezuri as the source for the *umdana* principle? The answer is that the *get* case (*kitvu get l'ishti*) is structurally different from what we need. In the *get* case, we are using the person's presumed intent to fill in a missing word — to read *kitvu* as *kitvu u'snu*. We are supplementing what he said, not negating what he did. But in the case of the *shechiv mera* — where the gift is voided because of the father's presumed frame of mind — we are using *umdana* to negate and undo an act that was already performed. That is a far more powerful application of the principle, and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's case provides a much closer precedent.

### Evidence Requirement

Conversely, the *gemara* asks why Rav Sheshet did not use Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's case as his evidence. The answer: *umdana d'mokeach shani* — an *umdana* that is entirely self-evident is a special case. In the father-and-son scenario, it is absolutely clear to everyone that the father gave the gift only because he thought his son was dead. This is a uniquely obvious *umdana*. Rav Sheshet preferred to derive the principle from a case where the *umdana* is less immediately self-evident — such as the critically ill person who does not use the precise legal formulation when directing that a *get* be written — in order to establish that we apply *azlinan batar umdana* even in contexts where the presumed intent is not quite so transparent.

### Sick Person Braita

The *gemara* then introduces another *braita* to determine which *tana* it follows. The case involves a person who is ill and lying in bed (*choleh u'mutal b'mitah*), whom the people around him ask about his property — *nechasyecha l'mi* — to whom should his property go? He responds by revealing his assumption: he says he had always believed he had a son overseas but now understands he does not, or that he had assumed his wife was pregnant but now learns she is not, and on that basis he directs his property to a third party. Subsequently it emerges that his original assumption was correct — the son was alive, or the wife was indeed pregnant. The *gemara* asks: is this gift voided?

### Explicit Statement

The *gemara* considers whether this *braita* must be attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and not to the Rabbis. The answer is: even the Rabbis could agree here, because this case is categorically different from the father-and-son case where the *tana kama* held the gift valid. There, the father said nothing — his frame of mind was purely internal, and *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim* applied. Here, the sick person actually stated his assumption out loud: *savur hayiti she-ein li ben* — I believed I had no son. That verbal articulation accomplishes two things simultaneously. First, it removes any doubt about what his frame of mind actually was — we are not guessing; he told us. Second, and more significantly, it transforms what would otherwise be an internal, legally inoperative mental condition into something approaching an explicit statement of condition. It is no longer purely *devarim she-ba-lev*; he said it. The *gemara* reinforces this by noting that one might have thought he was merely expressing his feelings — venting his distress at having no heir — rather than formally conditioning his gift. The *gemara*'s conclusion is that we read his words as contextualizing and conditioning the gift, not as a mere emotional aside.

---

## Biblical Sources

### Torah Source Query

After establishing the mechanics and doctrinal underpinnings of *matnat shechiv mera*, the *gemara* turns to a foundational question: Rav Zeira asks in the name of Rav — *minayin l'matnat shechiv mera min hatorah* — where in the Torah do we find the basis for this institution? The question is significant because throughout the earlier discussion the institution has been described in rabbinic terms, yet now the *gemara* appears to be reaching for a biblical derivation.

### V'Ha'avartem

Rav Zeira's proposed derivation draws on the verse in the laws of inheritance (*Bamidbar* 27): *v'ha'avartem et nachalato levitto* — you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter (in the absence of sons). The *gemara* asks: is there another type of active transfer analogous to this one? *Ve'eizo zo — matnat shechiv mera*. The Rashbam explains the *diyuk*: the verse could simply have stated *nachalato levitto* without using any verb, yet it employs the active verb *v'ha'avartem* — you shall transfer — which implies an active, directed conveyance. Since *yerusha* in the normal case requires no active act on anyone's part (the property simply devolves at death), the use of an active verb hints at a context in which a person can take a more active role in directing where his property goes. This, the *gemara* suggests, is the biblical hint for *matnat shechiv mera*.

### V'Natattem

Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuha, derives the principle from a different verse in the same passage: *v'netatem et nachalato le'achiv* — you shall give his inheritance to his brothers (in the absence of daughters). The same question is posed: is there another form of *netinah* analogous to this one? And again the answer: *matnat shechiv mera*.

### Verse Selection

One might ask why each *amora* chose a different verse. The *gemara* addresses this directly. Why did Rav Nachman not use the verse with *v'ha'avartem*? Because that verse is needed for a different *drashah* — the teaching of Rabbi (Rebi). As the *braita* records: in all other cases where the *parasha* discusses who receives the inheritance, the verb used is *netinah* — giving. But specifically when discussing the inheritance of a daughter in the absence of sons, the verse uses the word *ha'avarah* — transfer. This signals that the transfer to a daughter is peculiar, because a daughter, upon marriage, may bring the property into another tribe through her husband or son who inherits her. The use of *ha'avarah* — implying diversion — alludes to the transfer of *nachalah* from one tribe to another. Accordingly, that verse is occupied with Rabbi's *drashah* and cannot simultaneously serve as the source for *matnat shechiv mera*. Conversely, Rav Zeira did not use *v'netatem* because it is simply the normal way the verse speaks (*orcha dikra hu*) — an unremarkable verb that carries no special implication.

### Chizkiyahu Case

The *gemara* then turns from legal texts to narrative sources in *Tanach*. Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya derives support from the following verse: *bayamim haheim chalah Chizkiyahu lamut vayavo eilav Yeshayahu ben Amot vayomer eilav ko amar Hashem tzav leveitecha ki met atah* — in those days Chizkiyahu fell ill and was about to die, and the prophet Yeshayahu came to him and said: command your household, for you will die and you will not live. The instruction to *tzav leveitecha* — command your household — implies that a verbal directive issued in the context of anticipated death carries binding force. One might object that narrative passages in *Nach* do not ordinarily generate halachic norms. The answer is that they function at least as *giluy milta* — a reflection of existing practice — demonstrating that deathbed verbal commands were understood to be effective.

### Achitofel Case

The *gemara* anticipates a further objection: Chizkiyahu was a king, and the effectiveness of his verbal command might be attributed to royal authority rather than to the legal institution of *matnat shechiv mera*. To address this, Rami bar Yechezkel cites the case of Achitofel: *va'Achitofel ra'ah ki lo na'astah atzato vayachavosh et hachamor vayelech el beito el iro vayetzav el beito vayechaneik* — Achitofel saw that his counsel was not followed, saddled his donkey, went home, commanded his household, and hanged himself. The phrase *vayetzav el beito* — he commanded his household — establishes that a private individual's deathbed verbal command (*betzava'ah be'alma*) is likewise effective.

### Narrative Evidence

However, this case raises its own complications. Achitofel was not on a deathbed in the conventional sense; he was anticipating death because he was about to take his own life. This raises the question of whether the institution of *matnat shechiv mera* requires that the person be actually ill and dying, or whether it extends to anyone who has a reasonable anticipation of imminent death — such as someone entering a dangerous situation from which he may not return. Furthermore, the narrative might reflect only societal practice, not a binding legal institution. The *gemara* notes that Achitofel's case involves only *betzava'ah be'alma* — a verbal command alone, without a formal *kinyan* — which is precisely the *chiddush* of *matnat shechiv mera*. Whether these narrative proofs establish a *d'Oraita* institution or merely reflect an existing rabbinic practice that the *tanna'im* then read back into the verses will be addressed shortly.

---

## Achitofel & Weather

### Three Commands

A *braita* records three things that Achitofel commanded his sons before his death. First: *al tehyu bemachloket* — do not engage in strife and conflict. Second: *al timr'du b'malchus beit David* — do not rebel against the House of David, though rebellions against other kingships may be permissible. Both of these pieces of advice reflect the lessons of Achitofel's own catastrophic experience: he had joined the rebellion of Avshalom against David and the entire enterprise had collapsed. Third: if the *Yom Tov* of *Atzeres* (Shavuot) is a clear day (*barur*), plant wheat.

What is striking is that the *gemara* is now reading *vayetzav el beito* not as referring to the legal disposition of property — which was the earlier reading in the context of *matnat shechiv mera* — but as an ethical will: these are the pieces of advice and guidance Achitofel wanted to leave his children, not legally binding transfers of property. The tradition of writing or speaking an ethical will before death — conveying one's values and wisdom to one's descendants — is a practice with deep roots, and Achitofel's three commands represent a notable early instance.

### Weather Signs

The third of Achitofel's commands — to plant wheat if *Atzeres* is clear — immediately generates a dispute. One authority says the sign is a clear day; another says it is a cloudy day. The Sages of Nehardea then resolve the apparent contradiction: it is neither a day of perfect clarity nor one of complete cloud cover. Rather, even a partially cloudy day on which a north wind is blowing and scattering the clouds — *bahil ve'ruach tzafonit menasheves bo* — that too qualifies as the favorable sign (*zehu barur*).

### Holy Day Signs

The *gemara* then reports that Rav Papa told Rav Ashi: we do not teach this tradition about planting wheat in the context of Achitofel's commands. We teach it as a teaching of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi. And in that formulation, the relevant day is not Shavuot but rather *motzei Yom Tov acharon shel Chag* — the conclusion of the final *Yom Tov* of Sukkot, which is Shemini Atzeret. On that day, everyone would look to the smoke rising from the wood pile on the altar in the *Beit HaMikdash* to observe in which direction the wind was blowing, since the direction of the wind on that day was understood to forecast the character of the coming year's rainfall and agricultural conditions. The association with Shemini Atzeret is more logically coherent on several levels: it is the time when prayer for rain (*tefillat geshem*) begins, it is when one is approaching the planting season, and the judgment for water — critical for all crops — is associated with the festival of Sukkot.

### Wind & Crops

The *gemara* then elaborates on the significance of each wind direction as observed at the *maarchah* on the *mizbeiach*. If the smoke inclines toward the north (meaning a south wind is blowing it there): *aniyim smeichim u'ba'alei batim atzeivim* — the poor rejoice and the property owners are distressed. The reasoning: *gishmei shana merubim u'peirot markivim* — plentiful rain will cause the fruit to be abundant but prone to rapid spoilage, forcing sellers to lower prices quickly. This benefits the poor who buy cheap, but harms property-owning farmers whose produce deteriorates before it can command a good price.

If the smoke inclines toward the south (a north wind): *aniyim atzeivim u'ba'alei batim smeichim* — the poor are distressed and the property owners rejoice. Rain will be scarce, fruit less abundant but durable, prices high and sustainable — advantageous to the propertied class but harmful to the poor.

If the smoke inclines toward the east (a west wind): *hakol smeichim* — everyone is happy, as this signals a balance: sufficient abundance and good storage conditions. If toward the west (an east wind): *hakol atzeivim* — everyone is distressed, as this apparently signals scarcity combined with poor storage.

### Wind & Crops

A contradiction emerges from another source. That source states: *mizrachit olam yafeh* — the east wind is always good; *maaravit olam kasha* — the west wind is always bad. This directly contradicts the earlier ruling in which the east wind (causing smoke to go west) was described as bad for all. The *gemara* resolves the north-south contradiction by means of the famous mnemonic: *shulchan batzafon u'menorah badarom* — the table (*shulchan*), which held bread made from wheat, was in the north of the *Mishkan*, and the *menorah*, fueled by olive oil, was in the south. Accordingly, the north wind benefits wheat, the south wind benefits olives — *hai marbi dideih v'hai marbi dideih*, each promotes its own. The east-west contradiction is resolved differently: *ha lan v'ha lehu* — one ruling applies in the Land of Israel and the other in Babylonia. The Rashbam notes that Babylonia received ample rainfall, making an excess of rain counterproductive there, while conditions in the Land of Israel were different; which wind direction was favorable therefore depended on where one lived.

### Annual Forecast

A *braita* cited by Abba Shaul generalizes the principle: if the *Yom Tov* of *Atzeres* is a clear day, it is a favorable sign for the entire year. Rav Zevid then adds: if the first day of Rosh Hashana is warm, the entire year will be warm; if cold, the entire year will be cold.

### High Priest Practice

The *gemara* asks: *lemai nafka mina* — what practical difference does this make? The answer: *b'tzeluta d'Kohen Gadol* — it bears on the prayer of the *Kohen Gadol*. The *Kohen Gadol* observes the weather conditions on Rosh Hashana and uses them to calibrate his prayers when he enters the *Kodesh HaKodashim* on Yom Kippur. Knowing what kind of year is anticipated, he can direct his petitions with greater specificity and intention — whether praying for rain to moderate a hot year or for warmth to temper a cold one.

---

## Rabbinic vs. Biblical

### Rava's Position

With the extended digression on weather signs concluded, the *gemara* returns to the fundamental question of the status of *matnat shechiv mera*. Rava cites Rav Nachman: *matnat shechiv mera miderabanan be'alma hi* — the institution of *matnat shechiv mera* is purely rabbinic, not biblical. The reason: *shema titrof da'ato* — lest his mind become confused, a concern for *tiruf hadaas*.

### Rashbam Explanations

The Rashbam offers two distinct explanations of what *tiruf hadaas* means in this context. The first: if the Rabbis were to require a formal *kinyan* as a condition of the gift's validity, the dying person might not succeed in executing it in time — as people approach death they often lose mental clarity, and by the time the required formalities could be arranged, the person might no longer be capable of performing them. The institution was therefore created to spare him this obstacle.

The second explanation — and the one more widely cited — is a concern not for the person's mental capacity but for his physical welfare. If the Rabbis were to insist that a formal *kinyan* is required and that the dying person's verbal declaration alone is insufficient, the resulting anxiety, distress, and agitation could actually harm his health and hasten his death. The rabbinic institution was therefore created out of compassion for his condition: by making his words legally effective without further formality, the Rabbis ensured that his affairs could be settled without subjecting him to the emotional and physical strain of formal legal proceedings.

### Medical Autonomy

This second explanation has been applied by Rav Moshe Feinstein in several *teshuvot* addressing the question of patient autonomy in medical halachah. The challenge is well known: if there is a *mitzvah* to preserve life (*pikuach nefesh*), on what basis can a patient refuse treatment? Rav Moshe Feinstein finds an opening through this very principle.
