Just as the Rabbis instituted *matnat shechiv mera* out of concern that frustrating the dying person's wishes would itself constitute a threat to his life through *tiruf hadaas*, so too in certain medical situations, overriding a patient's self-determination and subjecting him to treatment against his will may cause him such distress that it actually hastens his death. In those cases, patient autonomy is supported not by an independent right of self-determination but through the back door of *pikuach nefesh*: granting the patient a measure of control is itself a life-preserving measure.

### Challenge: Debt Transfer

The *gemara* challenges Rav Nachman's position that *matnat shechiv mera* is purely rabbinic by citing a ruling attributed to Rav Nachman himself. The challenge involves a teaching of Shmuel about the sale of a debt document (*hamocher shtar chov l'chavero*).

### Shtar Chov Mechanics

Shmuel's ruling: if Reuven sells to Michael the debt that Shimon owes him, and subsequently Reuven forgives Shimon the debt (*vachazar umachalo*), the debt is indeed forgiven — *machul* — even though Reuven had already sold the document to Michael. The reason lies in the conceptual structure of debt transfer in halachah. A debt is a personal obligation; Shimon does not owe money to Michael directly — he continues to owe it to Reuven. What Michael has purchased is effectively the right to collect the debt and retain the proceeds; Michael is, in essence, Reuven's designated collector. Since the debt is still fundamentally owed to Reuven, Reuven retains the legal capacity to forgive it, even after having sold the document to Michael. The Rashbam notes that Michael's remedy in such a case is to pursue Reuven for damages under the principle of *diney d'garmi* — Reuven sold him something and then rendered it worthless — but Shimon is no longer obligated to pay Michael. Shmuel adds: *va'afilu yoresh mochel* — even if Reuven dies and his son inherits the debt, the son (as the continuation of the father) likewise retains the capacity to forgive it, and Michael would thereby lose his claim.

### Shechiv Mera Power

However, Shmuel himself rules that if a *shechiv mera* gave the debt to Michael as a *matnat shechiv mera* — rather than selling it in the ordinary fashion — then *eino yachol limchol* — Reuven can no longer forgive the debt even while still alive, and his son cannot forgive it either. The gift of the debt through *matnat shechiv mera* transfers it in a fundamentally more powerful way than an ordinary sale.

### Yerusha Model

The *gemara* now draws the implication. The more powerful transfer achieved through *matnat shechiv mera* is explicable only if the institution functions on the model of *yerusha* — inheritance. When a person dies and his son inherits, the debt is not merely assigned for collection; the son becomes the direct obligee, and Shimon owes the money to the son himself. If *matnat shechiv mera* is modeled on *yerusha*, then when the *shechiv mera* gives the debt to Michael, Michael becomes the direct obligee — equivalent to a *yoresh* — and neither Reuven nor his son can forgive it. But if *matnat shechiv mera* is a purely rabbinic institution built on the model of ordinary *kinyan*, it should produce no greater transfer than the ordinary sale of a debt document, in which case Reuven and his son would retain the capacity to forgive.

### Rabbinic as Biblical

The *gemara* resolves this tension with a formulation that is striking in its precision: *eima d'Rabbanan v'asu'uhu k'shel Torah* — it may be rabbinic in origin, yet the Rabbis structured it and gave it the legal mechanics of a biblical institution. Even though *matnat shechiv mera* is *d'Rabbanan*, it was constructed as if it were *d'Oraita* — specifically, as if it were *yerusha*. The gift therefore operates with the force of inheritance: the recipient becomes the direct obligee of the debt, and neither the original creditor nor his heirs can subsequently forgive it away. This formulation — *d'Rabbanan v'asu'uhu k'shel Torah* — reflects a broader phenomenon in halachah where rabbinic institutions are deliberately engineered to replicate the mechanics of biblical law, without being themselves biblical in origin.

### Internal Shmuel

It is important to note the scope of this resolution. The analysis of the debt transfer and the conclusion that *matnat shechiv mera* operates with the mechanics of *yerusha* is advanced specifically to reconcile Shmuel's position with itself — it is an internal resolution of what might otherwise appear to be a contradiction within Shmuel's own rulings. Other *amoraim* may not accept Shmuel's position on debt transfers, and accordingly the broader question of whether *matnat shechiv mera* is *d'Oraita* or *d'Rabbanan* remains a genuine dispute among the *amoraim*, not foreclosed by this particular resolution.

---

---

# Bava Batra 148

## Matnat Shchiv Mera Intro

### De-Oraisa Status

The daf opens in the midst of a fundamental debate about the nature of *matnat shchiv mera*: is it *de-oraisa* or *de-rabbanan*? Tosafos clarifies that when the Gemara uses the term *de-oraisa* in this context, it may not mean strictly biblical in origin — and yet the Gemara's own framing seems to pull in that direction.

### Shmuel Debt Transfer

The Gemara raises Shmuel's ruling on debt transfer as the crux of the difficulty. Shmuel holds that if the original creditor sells a *shtar chov*, he retains the ability to annul the debt through *mechila*. However, if he transferred the *shtar chov* via *matnat shchiv mera*, he loses that power of annulment. The Gemara presses: does this not indicate that *matnat shchiv mera* carries *de-oraisa* weight? If it were merely rabbinic, how could it operate with greater finality than a standard sale?

### Yerusha Model Foundation

The more satisfying explanation — and the one the discussion gravitates toward — is that the argument for *de-oraisa* is really an argument about the conceptual model underlying *matnat shchiv mera*. If *matnat shchiv mera* operates on the model of *kinyan*, the standard mechanisms of transaction apply: just as a creditor can annul a debt transferred by ordinary sale, so too by *matnat shchiv mera*. But if *matnat shchiv mera* is modeled after *yerusha* — inheritance — then the recipient stands in the position of an heir. And just as a son who inherits a debt owed to his father cannot have that debt annulled by the original creditor, so too the recipient of a *matnat shchiv mera* cannot have the transferred obligation undone. The force of the *de-oraisa* claim, then, is really a claim about which paradigm governs.

### Gemara Resolution

The Gemara resolves the tension by concluding that *matnat shchiv mera* is *de-rabbanan*, but the Rabbis consciously modeled it after *yerusha* rather than after standard *kinyan*. This distinction carries significant halakhic weight and will shape the entire subsequent discussion. Whether this means the Rabbis gave it the *force* of a *de-oraisa* institution, or that they modeled its internal logic after *yerusha*, the practical consequence is the same: for certain purposes, *matnat shchiv mera* behaves more like inheritance than like a commercial transaction.

---

## Abstract Transfers

### Rav Nachman Ruling

Rav Nachman now rules on a case that tests the limits of *matnat shchiv mera*. A *shchiv mera* on his deathbed says: "Let Reuven live in this house" (*yeidor ploni b'vayis zeh*), or "Let Reuven eat the fruit of this palm tree" (*yochal ploni peiros de-ikal zeh*). These seem like entirely natural expressions of a dying man's wishes — the kind of instruction one might imagine in any ethical will or final directive. And yet Rav Nachman rules: *lo amar klum* — these declarations have no legal effect.

Why not? Because neither statement transfers any concrete property. Dwelling in a house is an abstraction; the right to future fruit is a *davar shelo ba le-olam*, something that does not yet exist in the world. The family may choose to honor the dying man's wishes out of respect for his memory, but no legally cognizable gift has been made. The *shchiv mera* has not transferred anything.

### Property Transfer Requir…

To achieve the desired result, Rav Nachman specifies the required formulation: *tenu bayis zeh le-ploni ve-yeidor bo* — "Give Reuven this house so that he may live in it"; *tenu de-ikal zeh le-ploni ve-yochal peirosav* — "Give Reuven this palm tree so that he may eat its fruit." Once actual ownership of the object is transferred, the incidental benefits — dwelling, fruit — follow automatically. The explicit statement of purpose (*ve-yeidor bo*, *ve-yochal peirosav*) is not strictly necessary once ownership is conveyed, but the ownership transfer itself is indispensable. An intermediate option also exists — conveying the tree *le-peirosav*, transferring ownership for the specific purpose of its fruit — but even here, some concrete property right must be the subject of the transfer.

### Conditional Language Deb…

This raises a genuinely difficult question: can a *matnat shchiv mera* include conditional language — for instance, giving Reuven the house *letzorech dira*, for the purpose of dwelling, in a way that might limit what Reuven can do with it? The question cuts to the heart of the conceptual debate. A *kinyan* can certainly include conditions: one can transfer property *al tnai*, with a stipulation that reverts ownership if a condition is unmet. But a *yerusha* cannot be conditioned — one cannot inherit *b'tnai*. If *matnat shchiv mera* operates on the *yerusha* model, conditional transfers may be structurally unavailable. This remains an open and genuinely interesting question.

### Tanu Rabbanan

The Gemara now introduces a *braita* that, in the view of the discussion, demonstrates Rav Nachman's broader principle: *milta de-ita b'vari ita b'shchiv mera* — something that can be accomplished by a healthy person (*bari*) can be accomplished by a *shchiv mera*; *milta de-leita b'vari leita b'shchiv mera* — something a healthy person cannot do, a *shchiv mera* cannot do either. Giving over future fruit that does not yet exist is something a *bari* cannot accomplish. It remains a *davar shelo ba le-olam*, and the special status of *matnat shchiv mera* — which eliminates the need for a formal act of *kinyan* — does not transform the institution into some superhuman *kinyan* that overcomes all other halakhic limitations. It simply means that the words themselves function as the act. All other restrictions of the standard *kinyan* framework remain in place.

---

## Debt Transfer Power

### Rava Debt Transfer

Rava, citing Rav Nachman, now introduces what appears to be a direct challenge to this principle. A *shchiv mera* declares: "Give my debt — the money Reuven owes me — to Shimon." No *shtar chov* changes hands. There is no physical document, no formal act. And yet the ruling is that this transfer is effective. This is a striking Gemara. Even in the case of *shtar chov* transfer — where at least a physical document representing the debt is conveyed — the mechanism is already halakhically complex, requiring specific procedures to make the piece of paper constitute a genuine transfer of the underlying obligation. Here, there is not even a *shtar*. The debt is a purely abstract entity. A *bari* could not transfer a debt this way. And yet, by *matnat shchiv mera*, it works. This seems to contradict directly the principle just established: *milta de-leita b'vari leita b'shchiv mera*.

### Rav Pappa Yerusha Answer

Rav Pappa offers an elegant resolution. *Ho'il ve-yoresh yorsha* — since an heir inherits a debt. When a person dies, the money owed to the father passes to the sons, even if there is no *shtar*, even if the debt is a purely abstract obligation. The sons become the party to whom the debt is owed by operation of *yerusha*, not through any *kinyan*. So when a *shchiv mera* designates Shimon to receive the debt, he is in effect saying: Shimon is my heir with respect to this obligation. And since an heir inherits debts — without a *shtar*, without any formal act — *matnat shchiv mera*, modeled as it is on *yerusha*, can accomplish the same thing.

This answer is internally coherent and beautifully consistent with the earlier discussion. It also explains why, as Shmuel ruled, the original creditor cannot annul the debt after transferring it by *matnat shchiv mera*: the recipient stands in the position of the heir, and the debt is now owed directly to him. Crucially, however, this *yerusha* model does not extend infinitely. An heir does not inherit just the fruit of a tree without inheriting the tree itself. An heir does not inherit just the right to dwell in a house without inheriting the house. So the *yerusha* model explains the power of *matnat shchiv mera* to transfer debts while simultaneously preserving the earlier ruling that future fruit cannot be transferred in abstraction from the tree.

### Rav Acha Alternative

Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika offers an alternative approach that does not invoke the *yerusha* model at all. He maintains that even without *matnat shchiv mera*, a debt can in fact be transferred between healthy parties under certain circumstances — specifically through the rabbinic mechanism of *ma'amad sheloshtan*, the three-party transaction. Rav Huna in the name of Rav rules: if Reuven tells Shimon, "The hundred dinars you owe me — give them to Leah," and all three parties are present simultaneously, Leah acquires the debt and Reuven is no longer owed anything. This is already an established rabbinic *kinyan*. The *chiddush* of *matnat shchiv mera* is that it functions without requiring a formal *ma'aseh kinyan* — the words of the *shchiv mera* substitute for the act. By the same logic, just as *ma'amad sheloshtan* can transfer a debt among healthy parties, *matnat shchiv mera* — which is at least as powerful as any standard *kinyan* — can transfer a debt as well.

### Debt Transfer Conclusion

Both models thus remain viable. Whether *matnat shchiv mera* operates on the *yerusha* model or on the *kinyan* model, it can accomplish a debt transfer. The two approaches converge on this result while diverging in their reasoning — and the divergence matters: the *yerusha* model additionally explains why *mechila* is ineffective after such a transfer, whereas the *kinyan* model, standing alone, would not. What both models agree on is that *matnat shchiv mera* is not a blanket override of all halakhic limitations. It cannot transfer future fruit that does not yet exist, because neither *yerusha* nor any recognized *kinyan* can accomplish that. The institution has real but bounded power.

---

## Property Splitting

### Tree/Fruit Split Question

The Gemara now poses a more refined question (*iba'ya lehu*): what is the *halacha* if a *shchiv mera* assigns a palm tree to one person and its fruit to another? This question is read here following the approach of Tosafos rather than the Rashbam, whose reading is considerably more complex. The setup is this: we just ruled that a *shchiv mera* cannot give someone just the fruit of a tree, since the fruit does not yet exist and is a *davar shelo ba le-olam*. And yet, in the present case, the *shchiv mera* is not simply saying "give Reuven the fruit" — he is distributing the tree and its fruit as two separate items to two separate recipients. Perhaps when he designates the fruit to a second person, he actually means to convey the *makom peiri* — the place on the branches from which the fruit will grow — a concrete piece of the tree itself. The question is: *shiyer mekom peirot o lo shiyer?* Has the *shchiv mera* actually retained and conveyed a partial ownership interest in the tree, or is he doing nothing more than designating future fruit — which is no gift at all?

### Makom Peiri Principle

The concept of *makom peiri* is the critical analytical tool here. The question is not merely about what the *shchiv mera* intended but about what his words can legally accomplish. If designating the fruit to a second recipient is understood as conveying a portion of the tree — the physical location from which the fruit will emerge — then the transfer is of a concrete object and is valid. If it is understood as nothing more than granting entitlement to future fruit as an abstraction, then it remains a *davar shelo ba le-olam* and confers nothing. The challenge is determining which reading applies, and the Gemara suggests the answer may depend on who the designated recipient is.

### Self-Interest Distinction

Rav Amram citing Rav Nachman resolves the ambiguity by drawing a distinction based on the identity of the recipient. *Im timtza lomar dekel le-echad u-feirotav le-acher lo hashayir makom peiri* — if the *shchiv mera* splits the tree to one person and the fruit to someone else, we do not interpret his words as retaining or conveying the *makom peiri*. He is simply attempting to give the other person the future fruit, which does not exist yet, and the transfer fails. Charlie, as it were, gets nothing.

But *dekel le-echad ve-shayir peirotav l'atzmo* — if the *shchiv mera* gives the tree away and retains the fruit for himself, we do interpret that retention as constituting a genuine retention of *makom peiri*. The *shchiv mera* is treated as having held back a partial ownership interest in the tree itself, sufficient to sustain his entitlement to the fruit. *Mai ta'ama? Kol l'gabei nafshei b'ayin yafa meshayer* — when it concerns one's own interests, a person tends to retain more generously for himself. There is a greater presumption that the words carry full legal weight when the speaker is preserving something for himself than when he is attempting to confer an abstract benefit on a third party. One might also frame this differently: since the *shchiv mera* began as owner of the entire tree, it takes a clearer act of transfer to fully divest him of it; when his words are ambiguous, the inertia of ownership operates in his favor.

### House/Upper Floor Case

Rav Abba reports to Rav Ashi that this same distinction between conveying to another and retaining for oneself is actually taught in connection with a different case altogether — a ruling of Reish Lakish. Reish Lakish holds that if someone sells a house to another and says *al menat she-diyuta eliyona sheli* — "on condition that the upper story remains mine" — the seller retains the upper floor. The question then raised is whether selling the ground floor to one person and the upper story to a different person is equivalent, or whether there is a meaningful difference.

The Gemara rules: *im timtza lomar beita le-chad ve-dyuta le-chad lo havei shiyur* — if you divide the ground floor and upper story between two different recipients, you are not retaining any additional rights. But *chutz mi-dyuta havei shiyur* — if you are selling the house and explicitly reserving the upper story for yourself, that reservation carries additional air rights, including the right to extend protrusions (*zizin*) from the wall, following the view of Rav Zavid. The extra explicitness of the self-reservation language signals a broader retention. And the Gemara notes an analogy: *keivan de-amar chutz mi-peroseha makom peirot shiyer* — when a person declares "except for its fruit," perhaps we should similarly read that as a retention of *makom peirot*. That said, the analogy is imperfect — in the house case, the seller could have remained silent about the upper floor since the default rule (*mokher et ha-bayis lo mokher et ha-aliya*) would have protected it automatically, making the explicit reservation carry additional legal weight — whereas no such default operates in the tree case. The parenthetical comparison in the Gemara text is accordingly somewhat strained.

### Concrete Transfer Rule

The upshot of the entire discussion is a clean governing principle: even a *shchiv mera*, who possesses the power to transfer debts that a *bari* cannot transfer through ordinary *kinyan*, cannot transfer the fruit of a tree without transferring the tree itself. The extra power of *matnat shchiv mera* is real but specific: it can accomplish what *yerusha* accomplishes, and it can accomplish what *kinyan* mechanisms like *ma'amad sheloshtan* accomplish. What it cannot do is conjure a valid transfer of something that is neither concrete nor inheritable. If, however, the *shchiv mera* is retaining fruit for himself rather than conveying it to another, his words will be interpreted generously to preserve a meaningful ownership interest in the underlying property.

---

## Kol/Miktzat Nechasav

### Kol Nechasav Requirement

Rav Yosef bar Minyumi citing Rav Nachman now introduces the next major parameter of *matnat shchiv mera*. The two distinctive features of *matnat shchiv mera* — that words function as *kinyan* without any formal act, and that *amad chozer*, the gift reverts if the *shchiv mera* recovers — apply only when the gift is *kol nechasav*, all of the *shchiv mera*'s property. When a *shchiv mera* gives away only *miktzat nechasav*, a portion of his property, the gift is governed by ordinary *kinyan* rules. A formal act of *kinyan* is required, and if the *shchiv mera* recovers, the gift stands: *amad eino chozer*. The rationale is that a person who gives away only part of his property is not acting from the desperation of one who believes he is dying and has no further use for his possessions — he is making a regular gift that happens to occur while he is ill. The unique rabbinic institution applies only when the *shchiv mera* has divested himself of everything.

### Mechaleik vs. Nimlach

The practical application of this principle becomes complicated when a *shchiv mera* distributes his property not in a single statement but sequentially — giving one thing to Reuven, then the next day something to Shimon, and so on until all is distributed. The question is whether this sequential process is to be read as *k'mechaleik* — as a single unified act of distributing all one's property — or *b'nimlach* — as a series of separate reconsidered decisions, each of which constitutes only *miktzat* at the time it was made.

### Last Recipient Status

The *nafka mina* is significant. If the process is treated as *k'mechaleik* — one continuous act of comprehensive distribution — then every recipient's gift has *matnat shchiv mera* status: no *kinyan* is required and *amad chozer* applies to all. If, however, it is treated as *b'nimlach* — separate sequential decisions — then the early recipients received only *miktzat* at the time of their gifts, making those ordinary *kinyanim* that require a formal act and are not reversed by recovery. Only the final recipient, who received whatever was left when everything else had already been given away, received *kol nechasav* at the moment of his gift and thus holds a genuine *matnat shchiv mera* subject to *amad chozer*.

The Gemara attempts to provide a working standard: *stamei d'shchiv mera ma'ayan b'reisha ve-hadar yahiv* — typically, a *shchiv mera* thinks through his entire distribution in advance and only then begins allocating. If that is so, even a multi-day process of gifting reflects a single prior decision, and the *mechaleik* category applies. The Gemara acknowledges, however, that this standard is difficult to apply with confidence in practice — and the related question of whether a given *shchiv mera* even has the legal sophistication to frame his gifts correctly remains a genuine practical concern.

### Hidden Assets Concern

Rav Nachman raises what seems at first to be a devastating objection. Even when a *shchiv mera* appears to have distributed all his property, how can we ever be confident that we are truly in the category of *kol nechasav*? Perhaps he holds assets in another location — a forgotten account, an investment buried in paperwork, some property elsewhere. *Chashinan shema yesh lo nechasim b'medina acheret* — we must worry that he has property in another jurisdiction. If this concern is taken seriously, it would mean that virtually every case falls into *miktzat nechasav*, effectively eliminating the category of *kol nechasav* — and with it, the institution of *amad chozer* — almost entirely.

### Explicit Language Soluti…

Rav Chama resolves the difficulty: the category of *kol nechasav* is established when the *shchiv mera* explicitly uses the language *kol nechasai* — "all my property." When he frames his gift with that phrase, the hidden-assets concern is set aside because the gift is self-defining: whatever he owns, all of it, is being transferred. The concern about unknown assets does not override an explicit declaration of totality.

The Rashbam also cites a view in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel that extends this further: even when the *shchiv mera* specifies particular items — this house to one person, this vehicle to another, this account to a third — he may still achieve *kol nechasav* status by adding the clause that this constitutes all his property. Such a formulation combines the specificity of concrete itemization with the triggering language of comprehensive transfer. This approach has considerable practical appeal, since it allows a *shchiv mera* to be maximally concrete while still invoking the full protection of the institution. The Rashbam himself does not endorse this reading, though his precise objection is not entirely clear.

---

## Chazara B'Miktzat

### Retraction Question

The final major question of the daf: *chazara b'miktzat havi chazara b'kula o lo?* A *shchiv mera* has declared all his property to Reuven — a textbook *matnat shchiv mera*. The next day, he says that Shimon should receive the car. He has not said "I am revoking my prior gift." He has simply redirected one item. Is this partial modification a retraction of everything — *chazara b'kula* — leaving Reuven with nothing and Shimon with only the car? Or is it a limited revision — *chazara b'miktzat* — leaving Reuven with everything except the car and giving Shimon the car?

The *nafka mina* is concrete: if it is *chazara b'kula*, Reuven receives nothing and the original gift is entirely voided. If it is only *chazara b'miktzat*, Reuven retains approximately ninety-five percent of the estate and only the car shifts to Shimon. The further relevance of the principle *daitiki mevatelet daitiki* — a later will annuls an earlier one — frames the analysis: whenever a *shchiv mera* issues a new directive, it supersedes prior directives. The question is how broadly a new directive sweeps when it addresses only one item.

### Braita Evidence

The Gemara cites a *braita* that appears to resolve the question directly. *Kulam le-rishon u-v'miktzatam le-sheni — sheni kana, rishon lo kana.* When the *shchiv mera* first gave everything to the first recipient and subsequently redirected some portion to a second recipient, the second recipient acquires his portion and the first recipient acquires nothing. This seems to be a clear ruling of *chazara b'kula*: the partial modification to the second recipient completely voids the original gift to the first.

### Retention Hypothesis

The Gemara initially resists this reading. Perhaps, it suggests, the *braita* is not a case of *amad* followed by *chazara b'kula*, but rather a case where the *shchiv mera* recovered (*amad*) after the sequential gifts. Under that reading, Reuven still holds approximately ninety-five percent of the estate as a *matnat shchiv mera*, and Shimon holds his five percent — but if the *shchiv mera* recovered, the *amad* principle would reverse Reuven's gift (*amad chozer*) since it was *kol nechasav*, while Shimon's gift would survive as *miktzat nechasav* — a regular *kinyan* not undone by recovery. This reading avoids the conclusion that a partial modification produces *chazara b'kula*.

The Gemara supports this hypothesis by reference to the *seifa* of the *braita*: *miktzatan le-rishon ve-chulan le-sheni — rishon kana, sheni lo kana.* When a small gift was made first to Reuven, and subsequently everything remaining was given to Shimon, Reuven's gift stands and Shimon's does not. The Gemara reasons that this *seifa* must be a case of *amad*: if the *shchiv mera* died, both gifts would be valid and there would be no basis to deny Shimon his gift. Only if he recovered does it make sense that Shimon's gift — which was *kol nechasav* at the time it was given — reverts, while Reuven's earlier *miktzat* gift, a standard *kinyan*, remains valid.

### Amad Question

Rav Yimar presses Rav Ashi: if the *seifa* can be explained through *amad*, why not similarly explain the *reisha*? If *chazara b'miktzat* is not a *chazara b'kula*, then the *reisha* — where everything was given first and a little redirected to a second person — should also be resolvable through *amad*: the second person's *miktzat* gift remains (it was a standard *kinyan*), while the first person's *kol nechasav* gift reverts due to *amad chozer*. So neither the *sheni* losing nor the *rishon* losing requires *chazara b'kula*. But then the Gemara realizes the problem with this reasoning: if the original gift to Reuven (*kol nechasav*) and the subsequent gift to Shimon (*miktzat*) are both present and *amad* reverses the *kol nechasav* gift while preserving the *miktzat* gift, the entire estate should be divided accordingly — roughly ninety-five percent to Reuven reverting, five percent to Shimon standing. The *rishon* should not be left with zero. And yet the *braita* says *rishon lo kana* — the first recipient gets nothing. The *amad* explanation of the *reisha* cannot work unless one accepts that the partial modification to Shimon completely voided the prior gift to Reuven.

### Final Resolution

The Gemara concludes: *ve-hilcheta, chazara b'miktzat havi chazara b'kula.* Partial modification is total retraction. When a *shchiv mera* who has given all his property to one person subsequently redirects even a single item to someone else, the original comprehensive gift is entirely nullified. The first recipient receives nothing. The second recipient's gift, now a *miktzat nechasav*, is a standard *kinyan* — valid regardless of whether the *shchiv mera* lives or dies. And the *seifa* of the *braita* is accordingly confined to a case of *amad*: only when the *shchiv mera* recovered does the second person's *kol nechasav* gift revert, while the first person's earlier *miktzat* gift stands as a regular *kinyan*.

The practical implication of *chazara b'miktzat havi chazara b'kula* is striking and worth emphasizing: a *shchiv mera* who wishes to protect the integrity of a comprehensive gift cannot make any subsequent modification, however minor, without completely destroying the original gift and starting over. Conversely, if he wishes to revise, a single redirection of one item is sufficient to wipe the slate clean. The institution of *matnat shchiv mera* is as fragile as it is powerful — words both create it and dissolve it.

---

---

# Bava Batra 149

## Intro: Matnat Shchiv Mera

### Kol vs. Miktzat Nechasav

Today's daf is 149, and we continue our treatment of the different parameters of *matnat shchiv mera*. Yesterday's discussion centered on the fundamental distinction that determines whether a gift falls within the rabbinic category of *matnat shchiv mera*: namely, whether it constitutes *kol nechasav*, a gift of all one's assets, or *miktzat nechasav*, a gift of only some of one's assets. In the case of *kol nechasav*, the rabbinic institution of *matnat shchiv mera* applies, meaning that no formal *kinyan* is required and the operative principle of *amar chozer* — that if the *shchiv mera* recovers he may retract the gift — is in force.

### Amar Chozer Principle

The Gemara continued to probe the boundary between *kol nechasav* and *miktzat nechasav*, noting that even when a gift appears to involve all one's assets, there may be property whose existence is unknown, which would place many more situations within the category where the gift cannot be retracted upon recovery. The Gemara also addressed the more technical question of whether, when a *shchiv mera* gives away everything and then retracts, the retraction is full or partial — with all the attendant implications for which situations involve a straightforward *kinyan* and which involve the institution of *matnat shchiv mera*.

## Hedkesh, Hefker, Tzedakah

### Hedkesh Case

The Gemara now poses a series of questions beginning with the case of *hedkesh*: a person on his deathbed declares that all his property should be sanctified to the *Beis Hamikdash*. The question — *hikdish kol nechasav ve'amad mahu* — is whether, if he recovers, the principle of *amar chozer* applies and he may retract, or whether the dedication to *hedkesh* stands.

Two considerations pull in opposite directions. On one side: *kol lgabei hekdesh gamar u'makni* — perhaps, when it comes to the *Beis Hamikdash*, the person fully intends the dedication to take effect regardless of whether he survives. On the other side: *kol lgabei nafshei lo gamar u'makni* — at the end of the day, the person has his own financial needs, and we may assume he would not wish to be left penniless upon recovery. The Gemara leaves this unresolved.

### Hefker Case

The next case asks whether the same analysis applies when a *shchiv mera* declares *hefker* — that all his property should be ownerless, available to anyone who takes it. Here the argument for the dedication standing is framed somewhat differently: *keivan de'af le'aniym k'ashirim gamar u'makni* — since he is making his property available even to the poor, who are genuinely in need, perhaps his intent is wholehearted regardless of whether he survives. Against this: *kol lgabei nafshei lo gamar u'makni* — he too has his own needs, and if he recovers, we assume he did not intend for the renunciation to be irrevocable. Again, the Gemara leaves this unresolved.

### Tzedakah Case

The third case involves a *shchiv mera* who distributes all his property directly to the poor — *chilek kol nechasav le'aniym mahu*. The argument that this gift should stand unconditionally is strongest here: *tzedakah vadai migmar gamar u'makni* — when giving directly to the poor, who are genuinely destitute, surely his intention is complete and irrevocable. Against this, again: *kol lgabei nafshei lo gamar u'makni* — even charity does not override his own survival needs. The Gemara gives a *teiku*: the question is unresolved in all three cases.

### Psychology & Rashbam

How one reads the progression of these three cases is itself a matter of dispute. The natural reading of the Gemara suggests an escalating presumption in favor of the gift's irrevocability: even if we assume the *shchiv mera* would retract in the case of *hedkesh*, and even if we assume the same for *hefker*, perhaps by *tzedakah* — where the poor are directly and immediately helped — he genuinely intends the gift to stand. The Gemara's language for the *tzedakah* case, *tzedakah vadai migmar gamar u'makni*, sounds very much like the strongest argument in favor of irrevocability.

The Rashbam reads the progression in the opposite direction: even if we assume by *hekdesh* that the person wants the sanctification to stand, and even if we assume the same for *hefker*, perhaps by *tzedakah* he would ultimately want to retain his assets if he recovers. This reading does not sit easily with the Gemara's language. The underlying question — to which of these causes is a person psychologically most committed, to the point of being willing to part with his assets even upon recovery? — is genuinely interesting. One might observe that people often give more generously to prestigious institutions than to the poor, which would support reading the *tzedakah* case as the one where the person is least likely to have fully committed. But the Gemara's own language points the other way.

A student raised the question of whether *hedkesh* is a special case because, unlike a gift to the poor or a declaration of *hefker*, sanctification takes effect through speech alone, much as the *shchiv mera*'s words themselves effect a transfer. In response, it was noted that *hefker* similarly takes effect through speech, and that the entire force of *divrei shchiv mera* is precisely that his words function like an act of *kinyan* — so the distinction does not ultimately change the analysis in a clean way. A further version of these questions is cited more tersely — *hikdish kol nechasav mahu, hifkir kol nechasav mahu, chilek kol nechasav la'aniyim mahu, teiku* — and while it omits the arguments on each side, the fuller version better conveys the reasoning. What emerges from the discussion, in any case, is that *divrei shchiv mera* have legal force even in these unusual contexts — *hedkesh*, *hefker*, and gifts to the poor — sufficient to raise the question of whether the full transfer has been effected.

## Gift vs. Inheritance Lan…

### Valid Gift Terms

Rav Sheshet teaches that if a *shchiv mera* uses any of the following terms in his *tzava'ah* — *yitol*, *yizke*, *yachzik*, *yikne* — these are all valid formulations of a gift (*kulam lashon matanah hen*) and effect a proper *matnat shchiv mera*.

### Inheritance Language

A *baraita* adds that even the terms *yachsin* and *yeiraish* — both expressions drawn from the language of inheritance — are valid. This raises an important conceptual question: is *matnat shchiv mera* fundamentally a gift, or a pseudo-inheritance? The question has two dimensions — one concerns how the *shchiv mera* must frame his transfer, and the other concerns how the halakha treats its effects. We have already seen ways in which *matnat shchiv mera* operates like an inheritance, such as its capacity to transfer a loan; we will continue to see this. But does the person on his deathbed have to use the language of a *matanah*, even if the legal effect is structured like a *yerushah*?

### Rabbi Yochanan Exception

The Gemara qualifies the *baraita*'s ruling: *bera'uy leyorsho Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka hi*. The inheritance language is not a standard formulation for *matnat shchiv mera* in general; it is effective only within the framework of Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, who holds that a *shchiv mera* may use inheritance language when directing his estate to someone who qualifies as an heir in some degree. Within that view, there are further questions about whether the person must be a first-order heir or whether a more distant heir may be elevated to primary status — but the Gemara's point here is that inheritance language as a vehicle for *matnat shchiv mera* belongs to Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka's position, not to the standard halakhic framework. If we do not rule in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, the *shchiv mera* must use language of *matanah*, not *yerushah*.

This does not, however, close the question of whether we conceptualize the legal impact of *matnat shchiv mera* as ultimately resembling a *yerushah* or a *matanah*. The language required is that of *matanah*; but the structure of its effects, as we have already begun to see and will continue to see, has features that align with *yerushah*. It is a genuine hybrid. The distinction matters practically as well — a student noted that in many legal systems gifts and inheritances are taxed differently, and within halakha the rights of a widow and daughters to the estate differ depending on whether property was gifted, sold, or transmitted through inheritance.

## Ambiguous Benefit Langua…

### Yehana Bahen Question

The Gemara turns to a series of ambiguous formulations used by a *shchiv mera* and asks whether they constitute a full transfer. If the dying person says *yehana bahen* — let Ploni derive benefit from my property — what does this mean? Does it mean that Ploni should own the property outright, so that ownership itself is the source of his benefit? Or does it mean merely that Ploni should be allowed to derive some benefit — use the property periodically, for instance — without owning it?

### Other Ambiguous Terms

The same question applies to several related expressions. *Yeiraeh bahen* — let him be seen with the property — does this mean he should be recognized as the owner, or merely that he should have some occasion to appear with it? *Yaamod bahen* — let him stand upon it, in the sense of relying on it as a foundation — does this mean the property should be his, as one stands on and relies on one's own possessions, or does it merely mean some form of material support? *Yishaein bahen* — let him lean upon it — similarly: does this connote full ownership and support, or a more limited benefit?

### Teiku & Lo Kana

The Gemara leaves all of these formulations unresolved: *teiku*. The practical halakhic consequence, however, is clear. The Rambam rules *lo kana* — the recipient does not acquire — and the *Shulchan Aruch* in *Choshen Mishpat* 253:2 concurs, ruling straightforwardly *lo kana*. It is striking that a *teiku* resolves here in a definitive *lo kana* rather than a hedged position, though the logic is discernible: the *yorshim* are the *muchzak*, and the rabbinic institution of *matnat shchiv mera* should not be extended to ambiguous formulations without a clear basis. The resolution is stated without qualification, as a definitive ruling rather than merely a probabilistic outcome of doubt.

## Sale of All Assets

### Machar Kol Nechasav

The Gemara now asks a question one can readily imagine arising in practice: *machar kol nechasav mahu* — what is the rule if a *shchiv mera* sells all of his assets and then recovers? Does *amar chozer* apply, such that he can undo all the sales?

The grounds for *amar chozer* in standard *matnat shchiv mera* are rooted in *amdinan dateih* — we assess the person's intent and determine that he acted as he did only because he expected to die. If that assessment underlies the entire framework, then perhaps a *shchiv mera* who liquidates all his assets on the assumption of imminent death should similarly be able to reverse those transactions upon recovery.

### Devarim Shebalev Issue

Two powerful objections, however, cut against this. First, a sale is a two-sided transaction. The entire rationale for *amar chozer* — relying on the *shchiv mera*'s unexpressed intent — depends on the principle that in one-sided transactions, such as a *matanah* or a *get*, we may give legal weight to what was in the person's heart. But *devarim shebalev einam devarim* — unspoken conditions of the heart have no legal force — is precisely the rule that governs bilateral transactions, where a counterparty has entered the transaction in good faith without having stipulated to any condition of reversal. To undo a purchase because of the seller's undisclosed intent seems fundamentally unfair to the buyer.

Second, and relatedly, a person who has liquidated assets has not lost wealth — he simply holds it in a different form. He still has money with which to support himself and to leave to his heirs; it is simply now cash rather than property. There is no obvious harm to reverse.

Against these objections, one might argue that when everyone dealing with a *shchiv mera* knows his condition, the circumstances function not as *devarim shebalev* — purely private intentions — but as *devarim shebalev kol adam*, matters so universally understood that they operate more like explicit stipulations. A buyer purchasing assets from a dying person, in a face-to-face community context, arguably acquires with full awareness of the conditions. This would be a form of *anan sahadi*, where the communal knowledge is so evident that it stands in for an explicit declaration.

### Rav's Teaching

The Gemara records two versions of a ruling in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Rav — one holding *im amad eino chozer*, that recovery does not void the sale, and one holding *im amad chozer*, that it does. The Gemara reconciles these not as a dispute but as reflecting different circumstances: *ha de-is leh zuzei be-einaihu ve-ha de-parinehu be-chovo* — one ruling applies when the money from the sales remains on hand, and the other when the money was used to pay off debts.

If the proceeds were used to retire existing debts, then *amad eino chozer* — the transaction stands even if he recovers. The logic is that by applying the money toward a definite purpose — clearing liabilities — the *shchiv mera* demonstrated that the sale was genuinely intended to accomplish something real, not merely to transfer assets under the assumption of death. The funds are gone, the debts are settled; there is nothing to reverse and no basis to assume the sale was contingent. If, on the other hand, the money simply sits untouched, then *amad chozer* — he can reclaim it upon recovery — because the continued holding of the liquid proceeds suggests that his original intent was indeed predicated on dying, and upon recovery that predicate fails.

What remains striking, even with this reconciliation, is that the halakha entertains *amar chozer* even in the context of a bilateral commercial transaction. The typical force of *devarim shebalev einam devarim* would seem to preclude this. The resolution appears to rest on the quasi-public nature of a *shchiv mera*'s circumstances, in which the contingent character of his transactions may be sufficiently transparent to all parties to override the standard rule.

## Hoda'ah & Issur Giyora

### Shchiv Mera Hoda'ah

The Gemara now turns to a genuinely new question: *shchiv mera shehoda mahu* — what is the rule when a *shchiv mera* does not say "I want Ploni to have this field," but instead admits that the field has always belonged to Ploni? He claims, in effect, that what everyone assumed was his property is not his at all.

The concept at work here is *hoda'at baal din*, the admission of a litigant against himself. As a general principle, *hoda'at baal din kemeah edim dami* — a party's admission against his own interest is equivalent to a hundred witnesses. If a person stands before witnesses and, in a serious and deliberate context, declares that a specific piece of property belongs to someone else, that admission is binding regardless of whether it reflects objective reality. The admission, made under circumstances that exclude the possibility of idle joking, creates a legal reality that overrides even overwhelming contrary evidence. The person against whom the admission runs cannot subsequently retract by claiming it was false.

This mechanism is a powerful tool for transferring property without requiring a formal *kinyan*. By simply admitting that the property was always the other person's — even when this is counterfactual — one creates a binding legal entitlement in the other person. Why, then, is there even a question about whether this works for a *shchiv mera*?

The Rashbam explains that the question arises not because the *shchiv mera* lacks the power to make such an admission, but because there is a countervailing consideration specific to the deathbed context. The Gemara elsewhere records that if a *shchiv mera* says "I owe Reuven a million dollars," we do not necessarily credit that claim, because we suspect he is making it *shelo lehasbia et banav* — so that his children will not appear wealthy and thereby become targets for unscrupulous creditors or predators. The fear that strangers will try to take advantage of young heirs who appear to have inherited substantial wealth provides a motive for the dying person to make false debt claims. Given this, one might think that similar skepticism should extend to all admissions by a *shchiv mera*. The question is whether the skepticism is categorical or confined to claims of debt.

### Issur Giyora Story

The Gemara responds: *ta shema* — come and learn from the following episode. A convert named Issur — referred to as Issur Giyora — had in his early life taken captive a daughter of the sage Shmuel named Rachel, had relations with her, and she conceived. He subsequently converted while she was pregnant. The son born of this union was Rav Mari bar Rachel — known by his mother's name, since his father had been a non-Jew at the time of conception. Issur Giyora had twelve thousand *zuzei* deposited with Rava — apparently cash held in Rava's home for safekeeping.

### Rava's Dilemma

As Issur Giyora lay dying, Rava asked: *heichi kaninhu Rav Mari l'hanei zuzei* — how could Rav Mari acquire this money? Rava, who held the cash, was working through the available legal avenues. If Rav Mari should inherit it, the answer is that *lav bar yerusha hu* — he cannot inherit from his father. The Rashbam clarifies that the problem is patrilineal: since Issur Giyora was not Jewish at the time of conception, Rav Mari bears no halakhic relationship to him through patrilineal descent, which is the operative channel for inheritance. Although Rav Mari might in principle inherit through his mother, the relevant *yerushah* here is from father to son, and that relationship does not exist in halakha.

### Matnat Like Inheritance

This leads to the application of a principle we have been developing: *matnat shchiv mera k'yerushah shavyuha rabanan* — the Rabbis structured *matnat shchiv mera* to function like an inheritance. The consequence is: *kol heicha d'leisa b'yerusha leisa b'matana* — wherever inheritance is inapplicable, the rabbinic institution of *matnat shchiv mera* is equally inapplicable. If the mechanism depends on functioning like an inheritance, then a recipient who cannot stand in the position of an heir cannot receive through this vehicle.

### No Patrilineal Heir

The Rashbam reads the problem as applying to Rav Mari specifically: he is in a position of *leisa b'yerusha* through patrilineal descent, and therefore cannot receive a *matnat shchiv mera* from Issur Giyora. By extension, a *ger* who has no halakhic heirs, or any individual who bears no patrilineal relationship to the dying person, would be similarly excluded. This is a striking and somewhat counterintuitive limitation of *matnat shchiv mera*, underscoring how deeply the institution is structurally tied to the laws of *yerushah*, even though it requires the language of *matanah* to be effected.

### Failed Kinyan Methods

Rava proceeded to enumerate all possible methods by which Rav Mari might otherwise acquire the money:

Could Rav Mari simply come and take possession by *meshicha*? *Rachok migabei* — he is away at the yeshiva, and there is no time for him to come and physically take the money before his father dies.

Could the transfer be accomplished through *chalipin*, the symbolic exchange that effects a *kinyan*? *Ein matbe'a nikna bechalipin* — coins cannot be acquired through *chalipin*. That mode of acquisition works for land and movable goods but not for currency itself.

Could Issur Giyora transfer the money *agav karka* — by simultaneously conveying a piece of land, with the cash being transferred alongside? *Leit lei ara* — he has no land. Had he possessed even a tiny plot, he could have used it to effect the transfer of the cash.

Could a *ma'amad shelishtan* be arranged — the three-party standing meeting in which the creditor directs the depositor to transfer the funds to a third party, and the transfer is thereby effected? *Ishlach li lo azlina* — if Issur Giyora were to send for Rava to participate in such a proceeding, Rava would simply not go. This last point is deeply troubling. It makes plain that Rava was, at minimum as a matter of objective fact, obstructing the only remaining avenue by which the man whose money he held could direct it to his son. Whether Rava's motives were entirely proper is a question the Gemara invites us to confront.

### Udita Solution

At this point, Rav Ika bar Rav Ami objected and proposed a solution: *ve'odei Issur dehanei zuzei deRav Mari ninhu* — let Issur Giyora simply admit, before witnesses, that the money Rava is holding is not actually his. Let him declare that some time ago — a week, a year, whenever — he had already transferred the money to Rav Mari through a legitimate act of *kinyan*, perhaps a conveyance of land. This may be entirely counterfactual; Issur Giyora may never have done any such thing. But if he states it in front of witnesses, in a context that is clearly serious and deliberate, the admission is binding. *Hoda'at baal din kemeah edim dami* — his word against himself is worth a hundred witnesses, and what was Rava's claim to hold now becomes Rav Mari's property as a matter of law.

The mechanism is sometimes referred to as *kinyan udita* — acquisition through admission. It is not a standard mode of *kinyan* in the technical sense, but it functions in an analogous way: it creates a legal reality through a formal declaration, bypassing the need for actual physical transfer or any of the standard modes of acquisition. The fact that the Gemara frames it as *v'kaninu b'udita* — "let him acquire through the *udita*" — reflects the recognition that the admission serves as a practical substitute for a *kinyan*, even when everyone involved understands that the underlying factual claim is a legal fiction.

### Issur's Admission

Word of this solution reached Issur Giyora while the discussion was still ongoing, and he immediately made the admission before witnesses. The money was thereby transferred to Rav Mari bar Rachel. He had accomplished what he set out to do.

### Rava's Reaction

Rava was upset. His recorded reaction was: *ka magmrei ta'anta l'inshei umasdei li* — "you are teaching people claims and causing me a loss." The language is striking and, on its face, damning. The word *ta'anta* — claim, argument, legal stratagem — carries connotations of coaching a litigant in how to prevail in court, sometimes even through means that do not reflect the true underlying facts. And Rava explicitly identifies the result as a financial loss to himself. The plain reading of the episode is that Rava, holding money entrusted to him by a dying man who wished it to go to his son, was actively working to prevent that transfer and retain the money for himself through the operation of the rules governing a *ger shemet* — the property of a convert who dies without halakhic heirs, which becomes ownerless and is taken by whoever seizes it first.

### Rava Apologetics

The Soncino translation offers an extended apologetic note, arguing that Rava had no intention whatsoever of retaining the money, that the entire discussion of the available legal avenues was a pedagogical exercise for his students, that no one in his academy for a moment suspected the master of self-interest, and that his final exclamation of displeasure was nothing more than mild irony — the Soncino even arguing that Rava's public discussion of the matter, knowing that Rav Mari was himself a student and would hear of it, was actually evidence of his honor and good faith. The note concludes that Rava had intended to pass the money to Rav Mari as a generous personal gift rather than by legal compulsion, and was merely disappointed that the technical halakhic resolution preempted his own beneficent gesture.

This reading is, to put it plainly, extraordinarily strained. It is the kind of apologetics one associates with the ArtScroll tradition rather than with the more critical Soncino approach, a point that is all the more striking given the Soncino's usual tone. The apologetics were almost certainly shaped by the audience for whom the Soncino was written — a British public audience, including non-Jews, for whom the spectacle of a leading Talmudic sage apparently attempting to keep money entrusted to his care by a dying convert would have been acutely embarrassing.

One does note that a more charitable reading has some textual support: Rabbenu Yonatan of Lunel, an early Rishon, is quoted by Steinsaltz as holding that Rava did not intend to keep the money. And it is at least plausible that Rava's public airing of the issue, knowing that Rav Mari was present and would learn of it, reflects something other than pure self-interest. But the text remains what it is, and the discomfort is real.

### Debt vs. Property

What we do derive definitively from the story is that *hoda'ah* by a *shchiv mera* is effective. The Gemara uses this episode as the answer to its earlier question of *shchiv mera shehoda mahu*. And the Rashbam now addresses the apparent tension with the other *sugya* concerning *shelo lehasbia et banav*, where a *shchiv mera*'s claims of debt are regarded with suspicion.

The Rashbam distinguishes between two types of admission. A claim of debt — "I owe a million dollars to Reuven" — affects how the entire estate appears. A large apparent debt changes people's perception of the estate's worth, makes the heirs seem less wealthy, and thereby protects them from exploitation. The motivation of *shelo lehasbia et banav* is plausible and powerful in this context. Moreover, being known as heavily indebted carries social stigma, providing yet another incentive for a dying person to fabricate debt claims on behalf of his children's protection.

By contrast, an admission that a specific, identified piece of property belongs to a specific person is concrete and particularized. There is no general distortion of the estate's image, no social stigma, and the claim is much harder to attribute to an ulterior protective motive. When Issur Giyora admits that the twelve thousand *zuzei* held by Rava belong to Rav Mari, this is a targeted claim about a specific asset and a specific person, not a vague cloud cast over the entire estate. The Rashbam therefore holds that such targeted property admissions are binding even when made by a *shchiv mera*, while generalized debt claims remain subject to skepticism.

### Kinyan Udita

The upshot is the concept of *kinyan udita* — the recognition that formal admission before witnesses can function as an effective means of property transfer, even in the absence of any of the standard modes of *kinyan*. It almost operates as a species of *kinyan* in its own right, though technically it derives its force from the principle of *hoda'at baal din*. The practical significance is considerable: where all standard *kinyan* mechanisms fail — whether due to the absence of land, the impossibility of *meshicha*, the inapplicability of *chalipin* to coins, or the refusal of a necessary party to cooperate — a carefully constructed admission before witnesses can accomplish what formal *kinyan* cannot. The legal fiction is transparent to all parties, but its binding force is undiminished thereby.

## Shiyur: Leaving Over

### Shayar Karka Rule

We now turn to the question of *shiyur* — the requirement that in order for a *matnat shchiv mera* to be binding even upon recovery, the *shchiv mera* must have retained something. The basic rule: *shayar karka kol shehu matnaso kayemet* — if the *shchiv mera* left over even the smallest amount of land, his gift stands and cannot be retracted upon recovery. This is the rule of *miktzat nechasav* as opposed to *kol nechasav*.

### Kidei Parnasaso

The Gemara immediately asks: *vekama kol shehu* — how much is this "smallest amount"? The answer, given in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Rav, is: *karka kidei parnasaso* — land sufficient to support the person's livelihood. The *kol shehu* is not literally a token quantity. The reason a retained parcel of land renders the gift binding is that it demonstrates the *shchiv mera* understood that if he survived he would not be left destitute; he made provision for himself. Therefore the definition of a meaningful *shiyur* is not a nominal sliver but an amount sufficient to provide an ongoing livelihood. This could be a substantial figure — land that can produce enough to live on for potentially many years — and is calibrated to the person's individual circumstances and cost of living.

### Rabbi Zeira Reading

Rav Yirmiya bar Abba then extends the ruling: *metaltelin kidei parnasaso* — even if what remains is not land but movable property (*metaltelim*), so long as it is sufficient to support the person's livelihood, it qualifies as a meaningful *shiyur* and the gift is binding. The underlying rationale, as Rabbi Zeira articulates, is that the Mishnah's mention of *karka* reflects the classical role of land as a reliable source of ongoing sustenance — *de'i kai, samich alei* — something one can build upon and live off of indefinitely. But if the person retains sufficient *metaltelim* to provide the same ongoing support, the purpose is equally served. Rabbi Zeira praises this approach, noting how precisely attuned — *kama mechavnin shemaata desavei* — the teaching of these earlier sages is in reaching toward the deeper intention rather than being captive to the literal formulation.

### Rav Yosef Challenge

Rav Yosef objects sharply: *umai kavanaso* — what exactly is so precisely attuned about this? The extension to *metaltelim* involves simply disregarding what the Mishnah says. *Karka tenan* — the Mishnah says land. And in the same breath, redefining *kol shehu* to mean *kidei parnasaso* likewise ignores the plain meaning: *kol shehu tenan* — the Mishnah says any amount, however small. Two liberties have been taken simultaneously — replacing *karka* with *metaltelim* and replacing *kol shehu* with a substantial quantity — and Rav Yosef sees no warrant for either.

### Abaye's Precedent

Abaye responds by challenging the premise that *karka* in the Mishnah is always to be read with strict literalism: *vechol heicha detani karka karka davka* — is it true that every Mishnaic use of *karka* means only land and nothing else? He brings a proof from the Mishnah concerning a master who writes all his property to his slave. The slave goes free, because the slave is himself part of the property and thereby acquires himself. However, if the master says he is giving everything except for *karka kol shehu* — a small amount of land — the slave does not go free, because the *karka kol shehu* reserved can be understood to refer to the slave himself, who is treated as *karka* in halakha.

Rabbi Shimon, however, holds that if the master uses the specific word *karka*, he means land and does not mean the slave. The slave does not go free only if the master says "except for one ten-thousandth" without specification — which might refer to the slave — but "except for land" clearly refers to something other than the slave, and the slave is therefore freed.

Abaye then cites a further teaching of Rav Dimi bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *asu metaltelim shiyur etzel eved* — if the master says "except for a small amount of *metaltelim*," that too prevents the slave from going free, because a slave can be described as *metaltelim* as well, being mobile and not fixed like land. Thus the word *metaltelim* can, in context, refer to a slave. This demonstrates that the Mishnah's use of specific terminology about property is not always strictly limited to its literal meaning.

### Why Karka Mentioned

The Gemara, however, pushes back on the proof. The case of the slave-freeing Mishnah used *karka* in a context where the surrounding material had been discussing *karka* extensively. Specifically, the beginning of that Mishnah cited Rabbi Akiva's teaching that *karka kol shehu* — any smallest amount of land — entails obligations of *pe'ah*, *bikkurim*, the validity of a *prosbul*, and the capacity to transfer *metaltelim* alongside land. Since the entire preceding context was about *karka*, the subsequent use of *karka* in the exception clause naturally drew upon that context, even though the actual rule extends to *metaltelim* as well. The word *karka* was used, in other words, because it was contextually appropriate, not because it was strictly limited to land. *Mishum hachi tana karka* — because of the earlier context, the Mishnah said *karka*, though it was not literally exclusive.

The force of the pushback on Abaye's proof is this: the principle that a word can be used non-literally (*lav davka*) requires explanation — one must account for why the non-literal word was used. In the slave case, there is a clear contextual explanation: the Mishnah was already speaking of *karka*. But in the case of *shiyur* by the *shchiv mera*, what would explain the Mishnah's use of *karka* if it did not literally mean *karka*? Without such an explanation, the plain meaning stands.

### Kol Shehu Question

The Gemara concludes this amud with the question hanging: when the Mishnah says *shayar karka kol shehu*, does *kol shehu* always and invariably mean the smallest imaginable quantity, or might *kol shehu* in certain contexts refer to a specific type or category of something? This question will continue to be examined on the following daf.

---

# Bava Batra 150

## Karka & Kol Shehu

### Intro: All vs. Some

The *mishnah* on 150 establishes that the critical line separating a *matnat shechiv mera*—a deathbed gift that reverts if the giver recovers and requires no *kinyan*—from an ordinary gift is whether the giver transferred all of his property or only some of it. The *mishnah*'s specific formulation is *di-shiyar karka kol shehu*: if he retained even the smallest amount of land, the gift does not have the special status of a *matnat shechiv mera* and therefore remains binding even if he recovers.

### Rav Yehuda's Reinterpret…

Against this apparently straightforward reading, the *gemara* cites a statement in the name of Rav Yehuda Amar Rav and a parallel statement of Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba, proposing that *karka* in this context does not literally mean land, and *kol shehu* does not literally mean the smallest possible amount. Rather, according to this view, retaining any property sufficient to provide for one's ongoing support — whether land or otherwise — would suffice to remove the gift from the category of *matnat shechiv mera*. The reasoning is that when a person holds back enough to sustain himself, we understand that even if he recovers, the gift was intended as a genuine transfer, since he retained a basis for self-support.

### Eved Case Evidence

The *gemara* had attempted to bring evidence for the imprecision of the word *karka* from a *mishnah* concerning the freeing of a slave, where the term *karka* appeared to extend beyond literal land. This would support the claim that the *mishnah*'s use of *karka* need not be taken at face value.

### Context Argument

The *gemara* rebuffs this evidence, however, by arguing that context determines meaning. In the slave case, *karka* was used imprecisely because the broader surrounding discussion was already about *karka*, and the term was carried along by that context. But where a *mishnah* uses the word *karka* in isolation, without any surrounding context that would justify imprecision, it must be taken literally. The principle is sharp: if the *mishnah* is not responding to anything and is not embedded in a *karka* discussion, then *karka* means *karka*.

### First Shearer's Wool

A parallel challenge is then directed at the imprecision of the term *kol shehu*. The *gemara* asks whether it can really be claimed that every usage of *kol shehu* in rabbinic literature means a literally minimal amount, or whether sometimes that phrase, too, is imprecise. The proof case comes from the laws of *reshit hagez*, the obligation to give the first shearing of one's sheep to the *kohen*. Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas holds that the obligation requires the shearing of five sheep, each yielding a *maneh u'pras* — one and a half *maneh* — of wool. The Sages, by contrast, say that five sheep are required but that *kol shehu* from each suffices, meaning even the smallest amount per sheep is enough to trigger the obligation.

### Rav's Maneh Standard

The *gemara* then asks: how much is this *kol shehu*? Rav answers that it means a total of one *maneh u'pras* across all five sheep combined, with each sheep contributing at least a fifth of that total — that is, three-tenths of a *maneh* per sheep. This is not, in any ordinary sense, "the smallest possible amount." Rather, it is a defined and significant minimum. Yet the Sages called it *kol shehu*.

### Kol Shehu as Relative

The *gemara* resolves this by invoking the same contextual logic applied to *karka*. The Sages' use of *kol shehu* is not absolute — it is relative. Since Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas had established a very large standard (*maneh u'pras* per sheep, amounting to seven and a half *maneh* in total), the Sages, responding to that large figure with a dramatically smaller one, called their standard *kol shehu* — meaning: even a small amount suffices. The term is comparative, signaling a sharp departure from a large benchmark, not an assertion that there is literally no minimum at all.

### Literal Interpretation

The *gemara* then returns this logic to our *mishnah* about *matnat shechiv mera* and finds that neither of these imprecision arguments applies. Our *mishnah* is not embedded in a *karka* discussion, and it is not responding to any large competing standard. It stands alone, stating in a vacuum that *karka kol shehu* is the dividing line. In that context, there is no justification for reading *karka* as anything other than literal land, nor *kol shehu* as anything other than literally the smallest amount. The argument is, as the analysis acknowledges, a formidable one: the words must be taken at face value.

---

## Metaltelin Definition

### What's in Metaltelin

The *gemara* now turns to the question of what is included when a person — whether a *shechiv mera* or a healthy individual executing a *kinyan* — says, "All of my *metaltelin* should go to so-and-so." What does the word *metaltelin* encompass in *lashon bnei adam*, ordinary human speech?

The *gemara* answers: *manei tashmishtei kani* — the recipient acquires all the implements, objects, and possessions the person uses. This is an inclusive category of durable goods, broadly understood as "all his stuff." What is notably excluded, however, is food: wheat, barley, and by extension other foodstuffs. Even though legally — from a purely *halachic* standpoint — anything that is not land is *metaltelin*, the way people actually speak does not encompass food within that term. When a person says "*metaltelin*," they are thinking of durable objects, not their pantry. The Rashbam adds that livestock and presumably other animals are similarly excluded, since ordinary usage of *metaltelin* does not bring animals to mind either.

### Kol Metaltelin Expansion

When, however, a person says *kol metaltelin* — "all of my *metaltelin*" — the additional word *kol* operates to expand the category beyond what is ordinarily implied. *Kol metaltelin* includes even wheat, barley, and by extension other food. The extra word signals an intent to sweep in everything that is technically *metaltelin*, not merely what the word conventionally connotes.

### Millstone Distinction

The expansion introduced by *kol* goes further. *Kol metaltelin* includes even the upper millstone — *rechayim ha'elyona* — despite its great bulk and the fact that it would ordinarily not be thought of as a movable object. The reason it qualifies is that the upper millstone does in fact get transported on occasion: it might be removed for repair or resurfacing. Moreover, in its normal operation it moves in place. The lower millstone, *rechayim ha'tachtona*, is however excluded even from *kol metaltelin*, because it is never actually transported anywhere. If, on the other hand, one uses the phrasing *kol d'mitaltel* — anything that possesses the quality of being movable — then even the lower millstone is included, since it is theoretically capable of being moved.

### Slaves Classification

A pointed question is then raised regarding slaves. Legally, slaves have the *halachic* status of *karka* — they are acquired and treated in many respects like land and are excluded from numerous obligations that apply to *metaltelin*. Yet people do not typically think of slaves as land. The question is therefore: in *lashon bnei adam*, are slaves included in the word *metaltelin* or not — *kemakarkei o kemetalteli dami*? It is worth noting at the outset that these need not be mutually exclusive categories from the standpoint of ordinary usage. It is possible that people would include slaves under either term, *metaltelin* or *karka*, even if they are formally and exclusively one thing under *halacha*.

### Town Sale Case

An attempt is made to resolve the question from the *mishnah* in an earlier chapter of Bava Batra concerning the sale of a town. When a person sells a town, the sale includes houses, cisterns, wells, bathhouses, and olive presses — everything attached to the land — but does not include *metaltelin*. However, if the seller explicitly says he is selling the town and everything within it, the *mishnah* rules that even animals and slaves are included in the sale. This appears to suggest that animals and slaves normally fall into the *metaltelin* column rather than the *karka* column, since they require the expanded formulation "everything within it" to be transferred.

### Ambulatory Exception

The *gemara* pushes back on this inference. The word *afilu* — "even" — in the *mishnah*'s ruling about "everything within it" implies some novelty or difficulty about the inclusion of slaves and animals. If slaves and animals were simply ordinary *metaltelin*, no such emphasis would be needed. The *gemara* therefore proposes an entirely different framework: the reason slaves and animals are not automatically included in a sale of the town is not because of how they are categorized — as *karka* or *metaltelin* — but because they are ambulatory. *Metaltelin de-naydi* are fundamentally different from *metaltelin de-lo naydi*: objects that move on their own accord may not be "within" a place in any reliable sense, since they could walk out at any moment. Thus the *mishnah*'s special language about slaves and animals reflects their self-propelled nature, not their classification, and does not resolve the underlying question of whether slaves fall under *metaltelin* or *karka* in *lashon bnei adam*.

### Slave Freeing Case

A second attempt to resolve the question comes from Ravina's citation of the *mishnah* about freeing a slave. The *mishnah* states: *hakotev kol nechasav le'avdo, yatza ben chorin* — if a master writes to his slave, "All of my property goes to you," the slave goes free, because the slave is included in the master's possessions and thus receives himself. If, however, the master says "all my property except for a small amount of *karka*," the slave does not go free — perhaps because the retained *karka* is the slave himself, since slaves have the legal status of *karka*.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees with the first *tanna* on this point: he holds that *karka* means actual land, not a slave, and that the slave's legal classification as *karka* does not mean that ordinary speech would use the word *karka* to refer to a slave. For the slave to be excluded from the gift, the reservation would have to be of "one part in ten thousand" — an entirely abstract and undefined fraction — which could encompass the slave. But "except for a small amount of *karka*" would not, in Rabbi Shimon's view, be understood as excluding the slave.

The *tanna kamma*, however, holds that the word *karka* could be interpreted as referring to the slave, leaving open the possibility that the retained *karka* is the slave himself — and therefore the slave does not go free.

Now, crucially, Rav Dimi bar Yosef in the name of Rav Elazar states: *asu metaltelin shiyur etzel eved, ve-lo asu metaltelin shiyur etzel ketubah*. Retaining a small amount of *metaltelin* functions as a *shiyur* — a legally significant holding back — with respect to freeing a slave, just as retaining *karka* does. That is, if the master says "all my property except for a small amount of *metaltelin*," the slave also does not go free. This suggests that when a person says the word *metaltelin*, it is understood to potentially include a slave — the slave falls within that category in *lashon bnei adam* just as he falls within *karka*.

The second half of Rav Dimi's statement is that *metaltelin* does not function as a *shiyur* with respect to the *ketubah* case. This refers to the *halacha* whereby if a husband distributes all his property among his children and gives his wife a small amount of *karka*, this is treated as full payment of her *ketubah* — unless she objects — because the *ketubah* is fundamentally a lien on land. Since a *ketubah* is collected from *karka*, the small amount of *karka* given to the wife is seen as a *ketubah* payment. But if he gives her a small amount of *metaltelin* rather than *karka*, it is not treated as payment of the *ketubah*. The *ketubah*'s character as a land-based obligation means that *metaltelin* cannot substitute for *karka* in this context.

### Rava's Explanation

Rava explains to Rav Nachman why the two rules of Rav Dimi make sense together. By the slave: *avda metaltelin*, a slave is included in the term *metaltelin*; therefore, when the master retains "a little *metaltelin*," the retained quantity might be the slave himself, making it *metaltelin* for *metaltelin* — and that constitutes a legally significant *shiyur*. By the *ketubah*: *kesuvas isha mi-makarkei hu* — a *ketubah* is fundamentally collected from land; therefore, giving the wife *metaltelin* does not represent the kind of holding back from which she has lien rights, and hence it is not a *shiyur* in that context.

### Rav Nachman Kerisuta

Rav Nachman, however, challenges Rava's entire explanation of the slave case. He argues that the reason a slave does not go free when *metaltelin* is retained is not because a slave is classified as *metaltelin* in *lashon bnei adam*. The reason, rather, is *kerisuta* — the requirement that the document freeing the slave possess the quality of complete severance, analogous to a *get*.

This requires some unpacking. A *get* — a bill of divorce — operates not as a property transfer but as a change of status. It severs a relationship. We learn from the analogy to a *get* that the document freeing a slave must similarly be an instrument of complete severance, without any strings attached, whether physical or conceptual. The Talmud elsewhere discusses how if a *get* is given with a literal string attached by which the husband can retract it, it is invalid. Similarly, a *get* that contains a lifelong condition that contradicts full separation is invalid for lack of *kerisuta*.

Freeing a slave through the transfer of all one's property is unusual in that the mechanism is property transfer, yet it must also function as a status-altering document. When the master says, "I give you everything in this pile — which includes you — except for some undefined portion of it," that language introduces a quality of incompleteness into the document. Even if the retained portion does not refer to the slave himself, the statement "I am giving you everything but holding something back" prevents the document from being a complete severance. The result is not that the slave might be keeping himself — it is that the transfer is not absolute, and an instrument of manumission must be absolute.

Rav Nachman therefore concludes that the failure of the slave to go free when *metaltelin* is retained has nothing to do with whether slaves are categorized as *metaltelin* in ordinary speech. It has to do with the incompleteness of the act of severance when any undifferentiated portion of property is held back.
