Consequently, the question of whether slaves are included in the term *metaltelin* in *lashon bnei adam* remains unresolved.

---

## Five Categories

### Shechiv Mera

Rava in the name of Rav Nachman enumerates five categories of *halacha* in which there is a fundamental legal distinction — not merely a difference of degree — between transferring all of one's property and transferring only some of it. The principle is *chamisha ad sheyichtevu kol necheseihem*: in these five domains, the legal consequence shifts categorically depending on whether the entire estate is transferred or whether something is held back.

The first category is *shechiv mera*, which is the *mishnah* itself. *Shachiv mera she-katav kol nechasav le'acherim ve-shayer karka kol shehu*: if a deathbed person writes away all his property but retains even the tiniest amount of land, the gift remains valid even if he recovers, because it is treated as an ordinary gift, not a *matnat shechiv mera*. If, however, nothing is retained — no *karka kol shehu* is left over — then the full law of *matnat shechiv mera* applies and the gift is void upon recovery. We noted earlier that there was a debate in the *gemara* about whether *karka* in this formulation must be taken literally or whether *metaltelin* might also satisfy this condition; this point will be revisited.

### Eved Freedom

The second category is the slave. *Hakotev kol nechasav le'avdo, yatza ben chorin* — give the slave all your property and he goes free; *shiyar karka kol shehu*, retain a little *karka*, and he does not go free. We have discussed this at length: the two possible explanations are either that the retained *karka* might refer to the slave himself, or that the language lacks the complete severance required of an instrument of manumission. Either way, the distinction between 100 percent and anything less is halachically decisive. And it was agreed — in the course of the earlier discussion — that the same rule applies if *metaltelin* is retained: the slave does not go free.

### Wife Executor

The third category is a man's wife. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states: *hakotev kol nechasav le'ishto, lo asah ela apitropas* — if a man writes all his property to his wife, we do not read this as an actual gift to her. It would be inconceivable that a man would completely disinherit his children in favor of his wife; therefore, we interpret the transfer of 100 percent of the property to her as a designation of her as executor of the estate rather than outright owner. But this rule applies only when he gives her 100 percent. If he gives her 99 percent, she owns 99 percent. Here too — though the *gemara* does not spell it out fully in this context — if even a little *metaltelin* remains with the children or elsewhere, that presumably functions as a *shiyur* that prevents the rule from applying.

### Wife's Ketubah

The fourth category is the sons — or more precisely, the interaction between the distribution to the sons and the wife's *ketubah*. *Hakotev kol nechasav le-vanav ve-chotev le-ishto karka kol shehu, avda kesuvatah* — if a man distributes all his property to his children while giving his wife even the smallest amount of land, she loses her *ketubah* claim. Three elements combine to produce this result: the gift to her is *karka*, which is the classic medium for *ketubah* payment; she did not object; and the gift occurs in the context of a complete divestiture of all his property. In those circumstances, her silence is treated as acceptance of that *karka* as full satisfaction of her *ketubah*.

This rule, however, operates only when all the property is distributed. If 99 percent is distributed and the husband retains 1 percent for himself, the wife's *ketubah* rights remain intact — she can still collect from what he is holding back, and therefore we do not assume she has waived anything.

### Property Protection

The fifth category is *mavrachat* — the device used by a woman to protect her property from her husband. A woman about to marry, wishing to prevent her husband from enjoying the *peiros* (fruits) of her property during her lifetime and from inheriting from her after her death, would transfer all of her property to a trusted third party — say, to a friend. The *halacha* fascinatingly allows this arrangement to function precisely as intended: the property is shielded from the husband, yet the third party does not actually own it. The woman retains her own beneficial ownership, but vis-à-vis the marriage relationship, it is as though she has no property. This is a remarkable legal device: the law does not force an all-or-nothing conclusion of either "she really owns it, so the husband gets his rights" or "the friend really owns it, so the woman loses it."

However, this protective mechanism operates only when all the property is transferred. If the woman retains even a small amount, we cannot treat the transfer as a *mavrachat* — a protective fiction — and it is instead taken at face value as an actual gift, presumably with all the complications that entails. The Rashbam does note that a specific textual formula in the *shtar* — *mehayom ve-lichshe'ertza*, "from today and whenever I choose to void it" — can signal the protective intent even if not all the property is transferred; but absent such language, it is only the transfer of 100 percent that triggers the *mavrachat* rule.

### Metaltelin in Five

Having enumerated all five categories, Rav Nachman's ruling continues: *u-v'chulhu, metalteli havei shiyur* — in all of these categories, retaining *metaltelin* constitutes a *shiyur*, a legally effective holding back, just as retaining *karka* does. That is, if even a small amount of *metaltelin* is left over, the transfer does not have the *halacha* of 100 percent and none of the five rules apply — with one exception.

Going through the list: by *shechiv mera*, retaining *metaltelin* is a *shiyur*, as suggested by the earlier *gemara* analysis. By the slave, retaining *metaltelin* prevents him from going free, whether because of the *metaltelin* classification of slaves or because of *kerisuta*, as discussed. By the wife as executor, the *halacha* does not apply if *metaltelin* is left over for the children. By *mavrachat*, if the woman leaves over *metaltelin*, the transfer is not treated as a protective fiction.

### Ketubah Exception

The exception is the *ketubah*. In all other cases, *metaltelin* functions as a *shiyur*. By *ketubah*, it does not. The reasoning: *d'bimkarkei takinu rabanan, bimtalteli lo takinu rabanan* — the Rabbis established the *ketubah* as a lien on land, not on *metaltelin*. Therefore, since the wife has no lien rights over *metaltelin*, if the husband retains a small amount of *metaltelin* for himself while distributing everything else among the children and giving her *karka*, she cannot collect from that *metaltelin*. Since she has no rights against it, its retention is, as far as she is concerned, equivalent to his retaining nothing. The transfer is therefore treated as a full divestiture — and her acceptance of the *karka* given to her is still treated as *ketubah* payment.

This distinction can be drawn more sharply by separating two distinct questions. One question is: what is the man giving her — is it *karka* or *metaltelin*? For *ketubah* payment, it must be *karka*. The second and parallel question is: what is the man retaining for himself? If he retains *karka*, she still has lien rights over it and therefore has not waived her *ketubah* claims against it. If he retains *metaltelin*, she has no lien rights over it at all, and therefore it is as though he retained nothing of relevance to her *ketubah* — the distribution is treated as complete. This is a fundamentally different logical structure from the other four categories, where *metaltelin* does constitute a *shiyur*, because in those cases the question of liens is irrelevant.

It is worth noting the observation raised in this context: the *ketubah* case is the only one of the five in which the person holding the claim — the wife — holds it in the nature of a bond or creditor's lien, *shibudim*. In all the other categories, the relevant consequences have nothing to do with lien rights, and therefore the *metaltelin*/*karka* distinction does not affect those outcomes.

One might also ask whether the Geonic-era enactment extending *ketubah* collection to *metaltelin* would affect this *halacha*. After the *geonim*, *metaltelin* became subject to *ketubah* liens, and it may well be that this *halacha* would need to be revisited in light of that development.

### Amimar's Liens

Amimar adds a refinement. Even where the husband retains *metaltelin*, if those particular *metaltelin* are explicitly specified in the *ketubah* as subject to the wife's lien — *metaltalei di-chtivi bi-ktuva ve-itnhu be-'aineiyahu* — and they remain extant, then that retained *metaltelin* does constitute a *shiyur*. The reason is that, since she has explicit lien rights over these specific items, their retention by the husband means she still has something she can collect from. Once she retains that ability to collect, we do not treat the distribution as a full divestiture, and her acceptance of the small *karka* is not treated as waiver of the *ketubah*. It is a narrow but logically consistent carve-out from the general rule: the *metaltelin* exception applies only when the wife has no lien rights over the *metaltelin* in question. When she does, the general rule reasserts itself.

---

## Nechasim Definition

### Slaves in Nechasim

Having examined the scope of *metaltelin* and the five categories, the *gemara* now turns to analyze the scope of the word *nechasim* — possessions or property — particularly the phrase "all of my *nechasim*." How inclusive is this term? The discussion proceeds by identifying specific types of property and demonstrating that each falls within the word *nechasim*.

The first: slaves. *Avda ikri nechasai* — a slave is called *nechasim*. The proof: *hakotev kol nechasav le'avdo, yatza ben chorin* — as established earlier, if a master writes to his slave "all of my *nechasim*" go to you, the slave goes free, because he is included within the master's *nechasim* and thereby receives himself.

### Land in Nechasim

The second category: *ara'a ikri nechasai* — land is also called *nechasim*. One might have supposed that *nechasim* refers primarily or exclusively to movable possessions, not to real property. But the *mishnah* in the second chapter explicitly speaks of *nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayus* — property that has liens — which refers to land. Land is acquired through *kessef*, *shtar*, and *chazakah*. The *mishnah*'s use of the phrase *nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayus* to denote land confirms that the word *nechasim* encompasses real property.

### Metaltelin in Nechasim

Third: *gelima ikri nechasai* — even a garment, or movable property in general, is called *nechasim*. The same *mishnah* that speaks of property with liens continues with *nechasim she-ein lahem achrayus* — property without liens, which refers to *metaltelin* — and states that such property is acquired through *meshicha*, the act of drawing it toward oneself. The *mishnah*'s use of *nechasim* for *metaltelin* without liens thus confirms that *nechasim* includes chattels as well.

### Cash/Zuzim

Fourth: *zuzei ikri nechasai* — even cash is included in *nechasim*. One might have thought that "possessions" refers to tangible objects — land, goods, slaves — but not to coins or liquid currency. The *gemara* rejects this and demonstrates that cash falls within the word *nechasim* as well. The proof is derived from a *mishnah*'s statement that property without liens can be acquired together with property that has liens — through *kessef*, *shtar*, and *chazakah*. This mechanism — *kinyan agav* — allows the transfer of *metaltelin* and cash alongside a transfer of land. That the *mishnah* describes this as *nechasim she-ein lahem achrayus niknin im nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayus* shows that cash falls under the rubric of *nechasim*.

### Rav Pappa Story

The application of *kinyan agav* to the transfer of cash is illustrated by the well-known story of Rav Pappa. Rav Pappa was owed twelve thousand *zuzei* by a party in the distant locale of Bei Chuzai. Rav Shmuel bar Acha was traveling to that region, and Rav Pappa wished him to go and collect the debt on his behalf. To give him proper standing to do so — and to ensure that payment to Rav Shmuel bar Acha would discharge the debtors' obligation — a formal legal mechanism was required.

The mechanism used is *harsha'ah*, power of attorney, which in *halacha* operates not merely as an authorization but as an actual transfer of ownership: Rav Pappa transferred the debt to Rav Shmuel bar Acha so that Rav Shmuel bar Acha would be the legal owner of the claim and entitled to collect it in his own right, with a separate provision preventing him from keeping the funds for himself. The transfer of the cash claim was accomplished *agav asifa de-veiteh* — through the back porch of his house — meaning that Rav Pappa transferred a small amount of real property, and the monetary claim was transferred along with it via *kinyan agav*. When Rav Shmuel bar Acha returned successfully, Rav Pappa was so gratified that he went out to the town of Tavach to greet him. This story confirms that cash is considered *nechasim* and can be transferred through the *agav* mechanism alongside land.

### Shtarot/Documents

Fifth: *shtar ikrei nechasei* — writs, documents, and monetary instruments are also included in *nechasim*. The idea that documents representing debts owed to me — *shtarot* — are themselves a species of property that can be given away when one says "all of my *nechasim*" is established through a three-way discussion of types of *shtarot* connected to land.

Rav Abba bar Yitzchak identifies two such cases. In the first, a person instructs witnesses: "Take possession of this field for so-and-so, and write him a *shtar* documenting the gift." In this case, the gift of the field takes effect immediately through the *kinyan* the witnesses perform on the recipient's behalf, but the authorization to write the *shtar* can still be retracted — the *shtar* and the gift are severable. In the second case, the person says: "Take possession of the field for so-and-so on the condition that you write him the *shtar*." Here the gift is contingent on delivery of the *shtar*, and if the authorization is retracted before the *shtar* is written, the gift of the field itself can also be undone.

### Presigned Shtar

Rav Chiya bar Avin in the name of Rav Huna adds a third case. A seller, eager to finalize a transaction, instructs witnesses to write and sign a bill of sale transferring his field to the buyer — even in the buyer's absence, which the *mishnah* permits, since the *shtar* favors the buyer, and one may act on behalf of another to their benefit without their presence. The *shtar* is now signed and held. Later, the buyer performs a *chazakah* on the field. At the moment the *chazakah* takes effect, *nikna shtar kol makom she-hu* — the *shtar* is acquired by the buyer wherever it physically is. The buyer owns the *shtar* and can demand its delivery.

How do we know that the buyer's *chazakah* on the field carries with it ownership of the *shtar*? From the *mishnah*: *nechasim she-ein lahem achrayus niknin im nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayus be-kessef u-ve-shtar u-ve-chazakah*. The *mishnah* teaches that property without liens — here interpreted as a *shtar* — is acquired together with property that has liens, when the latter is acquired through the standard mechanisms. The *shtar* documenting the field sale is thus acquired automatically alongside the field when the buyer performs his *chazakah*.

This passage thus establishes that the word *nechasim* is broad enough to encompass *shtarot* — documentary instruments. The *amoraim* differ in how they interpret the phrase *nechasim she-ein lahem achrayus* in the *mishnah*: one reads it as referring to cash, another reads it as referring to *shtarot*. Either way, the breadth of the term *nechasim* to include both cash and documentary instruments is confirmed. The discussion of further items that may fall within *nechasim* continues into the subsequent daf.

---

---

# Bava Batra 151

## Nechasim Definition

### Daf 151 Intro

Daf 151 picks up four to five lines in, with the word *behema*, and continues the sustained inquiry into what types of property are encompassed by the term *nechasim* — possessions or property — as used throughout the relevant *mishnayot*. The broader context is the gift of a *shchiv mera*, a dying person, who declares that all his *nechasim* go to a particular recipient, as well as the parallel case of one who is not a *shchiv mera* but uses the same formulation. In the previous session, the *gemara* established that the word *nechasim* is inclusive enough to cover land, movable property (*metaltalin*), promissory documents (*shtarot*), and cash. The question now is what additional categories fall within that term, and whether anything falls outside it.

### Animals/Behema

The *gemara* states: *behema itkrei nechasai* — animals are called *nechasim*. One might have thought that livestock, being living creatures rather than static objects, occupy a different conceptual category. The *gemara* refutes this by citing the *mishnah* dealing with one who says *hamakdish nechasav* — I hereby consecrate all my possessions. The *mishnah* addresses the case where amongst his property are animals *re'ui legabei mizbeiach* — fit to be brought as a sacrifice on the altar.

The question that arises is how to understand the act of consecration in such a case. When a person declares *makdish* over his house, his furnishings, his tools — the proceeds go to *bedek habayit*, the general upkeep fund of the *Beis HaMikdash*. But what of an unblemished male animal that could itself be brought as a *korban*? Does the same declaration that sent his table to *bedek habayit* also transform this cow into a *korban*, or does it merely send the cow's monetary value to *bedek habayit* as well?

According to the *tanna kamma* of the *mishnah* — with the corrected *girsa* of the Bach reading *yimacheru letzorchei olot* — the resolution is as follows: the animal is technically *kodesh* for *bedek habayit*, since that is the operative meaning of *makdish* for all other property. However, since it would be inappropriate for an animal that is fit for the *mizbeiach* to be merely sold off for its monetary value, we arrange for it to be sold to someone who needs to bring an *olah*. That person pays its market value — those proceeds go to *bedek habayit*, redeeming the animal's *bedek habayit* status — and then consecrates it anew as an *olah* to be brought on the *mizbeiach*. Female animals, which cannot be brought as an *olah*, are sold for the purpose of *zivchei shelamim*. Males, who could in principle be a *shelamim*, are directed toward *olah* first, since an *olah* is entirely consumed on the altar and thus represents a more complete consecration than a *shelamim*, of which the owner eats a portion.

The central point for our purposes, however, is simply that when this person said *makdish* over his *nechasim*, the *mishnah* treats his animals as included. *Nechasim* extends to livestock.

### Birds/Ofos

The *gemara* continues: *ofos ikru nechasai* — birds are likewise called *nechasim*. A *baraita* is cited involving the same framework: *hamakdish nechasav*, someone who consecrates all his possessions, and *hayu vahen devarim harauyim legabei mizbeiach* — among those possessions are items fit for the altar. The *baraita* includes *yeinos shemanim* — wine and oil, which accompany sacrifices — and explicitly *ofos*, birds, which may be brought as offerings. The same logic of ensuring that altar-fit items reach the *mizbeiach* applies, and the conclusion is that birds too fall under the umbrella of *nechasim*.

### Tefillin

Having established animals and birds as *nechasim*, the *gemara* now asks about *mitzvah* objects. *Tefillin ikri nechasai* — *tefillin* are called *nechasim*. One might argue that objects designated for a *mitzvah* are not conceptualized as ordinary property — that they exist in a separate register in the owner's mind. The *gemara* rejects this from a *baraita*: when someone says *hamakdish nechasav*, the ruling is *ma'alim lo tefillin* — and his *tefillin* are subject to the consecration as well.

There are two interpretations of *ma'alim*. Rabbeinu Gershom understands it literally: the *hekdesh* administrators take the *tefillin* away from him. The *rashbam* understands it as: the value of the *tefillin* is assessed and he is expected to redeem them — effectively pressured to pay their monetary value so that he may keep wearing them — with that sum going to *hekdesh*. Either way, the *tefillin* are included within *nechasim*.

One might object: surely the person would not have intended to consecrate his *tefillin*, since doing so would prevent him from fulfilling the *mitzvah*. But this objection proves too much — one might equally say he would not have intended to consecrate his house, leaving himself homeless, or his food, leaving himself without sustenance. The declaration of *makdish nechasim* is all-encompassing, and the consequences for the declarant are his own concern. *Tefillin*, then, are unambiguously *nechasim*.

### Sefer Torah Question

At this point the *gemara* introduces an unresolved question: *Sefer Torah mai?* — what is the status of a *Sefer Torah*? Why might a *Sefer Torah* differ from *tefillin*? The *gemara* articulates the logic of each side. *Keivan d'lo mizdaben, va'asur lezabunei* — since a *Sefer Torah* is generally forbidden to be sold, perhaps it is not called *nechasim*. The concept of *nechasim* may be predicated on the ability to treat something as exchangeable property, something from which one can realize monetary value by selling it. An object that is categorically unsellable may fall outside that definition.

On the other hand, *o dilma keivan d'mizdaben lilmod Torah ule'nasah isha* — since there are recognized exceptions where one may sell a *Sefer Torah*, namely to fund Torah study or to enable marriage, perhaps that limited capacity to sell is sufficient to classify it as *nechasim*. The *gemara* concludes: *teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

### Rashbam Mitzvah Objects

The *rashbam* offers a striking analytical reframing of the *Sefer Torah* question that goes beyond the *gemara's* own formulation. He asks: *Sefer Torah mi mikrei nechasai k'tefillin dami* — is a *Sefer Torah* like *tefillin* and thus called *nechasim*, or perhaps *tefillin hainu ta'ama de'havei malbush* — the reason *tefillin* are included in *nechasim* is because you wear them, making them function like a type of garment or wearable object. A *Sefer Torah*, by contrast, is a *sefer mitzvah* — an object entirely defined by its identity as a sacred *mitzvah* object, not by any incidental personal use. Even granting that there are circumstances under which it can be sold, he argues, that does not determine the conceptual question of whether it is *nechasim*. Its essential character as a *mitzvah* object, not worn and not used in any way other than for its *mitzvah* function, places it in a distinct category.

The implication of the *rashbam's* analysis is significant: it would potentially extend the *Sefer Torah's* doubtful status to other *mitzvah* objects — a *lulav*, a *shofar* — which, unlike *tefillin*, are not worn, and whose sole function is the performance of a *mitzvah*. The *gemara* itself does not raise this question, but the *rashbam's* framing invites it.

There is also an additional dimension worth noting. *Tefillin* and a *Sefer Torah* both contain God's name and are therefore classified as *tashmishei kedusha* — objects of inherent holiness — unlike a *lulav* or *shofar*, which are *tashmishei mitzvah* and may ultimately be discarded with minimal ceremony. The *tashmishei mitzvah* objects have no *kedusha* and can be wrapped and disposed of; the *tashmishei kedusha* require *genizah*. The *gemara* does not explicitly invoke this distinction, but it adds conceptual texture: the very *kedusha* of a *Sefer Torah* — God's own *Torah* in a direct sense, not merely an instrument of a *mitzvah* — is another reason one might resist characterizing it as ordinary *nechasim*.

---

## Mivrachat Case

### Rav Zutra's Mother

The *gemara* now pivots to a different topic, though it remains organized around the question of *nechasim* and their transfer. *Imeih d'Rav Zutra bar Tuvia* — the mother of Rav Zutra bar Tuvia — *ktavin'hu l'nechasah l'Rav Tuvia* — wrote over all of her property to her son Rav Zutra bar Tuvia. The reason: *d'ba'aya l'minsaveih* — she was about to remarry. This is the *mivra'chat* scenario — a woman who, anticipating a new marriage, transfers her property to protect it from her future husband's access.

The story as presented involves the unnamed mother of Rav Zutra bar Tuvia. Her first husband had been Tuvia, and the son from that marriage was Rav Zutra bar Tuvia. She was now about to marry Rav Zivid. To protect her property from Rav Zivid, she transferred it all to her son. She married Rav Zivid — and then, demonstrating perhaps a well-founded caution, was divorced. She then sought to reclaim her property from her son.

### Rav Bibi's Ruling

The case came before Rav Bibi bar Abaye. His ruling was surprising: *mishum d'insuba hu v'insuba* — because she got married and she did get married, the son keeps it. Rav Bibi bar Abaye did not read this as a *mivra'chat* transfer at all. In his understanding, the mother was making a genuine gift to her son, to take effect upon her marriage — something like: given that I am entering a new chapter of life with Rav Zivid, I want my son from my earlier marriage to receive what I have now. Since she did get married, the condition was fulfilled and the gift is binding.

### Rav Huna Correction

Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua responded sharply: *mishum d'atu miMulai, amrisu milei mulaysa* — you come from Mulai, the *rashbam* identifies as the place associated with the descendants of Eli HaKohen, and you say blemished things. This is a pointed rebuke, playing on the name of the place.

His correction turns on a key distinction. *Afilu l'man d'amar mavra'chat kani* — even according to the opinion that the recipient of a *mivra'chat* transfer genuinely acquires it — *hani mili heicha d'lo galya da'ata* — that applies only where the woman does not explicitly articulate her intent. If she simply writes away all her property without saying why, there is a debate: is it a genuine gift or a protective transfer? Some hold that where all of the property is transferred and nothing is retained, we interpret it as *mivra'chat* without her needing to say so; others might read it as a real gift even then.

But in this case, *galya da'ata d'mishum insuba hu* — she made her intent explicit. She stated clearly: I am doing this because I am about to marry. That declaration removes any ambiguity. *V'insuba v'igirsha* — she married and was divorced — and therefore she gets it back. The transfer was never meant to be a permanent alienation of property; it was a protective device, now no longer needed.

The practical upshot is that the *mivra'chat* mechanism works most clearly in two ways: either through the transfer of *all* of one's possessions (which by itself signals the protective intent), or through an explicit statement of purpose regardless of how much property is transferred. Explicit expression of intent obviates any need to transfer the entirety.

### Tosafot Analysis

The *Tosafot* raise several incisive points about the mechanics of *mivra'chat*. First, regarding the threshold of *kol nechasim* versus *miktzas nechasim*: *Tosafot* argues, drawing on another *gemara* in Perek Kol Ha'isha Shenafelu, that when it is *kol nechasim*, all of the property, nobody disputes that it works as a *mivra'chat* — even without explicit statement. The debate exists only regarding *miktzas nechasim*, a partial transfer, where explicit articulation of purpose becomes necessary. This is the cleaner reading of what we established yesterday, and *Tosafot* is clarifying that it was never genuinely contested in the *kol nechasim* case.

The second and more searching question concerns the ownership structure during the interval of the marriage itself. The *girsa* that includes *v'igirsha* — she was divorced — might imply that while she was married to Rav Zivid, her son Rav Zutra in fact owned the property. *Tosafot* cites the R"I's objection to this reading, drawing on another *gemara* that makes clear that even while the woman is married, neither the husband nor the recipient truly owns the property. The *gemara* there asks: if the recipient does not own it, why does the husband not own it? The resolution — *takanta d'rabbanan she'asuha* — is that the Rabbis created an institution. It is a rabbinic enactment that treats the property as if it were in the recipient's possession for the purpose of shielding it from the husband, while in reality the woman herself retains ownership throughout.

*Tosafot* summarizes: *micol makom birshus mekabel matana heim ad shetisgaresh* — the property remains in some sense under the control of the recipient until she is divorced, but this does not reflect genuine ownership on his part. It is a legally constructed fiction designed to protect her. The question of who receives the *peiros* — the usufruct, the fruits of the property — during the marriage is left unresolved by *Tosafot*, though the logic of the institution would suggest it remains hers.

The conceptual challenge is real: either the son owns it or the husband does. There is no obvious middle ground in classical property law. What the Rabbis did was simply decree a protected category — something akin to a trust arrangement — in which neither the husband nor the recipient has genuine title, and the woman's effective ownership is preserved in a form that the husband cannot reach. It is a remarkable institution, though *Tosafot* does not spell out all of its details.

---

## Matnat Shchiv Mera

### Two Sons Case

The *gemara* now presents the story of the mother of Rami bar Chama. *Be'ursa kasivnah lenachasei le'Rami bar Chama* — in the evening, she wrote over all her property to Rami bar Chama, her son. *B'tzafra kasivnah le'Rav Ukva bar Chama* — the next morning, she wrote it over to Rav Ukva bar Chama, her other son. Both were sons of Chama. She was a *shchiv mera* — a dying person — throughout this episode. The question is which gift controls: the first or the second?

As a matter of intuition, most would answer: the last will and testament — the later one prevails. And indeed, the principle *dayatiki m'vatela dayatiki* — a later will voids an earlier one — is what ultimately governs. But this was not universally assumed, and the story maps out how that question was resolved.

### Rav Sheshet/Nachman

Rami bar Chama, the first recipient, came before Rav Sheshet, who awarded him the property. Rav Ukva bar Chama, the second recipient, came before Rav Nachman, who awarded it to him. Rav Sheshet then came to Rav Nachman to challenge his ruling.

Rav Sheshet's position was: *imi mishum dehadrabah* — if you say the mother retracted, *v'shchivah* — but she died. If the logic of *amad chozer* — if a *shchiv mera* recovers, the gift is voided — applies only because the gift was conditional on the person dying, then once she dies, the first gift is binding. What right did she have to supersede it with a second? She gave a gift on the condition she would die, she died, the first gift should therefore be binding. The ability to retract and give it to someone else in a second will is a separate and not obviously derivable claim.

### Chozer B'Matanto

Rav Nachman responded: *hachi amar Shmuel* — Shmuel taught: *kol she'ilu amad chozer, chozer b'matnato* — anyone whose gift would be voided if he recovered has the right to retract his gift and reassign it. The reasoning is that the entire frame of a *matnat shchiv mera* — a dying person's gift — is one of ongoing reassessment. A person in that condition who is divesting all of his property is doing so in the expectation of death and with the understanding that until death arrives, he retains a kind of continuing dominion over that process of divestiture. This is the principle of *chozer b'matnato*: within the dying person's frame, there is a right to continuously retract and redistribute until the end.

Rav Sheshet pushed back: perhaps Shmuel meant only *l'atzmo* — he can retract the gift entirely for himself, simply reclaiming his property and issuing no new will. That is more analogous to *amad chozer* — recovery likewise voids the gift and returns everything to him. But retraction in favor of a different recipient is a further step: it means the dying person can effectively keep issuing binding dispositions that supersede one another. That is not an obvious corollary of *amad chozer*.

Rav Nachman replied: *b'feyrush amar Shmuel bein l'atzmo bein l'acher* — Shmuel stated explicitly that the retraction applies both for the donor's own account and in favor of a different recipient. A later will does void an earlier one, and this is the operative rule.

### Later Will Voids

The principle *diatiki m'vatela diatiki* — a later will voids an earlier one — is hereby established and entrenched. It is worth marking how non-obvious this is. Simply because a gift is voided by recovery does not logically entail that a later will supersedes an earlier one. The two principles operate on different planes. But here both are affirmed as the *halacha*, and Rav Nachman's ruling in favor of Rav Ukva bar Chama — the second recipient — stands.

The underlying logic is coherent once articulated: the entire institution of *matnat shchiv mera* is structured around the anticipation of death. Everything is being done in that context. Just as recovery voids the whole because the context of anticipating death no longer obtains, so too within that context the dying person retains the right to continually refine and revise his dispositions. Both *amad chozer* and *diatiki m'vatela diatiki* are expressions of the same foundational principle: the dying person's ongoing sovereignty over his estate until the moment of death.

It is also worth noting at this point a principle that has been operative throughout but has not yet been stated explicitly in any *mishnah* or earlier *gemara*: *divrei shchiv mera k'chtuvim u'k'msurim dami* — the words of a *shchiv mera* are as if they were written and delivered. This is the principle that a *shchiv mera* requires no *kinyan* — the oral declaration itself constitutes the transfer. This principle has been implied all along by the institution of *matnat shchiv mera*, but it is formally introduced in the next episode.

---

## No Kinyan Principle

### Rav Amram Case

The mother of Rav Amram Chasida *hava lah meluga de-shatari* — had a satchel of promissory documents, outstanding debts owed to her. As she was dying, *amrah le-havei le-Amram beri* — she said: let them go to my son Amram. The brothers of Rav Amram came before Rav Nachman and argued: *halo mashach* — he did not take physical possession, he performed no *kinyan*. Since a satchel of *shtarot* is presumably not the entirety of her possessions, this is a *miktzas nechasim* transfer, not a *kol nechasim* transfer, and therefore it is not a *matnat shchiv mera* but rather a *matnat bari*, which would require a proper *kinyan*.

### Rav Nachman Ruling

Rav Nachman ruled: *divrei shchiv mera k'chtuvim u'k'msurim damu* — the words of a dying person are as if they were written in a document and physically handed over. No *kinyan* is needed. This is a striking ruling — and it is the first explicit articulation of this principle in the *gemara*. One could have read through all the *mishnayot* and all the *gemara* to this point and concluded that a *shchiv mera* must perform a *kinyan* like anyone else; the *mishnah's* discussion was solely about whether the gift is voided upon recovery (*amad chozer*), not about whether a *kinyan* is required. Rav Nachman is introducing this as a new and independent rule.

### Rashbam Interpretation

The *rashbam's* comment at this point is somewhat puzzling. He writes *kegon she'kanu mi'yadah* — as if they performed a *kinyan* from her hand — which would seem to reintroduce the *kinyan* requirement that Rav Nachman is precisely abolishing. The *Maharsha* already noted the difficulty. The *rashbam* then adds: *ei nami belo kinyan ve'kegon delo shayrei midi* — alternatively, without a *kinyan*, and assuming that she left over nothing, meaning this was indeed all of her possessions. The second reading makes better sense of the case: we are forced to assume that the satchel of *shtarot* constituted the entirety of her estate, putting it in the category of *kol nechasav* and thus a genuine *matnat shchiv mera* requiring no *kinyan*. On that reading, Rav Nachman's ruling flows from that premise.

---

## Metzaveh Machmas Misa

### Orchard Case

The *gemara* now presents the case of the sister of Rav Tuvi bar Rav Mattana. This is another in the remarkable series of stories about female relatives of named *amoraim* who manage their property as *shchiv mera*. *Havi lah piska d'pardisa* — she had a small plot of an orchard. *Kol eimas d'havya chalsha, havya maknya leh nihaleh* — whenever she became ill, she would transfer it to her brother as a *matnat shchiv mera*, and then *d'kayma, havya hadra* — when she recovered, it would be voided and she would retract. This cycle apparently repeated itself over the years.

One time, she fell ill again and sent word to her brother: come and do a *kinyan* on the orchard, take possession of it. Her brother — apparently at the end of his patience with this recurring deathbed drama — sent back: *lo ba'ina*, I do not want to come. She then sent a second message: come, do a *kinyan* in whatever form suits you. He came, and the resolution is elegant: *azal shiyer v'kana minah* — he left over a small portion of the orchard and performed a *kinyan* on the rest.

The significance of this maneuver is crucial. By doing a *kinyan* on *part* of the orchard — *miktzas nechasim* — rather than all of it, this is no longer a *matnat shchiv mera* but a *matnat bari* in structure: *im amad eino chozer* — even if she recovers, she cannot retract. And of course she did recover: *hadra bah* — she retracted.

### Rav Dimi Refusal

She brought the case before Rav Nachman. He sent word to Rav Dimi bar Yosef — the brother — to appear before the *beis din*. He refused: *lo ata* — he did not come. His reasoning, which he sent back, was: *ha shiyer v'kana minah* — she left over a portion and I performed a *kinyan*, therefore *amar einu chozer* — it cannot be retracted. He saw no need to appear, since his legal position was clear. Rav Nachman sent back: *ei lo atis, m'china lach b'silva d'lo mivza dama* — if you do not come, I will strike you with a nail that draws no blood, meaning I will place you in *cherem*. He came.

### Alas Oy Oy Oy

Rav Nachman asked the witnesses: *heichi havah ma'aseh* — tell me exactly what happened. They reported that she said: *oy oy oy, I'm about to die!* The *rashbam* notes that she said this particularly when her brother had failed to appear at her summons, expressing anguish that she would die without seeing him. What she said was an explicit, articulated expression of fear of imminent death — *metzaveh machmas misa*, giving instructions because she was dying.

### Rav Nachman Ruling

Rav Nachman ruled: *im kein, metzaveh machmas misa, u'metzaveh machmas misa chozer* — if that is the case, she was giving her instructions out of fear of death, and one who gives instructions because of fear of death also has the right to retract. This is a major *chiddush*. Until now, the dividing line between *matnat shchiv mera* and *matnat bari* seemed to be *kol nechasav* versus *miktzas nechasav*: give everything and it is a *shchiv mera* gift with all its attendant rules, give only part and it is a regular gift requiring *kinyan* and not retractable. Now a new category is introduced: *miktzas nechasav* paired with *metzaveh machmas misa* — a partial transfer, but one explicitly made out of fear of death — also qualifies as *matnat shchiv mera*. The transfer here, which was of *miktzas nechasim*, is pulled into the *shchiv mera* framework by the explicit expression of mortal fear, and therefore it is retractable after all.

### Abiyi Clarification

Abaye adds a clarifying point: the critical variable is whether the person explicitly expresses that they are acting out of fear of death. With *kol nechasav*, no such explicit statement is needed — the totality of the transfer itself, combined with the fact that the person is ill, suffices to establish *metzaveh machmas misa*. But with *miktzas nechasim*, explicit expression is required. The mere fact that a person is lying ill in bed and conducting some property transfer does not automatically make it a *matnat shchiv mera*. A person can be near death and still transact ordinary business. Only when they say — as this woman said, with her *oy oy oy, I'm about to die* — that this transfer is being made because they fear death does the *miktzas nechasim* transfer rise to the level of *matnat shchiv mera*.

This raises a further question: what of a person who is not ill at all, but is about to engage in a life-threatening activity — someone about to run into a burning building, for instance — and says, "if I don't survive, I want this property to go to this person and that property to that person"? Is that *metzaveh machmas misa*? The *gemara* does not resolve this, and it is genuinely unclear. The case in the *gemara* involves someone in a sickbed, in the active process of potentially dying. Someone about to engage in a dangerous activity is facing a contingent threat, not an ongoing physical deterioration. The *rashbam* uses the language of *haya mitonen al mitato* — the person is in a state of mourning for their own impending death — an *onen* for themselves. It is a striking formulation: the dying person inhabits a liminal state that mirrors the *onen's* interval between death and burial, poised between two worlds.

---

## Boundaries/Definitions

### Hybrid Category

The *gemara* now reports a teaching: *matnat shchiv mera b'miktzas* — a partial gift by a dying person — was attributed to Rav Nachman as establishing a hybrid category: *harei kematnat bari veharei kematnat shchiv mera* — it is in some respects like a *matnat bari* and in some respects like a *matnat shchiv mera*. *Harei kematnat bari she'im amad eino chozer* — like a *matnat bari* in that if the person recovers, the gift is not retracted. *Harei kematnat shchiv mera dlo ba'ei kinyan* — like a *matnat shchiv mera* in that no *kinyan* is required.

The logic of this hybrid construction is that since we have just established the principle that *divrei shchiv mera k'chtuvim u'k'msurim damu* — no *kinyan* is needed for a *shchiv mera's* declaration — and since *miktzas nechasim* with *metzaveh machmas misa* is now a species of *matnat shchiv mera*, perhaps the no-*kinyan* rule applies here too, even while the *amad eino chozer* rule (which tracks the *matnat bari* side) remains in force.

### Rava Correction

Rava rejected this emphatically: *lav amina lachu, lo tiplu buki seriki be-Rav Nachman* — have I not told you not to hang empty pitchers on Rav Nachman, do not attribute such nonsense to him. *Hachi amar Rav Nachman: harei hu kematnat bari u'ba'ei kinyan* — what Rav Nachman actually said is: it is entirely like a *matnat bari* and a *kinyan* is required. The two halves of the proposed hybrid — *amad eino chozer* and no *kinyan* needed — must both track the same model. If it is *matnat bari* in the sense that recovery does not void the gift, then it is *matnat bari* in every operative sense, and a *kinyan* is required.

### Summary Framework

The session's contribution to the overall architecture of *matnat shchiv mera* may now be summarized. What the *mishnah* established was one principle: *kol nechasav, amad chozer* — if all of one's possessions are given and the person recovers, the gift is voided. Everything else developed in today's *gemara* is an accretion beyond the *mishnah*:

The principle of *chozer b'matnato* — the right to retract a first gift in favor of a second, with *diatiki m'vatela diatiki* as its expression — was not in the *mishnah*. The principle of *divrei shchiv mera k'chtuvim u'k'msurim damu* — that no *kinyan* is needed — was not in the *mishnah*. The extension of *matnat shchiv mera* status to *miktzas nechasim* paired with *metzaveh machmas misa* — explicit expression of mortal fear — was not in the *mishnah*. And the firm ruling that *miktzas nechasim* without such explicit expression remains *matnat bari* in every respect — requiring *kinyan*, not voided by recovery — was also not in the *mishnah*, though it is now clearly entrenched.

The lines are now drawn. *Matnat shchiv mera* proper — *kol nechasav*, or *miktzas nechasim* with *metzaveh machmas misa* — requires no *kinyan* and is voided by recovery. *Matnat bari* — *miktzas nechasim* without explicit mortal intent — requires a *kinyan* and is not voided by recovery. The two sides of the board, as it were, remain entirely distinct.

---

---

# Bava Batra 152

## Matnat Shchiv Meira Basi…

### Kol vs. Miktzat

We pick up toward the bottom of 151b, in the middle of drawing together the general rules of *matnat shchiv meira*. The *mishna* itself distinguished between two fundamental categories: *kol nekhasav* — a gift of all one's property — and *miktzat nekhasav* — a gift of only part of one's property. These two categories serve as the baseline for the *halacha* of *amad chozer* and *amad eino chozer*, that is, whether recovering from one's illness voids the gift.

The *gemara*, however, introduces several additional distinctions that do not appear anywhere in the *mishna*, distinctions that many *bnei yeshiva* assume to be the ironclad rule of *shchiv meira* and yet which represent genuine *chiddushim*. Chief among these is the principle that a *shchiv meira* does not require a *kinyan*: *divrei shchiv meira ke-khtuvim u-ke-msurim damu*, the words of a dying person are treated as if they have already been written and transferred. This is not an assumption of the *mishna* and not everyone initially agreed to it.

### Kinyan Requirements

The *gemara* ultimately concludes that this special dispensation — the exemption from requiring a *kinyan* — is limited to the case of *kol nekhasav*. A gift of *kol nekhasav* does not require a *kinyan*. A gift of *miktzat nekhasav*, by contrast, does require a *kinyan*, because outside of the special *halachic* framework of *matnat shchiv meira*, such a gift operates like an ordinary *matnat bari* and must follow the standard rules of acquisition.

### Amad Chozer Rule

The *gemara* further introduces the rule of *chozer b'matnaso* and the parallel rule of *diatiki mevateles diatiki* — a later will overrides an earlier one. These two rules are related but distinct. The principle of *amad chozer* concerns the case where the donor recovers: because the entire gift was predicated on the assumption of impending death, if the person gets better, the gift is automatically voided. The rule of *diatiki mevateles diatiki* addresses a different scenario: the donor in fact dies, so one might think the original gift should stand; yet the *gemara*'s *chiddush* is that even so, a later will and testament can override an earlier one. Both of these rules — *amad chozer* and *diatiki mevateles diatiki* — are limited to the classic category of *matnat shchiv meira* of *kol nekhasav*.

### Metzaveh Makhmas Misa

The *gemara* also introduces the concept of *metzaveh makhmas misa* as a way of bringing a *miktzat nekhasav* case within the special *halacha* of *shchiv meira*. The mere fact that a person is bedridden does not automatically mean that every transaction they conduct is a *matnat shchiv meira*. A person may be ill for months and still be conducting ordinary business. It is therefore possible for someone lying on their deathbed to give away part of their property simply as a normal gift, operating fully within the *matnat bari* framework.

However, if the donor is explicit — if they say, in effect, "I am giving this because I fear I am about to die" — then even a gift of *miktzat nekhasav* is elevated into the *shchiv meira* category. The *gemara*'s example is the woman who, in her distress, gave away her necklace. When a person is thus explicit about giving *makhmas misa*, all the special *halachot* of *shchiv meira* apply even to a partial gift. The key point is that *metzaveh makhmas misa* requires an explicit verbal declaration; it cannot be inferred merely from context.

---

## Rava vs. Rav Nachman

### Shayar Karka Case

The *gemara* records that Rava challenged Rav Nachman on the question of whether *miktzat nekhasav* requires a *kinyan*. Rava had affirmed, and indeed defended forcefully, the position of Rav Nachman that *miktzat nekhasav* does require a *kinyan* — dismissing those who attributed the opposite view to Rav Nachman as saying something foolish. Having established that position, Rava then proceeds to challenge it from the *mishna*.

The *mishna* states: *shayer karka kol she-hu, matnaso kayyemet* — if the *shchiv meira* left over any amount of land for himself, his gift remains valid even if he recovers. This is the classic *miktzat nekhasav* case. Rava's challenge is: does this *mishna* not demonstrate that *miktzat nekhasav* is valid even without a *kinyan*? Just as *kol nekhasav* is valid without a *kinyan*, perhaps this case of *miktzat* is also valid without one?

### Shimuel's Answer

The *gemara* responds: *lo, de-kanu minei* — no, the *mishna* is speaking of a case where a *kinyan* was in fact performed. The *mishna* thus speaks of both categories with a *kinyan*: in the *miktzat* case the gift remains valid upon recovery, and in the *kol nekhasav* case the gift is voided upon recovery.

But this answer immediately raises a further difficulty. If the *mishna*'s case of *kol nekhasav* — where recovery voids the gift — also involved a *kinyan*, why does the *kinyan* not convert the transaction into a *matnat bari*, which would be *amad eino chozer*? If performing a *kinyan* defines the transaction as operating in the *matnat bari* mode, then recovery should not void it.

The *gemara* answers by quoting Shimuel's ruling: *shchiv meira she-kasav kol nekhasav la-acherim, af al pi she-kanu mi-yado, amad chozer* — a *shchiv meira* who gives all his property to others, even if a *kinyan* was performed, the gift is voided if he recovers. The reason, the *gemara* explains, is *bi-yadu'a she-lo haya kinyan ella makhmas ha-misa* — once one is in the *kol nekhasav* category, it is evident that the entire act, including the *kinyan*, was done in anticipation of death. The *kinyan* therefore does not shift the transaction into the *matnat bari* framework. Whether or not a *kinyan* accompanies a *kol nekhasav* gift, it remains a *matnat shchiv meira* in every respect: no *kinyan* is needed to make it effective, and even a *kinyan* does not prevent it from being voided upon recovery.

### Rochel Story

Rav Mesharsheya then challenged Rava on the requirement of a *kinyan* for *miktzat nekhasav* from a *ma'aseh*: the story of the mother of the sons of Rochel. This woman was ill and said, "Let my necklace be given to my daughter" — a necklace worth twelve *maneh*, which was thus a *miktzat nekhasav* gift. She then died. The *chachamim* upheld her words. Apparently, this was an entirely verbal gift with no *kinyan*, yet it was honored. This seems to demonstrate that even *miktzat nekhasav* does not require a *kinyan*.

### Metzaveh Response

The *gemara* answers: *hasam be-metzaveh makhmas misa* — that case involved an explicit declaration of *metzaveh makhmas misa*. The woman's cry of distress placed her squarely in the *shchiv meira* category even for a partial gift. It was precisely this explicit invocation of imminent death that elevated the *miktzat* gift into the special *halacha*, such that it required no *kinyan* and would likewise be voided upon recovery.

This answer, it must be said, begins to feel like a remarkably flexible tool: any time a *miktzat* case appears to function without a *kinyan*, one can always resolve the difficulty by invoking *metzaveh makhmas misa*. Yet the *gemara*'s consistent deployment of this answer reflects a principled distinction: every case where *miktzat nekhasav* appears to operate without a *kinyan* turns out, on examination, to involve either *kol nekhasav* or an explicit *metzaveh makhmas misa*. The *gemara* is insisting on a sharp line between the two categories.

It is worth pausing here to distinguish *matnat shchiv meira* from the related but distinct principle of *mitzvah le-kayyem divrei ha-meit* — the moral obligation to fulfill the wishes of the deceased. The latter is not a legal transfer; it does not cause property to change hands automatically. It is rather a moral charge upon the heirs, as in the case of David's final instructions to Solomon. *Matnat shchiv meira* operates as an actual legal acquisition. The question of which cases fall into which category — and whether the sons of Rochel may have been acting on *mitzvah le-kayyem divrei ha-meit* rather than on the legal force of *matnat shchiv meira* — is a separate discussion.

---

## Get vs. Money Case

### Get Comparison

Ravina challenged Rava from a *baraita* involving two parallel scenarios. In the first, a dying man says: "Give this *get* to my wife and this writ of manumission to my slave," and then dies. The *baraita* rules that the *get* and writ of manumission may not be given after death, because the man's legal capacity to divorce his wife or free his slave does not survive him; his wife has become a widow and his slave passes to his heirs. In the second scenario, the man says: "Give one hundred *maneh* to Reuven," and then dies. Here the *baraita* rules that the money is given after death.

### No Kinyan Assumption

How do we know there was no *kinyan* in the money case? The *gemara* reasons *dumya de-get*: it is analogous to the *get*. By a *get*, a *kinyan* is not the operative mechanism and would be irrelevant to its effectiveness. Since the *baraita* presents the monetary case in exact parallel to the *get* case, it would be incongruous to introduce a *kinyan* into the money scenario. The entire context of the *baraita* is one of verbal instructions alone, with no further act of acquisition. Yet the money transfer is upheld. This seems to demonstrate that a *miktzat* verbal gift without a *kinyan* is valid — directly contrary to what Rav Nachman and Rava maintain.

### Money Case Resolution

The *gemara* again answers: *hacha nami de-metzaveh makhmas misa* — here too the case involves an explicit *metzaveh makhmas misa*, which places the gift within the *shchiv meira* category even without a *kinyan*. Alternatively, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua adds a second resolution: *de-tani hani matnita be-machalek kol nekhasav* — the *baraita* is dealing with a case where the man was distributing all of his property. Either the hundred *maneh* constituted his entire estate, or he distributed this sum in the context of disposing of all his assets together. In either reading, the case falls under *kol nekhasav*, which requires no *kinyan* and is squarely within the *matnat shchiv meira* framework.

---

## Metzaveh Kinyan Need

### Rav Huna's Ruling

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua makes an important clarification at this point: *metzaveh makhmas misa b'alma ba'ei kinyan* — even a case of *metzaveh makhmas misa* requires a *kinyan* as a general rule. This is a significant qualification. One might have thought that invoking *metzaveh makhmas misa* entirely dissolves the requirement of a *kinyan* for any partial gift. Rav Huna corrects this impression. The *metzaveh makhmas misa* category indeed places the donor within the *shchiv meira* framework, with all that entails regarding *amad chozer*, but it does not per se eliminate the *kinyan* requirement.

### Distribution Defense

This then requires an explanation of the *baraita*'s money case, where apparently no *kinyan* was performed and yet the transfer is upheld. Rav Huna's answer is that the *baraita* speaks of a case of *machalek kol nekhasav* — distributing all one's property. It is this feature, the *kol nekhasav* character of the distribution, that exempts the gift from requiring a *kinyan*, not the *metzaveh makhmas misa* element alone. By being situated within a comprehensive distribution of all assets, even a particular bequest within that distribution acquires the status of a *matnat shchiv meira* of *kol nekhasav*.

---

## Halakhic Summary

### Kol Nekhasav Rules

The *gemara* now draws together its conclusions. In the category of *matnat shchiv meira* of *kol nekhasav*: no *kinyan* is required to make the gift effective. If the donor recovers, *amad chozer* — the gift is voided. This remains true even in the presence of a *metzaveh makhmas misa* declaration, which operates, for this purpose, on the same footing as *kol nekhasav*.

### Miktzat Kinyan Rule

In the category of *matnat shchiv meira* of *miktzat nekhasav*, by contrast, a *kinyan* is always required. Without a *kinyan*, the gift simply does not take effect — regardless of whether the donor subsequently dies. A *miktzat nekhasav* gift without a *kinyan* operates entirely within the *matnat bari* framework, and if no *kinyan* was performed, there is no acquisition. If there was a *kinyan* and the donor dies, the gift stands; if there was a *kinyan* and the donor recovers, *amad eino chozer* — the gift remains valid, because it was a *matnat bari* transaction from the outset.

### Kinyan Effect

This brings into focus the precise role a *kinyan* plays within the *kol nekhasav* category. Once a donor is in the *kol nekhasav* category — either because the gift encompasses all their property, or because of an explicit *metzaveh makhmas misa* — a *kinyan* does not alter the fundamental nature of the transaction. It does not transform the gift into a *matnat bari*. The gift remains a *matnat shchiv meira* whether a *kinyan* was performed or not. A *kinyan* in this category does not prevent *amad chozer*; if the person recovers, the gift is voided even where a *kinyan* took place, because the *kinyan* itself is understood to have been performed *makhmas ha-misa* — on account of the anticipated death — and does not operate as an independent act of acquisition of the *matnat bari* type.

One might ask: if the *kinyan* changes nothing, why would anyone perform one in the *kol nekhasav* category? The *gemara* will address this shortly, considering the possibility that in certain circumstances a *kinyan* — particularly when combined with a *shtar* — is intended to effect *amad eino chozer*. But that is the complication the *gemara* now proceeds to explore. The baseline established here is: in the *kol nekhasav* category, the presence or absence of a *kinyan* does not change the essential *halacha*; in the *miktzat nekhasav* category, a *kinyan* is constitutive of the gift's validity.

---

## Shtar + Kinyan

### Itmar Scenario

The *gemara* now introduces a more complex case, recorded with the word *itmar*: *matnat shchiv meira she-kasav bah kinyan* — a *matnat shchiv meira* in which a *kinyan* was performed and that fact was written into the *shtar*. The *gemara* thus contemplates a case where three elements converge: the donor is a *shchiv meira* operating in the *kol nekhasav* framework; a *shtar* was written recording the gift; and a *kinyan* was explicitly performed and memorialized within that *shtar*, in the manner that *shtarot* record, for instance, *v'kanina minei b'umana de-kasher le-miknaya beih*.

The question is whether this combination — the full formality of a *shtar* with an explicit *kinyan* written into it — changes the *halachic* character of the gift. We have already established that a *kinyan* alone does not transform a *kol nekhasav* gift into a *matnat bari*. We have also established that a *shtar* alone — a *diatiki* — does not prevent *amad chozer* or *diatiki mevateles diatiki*. But together, do they produce a different result?

The approach of the *Rashbam* is to treat this as re-opening the earlier discussion about a *kinyan* alone. The *Tosafot*, however, insist that the earlier question has been resolved: a *kinyan* alone does nothing to alter the *matnat shchiv meira* framework. The new question can only be about the combination of a *shtar* with an explicitly written *kinyan*, not merely a *kinyan* by itself. The following analysis follows the reading of *Tosafot*.

### Rav: Two Chariots

*Bei Rav* — the academy of Rav — said in the name of Rava: *arkvei atei richshei* — it is riding on two chariots. This vivid image captures the dual nature of such a gift: it partakes simultaneously of the character of a *matnat bari* and the character of a *matnat shchiv meira*. The formalities — the *shtar*, the explicitly recorded *kinyan* — give it the weight of a *matnat bari*. The circumstances — the donor lying ill in bed, the gift described explicitly as a *matnat shchiv meira* — keep it within the *shchiv meira* framework.

The practical consequence is that it operates like a *matnat bari* in one critical respect: *amad eino chozer* — if the donor recovers, the gift is not voided. This is the effect of the added formality. At the same time, it retains the power of a *matnat shchiv meira* in the following sense: a *shchiv meira* can transfer a debt directly to a third party without the need for *ma'amad sheloshtan*. Ordinarily, if one person owes money to another and the creditor wishes to transfer that debt to a third party, the only mechanism available — short of *ma'amad sheloshtan*, convening all three parties together — is to transfer the written *shtar chov*, which still leaves open the possibility of *mechila* by the original creditor. A *shchiv meira*, however, can transfer the debt directly to the recipient, bypassing *ma'amad sheloshtan* entirely and removing the creditor's ability to be *mochel*. This power is unique to *matnat shchiv meira* and cannot be replicated by ordinary *kinyanim*. So the gift with a *shtar* and *kinyan* retains this *shchiv meira* power while gaining the additional strength of *amad eino chozer*.

### Debt Transfer Power

The significance of this *shchiv meira* power over debts should not be understated. If a dying person has extensive outstanding debts owed to them, the ability to transfer those obligations directly to beneficiaries without *ma'amad sheloshtan* — and in a manner that the original creditor can no longer be *mochel* — represents a substantial practical advantage. The *matnat shchiv meira* thus continues to have distinctive legal force even in the beefed-up form under discussion.

### Shimuel: Unknown

Shimuel, however, says: *lo yadana mai adun bah* — I do not know how to treat it. The combination of *shtar* and *kinyan* creates such an ambiguous hybrid that Shimuel declines to assign it a clear *halachic* status.

### Shtar Delivery Limit

The reasoning behind Shimuel's uncertainty is this: *shema lo gamar le-haknoso ela be-shtar, ve-ein shtar le-achar mita* — perhaps by doing all of this the donor indicated that he only wished the gift to take effect through the *shtar*, and a *shtar* cannot operate after death. This principle of *ein shtar le-achar mita* operates on the model of *ein get le-achar mita*: just as a *get* cannot take effect after the husband's death, a *shtar* that is intended as the operative instrument of transfer cannot take effect if the donor has already died before it was delivered.

But the difficulty runs deeper than the question of whether the *shtar* was or was not delivered before death. Shimuel's concern, as explained by the *Rashbam* and accepted by *Tosafot*, is one of intent. The donor who surrounds his *shchiv meira* gift with all the apparatus of a *matnat bari* — a formal *shtar*, an explicitly recorded *kinyan* — may be signaling that he wants the gift to operate on the *matnat bari* track, taking effect after death. But a *matnat bari* cannot take effect after death. If I declare today, while in full health, that I wish someone to own my property after my death, that declaration has no legal effect; a transfer cannot be accomplished by a living person to take effect at the moment of death unless the person is operating within the special *shchiv meira* framework. If the donor is trying to use the *matnat bari* mechanism to achieve what is effectively a posthumous transfer, he gets neither: not a valid *matnat bari*, because it cannot take effect after death, and not a valid *matnat shchiv meira*, because he has chosen to operate on a different track. The result is total invalidity, and the property reverts to the estate.

So for Rav, the combined *shtar* and *kinyan* produces a beefed-up *matnat shchiv meira* — more powerful than the ordinary kind, but still recognizably a *matnat shchiv meira*, with its distinctive powers. For Shimuel, the same combination produces a failed *matnat bari* — an attempt to use *bari* mechanisms for a posthumous transfer, which collapses entirely.

---

## Self-Contradiction

### Rav Contradiction

Having established the positions of Rav and Shimuel, the *gemara* notes that each appears to contradict himself. The contradiction is introduced with the formula *v'rami de-Rav a-de-Rav v'de-Shmuel a-de-Shmuel*.

Rav's apparent self-contradiction: Rav said earlier that a *matnat shchiv meira* with a *shtar* and *kinyan* is a strengthened *matnat shchiv meira* — *amad eino chozer*. Yet a tradition transmitted from Rav through Rabbi Elazar to Rav Ravin and then to the exile says: *shchiv meira she-amar kisvu u-tnu maneh le-ploni u-meit, ein kosvin ve-nosnin* — if a *shchiv meira* said "write and give a hundred *maneh* to so-and-so" and then died before it was done, you do not write the *shtar* and give it. The reason given is *shema lo gamar le-haknoso ela be-shtar ve-ein shtar le-achar mita* — perhaps he only intended the gift to take effect through the *shtar*, and the *shtar* cannot operate after death. So here Rav seems to be saying that a *shtar* context undermines the *matnat shchiv meira* rather than strengthening it.

### Shimuel Contradiction

Shimuel's apparent self-contradiction: Shimuel said earlier that a *matnat shchiv meira* with a *shtar* and *kinyan* is ineffective — a failed *matnat bari*. Yet Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shimuel that the *halacha* is *kosvin ve-nosnin* — in the "write and give" case, you do write the *shtar* and give it. This seems to say that even a *shtar*-mediated *shchiv meira* gift is valid, the opposite of what Shimuel seemed to hold.

### Rav Resolution

The *gemara* resolves Rav's contradiction: *ha di-kanu minei, ha de-lo kanu minei* — the two cases differ in whether a *kinyan* was performed. When the *shchiv meira* said only "write and give" without a *kinyan*, Rav says the *shtar* has not yet been delivered, and without delivery — since the donor chose the *shtar* track — the gift cannot take effect after death. When, however, a *kinyan* was also explicitly performed and written into the *shtar*, Rav says this combination strengthens the *matnat shchiv meira* and effects *amad eino chozer*. The two cases are thus not contradictory but represent different factual scenarios.

This resolution, as *Tosafot* notes, raises its own question, because it seems to suggest that the distinction rests on whether the *kinyan* was merely performed alongside the *shtar* or was explicitly written into it. *Tosafot* reads *kanu minei* in the decisive case as referring specifically to the *kinyan* being recorded within the *shtar* itself — it is that integration of *kinyan* and *shtar* into a single instrument that gives the gift its enhanced standing. When the *kinyan* is absent altogether, the "write and give" instruction places the gift entirely on the *shtar* track, and *ein shtar le-achar mita* applies.

There is a relevant parallel to an earlier *mishna* where a will was found tied to a person's side — the *diatiki keshura al matno* — and yet was ruled ineffective because it had not been handed over. The principle that emerges is that when someone chooses the *shtar* path of *matnat shchiv meira*, delivery of the *shtar* becomes a necessary condition of the gift's taking effect. The verbal *matnat shchiv meira* path and the *shtar* path are distinct; choosing the latter means accepting its conditions.

### Shimuel Resolution

The *gemara* resolves Shimuel's contradiction by introducing the principle of *bi-myafes kocho* — when one makes clear through explicit language that the intent of the *kinyan* and *shtar* is to strengthen and supplement the *matnat shchiv meira* rather than to replace it or operate on a different track. When that explicit clarification is present, even Shimuel agrees that the gift is effective. When it is absent, Shimuel reads the combination of *shtar* and *kinyan* as an attempt to craft a *matnat bari* operative after death, and rules the gift void.

The two positions of the earlier Shimuel and the later Shimuel thus represent two different factual scenarios: without *bi-myafes kocho*, the gift is interpreted as a failed *matnat bari*; with *bi-myafes kocho*, even Shimuel recognizes it as a valid, strengthened *matnat shchiv meira*.

---

## Myafes Kocho Formula

### Kanina Mineih

The *gemara* now asks: *heichi dami myafes kocho* — what precisely does the explicit language of *myafes kocho* look like? Rav Chisda provides the formula: *kanina mineih* — we performed a *kinyan* with him — *mosif a-matnata da* — in addition to this gift. This is how the *shtar* should record the act.

### Mosif Keyword

The critical word, as Rav Chisda makes clear, is *mosif* — "in addition." This single word does all the work. It signals unambiguously that the *kinyan* is not the operative mechanism of the gift, not an attempt to shift the transaction onto the *matnat bari* track, but simply an addition to an already-valid *matnat shchiv meira*. The gift stands on its own as a *matnat shchiv meira*; the *kinyan* is being layered on top of it, supplementing it, strengthening it. Without that word, the *kinyan* and *shtar* together might be read as constituting an entirely different kind of transaction — a *matnat bari* — with all the problems that Shimuel identifies.

### Explicit Intent Effect

When the formula *kanina mineih mosif a-matnata da* is used, Rav Chisda says, he would agree with Rava's position. The explicit language removes Shimuel's concern entirely. There is no longer any ambiguity about which track the donor is riding. He is on the *matnat shchiv meira* track, and everything that follows — the *shtar*, the *kinyan* — is in service of that *matnat shchiv meira*, not in substitution for it. The gift is valid, *amad eino chozer*, and retains the distinctive powers of *matnat shchiv meira*, including the ability to transfer debts without *ma'amad sheloshtan*.

---

## Will Override Cases

### Simple Override

The *gemara* now turns to a related but distinct question: what happens when a *shchiv meira* writes one will and then writes a second will? The *gemara* presents this as *pshita* — apparently obvious — based on what has already been established. We know the rule of *diatiki mevateles diatiki*: a later will overrides an earlier one, operating on the same logic as *amad chozer* — since the entire gift was predicated on the anticipation of death, the donor retains the power to revise his instructions as long as he lives.

This is captured in the tradition that Rav Dimi brought from *Eretz Yisrael*: *de-asi kanina u-mevatel de-asi kanina* — a later *diatiki* cancels the earlier *diatiki*. This applies whenever the *matnat shchiv meira* is in the standard framework: either *kol nekhasav* or *metzaveh makhmas misa*.

### Rav: First Binds

The *gemara* then asks: what if the donor did not merely write a will twice, but in each case wrote it with full formality — *katav ve-zikah lo, ve-katav ve-zikah lo*? Here the *gemara* understands *zikah* as referring not merely to handing over the *shtar* — which would have been the case in the simple *diatiki* scenario as well, since an undelivered *shtar* would be ineffective — but to performing the gift together with a *kinyan*. The question is whether this added formality prevents the second will from overriding the first.

Rav rules: *rishon kana* — the first recipient has acquired the property, and the second will does not override it. Rav describes this as *harei hi ke-matnat bari* — it functions like a *matnat bari* — meaning that the effect of the added formality is that the gift cannot be retracted. This parallels precisely what Rav said in the earlier case of *matnat shchiv meira she-kasav bah kinyan*: the combination of *shtar* and *kinyan* creates an irrevocable gift, *amad eino chozer*, and similarly *eino chozer be-matnaso* — the donor cannot use a later will to override the earlier one.

### Shimuel: Second Overrides

Shimuel rules: *sheini kanah* — the second recipient acquires. Shimuel describes this as *harei hi ke-matnat shchiv meira* — it still operates like a *matnat shchiv meira*, which means the *kinyan* does not render it irrevocable, and the rule of *diatiki mevateles diatiki* continues to apply.

### Parallel to Shtar Case

The *gemara* immediately notes: *i-plegu vah chada zimna* — haven't they already disputed this exact question in the earlier case of *matnat shchiv meira she-kasav bah kinyan*? The parallel is precise: the question in both cases is whether a *matnat shchiv meira* accompanied by the formalities of *shtar* and *kinyan* is irrevocable, or whether it retains the full retractability of a standard *matnat shchiv meira*. Rav says it becomes irrevocable; Shimuel says it remains retractable.

### Why Both Cases Needed

The *gemara* answers: *tzricha* — you need both cases, because each teaches something the other does not. In the first case — *matnat shchiv meira she-kasav bah kinyan* — one might have thought Rav's ruling of *amad eino chozer* applies only because the *kinyan* was explicitly written into the *shtar*, making the connection between the two maximally clear. Without that written integration, one might have thought Rav would agree to Shimuel. By stating the ruling again in the *diatiki* case, the *gemara* teaches that even when the *kinyan* and *shtar* are not written together in one integrated document — even when they are conducted in parallel — Rav says *rishon kanah* and the gift is irrevocable.

Conversely, one might have thought that Shimuel's ruling of *sheini kanah* applies only in the *diatiki* case, where the *kinyan* was not written into the *shtar*; perhaps when the *kinyan* is written into the *shtar* as a single integrated act, Shimuel would agree with Rav. By stating Shimuel's ruling in both cases, the *gemara* teaches that even with full integration Shimuel maintains that *sheini kanah* — unless there is explicit *myafes kocho* language.

---

## Sura Query

### Query Details

The *gemara* concludes the *daf* with a report from the Academy of Sura. *Rav Yirmeya bar Abba* relates that they sent an inquiry from the house of Rav to Shimuel: *shchiv meira she-kasav kol nekhasav la-acherim ve-kanu mi-yado, mahu?* — a *shchiv meira* who wrote all his property to others and a *kinyan* was performed — what is the *halacha*? Note that here, no *shtar* is mentioned; the question concerns a *kinyan* alone accompanying a *kol nekhasav* gift.

### No Retraction

Shimuel's response was: *ein achar kinyan klum* — after a *kinyan*, nothing; there is no retraction. This seems to say that once a *kinyan* has been performed, the gift cannot be undone.

### Initial Misread

The initial understanding of this response was that it applied only to the case of someone writing another will to override the gift — *le-achar*, to another. But, reasoned those who first heard the ruling, surely if he recovered — *le-atzmo* — the gift would be voided, since *amad chozer* is a fundamental principle of *matnat shchiv meira* and a *kinyan* alone in the *kol nekhasav* category does not change this, as Shimuel himself ruled earlier.

### Chisda Correction

Rav Chisda corrected this misunderstanding, citing the clarification that Rav Huna brought from Kufi: *bein le-atzmo bein le-acherin* — whether regarding the donor himself recovering or regarding a subsequent will overriding the first, *amad eino chozer* and *eino chozer be-matnaso*. Once a *kinyan* was performed together with a *kol nekhasav* gift, the donation is irrevocable in both senses.

This, then, represents a point of agreement between Rav and Shimuel, at least according to this version. When a *shchiv meira* performs a *kinyan* alongside a *kol nekhasav* gift — even without a *shtar*, or at least without the full integration of *kinyan* into *shtar* — both authorities agree that the gift is strengthened to the point of *amad eino chozer*. Where they continue to disagree, according to the version that emerges from *Tosafot*'s reading, is in the case where *kinyan* and *shtar* are fully integrated into a single instrument without explicit *myafes kocho* language: Rav reads this as a beefed-up *matnat shchiv meira*, while Shimuel reads it as a failed *matnat bari*. The formula of *kanina mineih mosif a-matnata da* is the key that, even for Shimuel, resolves the ambiguity in favor of validity.

---

---

# Bava Batra 153

## Shchiv Mera Retraction

### Rav vs. Shmuel

We pick up at the top of 153, three lines from the top, at the words *hu d'kanu minei* — the conclusion of a lengthy discussion concerning a *shchiv mera* who gives away all of his property but also performs a *kinyan*. Rav holds that this combination means he cannot be *chozer* — he cannot retract the gift. Shmuel, by contrast, questions whether the gift is effective even if he dies.

### Rashbam & Tosafot

The Rashbam explains that the preceding discussion concerned a case of a *stam* *kinyan* — a straightforward act of acquisition — and argues that this does not fit well with the evidence presented earlier, which seemed to indicate that whenever a *kinyan* is performed, everyone agrees the gift takes effect, and that if he recovers (*amad*) the gift is revoked (*chozer*). Tosafot therefore explains that the case involves a *kinyan* that was specifically written into the *shtar* itself, which is what the *gemara* appears to indicate. This accounts for the range of opinions — from the view that the gift is fully effective and the donor cannot retract, to the view that it does not take effect at all.

### Rav Huna Case

The *gemara* now concludes this discussion with a practical illustration. The case is one where *kanu minei* — they performed this *kinyan* together with the *shtar* in the especially strong manner described — and presumably the donor subsequently recovered and sought to retract the gift.
