A clever buyer can always make a particular transaction look like a favorable one. The prohibition is categorical precisely to foreclose that manipulation.

### Gift Logic

The reason gifts are treated differently now becomes clear. When it comes to a gratuitous transfer, the temptation the Gemara worries about is simply not present. There is no one dangling money in front of the young person; there is no immediate exchange in which the senses are engaged by tangible gain. *Aval gabei matnah i'lav de'hava leh hana'ah mineh lo hava yahiv leh matnah* — were it not that the person received some genuine benefit from the recipient, he would not have given a gift. The absence of an immediate monetary temptation means that the young person's judgment is not being overridden by the same seductive force. The Gemara acknowledges, implicitly, that this logic has limits — one could imagine scenarios in which a young person is manipulated through gifts of hospitality or flattery into transferring land — but the structural concern, the categorical fear of the jingling coin, is simply not present in the same way.

### Chachamim Rationale

Even granting this reasoning, one might still ask: once the Sages have restricted the sale for the young person's protection, why not simply extend the same protection to gifts? Whatever the difference in risk level, the estate is still being given away for nothing. The Gemara adds a further consideration: *amru rabbanan tehei matnato matnah dilaavdu lei mili* — the Sages wanted people to be willing to do favors for the young person. If it were known that no gift he gave could ever be valid, people would have no incentive to invest socially in him. The very *possibility* that he might gift land to someone who has been generous to him creates a social dynamic in which people shower him with kindness. The Rashbam sharpens this point: *ligmol lo chesed u'lheitiv lo bechol inyanim* — to perform acts of kindness for him in all matters. The practical implication the Gemara seems to have in mind is that since gifts of *karka* are relatively rare even among adults, and the young person could in any event make gifts of *metaltelin* freely, the real significance of allowing gifts of land is primarily this incentive structure — preserving his social support network during the years before he reaches full transactional capacity.

## When Check Needed

### Verification Need

Having discussed the age thresholds for land transactions, the Gemara pivots to a broader discussion of when direct verification of adulthood is required. The triggering issue in the earlier narrative — the brother who proposed exhuming the body to check for pubic hair — raises the general question: when must one establish the presence of pubic hair through direct examination, and when may one rely on a presumption of adulthood based on age alone?

The framework here rests on what is known as *chazakah de'Rava* — Rava's presumption that once a boy reaches thirteen or a girl reaches twelve, we assume they have developed the requisite signs of adulthood. The halachic conclusion is that this presumption may be relied upon for matters that are *de'Rabbanan* in nature, but not for matters that are *de'Oraita*. This is why, at the rabbinic level, a thirteen-year-old boy may lead a congregation or receive an *aliyah*, since those functions rest on rabbinic frameworks. But for a *de'Oraita* obligation — such as *parashat zachor*, whose reading may be a Torah-level requirement — mere age is insufficient; one would need affirmative evidence of physical maturity. It should be noted, though not developed in this Gemara, that for boys, the presence of facial hair constitutes evidence of pubic hair and thereby avoids the need for more intrusive examination.

### Four Areas

Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel now provides a formal statement: *bodkin le'kiddushin le'geirushin le'chalitzah u'le'miunin* — we verify physical adulthood for four areas: *kiddushin*, *geirushin*, *chalitzah*, and *miun*.

For *kiddushin*: suppose a boy who was thirteen gave *kesef kiddushin* to a girl who is known to be an adult. Is the marriage valid? The answer has consequences in both directions. Being stringent and treating the marriage as definitely valid would mean that if she subsequently accepts *kiddushin* from a second man, her acceptance from the first forecloses the second. But treating the first as merely a *safeik* means she would need a *get* from both. Where consequences attach in both directions, the question cannot be resolved by simple stringency alone; one must establish the facts. Similarly, if a girl who has reached age twelve but whose physical maturity has not been verified accepts *kesef kiddushin* directly — not through her father — one must verify whether the *kiddushin* was definitively valid.

For *geirushin*: only a halachic adult can issue a *get*; therefore the husband's adulthood must be verified. The Gemara notes that since verifying for *kiddushin* and verifying for *geirushin* cover overlapping ground — once you have established adulthood for one purpose you have established it for the other — the separate mention of *geirushin* must be doing independent work.

### Yibum Issue

That independent work, the Gemara explains, concerns *yibum*. The Mishnah elsewhere establishes that a boy of nine years and one day who engages in intercourse with his deceased brother's widow has thereby *acquired* her through *yibum* — the act of intercourse creates the marriage-bond of *yibum* in a way that is almost purely factual rather than formal. Even if the parties did not fully understand the legal significance of the act, the Gemara contemplates that intercourse can create this bond. The woman is thus *de'Oraita* married through *yibum*. But *veino oseh get ad sheyagdil* — the boy cannot issue a *get* until he is an adult. So here is a scenario in which the boy may be legally bound to her through *yibum* and yet his ability to issue a *get* requires separate verification of adulthood — hence the need to check specifically for purposes of *geirushin* even where *kiddushin* was never the question.

### Chalitzah Debate

The statement that one must verify adulthood for *chalitzah* is noted as rejecting the position of Rabbi Yose. The verse governing *chalitzah* uses the word *ha'ish* — the man — in requiring that the male party be an adult, but does not explicitly impose the same requirement on the woman. Rabbi Yose, noting this textual asymmetry, holds that the woman need not be an adult for *chalitzah* to be valid, drawing an analogy to *geirushin*, where the woman is essentially a passive recipient of the *get* and need not be an adult herself. Rabbi Yose reads *chalitzah* similarly: whatever active role the woman plays in removing the sandal, the essential legal actor is the man. The ruling here — that we check *both* parties — rejects Rabbi Yose by equating the woman to the man: *demakshinan isha le'ish, shelo kerabbi yose*.

### Meiun Standard

The inclusion of *miun* in the list is noted as rejecting the position of Rabbi Yehuda. *Miun* is the right of a girl married off by her brothers or mother — in the absence of her father — to verbally reject her husband while she is still a minor, thereby dissolving the marriage without a *get*. Once she reaches adulthood and remains in the marriage, she requires a *get* to leave. Rabbi Yehuda holds that for purposes of *miun*, adulthood is defined not by the standard criterion of two pubic hairs but by a more developed standard: *ad sheyirbe shachor* — until the dark hair is abundant and, as another Gemara specifies, lies flat against the skin. By grouping the verification for *miun* alongside the standard verifications for *kiddushin* and *geirushin*, the ruling implicitly applies the ordinary definition of adulthood and thereby rejects Rabbi Yehuda's heightened standard: *delo kerabbi yehuda*.

### Age Twenty

Finally, the statement concludes: *ulimkor benichsei aviv ad sheyehe ben esrim* — for selling the father's estate, one must be twenty, and this rejects the position mentioned earlier that eighteen suffices. This provides a clean summary: the verification framework covers not only the personal-status areas of marriage and divorce but also the transactional context of inherited land, and it specifies that the threshold for land sales stands at a higher and distinct level from the physical markers of adulthood.

## Summary Rulings

### Twentieth Year

The Gemara now delivers a concentrated series of final halachic rulings. *Toch zman kilfnei zman* — during the twentieth year, the person is still considered to be under age; one must actually complete the twentieth year and enter the twenty-first. This rules out any argument that once the twentieth year has begun, the person has in some sense "reached" twenty.

### Savvy Exception

*Vehilchata kegiddel bar menashya* — the halacha follows Giddel bar Menashya, who held that a person who is demonstrably *yodea be'tiv massa u'mattan* — savvy in the ways of commerce — may have his transactions upheld even before reaching the age of twenty. The age threshold is the default rule; genuine demonstrated business acumen can override it.

### Testimony Split

*Vehilchata kemar zutra* — the halacha follows Mar Zutra's distinction between *metaltelin* and *karka*. A person under twenty whose transactions are valid for *metaltelin* may testify about *metaltelin*, but may not testify about *karka*. This is the combined ruling of the two-criteria framework: formal adulthood via *bar mitzvah*, plus the contextual judgment threshold appropriate to the subject matter.

### Gift Valid

*Vehilchata ke'ameimar* — the halacha follows Ameimar: a gift made by a person under twenty is valid, even though his sale of the same property would not be. Whatever the lingering puzzlement about this ruling — and the Gemara does not fully resolve the intuitive difficulty — this is the operative law.

### Verification All

*Vehilchata kerav nachman amar shmuel bekulhu* — the halacha follows the comprehensive framework of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel across all the cases enumerated: verification of physical adulthood is required for *kiddushin*, *geirushin*, *chalitzah*, and *miun*, and for land sales the threshold is twenty.

## Deathbed Gift

### Rabbi Elazar Rejects

The Gemara now arrives at the Mishnah that directly addresses the question that has been lurking throughout the tractate: does a *matnat shechiv meyra* require a formal *kinyan*, or does a verbal declaration suffice? This is, as the Gemara itself will make clear, the very foundation of the institution of *matnat shechiv meyra* as it is understood from the *yeshiva*-world perspective: the great *chiddush* is that *kechisuvim u'mesurim damu* — a *shichiv meyra's* verbal transfer is treated as if the property has already been written over and delivered. Rabbi Elazar, however, simply denies this. He holds that both a healthy person and a person on his deathbed are governed by the same rules: *echad bari ve'echad mesukan* — there is no special category.

### Property Types

According to Rabbi Elazar, the ordinary rules of *kinyan* apply without modification: *nechasim sheyeish lahem achrayut niknin bekesef beshtar uvachazakah* — property with *achrayut* (real property, which can serve as collateral) is acquired through money, a deed, or *chazakah*; and *she'ein lahem achrayut ein niknin ela bimshicha* — property without *achrayut* (movables) is acquired only through *meshicha*, drawing the object toward oneself. No verbal declaration, however sincere and however made on the threshold of death, substitutes for these formal modes of transfer. The consequence is clear: if the person distributes his estate verbally and then dies without a formal *kinyan* having been completed, the transfers are simply void.

This position is, from a traditional learning standpoint, almost heretical in its rejection of an institution the Sages are assumed to have established. The earlier Mishnah had addressed *matnat shechiv meyra* in terms of *chozer* — whether the gift reverts if the person recovers — but had taken for granted that a verbal transfer was at least effective in the first place. Rabbi Elazar rejects even that premise.

### Meroni Case

Rabbi Eliezer — and here the Gemara will debate whether this is indeed Rabbi Eliezer or Rabbi Elazar — attempts to support the requirement of a formal *kinyan* by citing a story about a man from Meron who was in Jerusalem with a large amount of movable property and wished to give it all away. The Sages told him: *ein lahem takkanah ad sheyiknem agav karka* — there is no way to effect the transfer properly unless he uses *kinyan agav*, the mechanism by which a person transfers movables along with a piece of land, so that the land serves as the anchor for the transfer. Since *meshicha* would be impractical for vast quantities of livestock and goods, *kinyan agav* was the recommended approach. He accordingly acquired a small plot of land near Jerusalem and transferred the northern portion to one person along with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels of wine, the southern portion to another with the same, and so on until he had distributed his entire estate. After his death, the Sages upheld his distributions. Rabbi Eliezer reads this as proof that even in the case of a *shichiv meyra*, a formal *kinyan* was necessary.

### Bnei Rochel Case

Against Rabbi Elazar's position, the Sages cite the case of the mother of the *Bnei Rochel* — the children of a man named Rochel. She was ill and said: "Give my necklace to my daughter." The necklace was worth twelve *maneh*, a substantial sum. She died, and the Sages upheld her words — despite the fact that no *kinyan* had been performed. When Rabbi Eliezer is confronted with this case, his response is striking: *bnei rochel tikberem imam* — let the sons of Rochel be buried by their mother. He does not accept the case as proof of a rule; instead, he suggests it was an exceptional outcome driven by the unworthiness of the sons. The necklace was given to the daughter not because the mother's verbal declaration was legally binding, but because the Sages chose not to allow it to go to sons who did not deserve it. The legal norm, Rabbi Eliezer maintains, has not changed.

## Meroni Debate

### Eliezer Version

The Gemara now unpacks the Meroni case more carefully. Rabbi Eliezer's version of events treats the man from Meron as a *shichiv meyra* who nonetheless needed — and performed — a formal *kinyan*. The very fact that a *kinyan* was done, in Rabbi Eliezer's telling, is what made the distributions valid. This is his proof that even a *shichiv meyra* cannot rely on mere verbal declaration.

### Kinyan Agav

The mechanics of what was done are worth noting. The man used *kinyan agav* — transferring movables by bundling them with a transfer of land. Since performing *meshicha* on hundreds of animals and barrels would be logistically impossible, the *kinyan agav* method allowed the entire transfer to be effected through the formality of the land transaction, with the movables riding along by virtue of being designated together with the land.

### Chachamim Response

The Sages, however, reject Rabbi Eliezer's framing of the Meroni case. *Meroni bari hayah* — the man from Meron was healthy when he made the distributions. He was not a *shichiv meyra* at all. He performed a *kinyan* not because the law of *matnat shechiv meyra* requires it, but simply because as a healthy person making a *matnat bari*, he was subject to ordinary rules of *kinyan*. The reason his distributions were upheld is precisely that he performed a valid *kinyan*. This case therefore proves nothing about what a *shichiv meyra* requires; it is simply a case of an ordinary healthy-person gift that was properly effected. Rabbi Eliezer's version of the story — that the man was a *shichiv meyra* — is disputed by the Sages, who say he was *bari*, and the two sides are in effect arguing about what kind of case this was.

## Thorns Vineyard

### Thorns Kilayim

With the Meroni case resolved, the Gemara returns to Rabbi Eliezer's dismissal of the *bnei rochel* case with the phrase: *mekayamei kotzim bekarem hayu* — "they were those who maintained thorn bushes in their vineyard." This requires explanation. The prohibition of *kilayim* in a vineyard covers the planting or maintenance of mixed species together with grapevines. The question is whether thorn bushes fall within this prohibition at all. A Mishnah elsewhere records a debate: *hamekayem kotzim bekarem, Rabbi Eliezer omer kidesh* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that if one allows thorn bushes to remain in one's vineyard, they become *kadesh*, sanctified as *kilayim*, and become *assur behanaa*, forbidden for any use, constituting a full transgression. *Vehachamim omrim lo kidesh* — the Sages disagree. In their view, *kilayim* applies only to something that people actively cultivate and intend to use as a crop — *davar shekamoho mekayemim*. Thorn bushes, being essentially weeds, do not qualify.

### Arab Practice

The Gemara asks what the basis for Rabbi Eliezer's position could be. *Kotzim lemai hazei* — what are thorns good for? If they serve no purpose, how can they be considered a cultivated species giving rise to *kilayim*? Rav Chanina provides the answer: *sheken ba'arvaya mekayemim kotzim besadot legamleihem* — the Arabs specifically maintain thorn bushes in their fields in order to feed them to their camels. Since camels do in fact eat thorns, and there are communities that intentionally cultivate them for this purpose, Rabbi Eliezer holds that thorn bushes are a legitimate crop and their maintenance in a vineyard constitutes *kilayim*.

### Sons Unworthy

With this background, the full logic of Rabbi Eliezer's dismissal of the *bnei rochel* case becomes clear. Rabbi Eliezer looks at the sons through the lens of his own ruling: maintaining thorn bushes in a vineyard is a violation of *kilayim*, making them *resha'im*. It was because of their wickedness — their halachic misconduct — that the Sages upheld the mother's verbal gift to the daughter. The mother's declaration was not legally binding under the normal rules; it was the sons' unworthiness that led the Sages to depart from ordinary legal procedure. The Sages, by contrast, follow their own ruling that thorn bushes do not constitute *kilayim*, and therefore see nothing wrong with the sons' conduct. In their view, the necklace was given to the daughter because the mother's verbal declaration was a valid *matnat shechiv meyra* — proof of the institution that Rabbi Eliezer denies.

## Verbal Kinyan

### Rav Levi Kinyan

The Gemara now states affirmatively, as the prevailing position: *konin kinyan mishechiv meyra* — a *kinyan* can be effected from a *shichiv meyra*. The statement itself is somewhat compressed, but its implication is that the verbal declaration of a *shichiv meyra* functions as a binding *kinyan*; the Sages' position that no formal act is required is adopted as normative.

### Shabbat Kinyan

Rav Levi then extends this principle: *konin kinyan mishechiv meyra afilu be'Shabbat* — one may perform a *kinyan* for a *shichiv meyra* even on *Shabbat*. This is noteworthy because *Shabbat* normally prohibits commercial transactions, and the prohibition is not trivially set aside. The question is: under what circumstances would a *kinyan* even be needed if the Sages have already ruled that a verbal declaration suffices? Recall that the Sages' ruling applies to a *shichiv meyra bekulo* — one who distributes his entire estate. A *shichiv meyra bemiktzat* — one who distributes only part — does require a *kinyan* to make the transfer irrevocable. There is also the consideration that even where the *kinyan* is technically unnecessary, the dying person may insist on one for peace of mind. The Rashbam understands the ruling as applying in both scenarios: whether the *kinyan* is fully necessary (as in the case of *miktzat nechasim*) or only for reassurance (as in *kol nechasim*), it may be performed even on *Shabbat*.

### Tiruf Daas

Why does the concern for *Shabbat* yield? The answer is: *shema titrof daato alav* — lest his mind become disordered. The Gemara's concern is that if the *shichiv meyra* is anxious about whether his dispositions will be legally binding, and that anxiety goes unaddressed, the resulting *tiruf daas* — mental anguish and agitation — may hasten his death. To prevent this, the Sages permit even a rabbinic prohibition of *Shabbat* to be set aside. The *kinyan* is performed not because it is legally necessary for the transfer to work, but because the dying person's psychological state requires it. This is a remarkable instance of rabbinic law yielding to the concrete human need of a specific individual.

### Medical Ethics

Rav Moshe Feinstein extracts a significant principle from this *sugya* and applies it to contemporary medical ethics. Halacha does not ordinarily recognize a robust right of patient autonomy in medical decisions: if one is obligated to preserve life, it is not obvious that a patient may simply refuse treatment that doctors agree is necessary. However, there are cases — such as high-risk procedures with uncertain benefit for a terminal patient — where the calculus of what *pikuach nefesh* requires is itself unclear, and autonomy finds a natural place in that gap. More broadly, Rav Moshe argues that where a patient actively and persistently refuses treatment, forcing the treatment upon them creates a risk of *tiruf daas* that may itself become a *sakanat nefashos* greater than the underlying medical risk. The principle does not ground an absolute right of autonomy; it grounds a *halachic* reason to take the patient's will seriously as a factor in the medical calculus. The basis in the *shichiv meyra* Gemara is this: there, to prevent mental anguish, we override *derabbanans* of *Shabbat*. Rav Moshe extends the principle, while noting — as the Gemara itself leaves implicit — that the *tiruf daas* concern in the Gemara overrides a *derabbanan*, not a *de'Oraita*, and that any extension to Torah-level prohibitions would require additional analysis.

## Shabbat Weekday

### Eliezer Shabbat

The final Mishnah of the daf introduces a position attributed to Rabbi Eliezer that creates a surprising internal tension with the opening Mishnah. Here Rabbi Eliezer says: *b'Shabbat devarav kayamim mipnei she'yachol likhtov, aval lo b'chol* — on *Shabbat* the *shichiv meyra's* verbal declarations are valid, because he cannot write a document; but on a weekday they are not valid. This is a significant qualification. It suggests that Rabbi Eliezer does not categorically reject the institution of *matnat shechiv meyra*; rather, he limits its verbal effectiveness to contexts where writing a document — and thereby performing a formal *kinyan* via *shtar* — is impossible. On *Shabbat*, writing is forbidden, so the verbal declaration must substitute. On a weekday, the option of writing is available, and therefore a verbal declaration alone will not suffice.

### Yehoshua Kal

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees by deploying a *kal vachomer*: *b'Shabbat amru, kal vachomer b'chol* — if the Sages permitted a verbal *kinyan* on *Shabbat*, when *all* forms of *kinyan* are unavailable, then certainly they would permit it on a weekday, when normal *kinyanim* are in full operation. The logic runs in the direction exactly opposite to Rabbi Eliezer's: the availability of formal *kinyanim* is not a reason to disallow the verbal alternative; rather, if the verbal alternative works even in an environment where *kinyanim* are categorically suspended, it works all the more in an environment where the ordinary legal framework is operational. The verbal *kinyan* of a *shichiv meyra* is not a last resort for when nothing else is possible; it is a valid institution in its own right.

### Zakhin Parallel

The Gemara notes a parallel dispute. Rabbi Eliezer holds: *zakkin l'katan v'ein zakkin l'gadol* — one may acquire a gift on behalf of a minor who is absent, but not on behalf of an adult. His reasoning tracks his position in the *Shabbat* case: the special dispensation applies only where the normal option is unavailable. A minor cannot acquire for himself, so the Sages allow someone else to do it for him; an adult can acquire for himself, so the dispensation is unnecessary and inapplicable. Rabbi Yehoshua inverts this: *l'katan amru, kal vachomer l'gadol* — if the Sages allowed acquisition on behalf of a minor even though the minor himself cannot act, then certainly they would allow acquisition on behalf of an adult, who can perfectly well ratify the transaction and is in effect using the acquirer as his agent. In both disputes, Rabbi Eliezer understands the special rule as a *b'dieved* accommodation for impossible circumstances, while Rabbi Yehoshua understands it as a positive institution that applies most naturally where the principal is a capable legal actor.

### Eliezer Elazar

This raises a textual problem. If the Rabbi Eliezer of this Mishnah accepts a verbal *matnat shechiv meyra* on *Shabbat*, is he the same person as the Rabbi Elazar of the opening Mishnah, who appeared to deny the institution categorically? Tosafot addresses this directly. Based on other Gemara sources, Tosafot concludes that the Rabbi Eliezer of the opening Mishnah does in fact categorically deny any verbal *matnat shechiv meyra* — whether on *Shabbat* or on a weekday. That absolute position cannot be reconciled with the nuanced *Shabbat*-versus-weekday distinction of this Mishnah. Tosafot therefore concludes that these must be two different Tannaim: the Rabbi Elazar of the opening Mishnah — spelled with an *ayin* — who absolutely denies the institution, and the Rabbi Eliezer of this Mishnah — spelled with an *alef* — who accepts it at least for *Shabbat*.

### Yerushalmi Version

The Yerushalmi preserves a different *girsah* — a different textual reading — of the Mishnah that distinguishes between *Shabbat* and weekdays. In the Yerushalmi's version, the position that verbal transfer is valid on *Shabbat* but not on a weekday is attributed not to Rabbi Eliezer at all, but to *vehachamim omrim* — the Sages. This creates a three-way picture. One view categorically denies verbal *matnat shechiv meyra* (Rabbi Elazar of the opening Mishnah, in Tosafot's reading). A second view accepts it on *Shabbat* but not on a weekday (the Sages in the Yerushalmi's reading, or Rabbi Eliezer in the Bavli's reading of this Mishnah). And the third, dominant view accepts it as a fully operative institution on *Shabbat* and weekday alike (Rabbi Yehoshua, and by implication the normative halacha). Whether this yields two distinct positions or three depends on how one reads the Tannaic attributions — a question the Gemara leaves open for the continuation of the sugya.

---

---

# Bava Batra 157

## Shchiv Mera Shabbat

### Rabbi Eliezer Shabbat

The daf begins at the bottom of 156b, picking up the *mishna* that was introduced at the close of the previous session. The *mishna* records the following: *Rabbi Eliezer omer beshabbos ve'al pi kayaman* — Rabbi Eliezer says that on Shabbat the verbal gift of a *shchiv mera* is effective. The apparent tension with the previous *mishna* requires some untangling. In that earlier context, an opinion — seemingly also attributed to Rabbi Eliezer — appeared to deny the entire institution of the *shchiv mera*'s verbal gift. Here, however, the same Rabbi Eliezer draws a distinction: specifically on Shabbat, the verbal gift is valid, *mipnei she'ein yachol lichtov* — because on Shabbat he cannot write, and therefore the Rabbis extended this mechanism to him. Within the broader framework of *lo tithrosh beiteih* and the concern not to leave the dying man's household destitute, the Rabbis had no other option but to allow it. *Aval lo bechol* — but on a weekday, when writing is perfectly available, they did not permit the verbal gift to substitute for a proper written instrument.

### Tosafot Clarification

Tosafot clarifies that the opinion in the earlier *mishna* and the opinion here are not necessarily the same person. One was Rabbi Elazar and the other Rabbi Eliezer — two distinct Tannaim. The Rif, by contrast, appears to read them as a single authority, treating the current *mishna* as a refinement of the position stated earlier. The Yerushalmi, for its part, attributes that earlier opinion to the *chachamim* generally. Regardless of how one resolves the attribution, the operative distinction being drawn here is between Shabbat and the weekday.

### Rabbi Yehoshua Kal Vacho…

Rabbi Yehoshua's response is structured as a *kal vachomer*: *beshabbos amru kal vachomer bechol* — they established the rule for Shabbat, and we may infer that it certainly applies during the week. The reasoning is as follows: Shabbat is a time when no *kinyanim* are normally operative, yet the Rabbis allowed the *shchiv mera*'s verbal gift to function as a form of *kinyan*. If it can work during a period when *kinyanim* are altogether suspended, then certainly it should work during the week, when ordinary *kinyanim* are fully available and this mechanism can be understood as a species of them. Rabbi Yehoshua thus extends the institution across both contexts.

### Zochin LeKatan

The *mishna* then presents a parallel dispute using the same logical structure. *Zochin lekatan ve'ein zochin legadol, divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that one may take possession of property on behalf of a minor, but not on behalf of an adult. The adult is capable of acting for himself; the Rabbis created this dispensation only where there was no other option, namely for a *katan* who cannot perform the *kinyan* independently. Rabbi Eliezer accordingly limits the principle to the case where it was originally taught.

### Zochin Principle

Rabbi Yehoshua counters with the same *kal vachomer* logic: *lekatan amru kal vachomer legadol* — if you can take possession on behalf of a minor who cannot act for himself at all, then certainly you can do so for an adult. After all, the adult's capacity to act is precisely what makes the case easier, not harder, to permit. According to this reading, Rabbi Yehoshua endorses the full principle of *zochin leadam shelo befanav* without restriction.

This is a striking *gemara*. The principle of *zochin leadam shelo befanav* — that one may acquire something on behalf of another in their absence — is treated elsewhere as virtually axiomatic. Similarly, the principle of *divrei shchiv mera kechtuvim uchemesurim damu* — that the words of a *shchiv mera* are treated as if written and delivered — is often invoked as though it were beyond dispute. Yet Rabbi Eliezer rejects both, save in narrow circumstances. One illuminating feature of Rabbi Eliezer's general approach is the *gemara*'s own characterization of him elsewhere: *le'olam lo amar davar shelo shama mipi rabo* — he never stated a teaching he had not received directly from his teacher. He consistently interpreted received traditions in their most conservative scope, neither abstracting nor innovating. This explains his position here: the teaching was given in the case of the *katan*; the teaching was given on Shabbat; he will not expand it beyond those specific contexts.

### Mishna Compilation

The *gemara* then identifies whose formulation our *mishna* follows: *matnitin mani Rabbi Yehuda hi* — our *mishna*, which frames the debate as Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagreeing about Shabbat versus weekday and *katan* versus *gadol* in the particular direction we have seen, is Rabbi Yehuda's version. A *braita* then introduces Rabbi Meir's version of the same dispute.

### Rabbi Meir Version

In Rabbi Meir's formulation, the entire structure is a mirror image. *Rabbi Eliezer omer bechol devarav kayamin mipnei sheyachol lichtov aval lo beshabbos* — Rabbi Eliezer says the verbal gift is valid on weekdays, because then it stands in place of a written *kinyan* at a time when *kinyanim* function, but it does not work on Shabbat, which is entirely excluded from the domain of *kinyanim*. Rabbi Eliezer still limits the institution; he simply limits it to the opposite scenario. Rabbi Yehoshua once again holds that it applies in both cases: *bechol amru kal vachomer beshabbos* — they established it for weekdays; certainly it applies on Shabbat when there is no alternative.

### Rabbi Meir Zochin

The parallel dispute about *zochin* is likewise inverted in Rabbi Meir's version. *Zochin legadol ve'ein zochin lekatan divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that one may take possession on behalf of an adult, because the adult could in principle appoint a *shaliach* and thus the acquisition can be conceived as an extension of his agency, but not for a minor, who cannot appoint an agent and for whom the very concept is therefore incoherent. Rabbi Yehoshua responds: *begadol amru kal vachomer lekatan* — if it works for an adult, it certainly works for a *katan* who has no other option. The two versions of the dispute thus present a genuine mirror image: Rabbi Eliezer always restricts the institution to one pole, Rabbi Yehoshua always extends it across both, and whether that pole is Shabbat or weekday, *katan* or *gadol*, depends entirely on which tradent — Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Meir — is reporting the debate.

---

## Collapsed House

### Case Setup

The *gemara* now transitions away from *shchiv mera* into a distinct set of questions about *yerusha* — not the ordering of heirs or the rabbinic will, but rather the factual question of who died when and what consequences flow from the sequence of death. The *mishna* presents the following scenario, using the names the Rashbam supplies: a house collapsed on Reuven and his father Yaakov. The *mishna* notes that the same analysis applies to any *morish* — anyone who would be in a position to bequeath property to Reuven, whether mother, brother, or uncle — but the paradigm case is father and son. Reuven, furthermore, had outstanding debts: *v'haysa alav kesubas isha u'va'al chov* — there was a creditor holding an IOU against him, and there was the claim of his ex-wife's *ketubah*. And crucially, Reuven had no money of his own.

### Competing Interests

The competing interests in this scenario are sharp and precisely defined. Yaakov has property. If Yaakov died first, his property would pass to Reuven; Reuven would then die, and his son Chanoch would inherit whatever Reuven had. The creditor wants exactly this sequence. If Yaakov's property passed through Reuven's hands, even momentarily, the creditor would have a lien on it by virtue of his outstanding claim against Reuven. He could then collect that debt from Chanoch as the heir who received encumbered property.

Chanoch, naturally, wants the opposite. He would prefer that Reuven died first — before inheriting anything from Yaakov — and that Yaakov died second, with the property passing directly from grandfather to grandson. In that scenario, the property arrives in Chanoch's hands via Yaakov, untouched by any of Reuven's liabilities. Either way, Chanoch ends up with the property; the question is which path it took through the family tree, and that path determines whether the creditor's lien attaches to it.

### Mishna Positions

*Yorshei ha'av omrim haben mes rishon* — the heirs of the father, in our simplified case Chanoch, claim that Reuven died first and Yaakov second, meaning the property came to them debt-free. *Uba'al chov omrim ha'av mes rishon* — the creditors claim the reverse, that Yaakov died first, the property passed to Reuven, and they therefore hold a lien on it.

### Beit Shammai Hillel

*Beis Shammai omrim yachloku* — Beit Shammai rules that they split the property. *Uveis Hillel omrim nechasim bechezkasan* — Beit Hillel rules that the property remains in its presumed possession, meaning in the hands of the family, not the creditors. The *gemara* here does not develop the full debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel at length — that is treated in another *gemara* — but the underlying logic of each position is clear. Beit Hillel's position is the most intuitive: regardless of which sequence of death occurred, Chanoch owns the property. The creditor is attempting to extract it on the basis of an alleged lien. *Hamotzi mechaveiro alav hara'ayah* — the burden of proof falls on the one seeking to take from the other. Since Chanoch is unquestionably *muchzak* in the property, the creditor who asserts a lien must prove it.

### Shtar Explanation

Beit Shammai's position, as the *gemara* elsewhere explains, rests on the principle of *shtar ha'omed ligvos kigavu dami* — a debt document that is standing to be collected is treated as though it has already been collected. Under this principle, if the property passed through Reuven's hands and the creditor held a *shtar* at that moment, it is as though the creditor had already taken possession. The situation is therefore not simply that Chanoch is *muchzak* and the creditor asserts an unproven lien — rather, if the property did pass through Reuven, the creditor's possession is itself treated as already established. From the creditor's side, Chanoch would then be the *motzi* attempting to extract from him. Because neither sequence of death can be verified, *yachloku* — they divide.

---

## Liens Property

### Shtar Liens Rules

The *gemara* now cites a ruling from elsewhere: *hamalveh es chaveiro bishtar goveh minechasim meshubadim* — one who lends to another with a *shtar* may collect from encumbered property, that is, real estate even after it has been sold to a third party. *Al yedei edim*, however — if the loan was witnessed but no *shtar* was written — *goveh minechasim benei chorin*, the creditor may collect only from free property, meaning property still in the direct control of the original debtor, not from any third-party purchaser.

The logic of the *shtar* creating liens is the following. When I borrow money and execute a *shtar* on a given date, that act of borrowing with a document creates, at that moment, liens on all the real property I presently own. Those liens travel with the property: if I subsequently sell it, the buyer acquires it subject to that prior encumbrance, and the creditor may reclaim it to satisfy the debt.

### Shmuel Future Liens

This sets the stage for Shmuel's question. What happens to property I acquire *after* the date of the loan? On January 1, I borrow money and execute a *shtar*. On January 15, I purchase a new plot of land. Does the creditor have liens on that new property? Logically, at the moment the lien was created, that property did not yet exist in my possession, so the lien could not have attached to it. But what if at the time of the loan I explicitly stated — as indeed the *ketubah* formula does, with the phrase *d'kanai u'd'asid ana lemiknei* — that I am hereby creating liens on property I currently own and on property I will come to own in the future? The *ketubah* language even specifies, *afilu glima d'al katfei* — even the cloak on his shoulder — and distinguishes between *nechasim* that carry *achrayus* and those that do not. Does such a declaration actually create enforceable liens on future-acquired property? That is Shmuel's question: *d'ikni d'asid ana lemiknei d'ikni* — future property, followed by an act of acquisition — *mahu*?

### Rabbi Meir Future

The question becomes most pressing in the position of the *Rabbanan*. *Aliba d'Rabbi Meir d'amar adam makneh davar shelo ba l'olam* — according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that a person can sell or transfer something he does not yet own, it is fairly clear that he should be able to create liens on future property as well. If you can effect a full transfer of something you do not yet possess, you can certainly encumber it with a *shibud*. The harder question is for the Rabbanan, who hold that one cannot be *makneh davar shelo ba l'olam*.

### Rashbam Reasons

The Rashbam provides two independent reasons why even according to the Rabbanan, future liens might be permissible. The first: *mi shani shibud mi'kinyan* — a *shibud* is qualitatively different from a *kinyan*. A full transfer of ownership in something not yet in one's possession is one thing; a *shibud* is a more abstract right, not a transfer of the thing itself, and perhaps that more abstract quality makes it possible to pre-create such a right before the underlying property comes into one's hands. The second reason, which the Rashbam introduces with *ei nami*: the Rabbis specifically legislated that *shibud* can attach to future property — *d'lo tinal delet bifnei lovin* — so as not to lock the door before borrowers. The policy concern is to facilitate lending. If creditors could never secure future-acquired property, their confidence in lending would be undermined; the Rabbis therefore empowered this mechanism to encourage commerce and the extension of credit.

### Rav Yosef Proof

Rav Yosef attempts to bring a proof from a *sugya* involving a dispute between Admon and the *chachamim*. The case: Michael presents an IOU showing that Dov owes him a sum of money, borrowed on January 1. Dov responds: that *shtar* is clearly a forgery, because on February 1 you sold me a plot of land for precisely that sum. If I truly owed you the money, why did you accept cash for the land instead of simply applying it to the debt? That is Admon's argument — the sale proves the debt cannot be real. The *chachamim* reject this: *zeh haya pikeach shemachar lo es hakarka mipnei sheyachol lemiashhkeno alav* — he was clever to sell him the land. The reasoning: Dov, if simply pressed for the money, would claim poverty. Cash is concealable. But a plot of land cannot be hidden. By selling Dov the land for cash — pocketing the money he knew Dov had — Michael converted Dov's liquid, concealable assets into real property that Michael can now collect against as a lien. The land purchased after the loan now stands as collateral for that prior debt.

Rav Yosef's point is that this demonstrates liens attaching to property acquired after the loan — which is precisely the principle under debate.

### Rava Pushback

Rava pushes back: *minei*? Collecting *from the debtor himself*? That was never in dispute. *Minei afilu miglima d'al katfei* — a creditor can collect from any property the debtor currently possesses, whenever he came into possession of it, even the shirt off his back. The question of liens concerns collection from *third parties* — from a *lokei'ach* who bought the property from the debtor after the loan. If Dov still holds the land, of course Michael can collect it. The issue arises only if Dov had since sold that land to someone else; does Michael's prior lien survive the transfer? The case of *d'ikni kana umachar* — future property acquired and then sold — or *d'ikni kana vehoreish* — future property acquired and then bequeathed — is what remains unresolved.

---

## Inheritance Liens

### Rav Chana Proof

Rav Chana attempts to bring proof from the collapsed house *mishna* itself. He reconstructs the scenario: *nafal habayis alav v'al aviv... yorshei ha'av omrim haben mes rishon... uba'al chov omrim ha'av mes rishon*. Recall the creditor's desired sequence of events: Yaakov dies first, his property passes to Reuven, and the creditor then uses that property to collect the debt from Chanoch. But this relies on liens attaching to property that Reuven came into possession of only *after* the loan. How else could the creditor lay claim to property that Yaakov owned when Reuven borrowed the money?

### Gemara Question

The *gemara* presses the question: *ve'i salka da'atach de'ikni kana umachar lo mishta'abed* — if you hold that future-acquired property does not become encumbered, then even if Yaakov did die first and the property passed to Reuven, on what basis would the creditor have any claim? The property was Yaakov's when the loan was made; it was not Reuven's property at all.

### Mitzvah Obligation

Rav Nachman Zeira answers: *mitzvah al hayesomim lifro'a chovos avihen* — there is an obligation upon orphans to repay their father's debts. The creditor does not necessarily need liens in the conventional sense. Even without liens on the inherited property, once Chanoch inherits from his father Reuven — even property that came to Reuven from Yaakov — there is an obligation upon Chanoch to use that property to discharge Reuven's debts.

### Two Degrees

Tosafot clarifies that there are two distinct degrees of this obligation, and the distinction is crucial. If a father dies leaving debts but no property — or leaving only *metaltelin* while the creditor holds liens only on *karka* — the children have no legal obligation to pay from their own resources. They have a moral obligation; some people of high scruple will indeed pay off a deceased father's debts from their personal funds, much as some bankrupted businessmen eventually repay creditors beyond any legal requirement. But *beit din* will not enforce it. However, if the children actually inherited property from the father, the obligation to repay the father's debts from that inherited property rises to the level of a legal, judicially enforceable duty. It is a personal obligation upon the heir, not a *shibud* on the property itself — but it is binding and actionable.

The subtle question, of course, is why one would need this *mitzvah* framework at all if the creditor already has proper liens. The *gemara* is operating on the premise that perhaps there are no liens in the usual sense — the obligation is what fills the gap.

### Rav Ashi Challenge

Rav Ashi challenges this construction: *milveh al peh hu* — if there are no liens, you have effectively reduced this claim to the status of an oral loan, a loan recorded only by witnesses and without a *shtar*. And Rav and Shmuel both rule that *milveh al peh eino goveh lo min hayorshim v'lo min halokechim* — an oral loan carries no liens and cannot be collected from heirs or from purchasers. The *gemara* understands this ruling to mean not only that there are no liens but that there is not even an enforceable *mitzvah lifro'a chov avihen* in this case. The *mitzvah* in its legally binding form applies only where actual liens exist; absent liens, the obligation reverts to the purely moral sphere that *beit din* will not enforce. The attempted answer thus collapses: if we posit no liens, the creditor's claim is unenforceable, and the scenario of Rav Chana's proof fails to establish what he intended.

---

## Shtar Dating

### Ha Mani Defense

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty with a single move: *ha mani Rabbi Meir hi d'amar adam makneh davar shelo ba l'olam*. Any proof one might adduce — from the collapsed house case, from the *shevach* case, from the postdated *shtar* — that shows liens attaching to property acquired after the loan can simply be attributed to Rabbi Meir's position. This becomes the *gemara*'s standing defense throughout this entire discussion. Whenever evidence accumulates that future liens are operative, the *gemara* deflects it with this attribution. The claim is: the *mishna* of the collapsed house works on the assumption that the *shtar* contained an explicit *d'ikni ana lemiknei* clause, and even so, it reflects only Rabbi Meir, not the *Rabbanan*. One cannot prove from it that future liens work according to everyone.

### Predating Invalid

The *gemara* then cites the rule: *shtarei chov hamukdamim pesulim vehamukharim kesherim* — predated loan documents are invalid; postdated ones are valid. The reason predating is *pasul* is straightforward. Suppose I borrow money on January 15 but write January 1 as the date. On January 1, the true date in the document, I had sold a plot of land to an innocent purchaser. That buyer performed a proper title search, confirmed there were no existing liens, and acquired the property in good faith. Now I am claiming retroactive liens from January 1 — and those fictitious liens reach back and undermine that innocent purchase. The predated *shtar* thus exposes third parties to liens they had no way to know about and no reason to anticipate. The document is therefore entirely disqualified. Tosafot raises whether the *pesul* invalidates the *shtar* entirely — including its use to collect from the debtor himself — or whether it merely strips away its liens while leaving the underlying debt intact. The plain meaning of *pesulim* suggests complete disqualification, though Tosafot entertains the possibility of a more limited reading.

### Postdating Benefit

Postdating, by contrast, is permissible, because the creditor is only harming himself by waiving liens for the interval between the true date and the written date. If I lend money on January 15 but write January 30 as the date, I am allowing the borrower to sell off property freely until January 30 without my liens attaching — a concession at my own expense. That is unobjectionable.

But the *gemara* observes that something more is happening. If the borrower purchases a new plot of land on January 25 — after the true date of the loan but before the written date — and the written date is January 30, then when the *shtar* is presented it appears that the loan was made on the 30th. Under a properly dated document, would the creditor have had liens on property bought on January 25? Only if future liens can be created. Yet by the postdating, the new property now falls squarely within the *shtar*'s apparent coverage — and this is treated as a benefit to the creditor.

### Inference Proof

The *gemara* presses: *ve'i salka da'atach de'ikni kana umachar lo mishta'abed* — if you hold that future-acquired property does not create liens, then why is the postdated *shtar* valid or even useful? Whatever benefit accrues to the creditor through postdating — the appearance of liens on intervening property — is only intelligible if there exists a mechanism by which future liens can be created. *Ha mani Rabbi Meir hi d'amar adam makneh davar shelo ba l'olam* — once again the answer: this postdating scenario works only according to Rabbi Meir's position. The defense holds, but the evidentiary weight is accumulating.

---

## Shevach Karka'ot

### Indeterminate Amounts

The *gemara* introduces a new category: *shevach karkaos* — improvements to land — as an illustration of a class of debts for which the Rabbis did not allow liens to operate against third parties. The general principle is that where the amount of the debt is indeterminate, it is unfair to expose innocent purchasers to unquantifiable liens they cannot foresee. A purchaser can inquire whether there are prior liens and calculate the risk. He cannot calculate a lien whose ultimate value depends on how much improvement the property will receive after he acquires it.

### Insurance Scenario

The concrete scenario: I sell Yisrael a plot of land, and I *insure* it. That is, I undertake an obligation of *achrayus* — if a creditor subsequently seizes the land on the basis of a prior lien, or if it emerges that the land was not mine to sell, I will reimburse Yisrael for his loss. This is the seller's standard guarantee. Yisrael, reasonably, wants more: he wants me to insure not just the value of the land itself but also the *shevach*, the improvements he invests in the property. If he builds and plants and develops, and then the land is seized, he does not want to receive back only what he paid for bare land. I agree to this extended insurance as well.

### Collection Rights

The *halacha* that emerges from this scenario is the following: when a creditor comes and seizes the land from Yisrael — *ke'she'hu goveh goveh es hakeren minechasim meshubadim* — the creditor collects the *keren*, the principal value of the land, from encumbered property, even from land I have since sold to others. But *ve'es hashevach minechasim benei chorin* — for the *shevach*, he can collect only from free property under my direct control. Yisrael's right to reimbursement from me follows the same structure: the principal creates liens, the *shevach* does not. Yisrael can therefore chase me through encumbered property for the principal, but for the improvements he can only collect from what I presently hold.

### Shevach Proof

What interests the *gemara* in this scenario, however, is not primarily where Yisrael can collect. The key question is: how did the creditor — call him Michael — get to take not just the land but the *shevach* as well? Michael's lien predates Yisrael's improvements. At the time the lien was created, the *shevach* did not exist. If Michael is entitled to collect his debt by taking the land together with the improvements that Yisrael made *after* the lien was created, this implies that Michael had liens extending to property or value that came into existence *after* the date of the loan. That is, it implies that future liens are operative. *D'ikni mah de'asid lemiknei* — the lien I created covers not just present property but future-acquired value.

The *gemara* again deflects: *ha mani Rabbi Meir hi d'amar adam makneh davar shelo ba l'olam*. Rabbi Meir's position accounts for this. The evidence continues to accumulate, the defense continues to be deployed, and the pattern itself — the sheer volume of cases in which the *gemara* finds it necessary to invoke this defense — signals that the underlying assumption of the entire legal system is that future liens are operative.

### Two Liens Priority

The *gemara* then poses a cascading hypothetical, introduced with *im timtzei lomar* — if you were to rule that future liens do work. The question: *lava lava vachazar vekana mahu* — suppose a debtor creates two separate future-lien agreements with two different creditors, and then subsequently acquires a new piece of property. Who has priority?

### Sequential Liens

The scenario is constructed as follows. On January 1, the debtor tells creditor one: future property I acquire will be encumbered to you. On January 15, he makes the same agreement with creditor two. On January 30, he acquires a plot of land. When that land comes into existence in his possession, both creditors' liens activate simultaneously. On pre-existing property, the principle is clear: *rishon kana* — the first lien in time has priority, because when the second lien was created the property was already partially encumbered. But here, neither lien was attached to anything at the time it was created. Both materialize at the same moment — when the property is acquired on January 30. Does the first creditor's temporal priority carry through? Or do both liens spring into existence simultaneously, giving them equal standing?

### Rav Nachman Debate

Rav Nachman reports that this question was sent to the scholars of Eretz Yisrael and the response that came back was *rishon kana* — the first creditor takes priority, analogous to the ordinary rule of liens. Rav Huna disagrees and rules *yachloku* — they divide equally. Rabba bar Avuha likewise rules *yachloku*.

### Rav Ashi Cycles

Ravina adds a historically notable detail: in Rav Ashi's first *madura* — his first cycle of teaching — he ruled *rishon kana*, first takes all. In his latter *madura*, he ruled *yachloku*, split equally. The term *madura kama* and *madura basra* refers to the two great cycles through which Rav Ashi reviewed all of his learning, a process that the Rashbam documents from responsa of Rav Hai Gaon and the commentary of Rabbeinu Chananel. Rav Ashi lived sixty years, and every year he devoted the two months of the *kala* — Nisan and Tishrei — to *chazarah*, public review of prior learning. After thirty years he had completed one full cycle of review; the second thirty years constituted his second cycle. The first cycle is *madura kama*, the second *madura basra*. This terminology was subsequently adopted by later *Rishonim* and *Acharonim* to describe first and revised editions of their own works, most famously the *Noda Biyehuda*, whose *kama* and *tinyana* are volumes one and two — though those are sequential volumes rather than revised editions of the same material.

### Hilchata Ruling

*Ve'hilchasa yachloku* — the *halacha* is that the two creditors split the liens equally. When future liens materialize simultaneously upon acquisition of the property, neither creditor has temporal priority over the other in the moment that matters, and they divide the encumbrance equally.

### Meisivei Question

The *gemara* now raises an objection (*meisivei*) from the *shevach karkaos* case. We said: Michael, the creditor, comes and seizes the land Yisrael improved, taking both the land and its *shevach*. But if future liens exist and split equally, then Yisrael — who himself has a future-lien claim against me for the *achrayus* on the principal — should have equal standing on the *shevach* alongside Michael. Why does Michael collect all of the *shevach*? Should not Yisrael share it?

### Split Resolution

The *gemara* resolves this: *lo mai goveh nami de'katani chatzi shevach* — that is precisely what the *mishna* means. Michael does not collect all the *shevach*. He collects half the *shevach*. Yisrael retains the other half as payment toward the principal he is owed. Once we acknowledge that both Michael and Yisrael hold future-lien claims that activate simultaneously on the *shevach*, the *hilchata* of *yachloku* applies: they split it equally, and Yisrael's half of the *shevach* is credited toward what I owe him.

One might ask why the *shevach* that Yisrael generated is treated as property that I came into possession of — which is the premise for my lien extending to it. The *gemara* does not fully develop this point, but it operates on that assumption.

The daf closes with the principle, supported by the full weight of the evidence marshaled throughout the discussion, that future liens are indeed operative — presumably for one of the two reasons the Rashbam identifies: either because a *shibud* is sufficiently abstract to be distinguishable from a full *kinyan*, such that one can pre-create it on property not yet in one's possession, or, more likely, because the Rabbis affirmatively legislated this power into existence — *d'lo tinal delet bifnei lovin* — so as not to lock the door before borrowers and thereby impede the extension of credit.

---

---

# Bava Batra 158

## Intro: Collapsed Houses

### Daf Overview

The daf of 158 continues a series of *mishnayot* no longer concerned with the *shchiv mera* — the deathbed bequest — but instead addressing a cluster of cases involving houses that collapse on multiple people simultaneously. Because the order of death cannot be determined, the question of who inherited from whom becomes legally significant and practically contested.

### Father & Son Case

The first *mishnah* in this series presented the case of a father and son. The question was: who died first? If the father died first, the property passed through the son, and a creditor's lien — which attached at the moment the son inherited — would affect it before it reached the grandson. If the son died first, the property passed directly from grandfather to grandson, bypassing the son entirely and defeating any liens.

### Beit Shammai/Hillel

*Beit Shammai* adopts his characteristic position: *yachloku* — split the disputed property. Where the order of death is unknowable and there is no way to presume one direction over the other, he divides the estate. *Beit Hillel* takes what seems to be the more principled stance: *nechasim bechezkatan* — property remains in its presumptive ownership. Since in either scenario the property is owned by the grandson *Chanoch*, and the only question is whether the creditor's lien applies, the burden of proof lies with the creditor. As the rule goes, *hamotzi mechavero alav harayah* — the one seeking to extract from another bears the burden of proof — and since the creditor cannot prove his lien attached, he loses.

---

## Man & Wife Case

### Case Setup

The *mishnah* on 158a turns to a new case: *nafal habayit alav ve-al ishto* — the house collapsed on a man and his wife. To clarify the stakes, consider *Yaakov* and *Rachel*. Rachel holds property that we care about. The question is: in what order did they die?

### Competing Claims

*Yaakov*'s heirs — say, his son *Reuven* from another wife — claim that Rachel died first. On that version, her property passed to Yaakov upon her death, and then from Yaakov to Reuven upon his death. Rachel's heirs — her father *Lavan*, assuming she left no other children — claim the opposite: Yaakov died first. With Yaakov out of the picture, Rachel died as a widow, and her property passed directly to Lavan's line without ever touching Yaakov's estate.

Note that this is not literally a courtroom argument in the sense of witnesses testifying to what they saw. Rather, the *beit din* must reason through what the outcome would be under each possibility. Each side is articulating the scenario that would make them prevail — effectively a *taanat shema*, a claim about what may have occurred, not a *taanat bari*, an assertion of direct knowledge.

*Beit Shammai omrim yachloku* — split it. Here, *Beit Shammai*'s position arguably makes even more intuitive sense than in the prior case, since the property either passed entirely through Yaakov or entirely bypassed him; there is no middle ground and no way to determine which occurred. *Beit Hillel omrim nechasim bechezkatan* — property remains in its presumptive ownership. But this immediately raises the question: whose *chazakah* are we speaking of? That will require the *Gemara*'s resolution, as neither owner is obviously the presumptive possessor.

### Three Property Types

Before addressing whose *chazakah* is at stake, the *mishnah* distinguishes among three categories of property relevant to a marriage: the *ketubah*, *nichsei tzon barzel*, and *nichsei milog*.

The *ketubah* — the 100 or 200 *zuz* (or the *tosefes*) — is a conditional debt: the husband's estate owes this sum to the wife if he predeceases her or divorces her. It was never her property to begin with; it is simply his obligation. *Nichsei tzon barzel* is the dowry property that she brought into the marriage and transferred to the husband's title, with the understanding that he would return its assessed value if he predeceased her or divorced her. *Nichsei milog* is the property she brought into the marriage but retained title to; he enjoyed the *peirot* — the usufruct — but she always remained the owner of the *guf*, the corpus.

### Ketubah Analysis

The *mishnah* rules: *ketubah bechezkos yorshei habaal* — the *ketubah* remains in the presumptive possession of the husband's heirs. Since the *ketubah* is a debt contingent on the husband dying first, and we do not know who died first, the debt may never have come due. The rule of *hamotzi mechavero alav harayah* applies: the wife's heirs cannot extract payment when they cannot prove the triggering condition. The *ketubah* goes unpaid.

### Nichsei Milog

The *mishnah* then states: *nechasim hanichnasim vehayotzim imah bechezkos yorshei haav* — the property that entered and exited the marriage with her, meaning the *nichsei milog*, is in the presumptive possession of her father's heirs. Even though she is deceased, the property is treated as having presumptively remained within her family line rather than having transferred to her husband's.

### Milog Reasoning

This ruling is not self-evident. One might ask: she is dead and both *Yaakov* and *Lavan* are potential heirs — why presume it goes to *Lavan*? After all, a husband does inherit from his wife, so *Yaakov*'s heirs have a claim. *Tosafot* addresses this and offers two explanations. The first is that a husband's inheritance from his wife is rabbinic in origin, not biblical. Therefore, in a case of doubt, we favor the biblical line of inheritance — the wife's own family — over the rabbinic one.

The second explanation, which arguably better reflects the language *chezkos yorshei haav* — note the *mishnah* says "father's heirs," not "wife's heirs" — is grounded in a principle of family structure. This is property that was given to her by her father for the sake of the marriage; it came from *Lavan*'s household and she retained title throughout. It is, in a sense, still labeled as her father's property. Unless it is established that she died first and the husband's inheritance clearly took effect, the presumption is that the property remains under the paternal family's ownership — it was given for the marriage and it stays on that side absent clear transfer.

A third related approach: precisely because it was brought as dowry, it is property identified with the *av*'s house, not the husband's. Unless it clearly passed over through her death while he lived, it stays.

### General Property

Once the *mishnah* has addressed the *ketubah* and the *nichsei milog* explicitly, *Beit Hillel*'s phrase *nechasim bechezkatan* must refer to a third category of property — one not yet addressed. The *Gemara* records the question: *bechezkos mi?* — whose *chazakah* is this? *Rabbi Yochanan* says *bechezkos yorshei habaal* — the husband's heirs. *Rabbi Elazar* says *bechezkos yorshei ha'ishah* — the wife's heirs. And *Bar Kappara* says *yachloku* — split it. *Bar Kappara* also taught this as a *baraita*: when both sides come to inherit, they divide.

### Rashbam Interpretation

The *Rashbam* reads this third category as *nichsei tzon barzel* — the dowry property transferred to the husband's title. This is the one category that does not fit neatly into either earlier ruling. On one hand, the husband owns it — she transferred title to him and he simply owes her its value in certain circumstances. That would suggest it should be treated like his property and remain with his heirs. On the other hand, it originated with her father, was brought into the marriage as her dowry, and would revert to her in value under specified conditions — suggesting it retains an association with her family. The three-way dispute among *Rabbi Yochanan*, *Rabbi Elazar*, and *Bar Kappara* reflects exactly this ambiguity: is this property identified with the husband's estate, with the wife's family, or is the doubt simply unresolvable?

### Tosafot Interpretation

*Tosafot*, while not explicitly disagreeing with the *Rashbam*, implicitly reads the third category differently. Reading the first *Tosafot* on the phrase *Beit Hillel omrim nechasim bechezkatan*, it becomes clear that *Tosafot* understands this as referring to general property she owned independently — not property brought as a dowry or listed in the *ketubah*, but property she earned on her own, through work or investment. Such property carries no special identification with her father's house. The argument for keeping *nichsei milog* within the father's family rested on its origin: it was given by *Lavan* for the sake of the marriage and she retained title, so it remained in that family's orbit. But property she earned independently has no such label. The question of who should be presumed to inherit it — her father or her husband — is genuinely open. That is why *Rabbi Yochanan* says the husband, *Rabbi Elazar* says the wife's family, and *Bar Kappara* says to split it.

---

## Son & Mother Case

### Case Setup

The next *mishnah* presents yet another variant: *nefla habayit alav ve-al imo* — the house collapsed on a son and his mother. The mother holds property and the question is again the order of death.

Working through a concrete example helps clarify the stakes. Take *Rachel* and her son *Yosef*, while *Reuven* is a paternal half-brother of *Yosef*. *Lavan* is Rachel's father and has no other grandchildren from Rachel's line. If Rachel died first, *Yosef* — her only son — inherited from her. Then *Yosef* died (leaving no children), and *Reuven*, his paternal half-brother, inherited from him. If *Yosef* died first, Rachel had no living children, and when she died her property passed to *Lavan*.

### Competing Claims

*Reuven* argues: Rachel died first, *Yosef* inherited from his mother, then *Yosef* died with no children, and I as his paternal brother inherited from him. *Lavan* argues: *Yosef* died first; with no surviving children, when Rachel died her estate went to me.

### Unanimous Split

In the earlier *man and wife* case, the dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* was structured around an argument from *chazakah*: there was at least a basis to say that one party was the presumptive possessor. Here, the *mishnah* states: *elu ve'elu modim sheyachloku* — both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* agree that the property is divided. The reason is that here there is no one who holds a better presumptive claim than the other. In the husband-and-wife case, one could argue for a *chazakah* in favor of the husband because the relationship of husband to wife has a special legal character — the husband is at least arguably a presumptive heir in a way that gives him a stronger position. Here, the competing heirs are all straightforwardly family members, each with a plausible inheritance claim depending solely on order of death. There is no basis to prefer one over the other, and so both schools agree: split it.

### Rabbi Akiva Dispute

*Rabbi Akiva* objects to this consensus. He says: *modeh ani bazo* — this is the very case in which I say that *nechasim bechezkatan* applies, that the property should not simply be divided but should remain in its presumptive ownership. The challenge, of course, is the same one we have seen before: *bechezkos mi?* — whose *chazakah*? That is precisely what is unclear, which is why the *Tanna Kamma* concludes it must be split.

### Ben Azzai Retort

*Ben Azzai* responds with some irony: *al hachlukim anu mitzta'arim* — we already suffer enough from the disputes in the earlier cases, where *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* were in disagreement. Here, finally, everyone agrees — and you want to introduce a new dispute? The irony is layered: the very thing everyone agrees upon is *yachloku*, to divide — and now *Rabbi Akiva* wants to divide the consensus as well. *Ben Azzai*'s willingness to address *Rabbi Akiva* in the second person — *she-bata* ("you came to divide") rather than referring to him in the third person as *Rabbeinu* — prompted a brief *Gemara* digression noting that *Ben Azzai* was a *talmid chaver* of *Rabbi Akiva*, a colleague-student whose scholarly stature had become sufficient to place him on more equal footing, such that a degree of familiar directness was appropriate between them.

### Rabbi Ila/Zeira

Having established the *mishnah*'s ruling, the *Gemara* asks *bechezkos mi?* — specifically with respect to *Rabbi Akiva*'s position that the property has a presumptive owner, but more broadly as a clarification of whose *chazakah* the property falls under. *Rabbi Ila* says *bechezkos yorshei ha'em* — the mother's heirs, meaning *Lavan*'s side. *Rabbi Zeira* says *bechezkos yorshei haben* — the son's heirs, meaning *Reuven*.

### Zeira Converts

The *Gemara* records that when *Rabbi Zeira* made *aliyah* to *Eretz Yisrael*, he changed his position and sided with *Rabbi Ila* — ruling that the property goes to *yorshei ha'em*. Upon making this switch, *Rabbi Zeira* himself commented: *shema mina avira de'Eretz Yisrael machkim* — from this we can infer that the air of *Eretz Yisrael* makes one wise. His change of mind upon arriving in the Land was itself the proof.

### Abaye Reasoning

What is the reasoning behind *Rabbi Ila*'s position, which *Rabbi Zeira* ultimately adopted? *Abaye* explains: *ho'il vehuchzeka nachalah be'oto shevet* — since the inheritance had been established within that *shevet*, that tribal or familial line. The property belongs to the mother's *shevet* and the presumption is that it remains there.

### Patriarchy Logic

This requires elaboration. One could argue the opposite: *Yosef* was the presumptive heir of his mother — in the normal course of events, the son outlives his mother and inherits her. So perhaps *Yosef*'s *chazakah* as heir gives *Reuven* his claim. But the counterargument, which is the deeper insight, runs as follows. The Torah operates within a patriarchal structure: *mishpachat av keruya mishpacha, mishpachat em eina keruya mishpacha* — the father's family is called a family; the mother's family is not technically called a family in the same juridical sense. A woman is defined within her father's patriarchal household. As long as Rachel has not died and passed her property on, she remains part of *Lavan*'s patriarchal house. *Yosef*, by contrast, belongs to a different patriarchal house — his father's. When Rachel's property eventually passes to *Yosef*, it will cross from one patriarchal family to another, from *Lavan*'s house to *Yaakov*'s. But until that moment of transfer, the property presumptively remains within the same patriarchal line from which it came. Moreover, with Rachel's husband deceased, the *pasuk* teaches *ve-hashiva el beit aviha kine'ureiha* — she returns to her father's house as in her youth. Without a living husband, her attachment is back to her father's patriarchal house. That is the *chazakah* that keeps the property on *Lavan*'s side absent proof that death occurred in the order that would have transferred it to *Yosef*.

---

## Presale of Inheritance

### Text Corruption

The *Gemara* introduces a teaching sent from *Eretz Yisrael* — *shalchu mi-tam* — which the *Gemara* itself immediately recognizes as textually corrupt. The original text reads: *ben she-lava be-nichsei aviv be-chayei aviv* — a son who borrowed against his father's property while his father was still alive. But this formulation is incoherent. How does a son borrow against property that is not his? And once we are told he borrowed, why does the ruling describe taking property *from purchasers* — where did purchasers enter the picture?

### Presale Case

The *Gemara* therefore corrects the text: *ben she-machar be-nichsei aviv be-chayei aviv* — a son who *sold* in his father's property while his father was still alive. According to the *Rashbam*'s reading, the case is that *Reuven*, anticipating his future inheritance from his father *Yaakov*, pre-sold his stake in that inheritance to a buyer, *Mordechai*. The inherent problem is immediately obvious: *ein adam makneh davar she-lo ba la-olam* — one cannot transfer ownership of something that has not yet come into one's possession. The future inheritance is not yet *Reuven*'s to sell.

### Transaction Sequence

Regardless of those complications, the *Gemara* describes the sequence of events. *Reuven* sold his anticipated portion to *Mordechai*. But it was not *Yaakov* who died first — it was *Reuven* who predeceased his father. Then *Yaakov* died. Now *Chanoch*, the son of *Reuven*, comes forward and seeks to reclaim the property from *Mordechai*, arguing that since his father was already dead when *Yaakov* died, the inheritance never passed through *Reuven* at all — it came directly from grandfather to grandson, and therefore *Reuven*'s purported sale never had a valid object.

### Initial Difficulty

The ruling is characterized as *kasha be-dinei mamonot* — a difficult ruling in property law, one that seems to go against logic. The apparent difficulty: *Mordechai* might reasonably protest that *Reuven* sold him this property, *Reuven* had as strong a claim to it as anyone, and now *Reuven*'s son is coming to invalidate a sale his own father made. That seems deeply unfair — hence the characterization of the ruling as "difficult."

### Direct Inheritance

The *Gemara* initially suggests this is not actually difficult to explain. *Chanoch* can legitimately say: *mikoach avuha de'abba ka'asina* — I am coming from the strength of my grandfather directly. The inheritance bypassed *Reuven* entirely because *Reuven* was already dead when *Yaakov* died. *Chanoch* is not standing in *Reuven*'s shoes; he is inheriting directly from *Yaakov* as if he were *Yaakov*'s son. The *pasuk* states *tachas avosecha yihyu vanecha* — in place of your fathers will be your sons — which the *Gemara* applies to mean that a grandson takes the place of a deceased son when inheriting from the grandfather.

### Solution Fails

But if *Chanoch* is getting it straight from grandfather, bypassing his father entirely, then this is actually a perfectly reasonable ruling — not *kasha* at all. The *Gemara* therefore rejects this as the true difficulty. *Ella ei kashya, ha kashya* — the real difficult ruling is the following.

### True Difficulty

The genuine *kasha be-dinei mamonot* involves a *bechor* — a firstborn. The case is: *ben bechor she-machar chelek bechorah be-chayei aviv* — a firstborn son who sells his double portion while his father is still alive. *Reuven* is the *bechor* and he sold not his regular *chelek* but specifically the *chelek bechorah*, the extra portion that accrues to a firstborn. Then *Reuven* died before *Yaakov*, and the question is whether *Chanoch* can take that *chelek bechorah* back from *Mordechai*.

### Gemara Response

Here the earlier solution breaks down. If *Chanoch* is taking the *chelek bechorah*, he cannot claim he is getting it directly from grandfather, bypassing his father. The *chelek bechorah* is not a portion that passes to a grandson from a grandfather on its own terms. *Chanoch* receives the *bechor*'s double portion precisely because he stands in his father *Reuven*'s place as the *bechor*'s heir — he inherits it *as* the son of the *bechor*, in his father's role. But if he is claiming his rights *as the son standing in the father's place*, then by the same logic, *Reuven*'s prior sale of that portion should be binding on him. If the sale would have been effective had *Reuven* lived, and *Chanoch* is claiming the *bechor* portion by virtue of being *Reuven*'s substitute, then the sale should pass through him to *Mordechai*. Yet the ruling is that *Chanoch* can take it back — which is what makes it *kasha*.

The *Gemara*'s response — that *Chanoch* can say simultaneously *mikoach avuha de'abba ka'asina* (I take from grandfather) *u-vimkom abba ka'imna* (but I stand in my father's place) — is frankly difficult to parse. If he bypasses his father to get it from grandfather, the *chelek bechorah* makes no sense; and if he stands in his father's place to claim the *bechorah*, the sale should follow. The *Rashbam* does not resolve the tension cleanly, and a careful reader will find the *Gemara*'s logic here strained.

### Tosafot Alternative

*Tosafot* resolves the difficulty by reframing the underlying case entirely. *Tosafot* is troubled by the basic premise: how can *Reuven* pre-sell an inheritance he does not yet own? *Ein adam makneh davar she-lo ba la-olam* is a fundamental principle, and *Tosafot* will not simply set it aside. *Tosafot* therefore reads the case differently: *Yaakov* himself, while still alive, transferred the *guf* — the corpus of the property — to *Reuven*, while retaining the *peirot* — the usufruct — for himself. This is a recognized mechanism by which a father can transfer ownership of property while alive, stipulating that he continues to benefit from it during his lifetime. On this reading, *Reuven* did hold actual ownership of the property; it was not merely an anticipated inheritance. He then transferred or sold it to *Mordechai*. But the transfer from *Yaakov* to *Reuven* was conditioned on *Reuven* coming into full possession — which would occur only when *Yaakov* died and the *peirot* ceased.
