Since *Reuven* predeceased *Yaakov*, he never came into full possession; the transfer never completed. Therefore, when *Yaakov* died, the property had never fully vested in *Reuven*, and *Chanoch* can claim it — the sale to *Mordechai* of something *Reuven* never fully owned is void. This reading has a certain elegance, though it requires reading considerable nuance into the *Gemara*'s formulation. The discussion of the full implications of *kasha be-dinei mamonot* continues onto the next daf.

---

---

# Bava Batra 159

## Inheritance Pre-Sale

### Kasha Shebidinei Mamonos

The daf opens at a peculiar juncture in the *Gemara*. We are told that a ruling was transmitted from *Eretz Yisrael* to *Bavel* accompanied by the declaration that it constituted a *kasha she-be-dinei mamonot* — one of the hardest, or at the very least a very hard, ruling in monetary law. The *Gemara* then proceeded to analyze the reasoning behind that ruling and concluded that it was, in fact, entirely straightforward. This conclusion sets the *Gemara* on a search: if that ruling is not genuinely difficult to understand, then what was the ruling that was actually sent, and why was it called *kasha she-be-dinei mamonot*?

### Chanoch's Reclamation

The ruling that was initially under discussion involved a son — call him Reuven, Yaakov's son — who pre-sold his anticipated inheritance to Mordechai. Reuven then died, and Chanoch, Reuven's son, came and reclaimed the property. The apparent difficulty is that Chanoch is receiving his inheritance *through* his father Reuven — or so it seems — and if that is the case, why should he be able to void the sale? The sale passed through Reuven, and Reuven had already disposed of the property. (Tosafot has a different way of learning the sugya altogether, though we bracket that issue for the moment.)

### Grandson Inheritance

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent difficulty by suggesting that a grandson may inherit directly from his grandfather, bypassing his father. If Chanoch inherits straight from Yaakov without the inheritance passing through Reuven at all, then Reuven's pre-sale becomes irrelevant to Chanoch's claim, and there is nothing surprising about Chanoch's reclamation. But that explanation dissolves the *kasha*: if the ruling makes perfect sense, it can hardly be called *kasha she-be-dinei mamonot*. The *Gemara* is therefore compelled to seek a different candidate for the ruling that was sent.

---

## Witness Signature Timing

### Gazlan Witness

The *Gemara* now proposes a different ruling as the true *kasha she-be-dinei mamonot*. The case is one of a witness who signed a *shtar* — say, a document recording that Charlie borrowed a thousand dollars from David — before becoming disqualified as a witness. At the time of signing, Reuven was a perfectly upstanding *kosher ed*. Subsequently, however, Reuven entered a life of crime and became a *gazlan*, which renders him halachically disqualified from giving testimony. The *shtar* now comes before *beis din*, but the signatures have not yet been validated (*mekuyam*). For David to use the *shtar* against Charlie, he must validate the signatures.

The most natural person to validate Reuven's signature would be Reuven himself, testifying that the signature on the document is his. But Reuven is no longer a *kosher ed* — he cannot testify at all. The *Gemara* states: *hu eno meid al ktav yado* — he cannot testify to his own signature. Yet *aval acherim meidim* — other people can come and attest that the signature is Reuven's. (Some versions of the text read *yecholim lekayem ktav yado* — others are capable of validating his handwriting.)

### Validation Paradox

At first glance this seems entirely reasonable, but the *Gemara* presses: *hashta ihu lo meheman acherim mehemani*? He himself cannot testify, yet others are believed? What makes this conceptually troubling is that when other witnesses validate Reuven's signature, they are essentially corroborating his testimony — but his testimony is inadmissible. One might respond that there is an obvious distinction: his testimony is inadmissible *today*, but the other witnesses are testifying to the fact that he gave his testimony *a year ago*, when he was still a *kosher ed*. The act of signing the *shtar* functions as the presentation of testimony, and that act occurred before he became a *gazlan*. Why should that be problematic?

### Predating Suspicion

The Rashbam explains the difficulty as follows. When other witnesses validate a signature, they are not testifying that the signatory gave testimony at a specific past date — they are only attesting to the identity of the handwriting. And therein lies the problem: given that we now know Reuven is a *gazlan*, a person who will transgress for money, we have reason to suspect that he may have forged the entire document. He could have written and signed it yesterday and simply predated it to a year ago, when he was still *kosher*. Merely confirming that the signature is Reuven's does not tell us *when* he signed it. If he is capable of dishonesty, why should the date on the document be trusted? Other witnesses validating the signature does not dispel the possibility of fraudulent predating.

### Prior Beit Din Viewing

The *Gemara* responds: *u-mai kushya* — why is this genuinely difficult? Perhaps the ruling is limited to a case where the *shtar* was already seen by *beis din* before Reuven became a *gazlan*. This is Tosafot's explanation: the *shtar* was brought before *beis din* a year ago while Reuven was still a valid witness. The signatures were not validated at the time, but the document was seen. Now that Reuven has become a *gazlan*, he cannot validate his own signature. But once other witnesses come and validate it, we know the signature was already present on the *shtar* when *beis din* saw it last year — at which point Reuven was still *kosher*. The forgery concern is thus neutralized by the prior *beis din* viewing. The ruling is sound, but it is confined to that circumstance. If the *shtar* appears before *beis din* for the first time today, the concern of predating would remain unresolved, and the validation by other witnesses would not suffice.

The *Gemara* thus concludes: if the difficulty was as described, then the ruling makes sense only when *beis din* had already seen the *shtar* — and that is not the kind of ruling one would call *kasha she-be-dinei mamonot*. The *Gemara* is again left without a satisfactory candidate, and presses on.

---

## Relative Witness

### Son-in-Law Status

The *Gemara* now proposes yet another ruling as the authentic *kasha she-be-dinei mamonot*. The case this time involves someone who possessed knowledge of a transaction and signed a *shtar* as a witness before he had any familial relationship to the parties. Subsequently — *ve-naaseh chotno* — he became the son-in-law of the relevant party. He is now a *karov*, a relative, and is therefore disqualified from giving testimony. Once again: *hu eno meid al ktav yado* — he cannot validate his own signature. Yet *aval acherim meidim* — others may attest to his signature.

### Prior Viewing Solution

The same conceptual problem recurs. If we are concerned that someone may have fabricated a document and forged a date, then confirming the identity of the signature does not help — he might have signed it yesterday and predated it to a time before he became a relative. So the *Gemara* offers the same response: perhaps here too the *shtar* was previously seen by *beis din* before he became a relative, so the prior viewing eliminates the predating concern.

### No Prior Viewing

But the *Gemara* now introduces a crucial distinction. *Ve-ha-amar Rav Yosef bar Minyumi amar Rav Nachman af al pi she-lo huchzak ktav yado be-veit din* — there is a received tradition that in the case of the son-in-law, the ruling applies even if the *shtar* first appears before *beis din* today, without any prior viewing. This is a striking departure from the *gazlan* case. Here we are told explicitly that even without the safeguard of a prior *beis din* viewing, the validation by other witnesses is sufficient. The question is: why?

---

## Gzeirat Hamelek

### Gazlan Dishonesty

To understand the distinction, the *Gemara* articulates a fundamental principle about the different categories of *psulei eidus* — those who are disqualified from testimony. A *gazlan* is disqualified because of a concern about dishonesty. Someone who will commit transgressions for money may well lie for money, may well forge documents for money. The *psul* of the *gazlan* is therefore rooted in a concern that he might not be telling the truth. Consequently, once we suspect him of potential dishonesty, confirming the identity of his signature without knowing *when* he signed it does not dispel the concern.

### Relative Formalism

The disqualification of a relative, by contrast, operates on entirely different grounds. The *Gemara* states: *dilma gzeiras ha-melekh hu* — perhaps the reason a relative is disqualified is not because we suspect him of lying, but rather because it is a formal, categorical exclusion — a *gzeiras ha-melekh*, a divine decree. On this view, we do not suspect the relative of being dishonest; his testimony is simply inadmissible as a formal matter. This has nothing to do with character or credibility.

This distinction is crucial. The *psul* of the *gazlan* and the *nogea ba-davar* (one who has a direct financial stake) is grounded in a concern about lying: if you will act corruptly for money, perhaps you will lie for money. But a relative — we might ordinarily assume — would lie for the sake of family loyalty. That would place the relative's disqualification in the same category as the *gazlan*, and the same predating concern would apply. The *Gemara* rejects this assumption.

### Moshe Aharon Proof

The *Gemara* offers a striking proof. *D'ei lo seima hachi, Moshe ve-Aharon le-chosanam* — if you insist that the disqualification of relatives is based on a concern about lying, consider: could Moshe and Aharon not testify for their sons-in-law? Would anyone suspect *them* of lying? Of course not. *Ela gzeiras Melech* — rather, it is simply a formal exclusion, a decree that relatives are categorically excluded from testimony — not because we suspect them of lying, but because that is the rule.

It is worth noting that some *rishonim*, when citing this principle, slightly reframe the *Gemara*'s example: they ask why Moshe and Aharon could not come together and testify as two witnesses on behalf of any party, given that they are brothers. There, the disqualification is not because they are relatives of the interested party, but because they are related to each other. That is an equally compelling illustration: of course Moshe and Aharon would never lie. *B'chayecha!* And yet they cannot testify together. The formal exclusion applies without regard to the actual likelihood of deception. It is a *gzeiras ha-kasuv*.

### Date Trustworthiness

This distinction resolves the puzzle of the son-in-law case perfectly. Since the disqualification of a relative is not rooted in any concern about dishonesty — it is purely formal — we have no reason to suspect that the witness forged the document and predated it. He is, on the contrary, a trustworthy individual whom we simply cannot allow to testify for technical, formal reasons. Once other witnesses confirm that the signature is genuinely his, we proceed on the assumption that a trustworthy person would have signed the document honestly and dated it accurately. The date is presumed truthful, and therefore we can infer that he signed it before he became a relative — at which point his testimony was fully valid.

In the *gazlan* case, by contrast, we cannot make this inference. Even after confirming the identity of the signature, we remain suspicious that he might have signed and predated the document fraudulently. The prior *beis din* viewing is the only mechanism by which that suspicion can be removed. In the son-in-law case, no such mechanism is needed, because the suspicion never arises in the first place. And *that* is why the ruling — that other witnesses may validate the signature of a man who has since become a relative, even without a prior *beis din* viewing — is genuinely *kasha she-be-dinei mamonot*. The result seems counterintuitive: he himself cannot testify, yet others can validate what is essentially his testimony. But once we understand that his disqualification is purely formal and carries no taint of dishonesty, the ruling becomes coherent — and its coherence is itself the source of the conceptual difficulty.

---

## Original Case Return

### Chanoch Presale

Having worked through the cases of the *gazlan* and the relative witness, the *Gemara* returns to its original discussion. *Ela amar Rava le-olam ke-da-amina me-ikara* — Rava says: in truth, the ruling that was sent was indeed the original ruling about Chanoch, who came to reclaim the property that his father Reuven had pre-sold to Mordechai.

### Through Father Paradox

And now the *Gemara* identifies precisely *why* this ruling is *kasha she-be-dinei mamonot*. Chanoch inherits in place of his father — he is receiving the inheritance *through* his father Reuven. That is what entitles him to the property at all. And yet, even though the inheritance passes through his father, the pre-sale that Reuven made to Mordechai is not valid against Chanoch. How can this be? The very thing that entitles him to the property — inheriting through his father — is what should make the sale binding on him. That paradox is the *kasha*.

---

## Grandson & Deaths

### Tachat Avotecha

The *Gemara* now turns to the verse *tachat avotecha yihiyu vanecha* — "in place of your fathers shall be your sons" — which was earlier cited in the discussion as a possible proof that a grandson inherits directly from his grandfather. Could this verse serve as a legal principle establishing that grandchildren bypass their fathers in the line of inheritance? The *Gemara* answers: *hahu be-vracha ketiv* — that verse is written in the context of a blessing, not as a halachic formulation. It speaks to the idea that grandchildren carry forward their grandparents' legacy and reputation, but it establishes no legal rule about the mechanics of inheritance. Inheritance passes through the son, and a grandson who receives an estate is conceptually receiving it through his deceased father, not directly from his grandfather.

### House Collapse Case

But this conclusion raises a difficulty. The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: *nafal ha-bayis alav ve-al aviv* — a house collapsed on a father and son. They both died, but the order of deaths is unknown. The son had debts: there was a woman holding a *kesuvas isha* and a *baal chov* to whom he owed money. The question of which death occurred first determines who receives the estate. The *ba'al chov* argues that the father died first and then the son, meaning the son briefly held the property — long enough for the creditor's lien to attach — before dying. Chanoch (the grandson) argues the opposite: that the son died first, then the grandfather, so the inheritance bypassed the son entirely and came to him directly from his grandfather. If this argument is valid, it seems to presuppose that a grandson *can* inherit directly from a grandfather, bypassing a deceased father — which would undermine the *Gemara*'s conclusion that the verse is only a blessing, not a legal principle.

### Baraita Dispute

The *Gemara* carefully reads the *baraita*. The phrase *yorshei ha-av* and *yorshei ha-ben* — the heirs of the father and the heirs of the son — at first seems to refer to a straightforward dispute between the son's descendants and the father's estate. But the *Gemara* points out that if the dispute were simply between the son's heirs and the father's heirs in the most natural reading, the order of death would not matter: everyone would receive their share regardless of who died first. There would be no genuine dispute, and no reason to divide.

### Grandfather Grandson

The *Gemara* therefore re-reads the *baraita*. The case is not between a father and son simpliciter, but between a grandfather and a grandson — where the father (*Reuven*) is not in the picture, having died previously, and the question is which of the other two — the grandfather (*Yaakov*) and the grandson (*Chanoch*, here Yaakov's grandson through Reuven) — died first. Alternatively, the *Gemara* considers a reading involving the father and an uncle (the father's brother), who is outside the house and unaffected by the collapse.

Working through the scenarios: if *Reuven* dies first, then *Yaakov* dies, the entire estate goes to *Yaakov*'s remaining son, *Shimon* — directly, with no passage through *Reuven*. If *Yaakov* dies first, half his estate passes to *Reuven* and half to *Shimon*; then when *Reuven* dies, his half passes on — but having passed through *Reuven*, it is subject to his creditors' claims. In that scenario, *Shimon* ultimately receives the property, but a portion of it traveled through *Reuven*, making it available to *Reuven*'s *baal chov*.

The *Gemara* ultimately concludes from this *baraita* that there is no proof that a grandson inherits directly from his grandfather bypassing the son. In fact, a grandson inherits through his father as a matter of principle — and the proof is that Chanoch also receives *Reuven*'s *chelek bechorah* (firstborn's portion), which demonstrates that he is standing *in his father's stead*, not bypassing him. The question of why, in that case, Reuven's pre-sale does not bind Chanoch remains the *kasha* — the *Gemara* never fully resolves the mechanics of how such a pre-sale could operate in the first place, and it seems that the very concept of pre-selling one's inheritance is inherently fragile, perhaps amounting to no more than a personal undertaking that cannot bind one's heirs.

---

## Son Mother Grave

### Rav Sheshet Query

Because the *sugya* has now established that a grandson inherits through his dead father — which means, in effect, that the son stands as the vehicle through which inheritance passes even after his death — the *Gemara* transitions to a related question about *inheriting through the grave*. The question is posed to Rav Sheshet: *ben mahu she-yirash et imo bakever le-hanchil le-achiv min ha-av* — can a son who has already died inherit from his mother in order to pass that inheritance on to his paternal half-brothers?

The scenario is as follows. Yosef, the son of Rachel, dies. Then Rachel dies. Had Yosef been alive when Rachel died, he would have inherited from her. The question is: does Yosef's death before Rachel's death sever any connection between Rachel's estate and Yosef's paternal half-brothers — Reuven, Shimon, and so forth — who are sons of Yaakov by Leah and are completely unrelated to Rachel? Or does Yosef, as it were, inherit from Rachel *bakever* — while already in the grave — and pass that inheritance to his half-brothers, who stand in his stead?

This is a critical question. We have established that a grandson can represent a dead father. Can half-brothers represent their dead brother to inherit from a woman to whom they have no relationship whatsoever?

### Mother Son House

The *Gemara* brings as evidence the classic case of *nafla ha-bayis alav ve-al imo* — the house that fell on a son and his mother. Both died; the order of death is unknown. The two possible sets of heirs dispute who receives the estate. The schools — *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* — agree that the estate is divided (*yachloku*) between the heirs of the mother and the heirs of the son, regardless of the order of death. This implies that the question of which death came first matters: the mother's relatives claim the son died first (leaving the estate with the mother, and thence to her relatives), while the son's heirs claim the mother died first (so Yosef inherited from her and then passed it to them).

### If Grave Permitted

But now the *Gemara* presses: *ve-im issa* — if it were true that a son can inherit from his mother *bakever*, even while he is already dead, then why does it matter who died first? Even if the son died first, let him inherit from his mother in the grave and pass the inheritance on to his paternal half-brothers. The dispute about the order of death would then be irrelevant: the half-brothers should receive the property in either scenario. But the *Gemara* treats the dispute as meaningful, which implies that when the son dies before the mother, the inheritance does *not* pass through him to his half-brothers.

### No Mother Grave

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ein ha-ben yoresh et imo bakever le-hanchil la-achin min ha-av* — a son does not inherit from his mother while in the grave in order to benefit his paternal half-brothers. Once the son is dead, his half-brothers cannot step into his shoes to claim from a woman to whom they are entirely unrelated. The inheritance does not travel through the grave in this direction.

---

## No Grave Inheritance

### Sibling Replacement

Abaye offers the conceptual reasoning. The principle is: *ne'emra sibah ba-ven ve-ne'emra sibah ba-ba'al* — the Torah articulates the mechanism by which inheritance can be diverted when it passes through a woman, and that mechanism involves either a son or a husband. The half-brothers are neither. They cannot step into the place of their dead brother to inherit from a woman who has no connection to them. A son can represent his dead father in the line of inheritance — the grandson-for-grandfather case — because the son *is* the legal continuation of the father in the chain of descent. But half-brothers do not stand in that relationship to their deceased brother.

### Husband Analogy

Abaye draws an explicit analogy: just as a husband does not inherit from his father-in-law once his wife has died — because the link that connected him to that estate has been severed — so too a son does not function as a conduit through the grave when the result would be to benefit parties who have no independent claim to the estate. *Ma sibah ha-amura ba-ba'al ein ha-ba'al yoresh ishto bakever, af sibah ha-amura ba-ven ein ha-ben yoresh imo bakever le-hanchil la-achin min ha-av.* The inheritance does not travel to people for whom the relationship has been cut — either because the wife died (severing the husband's connection) or because the son died (severing the half-brothers' connection). The estate in such a case returns to the mother's own kin, not to those whose only link to it was through a deceased intermediary who himself has no living descendants to represent him.

---

## Misc. Cases

### Bar Sisan Sale

The *Gemara* closes with a series of cases involving questions of possession and the burden of proof. In the first case, a man says to his fellow: *nichsei de-Bar Sisan mezavinna lakh* — I am selling you all the property of Bar Sisan that I possess. It turns out that among the properties under discussion there is one piece of land that is *called* "of the house of Bar Sisan" but was not actually acquired from Bar Sisan himself — it simply goes by that name. The question is whether that field is included in the sale.

### Rav Nachman Rule

The case came before Rav Nachman, and he ruled: *ve-ukmah be-yada de-loke'ach* — the property goes to the buyer. Since it is called *Bar Sisan*, it falls under the terms of what was sold.

### Rava Challenge

Rava challenged Rav Nachman: *dina hachi*? Is that really the ruling? The principle of *hamotzi me-chavero alav ha-ra'ayah* — he who seeks to remove property from another's possession must bring proof — should apply here. The buyer is the one seeking to take this field away from the seller's possession; it is the buyer who should have to prove his claim.

### House Case

But there is an apparent contradiction, because in a different case, Rav Nachman seems to take the opposite position. In that case, a man found someone occupying his house. The occupier claimed: I bought it from you and I have been *okhel* — using the property — for three years, establishing a *chazakah*. The original owner countered: I was living in the inner chamber of the house the whole time, so the *chazakah* is ineffective, since I was continuously present. The case came before Rav Nachman, who said: *zil berur achiltach* — go and prove that your use of the property was uninterrupted and without the owner's knowledge. Here Rav Nachman placed the burden on the person claiming the *chazakah*, which seems to favor the original owner.

Similarly, Rava himself seems to take contradictory positions: in the *Bar Sisan* case he argued that the burden falls on the buyer (who is removing from the seller's possession), yet in the house case he argued that once the occupier has established a prima facie *chazakah*, *he* becomes the *muchzak* (the one in possession), and the original owner then becomes the *motzi* who must bring proof.

### Muchzak Key

The *Gemara* resolves both apparent contradictions with a single elegant principle: do not ask who is the buyer and who is the seller — ask who is the *muchzak*, who currently holds the property. *Hacha mocher ka'i be-nichsei, hatam loke'ach ka'i be-nichsei* — in the *Bar Sisan* case, the seller is in possession of the disputed field; in the house case, the buyer (the one claiming *chazakah*) is in possession of the house. The *muchzak* is always favored; the burden falls on whoever is trying to dislodge him.

### Burden Context

This explains Rava's position perfectly: in both cases he invokes *hamotzi me-chavero alav ha-ra'ayah*, but the *motzi* is a different party in each case. In the *Bar Sisan* case, the buyer is the *motzi* — he is trying to take the field from the seller's possession. In the house case, the original owner is the *motzi* — once the occupier has demonstrated three years of *chazakah*, he becomes the *muchzak*, and it is the original owner who must now prove his claim.

As for Rav Nachman's apparently inconsistent rulings: in the *Bar Sisan* case, the seller is in possession and the field is called *Bar Sisan*, so the burden falls on him to prove that the term in the contract does not cover this field. In the house case, even though Rav Nachman places a demand on the *chazakah* claimant, this is not inconsistent — Rav Nachman treats the *chazakah* as functionally equivalent to a *shtar mecher*, a deed of sale. Just as a *shtar* that is challenged must be validated, so too a *chazakah* that is challenged — by the owner's claim that he was continuously present in the inner chamber — must be defended. The challenge need not be conclusive; it need only be serious enough to require a response. In both rulings, the *Gemara* concludes, Rav Nachman is operating from a consistent underlying logic once context and possession are properly understood.

With this, we conclude the ninth *perek*. *Hadran alach mi she-hotziu.*

---

---

# Bava Batra 160

## Get Pashut Intro

### Context & Connection

We begin the new *perek*, *Get Pashut*, the last *perek* of *Bava Batra*, which is devoted to the writing of *shtarot*. The connection to the preceding material is that the earlier discussion of deathbed bequests touched on questions of whether the disposition was written in a *shtar* or made orally, and whether the document reflected that the person was ill or healthy at the time. That thematic thread now opens into a full *perek* dealing with how *shtarot* must be written.

### Pashut vs. Mekushar

The *perek* opens with the *Mishnah* on 160a: *get pashut edav mitocho* — a simple, flat document has its witnesses signing on the same side as the text itself, at the bottom of the written content. This is the format familiar from a standard *ketubah*. The term *pashut* is used here in contrast to *mekushar*. A *mekushar* is a bound document in which the text is written in sections, each of which is folded over and sewn shut. For a *mekushar*, the *Mishnah* states *edav meachorav* — the witnesses sign on the back side, side B of the document.

### Bar Kokhba & History

The *Gemara* will explain that the institution of the *get mekushar* was originally established for *kohanim* who wished to divorce their wives. Because *kohanim* could be impulsive and would sometimes write and deliver a *get* in a moment of anger — after which reconciliation was impossible, since the wife became forbidden to her *kohen* husband as a divorcée — the Rabbis instituted the *get mekushar* to slow down the process. Writing the document section by section, folding and sewing each fold, required time and a degree of expertise, giving the husband a chance to reconsider.

By the time of *Rebbi* (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, at the end of the *Mishnaic* period), the *get mekushar* was already becoming unfamiliar, as we will see later in the *Gemara*. By the time of the *Rishonim*, it was entirely out of practice, and its structure had to be reconstructed from the textual sources. Interestingly, actual *mekushar* documents were found among the Bar Kokhba cave documents — not specifically *gittin* for divorce, but ordinary legal documents. This suggests that in the ancient world, folding and sewing a document was a standard method of securing it against tampering.

### Mishnah: Placement Rules

The *Mishnah* continues: *pashut she-katvu edav meachorav* — if one has a simple *pashut* document but placed the witnesses on the back as one would in a *mekushar*, or conversely, a *mekushar* in which the witnesses were placed inside alongside the text, *shehem pesulim* — both are invalid. The *Rashbam* explains that the invalidity follows from the fact that *Chachamim* established fixed parameters for each type of document, and failing to follow them renders the document invalid. *Tosafot* offers a different rationale: mixing the formats would distort the dating system, potentially creating what would be considered an antedated or postdated document — a *mukdam* or *me'uchar*. Other *Rishonim* offer additional explanations; the *Rashbam*'s position suffices as the working framework here.

### R. Chanina Leniency

Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel disagrees in one case: *mekushar she-katvu edav mitocho kasher mipnei she-yakhol la'asoto pashut* — a *mekushar* whose witnesses signed on the inside is still valid, because one can simply undo all the sewn folds and it becomes an ordinary flat document. Therefore it is not invalid, since it can be converted into a valid *pashut*. However, he does not extend this leniency to a *pashut* with witnesses on the back, because a *pashut* cannot easily be converted into a *mekushar* — and there are also concerns about the potential for forgery in such a configuration.

## Mekushar Structure

### Rashbam: Blank Lines

Before proceeding further, the *Gemara*'s discussion requires a clear picture of what a *mekushar* actually looked like. The *Rashbam* explains that one would write a line of text, leave a blank line beneath it, and then fold the written line down over the blank line, sewing that fold shut. Then one would move further down the document, write another line, leave another blank line beneath it, and fold and sew again. This produces an accordion-like structure of consecutive sealed folds — not a continuous fan from one end, but discrete separate folds, each consisting of a written line sewn against a blank one.

### Rashbam Problem

This model, however, runs into a difficulty from the *Mishnah* itself, specifically from Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's ruling that a *mekushar* with internal witnesses is valid because it can simply be converted into a *pashut*. If the *Rashbam*'s model is correct, then undoing the folds would leave the document with a blank line between every written line — a document with blank lines interspersed throughout would be entirely unacceptable, as those blank lines could be filled in with fraudulent additions. Such a document could not serve as a valid *pashut*.

### Tosafot: No Blanks

*Tosafot* therefore rejects the *Rashbam*'s model and argues that the entire document was written continuously, with no blank lines. The accordion folds were created by folding written line one over written line two, then written line three over written line four, and so on — each fold containing two lines of actual text with nothing blank in between. When unfolded, the result would be a complete, continuously written document without gaps. *Tosafot* derives this understanding specifically from Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's ruling, which only makes sense if undoing the folds would leave a usable, uninterrupted document.

## Scriptural Basis

### First Proof: Deut.

The *Gemara* asks: *mina hanei milei* — from where do we derive all these laws? Rabbi Chanina cites the verse from Jeremiah's land purchase narrative: *sadot ba-kesef yiknu ve-chatuv ba-sefer ve-chatom ve-ha'ed edim* — "fields shall be purchased for money, and it shall be written in a document and sealed, and witnesses shall testify." This verse is cited in other contexts as the scriptural basis for the legal validity of a *shtar re'ayah* — a documentary attestation as opposed to a *shtar kinyan*, which effects a transaction such as marriage, divorce, or purchase. The question of where the Torah legitimizes written testimony rather than oral testimony before a court is addressed through this verse.

### Two Types Derived

The *Gemara* on 160b attempts to derive both types of documents from this single verse. *Ve-chatuv ba-sefer* — "written in a document" — *zeh pashut*, this refers to a simple, straightforward document written in the manner of a book, everything on one side of the page. *Ve-chatom* — "and seal it" — *zeh mekushar*, this refers to a document that is folded over and sewn shut, i.e., sealed. *Ve-ha'ed edim* — "and witnesses shall testify" — since *edim* is written in the plural, the minimum count is two; but then a second instance of the word *edim* teaches that there can be three. This gives us the distinction in the number of witnesses: two for a *pashut*, three for a *mekushar*.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *ve-eifcha ana* — why not reverse the assignment and say two for the *mekushar* and three for the *pashut*? The answer is: *mitoch she-nitrabah bi-kshirah nitrabah be-adeha* — since the *mekushar* already bears greater demands in how it must be physically constructed, it stands to reason that it also bears the greater demand of requiring three witnesses rather than two.

### Second Proof: Jeremiah

Rafram cites a different verse, from Jeremiah's own account of executing the purchase he was commanded to perform: *va-ekach et sefer ha-miknah et ha-chatum et ha-mitzvah ve-ha-chukim ve-et ha-galui* — "I took the deed of purchase, the sealed one, and the laws and statutes, and the open one." Here, *sefer ha-miknah* — the deed of purchase — *zeh pashut*, that is the simple document; *et ha-chatum* — the sealed one — *zeh mekushar*, that is the sewn document.

### Pashut Shebim.

The verse then says *et ha-galui* — the open, explicit portion — and the *Gemara* identifies this as *zehu pashut she-bi-mekushar*, the flat portion of the *mekushar* document. This introduces an important concept: the *mekushar* consists of two distinct sections. The upper portion contains the *toref* — the essential particulars: the names of the parties, the amount, the date — written in folded and sewn sections. The lower portion, the *tofes*, contains the boilerplate language and is left flat and open, written in the ordinary manner. This lower flat portion is the *pashut she-bi-mekushar*. Finally, the verse adds *ha-mitzvah ve-ha-chukim* — the commandments and statutes — and the *Gemara* reads this as: *elu devarim she-bein pashut le-mekushar*, these are the detailed laws that distinguish between the two types of documents.

### Third Proof: Edim

Rami bar Yechezkel cites yet a third source: *al pi shnayim edim o al pi shlosha edim yakum davar* — "by the testimony of two witnesses or by the testimony of three witnesses shall a matter be established." The *Gemara* asks: if two suffice to establish testimony, why does the Torah add the possibility of three? *Le-omar lecha shnayim la-pashut shlosha la-mekushar* — to teach you that while two witnesses suffice for a *pashut*, a *mekushar* requires three. Again the reversal is challenged and answered with the same logic: the greater demands of the *mekushar* in its physical construction correlate with its greater demand for witnesses.

## Asmachta Disclaimer

### Rejection of Proofs

The *Gemara* then decisively rejects all three derivations: *ve-hanei le-hachi hu de-atu* — are these verses really coming to teach us about *pashut* and *mekushar*? No — *kol chad ve-chad le-miletei hu de-ata* — each verse comes to teach something entirely its own.

The first verse — *sadot ba-kesef yiknu ve-chatuv ba-sefer ve-chatom* — is *etzah tovah ka-mashma lan*: it is simply giving good advice. God commanded Jeremiah that, as an act of faith in Israel's return from exile, he should purchase a plot of land, write it in a document, seal it, and place it in a pottery vessel so that it should endure for many years. The verse is practical guidance for that particular act, not a source for legal categories.

The second verse — *va-ekach et sefer ha-miknah* — is *hachi havai ma'aseh*: it is simply narrating the story, reporting that Jeremiah did what he was commanded. The apparent superfluity of all the enumerated details does not carry the legal weight the *Gemara* had tried to assign to it. The *Gemara* acknowledges, in effect, that under ordinary interpretive principles one might press those extra words for legal content, but here it knows that the laws of *pashut* and *mekushar* do not actually derive from these verses.

The third verse — *al pi shnayim edim o al pi shlosha edim* — comes *le-hakish shlosha li-shnayim*, to equate a group of three witnesses with a group of two, establishing that even three witnesses constitute a single *kat* — a single testimonial unit. The practical implications of this equation are debated by Rabbi Akiva and the *Rabanan*: for instance, if three witnesses are subjected to *edim zomemim* proceedings, all three must be found conspiratorial — it does not suffice to disqualify only two of them. Similarly, if one of three is found to be *pasul*, the entire group is disqualified, rather than relying on the remaining two. These are distinct *halachot* discussed elsewhere in the *Gemara*, and the verse is fully occupied with them. It has nothing to do with *pashut* and *mekushar*.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *mekushar mi-derabanan* — the entire institution of the folded, sewn document is rabbinic in origin — *u-kerai asmachta be-alma* — and the verses cited above are mere *asmachta*, supports or allusions, not genuine derivations.

### Kohanim Takana

The *Gemara* then asks: *ve-ta'ama mai tiknu rabanan mekushar* — what was the actual reason the Rabbis instituted the *mekushar*? The answer: *asra de-kahanei hava* — this arose in a locale where *kohanim* were prevalent, *ve-havu kefidei tuva* — and those *kohanim* were quick-tempered and greatly agitated by small provocations, *u-mgarshi nishayhu* — and they would divorce their wives impulsively, and then regret it and find themselves unable to remarry them. The Rabbis therefore established the *takana* of the *get mekushar* specifically for *gittin*, so that the laborious process of writing, folding, and sewing — *ve-ad hachi ve-hachi maytva da'atayhu* — would allow sufficient time for the husband's temper to subside and for reconsideration.

### Extension to All

The *Gemara* then asks: *ha-tinach gittin, shtarot mai ika le-meimar* — understandable that the Rabbis made this institution for *gittin*, but why extend it to all *shtarot*? The answer: *kedei she-lo techalek bein gittin le-shtarot* — once the format was established for *gittin*, it became a recognized mode of document-writing, and one could not simply create a partition by which the same physical format would be valid in one legal context and unrecognized in another. Presumably, as well, the evidence from the Bar Kokhba caves confirms that this method of sealing documents was used in the broader world as a security measure, so extending it to all *shtarot* had practical justification.

## Witness Placement

### Rav Huna: Folds

The *Gemara* now turns to a specific and important practical question: *heichan edim chotmin* — where exactly did the witnesses sign on a *mekushar*? Rav Huna says: *bein kesher le-kesher* — between the folds. To understand this properly: imagining the accordion-folded document with all its folds on side A (where the text is), on side B — the back — the sealed folds appear as a series of raised ridges. Each fold, on side B, presents a strip of visible surface. Rav Huna's position is that one witness signed on each such fold-strip, so that three folds carry three witnesses, one per fold.

### R. Yirmeya: Back

Rabbi Yirmeya offers a different position: *achurei ha-ktav u-keneged ha-ktav mi-bachutz* — on the back of the document, facing the written text, on the outside. As the discussion develops, it becomes clear that Rabbi Yirmeya is referring to the *pashut she-bi-mekushar*, the flat lower portion of the document. On side B, directly behind the flat written section rather than behind the folded section, the witnesses would inscribe their names. This contrasts with Rav Huna's placement on the folded portion at the top of side B.

### R. Chama & Rabbi

Rami bar Chama poses a question to Rav Chisda concerning Rav Huna's position. He raises an assumption: *ka-salka da'atach bein kesher le-kesher mi-gavai* — one might have thought that when Rav Huna said "between the folds," he meant on the inside, on side A. Rami bar Chama adduces a proof from a story: a *shtar mekushar* was once brought before *Rebbi*, and *Rebbi* said *ein zman ba-zeh* — there is no date on this document. He was looking at the *pashut she-bi-mekushar*, the flat lower portion visible before him, and did not see the date, because the date was written in the sewn-up folds above it. Rabbi Shimon be-Rabbi said to him: *shema bein kashrav mufla* — perhaps the date is concealed in the folds. *Palyei* — he opened them — *ve-chazyei* — and the date was there. This story reveals that by the time of *Rebbi*, the *get mekushar* was already so unfamiliar that *Rebbi* himself did not recognize it when presented with one.

The *Gemara* uses this story to resolve the question about Rav Huna's position. If the witnesses had been on the inside of the folds — sewn up together with the text — then before *Rebbi* even raised the question of the missing date, he should have said: "Where are the witnesses?" A document without visible witnesses is simply not a valid *shtar*. The fact that *Rebbi* recognized it as a *shtar* and only questioned the date proves that the witnesses were visible on the outside. The *Gemara* therefore clarifies: *lo, bein kesher le-kesher mi-barai* — when Rav Huna said "between the folds," he meant on the outside, on side B, on each fold-strip as it appears externally.

## Anti-Forgery Problem

### Blank Space Risk

With the witnesses' placement established, the *Gemara* raises a serious structural problem. In an ordinary *pashut* document — such as a *ketubah* — the witnesses sign at the bottom, immediately after the final line of text. This configuration prevents forgery: there is no space to add lines after the witnesses have signed, and the standard closing formula *ha-kol sharir ve-kayam* signals that nothing follows. But in a *mekushar*, the witnesses are on side B up at the top of the document, associated with the folded section. The *pashut she-bi-mekushar* — the flat lower portion on side A — has no witnesses beneath it. This leaves the entire lower portion of the document open for fraudulent additions. A dishonest party could write additional obligations there — "and Reuven also owes Shimon one thousand dinars" — and the witnesses, being on side B above, would appear to attest to the entire document including the added text. The *Gemara* states the problem succinctly: *ve-neichosh dilma zayif ve-chasav mai de-ba'ei ve-chasmi sahadei* — let us be concerned that one might forge and write whatever one wishes, with the witnesses still appearing to corroborate it.

### Sharir V'kayam

The *Gemara*'s first answer is: *de-chasvi sharir ve-kayam* — they would write *sharir ve-kayam* at the end of the document. The formula *sharir ve-kayam*, meaning "this is established and confirmed," functions as a definitive termination marker. Anything appearing after it is automatically invalid. Writing this formula at the end of the *pashut she-bi-mekushar* would thus prevent any fraudulent additions from carrying legal weight.

### Two Sharir Problem

The *Gemara* immediately presses further: what if the forger writes the additional content and then simply adds a second *sharir ve-kayam* after it? The answer is straightforward: *chad sharir ve-kayam kasvinan, terei sharir ve-kayam lo kasvinan* — a document contains one *sharir ve-kayam*, never two. If a document bears two such formulas, the second is immediately suspect and renders the addition invalid. The presence of a second *sharir ve-kayam* is itself a red flag that something was improperly added.

### Erasure Risk

The *Gemara* escalates the challenge further: *ve-neichosh dilma makhakei lei le-sharir ve-kayam* — what if the forger simply erases the *sharir ve-kayam*, writes in the fraudulent addition, and then writes a new *sharir ve-kayam*? Now the document has only one *sharir ve-kayam* and appears entirely normal. Why should we not be concerned about this?

This question requires the *Gemara* to address the broader question of when we are concerned about document forgery through erasure. In general, an altered document can still be authenticated through a *kiyum* — a ratification written at the bottom of the document, before *sharir ve-kayam*, in which the scribes or witnesses note the correction explicitly: e.g., "in line three we inserted a *zayin*," and the witnesses sign beneath it. When they do so, the witnesses are attesting that the correction was made before they signed, not after. If a letter appears to be *taluy* — suspended or written above the line as a correction — this is acceptable if it is *mekuyam*, i.e., if the correction is explicitly noted and attested at the bottom before the signatures. Such a correction does not render the document invalid.

### Erasure Rules

Rabbi Yochanan establishes the governing rule: *tluyah me-kuyemet kesheirah, machuk pasul* — a suspended or floating correction that has been properly ratified is valid; an erasure (*machak*) is invalid. Critically, this applies even if the erasure is accompanied by a *kiyum* — *ve-af al pi she-mekuyam*. Why? Because the erasure might have been made precisely at the location where *sharir ve-kayam* had originally appeared, meaning the forger erased the closing formula, inserted fraudulent content, and then added a new closing. One can never be confident that an erasure in the relevant location did not erase the *sharir ve-kayam* itself.

The *Gemara* qualifies this rule: *ve-lo amru machak pasul ela bi-makom sharir ve-kayam* — erasure invalidates a document only when it occurs at the location in the document where one would expect *sharir ve-kayam* to appear, *u-ke-shiur sharir ve-kayam* — and when the erasure is of sufficient size to have accommodated that formula. Outside of that context and scale, erasures may still be ratified through a *kiyum*. Within that context, however, no *kiyum* can rehabilitate an erasure, precisely because the possibility of having erased the *sharir ve-kayam* itself can never be ruled out.

In the case of the *mekushar*, where there is extensive blank space at the bottom of side A below the main text, any erasure near the end of the document falls squarely within the problematic zone. There is no surrounding text that could limit the scope of the concern, and the entire area could have accommodated a *sharir ve-kayam* that was then erased and replaced.

### Conclusion

The *Gemara*'s conclusion is that the combination of two measures provides the anti-forgery protection that the *mekushar* requires in place of the conventional witness placement at the bottom. First, *sharir ve-kayam* is written at the end of the text on side A, marking definitively where the document concludes. Second, the rule that no document may contain two *sharir ve-kayam* formulas means that any addition after the first is immediately invalid. And the rule on erasures — that an erasure in the *sharir ve-kayam* zone cannot be rehabilitated even with a *kiyum* — means that erasing and rewriting the closing formula would itself render the document invalid. Together with the witnesses signed on the folds of side B, these measures constitute the structural integrity of the *mekushar* document. The question of how Rabbi Yirmeya's alternative placement — witnesses on the flat portion of side B rather than on the folds — handles the forgery concern will be taken up in the next session.

# Bava Batra 161

## Get Mekushar Intro

### Get Forms Review

The final *perek* of Bava Batra opens with a discussion of two fundamental forms of legal documents: the *get pashut*, a standard flat *shtar*, and the *get mekushar*, a document that is folded and knotted. The *gemara* explains that the *get mekushar* was originally enacted for *Kohanim*, who were prone to divorcing their wives in a sudden burst of anger and then regretting it — since once a *Kohen* divorces his wife, he cannot remarry her. The elaborate knotting process was designed to slow them down and give them time to reconsider. Over time, this form was extended as an option for writing general *shtarot*, though the precise reason anyone would prefer this more cumbersome format is not entirely clear — perhaps it lent greater weight or formality to the document.

### Tosafot: Mekushar Today

Having established the rationale for the *get mekushar*, Tosafot on 160b raises an obvious and pointed question: if this form was enacted specifically to protect *Kohanim* from hasty divorces, why is it no longer practiced today? No one in living memory has heard of a *Kohen* being required to use a knotted *get* when divorcing his wife.

### Tosafot Explanations

Tosafot offers three distinct answers. The first is that in principle the requirement remains in force, but since we are no longer sufficiently expert in how the *get mekushar* was written and executed — *mispaklan bizman hazeh* — it is better to use the standard *get pashut* that we know how to perform correctly than to attempt the knotted form and risk invalidating it.

The second answer is that perhaps the requirement was never universally binding; it may have applied only in that particular locale where *Kohanim* were especially prone to rash behavior, and was only an option elsewhere.

The third answer, attributed to *v'ri*, is the most conceptually interesting: *tiknu Rabbanan mekushar lo shehovah la'asot* — the Rabbis never actually required the *mekushar* form even in its original context. Rather, they created it as a legitimate form of *get* so that *Kohanim* who recognized their own impulsiveness could voluntarily opt into a process that would slow them down. It was a tool of self-restraint, not a compulsion. Once the form existed as an option, a *Kohen* who knew his own weaknesses — or a *sofer* advising him — could choose it for precisely that purpose.

## Signatures on Mekushar

### Rav Huna: Bein Kesher

The *gemara* turns to the technical question of where the witnesses' signatures are placed on a *get mekushar*. To understand the discussion, one must picture the physical structure of the document. The text is written across a parchment, which is then folded over and knotted repeatedly, producing a fan-like layered document. It should be noted that the Rashbam holds that the portion which gets folded over remains blank, while Tosafot maintains that writing appears on both the upper and lower portions before folding.

Rav Huna's position is that the signatures are placed *bein kesher l'kesher* — in the white space on the back of the document, between one knot and the next. According to this arrangement, the witnesses sign on the reverse side, each signature appearing in the exposed strip between consecutive knots.

### Adding After Signatures

This immediately raises a concern: if the signatures appear on the back of the document, what prevents someone from turning to the front side and adding text below the original content after the document has already been signed? In a standard *get pashut*, the signatures appear directly beneath the text, leaving no room for subsequent additions. But here, since the signatures are on the reverse, the front of the document could in principle be extended.

### Hakol Sharir V'Kayam

The *gemara* answers that the phrase *hakol sharir v'kayam* — "all is confirmed and established" — serves precisely this function. This closing formula signals the definitive end of the document; nothing may be added beyond it. The *gemara* then considers a further challenge: what if someone erases *hakol sharir v'kayam*, adds fraudulent content, and rewrites the formula? To this the *gemara* responds that erasures near the end of a document are themselves inadmissible — any erasure in that region would be treated with suspicion. The combination of *hakol sharir v'kayam* and the rule against accepted erasures after that point effectively closes the document against tampering.

## K'Neged HaKtav Method

### Rebbi Yirmiya bar Abba

The *gemara* presents an alternative view: that of Rebbi Yirmiya bar Abba, who holds that the signatures on a *get mekushar* run *achorei haktav u'k'neged haktav mibachutz* — on the outside of the document, parallel to the writing on the inner side. On this approach, the signatures on side B are aligned horizontally with the corresponding lines of text on side A, so that the endpoint of the signatures naturally corresponds to the endpoint of the writing.

### Forging Signatures Risk

Under this method, the concern about adding text after the fact is largely resolved, since the signatures already run parallel to — and thus visually "cap off" — the full extent of the writing. However, a different concern arises: *leichosh dilma kativ miguai mai d'ba'ei u'machtim sahadei yiteiri milvar* — perhaps one could write additional content on the inside and then obtain extra signatures on the outside, making it appear as though those signatures were part of the original document. The fraudster might then claim, *ana l'ravcha b'eidim hu d'avdi* — "I simply wanted the extra security of additional witnesses."

### Tosafot: Three Witnesses

Tosafot addresses this concern directly. The *halacha* is that for a *shtar mekushar* requiring three signatures, one need only validate (*lekayem*) three of them — not all of them. This means that if a forger adds extra lines of text and procures additional signatures alongside them, he gains nothing, because the court will simply validate the original three genuine signatures and disregard the rest. The forged extra signatures, lacking validation, will not strengthen the fraudulent additions. This asymmetry between genuine and forged signatures effectively neutralizes the scheme.

## Witness Signature Direct…

### Bottom-Up Signing

The *gemara* continues by introducing another protective mechanism: *eidim milmata l'mala chatmi* — the witnesses sign from the bottom upward. Based on the *Yerushalmi*, as understood by Tosafot and the Rashbam, this means the witnesses sign *lengthwise* — that is, each witness writes his name vertically along the side of the document rather than horizontally across it. If signatures run lengthwise in this fashion, there is no way to append an additional line of text below them, since any addition would have to cut across the vertical signature lines and would be immediately apparent.

Rabbeinu Gershom understands the phrase differently — that witnesses begin signing from the bottom line rather than the top — but this interpretation is difficult to sustain, since it would still leave the possibility of adding one more line below the last signature. The more convincing reading is the lengthwise interpretation, which physically forecloses any subsequent addition.

### Horizontal Name Integrity

The *gemara* raises a related concern: *leichosh dilma misramia reiusa b'shita achrona* — perhaps a damaging clause appears in the last line of the document. The interested party might then simply cut off that last line. If the witnesses have signed lengthwise, cutting away a line from the bottom of the text might also sever part of a signature — say, removing the word *Reuven ben*, leaving only *Yaakov eid*. Since *ben ish ploni eid* is a valid signature according to the *Mishna*, this truncated signature might still be accepted, and the fraudulent cut would go undetected.

The *gemara*'s response is that *Reuven ben* is written together in one column and *Yaakov eid* in the adjacent column, so that cutting away *Reuven ben* necessarily leaves the signature beginning with *Yaakov eid* — but the court would recognize that this is not Yaakov's signature at all; it is Reuven's handwriting. The *kiyum shtarot* process, which validates signatures by comparing them to known exemplars, would reveal the discrepancy.

The *gemara* pushes further: perhaps the witness himself signs using his father's name as a kind of symbol or family crest? After all, the *gemara* records that Rav would draw a fish as his signature, Rabbi Chanina would draw a palm tree, Rav Chisda would write the letter *samech*, Rav Hoshaiah an *ayin*, and Rabba bar Rav Huna a ship's mast. If rabbis could sign with such symbolic marks, perhaps a witness might use his father's name as his symbol? The *gemara* dismisses this: *lo khatzif inish v'shavi l'shmei d'avuh simana* — a person does not have the audacity to adopt his father's name as his own signature symbol. The social and familial inhibition is a sufficient safeguard.

### Mar Zutra: Justification

Having worked through a series of increasingly technical answers, Mar Zutra cuts through all of them with an elegant and straightforward solution: *mekushar she'ein yadav kalin b'shita achat pasul* — a *mekushar* document in which the signatures do not all conclude on the same line is invalid.

What this means, according to the Rashbam and Rabbeinu Gershom, is that all signatures must be fully justified — spread out so that each one begins and ends at precisely the same left and right margins. When names of different lengths are fully justified in this way, the spacing within each name will differ. Any fraudulent cut would therefore have to pass cleanly through all the signatures simultaneously, but since the internal letter spacing varies from name to name, a cut that aligns perfectly with one name will necessarily pass through the middle of letters in another. The irregularity makes the tampering immediately visible. This answer is so clean and obvious that one wonders why the *gemara* did not begin with it.

The sustained concern threading through this entire discussion is a single underlying problem: how does one prevent alterations to a document after it has been duly signed? The *gemara* has addressed this from multiple angles — the role of *hakol sharir v'kayam* in marking the document's terminus, the illegitimacy of erasures near the end, the physical arrangement of signatures, and the structural requirement that signatures be fully justified.

## Corrections & Erasures

### Listing Corrections

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol hamichakim kulam tzarich sheyichtov v'den kiyumeihon* — all erasures in a document must be enumerated and confirmed at the document's end. The question of whether the phrase *v'den kiyumeihon* — "and these are their validations" — must appear explicitly as a heading, or whether one need only list the corrections without that introductory phrase, is disputed. The version without *v'den kiyumeihon* is the practice endorsed by both Tosafot and the Rashbam: rather than a formal heading, one writes the substance of the corrections directly, noting in which line a *machak* occurred, whether a word was suspended (*tluya*), and so forth. This list appears before *hakol sharir v'kayam*, which then closes the document entirely.

Since no erasures are permitted after *hakol sharir v'kayam* has been written, and since that phrase itself signals the absolute terminus of the document, the listing of corrections before it carries full legal force and cannot be tampered with thereafter.

### Last Line Summary

The second requirement established by Rabbi Yochanan is *v'tzarich she'yachzor me'inyano shel shtar b'shita achrona* — the last line of the document must contain a recapitulation of the document's main substance. This does not mean rewriting the entire *shtar* in miniature. According to the Rashbam, the operative formula is something like *v'kanina min* so-and-so *al kol ma d'chtiv u'meforash le'eil u'mana de'kashrana le'makanya bei* — "we acquired from him regarding everything written and specified above, with an instrument fit for acquisition." This refers back to the whole of the *shtar* without restating it in full.

The rationale for this requirement becomes clear when one considers that witnesses, when signing, will inevitably leave some white space between the end of the text and their signatures. That gap creates an opportunity for fraud — a bad actor could insert an additional clause in that space. The solution is to fill the last substantive line with a formulaic summary that (a) leaves no ambiguity about where the document's content ends, and (b) is sufficiently standardized that any deviation from the expected boilerplate would be immediately apparent.

## Ein Lamedim Rule

### No Learning from Last

This requirement leads directly to the principle articulated by Rav Amram: *lefi she'ein lamedim mishita achrona* — no legally operative content may be derived from the last line of a document. The last line exists solely to close and summarize; it is structurally boilerplate. If someone manages to insert a substantive clause there — whether fraudulently or inadvertently — it carries no legal weight.

There is a dispute among the *rishonim* about how to understand this rule. The Rashbam holds that it is purely advisory: it instructs the drafter not to place anything of legal consequence in the last line, since the court will disregard it regardless. On this reading, the rule is about drafting practice — a warning, not a formal prohibition. Tosafot, drawing on other *Gemarot*, understands the requirement more stringently, suggesting that there is an affirmative obligation to include a substantive summary in that final line — and that the *ein lamedim* rule is then the logical corollary, since that line is inherently suspect as a potential site of tampering. The practical upshot is the same: the last line before the signatures must be standardized summary language, and nothing written there can serve as a source for independent legal inference.

### White Space Rule

Rav Nachman challenges Rav Amram: what is the source for this principle? Rav Amram replies from a *baraita*: *hirchik et ha'edim shnei shitin min hakatav pasul; shita achat kasher* — if the witnesses sign leaving two empty lines of white space between the text and their signatures, the document is invalid; one line of space is acceptable. The reason two lines is invalid is transparent: *dilma mezayef v'chatav* — the fraudster has room to insert an additional line of content in that space. But why is one line also not disqualifying, since one could theoretically insert something there as well? The *gemara* answers: *ela lav shema mina ein lamedim mishita achrona* — this must be because we rule that nothing written in that last line is legally operative. A forger gains nothing by inserting a clause there if the court will refuse to derive any ruling from it. The rule about white space and the principle of *ein lamedim mishita achrona* thus prove and reinforce each other.

## Modern Practice Explained

### Tosafot Observation

A substantial Tosafot at the end of the *sugya* confronts what is, on the face of it, a glaring discrepancy between the *gemara*'s framework and contemporary practice. The *gemara* operated in a world where *hakol sharir v'kayam* was not a standard feature of all documents — indeed, from the earlier discussion about the *mekushar*, one infers that it was the exception. Precisely because most *shtarot* lacked that closing formula, the entire architecture of the *sugya* — the prohibition on white space, the requirement that the last line be boilerplate, the rule of *ein lamedim mishita achrona* — was necessary to protect document integrity.

### Hakol Sharir Solves It

Tosafot observes: *b'yameihem lo haya katuv sharir v'kayam* — in their time, *sharir v'kayam* was not written in *peshutim*. It was precisely this absence that made all the protective measures necessary. But today, *sharir v'kayam* has become not merely conventional but obligatory — a *shtar* lacking it would be *pasul*. Once that phrase is universally required and its absence invalidates the document, all the concerns driving the *gemara*'s rulings dissolve. *Hakol sharir v'kayam* definitively seals the document; nothing written after it carries any force, and no erasure after that point is accepted. The fraudster has no opening.

### Corrections Before Final

This resolution also explains our practice regarding the placement of *kiyum machakim*. The *gemara* as analyzed by Tosafot would seem to require that corrections be validated before the summarizing last line — *kodem shita achrona* — so that nothing substantive appears after that boilerplate. Yet contemporary scribal practice places the *kiyum machakim* after the *v'kanina* formula, making the validation of corrections the last substantive element before the signatures, not something preceding the summary line.

Tosafot frames this as a genuine difficulty: *v'yeish litmoha — eich hurgalnu lichtov kiyum machakim achar v'kanina minei* — how have we become accustomed to writing the validation of corrections after the *v'kanina* formula? There is nothing more substantive than confirming erasures, and yet we place it precisely where the *gemara* says nothing of substance should appear. Tosafot's answer is that this concern evaporates entirely once *hakol sharir v'kayam* is universally mandated. Since the phrase is now required in every *shtar*, and since its presence absolutely bars any subsequent addition, the entire rationale for *ein lamedim mishita achrona* no longer applies. We can and do learn from the last line; we can place substantive content — including *kiyum machakim* — there, because *hakol sharir v'kayam* following it ensures the document is airtight. The *gemara*'s protective architecture was built for a world without that formula; in a world where it is obligatory, the rules governing the last line shift accordingly.
