# Bava Batra 162

## Two Blank Lines

### Blank Lines Rule

The *daf* opens on 162b with the established principle that a *shtar* is invalidated when two blank lines appear between the body of the document and the signatures of the witnesses. The concern is straightforward: people naturally leave some space when they sign, writing, say, *Yaakov ben Yitzchak*, *eid*, a bit below the last line of text. That gap creates an opportunity for a forger to insert an additional line of content. The first principle invoked is *ayn lamedin mishitah achronah* — we do not derive the terms of the document from the last line — meaning that even if a forged line were inserted just above the witnesses, it could be argued that we would simply disregard that last line. But if there are two blank lines, a forger could insert two lines of text, and we would then learn from the *second*-to-last line, which would not be covered by that principle. Hence the document becomes *pasul*.

### Ayn Lamedin

The principle of *ayn lamedin mishitah achronah* is thus the background assumption against which the entire discussion of blank lines must be understood. It protects against a single line of forgery, but it cannot protect against two, since we would then be forced to reckon with what appears above the last line.

### Line and Half

The *Gemara* raises the intermediate case: what about a space of a line and a half? The question is whether that much space is sufficient to enable a damaging forgery. If it is, the *shtar* should be *pasul*; if not, it should remain *kasher*.

### Tosafot Interpretation

*Tosafot* entertains a possible reading in which "a line and a half" refers to the height — that is, 1.5 times the normal line height. *Tosafot* initially considers whether this might mean that the *eidim* signed at a certain point, leaving a space of roughly one and a half lines in which something could be inserted. *Tosafot* then rejects this, noting that in such a case we would simply presume that neither the line above the *eidim* nor the line alongside them would be learned from. The more straightforward reading of "a line and a half" is that it refers to the vertical height of a line-and-a-half's worth of space — the question being whether a forger can squeeze two small lines into that height, or whether any attempt to do so would be obvious.

### Braita Evidence

The *Gemara* brings a *braitah* to resolve the matter: *hirchik et haeidim shtei shitim min haksav pasul* — if the witnesses are placed two lines away from the text, the *shtar* is *pasul*. Critically, the *braitah* does not introduce an intermediate figure; it simply states *pachot mikan*, anything less than two lines. This is far cleaner than the earlier formulation, which introduced the ambiguous case of a line and a half.

### Conclusion

The conclusion is therefore that anything less than two lines of distance is *kasher*, because any attempt to squeeze two lines into a smaller space would be detectable — it would be obvious that lines were inserted after the fact. Two full lines, by contrast, provide enough room for a natural-looking insertion, and the document is therefore *pasul*.

---

## Multiple Witnesses

### Multiple Witnesses Case

The *Gemara* next presents a distinct but related *halachah*: if four or five witnesses signed a *shtar* and one of them is found to be either a *karov* (a relative of one of the parties) or otherwise *pasul*, the testimony of the remaining valid witnesses stands — *titkayem eidut bashear*. This ruling is introduced here in close connection with the preceding discussion of blank lines, and *Tosafot* argues that it reads most naturally as a continuation of that discussion rather than a fully independent statement.

### Chizkiyah Ruling

The connection to the blank lines discussion becomes clear through the statement attributed to *Chizkiyah*: *miluo bikrovim kasher* — if one filled the white space in a *shtar* with *krovim*, the document is *kasher*. The principle is that when the document has been placed too far from the signatures, the problematic white space can be filled in with additional signatories, even if those signatories are *pasul*, and the *shtar* remains valid.

### Sukkah Analogy

The *Gemara* supports this with an analogy to *sukkah*: *avir sukkah pasul bisheloshah, schach pasul posel b'arba'ah* — a gap of air in the *sechach* of a *sukkah* invalidates it at three *tefachim*, whereas invalid *sechach* only creates a problem at four *tefachim*. The initial reaction to *Chizkiyah*'s ruling is naturally one of surprise: how can filling a *pasul* space with something itself *pasul* make the *shtar* more *kasher*? The *sukkah* analogy is invoked to show that such a result is not without precedent.

### Sukkah Details

To appreciate the analogy, consider a *sukkah* with only three walls, viewed from above. If there is a gap of three *tefachim* of air in the *sechach*, the *sechach* is no longer considered continuous. The *sukkah* effectively splits into two halves, each of which has only two walls — rendering both halves *pasul*. However, if instead of air there is *pasul sechach* — say, metal bars that cannot serve as valid *sechach* — the covering is still physically present and continuous. A gap of invalid material does not rupture the continuity the way air does. Therefore, up to four *tefachim* of *pasul sechach*, the *sukkah* remains *kasher*, because it is still treated as a single continuous entity. Only at four *tefachim* does the invalid material constitute its own independent section, effectively dividing the *sukkah* into three parts and rendering the whole *pasul*. Three *tefachim* is *kasher*; four *tefachim* is *pasul*.

### Logic Comparison

It must be said clearly: the logic in the two cases is entirely different, and the *Gemara* itself signals this with the words *v'al titamah* — do not be astounded. There is no genuine derivation from *sukkah* to *shtar*; it is purely an analogy meant to prevent surprise. In the *sukkah*, invalid material preserves continuity in a way that air does not — the physical presence of something, even something *pasul*, prevents a rupture. In the *shtar*, the operative concern is forgery. White space is dangerous because a forger can fill it with fabricated lines. Invalid signatories — *pasul eidim* — fill that white space physically and thereby remove the opportunity for forgery, even though what fills it is itself *pasul*. The logics are distinct: one is about structural continuity, the other is about eliminating the possibility of fraudulent insertion. *Tosafot* adds a further dimension by framing the *sukkah* comparison as a lesson against enacting a *gezeirah*: just as we do not prohibit three *tefachim* of invalid *sechach* out of concern that it will lead to permitting three *tefachim* of air, so too we do not prohibit *pasul eidim* filling the white space out of concern that it will lead to permitting blank space itself. But this *Tosafot* reading may not represent the core of *Chizkiyah*'s point.

### Ravad Tefillin

A fascinating *teshuvah* of the *Ravad* applies this same logic to *tefillin*. If the scrolls inside the *tefillin* contain a word that appears twice — for instance, a line ending with *l'vanecha* and the following line beginning again with *l'vanecha v'dibarta bam* — the *Ravad* rules that they are not *pasul*, and invokes precisely the same principle: *v'al titma*, do not be astounded. If blank space would have been *kasher*, then filling that space with a repeated word is also *kasher*. The logic is a striking extension of *Chizkiyah*'s ruling into the realm of *sifrei Torah* and *tefillin*.

### Tosafot Witnesses

Returning to the *shtar*, *Tosafot* raises the obvious difficulty: normally the rule is *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* — if one witness in a group is found to be a *karov* or *pasul*, all of the testimony is invalidated. Why does that rule not apply here to invalidate the remaining valid witnesses? *Tosafot* explains by focusing on the formal act that constitutes testimony. When witnesses appear before a *beit din* to testify, they undergo a process of formal acceptance — they declare their intent to testify, and the court receives them. At that moment they constitute a defined group, and if one member of that group is *pasul*, the entire group's testimony falls. The operative factor is that they all declared themselves witnesses together in that formal context.

### Invalid Permitted

With a *shtar*, however, there is no *beit din* formally accepting anyone's testimony at the moment of signing. There is only a person, a pen, and a document. In that context, it is possible to argue — and indeed the *halachah* does argue — that the *pasul* signer was not acting *lesheim eidus* at all.

### Intent Context

The question of intent is central here. The *Gemara* itself records, and the *Rema* confirms that this was actual practice, that additional people would sign a *shtar* or *ketubah* not as formal witnesses but as a form of *kavod* — honor. At a wedding, for example, people sign the *ketubah* to participate in and honor the *choson v'kallah*. If that is the context in which someone signs, they are not constituting themselves as *eidim* in the formal sense, and therefore the disqualifying logic of *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* never applies to them in the first place.

The argument becomes more subtle when one considers that signing a *shtar* is, on its face, an act of testimony — indeed, the *halachah* treats signatures on a *shtar* as equivalent to testimony received by a *beit din* (*k'mi shenichkra edutam b'veit din*). But there is a certain circularity here: a signature attains the status of formal testimony precisely because it is recognized as valid participation in the *shtar*. If the signer is *pasul*, the signature can never be so recognized, and therefore it never acquires the status of testimony in the first place. It is automatically excluded before the logic of group invalidation can even engage. One might test this in a hypothetical: what if the *pasul* witness signed fully intending to testify, unaware of his disqualifying status? Even then, it may be that the structure of *shtar* law is such that a *pasul* signature is by definition excluded from the document, and no subjective intent can change that.

### Witness Position

*Tosafot* raises a further question about the physical placement of the *pasul eidim* on the document. If we are to set aside the invalid signatures, which ones do we set aside? Consider a document in which the *kasher* witnesses signed above and the *pasul* witnesses signed below — or vice versa. Intuitively, one might think that the signatures closest to the body of the document are the more significant ones, as they directly address the question of whether the white space between the text and the signatures is impermissibly large. Those below, farther from the text, might seem more like afterthoughts. On the other hand, one could argue the opposite: the signatures below are closer to the *beit din*'s *kiyum hashtar*, which is appended at the bottom, and are thus more connected to the validation apparatus.

From the *sukkah* analogy, it would seem that the signatures filling the white space closer to the document are the ones doing the critical work of preventing forgery. Even if those are *pasul*, they are *kasher* by *Chizkiyah*'s ruling, since without them the *shtar* would have been *pasul* due to the white space. And if even those are acceptable, then certainly the *pasul* ones at the bottom, which are not filling the critical zone, would be acceptable.

### Karov Pasul

*Tosafot* then notes a further discrepancy in the sources: the *braitah* uses the phrase *nimtza karov o pasul* — a relative or an otherwise invalid witness — while *Chizkiyah*'s formulation mentions only *krovim*. Is there a meaningful distinction? A *karov* is someone who is disqualified only in relation to a specific case — in a different *shtar*, he would be a fully valid witness. A *pasul* in the broader sense — a *gazlan*, for instance — is disqualified in every context. *Tosafot* is uncertain whether *Chizkiyah* intends *krovim* precisely, or whether his ruling extends equally to any *pasul* signer. The majority position in *Tosafot* seems to be that the ruling extends to *pasul* witnesses as well, but the question is left without a definitive resolution.

---

## Women Ketubah

### Rama Practice

The *Rema* in *Hilchos Kesubot* records that the actual practice was for multiple relatives and others to sign the *ketubah* after the valid *eidim* had signed, specifically as a form of *kibbud* for the *choson v'kallah*. This practice was grounded in the principle that *miluhu bikrovim kasher* — filling the space with *krovim* is valid — and in the understanding that such additional signatories were signing for *kavod*, not *lesheim eidus*.

### Women Signatories

In our contemporary context, this question has acquired a new dimension. The question arises whether women may serve as additional signatories on a *ketubah* after the two valid male witnesses have signed. This is often asked by people who are unaware of the *Rema*'s ruling or the underlying *sugyah*, but who are, in effect, asking whether the traditional practice of adding *kavod* signatories can be extended to women.

### Woman Status

The question of a woman's status in this context is genuinely complex. One might argue that since a woman cannot serve as a valid *eid*, she is *pasul* in every context — even more so than a *gazlan*, who at least belongs to the category of potential witnesses and could theoretically become *kasher* through *teshuvah*. On this view, a woman is more disqualified than a *pasul*, and one might hesitate to include her even under *Chizkiyah*'s ruling.

However, the majority of *poskim* reason differently. A *pasul eid* is someone who is within the category of witnesses but currently disqualified. A woman, in traditional *halachic* analysis, is not a *pasul eid* — she is simply outside the category of *edim* entirely. She is not a disqualified witness; she is a non-witness. This distinction may actually make her signature *less* problematic for the *shtar*, not more: since she is not an *eid* at all, she cannot be *nimtza pasul*, and the rule of *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* does not engage with her signature in any way.

### Honor Line

In light of this analysis, a practical recommendation emerges for those who wish to have women sign the *ketubah* in addition to the valid witnesses. After the two *kasher eidim* have signed with the word *eid*, a separate line should be added in which the additional signatories — including women — sign beneath a phrase such as *v'gam anu chatamnu mata likvod hachoson v'hakallah*, "and we too have signed below in honor of the *choson v'kallah*." Critically, the word *eid* should not appear after their names. This achieves two things simultaneously: it replicates the historical *kavod* practice attested by the *Rema*, and it makes explicit that these signatures are not intended as *eidus* — thereby resolving *Tosafot*'s concern about whether the context of signing can be assumed to be *lesheim kavod* rather than *lesheim eidus*. In a society where this practice is not broadly familiar, it is harder to presume that context without explicit statement; making it explicit removes the ambiguity entirely.

---

## Two Lines Measurement

### With/Without Space

After the preceding discussions, the *Gemara* returns to the technical measurement of what constitutes "two lines" of space, and poses a careful question: *shnei shitin she'amru hen v'aviram o dilma hen v'lo aviram* — when the *halachah* says that two lines of distance renders the *shtar pasul*, does that measure include the normal intervening space between lines, or does it refer only to the height of the text itself, without that space?

To understand the stakes of this question, consider how a line of text actually occupies space on a page. If the text is written in a twelve-point font, say, each line has a certain height, but there is also a standard inter-line gap above and below it. When we say two lines of blank space invalidate the document, does that mean two text-heights plus the normal gaps — i.e., the full visual impression of two lines of writing — or only two text-heights with no additional space?

The practical difference is significant. If two full "natural" lines including their spacing constitute the danger zone, then anything that appears less than two naturally spaced lines is *kasher*. If the measure excludes the spacing, then the *pasul* threshold is reached more quickly. The concern in either case is that a forger will exploit the space to insert two new lines that appear to have always been there.

### Nachman Ruling

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* resolves the question: *nistavera d'hen v'aviram* — it stands to reason that the measure is the lines with their intervening space. His reasoning is elegant: if we were to say the measure excludes the spacing, then a single line of text without any following space would itself be a meaningful measure — but a line without any spacing after it is not a natural or functional unit of writing. The measure must therefore reflect actual writing practice, meaning the full height of a line as it would normally appear, including its spacing.

### Scribe Script

A further refinement is introduced by *Rav Chisda* in the name of *Chizkiyah*: *shnei shitin she'amru biksav yad eidim v'lo biksav yad sofer* — the two-line measure that renders a *shtar pasul* applies specifically to the handwriting size of non-professional witnesses, not to the smaller, more controlled handwriting of a professional *sofer*. The distinction is rooted in the different scales of writing. A trained *sofer* writes with precision and uniformity, producing smaller, tighter letters. An ordinary person writing in script produces larger, less uniform lettering.

### Forgery Risk

The entire concern about blank lines is that a forger will insert additional text after the witnesses have signed. For such an insertion to be dangerous, it must be capable of appearing natural — indistinguishable from the original. *Rav Chisda* reasons that the only person who could plausibly forge in a *sofer*'s handwriting is another *sofer*, and a *sofer* would not agree to participate in a forgery. Therefore, two lines of *sofer* script in a blank space do not create the same risk as two lines of ordinary script. The blank space is only *pasul* when it could plausibly accommodate the insertion of ordinary-sized lines.

One might object that even if the blank space contains ordinary script different from the *sofer*'s hand, that difference itself would signal a forgery. The response is that this is not necessarily so: it is perfectly plausible that an amendment or additional clause was written in by hand before the witnesses signed, without the *sofer* having written it. The discrepancy in handwriting styles does not, by itself, prove forgery.

### Lach Lach

*Rav Yitzchak ben Elazar* further refines the measurement with a concrete example: *k'gon lach lach zeh al gabi zeh* — imagine the word *lach* written one on top of the other. The word *lach* is written with a *lamed* and a *chof*. The *lamed* has an ascending stroke that rises above the normal line height, demanding an extra airspace above the line. The *chof* has a descending stroke that falls below the normal baseline, demanding an extra airspace below. When two such words are stacked, the visual footprint is therefore: the body of the first line, an airspace below for its *chof*, an airspace above for the *lamed* of the second line, and the body of the second line. This gives a total of two lines plus four airspaces — *shnei shitim v'arba'ah avirim* — as the full measure of what a forger would need to insert two lines of text that appear completely natural.

### Two Lines Four Air

To visualize this: the blank space above the witnesses, measured from the last line of the document's text, must span the full height of two naturally written lines — each with their ascenders and descenders accounted for. That amounts to two line-bodies and four airspaces. Anything less than this total height is considered *kasher*, because a forger could not squeeze in two full natural lines without it being apparent that they were added after the fact.

### Lamed Chof

*Rabbi Chiya bar Ammi* in the name of *Ulla* offers a slightly different account: one need only allow for the *lamed* above and the *chof* below, with a single normal space between the two lines — *shnei shitin v'shalosh avirim*, two lines and three airspaces. The point is that a skilled writer could avoid having both the descender of the upper line and the ascender of the lower line occupy space simultaneously; one can simply position the letters so they do not interfere with each other. The minimum natural arrangement requires only three airspaces rather than four.

### Single Line Two Air

*Abba* goes further still: *k'gon Baruch ben Levi b'shita achas* — take the name *Baruch ben Levi* written in a single line. *Baruch* contains a *chof* with a descender, and *Levi* contains a *lamed* with an ascender. Even within a single line, these letters demand airspace above and below. *Abba* therefore says: *shita achas u'shnei avirim* — only one line and two airspaces. This is a striking position, apparently arguing that even the threshold of two lines set earlier is not absolute — perhaps only a single line with the appropriate airspaces constitutes the danger zone. *Tosafot* notes that this seems to be a direct disagreement with the prior ruling.

### Before Hashrat

*Rav* adds a final qualification: *lo shanu ella bein eidim l'chsav* — the distance rule applies only to the space between the witnesses' signatures and the body of the *shtar*. However, *bein eidim l'ashrasa afilu tuvnami kasher* — between the witnesses and the *hashrat*, the court's validation of the document, even a large space is *kasher*. This distinction opens the discussion that occupies the final section of the *daf*.

---

## Witnesses Hashrat

### Space Permitted

The ruling of *Rav* — that a large space between the witnesses and the *kiyum hashtar* (the court's validation) is *kasher* — invites immediate scrutiny. The *kiyum hashtar* is appended by the *beit din* at the bottom of the *shtar* to certify that the witnesses' signatures are genuine. Why should white space in that location not create the same forgery concern as white space between the witnesses and the body of the document?

### Forgery Between

The *Gemara* itself voices this objection: *mai shena bein eidim l'chsav? dilma mezayef v'chasav mai d'ba'ei* — what is different about the space between the witnesses and the text? The concern is that a forger will write something in that space, and the witnesses' signatures below will appear to validate it. But, the *Gemara* continues, *bein eidim l'ashrasa nami* — should the same not be true between the witnesses and the *kiyum*? If there is a large blank space before the *beit din*'s certification, could a forger not insert text there and have the court's *kiyum* appear to validate it?

### Court Marks

The *Gemara* answers: *d'mitayeit lei* — what the *beit din* does is mark up or fill in the blank space between the witnesses' signatures and the *kiyum*. The court draws lines, marks, or other indications across that space, rendering it unusable. Any attempt to scrape those marks away and insert forged text would be visually apparent. With this practice in place, the blank space between the witnesses and the *kiyum* presents no forgery danger, and the *shtar* remains *kasher* even with a large gap in that location.

### Why Not Above

The *Gemara* then raises the obvious question: if such marking can solve the problem below, why not simply apply the same solution above? Mark the space between the witnesses and the body of the *shtar*, and the forgery concern is resolved there as well. If that worked, there would be no need for the strict two-line rule at all.

### Cannot Mark Above

The *Gemara* states that this solution cannot be applied above, between the witnesses' signatures and the text of the *shtar*.

### Signing Ambiguity

The reason is that if there are marks or designs in the space between the witnesses and the text, people will say — *amri, sa'adei atiyusa hu d'chasimi* — that the witnesses are signing on the design or marks, not on the *shtar* above. Once there is something other than blank space between the signatures and the document, the signatures no longer unambiguously attest to the document. They could be interpreted as attesting to whatever appears directly above them, which in this case would be the markings rather than the *shtar*'s content. This creates a fundamental ambiguity about what exactly the witnesses are validating.

### Court Clarity

Why does this problem not apply to the *kiyum hashtar* below? The *Gemara* answers: *bedina tiyuta lo chasimi* — no one would think that a *beit din* is signing its certification on a design or set of marks. It is universally understood that the *kiyum* of a *beit din* refers exclusively to the witnesses' signatures. Its referent is unambiguous: it certifies the identity and validity of the witnesses above it, nothing else. Therefore, even with marks between the witnesses and the *kiyum*, there is no confusion about what the court is validating.

The logic is admittedly not entirely symmetric, and a number of questions remain difficult to resolve. Why do we not simply mark the space between witnesses and text and then stipulate that the witnesses signed with reference to the document above? Why do we not say that the *kiyum* in any case only refers to the witnesses, and therefore even if forged content were inserted above the witnesses but below the body of the text, the *kiyum* would not be construed as validating it? The *Gemara* does not resolve these questions fully, and they remain points of difficulty in the *sugya*.

### No Blank Space

The conclusion is clear, however: no blank space is permitted between the witnesses and the body of the *shtar*. The space must contain either actual text — the continuation of the document's content — or, as *Chizkiyah* permitted, additional signatories even if they are *pasul*, since their physical presence removes the opportunity for forged insertion. What it may not contain is empty space, nor may it be solved by marks or designs, since those would undermine the unambiguous connection between the witnesses' signatures and the document above. The *kiyum* below may be separated from the witnesses by a marked space, since *beit din* practice ensures the area is filled and the court's certification unambiguously references the witnesses alone.

---

---

# Bava Batra 163

## Body-Witness Gap

### Two-line rule

The *gemara* on 163a continues its discussion of the white space between the body of a *shtar* and the signatures of the *eidim*. The central concern is straightforward: if too much blank space is left between the end of the document's text and the witnesses' signatures, a forger could insert an additional line of content — one line that would be incorporated into the *shtar* itself, followed by a second line of boilerplate — thereby altering the meaning of the document. For this reason, two full lines of gap are prohibited.

### One-line gap permitted

A single line of space, however, is permissible. The *eidim* need some room to sign; they cannot always be expected to inscribe their names immediately flush against the last line of text. Even if that one-line space were filled in, the principle that we do not derive legal force from the final line of a document means we would not act on whatever is inserted there.

### Dots prevent abuse

The *gemara* turns to the space between the witnesses' signatures and the *beit din*'s *kiyum* — its formal validation of those signatures. Why are we not afraid that someone will fill in the gap between the *eidim* and the *kiyum*, insert forged witnesses, and then exploit the *kiyum* as if it validates the inserted material? The answer is that the blank area is rendered unusable by filling it with dots and splotches, preventing that space from being written upon in any meaningful way.

## Erasure concerns

### Rav: erasure kasher

At the bottom of 163a, the *gemara* raises a deeper question. The dots and splotches prevent someone from simply writing in the blank space, but what about a more sophisticated attack: cutting away the top portion of the *shtar*, erasing the smudgy area, and then rewriting whatever one wishes? The obvious defense is that anything written on an erased background is suspect — but the *gemara* immediately complicates this by citing Rav's ruling: *shtar ha-ba hu v'eidav al ha-machak kasher* — a *shtar* in which both the body and the witnesses' signatures appear on an erased background is valid.

To appreciate why this ruling is relevant, one must understand that the *gemara* will establish later — though it is worth anticipating here — that a single erasure looks visibly different from a double erasure. With that principle in mind, consider what concerns might attach to a *shtar* written entirely on an erased background. One might worry that the document originally had different content written on a clean background, which was then erased and replaced. But if both the body and the *eidim* are on the erased background, there is nothing particularly alarming: even if the entire document was composed on a previously erased surface, the witnesses' genuine signatures are there, and the *shtar* functions normally. The forger cannot gain anything simply by using erased parchment.

### Full erasure risk

The more serious concern is this: since the background is already erased, a forger could erase the top portion a second time and rewrite it with different content, leaving the witnesses' signatures intact on their once-erased section. He would then present the document with a *kiyum* — and the *kiyum*, having been issued on the original signatures, would appear to validate his fraudulent version. This is not, however, a concern unique to the specific scenario involving smudgy space below the *kiyum*. It is a general challenge to Rav's ruling: whenever there is a *kiyum* on a *shtar*, what prevents someone from erasing the entire top, rewriting it, and reusing the *kiyum*?

The *gemara* addresses the internal tension. It notes that according to Rav Kahana, who transmits the ruling that *shtar chuv eidav al ha-machak kasher* in the name of Shmuel, there is no contradiction — because Rav himself may have held that a *shtar* with both body and witnesses on erased background is invalid. Under Rav's own view, then, such a forged *shtar* — with the rewritten top and the witnesses both on an erased background — would be disqualified, and the *kiyum* would be of no use. But according to Rav Tavyumi, who transmits this ruling in the name of Rav himself, the difficulty remains: if Rav considers such a *shtar* valid, how does he protect against the reuse of a *kiyum*?

### Validation voided

The *gemara* resolves this with a direct ruling: *kol ki hai gavna ein mekaymin oso min ha-asharta shebo ela min ha-eidim shebo* — in precisely this case, where the entire *shtar* is written on an erased background, one does not rely on the embedded *kiyum* at all. The *kiyum* is effectively voided. Instead, the witnesses must be validated directly before the court. The fear that someone erased the entire top and reused the existing *kiyum* is neutralized precisely because we will never rely on a *kiyum* when the full document appears on a *machak* background — we insist on direct testimony about the witnesses' authenticity.

## Witness-Validation Gap

### One-line doc valid

Rabbi Yochanan now introduces a set of distinctions about the permissible gap between the witnesses' signatures and the *kiyum*. He begins with a related rule: *lo shanu ela bein eidim le-chtav* — the rule permitting one line of space (and prohibiting two) applies between the body of the document and the witnesses. However, between the witnesses and the *ashrata* — the validation mark — *afilu shita achas pasul*: even a single blank line is invalid.

### Separate lines invalid

The concern with a one-line gap between the witnesses and the *kiyum* becomes clear with the *gemara*'s next question. Since Rabbi Yochanan holds that a one-line *shtar* — that is, a document whose entire content occupies a single line — with the witnesses signing on that same line is valid, even a one-line gap before the *kiyum* is dangerous. A forger could cut away the body of the document, write his own one-line *shtar*, place the *eidim* on the same line, and then exploit the *kiyum* that follows.

### Small doc concern

The *gemara* articulates this precisely: *dilma megayez lei le-ila'i ve-chasav hu ve-edav be-shita achas* — perhaps the forger will cut away the top and write a one-line document together with the witnesses all on a single line, thereby producing a valid *shtar* backed by an existing *kiyum*. Since one-line documents with witnesses on the same line are in principle valid, no gap at all may be left between the witnesses and the *kiyum*.

Tosafot raises the question of why the forger would not be exposed by the *machak* — if he cuts away and rewrites, the erased area would be visible. Tosafot answers that Rabbi Yochanan is addressing a different scenario than Rav. Rav's ruling concerns a case where the space before the *kiyum* has already been rendered smudgy, and any erasure would be detectable. Rabbi Yochanan is speaking of a case where the background is clean — no smudgy section separates the *eidim* from the *kiyum*. In that case, there is no *machak* evidence to expose the forgery, and even one clean blank line cannot be tolerated.

The Rashbam explains the underlying logic: since the Rabbis did not wish to define a minimum size for a *shtar*, a one-line document remains valid. But because a one-line *shtar* is possible, the single-line gap rule that applies between the body and the witnesses cannot be carried over to the gap between the witnesses and the *kiyum*. For the body-witness gap, we permit one line because witnesses need some space to sign. But permitting even one line between the witnesses and the *kiyum* would enable the precise fraud Rabbi Yochanan describes.

### Witness notation

The *gemara* then asks: since a one-line *shtar* with witnesses on the same line is valid, why isn't there a risk even when we allow one line between the *eidim* and the body? Could someone not cut that line off, leaving the witnesses' signatures intact, insert their own one-line document, and then present the valid witnesses alongside a *kiyum*? The *gemara* addresses this: *ve-kasavar shtar ha-ba hu ve-edav be-shita achas kasher* — yes, such a document is valid. But *shtar ha-ba hu be-shita achas ve-edav be-shita acheres pasul* — a one-line *shtar* with the witnesses signing on a *different* line is invalid.

The Rashbam explains: any full-sized *shtar* must allow one line of space for the witnesses to sign, because they cannot always be expected to crowd right up against the last line of text. Since one line must be permitted, we are in effect vulnerable to the attack of cutting off that line and using the witnesses elsewhere. Therefore, a one-line *shtar* with witnesses on a separate line is ruled invalid — exactly because this is the scenario the forger would construct. A one-line *shtar* with witnesses on the *same* line is safe, because then the *eidim* cannot be detached and reused: the forger would have to forge them himself, which exposes him in a different way.

### Extra witness risk

The *gemara* raises one further challenge. Given that a one-line *shtar* with witnesses on the same line is valid, could a forger not write his own one-line *shtar* with forged *eidim* on the same line, and then additionally present the genuine *eidim* whose signatures appear below, arguing he added extra witnesses? He would say: *ana l'rabot be-eidin hu d'avidna* — I was merely adding supplementary witnesses. He would then ask that the *kiyum* be applied to those additional witnesses, since they can be validated directly.

The *gemara* dismisses this: *katav be-che hai gavna ein mekaymin lei ela min eidim she-l'malah* — precisely because of this risk, we insist on relying only on the witnesses who appear on the same line as the one-line document, and we do not validate the supplementary witnesses below. The *kiyum* follows the witnesses on the shared line, and any witnesses appended below are disregarded.

## Erasure detection

### Visual difference

Having resolved the questions about white space, the *gemara* now turns formally to the topic introduced earlier — the principle that a single erasure looks different from a double erasure. The *gemara* states: *eino domeh nimchak pa'am achat le-nimchak shtei pe'amim* — a parchment erased once does not look the same as one erased twice. This principle is what permits Rav's ruling that a *shtar* with body and witnesses both on an erased background is valid, for if the top were re-erased and rewritten, the discrepancy would be visible.

### Double erase risk

The *gemara* challenges even this: *v'lichush dilma shadi deyuta amkom eidim me'ikara u'machik lei* — perhaps a forger will deliberately spill ink near the area where the witnesses will sign, erase it in their presence, and thereby arrange for them to sign on a background that has already been erased twice. Then when he erases the top and rewrites it, both sections will appear to have been erased twice, and no discrepancy will be visible.

### Witnesses witness erasure

Abaye resolves this by invoking a further principle attributed to Rav: *ein eidim chotmim al ha-machak ela im ken nimchak bifneihem* — witnesses may sign on an erased background only if the erasure was performed in their presence. The Rashbam explains: the witnesses will examine the full background before signing. If they observe any inconsistency — if the area where they are asked to sign looks different from the rest of the document — they will refuse to sign. Having seen the full document erased in their presence, they will know whether the background is uniform. A deliberate ink-spill and re-erasure, done immediately before signing, would produce a visible discrepancy that the witnesses themselves would notice and reject.

### Clean body valid

The *gemara* now presents a *baraita*: *hu al ha-niyar ve-adav al ha-machak kasher* — if the body of the document is on a clean, unerased background and the witnesses have signed on an erased background, the *shtar* is valid. What is there to fear? One might worry that there were previously different witnesses, whose signatures were erased and replaced with new ones — but this would be an absurd and harmful substitution from the forger's perspective, since it would only weaken rather than strengthen his document. So there is no obvious concern.

Yet the *gemara* probes further: this scenario seems to invite abuse. What prevents someone from writing a *shtar* on clean parchment, having witnesses sign on the erased bottom portion, and then immediately erasing the top and rewriting whatever he wishes? Once the top is erased, the entire *shtar* is on a *machak* background, and Rav's ruling validates it. The *gemara* responds that such a *shtar*, in the form described, requires a special notation: the witnesses write between their own signatures — *bein sahada le-sahada* — that the body of the document was written on a clean background while they signed on an erased one. This embedded notation protects the document: cutting it off would sever one witness's signature, and erasing it would produce a double erasure detectable by comparison to the once-erased section directly adjacent.

### Erased body invalid

The opposite configuration — *hu al ha-machak ve-eidav al ha-niyar pasul* — where the body is on an erased background and the witnesses sign on a clean background, is invalid. The reason is that this configuration shouts its own fraudulence: the most natural explanation for the top being erased while the bottom is clean is that the document originally had a legitimate text on a clean background, which was erased and replaced with a forgery.

### Notation solution

The *gemara* asks: why not apply the same solution here — have the witnesses insert a notation between their signatures stating that the body was on an erased background? This would explain the anomaly innocently. The *gemara* pushes back: if we allow this, we must address the concern that the top will be re-erased and rewritten — and the response, as before, is that a double erasure is visible. But then the *gemara* asks why the *pasul* ruling stands at all. Cannot the witnesses simply note between their signatures that the body was on a *machak*, and then we are protected against re-erasure by the double-erasure principle?

### Comparison needed

The *gemara* answers with a critical limitation: *hani milei heicha de-ichas sahadei a-machaka* — the double-erasure is detectable only when there is a basis of comparison within the same document. In the case where the witnesses sign on a *machak* background, the top can be compared to the bottom: if the top is re-erased, it will look different from the once-erased bottom. But where the witnesses are on clean parchment and the top alone is on a *machak*, there is no internal reference point for comparison. One cannot tell whether the top was erased once or twice when the only available comparison is clean parchment, not a once-erased section.

The *gemara* considers whether one could bring a separate scroll, erase a portion of it, and compare it to the top of the suspect document. This is rejected: *lo dami machaka de-hai megilta le-machaka de-hai megilta* — no two scrolls erase identically. The texture, age, and composition of each piece of parchment differ, so a once-erased patch on one scroll cannot serve as a reliable reference for detecting a twice-erased patch on another.

The *gemara* then asks whether one might validate the witnesses' signatures before the court, then erase those very signatures and use the resulting once-erased area on the same document as a comparison. If the top looks similar to this freshly erased area, the top was erased only once; if it looks different, the top was erased twice.

### Age of erasure

Rav Hoshaya rejects this: *ein domeh nimchak bein yomo le-nimchak bein shenei yamim* — a freshly erased area does not look the same as an area that was erased some time ago. The original erasure on the top of the document may have been performed months or years before the signatures were affixed. A fresh comparison erasure will therefore not produce a reliable match, yielding false positives and false negatives. One might propose waiting a period of time before making the comparison, allowing the fresh erasure to age to match the original — but this merely pushes the problem back, since we do not know how long ago the original erasure was made, and in any case an aged erasure on one scroll still cannot perfectly replicate the aging of another.

### Beit Din error risk

Rabbi Yirmiyah closes the discussion with a broader principle: *chiyshinan le-vei dina to'in* — once the analysis reaches this level of complexity, we are concerned that the *beit din* will err in making the required distinctions. A system of document validation that depends on comparing the visual texture of erasures, with all the variables of parchment type, erasure age, and comparison methodology, is simply too prone to judicial mistake. Accordingly, the invalid scenario remains invalid, and no notation between the witnesses' signatures can rescue it.

To summarize the full picture: a *shtar* with body and witnesses both on a *machak* background is valid, provided the *kiyum* is disregarded and the witnesses are validated directly. A *shtar* with a clean body and witnesses on a *machak* is valid, provided the witnesses insert a notation between their signatures. A *shtar* with the body on a *machak* and the witnesses on a clean background is invalid, and no notation can repair it.

## Dating systems

### Mekushar form

The *gemara* transitions to a new topic, returning to the *mekushar* — the tied or folded document. By way of reminder: a *get mekushar* is structured so that the text appears on both sides of the fold, with the witnesses signing on the outside. According to the standard ruling, witnesses on the inside of a *mekushar* disqualify it.

### Inside witnesses valid

Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel dissents: he holds that if the witnesses signed on the inside, the document remains valid, because one can simply undo the knots, open the document, and it will function as a standard *pashut* document. Tosafot notes that Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's position implies that the writing in a *mekushar* appeared on both sides of the fold — otherwise, when opened, the document would display large blank spaces and not resemble a normal *shtar*.

### Dating difference

Rabbi responds to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's position at the top of 164b: *she-lo eino domeh zemano shel zeh le-zemano shel zeh* — the date in one cannot be converted to match the date of the other, because the dating systems for a *pashut* and a *mekushar* differ. In a *pashut*, the standard reckoning applies: if a king has reigned for one year, the document says "year one"; if two years, "year two." In a *mekushar*, however, the system adds one: a king who has reigned for one year is recorded as "year two," and a king of two years is recorded as "year three." The Rashbam explains this increment as a form of *kavod* — a gesture of honor implying the king had already been ruling when the document was drawn. One might also suggest that the difference reflects competing conventions about whether "year one" means the king has completed one year or is currently in his first year — analogous to the ambiguity discussed in tractate *Rosh Hashanah*.

Whatever the precise origin of the discrepancy, the Rabbis deliberately maintained different systems for the two document types, as part of a broader policy of making *mekushar* and *pashut* documents as formally distinct as possible, to prevent confusion between them.

### Postdating risk

The practical danger of converting a *mekushar* to a *pashut* — as Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel would permit — is illustrated as follows. A borrower takes a loan from a lender during year one of a king's reign. A *mekushar* is drafted, and since *mekushar* dating adds one, the document reads "year two." The borrower repays the loan within the year and asks for his *shtar* back. The lender claims it was lost — *irchas li be-chutla iteyehiv* — and instead provides a receipt dated "year one" using standard *pashut* dating.

Now the lender waits. Once year two actually arrives, he opens the *mekushar* — since, according to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, opened witnesses can convert it to a *pashut* — and presents it as a *pashut shtar* purporting to establish a debt from "year two." The receipt the borrower holds says "year one," so it appears to predate the debt. The lender can now claim the debt was never repaid, seize property from purchasers who acquired land during year two, and harm innocent *lakuchot* who had no knowledge of a loan that never actually existed at that point.

The crucial asymmetry is that neither party necessarily acted in bad faith. The borrower accepted his receipt in good faith, not realizing that the dating systems would diverge when the *mekushar* was converted. A standard postdated *shtar* would have been flagged and rejected; this situation arises precisely because the postdating is structural and invisible.

### No receipts

The *gemara* resolves this by attributing to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel a consistent secondary position: *kasavar ein kotvin shovar* — he holds that receipts should not be written at all. The correct procedure when a loan is repaid is to demand the return of the original *shtar*; no receipt should substitute for it. If receipts are prohibited, the entire scenario collapses — the borrower's only protection is retrieving his *shtar*, and if the *shtar* is genuinely lost, the lender cannot open and repurpose it. The system remains internally coherent.

### Rabbi's learning

The *gemara* raises an intriguing question: did Rabbi actually know the details of *mekushar* dating well enough to make the objection he raised? The evidence suggests he did not, at least not initially. A *shtar mekushar* was once brought before Rabbi, and he declared it a *shtar me'uchar* — a postdated document — failing to recognize that what appeared to be a discrepancy was simply the standard *mekushar* dating convention. It was Zonim — the name of a person, perhaps related to the Baisos ben Zonim known elsewhere in the *gemara* — who informed him: *kach minhaga shel uma zu* — this is the practice of this nation; a king of one year is recorded as two, a king of two as three.

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction simply: *basar de-shamei mi-Zonim savra* — after Rabbi learned this from Zonim, he incorporated it into his reasoning. His later objection to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's ruling was informed by what he had learned from Zonim. The *gemara* treats this straightforwardly — Rabbi learned something during his life and applied it thereafter.

## Roman archon titles

### Archon dating

A *shtar* is presented to the court in which the date is recorded as "in the year of so-and-so the *arkan*." Tosafot notes that *arkan* does not literally mean king; it derives from the Greek *archon*, referring to an appointed official or governor — in the Roman context, roughly analogous to a consul. The document does not specify which year of this official's tenure; it simply names him and uses his title.

### Archon=year 1

Rabbi Chanina rules: examine when this official began his term in office — *eimasai amad arkan be-arkanutei* — and assume the document refers to the first year of that tenure. Since the title appears without qualification, it defaults to year one.

### Multiple terms

The *gemara* challenges this: *ve-dilma de-arich malchusei* — perhaps the official served for multiple years, and the document could refer to any one of them. How can we assume year one?

Rav Hoshaya resolves this by explaining the Roman convention: *kach minhaga shel uma zu* — this is the practice of this nation. During his first year in office, an official is called *arkan*. During his second year, he is called *digon* — from the Greek prefix *di-*, meaning two. Since the *shtar* uses the title *arkan* without qualification, it unambiguously refers to the first year.

### Term designation

The *gemara* raises one remaining difficulty: perhaps the official's original term ended, someone else served, and then he was reelected. In that case he would again be in his "first year" of a new tenure, yet the situation is not the same as his original first year. Rabbi Yirmiyah resolves this: *hahu arkan digon karu lei* — if an official returns to office after an interruption, he is not called simply *arkan* but *arkan digon*, signifying that this is his second term of office. The unmodified title *arkan* therefore reliably identifies the first year of his first continuous tenure.

## Greek geometry terms

### Shape-number terms

The *gemara* concludes with a brief but elegant discussion of Greek geometric terminology and its application in two distinct areas of *halacha*. The terms in question are: *acta* (one), *digon* (two), *trigon* (three), *tetragon* (four), and *pentagon* (five). These are shape names — polygon, triangle, square, pentagon — repurposed in Talmudic literature as numerical designations.

### Nazir multiplicity

Sumchus applies this vocabulary to *nazir* vows. If someone declares *hareini nazir acta*, he accepts one period of *nezirut* (the standard being thirty days). *Digon* means two periods; *trigon*, three; *tetragon*, four; *pentagon*, five. The Greek shape-names function as numerical shorthand within the context of vow-acceptance.

### Four corners needed

The *gemara* then cites a *baraita* applying the same geometric vocabulary to the laws of house impurity from *nega'im* — leprosy. A round house (*bayit agul*), a *digon* house (two-cornered), a *trigon* house (triangular), or a *pentagon* house (five-cornered) — *eino metamei be-nega'im*: none of these structures can become *tamei* through the leprosy impurity that afflicts houses. Only a *tetragon* — a four-cornered house — *metamei be-nega'im*.

### Four walls source

The *gemara* asks: what is the scriptural basis for requiring four walls and four corners? The *baraita* derives it from the verses in *Vayikra* governing house-leprosy: one verse refers to *kir* (a wall) and another to *kirot* (walls, plural). Each use of the plural implies at least two walls, and the combination of two such verses yields four walls — and with four walls comes the requirement of four corners. Hence the leprosy impurity applies only to a *tetragon* structure, completing the *gemara*'s excursion into Greek geometric terminology as applied to *halacha*.
