# Bava Batra 167

## Signature Display Rules

### Displaying Signature Loc…

The daf opens with a teaching of Abaye concerning the proper way to display one's signature to a *beit din*. The practical need for this arises from a scenario the Gemara describes: Reuven and Shimon have both signed a *shtar*, but Shimon has since died and no one in the world can identify Shimon's signature except Reuven and one other person. Since Reuven cannot both testify to Shimon's signature and validate his own — for that would mean three-quarters of the *shtar* is being validated through Reuven's testimony alone — a workaround is required. Reuven and the other witness testify to Shimon's signature, while Reuven contrives to let the *beit din* observe his own handwriting directly, without formal testimony. He enters the courtroom, begins practicing his signature, "accidentally" drops the paper, and walks away. The *beit din* then examines the writing on its own initiative, gaining firsthand familiarity with his signature without any testimonial act on his part.

This illustrates why one might wish to place one's signature on record before *beit din* in advance. Abaye's rule addresses how this should be done: *hai man deba'ei lemachvei chasimus yadei beveit dina, lilechei besof megilta* — whoever wishes to display his signature to *beit din* should sign at the top of a piece of parchment, not at the bottom.

### Blank Document Risk

The reason is straightforward and sobering. If one signs at the bottom of a blank piece of parchment, a finder could write above the signature whatever he wishes — a loan document, a sale, an IOU — and the signature would appear to authenticate the fabricated text. The Gemara reinforces this concern by invoking an established rule: *hotzi alav kesav yado shehu chayav lo, gova minechasim bnei chorin* — if someone produces another person's handwritten note acknowledging a debt, it may be used to collect from that person's unencumbered assets. The principle underlying this is *hoda'as ba'al din keme'ah edim dami*: a person's own admission is as effective as the testimony of a hundred witnesses. The note does not create a lien against property sold to third parties — it is, after all, only the debtor's own self-testimony and lacks the public notice of a witnessed document — but it does allow collection from freely available assets. Even if only the signature is in the debtor's hand and the body of the text was written by someone else, the signature is sufficient. This makes a signed blank page a genuinely dangerous instrument, and Abaye's rule is designed to prevent it.

### Tax Collector Story

The Gemara illustrates this with a memorable story. A certain *buzbina* — a tax collector — came before Abaye and made what sounded like a generous offer: he wished to see Abaye's signature so that when Torah scholars presented a note bearing Abaye's name, he would recognize it and exempt them from the tax. He handed Abaye a piece of parchment. Abaye began to sign at the top — leaving no blank space above — whereupon the tax collector began pulling the document, trying to maneuver Abaye into signing somewhere in the middle, where there would be blank space above the signature. Abaye recognized the trick immediately and said to him: *kvar kadmucha rabanan* — the Rabbis already anticipated you. The very rule that Abaye himself had taught had now saved him from being manipulated by the man asking him to apply it.

## Document Protection Rules

### Numbers at Line Ends

Abaye offers a second protective rule: *mitlat va-ad asara lo lichtov besof shita* — one should not write the numbers three through ten at the end of a line in a legal document. The concern is forgery by addition.

### Forgery via Yud Addition

The mechanism is elegant and troubling. In Aramaic, the numbers three through ten can each be multiplied by ten through the simple addition of a *yud* and a *nun* (or in some forms a *yud* and a *mem*): *tlat* becomes *tlatin* (thirty), *arba* becomes *arba'im* (forty), *chamesh* becomes *chamishim* (fifty), *shesh* becomes *shishim* (sixty), *sheva* becomes *shiv'im* (seventy), *tesha* becomes *tish'im* (ninety), *eser* becomes *esrim* (twenty). If the numeral falls at the end of a line, a forger can squeeze in a *yud-nun* in the margin or overhang — far less visibly intrusive than inserting an entirely new word like *me'ot* (hundreds), which would obviously stand out. One should note that *shmoneh* (eight) is apparently excluded from this concern, possibly because its terminal *hei* cannot be transformed into a *yud-nun* in the same way. Similarly, *echad* and *shnayim* cannot be inflated to *achad asar* or *esrim* by such a simple addition, so they pose no such risk. The range of three through ten is therefore the zone of vulnerability.

### Repetition Remedy

What if, despite best efforts, the number has already been written at the end of a line and nothing can be done about it? The Gemara prescribes a remedy: *mehadar lei lediburei t'rei vetlata zimni* — write the amount again two or three times later in the document. The principle is that we always follow the final repetition, analogous to how we write both numerals and words on a modern check, supplemented by a drawn line. The rationale is that among multiple repetitions, at least one will fall in the middle of a line, making forgery by marginal insertion impossible and thereby anchoring the authentic amount.

### Orchard Erasure Case

The Gemara now presents two case studies in forgery detection. In the first, a *shtar* recorded the sale of a *tilta b'pardisa* — a third of an orchard. The fraudster took the *bet* of *bi-pardisa* and erased both its roof (the horizontal top stroke) and its foot (the bottom stroke), leaving only a vertical line — transforming *bi-pardisa* into *u-pardisa*, "and the orchard." The document now appeared to convey not merely a third of one orchard but a third of some property *and* the entire orchard — a far more valuable transaction.

When the case came before Abaye, he examined the document and challenged the claimant: *mai ta'ama revach lei alma l'hai vav?* — why does this *vav* have so much room to breathe? Why is there such conspicuous space between the *vav* and the rest of the word *pardisa*? Had the *bet* originally stood there, the remaining vertical stroke would naturally be set apart from what followed, whereas a genuine *vav* would sit flush within the word. The physical spacing was telltale. Abaye had the claimant bound and administered lashes, and he admitted the forgery.

The Gemara leaves an important question unresolved, and it is worth pausing on it. What if the claimant had not admitted? Could Abaye — or any *dayan* — dismiss the *shtar* based solely on this visual anomaly? After all, a scribe might occasionally leave extra space inadvertently, and spacing alone is not conclusive proof. The Rambam, in *Hilchot Malveh v'Loveh* (27:12), addresses the obligation of careful scrutiny: *u'mitikun hashtarot l'hitbonen beshtar bevavin vezayinim shelo yihyu dechukim bein hatevot shema zayif vehosif zo* — it is a corrective institution of *shtar* law that one must carefully examine every *vav* and *zayin* in the document to ensure they are not squeezed between words, lest a forgery added them; *v'lo yihyu meruchakim*, and one must equally check that no letter is suspiciously separated from its neighbors, lest someone erased part of a letter — for example a *hei* or a *chet* — and left only one leg in the place of a *vav*. The Rambam's formulation makes clear that this scrutiny is mandatory, but it does not fully answer the threshold question: how much suspicion is sufficient for a *dayan* to dismiss a *shtar* outright? This remains a genuine gap in the analysis.

### Three Brothers Case

The second case involves a different kind of addition. A *shtar* read *manat Reuven v'Shimon achei* — the portion belonging to Reuven and Shimon, the brothers — which had been sold to a third party. Reuven and Shimon, it transpired, had a third brother named Acha. Reuven and Shimon jointly owned one field; all three brothers together owned a different, presumably more valuable field. The fraudster added a *vav* to the word *achei* — "brother" — transforming it into *v'Achi*, "and Acha," so that the *shtar* now read as if Reuven, Shimon, *and* their brother Acha had all sold together, which would convey the more valuable jointly-held field.

When this came before Abaye, he asked the same diagnostic question: *mai ta'ama dachik lei alma l'hai vav?* — why is this *vav* so crowded? Why is it squeezed so tightly against the surrounding letters? The compression was the giveaway. The man admitted after being bound. And here too the same open question stands: without a forced admission, what authority does the *dayan* have to act on visual suspicion alone, and what is the required threshold of proof?

## Forgery Detection

### Rambam's Scrutiny Rules

The Rambam's formulation quoted above — requiring the *dayan* to examine spacing both for suspicious compression and suspicious separation — captures the principle at work in both cases just described. The two anomalies are inverses of one another: a letter squeezed in (*dachik*) indicates an insertion; a letter standing conspicuously apart (*merubach*) indicates an erasure of the surrounding material. The Rambam instructs that this analysis must extend to the entire document and every form of writing. What the Gemara does not spell out, and what the Rambam likewise leaves implicit, is the operative standard of proof that translates a *dayan*'s suspicion into a definitive ruling — particularly when the party against whom the *shtar* is being used affirmatively claims forgery and the visual evidence is suggestive but not conclusive.

### Rava's Signature Case

A striking Gemara follows. A certain *shtar* bore the signatures of Rava and Rav Acha bar Adda. When it came before Rava in his capacity as *dayan* — itself an interesting question touching on the principle of *ed na'aseh dayan*, though the Gemara does not pursue it — Rava examined his own signature and said: *dein chatimat yada didi* — yes, this is my signature. *Mihu, kamei d'Rav Acha bar Adda lo chatmi li me'olam* — but I have never co-signed a *shtar* together with Rav Acha bar Adda. One possible reading of *kamei* ("before" or "in the presence of") suggests Rava's statement was more precise: he never signed a document prior to Rav Acha bar Adda — meaning he always signed only after his co-signatory, never first. This reading helpfully explains how Rava could be so confident: he would know from practice that he had never affixed his name to a document alongside this particular colleague.

The forger was bound and admitted the deed. Rava then turned to him with a sharp practical question: *bishlama didi zayafta* — perhaps I can understand that you forged my signature, if you are skilled enough. *Ela d'Rav Acha bar Adda* — but how did you replicate the signature of Rav Acha bar Adda, whose hand trembles with age or illness? The forger explained: *anchi yadai amitzra* — he placed his hand on a rope, like a suspension bridge, and as people walked across and the rope swayed and jiggled, he signed in that shaking motion. An alternate version has him suspended from a well-rope, swinging freely as he wrote. People will go to extraordinary lengths to produce a convincing forgery.

This prompts an important discussion. Once a *shtar* has been *mekuyam* — validated by *beit din* — does the signatory himself retain any *ne'emanus* to contest it? It seems clear that once witnesses have validated his signature and *beit din* has confirmed the document, the signatory's own subsequent claim that the signature is not his cannot simply override the validation. The principle of *keivan shehigid shuv eino chozer umagid* — once a witness has testified, he cannot retract — is relevant here, though the precise application is not fully worked out by the Gemara. What if independent witnesses later came forward claiming to have seen the forgery? That would function more like a *psul* external to the testimony itself, somewhat analogous to the process of *hazamah*, where witnesses are disqualified by a showing that they were elsewhere. These questions are raised but remain open.

## Documents Without Parties

### Get Without Wife

The Gemara transitions to a new Mishnah: *kotvin get l'ish af al pi she'ein ishto imo* — a *get* may be written for a husband even though his wife is not present. Since *get* is a unilateral act by the husband, the wife's agreement is not required; he will hold the *get* and present it to her when he is ready to divorce her. Of course, he must still authorize the writing himself.

### Tosafot on Dating Risk

Tosafot raises a difficulty: if the *get* is written now but delivered months later, it will appear that the divorce took effect at the earlier date. This creates at minimum the problem of protecting *lakuchos* — third-party purchasers — who may have acquired property from the husband after the date written in the *get* but before its actual delivery. If it appears the wife was divorced earlier, she might be deemed to have had usufruct rights (*peiros*) during that intervening period, prejudicing buyers who relied on the husband's ownership.

The *Ri* in Tosafot answers: *lo makish inish pur'anusa l'nafshei* — a person does not invite misfortune upon himself. Having a *get* written is considered a bad omen; no one does it in advance of genuine intent to divorce imminently. We therefore assume that whenever a *get* is written, it will be given very shortly thereafter. If there is specific evidence to the contrary — for instance, a *get* found on the floor under suspicious circumstances — suspicion may arise. But as a baseline assumption, we are not concerned. Tosafot further notes that for *gittin* transmitted from abroad (*gittei habaim mimedinas hayam*), the unavoidable delay is publicly known — the entire process of overseas transmission through *beit din* is notorious — so the apparent pre-dating creates no practical problem: *kala is lehu*, their circumstances are well known.

### Receipt Without Parties

The Mishnah continues: *v'hashover l'isha* — one may also write a *shover* (receipt for *ketubah* payment) for the woman even though her husband is not present. After a husband pays his wife's *ketubah*, the wife may either return the *ketubah* document itself or write a receipt acknowledging payment. If she comes to the scribes before payment and asks that a receipt be prepared in advance — to be handed over upon actual payment — the scribes may comply. The reasoning: the only person who might be hurt by a premature or fraudulent use of this receipt is the woman herself. If she gives the receipt before receiving payment, she loses her claim; no one else is injured. The Mishnah also specifies: *uvilvad sheyehu makirin* — provided the scribes recognize the relevant parties. Who precisely must be recognized, and in which direction, becomes the subject of Gemara discussion below.

As for scribal fees: *v'haba'al noten sachar* — the husband pays. This is consistent with the general principle that the beneficiary of the transaction pays. The husband benefits from the receipt because it extinguishes his *ketubah* obligation; that he pays is clear. Why he also pays the scribal fees for the *get* itself, given that the beneficiary of the *get* is less obvious, is left for the Gemara to work through.

### Debt Document Rules

The Mishnah proceeds: *kotvin shtar l'loveh af al pi she'ein malveh imo* — scribes may write a loan document for the borrower even without the lender present, since the borrower is only incriminating himself and the lender has no reason to object. Conversely, *v'ein kotvin l'malveh ad sheyehe loveh imo* — they may not write for the lender without the borrower present, since the lender could be fabricating a debt that the borrower never authorized. The borrower pays the fees: *v'haloveh noten sachar* — not because the borrower benefits from the *shtar* (it works against him), but because he benefits from the underlying transaction. He received money without paying interest; his is the financial gain.

### Sale Document Rules

The same logic extends to sales: *kotvin shtar l'mocher af al pi she'ein loke'ach imo* — a sale document may be written for the seller without the buyer's presence. If the seller wishes to have a document prepared stating that he sold his property to a named buyer, there is no harm; the buyer's interests are not prejudiced. But *v'ein kotvin l'loke'ach ad sheyehe mocher imo* — one may not write the document for the buyer without the seller, since the seller might deny the sale entirely and the document would be fraudulent. The buyer pays the fees: *v'haloke'ach noten sachar* — he is the transactional beneficiary. It might seem as though the seller benefits by receiving money, but it is the buyer who acquires property and for whom the documentary record provides protection.

### Two-Party Documents

Certain documents, however, are bilateral by nature, and neither party can initiate without the other. *Ein kotvin shtar eirusin v'nisuin ela mida'at shneihem* — a betrothal agreement (*tenai'm*) or marriage contract (*ketubah*) may be written only with the knowledge and presence of both parties, since both sides undertake obligations and both benefit. Similarly, *ein kotvin shtar arisut v'kablanut ela mida'at shneihem* — a sharecropping agreement (*arisut*) or a work contract (*kablanut*) requires both parties. A contract that specifies mutual obligations — payment on one side, labor on the other — cannot be prepared at the initiative of either party alone. The *m'kabel* (the one taking on the job) pays the fees in this case, being viewed as the more needy party who gains the employment opportunity. Likewise, *ein kotvin shitrei beirurin v'chol maaseh beit din ela midaat shneihem* — documents concerning the selection of judges or court proceedings that affect both litigants require the consent of both, and in that case *ush'neihem notnim sachar*, both parties share the cost.

### Two Copies Rule

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a practical observation about these two-party documents: *lishneihem kotvin shenayim, l'zeh l'atzmo ul'zeh l'atzmo* — for documents that affect both sides, two copies are prepared, one for each party. Since each side has obligations and rights recorded in the document, each side naturally needs its own copy. This point, while apparently obvious, is significant enough that it required explicit statement — since the earlier discussion of one-party documents did not address which party retains the single copy.

## Party Recognition Issue

### Recognition Initial Rule

The Gemara now explores the Mishnah's requirement that scribes recognize the parties. Rav Yehuda cites Rav: *uv'vada d'makir shem ha'ish b'get v'shem ha'isha b'shovar* — in the case of the *get*, the scribes need only recognize the man's name; in the case of the receipt (*shover*), they need only recognize the woman's name. The reasoning is intuitive. When a man comes to request a *get* for his wife, the scribes know him — that is sufficient. If he names his wife as Sarah, they will write that name. If he has no wife by that name, the document will be useless. What harm could come from not knowing the wife? Similarly, when a woman requests a receipt for her *ketubah*, the scribes recognize her; her husband's identity is not their concern, since the document only affects her and her husband.

### Identical Names Problem

Three Amoraim — Rav Safra, Rav Acha bar Rav Huna, and Rav Huna bar Chinana — sat together with Abaye present and raised an objection. Focusing on the *get*: *v'lichosh, dilma katav gita?* — why are we not concerned that the following fraud could occur? A man — not Reuven Jacobson, but someone else entirely — approaches the scribes and asks them to write a *get* naming his wife as Sarah. The scribes recognize this man as Reuven Jacobson and write accordingly. He then delivers this *get* not to his own wife, but to the wife of another Reuven Jacobson in the same town — a woman who also happens to be named Sarah. She now appears divorced when she is not, and may go on to collect her *ketubah* under false pretenses or worse. The parallel concern applies to the *shover*: a woman gives the scribes a false husband's name, the receipt is prepared, and it is delivered to a different man who shares that name, fraudulently extinguishing a real *ketubah* obligation.

### Both Names Required

Abaye responded that Rav had in fact said the opposite of what was initially quoted in his name: *shem ha'ish b'get vehu hadin leshem ha'isha* — both the husband's name and the wife's name must be recognized by the scribes when writing a *get*; *shem ha'isha b'shovar vehu hadin leshem ha'ish* — and both names must be recognized for the *shover* as well. The initial one-sided formulation was a misattribution or simplification. Recognition of both parties is required.

### Same City Same Names

This, however, does not fully solve the problem. The Gemara now raises the scenario of *shnei Yosef ben Shimon hadarim be'ir achas* — two couples in the same city where both the husbands and wives share identical names. Even if the scribes recognize that the man before them is indeed named Yosef ben Shimon and that his wife is indeed named Miriam, there may be another couple in the same city with precisely those names. A *get* written for one couple could be handed to the other.

It is worth noting a subtle but telling observation: the Gemara frames this problem entirely in terms of the husband's name — *shnei Yosef ben Shimon* — without mentioning the wives' shared names as part of the problem's description, even though the fraud being contemplated necessarily depends on the wives' names also matching. Tosafot raises a broader question at this point: perhaps a *get* or *shtar* is intrinsically *pasul* whenever its text could equally describe two different parties — regardless of any fraudulent intent — since it is ambiguous on its face. That question is bracketed by the Gemara here, which focuses on the practical concern of misuse rather than inherent invalidity.

### Both Couples Present Rule

Rav Acha bar Rav Huna cites Rav's ruling: *ein megarshin neshoseihen ela ze bifnei ze* — in a city where two couples share identical names, neither husband may divorce his wife except in the presence of the other couple. The logic, while not made fully explicit by the Gemara, appears to be that requiring both couples to appear together before *beit din* at the moment of divorce creates a verification mechanism. When the divorced woman later presents the *get*, she will need witnesses who can testify not only to the act of divorce but to the fact that the other couple was present and that she is indeed the correct recipient.

One might still question what this achieves. If a woman produces a *get* and claims divorce, the *beit din* knowing about the two identically named couples will presumably insist on witnesses who can testify to the circumstances of the divorce. What the requirement of both couples being present ultimately accomplishes is to make the act of fraud harder to execute without detection. But the honest challenge remains: a determined fraudster could still claim the required circumstances were satisfied and dare the court to disprove it. The Gemara does not fully resolve how this rule prevents rather than merely complicates fraud.

### Name Adoption Fraud

A further scenario: what if someone travels to a different city — where he is unknown — and begins representing himself as Yosef ben Shimon? His real name is something else entirely. He manages to establish this false identity, then approaches a *sofer* in that city, claims to be Yosef ben Shimon, and obtains a *get* written in that name. He returns to his home city and delivers this *get* to the wife of the real Yosef ben Shimon. When she presents it, the *beit din* of the home city will not even think to apply the two-couples rule, since to their knowledge there is only one Yosef ben Shimon in their town — the fraudster has constructed his identity in a different jurisdiction entirely.

### Thirty-Day Rule

Rav Huna bar Chinana cites Rav's response: *kol shehuchzak shemo ba'ir shloshim yom ein chosheshin lo* — a person whose name has been established in a city for thirty days, we are no longer concerned about this fraud. The Rashbam explains: if the ruse must be sustained for thirty days before a *get* can be written, the fraudster is exposed to a prolonged period during which his scheme might unravel — people might recognize him, word might travel back to his home city, or other circumstances might expose him. A fraud that can be executed in a single day is a practical threat; one that requires sustained impersonation over a month is sufficiently unlikely that we do not legislate against it. This does not mean the fraud is impossible; it means the risk is tolerable.

### Name Response Test

What if a stranger arrives in town and has not yet been there thirty days? The Gemara asks: *lo itchazak mai?* — what is the law when thirty days have not yet elapsed? Abaye proposes a test: *dekaru lei ve'ani* — call out the name and see if he responds. If someone walking down the street turns around when called by a name, that is evidence that the name is genuinely his. The reflex response to one's own name is deeply ingrained and is difficult to suppress or fake.

### Deceiver Objection

Rav Zvid rejects this: *ramai beramutei zahir* — a deceiver is careful in his deception. Someone who has gone to the effort of constructing a false identity will know to turn around when his assumed name is called; indeed, he will have been practicing and anticipating exactly this. The name-response test therefore provides no reliable information, and the conclusion follows: if a person has not been established in a city for thirty days, a *get* simply cannot be written for him there.

## Witness Retraction Case

### Woman Retraction Claim

The Gemara now presents a complex case involving Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba and a *shover* he had signed. A woman's husband produced the receipt in *beit din*, claiming that she had been paid her *ketubah*. The receipt bore Rav Yirmeyah's signature as a witness. The woman, however, claimed: *lav ana havai* — that was not me. She maintained that when Rav Yirmeyah and his co-witnesses signed the receipt, a different woman had appeared before them, falsely representing herself as the husband's wife.

### Witness Doubt Response

Rav Yirmeyah acknowledged that he himself had harbored doubts — that is, he had thought, even at the time the case came before *beit din*, that this woman did not appear to be the same woman from the earlier signing. *Ana nami amri lehu lav ihi* — I too said to my co-witnesses that she doesn't seem to be the same woman. But his co-witnesses had explained: *mikhashi dekhachsha* — she has simply grown thin, or aged; *uvagra lah kalah* — and her voice has deepened. It is the same woman, and she is lying.

### Torah Scholar Exception

Abaye addressed the question of whether Rav Yirmeyah's partial retraction could stand. The general rule is *keivan shehigid shuv eino chozer umagid* — once a witness has testified, he may not retract. Yet here the Gemara seems to permit the ultimate resolution in favor of the receipt's validity, grounded in a specific circumstance: *tzurba merabanan lav orchei lemidak* — a Torah scholar does not typically scrutinize women. Rav Yirmeyah had not been looking at her; he was listening to her voice, which had changed. His co-witnesses, who had looked at her, recognized her. His doubt was a product of his own *tzni'us* practices rather than genuine uncertainty about her identity. Under these circumstances, the final position — accepting the co-witnesses' explanation that she was the same woman — is allowed, because there is compelling circumstantial evidence explaining why Rav Yirmeyah's impression was mistaken.

### Unresolved Principles

This case leaves several important questions unresolved. First, on the principle of *keivan shehigid*: the rule is generally understood as an ironclad procedural bar — once testimony is accepted in *beit din*, it cannot be withdrawn regardless of subsequent explanations. Does this case establish that *keivan shehigid* can be overridden by sufficiently compelling circumstantial evidence explaining the error? If so, what is the threshold? This seems to cut against the formalistic understanding of the rule. Second, a more basic question: why is Rav Yirmeyah's initial doubt — his claim that this is a different woman — treated as significant at all? If the *shover* bears his validated signature, his subsequent second-guessing of his own signing would itself seem to trigger *keivan shehigid*; he would be retracting a previously established act of testimony. Part of the answer may lie in the distinction between formal testimony delivered in *beit din* and signatures on a *shtar*: the latter may not rise to the same level of *edut* for purposes of the *keivan shehigid* rule, and the question of whether the *shtar* had already been formally *mekuyam* before Rav Yirmeyah expressed his doubts is material. Whether the principle of *keivan shehigid* applies to witnesses retracting their signatures on documents, as distinct from their oral testimony before a court, and whether circumstantial evidence bearing on the reliability of that signature can reopen the question — all of this remains, as the Gemara closes, unresolved.

---

---

# Bava Batra 168

## Document Writing Rules

### Opening & Overview

Daf 168 finds us in the closing stretch of *Bava Batra*, engaged with the *gemara*'s treatment of a *mishna* concerning the writing of various legal documents: loan documents, *shovarim* (receipts), *ketubot*, *shtarei erusin*, and related instruments. The underlying questions are structural: for whose benefit may a document be written in the absence of the other party, and who bears the cost of the *sofer*? Only the party who is obligating himself may have a document written without the other party present — not the reverse. These principles will carry through the entire daf.

### Shovar Case

The *gemara* opens mid-discussion concerning the writing of a *shovar* — a receipt acknowledging payment of a *ketubah*. The case before us: there was a certain *shovar* bearing the signature of Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba. A woman declared, *lav ana havai* — this was not me, this was not my transaction. She was suggesting that her husband had arranged for some other woman to impersonate her and thereby obtain a fraudulent receipt attesting that her *ketubah* had been paid. Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba responded, *ivra at havait* — no, in truth it was you. I know it was you, and you will not deceive me.

Abaye then contextualizes this: even though the *gemara* concluded at the end of yesterday's discussion that *rabanan* do not typically scrutinize women closely — *lav orcha lemadak* — and that Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba could therefore have made an initial error of identification, here he is asserting positively that it was in fact this woman.

### Tosafot on Testimony

*Tosafot* raises a pointed question. We established yesterday that when Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba *initially* thought a woman was not the one named in the document, he could retract his testimony — because scholars do not ordinarily look at women closely, such initial uncertainty is understandable. *Tosafot* frames the logical implication: *kal va-chomer*, if one can retract testimony that contradicts the *shtar*, then surely when a witness affirms precisely what the *shtar* says — *zu hi* — he is believed, even though his ordinary practice is not to look at women carefully, *af al pi she-ein darko lehistakel ba-hen*. That is exactly what is written in the document; what else would one think?

*Tosafot* resolves the question as follows: *kivan de-dikdak*, once Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba stated definitively that it was her, *eino chozer umaggid* — he cannot subsequently claim he made a mistake. The point of the *gemara*'s discussion here is not to question his credibility but to establish that having made a firm identification, he is bound by it and may not retract.

## Talmidim & Document Costs

### Marriage Advice

Since the *gemara* has been discussing the fact that *talmidei chachamim* do not closely observe women, Abaye draws a practical lesson: *hai tzurba merabanan de-azal lekadesh iteta* — a Torah scholar who goes to betroth a woman should bring along an *am ha-aretz*, someone more familiar with the ordinary social world, *nidbar am ha-aretz bahadeih*. The concern is *dilma machlefu lah mineih* — perhaps they will swap the woman on him. Since the *talmid chacham* is not paying close attention, he may arrive at the *chuppah* and not recognize that a different woman has been substituted. The *am ha-aretz* will notice.

This is a striking sociological observation — one that inevitably evokes the *parshiyot* we are engaged with at this time of year, the story of Rachel and Leah, and the question of how such a substitution becomes possible at all. The *gemara* does not dwell on this, but the implication is significant.

### Get Costs

The *mishna* states that *ha-ba'al nosein sachar* — the husband pays the *sofer* to write the *get*. The reason is derived from the verse *ve-chasav ve-natan*: he must write it and give it. Since the *sofer* is acting as the husband's *shaliach*, his agent, the husband is naturally the one who pays. The one paying determines for whom the work is being done.

### Wife Pays Get

The *gemara* then asks: *veidach*, why does later practice diverge from this? By the time of the *gemara*, it had become standard for the wife to pay for the *get*. The explanation: *shadyu rabbanan a-isha ki heichi de-lo lishahai* — the Rabbis placed the financial burden on the wife so that the husband would have no monetary pretext to delay. This speaks directly to the tragedy of *agunah* situations: if the husband lacks funds to pay the *sofer* and is not eagerly seeking the divorce in the first place, the wife may be left waiting indefinitely. By having the wife absorb the cost, the impediment is removed.

What remains unresolved is how this squares with the principle that the *sofer* acts as the husband's agent. One might suggest it operates as a form of *hefker beis din hefker* — the rabbinic authority effectively assigns the payment in a way that is treated as though the husband is paying — but this is not entirely clear from the *gemara*'s language.

## Payment Responsibility

### Loan Docs

The *mishna* states: *kotvin shtar le-loveh af pi she-ein malveh immo* — you may write a loan document for the borrower even without the lender present, since the document only obligates the borrower himself. He may carry it and present it to the lender when ready. The *mishna* further states *ve-ha-loveh noten sechar* — the borrower pays the *sofer*. The *gemara* responds *pshita* — is this not obvious? The borrower is receiving a loan without paying interest; he is clearly the beneficiary of the transaction and should bear the cost.

### Iska Case

The *gemara* then says: *tzricha be-iska* — the ruling is actually needed for the case of an *iska*, a business investment arrangement that functions as half-loan and half-*pikadon*. Both parties benefit from the *iska*: the investor provides capital, the recipient invests it and shares the profit. One might have thought that since both benefit, both should share the cost. Nevertheless, since the recipient is the party without money who is more fundamentally in need of the arrangement, he is considered the primary beneficiary and pays the *sofer*'s fee — even though he currently lacks funds.

### Sale Docs

Similarly, *kotvin shtar le-mocher af pi she-ein lokeiach immo* — you may write a sale document for the seller without the buyer being present, since that document can only work against the seller's interests. The *mishna* states *ve-ha-lokeiach noten sechar* — the buyer pays. Again the *gemara* says *pshita*: who is benefiting? The *gemara* operates under the assumption that selling one's property — particularly ancestral land — is generally an unfortunate necessity rather than a commercial act. The buyer is therefore always the beneficiary.

### Field Quality

The *gemara* clarifies: *lo tzricha be-mocher sadehu mipnei ra'assa* — the ruling is needed for the case where someone is selling his field because it is of poor quality, a hardscrabble plot he is fortunate to unload. Here one might argue that the seller is the beneficiary, since he is rid of a liability. Nevertheless, the buyer still pays. The reasoning is either that in all cases of land acquisition the buyer is in the better position, or it reflects a principle of *lo plug* — once the rule has been established that the buyer pays for sale documents, we do not create distinctions between cases.

### Betrothal Docs

Regarding *shtarei erusin* and *nissuin*: *ein kotvin shtarei erusin* — you do not write betrothal documents or marriage contracts except when both parties are present, because it is a bilateral arrangement requiring mutual agreement. The *mishna* states *de-chassan noten sechar* — the groom pays. The *gemara* again says *pshita*. In a patriarchal framework, even though the groom takes on obligations of support, he is receiving a wife and is therefore considered the primary beneficiary. The *gemara* takes this so thoroughly for granted that it requires no elaboration.

The *gemara* then sharpens the ruling: *lo tzericha*, the ruling is needed even in the case of a *tzurba merabanan*, a Torah scholar, where *de-nichla ley le-chamuya le-kurvey* — the father-in-law actively desires him as a relative and derives significant social benefit from the match. Even so, the framing remains that the groom acquires the wife and he pays.

This passage invites substantial sociological reflection about how the *gemara* frames the question of who benefits in a marriage transaction — but the *gemara* itself moves on without dwelling on it.

### Sharecropping

*Ein kotvin shtarei arisut ve-kablanut* — one does not write sharecropping or rental agreements except with both parties present, and *ve-ha-mikabel noten sechar* — the one who receives the field to work it pays the *sofer*. That person is obtaining an opportunity to earn a livelihood; the field's owner merely has property. The *gemara* says *pshita* again, and notes it is needed for *bora* — a field requiring fallowing or heavy investment to be usable — where one might think the recipient is not clearly the beneficiary. Even so, he pays.

## Clarification Documents

### Berurin Definition

*Ein kotvin shtarei berurin ela mi-da'at shneihem* — one writes *shtarei berurin* only with the knowledge and consent of both parties. The *gemara* asks: *mai shtarei berurin* — what are these clarification documents? Two explanations are offered. In Babylonia it was explained as *shtarei ta'anata* — documents recording the claims and counterclaims of litigants that have been presented before the judges, a formal record of the positions each side has stated in court. Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba offers a different explanation: *ze borer lo echad ve-ze borer lo echad* — it refers to the process by which each litigant selects one of the judges who will adjudicate his case, as we will see elaborated in *Sanhedrin*. The two chosen judges then select a third. Once those selections have been made, they must be recorded and formalized. Either way, both parties pay equally since they are symmetric sides of the litigation.

### Copy Dispute

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* rules that you write two copies of the *shtar berurin* — *l'ze bifnei atzmo u-l'ze bifnei atzmo* — each litigant receives his own copy rather than sharing a single document.

### Midat Sodom

The *gemara* asks whether this dispute turns on the principle of *chofin al midat Sodom* — whether we compel a person not to adopt the posture of *midat Sodom*. *Midat Sodom* is the attitude of *sheli sheli ve-shelcha shelcha* — I keep mine and you keep yours, with no concession to shared arrangement. As *Pirkei Avot* characterizes it, this is at best a middling quality and at its worst the defining sin of Sodom. The *Rashbam* frames the case as follows: one litigant says, you keep your copy of the *shtar*, I want my own copy. I am not willing to pay half to share one document — I want one for myself. Is this *midat Sodom*, an insistence on keeping things separate at needless cost to both parties? The *chachamim* would say yes — it is wasteful to produce two documents when one would serve both, and we do not indulge such stubbornness.

### Privacy Concern

The *gemara* rejects this framing, however. *Lo* — the debate is not about whether we tolerate *midat Sodom*. Rather, *d'kulei alma kofin* — all would agree we do not simply accommodate someone who insists on separate arrangements when a shared one is practically adequate. The real issue, according to the *gemara*, is that there is a legitimate reason why sharing a document is not practically adequate here. That is the basis of *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s position: *lo nicha li de-tehevei zechutach gabei zechuti* — I do not want my rights, my claims, sitting alongside your rights in your possession. *De-damit alai ke-ari arava* — you are like a lion lying in wait. If you hold the record of my claims while litigation is still ongoing, you will have the opportunity to examine my arguments and prepare your counterattack. I do not want you holding a court record that contains what I have said.

### Separate Copies

The solution, on this reading, is that each litigant receives only the record of his own claims — you see your claims, I see mine. An alternative reading in the *gemara* is that the concern is not about examining the opponent's claims but simply about physical control: even if I could theoretically request access to the shared document, the fact that you hold it gives you unequal practical control. In either case, *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s ruling — that separate copies protect each party against the other's potential for deception — is vindicated.

## Asmachta

### Mishna Setup

The next *mishna*: *mi she-para mikzat chovo ve-hishlish et shtaro* — someone who has repaid a portion of a debt and places the original *shtar* in the hands of a trusted third party. The situation: Reuven owes a thousand dollars, pays two hundred and fifty, and cannot yet pay the balance. He does not have a receipt for the partial payment, and the *sofer* is unavailable. But he also does not want the creditor holding a *shtar* stating he owes the full thousand. They therefore agree to deposit the *shtar* with a mutually trusted intermediary.

### Penalty Clause

The terms of the deposit: *ve-im lo natati lecha mikan ve-ad yom ploni ten lo shtaro* — if by a specified date I have not paid you the remaining balance, you are empowered to return the *shtar* to the creditor, and I will owe the full thousand. This arrangement substitutes for a formal receipt: the third party knows a partial payment was made, and the penalty for non-payment of the balance is the restoration of the full debt obligation.

### Yosi v. Yehuda

When the time arrives and the borrower has not paid: *Rabbi Yossi omer yiten* — Rabbi Yossi says the third party should hand over the document as agreed, and the full debt is enforceable. *Rabbi Yehuda omer lo yiten* — Rabbi Yehuda says no. That agreement does not bind the third party to hand over the document. This is the paradigm case of *asmachta*.

### Asmachta Defined

*Be-mai kamiflagi*? The dispute turns on whether *asmachta kanyia* — whether an *asmachta* is legally binding. An *asmachta* is, broadly, a commitment made under the assumption that the triggering condition will never actually arise. The person making the promise is overcommitting — promising something he does not genuinely intend to give, something he does not believe the other party really deserves — precisely because he is so confident the condition will never come about. Because of this, there is no real *gemirat da'at*, no genuine settled intent to transfer. The promise is hollow. *Rabbi Yossi* holds *asmachta kanyia* — such a commitment is nonetheless binding. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds *asmachta lo kanyia* — it is not.

### Rav Nachman Ruling

*Amar Rav Nachman amar Rabbah bar Avuha amar Rav*: the *halacha* follows *Rabbi Yossi* — *asmachta* is binding. It should be noted that *Tosafot*'s *girsa* reads *ein halachah ke-Rabbi Yossi*, the opposite ruling. This ambiguity in the transmitted text makes the ultimate *psak* genuinely uncertain.

### Rabbi Ami

When cases of *asmachta* came before *Rabbi Ami*, he expressed a kind of reluctant constraint: *ve-chi me-achar she-Rabbi Yochanan melamedenu pa'am rishonah u-sheniyah halachah ke-Rabbi Yossi* — since Rabbi Yochanan teaches again and again that the *halacha* follows *Rabbi Yossi*, what can I do? *Ani mah e'eseh* — I am bound by that ruling. People may have hoped he would rule otherwise, but he could not depart from Rabbi Yochanan's repeated and explicit position.

### Final Conclusion

The *gemara* concludes: *ve-ein halachah ke-Rabbi Yossi* — but the *halacha* does not follow *Rabbi Yossi*. *Asmachta* is not *kanyia*. This reversal then opens the extensive discussions in *Tosafot* and the *Rishonim* about whether *asmachta* is categorically never binding or whether certain types of conditional commitments do acquire legal force. That is a major topic in its own right.

## Erased Documents

### Replacing Erased

The next *mishna*: *mi she-nimchak shtar chovo* — someone whose loan document has been erased. This situation arises in practice, including with *ketubot*, where the witnesses' signatures — written with materials that fade — may become illegible over time. A replacement is needed, and critically, it must bear the original date, since the original date establishes the liens from which the holder may collect. A new document dated to the present would forfeit those earlier liens.

### Procedure

The *mishna*'s procedure: *ma'amido la-eidim* — you station witnesses before the document while it is still legible, so they can testify to its contents before the text fades entirely. They then come before *beis din*, and *beis din* — according to most *Rishonim*, as opposed to the *Rashbam* who holds it refers to the witnesses themselves — creates a substitute *shtar* based on that testimony.

The language of the substitute document identifies the original holder, the date, and the original witnesses: *ish ploni ben ploni nimchak shtaro be-yom ploni u-ploni u-ploni eidav*. One might ask: who exactly are these witnesses being named? *Tosafot* explains that the document names all the relevant witnesses — both the original witnesses to the loan and the secondary witnesses who testified before *beis din* about what was written. The full record would read something like: Levi and Yehuda came before us and testified that this person held a loan document of one thousand dollars dated a certain day, with Reuven and Shimon as the original witnesses — and now we as *beis din* are creating this substitute. This is also the framework behind the *ketubah d'irkasa* and *ketubah d'nimchaka* — the formalized versions of substitute *ketubot* used when the original is lost or erased.

### Kiyum Language

The *baraisa* provides the precise language the *beis din* uses to certify the replacement: *be-moshav tlasa havina* — we were convened as a court of three. The *dayanim* identify themselves, and then record that *ploni ben ploni hotzi shtar machuk le-faneinu be-yom ploni*, so-and-so brought an erased promissory note before us on this date, with such-and-such witnesses. The *beis din* then records whether it observed the document while still legible, or whether secondary witnesses testified to its content.

### Evidence Standard

The *baraisa* continues: *ve-nimtzas eidusam mechuvenes* — and their testimony was found to be consistent and reliable. In that case, *goveh ve-eino tzarich le-havi raya* — the holder may collect on the basis of the substitute document and need bring no further proof. The substitute establishes the original date and the original liens. If, however, the content of the original *shtar* cannot be adequately established — the witnesses' accounts are insufficient or the original text is entirely illegible — then *tzarich le-havi raya*, further proof is required and the substitute alone will not suffice for collection.

### Torn Documents

*Nikra pasul* — if a loan document or *ketubah* is torn, it is invalid. Tearing may indicate payment: the creditor may have torn the document upon receiving payment, as was the customary sign of discharge. One cannot simply present a torn document and demand a replacement, since the tearing itself is evidence that the debt was settled. However, *nitkarei kasher* — if the document was torn on its own, as opposed to clearly ripped by human hands, it remains valid and a replacement may be written. Similarly, *nimchak o nishtatash* — if erased or smudged — *im shemo nikar kasher*: if the content remains discernible, even if the ink has faded, the document is valid.

### Beis Din Tearing

The *gemara* asks: *heichi dami nikra heichi dami nitkarei* — what precisely distinguishes a humanly torn document from one torn on its own? *Amar Rav Yehuda*: *nikra kera shel beis din* — the invalidating tear is specifically the tear administered by a *beis din* to mark a document as paid and discharged. *Nitkarei kera she-eino beis din* — the tear that does not invalidate is one that does not follow the pattern of a *beis din* tear.

How does *beis din* tear a *shtar*? *Rav Yehuda* says: *makom eidim u-makom ha-zman u-makom ha-torof* — they tear through the critical sections: the witnesses' signatures, the date, and the *torof*, the substantive body of the document, the actual terms and amounts. *Abaye* says: *shesi va-erev* — they make a crisscross cut across the document. This crisscross tearing is recognizable as an intentional act of invalidation. It is also the practice today when a *ketubah* has been delivered and received — the officiants make a crisscross cut to mark it as no longer operative as an independent legal instrument.

## Pumbedisa Story

### Coercion Context

A story is now related. *Hanu arvaei* — there were certain Arabs who came to Pumbedisa, *de-havu ka-antsi a-arata de-inshei* — who were coercing people and forcing them to hand over their deeds to their land. Landowners, anticipating that they might soon be compelled to surrender their title documents under duress, came to Abaye before this occurred. They presented their deeds to establish their legitimate ownership and made a request: *ve-lichtav lan mar shtar achrina alei* — could the master write them a duplicate deed? *De-im mintsis chad netinan chad biyadan* — that if they are forced to hand over one copy under coercion, they will retain the other and be able to prove their ownership.

This is not an unreasonable request on its face. But the potential for abuse is obvious: with two valid deeds in hand, a person could sell the land, pocket the proceeds, and then produce the second deed to claim ownership again. Or in cases involving *achrayus*, he could collect reimbursement twice if the land were seized by a creditor. Abaye was therefore unwilling to comply.

### Abaye Refuses

*Amar lehu*: *mai avid lachon* — what can I do for you? I cannot help you. *De-amar Rav Safra: ein kotvin shnei shtaros al sada achas* — Rav Safra ruled that one may not write two deeds on a single field. *Dilma teref ve-hadar teref* — the fear is that the holder will collect and then collect again.

### Double Collection

The *gemara* elaborates the mechanism of abuse: suppose Reuven sold a field to a buyer with an *achrayus* clause — if a creditor of Reuven's subsequently seizes the field to collect a prior debt, the buyer is entitled to be reimbursed by Reuven. Now suppose the buyer has two copies of the deed. The creditor seizes the field; the buyer collects reimbursement from Reuven's other assets — say, from another purchaser of Reuven's land. That purchaser demands the deed as evidence that the buyer has received his compensation. The buyer hands over one copy. But he still holds the second copy. He then approaches yet another purchaser of Reuven's land and presents the second deed as though he has never been reimbursed, and collects a second time. The prohibition against two deeds on one field exists precisely to prevent this.

### Invalid Document

The landowners continued to pressure Abaye. *Hava katardy lay* — they were pressing him. Abaye then said to his scribe: *zil ktov lahu hu al ha-machak ve-eidim al ha-niyar de-pasul* — go write them a document, but make it an invalid one. Write the deed itself on *klaf* that has been previously erased — *al ha-machak* — and have the witnesses sign on clean, unerased *klaf* at the bottom. As we have already learned, this configuration is invalid: when the body of the document is on erased parchment, we are suspicious that the original text was scraped away and new content substituted. The witnesses are signing something whose top may have been altered.

This solution is deeply troubling. Abaye was directing his scribe to produce a document that the recipients would believe to be valid but that was in fact legally worthless. One might raise serious concerns about *zilusa de-bei dina* — the dignity and integrity of the court — in authorizing such a deception. The *gemara* does not offer a defense of this conduct, and one is left to surmise that Abaye found himself in an impossible position under sustained pressure, and chose this as the least harmful path available.

### Rav Aha Objection

*Amar lay Rav Aha bar Minyumi le-Abaye*: there is a problem with this plan. He understood Abaye's instruction to mean that a valid existing *shtar* would be erased and the new deed written on top of that erased surface. He pointed to the *mishna*: *nimchak o nishtatash — im shemo nikar kasher* — if a document was erased or smudged but the original lettering remains visible, even faintly, the document is still valid. If the original *shtar* beneath is still partially legible, the document the people are receiving might inadvertently be valid — not because of the new text written on top, which is on *machak*, but because the original text beneath is still operative. They would then be holding a valid document after all.

### Abaye Clarifies

Abaye replied: *mi kamina shtar ma'alya? Aleph-beis be-alma kamina* — I never said to erase an actual valid *shtar*. What I said was: write out nonsense, *aleph-beis gimel dalet*, meaningless letters, and then erase that. Then write the deed on top of the erased nonsense, with the witnesses on the clean parchment below. There is no underlying valid document whose lingering legibility could rescue the result. The entire thing — deed on erased nonsense — is invalid, and that is exactly what Abaye intended.

The troubling nature of this entire episode remains. Abaye was knowingly issuing an invalid document to deceive people who were being victimized by coercive forces, and the *gemara* records it without editorial comment.

## Lost Documents

### Lost Note Rule

The *gemara* now turns to a *baraisa*: *harei she-ba ve-amar avad shtar hovi* — someone who comes and says he has lost his promissory note. *Af al pi she-amru eidim anu kasavnu ve-hasamnu ve-nasatnu lo* — even if the original witnesses come forward and say, we wrote it, we signed it, we gave it to him — *ein kotvin lo et ha-shtar* — you do not write a replacement *shtar*. How does this differ from the *mishna*'s case where witnesses testify to the content of an erased document and a substitute is written? The distinction is critical: in the *mishna*'s case, the original document is present, visible, and can be destroyed before the substitute is issued. Here, the original document is nowhere to be found. The claimant says he lost it — but perhaps he did not. Perhaps he will find it. If a replacement is issued and he subsequently produces the original, he will be able to collect the same debt twice.

### Double Collection Risk

This is the same concern that animated the prohibition against two deeds on one field: *dilma teref ve-hadar teref* — we fear he will collect once on the replacement and again when the original surfaces. The asymmetry between the erased-document case and the lost-document case is therefore not about evidentiary sufficiency — the witnesses in both cases may be equally credible — but about the physical control of the original instrument.

### Sale Exception

*Bamei devarim amurim* — when does this prohibition apply? *Be-shtarei halva'ah* — with promissory notes, for the reason just given. *Aval shtarei mekach u-mimkar kotvin chutz min ha-achrayus she-bo* — but with bills of sale, one may write a replacement, provided the replacement does not contain an *achrayus* clause. The absence of *achrayus* means the holder cannot use the document to collect reimbursement from others if the field is seized. Since the double-collection mechanism depends on *achrayus*, removing it from the replacement document eliminates the practical risk.

This seems, at first glance, to conflict with the Pumbedisa story, where Abaye refused to write a duplicate deed even for parties acting in evident good faith. One might ask: why not simply issue them a second deed without *achrayus*? The *gemara* will need to address this tension — and indeed, the two cases may not be as parallel as they appear, since the *baraisa* is discussing a lost document that may yet resurface, while the Pumbedisa case involves a deliberate duplication.

### Rabban Shimon

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* takes a stricter position: *af be-shtarei mekach u-mimkar ein kotvin* — even for bills of sale, no replacement document is written. His reasoning emerges from his broader view of how documents function in property transactions.

### Document Return

*Ve-chein haya Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer*: if someone gave a gift to another and the recipient returned the document to the giver, *chazra matanaso* — the gift is reversed. Returning the deed reverses the transaction. The *chachamim* disagree: *matanaso kayemet* — the return of the document does not undo the transfer.

This disagreement illuminates Rabban Shimon's stricter stance on replacement documents. In his view, the document is not merely evidence of a transaction — it has a constitutive role. If a seller claims he no longer has his *shtar* but in fact he returned it to the original seller (perhaps because the sale was reversed and he received payment for the reversion), a replacement *shtar* would allow him to claim the sale was never undone — that he lost the document, not that he gave it back. Rabban Shimon therefore prohibits replacement sale documents entirely, since their potential for enabling precisely this deception is too great. This will be unpacked further in the continuation of the discussion.

# Bava Batra 169

## Lost Documents Rule

### Braita Intro

The *braita* at the close of 168b is the subject around which the entirety of today's *daf* revolves. The *braita* opens with the following case: *harei sheba ve'amar avad shtar chovi* — someone comes forward and declares that he has lost the document recording a debt owed to him. Even if the original witnesses to that document come forward and testify — *af al pi she'amru eidim anu chasamnu venasanu bo* — that they were indeed the signatories and can vouch for the underlying transaction, *ein kosvin oso shtar*: we do not write him a replacement *shtar*.

### Why No Loan Rewrite

The reason is straightforward. Even granting that the claimant is entirely truthful about having lost the document, the risk of issuing a replacement is too great. He may yet find the original, leaving him with two *shtarot* each attesting that the same borrower owes him the same sum — and the temptation or opportunity to collect twice becomes real. Accordingly, no replacement *shtar* for a loan may be issued.

### Sale Docs Allowed

The *braita* continues: *bamei devarim amurim b'shtarei halvaa* — this rule applies specifically to loan documents. But *aval b'shtarei mekach u'mimkar kosvin chutz min achrayus shebo*: when the lost document was a bill of sale rather than a loan note, a replacement may be written — with one critical omission: the *achrayus* clause must be left out.

To appreciate why this distinction matters, consider the mechanics. If someone purchased a field from a seller and has lost his *shtar*, the core concern — that he owns the field — is not in doubt. Provided the witnesses testify to the original transaction and the replacement *shtar* bears the original date (not today's date, which would invite a separate abuse), what further danger remains? The answer lies in *achrayus*. Every bill of sale carries, explicitly or implicitly, a warranty: if the purchased field is subsequently seized by a creditor of the seller in satisfaction of a prior debt, the buyer is entitled to be reimbursed. Moreover, because the *achrayus* provision creates a lien dating back to the moment of the original sale, the buyer may collect that reimbursement not only from the seller directly but from anyone who subsequently purchased property from the seller — since those later buyers took their property already encumbered by this earlier lien.

The scheme that *achrayus* enables with a duplicate *shtar* runs as follows. Suppose the buyer produces one *shtar* — the replacement — and uses it to collect reimbursement from one of the seller's later buyers, claiming the field was seized from him in payment of the seller's debt. He then produces the original (which he "lost" but in fact retained) and uses it to collect again from a second buyer of the seller's property. The result is double collection from two different parties, each of whom thought he was buying free-and-clear property. To prevent this, the replacement *shtar* is issued without *achrayus*. A *shtar* lacking *achrayus* establishes the buyer's ownership of the field but confers no right of reimbursement whatsoever — *lo mimshabdei v'lo minichsei*, not from encumbered property and not from the seller's own assets. It is purely a title document. As a result, if the buyer were to produce both the original and the replacement, the replacement without *achrayus* would be useless for collecting from anyone, and the fraud is forestalled.

## Achrayus & Liens

### Liens on Sales

To understand how the *achrayus* mechanism actually operates, it is worth tracing the full chain of liability. A seller conveys a field to a buyer with *achrayus*. That *achrayus* places a lien on all property the seller subsequently sells: if the purchased field is one day seized to satisfy a debt the seller owed to some creditor, the buyer may demand reimbursement — and if the seller lacks personal assets, the buyer may seize property from those who bought from the seller after the original transaction, since their property was encumbered from the moment the earlier sale occurred. In practice, this means that the date of the original sale is determinative: any property the seller disposed of after that date is potentially subject to the buyer's lien.

### Double Collect

The double-collection scheme can now be reconstructed in detail. Let us call the original seller Reuven, the original buyer Dov, and the creditor Shimon. Reuven owes Shimon money. Shimon seizes the field Reuven had sold to Dov, in satisfaction of the debt. Dov, armed with his *shtar* containing *achrayus*, now goes to the people who purchased property from Reuven after Dov's original purchase — call them buyer number one and buyer number two — and seeks reimbursement. To do so, Dov must demonstrate to each of these buyers that the field was genuinely seized from him in payment of Reuven's debt; this typically requires Shimon to produce his court-issued authorization and confirm that he did indeed seize the field in satisfaction of a legitimate debt.

If Dov genuinely lost his *shtar* and was issued a replacement also bearing *achrayus*, he is now holding two *shtarot* both bearing the original date and both carrying the insurance clause. He uses the first to collect from buyer number one — a legitimate collection, since the field genuinely was seized. He then approaches Shimon: "Leave the field with me a while longer and we will go through the process again in a few years, and I will collect from buyer number two." After a suitable interval — long enough that courts and parties will have forgotten the earlier proceedings — Shimon again formally seizes the field, and Dov presents his second *shtar* to collect from buyer number two. The fraud succeeds because the two seizures are separated by enough time that nobody connects them.

## Lost Documents Rule (II)

### RSG Disagrees

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disputes even the leniency permitted by the Sages. *Ve-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer af shtar mecher shemachru ein kosvin* — not even a replacement bill of sale may be issued, even without the *achrayus* clause. His reasoning draws on a further ruling he articulates: *ha-noten matana l'chaveiro ve-hechezir lo es ha-shtar chazra matanaso* — one who gave a gift to another and subsequently returned the original *shtar* to the original owner has effectively reversed the gift. *Aval Chachamim omrim matanaso kayemes* — but the Sages disagree, holding that returning the *shtar* does not reverse the transfer.

### RSG Concern

The logic of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position is as follows. Just as a field may be acquired through the delivery of a *shtar*, so the return of that same *shtar* to the original owner functions as a reversal of the transfer, restoring ownership to him. If this is true, then when a buyer claims he has "lost" his *shtar*, the court cannot dismiss out of hand the possibility that the reason he no longer holds it is that he voluntarily returned it to the seller — thereby reversing the sale and restoring the field to the seller. If we write the buyer a replacement *shtar*, we may be enabling him to fabricate a claim of ownership in a field that is now legitimately the seller's again.

### Tosafos Solution

Tosafos raises a compelling difficulty with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position — one that he himself acknowledges is ripe for abuse. The *halacha* permits a seller to have a *shtar* drawn up by a scribe in anticipation of a sale, and this can be done without the buyer present. It is therefore possible for a seller, before delivering a *shtar* to the buyer, to have gone to one scribe and had one *shtar* prepared, and then gone to a second scribe and had an identical second *shtar* prepared. He delivers the first to the buyer. If the buyer later claims to have lost his *shtar*, the seller — according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — can simply produce the duplicate he had prepared from the second scribe and assert: "The reason the buyer no longer has his *shtar* is that he returned it to me, and I accepted it; that reversed the sale." The buyer cannot disprove this, because the seller is genuinely holding a copy.

The practical upshot, according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, is that the buyer must guard his *shtar* carefully. The Sages, by contrast, hold that returning a *shtar* does not reverse a sale — and therefore even if the seller produces a duplicate, it does not prove that the buyer voluntarily surrendered his ownership.

## Achrayus & Liens (II)

### Rav Safra Logic

The *Gemara* now turns to unpack the Sages' ruling. *Amar Mar: chutz me'achrayus shebo — mai ta'ama?* What is the precise rationale for disqualifying the *achrayus* clause from a replacement *shtar*? Rav Safra explains: *lefi she'ein kosvin shnei shtarot al sadei achat* — one simply does not write two *shtarot* for the same field both bearing *achrayus*. The concern is the double-collection scheme described above.

### Creditor Role

The mechanics of that scheme require some elaboration. Dov seeks reimbursement from buyer number one by claiming that the field was seized from him in satisfaction of Reuven's debt to Shimon. But buyer number one will not simply take Dov's word for it. He will want confirmation that the field was genuinely seized, that Shimon had legitimate court authorization to seize it, and that Dov is therefore truly entitled to reimbursement. This means Shimon must play a role in the process: he must produce the court documentation establishing his right to seize — the *beis din* authorization — confirming that Reuven failed to pay and that Shimon was entitled to collect from encumbered property. Only once buyer number one is satisfied on all these points will he accept Dov's claim and hand over reimbursement.

Now Dov approaches buyer number two with the second *shtar*. The same evidentiary demand will be made: prove that the field was seized. Dov again needs Shimon to cooperate — to appear or produce documentation confirming a second seizure. This is the scheme's critical vulnerability: Shimon must effectively seize the same field twice.

### Destruction Issue

This is where the scheme faces its most serious structural obstacle. From the moment Shimon moves to seize the field, Reuven — whose debt is being collected — will demand that the original *shtar chov*, the note establishing the debt, be torn up. It makes no sense for Reuven to allow Shimon to seize his property without receiving back the *shtar* that purports to obligate him, lest Shimon collect again later on a document that no longer reflects any outstanding obligation. The *Gemara* therefore asks: once the debt note has been torn up, how can Shimon go through the seizure process a second time? He no longer holds any documentation establishing that Reuven owes him anything.

## Seizure Process

### Tear Up Note

Rav Nachman resolves this by laying down a formal rule about how the seizure process operates: *kol tirfa delo kasiv beh kar'ina leshtara demilve lav tirfa hu* — any seizure document that does not itself state "we have torn up the original debt note" is not a valid seizure document at all. In other words, the court will not issue authorization for Shimon to seize property unless the original *shtar chov* is physically torn up at the moment the authorization is issued. This is a built-in safeguard: the very validity of the seizure documentation is conditioned on the destruction of the underlying debt note, ensuring that the same debt cannot be used to seize twice.

### Three Stages

The process of collecting on a debt through property seizure actually involves three sequential documents, each of which must explicitly reference and supersede the one before it.

The first is the *tirfa*. The *tirfa* is issued by *beis din* in response to the creditor's claim that the debtor has not paid. It authorizes the creditor to go out and identify property — whether still in the debtor's hands or in the hands of those who purchased encumbered property from him — that can satisfy the debt. At the moment the *tirfa* is issued, the original *shtar chov* is torn up; *kol tirfa delo kasiv beh kar'ina leshtara demilve lav tirfa hu*. Any *tirfa* that does not record the destruction of the original debt note is invalid.

The second document is the *adrachta*. Once the creditor has identified a specific piece of property that he wishes to claim, he returns to *beis din* and the *tirfa* is superseded by the *adrachta*, which specifies the particular field in question and formally authorizes seizure of that field. The *adrachta* must itself record that the *tirfa* has been torn up: *kol adrachta delo kasiv beh kar'ina letirfa lav adrachta hi*.

The third document is the *shuma*, the assessment. Even once the creditor holds an *adrachta* authorizing him to take a specific field, it remains to be determined how much of the outstanding debt that field actually satisfies — that is, what the field is worth relative to the total sum owed. The *shuma* is the formal valuation, and it likewise must reference the cancellation of the *adrachta*: *kol shuma delo kasiv beh kar'ina le'adrachta lav shuma hi*. Each stage in the chain therefore renders the prior stage null, ensuring that no document in the sequence can be reused to seize additional property.

### Original Ownership

Given this comprehensive system of document destruction, the *Gemara* asks: how is the double-collection scheme even theoretically possible? Once Shimon has gone through the entire process of seizing the field the first time, every document he held that gave him the right to do so has been torn up. He holds no *shtar chov*, no *tirfa*, no *adrachta*. On what basis could he claim the field a second time?

The *Gemara* answers: *lo tzricha d'ka'asi mi'koach d'avasai* — the concern arises not from a re-seizure on the basis of debt but from a claim of original ownership. Shimon (in our scheme, or whoever is playing his role) does not return as a creditor claiming Reuven owes him money. Instead he returns as a claimant who asserts that this field was always his — that it belonged to his fathers and was wrongfully taken from him, that Reuven essentially stole it. A claim of original ownership does not arise from the debt documentation at all; it is a separate cause of action that requires no *shtar chov* and is not affected by the destruction of the debt-collection documents. If such a claim is established, the field is removed from Dov's possession — and Dov, holding his second *shtar* with *achrayus*, is again entitled to seek reimbursement from buyer number two.

### Same Day Question

Rav Acha of Difti poses a question to Ravina: why bother with the elaborate scheme of waiting years before making the second claim? *V'lama lei l'meimar lei l'ba'al chov shofli v'behai ara v'eikum bah* — why does Dov need to say to Shimon "leave the field with me a while; hold off and then come claim it again in a few years"? Why not simply seize from buyer number one and buyer number two in rapid succession, effectively the same day? *Tipok lei d'keivan d'nakit teri shtarei taraf v'hadar taraf* — if he is holding two *shtarot* he could simply collect twice in immediate succession.

The *Gemara* answers: *im hachi nefishi lei ba'alei dinin* — if both collections happen at the same time or in very close succession, there will be a proliferation of litigants and word will spread quickly. People will discover that the same claimant is simultaneously asserting the field was seized in two different proceedings, and the fraud will be exposed. The scheme therefore depends on temporal separation: collect once, let the matter go quiet, and return years later before a different court that has no knowledge of the earlier proceedings.

## Receipt Solution

### Shovar Proposal

The *Gemara* now turns to whether there is any way to issue a replacement *shtar* with *achrayus* while still protecting the parties at risk. The proposal: *v'lichtov l'hai shtar ma'alya v'lichtov tavra l'mocher* — write the buyer a proper *shtar* with *achrayus*, and simultaneously write the seller a receipt — a *tavra*, or *shovar* — that explicitly invalidates any prior *shtarot*. The text of that receipt would read: *kol shtarei d'yaifku al ar'ah da psulin l'var min d'yaifuk b'zimna da* — any documents purporting to establish ownership of this field are invalid, except for the one issued at this particular time, i.e., the replacement *shtar*. The scheme is then foiled: the original *shtar*, should Dov try to produce it, is explicitly declared null by the seller's receipt. Only the designated replacement is valid.

The proposal also requires thinking through how the earlier scheme involved leapfrogging the seller. The earlier analysis assumed that Dov could proceed directly against buyer number one and buyer number two without involving Reuven at all — Reuven was not party to the scheme, and somehow could be bypassed. This new proposal imagines that Reuven will in fact always be drawn into any proceeding in which Dov attempts to collect, and once Reuven is involved he can produce the receipt that invalidates the original *shtar*. Rather than relying merely on Reuven verbally protesting — where it would be his word against Dov's — the receipt gives him documentation.

### Leapfrog Problem

This proposal was raised before Rav Pappa and before Rav Ashi. The *Gemara* rejects it, and the rejection turns precisely on the leapfrog problem. *D'dilma azil ba'al chov v'taref minei d'lokeach* — what happens if Dov simply goes directly to buyer number one and seizes from him without involving Reuven at all? Buyer number one, if he purchased his field with *achrayus*, will then want to seek reimbursement from Reuven, and Reuven will produce the receipt — but in the interim Dov has already seized the property. Moreover — and this is the *Gemara*'s more pointed objection — *v'shover gabi lekuchos leika*: the receipt is in the seller's possession, not in the possession of the buyers. The buyers do not have the receipt. If Dov can get to buyer number one or buyer number two before Reuven is pulled into the picture, the receipt does them no good.

The *Gemara* then anticipates an objection: surely the buyers will eventually bring the seller in, and once he is in the proceedings he will produce the receipt, the improper collection will be reversed, and Dov will be forced to return whatever he took. The *Gemara* dismisses this with a practical observation: *ad'hachi v'hachi shamit v'achil peiri* — in the meantime, while all the litigation is grinding forward, Dov has been living on that land or consuming its produce for years. By the time the matter is sorted out and a reversal ordered, those benefits have already been consumed and may be practically unrecoverable. The receipt mechanism is therefore not a satisfactory solution.

### Loan vs Land

One might press the point further: can the buyer simply leapfrog the seller in the first place? If someone purchased fields from the seller and has *achrayus*, are they not in a position to say — before handing over anything — "prove to us that you first exhausted your claim against the seller directly"? And if they insist on that, the seller would be involved from the outset, and the receipt would become effective. This question is not left unasked. The *Gemara* addresses it by distinguishing between loan cases and land cases.

In the loan case — where a creditor holds a *shtar chov* against a borrower, collects from the borrower, and then the borrower seeks to give him a receipt rather than getting the *shtar* back — the *Gemara* explains that the buyers of the borrower's property will naturally insist on involving the borrower before they yield their land. They will say: you are owed money; the primary obligor is the borrower; we are only a backup. Show us the borrower actually cannot pay before you come after our land. This forces the borrower into the proceedings, he produces the receipt, and the system functions.

### Land Not Cash

Here, however, the situation differs because what Dov is owed is not money but land. *Mi yad'ei de-man de-massik ara bezuzi lo m'fayis* — it is understood that a person whose entitlement is to land will not be satisfied with a monetary payment in lieu.
