The buyers therefore may recognize that they cannot simply point Dov to the seller and say "have him pay you in cash." Dov is owed land specifically, and that is why he may proceed directly against them. This is what enables the leapfrog, at least in the *Gemara*'s framing — though Tosafos himself raises the question sharply: if the seller does in fact have money, why should the buyers not insist that the seller pay first and thereby keep themselves out of the proceeding? If the seller can pay, why would the buyers allow their fields to be taken without first forcing the seller to be involved? Tosafos acknowledges the difficulty without resolving it fully, noting that the *Gemara*'s position seems to be that a person owed land may simply proceed against the encumbered property without first going to the seller, even if the seller might have assets. The matter remains somewhat difficult.

In any event, the conclusion stands: the *shovar* mechanism does not solve the problem, and therefore there is no way to issue a replacement *shtar* with *achrayus*. If the buyer loses his *shtar*, he may receive a replacement — but it will carry no *achrayus*. That is the price of carelessness with one's documents.

## Shtar Lo B'Achrayus

### Rava Default

The *Gemara* now turns to the broader question of what it means, in ordinary transactions, for a *shtar* to be written without *achrayus*. The question pivots on whether the absence of an explicit *achrayus* clause is itself meaningful or whether *achrayus* is always presumed as the default.

### Rav Ashi View

Rava and Rav Ashi dispute this directly. Rava holds: *achrayus ta'os sofer hu* — the omission of *achrayus* from a *shtar* is treated as a scribal error. *Achrayus* is always assumed to be intended; if it does not appear in the document it is because it was inadvertently left out, not because the parties wished to exclude it. Therefore, even a *shtar* that lacks an explicit *achrayus* clause is treated as if it contains one. Rav Ashi disagrees: *achrayus lav ta'os sofer hu* — the absence of *achrayus* is not a scribal error. If it was not written, it was not intended, and the *shtar* genuinely lacks warranty.

### Woman Story

An instructive case is recorded. A woman gave money to an agent to go purchase land on her behalf. The agent went and bought the land — but the *shtar* he obtained was written *shelo be'achrayus*, explicitly excluding the warranty. The woman came before Rav Nachman.

### Explicit Exclusion

Rav Nachman's position — consistent with his ruling that the *braita*'s replacement *shtar* must explicitly say there is no warranty, which itself proves that warranty is the default — is that the agent acted improperly. He was dispatched to act in the woman's best interest, and purchasing land without *achrayus* is simply not in anyone's best interest; it is never an acceptable outcome even if the agent secured a lower price, because the insurance on the land is a fundamental part of what the buyer needs.

### Nachman Solution

Rav Nachman does not, however, simply declare the original sale void and direct the parties to renegotiate from scratch. His remedy is more targeted: *zil zavna minei shelo be'achrayus vehadar zavnah nihala be'achrayus* — go buy the land from the original seller in your own name without *achrayus* (at the lower price the seller is willing to accept), and then turn around and sell it to the woman with *achrayus*. In other words, the agent must now personally absorb the risk: he buys the land without warranty and then resells it to the woman with full warranty, effectively providing the insurance himself out of his own obligation. This is a striking outcome — in effect, the agent is being penalized by being forced to stand behind the warranty personally — but it follows from the principle that an agent who acts outside the scope of his authorization cannot impose the consequences of that unauthorized act on his principal. This raises a broader point that recurs throughout the *Gemara*: the doctrine that a *shaliach* who acts contrary to the *meshale'ach*'s interests renders the *shlichus* void is in tension with the practical expectation that transactions conducted through agents will be stable. But that tension is not resolved here.

## Shtar Return Issue

### RSG Reversal

The *Gemara* returns to the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages regarding the effect of returning a *shtar*. *Ve-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer ha-nosen matana l'chaveiro ve-hechezir lo es ha-shtar chazra matanaso* — if one gives a gift to another and the recipient returns the *shtar* to the giver, the gift is reversed.

### Chachamim No Reversal

*Aval Chachamim omrim matanaso kayemes* — the Sages hold that the return of the *shtar* does not reverse the gift or sale. Ownership, once transferred, is not undone by the mere physical return of the document.

### Conditional Theory

The *Gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama de-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — what is the reasoning behind his position? Rav Assi suggests: *na'aseh ke-omer lo sade zu netuna lecha kol zman she-ha-shtar beyadecha* — the sale or gift is implicitly conditioned on the recipient holding the *shtar*. The transfer is, in effect, valid only so long as the recipient retains the document; returning it dissolves the condition and undoes the transfer.

### Rava Objection

Rava objects sharply: *i hachi nignav o avad nami* — if the ownership is conditioned on holding the *shtar*, then if the *shtar* is stolen or lost, the sale would equally be reversed. That is clearly an unacceptable result. Nobody would agree that losing a document voids a completed property transfer. Rava therefore rejects Rav Assi's explanation and offers his own.

## Kinyan by Mesira

### Mesira Transfer

Rava's alternative explanation reframes the entire dispute in terms of a fundamental *machloket* in the law of acquisition: *be-osiyos niknos be-mesira kamiflagi* — the underlying disagreement is whether the content of a *shtar* — the *osiyos*, the letters — can be transferred through *mesira*, the act of physically handing over the document. This principle is familiar in the context of transferring a debt: if Reuven holds a *shtar* establishing that Shimon owes him money, can Reuven sell that debt to a third party simply by handing over the *shtar*? The question is whether *osiyos niknos be-mesira* — whether the letters that constitute the legal content of the document are acquired by the very act of having the document handed to you.

### Rava Position

Rava holds that *osiyos niknos be-mesira*: yes, handing over the *shtar* does transfer what the *shtar* represents. This principle applies in the context of debt transfer, where the question is whether simply delivering the *shtar chov* to a new holder suffices to transfer the claim to that holder, or whether a new *shtar* must be written in the new holder's name.

### Return Property

The extension to *karka* is direct. If a seller once used a *shtar* as the instrument of *kinyan* to transfer a field to a buyer — delivery of the *shtar* being the very act that completed the buyer's acquisition — then the return of that same *shtar* to the seller operates as another *mesira*, another delivery. Just as the original delivery of the *shtar* from seller to buyer transferred the field to the buyer, the return of that *shtar* from buyer to seller transfers it back. The buyer, by handing the document back, is in effect re-executing the *kinyan* in the seller's favor. This is the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel according to Rava's analysis.

### Chachamim Pos

The Sages, by contrast, hold *ein osiyos niknos be-mesira* — the letters are not acquired through the mere act of handing over the document. A *shtar* for *karka* is the instrument of *kinyan* when executed as such, but the subsequent physical transfer of that document back and forth does not operate as a new *kinyan* with each exchange. Ownership, once vested, does not shift based on who is physically holding the *shtar* at any given moment. Accordingly, returning the *shtar* to the seller does not reverse the sale, and the Sages rule that the gift or sale remains in force. The discussion of this foundational *machloket* — and its many ramifications for the law of document transfer — will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Bava Batra 170

## Otiyot Niknas Bimesira

### Rabban Shimon on Doc Ret…

The sugya opens by revisiting a dispute from the preceding amud (169b) concerning whether the return of a sale document to the original seller reverses the transaction. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that it does, while the Rabbis disagree. The *gemara* now locates the source of that disagreement in a broader, foundational principle.

### Letters Acquired by Tran…

*Rabbah* identifies the crux of the dispute: *ba'otiyot niknas bimesira kamipligi* — the debate turns on whether documents are acquired, and their legal content transferred, by the mere act of physical handover. The classic illustration of this principle concerns a loan document: if Reuven holds an IOU establishing that Gloria owes him a thousand dollars, and he hands that document to David with the intent of transferring the debt, does David thereby become the new creditor? According to the position that *otiyot niknas bimesira* — letters are acquired by transfer — the answer is yes; the physical act of handing over the document accomplishes the legal conveyance, even though the document names a different obligee.

Here the *gemara* applies this principle not to a loan document but to a sale document. Suppose a deed records that in a given year Gloria sold her plot of land to Reuven, and ten years later Reuven hands that very document to David with the intent of conveying his interest. Even though the document names Gloria and Reuven, the act of transfer, according to those who hold *otiyot niknas bimesira*, accomplishes a new *kinyan*. This is a novel mode of acquisition: we are familiar with land being acquired through a *shtar* written in the buyer's name, but this would be a *kinyan* effected by the transfer of someone else's deed.

### Land Sale Application

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that *otiyot niknas bimesira* is operative — documents can be transferred by handover — and therefore, handing the sale deed back to the original seller functions precisely as a conveyance to a third party would: it transfers the land back. The Rabbis, by contrast, hold *ein otiyot niknas bimesira* — documents are not acquired by mere transfer. Consequently, returning the deed accomplishes nothing; to reverse the sale one would need either a new *shtar* or some other act of *kinyan*. Having established this framework, the *gemara* now turns to a second *baraita* to examine whether the same debate underlies it as well.

---

## Haba Lidon (Version 1)

### Shtar vs. Chazaka

The *baraita* states: *haba lidon bishtar uvachazaka* — one who comes to adjudicate by means of both a *shtar* and a *chazaka*. The *baraita* then records a dispute: *nidon bishtar* — Rabbi holds one must litigate by means of the *shtar* — while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says *bechazaka* — one litigates by means of the *chazaka*.

The terms *shtar* and *chazaka* are notably ambiguous here, and the *gemara* will offer several distinct readings of the *baraita* before arriving at its preferred interpretation. The straightforward reading might be that the *shtar* serves as proof of ownership while the *chazaka* refers to *chazakat gimmel shanim*, the presumption of ownership arising from three years of undisturbed possession — and indeed that is ultimately the most natural reading of the *baraita*, which the *gemara* will reach at the end. However, most of the intermediate interpretations read *shtar* and *chazaka* not as modes of proof but as modes of *kinyan* — acts by which possession of the land is formally acquired. The case: both parties agree that a sale was contemplated, but the seller now disputes whether the sale was ever finalized. The buyer claims he already acquired the land. The question is: through what act did he acquire it — a *shtar* or a *chazaka* (meaning some act of physical possession, such as making a small improvement to the property)?

On this reading, the *baraita's* question is not which form of proof should be presented in court, but which act of acquisition is valid. And the difficulty is immediately apparent: why would either mode of acquisition not be sufficient? Each one ordinarily establishes ownership perfectly well.

### Rav Dimi Explains

When Rav Dimi arrived from Eretz Yisrael, he explained that Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in this *baraita* are likewise debating *otiyot niknas bimesira*. On this reading, the seller had originally purchased the land from a prior owner — call her Gloria — and received a deed. He now wishes to transfer the land to the buyer by handing over Gloria's original deed, which of course bears Gloria's name and the seller's name, not the buyer's name. The question is: does the act of handing over this old deed — not written in the buyer's name — constitute a valid *kinyan*?

Rabbi says *nidon bishtar*: the old deed works, for *otiyot niknas bimesira* — the transfer of the document itself accomplishes the acquisition. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says *bechazaka*: handing over a deed not written in the buyer's name cannot effect a *kinyan*; the buyer must instead perform an act of physical *chazaka* to acquire the property.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye raises a pointed objection: if Rav Dimi's reading of the second *baraita* is correct, then the positions of Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel are reversed between the two *baraitot*. In the first *baraita*, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel held that *otiyot niknas bimesira* — handing back the deed reverses the sale. Here, on Rav Dimi's reading, it is Rabbi who holds *otiyot niknas bimesira* while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires a *chazaka* instead. The positions appear to have flipped.

Rav Dimi — or Rabbah — concedes the difficulty. *V'tisplog* — fine, this presents a problem for that interpretation. The point, Abaye clarifies, is that once Rabbah's reading of the first *baraita* is accepted (namely, that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position there rests on *otiyot niknas bimesira*), one cannot simultaneously use Rav Dimi's reading of the second *baraita* without generating a contradiction within Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's own rulings. Something must give — either the reading of the first *baraita* or the reading of the second. Abaye therefore sets out to offer a different interpretation of the second *baraita* entirely.

---

## Pasul Ed Interpretation

### Flawed Witness Problem

Abaye's first alternative reading: *kegon shenimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* — the case involves a new *shtar* written in the buyer's name, but one of the two witnesses who signed it turns out to be a relative or otherwise disqualified (*karov o pasul*). The debate between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then concerns whether the buyer can nonetheless use the *shtar* to effect a *kinyan*, or whether the flaw in the signatures renders it unusable, leaving the *chazaka* as the only viable mode of acquisition.

### Edei Mesira/Chatima

The argument maps onto the well-known dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar regarding *edei mesira* and *edei chatima*. Rabbi Elazar holds *edei mesirah karti* — it is the witnesses who observe the handover of the document who effect the legal act, not those who signed it. Rabbi Meir holds *edei chatimah karti* — the signatures on the document are what give it legal force.

On this reading, Rabbi in our *baraita* follows Rabbi Elazar: the *shtar* is valid for acquisition even with a disqualified signatory, because the witnesses who observed the delivery (*edei mesirah*) are the ones that matter. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel follows Rabbi Meir: only the signed witnesses (*edei chatimah*) are operative, and since one is disqualified, the *shtar* cannot be used; the buyer must resort to *chazaka*.

### Valid Handing Witnesses

To be precise about the scenario: the witnesses who signed the document are invalid (one is *karov* or *pasul*), but the witnesses who observed the physical act of handing over the *shtar* are perfectly valid. The debate is thus a clean application of the *edei mesirah/edei chatimah* controversy. However, the *gemara* raises an immediate difficulty from a ruling of Rabbi Abba: *modeh hayah Rabbi Elazar bimzuyaf mitocho shepasul* — Rabbi Elazar himself concedes that if the document is internally corrupted — that is, if the flaw appears within the body of the document itself — even he would declare it invalid. A disqualified signatory, it seems, would constitute precisely such an internal flaw, leaving no one who would validate such a *shtar*. This second reading therefore cannot stand as presented.

---

## Ein Alav Edim

### No Witnesses Written

A third reading (*okimta*) is therefore offered. Rather than positing a *shtar* with a disqualified witness, we posit a *shtar* that bears no signed witnesses at all — *ein alav edim klal*. This cleanly avoids the problem of *mizuyaf mitocho*, since there is nothing internally wrong with the document; it simply lacks signatures entirely.

### Rabbi Abba Principle

The principle of Rabbi Abba — that Rabbi Elazar concedes in a case of *mizuyaf mitocho* — is thereby resolved. Where the document has a positive flaw (a disqualified signatory written into it), even Rabbi Elazar would invalidate it. But where the document simply has no witnesses at all, there is no internal corruption; the absence of signatures is a gap that *edei mesirah* can fill, according to Rabbi Elazar's position.

### Mesira vs. Chatima

On this final version of the reading, the *baraita* describes a *shtar* without any signed witnesses, and the debate is once again between *edei mesirah* and *edei chatimah*. Rabbi holds like Rabbi Elazar — *edei mesirah karti* — so the *shtar* is effective for *kinyan* by virtue of the witnesses who observed the handover, even with no signatures. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds like Rabbi Meir — *edei chatimah karti* — so without signed witnesses the *shtar* is inoperative, and the buyer must use a *chazaka* instead.

This gives us, in summary, three ways of explaining what the *shtar's* defect is, all within the frame of debating the *maaseh kinyan*: (1) it is an old *shtar* written in someone else's name, raising the question of *otiyot niknas bimesira*; (2) it has a disqualified signatory, which the *gemara* rejected because of Rabbi Abba's principle; and (3) it lacks signed witnesses entirely, which the *gemara* accepts as a clean application of *edei mesirah* versus *edei chatimah*. Still, the *gemara* notes that all of these readings frame the question as one of *maaseh kinyan* — does the *shtar* validly effect an acquisition? There remains a further and ultimately more natural reading in which the question is not about *kinyan* at all but about proof of title, which the *gemara* now introduces.

---

## Modeh Bashetar

### Validity Questions

The *gemara* introduces yet another way of reading the *baraita*, one that shifts the entire frame from the act of acquisition to the question of evidentiary proof. The scenario: the sale was completed, Michael is in possession of the land, but the original seller now disputes not the signatures themselves but the delivery — he claims he never handed the *shtar* over to Michael, that it fell from his pocket and Michael picked it up without any *kinyan* having been made. Michael, holding the *shtar*, insists the transaction was properly completed.

### Modeh Principle

Here the *gemara* invokes the principle of *modeh bashetar shekatavo eino tzarich lekaymo* — if the original party admits that the document was legitimately written (i.e., he does not claim forgery), the holder need not have the signatures validated in order to rely on it. The original party is effectively conceding the document's authenticity even while contesting the delivery. The logic is that *Chazal* required validation (*kiyum*) only when the document's authenticity was challenged; in the absence of such a challenge, a *shtar* bearing unchallenged signatures has legal force by virtue of those signatures alone.

One might ask why the holder cannot simply rely on a *migu* — the argument that since the original party could have denied the signatures entirely (and thereby defeated the claim outright), his more limited denial should be believed. The answer is that *migu* is beside the point: according to the principle of *modeh bashetar shekatavo eino tzarich lekaymo*, the *shtar* does not require validation in the first place when its authenticity is conceded. The *migu* the original party theoretically had — denying the signatures — was never exercised, and the document therefore stands as valid testimony that the land belongs to its holder.

On this reading, the *baraita's* dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel concerns not whether the *shtar* effects a *kinyan* but whether it suffices as proof of ownership: Rabbi holds *modeh bashetar shekatavo eino tzarich lekaymo* — the conceded *shtar* proves Michael's title without requiring further validation; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds *tzarich lekaymo* — even when the original party admits the document was legitimately written, the holder must have the signatures formally validated before the *shtar* can serve as evidence.

### Document as Proof

A closer look at the mechanism reveals something important. The premise of the entire discussion is that Michael is holding a *shtar* that was signed by valid witnesses, those signatures have not been challenged, and the original party concedes both facts while claiming only that delivery never occurred. The holding of a *shtar* bearing valid, unchallenged signatures is, from the *halachic* standpoint, equivalent to those witnesses testifying in court to the facts stated in the document. The document testifies that Michael owns the field; the holder's possession of the *shtar* is the mechanism by which that testimony is placed before the court.

The complication — acknowledged openly — is that the signatures establish only that the document was signed, not that it was delivered. Delivery might have occurred a moment after signing or not at all. The *halachic* force of the *shtar*, however, is that its production in *beis din* by the person for whom it speaks is treated as the document's testimony to the reality it describes. *Edei mesirah*, when required, would close the factual gap regarding delivery; but even without *edei mesirah*, the *shtar* functions as evidence in the view of those who do not require it.

The principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav hare'ayah* operates here as well: Michael, holding a valid *shtar* whose authenticity is uncontested, stands in the position of the *muchzak*; the seller who wishes to dispossess him bears the burden of proof. The seller's claim that delivery never occurred is a contention against a document that is already testifying on Michael's behalf.

---

## Shnayim Achuzin

### Lender/Borrower Dispute

The *gemara* now cites a *baraita* that presents an apparent contradiction: *shnayim achuzin bashtar* — two people are holding onto the same *shtar* simultaneously. The lender says the document is his — he claims it is still active because the debt was never paid, that it fell from his possession and the borrower found it. The borrower says the document belongs to him as well — he concedes it was the lender's, but claims he paid the debt and the *shtar* fell from him after payment.

### Rabbi's Position

Rabbi rules *yitekayem hashtar bechosamav* — the signatures on the *shtar* must be validated. The implication is that once validated, the lender would be entitled to collect, or at minimum to some portion of the debt.

### Rabban Shimon Split

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules *yachloku* — they divide it. The scenario is analogous to the classic case of *shnayim achuzin bitallis*: each party swears he owns no less than half, and the disputed object is split. Here, the division means the borrower pays half the face value of the *shtar*.

The *gemara* asks: how can Rabbi's position make sense? Even after the signatures are validated, the borrower is holding one end of the *shtar*. Just as in the *tallis* case, should each party not be entitled to only half? Why does Rabbi prescribe validation as the remedy?

### Unvalidated Debate

Rav Nachman resolves the difficulty by establishing the precise terms of the debate. When the *shtar* is already *mekuyam* — when the signatures have already been validated — there is no dispute: all agree the parties divide it, just as in the *tallis* case. The debate arises only *beshe'eino mekuyam*, when the *shtar* has not yet been validated.

In that situation, the borrower is claiming he paid the debt — that is, he concedes the *shtar* was legitimately written, but insists it is no longer operative. This is precisely the case of *modeh bashetar shekatavo*: the borrower admits the document's authenticity while contesting its current validity. Rabbi holds *tzarich lekaymo* — even with the borrower's admission that it was validly signed, the *shtar* is legally inert until formally validated. Therefore, until the lender obtains *kiyum*, he cannot collect even half — the *shtar* is *chaspa be'alma*, a mere shard of pottery. Once he does obtain *kiyum*, he collects half. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, by contrast, holds *eino tzarich lekaymo* — the borrower's concession that the document was validly written is sufficient to give it legal force, and so the *shtar* is already operative without formal validation, entitling the lender to half immediately.

This means that the positions of Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in this *baraita* are the reverse of what was attributed to them in the reading of *haba lidon bishtar uvachazaka*: there, Rabbi was said to hold *eino tzarich lekaymo* (the *shtar* suffices), while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was said to require *kiyum*. Here it is Rabbi who requires *kiyum* and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who says it is unnecessary. The *gemara* resolves this either by reversing (*eifoch*) one of the attributions, or by preferring the final reading of the *baraita* — to which the discussion now turns.

---

## Better Evidence Case

### Verbal Admission

The *gemara* arrives at what is in all likelihood the most natural reading of *haba lidon bishtar uvachazaka*. On this final interpretation, the *shtar* and *chazaka* are not alternative modes of *kinyan* but alternative modes of proof, and both are available to the litigant. The *chazaka* here refers to *chazakat gimmel shanim* — the presumption of ownership arising from three years of undisturbed possession. The *shtar* refers to an ownership deed. The question is: if a litigant claims to have both, must he produce the superior evidence (the *shtar*), or may he simply rely on the *chazaka*, which ordinarily suffices on its own?

Rabbi says *nidon bashtar* — once you have told the court that a *shtar* exists, you are required to produce it. *Chazaka* is in principle a substitute for a lost *shtar*, something one relies upon when the deed is unavailable. If you are claiming the deed exists, the court demands to see it. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says *bechazaka* — the *chazaka* is independently sufficient and you may always elect to litigate on that basis, regardless of whether a *shtar* also exists. The rule of *halacha* is like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

The *gemara* illustrates the practical import of this debate with a case involving Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef, who had lent money to Rabbi Abba.

### Payment Claim

There was no *shtar* in this case — the loan had been made without a written document. Rabbi Abba admitted the loan but claimed he had already repaid it, specifying that the repayment occurred in the presence of Ploni and Almoni (two named witnesses).

### Witness Demand

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha, acting as the *dayan*, responded: let Ploni and Almoni come and testify that the repayment took place.

### Loan Admission

Rabbi Abba objected: if they cannot come, am I not believed even without them? The established principle is *hamalveh chaveiro be'edim eino tzarich lefar'o be'edim* — one who lends money with witnesses present need not repay in front of witnesses. Rabbi Abba had borrowed without any *shtar*; his mere claim of repayment would ordinarily have been sufficient to close the case (subject perhaps to a rabbinic oath, *shvuat hesset*, but in principle fully credited). By volunteering the additional information that specific witnesses were present, he had provided more than the law required. Must he now be penalized for that candor?

### Witness Demand

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha replied pointedly: *ana beha'i shmeita demar sevira li* — I rule in accordance with the very principle that you yourself have established. For it is Rabbi Abba who transmitted in the name of Rav Adda bar Abba the ruling of Rav: *ha'omer lechaveiro peraticha bifnei ploni uploni, tzarich yavo ploni uploni veye'eidu* — one who tells his creditor "I paid you in the presence of Ploni and Almoni" must have Ploni and Almoni come and testify. Rabbi Abba had himself ruled this very case in theory; he was now its subject in practice.

Rabbi Abba then invoked the ruling of Rav Gidel in the name of Rav: *halacha kedivrei Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — the law follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds (on this final reading of the *baraita*) that one may always rely on the sufficient evidence, even if better evidence exists. His simple claim of repayment suffices; he need not produce the named witnesses.

### Lechatchila Requirement

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha responded: *halacha keRabban Shimon ben Gamliel ve'af Rebbi lo amar ela levarer* — the law indeed follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and furthermore, even Rabbi only ever stated his requirement *lechatchila* — as a matter of proper procedure. Rabbi's position, properly understood through the reading of *Tosafot*, is not that failure to produce the better evidence results in losing the case *bedieved*. Rather, when a litigant informs the court that superior evidence exists, the court will demand to see all available evidence before ruling. If ultimately it cannot be produced, the litigant still prevails on the basis of the sufficient evidence he does have.

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha then added: *ana nami levarer ka'amina* — that too was all I was saying. When I demanded that Ploni and Almoni come testify, I was not ruling that Rabbi Abba would lose if they failed to appear. I was demanding, as a matter of *lechatchila* procedure, that all available evidence be placed before the court. The demand to produce witnesses one has named is a preliminary requirement, not a condition for victory.

The *Rashbam* reads the exchange differently, holding that *bedieved* — if the named witnesses cannot be produced — the claim of repayment fails and the borrower loses. *Tosafot* disputes this, noting that the entire tone of the exchange suggests the demand is procedural only, and pointing to a further irony the *Rashbam* himself acknowledges: a different sugya rules that if one names witnesses to a repayment and they come to court but testify that they did not see the repayment, the borrower still prevails — on the reasoning that they may simply not have been paying attention at the time. The result, on the *Rashbam's* reading, would be paradoxical: if the witnesses don't come, the borrower loses; but if they come and deny witnessing the payment, the borrower wins. This difficulty strengthens the *Tosafot* reading that the witness demand is *lechatchila* only.

---

## Partial Payment Case

### Yachlif vs. Shovar

The *gemara* transitions to a new *mishnah* dealing with partial repayment of a debt. When a borrower has repaid part of the principal, the parties must decide how to document that fact. Rabbi Yehuda says *yachlif* — replace the original document with a new one reflecting only the remaining balance. Rabbi Yosi says *yichtov shovar* — the lender should write the borrower a receipt for the amount paid, with the original *shtar* remaining in force for the full amount.

### Receipt Loss Risk

Rabbi Yehuda objects to the receipt solution: *nimtza zeh tzarich lihyot shomer shovaro min ha'achbarim* — the result is that the borrower is now required to guard his receipt against the mice, or face repaying the portion he has already paid. Rather than creating this burden, simply replace the thousand-dollar *shtar* with an eight-hundred-dollar *shtar* and eliminate the risk entirely. The borrower already had to guard his assets against the original *shtar*; creating a second document he must preserve introduces an additional and unnecessary risk of loss.

### Creditor Standing

Rabbi Yosi responds: *kach yafe lo* — let the borrower bear that responsibility; and *lo yeira kocho shel zeh* — we must not diminish the lender's standing. The substance of Rabbi Yosi's concern is that replacing a thousand-dollar *shtar* with an eight-hundred-dollar *shtar* causes the lender real harm — specifically, the loss of liens. A *shtar* creates a lien (*shi'abud*) on real property the borrower owned from the time the loan was made. If the original *shtar* is torn up and replaced with a new one dated today, the lender loses all the liens he had acquired over the intervening period. Property that changed hands since the original loan was made — which was subject to collection under the original *shtar* — would no longer be encumbered.

### Beis Din Solution

*Rav Huna* transmitting in the name of *Rav* rules: *ein halacha lo k'Rabbi Yehuda velo k'Rabbi Yosi* — we rule neither like Rabbi Yehuda nor like Rabbi Yosi. Instead, *beis din mekri'in hashtar*, the *beis din* tears up the original *shtar*, *vekotvim lo shtar acher mizman rishon* — and writes a new *shtar* for the reduced amount, but dated from the original date. This resolves both concerns: the borrower has no vulnerable receipt to guard (Rabbi Yehuda's concern is met), and the lender suffers no loss of lien because the new document bears the original date (Rabbi Yosi's concern is met). As *Tosafot* notes, the critical phrase in Rav's formulation is *mizman rishon* — from the original time.

### Edim Authority

Rav Nachman (and alternatively Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba) asks Rav Huna: had Rav heard the following *baraita*, would he have maintained his formulation? The *baraita* states: *eidim mekri'in et hashtar vekotvim lo shtar acher mizman rishon* — the witnesses tear up the *shtar* and write a new one from the original date. This *baraita* appears to express in the name of Rabbi Yehuda exactly what Rav said — that the replacement *shtar* is dated from the original time. Had Rav known of it, he might have simply said he was ruling like Rabbi Yehuda as clarified by this *baraita*, rather than departing from the *mishnah* entirely.

Rav Huna responds on Rav's behalf: Rav knew of the *baraita* and did not retract. The reason is that Rav's formulation contains an additional and decisive innovation — not merely the *mizman rishon* dating, but the insistence that this be done specifically by *beis din*, not by the witnesses themselves.

### Beis Din vs. Edim

*Bishlama beis dina alimei l'afkuei mamona* — it is understandable that *beis din* has the authority to create new financial realities: the principle of *hefker beis din hefker* gives the court power to restructure property and monetary obligations in ways that would otherwise be impossible. A *beis din* can therefore issue a new *shtar* bearing an earlier date, creating liens retroactively, because it acts within its institutional authority to do so.

But the *baraita* attributes this power to the *eidim* — the witnesses themselves. *Ella eidim she'asu shelichutam chozrim ve'osim shelichutam?* — after the witnesses have already performed their function by signing the original *shtar*, how can they be authorized to come back and perform it again in a different form, creating a new document of eight hundred dollars dated from the original time? Once witnesses have signed a *shtar*, their role is discharged. To issue a new predated *shtar* requires the authority of *beis din*, not merely that of the original signatories.

This, then, is Rav's *chiddush*: not the *mizman rishon* dating — the *baraita* says that as well — but the requirement that this procedure be carried out specifically by *beis din*. The witnesses who signed the original *shtar* lack the institutional authority to create a retroactively dated replacement document; only *beis din*, acting under the principle of *hefker beis din hefker*, possesses that power. The *gemara* leaves this issue open for the subsequent discussion.

---

---

# Bava Batra 171

## Rewriting After Partial…

### Mishna Debate

The daf opens with a question that arises from a common practical situation: a *shetar chov* has been written for a thousand dollars, and the *loveh* pays back two hundred. What is to be done with the existing document? The *mishna* records a debate on precisely this point. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the original *shetar* should be replaced with a new one reflecting the remaining balance of eight hundred. Rabbi Yosi disagrees and instead advocates writing a *shovar* — a receipt — for the amount paid.

### Positions Explained

The reasoning on each side flows from distinct concerns about who bears the burden of risk. Rabbi Yehuda objects to the *shovar* solution because it places an unfair responsibility on the *loveh*: he must now safeguard his receipt against loss, and if it is destroyed or stolen — proverbially, eaten by mice — he may find himself obligated to pay the full original sum again. Rabbi Yosi counters that this is not unreasonable: *kach yafeh lo*, it is appropriate that the *loveh* bear this responsibility, since after all it is he who incurred the debt. More importantly, Rabbi Yosi argues that rewriting the *shetar* in the manner Rabbi Yehuda proposes would damage the interests of the *malveh*. The implicit assumption underlying Rabbi Yosi's concern is that Rabbi Yehuda's new *shetar* would bear today's date — the date of rewriting — rather than the original date of the loan. Were that the case, the *malveh* would forfeit all the liens that had attached to the borrower's property from the time of the original transaction, a potentially devastating loss.

### Rav's Resolution

The *gemara* introduces Rav's ruling, transmitted through Rav Huna: the *halacha* follows neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosi as they had been understood. Instead, *beis din* tears up the old *shetar* and writes a new one *mizman rishon* — dated as of the original loan. This solution is elegant: the *malveh* loses nothing, retaining the full force of his liens from the original date, while the *loveh* is not burdened with the responsibility of guarding a receipt. The apparent third position introduced by Rav reflects his understanding that Rabbi Yehuda had meant only a *shetar* dated as of today, leaving the *malveh* worse off — and thus Rav stepped in to articulate a better path.

### Braita Clarification

At this point a challenge is raised. Rav Nachman — and some say Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba — asked Rav Huna: had Rav actually heard the *braita* that addresses this very dispute? For the *braita* teaches explicitly: *eidim* tear up the *shetar* and write a new one *mizman rishon*, stating clearly that even Rabbi Yehuda's position requires the original date. Had Rav known this *braita*, would he not simply have ruled like Rabbi Yehuda without introducing anything new?

The *gemara* responds that Rav had in fact heard the *braita* — and still did not retract. Why? Because the *chiddush* of Rav's ruling is not the *mizman rishon* principle, which the *braita* already attributes to Rabbi Yehuda. The *chiddush* is that writing a predated *shetar* — even in this legitimate case — requires the authority of a *beis din*. The *braita* had permitted the *eidim* themselves to rewrite the *shetar* from the original date. Rav rules that this is insufficient: only a *beis din* may authorize it.

### Beis Din vs. Witnesses

The *gemara* articulates why this distinction matters. *Bishlama beis din alima leafkuei mamona* — a *beis din* possesses the institutional authority to, in effect, extract monetary obligations and reconstitute them; *hefker beis din hefker*. But witnesses who have already signed a *shetar* and fulfilled their role — can they simply return and execute another? Writing a *shetar* dated as of today would present no difficulty: both *malveh* and *loveh* could agree to treat the original debt as discharged and execute a fresh $800 loan right now, no special authority needed. The problem arises precisely when the new *shetar* is to bear an earlier date. Creating liens retroactively — even to reflect a reality that genuinely existed — is not something witnesses and the parties can accomplish on their own. That is a form of predating a document, a *shtar mukdam*, and requires *beis din* to do it properly.

### Tosfot's Policy

Tosfot acknowledges the force of the conceptual question here: if the liens already exist, if the witnesses are not fabricating anything but merely re-attesting to a known fact, what is truly objectionable about allowing the *eidim* to rewrite the *shetar* themselves? Tosfot concedes that from a purely logical standpoint, this would not be invalid. The same witnesses who saw the original thousand-dollar loan can truthfully write that the *loveh* now owes eight hundred — that is not a lie. No new liens are being invented out of whole cloth; the liens have existed all along.

But Tosfot frames Rav's requirement of *beis din* as a matter of policy rather than strict legal impossibility. Allowing *eidim* on their own to write a predated *shetar*, even in a case where it reflects the truth and both parties consent, opens a dangerous door. Predating documents is inherently risky business, and Rav determined that it should only be done under the formal auspices of *beis din* — not because the liens cannot otherwise be said to exist, but because permitting private predating without judicial supervision invites abuse.

Tosfot also addresses a related scenario discussed earlier in the *gemara*: the case of a *shetar* being erased and requiring replacement. In that case as well, the question of whether *beis din* is needed — and at what level — turns on an additional factor. There, the *loveh* has not consented. He has not authorized the *eidim* to rewrite his *shetar*. Under ordinary circumstances, a *shetar* cannot be written against a party without that party's authorization — what the *gemara* calls *da'as mis'chayiv*, the consent of the one who is being bound. Here, in the partial payment case, both sides agree: the *loveh* has every reason to prefer a *shetar* for eight hundred over a *shetar* for a thousand, and he authorizes the *eidim* accordingly. That bilateral consent is what makes it comparatively manageable. But even so, Rav requires *beis din*, as a matter of policy, given the inherent danger of predating any document that carries liens.

---

## Deeds Without Liens

### Ten Deeds Ruling

The *gemara* now presses on its own conclusion with a question. Rav himself — the very authority who just ruled that *eidim* cannot rewrite a predated *shetar* without *beis din* — is also cited by Rav Yehuda as saying that *eidim kosvin afilu asara shtaros al sadei achas*: witnesses may write even ten replacement deeds on the same plot of land. How can both statements be Rav's? If *eidim* cannot rewrite a *shetar* independently, how can they produce ten replacement deeds?

### No Liens Exception

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction through two answers, one attributed to Rav Yosef and one to Rabba. Rav Yosef says the case of the ten deeds refers to a *shtar matana* — a gift deed. Rabba says it refers to a *shtar she'ein bo achrayus* — a deed that explicitly excludes the seller's liability. In either case, the key feature is the absence of *achrayus*.

The significance of this distinction is substantial. A standard deed of sale carries with it an implicit guarantee: if the property is subsequently seized by a prior creditor, the seller is obligated to compensate the buyer from his other assets — this is *achrayus*. It is this guarantee that generates the dangerous lien structure. A deed without *achrayus* — whether because it is a gift (where no such insurance is assumed by default) or because the parties explicitly waived it — cannot be used to seize property from third parties who purchased land in the interim. Therefore, even if such a deed is predated, there is no risk of defrauding earlier purchasers. The concern about *shtar mukdam* is precisely the concern that fabricated early liens will be used to dispossess innocent buyers. Where that risk does not exist, *eidim* may freely write replacement documents — even ten of them, even predated — without requiring the authority of *beis din*.

### Tosfot Caveat

Tosfot raises a subtle difficulty here. Earlier in the *gemara* there was a discussion of concerns about fraudulent schemes when replacement documents are involved — the worry being that a person might claim he "lost" a *shetar* when in fact he is setting up a double collection. How, Tosfot asks, could we even have entertained the idea that *eidim* would rewrite a document with *achrayus*, given all the concerns raised there?

Tosfot resolves this by drawing a crucial distinction: the earlier concern about schemes applied to a case where the original *shetar* was allegedly lost and its loss was unverifiable. In the case of the ten deeds, however, the situation is different — it is known with certainty that the original document was destroyed. Either the witnesses themselves observed it being burned, or its destruction is otherwise established beyond doubt. In that scenario, there is no concern that the *eidim* are participating in a scheme; the only question is whether they are technically authorized to produce a replacement. The answer, for documents without *achrayus*, is yes. It is only the loan document with liens — where predating creates real risk of prejudicing third parties — that Rav restricts to *beis din* supervision.

---

## Lost Document Case

### Lost Shetar Story

The *gemara* now turns to a related case involving a lost *shetar* and a dispute about whether a *shovar* must be written in its place. The narrative centers on Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef, who had lent money to Rabi Abba. The case came before Rabi Chanina bar Pappa. Rav Yitzchak demanded payment; Rabi Abba responded: *hav li shtarai* — return my *shetar* to me, and I will pay you. Rav Yitzchak said he had lost the *shetar*, and offered instead to write a *shovar* — a receipt — acknowledging that the debt had been discharged.

### Bavel vs. EY

Rabi Abba refused, citing the ruling of Rav and Shmuel, who both hold that *ein kotvin shovar* — one does not write a receipt. Under that position, the *loveh* is entitled to insist: if you want your money, produce the *shetar* and allow me to tear it up. The *loveh* should not be forced to accept a receipt and take on the burden of guarding it for the rest of time. Without the original *shetar*, the *malveh* cannot collect.

The *gemara* then introduces the opposing view: *man yeiv lan me-afrei de-Rav u-Shmuel ve-raminan be-einain* — who would give us the dust of Rav and Shmuel to place in our eyes, as it were. The formulation is striking: it acknowledges the towering authority of the Babylonian masters while also suggesting, gently, that their teaching may have obscured other valid positions. For Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish — the great Eretz Yisrael *Amoraim* — both hold that *kotvin shovar*, one does write a receipt. And when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael he transmitted in the name of Rabbi Ela'a that *kotvin shovar* as well. There is thus a genuine *machlokes* between Bavel and Eretz Yisrael on this point.

### Malveh's Loss

The *gemara* presses to establish which position ought to be followed. It brings a pointed argument in favor of writing the *shovar*: *avad shtaro shel zeh yochel haleh veyechadi?* — Because this person's *shetar* was lost, should the *loveh* consume the *malveh*'s money and rejoice? The *malveh* lent real money. He is owed it. If we say that without the *shetar* he cannot collect, then the loss of a piece of parchment destroys a legitimate debt — and the *loveh* profits from pure happenstance. That cannot be just. Therefore, the *malveh* must be able to write a *shovar* and collect even without the original document.

### Loveh's Loss

Abaye responds with a sharp counter-argument that mirrors the structure of the original complaint. Very well — but if we write the *shovar* and the *loveh* subsequently loses it, *avad shovro shel zeh yochel haleh veyechadi?* — should the *malveh* now go and rejoice and collect twice? The *malveh* still holds his original *shetar* — or claims it is "lost" while secretly retaining it — and the *loveh*, having paid and lost his receipt, stands exposed to a second demand for payment. The same logic that protects the *malveh* from the inequity of losing his *shetar* could equally be deployed to protect the *loveh* from the inequity of losing his *shovar*.

One must note the asymmetry in the two concerns, however. The scenario where the *malveh* "lost" his *shetar* and then produces it to collect twice requires the assumption that he is lying. The *loveh* who refuses to pay despite acknowledging the debt is not doing anything covert — he is openly exploiting the *malveh*'s misfortune. The moral weight of the two cases is not identical, even if their formal structure appears parallel.

### Loveh's Burden

Rava resolves the tension with a principled ruling. If a risk must be borne by one party, it should fall on the *loveh* — because *eved loveh l'ish malveh*, the *loveh* is a slave to the *malveh*. This is not a casual expression; it reflects a genuine *halachic* orientation. The entire network of *mitzvot* governing the creditor-debtor relationship — the prohibitions against pressuring the borrower, against entering his home to take collateral — exists precisely because the *malveh* holds structural power over the *loveh*, and the Torah seeks to check that power. Yet the underlying truth remains: the *loveh* is indebted. He received money he has not repaid. The *malveh* is out his funds and has received nothing in return. In any allocation of risk between the two, it is more appropriate that the *loveh* bear it.

The practical upshot is as follows. The *malveh*, if he has genuinely lost his *shetar*, may produce a *shovar* in its place and collect. We do not say that the accident of his loss extinguishes a legitimate debt. The *loveh*, once he pays, must guard his receipt — and if he fails to do so, the loss is his. From this case the *gemara* also establishes, against the view of Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua who had suggested that a *shovar* applies only to partial payment, that we write a *shovar* even for the *full* amount of the debt.

---

## Postdated Documents

### Predated Invalid

The *gemara* now transitions to a new *mishna* from *Shevi'it* bearing on the validity of misdated documents. The rule stated there is crisp: *shtarei chov hamukdamin psulin v'hameucharim ksherin* — predated loan documents are invalid, postdated loan documents are valid. The predated document is disqualified because it falsely extends the *malveh*'s liens backward in time, allowing him to collect from property sold after the actual loan was made but before the fabricated date. The postdated document, by contrast, merely means that the *malveh* is forfeiting some of his lien rights — he cannot collect from property sold between the actual date of the loan and the written date. That is a loss to no one but himself, and therefore the document remains valid.

### Loan vs. Sale

Rav Hamnuna refines the ruling: *lo shanu ela shtarei chov* — this leniency for postdated documents applies only to loan documents, not to sale documents. A postdated deed of sale is also invalid. The reason is a specific abuse that becomes possible when a sale deed is postdated. If Shimon sells land to Reuven in Nissan but the deed is written as of Tishrei, and in the intervening months Shimon raises funds and buys the land back from Reuven, then when Tishrei arrives Reuven can produce his postdated deed and claim that he purchased the land *then* — after the repurchase — creating the appearance of a second, independent sale and allowing him to assert ownership a second time. The *Rashbam* notes that such arrangements may even have been formalized with buyback clauses, making the scheme all the more plausible.

This fraudulent use is specific to sale documents. With a loan document, the argument might seem parallel: could a *malveh* not lend money in Nissan, postdate the *shetar* to Tishrei, accept repayment in the interim, lose the *shetar*, and then in Tishrei produce it and claim it reflects a new loan? The *gemara* considers exactly this scenario.

### Double Collection Risk

The *gemara* poses the parallel case with full force. Borrow a thousand dollars in Nissan; postdate the *shetar* to Tishrei. The *loveh* pays in the interim and asks for the *shetar* to be returned. The *malveh* claims he lost it and writes a *shovar*. Then when Tishrei arrives, the *malveh* takes out the *shetar* and says: you borrowed a thousand dollars from me again, just this month — this is a new debt. The *shovar* said he paid up a debt from months ago; this *shetar* is for a fresh loan. Pay up.

The *gemara* resolves this neatly: *kasavar ein kotvin shovar* — the concern only arises if we allow *shovarim* to be written. Under the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that *shtaros* must be returned and torn up upon repayment and that we do not write *shovarim*, there is no risk. The *loveh* will simply refuse to pay until the original *shetar* is returned. The *malveh* cannot hold onto the postdated *shetar* in secret and then produce it as evidence of a new loan, because the *loveh* can demand: give me the *shetar* before I give you the money. Once the *shetar* is surrendered and torn up, the postdated loan document cannot be misused.

The same protection, however, does not apply to sale documents. When the *loveh* pays off a loan, he can insist on receiving the *shetar* in exchange. But when a buyer repurchases land he had previously sold, he does not demand the original deed — he simply receives a new deed in his name. The original postdated deed thus remains in the seller's hands, available for future misuse. This is why postdated deeds of sale cannot be permitted, while postdated loan documents, under the regime that prohibits *shovarim*, are safe.

### Rav Abba Solution

The *gemara* arrives at a real-world problem. Rav Yeimar (and some say Rav Yirmiyah of Difti) raises the issue with Rav Kahana: *ve-haidna d'chatvinan shtarei meucharim ve-chatvinan shovar* — but in current practice, we write both postdated *shtaros* and *shovarim*. We have therefore returned to the very situation of potential double collection. Why do we do this?

The answer is that Rav Abba issued instructions to his scribes. When writing a postdated document, the *sofer* must include explicit language within the *shetar* itself: *shtara dnan lav b'zmanei chatavnuhu ela icharnu-hu u-chatavnu-hu* — this document was not written on its stated date; rather, we intentionally postdated it. This notation changes everything. Once it is explicit on the face of the *shetar* that the document is postdated, any subsequent *shovar* that the *loveh* holds can be matched to it. If the *malveh* tries to claim the *shetar* represents a new, later loan, the *loveh* simply points to the language within the *shetar* itself and says: look, it says right here that this was postdated. And since I have a *shovar* for a thousand dollars — the same amount — it must be going on this very *shetar*.

This is also why Rabbi Yosi, in the earlier *mishna*, permitted the Shabbos and Yom Kippur case: when it is manifest from the document itself that it is postdated — because no transaction could have been written on Shabbos or Yom Kippur — the *shovar* can be reliably correlated to it. The *Rashbam* adds an important practical note: once this system is in place, a *malveh* must be careful never to write another postdated *shetar* of the same amount for the same *loveh*, lest the *loveh* always be able to claim that any *shovar* he holds is matched to the new document.

---

## Practice Evolution

### Current Problem

The discussion takes another turn when the practice evolves still further. Rav Ashi raises the next problem with Rav Kahana: *ve-haidna d'lo chatvinan hachi* — but nowadays we do not even write that explicit notation in the *shetar*. We write postdated documents without any statement that they are postdated, and we write dated *shovarim*. This once again opens the system to abuse.

### Rav Safra Rule

Rav Safra addressed this by instructing his scribes differently. Rather than annotating the *shetar*, he focused on the *shovar*. When writing a receipt, the scribes should follow this principle: *i yaditu zimna d'shtara kisvu* — if you know the date of the *shetar*, write it on the *shovar*. So if it is known that the *shetar* is postdated to Tishrei and the *loveh* pays in Tishrei, simply date the *shovar* as of Tishrei. The *shovar* and the *shetar* will then carry the same date, making them clearly correspondent, and the risk of double collection disappears.

### Undated Receipt Risk

But what if the date of the *shetar* is not known? Rav Safra's instruction then is: write an undated *shovar* — *shetama*, without a date. An undated receipt can serve as a perpetual defense: whenever the *malveh* produces his postdated *shetar* and claims it reflects a current loan, the *loveh* produces his undated *shovar* and says he has already paid.

This solution, however, introduces new dangers of its own. An undated receipt is an extraordinarily potent instrument — essentially a blank check in reverse. If the *malveh* ever lends the same *loveh* the same amount again on a later occasion, the *loveh* can produce his undated *shovar* and claim it satisfies the new debt. Even more troubling: if the *malveh* later lends a larger amount, the *loveh* can produce the undated receipt and claim it represents partial payment of the new obligation, reducing what he owes. The *Rashbam* makes the practical implication explicit: once an undated receipt for a certain amount has been written, the *malveh* must be vigilant never to extend a loan of that exact amount to the same borrower again.

### Modern Practice

At the final stage of this development, Ravina poses the problem to Rav Ashi — and some attribute it to Rav Ashi addressing Rav Kahana — that current practice has reverted to a state where postdated *shtaros* are written alongside ordinarily dated *shovarim*, without any of the protective mechanisms described above. The system, as practiced, is exposed to the double collection risk that the entire preceding discussion was meant to prevent.

### Rabbis' Framework

Rav Ashi's response closes the discussion: *Rabanan takuni takuni* — the rabbis established the proper framework. They articulated the rules clearly: if you are going to write a postdated *shetar*, either explicitly annotate it as postdated within the document itself, following Rav Abba's instruction, or ensure that the *shovar* is undated, following Rav Safra's instruction. The system can work; the protections are available.

*Man d'avid avid* — one who follows the established procedure is protected. *Man d'lo avid ihu d'afsid anafshei* — one who does not follow it has caused his own loss. The *loveh* who pays a postdated debt, accepts a dated receipt, and fails to ensure that either the *shetar* is annotated or the *shovar* is undated has the tools of protection available to him and has simply not used them. The system places the responsibility squarely on the parties. The rabbis have done their part by establishing the framework; the *loveh* must do his part by insisting that the *sofer* follow it.

---

---

# Bava Batra 172

## Dating Sale Documents

### Known vs. Unknown Date

The daf opens with a ruling of Rava bar Rav Shila addressed to those who write *shtarei aknyata* — documents of acquisition. The Rashbam understands this term to refer not to a *shtar halva'ah* (loan document) but to a *shtar mekhar*, a deed recording the sale of land. The practical scenario is this: a *kinyan* took place on one date — say, November 1st — but the witnesses did not get around to writing the *shtar* until January 1st. How should they date the document?

Rava bar Rav Shila's instruction is clear: *im yiditu yoma dekannu bei, kisvu* — if you know the day that the *kinyan* was performed, write that date. *Ve'ei lo, kisvu yoma dematu bei* — and if you do not know that date, write today's date, *ki heichi dela mitchazi keshikra* — so that the document does not appear to be a lie. One might naturally ask: why not write both dates — noting both when the transaction occurred and when the *shtar* is being drafted? For all practical purposes, perhaps the standard practice does include both lines. But the critical *chiddush* here concerns the fill-in-the-blank for the original date. If one genuinely does not remember it, one might be tempted to reason: I know the transaction occurred before Thanksgiving, so let me simply write Thanksgiving as the date — at least that is a point before which I am certain the event took place. To this Rava bar Rav Shila says no: such an approximation is itself *mitchazi keshikra*, it has the appearance of a falsehood. If you do not know the precise date, write today's date — the one date of which you are certain — and do not guess.

### Land Sales & Liens

Beyond the question of which date to inscribe, the Rashbam identifies a second *chiddush* in this passage, one that is conceptually more significant. One might ask: in a case where the seller conveyed land to the buyer *with achrayus* — with a guarantee of security that creates liens on the seller's assets — is it not problematic to date the *shtar* two months retroactively to November 1st? Writing the *shtar* now but dating it to November 1st means that the buyer would hold liens stretching back two months. In that intervening period, however, people may have purchased land from the seller — the *lakuchot* — without any knowledge of those liens. Should we not be concerned that such a retroactively dated *shtar* would unfairly prejudice those subsequent buyers?

The Rashbam, reinforced by Tosafot, answers that in the case of land sales this concern does not arise. Sales of land are public and well-known events, especially when conducted before witnesses. We therefore assume that the *lakuchot* are already aware that the buyer acquired the land, even before any *shtar* is written, and they are expected to take that prior sale into account when purchasing land from the seller. The liens, in other words, are understood to exist from the moment of the sale — not from the moment of documentation — and buyers of land are presumed to know this.

### Loans Cannot Be Post-Dat…

The situation is starkly different when it comes to a *shtar halva'ah*. With a loan, liens on the borrower's property do not come into existence through the act of borrowing alone; they come into existence only when the *shtar* is written. This is a crucial legal distinction. If witnesses observed a loan on November 1st but did not write the *shtar* until December, they must write December — they are absolutely forbidden to write November, even though November is the accurate date of the transaction. To write November would be to create liens retroactively to a point when none legally existed, and such a document is a *shtar mukdam* — an antedated instrument — which is *pasul*.

This prohibition stands in deliberate contrast to the *shtar mekhar*. By land sales, the retroactive dating is permissible because the liens pre-exist the writing of the document. By a loan document, the liens are born with the *shtar* itself, and antedating it would therefore conjure liens out of thin air — a fraud against any *lakuchot* who acquired property from the borrower in the interval.

### Place of Writing & Event

Rav and Rav Huna each instructed their respective scribes on a related matter: *ki katbitu bi-Shili ve-af al gav de-mesiru lakhun mili be-Hini* — if you are writing the document in Shili, even though the testimony was given to you in Hini, write where you are at the time of writing. The Rashbam explains this to mean that one writes both: the place where you are sitting when drafting the document, and the place where the event itself occurred — *katavnu hakha mah she-rainu be-makom ploni*, "we have written here what we witnessed in such-and-such a place."

It may be asked: if one writes both lines anyway, what is the *chiddush*? Tosafot explains that Shili and Hini are like two villages immediately adjacent to one another — the Teaneck and Englewood of Babylonia, as it were — where the population moves freely between them. One might have supposed that since the two locales are functionally indistinguishable, it is acceptable to simply record the location of the event rather than the location where the *shtar* is being written. Rav and Rav Huna rule otherwise: no matter how close together these places are, you must write precisely where you are at the moment of drafting, distinct from where the underlying event took place.

---

## Receipts & Defective Doc…

### No Conversion: 100 to 50…

Having addressed the concerns that animate the *shover* (receipt), the Gemara now turns to a series of rulings by Rava concerning document conversion. Suppose a *malveh* holds a *shtar* for a hundred *zuz* and approaches the *beit din* with a seemingly reasonable request: since Michael is likely to pay in installments, could the court convert the single hundred-*zuz shtar* into two *shtarot* of fifty *zuz* each? The *malveh* would surrender the hundred-*zuz shtar* and receive two fifties in exchange, both bearing the same date. What could be the objection?

Ravina explains: *lo mashvinan lehu* — we do not make that conversion — because the current state of affairs, a single hundred-*zuz shtar*, carries distinct advantages for both parties, and we are not in the business of unilaterally dismantling those advantages.

The advantage for the *malveh* is one of leverage: *nicha lei le-malveh kedei she-yikof le-pora'o* — it is beneficial for the creditor in that it compels the debtor to pay. If the debtor pays fifty and receives a receipt, the *malveh* is still holding a hundred-*zuz shtar* against which the debtor must guard. That residual pressure creates an incentive for the *loveh* to pay off the remainder so that he does not remain exposed to a second claim.

The advantage for the *loveh* flows from a *halacha* about *shtar pagum* — a document that has been partially impaired. If the *malveh* comes to *beit din* with his hundred-*zuz shtar* and the *loveh* produces a receipt showing that fifty have already been paid, that partial payment creates a suspicion that perhaps the full debt has been discharged. The *shtar* is now *pagum* — like a *kiddush* cup from which some has been drunk — and the *malveh* cannot collect the remaining fifty without first taking a *shevuah* that the balance remains unpaid. This is a powerful position for the *loveh*: he compels the creditor to swear before collecting. If the *shtar* were converted into two fifties and the hundred-*zuz shtar* torn up, there would be no *shtar pagum*, no *chashash*, and no *shevuah* requirement. The *loveh* thus has a genuine interest in preserving the single hundred-*zuz shtar* even as it exposes him to continued liability. Since each scenario serves each party in different ways, we decline to alter it.

### No Conversion: 50+50 to…

Rava applies the identical reasoning in reverse. Suppose a *malveh* holds two *shtarot* of fifty *zuz* each, both dated on the same day, and asks the *beit din* to consolidate them into a single hundred-*zuz shtar*. Rav Adda bar Minyumi explains: *lo mashvinan lei* — we do not do it — because holding two fifties also carries distinct advantages for both parties.

The benefit to the *malveh* is that he can hand over one fifty-*zuz shtar* upon receiving partial repayment and retain the other fifty entirely intact — it is not *pagum* at all. And the benefit to the *loveh* is that *lo nikfayei le-pora'ei* — having paid off one fifty and received that *shtar* back, he is no longer under any coercive pressure with respect to that first fifty; only the second remains outstanding. Were the two fifties consolidated into a hundred and one fifty repaid, the *malveh* would still hold a hundred-*zuz shtar* with a receipt — a *shtar pagum* — and the *loveh* would face the leverage of that remaining instrument. Two fifties avoid that dynamic. The Rashbam notes that if both parties agree to the conversion, we would not stand in their way; it is only absent mutual agreement that the *beit din* refuses to act unilaterally.

### Fraud Prevention

Rav Ashi introduces a related prohibition that illuminates just how seriously the Gemara takes the potential for document manipulation. Suppose a *malveh* approaches the *beit din* and says: I have a hundred-*zuz shtar* against Michael, but poor Michael will never be able to pay the full amount, so please convert it to a fifty-*zuz shtar* — after all, *bichlal masayim maneh*, one who borrowed a hundred certainly borrowed fifty, so writing a fifty is not false. *Lo mashvinan lei* — we do not do it.

The reason is the following fraud scenario. Michael may have already paid off the full hundred-*zuz* debt, received a receipt from the *malveh*, and demanded his *shtar* back. The *malveh* told him: *irkas li* — sorry, I lost your *shtar* — and wrote him a *shover* instead. But the *malveh* still possesses the hundred-*zuz shtar*. Were he now to have it converted to fifty, he could produce the fifty-*zuz shtar* and claim it is a separate loan — *hai achrina hu* — distinct from the hundred-*zuz shtar* referenced in Michael's receipt. Michael's receipt would be useless against this new claim. This is why we refuse to perform such a conversion even when framed as an act of charity toward the debtor.

---

## Same-Name Identification

### Mutual Inability

The Mishnah now turns to a problem of a different character. If two people in the same city share the identical name — the classic case being *shenayim shehayu be'ir achat, shem echad Yosef ben Shimon veshem acher Yosef ben Shimon* — the result is a tangle of documentary uncertainty. Neither can bring a *shtar chov* against the other: I am Yosef ben Shimon, you are Yosef ben Shimon, and if I produce a *shtar* saying Yosef ben Shimon owes Yosef ben Shimon a hundred *zuz*, you can always claim it is you who are the creditor and I who have somehow come into possession of the document. Equally, a third party cannot bring a *shtar chov* against either of them, since the named debtor can always point to the other person of the same name and say the debt belongs to him.

The Mishnah further notes: *nimtza le'echad bein shtarotav shtar sheYosef ben Shimon parua* — if one finds a note among his own papers recording that the *shtarot* of Yosef ben Shimon are paid up, both individuals' *shtarot* are presumed discharged, since there is no way to determine which Yosef ben Shimon the memorandum referenced.

### Solutions: 3 Names & Sim…

*Keitzad ya'asu* — what, then, is to be done? *Yeshaleshu* — go three generations. Rather than identifying a party by father alone, include the grandfather's name as well. If the grandfathers also share the same name — *v'im hayu meshulashim* — then *yichtevu siman*, write an identifying characteristic: a physical description, some distinguishing feature, or the like. It is worth noting that the Mishnah makes no mention of a mother's name as a *siman*, even at this stage, before resorting to physical characteristics — a reflection of the patrilineal basis of formal identification in the legal tradition, though certainly a mother's name would qualify as a valid *siman* once that category is reached.

If even suitable *simanim* are lacking, the Mishnah suggests noting priestly or levitical status: *yichtevu kohen* — write that one is a *kohen* or *levi*. This does raise an eyebrow: one might have expected tribal status to appear earlier in the hierarchy, even before the three-generation name, since it is both stable and immediately known. And of course the solution fails if both men happen to be *kohanim* or both *leviyim*. The Mishnah's point, in the end, is simply that one must find *some* means of distinguishing between them; the specific tools it lists are illustrative of the principle rather than an exhaustive or rigidly ordered hierarchy.

---

## Bearer Bond Question

### Rav Huna's Challenge

The Gemara now presents a striking case that was brought before the *beit din* of Rav Huna. A *shtar* was produced that read: *ani ploni bar ploni liviti mimcha manah* — "I, so-and-so son of so-and-so, borrowed a hundred *zuz* from you." The *shtar* identified the debtor by name but left the creditor entirely open-ended: not "from Charlie" but simply "from you." Charlie arrives at *beit din* and says that "you" refers to him.

Rav Huna asks with evident skepticism: *mimcha afilu resh galuta?* — "from you" — would that mean even if the *resh galuta* were holding it? Even the *nishvor malka*, the Persian king? In other words, is it really sufficient that whoever is physically presenting the *shtar* at *beit din* gets to claim to be the "you" the document refers to? The question touches on a fundamental tension: either we read "from you" as identifying a specific but unnamed concrete person, in which case the challenge is how we determine who that person actually is, or we entertain the possibility — raised pointedly by Tosafot — that the document functions as what we would today call a bearer bond: the obligation runs not to a named individual but to whoever happens to be holding the instrument.

### Get Without Date

Rav Chisda instructs Rabbah to investigate the question, telling him that Rav Huna will be raising it that evening. Rabbah finds a relevant *beraita*: *get she-yesh alav eidim v'ein bo zman* — a *get* that bears witnesses but carries no date — is normally invalid. However, *Abba Shaul omer*: if the *get* contains the phrase *gerashtich hayom* — "I have divorced you today" — it is *kasher*.

The immediate implication seems strong: *alma hayom hahu yoma d'nafik bei mashma* — evidently, "today" is understood to mean the day on which the document is presented. And by analogy, *mimcha* — "from you" — should mean *me'hahu gavra d'nafik mitosei yadei mashma*, from the person from whose hand the document emerges when presented. Just as the *get* is treated as dated to the day it arrives at *beit din*, the *shtar chov* is treated as borrowing from the person who presents it. We do not ask what actually happened in the past; we interpret the document by the circumstances of its presentation.

### Tosafot's Bearer Bond Re…

Tosafot brings a deeper dimension to the comparison. In the case of the *get*, "today" does not merely identify a date after the fact; it is an operative legal term. When a husband on his deathbed says "here is your *get* if I die," there are complex questions about when the *get* takes effect and whether a conditional *get* that takes effect only upon death is valid. By writing *min yoma denan u'le'olam* — "from this day and forever" — the *get* takes legal effect as of today, neutralizing any concern that it activates only upon some future event. The Rashbam and Tosafot both note that standard *gittin* include this phrase for precisely that reason.

The parallel Tosafot draws to the *shtar* of "from you" is illuminating. Just as "today" in a *get* does not merely record a date but rather constitutes the operative moment of effectiveness — meaning the *get* takes effect on the day it is presented to *beit din*, whenever that may be — so too "from you" in a *shtar chov* might be read as constituting the operative identification of the obligee: the document creates an obligation running to whoever bears it at the time of presentation. On this reading, it is not a failure of identification but a deliberate legal structure, a *shtar* whose creditor is determined at the point of enforcement rather than at the point of creation. The debate, then, is whether such an open-ended formulation has legal force, and whether "from you" is properly read as invoking it.

### No Fear of Droppage

Abaye pushes back on the proof from *Abba Shaul*'s ruling about "today." He suggests that perhaps *Abba Shaul* holds like *Rabbi Eliezer*, who maintains *edei mesirah karti* — that the witnesses to the actual delivery of the *get* are the primary operative witnesses, and their presence at the moment of delivery supplies the date. On this view, "today" in the *get* does not function as a date at all; the *get* is valid not because the word "today" dates it but because the *edei mesirah* know when the delivery occurred. Abaye then adds the operative objection: *aval hacha leichush linfilah* — but here, in the case of the *shtar* that says "from you," we should be concerned that the original creditor dropped the document and Charlie found it, and "from you" therefore does not establish that Charlie is owed anything.

Rava responds directly: *linfilah lo chaishinan* — we do not entertain the fear of the document having been dropped and found. His proof is from the very Mishnah already learned: the case of the two men named Yosef ben Shimon establishes that *hahem al acheirim yecholim* — each of them *can* bring a *shtar chov* against a third party even though another person shares their name. If we were genuinely afraid of the *shtar* having been dropped and picked up, even a clearly named *shtar* would be suspect. The fact that the Mishnah permits such collection demonstrates that we do not operate with a fear of *nefilah*.

### Single vs. Multiple Drop…

Abaye distinguishes. *Linfilah dechad lo chaishinan* — we are not afraid that one specific person dropped the *shtar* and one specific other person found it. That scenario — the other Dov Linzer dropped his *shtar* and you happened to pick it up — is too implausible to take seriously. But *linfilah derabim chaishinan* — when the document uses an open-ended term like "from you," the universe of people who might theoretically have dropped it and from whom it might have passed to the current holder is unbounded. The *shtar* does not identify a specific person as the one who dropped it; anyone for whom such a *shtar* could have been written might be the source. That diffuse, open-ended possibility of loss among many is qualitatively different and cannot be dismissed.

The distinction is therefore not about probability but about structure: a named *shtar* implicates at most one other known individual, and that one-to-one coincidence we dismiss. An unnamed "from you" *shtar* potentially implicates any number of unknown creditors, and that open-ended quality sustains the concern.

### Same Name Affects Collec…
