The Gemara then introduces a *beraita* that complicates the picture: *keshem she'ein motzi'in shtar chov zeh al zeh, kach ein motzi'in al acheirim* — just as neither Yosef ben Shimon can bring a *shtar* against the other, so too neither can bring a *shtar* against a third party. This seems to contradict the Mishnah's ruling that *hahem al acheirim yecholim*. If we genuinely are not afraid of *nefilah dechad*, why does the *beraita* prevent the identically named parties from collecting even against outsiders? The outsider could simply claim: I don't know which Yosef ben Shimon this *shtar* belongs to; perhaps the one I borrowed from dropped it and the other picked it up.

### Acquisition by Delivery

The Gemara resolves the apparent conflict by locating it within a broader dispute: *be'osiyot niknot be-mesirah kamipalgei* — the debate turns on whether documents are acquired through delivery. According to the *tanna* of our Mishnah, *osiyot niknot be-mesirah* — the transfer of a *shtar* is legally effectuated by handing it over. If this is so, then even if the *shtar* was originally written in the name of one Dov Linzer and then physically delivered to the other, that delivery itself transfers the underlying *chov*. The holder can therefore claim: this *shtar* belongs to me because it was handed to me, regardless of in whose name it was originally written. The concern about *nefilah* is thus displaced: even if it passed through someone else's hands, delivery is the operative legal act, and if I am holding it, I am holding it rightfully.

The *tanna* of the *beraita*, by contrast, holds *ein osiyot niknot be-mesirah* — delivery of a *shtar* does not transfer ownership of the underlying debt. On that view, holding the document is not itself proof of entitlement. The *shtar* might have been dropped by the person to whom it was written, or that person may have asked someone to hold it for him — a *pikadon* — without transferring the debt. Since mere possession does not establish ownership, there remains genuine uncertainty about whether the person presenting the *shtar* is the rightful creditor. The discussion continues into the following daf.

# Bava Batra 173

## Identical Names Problem

### Two Dov Linzers

Daf 173 opens by continuing a discussion the Gemara had developed in the preceding pages concerning what might be called a "bare bond" — a document that says, in effect, "I, Dov Linzer, owe you a thousand dollars," where the identity of the creditor is determined by whoever happens to be holding the document. That discussion led the Gemara to confront the case of the *mishnah* that deals with two people who share an identical name. The *mishnah* implies that if I hold a document stating that Eli owes Dov Linzer a thousand dollars, and I am Dov Linzer, the document is valid and Eli cannot defeat my claim by pointing to the existence of another Dov Linzer in town. The mere fact that I am bearing the *shtar* creates a presumption that it was written in my name; we are not, as the Gemara put it, *chashinan lenifila dechad* — we do not entertain the concern that specifically that one other person with my name happened to drop it and I happened to find it.

### Otiyot Niknot Bimesira

At the top of 173a, however, the Gemara confronts a *braita* that complicates this picture considerably. The *braita* states: *keshaym she'ain motzi'in shtar chov zeh al zeh* — just as two people with identical names cannot use a debt document against one another, so too neither of them can use such a document against third parties. At first glance this seems puzzling. If I am Dov Linzer and I hold a *shtar* stating that Eli owes Dov Linzer a thousand dollars, why should the existence of another Dov Linzer prevent me from collecting?

The Gemara resolves this by explaining that the *mishnah* and *braita* disagree over the principle of *otiyot niknot bimesira* — whether the debt recorded in a document is transferred by the mere act of handing over the document. To appreciate how this principle bears on the two-Dov-Linzer problem, it helps to understand what *otiyot niknot bimesira* means in its clearest application. If I hold a *shtar* stating that Eli owes Dov Linzer a thousand dollars and I hand that *shtar* to Charlie, does Charlie now become the creditor, despite his name appearing nowhere in the document? According to the view that *otiyot niknot bimesira* — that a debt is transferred by delivery — the answer is yes. Whoever holds the *shtar* is presumed to be the party to whom the debt is owed, regardless of whose name is written in it.

This principle, once established, has an immediate consequence for the two-Dov-Linzer case. Even if we entertain the theoretical concern that the *shtar* may have originally been written for the other Dov Linzer, the very fact that I am holding it creates a legal presumption — either that it was written in my name, or that the other Dov Linzer transferred it to me by handing it over. If *otiyot niknot bimesira*, that theoretical concern is legally irrelevant. The *tana* of our *mishnah* therefore holds *otiyot niknot bimesira*, and the bearer of the *shtar* may collect. The *tana* of the *braita*, by contrast, holds *ein otiyot niknot bimesira* — a document cannot be transferred by mere delivery; a new *shtar* is required to effect any transfer. Without that mechanism, holding a *shtar* written in someone else's name proves nothing, and the concern that it originated with the other Dov Linzer therefore becomes legally operative.

### Proof of Transfer Debate

The Gemara then offers a second way to frame the same dispute. One might separate two distinct questions: (1) Does the act of handing over the *shtar* actually accomplish a transfer of the debt? (2) If it does, does holding the *shtar* constitute sufficient proof that such a transfer occurred? The Gemara introduces the formulation *ve-iba'is eima de-chulei alma otiyot niknot bimesira* — both *tanna'im* may agree that handing over a document does in fact transfer the debt. The dispute concerns only whether the holder of a *shtar* bearing someone else's name must *tzarich lehavi rayah* — bring additional proof that the transfer actually took place — or whether holding the document is itself a sufficient presumption.

The Gemara cites a direct dispute between Abaye and Rava on this question. Abaye holds *tzarich lehavi rayah*: even if *otiyot niknot bimesira*, a person appearing in court with a *shtar* written in the wrong name must bring corroborating proof — witnesses, an additional document, or other evidence — that the debt was actually transferred to him. Rava holds *eino tzarich lehavi rayah*: no additional proof is required; the fact of holding the *shtar* is itself the presumption.

Abaye derives his position from a *braita* dealing with one of several brothers who appears in court bearing a *shtar chov* written in his deceased father's name. The son claims the debt was assigned to him when the estate was divided; the *braita* rules that *alav lehavi rayah* — the burden of proof falls on him. Abaye reads this as evidence for a general rule that holding a *shtar* in the wrong name requires corroborating proof. Rava, however, rejects this inference: *shani achin de-shamtu mehadadi* — brothers are different, because they live together and have access to one another's documents, making the concern that one brother took the *shtar* illegitimately quite realistic. It is precisely in the brother case, where suspicion of improper access is elevated, that we require additional proof; with unrelated parties, who would have no such access to the other's *shtar*, no corroboration is needed.

The Gemara also records the *ikka d'amri* — the reverse version of the dispute — in which Rava himself cites the same *braita* about brothers as the source of his own position. In that version, Rava reads the *braita* as proof precisely because it speaks only about brothers: it is *achin hu de-shamtu mehadadi* — specifically brothers, where snatching is common, who must bring proof. Other people, by contrast, do not. Abaye would counter that even in the brother case one might have thought additional proof unnecessary — perhaps brothers are actually *more* careful with one another than with outsiders, so that a transfer among brothers would be presumed legitimate. The *braita* therefore needed to tell us that even among brothers, proof is required. But this is all within the framework of the general rule, which according to Abaye always requires additional proof.

Returning now to the case of two Dov Linzers: the *mishnah*'s position that I may collect using my *shtar* reflects either (a) *lo chashinan lenifila de-chad* — we simply do not worry about the remote possibility that the other person with my name dropped it, which is the most intuitive reading; or (b) even if we entertain that concern theoretically, once we accept *otiyot niknot bimesira* and *ein tzarich lehavi rayah*, any bearer of a *shtar* is the presumed creditor, regardless of whether the name matches. The *braita*'s stricter position — that neither Dov Linzer can collect — reflects both *chashinan lenifila de-chad* and *tzarich lehavi rayah*: we are concerned about the possibility of confusion, and holding the *shtar* alone does not establish entitlement.

## Same-Name Debts Allowed

### Braita Leniency

The Gemara then introduces a third text — still another *braita* — that is even more permissive than the *mishnah*. This *braita* states that *keshem shemotzi'in hen shtar chov aleihen kach motzi'in zeh al zeh* — just as the two people with identical names can use debt documents between themselves, so too can either of them use a document against the other. This is a striking position. If a *shtar* states that Dov Linzer owes Dov Linzer a thousand dollars, either party might claim to be the creditor and accuse the other of being the debtor. How could such a document ever be adjudicated?

The Gemara asks *be-mai kamiflegi* — what is the substantive legal question underlying this dispute?

### Writing Without Lender

The answer, the Gemara explains, is the principle of *kotvin shtar le-loveh af al pi she'ein malveh imo* — whether we permit a scribe and witnesses to write a promissory note for the borrower in advance, even without the lender present. The halachic background here is that the borrower, not the lender, is considered the party disadvantaged by the document, and it is therefore permissible, under certain views, to write the document at the borrower's request before the loan actually takes place. The borrower then holds the document until the lender hands over the money, at which point the borrower gives the *shtar* to the lender.

The *tana* of the *mishnah* holds that one *may* write the *shtar* for the borrower without the lender present. The problem this creates in an identical-name case is obvious: I go to the scribe and witnesses and say, "Write a *shtar* that Yosef ben Shimon borrowed from Yosef ben Shimon a thousand dollars — I am planning to borrow from my cousin who shares my name." I walk out with the document, and instead of giving it to my cousin when he lends me the money, I turn the tables and use it against him, claiming that he is the borrower and I am the creditor. Because the *mishnah* permits writing the *shtar* for the borrower in advance, this scheme is possible, and therefore neither Yosef ben Shimon can use the document against the other — each one can always claim the other is the debtor.

The *tana* of this permissive *braita*, by contrast, holds that one may *not* write the *shtar* for the borrower without the lender being present. If the lender must be there at the time of writing, both parties are present and the lender ensures that the *shtar* does not leave the room until the loan has been handed over. The risk of the scheme described above is therefore neutralized, and consequently the document can be used — even though both parties share an identical name.

### Receipt Ambiguity

The Gemara then cites a further clause that addresses what happens when a receipt (*shovar*) creates ambiguity. If a *malveh* finds among his own documents a receipt stating that Yosef ben Shimon's *shtar* has been paid up — *parua* — he cannot collect from either Yosef ben Shimon, since he cannot determine which one the receipt refers to. The Gemara asks an obvious question: why do we need the receipt to prevent collection? Even without it, the *mishnah* has already established that a bearer cannot enforce a *shtar* against either of two identically named parties, since each will claim the *shtar* refers to the other.

Rav Yirmiyah resolves this by explaining that the *shtaros* in question are *meshulashim* — written with three generations of names. One *shtar* says Reuven ben Shimon ben Yaakov owes a thousand dollars, and the other says Reuven ben Shimon ben Moshe owes five thousand dollars. With three-generation identification, both *shtaros* are individually valid and usable. The problem arises only because the *shovar* identifies the debtor using only two generations — "Reuven ben Shimon paid up his *shtar*" — and it is therefore ambiguous which of the two men it refers to. The receipt neutralizes both otherwise-valid documents.

The Gemara then asks: since the *shtaros* are *meshulashim* and thus distinguishable, why not simply look at which three-generation name appears in the receipt? Rav Oshaya answers: the *shtaros* went three generations, but the *shovar* was written with only two generations — *meshulashim be-shtar ve-ein meshulashim be-shovar*. That is the source of the ambiguity, and it is entirely plausible as a scribal oversight.

## Solutions to Ambiguity

### Three Generations

Abaye, however, offers a different reading of the *mishnah* altogether. He reframes the case: it is not the *malveh* who found the receipt — it is the *loveh* who produced it. The two Yosef ben Shimons are here the *creditors*, not the debtors; a single borrower took loans from each of them. Without any receipt, each Yosef ben Shimon could proceed independently: the one holding the *shtar* for a thousand dollars could collect his thousand, and the one holding the *shtar* for ten thousand could collect his ten thousand, since each *shtar* is presumed to belong to the person holding it. But the borrower produces a receipt — *shtar she-Yosef ben Shimon alai parua* — the *shtar* that Yosef ben Shimon holds against me is paid up. Since this receipt does not specify which Yosef ben Shimon's debt has been satisfied, neither can collect.

The Gemara asks: given this ambiguity, *keitzad ya'asu* — what should be done? *Yashalshu* — write three generations of names. If the *shtaros* themselves identify the creditors as Yosef ben Shimon ben Yaakov and Yosef ben Shimon ben Moshe, and the receipt says only "Yosef ben Shimon," we still have the problem of ambiguity in the receipt. Here the Gemara confirms the point: it is precisely when the *shtaros* are *meshulashim* but the *shovar* is not that the difficulty arises. The *mishnah* then adds that if both creditors happen to be *Kohanim* or both *Yisraelim* — such that the priestly designation cannot serve as a distinguishing marker and the family names happen to coincide through three generations — one must extend the identification to four or five generations until a distinction emerges. Notably, the Gemara nowhere considers using a mother's name or other identifiers as an alternative solution.

### Power of Attorney

The *Rashbam* adds a practical solution for the case of identical-name ambiguity with a shared receipt. If neither Yosef ben Shimon can individually collect his full amount — since the borrower will claim the receipt satisfies whichever *shtar* is being pressed — the two creditors can jointly execute a *shtar harsha'ah*, a power of attorney. One Yosef ben Shimon authorizes the other to act on his behalf, and that agent appears in court and argues: "You owe me at least a thousand dollars. Either you owe me a thousand dollars from my own claim, or you owe me even more because of the other Yosef ben Shimon's claim — and the receipt can have eliminated at most one of those two claims." By consolidating the two claims into a single court appearance rather than two separate proceedings, the agent can ensure that at minimum the lower amount is recovered. Individually, each creditor is defeated; together, they can collect the lesser sum.

## Deathbed Confession

### All Debts Nullified

A new case introduces the principle of an honest person's deathbed ambiguity. A man says to his son: *shtar bein shtarotai parua ve'eini yode'a eizehu* — one of the promissory notes among my documents has been paid up, but I cannot remember which one. The ruling is *shtarot kulam paruim* — all of the notes are treated as paid up, and the son cannot collect any of them.

One might ask what legal principle underlies this ruling. It appears to rest on *hoda'at ba'al din* — the admission of the litigant himself. The holder of the *shtaros*, while still alive, admitted that one of his claims had been satisfied. Even though his admission was in the form of a *safek* — an uncertainty — it is apparently sufficient to neutralize all of his *shtaros*. This is a somewhat surprising application of *hoda'at ba'al din*, since he did not admit to any specific debt being paid; nevertheless, once he acknowledged that one of the notes is void and cannot say which, the son is left unable to use any of them.

### Specific vs. General

Rava introduces a related but distinct case. If I say to Michael *shtar lecha beyadi parua* — "the *shtar* that I hold against you is paid up" — and it turns out I hold two *shtaros* against Michael, one for a large amount and one for a smaller amount, the ruling is *hagadol parua ve-hakatan eino parua*: I can still collect the smaller amount. The reasoning is that whichever *shtar* I meant to declare paid up, Michael certainly owes me at least the lesser sum. If the larger *shtar* is the one I admitted to be paid, he still owes me the smaller; if the smaller is the one I admitted to be paid, he certainly owes me the larger. Either way, the lesser amount is collectable.

However, if I say *hov shelecha beyadi parua* — "the *debt* you owe me is paid up" — using the word *chov* rather than *shtar*, the ruling changes: *shtarot kulan paruim*, all notes are voided. The word *chov* refers to the totality of the debt, not to a specific document, and therefore is read as an admission that the entire outstanding obligation has been satisfied.

### Burden of Proof

Ravina then challenges Rava: if we interpret indeterminate language so expansively in favor of the opposing party, should we not apply the same logic elsewhere? If a *shtar* states that Dov sold Michael "my field," and Dov owns multiple fields, should we assume Michael acquired the largest one — just as in the debt case we assumed the larger *shtar* was the one declared paid up? Or if the *shtar* says "the field I own," should we read it as encompassing all of Dov's fields?

Rava responds: *hatam yad ba'al ha-shtar al hatachtona* — in those cases, the burden of proof falls on the person wielding the *shtar*. The point is not that the ambiguous language has an inherent meaning; rather, every case of genuine ambiguity is resolved in favor of the party against whom the *shtar* is being asserted, following the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya*. In the debt case, Michael is being asked to pay, so we resolve the ambiguity in his favor by assuming it is the *larger* debt that was declared paid — leaving only the smaller obligation enforceable. In the sale case, Michael is trying to take Dov's field, so the ambiguity is resolved against Michael, and we assume only the smaller field was sold unless Michael can prove otherwise. The word itself does not determine the outcome; the allocation of the burden of proof does.

## Guarantor Institution

### Not First Creditor

The *mishnah* now opens an entirely new topic: the institution of the *arev*, the guarantor or co-signer. The *mishnah* rules *lo yifra min ha-arev techila* — the lender may not collect from the guarantor first. If I lend money to Michael and David serves as guarantor, I must first pursue Michael. Only if Michael defaults may I then turn to David.

Before analyzing the mechanics, it is worth noting the broader resonance of the term *arev*. The phrase *kol Yisrael arevim ze lazeh* — all of Israel are guarantors for one another — uses the same root in a non-legal, moral sense: just as a legal guarantor becomes responsible for another's debt, each Jew bears a form of responsibility for the religious conduct of fellow Jews. Here, of course, we are concerned with the strictly legal institution.

### Direct Collection Rights

The *mishnah* provides one exception to the rule of *lo yifra min ha-arev techila*: if the lender stipulated at the time of the loan *al menat she-efra mimi she-ertzeh* — on condition that I may collect from whomever I choose — then *yifra min ha-arev*, the lender may go directly to the guarantor. This stipulation must, of course, have been made with David's knowledge and consent; it is not a unilateral reservation by the lender.

### Visible Assets Exception

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a further qualification. Even if the lender made this stipulation, *im yesh nechasim la-loveh bein kach u-vein kach lo yifra min ha-arev* — if the borrower visibly has assets, the lender still may not bypass him and go directly to the guarantor. The underlying logic relates to the degree of the borrower's apparent solvency. There is a meaningful distinction between a borrower who clearly has accessible property — in which case even the stipulation does not permit going straight to the guarantor — and a borrower whose assets are not readily apparent, in which case the lender may need to choose between extended judicial proceedings and invoking the guarantor. The Gemara will elaborate on this distinction further.

### Ketubah Guarantor

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also addresses a separate scenario involving an *arev* in the context of a *ketubah*. If a husband could not persuade his prospective wife to marry him without a guarantor for the *ketubah*, and David agreed to co-sign — meaning that if the husband divorces her and lacks the funds to pay the *ketubah* settlement, David will cover it — a problem arises when the husband actually proceeds toward divorce. The concern is *she-ma ya'asu knunya al nechasim shel zeh ve-yahazir ishto* — that the husband and wife may be colluding to extract money from the guarantor and then remarry. The solution is *yadirenah hana'ah*: when divorcing, the husband must declare that he renounces all benefit from his ex-wife, making remarriage impossible and thereby eliminating the incentive for collusion. The *Rashbam* notes that this must be done through a *neder al da'at rabbim* — a vow formulated in a manner that cannot be annulled — to ensure the protection is real.

## Guarantor Mechanism

### Bail Bondsman Theory

The Gemara now asks *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason for the rule that I cannot collect from the guarantor first? Before addressing this, one might have asked an even more fundamental question: what is the basis for the institution of *areivut* at all? Why should David's verbal declaration that he will stand as guarantor create any legal obligation? That question will be addressed shortly; the Gemara begins with the narrower question of priority.

Rava and Rav Yosef together offer an explanation: *gavra ashlimit li gavra ashlimi lach* — you entrusted to me a person; I return to you that person. Under this theory, the guarantor's role is analogous to that of a bail bondsman: David's function is not to pay the debt but to ensure that Michael remains available and appears before the court. As long as Michael can be produced, David's obligation is discharged. Only if Michael has fled entirely and cannot be located does David become liable to pay.

Rav Nachman challenges this sharply: *hai dina de-Parsaye* — that is the law of the Persians, not ours. (The Gemara clarifies that the characterization is inverted: Persian law actually allowed the lender to go directly to the guarantor; it is the "bail bondsman" reading that is being called arbitrary and unfounded.) The objection is substantive: characterizing the guarantor's role as merely producing the debtor drastically and illogically narrows the institution. The whole point of a guarantor is that the lender can rely on *someone* for payment if the borrower defaults — not merely that someone will drag the borrower into court.

The Gemara therefore rejects the bail bondsman theory as the basis for the rule. Instead, the Gemara clarifies that *lo yifra min ha-arev techila* should not be read as "the lender can *never* collect from the guarantor" — which is what the words seem to say on a plain reading — but rather as *lo yitba areiv techila*: the lender may not *pursue* the guarantor first. The guarantor is fully liable; he is simply the second line of defense. A *braita* confirms this reading explicitly, using the language *lo yitba areiv techila* — the guarantor cannot be summoned first — while also preserving the exception when the lender stipulated discretionary collection rights at the outset.

### Biblical Source

The Gemara turns to the question of where the institution of *areivut* comes from in the first place. Rav Huna asks: *minayin le-areiv de-mishta'abed* — what is the source that a guarantor becomes legally obligated? The answer cited is a verse from Bereishit: *anochi e'erevenu mi-yadi tevakshenu* — "I will guarantee him; from my hand shall you seek him" (Bereishit 43:9). Yehudah's declaration to his father Yaakov is understood as establishing the paradigm of the *arev*: Yehudah accepts personal liability for Binyamin's return, such that if Binyamin is not returned, Yaakov may seek restitution from Yehudah himself.

### Kablanus vs. Areivus

Rav Chisda immediately challenges this proof: *ha kablanut hi* — what Yehudah did was not *areivut* but *kablanus*. The distinction is a significant one. *Areivut* is secondary liability: the guarantor stands in the background, and the lender's primary relationship is with the borrower. *Kablanus* is direct liability: the *kablan* inserts himself into the transaction as a primary party, effectively saying "lend the money to him and I will be the one responsible." The difference in practice is that a *kablan* — an *arev kablan* — can be pursued directly by the lender without first attempting to collect from the borrower, whereas an ordinary *arev* cannot. Rav Chisda points to the verse *tenahu al yadi va'ani ashivenu alecha* — "give him into my care and I will return him to you" — which uses language of direct personal responsibility, making it an instance of *kablanus* rather than background *areivut*, and therefore not a proof for the general institution.

Rav Yitzchak therefore offers a different biblical source, from *Mishlei*: *lakach bigdo ki areiv zar* — "take his garment, for he became guarantor for a stranger" (Mishlei 20:16). The verse reflects the practical reality that a guarantor's property can be seized when the debt is not paid — a clear indication that the guarantor bears genuine legal liability. Further verses from *Mishlei* (6:1–5) are cited, using the root *arev* in contexts that unmistakably connote binding financial obligation.

## How Liability Works

### Areivut vs. Asmachta

Having established the institution's biblical basis, the Gemara turns to the deeper question of *mechanism*. Even granting that the Torah endorses the idea of a guarantor, how does a purely verbal commitment — David saying "don't worry, I'll back the loan" — create a legal obligation? Normally, to obligate oneself to pay money to another person, one would need at minimum a *kinyan sudar* — a formal act of acquisition, taking hold of a garment or similar object — to effectuate the commitment. David performs no such act. He merely speaks.

Moreover, even if we could find a mechanism, there is the problem of *asmachta*. An *asmachta* is a conditional promise that the promisor does not genuinely expect to have to fulfill — an overcommitment made in the hope that the triggering condition never materializes. The classic ruling is *asmachta lo kanya* — an *asmachta* does not create a binding obligation, because there is no genuine intent (*gemirat da'at*) to pay. A guarantor is a paradigmatic case: David agrees to back the loan precisely because he expects Michael to repay it himself. He hopes, and perhaps genuinely believes, he will never have to pay. This looks like a textbook *asmachta*.

The Gemara frames this as a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose. Rabbi Yose holds *asmachta kanya* — an *asmachta* does create a binding obligation — and therefore an *arev mishta'abed*, the guarantor is legally obligated. Rabbi Yehuda holds *asmachta lo kanya*, and therefore *arev lo mishta'abed*, the guarantor does not become legally bound.

### Hana'ah of Reliance

This creates an immediate practical difficulty. Rav Ashi points it out to Ameimar: *hama'asim b'chol yom de-asmachta lo kanya* — the daily practice of the courts is to invalidate *asmachta* obligations. Yet *va'arev mishta'abed* — those same courts regularly enforce guarantor obligations. How can both be true simultaneously? If *areivut* is a form of *asmachta*, the courts should be throwing out guarantor claims just as they throw out other *asmachta* claims.

Rav Ashi himself resolves the paradox: *be-hai hana'ah de-kamheimin leh gemar u-mishta'abed nafsheh* — because of the benefit (*hana'ah*) that the lender is trusting him, the guarantor truly commits and becomes obligated. The word *hana'ah* here should not be read superficially as mere social prestige — "how nice that people trust me." The deeper point is this: the guarantor knows that the lender is extending the loan *solely because* of his commitment. He understands that his word is the operative cause of the transaction. A person of integrity who knows that someone else is relying on him — that the money changed hands only because of his promise — cannot truly say he did not mean it. He knows the lender is depending on the veracity of his commitment, and therefore he truly *does* commit, fully and without reservation. It is that genuine *gemirat da'at*, arising from the knowledge that the lender is relying on him, that distinguishes *areivut* from ordinary *asmachta* and renders the guarantor's obligation fully enforceable.

The discussion of who must be approached first — the borrower or the guarantor — will continue in the following daf.

---

---

# Bava Batra 174

## Arevim: Concept & Obliga…

### Opening & Overview

Today's *daf* is 174, and we pick up at the bottom of 173b at the two dots. We are in the *locus classicus* of the discussions of *arevim* — of guarantors. This is where the topic receives its central treatment in *Shas*, though naturally it arises in other places as well. The *Mishna* introduced the concept that a person may serve as a guarantor for another's loan, and the *Gemara* raised two foundational questions about this institution before we could proceed.

### Kinyan & Asmachta Issues

The *Gemara*'s two questions concern the very basis upon which a guarantor can be bound at all. The first question is: how can a person obligate himself merely through a verbal commitment, without performing a *kinyan*? As a general rule, one cannot create a legally binding obligation through words alone — a formal act of acquisition is required. We will see later in the *Gemara* that in certain circumstances a *kinyan* is indeed necessary, but in other circumstances — particularly when the guarantorship is undertaken at the moment the loan is extended — the verbal commitment alone suffices. The second question concerns *asmachta*: a guarantor's promise resembles a conditional undertaking that one hopes never to be called upon to fulfill. One commits to it in order to induce the lender to extend credit, and not out of genuine present resolve — precisely the structure that renders an *asmachta* non-binding.

### Trust & Integrity Soluti…

As to the first issue, the *Gemara* derives the institution of *areivut* from *psukim*, establishing that the Torah itself recognizes such an institution. The relevant *psukim* do not make entirely explicit that verbal agreement alone suffices — indeed, one of them speaks of a handshake, which is at least somewhat more than purely verbal commitment — but from these verses the institution is grounded. As to the *asmachta* problem, the *Gemara* initially entertains the possibility that guarantorship might indeed be unenforceable on grounds of *asmachta*, but then rejects this: since we rule that *asmachta* is not binding, and yet guarantorship demonstrably is binding, we must explain the distinction. The *Gemara* answers that the case of guarantorship differs from a standard *asmachta* because of the *hana'ah* — the benefit — the guarantor receives. One might frame this more precisely: when a lender extends money to the borrower on the strength of the guarantor's word, the guarantor has placed his own integrity and trustworthiness on the line. The lender's act of reliance transforms the guarantor's commitment from a speculative conditional promise into a genuine, wholehearted obligation. The guarantor truly means to commit, because the very trust reposed in him demands that he live up to it. Accordingly, even though *asmachta* is generally not *kanya*, in this context it is.

### Mishna: Order of Collect…

Having established the institution itself, the *Gemara* clarified one further point from the *Mishna*: when the *Mishna* says not to go to the *areiv*, it does not mean one may never go to the guarantor at all — it means one may not go to the *areiv* first. The *loveh*, the borrower, must be pursued first. The question now becomes: what precisely governs the ordering, and under what conditions may the guarantor be approached?

---

## Collection Order: Debtor…

### Mishna & Limitation

The *Mishna* states that if the lender stipulated — *al menat she-efra mi-mi she-ertzeh*, "on condition that I may collect from whomever I wish" — then the lender may go directly to the guarantor. *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* disagrees and holds that even with this retained right, the lender may not go to the guarantor if the *loveh* has property. *Rabbah bar bar Chana* then reports in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *lo shanu* — the rule permitting collection directly from the guarantor when the retained right was stipulated applies only *ella she-ein nechasim la-loveh*, when the borrower lacks property. But if the borrower has property, *lo yifra min ha-areiv* — one may not go to the guarantor first.

The *Gemara* immediately objects: but this is exactly the position of *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* stated at the end of the *Mishna*! If that is merely *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*'s view, the inference is that the *Tanna Kamma* holds that it makes no difference — even if the *loveh* has property and the retained right was stipulated, one may go straight to the guarantor. To accommodate *Rabbi Yochanan*'s ruling, the *Gemara* says *chisorei mechasra ve-hachi katani* — the *Mishna* is incomplete and must be read as containing an additional clause. The reconstructed *Mishna* reads: if you lend money through a guarantor without any stipulation, you may not go to the *areiv* first. If you stipulate that you may collect from whomever you wish, you may go to the *areiv* — but this applies only when the borrower has no obvious property. However, if the borrower does have obvious property, you must pursue the borrower first even when you retained the right to choose.

This raises a natural question. If the retained right permits you to go to the *areiv* only when the borrower lacks obvious property — then in the basic case without any stipulation, when exactly may the lender approach the guarantor at all? The answer requires careful attention to what "lacks property" means in each context. There appear to be two distinct levels of inability to collect. One is that there are simply no obvious, visible assets — no real estate, no apparent holdings. The second is that collection has genuinely proven fruitless: the borrower has been brought to court, his assets have been investigated, and nothing has been found; or he has fled; or he refuses to appear before the court. In the basic case without stipulation, the *areiv* may be approached only when collection from the borrower has truly proven impossible — one of these latter, more extreme scenarios. When the retained right is stipulated, the lender may approach the *areiv* already at the earlier threshold of no obvious assets.

### Five Gradations (Tosafot)

*Tosafot* formalizes these distinctions into a precise taxonomy, enumerating five gradations of guarantor status. This enumeration appears directly across from the *Rabbeinu Gershom* at the top of the page, beginning with the words *v'chamesh midos b'arevut* — there are five levels of guarantorship.

### Level 1: Basic Areiv

The first level is the basic guarantor — a case where someone becomes a guarantor without stipulating any retained right: *ha-malveh yedei areiv v'lo asni mi mi she-ertzeh*. In such a case, *toveah ha-loveh techilah b'veit din* — the lender must pursue the borrower first in court, whether or not the borrower appears to have assets. Only if it proves impossible to compel the borrower — *v'im lo yuchal l'khof et ha-loveh v'lo tza'is dina*, if he cannot be coerced or refuses to appear — may the lender then approach the guarantor's household.

### Level 2: Retained Right

The second level is a guarantor where the lender stipulated that he retains the right to collect from whomever he chooses — *im hisneh mi she-ertzeh efra* — and the borrower has no obvious assets, which *Tosafot* specifies as meaning primarily no *karka*, no real estate. In that case, *nifra min ha-areiv techilah* — the lender may go to the guarantor immediately. Critically, this is an option, not an obligation: *im yirtzeh ladun im areiv techilah, v'im yirtzeh min ha-loveh* — if the lender prefers to pursue the guarantor, he may; if he prefers to pursue the borrower, he may do that as well.

### Level 3: Debtor Has Asse…

The third level is also a guarantor with a retained right — but here the borrower does have obvious property, meaning real estate or other identifiable assets. In this case, *afilu asni, nifra min ha-loveh techilah* — even though the retained right was stipulated, the lender must pursue the borrower first.

### Level 4: Kablan Status

The fourth level is the *kablan*. A *kablan* is one who says, in effect: give the money to Michael and we will treat it as if you gave it to me — *ten lo va-ani nosein lecha*. By using this formulation, the *kablan* places himself on the front line: it is as if he himself is the borrower. Accordingly, *bein yesh lo nechasim la-loveh bein ein lo* — whether or not the borrower has obvious assets — *nifra min ha-areiv techilah*, the lender may go directly to the *kablan* first if he so chooses.

### Level 5: Direct Transfer

The fifth and final level is *nosei v'nosein b'yad* — where the lender actually hands the money to the guarantor, and the guarantor physically transfers it to the borrower. In this scenario, the legal relationship between the lender and the borrower is entirely severed. *Yifra min ha-areiv* — the lender's only recourse is to the guarantor — *v'lo min ha-loveh*, and not from the borrower at all, *she-ein malveh al ha-loveh klum* — the lender has no legal relationship whatsoever with the borrower.

The distinction between the fourth and fifth levels is worth pausing over. At the *kablan* level, the *kablan* says "give it to Michael and treat it as if I received it" — Michael is still in the room and receives the money directly from the lender, but the *kablan* by his formulation inserts himself as the primary obligor. In the *nosei v'nosein b'yad* case, the money passes through the guarantor's hands physically: the lender gives it to the guarantor, and the guarantor then hands it to the borrower. As a matter of *halakha*, what makes the difference is not who is present in the room but through whose hands the money actually passes. So long as the lender gives the money directly to the borrower, the borrower retains some legal relationship to the lender, even if secondary. Only where the money is genuinely first received by the guarantor and then conveyed is the borrower fully out of the picture.

*Tosafot*'s enumeration here is clearly motivated by *halakha le-ma'aseh*: practical guidance for real transactions. At the bottom of that same *Tosafot*, he even ventures into Old French to discuss certain linguistic markers relevant to categorization — noting, for instance, that one who does not use the language of a loan, *ela lashon pir'on*, is more in the *kablan* category — and he concludes by addressing the mechanics of performing a *kinyan* in this context, including the question of *keli shel makneh* versus *keli shel koneh*.

### Rav Huna: Language Test

With the conceptual structure in hand, the *Gemara* turns to a critical practical question: what precise language places a person in the category of *areiv* versus *kablan*? This is the ruling of *Rav Huna*. He teaches: if David says *halveihu va-ani areiv* — "lend him the money and I will be the guarantor" — that is the paradigmatic *areiv* formulation. And the same is true if instead of the word *areiv* he uses any of several variations: *halveihu va-ani poreia* ("lend him and I will pay"), *halveihu va-ani chayav* ("lend him and I will be obligated"), *halveihu va-ani eten* ("lend him and I will give") — *kullan lashon arevut hen*, all of these are the language of guarantorship. What they have in common is the verb *halveihu*: lend him, Michael, the money. By using the language of lending to Michael, David implies that Michael is the primary obligor — the one who owes the money — while David takes a secondary position.

Conversely, *ten lo va-ani kablan* — "give it to him and I will be the *kablan*" — is the paradigmatic *kablan* formulation. And similarly: *ten lo va-ani poreia*, *ten lo va-ani chayav*, *ten lo va-ani eten* — *kullan lashon kablanut hen*, all are the language of *kablanut*. The governing distinction, then, is the verb describing what the lender does with the borrower: "lend him" implies the borrower is the primary obligor; "give it to him" does not carry that implication. One can illustrate this intuitively: if a father accompanies his daughter to a store and says "give her a candy," the daughter is not the one who owes the storekeeper money — the father is. "Give it to him" does not inherently imply the recipient is the debtor.

### Amoraim Debate: Labels

The *Gemara* then raises the harder cases — the *ibayu lehu* — where the two key elements point in opposite directions. What if David says *halveihu va-ani kablan* — "lend him and I'll be a *kablan*"? Or inversely, *ten lo va-ani areiv* — "give it to him and I'll be a guarantor"? Now both the verb and the explicit label are each present, and they pull toward different categories. Which controls?

*Rav Yitzchak* rules: *lashon arevut arevut, lashon kablanut kablanut* — the label governs. If you explicitly called yourself an *areiv*, you are an *areiv*; if you called yourself a *kablan*, you are a *kablan*. This is a sensible position: when a person explicitly names his role, that declaration controls, regardless of what the surrounding verb might imply.

*Rav Chisda* takes the opposite extreme: *kulam lashon kablanut hen bar me-halveihu va-ani areiv*. Everything, including the cases in the *Baraita*, is to be treated as *kablanut* — with a single exception. The only case that qualifies as a basic *areiv* is the most paradigmatic one: *halveihu va-ani areiv*, both the verb "lend him" and the explicit label "I am an *areiv*." Any deviation from this exact formulation — lend him and I will pay, lend him and I will give, and certainly any formulation with "give it to him" — is categorized as *kablanut*. *Rav Chisda* thus defaults everything toward the *kablan* category, requiring a very specific double formulation to establish the more limited *areiv* role.

*Rava* takes precisely the opposite default: *kulam lashon arevut hen*, everything is *arevut*, *bar miten lo va-ani noten* — except the clearest *kablan* formulations, specifically "give it to him and I will give" or "give it to him and I am the *kablan*." Unless the language falls squarely within the *kablan* category — both the "give it to him" verb and the *kablan* framing — *Rava* treats the commitment as mere *arevut*. Any echo of the lending relationship, any language that implies the borrower owes the money, places the guarantor in the *areiv* category.

The underlying debate is about presumptions: what should we assume a guarantor intends when his language is ambiguous? One argument for defaulting to *kablanut* is societal — making it easier for a creditor to reach the guarantor encourages lending, precisely the rationale invoked in secular cosigning law. The counterargument runs the other way: why should we assume that David wishes to step in more than the minimum necessary? He agreed to stand behind Michael; why presume he meant to stand in Michael's place? The *Gemara* does not resolve which of these *Amoraim* we follow here.

### Direct Money = Debtor St…

One final clarification closes this sugya. *Mar bar Amemar* reports to *Rav Ashi* in the name of *Amemar*: if David says *ten lo va-ani noten* — "give it to him and I will give it to you" — or similarly the paradigmatic *kablan* formulation, then *ein la-malveh al ha-loveh klum*, the lender has no claim against the borrower at all. The *Gemara* immediately qualifies this: *v'la hi*, that is not so. *Lo miptar loveh minei de-malveh*, the borrower does not escape his obligation to the lender, *ad de-shakil v'yahiv be-yad* — unless and until the money was actually received by the guarantor and then physically handed over. This is precisely what distinguishes *kablan* from *nosei v'nosein b'yad*. As long as the lender gives the money directly to the borrower — whatever language David used — Michael retains some obligation. Only when the money genuinely passed through David's hands, with David receiving it and then conveying it to Michael, is Michael fully removed from the legal picture.

---

## Property as Guarantor

### Seized Property Case

The *Gemara* now turns to a related but conceptually distinct situation that illuminates a broader principle. A certain judge allowed a creditor to seize the debtor's property without first giving the debtor an opportunity to pay directly. The debtor was apparently absent — away visiting, so to speak — and the court allowed the creditor to proceed directly against his real estate. *Rav Chani brei de-Rav Yeiva* reversed the ruling, holding that the seizure was improper: the creditor had not first attempted direct collection from the borrower. *Rava* famously remarked that no one but *Rav Chani brei de-Rav Yeiva* would have had the insight to reverse the ruling in this way — it required real sharpness to recognize that the *beit din*'s decision needed to be overturned.

### Nichsei K'Areiv Concept

*Rava* then articulates the conceptual foundation: *nichsei de-var inish inun me'arvin leh* — a person's property functions as his guarantor. This is a striking idea and worth unpacking carefully. When a lender extends money to a borrower, the lender's confidence rests partly on the knowledge that the borrower has assets — a house, for example — which can ultimately be seized if he defaults. Those assets are, in a sense, the borrower's co-signer: they stand behind him and give the lender security. This is precisely the logic of liens. But if the borrower's property functions as his *areiv*, then the *halakha* of *areiv* applies to it: just as one may not go to the guarantor before attempting direct collection from the borrower, so too one may not go straight to the property — treating the lender-borrower relationship as if it is merely a relationship between the lender and the borrower's assets — before first attempting to engage the borrower directly.

The reasoning reflects a fundamental ordering of obligations. The lender's primary legal relationship is with the borrower personally — Michael owes the money. Only when that personal relationship breaks down, when Michael has defaulted and cannot or will not pay, does the lender's recourse shift to Michael's property, now operating as the backup guarantor. Seizing the property directly, bypassing the personal demand, skips over the primary relationship and moves prematurely to the secondary one. This is conceptually the same error as going to the *areiv* before trying the *loveh*. Property is the *areiv*; the borrower's personal obligation comes first.

### Attempt Direct First

The practical *halakha* that follows is therefore: before seizing a debtor's property, the creditor must first attempt direct collection from the borrower. Giving the borrower the opportunity to pay — even if he would pay by handing over his house — keeps the transaction within the primary lender-borrower relationship. Only after that relationship has failed, only after the borrower has defaulted and refused or been unable to respond, may the creditor bypass him and proceed directly against the property. This is not merely procedural courtesy; it reflects the conceptual architecture of the lien itself.

---

## Guarantor Reimbursement…

### Orphans Case: Rav Pappa

The *Gemara* now turns to the question of a guarantor who has actually paid the creditor and seeks reimbursement from the borrower's estate. The specific case involves a guarantor who had stood behind a father's loan; the father died, and the guarantor went ahead and paid off the creditor — but he did so before informing the orphans. He now seeks to recover from the orphans. *Rav Pappa* rules: *priat baal chov mitzvah* — repaying a creditor is a *mitzvah* — *ve-yatmi lav bnei ma'avid mitzvah ninhu*, and the orphans, being minors, cannot yet be compelled to perform this *mitzvah*, since they are underage.

### Rav Pappa: Two Readings

This ruling admits of two fundamentally different readings among the *Rishonim*, and the difference between them is substantial. The *Rashbam* reads *Rav Pappa* simply: the orphans owe the guarantor reimbursement, but because they are minors they cannot yet be brought to court to pay. The obligation exists; collection must wait until they come of age.

The *Rambam* and other *Rishonim* read the ruling very differently and more interestingly. On their reading, the problem is not merely procedural delay — it is that the debt to the creditor was not yet *actionable* at the time the guarantor paid. Minors cannot be compelled to pay the father's debts. Therefore, when the guarantor stepped in and paid the creditor, he was paying a debt that, at that moment, could not legally be demanded. And this matters: the right of a guarantor to seek reimbursement from the borrower is not a freestanding legal claim — it is embedded in the institution of *areivut* itself, and it is operative only when the guarantor acts *in the capacity of a guarantor*, discharging an obligation that was genuinely due. If the guarantor pays something that was not yet obligatory, he is not acting as a guarantor; he is simply doing a favor. And a person who voluntarily pays another's debt out of generosity has no legal claim for reimbursement. On this reading, the orphans owe the guarantor nothing — not merely not yet, but not at all.

The phrase *mikamei de-odienhu le-yatmi* — that he paid before informing the orphans — is accordingly of limited significance on either reading. Had he informed them, they might have chosen to pay voluntarily, but this would not change the legal analysis. The debt was either not yet actionable (second reading) or the orphans were simply minors who could not yet be brought to court (first reading).

### Rav Huna: Tzrari Issue

*Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua* offers a different reason entirely why the guarantor cannot collect from the orphans: *eimar tzerarei atfasei* — perhaps the father had already entrusted bound-up money to the creditor. The concern of *tzrari* is that a debtor may have already prepaid his loan in some form — perhaps he handed the creditor a valuable object with the understanding that it would cover the debt if other payment was not forthcoming — and we simply do not know. Since we cannot be certain the debt remained outstanding, and since we cannot trust the orphans' ability to investigate and contest their father's old business dealings, we do not allow the guarantor to collect from them.

This concern differs from the question of minority. One might ask: if the concern is simply that the orphans are minors, they will eventually grow up — and surely once they are adults, the *tzerarei* issue would be just as murky as it is now. If anything, the *tzerarei* concern seems equally problematic regardless of age. Accordingly, *Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua*'s rationale is not primarily about the age of the orphans at all — it is about the uncertain status of the debt itself. On the *Rashbam*'s reading of *Rav Pappa*, we also reach a similar conclusion: the concern over *tzerarei* means we cannot be confident the loan needed to be paid, so the guarantor who paid it cannot necessarily claim reimbursement. But the upshot differs: *Rav Pappa*'s version leads to a wait-until-they're-adults conclusion; *Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua*'s version points toward a more fundamental inability to collect at all if the debt's status is genuinely in doubt.

### When Can Collect

The *Gemara* identifies cases where the guarantor *can* collect from the orphans: *k'she-chayav modeh* — when the borrower, while alive, explicitly admitted that he still owed the money and had not prepaid — and *de-shamtuh u-meis be-shamta* — when the borrower was placed in *niddui* for failing to pay his debts and refusing repeated summonses to *beit din*, and he died while still under that *niddui*. In the latter scenario, the very fact of the *niddui* makes it evident he had not satisfied the loan: had he paid, he would have sought to have the *niddui* lifted. In both of these scenarios, the concern of *tzerarei* evaporates — we have certainty that the loan remained outstanding. Therefore, the guarantor who paid it was genuinely acting in his capacity as *areiv*, and the *Gemara* rules — citing a ruling sent from *Eretz Yisrael* — *hilchasa ke-Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua*: the law follows *Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua*, and in these cases the guarantor may collect from the orphans even if they are minors.

*Tosafot* raises a sharp structural point in this connection. If the orphans are minors and the guarantor is proceeding against their property, one might object: even if we treat the property as the borrower's *areiv*, don't we have to first try to engage the borrower — i.e., the orphans — directly before going to their property? *Tosafot* answers: the rule that you must try the borrower before going to the *areiv* presupposes a *loveh* who is available and capable of responding. Just as a creditor need not wait years for a borrower who has fled to France to return before approaching the guarantor, so too the creditor — or in this case the *areiv* seeking reimbursement — need not wait until the minors come of age before proceeding against their property. The inability to engage them now is functionally equivalent to the borrower having no available resources: the guarantor is entitled to proceed against the property immediately.

### When Cannot Collect

The *Gemara* then confronts a *baraita* that introduces a complicating element: *arev she-hayah shtar chov yotzei mi-tachas yado*, if the guarantor paid the creditor and received the original *shtar chov* as proof of payment, *eino goveh* — he cannot collect from the orphans. This is consistent with what we have established: the loan of minors was not yet actionable and the guarantor cannot collect. But the *baraita* continues: *v'im kasav bo hikbalti*, if the shtar contained a statement of *hikbalti* — "I have received payment" — then *hikbalti mimcha goveh*, the guarantor can collect.

The *Gemara* works through how this fits each position. For *Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua*, whose concern is *tzerarei*, there is a path: when the father admitted the debt (*chayav modeh*), the guarantor may collect even from minor orphans — though the *Gemara* acknowledges this does not fully explain why *hikbalti* specifically is required. The harder problem is for *Rav Pappa*: if the issue is that minors cannot be compelled to fulfill a *mitzvah*, how does the addition of *hikbalti* in the document change anything?

The *Gemara* answers: *shani hasam de-itarchi v-kasav lei hikbalti* — the creditor went to the effort of writing *hikbalti* precisely in order to enable the guarantor to collect from the orphans. The *Rashbam* explains: it is possible to collect on a *shtar* from minor orphans, just not on an oral debt. By writing *hikbalti* in the document and handing it to the guarantor, the creditor effectively transferred the documentary claim — creating for the guarantor a *shtar* against the orphans' estate that can be enforced even against minors. *Tosafot* finds this unsatisfying: if the fundamental problem is the orphans' minority, why should a *shtar* versus an oral claim make a difference? And what right does the creditor have to unilaterally confer collection rights against the orphans simply by writing a word in his document? *Tosafot* therefore reads the passage differently — that *hikbalti* was written not by the creditor but by the borrower himself before he died, in some form of pre-authorization empowering the guarantor to collect even in his absence. This reading is complex and the *Rishonim* acknowledge the difficulty.

---

## Non-Jews & Conclusion

### Non-Jew Creditor Case

The final section applies the *tzerarei* analysis to a case involving a non-Jewish creditor. A guarantor stood behind a Jewish borrower's loan to a non-Jew; the father died, leaving orphans. The guarantor paid off the non-Jewish creditor before proceeding against the orphans. Now — can he collect from the orphans?

### Rav Mordechai: No Tzrari

*Rav Mordechai* reports to *Rav Ashi* in the name of *Rav*: even according to those who would normally be concerned about *tzerarei* — that the father may have prepaid the loan — in the case of a non-Jewish creditor, *lo chashninan le-tzerarei*, we are not concerned. The reason: *kivan de-basar areva azil* — non-Jewish law allows the creditor to go straight to the guarantor. The father knew this. Would the father be foolish enough to prepay a loan to a non-Jew, knowing that the non-Jew would in any case go straight to the guarantor? Of course not. The dynamics of non-Jewish lending practice make the *tzerarei* concern inapplicable, because a rational borrower would have no incentive to prepay a non-Jewish creditor when the burden of collection would fall on the guarantor anyway. Therefore, the guarantor may collect from the orphans.

### Objection: Still Concern…

The *Gemara* rejects this reasoning decisively, and the counterargument is striking precisely because it flips the logic. *Adaraba* — on the contrary. Even according to those who would not normally be concerned about *tzerarei* with a Jewish creditor, we *are* concerned when the creditor is a non-Jew. Why? *Kivan de-danei basar areva azlei* — since non-Jewish law goes straight to the guarantor, no borrower would agree to have a guarantor for a non-Jewish creditor *unless* he had first given the creditor some form of collateral or prepayment — *tzerarei* — to protect the guarantor from immediate pursuit. *Ila de-atvei tzerarei, me-ikara lo hava mikabeli* — had the borrower not given the non-Jewish creditor some bound-up money or security, the guarantor would never have agreed to take on the role in the first place. No one would cosign for a non-Jewish creditor who can proceed directly against the cosigner without first trying the borrower, unless the borrower took steps to shield the guarantor. Therefore, when there is a non-Jewish creditor, we have a heightened concern that *tzerarei* existed — not a diminished one. The guarantor accordingly cannot collect from the orphans.

### Final Halakha & Shtar

The *Gemara* concludes with a comprehensive summary: *ve-hilcheta be-chulhu ke-Rav Pappa u-ke-Rav Huna berei de-Rav Yehoshua* — the law follows both *Rav Pappa* and *Rav Huna brei de-Rav Yehoshua* throughout, with three exceptions where the law diverges from *Rav Pappa*. These three exceptions are: the case of a non-Jewish creditor (where, contrary to *Rav Pappa*'s implied position, the guarantor cannot collect because we are in fact concerned about *tzerarei*); the case where the borrower died while in *niddui* (where the guarantor can collect from the orphans even though they are minors, since the debt is unambiguously established); and the case of *chayav modeh*, where the borrower admitted the debt before death (where again the guarantor may collect). In these latter two cases the law does not follow *Rav Pappa*'s position that the minority of the orphans categorically bars collection — when the debt's existence is beyond doubt, collection may proceed.

The *Gemara* then concludes with the opening clause of the next *Mishna*: one who lends to his fellow with a *shtar* may collect from *nechasim meshu'abadim* — liened property — while one who lends *al peh*, by oral agreement alone, may collect only from *nechasim bnei chorin*, unencumbered property.

---

---

# Bava Batra 175

## Arev Ketubah & Abaye

### Arev Ketubah Intro

The daf opens by picking up from 174b, approximately a third of the way down the page, in the context of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling in the *mishnah* concerning an *arev* for a *ketubah*. The *mishnah* addresses a scenario in which a guarantor underwrites the husband's obligation under the *ketubah* — that is, if the marriage ends in divorce or death and the wife cannot collect from the husband's estate, she may collect from the *arev*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if such a divorce actually takes place, the court must insist that the husband take a vow — *yadirana hana'ah* — prohibiting himself from deriving benefit from her, so as to forestall any collusive scheme whereby husband and wife manufacture a divorce, collect from the *arev*, and subsequently remarry. This ruling in the *mishnah* goes essentially uncontested.

### Moshe bar Atzri

The *gemara* then introduces a narrative involving a figure named Moshe bar Atzri, who had acted as *arev de'ketuvata de'khalatei* — guarantor of his daughter-in-law's *ketubah*, which is to say he guaranteed his own son's obligation under the *ketubah* to the son's wife. His son, Rav Huna, was a *tzurba me'rabanan* — a Torah scholar — who was suffering severe financial hardship and was unable to provide for his household.

### Divorce Scheme

Abaye, observing this situation, dropped a pointed suggestion — though notably without taking direct responsibility for the advice — that someone ought to go and inform Rav Huna that he should divorce his wife, allow her to collect her *ketubah* from her father-in-law, the *arev*, and then remarry her afterward. The scheme was technically within the legal framework, but its moral dimension is immediately troubling, and the *gemara* goes on to probe it from several directions.

### Rava's Objection

Rava raised an objection: but the *mishnah* of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires precisely that in such a case the man take a vow not to derive benefit from his divorced wife, which would prevent him from remarrying her. The scheme would not work. What is striking about Rava's objection is that it is purely practical — he raises no moral concern, only the question of feasibility.

### Unmarked Divorce

Abaye responded: *attu kol de-megarish dina de-megarish* — does every person who divorces his wife do so through a *beis din*? If the divorce were conducted without formal rabbinic oversight, who would enforce the requirement of the vow? This answer is deeply troubling on multiple levels. First, if the *halacha* demands *yadirana hana'ah*, then one is bound by that requirement regardless of whether a *beis din* is present to enforce it. Second, and more fundamentally, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's insistence on the vow makes plain that the underlying scheme is morally suspect — the *arev* did a kindness by guaranteeing the *ketubah*, and to exploit that guarantee through a sham divorce is precisely the sort of conduct the *mishnah* seeks to prevent. The question of how Abaye could advise such a course hangs heavily over the entire passage.

### Kohen Impediment

The *gemara* then relates: *u-sof igla'ei milta de-kohen hu* — in the end it emerged that Rav Huna, son of Moshe bar Atzri, was a *kohen*. Had he divorced his wife, he would have been permanently prohibited from remarrying her. Whether this was discovered before or after any action was taken, the scheme would have been undone in any case.

### Poverty Follows

Abaye responded with a folk saying: *basar aniya azla aniyusa* — poverty follows the poor. Even this attempt to help Rav Huna was foreclosed. The remark has an air of resignation — despite all efforts, misfortune kept closing off every avenue of relief.

### Scheming Principle

Now the *gemara* poses the serious question that was lurking all along: *mi amar Abaye hachi?* How could Abaye have made such a suggestion? Does not Abaye himself say elsewhere that the *eizehu rasha arum* — the wicked clever person — is one who gives advice enabling someone to sell property in the manner ruled upon by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in a different context?

That ruling concerns a case where one person gives a field to Reuven with the condition that after Reuven's death it passes to Shimon — *v'acharecha l'Shimon*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that if Reuven sells the field outright to a third party, Levi, that sale severs the chain and Shimon never receives the field. Since the field is worth more to Levi than to Reuven — Levi gets it permanently, while Reuven had only a life interest — Reuven could in fact profit by selling it. Reuven himself would be entirely within his legal rights to do this. But if a third party were to come and advise Reuven to take advantage of this legal right, that advisor is considered a *rasha* — because he is injecting himself into a *riv lo lo*, a dispute that is none of his business, benefiting Reuven at Shimon's expense, and subverting the clear intention of the original grantor.

Analogously, Abaye was advising Rav Huna to pursue a course that, while technically legal, was deceitful in its very structure and injurious to the *arev* who had done Rav Huna's family a genuine kindness. Even if legally the *arev* was liable, the whole enterprise was built on deception. How can this be reconciled with Abaye's own stated position?

### Son vs. Rasha

The *gemara* offers two answers: *bno shani v'tzurba me'rabanan shani*. First, the case is different because the money would ultimately be passing from a father to his own son. The *arev* for the *ketubah* was Moshe bar Atzri himself — Rav Huna's father. Unlike the field case, where one is diverting assets from a stranger to benefit another stranger against the grantor's intent, here the money moves within the family. The father may not have agreed to this precise mechanism, but there is no transfer from Reuven's pocket to an unrelated Shimon's pocket. That said, this answer is admittedly not fully satisfying. The father agreed to be an *arev* for a specific purpose and on specific terms; invoking those terms through a sham divorce is not what he contemplated.

Second, Rav Huna was a *tzurba me'rabanan*, a Torah scholar, and this distinguishes the case further. The intended point seems to be not that Torah scholars enjoy license to engage in deception, but rather that ensuring a *talmid chacham* can provide for his household is itself a matter of communal concern — not merely a private interest — and therefore Abaye's involvement was not the gratuitous meddling in another's affairs that characterizes the *rasha arum*. Even so, neither answer fully addresses the fundamental problem of the deception involved in the scheme itself, and the *gemara*'s resolution remains, on any honest reading, quite difficult.

---

## Arev Ketubah No Obligati…

### Father Liability

The *gemara* now shifts to a technical question that the preceding narrative itself raises: how could Moshe bar Atzri have been liable as *arev* for the *ketubah* in the first place?

### Arev Not Obligated

The *gemara* states the operative principle: *v'kaimalan arev d'ketubah lo mishtabed* — we have an established ruling that an *arev* of a *ketubah* does not in fact obligate himself. The reasoning is that in a normal loan transaction, the lender parts with money in reliance on the guarantor's commitment, and the borrower actually receives funds. The *arev*'s obligation is therefore grounded in real economic reliance. In the case of a *ketubah*, however, no money changes hands at the moment of the guarantee. The *arev* is stepping forward to help the couple get married, and his commitment is presumed to be more ceremonial than genuinely intended — he lacks *g'mar da'at*, the full, settled intention required to create a binding obligation. This ruling cuts directly against our *mishnah*, which presupposes that an *arev* of a *ketubah* is liable — otherwise Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would have no reason to require the vow against remarriage. The *gemara* does not attempt to reconcile this tension; it simply states the ruling.

This principle is troubling from a different direction as well. The *ketubah* was instituted by *Chazal* specifically to protect the wife's interests. She is not lending money, but she is committing herself — her life — to this man. The need to protect her interests is real and weighty. To say that the *arev* was not being serious undermines precisely the protection she believed she was receiving.

### Arev vs. Kablan

The *gemara* then resolves the question of how Moshe bar Atzri could have been liable at all: *kablan hava* — he was not merely an *arev* but a *kablan*, using the stronger language reviewed in the previous daf, whereby the guarantor speaks as though the debt comes directly to him. Rather than saying "I will guarantee your obligation," a *kablan* says, in effect, "I am taking this obligation upon myself as though I am receiving the money and will pay." This stronger formulation might be sufficient to create a binding obligation even in the case of a *ketubah*.

### Kablan Property Debate

But the *gemara* immediately qualifies even this: not everyone agrees that a *kablan* of a *ketubah* is fully obligated in all circumstances. One opinion holds that a *kablan* of a *ketubah* is obligated — *mishtabed* — even when the husband has no assets. Another opinion, however, holds that even a *kablan* of a *ketubah* is obligated only when the husband does have assets (*ais lei mishtabed*), but when the husband has no assets (*leis lei lo mishtabed*), the *kablan* is not bound.

This second position is paradoxical in a way that is difficult to accept. The very moment when a guarantor is most needed is precisely when the primary debtor cannot pay. Yet the *gemara* here suggests that it is in exactly that circumstance — when the husband is impecunious — that the *kablan*'s commitment may not be binding. The logic again returns to *g'mar da'at*: if the husband has no assets and the wedding would not otherwise take place at all, the *kablan* is presumed to be pledging his commitment merely to facilitate the marriage rather than from genuine intention to accept the obligation. If the husband already has assets, the *kablan*'s stepping forward was unnecessary — and therefore reflects genuine, deliberate assumption of liability. The woman, in the very circumstance where she most needs the protection, may find the guarantee legally void.

### Property Destroyed

The *gemara* offers two resolutions for how Moshe bar Atzri's obligation as *kablan* could have been operative. The first: *mehavei hava lei v'ishtadaf* — perhaps Rav Huna did have property at the time of the marriage and only afterward his assets were destroyed or depreciated. In that case, the *kablan*'s commitment was made when the husband had assets, satisfying the condition of the stricter opinion. The second: *amalgabei brei shibudei m'shabid nafshie* — because the *kablan* was the father of the husband, we may presume that a father genuinely intends to obligate himself when guaranteeing his son's *ketubah*, beyond the pro forma commitment that we might ascribe to an unrelated *kablan*.

---

## Arev/Kablan Dispute

### Universal Agreement

The *gemara* now presents the formal statement of the underlying debate that was referenced earlier. It begins with the points of consensus. Regarding *areiv diksuva* — one who serves as a standard *arev* for a *ketubah* — *divrei hakol lo mishtabeid*: all opinions agree, contrary to the apparent implication of our *mishnah*, that such a person does not obligate himself. The rationale is the one already discussed: no money changes hands, the *arev* is simply facilitating the marriage, and without *g'mar da'at* there is no binding obligation.

### Kablan Always Obligates

Conversely, regarding a *kablan* of a regular monetary debt — *kablan deba'al chov* — *divrei hakol mishtabeid*: all agree that such a person fully obligates himself. Here both factors reinforce one another: the language is the strongest possible form of guarantee, and real money is in fact changing hands in reliance on the guarantor's commitment.

### Mixed Cases Debate

The dispute concerns the two intermediate cases: a *kablan* who uses the stronger language but in the context of a *ketubah*, where no money changes hands; and a standard *arev* using the weaker language but in the context of a genuine monetary loan, *baal chov*. In these mixed cases, *pligi* — the opinions diverge.

### Property Condition

One view holds that in these intermediate cases, the obligation depends on whether the primary debtor (*loveh*) has assets. If the *loveh* has assets, the guarantor is bound; if not, he is not. The logic is that when the primary debtor has resources, the guarantor's intervention was superfluous — no one required him to step forward, and his doing so therefore reflects genuine, settled intention. But when the *loveh* has no assets and the transaction could not proceed without the guarantor, the guarantor's pledge is seen as instrumental — designed to make the transaction happen — rather than as a sincere assumption of liability.

This position is genuinely difficult to accept. From the creditor's standpoint, the guarantor's pledge is precisely what induced him to extend the loan. To say that the guarantee is legally void in the very circumstance where it was most needed — and where the creditor's reliance on it was greatest — seems to make the entire institution of guaranty unreliable.

### No Property Condition

The opposing view holds that in all intermediate cases, regardless of whether the *loveh* has assets, the guarantor is bound — *bein ais lei bein leis lei mishtabeid*. An additional curiosity in the presentation of this debate is that neither position is attributed to a named *amora*. The formulation is simply *mar savar* and *u'mar savar* — "one holds" and "the other holds" — without any identification of who stands behind each view. This is quite unusual for a named *tannaic* or *amoraic* dispute.

### Final Arev Ruling

The *gemara* concludes: *vehilchata* — and the law is as follows. In all cases of *arev*, regardless of whether the language used is that of *arev* or *kablan*, and regardless of whether the *loveh* has assets or not, the guarantor is obligated. The single exception carved out is *bar me'arev dekesubah* — the case of one who uses the weaker *arev* language in the context of a *ketubah*. There, *af al gav de'is lei l'ba'al lo mishtabeid* — even if the husband has assets, the guarantor is not bound. The reason: *mitzvah hu de'aveid velav midi chasrei* — he is merely performing a good deed, facilitating the marriage; the woman parts with nothing, and his commitment is therefore not taken as a genuine legal obligation. It is possible that in practice such a signing had become an honorific gesture — something akin to a ritual of participation in the wedding — rather than a genuine assumption of legal liability. Whether or not the *gemara* goes that far, the ruling stands, however unsatisfying it may seem from the perspective of the woman whose interests the *ketubah* was meant to protect.

---

## Deathbed & Hekdesh

### Separate from Hekdesh

The *gemara* transitions to a new topic with a statement of Rav Huna: if a *shchiv mera* — a person on his deathbed — distributes all of his assets to *hekdesh* (consecrated charity), but then states that a particular debt of one hundred *zuz* remains outstanding to Reuven, we believe him. *Chazaka ein adam oseh kenunyah al hekdesh* — there is a presumption that a person will not fabricate a claim in order to cheat *hekdesh* out of assets that he has already consecrated. The heirs must therefore honor this admitted debt and pay Reuven.

### Not Cheating Heirs

Rav Nachman challenged this reasoning. The very same logic, he argued, should apply to a person's own children: we similarly presume that a person does not wish to cheat his own heirs. Yet Rav and Shmuel — *amri tuvai* — both say that a *shchiv mera* who admits to owing Reuven money is only believed if he additionally says *tenu* — "give it to him." If he merely says "I owe Reuven a hundred *zuz*" without the directive to give it, the debt is not paid out.

### Tenu Requirement

The Rav and Shmuel ruling thus requires the affirmative directive *tenu* for the admission to be actionable. Why? Because without *tenu*, we apply the principle that *adam asui shelo lehasbi'a es banav* — a person acts in ways designed to prevent his children from appearing wealthy. A dying father may announce outstanding debts he does not actually owe so that creditors and others will not perceive his children as coming into a large inheritance and seek to exploit them. Unless he says *tenu* — a directive that implies a genuine, active intention to have the money transferred — we treat his statement as possibly motivated by this protective impulse rather than by truthfulness.

### Appearing Poor

This logic is then applied back to the case of *hekdesh*: *hacha nami adam asui shelo lehasbia es atzmo* — perhaps a person similarly acts to avoid appearing rich in his own right. If he is giving everything to *hekdesh*, he might claim a large outstanding debt to Reuven so that people do not think of him as a man of great wealth. This rationale is admittedly difficult to fully understand. A person on his deathbed who has already consecrated all his property has little practical reason to manage his public image in the days or weeks that remain.
