Yet this is the logic the *gemara* invokes, and it accordingly raises the question of whether *tenu* is required in the *hekdesh* case as well.

### Shetar Distinction

The *gemara* resolves the tension: *ki amar Rav Huna hatam denakat shtar* — when Rav Huna said the *shchiv mera* is believed, he was speaking about a case in which Reuven already holds a *shtar*. Why would the *shchiv mera*'s admission then matter if Reuven already has a *shtar*? Tosafot explains: when collecting from orphans, even a holder of a *shtar* — even one that is *mekuyam* (whose signatures have been verified) — is normally required to take an oath (*shvuah*) that the debt has not been repaid, since the orphans cannot have personal knowledge of their father's business affairs. If the father on his deathbed acknowledged the debt, this relieves the creditor of the need to take that *shvuah*. The admission is thus not creating the debt anew but confirming its continued validity for purposes of relieving the creditor of the *shvuah* requirement.

### Mekuyam & Tenu

This leads the *gemara* to ask whether Rav and Shmuel, who required *tenu*, were also discussing a case where Reuven holds a *shtar*. The *gemara* confirms: yes, both discussions involve a *shtar*. The distinction lies in whether the *shtar* is *mekuyam* — i.e., whether the witnesses' signatures have been formally verified. When Rav Huna said the admission is sufficient (without *tenu*), he was speaking of a *shtar mekuyam*, where the only remaining obstacle to collection from orphans is the requirement of a *shvuah*. In that case, the *shchiv mera*'s statement — even without *tenu* — suffices to waive the *shvuah* requirement. When Rav and Shmuel said *tenu* is required, they were speaking of a *shtar* that is not *mekuyam*, where the creditor would ordinarily need to go through the process of establishing (*mekayem*) the validity of the document's signatures. In that case, even the deathbed admission without *tenu* is insufficient — the creditor must still have the signatures verified. Only with *tenu* does the *shchiv mera*'s statement substitute for the formal process of *kiyum ha-shtar*.

This is a significant narrowing of the original statements, which sounded in their plain presentation as broad claims about belief and presumption. What emerges is a much more precisely calibrated set of rules governing the interaction between deathbed admissions, the existence of a *shtar*, and whether that *shtar* has been formally verified.

It is worth noting that as a matter of practical *halacha*, the rule that an oral loan (*malveh al peh*) cannot be collected from orphans was subsequently modified at the time of the *Geonim*, who established that even such loans may be collected from *yorshim*. This development protects creditors from a total loss in cases where no written instrument was ever executed.

### Tenu as Kiyum

Rav Pappa draws the principle together: when the *shchiv mera* says *tenu* — even where the *shtar* is not *mekuyam* — the *tenu* directive itself functions as a *kiyum* of the document. It is, in effect, a rabbinic substitute for the formal verification process. Without *tenu*, the unverified document remains without the necessary *kiyum* and cannot be used to compel the orphans to pay.

---

## Orphans & Payment

### Orphans Believed

Rava now introduces a related scenario. A *shchiv mera* states that he owes Reuven money, and afterward the orphans claim that the debt was paid. The *rishonim* understand this as involving a case where Reuven actually demanded payment and the *shchiv mera* acknowledged the debt, as distinct from a purely volunteered admission. If the father merely said he owed the money — without issuing a *tenu* directive — the orphans are believed when they say the debt was subsequently paid (*ne'emanin*).

### Tenu Bars Orphans

But if the father said *tenu* — give the money to Reuven — and afterward the orphans say they paid, they are not believed.

### Tenu More Credible

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *klapi laya* — the opposite seems to make more logical sense. If the father said *tenu*, that is a stronger and more explicit directive, and one can more readily assume the orphans acted on it and paid. *Ipcha mistabra* — the reverse is what logic suggests: when he said *tenu*, *keivan d'paska avuhon l'milsa*, since the father definitively commanded the matter, it is more plausible that they carried it out. When he merely said he owed the money without a directive, since he did not press the matter, there is less reason to assume they paid. The *gemara* thus reverses the initial presentation.

### Father Remembered

The *gemara* then presents the corrected version of the scenario: *shchiv mera she'amar maneh l'ploni biyadi v'amru yetomim chazar v'amar aba parati* — the *shchiv mera* said he owes Reuven money, and the orphans say not that they themselves paid, but that their father subsequently remembered or stated that he had already paid the debt before his declaration. In that case — where the father himself walked back his admission — *ne'emanin*, the orphans are believed.

### Father Said Remembered

The reason is *itkurei midkar* — he remembered. When a person merely says he owes money without issuing *tenu*, the statement is tentative enough that a subsequent recollection or correction by the father himself is credible. But if the father had said *tenu* — an unambiguous directive — and then the orphans report that the father said he remembered he had already paid, they are not believed: *d'im ita d'para lo hava amar tnu* — had he truly already paid, he would never have issued the affirmative command to give the money. The absolute certainty implicit in the *tenu* directive forecloses the possibility that the father was mistaken and later corrected himself.

The structure of the two scenarios thus runs in opposite directions depending on what the orphans are claiming. When orphans claim they themselves paid the debt: *tenu* makes them *more* believed, because the father's clear directive makes it plausible they acted on it. When orphans claim the father remembered he had already paid: *tenu* makes them *less* believed, because the father's unequivocal directive is inconsistent with any prior payment.

---

## Deathbed Admission

### Witnesses Needed

Rava raises several questions about the *shchiv mera*'s admission more broadly. The first: does a *shchiv mera* who admits a debt need to formally designate witnesses — saying *atem edai*, "you are my witnesses" — for his admission to carry legal force? Normally, an extrajudicial admission requires such a designation, since without it, we might treat the statement as casual or dismissive rather than as a formal acknowledgment.

### Automatic Shetar

A related question: if witnesses observe a *shchiv mera*'s admission without being explicitly commanded to record it, may they write it up as a *shtar* on their own initiative? Normally a person must explicitly instruct witnesses to reduce his words to writing; may that requirement be dispensed with in the case of a *shchiv mera*?

### No Joking at Death

The *gemara* answers both questions together: *batar d'ba'ei hadar pashatei* — after posing these questions, Rava himself resolved them. *Ein adam mashatei b'sha'at mita* — a person does not jest or speak carelessly at the moment of death. There is no concern that a *shchiv mera*'s admission is casual or dismissive; the gravity of the deathbed context endows every statement with seriousness.

### Force of Document

Correspondingly: *divrei shchiv mera k-ktuvin u-k-mesurin dami* — the words of a *shchiv mera* have the legal force of a written document and of a performed *kinyan*. Just as we say that a *shchiv mera*'s dispositions of property take effect by virtue of his words alone without requiring formal *kinyan* procedures, so too his admissions carry the weight of a formally executed *shtar*. He need not say *atem edai*, and witnesses may record his words as a *shtar* without any explicit command to do so.

---

## Loan Types & Collection

### Shetar Encumbered

The *mishnah* at the opening of 175b sets out a taxonomy of loan types and the corresponding scope of collection rights. A loan made with a *shtar* — *ha-malveh chavero b-shtar* — creates a lien on the borrower's properties and entitles the creditor to collect from *nechasim meshubadim*, encumbered property, including property the borrower has sold to third parties after the loan was made. The existence of the *shtar* provides the requisite public notice (*shibudim*) and, notably, even though the *shtar* may not explicitly state that there is a lien on the borrower's other properties, the principle of *achrayut ta'ut sofer* — that the omission of a guarantee clause is treated as a scribal error — means that such liens attach automatically.

### Witnesses Unencumbered

A loan made before witnesses but without a *shtar* does not create liens. The creditor in such a case may only collect from *nechasim bnei chorin* — unencumbered property currently in the possession of the borrower — and cannot reach assets the borrower has sold or transferred.

### IOU Unencumbered

If the debtor himself writes out an acknowledgment of debt — *ktav yado*, a handwritten IOU — that document may be used to compel payment, but because it was not executed before witnesses with the public formality of a proper *shtar*, it too creates no lien. Collection is limited to unencumbered property.

### Late Arev Unencumbered

Finally, if the *arev* affixed his guarantee to the *shtar* after the witnesses had already signed — *arev hayotzei le'achar chitum shtaros* — the creditor may collect from the *arev*, but only from the *arev*'s unencumbered property. Because the guarantee was added after the formal execution of the document, it does not benefit from the lien-creating effect of the witnesses' signatures, and is treated as equivalent to an oral or informal commitment.

---

## Arev Contingency

### Choking Parable

Ben Nanas illustrates the fundamental principle governing the *arev*'s obligation with a vivid parable: imagine someone who is choking another person in the marketplace, and a bystander says, "Release him and I will give you a hundred *zuz*." Such a promise, says Ben Nanas, is unenforceable. The bystander did not genuinely intend to transfer money; he was acting under duress, trying to save the victim, and no *g'mar da'at* — no settled intention — underlies that promise.

### Guarantee Causation

The parable maps onto the *arev* situation as follows: if the *arev* steps in and commits to the guarantee only after the loan has already been made and the money has already changed hands, then the lender did not extend credit in reliance on the *arev*'s commitment. Perhaps the *arev* is intervening to relieve pressure on the borrower — trying to stop the lender from pursuing him aggressively — but the loan itself was not made because of the guarantee. *Shelo al m'nas ken hilvahu* — he did not lend in reliance on this — and therefore *emunaso hilvahu*, the lender's willingness to extend credit was not based on the *arev*'s commitment. In consequence, the *arev* who signed after the fact cannot be compelled to pay.

### When vs. Before

The *mishnah* thus delineates the two cases sharply. *Halvahu va'ani noten lach* — "lend him the money and I will pay you": when the guarantee precedes the loan and the money is extended specifically because the *arev* has committed himself, the *arev* is *chayav* — fully obligated — because *al emunaso hilvahu*, the creditor acted in reliance on the *arev*'s word. But when the guarantee comes only after the money has already been lent, no such causal nexus exists, and the *arev* bears no obligation at all, collecting neither from encumbered nor from unencumbered property.

---

## Praise for Dinei

### Wisdom & Civil Law

The *mishnah* closes the tractate with a celebrated statement of Rabi Yishmael: *harotzeh sheyachkim ya'asok b'dinei mamanos* — one who wishes to acquire wisdom should devote himself to the study of civil law, *dinei mamanos*.

### Greatest Intellectual

The reason: *she'ein lach miktzoa baTorah yoser mehen* — there is no field in the entire Torah that demands greater intellectual capacity or that sharpens the mind more than *dinei mamanos*. The intricate interplay of principles, the layered distinctions between *arev* and *kablan*, the refined analysis of *g'mar da'at*, the fine calibrations of when a *shchiv mera*'s words do or do not carry legal force — all of this has been on full display in the pages of the tractate.

### Flowing Well

*V'hen k'mayan hanove'a* — they are like a flowing, springing well. There is no end to the new ideas, new applications, and new distinctions that emerge from sustained engagement with civil law. The well does not run dry.

### Shimon ben Nanas

And if one wishes to seriously take up the study of *dinei mamanos*, Rabi Yishmael recommends: *yeshamesh es Shimon Ben Nanas* — attend upon Shimon ben Nanas, who is exemplary not merely for his book knowledge but for his practical wisdom in applying the law — precisely the same Shimon ben Nanas whose parable about the man choking his fellow illuminated the foundational principle of the *arev*'s obligation. He is, in Rabi Yishmael's assessment, the master from whom one should seek to learn.

---

---

# Bava Batra 176

## Liens: דאורייתא vs. דרבנן

### Ulla: Liens from Torah

We open the final *daf* of Bava Batra with the *gemara* that follows the *mishna* on 175b. The *mishna* established two foundational principles that have been guiding our discussion: that a *shtar chov* — a written loan document — creates liens on the borrower's property, while an oral loan backed only by witnesses but no written document does not. The *mishna* also addressed the *areiv*, the guarantor, who signs at the bottom of the *shtar* after the witnesses have already signed: according to Rabbi Yishmael, such a guarantor is obligated, but his obligation carries no liens against his property; according to Ben Nanas, he is not even obligated at all. The *gemara* now explores the theoretical underpinning of these distinctions through a dispute between Ulla and Rabba.

*Amar Ulla*: Ulla holds that, *dvar Torah* — as a matter of Torah law — whether a loan was made with a written document or whether it was made purely orally, the lender would be entitled to collect from encumbered property. Liens exist as a matter of biblical reality. The act of lending money, in and of itself, creates the legal phenomenon of *shibud* — an encumbrance on the borrower's assets. No additional instrument is required to bring that encumbrance into existence.

### Rabba: Liens Rabbinic On…

Rabba disagrees entirely. According to Rabba, the Torah recognizes no category of liens at all. Whether the loan was documented in a *shtar* or was entirely oral, the Torah's default position is that a lender may collect only from *bnei chorin* — unencumbered property in the borrower's direct possession. It is worth noting, as Tosafot points out, that Rabba may be making an even more radical claim: that even if the document explicitly stipulated that the borrower's property should be encumbered, the Torah would recognize no such legal reality. The concept of a lien — the notion that a creditor holds a right in property even after it has been transferred to a third party — may simply not exist as a biblical category.

### Rationale & Policy

The two positions lead to opposite accounts of rabbinic intervention, and this is where the policy logic becomes illuminating. According to Ulla, since liens exist by Torah law, the rabbis had to step in and *remove* them in certain cases. Specifically, they removed the lender's right to collect from encumbered property when the loan was made without a written document. Why? *Mishum pseda de-lekuchos* — to protect the purchasers. A buyer who purchases land from the borrower has no way of knowing about an undocumented oral loan and cannot reasonably be expected to have investigated it. The rabbis therefore protected such buyers by effectively erasing the Torah-based lien in cases where no written record existed. When a *shtar* was written, however, the buyers bear responsibility for their own loss: *hasam inhu de'afsidu anafshayhu* — they brought the loss upon themselves, since the public document gave them the means to find out.

According to Rabba, the logic runs in the opposite direction. Since there are no Torah-based liens at all, the rabbis had to *create* them. Their motivation: *kedei shelo tin'ol deles bifnei lovin* — so as not to lock the door in front of borrowers, or more precisely, in front of lenders. The Torah already provides many disincentives for lending money; the rabbis needed to encourage the practice by ensuring that lenders had a reliable mechanism for recovering their funds. They therefore instituted the rabbinic creation of liens — but only when the lender takes the step of writing a *shtar*, because a *shtar* that is publicized gives the lender a way to protect himself without unfairly harming innocent purchasers. The *gemara* pushes back: why not extend rabbinic liens even to oral loans, in order to maximize the encouragement of lending? The answer: *hasam leis lei kala* — an oral loan has no public voice; there is no way for purchasers to discover it, and so the *pseda de-lekuchos* concern would immediately reassert itself. Moreover, once the rabbis have given lenders the option of writing a *shtar* and thereby securing full protection, they need not provide additional protection for lenders who decline to use that instrument.

It is worth pausing here to observe what is at stake conceptually. Both positions ultimately produce the same practical legal framework: a written loan carries liens, an oral loan does not. Yet the *gemara* clearly believes the theoretical difference is not merely academic. The question of whether *shibuda de-oraita* or *lav de-oraita* carries real legal consequences — and this is illustrated through a challenge from the laws of inheritance.

The *gemara* raises Rabba's own ruling elsewhere: *gavu karka yesh lo, gavu ma'ot ein lo* — if the heirs collect the outstanding debt in the form of land, a *bechor* (firstborn son) takes a double portion of that land; if they collect in cash, he does not. The principle governing a *bechor*'s double portion is that he collects *pi shnayim* only from property already in the estate at the father's death, not from property that subsequently flows into it — *ein ha-bechor notel pi shnayim b'ra'uy ke-va-muchzak*. The only way to explain why land collected after death is treated as if it was already part of the estate is to say that the estate always had a lien on it — its claws were already in that land — and therefore collection of it is not new property flowing in but the realization of an already-existing right. This logic presupposes *shibuda de-oraita*. But Rabba holds that liens are purely rabbinic! How could he issue such a ruling?

The *gemara* considers reversing the positions — assigning Rabba's *bechor* ruling to Ulla and vice versa — but is blocked by independent evidence for Ulla's position. *V'ha'amar Ulla, dvar Torah, ba'al chov dino b'ziborit* — Ulla said explicitly that a creditor collects from grade-C property by Torah law. The Rashbam sees this as proof that Ulla holds liens exist biblically, since the creditor is going to property. Tosafot, however, is not fully satisfied with this proof, noting that the rule about *ziborit* may concern direct collection from the borrower himself — which does not necessarily implicate the concept of a lien, i.e., the right to collect from a third party who purchased the land. For the Rashbam, any right to the borrower's property reflects the lien concept; for Tosafot, the lien specifically refers to the right against third-party purchasers, which is a distinct and more demanding category.

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction in Rabba by explaining that when Rabba issued his *bechor* ruling, he was not expressing his own view. *Rabba ta'ama de-vnei Ma'arava ka'amar v'lav sevira lei* — Rabba was there articulating the position of the sages of the West, *bnei Ma'arava*, not his own opinion. Rabba himself would not apply the *bechor* double-portion rule to land collected after the father's death, because for Rabba there was no pre-existing lien that would make that land "already" part of the estate.

### Liens as Ownership

This brings us to a conceptual framework that, while not stated explicitly in the *gemara* itself, helps illuminate what is at stake in the debate. Several *rishonim* and *acharonim* suggest two distinct ways of conceptualizing what a lien actually is.

The first model treats a lien as nothing more than an abstract legal right: because Michael owes me money, I have a right that allows me, under certain conditions, to go collect from Chanan who purchased Michael's land. But this model can seem arbitrary. Why should the fact that Michael owes me money create any rights against Chanan's property?

The second model is more intuitive: a lien represents a form of partial ownership in the land itself. From the moment of the loan, I held a certain stake in Michael's property. When Chanan bought that land, he bought it already encumbered by my pre-existing rights. This model makes the lien far more comprehensible — and it also points toward what a *shtar* might actually be doing. A *shtar* is, in other contexts, an instrument for transferring property rights. Perhaps the *shtar chov* functions similarly: it transfers a partial right in Michael's property to me, the lender, creating genuine partial ownership rather than a mere abstract entitlement. This would explain why, under this framework, *shibud de-oraita* has real legal consequences for the *bechor*: if the estate always held partial ownership in the land through the biblical lien, then collection of that land is not new property flowing in — it is the estate reclaiming what was always, in a sense, already its own.

---

## Heirs vs. Purchasers

### Rav & Shmuel Position

The *gemara* now introduces a related dispute with a third axis: the distinction between collecting from heirs and collecting from purchasers. This brings a new practical implication of the *shibud* debate into focus.

Rav and Shmuel both rule: *malveh al peh eino goveh lo min ha-yorshim ve-lo min ha-lekuchos* — an oral loan, with no written document, cannot be collected either from the borrower's heirs or from those who purchased the borrower's property. Their reasoning: *mai ta'ama, shibuda lav de-oraita* — since liens are not biblical, they exist only where the rabbis created them, and the rabbis created them only in the context of a written document. A lender who chose not to write a *shtar* forfeited the rabbinic protection entirely, including any claim against the heirs.

The logic here deserves reflection. One might have expected that even without a *shtar*, a lender could still collect from the heirs — after all, the concern that motivated the rabbis to remove liens for oral loans was the protection of innocent purchasers who paid money for the property not knowing of the undocumented debt. Heirs, by contrast, paid nothing; they simply received an inheritance. If the goal is to protect paying buyers, why should that protection extend to heirs who are not buying anything? This is precisely the argument one could construct from the *de-oraita* position: if liens exist biblically, there is no reason to protect heirs, and a lender should be able to collect from them even without a document. But Rav and Shmuel, who hold *shibuda lav de-oraita*, reason that since liens exist only where the rabbis explicitly created them — and the rabbis created them only when a *shtar* was written — without a *shtar* there is simply no lien to enforce against anyone, heirs included.

### R. Yochanan & Resh Lakish

Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish take the diametrically opposite position: *malveh al peh goveh bein min ha-yorshim u-vein min ha-lekuchos* — an oral loan allows collection from both heirs and purchasers. Their reasoning is *shibuda de-oraita*: liens are biblical, and the rabbis did nothing to interfere with them. This position, as the *gemara* notes, flatly contradicts everything the *mishna* has established. If you can collect from purchasers even without a written document, the entire edifice of the *mishna*'s ruling that oral loans have no liens collapses.

### Well-Digger Case

The *gemara* challenges Rav and Shmuel's position from a *baraita*. The case: someone who illegally digs a pit in the public thoroughfare, and an ox falls into the pit, killing the digger in the process while the ox also dies. The heirs of the pit-digger are liable to pay the owner of the ox for its value. But this debt — the obligation to pay damages — was never memorialized in any written document. How can the heirs be liable? According to Rav and Shmuel, without a *shtar*, you cannot collect from heirs.

The *gemara* resolves this through increasingly strained constructions. Rav Ila citing Rav says: the case is where the pit-digger had not yet died when a court session was held and judgment was rendered against him — and a court ruling is equivalent to a written document. The *gemara* objects: the *baraita* says the ox *killed* him. Rav Adda bar Ahava responds: he was rendered a *treifah* — fatally wounded but not yet dead — and survived long enough for a judgment to be issued. Then Rav Nachman offers a tradition that the *tanna* taught the case as one where the man died and was buried by the ox in the pit. To which the *gemara* answers: the *beit din* was sitting right at the lip of the well and issued their ruling before his last breath.

The *gemara* elsewhere offers an additional avenue of explanation: a debt whose obligation derives directly from Torah law — such as the obligation to pay damages — may be treated as if it were written in a document. *Milveh ha-ksuvah ba-Torah ki-ksuvah bi-shtar damya*. But the resolutions remain strained, and the middle position — that you can collect from heirs but not purchasers — is not yet stated here. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish meanwhile stand in tension with the *mishna*, and the *gemara* does not issue a formal refutation of their view at this juncture.

---

## Heirs vs. Purchasers (II)

### Rav Papa's Halakha

Rav Papa, on *daf* 176, issues the definitive ruling: *hilchesa, malveh al peh goveh min ha-yorshim ve-eino goveh min ha-lekuchos* — the halakha is that an oral loan allows collection from the heirs but not from purchasers.

Two reasons are given. Collection from the heirs is permitted *kedei shelo tin'ol deles bifnei lovin* — so as not to lock the door in front of lenders. Even though one could argue that a lender who chose not to write a *shtar* should have known the consequences, the scenario in which a borrower dies and his heirs receive the estate is a natural, predictable occurrence. It is fair to allow a lender to collect the debt in that scenario regardless of whether a document was written. The heirs, after all, have not expended any money; they are simply paying their father's debt out of an estate they received as a gift of inheritance. On the other side, collection from purchasers is forbidden — *de-leis lei kala* — because an oral loan has no public voice, and purchasers cannot be expected to have known about it.

As Tosafot notes, this split ruling does not resolve the underlying debate about whether *shibuda de-oraita* or *lav de-oraita*. Both sides can accommodate it: if *shibuda de-oraita*, then liens exist by default and the rabbis simply declined to erode them against heirs while removing them against purchasers. If *lav de-oraita*, then the rabbis instituted liens *kedei shelo tin'ol deles* even in the oral case when it comes to heirs, while declining to do so for purchasers. However, Tosafot observes that the *gemara* in the first chapter of Kiddushin explicitly associates this split ruling with the position of *shibuda de-oraita* — which makes intuitive sense, since if liens are biblical, there is a natural baseline from which the rabbis are making targeted exceptions, rather than creating entirely new rabbinic entitlements.

One further question arises: is a *shtar chov* itself a biblical institution? A *shtar* that effects a legal change — a *get*, a writ of manumission, a deed of sale — is certainly recognized by Torah law. But a *shtar* whose entire purpose is to serve as testimony, to create a written record of a transaction that has already occurred, may be only a rabbinic institution. This is a genuine debate among the *rishonim*, with the Ramban and Rambam holding differing views. If the *shtar chov* is itself only rabbinic, then the entire structure of rabbinic-versus-Torah liens takes on an additional layer: the instrument that triggers the rabbinic creation of liens may itself be a rabbinic creation.

---

## Document & Witness Rules

### Document + Witnesses

The *gemara* now proceeds to spell out a series of specific rules about when a loan document creates liens and when it does not. The baseline principle: both witnesses and a written document are required for liens to obtain. Without witnesses, a document alone does not create liens; without a document, witnesses alone do not create liens.

### Hand-Written IOU

*Hotzi alav ktav yado* — if the lender produces the borrower's own hand-written acknowledgment of the debt, he may use that to collect from the borrower directly, from *bnei chorin*. But this does not create liens on property sold to purchasers. A hand-written IOU, unsupported by independent witnesses, functions as evidence of the obligation but does not achieve the status of a full *shtar* with *shibud*.

### Beit Din Validation

A *she'ela* is posed by Rabba bar Rav Nachman to Rav Yochanan: *huchzak ktav yado be-veis din mai?* — what if the borrower's handwriting in the IOU was validated by a *beit din*, which affixed its seal confirming that the signature is authentic? Does this validation transform the document into one backed by witnesses, thereby creating liens?

The answer is no. Even if the *beit din* validates the borrower's handwriting, *eino goveh ela mi-nechasim bnei chorin* — he may still collect only from unencumbered property. The Rashbam explains that the *beit din*'s validation does not function as testimony to the loan itself; its purpose is only to prevent the borrower from later denying his signature. The *beit din* is not adding the weight of witness testimony to the *shtar*; it is simply removing the borrower's ability to claim forgery. The document remains exactly what it was before the validation, with no enhanced legal status vis-à-vis third-party purchasers.

### R. Elazar: Witnesses

The *gemara* introduces a *baraita* about three kinds of invalid *gittin* that are nevertheless *kasher be-di'avad* — if the woman remarried, we recognize the divorce as effective and the child of the new marriage is not a *mamzer*. The three cases are: a *get* written in the husband's own handwriting with no witnesses; a *get* with witnesses but no date; and a *get* with a date but with only one witness.

Rabbi Elazar then offers his ruling: even if there are no witnesses signed on the document, if it was delivered in the presence of witnesses — *eidei mesira karsai*, witnesses to the act of delivery are determinative — the *get* is fully valid, and not only valid but *goveh mi-nechasim meshubadim*. If we apply this principle to a loan document, then even a completely unsigned *shtar* handed over to the lender in the presence of two witnesses would create liens, because those witnesses to the delivery are the witnesses of the *shtar*.

This is a striking ruling. The *kol* — the publicity — that the *shtar* creates is achieved not by the signatures inscribed in the document but by the act of witnessed delivery. Two witnesses who saw the document handed over become, in Rabbi Elazar's view, the effective witnesses of that *shtar*, capable of generating full *shibud*.

### Document Effectiveness

This raises the obvious question for our earlier discussion: if witnesses present at the moment of delivery create liens even without anything written in the document, why does the subsequent validation of a hand-written IOU by a *beit din* — which involves three judges examining and certifying the document — fail to create liens?

The *gemara* answers with a principle of temporal priority: *shani hasam de-mishas kesiva hu de-shiabad nafshia* — in Rabbi Elazar's case, the *shibud* takes effect from the moment the *shtar* came into existence as a *shtar*. When does a *shtar* come into existence? At the moment it is handed over to the other side. And at that very moment, two witnesses were present and observing. The *shtar*, from its very inception as an operative document, had witnesses. The *shibud* attached simultaneously with the *shtar*'s creation.

By contrast, when Michael hands over his hand-written IOU and only later does the lender go to *beit din* to get the signature validated, the document became operative — was handed over and received — without any witnesses present at that moment. The witnesses, so to speak, arrived after the fact. Since the *shibud* must attach at the moment the *shtar* comes into being, and at that moment there were no witnesses, the subsequent validation cannot retroactively create a *shtar* that carries liens. The *beit din*'s seal does one thing: it prevents the borrower from denying that the signature is his. It does not transform the document into a *shtar* with *shibud*, because that would require witnesses present at the formative moment.

---

## Guarantor Obligations

### Before vs. After Witness…

The *gemara* returns to the case of the guarantor who signs on a *shtar*. Rav rules: if the guarantor's signature appears before the witnesses sign — that is, his commitment is embedded within the body of the document and the witnesses are then signing to attest to the whole — then the lender *goveh mi-nechasim meshubadim*, he has liens on the guarantor's property. If the guarantor's signature appears after the witnesses have already signed — as in the *mishna*'s case — then the lender *goveh mi-nechasim bnei chorin*, he can collect from the guarantor's unencumbered property but has no liens. This is essentially the ruling of Rabbi Yishmael in the *mishna*, now spelled out with its underlying rationale: the placement of the guarantor's commitment relative to the witnesses determines whether his obligation carries a *shtar* with *shibud*.

### Rav's Two Positions

Yet the *gemara* reports that Rav himself on other occasions ruled differently: *afilu kodem chitumei shtaros eino goveh ela mi-nechasim bnei chorin* — even if the guarantor signed before the witnesses, the lender still has no liens on the guarantor's property. This appears to be a direct contradiction within Rav's own rulings. The *gemara* announces: *la kashya* — this is no contradiction.

### Vav Distinction

The resolution turns on a single letter. If the *shtar* reads *ploni areiv* — "so-and-so is a guarantor" — then the guarantor's commitment stands as a separate statement, syntactically detached from the core content of the *shtar*. The witnesses who sign are signing to the main body of the document — the loan — not to this additional line about the guarantor. Consequently, even if the guarantor's name appears before the witnesses' signatures, his obligation does not have the status of a witnessed *shtar* and carries no *shibud*. But if the *shtar* reads *u'ploni areiv* — "and so-and-so is a guarantor," with a *vav* connecting it to what preceded — then the guarantor's commitment is syntactically integrated into one continuous statement. The witnesses are signing to the entirety of this unified document, including the guarantor's obligation, and therefore the guarantor's commitment carries *shibud*.

This is admittedly a formalistic distinction, and one that may leave the reader searching for the underlying policy. One possible explanation is an effort to protect the *areiv*: the guarantor is performing a generous act by standing up for the borrower, and the halakha perhaps wishes to limit the circumstances under which he will be fully exposed to liens on his own property. Another consideration is the protection of purchasers of the guarantor's property: the question is whether the *lekuchos* who buy from the guarantor have sufficient notice that his property is encumbered, and a tightly integrated *shtar* — marked by the conjunctive *vav* — may be seen as generating greater public notice than a loosely appended separate statement.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges this resolution by drawing a comparison to a *get* that is *pasul*. The case: a *get* that contains, at the end, the phrase *she'eilas shalom* — a greeting, asking how someone is doing — followed by the witnesses' signatures. We rule such a *get* invalid because we say the witnesses may have been signing only to the greeting, not to the body of the *get* itself — and testimony directed at a greeting has no legal effect on the *get*. Now Rabbi Abbahu clarifies: he heard this ruling from Rabbi Yochanan himself. If you say *she'ilu* — "ask after her" — the *get* is *pasul*. If you say *ve-she'ilu* — "and ask after her," with a *vav* — the *get* is *kasher*, because the *vav* makes it one continuous statement and the witnesses are signing to the whole.

The challenge to our resolution of Rav's two positions is this: in the *get* case, even a *vav* is insufficient to ensure that the witnesses are truly signing to the substance of the *get*, if there is extraneous matter present. So how can we say that a *vav* before the guarantor's name ensures that the witnesses are signing to his obligation? Surely the guarantor clause is less extraneous than a social greeting — it is legally significant content — but the comparison still raises a structural question.

### Unity of Statement

The resolution, as articulated by Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, turns on the direction of the concern. In the *get* case, when you say *she'ilu* without a *vav*, you have two entirely separate units: the *get* itself, and the greeting. We worry that the witnesses signed only to the greeting — an absurd thing, but formally possible — because the greeting stands as its own isolated statement. When you add the *vav*, it becomes one unified statement, the concern disappears, and the *get* is valid.

In the guarantor case, the parallel holds: *ploni areiv* without a *vav* creates a syntactic break, and we treat the guarantor clause as a separate unit, not directly attested by the witnesses. *U'ploni areiv* with a *vav* unifies the entire document, and the witnesses are signing to everything including the guarantor's obligation. Rabbi Yochanan's position, properly understood, is therefore identical to Rav's: the *vav* makes the difference. What we initially understood as Rabbi Yochanan saying that even a *vav* is insufficient turns out to be a misreading; he too holds that with a *vav* the guarantor's obligation carries *shibud*. The *gemara* concludes: *eima ve-chein amar Rabbi Yochanan* — simply say that Rabbi Yochanan said the same thing as Rav.

---

## Guarantor Liability

### Case of R. Ishmael

The *gemara* turns to a narrative that illuminates the final rulings about the guarantor's liability. A case came before Rabbi Yishmael in which the guarantor had signed at the bottom of the *shtar*, after the witnesses. Rabbi Yishmael's analysis: the guarantor is obligated to pay but his obligation carries no *shibud*, no liens. The obligation exists — one can collect from his *bnei chorin* — but there is no *shtar* against him personally that would allow collection from property he has sold to others.

### Ben Nanas Position

Ben Nanas disagreed fundamentally. He argued from a vivid and powerful analogy: imagine a creditor has grabbed a borrower by the throat — *chanok* — demanding payment. Another person steps forward and says: let him go, I will pay you. In such a case, says Ben Nanas, the bystander's promise is not a genuine acceptance of obligation. He is simply trying to stop the creditor's coercive pressure; his words do not reflect a considered decision to obligate himself. Therefore, when the guarantor signs at the bottom of an already-executed *shtar*, we infer that the loan had already been made, the lender was pressuring the borrower, and the guarantor stepped in to stop the pressure. His commitment is analogous to the bystander in the choking scenario — a reactive intervention, not a genuine acceptance of debt — and therefore he is not obligated at all.

### R. Ishmael's Praise

The *gemara* records that Rabbi Yishmael responded to Ben Nanas's argument with warm praise. He said: if you want wisdom, learn *dinei mamonos* — monetary law. And if you want to excel in *dinei mamonos*, apprentice yourself to Ben Nanas. The imagery Ben Nanas deployed was strikingly effective. Nonetheless:

### Actual Choking Case

The *gemara* then asks: *be-chanok ma lei amar Rabbi Yishmael?* — what about a case of literal choking? Not merely a metaphorical situation of financial pressure, but one where the creditor has literally grabbed the borrower by the throat. Does Rabbi Yishmael say even then the guarantor who steps in has obligated himself? One might think that in a case of genuine physical coercion, the guarantor's words are nothing more than a reflexive attempt to stop the violence, with no legal weight.

The answer comes from a tradition transmitted by Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *cholok haya Rabbi Yishmael af be-chanok* — Rabbi Yishmael would disagree with Ben Nanas even in a case of literal choking. Once a guarantor verbally accepts the obligation, regardless of what circumstances motivated him to speak those words, he has obligated himself. We do not look behind the words to evaluate the psychological state or external pressure that produced them. This is an interesting contrast to the earlier case where a guarantor for a *ketubah* is not liable because he is understood as simply trying to facilitate the marriage rather than genuinely accepting a debt. The distinction may rest on the principle of *lo plug*: we do not try to evaluate what motivated each individual guarantor; once the words of guarantee are spoken, the obligation attaches.

### Kinyan Requirement

The *gemara* now raises the question of *kinyan* — the formal act of acquisition that is typically required to create a binding legal commitment. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: chanok ve-kanu mi-yado* — in the choking scenario, where the guarantor steps in under pressure, his obligation is enforceable only if accompanied by a *kinyan*, a formal act such as the drawing of a handkerchief. The *gemara* derives from this, by implication, the converse principle: *mikhlal de-areiv be-alma lo ba'ei kinyan* — in a normal case, a guarantor does not require a *kinyan*. His verbal commitment alone is sufficient to create the obligation.

### Court-Appointed Guarantor

Rav Nachman introduces a qualification. He rules: *areiv de-bei din hu de-lo ba'ei kinyan* — specifically a guarantor whose role is assigned or supervised by a *beit din* does not require a *kinyan*. The logic: the honor and gravity of being designated by the court gives the guarantor's commitment such seriousness and weight that we need not require a formal act to confirm it. *De-be-hahi de-heiman lei gamar u-mishta'abed lei* — by the trust the *beit din* places in him, he fully resolves to accept the obligation and binds himself. But Rav Nachman holds that in an ordinary case — *ha de-alma* — a *kinyan* is indeed required. This conflicts with the earlier derivation from Shmuel, which suggested that only the pressure-induced guarantee (*chanok*) requires a *kinyan*, while all other guarantors are bound by words alone.

### Final Halakha

The *gemara* closes the *masechet* with the definitive ruling: *ve-hilchesa, areiv be-shas matan maos lo ba'ei kinyan* — a guarantor who accepts his obligation at the time of the loan, when the money is actually being transferred, does not need a *kinyan*. At that moment, the loan is being made *because of his guarantee*. The lender is extending credit in reliance on the guarantor's word. The guarantor's promise has genuine operative force — it is the immediate cause of the lender's action — and therefore creates a binding obligation through words alone.

*Achar matan maos ba'ei kinyan* — after the loan has already been made, the guarantor who steps in requires a *kinyan*. Here the money was already lent independently of his commitment; he is intervening after the fact, perhaps to relieve pressure on the borrower, and his words lack the same operative force. A formal *kinyan* is required to demonstrate the seriousness of his intention. This is precisely the Ben Nanas type of scenario: the guarantor who signs at the bottom of the *shtar*, after the loan has been made and the witnesses have signed.

*Areiv de-bei din lo ba'ei kinyan* — a court-appointed guarantor never requires a *kinyan*, regardless of timing. The weight of the *beit din*'s designation substitutes for the formality of acquisition.

With this ruling, Bava Batra reaches its conclusion. *Hadran alach Gett Pashut, ve-salikka lach Masechet Bava Batra.*

---

---

# Sanhedrin 2

## Textual Layout & Structu…

### Printer's Division

We open the Babylonian Talmud tractate of *Sanhedrin* on daf 2. The first striking feature of this daf is that the entire first *amud* is dominated by the *mishnah* — the *gemara* proper does not begin until later. This is worth pausing over, because it reflects a deliberate editorial choice by the publishers, not some intrinsic structure of the text itself.

The *mishnah* as it appears in printed editions of the Bavli was part of the manuscript tradition of the *gemara* — the two were not physically separate documents in the manuscripts. It was the printers, when moving from manuscript to the printed *Shas*, who decided how to divide the *mishnah* from the *gemara* and how large each presented unit of *mishnah* would be before its corresponding *gemara* followed. A printer could have divided the *mishnah* into many small chunks, each followed immediately by its relevant *gemara*, or into larger thematic blocks with correspondingly large sections of *gemara*. This was entirely a publisher's decision. Here, the printer chose to present the entire first chapter's *mishnah* as one continuous unit — most likely because it is unified by a clear thematic thread — and then to follow it with the *gemara* in full. It could just as easily have been divided into three-line segments with *gemara* interspersed.

### Transition & Ordering

We arrive at *Sanhedrin* coming directly from *Bava Batra*, making a natural thematic transition: from the substantive laws of property and commerce addressed in the *Bava*s to the laws of adjudication, courts, and judicial procedure in *Sanhedrin*. The general ordering of tractates within a *seder* in *Shas*, while the *gemara* sometimes offers thematic justifications, is primarily based on the number of *perakim* and overall size. The three *Bava*s together constitute *Nezikin* — thirty *perakim* as one unified tractate.

### Sanhedrin & Makkos

*Sanhedrin* and *Makkos* were originally a single tractate, just as the three *Bava*s were originally one. *Makkos* is a short tractate of only three *perakim*, while *Sanhedrin* runs eleven *perakim* in our editions — but properly speaking it is fourteen chapters, the remaining three being *Makkos*. They were separated because fourteen *perakim* was simply too large to remain as one tractate. The thematic coherence is evident: *Sanhedrin* deals with the court system and the administration of punishments, including capital punishment, while *Makkos* addresses the administration of lashes. The ordering of *Makkos* before *Shevuos* makes sense precisely because *Makkos* is organically part of *Sanhedrin*.

---

## Courts of Three

### Basic Categories

The *mishnah* opens: *dinei mamonos bishloshah* — monetary matters are adjudicated by a court of three. *Gezeilos vachavalos bishloshah* — theft and personal injury, likewise three. *Nezek vechatzi nezek, tashlumei kefel, tashlumei arba'ah vechamishah bishloshah* — full damages or half-damages (as in the case of a *tam* ox that gores), double payment in cases of burglary, and fourfold or fivefold payment when a stolen ox or sheep is subsequently slaughtered or sold — all of these, even though they move from compensation into the realm of monetary fines, are also adjudicated by a *beis din* of three.

Each ruling here carries its own element of surprise. One might have assumed that imposing monetary fines, which go beyond mere compensation, would require a larger court. The *mishnah* establishes that three suffice for the full range of monetary liability.

### Special Monetary Cases

The *mishnah* continues: *ha-onus veha-mefateh veha-motzi shem ra bishlosha* — the case of one who rapes an unmarried woman, one who seduces her, or a husband who falsely accuses his wife of not having been a virgin at the time of their marriage — these too are adjudicated by three judges. These cases fall within the category of fines: if the accuser is lying, he pays a monetary penalty, which is why they are grouped with the other fine-based cases.

### Slander Dispute

However, the *mishnah* immediately records a dissent: *divrei Rabbi Meir* — that is Rabbi Meir's position. *Vachachamim omrim ha-motzi shem ra b'esrim v'shlosha* — the Sages say the case of *motzi shem ra*, the false accusation of non-virginity, requires twenty-three judges, *mipnei she-yesh bo dinei nefashos* — because it contains within it the potential for a capital outcome. If witnesses emerge confirming that the wife did in fact commit adultery, the case becomes one of *dinei nefashos* and the woman's life is at stake. The Sages therefore require the full capital court.

### Lashes & Size

*Makos bishlosha* — lashes are administered on the basis of a *beis din* of three. This again is presented as a *chiddush*. If monetary fines required only three, one might well have assumed that corporal punishment — actual physical infliction of pain — demands a more substantial court. The *mishnah* says no, three suffice. *Mishum Rabbi Yishmael amru b'esrim v'shlosha* — Rabbi Yishmael, however, disagrees, holding that lashes are sufficiently analogous to a capital execution that they require a *beis din* of twenty-three. Bodily punishment, in his view, cannot be imposed by a mere three-judge court.

---

## Ritualistic Functions

### New Month Sanctification

The *mishnah* now shifts registers. We move from courts adjudicating disputes or imposing punishments to courts performing representational and ritualistic functions on behalf of the Jewish people. *Ibbur hachodesh bishlosha* — sanctifying the new month requires three. The *mishnah* uses the term *ibbur hachodesh* rather than *kiddush hachodesh* because the act in question is specifically the declaration that the outgoing month has concluded — that it was a twenty-nine-day month — thereby establishing when the new month begins. An important distinction must be drawn here: requiring only three judges does not mean any ad hoc *beis din* may perform this function. The size of the court and the question of who is authorized to represent the entire Jewish people in making this declaration are separate matters. *Kiddush hachodesh* must be performed by the designated court empowered to do so — it is simply that the minimum number of judges is three.

### Leap Year Declaration

*Ibbur hashanah bishlosha divrei Rabbi Meir* — declaring a leap year, that is, adding a thirteenth month to the calendar, requires three according to Rabbi Meir. *Mishum Gamliel amru bishlosha matchilin* — in the name of Rabban Gamliel, one may begin with three, *uv'chamisha nosin venosin* — debate the matter with five, given the many factors and considerations involved, *vegomrin beshivah* — and the final decision must be concluded with seven. *Ve-im nigmaru bishlosha me'ubaros* — but if in practice the final ruling was made by only three, it is nevertheless valid after the fact. This formulation raises an interesting question beyond the simple *lechatchilah u'bediavad* distinction: if seven are ultimately required and three suffice only *bediavad*, why not simply convene seven from the outset? And why the progressive escalation in the number of participants?

### Sin Offering Ritual

*Semichas zekenim* — this does not refer to the ordination of judges, as the name might suggest, but rather to the laying of hands by the elders upon the *par helam davar shel tzibbur*. When the *Beis Din HaGadol* issues an erroneous ruling and the majority of *Klal Yisrael* follows it and commits an inadvertent sin for which an individual would bring a *korban chatas*, the court upon recognizing its error brings a special communal *korban*. The laying of hands upon that *korban* requires only three. This is presented as a striking *chiddush*. This *korban* is the consequence of an error by the highest court of seventy-one. One would naturally expect that even if not all seventy-one members are needed, at least a more substantial representation of that court would be required. The fact that three suffice is genuinely surprising.

### Heifer Neck Breaking

*Va'arufas eglah bishlosha* — the ritual of *arifas eglah*, performed when an unidentified murder victim is found outside a city, requires three. In that ritual, the elders of the nearest city break the neck of a heifer, lay their hands upon it, and declare that their hands did not shed this blood. Here the *beis din* is not representing *Klal Yisrael* as a whole but rather the city. Still, one might have assumed that the full city court — ordinarily a *beis din* of twenty-three — would be required. The *mishnah* establishes that three representatives of that court suffice to stand in for the entire body. This, too, is a significant *chiddush*: three members of a court can represent the full court in performing a solemn communal ritual.

### Heifer Ritual Dispute

*Divrei Rabbi Shimon* — that is Rabbi Shimon's ruling that three suffice for *arifas eglah*. *Rabbi Yehuda omer b'chamisha* — Rabbi Yehudah disagrees, requiring five for this ritual.

---

## Status & Sanctification

### Chalitza & Refusal

Having surveyed courts that represent the people in ceremonial or representational capacities, the *mishnah* now turns to a third category: courts whose presence is required not to adjudicate a dispute, not to administer punishment, and not to represent the community at large, but rather to lend formal validity to a personal legal process. The closest analogy — though not cited in the *mishnah* because it was formulated later — is the requirement of a *beis din* for conversion. Here, the *beis din*'s role is to ritualize and validate the proceedings.

*Hachalitza v'ha-miunin bishlosha* — both *chalitza* and *miunin* require three. *Chalitza* is the process by which a *yavam* who declines to perform *yibum* releases his deceased brother's wife from the bond of *yibbum*: she removes his sandal, spits before him, and recites the prescribed declaration. The Torah itself specifies that this be done *le'einei hazekenim* — in the presence of elders. There is also arguably a representational dimension: the presence of the elders may serve to witness on behalf of the community that this woman is now released. The *beis din* of three is the minimum that satisfies this requirement.

*Miunin* — the refusal of marriage by a minor — applies when a girl below *bas mitzvah* was married off by her mother and brothers, a rabbinic institution created for cases where the father is absent and there is a clear societal and economic need to enable such a marriage. The Torah's marriage law vests this authority only in the father; the Rabbis extended a limited form of it to the mother and brothers specifically to address such situations. This rabbinic marriage carries with it the girl's right to refuse her husband at any point before she reaches *bas mitzvah* — once she attains *bas mitzvah* while living with her husband, it is too late. That act of refusal, like *chalitza*, must take place in the presence of a *beis din* of three.

### Value Assessment

*Neta revai u'maaser sheini she'ein damav yedua bishlosha* — when a person wishes to redeem his fourth-year fruit or his *maaser sheini* onto money and bring that money up to Jerusalem, and the precise value of the produce is not obvious or agreed upon, a *beis din* of three must assess the proper value. This differs from the case of items sanctified to the *Beis HaMikdash*, where the Temple treasurer is involved in the valuation. Here, the person is simply converting his own produce into money for his personal obligation to bring it to Jerusalem — but where the value is uncertain, a formal assessment by three judges is required.

### Sanctified Item Redempti…

*Ha-hekdeshos bishlosha* — when sanctified property is being redeemed, a *beis din* of three is required. *Ha-erachin ha-metaltelin bishlosha* — when one undertakes an *erech* in the sense of the valuation of movable property, this too requires three, though the *gemara* will investigate precisely what category of *erachin* the *mishnah* has in mind, since the primary usage of *erachin* in the Torah concerns the fixed valuations of human beings. *Rabbi Yehuda omer echad mehen kohen* — Rabbi Yehudah adds that in these cases involving *hekdesh*, since the proceedings have a ritual character connected to sacred property, one of the three judges must be a *kohen*.

### Land & Human Sanctificat…

*Ha-karkaos tisha v'kohen* — for the redemption of sanctified land, the court must consist of ten, with one of them being a *kohen*, for a total of ten. This number — ten plus one — no longer fits the standard *beis din* model, and the *gemara* will clarify its basis. *V'ha-adam k'yotzei bahen* — and similarly for the sanctification and redemption of persons; the *gemara* will note the surprising premise that a human being can be sanctified at all.

---

## Capital Crimes (23) (23)

### Capital Crime Baseline

The *mishnah* now returns to the classic judicial function: adjudicating criminal cases. Having worked through the range of courts of three and then the courts of five and ten for ritual purposes, we arrive at the next major threshold. *Dinei nefashos b'esrim u'shlosha* — capital crimes require a *beis din* of twenty-three.

### Animal Capital Crimes

*Ha-roveia v'ha-nirva b'esrim u'shlosha* — even when the capital proceeding concerns an animal rather than a human being, the same court of twenty-three is required. An animal used in an act of bestiality — whether the *roveia*, the penetrating animal, or the *nirva*, the one penetrated — must be formally judged by a *beis din* of twenty-three before it is executed. The *mishnah* provides its biblical basis: *she-ne'emar v'haragta es ha-isha v'es ha-beheima* — in a case involving a woman, the verse states "you shall kill the woman and the animal," and similarly, *v'omer v'es ha-beheima taharogu* — in the case involving a man, "the animal you shall kill." The execution of the animal is equated by the Torah with the execution of the human participant, and therefore the same procedural requirements apply.

It is noteworthy that this is the first point in the entire *mishnah* where a biblical verse is cited — and it is cited precisely to justify the formal judicial process for an animal. The intuitive response would be: it is an animal, simply kill it. The *mishnah* insists that a full *beis din* of twenty-three must adjudicate the matter.

### Goring Ox Dispute

*Shor haniskal b'esrim v'shlosha* — a goring ox that has killed a person and is to be stoned also requires a *beis din* of twenty-three. The *mishnah* again cites a verse: *v'hashor yisakeil v'gam be'alav yumas* — "the ox shall be stoned, and also its owner shall be put to death." The phrase about the owner's death is not literal — it indicates the degree of culpability — but the *mishnah* reads from it the principle of *k'mitat ba'al kach mitat hashor*: just as executing the owner would require a *beis din* of twenty-three, so too does executing the ox.

The *mishnah* then lists dangerous wild animals — the wolf (*ze'ev*), the lion (*ari*), the bear (*dov*), the leopard (*namer*), and the *bardelas* (hyena or polecat), as well as the snake — stating that *misasan b'esrim v'shlosha*, their execution also requires twenty-three, since they are functionally equivalent to a *shor haniskal*, even though they are not literally oxen.

Why mention these animals at all? Because it sets up the disagreement that follows. *Rabbi Eliezer omer* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that these animals, unlike a domesticated ox that momentarily lost control, are constant and ongoing threats to human life. Therefore, *kol ha-kodem l'horgan zachah* — whoever kills them first has done a meritorious act; one need not wait for a *beis din*. *Rabbi Akiva omer misasan b'esrim v'shlosha* — Rabbi Akiva disagrees: even these dangerous animals must go through the same formal procedure as a *shor haniskal*, requiring a *beis din* of twenty-three.

---

## High Court (71) (71)

### Tribe, Prophet, Kohen Ga…

*Ein danin lo es ha-shevet v'lo es nevi ha-sheker v'lo es kohen gadol ela al pi beis din shel shivim v'echad* — three categories of defendants can be tried only before the *beis din* of seventy-one: an entire tribe accused of *avodah zarah*, a false prophet, and a *kohen gadol*. The rationale in each case relates to the scope of the threat or the stature of the defendant. A false prophet poses an existential spiritual danger to the entire people, capable of leading all of Israel astray by misrepresenting the word of God. A tribe in collective rebellion against God is a communal catastrophe. The *kohen gadol* stands at the apex of the religious leadership of the nation. These are individuals and entities whose judgment must be rendered by the court that represents all of Israel.

### Discretionary Warfare

*V'ein motzin l'milchemet ha-reshut ela al pi beis din shel shivim v'echad* — one may not go out to wage a *milchemet reshut*, a discretionary war, without the authorization of the *beis din* of seventy-one. A *milchemet reshut* is distinguished from the obligatory wars of conquering the Land of Israel and — as the *Rambam* adds — defending Israel against enemies. A war of expansion or strategic choice, by contrast, requires the formal authorization of the *beis din* of seventy-one. This represents yet another role of the high court: not adjudicating a case, but authorizing a major national decision on behalf of the people, representing both the authority of the community and, through appropriate channels, the authority of God.

### Jerusalem Expansion

*V'ein mosifin al ha-ir v'al ha-azarot ela al pi beis din shel shivim v'echad* — one may not extend the halakhic borders of Jerusalem or expand the courtyard of the *Beis HaMikdash* without the authority of the *beis din* of seventy-one. The existing borders of Jerusalem and the *azaros* carry halakhic sanctity, and their formal expansion is a decision that affects the entire Jewish people and must be authorized by its highest representative body.

### Appointing Lower Courts

*Ein osin sanhedriyot l'shvatim ela al pi beis din shel shivim v'echad* — the appointment of *Sanhedrin* courts for the individual tribes, each of which consisted of twenty-three judges, requires the authorization of the *beis din* of seventy-one. The *Sanhedrin Gedolah* is the source of judicial authority in Israel, and the establishment of subordinate *sanhedriyot* flows from it.

### Idolatrous City

*Ein osin Ir Nidachas ela al pi beis din shel shivim v'echad* — the condemnation of an *ir nidachas*, an entire city that has been led into *avodah zarah* and is subject to total destruction, can only be decreed by the high court of seventy-one. The enormity of the act — wiping out an entire city — demands the highest level of judicial authority. The *mishnah* adds a brief but striking digression on the parameters of this law: one does not make an *ir nidachas* of a border city (*ein osin ir nidachas basfer*), since destroying a city on the frontier would create a dangerous opening for enemy attack. And one does not condemn three cities simultaneously as *ir nidachas*, as this would devastate the country. One or two cities, however, may be condemned.

---

## Biblical Derivations

### Seventy Elders

The *mishnah* steps back and restates the framework in summary: *Sanhedrin Gedolah haysa shivim v'echad* — the high court consisted of seventy-one members. *U'ktanah shel esrim u'shlosha* — the smaller courts, including the tribal *sanhedriyot* capable of adjudicating capital cases, consisted of twenty-three. Now the *mishnah* turns to biblical derivations.

*Minayin l'gedolah she'hi shivim v'echad* — where do we derive that the high court is seventy-one? *She-ne'emar esfa li shivim ish miziknei Yisrael* — "gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel," those who were to assist Moshe in leading the people. That body of seventy is understood as a deliberative court, not as seventy individuals each independently governing separate units of the population, but as a single representative body for all of Israel. *U'Moshe aleihem* — and Moshe was over them, bringing the total to seventy-one. This is a striking rereading of that narrative. *Rabbi Yehuda omer shivim* — Rabbi Yehudah holds the *Sanhedrin* consisted of only seventy, which immediately raises the objection that an even-numbered *beis din* is procedurally invalid. That issue will be addressed.

### Twenty-Three Derivation

*U'minayin l'ktanah she'hi esrim u'shlosha* — how do we know the smaller court is twenty-three? *She-ne'emar v'shaftu ha'eidah v'hitzilu ha'eidah* — "the community shall judge and the community shall save" — a verse applied to capital cases. The *derashah* reads the two occurrences of *eidah* as referring to two distinct groups within the *beis din*: *eidah shofetes*, the group that judges toward guilt — and *eidah matzeles*, the group that works toward acquittal. Each *eidah* consists of ten, giving us twenty.

How do we know an *eidah* is ten? *She-ne'emar ad masai la'eidah hara'ah hazos* — "until when shall I bear this evil community" — a verse referring to the spies. Yehoshua and Kalev were righteous; the remaining ten spies constituted the *eidah ra'ah*, the evil community. Thus an *eidah* is ten.

So we have ten arguing for guilt and ten arguing for innocence — twenty in total. This is specifically a capital case, which is why this verse applies to the derivation of the court size for *dinei nefashos*.

### Majority Rules

But we are still only at twenty, and a *beis din* for capital cases is twenty-three. *U'minayin l'havi od shlosha* — how do we get three more?

From the verse: *lo tihyeh acharei rabim l'ra'os* — "do not follow the majority to evil." This is read as a halakhic principle: a simple majority is insufficient to convict. The verse cautions against mechanically following the majority when the outcome is to find someone guilty. *Shome'a ani she-ye-hei imahem l'tovah* — from this I can infer that a simple majority is sufficient to acquit.

Then the *mishnah* asks: *im ken lamah ne'emar acharei rabim le-hatot* — if a simple majority suffices for acquittal, what need is there for the verse to state "follow the majority"? *Lo k'hatayascha l'tovah hatayascha l'ra'ah* — because the majority required to convict is not the same as the majority required to acquit. A simple majority of one is sufficient for acquittal. Conviction, however, requires a majority of two: *hatayascha l'ra'ah al pi shnayim*.

### Even Number Problem

Now the arithmetic follows. We have ten arguing for innocence. For conviction, the side arguing for guilt must exceed the innocence side by at least two. That means twelve must argue for guilt against ten for innocence, bringing the total to twenty-two. *V'ein beis din shakul* — but you cannot have an even-numbered *beis din*. *Mosivin aleihem od echad harei kan esrim u'shlosha* — therefore one more is added, giving us twenty-three.

The observant reader will immediately note a tension: if the *beis din* has twenty-three members, a majority of two requires thirteen votes for guilt against eleven for innocence — not twelve against ten. How this is resolved with the requirement of a two-vote majority will be addressed in the *gemara*.

### City Population

*V'kamah ye-hei b'ir v'teihei re'uyah l'Sanhedrin* — the *mishnah* now asks how large a city must be to merit its own *Sanhedrin* of twenty-three. *Me'ah v'esrim* — 120. This reflects the notion that the members of the *Sanhedrin* must be drawn from the general population, and the city must be large enough to support such a court while maintaining a viable population base.

### Rabbi Nechemiah's View

*Rabbi Nechemiah omer masayim u'shloshim k'neged sarei asaros* — Rabbi Nechemiah requires 230, reasoning from the institution of *sarei asaros*, the leaders of tens appointed on the advice of Yisro. The minimum rung of communal authority is authority over ten people. For each of the twenty-three members of the *Sanhedrin* to hold at least that minimum level of authority, the city must contain 230 adult males — ten per judge. Whether the judges themselves are counted within or apart from those ten is a question left open.

This concludes the entire sweep of *mishnayos* that make up the first *perek* of *Sanhedrin*. We now turn to the *gemara*.

---

## Theft vs. Civil Cases

### Enumeration Question

The *gemara* opens with a challenge to the structure of the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* states *dinei mamonos bishlosha* and then immediately adds *gezeilos vachavalos bishlosha* — monetary matters require three, then theft and personal injury require three. *Atu gezeilos vachavalos lav dinei mamonos ninhu* — but are theft and personal injury not themselves monetary matters? Why enumerate them separately? They would seem to be an obvious subset of the opening category.

### Rabbi Avahu's Interpreta…

*Amar Rabbi Avahu mah hen kasani* — Rabbi Avahu resolves this by reinterpreting the structure of the *mishnah*. The opening clause *dinei mamonos bishloshah* is not a general umbrella statement to which everything below is a specification. Rather, it is itself a definition. The *mishnah* is telling you what it means by *dinei mamonos*: *mah hen dinei mamonos — gezeilos vachavalos* — what is meant by "monetary matters"? Theft and personal injury. Nothing broader.

This reading has a striking implication. The most obvious cases of *dinei mamonos* — ordinary civil disputes, debts, loans, contract claims — are deliberately excluded from the *mishnah*'s category. *Aval hoda'os vehalva'os* — but admissions and loans, standard civil cases not involving torts, are not being included.

The *gemara* presents the double necessity for stating it this way. If the *mishnah* had said only *dinei mamonos bishlosha* without specifying *gezeilos vachavalos*, one might have understood it to include the full range of monetary disputes, certainly encompassing standard loans and civil claims. By explicitly saying *gezeilos vachavalos*, the *mishnah* signals that the category is restricted. Conversely, if the *mishnah* had listed only *gezeilos vachavalos* without the umbrella term *dinei mamonos*, one might have read it as illustrative — meaning *gezeilos vachavalos* are mentioned because that is where the derivation of "three" originates, but in practice everything, including civil cases, is included. The double formulation — umbrella statement plus specification — is therefore necessary to achieve precision: *dinei mamonos* means and is limited to *gezeilos vachavalos*, excluding ordinary loans and civil disputes.

It is worth noting that this reading is not the natural one. A straightforward reader of the *mishnah* would likely understand *dinei mamonos* as covering all civil matters, with *gezeilos vachavalos* then introduced as cases that might have been thought to belong to a different category. Rabbi Avahu is saying the opposite: the *mishnah* is restricting *dinei mamonos* to tort-like cases and deliberately leaving out ordinary civil litigation.

### Biblical Derivation

*Dechtiv* — and now the *gemara* explains where the requirement of three originates. The verse states *venikrav ba'al habayit el ha'elohim* — "the owner of the house shall be brought to the judges." This concerns the case of a *shomer*, a bailee, who denies that an object was ever entrusted to him, or who falsely claims it was damaged or lost, and then swears falsely to that effect. When witnesses expose the lie before a *beis din*, the *shomer* is liable. This is a case of *gezeilah*: the *shomer* actively possesses someone else's property and is keeping it from its owner.

*Rashi* draws an important distinction here. If someone fails to repay a loan and simply denies owing the money, he is certainly stealing in a moral sense — he is withholding money that belongs to another. But that is not *gezeil* in the technical sense, because there is no discrete object in his possession that belongs to the claimant. *Gezeil* requires that an identifiable object belonging to someone else is being actively withheld. The *shomer* who has the object in hand and lies about it is the paradigmatic case of *gezeil*, and it is from that case — *el ha'elohim*, to the judges — that we derive the requirement of three.

*Gezeilos* and *chavalos* are then treated as functionally analogous: *mah li chaval begufo mah li chaval bemamono* — whether you injured a person's body or injured his property, the underlying category is the same. Consequently, *gezeilos* is the classic source for the three-judge requirement. Since that is the derivation, one might have argued that the *mishnah* mentions *gezeilos* not to exclude civil cases but simply because *gezeilos* is the textual basis — yet in practice, everything, including loans and civil disputes, would require the same three. The *gemara* rejects this: *tani mah hen dinei mamonos gezeilos vachavalos* — the *mishnah* is specifically defining *dinei mamonos* as limited to *gezeilos vachavalos*, thereby excluding standard civil cases from the same halakhic framework.

### Loans Don't Need Status

*Aval hoda'os vehalva'os lo* — so civil disputes and loan claims are excluded. But excluded from what, exactly? *Ul'mai* — for what specific halakhic requirement? *Eilima d'lo ba'inan shlosha* — one might think the exclusion means they do not need three at all. But that cannot be right. *Veha amar Rabbi Avahu* — Rabbi Avahu himself ruled that *shnayim she'danu dinei mamonos, divrei hakol ein dineihem din* — a panel of two that adjudicated a monetary case has not rendered a valid judgment, according to all opinions. So even ordinary loans and civil disputes require three. Rabbi Avahu who formulated the exclusion of civil cases from the *mishnah*'s category is the same Rabbi Avahu who insists that anything fewer than three is invalid for monetary cases.

### Mumchin Concept

*Ella d'lo ba'inan mumchin* — the exclusion, therefore, is not from the requirement of three judges, but from the requirement that those three judges be *mumchin*. For *gezeilos vachavalos* — the cases enumerated by the *mishnah* — the three judges must be *mumchin*. For ordinary loans and civil disputes, while three judges are still required, they do not need to be *mumchin*.

What is a *mumche*? *Rashi* explains: *smuchim*, those who have received *semicha* — the formal chain of rabbinic ordination tracing back to Moshe Rabbeinu — and moreover, *venatlu reshut miNasi ladun*, those who have received political authorization from the *Nasi* to adjudicate. The full apparatus of formal judicial appointment is required for *gezeilos* and *chavalos*. For ordinary civil disputes, ordinary qualified judges suffice — three, but not necessarily *mumchin*. This distinction, and its far-reaching implications, will be developed in the *gemara* as we continue.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 3

## Dinei Mamonot Reading

### Rabbi Abbahu Exclusion

The *gemara* on Sanhedrin 3b opens by grappling with how to read the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states that *dinei mamonot* require a *beit din* of three, and then appears to enumerate specifics: *gezelot ve-chavalot* and so on. The difficulty is that this enumeration seems to pass over the classic cases of *dinei mamonot* — the ordinary civil disputes that the Bavli calls *hoda'ot ve-halva'ot*, admissions and loans. The simplest reading would be that the generic phrase *dinei mamonot* refers to precisely those ordinary disputes, and that *gezelot ve-chavalot* then covers the more non-standard cases of civil liability. Rabbi Abbahu, however, rejects this reading. He narrows the scope of *dinei mamonot* in the *mishnah* to refer only to the specific cases enumerated there, thereby deliberately excluding the classic civil disputes of *hoda'ot ve-halva'ot*. Why exclude them? Do they not also require a *beit din* of three? Rabbi Abbahu agrees that they do. The point of the exclusion, as the Bavli explains, is that while *hoda'ot ve-halva'ot* require three judges, they do not require *mumchin*.

### Mumchin Concept

What does *mumchin* mean? Rashi explains it as *semikhah* — the tradition of judicial authority passed down in an unbroken chain from Moshe Rabbeinu, combined with a form of political appointment by the *nasi*. This matters practically: a *beit din* today outside of Eretz Yisrael can issue rulings that carry religious force, but what political authority actually backs up the court's decisions? Rashi notes that *mumchin* possessed authority conferred by the *nasi*. The concept of *mumchin* is intimately linked to the word *elohim*. *Elohim* conveys the idea of representing God, of holding real power and authority — and it is from *elohim* that the requirement of *mumchin* is derived. What Rabbi Abbahu is saying is that this requirement of *mumchin*, rooted in *elohim*, applies to torts — but not to basic civil cases of loans and admissions. Those cases need three judges, but those three do not have to be *mumchin*.

### Eruv Parshiyot

The *gemara* now asks: what is the internal logic of this position? It frames the question sharply: *mai kasavar* — what exactly does the *tanna* of the *mishnah* hold? The *gemara* presents a dilemma grounded in the concept of *eruv parshiyot*. The classic source in the *Torah* for the requirement of a *beit din* of three is the *parshah* dealing with the case of a *shomer* — a bailee who claims that the object entrusted to him was stolen: *ki yiten ish el re'ehu kesef o kelim lishmor vegunav mibet ha'ish im yimatze haganav yeshalem shenayim im lo yimatze haganav venikrav ba'al habayit el ha'elohim im lo shalach yado bimlechet re'ehu* — and the passage continues with *al kol devar pesha al shor al chamor al seh al salma al kol aveda asher yomar ki hu zeh*, followed by *ad ha'elohim yavo devar sheneihem* and *asher yarshi'un elohim yeshalem shenayim lere'ehu*. Three occurrences of *elohim* — three judges. The question is what this *parshah* is actually about.

### Three Elohim

The phrase *ki hu zeh* — "this is it" — requires unpacking.
