The *gemara* understands this phrase as referring to *modeh b'miktzat*, a partial admission: I claim you owe me three objects, and you acknowledge owing only one of them. The question is whether *ki hu zeh* is addressing the *shomer* case or a loan case. In a standard *shomer* case, the *shomer* swears that something happened — that the item was taken, for instance — and the whole claim may be denied outright; partial admission is not structurally required. Partial admission — *ki hu zeh* — is precisely the mechanism that triggers an oath in the case of a loan: I lent you a hundred, you admit to fifty but deny the rest. This suggests that embedded within the *parshah* of *shomer* is actually a discussion of loan cases. That is *eruv parshiyot* — two distinct *parshiyot* interleaved: one about *shomrim* and one about loans, sewn together in the same passage.

### Gezelah Definition

Why is the *shomer* case a case of *gezelah*? Because the *shomer* is holding onto an object while falsely claiming it was stolen. As Rashi explains in the *mishnah*, if I simply fail to repay a debt, I am wronging the lender, but halachically that is not *gezelah*. The active retention of a specific, concrete piece of property that belongs to someone else — that physical hold — constitutes *gezelah*. The non-payment of a monetary debt, while wrongful, falls into a different category.

### Modeh B'Miktzat

Now the *gemara* returns to the dilemma it raised. If the *tanna* holds that there is *eruv parshiyot* — that loan cases are embedded within this *parshah* — then the word *elohim*, with its connotations of authority, applies to loans as well, and loans should require not only three judges but *mumchin*. If, on the other hand, the *tanna* holds there is no *eruv parshiyot* — that the entire passage is only about the *shomer* — then there is no *Torah* source teaching that loans require three judges at all. The *gemara* poses the challenge directly: *im kasavar eruv parshiyot katuv kan libei nami mumchin; ve'im kasavar ein eruv parshiyot katuv kan shlosha lamah li?* Make up your mind. The *gemara* resolves this by saying: *le'olam kasavar eruv parshiyot katuv kan* — yes, there is *eruv parshiyot*, and in principle loans do require *mumchin*. But the reason the *mishnah* excludes loans from the *mumchin* requirement is *mishum de-Rabbi Chanina* — by analogy to the teaching of Rabbi Chanina.

---

## Rabbi Chanina Analogy

### Derishah Chakira

Rabbi Chanina teaches: *dvar Torah, echad dinei mamonot ve'echad dinei nefashot b'drisha ve-chakira* — from a *Torah* perspective, both monetary cases and capital cases require rigorous cross-examination of witnesses — *drisha ve-chakira* — pinning down the precise time, place, and circumstances of the witnessed event. The source is *shene'emar mishpat echad yihyeh lachem* — one law for you — a verse that links *dinei mamonot* and *dinei nefashot* in a single standard of judicial procedure.

### Removing Obstacles

Why then did the rabbis remove the requirement of *drisha ve-chakira* from monetary cases? *Kedei shelo tin'ol delet bifnei lovin* — so as not to bolt the door before borrowers. The lender receives no interest and has no obvious benefit from lending. Any additional obstacle — an onerous judicial procedure, witnesses subject to rigorous cross-examination — becomes a plausible reason not to lend. So the rabbis paved the path by removing *drisha ve-chakira* from *dinei mamonot* entirely.

### Tosafot Extension

A natural question arises: does this dispensation apply only to loans, or does it extend across all *dinei mamonot* — including *gezelah*, *chavalot*, and other torts? From the language of Rabbi Chanina's statement, it sounds as though *drisha ve-chakira* is removed from all *dinei mamonot*. Tosafot explains that there is indeed good reason to extend the removal broadly. Just as the smallest obstacle can deter lending, so too with other forms of civil liability: if it becomes too difficult to prosecute someone who damaged your property, people will become careless. My ox will range freely if I know you cannot easily prove damages against me; I will not guard against incidental trespass on your property if I know prosecution is burdensome. *Gezel* will be rampant. So Tosafot reformulates: we remove *drisha ve-chakira* from *dinei mamonot* — including tort cases — *kedei lin'ol delet bifnei gazlanin*, to bolt the door before thieves, making it harder for wrongdoers to escape accountability. The analogy to the American legal system is instructive: criminal conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt, while civil liability requires only a preponderance of the evidence. Different thresholds apply to different proceedings.

By the same token, *mishum de-Rabbi Chanina*: just as *drisha ve-chakira* was removed from all *dinei mamonot* to facilitate civil society, the *mumchin* requirement is removed specifically from loan cases — not from all *dinei mamonot*, since *gezelah* and *chavalot* in the *mishnah* still require *mumchin*, but specifically from loans. Why only loans? Tosafot explains: with loans, I gain nothing from the transaction and the slightest obstacle deters me from lending. The removal of *mumchin* for loans is by rabbinic enactment, motivated precisely by the same concern for access to credit.

### Judicial Liability

The *gemara* then raises a sharp objection. *Ela me'ata ta'u lo yishalmu* — if you are trying to make it as easy as possible for a borrower to find a *beit din*, and you are not requiring *mumchin*, then you should also say that even if these non-*mumchin* judges rule incorrectly and cause a monetary loss, they should not be required to compensate for it. After all, if the judges face the threat of malpractice liability, no responsible person will want to serve. The *gemara* responds: *kol she-kein atana de-itta lifnei loveh* — on the contrary, this is an additional reason in favor of maintaining malpractice liability. If I know that the court handling my loan dispute is irresponsible and unreviewable, I will be that much more reluctant to lend in the first place. To encourage lending, the lender must have confidence that a court which mishandles his case can be held accountable. So even though malpractice liability may reduce the pool of willing judges, removing it would undermine lending even more decisively. This *sugya* thereby introduces, somewhat incidentally, the important principle that a *beit din* composed of *hedyotot* — non-expert judges — is subject to liability for erroneous rulings.

One of the functions of an opening *sugya* in the *gemara* is precisely this: it uses the apparently narrow question of how to read the *mishnah*'s first line to introduce the reader to a panorama of the major themes of the *perek*. In this short passage alone, we have encountered the word *elohim* as the basis for the *beit din*; the concept of *mumchin* derived from *elohim*; the exclusion of *hoda'ot ve-halva'ot* from the *mumchin* requirement; the distinction between *dinei mamonot* and *dinei nefashot* with respect to *drisha ve-chakira*; and the liability of a court composed of *hedyotot*. All of these themes will recur throughout the *perek*.

---

## Rava's Two Categories

### Challenging Exclusion

Having laid out Rabbi Abbahu's reading, the *gemara* now challenges it directly. *Iy hachi tarti katanei* — if you are going to say there are two different categories here, then why not read the *mishnah* as simply stating both? Read *dinei mamonot bishlosha hedyotot* — monetary cases, meaning loans, need three non-expert judges — and *gezelot ve-chavalot bishlosha mumchin* — torts need three *mumchin*. That is, why force a reading that excludes *hoda'ot ve-halva'ot* from the *mishnah*? Simply read *dinei mamonot* as referring to *hoda'ot ve-halva'ot* and treat the two phrases as two distinct categories, one not requiring *mumchin* and the other requiring *mumchin*.

The *gemara* adds a further challenge: *ve-od shlosha shlosha lamah li?* If *dinei mamonot* and *gezelot ve-chavalot* were meant to refer to the same category, why does the *mishnah* say *bishlosha* twice? The repetition of *bishlosha* strongly implies these are two separate rulings about two separate categories — not a single category with its examples. The plainest reading of the *mishnah*, the *gemara* presses, is that *dinei mamonot* means loans and *gezelot ve-chavalot* means torts, and both independently require three.

### Rava Resolution

*Ella amar Rava: tarti katanei* — Rava agrees: the *mishnah* does state both categories. *Dinei mamonot* refers to loans — three judges, without the *mumchin* requirement. *Gezelot ve-chavalot* refers to torts — three judges, with *mumchin*. The *mishnah* is not excluding loans; it is using *dinei mamonot* as its term for loans. Whether or not loans technically require *mumchin* is a separate debate — Rabbi Abbahu says they do not, and we have seen why — but the *mishnah* is not suppressing the category; it is naming it first. This is clearly the better reading of the *mishnah*, and the *gemara* adopts it through Rava.

### Minimum Size

Having clarified that loans require three judges who need not be *mumchin*, the *gemara* now opens up discussion of whether the requirement of three judges in loan cases is *de-oraita* or rabbinic. Rav Acha b'rei de-Rav Ika says: *mi-de'oraita chad nami kashar* — from the *Torah*'s perspective, even one judge suffices, at least for loan-type cases. The *Torah* source he cites is *be-tzedek tishpot amitecha* — "with justice you shall judge your fellow" — where *tishpot* is in the singular. As Rashi notes, this possibility flows naturally from the earlier discussion: if we concluded that when there is no *eruv parshiyot* loans have no explicit *Torah* source requiring three, then certainly one should be sufficient *de-oraita*.

### Yoshei Kranot

If one judge suffices *de-oraita*, why did the rabbis require three even in loan cases? *Ela mishum yoshei kranot* — because of the *yoshei kranot*, the idlers loitering on street corners. Rashi explains: *tagrin she-ein be-ki'in be-tiv dinin ve-yestu et ha-chayav ve-yachayavu et ha-zakai* — traders who are not expert in the proper conduct of cases, who will acquit the liable and convict the innocent. Once it was established that *mumchin* are not required for loan cases, anyone could volunteer to serve as a judge. Combining the absence of a *mumchin* requirement with the sufficiency of a single judge produces a court that could be, in practice, a single ignoramus. To counteract this, the rabbis raised the threshold to three: with three people convening as a court, at least one of them, presumably, has some idea of what he is doing. The *gemara* immediately asks: *atu be-telata mi lo havei yoshei kranot?* — can you not assemble three good-for-nothings just as easily as one? The *gemara* responds: *iy efshar de-la shechiach chad de-gamir* — it is unlikely that among three people willing to convene as a court, not a single one has any knowledge. One of the three, presumably, knows something. Whether that optimism is always warranted is another matter, but that is the rabbinic rationale.

The same *gemara* that raised the malpractice question earlier now raises it again in this context. If the goal is to encourage responsible people to serve on courts made up of *hedyotot*, perhaps malpractice liability should be removed — otherwise, only the irresponsible will agree to serve. The *gemara* inverts this: *kol she-kein ittefi yoshei kranot* — liability for error will actually deter the *yoshei kranot* from sitting in judgment. A person who recognizes he knows nothing will think twice before exposing himself to financial liability for a mistaken ruling. Far from chasing away the competent, malpractice liability weeds out the incompetent.

### Rava vs Rav Acha

What practical difference then exists between Rava and Rav Acha b'rei de-Rav Ika, if both ultimately require three non-*mumchin* judges for loan cases? The *gemara* answers: *ika beina'ihu de'amar Shmuel* — the difference lies in the ruling of Shmuel. Shmuel teaches: *shenayim she-danu dineihem din, ela she-nikra beit din chatzuf* — if two judges ruled, their ruling is valid after the fact, but they are called an impudent court. The question is whether *bidi'avad* — post facto — a court of fewer than three is valid.

According to Rava, the *Torah* itself requires three judges. Therefore, anything fewer than three — even two — is categorically invalid, and Shmuel's ruling does not apply. According to Rav Acha b'rei de-Rav Ika, who says that *de-oraita* one suffices and the requirement of three is rabbinic, Shmuel's ruling does apply: the rabbis required three, but if two ruled, the ruling stands *bidi'avad*, since the failure is merely rabbinic non-compliance. The court is *chatzuf*, but its ruling is not void. The question naturally arises whether, by the same logic, a single judge ruling *bidi'avad* would also be valid. The *gemara* suggests that even Rav Acha b'rei de-Rav Ika might not extend this *bidi'avad* leniency all the way to one. The principle that *al tehi dan yechidi she'ein dayan yechidi ela echad* — do not judge alone, for the only true sole judge is God — reflects a deep concern about the arrogance of a single person claiming total judicial authority. Moreover, a court of two that reaches a unanimous decision is functionally equivalent to two out of three: had a third been present, those same two would have prevailed. A ruling by two, while improper, mirrors the outcome of a proper court. A single judge has no analogous argument to make.

---

## Nezek Categories

### Nezek Mention

The *gemara* moves now to later phrases in the *mishnah*: *nezek va-chatzi nezek* — damages and half damages — need three. The *gemara* immediately asks: *nezek hainu chavalot* — isn't *nezek* already implicit in *chavalot*, personal injury? One of the payments in a case of personal injury is *nezek*, damage. And even if *nezek* is understood as property damage rather than bodily harm, if bodily harm requires three, obviously property damage does as well. Why state it separately?

The *gemara* answers: *mishum de-kava'ei le-misni chatzi nezek* — because the *mishnah* needed to teach the case of half damages. Half damages is a non-standard case that may be classified as a fine rather than as compensation. Because it had to introduce that exceptional case, the *mishnah* paired it with full damages in order to provide context, and taught *nezek* first as a transition.

### Chatzi Nezek Nature

The *gemara* then asks: even so, isn't *chatzi nezek* — half damages — still just a form of *chavalot*? It is still paying for damage, even if only half the amount. So why teach it separately? The *gemara* answers: *tani mamona ve-tani knasa* — no, the *mishnah* is distinguishing between monetary compensation and fines. The question of whether *chatzi nezek* is compensation or a fine is a classic debate in Bava Kamma. The case in question is an unhabituated ox that gores for the first time — or the first three times — before it is established as dangerous. The owner pays only half.

One view — *palga nizka mamona* — holds that the owner is genuinely negligent even in this case, and the payment is compensation. He is just over the threshold of liability, but fully liable; we simply went easy on him and required only half. On this view, half damages is still *mamona*. The other view — *palga nizka kansa* — holds that the owner was not quite negligent enough to be fully liable, but because he was so close to the line, the rabbis imposed a fine of half so that he would not escape entirely and become reckless. On this view, half damages is a *knas*, a fine that serves a deterrent function rather than a compensatory one. The *gemara* notes: if *palga nizka kansa*, then the separate mention of *chatzi nezek* makes perfect sense — it is a different legal category from standard compensation. But if *palga nizka mamona*, why mention it separately?

### Graduated Fines

The *gemara* resolves this: *ela aidi de-kava'ei le-misni tashlumei kefel ve-tashlumei arba'a va-chamisha* — because the *mishnah* needed to state the graduated fines of double payment (*kefel*), fourfold (*arba'ah*), and fivefold (*chamisha*). These are the fines for theft and for the theft-and-slaughter or theft-and-sale of an ox or sheep respectively, and everyone agrees these are *knasot* — pure fines, well in excess of compensation, of the category *de-mamona she'eino mishtalem be-rosh*, money that is not simply the base value of what was taken. Since those cases had to be taught, the *mishnah* drew *chatzi nezek* alongside them — even if technically it is *mamona* on one view, it shares the feature of being a non-standard, non-full payment. And once *chatzi nezek* was taught, *nezek* was taught alongside it as the natural transition from the territory of standard torts to the territory of fines. In this way, even under the view that *palga nizka mamona*, the literary structure of the *mishnah* is coherent: *nezek* and *chatzi nezek* serve as the bridge from *gezelot ve-chavalot* to *kefel ve-arba'ah va-chamisha*.

---

## Source: Three Elohim

### Pesukim Citation

Having worked through the structure of the *mishnah*, the *gemara* now turns to a question that has been implicit throughout: *shlosha minaalan* — where do we know you need three to constitute a *beit din*? The *gemara* cites a *baraita*. The source is the same *parshah* of the *shomer* we encountered earlier — the passage beginning *venikrav ba'al habayit el ha'elohim im lo shalach yado bimlechet re'ehu*, continuing with *al kol devar pesha asher yomar ki hu zeh*, then *ad ha'elohim yavo devar sheneihem*, and finally *asher yarshi'un elohim yeshalem shenayim lere'ehu*. The word *elohim* appears three times. Three *elohim*, three judges.

### Rabbi Yoshiya Count

This, says the *baraita*, is the position of Rabbi Yoshiya. He counts all three occurrences: *venikrav ba'al habayit el ha'elohim* — *harei kan echad*, that is one. *Ad ha'elohim yavo devar sheneihem* — *harei kan shenayim*, that is two. *Asher yarshi'un elohim* — *harei kan shlosha*, that is three. Three *elohim*, three judges.

### Rabbi Yonatan Object

Rabbi Yonatan disagrees: *rishon techilah ne'emar ve'ein dorshin techilot* — the first occurrence is simply the grammatical subject needed to introduce the passage; you do not count first occurrences for halachic derivation. Begin counting only from the second: *ad ha'elohim yavo devar sheneihem* — that is one. *Asher yarshi'un elohim* — that is two. And since a court cannot have an even number of members, *mosifin aleihem od echad harei kan shlosha* — you add one more and arrive at three. Both Tannaim reach the number three; they differ only on how they get there.

The *gemara* asks whether this reflects a general dispute about the hermeneutic principle of *dorshin techilot* — counting the first occurrence of a word. *Mar savar dorshin techilah*, one holds you do count it; *u-mar savar ein dorshin techilah*, the other holds you do not. That seems to be the debate. The *gemara* then says: perhaps not. *Dekulei alma ein dorshin techilah* — perhaps everyone agrees you do not count the first occurrence. How then does Rabbi Yoshiya justify counting it here? *Amar lach Rabbi Yoshiya*: the *Torah* could have written *ve-nikrav ba'al habayit el ha-shofet* — "the householder shall approach the judge" — and subsequently used *elohim*. Instead it used *elohim* all three times. That deliberate repetition of the same word signals that every occurrence is to be counted. Had the *Torah* not wanted us to count the first, it would have used a different word to introduce the subject. Rabbi Yonatan responds: *lishna de'alma nakat* — the *Torah* was simply speaking in a natural, echoing idiom. As people say: *man de'it lei dina likrav legabei dayana* — one who has a legal matter should approach a judge. The phrase uses *dina* and *dayana* — din and its cognate — for stylistic resonance, not because every instance of the word carries halachic weight. Similarly, the *Torah*'s repeated use of *elohim* is a matter of style, not instruction to count. Rashi offers a related explanation, and the *gemara* notes that the simpler reading remains that they are debating the general hermeneutic principle of *dorshin techilot*.

### Even Beit Din

The *gemara* now raises a striking question. If Rabbi Yoshiya derived three judges from the three occurrences of *elohim*, why did he not instead derive two from the second and third occurrences — and then, since a *beit din* cannot be of even number, add one to reach three? That is exactly what Rabbi Yonatan did. Does the fact that Rabbi Yoshiya needed to count three occurrences to reach three suggest that he holds it is in fact permissible to have a *beit din* of even numbers — and therefore two would not automatically yield three? The *gemara* cites a *baraita* in which Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Yosi ha-Gelili derives from the verse *lintos acharei rabim le-hatot* — "incline after the majority" — that a *beit din* must be structured so that it can *noteh*, tilt, that is, it must have an odd number of members in order for a majority to emerge. If this is a universal principle, then why did Rabbi Yoshiya not rely on it to move from two to three?

### Rabbi Yehuda Exception

The *gemara* proposes: *savar lah ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — perhaps Rabbi Yoshiya holds like Rabbi Yehuda. In our *mishnah* in Sanhedrin, Rabbi Yehuda says that the *Sanhedrin Gedolah* consisted of seventy members — *shivim*, not *shivim v'echad*. The standard *tanna kamma* says seventy-one. Rabbi Yehuda, who accepts an even number for the supreme court, might serve as the model for Rabbi Yoshiya's willingness to entertain an even-numbered *beit din*. The *gemara* is skeptical: is Rabbi Yehuda's allowance for an even *Sanhedrin Gedolah* a general principle, or a special ruling limited to that institution? The *gemara* demonstrates that it is strictly limited. A separate *mishnah* discusses *semikhah* — the laying of hands in the cases of *par helam davar* and *egla arufa*. Rabbi Shimon says three; Rabbi Yehuda says five. Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the verse says *ve-samkhu*, which implies two, plus *ziknei*, the elders, which implies another two — four in total. But since a *beit din* cannot be of even number, *ein beit din shakol*, we add one, arriving at five. Rabbi Yehuda, then, explicitly requires an odd-numbered court in this context. He never says that a standard *beit din* may be even-numbered. His ruling of *shivim* for the *Sanhedrin Gedolah* is an exceptional case driven by a specific *pasuk* — *shivim zekenim shivim ish* — not a general principle.

### Rabbi Yoshiya Even

How then can Rabbi Yoshiya be aligned with Rabbi Yehuda? The *gemara* resolves this: *Rabbi Yoshiya adifa mi-d'Rabbi Yehuda* — Rabbi Yoshiya's position is actually more radical than Rabbi Yehuda's. Rabbi Yehuda holds that even-numbered courts are permitted only for the *Sanhedrin Gedolah*, while all other *batei din* must have odd numbers — as proven by his ruling of five rather than four. Rabbi Yoshiya, by contrast, may hold that even-numbered courts are acceptable across all *batei din*. This is a striking inference. Since Rabbi Yoshiya derived three from three explicit occurrences of *elohim* rather than deriving two and adding one, we must conclude that he could not have relied on the *ein beit din shakol* principle to get from two to three — because for him, two would have been perfectly acceptable. He therefore needed the *Torah* to tell him three explicitly.

### Majority Rule

This leaves Rabbi Yoshiya with a textual problem. The verse *lintos acharei rabim le-hatot* — which Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Yosi ha-Gelili reads as requiring a *noteh*, tilting court, i.e., an odd-numbered court — how does Rabbi Yoshiya understand it? The *gemara* answers: *mookim lah b'dinei nefashot* — Rabbi Yoshiya applies that verse only to capital cases. Capital cases require an odd-numbered court. The *gemara* asks: does Rabbi Yoshiya then say that monetary cases do not follow a majority rule at all? But our *mishnah* explicitly states that if two say acquit and one says convict, he is acquitted — and vice versa. Majority rule clearly operates in *dinei mamonot*. The *gemara* resolves this: *afilu teima Rabbi Yoshiya — maisi lah b'kal va-chomer mi-dinei nefashot*. Rabbi Yoshiya derives the majority rule for *dinei mamonot* by *kal va-chomer* from *dinei nefashot*: *u-mah dinei nefashot de-chamiri amar Rachmana zil basar ruba, dinei mamonot lo kol she-ken* — if the *Torah* says that even a person's life is decided by majority rule, certainly monetary matters are decided by majority rule.

The crucial distinction the *gemara* is drawing is between the procedural principle that courts decide by majority vote — which applies universally — and the structural requirement that a court be constituted of an odd number of members so that a majority can always emerge. The verse *lintos acharei rabim* teaches the former, not the latter. A court of even numbers is structurally problematic — it can result in a deadlock — but Rabbi Yoshiya, on this reading, accepts that risk, at least in *dinei mamonot*, and relies on the derivation from the three occurrences of *elohim* to establish the minimum of three rather than on the structural necessity of an odd-numbered court. This is admittedly a position resting on thin evidence, and the *gemara* itself treats it with some tentativeness, but the logical structure is coherent: majority rule as a decisional principle is one thing, and the compositional requirement of an odd-numbered court is another.

---

# Sanhedrin 4

## Rabbi vs. Rabbis

### Rabbi's Five-Judge View

The *gemara* opens with a *beraisa* — apparently a *tosefta* — that states explicitly what the *Yerushalmi* had implied: *dinei mamonot bishlosha*, monetary cases require three judges, while *Rebbi omer bachamisha*, Rabbi maintains they require five. Rabbi's reasoning is that five judges are needed *kdei sheyigmor din bishlosha* — so that the final judgment (*gmar din*) is rendered by three.

One might object immediately: if you already have a *beis din* of three, surely the *gmar din* is rendered by all three — or at worst by two of them. Why would you need five for that purpose? The *gemara* clarifies: Rabbi's point is not that a *beis din* of three is incapable of reaching a verdict, but that the *pasuk* itself demands that three judges stand on the side finding for guilt or innocence. The *pesukím* referencing *Elohim* — the judges — require that the *gmar din* rest with a full three, not merely two out of three.

Rabbi's derivation proceeds as follows. The *pasuk* reads *asher yarshiun Elohim* — "whom the judges shall condemn" — where *yarshiun* is in the plural, indicating two judges find guilty. Separately, the *pasuk* opens with *ad ha'Elohim yavo devar shneihem* — "the matter of both of them shall come before the judges" — using *Elohim* for the *beis din* they come to. Since *yarshiun* implies two judges on the condemning side, Rabbi reads the *Elohim* above — the body they appear before — as also comprising two. But *ein beis din shakul*: a court cannot be evenly divided, so a court of two becomes a court of three. Now, since the lower *Elohim* (those finding guilt) corresponds to two, and the upper *Elohim* (the whole *beis din*) also corresponds to two, with one added for *ein beis din shakul*, the total is five: *mah lemata shnayim, af lemala shnayim*, two below and two above, and one added — *harei kan chamisha*.

### Rabbis' Three-Judge View

The Rabbis respond: *yarshi'an kesiv* — the word *yarshi'un* is in fact written without the *vav*. Because it is written in the defective spelling, you cannot derive from it that two judges are finding for guilt; you can only read it as referring to a single judge. With only one judge on the condemning side, the structure is one plus one plus one — three judges total, not five. The Rabbis thus hold the standard position: *dinei mamonot bishlosha*, three.

### Rabbi Abba's Challenge

Rabbi Abba — the same Rabbi Abba who raises this challenge in the *Yerushalmi* as well — objects forcefully to Rabbi's entire logic. If the principle is that the deciding side must comprise the full constitutionally required number, the consequences are absurd: the *sanhedrin gedola* of seventy-one would need a hundred and forty-one — enough that seventy-one could constitute one deciding side; the *sanhedrin ketana* of twenty-three would need forty-five — so that twenty-three could form the majority. No one accepts these conclusions.

### Resolved via Fixed Numbe…

The resolution is that these fixed numbers refer to the composition of the *beis din* as a whole, not to the numerical size of the deciding majority. The *Rachmana* said *esfi li shivim ish* — gather me seventy men — and the convocation is seventy, full stop. *V'shaftu ha'eida v'hitzilu ha'eida*: when the Torah speaks of "the congregation" judging or saving, it means the entire body — the ten and the ten and the twenty-three — not the winning side. Similarly, *v'nikrav ba'al habayit el ha'Elohim* — the litigant comes before the judges — means the body they come to is a body of three, *mishas kriva shlosha*. The full number describes the institution, not the voting bloc.

With this established, Rabbi's actual derivation becomes clearer. It is not the naive claim that three must sit on the deciding side. Rather, *asher yarshiun Elohim* uses *yarshiun* in the plural, indicating two. *Nemar Elohim lemata v'nemar Elohim lemala* — since *Elohim* appears both above and below, and the lower reference implies two, the upper reference — the body they come before — must also be two. But two is an even court, which is forbidden, so it becomes three. That gives us two (below) plus two (above, now raised to three), plus one for *ein beis din shakul*, yielding five. The Rabbis reply that since *yarshi'an* is written defectively, without the *vav*, the plural cannot be derived, and the whole structure collapses to three.

---

## Yesh Eim Lamikra

### All Agree: Reading Prior…

Having resolved the debate between Rabbi and the Rabbis, the *gemara* pivots entirely — occupying the remainder of the *daf* — to a question that the foregoing dispute has placed front and center: does one derive *halachic* conclusions from the way a *pasuk* is read aloud, or from the way it is written in the Torah?

The *gemara* opens with a sweeping statement attributed to Rabbi Yochanan: *Rebbi ve-Rabbi Yehuda ben Roeitz, u-veit Shammai ve-Rabbi Shimon ve-Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi, Rabbi Yehuda ben Roeitz, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Akiva — *kulu sevira lehu yesh eim lamikra*. All of these *Tannaim* hold that hermeneutic interpretation follows the reading (*mikra*), not the scribal tradition of spelling (*mesorah* / *mesoret*).

A brief terminological note: the word *mikra* means "reading," referring to our tradition of how the text is vocalized and pronounced. *Mesoret* means the scribal tradition of how the text is spelled — and counterintuitively, it is the *mesoret*, the "tradition," that refers to the written form, while *mikra*, "reading," refers to the oral pronunciation. This inversion of expectations is worth keeping in mind throughout.

### Yehuda ben Roeitz Story

The *beraisa* about Rabbi Yehuda ben Roeitz is a remarkably rich episode. His students posed to him what seemed like a genuine textual question: when the Torah says *ve'im nekeiva teled vetame'a shevu'ayim kenidasah* — that a woman who gives birth to a girl is *teme'ah* for *shevu'ayim* — the word is written without a *vav*, making it technically legible as *shivim*, seventy. Could it be that the mother of a girl is *teme'ah* for seventy days?

Rabbi Yehuda ben Roeitz answered them with an elegant *pshat* argument. The Torah establishes an exact parallel structure: by a male child there is a period of *tumah* (seven days) followed by a period of *dam tahor* (thirty-three days); by a female child those periods are precisely doubled — fourteen days of *tumah* and sixty-six days of *dam tahor*. The parallelism is unambiguous: *tima vetiher bezachar vetima vetiher banekeivah — mah shetihar bezachar banekeivah kiflayim*, just as the period of purity is doubled for a girl, so too the period of *tumah* is doubled. Two weeks, not seventy days.

The students left satisfied. But Rabbi Yehuda ben Roeitz ran after them: *iy atem zekukim lekach* — you don't even need that proof. The reason is simply *shevuayim karinan ve-yesh eim lemikra*: we read the word *shevuayim*, two weeks, and the principle of *yesh eim lamikra* determines the *halacha*. It does not matter that the defective spelling could theoretically support an alternative reading. The tradition of pronunciation takes precedence.

### The Principle Explained

The pedagogical structure of this episode is itself instructive. Rabbi Yehuda ben Roeitz taught the logical proof first and only then articulated the formal principle. This sequence carries a more powerful message than the reverse would have. Had he led with *yesh eim lamikra* and then offered the textual proof as corroboration, the listener might conclude that the principle of *yesh eim lamikra* requires independent textual backup. By demonstrating the elegant proof and then setting it aside, he conveys the opposite: even where I *can* prove it to you from the internal structure of the *pesukim*, that is ultimately beside the point. The tradition of reading is the anchor, and no alternative derivation is needed — or should be sought.

This connects to a foundational principle of *Torah she-baal peh*. The Talmudic enterprise of interpreting *Torah she-biktav* does not begin from the bare written letters in isolation, as if the reader had no prior knowledge of how those letters are meant to be read. The starting point is always the received tradition of vocalization and reading. Only from there does interpretation proceed.

---

## Beit Shammai vs. Hil (II)

### Shammai's Blood Analysis

The *mishnah* in question teaches: *kol hanitnin al hamizbe'ach hachitzon shenatan matanah achat kipper* — all blood applications that belong on the outer altar, if performed with only a single application, have achieved atonement *bedi'eved*. This applies to the *olah*, *shlamim*, *asham*, and the like. For the *chatat*, whose blood is applied to the *karnot hamizbeach* — the four corners (horns) of the altar — Beit Shammai rules that two applications suffice *bedi'eved*, while Beit Hillel rules that even a single application achieves atonement.

Rav Huna explains Beit Shammai's derivation. In the *parshiyot* toward the end of *Parshat Vayikra*, dealing with various *chataot*, the word *karnot* (corners) appears three times. The word *karnot* is plural, indicating a minimum of two each time. Three times two is six. But there are only four corners. Therefore: four is the prescribed *mitzvah*, and two is the minimum required (*me'akev*). Beit Shammai's derivation follows the reading (*yesh eim lamikra*): the word is read *karnot* in the plural, and from that plural they derive the number two.

### Hillel's Written Form

Beit Hillel, by contrast, notes that two of the three occurrences of *karnot* are written without the *vav* — *karnat* in defective spelling. Going by the written form (*yesh eim lamesoret*), two of the three instances mean only one, and one instance means two: one plus one plus two equals four. Of those four, three are the prescribed *mitzvah* and one is the minimum *me'akev*. Thus for Beit Hillel, only one application is minimally required *bedi'eved*.

The *gemara* raises an objection: if all four are the *mitzvah* component and the *me'akev* is zero, one might say no application is required *bedi'eved*. But *kapara belo netinah lo ashkechan* — we have no precedent for atonement being achieved without any blood application at all. Hence at least one is taken as *me'akev*, and three are the *mitzvah* portion.

---

## Sukkah Walls Debate

### Standard Ruling

The standard ruling, as taught in the *beraisa*, is *shtayim kehilchatan ve-shlishit afilu tefach*: a *sukkah* requires two full walls and a third wall of even a minimal *tefach*. This is the position of the *chachamim*.

### Rabbi Shimon's Position

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *shalosh kehilchatan ve-revi'it afilu tefach* — three full walls are required, with the fourth wall needing only a *tefach*. Elsewhere in the *gemara* his position is explained by the view that a *sukkah* must be a *dirat keva*, a permanent-style dwelling, requiring more complete walls. Here, however, the *gemara* frames the dispute as one of hermeneutics.

---

## Sukkah Walls Debate (II)

### Gemara's Analysis

The *gemara* explains the dispute as follows. The word *sukkot* appears three times in the relevant *pesukim*. According to *yesh eim lamesoret*, two of those appearances are written defectively — *basukat, basukat* — as singular, and one is written in the full plural form — *basukkot*. That yields: one plus one plus two equals four walls. One *pasuk* is needed to establish the basic topic of *sukkah* (the principle of *ein dorshin techilot* — you do not derive quantities from the opening word that introduces the subject). That leaves three, and a *halacha lemoshe misinai* reduces the third wall to even a *tefach*, yielding two full walls and a *tefach*. This is the position of the *Rabbanan*, who hold *yesh eim lamesoret*.

Rabbi Shimon holds *yesh eim lamikra*. All three appearances are read in the full plural, *basukkot*, yielding two each time — six total. Subtract one for *ein dorshin techilot*, leaving five. But five is two-and-a-half *sukkot*, which is meaningless as a count of walls; rather, the doubling reflects four walls from two *sukkot*. Subtract one more for *ein dorshin techilot* — now we have four. The *halacha lemoshe misinai* then reduces the fourth wall to a *tefach*, yielding three full walls and a *tefach*. The *gemara* notes that the identification of this *halacheta* as *halacha lemoshe misinai* is explicit in *Masechet Sukkah*.

---

## Beit Shammai vs. Hil (II)

### Reading vs. Writing Deba…

Having worked through the *sukkah* walls dispute, the *gemara* now revisits the *Beit Shammai–Beit Hillel* debate about blood application, clarifying that it too maps onto the *yesh eim lamikra* versus *yesh eim lamesoret* divide: Beit Shammai reads *karnot* by the oral tradition of the plural and derives six; Beit Hillel reads it by the defective written form and derives four. The *sukkah* analysis and the blood-application analysis thus operate by identical hermeneutic logic, with each *tannaitic* position consistently applying one principle across different domains.

---

## Blood from Corpses

### Rabbi Akiva's Reading

The *gemara* now presents Rabbi Akiva's position. The *beraisa* asks: *minayin lerevi'is dam sheba'ah mishnei meisim shemetame'ah b'ohel* — how do we know that a *revi'is* of blood that comes from two different corpses causes *tumah* under a tent (*tumah b'ohel*)?

The *halacha* is that a *revi'is* of blood — approximately three and a half ounces, the volume of blood needed to sustain a newborn — represents the person and therefore causes *tumah b'ohel*, like a *kezayit* of flesh or a certain number of bones. The question is whether this applies when the *revi'is* is composed of blood from two separate corpses, rather than a single one. If the rationale is that the blood represents an individual body, perhaps the blood must all come from a single *meis*.

Rabbi Akiva derives the answer from the *pasuk*: *al kol nafshot meit lo yavo* — do not come under the same roof as a dead soul. Since the word *nafshot* is read in the plural — two souls, two corpses — and the word *meit* is in the singular — one measure — Rabbi Akiva reads this as: the minimum measure from two different corpses is what the *pasuk* addresses. Blood representing two *nefashot* but comprising only one *shiur* still causes *tumah b'ohel*. His derivation follows *yesh eim lamikra*, going by the plural as read.

### Rabbis' Response

The Rabbis respond: *nafshat ketiv* — the word is written without the *vav*, in the defective spelling, making it singular. You cannot derive a plural meaning from a defective spelling. Going by the written form (*yesh eim lamesoret*), the *pasuk* refers to one dead body, and the blood must therefore come from a single *meis*.

---

## Challenge to Consensus

### Rav Acha's Objection

The *gemara* now challenges the sweeping claim that all of the listed *Tannaim* hold *yesh eim lamikra*. Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects: if everyone holds *yesh eim lamikra*, who would ever hold *yesh eim lamesoret*? Surely no *tanna* could reject the reading tradition altogether. A *beraisa* makes this vivid: the prohibition of *basar b'chalav* is derived from *lo tevashel gedi b'chalav imo* — do not cook a kid in its mother's milk. The word written is *chelev* (fat) and the word read is *chalav* (milk). The *beraisa* explicitly invokes *yesh eim lamikra* to establish that the prohibition is milk-based: because we have a tradition of how the word is read, we know that *chalav* means milk. Everyone accepts that *basar b'chalav* involves milk, not fat. Evidently, no *tanna* would dispute the primacy of the reading in such a case. So what does it mean to say some hold *yesh eim lamesoret*?

### Consensus on Reading

The *gemara* initially accepts the objection and states: *de-chulei alma yesh eim lamikra* — in truth, everyone agrees that reading takes primacy. The earlier debates among the *Tannaim* must therefore be based on something other than a fundamental disagreement about *yesh eim lamikra* versus *yesh eim lamesoret*.

The *gemara* then revisits each dispute in turn. The debate between Rabbi and the Rabbis about a *beis din* of five versus three is not about the general principle of reading versus writing; everyone reads *yarshi'un* in the plural. The debate is whether *yarshi'un Elohim* refers to a different *Elohim* than the one at the beginning of the *pasuk* (Rabbi's position), or to the same one (the Rabbis' position). Rabbi Yehuda ben Roeitz faced no actual halakhic dispute at all — he simply articulated *yesh eim lamikra* as the answer, and no one contested it. The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about blood application, the *gemara* now suggests, is actually rooted in a separate *drasha* — the series of *ve-chiper, ve-chiper, ve-chiper* in *Parshat Vayikra*. Each *ve-chiper* reduces the requirement by one, and the debate is about the logic of that reduction, not about *yesh eim lamikra*. Similarly, the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *Rabbanan* about *sukkah* walls may reflect a deeper disagreement about whether a *sukkah* is a *dirat keva* or *dirat arai*, not a hermeneutic dispute about reading versus writing. And in the case of Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis regarding blood from two corpses, the debate is over whether *nefashot* in the plural refers to two specific corpses (*Rabbi Akiva*) or simply uses a generic collective (*Rabbanan*) — not over the principle of reading.

But then the *gemara* pushes back in the opposite direction. *Ve-ha tanya letotafet letotafet letotafet harei kan arba* — the *beraisa* about *tefillin* derives four compartments for the *shel rosh* from the word *totafot*: twice written defectively (without the *vav*), yielding one each, and once in the full form, yielding two — total four. That is *yesh eim lamesoret*, explicitly. Rabbi Yishmael makes this *drasha*. Rabbi Akiva says it is unnecessary since *tat* in one language means two and *pat* in another means two — arriving at four by a different route — but he does not dispute the *drasha* in principle. So apparently there is a real dispute between *Tannaim* about *yesh eim lamikra* versus *yesh eim lamesoret* after all. The *gemara* withdraws the claim that everyone agrees and returns to the position that there is indeed a fundamental disagreement.

---

## When Debate Arises

### Divergence Required

With the dispute reinstated, the *gemara* must now address the *beraisa* about *basar b'chalav*, which seemed to demonstrate universal agreement. The resolution is the crucial conceptual distinction of this entire sugya: *ve-hani mili ki paligi heicha de-shani kra mi-mesoret* — the debate between *yesh eim lamikra* and *yesh eim lamesoret* only arises when the written spelling diverges from the oral reading. That is the precise condition under which a choice must be made.

Consider the examples: *yarshi'an* is written without the *vav* but read *yarshi'un*; *karnot* is written defectively in two of its appearances but read as the full plural; *totafot* is written without the *vav* but read *totafot* in the full form; *basukat* is written as singular but read *basukkot*. In each of these cases, the Torah could have spelled the word to match its pronunciation but chose not to. That divergence creates two legitimate data points — the reading and the spelling — and the question becomes which one to privilege for hermeneutic purposes. That is where the camps divide.

But when the written spelling and the oral reading correspond — when there was simply no other way to write the word — there is no divergence to adjudicate, and everyone agrees that the reading determines the meaning. The word *chalav* (milk) and the word *chelev* (fat) are spelled identically, using the same three letters. The Torah had no alternative spelling available. There is therefore no scribal "choice" to read into the defective or non-defective form, and everyone must defer to the tradition of how the word is read — which is *chalav*, milk.

### Yira'eh Example

The *gemara* raises a striking challenge to this resolution. The word *yira'eh* — appearing in the context of the commandment to appear before God in the *Beit HaMikdash* — is in the same position as *chalav*: it can be vocalized as *yera'eh* (shall appear, in the *nif'al*) or as *yir'eh* (shall see, in the *kal*), and both vocalizations use the exact same written letters. There is no alternative spelling that could have disambiguated them. Yet there is a *tannaitic* debate that exploits precisely this ambiguity.

The *beraisa* teaches: *ha-suma be-achat me-einav patur min ha-reiyah* — one who is blind in one eye is exempt from the obligation to appear in the *Beit HaMikdash* during the *regel*. The derivation by Yochanan ben Dahavai in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima is: *ki-derech she-ba lir'ot kach ba le-hera'ot* — just as one comes to see, so one comes to be seen. The word is read as the obligation to appear (*le-hera'ot*), but it is equally writable as the obligation to see (*lir'ot*). Since the requirement of sight — *bishtei einav*, with both eyes — is built into the word's alternate reading, one who cannot see with both eyes is also exempt from appearing. The Rabbis, however, do not accept this *drasha*; they read the word only as *yera'eh* (shall appear) and do not give weight to the alternate reading.

This is a case where the spelling did not diverge from the reading — yet there is a debate. Some *Tannaim* are willing to derive meaning from an alternate reading of the same letters even when that alternate is not the traditional pronunciation.

### Chalav Resolved

The *gemara* therefore revises its conclusion. It cannot be that the debate only arises from a spelling divergence. Perhaps those who hold *yesh eim lamesoret* always look for what the written letters *could* mean, even when there is no defective spelling.

Rav Acha son of Rav Ika resolves the case of *basar b'chalav* differently. The *pasuk* says *lo tevashel gedi* — do not cook a kid. *Derech bishul asrah Torah* — the Torah prohibits the normal manner of cooking. Cooking is done with liquids. Therefore the word must mean *chalav*, a liquid, and cannot mean *chelev*, a fat — at least not in its solid form. Even those who normally give weight to alternate readings cannot extract the meaning of *chelev* here, because the context of *bishul*, cooking, establishes that a liquid is intended. The restriction to milk is thus secured not by *yesh eim lamikra* alone but by the contextual logic of the cooking process itself.

With this, the sugya reaches its conclusion. The fundamental distinction is this: when there is a genuine spelling divergence between the written and the read form, there is a real dispute among *Tannaim* as to which to privilege for *drasha*. When there is no spelling divergence, the debate can still arise if the letters support an alternate vocalization — but in a case like *basar b'chalav*, the context of the *pasuk* independently resolves the ambiguity. Tomorrow the *gemara* returns to the substantive issues of *Sanhedrin*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 5

## Mumche L'Rabbim

### Definition of Mumche

The daf opens one line from the bottom of 4b. The *baraita* states: *dinei mamonos b'shlosha* — monetary cases require three judges. It then adds: *im hayah mumche l'rabbim, dan afilu yechidi* — if the judge was a *mumche l'rabbim*, an expert recognized by the public, he may judge even alone. This is precisely the principle left unresolved at the end of the previous discussion. The *Gemara* then asks: who qualifies as a *mumche l'rabbim*? Rav Nachman answers by citing himself — *kigon ana dan dinei mamonos b'yechidi*, "someone like me, who judges monetary cases alone" — and Rabbi Chiya says the same.

### Learning & Licensing

The *Gemara* then unpacks the question further. What exactly is required? The first component is *gmurna v'savirna* — erudition in received tradition combined with analytical acuity. One has both mastered the transmitted corpus and can reason through novel problems. But is that sufficient? The second component raised is *v'naktna rishusa* — that one has also obtained formal licensing, permission from the political head of the Jewish community. The *Gemara* asks whether the absence of this licensing renders a judgment invalid: *aval lo nakt rishusa dinei lo dina*, or whether a *talmid chacham* who simply knows the law may rule without such permission and have his ruling stand nonetheless.

To understand why licensing is even conceptually relevant here, one must recall the broader framework. The requirement of three judges for *dinei mamonos* is most likely a Torah-level requirement. The institution of the *dayan yechidi*, the single judge, is thus a rabbinic allowance, motivated by the principle of *lo tinol deles bifnei lovin* — not to shut the door before borrowers by making monetary adjudication impractical. Precisely because this is a rabbinic creation, the Rabbis could attach conditions to it. They required that the single judge be a *mumche l'rabbim*, and they may additionally have required formal licensing. The concept of *rishus* — licensing — fits naturally within a rabbinic framework: if the Rabbis are the ones permitting this departure from the standard three-judge requirement, they could also stipulate that recognized authorization from the appropriate communal authority be part of what confers that permission.

### Ramban's Distinction

At this point it is important to note that the term *mumche* appears elsewhere in the *Gemara* — including in Rashi's comments back on 2b — where it referred to *smicha*, the chain of rabbinic ordination extending back to Moshe Rabbeinu. That usage of *mumche* is the status required when the word *Elohim* in the verse demands representation of divine authority, as is necessary for cases of *dinei knasos*, *malkus*, or capital punishment.

The term *mumche l'rabbim* here is categorically different, and the *Ramban* makes this distinction with characteristic precision. Counterintuitively, *mumche l'rabbim* denotes a lower status than plain *mumche*. The phrase does not mean one is an expert in some intensified or broader sense; rather, it means one is recognized by the community as an expert — *baduk lahem*, tested by them through experience. The *Ramban* draws an analogy to the *mumche* who writes amulets: that term refers to someone the community has come to rely upon, not someone who holds a formal, objectively verifiable status. He writes: *shehakol yodim bo degamir vesavir* — everyone knows he is knowledgeable — *ve'eino mumche latorah she'eino samuch berabbi*, but he does not hold the *smicha* that confers the title Rabbi in the full traditional sense. Two usages, then: *mumche* as formal ordination going back to Sinai, and *mumche l'rabbim* as communal recognition of expertise, which is what authorizes the single judge in monetary cases.

### Mar Zutra Case

The *Gemara* now seeks to resolve whether licensing is strictly necessary. It brings the case of Mar Zutra, son of Rav Nachman, who issued a judgment — apparently without having obtained licensing from the *Reish Galuta* — and erred. He came before Rav Yosef, who ruled: *im kibluch aleiyhu lo teshalem* — if the parties had accepted his authority, he need not pay — *ve'ee lo zil shelim* — but if he imposed his authority on them without their consent, he must pay. This closely parallels what was seen in the Yerushalmi: acceptance of authority extends latitude, while imposed authority is held to a more objective standard.

What matters for the current question, however, is not the issue of payment but the status of the judgment itself. Even in the case where Mar Zutra imposed his authority — and we understand this was a case without formal licensing — the judgment stood. The payment question is secondary; the ruling was not invalidated. From this the *Gemara* concludes: *shema mina ki lo nakat reshuta dina dina* — even without licensing, the judgment is binding. That inference is accepted.

### Licensing & Liability

Rav then introduces a further practical dimension: *hai man deba'i lemidein dina ee ta'ei ba'ei lemiftera* — if one wishes to judge and also wishes to be exempt from liability in the event of error, there is a remedy: *lishkol reshuta mibei Reish Galuta*, obtain licensing from the *Reish Galuta*. Shmuel states the same ruling. The structure that emerges is therefore two-tiered. Being a *mumche l'rabbim* is sufficient for one's judgments to be binding — and perhaps even to impose authority — but it does not by itself confer immunity from liability if one errs. For that exemption, formal licensing from the *Reish Galuta* is required. One might wonder whether persistent errors would lead to revocation of that license, and who bears the authority to declare that a judge has erred in the first instance — questions the *Gemara* leaves for a later discussion.

---

## Jurisdiction: Bavel & EY

### Geographic Scope

Having established the role of *rishus* in conferring or protecting authority, the *Gemara* turns to the geographic scope of such authorization. The straightforward cases are clear: *me-hacha le-hacha* — authority granted in Bavel to judge in Bavel — and *me-hasam le-hasam* — authority granted in Eretz Yisrael to judge in Eretz Yisrael — these obviously work. The *Gemara* also states that authority granted in Bavel to judge in Eretz Yisrael — *me-hacha le-hasam* — likewise functions. The question is the reverse: what about authority granted in Eretz Yisrael to judge in Bavel?

### Staff & Lawgiver

The reason authority flows from Bavel to Eretz Yisrael is rooted in a *baraita* interpreting the verse *lo yasur shevet mi-Yehuda* — the staff shall not depart from Judah. The *baraita* identifies the *shevet*, the staff, with the *Roshei Galuyos* — the heads of the exile, the *Reish Galusa* — in Bavel, who exercise actual coercive power. *She-rodin es Yisrael be-shevet* — they govern Israel with a staff — meaning they had a genuine enforcement capacity backed by the surrounding government. The *mechokek*, the lawgiver, refers by contrast to the descendants of Hillel who teach Torah publicly in Eretz Yisrael. *Melamdim Torah be-rabbim* — they teach Torah to the many — but their authority is essentially one of persuasion and scholarship, not compulsion.

This distinction has direct relevance to the question of *rishus* in adjudication. The *Gemara*'s point is that since the *Reish Galusa* in Bavel holds the *shevet* — real coercive authority backed by the government — authorization from that office carries binding weight even beyond its immediate jurisdiction. This is why Bavel's authorization functions in Eretz Yisrael. There is a certain irony worth noting: the House of the *Nasi* in Eretz Yisrael, most famously Rebbe Yehuda HaNasi, combined both political and rabbinic authority in a single institution, whereas in Bavel the two were separate — political authority in the *Reish Galusa*, rabbinic authority diffused among the great Amoraim. Yet the *baraita* implies that in terms of coercive bindingness, the Babylonian political authority carried more practical weight. One might also note, as an aside, that Hillel himself was Babylonian — *Hillel HaBavli* — so that even the Torah authority of Eretz Yisrael ultimately traced its lineage to Bavel.

### Rabbah bar Chana

The *Gemara* now seeks a proof on the key unresolved question: does authority granted in Eretz Yisrael function in Bavel? It brings the case of Rabbah bar Chana, who — as will be detailed shortly — received his authorization from Rabbi Chiya in Eretz Yisrael before traveling to Bavel, specifically with Bavel in mind. He subsequently erred in a ruling he gave there, and came before Rabbi Chiya. Rabbi Chiya told him: *ei kibluch alayhu lo teshalem* — if the parties accepted his authority, he need not pay — *ve'ei lo zil shelim* — if not, go pay.

Now, the *Gemara* observes that Rabbah bar Chana did in fact hold authorization from Rabbi Chiya. If authorization from Eretz Yisrael were valid in Bavel, he should have been automatically exempt from payment regardless of whether the parties accepted him. The fact that Rabbi Chiya subjected him to the same test — did they accept you or not? — implies that the Eretz Yisrael authorization carried no weight in Bavel. *Shema mina me-hatam le-hacha lo mahani* — authority from there to here does not help.

### Rav Huna Defense

The *Gemara* challenges this conclusion by citing the behavior of Rabbah bar Rav Huna, a different figure. When Rabbah bar Rav Huna would clash with the house of the *Reish Galusa*, he would say: *lav minaichu nakitna reshuta* — do not think my authority derives from you. Rather, *nakitna reshuta mi-Abba Mari, ve-Abba Mari mi-Rav, ve-Rav mi-Rabbi Chiya, ve-Rabbi Chiya mi-Rebbi* — his authority derived from a chain going all the way back to Rebbe Yehuda HaNasi in Eretz Yisrael. This appears to be a direct claim that authorization originating in Eretz Yisrael carries weight in Bavel.

### EY Authority Invalid

The *Gemara* deflects this challenge with a pointed answer: *be-milta d'alma hu d'okim le-hu* — he was merely trying to get them off his back. He was dropping the names of great authorities to deter the *Reish Galusa*'s household from pressuring him, but his claim had no actual legal foundation. Authority from Eretz Yisrael genuinely does not function to grant exemption from liability in Bavel. It is worth pausing to note that from the Bavli's perspective, the asymmetry is complete: Bavel's authorization functions in Eretz Yisrael, but Eretz Yisrael's authorization does not function in Bavel. One wonders, as the lecturer notes, whether the Yerushalmi would have reached the same conclusion.

### Border Towns Exception

This leaves a question. If authorization from Eretz Yisrael confers no benefit in Bavel, why did Rabbah bar Chana bother obtaining it before he traveled there? The *Gemara* answers: *le-ayoti omdim al ha-gevulin* — there were towns situated along the border between the two jurisdictions, towns whose affiliation was ambiguous. In those regions, the Eretz Yisrael authorization was operative and conferred at minimum the exemption from liability. In the heartland of Bavel, the authorization was without legal effect in terms of liability; but at the margins, it retained practical value. This satisfies the question of why obtaining the authorization was not pointless, even given the *Gemara*'s ruling.

---

## Rabbah & Rav Story

### Authority to Rabbah

The *Gemara* now presents the background story that illuminates how Rabbah bar Chana received his authorization, and in doing so introduces terminology that has become the foundation of all subsequent rabbinic licensing. When Rabbah bar Chana was preparing to go down to Bavel — note the traditional usage of *yored*, descending, when one travels from Eretz Yisrael — Rabbi Chiya went to Rebbe and said: *ben achi yored le-Bavel*, my nephew, my brother's son, is going to Bavel.

He then asked three questions and received three answers. *Yoreh?* — does he have the authority to rule on questions of *issur ve-hetter*, permitted and forbidden? *Yoreh* — yes. *Yadin?* — does he have the authority to adjudicate *dinei mamonos*? *Yadin* — yes. *Yattir bechorot?* — does he have the authority to examine blemishes on firstborn animals and rule on whether they are permanent blemishes that would permit the animal to be eaten rather than offered as a sacrifice? *Yattir bechorot* — yes, he has that authority as well.

### Rav Denied Authority

When Rav was similarly preparing to go to Bavel — also a nephew of Rabbi Chiya — Rabbi Chiya went to Rebbe and asked the same sequence of questions: *ben achoti yored le-Bavel*, my sister's son is going to Bavel. *Yoreh? Yoreh. Yadin? Yadin. Yattir bechorot? Al yattir* — this authority he was not granted.

### Family Relations

Before examining why Rav was denied this particular authorization, the *Gemara* pauses to address an apparent inconsistency. Rabbi Chiya referred to Rabbah bar Chana as his brother's son, but to Rav as his sister's son. Were they not both his nephews through brothers? The *Gemara* confirms from a tradition that Rabbi Chiya, along with Aivo, Chana, Shila, and Marta, were all sons of Abba bar Acha Carsela of Kafri — all siblings. Chana was the father of Rabbah bar Chana, making him unambiguously a brother's son. Aivo was Rav's father, which should make Rav also a brother's son. Why then did Rabbi Chiya call Rav his sister's son?

The *Gemara* offers two answers. The first is that Rav was both his brother's son and his sister's son — that is, his parents were a half-brother and half-sister of Rabbi Chiya who were not themselves related to each other, so that Rav stood in both relationships simultaneously. Rabbah bar Chana was only a brother's son. The second answer is that Rabbi Chiya called Rav his sister's son as an expression of Rav's exceptional wisdom — *al shem chochmato* — based on the verse *emor la-chochmah achoti at*, "say to wisdom: you are my sister." By calling him the son of his sister, Rabbi Chiya was poetically indicating that Rav was a man of surpassing *chochmah*.

### Rav's Expertise

This second answer, however, immediately generates a problem. If Rav was the greater scholar, why was he denied the authorization to rule on blemishes of firstborn animals? The *Gemara* considers and rejects two obvious explanations. Perhaps he was not so learned? — but we just established he was the greater intellect. Perhaps he lacked practical familiarity with blemishes? — but the *Gemara* cites Rav's own statement: *shmonah asar chodashim gadalti etzel ro'eh behemah le-ida eizeh mum kavua v'eizeh mum over* — he spent eighteen months apprenticed to shepherds specifically to learn the difference between a permanent blemish and a transient one. He possessed both the theoretical knowledge and the practical experience.

The *Gemara* offers two answers. The first is *lachaloik lo kavod le-Rabba bar Chana* — it was done to ensure that Rabbah bar Chana would receive sufficient honor. Rav's stature was already so great that he needed no additional credential; he would command respect regardless. But Rabbah bar Chana needed something distinguishing, and by granting him an authorization withheld even from Rav, Rabbi Chiya ensured that the community would accord Rabbah bar Chana the deference he required.

The second answer is more striking: *mishum ha gufa* — precisely because of Rav's expertise, he was not given the authorization. *De-Rav baki be-mumin tefei, de-sharei mumin d'lo yad'ei inshi* — Rav was so expert in blemishes that he would sometimes permit blemishes that to ordinary observers did not appear to be blemishes at all. *V'atu lemishrei mum over* — people watching would not understand the fine distinctions he was drawing, and would take his lenient rulings as precedents for cases involving transient blemishes, which are not grounds for permitting the animal. Sometimes, the *Gemara* implies, one can be too expert for the public good.

---

## Yoreh Yoreh

### Licensing Question

Having introduced the phrase *yoreh yoreh* in the context of Rabbah bar Chana's authorization, the *Gemara* now examines the underlying rationale for requiring licensing specifically for *hora'ah* — ruling on questions of permitted and forbidden. This is counterintuitive. The case for licensing in *dinei mamonos* is clear: either to make rulings compellable, or to exempt the judge from liability. But *hora'ah* involves neither. If someone brings a chicken to a rabbi and asks whether it is *kosher*, no one is being compelled, and there is no framework of liability for an incorrect ruling. Why then should a *talmid chacham* who knows the *halacha* need any license at all?

### Dough Story

The *Gemara* answers: *mishum maaseh shehayah* — because of an incident that occurred. A *baraita* relates that Rebbe once visited a certain place and found the people kneading their dough in a state of *tumah* without apparent concern. He asked them why. They explained that a certain scholar had once come and ruled for them: *mei bitzaim ein machshirin* — water from eggs does not render food susceptible to *tumah*. Since they were using water that did not constitute *mayim* in the relevant sense, they had concluded they could knead freely without concern for *tumah*.

### Misinterpretation

The *Gemara* explains what had actually happened. The scholar had told them *mei beitzim darash lehu* — he had ruled about egg water, meaning that dough kneaded with eggs rather than water would not be susceptible. But the community heard *mei bitzaim* — water from marshes or ditches — and assumed that such water did not render food susceptible. Adding to the confusion, a *tanna* had indeed taught that the waters of certain rivers were invalid for use in the *parah adumah* purification process because they were like ditch water. The community reasoned: since this water is disqualified even for the *parah adumah* process, surely it cannot function as water in any halachic sense — and therefore *achshurei nami lo machshiri*, it cannot render food susceptible to *tumah* either. This reasoning is incorrect: the *parah adumah* requires *mayim chayim*, genuinely fresh water, whereas *hechsher tumah* — rendering food susceptible — is triggered by virtually any liquid. The two categories are distinct.

The core point, however, is not this particular *halachic* detail but what the incident reveals about the practical responsibilities of *hora'ah*. It is not sufficient to know the law; one must know how to communicate a ruling to a community, anticipate how it will be received, and bear responsibility for how it will be applied. The scholar in this case was apparently not irresponsible in terms of his knowledge, but his ruling was misunderstood in a way that led to widespread violation, and he had no mechanism of accountability.

### Licensing Decree

As a result of this incident, a decree was issued: *talmid al yoreh ela im kein notal reshusa mei-rabbah* — a student may not issue rulings unless he has obtained permission from his teacher. This represents the origin of professional licensing in the rabbinic context. Unlike the *rishus* from the *Reish Galusa* discussed earlier — which was about coercive authority in *dinei mamonos* or about exemption from liability — this decree is about communal responsibility. The concern is that people should not accept a rabbi as their *posek* unless someone within the professional community has vouched for him. Just as one should not accept a physician based solely on a persuasive manner, one requires confirmation from those already within the field that the candidate has been properly trained and evaluated.

### Community Trust

This is the origin of *yoreh yoreh* as a phrase of rabbinic licensing. In the absence of *smicha* in its classical sense — the chain of ordination extending back to Moshe Rabbeinu — the phrase *yoreh yoreh* became the formulation by which a rabbi's teacher communicated to the community that this individual was authorized, responsible, and trustworthy in rendering *hora'ah*. It is not, strictly speaking, a *halachic* requirement in the sense of *d'oraisa* or even a formal rabbinic enactment in the mold of the three-judge requirement. It is a communal institution: the profession certifies one of its own, and the community is thereby assured that it can rely on his rulings.

The question of *yadin yadin* — whether the authorization for *dinei mamonos* similarly served a purpose, given that Eretz Yisrael authorization did not help in Bavel — remains open, and will be taken up in the continuation of the *sugya*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 6

## Yoreh Yoreh & Licensing

### Yoreh Yoreh Origins

The daf opens by revisiting the discussion begun on the previous amud concerning the origins and purpose of *yoreh yoreh*. The Gemara had established that rabbis require authorization — *notel reshut* — in order to be exempt from liability if they issue an incorrect ruling in *dinei mamonot*. The Gemara further noted that authority granted from Eretz Yisrael does not extend to Bavel. Against that backdrop, the stories of Rabbi Chiyya's nephews traveling between Eretz Yisrael and Bavel provide the classical basis for the institution of *yoreh yoreh* and *yadin yadin* — the formal authorization to rule on *issur v'heter* and *dinei mamonot* respectively.

### Licensing Purposes

The question that naturally arises is: if authority from Eretz Yisrael does not help for Bavel, why was the licensing of *yoreh yoreh* needed at all for communities outside that framework? The Gemara resolves this by noting that the original context concerned border communities, for whom such licensing was specifically relevant.

This, however, points to a broader purpose of *yoreh yoreh* that has nothing to do with *dinei mamonot* or the compulsion of litigants to appear before a court. When someone comes to a rabbi with a *halachic she'elah* in *issur v'heter*, there is no question of exemption from payment for an erroneous ruling. Rather, the licensing serves a different function entirely: it is a verification of competence and fitness to serve. Not every *talmid chacham*, however knowledgeable, is necessarily fit to serve as a communal rabbi and to *pasken* for others. The Gemara illustrates this with the story of a rabbi who articulated his words imprecisely and thereby misled people into error. The institution of *yoreh yoreh* thus emerged as a mechanism by which the community could be assured that a person presenting himself as a rabbinic authority had been vetted and licensed by his own *rav*.

### Rabbi's Inspection

The Gemara presents the story of *Rebbi* arriving in a community and discovering that the local rabbi had been ruling incorrectly. The text picks up with the phrase *be-osa sha'ah gazru*: at that moment they established the rule, *talmid al yoreh ella im ken notal reshut mi-rabbo* — a student may not issue rulings unless he has received explicit authorization from his teacher. The framing here is personal and individual: it is not primarily a communal concern but a personal prohibition incumbent on the student himself. Regardless of how great a *talmid chacham* one may be, the authority to *pasken* for others must be formally conferred by one's *rav*, who thereby testifies that the student possesses not only the necessary knowledge but also the judgment and communicative skill to render rulings reliably.

### Tanchum Story

A further dimension of this principle is illustrated by the story of Tanchum the son of Rabbi Ami, who arrived in the town of Chasor and taught publicly that it is permitted to rinse grain on Pesach — a process of wetting the grain to loosen the husk — without concern that this would cause the grain to become *chametz*. The townspeople, remarkably well-versed in their *halacha*, challenged him by citing a *braita*: *talmid al yoreh halacha be-makom rabbo* — a student may not issue rulings in the place of his *rebbe*. They identified that Rabbi Mani of Tzor was present in that very town. Tanchum replied: *lav ada'ati* — I was unaware that my *rebbe* was here; had I known, I would not have ruled.

### Distance Requirement

The *braita* the townspeople cited is precise: the prohibition applies unless the student is at least three *parsas* distant from his *rebbe*, corresponding to the breadth of the entire camp of Israel in the wilderness. This demonstrates that the restriction on issuing rulings is not merely a matter of not contradicting one's teacher face-to-face; it extends across an entire geographic zone defined by that three-*parsa* radius. Even a student who has been fully licensed and authorized is nonetheless prohibited from *paskening* within his *rebbe*'s domain, as doing so is considered a breach of respect for the *rebbe*'s authority. Tanchum's immediate acknowledgment of this principle reflects how deeply embedded the norm was in rabbinic culture.

This raises the further question of what precisely constitutes *psak* for these purposes — and whether there exists a form of authorization that would permit a student to rule even within his *rebbe*'s presence. Some understand the deeper significance of *semicha* — ordination — precisely in these terms: not merely as a license to *pasken* at all, but as a grant of authority sufficient to permit *paskening* even in the *rebbe*'s domain.

### Conditional Authority

Having established that partial authority is valid — as seen from the earlier case where one could be authorized for *dinei mamonot* but not for *matir bechorot* — the Gemara turns to a related question: what about conditional authority, such as a license limited by time or by circumstance?

The Gemara cites a proof: Rabbi Yochanan said to Rav Shemen, *harei ata bi-reshutenu ad she-tavo etzelenu* — you have our authority until you return to us. This is, on its face, a geographically bounded grant: you are authorized to rule while you are away from us. The Yerushalmi reads this more broadly, however, treating all forms of limitation — whether by time, place, or subject matter — as equivalent expressions of partial or conditional authorization. One might have thought that since the act of granting *reshut* constitutes an acknowledgment of the student's competence, it should not be possible to confine that competence by time or geography. The Gemara and Yerushalmi, however, see all of these as structurally identical: they are variations of a limited grant, and they are all valid.

This concludes the Gemara's discussion of licensing and the granting of rabbinic authority.

---

## Court Composition

### Shmuel's View

The Gemara returns to the question of how many judges are required to constitute a valid *beit din* for *dinei mamonot*. Shmuel states: *bei shenayim she-dannu dineihem din ella she-nikra beit din chatzuf* — if two people judged, their judgment is binding, but they are called an impudent court. The position of Shmuel is thus that two judges, while not ideal and technically contemptuous of proper procedure, nonetheless produce a legally valid ruling after the fact.

### Unknown Judge

The Gemara opens a challenge against Shmuel's position by citing a ruling of Rav Nachman. The case is as follows: if a *beit din* of three is constituted and two of the three rule one way — whether to acquit or to obligate — while the third says *eini yodea*, "I don't know," the judges must be supplemented with additional members. The challenge to Shmuel is straightforward: if two judges suffice, why does a panel of three devolve into an invalid court simply because one member declares himself unable to rule? Even if the third voted the opposite way, two against one would still resolve the case — so why should the declaration of ignorance require expanding the panel?

The Gemara answers: *shani hatam de-me'ikara da'ata di-tlata yasvi* — that case is different, because from the outset the court was constituted as a unit of three. When you define the adjudicating body as three, the outcome must emerge from that entire unit. The statement of *eini yodea* is not a vote; it is an abdication, and it leaves the court functionally incomplete even if two valid votes remain. As the Gemara puts it, this is worse than beginning with two: a court that starts as three and is reduced to two effective voices has not concluded its deliberation. By contrast — *hacha lav ada'ata di-tlata yasvi* — when one begins with only two and never constituted the panel as three, Shmuel's ruling applies and the judgment stands.

### Shimon ben Gamliel

A further challenge is raised from a *braita* in which Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states: *ha-din bi-shelosha, peshara bi-shenayim* — formal judgment requires three, while compromise (*peshara*) requires only two. He adds, *yafeh koach peshara mi-koach ha-din* — the power of compromise exceeds that of judgment in one respect: if two judges issued a formal ruling, the litigants may withdraw from it since it lacks binding force, whereas if two judges effected a *peshara*, the litigants cannot retract, since they have accepted those two as their arbiters. This directly contradicts Shmuel, who holds that formal judgment by two is binding. According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, judgment by two is explicitly non-binding.

One might attempt to save Shmuel by arguing that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view is disputed and that Shmuel rules in accordance with the opposing opinion. The Gemara preempts this.

### Abbahu Disputes

Rabbi Abbahu declares: *shenayim she-dannu le-divrei ha-kol ein dineihem din* — if two judged, their judgment is universally invalid. Rabbi Abbahu thus frames Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position not as a minority opinion but as a universal ruling with which all authorities agree. This forecloses Shmuel's escape route: one cannot claim that Shmuel follows an opposing opinion if, as Rabbi Abbahu maintains, there is no opposing opinion.

The Gemara responds with characteristic directness: *gavra agavra karemita* — you are simply pitting one authority against another. Rabbi Abbahu holds that two is universally invalid; Shmuel holds that two is valid though contemptuous. These are two Amoraim in genuine dispute, and the Gemara leaves them as such.

The landscape of *beit din* composition thus stands as follows: three is the classical and undisputed standard; two is debated, with Shmuel permitting it as *beit din chatzuf* and others rejecting it entirely; and one — specifically, a *yachid mumche* — was addressed in an earlier Gemara in a way that seemed to permit it by consensus.
