Tosafot explains the earlier ruling of *yachid mumche* as a special rabbinic enactment (*takanat de-Rabbanan*) designed to expand access to *dinei mamonot* adjudication, which is why that Gemara specifically emphasized the requirement of *mumche*. The present discussions of two and three do not concern the *mumche* case at all.

---

## One Judge Valid?

### Kiblu Aleihu

The Gemara now introduces a *braita* that complicates the picture. The text reads: *dan et ha-din, ve-zikah et ha-chayav, ve-chiyav et ha-zakai, timei et ha-tahor, ve-tiher et ha-tamei* — someone rendered judgment and cleared the guilty, convicted the innocent, declared impure what was pure, or declared pure what was impure. The ruling continues: *mah she-asah asui u-meshalem mi-beito* — what he has done is done, and he must compensate from his own property. The verbs throughout are in the singular, pointing to a single judge. How can a single non-*mumche* individual issue a binding ruling?

The Gemara resolves this with a principle that should resonate from the Yerushalmi: *de-kiblu aleihu* — the litigants accepted this individual's authority. Acceptance by the parties (*kiblu aleihu*) grants jurisdiction to an individual who would otherwise have none.

### Error & Liability

A difficulty immediately presents itself. If the parties accepted this person's authority, why does the Gemara speak of error and financial liability at all? Acceptance of an arbitrator's authority normally renders the outcome binding, much like contractual arbitration. If *kiblu aleihu* places the matter in the hands of this individual, why is his ruling subject to challenge on grounds of error?

### Din Torah Requirement

The Gemara provides the key: *de-amru leih dayant lan din Torah* — the parties accepted his authority, but they stipulated that he must adjudicate according to objective Torah law. They did not surrender themselves to his personal discretion. The acceptance grants him jurisdiction; the demand for *din Torah* preserves the objectivity of the outcome. Because they required *din Torah*, it remains possible to identify an error, and the judge remains exposed to financial liability if he rules incorrectly. The ruling is not automatically insulated by the acceptance, because the acceptance itself was conditional on the application of objective *halacha*.

### Reconciliation

The full framework can now be articulated. There are three distinct scenarios. First, the *yachid mumche*: an established expert judge, ideally holding *notel reshut*, who can adjudicate even without the parties' consent, is exempt from payment (*patur mi-leshalem*) if he errs, since his authority derives from his recognized expertise and formal authorization. Second, a panel of two, which Shmuel considers binding though contemptuous and others consider invalid altogether — these discussions address compelled jurisdiction, independent of whether *kiblu aleihu* applies. Third, the *yachid she-eino mumche* who adjudicates by virtue of *kiblu aleihu* with a demand for *din Torah*: the acceptance gives him jurisdiction, but the requirement of objective law means that an incorrect ruling creates liability (*chayav le-shalem*). This is contrasted with *peshara* or *bitzua*, where *kiblu aleihu* without a demand for *din Torah* means whatever the arbitrator decides is fully binding, with no exposure to liability for error.

---

## Errors in Rulings

### Taah Bidvar Mishna

The Gemara now turns to the internal analysis of the *braita*'s case. Rav Safra poses the question to Rabbi Abba: *de-ta'ah be-mai* — in what kind of error are we dealing? The Gemara considers first the case of *ta'ah bi-dvar mishna* — an error in black-letter law, something explicit and settled. In such a case, Rabbi Sheshet citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi rules: *ta'ah bi-dvar mishna, chozer* — the ruling is reversed. If the judge made a clear, demonstrable error against settled law, the judgment is not merely voidable; it is undone entirely. The consequence is that the judge does not pay from his own pocket, because there is no loss to compensate — the original legal situation is restored by reversing the erroneous ruling. David gives the money back to Michael; Michael never suffers a final loss.

One might ask who determines that the error occurred. The Gemara does not specify a formal appeals mechanism. It may be that the judge himself recognizes the mistake, or that the broader rabbinic community identifies it — the Gemara leaves this question open. What is clear is that the reversal is the operative remedy: *chozer*.

### Shikul Hadaat Error

The Gemara then considers the alternative: *ela de-ta'ah be-shikul ha-da'at* — an error in judgment, a discretionary call. Rav Papa explains the case: it involves a dispute between two *tannaim* or two *amoraim* of equal weight, where neither position has been formally designated as authoritative — *ve-lo ismar hilcheta lo ke-mar ve-lo ke-mar*. In such a situation, ruling in accordance with either opinion seems entirely legitimate as a matter of personal judgment. So what makes the ruling an error?

The answer: *ve-sugya de-alma aliba de-chad mineihu* — the general practice among judges (*hiluch dina*, as Rashi explains) has settled, without formal canonization, in favor of one of the opinions. The judge went and ruled according to the other one — *ve-zal ve-avad ke-idach*. That is what the Gemara means by a *shikul ha-da'at* error.

### Error Paradox

This answer, however, is genuinely puzzling. If there has been no formal ruling and both positions remain technically live, on what grounds is the judge's ruling an error? One possible reading is that the judge was simply unaware of the prevailing practice among his contemporaries — had he known, he might well have followed the consensus. But if he was aware and consciously chose the minority position, it is not at all obvious why that constitutes a punishable mistake, since he is following a legitimate opinion in a non-settled dispute.

The Gemara's conclusion is that this type of error is *not chozer* — the ruling stands, because it cannot be characterized as plainly wrong. Yet the judge is *chayav le-shalem* — liable to compensate — because the ruling is sufficiently deviant from accepted practice to constitute culpable error. Exactly where the threshold lies between legitimate minority ruling and actionable mistake remains, even after all analysis, genuinely difficult to pin down.

### Canonization

This Gemara and the *rishonic* discussion surrounding it carry implications that extend far beyond the immediate case. The distinction between *ta'ah bi-dvar mishna* and *ta'ah be-shikul ha-da'at* becomes the framework within which later authorities discuss the binding force of different levels of legal tradition. A fundamental question debated among the *rishonim* is whether ruling against a consensus of the *geonim* constitutes *ta'ah bi-dvar mishna* — and therefore triggers automatic reversal — or merely a *shikul ha-da'at* deviation. This is ultimately a question about the canonical authority of the *geonic* tradition. Similarly: can a *rishon* such as the Rambam or Ramban rule against geonic consensus without being characterized as having erred in black-letter law? Can one rule according to the Yerushalmi against the Bavli, or against the *Shulchan Aruch*? Each of these questions is, at its root, a question about what counts as *dvar mishna* — what has been sufficiently canonized that departing from it is not an exercise of judgment but an error. The Gemara does not answer these questions, but by constructing this category, it supplies the vocabulary and conceptual structure within which *poskim* across the centuries have conducted precisely this debate.

---

## Peshara vs Din

### Parallel Requirements

The Gemara now proposes to link the Tannaitic debate about *peshara* to the underlying question of court composition for *din*. The suggestion is that the dispute about how many judges are required for *peshara* may reflect a parallel disagreement about how many are required for *din* itself — the assumption being that *peshara* and *din* are governed by the same compositional rules.

### Three Peshara Views

The Gemara presents three positions. Rabbi Meir holds that *bitzoa* — compromise, binding arbitration — requires three judges. The *Chachamim* hold that *peshara* requires only one. And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, as noted earlier, holds that *peshara* requires two. If one assumes that the court composition requirements for *peshara* mirror those for *din*, the positions would map onto one another: Rabbi Meir's three for *peshara* reflects three for *din*; the *Chachamim*'s one for *peshara* reflects one for *din*.

The Gemara rejects this inference, however. One cannot conclude from Rabbi Meir's position that he requires only two for *din* simply because the *Chachamim* who require one for *peshara* implicitly require one for *din*. Rather, the Gemara says, *de-chulei alma din bi-shelosha* — everyone agrees that formal *din* requires three. The debate among the *tannaim* is not about the compositional requirements of *din* at all, but about whether *peshara* is analogous to *din* in this respect.

### Two as Witnesses

The position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — that *peshara* requires two — receives an important clarification. Rabbi Acha the son of Rav Ika (or, in another version, Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya) explains: the one who says two for *peshara* in fact concedes that one would suffice. The reason two is recommended is not structural necessity but practical wisdom: *kedei le-hava lei sahidei* — so that witnesses will be available. Without a second person present, each litigant may walk away from the proceeding claiming that the arbitrator ruled differently, and there will be no one to confirm what the actual decision was. Having a second participant allows the two of them to serve as witnesses to the ruling's content. Two, in this view, is not a compositional requirement but a procedural safeguard.

### Peshara Summary

The Gemara thus arrives at a settled picture. When it comes to *din*, three is the universally acknowledged standard; the debates about two and one apply within that framework, with the *yachid mumche* representing a special rabbinic dispensation. When it comes to *peshara*, the operative positions reduce to two: three, which assimilates *peshara* to *din* and demands a full *beit din*, reflecting a view that *peshara* involves genuine legal evaluation of the merits; and one, which treats *peshara* as a distinct process that does not require a formal court. Two is not a genuine third option but rather a procedural recommendation — to have a witness — layered over the substantive position that one suffices. The tension between these views reflects a deeper question about the nature of *peshara* itself: whether it is a form of adjudication that happens to be more flexible, or whether it is something categorically different from *din*, demanding different rules altogether.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 6b

## Peshara & Kinyan

### Rav Ashi: No Kinyan

The daf opens mid-discussion, picking up from the debate over *peshara* versus *din* — whether compromise, understood as binding arbitration, constitutes a form of judicial rendering or merely a contractual arrangement. That underlying question determines whether *peshara* requires three judges or one. It is in this context that Rav Ashi offers his inference: *shema mina peshara eina tzricha kinyan* — from the very fact that there is a debate between one and three judges, we may conclude that *peshara* does not require a *kinyan*.

The logic runs as follows. Were *peshara* to require a *kinyan* — the formal act of acquisition by which one obligates oneself to a decision — then the entire debate over requiring three judges would collapse. Once a *kinyan* is performed, the parties have already contractually bound themselves to accept whatever the arbitrator decides. In that case, even two witnesses should suffice to validate the arrangement, and no one would argue that three judges are necessary. The fact that an opinion exists requiring three demonstrates that we are not operating within a purely contractual framework; something more judicial is at play.

### Hilcheta: Kinyan Required

The *Gemara* then reaches a surprising conclusion. Despite the apparent force of Rav Ashi's inference, the *halacha* is stated plainly: *v'hilcheta peshara tzricha kinyan* — *peshara* does in fact require a *kinyan*. The question then reasserts itself: if a *kinyan* is performed, why would anyone still require three judges?

Tosafot addresses this directly. The requirement for three judges persists even when a *kinyan* is performed because a *kinyan* made before an illegitimate panel would be tantamount to a *kinyan* made in error. The parties are not agreeing to submit themselves to an arbitrary result; they are committing themselves to a genuine and responsible *peshara*. Anything less than three judges risks producing a decision that lacks the requisite legitimacy, and therefore the agreement itself would be built on a flawed foundation. Hence, three judges remain necessary even in the presence of a *kinyan* — not to enforce the contractual obligation, but to ensure that what the parties are obligating themselves to constitutes a real and defensible form of compromise.

---

## Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

### Baraita: 3 Judges, No Po…

A *baraita* is introduced: just as *din* requires three judges, so too *bitzua* — compromise — requires three. This confirms that *peshara* is understood, at least procedurally, as a form of adjudication rather than a purely private arrangement. The *baraita* further establishes that once *gmar din* — the finalized judgment — has been pronounced, *bitzua* is no longer permitted.

### R. Eliezer: Assur

Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yose HaGalili goes further. In his view, *assur livtzoa* — it is forbidden to compromise — and one who does so is a sinner, perverting the truth. More strikingly, *kol hamevarech et habotzea harei zeh menaetz* — anyone who praises the one who arranged the compromise is as one who blasphemes God. The verse invoked is *botzea berech ni'etz Hashem* — the one who blesses the *botzea* blasphemes God — which the *Gemara* reads not in its plain sense of ill-gotten gain but as a condemnation of judicial compromise. The imperative that follows is *yikov hadin et hahar* — let the law pierce the mountain. No obstacle is large enough to justify bending the truth of justice. The basis is *ki hamishpat lElokim hu* — the judgment belongs to God, and to distort it is to act against God Himself.

This position is reinforced by contrasting Moshe and Aharon. Moshe is associated with *yikov hadin et hahar* — the unbending administration of divine law. Aharon, by contrast, is described as *ohev shalom verodef shalom*, one who loved peace and pursued it, making peace between people, with truth on his lips and uprightness in his conduct. The verse cited is from the passage beginning *ki siftei kohen yishmeru da'at*, affirming Aharon's prophetic role.

One might ask: if compromise is *assur*, how is Aharon's conduct praiseworthy? The very qualities attributed to Aharon — making peace, speaking truth — sound like exactly the behavior Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yose HaGalili condemns.

### Rashi: Before Court

Rashi resolves this tension precisely. The prohibition of *livtzoa*, in Rashi's reading, applies specifically *mi sheba ledin* — once the parties have come before the court seeking judgment. At that point, the judges are obligated to administer justice and may not redirect the proceedings toward compromise. Aharon's conduct was entirely different: he pursued peace *before* disputes ever came before him as a judge, *kodem sheyavo'u lefanav ledin*. When he heard of a conflict, he would run after the parties and establish peace between them before they reached the stage of formal litigation. This is the essential distinction — Aharon's peacemaking was pre-litigation, and it is precisely that which is praiseworthy. Once the parties stand before the court, a different standard applies.

### Stolen Goods & Judah

The *Gemara* then digresses briefly from the main discussion. A teaching of Rabbi Eliezer considers the case of one who stole grain, ground it, baked it, and then separated *challah* from the loaf. How can such a person recite a blessing? The answer is that he cannot — *ein zeh mevarech ela menaetz*, it is not a blessing but a blasphemy, a case of *mitzvah haba'ah be'aveirah*, the performance of a commandment through sin. The verse *uvotzea berech ni'etz Hashem* is again invoked, here reading *botzea* in its literal sense of one who breaks bread.

Rabbi Meir then offers another reading of the verse, applying *botzea* specifically to Yehuda's proposal regarding Yosef. When Yehuda said to his brothers *mah betza ki naharog et achinu*, "what profit is it that we kill our brother?" — he was not the hero some might make him. Yehuda had it in his power to call for Yosef's release and return to their father. Instead he settled for a half-measure, selling him to the Ishmaelites. Rabbi Meir insists that praising Yehuda for this falls into the same category of *botzea berech ni'etz Hashem* — one who blesses a compromise that fell far short of what was possible is blaspheming. The comparison is pointed: a position of moral authority carries with it the obligation to act on it fully, not to negotiate it away.

### R. Yehoshua: Mitzva

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha takes the opposite position. Not only is *peshara* permitted even after the parties have come before the court, but *mitzva livtzoa* — it is a positive obligation to seek compromise. His proof is the verse *emet umishpat shalom shiftu beshaareichem* — judge truth and a judgment of peace in your gates. The apparent tension between *mishpat* and *shalom* — between strict law and peace — is itself the key. If you apply strict law, you do not necessarily achieve peace; if you pursue peace, you may compromise justice. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha resolves this by saying that *bitzua* is precisely the form of judgment that contains peace within it. It is not a departure from justice but a form of it — a *din berachamim*, judgment infused with compassion — which is why it properly requires three judges just as *din* does.

### David's Tzedakah Model

The *Gemara* cites the verse describing David: *vayehi David oseh mishpat utzedakah lechol ammo* — David performed *mishpat* and *tzedakah* for all his people. The parallel tension arises: where there is *mishpat*, how can there be *tzedakah* in the charitable sense, and vice versa?

One reading would see this as analogous to the *mishpat shalom* formulation — a judgment that incorporates *tzedakah*, understood as *chesed* and contextual sensitivity. The *Gemara*, however, reads *tzedakah* more literally, in the rabbinic sense of actual charity, and aligns the verse with the position of *assur livtzoa*: David would render strict justice, and then, if the poor party suffered financially as a result, David would personally compensate him from his own resources. The judgment was pure *mishpat*, and the subsequent payment from his own pocket was the *tzedakah*. These are two distinct acts, not one integrated ruling.

The *Gemara* makes this explicit: *dan et hadin, zikah et hazakai, vechiyav et hachayav* — he rendered the judgment, acquitting the innocent and obligating the liable — *vera'ah shenitchayev ani mamon, veshilam lo mitoch beito* — and when he saw that a poor person was financially ruined by the outcome, he paid him from his own household. *Zehu mishpat utzedakah* — that is both *mishpat* and *tzedakah*: *mishpat* for the winning party who received justice, and *tzedakah* for the poor party who received personal assistance from the judge.

A difficulty is then raised: if the *tzedakah* component only applied when the losing party happened to be poor, how does the verse say David acted this way *lechol ammo* — for all his people? In response, Rebbi offers a reading that does not require the losing party to be impoverished. Even without any financial payment from the judge's pocket, the outcome itself constitutes both *mishpat* and *tzedakah*: *mishpat* for the winning party, who had his property restored, and *tzedakah* for the losing party — *she'hotzi gezeila mitachat yado* — because the judgment removed from his hands money or property that was not rightfully his. Being compelled to return what one wrongfully holds is itself a form of *tzedakah*, a benefit to the one who is corrected, since he is no longer in possession of ill-gotten goods. In this way, every litigant receives *mishpat* and *tzedakah*, which accounts for *lechol ammo*.

### R. Shimon: Before Clarity

Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya introduces a third position. Two parties come before you. Either before you have heard their arguments at all, or after hearing them but before it is clear to you which way the judgment is likely to go — in both of these situations, *ata rashai lomar lahem tze'u u'bitzu*, you may tell them to go and work out a compromise. However, once you have heard the claims and you *do* have a sense of which way the judgment will lean, *i ata rashai lomar lahem tze'u u'bitzu* — you may no longer direct them toward compromise.

The proof text is *poter mayim reshit madon* — one who releases water is the beginning of strife. Rashi reads this as: if you wish to exempt yourself from the waters of judgment, from the controversy, you may do so *reshit madon* — at the beginning, before the dispute has been laid open before you. *V'lifnei hitgala hariv* — before the conflict is revealed, you may *nitosh*, abandon it. Once *nitgala hariv* — once it becomes clear — *i ata yachol lintosho*, you can no longer walk away from it.

The language here is notable. This formulation does not frame *bitzua* as an alternative form of judgment the court is exercising; rather, it speaks of exempting oneself, stepping back. This is more consistent with the idea that at a certain stage, a judge simply cannot abandon his responsibility. Once the trajectory of the case is visible, justice demands that he see it through. The result is three positions: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yose HaGalili forbids *bitzua* once the parties come before the court at all; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha permits and even requires it to be offered even at late stages, understanding it as a legitimate form of *din*; and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya permits it until the judgment's direction becomes clear, after which it is foreclosed.

---

## Recusal & Responsibility

### Reish Lakish: Before Cla…

Reish Lakish — some have the reading *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Lakish* — applies a closely related analysis to the question of judicial recusal. Two parties come before the court: one is *rach*, gentle and accommodating, and the other is *kasheh*, firm and potentially aggressive. The judge is concerned that whichever way he rules, the firm party will make his life difficult if he loses. The question is whether the judge may recuse himself from the case entirely.

Reish Lakish rules that before the judge has engaged the parties, or after hearing them but before the direction of the judgment is apparent, *ata rashai lomar lahem eini nizkak lachem* — the judge may say, "I am not taking on this case." The concern motivating this is explicit: *shema yitchayev chazak venimtza chazak rodfo* — lest the firm party be found liable and proceed to pursue the judge who ruled against him. This is a real human concern, and Reish Lakish acknowledges it by permitting early recusal.

### 'Lo Taguru' Obligation

However, once the judge has heard the parties and knows where the judgment is heading, that option is foreclosed. *Mishetishma divreihen ve'ata yode'a leheichan hadin noteh, i ata rashai lomar lahem eini nizkak lachem.* The proof is the verse *lo taguru mipnei ish ki hamishpat lElokim hu* — do not be afraid of any man, for the judgment belongs to God. The *chiddush* of Reish Lakish is therefore not that judges must be fearless at every stage, but that early recusal — before the case is engaged — is permissible. Once engagement occurs and the trajectory is clear, fear is no longer a valid reason to step away.

---

## Witnesses & Judges

### Student Must Speak

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha extends the responsibility of speaking truth in the courtroom beyond the judges themselves. If a student is sitting before his *Rebbe* and observes the proceeding — and he sees a point of merit in favor of the poor party, or something that would weigh against the rich party — *minayin shelo yishtok*, how do we know he may not remain silent? The source is *lo taguru mipnei ish* — do not be afraid of any person. Here *taguru* is read as a form of *agur*, to gather or hold in. Do not gather in your words; do not withhold them out of deference to the *Rebbe* presiding over the court or out of fear of the powerful litigant.

### Don't Withhold Words

Rabbi Chanina formulates the same principle more directly: *lo tachnis devarecha mipnei ish* — do not cause your words to be held back because of any person. The obligation to speak the truth in a judicial context falls on everyone present who has relevant knowledge or insight, not only on the judges themselves.

### Witness Awareness

The *Gemara* then turns to witnesses. *V'hayu ha'edim yodim et mi hem mei'idim v'lifnei mi hem mei'idim umi atid lipara mehem* — the witnesses must know before whom they testify, against whom they testify, and who will exact payment from them. The verse cited is *v'amdu shnei ha'anashim asher lahem hariv lifnei Hashem* — the two people who have the dispute shall stand before God. This is read not as referring to the litigants but to the witnesses, who are presenting themselves before God Himself.

Rashi explains the phrase *et mi hem mei'idim* — against whom they testify — in a striking way. False witnesses are, in a sense, testifying against God. By testifying falsely, they cause an unjust outcome that God would then have to correct through other means, compelling the wronged party to receive back what is his through divine intervention rather than through the court. The witnesses are therefore, as it were, making God Himself work harder, and their false testimony acts as a kind of affront to the divine justice they have circumvented.

### Judge's Fear & Assurance

The same framework applies to the judges. *V'hayu hadayanim yodim et mi hem danim v'lifnei mi hem danim umi atid lipara mehem* — judges must know before whom they judge and who will exact from them. The verse *Elokim nitzav ba'adat El* — God stands in the congregation of the judges — establishes that divine presence is real and active in the court. The same teaching is found in Yehoshaphat's address to the judges: *re'u mah atem osim ki lo l'adam tishpetu ki laShem* — see what you are doing, for you judge not for man but for God.

Lest this awareness become paralyzing — lest a judge say *mah li betzaar zeh*, why should I take on this burden — the *Gemara* offers the counterbalancing assurance: *imachem bidvar mishpat*, God is with you in the matter of judgment. *Ein lo l'dayan ela mah she'einav ro'ot* — a judge is accountable only for what his eyes can see. He is not expected to transcend his human limitations; he is expected to bring integrity, rigor, and honesty to the process. If he does, God accompanies him, and his ruling carries legitimacy even if it is not perfect. This principle finds an echo in the teaching of Rav Moshe Feinstein regarding *psak halacha*: when a decisor goes through the process with genuine integrity, whatever he concludes is a legitimate ruling.

---

## Gmar Din & Ruling

### Gmar Din Definition

Returning to the threshold at which all opinions agree compromise is foreclosed, the *Gemara* defines *gmar din*. Rav Yehuda citing Rav states: *ish ploni atah chayav, ish ploni atah zakai* — when the court declares, "So-and-so, you are liable; so-and-so, you are exempt" — that is *gmar din*. At that moment, no further *peshara* is possible under any opinion.

### Halacha: Equal Option

The *halacha* is ruled like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who said *mitzva livtzoa*. However, the *Gemara* clarifies the precise scope of this ruling. The *mitzva* does not mean the judge is obligated to actively encourage compromise or steer the parties toward it. Rather, *mitzva lemeimar lehu ee dina bayisu ee pshara bayisu* — it is a *mitzva* to present both options equally: do you want *din* or do you want *pshara*?

### Rav Huna's Practice

This was the actual practice of Rav Huna, a student of Rav. When litigants came before him, he would ask: *ee dina be'itu ee pshara be'itu* — do you want judgment or do you want compromise? Both were offered as equal possibilities, neither promoted over the other. This reflects the ruling *le'ma'aseh*: the judge fulfills his obligation by making the option known, not by advocating for it.

### Mitzvah vs. Permitted

The *Gemara* then asks whether this ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha is not simply identical to the *tanna kamma* who opened the *baraita*. After all, the *tanna kamma* said that *bitzua* requires three judges as *din* does, and that it is forbidden after *gmar din* — implying it is permitted beforehand. Is that not what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha is saying?

The *Gemara* answers: *ika beina'ihu mitzva* — the difference is precisely the characterization of *bitzua* as a *mitzva*. The *tanna kamma* treats *bitzua* as *reshut* — permissible if the parties request it, but not something the judge needs to raise. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha holds that the judge has an affirmative obligation to present the option proactively, even if he must not push it as the preferred path.

A further comparison is drawn to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya. Is the *tanna kamma* not equivalent to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, who allowed *bitzua* until the direction of the judgment was clear? The *Gemara* responds: *ika beina'ihu mishetishma divreihem ve'ata yode'a heichan hadin noteh*. According to the *tanna kamma*, the option of *bitzua* remains available — if requested — right up until *gmar din*, even after the direction is apparent. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya closes that window earlier, once the judge perceives which way the case will go. So the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya differ on timing, and the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha differ on whether proactive suggestion is obligatory or merely permitted.

---

## Golden Calf Compromise

### Tanchum: Egel Context

The *Gemara* now introduces a dissenting interpretive voice. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai argues that the verse *botzea berech ni'etz Hashem* — which has been used throughout this discussion to anchor the debate about judicial compromise — was never about *peshara* in court at all. *Lo ne'emar mikra zeh ella keneged ma'aseh ha'egel* — this verse was said only in reference to the sin of the golden calf. Rashi explains: Aharon made a *peshara* with his own conscience, permitting himself to build the *eigel*, and it is that compromise — internal, private, a *horeh heter le'atzmo* — to which the verse refers.

### Aharon's Reasoning

The *Gemara* cites a *midrashic* reading of the verse *vayar Aharon vayiven mizbeiach lefanav* — and Aharon saw and built an altar before it. What did Aharon see? Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet citing Rabbi Elazar: *ra'ah Chur shezevuach lefanav* — he saw that Chur had been slaughtered before him. Moshe had left Aharon and Chur in charge. When Moshe returns, Chur is gone. The *midrash* understands that the people killed Chur when he refused to cooperate. Seeing this, Aharon reasoned: *ilu shama'nu lehu, hashta avidu li kedavdu veChur* — if I refuse them as Chur did, they will do to me what they did to Chur.

But Aharon's reasoning was more than simple self-preservation. He calculated that if *he* — a *kohen* and a *navi* — were slaughtered at what would become the site of the *Mikdash*, the sin would be so catastrophic, so beyond repair, that *lo havi lehu takana le'olam* — they would have no possibility of atonement ever. Whereas if he built the *eigel*, grievous as that was, *efshar havi lehu takana be'teshuva* — there remained the possibility of *teshuva*. It was, in Aharon's calculus, a compromise between two terrible outcomes, choosing the one that left the door to repentance open.

The *Gemara* does not absolve Aharon of responsibility for this reasoning. The language of *peshara beino levein atzmo* — compromise with his own conscience — signals that this was a rationalization, or at best a morally fraught calculation, not a clear justification. The parallel to Yehuda's half-measure regarding Yosef, raised earlier in the *sugya*, hovers in the background: is a partial intervention that averts the worst still praiseworthy, or is it a failure to do what was fully required?

### Water = Torah

The *Gemara* then addresses the other *tanna'im* who interpreted the verse *poter mayim reshit madon* not in terms of judicial withdrawal but in a different context entirely. They read it according to the principle of Rav Hamnuna: *ein techilat dino shel adam nidon ella al divrei Torah* — a person is first judged in the heavenly court on the basis of his relationship to Torah. *Mayim* — water — represents Torah, as in the verse *hoi kol tzame lechu la-mayim*. Therefore, *poter mayim reshit madon* means that exempting oneself from Torah study is the *reshit*, the beginning, of one's judgment. The *tanna'im* who apply the verse this way are not ignoring the *peshara* discussion; they simply read this particular *pasuk* as pointing elsewhere.

---

## Folk Sayings & Verses

### Aphorisms Cited

The *Gemara* now presents a series of folk sayings, each matched by Shmuel to a biblical verse, as a way of showing that common wisdom is already embedded in *pesukim*. These exchanges are framed as Shmuel speaking to Rav Yehuda.

The first aphorism: *tuvya de-shama ve-adish, chafua bei shtei me'ah* — it is good for one who hears insults hurled at him and remains silent; a hundred misfortunes will not befall him. Shmuel responds that the verse says *poter mayim reshit madon* — releasing the waters of strife is the beginning of a hundred judgments. By reading *madon* in its *gematria* value — Rashi notes that *madon* equals one hundred — one who releases strife frees himself from a hundred litigations. The aphorism and the verse, differently approached, point to the same wisdom: letting conflict go spares enormous consequence.

The second: a person who commits a sin two or three times without evident consequence begins to think he will escape punishment. Shmuel cites the verse *al shlosha pishei Edom ve'al arba lo ashivenu* — for three transgressions of Edom and for four I will not turn back the judgment. Beyond a certain point, accumulating sins will bring their reckoning; repeated transgression does not signal impunity but accumulating debt.

The third: seven pits are laid for a man of peace and he avoids them all, while for a wicked person a single pit suffices to bring him down. Shmuel cites *ki sheva yipol tzadik ve-kam* — the righteous man falls seven times and rises, while the wicked stumble in evil. The verse as it actually reads, noted in the margin, has *ve'rasha'im yikashlu be-ra'ah*, not quite the formulation given in the *Gemara* — a small textual discrepancy, but the point holds.

The fourth: one who leaves court having had his cloak taken from him should sing and go on his way. Shmuel cites *ve'gam kol ha'am hazeh al mekomo yavo ve-shalom* — all this people will go to their place in peace. The idea echoes the earlier discussion of *tzedakah* to the losing party: being compelled to return what does not belong to you is not merely a loss, but a restoration of right order. Justice brings peace even to those who are ruled against.

The fifth: a woman carrying a basket on her head who dozes off will drop it — inattention leads to ruin. Shmuel cites *be-atzaltaim yemach ha-mikre* — through laziness the rafters will collapse. Negligence, whether physical or spiritual, produces structural failure.

The sixth: the person I relied upon raised his fist against me — the pain of betrayal by someone trusted. Shmuel cites *ve-gam ki ish shlomi asher batachti bo* — even the man of my peace in whom I trusted — the verse goes on to describe how that person turned against the speaker. The aphorism has its parallel in the *pasuk*: betrayal by the trusted is an ancient and recurring human experience.

The seventh and final aphorism is the most poignant: when our love was strong, we could sleep on the edge of a sword — the narrowest space felt spacious. Now that our love has weakened, a bed of sixty *amos* is not wide enough for us. The quality of a relationship transforms the conditions within it.

### Shechina Withdrawal

Rav Huna responds to this last aphorism with a *pasuk*. Originally, God said *ve-no'adti lecha sham ve-dibarti itcha me'al ha-kaporet* — I will meet you there and speak with you from above the *kaporet*. A *baraita* establishes that the *aron* was nine *tefachim* tall and the *kaporet* one *tefach*, making ten *tefachim* total. God's presence was contracted, as it were, to within ten *tefachim* of the ground — intimate, immediate, pressing close to the human space.

Later, however, the verse describes the *Beit Hamikdash* that Shlomo built: sixty *amos* long, twenty *amos* wide, thirty *amos* high. And after Israel sinned, God declared *ko amar Hashem ha-shamayim kis'i ve-ha'aretz hadom raglai, ei zeh ha-bayit asher tivnu li* — the heavens are My throne and the earth My footstool; what house will you build for Me? God, who had once compressed His presence into ten *tefachim* alongside His people, could no longer dwell even in a thirty-*amah* sanctuary when the relationship had deteriorated. The analogy to the aphorism is precise: when love is strong, the narrowest space suffices; when it is not, no space is adequate.

### 'Lo Taguru' Meaning

The *Gemara* concludes by returning to the phrase *lo taguru mipnei ish*, which has been used several times to derive the obligation not to withhold one's words in a judicial context. The question is the *lashon*: what does *taguru* mean such that it can be read as "do not hold back your words"?

Three sources are offered. Rav Nachman derives it from the verse *ve-yayin lo tishteh ve-lo te'egor* — wine you shall not drink and you shall not gather in — where *te'egor* means to gather or store up. Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives it from the verse about the ant, *tachin ba-kayitz lachmah, agra ba-katzir ma'achalah* — she prepares her food in summer, she gathers her stores in the harvest. And Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika derives it from *oger ba-kayitz ben maskil* — a wise son gathers in summer. In all three cases, *oger* or *agar* means to gather, to store up, to hold in. The prohibition of *lo taguru* is therefore a prohibition against gathering in one's words, against withholding them. The one who possesses truth in a court of justice — witness or bystander alike — must not hoard it.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 7

## Pshara & Kinyan

### Pshara: No Kinyan Needed

The daf opens with a discussion that was already underway, examining the relationship between *pshara* (compromise) and *din* (strict judgment), specifically whether *pshara* constitutes a form of binding arbitration — a type of *din* — or merely a contractual agreement between the parties. This question is intimately connected to the debate about whether *pshara* requires one judge or three: if it is a form of *din*, it may well require three, as *din* does; if it is merely a contractual mechanism, one might suffice.

Now Rav Ashi draws an inference. *Amar Rav Ashi shma minah pshara eina tzricha kinyan* — from this very debate between those who require three judges and those who require only one, we may infer that *pshara* does not require a *kinyan* (a formal act of acquisition or obligation, such as a *kinyan sudar*, the handkerchief exchange). The reasoning runs as follows: *di salka daitach tzricha kinyan* — were you to maintain that *pshara* requires a *kinyan*, then the position that three judges are necessary would be incomprehensible. If the parties are binding themselves through a formal *kinyan* to accept whatever decision emerges, then two witnesses would suffice — there is no need for a judicial panel of three. The very existence of an opinion requiring three judges indicates that we are not operating within a framework of contractual self-obligation, but within something more akin to a judicial proceeding.

### Three Judges & Kinyan

The Gemara's inference seems compelling — yet it then reaches a surprising conclusion. Despite the apparent logic that a *kinyan* would render three judges unnecessary, the Gemara rules: *v'hilchata pshara tzricha kinyan* — the *halacha* is that *pshara* does in fact require a *kinyan*. This is unexpected. If a *kinyan* is performed, why would anyone require three judges? The parties have already obligated themselves to the outcome through the formal act of *kinyan*; whatever one judge decides ought to be binding.

### Tosafot: Legitimacy

Tosafot addresses this directly. Their language is precise: *v'ha d'lo sagi bitrei mishum d'havei k'kinyan b'ta'us d'lo b'ki b'pshara shapir* — the reason three are nonetheless required is that a *kinyan* executed toward an irresponsible or illegitimate *pshara* would be akin to a *kinyan ba-ta'ut*, a *kinyan* made in error, and therefore not truly binding. The parties are not agreeing in the abstract to accept whatever random words emerge from a single individual; they are committing themselves to a genuine, well-reasoned compromise. For such a commitment to be meaningful, the *pshara* itself must be arrived at responsibly and with appropriate deliberation. Three judges provide precisely that legitimacy. Fewer than three raises the concern that the process was insufficiently rigorous to justify binding both parties to a decision that departs from strict law.

### Baraita: Three & Gmar Din

The Gemara then cites a *baraita*: *k'shem she'adin b'shlosha kach bitzua b'shlosha* — just as *din* requires three judges, so too does *bitzua* (the act of compromise/binding arbitration). This establishes that *pshara* or *bitzua* functions as a parallel process to *din* in its procedural requirements. However, once *gmar din* — the finalized judgment — has been rendered, *bitzua* is no longer permitted: *nigmar hadin i ata rashai livtzo'a*. What constitutes *gmar din* will be defined later; Rashi's formulation is that it occurs when the court explicitly declares *ish ploni atah zakai, ish ploni atah chayav* — "so-and-so, you are exempt; so-and-so, you are liable." Once those words are spoken, compromise is foreclosed.

---

## R. Eliezer: Assur

### Assur Livtzoa

With the procedural framework in place, the Gemara now turns to a fundamental dispute among the Tannaim about whether *pshara* is desirable at all. The tension at its core is between *emet* (truth) and *shalom* (peace). Strict *din* may yield the most legally correct outcome, but it does not always leave all parties at peace. *Pshara* aims at *shalom* but may require some concession from strict *emet*. Which is to be preferred — and at what stage of the proceedings?

Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yossi HaGlili takes the most stringent position: *assur livtzoa* — it is forbidden to engage in *bitzua*. Not only is it forbidden, but *vechol habotzeia harei zeh chotei* — one who does so is considered a sinner, perverting truth. Moreover, *vechol hamevarech et habotzeia harei zeh mena'etz* — one who praises the judge who engaged in *bitzua* is blaspheming God. The prooftext is *botzeia bereich ni'etz Hashem* — "the *botze'a* who blesses desecrates God." On its plain meaning, *botze'a* refers to one who takes ill-gotten gains; here it is read as the one who compromises between litigants, and one who blesses such a person thereby desecrates the divine name. The underlying principle is *ela yikov hadin et hahar* — let judgment pierce the mountain. No matter how formidable the obstacle, justice must prevail. *Ki hamishpat lelokim hu* — the judgment belongs to God, and to compromise it is to pervert God's own mandate.

### Moshe vs. Aharon

To illustrate the contrast, the Gemara juxtaposes Moshe and Aharon. Moshe embodies the principle of *yikov hadin et hahar* — uncompromising, piercing justice, brooking no deviation from the law that descended from Sinai. Aharon, by contrast, is characterized as *ohev shalom verodef shalom umesim shalom bein adam lechavero* — a lover of peace, a pursuer of peace, one who made peace between people. The verse in his praise reads: *torat emet hayta bepihu ve'avla lo nimtza bisfatav* — "a teaching of truth was in his mouth and perversion was not found on his lips." He walked in peace and on the straight path, *verabim heshiv me'avon* — and he turned many away from sin.

This sounds thoroughly praiseworthy of Aharon — yet Rabbi Eliezer has just declared *bitzua* to be forbidden. Is there a contradiction?

### Rashi: Before Din

Rashi resolves this cleanly. The prohibition of *assur livtzoa* applies specifically once the litigants have brought their case before the judges: *mi shebau ledin assur ladayanim livtzoa* — once they have come to the court of justice, the judges are obligated to administer justice. What Aharon did was entirely different: he would pursue peace *before* people came to him for *din*. Rashi makes this explicit: *vekeivan shehaya shomeia machloket beineihem kodem sheyavou lefanav ledin haya rodef achareihem umetil shalom beineihem* — when he would hear of a dispute between people, before they came before him for judgment, he would pursue them and make peace between them. There is no tension, then, between Aharon's conduct and Rabbi Eliezer's ruling: pre-litigation peacemaking is praiseworthy; perverting the judicial process once it has begun is forbidden.

### Stolen Goods & Bracha

The Gemara now digresses, picking up on the *botze'a berech* theme in a different context. Rabbi Eliezer teaches: if someone steals a measure of grain, grinds it, bakes it, and then separates *challah* from it — how can such a person recite a blessing? *Ein zeh mevarech ela mena'etz* — this is not a blessing but a desecration. Invoking God's name over the fruit of theft is a case of *mitzvah haba'ah be'aveirah* — a mitzvah performed through the means of a sin. Here too, *botzeia berech ni'etz Hashem* applies: the one who blesses over ill-gotten gains desecrates God.

### R. Meir & Yehuda

Rabbi Meir extends the *botze'a* teaching in yet another direction: *lo ne'emar botzeia ela keneged Yehuda* — the *botze'a* verse was said specifically in reference to Yehuda's role in the sale of Yosef. The verse reads: *vayomer Yehuda el echav mah betza ki naharog et achinu* — "And Yehuda said to his brothers, what profit is there that we should kill our brother?" He proposed selling Yosef to the Ishmaelites rather than killing him, and the brothers listened. Some have praised Yehuda for thereby saving Yosef's life. Rabbi Meir rejects this framing entirely: Yehuda was in a position of influence and could have convinced the brothers to return Yosef outright. By settling for the half-measure of selling him — preventing murder while still enabling enslavement and exile — Yehuda acted as a *botze'a*. *Vechol hamevarech et Yehuda harei zeh mena'etz* — praising Yehuda for this is blaspheming God. And the verse confirms it: *uvotzeia berech ni'etz Hashem*.

---

## R. Yehoshua: Mitzvah

### Emes Umishpat Shalom

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha takes the diametrically opposite position: *mitzvah livtzoa* — it is a *mitzvah* to engage in *bitzua*, and this applies even after the litigants have come before the *beit din*. His prooftext is: *emes umishpat shalom shiftu besh'areichem* — "truth and a judgment of peace you shall judge in your gates." Even at the gates of the court, the verse instructs judges to seek out a judgment that incorporates peace.

### Judgment with Peace

But here lies a paradox, which the Gemara articulates: *vehalo bimkom sheyesh mishpat ein shalom, bimkom sheyesh shalom ein mishpat* — where there is strict judgment, there is no peace, and where there is peace there is no strict judgment. These are in tension by their very nature. So how can the verse call for a "judgment of peace"? The resolution: *ela eizehu mishpat sheyesh bo shalom hevei omer ze bitzua* — what is the kind of judgment that contains within it peace? That is *bitzua*. *Bitzua* is not a departure from judgment but a form of it — one that applies law with sufficient flexibility to attend to context, to the needs of both parties, and to the production of a genuinely satisfactory and peaceful outcome. This reading also bears on the earlier debate about whether *bitzua* requires one or three judges: if *bitzua* is indeed a form of *mishpat*, it has an inherent dignity and structure that demands the full judicial apparatus.

### David's Mishpat & Tzedaka

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha adduces a further proof from David: *vayehi David oseh mishpat utzedakah lechol amo* — "And David did *mishpat* and *tzedakah* for all his people." But the same paradox applies: *vehalo kol makom sheyesh mishpat ein tzedakah, vechol makom sheyesh tzedakah ein mishpat* — where there is *mishpat* there is no *tzedakah* (charity or generosity), and where there is *tzedakah* there is no *mishpat*. If a wealthy creditor is legally entitled to the full sum and the court rules in his favor, the poor debtor is left penniless — that is *mishpat*, but it is not *tzedakah*. If the judge shows leniency to the poor debtor, that may be *tzedakah*, but it is not strict *mishpat*.

The Gemara, however, shifts interpretive tracks here, reading *tzedakah* not as a metaphorical dimension of *mishpat* but in its more literal, rabbinic sense — charity in the form of personal financial giving. On this reading, David would administer strict justice — declaring the innocent exempt and the liable party guilty — and then, if a poor person had suffered a financial loss as a result of the judgment going against him, David would personally pay him out of his own pocket. *Ze mishpat utzedakah*: *mishpat* for the one who prevailed in law, and *tzedakah* for the one who lost but was made whole through David's personal largesse. This reading places the *baraita* in alignment with the position of *assur livtzoa* — David did not compromise the judgment itself, but supplemented it from his personal resources to achieve a just outcome for all.

### Judgment as Tzedakah

Yet this reading raises an objection: the verse says David did *mishpat utzedakah lechol amo* — for *all* his people. If *tzedakah* here means personal charitable payment to the losing poor party, this would apply only to a subset of cases — those where the losing party happened to be poor. *Rebbi* resolves this by offering an alternative reading that does not require David to dip into his own pocket at all: *af al pi shelo shilem mitoch beito zehu mishpat utzedakah*. How so? *Mishpat laze shehechziru lo mamono* — it is *mishpat* for the party who won and had his money restored, *utzedakah laze shehotzi gzeila mitachat yado* — and it is *tzedakah* for the party who lost, because the judgment freed him from holding on to money that was not rightfully his. By compelling him to return the ill-gotten funds, the court performed a kindness for him — it restored his integrity and released him from the weight of wrongful possession. On this reading, every judgment, regardless of the financial circumstances of the parties, constitutes both *mishpat* and *tzedakah* — for every winner and every loser alike. This is how *lechol amo* is satisfied.

---

## R. Shimon: Conditional

### Before Clarity

Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya offers a position that mediates between the two poles. When two litigants come before a judge — before he has heard their claims and counter-claims, or even after he has heard them but has not yet formed a sense of which way the judgment will lean (*v'ee ata yodea leheichan hadin noteh*) — *ata rashai lomar lahem tze'u uvitz'u*: the judge may tell them to go and work out a compromise. The language here is notable: the judge is not conducting the *bitzua* himself as a form of *din berachamim* but suggesting that the parties go and reach their own compromise. This positions *bitzua* more as a contractual resolution between the parties than as a judicial act.

### After Clarity: Forbidden

Once, however, the judge has heard the claims and formed a clear impression of which way the judgment is leaning — *leheichan hadin noteh* — he may no longer suggest compromise. The prooftext is *poter mayim reishit madon* — "releasing water is the beginning of contention." Rashi reads this as: if you wish to exempt yourself, to withdraw from the judgment, you may do so *reishit madon* — at the beginning, before the dispute has been fully exposed and revealed. *Kodem shenitgala hariv ata yachol lintoshov* — before it has become revealed you may withdraw, but *mishenitgala hariv ee ata yachol lintoshov* — once it has become revealed, you may not.

There is a meaningful distinction between this position and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's. For Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, suggesting that parties seek their own compromise is a form of the judge stepping away — exempting himself from administering *din*. Once the judge's judgment is engaged — once he knows where it is heading — he cannot step away without perverting justice. The image is not of *bitzua* as a superior form of *mishpat* but as an exit from the judicial obligation, one that is only permissible before that obligation is fully activated.

This yields three distinct positions: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yossi HaGlili forbids *bitzua* once the parties appear before the court. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha permits — indeed encourages — offering *bitzua* even well into the proceedings. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya permits suggestion of *bitzua* until the judge discerns which way the judgment leans, at which point it is forbidden.

---

## Recusal Before Clarity

### Recusal Early Stage

Reish Lakish (some versions say Rabbi Yehoshua ben Lakish) introduces a related scenario. Two litigants come to court — one soft-spoken, one aggressive and intimidating. The judge is concerned: if the aggressive party is found liable, he may come after the judge. Reish Lakish rules: *ad shelo tishma divreihen o mishetishma divreihen v'ee ata yodea leheichan hadin noteh ata rashai lomar lahem eini nizkak lachem* — before hearing their claims, or after hearing them but without yet knowing which way the judgment will lean, the judge may recuse himself. He may say: I am not available to deal with you.

This parallels Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's position on *bitzua*: before the judicial obligation is fully activated — before *leheichan hadin noteh* is known — the judge retains some latitude. The threat of intimidation from a firm and potentially dangerous litigant is acknowledged as a human reality. Indeed, the Torah's command of *lo taguru mipnei ish* — do not be afraid of any person — already implies that the temptation to fear exists. The *chidush* of Reish Lakish is that before the judgment's direction is clear, the judge may act on that fear by recusing rather than by staying and being corrupted.

### No Recusal Late Stage

Once the judge knows which way the judgment is leaning, however, recusal is forbidden. *Mishetishma divreihen v'ata yodea leheichan hadin noteh ee ata rashai lomar lahem eini nizkak lachem* — at that stage, the judge cannot withdraw. The prooftext is now invoked in full force: *lo taguru mipnei ish ki hamishpat lelokim hu* — do not fear any man, for the judgment belongs to God. When the judge is already in possession of where justice lies, his obligation to see it through is absolute. The verse does not merely permit courage — it mandates it.

---

## Obligations to Justice

### Student's Obligation

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha now adds a dimension that extends the obligation of speaking truth beyond the judges themselves. The verse *lo taguru mipnei ish* is applied to a student sitting before his teacher during court proceedings. If that student perceives a *z'chut* (a merit or legal argument) that favors the poor party, or a fault with the rich party's position, he cannot remain silent — *minayin shelo yishtok* — and the verse commands him to speak. *Lo taguru* is read here not in the sense of fearing but in the sense of withholding, gathering in: *lishana dekinnushei* — the language of gathering in and holding back. Do not gather your words inside yourself out of fear of your teacher or of the powerful party before the court.

### Speaker's Obligation

Rabbi Chanina broadens this further: *lo tachnis devarecha mipnei ish* — do not hold your words back because of any person. This applies even to one who is not a judge and not a student in any formal capacity. If you observe a judicial proceeding and perceive something relevant to justice, you bear an obligation to speak. The scope of the obligation, then, extends from the judges themselves outward to students, observers, and bystanders.

### Witness Awareness

The Gemara turns to witnesses. They too must internalize who they are testifying about, before whom they testify, and who will ultimately exact payment from them: *v'hayu edim yod'im et mi hem me'idim v'lifnei mi hem me'idim u'mi atid lipara mehem*. Testifying before a human court is testifying before God. And who are they testifying about — to some degree, as we shall see, also God.

### Witnesses Before God

The verse is cited: *v'amdu shnei ha'anashim asher lahem hariv lifnei Hashem* — "and the two men who have the dispute shall stand before God." This is read as referring not merely to the litigants but to the witnesses, who present themselves before God. Rashi's comment on *mi hem me'idim* is striking: false testimony is *ke'ilu hen me'idim b'Hakadosh Baruch Hu she'matrichin oto lehachazir mamon l'ba'alo* — as if they are testifying against God Himself, forcing God to work harder to restore money to its rightful owner through other means. By corrupting the judicial process, false witnesses shift the burden of justice back onto the divine. In that sense, they are testifying against — and burdening — God.

### Judge Awareness

The same framework applies to judges. *V'hayu hadayanim yod'im et mi hen danin v'lifnei mi hen danin u'mi atid lipara mehem* — judges must know who they are judging, before whom, and who will exact from them. The prooftext: *Elokim nitzav ba'adat El* — God stands in the assembly of the divine, meaning God is present among the judges. The precedent from Yehoshaphat reinforces this: *r'u mah atem osim ki lo l'adam tishpotu ki l'Hashem* — see what you are doing, for you judge not for man but for God.

### Judge's Responsibility

One might think that this overwhelming weight of divine accountability would paralyze a judge. Lest the judge recoil and say *mah li b'tzar zeh* — why do I need this anguish? — the verse adds: *imachem bidvar mishpat* — God is with you in the matter of justice. And the corollary: *ein lo l'dayan ela mah she'einav ro'ot* — a judge is only accountable for what his own eyes can assess. If the judge proceeds with integrity, rigor, and honesty, the obligation is fulfilled. The outcome is not entirely in his hands; the process is. This principle is the basis for Rav Moshe Feinstein's approach to *psak halacha*: if the process is undertaken with integrity, whatever conclusion emerges is legitimate. *Lo bashamayim hi* — the Torah is not in heaven; it is entrusted to human judgment exercised with good faith.

---

## Gmar Din & Halacha

### Definition of Gmar Din

Returning to the earlier point that once *gmar din* is reached *bitzua* is universally forbidden, the Gemara now defines *gmar din* precisely. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: *ish ploni atah chayav, ish ploni atah zakai* — when the court explicitly declares "so-and-so, you are liable" or "so-and-so, you are exempt," that is *gmar din*. At that moment, the judgment is final and compromise becomes irrelevant.

### Halacha: Mitzvah

The Gemara then rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who held *mitzvah livtzo'a*, that engaging in *bitzua* is a *mitzvah*. The evidence is Rav Huna, who was a student of Rav. When litigants came before Rav Huna, he would say to them: *i dina ba'itu o pshara ba'itu* — do you want me to adjudicate strictly according to law, or do you want *pshara*? He would offer both options. This practice reflected the ruling in favor of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.

### Mitzvah: Inform Options

But does "it is a *mitzvah*" mean the judge should actively promote *bitzua*? The Gemara clarifies: *mitzva lemeimar lehu i dina ba'itu pshar ba'itu* — the *mitzvah* consists in informing the litigants of both options equally, as Rav Huna did. It is not a mandate to encourage compromise specifically, but to present it as an equally legitimate path alongside strict *din*. The judge lays out the choice without tilting the litigants toward one option or the other.

### Mitzvah: Inform Options

If Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha merely requires that the judge present *bitzua* as an option, how is this different from the *Tanna Kamma* who implied that *bitzua* is available but never said the judge must affirmatively offer it? The Gemara's answer: *ika beinaihu mitzvah* — that is precisely the difference. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that *bitzua* is *reshut* — permissible if the parties seek it, but the judge need not proactively raise it. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha holds it is *mitzvah* — the judge must affirmatively inform the parties that this option exists. The word *mitzvah* here signals not enthusiasm for *bitzua* as the superior outcome, but an active obligation to make it known as a real possibility.

### Difference: Proactive

One further question: if the *Tanna Kamma* permits *bitzua* before *gmar din* and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya permits it before *leheichan hadin noteh*, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha holds it is a *mitzvah* — what exactly separates Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya from the *Tanna Kamma*? The Gemara answers: *ika beinaihu mishetishma divreihem v'atah yode'a leheichan hadin noteh ee atah rashai lomar lahem tze'u uvitz'u* — the point of difference is precisely this: once the judge knows which way the judgment is leaning, Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya forbids even mentioning *bitzua*, while the *Tanna Kamma* permits it up until actual *gmar din*. The positions, in sum, cascade as follows: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha — *mitzvah* to offer *bitzua* even after hearing the parties and knowing the direction; *Tanna Kamma* — permissible to allow *bitzua* if sought, up through just before *gmar din*; Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya — *bitzua* may be suggested only until *leheichan hadin noteh* is known; Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yossi HaGlili — forbidden from the moment the litigants appear before the court.

---

## R. Tanchum: Eigel

### Botze'a = Eigel

The Gemara now introduces a dissenting interpretation of the *botze'a berech* verse. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai argues: *lo ne'emar mikra zeh ela keneged ma'aseh ha'eigel* — this verse was not said about *pshara* at all, but specifically about the episode of the Golden Calf, where Aharon made a *pshara* — a compromise — with his own conscience. The *botze'a* who blessed and thereby desecrated God was Aharon himself.

### Aharon's Rationale

The Gemara presents Aharon's reasoning. When the people demanded a golden calf, Aharon looked and saw that Chur had been slaughtered before him — *ra'ah Chur shezavuach lefanav*. He understood: *ilo shamana lehu hashta avdu li kide'avdu beChur* — if I do not comply, they will do to me what they did to Chur. But his reasoning was more than simple self-preservation. He feared the compounding horror of *im yehareg bemikdash Hashem kohen venavi* — if a *kohen* and *navi* were to be murdered, the sin would be of an entirely different and irremediable order. *Mutav deya'avdu la'egel* — better that they engage in idol worship around a calf, *efshar havi lehu takanah betshuvah* — for that there can be a path of *teshuvah*. The sin of murdering a *kohen* and *navi* would be *velo havi lehu takanah le'olam* — without remedy. So Aharon compromised: he enabled the *eigel* to prevent something far worse. He told himself he was not acting out of fear for his own life but out of concern to channel the people's energy toward a remediable sin rather than a catastrophic one.

### Critique of Justification

The Gemara does not entirely accept this rationalization. Aharon built the calf and blessed the proceedings — *vayar Aharon vayiven mizbe'ach lefanav* — and the Gemara's implicit critique is that whatever his motivations, his self-justification may have been precisely that: a self-justification. He may genuinely have believed he was preventing a greater sin, but perhaps he was also, on some level, making peace with his own fear by dressing it in more noble rationale. The connection to Yehuda's half-measure in the sale of Yosef is not far in the background — the question of whether a compromise that averts the worst is genuinely praiseworthy, or whether it is a *botze'a* that blesses its own accommodation.

---

## Stages of Conflict

### Torah Study Focus

The *Tanna'im* who reject the reading of *poter mayim reishit madon* as a license for early-stage recusal or *bitzua* must find an alternative application for the verse. The Gemara tells us they read it in line with Rav Hamnuna.

### Rav Hamnuna's Reading

*Damar Rav Hamnuna: ein techilat dino shel adam nadon ela al divrei Torah* — the first thing on which a person is judged is *divrei Torah*, whether he was *mevatel* from Torah study. *Poter mayim reishit madon*: releasing from *mayim* — and Torah is compared to water, as the verse says *hoy kol tzamei lechu lamayim* — is the very beginning of all judgment against a person. The failure to engage with Torah is not a minor sin tucked away in the middle of the divine accounting; it is the first question asked.

### Cracked Hose Metaphor

Rav Huna offers an image for the dynamics of interpersonal conflict: *hai tigra damya letzinora debitka damya* — a quarrel is like a cracked pipe. *Keivan deravach ravach* — once the crack widens, it continues to widen. A conflict that is not addressed early will expand and deepen until it becomes irreparable. The implication is that early intervention — whether through *pshara*, through making peace before the *beit din* on the model of Aharon, or through any other means — is critical precisely because the window of opportunity closes rapidly.

### Bridge Board Metaphor

Abaye Kishisha offers a contrasting image: *dami leguda degamla* — a quarrel is also like a board of a bridge. *Keivan dekam kam* — once it is set in place, it holds firm. Once a dispute has become entrenched, it is as stable in its hostility as a bridge board is in its position. Reconciliation becomes progressively harder with time. Together, the two images reinforce the same practical message from different angles: the cracked pipe speaks to how quickly conflict escalates if unchecked, while the bridge board speaks to how stubbornly it persists once established.

### Folk Wisdom & Verses

The Gemara at this point collects a series of aphorisms — folk sayings from oral tradition — each accompanied by a corroborating verse that Shmuel identifies for Rav Yehuda. The rhetorical pattern is consistent throughout: someone was going around repeating a saying, and Shmuel would demonstrate to Rav Yehuda that the saying is already encoded in Scripture — *kra ktiv*, it is written in a verse.

### Ignoring Insults

The first: *tuvya deshama ve'adish, chafu beih me'ah bishta* — good is the one who hears insults and lets them pass without response; a hundred misfortunes will not befall him. Shmuel identifies the verse: *poter mayim reishit madon* — releasing, letting go of the waters of dispute is the beginning of *madon*, which Shmuel reads as *reish me'ah dinei* — the beginning of a hundred litigations. Rashi adds that *madon* in *gematria* equals one hundred. If you release the strife — if you let the insult wash off rather than grabbing hold of it — you spare yourself from a hundred judgments, a hundred entanglements.

Another aphorism notes that a person is not struck down for the first transgression, or the second, or the third — seeming impunity can breed complacency. Shmuel cites the verse: *al shlosha pishei Adam v'al arba'a lo ashivenu* — on three transgressions and on four I will not hold back; beyond a certain threshold, judgment arrives. The impunity is not permanent.

A third: for a person of peace, seven pits are set out and he navigates them all; for the wicked, a single pit will suffice to bring him down. Shmuel cites: *ki sheva yipol tzaddik v'kam* — a righteous person will fall seven times and rise; *u'resha'im yikashlu b'ra'ah* — and the wicked will stumble in evil.

A fourth: someone going from court having had his cloak taken from him in judgment should sing a song on his way — because he is no longer holding ill-gotten goods. This returns to the theme from the discussion of David's *mishpat utzedakah*: even the losing party has had a kindness done for him by being freed from wrongful possession. Shmuel cites: *v'gam kol ha'am hazeh al mekomo yavo v'shalom* — all this people shall go to their place in peace. Good judgment, even when its verdict stings, produces peace.

A fifth: if a woman carrying a basket on her head nods off, the basket falls — inattention and laziness lead to loss and collapse. Shmuel cites: *ba'atzaltayim yemach hamikreh* — through laziness the roof-beam warps and sinks.

A sixth: the man I relied upon raised his fist against me — the pain of betrayal by someone trusted. Shmuel cites: *v'gam ki ish shlomi asher batachti vo* — even the man of my peace, in whom I placed my trust, lifted against me.

### Love vs. Wealth

The final aphorism in the series is the most evocative: *ki rechimtin havai aziza a'putya d'safsira shchivan* — when our love was strong, we could sleep on the blade of a sword. In the early days of love, poverty is no obstacle; the bond itself sustains everything. *Hashta d'lo aziza rechimtin, purya bar shitin garmida lo sagi lan* — now that our love has weakened, a bed of sixty *amot* is not enough for us. Physical comfort and material wealth cannot substitute for genuine closeness.

### God's Presence & Sin

Rav Huna extends this teaching into theology. *Me'ikara ksiv v'noadeti lecha sham v'dibarti itcha me'al hakaporet* — originally God said He would speak from above the *kapporet* of the Ark, which stood ten *tefachim* from the ground. God's presence was concentrated and immediate, dwelling within the intimate space of ten *tefachim*, right at human height. The *baraita* corroborates: the *aron* was nine *tefachim* tall, the *kapporet* one *tefach*, totaling ten — and God was right there.

Then came the *Beit HaMikdash* of Shlomo: *vehabayit asher bana Shlomo la'Hashem shishim ama orko, ve'esrim rochvo, u'shloshim ama komato* — sixty *amot* long, twenty wide, thirty tall. Already God's presence required a far more expansive structure. And finally, when Israel sinned: *koh amar Hashem hashamayim kisi veha'aretz hadom raglai eizeh bayit asher tivnu li* — the heavens are My throne and the earth My footstool; what house could you build for Me? God withdrew entirely; not even a thirty-*amah* ceiling could contain the *Shechina* that had been estranged by sin. The progression is devastating: from ten *tefachim* of intimate closeness, to a thirty-*amah* building, to the infinite expanse of heaven and earth — and God declaring that no human structure could any longer serve as His home.

---

## Lo Taguru Etymology

### Taguru = Gather

The Gemara circles back to the word *taguru* in the verse *lo taguru mipnei ish*, the command not to withhold one's words or testimony out of fear. The question is the derivation: *mai mashma dehai lo taguru lishana dekinnushei hu* — what is the evidence that *taguru* means to gather in, to withhold? The prooftext: *veyayin lo tishteh velo te'egor* — wine you shall not drink and you shall not gather in. The root *aleph-gimel-reish* clearly means to accumulate or gather, and this confirms that *lo taguru mipnei ish* means do not gather in your words before any man — do not hold them back.

### Ant's Gathering

Rav Acha bar Yaakov cites the verse about the industrious ant: *tachin bakayitz lachma, agra bakatzir ma'achala* — it prepares its bread in the summer, it *gathers* (*agra*) its food in the harvest. The root again is *ayin-gimel-reish*, the same sense of gathering and accumulating, confirming that *oger* means to gather up and store.

### Wise Son Gathering

Rav Acha son of Rav Ika cites a third verse: *oger bakayitz ben maskil* — the wise son gathers in the summer. Here the word *oger* is explicit and unmistakable in its meaning. From all three prooftexts, the linguistic case is closed: *taguru* in *lo taguru mipnei ish* means to gather in, to hold back, to withhold. The command is therefore not merely about personal courage in the face of fear — it is a prohibition against the act of withholding one's words or testimony when justice demands that they be spoken.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 7b

## True Justice & Shechina

### Emes L'Amito

The daf opens with a statement of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: *kol dayan shedan din emes l'amito, mashre Shechina beYisrael* — any judge who judges with *emes l'amito*, truth to its truth, causes the Divine Presence to dwell among Israel. The double formulation — truth to its truth — is striking, and recalls the *Yerushalmi*'s treatment of how part of the idea of truth concerns process and not merely result. The proof-text is *Elokim nitzav ba'adat El, bekerev Elokim yishpot*: God stands in the assembly of God, for in the midst of God do you judge. When justice is properly executed, God is able to dwell on earth.

### Perverting Justice

The converse follows immediately: *vekol dayan she'eino dan din emes l'amito, gorem laShechina shetistalek miYisrael* — the judge who fails to judge truth to its truth causes the Divine Presence to be withdrawn from Israel. The supporting verse is *mishod aniyim me'ankat evyonim, ata akum yomar Hashem* — from the despoiling of the poor and the outcry of the needy, now I will rise up, says God. The *gemara* reads "rise up" not as rising to take vengeance, but as rising to depart — to withdraw the Divine Presence from a people whose courts have abandoned justice. The verse evokes the judge who, rather than ruling correctly, recuses himself to avoid antagonizing powerful litigants, thereby ignoring the outcry of those who have been wronged.

### Theft in Judgment

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani continues in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: *kol dayan shenotel mizeh venoten lizeh shelo kedin* — any judge who takes from one and gives to the other in a manner contrary to law — *Hakadosh Baruch Hu notel mimenu nafsho*, God will demand his soul. The proof-text is *al tigzol dal ki dal hu ve'al tedake ani basha'ar* — do not steal from the poor because he is poor, and do not crush the poor person in the gate. The word *sha'ar*, gate, evokes the place of justice — as in *Lot yoshev bisha'ar Sedom* — connecting the verse to the judicial context. *Ki Hashem yariv rivam, vekava es koveihem nafesh*: God will come to fight their fight and rob the soul of those who rob them. The weight of responsibility incumbent upon the judge could not be stated more sharply.

---

## Fear & Burden

### Sword & Gehinnom

A third teaching from the same chain: *le'olam yireh dayan atzmo k'ilu cherev munachas lo bein yarchosav, veGehinnom pesucha lo mitachtav* — a judge should always see himself as though a sword is placed between his thighs and *Gehinnom* lies open beneath him. The consequences of judging incorrectly are that severe. This is, to put it plainly, not an encouraging portrait of what it means to hold judicial office — but the *gemara*'s point is precisely that one must enter that role with full awareness of what is at stake.

### Shlomo's Bed

The proof-text is the verse describing Shlomo's bed: *hinei mitaso shelishlomo shishim gibborim seviv la, migibborei Yisrael, kulam achuzei cherev, melumdei milchama, ish charbo al yerecho, mipachad baleilos* — behold the bed of Shlomo, sixty mighty warriors surrounding it, from the warriors of Israel, all gripping a sword, expert in battle, each man's sword upon his thigh, because of the fear of the night. The *gemara* reads *mipachad baleilos* as *mipachada shel Gehinnom shedomeh lalaylah* — from the fear of *Gehinnom*, which resembles the night. Rashi connects the *gibborim* to *talmidei chachamim*, and *melumdei milchama* to *milchamta shel Torah*, grounding the verse in the world of Torah scholarship — but the specific application here is to the consequence awaiting the judge who rules incorrectly.

---

## Morning Light Test

### Clarity Standard

The *gemara* cites a verse: judge justice in the morning and save the one being robbed from the hand of the oppressor. The obvious question is posed: *vachi baboker danni vechol yoma ein danni* — do you only judge in the morning? Don't you judge the entire day? The answer offered: *ella im barur lach davar kaboker amreihu* — if the matter is as clear to you as the morning, when the break of dawn makes everything vivid and the distinction between light and darkness unmistakable, then say it. *Ve'im lav al tomreihu* — and if not, do not say it.

### Tension: Certainty

This principle is immediately recognized as generating a real tension. If a judge is not one hundred percent certain which party is right, does that mean he must refrain from ruling? That cannot be the practical requirement, since *halacha* has mechanisms for handling doubt — *hamotzi mechaveiro alav harayah*, the burden of proof rests on the claimant — yet applying that rule may itself produce an unjust result if the judge suspects the claimant is actually correct but cannot be certain. One might also ask: what about the earlier principle that *ein lo ladayan ela mah she'einav ra'ot* — a judge has nothing but what his eyes see? That principle is understood to mean that a judge must rule based on his best assessment of the facts as he can evaluate them. These two principles — that one must be certain as the morning before ruling, and that a judge has only what his own eyes show him — live in genuine tension with one another, and both must be held together.

### Wisdom as Sister

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives the same principle from a different verse: *emor lachochmah achoti at* — say to wisdom, you are my sister. The *drasha*: if the ruling is as clear to you as the prohibition against relations with one's sister — which admits of no ambiguity whatsoever — *amreihu*, then deliver the judgment. *Ve'im lav al tomreihu* — and if not, withhold it.

---

## Shared Responsibility

### Ten Judges

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states: *asarah sheyoshvim badin, kulo talui betzavar kulan* — when ten people sit in judgment, the yoke hangs on all of their necks.
