One might ask why the number ten, since ten is not a standard size for a *beit din*. The *gemara* anticipates the objection that of course all judges bear shared responsibility — *peshita*. The novel teaching is *lo tzericha ela letalmid hayosheiv lifnei rabbo*: even a student who is present before his teacher and could have spoken up but did not bears some portion of that responsibility. The practical implication is that being part of a large group does not displace one's individual responsibility for an incorrect ruling. If a group reaches a wrong decision, the presence of many participants is no excuse for any one of them.

### Splinter of Beam

At the same time, the *gemara* presents the complementary principle through a practice of Rav Huna. When a case would come before him, *michneif umaitei asarah rabanan* — he would gather ten rabbis from the *yeshiva*, so that *ki heichi de'limtiyei shiva mikashura* — a splinter of the beam should go to each of them. The burden of responsibility should be shared across many.

This practice finds its parallel in the conduct of *poskim* who, when ruling on a difficult case, will decline to issue a ruling unilaterally and instead seek the signatures of multiple colleagues — not because they lack the authority, but in order that the weight of the decision be collectively borne. There is also something worth examining sociologically: it might be assumed that group decision-making produces more conservative outcomes, since competing views balance one another out. But the reality is more complicated — individuals can exert influence on group outcomes while simultaneously diffusing personal accountability for the result. The deeper point, which this practice embodies, is the principle not to be a *dayan yachidi*, not to think that all truth resides with oneself alone. If you are about to make an important decision, bring in other perspectives.

### Rav Ashi & Shochtim

Rav Ashi's parallel practice is more illuminating still. When a question of *tereifa* would come before him, *makhnif u-maiti lehu le-khulhu tavkhei de-Mata Mechasya* — he would gather all the *shochtim* of the city of Mata Mechasya, so that everyone should receive a *shiva mi-kishora*, a splinter of the beam. This case is instructive on multiple levels. First, the *shochtim* are precisely the people most affected by the ruling — bringing them in means hearing their concerns directly, and sometimes a *psak* must be understood in relation to how it impacts those subject to it. Second, they bring genuine expertise that the *posek* himself may not possess in the same form. Rav Ashi was certainly capable of ruling on his own, but he wanted to hear all perspectives and ensure that every relevant form of knowledge was brought to bear. This is not ignorance requiring consultation; it is wisdom choosing to consult.

---

## King vs. Kohen

### Self-Sufficiency

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported a *drasha* of Nachman bar Kohen — who was himself, notably, *bar Kohen*. The verse: *melech be-mishpat ya'amid aretz ve-ish terumot ye-hersena* — a king through justice establishes the land, but a man of gifts will destroy it. Reading *terumot* as an allusion to the *kohen* who goes from threshing floor to threshing floor collecting his portion, the *drasha* proceeds: *im dayan domeh le-melech she-eino tzarich le-khlum* — if the judge is like a king who needs nothing from anyone, *ya'amid aretz*, he will establish the land. *Ve-im domeh le-kohen she-mechazer be-veit ha-granot* — but if he is like a *kohen* who must make his rounds to collect, *ye-hersena*, he will destroy it.

### Knowledge vs. Questions

What exactly does this analogy describe? *Tosafot* understands it in terms of material independence — a wealthy judge who requires no one's favor can rule without fear of compromising his judgment, while a judge who is financially dependent on the goodwill of others will inevitably find that independence compromised. But Rashi reads differently. Looking at Rashi's narrow column, the contrast is: *im domeh dayan le-melech she-baki be-tiv dinim* — if the judge is like a king in the sense of being thoroughly expert in the substance of the law — *male chochma*, full of wisdom — he will establish justice. But if he must constantly go around asking *shaylos*, like the *kohen* going from threshing floor to threshing floor seeking his portion, he will destroy it.

This Rashi must be held in tension with what was said earlier about gathering others to share the burden of judgment. The resolution lies in the difference between genuine expertise that chooses to consult, and ignorance that must always ask because it lacks the foundational knowledge to rule at all. A world-class surgeon who recommends a second opinion does so not because he lacks competence but because the case warrants it. One can be an expert who consults, or one can be someone who fundamentally does not know the material required to adjudicate properly.

### Unqualified Judge

The *gemara* illustrates the problem. *Debei nesi ukmei dayana delo hava gmir* — the house of the *nasi* appointed a judge who was not learned. This connects back to the concept of *yachid mumche*, which requires *gmir vesavir* — both thorough knowledge and analytical capability. Once a system of political appointment (*netilat reshut*) is in place, the *nasi* or *reish galusa* grants judicial authority — but the conditions are ripe for appointment without knowledge. They told Yehuda bar Nachmani, who served as the translator and announcer (*amora*) of Reish Lakish, to go serve as this judge's *amora*. He rose and leaned toward him — but the appointed judge had nothing to whisper, because he knew nothing. The *amora* received silence.

---

## Empty Vessel

### Innkeeper Judge

So Yehuda bar Nachmani opened and, improvising as though he were transmitting what had just been whispered, declared: *hoi omer la'etz hakitza, uri le'even domem* — woe to the one who says to the wood "wake up," stir yourself, O silent stone — *hu yoreh hinei hu tafus zahav vachesaf vechol ruach ein bekirbo* — should he be the one to judge? Behold, he holds gold and silver, and there is no spirit within him. Like the classic story of the rabbi and the wagon driver — the wagon driver memorizes the *drasha* and delivers it convincingly until someone asks a question — here the *amora* covered for the empty vessel, but delivered his critique through the covering itself.

The *gemara* concludes that God will ultimately exact payment not only from the unfit appointee but from those who do the appointing: *atid Hakadosh Baruch Hu l'hipara mimamidim* — from those who install such people. The verse: *v'Hashem b'heichal kodsho has mipanav kol ha'aretz* — God is in His holy sanctuary; silence before Him all the earth. When false speech and empty authority have filled the land, God will rise to silence it.

### Asherah Comparison

Reish Lakish states: *kol hamaamid dayan she'eino hagun ke'ilu noteia asherah b'Yisrael* — anyone who appoints an unfit judge is as though he has planted an *asherah*, an idolatrous tree, in Israel. The connection is not arbitrary. We have seen that when justice is executed properly, it draws the *Shechina* into the world — the judge is, as it were, doing God's work and establishing the world according to the divine sense of right and wrong. The judge who knows nothing is like an idol: authority without substance, worship of something empty. And the one who installs such a person is actively driving out the Divine Presence and importing idolatry in its place. The proof-text proceeds by *semichut*: the Torah places the appointment of judges immediately adjacent to the prohibition of planting an *asherah* — *shoftim v'shotrim titein l'cha*, and directly following, *lo tita l'cha asherah kol eitz*.

### Beside Altar

Rav Ashi extends the severity further: *uv'makom sheyesh talmidei chachamim* — where there were qualified scholars who could have served as judges and were bypassed, *ke'ilu netao eitzel mizbeach* — it is as though the *asherah* was planted right next to the altar. The verse: *eitzel mizbeach Hashem Elokecha* — do not plant this beside the altar of God. When the seat of justice sits alongside qualified *talmidei chachamim* who are ignored in favor of a political appointee, the affront to God's presence is direct and unmistakable.

### No Gods for Money

The *gemara* now turns to the verse *lo taasun iti elokei cheseph v'elokei zahav* — do not make gods of silver and gold. An obvious question: does this imply that gods of wood are permitted? Rav Ashi explains: *eloah haba bishvil cheseph* — do not appoint an authority over you who holds that position because of money paid. The judge is, in a sense, a *god* on earth — an authority representing the divine order of justice. That position must not be one that is bought. The *gemara* acknowledges the reality it was addressing.

---

## Humility & Honor

### Rav's Declaration

Having addressed the grave weight and spiritual stakes of rendering judgment, and the particular corruption of political appointment, the *gemara* now turns to how a righteous judge deals with the honor that can accompany the role. Rav, when he would come to the *beit din* to serve as judge, would recite a declaration: *b're'ut nafshiah l'katla nafik* — through my own desire I am going out to death. If I judge incorrectly, I deserve to die; I am walking into that exposure voluntarily. *Utzvei beiteih leit hu avid* — and I am not attending to my family's needs. I am not working, I am not earning, I am not bringing home any material gain. *V'reikan l'beiteih ayeil* — I will return home empty-handed. *Velivai shetehei biah kiyitziah* — and I only hope that my going in is like my going out, meaning that I return without having made things worse.

### Rise to Heaven

This declaration, one imagines, was intended to pre-empt both the temptation of honor and others' perception that honor was sought. Yet it apparently did not prevent crowds from gathering to follow Rav when he would leave the court. When he would see the *ambua* — the crowd — gathering behind him, he would say to himself: *im yaaleh lashamayim seo, kegilalo lanetzach yoved* — if you rise to heaven, like your dung you will ultimately be destroyed. Whatever honor accrues in this world is passing and without ultimate significance; this was how he kept himself from being consumed by it.

### Mar Zutra

Mar Zutra the *chasid* faced a similar challenge. On the *Shabbos* before the *regel*, when he would deliver public *drashos* to large crowds, people would carry him on their shoulders to bring him quickly through the assembled masses to the front. The physical experience of being borne aloft while everyone else sat below was its own form of *kavod*, however practically motivated. When they would do this, he would recite to himself: *ki lo leolam chosen veim nezer lador dor* — wealth is not forever, and glory is not for all generations. Honor, position, elevation — all of it passes.

---

## Steps in Judgment

### No Leaping

The *gemara* now turns to the verse *lo saaleh bemaalos* — do not go up in steps — and reads it in proximity to *ve'eileh hamishpatim asher tasim lifneichem*. Bar Kappara asks: from where do we derive the rabbinic teaching of *hevei masun badin*, be deliberate in judgment? From this verse. Steps, as opposed to a ramp, involve leaping over intermediate points in a process. The judge must not skip stages; every step of the deliberative process must be covered. Rabbi Elazar adds a further derivation: from where do we know that a judge may not step over the heads of the assembled people — physically stride over those sitting — since this projects a sense of superiority, as though towering above them? From the same verse and its *semichut* to the laws of judgment.

### Instruments

The *gemara* then asks why the verse says *asher tasim* — which you shall place — rather than *asher telamdem*, which you shall teach. Rabbi Yirmiyah, and some say Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, explains: *eileh klei hadayanim* — these are the instruments of the judges, placed before them to maintain order and project authority. When Rav Huna would go out to judge, he would say: *afiku li manei chanusai* — bring me the vessels of my store, my professional instruments. These were: a *makel* and *retzuah*, a staff and a leather strap for administering lashes; a *shofar* for imposing *cherem*; and a *sandal*, which Rashi explains as used for *chalitzah*. That last item seems somewhat out of place alongside the others — the staff, strap, and *shofar* all belong to the same category of judicial enforcement, while *chalitzah* is a distinct procedure — but it is apparently included among the instruments associated with the court's authority.

### Severity & Restraint

Rabbi Yochanan derives from *va'atzaveh es shofteichem ba'es hahi* — and I commanded your judges at that time — an instruction regarding the staff and strap: *keneged makel u'retzuah tehei zariz*, regarding the staff and strap be zealous. But what exactly does *tehei zariz* demand? Rashi reads it as owning the responsibility to make people properly fearful and respectful of the court's authority — *sheyihyu metilin eimah al hatzibur leshem shamayim*. If you carry the instrument, people need to know you are serious about using it. *Tosafot*, however, reads it in nearly the opposite direction: *shelo lehatil eimah al hatzibur leradosam yoser midai* — be careful not to impose excessive fear on the public, not to go too far. The two readings, taken together, describe the balance a judge must strike: owning the authority fully while not abusing it.

---

## Both Parties Present

### Shamoa Bein

Returning to the *pesukim* at the opening of *Devarim*, the *gemara* examines *shamoa bein achichem ushfatetem tzedek* — hear between your brethren and judge righteously. Rabbi Chanina derives two obligations from this phrase. First, *azharah l'beis din shelo yishma divrei baal din kodem sheyavo baal din chaveiro* — a prohibition on the court to hear one litigant's arguments before the other litigant has appeared. Second, *va'azharah l'vaal din shelo yat'im devarav l'dayan kodem sheyavo baal din chaveiro* — a parallel prohibition on the litigant himself from presenting his case to the judge before his counterpart arrives. The verse supports both: reading *shamoa* not only as "hear" but as "make heard" — *kari beih nami shama bein achichem* — when you make your case heard, both parties must be present.

### Anchoring Effect

Rashi's comment here is particularly incisive. When a litigant appears before the judge without his opponent present, *shema mesader divrei sheker kedivrei emes* — he will arrange false claims to sound like truth, because *ein machshisho* — no one is there to contradict him. And critically: *mikeivan shelev hadayan noteh lo lizkot, shuv ein bo mahapech bizchut hasheni kol kach* — once the judge's mind has tilted toward acquitting the first litigant, it is much harder to achieve a full reversal in favor of the second once the other side is heard. The first presentation anchors the judge's perception of the case; it becomes the default frame through which all subsequent information is processed. Even once both sides are present and both arguments heard, the asymmetry introduced by hearing one side first does not simply disappear. This is why the rule applies not only to the court but to the litigant himself: a litigant appearing before a judge when his opponent is absent will not spin out a complete fabrication as readily if the opponent were present, and in any case the judge's mind would already be framing the situation as one with two sides to hear. The rabbi or judge must always keep in mind, when hearing one party's account alone, that this is one version of a story and no more.

---

## False Reports

### False Reports

Rav Kahana derives from *lo tisa shema shav* — do not lift up a false report — a prohibition that extends beyond the context of oaths. Reading *lo tasi* (do not carry) alongside *lo tisha* (do not take up), the verse prohibits not only making a false claim but receiving and carrying one. *Al tashet yadcha im rasha lihyot ed chamas* — do not place your hand with the wicked to be a witness of violence — confirms that the prohibition encompasses the acceptance of false testimony, not only its production.

---

## Tzedek Din

### Know First

Back to *ushfatetem tzedek* — and you shall judge righteously. Reish Lakish states: *tzedek et hadin v'achar kach chatcheihu* — justify the judgment, and then cut it — meaning, deliver it. Know what the ruling is before you issue it; do not announce a *psak* before you have fully worked through your reasoning and reached a conclusion. Rashi does not fully explicate what *tzedek et hadin* demands beyond the general obligation of proper deliberation. One reading would have the judge articulate his reasoning before announcing the ruling, presenting the analysis and then the conclusion. But there is a countervailing consideration: a ruling prefaced by its entire reasoning has a different psychological weight than one stated directly, and one might argue the ruling should come first — *Reuven is right*, with reasoning available thereafter. In any event, the core principle of *tzedek et hadin v'achar kach chatcheihu* appears to require that the judge be fully certain of the *psak* before he states it publicly — know the result before you cut it loose.

---

## Among Relatives

### House & Chamber

*Bein ish u'vein achiv u'vein gero* — between one man and his brother and his sojourner. Rav Yehuda derives: *afilu bein bayit l'aliyah* — even between the house and the upper chamber. If two brothers inherit a property, do not summarily divide it by telling one to take the ground floor and the other the upper story. Those two portions may differ in value, and if so, real justice requires calculating the difference and having the one who receives the more valuable portion compensate accordingly. Similarly, if household items are divided, one item may be worth more than another, and splitting evenly by category rather than by value fails to deliver true justice. Even in cases between close relatives, even in cases that appear simple and easy to resolve, the obligation is to execute genuine justice, not an approximate or lazy approximation of it.

---

## Recognition & Bias

### No Favor

*Lo takiru fanim bamishpat* — do not recognize faces in judgment. Rabbi Yehuda reads this straightforwardly: *lo takiruhu* — do not recognize someone and on the basis of that recognition show them favor. This is the plain meaning.

### Balance

Rabbi Elazar adds a refinement: *lo tenakruhu* — but do not make a stranger of him either. Rashi explains: if someone before you in judgment is a person you dislike, do not treat him as though he were a foreigner with whom you have no connection, as though you owed him nothing and could rule against him freely. The obligation is to maintain genuine objectivity — neither favoring the familiar nor penalizing the disliked.

### Innkeeper Case

A story illustrates how even the act of acknowledging a connection can compromise judicial integrity, quite apart from any actual favoritism. The innkeeper where Rav was lodging came before Rav for a judgment. When the innkeeper saw Rav, he greeted him: *lav ushpixini at* — are you not my lodger? Rav confirmed that he was. The innkeeper then said he had a case to bring. Rav responded: *psilna lach l'dina* — you have disqualified me to be your judge. Rashi explains that it was the act of *mentioning* the connection — *shehizkartani tovascha* — that created the problem. Had the innkeeper not raised it, there might have been no disqualification. *Tosafot* notes that technically this does not rise to the level of *shochad* that invalidates a ruling, and Rav was distancing himself beyond the letter of the law; but once the connection is surfaced in the courtroom, the appearance and the reality of impartiality are both compromised.

Rav therefore said to Rav Kahana: *puk dayneih* — go and judge his case, since I cannot. Rav Kahana saw that the innkeeper was behaving with excessive familiarity, apparently assuming that his social connection to Rav's circle gave him an advantage. Rav Kahana warned him: *itsaisa itsaisa* — listen and show proper deference. *Ve'i lo, nafkina lach Rav me'onecha* — if you continue, I will pull Rav out of your ear, meaning, Rashi explains, I will make it clear that Rav cannot come to your aid by placing you in *cherem* — a finding of contempt of court.

### Deference

The case illustrates that the problem of *lo takiru fanim* is not limited to the judge's internal disposition. The litigant's conduct in the courtroom — his assumption of familiarity, his failure to show proper deference to the proceedings — is itself a corruption of the judicial process, and the court has both the authority and the obligation to address it directly.

---

## Small vs. Great

### Equal Attention

*Ke-katan ke-gadol tishme'un* — like the small and the great you shall hear. Reish Lakish interprets: *she-chaviv alecha din shel peruta ke-din shel me'ah maneh* — a case involving a *peruta* should be as important to you as a case involving a hundred *maneh*. The principle applies not only to the social status of the parties but to the magnitude of the case itself.

### First Come

The *gemara* asks: *le-mai hilcheta*? If the instruction means to give equal deliberation and care to small and large cases, that is already obvious from the basic obligation of justice. The novel ruling, therefore, concerns priority: even when it comes to which case to hear first, do not set aside a small case in order to deal with the large one first. Whatever came before the court first is dealt with first — *le-akdomei*, to prioritize — regardless of the relative size of the claims at stake.

---

## Independence

### Fear None

*Lo taguru mi-pnei ish* — do not fear any person. Rav Chanan reads this expansively: *al tachnis devarecha mi-pnei ish* — do not hold back your words because of anyone. This applies not only to the judge but to the court clerk or any officer of the court who might be in a position to suppress a message or a ruling out of deference to a powerful figure.

### God's Justice

*Ki ha-mishpat le-Elohim hu* — because justice belongs to God. Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina derives: *lo dayam la-resha'im she-notlin mi-zeh mammon ve-notnin le-zeh she-lo ke-din* — it is not enough that the wicked — and here the term encompasses the corrupt judges alongside ordinary wrongdoers — take money from one and give it to another against the demands of justice. Beyond the immediate injustice, *ela she-matrichin oti le-hachzir mammon le-ba'alav* — they force upon God the burden of restoring the money to its rightful owner. This returns to the earlier principle that unjust judgment is not only a wrong done to the parties; it is a wrong done against God, who is left to clean up the corruption of His world.

*Ve-ha-davar asher yiksheh mi-chem takrivun elai u-shmati-v* — and the matter that is too difficult for you, bring it to me and I will hear it. Rabbi Chanina, and some say Rabbi Yoshiya, teaches that Moshe was punished for this declaration — for presenting himself as the ultimate arbiter who would always have the answer, rather than saying he would bring it to God. The case of *Benot Tzelofchad* demonstrates this: they came with a question, and Moshe had to bring it before God.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges: the verse does not say *ashmi'achem*, I will tell you the ruling. It says *u-shmati-v*, I will hear it. Perhaps Moshe meant only that he would hear the question and then go to receive the ruling from God — not that he would always have the answer himself. *Ei gemirna gemirna* — if I know the ruling I will give it; *ve'i lo, azlina ve-gemirna* — if not, I will go and learn it from God. On this reading, Moshe said nothing wrong, and the fact that *Benot Tzelofchad* required him to ask God was not a form of punishment.

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty differently. *Re'uya parashat nachalot she-tikatev al yedei Moshe Rabbeinu* — the section of inheritance was destined to be written through Moshe regardless of whether *Benot Tzelofchad* had ever come to him. Had they never raised the question, at some point within the forty years the ruling would have been issued anyway. *Ella shezachu Bnot Tzelafchad venichteva al yadan* — but they merited, and so it was written in conjunction with them, because they stood up for what was right and approached Moshe in the proper way. Similarly, *re'uya hi parshat ha-mekoshesh* — the portion concerning the one who gathered wood on *Shabbat* would have been written regardless, conveying the punishment for *chilul Shabbat*; but because that particular individual was guilty, *nitchayev mekoshesh venichteva al yado*, the section was attached to him. *Megalgelin chovah al yedei chayav vezachut al yedei zakai* — liability gravitates toward those who are guilty, and merit gravitates toward those who are righteous. The *mekoshesh* is forever associated with the *parasha* of *chilul Shabbat*'s punishment; *Benot Tzelofchad* are forever associated with the *parasha* of women's inheritance.

---

## Bear Complaints

### How Long?

*Va'atzaveh es shofteichem ba'es hahi* and *va'atzaveh etchem ba'es hahi* — I commanded your judges at that time, and I commanded you at that time. Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Simlai derives from the dual formulation two distinct obligations. *Azharah la-tzibur shetehei eimat dayan aleihem* — the public must maintain proper fear and deference toward the judges. *Va'azharah la-dayan sheyisbol et ha-tzibur* — and the judge must bear the burden of the public. Both sides have their obligations in the relationship between judge and community.

### Nursemaid

To what extent must a judge tolerate the friction and complaints that come from those he serves? Rabbi Yochanan, and some say Rav Shavtai, answers: *ka'asher yisa ha-omen et ha-yonek* — as a nursemaid bears a crying infant. The obligation of patience with the community's burden and complaint is without limit in this formulation, even as we know that Moshe himself protested the weight of the people's demands and was granted the *shivim zekeinim* in response.

---

## One Voice

### Go With Elders

When Moshe spoke to Yehoshua before the people's entry into the land, the verse reads: *ki ata tavo et ha-am ha-zeh* — for you will go with this people. Rabbi Yochanan explains: Moshe was telling Yehoshua that he would lead together with the elders of the generation, not as sole authority. *Ata u-zekeinim shebador imahem* — you and the elders of the generation together with them.

### One Leader

But God's instruction to Yehoshua uses a different formulation: *ki ata tavi* — for you will bring them. God told Yehoshua: *tol makeil vehach al kadkodam* — take the staff and strike them on the head. Do not be so retiring; you are the leader. *Dabar echad lador ve'ein shenei devarim lador* — one voice for a generation, not two. Consultation with the elders is appropriate; indeed, Rav Huna's practice of gathering colleagues precisely reflects the wisdom of hearing multiple perspectives. But leadership requires one person who owns the final authority. Even if Yehoshua consults with the *zekeinim*, he must lead, because a generation cannot have two overlapping authorities — they will climb on each other's heads. *Ata tavi* — you, singular, will bring them.

---

## Zimmun

### Full Court

A *tanna* teaches: *zimmun bishlosha* — a *zimmun* requires three. The *gemara* asks what this *zimmun* means, since *birkat zimmun* — the invitation to *bentch* — is already known to require three, and this teaching seems to add nothing. The *gemara* therefore concludes that this is a different *zimmun* altogether: *azmuni l'din* — summoning someone to appear in court. That judicial summons must be issued through the *beit din*, three judges.

### Non-Court Days

Rava explains the practical rule: if the three judges of a *beit din* are sitting and a court messenger goes to summon someone, but issues the summons *mishmei d'chad* — in the name of only one of the judges — *lo amar klum*, he has said nothing effective and the recipient is not obligated to respond. The summons is only valid when issued *mishmei d'chulhu* — in the name of the entire court, all three judges. This applies on days when the court is not formally sitting — that is, not on Mondays and Thursdays, when the court convenes by established practice.

### Court Days

*Aval beyoma d'dina* — but on a day when the court is formally sitting, *mishmei d'chad* does suffice. When it is a day of judgment and the court is in session, a summons issued in the name of one judge is understood to carry the authority of the full sitting *beit din* — the single judge's name implies the entire court behind him. Outside of court days, that inference cannot be drawn, and the summons must therefore explicitly invoke all three.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 8

## Divine Presence & Justice

### Truth Brings Shechinah

We pick up at the bottom of 7a, where the *Gemara* has just concluded a discussion about *bitzua* versus *din* — binding arbitration and compromise as opposed to strict justice — along with some digressions connecting popular sayings to verses. The *Gemara* now transitions to a series of statements transmitted by Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, each bearing on the spiritual weight of judicial integrity.

The first teaching: *kol dayan shedan din emes l'amito, mashre Shechina b'Yisrael* — any judge who renders true judgment, truth to its truth, causes the *Shechina* to dwell among Israel. This is not the earlier question of choosing between *din* and compromise; we are now operating squarely within the framework of justice and asking what it means to do it correctly. The double language — *emes l'amito*, truth to its truth — is striking. It calls to mind the *Yerushalmi*'s discussion of how authentic truth encompasses not only the result but the process by which it is reached. When justice is genuinely done, the verse confirms: *Elokim nitzav ba'adas E-l, bekerev elokim yishpot* — God stands in the congregation of God; in the presence of God they judge. The divine presence rests on earth precisely when justice is being enacted.

### Perversion Removes Shech…

The converse follows immediately. Any judge who does not render *din emes l'amito* causes the *Shechina* to withdraw from Israel — *gorem l'Shechina shetistalek miYisrael*. The prooftext is: *mishod aniyim me'ankat evyonim, ata akum yomar Hashem* — from the despoiling of the poor and the outcry of the needy, now I will rise up, says God. The word "rise up" here carries a double valence: God rises to take vengeance, but also, as it were, withdraws His presence. This verse speaks to the judge who perhaps ignores injustice being done, or who recuses himself to avoid trouble with the powerful, thereby abandoning the outcry of the poor.

### Unjust Judgment Fatal

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani then transmits a further teaching in Rabbi Yonatan's name: *kol dayan shenotel mizeh venosein lizeh shelo k'din, Hakadosh Baruch Hu notel mimenu nafsho* — any judge who takes from one party and gives to the other in a manner contrary to law, God will demand his soul. If the previous verse addressed a judge who ignored injustice, this one targets the one who actively perverts it. The prooftext — *al tigzol dal ki dal hu, v'al tedakeh ani b'sha'ar* — do not steal from the poor because he is poor, and do not trample the poor person in the gate — identifies the *sha'ar*, the gate, as the locus of judicial proceedings, evoking *Lot yoshev b'sha'ar Sdom*, where justice was administered. *Ki Hashem yariv rivam, v'kava es koveihem nafesh* — God will fight their fight and take the soul of those who rob them.

### Fear of Judgment

A third teaching from the same tradent: *l'olam yireh dayan es atzmo k'ilu cherev munachas lo bein yarchosav, v'gehinnom pesucha lo mitachtav* — a judge should always see himself as if a sword is placed between his thighs and *gehinnom* is open beneath him. This is hardly an encouraging recruitment pitch, but the point is serious: the consequences of judging incorrectly are severe. The prooftext is taken from the description of Shlomo's bed: sixty mighty warriors surrounding it, each with his sword at his thigh, *mipachad balaylos* — fear of the night. The *Gemara* reads this as *mipachda shel gehinnom shedomeh lalaylah* — fear of *gehinnom*, which is likened to night. Rashi explains *melumdei milchama* as *milchamta shel Torah*, those engaged in Torah learning, evoking the classic image of the *beis medrash* — but here the teaching is specifically applied to the consequence of incorrect adjudication.

---

## Clarity Standard

### Morning Clarity Test

Rav Yoshaiya — or some say Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak — expounds the verse: *Beit David ko amar Hashem dinu laboker mishpat v'hatzilu gazul miyad oshek* — O House of David, thus says God: judge justice in the morning and rescue the robbed one from the hand of the oppressor. The immediate question is: *v'chi baboker danin uv'chol yoma ein danin?* Do you only judge in the morning? Surely one judges throughout the day. The answer: *im barur lach hadavar kaboker amrehu* — if the matter is as clear to you as the morning light, say it. *V'im lav al tomrehu* — and if not, do not say it.

This raises an immediate challenge. If the standard for issuing a ruling is that the matter must be crystal clear — as obvious as the difference between light and darkness at dawn — what happens when a judge is not entirely certain? Does it mean justice will go unserved? *Halacha* has mechanisms for situations of doubt: *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya* — the burden of proof rests on the claimant, so if the judge is uncertain, the case defaults to the party in possession. But that default might itself be a perversion of justice for all one knows.

### Certainty vs. Practice

This tension must be read alongside another *Gemara* that states *ein l'dayan ella mah she'einav ro'ot* — a judge has only what his own eyes can see. These two principles live in productive tension with one another. A judge must be genuinely afraid of judging wrongly; yet if he does his honest best with the information available, he is not culpable. The statement about absolute morning clarity does not demand omniscience but rather a prohibition against ruling when the judge privately knows he is operating in the dark. Certainty and conscientiousness are the demand; *ein l'dayan ella mah she'einav ro'ot* provides the relief when honest effort falls short of perfect knowledge.

### Wisdom Sister Analogy

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba transmits in the name of Rabbi Yochanan an analogous formulation from a different source: *emor lachochma achoti at* — say to wisdom, you are my sister. If the ruling is as clear to you as the prohibition against relations with one's own sister — *im barur lach hadavar k'achotcha shehi asura lach* — then give the judgment. *V'im lav al tomrehu* — and if not, do not say it. The analogy is arresting: the certainty required for judgment is compared to one of the most self-evident prohibitions in the Torah, something no person would ever need to deliberate about or second-guess.

---

## Shared Responsibility

### Ten Judges Yoke

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches: *asara sheyoshvin bedin, kola taluy betzavra d'chulhu* — ten people who sit in judgment, the yoke hangs around all of their necks. The number ten is notable; it is not a standard *beis din* composition. The *Gemara* immediately presses: is this obvious? Of course everyone shares responsibility. The teaching adds a less intuitive extension: *tzricha ella l'talmid hayoshev lifnei rabbo* — it applies even to a student sitting before his teacher. Rashi ties this back to earlier discussion: if a student was present and could have spoken up but did not, he bears a share of responsibility for the erroneous outcome. Being part of the process — even as a subordinate — means one cannot disclaim responsibility by pointing to the many others present. The crowd does not dilute the obligation.

### Rav Huna Ten Rabbis

The *Gemara* now pivots to a complementary application: not responsibility-sharing as an excuse, but responsibility-sharing as a safeguard. *Rav Huna ki havai ati dina l'kameih, michnaf umayti asara rabbanan* — when a case would come before Rav Huna, he would gather ten rabbis from the *yeshiva*. His stated reason: *ki heichi d'limtei shiva mikashura* — so that a splinter from the beam should reach everyone, meaning the weight of responsibility should be distributed across multiple shoulders.

This is the reverse of the prior teaching's concern. There the warning was: do not use the presence of others to evade personal responsibility. Here: when you carry a difficult ruling, bring in others so that no one person bears the full burden alone. This practice is attested among *poskim* as well — some will explicitly state that they will not issue a ruling on a sensitive matter unless they can secure the agreement of several other rabbinic colleagues, so that the *shiva mikshura* is shared.

One might question how much genuine deliberation occurred when Rav Huna assembled ten unnamed rabbis from the yeshiva. In all likelihood they deferred to him. The sense that many unnamed disciples mostly follow the lead of the senior authority does somewhat undercut the claimed benefit of shared decision-making. Indeed, sociological research into group decision-making has found that groups do not necessarily produce more balanced outcomes; individuals can still exert influence over group decisions while simultaneously avoiding personal accountability for them. Nevertheless, the underlying principle is sound: *al tehi dan yechidi* — do not judge alone — and the counsel to hear other perspectives and not assume that all truth rests with oneself.

### Consulted Slaughterers

A contrasting and in some ways more compelling example follows. *Rav Ashi ki hava atei tereifta lekamei, machneif umeisei lehu lekulhu tavchei demasa* — when a question about a *tereifta* would come before Rav Ashi, he would gather all the *shochtim* of the city of Masa Machasya, and he too would invoke the principle of *ki heichi delimteiyan shiva mikshura* — so that a splinter of the beam reaches everyone.

This case is substantively different from Rav Huna's practice and, in fact, more instructive. Rav Ashi was not summoning random students; he was bringing in the very people whose livelihoods and expertise were most directly at stake. First, the *shochtim* are the ones upon whom the *psak* will have practical impact — hearing their concerns might legitimately reshape how the ruling is framed. Second, they bring technical expertise that no single *posek*, however learned, necessarily possesses in full. This is not a case of insufficient knowledge on Rav Ashi's part; rather, it reflects the principle that different practitioners bring different dimensions of knowledge and perspective to any ruling, and the *posek* who draws on those perspectives before issuing a *psak* is serving justice more fully than one who rules in isolation.

---

## Unfit Appointees

### King vs. Kohen

*Ki ata Rav Dimi amar, darash Nachman bar Kohen* — when Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he quoted a teaching of Nachman bar Kohen — and note that the teacher himself bears the name "bar Kohen," which will prove relevant. The verse: *melech bemishpat ya'amid aretz, ve'ish terumos yeherosena* — the king with justice will establish the land, but a man of gifts will destroy it. Reading *terumos* as an allusion to the *kohen* who goes from threshing floor to threshing floor collecting his *terumah*: if the judge is like a king who needs nothing from anyone — *sheino tzarich leklum* — he will establish justice. But if he is like a *kohen* dependent on others' goodwill, going door to door for his grain, he will destroy it.

Tosafot understands this in material terms: a financially independent judge who needs no one's favor can rule freely, whereas a judge dependent on others' support will inevitably be compromised. Rashi, however, reads it differently. Looking at Rashi's second narrow column: *im domeh dayan lemelech shebaki betiv dinim* — if the judge is like a king who is expert in the nature of legal cases, *umaleh chochma* — and full of wisdom — as opposed to the *kohen* who must go around asking for his *terumah* — *shetzarich lachzor lishol ba'ish*, who must keep asking others — if the judge must constantly seek guidance because he lacks the knowledge, he will destroy it.

Rashi's reading should be balanced against what we have just learned about consulting others. The difference is clear: a genuine expert who chooses to consult is not the same as someone who lacks fundamental competence and must ask because they do not know. As in medicine, a skilled surgeon who recommends a second opinion is not confessing ignorance; rather, the seriousness of the matter warrants additional expert input. That is entirely different from a practitioner who lacks the training to know what they are doing.

### Empty Vessel Judge

The *Gemara* now arrives at a famous and darkly comic episode. *Devei nasi ukmei dayana delo hava gamir* — the house of the *Nasi* appointed a judge who did not know. This echoes directly back to the requirement for a *yachid mumcheh* to be *gamir vesavir* — knowledgeable and possessed of sound analytical capacity. Once a system of political appointments was established (*netilat reshut* from the *Nasi* or from the *Resh Galuta*), the predictable failure mode emerged: political connections substituting for competence.

Someone said to Yehuda bar Nachmani — the *meturgeman*, the announcer of Reish Lakish — *kum alei be'amora*, go serve as this judge's *amora*. Here the word *amora* does not refer to the rabbinic era but to its other meaning: the one who stood before large crowds and projected the speaker's words. The scholar would whisper his teaching and the *amora* would boom it out to the assembled. The incompetent judge was apparently meant to whisper something to Yehuda bar Nachmani, who would then pronounce it publicly.

What followed is almost farcical. *Kam gachin alei velo amar leh velo midi* — the judge leaned in and whispered to Yehuda bar Nachmani, but said nothing at all, for he had nothing to say. So what did Yehuda bar Nachmani announce? He improvised, and what he chose to recite was devastating: *hoi omer la'etz hakitza, uri la'even domem, hu yoreh, hineihu tafus zahav vakesef, vechol ruach ein bekirbo* — woe to the one who says to wood, wake up, stir yourself to the mute stone — he is the one who should judge? Behold he holds gold and silver, and there is no spirit within him. The empty idol, the silent stone that cannot speak: this is the image deployed for the unfit judge. It had the appearance of being the ruling whispered to him; in reality, it was a public condemnation of the judge himself.

*Amar Hakadosh Baruch Hu lifroa mihamaamidim* — God will ultimately exact payment not only from the incompetent appointee but from those who did the appointing. The verse: *v'Hashem b'heichal kodsho has mipanav kol ha'aretz* — God is in His holy sanctuary, silence before Him, all the earth. What follows that image of empty idols that speak nothing — the wood and the stone that hold gold and silver but have no spirit — is the silence of divine reckoning.

### Unfit Judge Idolatry

Reish Lakish draws the theological conclusion: *kol hama'amid dayan she'eino hagun, ke'ilu noteia asherah b'Yisrael* — whoever appoints an unfit judge is as if he planted an *asherah*, an idolatrous tree, among Israel. The connection to the image of the empty idol from the previous episode is direct: the unfit judge is an empty vessel, like a statue of gold and silver that has no inner life. Just as rendering true justice brings the *Shechina* to dwell among Israel, appointing someone who cannot render true justice is idolatry — it drives the divine presence away. More than that: justice is God's work on earth, and the judge is meant to be God's agent. Handing that authority to someone unworthy is to install a false god in God's place.

The *semichus* — the proximity of verses — makes this explicit: *shoftim veshotrim titein lecha* is immediately followed by *lo tita lecha asherah kol etz* — you shall set up judges and officers, and do not plant an idolatrous tree. Appointing unfit judges is the functional equivalent of spreading idolatry.

### Against the Altar

Rav Ashi adds a further gradation: *uv'makom sheyesh talmidei chachamim* — if there were qualified Torah scholars available who could have served as judges and were passed over, *ke'ilu nata eitzel mizbei'ach* — it is as if the *asherah* were planted right next to the altar itself. The verse: *lo tita asherah eitzel mizbei'ach Hashem Elokecha*. This is not merely the wrong choice; it is direct defiance, an insult planted in the very precincts of holiness.

### Gods of Silver/Gold

The *Gemara* then addresses the verse *lo taasun iti elohei chesef ve'elohei zahav* — do not make gods of silver and gods of gold alongside Me. A question is posed: surely this obviously means do not make idols of silver and gold — do we need to say this? Does it follow that idols of *wood* would be permitted? Rav Ashi resolves this: *elo'ah haba bishvil kesef* — a god that comes because of money. The verse is warning against appointing someone to a position of authority — one who functions like a god on earth, executing divine justice — simply because they paid for the position. The word *elo'ah* here encodes the judicial role: the *shofet* represents divine authority on earth. When that position is purchased rather than earned through knowledge and integrity, it is the creation of a false god. The *Gemara* clearly acknowledges the realities of the political-appointment system of its era.

---

## Honor & Humility

### Rav's Declaration

Having treated the weight of judicial responsibility and the corruption of unfit appointees, the *Gemara* now turns to a connected but distinct problem: the honor that attaches to the position of judge, and how a person who holds that position righteously navigates the risk of being corrupted by the honor itself.

*Rav ki hava ati l'vei dina, amar hachi* — when Rav would come to court to serve as a judge, he would make the following declaration: *bire'ut nafshiah l'katla nafik* — through my own choice I am going out to be killed, meaning if I judge incorrectly I will deserve death. *V'tzvi beiteiah leit hu avid* — I am not attending to my family's needs by being here; I will earn nothing. *V'reikan l'beiteiah ayil* — I will return home empty-handed. *Veluai shetehei biati kiyetziati* — and I only hope that when I am finished, my entering was like my leaving, meaning I have not made things worse. This declaration — addressed to himself, to others present, to anyone who would hear — was Rav's way of making explicit that he was not doing this for *kavod*, not for financial gain, not for any benefit to himself.

### Heaven & Dung

Yet *ki hava chazi ambua basreih* — when Rav would leave the court and see that crowds of people were gathering to follow him, that despite everything, honor was still accruing to him, he would say to himself: *im yaaleh lashamayim se'o, kegilalo lanetzach yovad* — even if your glory rises to heaven, in the end, like your own dung, you will be destroyed and pass away. The Hebrew is pointed and deliberately deflating. Whatever honor the crowd conferred, Rav chose to see it through the lens of ultimate insignificance: all human glory ends the same way.

### Mar Zutra Humility

The *Gemara* records a parallel practice from Mar Zutra Chasida. On *shabsa deregla* — the Shabbat before a *regel* when large masses would gather to hear Torah — people would carry him on their shoulders (*katef*) to move him quickly to the front of the assembly. Rashi explains that walking slowly through the seated crowd would require everyone to stand repeatedly, so he was carried aloft. But in that position — elevated above everyone, being physically carried by others — the risk to one's sense of proportion was acute. So Mar Zutra would say to himself: *ki lo leolam chosen, ve'im nezer ledor dor* — because wealth is not forever, and honor does not pass from generation to generation. This too will pass; whatever elevation I now experience is temporary and ultimately meaningless.

---

## Judicial Deliberation

### No Steps in Justice

Bar Kappara expounds: where do we derive the rabbinic principle of *hevei masun badin* — be deliberate in judgment? From the verse *lo saaleh bemaalos* — do not go up in steps — which is immediately followed by *ve'eleh hamishpatim asher tasim lifneihem*, these are the laws you shall place before them. Going up steps rather than a ramp involves skipping the intervening space — jumping over sections of the process. Deliberation in judgment means touching every point, moving slowly, not leaping to conclusions. A ramp forces one to traverse every inch; steps allow gaps. The judge must be like one ascending a ramp.

### Not Over Heads

Rav Elazar adds a further derivation from the same verse: *minayin ledayan shelo yifsa al rashei am kodesh* — how do we know that a judge should not step over people's heads? The image is literal: when a judge must move through a seated assembly to reach his place, stepping over seated people makes it appear as though he is literally stepping on them, asserting his elevation over the holy people. The verse *lo saaleh bemaalos* followed immediately by *ve'eleh hamishpatim* teaches again: the judge who represents justice must not comport himself in ways that visually assert superiority over those he serves.

### Judge's Instruments

The *Gemara* notes that the verse *asher tasim lifneihem* uses the word *tasim* — you shall place — rather than the expected *tilmedem* — you shall teach them. Rabbi Yirmiyah (or some say Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba) explains: *elu klei hadayanim* — these are the instruments of the judges. The placing refers to the tools the judge employs. Rav Huna, when going out to judge, would call for *manei chanutai* — the vessels of his trade: *makel v'retzuah, v'shofra v'sandala* — a staff and a leather strap, a *shofar*, and a sandal. The staff and strap are for the administration of lashes; the *shofar* is for *cherem*, excommunication; and the sandal, Rashi explains, is for *chalitzah*. The *shochtim* were the ones who physically administered lashes — the judge himself wielded the symbolic authority — but the point is that the responsibilities of justice are not only deliberative. They include the willingness to enforce.

### Staff Strap Balance

Returning to the verse *va'atzaveh et shoftechem ba'et hahi* from the beginning of Devarim, Rabbi Yochanan reads *va'atzaveh* as an instruction about *makel v'retzuah*: *keneged makel v'retzuah tehei zariz* — be punctilious about the staff and the strap.

Rashi and Tosafot differ on what *tehei zariz* demands. Rashi: *tehei zariz al hamakel v'al haretzuah she-hayu matilin eimah al hatzibur l'shem shamayim* — be diligent about the staff and strap, which instill proper fear in the public for the sake of Heaven. The judge must own that aspect of the role; people must sense that the authority to enforce is real and will be exercised. Tosafot reverses the emphasis: *shelo lehatil eimah al hatzibur l'rodotam yoter midai* — be careful not to impose fear upon the public excessively, not to go too far. The balance between these readings is the balance demanded of the judge: sufficient authority to be taken seriously, restraint enough not to become oppressive.

---

## Procedural Safeguard (II)

### Both Parties Present

The *Gemara* continues through the *pesukim* at the opening of Devarim. *Shamo'a bein acheichem ushfatetem tzedek* — hear between your brethren and judge righteously. Rabbi Chanina derives: *azharah l'Beis Din shelo yishma divrei ba'al din kodem sheyavo ba'al din chaveiro* — a prohibition on the court from hearing one litigant's words before the other litigant arrives. The obligation cuts both ways: *v'azharah l'ba'al din shelo yateim dvarav l'dayan kodem sheyavo ba'al din chaveiro* — a litigant is also prohibited from presenting his case to the judge before the opposing party appears. *Kari bei nami shema bein acheichem* — the word can also be read as "make heard": when you make your case heard, it must be in the presence of your counterpart.

### Anchoring Effect

Rashi's comment here is particularly penetrating. Why does it matter so much that both be present simultaneously? *K'sheyavo'u shneihem yachad, shimu divreihem, v'lo tishme'u divrei zeh belo zeh* — hear them together, do not hear one without the other — *shema mesader divrei sheker k'divrei emet* — because when his opponent is absent, a person will lay out his false claims as if they were true: *lefi shehamach'shio eino sham* — since the one who would contradict him is not there.

Moreover, once the judge has heard only one side, that framing becomes the default lens through which everything subsequent is processed. When the second party's case is presented, the judge hears it against the backdrop already established by the first. This is the *anchoring* effect: the initial piece of information structures all subsequent evaluation. Requiring both parties to be present from the outset mitigates — though does not eliminate — this distortion. Someone will inevitably speak first; but if the judge frames the situation from the beginning as one with two competing versions, and if the first speaker knows the second is present and less likely to fabricate freely, the anchoring is diminished. A rabbi must be especially vigilant about this: when a congregant comes privately with a detailed account that sounds entirely persuasive, one must always hold in mind that this is one person's version, and the absent party has not yet been heard.

---

## Impartiality

### No Recognition

*Lo takiru fanim bamishpat* — do not recognize faces in judgment. Rabbi Yehuda interprets *lo takireihu* straightforwardly: do not show favor to someone you recognize. But the verse may carry a further dimension. Showing recognition itself — independent of any actual favoritism — creates a procedural problem. A practical illustration: when a woman came to a *beis din* for a *get* and the judges greeted her husband by name, remarking warmly on how long it had been, the message received by the woman — regardless of how the case was ultimately decided — was that the court had a pre-existing relationship with her husband that she did not share. That perception alone compromises the litigant's sense that her case will receive fair hearing.

Rabbi Eliezer reads the verse differently: *lo tinakruhu* — do not make him a stranger. If the party before you is someone you dislike, you must not treat him as a foreigner or an outsider by way of bias against him. But the practical balance is fine: you should not warmly acknowledge someone you know (*lo takiru*), yet you should not pointedly ignore them to demonstrate your impartiality (*lo tinakruhu*). The correct posture is measured evenhandedness — neither warmth nor conspicuous coldness.

---

## Procedural Safeguard (II)

### Innkeeper Disqualificati…

The *Gemara* illustrates with a story. The innkeeper where Rav was staying came before Rav to bring a legal matter. The innkeeper, seeing Rav, said: *lav ushpizichna at* — are you not my tenant? Rav responded: yes, I am. The innkeeper then said he had a case to bring. Rav replied: *psilina lach l'dina* — you have disqualified me from judging your case.

The mechanics here are worth examining. Rav was paying for his lodgings; the innkeeper was not providing charity. So the issue is not *shochad* — bribery in the conventional sense. Rashi explains: *shehizkarta li tovatecha* — because you mentioned your connection to me. Had the innkeeper said nothing, Rashi implies, it would not have been a problem. Tosafot frames it differently: *marchik hava atzmo aval midina lo mipsil* — he was distancing himself out of scrupulousness, but strictly speaking it would not have been an invalidation. The procedural problem arises precisely because the connection was surfaced; once it is named, it cannot be un-named.

### Rav Kahana Warning

Rav said to Rav Kahana: *puk dainei* — go, you take this case, since I cannot. Rav Kahana then observed that the innkeeper was behaving with excessive familiarity, projecting confidence as if his relationship with Rav guaranteed a favorable outcome. Rav Kahana warned him: *tzeita tzeita* — pay attention and show proper deference — *v'i lo, nafekna lach Rav me'unach* — if not, I will pull Rav out of your ear: Rashi explains this as a declaration that Rav's relationship with the man would not help him, and indeed Rav Kahana would put him in *cherem* — a public declaration that the court viewed him as in contempt of judicial process.

---

## Impartiality (II)

### Equal Care

Returning to the *pesukim* in Devarim: *k'katan k'gadol tishme'un* — like the small and the great you shall hear. Reish Lakish explains: *she'chaviv alecha din shel prutah k'din shel me'ah maneh* — the case of a *prutah* should be as dear to you as a case of a hundred *maneh*. The *Gemara* immediately asks: if this means that each case deserves equal deliberation and care, *pshitah* — that is obvious, at least from the perspective of *halacha*. Of course justice is justice regardless of the amount at stake. The psychological reality is another matter — a judge will naturally invest more effort in a high-stakes case — but the normative demand is clear.

The *Gemara* therefore identifies a less obvious application: even regarding which case to take up first, one may not set aside a small case to prioritize a large one. Whichever case arrives first is taken first. This is the practical content of *ke'katan kegadol*.

### No Fear

*Lo taguru mipnei ish* — do not fear any person. Rav Chanan adds: *al tachnis devarecha mipnei ish* — do not withhold your words before anyone. Even a court officer or clerk who is aware of relevant information must not suppress it out of fear of the powerful.

### Justice God's

*Ki hamishpat l'Elohim hu* — for justice belongs to God. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina reads this as a divine complaint: it is not sufficient punishment for the wicked — and here the wicked are the judges who pervert justice, not merely ordinary thieves — that they take from one and give unjustly to another. Beyond that, *shematrichin oti lehachzir mamon l'ba'alav* — they burden Me with having to rectify their mess, returning the money to its rightful owner. When a judge rules falsely, he is in effect compelling divine intervention to clean up what human perversion has corrupted. This is the full weight of *ki hamishpat l'Elohim hu*: justice is God's domain, and to violate it is to make God responsible for the repair.

---

## Difficult Cases

### Difficult to God

*Ve'hadavar asher yiksheh mikem takrivun elai ushm'ativ* — and the matter that is too difficult for you, bring to me and I will hear it. Moshe presents himself here as the ultimate arbiter: if something is beyond you, bring it to me and I will resolve it. Rabbi Chanina (or some say Rabbi Yoshiyah) says: *al davar zeh ne'enash Moshe* — for this, Moshe was punished. The claim to be able to hear and resolve all cases set him up in a way that was not fully warranted.

### Moses Not Punished

This is challenged immediately: *mi ktiv v'ashmi'achem?* — does the verse say "I will tell you"? No, it says *ushm'ativ* — I will *hear* it. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reads this as: I will hear it from God and relay the answer. *Ei gemirna gemirna* — if I already know the ruling, I will tell you; *v'i lo, azlina v'gemirna* — and if not, I will go and learn it from God. Under this reading, Moshe's statement contained no arrogance; he was simply saying that the hardest cases would ultimately be referred upward. Moshe was not punished.

### Zelophehad Merit

If Moshe was not punished — if the *parasha* of inheritance did not emerge because he overstepped — why did the case of the daughters of Zelophehad require their petition to Moshe and his subsequent inquiry to God? The *Gemara* explains: *re'uyah parshat nachalot sheticatev al yedei Moshe Rabbeinu* — the laws of inheritance were already destined to be written through Moshe regardless. Had the daughters never come forward, the ruling would have been issued anyway. *Ella shezachu Benot Zelophehad venichtava al yadan* — but they merited, because they spoke up at the right moment in the right way, that this portion of Torah was recorded through them. Their advocacy linked their names to the *parasha* in perpetuity.

This principle — *shemegalgelin chova al yedei chayav vezachut al yedei zakai* — that burdens fall upon those who bear guilt and merits upon those who are worthy — is illustrated through a parallel case. The *parasha* of the *mekoshesh*, the person who gathered wood on *Shabbat*, was likewise inevitable: the laws of *chilul Shabbat* would have been recorded regardless. But because this individual transgressed, his act became the vehicle through which the punishment was written down, and his transgression is embedded in the text forever. The merit of the daughters of Zelophehad and the guilt of the *mekoshesh* each determined the occasion and context through which God's will entered the Torah record, even though both teachings were destined to be recorded in any case.

---

## Leadership Balance

### Joshua's Dual Role

The *Gemara* addresses a tension in the *pesukim* concerning Yehoshua. In one place it says *ki ata tavo et ha'am hazeh* — for you will go with this people; in another, *ki ata tavi* — for you will bring them. Rabbi Yochanan explains: Moshe said to Yehoshua, *ata u'zekeinim shebador imahem* — you and the elders of the generation shall go together. That is what Moshe said. But the Holy One Blessed be He said to Yehoshua: *tul makel vehach al kadkadam* — take the staff and strike them on the head. *Ata tavi.* You lead; you do not merely accompany.

### One Leader

*Davar echad ledor ve'ein shenei devarim lador* — one leader for a generation, not two. Even though Yehoshua is not Moshe, he is the leader of his generation, and that role cannot be shared with the council of elders, even a distinguished one. He may and should consult; but he must own the leadership. The staff is his to wield. The public requires a single clear address of authority, not a committee.

---

## Court Summons

### Zimun Definition

The *Gemara* concludes with a *baraita*: *zimmun bishlosha* — a *zimmun* requires three. The immediate question: *mai zimmun?* — what is this *zimmun*? If it refers to *birkat zimmun* — the invitation to bentch together — that is already well known and not in need of restatement here. And if the *baraita* is simply elaborating by distinguishing *zimmun* from *birkat zimmun*, that distinction is immediately undermined by another *baraita* that lists them as one: *zimmun uvirkat zimmun bishlosha*. The *Gemara* therefore concludes that the *zimmun* under discussion here refers to something else entirely: *azmunei ledin* — summoning someone to a rabbinic court. This form of *zimmun* must be issued by, or in the name of, the full *beis din* of three.

### One Judge Summons

Rava's ruling establishes the operative rule: if the court is sitting and the court's messenger goes out and summons a party to appear *mishmeia dechad* — in the name of one judge only — *lo amar klum* — this counts for nothing. The summons is invalid and the recipient need not respond.

### Full Court Zimun

A valid *zimmun* to court requires the messenger to invoke the authority of *mishmeia dekulhu* — all the judges. A summons issued in the name of only one member of the *beis din* does not constitute a legitimate court summons and carries no binding obligation on the recipient.

### Court Days Presumption

There is, however, an important qualification. *Hanei mili belo yoma dedina* — the above applies when it is not a court day. On a regular day, a summons in the name of only one judge is insufficient because there is no presumptive understanding that the full court stands behind him. But *aval beyoma dedina* — on a day when the court is formally sitting (Rashi specifies Mondays and Thursdays, the regular court days) — even a summons issued *mishmeia dechad* is valid, because on that day it is understood that any message from a judge speaks on behalf of the sitting *beis din* as a whole. The context of the sitting court confers collective authority on the individual voice.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 8b

## Motzi Shem Ra Intro

### Case Classification

The daf begins near the bottom of 8a, approximately five lines from the end of the amud, dealing with the case of *motzi shem ra* — the husband who defames his wife by claiming she was not a virgin at the time of their marriage. The central question is how to classify this case for purposes of judicial composition: how many judges are required?

### Yerushalmi Two Views

The *Yerushalmi* offers two distinct explanations of the underlying dispute. The first frames the debate as concerning the case against the woman: the proceedings begin as *dinei mamonot*, a monetary case, but carry within them the potential to escalate into *dinei nefashot*, a capital case. The second frames it as concerning the case against the man — where from the outset there are two simultaneous dimensions, *dinei nefashot* against the witnesses (who, if proven *zomemim*, face execution) and *dinei mamonot* against the husband himself. These two framings provide a clean and transparent structure for the debate. As we shall see, the *Bavli*'s treatment of the same dispute is considerably more opaque.

---

## Ulla & La'az Debate

### Bavli Position

The *Bavli* records the dispute tersely: *ve-chachamim omrim motzi shem ra be-esrim u-shlosha* — the Sages hold that the case of *motzi shem ra* requires a court of twenty-three, while Rabbi Meir holds that three suffice. The *Gemara* immediately challenges the Sages' position: granted that there is an element of *dinei nefashot* embedded in this case, but so what? We are dealing with the *dinei mamonot* aspect of the proceedings, not the capital dimension. Why should that require twenty-three?

### Ulla's Framework

Ulla offers the following resolution: *chosheshin la-la'az kamipalgi* — the dispute turns on whether we are concerned about *la'az*, a kind of escalating rumor or public disclosure. Rabbi Meir holds *ein chosheshin la-la'az*, that there is no such concern, while the Sages hold *chosheshin la-la'az*, that there is. The *Bavli*, compared to the *Yerushalmi*, is far more cryptic here. The meaning of Ulla's formulation requires unpacking, and Rashi and Tosafot read it in fundamentally different ways.

### Rashi's Reading

Rashi understands the case as being against the woman. The proceedings begin as a monetary case adjudicated before three judges — that is Rabbi Meir's position. The Sages, however, are concerned that once word gets out — once people begin hearing that there is a case against this woman alleging she was not a virgin on her wedding night — witnesses may come forward and testify that she actually committed adultery. If that occurs, the case transforms from a monetary proceeding into a full capital case, requiring twenty-three. Rabbi Meir is not troubled by this possibility: if it happens, one can simply add judges at that point. The Sages, by contrast, say we must start with twenty-three now, because we are concerned the case will evolve into *dinei nefashot*. On this reading, *chosheshin la-la'az* means something like: we are worried that the word will spread and draw out witnesses, turning the case into a capital one.

### Tosafot Disputes

Tosafot is deeply dissatisfied with Rashi's reading on several grounds. First, Tosafot objects to Rashi's translation of the term *la'az* itself. Second, and more fundamentally, Tosafot insists that the phrase *motzi shem ra* throughout the *Gemara* refers specifically to the case against the man — not the case against the woman. This objection will be recognized immediately by anyone who has just studied the *Yerushalmi*: the identical pushback appears there, where the second opinion in the *Yerushalmi* protests that *motzi shem ra* means the case against the man, not against the woman. Rashi, in effect, reads like the first opinion in the *Yerushalmi*; Tosafot reads like the second.

### Tosafot Zomemin Theory

Tosafot therefore reframes the entire case as being against the man. But this creates a significant difficulty, because in the standard case against the man, his witnesses are proven *zomemim* — and it is in that moment that the man faces both lashes and monetary liability. If the witnesses are already definitively *zomemim*, there is nothing merely monetary about the initial proceedings; the capital dimension of the witnesses' fate is already established. To resolve this, Tosafot advances a bold and acknowledged *chidush*: he posits a case in which the husband's witnesses were not made *zomemim* but were instead neutralized — that is, contradicting witnesses came forward and testified on the woman's behalf, and the result was a standoff, two against two, with neither set of witnesses definitively discredited. In this scenario, Tosafot argues, the husband would still be required to pay the fine and receive lashes — despite the fact that it is entirely unclear he was lying, since it was simply a case of contradictory testimony. This is, Tosafot concedes, a remarkable position. But it allows Tosafot to construct a case in which the proceedings against the man begin as *dinei mamonot* while retaining the potential to become *dinei nefashot* if the husband's witnesses are subsequently proven *zomemim*.

### La'az Meanings

On Tosafot's reading, what does *chosheshin la-la'az* mean? Here, a crucial distinction emerges between two possible meanings of the phrase. The first meaning — Rashi's reading — is that *la'az* refers to the fear that news of the case will spread and attract witnesses, causing the case to escalate into a capital proceeding. This, one might note, is not obviously a bad thing. The second meaning, which Tosafot prefers and which was raised in discussion, is that *la'az* refers to concern for the honor of the original judges: if a court of three initially convenes and then it later becomes necessary to convene a court of twenty-three, people may say that the original judges were somehow inadequate — an embarrassment to the *beit din*. Under both meanings, the underlying question is the same: whether a *dinei mamonot* case might evolve into a *dinei nefashot* case. But they diverge on what specifically is feared about that evolution. Rabbi Meir, under the second reading, says: if we have to add judges, we will add them then — *ein chosheshin la-la'az*, we are not troubled by how that looks. The Sages say: we are troubled, and therefore we begin with twenty-three.

### Bavli-Yerushalmi Parallel

Tosafot makes an observation of striking methodological importance. Near the end of the extended Tosafot on 8b, in the passage beginning *ve-heivi ha-av edim ve-hizimum*, Tosafot cites a finding by the *Rashba* — here referring to Rabbi Shimshon, not the later Sefardic authority — that in the *Yerushalmi*, the very dispute between Rashi and Tosafot about how to read the *Bavli* is explicitly present as a dispute between *Amoraim*. One opinion in the *Yerushalmi* explains the case as being about the *kesubah*, paralleling Rashi's reading of the case against the woman; another explains it as being about the hundred-*sela* fine, paralleling Tosafot's reading of the case against the man. What this reveals is that the *Bavli*'s cryptic formulation is not merely ambiguous prose — it reflects an inherent ambiguity in the *sugya* itself. The *Yerushalmi* preserves that ambiguity transparently, as an explicit dispute; the debates of the *Rishonim* on how to read the *Bavli* are effectively the same debate, mapped onto a different layer of tradition. It is a pattern one encounters repeatedly: implicit divergences in reading a *Bavli* text turn out to parallel explicit disagreements recorded in the *Yerushalmi*.

---

## Rava's Honor Theory

### Rava Reframes

Rava offers a fundamentally different reading of the dispute. He opens with a broad claim: *kuli alma la-la'az lo chashinan* — everyone agrees that we are not concerned about a court of three devolving into or evolving into a court of twenty-three by virtue of public rumor. That question is off the table. The real dispute, Rava says, lies elsewhere.

### Honor of Judges

According to Rava, the debate concerns *chosheshin li-khodan shel rishonim* — concern for the honor of the original judges. This sounds superficially like one of Ulla's readings of *la'az*, but Rava inverts the direction of the problem entirely. It is not about adding judges; it is about dismissing them.

### Dispersal Scenario

The case Rava constructs is the following: a full court of twenty-three has already assembled to adjudicate what began as a potential capital case — the husband claimed his wife committed adultery and sought to bring witnesses to prove it. The court gathered *le-midon dinei nefashot*, to try a capital matter. But the case collapsed — the witnesses could not substantiate their claim — and the court began to disperse. At that point the husband calls out: do not all leave! Even if I cannot prove adultery, at least adjudicate the monetary question, whether my wife is entitled to her *kesubah*.

### Dismissal Dispute

Now the question is inverted: do we need to keep all twenty-three judges to hear a monetary question, or may the plaintiff make do with three, dismissing the other twenty? Rabbi Meir says twenty may be released; three remain to hear the *dinei mamonot*. The Sages say: since we started with twenty-three, we keep twenty-three — dispersing the majority of the court would be a slight to their honor. Ulla's reading strikes this analysis as more intuitive than Rava's, but Rava's reframing provides a coherent and internally consistent account of the dispute.

---

## Baraita & Cases

### Baraita Statement

The *Gemara* challenges the foregoing discussion by citing a *beraita*: the Sages say, if a monetary claim is brought, a court of three suffices; if a capital matter is brought, twenty-three are required. This *beraita* attributes to the Sages a position that sounds remarkably like Rabbi Meir's position in the *Mishnah* — namely, that a monetary case requires only three.

### Ulla's Problem

The difficulty is most acute for Ulla. Ulla's account of the debate is that the Sages and Rabbi Meir are arguing specifically about what happens when the case *begins* as a monetary proceeding — Rabbi Meir says three, the Sages say twenty-three because it may escalate. But now the *beraita* presents the Sages themselves as agreeing that a monetary case requires only three. How can Ulla's reading be sustained?

### Rava's Solution

Rava responds — identifying himself as one who explained this alongside *ari she-ba-chavura*, the lion of the group, Rabbi Chiya bar Avin — that the *beraita* must be read in a very specific context. The case is one in which the husband brought witnesses that his wife committed adultery, and then the father brought witnesses to prove those witnesses were *zomemim*. The proceedings have now shifted: we are no longer dealing with a case against the woman but with a case against the man. The question before the court is whether to extract money from the husband.

### Man vs Woman Cases

In the case against the man, Rava explains, a court of three is always appropriate. The husband is never going to face a capital proceeding — whatever happens, his liability is monetary. It is therefore accurate for the Sages to say: when the case is a *dinei mamonot* case against the man, three suffice. The phrase *u-vimkom nefashot be-esrim u-shlosha* — and where there is a capital dimension, twenty-three — most naturally refers to the case involving the witnesses or, alternatively, to the case against the woman, who genuinely risks a capital outcome if the proceedings against her take a certain turn. The *beraita*'s formulation thus does not contradict Ulla at all: it is simply addressing a different sub-case, the case against the man, where the Sages willingly grant that three suffice.

### Yerushalmi Parallel

This explanation closely mirrors the structure of the *Yerushalmi*, which we had already studied. The *Yerushalmi* oscillates between two framings: the case against the woman, where a capital outcome is always in the background and the Sages therefore insist on twenty-three, and the case against the man, where the monetary dimension is primary and a court of three is appropriate. Reading the *Bavli*'s *beraita* in light of the *Yerushalmi* now renders the passage considerably more transparent. The Sages who insist on twenty-three when the case is against the woman — because she herself could be subjected to capital punishment if adultery is proven — readily concede that when the case is against the man, who will never face a capital proceeding, three are sufficient. The *Yerushalmi*'s two framings and the *Bavli*'s resolution of the *beraita* are telling the same story.

---

## Alternative Readings

### Abaye & Hatra'ah

At this point the *sugya* takes a dramatic turn. The *Yerushalmi* would stop here; the *Bavli* does not. Having established the core positions, the *Gemara* deploys a characteristic move: it uses the ambiguity of the dispute in the *Mishnah* as an invitation to import a series of entirely distinct legal debates and read them into the disagreement between Rabbi Meir and the Sages. Each of the following readings is offered by a later *Amora* and is, as will become apparent, quite distant from what the *Mishnah* most plainly seems to be discussing.

Abaye offers the first alternative reading. He sets aside both the *la'az* question and the concern for the honor of the judges, asserting that everyone agrees on those points. The real dispute, Abaye says, concerns the specificity required in a *hatra'ah* — the formal warning that must be delivered to a defendant before a capital sentence can be imposed. The case, Abaye maintains, is one where the witnesses warned the woman that adultery is forbidden and punishable by death, but did not specify *which* form of death she would incur.

### Baraita Death Rules

The *Gemara* cites a *beraita* that establishes the general rule for capital cases: all those liable for death penalties in the Torah require a full court (*edah*) of twenty-three, open witnesses (not concealed, as in the case of the *meisit u-madiach*), and explicit *hatra'ah* — a warning that makes clear the person faces capital liability before the *beit din*. The ordinary standard is that the defendant must be informed he faces a death penalty.

### Meir No Capital

But Rabbi Yehuda — cited in that same *beraita* — goes further: the warning must specify *which* form of execution the person faces, not merely that death is at stake. Abaye maps this debate onto the *Mishnah*.
