Rabbi Meir holds that the warning here was delivered in the general form — death, without specification — and therefore, adopting the stringent position of Rabbi Yehuda, no valid capital case can proceed. Without a capital case, the proceedings are purely monetary, and three judges suffice. The Sages, by contrast, hold that the general-form warning is sufficient to support a capital proceeding, and therefore twenty-three are required. Whatever one thinks of this reading's fidelity to the *Mishnah*'s plain meaning, it is internally coherent.

### Pappa Chaverah

Rav Pappa offers yet another reading. He proposes that the case concerns a woman who is a *chaverah* — a learned woman, familiar with Jewish law. The dispute, he says, parallels the debate between Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages on the question of whether a *talmid chakham* requires *hatra'ah* at all before being subjected to capital punishment.

The reasoning behind the exemption from *hatra'ah* for a scholar is that the entire purpose of *hatra'ah* is to establish that the person acted with full intentionality — to distinguish *shogeg* from *mezid*. If someone is demonstrably learned, they obviously know what they are doing, and the warning adds nothing, much as one would not need to warn a criminal lawyer that what they are doing is a crime. The counterargument — which the other Sages maintain — is that *hatra'ah* serves purposes beyond establishing intent. One reason is that people can forget in a moment of passion, even if they know the law. Another, deeper rationale is that the warning converts the act into one of defiance: being told explicitly and still proceeding is an act of willful rejection of the law. The *Gemara* later in Sanhedrin will develop this further, articulating the principle of *ad she-yatir atzmo le-oso mita* — the requirement that the person effectively accept upon themselves the capital liability as a condition of the court's authority to execute. On Rav Pappa's reading, Rabbi Meir holds that a *chaverah* does not require *hatra'ah* and therefore is never rendered liable for death — the case remains monetary and three suffice. The Sages hold that even a *chaverah* requires *hatra'ah*, and since she received it, the case is a capital one requiring twenty-three.

### Ashi Wrong Warning

Rav Ashi proposes a different variant: the warning was delivered, but the content was wrong. The witnesses warned the woman that she faced *malkus* — lashes — not death. Since the warning was incorrectly formulated, she can never be subject to the death penalty. But the question then becomes: does a case of *malkus* require three judges or twenty-three? The *Gemara* notes that this parallels the dispute recorded later in our own *Mishnah*: the Mishnah there states that *malkus* requires three judges, but in the name of Rabbi Yishmael it was taught that it requires twenty-three. On Rav Ashi's reading, Rabbi Meir adopts the position that *malkus* requires three, and the Sages adopt the position that it requires twenty-three. This reading, one must acknowledge, fits the language of the *Mishnah* very poorly: the *Mishnah*'s Sages explicitly invoke *dinei nefashot* as the reason for requiring twenty-three, yet on Rav Ashi's reading the case has nothing to do with *dinei nefashot* at all. One could perhaps have read this more naturally as a case against the husband — who pays a hundred *shekel* and receives *malkus* — and then framed the debate simply as whether *malkus* requires three or twenty-three. But as it stands, the reading is notably strained.

### Ravina Relative

Ravina offers a final alternative in this series. The case, he says, involves three witnesses, one of whom turns out to be a relative — *karov* — or otherwise disqualified. The question is whether the presence of the invalid witness nullifies the testimony of the remaining two for purposes of a capital case, or whether the two valid witnesses can still function. Rabbi Meir says they cannot: following the position of Rabbi Yosi, the two valid witnesses may still testify in a monetary proceeding, but the invalid witness disqualifies the entire group from serving in *dinei nefashot* — leaving the case as a purely monetary matter, with three judges. The Sages say the case remains a capital one, paralleling the position of Rabbi (Rebbi), who, as we shall see in the following section, holds that an invalid witness disqualifies the group only under certain conditions of active participation.

---

## Akiva & Witnesses

### Akiva Third Witness

The foregoing discussion of *karov* and *pasul* draws the *Gemara* into a broader analysis of Rabbi Akiva's position on the relationship between multiple witnesses. Rabbi Akiva addresses the verse *al pi shnayim eidim o shlosha eidim yumat ha-met* — "by the mouth of two witnesses or three witnesses shall the dead be put to death." The redundancy is striking: if two witnesses suffice to impose capital liability, why mention three? Rabbi Akiva explains that the verse comes to be *machmir* — strict — with respect to the third witness, teaching that he receives the same punishment as the first two if they are all found to be *zomemim*. The argument that the third witness might raise — that his testimony was superfluous, that even without him the first two had already established the defendant's liability, and therefore he should not be punished — is rejected. The Torah links two and three witnesses together, treating the third as fully culpable alongside the first two.

The further implication Rabbi Akiva draws is a moral one: if the Torah treats one who peripherally attaches himself (*nitepal*) to sinners as bearing the full liability of the principal sinners, then all the more so should one who attaches himself to those performing a *mitzvah* receive the full reward of the principal actors. It is a finely structured *derash*.

### All Void Principle

Rabbi Akiva proceeds to derive from this linkage of two and three a broader principle of witness invalidation. Just as with two witnesses — if one of them is found to be *karov* or *pasul*, the entire testimony is void — so too with three: *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul, eidusam batelah*, if one of three witnesses is disqualified, the entire testimony is nullified. And this extends further: even if there are a hundred witnesses, and one proves to be invalid, all are disqualified. The verse's use of the word *eidim* — witnesses — treats the entire group as a single unit.

### Yosi Distinction

Rabbi Yosi limits this principle. He holds that *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* applies exclusively to *dinei nefashot* — capital cases. In *dinei mamonot* — monetary cases — if one of multiple witnesses is invalid, the remaining valid witnesses may continue to testify and their testimony stands. The invalid witness does not drag down the entire group in a monetary context.

### Rabbi Active Witness

Rabbi (Rebbi Yehuda ha-Nasi) takes a different approach. He holds that the principle applies to both *dinei mamonot* and *dinei nefashot* — the invalid witness can theoretically nullify the group in monetary cases as well. However, Rebbi qualifies his position: *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* applies only *be-zman she-histru bahen* — when the other witnesses actively demonstrated their participation, such as by delivering the *hatra'ah* warning. If they merely happened to be present and observed the event passively, without actively presenting themselves as witnesses, they are not treated as part of a unified group, and the invalidity of one does not contaminate the others.

Rebbi illustrates this with a case: two brothers are walking down the street with a third person and they witness a murder. If the brothers — who are *krovim* to each other and hence mutually disqualified — observed the event alongside the third witness, does that invalidate the third witness's testimony? Rebbi's answer is no, because passive observation does not constitute active membership in a witness group. The logic is that *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* presupposes a unified group of witnesses; passive co-presence does not create such a group.

### Tosafot Yichud

Tosafot on 9a raises the practical implications of Rebbi's principle for everyday life, asking why weddings and other public events at which relatives are present do not render the valid witnesses who also attend permanently disqualified, if those relatives intended to serve as witnesses. Tosafot resolves this by pointing to the principle of *yichud eidim* — the formal identification of witnesses as a distinct unit — and by citing the ruling in the first chapter of Makkot: a witness is only considered to have formally joined the witness group if he actively appears before the *beit din* to testify, not merely by intending to testify at the time of the witnessed event. Even the intention to serve as a witness at the time of the act, without subsequently appearing before a court, is insufficient to constitute one a formal member of the witness group. As Tosafot clarifies: *she-holchin u-me'idin kulam be-veit din* — they must actually go and testify before the *beit din* — and mere intent at the time of witnessing falls short of this threshold.

---

## Invalid Witness Reading

### Meir One Invalid

Returning to the application of these principles to the *Mishnah*, the *Gemara* now works through Ravina's reading in greater detail. The case has three witnesses, one of whom is *pasul*. Rabbi Meir, on this account, holds that the presence of the invalid witness means that the remaining two valid witnesses cannot serve in a capital case — the group is treated as invalidated for *dinei nefashot*. However, following Rabbi Yosi's distinction, the two valid witnesses can still function in a monetary proceeding. The case is therefore only a *dinei mamonot* case, and three judges suffice.

### Chachamim Two Valid

The Sages, by contrast, follow Rebbi's position. They argue that the invalid witness did not give the *hatra'ah* warning and did not actively participate in the witness group in the manner required by Rebbi's standard — he was not, in the relevant sense, an active member of the witness group at all. Accordingly, the remaining two valid witnesses are unaffected by his disqualification and can serve fully in a *dinei nefashot* proceeding. The case therefore remains a capital one, requiring twenty-three.

### Non-Witness Warning

Another variant is offered: the warning was given not by the witnesses themselves but by bystanders — others who were present but who were not testifying in the case. This too bears on whether the case can proceed as a capital matter. The debate is framed as paralleling Rabbi Yosi's position that *l'olam eino neherag ad she-yiyu pi shnayim eidim matrin bo* — the person can only be executed if the witnesses themselves delivered the warning, based on the verse *al pi shnayim eidim*, "by the mouth of two witnesses," implying that the warning must come from the mouths of those who are also testifying. Rabbi Meir holds that the warning delivered by non-witnesses does not suffice for a capital proceeding, and therefore the case remains monetary, with three judges. The Sages hold that the warning is valid regardless of who delivered it, and the case may proceed as a capital matter.

### Bedikos Contradiction

A final variant: the witnesses contradicted one another not in the *chakiyrot* — the core examination of when and where the event took place — but in the *bedikot*, the supplementary questioning on ancillary details. The *chakiyrot* are the examinations that can render witnesses *zomemim*: if witnesses cannot agree on the time and place of the event, their testimony is invalidated as a capital matter. But a contradiction in the *bedikot* — say, a discrepancy about the precise description of the fig tree under which the event occurred — is a different matter. The *Gemara* cites the famous case of Ben Zakkai, who would press witnesses on minute details such as the direction of the fig stems, seeking any inconsistency to disqualify them from capital testimony. The debate between Ben Zakkai and the Sages is whether such contradictions in the *bedikot* suffice to invalidate testimony for *dinei nefashot*. Rabbi Meir follows the view that they do — the testimony is void as a capital matter, leaving only a monetary case with three judges — while the Sages hold that such minor inconsistencies do not disqualify the witnesses, and the case proceeds as a capital matter with twenty-three.

It is worth pausing to take stock. The *Bavli* has now generated approximately ten distinct readings of the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages in the *Mishnah*. Of these, perhaps two — the ones paralleling the *Yerushalmi*'s explicit framings — are genuinely grounded in what the *Mishnah* most plainly seems to be debating. The remaining readings are, transparently, imports from other areas of the law, used to populate an ambiguous dispute with content drawn from elsewhere. This is the *Bavli* at its most characteristic: treating the uncertain space within a cryptic *Mishnaic* dispute as an opportunity to explore a range of other legal questions and to map the contours of broader principles across an array of connected domains.

---

## Double Aveira

### Classic Setup

The *sugya* concludes with a passage from Rav Yosef that returns to the classical scenario of *motzi shem ra*: the husband brings witnesses that his wife committed adultery; the father then brings witnesses who prove the husband's witnesses were *zomemim* — that is, that they were lying about the time or place of the alleged adultery and therefore could not have seen what they claimed to have seen.

### Witnesses Executed

The immediate consequence: the husband's witnesses are executed, since they sought to have the woman put to death and the law of *eidim zomemim* requires that they receive the punishment they sought to impose. However — and this is where *kim lei* enters — even though their false testimony would also have cost the woman her *kesubah*, the witnesses do not additionally pay the monetary amount. As Rashi reads it, this is an application of *kim lei*: the capital penalty they face is the greater punishment, and it subsumes the monetary liability.

### Reversal Case

Now the scenario reverses. The husband himself goes on the offensive: he brings a new set of witnesses who prove that the father's witnesses — the ones who had just gotten the husband's first witnesses condemned as *zomemim* — were themselves lying. The father's witnesses, it turns out, were the false ones all along.

### Both Penalties

The father's witnesses are now executed: they attempted to have the husband's legitimate witnesses condemned and killed as *zomemim*, and the law of *eidim zomemim* applies to them in kind. But crucially, they are also required to pay money to the husband — specifically, the hundred *shekel* that is the penalty of *motzi shem ra*. The husband's first witnesses, when they testified, faced the potential consequence of the hundred-*shekel* fine being imposed on the husband. When the father's witnesses falsely negated that testimony and caused the husband's witnesses to be condemned, they created a monetary liability for the husband. They now owe that money to him.

### Separate Crimes

Why does *kim lei* not apply here, allowing the father's witnesses to escape the monetary penalty by virtue of being executed? The answer is *mammon le-zeh ve-nefashot le-zeh* — the money is owed to one party and the capital liability is to another. The crime against the witnesses is adjudicated as a capital matter: the father's witnesses tried to have the husband's witnesses killed, and for that they are executed. The crime against the husband is adjudicated as a separate monetary matter: the father's witnesses caused the husband to incur a financial loss by falsely discrediting the testimony that would have established his right to the hundred-*shekel* payment. Because these are separate offenses against separate parties — each adjudicated independently — there is no single proceeding in which *kim lei* can operate to override the lesser penalty. Both penalties stand: the father's witnesses (or their estates) owe the husband one hundred *shekel*, and the father's witnesses are also put to death. The elegance of *mammon le-zeh ve-nefashot le-zeh* lies precisely in this separation: by disaggregating the offenses, the law ensures that neither the capital victim nor the monetary victim is left without remedy.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 9

## Yerushalmi Framework

### Woman vs. Man

Today's daf is 9, though we began at the bottom of 8a, approximately five lines from the bottom, where the Gemara deals with *motzi shem ra*. We have just seen the Yerushalmi present two explanations of the underlying debate. The first frames it as a case against the woman, which begins as *dinei mamonot* and may draw close to *dinei nefashot*. The second frames it as a case against the man, where from the outset there are simultaneously *dinei nefashot* — against the witnesses — and *dinei mamonot* against the man himself. Those are two distinct ways the Yerushalmi frames the question, and it presents them in clear, well-ordered terms. Let us now see what the Bavli has to say.

### Yerushalmi's Debate

The Mishnah records: *v'chachamim omrim motzi shem ra b'esrim v'shlosha* — the Chachamim say the case of *motzi shem ra* requires twenty-three judges, while Rabbi Meir holds it requires only three. The Gemara on 8a, five lines from the bottom, immediately challenges this: *v'chi yesh bo dinei nefashot mai havei?* — so what if there is an element of *dinei nefashot* in it? We are dealing with the *dinei mamonot* aspect. Why should that aspect require twenty-three?

The Bavli's response to this question, it must be said, is considerably more cryptic than the Yerushalmi's. The Gemara records: *amar Ulla bechoshshim l'la'az miflagi* — the debate between Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim turns on the question of whether we are concerned about *la'az*, about rumor or ill repute. Rabbi Meir holds *ein choshshim l'la'az* — we are not concerned about rumor. The Chachamim hold *choshshim l'la'az* — we are indeed concerned. But what exactly does this mean?

## Three vs. Twenty-Three

### Basic Positions

Reading with Rashi, who is easier to follow, the case is against the woman. Rabbi Meir says you begin with a court of three, since the immediate matter is one of *dinei mamonot*. The Chachamim say you must begin with twenty-three.

### Ulla's Choshshim L'la'az

Ulla's explanation is that the concern is this: once people begin hearing that there is a case against this woman — that she was not found to be a virgin on her wedding night, or whatever the allegation — that very publicity might cause witnesses to come forward and actually testify that she committed adultery after her betrothal. The case could thus evolve from a *dinei mamonot* proceeding into a capital one requiring twenty-three. Rabbi Meir says we need not worry about that possibility; it is a *mamonot* case and three judges suffice. The Chachamim say: precisely because it could become *dinei nefashot*, we must begin with twenty-three.

### Rashi's Reading

This, then, is Rashi's understanding: the debate is about whether a *dinei mamonot* case against the woman might evolve into a *dinei nefashot* case, and the term *choshshim l'la'az* captures the concern that the rumor will spread and bring witnesses forward. It is an admittedly curious use of *la'az*, since the "rumor" in question is not quite a slander — it is more about the word getting out and drawing additional witnesses. Nevertheless, that is how Rashi reads it.

### Tosafot's Critique

Tosafot is deeply unsatisfied with this reading on multiple grounds. First, Tosafot argues that *la'az* does not carry this meaning. Second — and here we hear a direct echo of the Yerushalmi — Tosafot maintains that the phrase *motzi shem ra* always refers to the case against the man, not against the woman. This is precisely the objection raised in the Yerushalmi against its first opinion: what do you mean the debate is about the woman? *Motzi shem ra* means the case against the man.

Tosafot therefore insists that the entire discussion concerns the case against the man. But then what is the *choshshim l'la'az* type of concern? To arrive at an answer, Tosafot performs considerable interpretive acrobatics. He proposes that there can be a case against the man even without the witnesses becoming *chayav misa*. How? Suppose the husband brought witnesses who testified that his wife committed adultery, and then other witnesses came and contradicted them — not as *zomemim*, not by saying "you were elsewhere," but simply by testifying to the contrary, thereby neutralizing the first set. Tosafot makes the striking claim — which he himself acknowledges is a significant *chiddush* — that even in such a case, where the witnesses are merely neutralized rather than refuted through *zomemut*, the husband would still be liable to pay the fine and receive lashes. The case thus begins as *dinei mamonot* against the man — his witnesses were neutralized — but could potentially turn into *dinei nefashot* if those witnesses were subsequently proven to be *zomemim*.

### Two Meanings

This discussion surfaces two distinct meanings of *choshshim l'la'az*. The first, which can be attributed to Rashi's approach, is that the rumor will spread and the case will actually turn into a capital one. The second is more subtle: even granting that the case might evolve, we are concerned about what it would look like to add judges after the fact — *k'vod* for the original judges. If we started with three and then had to augment to twenty-three, people might say: something must have gone wrong with the original court. Rabbi Meir says *ein choshshim l'la'az* — if we have to add judges later, we add them and we do not worry about how it reflects on the original three. The Chachamim say *choshshim l'la'az* — to avoid that indignity to the first judges, we begin with twenty-three from the outset.

What both meanings share is the underlying concern that a *dinei mamonot* case might become a *dinei nefashot* case. The question that divides them is: does that possibility require us to start with twenty-three from the beginning, or can we deal with it if and when it arises?

An important observation emerges at the end of this Tosafot, on 8b. Tosafot writes: *u'vi'Yerushalmi matza Rashba* — that Rav Shimshon found in the Yerushalmi a debate among Amoraim. Some explain it in terms of the case against her — *k'id'mifaresh b'kuntres*, as Rashi explains — and some explain it in terms of the case against him — *k'id'mifaresh Rabbeinu Tam*. Tosafot is pointing out that the very debate between Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam over how to read the Bavli is itself the same debate recorded explicitly in the Yerushalmi. This is a pattern that recurs throughout the literature: disputes among the *Rishonim* about how to read the Bavli reflect ambiguities in the Bavli's text itself, ambiguities that may be spelled out explicitly in a parallel Yerushalmi passage. The Yerushalmi, then, actually provides a far clearer framing of the underlying question. In our Gemara it is much less transparent. But let us return to the Bavli.

## Rava's Framework

### Rava's Reversal

Four lines from the bottom of 8a, we pick up again: *amar Ulla b'chosheshin l'la'az kamipalgi* — and then the Gemara introduces Rava's alternative. *Rava amar kuli alma l'la'az lo chashinan* — everyone agrees we are not concerned about three becoming twenty-three. The debate, says Rava, is something altogether different.

### Honor Concern

*V'hacha b'chivodan shel rishonim kamipalgi* — the dispute is about concern for the honor of the first judges, but in a scenario that is the reverse of what Ulla described. *V'hacha b'mai askinan k'gon d'ichnisu bei esrin v'tlasa* — the case began with a court of twenty-three, assembled *l'meidan dinei nefashos*. Then *v'izdu* — the court dispersed, because it became apparent that the husband would not be able to produce proof that his wife committed adultery. At that point the husband says: fine, I cannot prove adultery, but at least adjudicate the monetary question and let me establish that she forfeits her *ketubah*. So the question becomes: can twenty of the judges go home, leaving three to handle the *dinei mamonot*? *Rabbi Meir says yes — let twenty go and three remain. The Chachamim say: since we began with twenty-three, we keep twenty-three. To dismiss twenty of them would be a slight to their dignity. That is the *la'az* here — not that people will gossip about the woman, but that it would be disrespectful to dismiss the majority of a court that was properly convened. This is a fascinating read, though perhaps less intuitive than Ulla's.

## Baraita Reconciliati (II)

### Apparent Contradiction

The Gemara then raises a challenge from a *braisa*: *v'chachamim omrim tavo'u mammon* — three; *tovu nefashos be-esrim ushlosha* — twenty-three. This sounds as though the Chachamim agree with Rabbi Meir: if the case involves only *dinei mamonot*, three suffice. But that seems to be exactly what Rabbi Meir said. In what sense, then, do the Chachamim disagree at all? This *braisa* appears to undermine Ulla's entire reading of the debate.

## Rava's Framework (II)

### Resolution

The Gemara notes: *bishlama le-Rava* — for Rava, this *braisa* works nicely. *Tovu mamon techila* — if the case began as a *dinei mamonot* matter from the start, everyone agrees: three. *Tovu nefashos techila* — if it began as a capital case but the witnesses did not materialize and you are left with a monetary question, then even for that remaining monetary matter you keep twenty-three, because it was initiated as a capital case. For Rava, this resolves cleanly: the Chachamim are saying precisely that — if it started as *mamonot*, we agree to three; if it started as *nefashot*, we keep twenty-three even if all that remains is a monetary issue. But *ella le-Ulla kashya* — for Ulla it is difficult. On Ulla's reading, the whole point is that the case starts as *mamonot* and might evolve into *nefashot*, and that is precisely what causes the Chachamim to require twenty-three. How then does this *braisa* show the Chachamim agreeing to three when it begins as *mamonot*?

## Baraita Reconciliati (II)

### Rava & Chiya Bar Abba

The Gemara records Rava's response: *ani ve-arya she-bachabura* — "I and the lion of our group have explained this *braisa* consistently with Ulla." Who is this lion? *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba*.

### Case Against Man

Here is the resolution: *hacha be-mai askinan she-heivi ha-ba'al eidim she-zinta ve-heivi ha-av eidim ve-hizimum* — the husband brought witnesses that she committed adultery, and the father brought witnesses who proved those witnesses were *zomemim*. We have now shifted from a case against the woman to a case against the man. His witnesses have been exposed as *zomemim*, and the question is how to adjudicate the monetary claim against him. *Ba likvos mamon mi-ba'al bishlosha* — when the court is convened to extract money from the husband, that requires three. The reason is that a case against the man himself can never escalate into *dinei nefashot*; it will always remain monetary. So the Chachamim readily agree: when it is the case against the man, three suffice.

### Case Against Woman

*U've-makom nefashos be-esrim ushlosha* — but when the case is against the woman, in a setting where *nefashot* are implicated, it requires twenty-three. Because the woman herself could potentially face a death penalty if the case evolves into one of capital adultery, we always demand twenty-three from the outset.

### Yerushalmi Mirroring

What the Bavli has now arrived at is precisely the same two-way framework the Yerushalmi laid out explicitly at the start. The Yerushalmi's first approach: it is a case against the woman, which begins as *mamonot* but may evolve toward *nefashot* — and therefore we debate whether to start with three or twenty-three. The Yerushalmi's second approach: it is a case against the man, which has *nefashot* implications for his witnesses but is always only *mamonot* for him — and therefore the debate is resolved differently depending on whom we are adjudicating against.

The Bavli arrives at this same bi-directional framework, but through a far more labyrinthine route. Once we have read the Yerushalmi, the Bavli's final resolution reads much more clearly. The case against the man is always three; the case against the woman, who might herself be condemned to death, is always twenty-three. Just as in the Yerushalmi, one could argue either direction — the woman's case more urgently demands twenty-three because she herself faces death; conversely, in the man's case someone is always going to be executed (his witnesses), suggesting that too should require twenty-three. The Bavli resolves it by distinguishing which party is actually being adjudicated.

A brief clarification is worth noting here: if she is found not to have been a virgin, that alone does not bring a death penalty. The death penalty applies only if she committed adultery after the betrothal — *kiddushin* — meaning during the year or so between betrothal and the actual marriage (*nisu'in*), when she was already legally bound to her husband. If the act occurred before the betrothal, it is only a question of *ketubah*. And of course the *sotah* procedure, triggered by a husband's jealousy, is an entirely separate framework — one that involves a ritual outcome rather than a judicial death sentence, though witnesses to actual adultery could always bring a capital case independently.

## Alternative Readings

### Abaye's Warning

At this point the Gemara could have stopped. The Yerushalmi stops here, having established the two primary frameworks for understanding the debate. But this is where the Bavli's distinctive character asserts itself. Because the underlying dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim is not fully transparent from the text of the Mishnah alone, the Bavli — particularly its later Amoraim — takes the opportunity to import other debates entirely and propose that our Mishnah's dispute might really be about any number of other legal questions. These readings are, frankly, imported from elsewhere and are largely absent from the Yerushalmi, but they allow the Gemara to expand the discussion in characteristic Babylonian fashion.

*Abaye amar dechulei alma chaishinan l'la'az* — Abaye says forget the question of whether we are concerned about *la'az*, and forget the question of the honor of the original judges. *Hacha b'mai askinan kegon d'atru bah stam* — the case is against her, as we have been assuming, but those who warned her gave the *hatra'ah* generically, without specifying which mode of death she would deserve if convicted. They simply said: if you commit adultery you are *chayav misa* — they did not specify which *misa*.

### Death Penalty Baraita

This distinction is grounded in the following *braisa*: the *Tosefta* discusses the *mesit u'madiach* — the one who seduces others to idolatry — where a uniquely concealed form of warning is used, almost entrapment-like. But regarding all other capital crimes in the Torah, *v'sha'ar kol chayavei mitot she-baTorah ein mamitim otam ela b'edah* — a full court of twenty-three is required — *v'edim* — witnesses who are present openly, not hidden — *v'hatra'ah* — and explicit warning — *v'ad sheyodi'uhu shehu chayav mitah b'veit din* — and the warning must convey not merely that the act is forbidden but that it carries a court-administered death penalty.

*Rabbi Yehuda omer ad sheyodi'uhu b'eizo mitah hu neherag* — Rabbi Yehuda goes further: it is not enough to say you will be *chayav misa*; the warning must specify which form of death. This is the crux of the debate Abaye is importing. According to Rabbi Yehuda, if the warning did not specify the mode of death, there can be no capital sentence. So on this reading, Rabbi Meir holds like Rabbi Yehuda: the witnesses warned her only that she would be *chayav misa* without specifying the method, and therefore she can never actually be executed — the case will only ever result in a monetary outcome, and three judges suffice. The Chachamim disagree: even a generic warning suffices for a capital sentence, and therefore the case could result in death, warranting twenty-three. This has nothing to do with the plain meaning of the Mishnah's dispute, but it is a coherent legal reading.

### Rav Pappa's Chaverah

*Rav Pappa amar hacha b'ishah chaverah askinan* — Rav Pappa says: the case involves a *chaverah*, a learned woman, and no warning at all was given to her. The debate then maps onto the dispute between Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbanan: *chaver ein tzarich hatra'ah* — a *talmid chacham* does not require warning, because the purpose of *hatra'ah* is to distinguish intentional from unintentional sin, and a knowledgeable person clearly understands the gravity of what they are doing. One does not need to warn a criminal lawyer that what they are doing is illegal. The Rabbanan disagree and require warning even for the learned, for any of several reasons: one might forget even what one knows in a moment of passion; or the purpose of *hatra'ah* is not merely to establish intent but to make the sin an act of defiance — *af al pi chen*, the person says, I proceed anyway; or, as the Gemara will develop later in Sanhedrin, *ad she'yatir atzmo le'otah mita* — the person must effectively grant the court license to take their life, which the explicit acceptance of the warning accomplishes.

On this reading: Rabbi Meir holds that a *chaverah* requires no warning, and therefore without *hatra'ah* she will never be found liable to death — three judges. The Chachamim require warning even for the learned, so she could in principle be executed — twenty-three.

### Rav Ashi's Lashes

*Rav Ashi amar kegon de'asru bah bemalkut velo asru bah bekatalah* — Rav Ashi proposes yet another scenario: the witnesses warned her that she would receive *malkut* — lashes — but did not warn her of the death penalty. Since one cannot be executed on the basis of a warning about a lesser punishment, she can never receive the death penalty. The question then becomes: does *malkut* require three judges or twenty-three? This maps onto the later Mishnah in our tractate: *malkut bishloshah mishum Rabbi Yishmael amru be'esrim ushloshah* — lashes normally require three, but Rabbi Yishmael says twenty-three. This is a very weak reading, it must be said, because the language of the Mishnah itself attributes the Chachamim's position to the presence of *dinei nefashot* — and on this read, there is no *nefashot* dimension at all. One might wonder why the Mishnah did not simply frame this as a debate about the case of the man, who also receives *malkut* and pays the hundred-shekel fine. But Rav Ashi is simply adding yet another possibility to the growing list.

### Ravina's Invalid Witness

*Ravina amar kegon shenimtza echad min ha'edim karov upasul* — Ravina proposes that the case involves three witnesses who testified that she committed adultery, and one of them turned out to be a relative and therefore disqualified. Is she then liable to the death penalty, or is the capital dimension eliminated entirely?

## Invalid Witnesses

### Rabbi Akiva Principle

This question leads into a substantial independent discussion. The background is the principle derived by Rabbi Akiva. The Torah says *al pi shenayim edim o sheloshah edim yumat hamet* — why mention three witnesses if two already suffice to impose a death sentence? Rabbi Akiva answers: it comes to be strict regarding the third witness. If Reuven, Shimon, and Levi all testified and were later proven to be *zomemim*, Levi might argue: even without my testimony, Reuven and Shimon had already made the defendant *chayav misa* — my addition changed nothing, so why should I be punished as a *zomem*? The Torah therefore links three to two to say: Levi receives the same punishment as the other two, even though his testimony was not strictly necessary. By the same logic, *nitpal le'ovrei averah ke'ovrei averah* — one who attaches himself peripherally to wrongdoers is treated as a principal wrongdoer. And by *kal v'chomer*, one who attaches himself peripherally to a group performing a *mitzvah* — say, joining twenty others on their way to do *bikur cholim* — receives the same reward as the principal actors.

Beyond the individual witness, this reasoning establishes that when witnesses are linked — two or three or even one hundred — they function as a single unit. And therefore: *u'mah shnayim nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul eidusam bateilah* — just as with two witnesses, if one is disqualified the entire testimony is void (since you are left with only one), so too with three — if one is disqualified, all are void. *V'minayin she-afilu meiah* — and how do we know this extends to a hundred? *Talmud lomar eidim* — "witnesses" — they are treated as one indivisible unit.

### Yosi vs. Akiva

But how far does this principle extend? Here the debate opens. *Amar Rabbi Yose: b'meh devarim amurim b'dinei nefashos* — Rabbi Yose limits the principle of *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul* to capital cases. *Aval b'dinei mammonos tiska-yeim eidus b'sha'ar* — but in monetary cases, the valid witnesses among the group retain their validity even if one of them is disqualified. They are not treated as a single unit; the kosher ones stand on their own.

### Rabbi's Conditions

Rabbi (*Rebbi*) disagrees with the very distinction Rabbi Yose draws. *Echad dinei mammonos v'echad dinei nefashos* — even in monetary cases, if one witness is disqualified, all are invalidated. However, Rabbi introduces his own qualifier: *v'eimasai? Bizman she-hisru bahen* — this applies only when the witnesses actively participated by delivering the *hatra'ah*, the warning. This active participation identifies them as a unified witness group, and the disqualification of one then invalidates all. The corollary is that if they did not give the warning — if there was no act that singled them out as a collective — then the disqualification of one does not sweep away the rest, since they were never constituted as a unit in the first place. Rabbi's famous illustration: *mah ya'asu shnei achim b'soch echad she-harag es hanefesh* — what should two brothers do who happen to be walking with a friend when a murder is committed before their eyes? They did nothing to identify themselves as witnesses. Their mere passive presence should not disqualify the third witness by making all three a unit that collapses when the two brothers are disqualified as relatives.

### Tosafot's Questions

Tosafot picks up on this and raises a critical question. Tosafot notes that the mechanism of warning works to identify a group as a collective *eidut* — but warning is relevant only in capital cases. How does this operate in monetary cases or in matters like *gittin* and *kiddushin*? The Gemara in the first chapter of Makkot supplies a partial answer: the court would ask the witnesses, *l'as-hodei asisu o l'michzei asisu* — did you come to testify or did you come merely to observe? If they declared their intention to testify, then *nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul eidusam bateilah* — the group is constituted as a unit and the disqualification of one invalidates all. If they said they came only to watch, then *mah ya'asu shnei achim* applies — they are not a collective.

But the Ri (*Rabbeinu Yitzchak*) goes further: even the declaration of intent to testify is not sufficient. *Nira l'Ri de-mishum she-nis-kavnu l'ha-id lo amrinan nimtza echad meihem karov o pasul eidusam bateilah* — merely intending to bear witness, even consciously, does not create the collective unit. What is required, says the Ri, is that they actually appear in *beit din* together and testify: *ela she-holchin u'me-idin kulam b'Beis Din* — it is their joint appearance in court that fuses them into a single *eidut*. For *re'iyah l'chudei* — mere seeing of the event, even with conscious intent to serve as a witness — does not suffice. The Ri's proof: *d'ei lo teima hachi kol gittin keshenosnim osam bifnei krovim o psulim yihyu psulim im nis-kavein ha-echad* — if intent alone were enough to form a collective, then any *get* given in the presence of relatives who happened to intend to observe would be invalidated whenever one of them is disqualified. That is clearly untenable.

This opens a rich question in the *Rishonim*: what exactly is the threshold that constitutes a person as a *witness* for purposes of *nimtza echad karov o pasul*? Is it passive presence? Conscious intent? Delivery of a warning? Appearance in *beit din*? These conditions operate differently across different legal contexts — capital cases, monetary cases, *kiddushin*, *gittin* — and no single answer covers them all.

### Applied to Mishnah

Returning to our Mishnah: on Ravina's reading, there were three witnesses. One was a relative and disqualified. Rabbi Meir holds like Rabbi Yose — the invalid witness eliminates the capital dimension but leaves the monetary case intact. The two remaining valid witnesses can still function as *eidim* for a *dinei mamonot* claim, so the case is adjudicated before three judges. The Chachamim hold like Rabbi (*Rebbi*): the invalid witness does not sweep away the remaining two for *dinei nefashot*, provided the invalid witness did not actively participate in the warning. Since the disqualified witness did not give *hatra'ah*, the other two are not constituted together with that witness as a unified group. They retain full validity for *dinei nefashot*, and therefore the case requires twenty-three.

## Further Readings

### Warning Source

*V'ee ba'is eima she'hisru ba'acherim v'lo hisru ba'edim* — yet another proposed reading: others gave the warning, but the witnesses themselves did not. The question here is whether the witnesses must deliver the *hatra'ah* personally. This debate maps onto Rabbi Yose, who derives from *al pi shenei edim* that the witnesses themselves must be the ones to warn: *l'olam eino neherag ad she'yiyu shenei edim masrin bo* — a person can never be executed unless two witnesses delivered the warning themselves. On this reading, Rabbi Meir holds like Rabbi Yose — the warning delivered by others is invalid and there can be no death sentence, so three suffice. The Chachamim disagree and hold that a warning from others is adequate, making a capital case possible and requiring twenty-three.

### Contradiction Types

*D'iskachashi b'vedikos v'lo iskachashi b'chakirosh* — a final proposed reading: the witnesses contradicted one another in the *badikos*, in the circumstantial details of what happened, but not in the *chakirot*, the essential interrogation about when and where. The distinction is significant. It is the *chakirot* — the time and place — that are fundamental to testimony, and it is contradiction there that renders witnesses invalid; moreover, it is consistency on time and place that opens the door to *zomemut*, since counter-witnesses can claim "you were elsewhere at that time." Contradiction in *badikos*, the fine details, is a different matter.

### Ben Zakkai Method

*Ma'aseh u'vadak Ben Zakkai b'uktzei te'einim* — the Gemara recalls that Ben Zakkai would probe witnesses with minute questions: if the alleged crime occurred under a fig tree, he would ask whether the stems of the figs pointed north or south, whether they were sharp or smooth. The point was to find any discrepancy that might unravel the testimony, since the Gemara is always cautious about *dinei nefashot*. The question is whether a contradiction in such picayune details — *badikos* rather than *chakirot* — is sufficient to disqualify witnesses entirely. Ben Zakkai says yes; the Chachamim say no. On this reading of our Mishnah, Rabbi Meir holds like Ben Zakkai: the contradiction in *badikos* disqualifies the witnesses for capital purposes, leaving only a monetary case — three. The Chachamim say a contradiction in *badikos* does not disqualify them, the testimony stands for capital purposes, and twenty-three are required.

In all, this gives us approximately ten different readings of the Mishnah's dispute, of which the vast majority are imported from entirely other legal debates. The genuine interpretive work was done with Ulla and Rava at the outset, paralleling what we saw in the Yerushalmi. Everything that follows is the Bavli's characteristic mode of using a textual ambiguity as a canvas on which to project and explore the full range of relevant legal debates — with no pretense, in many cases, that this is what the Mishnah was originally about.

## False Witnesses

### First Inversion

The Gemara concludes with a compact but striking discussion of the *zomemim* scenario at the heart of *motzi shem ra*. The husband brings witnesses testifying that his wife committed adultery. The father brings witnesses who prove that the husband's witnesses are *zomemim* — false witnesses. *Eidei haba'al neheragin* — the husband's witnesses are executed, since they tried to have her killed.

### First Consequence

*Ve'ein meshalmin mammon* — they do not also pay money. Even though their testimony, had it stood, would have also caused her to forfeit her *ketubah*, they are not liable for that monetary harm as well. Rashi explains this on the basis of *kim lei* — when one is liable to death, the monetary obligation is subsumed within the greater penalty.

### Second Inversion

*Chazar ve'hevi haba'al eidim ve'hizimum le'eidei ha'av* — the case then reverses again. The husband produces a new set of witnesses who prove that the father's witnesses — the very ones who had the first group condemned as *zomemim* — were themselves lying. The father's witnesses had falsely accused legitimate witnesses of being *zomemim* and had tried to have those witnesses killed.

### Second Consequence

*Eidei av neheragin* — the father's witnesses are now executed. *U'meshalmin mammon* — and they also pay money, namely one hundred shekels to the husband. Their false testimony, if accepted, would have exposed the husband's legitimate witnesses to death and forced the husband himself to pay the hundred-shekel fine of *motzi shem ra*. Now that they are proven to be *zomemim*, they pay that fine themselves — and are also executed.

### Two Crimes

Why do the father's witnesses pay money in addition to being executed, when the husband's witnesses in the first round did not? The answer is *mammon le'zeh u'nefashos le'zeh* — the monetary crime and the capital crime were committed against two different parties. The father's witnesses committed a capital offense against the husband's witnesses — they tried to have them executed. And they committed a monetary offense against the husband — they tried to impose a hundred-shekel fine upon him. These are two entirely separate wrongful acts, directed at two different victims, adjudicated in two separate proceedings. There is therefore no *kim lei*; the cases do not collapse into one another. Each must be answered for independently — and accordingly, the father's witnesses both lose their lives and, before that sentence is carried out, their estate pays the hundred shekels to the husband.

# Sanhedrin 10

## Palginin Dibbura

### Rav Yosef Intro

The daf opens — five lines from the bottom of amud bet — with a continuation of Rav Yosef's rulings concerning *edim zomemin*. The previous teaching had established that when false witnesses attempt both to execute a woman and to cause her to forfeit her *ketubbah*, and both consequences fall upon the same victim, the principle of *kim lei b'drabba minei* applies: only the weightier punishment — death — is imposed and the monetary obligation is absorbed. However, where the monetary obligation runs to a different party than the one for whom the witnesses face execution, the principle of *mamon vezeh v'nefashos zeh* obtains, and both consequences are enforced simultaneously. It is against this backdrop that Rav Yosef now introduces a related but distinct case.

### Mishkav Zachar Victim

*V'amar Rav Yosef: ploni riv'o l'onsho* — Reuven comes forward and testifies that Shimon subjected him to anal intercourse against his will, that is, he was raped. The sin at issue is *mishkav zachar*, and the preliminary question is whether Reuven himself is a qualified witness. Since the event involved him directly, is he not in the position of a *karov* — a relative or interested party — whose testimony about that very event is inadmissible?

Rav Yosef rules: *hu v'acher mitztarfin l'horgo* — Reuven and one additional witness may combine their testimony and bring Shimon to execution. The victim of a sexual violation is not disqualified as a witness against the perpetrator. Surprisingly, the victim is not considered a *pasul* witness, not regarded as a *karov* to the case. The reasoning appears to be connected to the nature of the transgression: the sin of *mishkav zachar* is not fundamentally a harm done *to* the victim — its prohibition inheres in the act itself. The victim who was coerced is therefore not truly a party to the offense in the legal sense, and his testimony against the perpetrator is valid.

### Willing Participant

The *Gemara* immediately introduces the contrasting scenario: *im b'retzono* — what if Reuven testifies that Shimon had intercourse with him and that he was a willing participant? In that case, *rasha hu*: Reuven is by his own testimony confessing to a transgression for which he himself bears liability, one that carries *chiyuv mita*. The Torah states *al tashes rasha ed* — do not place a wicked person as a witness — and since accepting his testimony about Shimon necessarily entails accepting his testimony about himself, and that testimony renders him a *rasha*, he is disqualified. Both aspects of this ruling make sense: the greater *chiddush* is the first case, where the victim's standing as a valid witness is established despite his direct involvement in the events described.

### Rava's Doctrine

Rava now introduces his pivotal principle: *adam karov eitzel atzmo v'ein adam meisim atzmo rasha* — a person is considered *karov* to himself, just as one cannot testify concerning a close relative, one cannot testify concerning oneself. Therefore, that portion of Reuven's statement in which he declares his own willing participation is legally inadmissible — not merely unreliable, but structurally excluded from consideration, as though it were never said. What remains is his testimony concerning Shimon alone. This is the doctrine the *Rishonim* identify as *palginan dibura*: we split his words, discard the self-incriminating portion as legally null, and accept the remainder as valid testimony against Shimon. By this mechanism, Shimon may be convicted on the basis of Reuven's testimony combined with that of another witness, because as far as the court is concerned, Reuven testified only about Shimon — what he said about himself never entered the evidentiary record.

It bears acknowledgment that reading these *Gemaros* today — with an understanding of same-sex attraction and the genuine personal struggles faced by a portion of the community — these discussions cannot remain purely abstract. They speak to real human lives and profound challenges, and that dimension deserves to be acknowledged.

### Adultery Case

Rava continues with a parallel case involving adultery: *ploni ba'al ishti* — a husband testifies that a certain man, Shimon, had intercourse with his wife. Rava rules: *hu v'acher mitztarfin lehorgo aval lo leharga* — he and another witness may combine to execute Shimon, but the wife may not be executed on the basis of the husband's testimony. The husband is a *karov* to his wife and cannot testify against her. The *chiddush*, however, is that his disqualification vis-à-vis his wife does not contaminate his testimony vis-à-vis Shimon. Once again, *palginan dibura*: what he says about Shimon stands on its own, while what he says about his wife is simply set aside.

### Doctrine Debate

The *Gemara* challenges: *mai kamashmalan?* Is this not identical to what was already established? The *Gemara* responds that the new case is needed to forestall a possible objection: one might have thought that while *adam karov eitzel atzmo* holds — a man is considered *karov* to himself — we would not say *adam karov eitzel ishto* for the purposes of *palginan dibura*. That is, perhaps the principle that renders self-incriminating testimony completely inadmissible does not extend to testimony concerning one's wife. Hence the case is needed to teach that it does.

This raises a further question: what exactly would the *halacha* have been had we *not* applied *palginan dibura* here? Rashi and Tosafos take a surprising position: without *palginan dibura*, the husband's testimony would actually have been accepted in its entirety — both against Shimon *and* against the wife, and she would have been executed. The reasoning would be that since the testimony against Shimon is valid, and the wife is a separate individual rather than the husband himself, a kind of *migu* logic would operate and the testimony would be bundled together and applied to both. This reading is widely acknowledged to be extremely difficult: how could testimony that is fundamentally inadmissible against the wife somehow become valid through this bundling mechanism? Using *migu* to take a person's life in this manner seems unacceptable.

Other *Rishonim* take the opposite position. Without *palginan dibura*, the testimony would be thrown out entirely. The logic: testimony about oneself is not merely *pasul* — it is not testimony at all, because *adam karov eitzel atzmo* renders it structurally non-existent. Testimony about one's wife, however, though *pasul*, is still *an act of testimony* — it is a real statement about another person, albeit an inadmissible one. Therefore, unlike the case involving oneself, the husband's words about his wife cannot simply be ignored; they constitute a flawed act of testimony. And since that flawed testimony is part of the very same statement as his testimony against Shimon, the entire statement becomes tainted, and Shimon goes free. *Kamashmalan*, therefore, is that *palginan dibura* applies: we excise the inadmissible portion — whether it concerns the witness himself or his wife — and allow what remains to stand as valid testimony against Shimon.

A further case bearing on *palginan dibura* involves the *na'ara me'orasa*. Rava rules: if witnesses testify that Shimon had intercourse with a *na'ara me'orasa* without specifying which woman, and those witnesses are subsequently found *zomemin*, they are executed but pay no money — there is no identified person to whom a monetary payment would be owed. But if they say *bito shel ploni* — they specifically identify Levi's daughter — then the case changes: *neheragin u'meshalmin mamon*, they are executed and also pay. Why? Because the daughter faces execution for her own alleged willing participation, while the *ketubbah* benefit that would have been destroyed by the testimony belonged not to her but to her father. Since the betrothal has not yet ripened into full marriage, *kol shevach ne'ureiha le'aviha* — all benefit from the daughter in her youth belongs to the father. The person for whom they are executed — Shimon and the daughter — is different from the person to whom they owe money — the father. This is *mamon lazeh v'nefashos lazeh*, and *kim lei* does not apply.

### Bestiality Case

Rava introduces a further ruling: *ploni rava ha-shor v'huzmu* — witnesses testify that Shimon committed bestiality with Reuven's ox, and they are found *zomemin*. In that case, *neheragin u'meshalmin mamon*: they are executed for having sought to have Shimon put to death, and they pay money for having sought to deprive Reuven of his animal. Again the twin principles apply: *mamon lazeh v'nefashos lazeh*, and so both consequences are enforced.

The *Gemara* asks: *ha tu lama li?* Why was this additional case necessary given what was already established? The answer is that this case was included not for its own ruling — which is indeed straightforward — but because it serves as the necessary foundation for Rava to pose a related but unresolved question, the case of *palginan dibura* when property is at stake.

### Property Question

*De'va'ei Rava: ploni rava shori mahu?* — Reuven himself, together with another witness, testifies that Shimon committed an act of bestiality with Reuven's own ox. Here the question crystallizes: we have established that *adam karov eitzel atzmo* — a person is *karov* to himself — and that *palginan dibura* allows us to split his testimony and ignore what implicates him directly or through his wife. But what about testimony that causes harm to his own property? The *Gemara* frames it as two possibilities: *mi amrinan adam karov eitzel atzmo v'ein adam karov eitzel mamono* — do we say that a person is *karov* to himself but not to his property? Or do we say *adam karov eitzel mamono* — that a person is also considered sufficiently close to his property that the same principle applies?

The stakes require clarification. The *Gemara* notes that the execution of the ox is not merely a monetary matter — *kemitat habalim kach mitat hashor* — the animal's death is a form of *dinei nefashos*, parallel to the capital liability of the human perpetrator. So the question is not simply whether he is prejudiced financially. He is testifying about an event that will cause the destruction of his own property through a legal process analogous to capital punishment. Does *palginan dibura* operate in such a case — separating his testimony about Shimon from its consequences for his own ox — or does the witness's connection to his property prevent that separation?

### Resolution

*Hadar pashata be'aya* — Rava himself resolved his question: *adam karov eitzel atzmo v'ein adam karov eitzel mamono*. The principle of *palginan dibura* applies when testimony implicates the witness himself or his wife — those are cases where the inadmissible portion is treated as though it does not exist as testimony. But when testimony damages the witness's property, we do not say the same. The witness is *nogea badavar* with respect to his ox, and that connection is real — but it is not the kind of connection that renders his words legally null. His statement about the ox constitutes actual testimony; it is simply *pasul* testimony. And as the earlier analysis showed, testimony that is *pasul* — as opposed to legally nonexistent — cannot simply be ignored; it contaminates the whole.

According to Rashi and Tosafos, the consequence of *not* applying *palginan dibura* would be the opposite: since the testimony about Shimon is accepted, and the witness is not sufficiently close to his property to render that portion of the testimony null, the entire statement is accepted, and the ox is executed as well — a bundling of the testimony that works in favor of conviction. The alternative reading, consistent with the other *Rishonim*, is that because the portion concerning the ox is *pasul* testimony rather than a legal nullity, it invalidates the entire testimony, and Shimon escapes liability. These are two fundamentally different understandings of what it means when *palginan dibura* does not apply.

---

## Makkot & Beit Din

### Three Judges Source

The *Mishnah* continues its enumeration of matters requiring a *beit din* of three, adding the case of administering lashes — *makkot bishelosha*. Notably, the *Gemara* did not ask for a source when the *Mishnah* earlier required three judges for monetary penalties such as *kefel* and *arba'a vachamisha*. Here, however, where the matter involves physical punishment of a person's body, the *Gemara* does ask: *mena hanei milei?*

### Shoftim Source

*Amar Rav Huna amar kera*: the verse in the *parasha* dealing with lashes says *ushfatam* — "and they shall judge them" — written in the plural. Since a court cannot have an even number of judges, that plural implies two; and since two is an even number and *ein beit din shakul*, we add one more, arriving at three: *harei kan shelosha*. This is the source for requiring a *beit din* of three for lashing.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges: the same passage also contains *vehitzdiku es hatzadik vehirshiu es harasha* — "and they shall acquit the innocent and convict the guilty" — both expressed in the plural. If each such phrase implies an additional pair of judges, one arrives at six, and since six is even, seven — *harei kan shiva*. Why should we not require a *beit din* of seven for lashes? The *Gemara* answers that those additional phrases are not needed for deriving the composition of the court. They are needed for something else entirely — for what Ulla teaches.

### Ulla's Teaching

*De'amar Ulla: remez le'edim zomemin she-lokin minayin?* Where is there a hint in the Torah to the principle that *edim zomemin* receive lashes? The *Gemara* immediately interrupts: surely there is an explicit *parasha* — *ka'asher zamam* — one does to them as they plotted to do! Ulla's question must therefore concern those situations where *ka'asher zamam* cannot be applied. The classic example, familiar from the opening of tractate *Makkos*, is where false witnesses attempt to disqualify a *kohen* as a *ben gerusha ben chalutza* — a status that cannot be retroactively imposed on the witnesses themselves. In such cases, the punishment is *malkos* in lieu of *ka'asher zamam*. *Ulla's* question is: where does the Torah hint that lashes serve as the substitute when *ka'asher zamam* is unavailable?

His answer: from *vehitzdiku es hatzadik vehirshiu es harasha* — "and they acquitted the righteous and convicted the wicked" — followed by *vehaya im bin hakos harasha*, "and if the wicked one is liable to be struck." The narrative connection between these verses is at first puzzling: why should acquitting the righteous and convicting the wicked lead to lashes? Ulla explains that this entire passage is actually describing a case of *edim zomemin*. The sequence unfolds as follows: the false witnesses initially testify against the innocent man, attempting to make the righteous appear wicked. New witnesses then arrive, expose the original witnesses as *zomemin*, restore the innocent man's status — *vehitzdiku es hatzadik* — and reveal the original witnesses as the true *resha'im* — *vehirshiu es harasha*. Having straightened out the record — *vehitzdiku es hatzadik deme'ikara* — the Torah then continues: *vehaya im bin hakos harasha*, the newly identified wicked ones receive lashes. This is a brilliant reading of the narrative in the Torah: the passage is not describing a simple trial but specifically the aftermath of uncovering false witnesses, and from it we derive that *edim zomemin* receive lashes when *ka'asher zamam* cannot be applied.

The *Gemara* then asks: why not derive the lashing of *edim zomemin* simply from their violation of *lo ta'aneh* — the prohibition of bearing false witness? The answer: *mishum de'hava lei lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — testimony is speech, not a physical act, and a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* does not ordinarily carry *malkos*. The special derivation from *vehitzdiku* and *vehirshiu* is therefore needed to establish that lashes apply despite the absence of a physical act, or alternatively, to clarify the relationship between the lashes for the *lav* and the distinct mechanism of *ka'asher zamam*. The precise nature of that relationship is a full *sugya* in the opening of tractate *Makkos*.

### Lav She'Ein Bo

The *Gemara*'s observation that testimony constitutes a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* raises the broader question of what the *Gemara* means to teach by invoking this category. The claim is that ordinary violations of *lo ta'aneh* would not generate *malkos* precisely because the prohibition is violated through speech alone, without any accompanying physical action. The special derivation from the verses in *Parashat Shoftim* therefore functions either to override that limitation or to ground the punishment on a basis independent of the ordinary mechanism by which *malkos* is assigned for violated *lavim*.

### Rabbi Ishmael View

*Mishum Rabbi Yishmael amru be'esrim ushelosha* — in the name of Rabbi Yishmael it was taught that lashing requires a court of 23, the same as capital cases. *Mai ta'ama de'Rabbi Yishmael?* asks the *Gemara*. *Amar Abaye: asya rasha rasha michayevei misos* — a *gezeira shava*. The verse concerning lashes calls the subject *rasha* — "and it shall be if the wicked one is liable to be struck" — and a separate verse speaks of one who is *rasha la'mus*, wicked and deserving of death. Since both employ the term *rasha*, Rabbi Yishmael applies the same requirement: just as capital cases require 23, so too does lashing.

### Rava's View

Rava disagrees and offers a conceptually different rationale: *malkos bi'mkom misa omedes* — lashes stand in place of death. Rava's understanding, as elaborated by Tosafos, connects to the principle that all violations of divine command carry an inherent capital dimension — *bnei Noach* are liable to death for any violation of their *sheva mitzvos*, which suggests that at some fundamental level every transgression is deserving of death. When the Torah prescribes *malkos*, it is assigning a kind of partial or symbolic death: an act of violence against the body that stands in for the ultimate penalty. The person receiving lashes is in some sense *chayav misa*, and the *malkos* is that death — diminished, survived, but real. This is a harsh and striking understanding of corporal punishment, but it is what Rava means when he says that lashes stand in the place of death and therefore require the same court of 23.

### Challenge to Rava

*Amar Rav Acha brei de'Rava le'Rav Ashi*: if Rava is right — if at some conceptual level the recipient of lashes is *chayav misa* and the *malkos* is simply the form that death takes — then why does the court bother to assess how many lashes the person can withstand? The standard procedure, discussed at length in tractate *Makkos*, is that the court evaluates whether the person can safely receive the full 39 lashes, and if not, the number is reduced to the largest multiple of three that falls within his capacity. But if he is *chayav misa* in any case, why not simply give him the full 39 and let him die if that is what happens? *V'ei mayis leimus* — if he dies, let him die; he was *chayav misa* anyway.

### Nikla Achicha

The *Gemara* answers from a verse: *amar kra veniklah achicha le'einecha* — "and your brother shall be diminished before your eyes." The *Gemara* reads this as requiring that when the lashes are administered, the subject must still be *your brother* — that is, still alive. *V'ki machyas agaba de'chaya machyas* — you are striking the back of one who is living. This implies that he must be alive throughout the lashing and must survive it.

The *Gemara* presses further: could one not simply stop lashing the moment the person dies? The answer lies in the practical difficulty of rounding up to the nearest multiple of three. If the assessment establishes that a person can survive 20 lashes, one cannot give 21 — even though 21 is the nearest multiple of three above 20 — because the 21st lash might kill him. The verse requires not merely that the lashes be given while the person is alive, but that after the lashes — *achar shelaka* — he remains *achicha*, your brother, still living. The lashing must leave him alive. *Veniklah* is read as *laka* — he received lashes — and *achicha* follows: he is still your brother, still among the living. Even if *malkos* conceptually represents a form of the death penalty, the Torah insists that this particular death be one from which the recipient emerges alive. This is a fascinating and deeply significant way of understanding the nature of *malkos*.

---

## Calendar Matters

### Calendar Intro

The *Mishnah* now turns from judicial penalties to matters of the calendar, teaching that additional items requiring a court of three include calendar determination — specifically *ibur hachodesh* and, as will soon emerge, *ibur hashana*. The transition is striking: the *Mishnah* moves from cases involving punishment of individuals to the national and sacred institution of the calendar, both requiring the same minimal *beit din* of three.

### Ibur vs Kiddush

The *Gemara* immediately notices a terminological difficulty in the *Mishnah*'s language. The *Mishnah* says *ibur hachodesh* — making the month "pregnant," or full — which would seem to refer to the act of extending a month to 30 days rather than allowing it to end after 29. But this term is puzzling on two counts. It is not *chishuv*, the *Gemara* notes — it does not mean the calendrical computation involved in deciding whether to manipulate the month's length. Nor is it *kiddush hachodesh* — the formal ritual sanctification of the new month, the declaration of *mekudash mekudash mekudash* that the *beit din* pronounces. So what exactly does *ibur hachodesh* denote, and what act is it that requires three judges?

The *Gemara* presses the difficulty: making a month into a full month — an *ibur* — happens passively, by the court's *failure* to act. If day 30 arrives and the court does not accept witnesses or does not perform the act of *kiddush*, then day 30 passes without becoming *Rosh Chodesh*, and automatically — *mimeila me'ubra* — the month becomes a full 30-day month, and day 31 becomes *Rosh Chodesh*. If *ibur hachodesh* is simply what happens when no *kiddush* is performed, then nothing is done, no court convenes, and there is nothing requiring three judges. The *Mishnah*'s formulation requires clarification.

### Abaye's Fix

*Amar Abaye: tani kiddush hachodesh* — Abaye proposes that the *Mishnah*'s text should simply be emended. The correct reading is *kiddush hachodesh*, not *ibur hachodesh*. It is the formal act of sanctifying the month — whatever day that is performed — that requires a *beit din* of three. Abaye supports this from the *Tosefta*, which reads *kiddush hachodesh v'ibur shana bishelosha* — using *kiddush* for the month and *ibur* for the year. If the *Tosefta* in the name of Rabbi Meir uses *kiddush hachodesh*, that is the proper formulation and the *Mishnah* should be corrected to match.

### Rava's Day 30

Rava is unwilling to emend the text: *v'hai ibur katani* — the *Mishnah* deliberately chose the word *ibur*, and one cannot simply discard the *Mishnah*'s precise language. Instead, Rava offers a reading that preserves the text: *kiddush b'yom ibur bishelosha, achar ibur leika kiddush* — when *kiddush hachodesh* is performed on day 30 — the day called *yom ibur*, the day that could make the preceding month a full one — that act requires a *beit din* of three. But if day 30 passes without being declared *Rosh Chodesh*, so that the month becomes a full 30-day month by default, and day 31 then becomes the new month, there is no formal *kiddush* at all on day 31, because it is self-evidently *Rosh Chodesh* — nothing more needs to be declared. Thus, the word *ibur* in the *Mishnah* qualifies which *kiddush* requires three: specifically, *kiddush* performed on *yom ibur*, day 30 itself. It is an active determination against the natural flow — declaring day 30 to be *Rosh Chodesh* rather than allowing the month to run its full course — and that active intervention requires three judges.

### Rabbi Elazar View

*Umani Rabbi Elazar berabi Tzadok hi* — Rava identifies this reading of the *Mishnah* as consistent with the position of Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Tzadok, as recorded in a *baraisa*. Rabbi Elazar berabi Tzadok teaches: if the new moon was not seen *bizmano* — in its natural time, meaning on day 30 — then *ein mekadshin oso shekvar kidshuhu bashamayim*: there is no need for the *beit din* to sanctify it, for heaven has already sanctified it. Once day 30 passes without a sighting that warrants *kiddush*, the lunar cycle itself has ordained that day 31 is *Rosh Chodesh*; the court has nothing to add. Conversely, when the new moon is seen on day 30 and the *beit din* actively declares it *Rosh Chodesh*, that is the case where a court is needed and where Rava's reading applies.

### Rav Nachman View

Rav Nachman takes the opposite position: *kiddush achar ibur bishelosha, b'yom ibur leika kiddush* — it is specifically when the court performs *kiddush* on day 31, after the month has already become an *ibur* month, that three judges are required. On day 30 itself, no formal ritual of *kiddush* is performed at all. This position is, as the *Gemara* acknowledges, highly counterintuitive. The idea that an active declaration of *Rosh Chodesh* is unnecessary on the very day when the determination is most consequential — and necessary only the following day, once the matter has resolved itself — is difficult to understand. Rav Nachman associates this view with the teaching of Pleimo, who states: *bizmano ein mekadshin oso, shelo bizmano mekadshin oso* — when the month appears in its natural time (day 30), no sanctification is performed; when it appears outside its natural time (day 31), sanctification is performed. This is the exact inversion of the position one would expect, and it stands as recorded without further justification in this context.

### Rav Ashi Resolution

Rav Ashi takes a step back from the entire debate and restores the original meaning of the *Mishnah*'s language: *le'olam chishuv katani* — actually, *ibur hachodesh* in the *Mishnah* does mean *chishuv*, computation. The word *ibur* in this context refers to the process of deliberating and calculating whether to extend the month, not to any ritual act of *kiddush*. Why then does the *Mishnah* say *ibur* rather than *chishuv*? *U'mai ibur — chishuv de'ibur*: the word *ibur* is used because the specific computation in question is the deliberation over whether to make a month into an *ibur* month — a full 30-day month. *V'aiidi de'tana ibur shana, tana nami ibur chodesh*: since the very next clause of the *Mishnah* discusses *ibur hashana* — adding a leap month to make a leap year — and uses the word *ibur* naturally in that context, the same word is borrowed for the monthly calendar deliberation to create linguistic parallelism.

The *Gemara* then asks: does this mean that *kiddush hachodesh* — the formal act of sanctification — does not require three judges, and only the computation does? *Mani Rabi Eliezer hi* — this reading aligns with the view of Rabbi Eliezer, who teaches: *bein bizmano bein shelo bizmano ein mekadshin oto* — whether the moon appears on day 30 or day 31, no formal ritual of *kiddush* is ever performed. The *beit din* determines when *Rosh Chodesh* falls — accepting witnesses, deliberating, and issuing its ruling — but there is no ceremony of *mekudash mekudash mekudash*. Rabbi Eliezer derives this from the verse *vekidashtem et shnat hachamishim shana*: you sanctify the *Yovel* year — meaning years are subject to sanctification, not months. Rashi and Tosafos clarify that Rabbi Eliezer does not mean the *beit din* plays no role; rather, the court accepts witnesses and makes its formal determination, but without the ritual proclamation. Therefore, since there is no act of *kiddush* for the month, the *Mishnah* rightly uses only the language of *ibur* and *chishuv*, and Rav Ashi's reading is fully consistent with Rabbi Eliezer's position.

---

## Ibur HaShana

### Framework

The *Mishnah* teaches that *ibur hashana* — the intercalation of the year, adding a thirteenth month to create a leap year — also requires a *beit din* of three. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then elaborates that this is not a simple requirement of three judges from start to finish, but a structured process in which the court expands in stages: one begins with three, continues with five, and concludes with seven.

### Stage One: Three

The *baraisa* elaborates on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's framework. The process begins with the three recognized authorities who have standing to deal with calendar matters on behalf of the entire nation. These three convene to determine whether it is even worth discussing whether to intercalate the year — that is, whether there are sufficient grounds to open the question at all. The vote at this stage concerns only the threshold question: shall we sit and examine this? If one of the three says yes, we should convene and discuss, and two say no, the minority is negated by the majority — *batel yachid bemiyuto* — and the matter is closed; there will be no intercalation that year. If two say yes and one says no, the two prevail and the process moves forward.

### Stage Two: Five

Once the decision is made to proceed with deliberation, the court is expanded by two additional members, bringing the total to five. These five then engage substantively with the question — *nosin venosnin badavar*, examining the relevant considerations and debating whether the year warrants intercalation. A vote is then taken: should an extra month be added? If two say yes and three say no, the two are negated and the process ends without intercalation. If three say yes and two say no, the three prevail.

### Stage Three: Seven

When the majority of the five determine that intercalation is warranted, two further members are added, bringing the total to seven. These seven issue the final formal determination. As the *baraisa* specifies, *she'einam pechutim mishiv'ah* — the final ruling must be issued by no fewer than seven. The purpose of the final expansion, as the structure implies, is not to re-examine the question but to ensure that the solemn declaration of intercalation is issued with the full weight of a *beit din* of seven — appropriate to a matter of national consequence.

### Sources Debate

The *Gemara* asks: *hani shelosha chamisha veshiv'ah kineged mi?* What is the basis for these specific numbers? A debate is recorded between Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani and his colleague — identified as Rav Shimon ben Pazi — though the *Gemara* notes uncertainty about which name goes first, presenting both orderings: some attribute the more prominent position to Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani and identify Rav Shimon ben Pazi as his colleague, and others reverse the attribution.

One opinion derives the numbers from *birchas kohanim*: the first verse of the priestly blessing contains three words, the second five, and the third seven. The calendrical court mirrors the expanding cadence of the priestly blessing — both relate to something of national sacred significance, even if the precise connection between *birchas kohanim* and *ibur hashana* is not spelled out further.

The other opinion derives the numbers from the ranks of royal officers described in *Tanach*: those who guard the threshold — three in number; those who behold the king's face at a lower level — five; and those who behold the king's face at the highest level — seven. Rashi notes that the verse concerning seven officers who behold the king's face refers to the court of Achashverosh, and the *Gemara* is at pains to indicate that the derivation is not from Achashverosh but from a parallel passage describing a Jewish king.
