The connection to royalty makes sense conceptually: the determination of the calendar is an act of national governance, a royal function as it were, and the structure of the *beit din* for *ibur hashana* is therefore modeled on the hierarchical ranks of those who serve and counsel the king.

### Rav Yosef & Abaye

Rav Yosef taught a *baraisa* that presents the second derivation — three corresponding to those who guard the threshold, five to those who behold the king's face at a lesser degree, and seven to those who behold the king's face at the highest level. Following this teaching, Abaye said to Rav Yosef: *ad ha'idna mai ta'ama lo parish lan mar hachi?* — until now, why had Rav Yosef never shared this reasoning with them? They had studied this material before and Rav Yosef had not explained the basis for the numbers three, five, and seven.

Rav Yosef replied: *lo hava yadana detzrichitu* — I did not know that you needed it, or that you did not already know the reason. *Mi be'itu minai milta velo amri lachut?* — did you ever ask me something that I did not tell you? The exchange is gently reproachful in both directions: Abaye wondering why the teacher withheld an explanation, the teacher wondering why the student never asked. It is a fitting note on which the daf closes — a reminder that in the study of Torah, the responsibility to seek out understanding rests as much on the student as on the teacher, and that much that is known goes untransmitted simply because the question was never asked.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 11

## Appointment & Shmuel HaK…

### Leap Year Requirement

The *daf* opens on 10b with a *tanna rabbanan* addressing the laws of *ibbur hashana* — the intercalation of the year. The *baraita* states: *ain me'abrin et hashana ella bimezumamin* — the year may only be intercalated by those who have been specifically appointed. This principle was already encountered in the Yerushalmi, and the Bavli now takes up the same point, moving rapidly given that familiarity.

### Rabban Gamliel Story

The *baraita* continues with a *ma'aseh* involving Rabban Gamliel. He instructed his attendants: *hishkimu li shiva l'aliyah* — rise early and bring me seven people to the upper chamber. The word *hishkimu* is notable; it implies that the proceedings were to begin at first light. When Rabban Gamliel arrived, however, he found that eight people had gathered. He declared: *mi hu she'ala shelo birshut yeired* — whoever came without permission must leave. The rule is firm: only those formally appointed may participate in the intercalation.

### Shmuel HaKatan

At that moment, Shmuel HaKatan rose and declared: *ani hu she'aliti shelo birshut* — it is I who came without being called. He explained that he had not come to participate in the *ibbur hashana* itself, but rather *lilmod halacha lema'aseh hitztarchti* — he needed to observe the proceedings in order to learn practical *halacha*. Rashi notes that the phrasing here is somewhat vaguer than the parallel in the Yerushalmi, and understands it to mean that Shmuel HaKatan simply wished to observe how the process was conducted.

Rabban Gamliel responded warmly: *shev bni shev* — sit, my son, sit. *Re'uyin kol hashanim kullan lehitabber al yadecha* — all the years would be fit to be intercalated by you. Nevertheless, the sages have ruled that the *ibbur hashana* may only be performed by those who were formally appointed, and this rule cannot be set aside even for someone as worthy as Shmuel HaKatan.

The Bavli then adds a clarifying remark — signaled by the shift from Hebrew into Aramaic — that it was not in fact Shmuel HaKatan who had entered uninvited: *velo Shmuel HaKatan hu, ella inish achrini* — it was another person entirely. *Umachmat kisufa hu de'avid* — Shmuel HaKatan acted as he did purely out of concern for the other person's embarrassment. He took the blame upon himself to spare the actual intruder from humiliation. This detail illuminates and completes the story as it appeared in the Yerushalmi.

---

## Ethos of Modesty

### Rabbi Chiya & Garlic

The Gemara now pivots to explore more broadly the ethos of protecting others from embarrassment, even at personal cost — what one might call the ethics of not pointing the finger. A further story is introduced: *ki ha de-yatv Rabbi* — there was an incident when Rabbi (Rebbi) was sitting and delivering his *shiur*, and he detected the smell of garlic. He announced: *mi she'achal shum yetzei* — whoever ate garlic must leave. At that point, *amad Rabbi Chiya veyatza* — Rabbi Chiya rose and left. Once Rabbi Chiya left, *amdu kullan veyatzu* — everyone else rose and departed as well.

The following morning, Rabbi Shimon b'Rabbi — Rebbi's son — encountered Rabbi Chiya and said to him: *ata hu shetziaarta le'abba?* — Was it you who caused my father this anguish by coming to the *shiur* having eaten garlic? Rabbi Chiya replied: *lo tehei kazot beYisrael* — God forbid that such a thing should be.

Rashi understands the son's question as a genuine accusation: *she'achalta shum venadaf harei'ach* — that Rabbi Chiya had been the one who ate the garlic. But there is also a compelling alternative reading: the son was not accusing Rabbi Chiya of eating garlic, but rather of disrupting the entire *shiur* by rising and causing everyone else to follow. On this reading, Rabbi Chiya's response — *lo tehei kazot beYisrael* — means that it would have been worse to allow an innocent or guilty party to be shamed publicly than to endure the disruption of the class.

### Justice vs. Dignity

This alternative reading carries a pointed implicit critique of Rebbi himself. By choosing to leave, Rabbi Chiya was in effect registering a position: one should not publicly call out an individual and demand that a guilty party expose himself. The tension here is real and worth pausing over. We are in a tractate fundamentally concerned with *din* — with guilt, innocence, and judicial process — and yet here the Gemara is celebrating someone who actively shielded a wrongdoer from accountability. The juxtaposition is not accidental.

The resolution is that not everything rises to the level of a matter for the court. This is an interpersonal and communal setting, not a formal judicial proceeding. Human relationships and communal life cannot and should not operate solely on the logic of establishing guilt. There are moments when protecting a person's dignity is the more urgent value, even if it means that accountability is deferred or foregone. The question of when to speak and when to remain silent — the ethics of not snitching versus the ethics of truth-telling — is genuinely complex, and the Gemara's interest in establishing precedent for Rabbi Chiya's behavior suggests that this position requires defense precisely because it is not self-evidently correct.

### Rabbi Meir Precedent

The Gemara asks: *meheicha gamar lah mi-Rabbi Meir* — from where did Rabbi Chiya learn to act this way? He learned it from Rabbi Meir. A *baraita* is cited: a woman came to the *beis midrash* of Rabbi Meir and declared that one of the men present had married her through an act of sexual intercourse — a form of *kiddushin* that, while technically effective, is entirely improper. *Amad Rabbi Meir ve-chasav lah get krisus* — Rabbi Meir stood up and wrote her a *get*. Once he did so, *amdu ve-chasvu kulam ve-nasnu lah* — all the other members of the *beis midrash* rose and each wrote her a *get* as well, providing cover for the actual party so that no individual would have to come forward and be identified.

This case is in important respects different from the garlic story, because here the action was not merely protective of someone's dignity but also practically beneficial to the woman. Had no one come forward, she would have remained an *agunah* — unable to remarry. Rabbi Meir's stratagem simultaneously protected the guilty party from exposure and ensured that the woman received her *get*. One might also note with some amusement that Rabbi Meir was himself a scribe, and that the *baraita* says all of them wrote — perhaps the school had a scribal dimension and they were all capable of drafting a *get* independently.

### Chain of Learning

The Gemara then traces a chain of tradition: *Rabbi Meir meheicha gamar leh? Mi-Shmuel HaKatan* — and from where did Rabbi Meir learn? From Shmuel HaKatan. *Mi-Shmuel HaKatan meheicha gamar leh? Mi-Shechaniah ben Yechiel* — and Shmuel HaKatan learned from Shechaniah ben Yechiel. The verse cited is from Ezra: *va-ya'an Shechaniah ben Yechiel mi-benei Elam va-yomer le-Ezra anachnu ma'alnu be-Eloheinu* — Shechaniah spoke in the collective first person, "we have betrayed our God," even though he himself had not taken a foreign wife. By speaking in the plural, he avoided singling out the guilty parties and dividing the community into the righteous and the wicked.

*Shechaniah ben Yechiel meheicha gamar leh? Mi-Yehoshua* — and Shechaniah learned from Joshua. When God said to Joshua, *kum lach lamah zeh atah nofel al panecha chata Yisrael* — Israel has sinned (this in the context of Achan's violation of the *cherem*) — Joshua asked: Master of the Universe, who sinned? And God replied: *ve-chi diltor ani lach?* — Am I your *diltor*? The word *diltor* almost certainly derives from the Latin *delator*, meaning an informer or denouncer. God said: I am not your tattletale. *Hatel goralos* — cast lots and find out for yourself.

This is the most striking case in the chain, because here it is God Himself who declines to identify the wrongdoer, even though the situation ultimately required resolution and Achan had to be found out. The Gemara does not resolve the tension — ultimately a process of lot-casting was used, and perhaps the point is that the process itself gave Achan the opportunity to come forward voluntarily. The collective language also has a darker side: if the wrongdoer is not identified, the entire community bears the burden, and the rhetoric of *chata Yisrael* — Israel sinned — can shade into collective punishment, which is its own moral difficulty.

The chain continues: *ve-iba'is eima mi-Moshe* — or alternatively, the tradition traces back to Moses. When Moses declared *ad anah me'antem* — how long will you refuse to observe God's commandments? — referring to those who had gone out to collect *manna* on Shabbat, he addressed the entire nation collectively even though only a minority had actually transgressed. Here again the use of collective language shields the individuals while holding the community as a whole to account.

---

## Shmuel HaKatan Merit

### Bat Kol & Hillel

The Gemara now introduces a *tanna rabbanan* on an adjacent theme, prompted by the prominence of Shmuel HaKatan in the preceding discussion. After the last of the prophets — Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi — *nistalka Ruach HaKodesh mi-Yisrael*: the spirit of holiness departed from Israel. Nevertheless, *hayu mishtamshim be-bat kol* — the sages would still make use of the *bat kol*, the heavenly echo, some attenuated form of divine communication short of full prophecy.

On one occasion, the sages were gathered in the upper story of a certain Beit Gorya in Jericho, and a *bat kol* issued from the heavens declaring: *yesh kan echad she-ra'uy she-tishreh alav Shechinah ke-Moshe Rabbeinu* — there is one person here who is worthy of having the divine presence rest upon him as it rested upon Moses. Some authorities omit the comparison to Moses, feeling it is theologically untenable given the principle that *lo kam navi od be-Yisrael ke-Moshe* — no prophet like Moses has arisen in Israel. The heavenly voice, however, was not necessarily claiming equivalence of prophetic degree; it was speaking of the worthiness of the individual for divine presence. *Ela she-ein doro zakai le-kach* — but the generation does not merit it. *Ve-natnu chachamim et eineihem be-Hillel HaZaken* — the sages cast their eyes toward Hillel the Elder as the person being indicated. When Hillel died, they eulogized him: *hai chasid hai anav* — alas, the pious one; alas, the humble one — *talmido shel Ezra*, the disciple of Ezra. It is notable that they called him a disciple of Ezra rather than of Moses: Ezra represents the world of rabbinic, post-prophetic Judaism, which is the world Hillel inhabited and shaped.

### Shmuel Worthy of Prophecy

On another occasion, the sages were gathered in an upper chamber in Yavne, and a second *bat kol* emerged with the same declaration: *yesh kan echad she-ra'uy she-tishreh Shechinah, ela she-ein doro zakai le-kach* — one person here is worthy of the divine presence, but the generation does not merit it. *Ve-natnu chachamim et eineihem bi-Shmuel HaKatan* — the sages looked toward Shmuel HaKatan. This is why the tradition about him was introduced here. His very name — *HaKatan*, the small one — may reflect his extraordinary modesty, the same quality that caused him to rise and take blame for an uninvited intruder rather than expose that person to humiliation. And yet, beneath that apparent smallness, he was in reality one of the most spiritually exalted figures of his generation.

When Shmuel HaKatan died, they eulogized him with the same words used for Hillel: *hai chasid hai anav, talmido shel Hillel* — alas, the pious one; alas, the humble one — disciple of Hillel. The chain continues: Hillel is the disciple of Ezra, and Shmuel HaKatan is the disciple of Hillel.

### Shmuel's Prophecy

*Af hu amar bi-sh'at mitato* — even Shmuel HaKatan himself, at the moment of his death, gave expression to something like prophetic vision. He declared: *Shimon ve-Yishmael le-charba* — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael the Kohen Gadol will fall by the sword. *Ve-chavrohi le-katla* — their colleagues, including Rabbi Akiva and those who were killed alongside him, will be put to death by other means. *Ve-sha'ar ama le-viza* — the rest of the people will be despoiled. *Ve-akan sagiyan atidin le-meiti al alma* — and great suffering will befall the world. This was a vision of the Hadrianic persecution that would come. The fact that this prophecy emerged at the moment of Shmuel HaKatan's death serves as confirmation of what the *bat kol* had declared: he was indeed one in whom the *Shechinah* was worthy of resting, and at the threshold of death, when the soul draws closest to its source, this capacity briefly manifested.

### Yehuda ben Bava

The Gemara adds that they wished to offer the same eulogy — *hai chasid hai anav* — for Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, but *nitrefa sha'ah* — the moment was snatched away from them. *She-ein maspidin al harugei malchut* — one may not deliver a formal *hesped* for those killed by the Roman government, for fear of drawing the authorities' wrath. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava was among the *harugei malchut*, and so the eulogy that would have honored him could not be publicly delivered.

---

## Nasi Authority

### Nasi Consent

Returning now to the laws of *ibbur shanah*, the Gemara introduces another *tanna rabbanan*: *ein me'abrin et ha-shanah ela im ken yirtzeh Nasi* — the year may not be intercalated unless the *Nasi* consents. It is not sufficient that the *Nasi* appoint the members of the court; he must also affirmatively agree to the decision to add the month. Appointment of the participants and ratification of the outcome are two distinct requirements.

### Retroactive Validation

A *ma'aseh* illustrates how this requirement was navigated in practice. Rabban Gamliel traveled to obtain some authorization from a Roman official in Syria and was delayed in returning to Eretz Yisrael. In his absence, the appointed court proceeded with the *ibbur shanah* — but conditionally: *al menas sheyirtzeh Rabban Gamliel* — on the stipulation that Rabban Gamliel would ratify the decision upon his return. When he returned, already into Adar Sheni, he declared *rotzeh ani* — I consent — and *nimtza shana muberet* — the intercalation was thereby retroactively validated. The *chiddush* here is that ratification after the fact, provided it was stipulated from the outset as a condition, suffices to validate the court's action. Had Rabban Gamliel returned and withheld his consent, the intercalation would have been retroactively invalid — and the community would have found itself, one imagines, suddenly in the middle of Nissan.

---

## Grounds for Intercalation

### Valid Reasons

The Gemara presents a *tanna rabbanan* enumerating valid reasons for intercalating the year. The year may be intercalated *mipnei haderachim* — because the roads are impassable due to mud, making *aliyah l'regel* impossible — *umipnei ha-gisharim* — because bridges have been washed out — *umipnei tanurei pesachim* — because the outdoor ovens used to roast the *korban pesach* are still waterlogged and have not dried out. An additional valid reason is that diaspora communities — *galuyot Yisrael* — have set out on the pilgrimage but circumstances have delayed them and they will not arrive in time for Pesach.

### Invalid Reasons

By contrast, the *baraita* identifies reasons that are insufficient. *Aval lo mipnei hasheleg* — but not because of snow during the Nissan period; people will make the journey even through snow. *Ve-lo mipnei hatzina* — nor because of cold; that alone is not grounds for adding a month. *Ve-lo mipnei galuyot Yisrael shelo akru mimkomam* — nor because diaspora communities have not yet mobilized from their places of origin. If the people have simply failed to begin their journey when they should have, that delinquency on their part does not justify intercalation.

### Animals & Birds

A further *tanna rabbanan* addresses the status of animal and bird maturity as grounds for intercalation. One does not intercalate the year because the kids (*gedayim*) or lambs (*tela'im*) are too small — that is, one does not add a month to allow them to grow larger for the *korban pesach*, even though these are precisely the animals brought as the *paschal* offering. Similarly, one does not intercalate because the young birds (*gozalot*) have not yet matured — women in particular would bring bird offerings for post-childbirth sacrifices and would consolidate these obligations for *aliyah l'regel*, but the immaturity of the birds is not a sufficient basis for adding a month.

However, *aval osin otam se'ad lashana* — these considerations may be adduced as supporting factors. They cannot stand alone as the reason for intercalation, but once a valid reason exists, the smallness of the animals or birds may be cited as an additional rationale.

---

## Official Declaration

### Aramaic Edict Text

Rabbi Yanai transmits in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the actual Aramaic text used when issuing the declaration of intercalation — a remarkable survival of what appears to be an authentic official edict:

> *Mehodinan anachna lachon d'gozlanaya rakikin, v'imraya d'arkin, v'zimna d'aviva lo mata, v'shapir miltza b'anpai, v'osifna al shata da tlatin yomin.*

We hereby inform you that the birds are still tender, the flock is still small, the time of the *aviv* — the ripening of the grain — has not yet arrived, and the matter is good in our eyes; we have therefore added thirty days to the year.

This text is a precious document. The primary operative reason is that Nissan must coincide with *chodesh ha-aviv* — the month of ripening grain — and this astronomical-agricultural condition has not yet been met. The birds and the flocks are cited as *se'ad* — supporting considerations — but the *aviv* is the essential basis. The declaration was composed in Palestinian Aramaic, the vernacular of the period. While the formal literary language of rabbinic rulings was Mishnaic Hebrew, official edicts addressed to the broader population — and particularly to the diaspora communities — would naturally have been issued in Aramaic, and it is this edict-text that the Gemara preserves.

### Month Length

One might ask: the edict specifies thirty days, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is recorded elsewhere as holding that *ibbur hashana* is *chodesh* — a month, which is twenty-nine days. Is there a contradiction? Rav Papa resolves this: *ratzu chodesh ratzu shloshim yom* — one may choose. Adar Sheni may be constituted as either twenty-nine or thirty days; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel does not insist that it must be only twenty-nine, but rather that both options are available.

---

## Father & Son Contrast

### Mighty vs. Humble

Having cited Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's declaration, the Gemara pauses to note a striking irony: *ta chazi ma ika bein takifaya kadmaya l'invatnusaya batrayei* — come and see the difference between the mighty early ones and the humble later ones. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's edict reads *v'shapir miltza b'anpai* — the matter is good in my eyes — using a first-person royal formulation. He is speaking as the sole authority whose assent makes the intercalation valid. This is the son, the later and ostensibly "humbler" generation.

Compare this to the earlier generation — the father — Rabban Gamliel, who is generally remembered for his forthright exercise of authority: it was he who compelled Rabbi Yehoshua to appear before him on what Rabbi Yehoshua maintained was Yom Kippur by his own reckoning, and who made a point throughout his tenure of asserting the supremacy of the *Nasi*. Yet, as the Gemara now shows, Rabban Gamliel's own written edict speaks in the first-person plural: *v'shapir miltza b'anpai u-ve-anpei chaverai* — the matter is good to me and to my colleagues. The seemingly more authoritarian father used the more collegial formulation; the son who came after him spoke in terms of his individual authority.

### Three Letters

The Gemara cites a *baraita* describing Rabban Gamliel seated on the steps of the Temple Mount, with his scribe Yochanan standing before him and three pieces of cloth already prepared for writing. He directed Yochanan to take each cloth in succession and compose three separate letters.

### Galilee & South Letters

The first letter was addressed to the communities of Upper and Lower Galilee: *le-achana benei Galila illa'ah, le-achana benei Galila tatta'ah* — to our brothers in the upper Galilee and to our brothers in the lower Galilee — *shelomchon yisge* — may your peace be increased. *Mehode'in anan lechon di-zman bi'ura mata* — we inform you that the time of *bi'ur* has arrived — the obligation, which falls every third year of the *shemita* cycle, to remove all *ma'aser* from one's home. In the Galilee the principal crop was olives, and so the letter specified: *leafrushei ma'asra mi-ma'atana de-zeita* — to separate *ma'aser* from the presses of olives.

The second letter was addressed to the communities of the south: *le-achana benei daroma* — to our brothers in the south — with the same blessing of peace and the same notification of *bi'ur*. In the south, the dominant crop was grain rather than olives, and so the letter read: *leafrushei ma'asra mi-umrei shivla* — to separate *ma'aser* from the bundles of wheat.

### Diaspora Letter

The third letter was addressed to the diaspora: *le-achana benei galvasa be-Bovel ve-le-achana de-vi-Madai ve-lish'ar kol galvuta de-Yisrael* — to our brothers of the exile in Babylonia and in Medai and to all the exile-communities of Israel. The greeting is notably extended: *shelomchon yisge le-alam* — may your peace be increased forever — with the word *le-alam* added, perhaps befitting communities at a greater remove who needed a more expansive expression of connection.

The body of this letter contains the intercalation notice in the same Aramaic formula: *de-gozalaya rakikin ve-imraya adkin ve-zimna de-aviva lo mata* — the birds are tender, the flock is small, the time of the *aviv* has not arrived — *ve-shafra milta be-anpai u-ve-anpei chaverai* — and the matter is good to me and to my colleagues — *ve-osifat al shatta da yomin tlatin* — and we have added thirty days to the year.

This document has the character of a genuine historical record, and indeed the *tanna* transmitting it in the Tosefta appears to have preserved the actual Aramaic text of these letters. It stands apart from nearly everything else in this section of the Gemara.

### Humility Explained

The Gemara raises what is now an apparent paradox: Rabban Gamliel, known for his assertiveness in maintaining the authority of the *Nasi*, here defers to collegial language — *me and my colleagues* — while his son Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel speaks in the singular. The Gemara offers one resolution: *dilma batar de-avruha* — perhaps this letter was written after the period when Rabban Gamliel was temporarily removed from his position as *Nasi* for overstepping. Having been deposed and reinstated, he may have emerged chastened and more inclined toward humility.

Tosafot, however, offer a more structural explanation in a single sentence: *peirush de-hayah lo chaver Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya she-hayah nasi imo* — after the incident of his removal, Rabban Gamliel did not rule alone; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya was appointed as co-*Nasi* alongside him. On this reading, Rabban Gamliel's use of collegial language was not merely a rhetorical gesture of modesty, but an accurate reflection of institutional reality: he now shared authority, and *u-ve-anpei chaverai* — and my colleagues — referred quite literally to his co-leader. The apparent humility of the father, then, was in part a consequence of the political circumstances that followed his earlier exercise of unilateral authority.

The daf thus closes with the theme of *nasi* authority held in tension with collegial governance — a theme that will continue into the next *daf*, where the Bavli will take up the third major principle encountered already in the Yerushalmi: the requirement that intercalation be performed specifically in Eretz Yisrael.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 12

## Chaverim & Ibur

### Chaverim & Festivals

Today's *daf* in the Bavli is 12. We pick up in the middle of 11b and continue with the issue of *ibur hashana*. A point worth noting — raised in connection with the Yerushalmi — is the question of whether a *chaver* is permitted to be present in the *beit din* when they perform *kiddush hachodesh* or *ibur hashana*.

### Chaverim Phrase

This connects naturally to something familiar from the synagogue liturgy. When we make the announcement of *rosh chodesh* in *shul*, we say *chaverim kol Yisrael v'nomar amen* — "all Israel are *chaverim*, and let us say amen." The instinct is to read *chaverim* colloquially, as simply meaning "friends" or "companions." But there may be a more precise technical meaning here: the term *chaver* as a distinct status in matters of *tumah v'tahara*, referring to individuals trusted in ritual matters. The Yerushalmi's conclusion was that a *chaver* could be *min haminyan* — counted among those participating in the proceedings of calendar-making — though this was debated.

The Gemara elsewhere invokes a related idea: during the *regel*, many concerns about *tumah v'tahara* were waived, based on a *pasuk* indicating that when all Israel gathers for the festival, everyone is treated as a *chaver* in matters of ritual purity. This is a *mishnah* in Chagigah. So when we say *chaverim kol Yisrael*, it may be evoking this same concept — that we all come together as one people. There is also a broader question here about *kiddush hachodesh* in our own time: we have no *beit din*, no witnesses appearing before a court, and yet Hillel the Second established the fixed calendar, and somehow it is by communal recognition — by acclamation — that the *kiddush hachodesh* takes effect.

---

## Three Criteria

### Reasons & Requirements

The *Tnu Rabbanan* at the bottom of 11b, approximately ten lines above the wider section, states: *al shlosha devarim me'avrin et hashana* — for three reasons one intercalates the year: *al ha'aviv*, *v'al peirot ha'ilan*, *v'al hatkufa*. The *aviv* refers to whether the grain has sufficiently ripened; the *tkufa* refers to whether the seasons are properly aligned — whether spring is arriving at the right time, which logically is often connected to *aviv*; and the third factor is whether the fruit will be ready in time for *shavuot* so that people can bring their *bikkurim*.

The *Tnu Rabbanan* then states: *al shnayim me'avrin* — two of these factors are required to intercalate the year; *v'al echad mehem ein me'avrin* — one factor alone is insufficient. Unlike what was said in the Yerushalmi — that *bedieved* one factor might be enough — this *braita* makes no such qualification.

### Aviv & Happiness

*Ubizman she'aviv echad mehem hakol smechim* — when *aviv* is one of the two factors driving the intercalation, everyone is very happy. Rashi explains: *she'ein choshim bit'chilat Pesach* — they are not anxious about Pesach being pushed off, *lefi she'ein tevuah reuyah* — because the grain is not yet ready. If the grain has not ripened, there is no hardship in waiting another month. The new grain cannot be eaten anyway before the *omer* is brought, and since it is not yet ripe, there is no grain sitting ready that people are forbidden from eating.

But if *aviv* is not one of the factors — meaning the grain *has* ripened — and the year is still being intercalated for the other two reasons, then everyone is unhappy: *atzeivim*, grieved, because the *omer* is being delayed a month despite the grain being ready, and the prohibition of *chadash* weighs upon them.

### Tkufa Debate

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: *al hatkufa* — regarding the *tkufa*. The Gemara raises an ambiguity: *al hatkufa smechim* — does he mean that the *tkufa* factor makes everyone happy? Or does he mean *o al hatkufa me'avrin* — that the *tkufa* alone is a sufficient reason to intercalate? The Gemara concludes *teyku* — the question is unresolved.

Rashi's explanation of why the *tkufa* would generate happiness is as follows: if the *tkufa* is properly aligned and the seasons are in the right time — even though it is not one of the factors driving intercalation — then it means the weather will be ideal for the *chagim*. Everyone who goes to Israel for *Sukkot*, for example, loves the perfect autumn weather. If the *tkufa* is synced, the *olei regel* travel to Israel at a beautiful time. But if the *tkufa* is not a factor, it means the seasons are misaligned — it will be too cold or too hot — and the *aliya l'regel* becomes uncomfortable.

---

## Geographic Regions

### Lands & Requirements

The next *Tnu Rabbanan* addresses the geographic dimension of *ibur hashana*: *b'shalosh aratzot ma'avrin et hashana* — on the basis of three different regions one assesses whether the conditions for intercalation exist: Yehuda, Ever HaYarden, and the Galil. *Al shtayim hen ma'avrin* — if the conditions exist in two of the regions, one intercalates; *v'al achas meihen ein ma'avrin* — but if only one region shows the signs, one does not.

### Yehuda Priority

*Ubizman she'Yehuda achas meihen hakol smechim* — when Yehuda is one of the two regions confirming the readiness, everyone is very happy, because *she'ein Omer ba ela miYehuda* — the *omer* comes only from Yehuda. Rashi clarifies that this does not mean literally that the *omer* cannot come from elsewhere, but rather that the proper practice is to bring it from Yehuda. So when the conditions in Yehuda allow us to bring the *omer* from its ideal source, there is general rejoicing.

### Authority in Yehuda

The next *Tnu Rabbanan* addresses where the act itself must take place: *ein ma'avrin et hashana ela b'Yehuda* — one may only intercalate the year in Yehuda. *V'im ivruha baGalil me'uberet* — but if they did it in the Galil, it is nonetheless valid.

### Chananya's Testimony

Against this, *He'id Chananya Ish Ono*: if they intercalated in the Galil, *einah me'uberet* — it does not take effect. This is framed as testimony, not merely as his opinion — presumably he had a tradition, or witnessed a case in which an intercalation performed in the Galil was voided.

Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, then asks: *mai ta'ama d'Chananya Ish Ono* — what is the reasoning behind Chananya's position? Interestingly, he frames the question not as "why should Yehuda be required in the first place?" but rather "why does he say it doesn't even work *bedieved*?"

---

## Authority: EY vs Bavel

### Eretz Yisrael Req.

The question is: what is the reason that even *bedieved*, intercalating outside of Yehuda fails? Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi's answer draws on the verse: *l'shichno tidreshu uvasa shamah* — "to His dwelling place you shall seek, and there you shall come."

### Lechono Tidreshu

*Kol drisha she'atah doresh lo yehei ela b'shichno shel makom* — any act of religious seeking must be performed in the proximity of God's dwelling, meaning in Yehuda, in the orbit of Jerusalem and the *Beit HaMikdash*. The question arises: in what sense is *ibur hashana* an act of *derisha* — of seeking? The connection becomes clearer through a second verse: *eretz asher Hashem Elohecha doresh otah* — "a land which the Lord your God seeks out," *mereishit hashana v'ad achrit shana* — "from the beginning of the year to its end." The idea is that assessing the year — determining its seasons, its agricultural conditions, its calendar — is itself an act of *derisha* of the land, a seeking out of its condition from beginning to end. This is an elegant reading.

### Tosafot Exceptions

Tosafot raises an immediate challenge: *v'hadar Rabbi Akiva iver shana b'Nehardea* — Rabbi Akiva performed an intercalation in Nehardea, which is not only outside Yehuda but outside Eretz Yisrael entirely. Tosafot, citing the beginning of the chapter *HaIsha Shalom* and the end of Berachot, answers: *shelo hiniach kamoso b'Eretz Yisrael* — Rabbi Akiva left no equal to himself in the Land of Israel. The principle is that if the greatest *talmid chacham* is situated outside Eretz Yisrael, the requirement to perform the intercalation specifically in Eretz Yisrael does not apply — because religious authority follows the greatest Torah scholar.

Tosafot further notes, citing the Yerushalmi explicitly: *d'cheshe'ein yecholim l'avrah b'Eretz Yisrael ma'avrin osah b'chutz la'aretz* — when it is impossible to intercalate in Eretz Yisrael, one may do so outside the Land. The case differs from Rabbi Akiva's: there it was a question of where the greater authority resided; here it is a question of political impossibility. The Yerushalmi cites Baruch ben Neriah and Yechezkel as examples of intercalations performed outside the Land, and the passage leads into the famous story of Chananya.

### Geonic Authority Shift

This entire discussion bears directly on one of the most significant questions in the history of Jewish law: why do we follow the Bavli rather than the Yerushalmi? Some wish to say it is because the Bavli was redacted a century later and therefore assessed all that the Yerushalmi had said — though whether the Bavli's editors actually knew the Yerushalmi as a text is itself quite questionable. The real reason is historical and sociological: the center of Torah had been shifting progressively to Bavel, and as the *Geonei Bavel* became the preeminent Torah authorities, communities throughout the Jewish world turned to them with their *halachic* questions. The *Geonei Bavel* used the Bavli; hence the Bavli became the determinative *Talmud* for all of Jewry.

But the picture was not so clean. Communities in Eretz Yisrael continued to turn to the *Geonei Eretz Yisrael*. There was not one undisputed center of authority. The decisive moment — what one might call the *maka b'patish*, the final hammer blow that settled the question — was a dispute in the Geonic period (eighth or ninth century) over the calendar itself, likely involving *rosh chodesh Tishrei*, when Bavel and Eretz Yisrael were determining different dates. One could live with disputes about the permissibility of various actions on *Shabbos*, but one cannot have Bavel observing one calendar and Eretz Yisrael another — that would fracture the people entirely. When the *Geonei Bavel* won that dispute by invoking the principle of *lo hiniach kamoso* — that greater Torah authority may relocate the seat of religious power — they definitively established Bavel as the locus of *halachic* authority, and with it, the Bavli as the authoritative *Talmud*.

Even so, the picture remained nuanced. Many of the Rambam's *psakim* that seem puzzling are explicable as reflecting the Yerushalmi. And Ashkenazic *minhagim* often diverge from the Bavli, a point Tosafot itself makes: Ashkenazic Jewry derived from Eretz Yisrael and carried with them the *minhagei Eretz Yisrael*, so that *minhagei Ashkenaz* sometimes track the Yerushalmi rather than the Bavli. Tosafot's own methodology is to work through the texts of the Bavli and render them consistent — not to systematically reconcile the Bavli with the Yerushalmi. When Tosafot encounters an Ashkenazic practice out of sync with the Bavli, it sometimes offers a reading of the Bavli that accommodates it, and sometimes simply acknowledges that the practice follows *minhag Eretz Yisrael* and diverges from the Bavli.

The entire question of *kiddush hachodesh* and *ibur hashana* — where it must be performed, who has authority to perform it — is in essence a question about where the seat of religious authority lies. That is what makes these *sugyot* so historically consequential.

---

## Time Restrictions

### Daytime Req.

The next *Tnu Rabbanan* introduces a temporal requirement: *ein ma'avrin et hashana ela bayom* — intercalation may only be performed during the daytime. *V'im ivruha balaila, eina me'uberet* — if they did it at night, it has no effect. Similarly, *v'ein mikadshin et hachodesh ela bayom* — *kiddush hachodesh* must also occur during the day. *V'im kidshuhu balaila, eino mekudash* — if they sanctified it at night, it is not sanctified. This is striking, given that the new moon is actually visible at night — and yet the active *kiddush* must occur in daylight.

### Daytime Proof

Rabbi Abba asks: *mai kra* — what is the scriptural basis? *Tiku bachodesh shofar bakeseh l'yom chageinu* — "Blow the shofar in the new month, at the covering, on our festival day." The Gemara asks: *eizehu chag shehachodesh mitkasseh bo* — which is the only festival on which the moon is concealed? The answer is *Rosh Hashanah*, since it falls on the first of the month when the moon is not yet visible. And the verse identifies this as *mishpat l'Elohei Yaakov* — a "judgment" belonging to the God of Yaakov. *Mah mishpat bayom* — just as judicial proceedings of *beit din* occur during the day, *af kiddush hachodesh bayom* — so too *kiddush hachodesh* must occur during the day.

---

## Famine Restrictions

### Famine Ban

We now arrive at 12a. *Ein me'avrin et hashana bishnei ra'avon* — one does not intercalate the year during a period of famine. The reason is that however compelling the other factors may be, one does not wish to delay the bringing of the *omer*, because people who are suffering from famine need access to grain as early as possible. Delaying *Pesach* by a month means delaying the *omer* and, with it, the permission to eat the new grain.

### Elisha Story

A *braita* is cited in which Rabbi offers a proof from a narrative about Elisha. A man came from Baal Shalisha and brought to the man of God — Elisha — *lechem bikkurim esrim lechem se'orim*, ripened bread of twenty barley loaves. The *braita* notes: *v'ein l'cha kala bechol Eretz Yisrael l'vashel peiroseha yoter miBa'al Shalisha* — there is no region in all of Eretz Yisrael where produce ripens more quickly than Ba'al Shalisha. And yet, *v'af al pi chein lo bikra ela min echad* — only one type, the barley, had ripened. The wheat had not yet ripened.

One might suggest that this was because the episode occurred before the *omer* — early in the spring season, when only barley ripens. But the *braita* counters: *talmud lomar ten l'am veyocheilu* — Elisha said "give to the people and let them eat," which indicates that this was *after* the *omer*, when eating was already permitted. So even after the *omer*, in the fastest-ripening region of Eretz Yisrael, only the barley had ripened and the wheat had not yet begun. *Haya omer me'atah re'uya haysa zo shana shetistabeir* — one would have said that this year truly should have been intercalated, that *Pesach* should have been pushed off so that more grain — including wheat — would ripen before the festival.

*U'mipnei mah lo ibra* — so why did Elisha not intercalate? *Sheshnas batzores haysa* — because it was a famine year. *V'hayu hakol ratzin l'veit hagranos* — and everyone was running to the granaries, desperately needing grain. One could not delay the bringing of the *omer* and thereby delay people's access to the new grain, even though from a purely agricultural standpoint the conditions might have warranted intercalation.

This passage also yields an important subsidiary observation. One might have assumed that *aviv* as a criterion for *Pesach* means only that the barley has ripened, since the *omer* brought on *Pesach* is from barley, while the *shtei halechem* of *Shavuot* is from wheat. But the *braita*, and Rashi explicitly, indicate that the ideal *aviv* condition for *Pesach* includes the beginning of the wheat's ripening as well — at least in some regions.

---

## Time Restrictions (II)

### Before RH Ban

The next *Tnu Rabbanan*: *ein me'avrin et hashana lifnei Rosh Hashanah* — one may not intercalate the year before *Rosh Hashanah*. A clarification is needed here: *Rosh Hashanah* in this context means the midpoint of the year, not the *Rosh Hashanah* twelve months prior. Since *ibur hashana* concerns *Adar* and *Nissan*, the relevant *Rosh Hashanah* falls mid-year. The intercalation must be done in the second half of the year, not the first. *V'im ivruha, eina me'uberet* — even if one did intercalate before *Rosh Hashanah*, it is not valid.

*Aval mipnei hadochak* — however, if there is pressing political constraint (Rashi suggests Roman governmental pressure, since *ibur hashana* was an exercise of religious authority and therefore sometimes subject to political interference), then *ma'avrin osa achar Rosh Hashanah miyad* — one may intercalate immediately after *Rosh Hashanah*. The preference is to do it closer to the relevant time both because the data about conditions will be more accurate and because people will take greater notice of it. But if compelled by circumstance, one may do it right after *Rosh Hashanah*.

### Adar Only

Even so: *v'af al pi chein ein me'avrin ela Adar* — regardless of when the decision is made, the only month one may add is *Adar*. The Gemara itself never explains why this is so. The intuitive answer would be that the Torah commands *Pesach* to fall in *chodesh ha'aviv*, and therefore the only way to properly situate *Pesach* is to fix the month immediately preceding it — which is *Adar*.

Tosafot, however, offers a different reason entirely. The *pasuk* in Esther states *b'chodesh shenayim asar hu chodesh Adar* — "in the twelfth month, which is *Adar*." The Torah similarly fixes *Nissan* as the first month and *Tishrei* as the seventh. These numerical designations are anchored. If one were to add a month other than *Adar*, all those fixed numberings would shift, and *Adar* could no longer be the twelfth month. The only way to preserve the numbering is to add a thirteenth month at the end — a second *Adar* — without displacing any of the others. This is a fascinating reason, and it is noteworthy that the Gemara itself does not state it.

---

## Political Constraints

### Coded Message

The Gemara then raises a challenge: *v'ha shalchu lei l'Rava* — but they sent to Rava the following message. The message is cryptic, evidently designed so that Roman authorities would not understand it. *Zug ba mi-Rakat* — a pair has come from *Rakat*, which Rashi identifies as Tiberias, meaning two *talmidei chachamim*. *V'tafso nesher* — and the eagle has seized them. The eagle, of course, is Rome, whose legions bore the eagle as their standard. *U'vi'yadam devarim ha-na'asim b'Luz* — and in their hands were things produced in Luz. The Gemara interjects: *u'mai nihu techelet* — what is this? *Techelet*. *Techelet* was produced in Luz. Rome had a vested interest in *techelet* as a controlled substance — it was the royal blue — and so these scholars may have been seized for violating some edict or for evading duties on it. *U'vizchut ha-rachamim u'vizchutam yatz'u b'shalom* — through divine mercy and their own merit, they came out unharmed.

### Rome's Prevention

*V'amusei yarchei Nachshon* — and those who carried the lineage of the loins of Nachshon, meaning *Nachshon ben Aminadav*, i.e. the house of Yehuda and ultimately the *nasi*'s household. *Bikshu likvo'a natziv* — they sought to establish a *natziv*, which we will shortly see is a term for an intercalated month. *V'lo hinicha'an adomi ha-laz* — and this Edomite — Rome — did not allow them. The Roman government prevented them from performing the *ibur hashana*.

### Decision in Av

*Aval ba'alei asupot ne'esfu v'kav'u lo natziv echad b'yerach she-met bo Aharon haKohen* — but those who gather — the *talmidei chachamim* — gathered and established an extra month in the month in which Aaron the *Kohen* died, which is Av. Now this seems problematic: how could they do *ibur hashana* in Av, which is before *Rosh Hashanah*? The Gemara resolves this: *chashuvei machshvei, galuyei lo me-galu* — they performed the calculations, and they determined that an intercalation would be required. But they did not make the formal announcement, or alternatively they did not perform the official act creating the intercalation — they merely resolved upon it and completed the calculation. The public proclamation was reserved for the proper time.

### Natziv Terminology

The Gemara then asks: *mai mashma d'hai natziv lishna d'yarcha hu* — how do we know that the word *natziv* in this coded message means a month? The source is the verse: *u'li-Shlomo shenayim asar netzivim al kol Yisrael v'chalkelu et ha-melech v'et beito chodesh ba-shanah* — Solomon appointed twelve officers over all Israel, and each one provided sustenance for the king's household during one month of the year. The association of a *natziv* — an officer — with a monthly appointment is what gives the term its meaning as a month in the coded communication.

The Gemara then cites a verse indicating that there was *v'natziv echad asher ba'aretz* — one *natziv* over the land. Two opinions are offered: one says this was a superintendent over the twelve; the other says *keneged chodesh ibur* — this was the officer corresponding to the intercalated month, the second *Adar*, whose role only arose in a leap year.

---

## Shemita & Consecutive

### No Consecutive Years

The next *Tnu Rabbanan* addresses a different set of restrictions: *ein me'avrin et hashana lo mishanah l'chaverta* — one does not intercalate from one year to the next. The precise meaning of this is debated between Rashi and Tosafot. Rashi understands it to mean that one may not intercalate this year for the sake of the *next* year's seasons — intercalation must address a problem of the *current* year. Tosafot understands it differently: one may not even make the calculation more than a year in advance. This would explain the apparent redundancy with the rule that one cannot intercalate before *Rosh Hashanah* — Tosafot's reading extends the prohibition to the calculation itself, not merely the act, since so many relevant factors are unknown that far in advance.

*V'lo shalosh shanim zo achar zo* — and one may not intercalate three years in a row, as that would distort the calendar entirely.

Rabbi Shimon then introduces a story: *ma'aseh b'Rabbi Akiva shehayah chavush b'veit ha'asurim* — there was an episode involving Rabbi Akiva while he was imprisoned, in the period leading up to his martyrdom. *V'iber shalosh shanim zo achar zo* — and they effectively calculated three consecutive leap years, sending a delegation to consult with Rabbi Akiva in prison. This seems to directly contradict the prohibition.

The Gemara responds: *amru lo misham ra'ayah?* — you want to bring a proof from there? *Beit din yashvu v'kav'u achat achat bizmanah* — the court sat and established each one in its proper time. The resolution is not entirely clear. One reading is that the three leap years Rabbi Akiva calculated were not actually consecutive — they were the next three occasions on which intercalation would be required, but spread out over a longer period. Another reading is that even if three consecutive leap years were warranted, what is prohibited is the advance determination that they will all be intercalated, without reassessing each one in its proper time — whereas here, each year was independently assessed when it arrived. The precise parameters of the prohibition and the precise force of the resolution thus remain somewhat open.

### Shemita Bans

*Ein me'avrin et hashana lo bishvi'it v'lo b'motza'ei shvi'it* — one does not intercalate during *shemita* and does not intercalate in the year immediately following *shemita*. The reason for the *shemita* year is obvious: intercalating extends the period in which one cannot plant. The reason for the year after *shemita* is that people have been waiting anxiously for the *omer* to be brought as soon as possible so that they may begin eating grain from the fields they have just resumed planting. Delaying *Pesach* by an extra month makes that wait even longer.

### Preferred Timing

*Eimatai regilin l'aber* — when was the preferred time to intercalate? *Erev shvi'it* — the year before *shemita*. This makes sense: giving people an extra month of planting and harvesting before *shemita* arrives is a genuine benefit.

### Vegetable Imports

*Shebeveit Raban Gamliel hayu me'avrin b'motza'ei shvi'it* — in the house of Raban Gamliel they would intercalate in the year after *shemita*. How could they do this if it would delay people's access to new grain? The Gemara explains: *uv'plugta d'hani tanna'ei* — this reflects a tannaitic dispute. The underlying debate is: *ein mevi'in yerak michutz la'aretz* — one may not import vegetables from outside Eretz Yisrael, while *v'raboteinu hitiru* — the sages permitted it. The question between them, as Rabbi Yirmiyah explains, is whether one is concerned about the soil that adheres to the vegetables, since the soil of *chutz la'aretz* is *tamei* and importing it could create *tumah* problems.

The house of Raban Gamliel held that vegetables may be imported. If so, food could be brought in from *chutz la'aretz* to compensate for the delay, making intercalation after *shemita* tolerable. It is worth noting that this logic — intercalating a leap year and relying on imports to supply food — reflects a trade-off between *halachic* concerns and economic priorities, specifically whether it is appropriate to make calendar decisions on the assumption that agricultural self-sufficiency can be supplemented by imports.

---

## Tumah Exception

### Tumah as Reason

The next *Tnu Rabbanan*: *ein me'avrin et hashana mipnei hatumah* — one does not intercalate the year on account of *tumah*. The case would be: there is concern that people are *tamei* and unable to bring the *korban Pesach*; if we add a month, people will have time to become *tahor* and be able to participate. Nevertheless, this is not a valid reason. *Rabbi Yehuda omer me'avrin* — Rabbi Yehuda says it is a valid reason.

### Chizkiyahu Story

Rabbi Yehuda then adds: *ma'aseh b'Chizkiyahu melech Yehuda she'eibur et hashana mipnei hatumah* — there was an episode in which Chizkiyahu, king of Yehuda, intercalated the year because of *tumah*. *U'vikeish rachamim al atzmo* — and he then sought divine forgiveness for himself.

This is immediately puzzling. Rabbi Yehuda first says intercalating for *tumah* is permitted, then cites Chizkiyahu as support, but then reports that Chizkiyahu sought forgiveness — which would imply it was wrong. The Gemara will need to unravel what Rabbi Yehuda is actually saying.

The scriptural basis for the episode is the verse: *ki marbit ha'am rabat me'Ephraim u'Menashe Yissachar u'Zevulun lo hitaharu* — the vast majority of the people from those tribes were not ritually pure when Chizkiyahu convened the great *korban Pesach* revival. A subsequent verse states: *ki achlu et haPesach b'lo kakatuv* — they ate the *Pesach* offering contrary to what is written. The plain reading of these verses is that they ate the *korban Pesach* in a state of *tumah*. But the Gemara does not read it that way.

First, if the majority of the people were *tamei*, the principle of *tumah hutra b'tzibbur* would apply, and eating the *korban Pesach b'tumah* in that case would be permitted. So that cannot be what "contrary to what is written" refers to. Second, the Gemara chooses to understand the violation differently: Chizkiyahu, seeing that the people were *tamei*, decided to solve the problem by intercalating the year — adding a month to give people time to become *tahor*. It was this act of intercalation that was the violation. The people's eating of the *korban Pesach* at the wrong time was the consequence — they observed *Pesach* at what should not have been the correct time, because the *ibur hashana* had been improperly performed. *Ki hitpalel Chizkiyahu aleihem leimor Hashem hatov yichaper b'ad* — Chizkiyahu then prayed for forgiveness on their behalf.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees entirely: *im mipnei hatumah ibrunah me'uberet* — if they intercalated because of *tumah*, the intercalation is valid. So what was Chizkiyahu praying for forgiveness for? *She'ein me'avrin ela Adar v'hu iber Nissan b'Nissan* — because one may only add *Adar*, and Chizkiyahu made his decision when *Nissan* had already arrived. He effectively added a second *Nissan* and pushed *Pesach* to the second *Nissan* rather than the first.

Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda then offers yet another reading in the name of Rabbi Shimon: Chizkiyahu's sin was that he directed all the *tamei* people to go and bring a *Pesach sheini* — the second *Pesach* observed a month later for those who could not bring the offering in *Nissan*. This was wrong because since the majority of the people were *tamei*, *tumah hutra b'tzibbur* should have applied, and they should have been permitted to bring the *Pesach rishon* together with everyone else.

### Tumah Hutra/Dechuya

The Gemara now works through the conceptual structure underlying this dispute. *Amar mar Rabbi Yehuda omer me'avrin — alma sevira lei l'Rabbi Yehuda tumah dechuya hi b'tzibbur* — the Gemara infers that Rabbi Yehuda, by saying intercalation is warranted, must hold that *tumah* is merely *dechuya* — overridden but still a violation — in the case of a *tzibbur*. If *tumah* is only overridden and not fully permitted, then we should prefer to avoid the conflict altogether by adding a month, rather than having people eat the *korban* in a state of *tumah* even under permitted circumstances.

But a challenge arises: there is a *braita* concerning the *tzitz* — the golden headplate worn by the *Kohen Gadol* — which atones for *korbanot* brought in *tumah*. The dispute there concerns whether the *tzitz* operates to make such a *korban* acceptable only while the *Kohen Gadol* is actively wearing it on his forehead (*divrei Rabbi Shimon*) or whether its presence in the *mishkan* is sufficient even if he is not wearing it (*Rabbi Yehuda*). Rabbi Shimon challenges Rabbi Yehuda: what about the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur*, when he wears white garments and is not wearing the *tzitz*, and yet we know that *korbanot* brought in *tumah* on *Yom Kippur* are acceptable? Rabbi Yehuda responds: *henach l'Yom Hakippurim she-tumah hutra b'tzibur* — do not cite *Yom Kippur* to me, because on *Yom Kippur* the *tumah* is *hutra* — fully permitted — for the *tzibbur*, and that is why those *korbanot* are acceptable, not because of the *tzitz*.

This is decisive: Rabbi Yehuda himself says *tumah hutra b'tzibbur*, not *dechuya*. But if *tumah* is fully permitted for the *tzibbur*, there is no basis for intercalating the year in order to avoid the situation. Why, then, did Rabbi Yehuda say intercalation is warranted?

### Emendation of View

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *ela chisuri michsera v'hachi katani* — the *braita* must be emended, and this is how it should be read: *ein me'avrin et hashana mipnei hatumah v'im ibru me'uberet* — one does not intercalate because of *tumah*, but if one did, *bedieved* it takes effect. *Rabbi Yehuda omer eina me'uberet* — Rabbi Yehuda says it does not take effect even *bedieved*.

This is a striking reversal. Rabbi Yehuda has been moved from one extreme to the other: from being the one who says *lechatchila* one may intercalate for *tumah*, to being the one who says even *bedieved* it does not work. But now the positions are internally consistent. Rabbi Yehuda holds *tumah hutra b'tzibbur* — there is no violation, hence no motivation to intercalate, and an intercalation performed for that reason is nullified even after the fact. And now Rabbi Yehuda's citation of Chizkiyahu also makes sense: Chizkiyahu added a month because of *tumah* and asked for forgiveness precisely because it was invalid — consistent with Rabbi Yehuda's position that such intercalation is ineffective.

The Gemara then asks: *ei hachi Rabbi Shimon omer im mipnei hatumah ibrunah me'uberet — hainu tanna kamma* — if this is how we read the positions, then Rabbi Shimon, who says *bedieved* the intercalation works, is identical to the first *tanna*, who also says *bedieved* it works. *Amar Rava lechatchila ika beinaihu* — Rava resolves this: the debate between them is about *lechatchila*. The first *tanna* holds that *lechatchila* one does not intercalate for *tumah*, but *bedieved* it takes effect. Rabbi Yehuda holds it does not take effect even *bedieved*. And Rabbi Shimon holds that one may even do so *lechatchila*. A supporting *braita* confirms this three-way structure.

### Fixed-Time Principle

Before proceeding, Tosafot makes an important clarifying observation about the phrase *tumah hutra b'tzibbur*. The formulation implies that the leniency is a function of the *tzibbur* — communal — nature of the offering. But Tosafot insists this is not precise. *Ein ha-davar talui b'tzibbur* — the matter does not depend on whether the offering is a *korban tzibbur*.

Tosafot cites the *mishnah* in the chapter *Hotzi'u*: the *par* of *Yom Kippur*, the *chavitei Kohen Gadol*, and *Pesach* — all of which are technically *korbanot yachid*, individual offerings — override both *Shabbos* and *tumah*. On the other hand, the *par he'elam davar shel tzibbur*, the *se'irei avoda zara*, and *chagiga* — all *korbanot tzibbur* — do *not* override *Shabbos* and *tumah*. So the distinction between *tzibbur* and *yachid* does not map onto the question of whether *tumah* is permitted.

Tosafot then states the true principle: *kol she-zmano kavu'a docheh* — any *korban* whose time is fixed overrides *Shabbos* and *tumah*, even if it is a private offering; *v'chol she-ein zmano kavu'a eino docheh v'afilu de-tzibur* — and any *korban* whose time is not fixed does not override, even if it is a communal offering. The phrase *tumah hutra b'tzibbur*, which is so commonly invoked, is thus a shorthand that is, strictly speaking, imprecise — it is really about fixed-time *korbanot*, not about the communal versus individual distinction.

---

## Chizkiyahu's Error

### 30th Adar Error

The Gemara now returns to Chizkiyahu's specific error. *Amar mar she-ein me'avrin ela Adar v'hu iber Nissan b'Nissan* — the claim is that Chizkiyahu did not add an extra *Nissan* in the straightforward sense. Rather, he declared a second *Adar* — but he did so on the 30th day of *Adar* itself. The violation was thus not adding *Nissan* per se, but declaring the intercalation when it was already the 30th of *Adar*.

### Shmuel's Ruling

This is based on Shmuel's ruling: *de-amar Shmuel ein me'avrin et hashana b'yom shloshim shel Adar* — even if *Adar* is a 30-day month, one may not perform the intercalation on *Adar* 30. The reason is that *Adar* 30 *hu ra'uy l'kovo Nissan* — that day is potentially *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*. Once a day is capable of being *Nissan*, the window for declaring an intercalation has closed.

Chizkiyahu's mistake was that he reasoned: *v'hu savar chov v'ra'uy lo amrinan* — he thought that the rule *ra'uy*, "potentially," does not close the window. He believed that as long as *Nissan* had not been formally declared, there was still time to add a second *Adar*. That was his error, and it is what required his seeking of forgiveness.

### Tannai Debate

The Gemara confirms Shmuel's ruling with a supporting *braita*: *ein me'avrin et hashana b'yom shloshim shel Adar hu ra'uy l'kovo Nissan* — one may not intercalate on *Adar* 30 since that day is eligible to become *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*. With this, the Gemara has assembled all the opinions regarding Chizkiyahu's sin: according to Rabbi Yehuda (as re-read), his sin was adding a month because of *tumah* when that is not a valid basis; according to Rabbi Shimon, his sin was that he did so on *Nissan* itself — specifically on *Adar* 30, which can already be the beginning of *Nissan*; and according to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon, his sin was directing *tamei* individuals to bring *Pesach sheini* when they should have been permitted to bring *Pesach rishon* along with the majority.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 13

## Chizkiyahu & Tumah

### Chizkiyahu Overview

The daf opens at the bottom of 12b, continuing the discussion of Chizkiyahu and his controversial *korban Pesach*. The verse describes the people as having brought the *korban Pesach* *she'lo kakatuv* — not in accordance with what the Torah requires — and one of the reasons given is that Chizkiyahu added an extra month on account of *tuma*. The underlying question is whether *tuma* is a legitimate grounds for *ibur shana* in the first place, and whether the famous principle of *tuma hutrah betzibbur* or *dechuyah betzibbur* is relevant. An additional possibility is that Chizkiyahu acted on the thirtieth of Adar, which was already a day eligible to be designated as Nissan — and we encountered both of those positions earlier.

Now the Gemara continues, three lines into the wide-lined text. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon: the problem was that Chizkiyahu caused Israel to bring *Pesach Sheni*, delaying the *korban* to the second Pesach when they could have brought it on *Pesach Rishon* despite their *tuma*.

### Half Impure & Women

The Gemara asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly was the situation, and why was there any ambiguity? Rav Ashi explains: the case was one where Israel was exactly half *tamei* and half *tahor* — or perhaps slightly less than half *tamei*, since triggering *tuma hutrah betzibbur* requires a *rov tamei*. Chizkiyahu's error was factoring in the women. When women were included in the count, the *tahorim* became the majority, and Chizkiyahu concluded that since the majority was *tahor*, the *tamei* minority should be deferred to *Pesach Sheni*. But the rabbis disagreed: even if women bring the *korban Pesach*, the determination of whether *rov tzibbur* is *tamei* is made by counting men alone.

### Women's Status Shift

The Gemara explains that Chizkiyahu's position actually evolved. Initially — *me'ikara* — he held that women are *obligated* in *Pesach Rishon*, and therefore they are included in the count: when factored in, the *tamei* were a minority and were pushed to *Pesach Sheni*. Ultimately — *levasof* — he concluded that women have *reshut* to bring the *korban Pesach* on *Pesach Rishon* but are not obligated, and therefore they are not counted in determining the ratio. Under that reading, the *tamei* were in fact the majority, and the majority does not defer to *Pesach Sheni* but must bring on *Pesach Rishon*. The Gemara uses this as the *gufa* of the passage and then transitions to the separate topic of *ibur shana*.

---

## Ibur Shana Timing

### No Ibur on Adar 30

The Gemara, after closing out the Chizkiyahu discussion, records: *amar Shmuel*, you do not perform *ibur shana* on the thirtieth day of Adar, because that day is already eligible to be designated as Nissan. As we learned in the Yerushalmi, this day would normally become *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*.

### Ulla's De Facto

The Gemara then asks: *ibruha mai* — if *bedi'avad* you did carry out the intercalation on the thirtieth of Adar — say by not formally designating the month but simply treating it as a second Adar — would it take effect? One might think not, since this appeared to be the very mistake of Chizkiyahu according to one opinion. Ulla answers: you do not perform *kiddush hachodesh* — you do not formally declare "today is *Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni*." Rashi explains this clearly: since the day is eligible to be Nissan, we say "this is Nissan and there is nothing after Nissan." Instead, one remains silent, and when the next *Rosh Chodesh* arrives, one sanctifies it as Nissan. So Ulla's solution is that *de facto* intercalation can be accomplished without a formal declaration. That resolves the *bedi'avad* question.

### Rava vs. Nachman

But what if one *did* formally declare — on the thirtieth of Adar — "today is *Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni*"? Rava says: *batel ha'ibur* — the intercalation is void. This is, again, precisely what one opinion identified as Chizkiyahu's error. Rav Nachman, however, says: *me'ubar umekudash* — it is both intercalated and sanctified, and the declaration stands.

### Purim-Pesach Gap

Rava presses Rav Nachman with a practical objection. From Purim to Pesach is thirty days, and we begin teaching and asking about the laws of Pesach thirty days before Pesach — as the Baraita states: *sho'alin vedorshin be'hilchos haPesach kodem haPesach shloshim yom*, with Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel giving the opinion of two weeks. If *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* is only announced when it is already *Rosh Chodesh* — so late in the process — people will still be operating under the assumption that Pesach follows thirty days after Purim. When they suddenly hear a late announcement of *ibur*, they will not absorb it in time. They may already be treating chametz leniently (*mezalzel bechametz*) because they believe Pesach is a month later than it actually is.

### Computation Known

Rav Nachman responds: people know. The intercalation of the year depends on computation — *bechushbana talya milta* — and the public understands that the rabbis may not have completed their calculations until late in the month. People will not dismiss a late announcement of *ibur shana*; they will accept it and conduct themselves accordingly. There is therefore no practical concern.

---

## Tekufah & Ibur

### Majority Month Rule

The Gemara now introduces a ruling attributed to Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel — wrapping up the preceding subject and transitioning to a topic that will occupy the remainder of the daf: *ein me'abrin et hashana ela im ken hayta tekufah chaseira rubo shel chodesh* — one does not intercalate the year unless the *tekufah* is off by the majority of a month. The context here is not the agricultural consideration of *chodesh ha'aviv* and the ripening of grain, but the solar-calendrical requirement: *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* is supposed to coincide with the vernal equinox, and *Rosh Chodesh Tishrei* with the autumnal equinox. If the equinox is displaced far enough into the month — if the solar season is starting too late relative to the calendar — a month must be added to realign them. The question is how far off the *tekufah* must be before intercalation is required.

### Rabbi Yehuda: 16 Days

Shmuel's rule specifies a majority of a month, and the Baraita then asks: how much is the majority of a month? *Shishah asar yom* — sixteen days, according to Rabbi Yehuda. The reasoning is that Pesach must fall during the spring, and when the *omer* is brought, the season should be in effect. If the vernal equinox is displaced sixteen days past *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*, Pesach will no longer fall within the proper seasonal window, and intercalation becomes necessary.

### Rabbi Yose: 21 Days

Rabbi Yose says: *echad ve'esrim yom* — twenty-one days. Both opinions derive from the same verse, and the Bavli is striking in its choice of locus: rather than focusing on Nissan and Pesach as the Yerushalmi does, it examines the pasuk about Sukkot.

---

## Tekufah Interpretation

### Chag Ha-Asif Views

Both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose expound the same verse: *chag ha'asif tekufat hashana* — the festival of the ingathering, at the *tekufah* of the year. The dispute turns on what "the festival of the ingathering" requires with respect to the new season. One opinion holds that *kulo chag ba'inan bi'tekufah chadasha* — all of *chag ha'asif* must be within the new *tekufah*. As Rashi explains, *chag ha'asif* refers to *Chol HaMoed*, the intermediate days of Sukkot, when labor — including the gathering of the harvest — is actually permitted. *Chol HaMoed* spans seven days: the days between the first *yom tov* and *Shemini Atzeret*, running from the 16th through the 21st of Tishrei. The other opinion holds that only *miktzat chag*, some portion of *Chol HaMoed*, need fall in the new season.

To illustrate: picture the month of Tishrei, with the autumnal equinox meant to coincide with *Rosh Chodesh*. If the equinox has shifted forward — if the fall season, calendrically speaking, now begins on day 17 rather than day 1 — then only if it begins by day 16 is all of *Chol HaMoed* guaranteed to fall within the fall. If the equinox begins on day 17, the 16th of Tishrei — the first day of *Chol HaMoed* — was still part of the summer, and the requirement that all of *chag ha'asif* fall in the new season has been violated. That is the opinion requiring intercalation when the *tekufah* is sixteen days off. The other opinion requires only that some portion of *Chol HaMoed* begin within the new season: even if the first days of *Chol HaMoed* were in the old season, as long as the 21st of Tishrei — the last day of *Chol HaMoed* — begins in the fall, that suffices. That permits being up to twenty days off before intercalation is required.

### Yom Tekufah Debate

The Gemara probes the assumptions behind these positions. The equinox does not fall at the precise start of a calendar day; it can occur at any hour. The question therefore arises: does the day on which the equinox falls count as the final day of the outgoing season (*yom tekufah gomer*) or the first day of the incoming season (*yom tekufah matchil*)? The Gemara reasons that both opinions must hold *yom tekufah matchil* — the equinox day inaugurates the new season — because if they held *yom tekufah gomer*, neither position would work. If the equinox day still belongs to the old season, then even being fifteen days off would be problematic under the first opinion, since the sixteenth day of *Chol HaMoed* would still be in the prior season. The only way either threshold makes sense is if the day of the *tekufah* is already part of the new season.

A contradiction is then raised from a Baraita: *yom tekufah gomer — divrei Rabbi Yehuda; Rabbi Yose omer yom tekufah matchil*. This is a direct contradiction of the Gemara's assumption that both held *matchil*. Moreover, a second Baraita contradicts Rabbi Yehuda's position of sixteen days: there, Rabbi Yehuda says *shtei yadot* — two thirds of a month, which is twenty days — not sixteen.

### Rabbi Yehuda Contradicti…

The Gemara notes this second contradiction baldly. In the first Baraita, Rabbi Yehuda says sixteen days. In the second Baraita, Rabbi Yehuda says twenty days. The Gemara leaves this unresolved: *kashya*.

### Matchil/Gomer Resolution

However, having introduced the second Baraita, the Gemara now turns to explaining the relationship between its opinions. Rabbi Yehuda says twenty days; Rabbi Yose says that one calculates sixteen days before Pesach — if the *tekufah* is sixteen days off at Pesach time, one intercalates; but sixteen days before Sukkot, one does not intercalate. The Gemara notes that twenty and twenty-one seem to be saying essentially the same thing, and asks whether Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose are simply agreeing. The answer: *yom tekufah gomer ve'yom tekufah matchil ika beinihu* — the difference between them is precisely the dispute about the equinox day. Rabbi Yose holds *matchil*: if the *tekufah* is twenty days off, the twenty-first day itself begins the new season and that last day of *Chol HaMoed* is fine. Rabbi Yehuda holds *gomer*: even at twenty days off, the twenty-first day is still the old season, so you can only tolerate being nineteen days off — i.e., twenty days is already a problem, which is why he says twenty.

### Five-Day Shift

The Gemara then addresses the seemingly anomalous language of Rabbi Yose, who speaks of sixteen days before Pesach rather than twenty-one days before Sukkot. The explanation involves a five-day differential between the lunar calendar and the solar seasons. There are ninety-one days to each *tekufah* (four times ninety-one equals three hundred sixty-four, approximately a solar year). But the distance from Tishrei to Nissan on the lunar calendar — six months averaging twenty-nine and a half days each — works out to approximately a hundred and seventy-seven days, while the seasonal distance is one hundred and eighty-two days (two times ninety-one). The five-day difference means that whatever the seasonal displacement is at Nissan time, it will have grown by five more days by Sukkot. If the *tekufah* is sixteen days off at Nissan, it will be twenty-one days off by Tishrei. Rabbi Yose is therefore expressing the same twenty-one-day threshold — but keyed to the Nissan calculation rather than the Tishrei one. His formulation says: if you are sixteen days off at Pesach time, you know the Sukkot *tekufah* will be twenty-one days off, which is beyond the threshold, and you intercalate. But if you are only sixteen days off *at Sukkot time*, that is within the twenty-one-day tolerance, and you do not intercalate. The reason he uses the number sixteen in both places is stylistic symmetry — the Baraita mentions sixteen before Pesach, and so it also says sixteen before the *chag*; but in reality, the threshold at Sukkot is anywhere up to twenty days off.

### Acheirim: 14 Days

*Acheirim* offer yet another threshold: *mi'uto* — even a minority of the month is sufficient to require intercalation. *Vechama mi'uto?* Fourteen days. The Gemara asks what the underlying reasoning is. To get to a threshold of fourteen, one must hold two things simultaneously: first, that all of Sukkot proper — including *yom tov rishon*, not merely *Chol HaMoed* — must fall within the new season; and second, that the equinox day belongs to the old season (*gomer*). If the *tekufah* is fourteen days off, it falls on the fifteenth of Tishrei — the first day of Sukkot itself. If that day is still part of the old season, the festival has not begun in the new season, which triggers the requirement to intercalate. The Gemara confirms this: *ei kasavri yom tekufah gomer ve'chulei chag ba'inan* — if we assume *gomer* and require the entire *chag* (including *yom tov rishon*) to be in the new season, then fourteen days off is indeed a problem.

### Pesach Reference

The Gemara turns back to Rabbi Yose's language about computing sixteen days before Pesach and asks: why does Rabbi Yose reference Pesach at all, if the underlying standard is about Sukkot? And, more sharply: if Sukkot is the operative framework, Rabbi Yose should say that up to twenty days off at Sukkot time is permissible — why does he say sixteen? The Gemara answers that the phrasing is driven by the parallel structure of the Baraita: because the opening clause says sixteen days before Pesach, the concluding clause uses sixteen before the *chag* as well. But substantively, Rabbi Yose's position permits being up to twenty days off at Sukkot without intercalating; it is only when the displacement reaches twenty-one — detectable already at Pesach as a sixteen-day offset — that intercalation is required. The number sixteen appears at the *chag* because it mirrors the formulation of the *reisha*, not because it independently represents a threshold there.

### Waxing Moon

Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak offers a distinct explanation for the *acheirim* position, one that does not depend on Sukkot at all but instead invokes the verse about Nissan: *shamor et chodesh ha'aviv* — guard the month of the ripening. He reads *chodesh* in the sense of *chadash* — renewal, the waxing of the moon. The injunction is that the *tekufah* of spring must occur while the moon is still *chadash*, still waxing. The moon waxes from the first of the month through the fourteenth, and becomes full on the fifteenth — at which point it is no longer waxing. If the spring *tekufah* is fourteen days off, it falls on the fifteenth of Nissan, when the moon is already full. That means the equinox arrives when the month is no longer waxing, violating the requirement of *chodesh ha'aviv*. Hence, if displaced by fourteen days, intercalation is necessary.

The Gemara then asks: but if you are only slightly off — say, one day — why must you add an entire extra month? Why not simply add one day to Adar? The Gemara answers through Rav Acha bar Yaakov: the *tanna*'s formulation counts downward rather than upward. When *acheirim* say *mi'uto*, fourteen days, they mean that *up to and including* fourteen days you do not intercalate; only from fifteen onward is intercalation required. This resolves the question about adding a single day: a single day's displacement does not trigger intercalation at all.

### Ravina & Tishrei

Ravina offers an alternative reading: *l'olam acheirim beTishrei kaimei* — the *acheirim* are actually speaking about Tishrei all along, not Nissan. One might ask: if the *tekufah* falls on the fifteenth of Tishrei, all of *Chol HaMoed* still falls within the new season — so why should being fourteen days off be a problem? Ravina answers: *acheirim* require not only that *Chol HaMoed* begin in the new season, but that *yom tov rishon* itself must begin in the new season — *kulei chag ba'inan ve'yom tov rishon*. If the *tekufah* is fourteen days off and falls on the fifteenth, and if we hold *yom tekufah gomer* — that the equinox day still belongs to the prior season — then the first day of Sukkot was the last day of the old season. The Gemara objects: can *yom tov rishon* really be included in *chag ha'asif*? One cannot do agricultural labor on *yom tov* itself. The Gemara answers: *chag haba biz'man asifah* — the verse means the *chag* that arrives during the time of gathering. Even if the gathering cannot actually occur on *yom tov*, the verse intends that the festival itself must fall within the season of the ingathering, which encompasses *yom tov rishon* as well.

The cumulative picture that emerges is this: there are three interlocking variables — which portion of Sukkot must fall in the new season (*yom tov rishon*, the first day of *Chol HaMoed*, or the last day of *Chol HaMoed*); whether *yom tekufah* is *matchil* or *gomer*; and whether the computation is keyed to Nissan or Tishrei. The interplay of these variables generates the range of thresholds: fourteen, sixteen, twenty, and twenty-one days.

---

## Smicha Zekenim

### Elders Defined
