With the *tekufah* discussion concluded, the Gemara turns to the second topic of our *Mishnah*: *semichat zekenim*, the placing of hands by the elders on the *par he'elam davar shel tzibbur* — the communal *korban* brought when the Great Sanhedrin issued an erroneous ruling and the majority of the Jewish people acted upon it. The Baraita opens: *v'samchu ziknei* — "and the elders shall lay their hands." One might think the word *zekenim* simply means older men, perhaps communal figures one might encounter in the marketplace. The Baraita therefore derives from the word *edah* that these must be the elders of the congregation — the *Sanhedrin*. And since the plain meaning of *edah* could encompass even a small *Sanhedrin* of twenty-three, the Baraita adds *ha'edah hameyuchadim she'ba'edah* — the preeminent court over all of Israel, meaning the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one.

### 5 vs. 3

How many of the Great Sanhedrin actually perform the *semichah*? The verse uses the word *v'samchu*, which is plural — implying two — and *ziknei*, also plural — implying another two. Since a court cannot be even-numbered, one additional member is added, yielding five. This is the position of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Shimon says three: *ziknei* implies two, an even court cannot stand, so a third is added. That gives three.

### Vayasmchu Debate

The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon turns on whether the word *v'samchu* is exegetically available. Rabbi Yehuda reads it as adding two additional members beyond the two already derived from *ziknei*, yielding five. Rabbi Shimon objects: *v'samchu* is not extra — it is the essential verb of the sentence, telling us what the elders actually do. Had it been omitted, the text would have read "the elders of the congregation, their hands upon the head of the calf" — the verb *samach* would have been understood implicitly from context. Rabbi Shimon therefore says the word is necessary for its own meaning and cannot be used as a derivation.

Rabbi Yehuda rejoins: *lichtov ziknei ha'eidah yedeihem al rosh hapar* — the Torah could simply have written "the elders of the congregation, their hands on the head of the ox," and we would have understood from the context of *semichah* (as derived from *gezeirah shavah* of *rosh rosh* from an *olah*) that "their hands" means pressed upon the head. The verb *v'samchu* is therefore genuinely extra, and Rabbi Yehuda uses it to derive two additional elders. Rabbi Shimon counters that without the verb, he would have understood *al rosh* to mean merely in proximity to the head, not actually resting hands upon it. He does not accept the *rosh rosh* derivation as making the verb superfluous. The dispute ends there.

---

## Semichah Authority

### Two Types

A Baraita records: *semichah u'semichas zekeinim bishloshoh* — both *semichah* (the granting of rabbinic authority) and *semichas zekenim* (the placing of hands on the communal *korban*) require three.

### Semichah Definition

The Gemara asks: *mai semichah u'mai semichas zekeinim* — what distinguishes these two? Rabbi Yochanan answers: *mismach savi* — *semichah* here means the ordination of sages, the transmission of rabbinic authority. This is a distinct institution from the *semichah* of the elders on the *korban*, even though the same Hebrew root is used for both.

### Moshe & Yehoshua

Abaye then addresses Rav Yosef: where do we learn that this *semichah* of ordination requires three? He raises the obvious source: *vayismoch et yadav alav* — Moshe lays his hands upon Yehoshua. This is the paradigmatic model for the transmission of authority: Moshe received Torah at Sinai and transmitted it to Yehoshua, Yehoshua to the elders, and so down through the generations.

### One or 71?

But if Moshe is the model, the number derived is one — Moshe did it alone. If one argues that Moshe stood in the place of the entire Sanhedrin, then one needs seventy-one. How does one arrive at three? The Gemara leaves this unresolved: *kashya*.

### Semichah by Name

Rav Acha, son of Rava, asks Rav Ashi: is *semichah* performed by literally placing hands on the recipient's head, as Moshe did with Yehoshua? Rav Ashi responds: no — *samchinan lei bishmah*, it is done by conferring a name or title. The recipient is called *Rebbi*. This explains why some *tanna'im* and *amora'im* carry the title *Rebbi* and others do not — and this also reflects, in part, the distinction between sages ordained in Eretz Yisrael and those in Bavel — since this chain of *semichah* ultimately goes back to Moshe and is rooted in the land.

### Dinei Knasos

The practical legal effect of receiving this *semichah* is the authority to adjudicate *dinei knasos* — monetary fines. Rashi's comment is illuminating: the verse *ad ha'Elohim* — going back to the first *daf* of Sanhedrin — establishes that a *beis din* must *represent* God in some meaningful sense. To adjudicate cases involving penalties and compulsion — *knasos*, *malkus*, *misah* — rather than mere restitution, requires a *beis din* bearing this chain of authority traceable to Moshe Rabbeinu. These are matters of imposing force and punishment, not merely compensating a plaintiff. *Dayyanim mumchin*, ordained judges in this sense — *hainu semuchim* — are required for such cases. For ordinary monetary disputes, the rabbis were lenient, partly because of the principle of *ne'ilas deles* and partly through the mechanism of *shlichusayhu ka'avdinan* (acting as agents of ordained courts), which will be elaborated later. But fines and punishments remain reserved for those who carry this *semichah* tracing back to the *ad ha'Elohim* of the original divine mandate.

### One Person?

The Gemara then raises a new question: *vechad lo samich* — can a single individual grant *semichah* alone? This leads into a well-known narrative about *semichah* that the Gemara will take up beginning on the next daf.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 14

## Semikhat Zekeinim: 3 vs 1

### Can One Person Give Semi…

The *mishnah* established that *semikhat zekeinim* — the classical *semikhah* tracing its lineage all the way back to Moshe Rabbeinu, conferring the authority to represent God, to be called a *beit din* of *Elohim*, and to adjudicate *dinei kenasos*, administer *malkos*, and carry out *misos beit din* — requires three participants. The *gemara*, picking up four lines from the bottom of 13b, immediately challenges this: *v'chad lo samikh?* Is it truly impossible for a single individual to confer *semikhah*?

The challenge is rooted in a tradition cited by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *baram zakhor oso ish letov, v'Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava shemo* — this man should be remembered for good, and his name is Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava — *she-ilmalei hu nishtakhu dinei kenasos mi-Yisrael*, for were it not for what he did, the laws of *kenas* would have been forgotten among the Jewish people.

The *gemara* immediately presses the language: what does it mean they would have been "forgotten"? Surely the laws themselves could simply be relearned. The answer: the word *nishtakhu* must be understood not as a forgetting of legal content but as a complete cessation of authority — *batlu dinei kenasos mi-Yisrael*. The entire chain of *semikhah*, and with it the power to actually adjudicate *kenasos*, administer *malkos*, and carry out *misos beit din*, would have been irrevocably severed.

### Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's…

The historical context is the Hadrianic persecutions, the period of Rabbi Akiva and his students. The Roman government had issued a series of sweeping decrees: anyone who confers *semikhah* will be killed; anyone who receives *semikhah* will be killed; any city in which *semikhah* takes place will be laid waste; and anything within the city limits of those cities will be uprooted.

Confronted with this existential threat to the chain of *semikhah*, Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava acted with extraordinary ingenuity and courage. He positioned himself *bein shnei harim gedolim u-vein shtei ayaros gedolos u-vein shnei techumei Shabbos* — between two large mountains, between two large cities, and between the *techumim* of two population centers: *bein Usha l'Shefaram*. Usha, of course, was itself a major seat of the *beit din*. By situating himself in open territory between cities, no single city could be destroyed, and the sheer impracticality of simultaneously destroying two major cities offered a measure of protection to the cities themselves, if not to the participants directly.

There he conferred *semikhah* upon five elders: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yosi, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua — the classic generation of *talmidei Rabbi Akiva*, as we shall see momentarily. Rav Abba adds that Rabbi Nechemiah was also among the recipients.

When the enemies discovered what was happening — and one wonders about the historical realities that prevented this from being conducted in secrecy — Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava urged those who had received *semikhah* to flee: *bnai rutzu*. When they asked what would become of him, he answered, *hareini mutal lifneihem k'even she-ein lah hofkhin* — I will stand before them as an immovable stone. The story ends with a stark image: *v'asu oto k'khivra* — they made him like a sieve, pierced by three hundred iron lances. The precise mechanics of how he held off the soldiers long enough for the others to escape, and why the *semikhah* could not be conducted covertly, are not elaborated upon by the *gemara*, though one can speculate about the historical realities of that moment.

### Three Were Present

This powerful story seems to present a difficulty: it sounds as though Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava acted alone, yet the *mishnah* requires three for *semikhah*. The *gemara* resolves this cleanly: *achrini hava bahadei* — there were two others with him. *V'hai d'lo khashiv lehu mishum kevodo d'Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava* — the reason they are not mentioned is out of deference to his honor. He was the one who mattered; the story wanted to be told about him. The other two, who must themselves have possessed *semikhah*, accompanied him and participated, but they were secondary figures in what was fundamentally his act of heroism. One wonders, of course, what became of those two as well.

### Rabbi Meir's Semikha Cha…

The *gemara* now turns to a detail within the story: was it truly Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava who conferred *semikhah* upon Rabbi Meir? Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol ha'omer Rabbi Meir lo samcho Rabbi Akiva eino ela to'eh* — whoever says that Rabbi Akiva did not give *semikhah* to Rabbi Meir is simply mistaken. This is a striking formulation, clearly directed against some tradition or claim to the contrary, and it underscores that these figures were all, at their core, *talmidei Rabbi Akiva*.

The resolution: Rabbi Akiva did indeed confer *semikhah* upon Rabbi Meir, but *lo kibluhu* — the community did not accept him. Rashi explains, three lines from the top of 14a: *l'fi she-adayin haya bachur* — perhaps Rabbi Meir was still too young, or had the learning but not yet the gravitas, and the community was not prepared to recognize his authority. Subsequently, when Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava conferred *semikhah* upon him — *samchei Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava v'kibluhu* — the community accepted it. Perhaps Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's standing was of a different order, or perhaps Rabbi Meir had by then matured to the point where the community was ready to recognize him. This also may shed light on how the ceremony became known to the Romans: once someone is elevated to a position of authority and publicly recognized as such by a community, it is difficult to keep that quiet.

---

## Semikha Outside Eretz Yi…

### No Semikha in Chutz LaAr…

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi now asserts a geographic restriction: *ein semikhah b'chutz la'aretz* — *semikhah* cannot be conferred outside of the Land of Israel. This is somewhat analogous to the principle that *nevuah* is fundamentally rooted in *Eretz Yisrael*: the authority being transmitted traces back to Moshe and ultimately represents a kind of divine presence, and the source of that presence is anchored in the Land.

But what precisely does *ein semikhah b'chutz la'aretz* mean? One might have thought it means that even *semikhah* conferred in *Eretz Yisrael* does not grant its holder the authority to adjudicate once he is in *chutz la'aretz*. That reading is immediately rejected: *v'ha tnan* — the *mishnah* in Makkos states explicitly that *Sanhedrin noheget bein ba'aretz bein b'chutz la'aretz* — the *Sanhedrin* can function in *chutz la'aretz*. Indeed, the concept of *shlikhuta'ihu kavidnan* — even where full *semikhah* no longer exists, we act as agents of a prior *beit din* that did possess it — and certainly a holder of actual *semikhah* retains his authority wherever he goes.

The correct reading of the restriction, therefore, is simply this: *d'lo samkhinan b'chutz la'aretz* — the act of conferring *semikhah* itself must take place in *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Proximity Requirement

But is the rule really about *Eretz Yisrael* as such, or is it about something else? The *gemara* presses further. One obvious case is already clear: if those conferring *semikhah* are in *chutz la'aretz* and those receiving it are in *Eretz Yisrael*, the absence of the *mesmakhim* from the Land plainly disqualifies the act. That is *peshita* — obvious, since the authority must flow from within *Eretz Yisrael*.

The more interesting question is the reverse: *somkhin ba'aretz v'nismakhin b'chutz la'aretz* — the conferring authorities are in *Eretz Yisrael*, and the recipients are in *chutz la'aretz*. Given that the *gemara* elsewhere noted that *semikhah* does not require physical hand-laying — *samchinan lei bishmei*, one simply declares the person a *rebbe* — one might envision a scenario where the grantors in *Eretz Yisrael* confer *semikhah* by declaration upon someone across the border. Would this work, since the source of authority is firmly in the Land?

The *gemara* poses this question, and the evidence suggests that the real issue is not the geographic category of *chutz la'aretz* per se, but rather the requirement of physical proximity between the grantor and the recipient.

### Physical Presence Exampl…

Several narratives converge to establish this point. First: *Rabbi Yochanan hava mitzta'er alei de-Rav Shemen bar Abba d'lo hava gabei d'lismachiei* — Rabbi Yochanan was deeply anguished that Rav Shemen bar Abba was never in the same location as him and that he was therefore never able to confer *semikhah* upon him. The very fact that Rabbi Yochanan's anguish was precisely that they were never together — and not that he simply sent a letter of appointment — demonstrates that physical co-presence is a prerequisite.

A second set of narratives follows. Rabbi Shimon ben Zirod and Rabbi Yonatan ben Achmai — with some versions of the tradition reversing which name belongs to which role — both sought *semikhah*. The one who was present at the time received it; the one who was not present did not. Here too the *gemara* notes that the verb *samchuhu* is in the plural, indicating that the story is not specifically about Rabbi Yochanan but about whoever the *mesmakhim* were in that setting — and in both cases, presence determined the outcome.

A third narrative: Rabbi Yochanan was working to confer *semikhah* upon Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya — *havu kamishtadlei Rabbi Yochanan lemismachinhu* — yet *lo hava mistaya milta*, it simply never came together. Rabbi Yochanan was anguished. At this point, Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya themselves told him not to be distressed, because they were descendants of the house of Eli: *d'anan m'devei Eli katinan*. And Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan that we know from the verse *velo yihyeh zaken b'veitcha kol hayamim* — there will not be an elder in your house all the days — that no descendant of Eli's house would ever attain *semikhah*.

The *gemara* asks what *zaken* means here. If it means literally growing old in years — well, the verse already says elsewhere that the men of his house would die while still young men. Rather, the curse refers specifically to the status of *zaken* as elder and authority: *ela semikhah* — no one of the house of Eli would ever receive *semikhah*. So Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya were telling Rabbi Yochanan: the obstacle was not logistical, it was metaphysical — it was simply not meant to be.

---

## Rabbi Zeira & Authority

### Zeira's Reluctance

*Rabbi Zeira hava mitmar lemismichei* — Rabbi Zeira was hiding so as not to receive *semikhah*. His reluctance was grounded in the teaching of Rabbi Elazar: *le'olam hevei kabil v'kayam* — always be inconspicuous, dark, and you will survive. The implicit logic: positions of authority bring exposure, responsibility, and *tzaros*. With *semikhah* comes not only the power to adjudicate *dinei kenasos*, but the full weight of public rabbinic authority, of representing the tradition with all that entails. Rabbi Zeira preferred to remain in the shadows.

### Authority & Atonement

But when Rabbi Zeira then encountered a different teaching attributed to Rabbi Elazar — *ein adam oleh ligdulah ela im ken mochlin lo al kol avonotav* — that no one ascends to a position of authority unless Heaven has forgiven all his sins — the calculus changed. If accepting authority is itself a vehicle for *kaparah*, then the willingness to shoulder that burden is not merely sacrifice; it carries a profound spiritual benefit. Upon hearing this, *amtzei lei anafshei* — Rabbi Zeira made himself available to receive *semikhah*.

### Song for Rabbi Zeira

At the ceremony of *semikhah*, songs were composed in honor of the recipient. For Rabbi Zeira — the one who had been reluctant, the one who did not seek the honor — they sang: *lo kachal v'lo srak v'lo pirchus v'ya'alat chen* — without eye shadow, without rouge, without hair adornment, and yet the *kallah* is beautiful. The natural beauty shines through. Rabbi Zeira, unpretentious and genuinely a *talmid chacham*, needed no adornment; his inner qualities were self-evident.

### Community Acceptance

The songs varied depending on the recipient. For Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, the community sang: *kol min dein kol min dein somchu lana* — anyone like this, anyone like this, give *semikhah* for our sake. The community was celebrating not merely the individual but the quality he represented, expressing the wish that more such figures would receive *semikhah*. The flip side was also expressed: *lo tismchu lana lo misarmitin v'lo misarmisin* — do not give *semikhah* for our sake to the unworthy. Rashi explains these terms as referring to people who are puffed up but empty of *Torah*, or who pervert its teachings. Another version of the formula: *lo machmisin v'lo matremisin* — not those who withhold *Torah*, not those who compromise their integrity, with the last term left unclear even by Rashi. The community is declaring its investment in the quality of those who receive the mantle of authority.

Finally, a vivid vignette: when Rabbi Abbahu would come from the *yeshiva* to the Caesar's house — we have seen in other contexts that certain rabbis had dealings with the Roman government — the matrons of the imperial household would come out and sing in his honor: *rabba d'amei, midbarna d'umsei, botzina d'nehura, brich maseich l'shalom* — the great one of his people, the leader of his nation, the candle of light, blessed is your coming in peace. This language, notably, is the Aramaic that will later be used extensively in the *Zohar*. One imagines the women sang in Greek or Latin rather than Aramaic, but the content has been preserved in these terms.

With that, the *gemara*'s treatment of *semikhat zekeinim* concludes.

---

## Arifat Egla: 3 vs 5

### Basic Dispute

The *mishnah* stated: *semikhat zekeinim va'arifat egla bishlosha divrei Rabbi Shimon; Rabbi Yehuda omer b'chamisha* — *arifat egla* requires three according to Rabbi Shimon, and five according to Rabbi Yehuda. A *beraita* now unpacks the derivations on both sides.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Position

The verse reads: *v'yatzu zekeinecha v'shofte-cha* — your elders and your judges will go out. Rabbi Yehuda reads: *zekeinecha* — two; *v'shofte-cha* — two more; and since a *beit din* cannot be evenly numbered, one more is added — *harei kan chamisha*, a total of five.

### Rabbi Shimon's Position

Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, reads only *zekeinecha* — two — and since a *beit din* cannot be even, adds one more — *harei kan shlosha*, a total of three. He does not derive an additional two from the word *shofte-cha*.

The *gemara* immediately asks: what does Rabbi Shimon do with the word *shofte-cha*? He requires it to teach something else: *miyuchadim she-b'shofte-cha* — it is the select ones among your judges, meaning this must come from the *beit din hagadol*, not from an ordinary court.

And what does Rabbi Yehuda do to derive *beit din hagadol* without relying on *shofte-cha* for that purpose? He derives it from *zekeinecha* itself: since the verse could have written the simpler *ziknei* and instead wrote the possessive *zekeinecha*, that indicates the special, select elders — the *beit din hagadol*.

Rabbi Shimon responds: he needed *zekeinecha* precisely because without it he would have read *ziknei* to mean merely elderly people from the marketplace — *ziknei hashuk* — not judges at all. So *zekeinecha* establishes that these are genuine judicial authorities, but not necessarily the *beit din hagadol* — it would have implied only the smaller *sanhedrin* of twenty-three. It is the word *shofte-cha* that elevates the requirement to the *beit din hagadol* through the phrase *miyuchadim she-b'shofte-cha*. Rabbi Shimon therefore cannot use *shofte-cha* to add two more judges; it is fully occupied with its other function.

Rabbi Yehuda, for his part, derives *beit din hagadol* through a *gzera shava*: *gamir ziknei ziknei* — there is a verbal analogy between *ziknei* here and *v'samchu ziknei ha'eida es yadeihem* by the *par helam davar shel tzibur*, the case where the *beit din hagadol* errs in its *hora'ah*. That context unambiguously involves the *beit din hagadol*, and the shared term *ziknei ha'eida* — the ה' indicating "the special ones of the congregation" — establishes that the *zekenim* of our verse are likewise the *beit din hagadol*. Having derived *beit din hagadol* from the *gzera shava*, Rabbi Yehuda can then use *shofte-cha* for its numerical function: the *vav* of *v'shofte-cha* adds two more judges to the count.

The *gemara* raises a further question: if Rabbi Yehuda is making a *gzera shava* to *par helam davar*, why not derive the number itself from there as well, making *shofte-cha* unnecessary? The answer: it is specifically the *vav* of *v'shofte-cha* — the conjunctive prefix — that Rabbi Yehuda reads as a numerical signal, adding two to the count. Rabbi Shimon does not interpret the *vav* this way — *Rabbi Shimon vav lo darish* — and therefore draws no numerical inference from it.

The *gemara* then raises an arithmetical challenge to both positions: the verse also uses the verbs *v'yatzu* — they went out — and *u'madedu* — they measured — each of which could similarly be read as implying two additional participants, driving the totals to nine and seven respectively. The *gemara* responds that these verbs are required for a different teaching entirely: *v'yatzu hein v'lo shluchan* — they themselves must go out and perform the measurement; they cannot send representatives. And *u'madedu* teaches that even when the proximity of the body to a particular city is obvious — *she'afilu nimtza be'alil l'ir* — the act of measuring is still obligatory as a *mitzvah*. This discussion carries into the top of 14b.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov

### Eliezer ben Yaakov's View

Having established the three-versus-five dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda, the *gemara* notes that the *mishnah* does not accord with a third *tanna* altogether: *matnitin d'lo ki hai tanna*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds an entirely different position. Reading the same verse — *v'yatzu zekeinecha v'shofte-cha* — he interprets *zekeinecha* not as a small delegation but as the full *Sanhedrin*: *zekeinecha zu Sanhedrin*. And *shofte-cha* — your judges — refers not to additional judicial members but to the political and religious leadership of the nation: *zeh melech v'kohen gadol* — a king and a *kohen gadol*.

The king is derived from the verse *melech b'mishpat ya'amid aretz* — the king through justice establishes the land — associating royal authority with the judicial process. The *kohen gadol* is derived from *u'vata el ha-kohanim ha-leviyim v'el ha-shofet* — which is admittedly a somewhat unusual reading, since that verse distinguishes the *kohanim* from the *shofet*, but the association is drawn nonetheless. For Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, the gravity of *egla arufa* — a case of unresolved death with no perpetrator found, and the communal responsibility to declare that one's hands did not shed this blood — demands the presence of the entire national leadership: the *Sanhedrin*, the king, and the *kohen gadol*.

### Whole Sanhedrin Needed?

A question is then raised: does Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov dispute only on one point or on two? *Bachada pligi o bitartei pligi?* Does he merely add the king and the *kohen gadol* while otherwise agreeing with either Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon regarding the number of judges — accepting three or five as the representative *beit din* — or does he additionally require that the entire *Sanhedrin* be present? *O dilma b'Sanhedrei nami pligi d'amar kula Sanhedrei ba'inan?* Given his reading of *zekeinecha zu Sanhedrin*, it would seem to imply the latter.

### Zaken Mamre Proof

Rav Yosef proposes a proof from the laws of *zaken mamre*. The *mishnah* teaches: if a rebellious elder — one who defies the ruling of the court and continues his own teaching — encounters the *Sanhedrin* outside of the *Beit Hamikdash*, at *Beit Pagi*, which is within Jerusalem but clearly not on the *Har Habayit*, and he rebels against them there — one might think his defiance still constitutes the offense of *zaken mamre*. But *talmud lomar: v'kamta v'alita el ha-makom* — you shall arise and go up to the place — *melamed she-hamakom gorem*: it is the location that determines the status. The rebellious elder acquires the designation of *zaken mamre* only if he defies the *Sanhedrin* while they are seated in their place of authority in the *Lishkat Hagazit*.

This raises the question: *d'nafak man?* — who exactly is not in the *Lishkat Hagazit*? If only some members have left, then *dilma hanach d'ika gava'i kaimi kavatei* — perhaps those remaining inside would have sided with him, and one cannot characterize his position as a defiance of established authority when the full court has not rendered a unanimous position. For the designation of *zaken mamre* to be meaningful, it must be the case that the entire *Sanhedrin* has departed — and therefore the scenario of *Beit Pagi* presupposes a situation where all of them are outside together.

### Why Sanhedrin Left

But why would the entire *Sanhedrin* be outside together? If it is for a personal, optional matter — *lidvar reshut* — the *gemara* objects: they cannot simply leave, because of the verse *sharreich agan ha-sohar al yichsar ha-mazeg* — your navel is like a round goblet, the mixed wine shall not be lacking. This phrase from *Shir Hashirim* is read as establishing that the *Lishkat Hagazit* must always maintain a minimum quorum. Rashi explains: if one member needs to leave, there must remain at least twenty-three — the equivalent of a *sanhedrin ketana*. Tosafos adds a *gematriya*: *mazeg* (מזג) equals fifty; *al yichsar ha-mazeg* means one may not be lacking fifty, leaving a minimum of twenty-two, which rounds up to twenty-three since *ein beit din shakul*. Either way, the principle holds that the *Lishkat Hagazit* cannot be vacated for a discretionary purpose.

It follows that if the entire *Sanhedrin* is absent from the *Lishkat Hagazit*, it must be for a *dvar mitzvah* — a mandatory communal purpose. And what *mitzvah* would require the entire *Sanhedrin* to convene outside? *Heichi dami lav l'medidas egla* — it must be for the measuring and the *egla arufa* procedure. This proves that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires the full *Sanhedrin* for *arifat egla* — not merely three or five representatives.

Abaye, however, deflects this proof: the *Sanhedrin* might have departed together for a different *mitzvah* entirely — *sheyatzu lehosif al ha'ir v'al ha'azarot* — to expand the boundaries of Jerusalem or of the *azaros* of the *Beit Hamikdash*, which, as the *mishnah* elsewhere states, requires a *beit din* of seventy-one. A second *beraita* then affirms Rav Yosef's position explicitly, spelling out that the scenario where the *zaken mamre* finds the court at *Beit Pagi* encompasses two cases: the court had left either for the measuring of the *egla* or to expand the city and *azaros* boundaries.

---

## Minimum Sanhedrin Present

### Cannot Lack Minimum

With the conclusion that the entire *Sanhedrin* must not be absent from the *Lishkat Hagazit* for a discretionary purpose, the *gemara* articulates the underlying principle: one cannot simply walk out and reduce the assembly below a certain threshold.

### Mixed Wine Metaphor

The source is the verse from *Shir Hashirim*: *sharreich agan ha-sohar al yichsar ha-mazeg* — your navel is like a round goblet; the mixed wine shall not be lacking. Rashi explains the application directly: if one of the *Sanhedrin* must leave, it is permitted only if there remain at least twenty-three, corresponding to the *sanhedrin ketana*; if not, he may not leave.

Tosafos develops the image of mixed wine further. *De'al chad terei* — mixed wine is one part wine to two parts water. Just as the wine remains the essential component — the minimum that must be present to call the mixture wine at all — so too the minimum essential core, the *sanhedrin ketana* of twenty-three, must remain in the *Lishkat Hagazit*. The *gematriya* of *mazeg* adds a complementary derivation: fifty, the number one may not be "lacking," meaning one may not remove fifty members, leaving at least twenty-two — which, given the rule of *ein beit din shakul*, becomes twenty-three.

The practical upshot is that the *Sanhedrin* as a body can leave the *Lishkat Hagazit* only for a genuine *dvar mitzvah*, such as the *egla* measurement or the expansion of the city's sacred boundaries, and even then the *Lishkat Hagazit* must retain a *sanhedrin ketana*.

---

## Neta Revai & Maaser Sheni

### Uncertain Value Produce

The *mishnah* states that *neta revai* and *maaser sheni* of uncertain value require three parties for redemption. To clarify: *maaser sheni* — the second tithe taken in years one, two, four, and five of the *shemitah* cycle — was ideally brought to Jerusalem. If the owner did not wish to transport the produce, he could redeem it onto money and bring the money to Jerusalem to spend there. Similarly, *neta revai* — the fruit of the fourth year of a tree's growth, following the three years of *orlah* — could be redeemed. The *gemara* now explains what the *mishnah* means by "uncertain value."

The *beraita* specifies: *eizo hu maaser sheni she'ein damav yedu'in?* What constitutes *maaser sheni* of uncertain value? Three cases: produce that has rotted — *peiros she-hirkivu* — and can now be sold only as animal fodder; wine that has developed a film — *yayin she-hikrim* — making it substandard; or coins that have become rusted — *ma'os she-hechlidu*. In each case, there is no standard market price, and judgment is required to assess value. The fear is that without external oversight, the owner may not be fully objective in his assessment.

### Three Assessors, Not Jud…

The *beraita* then clarifies who these three must be: *maaser sheni she'ein damav yedu'in, podno oto b'shlosha lakuchos* — one redeems it with three buyers, meaning three commercial experts who are practiced in assessment. Rashi defines *lakuchos* as *socharim b'ki'in b'shuma* — merchants who are skilled in appraisal.

This is striking, because the entire context of the *mishnah* is the authority of *beit din*, yet here the "three" has nothing to do with a *beit din* at all — it is simply a panel of independent assessors. Two proofs confirm this: first, the *beraita* states *aval lo b'shlosha she'einan lakuchos* — three non-experts will not suffice, regardless of their judicial standing; second, and definitively, *v'afilu nochri echad meihem* — a non-Jew can serve as one of the three. Since a non-Jew cannot be part of a *beit din*, this conclusively establishes that what we are dealing with is not a judicial panel but an objective commercial appraisal. The inclusion of this *halakhah* under the heading of the *mishnah*'s discussion of *beit din* numbers is therefore noteworthy. Finally, the *beraita* permits even one of the three to be the owner himself — *v'afilu echad meihem ba'al ha-bayit* — since he presumably has expertise in his own produce; but he alone cannot assess, as his objectivity cannot be assumed, and he therefore requires two independent parties alongside him.

### Shared Interests Question

Rabbi Yirmiyah raises a question: *shlosha u-matilin l'toch kis echad mahu* — what if the three assessors all pool their income into a single fund, meaning they are business partners? Does that still constitute three independent assessments?

The *gemara* brings a potential answer: *ish u-shtei nashav podin maaser sheni* — a man and his two wives can redeem *maaser sheni* together. Here is a case of three people who are functionally one household, and yet it is permitted. However, the *gemara* resists treating this as a complete proof. *Dilma k'gon Rav Papa u-vas Abba Sura* — perhaps it refers to a case like Rav Papa and the daughter of Abba Sura: Rashi, citing the tractate Ketubot, notes that she earned her own income independently and did not rely on her husband's resources. In such a case, the wife is economically independent and constitutes a genuinely separate party. The question of whether three assessors who are fully intertwined economically — who truly pool everything — can constitute an acceptable panel thus remains unresolved.

Tosafos adds that some hold the mechanism here to be auction — going by the highest bid — but notes that the discussions about wives and shared funds do not necessarily support that interpretation.

---

## Hekdesh Redemption

### Ten for Any Hekdesh

Having treated *neta revai* and *maaser sheni*, the *mishnah* moves to *hekdesh* — dedicated property. Here the dynamic is different: whereas *maaser sheni* is the owner's property being transferred onto money, *hekdesh* belongs to the *Beit Hamikdash*, and the transaction removes it from the domain of *hekdesh* by assessing and paying its value. The *mishnah* states that redemption of *hekdesh* requires three. But the *gemara* immediately notes: *matnitin d'lo ki hai tanna* — the *mishnah* does not accord with a competing *tanna*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — again this figure — holds that even to redeem something as minor as a small utensil of *hekdesh*, a fork perhaps, *tzricha asara bnei adam lifdosa* — ten people are required.

### Counting Kohen in Parsha

Rav Papa said to Abaye: *bishlama l'Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov d'amar k'Shmuel* — I understand where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov gets the number ten. He holds like Shmuel, *d'amar Shmuel asara kohanim kesuvin b'parsha* — Shmuel taught that the word *kohen* is written ten times in the relevant *parasha*.

This *parasha* is at the end of *Bechukotai* in *Vayikra*, chapter 27, which discusses the redemption of things dedicated to *hekdesh*. The word *kohen* appears in three different subsections. In the subsection dealing with the poor person who cannot pay his *erekh* — the fixed Torah valuation — the verse (27:8) repeats *kohen* three times: *v'he'emido lifnei ha-kohen, v'he'erich oso ha-kohen, ya'aricenu ha-kohen*. In the subsection dealing with a non-sacrificial animal dedicated to *hekdesh* (27:11), *kohen* appears three more times. And in the subsection dealing with land dedicated to *hekdesh*, the word *kohen* appears four times. Three plus three plus four equals ten. While this does not require ten *kohanim* — as will be clarified on the next *daf*, where we will see that only one of the ten must be a *kohen* — the ten appearances of the word establish the number ten as the required quorum for the redemption assessment.

### Rabbis Say Three

Having understood Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position, the obvious question is: *ela rabanan shlosha mna lehu* — from where do the Rabbis derive their number of three? The natural answer would seem to be that since the relevant subsection for *hekdesh* (the non-sacrificial animal) contains three mentions of *kohen*, three is the applicable number for that category.

### Land vs Hekdesh Numbers

But this creates an immediate difficulty: *vechi teima dechsivi behu shlosha shlosha, karka'os dechsivi behu arba'ah tisgei be'arba'ah* — if the subsection for *hekdesh* says *kohen* three times and therefore three suffices, then for land, where *kohen* appears four times, four should suffice. Yet everyone agrees that the redemption of dedicated land requires ten judges. The *gemara* responds that for land, one does not count only the mentions within the land subsection but accumulates all previous mentions as well, reaching a running total of ten by that point.

The *gemara* then presses: if we adopt that cumulative counting methodology, then by the time we reach the *hekdesh* subsection, the running total of *kohen* appearances is already six — *hekdesh de-ishtalmu bo shita libei shita* — and therefore *hekdesh* should require six, not three. The Rabbis' derivation of three remains unexplained. The *gemara* concludes: *kashya* — this is a difficulty, and it is left unresolved.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 15

## Erchin Metaltelin

### Definition & Grammar

The *mishnah* on 14b introduces the concept of *erchin ha-metaltelin* — movable *erchin*. To understand what this means, one must first recall the nature of *erech* itself: when a person declares "the *erech* of so-and-so is upon me," the *Torah* assigns fixed valuations based on the subject's age and sex, and those sums are owed to the *Beis Hamikdash*. The question is what it means for *erchin* to be "movable."

### Rav Gidal Vessels

Rav Gidal citing Rav explains: *ba-omer erech kli zeh alai* — someone who declares the *erech* of a vessel upon himself. Of course, the *Torah*'s system of *erech* does not apply to vessels at all; *erech* exists only for persons. What then does such a declaration mean? Rav Gidal teaches that since a person knows full well that *erech* has no technical application to a vessel, when he uses that language he must have meant its market value — *damim*. He concludes his vow and intends to pay the object's worth. Therefore *noten damav* — he pays its monetary value. And because we are now speaking of assessing the value of movable property, a *beis din* of three suffices.

This phenomenon — using a term loosely and having the law interpret it according to intent rather than strict terminology — appears in other halachic contexts as well. The Gemara in tractate *Nedarim* discusses *neder bi-leshon shvuah* and *shvuah bi-leshon neder*: people often employ technically incorrect vocabulary, and the halacha asks what they actually intended. Here the principle is the same: *adam yode'a she-ein erech le-kli* — a person knows a vessel has no *erech*, and so *vegamar ve-amar leshum damim* — he concluded and spoke for the purpose of monetary value.

### Metaltelin Designated

The *Gemara* then raises a grammatical objection: the phrase *erchin ha-metaltelin* seems to say that the *erchin* themselves are movable, whereas what is intended is *erchin shel metaltelin* — the *erech* of movable property. One resolution is simply to emend or reread the *mishnah* as *erchin shel metaltelin*. This is offered in the name of Rav Chisda citing Avimi, who explains the case as *be-matpis metaltelin le-erchin* — one who designates movable goods toward the satisfaction of an *erech* obligation. Having said "the *erech* of a person is upon me," one sets aside cattle or household items as the means of payment. The question of how to value those items requires a *beis din* of three.

### Abbahu & Yerushalmi

Rabbi Abbahu offers a third reading: *ba-omer erki alai be-karka ligvot mimena metaltelin* — one who declared an *erech* upon himself and is being collected from via movable property or land. This corresponds to the *Yerushalmi*'s approach: if one pays up with *metaltelin*, a *beis din* of three is needed to assess value; if one pays with *karka*, a *beis din* of ten is required. This better parallels the standard framework of redeeming sanctified property, though here the distinction turns on what one is paying *with*, not what has been sanctified.

### Rav Acha Three Din

Rav Acha of Difti challenges Ravina on this point. The three-versus-ten distinction makes intuitive sense when one is *redeeming* from *hekdesh* — taking something out — because *hekdesh*'s interests need representation, and a larger *beis din* protects against undervaluation of land. But what about when one is simply *giving to hekdesh* — *le-ayulei le-hekdesh*? Why would one need a *beis din* at all? There is no adversarial party whose interests require protection. *Le-ayulei le-hekdesh shlosha lama li?*

### Beis Din Purpose

The response is elegant: *svara hu* — it is self-evident. *Mah li le-ayulei mah li le-apukei* — what difference does it make whether you are giving to or taking from *hekdesh*? The reason a *beis din* is required in either case is not primarily ritualistic but practical: *di-oma* — you might make a mistake in estimating value. Whether you are redeeming *karka* from *hekdesh* or paying the value of *karka* to satisfy an obligation, land is difficult to appraise. You need a larger body — not because it ritualizes the redemption, but because more expert eyes ensure the valuation is correct. One might therefore ask whether this is truly a *beis din* in the juridical sense or more like an appraisal panel. That question will resurface as we examine who must constitute this group.

---

## Kohen Requirement

### Rabbi Yehudah Kohen

Rabbi Yehudah holds that a *kohen* must be one of the three who assesses *metaltelin* or *erchin*. This is his distinctive position: even for the smaller *beis din* of three, one member must be a *kohen*.

### Rav Pappa Question

Rav Pappa asks Abaye: *bishlama le-Rebbe Yehudah hayinu dikesiv Kohen* — granted, according to Rabbi Yehudah, the Torah's repeated mention of *kohen* in these passages is intelligible, since he requires a *kohen* even for the three. But *ela le-rabbanan Kohen lamah li?* — according to the *rabbanan*, who ultimately do not require a *kohen* even for the ten, why does the Torah mention *kohen* at all in these passages? This question is left standing: *kashya*.

### Ten Kohenim Count

The *Gemara* then asks how we know that for *karka*, one needs ten, and that at least one of those ten must be a *kohen*. Shmuel answers: *asarah Kohanim kesuvim ba-parsha* — the word *kohen* appears ten times in the relevant section of the Torah. One occurrence establishes the requirement of a *kohen* — *chad le-gufo*. The remaining nine repetitions create a sequence of *miyut achar miyut* — limitation after limitation — and the hermeneutical principle is *ein miyut achar miyut ela le-rabbos*: each successive limiting term actually expands the category. So the cascading repetitions of *kohen* come to teach that even a non-*kohen*, a *Yisrael*, may fulfill that role. The upshot is *va-afilu tish'ah Yisrael ve-echad Kohen* — nine Israelites and one *kohen* suffice, meaning the *kohen* is one of the ten, not an addition to them.

### Five Kohenim Five

Rav Huna son of Rav Nassan objects to this reading: why must the alternation work in only one direction? The first mention of *kohen* requires a *kohen*; the second, as a *miyut achar miyut*, opens the category to a *Yisrael*; the third reverts to requiring a *kohen*; the fourth again expands to *Yisrael* — and so on, yielding five *kohanim* and five Israelites.

### Kashya Consensus

The *Gemara* leaves this *kashya* unresolved. Nevertheless, the consensus position for *karka* cases is clear: ten are required, at least one of whom is a *kohen*.

---

## Adam Kadosh

### Abbahu Adam Value

The *mishnah* includes *adam* — a person — in the list of cases requiring a *beis din* of ten. But as the *Gemara* asks: *Adam mi kadosh?* Since when does a free person become sanctified? One cannot sanctify a free person. The *Yerushalmi* suggested this referred to a slave; the *Bavli* takes a different approach. Rabbi Abbahu explains: *ba-omer demay alai* — one who declares "my value is upon me," or the value of another person. Crucially, this person did not say *erech*, invoking the Torah's fixed valuation tables, but *damim* — the market value.

### Slave Market Price

How does one assess the market value of a free person? The *beraita* teaches: *ha-omer demay alai shamin oso ke-eved ha-nimkar ba-shuk* — one appraises how much that person would fetch if sold as a slave. And because *eved itkes le-karka'os* — slaves are halachically equated with land — this assessment is treated like an assessment of land, and therefore requires a *beis din* of ten. Notably, the person has not been sanctified; one has merely committed to paying a sum equivalent to the person's slave-market value. And yet, just as paying with or for land requires ten even when the land itself has not been formally sanctified, so too here.

### Tosafot Slaves

*Tosafot* raises the obvious question: if the case involves assessing someone like a slave, why does the *mishnah* use the word *adam* — a free person — rather than simply saying *avadim*? *Tosafot* answers that *adam* does not naturally connote a slave; had the *mishnah* meant a slave it would have said *avadim ke-yotzei ba-hem*. Additionally, there is the view of Rabbi (Rebbi) that if one sanctifies his slave, the act of sanctification liberates the slave — making the whole framework of "sanctified slave" conceptually fraught from the outset.

### Sanctified Valuations

The combined picture, then, is this: the *Yerushalmi* began by assuming *adam* referred to a slave, then retreated to a free person but did not fully explain the mechanism. The *Bavli* through Rabbi Abbahu and the *beraita* fills in the gap: you have committed to paying the equivalent of a person's value as assessed on the slave market, no actual sanctification of a person occurred, and you need a *beis din* of ten to conduct that assessment — parallel to the appraisal of land.

---

## Hair Cutting

### Hair Valuation

Rabbi Avin poses a question that grows naturally from the foregoing: *se'ar ha-omed ligzoz be-kama* — if someone declared the value of a person, and that person's hair is ready to be cut, do you include the hair's value in the assessment? And if the hair is included as a distinct item, what size *beis din* is needed to assess it? Is the hair considered like *gazuz* — already cut, hence *metaltelin* — requiring three? Or is it *ke-mechubar* — like something still attached to the body, which is equated with land — requiring ten?

### Meila Hair Laws

To resolve this question, the *Gemara* brings a parallel from the laws of *me'ilah*. When one sanctifies a slave, the slave himself is not subject to the full laws of *me'ilah* — misappropriation of *hekdesh* property — because slaves are equated with *karka*, and *me'ilah* does not apply to land. But what of the slave's hair?

### Meila Applies

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules: *mo'alin bi-se'aro* — the laws of *me'ilah* do apply to the hair of a sanctified slave. The underlying debate, the *Gemara* establishes, turns precisely on the status of hair that is ready to be cut: *de-bi-se'ar ha-omed ligzoz pligi* — that is the contested case. According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, hair ready to be cut is not considered part of the slave's body for purposes of *me'ilah* — it is functionally detached, hence *metaltelin*, and *me'ilah* applies. The *Gemara* concludes that the very same dispute governs Rabbi Avin's question: the tannaim who debate *me'ilah* for the hair are debating whether it requires a *beis din* of three or ten. *Shema mina*.

It is worth noting that a similar question surfaces in the *poskim* regarding *chatzitzah* before *mikveh*: when hair or fingernails are ready to be cut, is the portion that would be exposed upon cutting already considered extraneous, creating a *chatzitzah* on what lies beneath it? The general ruling is that there can be no *chatzitzah* on a part of the body not yet exposed, but the conceptual parallel to our *Gemara* is evident.

### Grapes Harvest

The *Gemara* attempts to identify whether the *tannaim* debating the hair's status are the same as those in a separate dispute. The *mishnah* elsewhere records that Rabbi Meir holds: *yesh devarim she-hen ke-karka ve-einam ke-karka* — there are things that are like land but not fully like land. His illustrative case: one who deposits ten laden vines — *gafnim te'unot* — with another, and the bailee claims there were only five. Is this a *modeh be-miktzat* requiring an oath, or is the oath-exemption for *karka* disputes applicable? Rabbi Meir rules that an oath is required, while the *chachamim* hold *kol ha-mechubar la-karka harei hu ke-karka* — whatever is attached to the ground is treated as land, exempt from oath.

Rabbi Yossi son of Rabbi Chanina clarifies: *be-anavim ha-omdot li-vatzer askinan* — the case concerns grapes ready to be harvested. Rabbi Meir holds they are *ki-vtzurot* — as if already harvested, hence movable; the *chachamim* hold they remain *mechubar* and are treated as land.

### Hair Grapes Differ

The *Gemara* rejects the identification of these disputes. One might have supposed that Rabbi Meir, who considers harvest-ready grapes equivalent to harvested ones, would similarly consider cut-ready hair equivalent to cut hair. But this does not follow. *Ad kan lo ka-amar Rabbi Meir hatam ela kol kama de-shabak lehu mikachshi* — Rabbi Meir's reasoning in the grape case is that leaving the grapes on the vine past their time causes them to deteriorate; there is a practical imperative to harvest them immediately, and thus they are treated as already detached. *Aval hacha* — but with hair, *kol kama de-shabak lehu ashbuchei mashbechei* — the longer the hair remains on the head the more it grows and the better it becomes. There is no imperative to cut it now. Therefore, even Rabbi Meir might agree that uncut hair is considered *mechubar* to the person, not yet detached, and the entire body of tannaitic opinion might hold that such hair requires a *beis din* of ten rather than three.

---

## Bestiality Rova

### Rova Nirva

The *mishnah* lists cases of *rova ve-nirva* — a male animal that performed an act of bestiality and a female animal subjected to such an act — as requiring a *beis din* of twenty-three. The *Gemara* notes that the *mishnah* draws no distinction: *lo shena rova zachar* — it makes no difference whether the male animal penetrated a male, *ve-lo shena rova nekevah* — or a female.

### Male Penetrator

The female case is textually straightforward: the Torah says *ve-haragta et ha-ishah ve-et ha-behemah* — you shall kill the woman and the animal — making clear that both parties are executed, with the standard *beis din* of twenty-three governing the animal's death. But the case where the male animal was the penetrator — *rova zachar* — is not explicitly stated. The source is derived from the verse *kol shochev im behemah mot yumat* — anyone who lies with an animal shall be put to death. This refers to a man as penetrator. Yet there is a parallel verse in *Vayikra*: *ish asher yiten shichavto* — a man who gives forth his seed — describing the same scenario. Since both verses describe an identical case, one of them is superfluous for that case.

### Textual Parallelism

*Im eino inyan le-shochev* — since one verse is not needed to teach the case of the human as penetrator — *tanehu inyan le-nishkav* — apply it to the case where the human is the one penetrated, i.e., where the male animal is the *shochev* and the man is the *nishkav*. But why frame the reversed-role case in the language of *shochev*? *Va-afkeih Rachmana bi-leshon shochev le-akushei nishkav le-shochev* — the Torah expressed it in the language of the active role in order to create a textual equation between the two cases. *Mah shochev hu be-Beis Din shel esrim u-shloshah* — just as the case where the human is the penetrator requires a *beis din* of twenty-three for the animal, *af nishkav hu be-Beis Din shel esrim u-shloshah* — so too the reversed case. The repetition of the verse, framed in the language of the active role even when describing the passive scenario, links the two cases and establishes identical procedural requirements.

---

## Shor Haniskal

### Owner Ox Parallel

The *mishnah* rules that the *shor ha-niskal* — a goring ox sentenced to death — is judged by a *beis din* of twenty-three. The textual basis: *ha-shor yisakel ve-gam ba'alav yumat* — the ox shall be stoned and also its owner shall be put to death. *Ke-mitat ha-ba'alim kach mitat ha-shor* — the same way you would execute a person, with a *beis din* of twenty-three, so too you execute the ox.

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye challenges Rava: how do we know that *ve-gam ba'alav yumat* is teaching that the ox requires a *beis din* of twenty-three? Perhaps the verse should be read literally — *yumat* means the owner himself is put to death.

### Lighter Penalty

Indeed, the *Gemara* entertains a sophisticated *peshat* reading of the verse: *ve-gam ba'alav yumat* could mean the owner faces a death penalty, but a lighter one than he would have received had he himself done the killing. If a person kills directly with his own hands, his execution is by the sword. Here, since it was his ox that killed, *yumat* — he is executed — but by *chenek* (strangulation), a lighter form of execution. This yields a coherent reading: the owner receives a diminished death penalty commensurate with his indirect responsibility.

### No Death Kofer

The *Gemara* begins to dismantle this reading. It first proposes that even without the word *yumat*, one would never have read *ha-shor yisakel ve-gam ba'alav* to mean *skilah* (stoning) for the owner, because *katil ihu be-sayif* — if he himself had done the killing his penalty would have been the sword — and *mammona be-skilah salka da'atach?* — would you impose a more severe penalty on someone for his ox's act than for his own? That is inconceivable, so *yumat* is not needed to prevent us from reading *skilah*. Yet the *Gemara* then presses further: perhaps *yumat* comes to tell us the owner receives *chenek* rather than the sword — a lenient death rather than no death. What rules this out?

The answer comes from the verse that explicitly authorizes a *kofer* payment: *im kofer yushat alav* — if a ransom is imposed upon him. The *Gemara* initially suggests that this availability of *kofer* proves the owner is not truly subject to execution. But then an audacious counterargument emerges: *adaraba mishum hi gufa* — on the contrary, the *kofer* clause makes perfect sense precisely *because* the owner deserves death. *Lo tikchu kofer le-nefesh rotzeach* — we do not accept a monetary ransom for a murderer who killed with his own hands. But *katal shoro* — when his ox killed, *li-prok nafshaya be-mammona* — then he may redeem himself with money. This is in fact a beautiful *peshat* of the two verses read together: *ve-gam ba'alav yumat* — the owner deserves death — but *im kofer yushat alav* — since he did not do it himself, we permit monetary redemption, which we would otherwise forbid for a killer.

### Chizkiyah Yomus

Chizkiyah resolves the impasse with a teaching from his school: *amar kra yumat ha-makeh rotzeach hu* — the Torah says "he who strikes shall be put to death, for he is a murderer." *Al retzichato atah horgo* — you execute him for *his own* murder. *Ve-i atah horgo al reziichat shoro* — but you do not execute him for his ox's killing. So *yumat* in the *shor ha-niskal* passage cannot be literal execution of the owner; it means something else — namely, that the same procedural standard applied to human capital cases (*beis din* of twenty-three) governs the ox's execution.

### Policy Reasoning

Beyond the textual derivation, it is worth pausing to consider why *chazal* were motivated to resist the *peshat* reading so strongly. The literal reading would mean that a wealthy owner could buy his way out of execution while a poor owner would be put to death — a troubling inequality before the law. Moreover, it would impose capital punishment for negligence rather than deliberate murder, eroding the principle that *al retzichato atah horgo* — only for one's own act is execution warranted. Some *rishonim* suggest that even according to *chazal*'s reading, *ve-gam ba'alav yumat* retains moral force: the owner is *deserving* of death, but the legal system will never impose it, imposing *kofer* instead — analogous to some explanations of *ayin tachat ayin* (monetary compensation rather than literal retaliation), where the verse expresses the moral claim while the practical implementation is monetary.

---

## Shor Sinai

### Sinai Beis Din

The *Gemara* closes with a question regarding *shor Sinai* — an ox (or person) that drew too close to Mount Sinai during the revelation. The Torah declares *im behemah im ish lo yichyeh* — whether animal or human, it shall not live. The question posed: *shor Sinai be-kama?* — would executing such an animal require a *beis din* of twenty-three?

### Peshat Killing

The *peshat* of the relevant verses is that transgressors at Sinai were to be killed immediately and at a distance — stones hurled or arrows shot — because no one was permitted to touch the mountain: *ki sakol yisakel o yaro yiyareh*. The Rabbis, however, read those same words as establishing the standard punishments of *skilah* (throwing from a height and then stoning) applicable in later generations, and the implication is that even at Sinai those who drew close would have been judged by a *beis din*. The question then is whether the animal would similarly require a *beis din* of twenty-three.

### Rami Yechezkel

Rami bar Yechezkel resolves the question with a *beraita*: *im behemah im ish lo yichyeh* — *mah ish be-khaf-gimel* (23), just as a person is never executed without a *beis din* of twenty-three, *af behemah be-khaf-gimel* — so too an animal. This *drashah* extends the rule from that singular moment at Sinai to all future generations: the procedural requirement of twenty-three for capital cases involving animals is derived from the parallel phrasing that equates the fate of animal and human at Sinai. We will continue from here tomorrow.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 16

## Wild Animals & Beis Din

### Opening & Context

Daf 16 opens in the middle of a discussion that begins on 15b, concerning the case of *ha'ari vehaze'ev* — the lion and the wolf. The Gemara has been treating the *shor haniskal*, the ox condemned to stoning, as requiring a *beis din* of twenty-three. This leads the Mishnah to extend the discussion to wild animals more broadly, a topic also addressed in Bava Kamma.

### R. Eliezer Opinion

The Mishnah presents two views. Rabbi Eliezer says: *kol hakodem lehorgam zachah* — whoever kills these dangerous animals first has thereby merited. Rabbi Akiva says: *misasan be-beis din shel sheloshah* — their death requires a court of three. The underlying premise of Rabbi Eliezer's opinion is that these creatures — lions, bears, and similarly fierce animals — are not like an ox that has gored three times and thus acquired a dangerous history. They are fundamentally, inherently dangerous, and therefore one need not wait for a *beis din* at all.

### Reish Lakish Position

Reish Lakish qualifies: *vehu shehemitu* — this dispensation to kill without a court applies only if the animal has already killed. If the animal has not yet taken a human life, one may not simply destroy it. The underlying rationale, the Gemara explains, is *al-ma kasavar yesh lahem tarbus veyesh lahem be'alim* — Reish Lakish holds that these animals can, in principle, be domesticated. It is exceedingly difficult, but it is possible to keep a lion or a bear as a pet, and therefore such animals can have owners. Until they have demonstrated by actually killing that they are reverting to their wild nature, an owner's rights must be respected and one cannot simply kill the animal.

Once the animal has killed, however, its danger is considered to exceed even that of a *shor haniskal*, and one may proceed to kill it without waiting for a court proceeding.

### R. Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan takes a more sweeping position: *af al pi she-lo hemitu* — even if the animal has not yet killed, one may go ahead and kill it. *Al-ma kasavar ein lahem tarbus ve-ein lahem be'alim* — Rabbi Yochanan holds that these animals cannot truly be domesticated, and therefore no one is genuinely their owner in any meaningful legal sense. At their core they are wild, and killing them is simply a service to society.

### Merit Explained

This dispute generates a precise question about what Rabbi Eliezer means when he says the first to kill *zachah* — merits. The Gemara works this out according to each position. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the answer is straightforward: *zachah le-oran* — the killer merits the hide of the animal. Since the animal cannot truly be owned, the one who kills it acquires its skin, an established principle that the killer of such an animal keeps its hide. This provides a clear incentive to perform the socially beneficial act of eliminating a dangerous creature.

According to Reish Lakish, however, the question is sharper. Since Reish Lakish maintains that these animals do have owners, killing the animal would normally leave the skin with the owner, not the killer. So what does the first killer merit? The Gemara answers: *kevan shehemitu* — since Reish Lakish requires that the animal have already killed before it may be slain, we are in effect treating these animals within the conceptual framework of a *shor haniskal*. And a *shor haniskal* is forbidden in benefit — *assur be-hana'ah*. Consequently, the killer cannot acquire the hide as property. *Mai zachah?* What then does one merit? *Zachah lishmaya* — one merits the spiritual reward of having performed a *mitzvah*.

### Tanya & Reish Lakish

A *baraisa* is then cited in support of Reish Lakish's position: *echad shor shehemit ve-echad behemah vechayah shehemitu be-esrim ushloshah* — both an ox that killed and other domesticated or wild animals that killed require a court of twenty-three. Rabbi Eliezer adds, in a notably expansive formulation, that for all animals other than an ox — including any *behemah* or *chayah* — once they have killed, *kol hakodem lehorgam zachah bahen lishmaya*, whoever kills them first merits, and that merit is explicitly *lishmaya*, meaning one does not acquire the hide. The *tanya* thus confirms the Reish Lakish position, and also broadens the category considerably beyond what was initially stated.

### R. Akiva & Beis Din

Rabbi Akiva's position is that even these animals require a *beis din* of twenty-three. The Gemara asks: is this not identical to the view of the *tana kamma* of the Mishnah? The answer is that there is a practical difference between them regarding a snake. The *tana kamma* would require a *beis din* of twenty-three even for a snake, whereas Rabbi Akiva — consistent with other *mishnayos* in Bava Kamma — might concede that a snake, being particularly and distinctively lethal, does not require a court at all.

---

## Shevet & Avodah Zarah

### Shevet Intro

The Mishnah teaches that a *shevet* — an entire tribe of Israel — that sins requires a *beis din* of seventy-one to adjudicate the matter. The Gemara now seeks to understand this ruling in detail.

### Tribe's Sin

The first question is: *hai shevet dechata be-mai?* — in what sin did this tribe engage? The Gemara considers whether an ordinary transgression, such as *chilul Shabbos*, could be the subject of this ruling. The answer is that the Torah distinguishes between individuals and multitudes specifically in the context of *avoda zara*, idolatry — that is the realm in which the Torah treats a community as a corporate religious entity rather than a mere aggregation of individuals. By other *mitzvos*, the Torah does not apply this communal framing. Therefore the tribe in question must have committed *avoda zara*.

### Ir Hanidachas Model

Having established that the tribe committed *avoda zara*, the Gemara considers the obvious interpretation: the tribe is simply being treated as a large *ir hanidachas*, a wayward city, and since *ir hanidachas* requires a court of seventy-one, a tribe that similarly commits mass idolatry would also require seventy-one. But the Bavli presses further and demonstrates that this reading is not only obvious — it is in fact legally impossible. The *ir hanidachas* framework cannot actually apply to a whole tribe, because there are size limits beyond which a city loses its status as an *ir hanidachas*.

### City Size Debate

A *baraisa* records a debate between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonasan. Rabbi Yoshiya holds that an *ir hanidachas* must have between ten and one hundred inhabitants. A community smaller than ten or larger than one hundred does not qualify. Rabbi Yonasan holds that the range extends from one hundred up to the majority of a tribe, *rubo shel shevet* — but once the city encompasses a majority of a tribe, it is no longer treated as a city at all, and reverts to the status of individuals who happened to commit *avoda zara*. Tosafos notes that the figures of ten and one hundred appear in a verse in Amos.

Critically, even Rabbi Yonasan only goes as far as a majority — *rubo*. If it is literally the entire *shevet*, he would not apply the *ir hanidachas* model at all. One might invoke the principle of *rubo ke-kulo*, majority as equivalent to totality, but a literal entire tribe would fall outside Rabbi Yonasan's formulation. The result is a pointed irony: the case of the whole tribe committing *avoda zara* would paradoxically revert to being judged as individuals, which is clearly not what the Mishnah intends. The Gemara therefore rejects the *ir hanidachas* model entirely as the basis for the Mishnah's ruling, and seeks alternative explanations.

### Rav Masnah Answer

Rav Masnah offers the first answer: *hacha be-nasi shevet she-chata askinan* — the Mishnah is dealing not with the entire tribe but with the *nasi* of the tribe, its leader, who sinned.

### Moses as Source

The basis for this is drawn from the principle already stated elsewhere by Rabbi Adda bar Ahava: the verse in Yisro says *kol hadavar hagadol yavi'u eilecha* — every great matter shall be brought to you, Moses. This is read as *devarav shel gadol* — matters pertaining to a great person. Moses represents the *beis din* of seventy-one, so matters involving a great personage go to a court of seventy-one. Accordingly, the head of a tribe — a *nasi* — is such a great personage, and any capital matter involving him goes before the *sanhedrin* of seventy-one.

### Ulla: Boundaries

Ulla, citing Rabbi Elazar, offers a second answer: the Mishnah refers to disputes *al iskei nachalos*, concerning tribal inheritances and the boundary lines of the land of Israel. When *shevatim* dispute which territory belongs to whom, a court that stands above the *shevatim* is required, and since the original apportionment of the land was conducted with a *beis din* of seventy-one, boundary disputes among tribes similarly require seventy-one. The Gemara then pushes back: if we are reconstructing the original division, should we not also require the *kalfi* — the lottery — the *urim ve-tumim*, and the presence of all of Israel? That would obviously be absurd. The Gemara therefore rejects the extreme form of this argument and concludes that Rav Masnah's formulation is the cleaner and more well-established answer.

### Ravina Answer

Ravina offers a third answer: *le-olam be-shevet she-huda'ach* — in fact the Mishnah does refer to a tribe that committed *avoda zara*. And the earlier objection — that we cannot treat them as a corporate entity because they would not qualify as an *ir hanidachas* — is met as follows. *In* — yes, indeed we are judging them *bedina de-rabim*, with the framework applicable to a mass collective. *Af al gav de-katlinan be-yachid* — even though the actual mode of execution is as individuals, not as a collective destruction of a city, nevertheless the *type of court* that hears the case is the court that would apply to a corporate entity. The judgment is individual; the court is communal.

### R. Chama Source

This is supported by a teaching of Rabbi Chama bar Yosei citing Rabbi Oshaya, which explains how we know that an *ir hanidachas* requires a *beis din* of seventy-one. The verse concerning *avoda zara* by an individual says *vehotzeisa es ha-ish hahu oh es ha-ishah hahi el she'arecha* — you shall bring that man or that woman out to your gates, meaning the *beis din* of the city. The Gemara derives: *ish ve-ishah ata motzi lish'arecha* — individuals you bring to the city gates; *ve-i ata motzi kol ha-ir kulo lish'arecha* — but if the entire city has sinned, you do not bring them to the city's own *beis din*. Instead they go before the *beis din* of seventy-one, the court of *Klal Yisrael*. By the same token, *ish ve-ishah ata motzi lish'arecha ve-i ata motzi kol shevet kulo lish'arecha* — if the entire tribe has sinned, it too requires a different and higher court, even though the judgment rendered is individual in nature. This also suggests that the rule is not limited to *avoda zara* specifically: once one adopts the principle that a sufficiently large portion of the population demands a court of seventy-one, that logic could extend to any mass communal sin. The Gemara leaves this as a point worth noting.

---

## Navi Sheker & Zakein

### Navi Intro

The Mishnah teaches that a *navi sheker*, a false prophet, is also judged before a *beis din* of seventy-one. The Gemara seeks the scriptural basis for this ruling.

### Hazada Problem

Rabbi Yosei berabbi Chanina says: this is derived through a *gezeirah shavah* — a verbal analogy — of *hazada hazada* from *zakein mamre*. The verse concerning a false prophet uses the word *yazid*, a form of *zadon* — presumption or willful rebellion. The verse concerning a *zakein mamre* likewise uses the word *bezadon*. Just as the *zakein mamre* is associated with a court of seventy-one, so too the false prophet is judged by seventy-one.

At this point the Bavli, departing from the simpler treatment in the Yerushalmi, raises an important problem. The verse using *zadon* in the context of *zakein mamre* — *veha-ish asher ya'aseh bezadon levilti shmo'a el ha-kohein... u-meis ha-ish hahu* — is referring specifically to the moment of his *execution*. And the execution of a *zakein mamre* takes place before a *beis din* of *twenty-three*, not seventy-one. A *zakein mamre* must rebel against the *sanhedrin* of seventy-one, but he is actually tried and executed by a *beis din* of twenty-three. This is a striking and counterintuitive point: the *zakein mamre* rejects the authority of seventy-one but is himself judged by twenty-three. Thus the word *zadon* in the verse about *zakein mamre* maps onto a court of twenty-three, not seventy-one. Linking the false prophet's *zadon* to the *zakein mamre*'s *zadon* would therefore yield twenty-three — the opposite of what is intended.

### Gezeirah Shavah

Reish Lakish therefore proposes a different *gezeirah shavah*: *davar davar*, a link through the word *davar* — matter. In the passage dealing with the *zakein mamre*, the verse reads *ve-asisa al pi ha-davar asher yagidu lecha* — you shall act according to the matter that they tell you. This *davar* situates itself in the context of the *zakein mamre* defying the *sanhedrin* of seventy-one. By linking the word *davar* in the false prophet's verse — *asher yazid ledaber davar bishmi* — to the *davar* in the *zakein mamre* passage, we connect the false prophet not to the *zakein mamre*'s execution (which involves twenty-three) but to the *zakein mamre*'s act of rebellion against seventy-one. From this we derive that the false prophet is judged by seventy-one.

### No Reverse Link

A natural follow-up question arises: now that we have the false prophet pegged at seventy-one via the *davar davar* link to *zakein mamre*, can we close the circle? Can we take the *hazada hazada* link and use the false prophet's seventy-one to elevate the *zakein mamre* to seventy-one as well? The Gemara answers: *davar davar gamir, hazada hazada lo gamir* — we have a received tradition of the *davar davar* analogy operating in one direction only. We do not have a tradition for the *hazada hazada* link to operate in the other direction. A *gezeirah shavah* works only where there is a received tradition, and we cannot simply reverse its direction at will.

### Zakein Irony

The Gemara thus arrives at a formally ironic position: the *zakein mamre* defines his sin by rejecting the authority of the *sanhedrin* of seventy-one, yet he himself is judged by a *beis din* of only twenty-three. The *halacha* of a *zakein mamre* is that after his case is heard by the *sanhedrin* of seventy-one, he returns to his city and continues to rule according to his dissenting opinion. The sin that seals his death warrant is his continuing to rule and teach in his city in defiance of the Great Court. It is therefore the *beis din* of his own city — a court of twenty-three — that ultimately hears his case. The logic of the *halacha* carries its own internal coherence, even if the result is striking.

---

## Kohen Gadol & 71

### KG Intro

The Mishnah also teaches that a *kohen gadol* is judged only before a *beis din* of seventy-one. The Gemara again asks for the scriptural source.

### Yitro Source

Rabbi Adda bar Ahava cites the verse from the episode of Yisro's counsel to Moses: *kol ha-davar ha-gadol yavi'u eilecha* — every great matter they shall bring to you. This is read as *devarav shel gadol* — matters concerning a great person. Moses standing in for the *sanhedrin* of seventy-one, the verse establishes that matters involving figures of great stature go before a court of seventy-one.

### Gadol vs. Kashe

A *baraisa* then challenges this reading. Perhaps *davar gadol* simply means a difficult matter — *davar kashe* — which is the plain sense of the verse. After all, the *baraisa* itself entertains the question: *atah omer davar kashe o eino ela devarav shel gadol?* A later verse confirms that the people brought *davar kashe* — the difficult matters — to Moses. Since this parallel verse uses *davar kashe* to describe the same practice, and since both verses describe Moses's role, one might conclude that *davar gadol* and *davar kashe* are synonyms, both meaning simply difficult matters. The interpretation of *devarav shel gadol* would then be excluded.

### Two Concepts

The Gemara resolves this by appealing to another *baraisa* that reads the two terms in precisely the opposite way: *davar gadol* means *devarav shel gadol*, matters of a great personage, while *davar kashe* means a difficult matter. The two verses use different words deliberately, and the divergence in terminology communicates two distinct legal concepts: difficult matters go to Moses — that is, to the *sanhedrin* of seventy-one — and matters involving great personages also go to Moses. One verse communicates one principle; the other communicates the other.

The Gemara presses further: if both terms convey the same point, why change terms at all? The answer that both verses refer to the same instruction but one is the command and one is its execution is formally adequate but does not explain the lexical variation. The better answer is *shema mina tartei* — infer from this two separate teachings. Both concepts are intentionally embedded in the Torah's use of different language.

### Abaye: Monetary

The Gemara then raises a question attributed to Rabbi Eliezer about the *kohen gadol*: if *kol ha-davar ha-gadol* means all matters involving a great personage, does this include monetary cases? Would even a routine financial dispute involving a *kohen gadol* require a *beis din* of seventy-one? Abaye responds: the very fact that the question focuses on an ox — *shoro shel kohen gadol* — and notes that monetary matters are *peshita*, obviously not requiring seventy-one, already concedes that a straightforward monetary claim against a *kohen gadol* would go to an ordinary court. The matter pertains to his property, not to his person.

### Open Questions

The Gemara notes that the question is not fully resolved, however, regarding the broader range of cases that fall between monetary matters and capital crimes. What about *malkus* — lashes? What about *knas* — a financial penalty that is punitive in nature? The scope of the *beis din* of seventy-one's exclusive jurisdiction over the *kohen gadol* beyond capital crimes remains an open question at this stage.

---

## Milchemet Reshut

### War Intro

The Mishnah states that going out to an optional war — *milchemet reshut* — requires the authorization of a *beis din* of seventy-one. It is notable that this halakhic requirement is not addressed in the Yerushalmi. One might speculate — though the Gemara does not say so explicitly — that in the wake of the Bar Kochva revolt and the Hadrianic persecution, the Sages of the land of Israel may have been reluctant to engage with topics touching on Jewish sovereignty, kingship, and the prospect of going to war. The Bavli addresses the topic directly.

### Joshua & Urim

Rabbi Abbahu cites a verse from Bamidbar concerning Joshua: *ve-lifnei Elazar ha-kohen ya'amod ve-sha'alu be-mishpat ha-urim lifnei Hashem al piv yetze'u ve-al piv yavo'u* — he shall stand before Elazar the priest, who shall inquire for him through the judgment of the *urim* before God; at his word they shall go out and at his word they shall come in. This verse describes Joshua consulting the *kohen* who bears the *urim ve-tumim*, clearly establishing the role of divine consultation in going to war.

### Verse Parsing

The Gemara then parses additional phrases from the surrounding verses to identify each component required for *milchemet reshut*. *Ya'amod* — he shall stand — refers to Joshua, representing the king. *Ve-chol bnei Yisrael ito* — all of Israel with him — is read as referring to the *mashuach milchama*, the kohen anointed for war, whose role it is to lead and address the troops. *Ve-chol ha-edah* — and all the congregation — the word *edah* being a key term that the Gemara consistently reads as signifying the *sanhedrin*, represents the seventy-one.

### Urim Authority
