The Gemara raises an alternative reading: perhaps the verse is not specifically about the requirements for going to war, but rather about who has standing to consult the *urim ve-tumim* in general — whether it is a king or the *sanhedrin* that has this authority. The Gemara sets this aside and moves to an alternative derivation.

### David Story

The alternative is a well-known *midrash* from Berachot. Rav Yitzchak bar Bizna cites Rabbi Shimon Chasida: David had a *kinor* hanging above his bed. At midnight, a northern wind would blow through it and cause it to play on its own — his natural alarm. David would arise immediately and engage in Torah study until the first light of dawn. When dawn broke, the sages of Israel would come before him and say: *Adoneinu ha-melech, amecha Yisrael tzrichim le-farnasa* — our lord the king, your people Israel need sustenance. He would tell them to sustain themselves from one another through commerce. They would respond: *ein ha-kometz masbia et ha-ari* — a handful does not satisfy a lion. The resources are insufficient for internal trade alone to meet the people's needs. *Ve-ein ha-bor mitmale me-chulyato* — and a pit does not fill from its own cavity. Rashi interprets this phrase as meaning that dirt excavated from a pit, if replaced, does not fully fill it back in. Tosafos suggests instead that a well does not fill with water from its own opening. In either case, the point is that recirculating insufficient resources among the people yields nothing. David would then say: *lechu pish'tu yadeichem bi-gdud* — go extend your hands in battle, go to war.

### David Breakdown

The Gemara then shows that what follows in the verse describing David's court maps onto the three required elements. Rav Yosef cites the verse: *ve-acharei Achitofel Benayahu ben Yehoyada ve-Evyatar ve-sar tzava la-melech Yoav* — after Achitofel came Benayahu ben Yehoyada and Evyatar, and the commander of the king's army was Yoav. The breakdown is as follows: *Achitofel zeh yoetz* — Achitofel was the king's personal advisor. *U-Bnayahu ben Yehoyada zo Sanhedrin* — Benayahu ben Yehoyada represents the *sanhedrin*. *Evyatar elu urim ve-tumim* — Evyatar represents the *urim ve-tumim*, the divine consultation. Only after all three — advisor, *sanhedrin*, and *urim ve-tumim* — had been consulted did the king proceed to war under the command of Yoav.

### Kereti & Peleti

The identification of Evyatar with the *urim ve-tumim* is buttressed by another verse: *u-Bnayahu ben Yehoyada al ha-Kereti ve-al ha-Peleti* — Benayahu ben Yehoyada was over the *Kereti* and the *Peleti*. For *Chazal*, *Kereti* and *Peleti* are designations for the *urim ve-tumim*. *Kereti she-korin divreihem* — they cut their pronouncements with precision, like a definitive divine word. *Peleti she-mufla'im ma'aseihem* — their workings are wondrous, describing the miraculous way the divine word emerges from the *urim ve-tumim*. Having established that *Kereti* and *Peleti* refer to the *urim ve-tumim*, and that Benayahu is juxtaposed to them in one verse, while Evyatar is paired with Benayahu in the other, the Gemara maps Evyatar onto the *urim ve-tumim* — thus confirming that all three elements (advisor, *sanhedrin*, divine oracle) were present before David went to war.

### David's Harp

Rav Yitzchak bereih de-Rav Adda — and some say Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi — provides the scriptural basis for David's harp waking him at midnight. The verse reads: *urah kviudi, urah ha-nevel ve-chinor, a'irah shachar* — awake my glory, awake harp and lyre, I will wake the dawn. David does not say that the dawn woke him; he says he will wake the dawn — indicating that it is he who rises before first light, prompted by the instrument that plays on its own.

---

## City Expansion & Judges

### City Walls

The Mishnah teaches that one may not expand the walls of the city — *ein mosifin al ha-ir* — without the authority of a *sanhedrin* of seventy-one. The Gemara asks for the source.

### Mosaic Model

Rav Shimi bar Chiyya cites the verse: *ke-chol asher ani mareh otcha et tavnit ha-mishkan ve-chen ta'asu le-dorot ha-ba'im* — precisely as I show you the pattern of the Tabernacle, so shall you do for future generations. The construction of the *mishkan* was supervised by Moses, and Moses represents the *sanhedrin* of seventy-one. The verse's instruction to replicate the process for future generations thus implies that analogous acts of national significance — such as expanding a city — require that same level of authority.

### Mishkan Vessels

Rava challenges this derivation from a *baraisa*: *kol ha-kelim she-asah Moshe meshichatan mekadashtan* — all the vessels that Moses made for the sanctuary, their anointing with the *shemen ha-mishchah* consecrated them. But *mikan va-eilach* — from that point on and for future generations — *avodatan mechanchtan*, they are consecrated through being put to use in the service of the sanctuary. This raises a question: if the verse says *ve-chen ta'asu le-dorot*, meaning do as Moses did for all generations, then future generations should also have to anoint their vessels with *shemen ha-mishchah* — just as Moses did.

### Vessel Sanctification

The Gemara resolves this from another verse: *va-yimshachem va-yikadesh otam* — and he anointed them and sanctified them. The word *otam* — them, specifically — implies that it was those particular vessels that were consecrated through anointing, and not the vessels of future generations. *Otam bi-meshichah ve-lo le-dorot bi-meshichah* — those vessels through anointing, but not for future generations through anointing.

The Gemara pushes back: perhaps *otam* is not exclusive, and in future generations one has the option of consecrating through anointing *or* through use? Another verse resolves this: *asher yeshartu bam ba-kodesh* — that they will be used in sanctity — implying that use is the operative mechanism for future consecration. The Gemara then asks: if a separate verse already establishes that future vessels are consecrated through use, why is *otam* needed at all? The answer is that without *otam*, one might have thought — given the instruction of *ve-chen ta'asu* — that future generations require *both* anointing and use, since they are told to follow Moses's model. *Otam* comes to teach that future vessels require anointing specifically in their generation, not going forward; and going forward, use alone is sufficient. This excursion into the laws of *mishkan* vessels arises directly from the effort to establish the limits of the principle that future generations must replicate Moses's process.

---

## Judge Hierarchy

### Judges Mitzvah

A *baraisa* establishes the scriptural basis for the entire system of appointing judges throughout Israel. *Minayin she-ma'amidin shoftim le-Yisrael* — how do we know there is a *mitzvah* to appoint judges for Israel? *Talmud lomar shoftim titen* — the verse says you shall appoint judges.

### Police Force

*Shotrim le-Yisrael minayin* — how do we know there is an obligation to establish a police force, officers who enforce the law? *Talmud lomar* — the verse says *shotrim*, officers, alongside the judges.

### Tribal & City Courts

*Shoftim le-chol shevet ve-shevet minayin* — how do we know that each individual tribe must have its own judges and its own *sanhedrin* standing over it, rather than just a single federal-level court? The *baraisa* derives this from the full verse: *shoftim ve-shotrim titein lecha be-chol she'arecha asher Hashem Elokecha notein lecha le-shivtecha* — you shall appoint judges and officers in all your gates that the Lord your God gives you, according to your tribes. The word *le-shivtecha* — for your tribes — indicates that each tribe is to have its own judicial structure. Similarly, *shotrim le-chol shevet ve-shevet* — a police force for each tribe — and *shoftim le-chol ir ve-ir* — judges for each and every city — and *shotrim le-chol ir ve-ir* — officers for each city — are each derived from the relevant terms in the verse. The word *she'arecha*, your gates, means every city, requiring each city to maintain its own local *beis din* of twenty-three.

### R. Yehudah Head

Rabbi Yehudah adds: *echad memuneh al kullan* — there is one appointed over all of them. Rashi understands this as referring to the *sanhedrin gedolah* that presides over the entire court system. Tosafos interprets it more modestly, as indicating that each *beis din* has a single head or presiding officer, derived from the verse's phrase *titein lecha*, which implies a singular appointment at each level.

### RSbG Tribal Authority

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel concludes: *leshivtecha ve-shaftu — mitzvah be-shevet ladun es shivto* — the verse *leshivtecha* teaches that it is a *mitzvah* for each tribe to judge matters pertaining to its own tribe. Each tribe, as it were, handles its own internal affairs. Only specific matters of national import — those requiring the *sanhedrin gedolah* of seventy-one — are brought before the highest court. The question of who originally appointed the members of the *sanhedrin gedolah* itself is left without a formal answer.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 17

## Ir Nidachas

### 71 Judges Required

The Mishnah rules that an *ir nidachas* — a condemned city — requires a *beis din* of 71 judges. The Gemara opens by asking *mena hani mili*, what is the scriptural source for this requirement? Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef citing Rabbi Oshaya derives it from the verse: *v'hotzeisa es ha-ish ha-hu o es ha-isha ha-hi asher asu es ha-davar ha-ra ha-zeh el sharecha* — "and you shall bring out that man or that woman who committed this evil thing to your gates." The verse indicates that individual defendants are judged at the gates by a local *sanhedrin*, but an entire city — a *rabbim* — cannot be judged by a local court. It must be brought before the *Sanhedrin Gedola*.

### Geographic Limits

The Gemara next addresses the geographic restrictions on an *ir nidachas*. The rule is that one does not declare a border city a condemned city. The reason: the Torah says *mikirbecha* — "from your midst" — implying the interior of the land, *v'lo min ha-sefar*, not from the border. The city must be located in the middle of the land.

### Number of Cities

Nor may three cities be condemned together. The verse uses the word *achas* — "one city" — suggesting a limitation. But the Gemara raises the question: perhaps you cannot even condemn two simultaneously? After all, the verse says *achas*. The answer is that elsewhere the verse reads *arecha* — "your cities" — in the plural, which implies that two is permissible. The word *achas* then comes to exclude three, not two. Thus the rule is: one or two cities may be condemned simultaneously, but not three.

### Karcha Issue

The Gemara then records a further tradition. Rav states that one *beis din* may not rule on more than one *ir nidachas* at a time, though if a different *beis din* convenes — Rashi understands this to mean a later generation of judges after the previous ones had died — the process could apply anew. Yet in another formulation, Rav states that even across multiple courts it may never be done simultaneously.

What is Rav's reason? *Mishum karcha* — because it would leave a bald spot in the land of Israel. Reish Lakish qualifies: the *karcha* concern applies only when the cities are in the same geographic area. If they are in two or three separate regions, the objection falls away. Rabbi Yochanan, however, maintains that the *karcha* concern stands regardless, and a *baraisa* is cited in support of his position: one may not condemn three cities in *Eretz Yisrael* as condemned cities. However, two may be condemned if each is in a different region — for instance, one in Yehudah and one in the Galil. But two in Yehudah and two in the Galil — that cannot be done, precisely because of the *karcha*. It thus emerges that there are two distinct limitations operating here: the *achas v'lo shalosh* exclusion, which may operate even across scattered locations, and the *karcha* principle, which prohibits even two condemned cities within the same region.

### Border Restrictions

The Gemara then returns to the border restriction: even a single condemned city cannot be declared on the border of the land. Why? *Shema yishmu nochrim v'yacharivu es Eretz Yisrael* — lest the nations hear of the destruction and take the opportunity to attack. One might ask: if the verse already says *mikirbecha* — "from your midst" — excluding the border, why supply a rational explanation? The answer is that this is Rabbi Shimon, who characteristically explicates the reasons behind the *psukim*. Here, it would appear, he is not using the reason to expand or contract the halacha in a novel way, but rather his concern for the security of the land motivates his reading of the word *mikirbecha* in the first place.

---

## Great Sanhedrin

### Moshe's Count

The Gemara now turns to the composition of the *Sanhedrin Gedola*, which was 71. What is the Rabbanan's reason for saying that Moshe is counted as part of the 71 rather than standing apart from the 70 elders? The verse states *v'hisyatzvu sham imach* — they shall stand there with you — indicating that Moshe is grouped together with the 70 elders as part of a single body. Furthermore, the verse says *v'nasu itach b'masa ha'am* — "and they shall carry the burden of the people with you" — meaning all of them together, the 70 plus Moshe, form the collective that bears the burden, yielding a court of 71.

Rabbi Yehudah disagrees. The word *imach* in the verse does not mean Moshe is counted as part of the same group; rather, *itach b'domeh lach*, it means that the elders must be as similar to Moshe as possible in terms of personal character and wisdom. We already have an instance of *itach* from the section concerning Yitro — referring to the smaller *sanhedrin* — which conveys the standard of resembling Moshe. The additional *itach* in the context of the 70 elders therefore teaches something new: that Moshe is included in the count, making the total 71.

### Lottery Selection

The Gemara records a *baraisa* about how Moshe actually selected the 70 elders. When the Holy One told Moshe to gather 70 elders from among Israel, Moshe faced an arithmetical challenge: if he took six from each of the twelve tribes he would have 72 candidates — two too many. If he took five from each tribe he would have only 60 — ten short. And if he took six from some tribes and five from others he would create jealousy among the tribes.

What did Moshe do? He selected six men from each of the twelve tribes, yielding 72 candidates. He then prepared 72 lots: on 70 he wrote the word *Zaken* (elder), and two he left blank. He mixed them in a box (*kalfi*) and told each candidate to come and draw his lot. Whoever drew *Zaken* was told: heaven has already sanctified you. Whoever drew the blank was told: *Hamakom lo chafetz becha* — God does not desire you; I can do nothing for you. The Gemara draws a parallel to how Moshe resolved the redemption of the 273 extra *bechorim* over the number of Levites: he prepared 22,000 lots inscribed with *ben Levi* and 273 inscribed with *chamesh shekalim* — five shekel — mixed them, and had the *bechorim* draw, so that no individual could complain that Moshe had singled him out.

### Eldad & Medad

The Gemara now addresses the famous story of Eldad and Medad, who "remained in the camp." One opinion (*yesh omrim*) holds that they remained because of the lottery (*bakalfi nishta'yeru*): they drew the blank lots and were thereby excluded. This reading is consistent with the lottery narrative just described, and if so Eldad and Medad were among the original 72 candidates.

A close reading of Rashi here, however, reveals a nuanced interpretation distinct from the well-known account in Rashi's commentary on the Torah. Rashi on the Gemara explains that Eldad and Medad did not go to draw their lots because they feared that blank lots would come up in their hands. They preferred to disqualify themselves from the process rather than risk drawing the blank and having Moshe tell them, *Hamakom lo chafetz becha*. This portrayal is more ambiguous than the familiar Rashi on the Torah, where they are praised for their humility in voluntarily withdrawing out of deference. Here the motivation is closer to reluctance to face public rejection — which, as the Gemara will develop, leaves open the question of their virtue.

Rabbi Shimon offers a second opinion: Eldad and Medad chose on their own initiative to remain in the camp. When the Holy One told Moshe to bring 70 elders, Eldad and Medad said: *einenu re'uyim l'ota gedolah* — we are not worthy of this greatness. The Holy One responded: because you have made yourselves small, I will add greatness upon your greatness. And what was that greatness? All the other 70 elders prophesied and then stopped — *vayitnabu velo yasafu*; but Eldad and Medad began to prophesy and did not stop. They continued prophesying within the camp.

### Their Prophecy

What did Eldad and Medad prophesy? The Gemara offers several opinions. One view holds that they prophesied: *Moshe mes v'Yehoshua machnis es Yisrael l'aretz* — Moshe will die and Yehoshua will bring Israel into the land. This is inferred from the context: Yehoshua became agitated at their prophesying, which makes most sense if their prophecy touched on a matter involving Moshe's honor — specifically, the announcement of his death and succession.

Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer offers a second view: they prophesied about the *slav* — the quail that was to come — saying *ali slav, ali slav*.

Rav Nachman proposes a third interpretation: they prophesied about Gog and Magog, the eschatological war at the end of days. The source is the verse in Yechezkel: *ha'atah hu asher dibarti b'yamim kadmonim beyad avdai nevi'ei Yisrael* — "Are you the one of whom I spoke in former days through my servants, the prophets of Israel?" The word *shanim* in the verse can be read not as "years" but as *shnayim* — two — referring to two prophets who prophesied the same prophecy at the same time in the same place. Who are those two prophets? Eldad and Medad.

### Content Debate

The Gemara now examines the coherence of each of these three opinions against the textual clues. The opinion that they prophesied about Moshe's death fits naturally with the narrative: Yehoshua urges Moshe, *Adoni Moshe kela'em* — my master Moshe, restrain them — and the context clearly involves protecting Moshe's dignity. If they announced his death and succession by Yehoshua, Yehoshua's protective reaction is entirely understandable.

The two other opinions — the *slav* and Gog and Magog — raise a difficulty: what exactly was Yehoshua objecting to? Why would a prophecy about quail or an end-of-days war provoke him to try to silence them? The Gemara answers: *lav orach ar'a* — it is simply not proper conduct for students to prophesy in the presence of their master. Eldad and Medad were in some sense disciples in Moshe's orbit, and to deliver public prophecy while Moshe was present was like a student who rules on halacha in the presence of his teacher. That alone was reason enough for Yehoshua's distress.

### Silencing Them

The Gemara then addresses the converse problem for the first opinion — that they prophesied Moshe's death. If that was the content of their prophecy, how do we understand Moshe's response of *mi yiten ki yitein Hashem rucho aleihem* — would that all of God's people were prophets? Why would Moshe express such a noble, generous sentiment upon hearing that he was about to die?

The Gemara answers: *lo siyumuha kamei* — they did not tell Moshe the content of the prophecy. Moshe only knew that they were prophesying; he did not know what they said. Yehoshua, presumably, knew.

### Moshe's Response

What then did Yehoshua mean by *kela'em* — restrain them? Various interpretations appear. One reading is that he meant: lock them up or punish them. But the Gemara offers a more pointed interpretation: *hatil aleihem tzorchei tzibur* — place communal responsibilities upon them, and *v'hein kalin mei'aleihen* — the demands of public leadership will destroy them on their own. Tosafos explains: the *shechinah* does not rest amid sadness, only amid joy. The pressures of communal administration bring anguish and preoccupation, and that alone would extinguish the *nevuah* without any active intervention.

Moshe's response, *mi yiten ki yitein Hashem rucho aleihem*, is thus the expression of a man who genuinely desires that all of Israel be *nevi'im* — who shows no possessiveness about divine inspiration, even when told (as far as Yehoshua knew) that others were prophesying. This quality of *anivus* is itself what the Gemara highlights as the greatness of Moshe's character.

---

## Sanhedrin Makeup

### I Don't Know

The Gemara now turns to the procedural and compositional requirements of the *Sanhedrin*. One issue concerns a judge who says *eini yodeia* — I do not know. Such a judge is effectively recused, treated *k'man d'leiseih damei* — as if he were not there. Importantly, even if that judge subsequently wants to offer a reason and participate in the second round of deliberations after additional judges have been added, we do not hear from him — *lo sham'inan lei*. This is a striking rule: not only can he not vote, but his voice is entirely removed from the proceeding.

### Odd Numbers

This leads to the question of why the *Sanhedrin* must have an odd number of judges. The requirement is rooted in the rules of *dinei nefashos*: a conviction requires a majority of two. But as the Gemara demonstrates, with 23 judges you can never achieve a majority of two through the standard configuration if one judge says *eini yodeia*. If one judge recuses himself and we are now effectively at 22, and we add pairs to restore odd numbers — we go to 24. Now a vote of 13 to 10 yields a majority of three, but a vote of 12 to 10 yields a majority of two. That case — 12 against 10 — is precisely the case of *mosifin*, the case where judges were added, and according to all opinions this is achievable. Rabbi Abbahu notes that in the *Sanhedrin Gedola* according to Rabbi Yehudah — who holds the larger court has 70, not 71 — the same logic applies: you can achieve 36 against 34 through the same mechanism.

Rabbi Abbahu further rules that when adding judges in the *mosifin* process, one may create a *beis din shakul* — an evenly divided court — as an acceptable *lechatchila* in that situation. One might have thought that the judge who said *eini yodeia* is still counted as present (*k'man d'iseih damei*), keeping the effective total at 23 and preserving odd numbers. The Gemara clarifies: no — once he says *eini yodeia* he is treated as entirely absent, which is precisely why we add judges and why an even division becomes permissible in that context.

### Unanimous Guilty

Rav Kahana states a rule familiar to many: if the entire *Sanhedrin* immediately voted that the defendant is guilty — *rau kullan le-chovah* — the defendant is acquitted (*potrin oso*). The rationale reflects the principle of *halanas din*, the requirement to deliberate overnight before imposing a capital verdict, precisely so that one or more judges can reconsider and perhaps find some argument in the defendant's favor. A unanimous instant guilty verdict is itself evidence that no one is genuinely arguing on his behalf. Since the Torah demands that someone advocate for the accused — as expressed in the formula *v'shafetu ha-eidah v'hitzilu ha-eidah* — a court in which every member immediately condemned the defendant has, by definition, failed to fulfill this function.

### Physical & Wisdom

Rabbi Yochanan enumerates the ideal qualifications for members of the *Sanhedrin*: they must be *ba'alei komah* — people of notable stature; *ba'alei chochmah* — learned and wise; *ba'alei mareh* — of good appearance; *ba'alei ziknah* — advanced in years and presumably in sagacity; and *ba'alei kishafim* — knowledgeable in the ways of witchcraft, so as to be able to counteract sorcery that defendants might employ, as Rashi explains. These qualifications include explicitly physical traits alongside intellectual ones — a recognition that human beings respond to appearance and bearing, just as the beauty of the *Beis ha-Mikdash* serves a purpose beyond the purely spiritual.

### 70 Languages

They must also be *yod'im b'shiv'im lashon* — knowledgeable in 70 languages. The Gemara clarifies that this requirement does not mean every member of the *Sanhedrin* must personally know all 70 languages; rather, enough members must know them so that the court does not have to rely exclusively on a translator. *Shelo tehei Sanhedrin shoma'as mipi hamisurgeman* — the *Sanhedrin* should not be entirely dependent on hearsay translation. At minimum, some members must hear testimony directly in the original language.

### Sheretz Argument

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds another memorable qualification: one may not seat on the *Sanhedrin* anyone who cannot argue that a *sheretz* — one of the eight categories of small creeping creatures that transmit *tumah* — is in fact *tahor* according to the Torah, at least as a counterfactual. Rav himself demonstrates: a snake kills people and animals, generating *tumah* through the resulting corpse, yet the snake itself is *tahor*. If so, a *sheretz* — which does not kill — should certainly be *tahor* by a *kal vachomer*. The Gemara immediately rejects this argument: *midi dehavei akoitz b'alma* — a thorn also kills and is *tahor*, so clearly lethality is irrelevant to *tumah* status. The *kal vachomer* therefore fails.

Yet the requirement itself remains. What is its point? Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafos asks why we would want judges who can construct invalid counterfactual arguments. The deeper lesson, as the Gemara implies, is that the very capacity to construct clever arguments from sources — even arguments that are ultimately wrong — could, in the wrong hands, pervert the law. Anyone can invoke the same texts and methods to reach a wrong conclusion. What distinguishes a proper *dayan* is not cleverness alone, but integrity, fidelity to the *Torah*, and an honest sense of what the law truly means. The ability to argue a *sheretz* is *tahor* tests whether someone understands the difference between argumentation and truth.

### City Language Needs

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav further rules: a city that does not have two people who can speak a foreign language and one additional person who can understand it may not seat a *Sanhedrin*. This is a minimum linguistic infrastructure requirement. The reason is consistent with the broader concern: members of the court must be able to directly communicate with and understand parties who appear before them.

### Beitar & Yavneh

The Gemara illustrates this with historical examples. In Beitar there were three individuals capable of meeting this standard; in Yavneh there were four: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva, and Shimon haTimni. Shimon haTimni is notable — he did not bear the title *Rabbi*, having not received *semikhah*, and he sat on the ground (*dan lifneihem b'karka*), participating in deliberations without being a fully ordained member of the court. The Gemara then records a tension: a *baraisa* suggests that three who know languages is praiseworthy, and four is unparalleled — yet we said that two who speak and one who understands is the minimum. The resolution is that this *tanna* follows the position that three is praiseworthy and two is already a mark of wisdom, consistent with the figures at Beitar and Yavneh.

---

## Rabbinic Titles

### Learning vs. Deliberating

The mention of *dan lifneihem b'karka* — deliberating before the sages on the ground — prompts the Gemara to identify a series of technical phrases used throughout the Talmud, each of which designates a specific sage or group of sages. This is not a pure digression: the Gemara is operating in the context of *Sanhedrin* composition, and understanding the different statuses of sages — those who deliberated, those who merely learned, those with and without *semikhah* — is directly relevant.

When a Talmudic passage says *lemidim lifnei chachamim* — someone who was learning before the sages — this refers to Levi, who studied under Rebbi. When a passage says *danim lifnei chachamim* — deliberating before the sages — it refers to Shimon ben Azzai, Shimon ben Zoma, Chanan haMitzri, and Chananyah ben Chakinai. Significantly, none of these bear the title *Rabbi*: they were brilliant students who participated in the deliberations of the *Sanhedrin* without having received formal ordination. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds a fifth to this group: Shimon haTimni, already mentioned in connection with Yavneh, bringing the total to five.

### Regional Sages

The Gemara continues with regional designations. *Rabboseinu she'be-Bavel* — our teachers in Babylonia — refers to Rav and Shmuel. *Rabboseinu she'be-Eretz Yisrael* — our teachers in the land of Israel — refers to Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Ami. *Dayyanei golah* — the judges of the exile — refers to Karna. *Dayyanei Eretz Yisrael* — the judges of the land of Israel — refers to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi. *Dayyanei de'Pumbedisa* — the judges of Pumbedisa — refers to Rav Pappa bar Shmuel alone. *Dayyanei de'Neharde'a* — the judges of Nehardea — refers to Rav Adda bar Minyumi.

### Amoraim Roles

The identifications continue with the Babylonian academies. *Sabei de'Sura* — the elders of Sura — refers to Rav Huna and Rav Chisda. *Sabei de'Pumbedisa* — the elders of Pumbedisa — refers to Rav Yehudah and Rav Eina. *Charifei de'Pumbedisa* — the sharp ones of Pumbedisa — refers to Eifa and Avimi the sons of Rechava. *Amora'ei de'Pumbedisa* — the Amoraim of Pumbedisa — refers to Rabba and Rav Yosef, the leading Amoraim of that academy. *Amora'ei de'Neharde'a* — the Amoraim of Nehardea — refers to Rav Chama of Neharbal.

The phrase *masni* — he taught — refers to Rami bar Berabi. *Amri bei Rav* — they say in the house of Rav — the Gemara first suggests this refers to Rav Huna, but immediately raises a challenge: we have a tradition that Rav Huna himself said *amri bei Rav*, citing the academy. Rav Huna therefore cannot himself be the referent of that phrase. The Gemara revises: *amri bei Rav* refers to Rav Hamnuna, though Rashi and Tosafot debate whether Rav Hamnuna is himself the referent or whether he is the one who transmitted sayings in the name of Rav Huna's academy.

*Amri be'ma'arava* — they say in the west, meaning in Eretz Yisrael — refers to Rabbi Yirmiya. *Shalchu misam* — they sent from there — initially attributed to Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina, and *machaku aleih be'ma'arava* — they mocked this in the west — attributed to Rabbi Elazar. But the Gemara challenges this assignment: we have a case where *shalchu misam* is followed by an opinion cited in the name of Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explicitly, so clearly that phrase cannot refer to him. The Gemara resolves: reverse the assignment — *shalchu misam* is Rabbi Elazar, and *machaku aleih be'ma'arava* is Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina.

---

## City Population

### 120 People

The Gemara now addresses the minimum population required for a city to establish its own *Sanhedrin ketana* of 23. The *chachamim* require a city of 120 people. The Gemara asks *mai avidtaihu* — how is this figure derived? The calculation proceeds as follows: the court itself requires 23 judges. Beyond that, the *Sanhedrin* in session was accompanied by three rows of 23 scholars each — qualified replacements who could be elevated to the bench if a judge needed to be replaced or recuse himself. That gives 23 plus 69, totaling 92. Add to that 10 *batlanim* — communal functionaries permanently available to ensure a *minyan* in the synagogue — and the total reaches 102. The remaining positions include two scribes, two court attendants, two litigants, two witnesses, two witnesses who could render the first pair *zomemin*, and two who could render those *zomemin* — adding another 10, bringing the total to 112 and eventually 120 once the full tally is complete, though a separate *baraisa* accounting for various communal roles brings the count to 140, which Rashi reconciles by noting that one person can hold multiple roles.

### Ten Services

The *baraisa* teaches: any city that does not have these ten things, a Torah scholar is not permitted to reside within it. The ten are: a *beis din* empowered to flog and to punish; a *kuppah shel tzedakah* — a communal charity fund, collected by two people and distributed by three; a *beis knesses* — a synagogue; a *beis ha-merchatz* — a bathhouse; a *beis ha-kisei* — a privy; a physician; a *uman* — a bloodletter; a *lavlar* — a scribe; a *tabbach* — a butcher (according to the version that includes this); and a *melammed tinokos* — a teacher of young children. Rabbi Akiva adds: the city must also have various species of fruit, because the different varieties of fruit brighten the eyes and help maintain the clarity of mind needed for Torah study.

### Alternative Minimums

Rabbi Nechemiah sets the minimum population at 230, so that each person is fit to serve as a commander of ten — an allusion to the organizational structure Moshe established in the wilderness. Rebbi sets the figure at 277, and a *baraisa* cites Rebbi as requiring 278. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between 277 and 278 by reference to the disagreement between Rabbi Yehudah and the *chachamim* about whether the *Sanhedrin Gedola* consists of 70 or 71: the court of 23 may need to grow by adding judges until it reaches the size of the larger court, and the different totals reflect whether one counts 70 or 71 at the top.

---

## Census Count

### Military Hierarchy

The Gemara concludes the chapter by drawing on the organizational hierarchy that Moshe established among the people. The *baraisa* cites the verse listing the military commanders: *sarei alafim* — commanders of thousands; *sarei meos* — commanders of hundreds; *sarei chamishim* — commanders of fifties; *sarei asaros* — commanders of tens.

### Total 78,600

The calculation unfolds as follows. *Sarei alafim* — 600,000 divided by 1,000 yields 600 commanders of thousands. *Sarei meos* — 600,000 divided by 100 yields 6,000 commanders of hundreds. *Sarei chamishim* — 600,000 divided by 50 yields 12,000 commanders of fifties. *Sarei asaros* — 600,000 divided by 10 yields 60,000 commanders of tens. Adding these together: 600 plus 6,000 plus 12,000 plus 60,000 equals 78,600. Thus the total number of judges of Israel appointed by Moshe was *sheva ribo u'shmonas alafim v'shesh meos* — 78,600. And with that calculation, the first chapter of *Sanhedrin* comes to a close.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 18

## Character & Integrity

### Intro & Tisha B'Av Review

We begin today in the *Bavli* on daf 18, at the opening of the second *perek*. By way of introduction, it is worth noting that a pre-recorded shiur on Sanhedrin for Tisha B'Av has been posted, covering material from both the *Bavli* and the *Yerushalmi* on the qualifications for membership on the *Sanhedrin gedolah*. Two points from that recording bear mention here.

The first concerns a requirement discussed in the *Bavli*: to serve on the *Sanhedrin*, one must be fluent in multiple languages so as to hear the testimony of witnesses and litigants directly, without relying on an interpreter. The concern is not merely about conscious misrepresentation but about the subtle loss of nuance and emphasis that even a well-intentioned translation inevitably introduces. The second point, equally famous, is that a judge cannot sit on a *beit din* unless he is capable of constructing an argument that a *sheretz* — an otherwise quintessentially impure creeping creature — is *tahor*. *Tosafot* famously asks: *mah lanu ledrashot shel hevel* — what is the value of such demonstrably hollow argumentation? What does it prove?

### Integrity > Intellect

The capacity to demonstrate intellectual virtuosity — to prove a counterfactual conclusion through sheer command of texts and logic — is indeed part of what this requirement tests. But the deeper question it raises is precisely that intellectual prowess alone is not sufficient, and is perhaps even dangerous. If a person is clever enough and knows the sources well enough, he can reach virtually any conclusion he sets out to reach. The ability to win an argument does not establish the integrity of a decision.

What is truly striking, when one examines the criteria for who may serve on the *Sanhedrin* in both the *Bavli* and the *Yerushalmi*, is that it is not intellectual ability or breadth of knowledge that leaps out at you — it is *character*. Humility, probity, *yiras shamayim*, moral integrity: these are the qualities that dominate the lists of qualifications. This remains relevant to the question of how one evaluates *poskim* today. In theory, one could construct a halakhic argument leading to virtually any conclusion. The degree to which we can trust a ruling is bound up with our confidence in the decisor's integrity and fidelity — not merely in his erudition.

### Torah Models

The second noteworthy point from the Tisha B'Av recording concerns a famous and lengthy *Tosefta* discussed in the *Yerushalmi*, which describes an era when there was never any unresolved debate. Whenever a *beit din* did not know the answer to a question, it would refer the matter to the next higher court — and so on, up through the hierarchy, until the question reached the *Sanhedrin*. The *Tosefta* describes each level of the process with the same formula: *im shamu amru lahem* — if they had a tradition, they transmitted it; *ve-im lo shamu* — if they did not have a tradition, they referred the matter upward. At the level of the *Sanhedrin* itself: *im shamu amru lahem, ve-im lo shamru amdu leminyan* — if they had a tradition they transmitted it, and if they had no tradition, they took a vote. What is conspicuously absent at every stage is any notion that a court, lacking a received tradition, would turn to its own creative analysis to work out the answer.

This reflects a particular model of *Torah she-ba'al peh*: it is entirely transmission. Debate is not a sign of intellectual vitality but of uncertainty — a failure in the chain of tradition. The *Tosefta* praises the era when there was never any debate precisely because it meant the tradition was intact and the *halacha* was always known.

This stands in sharp contrast to what might be called the *Hillel* or the *Rabbi Akiva* model of *Torah she-ba'al peh*, in which any tradition and any text is inherently limited and cannot be expected to address every future question. In that model, debate is not a symptom of failure but a natural and indeed positive feature of a living tradition — a space for human intellect, creativity, and development to operate. These two visions of the nature of *Torah she-ba'al peh* are worth holding in mind as we proceed, for we will encounter the same *Tosefta* discussed at length in the *Bavli* as well.

---

## Kohen Gadol Status

### Perek 2 Opening

The second *perek* opens with the topic of the *kohen gadol* and the *melech*. One might note that this represents a degree of digression from the organizational logic of the first *perek*, which was organized around the question of court sizes. But it is not really such a great digression, since the underlying question is one of fundamental importance: is anyone above the law, and who receives special treatment within the legal system? It is worth noting, however, that even within the *Mishnah* of the first *perek* there were puzzling digressions — including a discussion of *ir nidachat* that is difficult to account for. The digressions here, as we will see, are more understandable.

### Kohen Gadol Judged

The *Mishnah* opens: *kohen gadol dan vedanin oto* — a *kohen gadol* may serve as a judge, and he himself may be judged. As we saw in the previous *perek*, when he is judged, it is before a *beit din* of seventy-one — *kol hadavar hagadol yavi'u eilecha*, the cases involving great personages are brought before the highest court. Nevertheless, he is judged. He is not above the law.

### Testimony Rules

*Me'id ume'idin oto* — he may testify, and others may testify against him. This is perhaps obvious: if he can be brought to court and judged, it follows that testimony must be admissible against him.

### Family Law

The *Mishnah* continues: *choletz vecholtzin le'ishto* — he may perform *chalitzah*, and even though that involves his sister-in-law spitting at him, this applies. And if he dies, his wife may undergo *chalitzah* with his brother. *Umeyabmim et ishto* — if he dies, his brother may perform *yibum* with his wife. *Aval hu eino meyabem* — but he himself cannot perform *yibum* with his brother's widow, *mipnei shehu asur be'almanah* — because a *kohen gadol* is forbidden to marry a widow.

This immediately raises a question: if he is categorically forbidden from *yibum*, why is he obligated in *chalitzah* at all? He should seemingly be excluded from the entire institution. The answer relates to the status of his brother, who is a *kohen* but not a *kohen gadol*. A standard *kohen* is forbidden to marry a *gerushah* but is permitted to marry an *almanah*. It is only the *kohen gadol* who is uniquely forbidden to marry a widow — contrary to what a surface reading of *Yechezkel* might suggest, since *Yechezkel* implies that *kohanim* generally cannot marry a widow. But that is one of those places where the *Yerushalmi* notes that *Yechezkel* appears to contradict received *halacha*. The operative *halacha* is that an ordinary *kohen* may marry an *almanah* but not a *gerushah*. So his brother, being a regular *kohen*, is eligible for *yibum*, and because *yibum* is available through the brother, *chalitzah* remains relevant.

### Mourning Rules

*Mes lo mes* — if an immediate relative of the *kohen gadol* dies: *eino yotzei achar hamitah* — he does not directly follow the coffin. Rather, *ela hen nichnasim vehu nigleh, hen niglin vehu nichseh* — as the procession turns from one street onto another, he appears on the street they have just left; when they appear on a new street, he withdraws from it. He is always at a distance, never on the same street as the coffin. *Veyotzei imahen ad petach sha'ar ha'ir* — in this manner he accompanies the procession, maintaining this careful distance, until it reaches the city gate, since the burial takes place outside the city. This is the view of *Rabbi Meir*.

The reason for this protocol is that even though an ordinary *kohen* is permitted — and indeed has a *mitzvah* to become *tamei* for his immediate relatives — a *kohen gadol* is not. The verse in *Emor* states explicitly: *ve'al kol nafshot met lo yavo, le'aviv ule'imo lo yitama* — he may not become *tamei* even for his father or his mother. Similarly, the *nazir* shares this same restriction. The *kohen gadol* must therefore keep his distance to avoid accidentally incurring *tumah*.

*Rabbi Yehuda* takes a stricter and more literal position: *eino yotzei min hamikdash* — he does not leave the *Beit HaMikdash* at all, based on a literal reading of the verse *u'min hamikdash lo yetzei*. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, the *kohen gadol* continues performing the *avodah* even while his relative is being buried. *Rabbi Meir* reads the verse differently — not as a prohibition on physically leaving the *Beit HaMikdash*, but as a prohibition on compromising his *kedushah* — *min hakedusha lo yetzei* — and therefore allows him to leave, provided he avoids *tumah*.

### Consolation Rituals

The *Mishnah* then describes the protocols that apply to the *kohen gadol* in the context of consolation — both when he is consoling others and when others are consoling him.

When he consoles others: *derech kol ha'am ovrim ze achar ze* — all the people pass before him in a line, and *vehamemuna memutza beino uvein ha'am* — the *memuna*, his deputy, stands as a kind of buffer between him and the passing mourners. *Rashi* explains that this means the *memuna* stands to his right while the people pass on his left.

When he himself is the mourner receiving consolers: *kol ha'am omrim lo anu kaparat'cha* — all the people say to him, "We are your atonement," meaning: let whatever bad that might befall you befall us instead. This formula reflects a theological assumption that a death represents the need for atonement — whether for the sins of the deceased, or because the loss itself is a sign that something must be spiritually rectified. One encounters a similar formula in the practice of saying *hareini kaparat mishkavo* upon the death of a relative. Here it is the community that takes upon itself, as it were, to serve in the *kohen gadol*'s stead.

The *kohen gadol* responds: *titvarchu min hashamayim* — may you be blessed from heaven.

When the *kohen gadol* is served the *havra'ah* — the meal given to a mourner following the burial: *kol ha'am mesubin al ha'aretz vehu meisev al hasafsal* — all the people sit on the ground as mourners would, while he sits on a bench. This is a kind of reversal of the usual practice, in which the mourner sits below and the consolers sit above. Here, out of honor for the *kohen gadol* and as an expression of *anu kaparat'cha*, the community takes on the posture of mourning while he is elevated above them.

---

## King's Exemption

### King Not Judged

In stark contrast to the *kohen gadol*, the *Mishnah* states: *hamelech lo dan velo danin oto* — the king does not judge, and he is not judged. It should be noted that in an earlier discussion we mentioned that the phrase *kol hadavar hagadol yavi'u eilecha* extends a *beit din* of seventy-one to the heads of tribes — and at that point it was perhaps suggested, implicitly, that a king might be included. But this *Mishnah* makes clear that a king stands outside the judicial system entirely. This is, in some respects, troubling. The *Torah* explicitly requires the king to write a *Sefer Torah* and carry it with him — *velo yasur levavo mei'achav* — to constantly reinforce that he is not above his fellows. He is clearly bound by *Torah* law. Yet here he is excluded from the court system.

The *Gemara* will resolve this by explaining that this exclusion applies specifically to *malchei Yisrael* — the kings of the northern kingdom, who were not seen as consistently submissive to *Torah* authority. Bringing such kings to court would only cause harm to the judicial system; the confrontation would not end well. But the *Gemara* will go on to say that this does not apply to *malchei Yehuda*. So the earlier suggestion was not entirely wrong. But from the *Mishnah*'s plain presentation, the king is excluded both from judging and from being judged.

There is something worth noting here: the exclusion cuts both ways. If the king cannot be judged, he also cannot judge. He is not operating a parallel system in which he enjoys immunity while wielding authority over others. He is simply outside the system altogether. This is at least partially analogous to certain modern conventions — such as the question of whether a sitting head of state can be subpoenaed as a witness in a civil dispute, a matter that courts have engaged with in various ways. The underlying tension between sovereign authority and judicial accountability is not unique to the *halacha*.

### King Restrictions

*Lo dan velo danin oso, lo me'id velo me'idin oso* — the king does not testify and you cannot testify against him. *Lo choletz velo choltzin le'ishto* — he does not perform *chalitzah*, which would require his sister-in-law to spit at him, and if he dies, *chalitzah* is not performed on his wife. *Lo meyabem velo meyabemin le'ishto* — he does not perform *yibum* with his brother's widow, and if he dies, *yibum* is not performed with his wife.

*Rabbi Yehuda* says: *im ratza lachlotzo leyabem zachur letov* — if he voluntarily wishes to perform *chalitzah* or *yibum*, he will be remembered favorably. This implies, according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, that the restriction is merely that we do not compel him, but that voluntary participation is praiseworthy. The *tanna kamma*, however, holds that we do not permit it even if he wishes to waive his honor: *shemachal al kevodo, ein kevodo machul* — even when he waives his own honor, his honor as king is not his to waive, for it represents the dignity of the entire nation. The troubling implication of the *tanna kamma*'s view, of course, is that his brother's widow would remain an *agunah*.

### Royal Marriage

*Ve'ein nosin almanaso* — one may not marry the king's widow. This reflects a reality familiar from *Tanach*, where a king's widows are treated as off-limits to others. *Rabbi Yehuda* adds: *nosei hamelech almanaso shel melech* — a king may marry the widow of a previous king, since we find that David married Saul's widow, as the verse states: *va'etna lecha et beit adonecha ve'et neshei adonecha becheikecha*.

---

## Talmudic Analysis

### Self-Judgment First

The *Gemara* opens its analysis with what appears to be an obvious question: *kohen gadol dan* — of course a *kohen gadol* can serve as a judge. Why would we think otherwise? Perhaps, one might suggest, because the next *Mishnah* will exclude the king from judging, and we might have assumed the same of the *kohen gadol* by analogy. But then comes the real question: *vedanin oto* — that he himself may be judged — is that not equally obvious? Why does the *Mishnah* need to state it?

The *Gemara* answers: *ei lo dayninan lei, ei ihu heichi dayan* — if we would not allow him to be judged, how could he himself judge others? The verse states *hitkosheshu vakoshu*, which *Resh Lakish* expounds by reading *hitkosheshu* through the root *kshot* — to adorn or perfect. The *Gemara* renders: *kshot atzmecha, ve'achar kach kshot acherim* — first perfect yourself, and only then set about perfecting others. The ethical principle embedded here is a powerful one: you cannot stand in judgment over others unless you yourself are open to being judged. One must first be subject to the law before exercising authority within it. As the *kohen gadol* must atone for himself before atoning for the nation on *Yom Kippur*, so too a judge must be open to judgment before he can legitimately judge.

Since the *Gemara* establishes that the *kohen gadol*'s being judged is logically entailed by his being a judge, it adds: *ella aidi dikba'ei lemitni melech lo dan velo danin oto* — the reason both sides are stated explicitly (*dan vedanin oto*) is that since the *Mishnah* must state both elements by the king in the negative, it states both explicitly by the *kohen gadol* as well, for symmetry.

Alternatively, the *Gemara* offers a further reason: *kedetanya* — as taught in a *baraita*: *kohen gadol sheharag et hanefesh, bemezid neherag, beshogeg goleh* — a *kohen gadol* who kills someone is executed if he acted intentionally, and is sent into exile if he did so unintentionally. *Ve'over al asei ve'al lo ta'aseh, vaharei hu kehedyot lechol devarav* — and he transgresses a positive and a negative commandment, and he is treated as a commoner in all other matters.

### Murder Baraita

The *Gemara* proceeds to analyze each clause. That he is executed for intentional murder — *pshita*, that is obvious, once we have established that he can be judged. The *chiddush* is specifically that *beshogeg goleh* — he is exiled for unintentional killing. Why might we have thought otherwise?

### Permanent Exile

*Salka datach amina*: I might have thought that since the release from exile is conditioned on the death of the *kohen gadol* — *veyashav bah ad mot hakohen hagadol* — and since this *kohen gadol* is himself the *kohen gadol*, there is no death of a *kohen gadol* that will ever free him. And therefore, *kol de'it lei takanta bachazara lighlot* — exile applies only to those for whom there is a mechanism of release; *vechol deleit lei takanta bachazara lo lighlot* — those for whom there is no mechanism of release should not be exiled. So I would say he should not go into exile at all.

This brings up a remarkable question: can a *kohen gadol* continue to serve in that capacity even from exile, after having committed an unintentional killing? It sounds very much from the *Gemara* here as if the answer is yes — that he would remain *kohen gadol*, and that this is precisely the source of the problem, since his own death would be required to free himself. 

The *Mishnah* at the beginning of daf 18b states: *ha-horeg kohen gadol o kohen gadol she-harag et hanefesh, eino yotzei misham le-olam* — both one who kills a *kohen gadol* and a *kohen gadol* who kills someone are never released. *Rashi* explains the two cases somewhat differently. In the first case — one who kills the *kohen gadol* — since at the time of exile there was no *kohen gadol* in office (the position had just been vacated by the very killing), there is no one whose death can anchor the exilee's release. Even if a new *kohen gadol* is subsequently appointed, *Rashi* maintains that it is the *kohen gadol* in office *at the time of exile* that determines release — and that position was empty. In the second case — the *kohen gadol* who commits the killing — the problem is simply that it is his own death we would be talking about.

*Tosafot* refines the first case: *eino yotzei misham le-olam* applies specifically when no replacement *kohen gadol* was appointed before the judgment was concluded. Had a new *kohen gadol* been installed before the exilee's sentence was finalized, that *kohen gadol*'s eventual death would serve as the release mechanism. *Tosafot* further notes that in addition to a sitting *kohen gadol*, a *mashuach she-avar* — a former *kohen gadol* who had vacated the position — or a *mashuach milchama* can also function as the relevant figure, meaning there may be other quasi-equivalents whose death could free the exilee.

In the case of the *kohen gadol* who himself commits the killing, the *Rashi* is somewhat ambiguous: *bemisas mi yashuv? Halekha Kohen Gadol* — by whose death would he return? He is himself the *kohen gadol*. This could be read either as meaning that he remains *kohen gadol* throughout his exile and hence there is literally no one else's death that could free him, or that he has effectively ceased functioning as *kohen gadol* but no replacement has yet been appointed. The question of whether a *kohen gadol* who commits an unintentional killing would be removed from office or retained is not definitively resolved here, though the plain sense of the *Gemara* is that he remains *kohen gadol*.

The *Gemara* then asks: could we simply say he should not be exiled at all? *Amar kra: venas shama kol rotzeiach* — the verse says "every murderer shall flee there," and *afilu kohen gadol bemashma* — even a *kohen gadol* is included in "every."

### Non-Capital Crimes

The *baraita* concludes: *ve'over al asei ve'al lo ta'aseh, vaharei hu kehedyot lechol devarav* — he is treated as a commoner in all his affairs. The *Gemara* asks: is that not obvious? But no — one might have thought otherwise, given the rule established in the first *perek* that *ein danin lo et hashevet velo et navi hasheker velo et kohen gadol ela al pi beit din shel shivim ve'echad* — only a *beit din* of seventy-one may judge the *kohen gadol*. And *Rabbah bar bar Chana* derived this from *kol hadavar hagadol yavi'u eilecha* — all matters relating to this great personage come before the highest court. One might therefore have thought that even monetary disputes or cases of *malkus* require a *beit din* of seventy-one for the *kohen gadol*.

The *Mishnah* therefore teaches that for anything short of a capital crime, he is treated entirely as a commoner and receives a standard *beit din* of three. The textual basis for limiting the elevated *beit din* to capital matters is the phrase *hadavar hagadol* — the *great* matter — which implies not merely matters *relating to* a great person, but matters that are themselves of great import. A non-capital case, even involving the *kohen gadol*, does not meet that threshold.

It is worth noting that the *Yerushalmi* actually takes a different view: it holds that for non-capital crimes, the *kohen gadol* is given a *beit din* of twenty-three rather than three. The *Yerushalmi* thus maintains an intermediate position — he is not treated entirely as a commoner in non-capital matters, even if he does not receive the full *beit din* of seventy-one.

---

## Testimony Exceptions

### Lost Property Principle

The *Mishnah* states that a *kohen gadol* may testify, *me'id ume'idin oso*. But the *Gemara* raises a challenge from a *baraita*: *vehisalamta meihem* — the verse says "and you shall hide from them," implying that there are times when one is actually supposed to look away, to passively not fulfill certain positive *mitzvot*, when fulfilling them would compromise one's dignity. The specific model is the *mitzvah* of returning a lost object. The verse states *lo tireh et shor achicha o et seyo nidachim vehisalamta meihem* — do not see your brother's ox or sheep going astray and hide from it. The Rabbis, in their characteristically precise reading, focus on *vehisalamta meihem*: there are times when you should hide from it. When? When it would not be befitting your dignity — when stooping to recover and return the object would represent a genuine compromise of a person's station.

This principle of *kevod habriyot* — human dignity — is capable of overriding rabbinic enactments and even, in the case of the passive non-performance of a positive *mitzvah*, potentially biblical obligations. Three cases are enumerated in the *baraita* for when one may be exempt from returning a lost object: a *kohen* who would have to enter a cemetery to retrieve it; an elder for whom the physical act of retrieving it would not be befitting his dignity (*zaken ve'eino lefi kevodo*); and a case where the monetary value of the time one would lose from one's own work exceeds the value of the object (*melachto merubah mishel chaveiro*).

This last case reflects a broader and critically important principle in *bein adam lachaveiro*: *chayecha vechayei achicha chayecha kodmim* — your life and wellbeing take precedence over your fellow's. This is not merely about life-or-death situations; it applies to economic interests as well. My primary obligation is to my own needs before those of my fellow. Why should protecting your property come at a greater cost to me than the property is worth to you? If there are two lost objects and I can only retrieve one, I am permitted to prioritize my own. This principle has significant implications for domains well beyond *aveida* — including, crucially, questions about *kibbud av va'em* in the context of difficult or harmful parental relationships. The genuine exemption in such cases is not derived from characterizing the parent as a *rasha* — a categorization that has traditionally been applied only to those who reject *Torah* observance, not simply those who behave cruelly — but from the fundamental principle that a person's own psychic and emotional wellbeing takes precedence over the obligation to honor a parent. That message is too often lost, but it is an authentic and important *halachic* position.

Returning to the *Gemara*'s question: if testifying is a positive obligation, and if *kevod habriyot* can exempt a person from a positive obligation when its performance would compromise his dignity, should a *kohen gadol* not be exempt from appearing to testify? The *Gemara* is raising this as a genuine challenge to the *Mishnah*'s statement that the *kohen gadol* may testify.

### Royal Testimony

*Amar Rav Yosef*: the *kohen gadol* testifies before a king — meaning in a case involving a king, that would be befitting his dignity. But the *Gemara* immediately objects: how does a king get into a court case at all? The *Mishnah* said *lo dan velo danin oso, lo me'id velo me'idin oso* — a king is neither judged nor testified against. So in what scenario would the *kohen gadol* be testifying in a matter involving a king?

### Prince Halakhic Status

*Ela amar Rav Zeira*: perhaps the *kohen gadol* is testifying in a case involving the king's son — the prince. That would be a person of sufficient dignity that appearing as a witness would be befitting the *kohen gadol*'s honor.

But the *Gemara* objects immediately and strikingly: *ben melech hedyot hu* — the king's son is a commoner. This is a genuinely arresting statement. There is no *halachic* status of prince. The person may stand next in line to the throne, but from a *halachic* standpoint he carries no special standing. The *Gemara* therefore holds that testifying in a case involving a prince would not be sufficiently dignified to bring out the *kohen gadol*. One might ask: surely *kavod* is a social reality, not a purely technical *halachic* one — and who would say that a prince commands no special respect? Yet the *Gemara* insists on a *halachically* recognized status as the threshold.

### King's Brief Attendance

*Ela meid bifnei hamelech* — the *Gemara* revises: perhaps what is meant is that the *kohen gadol* testifies in a case being held *in the presence of* the king. The king is not serving as a judge — that would be excluded by the *Mishnah* — but the proceedings are taking place before him.

The *Gemara* then notes: *ve'ein moshivin melech be'Sanhedrin* — but you cannot have a king sitting in the *Sanhedrin*, even in a non-judicial, presiding role. The reason, which will be stated explicitly in the next passage, is the principle of *lo sa'aneh al rav* — one cannot freely argue once a higher authority has expressed a view. The presence of the king, even as a passive observer, would effectively silence debate and compromise the *Sanhedrin*'s independence. The separation of judicial and royal authority is not merely formal but functional.

The *Gemara* then resolves the tension: *mishum yikra d'kohen gadol asa veyasiv* — in order to honor the *kohen gadol* and enable him to appear as a witness without it being beneath his dignity, the king would come and briefly sit — because it is his son who is involved in the case. His attendance is not a participation in the judicial process but a courtesy. *Mekabli minei sahadusa* — the court accepts the testimony of the *kohen gadol*. *Kai ve'azil* — and then the king immediately departs, leaving the court to conduct its deliberations without royal presence. *U'mashkali u'matrinan be'dina* — and the judges then engage in the normal course of judicial deliberation.

The net effect of this entire discussion is that the *Gemara* has effectively narrowed to near-vanishing the circumstances in which a *kohen gadol* would actually testify. The only viable scenario turns out to be a highly unusual and orchestrated one: a case involving the king's son, in which the king makes a brief formal appearance to lend sufficient honor to the proceedings that the *kohen gadol*'s appearance is not beneath his dignity. In any ordinary case, the *kohen gadol* could decline to testify on grounds of dignity, just as an elder is exempt from returning a lost object when it would compromise his station.

---

## Sanhedrin Exclusions

### King on Sanhedrin

*Gufah* — taking up the statement itself: *ein moshivin melech be'Sanhedrin* — a king may not sit on the *Sanhedrin*. This means not only that he does not serve formally as a judge but that he should not even be present in a presiding or supervisory role during deliberations. The reason is the verse *lo sa'aneh al riv* — do not respond against a *rav*, a greater authority. The presence of the king would suppress honest debate. This is precisely why in capital cases the *Sanhedrin* begins deliberations from the most junior members — so that no one is silenced by deference to authority. A king in the room would fatally compromise that independence. The principle here is, in modern terms, one of separation of powers — judicial independence requires that the royal presence be entirely excluded from the deliberative process.

### Leap Year Conflicts

*Ve'lo melech ve'kohen gadol be'ibur shana* — neither the king nor the *kohen gadol* may participate in the *beit din* that determines whether a leap year should be declared. The concern regarding the *kohen gadol*: *mishum tzina* — because of cold. *Rashi* explains that the concern is that he will be cold on *Yom Kippur*, when he must immerse five times. *Tosafot* disagrees, noting that the *mikvah* water would be heated, and suggests instead that the concern is that the stone floor of the *Beit HaMikdash*, which he must traverse barefoot, would be unbearably cold. Either way, the *kohen gadol* has a personal, self-interested stake in ensuring the leap year is not declared in a way that places *Yom Kippur* in a cold month — and that self-interest disqualifies him from the decision.

### King's Money Interest

The king's disqualification is similarly rooted in self-interest: *mishum afsanya* — because of the wages paid to his troops. An intercalary year gives the king an extra month of labor from the soldiers and officials on his payroll, since they are paid an annual salary. The king would therefore have a financial stake in declaring a leap year, and that conflict disqualifies him from participating in the decision. This is a striking example of how rigorously the *halacha* guards the integrity of decisions of public moment against even structural conflicts of interest.

### Year Calculations

*Amar Rav Pappa: shma mina* — we may infer from this discussion that *shata basar yarcha azla* — the year follows the months. *Tosafot* explains that this means the primary basis for declaring a leap year is the calculation of the *tekufah* — the solar season, the position of the sun — rather than the agricultural state of the crops. This is why the *kohen gadol*'s concern about cold is relevant: cold versus warm is fundamentally a function of where the sun is, i.e., the *tekufah*. The question of *aviv* — the actual agricultural ripeness of the grain — is, in this framework, secondary.

### Shepherds & Tekufah

This inference is supported by a story in the *Gemara*. Three cowherds were overheard conversing, and the Rabbis who heard them subsequently declared an intercalary year based on what they had heard. The three men offered different criteria for identifying the month of *Adar*. The first said: if the early grain and the late grain sprout simultaneously, then it is *Adar*; if not, it is still *Shevat*. The second said: if in the morning an ox might freeze to death, and by midday the same ox can lie down in the shade of a fig tree to escape the heat, then it is *Adar*; otherwise it is still *Shevat*. The third said: if the east wind is so strong that when you breathe out you can see your breath, then it is *Adar*; otherwise it is not yet *Adar*.

The Rabbis, having heard these observations, then declared that year a leap year — inferring that it was not yet truly *Adar* but still *Shevat*, and that an additional *Adar* was needed.

The *Gemara* immediately asks: *vetisbera rabanan arevusa samchi* — do you really think the Rabbis relied on the observations of shepherds? *Ela rabanan achushbenayehu samchi* — no, the Rabbis relied on their own calculations of the *tekufah*. *Vero'ei bakar isyuhi de'istaye milta* — the observations of the cowherds merely served to support and confirm what the Rabbis had already determined through calculation. The testimony of the shepherds was corroborative, not determinative.

The conclusion, as *Tosafot* understands it, is that the *tekufah* — the solar calculation — is primary in determining whether a leap year is needed, while agricultural observation serves a secondary, confirmatory role. This also illuminates the reason for the *kohen gadol*'s disqualification from leap year deliberations: since the decision turns primarily on questions of heat and cold, i.e., the solar season, the *kohen gadol*'s personal stake in avoiding cold at *Yom Kippur* time creates a direct and disqualifying conflict of interest.

# Sanhedrin 19

## Kohen Gadol & Yibum

### Perek Overview

We begin the second *perek* of Masechet Sanhedrin, on 19b, starting three lines down from the word *kapasik vetani*. The *perek* is broadly concerned with the special laws governing the dignity and personal status of the *kohen gadol* and the *melech*. The *mishnah* established that the *kohen gadol* does not perform *yibbum*. More precisely, the *mishnah* states: *kohen gadol dan vedannin oto, meid umeidim oto, choletz vecholtzin le-ishto umeyabmin et ishto* — the *kohen gadol* is judged and judges, testifies and others testify against him, performs *chalitzah* and others perform *chalitzah* for his wife, and others may perform *yibbum* with his wife. *Aval hu eino meyabbem* — but he himself does not perform *yibbum* if his brother dies without children. The reason given is *mipnei shehu assur be-almanah*: one of the prohibitions incumbent upon the *kohen gadol* is that he may not marry a widow, and once his brother dies, the sister-in-law becomes an *almanah*, making *yibbum* impossible for him.

### Kohen Gadol Status

The *kohen gadol* bears two distinct laws concerning his personal status in marriage. First, he is prohibited from marrying an *almanah* — a widow. All *kohanim* are prohibited from marrying a divorcee, and the *kohen gadol* bears the additional prohibition against marrying a widow. Second, stated in the form of a positive commandment, the Torah requires him to marry a *betulah*: *betulah yikach*. These two obligations — the *lo ta'aseh* of *almanah lo yikach* and the *aseh* of *betulah yikach* — combine to create the complex halachic tension that the *gemara* proceeds to analyze.

### Erusin vs Nisu'in

The *gemara* opens with the observation that the *mishnah* made no distinction between a brother who had reached the stage of *erusin* — the initiation of marriage, equivalent to *kiddushin*, where the marriage has not yet been consummated — and the stage of *nisu'in*, where the marriage is fully completed. The *mishnah* categorically prohibits the *kohen gadol* from performing *yibbum* in both cases.

## Erusin Nisu'in Debate

### Aseh vs Lo Taseh

The *gemara* explains why the categorical ruling is understandable in the case of *nisu'in*: *bishlama min ha-nisu'in havi aseh velo ta'aseh* — in the case of *nisu'in*, we have both an *aseh* and a *lo ta'aseh* arrayed against the *mitzvah* of *yibbum*. The *mitzvah* of *yibbum* is itself an *aseh*, but the *kohen gadol* faces the *lo ta'aseh* of *almanah lo yikach* and the *aseh* of *betulah yikach* working against him. *Ve-ein aseh docheh lo ta'aseh va-aseh* — the general principle is that a positive commandment does not override the combination of a *lo ta'aseh* and an *aseh*. So in the case of *nisu'in*, the *kohen gadol* faces two prohibitions standing against one *mitzvah*, and the case for prohibiting *yibbum* is clear.

### Aseh Docheh Principle

The difficulty arises with *erusin*. At the stage of *erusin*, we presume the woman is still a *betulah* — she has not had relations with her husband. If we remove the *aseh* of *betulah yikach* from the equation, what remains is simply an *aseh* of *yibbum* against a *lo ta'aseh* of *almanah lo yikach*. And there is a well-established principle — derived from *psukim* in Yevamos — that *aseh docheh lo ta'aseh*, a positive commandment overrides a negative one. If so, the *mishnah* should have drawn a distinction: in the case of *erusin*, the *kohen gadol* should be permitted to perform *yibbum*, since the *mitzvah* of *yibbum* as an *aseh* would override the *lo ta'aseh* alone. Why does the *mishnah* state the prohibition categorically?

### Gzerah Biah Rishonah

The *gemara* answers: *gzeira biah rishonah atu biah shniyah*. There is in fact no biblical prohibition preventing the *kohen gadol* from performing *yibbum* with a *yevamah* from *erusin* — the prohibition is rabbinic. The *chachamim* were concerned that if the first act of *biah* — which is itself the *mitzvah* of *yibbum*, as the *psukim* make clear — were permitted, the couple would continue with a second *biah*. The second *biah* is not a *mitzvah*, and therefore the considerations of *betulah yikach* and *almanah lo yikach* reassert themselves in full force. At that point the *kohen gadol* faces both the *aseh* and the *lo ta'aseh* against him, and the *aseh* of *yibbum* cannot overcome that combination. In order to prevent the *kohen gadol* from arriving at that forbidden second *biah*, the *chachamim* issued a *gzeira* prohibiting even the first *biah*.

The *gemara* notes that a *baraita* supports this position: *im kadmu u-va'alu biah rishonah, kanu* — if the *kohen gadol* went ahead and violated the *gzeira* and had the first *biah*, the marriage takes effect (*kanu*), but they are thereafter prohibited from continuing with a second *biah* and the relationship must be dissolved.

## Funeral Procession

### Rav Meir Position

The *gemara* now turns to the *mishnah*'s discussion of how the *kohen gadol* conducts himself in relation to a funeral procession. The *mishnah* records a debate between Rav Meir and Rav Yehudah. Rav Meir holds that when the *kohen gadol* has a death in his family — *meis lo meis* — he does not follow the funeral procession directly. Instead, the two processionals alternate their visibility: *hen nichsin v'hu nigleh, hen niglin v'hu nichseh* — when the funeral party is hidden from view, he appears, and when they emerge, he withdraws. The two processionals thus remain perpetually separate. Nevertheless, he does accompany the procession up to the gate of the city: *v'yotzei imahen ad pesach shaar ha-ir*.

### Rav Yehudah Position

Rav Yehudah takes a stricter position: *eino yotzei min ha-Mikdash* — the *kohen gadol* may not leave the Temple precinct at all. The *gemara* quotes the *baraita* which presents the *pasuk* underlying Rav Yehudah's ruling: *u-min ha-Mikdash lo yeitzei* — "and from the Temple he shall not depart" (in *Parshas Emor*, in the laws of *aveilus* for the *kohen gadol*). The *baraita* itself, however, reads the *pasuk* in the manner of Rav Meir: *lo yeitze imahen* — he shall not go out *with them*, but *aval yotzei hu achareihem* — he may follow behind them. *Keitzad? Hen nichsin v'hu nigleh, hen niglin v'hu nichseh* — the same alternating arrangement described in the *mishnah*.

The *gemara* says *shapir ka'amar Rav Yehudah* — Rav Yehudah is at least quoting a *pasuk*, and the plain words of that *pasuk* seem to support his position. Rav Meir then offers his *reductio*: *amar lach Rav Meir, i hachi, levayto nami lo* — if Rav Yehudah's concern is that the *kohen gadol* not leave the Temple, then by the same logic he should be prohibited from returning to his home, lest he encounter *tumah* of a corpse along the way. Since we know he is obviously permitted to go home, that reading of the *pasuk* is untenable.

### Rav Meir Pasuk

How then does Rav Meir read *u-min ha-Mikdash lo yeitzei*? *Ela hachi ka'amar: min ha-Mikdash lo yetzei — mikedushato lo yetzei* — the *pasuk* means not that he may not physically leave the Temple building, but that he must not depart from his state of sanctity. The concern the *pasuk* addresses is *tum'at meit*. The *kohen gadol* is prohibited from contracting corpse *tumah*, and the *pasuk* is warning him to guard his sanctity in that regard. *V'keivan de-is lei hekera* — and since he has a *hekera*, a visible act of distinction that separates him from the funeral party, that is sufficient. When a person is publicly and visibly acting in a manner distinct from the procession, he will be reminded to remain on guard and *lo ati leminga* — he will not come to touch anything that is *tamei meis*.

### Yehudah Concern

Rav Yehudah's counter-position is that this *hekera* is inadequate: *agav merira dilma mikrei ve-ati venaga* — in the midst of grief, a person's judgment is diminished, and he may come to inadvertently touch something that causes *tum'at meit*. The visible separation of the two processionals is therefore not a sufficient safeguard. Rav Yehudah thus requires the *kohen gadol* to remain within the Temple entirely.

## Nichimat Avelim

### Temple Officials

A *baraita* now describes the physical arrangements for *nichum avelim* involving the *kohen gadol*. *Tanu rabanan: keshehu over ba-shura lenachem et acherim* — when the *kohen gadol* passes along the *shura*, the line of comfort extended to mourners, the ceremonial attendants accompanying him are: the *sgan* — the assistant to the *kohen gadol* — and the *mashuach she'avar*, both positioned to his right. Rashi explains that the *mashuach she'avar* is a former *kohen gadol* who was temporarily removed from service due to some *psul* — a disqualification — and who was replaced for the interim, but who retains his status and returns to his service when the *psul* passes. To the left of the *kohen gadol* stands the *rosh beis av* — the head of the mourning family — and then *vechol ha'am mismol*, all the people arrayed to the left.

### Kohen Comforts

The physical arrangement thus places the *kohen gadol* at the center, with the *sgan* and *mashuach she'avar* to his right and the mourning family and community to his left.

### Kohen Mourns

The *baraita* then turns to the reverse situation: *keshehu omed ba-shura u-misnachem me-acherim* — when the *kohen gadol* himself is the mourner and receives comfort from others. Here the *sgan* is to his right, and to his left stands the *rosh beis av* and all the people. A careful reader will notice that someone is conspicuously absent from this list: the *mashuach she'avar*, who was present in the previous scenario, does not appear when the *kohen gadol* is the mourner.

### Mashuach Concern

The *gemara* raises the question: *aval mashuach she'avar lo asi gabei?* — does the *mashuach she'avar* not come to visit the *kohen gadol* when he is in mourning? The answer given is: *chalsha date-ih, savar kachadi bi* — the *kohen gadol's* spirit would be weakened by his presence; he would think that the *mashuach she'avar* is inwardly pleased at his misfortune. The logic is that the *mashuach she'avar* was displaced from the position of *kohen gadol* due to his temporary *psul*, and during that interval he fills the role. If something befalls the current *kohen gadol*, the *mashuach she'avar* steps in. There is thus a structural tension between the two — not necessarily personal animosity, but an objective conflict of interests — and the *kohen gadol* in his grief might naturally suspect the *mashuach she'avar* of *schadenfreude*. To protect the *kohen gadol* from this weakening of spirit, the *chachamim* ruled that the *mashuach she'avar* does not attend the mourning house of the *kohen gadol*.

## Pappa's Inferences

### Sgan Mamona

Rav Pappa states: *amar Pappa, shma mina tlat* — from this *baraita* we derive three things. First: *hainu sgan hainu mamona* — the *sgan* is the same figure referred to elsewhere as the *mamona*. Another *baraita* uses the term *mamona* for this official, and Rav Pappa confirms that the two terms refer to the same person.

### Original Practice

Second: *avelim omdim ve-chol ha'am ovrim* — we learn from here that the original procedure for *nichum avelim* was for the mourners to stand and the community to pass by them.
