### Positioning Rules

Third: *avelim li-smol ha-menachamim hen omdim* — we learn that the mourners are positioned to the left of those providing comfort, and those providing comfort are the ones standing.

## Historical Development

### Two Families Dispute

A *baraita* now provides the historical context for why the procedure was changed. *Tanu rabbanan: be-rishona hayu avelim omdim ve-chol ha'am ovrim* — originally, the mourners stood and the community passed by. *Ve-hayu shtei mishpachot bi-Yerushalayim mitgarot zu ba-zu* — but there were two families in Jerusalem who would quarrel with one another. *Zot omeret ani overet techila, zot omeret ani overet techila* — each one would insist that she had the right to pass by the mourners first, each claiming priority of honor.

### Takana Reversal

To eliminate this conflict, the *chachamim* instituted a *takana*: *hitkinu she-yihiyu ha-am omdim ve-avelim ovrim* — they reversed the procedure, making the community stand and the mourners pass by. Even though this reversal is, in some sense, not the ideal arrangement for the procedures of *halachos aveilus*, the values of *kavod ha-briyos* and the prevention of dispute were deemed sufficient grounds to alter the practice. The awareness that *shalom* is built into the historical origins of this reversal is something worth carrying in mind.

## Rabbi Yosi Takanos

### Shura Restoration

Rabbi Bar Abba reports: *hechzir Rabbi Yosi et ha-davar le-yoshno be-Tzipori* — Rabbi Yosi restored the original procedure in Tzipori, instituting that the mourners would stand and the community would pass by, returning the *shura* to its original form.

### Child Safety Takana

Rabbi Yosi enacted a second *takana* in Tzipori: *shelo tehei isha mehalacḥet ba-shuk u-vnah achareha* — a woman should not walk through the marketplace with her child walking behind her. The reason: *mishum ma'aseh she-hayah* — because of an incident that occurred. Rashi supplies the details of that incident: kidnappers seized the child from behind his mother. When she turned around and did not see him, she began to cry out. One of the kidnappers approached her and said, come, I will show you where he is. When she followed him in, she was assaulted. The *takana* thus requires that the child walk close to the mother rather than trailing behind, to prevent the exploitation of that physical separation.

### Bathroom Yichud

Rabbi Yosi's third *takana* in Tzipori: *sheyihiyu nashim mesaprot be-veit ha-kisse mishum yichud* — women should speak aloud to one another while in the bathroom, on account of the laws of *yichud*. The underlying concern, as Rashi explains, is that a man might approach and, hearing no sound indicating who is present, enter and create a situation of *yichud*.

The Talmud cites the *mishnah*: *lo yityached adam im shtei nashim* — a man may not have *yichud* even with two women. So the remedy is for the two women to speak to each other, thereby alerting any approaching man that two women are present and thus removing the concern of *yichud*.

There is a notable analytical tension here concerning the time element of *yichud*. Ordinarily, *yichud* requires the elapse of a duration equivalent to *zman biah* — perhaps five or six minutes — not merely the existence of a situation. According to Rashi's framing, however, there is no mention of any such time threshold; the setting itself appears to constitute the problem. The Yad Ramah addresses this difficulty and takes a different approach: he understands the women's speaking aloud not as a *halachic* fix for *yichud* in the technical sense, but as a practical deterrent — the noise creates an impression that many people are present, and anyone with harmful intent will be dissuaded. For Rashi, the concern appears to be the *halachic* category of *yichud* itself; for the Yad Ramah, it functions more as an anti-assault protection.

## Shura Requirements

### Ten Person Minyan

Rav Menashya bar Shlub reports: Rav Yosef asked Rav Yoshiya Rabbah this question at the cemetery in Hutzal, and he was told: *ein shura pechuta me-asara bnei adam* — the *shura* of *nichum avelim* requires a minimum of ten people. *Ve-ein avelim min ha-minyan* — and the mourners themselves do not count toward the ten. This is intuitive: the entire purpose of the *shura* is for the community to gather around the mourners and comfort them. The mourners are the center of the ritual, not participants who constitute it.

### Flexible Arrangement

The same authority ruled: *bein she-avelim omdim ve-chol ha-am ovrim, bein she-avelim ovrim ve-chol ha-am omdim* — whether the mourners stand and the community passes by, or the mourners pass and the community stands, both arrangements are acceptable. The essential requirement is the gathering of ten, not the specific physical choreography.

## Comfort Formula

### Formula Question

The *mishnah* described what is said to the *kohen gadol* when he is in mourning, but did not address what the *kohen gadol* himself says when he performs *nichum avelim* for others. The *gemara* raises this question: *ki menachem hu achrinei, heicha amar lehu?* — when the *kohen gadol* comforts others, what does he say to them?

### Titnachwmu Formula

The *gemara* offers: *ta shema, ve-hu omer titnachamu* — come and hear, for he says *titnachamu*, "you shall be comforted." The *gemara* then pauses to clarify: *heichi dami?* — in what case is this said?

The *gemara* considers the possibility that *titnachamu* is said when others are comforting him and he responds. But this reading is rejected immediately: *nechasha ka-rami lehu?* — if he is the mourner and others are comforting him, and he responds with "you shall be comforted," that sounds like a curse. It would be as if a mourner, upon receiving comfort, turns to the comforters and wishes upon them that they too should need to be comforted. This cannot be the intended reading.

### Comforter Context

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ela ki menachem le-achrinei, amar lehu titnachamu* — rather, it is when the *kohen gadol* is himself the active comforter of others that he pronounces the phrase *titnachamu*. *Shma mina* — and from this we derive the formula.

One observation worth noting: the word *titnachamu* is in the plural. This is structurally analogous to the standard formula in use today — *ha-Makom yenachem etchem* — which is likewise phrased in the plural even when addressing a single mourner. The formula *titnachamu* similarly uses the plural regardless of the number of mourners present, suggesting that the conventional use of a *lashon rabbim* in the comforting formula may have deep roots in this very practice.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 19b

## Melech Lo Dan

### King's Status

We have been discussing the laws of royalty as presented in the *mishnah* and comparing them to the laws of the *kohen gadol*. The king occupies a higher status, and this affects numerous areas — including testimony and adjudication. One of the central rules is *melech lo dan v'lo danin oto*: the king neither judges nor is judged. In contemporary terms, one might compare this to diplomatic immunity on one side, and exemption from jury duty on the other.

This is, at first glance, somewhat surprising, given that *shefatenu malkenu* — judging the nation — is itself listed among the prerogatives of kingship in *mishpat hamelucha*. The resolution appears to be that the king does adjudicate in various senses, but he does not participate in the formal legal process of the *sanhedrin*. He may govern by royal decree, or he may legislate broad state policy, but he does not sit and adjudicate cases through the procedural framework of *din Torah* in the traditional manner. There may also be a distinction between *din* — the process of adjudicating a specific case under existing law — and *lishpot* in the broader sense of formulating national policy, though this remains somewhat speculative.

### Israel vs. David

*Amar Rav Yosef: lo shanu ela Malkhei Yisrael, aval Malkhei Beit David dan v'danin oto.* Rav Yosef teaches that this exemption applies only to the kings of Israel — that is, the northern kingdom — but not to the kings of the Davidic dynasty. This is counterintuitive. One would have expected the more traditionally legitimate dynasty, the line of David, to enjoy greater immunity, while the kings of Israel, who split off from that line, would face stricter standards. Yet the rule runs in precisely the opposite direction.

How do we know that kings of the House of David may judge and be judged? *De-ketiv: Beit David ko amar Hashem dinu la-boker mishpat* — "House of David, thus says God: judge righteous judgment in the morning." God explicitly addresses the Davidic kings with a command to adjudicate *mishpat*, which demonstrates that they are, in principle, participants in the legal process.

From this same *pasuk* one might ask: we can derive that the Davidic king judges — but how do we learn that he is also subject to being judged? The answer follows the same logic employed earlier in the *gemara*: *ve-ketiv hitchosheshu va-khoshu* — "Gather yourselves together, and gather." If one must impose discipline on others, one must first submit to it oneself. *Amar Reish Lakish: kshot atzmekha ve-ahar kshot acherim* — prepare yourself first, and only thereafter prepare others. The same standard applies reciprocally.

### Yannai Slave Case

This brings us to the *ma'aseh* that established the rule for the kings of Israel. The *gemara* explains: *mai ta'ama lo mishum ma'aseh shehayah* — the reason this exemption applies to *Malkhei Yisrael* is because of a specific incident. The incident involved the slave of King Yannai — *Yannai Malka*, who appears frequently throughout *Shas*, often alongside Shimon ben Shatach, who was, according to tradition, his brother-in-law — whose slave killed a person. Shimon ben Shatach addressed the *chachamim*: *tnu eineichem bo venidunenu* — "Turn your eyes to him and let us judge him."

They sent word to King Yannai: *avdach katal nafsha* — "Your servant has killed a person." They instructed him to send the slave to be judged. Then they went further and summoned the king himself: *ta ant nami lehacha* — "You must come here as well." The legal basis for this is the principle of *ve-hu'ad biv'alav*: *amrah Torah yavo ba'al ha-shor ve-ya'amod al shoro* — the Torah requires that the owner of an ox be present at the trial of a *shor haniskal*. The comparison of the slave to the ox is, admittedly, a discomfiting one, but the legal principle being invoked is that one whose property causes harm bears a legal stake in the proceedings and must be present. This concept has obvious parallels in the legal doctrine of *respondeat superior*, where an employer bears liability for harm caused by an employee acting in the course of his duties — though the precise contours of that parallel are a separate discussion.

### Shatach & Yannai

King Yannai came and took his seat. Shimon ben Shatach then addressed him directly: *Yannai HaMelech, amod al raglecha ve-ya'idu bach* — "King Yannai, stand on your feet, and let them testify against you." The legal basis for this demand is the *pasuk*: *ve-amdu shnei ha-anashim asher lahem ha-riv lifnei Hashem* — the litigants must stand before God. Shimon ben Shatach was careful to add: *ve-lo lifneinu atah omed ela lifnei mi she-amar vehayah ha-olam atah omed* — "It is not before us that you stand, but before the One who spoke and the world came into being." He is deflecting any suggestion of personal presumption: the king is not being required to stand out of deference to the judges themselves, but because God is the ultimate backdrop of all judicial proceedings.

King Yannai replied: *lo keshetomar atah ela kemah sheyomru chaveirecha* — "I will not act on your word alone; I want to hear what your colleagues say." Shimon ben Shatach turned to the right. The judges averted their eyes downward — *ve-chavshu pneihem bakarka* — burying their faces toward the ground. He turned to the left; the same silence. Shimon ben Shatach said to them: *ba'alei machshavot atem* — you are full of thoughts, but you do nothing. *Yavo Ba'al Hamachshavot*, the ultimate Reader of thoughts, which is God, *ve-yifra mikem* — and He will exact justice from you. And indeed, *miyad ba Gavriel ve-chavatan bakarka va-metu* — the angel Gabriel immediately came and struck them to the ground, and they died.

*Ve-otah sha'ah amru: melech lo dan ve-lo danin oto, lo meyid ve-lo meyidin oto.* It was at that hour that the Sages declared: a king neither judges nor is judged, neither testifies nor is testified against.

The reasoning is striking. One might have expected this rule to have been generated by something directly involving the king's own dignity or conduct. Instead, it arose from a case involving a slave — the king's property. And yet that makes the point even more powerfully: even an indirect connection to the king, even a matter involving his property, was sufficient to paralyze the court. When the king's presence intimidates the judges to the point where justice cannot be administered, the process itself becomes meaningless. Hence the sweeping ruling.

It is worth noting that even if one takes this *ma'aseh* as the origin of the rule, it applies only to *Malkhei Yisrael*, since that is the context in which it occurred. The *malkhei Beit David* remain bound by the *pasuk* requiring them to judge and be judged, and a *ma'aseh shehayah* is generally interpreted narrowly — it governs only the circumstances that produced it, especially where there is countervailing scriptural evidence.

---

## King vs. Scholar

### Judging Authority

Turning to the *Tosafot* on 19a, the third *Tosafot* raises a difficulty: if *Malkhei Beit David dan v'danin oto* — they can judge and be judged — how can this be, given that we established earlier that one does not seat a king in the *sanhedrin*? The basis for that prohibition is the *pasuk*: *lo ta'aneh al riv* — interpreted to mean that one does not contradict the *mufla shebebeit din*, the most senior authority on the court. If the king is present, the other judges may be reluctant to disagree with him, which undermines the integrity of the process.

The *Tosafot* resolves this by distinguishing between types of cases: *hacha mairi davka ledun dinei mamonot* — this refers specifically to monetary cases. In *dinei mamonot*, the stakes are lower, and judges feel less constrained about contradicting even a king. By contrast, in *dinei nefashot* — capital cases — the matter is different, and even standard procedure requires that deliberation begin with the most junior judge rather than the most senior, precisely to avoid undue influence. So the king's participation is permitted, but only in *dinei mamonot*.

### Standing Honor

The adjacent *Tosafot* takes up a conceptual comparison between the *talmid chacham* and the *melech* with respect to the obligation to stand. The premise of the question is: a *talmid chacham* is not required to stand before others in certain contexts; should it not follow, *kal vachomer*, that the king, who is even more exalted, is equally exempt? The *Tosafot* rejects this framing. The answer lies in the *pasuk* cited earlier: *som tasim alecha melech she'tehei eimato alecha* — you must appoint a king over you, and his *eimah* — his aura of authority — must rest upon you at all times. This obligation is constant and cannot be waived.

### Torah Acquisition

Why, then, can the *talmid chacham* be *mochel* on his *kavod* — waive the honor due him — while the king cannot?

The *Tosafot* offers a penetrating distinction: *ki kevodo ba lo mishum de'mitvat hamakom kach hu* — the king's honor is extrinsic. It does not originate in the king himself; it is conferred upon him by divine command. One inherits kingship; it descends through lineage, not through personal achievement. Since the *kavod* comes from God, the king cannot unilaterally *hafkiah mitvat hamakom* — annul a Divine obligation. It is not his to waive.

The *talmid chacham*, by contrast, possesses *torato dilei* — his Torah is his own. He has struggled, invested, and acquired it through personal effort. As the *pasuk* puts it: *ki im betorat Hashem cheftzo* — initially, Torah is described as God's Torah; *uvetorato yehgeh yomam valaylah* — but once one has truly acquired it, it is called his Torah. *Bitechilah nikret al shemo shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu, ulevasof nikret al shemo* — first it is called on God's name, and ultimately it is called on the name of the one who learned it. Since the *talmid chacham* earned this status through his own toil, he has standing to relinquish it as he sees fit — *shelo hi*, it is genuinely his. The king's honor, by contrast, belongs to God. This is, one might note, a striking conceptual asymmetry: earned accomplishment carries with it the prerogative of renunciation, while inherited or externally imposed status does not.

---

## Mitzvot Exemptions

### Chalitzah

The *mishnah* continues: *lo chalitzah ve-lo choltzin* — a king neither performs *chalitzah* nor does anyone perform *chalitzah* with him. *Chalitzah*, as is well known, involves a degree of public humiliation — the widow removes the *yavam*'s sandal and spits, if not directly at him then in his direction and before the court. This does not comport with the *kavod* of kingship.

A *beraita* is cited: *amar Rav Ashi, afilu man d'amar nasi shemachal al kevodo kevodo machul, melech shemachal al kevodo ein kevodo machul* — even according to the opinion that a *nasi* who waives his honor, his honor is considered waived, a king who waives his honor — his honor is not waived. The source is again *som tasim alecha melech she'eimato alecha*: the *pasuk* demands that the king's *eimah* rest upon the people at all times, which means his *kavod* must remain intact regardless of his own wishes.

One might object: even if this applies in ordinary situations, surely a *mitzvah* should override the concern for royal dignity — *mitzvah shani*. This argument does appear as a position in the *mishnah*. *Rabbi Yehudah omer: im ratzah lachlots o le'yabbem, l'zachur latov* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that if the king wishes to perform *chalitzah* or *yibbum*, he is to be remembered favorably for doing so. The *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda thus disagree on whether the concern for royal dignity overrides even a *mitzvah* obligation.

### King's Widow

Similarly, *ve-ein nos'im almenato* — one does not marry the widow of a king. This, too, is connected to the inviolability of royal *kavod*. In the ancient world, taking the wives of a predecessor was a well-understood symbol of usurpation. When Avshalom rebelled against David, his attempt to take David's wives was a declaration of sovereignty — those were fighting words, a coup in symbolic form.

*Rabbi Yehudah omer: nosei melech almenato shel melech* — Rabbi Yehuda permits one king to marry the widow of another king, not a commoner. His proof text: *ve-etnah lecha et beit adonecha ve-et neshei adonecha b'cheikecha* — God said to David, "I will give you the house of your master and the wives of your master into your lap." The word *neshei adonecha*, on a straightforward reading, refers to wives — *eshet cheiko*, the language of marital intimacy.

The response to Rabbi Yehuda is: *nashim eten lecha mibeit hamelech* — the word *nashim* here means women, not wives specifically. *U'mani hu? Merav u'Michal* — and who are these women? Merav and Michal, the daughters of Shaul. So the *pasuk* does not authorize marrying a king's widows at all; it refers to David being given Shaul's daughters in marriage. This reading, admittedly, is counterintuitive at first glance — *beit adonecha* and *neshei adonecha b'cheikecha* would naturally evoke a different meaning — but that is the *gemara*'s resolution. And once this *pasuk* is repurposed to refer to Merav and Michal, it opens the door to a broader discussion of David's marriages to Shaul's daughters.

---

## David & Saul's Daughters

### Merav & Michal

Shaul had two daughters: Merav, the elder, and Michal, the younger. The *gemara* now proceeds to untangle the complex and somewhat tortured history of David's relationship to both of them.

The immediate question is: if *nashim* in the *pasuk* refers to Merav and Michal, and David married both of them, how is that possible? They were sisters. The Torah prohibits marrying two sisters while both are alive — *shnei achayot b'chayeihen*.

Two answers are offered. *Amar lei: Michal achar mot Merav nasa* — the first answer is that David married Michal only after Merav had died, so the two marriages did not overlap. The second answer, offered by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, is that one of the betrothals was a *kiddushei ta'ut* — a mistaken or flawed betrothal — and therefore David was never fully married to one of them.

### Sisters Issue

The *gemara* pursues the question of which betrothal was the problematic one and what exactly rendered it defective. The proof that there was something wrong with the *kiddushin* to Merav is derived from a *pasuk*: *shene'emar tena et ishti et Michal asher erasti li beme'ah orlot Plishtim* — "Give me my wife Michal, whom I betrothed with a hundred foreskins of the Philistines." David says *ishti et Michal* — my wife, Michal. *Amar Pappa: Michal ishti, lo Merav ishti* — he is specifying Michal as his wife, thereby implying that Merav is not his wife. This supports the position that the betrothal to Merav was invalid.

### Goliath Prize

What was the background of the betrothal to Merav? The *pasuk* records: *vehayah ha'ish asher yakenu ya'asrenu hamelech osher gadol* — whoever defeated Goliath would be greatly enriched by the king, and the king would give his daughter to that man as a wife. David killed Goliath. So far so good — the betrothal should have been valid.

The problem is the mechanics of the *kiddushin*. *Kiddushin* requires *kesef, shtar*, or *biah* — money, a document, or cohabitation. In this case, David proposed to use the *osher gadol* — the prize money that Shaul owed him — as the *kesef kiddushin*. But he never actually received the money. The money remained a debt owed to him. *Amar lo: milve yesh li gavach, hamekadesh b'milve eina mekudeshet* — one who betroths a woman with a loan owed to him has not effected a valid *kiddushin*. Since the money never passed through David's hands, it could not serve as the consideration for the betrothal.

Shaul, in the meantime, gave Merav to someone else entirely. *Dichtiv: vayehi be'et tet et Merav bat Shaul leDavid vehia nitna l'Adriel haMechollati l'isha* — Merav was given to Adriel the Mecholathite as a wife.

### Foreskins Value

The story then continues. Shaul made a second offer: if you want Michal, go and bring me a hundred foreskins of the Philistines — *zil aiti li me'ah orlot Plishtim*. David went and brought them. Now, David had two things to offer for the *kiddushin*: the *milveh* — the outstanding debt from the Goliath affair — and the *pruta*, meaning the foreskins themselves.

*Amar lei: milve upruta it lach gavai* — "You have a loan and a *pruta* owed by me." The question becomes: what was David's *da'at* — his intent — when he offered these two items? *Shavyah milve upruta da'ateih amilve* — if he had in mind primarily the *milveh*, then the *kiddushin* still fails, since the *milveh* cannot serve as *kesef kiddushin*. *Milve upruta da'ateih apruta* — but if his intent was focused on the *pruta*, i.e., the foreskins themselves, then the *kiddushin* succeeds, provided the foreskins have the minimum value of a *pruta*.

And here is where Shaul and David disagreed. Shaul held *lo chazi l'midei* — the foreskins are worthless, not even worth a *pruta*. What use does anyone have for two hundred foreskins? David held *chazu lei, chavi l'shunrei* — they are worth something; you can feed them to household animals, which saves you the cost of their feed. Meat is meat.

This is a relevant conceptual point for *kiddushin* more broadly. The reason the practice under the *chuppah* is to use a plain gold ring rather than an elaborate gemstone is related to this concern. If a bride believes the ring is worth ten thousand dollars and it is actually a cheap imitation worth far less, questions arise about whether her consent was given on accurate information, which could affect the validity of the *kiddushin*. By using a simple ring of known minimal value and having witnesses confirm it is worth at least a *pruta*, these concerns are preempted from the outset.

### Merav Bore

We now return to Rabbi Yose, who holds the first position: that David actually married both Merav and Michal sequentially — Merav first, and after her death, Michal. According to this view, there is no *kiddushei ta'ut*; the betrothal to Merav was valid. But then what does David mean when he says *et ishti et Michal* — singling out Michal as his wife? Rabbi Yose would say he is simply being specific, as Yaakov said *Rachel bitcha haktana* — specifying which daughter he wanted.

*Rabbi Yose l'ta'amei: d'tanya, Rabbi Yose haya doresh mikra'ot m'rubavin* — Rabbi Yose was known for interpreting verses that appear mixed or interchanged, reading them as internally rearranged in order to yield a coherent meaning.

### Proof Method

The *gemara* cites the verse: *vayikach hamelech et shnei bnei Ritzpah bat Ayah asher yalda l'Shaul et Armoni v'et Mephiboshet, ve-et chameshet bnei Michal asher yalda l'Adriel haMechollati* — the five sons of Michal that she bore to Adriel the Mecholathite. This is immediately problematic. Merav was given to Adriel, not Michal. Michal was given to Paltiel ben Laish. The verse has apparently transposed the daughters.

The *gemara* uses this transposition as a *hekesh* — a textual analogy: *makish kiddushei Merav l'Adriel l'kiddushei Michal l'Palti* — just as Michal's marriage to Palti was *ba'aveirah*, a transgression (since she was really David's wife), so too Merav's marriage to Adriel was *ba'aveirah* (since she too was really David's wife). The point of the comparison is not to excuse either marriage, but to demonstrate through the juxtaposition that David's betrothal to both women was valid — which in turn establishes that he was married to both, and consequently that one must have died before he married the other.

### Korcha's View

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha asks his own question on this *pasuk*: *ve-chi Michal yalda? Halo Merav yalda* — did Michal give birth to these children? Surely it was Merav who bore them, not Michal! Michal, as the text elsewhere records, had no children. The resolution is: *Merav yaldah, Michal giddelah, ve-kach nikreu al shemah* — Merav bore these children, and Michal raised them as an orphaned aunt after Merav died, and therefore they are called after Michal's name.

This brings the *gemara* to a broader principle.

---

## Raising Orphans

### Raising Teaches

*Lelamedcha: shekol hamigadel yatom betoch beito, ma'aleh alav hakatuv ke'ilu yelado* — this teaches us that whoever raises an orphan in his home, the Torah accounts it to him as if he had given birth to that child. Michal's raising of Merav's children is the proof text for this principle, and the *gemara* proceeds to elaborate upon it through a series of expansions.

### Ruth Naomi

Rabbi Chanina derives the same principle from the Book of Ruth. *Vatikerena lo hashenot shem lemor: yulad ben le-Naomi* — the neighbors declared, "A son has been born to Naomi." But the son was born to Ruth, not to Naomi. So why is he called Naomi's son? *Ruth yalda, Naomi gidla, u'lefikach nikra al shemah* — Ruth bore him, Naomi raised him, and therefore he was called after Naomi's name.

One might wonder what exactly Ruth's role was in all this, since she was very much alive. Perhaps there is something to the suggestion that Ruth's status as a *Moaviyah* made the community reluctant to credit her publicly, and so the child was attributed to Naomi, the Israelite grandmother. But in any case, the principle holds: the one who raises a child receives the credit, even when the birth mother is still living.

### Bitya Moses

Rabbi Yochanan draws the same principle from a verse in Chronicles. *Ve-ishto ha'Yehudiyah yalda et Yered avi Gedor* — his Jewish wife bore Yered, and the text continues listing names that the *gemara* identifies as epithets for Moshe. The *Yehudiyah* is identified as Bitya bat Paroh.

The chronology here is dizzying. Calev ben Yefuneh, who married Bitya bat Paroh, was forty years old among the *meraglim* and was sustained for another forty years in the wilderness — as the *pasuk* records, *kechochi az kachochi ata*, his strength was undiminished. Moshe was eighty years old when he stood before Paroh — *Moshe ben shemonim shanah ve-Aharon ben shalosh u'shemonim shanah b'daberam el Paroh*. So Moshe was twice Calev's age, and yet Bitya bat Paroh, who had drawn Moshe from the Nile when he was an infant, was, on this reading, eventually married to someone far younger than Moshe himself. The timelines do not resolve easily.

Regardless: *Yocheved yalda, Bitya gidla, u'lefikach nikra al shemah* — Yocheved bore Moshe, Bitya raised him, and therefore Moshe is reckoned as her child. This is the principle at work. Note that in this case, Moshe was not an orphan — his birth mother was alive and was even, unknowingly, hired as his nursemaid. The principle of raising conferring parenthood applies even when the birth parent is living.

### Support & Teach

The principle now expands beyond literal orphan-raising. Rabbi Elazar cites the verse: *ga'alta bizroa amecha b'nei Yaakov v'Yosef sela* — "You redeemed with Your arm Your people, the children of Yaakov and Yosef." Why does Yosef appear alongside Yaakov? *V'chi Yosef yalad? Ela Yaakov yalad v'Yosef kilkel* — Yosef did not father these people; Yaakov did. But Yosef *kilkel* — he sustained and supported the entire family when they descended to Egypt. *Lefikach nikru al shmo* — therefore they are called after his name as well.

The principle has now extended beyond raising to merely providing for someone's sustenance. Supporting a person financially — *kilkul* — is sufficient to render one, in a sense, their parent.

### Torah Teaching

*Amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yonatan: kol hamelamed ben chavero Torah, ma'aleh alav hakatuv ke'ilu yelado* — whoever teaches his fellow's son Torah, the verse accounts it to him as if he gave birth to him. The source: *ve-eleh toldot Aharon u'Moshe* — "These are the generations of Aharon and Moshe." But then the text continues only with the names of Aharon's sons, making no mention of Moshe's children. The answer: *Aharon yalad u'Moshe limed, lefikach nikru al shmo* — Aharon fathered them biologically, but Moshe taught them Torah, and therefore they are also called Moshe's generations.

### Joseph & Jacob

The expansion continues with one further example. *Ve-chen hu omer: asher padah Avraham* — "who redeemed Avraham." The verse associates Yaakov with having redeemed Avraham. But in what sense did Yaakov redeem Avraham? *Amar Rav Yehuda: she'pado m'tza'ar gidul banim* — Yaakov freed Avraham from the anguish of childbearing. God had promised Avraham that he would father multitudes. From Sarah, he had only one child. Yaakov, by producing the twelve *shevatim*, fulfilled that promise in Avraham's stead — he bore the generational burden that Avraham could not complete on his own. In this sense, Yaakov redeemed Avraham from the unmet obligation. Therefore, *lo ata yeivosh Yaakov me'aviv, ve-lo ata panav yeichavaru me'avi aviv* — Yaakov will not be ashamed before his father Yitzchak, nor before his grandfather Avraham — because he fulfilled what they could not.

---

## Palti Restraint

### Name Meaning

The *gemara* now returns to Palti ben Laish, the man to whom Shaul gave Michal after taking her from David. *Kesiv Palti u'chesiv Paltiel* — the text alternates between the names *Palti* and *Paltiel*. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan: lamah nikra shemo Paltiel? She'pelato E-l* — God saved him, *palat*, from an *aveirah*. The *aveirah* in question was the prohibition against sleeping with a married woman — and according to the view that David's *kiddushin* to Michal was valid, she remained his wife even while living in Palti's house.

### Sword Between

How was Palti saved? *Mah asah? Na'atz cherev beino l'veinah* — he took a sword and drove it into the ground between himself and Michal. *Amar: kol ha'osek b'davar zeh yidaker b'cherev zeh* — he declared: whoever reaches toward the other for the purpose of relations will be pierced by this sword. Through this means, they coexisted in the same household without transgressing.

The verse then records: *vayeilech itah ishah bacho* — her husband walked after her weeping. One might ask: if they never had relations, in what sense was he her *ish*, her husband? The answer is *ishta d'lah hi* — he regarded her as his wife in his heart. And why was he weeping? *Al mitzvah d'azla mineih* — he was crying over the *mitzvah* that was departing from him. He had sustained himself through an extraordinary test of restraint, and as she was taken from him, he mourned not the loss of a woman, but the loss of the ongoing opportunity to perform this *mitzvah* of self-discipline. *Vayeilech achareiah ad Bachurim* — he followed her until *Bachurim*, and the *gemara* notes: *Bachurim* can be read as suggesting *bachurim* — young people — *she'na'asu sheneihem k'vachurim shelo ta'amu ta'am bi'ah* — for both of them had remained like youths who had never experienced relations with one another.

### Trial Compare

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan: tokpo shel Yosef anvetanuto shel Boaz, v'tokpo shel Boaz anvetanuto shel Palti ben Laish* — the great trial that Yosef withstood was easy by comparison to what Boaz overcame, and what Boaz overcame was easy by comparison to the ongoing trial of Palti ben Laish.

How so? Yosef resisted the advances of his master's wife — a married woman, a single incident, a moment of acute temptation. Boaz faced a different trial. The verse in Ruth records: *vayehi bachatzot halaylah vayecherad ha'ish vayilafes* — in the middle of the night, Boaz trembled and recoiled. *Mai vayilafes? Amar Rava: she'na'asa b'saro k'roshei lefasos* — his flesh reacted involuntarily. But Boaz's trial involved a single woman — Ruth — and a single night — and she was not married. That was Boaz's trial.

Palti ben Laish, by contrast, lived with Michal night after night, year after year. She was, on this account, a married woman — another man's wife. He overcame this trial not once, but continuously, over an extended period of time. That, the *gemara* tells us, was a greater *nisayon* than anything Yosef or Boaz faced.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 20

## Proverbs 31:29 Aggada

### Yosef, Boaz, Palti

The daf opens in the midst of an extended *aggadic* passage that grew out of a *mishnah* concerning a king's marriages. The discussion turned to David, Saul, and Michal — and specifically to Palti ben Laish, to whom Michal had been given in marriage until she was returned to her rightful husband David. Rabbi Yochanan now draws on that narrative to expound the verse in Proverbs 31: *rabos banos asu chayil v'at alis al kulanu* — "Many daughters have done valor, but you have surpassed them all."

*Rabos banos asu chayil*, Rabbi Yochanan teaches, refers to Yosef and Boaz, who withstood sexual temptation. As the *gemara* discussed on the preceding daf, however, their restraint was qualified in certain respects: Boaz resisted temptation for only a single night, and the woman in question was unmarried; Yosef faced a married woman and a more sustained situation, yet she was not actually lying beside him. *V'at alis al kulanu* — "but you have surpassed them all" — this is Palti ben Laish, who lived as Michal's husband for years and, according to the *gemara*, never engaged in marital relations with her throughout that entire time.

It is striking that a verse explicitly praising women is here applied entirely to men and their resistance of temptation. The question of Michal's own restraint — and her own moral achievement — is conspicuously absent from the *gemara*'s discussion.

### Charm, Vanity, Fear

Rabbi Yochanan offers a second interpretation using the verse *sheker hachen v'hevel hayofi, yiras Hashem hi tishallal* — "False is charm and vain is beauty; a woman who fears God, she shall be praised." *Sheker hachen* — false charm — is Yosef; the quality was ultimately superficial in the sense that the woman he refused was married and not physically beside him. *V'hevel hayofi* — vain beauty — is Boaz; what he did appears admirable but lacks the ultimate depth of achievement. *Yiras Hashem hi tishallal* — the one who truly fears God — is Palti ben Laish. Once again, a verse framed around a woman's virtue is read as a portrait of male restraint, and once again the asymmetry in the *gemara*'s attention is remarkable.

### Generations Comparison

The *gemara* then offers an alternative interpretation (*davar acher*) of the same verse, now shifting from personal moral restraint to the domain of *Torah* study. *Sheker hachen* refers to the generation of Moshe, and *v'hevel hayofi* to the generation of Yehoshua — both represent great eras that nonetheless, for all their outward glory, do not represent the ultimate achievement in *Torah* learning. *Yiras Hashem hi tishallal* refers to the generation of Chizkiya, during which, the *gemara* reports elsewhere, a search from Dan to Be'er Sheva turned up no *amei ha'aretz* whatsoever — even children possessed remarkable Torah knowledge. We tend to romanticize the generations of Moshe and Yehoshua, but the *gemara* insists that the genuine flowering of *talmud Torah* came under Chizkiya.

### Yehuda bar Ilai Era

A second *davar acher* goes further still. Now the generations of Moshe and Yehoshua together are classified as *sheker hachen*, and the generation of Chizkiya itself is demoted to *hevel hayofi*. The true *yiras Hashem hi tishallal* is the generation of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai. About him it was said: six students would cover themselves with a single *tallis* — they were so impoverished they could not afford separate blankets — and yet they would engage in Torah study.

### Mesirut Nefesh Analysis

This raises an important conceptual distinction. The praise of Chizkiya's generation centered on the breadth and depth of Torah knowledge — its penetration into every corner of the population. The praise of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's generation, by contrast, centers on *mesiras nefesh*, the self-sacrifice for *Torah* learning demonstrated through dire poverty. These are two different criteria of greatness, and the *gemara* seems to apply them differently to different generations. Chizkiya's era remains the paradigm of Torah knowledge as a mass achievement; Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's era exemplifies what it means to sacrifice everything for learning.

The lecturer notes that in our own time, the *mesiras nefesh* of that kind of grinding poverty is largely absent. Yet in terms of the sheer number of Jews engaged in *Torah* study and the number of *yeshivos* in existence, the present era may rival or exceed every historical period — with the possible exception of the generation of Chizkiya.

---

## Royal Mourning Laws

### King Confinement

The *gemara* turns to the next *mishnah*, which addresses the laws of mourning as they apply to a king. Unlike the *kohen gadol*, for whom the relevant law derives from a *pasuk* — *min hamikdash lo yeitzei* — the restrictions on a king are rooted in the practical need to protect and affirm his royal status as a public figure. Accordingly, if an immediate relative of the king dies, he does not leave the entrance of his palace. Even during mourning, his public persona must remain intact; private grief does not transform the king into a private individual.

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: if the king wishes to accompany the funeral bier, he may do so, since we find that David followed the bier of Avner. Avner had been the general under Saul who had come over to David's side, before being treacherously killed by Yoav ben Tzeruya. The verse states: *vehamelech David holeich achar hamita* — King David walked after the bier.

### David & Avner Case

The *chachamim* respond: that was a special exception — *lo hayah hadavar ela lefayeis et ha'am*. David needed to appease the people, who suspected him of complicity in Avner's death. Avner had been on the verge of bringing all of Israel over to support David's realm during the interregnum under Ishboshet, Saul's son. His murder therefore threatened David's entire ascension to the kingship, and public suspicion was a genuine political danger. The action was therefore exceptional and cannot serve as a normative proof. This dynamic parallels the earlier *mishnah*, where Rabbi Yehuda similarly cited a verse only to receive the reply that it was a unique circumstance.

### Consolation Meal

The *mishnah* also addresses the *seudat havra'ah* — the consolation meal that mourners are fed by those who come to comfort them. When the king is fed this meal, all of the people recline on the ground while he reclines on the *dargash*. Just as in the case of the *kohen gadol* a *safsal* (a low bench) was used, so too the king occupies a position that is closer to the ground than normal seating but not directly on the floor as the other mourners are. Even in his grief, the distinction of his rank is preserved.

### Procession Order

A *baraita* addresses the arrangement of men and women in funeral processions. Where the local custom was for women to follow behind the coffin and men to walk in front, that custom is followed; where the custom was the reverse, that is followed. Rabbi Yehuda, however, maintains that women should always walk in front of the coffin — and once again he derives this from David's following of Avner's bier, reasoning that since David walked behind, the women must have been in front.

Once again the *chachamim* respond: *lo hayah hadavar ela lefayeis et ha'am* — this was an exception for the specific purpose of appeasing the people, and no general rule may be derived from it.

### David's Strategy

The *gemara* explains more precisely how David succeeded in this appeasement. He did not remain with one group of mourners in the procession but moved back and forth — leaving the men to go among the women, then returning from the women to go among the men — so that everyone could see that he was personally and conspicuously mourning for Avner. Because he was constantly shifting between groups, no conclusion can be drawn about which group — men or women — was positioned in front or behind. The verse confirms his success: *vayedu kol ha'am vechol Yisrael ki lo hayta mehamelech lehamis et Avner* — all the people and all Israel knew that it had not come from the king to put Avner to death.

The *gemara* also notes that the concern regarding the placement of women in front of men — specifically, whether men might gaze at women during the procession — does not appear to have been treated as decisive here. The accepted practice, wherever it exists, is followed in either direction.

### Havra'ah Wordplay

Rava expounds a further dimension of the episode. The verse states: *vayavo kol ha'am lehavrot et David* — all the people came to give David the *havra'ah*, the consolation meal. The word *lehavrot* as written in the text is similar to the word *lehachrot*, to cut down or destroy. Rava reads this as a *ketiv-keri* nuance: *techilah lehachroto* — initially the people came with the intent to destroy him, suspecting him of having ordered Avner's death — *ul'vasof lehavroto* — but in the end, after witnessing his mourning, they came to give him the proper consolation of *havra'ah*. The word carries both meanings simultaneously, capturing the transformation that David's public behavior achieved.

---

## Avner's Punishment

### Avner's Protest

The *gemara* asks: *mipnei mah ne'enash Avner?* — why was Avner punished? The presumption is that even a treacherous death implies some divine accounting. The answer given: *mipnei shehayah lo limchot beShaul velo michah* — because he had the ability and standing to protest Saul's massacre of Nov, the city of Kohanim, and he did not speak up. The *gemara* draws on the broader principle, stated in multiple places, that a bystander who has the power to protest and remains silent bears responsibility.

Rav Yitzchak disputes this: Avner did protest, but *lo ne'enah* — he was not heeded. His protest was ineffective, and therefore if he was punished, the reason must lie elsewhere.

### David's Eulogy

Both opinions derive their position from the same verse — David's eulogy over Avner: *hayakemot naval yamut Avner, yadecha lo asurot veraglecha lo linchoshtayim hugashu* — "Should Avner die the death of a degenerate? Your hands were not bound, your feet were not put in chains."

According to the view that Avner did *not* protest, David's words are not an expression of astonishment at injustice, but rather an indictment: your hands were not bound, your feet were not chained — no one was stopping you — *mai ta'ama lo machita?* — why then did you not protest? And therefore *kinfol lifnei bnei avla nafaltah* — you fell as one falls at the hands of the treacherous — meaning this is why it happened to you.

### Injustice Reading

According to the view that Avner *did* protest, the same words are read differently. David is *itmuhei mitamei* — genuinely astounded at the injustice. Your hands were free, your feet were unbound — you acted as you should have acted, you lived a righteous life — *mai ta'ama kinfol lifnei bnei avla nafaltah?* — how could it be that you suffered such a disgraceful death? The eulogy, on this reading, is an authentic lament over incomprehensible injustice.

### Delayed Kingship

If Avner did protest Saul, the *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama ye'anesh* — why was he then punished at all? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers: *sheshaha malchus beis David shtei shanim u'mechtza* — because Avner delayed the establishment of the house of David by two and a half years, during which he supported Mephibosheth rather than throwing his considerable influence behind David's kingship. Rashi and Tosafot discuss the precise chronology, noting that seven and a half years elapsed between Saul's death and David's accession over all Israel, and debating how the two and a half years of Mephibosheth's rule fit into that period. But whichever the exact reconstruction, the core point is clear: Avner supported the wrong claimant when he should have supported David.

---

## Dargash Definition

### Luck Bed

Having established that the king reclines on the *dargash* while the other mourners sit on the floor, the *gemara* now asks: *mai dargash?* — what exactly is a *dargash*? Ulla answers: *arsa degada* — a bed of luck. As Rashi explains, *gad* here relates to the concept found in Tanakh of setting a table for *gad*, an idol or symbol of fortune. The *dargash*, on this reading, was a decorative bed placed in the home for good fortune — similar in function to a symbolic ceremonial object — on which no one would normally sit. Its low, decorative character would make it appropriate for a mourner.

### Functionality Challenge

The *rabbanan* immediately challenge Ulla: *mi ika midei d'ad ha'idna lo oshvinei v'hashta moshvinei leh?* — is it sensible that something which has never been sat upon, existing purely as decoration, should now suddenly be appropriate to sit on? What is the significance of placing a mourner on an object that is not functionally a seat?

### Mourning Context

Rava deflects the challenge: *dilma midei d'havah achila ushtiya* — perhaps it is no different from the general inversion that the *seudas havra'ah* represents. Normally, the mourner feeds himself; now others feed him. The entire framework of mourning involves doing things differently, creating a *topsy-turvy* quality that reflects the disrupted world of *aveilus*. That something is normally not used as a seat is therefore not itself a sufficient reason to say it cannot serve as a mourner's seat.

### Bed Overturning

Rava then redirects the challenge more precisely. The real difficulty with Ulla's definition is posed by a *baraita*: *dargash eino tzarich lichfoso ela zokfo* — for a *dargash*, one does not need to overturn it as one overturns beds during mourning; instead, one stands it on its head, tilting it ninety degrees. If the *dargash* were simply a decorative non-functional bed, why would this distinction apply?

The general rule from the *baraita* is that the overturning of beds extends to all beds in the house: *hachofeh mitato lo mitato bilvad hu kofeh ela kol mittes sheyesh b'soch beiso kofeh*. Why would this decorative bed be exempt from standard overturning?

The *gemara* answers: this poses no difficulty. Just as a bed designated for storing *keilim* — utensils — rather than for sleeping is not subject to the overturning requirement (*im hayta myuchedes l'keilim eino tzarich lichfoso*), so too a decorative bed that is not made for sleeping would be similarly exempt. The *dargash* is therefore tilted rather than fully overturned: still an expression of *kefiyat hamita*, but in a modified form.

### Strap Release

Nevertheless, the *gemara* identifies a deeper difficulty. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules: *dargash matir karbitin v'hu nofel me'elav* — for a *dargash*, one simply releases the straps and it falls of its own accord. This implies that the *dargash* is a bed or chair whose surface is held up by straps, and that releasing those straps constitutes the required mourning practice in lieu of full overturning. But if the *dargash* were simply a decorative non-functional bed, *karbiti mi ika* — would such a bed even have straps in the first place? The structural feature that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel describes is inconsistent with a purely decorative object.

### Leather Bed

The *gemara* therefore turns to a different definition entirely. When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported in the name of one of the rabbis — Rav Tachlifa, who was frequently present in the marketplace of the tanners (*shuka d'gilda'ei*) and therefore had direct knowledge of such objects — that a *dargash* is an *arsa d'tzala*, a leather bed. Specifically, it is a bed frame onto which a leather hide is strapped as the sleeping surface. This explains the straps mentioned by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rashi explains why such a bed would be tilted rather than fully overturned: its frame has no posts extending above the height of the leather surface, so if it were flipped upside down, the leather would be pressed against the ground and ruined. One therefore tilts it onto its side rather than inverting it completely.

### Strap Placement

Rabbi Yirmiyah, citing Rabbi Yochanan, adds a further structural distinction: *dargash sirugo mitocho* — the straps of a *dargash* pass through holes located within the interior of the frame or legs, with the straps threaded through and knotted from the inside. A regular *mitah*, by contrast, was strung with ropes that went over the top of the frame — *siruga me'al gabah* — crisscrossing on the exterior surface to form the lattice on which a mattress or hay would be placed.

### Wood Finishing

The *gemara* raises a challenge from a *mishnah* concerning the point at which wooden utensils become susceptible to *tumah*. It teaches that a bed or *arisa* becomes complete — *gmar melacha* — when it is smoothed with fish skin (the ancient equivalent of sandpaper). But if a regular *mitah* has its ropes wrapped around the exterior of the frame, the frame itself would be entirely hidden and there would be no reason to polish it to a smooth finish. The visible wood would never be exposed.

### Both Have Holes

The *gemara* resolves the challenge simply: both the *dargash* and the regular *mitah* have their straps or ropes threaded through interior holes. The earlier distinction — that one goes through internal holes and the other over the exterior surface — cannot be the point of differentiation between them.

### Rings vs Holes

The actual structural distinction, the *gemara* concludes, lies elsewhere. In a regular *mitah*, the ropes go *in and out* through simple holes bored in the frame — one might imagine a pattern not unlike the eyelets in a shoe, with a rope passing back and forth through holes to create the crisscross surface. In a *dargash*, by contrast, the straps are attached to *afkasa* — external rings fixed to the frame — through which the leather straps are tied. The *dargash* uses rings; the regular bed uses holes. This accounts for why Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel can describe the release of straps as the operative mourning action: the rings holding the leather surface can be untied, causing it to fall.

### Halacha Ruling

Rav Yaakov, in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, rules: the *halacha* follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — for a *dargash*, one simply releases the straps rather than overturning the bed.

### High Posts

Rav Yitzchak bar Ami adds a related ruling: if a regular bed has tall posts (*naklitei*) projecting upward from the headboard or footboard — the type used to support a canopy or draped sheet — then fully overturning the bed would still leave it elevated far off the ground, defeating the purpose of *kefiyat hamita*. In such a case, one does as with the *dargash*: one tilts it ninety degrees onto its side, standing it on its head, and that is sufficient.

---

## Royal Prerogatives

### War & Roads

The *gemara* moves to the next *mishnah*, which outlines further royal prerogatives. The king may take the nation out for an *optional war* — *milchemes hareshut*, a war of expansion beyond the conquest of the Land — but only with the authorization of the *beit din* of 71. A war of self-defense or the original conquest of Eretz Yisrael does not require this; it is specifically the discretionary expansion of territory that demands the consent of the *sanhedrin* as representative of the people.

The king may also break through fences and property in order to make a path, and no one may prevent him — *v'ein mamchin b'yado*. Rashi reads this not as the king passing through on a royal journey, but specifically as securing access to his own fields. The *derech hamelech* — the king's road — has no fixed minimum width; it may be as wide as necessity requires.

Additionally, when the people take spoils in war, the king receives the first choice of the plunder — *notel chelek b'rosh*. Rashi adds that the king also receives the finest portion and takes half of the total spoils.

### Seventy-One

The *gemara* notes that the requirement of 71 for optional war was already taught in the very first *mishnah* of this *masechet*. It answers: since this chapter is devoted to a comprehensive treatment of the laws of *kohen gadol* and *melech*, the laws of the king are being gathered and restated in full, including those already mentioned elsewhere. The repetition is purposeful — it belongs to the complete picture of royal law being assembled here.

---

## Royal Powers Debate

### Powers Permitted

The *gemara* now enters one of its most famous debates regarding the nature of monarchy. Rav Yehuda, in the name of Shmuel, states: *kol ha'amur b'parshas melech melech mutar bo* — everything enumerated in the *parshas hamelech* in 1 Samuel 8 — Shmuel's warning to the people about what a king will do to them — those are actual, legitimate royal powers. When Shmuel told the people that the king would conscript their sons, seize their daughters, appropriate their fields, and exact tithes of their produce, this was not a warning of abuse but a description of rights genuinely belonging to the king.

### Fear, Not Rights

Rav disagrees fundamentally: *lo ne'emra parsha zu ela l'ayem aleihem* — this entire passage was stated only to instill fear, not to grant the king actual authority to do these things. As Rashi explains Rav's position: the purpose was that *eimas melachim* — the awe of kingship — should rest upon the people, but the king does not in fact possess those powers as legal entitlements. If one were to call his bluff, there would be no *halachic* basis for the king to enforce them.

A careful reading of the passage in Shmuel itself makes it difficult to sustain Rav's interpretation in its straightforward sense: after Shmuel delivers the entire warning, the text records explicitly that the people refused to listen — *vayema'anu ha'am lishmo'a b'kol Shmuel* — and insisted they wanted a king anyway. The pedagogical force of the passage seems to have been aimed at changing their minds, not at establishing the *eimas* of an already-existing monarchy. Nevertheless, Rashi follows Rav's formulation: the passage was stated so that when they would eventually have a king, the proper fear of royal authority would be in place.

### R. Yose & R. Yehuda

The *gemara* identifies this as a *tannaitic* dispute. Rabbi Yose holds that everything stated in *parshas hamelech* the king is actually permitted to do — corresponding to the position of Shmuel. Rabbi Yehuda maintains that the *parsha* was stated only in order to instill fear — *som tasim alecha melech shetehei eimaso alecha*, "you shall set upon yourself a king that his fear shall be upon you" — and this is where Rashi locates the textual basis for that reading. On Rabbi Yehuda's view, the purpose of *parshas hamelech* is to ensure that the institution of kingship carries real psychological weight and authority, not to enumerate actual legal powers.

It should be noted that it is this same Shmuel who established the principle of *dina d'malchuta dina* — the law of the [ruling] kingdom is the law — and some have sought to connect that principle to Shmuel's position here recognizing the breadth of royal authority.

### Three Commandments

The *gemara* cites an additional ruling associated with Rabbi Yehuda. He teaches: *sheloshah mitzvos nitztavu Yisrael bichnisatan la'aretz* — three commandments were given to Israel upon their entry into the Land, and these are collective national obligations tied to the establishment of sovereignty and the ordering of national life. The first is *leha'amid lahem melech* — to establish a king. The second is *ulimchot zaro shel Amalek* — to eradicate the seed of Amalek. The third is *velivnot lahem beit habechirah* — to build the Temple. These three form a progression: establish the governing authority, eliminate the archetypal enemy, and erect the center of divine worship.

### Response to Complaint

Rabbi Nehorai takes a sharply different position. He maintains that *parshas hamelech* was stated only *keneged taro'umtan* — in response to their complaint — as indicated by the verse *ve'amarta asimah alai melech*, "and you will say, let me set a king upon myself." For Rabbi Nehorai, appointing a king is not a *mitzvah* at all; it is a concession to popular demand. Rashi makes explicit that on this view even *som tasim alecha melech* in the Torah is not a commandment but rather a description of what will happen when the people demand it. This tension — is *malchus* an ideal or merely a permitted accommodation? — runs through Shoftim, Samuel, and the entire *sugya*.

### Elders vs. People

A *baraita* cites Rabbi Eliezer, who offers a nuanced middle position. The request for a king was not monolithic: *zkeinim shebador kahogen sha'alu* — the elders of the generation asked properly. Their request — *tnah lanu melech lishofteinu*, "give us a king to judge us" — was rooted in the desire for justice, strong central authority, and proper governance. It was the *amei ha'aretz*, the common people, who *kilkelu* — who corrupted the request — as expressed in the verse: *vehayinu gam anachnu kechol hagoyim ushfatanu malkeinu veyatza lefaneinu v'nilcham milchamoseinu* — "and we shall be like all the nations, and our king will judge us and go out before us and fight our wars."

Rashi identifies two elements in the people's flawed motivation. The phrase *kechol hagoyim* reflects a desire for assimilation, for Israel to be a nation like any other rather than a people defined by its unique relationship with God. And *veyatza lefaneinu* — "he will go out before us" — reflects an improper emphasis on military conquest and expansion. The elders sought justice and governance; the people wanted military glory and national normalcy. Both are in the same verse, but they represent fundamentally different visions of what a king is for.

---

## Order of Commandments

### Sequence Logic

Rabbi Yose (here teaching the same tradition as Rabbi Yehuda regarding the three commandments) notes that while the three obligations are clear — establish a king, destroy Amalek, build the Temple — their *sequence* requires derivation. He states: *eini yode'a eizeh mehem techila* — I do not know which comes first. The question is resolved through careful attention to specific biblical texts.

### King First

The verse states: *ki yad al kes Ya milchama l'Hashem b'Amalek* — "for a hand is upon the throne of God; a war of God against Amalek." The word *kisei* — throne — signifies a king, as demonstrated by the verse describing Solomon: *vayeshev Shlomo al kisei Hashem lemelech* — Solomon sat upon the throne of God as king. Therefore, before the war against Amalek can be waged, there must be a throne — and a throne means there must first be a king. The sequence of the first two commandments is thus established: first appoint a king, then destroy Amalek.

### Historical Order

The remaining question is whether building the Temple should precede the destruction of Amalek. This is resolved from the verse: *v'heniach lachem mikol oyveichem* — "and He will give you rest from all your enemies" — only after which comes the obligation to build the *beit habechirah*. Peace from enemies must precede the Temple's construction.

The historical record confirms this sequence exactly. Saul was appointed king first. God then commanded Saul to destroy Amalek. Only after David had subdued Israel's enemies — as recorded in the verse *vayehi ki yashav hamelech David b'veiso v'Hashem hiniach lo misaviv*, "and it came to pass that King David sat in his house and God had given him rest from all his enemies round about" — did the initiative to build the Temple arise, ultimately fulfilled by Solomon. The *gemara* concludes by citing David's words to the prophet Nathan, in which he expresses his discomfort at dwelling in a house of cedars while the Ark rests in a temporary shelter — the opening of the sequence that would culminate in Solomon's construction of the *beit habechirah*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 21

## Solomon's Declining Power

### Reish Lakish Overview

The daf opens with a teaching from Reish Lakish tracing the gradual diminishment of King Solomon's authority. The tradition he cites follows an arc of progressive contraction, beginning at the heights of cosmic dominion and ending in near-total loss.

### Heavenly to Earthly Rule

Reish Lakish teaches: *batichila malach Shlomo al elyonim* — in the beginning, Solomon reigned even over the celestial sphere, over the angels and demonic forces, as it is written, *vayeshev Shlomo al kisei Hashem* — Solomon sat upon the throne of God. Yet ultimately, *u-levasof malach al tachtonim* — he came to reign only in the temporal, physical world. The verse cited is *ki hu rodeh bechol ever hanahar mi-Tifsach ve-ad Azah* — he ruled over the entire *ever hanahar*, from Tifsach to Azah.

Rav and Shmuel each expound upon this same point while arriving at it differently. One holds that Tifsach and Azah were at opposite ends of the world — *sofa olam* — so that ruling from one to the other means ruling over everything between. The other holds that Tifsach and Azah were situated adjacent to one another, *bahadei hadadi havu yatevei*, and that ruling over both therefore implies ruling over all that lies in every direction around them — analogous to the formulation *me-Hodu ve-ad Kush*. Either way, the conclusion is that Solomon had once ruled over the entire world.

### Israel to Jerusalem

From there the decline continues. *U-levasof malach ela al Yisrael* — ultimately he reigned only over Israel, as the verse says, *ani Kohelet hayiti melech al Yisrael*. The identification of Kohelet with Solomon is assumed throughout. And then further still: *u-levasof malach ela al Yerushalayim* — he reigned only over Jerusalem, as it is written, *Divrei Kohelet ben David melech bi-Yerushalayim*.

### Throne to Staff

The contraction does not stop at geography. *U-levasof malach ela al mitato* — in the end, all Solomon had dominion over was his own bed, as it is written, *hinei mitato sheli-Shlomo*. And at the very last stage: *u-levasof malach ela al maklo* — he held authority over nothing but his staff, derived from the verse *ze hayah chelki mikol amali* — this is all I had from all my toil. The connection between *ze* and a staff is that *ze* implies something one can physically point to or hold. Rav and Shmuel dispute what exactly this refers to: one says *maklo*, his staff; the other says *gundo*, his cloak. In either interpretation, the king had been reduced to virtually nothing. This episode is connected in a note to the story of *Ashmedai*, the demon king, who assumed Solomon's form and expelled him from his throne — a narrative recalled from tractate *Gittin*.

### Restoration Question

The Gemara then raises the question *hadar lo hadar* — did Solomon ultimately recover his former stature? Rav and Shmuel again divide: one says *hadar*, he was restored; the other says *lo hadar*, he was not. According to the view that he was not restored: *malach ve-hediyot* — he was a king who became a commoner. According to the view that he was restored: *malach ve-hediyot u-malach* — king, commoner, and king again.

---

## Royal Spoils & Treasure

### Treasure Distribution

The Gemara proceeds to discuss the king's portion of war booty. A *baraita* teaches: *otzrot melachim la-melech* — the treasure houses of conquered kings go to the victorious king. *Ve-shear biza shebozezin, mechetza la-melech u-mechetza la-am* — and the remainder of all spoils taken are split equally between the king and the people. Being the winning king, in short, is extremely lucrative.

### Abaye's Question

Abaye raises a challenge to Rav Dimi (or, in another version of the text, to Rav Acha): *bishlama otzrot melachim la-melech, orcha de-milta hi* — it is understandable that the conquered king's treasury goes to the victor, for that is simply the way of things. But from where do we derive that even the remaining general spoils are split with the king getting half? The source, the Gemara answers, comes from a verse: *vayimshchu l'Hashem le-nagid u-le-Tzadok la-kohen* — they anointed Solomon as ruler and Tzadok as *kohen*.

### Solomon-Tzadok Parallel

From this juxtaposition, a *hekkesh* is drawn: the king (*nagid*) is compared to Tzadok the *kohen*. *Makish nagid le-Tzadok* — just as Tzadok the *kohen* receives half of something, so too the king receives half.

### Priestly Share Source

The Gemara then asks: *ve-Tzadok gufei mena lan* — but from where do we know that the *kohen* gets half? The answer comes from a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi: when the Torah speaks of the *lechem ha-panim* and says it shall be *le-Aharon u-le-vanav* — for Aaron and his sons — this is not simply referring collectively to the *kohanim*. Rather, Aaron himself receives half and his sons collectively receive the other half. This principle is then extended more broadly.

A parallel is noted from *Matot*, where the spoils of the war against Midyan were divided between the fighters and the rest of the nation, with the fighters contributing one out of five hundred to Elazar and the people contributing one out of fifty — far from a half-and-half split. No king existed at the time; the role was filled by Yehoshua. The proportions there are quite different, and the Gemara does not draw on that precedent for the present *halacha*.

---

## Royal Wives Limit

### Eighteen Wives Rule

The *mishnah* states: *lo yarbeh lo nashim ela shemoneh esrei* — the king may not have more than eighteen wives.

Before addressing the *machloket* between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon, the broader *parashah* of *Shoftim* is examined, as it provides the scriptural grounding for the entire discussion. The relevant passage in Devarim 17:14 begins with the people anticipating their entry into *Eretz Yisrael* and saying *asim alai melech ke-chol ha-goyim asher svivotai* — let me appoint a king like all the nations around me. This phrasing is notable because it echoes the complaint lodged against the people's request for a king elsewhere — that they asked *ke-chol ha-goyim*, which was seen as the wrong framing. Yet the Torah itself uses this formulation here, which leaves the question of whether kingship is ideal or merely permitted as a genuine *machloket*.

The passage continues: *som tasim alecha melech* — you shall appoint a king over yourself — which the Gemara reads as requiring that the king's authority be felt, that one hold him in genuine awe. *Mikerev achecha tasim alecha melech* — he must be from among your brethren; *lo tuchal latet alecha ish nochri asher lo achecha hu* — a foreigner cannot serve as king, which is the root of the problem with Hordus, who was a slave. The sages of that era were criticized for flattering him — being *machnif* — when they should not have been.

The passage then lists restrictions: *rak lo yarbeh lo susim* — he may not accumulate too many horses — and this prohibition extends to bringing the people back to Egypt to acquire them. The verse adds: *ve-lo yarbeh lo nashim ve-lo yasur levavo* — he should not have too many wives so that his heart not be led astray — *ve-chesef ve-zahav lo yarbeh lo me'od* — and he should not accumulate excessive silver and gold. The verse provides a reason for the horses restriction (not returning to Egypt), and a reason for the wives restriction (*ve-lo yasur levavo*), but states the money restriction without any stated rationale — presumably because the reason is self-evident.

The verse that anchors the number eighteen is the passage from Shmuel 2, chapter 12, where the prophet Nathan, rebuking David over Batsheva, conveys God's words: *va-etna lecha et beit adonecha ve-et neshei adonecha be-cheikecha* — I gave you the house of your master and the wives of your master — and adds: *ve-im m'at ve-osifa lach kahena ve-kahena* — and if that was too little, I would have given you more, *kahena ve-kahena*, here and here. Since David at that point had six wives — born to him in Chevron as enumerated in Shmuel 2, chapter 3 — each *kahena* is taken to equal six. Six plus six plus six equals eighteen.

### Yehudah: Conditional

Rabbi Yehudah holds that the king *may* have more than eighteen wives, provided that they do not turn his heart astray: *marbe hu lo u-vilvad she-lo yehu mesirot libo*. In his view, the prohibition is triggered not by the number but by the consequence.

### Shimon: No-Astray Rule

Rabbi Shimon takes the opposing position: *afilu achat u-mesira et libo harei zu lo yisana* — even one wife who will turn his heart astray, he may not marry. *Im ken lama ne'emar ve-lo yarbeh lo nashim* — if so, what does the Torah add by saying he should not *multiply* wives? *D'afilu ke-Avigayil* — even if they are all as righteous as Avigayil, having too many is still prohibited.

### Dispute Resolution

The Gemara asks: does this mean Rabbi Yehudah is the one who *darish ta'ama de-kra* — who interprets the law through its underlying reason — while Rabbi Shimon does not? This appears to invert the usual alignment, since Rabbi Shimon is famously associated with *derisha ta'ama de-kra* elsewhere. The classic example is the law of *lo tachbol beged almana* — one may not take a cloak as collateral from a widow. Rabbi Yehudah holds that this applies whether the widow is rich or poor — he does not look to the reason and applies the law categorically. Rabbi Shimon holds that a rich widow's cloak *may* be taken as collateral, since the reason for the prohibition — that she is poor and will be embarrassed going to retrieve it from her creditor — does not apply to a wealthy woman. Rabbi Shimon elaborates: if one does take a *mashkon* from a poor widow, she will inevitably return to retrieve it, and her neighbors will draw unseemly conclusions about why she is constantly visiting a man's home, damaging her reputation. For a rich widow, this dynamic does not arise. Thus Rabbi Shimon *is* the one who reasons from *ta'ama de-kra*, and Rabbi Yehudah is not.

How, then, do we reconcile the reversal apparent in the king's wives case? The answer given is: *shani hacha de-mefaresh ta'ama de-kra* — this case is different because the Torah itself explicitly states the reason. In the widow case, no reason is given, so Rabbi Shimon infers one. Here, the Torah openly states *ve-lo yasur levavo*. Given that explicit reason, Rabbi Yehudah naturally incorporates it into his ruling: so long as the wives will not turn the king's heart astray, the prohibition does not apply. Rabbi Shimon, for his part, says: precisely because I generally derive reasons myself, I know that if the Torah had intended to convey only this principle it could simply have written *lo yarbeh lo nashim* and remained silent — *ve-lishtok*. I would have inferred the reason myself. Since the Torah went out of its way to add *ve-lo yasur levavo*, it must be teaching something beyond what I would have derived on my own: namely, that even one wife who will lead him astray is forbidden. And since that is the lesson of the added phrase, the main prohibition of *lo yarbeh* must teach something distinct: *afilu ke-Avigayil* — even if all the wives are righteous, exceeding the number is still prohibited.

### Kahena Calculation

The derivation of eighteen from the *kahena ve-kahena* formula is that since David had six wives at the time of Nathan's rebuke, each *kahena* equals six. The *tanna de-didan* holds that the two instances of *kahena* each add six, bringing the total to 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. This is supported by a principle that the second *kahena* is linked to the first: *makish kaheina basra le-kaheina kamma, mah kaheina kamma sheis af kaheina basra sheis*.

### Higher Wife Counts

Alternative readings produce higher totals. If the second *kahena* is taken as doubling all that came before rather than adding a flat six, then 6 + 6 = 12, and *kahena* again doubles to yield 24. A *baraita* is cited in support: *lo yarbeh lo nashim ve-yoter me-esrim ve-arba* — he may not have more than twenty-four. Alternatively, taking the doubling principle further: 6 + 6 = 12, then a *kahena* equivalent to all of that is 12, so 12 + 12 = 24, and a final *kahena* equal to 24 produces 48. Another *baraita* is cited in support: *lo yarbeh lo nashim ve-yoter me-arba'im u-shemoneh* — he may not have more than forty-eight.

---

## Michal & David's Wives

### Michal as Eglah

Among the six wives listed in Shmuel 2, chapter 3 is a woman named *Eglah*, which is an unusual name. The Gemara, citing Rav, identifies this as Michal: *amar Rav, Egla zu Michal*. The epithet *egla* is a term of endearment — *she-havivah alav ke-egla*, she was beloved to him like a calf. A parallel is drawn to Shimshon's riddle: *lulei charashtem be-eglati lo metzasem chidosi* — had you not plowed with my *egla*, meaning extracted the answer through my wife, you would not have solved the riddle.

### Michal's Children Problem

This identification immediately raises a difficulty: *u-mi havu le-Michal banim?* Did Michal actually have children? The verse in Shmuel explicitly states: *u-le-Michal bat Shaul lo hayah lah yeled ad yom motah* — Michal the daughter of Shaul had no child until the day of her death. This verse follows the episode in which Michal rebuked David for dancing before the *aron*, saying *mah nichbad hayom melech Yisrael*, accusing him of demeaning himself by dancing before everyone *ke-higlot niglot achad ha-reikim* — like one of the empty commoners. David responded that he would humble himself even further and would be held in esteem by the *shfachot*. After this exchange, the verse records that Michal had no offspring until her dying day.

### Hebron vs Jerusalem

Two resolutions are offered. Rav Chisda proposes: *ad yom motah lo hayah lah, be-yom motah hayah lah* — she had no child *until* the day she died, meaning she gave birth on the very day of her death, presumably dying in childbirth from the son Yitream listed among David's Chevron children. The second resolution notes that the children enumerated in Shmuel 2:3 were born to David in *Chevron*, whereas the entire incident with Michal and the dancing before the *aron* took place in *Yerushalayim* — as the verse explicitly places the scene there. Therefore *mipnei baneha she-chashavu be-Chevron* — the children attributed to her were conceived in Chevron — and *ve-ilu ma'aseh de-Michal be-Yerushalayim havah* — the episode that resulted in her barrenness occurred only afterward in Yerushalayim. Rav Yehudah (or Rav Yosef) adds that she was punished for her words to the king: *shekaltah Michal de-mitrefah*. The fuller formulation reconciles the texts: *ad oto ma'aseh hayah lah, mi-kan ve-eilach lo hayah lah* — until that incident she had children; from that point on she did not.

This resolution is coherent: David reigned first in Chevron with a more limited kingdom, then consolidated power and moved to Yerushalayim. The children, including the one born of Michal (*Eglah*), predate the Yerushalayim episode.

### Merav-Michal Solution

The Gemara also addresses the verse in Shmuel 2, chapter 21 that refers to *chameshah bnei Michal bat Shaul* — five sons of Michal the daughter of Shaul — which seems to attribute even more children to her. One possible resolution, already noted on 19b, is: *Merav yaldah, Michal giddelah, be-chach nikreu al shemah* — Merav bore them, Michal raised them, and therefore they are called by her name. The word *yaldah* would normally imply she gave birth, but the Gemara is willing to entertain the principle that raising children can render them attributable to the one who raised them. This provides an alternative avenue of resolution independent of the Chevron-versus-Yerushalayim answer, though the Gemara employs both.

---

## Concubines & 400 Children

### Concubine Definition

The verse in Shmuel 2, chapter 5 states that David took additional *pilagshim* and *nashim* in Yerushalayim — *vayikach David od pilagshim ve-nashim mi-Yerushalayim*. The Gemara asks: *mai nashim mai pilagshim* — what distinguishes a wife from a *pilegesh*? Rav Yehudah citing Rav explains: *nashim be-ketubah u-ve-kiddushin* — wives have a *ketubah* and *kiddushin*; *pilagshim belo ketubah u-velo kiddushin* — concubines have neither. The relationship is essentially a sexual one, without the formal legal structure of marriage. Whether such an arrangement is normatively permissible, and under what conditions — whether it was specific to kings, to the biblical period, or to the very wealthy — is not addressed here; the Gemara only records what the distinction is.

### 400 Yefat Toar Children

Rav Yehudah citing Rav teaches: *arba me'ot yeladim noldu le-David ve-khullam bnei yefat to'ar hayu* — four hundred children were born to David, and all of them were sons of *yefat to'ar*. The *yefat to'ar* is the beautiful captive discussed in *Ki Tetzei*: a non-Jewish woman captured in war whom a soldier desires.
