David was a highly martial king who fought many wars, and he apparently desired women captured in those campaigns, with the result that four hundred children were born from such relationships. These children all had *beloriot* — the braided hairstyle associated with non-Jewish culture — and they would sit in golden chariots, *bekronot shel zahav*, and lead the troops. They were the powerful fighters of the house of David: *ba'alei egrofim shel beit David*.

### Blorit Hair Problem

This creates a serious halakhic problem. The *belorit* is not merely a foreign aesthetic; it falls squarely within the prohibition of *chukkot ha-goyim* and possibly even *avodah zarah*. The Rambam in *Hilchot Avodah Zarah*, chapter 11, *halacha* 1, lists among the prohibited acts: *lo yilbash malbush ha-miyuchad lahem* — one may not wear clothing distinctive to them; *ve-lo yigadel tzitzit kemo tzitzit rosham* — one may not grow hair in the style of their hair; *ve-lo yegalach min ha-tzdadim ve-yaniach ha-se'ar be-emtza, kemo she-hem osim* — one may not shave the sides and leave hair in the center as they do. And: *ve-zehu ha-nikra blorit* — this is what is called *blorit*. According to the Rambam, violating these prohibitions incurs *malkut*.

### Rambam's Close-to-Royalty

The Rambam himself provides a limited dispensation: *Yisrael she-hayah karov la-malchut ve-tzarich liyeshev lifnei malcheihem ve-yehei gnai im lo yidameh lahen* — a Jew who is close to the royal court and must appear before non-Jewish kings, for whom it would be demeaning not to resemble them, *harei zeh mutar lilbosh ke-malbushan u-le-galach ha-se'ar keneged panav ke-derech she-hem osim* — he is permitted to dress as they dress and to style his hair as they do.

### Kesef Mishneh Defense

The *Kesef Mishneh* cites the case of Avtulos bar Reuven, who was permitted to have a *komi* haircut — a non-Jewish style — because he was *karov la-malchut*, in proximity to royalty. From this the Rambam derived the broader dispensation for dress as well.

But the *Kesef Mishneh* presses further: if the Rambam rules that one incurs *malkut* for these acts, how could the *chachamim* permit them even for those close to royalty, given that such proximity does not ordinarily override a *lav* of the Torah? The answer offered by the *Kesef Mishneh* is: *mishum hatzalat Yisrael hu de-sharu* — it was permitted on grounds of saving Jewish lives. Those who served as emissaries or advisors to kings were in a position to protect the Jewish people, and thus the allowance falls under the principle of *pikuach nefesh*. The *Kesef Mishneh* then applies this reasoning directly to the four hundred children: *nami hatzalat Yisrael hu de-havu meva'atim et ha-oyvim* — this too was permitted for the sake of *hatzalat Yisrael*, because these men, placed at the forefront of battle looking entirely non-Jewish, would strike fear into the enemy. Seeing what appeared to be an enormous, non-Jewish-looking army advancing against them, the enemy would lose heart — even their own population appeared to oppose them. The *belorit* served a strategic military function of psychological intimidation, and on that basis the *Kesef Mishneh* justifies it.

An alternative formulation is also raised: *she-ha-Torah lo partah davar ela amrah uvechukoteihem lo telechu* — the Torah did not specify the precise content of this prohibition, only stating the general rule not to follow their customs. The Torah entrusted the details to the *chachamim*, and the *chachamim* determined that it does not apply to those close to royalty. Under this reading there is no true *Torah*-level prohibition being overridden; the *chachamim* have simply defined its scope.

---

## Amnon & Tamar Incident

### Tamar as Yefat Toar

Rav Yehudah citing Rav teaches: *Tamar bat yefat to'ar hayeta* — Tamar was the daughter of a *yefat to'ar*. This is derived from her own words during the assault, when she pleaded with Amnon: *ve-atah daber na el ha-melech ki lo yimna'eni mimecha* — speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you. How could Tamar have suggested that the king would permit her marriage to Amnon, given that they were half-siblings sharing the same father? The answer is that she must have been a *bat yefat to'ar* — a daughter born of a captive woman — and thus there was a question whether her status as David's daughter was halakhically equivalent to a full sister. *Michdei bat achva me-nisuin hava, achva hi ve-i sharei lei?* — she was indeed his sister through their father. The very fact that she could plausibly argue the king might permit it indicates she knew there was a technical basis for such a position, and that basis is her being a *bat yefat to'ar*.

This raises a further question addressed in *Tosafot*. The *Yerushalmi* records a *machloket* between Rav and Shmuel: *Rav amar eina muteret ba-milchamah ela bi'ah rishonah* — Rav holds that relations with a *yefat to'ar* are permitted once, in the heat of battle, before the full conversion process. *Ve-Shmuel amar af lo bi'ah rishonah* — Shmuel holds that even the first act of relations is not permitted until the conversion ritual is complete. According to Shmuel's position, by the time a man could have legitimate relations with a *yefat to'ar*, she would already be Jewish — so how could Tamar have been born before her mother converted?

*Tosafot* offers two answers. First: *she-imah kvar hayeta uberet ke-she-ba'ah la-milchamah* — Tamar's mother may have already been pregnant with Tamar from her previous non-Jewish partner at the time she was captured. David then performed the *yefat to'ar* ritual and formally married her, but Tamar herself was conceived before that. Thus, even according to Shmuel, David never had relations with Tamar's mother before she was Jewish — he only did so after the conversion — but Tamar herself was conceived by a different father beforehand. Second: *mitoch she-gadlah be-cheiko shel David karu lah bat ha-melech* — since Tamar grew up in David's household, she was called the king's daughter, even if David was not her biological father. This reading can absorb the textual reference to her as David's daughter without requiring that David fathered her at all. Neither answer forecloses the other, and together they demonstrate that the *Tamar* narrative cannot serve as definitive proof in either direction regarding the *bi'ah rishonah* question.

### Yonadav's Evil Advice

The narrative returns to the incident itself. The text introduces Amnon's associate: *ve-le-Amnon rei ve-shmo Yonadav ben Shima achi David* — Amnon had a friend named Yonadav, the son of David's brother Shima, making him David's nephew. He is described as *ish chacham* — a clever man. Rav Yehudah citing Rav glosses: *ish chacham hayah le-rish'ah* — he was clever in wickedness, for he devised the scheme. Yonadav advised Amnon: *shechav al mitatecha ve-hitchala* — lie on your bed and feign illness. When people come to you, say that only Tamar's cooking can restore you. Rav Yehudah citing Rav adds that what Tamar made was *minei tigun* — fried foods. The reason the ruse required Tamar to cook in front of him specifically was that fried food must be served immediately; it loses its quality if it sits. He could therefore legitimately demand that it be prepared fresh in his presence, providing the pretext to clear everyone else from the room.

### Amnon's Hatred

After the assault, the verse states: *vayisna Amnon sin'ah gedolah me'od* — Amnon hated her with a very great hatred. The reversal of passion into revulsion is noted without extended commentary. The hatred he felt was likely intensified by the sight of Tamar, which confronted him constantly with his own transgression.

### Tamar's Pubic Hair Issue

The Gemara then addresses a strange textual issue. The phrase *mai Tamar* is read to suggest that Tamar did something involving a strand of hair tied in a knot, and this caused Amnon to become a *k'rut shofcha* — one whose generative capacity is severed or destroyed. The verse is read: *kashra lo nima ve-asta lo k'rut shofcha* — she tied a hair-strand around him and thereby rendered him sterile. It is understood here as her act of resistance — she managed to strike back at her attacker in some way, leaving him permanently incapacitated.

This raises an apparent contradiction with a statement of Rava, who teaches from the verse *vayeitzei shemech ba-goyim be-yofyeich* — your fame went out among the nations for your beauty — that Jewish women do not have hair in the underarm or the pubic area: *she-ein lahem li-vnot Yisrael lo sarchat ha-shachi ve-lo beit ha-erva*. If Jewish women lack pubic hair, how could Tamar have used one? The resolution proposed is that Jewish women of that era were scrupulous about shaving — they did grow hair naturally, but maintained careful grooming such that they were smooth. This is not a claim that Jewish women biologically lack body hair (*nishtana ha-teva* is not invoked), but rather a description of their customary practice. How then could Tamar have done this? *Ve-shani Tamar de-bat yefat to'ar havi* — Tamar, as the daughter of a *yefat to'ar*, was not in the same category. Alternatively, since she was an unmarried woman who was not having sexual relations, she would have had no occasion or reason to shave, and so she was in a different practical situation than married women.

### Yichud Decree on Women

The narrative concludes with a communal consequence. The verse describes Tamar placing ash on her head and rending her garment of many colors in mourning. A *tanna* in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha teaches: *gader gadol gadrah Tamar be-otah sha'ah* — Tamar erected a great fence through this incident. The reasoning: *amru bnot melachim kach, bnot hedyotot al achat kama ve-chama; im li-tzenu'ot kach, li-frutzot al achat kama ve-chama* — if this could happen to the modest daughter of a king, *kal ve-chomer* to anyone; if even a modest woman was vulnerable, certainly an immodest one would be.

Rav Yehudah teaching: *ba-otah sha'ah gazru al ha-yichud ve-al ha-penuyah* — at that time they decreed regarding *yichud* and regarding the unmarried woman. The Gemara clarifies: is *yichud* not already prohibited from the Torah? Yes — *yichud de-Oraita hu* — seclusion with a married woman is a Torah-level prohibition, derived from the verse *ki yesitcha achicha ben imecha*: the Torah specifies "the brother, the son of your mother" rather than simply "your brother" to convey that only a son may be secluded with his own mother; any other pairing involving the forbidden relations of the Torah falls under *yichud*. That derivation is attributed to Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak.

If *yichud* was already prohibited, what was new in the decree? The Gemara clarifies: *ela eima gazru al yichud de-penuyah* — the decree addressed *yichud* with an unmarried woman. Until that point, an unmarried man and an unmarried woman could be alone together, since neither was technically *arayot* to the other. After the incident with Tamar — which demonstrated the danger even in a royal, modest setting — the rabbis extended the prohibition to cover seclusion between unmarried men and women as well.

---

## Adoniyah's Rebellion

### Failed Coronation

The *mishnah* concludes with Adoniyah the son of Chagit, who declared *ani emloch* — I shall be king — and made an attempt to claim the throne. Rav Yehudah citing Rav interprets this: *melamed she-bikkesh le-holmo ve-lo holmato* — the text teaches that he sought to have the crown placed on his head, and it did not fit.

### Speedy Runners Enhanceme…

The verse records that Adoniyah prepared a chariot and cavalry and fifty runners to go before him. The Gemara asks: is that remarkable? Many princes have entourages. The answer is what distinguished these fifty men: *kulam ntulei tchol ve-chakukei kipot raglayim hayu* — they had all undergone spleen removal, and their foot-soles had been treated — literally, carved. The spleen removal was apparently understood to enhance running endurance. The treatment to the feet refers to the deadening of nerve endings: since runners of that era ran barefoot, they would be slowed or stopped by sharp thorns and rocks underfoot. By killing the nerve endings in the soles of their feet, these runners could traverse any terrain without pain, enabling them to travel greater distances at greater speed. These were deliberately engineered elite runners, prepared through what amounts to surgical intervention.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 22

## Horses & Wealth

### Intro: Horses & Money

The *mishnah* on 21b introduces a set of royal restrictions that extend beyond the prohibition on excessive wives discussed previously. The *mishnah* states: *lo yarbeh lo susim ella k'dei mirkavto v'chesef v'zahav lo yarbeh lo me'od ella k'dei litein aspanya* — the king may not accumulate too many horses beyond what is needed for his chariots and cavalry, and he may not accumulate excessive silver and gold beyond what is needed to fund his army and the operating needs of the crown. The underlying principle is that while some subjective threshold exists, once horses or wealth become genuinely extraneous — serving no present or even potential function — the prohibition applies.

### Extraneous Horses

The *gemara* refines this with a *baraita*: *tanu rabbanan lo yarbeh lo susim yachol afilu k'dei mirkavto ufarashav talmud lomar lo* — one might have thought that even the horses needed for the king's military forces are prohibited. The word *lo* — "for himself" — teaches otherwise: he may not accumulate horses for personal, extraneous purposes, but he may certainly maintain whatever is necessary for his cavalry and chariots.

What, then, is actually prohibited under the word *susim*? The *gemara* answers: *susim batlanin* — idle horses, horses running in front of the royal procession purely for show, serving no military or functional role whatsoever. The *gemara* further asks: how do we know that even a single idle horse, *sus echad v'hu batel*, falls under *lo yarbeh*? From the verse *l'ma'an harbot sus* — the word *l'ma'an* comes to include even one such horse. But then, once we know that even a single idle horse is already prohibited, what additional work does the plural *susim* do? The answer is *la'avor b'lo ta'aseh al kol sus v'sus* — each and every extraneous horse constitutes its own independent transgression. The accumulation of additional idle horses does not merely deepen a single *issur*; rather, each one is a separate violation.

### 'Lo' Teaches Limit

The *gemara* then addresses the textual role of the word *lo* more precisely. Had the Torah not written *lo*, one might have thought the prohibition extended even to horses maintained for the army itself. The word *lo* therefore comes to carve out that military horses are entirely permitted — and indeed, the king must ensure he has adequate forces. The *lo* limits the prohibition sharply to personal, extraneous accumulation.

### Silver & Gold

The same structure is applied to silver and gold. The *baraita* states: *lo yarbeh lo — lo eino marbeh aval marbeh hu kedei liten aspanya* — the word *lo* teaches that a personal stockpile is prohibited, but accumulation for military pay and the needs of the kingdom is permitted. The *gemara* raises the obvious question: would anyone have thought the king cannot maintain funds to pay his army? The answer is that the word *lo* comes to emphasize that the permission for expanded royal wealth is genuinely limited to those functional needs — *lo tzricha le-harchavah* — and that any accumulation beyond them, even in anticipation of future needs, is restricted to the personal sphere.

The *gemara* then connects this back to the earlier prohibition of *lo yarbeh lo nashim*, noting that the *lo* in that context serves a different function: *lemiut hedyotot* — to distinguish the king's restrictions from those of a commoner, who is not limited in the number of wives he may marry.

---

## Solomon's Wealth

### Conflicting Verses

Rabbi Yehuda notes an apparent contradiction between two verses regarding Solomon's stables. One verse states that Solomon had *arbaim elef urvot susim* — forty thousand stable-units for his horses — while another states *arba'at alafim* — four thousand. The resolution offered is that these figures describe different levels of organization: either there were forty thousand stable complexes each containing four thousand individual stalls, or four thousand complexes each containing forty thousand stalls. Either way, the total number of horses involved is staggering.

### Silver Contradiction

Rabbi Yitzchak raises a parallel tension regarding silver. One verse says *ein kessef nechshav bimei Shlomo le'me'umah* — silver was not considered significant in Solomon's days — implying a kind of devaluation or scarcity of prestige. Another verse states that Solomon made silver as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones. These two descriptions seem irreconcilable.

### Pre/Post Marriage

The *gemara* resolves both tensions through the same chronological key: *lo kashya kan kodem shenasa Shlomo et bat Paroh kan le'achar shenasa Shlomo et bat Paroh* — one verse describes the period before Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter, and the other describes the period after. It is worth noting that there is an additional tradition that the king may not accumulate wealth through taxation, but gifts — such as a royal dowry — would be permitted, which may help explain the dramatic shift in the kingdom's financial character following the marriage.

### Rome Foundation

A striking *midrash* is introduced here: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that at the very moment Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter, the angel Gabriel descended and drove a reed into the sea. From the sandbank that arose, the great city of Rome was eventually built. The implicit reading is that Solomon's sin in this marriage planted the seed of Israel's greatest future enemy. A tradition also cited in this context holds that Pharaoh's daughter brought with her musical instruments associated with idolatrous worship, introducing practices that God would ultimately punish through the Roman destruction of the Temple. The very act by which Solomon built the Temple thus contained within it the conditions for its destruction.

### Hidden Reasons

Rabbi Yitzchak draws a broader lesson from Solomon's failures: *mipnei mah lo nitgalu ta'amei Torah* — why are the reasons for *mitzvot* generally not revealed in the Torah? Because the two cases where reasons are given — don't multiply wives, lest your heart be led astray; don't multiply horses, lest you return to Egypt — both led to disaster. Solomon reasoned that the reasons would not apply to him: *ani arbeh velo asur* — "I will multiply and not be led astray." In both cases, the Torah's feared outcome came to pass. The lesson is that once reasons are known, individuals will construct arguments for why those reasons do not apply to their circumstances. This connects to a broader *machlokes* discussed earlier in the *masechta* about whether one *doresh ta'ama de'mitzvot*, since even where reasons are given by *Chazal* at a later stage, the same risk emerges: a person identifies with one side of a *chakira* and concludes the prohibition does not apply.

---

## Sefer Torah

### Own Sefer Torah

The *mishnah* states that the king must write a *sefer torah* for himself — *v'chotev lo sefer torah lishmo* — and this *sefer torah* accompanies him everywhere. When he goes out to war, it goes with him; when he returns, it returns with him. When he sits in judgment, it sits beside him, as the verse states *v'haytah imo v'kara bo kol y'mei chayav* — it shall be with him and he shall read from it all the days of his life. The *sofrim* of antiquity were capable of writing with extraordinary precision in miniature form, making it plausible that the king carried something approaching a portable *sefer torah*.

### Braita: Others' Torahs

A *baraita* refines the *mishnah*'s ruling. When we say the king must write his own *sefer torah lishmo* — and that he should not make use of one that is not his — the disqualification is not of an inherited *sefer torah* but of one written for someone else. For the king (*melech*), the requirement to have his own applies; for a commoner (*hedyot*), it does not. Yet separately, the rule that one must write his own even if he inherits one applies to everyone, based on the verse *ve'ata kitvu lachem et hashirah*.

### Two Torahs

The *baraita* continues: the king actually requires two *torahs*, as derived from the verse *v'chatav lo et mishneh ha-Torah ha-zot*. One accompanies him in and out — a travel *sefer torah* — and one remains in his treasury, *veit genazav*.

### Torah as Amulet

The *sefer torah* that travels with the king is fashioned into a kind of receptacle that can be attached to his arm, *kemin kame'a vetoleh bizro'o*, evoking the verse *shiviti Hashem l'negdi tamid* — I have set God before me always. It is worth noting the *tefil'in*-like character of this practice. However, this portable *sefer torah* is not taken absolutely everywhere: *eino nichnas bah lo le-veit hamerchatz velo le-veit hakisei* — it does not accompany him into the bathhouse or the bathroom.

### Inner/Outer Torah

The image of two *torahs* — one that goes out into the world and one kept in the *genizah* — invites reflection on different modes of Torah engagement. The *torah* one presents to the world and the *torah* one maintains internally need not be identical in character; there is a *torah* for public life and a *torah* for the private inner realm. The verse *v'hayeta imo v'kara bo* — he shall read from it — is limited by the phrase *makom hara'ui likro bo*, a place appropriate for such reading, which restricts the portable *sefer torah*'s use to fitting contexts.

---

## Torah Scripts

### Original Script

Mar Zutra, and some attribute this to Mar Ukva, teaches: *batchila nitna torah le-Yisrael bichtav Ivri u-leshon hakodesh* — the Torah was originally given to Israel in *ktav Ivri* and *leshon hakodesh*.

### Ezra's Change

In the time of Ezra, the script was changed: *chazra venitna lahem bimei Ezra bichtav Ashurit u-leshon Aramit* — it was reissued in *ktav Ashurit* with *leshon Aramit*. The refined formulation is that the Jewish people ultimately retained *ktav Ashurit* with *leshon hakodesh* — which is our current form — while *ktav Ivri* and *leshon Aramit* were left for the *hedyotot*. Who are the *hedyotot* here? Rav Chisda says: the *Kuta'ei*, the Samaritans.

### Ktav Names

What is *ktav Ivri*? Rav Chisda says it is *ktav libona* — script associated with a place called Libona, the precise identification of which remains unclear. As for *ktav Ashurit*, the *gemara* will shortly address its etymology.

### Ezra & Moses

A *baraita* records a remarkable statement: Rabbi Yosei says, *raui haya Ezra she-tinaten torah al yado le-Yisrael ilmalei lo* — Ezra was worthy of having the Torah given through him, had Moses not preceded him.

### Moses Parallels

The *gemara* then develops a series of textual parallels between Moses and Ezra. Moses *alah el ha-Elohim* — went up to God; Ezra *hu oleh mi-Bavel* — ascended from Babylon. The shared language of *aliyah* in both cases implies a parallel spiritual significance, and one might further read here an early Zionist resonance: the ascent to the Land of Israel is equated with the ascent to receive Torah. Moses was commanded to teach *chukim u-mishpatim* to Israel; of Ezra it is written that he prepared his heart *lidrosh et Torat Hashem ve-la'asot u-le-lamed be-Yisrael chok u-mishpat* — virtually identical language. And yet, though the Torah was not transmitted through Ezra's hand, the script nonetheless changed through him — *nishtanah al yado ha-ktav* — as attested by verses in *Sefer Ezra* and *Daniel* that point to changes in written form, and a verse in *Devarim* which the *gemara* reads as implying a script *ra'uy le-hishtanot* — fit to be changed.

---

## Script Changes

### Sin/Repentance

*Rebbe* offers a different framing of the script changes. He argues that one should not understand these changes as innovations introduced in the time of Ezra. Rather, *bi-tchilah ktav zeh nitenah Torah le-Yisrael* — the Torah was given in this script from the beginning. When Israel sinned, the script was transformed against them; when they repented, it was restored. The proof-text is *shuvu le-vitzaron asirei ha-tikvah gam hayom magid mishneh ashiv lach* — the word *mishneh* implying a doubling back or restoration. This framing is significant: if the different scripts already existed as modes at *Har Sinai*, then Ezra's changes feel far less theologically destabilizing. One need not view them as a later editorial intervention but as a restoration of an earlier state.

### Ashurit Name

The *gemara* asks: *lamma nikra Ashurit* — why is the script called *Ashurit*? Two answers emerge. One: *she-alah imahem me-Ashur* — because these letters came up with the returning exiles from Assyria. A second etymology: *she-me'usheret bi-chtav* — because it is a particularly rich, embellished script.

### No Change View

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Perata, in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i, takes the strongest position: *ktav zeh lo nishtanah kol ikar* — this script never changed at all. His proof is the verse *vavei ha-amudim* — the pillars. Just as the columns of the *sefer torah* never change, so too the *vav* — the shape of the letter *vav* — never changed. A further proof: the verse in *Esther* reads *ki-chtavam ve-khilshonam* — just as their language did not change, so too their writing did not change. One must acknowledge, however, that in practice many *torahs* have different column configurations, so the absolute stability of columns is itself not uncontested.

According to this view, the verse *mishneh ha-Torah ha-zot* does not refer to a script change at all, but to the two *torahs* the king writes — one that accompanies him and one kept in storage. The portable *sefer torah* is made like an amulet, *kemin kame'a ve-toleh bi-zro'o*, based on *shiviti Hashem le-negdi tamid*. Those who do not read this verse as referring to the portable *sefer torah* apply it instead to the teaching of Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida: *hamispallel tzarich sheyireh atzmo ke'ilu Shechina kenegdo* — one who prays must imagine the *Shechina* standing before him, as it says *shiviti Hashem l'negdi tamid*.

### Gimatriya Code

The *gemara* addresses how Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds the script never changed, handles the verse from *Daniel* — *lo kahalin kesava le-mikra* — which implies that the writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast could not be read by the Chaldean wise men. Rav answers: *be-gimatriya* — it was a cipher. The words were written in a code in which each letter is replaced by its counterpart from the opposite end of the alphabet (*alef* for *tav*, *bet* for *shin*, *gimel* for *reish*, *dalet* for *kuf*, and so forth). The apparently nonsensical letters *itat itat adach pugachmat* thus decode into *mene mene tekel upharsin*. Various Sages — Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Ashi — offer additional interpretations of the cipher according to different decoding schemes, each arriving at somewhat different readings of the underlying text.

---

## Royal Dignity

### Horse & Seat

The *mishnah* continues with a series of prohibitions protecting the dignity of the king: *ein rochvin al suso* — one may not ride the king's horse; *ve'ein yoshvin al kiso* — one may not sit on his throne; *ve'ein mishtamshin be-shravito* — one may not use his scepter.

### Visibility Rules

Similarly: *ve'ein ro'in oto keshehu mistaper* — one may not observe the king while he is getting his haircut, *velo keshehu arum* — nor while he is naked, *velo keshehu be-veit hamerchatz* — nor while he is in the bathhouse.

### Eimah Principle

The source and reason for all these prohibitions is the verse *som tasim alecha melech* — you shall surely set a king upon yourself — which the *gemara* reads as *she-tehe eimaso alecha* — that his *eimah*, his awe-inspiring quality, should rest upon you. All these activities — riding his horse, sitting in his chair, seeing him in a compromised state — erode the royal dignity and undermine the subject's appropriate sense of reverence toward the king.

---

## Avishag Story

### Avishag & Kings

Rav Yaakov, citing Rabbi Yochanan, addresses the case of Avishag HaShunamit: she was permitted to Solomon but forbidden to Adoniyah. She was permitted to Solomon because he was himself a king, and a king may make use of the property or prerogatives of a previous king — *melech mishtamesh be-shravito shel melech*. She was forbidden to Adoniyah because *hedyot hu* — he was a commoner.

### Caregiver Role

The *gemara* explains who Avishag was. The verses from *Melachim* describe how King David had grown old and cold, and his servants sought a young woman to serve as his companion and caretaker. Avishag was found — exceptionally beautiful — and she served the king. At some point she said to David: *ninsavin* — marry me. David refused, saying it was forbidden for him to do so. She accused him of using *halacha* as a pretext, suggesting that he was really afraid of his own diminished capacity — *chasra d'ganav v'anafshaih l'shlama nakit* — that he was hiding his weakness behind religious scruple.

### Bathsheva Act

David rejected this accusation decisively. He instructed his servants: *karu li l'Batsheva* — bring Bathsheva to me. The verse records that Bathsheva came to the king in his chamber. Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, teaches: *b'ota sha'ah kincha Batsheva b'shlosh esrei mapot* — at that moment, Bathsheva cleaned herself with thirteen cloths, corresponding to the thirteen words in the verse describing the scene and indicating, per Rashi, that they had relations thirteen times in succession. David's purpose was unambiguous: to demonstrate that his earlier refusal of Avishag was entirely on *halachic* grounds and not on account of any personal failing.

### Divorce Hard

Rav Shemen bar Abba draws a striking lesson from this episode: *bo u're'eh kamah kashin gerushin* — come and see how difficult divorce is. David, who had as many as eighteen wives, was not permitted to divorce one of them in order to marry Avishag. Instead, the authorities permitted him the more delicate arrangement of *yichud* with a woman who remained forbidden to him — rather than sanction the dissolution of an existing marriage. This illustrates how deeply resistant *halacha* is to divorce even when there might seem to be good reason for it.

---

## Marriage & Divorce

### First Wife

Rabbi Elazar states: *kol hamgaresh et ishto rishonah afilu mizbe'ach morid alav dmaot* — whoever divorces his first wife, even the *mizbe'ach* weeps for him. The *pesukim* from *Malachi* are cited: the *mizbe'ach* is covered with tears; God testifies between a man and the wife of his youth — *eshet ne'urecha* — whom he has betrayed, and who was his companion and the wife of his covenant. These are presented as experiential and *agadah*-level observations rather than purely prescriptive *halacha*, though they are no less serious for that.

### Wife Death

Rabbi Yochanan — and some attribute this to Rabbi Elazar — teaches that a man's wife dies only when he faces debts he cannot repay: *im ein lecha l'shalem lamah yikach mishkavcha mitachtecha* — if you cannot pay, why should your bedfellow be taken from beneath you. This is a striking *gemara*. Rabbi Yochanan then adds: *kol adam shemeta ishto rishonah k'ilu charav Beit HaMikdash b'yamav* — for any man whose wife dies before him, it is as if the *Beit HaMikdash* was destroyed in his days. The proof comes from *Yechezkel*, where the prophet is told that God will take away *machmad eineicha* — the delight of your eyes — in a plague, and where the Temple itself is called *machmad eineichem*. The death of Yechezkel's wife and the destruction of the *Mikdash* are juxtaposed explicitly in those verses. Clarifying the phrase *ishto rishonah*: it refers not to a first wife as opposed to a second, but to the wife who dies before her husband — that is, whose death he lives to experience.

### Darkness

Rabbi Alexandri adds: *kol adam shemeta ishto b'yamav olam chashach ba'ado* — for any man whose wife dies in his days, the world grows dark around him, as the verse says *or chashach b'oholo v'nero alav yidach* — the light darkens in his tent and his candle is extinguished over him. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that such a man's stride shortens — *pisiotov mitkatzrot* — one can almost picture the diminished, shuffling gait of grief. Rabbi Abahu adds that *itzato nofelet* — his counsel fails him, his judgment and capacity for wisdom become unreliable.

### Shidduchim

Rabbah bar Bar Chana, citing Rabbi Yochanan, states: *kasheh lezivugam kepriat yam suf* — making a match is as difficult as the splitting of the sea. The verse *elohim moshiv yechidim baitah* is read with *bakosharot* parsed as *bechi veshirut* — with weeping and with song. One might ask: is this really true? After all, we know that Rav Yehuda teaches in the name of Rav that forty days before a child is formed, a *bat kol* goes out and declares *bat ploni l'ploni* — the daughter of so-and-so for so-and-so. If the match is preordained at birth, how can it be as difficult as splitting the sea?

The *gemara* resolves the tension: *lo kashya ha bezivug rishon ha bezivug sheni* — there is no contradiction. The first marriage is preordained from before birth and in that sense is not hard at all. It is the *zivug sheni* — the second marriage — that is as difficult as splitting the sea. The weight of this discussion is palpable. These are texts that are difficult to read without thinking of people in one's own life — those who have lost spouses, those who are seeking a match — and that dimension of personal resonance deserves acknowledgment.

### Eshet Neurim

Shmuel bar Nachman teaches: *lakol yesh tmurah chutz me'eshet neurim* — for everything there is a substitute or replacement, except for the wife of one's youth, the *eshet neurim*. The verse in Isaiah — *ve'eshet neurim ki timas* — is read as a rhetorical question: can the wife of your youth truly become despicable to you? Rav Yehuda teaches his son Rav Yitzchak that a person achieves true *korat ruach* — contentment and equanimity — only through his first wife, citing the verse *yehi mekorecha varuch usmach me'eshet neurecha*. When Rav Yitzchak asks for a concrete example, Rav Yehuda replies: *kegon imach* — like your mother. This is, one might observe, the first recorded your-mother joke in the *gemara*.

Rav Yitzchak then pushes back: but didn't Rav Yehuda himself teach from *Kohelet* the verse *u-motze ani mar mi-mavet et ha'isha* — I find the woman more bitter than death? Rav Yehuda's response: *kegon imach — mitzvavcha kefifa iburei ma'avra ummilla* — like your mother: there are times it is as constricting as a basket, but that too passes and the goodness returns. The picture of marriage that emerges here is not of unvarying bliss but of something that encompasses both bitterness and sweetness, and whose depth of satisfaction, over time, is irreplaceable.

---

## Kohanim Grooming

### Haircut Times

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita* laying out the haircut schedule for the three levels of sacred personnel: the king receives a haircut every day — *melech mistaper bechol yom* — because the verse says *melech be-yofyo techazenah eineicha*, a king should be seen in his beauty. The *Kohen Gadol* receives a haircut *me'erev Shabbat le'erev Shabbat* — once a week, every Friday. The ordinary *kohen* receives one *achat lishloshim yom* — once every thirty days.

### Mishmar Rotation

The reason the *Kohen Gadol* cuts his hair weekly is connected to the rotation of the *mishmarot* — the priestly divisions. Each week a new group of *kohanim* arrives at the *Mikdash* to begin their term of service, and the *Kohen Gadol* must appear dignified and well-groomed to receive them on that first day.

### 30-Day Cycle

The thirty-day cycle for the ordinary *kohen* is derived from a *gezeirah shavah* using the word *pera*. In *Yechezkel*, the verse reads *rosham lo yifrau ufera lo yeshalchu kasom yichsemu et rosheihem* — they shall not grow their hair in a disordered way but shall cut it regularly. And in the laws of *nazir*, the verse uses *gadel pera se'ar rosho*. The shared word *pera* links the two contexts: just as the minimum period of *nezirut* — and thus the minimum period over which *pera* can grow — is thirty days, so too the *kohen* must cut his hair at thirty-day intervals. The basis for the thirty-day minimum of *stam nezirut* is itself derived by Rav Matnah from *gematriya*: the verse *kadosh yihyeh* — *yihyeh* being *yud-heh-yud-heh*, which equals ten plus five plus ten plus five, totaling thirty.

### Challenge

Rav Pappa raises a challenge to Abaye: perhaps the instruction *pera lo yishalchu* should be read as requiring haircuts more often than every thirty days, or even as prohibiting any *pera* growth at all — that is, the *kohanim* should keep their heads entirely shorn at all times, not merely trim them periodically.

### Service Time

Abaye responds: the prohibition against *parua rosh* applies only *bizman biah* — at the time of entering the *Mikdash* for service. Outside of active service, it is no longer applicable. The analogy is to wine: just as wine is forbidden to a *kohen* only at the moment he is about to enter the *Mikdash* for service, and is entirely permitted to him when he is not serving, so too the prohibition on unkempt hair is tied exclusively to the moment of *biat haMikdash*.

---

## Wine & Service

### Wine Permitted

Since the prohibition on *parua rosh* applies only at the time of entering the *Mikdash*, the same is clearly true of wine: *kohanim* who are not currently on their *mishmar* and not entering the *Mikdash* to serve may drink freely.

### Yehuda View

Rabbi Yehuda dissents: *omer ani Kohanim assurim lishtot yayin l'olam* — I maintain that *kohanim* are forbidden to drink wine at all times, not only during service. Yet he concedes the practical reality: *aval mah e'eseh shetakanto kalkalato* — but what can I do? The very measure that would fix the situation is what ruins it.

### Future Ban

The logic of *takanto kalkalato* is striking. *Kohanim* currently drink wine — that is the established custom — and Rabbi Yehuda acknowledges this. But if the *Beit HaMikdash* were rebuilt — which is what all Jews pray for — the ban on wine would presumably resume. The incentives are, as one might observe, entirely backward: the thing that *kohanim* would presumably be praying for would result in their no longer being able to drink wine. Abaye identifies the relevant position: it is Rabbi Yehuda's view that permits current *kohen* wine-drinking, since in his framework the restriction is absolute in principle but deferred in practice due to the absence of the Temple. The majority opinion (*rabanan*), by contrast, restricts the prohibition to times of actual service, making the question of the Temple's rebuilding somewhat less dramatic in its practical implications. The reason the *rabanan* nonetheless do not require *kohanim* to maintain their haircuts every thirty days today is the same as the logic for wine: *meheira yibaneh Beit HaMikdash u-vainan Kohen haraoy l'avoda v'leika* — the Temple may be rebuilt at any moment, and we will need a *kohen* ready to serve. He can simply get a haircut and enter — *efshar d'mistaper v'ayel*.

### Drunkenness Cure

The *gemara* discusses the possibility of having a *kohen* sober up quickly in order to serve. Rav Acha teaches: *derech mil v'shaina kol shehu mefigin et ha-yayin* — walking a *mil* or taking even a brief nap will abate the effects of wine. However, Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuha, qualifies this significantly: *lo shanu ela sheshata k'dei revi'it* — this applies only if he drank up to a *revi'it*. If he drank more than a *revi'it*, walking and sleeping will in fact intensify the intoxication rather than mitigate it.

---

## Profaning Service

### Death Penalties

The *gemara* now establishes that entering the *Mikdash* in a state of intoxication carries the death penalty. The source is explicit: the verse in *Vayikra* states *yayin ve-shechar al tesht atah u-vanecha itach velo tamutu* — do not drink wine or strong drink, you and your sons with you, lest you die. What of *parua rosh* — entering without the proper haircut? That prohibition is explicitly stated in *Yechezkel*: *rosham lo yifrau u-fera lo yeshalchu*. The *gemara* derives that just as intoxication in the Temple carries the death penalty, so too does officiating with unkempt hair, via the *heikesh* — the juxtaposition of the two prohibitions in the verse.

### Profaning Avodah

The *gemara* further derives that both wine and *parua rosh* profane the *avodah* — *machil avoda*. The verse draws together both prohibitions, and the parallel structure implies that just as serving drunk constitutes *chilul ha-avodah*, so too does serving with disordered hair.

### Before Yechezkel

Ravina poses a classic question to Rav Ashi: *hai ad delo ata Yechezkel man amrah* — before *Yechezkel* recorded these verses, what was the source for these *halachot*? This is a recurring concern in the *gemara* whenever a *halacha* appears to rest on a late prophetic text: were these rules simply unknown beforehand?

### Mesorah

Rav Chisda answers: *davar zeh mi-torat Moshe Rabbeinu lo lamdanu ad sheba Yechezkel ve-limdanu* — this matter was not taught to us explicitly from the Torah of Moses our teacher until Yechezkel came and taught it. The tradition itself existed — *gemara gemiri lah* — as an oral *mesorah* going back to Sinai. Yechezkel did not innovate the *halacha*; he gave it explicit textual grounding. The *gemara* draws an analogy: just as Yechezkel grounded other long-standing oral traditions in written verse, so too here — *ve'ata Yechezkel ve'asmachah akra* — he came and anchored the received tradition to a *pasuk*.

---

## High Priest Hair

### Lulianit Style

The *gemara* now asks: what exactly is the *tisporet* described in the verse *rosham lo yifrau u-fera lo yeshalchu*? The *tana* answers: *kemin tisporet lulianit* — something like the *lulianit* haircut. What is the *tisporet lulianit*? Rav Ashe explains: *rosho shel zeh betzad ikaro shel zeh* — the tip of one hair lies adjacent to the root of the next. This seems to describe a style in which the hair is so uniformly and carefully cut that each hair's end is flush with the base of the next — suggesting either an extremely precise, closely-cropped look, or perhaps a layered, curved arrangement. The *Rambam* describes it as hair cut uniformly short so that no hair folds over another, resembling a closely harvested field. Some have suggested the term *lulianit* — related to the word for a trapeze or acrobat — implies a curved, looping style where each hair arcs back toward the scalp. The precise visual remains somewhat elusive.

### Ben Alasha

When Rabbi was asked to describe the *Kohen Gadol*'s haircut, he did not attempt a verbal description but instead directed his questioners: *tze'u ur'u mi-tisporet shel Ben Elasha* — go out and observe the haircut of Ben Alasha. Ben Alasha apparently maintained this distinctive style in his own appearance, making him a living demonstration of the *Kohen Gadol*'s haircut.

### Display Purpose

A *baraita* records Rebbe's explanation of why Ben Alasha spent lavishly on his haircuts: *lo al chinam pizer Ben Elasha mamon rav ela kedei lehar'ot bo tisporet shel Kohen Gadol* — it was not for vanity that Ben Alasha spent so much money on his hair, but specifically to display and preserve the knowledge of what the *Kohen Gadol*'s haircut looked like. In a world without a functioning Temple, without a *Kohen Gadol* actively serving, Ben Alasha took it upon himself to embody and transmit this *halacha* through his own appearance — a remarkable act of living *mesorah*. The very fact that such concerns were maintained with such care speaks to the seriousness with which the restoration of the *Beit HaMikdash* was anticipated.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 23

## Perek III Intro

### Context & Opening

Sanhedrin 23a opens the third *perek* of the tractate, and in doing so circles back to the very beginning of *Masechet Sanhedrin*. The first three words of the new *mishna* — *dinei mamonot bishlisha*, monetary cases require three judges — are of course familiar, since that is precisely how the entire tractate began. The *Rambam* explains that the reason this phrase recurs here is that the second *perek* took us on something of a detour, addressing the relationship of the *kohen gadol* and the *melech* to the *beit din*. Now we return to *dinei mamonot bishlisha*, and this *perek* will focus on a different question: how does one actually constitute such a court? Who gets to be among the three who sit in judgment over these monetary cases?

### Mishna Translation

The *mishna* itself is not entirely clear, and as it turns out, the *gemara* will spend considerable time — across multiple *amudim* — simply trying to determine what the *mishna* means. For that reason, it is worth reading and translating it first before attempting any deeper analysis.

*Dinei mamonot bishlisha* — monetary cases require three *dayanim*. *Zeh borer lo echad vezeh borer lo echad* — this litigant chooses one, and the other litigant chooses one. The *gemara* will address what exactly "one" refers to. *Ushneihem borerim lahen od echad* — and the two of them choose one more. The question of who precisely "the two of them" refers to will likewise depend on how the *mishna* is read. *Divrei Rabbi Meir* — this is Rabbi Meir's position. *Vachachamim omrim shnei dayanim borerim lahen od echad* — the Sages say that the two *dayanim* choose one additional *dayan*. From this formulation, it becomes clear that in the *reisha*, "the two of them" who each choose one *dayan* must be the two litigants — since the *Chachamim* explicitly say it is the two *dayanim* (not the litigants) who choose the third.

*Zeh posel dayno shel zeh vezeh posel dayno shel zeh, divrei Rabbi Meir* — this litigant can invalidate the other's *dayan*, and vice versa; this is Rabbi Meir's view. *VeChachamim omrim eimatai bizman shemevi aleihem ra'ayah shehen kerovim o pesulim* — the Sages say: when can he do this? Only when he brings proof that the *dayan* is related to the other litigant, or is *pasul* for some other reason. *Aval im hayu kesherim, eino yachol leposlan* — but if they are *kosher*, he cannot disqualify them.

The *mishna* continues with a parallel ruling regarding witnesses. *Zeh posel ido shel zeh vezeh posel ido shel zeh, divrei Rabbi Meir* — each litigant can invalidate the other's witness; this is Rabbi Meir's view. The *Chachamim* repeat their position: only when he can prove they are related or *pesulim* for another reason; but if they are *kesherim*, he cannot *posel* them.

---

## Mai Zeh Borer

### Gemara Question

The *gemara* opens with the question *mai zeh borer lo echad vezeh borer lo echad, bitlata sagi* — what does this mean, "this one chooses one and this one chooses one"? Three *dayanim* would suffice; why does the *mishna* speak of this elaborate procedure of choosing? According to Rashi's reading, the *gemara*'s initial assumption is that *echad* in the *mishna* means one entire *beit din* of three judges — meaning each litigant selects a full *beit din*, yielding six judges, and then together they choose a third *beit din*, yielding nine. The *gemara* finds this puzzling: we only need three.

---

## Perek III Intro (II)

### Rashi: Full Beit Din

Rashi explains the *pshat* of the *mishna* as follows: *zeh borer lo beit din echad shehem shlosha, vezeh echad, harei shisha* — this one chooses one full *beit din* of three, and the other chooses another, giving six. *Ushneihem borerim lahen od echad, harei tisha* — and together they choose a third *beit din*, giving nine. And that, says Rashi, is precisely the force of the *gemara*'s surprised question: *mai zeh borer, ha bitlata sagi* — why go through all of this when three judges are sufficient?

### Tosafot Dispute

Tosafot disagree with Rashi's reading of the *mishna*'s *pshat*. They maintain that the *gemara* knows from the outset that *echad* simply means one *dayan*, not one *beit din*, and that the straightforward reading of the *mishna* is that each litigant chooses one judge and together they choose a third. According to Tosafot, the *gemara*'s question is not asked out of genuine puzzlement about the *mishna*'s meaning; rather, it is posed as a kind of leading question in order to introduce an additional ruling — namely, the scenario in which one litigant selects a *beit din* and the other rejects it, and they must then choose a third *beit din* together. The *gemara* asks the question in order to bring that case as an answer, even though it already knows that is not the primary *pshat* of the *mishna*.

---

## Mai Zeh Borer (II)

### Beit Din Rejection

With this framework in place, the *gemara* proceeds to answer its own question. *Hachi ka'amar* — this is what the *mishna* means: when Reuven selects a *beit din* and Shimon objects, and then Shimon proposes a different *beit din* and Reuven objects, neither of those first two courts is used. Instead, *shneihem borerim lahen od echad* — together they choose a third *beit din*. This is the scenario the *gemara* had in mind when it asked *mai zeh borer*.

### Debtor Power Issue

The *gemara*, however, immediately raises a difficulty against this proposed answer. It notes the apparent contradiction with a ruling of Rav Elazar cited later in the tractate: *lo shanu ela malve, aval love kofin oto vedan be'iro* — the rule that a litigant may reject the other's *beit din* applies only to the creditor (*malve*), but the debtor (*love*) is compelled to appear before the court in his own city. If the *love* has no power to reject the *malve*'s *beit din*, how can the *mishna* contemplate a scenario in which the *love* does exactly that?

### Rabbi Elazar Ruling

Rav Elazar's ruling thus creates a problem for the reading of the *mishna* just proposed: the *mishna* seems to assume that either litigant may reject the other's court, while Rav Elazar limits that power to the creditor alone.

### R. Yochanan: Non-Expert

The *gemara* resolves this tension through Rabbi Yochanan's ruling in a different context: *be'arkaot shebe'Surya shanu* — our *mishna* is speaking specifically about non-professional courts. When the *beit din* consists of three *dayanim* who are not *mumchin* — who are not well-versed experts in *dinei mamonot* — then even the *love* can legitimately object, because there is valid grounds for preferring a different court. The *love* is not acting capriciously; he has a substantive reason to reject *dayanim* who are not professionally competent. *Aval mumchin lo* — but if the *dayanim* are expert professionals, the *love* cannot reject the creditor's court, and we revert to Rav Elazar's ruling.

### Rav Pappa Clarif.

Rav Pappa offers a further nuance. Even if one assumes the *mishna* is speaking of expert courts — *afilu teima mumchin*, such as the courts of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda — the *love* may still object, on the grounds that *mi ka matrachna lach* — I am not causing you a significant burden (*tircha*) by asking you to go to the other *beit din*, because both courts are equally accessible. Rashi explains that Rav Elazar's ruling — that the *love* cannot impose on the *malve* — is premised on the *love* causing undue *tircha*, such as requiring the *malve* to travel to a different city. But where both courts are located in the same city, no such *tircha* is imposed, and even the *love* may insist on a different court. Tosafot extend this somewhat, suggesting that even courts within a certain distance — less than three *parsaot* — would satisfy this condition.

---

## Reject Beit Din Interp.

### Logic Problem

Having explored the reading of the *mishna* as referring to *batei din*, the *gemara* now returns to reject this interpretation entirely. The *mishna* states: *vachachamim omrim shnei dayanim borerim lahen od echad* — the Sages say the two *dayanim* choose a third. If the earlier part of the *mishna* meant that each litigant chose an entire *beit din*, it would make no sense for those two *batei din* — having rejected each other — to then convene together and choose a third *beit din*. *Beit din batar depasli lehu azlu uvararu lehu beit dina achrina* — two courts that have just invalidated each other are not going to collaborate on selecting a third. The scenario is logically absurd.

### One Judge Each

There is also a linguistic problem with the *beit din* reading. The *mishna* uses the word *echad* — one. One does not mean one *beit din*; *echad* means one *dayan*. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ela hachi ka'amar* — this is what the *mishna* actually means. *Keshezeh borer lo dayan echad vezeh borer lo dayan echad, shneihem borerim lahen od echad* — when this litigant chooses one *dayan* and the other litigant chooses one *dayan*, the two of them together choose a third.

### Fairness Purpose

The *gemara* then asks *mai shena de'avdi hachi* — why is this the proper procedure? The answer comes from the *amora'im* in the West (*amri bema'arava*) in the name of Rabbi Zeira: *mitoch shezeh borer lo dayan echad vezeh borer lo dayan echad ushneihem borerim lahen od echad, yetzei hadin la'amito* — because this arrangement produces the truest and most reliable judicial outcome. Both Rashi and the Rambam emphasize that this structure is the surest guarantee of a fair result, and it also puts the losing litigant's mind at ease. Whoever loses will be able to say: I chose my own *dayan*, and he tried his best to rule in my favor; the fact that the court ruled against me means the *din* must be correct.

---

## Rabbi Meir Dispute

### Judges' Knowledge

With the *pshat* of the *mishna* now established — each litigant chooses one *dayan*, and together they choose a third — the *gemara* turns to the *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* regarding who selects that third *dayan*. The *gemara* wonders whether this dispute might be rooted in an earlier *machloket* between Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rav: *ein ha'eidim chotmin al hashtar ela im ken yod'im mi chotam imahen* — witnesses should not sign a document unless they know who else is signing with them. Rashi explains the reason: *shema yachtimu imahem ed echad pasul* — lest an invalid witness sign alongside them, thereby invalidating the entire testimony and causing them embarrassment.

This ruling is supported by a *baraita*: *kach hayu niki'ei hada'at shebe'Yerushalaim osin* — this was the practice of those of refined sensibility in Jerusalem. They would not sign a document unless they knew who was signing with them; they would not sit in judgment unless they knew who their fellow *dayanim* would be; and they would not enter a *se'udah* unless they knew with whom they would be *meisav*. The first two practices follow naturally from legal and halakhic concerns. The third — not dining without knowing one's company — reflects something beyond the strictly legal: the importance of the company one keeps, the dignity associated with a formal meal in rabbinic culture. Rashi's comment suggests this reflects concern for the honor of Torah scholars, though the text uses the term *niki'ei hada'at* rather than *chachamim*, which raises the question of whether this is a distinct category with only partial overlap.

### R. Meir: Full Consent

The *gemara* proposes that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* tracks precisely this earlier *machloket*. Rabbi Meir — who holds that both litigants together choose the third *dayan* — would *not* hold like Rabbi Yehuda's ruling in the name of Rav. In other words, Rabbi Meir is not concerned that the two *dayanim* might be embarrassed by the third turning out to be *pasul*. Rather, Rabbi Meir's position reflects a different concern: that the litigants themselves must have full buy-in (*da'at ba'alei dinim*) into the composition of the *beit din*. According to Rabbi Meir, a *beit din* requires the consent of both litigants to all three *dayanim*; without that, the court lacks proper authority.

### Chachamim: Judges Agree

The *gemara* rejects this proposed alignment. *De'chulei alma is lehu deRabbi Yehuda amar Rav* — everyone agrees with Rabbi Yehuda's ruling in the name of Rav that witnesses (and by extension *dayanim*) must know who their counterparts are. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* is not about whether the *dayanim* need to know who the third *dayan* is — all agree they do — but rather about whether the *litigants* also need to know and consent to the third *dayan*. *Rabbi Meir savar da'at ba'alei dinim nami ba'inan* — Rabbi Meir holds that the litigants' consent is also required. *VeRabbanan savri da'at hadayanim ba'inan da'at ba'alei dinim lo ba'inan* — the *Chachamim* hold that the *dayanim*'s agreement on the third is sufficient; the litigants need not consent.

This surfaces a broader theme that runs throughout this entire *sugya*: whence does a *beit din* derive its authority? If three people simply sit down and declare themselves a *beit din*, does that automatically grant them judicial power? The emerging principle seems to be that a *beit din* of recognized professionals (*mumchin*) established in a town possesses authority automatically. But where the *dayanim* are not *mumchin*, the court requires the buy-in of the litigants — without it, the *beit din* has no real power over them.

### Language Analysis

The *gemara* then cites the later part of the *mishna* to further examine this question — *gufah*, returning to the *baraita* quoting Rabbi Yehuda's ruling — *ein ha'eidim chotmin al hashtar*, and confirming that this is cited as support. At this point the *gemara* begins addressing the second part of the *mishna* — the disqualification of witnesses — a subject which introduces its own complexities.

---

## Witness Disqualif.

### Disqualif. Problem

The *mishna* states, according to Rabbi Meir, that *zeh posel dayno shel zeh* — one litigant may invalidate the other's *dayan*. The *gemara* asks: *kol keminei depasil dayanei* — can anyone simply come along and disqualify a judge at will? This seems untenable. The *gemara* invokes Rabbi Yochanan's answer: *be'arkaot shebe'Surya shanu* — the *mishna* is speaking of non-professional courts, courts in which the *dayanim* are not *mumchin*. In those cases, a litigant may object. *Aval mumchin lo* — but for professional *dayanim*, no, one cannot simply disqualify them.

However, the *gemara* immediately challenges this reading from the *seifa* — the latter clause — of the *mishna* itself: *VeChachamim omrim eimatai bizman shemevi aleihem ra'ayah shehen kerovim o pesulim, aval im hayu kesherim umumchin mipi beit din eino yachol leposlan* — the *Chachamim* say that one may only disqualify where he brings proof that the *dayanim* are *kerovim* or *pesulim*, but if they are *kesherim* and *mumchin*, he cannot. This formulation implies that Rabbi Meir is indeed talking about *mumchin* — for the *Chachamim* respond specifically that *mumchin* cannot be disqualified. If Rabbi Meir were only talking about non-*mumchin*, the *Chachamim*'s response would be oddly framed.

The *gemara* attempts to defend the *arkaot shebe'Surya* reading by reinterpreting the *Chachamim*'s clause: *aval im hayu kesherim na'asu kemumchin mipi beit din ve'eino yachol leposlan* — if they are otherwise *kosher*, they become *like* certified *mumchin* by virtue of a *beit din*'s endorsement, and therefore cannot be disqualified. Under this reading, Rabbi Meir is saying that even technically *kosher* non-*mumchin dayanim* can be invalidated by a litigant, while the *Chachamim* say that once a *beit din* has endorsed them as *like mumchin*, they cannot be touched.

The *gemara* proceeds to reject even this reading. A *baraita* is cited: *ta shema* — Rabbi Meir's opponents say to him, *lo kol heimenu sheposel dayan shemumche larabbim* — not everyone may disqualify a judge who is publicly acknowledged as an expert. This implies that Rabbi Meir is indeed speaking about *mumchin*, and even so he allows disqualification. A further formulation — *lo kol heimenu sheposel dayan shehimchu rabbim aleihem* — clarifies: this refers not to the most elite expert, but to one whom the community has collectively invested with judicial authority, even without formal expertise in *dinei mamonot*. The *baraita* then states explicitly: *le'olam posel vehole'ch ad sheyekabel alav beit din shemumche larabbim, divrei Rabbi Meir* — according to Rabbi Meir, a litigant may continue disqualifying proposed *dayanim* until a *beit din* that is publicly recognized as authoritative is agreed upon.

This now makes it clear that the *arkaot shebe'Surya* reading cannot account for Rabbi Meir's position in the *mishna*. Rabbi Meir is speaking precisely about *mumchin*, and still permitting disqualification. The problem then sharpens when we turn to witnesses, since witnesses are always treated as *mumchin* by default — *eidim ke'mumchin dami* — and yet Rabbi Meir says *zeh posel edav shel zeh*: each litigant may invalidate the other's witnesses. If witnesses are automatically *mumchin*, and Rabbi Meir still allows invalidation, it cannot be that Rabbi Meir's *chiddush* is confined to non-*mumchin*. Even by *mumchin* — even by *dayanim* — Rabbi Meir must be saying the same thing.

### Reish Lakish

This leads to the striking intervention of Reish Lakish: *peh kadosh yomar davar zeh* — could a holy mouth such as Rabbi Meir say something so extreme, that a litigant may simply invalidate the other's *dayanim* and witnesses at will? Reish Lakish offers a radical re-reading: *tani edo edo* — read the *mishna* as saying *edo* (his one witness) rather than *edav* (his two witnesses). The *mishna* is not speaking about disqualifying multiple witnesses; it is speaking about one witness.

### One vs. Two Witnesses

The *gemara* immediately asks: *lemai* — to what end? *Ilima lemamon, Rachmana paslei* — if we are talking about monetary cases, a single witness is already invalidated by the Torah; one witness accomplishes nothing in a *din* of *mammon*. The *gemara* therefore suggests: *i lishvuah, heimnu heman ke'vei terei* — if we are talking about the case where a single witness obligates an oath (*shvuah*), then once the witness swears, he is believed like two witnesses — and in that case there would be no power to renege. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *le'olam lemamon, lo tzricha dekablei alei kevei terei* — we are in fact talking about a monetary case, but one in which the opposing litigant voluntarily accepted the single witness as though he were two witnesses. Just as a litigant may accept a *beit din* of non-*mumchin*, he may also accept a single witness in lieu of two. The *chiddush* of Rabbi Meir, according to Reish Lakish, is that even after making such an acceptance, and even after that witness has testified, the litigant may retract his acceptance. The *Chachamim* disagree: once the acceptance has been made, it cannot be revoked.

The scenario unfolds as follows: Reuven brings one witness. Shimon says, "I accept your single witness as valid." The witness testifies. Shimon then says, "I have changed my mind; I no longer accept him." Rabbi Meir says this retraction is effective. The *Chachamim* say it is not. One might observe that reneging in this situation is not without cost: the *dayanim* may well draw negative inferences from a litigant who rejects a witness only after hearing unfavorable testimony. Nevertheless, Rabbi Meir maintains the retraction is legally operative.

### Judge Acceptance

The *gemara* asks: *mai kamashma lan* — what is the *chiddush* here, given that this principle seems already to have been taught in an earlier *mishna*? That *mishna* states: *amar lo ne'eman alai aba, ne'eman alai avicha, ne'emanin alai shlosha roei vakar* — if one litigant says to the other, "I accept your father as a *dayan*," or "I accept my father," or "I accept these three cattle-herders" (who are ordinarily unqualified), *Rabbi Meir omer yachol lachazor bo* — Rabbi Meir says he may retract. *VeChachamim omrim eino yachol lachazor bo* — and the *Chachamim* say he may not. This is identical in structure to what Reish Lakish read in our *mishna*. What, then, does our *mishna* add?

### Both Mishnayot

*Tzricha* — both *mishnayot* are necessary. If we only had the *mishna* of *aba ve'avicha* — the father cases — we might have thought the *Chachamim* said he cannot retract specifically there because *aba ve'avicha*, for everyone else in the world who is not their child, would be *kesher* witnesses. Perhaps the *Chachamim* only restrict retraction when the accepted witness is one who is *kosher le'alma* — universally valid — just not for this particular litigant due to their familial relationship. But one might then think that for a single witness accepted as two — who is *pasul de'Oraita* for the entire world, not just for this litigant — even the *Chachamim* would agree with Rabbi Meir that retraction is possible. The case in our *mishna* is therefore necessary to teach that the *Chachamim* disallow retraction even there.

Conversely, if we only had our *mishna* — the case of one witness accepted as two — we might think Rabbi Meir only permits retraction in that case, since a single witness is universally *pasul* and the acceptance is inherently tenuous. But in the *aba ve'avicha* case, where the accepted individual would be *kosher* for everyone else, we might have thought Rabbi Meir agrees with the *Chachamim* that retraction is unavailable. The earlier *mishna* teaches that Rabbi Meir permits retraction even there. Both *mishnayot* are thus indispensable.

---

## Two Sets Witnesses

### Reject Reish Lakish

Having explored Reish Lakish's reading, the *gemara* now formally rejects it. *Ha midiktani reisha dayano vesifa eidav, alma davka katani* — the *reisha* of the *mishna* uses the word *dayano* (his *dayan*) and the *seifa* uses *eidav* (his witnesses). The *mishna* is clearly deliberate and precise in its language, shifting terms intentionally. If Reish Lakish were correct that *eidav* really means *edo* — one witness — the *mishna*'s precision in distinguishing *dayano* from *eidav* would be undermined. The linguistic evidence points against Reish Lakish's emendation.

### Family Flaw

Rabbi Elazar offers yet another explanation of our *mishna*. He says: *bevah hu ve'echad leposlan* — the litigant comes together with one other witness in order to disqualify the other's witnesses. That is, Shimon himself, along with a second witness, testifies that Reuven's witnesses are *pasul*. The immediate problem: *kol deminei nogea be'eduto* — Shimon is a *nogea badavar*, a party with a direct interest in the case. He stands to benefit from the disqualification of Reuven's witnesses, so how can he serve as one of the witnesses to their invalidity?

Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika answers: *kegon shekara alav arar* — this applies where there is already a public claim (*arar*) circulating that there is some flaw in the witness's status. Rashi defines *arar* here as a rumor — *shemetz shel pasul* — a hint or suggestion of *pesul* already in the air. The *gemara* then asks: *arar demai* — a rumor about what? If the rumor concerns theft — *arar degezelanuta* — Shimon is still *nogea be'eduto*, still a party with an interest. But if it is *arar depgam mishpacha* — a rumor concerning the witness's family status, perhaps that he is a slave, or that his lineage is not fully Jewish — then perhaps Shimon can bring a second witness to testify about this man's family.

### Family Bias Dispute

The *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* in this explanation turns on whether Shimon is still considered *nogea badavar* when he testifies about the witness's family. *Rabbi Meir savar hanei amishpacha ka mashadei vehu mimela ka pasil* — Rabbi Meir holds that Shimon is only testifying about the family; the disqualification of the witness follows automatically, as a byproduct. Since his testimony is about a matter external to the case itself — the man's lineage — he is not *nogea be'eduto* in a meaningful sense. *VeRabbanan savrei sof sof nogea be'eduto hu* — the *Chachamim* hold that at the end of the day, the practical effect of his testimony is to alter the outcome of his own case, and therefore he remains *nogea badavar* regardless of what he is formally testifying about.

### Rav Dimi Intro

At this point, Rav Dimi arrives from Eretz Yisrael with yet another reading of the *mishna*. He brings in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *machloket bishtei kitei eidim* — the *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* concerns a case involving two sets of witnesses. *DeRabbi Meir savar tzarich levarer veRabbanan savrei eino tzarich levarer* — Rabbi Meir holds that examination and verification (*levarer*) is required, while the *Chachamim* hold it is not. There are several ways to understand this, and the *gemara* will proceed to elaborate through the framework of the Rambam's reading.

---

## Rambam: Four Witnesses

### Multiple Witnesses

The Rambam's explanation — which is the clearest and most coherent reading of this *sugya* — sets up the case as follows. Reuven and Shimon have a monetary dispute. Reuven brings two witnesses who testify in his favor. Subsequently, Reuven brings two additional witnesses who corroborate the first two. Shimon then claims that one or more of these four witnesses is *pasul*.

### R. Meir: Prove Kosher

According to Rabbi Meir, *shomin lo* — we listen to Shimon's claim — *vene'emar leReuven hava re'ayah shehem kesherim* — and we require Reuven to prove that all four of his witnesses are *kosher*. The rationale: if Reuven had confidence in his witnesses, why would he bring two full sets? The very fact that he brought four witnesses testifying to the same matter suggests he knew one set was potentially compromised. Shimon's suspicion is therefore credible, and Reuven bears the burden of establishing the validity of his witnesses.

### Chachamim: No Proof

The *Chachamim* are not troubled by this inference. They hold *eino tzarich levarer* — Reuven need not prove the *kashrus* of his witnesses. The fact that he brought two sets of witnesses does not imply knowledge of a defect in one of them; a litigant may simply wish to strengthen his case with additional testimony. Reuven is presumed to have brought four witnesses in good faith, and Shimon's unsupported claim cannot compel an investigation. *Aval bekat achat divrei hakol eino yachol leposlan* — if Reuven brought only one set of witnesses, everyone agrees that Shimon cannot challenge their *kashrus* without proof.

### R. Yochanan Clarif.

The discussion continues in the context of Rav Dimi's report from Eretz Yisrael. Rav Ami and Rav Assi pose a question to Rabbi Yochanan: *ein sham ella kat achat mahu* — if only one set of witnesses is present, what is the *din*? Rabbi Yochanan notes that this has already been answered: with only one *kat*, everyone agrees the litigant cannot disqualify. The question is then refined: *ella nimtzeit kat sheniya krovim o psulim mahu* — what if Reuven brings two sets of witnesses, and one set turns out to be *pasul* or *karov* — can Shimon still press his claim and compel Reuven to prove the remaining two witnesses are *kosher*?

The Rambam suggests two possible readings of Rabbi Meir's position here. On one view, Rabbi Meir would say yes — since Reuven initially brought four witnesses, Shimon's suspicion remains operative even after one set is found to be invalid; Reuven must still prove the remaining two are *kesherim*. Alternatively, one might say that once we have identified *which* witnesses were *pasul*, the concern is resolved, and Reuven need not prove the validity of the remaining *kat*. The *gemara*'s resolution — *amar lahem kvar he'idu eidim harishonim*, the first witnesses have already testified — leaves some ambiguity, and Rashi notes it could be read either way. A parallel statement is attributed to Rav Ashi as well: *ika de'amri amar Rav Ashi kvar idu edut rishonim*.

---

## Bava Batra Parallel

### Document vs. Possess.

The *gemara* now proposes that the *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* in our *sugya* might parallel an older dispute from *Bava Batra*. *Nima biplugta deRabbi veRabban Shimon ben Gamliel ka miflegi* — perhaps Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* are disputing the same underlying principle as Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. The case from *Bava Batra*: a litigant comes to court with both a *shetar* (document of sale) and a claim of *chazaka* (three years of uninterrupted possession). These are analogous to two sets of witnesses: the *shetar* functions as one set of witnesses, and the *chazaka* as another.

### Rabbi: Document Wins

*Haba lidon be'shetar uve'chazaka, nidon be'shetar, divrei Rabbi* — Rabbi holds that when a litigant presents both a *shetar* and *chazaka*, he must adjudicate through the *shetar*. The *shetar* is the stronger and more primary form of proof. By claiming both, the litigant implicitly concedes the *shetar* is his fundamental basis, and he must rely on it.

### Rabban Shimon

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel nidon be'chazaka* — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says he may use *chazaka*. The *gemara* asks: does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel really mean the litigant *cannot* use the *shetar* if he has one? That would be strange. *Ela eima af be'chazaka* — rather, read it as: even *chazaka* suffices. He may use either the *shetar* or the *chazaka*; he is not compelled to produce the *shetar* simply because he mentioned it. The parallel to our *sugya* is thus: according to this reading, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds *eino tzarich levarer* — once the litigant has one valid form of proof, there is no obligation to verify the other. *VeRabbi Meir keRabbi* — Rabbi Meir in our case holds *tzarich levarer*, like Rabbi in *Bava Batra*: the existence of two sets of evidence creates an obligation to examine them both.

### Reconciliation

The *gemara* ultimately rejects this proposed alignment. *Lo, aliba deRabban Shimon ben Gamliel kuli alma lo peligi* — both Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* in our case agree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. *Peligi aliba deRabbi* — the *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* is entirely within the framework of Rabbi's position. *DeRabbi Meir keRabbi* — Rabbi Meir agrees with Rabbi that *tzarich levarer*. *VeRabbanan amri lach, ad kan lo ka'amar Rabbi hatam, ela be'chazaka demikoach shtara ka'atei* — the *Chachamim* say: Rabbi only required verification in *Bava Batra* because the *chazaka* there *emerged from* the *shetar*. There is an A-then-B relationship: the *chazaka* is grounded in and derived from the *shetar*, and therefore when a litigant claims *chazaka*, he is implicitly relying on the *shetar* as its source. Rabbi says we must therefore examine the *shetar* directly.

### Independent Witnesses

*Aval hakha, dehanei eidim lav mikoach eidim achrinei ka'atei, afilu Rabbi modeh de'eino tzarich levarer* — but in our case, two sets of witnesses are not A-then-B. One set of witnesses did not produce or generate the other. They are two independent, parallel testimonies. Therefore, even Rabbi — say the *Chachamim* — would agree that when a litigant brings two independent sets of witnesses, there is no obligation to verify both sets. The existence of one valid *kat* is sufficient; the other can simply be disregarded. There is no structural dependency between them that would obligate further examination.

We will stop here and resume with yet another explanation of our *mishna*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 24

## Witness vs Judge Disqual…

### Rav Dimi Intro

The daf opens at the bottom of 23b, with the *gemara* presenting two distinct traditions — brought by *tanna'im* who traveled from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel — regarding Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of the *mishna*'s ruling that *zeh posel dayano shel zeh ve-zeh posel dayano shel zeh*, "this one disqualifies the other's judge and the other disqualifies his judge." Yesterday's discussion established the interpretation of Rav Dimi, read through the Rambam's *pshat*: the *mishna* is addressing a case where a litigant brings two sets of witnesses. Since he has done so, it is apparent that he himself knows at least one set is *pasul*, and therefore if the opposing litigant challenges one of the witnesses as invalid, the burden of proof falls on the one who brought four witnesses to demonstrate that all of them are *kosher*.

### Ravin Migo Logic

A second tradition arrives with Ravin, who likewise cites Rabbi Yochanan: *ki ata Ravin amar Rabbi Yochanan: reisha be-edim pesulin ve-dayanim kesherin, migo de-paslei edim paslei nami dayane* — the *reisha* of the *mishna*, "this one disqualifies the other's judge," is a case where the witnesses are *pasul* and the judges are *kosher*, and yet, because (*migo*) we disqualify the witnesses, we disqualify the judges as well. Conversely, the *seifa* — *migo de-paslei dayane paslei nami edim* — addresses a case where the judges are *pasul* and the witnesses are *kosher*, and since we disqualify the judges, we disqualify the witnesses as well, because the entire proceeding has been rendered *pasul* and must begin from scratch.

This requires explanation, because at first glance the logic seems strange: what does the *pasul* status of witnesses have to do with the judges, who perform an entirely different function? Rashi addresses this under the heading of Ravin: the underlying principle is *migo be-alma*, here meaning not the familiar *migo* of monetary law (where we believe a claim because a stronger claim was available), but simply "since" or "because." The mechanism, as Rashi explains in the *seifa* of the *dibbur hamatchil*, is that once the challenging litigant has proven the truth of one of his claims — say, that the *edim* are *pasul* — we extend credibility to his remaining claim, namely that the *dayanim* are likewise *pasul*. The principle is that *she-nimtzu devarav emet*, since his words have proven true about one matter, we believe him regarding the other. This is the position of Rabbi Meir. If, conversely, the opposing party brings proof that the *dayanim* or *edim* in question are in fact *kosher*, that proof might suffice to rebut the claim even according to Rabbi Meir — but the *gemara* does not press that point.

### Rava Challenge

Rava challenges the *migo* logic: *bishlama migo de-paslei edim paslei nami dayane* — it is understandable that disqualifying the witnesses would also disqualify the judges, because *ika bei dina achrina*, one can always find other judges. The case is analogous to a mistrial in secular law: the proceeding is voided and begins anew, perhaps with a different panel, as the judges are not the evidentiary foundation of the case. But *ela migo de-paslei dayane paslei nami edim, ve-ha edim tafi leika* — how can we say that because the judges are *pasul*, the witnesses are also *pasul*, when there may simply be no other witnesses available?
