Everything rests on the witnesses; they are the *ikar* of the case. If the witnesses are disqualified solely by virtue of this *migo*, the claimant may be left with no legal recourse whatsoever.

The *gemara* resolves this: *lo tzricha, d'ika kat acher* — this ruling applies only where there is another set of witnesses available. The disqualification of the witnesses via the *migo* of the judges' *pasul* status is only operative when replacement witnesses exist. The question is then asked: *ha leika kat acher, mai?* — what is the law if no other set of witnesses exists? The answer: *hachi nami d'lo matzi paslei* — in that case as well, even if one of the judges is proven *pasul*, the witnesses are not automatically disqualified.

### Dimi vs Ravin

The *gemara* then observes: *hainu d'Rav Dimi* — this is essentially the same position as Rav Dimi, who held that Rabbi Meir's ruling (that a litigant can disqualify the other's witnesses or judges) only applies in a case involving two sets of witnesses. The *gemara* concludes: *ika beiniyahu migo* — the practical difference between Rav Dimi and Ravin lies precisely in whether we invoke this *migo* principle. Rav Dimi holds *lo amrinan migo* in this context; Ravin, citing Rabbi Yochanan, holds *amrinan migo*. According to Ravin, the *migo* is operative and therefore one litigant's proof of *pasul* status regarding one element of the proceeding extends credibility to his claim about the other element as well.

---

## Reish Lakish Solo Witness

### Reish Lakish Intro

The *gemara* returns (*gufa*) to a statement cited earlier. One interpretive approach to the *mishna* renders it as *zeh posel edo shel zeh ve-zeh posel edo shel zeh* — "this one disqualifies the other's witness," referring to a single witness. In other words, if one litigant brought only one witness, the opposing litigant, even after having accepted that witness as valid, may still declare him *pasul*. This reading was attributed to Reish Lakish.

### Reish Lakish Challenge

The *gemara* challenges this attribution: *ini?* — is this really what Reish Lakish said? The challenge arrives via a statement of Ulla: *ha-ro'eh et Reish Lakish be-veit ha-midrash ke-ilu oker harim ve-tochenan zeh ba-zeh* — one who observed Reish Lakish in the *beit midrash* was as though watching someone uproot mountains and grind them against one another. Rashi explains this as meaning that Reish Lakish rendered everything coherent and straightforward — *matiach u-makish zeh ba-zeh*, he would strike his arguments together with such force and clarity that nothing remained unclear. Rashi adds that Reish Lakish was known to be exceedingly *charif*, sharp in his analysis, yet it was said of him *derech anavah*, out of humility, that he praised Rabbi Meir with the phrase *peh kadosh*, "a holy mouth." The *gemara*'s *ini* is therefore not about the substance of *tani edo* but about the phrase *peh kadosh yomar davar zeh* — the surprise is that one as formidable as Reish Lakish would speak with such deferential praise of another. The transition into the aggadic passage that follows emerges from this observation.

---

## Eretz Yisrael vs Bav (II)

### Mutual Respect Comparison

Ravina resolves the rhetorical surprise of Reish Lakish's humble praise by reframing the *gemara*'s *ini* entirely: the point is not that Reish Lakish said something surprising, but that both Reish Lakish and Rabbi Meir — about whom Ulla said the same thing, *ke-ilu oker harei harim ve-tochenan zeh ba-zeh* — praised one another so extravagantly. *Hachi ka'amar*: come and see, *bo u-re'eh kama mechabevin zeh et zeh*, how much the scholars of Eretz Yisrael love and respect one another — unlike the scholars of Bavel, who are *charif* and harsh with one another.

### Rabbi Yossi Humble Defer…

The *gemara* illustrates *mechabevin zeh et zeh* with a concrete case. There was a time when Rabbi — referring to Rebbe, the *Nasi* — declared that it is *asur* to *lehatmin*, to insulate, cold food before *Shabbat*. Rashi explains the reasoning: insulating cold food might lead to insulating hot food, which is *asur de-rabbanan*. Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yossi then said to him: my father, Rabbi Yossi, *hitir lehatmin et ha-tzonen* — explicitly permitted the insulation of cold food. Upon hearing this, Rebbe immediately retracted: *kvar hora zaken* — "a *zaken* has already ruled on this matter," and he accepted Rabbi Yossi's position. This is the model of *mechabevin zeh et zeh*: even though Rebbe held his own ruling, out of respect for Rabbi Yossi and love for his fellow scholars, he deferred.

Rav Pappa adds a further observation: *bo u-re'eh kama mechabevin zeh et zeh* — and here is additional proof of how they respected one another. *De-ilu Rabbi Yossi kayam, haya kafuf ve-yoshev lifnei Rabbi* — had Rabbi Yossi still been alive, he himself would have sat before Rebbe in a posture of deference, bent and subordinate, *de-ha Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yossi memale makom avotav* — as is demonstrated by the fact that Rabbi Yishmael, who filled his father's place (*chashuv ke-aviv*, as Rashi says, he was regarded as important as his father), himself sat humbly before Rebbe. Yet here is what is striking: according to one reading, Rabbi Yossi was in fact a greater Torah scholar than Rebbe, and yet he would have deferred to Rebbe because Rebbe held the position of *Nasi*. The deference was not a function of inferior learning but of respect for institutional position. And still, when Rabbi Yishmael conveyed his father's ruling, Rebbe accepted it without contest — *kvar hora ha-zaken*.

### Noa'im vs Chovelim

Rav Oshaya opens a *midrashic* reading of a verse from Zechariah: *va-ekach li et shenei maklot, karati le-no'am u-le-echad karati le-chovelim* — "I took for myself two staffs; one I called *no'am* and one I called *chovelim*." *No'am*, pleasantness: *elu talmidei chachamim she-be-Eretz Yisrael, she-man'imin zeh la-zeh ba-halacha* — these are the Torah scholars of Eretz Yisrael, who are pleasant to one another in *halacha*. *Chovelim*, destructive or harsh: *elu talmidei chachamim she-be-Vavel, she-mechavelim zeh la-zeh ba-halacha* — these are the Torah scholars of Bavel, who are harsh with one another in *halacha*. Rashi notes that this harshness — *de-kamnatzchi zeh la-zeh be-divrei baraita u-shemu'ata* — because they compete and contend with one another over *baraitot* and *shemu'ot*, they actually lose something in their learning. The productive tension of genuine dialogue is replaced by combative disputation, and Torah is thereby diminished.

A second verse from Zechariah is then read: *u-shnei zeitim aleha* — the two olive trees alongside the menorah — interpreted by Rabbi Yitzchak as *elu talmidei chachamim she-be-Eretz Yisrael, she-nochin zeh la-zeh ba-halacha ke-shemen zayit* — the scholars of Eretz Yisrael are gentle with one another like olive oil. By contrast, *elu talmidei chachamim she-be-Vavel she-meririn zeh la-zeh* — the scholars of Bavel are bitter to one another, like a raw olive eaten directly from the tree, whose bitterness clings in the mouth for many minutes.

A third passage from Zechariah describes two women carrying a tub (*eifah*) between sky and earth, with stork's wings and wind within them. The destination of this tub is *Eretz Shinar*. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai interprets: *zo chanufah ve-gasut ruach she-yardu le-Vavel* — this is flattery and arrogance that descended to Bavel. The *gemara* immediately challenges: there is a tradition that *asarah kabin gasut yardu la-olam, tishah natlah Elam ve-achat kol ha-olam kulo* — ten measures of arrogance descended to the world, nine were taken by Elam (Persia) and one by the rest of the world combined. This seems to contradict the claim that *gasut ruach* went to Bavel. The *gemara* resolves: *ve-ishtarbovei de-ishtarbav le-Elam* — they became confused in transit and ended up in Elam. The proof is in the verse itself: *livnot lah bayit be-Eretz Shinar*, the *heh* in *lah* lacks a *mapik heh*, hinting that the destination was not firmly established — they were headed for *Shinar* but ended up in Elam. A further tradition is cited: *siman le-gasut ha-ruach, aniyut* — the marker of arrogance is poverty — and *aniyut le-Vavel nachit*, poverty did descend to Bavel. The *gemara* resolves: *mai aniyut? aniyut Torah* — this is poverty of Torah, as the verse says *achot lanu ktana ve-shadayim ein lah* — "we have a little sister and she has no breasts," referring, as Rashi indicates, to Daniel in Elam: *she-zachata lilmod ve-lo zachata lelamed* — she merited to learn but not to teach, meaning Daniel received Torah but had no disciples to whom he could transmit it.

---

## Eretz Yisrael vs Bav (II)

### Bavel Belula Meaning

The *gemara* asks: *mai Bavel?* — what is the meaning of the word *Bavel* itself? Rabbi Yochanan answers: *belula be-Mikra, belula be-Mishna, belula be-Talmud* — "mixed together" with Scripture, *Mishna*, and *Talmud*. The very name *Bavel* contains a pun on *belula*, meaning mixed or combined, and this is now offered as a compliment: the *Talmud Bavli* integrates all three sources of Torah — *pesukim*, *Mishna*, and *Talmud* — simultaneously. Rabbeinu Tam, cited in *Tosafot*, develops this further: the Sages taught that one should divide one's learning time three ways — one third *Mikra*, one third *Mishna*, one third *Talmud*. Because the *Talmud Bavli* incorporates all three, one who learns it is *yotzei* all three obligations without needing to divide one's time separately.

Against this stands Rabbi Yirmiya's reading of *ba-machshakim hoshivani ke-metei olam* — "He made me sit in darkness like the eternal dead" — which he applies to the *Talmud* of Bavel: *she-ein nochin zeh im zeh ve-talmuda safek be-yadam* — because the scholars are harsh with one another and in constant contradiction, their Torah is consequently diminished, sitting in darkness.

---

## Creditor Accepts Invalid

### Mishna Setup

The *gemara* now transitions to the next *mishna*, which had already been cited in the previous discussion. The *mishna* teaches: if one litigant says to the other, *ne'eman alai avikha, ne'emanin alai shlosha ro'ei bakar* — "your father is trusted by me," or "these three cowherd are trusted by me" — to serve as witnesses or judges even though *mi-ikar ha-din* they are *pasul*, Rabbi Meir says *yachol lachzor bo*, he may retract his acceptance, while the Sages say *eino yachol lachzor bo*, he may not retract. A second clause teaches: if one litigant is required to take a *shevua* and the other says *dor li be-chayei roshecha* — "swear to me on your life" — rather than the more severe *shevua* invoking the name of God, Rabbi Meir says he may retract and the Sages say he may not.

### Shmuel Creditor Debtor

The *gemara* opens with a statement of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: *machloket be-machul lach, aval be-eten lach divrei hakol yachol lachzor bo* — the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages concerns *machul lach*, the case where the creditor says "I forgive your debt" conditional on the *pasul* witnesses testifying. But in the case of *eten lach* — where the debtor says "I will pay you" upon the testimony of the *pasul* witnesses — everyone agrees he can retract, because *mi-de'oraita*, the rule of *ha-motzi me-chaveiro alav ha-ra'aya* means the burden of proof rests with the one extracting the money. Since the *pasul* witnesses cannot truly discharge that burden *mi-de'oraita*, the debtor's acceptance is not binding and all agree he may go back.

### Rabbi Yochanan Both Cases

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *be-eten lach machloket* — the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies specifically to the case of *eten lach*, where the debtor says "I will pay you" upon the testimony of the *pasul* witnesses. It is that acceptance — of the debtor himself — that is contested.

### Question Both or One

This raises a further question: according to Rabbi Yochanan, who places the *machloket* in the case of *eten lach*, what is the rule regarding *machul lach*? Is there also a *machloket* there, or does everyone agree that the creditor's acceptance is binding and he cannot retract? Or perhaps, as the other possibility holds, there is a *machloket* in both cases — both *eten lach* and *machul lach*.

---

## Rava Three Positions

### Rava Oath Case

Rava teaches: *machloket be-eten lach, aval be-machul lach divrei hakol ein yachol lachzor bo* — the *machloket* exists in the case of *eten lach*, but in the case of *machul lach* everyone agrees that one cannot retract. If one accepts this as Rabbi Yochanan's position — that the *machloket* is in *eten lach* alone, while *machul lach* is universally binding — then Rava's ruling aligns with Rabbi Yochanan. But if one says the *machloket* applies in both cases, then *Rava de-amar ke-man?* — whose opinion does Rava follow? In that case, *Rava ta'ama de-nafshei ka'amar* — Rava is expressing his own independent position, yielding a three-way dispute: some hold the *machloket* applies only to *machul lach* (Shmuel); some hold it applies only to *eten lach* (Rabbi Yochanan); and some hold it applies to both.

### Rav Acha Objection

Rav Acha bar Tachlifa raises a challenge to Rava from the second clause of the *mishna*: if one is obligated to take a *shevua* and the other says *dor li be-chayei roshecha*, Rabbi Meir says he may retract and the Sages say he cannot. Rava had said the *machloket* is in *eten lach* but not in *machul lach*. The question: does not this case of the *shevua* involve *machul lach* — the creditor effectively saying "take this lighter oath and I release you" — which would mean there *is* a *machloket* by *machul lach*, contradicting Rava?

### Nishba'in Cases

The *gemara* resolves by distinguishing two types of oath-takers. There are those who are *nishba'in ve-lo meshalmin* — they take an oath and are thereby exempted from payment. In that case, the creditor is saying: swear on your life and I will forgive the debt — which is structurally *machul lach*. But Rava's ruling in the *shevua* case concerns *nishba'in ve-notlin* — those who take an oath and then collect, such as a paid guardian (*shomer sachar*) from whom the object was stolen, who swears that it was stolen and thereby collects. The debtor in such a case is saying: I accept this lighter oath, and *eten lach* — I will pay you — which is structurally *eten lach*. Therefore the *shevua* case poses no contradiction to Rava.

### Both Clauses Needed

The *gemara* then addresses a potential redundancy: if the *seifa* of the *mishna* (the *shevua* clause) is also about *eten lach*, why do we need it when the *reisha* already established the *machloket* in *eten lach*? The answer is that *tanna tole be-da'at acherim* and *tanna tole be-da'at atzmo* — we need both because they differ in a critical way. The *reisha* (*avikha*, *avicha*, the cowherd witnesses) involves an acceptance that depends on others' intentions — the litigant is accepting witnesses or judges who are not himself, and Rabbi Meir might say he can retract because *mi yeimar de-mazkei lei*, perhaps he assumed they would testify in his favor and was not truly *gomer* in his commitment. But in the *seifa*, the case is *tole be-da'at atzmo* — the debtor himself decides to swear on his own life, which is his own *da'at*, and one might think he is fully committed and even Rabbi Meir would agree he cannot retract. Conversely, if we only had the *seifa*, we might think the Sages agree he can retract in the *reisha* because the acceptance was based on others' intentions and therefore was never fully binding. Both clauses are therefore necessary, *tzericha*.

---

## Before vs After Judgment

### Reish Lakish Position

A parallel structural debate now emerges, this time concerning the temporal dimension of the *machloket*. Reish Lakish says: *machloket lifnei gmar din, aval le-achar gmar din divrei hakol ein yachol lachzor bo* — the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages concerns what happens *before* the judgment is finalized. Once *gmar din* has occurred, everyone agrees that neither party can retract their acceptance of the *pasul* witnesses or judges. Concretely: if Reuven brings his father as a witness, Shimon accepts him, the father testifies, and Shimon loses the case, according to Reish Lakish Shimon can no longer invoke Rabbi Meir's position to challenge the father's testimony — the judgment is final.

### Rabbi Yochanan Dispute A…

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *le-achar gmar din machloket* — even after the judgment has been rendered, the *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the Sages remains live. That is, Rabbi Meir would hold that even after the judgment is finalized, a party could still challenge the *pasul* witnesses or judges he had previously accepted.

### Rava Temporal Proof

The *gemara* raises a question about Rabbi Yochanan's position: *le-achar gmar din machloket, aval lifnei gmar din divrei hakol yachol lachzor bo?* — does Rabbi Yochanan mean the *machloket* applies only after *gmar din*, while before *gmar din* everyone agrees one can retract? Or perhaps there is a *machloket* both before and after?

Rava provides an answer: *kibel alav karov o pasul lifnei gmar din yachol lachzor bo, le-achar gmar din ein yachol lachzor bo* — if someone accepted a relative (*karov*) or otherwise *pasul* witness before the conclusion of the judgment, he may retract; after *gmar din*, he cannot.

### Question Temporal Scope

This teaching of Rava now becomes a proof. The *gemara* reasons: if one takes the position that the *machloket* is only after *gmar din*, while before *gmar din* everyone agrees one can retract — then Rava's ruling reflects Rabbi Yochanan's position, specifically the opinion of the Sages (*aliba de-rabbanan*). Before *gmar din*, even the Sages agree one can retract (*yachol lachzor bo*); after *gmar din*, the Sages hold one cannot (*ein yachol lachzor bo*), and it is only there that Rabbi Meir would disagree. Rava's ruling — before *gmar din* one can retract, after *gmar din* one cannot — fits precisely with Rabbi Yochanan as understood according to the Sages.

But if one says the *machloket* exists both before and after *gmar din*, then *Rava de-amar ke-man?* — Rava's ruling cannot be attributed to any consistent position, since he holds one can retract before *gmar din* but not after, which would mean he follows the Sages on one side and no one in particular on the other.

### Conclusion After Judgment

The *gemara* concludes: *ela lav, shema mina le-achar gmar din machloket* — we must therefore conclude, according to Rabbi Yochanan (as demonstrated by Rava), that the *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies only after *gmar din*. Before *gmar din*, the rule is *divrei hakol yachol lachzor bo* — all agree that one may retract his acceptance of a *pasul* witness or judge. *Shema mina*.

---

## Geonic Rulings Kinyan

### Nachman Correspondence

The *gemara* records a correspondence: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda sent a question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: *yelamdenu rabbeinu* — teach us, our master — *lifnei gmar din machloket o le-achar gmar din machloket?* Is the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages located before *gmar din*, as Reish Lakish holds, or after *gmar din*, as Rabbi Yochanan holds? And what is the practical *halakha*?

### Halakha Chachamim

The reply: *le-achar gmar din machloket*, the *machloket* is after *gmar din* — following Rabbi Yochanan. *Ve-halakha ke-divrei chachamim*: the *halakha* follows the Sages, which means that after *gmar din* one may not retract the acceptance of a *pasul* witness or judge.

### Rav Ashi Question

Rav Ashi reports that the question sent was actually framed differently: *be-eten lach machloket o be-machul lach machloket?* — is the *machloket* in the case of *eten lach* (the debtor accepting the *pasul* testimony as grounds for payment) or in the case of *machul lach* (the creditor accepting it as grounds for forgiveness)? And who is the *halakha* like?

### Rav Ashi Answer

The reply: *be-eten lach machloket* — the *machloket* is in the case of *eten lach*, following Rabbi Yochanan. *Ve-halakha ke-divrei chachamim* — the *halakha* follows the Sages, meaning that once the debtor has said *eten lach* and the case has proceeded, he cannot retract.

### Kinyan Exception Final

The *gemara* then notes a distinction between the academies of Sura and Pumbedita. In Sura they taught as above. In Pumbedita, Rav Chanina bar Shalmaya relates that a question was sent from the *bei rav* to Shmuel: *yelamdenu rabbeinu, lifnei gmar din ve-kanu mi-yado, mai?* — if all of this occurred before *gmar din* but an act of *kinyan* had been performed — what is the *halakha*? The reply: *ein le-achar kinyan klum* — after a *kinyan* has taken place, nothing can be undone. Once a *kinyan* is performed, even Rabbi Meir agrees with the Sages that the acceptance is fully binding and there is no further possibility of retraction. The reasoning becomes clear: *kinyan* constitutes *gmar da'at* — a decisive, finalized act of will — and once the debtor has both declared his acceptance and performed an act of acquisition, his commitment is unambiguous and irrevocable.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 25

## Intro & Psulei Edut

### Opening Remarks

The Mishna on Sanhedrin 25a introduces a category of individuals who are *pasul* — disqualified — both for *edut* (bearing witness) and for *dayanut* (serving as judges). The Mishna appears as a continuation of the preceding discussion: having established in the previous Mishna that one may in certain contexts rely on a technically disqualified witness, the Mishna now proceeds to identify precisely who those disqualified individuals are.

### Rashi's Framework

Rashi, in his comment under the *dibur hamatchil* of *hamasachek be-kubiya*, offers a general introduction to the entire Mishna: *kulan me'ein gazlanim hen* — all of these individuals are, in some sense, akin to thieves. The Torah states *al tashet rasha ed* — do not place a wicked person as a witness — and Rashi derives by *kal va-chomer* that all the more so, a *rasha* may not serve as a *dayan*. This framework of quasi-theft governs the Mishna's logic throughout.

### Categories Listed

The Mishna enumerates the following disqualified individuals: *hamasachek be-kubiya* — one who plays dice or engages in this gambling game (in modern Hebrew, *kubiyot* are dice, though the Gemara will clarify the precise nature of this game); *hamalveh be-ribit* — one who lends money on interest; *mafrichei yonim* — those who fly pigeons or doves, the precise meaning of which the Gemara will explain; and *sochrei shevi'it* — those who trade commercially in produce of the *shemita* year, one of whose stipulations is that one may not profit from produce grown that year.

The Mishna adds a statement of Rabbi Shimon: at first these individuals were called *osvei shevi'it* — those who merely gathered *shevi'it* produce — but once tax collectors proliferated, the designation shifted to *sochrei shevi'it*, traders in *shevi'it* produce. The Gemara will explain what lies behind this shift in terminology.

### R. Yehuda's Condition

Rabbi Yehuda qualifies the preceding list: *eimatai* — when does the disqualification apply? Only *bizman she'ein lahem omanut ela hu* — when these activities are their sole occupation and they have no other trade. But if they do have another legitimate occupation, they are *kasherin*. The Gemara will address at length whether Rabbi Yehuda is here disagreeing with the *tanna kamma* of the Mishna or merely clarifying and elaborating upon it.

---

## Dice Player Debate

### Rami: Asmakhta Theory

The Gemara opens its analysis with a question: *hamasachek be-kubiya mai ka'avid* — what exactly has the dice player done wrong? Rami bar Chama answers: *mishum de-hava asmakhta ve-asmakhta lo kanya* — because it constitutes an *asmakhta*, and an *asmakhta* does not effect a legal acquisition. The principle of *asmakhta*, encountered in Bava Batra and elsewhere, holds that when a person makes a stipulation predicated on an assumption — typically that a certain outcome will obtain — the underlying transfer of ownership is not halachically valid, because the person never genuinely resolved to relinquish his money. The classic case is one who owes a debt and says: if I do not repay by a certain date, I will pay double — he assumes he will pay on time and never truly commits to the penalty. So too, says Rami bar Chama, each gambler assumes he will win, and therefore never truly relinquishes ownership of the money he stakes. When the other party collects, he is taking money whose ownership was never genuinely transferred — rendering him, in effect, a thief.

### Rav Sheshet: Yishuvo

Rav Sheshet disagrees: *kol ki hai gavna lav asmakhta hi* — this type of case is not an *asmakhta* at all. Rashi explains the distinction carefully: a true *asmakhta* is one where the person relies on some anticipated event and mistakenly believes it will not occur — *to'eh ve-savar lo yavo lidei kach*. But in the gambling context, the gambler does not know whether he will win or lose. Because the outcome is entirely uncertain, and he stakes his money regardless, we say that *mi-sfeika gamar ve-aknei* — he fully resolves, even out of uncertainty, to transfer ownership. There is therefore no *asmakhta* problem, and the money is legitimately acquired by the winner.

Instead, Rav Sheshet offers an entirely different rationale for the disqualification: *ela le-fi she-ein asukin be-yishuvo shel olam* — it is because gamblers are not engaged in productive activity that benefits the world. The disqualification is not a function of the mechanics of acquisition but of the character of the person's occupation.

### Practical Difference

The Gemara identifies the practical difference between the two opinions: the case where the gambler has also learned another legitimate trade. According to Rav Sheshet, whose disqualification rests on non-productive activity, such a person would be *kasher* for testimony and judgment — he is, after all, contributing productively to society through his other trade. According to Rami bar Chama, however, whose disqualification rests on the *asmakhta* doctrine and the quasi-theft involved, the existence of another trade is irrelevant — the gambler remains, in effect, a thief regardless of his other occupation.

One might ask whether a *batlan* — a person who is simply idle and does nothing — would similarly be disqualified under Rav Sheshet's reasoning. The answer is probably not, because *asukin be-yishuvo shel olam* implies not merely the absence of productive activity but the presence of something actively harmful alongside that absence.

### Mishna Challenge

The Gemara raises a powerful challenge to Rami bar Chama from the Mishna itself: Rabbi Yehuda says *eimatai* — the disqualification applies only when the person has no other occupation, but if he does, he is *kasher*. This strongly implies that the rationale underlying the Mishna is indeed *yishuvo shel olam* — lack of productive engagement — which would support Rav Sheshet and contradict Rami bar Chama.

### Amatai = Clarification

The Gemara responds that one might think Rabbi Yehuda is arguing against the *tanna kamma*, but two Amoraic principles preclude this reading. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught: *kol makom she-amar Rabbi Yehuda eimatai u-vemah eino ela le-fareish divrei chachamim* — wherever Rabbi Yehuda says *eimatai* or *u-vemah*, he is coming to clarify and elaborate upon the position of the *chachamim*, not to dispute them. Rabbi Yochanan refines this: *eimatai* always signals clarification, while *u-vemah* signals disagreement. Since our Mishna uses *eimatai*, everyone agrees that Rabbi Yehuda is merely explicating the *tanna kamma* — and the Mishna therefore implies that the reason for disqualification is *yishuvo shel olam*, which is difficult for Rami bar Chama.

The Gemara resolves this by noting that Rami bar Chama may simply disagree with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan on the interpretive principle itself — *mar savar pligei u-mar savar lo pligei* — and maintains that Rabbi Yehuda's *eimatai* does signal genuine disagreement with the *tanna kamma*.

### Tarfon's Nezirot

The Gemara then introduces a *beraita* that initially seems to support Rami bar Chama's opponent but ultimately vindicates him. The *beraita* records Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Tarfon: two men are seated and a third passes by. One says, "I hereby become a *nazir* if that passerby is a *nazir*," and the other says, "I hereby become a *nazir* if he is not a *nazir*." After they discover the truth, one of them has evidently stated the correct condition — yet Rabbi Tarfon rules that *neither* of them becomes a *nazir*. The reason: *she-al ha-safek amar devarav techilla* — each spoke his declaration initially from a position of uncertainty. Since the verse requires *le-hafla* — an explicit, unequivocal declaration — and neither spoke with that certainty, neither achieves *nezirut*.

### Beraita Support

The Gemara draws the implication: according to Rabbi Tarfon, even when a person makes a conditional declaration regarding something that is entirely beyond his control and about whose outcome he is wholly ignorant, it is still an *asmakhta* — *afilu hachi havya asmakhta*. And we do not say *mi-sfeika gamar ve-aknei* — that the uncertainty itself generates a full resolve to transfer ownership or commit to the condition. This *beraita*, which represents the position of Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Tarfon, is thus a third opinion distinct from the *tanna kamma* of our Mishna, and it directly supports Rami bar Chama's position that gambling transactions are *asmakhta* and that the *masachek be-kubiya* is disqualified on those grounds.

---

## Interest Lender

### Rava on Borrower

The Mishna lists *hamalveh be-ribit* — the lender on interest — among the disqualified. Rava adds: *loveh be-ribit pasul* — not only the lender but also the borrower who takes a loan on interest is *pasul* for testimony. The Gemara challenges this from our Mishna, which specifies only *malveh*, the lender. Rava responds that the Mishna should be read as *milveh be-ribit* — a loan that comes with interest — indicating that anyone involved in an interest-bearing loan is disqualified. This would include both creditor and debtor, and there is a *machloket Rishonim* as to whether Rava's ruling extends further to the guarantor and the witnesses to the loan document — all of whom, according to the Mishna in Bava Kamma, transgress a *lav* by their involvement.

### Bar Binyatus Case

The Gemara presents a case: two witnesses came and testified about a man named Bar Binyatus. The first said, "In my presence, Bar Binyatus lent money with interest." The second said, "He gave *me* a loan with interest." Rava disqualified Bar Binyatus on the strength of this testimony.

### Self-Disqualification

The question arises: Rava himself ruled that a borrower who takes a loan with interest is *pasul* for testimony — meaning the second witness has himself admitted to a transgression that renders him a *rasha*. How, then, can his testimony be valid? The answer rests on Rava's own principle, stated elsewhere: *adam karov etzel atzmo ve-ein adam mesim atzmo rasha* — a person is considered his own *karov*, his own relative, and therefore cannot render himself a *rasha* through his own testimony. When the second witness says "he lent *me* money with interest," that portion of his statement cannot disqualify him personally — one cannot bear testimony against oneself in a manner that produces legal consequences for the speaker. However, the part of his testimony that pertains to Bar Binyatus — namely, that Bar Binyatus engaged in interest-lending — remains valid. Thus Rava accepts the testimony with respect to Bar Binyatus while disregarding its self-incriminating dimension.

---

## Shochet & Teshuva

### Shochet Caught

The Gemara relates an incident involving a *shochet* — a ritual slaughterer — who was found to have been selling *tereifot*, animals with pre-existing injuries that rendered them non-*kosher*, while passing them off as permissible meat. Rav Nachman disqualified him for testimony and removed him from his position as *shochet*. The *shochet* subsequently let his hair and fingernails grow as visible signs of contrition.

### True Repentance

Rav Nachman considered reinstating him. Rava intervened: *dilma iyarumei ka-mairim* — perhaps this is mere subterfuge. A man who knows what contrition looks like can simulate it. If external signs of mourning are insufficient, how does one genuinely establish *teshuva*? Rava cites Rav Idi bar Abin: a *shochet* suspected of selling *tereifot* has no remedy until he goes to a place where nobody recognizes him — where performance for an audience is impossible. There, he must demonstrate changed character through action: either he finds a valuable lost object and returns it to its owner — thereby demonstrating that he is no longer unscrupulous with money — or he identifies a *tereifa* among his own animals, an expensive one, and comes forward to declare it non-*kosher*, thereby absorbing a substantial financial loss in the service of honesty. Either act, performed without audience or incentive, constitutes credible evidence of genuine *teshuva*.

---

## Pigeon Flyers

### Two Interpretations

The Mishna lists *mafrichei yonim* among the disqualified. The Gemara asks: *mai mafrichei yonim* — what precisely is this? Two interpretations emerge. In Bavel, the term is understood to refer to pigeon racing: *i tadmi yonecha le-yon* — if your pigeon arrives before mine at a certain destination, you win a stipulated sum. This is a form of gambling.

### Arah Interpretation

Rabbi Chama bar Oshaya, from Eretz Yisrael, interprets the term as referring to an *ara* — a trained bird used to lure and attract other people's pigeons to the owner's home against their will. Rashi explains that this practice is not technically *gezel de-oraita*, since pigeons cannot be formally owned in the way that other property can, but the *chachamim* prohibited it as a form of theft — either as *tikkun olam* or as *darchei shalom*. Because it is only a rabbinic prohibition, the Mishna had to state it explicitly; had it been full biblical theft, the person would already be disqualified on those grounds without special mention.

### Reconciliation

The Gemara then asks: why does the Mishna list both *masachek be-kubiya* and *mafrichei yonim*? If *mafrichei yonim* means pigeon racing, it is essentially the same as gambling — why mention it separately? And conversely, if *mafrichei yonim* refers to *ara*, why mention *masachek be-kubiya* separately when pigeon racing would be subsumed under gambling? Each opinion responds symmetrically: the proponent of pigeon racing says that *ara* is only a rabbinic prohibition rooted in *darchei shalom* and would not on its own suffice to generate full disqualification — thus the Mishna would have had no reason to include it; the proponent of *ara* says that pigeon racing is no different from *kubiya* gambling and the Mishna would not have needed to repeat it.

### Dependency Analysis

The Gemara adds that even if both interpretations were accepted simultaneously, it would be necessary to teach both cases. The gambler at dice depends entirely on his own judgment and skill — *toleh be-da'at atzmo* — and therefore never fully resolves to relinquish his money, since he trusts in his own superiority. The pigeon racer depends on his pigeon — *toleh be-da'at yonah* — but he too may believe he knows how to bang the instruments that urge his pigeon on better than his opponent: *ana yad'ana le-nakushei tefei*. Conversely, if we knew only about the pigeon-dependent case, we might think the self-dependent gambler does fully resolve to transfer ownership since he is genuinely uncertain about his own capacities. And if we knew only about the self-dependent case, we might think the pigeon case involves a more genuine transfer. Both must therefore be taught: *tzricha*.

### Animal Fighting

A *beraita* from the Tosefta extends the categories. *Masachek be-kubiya* is defined as those who play with *fisfasin* — pieces of wood — but also with nutshells and pomegranate shells, reflecting various gambling implements. Repentance (*teshuva*) requires that they break their gambling tools and undertake *chazara gemura* — complete return — such that they would not even play the game for free, without money at stake.

*Milveh be-ribit*, the interest-bearing loan, applies to both creditor and debtor. Repentance requires tearing up the loan documents and resolving not to lend on interest even to a *nochri* — to whom lending with interest is technically permitted. Similarly, *mafrichei yonim* who fight pigeons — and the *beraita* extends the prohibition to those who fight other animals as well: *behema*, *chaya*, and *of*, domesticated animals, wild animals, and birds — must break their fighting implements (*pigmeihen*) and resolve not to engage in animal fighting even in the *midbar*, the wilderness, where there is no settled community to harm.

### Rashi's Caveat

Rashi notes that the *chazara gemura* clauses — requiring the offender to go beyond the letter of the law to demonstrate repentance — are not original parts of the *beraita*. They are later additions by the *stam* of the Gemara. Rashi's evidence for this is linguistic: the word *mozfei*, used in connection with the interest-lender's repentance (not lending even to a *nochri*), is Aramaic rather than Hebrew — it is not the vocabulary of a Tannaitic source. Similarly, the clause about not fighting animals even in the *midbar* is, Rashi observes, added to defend the interpretation of *ara*: if one races or fights pigeons, the locale would be irrelevant to the prohibition, but if the issue is luring other people's birds to one's home, then even in the *midbar* — where there are no other people's animals to steal — one must demonstrate restraint as a sign of full repentance.

---

## Shviit & Taxes

### Shviit Traders

The *beraita* continues with *sochrei shevi'it* — those who trade in *shemita* produce. Their repentance requires waiting until the next *shevi'it* year arrives and then refraining from the prohibited commerce. The wait of up to seven years reflects the severity of the offense and the need to demonstrate that the change in behavior is genuine rather than circumstantial.

### Monetary Repentance

Rabbi Nechemia adds that repentance in this domain requires not merely behavioral change but *chazarat mamon* — monetary restitution. The offender must declare explicitly: "I, so-and-so, have collected two hundred *zuz* through trading in *shevi'it* produce, and these funds are hereby given as a gift to the poor." The rationale is that *shevi'it* produce is designated for the poor to eat freely; the money derived from its illicit sale must therefore be directed to *aniyim*.

### Thieves & Chasmans

The *beraita* further records that the Sages added *gazlanim* — thieves — and *chamsanim* — violent takers — to the list of the disqualified. A *chamsan* is one who takes an item from another even when the owner objects, but pays for it nonetheless. The *gazlan* disqualification requires explanation: a *gazlan* commits an *issur de-oraita* and would obviously be *pasul* without any new ruling.

### Finding from Incapacitated…

The answer is that the ruling is necessary specifically for the case of one who takes a found object belonging to a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, or *katan* — a deaf person, a fool, or a minor. Since none of these three can halachically perform an act of *kinyan*, they technically cannot acquire a found object, and taking it from them would not constitute biblical theft. Nevertheless, the *chachamim* instituted a rabbinic prohibition against this *mipnei darchei shalom* — for the sake of social peace. Originally, the Sages did not include such a person among the disqualified for testimony, reasoning that the situation was uncommon. Ultimately, however, since this person is demonstrably unscrupulous with money, the Rabbis extended the disqualification to him as well.

As for the *chamsan*: originally the Sages reasoned that since he pays for what he takes, his behavior is merely objectionable — *akrai be-alma hu* — but not an expression of financial unscrupulousness. Once they observed that people were brazenly grabbing others' property and forcing payment — *kachatfei* — the Rabbis decreed the disqualification.

### Shepherds Added

The *beraita* records that shepherds (*ro'im*) were added to the disqualified list as well, along with two categories of tax collectors (*gabba'im* and *mochsin*). Regarding shepherds: originally the Sages assumed that when a shepherd's flock grazed in another's field, it was accidental — *akrai be-alma hu*. Once they observed that shepherds were deliberately guiding their animals into others' fields — as Rabbeinu Chananel explains, even throwing food ahead of the animals to lead them there — the Rabbis imposed disqualification.

### Tax Collectors

Tax collectors were originally trusted: the assumption was that they collected only what the ruler had assessed. Once it became clear that they were routinely taking more than their authorized quota — essentially stealing under cover of official authority — the Rabbis decreed them *pasul* for testimony.

---

## Shepherds Geography

### Rava's Claim

Rava rules that the disqualification of shepherds applies equally to shepherds of small animals (*behema dakka*) and shepherds of large animals (*behema gassa*).

### Contradiction Found

A contradiction is immediately raised: Rava himself stated elsewhere that a shepherd of small animals in Eretz Yisrael is *pasul*, whereas outside of Eretz Yisrael such a shepherd is *kasher*. And regarding large animals, Rava said that even in Eretz Yisrael such a shepherd is *kasher*. This appears to contradict his blanket ruling above.

### Resolution via Context

The resolution: Rava's second, more lenient statement — which permits the shepherd of small animals outside Eretz Yisrael and the shepherd of large animals everywhere — was stated in the context of *megadalim*, those who raise their animals domestically, within the home or city. A person who raises an animal in his own home is far less likely to allow it to graze in others' fields, and so the concern for unscrupulousness does not arise in the same way. The stricter ruling — disqualifying shepherds who take animals out to pasture — applies to those who actually work in the field.

### Rashi's Reason

Rashi explains why the rules differ between Eretz Yisrael and *chutz la-aretz* for small-animal shepherds: *be-Eretz Yisrael chamira tefei mishum yishuv Eretz Yisrael* — in Eretz Yisrael the matter is more serious because of the importance of *yishuv Eretz Yisrael*, the settled and flourishing habitation of the Land. Preventing the invasion of neighbors' fields preserves the quality of life and the integrity of land use in the Land of Israel, making the Rabbis more stringent about whom they regard as trustworthy.

### Mishna Support

The Gemara finds support for Rava's position in the previous Mishna, which stated: *ne'emanim alai sheloshah ro'ei vakar* — three cattle herders are trusted by me. The Gemara asks: trusted for what purpose? For bearing witness? The Gemara answers: no — *lo le-dina* — for serving as *dayanim*, judges.

### Three Herders Rule

The implication of the Mishna's language is that these three herders are technically *pasul* — for otherwise the Mishna would not have needed to say they are "trusted." The phrase signals that despite their technical disqualification, the litigants may accept them. And the Gemara notes that the number three is specified because it is *dayanim* under discussion: for *edut*, bearing witness, you would not need three; but for *dayanim* you need a court of three. Furthermore, the Mishna's particular mention of these *ro'ei vakar* teaches that even individuals who are maximally removed from settled life, rarely exposed to monetary transactions, and likely unversed in the law can be accepted as a court of three — *afilu hanei de-la shechichi be-yishuv* — if the litigants so agree.

---

## Stam Roeh vs Gabbai

### Default Rules

Rav Yehuda concludes with a practical ruling governing presumptive status: *stam roeh pasul* — a random, undifferentiated shepherd is presumed *pasul* for testimony unless proven otherwise. *Stam gabbai kasher* — a random tax collector, by contrast, is presumed *kasher* until the opposite is demonstrated. The burden of proof runs in opposite directions for the two figures: the shepherd begins with a presumption of disqualification, while the tax collector begins with a presumption of validity.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 26

## Tax Collectors & Shevi'is

### Rabbi Zeira's Father

The *daf* opens, properly speaking, three lines from the bottom of 25b, with a story offered as an exemplar of what a truly righteous tax collector looks like. The Gemara relates that the father of Rabbi Zeira served as a tax collector for the government for thirteen years. As we learned in the preceding discussion, a *stam* tax collector — one about whom nothing is known — is *kosher* until there is evidence that he is pocketing more than his due.

The story illustrates how this particular man managed to protect the townspeople he served. Whenever the regional official — the *reish nahara*, the head of the locale — came to town on a surprise visit, the father of Rabbi Zeira understood that this official would press him to collect higher taxes. He had apparently been reporting very low yields and demanding very little from the people. So what would he do when he saw that a visit was imminent? When he saw the rabbis out in the street, he would say to them cryptically: go back into your rooms. Let no one see you lest the visiting official notice all these people who might be exempt from taxation — or at least begin demanding more from them. His message to the rabbis was deliberately indirect; he did not want to be caught giving explicit instructions to hide. By contrast, when he saw the ordinary townspeople, he was somewhat more explicit, announcing: the boss is coming, and a father will be slaughtered in the presence of his son and a son in the presence of his father — meaning, the official will be furious and will impose crushing taxes upon everyone. The result in both cases was the same: *u-miglaz kulei alma*, everyone scattered and hid.

When the official finally arrived and demanded to know why so few taxes had been collected, the father of Rabbi Zeira replied: from whom should I collect? The town has been abandoned; there is no one here. And so the excuse held.

When he was on his deathbed, the father of Rabbi Zeira made a final request: take these thirteen *ma'ah* that I have bound up in my kerchief and return them to so-and-so, for I collected them from him as a tax payment, and in the end I did not need them — I managed to protect the people without using the money. The Gemara presents this as the portrait of a truly upright tax collector: someone who not only avoids personal enrichment but who goes to extraordinary lengths to protect those under his charge, and who in his final moments ensures that not a single coin was wrongfully retained.

### Otzrei vs. Sochrei Shevi'is

The Gemara now turns to explain a shift in terminology that appeared in the *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* originally referred to those disqualified from testimony in connection with *shevi'is* as *otzrei shevi'is* — those who gather and hoard *shevi'is* produce — and then later referred to them as *sochrei shevi'is*, those who conduct commerce in *shevi'is* produce. The Gemara asks: what does this shift mean?

Rav Yehuda explains it as follows. Originally, the rule was that *otzrei shevi'is* — those who merely gathered the produce for personal use — were *kosher*, while *sochrei shevi'is* — those who actually conducted commerce in it — were *pasul*. The reasoning was that while gathering up one's own produce and keeping it, even past the *zman habiyur*, was not ideal, it did not constitute the kind of commercial violation that disqualifies a witness. However, people then discovered a workaround: they would pay poor people to go out and gather the *shevi'is* produce on their behalf. The poor people could argue they were merely gathering for personal use, but effectively they were collecting on behalf of someone engaged in commerce. Once this practice spread, the ruling changed: *chazru lomar echad zeh v'echad zeh psulim* — both the gatherer and the merchant are now *pasul*.

The *b'nei Rechav* objected to this reading of the *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* uses the phrase *mishe-rabu ha-annasim*, "when the forceful ones multiplied," which they argued should have read *mishe-rabu ha-tagari*, "when the merchants multiplied," if the concern was simply commercial expansion. So Rava offers a different reading. Originally, the rule was that both gatherers and merchants were *pasul*. Then, *mishe-rabu ha-annasim* — when the strong-arm of the government increased its demands — the ruling changed. This refers to *arnona*, the government tax burden. At that point, as Rabbi Yannai publicly proclaimed: *puku v'ziru b'shevi'is* — go out and plant during *shevi'is*, because of the necessity of paying taxes. If people were being compelled to work their fields and harvest their crops in order to meet government demands, one could no longer declare that a gatherer is *pasul*. So *chazru lomar oskim ksheirim* — those who plant and gather are now permitted, even though this would ordinarily constitute a direct violation of *shemitah*. However, *sochrim psulim* still stands: if one is actually conducting commerce in *shevi'is* produce, one remains *pasul*.

### Arnona & Permissibility

This ruling raises an important question. How could *arnona* justify what would otherwise be a *d'oraysa* prohibition? *Tosafos* addresses this directly. The question is: *mishum arnona hitiru lachrosh velizro'a dehavai issur d'oraysa* — did they really permit a biblical violation merely because of tax demands?

*Tosafos* offers two answers. The first: perhaps this discussion concerns *shevi'is* in the present era, which may be only *d'rabbanan* in force, depending on various considerations regarding the sanctity of the land. If so, there would be room to permit it under significant economic pressure. The second answer: *ee nami, pikuach nefesh hu* — there was an element of mortal danger involved. The king sent a tax demand, they had nothing with which to pay, and they faced imprisonment at the king's hands, which could lead to death. *Tosafos* adds that the *Yerushalmi* states this explicitly in terms of *chayei nefesh*, preserving life.

It is striking that the *Bavli* includes no such explicit reference to life-threatening danger, whereas the *Yerushalmi* makes the mortal stakes clear. This creates two quite different interpretive frameworks: either this was a matter of *pikuach nefesh*, which would justify even a *d'oraysa* violation, or it was a *d'rabbanan* violation that was set aside because of severe and genuine economic pressure even without an immediate threat to life.

This *Gemara* becomes significant in the later discussions of *heter mechira*. Rav Kook invokes it substantially, because if we accept *Tosafos*'s first reading — that *shemitah* in the present era is *d'rabbanan* and that they permitted direct violation because of economic compulsion — then that framework can be applied to argue that under similar pressures, and given the rabbinic nature of the prohibition, other mechanisms such as the sale of land are certainly no less permissible. In fact, the argument would run: here they permitted the violation directly; a workaround like a land sale is even more lenient.

## Ibur Shana Story

### Encounters & Excuses

With the halachic background established, the Gemara introduces a narrative that bears directly on the question of *shevi'is* and the fitness of those who tolerate its violation to serve in rabbinic roles. Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnuki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak were traveling to perform an *ibur shana* — to add an intercalary month to the year — in Asya, which is outside of *Eretz Yisrael*. *Tosafos* raises the question that one is generally not supposed to extend a *shemitah* year, and also that *ibur shana* is not supposed to be performed outside of *Eretz Yisrael* — and indeed, it may be that the intercalation was being calculated for the following year, not the current one.

Reish Lakish encountered them on the road and asked to accompany them, saying he wished to observe how such a proceeding was conducted. As they traveled — presumably still within *Eretz Yisrael* — he saw a man plowing. He exclaimed to the two rabbis: this man is plowing during *shemitah*! They replied that he could say he was an *agiston*, an imperial worker — meaning either that he was working land belonging to a non-Jew (which raises its own questions about whether a Jew may work a non-Jew's land in *Eretz Yisrael* during *shemitah*), or, as *Tosafos* prefers, that he was effectively conscripted — compelled to work the land as a government laborer in order to pay the *arnona*. Under those circumstances, as we have seen, the violation might be condoned.

Continuing on, Reish Lakish saw a *kohen* pruning a vineyard. He exclaimed: a *kohen*, and he is pruning on *shemitah*?! They replied that he could say he was pruning not to tend the vines but to obtain the wood for his olive press. To this, Reish Lakish responded: *ha-lev yodeia im l'akel im l'akalkalot* — the heart knows whether you are genuinely in need of the wood or whether this is simply a pretext.

The Gemara then asks: which of these two incidents occurred first? If one thinks it was the plowing incident, a difficulty arises: once they had given Reish Lakish the answer about the *agiston*, he should have realized — or they should have known to tell him — that the same kind of justification could apply to the pruning. The fact that they did not suggests the pruning came first. Indeed the Gemara concludes: the vineyard incident happened first, and then came the plowing, at which point they offered the *agiston* excuse.

The Gemara then asks: why did Reish Lakish specifically note that the pruner was a *kohen*? One might assume it was simply to add moral emphasis — a *kohen* is expected to be particularly scrupulous, so the violation was all the more striking. But the Gemara offers a different answer: *mishum d'chashidei a'shvi'is* — *kohanim* as a group were specifically suspected of laxity regarding *shemitah*. Rashi explains that they rationalized their behavior: since they were permitted to use *terumah* — produce with a degree of sanctity — they concluded that they were entitled to work the land on *shemitah* and benefit from its produce as well. If the *Torah* grants us access to sanctified produce, they reasoned, surely we may also work the sacred soil.

The Gemara cites a *tanna* in support of this inference. If a *seah* of *terumah* falls into one hundred *seah* of *shevi'is* produce, it is *battel*. But if there is less than one hundred, the entire mixture must be allowed to rot. The Gemara asks: why must it rot? One might suggest selling the whole mixture to a *kohen* at the price of *terumah*, since he must treat it all as *terumah* — he must be *tahor* and careful with it, but at least it would not go entirely to waste. Why not do that? Rabbi Chiyya in the name of Ulla answers: *nechsh'du kohanim a'shvi'is* — *kohanim* are not trusted with *shevi'is* produce. If you sell it to a *kohen*, he will eat it past the time when it is permitted. From this we learn that *kohanim* were under general suspicion regarding *shevi'is*.

It should be noted that while the suspicion in this source concerns eating *shevi'is* produce past the time of *biyur*, the incident in the story involves a *kohen* actually working the land — a far more overt violation. Yet Rashi's explanation ties it all together: the underlying rationalization — that the *Torah*'s allowance of sanctified produce extends to *shemitah* — led *kohanim* to be lax across the range of *shevi'is* prohibitions.

*Tosafos* raises a related question: how could one even consider selling the mixture to a *kohen*, given the prohibition against doing business with *shevi'is* produce? *Tosafos* answers by distinguishing between commercial activity — ongoing, profit-driven trade in *shevi'is* — and a one-time, incidental sale. If someone gathered *shevi'is* produce for personal use, consumed most of it, and then sold a small remainder, that does not constitute doing business with *shevi'is*. It was a chance occurrence, not a commercial enterprise. The prohibition on *sechorah* with *shevi'is* produce targets systematic commercial activity, not isolated transactions.

### Reish Lakish's Critique

When they finally arrived at their destination, Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnuki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak went up to the attic to conduct the *ibur shana* proceedings, and they arranged to leave Reish Lakish out. They had decided he was *turda* — a nuisance, a headache — for holding them to such a rigorous standard while they were trying to navigate the realities of the time.

Reish Lakish went to Rabbi Yochanan and asked: are people who are *chashudim* on *shevi'is* fit to perform *ibur ha-shanah*? This question resonates directly with the *Mishnah* under discussion, since among those disqualified are *sochrei shevi'is*. These rabbis were not themselves violating *shemitah*, but they were passively condoning violations they witnessed on the road — and Reish Lakish argued that this compromised their fitness for so significant a rabbinic function.

Reish Lakish then attempted to walk back his own critique. Perhaps, he suggested, they could be like the cowherds in the famous story where three cowherds were observed talking about agricultural conditions and their observations were used by the rabbis to determine whether the year warranted intercalation. Those cowherds were not themselves rabbinic authorities, yet the rabbis relied on what they said. Similarly, perhaps Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnuki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak could be said to serve in a merely evidentiary role. This echo is pointed: the *Mishnah* mentions *ro'ei tzon* — shepherds — and *ro'ei bakar* — cowherds — among those who are *pasul*, and here the comparison is being made deliberately.

But Reish Lakish rejected his own analogy. *Lo dami* — it is not comparable. In the case of the cowherds, the rabbis heard what they said and then convened separately and performed the *ibur shana* themselves, based on their own *cheshbon*. The cowherds were merely a source of information, not participants in the proceeding. Here, the very rabbis who tolerated the violations of *shemitah* are themselves conducting the *ibur shana*. That is categorically different: *kesher resha'im hu* — it is a band of wicked people. *Ve-kesher resha'im eino min ha-minyan* — a band of wicked people cannot be counted toward the convocation required to perform the intercalation.

### Kesher Resha'im

Rabbi Yochanan's response was pointed in a different direction: *da'aka* — that hurts. To call these rabbis *resha'im* goes too far. That was his only objection.

When Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnuki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak subsequently came before Rabbi Yochanan, they complained: Reish Lakish called us *ro'ei bakar* — cowherds — and you said nothing. You only defended us when he called us *resha'im*. Rabbi Yochanan replied: if he had called you *ro'ei tzon* — shepherds, which the tradition considers worse than cowherds, as we saw in the preceding material — what would I have said? He would have been right. You were tolerating violations of *shemitah*. You are not *resha'im*, but you bear responsibility for not doing more.

What is striking here is the contrast between the *Yerushalmi* and the *Bavli* in their handling of this reality. The *Yerushalmi*, living within the circumstances of *Eretz Yisrael*, presents the situation as an unambiguous matter of *pikuach nefesh* and raises no hint of criticism toward those who tolerated the violations. The *Bavli*, by contrast, contains no suggestion that lives were at risk — which is why *Tosafos* raises the alternative explanation that *shemitah* may have been *d'rabbanan* at the time. And the *Bavli's* narrative concludes with sharp, if nuanced, criticism: Reish Lakish's critique of the rabbis for their passivity is vindicated at least in part, even if calling them *resha'im* was a step too far. This distance from the circumstances — being outside the land, outside the immediate pressures — makes it easier to hold a more demanding standard.

## Shevna Narrative

### Shevna's Plot

The discussion of *kesher resha'im* — the band of wicked people who cannot be counted toward a *minyan* — now prompts an *aggadic* digression into the source of this principle. Where does the idea come from that a *kesher resha'im eino min ha-minyan*?

The Gemara introduces Shevna, who served as a senior official in the court of King Hezekiah. Shevna would teach *Torah* publicly, and his classes drew thirteen myriads — 130,000 attendees. Hezekiah himself commanded only eleven myriads. On the strength of his larger following, Shevna regarded himself as the more consequential figure.

When Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem, Shevna wrote a note, fired it out of the city on an arrow to Sennacherib's camp, and in it declared: Shevna and his faction have already made peace with you and are prepared to open the gates of Jerusalem and submit. Hezekiah and his faction refuse to surrender. The Gemara derives this from the verse in Psalms: *ki hinei ha-resha'im yidrechun keshet* — the wicked bend the bow; *konennu hitzam al yeter* — they aim their arrow at *yeter*, which Shevna read as a reference to his superior numbers. He was betting on his majority.

Hezekiah was frightened. He worried that God might, as it were, side with the majority — invoking the principle of *acharei rabim le-hatot*, following the majority. If Shevna commanded more followers, perhaps the divine calculus would follow the larger number.

The prophet came to Hezekiah and reassured him with the verse: *lo tomrun kesher le-chol asher yomar ha-am ha-zeh kesher* — do not call it a band in the way this people calls it a band. In other words: yes, they may be numerically larger, but *kesher resha'im hu* — it is a band of wicked people. *Ve-kesher resha'im eino min ha-minyan* — and the wicked do not count toward the majority. Hezekiah need not fear: the true majority is on his side.

The Gemara then continues the story of Shevna's downfall. Thinking himself the equal of kings, Shevna had gone ahead and carved out a sepulchre for himself among the tombs of the Davidic dynasty. The prophet confronted him: *ma lecha po u-mi lecha po* — what gives you the right to be here, among the graves of kings? And then God's punishment is described: *hinei Hashem metaltelecha taltela gaver* — God will send you into exile with the exile of a man. Rav observes from the word *gaver* that exile is harder for a man than for a woman.

Furthermore, *va-atecha ata* — you will be covered with a covering. Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Chanina interprets this through a *gezerah shavah*: just as the *metzora* covers his upper lip, so too Shevna was struck with *tzara'as*.

The verse concludes: *tzanof yitznefecha tznifa ka-dur el eretz rachavat yadayim* — you will be hurled like a ball across a wide land. *Tosafos* explains this as being rolled like a ball across the open country.

The Gemara also states: *hu bikesh kalon beis adonav* — he sought to bring shame upon the house of his master, Hezekiah, and therefore *kvodo le-kalon nehpach* — his own honor was turned to disgrace.

When Shevna finally tried to go out with his 130,000 followers to surrender to Sennacherib, the angel Gabriel appeared and closed the gate, cutting him off from his entire entourage. He went out alone. When Sennacherib's troops asked him where his people were, he claimed they must have abandoned him. They replied: then you have made a mockery of us — you promised us 130,000 people and you appear alone. They pierced his heels, suspended him from the tails of their horses, and dragged him across thorns and thistles.

Rabbi Eliezer notes that Shevna was a man driven by sensual pleasure — the Talmud reads the description of his role through a verbal parallel to Avishag the Shunamite, who served King David. The verse *lech bo el ha-sochen* is linked by the word *sochen* to *va-tehi lo sochenes*, associating Shevna's position with physical indulgence. He was, in a word, a hedonist.

### Foundations & Torah

The Gemara now turns to a verse that connects this narrative to a broader theological and philosophical reflection: *ki ha-shatos yeharesun tzaddik mah pa'al* — if the foundations are destroyed, what will the righteous one have done? What does this verse mean in this context?

Rav Yehuda and Rav Ina offer two interpretations. One says: the verse is asking — had Hezekiah and his circle been destroyed, had Shevna succeeded in handing over the city, what would God have had left to give Hezekiah for his righteousness? The word *shatos*, foundations, refers here to Hezekiah and his followers, who are the foundational pillars upon which the world rests. The other says: the verse refers to the *Beis Ha-Mikdash*. Had Sennacherib entered and destroyed the Temple — with Shevna's treachery enabling this — where would God's promises have stood? What would have remained of divine providence?

Ulla offers a third interpretation that runs in the opposite direction: the *shatos* that needed to be destroyed were the schemes of Shevna himself. *Eilu machshavosav shel oso rasha einam neharasos* — had the plot of that wicked man not been destroyed, *tzaddik mah pa'al* — where would have been God's intervention on behalf of the righteous?

The Gemara explains the linguistic connections. For those who understand *shatos* as referring to Shevna's schemes, Rashi explains the word as related to *lo shas libo* — placing one's heart, i.e., one's plans and intentions. For those who understand *shatos* as referring to the *Beis Ha-Mikdash*, the connection is to the *even shesiyah* — the foundation stone — as recorded in the *Mishnah* about the stone that stood in the Temple from the days of the early prophets and was called *shesiyah*. For those who understand it as referring to Hezekiah and his circle, the Gemara asks: where do we find the righteous described as *shatos*? From the verse *ki l'Hashem metzukei eretz va-yashes aleihem tevel* — God has the pillars of the earth and places the world upon them. The righteous and the scholars of Torah are those pillars; the world is sustained upon them. And there is a further proof-text: *hifli eitzah higdil tushiyah* — the counsel is great, the *tushiyah* is great — where *tushiyah* refers to Torah. Torah is the foundation. And therefore Hezekiah and those who study and uphold Torah are themselves the foundations upon which the world stands.

### Machshavah & Learning

This leads the Gemara to a series of reflections on *tushiyah* — the term the *Torah* uses to describe understanding or wisdom — and why the *Torah* itself might be called by this name.

Rav Chanan asks: *lamah nikra shemah tushiyah* — why is Torah called *tushiyah*? *Mipnei she-hi masheshes kocho shel adam* — because it weakens a person. The pursuit of Torah study is demanding; it taxes one's physical and mental strength.

Another interpretation: *tushiyah she-nisnah be-chashai* — it was given quietly, in private, not with the thunderous public revelation one might expect. This is because of *ha-satan*, the prosecutorial force in the divine realm. The second giving of the *Torah*, in particular, is associated with this quality of quiet transmission, echoed in the *kol demamah dakkah*, the still small voice.

A third interpretation is the most philosophically striking. *Tushiyah devarim shel tohu she-ha-olam mishtates aleihem* — Torah consists of words that are, physically speaking, of the category of *tohu*, nothingness. Words have no material form; they are, in a physical sense, nothing. Air. And yet the world is sustained upon them. The very thing that seems most insubstantial — the spoken and studied word of Torah — is what underlies all of reality. As one might observe: if God Himself, whose word has no physical form, created the entire world through speech, it is of a piece that the words of Torah, equally incorporeal, should be the foundation upon which the world stands.

Finally, Ulla makes a practical observation: *machshavah mo'eles afilu le-divrei Torah* — troublesome thoughts have an effect even upon words of Torah. As wonderful and foundational as Torah study is, a person who is perpetually anxious and preoccupied with worries will find that those thoughts impair even their ability to learn. The proof-text: *mefir machshavos arumim velo ta'asena yedeihem tushiyah* — God undoes the schemes of the clever, and their hands cannot achieve *tushiyah*, cannot reach Torah wisdom. Anxiety and preoccupation can foreclose the very engagement with Torah that gives the world its foundation.

Rava qualifies this: *osukim lishmah einam mo'eles* — if one is learning Torah *lishmah*, for its own sake, then the troublesome thoughts will not prevail. *Rabos machshavos be-lev ish va'atzas Hashem hi sakum* — a person may have many thoughts in their heart, but it is God's counsel — *etzas Hashem*, that which is dedicated entirely to God — that will endure. If one's learning is genuinely oriented toward the divine purpose and not toward other ends, then the distractions and anxieties of the world will not succeed in disrupting it. The Torah, studied *lishmah*, remains standing.

# Sanhedrin 27

## Psulei Eidus Overview

### Mishna: Gambled & Lenders

The *daf* opens in the middle of a discussion on 26b, with the words *amar Rav Yehuda eimatai*, building on the *mishna* that lists categories of people disqualified from serving as witnesses — *psulei eidus* — on account of various transgressions. The common denominator running through the *mishna's* list is that all of these individuals are engaged in sins committed for the sake of financial gain.

The *mishna* enumerates: *misachek be-kubiya* (gamblers), *malveh be-ribbit* (one who lends money with interest, which is a clear *issur de-oraita*), *mafrichai yonim* (a type of gambling involving pigeons), and *sochrei shevi'it* (those who conduct commerce with *shemitah* produce). Some of these are *de-oraita* prohibitions, while others are *de-rabbanan*. Gambling, for example, is *de-rabbanan*, stemming from either the problem of *asmachta kanya lo kanya* — the view that a transaction based on a conditional wager is not legally binding — or, as *Tosafot* notes, the concern that such individuals are not *oskim be-yishuvo shel olam*, that is, they are not engaged in productive labor that sustains society. The underlying worry in all these cases is that a person willing to transgress — whether *de-oraita* or *de-rabbanan* — for monetary gain may be susceptible to accepting a bribe in exchange for false testimony. That is the essential common denominator.

### De-Oraita vs De-Rabbanan

When an individual knowingly and willingly violates a *de-oraita* prohibition for financial gain, his disqualification as a witness is itself *de-oraita*. The verse *al tashet yadcha im rasha lihyot eid chamas* — "do not put your hand with the wicked to be a false witness" — establishes the category of *eid chamas*, understood to refer to one who is motivated by financial gain. One who deliberately transgresses a *de-oraita* prohibition for such gain is *pasul de-oraita*.

However, the *mishna's* cases are all assumed to carry only *de-rabbanan* disqualification. Either the underlying problem is itself only rabbinic — such as *asmachta lo kanya* or the failure to be *oskim be-yishuvo shel olam* — or, as *Tosafot* explains for the case of *malveh be-ribbit*, either we are dealing with *ribbit de-rabbanan*, or the person has rationalized the behavior and does not truly view himself as willfully transgressing a *de-oraita* prohibition. After all, the borrower entered the arrangement consensually, with a contract — so it does not feel like genuine theft. Similarly, *shemitah* in the Babylonian context is *de-rabbanan*, rendering these cases all *de-rabbanan*. Nevertheless, an individual who transgresses a *de-oraita* prohibition knowingly, willingly, and for monetary gain would incur a *de-oraita* disqualification.

### Rav Yehuda's Condition

Rav Yehuda's qualifying statement — that these individuals are invalid only when they have no other gainful employment — appears to apply specifically to the gambling cases (*misachek be-kubiya* and *mafrichai yonim*) and does not straightforwardly extend to the other two categories.

---

## Hachraza Principle

### Rav Elazar Rule

The *gemara* then cites Rabbi Abahu in the name of Rav Elazar: *halacha ke-Rav Yehuda* — we follow Rav Yehuda at least in the gambling cases, where a person who has other gainful employment may not be disqualified. Rabbi Abahu then adds a second ruling in the name of Rav Elazar: *kullan tzerichin hachraza be-veit din* — all those listed in the *mishna* require a formal court announcement before their disqualification takes effect. This principle applies specifically to *psul de-rabbanan*.

The logic is as follows. When a *de-oraita* disqualification applies — say, someone committed an act of *gezeila* (robbery) in January and thereby became *pasul de-oraita* — his disqualification is effective from the moment of the transgression. If witnesses come in July and establish that he was a *gazlan* back in January, every testimony he gave from January onward is retroactively invalid. But when the disqualification is only *de-rabbanan*, the Rabbis have the authority to define when the *psul* takes effect, and they rule that it begins only once a formal announcement — *hachraza be-veit din* — has been made publicly. Until that point, all prior testimony stands. This is a critical and far-reaching principle in the laws of *psulei eidus de-rabbanan*.

### Shepherd Debate

The *gemara* turns to the case of a shepherd. It was previously established that shepherds are *pasul de-rabbanan* because they tend to graze their flocks on land that does not belong to them. The question is whether even a shepherd requires *hachraza be-veit din* before his disqualification takes effect. Rav Acha and Ravina dispute this. One holds that *hachraza* is required; the other holds it is not. *Rashi* explains why a shepherd might be different from the other cases: whereas a gambler's activity may be known only to a small circle, a shepherd's profession is public knowledge, observed daily. If everyone already knows he is a shepherd, one might argue that no formal announcement is needed — his status is self-evident.

### Stam Ro'eh Explained

The *gemara* raises an apparent difficulty: there is a teaching attributed to Rav in the name of Rav Yehuda that *stam ro'eh pasul* — a shepherd is presumed invalid without requiring any additional investigation. This fits well with the view that no *hachraza* is required, since the shepherd's status is publicly known. But according to the view that even a shepherd requires *hachraza be-veit din*, what meaning does *stam ro'eh pasul* carry? His disqualification does not arise automatically.

The *gemara* resolves this: *de-bistama machrizan alei* — the statement does not mean the general public may simply assume the shepherd is invalid. Rather, it means that when a *beit din* is required to make an announcement, it will issue one regarding any shepherd who has not affirmatively established his innocence. The presumption of guilt shifts the burden of proof onto the shepherd, but the actual *psul* still takes effect only through the announcement. The phrase *stam ro'eh pasul* thus describes the evidential posture of *beit din* — the shepherd bears the burden — but not an automatic, announcement-free disqualification.

---

## Gazlan Invalidity

### Rav Pappa Case

A practical case illustrates the stakes. A certain document had been signed by two witnesses who were *gazlanim*. Rav Pappa bar Shmuel was inclined to uphold the document's validity on the grounds that no *hachraza be-veit din* had been issued regarding these witnesses, and therefore they had not yet been formally disqualified.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenged this reasoning sharply: *nehi da-beinan hachraza be-gazlan de-rabbanan, be-gazlan de-oraita mi beinan hachraza?* — granted, we require *hachraza* for a *de-rabbanan* disqualification, but does a *de-oraita* disqualification require *hachraza* as well? Certainly not. A genuine *gazlan* — one whose robbery constitutes a *de-oraita* transgression done knowingly and for gain — is *pasul* from the moment he committed the act, regardless of whether any court announcement was ever made. The *hachraza* requirement is a rabbinic mechanism to protect previously accepted testimony, and it applies only where the *psul* itself is rabbinic. This distinction between *de-oraita* and *de-rabbanan* invalidity will resurface in the discussion of *eidim zomemim*.

---

## Davar Acher Case

### Rav Nachman Rule

The *gemara* records that Rav Nachman said: *ochlei davar acher psulin le-eidus* — those who eat *davar acher* are invalid as witnesses. The phrase *davar acher*, ordinarily a euphemism for pig meat, is explained by *Rashi* — and endorsed by *Tosafot* — as referring here to Jews who sustain themselves from charitable funds distributed by non-Jews. This was considered a *chillul Hashem*, an affront to communal dignity. *Rashi* frames the disqualification under the rubric of *rasha de-chamas*: such a person is willing to compromise their dignity and integrity when under financial pressure, and we therefore fear they may be susceptible to giving false testimony for money. This would be a *de-rabbanan* invalidity.

### Public vs. Private

The *gemara* immediately qualifies the ruling. *Hani mili be-farhesya aval be-tzina lo* — this applies only when the individual accepts these funds openly and publicly. If done quietly, the person demonstrates sensitivity to social norms and does not thereby compromise their credibility. Furthermore, even when it is done publicly, disqualification applies only if the person had a more discreet alternative: *de-efshar leih le-izonei be-tzina* — if they could have managed this privately and chose not to, their willingness to humiliate themselves publicly for money *— ve-kamvazyei nafshai be-farhesya —* reveals the kind of character that might compromise testimony for financial benefit. But if there was no alternative — *lo efshar leih* — and the only way to obtain subsistence was through public acceptance of non-Jewish charity, then *chiyyusei hu*: people do what they must to survive, and the fact of their need does not translate into a readiness to accept bribes. One does not leap from dignitary compromise born of desperation to the willingness to testify falsely.

---

## Sexual Transgression

### Chashud Arayos Valid
