The point rather is: *zeh she'hayah karov v'nitrachak* — the verse addresses the one who was once a relative and became distant. *B'yamim ha'hem* — if at the time of judgment he is no longer a *karov*, he is eligible to judge, even though he was previously disqualified. On this formulation Rabba bar bar Chana reports: *amar Rabbi Yochanan halacha k'Rabbi Yose HaGlili* — we rule that *karov v'nitrachak* is *kasher*, without the qualification that Rabbi Yehuda introduces for surviving children.

### Mar Ukva's Case

A case is then brought involving Mar Ukva. *B'nei chamu'eh d'Mar Ukva* — the sons of Mar Ukva's mother-in-law, who are Mar Ukva's brothers-in-law, came before him for a *din*. These brothers-in-law had been *krovim* to him through his wife and had become *nitrachku* — distanced — when his wife passed away. The question was whether they remained *pesulim* to appear before him. Under Rabbi Yehuda's view, if there are surviving children, the *pesul* persists — the brothers-in-law are now his children's uncles, even if they are no longer related to him directly. Under the majority position, the *pesul* has lapsed entirely.

*Atu l'kamei l'dina* — they came before him for judgment. Mar Ukva declared: *psilna l'chu l'dina* — I am *pasul* to judge your case.

### Real Reason: Troublemake…

The brothers-in-law protested: *mai daitach k'Rabbi Yehuda* — do you really rule like Rabbi Yehuda, finding yourself disqualified merely because you are still their children's uncle? *Anan maitina igarta mi'Maarava* — we will obtain a letter from the west, from Eretz Yisrael, attesting that *ein halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda*, and you should be fully eligible to judge us.

Mar Ukva responded with force: *atu b'kafta d'dikula idbakna b'chu* — do you think I am bound to you like wax? The point was not kinship at all. *Lo kamina psilna l'chu l'dina — ela mishum d'la tzyyitu l'dina* — I declared myself *pasul* not because of any formal disqualification arising from relationship, but because you are troublemakers who refuse to accept the rulings of the court. He was, in effect, recusing himself — and the brothers-in-law's immediate maneuvering to counter-argue the *pesul* of kinship only confirmed his assessment. The episode concludes without a *psak* on the merits.

---

## Ohev & Sonei

### Ohev Narrowly Defined

Having completed the discussion of *krovim*, the *mishnah* addresses the categories of *ohev* — a close friend — and *sonei* — an enemy — as additional grounds for disqualification. The *mishnah* defines *ohev* with striking specificity: *echad ha'shoshvinim* — one of the groomsmen, a member of the wedding party. This already narrows the category considerably.

The *Gemara* further qualifies how long this status persists: *amar Rabbi Abba amar Rabbi Yirmiyah amar Rav — kol shivat yemei ha'mishteh* — for the full seven days of the wedding celebration. Beyond that week, the fact of having been a groomsman no longer creates a *pesul*. The *Rabanan*, citing Rava, go further: *afilu mi'yom rishon v'eilach* — even from the day after the wedding, the *ohev* disqualification no longer applies.

This extraordinary narrowness reflects a broader principle: *lo nechshadu Yisrael al kach* — we do not suspect Israel of falsifying testimony on account of friendship or animosity. The formal *pesul* of relatives is a structural rule, not a judgment about individual character. To then expand it to encompass friends and enemies would require much stronger grounds.

### Witnesses vs. Judges

This narrowing, however, applies specifically to witnesses. The *Gemara* develops a crucial distinction: the rules governing *ohev* and *sonei* operate differently when one is serving as a judge rather than a witness. The logic is instructive. A witness is called upon to report facts directly observed — what he saw, heard, or perceived. The concern that friendship or enmity might distort testimony, while real, is already filtered by the structural question of what happened. A judge, by contrast, must actively argue both sides of a case, probe the evidence, construct arguments on behalf of each party, and exercise independent evaluative judgment. In that role, even a subtle pull of loyalty or antipathy can fundamentally compromise the process — not merely at the level of individual bias in reporting, but at the level of the entire deliberative exercise. The requirement of impartiality is therefore correspondingly more demanding for judges.

It follows that *ohev* and *sonei* retain a broader disqualifying effect for *dayanim* than for *edim*. As a witness, the category of *ohev* is limited to the groomsman during the wedding week; as a judge, the standard of freedom from bias is more expansive.

### Sonei Definition

*Sonei* is defined more broadly than *ohev*. The *Gemara* states: *ha-soneh kol she-lo diber* — whoever has gone without speaking to the other party because of a quarrel is in the category of *sonei*. The minimum threshold is three days of non-communication due to enmity. As long as the parties remain estranged and unreconciled, the *pesul* of *sonei* applies.

It is notable that this category, grounded in ongoing conflict, can in practice encompass a far wider range of people than the narrowly defined *ohev*. Anger and enmity, as a matter of human experience, tend to be more durable motivators than affection — they drive people more forcefully and persistently.

### Ohev from Pasuk

The *Gemara* now seeks the biblical source for these disqualifications. The *pasuk* that emerges is from the laws of the *ir miklat*: *v'hu lo oyev lo v'lo mivakesh ra'ato* — and he was not his enemy and was not seeking his harm. The verse speaks of an unintentional killer who fled to a city of refuge. Rereading it through the lens of testimony and judgment, the *Gemara* derives: *lo oyev lo* — if he is not the enemy of the subject, *ye'idenu* — he may testify about him; *v'lo mivakesh ra'ato* — and if he does not seek the man's harm, *yadinenu* — he may judge him.

From *sonei* we thus have an explicit *pasuk*. But *ohev* is not found there. The *Gemara* suggests reading it into the gaps: *v'lo ohev... v'lo tovaso* — and not a lover, and not one seeking his benefit. But the *Gemara* immediately objects: *midi ohev ktiv*? Is the word *ohev* actually written there? It is not. The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ella sevara hu* — it is a matter of *sevara*, logical reasoning. *Ohev mai ta'ama*? Why is *sonei pasul*? Because *de'marchaka da'ateih* — his thinking is distorted against the subject. *Ohev nami mikrava da'ateih* — and one who loves is equally distorted in the subject's favor. The disqualification of *ohev* flows from the same principle, derived by analogy.

### Judges Need Impartiality

With both categories established, the *Gemara* accounts for the position of the *Rabanan* who held that *ohev* and *sonei* do not disqualify witnesses at all — relying on the principle *lo nechshadu Yisrael al kach*. If witnesses are always *kasher* as *ohev* or *sonei*, what becomes of the *pasuk*? *Chad ledayan* — one application is to the judge. The *Rabanan* use the verse exclusively to disqualify *dayanim*, where the need for impartiality is more demanding, while leaving witnesses *kasher*. The companion phrase of the *pasuk* then covers *ohev* by the same logic applied to a judge.

*Amar Rabbi Yossi beRabbi Yehuda*: from the same verse — *v'hu lo oyev lo v'lo mivakesh ra'ato* — we derive *mikan lishnei talmidei chachamim she'son'im zeh et zeh she-ein yoshvin badin ke'echad* — two scholars who are enemies of one another may not sit together as a panel of judges. The prohibition is not only about judging someone one hates, but about sitting *alongside* someone one hates.

### Enemies Can't Sit Togeth…

This last point requires a distinction. Two judges who are close friends may serve together on a *beit din* — friendship does not impair the deliberative dynamic between them; they can disagree vigorously and reconcile warmly, as the model of *chavruta* study illustrates. Two judges who are enemies, however, cannot function together. Each will reflexively oppose the other's reasoning, resist listening, and subvert the open atmosphere the court requires. The *pesul* of enemies sitting together is therefore real and distinct from the general disqualification of *sonei* when judging the person one hates. Enemies cannot sit together as a panel. Regarding friends on a shared panel, no analogous concern applies.

---

## Witness Examination

### Frightening Witnesses

The *mishnah* turns to the procedure for examining witnesses in civil cases: *keitzad bodkin et ha-edim* — how does one examine the witnesses? The procedure begins with *hachnisan lacheder* — bringing the witnesses into a room — and *umaimin aleihem* — frightening them, impressing upon them the gravity of false testimony. By *dinei nefashot* we know the specific content of this admonition; the *mishnah* here does not specify it for civil cases, as we shall see shortly. The bystanders are then cleared from the chamber.

### Individual Examination

The *mishnah* records: *umshayirin et hagadol shebahen* — the senior witness is retained while the others are removed. He is questioned individually: *emor heich atah yodea shezeh chayav lazeh* — tell us how you know that this person owes something to the other. The witnesses are examined one by one, in isolation from one another.

### Hearsay Rejection

What types of answers will not suffice? If the witness says *hu amar li she-ani chayav lo* — the debtor himself told me in passing that he owed the money — *lo amar klum*, that amounts to nothing. Similarly, if he reports that a third party told him about the debt, that is pure hearsay and equally inadmissible. Even a first-person statement heard in casual conversation does not qualify, because such statements can be made without real seriousness — perhaps the speaker wished not to appear overly wealthy, or was simply making conversation.

### Admission Standard

The only admission that carries legal weight is: *befanenu hodeh lo she'hu chayav lo matayim zuz* — I was present when the debtor directly admitted to the claimant himself, in my presence, that he owed him the money. The admission must be made face-to-face between the parties, with the witness actually observing the moment of acknowledgment.

### Verdict Process

Once both witnesses have been examined separately, *ve'achar kach machnisin et hasheni u'vodkin oto* — the second witness is brought in and examined in the same fashion. *Im nimtzeu divreihem mechuvanim* — if their accounts align, *nosim ve'nosim ba'davar* — the judges deliberate and discuss the matter.

### Unanimity or Add Judges

The *mishnah* then addresses the voting: two saying *zakai* and one saying *chayav* yields *zakai*; two saying *chayav* and one saying *zakai* yields *chayav*. If two judges have reached a clear majority but the third says *eini yodea* — I do not know — that judge is effectively removed from the panel; one cannot maintain a functioning *beit din* of three with an abstaining member. *Yosifu ha'dayanim* — additional judges must be added, in pairs, until a proper majority is reached.

### Announcing Verdict

Once a conclusion is reached, the litigants are brought back in. The deliberations were conducted outside their presence. The most senior judge then speaks: *ish ploni atah zakai, ish ploni atah chayav* — so-and-so, you are exempt; so-and-so, you are liable. The court speaks in a single, unified voice through its most senior member.

### Secrecy of Votes

The *mishnah* then asks: *u'minayin she'kesheyeitzei lo yomar* — how do we know that after the case is concluded a judge may not approach the losing litigant and say privately: I voted in your favor, but my colleagues outvoted me, *aval mah eseh she'chaverai ravu alai* — what could I do, they were the majority? The source: *lo telech rachil beamecha* — do not go as a talebearer among your people — and the further verse: *holech rachil megaleh sod* — the talebearer reveals secrets.

The court must speak with a unified voice. There is a meaningful difference between preserving a *daat yachid* as an abstract legal position — which the tradition values, as minority opinions may later be relied upon — and revealing one's personal vote in a specific, concluded case. The latter undermines the authority of the court, invites partisanship, opens the door to after-the-fact pressure and influence, and compromises the integrity of the deliberative process. Just as parents speaking with one voice on a disciplinary matter protect the integrity of the household, so the court speaking with one voice protects the integrity of its judgment.

---

## Deterring False Testimony

### Clouds & Rain Warning

Having established that witnesses in civil cases are brought in and frightened, the *Gemara* asks: *heichi amrinan lehu* — what exactly do we say to them? This is a case of *dinei mamonot*, not *dinei nefashot*; you cannot invoke the weight of a human life. *Amar Rav Yehuda hachi amrinan lehu* — Rav Yehuda says we say to them the verse *nesi'im ve'ruach ve'geshem ayin, ish mithallel be'matat shaker* — clouds and wind and then no rain: a man who boasts of a false gift. False testimony, like clouds that promise rain and deliver none, will result in drought. The implication is that false testimony brings about a world in which there is no rain.

Rava objected: *yachil lemeimar* — the witness could simply say, *sheva shani havei kafna, de'bava umna lo chalif* — there can be a famine for seven years, but it never passes through the craftsman's door. If he is not a farmer, the threat of drought is no personal deterrent.

### Sword & Arrow Warning

*Ela amar Rava amrinan lehu* — Rava therefore proposes a different verse: *mafitz ve'cherev ve'chetz shanun ish onneh ve're'ehu ed shaker* — like a club, a sword, and a sharpened arrow is the man who bears false witness against his fellow. The consequence here is war and bloodshed. *Amar Rav Ashi* — but Rav Ashi noted the same objection applies: *yachil lemeimar sheva shani havei motna, ve'inash belo shnei lo shachiv* — there can be pestilence for seven years, but no one dies before his appointed time. The threat of death and war remains abstract.

### Despised Witnesses

*Ela amar Natan bar Mar Zutra amrinan lehu* — Natan bar Mar Zutra proposes the decisive warning: *sahadei shikrei ogreihu zilei* — false witnesses are despicable even to those who hire them. The verse cited is from the case of Navot's vineyard: the king arranged for *shnayim anashim bnei beliya'al* — two men of *beliya'al* — to testify falsely against Navot. Even Ahab, who commissioned the false testimony, regarded these witnesses as men of corrupt character. The warning is thus personal and immediate: whatever payment you receive, you will be viewed with contempt even by the one who paid you.

---

## Admissions & Retractions

### Direct Admission Required

The *mishnah* has established that the only valid admission is one in which the debtor acknowledged the debt *befanenu* — in the presence of the witnesses, directly to the claimant. Casual statements made in conversation, even to the claimant himself, do not rise to this standard, because they may not have been intended seriously.

### Yehuda's Strict Rule

Rav Yehuda takes this further, citing a ruling of Rav: *tzarich she'yomar atem edai* — it is not sufficient that witnesses happened to be present when the admission was made; the admitting party must explicitly designate them as his witnesses. Without that designation, the admission, even if made directly to the claimant before observers, does not create binding legal liability. The statement is supported by a parallel *braisa* cited immediately after: *mesaye'a lei le'Rav Yehuda*.

### Jest Retraction

The *Gemara* then introduces the claim of *meshateh ani bach* — I was only joking. *Amar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba amar Rabbi Yochanan*: if a person acknowledged a debt of one hundred *zuz* and the following day, when asked to pay, said *meshateh ani bach*, he is *patur* — exempt. The claim of having been insincere is believed, even in the presence of witnesses who heard the original admission.

A *braisa* confirms this, and goes further: even where the claimant had anticipated the retraction and hidden witnesses behind a wall to capture the admission — *hichmin lo edim achorei ha'geder* — and the debtor acknowledged the debt but then explicitly said he would not admit it formally because he feared being brought to court — even so, if the next day he claimed *meshateh ani bach*, he is *patur*. Remarkably, even the statement that he would not admit in front of witnesses because of the legal consequences does not strip him of the *meshateh* defense.

The *Gemara* adds a procedural point: *im lo ta'an ein to'anin lo* — if the defendant does not himself raise the claim of jest, the court does not raise it on his behalf. Where witnesses have attested to the admission, we treat it as genuine unless the defendant himself says otherwise. The court will not volunteer a defense the party has not made.

### Capital Cases Defense

In capital cases, however, the rule is reversed: *u've'dinei nefashot af al gav d'lo ta'an to'anin lo* — even if the defendant does not raise a potentially exculpatory claim, the court argues it on his behalf. Where a person's life is at stake, the court assumes an affirmative responsibility to explore every possible ground for acquittal.

### Mesit Exception

There is one exception to this rule of capital advocacy: *ve'ein to'anin le'masit* — the court does not argue on behalf of the *mesit*, the one who seduces another to idolatry. The *Gemara* questions: since when were we discussing a *mesit*? This leads to the observation that the text is missing an intermediate passage, *chassurei mechassra ve'hachi katni*, and the full rule is reconstructed: ordinarily, if a defendant does not raise a defense, the court does not raise it for him; in capital cases the court does raise it; but for the *mesit*, even in a capital case, the court does not raise defenses on his behalf.

The reason is explicit in the verse: *lo tachmol ve'lo techaseh alav* — have no compassion and do not cover for him. The *mesit* who seduces to *avodah zarah* presents so grave a threat to the community and to divine authority that the ordinary protections extended to a capital defendant are suspended. The tension with the general obligation to protect individual rights is intentional and acknowledged: the interest of the community in suppressing this particular threat outweighs the standard commitment to maximizing the individual's defenses.

### Mesit & Serpent

The *Gemara* derives this further from the case of the primordial serpent. *Amar Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yonatan*: we learn that the court does not argue on behalf of the *mesit* from the serpent of Eden. *Amar Rabbi Simlai*: the serpent had many arguments it could have made in its own defense after God confronted it — *harbeh ta'anot hayah lo la'nachash lit'on* — and it did not make them. More pointedly, God Himself did not argue the serpent's case. Why? *Lefi she-lo ta'an hu lo ta'an lo* — because the serpent did not argue for itself, God did not argue on its behalf. The serpent was a *mesit*, seducing Adam and Chava to the primordial act of defying divine authority, and so the rule holds: *lo ta'aninan le'masit*.

What argument could the serpent have made? *Divrei ha'Rav ve'divrei ha'talmid, divrei mi shom'in* — if the master commands one thing and the student commands another, whose word does one obey? The master's, of course. The serpent could have argued: I told them to eat; God said not to eat; they should have listened to God, not to me. That is precisely the defense every *mesit* could offer, and it is why the *Gemara* notes that these arguments existed but were not accepted.

### Adding Takes Away

*Amar Chizkiyah*: from where do we know that *kol ha'mosif goreia* — whoever adds takes away? From the serpent's own case. The verse records Chava telling the serpent that God said not to eat *and not to touch* the fruit of the tree. God had in fact prohibited only eating; Chava added the prohibition of touching. The serpent thereupon pushed her against the tree, demonstrating that she could touch it without consequence — and used that as a basis to argue that eating would similarly be harmless. The addition to God's word became the instrument of the transgression.

The *Gemara* notes a remarkable tension here. The *Anshei Knesset Ha'Gedolah* teach in *Pirkei Avot* to *asu siyag la'Torah* — make a fence around the Torah. And *Avot D'Rabbi Natan* explicitly counts Adam's instruction to Chava not to touch as such a *siyag*. Yet here the same act is taken as the source for *kol ha'mosif goreia*. The tension is left unresolved — the two principles stand alongside one another, and the balance between making protective fences and the danger of adding to God's word is itself a subject for deeper reflection.

Additional derivations of the principle are cited: *Rav Mesharshiya* from the word *amatayim vachatzi* — two and a half cubits — arguing that the additional *alef* reduces the apparent measure; *Rav Ashi* from *ashtei esrei yeriot* — eleven curtains — arguing that the *ayin* reduces the count from twelve to eleven.

### Jest vs. Denial

*Amar Abaye lo shanu ela de'amar mishteh ani bach* — Abbaye clarifies the scope of the *meshateh* rule. The claim of jest is available only as long as the defendant affirmatively says *meshateh ani bach*. If instead the defendant says *lo hayu devarim me'olam* — it never happened — and witnesses then attest that it did happen, he is *huchzak kafran* — established as a proven liar. His credibility is destroyed; he can no longer make the *meshateh* claim having first denied the event entirely. According to Rashi, this *kafran* status would also preclude him from taking an oath.

### Papa: Jest & Forgetfulne…

Rav Papa, however, disagrees. His ruling is cited in the name of Rava: *kol midei de'chadi lo dachir inash* — things that are of no serious consequence people do not remember. The same lack of seriousness that underlies the claim of *meshateh* — the statement was made carelessly, without weight — also explains why the defendant might fail to remember having made it at all. His initial denial that the statement ever occurred is therefore not to be treated as a lie; it is equally consistent with having genuinely forgotten something that was said in passing without intent. Just as he may claim *meshateh*, so too may he claim *lo dachir* — I simply do not recall — and neither amounts to *huchzak kafran*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 29b

## Atem Edai Requirement

### Awareness of Witnesses

The Gemara opens on 29b with a continuation of the discussion concerning the requirement of *atem edai* — the formal designation of witnesses — as a prerequisite for a binding admission. The background to this discussion involves a case where a borrower was unaware that witnesses were present when he made an admission, and those witnesses were subsequently produced in court. The Gemara had already established that such a person is not considered *huchzak kafran* — not deemed a proven liar for having denied the debt — since, absent any awareness that witnesses were present, a person does not treat casual admissions as serious or memorable. The related point from the Yerushalmi was that in such a case, the debtor would need to actively declare *meshahta ani bach* — "I was only joking" — in order to escape liability; if he fails to say so explicitly, we do not supply that argument on his behalf, though the Yerushalmi was somewhat more willing to do so.

### Canopy Bed Case

The Gemara now advances to a new case. A person concealed witnesses against his fellow inside a canopy bed — hidden behind its curtains. The concealing party then said to the other: "What do you owe me?" The respondent confirmed the debt, saying yes. At that point, the questioner asked: "Are you prepared that all those living and asleep should serve as witnesses against you?" — framing the question so as to include the hidden witnesses without revealing their presence. The respondent replied: no, he was not prepared for anyone to serve as witnesses.

Rav Kahana rules that even though the witnesses heard the admission, since the admitting party was unaware of their presence and explicitly declined to have anyone serve as witnesses, this does not constitute a valid admission. Rather than inferring that the denial only demonstrates an attempt to conceal an actual debt, the Gemara returns to the formal principle: unless a person explicitly accepts the witnesses as such — whether by saying *atem edai* or by awareness and acceptance of their presence — the admission carries no legal force.

### Graveyard Case

A parallel case is presented: someone concealed witnesses inside a grave — presumably an open grave or a mausoleum — and then asked his fellow to admit a debt in that setting. The fellow admitted, and the questioner then asked: "Are you prepared that the living and the dead should be witnesses against you?" — an absurd formulation designed to trick the admitting party into accepting the concealed witnesses as testimony. The admitting party, thinking this a jest about dead witnesses, responded: no.

Rav Shimon rules that since the person said no, this does not constitute *atem edai*. The more striking implication, however, runs in the opposite direction. Had the admitting party said yes — even without seeing any witnesses, even treating the question as idle talk — that affirmative response would have constituted valid *atem edai*, and the hidden witnesses in the grave would have been duly designated. This is a significant *chiddush*: the formal requirement of *atem edai* operates independently of the subjective seriousness with which the admitting party treats the designation. Once created, the formal act of witness designation is binding even if the designating party assumed it was meaningless. One might then ask whether the admitting party could later claim *meshahta ani bach* — that he was obviously not serious. The answer appears to be no. The Gemara's reasoning seems to be that once the formal requirement of *atem edai* is established as the operative standard, the law deals in formal categories rather than contextual readings of intent. Having erected a demanding formal threshold, the law correspondingly allows that threshold to be satisfied in formal rather than intuitive terms.

### Formal Requirements

Rav Yeivi — and some attribute it to Rav Papa — draws the following inference from these cases: the requirement articulated by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, that one must say *atem edai*, applies equally whether it is the borrower who initiates — approaching the witnesses and designating them himself — or whether it is the lender who initiates by asking: "Are you willing for Michael and David to serve as witnesses?" and the borrower responds affirmatively. In either formulation, the formal requirement of *atem edai* is satisfied.

### Silence as Consent

The Gemara extends this principle one step further: not only does an affirmative response suffice when the lender initiates the designation, but even silence — a failure to respond either way — constitutes acceptance. The Gemara makes this explicit: the only reason the graveyard case failed was that the admitting party actively said no. Had the party simply remained silent, that silence would have operated as *shtika ke-hoda'ah* — silence as admission — and would have constituted a valid *atem edai*.

This represents a notable internal tension within the Bavli's treatment of witness designation. On one hand, the Bavli imposes a stringent formal demand — *atem edai* must be established, more so than the Yerushalmi requires. On the other hand, having established that demanding standard, the Bavli simultaneously lowers the threshold for what satisfies it: a hidden witness scenario, a fanciful formulation about the living and the dead, an ambiguous designation initiated entirely by the opposing party, and even sheer silence — all suffice. The formalism cuts in both directions.

---

## Deathbed Admissions

### Kav Rashu Case

The Gemara introduces the case of a person known by the nickname *kav rashu* — literally a measure of wickedness, but Rashi explains it as someone against whom there exists a bundle of promissory notes, a person so thoroughly in debt that this became his very identity. When challenged about his many debts, this person responded dismissively: "Who has ever lent me money? No one — except so-and-so and so-and-so." Those named creditors then came before Rav Nachman and argued that even his own mouth had confirmed the debt.

Rav Nachman rejected the claim on the basis of the principle *adam asui she-lo le-hasbiya et atzmo* — a person naturally acts so as not to make himself appear wealthy. This requires some explanation, because on its face the principle seems ill-fitted to a case where the person was trying to appear poor, not wealthy. The deeper logic, however, appears to be that the principle underlies the very requirement of *atem edai*: even a contextually plausible-seeming admission, made without formal witness designation, carries no legal weight, because we can always construct a reason why someone might have said such a thing without intending it as a binding acknowledgment. Here, for instance, the person may have named specific creditors precisely to make himself look burdened with debt rather than flush with assets. The admission, lacking *atem edai*, is thus not binding.

### Miser on Gold

A second case: a person whose nickname was *achbara de-shachiv a-dinarei* — the rat who sleeps on his gold coins, a miser who hoards wealth. When this person was dying, he declared that Reuven and Shimon had lent him money and he owed them repayment. Reuven and Shimon then came to collect — but after his death, from the heirs. The question was whether a deathbed admission should be treated differently from an ordinary admission.

### Deathbed Dispute

The case came before Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosi. He ruled in favor of the creditors: the principle of *adam asui she-lo le-hasbiya et atzmo* — that a person avoids making himself look wealthy — applies only to the living, *hani mili mechayim*. A dying person, *achar misah*, has no further interest in appearances and will speak truthfully. Therefore, even without *atem edai*, a deathbed admission is accepted, and the creditors may collect from the heirs. Half the debt was paid.

### Living vs. Deathbed

When the creditors sought to collect the remaining half, Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosi was unavailable and they appeared before Rabbi Chiya, who explicitly disagreed with the prior ruling. Just as a person avoids making himself look wealthy, said Rabbi Chiya, so too a person avoids making his children look wealthy — *adam asui she-lo le-hasbiya banav*. A dying man may say that he owes debts precisely to prevent the world from knowing how much his heirs are about to inherit, lest creditors — real or fabricated — descend upon them. Therefore, even a deathbed admission, absent *atem edai*, is not binding on the orphans.

The creditors themselves, acting with integrity, asked whether they should return the half already paid. Rabbi Chiya responded: *kvar hora zaken* — a sage has already ruled. The ruling of Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yosi on the first half stands, since it was a legitimate *psak* and is not to be reversed retroactively. As for the second half, however, Rabbi Chiya's ruling prevails: the deathbed admission without *atem edai* is insufficient, and the heirs need not pay.

---

## Writing Documents

### Two Witnesses Kinyan

The Gemara turns to the question of when witnesses who heard an admission are authorized to memorialize it in a *shtar*. The advantage of a *shtar* over an oral admission is considerable: the creditor need not produce the witnesses in person at trial, and the debtor cannot easily claim subsequent repayment while the creditor holds the document. However, a *shtar* can only be written with the authority of the obligated party.

The Gemara rules: if the debtor admitted in front of two witnesses *and* performed a *ma'aseh kinyan* — a formal symbolic act of acquisition — *kosevin*, the witnesses may write a *shtar*. Without the *kinyan*, they may not.

### Three Without Kinyan

The question then arises regarding admission before three individuals, without any *kinyan*. Three constitutes a *beis din*, and when a court issues a judgment it writes a *shtar* on its own authority without requiring the losing party's consent. If this admission occurred before something resembling a court, perhaps the three may write a *shtar* even without a *kinyan*.

### Rav Ami vs Rav Assi

On this question Rav Ami and Rav Assi dispute. Rav Ami holds *kosevin* — the three may write a *shtar* even without a *kinyan*. Rav Assi holds *ein kosevin* — they may not. When a case arose in practice, Rav deferred to the position of Rav Assi and did not permit writing the *shtar*.

Rav Adda bar Ahava, however, introduces a nuance: *zimnin kasvinan ve-zimnin lo kasvinan* — sometimes they write and sometimes they do not, depending on the circumstances. The distinction is as follows. If the three happened to be sitting together and the admission occurred in their presence without any prior arrangement, they lack the status of a *beis din* and may not write a *shtar*. But if the parties specifically convened the three — whether creditor or debtor who gathered them for the purpose of making or receiving the admission — then they function as a *beis din*, and the *shtar* may be written without a *kinyan*.

It is worth noting that a related concept, *odaysa*, bears mention here. In halakhic practice, an *odaysa* — a formal admission — can function as a vehicle for creating new legal realities in monetary matters: a person may admit before witnesses to a transaction that never occurred, and that admission itself effectuates the transfer. This broader concept underlies the Gemara's careful attention to the conditions under which a *shtar* of admission may be written.

### Rava's Requirement

Rava adds a further condition: even if the three were deliberately convened, the *shtar* may not be written unless the admitting party explicitly says *havu alai dayanei* — "serve as my judges." Without that verbal designation of the three as *dayanim*, their convening alone is insufficient.

### Mar Bar Rav Ashi

Mar bar Rav Ashi goes furthest of all: even explicit verbal designation as judges is not enough. A *shtar* may only be written by an actual established court — one that has a fixed location, hears cases on an ongoing basis, and formally summons parties through a written notice. Only such an institution has the standing of a *beis din* capable of writing a *shtar* on the basis of an admission. In his view, the entire framework of treating convened individuals as a quasi-court is a legal fiction that he declines to accept. If a genuine court is hearing the case, let the court write its judgment; if there is no genuine court, then a *kinyan* is required, and without it no *shtar* may be written.

---

## Chattels vs Land

### Chattels Kinyan

The Gemara now articulates a further distinction between different types of subject matter. Regarding movable property — *metaltlei* — the rule is as stated: admission before two witnesses with a *kinyan* allows writing a *shtar*; without a *kinyan*, it does not.

### Land No Kinyan

Land — *karka* — presents a different case. When a debtor admits that a particular piece of land belongs to the creditor, the situation differs from a monetary debt. A monetary debt in movables must still be extracted through legal process; there is a gap between the admission and the actual transfer of value. Land, by contrast, simply sits there. Once the debtor admits it belongs to the creditor, there is nothing further to extract — *lo mechasar guvaina*. Rashi formulates the distinction precisely: with movables and a loan, it is still a debt, it still requires delivery, and there is a meaningful difference between an oral debt and a debt documented by a *shtar* — the *shtar* gives the creditor enhanced enforcement power over encumbered properties, which is something the debtor has reason to resist granting. But with land, writing the *shtar* is merely *gilui milta* — revealing and memorializing what is already an established fact. The question, then, is whether this distinction justifies writing a *shtar* regarding land without any *kinyan*.

### Amemar vs Zutra

Amemar holds *ein kosevin* — even for land without a *kinyan*, no *shtar* may be written. Mar Zutra holds *kosevin* — it may be written. The Gemara rules: *ve-hilchasa kosevin* — the *halacha* follows Mar Zutra, and a *shtar* is written for land even without a *kinyan*, because the admission alone establishes ownership of something that needs no further extraction.

### Concrete Chattels

Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna of Damarya raised a question before Ravina: the foregoing analysis distinguishes land from movables on the basis of the need for extraction. But what of concrete, physical chattels that are present and identifiable — *metaltlei ve-isnahu b'einaihu*, movables that are right there before one's eyes? If Gloria admits that the car in her driveway is mine, that is not an abstract debt; it is a specific, identifiable object, not requiring the legal processing that a monetary debt requires. Perhaps such concrete movables should be treated like land?

### Rav Ashi Disagrees

Rav Ashi disagrees. Even in the case of a specific, present chattel, *keivan de-mechassrei guvaina* — since it still requires extraction, it is not like land. To obtain the car, I must compel Gloria to deliver it; I cannot simply walk up and take possession as I can with land once the admission is made. Therefore, concrete chattels remain categorized with *metaltlei* for this purpose, and a *shtar* may not be written without explicit authorization — that is, without a *kinyan*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 30

## Witness Authorization

### Doc Without Auth

The Gemara at the bottom of 29b introduces a case involving a *shtar* of admission — a document recording that a debtor acknowledged his obligation — in which the *shtar* did not contain the explicit language stating that the *eidim* had been authorized to write and sign it: *amar lanan kisvu v'chasmu v'havu lei*, "he said to us, write, sign, and give it to him." The problem is one we have already encountered: witnesses cannot create a *shtar* on their own initiative following an admission. They require explicit authorization from the admitting party. Yet here that authorization language is absent. What is the legal status of such a document?

### Reish Lakish Rule

Abaye and Rava both rule that we apply the principle of Reish Lakish: *chazaka ein eidim chotmim al ha-shtar ela im kein na'aseh gadol* — there is a presumption that witnesses do not sign a *shtar* unless the transaction was performed properly. The original context of this rule in Bava Basra concerns whether a seller of ancestral land was old enough to do so validly; we presume the witnesses would not have signed unless the seller had reached majority. Abaye and Rava apply the same reasoning here: we presume the witnesses would not have composed and signed the *shtar* without having received proper authorization, even if the *shtar* itself does not record that authorization explicitly.

### Rav Pappa Object

Rav Pappa — and some attribute the objection also to Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua — challenges this application. The rule of Reish Lakish works when what is presumed is something universally understood. But the entire question of when witnesses must be authorized to write a *shtar* following an admission was itself the subject of extended Talmudic deliberation. If the matter was not obvious even to the scholars who debated it at length, can we assume that court scribes — *safrei d'bei dina* — automatically know this *halakha*? The scribe is, after all, the natural gatekeeper who would flag an improperly convened writing. If we cannot rely on him to know the requirement, then the absence of authorization language cannot be cured by presumption, and the *shtar* would be invalid.

### Scribes Test

The Gemara reports an empirical resolution: they actually went and tested the scribes of Abaye — and those scribes knew the *halakha*. They then tested the scribes of Rava — and those scribes knew as well. It is, of course, worth noting that it is Abaye and Rava themselves who invoke Reish Lakish's principle, and it is their own scribes who pass the test. There is something inherently circular about this; one might fairly observe that not every *beis din*'s scribes would necessarily be as well-trained. Nevertheless, the Gemara's conclusion stands: although explicit authorization language is preferred, its absence does not invalidate the *shtar*, since we may presume the scribes ensured the proper procedure was followed.

---

## Two Sig Confusion

### Mixed Signals

The Gemara now introduces a more complex case of an ambiguous *shtar*. This document was written using all the linguistic hallmarks of a *beis din* document — *duchran pisgamei*, a formal record of proceedings, and language structured in the manner of *lishnei d'bei dina*, the formulaic style courts use — as opposed to the style of *anan sahadi*, "we testify," which is characteristic of individual witnesses. The significance of this distinction is that an admission made before a *beis din* of three requires no authorization for a *shtar* to be written; authorization is only needed when witnesses are acting independently.

The problem is that despite all these signals pointing toward a *beis din* document, only two signatures appear at the bottom. A *beis din* requires three judges. One could imagine a scenario in which a third member died or was otherwise unavailable after the proceedings, in which case the proper practice would be to include a notation: *b'mosav tlata havina v'chad leiseih* — "we were convened as three, and one is no longer present." But no such notation appears. The document thus contains contradictory signals: the language of a *beis din* on one hand, and only two signatures without explanation on the other.

### Ravina View

Ravina proposes to resolve the ambiguity in favor of validity. He would apply Reish Lakish's presumption here as well, reasoning that we assume the *shtar* was done properly — that there was indeed a full *beis din* of three, and that the third member's absence from the signatures was simply an oversight, perhaps because he had passed away.

### Fear Error

Rav Natan bar Ami objects, citing a ruling in the name of Rava: *kol ki hai gavna chaishinan l'Beis Din to'eh* — in a case like this, we are concerned that this was a *beis din* in error, meaning that it may have operated with only two members who mistakenly considered themselves a proper *beis din*. The distinction from Reish Lakish's standard application is critical. Reish Lakish's presumption operates when everything in the *shtar* looks correct and there is no internal evidence of a problem. Here, however, the document itself provides affirmative evidence of a deficiency: there are only two signatures. This is not merely an absence of confirming language — it is a positive indication that something may be wrong. Accordingly, we cannot simply presume regularity.

### Explicit Language

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak refines the analysis. If the *shtar* explicitly contains the language *bei dina* — "the court" — indicating that the signatories identify themselves as acting in the capacity of a *beis din*, then even with only two signatures, Reish Lakish's presumption may be applied. The reasoning is that anyone who writes *bei dina* understands that a *beis din* requires three members, and therefore some explanation must account for why only two signed. We may presume the third member was present but did not sign for some reason.

### Two Valid

But the Gemara raises a further complication. Perhaps it was indeed only two judges who referred to themselves as a *beis din*, relying on the opinion of Shmuel: *shnayim she'danu dineihem din* — if two people adjudicate, their ruling is valid, though they are called a *beis din chatzuf*, an impudent court. If we rule like Shmuel, might these two have legitimately considered themselves a *beis din* entitled to use that language?

### Two Not Auth

The problem with this reasoning is that even granting Shmuel's position, two judges would not suffice for the specific purpose of authorizing a *shtar* to be written following an admission. As we have established, that requires a *beis din* of three. So even if two can validly adjudicate in general, they cannot serve as the forum before which an admission is made in a manner that permits a *shtar* to be written without separate authorization. The document's validity therefore remains in question.

### Rav Ashi Case

The Gemara resolves the matter by reference to a specific case: the *shtar* contains the words *bei dina d'Rav Ashi* — the court of Rav Ashi — or alternatively, *v'amar lan Rav Ashi*, that Rav Ashi himself instructed the court members to serve and to write the *shtar*. Under these circumstances, no one would assume that the court of Rav Ashi would conduct itself in a manner that merited the characterization of *chatzuf*. We therefore presume that the *beis din* was composed of a full three members, and that the third simply did not sign — an oversight — while the substance of the proceeding was entirely proper.

---

## Binding Admit

### Hidden Money

A *baraita* introduces a set of cases concerning the evidentiary weight of a statement made not in the context of a formal legal proceeding, but rather a private disclosure about the nature of hidden assets. The case: one person says to heirs, "I saw your father hide money in a chest, box, or cabinet, and he said that this money belongs to so-and-so" — or that it is *ma'aser sheni* funds. The question is not whether the heirs are being sued; no one is demanding they hand the money over. Rather, the heirs want to act correctly and need to know whether they are obligated to treat that money as belonging to another or as consecrated funds. Should they believe this single witness?

### Benefit Desire

The resolution turns on two factors: whether the person disclosing has the practical ability to benefit from what he is describing, and whether his disclosure reflects a genuine intent to inform. These two considerations together determine whether the statement carries evidentiary weight sufficient to obligate the heirs to act upon it, even though the speaker is only a single witness and the declaration was not made before a *beis din* or in the formal context of an admission to an interested party.

### House vs Field

The *baraita* distinguishes between two scenarios based on where the money is hidden. If the witness says the money is concealed in the house — *be-bayit* — his words carry no weight: *lo amar klum*. The circumstances leave open too many possibilities; there is no corroborating factor that lends credibility to his claim. However, if the witness says the money is hidden in the field — *be-sadeh* — under a specific rock, for instance, then his words do carry weight: *devarav kayamin*.

### Migo Principle

The reason for the distinction lies in the principle of *migo*: if I could have gone to the field when no one was watching and taken the money for myself, the fact that I am instead disclosing its whereabouts and its true ownership is strong evidence that I am telling the truth. Why would I fabricate a story that actually works against my own material interest? The general principle is stated explicitly: *kol she-beyado litol devarav kayamin; ein beyado litol lo amar klum* — wherever the claimant has the practical power to take the asset himself, his words stand; where he lacks that power, his statement carries no legal weight.

### Children Witness

A further case: the heirs themselves saw their father hide the money, and the father declared in their presence that it belonged to someone else or was *ma'aser sheni*. One might think this is even more clearly binding — the children are direct witnesses to both the hiding and the declaration. Yet the *baraita* does not treat this as automatically conclusive, because the father's declaration was not made as an admission to the interested party, and questions arise as to whether the statement should be taken at face value.

### Sincere vs False

The *baraita* resolves this through an inquiry into the father's intent. If he spoke *ki-mesaper* — in the manner of someone genuinely informing the listeners because he wants the matter handled correctly — then *devarav kayamin*, his words are binding. The heirs must treat the money accordingly. However, if it is evident that he was being *ma'arim* — scheming or maneuvering — for instance, by fabricating a story to discourage his children from spending the money on themselves, then *lo amar klum*, his declaration carries no legal force. The threshold question is whether the declaration was a sincere disclosure or a strategic deception, and the answer depends on the surrounding circumstances.

### Dreams No Weight

A final variation: the heir was distressed because he knew his father had accumulated substantial sums but could not locate where the money was hidden. A figure appeared to him in a dream and told him precisely: this amount, in this location, and — the money is *ma'aser sheni*. The heir arose the next morning, looked in the specified place, and found exactly the sum that had been described. Everything about the dream's content was verified — except for the *ma'aser sheni* status. Must he treat the money as *ma'aser sheni*?

The Gemara reports: *ze haya ma'aseh* — this actually occurred — *v'amru divrei chalomot lo ma'alin ve-lo moridin*. Dreams have no legal standing. They neither establish nor undermine a halakhic claim. The fact that the amount and location turned out to be accurate is remarkable but does not transform the dream into a valid evidentiary source. Perhaps it was coincidence; perhaps it was the dreamer's own subconscious knowledge emerging — though one might wonder why the subconscious would also have concluded that the money was *ma'aser sheni*. Nonetheless, the *halakha* is clear: one may not selectively credit a dream for purposes of legal obligation.

---

## Court Dissent

### Write Judgment

Having concluded the discussion of what constitutes a binding admission, the Gemara turns to the process of rendering and recording a court judgment. The *mishnah* has established that when two judges vote for acquittal and one votes for conviction, the ruling is acquittal — and that the dissenting judge may not go to the losing party afterward and express private sympathy with his position, since doing so constitutes *holech rachil*, talebearing. This raises a procedural question: when the court's ruling is formally written out and issued as a judgment document, what exactly do they write in the case of a two-to-one decision?

### Yochanan View

Rabbi Yochanan rules that the document is written in a unified voice: simply, that the court has found the party innocent — *zakai*. The entire court speaks as one body, and no trace of the internal division appears in the written record.

### Lakish View

Reish Lakish disagrees. He holds that the minority opinion must be recorded explicitly: *ploni u-ploni mezakin u-ploni mechayev* — judge A and judge B ruled for acquittal, and judge C ruled for conviction. The actual positions of the individual judges are recorded in the written judgment.

### No Talebear

The Gemara raises the obvious tension: how does Reish Lakish's position square with the *mishnah*'s prohibition of *lo telech rachil be-amecha* — the verse forbidding talebearing, which the *mishnah* invokes to prohibit a dissenting judge from privately expressing his disagreement to the losing party? If a dissenting judge may not reveal his minority position privately, how can it be written in the official judgment?

The Gemara does not make the reconciliation entirely explicit, but the natural distinction is between two fundamentally different modes of disclosure. What the *mishnah* prohibits is a judge going privately to one of the litigants and expressing personal allegiance to that party — sowing dissent, undermining the authority of the majority ruling, and signaling that the dissenter sided with one party against the other. This is what constitutes *rachilut*. By contrast, what Reish Lakish permits — indeed requires — is an official, transparent record in which the full court speaks with institutional authority, recording how each member voted as a matter of fact. The court document does not express sympathy or pick sides; it records the deliberation of the tribunal as a whole.

The underlying values driving each position can also be identified. Rabbi Yochanan insists on a unified voice in order to prevent any form of dissent-sowing — *mishum lo telech rachil*. Reish Lakish insists on accuracy because to write that all three judges ruled for acquittal when one did not would be *meiחzi ke-shikra* — it would have the appearance of falsehood. Beyond the prohibition of falsehood, there is also a positive reason to preserve the dissenting voice: minority opinions are recorded throughout the *Mishnah* so that future courts and future *halakhic* deliberations can draw upon them. The same logic may apply here, though the Gemara in this context focuses primarily on the *meiחzi ke-shikra* concern.

### Liability Issue

The Gemara explores what practical difference might follow from the dispute regarding how to write the judgment. One possibility: if the court is subsequently found to have ruled incorrectly — which in certain categories of law triggers an obligation on the *beis din*'s part to compensate the injured party — does the dissenting judge who had voted correctly share in the financial liability?

The initial proposal is that according to Rabbi Yochanan, who requires the minority opinion to be subsumed into a unified ruling, the dissenting judge would be obligated to pay his share, since the written judgment reflects all three judges as having ruled together. But this seems deeply unjust: the dissenting judge can turn to his colleagues and say, *ilu didi tzaitan, atun nami lo shalumtun* — had you listened to me, you would not be paying either. He was right all along and only the coercive logic of majority rule required him to have his voice formally absorbed into the ruling.

Conversely, under Rabbi Yochanan's framework, the two majority judges might argue that they should not be required to pay the full amount of compensation alone, since the judgment was rendered by a court of three, not two — the dissenter's participation in the court is what gave the ruling its formal validity. Without his presence the court could not have reached a *psak din* at all.

The Gemara's resolution to this impasse is that in either view, the liability question ultimately resolves similarly: what differs is whether the two majority judges pay the full amount or only two-thirds. If the judgment was recorded in a unified voice — with the dissenter formally included in the ruling — then the majority judges, as those who actually drove the erroneous conclusion, absorb the full weight of the compensation, since it is properly their *psak* that is being attributed to all three. If the dissenting opinion is recorded separately, the two who voted erroneously bear only two-thirds of the liability, their specific portion.

The Gemara steps back from this entire line of reasoning. Given the back-and-forth, the only real and stable *beinaihu* — practical difference — between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is the concern about *lo telech rachil be-amecha* itself: how concerned is each authority that recording the minority opinion, even in an official document, risks crossing into the territory of talebearing and undermining the integrity of the judicial process?

### Elazar Middle

Rabbi Elazar offers a compromise position that is sensitive to both concerns simultaneously. He rules that one writes: *mi-divreichem nizdaka ploni* — "from our deliberations, so-and-so has been found innocent." This formulation is notable for what it implies without stating explicitly. The phrase "from our deliberations" signals to any careful reader that there was a deliberative process — that the ruling was not self-evident, that some debate occurred — without identifying who voted which way or recording anyone's individual position. It preserves the unified voice of the court while hinting at the existence of internal disagreement.

Rabbi Elazar is thus concerned about both *lo telech rachil* and *meiחzi ke-shikra*: he will not simply write that all three unanimously ruled innocent when they did not, but he will not expose the particulars of individual votes either. Whether this language would be used even in cases of unanimous decisions — in which case it signals nothing — or only when there was a dissent — in which case it functions as a coded signal — is left open by the Gemara.

---

## Court Process

### Bring Parties

The *mishnah* states that once the judges concluded their deliberations, they would bring in the parties. The Gemara asks: who exactly had been outside during the deliberation and is now being brought back in? If it refers to the litigants — *baalei dinim* — then the implication is that the litigants were excluded from the deliberations, which actually accords with what we would expect, given the concern about judges expressing opinions in front of the parties. Yet there is no explicit statement earlier in the *mishnah* that the litigants were removed before deliberations began.

Alternatively, if the *mishnah* is referring to the witnesses being brought back in after deliberations, that would require explanation: why would witnesses need to be brought in at the conclusion? The Gemara suggests this would make sense only according to the view that witnesses must testify together in court simultaneously — that is, not like Rabbi Natan, who holds that witnesses may testify on separate days. Under that view, having heard the witnesses separately, the court would need to convene the witnesses together for a formal joint presentation of their testimony, and that would be the final act of "bringing them in" before the *psak* is issued.

The Gemara quickly sets aside this reading. In fact, the *mishnah* refers to the litigants being brought back in — not the witnesses. The litigants were removed during deliberations, and they are brought back in to receive the ruling. A separate *baraita* that specifically emphasizes bringing the witnesses back in after deliberations would, the Gemara concludes, represent a different view — one that does not follow Rabbi Natan — and is not the source text under discussion.

### Jerusalem Custom

The refined practice of Jerusalem is described by Rabbi Nechemia in a *baraita*: *kach hayu minhagam shel nekiyei ha-da'as she-bi-Yerushalayim* — this is how the people of clarity conducted themselves in Jerusalem. The proper sequence was as follows: first, the litigants are brought in and the court hears their respective claims; then the witnesses are brought in and their testimony is heard; then everyone — litigants and witnesses — is sent outside; the judges then deliberate; and when deliberations conclude, all parties are brought back in to receive the *psak*. This is presented as the most orderly and careful way to conduct the proceedings, ensuring that witnesses and litigants are not present during the judges' private deliberation and that all parties receive the ruling together in a formal setting.

---

## Witness Combine

### See Together

The Gemara now turns to a fundamental question in the law of testimony: when two witnesses observed related events — for instance, each witnessing the same defendant borrow money, but on different occasions — can their testimonies be combined to constitute valid proof? The *tanna kamma* holds that testimonies cannot combine unless both witnesses observed the same event together: *ein eidut mitztarefet ad she-yiru sheneihem ke-echad*.

### Sequential OK

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha disagrees: *afilu b'zeh achar zeh* — testimonies combine even when the witnesses observed events sequentially, not simultaneously. His ruling extends to both the viewing of the events and the presentation of testimony in court.

### Same Time

The Gemara asks: what exactly is the dispute? The disagreement may be grounded in either a textual argument from a *pasuk* or in a pure *svara*, a logical argument. It is worth pausing here to appreciate the Gemara's equanimity in presenting these alternatives. The formulation *i ba'it eima kra, i ba'it eima sevara* — "if you wish, cite the verse; if you wish, cite the logic" — and the fact that the *svara* is presented first, reflects something of the radical nature of *Torah she-ba-al peh*: a purely logical argument is treated as equally authoritative as a scriptural derivation. The Gemara elsewhere goes even further, asking *lama li kra, sevara hu* — why do I need a verse at all when logic alone suffices?

### Ed as One

If one prefers the textual derivation: the verse in Vayikra states *ve-hu ed o ra'ah o yada* — "and he is a witness, whether he saw or he knew." A related verse states *lo yakum ed echad* — "a single witness shall not stand up." From the fact that the Torah uses *ed echad*, specifying "one witness," the Gemara derives that the word *ed* by itself — without the word *echad* — would already connote two. This is established through the principle that wherever the Torah says *ed*, read it as referring to two, unless the text specifies *echad* and means a single individual. The implication of using a singular noun — *ed* — to refer to the minimum quorum of two witnesses is that the two must function as one: they must have witnessed the same event at the same time, such that they are, in testimony terms, a single unified entity. This is the textual basis for the *tanna kamma*'s view.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha reads the same phrase — *o ra'ah o yada*, "whether he saw or he knew" — as indicating that the Torah is expansive about the mode of knowledge: *however* a witness came to know, it qualifies. The disjunctive *o* — "or" — signals that the specifics of how or when the knowledge was acquired are not determinative.

### Testify Together

The *mishnah* contains a second clause: *ein eidutan mitkayemet be-veit din ad she-ya'idu sheneihem ke-echad* — testimony is not established in court unless both witnesses testify simultaneously. Rabbi Natan dissents: *shome'in devarav shel zeh hayom u-che-she-yavo chaveiro le-machar shome'in devarav* — one may hear the testimony of one witness today, and when the second witness arrives tomorrow, one hears his testimony separately. The question of whether witnesses must testify together in court is distinct from whether they must have observed the events together.

### Context Later

The logical debate underlying this question can be framed as follows. The *tanna kamma* reasons: if only one witness appears before the court on a given day, at that moment his testimony functions as that of a single witness — which under biblical law creates not a monetary obligation but an obligation on the defendant to take an oath. If his role is thus defined at the moment of his testimony as that of an *eid* for a *shvu'ah*, one cannot subsequently redefine it as an *eid* for monetary purposes when the second witness arrives.

Rabbi Natan's counter-argument is incisive: even when two witnesses appear together on the same day, they do not literally testify with one mouth simultaneously. The first speaks and then the second speaks. By the same logic one might say that when the first speaks, he is a lone *eid* whose testimony obligates an oath, not money — yet we do not say this. Rather, we say that what will come afterward provides the context for what was said first: the subsequent testimony of the second witness retroactively frames the first witness's testimony as part of a valid two-witness evidentiary unit. If we accept that principle when both come on the same day, the same logic should apply when they come on different days.

### Smicha Story

The Gemara relates a story that, beyond its narrative interest, bears on which ruling we follow. Rav Shimon ben Elyakim had long been trying to secure *smicha* — ordination — for Rabbi Yose berabbi Chanina, but without success. One day, Rabbi Yochanan posed a question to those assembled: does anyone know whether the *halakha* follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha or not? Rav Shimon ben Elyakim indicated that Rabbi Yose berabbi Chanina possessed that knowledge. Rabbi Yochanan asked that he be told. Rav Shimon ben Elyakim replied: if you want him to participate in the deliberations, grant him *smicha* first — and then he will tell you. Rabbi Yochanan granted Rabbi Yose berabbi Chanina *smicha*, and then asked him how he had heard the ruling.

Rabbi Yose berabbi Chanina responded: *kach shamati she-modin Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha le-Rabbi Natan* — I heard that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha concedes to Rabbi Natan. That is, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who permits witnesses to observe events separately, would certainly agree that witnesses may also testify separately — since if sequential observation is valid, sequential testimony is at least as permissible.

Rabbi Yochanan's response was sharp: *lezeh hutzrachti?* — for this I went to the trouble? The inference that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha would agree with Rabbi Natan is obvious: *uma ikar re'iyah be-hada de-amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha lo bainan, hagada mibaiya?* — if even the primary act of seeing does not need to be simultaneous according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, is it even a question that the testifying does not need to be simultaneous? Rabbi Yochanan expected something that actually settled the disputed question of the *halakha*, not a trivially obvious implication.

Nonetheless, Rabbi Yochanan told him: *ho'il ve-alita lo tered* — since you have already been elevated, you shall not descend. The *smicha* stands. Rabbi Zeira draws a lesson from the episode: *gavra raba, kivan de-isamech samech* — once a great person has granted *smicha*, that ordination is firm and is not revoked, even if the occasion for which it was granted turns out to have yielded less than anticipated.

It is worth noting that the cast of characters in the parallel account in the Yerushalmi differs: there it is Rabbi Yonatan rather than Rabbi Yochanan, and the roles of Rav Shimon ben Elyakim and Rabbi Yose berabbi Chanina appear to be reversed. The *Bavli* and *Yerushalmi* versions thus present strikingly different portraits of the same underlying event.

### Practical Rule

Rabbi Chiya bar Avin cites Rav: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha* — the practical ruling follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha — *bein be-karka bein be-metaltelin*, whether regarding land or movable property. The ruling applies across the board: even when two witnesses testify about events that occurred on different occasions, their testimonies may be combined.

### Ulla Limits

Ulla limits this ruling: we follow Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha in cases involving *karka* — land — but not in cases involving *metaltelin* — chattel. Abaye objects to this formulation: if Ulla says we rule like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha for land, that implies there is a debate regarding land and that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha does not automatically prevail there. But a tradition in the name of Rav — *modim chachamim le-Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha be-edut karka* — holds that when it comes to land, the *chachamim* themselves concede to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. The reason is straightforward: when two witnesses both testify that Reuven owns a particular parcel of land, they are by definition testifying about the same object. The testimonies inherently concern a single, identifiable thing. This is categorically different from two witnesses each testifying about a separate monetary transaction. According to this tradition, the question of combining testimonies is not disputed at all with respect to land.

A *baraita* attributed to Rabbi Idi bar Avin in the *yeshiva* of Karna confirms: *modim chachamim le-Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha be-edut bechor, u-ve-edut karka, u-ve-edut chazaka* — the sages concede to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha in cases of testimony about a firstborn (whether of an animal or, according to Tosafot, whether a person is a firstborn son entitled to a double inheritance share), about land, and about *chazaka* — the established presumption of land ownership. In all these cases, the object of testimony is singular and identifiable, and so there is no dispute: the testimonies combine even if the witnesses observed different aspects at different times.

The Gemara acknowledges that this *baraita* and Ulla's ruling represent different positions held by different authorities — *gavra a-gavra ka ramis* — and does not attempt to harmonize them further. One authority holds that land is contested and Rav rules for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha; another holds that land was never in dispute.

### Combination Examples

The Gemara then presents Rav's own view on when testimonies combine in monetary cases. Rav rules: *hodaah achar hodaah, hodaah achar halvaah mitztarfi* — an admission following an admission, or an admission following a loan, can be combined. If one witness testifies that he heard the defendant admit to owing a sum on one occasion, and another witness testifies that he heard a similar admission on a different occasion, they may be combined, since the defendant may well have been admitting to the same underlying debt on both occasions. Similarly, if one witness testifies to having witnessed the loan itself, and another testifies that the defendant subsequently admitted to that loan, the two testimonies concern the same event and combine.

However, *halvaah achar halvaah lo mitztarfi* — a loan after a loan does not combine. If one witness says he saw money lent on Monday and another says he saw money lent on Wednesday, they are clearly testifying about two separate transactions. Nor does *halvaah achar hodaah* — a loan witnessed after an admission — combine, since in that configuration the sequence indicates that the admission on Monday concerned a prior debt, and the loan on Wednesday was a new and separate transaction.

### Know Same Thing

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak pushes back against even the permissive cases. He asks: if the reason a loan-after-a-loan does not combine is that *maneh d'kahazi hai lav kahazi hai* — the sum witnessed by the first witness is not the same sum witnessed by the second — then the same logic applies to an admission after an admission. The sum admitted before the first witness is not the same sum admitted before the second witness. The mere possibility that the defendant was admitting to the same debt on both occasions is insufficient; how do we know he was not admitting to two different debts?

The Gemara suggests that the combining case involves a specific circumstance: when the defendant himself, in his second admission before the second witness, explicitly identified the prior admission — "this debt that I am admitting to you now, I also admitted before that other witness." In that case, there is no ambiguity about which debt is being discussed.

The Gemara then adds a further requirement: not only must the second witness know that the admission he heard concerned the same debt the first witness heard about, but the first witness must also know this. This would require the defendant to have subsequently informed the first witness: "the debt I admitted to you, I have now also admitted before a second witness." The need for each witness to independently know that both testimonies concern the same obligation is what the Gemara here demands.

### Rava Critique

Rava — some versions say Rav Sheshes — objects sharply to this structure. If you require this entire machinery of mutual cross-notification even in the case of admission-after-admission, the same requirement would logically have to apply even to the simpler case of *hodaah achar halvaah* — an admission after a loan — which Rav himself treated as unproblematically combinable. Must the witness to the loan go inform the witness to the admission, and vice versa, before their testimonies can be joined? That would make Rav's original distinction between loan-after-loan (which does not combine) and admission-after-admission (which does) practically meaningless.

The respondent acknowledges the force of this critique with an idiom: *d'ramisu diklei ve-zakifisu lehu* — you chopped down trees to use for construction, and now you are taking them and replanting them. The vivid image captures the frustration: an elegant framework was built up and then effectively dismantled by the very person who constructed it. The Gemara recognizes that the attempt to limit Rav's ruling to cases of absolute certainty — where every witness knows precisely what the other witnessed — goes far beyond what Rav himself ever required. Rav's original ruling is more straightforward: testimonies combine when it is possible they concern the same event, and they do not combine when it is clear they concern different events.

### Nehardai All

The scholars of Nehardei take the broadest possible position: *bein hodaah achar hodaah bein hodaah achar halvaah bein halvaah achar halvaah bein halvaah achar hodaah, mitztarfin* — all combinations, in every sequence, combine. Whether the witnesses observed admissions, loans, or any mixture thereof, and whether they did so simultaneously or at different times, the testimonies are joined. This is a straightforward and unqualified ruling in accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, without the additional distinctions introduced by Rav or the further restrictions proposed in the preceding discussion. The essential question is simply whether the combined testimonies establish that the defendant owes the amount claimed — and if they do, they are valid proof.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 31

## Contradictory Testimony

### Witnesses Combination

The daf opens by picking up where the previous discussion left off: the question of combining the testimony of two witnesses who each observed different aspects of a case. The paradigmatic issue is that of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who permits combining witnesses who testified about the same underlying obligation but observed it at different times — one seeing the loan on Monday, the other on Wednesday. The *gemara* now extends this inquiry into a related but distinct problem: what happens when two witnesses testify about the same case, but their accounts contradict each other on certain details?

### Bedikot vs. Chakirot

Rav Yehuda establishes a foundational distinction. There are two categories of questions put to witnesses: *chakirot*, which are the foundational questions of time and place — when and where did the event occur — necessary to establish the possibility of rendering the witnesses *edim zommim*; and *bedikot*, which are questions about the particulars and circumstances of the case itself. Regarding *chakirot*, witnesses may not respond *eini yodeia* — "I do not know" — whereas regarding *bedikot* they may. The critical ruling Rav Yehuda now introduces is: *edut hamacheshet zo et zo b'dikot, k'sherah b'dinei mamonot* — testimony that contradicts itself in *bedikot* is valid in civil cases. If one witness says the borrower was wearing a red shirt and the other says black, that inconsistency does not invalidate the testimony in *dinei mamonot*. In *dinei nefashot*, however, such contradictions would be disqualifying.

### Trivial vs. Substantive

Rava clarifies and refines Rav Yehuda's principle. The distinction is not merely between *chakirot* and *bedikot*, but between contradictions in genuinely trivial peripheral detail versus contradictions that go to the substance of the transaction itself. Rava's example: if one witness says the borrower's wallet was black and the other says it was white, that is trivial — an *arnaki shechorah* versus an *arnaki levanah* — and the testimony stands in *dinei mamonot*. But if one says the coins lent were old and tarnished while the other says they were new and shiny — *mana shachor* versus *mana lavan* — while this does not change the amount of the loan, it touches on the substance of the transaction itself. In that case, Rava holds, the testimonies cannot combine: *ein mitztarfin*.

The *gemara* then presses: does Rav Yehuda mean that even a trivial detail like the *arnaki shechorah* case would invalidate testimony in *dinei nefashot*? This seems harsh. The *gemara* raises the position of Rav Chisda, who states that one witness saying he was killed with a sword (*sayif*) and another saying with a spear are not in accord and thus inadmissible — *ein zeh nachon* — but if one says the killer was dressed in black and the other says in white, *harei zeh nachon*, that is acceptable even in *dinei nefashot*. So Rav Chisda himself does not invalidate trivial details in capital cases. The *gemara* responds: *gavra gavra rami* — this is simply a debate between Rav Yehuda and Rav Chisda. Nardea'ei then weigh in: even if witnesses contradict on the substantive details of the transaction itself in *dinei mamonot*, they may still combine. The *gemara* asks: is this then like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha? The answer is no — Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's principle applies where witnesses are not contradicting each other at all, merely testifying to separate but similar events that can be abstracted together. Where witnesses genuinely contradict about the same event, even Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha would not combine them. The Nardea'ei must therefore be going on the basis of a different *tanna*.

### Overlap Principle

That *tanna* is Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who states: *lo necheleku Beit Shammai u'Beit Hillel al shtei kitei edim she'achat omeret masayim ve'achat omeret maneh* — there was no dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel in the case of two *groups* of witnesses, one saying the borrower owes two hundred and the other saying one hundred. All agree we accept the lower figure, invoking the principle *yesh bichlal masayim maneh* — one hundred is subsumed within two hundred, so all witnesses agree at minimum to the lower amount.

The debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar explains, concerned a single group of witnesses internally contradicting — one witness saying one hundred and another within the same group saying two hundred. Beit Shammai holds that since the group's testimony is divided, the entire testimony is voided: *nechelekah edutan*. Beit Hillel applies the principle of *yesh bichlal masayim maneh*: since two hundred contains one hundred, the group is unanimously testifying to at least one hundred, and that amount is accepted. This represents an even greater *chiddush* than Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's ruling: here witnesses are contradicting about the substantive terms of the very same case, and we nonetheless find the overlap and accept it.

### Application Cases
