Two illustrative cases then appear. First: one witness says it was a barrel of wine (*chavit shel yayin*) and the other says a barrel of oil (*chavit shel shemen*). This incident came before Rav Ami, who ruled that the defendant must pay at least the value of wine — the lesser of the two — since all witnesses agree at minimum to that value. The *gemara* challenges: is this going like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar? The principle of *yesh bichlal masayim maneh* works because two hundred literally contains one hundred. But wine and oil are entirely different commodities; it cannot be said that oil "contains" wine in the way two hundred contains one hundred. The *gemara* retreats: the case must be reframed in terms of monetary value — one witness assessed the obligation at the value of wine, another at the value of oil — returning it to a standard high-low numerical dispute. The simpler reading of one commodity versus another is thus more difficult to sustain under the Beit Hillel principle.

The second case: one witness says the transaction occurred on the upper balcony (*diyuta ha'elyona*) and another on the lower balcony (*diyuta hatachtona*). Rabbi Chanina reports that such a case came before Rabbi, who combined their testimony — a ruling that seems relatively unsurprising, since the location of the event within a building is as trivial a detail as one could imagine.

---

## Privacy & Disclosure

### Dissenting Opinions

The *gemara* now turns to a section of the *Mishnah* addressing the prohibition on judges disclosing what transpired within the court. The *Mishnah* states: *minayin lechesheyetze lo yomar hareni mezakeh vachaverai mechayivin* — from where do we know that when a judge leaves court, he may not say "I voted to acquit but my colleagues outvoted me"? He may not go around cultivating sympathy outside the court, telling a litigant that he personally favored him. *U'mah a'aseh shechaverai rabu alai* — "what could I do, they were the majority against me?"

### Lo Telech Rachil

The biblical source is *lo telech rachil b'amecha* — do not go as a talebearer among your people. The *gemara* adds the verse *holech rachil megaleh sod* — one who goes and spreads tales reveals private matters. Judicial deliberations are precisely the kind of private matters this prohibition encompasses.

### Student Story

A striking episode then follows. There were reports circulating that a certain student had revealed things that had been said in the *beit midrash* twenty-two years earlier — effectively writing a tell-all account of private discussions that had occurred decades prior. One might think that after so many years a kind of statute of limitations would apply. Nevertheless, Rav Ami expelled him from the *beit midrash*, declaring: *dein galya raza* — this man reveals secrets. The passage of twenty-two years provides no exemption from the prohibition of *galya raza*.

---

## Reopening Cases

### 30-Day Limit Debate

The *Mishnah* teaches: *kol zman shemeivi raya soter et hadin* — any time a litigant produces new evidence, it can overturn the judgment. The court may attempt to place a limit on this: "bring whatever evidence you have within thirty days." If evidence is found within thirty days the case can be reopened; after thirty days it cannot. This is the position of the *Tanna Kamma*. The practical reasoning is clear: once a ruling has been issued and the prevailing party has acted on it — investing in property, developing land, entering into new arrangements — the other party cannot be permitted to unravel everything at any future moment.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: *ma ya'aseh zeh shelo matza besoch shloshim umatza le'achar shloshim* — what is the person to do who simply did not find his evidence within thirty days but found it afterward? The court cannot impose such a cutoff. A person always retains the right to reopen a case with newly discovered evidence. This debate concerns *dinei mamonot*; in *dinei nefashot*, the door to reopening in favor of the accused is always kept open until the very last moment.

### Forfeiture Principle

A distinct scenario: during the court proceedings themselves, the court asks the litigant to bring witnesses, and he says *ein li edim* — I have none. The court asks for documentary proof, and he says *ein li raya* — I have none. Subsequently he produces witnesses or evidence. Has he forfeited his right to bring them by explicitly declaring he had nothing? The *Tanna Kamma* says yes — by declaring before the court that he has no evidence, he has effectively testified to that fact and forfeited his ability to produce it later. *Harei zeh eino klum* — it is of no effect.

### Unknowingly Unavailable

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: *ma ya'aseh zeh shelo haya yodeia sheyeish lo eidim umatza eidim* — what is to be done for one who genuinely did not know he had witnesses, and then found them? He made an honest mistake. The practical lesson for the litigant under the *Tanna Kamma*'s ruling is clear: never state categorically before the court that you have no witnesses; always say "as far as I know I have none, but I cannot be certain without further inquiry."

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel himself, however, acknowledges a limiting case: if the circumstances make it evident that something suspicious is occurring — the litigant said he had no evidence, then immediately as the ruling appeared to go against him, he produced witnesses from among those present (*kirvu ploni u'ploni veya'iduni*) or extracted a proof document from his own sack — then even he agrees the evidence cannot be accepted. When the duplicity is manifest, *harei zeh eino klum*.

### Halacha: First Case

Rabbah bar bar Chana states: *halacha keRabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — the law follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the first case, namely that the court cannot impose a thirty-day limit on producing new evidence. One cannot simply infer this from the ruling in the first case, the *gemara* notes, because one might argue that *lechatchila* we advise courts not to impose such limits, but *bedi'avad*, if a court did impose a limit and then refused to hear new evidence, its ruling might stand. Therefore it is stated explicitly: *de'ahadori mehadreinan leih* — we reverse any such ruling. The right to produce new evidence and reopen a case is fully intact regardless of any court-imposed deadline.

### Halacha: Second Case

Rava bar Rav Huna said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *halacha k'divrei chachamim* — the law follows the *Chachamim* in the second case. Once a litigant has declared before the court that he has no witnesses, he may not subsequently produce them. And symmetrically: *ein halacha k'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* in this case. The *gemara* notes the apparent redundancy of stating both sides, and resolves it: the emphasis on *ein halacha k'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* here is deliberate, because in virtually every other instance in the *Mishnah* where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel appears, the *halacha* follows him. This is the exceptional case, and it needed to be called out explicitly.

---

## Sealing Claims

### Three Exceptions

Rabbah bar bar Chana further cites Rabbi Yochanan's general rule: *kol makom sheshana Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel b'mishnatenu halacha k'moto* — wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel appears in our *Mishnah*, the *halacha* follows him, *chutz* — with three exceptions: *arev*, *Tzidan*, and *ra'aya achrona*.

*Arev* refers to the case at the end of Bava Batra concerning the guarantor — the co-signer — and the rules governing whether the creditor must first pursue the primary debtor or can go directly to the guarantor, depending on whether the guaranty was issued *b'sha'at matan ma'ot* or *achar matan ma'ot*. *Tzidan* refers to a case involving criticism of witnesses — a claim that witnesses were in a particular location — where the *halacha* departs from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. And *ra'aya achrona* — the "final evidence" — refers precisely to our case. It is called the final *ra'aya* because our *Mishnah* presents two scenarios involving a litigant's claim of having evidence. In the first scenario (the thirty-day limit), we rule like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. In the second scenario (the litigant who declared he had no witnesses), we do not. *Ra'aya achrona* refers to that second scenario in our *Mishnah*.

---

## Child's Case

### Child Case Details

A case: a child (*yanuka*) was brought before Rav Nachman for judgment. Rav Nachman asked him: *it lakh sa'adei?* — do you have witnesses? The child said no. *It lakh ra'aya?* — do you have evidence? Again, no. Rav Nachman ruled against him. The child left in tears. Certain bystanders who heard the child crying asked what had happened, and upon learning the circumstances, said: *anan yad'inan b'milei de-avukh* — we know about your father's business dealings; we have relevant evidence to offer.

Tosafot raises a preliminary question about whether testimony may be accepted in the absence of the other party, *shelo befanav*, noting that this issue had been explored in the *Yerushalmi*. The *gemara* here does not address that question directly.

### Children Unaware

Rav Nachman rules: *b'ha afilu rabanan modu de-yanuka b'milei de-avuhu lo yada* — even the *Rabbanan* who rule against Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the *ra'aya achrona* case would concede here. The reason is not merely general circumstantial evidence suggesting the child was unaware; rather, it is that *as a matter of general principle* we do not assume that children know the details of their father's business affairs. When the child said he had no evidence, that statement cannot be treated as a categorical forfeiture, because it reflects a structural epistemic limitation inherent to the child's position, not a deliberate claim. The new evidence produced by the bystanders may therefore be accepted.

This raises the broader question of how far the principle extends. Is it limited to an *yoresh* — an heir who is not the direct *baal din* but is representing his father's estate — or would it apply in other circumstances where a litigant's unawareness of evidence is demonstrable? The *gemara* leaves this open.

---

## Receipt & Migo

### Woman & Receipt

A woman produced a *shetar* — a loan document — that was in her possession. She declared: *yada'ana b'hai shetara depari'a hava* — I know that this loan document has already been paid. In other words, the document evidences a debt that David ostensibly owes Michael, and the woman, who had been holding the document, claims the debt was in fact discharged, though there is no receipt.

### Rav Nachman Believes

Rav Nachman believes her declaration.

### Rava's Objection

Rava challenges Rav Nachman: *keman?* — on whose view are you relying? Is this going like Rabbi, who holds that *otiyot niknot b'mesirah* — a *shetar* can be transferred through physical delivery? If so, since the woman was holding the *shetar*, she could have claimed the debt as her own. But the *gemara* does not accept that reasoning.

### Validated in Court

Rav Nachman explains his ruling differently: *shani hacha de-i ba'ya kaltah* — what is distinctive here is that she could have simply destroyed the document. Since she chose to produce it rather than burn it, we believe her claim that it was paid, on the basis of *migo* — had she wanted to conceal that the debt existed, she could have destroyed it, so her producing it and simultaneously claiming payment is credible. 

The *gemara* then presents an alternative version of the exchange. In this version, Rav Nachman does *not* believe her, and it is Rava who raises the *migo* argument: surely she could have destroyed it? Rav Nachman responds: *keivan de-itchazei b'bei dina i ba'ya kaltah lo amrinan* — once the *shetar* had been validated before a *beit din*, we no longer apply the *migo* of "she could have destroyed it." Rashi explains the reason: the principle is *edim hachatumim al hashetar kemi shenechkerah edutam b'beit din* — witnesses whose signatures appear on a document are treated as if their testimony had been formally examined in court. Accordingly, we have witnesses attesting that the debt exists; a *migo* is insufficient to override the testimony of witnesses. Tosafot questions this: even if the *shetar* was validated, she still *could* have destroyed it, and the *migo* argument should remain valid on its own terms. Tosafot therefore explains that *itchazei b'bei dina* means the *beit din* had previously seen the *shetar* in her possession, so it was already known to exist — burning it was no longer an option.

### Receipt Challenge

Rava then poses a challenge to Rav Nachman's position. Consider the case of a *simpon* — a receipt — that bears signatures: if an unsigned receipt is produced by the person holding the *shetar*, together with the *shetar* itself, the *shalish* — the trustee holding the documents — is believed. An unsigned receipt is normally worthless, yet since the person is producing both the *shetar* and the receipt, they are believed to say the *shetar* was paid. This apparently contradicts Rav Nachman's view that producing a document cannot lend credibility to an accompanying claim.

### Migo Resolution

The resolution: the act of producing the *shetar* itself creates a *migo*. By bringing the document forward, the holder demonstrates that if she had wanted to simply make the debt disappear she could have destroyed it. Therefore, when she produces it and simultaneously declares it paid, she is believed — even on the basis of an unsigned receipt. The *tiyuvta* against Rav Nachman's first position stands.

---

## Sealing Claims (II)

### Until Claims Sealed

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he cited Rabbi Yochanan: *le'olam mevi ra'ayah vesoter* — one can always produce evidence and reopen a case, *ad she'yistatemu ta'anotav* — until his claims have been sealed off. The *gemara* initially puzzles over this formulation, because no external sealing mechanism has been identified in the *Mishnah*. The phrase *yistatemu ta'anotav* seems to refer to the litigant's own declaration — *ein li ra'ayah* — which is precisely what seals his claims and triggers the *Rabbanan*'s rule against further evidence.

The *gemara* then examines an apparent internal contradiction. On one reading, once claims are sealed — by saying *ein li edim*, *ein li ra'ayah* — the *Rabbanan*'s rule applies and no further evidence is admitted. But another formulation attributed to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel suggests evidence is inadmissible only when the circumstances are clearly suspicious — the moment he said he had nothing and immediately called for witnesses (*ploni u'ploni ye'iduni*). These are different standards. Could the entire *sugya* be read as following Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, with *yistatemu ta'anotav* interpreted narrowly to mean only the case of obvious manipulation? The *gemara* rejects this: Rabbi Yochanan had explicitly stated that the *halacha* follows the *Chachamim* and not Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the *ra'aya achrona* case. One cannot construe the ruling as being in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

The resolution comes when Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda cites Rabbi Yochanan with greater precision: *le'olam mevi ra'ayah vesoter ad she'yistatemu ta'anotav* — one may always produce evidence, until he seals his own claims by declaring *ein li edim, ein li ra'ayah*. At that point we rule like the *Rabbanan* and no further evidence is accepted. The phrase *u'veyomar kirvu ploni u'ploni ve'ha'iduni* describes the case where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel himself would reject the evidence — when the suspicious circumstances are manifest — and this represents a separate ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, not the general standard.

### Exception Cases

Even after claims have been sealed by the declaration *ein li edim*, there remain certain exceptional circumstances in which evidence may still be admitted. First: *aval bau edim m'medinat hayam* — if witnesses arrived from overseas after the litigant had declared he had no witnesses, since there is a clear reason the litigant could not have known of their availability, their testimony may be admitted. Second: *o shehayah diskaya shel aviv mufkedet b'yad acher* — if the father's collection of documents and proofs was being held by a third party, and those documents came to light only later, that evidence may be brought. Importantly, this second case demonstrates that the exception is not limited to the specific case of a child and his father's affairs; it extends to any situation where there is demonstrable reason the litigant was unaware of available evidence, even in one's own affairs.

---

## Venue & Jurisdiction

### Court Location

When Rav Dimi came and cited Rabbi Yochanan, he also transmitted the following ruling: *hatokef et chavero b'din* — when one party seeks to bring another to court, and one says *nidon kan* — let us litigate here locally — while the other says *neilech l'makom hava'ad* — let us go to the major court — the rule is *kofin oto veyelech l'makom hava'ad*: the party who wants to go to the major court can compel the other to go there.

### Lender Dictates

Rabbi Elazar raises an objection before Rabbi: *mi she'nosheh b'chavero maneh yotzi maneh al maneh?* — if Michael is the lender and I the borrower, are you saying Michael must spend one hundred to recover one hundred, traveling at his own expense to a distant court because I insist on it? Rather, the *halacha* is: *kofin oto vedan b'iro* — the borrower can be forced to litigate in the lender's locale.

Rav Safra adds a complementary ruling: where two parties are being obstinate and disputing the venue, we rule that the case is heard locally, *d'im hutzrach davar lishol* — and if the local *beit din* needs to refer a question to the larger court, *kotvin vesholchin* — they write to them and receive their guidance. The mere existence of a major court does not require parties to travel there; the local court can access the major court's authority through written correspondence.

---

## Judgment Reasons

### Upon Request

In this same context, the *gemara* states: *ve-im amar kisvu usnu li me-eizeh ta'am dantuni, kosvin venosnin lo* — if the losing party requests that the court commit to writing the reasoning behind its judgment, the court writes it out and provides it to him. The structure of this ruling implies two things: first, the court does not routinely provide written reasoning absent a request; second, the right to request written reasoning appears to arise specifically in this context — where a party has been compelled to litigate before a local court over his objection.

### Tosafot Question

Tosafot addresses this directly: *davka heicha denis-atzmu ladin vekafu ladun kan* — this provision applies specifically where the parties contended about venue and the party was compelled to litigate before the local court. In that circumstance alone does the losing party have the right to demand a written statement of reasons — *aval b'alma lo*, but not in the ordinary case. Tosafot notes a possible alternative reading, suggesting that perhaps in such a case the court must in any event notify the losing party of the grounds of the decision even without his asking, while in general cases written reasons are provided only upon request. The Tosafot's discussion also raises the implicit corollary: if the losing party in a local court obtains a written statement of reasons, could he then bring that document to the major court and argue that the local court erred? This connects to the broader framework of *ta'ah bidvar mishnah* and *ta'ah bidvar halacha* — categories of judicial error that are reversible — though the *gemara* does not spell this out.

---

## Venue & Jurisdiction (II)

### Yibum Case

The *gemara* introduces a case from *yibum*: *vehayevamah holeches achar yavam* — the *yevamah* (sister-in-law) must follow the *yavam* (brother-in-law) to his location in order to perform either *yibum* or *chalitzah*; she cannot demand that he come to her. Rabbi Ami states: this applies even from Tiberias to Sepphoris. Rashi explains the significance: even though Tiberias is the larger city, the *yevamah* must travel to the smaller location of the *yavam* and cannot insist that he come to the larger city.

The biblical basis is derived by Rav Kahana: *veyikre'u lo ziknei iro* — the elders of *his* city are called, not the elders of *her* city. Accordingly, the proceedings take place in his city. This also means that if the *yavam* is away from his home, his city's court can summon him back — the *yevamah* is required to come to his city, not to wherever he happens to be at the moment.

### Lender-Borrower

Meimar rules: *halacha holeches, kofin oto veyelech l'makom hava'ad* — in the *yibum* case, the *yevamah* can compel the *yavam* to go to the major court. Rav Ashi challenges this on the basis of Rabbi Elazar's ruling that a party can be compelled to litigate locally. Rav Ashi resolves the apparent conflict: *hani mili heicha dekamar loveh le-malveh* — the principle that one goes locally applies when it is the borrower making demands of the lender. The underlying rationale is *malveh eved loveh le-ish malveh* — the borrower is in a position of subservience to the lender. It is therefore the lender who dictates the terms of where litigation occurs. If the lender wishes to remain local, the borrower cannot force him to the major court. If the lender wishes to bring the borrower to the major court, he may compel him to go. In any case, the lender's prerogative governs. The *yibum* case, involving different dynamics, is therefore distinguishable.

---

## Ukvin Case

### Letter to Mar Ukva

The *gemara* records that a letter was sent to Mar Ukva in highly poetic terms, referencing the luminosity associated with *Moshe Rabbeinu* — *karan or panav* — and applying the imagery to Mar Ukva as one who shines like the son of *Batya* (daughter of Pharaoh who raised Moshe). The letter conveyed that a certain *Ukvan HaBavli* had brought a complaint against someone — identified as *Yirmiyah achi* — claiming that he had wronged him: *he'evir alai et haderech*. The letter told Mar Ukva to judge the case, and instructed the defendant to appear before the court in Tiberias.

The *gemara* notes an apparent internal contradiction in the letter: on one reading it says "you judge him," while on another it says "have him appear before us in Tiberias." *Hagufa kashya* — the passage itself is difficult. The resolution: the message to Mar Ukva was structured as follows — *daynu atun*, we are asking you to judge him; *ei tzyat tzyat*, if you can get him to comply and submit to your judgment locally in Bavel, fine; *v'ei lo, hatzivu v'harei paneinu beTverya*, and if you cannot get him to submit, then have him appear before us here in Tiberias and we will hear it.

### Knas Explanation

Rav Ashi offers an alternative interpretation: *dinei knasot hava* — this was a case involving a *knas*, a penalty. In Babylonia, *dinei knasot* are not adjudicated — *u'vei b'Bavel lo dayni dinei knasot*. Therefore, the case was never going to be heard before Mar Ukva in Bavel at all; it was always going to be tried in Eretz Yisrael.

### Honoring Mar Ukva

If that is so, why was the letter sent to Mar Ukva at all? The *gemara* answers: *kedei lachlok kavod leMar Ukva* — to honor Mar Ukva. The Eretz Yisrael *beit din* reached out to the great Babylonian leader out of respect, informing him of the case and of their intention to hear it in Tiberias. The elaborate and poetic formulation of the letter was itself an expression of that honor.

---

## Court Costs

### No Expense Payment

Tosafot closes the daf with a significant observation arising from the earlier discussion of *mi she'nosheh b'chavero maneh yotzi maneh al maneh* — the concern that the lender would have to spend money to recover his money. One might ask: why not simply have the lender travel to the borrower's preferred venue and then require the guilty party to reimburse the lender's travel expenses? Tosafot answers: *mikan lemi shechayav badin d'lo m'shaleim l'idach yitziotav* — this very *gemara* is the source for the principle that even a party who is found liable in litigation does not pay the opposing party's expenses, *af al pi shemazkiko leilech ladun b'ir acheret*, even when the litigation required the other party to travel to a different city to pursue the case. The *gemara* never suggested that possibility as a solution, and that silence is itself the ruling.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 32

## Perek Intro & Structure

### Opening & Transition

Today's *daf* is 32, and with it we begin the fourth *perek*, *Echad Dinei Mamonot*. The first three *prakim* laid essential groundwork: the first *perek* established which cases require a court of three, of twenty-three, or of seventy-one — reflecting the fundamental distinction between civil and capital cases. The second *perek* digressed to address the special status of the *Kohen Gadol* and the king. The third *perek* returned to the core questions of what constitutes a valid court, how judges are defined, what renders witnesses valid or invalid, and at what stages a litigant may still bring proofs to overturn a decision. There it was established that in monetary cases a majority of one suffices to reach a verdict, and the framework for when evidence may be brought to reverse a judgment was laid out. These serve as the building blocks for the present *perek*.

### Drishah V'Chakirah

The *perek* opens with the principle that *dinei mamonot* and *dinei nefashot* share certain fundamental requirements. Specifically: *echad dinei mamonot v'echad dinei nefashot b'drishah uv'chakirah* — whether in civil or capital cases, both require *drishah v'chakirah*. *Drishah* refers to the type of questioning that establishes the precise facts of what occurred and verifies that the witnesses are telling a consistent story. *Chakirah* refers to the seven specific interrogative questions — six concerning when the event occurred and one concerning where — which create the legal basis for a finding of *edim zomemim*. If other witnesses come forward and testify that the original witnesses could not have been present at the stated place and time — because they were elsewhere in the company of these new witnesses — the original witnesses are disqualified as *edim zomemim*. Both *drishah* and *chakirah* are required in *dinei nefashot* and, according to the *Mishnah*, in *dinei mamonot* as well. The scriptural basis is *mishpat echad yihiyeh lachem* — there shall be one standard of justice, whether the case is capital or civil.

### Key Differences

Notwithstanding this shared foundation, the *Mishnah* proceeds to enumerate the differences between *dinei mamonot* and *dinei nefashot*. The first difference already noted in the first *perek* is that civil cases require a court of three while capital cases require twenty-three. This distinction in court size does not constitute a violation of *mishpat echad*; the underlying rules remain the same.

The more substantive differences are as follows. With respect to how deliberations are opened: in *dinei mamonot*, the court may open by arguing either toward innocence or toward guilt — *potchin bein l'zechut bein l'chovah*. In *dinei nefashot*, however, the court may only open by arguing toward the accused's innocence — *potchin l'zechut v'ein potchin l'chovah*. The reason is the principle of *v'hitzilu ha'edah*: the court bears a special mandate to exert extraordinary effort to protect a possibly innocent life from wrongful capital punishment.

*Tosafot* makes a further observation: some of these distinctions can only apply to *dinei nefashot* in the first place, because in monetary cases there is no pure category of innocence or guilt. One party's innocence is the other party's loss; one party's liability is the other's gain. The concepts of *zechut* and *chovah* in monetary cases are always relative to the two competing parties, making an absolute *potchin l'zechut* structurally impossible. In *dinei nefashot*, by contrast, there is a straightforward distinction: arguments toward the accused's guilt constitute *chovah*, and arguments toward innocence constitute *zechut*.

### V'Hitzilu Ha'edah

The *Mishnah* continues: with respect to majority requirements, *dinei mamonot* may be decided by a simple majority of one — *matin al pi echad* — whether the verdict favors or disfavors either litigant. In *dinei nefashot*, a majority of one suffices to acquit, but a majority of two is required to convict. Since in capital cases there is a true *chovah* — the punishment of the accused — the *Torah* requires a heightened threshold before that verdict may be rendered.

### American Law Comparison

This structure invites comparison to American law, though the differences are significant. In American criminal proceedings, the standard of proof itself already differs: civil cases operate on a preponderance of the evidence, while criminal cases require proof beyond a reasonable doubt — a distinction that has no precise parallel in the *Mishnah*'s framework. More strikingly, American law in both capital and criminal cases requires a unanimous jury — not merely a majority of two — and in most civil jurisdictions unanimity is similarly required, though certain jurisdictions permit majority verdicts. The *Talmudic* framework, which imposes a mere majority of two for capital convictions, thus diverges markedly from contemporary practice, even while sharing the underlying intuition that the threshold for finding someone guilty of the gravest offenses must be meaningfully higher.

### Case Reversal Rules

With respect to reversibility of verdicts: in *dinei mamonot*, the court may revisit a case and reverse its decision in either direction — *machzirin bein l'zechut bein l'chovah* — whether new evidence or a recognized error would benefit or harm either party. Since hurting one side always benefits the other, a reversal is necessarily both *zechut* and *chovah* simultaneously.

In *dinei nefashot*, however, a verdict may only be reversed to find the accused innocent — *machzirin l'zechut v'ein machzirin l'chovah*. Once someone has been acquitted, no new evidence may be brought to reinstate their guilt. This is analogous to the principle against double jeopardy in American law, which similarly bars retrial of an acquitted defendant.

### Who Can Argue

In *dinei mamonot*, anyone present — including students and non-judges, the *talmidim* who sit in the court as observers or apprentices — may argue on either side of the case. In *dinei nefashot*, students and non-judges may voice arguments in defense of the accused — *hakol melamdim zechut* — but arguments toward guilt may only come from the judges themselves — *v'ein hakol melamdim chovah*.

### Argument Switching

The *Mishnah* addresses the ability of judges to switch their argumentative position during deliberations. In *dinei mamonot*, any judge who has argued on one side may freely switch to arguing the opposite position. In *dinei nefashot*, if a judge has been arguing toward the accused's guilt, he may change his position and argue for innocence. However, if a judge has already argued toward the accused's innocence, he may not subsequently argue toward guilt. *Rashi* clarifies that this restriction applies only to the deliberative arguments, not to the final vote: a judge who argued for innocence may ultimately vote for guilt if that is his sincere conclusion. The logic, however, is that since the judge has already publicly invested himself in the argument for innocence, that commitment will press him to search even more rigorously for grounds on which to exonerate the accused — and that pressure is precisely what *dinei nefashot* is designed to create.

### Timing Requirements

Regarding timing: *dinei mamonot* may be opened during the day and concluded at night — that is, deliberations begun during daylight hours may be finalized on the following evening. *Dinei nefashot*, however, must not only begin during the day but the *gemar din*, the final pronouncement of the verdict, must also occur during the day. While it may take place on a subsequent day, it may never be rendered at night.

Furthermore, in *dinei mamonot* the entire proceeding may be completed in a single day regardless of the outcome. In *dinei nefashot*, a verdict of innocence may be rendered on the same day the case opened, but a verdict of guilt may not. If the court is inclined toward conviction, judgment must be deferred until the following day — giving the judges time to sleep on the matter, reflect further, and avoid any rush to condemn a defendant in a capital case.

### Holiday Restrictions

It follows from the above that a capital case may not be initiated on *Erev Shabbat* or *Erev Yom Tov*. Since a guilty verdict requires a second day of deliberation, and *din* cannot be conducted on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*, beginning a case on *Erev Shabbat* would force an unacceptable delay in rendering judgment. Such delay constitutes *inuy hadin* — the wrongful prolongation of a judgment — and is therefore prohibited.

### Tahor V'Tamei

The *Mishnah* then addresses the order of arguments among judges. In *dinei mamonot* — and here, interestingly, the *Mishnah* adds cases of *tumah v'taharah*, which raises the question of why a matter of *tumah v'taharah* would come before a *beit din* rather than simply being referred to a rabbi for a *psak*. One would have to construct a case in which there was an attendant *malkus* or *mamonot* dimension — perhaps someone claimed that another rendered his grain *tamei* and thus owes compensation. The exact case is not spelled out, but in any event the principle is that deliberations begin with the senior judge, since in non-capital contexts there is no concern that the elder's view will suppress genuine debate.

In *dinei nefashot*, however, deliberations begin from one of the more junior judges — *matchilin min hatzad* — precisely because if a senior judge were to argue first for conviction, his voice might dominate and chill the deliberations. The *Mishnah* ensures that real debate and vigorous advocacy for innocence have every opportunity to unfold before the most authoritative opinions are heard.

It is worth noting that *malkus* cases have not been explicitly addressed. The *Mishnah* mentions twenty-three as the size of the court only for genuine *dinei nefashot*. It would appear that cases that fall between pure *mamonot* and *nefashot* — including *malkus* — are in many respects treated in the *mamonot* category, though this will require further analysis as the *Gemara* proceeds.

### Judge Eligibility

Finally, the *Mishnah* addresses who is qualified to serve as a judge. Anyone — notwithstanding various disqualifications such as family relationship, *avadim*, and the like, and setting aside the broader question of whether women may serve — may sit as a judge in *dinei mamonot* regardless of lineage. In *dinei nefashot*, however, only *Kohanim*, *Levi'im*, and *Yisraelim* of sufficiently established *yichus* to be fit for marriage into *kehunah* may serve as judges. *Rashi* notes the practical implication: a *mamzer* may serve as a judge in *dinei mamonot* but not in *dinei nefashot*.

---

## Drishah Challenge

### Initial Question

With the *Mishnah* before us, the *Gemara* immediately raises a challenge: *dinei mamonot mi ba'inan drishah v'chakirah?* Is it really true that monetary cases require *drishah v'chakirah*? Those familiar with earlier sections of the *masechet* will recall that this is, at the very least, not straightforwardly true. The *Gemara* now probes how to demonstrate this, and from which source.

### Postdated Document

The *Gemara* introduces a *Tosefta* as its challenge. Consider the following case: a *shtar* bears a date of the first of Nisan in a *Shemitah* year. The end of that year will annul outstanding loans. Witnesses then come forward in what appears to be a textbook case of *hazamah* — they claim that the witnesses who signed the document could not have done so on the stated date, because on that very day the signatories were in an entirely different location, in the company of these new witnesses.

The *halacha* in this case is that the *shtar* remains valid and the original witnesses retain their credibility — *shtar kasher v'adav kisherim*. Why? Because *chayishinan shema icharu v'chasavu* — we entertain the possibility that the document was post-dated. Postdating a loan document is entirely permissible; it means that the liens associated with the loan will not take effect until the later date specified in the document. The loan itself may have been extended in an earlier year, with the document dated forward to allow the borrower more time before liens could be collected — and to give the approaching *Shemitah* less opportunity to annul the debt. Because postdating is permitted, the date inscribed in the *shtar* cannot be taken as definitive proof of when the transaction occurred, and *hazamah* is therefore not available as a mechanism in this case.

### Postdate Inference

The *Gemara* now articulates the inference: if *dinei mamonot* truly required *drishah v'chakirah* — and specifically *chakirah*, the rigorous establishment of place and time — then postdating would never be permissible in the first place, because the permissibility of postdating presupposes that the time stated in a document need not be taken as authoritative. The existence of postdating as a legitimate practice thus demonstrates that *chakirah* is not operative in *dinei mamonot*, at least as it relates to documents.

### Mishnah Contradiction

The *Gemara* responds to this proof by noting that the challenge could have been posed even more simply, directly from the *Mishnah* itself, without resorting to the *Tosefta*. For the *Mishnah* states the general rule: *shtarei chov hamukdamim psulim hamucharim ksheirim* — predated loan documents are invalid, because they create liens earlier than the transaction actually took place; postdated loan documents, however, are valid. If you truly required *drishah v'chakirah* and insisted on firmly establishing the time of a transaction, how could a postdated document — one in which the stated date is by design not the actual date — ever be valid?

The *Gemara* then defends the choice of the *Tosefta* over the *Mishnah* as the stronger proof. The *Mishnah* merely permits postdating in the abstract. The *Tosefta*, however, goes further: it constructs a case in which postdating is permitted even in a situation where it is distinctly unusual and would ordinarily raise eyebrows — namely, a document dated to the first of Nisan of a *Shemitah* year, a time when virtually no one would lend money, since the end of that very year will annul the loan. One might have thought that in such a peculiar case, where postdating is so unlikely, we would treat the stated date as genuine and allow *hazamah* to operate. The *Tosefta* teaches that even in such a case — *afilu hachi*, even so — since *Shemitah* annuls only at the year's end, the document remains valid, and we still do not treat the date as authoritative enough to support *hazamah*. The *Tosefta* thus demonstrates that the irrelevance of the date in a *shtar* is not merely a practical accommodation but a thoroughgoing principle: even in the most unlikely of postdating scenarios, the time is not treated as firm.

The *Gemara* concludes: *mikol makom kashya* — in any event the difficulty stands. The practice of postdating, particularly in such an extreme case, demonstrates that *chakirah* simply does not function in *dinei mamonot* in the way the *Mishnah* seems to imply. And while one might have tried to limit this conclusion to *shtarot* specifically — since a *shtar* is processed differently from live oral testimony before the *beit din* — the *Gemara* does not accept that limiting move. The exception is more general.

### Rabbi Chanina Answer

Rabbi Chanina resolves the tension as follows: *dvar Torah echad dinei mamonot v'echad dinei nefashot b'drishah v'chakirah* — at the level of *d'Oraita*, the *Torah* indeed imposes the same requirement of *drishah v'chakirah* on both civil and capital cases, as the *Mishnah* states, grounded in the verse *mishpat echad yihiyeh lachem*. The *Mishnah* is accurately describing the *d'Oraita* framework.

### Lo Tin'ol Daltot

The question then becomes: why did the Sages waive *drishah v'chakirah* in *dinei mamonot* in practice? The answer is *kedei shelo tin'ol daltot bifnei lovin* — so as not to lock the door before borrowers. In the *Torah*'s economic system, lending money is already an unattractive proposition: one may not charge interest, the borrower may deny the debt, collection requires litigation, and *Shemitah* threatens to annul the loan entirely. To impose additionally the full rigors of *drishah v'chakirah* — making it harder to collect in court — would be to discourage lending altogether and thereby harm the very borrowers the system seeks to protect. The Sages therefore waived these requirements to keep the lending market viable.

The *Gemara* then raises an objection: if the basis for the waiver is *lo tin'ol daltot bifnei lovin*, could the judges of a *beit din* that errs in a monetary case use the streamlined process as a defense — arguing that since *drishah v'chakirah* was not required of them, they cannot be held liable for the mistake? The *Gemara* rejects this: *kol shekein she-tin'ol daltot bifnei lovin* — if judges were freed from liability for errors precisely because *drishah v'chakirah* was waived, the result would be even more chilling for lenders, who would have no recourse if the court wrongly decided against them. The protections for lenders must therefore remain intact.

### Rava's Distinction

*Rava* offers a different resolution. He accepts that in practice *drishah v'chakirah* has been waived for standard monetary cases. Our *Mishnah*, however, which states that *dinei mamonot* do require *drishah v'chakirah*, is not speaking of ordinary loans and admissions — *hoda'ot v'halva'ot* — but rather of *dinei knasot*: monetary fines imposed as punishment. Fines occupy a different category from ordinary civil claims; they function more like sanctions than like contractual remedies, and their punitive character brings them closer to *malkus* and *misah* than to ordinary commerce. Accordingly, the *Torah*'s requirement of *drishah v'chakirah* was never waived for *dinei knasot*, even as it was relaxed for routine monetary cases.

### Reish Lakish Principle

*Rav Pappa* agrees that the waiver applies to ordinary *hoda'ot* and *halva'ot*, and that the *Mishnah* is therefore to be understood along one of the lines already proposed. He then cites *Reish Lakish*, who raises a different principle from a different scriptural source. The verse *betzedek tishpot amitecha* — judge your neighbor with righteousness — stands alongside the emphatic *tzedek tzedek tirdof* — justice, justice shall you pursue. Why the repetition? *Reish Lakish* resolves it: *kan b'din merumah kan b'din she-eino merumah* — the first formulation addresses an ordinary case, while the doubled emphasis of *tzedek tzedek tirdof* addresses a case where the judge suspects that something fraudulent is taking place. *Tosafot* notes that if fraud is definitively established but cannot be identified, the court should simply refuse to adjudicate the case. But where fraud is merely suspected, the court must impose *drishah v'chakirah* with particular rigor, pressing hard to uncover the deception. Thus the *Mishnah*'s statement that *dinei mamonot* require *drishah v'chakirah* may refer specifically to suspicious cases.

### Rav Ashi Tzedek

*Rav Ashi* adds a further layer. He accepts that the *Mishnah*'s *drishah v'chakirah* requirement is addressed by one of the foregoing answers. But he observes that the doubled language of *tzedek tzedek tirdof* carries an additional teaching beyond the suspicious-case principle of *Reish Lakish*: *echad l'din v'echad l'pshara* — one instance of *tzedek* refers to formal adjudication, and the second refers to compromise. The verse is teaching that the same standard of justice and rigor that governs a court ruling must also govern a *pshara* — a negotiated compromise. Even when the parties agree to settle rather than receive a formal verdict, the arrangement must be constructed with fairness and genuine moral seriousness, not merely with whatever is expedient.

---

## Ships & Camels

### Ships Case

A *Baraita* is cited to illustrate the principle of *tzedek* in *pshara*. Two ships are traveling through a body of water and arrive simultaneously at a narrow strait. If both attempt to pass at once, both will sink. If they take turns — one going first — both can pass safely.

### Camels Case

The parallel case: two camel-drivers are ascending the narrow mountain path of *Beit Choron* and encounter one another face to face. If both try to proceed simultaneously, both will fall. If one yields and they go one at a time, both reach their destination.

### Priority Principles

The *Baraita* then establishes the principles for determining who goes first. If one vessel or camel is laden with goods and the other is not, the laden one takes priority — *tidacha she-eina te'una mipnei te'una* — because the economic cost of delay is greater for the party carrying cargo. If one is far from its destination and the other is close, the one that has a longer journey ahead takes priority — *tidacha krova mipnei she-eina krova* — because making the farther party wait imposes a greater burden. These are not arbitrary choices; they reflect a principled assessment of relative need and cost.

### Compromise Payment

If the two are equal in all relevant respects — both close, or both far, both laden, or both unladen — then a *pshara* is arranged between them. But the *Baraita* adds a critical element: even within the *pshara*, fairness demands that the party who goes first compensate the party who yields — *ma'aleh s'char zu l'zo*. The one who benefits from going first pays for that privilege. How the precise amount is calculated, or what happens when both parties wish to pay for the right to proceed first, is left open — but the underlying principle is clear. Even compromise must be structured, principled, and fair. This is what *tzedek tzedek tirdof* demands even in the domain of *pshara*.

---

## Best Courts Pursuit

### Excellent Courts

The *Gemara* offers yet another reading of *tzedek tzedek tirdof*, this one addressed not to courts but to litigants. *Halach achar beit din yafe* — seek out the finest court available to you. The verse is read as a mandate for parties to a dispute to pursue not merely the nearest or most convenient judicial forum, but the best one, even if that requires traveling.

### Sages' Locations

The *Gemara* illustrates this by listing the great sages of the era and their locations: *achar Rabbi Eliezer l'Lod* — follow Rabbi Eliezer to Lod; *achar Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai l'Bror Chayil* — follow Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai to Bror Chayil. Make the journey to wherever the greatest scholars have established their courts.

---

## Brit Milah Customs

### Mill Sound Signal

The mention of Bror Chayil occasions a *Baraita* that digresses into local customs of that region and its neighbor Borni. The *Baraita* teaches: *kol recheiyim b'Borni shavua ben* — the sound of a mill grinding in Borni is a signal that a *brit milah* is taking place. *Rashi* explains that *shavua ben* was a phrase used to refer to a *brit milah*, derived from the fact that it occurs at the end of seven days. *Rashi* further suggests that this was a period of persecution, and the sound of the mill served as a covert announcement that a *brit milah* was being performed.

### Candle Lighting

The parallel custom for Bror Chayil: *ha-ner b'Bror Chayil mishteh sham* — if candles are seen burning in Bror Chayil, it signals that a celebration is taking place. *Rashi* indicates that this, too, refers to a *brit milah* rather than a wedding, though *mishteh* can refer to either.

### Candles & Sheet

*Tosafot* raises an obvious question: since candles burn at night in general, how does one know that the candles in Bror Chayil specifically signal a celebration? Perhaps it refers to a conspicuous number of candles, or to candles kindled during the day. *Tosafot* then draws a normative conclusion from this passage: *mikan nahagu lehadlik ner b'milah* — from here derives the custom of lighting candles at a *brit milah*. *Tosafot* also notes an attendant custom: *umah shenahagu lifros hamapal hapetach* — the practice of hanging a sheet or cloth over the doorway at a *brit milah*, which derives from a tradition that in earlier times in Jerusalem, when a cloth was spread over the entrance of a home, it signaled an open house — a *seudat mitzvah* to which guests were invited to enter. Both customs — candle-lighting and the hanging of the cloth — are thus traced by *Tosafot* to this passage.

---

## Best Courts Pursuit (II)

### More Locations

The *Gemara* continues the list of sages and their locations, now introducing a second *Baraita* that elaborates further. In addition to Rabbi Eliezer in Lod and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai in Bror Chayil, the list includes Rabbi Yehoshua in *Peki'in*, Rabban Gamliel in Yavneh, Rabbi Akiva in Bnei Brak, *achar Rabi Matya le-Romi* — Rabbi Matya in Rome (a striking reminder that the community of great Torah scholarship extended even to Rome), Rabbi Chananyah ben Teradyon in Sichni, Rabbi Yosi in Tzippori, and *achar Rabi Yehudah ben Beteira le-Netzivin* — Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira in Netzivin. The list also includes, in some versions, Rabbi Chanina in *Golah*, which *Rashi* identifies as Pumbedita, and Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] in Beit Shearim — which one can visit in Israel today, where significant archaeological remains have been excavated.

### Lishkat HaGazit

The list culminates with the ultimate venue: *achar chachamim le-Lishkat HaGazit* — follow the great Sages to the *Lishkat HaGazit*, the Chamber of Hewn Stone, seat of the *Sanhedrin HaGedolah*. The word *tirdof* is thus read with full literalness: not merely pursue justice as an abstraction, but physically run, travel, relocate to wherever the greatest justice can be obtained.

---

## Opening in Defense

### Apparent Contradiction

Having established that in *dinei nefashot* one opens the deliberations in defense of the accused — *potchin l'zechut* — the *Gemara* now confronts a practical difficulty. What exactly does this mean when the witnesses have just testified and their testimony appears clear and damning? How does one "open for innocence" in the face of seemingly unambiguous evidence of guilt?

### Rav Yehudah Answer

*Rav Yehudah* proposes the following: we address the witnesses directly after their testimony and say, *mi yomar kidamretun* — is there anyone else who says what you said? Do you have further corroboration? *Rashi* explains that we greet even accepted testimony with a note of skepticism.

### Ulla's Concern

*Ulla* objects: *ve-achasminhu lehu?* Would this not silence the witnesses? Once their testimony has been accepted, is it appropriate to challenge it so explicitly? *Rashi* suggests this might work through *toch kedei dibbur* — a retraction within the brief moment immediately following the testimony. *Tosafot* notes that the conversation might concern testimony not yet formally accepted, though he concedes from other passages that the scenario appears to involve testimony that has already been received. In any event, the concern is that explicitly challenging the witnesses in this way either pressures them to retract what they have already said, or — if we are preemptively issuing the challenge before they testify — discourages witnesses from coming forward at all.

### Direct vs Indirect

The *Gemara* responds to this concern by distinguishing between two types of deterrence. The practice cited elsewhere — of moving witnesses from room to room before their testimony in capital cases in order to unsettle them and cause them to have second thoughts — achieves its effect *mimila*, indirectly. The witnesses themselves decide to withdraw; no direct pressure is applied. What *Rav Yehudah* proposes, by contrast, is a direct challenge to the witnesses — *kadchinan lehu beyadayim* — and that crosses a line. Once the court begins actively impugning the witnesses through direct confrontation, it has moved from protecting the accused to undermining the judicial process itself.

### Raba's Proposal

*Rava* then proposes a different approach to *potchin l'zechut*: instead of challenging the witnesses, we address the accused and say, *yesh lacha edim lehaziman?* — perhaps you have witnesses who can establish that the testifying witnesses are *edim zomemim*, that is, that they were elsewhere at the time they claim to have witnessed the act, and thus could not have seen what they claimed to see. This appears to open genuinely in the accused's defense without directly impugning the witnesses who have already testified.

### Hazamah Timing

*Rava*'s proposal is immediately challenged. The difficulty is this: by planting the idea of *hazamah* in the accused's mind before *gemar din*, we may be inadvertently creating a scenario in which the accused waits until after *gemar din* before producing *edim zomemim*. The *halacha* is that *edim zomemim* are not executed until after *gemar din* — *ein edim zomemim neheragim ad sheyigmar hadin*. If the accused produces *edim zomemim* after the verdict is already final, the witnesses will be subject to death, and we will have, through our opening statement, contributed to that outcome. We will have opened in defense of the accused in a way that brings *chovah* — serious liability — upon the witnesses who testified.

### Raba Refined

*Rava* refines his proposal in response: the court should say instead, *yesh lacha edim lehach-chishan?* — not do you have witnesses to make the testifiers *edim zomemim*, but simply do you have witnesses who can *contradict* what they said. Contradicting witnesses do not create *hazamah*; *hazamah* requires the specific claim that the testifying witnesses were elsewhere at the time in question. Contradicting witnesses merely offer a competing account of the facts. This achieves the goal of opening in the accused's defense — inviting him to produce exculpatory evidence — without creating any risk of *chovah* for the original witnesses.

### Anchoring Effect

*Rav Kahana* takes a different approach, less focused on adducing counter-evidence and more focused on how the court frames its own deliberations. He says: *m'divreichem nizdaka ploni* — after the witnesses testify, the very first statement the court makes is: "Based on everything that has been said, it appears that the accused is innocent." This flies in the face of the testimony just received, but the effect is powerful: by anchoring the deliberation in that direction, the court shapes the subsequent conversation to think in terms of innocence first. The psychological phenomenon of anchoring — the power of an initial framing to condition all subsequent analysis — is operative here. Whoever frames the opening position exercises disproportionate influence over where the discussion goes.

### Reassurance Method

*Abaye* and *Rava* both propose yet another method: *amrinan lei i lo katalt lo tidchal* — we say to the accused, "If you did not kill anyone, do not be afraid." This seems at first glance to be less a legal technique than a pastoral reassurance. But it serves a dual function. First, it puts into the court's own consciousness the genuine possibility that the accused is innocent, and by articulating that possibility directly, the judges begin to internalize it in their deliberations. Second, an accused person who feels presumed guilty may comport himself in ways that inadvertently influence the judges against him; by reassuring him that innocence means no cause for fear, we level the psychological playing field.

### Public Announcement

*Rav Ashi* proposes the most practical approach: *kol mi sheyodeia lo zechut yavo v'yilamed alav* — make a public announcement in the court inviting anyone who possesses exonerating evidence, testimony, or relevant facts to come forward. This directly and concretely opens the possibility of vindication. Even if no one comes forward, the announcement itself orients the deliberations toward the possibility of innocence and signals to all present that the court is actively seeking grounds for acquittal.

### Sotah Support

A *Baraita* is then cited in support of *Abaye* and *Rava*'s method, drawn surprisingly from the context of *sotah*. The verse states: *im lo shachav ish otach v'im lo satit tumah tachat ishech hinaki mi'mei hamarim hamarerim* — if no man has lain with you, and you have not gone astray under your husband, be cleared by the bitter waters. Only after this statement of innocence does the verse address the possibility of guilt: *v'at ki satit* — but if you did stray, then the consequences follow. From the structure of the *sotah* procedure — itself a remarkable case study in the intersection of judicial and ritual process — the *Gemara* derives the principle that even in a capital-adjacent proceeding, one opens by articulating the possibility of innocence before turning to the possibility of guilt. *Mikan shepotchin b'dinei nefashot techilah l'zechut* — from here we learn that in capital cases, the deliberations must always open with a statement favoring the accused's innocence.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 33

## Dinei Nefashos vs Mamonos

### Opening & Framework

Sanhedrin 33 opens in the midst of the discussion distinguishing *dinei nefashos* from *dinei mamonos*. The previous daf had already introduced several such distinctions, and we now continue with two further differences: how a case is opened, and whether a ruling may be reversed.

### Opening Procedure

In *dinei mamonos*, a case may be opened *bein lizchus bein lichova* — whether to find the party exempt or obligated. In *dinei nefashos*, the case must be opened *lizchus* — first arguing in the defendant's favor, seeking reasons for acquittal, as was discussed on the preceding daf.

### Reversibility Rules

The *mishna* then addresses the question of reversibility. In *dinei mamonos*, the court may reverse its ruling in either direction — whether to find someone liable who had been exempted, or to find someone exempt who had been found liable. In capital cases, the asymmetry is striking: if a defendant was found innocent, the ruling cannot be reversed — there is no double jeopardy. However, if a defendant was found guilty, the ruling can be reversed in his favor, functioning as a kind of appeal for a guilty verdict.

The *gemara* notes an apparent contradiction. Our *mishna* states that civil rulings may be reversed, yet an earlier source — quoted already in the first *perek* — states: *dan es hadin, zika es hachayav, chiyav es hazakai, tima es hatahor, tahar es hatamei* — if a judge rendered a ruling in error, whether finding the liable party exempt or the exempt party liable, or declaring something pure that was impure or impure that was pure, then *ma she'asa asa* — what is done is done — and the judge must pay damages from his own resources.

Several important issues converge here. One is the question of tortious liability: is the judge's error a form of *mazik biyadayim*, or is it rather an indirect cause, a *grama*, perhaps falling under the category of *hezek de'garmi* as discussed in Bava Kamma? Another is the question of who determines that a mistake was made at all. But the issue most immediately relevant to our passage is the principle of *ma she'asa asa* — that the ruling is not reversible — which stands in direct tension with our *mishna*'s statement that civil rulings may indeed be reversed.

---

## Mumche Framework

### Mumche Distinction

Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — kan bemumcheh, kan beshe'eino mumcheh*. The difference turns on whether the judge is an expert, a *mumche*, or not. We will follow Rashi's reading and interpretation of this sugya.

### Rashi's Logic

Rashi's explanation throughout this passage rests on a structural observation about the nature of judicial reversal in civil cases. Any reversal of a ruling necessarily helps one litigant and harms the other. If, for example, the court initially found Reuven liable to pay Shimon a hundred dinars, and now the judge wishes to reverse that ruling and exempt Reuven, Shimon has every reason to object. He can reasonably say: you were wrong once, why should I believe you are wrong now rather than then? You found in my favor originally — perhaps that was correct and the reversal is the mistake.

This is precisely why *ma she'asa asa* applies, and why a judge who now admits his error nonetheless bears financial liability to the party his incorrect first ruling harmed. As Rashi states (*bemumche*): *yesh bo koach lachzor velo matzi lemimar leh avdin ana ketaama kama didach avdina* — if he is an expert, the other litigant cannot simply say "I will act on your first ruling," because the expert's reconsidered opinion carries genuine authority. The second judgment, coming from an acknowledged expert, has weight sufficient to override the first.

But if the judge is not a *mumche*, the other litigant may say: *mi yeymar detaama batra didach ikkar — dilma kama ikkar uvehai hu detaita* — who says your later reasoning is the authoritative one? Perhaps the first was right and this is the new mistake. Since there is no expertise establishing that the second judgment should be credited over the first, the original ruling stands, and the only remedy is financial liability on the part of the judge.

### Liability & Mumche

The *gemara* presses further. The very same *tosefta* that declared *ma she'asa asa* also ruled: *haya mumche leveit din — patur melashalem* — if the judge was a court-recognized expert, he is exempt from paying damages. This seems to say that even for a *mumche*, *ma she'asa asa* applies, and the only distinction between a *mumche* and a non-expert is whether there is liability. For an expert, erroneous rulings happen without negligence — it is an accident rather than a failure of due care — and therefore no payment is required. But in both cases, the ruling appears to remain binding.

### Higher Authority

Rav Nachman offers a different resolution: *kan sheyesh gadol heimenu bechochmah uvevinyan, kan she'ein gadol heimenu bechochmah uvevinyan* — the distinction is whether there exists someone of greater authority who can endorse the reversal. The phrase *gadol bechochmah uvevinyan* is itself somewhat puzzling, since all senior courts share the same fixed size of seventy-one; some interpret *minyan* as referring to the number of students, others to the judge's seniority in years.

In any case, Rav Nachman's position — understood through Rashi — is that even a *mumche* cannot unilaterally reverse his own ruling simply on the strength of his own reconsideration. The litigant who benefited from the first ruling can still say: perhaps the error is now, not then. However, if there is a figure of even greater authority who validates the reversal — confirming that the later decision is the correct one — then the second judgment overrides the first. The *mumche* himself performs the reversal, but it is the backing of superior authority that gives it force. Where there is no such higher authority, even the *mumche*'s reversal cannot stand. And in either case, a *mumche* whose error caused a loss bears no liability — that exemption holds regardless.

---

## Dvar Mishna vs Shikul Ha…

### Rav Sheshet's View

Rav Sheshet offers an entirely different resolution, one that cuts across the *mumche* distinction altogether: *kan shetaah bidvar mishnah, kan shetaah beshikul hadaat* — the critical variable is not the judge's level of expertise, but the type of error he made. Did he err in *dvar mishnah* — black-letter law — or in *shikul hadaat* — a judgment call?

As Rav Sheshet states, citing Rav Assi: *ta'ah bidvar mishnah — chozer; ta'ah beshikul hadaat — eino chozer*. If the error was in established black-letter law, the ruling is reversed. If the error was a matter of judgment, the ruling stands. The *mumche* distinction, on this view, is relevant only to the question of liability — whether the judge pays — not to reversibility.

The logic is compelling. A ruling that contradicts accepted, unambiguous law was never a legitimate ruling to begin with. It had no valid basis, and therefore it can be undone. A ruling that was a reasonable judgment call, even if the judge now wishes he had decided otherwise, was legitimate when rendered. The party who prevailed under that ruling has a valid claim to rely on it, and it cannot be retracted.

### What is Dvar Mishna

The *gemara* immediately probes the scope of *dvar mishnah*. Does it refer literally only to something recorded in a *mishna*? What if the error concerns a ruling in the *Tosefta* — the work of Rav Chiya and Rav Oshaya? The answer is *in* — yes, a clear ruling in the *Tosefta* also qualifies as *dvar mishnah* for these purposes. What about a ruling of the *Amoraim*, after the *mishna* itself? *Afilu bidvar Rav u'Shmuel* — yes, even a ruling of Rav and Shmuel counts. The *gemara* then pushes further: *afilu bdidi u'vdidach* — what about our own rulings, asks Ravina (or Rav Ashi) — do rulings of the last generation of *Amoraim* also have *dvar mishnah* status? The response is characteristic: *atu anan k'kitzay d'kanay b'agma nan* — are we like reeds cut from a swamp? Our rulings equally carry that authoritative weight.

### What is Shikul Hadaat

Rav Pappa defines *shikul hadaat*: *k'gon tray tannay o tray amoray d'pligi ahadadi* — cases where two *tannaim* or two *Amoraim* dispute the matter, *v'lo itmar hilchata lo k'mar v'lo k'mar* — and no authoritative ruling was ever rendered as to which position is the *halacha*. The judge then decided to side with one of the opinions, *v'ikri v'avid k'chad minayhu*, but the *sugya d'shma'ta* — the general drift of *halachic* practice — ran in the other direction. That is *shikul hadaat*: a mistake in judgment, even though the position adopted was one that a legitimate authority had maintained.

### Implication & Logic

This requires some reflection. Why is it called an error if the judge sided with a recognized opinion in a genuine dispute? The answer appears to be that as long as the judge stood by his decision it would have been entirely legitimate — no one could compel him to change or find him liable. The ruling is called a *shikul hadaat* mistake only in retrospect, when the judge himself concedes that he should have ruled with the majority weight of opinion. At that point, his original ruling had legitimacy and remains binding, but he acknowledges it as a mistake, which may create financial liability — from which he is exempt if he was a *mumche*. The contrast with *dvar mishnah* is sharp: there, the original ruling had no legitimacy whatsoever, it was simply wrong, and it is therefore reversed entirely.

### Canonization Issues

This framework raises a fascinating question that occupied the *Rishonim*: how far does the category of *dvar mishnah* extend beyond the *Amoraim*? If a judge ruled in a manner contradicted by a clear consensus of the *Geonim*, does that constitute *ta'ah bidvar mishnah*? There are different positions among the *Rishonim* on the authority of the *Geonim*. Some distinguish between a judge who was simply unaware of the *Geonic* ruling — in which case it might qualify as *ta'ah bidvar mishnah*, since his error stemmed from ignorance of available authoritative material — and a judge who knew the *Geonic* position and chose to rule otherwise, in which case it remains within his prerogative, just as one *amora* could legitimately rule against another *amora*. These are profound questions about what gets canonized, what constitutes authoritative *halachic* knowledge at any given era, and where the threshold of *dvar mishnah* stops.

---

## Parah Case Study

### Story Setup

The *gemara* now records a challenge that Rav Hamnuna posed to Rav Sheshet's framework, based on a famous incident. *Maaseh b'parah she-nitlah em shelah* — there was a case involving a cow from which the uterus had been surgically removed. Rabbi Tarfon ruled the animal a *treifah* — reasoning that an animal missing such an organ could not survive — and accordingly it was slaughtered and *he'echilah l'klavim*, fed to the dogs. The matter was subsequently brought before the sages at Yavneh, *u-va maaseh lifnei Chachamim be-Yavneh*, and they permitted such animals, because Todos the physician testified: *ein parah ve-chazirah yotzet me-Alexandria shel Mitzrayim ela im ken chotchin ha-em shelah* — no cow or sow leaves Alexandria in Egypt unless its uterus has been removed. The Egyptians wished to protect their livestock as a commercial asset and prevent others from breeding their animals, so they surgically removed the uteruses of animals exported from Alexandria — and those animals plainly survived. The *mishna* thus records that an animal without a uterus is not a *treifah*. Rabbi Tarfon had ruled against a clear *mishna*-level halachic position, making this a textbook case of *ta'ah bidvar Mishna*.

### Akiva's Solution

Upon realizing his error, Rabbi Tarfon exclaimed: *hacha chamor Tarfon* — he feared that he had effectively lost the equivalent of a donkey's load in liability, having caused a loss to the animal's owner through his erroneous ruling. Rabbi Akiva responded: *patur atah — she-kol ha-mumcheh l'rabbim patur milishalem* — you are exempt, because any recognized communal expert is exempt from paying damages.

### Gemara's Challenge

Rav Hamnuna's challenge to Rav Sheshet now comes into focus. If *ta'ah bidvar mishnah chozer* — if an error in black-letter law automatically reverses the ruling — why did Rabbi Akiva respond only by invoking Rabbi Tarfon's status as a *mumche* to exempt him from liability? He should have said: your error was *ta'ah bidvar Mishna*, and therefore your ruling was never binding in the first place, which means the owner who fed the cow to the dogs did so on his own initiative, and you bear no responsibility for his consequent act.

### Resolution

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies the challenge. He asks: *mai ka-moteiv Rav Hamnuna le-Rav Sheshet mi-parah* — what was the force of this challenge? After all, the cow had already been fed to the dogs; there is nothing to reverse. The answer is that the challenge was not about reversibility per se, but about liability. *Ei amart bishlama Toeh b'dvar Mishna eino chozer* — if we were to say that even a *ta'ah bidvar Mishna* cannot be reversed, then *kam dina* — the ruling was binding the moment it was issued, and Rabbi Tarfon had reason to fear liability, which is exactly why Rabbi Akiva's assurance that he is a *mumche* and therefore *patur* was the relevant and necessary response.

### Practical Limits

But if we rule — as we do — that *ta'ah bidvar Mishna chozer*, then Rabbi Akiva had an additional and perhaps stronger argument available to him: *keivan de'ilu havei para dina lav dina* — had the cow still been alive, the ruling would have had no binding force, it would have been reversed, and the cow would have been permitted. Since that would have been the result, Rabbi Tarfon's ruling itself produced no halachic consequence; it was the owner's subsequent decision to feed the cow to the dogs — not the ruling — that caused the loss. Rabbi Tarfon should therefore be exempt not merely because he is a *mumche*, but because his ruling itself did nothing actionable, and any subsequent loss traces to the owner's own act.

The *gemara* accepts this: *chada ve-od ka-amar* — Rabbi Akiva was making two cumulative arguments. First, this was a *ta'ah bidvar Mishna* and the ruling was therefore never binding. Second, even if we were to treat the error as a *shikul hadaat* mistake and the ruling were binding, Rabbi Tarfon is still a *mumche lerabbim* and exempt from paying. Both grounds converge to exempt him. The upshot of this passage is thus to confirm Rav Sheshet's framework while also demonstrating that the *mumche* exemption from liability remains relevant in its own domain.

---

## Nital Venatan Beyad

### Rav Chisda's Principle

Rav Chisda proposes yet a further distinction to resolve the contradiction between the *mishna* and the earlier *tosefta*: *kan shenatal venatan beyad, kan shelo natal venatan beyad* — the difference is whether the judgment was physically executed, whether the money was literally taken from one party's hand and placed in the other's. When the judge physically transferred the funds — *natal venatan beyad* — the matter is final and irreversible, and the question becomes only whether the judge is liable for the damage he caused. When the judge merely issued his verbal ruling without physically effecting the transfer, the ruling may still be reversed.

This distinction concerns reversibility, not liability. The *gemara* does not fully articulate the conceptual basis for this distinction, though a consideration of *ziluta debei dina* — the dignity and finality of the court — may be at work. Once the judge has acted in a manner that concretizes and finalizes the ruling, it takes on a definitive character that verbal rulings alone do not possess.

### Tosefta Context

The *tosefta* that said *ma she'asa asa* and imposed liability was accordingly describing a case of *natal venatan beyad*, where the ruling had been physically executed. That is the scenario where what is done cannot be undone, and where the question of liability becomes pressing.

Working through the individual cases: *chiyav es hazakkai* — where the judge found the innocent party liable and took money from him to transfer to the other — this is readily intelligible as *natal venatan beyad*. But *zikah es hachayav* — where the judge exempted the truly liable party — how is this *natal venatan beyad*? The judge merely said "you are exempt"; there was no money to transfer.

### Mishna Context

The *mishna* that says civil rulings may be reversed is describing the case of *lo natal venatan beyad*, where the money was not yet physically transferred. In that case, the ruling remains open to reconsideration: if the judge had said *chayav ata* but not yet taken the money, he may call the case back and reverse it.

### Patur Problem

The difficulty is with the case where the judge said *patur ata* — "you are exempt" — and nothing remained to be physically transferred. How does this fit either category?

The *gemara* states: *keivan d'amar patur ata k'man d'naso v'nasav biyod dami* — since once you declared someone exempt and the parties went home with nothing further to do, that is functionally equivalent to *natal venatan beyad*. The finality of *patur ata* is total: nothing remains to be done, the case is complete, and that completeness mirrors the physical finality of an actual transfer.

This creates a problem for the *mishna*, however. The *mishna* says that civil rulings may be reversed *bein lizchus bein lichova* — both to exempt and to obligate. But if *patur ata* is already equivalent to *natal venatan beyad*, how can the *mishna* say we may reverse a ruling that initially exempted someone and now find him liable?

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this by reading the *mishna* as presenting only one case: *dinei mamonos machzirin l'zchus shehi chova* — when it says "reverse to exempt," it means a single case in which the original ruling of *chayav ata* is reversed to *patur ata*, and by that single reversal, the party previously found liable is now freed, while the party previously found in favor is now disadvantaged. The *mishna*'s "both ways" reflects the double impact of one ruling on two parties, not two separate proceedings.

But this resolution fails under scrutiny, because the parallel ruling for *dinei nefashos* — *machzirin l'zchus v'ein machzirin l'chova*, that in capital cases we reverse only toward innocence and not toward guilt — cannot similarly be read as a single case with two sides. *Machzirin l'zchus zechus geridasa* — reversing to find someone innocent in a capital case is simply finding that one person innocent, not necessarily hurting anyone else. And *v'ein machzirin l'chova* means we will not reopen the case to find the defendant guilty even if there is now a basis to do so. One might theoretically suggest that finding a murderer innocent harms the *goel hadam* — the blood-redeemer — and for that reason should also be prohibited. The *gemara* summarily dismisses this: *mishum chovasi d'goel hadam katlinan lei lehai* — we would not execute an otherwise innocent person in order to spare the *goel hadam* from disappointment. And further, the language *bein bein* — "whether... whether" — clearly signals two separate cases, not one case with dual impact. So the *gemara* acknowledges the difficulty: *kashya*.

### Ravina's Clarification

Ravina offers a more precise and satisfying account. The *natal venatan beyad* in a case of *patur ata* need not be a legal fiction. It describes a specific physical act: *kegon dehava lei mashkon unetalo heimenu* — where Reuven held collateral belonging to Shimon as security against the claimed debt, the judge declared Shimon exempt, and then physically took the collateral from Reuven's hand and returned it to Shimon. That physical return of the collateral is the *natal venatan beyad* that renders the ruling final. Where no such physical act occurred — where the judge merely said "you are exempt" without taking and transferring anything — the ruling is *lo natal venatan beyad* and may still be reversed.

This resolves the problem cleanly. A ruling of *patur ata* is not automatically equivalent to *natal venatan beyad*. It becomes final only when accompanied by a physical act, specifically the return of collateral. Without that act, reversal remains possible.

### Other Examples

The *gemara* extends this analysis to purity rulings. *Timas es hatahor* — declaring something pure to be impure — when is that *natal venatan beyad* such that it cannot be reversed? *Daadi bei sheretz* — if the judge actually took an insect (*sheretz*) and threw it onto the *terumah* to demonstrate and physically instantiate his ruling of impurity, that is *natal venatan beyad*. The ruling is now irreversible.

Conversely, *tihartas es hatamei* — declaring something impure to be pure — how does one physically demonstrate such a ruling *biyadayim*? *Sheiravan befirotav* — the judge mixed the suspected impure item into the person's other produce, thereby physically expressing his confidence in its purity. That physical act of mixing constitutes *natal venatan beyad* and renders the ruling final.

In sum, three frameworks are presented for when *dinei mamonos* rulings may be reversed. First, the *mumche* who is backed by someone of even greater authority — his second ruling, thus supported, can override his first.
