What about Chizkiah? *Havai Shevna*, a great Torah authority — who was subsequently killed. Same analysis applies. What about Ezra? *Havai Nechemiah ben Chakalyah*, again a competing political and Torah figure.

### Adda Bar Ahava: Rabbi to…

Adda bar Ahava then offers a parallel observation: *mi-yemot Rabbi ve-ad Rav Ashi lo matzinu Torah u-gedulah be-makom echad* — from the time of Rabbi until Rav Ashi, we do not find Torah greatness and political greatness combined in one person. Rav Ashi himself apparently held both. The *Gemara* challenges: was there not Huna bar Natan, who was very close to the royal court and thus wielded political influence? As *Tosafos* notes, Huna bar Natan had significant proximity to power. The *Gemara* responds: *Huna bar Natan mikaf hava kayaf le-Rav Ashi* — he submitted to and deferred to the authority of Rav Ashi. He was therefore not the supreme authority in the Torah domain; that remained with Rav Ashi exclusively.

---

## Lo Ta'aneh Source & Logic

### Lo Ta'aneh Verse Source

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Bavli*'s own presentation of the source for the procedural rules of capital and monetary cases. The *mishnah* states: in capital cases one begins from the junior side. Where does this come from? Rabbi Acha bar Papa cites the verse: *lo tateh mishpat evyoncha be-rivo* — do not pervert the judgment of the poor person in his dispute — and reads *rivo* as *rabo*, his elder. Do not respond after the elder has spoken.

### Monetary: Respond or Not?

This immediately raises a question: does the same prohibition apply in monetary cases? If it does, then the monetary *beit din* effectively becomes a court of one, because once the elder speaks, no one may respond. And yet we know that in monetary cases you do afford honor by letting the elder speak first — implying that others do speak afterward. How can both things be true?

### Tosafot's Two Solutions

*Tosafos* offers two answers. The first: in monetary cases one may respond, but only in the form of a question — not by stating outright "I disagree," but by asking "might it not be the case that...?" This approach would still substantially hamper free debate, which makes it somewhat unsatisfying. The second answer of *Tosafos* is that the prohibition against responding altogether is confined to capital cases and does not apply to monetary cases at all. The precise reasoning for this limitation is not fully spelled out, but the functional result is the mirror image structure that we described.

### Yerushalmi Alternative

The *Yerushalmi* offers a cleaner resolution. On its reading, *lo ta'aneh* does not mean "do not respond after the elder"; it means "do not speak up before the elder" — that is, afford him the honor of speaking first, and thereafter others may freely offer their opinions. This interpretation preserves the full integrity of monetary-case deliberation without any chilling effect on subsequent speakers.

### Mirror: Respect Mechanis…

The mirror image is then fully explained. In monetary cases, the elder speaks first — that is the honor afforded to him — and the junior members may respond and share their views freely thereafter. In capital cases, the concern for the accused's innocence demands that even after the elder speaks, no one feel inhibited from disagreeing. The way the system ensures this is by having the elder speak last. And the way the elder's honor is maintained is through the rule that one may not respond once he has spoken — his word carries finality. By speaking last and having his word stand, the elder retains his dignity, while the process of reaching that point has been an entirely open deliberation. The two systems are thus symmetrical expressions of the same underlying respect for both honor and justice.

---

## Teacher-Student Voting

### Rabbah: Student Negates…

The *Gemara* cites Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, deriving from the same verse about David and his men girding their swords — understood as a metaphor for deliberation before the judgment of Naval — that *shoneh adam le-talmido ve-dan imo be-dinei nefashos*: a person may teach his student and the student may then count as a distinct vote alongside his teacher in a capital case. Rashi explains this explicitly as meaning the student is counted as a separate vote. This is in itself a striking statement, because ordinarily one cannot simply add a person to the *Sanhedrin* ad hoc; the student would have to be a duly constituted member. But beyond the question of how the student gets to vote at all, the *Gemara*'s focus is on a different and more subtle question: why does the student's vote count as a *separate* vote, and not merely as a second expression of his teacher's view?

### Challenge: Purity Cases

The *Gemara* raises a challenge from *halakhic* sources dealing with *taharos* and *tumaos* — matters of purity and impurity, kashrut questions — where, since a single rabbi can render the ruling without a formal *beit din*, the rules of counting are much more relaxed. In those contexts, a father and son, or a rabbi and student, may indeed be counted as two, because there is no rigorous requirement of a distinct formal vote from each member.

### Formal Cases: One Count

However, the source continues: *aval dinei mamonos u-dinei nefashos u-dinei makos kiddush ha-chodesh ve-ibbur ha-shanah* — but in monetary cases, capital cases, lashes, sanctification of the new month, and intercalation of the year — *av u-veno ha-rav ve-talmido ein monin lahem ela echad* — a father and son, or a rabbi and student, count only as one, because one naturally assumes the student is simply following his teacher's lead. Unless, of course, they actually voted differently — in which case they plainly are distinct voters — but when they agree, the default assumption is that the student's agreement is not independent.

One might ask: how can a father and son both be on a *beit din* at all, when relatives are ordinarily disqualified from sitting together? Rashi resolves this by saying precisely this rule is the operative disqualification — they can never count as two — and effectively they do not both sit as full independent members. *Tosafos* suggests the case may involve *kiddush ha-chodesh*, for which relatives may be eligible. The father-son question can be set aside; the core issue is the rabbi-student relationship.

### Papa: When Independent?

The *Gemara* on 36b resolves the tension by drawing a crucial distinction. When did Rav say that a rabbi and student count as a separate vote? Only in a case where the student possesses genuine intellectual independence from his teacher.

### Kahana & Ashi Model

The paradigm offered is Rav Kahana and Rav Ashi in relation to Rav. They needed Rav's *gemara* — his transmitted traditions and teachings — because in that era, without written texts, all received knowledge had to be obtained directly from one's teacher. They depended on their teacher for the *material*. But they did not need their teacher's *analysis*: *li-svarei de-Rav lo havu tzerikhi* — they worked through the reasoning independently. If a student truly brings his own analytical capacity and can reach conclusions without being guided by his teacher's reasoning, then his vote is genuinely distinct and counts separately.

This point has interesting resonances beyond the specific *Sanhedrin* context. In determining how many *poskim* hold a particular position, one must ask whether a series of later authorities — *Tosafos*, the *Rosh*, the *Mordechai*, the *Terumat HaDeshen* — are truly independent voices or whether they are all flowing from the same source, in which case they may represent, in some sense, a single opinion that has been amplified rather than independently corroborated. Genuine independence of analysis is what creates a genuinely separate vote.

---

## 10 Differences: Mamo (II)

### Abbahu: Ten Differences

Rabbi Abbahu states: there are ten differences between *dinei mamonos* and *dinei nefashos* enumerated in our *mishnah*, and all of them do not apply to a *shor haniskal*. The *shor haniskal* requires a *beit din* of 23 because we formally liken its execution to that of a person, but every other protective rule that makes *dinei nefashos* distinct from *dinei mamonos* — the super-majority requirement, the order of deliberation, the prohibition on completing judgment the same day — none of those apply. Quite the opposite: the goal in the case of a *shor haniskal* is to effectively remove a potentially dangerous animal from society, not to protect it from conviction.

### Challenge: Only Nine?

The *Gemara* immediately challenges Rabbi Abbahu: *ha tish'a havyan* — there are only nine in our *mishnah*, not ten. This is a striking moment because the *Yerushalmi* similarly counted nine.

### Resolution: Criteria Uni…

The *Gemara* then responds with an equally pointed counter-challenge: *ha asara havyan* — there are actually ten! The dispute is about how to count. The *Gemara* resolves it by explaining: *mishum de-ein hakol kesherin le-esrim u-shelosha khada hi* — the criterion of who may judge and the requirement of 23 are a single unified point, not two separate distinctions. Once you establish that this is a *Sanhedrin* of 23, the eligibility requirements for who may serve on it are implicitly determined. They are two sides of the same coin, and so they count as one difference, not two. Once we recalibrate and treat that as nine, Rabbi Abbahu's claim of ten requires identification of a tenth difference.

### Zaken & Saris Rule

The *Gemara* supplies it: *ain moshivin be-Sanhedrin zaken ve-saris* — one does not seat on the *Sanhedrin* an elderly person or a *saris*. Rashi explains that someone so advanced in age has forgotten, *she-shakhakh kevar tza'ar giddul banim* — the experience and pain of raising children — and may lack the emotional sensitivity required. A *saris*, and similarly anyone who has never had children, has not undergone those formative experiences. As we noted earlier, these are sweeping generalizations, but they function as protective rules to reduce the risk of unjust convictions in capital matters.

### Yehuda: Cruelty Criteria

Rav Yehuda adds that the cruel — *achzarim* — are also excluded from the *Sanhedrin*. This is the exclusion one would most intuitively want, though it is also the hardest to quantify. And there is an interesting inversion: *ve-chilufeihen be-meisis* — the opposite rule applies in the case of a *meisis*, one who seduces others to idolatry. There, precisely, you would want the stern and unyielding judges, because the Torah explicitly commands *lo tachmol ve-lo techakeh alav* — do not have compassion, do not conceal anything in his favor. The *Sanhedrin* for that case is intended to achieve conviction, not to protect the accused, and the composition of the court reflects that goal.

---

## Money: Mamzer & Ger Incl…

### Hakol Kasherim Scope

The *mishnah* says *hakol kesherim ladun dinei mamonos* — everyone is eligible to judge monetary cases. The *Gemara* asks: *hakol le-asuyei mai* — what does "everyone" come to include beyond what we already know?

### Rav Yehuda: Mamzerim OK

Rav Yehuda answers: *le-asuyei mamzer* — to include a *mamzer*. In capital cases, those who are disqualified from the lineage perspective are anyone who cannot marry into the Jewish community in the standard way — such as a *chalal*. But for monetary cases, the circle is wider still: even a *mamzer*, who cannot marry another Jew at all, is nonetheless eligible to sit in civil judgment.

### Already Taught Mamzerim

The *Gemara* objects: *ha tanyina chada zimna* — we have already taught this. An earlier *mishnah* states that anyone fit to judge capital cases is fit to judge monetary cases, and there are those fit for monetary but not capital — and Rav Yehuda himself already explained that this category includes a *mamzer*. So what is Rav Yehuda adding by saying it again?

### Ger vs. Mamzer Logic

The *Gemara* resolves: *chada le-asuyei ger, ve-chada le-asuyei mamzer* — one teaching comes to include a *ger*, a convert, and the other to include a *mamzer*, and *tzericha* — both are necessary. Each teaches a distinct principle that cannot be derived from the other. Had we only been told that a *ger* may judge monetary cases, one might have thought: true, a *ger* can marry a Jew, so his inclusion makes sense — but a *mamzer*, who cannot marry a Jew at all, might be seen as too far outside the community to be included. Conversely, had we only been told about a *mamzer*, one might have reasoned: a *mamzer* comes from Jewish parents, *mi-tipa kesheira*, so he retains a Jewish identity connection — but a *ger*, who does not come from Jewish parentage at all, might be excluded. Each ruling thus does genuine work, and both are needed.

### Ger Jurisdiction Dispute

There is an interesting dispute between Rashi and *Tosafos* on the precise scope of a *ger*'s eligibility. Another *Gemara* states that a *ger* may sit in judgment on a case involving a fellow *ger*. The question is whether the two teachings — the general inclusion of a *ger* in *dinei mamonos*, and the specific allowance to judge a fellow *ger* — are alternatives or cumulative requirements. Rashi reads them as alternatives: a *ger* may judge any monetary case, or may even sit in capital cases when the accused is also a *ger*. *Tosafos* reads them as cumulative and highly restrictive: a *ger* may only sit in monetary cases, and even then only when the case involves another *ger* — which is not at all what the plain reading of this *Gemara* suggests, and which is quite a dramatic limitation.

---

## 10 Differences: Mamo (II)

### Purity from Song of Songs

The *Gemara* asks: what is the verse source for the requirement that members of the *Sanhedrin* for capital cases be free from lineage blemish? The *Gemara* cites Ameimar: *kulach yafa ra'ayati u-mum ein bach* — you are entirely beautiful, my beloved, there is no blemish in you — drawn from *Shir HaShirim*. This is applied to the *beit din*: as they must be pure in righteousness, so too they must be free from *mum*, understood here as a lineage blemish. The *Gemara* raises the possibility that *mum* here means a physical blemish rather than a lineage one. But that possibility does not survive scrutiny.

### Yitro's V'Nisu Source

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative derivation: *ve-nasu itach* — from the passage in which Yisro advises Moshe to appoint judges who will carry the burden together with him. *Itach*, "with you," is read as *be-domin lach* — ones who are similar to you. In that context, the similarity is understood to pertain to lineage purity rather than physical characteristics. And crucially, unlike the *Shechina* argument that could have been raised against the *Shir HaShirim* source — perhaps the need to resemble Moshe was specific to the context of divine presence resting on the seventy elders — here in Yisro's practical counsel to Moshe about ordinary judicial appointments, the same standard of *be-domin lach* applies, making it a more generalizable rule.

---

## Sanhedrin Seating Layout

### Half-Circle Design

The next *mishnah* describes the physical structure of the *Sanhedrin*. *Sanhedrin haysa ke-chatzi agula goren agula* — the *Sanhedrin* sat in the shape of half a threshing floor, which is to say, a half-circle. The threshing floor itself was round; the court replicated half of that form.

### Visibility Purpose

The purpose of this arrangement was *ke-dei she-yiyu ro'im zeh et zeh* — so that the judges could all see one another. This served multiple functions simultaneously: it enabled equal visibility among all the judges, gave each member an equivalent view of the witnesses and the litigants, and created a sense of equality in the deliberative body even while a hierarchy was maintained within it. No judge was behind another or out of sight.

### Two Scribes System

*U-shnei sofrei ha-dayanim omdim lifneihem* — two scribes of the court stood before the judges, one on the right and one on the left at the edges of the half-circle. They would write everything: *divrei ha-mezakkim ve-divrei ha-mechayevim* — the arguments for acquittal and the arguments for conviction — producing duplicate records so that each could serve as verification of the other.

### Yehuda: Three Scribes

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and says there should be three scribes. Writing everything is burdensome, so the labor should be divided: one scribe records only the arguments for acquittal, a second records only the arguments for conviction, and the third — with the most demanding role — writes everything. This third record serves as the master verification: in any case of doubt about what was actually argued, the comprehensive record provides the authoritative check. The workload of the primary recording is thus distributed while the integrity of the full record is maintained.

### Three Student Rows

Beyond the half-circle of judges, there were three additional half-circles seated in front of the court: three rows of *talmidei chachamim*. These were concentric, one inside the other, forming a nested series of arcs. This is not merely an arrangement for observers; as the *Gemara* will make clear shortly, these rows served a specific function in the process of adding members to the *Sanhedrin* when necessary.

### Hierarchy & Place

Despite the egalitarian geometry of the half-circle, *kol echad ve-echad makir et mekomo* — every person knew his place. There was a clear hierarchy: which of the three rows you sat in, where within your row you were positioned — all of this was understood and observed. The egalitarianism of the circle, where every judge can see every other, coexists with a precise and acknowledged order of rank. As we will see in the next *mishnah*, this hierarchy has practical procedural consequences.

---

## Adding Judges & Semicha

### Replacing a Judge

If a judge was required to leave the court — whether because he died, had to recuse himself, or declared *eini yode'a*, I do not know — and the *Sanhedrin* needed to bring in a replacement, a formal process was required.

### Semicha from Moshe

It becomes clear here, with a subtlety that could easily be overlooked, that placing someone on a *Sanhedrin* for capital cases requires granting them *semicha*. This is the ordination that traces back to Moshe Rabbeinu — the authority of *elohim*, representing in some sense divine delegated authority. Without that formal chain of ordination, a judge cannot adjudicate a capital case. So when a vacancy arises, the replacement must be given *semicha* before taking his seat.

### Somchin Min HaRishona

*Somchin min ha-rishona* — one ordains from the first row, that is, from the innermost of the three rows of students seated before the court. Within that inner row, the candidate is the one who is at the head — the front of the half-circle as defined by its internal hierarchy.

### Promotion Cascade

What follows is a cascade of promotions. Once the top person from the inner row is elevated to the *Sanhedrin*, everyone in the inner row shifts forward one position. This creates a vacancy at the end of the inner row. The top person from the second row then moves up to fill that last seat in the inner row. This in turn creates a vacancy at the end of the second row, which is filled by the top person from the third row, leaving a vacancy at the end of the third row.

### Selection from Community

*Borim lahem od echad min ha-kahal* — one selects an additional person from the broader community, someone who has now been identified as worthy of entering this circle of students and potential future judges. This person is brought in to fill the newly opened seat.

### Proper Placement Rule

The person selected from the community does not simply sit in whichever seat is vacant. *Ela yoshev ba-makom ha-rauy lo* — he sits in the place appropriate to his level. The empty seat at the end of the third row happens to be the bottom of the hierarchy, which is in fact where a newcomer belongs. But the principle is stated as a general rule: you do not tell someone to jump to a seat that is not his by rank simply because it happens to be empty. The cascade ensures that everyone advances properly, and the newcomer enters at the position befitting him. The *mishnah* closes with the observation that egalitarianism and hierarchy are not in tension here — they are two aspects of a single, carefully ordered system.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 37

## Sanhedrin Layout

### Semicircular Seating

The *mishnah* that opens our discussion actually begins at the bottom of daf 36, and it describes the physical arrangement of the *sanhedrin*: *sanhedrin hayetah kechatzi goren agulah kedei sheyihiyu ro'in zeh et zeh* — the *sanhedrin* was arranged like half of a circular threshing floor, so that all of the judges could see one another. The semicircular shape was not merely aesthetic; it served the functional purpose of ensuring mutual visibility among all who sat in judgment.

### Court Scribes

The *mishnah* continues: *ushenei sofrei hadayanin omdim lifneihem echad miyamin ve'echad mismol* — there were two court scribes standing before the judges, one on the right and one on the left. These scribes recorded the arguments on both sides: *vekotvin divrei mechaivin vedivrei mezakin* — they wrote the words of those arguing for conviction and the words of those arguing for acquittal.

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and holds that there were in fact three scribes: one dedicated to recording the words of those arguing for acquittal, one dedicated to recording the words of those arguing for conviction, and a third who recorded both. Rashi explains that this third scribe served as a checker, providing a built-in safeguard against errors that might arise when a single scribe attempts to record both sides simultaneously — the workload being simply too great to do accurately.

### Three Rows of Scholars

Beyond the judges themselves and the scribes, the *mishnah* describes three rows of *talmidei chachamim* seated before the court: *veshalosh shurot shel talmidei chachamim yoshvin lifneihem kol echad ve'echad makir et mekomo* — three rows of scholars sit before them, and each individual knows his place.

Rashi clarifies that each of these three rows contained twenty-three scholars — the same number as the judges of the *sanhedrin ketanah* itself. The reason for maintaining this number, as Rashi explains, is rooted in the *halachic* mechanics of capital cases. In a capital case, a verdict cannot be rendered on the basis of a single-vote majority for conviction; at least two additional votes for conviction over acquittal are required. If the court of twenty-three becomes deadlocked in a configuration such as twelve for conviction and eleven for acquittal, they are unable to proceed. In such a case, they augment the court by bringing in additional judges from the first row of scholars seated before them.

### Adding Judges

The process of augmenting the court works as follows: *hutzrechu lismoch somchin min harishonah* — if they need to appoint additional judges, they draw from the first row. When someone from the first row is elevated to the bench, someone from the second row advances into the first, and someone from the third row advances into the second. And since one of the three rows now has a vacancy, *uvorerin lahem od echad min hakahal* — they select an additional individual from the general public watching the proceedings and seat him in the third row.

Importantly, *velo hayah yoshev bimkomo shel rishon ela yoshev bimkom haraui lo* — the newcomer does not take the specific seat vacated by the person who was elevated; rather, everyone shifts forward in an orderly fashion and the new person takes the position appropriate to him at the end of the row.

One might ask: why not simply maintain rows of twenty-three, twenty-three, and two, which would sum neatly to the maximum of seventy-one judges? Rashi addresses this: it would be disrespectful to seat only two people in what is meant to be a full row. The aesthetic and honorific consideration demands that all rows be equal in number. This admittedly creates the somewhat curious situation where most of the scholars seated in these rows — particularly those deeper in — will realistically never be called upon to serve as judges. Nevertheless, the rows must be maintained and filled.

---

## Biblical Derivation

### Shorerech as Navel

The *gemara* now asks: *mena hani milei* — what is the scriptural derivation for the semicircular arrangement? Rabbi Akha bar Chanina answers by citing a verse from *Shir Hashirim*: *shorerech aggan hasahar al yechsar hamazeg* — your navel is like a crescent basin; may its mixed wine never be lacking. The *gemara* proceeds to expound each term of this verse as a reference to the *sanhedrin*.

*Shorerech* — your navel — *zo sanhedrin*: this refers to the *sanhedrin*. Why is the *sanhedrin* compared to the navel? *She-hi yoshevet be-tiburo shel olam* — because the *sanhedrin* sat in the navel of the world, a phrase associated with the Temple in Jerusalem, which other *midrashim* similarly describe as the world's center.

### Aggan & Hasahar

*Aggan* — basin — *she-hi megina al kol ha-olam kulo*: the word *aggan* is read as a reference to protection (*haganah*), because the *sanhedrin* protects the entire world. *Hasahar* — the crescent — *she-hi domah le-sahar*: this is the element most directly relevant to the *mishnah*, for it teaches that the *sanhedrin* is shaped like a crescent moon.

### Mazeg Requirement

The final clause of the verse — *al yechsar hamazeg*, may the mixing not be lacking — is interpreted as follows: *im hutsrach echad mehem latzet ro'in im yesh esrim u-shlosha keneged sanhedrei ketana yotze ve-im lav eino yotze*. If one of the judges must leave during the proceedings, they first check whether there are twenty-three individuals present in the crowd — corresponding to the number of a *sanhedrin ketanah*. Only if that minimum is present may the judge excuse himself; otherwise, he may not leave. The reference to *mazeg*, the mixing of wine, alludes to the maintenance of this quorum.

---

## Jewish Trustworthiness

### Wheat Mound

The *gemara* continues to expound the verses of *Shir Hashirim* in connection with the *sanhedrin* and with the Jewish people more broadly. The verse *bitnech aremat chitim* — your stomach is like a mound of wheat — is interpreted: *mah aremat chitim ha-kol nehenin mimena af sanhedrin ha-kol nehenin mi-ta'amehem* — just as everyone benefits from a mound of wheat, so too everyone benefits from the reasoning and legal rulings of the *sanhedrin*.

### Rose Hedge

The verse *suga bashoshanim* — hedged with roses — is interpreted as a metaphor for the Jewish people's resistance to transgression: *she-afilu ke-suga shel shoshanim lo yifretzu bahen pratzot* — even a barrier as thin and penetrable as a hedge of roses, the Jewish people will not break through it.

### Niddah & Yichud

The *gemara* illustrates this principle with a remarkable exchange. A heretic approached Rav Kahana and challenged him: *amritu nida shari le-yichudi bahadei gavra* — you say that a *nidah* is permitted to be in *yichud* with her husband? *Efshar esh be-no'oret ve-eina mehabhevet* — is it possible that fire can be placed among flax and not singe it? Surely such proximity will inevitably lead to transgression.

Rav Kahana responded: *ha-torah he'idah aleinu suga bashoshanim* — the Torah has testified about us through this verse, that even a barrier as weak as a hedge of roses will not be breached. The Jewish people will not transgress even in circumstances that appear to invite it.

This exchange prompted a *halachic* observation by *Tosafot*, who notes a difficulty: if the prohibition of *yichud* is *de-oraita*, how can a verse from *Shir Hashirim* be invoked to override it? *Tosafot* resolves this by explaining that the *de-oraita* prohibition of *yichud* applies only in cases where the two individuals involved are categorically forbidden to one another — such as close relatives or other *arayot* — but not in the case of a husband and wife between whom *yichud* is not absolutely prohibited under Torah law in all circumstances.

### Pomegranate Verse

Resh Lakish offers an alternative source for the same principle. He cites the verse *ke-felach harimon rakatech* — like a wedge of pomegranate is your temple — and expounds: *afilu rikanim sheback male'im mitzvot karimon* — even those who are the most empty among you, the lowest of the low, are full of *mitzvos* like a pomegranate is full of seeds. This too serves as a basis for trusting in the essential spiritual integrity of every Jew.

### Fragrant Clothes

Rabbi Zeira derives the same idea from yet another source, citing the verse *vayarach et reiach begadav* — and he smelled the smell of his clothes — from the episode in which Yitzchak smells the garments of who he believes to be Eisav. Rabbi Zeira reads *begadav* not as "his clothes" but as *bogdav* — his traitors, or those who mislead. The point is striking: even when reading the verse as referring to deceivers, Yitzchak smells and finds them fragrant. The Torah makes explicit that the smell was pleasing — *kerei'ach sadeh asher beraco Hashem* — like the smell of a field that God has blessed. Even those who are in some sense dishonest or misleading carry within them something of genuine worth and beauty. The trust we extend to Jews even in compromised situations is grounded in this assurance.

### Rabbi Zeira & Thugs

The *gemara* then recounts a story that illustrates this principle in practice. There were certain thugs (*biryonei*) in the neighborhood of Rabbi Zeira. Rather than avoiding them, *de-hava mekarev lehu* — he would associate with them, in the hope that his proximity would bring them to *teshuvah*. The *Rabbanan* were displeased with this conduct.

When Rabbi Zeira died, these same thugs said: *ad ha-idana hava haricha ketin shakei de-hava ba'ei alan rachamei hashta man ba'ei alan rachamei* — until now the singed small legs — their nickname for Rabbi Zeira, who according to Rashi had subjected his legs to heat as part of his ascetic practices, and who was known for his short, unimposing stature — would pray for us; who will pray for us now? *Hirhiru belibehu ve-avdu teshuvah* — they searched their hearts and did *teshuvah*. The connection to the theme of the section is clear: even the most apparently lowly and coarse among the Jewish people carry within them the capacity for genuine repentance and spiritual ascent.

---

## Judge Advancement

### Advancement Process

Returning to the three rows of scholars, *Abaye* derives a principle about how movement through the rows operates. When a scholar is elevated from the rows into the court, all others advance to fill the vacated positions, so that no empty space is left standing.

### Tail vs Head

This raises an apparent difficulty. Imagine a scholar who holds the first position in the second row — the most prominent seat in that row. When the court is augmented and everyone shifts forward, this individual is moved up into the second row of the first row, but he now occupies the last position there — the least prominent seat. He might reasonably object: *until now I was at the head; now you are placing me at the tail?*

Abaye responds with a well-known principle: *havei zanav la-arayot ve-al tehi rosh la-shu'alim* — be a tail among lions rather than a head among foxes. It is better to occupy the lowest position among a more distinguished group than the highest position among a lesser one. This resolves the objection: being last in the company of greater scholars is itself an elevation, not a demotion.

---

## Witness Warning

### Bringing Witnesses

The *mishnah* now turns to the procedure for warning witnesses in capital cases. *Al edei nefashot hayu machnisin otan u'me'aymin aleihem* — when dealing with witnesses in capital cases, they would bring them into the *sanhedrin* and impress upon them the gravity of their testimony.

### Direct Evidence

The witnesses are warned against several categories of invalid testimony: *shema tomru me'omed u'mishmua mipi ed v'ed mipi ed u'mipi adam ne'eman* — lest you base your testimony on an assumption, on something you heard, on what one witness told you another witness said, or on the word of someone you consider trustworthy. None of these suffice. Only direct personal observation constitutes valid testimony in a capital case. And the witnesses are reminded that the court will subject them to thorough *drisha u'vchakira* — the formal set of interrogatory questions designed to probe the precise circumstances of their claimed observation.

### Civil vs Capital

The witnesses are further instructed: *havu yodim shelo k'dinei mamonot dinei nefashot* — know that capital cases are not like civil cases. In a civil case, *adam noten mamon u'mitkaper lo* — a person can give money and be atoned; the wrong can be undone materially. Moreover, even a witness who testified falsely in a civil case can make restitution. But in a capital case, *damo ve-dam zariyotav taluy bo ad sof ha-olam* — if someone is executed on the basis of your testimony, his blood and the blood of all of his potential descendants hang upon you forever.

### Cain & Abel

The *mishnah* illustrates this with the story of Kayin: *sheken matzinu be-Kayin she-harag et achiv shene'emar dmei achicha tzo'akim* — as we see with Kayin who killed his brother, where the verse says "the bloods of your brother cry out." The deliberate use of the plural *dmei* — bloods — rather than the singular *dam* is significant. *Eino omer dam achicha ela dmei achicha* — it does not say "the blood of your brother" but "the bloods of your brother" — implying both his own blood and the blood of all his descendants who would never come into existence.

A *davar acher* adds: perhaps the plural refers to the fact that Hevel's blood was scattered across the trees and stones, sprayed in multiple places.

### Single Human Value

The *mishnah* then draws a profound theological lesson from the fact that all of humanity descends from a single ancestor, Adam HaRishon: *lefikach nivra adam yechidi* — therefore man was created singular. The lesson this conveys is that *kol ha-me'abed nefesh achat mi-Yisrael ma'aleh alav ha-katuv ke'ilu ibed olam malei* — anyone who destroys a single soul is treated by the Torah as though he has destroyed an entire world.

It is worth noting that the words *mi-Yisrael* — "from Israel" — do not appear in the earliest printings of the text, including the text as cited by the Rambam and in the old versions of Rashi. The original formulation appears to have applied universally to any human soul, without the specification of Jewish identity.

### Soul = World

Correspondingly, *ve-chol ha-mekayem nefesh achat mi-Yisrael ma'aleh alav ha-katuv ke'ilu kiyem olam malei* — anyone who sustains a single soul is treated by the Torah as though he has sustained an entire world. Rashi explains the practical implication of the statement *bishvili nivra ha-olam* — the world was created for my sake: *klomar chashuv ani ke-olam malei* — it means I consider myself to be like an entire world. This mindset carries with it a sense of cosmic responsibility: *lo etred et atzmi min ha-olam ba-aveira achat* — I will not cast myself out of the world through a single transgression.

### Creation Reasons

The *mishnah* enumerates additional reasons why God chose to create humanity through a single ancestor. *U-mipnei shalom ha-briyot shelo yomar adam le-chavero abba gadol mei-avicha* — for the sake of peace among human beings, so that no person could claim to his fellow that his lineage is superior, since all share the same first ancestor. *Ve-shelo yihyu ha-minim omrim harbeh rashuyot ba-shamayim* — so that heretics could not argue that multiple divine powers created different peoples, with each people's god responsible for their first ancestor. *U-lehagid gedulato shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — and to declare the greatness of God: whereas a human craftsman stamps many coins with the same mold and they all come out identical, God stamps every human being with the stamp of Adam HaRishon and yet no two are alike.

---

## Witness Warning (II)

### Personal Responsibility

The *mishnah* concludes: *lefikach kol echad ve-echad chayav lomar bishvili nivra ha-olam* — therefore each and every individual is obligated to say: the world was created for my sake. As Rashi makes clear, this is not an expression of arrogance but of moral seriousness — an awareness that one's own life is of infinite worth, and that the destruction of any life is therefore an act of cosmic devastation.

---

## Witness Concerns

### Fear of Involvement

After being told all of this, the witness might understandably recoil: *shema tomru ma lanu u-la-tzara ha-zot* — perhaps you will say, what do we want with all this trouble? The gravity of the situation — the weight of being responsible for a verdict that could result in someone's death — might cause a witness to retreat from testifying altogether.

### Rejoicing in Justice

The *mishnah* addresses this concern on two levels. First, there is a positive obligation: *halo kevar ne'emar ve-hu ed o ra'ah o yada im lo yagid* — the Torah has already stated that if one is a witness and has seen or knows something, he must come forward and testify. Second, the witness need not fear moral complicity in a justified execution: *halo kevar ne'emar be'avod resha'im rinah* — the Torah has already stated that when the wicked are destroyed, there is rejoicing. Participating in a just verdict against someone truly guilty is not a burden to be feared but an act of righteousness to be embraced.

---

## Circumstantial Evidence

### Assumption Defined

The *gemara* now asks: *keitzad me'umad* — what exactly is an *umdana*, an assumption or circumstantial inference? The *baraita* explains with a concrete case: *omer lahem shema kach re'item sheratz echad achar chaveiro lechorba* — perhaps this is what you saw: one person running after another into a ruin. *Ve-ratztem acharav* — and you ran after him.

### Sword & Blood

*U-matzatem sa'if beyado u-damo metaptef ve-harug mefarfer* — and you found a sword in his hand, blood dripping from it, and a dead body nearby in its final convulsions. *Im kach re'item lo re'item klum* — if that is what you saw, you have seen nothing admissible. No matter how overwhelming the circumstantial picture, this does not constitute valid testimony in a capital case.

### Shimon ben Shatach

The *baraita* then cites a first-person account from Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach. He attests — using the formula *er'eh be-nechama im lo ra'iti*, an oath of uncertain precise meaning — that he himself witnessed exactly this scenario: one man running into a ruin, the rabbi running after him, finding a sword in hand, blood dripping, and a dead body convulsing. He confronted the man directly: *amarti lo rasha mi harago lazeh o ani o ata* — wicked one! Who killed this person? Either I did or you did, and obviously it was not I. Yet, *aval ma e'eseh she-ein damcha masur beyadi* — what can I do? Your blood is not in my hands. *She-harei amra torah al pi shnayim edim yumat ha-met* — for the Torah has said: it is on the testimony of two witnesses that the death sentence is carried out.

This passage is somewhat puzzling, as the rishonic commentators note: the *mishnah*'s case concerns *umdana* — the requirement of direct observation versus circumstantial inference — while Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach's formulation invokes the requirement of two witnesses, a distinct principle. *Tosafot* addresses this by suggesting that Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach was not alone — there were other observers present — and that he is in fact deriving both the requirement of direct sight and the requirement of two witnesses from the same verse. The *gemara* acknowledges that this is somewhat strained (*ra'uh*), reflecting the genuine difficulty in the way the sources align.

### Divine Punishment

Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach concludes his account: *ha-yodea machshavot yipara me'oto ish she-harag et chaveiro* — may the One who knows all thoughts punish this man who killed his fellow. *Amru lo zazu misham ad sheba nachash ve-hikisho* — they said: they had not even moved from that place before a snake came and bit him, and he died. Divine justice was carried out where human justice could not reach.

---

## Post-Destruction Judgment

### Four Death Penalties

This brings the *gemara* to a remarkable principle stated by Rav Yosef and corroborated in the school of Chizkiyah: *miyom she-charav Beit HaMikdash af al pi she-batla Sanhedrin arba mitot lo batlu* — from the day the Temple was destroyed, even though the *sanhedrin* was nullified, the four death penalties were not annulled.

### Sanhedrin Cessation

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *lo batlu? ve-ha batlu!* — they were not annulled? But they clearly were nullified! The response is that the *din* — the legal principle and its implementation — was not annulled; it is simply that God now carries out these sentences through natural means rather than through a human court.

*Tosafot* raises a further difficulty: it is known that the *sanhedrin* ceased to adjudicate capital cases forty years *before* the destruction of the Temple. Why then does the *gemara* speak specifically of the day the Temple was destroyed rather than the earlier date?

### Special Cases

*Tosafot* explains, citing the passage in *Perek Hayu Bodkin*, that even after the *sanhedrin* went into a form of exile and ceased its regular functioning, it would still reconvene *letzorech sha'ah* — for special cases requiring it — and would return to the *Lishkat HaGazit* in the Temple precinct. *Tosafot* mentions in this connection a case that appears in uncensored versions of the text as *hahu uvda de-Yeshu* — the case of Jesus — which was subsequently removed by censors, likely to avoid provoking Christian hostility. Whether this reflects an independent Jewish tradition of such a trial or represents a textual intrusion from external sources is itself a question worth noting.

### Natural Death Means

The *gemara* then enumerates how each of the four death penalties continues to be administered through natural agency. One deserving death by stoning (*sekilah*) will either fall from a roof or be killed by a wild animal. One deserving death by burning (*sereifah*) will fall into a fire or be bitten by a snake. One deserving death by sword (*harigah*) will be handed over to the non-Jewish authorities or will be killed by bandits. One deserving strangulation (*chenek*) will drown in a river or die of *serunchi*, some form of disease.

### Multiple Penalties

This raises a question about the snake in Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach's case. If the man was a murderer, his punishment should have been *harigah* — death by sword. Why then was he killed by snakebite, which corresponds to *sereifah*? *Amrei hahu chata acharini havah beih* — the answer is that he had another sin as well, one that carried the penalty of *sereifah*. *De-amar mar mi she-nitchayev shtei mitot beit din nidon ba-chamurah* — as the principle states, one who is liable for two different death penalties is judged by the more severe of the two. Since *sereifah* is considered more severe than *harigah*, it was the penalty of *sereifah* that was visited upon him through the snakebite.

---

## Evidence Standards

### Capital Restriction

The *gemara* now returns to analyze the *mishnah*'s broader evidentiary framework. The *mishnah* explicitly states that *umdana* is invalid in capital cases, which implies by inference that *umdana* is valid in civil cases.

### Camel Example

The *gemara* identifies this as aligning with the view of Rabbi Akha: *tanya Rabbi Acha omer gamal ha'ochez bein ha-gamalim ve-nimtza gamal harug be-tzido ve-yadu'a she-zeh harago* — Rabbi Akha taught that if there is a camel — described by a term (*ha'ochez*) that Rashi explains with some uncertainty, perhaps meaning one in heat or one that is agitated — in the midst of other camels, and a dead camel is found alongside it, it is known that this camel killed the other, and the owner bears civil liability accordingly. This is a straightforward application of *umdana* to civil cases.

### Evidence Consistency

A challenge is raised: if the logic of the *mishnah* is that whatever is invalid in capital cases is thereby valid in civil cases, this would imply that *ed mipi ed* — secondhand testimony — which the *mishnah* also lists as invalid in capital cases, should similarly be valid in civil cases. But this is clearly untenable.

### Secondhand Testimony

The *gemara* resolves this by rejecting the premise: *ed mipi ed* is invalid in *both* civil and capital cases. The *mishnah* cites it in the context of capital cases for completeness, not to imply that it is permissible in civil cases. The *gemara* cites a *mishnah* from elsewhere: if a person claims that his fellow told him he owes money to a third party, that testimony is worth nothing — the obligation must be admitted directly before witnesses with a specific acknowledgment of the sum owed. This confirms that secondhand testimony is disqualified across the board. Consequently, one cannot derive from the *mishnah*'s treatment of *umdana* in capital cases a blanket rule that everything listed there is permissible in civil cases; each category must be analyzed independently.

---

## Bloods Plural

### Kayin's Strikes

Returning to the phrase *dmei achicha* — the bloods of your brother — the *gemara* offers additional interpretations. Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Hiyya teaches: *melamed she-asa Kayin be-Hevel achiv chaburot chaburot petza'ot petza'ot* — this teaches that Kayin inflicted blow after blow and wound after wound upon his brother, *she-lo haya yodea me-heichan neshama yotzet* — because he did not know from where the soul departs, *ad she-higi'a le-tzavaro* — until he reached his neck and realized that was the means of death. The plural "bloods" thus reflects the multiple wounds inflicted in this act of primordial violence.

### Blood & Descendants

Rav Yehuda bar Rav Hiyya offers a further teaching: *mi-yom she-patcha ha-aretz et piha ve-kibla et damo shel Hevel shuv lo patcha* — from the day the earth opened its mouth and received the blood of Hevel, it never opened its mouth again. The proof is from the verse *mi-kenaf ha-aretz zemirot shamanu tzevi la-tzaddik* — from the edges of the earth we heard song, glory to the righteous. The verse says *mi-kenaf ha-aretz* — from the edges — and not *mi-pi ha-aretz* — from the mouth of the earth — indicating that the earth's mouth was no longer available for this purpose.

### Earth's Mouth

His brother Chizkiyah challenged this: *va-tiftach ha-aretz et piha* — the earth did open its mouth, in the episode of Korach! The response: *le-ra'ah patcha le-tova lo patcha* — it opened its mouth to receive an evil person, not to benefit the righteous. That is a different matter entirely.

---

## Exile Atonement

### Half Atonement

Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Hiyya further teaches that *galut mechaper avon mechtza* — exile atones for half of the sin. The proof is from Kayin's punishment: initially the verse describes his fate as *ve-hayiti na va-nad* — I will be both a wanderer (*na*) and a rover (*nad*). Yet subsequently it is written *va-yeshev be-eretz Nod* — and he settled in the land of Nod. Nod retains the root of *na* or *nad*, but the doubling is gone: only one form of wandering remains, suggesting that exile atoned for half of his sentence.

### Three Attone

A distinct Rav Yehuda — a different *amora* — teaches that exile atones for three specific things, citing the verse: *ha-yoshev ba-ir ha-zot yamut ba-cherev u-va-ra'av u-va-dever ve-ha-yotzei ve-nafal al ha-kasdim ha-tzarim aleichem yichyeh ve-hayeta lo nafsho le-shalal* — he who dwells in this city will die by sword, by famine, and by pestilence, while he who goes out and surrenders to the besieging Kasdim will live, and his life will be as loot to him. The one who chooses exile — entering the hands of the besieging enemy — is spared from the three fates of sword, famine, and pestilence. Thus exile atones for three things: preservation from violent death, from starvation, and from plague.

### Complete Atonement

Rabbi Yochanan goes further: *galut mechaperet al ha-kol* — exile atones for everything. His proof is from the case of Yechonya, the last king of Judah before the Babylonian exile. The prophet declared: *kitvu et ha-ish hazeh ariri* — write this man off as childless, and further that no descendant of his would sit on the throne of David or rule in Yehudah. His line appeared to be utterly and permanently severed. Yet after his exile, *ketiv uvnei Yechanya* — it is written that Yechonya had children. The exile atoned for the decree against him and restored what had been taken away.

### Shealtiel Birth

Why is one of Yechonya's sons called *Assir*? *She-ibrato imo be-veit ha-asurim* — because his mother conceived him while in jail, and *Assir* is connected to *asurin*, the imprisoned. The constraints of incarceration — according to Rashi, the confined space forced an unusual posture for conception, since a woman does not ordinarily conceive while standing — are reflected in this unusual name.

### Zerubbabel

Yechonya's grandson Zerubbabel, who led the Jews back from Babylonian exile and oversaw the early stages of the Second Temple's construction, bears a name that the *gemara* unpacks: *she-nizra be-Vavel* — he was seeded, i.e., conceived, in Babylon. His very name encodes the geography of exile and return.

### Name Identities

*She'altiel* — Zerubbabel's father — is expounded in two ways. First: *she-lo kederech ha-neta'im* — he was not planted in the normal manner of plantings, reflecting his unusual circumstances of conception in jail. Second, a *davar acher*: *she-nish'al al alato el* — God dissolved or absolved the oath that had been made concerning his father Yechonya, releasing the curse.

The *gemara* then states that Zerubbabel's actual name was Nechemia ben Chachalya. This identification — equating Zerubbabel with Nechemia — is noted as puzzling by at least one of the commentators (*Margoliyot*), since they appear to be distinct figures elsewhere in Tanach. Yet here the *gemara* presents them as the same individual, and thus ends the discussion of daf 37.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 38

## Intro & Yerushalmi

### Civil vs. Capital

We are situated in *Sanhedrin*, *perek* 4, *echad dinei mamonot*, which deals with the ten differences between *dinei mamonot* and *dinei nefashot* — civil monetary cases and capital cases. The *mishnah* on the previous page taught how witnesses in capital cases are warned and, in effect, guilt-tripped: they are reminded of the weight of their testimony and the justice and righteousness that demands they speak the truth. The *aggadot* that follow shift the register entirely, moving from legal procedure to the cosmic stature of the human being — because if we are dealing with life and death, we must first understand what is at stake when the life of even one person hangs in the balance.

### Yerushalmi: Adam

Before entering the *Bavli* proper, it is worth surveying the *Yerushalmi*, which compresses into five and a half lines much of what the *Bavli* will expand at length. We are looking at *Yerushalmi Sanhedrin* 23b, *perek* 4, *halacha* 9, beginning with the words *keitzad me'umad*.

The *Yerushalmi* opens with the statement *adam nivra be'erev Shabbat* — the human being was created on *erev Shabbat*, Friday afternoon — *kedei sheyikanes techila lemitzvah*, so that he would immediately be able to perform a *mitzvah*. That is one reason. A second reason is offered in the form of a *mashal*: *mashal lemelech she'asa se'udah* — this is like a king who made a meal. *Keshematkin hase'udah mazmin ha'orchim* — first he sets out the meal, and only then does he invite the guests, rather than allowing the guests to witness the disorder of the preparations. The *Bavli* will expand this parable.

The *Yerushalmi* then brings a *pasuk* from *Mishlei*: *chochmot banta beita* — wisdom built her house. The *Yerushalmi*'s treatment is cryptic and fragmented, but the identification is clear: this is like God, who built the world *be-chochma*, with wisdom, as another *pasuk* confirms — *bechochma yasad aretz*. The *Yerushalmi* then reads the continuation of the *Mishlei* passage: *chatzva amudeiha shiva* — she carved her seven pillars — which alludes to *shivat yemei bereishit*, the seven days of creation. The preparations of the meal and the mixing of wine allude to *yamim veneharot ve-chol tzorchei ha'olam*, the seas, the rivers, and all the needs of the world. When the *pasuk* continues with *mi peti yasur henna* — who is the fool who will come here — that alludes to *Adam ve-Chava*.

### God's Joy

The *Yerushalmi* then takes a surprising turn and brings a *pasuk* from *Melachim* in the context of the death of *Achav*, king of *Yisrael*: *vaya'avor harina bamachane* — and the *rinah* passed through the camp. The question posed is *mahu harina* — what is the nature of this *rinah*? *Rinah* can mean joy, and the implication is that God rejoiced at the downfall of an evildoer. But the *Yerushalmi* immediately contrasts this with a *pasuk* from *Divrei HaYamim*, where *hodu la'Hashem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo* is said — *chesed* is invoked but not *tov*, joy, in the full sense. The tension between these two verses drives the conclusion: *l'lamdecha she'af mapalat ha-resha'im eina simcha lifnei ha-makom* — to teach us that even the downfall of evildoers is not truly joyful before God. This is a tension that will appear again in our *daf*.

---

## Sons of R. Chiya

### Wine & Secrets

We now turn to the *Bavli*, beginning a few lines from the top of 38b. The discussion of the sons of *Rabbi Chiya* connects directly to the preceding material about the weight placed on testimony and the significance of a single human being. We are told: *Yehuda ve-Chizkiya b'nei Rabbi Chiya havu yatvei be-seudata kamei de-Rabbi* — Yehuda and Chizkiya, the sons of *Rabbi Chiya*, were sitting at a meal in the presence of *Rebbi*. *Ve-lo havu ka'amrei ve-lo midi* — they did not speak a word. *Rebbi* then instructed his servants: *ashkuhu chamra le-dardakei* — give more wine to these young men — *ki heichi de-limru milta* — so that they will say something. As the *Gemara* will shortly make explicit, wine has the effect of loosening speech and drawing out what lies within.

### Two Institutions

Once the wine took effect — *keivan de-ivsum*, when they became inebriated — they opened with the following teaching: *ein Ben David ba ad she-yichlu shnei batei avot mi-Yisrael* — the *Mashiach* will not come until two institutions cease from the Jewish people. *Ve-elu hen*: the *resh gola she-be-Bavel* — the head of the diaspora in *Bavel* — and the *nasi she-be-Eretz Yisrael* — the *nasi* in the Land of *Yisrael*.

Now consider the situation: the *nasi* in *Eretz Yisrael* is *Rebbi* himself, seated right before them. These two young scholars, in their father's presence, with the servants and the wine, declare that the coming of *Mashiach* depends on the cessation of the very institution their host represents. The teaching is supported with a *pasuk* from *Yeshayahu* 8: *ve-haya le-mikdash u-le-even negef u-le-tzur michshol li-shnei batei Yisrael* — he will be a *mikdash*, but also an *even negef*, something that causes tripping, and a *tzur michshol*, a stumbling block, for the two houses of *Yisrael*.

The underlying tension is striking: we are waiting for the *Mashiach*, and yet the very institutions that sustain communal life in the interim — the *nasi* and the *resh gola* — are, according to this teaching, among the conditions that delay his coming. As long as these institutions are in place, the *Mashiach*'s role is, in a sense, already occupied. And yet we cannot simply relinquish what we have. The tension between living within existing structures and anticipating their transcendence is real and unresolved.

*Rebbi* responds — and the text is ambiguous as to whether his words are a statement or a question: *banai, kotzim atem matilin li bein einai* — my sons, you are throwing thorns between my eyes. Whether he intends a declaration of pain or an incredulous challenge, the thrust is clear: this teaching stings.

### Gematria Wine

*Rabbi Chiya* then intercedes on behalf of his sons: *Rebbi, al yera be-eineicha* — do not be upset. *Yayin nitan be-shiv'im otiyot ve-sod nitan be-shiv'im otiyot* — wine is spelled with letters that sum to seventy, and *sod* — secret — is also spelled with letters that sum to seventy. The *gematria*: *yayin* — *yud* (10), *yud* (10), *nun* (50) — equals 70. *Sod* — *samech* (60), *vav* (6), *dalet* (4) — also equals 70. *Nichnas yayin yatza sod* — when wine enters, secrets emerge. The image is of a narrow pipe: when wine flows in, it pushes the secrets out, because there is no room for both. *Rabbi Chiya*'s defense is elegant — you gave them the wine, and the wine produced the truth. Notably, *Rebbi* does not dispute the content of the teaching. He does not argue against the statement itself; he simply receives *Rabbi Chiya*'s explanation. The *sod* of the *sod*, one might say, has been confirmed.

---

## God's Righteousness

### Hastening Evil

*Rav Chisda* cites either *Mar Ukva* or *Mari bar Mar* — the transmission is uncertain — raising the following question: *Mai de-chtiv, vayishkod Hashem al hara'ah vayevi'eha aleinu ki tzaddik Hashem Elokeinu* — what is the meaning of this verse in *Daniel*, which says that God was diligent to bring evil upon us because He is righteous? The question the *Gemara* asks is pointed: is it because of God's righteousness that He hastened evil upon us? That is a deeply counterintuitive claim — that divine justice itself is the mechanism by which suffering is accelerated. The *Gemara* answers: *in* — yes — and proceeds to illustrate with examples.

### Yechanya Exile

The first example concerns the exile of *Yechanya*. The setting is the period of the first *Beit Hamikdash*. The destruction did not occur all at once; there were three stages of exile, *galuyot*, before the final one. *Yechanya* was a king of *Yehuda* who was exiled first by Nevuchadnezzar and the Neo-Babylonians. *Tzidkiyahu* was then installed in his place, and only later was he exiled as well. This means that when the later exiles arrived in *Bavel*, the earlier ones were already there — a welcome committee, in effect. God's "hastening" of the first exile was therefore an act of *tzedakah* toward those who came later, for they arrived to find an established community.

The proof text is the *pasuk*: *hecharash vehamasger elef* — the craftsmen and the smiths, a thousand. The *Gemara* reads *charash* not as craftsman but through the root of *cheresh*, deaf: *keivan shepotchin hakol na'asu ke-chershin* — when this group opened a *Torah* text, everyone around them fell silent like the deaf, having nothing to add. *Masger*, similarly, is read through the root *sagur*, closed: *keivan she-sogrin be-halacha shuv ein potchin* — when they closed a halachic matter, no one could reopen it. And they numbered a thousand — a substantial, learned community already established in *Bavel* to receive the later exiles.

### 852 Years

*Ulla* provides a second illustration. He says: *she-hikdim shtei shanim le-noshantem* — that God subtracted two years from the calculation implied by the word *venoshantem*. The *gematria* of *venoshantem* — *tav* (400), *shin* (300), *nun* (50), *tav* (400) — wait, reckoned as the *Gemara* reckons it — yields 852. The *pasuk* in *Devarim* uses the word *venoshantem*, and the continuation of the verse implies that if Israel remained in the land for 852 years and then acted wickedly, *va-avadetem* — they would be lost. According to *Ulla*, God in His mercy brought the exile after only 850 years, so that the full 852-year threshold stipulated in the verse would never be reached, and the threatened consequence would therefore not apply. God shortened the tenure so that the curse attached to its completion could not be triggered. Lengthy discussions exist as to how exactly the 850 years are calculated — whether *Mitzrayim* and the forty years in the desert are included or not — and we will not resolve them here.

*Rav Acha bar Yaakov* adds a further point: the next *pasuk* in *Devarim* uses the word *maher* — quickly. From this, *shema mina mehera* — we understand that for *Hashem*, 852 years qualifies as quickly, as the verse teaches: *ki elef shanim be-einecha ke-yom etmol* — for God, a thousand years is like yesterday. In divine reckoning, 852 years passes in no time at all.

---

## Adam Created Alone

### No Partnership

Returning now to the *mishnah* on 37a — *lefikach nivra adam yechidi* — we turn to the *midrashim* and explanations for why the human being was created alone. *Tanu rabanan*: *adam yechidi nivra* — the human was created as a single individual. *Mifnei mah?* Why? *She-lo yehu ha-minim omrim, harbeh rashuyot ba-shamayim* — so that the *apikorsim* would not say there are many powers in the heavens. If there had been two first humans, one might claim that two divine entities created them respectively.

Additional reasons follow. Another explanation: because of the righteous and the evildoers. *She-lo yehu ha-tzadikim omrim anu bnei tzadik ve-reshaim omrim anu bnei rasha* — so that the righteous would not say "we are descended from the righteous one" and the wicked would not say "we are descended from the wicked one." All are descended from a single common ancestor. Another explanation: *mifnei ha-mishpachot* — because of family rivalries. *She-lo yehu mishpachot mitgarot zo be-zo* — so that families would not provoke one another. And the *Gemara* notes pointedly: even now that only one Adam was created, families still quarrel; had there been two, all the more so. Similarly: *mifnei ha-gazlanim u-mifnei ha-chamsanim* — because of thieves and robbers. Even now that Adam was created alone, people steal; in a sense, we are stealing from ourselves. Had there been two, this would have been far worse.

### Stamp Metaphor

These reasons all concern human benefit. There is another dimension entirely — the greatness of God. *Tanu rabanan*: *le-hagid gdulato shel melech malchei ha-mlachim, ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — to proclaim the greatness of the King of kings, the Holy One, Blessed be He. *She-adam tovea kamah matbe'ot be-chotam echad ve-kulam domim zeh la-zeh* — a human being mints many coins in a single stamp and they all look identical. *Aval ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu tovea kol adam be-chotamo shel Adam ha-Rishon ve-ein echad me-hem domeh le-chavero* — but the Holy One, Blessed be He, stamps every human being from the mold of the first Adam, and yet no two are alike. The prooftext, remarkably, comes from *Iyov*: *titehafech ke-chomer chotam ve-yityatzvu ke-mo levush* — the material turns like a stamp and yet they are each clothed differently, each bearing a distinct exterior.

One might then ask: why, specifically, do faces differ? *U-mifnei mah ein partzufin domim zeh la-zeh?* The answer: *she-lo yireh adam dirah na'ah ve-ishah na'ah ve-yomar sheli* — so that a person will not see a beautiful home or a beautiful woman and say "those are mine," mistaking another's possessions or spouse for his own. The differences in appearance are a structural safeguard against moral disorder.

### Three Differences

*Rabbi Meir* teaches: *bishlosha devarim adam nishtaneh me-chavero* — in three things a person differs from his fellow. *Bekol u-ve-mareh u-ve-da'at* — in voice, in appearance, and in mind. *Bekol u-ve-mareh mishum ervah* — voice and appearance differ so that people will not come to immorality: at night, one can identify one's spouse by voice; by day, by sight. *Rashi* notes this prevents confusion and the moral violations that could result. *U-ve-da'at mipnei ha-gazlanim ve-ha-chamsanim* — and minds differ, *Rashi* explains, because each person conceals their valuables differently and cannot read another's mind. This limitation of mutual mental transparency is, as the lecturer notes, disappointing but important.

### Gnat Before

*Tanu rabanan*: *adam nivra be-erev Shabbat* — the human was created on *erev Shabbat*. *She-lo yihyu ha-minim omrim, shuttaf haya lo le-Hakadosh Baruch Hu be-ma'aseh bereishit* — so that the *apikorsim* would not say God had a partner in creation. By creating Adam last, there was no entity present to serve as a co-creator. Another reason: *she-im tazuach da'ato alav, omer lo, yatush k'damcha be-ma'aseh bereishit* — if Adam becomes *zachuach*, overly self-important, God can say to him: even the mosquito preceded you in the order of creation. The smallest creature was here before you.

### King's Parable

Two further reasons parallel what we saw in the *Yerushalmi*: *k'dei sheyikanes le-mitzvah miyad* — so he would immediately be able to perform a *mitzvah* (which *Rashi* identifies as *Shabbat*); and *k'dei sheyikanes le-seudah miyad* — so he would immediately enter into a prepared meal, finding everything ready. And now the *mashal* expands: *mashal le-melech basar va-dam she-bana paltarin ve-shichlalan ve-hitkin seudah, ve-achar kach hichnis orchim* — like a human king who built a palace, improved it, set out a meal, and only then brought the guests. The world was made ready before the guest of honor arrived.

---

## Wisdom's House

### Seven Pillars

The *mashal* is now grounded in the *psukim* of *Mishlei*. The *Gemara* brings three consecutive verses: *chochmot banta beita chatzva amudeiha shiva* — wisdom built her house, she carved her seven pillars. *Tavcha tivcha mascha yeina af archa shulchana* — she slaughtered the meat, mixed the wine, and set the table. *Ve-shalcha naaroteiha tikra al gappei meromei karet* — she sent her maidens to call, from the heights of the city. Now each element is decoded. *Chochmot banta beita* — this is the wisdom with which the Holy One, Blessed be He, built the entire world: *zu midato shel ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu she-bana et kol ha'olam kulo be-chochma*. It is striking, and worth noting, that the divine act of creation is here modeled on the image of a woman who builds her house.

*Chatzva amudeiha shiva* — she carved her seven pillars — *elu shiva yemei bereishit*, these are the seven days of creation.

### Meal & Rivers

*Tavcha tivcha mascha yeina af archa shulchana* — the preparation of meat and wine and the setting of the table — *elu yamim ve-neharot ve-chol tzorchei ha'olam* — these are the seas and rivers and all the needs of the world, everything laid out in advance for the arriving guest.

*Ve-shalcha naaroteiha tikra* — she sent her maidens to call — *zeh Adam ve-Chava*, this refers to *Adam ve-Chava*, the guests who are now invited into the prepared world. *Al gappei meromei karet* — from the heights of the city.

*Rabba bar Chana* then raises a challenge: one verse says *al gabei* — on high — and another says *al kisse* — on the seat or throne. The *Gemara* resolves: *be-techila al gabei u-le-vasof al kisse* — initially Adam was on high, but ultimately he ended up on the seat. Some understand the seat as the wedding seat when *Chava* is brought to him.

### Fool Tempted

The introduction of *Chava* immediately evokes a difficult *pasuk* from *Mishlei*: *mi peti yasur henna chasar lev* — who is the fool, or the one susceptible to enticement, who will come here? He lacks a heart, lacks understanding. The *Gemara* applies this to Adam: *amar ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu* — what tempted him? *Isha amrah lo* — the woman told him. A further verse about the *no'ef*, the adulterer, who is *chasar lev* — lacking a heart — is then invoked in comparison with Adam. The section is terse and difficult; we note it and move on.

---

## Adam's Composition

### Dust Gathered

*Rabbi Meir* teaches: *adam ha-Rishon mi-kol ha'olam kulo hutzbar afaro* — the first human being's dust was gathered from the entire world. The name *adam* itself shares a root with *adamah*, earth, and the imagery here is that the very material substance of the first person was drawn from everywhere on earth. The supporting *pasuk*: *golmi rau einecha* — your eyes saw my raw material. The parenthetical note in the *Gemara* adds: *ki Hashem einav meshotetvot be-chol ha'aretz* — because God's eyes sweep over the entire world, and from the choicest places He gathered the raw material for Adam's body.

### Body & Head

*Rav Oshaya* in the name of *Rav* provides a geographic breakdown: *Adam ha-Rishon gufo mi-Bavel ve-rosho me-Eretz Yisrael ve-eivarav mi-she'ar ha-aratzot* — his body was from *Bavel*, his head from *Eretz Yisrael*, and his limbs from the other lands. *Rashi* explains the head's origin in *Eretz Yisrael* because it is the highest and most esteemed of all lands — *she-hi gvohah ve-chashuva mi-kol ha-aratzot*. The body, the material dimension, comes from *Bavel*; the head, the spiritual apex, from *Eretz Yisrael*. *Rav Acha* adds that *agvotav* — the buttocks — come from *Akra d'Agma*, one of the lakes of *Bavel*, a location mentioned in other passages as well. The human being is literally composed from the whole world.

---

## Twelve Hours

### Hours 1-4

*Rabbi Yochanan bar Chanina* teaches: *shtem-esrei sha'ot havei ha-yom* — the day has twelve hours. The first day of Adam's existence was divided as follows. In the first hour, *hutzbar afaro* — his dust was collected. In the second, *na'asa golem* — he became a *golem*, a shapeless mass, like the stage before the creature takes final form, like dough that has received its yeast but has not yet risen. In the third hour, *nimtechu eivarav* — his limbs stretched out. In the fourth, *nizreka bo neshama* — the soul was, as it were, injected into him; the word *mazrek* in modern Hebrew means a syringe, and the image is of the soul being shot or thrown into the prepared body.

### Hours 5-8

In the fifth hour, *amad al raglav* — he stood on his feet. In the sixth, *kara shemot* — he named the animals. In the seventh, *nizdavga lo Chava* — *Chava* was paired with him. In the eighth, *alu la-mita shnayim ve-yardu arba'ah* — they went to bed as two and came down as four. Some understand this as referring to *Kayin* and his twin sister, others to *Kayin* and *Hevel*.

### Hours 9-12

In the ninth hour, *nitztave shelo le-echol min ha-ilan* — he was commanded not to eat from the tree. In the tenth, *sarach* — he sinned. In the eleventh, *nidon* — he was judged. In the twelfth, *nitrad ve-halach lo* — he was expelled and departed. The prooftext: *adam bi-yekarot bal yalin* — Adam did not sleep even one night in his place of glory. He did not remain in the Garden of Eden long enough to see a night's sleep.

---

## Adam Epicurus

### Adam Heretic

*Rav Yehuda* says in the name of *Rav*: *adam ha-Rishon min haya* — the first human being was an *epikoros*, a heretic. How is this known?

### Heart Wandered

The proof is from the verse: *vayikra Hashem Elohim el ha-Adam vayomer lo ayeka* — God called to the human and said to him, *ayeka* — where are you? One might wonder what it means for God to ask Adam where he is, since God surely knows. The *Gemara* explains that the real content of the divine question is: *an nata libcha* — where has your heart wandered? It is not a question about physical location but about attention, orientation, inner life. The fact that God had to stop Adam and ask "where are you?" implies that Adam's mind had already drifted, that the wholeness of his awareness had fractured. Already there was a split — he no longer apprehended the oneness of God in an undivided way. Something had leaked in.

*Rabbi Yitzchak* adds a further indication that Adam was a *min*: *moshech be-orlato haya* — he was pulling at his foreskin. The *Gemara*'s reasoning: Adam was created perfect, which the tradition understands as meaning he was created already circumcised. The act of pulling at the foreskin to conceal the *brit* is a gesture associated with those who sought to mask their Jewish identity. The *pasuk*: *ve-hema ke-adam avru brit* — and they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant — is paired with another verse, *et briti hefer* — he broke my covenant.

### Denied Principle

*Rav Nachman* goes further: *kofer be-ikar haya* — he denied the fundamental principle of faith. The same *psukim* are adduced, connecting the language of transgressing the covenant with the word *adam*, from which the sages infer that Adam had already harbored doubts about his covenant relationship with God.

---

## Heretics

### Learn Torah

This discussion of Adam's heresy opens naturally into a broader discussion of how one should respond to *apikorsim*. The *Gemara* cites a teaching from *Pirkei Avot*: *Rabbi Elazar omer, hevei shakud lilmod Torah ve-da ma she-tashiv le-apikores* — be diligent in the study of *Torah* and know what you will answer to the *apikores*. The emphasis on *Torah* is deliberate: the *apikores* does not accept the *Torah sheba'al peh*, the oral tradition, so there is no point engaging him on that ground. Instead, master the written *Torah* so thoroughly that you can meet him on the terrain he acknowledges.

### Internal Heretics

*Rabbi Yochanan* qualifies: *lo shanu ela apikores shel ovdei kochavim, aval apikores shel Yisrael, kol she-ken de-pakir tfei* — this applies to the *apikores* among the idolaters, but the *apikores* from within the Jewish people is far more argumentative. Why? Because he sat in the same classes, studied the same material, and arrived at his conclusions knowing all the answers in advance. You must therefore be genuinely prepared, not merely armed with standard responses.

*Rabbi Yochanan* adds a broader principle: *kol makom she-pakru ha-minim, teshuvatan be-tzidam* — in every place where the *minim* launch their challenges, the answer is right next to the challenge in the text itself.

### Answer Beside

The examples: *na'aseh adam be-tzalmenu* — let us make man in our image — the plural. Immediately the text continues: *vayivra Elohim et ha-adam be-tzalmo* — and God created the human in *his* image, singular. The challenge and the response sit side by side. Similarly: *hava nerda ve-navla sham sfatam* — let us go down and mix their language — again plural; but: *vayered Hashem lirot et ha-ir ve-et ha-migdal* — and God went down, singular. And: *ki sham niglu elav ha-Elohim* — for there *Elohim* was revealed to him, a plural construction for God. The same tension appears in *Daniel*: *ad di chorsevan* — until thrones, plural, were set — but *ve-atik yomin yetiv* — and the Ancient of Days sat, singular.

The *Gemara* addresses this last case: *hanach lama li* — but why do I need this? The answer is given in the spirit of *Rabbi Yochanan*, who taught: *ein ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu oseh davar ela im ken nimlach be-famalya shel ma'ala* — God does not do anything without consulting the heavenly court, as the *pasuk* in *Daniel* states: *be-gezirat irin pitgama u-ve-ma'amar kadishin she'elta*. All the plural formulations reflect this dynamic of divine consultation, not a plurality of divine beings. This resolves the challenge in each case regarding divine actions. But the case of the thrones in *Daniel* presents a different kind of problem — not about actions but about the physical thrones themselves. How can there be two?

---

## Two Thrones

### Akiva: Two

The *Gemara* provides the answer: *echad lo ve-echad le-David* — one throne for God and one for David. This is *divrei Rabbi Akiva* — the opinion of *Rabbi Akiva*, who holds that the two thrones mentioned in *Daniel* are one for God and one for the *Mashiach*, identified here as David. It is worth bearing in mind *Rabbi Akiva*'s well-known association with *Bar Kochba* as a messianic figure; for *Rabbi Akiva*, a throne for the *Mashiach* is not merely homiletical but carries deep practical weight.

### Yosi Challenge

*Rabbi Yosi* objects: *Akiva, ad matai ata oseh shechina chol* — Akiva, how long will you make the *shechina* mundane, *chol*? That interpretation is not acceptable. Rather, *echad le-din ve-echad le-tzedaka* — one throne is for justice and one is for righteousness. The *Gemara* then asks whether *Rabbi Akiva* accepted this rebuke or did not. It finds that elsewhere *Rabbi Akiva* is cited as agreeing with the formulation *echad le-din ve-echad le-tzedaka*, suggesting that he did in fact accept the correction.

### Footstool

*Rabbi Elazar ben Azaria* then offers a third resolution: *echad le-kise ve-echad le-shrafraf* — one is the throne and one is the footstool. When God, as it were, sits at the end of the day, He sits on the chair — *kise la-shevet alav* — and rests His feet on the stool — *shrafraf le-hadom raglav*. *Rabbi Elazar ben Azaria* even addresses *Rabbi Akiva* directly: *Akiva, ma lecha etzel aggada? Kelach etzel nega'im ve-ohalot* — what business do you have with *aggadata*? Go back to your specialty in *nega'im* and *ohalot*, purity and impurity law, where you are a master. The *aggadata* is not your strong suit.

---

## R. Idi Expert

### Only Rav Idi

*Rav Nachman* now introduces a principle for the extended discussion of responses to *minim* that follows: *hai man de-yada le-ahadori le-minim ke-Rav Idi leihadar, ve-i lo, lo leihadar* — whoever knows how to respond to the *minim* as *Rav Idi* did, let him do so; and if not, let him not try. *Rav Idi* knew not merely what to answer but how to answer — in a manner that was both textually grounded and rhetorically measured. The implication is that an ill-prepared response can do more harm than silence.

---

## Heretic Challenges

### Metatron Q

A *min* poses a challenge to *Rav Idi*: there is a verse, *ve-el Moshe amar, aleh el Hashem* — and to Moshe He said, go up to God. The challenge: if God is speaking, He should have said *alei elai*, come up to me. Why does God speak of Himself in the third person, saying "go up to *Hashem*"? The implication is that the entity speaking to Moshe is distinct from the entity called *Hashem* — raising the possibility of two powers.

### Metatron A

*Rav Idi* responds: *zehu Metatron she-shmo ke-shem rabo* — this is *Metatron*, whose name is like the name of his Master. The *pasuk* affirms this: *ki shmi be-kirbo* — my name is within him. *Metatron*'s *gematria* is 314, which equals the *gematria* of *Shaddai* — *Shin* (300), *Dalet* (4), *Yud* (10) — and this is how *Metatron* bears God's name within him.

The *min* presses: if so, *niflahu leh* — perhaps we should worship him? *Rav Idi* responds: *ktiv al tamer bo* — the verse says do not defy him. The Rabbis read the verb *tamer* not only as "defy" but as *al temireni bo* — do not replace me with him. And: *im ken lo yissa le-fish'achem lama li* — why then does the verse continue to say that he will not carry your sins? If *Metatron* were a valid intermediary, he would forgive sins. But he cannot. The conclusion: *haymanuta be-yadan ve-afilu be-farvanka nami lo kablinei* — we reject *Metatron* entirely. Not only do we not accept him as a divine being who carries our sins, but even as a guide along the way we do not accept him. As Moshe himself said: *im ein panecha holchim* — if You yourself do not go with us, we are not going. We want *Hashem* directly, not an intermediary.

### Sodom Q
