A *min* poses a challenge to *Rabbi Yishmael* from *Rabbi Yosi*: the verse reads, *ve-Hashem himtir al Sedom ve-al Amora gofrit va-esh me-et Hashem* — and God rained down fire and brimstone on *Sedom* and *Amora* from God. The challenge is parallel to the previous one: if God is the one raining, the verse should say *me-ito* — from Him. The phrase *me-et Hashem* again implies two distinct entities.

### Lemech A

A *koves* — a launderer, remarkably — says to *Rabbi Yishmael*: leave it, I will respond to him. And he answers with a verse from *Bereishit*: *vayomer Lemech le-nashav Ada ve-Tzila, sheman koli neshei Lemech* — Lemech said to his wives Ada and Tzila, listen to my voice, wives of Lemech. If Lemech is speaking, he should have said "my wives," *neshai*. Instead he refers to them in the third person as "wives of Lemech." *Ela mishtaye kra hachi* — this is simply how the text speaks. And the same principle applies to the verse about *Sedom*: *hacha nami mishtaye kra hachi* — here too the text speaks in this manner. That is a recognized literary pattern in *Tanach* — speaking of oneself in the third person — and it resolves the challenge.

### R. Meir Learning

*Rabbi Yishmael* is impressed that the *koves* can answer this way and asks: *minalach* — where did you learn this? The *koves* replies: *ha mi-pirkei de-Rabbi Meir shmiya li* — I have heard this from the teachings of *Rabbi Meir*. This sets up the final passage of the *daf*.

---

## R. Meir Parables

### Teaching Division

*Rabbi Yochanan* teaches: *ki hava darish Rabbi Meir be-pirkei, hava darish tilta shamata* — when *Rabbi Meir* would deliver his public discourses, a third was *halakha*, a third was *aggadata*, and a third was *meshalim* — parables.

### Fox Parables

*Rabbi Yochanan* further teaches: *shlosh me'ot mashal shu'alim hayu lo le-Rabbi Meir* — *Rabbi Meir* had 300 fox parables. He was extraordinarily rich in parabolic wisdom. And yet: *ve-anu, ein lanu ela shalosh* — and we, we possess only three of them. Three fox parables from that vast treasury of 300 have survived to us. Those three parables await us at the opening of the next *daf*, and they are, by all accounts, worth the anticipation.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 39

## Fox & Wolf Parables

### Intro & Rashi

The Gemara at the top of 39a concludes its discussion of Rabbi Meir by noting that although he composed three hundred parables involving foxes, we possess only three. These three parables are introduced cryptically — without context or narrative — and a careful reading of Rashi is necessary before any of them makes sense.

Rashi on the opening words — *avot yochlu boser* — explains that the three parables are embedded within a single story: the fox tricked the wolf into entering a Jewish quarter on *erev Shabbat* in order to help prepare the Shabbat meal and eat with them. When the wolf arrived and the townspeople set upon him with clubs, he turned to the fox in alarm. The fox reassured him: "They are not beating you for your own sins. They are beating you because of your father, who once came here, began helping them prepare the meal, and then ate all the choice portions himself, leaving nothing." The wolf protested — *uvishvil aba ani loke?* — "For my father's sin I am being beaten?" The fox replied simply: yes. This is the first parable: *avot yochlu boser v'shinei banim tikhenah* — "the fathers ate sour fruit and the teeth of the sons became dull." The phenomenon by which a parent's actions visit consequences upon a child is ancient and deeply human, and here it is given a parable's concise, unsettling form.

### Sour Fruit Parable

Having delivered this explanation, the fox continues: come with me, I will show you a place where you can eat and be satisfied. This transition leads directly into the second and third parables, both of which are contained within the same escapade at the well.

The identification of the wolf as the consuming, ungrateful figure and the fox as the clever one is precisely the conceit our rabbis are drawing on. Yet even accepting this, the reader is left with a question: how exactly did the fox manage this trick, and how does it connect to the remaining two *psukim*?

### Well Bucket Story

The fox leads the wolf to a well. Over the mouth of the well lies a piece of wood from which a rope is suspended, with a bucket tied to each end — the classic two-bucket pulley system, in which the weight of a descending bucket draws the other upward. The fox climbs into the upper bucket. His weight carries him down. As he descends, the other bucket rises. He calls up to the wolf: there is meat and cheese down here — eat and be satisfied! To make the claim convincing, he points to the reflection of the moon in the water below, which shimmers like a round of cheese.

The wolf asks how he can descend. Simple, says the fox: climb into the upper bucket. The moment the wolf — heavier than the fox — steps in, his weight carries him down and the fox rises up. Now the wolf is trapped at the bottom of the well. He calls out: how do I get back up? And the fox, now safely at the top, quotes him the *pasuk* from Mishlei: *tzadik mitzara nechelatz v'yavo rasha tachtav* — "the righteous man is rescued from trouble, and the evildoer comes under him." *Lav kach ktiv?* Is that not what is written? This is the third parable.

The second parable — *moznei tzedek avnei tzedek*, scales of justice and weights of justice — is also woven into this moment, referring to the precise calibration by which the scheme was arranged and executed.

### Maharsha Stones

The Maharsha, writing in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, raises a practical difficulty with the story: the fox weighs less than the wolf. Left to his own weight alone, would the fox even succeed in pulling the bucket down far enough to go to the bottom? And once down, if the wolf chooses not to get in, how does the fox get back out? The fox would be trapped regardless.

The Maharsha answers that the fox placed two stones in his bucket before descending — stones whose combined weight with the fox exceeded the fox's weight alone, but was still less than the wolf's weight. This is the *moznei tzedek*, the precise calibration of weights. If the wolf cooperated, his weight would bring the fox up. If the wolf refused, the fox could remove one of the stones, and the remaining stone — heavier than the fox himself — would tip the balance and raise the fox out. It is a clever and self-insuring arrangement, and the Maharsha's observation makes the ingenuity of the scheme complete.

---

## Heretic Challenges

### God Thief Challenge

We now move squarely onto 39a, which presents ten exchanges between a *kofer* — understood by the commentators as the emperor or Roman ruler — and various *Tanna'im* and *Amora'im*. Each exchange reflects a genuine theological challenge rooted in a misreading or provocative reading of a *pasuk*, and each response turns the challenge on its head.

The first challenge is addressed to Rabban Gamliel. A *kofer* declares: your God is a thief. The proof text: *vayapel Hashem Elokim tardemah al ha'adam vayishan* — God caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam and he slept. While Adam slept, God took his rib and fashioned woman from it. Stealing, the challenger insists, while the victim is unconscious.

Before Rabban Gamliel can respond, his interlocutor's own daughter intervenes. She says to Rabban Gamliel: sit, I will answer him. She then demands a judge from her father, alarming him. Why do you need a judge? Because, she says, robbers came to us last night. They took away a vessel of silver and left behind a vessel of gold. Her father replies: *ulevai sheyavo aleinu bechol yom* — would that such robbers came to us every day! She turns to him: was it not the same for Adam? They took one rib and gave him a *shifchah leshamsho*, a partner to serve him. He lost nothing and gained everything.

The emperor is not fully satisfied. *Hachi kamina*, he says — I understand the point, but the issue is not the exchange itself; it is that it was done covertly. Why did God not do this openly while Adam was awake? The daughter's response is as elegant as it is practical. She asks that a piece of raw meat be brought. She prepares it over the fire and coals, and presents it to her father. He recoils: *me'isa li* — it is revolting to me. She says: had Adam watched the entire process — the taking of the rib, the fashioning of flesh and bone — it would have been equally repulsive to him. It was better that it was done in concealment. This answer effectively closes the challenge.

### God Location Challenge

The second challenge, again to Rabban Gamliel. The emperor says: I know what your God is doing — and where He sits. Having made this boast, he then becomes visibly restless and sighs. Rabban Gamliel asks: what is the matter? The emperor replies: I have one son somewhere across the sea, and I miss him greatly. Rabban Gamliel says: show him to me. The emperor replies: how would I know where he is? He is somewhere in the world. Rabban Gamliel responds: *de'ika be'ara lo yad'at, de'ika bishmaya yad'at?* — what is happening on the earth you do not know, and yet you claim to know what is happening in the heavens?

### Stars Counting

Third challenge. The emperor says to Rabban Gamliel: it is written that your God can count the stars. What is so remarkable about that? *Ana mtzana lemeiman kochvei* — I too can count the stars. The practical difficulty with refuting this claim is obvious: if someone tells you there are twenty-three billion stars, you cannot immediately contradict them. You cannot count them on the spot.

Rabban Gamliel responds with a demonstration rather than an argument. He produces quinces and throws them into a spinning mixer, then turns to the emperor and says: *minyaneihu* — count them. The emperor says: stop the mixer and I will count them. Rabban Gamliel replies: *rakia nami hachi hadra* — the sky too is turning while you are counting. If you cannot count fruit whirling in a basin before your eyes, how do you propose to count the stars as the heavens revolve?

An alternative version of this exchange is recorded: the emperor challenges Rabban Gamliel to count the stars. Rabban Gamliel turns it around and asks: tell me first how many teeth and molars are in your mouth. The emperor immediately puts his hand to his mouth and begins counting. Rabban Gamliel says: *deika b'pumeich lo yad'at, deika b'rakia yad'at?* — what is inside your own mouth you do not know, and yet you claim to know what is in the heavens?

### Creators Debate

The fourth challenge introduces a more philosophically layered claim. The emperor says to Rabban Gamliel: the one who created the mountains did not create the wind. The proof text comes from the prophet Amos: *ki hinei yotzer harim u'vorei ruach* — "for behold, He who forms the mountains and creates the wind." Two different verbs are used — *yatzar* and *bara* — and the challenger reads this as evidence of two distinct creators: one who fashioned the mountains and one who created the wind.

The distinction between these verbs is significant. *Yetzira* — formation — describes shaping something from pre-existing material. *Bri'ah* — creation — describes bringing something into existence from nothing, an act uniquely available to God. People can be *yotzrim*, artisans and creators in a derived sense, but they are not called *bor'im*. That capacity belongs to God alone. The challenger's point rests on reading the two verbs as marking two separate agents rather than two distinct modes of the same divine creative act.

Rabban Gamliel responds: if this is so, then consider what is written about the creation of the human being — both *vayivra* and *vayitzer* appear. Does that mean two different creators fashioned Adam? The Gemara understands the *bri'ah* as producing the raw material — something from nothing — and the *yetzira* as shaping that material into human form. But the challenger's logic, if pressed, would require multiple creators for the human being.

Rabban Gamliel presses the absurdity further: *tefach al tefach yesh bo b'adam u'shnei nekavim yesh bo* — a human being is constructed composite, from part upon part, with multiple openings. Do you really mean that each was created by a separate being? He brings a *pasuk* from Tehillim: *hanotea ozen halo yishma, v'im yotzer ayin halo yabit* — "He who plants the ear, does He not hear? He who forms the eye, does He not see?" Does this mean the one who planted the ear and the one who formed the eye are different persons? The emperor confirms: yes, that is what I mean.

Rabban Gamliel then delivers the decisive line: *u'vishkat mita kulan nitpaisu?* — when the time comes for a human being to die, did all these various creators make peace with one another and agree that now is the moment? If there are multiple creators each responsible for a different organ or faculty, what happens at death? The composite would collapse incoherently, with each part departing on its own schedule. Yet people die as whole beings. This observation — delivered in one line — refutes both the Greco-Roman polytheism with its pantheon of non-omnipotent gods and the emerging Christian theology of distinct powerful divine figures, all in a single argument.

### Dualism Challenge

A *magush* — Rashi glosses this as a *mechashef*, a sorcerer, and some understand it as a Persian priest — says to Ameimar: from your waist upward, you belong to Ormazd; from your waist downward, you belong to Ahurmiz. This is a Zoroastrian dualism in which two distinct divine powers govern different domains. Applied to the human body, the upper half belongs to one god and the lower half to another.

Ameimar's refutation is immediate and practical: *i hachi, heichi shabkeih Ahurmiz le-Hurmiz l'avorei maya be-ar'eih?* — if so, how does Ahurmiz permit Ormazd's territory to pass water through its domain? One god controls the intake, the other controls the output, and they must share the body's infrastructure. This is not a tenable arrangement. The argument dissolves the dualist claim by pointing to the body's functional unity.

### Unity Challenge

The emperor says to Rabban Tanchum: come, let us all be one people. The proposal sounds generous. Rabban Tanchum replies with a smile: we would gladly oblige, but there is one small obstacle — *anan de-mahalinan lo matzinan mihvei kevataichu*. We practice circumcision and cannot simply become like you. However, you are welcome to become like us: *atu mahlitu ve-hevu kevatan*.

The emperor pronounces this an excellent answer — and then adds that anyone who bests the king in argument will be thrown to the animals. Rabban Tanchum is cast into the arena, and the animals do not eat him. A *min* who is watching says: the animals are simply not hungry — that is why he was spared. So they throw the *min* in, and the animals devour him. The parallel to the story of Abraham and to the story of Daniel is not lost on the Gemara.

### Shekhinah Minyan

A *kofer* challenges Rabban Gamliel: you say that wherever ten people assemble — wherever there is a *minyan* — the *shekhinah* dwells. How many *shekhinah*s can there be? If every *minyan* that gathers has its own *shekhinah*, the number becomes impossibly large.

Rabban Gamliel calls over the emperor's servant and strikes him across the back. The emperor demands an explanation. Rabban Gamliel says: I am upset because you let the sun into the emperor's house. The emperor replies: the sun shines across the entire world — how could we keep it out? Exactly, says Rabban Gamliel. If the sun — which is but one among thousands upon thousands of creations of the *kadosh baruch hu* — can illuminate the whole world simultaneously, then *al achat kama ve-kama*: all the more so can the *shekhinah* of the *kadosh baruch hu*, which is not a physical object, be present in every place at once. The argument also makes a subtler point: Rabban Gamliel demonstrates that even a physical entity can be present everywhere, which makes the omnipresence of a non-physical divine presence that much more comprehensible.

### Yechezkel Suffering

A *min* challenges Rabbi Abbahu: your God is inconsistent — He says to Yechezkel "lie on your left side," yet elsewhere it is written "you shall lie on your right side." What does He want?

At the same moment, a student arrives and asks Rabbi Abbahu: what is the reason for *shemitah*? Rabbi Abbahu responds: I will now give you an answer that addresses both questions — though he notes in advance that it will connect Yechezkel to *shemitah* while still leaving much unsaid.

Here is the answer. God said to Israel: sow for six years and let the land rest on the seventh, so that you will know that the land is Mine. They did not do so; they sinned and were exiled. Now consider how an earthly king responds to a rebellious province. If he is cruel, he kills everyone. If he is merciful, he kills half. If he is full of compassion, he singles out the great ones among them and inflicts suffering upon them alone. That is what the *kadosh baruch hu* did: all of Israel had transgressed in the matter of *shemitah*, but He afflicted only Yechezkel — *meyaser et Yechezkel* — in order to cleanse the transgressions of Israel.

This raises a profound and difficult question. Is this the trope of the suffering servant — a single righteous person bearing the burden of collective sin? The concept exists in our tradition: the suffering of the righteous can carry atoning weight for the many. But there are important distinctions. In this reading, Yechezkel is not an innocent party sacrificed in the people's place; he is the *gadol* among them, the leader of the *galut*, arguably the most responsible figure among those who failed to uphold *shemitah*, and his suffering reflects that responsibility. This differs from the Christian theological claim in which the atoning figure is entirely innocent and wholly outside the community of sinners. Here the connection between Yechezkel's leadership and the nation's failure is precisely what makes his suffering meaningful rather than arbitrary. The restlessness and discomfort described in the account of Yechezkel may itself be a reflection of that burden — the leader of exile carrying the weight of what exile represents.

### Priest Challenge

A *min* says to Rabbi Abbahu: your God is a *kohen*. The proof: *v'yikchu li terumah* — "and they shall take for Me *terumah*." If God receives *terumah*, He must be a *kohen*. But a *kohen* who buries a corpse becomes *tamei* and must immerse. Since God buried Moshe — *ki kavrei l'Moshe* — what *tevilah* did He perform afterward? And if you say He immersed in water, the *pasuk* from Yeshayahu refutes that: *mi madad b'sha'alo mayim* — God is so vast that the waters of the entire world would barely cover His hand. There is no body of water sufficient for such an immersion.

Rabbi Abbahu responds: *b'nura tavil* — He immersed in fire. The proof text: *ki hinei Hashem ba'esh yavo* — "for behold, God comes in fire."

The *min* objects: can fire really serve as a valid medium for immersion? Rabbi Abbahu replies: *adraba* — on the contrary. *Ikar tviluta b'nura* — immersion in fire is the superior form. The proof comes from Bamidbar, where the Israelites are instructed on purifying the vessels they acquired from Midian: *v'chol asher lo yavo ba'esh ta'aviru va-mayim* — anything that cannot pass through fire shall pass through water. The implication is clear: fire is the preferred and primary medium; water is the fallback for what cannot withstand fire. Rabbi Abbahu does not reject the premise that God is a *kohen* or that He buried Moshe. He simply explains how the necessary purification was accomplished.

### Nations Uniqueness

A *min* says to Rabbi Avina: it is written *mi k'amcha Yisrael goy echad ba'aretz* — "who is like your people Israel, one nation in the land?" What is so distinctive about you? On one hand, you are a *goy* like any other nation. On the other hand, the *pasuk* says *kol hagoyim k'ayin negdo* — all nations are as nothing before Him. Which is it? Are you elevated or are you, together with all nations, simply nothing?

One of the most striking features of this exchange is Rabbi Avina's response, or rather the response embedded in the Gemara's resolution. The answer is not to choose one side of the tension but to hold both. Israel is a *goy* — a people, a nation — and in that sense shares a category with all nations. And Israel is *goy echad*, uniquely one, set apart in a way that Bilam himself proclaimed: *uvagoyim lo yitchashav* — it shall not be reckoned among the nations. The power of the Jewish teaching, as is observed here, lies precisely in this refusal to collapse the tension. If the answer were only one way, something would be lost. Because it is both, something is preserved.

Rabbi Elazar then juxtaposes two *psukim* that seem to contradict each other. One says *tov Hashem lakol* — God is good to all. Another says *tov Hashem lekovav* — God is good to those who hope in Him. The *shoresh* *kuf-vav-heh* carries the connotations of gathering, hope, and waiting — *tikvah*, hope, and *mikveh*, a gathering of waters, share this root. The parable offered to resolve this: a person who has an orchard. When he waters, he waters the whole orchard — everyone benefits equally. But when he tills and tends to each tree individually, he does not tend to all of them indiscriminately; he gives particular care only to the good ones, the ones that will bear fruit. So too with God: His general sustenance extends to all creation, but His intimate, individualized attention is directed toward those who seek and hope in Him.

---

## Ahab Downfall

### Witness Mishnah

The Mishnah at 37a closes the chapter with the statement: *lefikach kol echad ve'echad chayav lomar bishvili nivra ha'olam* — therefore every single person is obligated to say, for my sake the world was created. This is connected to the testimony requirement in capital cases: witnesses might think, what is all this trouble to us? But the Torah says you must testify. And witnesses might also think, why should we be responsible for this person's blood? The Mishnah addresses this by citing the *pasuk* from Mishlei: *ba'avod resha'im rinah* — when evildoers are lost, there is joy. The implied message to potential witnesses is that when testimony leads to the conviction and death of a genuine evildoer, this is not a cause for guilt but for *rinah*.

This *pasuk* now becomes the entry point for the Gemara on 39b, which picks up the word *rinah* and subjects it to close analysis.

### No Joy Rejoicing

The Gemara notes a similar word in the account of King Ahab's death in the book of Melachim: *vaya'avor harinah bamachaneh* — a proclamation of joy passed through the camp. But the text does not say *vaya'avor rinah*; it says *vaya'avor ha-rinah*, with the definite article *heh*. For our commentators, a *heh* here is significant — it can function as a reference to *Hashem*.

Rabbi Avicha bar Chanina teaches: *ba'avod resha'im rinah* — when evildoers are lost, there is joy — and the example given is the loss of Ahab ben Omri. One might then ask: is this plural *resha'im* justified when we are speaking of a single person? Some explain that it includes Ahab's wife Izevel and the rest of his household, and extends — as we learned in the context of Kayin and Hevel — to his offspring as well.

But a serious problem immediately arises. *U'mi chadei Kudsha Brich Hu bemapalatan shel resha'im?* — Does God actually rejoice at the downfall of evildoers? This is theologically fraught. The Gemara brings a *pasuk* from Divrei Hayamim: *betzet lifnei hachalutz ve'omrim hodu Lashem ki le'olam chasdo* — when the armies went out, they said, give thanks to *Hashem*, for His kindness endures forever. The formulation conspicuously omits the usual phrase *ki tov* — "for He is good." Rabbi Yochanan explains: *mipnei mah lo ne'emar behoda'ah zu ki tov?* — Why was *ki tov* not said in this thanksgiving? Because *ein Hakadosh Baruch Hu same'ach bemapalatan shel resha'im* — the *kadosh baruch hu* does not rejoice at the downfall of evildoers.

### Angels Song

The same principle is illustrated in one of the most famous *aggadot* in the Talmud, cited here by Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan. At the crossing of the sea, it is written: *velo karav zeh el zeh kol halaila* — the forces did not come close to one another all night. During that night of separation, the *mal'achei hasharet* came before the *kadosh baruch hu* to sing a song of praise. God said to them: *ma'aseh yadai tove'im bayam ve'atem omrim shira lefanai?* — My creations are drowning in the sea and you wish to sing a song before Me?

There is considerable discussion in the commentaries about which *shirah* is meant here — whether it is the *Az Yashir* that Israel sang at the sea, or whether it refers to the *Hallel*, and which contexts of incomplete *Hallel* trace back to this moment. These are rich threads, but the core teaching is clear: God's sorrow at the death of His creations — even the Egyptians who oppressed Israel — precluded a posture of celebration.

### Hif'il Grammar

Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina adds a grammatical precision that sharpens the point. He teaches: *hu eino sas, aval acherim masis* — He Himself does not rejoice, but He causes others to rejoice. The proof lies in the verb form. The text uses *yasis* — the *hif'il*, causative stem — rather than *yasus*, the simple *kal* form. In the *hif'il*, the subject causes something in others rather than experiencing it directly. God is in the causative position: He brings about joy in others at the passing of evildoers, but He does not Himself rejoice.

This creates a carefully calibrated theological position. The Mishnah is correct that there is *rinah* — joy — when evildoers are lost. The Gemara in Pirkei Avot is also correct that one should not rejoice when one's enemy falls. Both teachings are true simultaneously. As is observed here: whenever one asks whether a Jewish teaching points this way or that way, the answer is almost invariably yes. The capacity to hold two truths in tension without forcing a resolution is one of the most characteristic features of Jewish thought, and this discussion is a striking illustration of that disposition.

### Ahab Death

Since the Gemara has introduced Ahab in this context, it now turns to explore a peculiarity in the narrative of his death. The text in Melachim tells us that Ahab was killed by a stray arrow — *v'ish mashach b'keshet l'tumo vayakeh* — someone drew his bow randomly and the arrow found Ahab. The word *l'tumo* is ambiguous. Rabbi Elazar reads it simply: *lefi tumo* — innocently, without aim or intention. But Rava reads it differently: *letamem* — to complete, to bring to wholeness — because *tam* carries the sense of completion, as in *Yaakov ish tam*.

Rava's reading connects to a deeper problem: at the time of Ahab's death, two prophecies about him appeared to contradict one another. Michayahu had prophesied that Ahab would fall somewhere other than where Eliyahu had prophesied — Eliyahu had designated the place where the dogs had licked Navot's blood, while Michayahu's prophecy pointed elsewhere. Geographically, one points toward the Gilad region to the southeast of the Kinneret, and the other toward Shomron, the capital of Ahab's kingdom. Rava reads the stray arrow — *l'tumo* — as the instrument by which both prophecies were simultaneously fulfilled.

### Zonot Interpretations

The verse describing Ahab's death includes the phrase *v'hazonot rachatzu* — the *zonot* washed. The surface meaning (*peshat*) is that harlots washed in the pool where Ahab's blood-drenched chariot was cleansed, signifying a degraded and ignominious end for the king: his blood was licked by dogs and washed away by prostitutes.

Rabbi Eliezer, however, reads *zonot* not as prostitutes but as *hezyonot* — visions, prophecies. His reading: the washing at the pool of Shomron served to cleanse, to reconcile, the two contradictory *hezyonot* — the vision of Michayahu and the vision of Eliyahu. The chariot carried his blood from the place where he fell to Shomron, allowing the blood to be licked by dogs at the location Eliyahu had designated while also arriving at the Shomron pool that Michayahu's prophecy had pointed to. Both prophecies were thus upheld.

Rabba, by contrast, maintains the plain sense: *zonot mamash* — real prostitutes. He explains that Ahab, whose name in later Hebrew is associated with being *metsunan* — cold, frigid — had little interest in intimate relations. Izevel, his wife, had placed images of harlots on his chariot in the hope of arousing him. These are the *zonot* of the verse.

---

## Ovadiah Stories

### Blessing Lineage

Since the Gemara has been discussing Ahab, it turns now to an episode that illuminates his relationship with his servant Ovadiah. The *pasuk* reads: *vayikra Achav el Ovadyahu asher al habayit ve'Ovadyahu haya yere Hashem me'od* — Ahab called to Ovadiah who was over his household, and Ovadiah feared God greatly. The word *me'od* — greatly — will carry significant weight.

The question the Gemara raises is: what is the narrative connection between the fact that Ahab calls Ovadiah and the fact that Ovadiah fears God greatly? They appear as two unrelated facts placed side by side without explanation.

Rabbi Yitzchak supplies the subtext of what Ahab said to Ovadiah. Ahab was invoking a lineage of blessing. In the story of Yaakov, Lavan acknowledged: *nichashti vayivarchani Hashem biglalecha* — I have divined that *Hashem* blesses me on your account; because you are with me I am blessed. In the story of Yosef, it is written: *vayivarech Hashem et beit hamitzri biglal Yosef* — *Hashem* blessed the Egyptian household because of Yosef. Ahab was therefore saying to Ovadiah: you fear God greatly, so the house of anyone who shelters you should be blessed as Lavan's was blessed through Yaakov and as Potipha's house was blessed through Yosef. But my house is not being blessed — *beiteih dehai gufra lo hava mivarech*. Perhaps you are not truly fearing God as I thought.

Ahab's construction of this lineage is deliberate. The kingdom of Israel rested over the territories of Ephraim and Menashe, the sons of Yosef. Ahab was positioning himself as the successor to the Yaakov–Yosef line rather than to the Davidic line from Yehudah, establishing a claim to dynastic blessing through Ovadiah's presence in his house.

The *bat kol* responded: *ve'Ovadyahu haya yere et Hashem me'od* — Ovadiah indeed feared *Hashem* greatly. The blessing, however, would not reach Ahab's house. *Aval beito shel Achav eino mezuman livracha* — Ahab's household is simply not positioned to receive blessing. No amount of Ovadiah's righteousness could overcome the weight of Ahab's own conduct.

Rava adds a further dimension: the greatness attributed to Ovadiah in this verse actually exceeds what was said of Avraham. In the verse describing Avraham's fear of God, the word *me'od* does not appear; in the verse about Ovadiah it does. Yet even this extraordinary level of *yirat Hashem* was insufficient to unlock blessing for the house of Ahab.

### Ovadiah Prophets

The Gemara now examines the role Ovadiah played during Izevel's campaign against the prophets of *Hashem*. The *pasuk* recounts: when Izevel was cutting down *Hashem*'s prophets, Ovadiah took a hundred prophets, hid them fifty to a cave, and provided them with bread and water.

Why fifty per cave rather than all one hundred in a single place? Rabbi Elazar answers: *mi'Yaakov lamad* — he learned this from Yaakov. When Yaakov approached danger from Esav, he divided his camp into two, so that if one was struck the other might survive: *vehayah hamachaneh hanishar lifleitah*. By dividing the prophets, Ovadiah ensured that the capture of one group would not doom the other.

Rabbi Abbahu offers a more prosaic explanation: a cave simply cannot hold more than fifty people. Practicality, not spiritual strategy, dictated the division.

### Convert Prophet

The question then arises: why did Ovadiah, specifically, merit the gift of prophecy? According to tradition, Ovadiah was a convert — an Edomite by origin. There is a principle rooted in the *pasuk* that God's covenant extends to Israel and to their offspring after them, and this has been understood by some as limiting prophecy to those of Israelite lineage. A convert lacks that genealogical chain. How, then, did Ovadiah become a prophet?

One answer given is precisely his act of protecting the hundred prophets. By risking his position in Ahab's court — and his life — to conceal them in the caves, Ovadiah demonstrated a fidelity to *Hashem*'s prophets that merited prophetic standing in return.

### Edom Prophecy

The opening words of the book of Ovadiah read: *chazon Ovadyahu, koh amar Hashem Elokim le'Edom* — the vision of Ovadiah; thus says *Hashem* God to Edom. Why should Ovadiah, of all prophets, be the one to deliver a prophecy against Edom?

Rabbi Yitzchak explains in the name of the *kadosh baruch hu*: let Ovadiah — who lived between two evildoers, Ahab and Izevel, and did not learn from their conduct — come and prophesy against Esav the evildoer, who lived between two righteous ones, Yitzchak and Rivka, and did not learn from their conduct. The contrast is precise and structurally elegant: Ovadiah withstood malign influence from within the palace of the wicked; Esav could not absorb righteous influence even from within the home of the righteous. Each is measured by the environment they inhabited and how they responded to it.

Ephraim Maksha'ah, a student of Rabbi Meir, transmits in Rabbi Meir's name that Ovadiah was indeed of Edomite origin, a *ger Edomite*. This brings the Gemara to the proverb: *mineih uveih abba nizal beih narga* — from it and within it, the father, the axe handle goes into it. The axe handle is made from the very forest it is used to cut down. Destruction sometimes comes from within: the means of a thing's undoing is drawn from its own substance. In Ovadiah's case, an Edomite becomes the instrument of Edom's prophetic condemnation.

---

## David Moab Tension

### David Moab War

The Gemara brings this proverb again in the name of Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, now applied to a different case. The *pasuk* from Melachim recounts: *vayach et Mo'av vayimadedem bechevel hashkev otam artzah* — King David struck Moav and measured them with a rope, laying them on the ground. David waged war against Moav. What makes this notable is that David himself traces his lineage through Moav — his ancestor Rut was a Moabite. Here too, the axe handle comes from the forest. The instrument of Moav's judgment was formed from within Moav's own line.

### Customs Contradiction

The Gemara then presents another episode and a further biblical tension. A king takes his firstborn son — the one who was to reign after him — and offers him as a burnt-offering upon the wall. Rav and Shmuel disagree about the motivation: one says it was *leshem shamayim* — for the sake of heaven; the other says it was for the sake of *avodah zarah*.

Both positions bring a proof text. The one who says it was for the sake of heaven cites the verse *vayehi ketzef gadol al Yisrael* — a great anger came upon Israel — and explains this through a teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who juxtaposes two apparently contradictory verses. One verse says: *u'chemishpetei hagoyim asher svivoteichem lo asitem* — you have not done like the laws and customs of the nations around you. Another verse says: *ki chemishpetei hagoyim asher svivoteichem asitem* — for you have done like the laws and customs of the nations around you. Which is it? Did Israel follow the ways of the nations or not?

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *kamukanim shebahem lo asitem, kemkulkalim shebahem asitem* — the good customs of the surrounding nations, you did not adopt; the corrupted ones, you did. Israel selectively absorbed the worst of their neighbors while failing to learn from the best.

### Evildoers Depths

Following the departure of the nations from the king who sacrificed his son — *vayisu me'alav vayashuvu la'aretz* — Rabbi Chanina bar Papa teaches: *be'otah sha'ah yardu resha'im shel Yisrael l'madregah tachtona* — at that moment, the evildoers of Israel descended to the lowest level. The *pasuk* cited describes the *na'arah* as *yafah ad me'od* — beautiful up to very much.

Rabbi Chanina bar Papa adds a closing qualification: *adayin lo higiya l'chatzi yafyah shel Sarah* — they still did not reach even half the beauty of Sarah. The word *ad me'od* — "up to very much" — means they reached *until* the threshold of *me'od*, but did not cross into it. *Me'od bichlal* they did not attain. In descending to the lowest depths, the evildoers of Israel still, perhaps by some mercy, stopped short of the absolute limit. That the chapter closes on this note — finding even in the most extreme descent a margin of restraint — is itself a kind of commentary on the unbounded quality of divine measure.

*Hadran alach echad dinei mamonot.* We conclude the fourth chapter of Sanhedrin.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 40

## Intro: Witness Inte (III)rroga…

### Transition & Topic Intro

The fifth *perek*, *Hayu Bodkin*, opens at the top of Sanhedrin 40a with the *mishnah*. Having dealt in the previous *perek* with the early stages of the court process — accepting witnesses and the general framework of capital proceedings — the *mishnah* here addresses specifically the rules governing the *chakiros* and *drishot*, or *bedikos*: the different types of questions the court must put to witnesses. Some of these questions are mandatory; others are discretionary. Some are sufficiently precise that if the witnesses err in answering them, the entire testimony is disqualified; others leave room for ignorance or even contradiction without invalidating the testimony. Crucially, this framework of *drisha ve-chakira* applies only to *dinei nefashot* — capital cases. As established in the first *perek*, the Rabbis did not apply this regime to *dinei mamonos*, civil suits, not because it would not be required by Torah law but because the rigors of the process would make it impractical for people to resolve monetary disputes. The economic cost of making litigation too cumbersome was a serious concern the Rabbis sought to avoid.

## Seven Chakiros: Tim (III)e/Pla…

### Seven Questions Listed

The *mishnah* states: *hayu bodkin otan be-sheva chakirot* — the judges would interrogate the witnesses with seven distinct categories of questions. These are: *be-eizo shavua* — in which cycle of seven years within the *yovel* cycle? Here *shavua* refers not to a week of days but to a *shemita* cycle, a seven-year period; *be-eizo shana* — which year within that seven-year cycle? *Be-eizo chodesh* — which month of the year? *Be-khamma ba-chodesh* — which day of the month? *Be-eizo yom* — which day of the week? *Be-eizo sha'ah* — at what hour of the day? And the seventh: *be-eizo makom* — in what place? Six of the seven questions concern time, and the seventh concerns location. The question of how precise the answers need to be — whether "in New York City" suffices or whether the floor of a particular building must be specified — is itself a matter the *gemara* will probe.

### Rabbi Yosi: Three Only

*Rabbi Yose omer be-eizo yom be-eizo sha'ah be-eizo makom* — Rabbi Yosi holds that only three *chakiros* are required: which day of the week, at what hour, and in what place. His position stands in direct contrast to the majority view of seven, and the question of what drives this disagreement will become central to the *gemara*'s later analysis of the biblical sources.

### Act Details: Idol & Meth…

The *mishnah* continues with a set of questions that the *Rambam*, in his *Perush ha-Mishnayos*, regards as even more fundamental than the *chakiros* proper — so fundamental, in fact, that without them there is no testimony at all, since they go to the very content of the act being testified about. These are: *makirin atem oto* — do you, the witnesses, recognize him? This includes whether they could identify the defendant as a Jew, since Jewish identity bears on culpability. *Hitartem bo* — did you administer a warning (*hatra'ah*) about the consequences of the act? In *dinei nefashot* the witnesses must have warned the person that the specific act he was about to perform carries a death penalty. In the *mishnah*'s context of idolatry, they would have had to say explicitly: if you worship this idol you will be liable to *skila*.

Beyond these preliminary questions, if the case involves *avodah zarah*, the court asks *et mi avad* — which idol did he worship? — and *u-ve-mah avad* — by what mode of worship? This second question matters because *avodah zarah* has two distinct tracks of culpability. First, four categories of worship — sacrifice, libation, incense-offering, and prostration — are forbidden regardless of what the idol's normal mode of worship is, because these replicate the modes of divine service. Second, if an idol has a characteristic mode of worship native to it, performing that mode is likewise prohibited. The *gemara*'s classic example is *Markulis*, likely the Roman god Mercury, worshipped by throwing or placing stones at the idol's location or at crossroads. Even one who throws a stone at *Markulis* sarcastically, intending it as an act of contempt, has nonetheless performed its characteristic form of worship and is culpable. The question *bameh avad* therefore needs to establish which of these tracks applies.

## Intro: Witness Inte (III)rro…

### Purpose: Hazimah

*Rashi* makes a point of emphasizing the fundamental purpose of the *chakiros*: they exist specifically in order to create testimony that is *edut sheyachol lehazimah* — testimony susceptible to being exposed as conspiratorial. The mechanism of *hazimah*, the disqualification of *eidim zomemim*, which we will reach in the first *perek* of *Masechet Makkos*, works by a counterclaim of *imanu hayitem* — "you, the witnesses, were with us elsewhere at the very time you claim to have witnessed the crime." For such a counterclaim to be possible, the testimony must be anchored to a specific time and place. Without those coordinates, there is no basis for *hazimah*. *Rashi*'s point is therefore that the *chakiros* are not merely procedural safeguards but are constitutive of valid testimony in capital cases: the time and place of the event are not themselves elements of the *aveira* but are essential to the testimonial quality that allows the judicial process to function with integrity.

## Seven Chakiros: Tim (III)e/P…

### Bdikot Example

The *mishnah* continues: *kol hamarbeh bivdikot harei zeh meshubach* — one who multiplies *bedikot* questions is praiseworthy. The *bedikot* are the discretionary questions, left to the court's judgment, and an illustrative case is cited: *maaseh uvadak Ben Zakkai be'uktzei te'einim* — there was an incident in which Rabbi Yochanan Ben Zakkai examined witnesses about the fig stems at the site of a murder committed under a fig tree. Different varieties of figs have stems of different thicknesses, and Ben Zakkai asked the witnesses to describe them. This *bdikah* was designed to verify whether two witnesses were truly describing the same tree and the same scene. Naturally, each witness was examined separately — the entire system of interrogation requires the witnesses to be questioned apart from one another so that they cannot coordinate answers — and if one described thick stems while the other described thin ones, their accounts would be revealed as incompatible, exposing the inconsistency in their testimony.

## Intro: Witness Inte (III)rro…

### Chakiros vs. Bdikot

*Mah bein chakiros livdikot* — what is the difference between *chakiros* and *bedikot*? The *mishnah* answers: for *chakira* questions, if even one witness says *eini yodea* — "I don't know" — *edutan beteilah*, the testimony is entirely invalidated. The logic follows from *Rashi*'s principle: if a witness cannot specify when and where the event occurred, the testimony loses its quality of *edut sheyachol lehazimah*. A witness who says "I don't know what day of the week it was" has left an opening that prevents any subsequent *hazamah*.

For *bedikot*, by contrast, *afilu shenayim omrim ein anu yode'im edutan kayemet* — even if both witnesses say they do not know, the testimony stands. *Bdikot* are designed to catch witnesses in a contradiction, not to affirm the factual foundation of the testimony. So if one witness says the stems were thick and the other says he was not paying attention to the stems at all, that is perfectly acceptable — there is no contradiction and no deficiency in the core testimony. The *mishnah* then adds that both *chakiros* and *bedikot* share one rule: *bizman shemachchishim ze et ze edutan beteilah* — if the witnesses contradict one another, the testimony falls regardless of which type of question produced the contradiction.

## Seven Chakiros: Tim (III)e/P…

### Month/Day Errors

*Echad omer bishnayim ba-chodesh ve-echad omer bishlosha ba-chodesh* — if one witness says the event occurred on the second of the month and the other says on the third, *edutan kayemet*. The testimony stands, because *sheze yodea be-iburo shel chodesh veze eino yodea be-iburo shel chodesh* — one witness may have known whether the previous month had thirty days or only twenty-nine, while the other did not. Months varied in length, and early in the month, when the precise day count since the month's beginning was not yet settled in everyone's mind, an off-by-one error is a reasonable human mistake. Notably, *Elul* was the one exception — since the time of Ezra, *Elul* never carried thirty days and was always twenty-nine — so there could be no ambiguity about *Elul* dates. But for other months, a one-day discrepancy at the beginning of the month is treated charitably.

*Ze omer bishlosha ve-echad omer bachamisha* — but if one witness says the third and the other says the fifth, *edutan beteilah*. A two-day discrepancy is not a reasonable error, because months are always either twenty-nine or thirty days, never more. A person of the sort who would come to testify in court is expected to track the passage of days of the month, and being off by two days exceeds the latitude the court extends.

### Hour Errors & Pesach

*Echad omer bishtei sha'ot ve-echad omer bishalosh sha'ot* — one says it was during the second hour, the other says during the third hour: *edutan kayemet*. Without mechanical timepieces, witnesses tracked the hour by the sun's position, and a one-hour error is an ordinary human mistake. *Echad omer bishalosh ve-echad omer bachamesh* — one says the third hour, the other says the fifth: *edutan beteilah*. A two-hour discrepancy, being off by one hour in either direction, is beyond reasonable error.

*Rabbi Yehuda omer kayemet* — Rabbi Yehuda, however, holds that even a two-hour discrepancy leaves the testimony valid, because Rabbi Yehuda's view is that a two-hour error is within the range of normal human imprecision. This position has interesting implications for *Pesach*-related questions that *Tosafot* raises. The *de'oraita* prohibition on eating *chametz* takes effect at noon on *erev Pesach*. The Rabbis added a prohibition at the sixth hour to safeguard against encroaching on the seventh. They further prohibited eating *chametz* during the fifth hour — the concern being that on a cloudy day one might confuse the fifth hour for the sixth. This yields an apparent difficulty: we generally do not issue a rabbinic decree to protect another rabbinic decree, *gezeira al ha-gezeira*. Various resolutions are offered; perhaps the fifth-hour prohibition is actually safeguarding the seventh hour, the *de'oraita* threshold, which would make it a two-hour protective buffer. Yet according to the *chachamim* who reject Rabbi Yehuda's position, a two-hour error is not a normal human mistake — so why enact a two-hour buffer? These are among the questions the issue raises.

### 5th-7th Hour Boundary

*Echad omer bachamesh ve-echad omer besheva* — one says the fifth hour and the other says the seventh: *edutan beteilah*, even according to Rabbi Yehuda, because *shebachamesh chama bamizrach u-vesheva chama bama'arav* — in the fifth hour the sun is in the east, while by the seventh hour it has already crossed to the western half of the sky. No reasonable person could mistake one for the other, since the sun's position has shifted unmistakably from one side to the other. This marks the outer limit beyond which even Rabbi Yehuda concedes the discrepancy is fatal to the testimony.

## Post-Interrogation P (II)

### Acquittal Presumption

After the *chakiros* and *bedikot* have been conducted and the witnesses' answers found consistent — *im nimtze'u divreihem mechuvannim* — the court proceeds to deliberation. Even at this point, with two witnesses testifying to the defendant's guilt, the *mishnah* prescribes *poteach bizchut* — the proceedings open with a presumption toward acquittal. The court actively seeks reasons to find the defendant innocent before rendering any judgment.

If one of the witnesses then says he has a reason to argue in the defendant's favor, or if one of the *talmidim* — junior observers seated in the courtroom — says he knows a reason to find the defendant liable, both are silenced: *meshatakin oto*. The witness who originally came to testify to guilt cannot now offer exculpatory arguments. This flows in part from the general principle of *keivan she-higid shuv eino chozer u-magid* — once a witness has entered testimony into the record, he cannot retract it and return with supplementary testimony. There is also an inherent implausibility to a witness who testified that the accused committed a capital crime now claiming to know grounds for acquittal. For the observing *talmid* who wants to argue for conviction, he is silenced because the court's formal deliberation must begin from the side of innocence, not guilt.

### Student Elevation

If, by contrast, one of the *talmidim* says *yesh li lelamed alav z'chut* — he has a reason to find the defendant innocent — *maalin oto*, the court brings him up and seats him among the judges for the remainder of the day. The entire proceeding in *dinei nefashot* reflects the obligation of *v'hitzilu ha-edah* — the community's affirmative duty to seek the defendant's acquittal — a principle derived from the laws of *ir miklat* but applied across all capital cases.

*Im yesh mamash b'divrav* — if there is genuine substance to what the *talmid* says, *shom'in lo*, the court listens to him. Remarkably, *afilu hu omer yesh li lelamed al atzmi z'chut* — even if the accused himself raises a ground for his own defense — *shom'in lo*, the court may hear him, *u-vilvad she-yesh mamash b'divrav*, provided there is actual substance to the claim. The accused is not presenting himself as a witness and is not testifying about facts; he is offering, in something like a hybrid procedural role, a ground that might tip the scales toward innocence. The *rishonim* debate exactly what legal role the accused plays in this moment, but the principle is clear: any opening toward acquittal is to be pursued. The courts will not, however, let this become a mechanism for indefinitely prolonging proceedings through empty claims — once a pattern of groundless assertions emerges, the court will cease to engage.

### Adjournment & Pairs

*Im matzu lo zechu petaruhu* — if they find a reason to acquit, they release him. *Ve-im lav, maavirin oto lemachar* — if they have found no exculpatory reason, they still do not render a final judgment. They adjourn until the following day. In the interim, *mizdavvegim zugot zugot* — the judges pair off with one another. Given that the court must have an odd number of members, at least one group of three must have formed.

### Judge Restrictions

During this interlude the judges observe certain austerities. *Hayu memaatim bemaachal* — they eat less, avoiding any suggestion of indulgence while bearing the weight of a capital decision. *Velo hayu shotin yayin kol ha-yom* — they drink no wine throughout the entire day, since a judge is disqualified from rendering a decision after consuming wine, and this rule remains in force across the entire deliberative period. *Kol ha-yom ve-nos'in ve-notenim kol ha-layla* — they engage in deliberation throughout the day and the entire night. Whether *kol ha-layla* means they must remain entirely awake throughout the night or means only that they should be occupied in discussion as much of the night as possible is a question raised by commentators. There is a suggestive parallel to the *Kohen Gadol*, who must remain awake the entire night before *Yom Kippur* — perhaps a broader parallelism exists between the *Kohen Gadol*'s entry into the *avoda* on *Yom Kippur* and the judges' entry into capital deliberation.

### Day Two: Positions

*U-le-macharot*, on the second day, *mashkimim u-va'in le-veit din* — the judges rise early and return to the *beit din*. Each judge then declares his position. *Hamezakeh omer: ani mezakeh u-mezakeh ani bi-mkomi* — one who votes for innocence declares: "I find him innocent and I remain in my place," meaning his position has not changed. *Ve-hamachayev omer: ani machayev u-machayev ani bi-mkomi* — one who votes guilty makes the corresponding declaration of consistency.

### Verdict Asymmetry

A judge who previously said guilty may now have been persuaded to say innocent — that switch is permitted. But *hamlamed zechut eino yachol lachzor lelamed chova* — a judge who previously argued for innocence cannot change to guilty. Even from the first day's deliberations, this asymmetry is operative: verdicts may only move in one direction, from conviction toward acquittal, never the reverse.

This creates a striking catch-22. If on the first day the entire court unanimously found the defendant guilty, and the following day some judges switch to innocent, that switch — although formally permitted — would actually move the verdict from the status of non-execution (since a unanimous guilty verdict results in acquittal) to possible execution. The precise *psak* in such a case is genuinely unclear.

## Voting & Court Expan (II)

### No Unanimous Guilt

The rule that a unanimous guilty verdict results in acquittal rather than execution warrants attention. If all twenty-three judges find the defendant guilty, he is paradoxically set free. The concern underlying this rule is *groupthink* and the fear of external pressure — if every single member of a court has been convinced unanimously, something may be distorting the deliberation. Whether the basis is *gezeirat ha-katuv* or grounded in a realistic assessment of how consensus-without-dissent emerges, the rule reflects a deep suspicion of unanimity in capital cases. Statistical analysts in other contexts have similarly noted that 100% agreement itself is a signal that something is amiss in the process.

## Post-Interrogation P (II)

### Scribes' Role

*Shenei sofrei ha-dayanim mazkirin oto* — two court scribes keep the record of each judge's declared position, and their role is specifically to prevent a judge from switching his verdict in the prohibited direction. If a judge who had voted innocent attempts to shift to guilty, the scribes' record serves as the check against that impermissible change.

## Voting & Court Expan (II)

### First Vote

After all deliberations, *omdim le-minyan* — the court rises to a formal vote count. *Im matzu lo zechut petaruhu* — if they find grounds for innocence, he is freed. *Ve-im lav* — if not (note again the circuitous phrasing, avoiding the direct statement that he is guilty) — *omdim le-minyan* — they proceed to the formal tally.

### 23-Judge Voting

*Shenayim asar mazakin ve-achad asar mechayavin* — if twelve say innocent and eleven say guilty, *zakai*, he is acquitted, since twelve constitutes a majority. *Shenayim asar mechayavin ve-achad asar mazakin* — if twelve say guilty and eleven innocent, that is likewise inconclusive as a final verdict: conviction requires a majority of three, meaning at least thirteen against ten in a court of twenty-three. *Ve-afilu achad asar mazakin ve-achad asar mechayavin ve-echad omer eini yodea* — even if it is eleven to eleven with one abstention, *afilu esrim u-shenayim mazakin o mechayavin ve-echad omer eini yodea* — or even if twenty-two vote one way and one judge says *eini yodea*, I cannot decide — then *yosifu ha-dayanim*, more judges must be added. It may seem puzzling that adding judges resolves the difficulty created by one judge who abstains: the abstaining judge's own position will not be changed by the addition of new judges. How this actually resolves the problem is itself a question the *gemara* will address.

### Adding Judges

*Ve-chamah mosifin — shenayim shenayim* — judges are added two at a time, since the court must always remain odd-numbered. The court expands incrementally in pairs.

### 71-Judge Court

*Ad shivim ve-echad* — until the court reaches seventy-one members, the maximum permitted. At seventy-one: *sheloshim ve-shisha mazakin u-sheloshim ve-chamishah mechayavin* — thirty-six for innocence and thirty-five for guilt yields an acquittal. *Sheloshim ve-shisha mechayavin u-sheloshim ve-chamishah mazakin* — thirty-six for guilt and thirty-five for innocence produces a deadlock, because to execute one needs a majority of three, meaning thirty-seven against thirty-four, and thirty-six against thirty-five is insufficient. Yet a majority also cannot simply acquit since more judges voted for guilt. In this deadlock, *danin elu keneged elu ad she-yireh echad min ha-mechayavin divrei ha-mazakin* — the two sides argue with one another until one of those voting guilty is persuaded to shift to innocent. It is, in effect, a procedural filibuster: the court cannot proceed to execution without achieving the required supermajority, and the burden falls on the side of guilt to yield.

## Biblical Source: Gezeirah

### Three Contexts

The *gemara* now turns to the biblical derivation of the seven *chakiros*. *Mena hanei milei* — where is this learned from? *Amar Rav Yehudah d'amar kra* — Rav Yehudah the *amora* derives it from three distinct biblical passages, two of which appear in last week's *parasha* and one in this week's. The three contexts are: *ir ha-nidachat* — the wayward city that turns to *avodah zarah*; an individual case of *avodah zarah*; and the case of *eidim zomemim* — conspiring witnesses. Before the biblical analysis, however, the *Rambam* in the first chapter of *Hilchot Edut* should be noted. *Halacha* 4 states: *mitzvat aseh lidrosh ha-edim ve-lachkor otam* — there is a positive *mitzvah* on the court to conduct the *derishah* and the *chakirah*. *U-leharbot bi-she'elatan* — to multiply the questions. *U-medakdekin aleihem* — to be exacting with the witnesses. *U-masi'in otam me-inyan le-inyan betoch ha-she'elah* — to move fluidly between topics during the questioning in order to disorient witnesses who are fabricating testimony, since such interrogation techniques — familiar from any serious investigative context — are effective at revealing inconsistency and deception. The *Rambam* adds that the *dayanim* must be careful not to inadvertently coach the witnesses by revealing information that could help them construct a more coherent false account. The *Rambam* then enumerates the seven *chakiros* as in our *mishnah*, adding that there are further questions beyond the seven that also carry the status of *chakiros* — though, as noted, in his *Perush ha-Mishnayos* the *Rambam* seems to treat those additional questions as a separate category, raising interesting questions about the consequences of a witness's failure to answer them.

### Gezeirah on 'Heitiv'

The three *pesukim* are: *ve-darashta ve-chakarta ve-sha'alta heiteiv* — regarding *ir ha-nidachat*, in which the requirement to investigate, search further, and ask very well uses three distinct verbs plus the word *heiteiv*; *ve-hugad l'cha ve-shamata ve-darashta heiteiv* — regarding individual *avodah zarah*, where the court is told it was reported, you heard, and you investigated thoroughly; and *ve-darshu ha-shoftim heiteiv* — regarding *eidim zomemim*, where the judges are required to investigate very well.

If we simply count the operative words across the three *pesukim*, we might say each passage contributes its own set of requirements independently. One might then ask: why not treat each passage in isolation and conclude, as Rabbi Yosi does, that each contributes only three requirements? *De-im kein l'chitivinhu Rachmana b'chada* — the *Torah* could have stated the requirement of investigation once, in a single place. The fact that all three appear in separate *halachic* contexts, each with its own word *heiteiv*, signals that they are meant to be read together — *keivan d'culhu bahadi hadadi ktivi, mehadadi yalfei* — and since they are learned from one another, it is *k'man d'chtiv b'chada dami*, as though written together as a unified law. This is not quite a *binyan av* but something related — splicing together three separate *pesukim* to generate the number seven.

### Case Distinctions

The obvious objection is that the three cases are not analogous, and ordinarily we would not combine non-analogous cases into a single legal construct. A *siman* captures the three differences: *palat, sayif, hatra'ah* — property, sword, and warning.

*Ir ha-nidachat l'hanach tarti lo damya* — *ir ha-nidachat* is unlike the other two: *sheken mamonam palat* — in *avodah zarah* and *eidim zomemim* the participants' property is preserved, but in *ir ha-nidachat* the property of the city's inhabitants is incinerated along with the city itself.

*Avodah zarah l'hanach tarti lo damya* — *avodah zarah* is unlike the other two: *sheken b'sayif* — both *ir ha-nidachat* and *eidim zomemim* (in the context of a murder conviction) are executed by beheading with a sword, while *avodah zarah* carries execution by *skila*, stoning.

*Eidim zomemim l'hanach tarti lo damya* — *eidim zomemim* is unlike the other two: *sheken tzrichim hatra'ah* — both other cases require that the offender be warned in advance, but *eidim zomemim* famously does not require *hatra'ah*. This is nearly unique among capital crimes; presumably the nature of a conspiracy to corrupt the judicial process is such that a formal warning is considered superfluous or inapplicable.

Since each of the three cases has a distinctive feature that sets it apart from the other two, we cannot simply combine them as parallel cases through a general literary construction.

### Gezeirah Mufneh

*Be-heiteiv heiteiv yalfinan mehadadi u-gzeirah shavah mufneh* — the resolution is that the word *heiteiv* appears in each of the three contexts, enabling a *gezeirah shavah* that equates the three cases despite their differences. A *gezeirah shavah* operates on a different principle than a *binyan av*: it does not require the cases to be similar; it requires only that the identical word appear in each context, with a *masorah* supporting the connection. Because it is a *gezeirah shavah*, the underlying dissimilarities between the cases do not defeat the *drasha*.

The *gezeirah shavah* must be *mufneh* — open-ended, meaning the word used in the comparison is extraneous to its immediate context, present specifically to be available for the *drasha*. *Rashi* explains: a *gezeirah shavah ha-mufneh lemedim ve-ein meshivin* — a *gezeirah shavah* that is *mufneh* cannot be challenged; it is as watertight a proof as exists in the system of *drashot*. But if it is not *mufneh*, it is open to refutation, which would explain how Rabbi Yosi can disagree.

How is *heiteiv* shown to be extraneous? In two of the three cases the word is obviously unnecessary: the *pesukim* already have *ve-darashta ve-chakarta* — "you shall investigate and you shall search" — and adding *heiteiv*, "very well," is redundant. The *Torah* could have said *darosh tidrosh* or *chakor tachkor*, using the doubled-verb form that Hebrew uses for emphasis, and the requirement to investigate thoroughly would have been conveyed. By choosing *heiteiv* instead, the *Torah* signals that this word is present specifically to be available for the *gezeirah shavah* — *shma mina le-afnu'ei*.

One might object that *heiteiv* is extraneous only in two of the three *pesukim*, not all three — making it *mufneh mitzad echad*, open-ended from only one side. The *gemara* responds: *bishlama hanech tarti mufneh* — the two cases of *avodah zarah* and *eidim zomemim* are clearly *mufneh* given their alternative formulations. For *ir ha-nidachat*, however, *mai havah leih le-michtav* — what alternative phrasing would have been available that would not have used *heiteiv*? The answer is the same: it could have used the doubled-verb form, *darosh tidrosh* or *chakor tachkor*, for emphasis. Since it did not, and instead chose *heiteiv*, that too is *mufneh* — *shma mina le-afnu'ei* — open for use in the *drasha*.

Having established the *gezeirah shavah mufneh* and combined the three *pesukim*, the three *pesukim* yield the following words with independent semantic weight: seven operative words across the passages, producing the seven *chakiros*. Three uses of *heiteiv* provide the basis for the *gezeirah shavah* itself. The next matter is whether the cases of *nechnakin* — strangulation — and *nisrafin* — burning — can be derived from these same sources or require further derivation. *Ve-atu nechnakin be-kal va-chomer mi-skilin u-miharugin* — those executed by strangulation can be learned by *kal va-chomer* from the contexts of stoning and beheading. *Ve-atu nisrafin be-kal va-chomer mi-skilin* — burning is learned by *kal va-chomer* from stoning.

The structure of this *kal va-chomer* deserves attention. The argument is: if even in cases of the most severe punishment, where we might be most motivated to convict, we nonetheless impose the rigor of *drisha ve-chakira* that works to protect the accused, then *kal va-chomer*, in cases of lesser punishment where we have less motivation to convict, the same requirement certainly applies. The direction is perhaps counterintuitive — learning from the more severe to the less severe in a way that appears to impose *additional* requirements — but the logic holds when the *drisha ve-chakira* is understood as a protective mechanism rather than as a precondition for punishment.

*Ha niicha le-Rabbanan d'amri skila chamura* — this *kal va-chomer* works smoothly according to the Rabbis, who hold that *skila* is the most severe form of capital punishment, so learning from stoning to burning presents no difficulty. *Ella le-Rabbi Shimon d'amar sreifa chamura* — but Rabbi Shimon holds that burning is the most severe execution. If burning is more severe than stoning, then the *kal va-chomer* from stoning to burning cannot work, since one cannot learn from a less severe case to a more severe one in this direction. *Mai ika le-meimar* — how does Rabbi Shimon account for *nisrafin*?

### Rav Yehudah: 11 Words

*Ella amar Rav Yehudah: ve-hinei emet nachon ha-davar* — Rav Yehudah now offers an alternative *drasha*. The *pasuk* says *ve-hinei emet nachon ha-davar* — "and behold, the matter is true and established" — which adds additional words to the count of operative terms across the three *pesukim*. Tallying carefully: *sheva le-sheva chakirot* — seven of the eleven words derived from the combined *pesukim* provide the source for the seven *chakiros*. *Tlat le-gezeirah shavah* — three words (the three appearances of *heiteiv*) are reserved for the *gezeirah shavah*. *Pash lihu chada le-Rabbi Shimon le-atuyei nisrafin* — one word remains, and this remaining word serves, for Rabbi Shimon, as the explicit textual inclusion of *nisrafin*, since Rabbi Shimon cannot use the *kal va-chomer* that the Rabbis rely upon.

For the Rabbis, who could have learned *sreifa* by *kal va-chomer*, the fact that the *Torah* explicitly includes it anyway reflects the general principle that *milta d'atya be-kal va-chomer tarach ve-chatav lah kra* — the *Torah* sometimes writes out explicitly even what could have been derived logically, and the Rabbis simply count that explicit inclusion as an expression of the same principle. The concern about *ein onshin min ha-din* — that one cannot derive punishments from *kal va-chomer* — does not apply here, since the *drisha ve-chakira* regime is itself oriented toward acquittal rather than punishment; its purpose is to protect the accused, not to impose liability.

### Rabbi Abbahu Challenge

*Megaded beh Rabbi Abbahu* — Rabbi Abbahu challenges Rav Yehudah's accounting. If the Rabbis have an eleventh word available and use it to explicitly include *nisrafin* even though they could have derived it by *kal va-chomer*, why not instead use that eleventh word to generate an *eighth chakira* rather than seven? Rabbi Abbahu's question is pointed: Rav Yehudah's resolution of the problem for Rabbi Shimon works only if the Rabbis commit that eleventh word to *nisrafin*. But why is that the necessary use of the word rather than expanding the number of *chakiros*?

### Baraita: 8 Chakiros

*Shmoneh chakirot mi ika* — the *gemara* asks whether there is any *tanna* who actually holds that there are eight *chakiros*. *Ve-ha ika le-atuyei b'khama b'sha'ah* — the answer is: there is indeed a possible eighth question, namely how far into the hour the event occurred. Beyond the hour itself, one could ask witnesses to specify how many *dakin* or *chalakim* — the Rabbis' more precise sub-hour units — had elapsed. *Chalakim* are units of three and a third seconds each, too fine for any witness to track in a criminal event, but some sub-hourly precision might in principle be demanded.

*Ve-tanya nami hachi* — and indeed there is a *baraita* that reflects this position: *hayu bodkin oto bi-shmoneh chakirot* — they would examine him with eight questions. *Ha nicha le-Abaye aliba de-Rabbi Meir d'amar ein adam toeh ella khlum* — this works well according to Abaye's reading of Rabbi Meir, which is that a person knows precisely what time it is, even within the hour. *U-le-hach lishna nami d'amar adam toeh mashehu* — and it also works under the version that holds a person might err by only a small amount within the hour. *Ella le-Abaye aliba de-Rabbi Yehuda d'amar adam toeh chatzi sha'ah* — but according to Abaye's reading of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a person can err by as much as half an hour, and *u-le-Rava d'amar ta'u inshei tuvei* — according to Rava, who interpreted the *mishnah*'s handling of a two-hour discrepancy as reflecting that people err substantially — how could an eighth question about the sub-hourly interval even be asked if witnesses routinely cannot be held to precise hour-level accuracy?

## Yovel Year Question

### 8th Q: Yovel Cycle

The *gemara* proposes another candidate for a possible eighth *chakira*: *ela le-atuyei b'eizeh yovel* — perhaps the eighth question is not about the sub-hourly time but rather about which *yovel* cycle it is. The first *chakira* already asks *be-eizo shavua*, in which seven-year cycle within the *yovel* period. A logically distinct question would be *be-eizeh yovel* — in which fifty-year *yovel* cycle, counting from the inception of the *yovel* system, did this event occur? The *gemara* then considers whether this is truly a distinct question from *be-eizo shavua* — and concludes that it is: *hainu be-eizeh shavua* is asking about the position within a *yovel* cycle, while *be-eizeh yovel* asks which *yovel* cycle altogether.

### Yovel Tracking Ended

However, this eighth question is not asked in practice, and the reason is historical. *Keivan d'amar be-eizeh shavua lo ba'ei be-eizeh yovel* — since after a certain point in history, no one was tracking which *yovel* cycle they were in, the question becomes unanswerable and therefore moot. Already during the *Bayit Rishon* period there are indications that tracking of *yovel* years had lapsed — though there is some debate about precisely when — and certainly by the *Bayit Sheni* period the *yovel* was not observed. A question no witness could be expected to answer cannot form part of the mandatory *chakiros*. There is perhaps also a polemical dimension here: the authors of *Sefer Yovelot* — the Book of Jubilees, a work associated with sectarian groups outside the rabbinic tradition — placed enormous emphasis on tracking *yovel* cycles. A quiet rabbinic dismissal of *be-eizeh yovel* as an unanswerable question may carry some polemical resonance against those groups.

### Yosi Rejoinder

*Tanya, amar lahem Rabbi Yosei la-chachamim* — the *baraita* then records Rabbi Yosi's rhetorical challenge to the *chachamim*: *le-divreichem mi sheba ve-amar emesh harag* — according to your position, if a witness comes to court and says "yesterday he committed murder," do you intend to ask him *be-eizeh shavua be-eizeh shana be-eizeh chodesh be-kama ba-chodesh* — which seven-year cycle, which year, which month, which day of the month? The questions are plainly unnecessary when the event occurred *yesterday*; asking which year or which month is ludicrous when there is no ambiguity whatsoever.

*Amru lo* — the Rabbis respond in kind: *le-vareicha mi sheba ve-amar achshav harag* — according to *your* position, Rabbi Yosi, if someone comes to court and says "he murdered him just now, today," would you still ask *be-eizeh yom be-eizeh sha'ah be-eizeh makom* — which day of the week, at what hour, in what place? The questions are equally unnecessary in such a case; it happened moments ago in an identifiable location. Each side, Rabbi Yosi's and the Rabbis', can identify a scenario where the other's required questions are pointless.

### Pressure Witnesses

*Ela af al gav de-lo tzarich, raminin alei* — the Rabbis' answer is that even when the questions are technically unnecessary, the court imposes them regardless, *ke-di'Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* — in accordance with the principle stated by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. *Lehatricham* — the purpose is to put pressure on the witnesses. *De-amar mesin hayu et ha-edim mi-makom le-makom* — Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's teaching is that part of the formal court proceedings involved moving witnesses from place to place, physically relocating them during the process as a form of deliberate pressure. Formal interrogation, even with questions whose answers are already known, serves the same function: the atmosphere of scrutiny and the demand to answer precisely creates psychological pressure that exposes deception in ways that a more casual inquiry would not.

Rabbi Yosi, however, distinguishes between the two scenarios: *emesh harag shachiach le-rov edyot* — "yesterday he committed murder" is a type of testimony that actually arises with some frequency in ordinary court proceedings; a witness who saw something yesterday and comes today to testify is a common occurrence. *Achshav harag lo shachiach le-rov edyot* — "he committed murder right now, this instant" is not a normal form of testimony. Because the scenario of "yesterday" is common in practice, Rabbi Yosi is willing to concede that it requires the formal procedure even when technically redundant. The extreme edge case of the murder that literally just occurred does not shape the formal rule.

---

# Sanhedrin 41

## Witness Recognition & Ha…

### Makirim Atem Oto

We pick up six lines from the bottom of 40b. The *mishnah* arrives at the next stage of examining the witnesses: *makirim atem oto* — do you recognize the person? Just as in a police lineup, the witnesses must be able to confirm that the individual standing before the court is indeed the one who committed the crime.

A *baraita* then expands on the questions that were posed. *Makirim atem oto* — do you recognize him? Then: *nochri harag Yisrael harag* — if he killed someone, do you know whether the victim was a Jew or a non-Jew? One sees him commit a killing, but only when a Jew kills another Jew does the death penalty apply. Next: *hitretem bo* — did you give him *hatra'ah*, a warning? As we know from the *mishnah*, a warning must be administered before any punishment can be imposed in court.

The *baraita* now introduces several additional requirements that make conviction exceptionally difficult. *Kibel alav hatra'ah* — it is not enough that a warning was issued; the perpetrator must have acknowledged it. He must have said, in effect, "Yes, I know, and I intend to do it anyway." Can the witnesses attest to that? Then: *hitir atzmo lemitah* — did he permit himself, did he open himself up, to execution? As the *gemara* will explain, it is not sufficient merely to say "I know this is forbidden." He must declare that he knows it is forbidden and that he accepts upon himself the death penalty as a consequence. This concept of *hitir atzmo lemitah* addresses, in some sense, the fundamental question of by what right a court may do violence to another person and impose such a punishment. The answer the *mishnah* offers is: he willingly accepted it upon himself.

Then: *hemit b'toch k'dei dibur* — even after all of the above, he must actually commit the crime within *toch k'dei dibur*, within approximately three seconds of accepting the warning upon himself. If he does not, the concern is that perhaps he forgot. That may seem almost absurd — can one truly forget within three seconds? A more satisfying reading may be that if the act is not carried out in immediate temporal proximity to the acceptance, it is no longer performed in the context of the total defiance that *hitir atzmo lemitah* requires, and thus does not grant the court the license to execute.

### Jew or Non-Jew; Avodah Z…

The *baraita* then turns to a case not of murder but of *avodah zarah* — idolatry. Here the witnesses are asked: *et mi avad* — which deity did he worship? Was it Pe'or, was it Markolis? Unlike the distinction between Jew and non-Jew in the murder case — where the identity of the victim determines whether the death penalty applies at all — here the identity of the deity serves a different purpose. What matters is whether the form of worship performed is the form specific to that deity, which is necessary for determining *chayav mitah*.

The witnesses are also asked *uvameh avad* — how did he perform the worship? Was it through *zibuach* (slaughtering an animal), *kitur* (burning incense), *nisuch* (pouring a libation), or *hishtachavayah* (prostration)? These four constitute the generic standard forms of divine service, and performing any one of them renders one liable for *avodah zarah* regardless of whether that particular form is native to the specific deity in question. The inquiry is thus not essential to establishing liability, but forms part of the *chakirot* — the broader effort to interrogate the witnesses, establish all the facts, and potentially expose inconsistencies or contradictions between them.

### Ulla: Source for Hatra'ah

Having introduced the requirement of *hatra'ah*, the *gemara* now asks: *minayin le'hatra'ah min haTorah* — where in the Torah is *hatra'ah* derived? *Ulla* cites the verse: *v'ish asher yikach et achoto bat aviv o vat imo v'ra'ah et ervatah* — if a man takes his sister, the daughter of his father or his mother, and sees her nakedness.
