This is the sin of sexual relations with a sister, which is punishable by *karet*.

The *gemara* immediately asks: *atu b're'iyah talya miltah* — is the prohibition really about seeing? The act that is forbidden is intercourse, not vision. Rather, *ela ad she'yireh re'iyuto shel davar* — the verse teaches that the transgression must be performed, so to speak, in the open: the fact of the transgression must be blatant to the transgressor before punishment follows. In other words, the person must have seen — that is, clearly recognized — that what he was doing was wrong.

The *gemara* then asks: *im eino inyan l'karet* — but this verse is speaking of *karet*, divine punishment. *Karet* is administered by Heaven, and God knows whether one acted willfully or not. The entire framework of *hatra'ah* — establishing *mezid*, confirming a posture of defiance — is relevant only to a court-imposed sanction. So this teaching about *ra'ah*, about the transparency of the act, is not needed for *karet* itself, and must therefore be applied elsewhere.

### Hatra'ah for Lashes & Ca…

The top of 41a concludes this point: *tanya inyan lemalkos* — the verse is applied to lashes. When a court-imposed punishment of *malkos* is on the table, it must be established that the transgressor acted with full awareness. Thus we learn that *hatra'ah* is at minimum required for lashes.

The *gemara* then brings three additional sources extending this principle to capital cases. The school of *Chizkiya* teaches from the verse *vechi yazid ish al re'ehu lehargo be'arma* — when a man acts willfully against his fellow to kill him by treachery — *shehitru bo ve-adayin hu mezid*: that even after being warned, he remained *mezid*, willful. *Rashi* explains that *vechi yazid*, as opposed to *im yazid*, conveys that the dimension of *mezid* is vividly and continuously present in the act itself.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives *hatra'ah* from the incident of the *mekoshish*, the wood gatherer: *hamotzim oto mekoshesh etzim* — those who found him gathering wood. The verse does not say merely that they found someone who had been gathering; it says they found him still in the act of gathering — *adayin hu mekoshesh* — even in the presence of the witnesses. This again conveys an ongoing, defiant posture.

The school of *Rebbi* derives it from the verse *al devar asher ina et eshet re'ehu* — on account of the matter of his having violated his fellow's wife. The phrase *al devar* rather than *al asher* points to an element of speech — *al iskei dibbur* — that must accompany the act. Notably, several of these sources seem to point toward something beyond establishing mere mental state. The *mekoshish* continuing to gather in the witnesses' presence, the explicit *al devar dibbur* — these suggest an element of defiance and public declaration, not only a determination of intent.

The *gemara* then explains why all these different verses are necessary. Had the Torah stated only the case of the sister (*karet* punishable by *malkos*), one might have thought *hatra'ah* is required for the lighter sanction but not for capital punishment, since the gravity of the offense might argue for punishing even without formal warning. Hence we need *vechi yazid* for the case of the sword (*sayif*). But had we only the case of *sayif*, which is considered a lesser form of execution, one might have excluded *skila*, the weightiest — perhaps such a severe punishment requires no *hatra'ah*, or perhaps the greater severity demands it. Hence additional verses are required. And the *gemara* ultimately acknowledges: one might argue that the *sukim* could have stated *skila* alone and all lighter cases could have been derived by *kal vachomer* — but *milsa de'asya bikal vachomer tarch va-kasav lah kra*, even something derivable by *kal vachomer* sometimes receives its own explicit verse.

---

## Hitir Atzmo Lemita

### Rava: Hamet Status

The *gemara* now turns to the further requirement of *hitir atzmo lemitah*. The preceding requirement — *kibel alav* — that he acknowledged and accepted the warning, is treated as self-evident: without confirmed receipt of the warning, the accused can always claim he did not hear it. But where is the requirement of *hitir atzmo lemitah* itself derived?

*Rava* — and some say *Chizkiya* — cites the verse *yumat hamet*, "the dead shall be put to death." The seemingly redundant word *hamet* — the dead — teaches that the defendant must already have made himself into *hamet*, the walking dead, before the court can execute him. He must have explicitly accepted that his action renders him deserving of death. This formulation reinforces the sense that the court is not imposing something alien upon him; rather, it is actualizing a status he himself accepted.

### Rav Chanan: Edim Zomemim

*Rav Chanan* teaches: *edei na'ara hame'urasa shehuzmu ein neheragin* — witnesses who testified that a *na'ara hame'urasa* (a young betrothed woman) had committed adultery and were subsequently found to be *edim zomemim* — conspiring false witnesses — are not executed, even though adultery is a capital offense and the principle of *ka'asher zamam* would normally dictate that they receive the punishment they sought to impose.

The reason: *mitoch she'yecholim lomar le'osra al ba'alah banu* — since they could claim "our only purpose was to render her forbidden to her husband," and not to have her executed. The principle of *edim zomemim* is grounded in *asher zamam la'asot le're'eihu* — what they actually intended to accomplish. The false witnesses may argue, in effect, that getting her killed was not their goal; forbidding her to her husband was. This remains striking, because by the time a case reaches the point of capital testimony, it will have been made abundantly clear that the consequence of their testimony is her execution — yet they can still make this claim and thereby escape the penalty of *edim zomemim*.

The *gemara* immediately raises an objection. For *Rav Chanan*'s ruling to be meaningful, she must have been on the verge of execution based on their testimony. But how could she have been executed on their testimony if they testified that they gave her *hatra'ah*? If they testified to *hatra'ah*, then their intent to have her killed is obvious — how can they claim they only came to forbid her to her husband? The *gemara* answers: *dilo asru bah* — in fact, they did not claim to have warned her. But then the *gemara* objects further: if they did not testify to *hatra'ah*, how could she ever be executed? This makes *Rav Chanan*'s ruling apparently trivial.

The *gemara* resolves this: *be'isha chavera* — we are speaking of a woman who is a *chavera*, someone learned and scrupulous in *taharot* and *trumos*, and the ruling follows the opinion of *Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda*. Thus the *gemara* introduces the pivotal *baraita*.

### R. Yosi b. R. Yehuda: Ch…

*Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda omer: chaver ein tzarich hatra'ah* — a *chaver*, a person who is learned in *halacha*, does not require *hatra'ah* before being put to death. Why? *Lefi she'lo nitna hatra'ah ela lehavchin bein shogeg lemeizid* — the only purpose of *hatra'ah* is to distinguish between *shogeg* (unintentional transgression) and *mezid* (intentional). A person who is knowledgeable in *halacha* is self-evidently aware of what they are doing and is self-evidently *mezid*; no formal warning is necessary to establish that.

This is a striking position, and it carries profound implications. Until this point in the sugya, one might have assumed that *hatra'ah* is a formal procedural requirement — a mandatory step in the capital process independent of its evidentiary function. *Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda* is saying not only that it is not a formal requirement, but that its entire and exclusive purpose is to arrive at the defendant's state of mind. *Tosafos* notes that according to this view, the additional requirement of *hitir atzmo lemitah* — which plainly concerns something beyond the *mezid* component — would not apply.

This also illuminates the range of positions that have emerged in this sugya. Some of the Scriptural sources cited earlier — the *mekoshish* still gathering in the witnesses' presence, the requirement of *al devar dibbur* — suggested that *hatra'ah* serves functions beyond simply diagnosing intent: creating a context of open defiance, or providing the quasi-consensual basis (*hitir atzmo lemitah*) that licenses the court to act. *Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda* rejects all of that, reducing *hatra'ah* to a single epistemic function.

The *gemara* returns to *Rav Chanan*'s ruling. The *gemara* notes: if witnesses testify that an *isha chavera* committed adultery without any *hatra'ah* — and since, following *Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda*, she could be executed without it — and they are then found to be *edim zomemim*, can they be executed? They would claim *le'osra al ba'alah banu*. And once we establish that they cannot be executed as *zomemim*, the *gemara* presses further: if they cannot be made into *edim zomemim*, then their testimony against her is *eidus she'ein ata yachol lehazimah* — testimony that cannot be subjected to *hazama* — and *kol eidus she'ein ata yachol lehazimah lo shemah eidus*: such testimony is not testimony at all and cannot be used to convict her either. The *gemara* confirms: that was indeed *Rav Chanan*'s intent. First establish that the witnesses cannot themselves be executed (because of the *le'osra* claim), and from that it follows that their testimony cannot convict her either.

### Chaveira: Twice or Forbi…

The *gemara* then challenges: if that is so, according to *Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda*, how can an *isha chavera* who commits adultery ever be put to death? The *gemara* answers: *keshe-zinta v'chazra v'zinta* — in a case where witnesses testify that she committed adultery twice. After the first act, she is already forbidden to her husband; thus the second testimony cannot be aimed at making her forbidden again. Its only operative effect must be to have her executed. The witnesses cannot claim *le'osra al ba'alah banu* regarding the second act.

The *gemara* objects: perhaps the witnesses' purpose with the second testimony was *le'osra al bo'al hasheni* — to render her forbidden to her second lover, since a woman who commits adultery is forbidden both to her husband and to the man with whom she sinned. The *gemara* therefore specifies: *keshe-zinta miboa'l rishon* — the second act was with the same man as the first. At that point she is already forbidden to him from the first act; the second testimony serves no purpose other than execution. And the *gemara* adds: if the second act was with a relative — a prohibited relation — she is already forbidden to him by Torah law regardless, so again the only purpose of the testimony could be her execution.

The *gemara* closes this passage by asking why *Rav Chanan* used the specific case of the *na'ara hame'urasa* — a young betrothed woman who has not yet begun living with her husband. The *gemara* answers that this is precisely the *chiddush*: even here, where she has not yet been living with her husband and one might have thought that forbidding her to him is no longer a live concern given that the relationship is not yet consummated, the witnesses can still invoke the *le'osra* claim. Even that far-removed purpose is sufficient to shield them from the consequences of *edim zomemim*.

---

## Bedikot vs. Chakirot

### Rav Chisda: Central vs.…

*Rav Chisda* teaches the following principle: *echad omer be-sayif harago ve-echad omer be-aririn harago* — if one witness says he was killed with a sword and the other says with an awl or similar instrument, this is not *nachon* — their testimony is not aligned, and it is disqualified. That accords with the *mishnah*: if the *bedikot* contradict one another, the testimony is invalid. The *chiddush* of *Rav Chisda* comes in the next ruling: *echad omer kelim shechorim ve-echad omer kelim levanim harei zeh nachon* — if one witness says the perpetrator was wearing black clothes and the other says white clothes, this *is* considered *nachon*. Contradictions in *bedikot* that are peripheral to the actual act — what color clothing the defendant was wearing — do not disqualify the testimony. What matters is that the witnesses are aligned on the central defining facts of the transgression itself.

This is an interesting observation in its own right. We know from real-world experience that eyewitness testimony is notoriously unreliable on peripheral details; the *halacha* here seems to reflect a similar intuition — that noise in peripheral observation does not undermine the core evidentiary weight of testimony. Nevertheless, the witnesses must agree on the substance of the act itself.

The *gemara* challenges this from a *baraita*: *echad omer be-sayif harago ve-echad omer be-aririn harago echad omer kelim shechorim ve-echad omer kelim levanim ein zeh nachon* — a *baraita* that explicitly states that even disagreement on the color of clothing disqualifies testimony. *Rav Chisda* resolves this: *be-sudar she-chanku bo* — the *baraita* is not speaking of clothing worn by the defendant; it is speaking of the handkerchief or cloth used as the murder weapon in a strangulation. In that case the color of the cloth is directly part of the act of killing, comparable in nature to whether it was a sword or an awl. The *gemara* concedes that this interpretation is difficult — it does not sit easily with the plain reading of the *baraita* — but proceeds with it.

A further *baraita* states: *echad omer sandalo shechorim ve-echad omer sandalo levanim ein zeh nachon* — disagreement about the color of the defendant's shoes also disqualifies. The *gemara* responds: *she-va'at bo be-sandalo ve-harago* — the shoe was the murder weapon; he kicked the victim with his shoe and killed him. Again, this is plainly not the *pshat* of the *baraita*, but the *gemara* continues to strain toward consistency with *Rav Chisda*'s principle.

### Ben Zakkai: Fig Twigs

A further challenge emerges from the *mishnah* itself, which records that Ben Zakkai once examined witnesses on the question of *uktzei te'einim* — the twigs or stems of fig trees. This seems entirely peripheral — how can such a detail be a legitimate basis for invalidating testimony? This sits uncomfortably with *Rav Chisda*'s distinction between central and peripheral *bedikot*.

*Rami bar Chama* proposes: perhaps the case was not one of murder at all, but of someone who plucked a fig on *Shabbat* — *de-aktaf te'ena be-Shabbat* — in which case the fig itself is part of the transgression and the examination of its characteristics is directly relevant to the act.

The *gemara* objects: the *baraita* explicitly states *tachat te'ena harago* — he killed him under a fig tree — which places the case squarely in the domain of murder. *Rami bar Chama* then offers an alternative: *she-shafto be-yichur shel te'ena* — he speared the victim with the twig of the fig. This, too, is acknowledged to be a highly strained reading — a fig twig seems hardly sufficient to kill anyone, and the *gemara* is, as the lecturer notes, doing somersaults to maintain *Rav Chisda*'s position against the plain testimony of these sources.

A further question is then posed: if the fig was the murder weapon, why does the *mishnah* also ask whether the figs were black or white (*te'einim shechorot, te'einim levanot*)? There is no conceivable way a fig itself could kill someone. This truly cannot be explained by the murder-weapon theory.

The *gemara* concludes: *mibei Ben Zakkai lo tosif inish* — one should not derive rules from Ben Zakkai. *Shani Ben Zakkai de-bedikot ke-chakirot mashvei lehu* — Ben Zakkai treated *bedikot* as though they carried the same weight as *chakirot*. That is, he held that any contradiction in a *bedikah* — even the most peripheral — is sufficient grounds to invalidate the testimony, just as in the *chakirot*. This represents a minority position, and *Rav Chisda*'s ruling reflects the majority view: only contradictions in *bedikot* that are central to the act of the transgression disqualify the testimony; peripheral contradictions do not.

### Ben Zakkai Identification

The *gemara* asks: *man Ben Zakkai* — who exactly is this Ben Zakkai? If it is the famous Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, *mi hava be-Sanhedri* — how could he have served on the *Sanhedrin* in a capital case?

A *baraita* records that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai lived 120 years, divided into three periods of forty years each: forty years in business, forty years learning, and forty years teaching. Only in his final forty years did he attain the stature of a leading *rav* capable of sitting on a *beis din* in a capital case. But another *baraita* teaches: *arba'im shana kodem churban ha-bayit galta Sanhedrin ve-yashva la be-chanut* — forty years before the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*, the *Sanhedrin* relocated from the *Lishkat HaGazit* to one of the chambers adjoining the *Beis HaMikdash*, and ceased adjudicating capital cases. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi clarifies: the relocation signified that they no longer judged *dinei nefashot* — capital crimes — since such adjudication requires the *Beis Din HaGadol* to be seated in the *Lishkat HaGazit*.

Since Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai survived the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*, and since the *Sanhedrin* stopped hearing capital cases forty years before that destruction, it follows that his entire final forty-year period of teaching and public leadership fell after the *Sanhedrin* had ceased capital jurisdiction. He could therefore never have participated in such a case. A *mishnah* further confirms that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai instituted *takanos* after the *churban*, placing him clearly in the post-destruction era.

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ella Ben Zakkai d'alma* — this must have been some other Ben Zakkai, perhaps a brother or relative, not the famous Rabban. And indeed, the text of the *mishnah* refers to him simply as "Ben Zakkai" without the title *Rabban* — itself evidence that it cannot be Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. *Hachi nami mistavra* — this also makes logical sense: had it been Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, he would surely have been referred to with his full title.

But the *gemara* then adduces a *baraita* that explicitly attributes this examination of the fig twigs to *Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* — by name and title. This creates a direct contradiction. How can the *mishnah* attribute it to a nameless "Ben Zakkai" while the *baraita* attributes the same act to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai?

The *gemara* resolves both problems with a single elegant answer: *talmid hayoshev lifnei rabbo hava* — at the time of this incident, Yochanan ben Zakkai was still a student sitting before his teacher. This places the event during his middle forty years of study, before he had received *semikhah* and the title *Rabban*, and at a time when the *Beis Din* was still seated in the *Lishkat HaGazit* and still hearing capital cases. He had not yet become *Rabban*; he was present in the *beis din* as a student. He suggested examining the witnesses on the fig-twig details, the court found it compelling, and *ukeva'uha bishmeih* — the practice was formally attributed to him.

As for the discrepancy in names: *ki hava lomed Ben Zakkai hava kari leh* — during his years of study he was called simply "Ben Zakkai," as befitting a student. *Ki hava melammed Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai hava kari leh* — when he was teaching and had received *semikhah*, he bore the title Rabban. The *mishnah*, in calling him "Ben Zakkai," uses the name current at the time of the incident itself. The *baraita*, in calling him "Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai," uses the name by which he was universally known at the time the *baraita* was composed. Both are accurate; they simply operate from different temporal reference points.

### Chakirot & Hazama vs. Be…

The *mishnah* asks: *mah bein chakirot l'bedikot* — what is the difference between *chakirot* (examination on time and place) and *bedikot* (examination on circumstantial details)? By *chakirot*, if even one witness says *eini yodea* — I do not know — the testimony is invalidated. By *bedikot*, even if both witnesses say *eini yodea*, the testimony stands.

The *gemara* explores whether there is anything genuinely novel in the further formulation *afilu shnayim omrim ein anu yodeim edutan kayemes* — even if both say they do not know, the testimony is still valid. *Pishita* — surely that is obvious: if one person's *eini yodea* on a *bedikah* does not invalidate, then two saying so is equally inconsequential. There are only two witnesses; if each individually saying *eini yodea* is not a problem, there is no one left to make it one.

*Rav Sheshet* proposes reading the clause as pertaining to the *chakirot* rather than the *bedikot*, and furthermore as a case involving a third witness. When three witnesses testify together as a single *kat* (group) and two affirm that they do know the time and place while one says *eini yodea*, the entire testimony is invalidated — *edutan beteila* — because all three form a single testimonial unit and one member's ignorance compromises the whole. *Keman* — like whom? Like *Rebbi Akiva*, who teaches by analogy to *shnayim* from *shlosha*: just as with two witnesses, a *pasul* invalidates the entire group, here *eini yodea* functions as a disqualification of that witness, and that disqualification cascades to the others.

*Rava* objects: the *mishnah* says *edutan kayemes* — the testimony stands — yet *Rav Sheshet* has converted it into a ruling that it does not. That is too violent a departure from the plain text. *Rava* therefore offers his own reading. He accepts many of *Rav Sheshet*'s departures from *pshat* — that we are speaking of *chakirot*, that two witnesses are saying *yadanu* (we do know) rather than *eini yodea*, and that the third says *eini yodea* — but he maintains the *mishnah*'s conclusion: *afilu b'chakirot shnayim omrim yadanu v'echad omer eini yodea edutan kayemes* — even in the *chakirot*, even when one of the three says *eini yodea*, the testimony of the other two stands. *Keman d'lo k'Rebbi Akiva* — not like *Rebbi Akiva*, for whom the *eini yodea* would collapse the entire group's testimony. Both readings, as noted, depart substantially from the plain sense of the *mishnah*.

### Rav Kahana & Rav Safra

*Rav Kahana* and *Rav Safra* were studying *Sanhedrin* in the *yeshiva* of *Rabba*. *Rami bar Chama* encountered them in the street and asked: I hear you are learning *Sanhedrin* — what *chiddush* did *Rabba* teach you? Rather than immediately answering, they replied: tell us first what you generally say about the topic, and what difficulty it raises for you — then we will tell you if we have heard something relevant.

*Rami bar Chama* posed the question from our very *mishnah*: *mah bein chakirot l'bedikot* — both are derived from biblical verses, *idi v'idi d'oraisa*; why should *eini yodea* invalidate testimony in *chakirot* but not in *bedikot*?

*Rav Kahana* and *Rav Safra* answered: the distinction is rooted in *hazama*. By *chakirot* — questions of time and place — the legal mechanism of turning witnesses into *edim zomemim* depends on other witnesses coming and saying "you were not there at that time and place." If one of the witnesses says *eini yodea* regarding the time or place, it becomes impossible to subject them to *hazama*, and testimony that cannot be subjected to *hazama* is not valid testimony at all — *eidus she'ei ata yachol lehazimah lo shemah eidus*. By contrast, the *bedikot* bear on the question of *nachon* — the internal consistency and alignment of testimony. Saying *eini yodea* regarding a peripheral circumstantial detail does not create any inconsistency; the witnesses can still be subjected to *hazama* on the central facts of time and place. Their testimony therefore remains valid.

*Rami bar Chama* responded: *ei hachi amritu bah tuva* — oh, if that is what you are saying, you have said something very significant. *Rav Kahana* and *Rav Safra* replied with characteristic wit: *minichuta d'mar amrinan bah tuva* — it was precisely because you were so generous and kind in your manner of asking — you invited us to share what we had learned, rather than positioning yourself to find fault with it — that we responded in kind and shared our *torah* with you. *Minizihuta d'mar lo amrinan bah v'lo chada* — had you been combative, angling to challenge us or expose a weakness in what *Rabba* had taught, we would not have said a word. The exchange captures something of the human texture of the *beis midrash*: the willingness to share *torah* openly is connected, in this telling, to the spirit in which it is sought.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 42

## Calendar Discrepancy

### Investigation Methods

The fifth chapter of Masechet Sanhedrin, *hayu bodkim*, concerns the examination of witnesses. The tradition presents three distinct frameworks for this examination. *Chakirot* are the formal investigations into the circumstances of the alleged crime: in which week, in which year, on which day. *Drishot* are inquiries into the defendant himself — who is he, what does he do? *Bdikot* are the more general questions put to witnesses. The precise boundary between these three categories was itself a matter of debate among the Rabbis, and the uncertainty about where one ends and the next begins is itself instructive.

### Mishnah Discrepancy Rule

The *mishnah* underlying our *gemara* (from the previous *amud*) addresses discrepancies in testimony concerning the day of the month. If one witness says the event took place on the second of the month and another says it was the third, *edutan kayemet* — their testimony stands. The *mishnah* explains: *shezeh yode'a be'iburo shel chodesh vezeh eino yode'a be'iburo shel chodesh* — one witness knows precisely when the new moon was declared, and the other does not, which accounts for the one-day discrepancy. However, if one witness says the third of the month and the other says the fifth, *edutan beteilah* — their testimony is void.

### Rabbi Yochanan

The *gemara* asks: *ad kama?* — how far into the month does this leniency apply? Rabbi Acha bar Chanina said in the name of Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ad rubo shel chodesh* — up to the majority of the month, roughly the middle. Beyond that point, a person ought to know which day it is, and a discrepancy of even a day or two can no longer be excused by ignorance of the new moon's declaration.

### Rava's Analysis

Rava observes that this principle is already implicit in the *mishnah* itself: *af anan nami tanina* — we also teach this. He presses the point: why should a discrepancy of two days — saying the third versus the fifth — invalidate testimony? Could we not say that one witness knows about two consecutive intercalations and the other knows only one? The *gemara* responds: *le'olam eima lach beruba nami lo yadat* — it is entirely possible for a person not to know which day of the month it is throughout most of the month. The crucial factor is the *shipura*, the *shofar* blast announcing the new moon. If there was only one day of *Rosh Chodesh* with one *shofar* blast, it is reasonable that someone missed it. But two blasts — *betrei shipura lo amar detei* — it is no longer plausible that a witness failed to register two separate announcements.

Tosafot addresses a difficulty with this entire framework. The purpose of witness examination is to protect the defendant, yet we are being asked to invalidate testimony over calendar discrepancies that might be perfectly innocent. Tosafot resolves the matter by focusing on what the two witnesses actually agree upon: if both are certain the event occurred on, say, a Monday, and they simply disagree about whether that Monday was the 27th or the 28th of the month, the testimony is accepted — they are speaking of the same day of the week, however uncertain about its numerical date. But if the discrepancy is such that there is genuine uncertainty about which day of the week the event occurred, the testimony is disqualified as insufficiently reliable.

---

## Birkat Levana

### Days for Blessing

Transitioning naturally from the discussion of the month and the calendar, the *gemara* addresses *birkat levana* — the blessing recited upon the renewal of the moon. The same chain of tradition — Rabbi Acha bar Chanina in the name of Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — addresses how many days after *Rosh Chodesh* one may still recite this blessing: *ad she-titmale pegimata* — until the defect of the moon is filled. The moon at the beginning of the month is incomplete — *pagum* — and the question is when the *miluy*, the filling of that defect, is considered complete.

### Moon's Shape

Rav Yaakov bar Iddi said in the name of Rav Yehuda: *ad shiva* — until the seventh day of the month. The sages of Neharde'a say: until the sixteenth, the middle of the month. Both opinions are understood to be consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's formulation, differing only in their definition of when the moon is considered "filled." One opinion holds that the moon must achieve the shape of a *yeter* — the string of a bow, a slight arc — while the other requires the shape of a *nafya* — a full round sieve, meaning the complete full moon.

### HaTov VeHaMeitiv

Rav Acha of Difti posed a question to Ravina: since we recite *mechadesh chodashim* only for perhaps seven days — the period of the moon's filling — should we not also recite *HaTov VeHaMeitiv*, the blessing reserved for especially beneficial news, in response to the moon's growth? And conversely, when the moon wanes, should we not say *Dayan HaEmet*, the blessing recited upon receiving bad news?

The *gemara* responds that both blessings could in principle be said — *levarechin'hu le-travaihu*. But then it adds the decisive qualification: *keivan de-hainu orchei lo mevar'chinan* — since this is simply the way of the world, we do not recite them. Rashi explains the distinction precisely: the blessing for the moon is an act of acknowledging *Hashem*'s creation — a recognition that the world operates according to its established order. It is categorically different from *HaTov VeHaMeitiv*, which is recited when something personally beneficial has occurred to a person. When we recite *birkat levana*, we are not recipients of a personal gift; we are observers of the ongoing wonder of creation. The moon's renewal is not something done *for* us — it is something we witness and attest to. *HaTov VeHaMeitiv*, by contrast — such as when a second bottle of wine is brought to one's table — is a response to a personal act of kindness. The two categories do not mix.

### Shechinah

Rabbi Acha bar Chanina said in the name of Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol hamevarech al hachodesh bizmano ke'ilu mekabel pnei Shechinah* — whoever blesses the new moon in its proper time, it is as though he receives the face of the *Shechinah*. This is a striking statement. Why should *birkat levana* carry such spiritual weight? Several possibilities suggest themselves. *Kiddush hachodesh* — the sanctification of the new month — was the very first *mitzvah* given to the Jewish people as a nation. There is something profound about a *mitzvah* that requires presence: not merely physical compliance, but awareness of time, awareness of the moment. So many hours pass in which we are not truly present; here we are called to *mamash* be present.

The *gemara* supplies a textual proof by *gezeirah shavah*. In the passage concerning the new month, the Torah uses the word *hazeh* — "this." In another context, we encounter *zeh Eli ve'anvehu* — "this is my God and I will glorify Him" — a verse from *Shirat HaYam*. What was the greatness of *Shirat HaYam*? The tradition teaches that *ra'ata shifcha mah shelo ra'ah Yechezkel ben Buzi* — even the maidservant at the Sea witnessed what the prophet Ezekiel, in all his sublime visions, did not see. At the Sea, the *Shechinah* was accessible to all. By the same *gezeirah shavah*, when one greets the new moon with its blessing at the right moment, one taps into something of that same direct encounter with the divine presence.

### Tana d'vei R. Yishmael

A teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael makes this point with characteristic force: *ilmalei zachu Yisrael ela lehakebil pnei avihem shebashamayim kol chodesh vechodesh dayam* — if Israel had merited nothing other than to welcome their heavenly Father each and every month, that alone would be sufficient. The language is striking — *lehakebil pnei* — to receive the face, as one would welcome a distinguished guest. If the entirety of Jewish achievement had been only this monthly encounter, it would have been enough to justify our creation.

### Standing Requirement

Abaye derives a practical ruling from this: *hilkach nimrinhu me'umad* — therefore, we recite *birkat levana* standing, not sitting, in recognition of the *Shechinah*-like quality of the moment. Merimar and Mar Zutra, who were elderly, would lean upon support — some say upon one another, some say upon their servants — specifically in order to fulfill this requirement of standing. The custom thus reflects the halakhic ruling directly.

Regarding the question of whether women are obligated in *kiddush levana*: the *gemara* raises it — *hani neshei didan nami mevarchi*, implying that women too should recite the blessing — but then sets the discussion aside without resolution, much as happens in a live *shiur* when a question opens onto a thicket of connected issues. The moon's cycle, the timing of women's marriages (traditionally on Wednesday, the fourth day of the week, the day the *me'orot* were created and the moon was diminished), and the question of *mitzvat asei shehazman grama* (time-bound positive commandments from which women are generally exempt) are all interlocked. The custom has become for women not to recite *kiddush levana*, but the full analysis of the sources behind that custom goes beyond what the *gemara* resolves at this point.

### Blessing Text

Rav Acha said to Rav Ashi: in the west — that is, in Eretz Yisrael — they conclude the blessing with *baruch mechadesh chodashim*, which is in fact the *chatima*, the signature formula, of our own *birkat levana*. The full text of the blessing as it appears here is deeply moving:

> *Asher bema'amaro bara shechakim, uveruach piv kol tzeva'am, chok uzman natan lahem shelo yeshanu et tafkidam, sasim vesamechim la'asot retzon konam, po'alei emet shepe'ulatam emet. Velalevana amar shetitchadesh ateret tiferet le'amusei vaten, shehen atidim lehitkhadesh kemotah, ulefa'er leyotzram al shem kevod malchuto. Baruch Atah Hashem mechadesh chodashim.*

In His utterance He created the heavens; by the breath of His mouth, all their hosts. He gave them law and time so that they would not deviate from their appointed task. They are joyous and glad to do the will of their Creator — truthful workers whose deeds are truth. And to the moon He said: be renewed as a crown of glory for those laden from the womb, for they are destined to be renewed like her, and to glorify their Creator for the glory of His kingship. Blessed are You, *Hashem*, who renews the months.

The connection between the moon's renewal and the renewal of the Jewish people — *shehen atidim lehitkhadesh kemotah* — gives the blessing its emotional resonance. We are not merely observers of an astronomical phenomenon; we see in the waxing moon a reflection of our own destiny.

---

## Torah's Wars

### Mishnah Bundles

The *gemara* asks: *bemi atah motzei milchamtah shel Torah?* — in whom do you find someone capable of fighting the Torah's battles? The answer: *bemi sheyesh beyado chavilot shel Mishnah* — in the one who possesses bundles of *Mishnah*. Why *Mishnah* specifically, rather than *Torah* itself? Because the *Torah* contains apparent contradictions and repetitions, and it is the *Mishnah* that provides the tools to reconcile those tensions and harmonize what might otherwise appear inconsistent. One cannot fight for the *Torah* without the *Mishnah* as the instrument of reconciliation.

The *gemara* applies this to Rav Yosef himself — *k'Rav Yosef anafshei* — who said this of himself, citing the verse *verav tevuot be'choach shor*: *tevuah*, grain, is a reference to *Torah*, and *shor*, the ox, is the symbol of the tribe of Yosef. Rav Yosef thus understood himself as one who brought forth great *Torah* like the strength of an ox.

---

## Hourly Discrepancy

### Sunrise Boundary

The *mishnah* now addresses discrepancies not in the day of the month but in the hour of the day. If one witness says the event occurred at the second hour and another says the third, the testimony is generally accepted. Minor variations in time estimation do not disqualify witnesses. The critical exception, however, is when the discrepancy straddles *neitz hachamah* — sunrise. If one witness says the event occurred before sunrise and another says after sunrise, *edutan beteilah* — their testimony is void. The *gemara* extends this: even if one says it occurred right before sunrise and another says during sunrise itself, the testimony is still disqualified.

### Location Factor

Rav Shimi bar Ashi offers a penetrating observation. One might think the issue is simply the hour discrepancy between "before" and "after" sunrise. But the underlying problem is geographic. To have seen the sun rise while another person, present at the same event, had not yet seen it, the two witnesses must have been standing in different locations — perhaps one on higher ground, or one in a place with an unobstructed eastern horizon and the other not. That difference in location is itself what invalidates the testimony. The witnesses must have been in the same place observing the same event; if their reports of sunrise diverge, their physical positions diverge, and the testimony collapses.

---

## Court Procedure

### That Day Rule

The *mishnah* states that testimony is heard *oto hayom* — on that day, the day the defendant is present in court. The *gemara* immediately challenges this formulation: *oto hayom v'tu lo?* — only on that day and nothing more? The *mishnah* elsewhere teaches: if someone — whether a student or anyone present — says *yesh li lelamed zechut*, "I have something to say in his merit," he is brought up and seated among the judges, and *lo hayah yored misham kol hayom kulo* — he does not leave from there the entire day. Furthermore, a *beraita* teaches: *im yesh mamash bidvarav lo hayah yored misham le'olam* — if his words have genuine substance, he does not leave from there ever, meaning the court continues as long as he has something meaningful to contribute.

These are not the prosecution witnesses but character witnesses — not witnesses to the event itself, but those who wish to speak on behalf of the defendant's merit. The *talmidim* who are permitted to speak in favor of the defendant (*lelamed zechut*) may not speak to condemn him (*lelamed alav chovah*).

### Abaye Reconciles

Abaye reconciles the apparent tension between the sources. The key is the phrase *mamash bidvarav* — whether there is genuine substance to what the character witness is saying. If a person rises to speak and his remarks are substantively relevant to the defendant's case, he remains as long as necessary. If his remarks amount to nothing material — if, for instance, he can say only that the defendant bakes cookies — we would not keep him there, but we also do not simply dismiss him: *kedei shelo tehei aliyaso yeridah lo* — so that his having been called up should not become a humiliation for him. Abaye's reconciliation is thus that *oto hayom* describes the outer limit of the day, while the substantive standard of *mamash bidvarav* governs how long a character witness remains.

### Wine Prohibition

The *mishnah* notes that neither the witnesses nor the character witnesses may drink wine throughout the day of proceedings. The *gemara* asks: why is wine specifically mentioned? Rabbi Acha bar Chanina cites a verse from Mishlei: *vela-roznim ei shachar* — do not give strong drink to rulers. The word *roznim* carries the Hebrew root for *raz*, secret. The principle invoked is the well-known *nichnas yayin yatza sod* — when wine enters, secrets exit. Those who are dealing with matters of such gravity — the secrets of life and justice — must not compromise their discretion with drink.

---

## Hung Courts

### Dismiss or Add

When the court finds no merit in the defense and the vote stands without the required majority for conviction, what is the procedure? The *mishnah* discusses a split of 35 to 36 in a court of 71 — a genuinely hung court. And separately, what if the court of 23 stands at 12 to 11? There is not yet sufficient majority, but one could either add judges (the court may expand from 23 up to 71) or simply dismiss the defendant. Rav Pappa raises the question to Abaye: should we not simply dismiss him immediately?

### Rav Pappa/Yosef

The *gemara* presents two versions of the answer. In one version, Rav Pappa conveys in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *potrim oto* — dismiss him. The reason: *kedei shelo yetzu mibeis din me'urvavin* — so that the *beis din* should not emerge in a state of confusion without a clear decision. If no majority can be reached, the defendant goes free.

In the alternative version, Rav Pappa asks: but the *mishnah* speaks of adding judges — why add? Rav Yosef responds: *tei kavatach* — both approaches are valid. As a *beraita* establishes from Rabbi Yosi: just as the *beis din* of 71 cannot be expanded further when it reaches a hung vote of 35-36 — the defendant is dismissed — so too the *beis din* of 23 need not necessarily expand. If extra judges happen to be available, they may be added; if not, or if the deliberation is already sufficiently extended, the defendant may be dismissed.

---

## Aged Judgment

### Difficult Judgment

The *gemara* discusses the phrase *nizdaken hadin* — the judgment has "aged." A *beraita* states that in *dinei mamonot*, civil cases, one may say the judgment has become aged or difficult, but in *dinei nefashot*, capital cases, one may not say this. The *gemara* immediately objects: *ipcha mibei lei* — should it not be the opposite? A capital case is far weightier than a civil case; should the threshold not be higher, not lower? The *gemara* considers that *nizdaken* might mean *chacham dina* — the judgment has become wise, ripened through deliberation — rather than simply "grown difficult."

### Chief Judge's Role

The *mishnah* specifies that it is the *gadol she-ba-dayanim*, the senior judge of the *beis din*, who pronounces this formula. A challenge is raised: if the formula means *chacham dina* — the judgment is wise — then it is fitting for the *gadol* to declare it, as a statement of confidence in the deliberation. But if the formula means *kash dina* — the judgment has been difficult — is it appropriate for the *gadol* to say so? Would that not be embarrassing?

The *gemara* turns the question around. *Eino domeh mitbayesh me-atzmo le-mitbayesh me-acherim* — it is not the same to be embarrassed by oneself as to be embarrassed by others. If the *gadol* himself says the judgment was difficult, he has chosen his own embarrassment, which is more manageable than having others expose it. Conversely, if *nizdaken* means *chacham dina*, the *gadol* might appear to be praising himself — and we have the principle *yehalelcha zar ve-lo picha*, a stranger should praise you, not your own mouth.

### Self-Praise

The verse *yehalelcha zar ve-lo picha* — let a stranger praise you, not your own mouth — would seem to prohibit the *gadol* from declaring the judgment wise. A playful modern reading of the verse changes the vowel on the *vav*, yielding *ve-ilo picha* — "and if there is no stranger, then your mouth" — but this is of course a *derashah* for rhetorical effect, not a ruling.

The *gemara* resolves the tension with the principle *shani milta de-bei dina* — the matter of the *beis din* is categorically different. The *gadol* is not speaking about himself; he is serving as a conduit — *de-gadol ramya*, the responsibility rests upon him — and the pronouncement of the judgment flows through him regardless of how it reflects on his personal standing. This is established from the *mishnah* itself: *gamru et hadavar hayu machnisim otam* — when the deliberation concluded, they brought in the parties, and *gadol she-ba-dayanim omer*, the senior judge pronounces: *ish ploni ata zakai*, so-and-so you are acquitted; *ish ploni ata chayav*, so-and-so you are liable. The *gadol* must make this pronouncement whether it redounds to his credit or his embarrassment, because the role transcends the individual.

---

## Trial Conclusion

### Hadran

*Hadran alach hayu bodkim* — we complete the fifth chapter of Masechet Sanhedrin, the chapter of witness examination. We now proceed to the sixth chapter, *perek shishi*, which opens with the words *nigmar hadin* — the judgment has been concluded — and takes up the question of what happens after conviction: where and how is the condemned person executed?

---

## Stoning Location

### Stoning House

The *mishnah* at the top of 42b opens the sixth chapter: *nigmar hadin* — after the verdict has been rendered, the condemned man is taken out. *Beit hasekila haya chutz l'beit hadin* — the stoning house was outside the *beis din*. The source text is from Leviticus, the end of *Parshat Emor*, in the incident of the *mekalel*, the one who blasphemed: *hotze et hamekalel el michutz lamachaneh* — take the curser outside the camp. *V'samchu kol hashomim et yadeihem v'ragmu oto kol ha'edah* — all who heard lay their hands upon him, and the entire congregation stones him.

### Signal System

The procedure described in the *mishnah* is elaborate. Once the condemned man is being led away, one person remains stationed at the entrance of the *beis din* with a *sudarin* — a cloth or scarf — in his hand. Rashi notes some ambiguity about the precise distance: *chutz l'beit hadin rachok m'beit hadin kzat* — outside the *beis din*, somewhat distant. A horse is stationed at a sufficient distance from this person so that the man at the entrance can be seen by the rider. If at any moment someone comes forward with new testimony in the defendant's favor, the man at the entrance waves the cloth, and *hasus ratz u'ma'amidan* — the horse races and the procession halts.

### Last Chance

Even the condemned man himself may speak: *v'afilu hu omer yesh li lilamed al atzmi zechut* — even if he himself says he has something to say in his own favor. *Machzirin oto afilu arba v'chamesh pe'amim* — they bring him back as many as four or five times, *u'vilvad she'yesh mamash bidvarav* — provided there is genuine substance to what he says. The court is not obligated to entertain every last-minute claim, but the principle is clear: we return him as many times as necessary to hear anything that might save his life.

### Karoz

The condemned man does not walk to the execution site in silence. A *karoz* — a herald, an announcer — walks before him and proclaims publicly: this man, son of this man, is being executed for this offense, committed at this hour, in this place; anyone who has testimony in his behalf should come forward. The public nature of the announcement, combined with the signal system at the *beis din* entrance and the capacity to return the condemned man multiple times, reflects the halakhic system's deep reluctance to bring a person to execution. The community is enlisted as a last court of appeal.

### Outside Camp

The *gemara* now confronts a contradiction. The *mishnah* says *beit hasekila haya chutz l'beit hadin* — outside the *beis din*. A *beraita* says *beit hasekila haya chutz l'shalosh machanot* — outside three camps. Which is it? And what do these "three camps" correspond to?

In the context of the desert, the layout was: the *Mishkan* at the center, corresponding to the *Beit Hamikdash* — this is the innermost camp. Surrounding it was *Machaneh Leviyah*, the camp of the Levites. Outside that was *Machaneh Yisrael*, the camp of Israel generally. The question is whether the verse's phrase *michutz lamachaneh* — outside the camp — means merely outside the innermost precinct, or outside all three concentric camps. If the *beis din* itself is situated somewhere outside these camps, does the condemned man still need to be taken further?

### Appearance

The *gemara* offers two reasons for requiring the execution site to be distant from the *beis din* itself. The first: *ki heichi dela mitchazi beis din rotzchin* — so that the *beis din* should not appear to be a house of murderers. Rashi states it plainly: *ki heichi dela litchazi beis din rotzchin, de-genai hadavar* — it is a disgrace for the *beis din* to appear as an execution ground. The *mishnah* in Makkot already teaches that a *Sanhedrin* that executes even once in seven years is called *chavlanit* — violent. How much more so if executions appear to take place at the *beis din*'s front door? The *beis din* must remain a house of justice, not a place of *ibud nefashot*, destruction of souls.

### Opportunity

The second reason: *inami ki heichi detihavei lei hatzala* — so that there will be an opportunity for *hatzala*, for saving the condemned man. The greater the physical distance between the *beis din* and the execution site, the more time the *karoz*'s announcement has to reach potential witnesses who might come forward with exculpatory testimony. Distance is not punitive; it is protective. It is one more structural provision aimed at preventing an irreversible outcome.

---

## Biblical Passages

### Curser

With both reasons established, the *gemara* now turns to the textual analysis. The *beraita* teaches: *hotze et hamekalel el michutz lamachaneh* — take the curser outside the camp. The *gemara* asks: when the Torah says *michutz lamachaneh* about the *mekalel*, does it mean outside one camp, or outside all three camps? Could we establish that it means three from the analogy to *parim nisrafim*, the communal sin-offering bulls that are burned outside? We know *parim nisrafim* are taken outside all three camps — so *mah lehallan chutz l'shalosh machanot, af kan chutz l'shalosh machanot*: just as there outside three camps, so too here. But the analogy immediately runs into a problem.

### Burned Bulls

How do we know that the *parim nisrafim* themselves must be taken outside three camps? The Torah says about them, too, only *michutz lamachaneh* — in the singular. So we cannot use *parim nisrafim* to prove three camps for the *mekalel* if we have not yet established that the *parim nisrafim* themselves require three camps. The *gemara* must first derive the three-camp requirement for *parim nisrafim* on independent grounds.

### Incremental Camp

A second *beraita* addresses the *parim nisrafim* directly: *ve-hotzi et kol ha-par el michutz lamachaneh* — and take the entire bull outside the camp. Again: *atah omer chutz l'shalosh machanot o eino ela chutz l'machaneh achat?* — does this mean three camps or one? The *gemara* resolves this by noting that the Torah uses the phrase *michutz lamachaneh* in three separate sacrificial contexts, each one incrementally adding a camp. First: in the context of *parim nisrafim* — that gives us the first camp. Second: regarding *par ha-edah*, the communal atonement bull, the Torah says *el michutz lamachaneh* again — but we already know from the earlier verse that one applies to the other (*saraf oto ka-asher saraf et ha-par ha-rishon*), so this second mention must come to add a second camp. Third: in *Parshat Tzav*, when the Torah instructs the *kohen* to remove the *deshen*, the ashes of the altar, *al michutz lamachaneh* — again, we already know the ashes are removed outside the camp; this third mention must add the third camp. Through this technique of incremental inclusion — each additional mention of *michutz lamachaneh* extending the requirement by one more camp — the *gemara* establishes that *parim nisrafim* must indeed be taken outside all three camps.

### Wrong Slaughter

One might object: there is another case in the Torah where the phrase *michutz lamachaneh* appears — *shochutei chutz*, the case of sacrifices slaughtered outside the designated sacred precinct. In that case too the words *michutz lamachaneh* appear, and there it refers to a single camp. Should we not learn the rule for the *mekalel* from *shochutei chutz*, which would give us only one camp? The *gemara* frames the question directly: there are (at least) four features the *mekalel* shares with *parim nisrafim* — the verb *hotze* (taking out), the phrase *michutz lamachaneh*, the character of *machshir* (enabling or atoning for something), and the making-right of a transgression. There are also features the *mekalel* shares with *shochutei chutz*: a human actor (*adam*), the element of sin (*chotei*), the involvement of a *neshamah*, and a quality of *pigul* — abomination or fundamental wrongness.

### Machshir

The *gemara*'s resolution is elegant: *machshir mi'machshir adif* — it is preferable to learn from something that atones or validates (*machshir*) rather than from something defined by its transgression. The *parim nisrafim* are taken outside as part of a holy atonement process; *shochutei chutz* represents a wrongful act — a sacrifice offered where it should not have been. We do not derive the proper place of execution from the case of a transgression. We derive it from the case of sacred atonement.

### Moshe's Location

Rav Pappa offers a further proof that the execution site must be outside all three camps, and it operates on entirely different grounds. He asks: *Moshe heicha havah yasiv?* — where was Moshe sitting when *Hashem* commanded him to take out the *mekalel*? Moshe sat in *Machaneh Leviyah*, the second camp. When *Hashem* said *hotze et hamekalel el michutz lamachaneh*, that command was issued from within *Machaneh Leviyah* — so taking the man outside the camp means, first, outside *Machaneh Leviyah*: one camp. Then the Torah continues: *vayotziu et hamekalel el michutz lamachaneh* — and they took the *mekalel* outside the camp. But he was already outside *Machaneh Leviyah*. The fact that the Torah records a second act of taking him out means they took him yet further — outside *Machaneh Yisrael*, the third camp. The *gemara* anticipates the objection that this second verse is simply describing the execution of the command rather than adding a second movement, but responds: the verse *u'vnei Yisrael asu ka'asher tzivah Hashem et Moshe* — the children of Israel did as *Hashem* commanded Moshe — already covers the execution of the command. The second *vayotziu* must therefore be teaching something additional: namely, that the *mekalel* was taken past *Machaneh Leviyah* and past *Machaneh Yisrael*, so that the execution site lay beyond all inhabited camps. Even if the *beis din* itself happens to be located outside any of those camps, the stoning house must be further still. With that, the *gemara* sets the stage for the opening of 43a.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 43

## Skilah Location

### Skilah Outside Beit Din

The *mishna* establishes that once a capital verdict has been rendered, the condemned is taken *chutz l'beit din* — outside the court. The *gemara* will discuss precisely what that means geographically. As we noted previously, drawing on the structure of the desert encampment, the *beit hamikdash* (corresponding to the *mishkan*) stands at the center, the *machaneh leviyim* surrounds it, and the *machaneh yisrael* occupies the outermost ring. *Skilah* takes place outside all three of these camps, at the *even hachitzon* — the place of the stone, or, as we will discuss, possibly a single stone.

### Three Camps Structure

This geography of the three camps — *beit hamikdash*, *machaneh leviyim*, and *machaneh yisrael* — provides the structural backdrop for the entire discussion of where capital punishment is carried out. The condemned must be taken beyond the furthest boundary, outside *machaneh yisrael* entirely.

### Rav Pappa's Source

Picking up from the bottom of 42b, after the discussion of *makshir mimakshir*, Rav Pappa offers an independent source for the requirement that *skilah* takes place outside all the camps, drawing from the narrative of the *mekallel* — the blasphemer described in *Vayikra*.

The *gemara* asks: where was Moshe sitting? *B'machaneh leviyah* — in the *machaneh leviyim*, the second concentric ring. When God instructed Moshe, *hotzei et hamekallel el michutz lamachaneh* — take the blasphemer outside the camp — what Moshe understood was that he should take him outside the camp in which Moshe himself was sitting, namely the *machaneh leviyim*, placing the *mekallel* in *machaneh yisrael*. Then *bnei yisrael* subsequently took him further, *michutz lamachaneh* — outside the camp he was now in — which brought him beyond *machaneh yisrael* entirely. That outermost location is where the stoning occurred. This is derived from the verse *vayotziu et hamekallel el michutz lamachaneh* — they took the blasphemer outside the camp — meaning outside *machaneh yisrael*.

### Two Verses Analysis

At this point the *gemara* raises an objection. If everything that God commanded Moshe is already accounted for by the verse *u'venei yisrael asu ka'asher tziva Hashem et Moshe* — the *bnei yisrael* did as God commanded Moshe — then we already know they carried out the execution outside the camp. The verse *vayotziu et hamekallel el michutz lamachaneh* would be redundant for the purpose of telling us the action occurred, and therefore it must be teaching us something additional: that they took him specifically outside *machaneh yisrael*, as Rav Pappa derives.

But then the *gemara* notes a further redundancy: what do we do with *vayirgemu oto ba'even* — they stoned him with a stone? If the general verse already tells us they did everything commanded, this verse too is superfluous for establishing the bare fact of execution. The *gemara* answers: *ha mibayei likde'tanya* — this verse is needed for what we learn in the following *baraita*.

## Smicha & Dechiya

### Even vs. Avanim

The *baraita* derives two teachings from this verse. *Vayirgemu oto ba'even* — *oto*, "him," and not while he is clothed; and *even*, in the singular, teaches that if he died from a single stone, the obligation has been fulfilled. This raises an immediate question: in two different places the *Torah* describes the stoning of a condemned person — one instance uses *even* (singular) and another uses *avanim* (plural; the parallel verse appears in *Bamidbar*, regarding the *mekoshesh etzim*). Why does the *Torah* use both forms?

### One Stone Teaching

The *gemara* explains the necessity of each form. Had the *Torah* written only *even*, I might have thought that if the condemned person does not die from the first stone, no further stone may be brought to complete the execution. Therefore the *Torah* also writes *avanim* in the plural, to teach that additional stones may be brought if needed. Conversely, had the *Torah* written only *avanim*, I might have thought that *lechatchilah*, from the outset, you must bring multiple stones. Therefore the *Torah* also writes *even* to establish that you begin with one stone, and bring more only if the person has not died.

### Both Forms Needed

Both the singular *even* and the plural *avanim* are thus indispensable. The singular establishes the procedure — begin with one stone — while the plural preserves the obligation to complete the execution if the first proves insufficient. Each form addresses a possible misunderstanding that would arise from reading only the other.

### Rav Pappa vs. Tanna

The *gemara* then steps back and considers a broader difficulty. The teachings Rav Pappa derived from the *mekallel* narrative — that *skilah* takes place outside all three camps — were, at the outset of the *gemara*'s discussion, already established through *gezeirot shavot* by the *tanna'im*: the verbal analogy connecting the *mekallel* to *parim hanisrafim* and to *shochutei chutz*, all of which use the language of *michutz lamachaneh*. If the *tanna'im* already had this derivation, why did Rav Pappa need to introduce his own?

The *gemara* answers: *ne'emar ka'amar* — the *tanna* was not asserting that the *gezeirah shavah* is in fact the operative source. Rather, he was saying: *ilu lo ne'emar kra* — had the more direct verse that Rav Pappa uses not existed, I would have resorted to the *gezeirah shavah*. But *hashta de'ne'emar kra gezeirah shavah lo tzarich* — now that the direct verse exists, the *gezeirah shavah* is unnecessary. The entire exercise in *gezeirah shavah* was thus a kind of *bedi'avad* demonstration: this is what we would have done without the better source. This makes the *sugya* an instructive case study in the methodology of *gezeirah shavah* itself.

## Rav Ashi's View

### Rav Ashi's Setup

Rav Ashi offers yet another reading of the *mekallel* verses to establish the same geographic requirement. He begins from the same premise: Moshe was sitting in *machaneh leviyim*. God says to him, *hotzei et hamekallel chutz lamachaneh* — take the blasphemer outside the camp — which Rav Ashi understands as referring to *machaneh leviyim*.

### Verse Splitting

Rav Ashi then splits the verse differently from Rav Pappa. He reads *hotzei* as commanding that the *mekallel* be removed from *machaneh leviyim*, while *el michutz lamachaneh* refers to the next boundary — outside *machaneh yisrael*. Thus the single verse itself encodes both stages of removal: out of the inner camp and then out of the outer one.

### Action Occurred

On this reading, *vayotziu et hamekallel el michutz lamachaneh* — the verse recording that they actually carried out the action — is used simply to teach that the execution took place as commanded, and does not carry the additional geographic teaching that Rav Pappa derived from it.

## Smicha & Dechiya Details

### Unexampled Actions

The *gemara* then raises a difficulty against Rav Ashi's approach. On his reading, the verse *u'venei yisrael asu ka'asher tziva Hashem et Moshe* — they did as God commanded — must be doing additional work, since *vayotziu* is already accounting for the bare fact that the execution occurred. What does this verse teach?

The *gemara* answers: *ha mibayei leh chad l'smicha v'chad l'dechiya* — one is needed for *smicha*, the laying of hands upon the condemned before execution, and one for *dechiya*, pushing the condemned off from a height.

One might ask: why would we need a verse to establish these actions at all? The answer is that both *smicha* and *dechiya* go beyond what is explicitly commanded. If everything commanded is already accounted for by the general verse, then the additional verse teaches that *bnei yisrael* performed even these additional acts — which requires us to explain what those acts are and where they come from.

### Smicha vs. Dechiya

As for *smicha*, it is in fact stated explicitly in the text: *v'samchu kol hashom'im et yedeihem al rosho* — all those who heard him blaspheme lay their hands upon his head. So *smicha* does appear in the commandment.

*Dechiya*, however, is not stated explicitly in the execution command at all. Where does it come from? The *gemara* answers: *dechiya lav hacha ksiva ela misinai* — it is not written here in the text but is a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*, derived from *yareh yareh*, the phrase in *Har Sinai* that indicates either stoning or shooting — *o sakol yisakeil o yareh yareh*. Chazal understand *yareh yareh* as teaching that one of the witnesses comes and pushes the condemned off the *beit haskilah*.

### Beit Skilah Structure

The *beit haskilah* — the stoning structure — is two stories high, *gavoha shtei komot*. One of the witnesses comes and pushes the condemned off the top, so that he falls to the ground below. This is the *dechiya*. If he does not die from the fall, then the stoning with *even* or *avanim* proceeds as described.

The *gemara* thus groups *smicha* and *dechiya* together because both represent actions that, while either stated or derived elsewhere, required confirmation that *bnei yisrael* actually performed them in the case of the *mekallel*. The general verse *u'venei yisrael asu ka'asher tziva Hashem et Moshe* provides that confirmation: they did indeed perform *smicha* and *dechiya* just as required.

### Hotzei Objection

The *rabbanim* raise an objection against Rav Ashi. If he is reading *hotzei* in the *mekallel* narrative as implying *dechiya* or some similar additional content, then in every case in the *Torah* where the word *hotzei* appears — including the passages concerning *parim hanisrafim*, the burned cattle — one would have to derive a *derasha* from it as well. The *gemara* concludes: *kashya* — this is indeed a strong difficulty, and Rav Ashi's reading is apparently not accepted.

## Communal Ownership

### Rav Huna's Rule

The *mishna* introduces the role of the person who stands at the entrance of the *beit din* with *sudarin* — signal flags — in hand, ready to wave them if an appeal for acquittal is raised while the condemned is being led out. Rav Huna then teaches a broader principle: it is obvious to me (*peshita li*) that the stone used for *skilah*, the tree used for hanging, the sword used for execution by *sayif*, and the cloth used for *chenek* (strangulation) must all belong to the *tzibur* — the community.

### Rationale

The reason is straightforward: we do not say to the condemned, *zil v'aytei veniktal nafshech* — go fetch your own stone and we will kill you with it. The instruments of execution are not the condemned person's obligation to provide. They belong to the community, whose court has decreed the execution.

### Signal Cloth & Horse

Rav Huna then raises a question about two other items. The *sudar* used to signal — waved to halt the procession if an appeal is raised — and the horse kept ready to ride out and stop the execution if needed: whose property are these? On one hand, since both exist for the purpose of potentially saving the condemned person's life, perhaps they should be his responsibility to provide. On the other hand, since the *beit din* is obligated to halt the execution if a valid appeal arises, perhaps the *beit din* — and thus the *tzibur* — bears this responsibility. The *gemara* leaves this as an unresolved question.

### Frankincense Wine

Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Ashi in the name of Rav Chisda teaches: *hayotzei lahareg mashkin oto koret shel levonah bekos shel yayin* — the person being led out to execution is given *levonah* (frankincense) mixed into a cup of wine. The purpose is *kedei shetitaref da'ato* — so that his mind becomes confused and disordered. As Rashi explains, *titaref da'ato velo yidag veyitmahmeha baharigato* — his mind is unsettled and he does not fully comprehend what is happening to him, sparing him the full psychological anguish of his execution. The scriptural basis offered is the verse, *tenu shechar le'oved veyayin lemarei nafesh* — give strong drink to one who is lost and wine to one who is bitter of soul.

### Women Volunteers

A *baraita* records that the distinguished women of Jerusalem — *nashim yekarot shebiyerushalayim* — used to voluntarily prepare and bring this mixture of their own accord, as an act of communal *chessed* toward those condemned.

### Tzibur Provides

This prompts the question: if the precious women of Jerusalem did not volunteer, from whose resources should the mixture come? The *gemara* answers that it is clearly reasonable it should come from the *tzibur*, drawing on the fact that the scriptural verse uses the plural command *tenu* — "give" — indicating a communal obligation.

## Appeals & Silence

### Appeal Rights

The *mishna* establishes that the condemned person may appeal his own sentence — *afillu hu omer yesh li l'lamed al atzmi zechut* — even he himself can claim to have a *limud zechut*, and he is brought back, even four or five times, *u'bilvad sheyesh mamash bidvarav* — provided there is substance to what he says.

### Silent Student

This gives rise to the question posed by Rav Acha bar Huna to Rav Sheshet: what if one of the students says he has a *limud zechut* on the condemned and then goes silent — *nishtatek*? Rashi explains *nishtatek* as *ne'elam*, meaning he forgot what he was going to say. He got as far as declaring that he had an appeal but could not articulate it. Is the signal flag waved and the procession halted?

### Blowing Wind

Rav Sheshet's response is pointed: he waved his hand dismissively, indicating *ruach hu zeh she'amarta* — it is merely blowing wind. *Keivan denishtatek mah ho'il* — since he went silent, what purpose does his initial claim serve? An appeal that cannot be stated is no appeal at all.

### World-Wide Objection

The *gemara* then raises a challenge to this position. If we were to treat a claim that goes silent as sufficient cause to halt proceedings, we should logically worry about everyone in the world: *afilu echad besof ha'olam nami* — perhaps someone at the ends of the earth knows a *limud zechut* on him. If the mere possibility of an unvoiced appeal is grounds for delay, no execution could ever proceed.

### Claims Only Count

The resolution is that we care only about claims actually made. *Hatam lo ka'amar hacha ka'amar* — there, nobody has said anything; here, this person did say he had an appeal. But the point of the objection stands as a reductio: the reason we do not halt proceedings for the person who *might* have a claim is that no claim has been made. By the same logic, the student who said he had an appeal but then went silent has not actually made a claim in any actionable sense. His initial statement, unaccompanied by any substantive content, is treated as nothing.

## Student Dies Mid-Appeal

### Completed Appeal

Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina teaches: if one of the students articulated a *limud zechut* — *shezika*, meaning he completed his appeal — and then died before the court could vote on it, *ro'in oto ke'ilu chai v'omed bimkomo* — we regard him as though he were alive and standing in his place.

### Substitute Voting

Practically, this means we substitute another person to occupy his position for the vote. The deceased student's completed *limud zechut* retains its standing; his death does not invalidate what he articulated. A replacement voter is seated and the deliberation proceeds as if the original student were present.

### Censored Text

At this point in the text, there is a section that was removed by censors. The printed versions available to us preserve only a truncated *gemara*, though other printings make clear that the censored passage deals with Jesus and the eve of Passover. We will return to this if time permits.

### Unfinished Appeal

The *gemara* then distinguishes: *zika in, lo zika lo* — if he completed his *limud zechut*, yes, we place someone in his stead; if he did not complete it, no, we do not. This creates the direct connection back to Rav Sheshet's ruling: a student who said only that he had an appeal and then fell silent — or died before articulating anything — is treated identically. The bare statement of intention, unaccompanied by substantive argument, generates no procedural consequence. *Zika peshita li* — if he completed it, that is obvious; *lo zika tiba'i lach* — the question is specifically about the case where he did not complete it.

## Appeals & Silence (II)

### Baraita Timing

Rav Pappa explains the apparent tension between our *mishna* — which says the condemned may be brought back even four or five times *provided there is substance to his claim* — and the *baraita*, which states that the first and second time he claims to have an appeal, he is brought back *whether or not* there is substance to his words. Rav Pappa resolves this by explaining that our *mishna* is speaking from the second or third time onward. The requirement of *mamash bidvarav* — substantive content — applies only from the third appeal onward; the first two times, the court brings him back unconditionally.

Abaye adds a practical dimension: from the third time onward, how does the court determine whether there is *mamashut* to the claim? A pair of rabbis accompanies the condemned and listens to what he intends to say. *Ei ika mamash bidvarav in, ei lo lo* — if there is substance, he is brought back; if not, he is not. One might ask why this procedure is not applied from the very first appeal. The *gemara* answers: *agav d'ba'it lei* — because the condemned is frightened and may not be able to fully articulate his claim under that duress, the court gives him unconditional latitude for the first two attempts.

## Pre-Execution Announceme…

### Announcer Role

A new *mishna* teaches: *matzu lo zechut pat'ruhu* — if a meritorious claim is found, he is acquitted; if not, he is brought out to be stoned. And *charoz yotzei lefanav* — an announcer goes out before him, publicly declaring: *ish ploni ben ploni yotzei lisakel* — so-and-so is being brought out to be stoned — *al she'avar aveira ploni* — for having committed such-and-such a transgression — *u'ploni u'ploni edav* — and so-and-so are his witnesses. The announcement concludes with an open invitation: *kol mi sheyodea lo zechut yavo vyelamed alav* — anyone who knows a reason to acquit him should come forward and do so.

### Details Announced

Abaye adds that the announcer must also specify the day, the hour, and the place where the transgression occurred: *b'yom ploni u'v'sha'ah ploni u'v'makom ploni*. The reason is practical and procedurally significant — *dilma ika did'u v'atu u'mazmin lei* — perhaps there are those who know that the named witnesses were not actually present at that location at that time, and can come forward to render them *edim zomemin*, conspiring witnesses, thereby invalidating their testimony entirely.

### Why Not Earlier?

The *gemara* then raises what should be an obvious question: the *mishna* says the announcer goes out *before him* — in front of the condemned as he is being led to execution. But does this mean that from the beginning of the trial, no such announcement was made? Surely it would make more sense to publicize the proceedings from the outset, giving potential witnesses or appellants the maximum time to come forward.

### Censored Jesus Text

The *gemara* does not answer this question in our printed text, because this is precisely where the censor intervened. The passage continues with a *baraita*: *v'ha tanya b'erev hapesach taluhu l'Yeshu* — but we learn in a *baraita* that on *erev Pesach* they hanged Jesus. The *gemara* proceeds from there, but the text in standard printed editions is cut off. One printed version notes explicitly that what follows here was removed by the censors and added according to the Venetian printing. The *baraita* about Jesus appears to have been the *gemara*'s response to the question of why no earlier announcement was made — the implication being that in that case, announcements *were* in fact made over an extended period beforehand. We will return to this passage if time allows.

## Confession Before Death

### Yetzer Sacrifice

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches: *kol hazove'ach et yitzro u'mitvadeh alav ma'aleh alav hakatuv ke'ilu kibdo l'Hakadosh Baruch Hu bishnei olamim* — anyone who slaughters his *yetzer hara* and confesses upon it, the verse accounts it as though he honored God in both worlds, this world and the world to come. The *drashah* is drawn from the verse *zove'ach todah yechabdaneni* — he who offers a *todah* sacrifice honors Me — and the word *todah* shares its root with *mitvadeh*, to confess. The double *nun* in *yechabdaneni*, where the simpler form *yechabdani* would have sufficed, yields one *nun* for *olam hazeh* and one for *olam haba*.

### Sacrifices & Reward

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi continues: when the *beit hamikdash* stood, a person who brought an *olah* received reward for the *olah*, and one who brought a *minchah* received reward for the *minchah*.

### Lowered Mind

But now — *aval mi sheda'ato shiflah* — whoever lowers his mind and humbles himself, *ma'aleh alav hakatuv ke'ilu hikriv kol hakorbanot kulan* — the verse accounts it as though he offered all the sacrifices combined. The prooftext is *zivchei Elohim ruach nishbarah* — the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. And moreover, his prayer is not rejected: *lev nishbar venidkeh Elohim lo tivzeh* — a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.

### Ten Amot Rule

The *mishna* now addresses the procedure immediately before execution. When the condemned is approximately ten *amot* from the *beit haskilah*, they say to him: confess your sins — *hitvadeh* — for it is the practice of all those who are put to death to confess, and anyone who confesses has a portion in the world to come.

### Achan Example

The basis for this is the case of Achan, who took consecrated property from Yericho in violation of the *cherem*, committing *me'ilah*. Yehoshua said to him before his execution: *b'ni sim na kavod la'Hashem Elohei Yisrael viten lo todah* — my son, please give honor to the God of Israel and confess. Achan responded: *omnah anochi chatati v'chazot v'chazot* — truly I have sinned, and he confessed in detail. Yehoshua then said to him: *bayom hazeh ata achur v'ee ata achur l'olam haba* — today you are *achur* (the opposite of *zach*, pure — murky, blemished, unclean), but in the world to come you are not *achur*. The confessed sin was forgiven and his portion in the world to come was secured.

### Default Confession

For someone who does not know how to formulate a confession, the *mishna* prescribes a simple formula: *emor tehei mitati kapara al kol avonotai* — say, let my death serve as atonement for all of my sins.

### Innocent Exception

Rabbi Yehuda adds a qualification: if the condemned person knows that he is *mezumam* — that he is innocent of this particular charge — he should say: *tehei mitati kapara al kol avonotai chutz me'avon zeh* — let my death be atonement for all my sins, except for this one.

### Innocence Claim

The *rabbanim* object to Rabbi Yehuda's position: *im kein yehu kol adam omer kein kedei l'nakot atzmo* — if that is the case, everyone will say this in order to appear clean before the public after their death. The force of this objection is striking. The *rabbanim* are effectively assuming that a person facing death will prioritize his posthumous reputation over the *kapara* that confession and death together could provide. One who confesses knows his death will atone for his sins; yet *rabbanim* predict that he will deny the sin anyway, apparently caring more about how he is perceived than about the spiritual benefit of honest confession. Whether this reflects a concern about wrongful conviction — the truly innocent claiming innocence — or a more cynical reading of human nature in extremis, is itself a matter worth reflection.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 44

## Achan & Confession

### Daf Overview

The daf begins at the top of 44a with the *mishnah* that speaks about encouraging a condemned person to perform *viduy* — confession — before execution.
