The narrative of *Achan* serves as the biblical basis for this practice: he offered a confession before being put to death by *Yehoshua*. As we saw in the previous daf, *Yehoshua* engaged in *shichto bidvarim* — he encouraged, even enticed, *Achan* to confess, apparently under the impression that doing so might save him.

### Viduy & Atonement

This dynamic raises an important theological question about the nature of *viduy*. There is no doubt that a central dimension of the practice is the principle of *mita hi kappara* — that death itself serves as atonement. The *beis din*, in this framework, functions as God's agent. The act of execution is not merely a legal sanction but a vehicle for the condemned person's spiritual rectification. Encouraging confession, then, is an act of genuine concern for the person's soul.

### Public vs. Private

Yet there is simultaneously a public dimension to *viduy* that cannot be ignored. The *beis din* must also be seen to be acting correctly. One might compare — though emphatically not equate — the forced confessions extracted by totalitarian governments, which serve to exonerate the regime rather than benefit the accused. The concept of *shichto bidvarim* becomes more complex if the sole purpose of confession were the condemned person's personal *kaparah*: the public acknowledgment carries its own institutional weight, making clear to all observers that justice is being done transparently and legitimately.

### Confession & Hatra'ah

This public dimension parallels, in a certain sense, the requirement of *hatra'ah* — the formal warning given before a transgression. The formula *ad she-yatir atzmo la-mitah*, that the perpetrator must "release himself to death," *al menas ken*, on the condition of accepting the consequence, means that the perpetrator actively acknowledges and accepts the death penalty upon himself. This, too, addresses the deeper question of how a *beis din* can be justified in carrying out a violent act against another person. Part of the answer is *ki ha-mishpat l'Elokim* — the court represents divine justice. But part of the answer is also that the person himself, through his knowing and willing acceptance, has in a real sense consented to what follows. *Viduy* and *hatra'ah* thus function in parallel as structures through which both the perpetrator's inner acceptance and the court's outer legitimacy are established.

---

## Five Charamim

### Five Instances

The *gemara* at the bottom of 43b opens a broader inquiry into *Achan*'s sin. Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon, enumerates *chamisha* — five instances of *mo'al b'charamim*, of taking benefit from property that had been placed under a *cherem* (ban). Four of these occurred during the time of *Moshe*, when various battles were fought and property was explicitly declared *cherem*. One occurred in the time of *Yehoshua*, and that is *Achan*'s sin. The derivation of the number five comes from the verse in which God reveals *Achan*'s guilt: *anochi chatasi v'chazos v'chazos asisi* — "I have sinned, and done such and such." The doubled *chazos* yields four, plus the instance already established, arriving at five. *Tosafos* notes that one could arithmetically derive an even higher number from the language, but since there were not that many relevant wars, the count cannot exceed five.

### Delayed Punishment

This enumeration raises an immediate question: if *Achan* sinned during the period of *Moshe*, why was he not punished then? More precisely — and this is the correction that sharpens the question — why were the *Jewish people* not punished collectively during *Moshe*'s time? The deaths at the battle of *Ha-Ai* represent a form of collective punishment visited upon Israel for *Achan*'s transgression. Why did this collective consequence only materialize after the crossing of the *Yarden*?

### National Identity

Rabbi Yochanan, again in the name of Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon, explains: *lo anash al ha-nistarot ad she-avru Yisrael et ha-Yarden* — collective punishment was not applied for hidden sins until Israel crossed the *Yarden*. The *pasuk* in *Devarim* — *ha-nistarot l'Hashem Elokeinu veha-niglot lanu u-levaneinu* — "the hidden things belong to the Lord our God, and the revealed things belong to us and to our children" — carries an unusual scribal notation: dots appear over the words *lanu u-levaneinu* and over the *ayin* of *ad*. Rabbi Yehuda derives from this notation that the responsibility for *nistarot*, hidden sins, was subject to a temporal limit: it did not apply until the crossing of the *Yarden*.

This is a striking and difficult idea. What is the conceptual basis for it? It cannot simply be about fault, because the people cannot be faulted for what they did not know. The better framework is one of collective *identity* rather than individual blame. Before the crossing of the *Yarden*, Israel functioned as a people in a more individualist mode — what one person did privately was, in a sense, his own business. After crossing, they became a *nation*, a collective unity. And as a collective unity, they bear responsibility — not necessarily blame — even for what one of their members does in private. An analogy: if a child breaks a store window, the parent may not be at fault but is nonetheless responsible. The shift from *am* to *goy*, from a people to a nation, is what creates this new framework of corporate accountability.

### Preventable Sins

Rabbi Nechemia takes a sharply different position. He cannot accept the idea that people die for sins they could not have prevented or even known about. He therefore inverts the reading: *keshem she-lo anash al ha-nistarot, kach lo anash al ha-niglot* — just as there was no collective punishment for hidden things, there was equally no collective punishment for public things — until the crossing of the *Yarden*. For Rabbi Nechemia, the dotted letters indicate not that the threshold for hidden sins was lowered after crossing, but that *both* categories — hidden and revealed — were only subject to collective consequence once the national identity was established. And crucially, even then, collective responsibility applies only to *niglot*, to public, preventable sins — things that the community could have known about and acted upon. The more palatable moral intuition here is clear: we can accept communal responsibility when we had the means to do something about it.

### Unity vs. Blame

The contrast between the two positions thus maps onto two distinct conceptions of collective responsibility. Rabbi Yehuda holds a more metaphysical view: once Israel crosses the *Yarden* and becomes a nation, they are one unity and bear the consequences of that unity even for what is beyond their knowledge. Rabbi Nechemia insists on a more pragmatic, action-based standard: communal responsibility attaches only where the community could have intervened. Before the crossing, even the *niglot* were not subject to collective sanction. After, they are — but only those.

### Family Knowledge

Having resolved why *Yisrael* as a whole suffered at *Ha-Ai* even according to Rabbi Nechemia's framework, the *gemara* still needs to explain how *Achan*'s sin — which was, after all, conducted in secret — could qualify as a *niglah*, a revealed sin, triggering collective responsibility. The answer offered is: *mishum de-havu yad'ei bei ishto u-vanav* — because his wife and children knew. The knowledge of the family introduced a public dimension into what had otherwise been a hidden act. Since those who were aware could have come forward and did not, the sin acquired something of the character of a communal failure to act. This is admittedly a difficult answer, and the *gemara* strains to reach it. Questions arise naturally: how many people must know before a sin becomes effectively public? Does some person in a position of authority need to have been in a position to discover it? The *gemara* does not fully resolve these tensions, but the thrust of the reasoning is that once family members who could have disclosed the sin chose not to, the community's failure of oversight becomes operative.

---

## Achan's Sins

### Jewish Identity

The *gemara* cites the *pasuk*, *chata Yisrael* — "Israel has sinned" — as God's announcement to *Yehoshua* even before *Achan* is identified through the casting of lots. Rabbi Abba bar Zavda draws from these words a fundamental *hashkafic* principle: *af al pi she-chata, Yisrael hu* — even though he sinned, he is still *Yisrael*. The *pasuk* does not say "Israel sinned and is no longer Israel." It says *chata Yisrael* — "Israel sinned" — the name *Yisrael* remains attached to the sinner even after the transgression.

The classic illustration cited is the verse about *Reuven*: *vayishkav et Bilhah pilegesh aviv vayihyu b'nei Yaakov shneim asar* — even after *Reuven*'s grave sin, the count of *Yaakov*'s sons remained twelve. He was not excised from the tribal register. The analogy from folk wisdom: *asa d'kai beini chilfei, asa shemei* — a *hadas* (myrtle) growing among thorns is still called a *hadas*. One student offered a deeper reading: the *hadas* itself hasn't changed, only its surroundings. But here *Achan* himself sinned. The response is that perhaps the *neshama* — the soul, the *pintele Yid* — is like the *hadas*, while the outer conduct has become corrupted. The core Jewish identity remains intact.

This *aggadic* passage became the textual basis for a major *halachic* claim. *Rashi*, in a *teshuva* dealing with apostasy, invoked this *gemara* to argue that regardless of how severely a person sins — even if they convert to another religion — their Jewish status remains intact *al pi halacha*. Strictly speaking, *Rashi* was not innovating without precedent, since there is no source anywhere in *Shas* suggesting that sin can strip a person of Jewish identity. But the rhetorical and *halachic* force of citing this *gemara* was powerful. It is worth noting that some *Geonim* held that apostasy does trigger some form of status change, and the question of whether there are perhaps two dimensions to Jewish identity — one inalienable and one that can be affected by apostasy — was taken up by *Rav Aharon Lichtenstein* in his discussion of the famous Brother Daniel case in Israel.

### Five Books

God's indictment of *Achan* is conveyed to *Yehoshua* through a verse heavy with repetition: *v'gam avru et briti asher tziviti otam, gam lakchu min ha-cherem, gam ganvu, v'gam kichu'shu, v'gam samu vi-kleihem* — the word *gam* ("also" or "and also") appears five times. Rabbi Ila, in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Masparta, derives from this: *melamed she-avar Achan al chamisha chumshei Torah* — *Achan* transgressed all five books of the Torah. This reflects the *gemara*'s characteristic tendency to portray the paradigmatic *rasha* as having committed the full spectrum of possible transgressions.

### Brit Milah

Rabbi Ila further teaches that *Achan moshach be-orlaso hayah* — *Achan* even attempted to reverse his *bris milah* by stretching his foreskin. The textual link is *gezeirah shavah*: the verse here reads *v'gam avru et briti*, and a verse elsewhere reads *et briti heifar* — both use the word *briti*, which is a coded reference to *bris milah*. The *gemara* preempts the objection that this is obvious — since he violated all of the *taryag mitzvos*, of course he violated this one too. The answer: *mahu de-seima, be-mitzvah gufei lo pakar* — one might have thought that even a person who transgresses all other commandments would not do something that compromises his very bodily identity. Therefore the verse teaches us: even that he did.

### Na'arah Me'orasah

Rabbi Abba bar Zavda adds another transgression inferred from the indictment: *melamed she-ba Achan al na'arah ha-me'orasah* — *Achan* had intercourse with a betrothed maiden. The derivation is again a *gezeirah shavah*: the verse says *ki asah nevalah* about *Achan*, and a verse elsewhere uses the same phrase *ki asah nevalah* in the context of a *na'arah ha-me'orasah*. Once more the *gemara* raises the objection: this is obviously included in the general sin of violating all *taryag mitzvos*. The response — citing *Rashi* — is that intercourse with a *na'arah ha-me'orasah* is particularly egregious because it renders her *asur* to her husband, thus actively harming a third party. One might have thought *Achan* would not go quite that far. The verse teaches us: even that.

### Sekilah Punishment

*Ravina* offers a clarification: the specific mention of a *na'arah ha-me'orasah* is not simply about cataloguing *Achan*'s sins, but about explaining his mode of execution. *Dinei k'na'arah ha-me'orasah* — his judgment was like that of a *na'arah ha-me'orasah*. Just as a *na'arah ha-me'orasah* who sins receives *sekilah* (stoning), so too *Achan* received *sekilah*.

---

## Family Punishment

### Challenge to Justice

*Reish Galusa* posed a challenge to *Rav Huna*: the verse states that *Yehoshua* took *Achan ben Zerach* along with the silver, the cloak, the bar of gold, his sons, his daughters, his ox, his donkey, his flock, his tent, and all that was his — and had them all executed. The question is sharp: *im hu chata, banav u-venosav mah chatu?* — if *Achan* sinned, what did his sons and daughters sin? We are dealing here not with God's inscrutable justice but with a *beis din* carrying out a sentence. The principle of *lo yumsu avos al banim* — fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers — is explicit in the Torah.

*Rav Huna* responds with a rhetorical counter: if you ask about the sons and daughters, the same question applies to *kol asher lo* — all his possessions. What did his possessions do wrong? The verse *v'chol asher immo* refers, in context, not to their being punished but to their being brought and present at his execution. The point of bringing all of them — family, property, and livestock — was *ela lirdosam*, to bear down upon the people, to send an unmistakable message. The execution was public precisely because it was meant to deter all of Israel. And it is in that same framework — *kol Yisrael lirdosam* — that the sons and daughters, and all his possessions, were brought to the scene.

### Public Deterrence

The answer, then, is that the killing of *Achan*'s children and the destruction of his property were not punishments in the retributive sense but public acts of institutional messaging. *Ela lirdosam* — to impress upon Israel the gravity of what had occurred. Just as the *sotah* ritual is performed publicly to serve as a deterrent to others, the totality of *Achan*'s destruction — family, property, animals — served a communal pedagogical function.

### Disproportionate Punishm…

The *Ramban* identifies a pattern that runs through this week's *parasha*: in several cases, the punishment appears to exceed what simple retributive justice would demand. The *zaken mamre* who rules against the *Sanhedrin* is put to death; *edim zomemim* are executed; the *ben sorer u-moreh* is put to death for what is, in strict terms, very minor misconduct; the *navi sheker* is executed. In each of these cases, the Torah appends the phrase *v'chol Yisrael yishme'u v'yira'u* — and all Israel will hear and fear. The *Ramban* points out that this phrase itself is the justification. The institutions being protected — the authority of interpretation (*zaken mamre*), the integrity of the court system (*edim zomemim*), the structure of parental authority (*ben sorer u-moreh*), the authority of divine communication (*navi sheker*) — are of such foundational importance that their protection warrants punishments that would otherwise be disproportionate.

### Institution Preservation

This principle, that innocent or minimally guilty lives may be taken for the sake of institutional preservation and public message, sits in profound tension with the broader ethos of *masechet Sanhedrin*, which strains throughout to minimize capital punishment. One might fairly ask: which tendency serves as the normative model and which is the exception to be explained? The tension is real, and the *gemara* does not resolve it. What can be said is that the *Ramban*'s principle applies specifically to cases where *v'chol Yisrael yishme'u v'yira'u* is explicitly invoked — suggesting that the justification for disproportionate punishment is anchored in the protection of irreplaceable communal structures, and that without that explicit biblical warrant, the ordinary rules of proportionality govern.

---

## Sreifa & Sekilah

### Two Punishments

The verse records that after *Achan* and his household were condemned, *v'yisrefu otam ba-esh v'yiskelu otam ba-avanim* — they were both burned and stoned. The question is immediate: *b'tarti?* — both? Once a person is dead from one form of execution, what is the point of a second? And further: which punishment applies — *sreifa* or *sekilah*?

### Different Penalties

*Ravina* resolves this: *ha-ra'uy li-sreifa, sreifa; ha-ra'uy li-skila, skila* — each category received the punishment appropriate to it. The *property* — the cloak, the silver, the gold — was burned, as material objects designated for destruction by fire. The *people* — *Achan* and his family — were stoned, since *sekilah* is the applicable mode of execution for *Achan*'s capital offense (as established earlier from the comparison to a *na'arah ha-me'orasah*). The two punishments were not applied simultaneously to the same person but were differentiated according to the category of the condemned.

---

## Confession & Challenge

### Achan's Theft

The *gemara* now turns to *Achan*'s own confession. He declares: *va-ere ba-shalal, aderet shinar achat tovah, u-matayim shekalim kesef* — I saw in the spoils a fine cloak from Shinar, and two hundred shekels of silver, as well as a bar of gold.

### Garment Type

*Rav* and *Shmuel* debate the nature of the garment. *Rav* identifies it as *itztala d'milta* — a cloak of silk. *Shmuel* describes it as *sarvla d'tzrifa* — a heavier garment of fine wool, or according to some readings, a dyed wool cloak.

### Pouring Out

The verse then says *va-yatzikum lifnei Hashem* — he poured out before God what he had stolen. The word *va-yatzikum* is unusual; *lehatzik* is the word for pouring a liquid, not for placing objects. *Rav Nachman* therefore re-reads it: *ba v'chavtam lifnei ha-Makom* — he went and slammed them down before God. The image is one of force and anger, not reverent presentation.

### Joshua's Challenge

*Rav Nachman* goes further: the subject of this action is not *Achan* but *Yehoshua*. It is *Yehoshua* who slammed the stolen goods before God and said: *Ribono shel Olam* — Master of the Universe — the verse says *vayaku meihem anshei ha-Ai kishloshim v'shisha ish* — thirty-six men of *Ha-Ai* struck them down. A *baraita* records the debate: Rabbi Yehuda says this means literally thirty-six people died. Rabbi Nechemia says — but the verse says *kishloshim v'shisha*, *like* thirty-six, not exactly thirty-six. Rather, it was one person, *Yair ben Menashe*, who was equivalent in worth to the majority of the *Sanhedrin*, making him count as thirty-six. In some measure, narrowing the number to one person, rather than thirty-six, modulates the starkness of the collective punishment — though one innocent life remains one innocent life.

*Yehoshua*'s challenge to God is itself given voice through a further verse: *Rav Nachman* cites the *pasuk*, *tachanunim yedaber rash v'ashir ya'aneh azut* — a poor man speaks with supplications, while a rich man answers harshly. *Tachanunim yedaber rash zeh Moshe* — *Moshe* is the poor man who spoke softly and supplicated before God. *V'ashir ya'aneh azut zeh Yehoshua* — *Yehoshua* is the rich man who answered God harshly. The *gemara* thus frames *Yehoshua*'s confrontation with God as something qualitatively more aggressive than *Moshe*'s characteristic mode of petition. This is also the *gemara*'s way of giving voice to what *Chazal* themselves find troubling: thirty-six people died — or even one equivalent — for one man's hidden sin. *Yehoshua*'s challenge is the vehicle through which that disquiet is expressed.

### Other Challenges

The *gemara* raises a challenge: if the *drasha* that *Yehoshua* "slammed" the items before God is what establishes his harshness, was *Pinchas* not guilty of the same? The verse about *Pinchas* reads *va-ya'amod Pinchas vayifaleil* — and *Pinchas* stood and *vayifaleil*. Rabbi Elazar notes: the verse does not use the *hitpaleil* form, which would mean he prayed, but the *piel* form *vayifaleil*, from the root *plilim*, meaning judges — implying he held God to account. *Pinchas* said: *Ribono shel Olam*, twenty-four thousand people died in the plague — as the verse records *vayihyu ha-meitim ba-magefah arba'ah v'esrim elef* — and held God to task for it. And *Moshe* himself, the supposed model of gentle supplication, also challenged God — as the verse *v'lu ho'alnu va-neshev b'ever ha-Yarden* shows: *Yehoshua* said had we only remained on the other side of the *Yarden*, we would have been better off. This is something stronger than challenging God's decision; it is a near-rejection of the entire enterprise of entering the land. The *gemara* parallels it to *Moshe*'s cry of *lamah hare'ota la'am hazeh* — why have You dealt harshly with this people? Such challenges, the *gemara* implies, are not unique to *Yehoshua*, nor are they outside the range of acceptable discourse with God.

---

## God's Response

### Joshua's Sin

God's response to *Yehoshua*'s prostration and lamentation is *kum lach* — get up, deal with this. *Darash Shila* interprets God's words to *Yehoshua* as containing an implicit rebuke: *shelcha kasha mi-shelahem* — what is yours, your responsibility, is harsher than theirs. The people died at *Ha-Ai* not only because of *Achan*'s sin but also because of something *Yehoshua* himself had done — or failed to do.

### Delayed Altar

The specific charge: *ani amarti, ve-hayah be-ovrechem et ha-Yarden takimu* — God had commanded that immediately upon crossing the *Yarden*, certain stones were to be erected. *Ve-atem richaktem shishim mil* — and you delayed sixty *mil* before erecting them, going all the way to *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eval*. *Yehoshua*'s sin, in this reading, was that he did not fulfill the commandment with the immediacy God intended.

### Tosafot Resolution

*Tosafos* raises an obvious difficulty: the Torah itself specifies that the stones were to be erected at *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eval*. How could *Yehoshua* have been expected to erect them immediately upon crossing the *Yarden*, when those mountains were sixty *mil* away? *Tosafos* resolves this through a debate in the *Yerushalmi*. One opinion (attributed to Rabbi Elazar) holds that the commandment was to erect the stones immediately upon crossing — and that *Yehoshua* was therefore supposed to build two small mounds of earth right there, symbolically calling one *Har Gerizim* and the other *Har Eval*: *de-asu shushi de-afra, ve-karu le-achat Har Gerizim u-le-achat Har Eval*. The second opinion (Rabbi Yehuda) holds that the commandment referred to the actual mountains, but that *Yehoshua* fulfilled it on the very day of the crossing — *shishim mil halchu be-oto ha-yom* — covering sixty *mil* in a single day. According to the *Yerushalmi*, then, either *Yehoshua* made symbolic mounds immediately, or he reached the real mountains the same day. In both cases he did what was required. *Tosafos* explains that *Darash Shila* here holds that the commandment was meant like Rabbi Elazar — immediate erection upon crossing — and that *Yehoshua* erred by going to the real *Har Gerizim* and *Har Eval* instead of constructing symbolic ones on the spot.

### No Sin, Contribution

*Rav* responded to *Darash Shila*'s position by having an *amora* publicly expound: *ka-asher tzivah Hashem et Moshe avdo, ken tzivah Moshe et Yehoshua, ve-chen asah Yehoshua, lo he-sir davar mi-kol asher tzivah Hashem et Moshe* — as God commanded *Moshe* His servant, so *Moshe* commanded *Yehoshua*, and so *Yehoshua* did; he did not deviate from anything God had commanded *Moshe*. *Rav* thus rejected the claim that *Yehoshua* had sinned in any direct sense. And yet the *gemara* preserves the force of God's words: *attah geramta lahem* — you contributed to this. Not through transgression, but through *gerama*, indirect causation. *Yehoshua* had placed the spoils of *Yericho* under *cherem* — and it was the existence of that *cherem* that created the opportunity and temptation for *Achan*'s sin. Nobody asked *Yehoshua* to impose that *cherem*. He created the prohibition that *Achan* then violated.

### Learned Lesson

The *gemara* closes this thread by noting that God's subsequent command about the city of *Ai* carries an implicit lesson. The verse regarding *Ai* says to do to it and its king as was done to *Yericho* — but the end of the verse, which is not fully quoted, specifies: except do not place the spoils under *cherem*. The ellipsis is pointed: the lesson is built into the instruction. The tragedy at *Ha-Ai* was in part the consequence of an overly strict *cherem* on *Yericho*'s spoils. With *Ai*, that mistake is corrected.

---

## Angel & Talmud Torah

### Angel Encounter

Before the events of *Ha-Ai*, while *Yehoshua* was encamped near *Yericho*, he encountered an *ish omed l'negdo* — a man standing opposite him. This figure declared: *lo, ki ani sar tzeva Hashem atah bati* — no, I am the commander of God's army, and I have come now. *Yehoshua* fell on his face to the ground and prostrated himself.

### Greeting at Night

The *gemara* asks: *heichi avid hachi?* — how could *Yehoshua* have done this? Rabbi Yochanan teaches that *asur lo le-adam she-yiten shalom le-chavero ba-lailah* — it is forbidden for a person to greet another at night. The concern is *chaishinan shema shed hu* — we worry that the figure may be a demon. And since *shalom* is one of God's names, one cannot invoke God's name on a demon. Prostrating before an unknown figure at night would be equally problematic.

### Angel Identity

The resolution is that the figure identified himself by name as *sar tzeva Hashem*. By announcing himself as an agent of God, he established that he was not a demon. The *gemara* considers the counter: but perhaps he was a demon who was lying? The response: *gemiri d'lo mafkei shem shamayim le-vatalah* — we have a received tradition that demons will not invoke God's name. One who says *ani sar tzeva Hashem* is therefore either a human being or an angel. The identity of a demon is ruled out.

### Two Failures

The angel then articulated two distinct failures. First: *emesh bitaltem tamid shel bein ha-arbayim* — at the close of day (*Rashi* notes that *emesh* here refers to just before nightfall), they had been so preoccupied with the encampment of *Yericho* that they neglected to bring the daily *korban tamid*. Second: *v'achshav bitaltem Talmud Torah* — now, in the nighttime, they were maintaining the siege when no military activity was needed. The night hours should have been devoted to Torah study, not to an encampment with no immediate tactical purpose.

### Talmud Torah Greater

*Yehoshua* then asked: *al eizeh mehen bata?* — which of these sins brought you here? The angel answered: *atah bati* — now, referring to the current violation: the *bittul Talmud Torah* was the greater sin. The neglect of Torah study was what prompted the angel's appearance.

### Joshua Corrects

*Yehoshua* immediately responded: *mi-yad vayalen Yehoshua ba-lailah ha-hu be-toch ha-emek* — that very night, *Yehoshua* went and spent the night in the valley. Rabbi Yochanan adds: *melamed she-lan be-umkah shel halachah* — this means he went into the depths of *halachah*, immersing himself and his people in profound Torah study through the night.

### Explicit Teaching

*Rav Shmuel bar Unya* in the name of *Rav* draws the explicit conclusion: *gadol Talmud Torah yoter me-hakravat temidim* — *Talmud Torah* is greater than bringing the daily sacrifices. The proof: *she-ne'emar atah bati* — the angel said "now I have come," pointing to the *bittul Talmud Torah* as the primary offense, even over the neglect of the *tamid*.

---

## Secrets & Shame

### Dispute Verse

*Abaye* asked *Rav Dimi*: how is the verse *al taitzei la-riv maher, pen mah ta'aseh be-acharitah be-hachlim otcha re'acha* — "do not rush into a dispute, lest you not know what to do at the end when your friend shames you" — applied in *Eretz Yisrael*? He suspected there was a particular *derasha* in the west attached to this verse.

### Yechezkel's Protest

*Rav Dimi* related the following *midrash*: when God told *Yechezkel* to go and say to Israel, *avichem ha-Emori ve-imchem Chittit* — your father is an *Emori* and your mother is a *Chittit*, meaning you have behaved as children of Canaanites — a certain spirit of judgment rose up and protested before God: *Ribono shel Olam, im yavo Avraham ve-Sarah ve-ya'amdu lefanecha* — if *Avraham* and *Sarah* were standing right here before You, and You said this to them, would You embarrass them? *Umachlim otam* — and shame them publicly?

### Secret Principle

The connection to the verse is then made explicit: *rivcha riv et re'acha* — if you have a complaint to press against *Bnei Yisrael*, fight it out with them, address it directly. But *ve-sod acher al tegal* — do not reveal another's secret. The "secret" here is the ancestral lineage that connects *Avraham* and *Sarah* to peoples who were not Jewish; bringing that into the argument to shame Israel is not a legitimate move. Even if there is a case to be made against *Bnei Yisrael*, that case should not be made by embarrassing their forebears.

### Angel's Names

The *gemara* then addresses the question of whether this figure — identified as *ruach paskonit*, which *Rashi* understands as *Gavriel* — has the standing to challenge God in this way. The answer is yes, and the *gemara* explains through three names. *Rav Yose be-Rabbi Chanina* teaches: this angel has three names: *Piscon* — *she-posek devarim klapei ma'alah*, he has the authority to cut and deliver sharp words before God on behalf of Israel; *Itmon* — *she-otem avonoseihem shel Yisrael*, he seals and closes up the sins of Israel, protecting them from full prosecution; and *Sigron* — *ki-van she-soger, shuv ein pote'ach*, once he closes a matter, no one can reopen it. The angel's license to intercede on Israel's behalf is thus established through the very nature of his office.

---

## Prayer & Intercession

### Prayer Before Calamity

Rabbi Elazar teaches: *le-olam yakdim adam tefillah le-tzarah* — a person should always anticipate calamity with prayer, placing his prayers before the trouble arrives rather than after.

### Abraham's Altar

The paradigmatic example is *Avraham*: *she-imalai hikdim Avraham tefillah le-tzarah bein Beis El u-vein ha-Ai* — because *Avraham* built a *mizbe'ach* and prayed between *Beis El* and *Ha-Ai* — the very location where Israel later suffered defeat — his prayer a millennium earlier provided protective merit. Had *Avraham* not prayed there, *lo nish'ayar mi-sonei Yisrael sarid u-palit* — not a single survivor of Israel's enemies (a reverential circumlocution for Israel itself in times of danger) would have remained. Far more than thirty-six — or even one — would have died at *Ha-Ai*.

### Prayer Exertion

*Reish Lakish* reads the verse differently: *kol ha-ma'amitz atzmo be-tefillah mi-lemata, ein lo tzarim mi-lema'alah* — whoever exerts himself in prayer below, in this world, will have no adversaries pressing against him from above. The verse *ha-ye'aroch shuva'cha velo ba-tzar* — set out your prayer, not in distress — becomes a statement about the timing and intensity of prayer: commit to it before adversity strikes.

### Divine Support

Rabbi Yochanan adds a final teaching: *le-olam yevakesh adam rachamim she-yehu kol ma'amitzos kocho* — a person should always pray that all heavenly forces strengthen him, *ve-al yehu lo tzarim mi-lema'alah* — and that no one on high stand against him. The goal of prayer is not only to avert specific catastrophes but to ensure that the entire heavenly apparatus is aligned in one's favor rather than arrayed in opposition.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 45

## Achan's Confession

### Achan Atonement Source

The daf begins at the bottom of 44b, picking up with a *baraita* that asks: *minayin shekiper lo viduyo* — how do we know that Achan's confession atoned for him? The source is the verse in which Yehoshua says to Achan: *ma achartanu ya'acharcha Hashem bayom hazeh* — "as you have troubled us, so shall God trouble you this day." The *drash* is that the word *hayom hazeh* — "today" — implies a limitation: today you are cursed, but not for *olam haba*. Because he confessed, Achan retains his portion in the World to Come.

A second verse confirms this. The sons of Zerach are listed: *Zimri, Eitan, Heiman, Calcol, and Dardah* — and they are counted as five. Since we know that Achan was *Achan ben Zerach*, he must appear somewhere in that list. The Gemara concludes that *Zimri* is a name for Achan. Just as the verse about Yaakov's sons — *vayihyu venei Yaakov shneim asar* — treats all twelve sons as equal in their standing, so too here: *ma kulam chamisha kulam chamisha l'olam haba* — just as all five brothers share equally in *olam haba*, so too does Achan.

### Zimri/Achan Names

This leads directly to the question of the dual naming. The verse is written as *Zimri* and yet elsewhere as *Achan*. Rav and Shmuel dispute the matter.

### Rav/Shmuel Dispute

One opinion holds that Achan was his true name, and he was called *Zimri* because *she'asa ma'aseh Zimri* — he acted like Zimri, committing a grievous sin that brought death upon the Jewish people. The other opinion holds that Zimri was his true name, and he came to be called Achan because *she'hichin avonoteihem shel Yisrael* — he set in motion, or caused to roll upon Israel, the punishment for their sins. Rashi explains the word *hichin* through the image of *ke'achna* — like a serpent — evoking the sense of one who causes consequences to come crashing down upon others.

---

## Execution Confession

### How to Confess

The *Mishnah* teaches that if a condemned person does not know how to perform *viduy*, the court teaches him what to say. Rabbi Yehuda goes a step further: if the person knows that the witnesses against him were *mezuman* — properly warned and gathered — he may say, "Let my death be an atonement for all my sins, except for this one, of which I am innocent."

### Rabbis' Objection

The Rabbis, however, do not permit this formulation. At first glance, the objection seems odd — if only a truly innocent person would say such a thing, why not allow it? But the reasoning becomes clear: the concern is not primarily about the guilty borrowing the language of the innocent. Rather, we do not want to introduce any formulation that casts ill repute upon the *beis din*, making it appear that they are executing an innocent person. The Gemara states this explicitly: *kedei shelo l'hotzi la'az al batei dinim* — so as not to bring disrepute upon the courts — and adds *v'al ha'edim* — and upon the witnesses as well.

### Man Exonerates Beis Din

A *baraita* then relates a striking case. A man being led out for execution declared: "If I am guilty of this sin, let my death not atone for any of my other sins. But if I am innocent of this sin, let my death atone for all my sins — the *beis din* and all of Israel are absolved, and the witnesses who bore false testimony against me should never receive atonement." The power of this statement lies in its structure: he is willing to forfeit atonement for his other sins in order to make his declaration of innocence. He does not blame the *beis din* — he absolves them entirely, placing the responsibility squarely on the witnesses. This sounds entirely sincere. And of course, once a person learns how to sound sincere, others may imitate the form without the substance.

### Cannot Reverse Verdict

When the Sages heard this, they were shaken. Nevertheless, *amru l'hachziro ee efshar shekvar nigzar gzeira* — to reverse the ruling was impossible, for the verdict had already been rendered. Without new admissible evidence, a verdict cannot be reversed. So the decision was: *yeihareg* — he must be executed — *vekola taluy betzavar edim* — and let the weight of it hang around the necks of the witnesses.

Even though one might imagine that, at least in principle, permission should have been sought before making such a declaration, the fact is that even had he asked, we likely would not have permitted it — because even a statement that explicitly exonerates the *beis din* still reflects poorly on them if it becomes known that they executed someone who proclaimed his innocence in so compelling a manner. But he said it, and now what is to be done? The possibility that an innocent person is being executed cannot be acted upon once procedure has run its course.

### Testimony Irreversible

The Gemara then sharpens the point. One might think the whole discussion is obvious — of course we proceed, since his word alone cannot reverse a verdict. So the Gemara clarifies: *lo tzricha d'hadri behu sahadei* — the novel case is where the witnesses themselves have retracted their testimony. Even so, the principle of *keivan shehigid shuv eino chozer umagid* — once testimony has been given, it cannot be withdrawn — applies. A retraction of testimony is not admissible.

The Gemara pushes further: the case is even more extreme — *af al gav d'ka yahavi ta'ama l'milsaihu* — not only do the witnesses retract, but they provide a convincing explanation of why they testified falsely, and all the surrounding circumstances support the claim that their original testimony was fabricated. Even then, procedure binds us. This is a deeply uncomfortable conclusion. In monetary cases, a judge has considerably more latitude — *ein l'dayan ela mah she'einav ro'os* — but in capital cases, the formal rules govern even when the outcome seems manifestly unjust.

### Baya & Shimon Story

The Gemara here includes — in some versions in brackets, suggesting it may be a later insertion — the story of *Baya machsa*, the tax collector, and Shimon ben Shatach. The story, reconstructed largely from the Yerushalmi, runs as follows: an evil tax collector and a great *tzaddik* died on the same day. During the commotion of the funeral, their bodies were switched and each was buried in the other's grave. The *talmid* of the *tzaddik* was distraught, wondering what his *rebbi* could have done to deserve burial in the grave of a *rasha*. The *rebbi* appeared to him in a dream and explained that there had been one sin on his part and one exceptional *mitzvah* on the tax collector's part that had resulted in this reversal — but in *olam haba*, the *tzaddik* was in a good place and the tax collector was suffering in *gehinnom*, with the hinge of the *gehinnom* gate resting upon him.

The *talmid* asked how long the tax collector would remain there, and was told: until Shimon ben Shatach dies and takes his place. This led to the question of what Shimon ben Shatach had done wrong — the answer being that he had failed to act against a group of witches. This detail feeds directly into the next *mishnah*. Shimon ben Shatach then devised a plan to capture and hang all the witches at once.

The relatives of the executed witches, enraged, hired false witnesses to testify against Shimon ben Shatach's son, accusing him of a capital crime. The witnesses could not be refuted through the standard procedure, and so he was led out to be executed. At the last moment, the witnesses themselves admitted they had been paid to lie, and it was evident to everyone that the testimony was fabricated. And yet — they could not halt the execution. Shimon ben Shatach's son was killed. This is the paradigm case for the Gemara's ruling: even when it is all but certain that the witnesses lied, once testimony has been given, it cannot formally be retracted, and procedure takes its course.

This is, as the Gemara acknowledges, deeply troubling. The counter-consideration is equally sobering: once you allow discretion to interrupt procedure when things seem obviously wrong, what prevents that discretion from being catastrophically abused? The formal rules exist precisely because we cannot trust case-by-case intuitions, however compelling they appear in the moment. A similar logic applies to the case of *eidim zomemin*: if a pair of alibi witnesses comes forward to counter the original testimony — *imanu heyitem* — we formally credit the *mezimim* even if many others could theoretically provide the same alibi. We follow formal rules. It is hard to live with in capital cases, and it will be a theme to which the tractate returns.

---

## Clothing at Stoning

### Strip Dispute

The *Mishnah* rules that when the condemned person is four *amot* from the *beis hasekila*, he is stripped of his garments. Rabbi Yehuda holds that a man is covered only in front, and a woman is covered both in front and behind — the operative word being that in both cases they are essentially brought to the place of execution nearly naked. The Sages disagree: *haish niskal arom* — the man is stoned naked — *ve'ein haisha niskal aruma* — but the woman is not stripped at all.

The *baraita* specifies the practical details: for the man, *perek echad milfanav* — one expanse of cloth in front. For the woman, *shenei prakim bein milfanav bein machoreha* — two pieces of cloth, front and back. The reason offered for the additional covering of the woman, in Rabbi Yehuda's formulation, is *mipnei shekula erva* — because the entire body of a woman is considered *erva*, invoking the principles of *sear be'isha erva* and *tefach be'isha erva*. This creates an immediate paradox: if every part of her body is considered nakedness, why strip her at all? And yet Rabbi Yehuda does strip her, while adding more covering than he provides the man. It is a strange balancing act.

On the distinction between objective and subjective *erva*: the question of whether one may recite a *bracha* in the presence of an exposed body part concerns the objective, formal category of nakedness — and in that context, for men, essentially only the genitals are at issue. For women, there is a distinction between the formal-objective category and the subjective dimension — what is considered nakedness in the presence of men, which shifts the analysis considerably. These are matters for a separate discussion.

### Sexual Concern

The Gemara now asks: *mai taama d'rabbanan* — what is the Rabbis' reason for not stripping the woman? The Gemara answers from the word *oto* in the verse *veragmu oto* — "you shall stone him." One might read *oto* as excluding women from stoning altogether, but this cannot be right since another verse explicitly includes women: *vehotzeta et haish hahu o et haisha hahi*. Rather, *oto belo ksuto* — "him, without his garment" — means the man is to be stoned stripped. *Ve'ota bichsuta* — but "her," it implies, is to be stoned with her garments on.

Rabbi Yehuda reads *oto belo ksuto* as meaning nakedness is required — *lo shena ish velo shena isha* — regardless of male or female. The question then becomes: what is actually driving this disagreement about how to read the verse?

The Gemara makes the underlying motivation explicit. The Rabbis read it to exclude stripping the woman because *rabbanan chaishi l'hirhura* — they are concerned about sexual thoughts arising in the onlookers. Rabbi Yehuda, who speaks in terms of *kulo erva*, is by contrast *lo chaishi l'hirhura* — not concerned about *hirhur* among those present. It should be stated plainly: the concern the Gemara voices is entirely about men viewing a woman's body and experiencing sexual thoughts. The Gemara expresses no corresponding concern about the reverse. This asymmetry is built into the framing, and it should be acknowledged rather than explained away.

### Sotah Comparison

This creates an apparent contradiction. In the laws of *sotah*, the *kohen* holds the woman's garments and tears them — *im nikre'u nikre'u v'im nifremu nifremu* — until her heart, meaning her breast, is exposed, and her hair is undone. There, Rabbi Yehuda says: *im hayah libah naveh lo hayah megalehu* — if her breast was attractive, he would not expose it. *Im hayah se'arah naveh lo hayah soisro* — if her hair was attractive, he would not undo it. So in the case of *sotah*, Rabbi Yehuda is concerned about *hirhur*, and the Rabbis apparently are not. Here, their positions appear reversed.

### Death Changes Stakes

Rabbah resolves the contradiction for Rabbi Yehuda: *hasam hainu ta'ama shema taitzei m'beis din zaka'ah v'yisgaru bah pirchei kehuna* — there, in the *sotah* case, there was concern that she might be exonerated and leave the court, having already been publicly exposed. The young priests who had seen her body or hair would then pursue her, and that pursuit would be able to find its footing precisely because she had already been publicly displayed in that state. So Rabbi Yehuda's concern is not her dignity as such — it is the concrete consequence: that men who have seen her body will be provoked to pursue her. If she is attractive, and she is exonerated and goes out into the world, those men will act on what they saw. Here, at the execution, she will not go out. There is no subsequent action to be feared.

But then what of the concern that seeing one woman stripped will provoke lust toward other women? Rabbah answers: *ein yetzer hara sholet ela b'mah she'einav ro'os* — the *yetzer hara* — here meaning specifically the sexual drive — has power only over what a person is actually seeing. It does not transfer: a man who sees a woman in one context does not, by virtue of that encounter, go on to pursue someone else. The *yetzer hara sholet* is specifically the impulse that leads to action, and action is bounded by the present visual experience.

This is a significant distinction. The Gemara elsewhere is concerned that a man who sees something sexually provocative may experience *hirhur* that leads to nocturnal seminal emission — which is a concern even when no overt action results. But apparently that level of concern is not sufficient to alter execution procedure. It is only the *yetzer hara sholet* — the drive that leads to actual transgression — that we must prevent, and that drive is bounded by *mah she'einav ro'os*. This principle has ramifications for later discussions, including the question of *kol isha* — one hears on the radio but does not see — but those discussions belong elsewhere.

The resolution for the Rabbis runs parallel: in the *sotah* case, the Rabbis are not concerned about *hirhur* because the verse itself mandates the public exposure — *venivasseru kol hanashim velo taasena kizmizatchena* — "and all women will be chastened and not do as she has done." There, public shaming serves the purpose of the verse's own imperative. Here, at the execution, *ein lecha yissur gadol mizeh* — there is no greater rebuke than death itself. The execution teaches the lesson; no additional shaming is required.

### Dignity vs Pain

This raises a final question: if not stripping the woman is appropriate, why then strip the man? Does *v'ahavta lere'acha kamocha* not apply equally? The Gemara insists it does. Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha says: *v'ahavta lere'acha kamocha — beror lo misah yafa* — you shall love your neighbor as yourself: choose for him a good death. This is a remarkable application. The person being executed is, at the very moment of execution for a grave sin, still the subject of *v'ahavta lere'acha kamocha*. The obligation to treat him as one would wish to be treated does not lapse. Even if there is value in a deterrent lesson for others, introducing gratuitous shame is foreclosed by this principle.

The Gemara therefore frames the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages as a disagreement not about whether *v'ahavta lere'acha kamocha* applies — everyone agrees it does — but about what a person actually prefers. *Mar savar bizyoni de'inish adif leh tefei minei nicha degufa* — one holds that a person cares more about avoiding shame than about avoiding physical pain, such that stripping him and causing the added discomfort of execution without garments is preferable to the shame of being exposed. *Umar savar nicha degufa adif mibizyonei* — the other holds that physical ease outweighs shame, so stripping him to allow a smoother, less friction-laden execution is the greater act of *mita yafa*.

The difference between men and women, then, is not that *v'ahavta lere'acha kamocha* applies only to one. It is that the calculation of *mita yafa* differs. For the man, the shame of stripping is not as acute — or the physical benefit of stripping outweighs the shame — and so stripping serves *mita yafa*. For the woman, according to the Sages, the shame overwhelms any physical benefit, and so *mita yafa* requires keeping her clothed. And beyond this, the verse *oto belo ksuto* provides an independent textual anchor.

---

## Stoning Procedure

### Platform Height

The *Mishnah* states that the *beis hasekila* — the stoning platform — was two heights of a man. One of the witnesses would push the condemned off by the hips; if he flipped and landed on his back, the witness would push him again. *Ve'im mes bah yatza* — if this killed him, good. If not, the second witness would take the stone and place it on his chest. If that killed him, good; if not, *regimaso bechol Yisrael* — the entire community would participate in stoning him, as the verse states: *yad ha'edim tihyeh bo barishona lehamiso veyad kol ha'am ba'achrona*.

But why exactly two heights? A *baraita* adds that if the person's own height is included, we arrive at three heights total. And the Gemara asks: *umi bainan kulei hai* — do we really need all that height? After all, a pit capable of killing is defined as *asara tefachim* deep, far less than the height implied here. The resolution is: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha says — again — *v'ahavta lere'acha kamocha: beror lo misah yafa*. The height is not merely sufficient to cause death; it is chosen to cause death quickly and certainly. Rashi says *sheyamus maher* — so that he will die quickly. A greater height ensures a faster death.

### Don't Deform Body

Then why not make it even higher — so that death on impact would be virtually instantaneous? The Gemara answers: *mishum deminuval* — because the body would become deformed. Even the condemned person would not want his body completely shattered and disfigured. This too falls under *v'ahavta lere'acha kamocha*: even a faster death is not worth purchasing at the cost of the body being destroyed in that manner. The height, therefore, is calibrated precisely — high enough for a quick death, not so high as to deform the body.

### Push vs Stone

A *baraita* derives the different stages of the execution procedure from the verses dealing with *Har Sinai*. *Yaroh yerah* — "he shall surely be shot" — is read as referring to pushing off the platform. *Sakol yisakel* — "he shall surely be stoned" — refers to actual stoning. The combination of the two terms teaches that both methods are to be used if necessary. The word *o* — "or" — teaches that if the pushing alone caused death, the second stage is not required. The fact that pushing comes first, rather than the more intuitive stoning, reflects the overarching desire to reduce the violence of the procedure and its character as a public mob event. The dual form *sakol yisakel* with its future-tense *yud* establishes that this procedure applies not only at *Har Sinai* but for all generations.

### Second Witness Stone

Returning to the *Mishnah*: if the push did not kill the condemned, the second witness takes the stone. The Mishnah's language of *notel* — taking — is relatively spare. A *baraita* of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar specifies that *even haytah sham masui shenei benei adam* — the stone was of a size requiring two people to lift. The *baraita* then says the witness *notlah venosnah al libo* — takes it and places it on his chest — which seems to imply one person. The Gemara resolves this: two people lift the stone together, and then one of them holds it while *veshadei lei ihu* — the other throws it down alone — *ki heichi detisei mizayar* — so that it comes down with force and velocity. Two people throwing together cannot generate the same directed force as one person casting alone.

This is, frankly, a more violent image than the simple *Mishnah* language suggests. The stone requires two men to lift it; it is not merely rested on the man's chest — it is hurled down upon him. The design serves *mita yafa*: swift and decisive. If even this does not kill him, *regamuhu kol Yisrael* — the community participates — but by that point the condemned is already lying on the ground, so this is far removed from the image of a mob chasing a person.

### People Never Stoned

A *baraita* then states: *me'olam lo shanah bah adam* — it never actually came to a second stoning by the community. The push and the witnesses' stone always sufficed. This sits alongside similar rulings in the tractate — *ir hanidachat*, *eidim zomemin* — where the Gemara notes *lo hayah velo nivra*: the case never occurred or was never implemented. Here too, the community stoning remained a theoretical final stage that was never reached in practice.

The Gemara clarifies: *mi kamina de'avid* — who said it ever happened? *De'mitzrich kamina* — the *Mishnah* is speaking hypothetically. It lays out the theoretical procedure should each stage fail, but in practice it never progressed to community participation.

### Bury Instruments

A *baraita* teaches that all the instruments used in the execution — the stone by which he was stoned, the wood of the gallows, the sword, the *sudar* used for strangulation — *kulan nikbarim imo* — all are buried with the condemned. The principle behind this is striking: we do not maintain a standing collection of execution instruments, as though execution is a routine feature of communal life. The instruments are buried, the memory of the event is put away. It had to be done; it should not define who we are.

A second *baraita*, however, seems to say *ein nikbarim imo* — they are not buried with him. Rav Pappa resolves the apparent contradiction: *mai imo* — what does "with him" mean? Not in the same grave, but *b'arba amot shelo* — within his four *amot*, in his immediate area. The instruments are buried near him but not placed in his grave. He is not interred with the symbols of his execution upon him. They are removed from circulation, buried out of sight, but they do not accompany him into the grave itself.

# Sanhedrin 46

## Shmuel: Disabled Witness…

### Severed Hands Rule

The daf opens on 45b, approximately ten lines from the bottom, with a statement of Shmuel bearing on the laws of *skilah*: *niktata yad ha'edim patur* — if the hands of the witnesses are severed after the *gmar din*, the person who was condemned to death goes free.

### Witnesses' Hands Require…

The reason is rooted in a scriptural requirement: *yad ha'edim tihyeh bo barishona* — the hands of the witnesses must be the first to cast the stone. If those hands no longer exist, the execution cannot proceed as prescribed, and the condemned is therefore released from this sentence. All the formal technical requirements of the procedure must be in place; if they are not, execution cannot be carried out.

### Pre vs Post Disability

One might immediately ask whether this principle extends to its logical extreme: what if the witnesses had amputated hands *from before the crime was committed* — *edim gidimim d'me'ikara* — would they also be disqualified? The answer is no. The verse specifies *yad ha'edim* — the hand of the witnesses — referring to a hand that *already existed* at the time of the crime. A pre-existing amputation does not create a *psul*. It is only when the witnesses possessed hands at the time of the crime, and those hands were severed afterward, that a disqualification arises. The hand that was present at the moment of witnessing is the hand that must cast the first stone, and its subsequent loss removes the possibility of fulfilling that requirement.

## Meitvei Challenge

### Court Observers Testify

The Gemara raises a *meitvei* — a challenge to Shmuel's position — from the following *braita*: if two people come to a court and testify, "We are witnesses that this person received a *gmar din* in another *beit din*, with these specific witnesses and these specific charges," and the person had fled before execution — *harei zeh yehareg* — he should be put to death by this court. The implication of the *braita* is striking: the two individuals testifying never witnessed the crime themselves; they only observed the prior court proceedings. Yet their testimony would apparently be sufficient to carry out the execution.

This creates a direct tension with Shmuel's rule. If such court-observer testimony were valid, then even in a case where the original witnesses had their hands severed, two others who had merely watched the original proceedings could walk into a different court, testify to the conviction, and bring about execution — effectively circumventing the disqualification Shmuel describes.

### Same Witnesses Required

Shmuel resolves this tension with the interpretation *b'hen hen edav* — it must be that the very same original witnesses came to testify in the second court. The *braita* is not describing a case where independent observers testify to having watched a court case; it is a case where the original witnesses themselves appeared before the new tribunal. This is not a minor technical point. Shmuel's position rests on a fundamental principle: the witnesses who execute the convicted person must be the very same witnesses who saw the crime committed. Court-observer testimony — no matter how reliable — cannot substitute for this. Even according to Shmuel, the original witnesses must come forward, and the second court would conduct at least some form of proceeding, though given that they are testifying that a *gmar din* was already reached, the process would presumably be abbreviated.

## Execution Alternatives

### Backup Execution Methods

The Gemara now turns to a broader question, prompted by a *braita*: the verse *mot yumat ha-makeh rotze'ach hu* establishes that a murderer must be put to death according to the prescribed method. But what if it is impossible to carry out the assigned form of execution? *Minayin she-im ee atah yachol le-hamito be-mitah ha-ktuvah bo* — from where do we know that if you cannot execute someone by the prescribed method, you may use any other available means? The answer: *talmud lomar mot yumat ha-makeh mikol makom* — the verse teaches that he must be executed regardless. The obligation to carry out the death sentence overrides the obligation to follow the specific prescribed form. This would suggest, for instance, that if the witnesses had their hands cut off and *skilah* could not be performed, one might still execute the person by another method — which would undermine Shmuel's ruling entirely.

### Murder Exception

The Gemara rejects this line of reasoning, however, by noting that the general principle drawn from *mot yumat* cannot be universally applied. The rule allowing execution by alternative means is derived specifically in the context of *rotze'ach* — the murderer — and *goel ha-dam* — the blood redeemer. These are two distinct contexts, and together they form *shnei ktuvim ha-ba'im k'echad* — two scriptural examples that appear to establish a common rule.

### Two Examples Rule

This brings us to a fundamental hermeneutical principle: *shnei ktuvim ha-ba'im k'echad ein melamdin* — when two verses come together to teach the same principle, we do not extrapolate a general rule from them to apply across all of Torah. The principle that one may execute by alternative means if the prescribed method is unavailable is therefore limited to the two specific cases from which it is derived: murder (*rotze'ach*) and the *goel ha-dam*. It cannot be extended to, say, a case of *chillul Shabbat* or *avodah zarah* where the witnesses' hands have been severed. For those crimes, Shmuel's rule stands: if the specific requirements cannot be met, the person goes free.

## Goel HaDam Principle

### Blood Redeemer Role

The Gemara clarifies the scriptural basis for the *goel ha-dam*'s authority to use alternative means: *goel ha-dam yamit et ha-rotze'ach* — the blood redeemer may kill the manslayer. This is framed as a *mitzvah*: it is a positive obligation for the *goel ha-dam* to pursue the manslayer. The *goel ha-dam* is a close relative of the person who was killed, and the Torah grants him a special dispensation to pursue and kill the manslayer — even without a formal court procedure — so long as the manslayer has not yet reached sanctuary in an *ir miklat*.

### Court Appoints Redeemer

A remarkable principle follows: *u-minayin she-im ein lo goel she-beit din ma'amidin lo goel* — if the victim has no *goel*, from where do we know that the *beit din* appoints one on his behalf? The verse *bifig'o bo* — "when he encounters him" — is read expansively: *mikol makom*, any person authorized to do so may act as the *goel ha-dam*, regardless of familial connection.

What is striking about this is the transformation the institution undergoes. Reading the verses in the Torah, the *goel ha-dam* appears to be a purely spontaneous, extra-legal expression of family grief and honor — *yecham levavo*, his heart burns with vengeance. It is a special dispensation granted because of the emotional bond between family members and their slain relative. And yet here the Gemara presents it as a legislated, institutionalized component of the juridical process: if no family member steps forward, the court itself appoints an official surrogate. The principle is that manslaughter law, as constructed by the Torah, requires there to be a *goel ha-dam* — otherwise the entire framework of the *ir miklat* loses its force, since without the threat of the *goel ha-dam* there is no compelling reason for the manslayer to flee to sanctuary in the first place.

## Necessary Conditions

### Ben Sorer Parents

The Gemara now addresses the broader question of whether Shmuel's principle — that missing necessary conditions nullify the execution — requires a specific scriptural source, or whether it might be derived from a more general rule. A *mishna* is cited: if either parent of a *ben sorer u'moreh* is *gidem* (has an amputated hand), *ilem* (mute), *chiger* (lame), *suma* (blind), or *cheresh* (deaf), the son cannot be executed as a *ben sorer u'moreh*. Each of these disqualifications is derived from the specific language of the relevant verses: *vetafsu bo* — "and they shall seize him" — requires functioning hands; *vehotziu oto* — "and they shall bring him out" — requires the ability to walk; *ve'amru* — "and they shall say" — requires the ability to speak; *benenu zeh* — "this is our son" — requires the ability to point and see; *einenu shome'a bekolenu* — "he does not heed our voice" — requires that the parents themselves can hear.

The question raised is: why not simply say that even if the parents are disqualified in one of these ways, the son is still deserving of death and should be executed by an alternative means? The answer is that these requirements are special additional conditions legislated specifically for *ben sorer u'moreh* based on its own *psukim*, and cannot be overridden by a general backup principle. They are necessary conditions whose absence simply prevents the application of this particular law.

### Ir HaNidachat Square

A further proof is brought from the laws of *ir ha-nidachat*: if a city condemned as an idolatrous city has no *rechov* — no public city square — it cannot be treated as an *ir ha-nidachat*, according to Rabbi Yishmael. The Torah requires that all the property of the condemned city be gathered into the *rechov* and burned there. Without such a square, the defining act of the procedure cannot be carried out.

Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *osin la rechov* — if there is no city square, one is created. The only dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is whether the *rechov* must have pre-existed the city's designation as *ir ha-nidachat*, or whether one constructed after the fact is equally valid. But both agree — *dechulei alma ba'inan kra kideichtiv* — that a *rechov* is an indispensable requirement, as written in the Torah. No alternative procedure exists to circumvent it. This is another demonstration that necessary conditions on capital and related laws cannot be bypassed by appealing to a general principle of alternative enforcement.

The discussion is also an occasion to note the parallel with certain questions in the laws of *eruvin*, where modern *poskim* — notably the *Aruch HaShulchan* — debate whether contemporary cities, with their many streets and no single dominant thoroughfare, possess what the Gemara considers a *reshut ha-rabbim*. Rabbi Yishmael's position here, that the city's *rechov* must be the particular kind of public square the Torah envisions, touches on related conceptual terrain.

### Metzora Requirements

The Gemara then raises a *machlokes tanna'im* that reveals the dispute over necessary conditions to be an ancient one. The purification process of the *metzora* requires the application of blood and oil to three specific points: the right thumb, the right big toe, and the right ear. If the *metzora* lacks any of these — *ein lo bohen yad bohen regel ozen yemanit* — what is to be done?

The *Mishnah* records that he has no purification available to him ever — *ein lo taharah olamit*. Rabbi Eliezer, however, says one places the blood and oil *al mekomo* — on the place where the limb once was, or where it would have been — and that fulfills the requirement. Rabbi Shimon offers a different alternative: *noten al smolo veyotze* — one places it on the left side instead. Both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon maintain that a backup procedure exists, differing only on its nature. Rabbi Eliezer's approach suggests that the essential act concerns the specific location regardless of whether the limb is present; Rabbi Shimon's approach suggests that right-sidedness is essential but that the left can serve as a substitute. Worth noting is the deep structural parallel between the purification of the *metzora* and the inauguration of the *kohanim* in the *miluim*: both involve the same application of blood and oil to thumb, big toe, and ear — reflecting the conceptual symmetry between the transition from ordinary *Yisrael* to *kohen* and the transition from *metzora* back to ordinary *Yisrael*.

## Hanging After Execution

### Eliezer: All Stoned

The next *mishna* opens a new topic: *telihah* — the display of the body after execution by hanging it on a post. This is emphatically not execution by hanging; it is a post-mortem display of the corpse. *Kol haniskalin nitlin divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that everyone executed by *skilah* must also have their body hanged for display.

### Chachamim: Two Cases

The *Chachamim* disagree: *eino nitlah ela ha-migadef ve-oved avodah zarah* — only the blasphemer (*megadef*) and the idolater are subject to post-mortem hanging. On the question of orientation, the *Mishnah* records that a man is hung facing outward toward the public — *panav klapei ha'am* — while a woman, according to Rabbi Eliezer, faces the wooden beam. The *Chachamim* go further and hold that women are not hanged at all.

### Shimon ben Shetach Case

Rabbi Eliezer challenges the *Chachamim* with a historical precedent: *vehalo Shimon ben Shetach talah nashim be'Ashkelon* — did not Shimon ben Shetach, from the period of the *Zugot*, hang women in Ashkelon? The *Chachamim* respond that he hung eighty women on a single day — *ve'ein danim shnayim beyom echad* — and one cannot adjudicate two cases on the same day. The very fact that his conduct raised this procedural objection is itself noteworthy, and the Gemara will shortly examine precisely what the prohibition against judging two cases in one day entails.

## Hanging Derasha Methods

### Kilelat Elohim Pasuk

The Gemara examines the *drashot* underlying the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim*. A *braita* opens the discussion: *vehumat vetalita* — "he shall be put to death and you shall hang him." This might suggest that every form of execution is followed by hanging — *yachol kol ha-mumatin nitlin*. The verse then provides a limiting phrase: *ki kilelat elohim taluy* — "for it is a curse of God that he hangs." The practical consequence of this prohibition is significant: the body must be buried before nightfall. In practice, the *beit din* would carry out the hanging only moments before sunset and untie the body almost immediately — the display lasting mere seconds — so as not to violate the prohibition against leaving the body overnight.

The connection between *kilelat elohim* and the *megadef* is the pivot of the *drashah*: the word *kilelat* — curse — refers to the one who cursed God, that is, the *megadef*, who is executed by *skilah*. The Gemara unpacks the logic of this linkage and its implications for how the verse is read by each side.

The *Rambam* in *Hilchot Avodah Zarah*, Perek 2, famously explains why he included the laws of *megadef* within the laws of *avodah zarah*: it is precisely because of this Gemara that connects the two. One who blasphemes God has, in the deepest sense, denied divine sovereignty — *kafar be'ikar* — just as one who worships idols has denied God. The connection is not merely formal but conceptual: both the *megadef* and the *oved avodah zarah* represent a fundamental rupture with the foundational belief in one God.

### Klal U'Prat Method

The *Chachamim* derive their position through the *klal ufrat* hermeneutical method. *Vehumat vetalita* is the *klal* — the general principle; *ki kilelat elohim taluy* is the *prat* — the specific case. In the *klal ufrat* method, the *prat* functions as an explanation and limitation of the *klal*: *ein baklal ela mah shebaprat* — the *klal* applies only to what is specified in the *prat*. Even something similar to the *prat* cannot be included, because the *prat* is extremely limiting.

However, because the *klal* and *prat* here are not in the same verse — *lo talin nivlato al ha'etz* comes with some textual distance from *vehumat vetalita* — the *Chachamim* expand slightly beyond the pure *klal ufrat* rule. Since they are separated, *ata hani leribuyei* — the general clause comes to include one additional case. *Avodat kochavim*, which is similar to *megadef* in every meaningful way — both represent *kefira be'ikar*, denial of fundamental belief — is therefore included alongside the *megadef*.

### Ribui U'Miut Method

Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, employs the *ribui umiut* method. Here, *vehumat vetalita* is a *ribui* — a broad inclusion — and *ki kilelat elohim* is a *miut* — a limitation. Rashi explains the critical difference between the two approaches: in *klal ufrat*, the *prat* uproots the *klal* from its broad application and restricts it precisely to what the *prat* specifies — nothing more, even if similar. In *ribui umiut*, the *miut* merely narrows the range of application without entirely displacing the broader principle; there remains more room for inclusion. The *miut* does not eliminate the *ribui* but limits it.

Under Rabbi Eliezer's *ribui umiut* reading, because the two clauses are separated in the text, the *miut* — which on a closer reading would have limited application only to *avodah zarah* as similar to *megadef* — is understood to expand further, reaching *kol haniskalin*, all those executed by *skilah*. Had the clauses been closer together in the text, Rabbi Eliezer would have limited the expansion to *avodah zarah* alone, as most similar to *megadef*; the textual distance licenses the broader inclusion. In general, the *ribui umiut* method is the more expansive of the two, which accounts for the characteristic difference between the positions: the *Chachamim* using the more restrictive *klal ufrat* arrive at only two cases, while Rabbi Eliezer using the more expansive *ribui umiut* arrives at all cases of *skilah*.

## Gender in Hanging

### Face Directions

The Gemara now addresses the *machlokes* regarding orientation of the hanged body. The *Chachamim* derive from the verse *vechi yihye be'ish chet* — "when there is in a man a sin" — that the verse speaks of *ish*, a man, but not *ishah*, a woman: *oto velo otah*. Rabbi Eliezer, who cannot use this derivation to exclude women (since he holds women are hanged as well, differing only on orientation), reads *oto velo ksuto* — "him but not his garment" — deriving that the hanging is performed without clothing. This too has a rationale: part of the purpose of the post-mortem display is to shame the person for their transgression, and accordingly the body is displayed without garments, consistent with the practice at the time of *skilah* when clothing is removed to facilitate the execution.

### Women Not Hanged

The *Chachamim* then derive from a separate verse — *vechi yihye be'ish chet*, *ish velo ishah* — that women are categorically exempt from *telihah* altogether. Rabbi Eliezer uses this verse differently, as will be seen below.

### Ben Sorer Exception

Reish Lakish raises the question of *ben sorer u'moreh*: according to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that *kol haniskalin nitlin*, one executed by *skilah* is also hanged, does this apply to a *ben sorer u'moreh* as well? He argues that the verse *vechi yihye be'ish chet* — specifically the word *ish* — comes to exclude *ben sorer u'moreh*, who is not yet a man. Since he is a minor, the verse does not apply to him.

But a *braita* is cited that appears to attribute to Rabbi Eliezer the view that *ben sorer u'moreh niskal ve-nitla* — he is both stoned and hanged. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this by reading the verse differently: *ish velo ben* — the exclusion of *ben* is derived; but then *chet* is the operative word — *mi she-al chet neherag*, one who is killed for his sin. *Ben sorer u'moreh* is executed not for any sin he has actually committed but *al shum sofo* — on account of his projected future. He is *nidon al shem sofo*, preemptively sentenced. Since he is not killed for a *chet* in the full sense, he is excluded from the principle of *vechi yihye be'ish chet*. This produces a *miut achar miut* — a double exclusion — which, as a rule of *drashah*, comes to *lerabot*, to include: *ben sorer u'moreh* is therefore included in *telihah* even according to Rabbi Eliezer.

The discussion of *ben sorer u'moreh* being executed *al shem sofo* — preemptively, for what he will become rather than what he has done — evokes the theological principle of *ba'asher hu sham*: God judged Yishmael according to who he was at that moment, not according to what he would become. The *ben sorer u'moreh* represents a deliberate statutory exception to that principle, and its full treatment awaits *Perek Ben Sorer u'Moreh*.

## One Case Per Day Rule

### Two Cases Rule

Returning to the conclusion of the *mishna* — *ein danim shnayim beyom echad* — the Gemara examines what exactly is prohibited. The *mishna* cited Shimon ben Shetach's hanging of eighty women in Ashkelon as a case where this rule was apparently violated, or at least raised as a concern.

### Different Execution Types

Rav Chisda proposes a narrow reading: *lo shanu ela bishtei mitot* — the prohibition against judging two cases in one day applies only when the two cases involve two different types of execution. *Aval bemita achat danin* — if both cases involve the same form of execution, two cases may in fact be judged on the same day. Since Shimon ben Shetach's case involved women all subject to the same *mitah*, it would fall within what is permitted according to this reading.

The Gemara then revises even this formulation: *lo shanu ela bemita achat ke'ein shtei mitot* — the prohibition applies even to a single type of execution that is, in some respect, like two. This means two different *aveirot* that happen to carry the same capital punishment. *Aval bemita achat va'aveirah achat danin* — two entirely identical cases — same crime, same punishment — may be heard together on the same day.

### Adultery Challenge

Rav Ada bar Ahava challenges this: *ein danim shnayim beyom echad afilu benoef venoefet* — even a male and female adulterer cannot be judged on the same day. This is a powerful challenge: not only is it the same crime and the same punishment, it is literally the same act committed together. One would think this is the clearest possible case of *bemita achat va'aveirah achat*. Yet the *braita* rules that even this falls under *ein danim shnayim beyom echad*.

### Bat Kohen Resolution

Rav Chisda resolves the challenge: the case must involve a *bat kohen* and her lover. A *bat kohen* who commits adultery is executed not by *chenek* — the standard form of execution for adultery — but by *sreifah*, one of the relatively rare instances where burning applies. Her male partner, however, is executed by *chenek*. Thus even though it is the same act and technically the same crime, the two parties face different forms of execution — and that is why they cannot be judged together on the same day.

Alternatively, the case involves *bat kohen* and *zomemei zomemeha* — the false witnesses who had conspired against her being themselves exposed by a third set of witnesses. In such a case, she would be executed by *sreifah* while the exposed false witnesses would be executed by *chenek* — since the principle of *va'asitem lo ka'asher zamam* would, by some views, prescribe *sreifah* for the first set of witnesses but the second set, who were trying to discredit true witnesses, would receive the ordinary punishment of *chenek*. In either formulation, the result is two different *mitot*, which is why the prohibition applies.

## Beit Din Elastic Power

### Rabbi Elazar Statement

A *braita* records the well-known statement of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov: *shamati shebeit din makin veonshin shelo min haTorah* — I have heard that a *beit din* may administer lashes and punishments that are not prescribed by Torah law. This is a foundational principle for the concept of extra-legal judicial authority, one that has generated extensive discussion in later literature — notably in a *drashah* of the *Ran* and in a responsum of the *Rosh* arising from a case in Spain where an informant had endangered the Jewish community. The *Rosh*, drawing on this principle, argued for the power of contemporary rabbinic authority to impose punishments not found explicitly in Torah law, and reportedly suggested that the informant's tongue be cut out — a punishment with no basis in the *Written Torah* — precisely because of this extra-legal elastic authority.

### Syag LaTorah Purpose

The critical qualification is that this authority does not license acting *against* Torah law: *velo la'avor al divrei Torah* — it is not a license to transgress.
