The entire purpose is *kedei la'asot syag la-Torah* — to build a protective fence around Torah law, to deter violations when ordinary enforcement mechanisms are insufficient or when social conditions demand a more forceful response.

### Horse Riding Example

The first illustration: *umaseh be-echad sherachav al sus be-Shabbat bimei Yevanim* — there was a case of a man who rode a horse on *Shabbat* during the Hellenistic period. He was brought before the *beit din* and stoned to death. Now, riding a horse on *Shabbat* is a *de-rabbanan* prohibition — specifically a *shvut*, a rabbinic decree enacted as a *gezirah* lest one break off a branch to use as a whip. Stoning is, of course, a capital punishment reserved for the most severe Torah violations. By any standard measure, this man's offense carried no capital punishment at all.

The Gemara explains: *lo mipnei she-ra'uy lekach ela she-ha-sha'ah tzericha lekach* — not because this was the fitting penalty, but because the hour required it. The Hellenistic period was one of intense social and religious pressure; observance of rabbinic enactments around *Shabbat* was being eroded. The *beit din* of that generation determined that radical enforcement was necessary to impress upon the community the seriousness of even rabbinic-level *Shabbat* violations. One might imagine that the relevant *de-rabbanans* had only recently been legislated, and that without dramatic enforcement they would remain a dead letter. The principle underlying the enforcement is extra-legal authority deployed precisely because the *hora'at sha'ah* — the need of the hour — demanded it.

### Public Relations Example

The second illustration: *ma'aseh be-adam echad she-hitiach im ishto tachat ha-te'enah* — there was a case of a man who engaged in sexual relations with his wife in public, beneath a fig tree. He was brought to *beit din* and given lashes. There is, in fact, no *halacha* that prohibits marital relations per se; only the public nature of the act made it objectionable. Technically, no punishment attaches to this conduct. Yet here again, *lo mipnei she-ra'uy lekach ela she-ha-sha'ah tzericha lekach* — the generation required a strong public response to conduct that, while not halakhically prohibited in the strict sense, was socially destructive and publicly disgraceful.

## Hanging Methods

### Hanging Procedure

The *mishna* turns to the practical procedure of *telihah*. How is the hanging carried out? *Meshaki'in et ha-korah ba-aretz* — a vertical beam is planted in the ground. *Ve-ha-etz yotzei* — a horizontal board extends from it. The condemned person's two hands are bound together — *makif shtei yadav zo al gav zo* — and the body is suspended from the beam in that posture, hands crossed behind the back.

### Yosei Alternative

Rabbi Yosei offers an alternative: *ha-korah mutal al ha-kotel* — rather than planting the beam in the ground, one leans a beam against the wall. *Ve-toleh oto ke-derech she-ha-tabachim osim* — the body is then hung in the manner that butchers use when hanging an animal that is being flayed. This is a more practical method requiring less preparation, and it serves the same purpose of briefly displaying the body.

### Immediate Removal

Whatever the method employed, the requirement is unambiguous: *u-matirin oto mi-yad* — they untie him immediately. The moment the body has been hung, it is taken down. This near-instantaneous display is the fulfillment of the *mitzvah* of *telihah*; leaving the body up even briefly longer than necessary begins to encroach on the prohibition of *lo talin*. If the body is left overnight, *over alav be-lo ta'aseh* — one has violated a negative commandment of the Torah.

## Criminal Burial Laws

### No Overnight Hanging

The prohibition is stated explicitly in the verse: *lo talin nivlato al ha'etz* — you shall not leave his corpse hanging on the wood overnight. This is accompanied by a positive commandment — *ki kavor tikberenu* — you shall certainly bury him.

### Divine Curse Reason

The verse gives its own reason: *ki kilelat elohim taluy* — for it is a curse of God to leave the body hanging. The plain sense of the verse (*pshat*) is that leaving a corpse on display is repulsive and degrading — an affront to human dignity and, by extension, to God whose image humanity reflects. The *derash* adds another dimension: this person had *beirach et HaShem* — cursed God — and *nimtza Shem Shamayim mitchalel* — God's name becomes desecrated if the display of this curse becomes too public. There is a tension built into the law: the display must occur, because it serves as a deterrent and gives expression to the gravity of the crime; but it must not persist, because prolonging it risks further desecrating the divine name by publicizing the terrible act that was committed.

### Rabbi Meir Suffering

Rabbi Meir draws a profound theological teaching from this verse. When a person suffers, the divine presence responds as if in sympathy: *lashon omeret kallani me-roshi kallani me-zero'i* — the language of the *Shechinah* says, as it were, "my head aches, my arm aches." This is a striking expression of the principle that God's presence is implicated in human suffering, even the suffering of the wicked. If this is true of the suffering of a condemned criminal, *kal vachomer* — how much more so — is God pained by the spilling of the blood of the righteous.

### Honor Exception

The prohibition against leaving a body overnight is not limited to executed criminals: *kol ha-malin et meto over be-lo ta'aseh* — anyone who leaves any corpse unburied overnight transgresses a negative commandment. This applies to all the dead, not only those executed by *beit din*.

However, there is an important exception: *she-hilinhu l'chevodo* — if the body is left overnight for the *kavod* of the deceased, there is no violation. *Le-havi lo aron ve-tachrichin* — to allow time to procure a coffin or shrouds — that delay is permitted, because the delay itself constitutes an act of respect. The underlying principle is that the prohibition targets delay that reflects disregard for the dead; delay undertaken in service of the deceased's honor is not only permitted but appropriate. In contemporary practice, this principle is invoked when families need to wait for relatives to travel from afar — from overseas, from distant cities — in order to be present at the funeral. Such waiting is considered *she-hilinhu l'chevodo* and does not violate the prohibition.

### Burial Plot Types

Executed criminals were not buried in their families' ancestral burial plots: *velo hayu kovrin oto be-kivrot avotav* — he was not buried with his fathers. Instead, the *beit din* maintained two dedicated criminal cemeteries: one for those executed by *hereg* and *chenek*, and a separate plot for those executed by *skilah* and *sreifah*. The separation reflects the relative severity of the different forms of capital punishment — the more severe and the less severe are kept distinct.

### Bone Gathering

Once the flesh had decomposed — *nit'akel ha-basar* — the practice was *melaktin et ha'atzamot*, gathering the bones for secondary interment *be-mikoman*, in their place. Whether *be-mikoman* refers to reburial in the same criminal cemetery or eventual transfer to the ancestral family plot is itself a subject of debate. The practice of *likut atzamot* — secondary bone-gathering — was the standard burial practice of the *mishnaic* period, discussed extensively in *Moed Katan*: bodies were first interred in a cave or rock tomb, and after a year or so when the flesh had decomposed, the bones were gathered and placed in an ossuary for permanent burial. This two-stage burial practice, common throughout the land of Israel in the Second Temple and *Tanna'itic* periods, is not the norm today, reflecting one of the more significant shifts in Jewish burial practice over the centuries.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 46b

## Burial & Cemeteries

### Burial Overview

The *mishna* at the close of 46a addresses the post-execution treatment of the condemned. After carrying out the death penalty, the court would not bury the executed person in the family cemetery. Instead, two separate graveyards were maintained: one for those executed by the more stringent forms of execution, and one for those executed by the more lenient forms. This distinction ensures that even in death, the gradations of punishment are preserved, and that those who violated the law in the most severe ways are not interred alongside family members.

### Bone Collection

The *mishna* further states: *nis'achal habasar, m'laktin et ha'atzamot v'kovrin otan bimkoman* — once the flesh had decomposed, they would gather the bones and rebury them in the family plot. This practice of *likut atzamot* — the secondary collection and reburial of bones after decomposition — was common in that era more broadly, and the *mishna* here specifies that it was available even for the executed criminal, allowing eventual return to the family burial ground once the flesh had run its course.

### Relatives & Mourning

The *mishna* then describes a striking social ritual: *v'hakerovim ba'im v'sho'alim bishlom hadayanim uvishlom ha'edim* — the relatives of the executed person would come and greet the judges and witnesses, as if to say, "We hold no grudge; we believe this judgment was just." This practice served to protect the honor of the court and to prevent lingering communal strife and resentment.

Regarding mourning, the *mishna* rules that the relatives would not observe *aveilus* for the executed person, but they would be *onenim*. The distinction is important. *Aninut* — the acute state of inward devastation — is a feeling, and as the *mishna* concludes: *she'ein aninut ela balev*, *aninut* is only in the heart. No one can legislate emotion, and the family may naturally feel the weight of the loss. But *aveilus* — the formal, public practice of mourning — is an expression of honor to the deceased, and that the family may not perform. Rashi frames this positively: the relatives refrain from *aveilus* not because the executed person is beneath its dignity, but because the absence of *aveilus* itself constitutes an additional disgrace, and that disgrace functions as *kapara* — atonement — for the condemned.

---

## Execution Procedures

### Hanging Method

A *baraisa* clarifies what the Torah means when it speaks of hanging. One might read the verse *v'talita v'humat* as mandating crucifixion in the Roman manner — hang the person and the hanging itself kills him. The *baraisa* corrects this: *talmud lomar v'humat v'talita* — first you put the person to death by the court's prescribed method, *and then* you hang the body. The hanging is a post-mortem act, not the execution itself.

### Sunset Timing

The *baraisa* continues: *mashhinin oto ad samuch lishki'at hachama* — you wait until close to nightfall before completing and announcing the final judgment. This seems puzzling at first glance, since *halanat hadin* — postponing the verdict — is itself forbidden. The resolution is that the prohibition of *halanat hadin* applies after the judgment has been formally declared; what is being delayed here is the moment of public announcement and execution, not the deliberative process. And the reason for timing it so close to sunset becomes clear from Rashi: if you hang the body in the morning, there is every reason to be complacent about taking it down — hours remain before nightfall, and, like the woman in the parable who had but one task and never accomplished it precisely because she had all day, the duty to remove the body might be forgotten or procrastinated until it becomes nightfall without having acted. *Shema yitrashlu bikvuraso veyavo lidei shikcha* — perhaps they will be negligent about burial and it will be forgotten. By timing the execution to occur just before nightfall, you guarantee urgency: the body must come down immediately.

### Body Removal

This urgency is codified directly: *echad koveish v'echad matir* — one person ties and another unties simultaneously, or in immediate succession. The hanging becomes the most perfunctory of acts, done purely to fulfill the technical *mitzvat teliyah*, with none of the punitive public display that ordinarily accompanies hanging. The Rabbis are quite openly reshaping what the broader purpose of hanging might be. Just as the Rabbis found ways to make capital punishment nearly impossible to carry out, here too the logic of *kilalat Elokim taluy* — that it is a disgrace before God to leave a body hanging — drives the entire procedure toward minimizing the duration of exposure as much as possible. The timing close to sunset is designed not merely to avoid transgressing the prohibition of leaving the body overnight but to reduce the period of hanging to the absolute minimum, even if that creates complications around *inuy hadin* and the possibility of a last-minute reversal while taking the condemned out for execution.

---

## Source & Ground

### Tree vs. Post

A second *baraisa* addresses the biblical text's use of the word *etz* — wood or tree. One might think that the verse permits hanging on either a detached beam or a tree still connected to the ground. The *baraisa* derives from the juxtaposition of *ki kavor tikberenu* — you shall surely bury him — that the instrument of hanging must be such that burial can follow immediately afterward. This means: *mi she'eino mechusar ela kevurah* — something that requires nothing further before burial can occur. A tree connected to the ground requires cutting it down first; that intermediate act disqualifies it. The Sages hold that simply uprooting a stake from the ground — *tlishah* — is trivial and does not count as an intervening step, so a post embedded in the ground would still be permitted. Rabbi Yosi goes further, maintaining that even pulling a stake from the ground is a meaningful act, which would seem to leave one uncertain about what method he would endorse, as the *gemara* notes without resolution.

### Twin Brothers

The *gemara* then cites a *tanya* presenting a parable from Rabbi Meir that expands and deepens the concept of *kilalat Elokim taluy*. Until this point, the phrase might have been read narrowly — the one hanged is the blasphemer, who is executed *because* he cursed God. Rabbi Meir offers a broader reading: *mashal l'mah hadavar domeh l'shnei achim te'omim b'ir achat* — consider two twin brothers in the same city. One becomes king; the other becomes a bandit. The king orders his twin brother hanged. Anyone who passes and sees the body hanging remarks: the king is hanged. The visual identification is so complete that the dignified twin is implicated in the indignity of the condemned one. So too, human beings are created in the image of God. When a human body hangs in disgrace, it is as though the divine image itself is on display in humiliation. This is what *kilalat Elokim taluy* means in its fullest sense. God, as it were, commanded that the condemned be executed — just as the king commanded his brother's death — but the ongoing presence of the hanging body is a disgrace to the image in which all human beings are formed.

### God's Anguish

The *mishna* itself contains the *derasha*: *kalani me-roshi, kalani mi-zero'i* — God, as it were, says: my head is heavy upon me, my arm is heavy upon me. This anthropomorphizing language — God speaking of his own distress — intensifies the identification between the divine and the human being made in the divine image. When the hanged body remains on display, God experiences anguish. The *gemara* then parses the precise wordplay underlying *kilalat Elokim*. Abaye reads *kilalat* as suggesting that things are light — *kales kales* — which is taken to mean that things that should feel weighty now feel insubstantial, conveying heaviness through irony. Rava objects: if that is the intent, the verse should have said *kaveda alai roshi*, "my head is heavy" — why speak of lightness? Rava instead reads it as *ki alima* — the world feels light, which is likewise an expression of existential heaviness. The *gemara* then raises the question of how much work this play on *kilalat* is doing: the verse needs at minimum to establish that a blasphemer is the paradigm of the one who is hanged. Perhaps the entire verse is consumed by that teaching alone. The *gemara* replies that if that were the sole purpose, the verse would have said simply *mekallel*; the double *lamed* of *kilalat* yields two teachings simultaneously — the blasphemer, and God's anguish. Throughout this passage, Chazal give pointed expression to their profound discomfort with the entire practice of hanging.

---

## Universal Burial

### Biblical Basis

The *gemara* broadens the discussion: *v'lo zu bilvad* — not only the executed criminal must be buried promptly; the prohibition extends to any corpse. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rashbi derives this from the verse *ki kavor tikberenu bayom hahu* — you shall surely bury him on that day — reading *bayom hahu* not as limited to the executed criminal but as establishing a general norm: leaving any body unburied overnight constitutes a violation of a *lo ta'aseh*. The *gemara* then pivots from the prohibition against leaving the body overnight to a more fundamental question: where does the obligation to bury at all come from?

### Shapur's Challenge

The *gemara* reports that the Persian king Shapur posed this challenge to Rav Chama: *kvurah min haTorah minayin* — where does the Torah require burial? In Zoroastrian practice, bodies were left exposed in the open. Rav Chama was silent — he had no ready answer. Rav Acha bar Yaakov expresses astonishment: *imsar alma b'yadei d'tifshai* — has the world been handed over to fools? Could Rav Chama not cite *ki kavor tikberenu*? The *gemara* answers that Shapur could have deflected even that: perhaps *kavor tikberenu* only specifies *how* you handle a body — by placing it in a box — rather than mandating burial in the ground. The doubling of the root could mean burial *properly*, not burial *in earth*, and Shapur would not have been persuaded by the double language alone.

Attempts to derive the obligation from the practice of the *tzaddikim* — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah — all buried in the ground — are dismissed: that merely reflects *minhaga be'alma*, ancient custom, not religious obligation. Even the fact that God Himself buried Moshe proves only that God did not want Moshe to be treated differently from common practice. None of these demonstrations establishes a *chiyuv*.

### Doubling of Bury

The result is that the *gemara* can only offer *remez l'kvurah min haTorah* — a *hint* in the Torah — rather than an explicit commandment. The word *remez* here is not merely rhetorical modesty; it is a halachically significant categorization.

### Rabbinic Obligation

This brings us to a striking conclusion noted by Rabbeinu Chananel in his commentary to 47a. After canvassing all of the attempted proofs and finding them inadequate to convince even Shapur, Rabbeinu Chananel states plainly: *mitzvah zo miderabbanan hi* — this *mitzvah* is rabbinic in origin, not biblical. The general assumption of halachic discourse is that there is a *de'oraita* obligation of *kevurah* and a *lo ta'aseh de'oraita* of leaving a body unburied overnight. Rabbeinu Chananel appears to read the *gemara* as concluding otherwise. One might add that the *remez* language could reflect a different limitation as well: perhaps the verse in context is speaking specifically about the executed criminal and the need to prevent the ongoing *bizayon* of hanging, rather than articulating a free-standing universal obligation of burial. What precisely constitutes a *de'oraita* obligation of *kevurah*, and whether burial specifically in the earth — as opposed to some other form — is itself biblically mandated, remains a genuinely open question that this *sugya* does not resolve with finality.

---

## Purpose of Burial

### Disgrace vs. Atonement

The *gemara* now poses a question that, as the analysis unfolds, reveals considerable halachic depth: *kevurah mishum bizyona hu o mishum kapara?* — is the purpose of burial to protect the body from disgrace, or to provide atonement for the deceased? Rashi notes that the *bizayon* at stake is not merely relative — not simply that burial is the norm and its absence therefore a deviation. It is also that a body left unburied decomposes visibly and becomes repulsive, producing an experience of degradation for all who witness it.

### Refusal Implications

The practical difference between the two rationales is sharpest when the deceased has expressed a preference not to be buried: *de'amar lo be'ina likvura le'hahu gavra*. If burial is to prevent *bizayon*, then the deceased has no standing to waive it — *lav kol kimeineih* — because the concern is not his alone. It implicates the family who survives him, and more broadly, it implicates the dignity of the divine image instantiated in every human body. One cannot be *mochel* on a *bizayon* that is not entirely one's own to waive. But if the reason is *kapara* — atonement for the soul — and the person declares *lo be'ina kapara*, I do not want atonement, does he then have the ability to waive it?

This is a striking methodological problem in its own right. If *kevurah* is *de'oraita*, the standard principle of *lo darshinan ta'ama de'kra* — we do not allow the rationale behind a commandment to exempt individuals from its application — would seem to foreclose any *nafka mina* based on motive. The *poskim* address this tension directly. Some commentators see in this very analysis a further indication supporting Rabbeinu Chananel's view that the obligation may be rabbinic, since a *de'oraita* obligation would not typically be undone by identifying its purpose and finding it inapplicable to a particular case.

### Righteous Burial

One might ask: if burial is for *kapara*, why are *tzaddikim* buried? Do the righteous require atonement? The *gemara* answers with the verse: *adam ein tzaddik ba'aretz asher ya'aseh tov v'lo yecheta* — there is no one so righteous on earth who does only good and never sins. Even the greatest *tzaddik* has some need of *kapara*, and burial provides it.

---

## Eulogies

### Hesped Purpose

The *gemara* raises a parallel question regarding the *hesped*: *yikara de'chayei havei o yikara de'shichvei havei?* — is the eulogy for the honor of the living, or the honor of the dead? It is worth noting at the outset that *hesped* in the Talmudic context is not simply a formal oration praising the deceased. It was performative — mourners would wail, *mekonenot* would compose elegies — and it was understood to be a powerful social ritual. The question of whose honor it serves is thus not merely theoretical.

### Abraham & Sarah

The *gemara* brings its first proof: *va-yavo Avraham lispod le-Sarah v'livkotah* — Abraham came to eulogize Sarah and to weep for her. If the *hesped* is for the honor of the living, why was the burial of Sarah postponed until Abraham arrived? Delaying burial — which creates its own concerns of *bizayon* to the body — can only be justified for the sake of the deceased. The *gemara* deflects this proof: *Sarah gufa nicha lah ki heichi de'miyaker be'Avraham* — Sarah herself would have wanted this, because she would have wished Abraham to receive the honor that comes to those whose loved ones are properly eulogized. The *hesped* is still framed as being in service of the living, but the justification for postponing the burial is that the *meis* herself desired this honor for her survivors.

### Yerovam's Son

The *gemara* next cites the case of Aviyah ben Yerovam: only this one among the descendants of Yerovam would be properly buried and eulogized, the others being left unburied as punishment for the sins of their lineage. If *hesped* is for the honor of the living, why would the surviving family — themselves *resha'im* — be denied that honor? They need the *hesped* as much as anyone. The *gemara* answers: *nicha leh le'tzaddika de'miyakru beih inshi* — the righteous young man himself would have wanted to be properly honored, and for his sake the *hesped* is done, even though his surviving relatives are unworthy. The honor flows toward the living — that is what *hesped* does — but the motivation for giving it can derive from what the deceased would have wanted.

### Chizkiyahu

The discussion expands beyond *hesped* to encompass all funeral proceedings. The case of Chizkiyahu is invoked: *shegirer atzmos aviv al mita shel chavalim* — Chizkiyahu dragged the bones of his father Menashe on a bed of ropes when Menashe died, thereby actively disgracing the body, in order to bring *kapara* for his wicked father. If funeral proceedings are for the honor of the living, why would Chizkiyahu do something that reflects so badly on himself and on the Jewish people? The *gemara* answers that *Yisrael gufaihu neicha lehu d'michli yeikara'ihu legabei* — Israel themselves were willing to forgo their own honor for the sake of the *kapara* that their king would thereby achieve.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, in his final instructions, directed that his bier not be stopped in the small villages as it was carried from Tzippori to Beit She'arim. If *hesped* is for the honor of the living, the people of those small towns might benefit from the opportunity to eulogize Rabbi. Why would Rabbi deny them that? The *gemara* answers: *nefisha behu Yisrael tfei* — the aggregate honor of all of Israel is greater when large crowds gather in major cities than when dispersed efforts are made village by village. Even according to the view that *hesped* honors the living, Rabbi's instruction was an expression of that same principle — more honor to more people through concentration.

### Conclusion

After all of these exchanges, the *gemara* arrives at a definitive conclusion from a *baraisa*: *kol ha-oseh eino ela lichvodo shel meis* — everything done in funeral proceedings is for the honor of the dead. The *gemara* then challenges this from the example where burial was postponed for a legitimate reason connected to the living: how can postponement be justified if everything is for the dead? The *gemara* responds: *kol ha-oseh lichvodo shel chai ein bo bizayon la-meis* — anything done for the honor of the living does not constitute *bizayon* to the dead. And a final proof arrives: *siman yafeh la-meis she-nifrain mimenu le-achar misah* — it is actually a good sign for the deceased when bad things happen to the body after death, such as no eulogy, no burial, or animals dragging the body, because these disgraceful occurrences bring *kapara*. Since these things are "good" by virtue of what they do for the *meis*, it is clear that everything surrounding the body is understood in terms of honor and disgrace to the dead, not to the living. *Shma minah yikara de-shachvei hu, shma minah* — this is the conclusion.

It is worth pausing to note that the *mishna*'s ruling — that relatives do not observe *aveilus* for the executed — now raises a related and unresolved question: whose honor is *aveilus* for? If, as we have now concluded, funeral proceedings honor the dead, then the prohibition of *aveilus* for the executed must be because *aveilus* too is an expression of honor for the deceased, honor that the executed does not yet deserve. This would also imply that a person who instructs his children not to sit *shiva* for him could in principle be obeyed, since *aveilus* is primarily in service of the dead. This question is discussed by the *poskim* and remains live.

---

## Postponement

### Disgrace Definition

The *gemara* now draws together the threads of the preceding analysis. Postponing burial is prohibited when it constitutes *bizayon* to the body. But *bizayon* is not an absolute category — it is contextual. The prohibition against leaving a body overnight, derived from the verse *lo talin nivlato al ha-etz*, applies *dumya de'talui d'it bei bizayon* — in circumstances resembling those of the hanged body, where there is genuine disgrace. Where burial is delayed for a legitimate purpose, and that purpose removes the character of neglect or contempt from the delay, there is no *bizayon* and therefore no prohibition.

### Legitimate Delays

The *gemara* identifies specific categories of permissible delay: *lehavi lo aron v'tachrichin* — waiting to procure a coffin or burial shrouds; *lishmoa alav ayarot* — waiting so that surrounding towns can come to participate in the burial; *lehavi lo mekonenot* — waiting to bring wailers or eulogizers. In all of these cases, *eino over alav* — one does not violate the prohibition. The *gemara* makes explicit that the key principle is that any act done *lichvodo shel chai* — for the honor of the living — does not constitute *bizayon la-meis*, and thus any such purpose can justify postponement, without needing to be framed as what the deceased would have wanted.

This gives somewhat broader latitude than the framework articulated in the conclusion about *hesped*. There, the ultimate principle was that all funeral proceedings honor the dead. Here, the *gemara* justifies delay even for the living's honor, on the grounds that purposeful, dignified delay is not *bizayon*. The practical consequence is significant: one does not have to demonstrate that this is what the deceased would have wanted, or that it is directly for the deceased's honor. As long as there is a genuine reason and the delay is not mere neglect, it falls outside the prohibition.

---

## Atonement

### Abaye vs. Rava

The *gemara* turns to a dispute that bears directly on the question of when *kapara* is achieved for the executed criminal, and by extension why the family cannot observe *aveilus*. The immediate context is a statement about what happens to *kodshei mizbei'ach* — sanctified animals designated for offerings — belonging to inhabitants of an *ir hanidachat*, a condemned city whose people are executed for collective apostasy. The *gemara* asks: once those people are executed, have they achieved *kapara*? If so, they are no longer *resha'im*, and their offerings — normally disqualified because they are offerings of the wicked — should in principle be eligible for the altar. The answer invokes the principle of *dichuy*: once the offerings were disqualified, they remain permanently disqualified even if the owners' status changes. But this raises the underlying question: does execution confer *kapara* at all?

Abaye challenges the assumption: *mi savrat mes mitoch risho havei lei kapara?* — do you think dying in one's state of wickedness produces atonement? Abaye holds that *mes mitoch risho lo havei lei kapara* — death occurring while the person is still in their unrepentant, unatoned state does not bring atonement.

### Death Types

Rava responds with a crucial distinction: one must not conflate dying naturally in a state of wickedness with being executed. *Mes mitoch risho ki orchei ka mayes, lo havei lei kapara* — natural death occurring in the ordinary course of things does not confer atonement; the mere biological fact of dying is not redemptive. But *neherag mitoch risho, keivan d'lav ki orchei mayes, havei lei kapara* — execution, which is not the natural course of events, does constitute *kapara*, because the violent, imposed quality of the death itself is the redemptive mechanism. Notably, the *gemara* does not at this point require *viduy* or *teshuvah* as prerequisites; the act of being executed by itself appears sufficient. Rava also observes that the category of *neherag* would appear to include violent death more broadly — not only judicial execution.

This is borne out by a proof from *Mizmor L'Asaph* (Tehillim 79): the verse speaks of *nivlas avadecha* and *basar chasidecha* — the bodies of God's servants and the flesh of His pious ones — given over to the birds and beasts by foreign conquerors. These people were not the truly righteous; the verse distinguishes *chasidecha* from *avadecha*, and the latter are people who *mechayvei dina de'ikra* — who were deserving of death. Yet once they were killed, they are called God's servants. Violent, unjust death achieves *kapara* and removes the designation of *rasha*.

### Court Execution

Abaye now introduces a further distinction: *mi kamidames harugei malchus l'harugei Beis Din?* — can you really compare those killed by a foreign government to those executed by the court? *Harugei malchus, keivan d'shelo bedin kamikteli, haveu lehu kapara* — those killed unjustly, outside any legal process, achieve *kapara* precisely because the injustice inflicted upon them is such a violent rupture of the moral order that it itself becomes redemptive. But *harugei Beis Din, keivan devedin kamikteli, lo havei lehu kapara* — those executed by the court, through an ordered and legitimate judicial process, do not achieve *kapara* through the execution itself.

This is a striking and counterintuitive conclusion. One would have supposed that judicial execution, carried out as the sanction for a specific sin after due process — accompanied by confession and formal procedure — would be the paradigmatic case of atonement through punishment. Yet the *gemara* holds that it is precisely the orderly, lawful character of the execution that prevents it from functioning as *kapara*. The violent, unjust death of an enemy's victim has more redemptive power than the lawful execution of a convicted criminal. The proof that *harugei Beis Din* do not achieve *kapara* through execution alone comes from the *mishna* itself: *lo hayu kovrin oso bekivros avosav* — they were not buried in the family cemetery. If execution alone had conferred *kapara*, there would be no reason to continue treating the deceased as a *rasha* through separate burial.

### Decomposition

The *gemara* then considers the response that perhaps *kapara* requires both death *and* burial: *misah ukevurah bainan*. The execution alone is insufficient; burial is also necessary. On this view, a person executed by the court will eventually achieve *kapara*, but only after burial — which is why separate burial is still required at the moment of interment (since *kapara* has not yet occurred), but in principle, once buried, the person's status changes. Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges this from the *mishna*: if burial produces *kapara*, why can the family not observe *aveilus* after the burial? The *gemara* answers: *bainan nami ikul basar* — you need not only death and burial but the decomposition of the flesh. *Kapara* does not arrive at the moment of burial; it arrives only as the body begins to break down underground.

### Time Gap

Rav Ashi offers a more refined formulation. *Aveilus* begins *mistimas hagolel* — from the sealing of the grave. *Kapara* begins *mikeichazu tzara dekivra purta* — when the first traces of the pain of the grave begin, a little while after burial, when the first stages of decomposition commence. The difficulty is that there is an irreducible time gap: at the moment *aveilus* would normally begin, *kapara* has not yet occurred, and the deceased is still classified as a *rasha*. Therefore the family is not obligated to observe *aveilus*. Once *kapara* arrives, shortly thereafter, the *chiyuv* of *aveilus* has already been displaced — *ho'il v'idchu yidchu*, just as the disqualified *korbanos* of the *ir hanidachat* remain permanently disqualified once they have been pushed off. The parallel to *dichuy* thus turns out to have been the very key to the discussion from the beginning.

The result is two competing explanations for why *aveilus* is not observed: either *kapara* arrives only after full decomposition — a year or more later — making *aveilus* permanently inapplicable; or *kapara* arrives an hour or so after burial, but it comes too late for *aveilus* to begin, and the principle of *dichuy* forever bars it. A further implication: if a relative was not aware of the execution until after the burial had taken place, it is possible that according to the second view, *aveilus* could be observed at that point — the *chiyuv* beginning upon hearing the news, by which time *kapara* may already have been achieved.

---

## Forbidden Benefit

### Grave Soil

The *gemara* now turns to the question of *issurei hana'ah* — prohibitions on deriving benefit — as they apply to things associated with a *meis*. The background case is that people would take dirt from Rav's grave as a *segula* for treating a day-old fever. When Shmuel was told of this practice, he expressed no concern. The *gemara* frames the question: is the soil of a grave *assur behana'ah*?

### Ground Analogy

The answer is that *karka olam* — the earth itself — does not become forbidden. The principle is derived by analogy to *avodat kochavim*: the verse states *al he-harim eloheihem v'lo he-harim eloheihem* — their gods are on the mountains, but the mountains are not their gods. If one worships a mountain, the mountain itself does not become a forbidden idol, because ground cannot be made *assur*. The *gemara* extends this: just as *avodat kochavim bemachubar lo mitzra* — an idol attached to the earth cannot become forbidden — so too burial in the earth does not render the surrounding earth *assur behana'ah*.

### Mausoleums

However, things change when we move from bare ground to constructed structures. A mausoleum or built grave — *kever binyan* — stands in a different category. Something that was originally detached and subsequently attached to the ground retains enough independence from the earth that it can acquire the halachic status of *issurei hana'ah*. Several challenges from the *gemara* — a grave dug for a father but used elsewhere; a new grave into which a *nefel* was placed — are all resolved by the *gemara* as referring to constructed graves, not bare earth. The distinction is somewhat strained in *pshat*, since a mausoleum that is "found" unexpectedly or whose provenance is unknown seems implausible. Nevertheless, the *gemara* expends considerable effort sustaining the principle that earth itself cannot be made *assur behana'ah*, and that only constructed elements qualify.

### Grave Types

The *gemara* closes with a *baraisa* enumerating three categories of graves with respect to moving a body. A *kever hanimtza* — a body discovered buried in one's field without the owner's knowledge — may be moved, and once moved, the location is *tahor* and *mutar behana'ah*, because one cannot render another's property *assur* without his consent. A *kever hayadua* — a grave intentionally placed in a location — may not be moved, and even if moved, the location remains *tamei* rabbinically and *assur behana'ah*, since the deceased had a legitimate claim to that space. A *kever hamazik et harabbim* — a grave whose location causes harm to the public, because of *tum'ah* or otherwise — may be moved in deference to communal welfare. In that case the location becomes *tahor*, since the rabbinic extension of *tum'ah* does not apply after the body is gone, but the space remains *assur behana'ah*, since the original burial was with permission and the body had legitimately belonged there. The *gemara* applies the *kever binyan* reading to all three cases, maintaining throughout that bare earth cannot become *assur*.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 48

## Context & Overview

### Previous Daf Review

Sanhedrin 48 picks up at the bottom of 47b, at the line beginning *itmar*, ten lines from the bottom of the page. The daf arrives in the middle of a sustained treatment of *misat beit din* — execution by rabbinic court — and the rules governing what happens afterward. The prohibition of *halanas hameis*, leaving the body overnight, which applies to one who has been hanged, opens a broader conversation about the general obligation of burial. That discussion branches into the question of the halakhic basis for *kevurah* in the first place, which then generates its own set of *nafka minos*.

### Purpose of Burial

One central question is whether the purpose of *kevurah* is primarily to achieve *kaparah* — atonement — for the deceased, or whether it is driven by the concern that leaving a body unburied constitutes *bizayon*, a degradation and disgrace. The Gemara draws practical consequences from this distinction.

### Aveilus & Kaparah

Connected to this is the question of timing: when precisely does *aveilus* begin, and when does the *kaparah* take effect? The discussion from the previous daf establishes that *aveilus* begins at *stimas hagolel* — Rashi understands this as the closing of the coffin lid, while Tosafos understands it as the placement of the headstone, where there is one.

### Issurei Hana'ah

The Gemara then moved into the question of *issurei hana'ah* — the prohibition on deriving benefit from a corpse. A corpse is itself forbidden in *hana'ah*, and the Gemara addressed a case involving soil taken from the burial site of Rav. Shmuel ruled that such soil is permissible, since it is *karka olam* — the ground itself — as distinct from something that was *talush u'levsof chibro*, originally detached and subsequently reattached to the ground, which, when placed there for the corpse, is conceptually connected to it and thus forbidden. This leads directly into the central question of the current daf: at what stage does something become connected to the corpse and thereby forbidden in *hana'ah*? This is the question of *hazmanah milsa* — whether designation alone, prior to actual use, suffices to confer a halakhic status.

---

## Hazmanah Milsa

### Abaye vs. Rava

The Gemara opens with a case: *ha'oreg beged l'meis* — one who is weaving a garment to serve as a shroud for a corpse (and it is crucial that the person is already dead). Does the act of weaving for the sake of the deceased render the garment already connected to and forbidden on account of the corpse, or must it await actual use? Abaye says it is forbidden; Rava says it is permitted.

### Abaye's Position

Abaye rules *asur*, explaining his position with the phrase *hazmanah milsa* — designation is halakhically meaningful. It should be noted that Abaye is not speaking of mere verbal intent; the designation must come through an action, in this case the act of weaving. Nevertheless, the point is that preparing something, even before it is put to use, is sufficient to confer its halakhic status.

### Rava's Position

Rava rules *mutar* and holds *hazmanah lav milsa* — designation without actual use is of no halakhic consequence. The status attaches only when the item is actually employed for its designated purpose.

### Models Compared

The Gemara then probes the reasoning behind each position. *Mai ta'ama d'Abaye?* — What is Abaye's source? He derives it through a *gezerah shavah* of *sham sham* from *eglah arufah*. By the *eglah arufah* — the calf brought to the wadi in the case of an unsolved murder — the Torah uses the word *sham*, "there," indicating that the calf is left in the wadi. The same word *sham* appears in connection with death, in the verse *vatamas sham Miriam*. From the *eglah arufah* the rule emerges that the calf becomes forbidden in *hana'ah* already when it descends into the *nachal eitan*, the hard wadi, even before its neck is broken. As Rashi explains: *yeridata lenachal eitan hi osartah* — the mere descent into the wadi, which is the act of designation, suffices to forbid it. So too, by analogy, when something is designated for the dead, the designation itself is sufficient. Whether this applies as a general principle across all areas of *halakha* or specifically to matters involving the dead remains an open question at this stage.

Rava, for his part, also employs the *gezerah shavah* of *sham sham*, but draws his analogy from *avodah zarah*. The verse by *avodah zarah* uses the term *asher avdu sham hagoyim*, and from this comes the principle that there is *ein hekdesh l'avodah zarah* — one cannot formally consecrate something to an idol through designation alone. If one declares that a house or an ox is donated to *avodah zarah*, the declaration confers no status; the object is not forbidden until it is actually put to use with the idol. Correspondingly, the corpse is forbidden in *hana'ah*, and something becomes connected to it — becoming an appurtenance of it — only when it is actually employed in connection with it, not when it is merely designated.

### Rava's Model

The Gemara now asks why Rava does not also learn from *eglah arufah*, and why Abaye does not learn from *avodah zarah*. Rava answers: *mishamesh mi'meshamesh gamrinan* — the relevant analogy is between one appurtenance and another appurtenance. Both the items designated for *avodah zarah* and the garments made for a corpse share the structural characteristic of being appurtenances of a forbidden object, rather than being that primary forbidden object itself. The question in both cases is: when does an accessory acquire the status of connection to the main forbidden thing? The answer, from *avodah zarah*, is: only when it is actually used together with it. This is not comparable to the *eglah arufah*, where one is making the thing itself forbidden — not an appurtenance of it. When a primary object is being forbidden, that may occur at an earlier stage, just as an object actually designated to be an idol itself becomes forbidden immediately upon designation. But for the status of an appurtenance, actual use is required.

### Abaye's Model

Abaye responds: *midi d'orcha mi'midi d'orcha* — one should compare matters of the same normative character. The *eglah arufah* and the shroud for a corpse are both things carried out within the ordinary halakhic framework, operating within the realm of things people are supposed to be doing — or at least things that fall within the normal universe of *halakhic* obligation and practice. When one acts within that framework, designating something for its purpose suffices to confer status, since the *hazmanah* flows from a commanded or at least normatively appropriate act. *Avodah zarah*, by contrast, is something nobody should be doing — not Jews, and indeed not non-Jews either. One does not give earlier or fuller effect to designations that should never have been made in the first place. Hence the analogy from *avodah zarah* is rejected; *eglah arufah*, which operates within the halakhic order, is the appropriate model.

The Gemara also establishes that the phrase *hazmanah milsa* and *hazmanah lav milsa* is a general formulation, not limited to cases involving the dead. Even though the *gezerah shavah* was anchored in the context of *meis*, what is found in that context becomes the general rule throughout *halakha*: either, following Abaye, designation suffices to confer status across the board, or, following Rava, only actual use does.

---

## Rav Chisda's Test

### Kerchief & Sefer

The Gemara raises a challenge from a case involving a *kippa she'tamei midras* — a headscarf that has contracted *tumah* of *midras*, the type of impurity generated when a *zav* or *zava* lies on or sits on something susceptible to that form of *tumah*. Because such a headscarf can double as a pillow, it is susceptible to *midras tumah*. Now if one then redesignates this scarf to serve as a wrapping for a *sefer Torah* or any other book — a use that is wholly incompatible with the function of sitting or lying upon — the scarf becomes *tahor min hamidras*. It can no longer be a *mishkav* or *moshav* since it is no longer used for that purpose. However, it remains *tamei maga midras* — impure through contact with a *midras* — and is thus a *rishon l'tumah*. The mechanism of that residual *tumah* is subtle: at the moment of its transition from *midras* to *sefer* covering, it ceases to be a *midras* object itself, but in that same instant, as an ordinary vessel, it has touched something that was a *midras* — namely itself in its prior state — and thereby contracts one degree of *tumah*. The relevant point is that the redesignation alone, apparently without any actual use as a *sefer* wrapping, changes the object's status. This seems to constitute proof that *hazmanah milsa*, supporting Abaye.

There are, however, two difficulties with this reading. First, even Abaye was speaking of a *hazmanah* effected through an action — weaving the garment — not through bare verbal declaration. Second, the general principle in the laws of vessels holds that *kol hakelim yordim lidei tumasan b'machshava v'ein olim midei tumasan ela b'shinui ma'aseh* — vessels acquire *tumah* through *machshava* (thought or intent), but they are not purified from their *tumah* except through an actual physical change to the object. These two difficulties may be mutually resolving. Tosafos suggests that the phrase *nasnu l'sefer* — "and he designated it for the *sefer*" — implies that some physical change was made to render the scarf suitable for use as a *sefer* covering, even though it has not yet actually been used. Thus the case demonstrates that designation through an action is sufficient to change status even absent actual use — a proof for Abaye, and, importantly, the principle appears to extend beyond the specific context of the dead.

### Rav Chisda Case

Rava, however, contests this reading. He insists that *nasnu v'karcho* — "he designated it and wrapped the *Sefer Torah* with it" — means that both steps occurred: the designation and the actual wrapping. The Mishnah mentions the designation specifically because, as Rav Chisda teaches, both designation and use are necessary.

### Both Required

Rava's position is thus clarified by the principle of Rav Chisda: *hai sudra d'azmanei l'meitzar bei tefillin v'tzar bei tefillin, assur l'meitzar bei peshitei* — a kerchief that one designated as a bag for *tefillin* and then actually used to wrap *tefillin* becomes *tashmishei kedushah* and may not thereafter be used to wrap coins. But Rav Chisda specifies both conditions. *Azmanei v'lo tzar bei* — if one designated the kerchief without ever actually wrapping *tefillin* in it — that is *hazmanah lav milsa*, insufficient by itself. *Tzar bei v'lo azmanei* — if one wrapped *tefillin* in it ad hoc, without any prior designation — it may still be used for money. The reason is that casual, unreflective use — without the intention that this is now one's designated *tefillin* bag — confers no status. Something is not committed to *tashmishei kedushah* by accident. For something to acquire the status, therefore, both intentional designation and actual use are required. This is why the Mishnah mentions the designation alongside the use.

### Designation Alone

Abaye, who holds *hazmanah milsa*, does not accept Rav Chisda's requirement of dual conditions. For Abaye, what matters is the designation. *Azmanei af al gav de'lo tzar bei* — designating it, even without ever wrapping *tefillin* in it, suffices to give it the status of *tashmishei kedushah*. Actual use is neither needed in addition to designation nor does it accomplish anything by itself. *Tzar bei ei azmanei* — if one used it: did one designate it? If yes, it has the status; if not, it does not. The designation is the sole operative factor. The result is that for Abaye the only question is whether a genuine *hazmanah* was performed; for Rava, the only configuration that confers status is designation followed by actual use.

---

## Graves & Structures

### Tombstone Case

The Gemara brings another test case. *Nefesh she'banao le'shem chai* — if someone constructs a structure, a kind of tombstone or funerary monument, over a grave site intended for someone still alive. Since that person is still living, there is as yet no corpse with which the structure could be connected. Accordingly, *mutar b'hana'ah* — benefit may be derived from it, because the object to which it would be connected does not yet exist.

### Addition After Death

After this structure is built and while it remains permissible — the person then dies, and at that point someone adds *dimos echad l'shem meis*, a single row of bricks with the corpse now in existence — that addition renders the entire structure forbidden in *hana'ah*. This seems to support Abaye: the act of adding bricks, which constitutes designation through action, combined with the presence of a corpse, suffices even before anything is fully "used" in the ordinary sense.

### Resolution

The Gemara deflects by establishing that the case concerns a body already interred: *hacha b'mai askinan de'ramya bei meis* — we are dealing with a situation where the corpse has actually been placed in the grave. This invites a further objection: if the body is already in the grave, why does the addition of the new row of bricks matter at all? Why should the original tombstone not already be forbidden simply by virtue of the buried body? The answer is that the case involves the body having subsequently been removed — *af al gav de'panya*. This now maps precisely onto the structure of the *tefillin* case. The tombstone was used alongside a corpse — the body was in the grave — but it had never been genuinely designated for that purpose, since at the time of original construction the intended occupant was still alive. Absent designation, even use creates only a transient status: the object is forbidden while in use but reverts to its original permissible state once the corpse is removed, just as the kerchief used ad hoc to wrap *tefillin* remains eligible for use as a money pouch. If, however, the row of bricks is added after the person's death — constituting a genuine designation at a time when there is a corpse — then the full status attaches, and the structure remains forbidden even if the body is later removed.

### Reversing Status

Rav Pappa bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda adds a further teaching: *im hayah mekiro chotzo mutar* — if one can identify the specific bricks that were added by way of designation, one may remove them, and in doing so reverse the act of designation. With the designation undone, the structure reverts to its prior permissible status. This reinforces that the operative mechanism is the act of designation through a physical action — laying the bricks — and that undoing that act undoes the designation.

---

## Father's Grave

### Father's Cave

The Gemara brings yet another case: *ha'chotzev kever l'aviv* — one who has hewn a cave for his father's burial. He carves it out, but ultimately the father is interred elsewhere. The ruling is *lo yikaver bo olamis* — no one may ever be buried in that cave. The Gemara's initial assumption is that this prohibition stems from *issur hana'ah*, and is a function of *hazmanah milsa* — the designation of the cave for the father is sufficient to connect it to the deceased and to make burial of another therein a form of forbidden *hana'ah*.

### Hazmanah vs. Honor

This initial reading is puzzling on multiple grounds. The cave is *karka olam*, ground, and the Gemara itself noted earlier that ground is generally not subject to *issur hana'ah*. Moreover, even if we were to say it is forbidden, why would using the cave for a different corpse constitute *hana'ah* forbidden to the living? Burying anyone in it is serving the dead, not the living. And if it is designated for the dead in general, any corpse should be eligible. The Gemara resolves both of these tensions by rejecting the *hazmanah milsa* reading: *hatam mishum kevod aviv* — the prohibition here is not about *issur hana'ah* at all, but about the personal honor owed to one's father. It is socially and morally disrespectful to use a grave carved specifically for one's father for a different person. The restriction is particular to the relationship; if the cave had been carved for Reuven and Reuven was ultimately buried elsewhere, Shimon could certainly be interred there.

### Stones Quarried

The Gemara adds that this reading is supported by the ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the continuation of that Mishnah: *af ha'chotzev avanim l'aviv* — even one who quarries stones intended to build a burial structure for his father, and the father is ultimately interred elsewhere, those stones may not be used for another corpse. This extension makes perfect sense if the reason is *kevod ha'av* — respect for one's father — since even preparing stones in honor of a parent creates a social and moral restriction on using those materials for another. The father's honor attaches to anything expressly prepared in his memory.

### Honor Principle

If, by contrast, the prohibition were a function of *hazmanah milsa* and *issur hana'ah*, this extension would be impossible to sustain. Abaye's position holds that designation through action — *hazmanah* — confers status, but this requires that the designated object already be in a state ready for use. A finished garment designated as a shroud is in a ready state; quarried stones awaiting construction are the equivalent of thread before it is woven into a garment. No one would argue that spinning thread gives it the status of a burial garment. Hence Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling cannot be grounded in *hazmanah milsa* and must be understood purely in terms of *kevod ha'mais* and *kevod ha'av*. The prohibition is one of dignity and honor, not of *issurei hana'ah*.

---

## New Grave Case

### Used vs. Unused

The Gemara brings a further source: *kever chadash mutar b'hana'ah* — a new grave is permissible in benefit. The assumption here is that "new" means it was dug for a corpse but has not yet been used. *Nitna bo nefel assur b'hana'ah* — once even a *nefel*, a miscarried fetus, has been placed in the grave, it becomes forbidden. The bracketed issue of *karka olam* and how this applies to ground is noted but set aside.

### Supports Rava

On its plain reading, this passage appears to be a strong proof for Rava. The grave was dug — it was designated for a corpse — and yet it remains permitted until a body is actually placed in it. The operative factor is *heitil*, placing the body in, not the prior designation: *heitil in, lo heitil* — only when one has placed [the body], and not before.

### Fetus Exception

The Gemara rejects this straightforward reading by offering an alternative. What the teaching actually comes to establish is not the general rule of *hazmanah lav milsa*, but rather to controvert the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that a *nefel* — a miscarried fetus — does not *tofes* the grave, does not affix the status of a used burial site to it. The baraita is saying that even a fetus does create that status, against Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. On Abaye's reading, *kever chadash* does not mean a grave dug but not yet used; it means a grave prepared for someone still living, which is why it is permissible — not because the grave has not yet been used, but because there is no corpse with which it can be connected. Once it is designated for a dead person, even a fetus, it is forbidden. The Gemara acknowledges that this reading of *kever chadash* is strained but maintains it in order to preserve Abaye's position.

---

## Money Collection

### General vs. Specific

The Gemara introduces a distinction from a Mishnah in tractate Shekalim: *mosar hamaisim lamaisim* — if funds are collected generally for burial costs of the poor, leftover funds remain available for future burial needs. *Mosar hamais l'yorshav* — if funds are collected specifically for a named individual who has died, any surplus after covering the burial expenses goes to the heirs. The question is whether the designation of money for a specific corpse confers on those funds a status connected to the deceased that would preclude their ordinary use — and the ruling that the heirs receive the surplus suggests that it does not.

### Braisa Debate

A *braisa* is cited to elaborate. *Gavu l'maisim stam* — if one collected for burial costs in general, without specifying any individual, the surplus is available for *maisim stam*, any burial need. *Gavu l'mais zeh* — if one collected specifically for this corpse, for Reuven after his death, that is a case of *mosar hamais l'yorshav*, and the surplus goes to the heirs. This shows that designating money for a particular corpse does not render it permanently connected to that corpse in the manner of *issurei hana'ah*. Tosafos notes that one might object that money is too fungible to serve as a test case for *hazmanah milsa*, since it is not yet in the state of the final object. Tosafos responds that precisely because money can be readily converted into whatever burial necessity is required, it is considered in a state of readiness — analogous to a completed garment rather than raw thread — and is a valid test case for the principle.

The dispute among the Tannaim in the baraita involves the *Tanna Kamma*, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Nosson.  Rabbi Meir says *lo yiga bahen olam ad sheyavo Eliyahu* — no one should touch the surplus funds at all until Elijah comes to resolve the question. Rabbi Nosson says *ya'asenu dimus al kivro* — use the surplus to build a finer monument on his grave, *o ziluf lifnei mitaso* — or for sprinkling incense or wine around his bier; in other words, apply the funds to the benefit of that same *mais*.

### Abaye Explains

Abaye maintains that all positions in this dispute are compatible with *hazmanah milsa* — all agree that designation confers meaningful status. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that *dechazu letaphis* — only the funds that were actually required by the burial are retroactively considered designated. The surplus, which in hindsight was never needed, is understood to have never been included in the *hazmanah*. This is a principle akin to *breira*: the designation is clarified retroactively by what was actually necessary. Rabbi Meir holds that since at the time of collection the donors assumed everything collected would be needed, perhaps all the funds were fully designated for the *mais* — *tafi*, it designated — or perhaps not — *lo tafi* — since retroactively not all of it was used. His uncertainty on this point leads to the ruling of *lo yiga bahen ad sheyavo Eliyahu*. Rabbi Nosson holds unambiguously that yes, since the money was collected for this *mais* while the collection was taking place, it is fully designated — *peshita lei devadai taphis* — and must therefore be applied to the benefit of that *mais*.

### Rava Explains

Rava explains the same dispute entirely within his own framework: *lechulei alma hazmanah lav milsa hi* — all agree that designation is of no halakhic consequence. The entire debate, therefore, has nothing to do with *issurei hana'ah* and everything to do with *kevod hamais* — the honor of the deceased. It would be disrespectful for money collected in a person's memory, for his funeral, to be taken home by his heirs and spent on their own needs. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that the deceased would have wanted his heirs to benefit and would forgive the indignity — *machil zilutei gabei yorshim*. Rabbi Meir is uncertain whether the deceased would forgive that disrespect or not — *mesafke lei machil o lo machil* — and so rules that no one should touch the funds. Rabbi Nosson holds that the deceased would certainly not forgive such indignity — *peshita lei delo machil* — and therefore the funds must be spent on something honorable for him, namely the grave monument or sprinkling.

---

## Parents' Grief

### Prevention Duty

The Gemara brings a final test case in this series: *hayu aviv ve'imo mizarkin bo kelim* — the mother and father of a deceased child, overwhelmed with grief, are throwing their belongings — clothing, jewelry, and various objects — into the coffin or onto the body. The ruling is *mitzvah aleichem lehatzilan* — it is obligatory for bystanders to prevent these items from entering the coffin, to rescue them. The reason is practical and compassionate: the parents, in their immediate anguish, will later be grateful for the intervention once they have recovered from the initial shock of grief. Rashi clarifies that *lehatzilan* refers to removing objects that the parents have already thrown into the coffin before they are buried together with the corpse.

The question is what this teaches about *hazmanah milsa*. If the items become forbidden only once they actually come into contact with the body and are buried with it, then *hazmanah lav milsa* and Rava is supported. One should be able to retrieve them at any point before actual interment, since no status has yet attached.

### Fevered State

Abaye's response to this proof is *hatam mishum merirayhu* — in that situation the parents are acting out of a state of *merirut*, profound bitterness and anguish. Their casting of items into the coffin does not constitute a genuine, reflective *hazmanah*. It is an impulsive act of grief, not a considered designation. Therefore it carries no halakhic weight as *hazmanah*, even for Abaye.

### Gezera Reason

The Gemara, however, questions whether Abaye's answer is sufficient to explain the teaching of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says: *bameh devarim amurim shelo nag'u bamittah — aval nag'u bamittah assurin* — when is it that we can rescue these items? Only if they have not yet touched the funeral bier. Once they have touched the bier, they are forbidden. This means that for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the combination of the parents' intent and contact with the bier is sufficient to confer forbidden status — regardless of the fevered state of the parents. If their designation is meaningless due to *merirut*, the touching of the bier should also be irrelevant. Evidently, for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, even a fevered *hazmanah* carries some weight when combined with physical contact. And for the *Tanna Kamma*, even touching the bier is not enough to forbid the items, which aligns with Rava.

The Gemara resolves this through Ulla's teaching: *targemah Ulla bemittah hanikberet imo* — the case of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel concerns a bier that is actually going to be buried together with the deceased. The issue is not *hazmanah milsa* at all; the ruling is a *gezeirah* — a rabbinic protective decree — based on the concern that if one were permitted to retrieve items thrown onto the bier while the bier itself is going to be interred, people would infer that the actual *tachrichin*, the burial shrouds, may also be retrieved and removed from the dead. Permitting the removal of items from the bier would thus create a dangerous precedent regarding the shrouds themselves. The *Tanna Kamma* and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel therefore disagree not about *hazmanah milsa* but about the scope of this protective decree.

---

## Tefillin & Sefer

### Ad Hoc Use

The Gemara brings a further teaching: *kis she'asao lehaniach bo tefillin, assur lehaniach bo ma'ot* — a bag that one has made to hold *tefillin* may not be used as a money pouch. However, *heniach bo tefillin, yaniach bo ma'ot* — if one has merely placed *tefillin* in it ad hoc, without designating it as one's *tefillin* bag, one may use it for money afterward. This appears to be an explicit statement that designation alone — making the bag *for tefillin* — suffices to give it the status of *tashmishei kedushah*, while ad hoc use without designation does not. This would be a clear proof for Abaye.

### Both Required

The Gemara deflects: *eima asao veheniach bo tefillin assur lehaniach bo ma'ot k'derav Chisda* — the teaching should be read as: he designated it *and* placed his *tefillin* in it, and only then is it forbidden as a money pouch, following Rav Chisda's requirement of both designation and use. The designation mentioned in the text is not sufficient on its own; the text is compressed, and the actual use is implied. This is admittedly not the plain meaning of the text, but it is how Rava reads it.

### Craftsman Case

The Gemara then brings an explicit and unambiguous teaching: *amar le'uman aseh li tik shel sefer o nartik shel tefillin* — if one instructs a craftsman to make a covering for a *Sefer Torah* or a case for *tefillin*. *Ad shelo nishtamesh bahen kodesh, mutar lehishtamesh bahen chol* — before one has actually used them for the holy objects, one may use them for mundane purposes. *Nishtamesh bahen kodesh, assur lehishtamesh bahen chol* — once one has used them for the holy purpose, they become *tashmishei kedushah* and may no longer be used for mundane purposes. This is an explicit ruling like Rava: designation and commission alone are insufficient; actual use for the sacred object is required.

### Tannaic Dispute

Faced with these conflicting indications from various *braisos* and Mishnaic sources, the Gemara concludes: *tannai hi* — it is a dispute among Tannaim. The evidence from earlier suggested Tannaim who hold that *hazmanah* alone, or *hazmanah* through action without actual use, suffices; the final teaching cited clearly requires actual use. Rashi explains the final *baraisa* about tanning leather *lishma* — for the sake of *tefillin* — in light of *hazmanah lav milsa*: since designation does not confer status, preparing the leather without *ibud lishma* is irrelevant, and only actual proper preparation for the sake of *tefillin* matters. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the leather of a kosher animal is invalid for *tefillin* unless the tanning process was done *lishma*, for that purpose. Tosafos, in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, explains the linkage in reverse: Rava, who holds *hazmanah lav milsa*, corresponds to the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that *ibud lishma* is required, since designation alone is insufficient and a more substantive act of preparation is needed. Abaye, who holds *hazmanah milsa*, would not require *ibud lishma*, since the designation through the act of preparation gives the leather its status. The Gemara acknowledges that the connection between the *lishma* requirement for leather and the *hazmanah* debate is not straightforward — in particular, even Rava requires both *hazmanah* and use to confer status, so one could argue that even for Rava one should need *ibud lishma* plus actual use — but the Gemara draws the conclusion that at minimum there is a *machloket Tannaim* underlying the debate of Abaye and Rava.

---

## Final Ruling

### Opinions

The *sugya* concludes with a statement of the practical *halakha*. *Darash Mareimar hilkhata k'vatei de'Abaye* — Mareimar ruled publicly that the *halakha* follows Abaye. *Ve'rabbanan amri hilkhata k'vatei de'Rava* — the Rabbis say the *halakha* is in accordance with Rava.

### Accepted Law

*Ve'hilkhata k'vatei de'Rava* — and the accepted *halakha* is like Rava. This is not one of the well-known exceptional cases — the *ya'al kegam* — in which we rule against Rava. The practical consequence is that *hazmanah lav milsa*: designation alone does not confer status. What is required is both *hazmanah* — a genuine, intentional designation through action — and actual use. Only the combination of both conditions causes an object to acquire its new halakhic status.

---

## Execution & Property

### Property Rights

With the conclusion of the *sugya* on *hazmanah milsa*, the Gemara pivots back to the topic of court-ordered executions and the laws governing property. *Harugei malkhut nikhseihem l'melekh* — the property of those executed by the king reverts to the king, presumably in the context of *mored b'malkhut*, rebellion against the crown. *Harugei beit din nikhseihem l'yorshim* — those executed by the court leave their property to their heirs. This latter principle is unremarkable: regardless of the circumstances of death, the estate passes to heirs in the ordinary course. The *chiddush* is the claim that property is seized by the king in the case of a royal execution.

### Dissent

Rabbi Yehuda dissents: *af harugei malkhut nikhseihem l'yorshim* — even those executed by the king leave their property to the heirs. Rabbi Yehuda challenges the premise that any government body acquires rights to the property of an executed person.

### Navot Case

The Rabbis cite a proof against Rabbi Yehuda from the story of Navot: *hinei b'cherem Navot asher yarad sham l'rishto* — "Behold, he is in the vineyard of Navot, where he went down to take possession of it." The word *l'rishto* — "to inherit it" — suggests that Achav acquired Navot's vineyard through a recognized mechanism of inheritance following Navot's death at the king's behest, implying that the property of one executed by the king passes to the king.

### Resolution

Rabbi Yehuda responds: *ben achei aviv hayah v'raui l'yorsho hayah* — Achav was Navot's cousin, and the vineyard came to him through ordinary family inheritance, not through any royal prerogative over the property of the executed. The Gemara objects: but Navot had many sons; why would it pass to a cousin? Rabbi Yehuda answers: *oso v'es banav harag* — Achav had Navot and all of his sons killed, removing them from the line of succession. With the direct heirs eliminated, Achav as a collateral relative inherited the vineyard in the normal course of inheritance law. It was not royal confiscation; it was the result of a systematic and horrific elimination of all closer heirs.

The Rabbis counter that this reading of "his sons" refers to *banim hare'oyim l'tzeis mimenu* — the future children Navot never had the opportunity to father — but that Achav did not actually kill the existing sons. The point of contention is thus whether *banav* refers to actual sons killed or potential progeny denied.

### Blasphemy Charge

The Gemara observes that the position holding *nikhsei l'melekh* gains particular support from the specific accusations fabricated against Navot: *beirach Navot Elohim vaMelekh* — that he blasphemed both God and the king. If the king's property claim over the executed requires that the charge be *mored b'malkhut* — rebellion against the king — this explains why the false witnesses were instructed to accuse Navot of blaspheming the king: to establish the legal predicate for royal confiscation of the vineyard.

Rabbi Yehuda, however, is confronted with a question: even on his view, if the property would have gone to Achav in any event through inheritance, why did they need to fabricate the charge of blaspheming the king? And more fundamentally, why include the charge of blaspheming God at all? This charge was entirely unnecessary for any legal purpose related to property acquisition. The Gemara answers: *l'afushei ritcha* — to inflame the judges' anger. Adding the charge of blasphemy against God was designed to make the accusation maximally outrageous and ensure that the judges — who would otherwise need to be manipulated into convicting an innocent man — would be so enraged that they would convict without scrutiny. The same reasoning applies for Rabbi Yehuda's position: even without needing the legal framework of *mored b'malkhut* for property purposes, the false charge against the king was added alongside the charge against God purely to inflame the court. The *sugyah* breaks off at this point.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 49

## Yoav's Execution

### Yoav narrative intro

Daf 49 picks up on 48b, continuing the discussion of who inherits the property of one executed by royal decree — do the heirs inherit, or does the king expropriate it? The daf arrives at this question through the story of *Yoav ben Tzeruyah*, and to understand what follows, it is necessary to reconstruct the broader narrative.

*Yoav* was a military leader, a son of *Tzeruyah*, and one of the central figures in the court of *David HaMelech*. The daf is, in a real sense, a continuation of discussions begun on earlier pages — involving *Michal*, the daughters of *Shaul*, *Avner ben Ner*, and *Ish-bosheth*. All of these figures orbit a central drama: the fragile consolidation of David's kingship in the wake of Shaul's death and the rival claims of other factions.

### Asahel & Avner clash

*Avner ben Ner* had backed *Ish-bosheth*, Shaul's son, essentially installing him as a rival king. Meanwhile, *Asahel* — a brother of *Yoav* and famously fleet-footed — pursued *Avner* in battle. *Avner* warned Asahel to desist; Asahel did not, and *Avner* killed him, striking him in the fifth rib with the blunt end of his spear. This moment — a brother's death — lodged itself permanently in *Yoav's* memory and would eventually cost *Avner* his life.

### David's mourning

When news of Avner's subsequent killing reached *David*, he staged a conspicuous and heartfelt public mourning. The narrative in *Shmuel* makes clear that his purpose was, at least in part, political: the people had been suspicious of *David's* involvement, and by mourning visibly and sincerely, he won them over. The *Gemara* treats this mourning as genuine but also strategically consequential.

### Yoav's rebellion

The *pesukim* that open the *Gemara's* discussion come from *Melachim*. By the time of *Shlomo's* reign, *David* had died. Among the events leading up to the end of *David's* reign were a series of rebellions from within his own household. His son *Adoniyah ben Chaggit* declared *ani emloch* — "I shall reign" — and sought to seize power. His son *Avshalom* had earlier mounted the famous and devastating rebellion that forced *David* to flee *Yerushalayim*.

*Yoav*, for his part, threw his support behind *Adoniyah*. The *pasuk* states explicitly: *ki Yoav natah acharei Adoniyah* — that *Yoav* turned and followed *Adoniyah*. This was not a trivial act; *Yoav* was the commander of the army. The *pasuk* notes that he did not follow *Avshalom*, and this contrast will become significant. Having backed *Adoniyah*, *Yoav* found himself on the losing side when *Shlomo* became king. He fled and took hold of the horns of the *mizbe'ach*: *vayanos Yoav el Ohel Hashem vayachazek bekarnot hamizbe'ach*. This is the ancient claim of sanctuary — clinging physically to the altar's four horns.

### Shlomo orders execution

*Shlomo* was informed that *Yoav* had fled to the *mizbe'ach*. His response was swift: he dispatched *Benayahu ben Yehoyada* with the command *lech pega bo* — go and strike him down. *Benayahu* entered the precincts of the *Ohel Hashem* and conveyed the king's order: *tze* — come out. *Yoav's* answer was terse and resolute: *lo ki po amut* — no, for I will die here.

### Biblical text analysis

*Benayahu* returned to the king and reported back — and this is where the *Gemara* pauses. The *pasuk* says *koh diber Yoav vechoh anani* — "thus spoke *Yoav* and thus he answered me" — implying a full conversation. Yet what actually appears in the text amounts to four words: *lo ki po amut*. This discrepancy signals to the *Gemara* that there was a much more substantial exchange behind those four words, a conversation that the *pasuk* compresses. The remainder of the *sugya* will unpack what that conversation actually contained.

*Shlomo* responded: *aseh ka'asher diber* — do as he said — and ordered *Yoav* killed and buried. At the simplest level of *pshat*, this seems to mean: kill him where he stands, at the *mizbe'ach*. But the *Gemara* will read it very differently.

---

## Yoav's conditions

### Curse conditions

The *Gemara* now reconstructs the hidden conversation. *Yoav* said to *Benayahu*: do not be involved with this man. Then he laid out his terms with stark logic — *tarte*, two conditions: either accept his curses upon yourself and kill him, or leave him alive with his curses. It is not acceptable to do both — to kill him and leave the curses in force.
