The backstory here is that when *David* discovered *Yoav* had killed *Avner*, he responded with a series of formal execrations — curses — against *Yoav* and his household. These curses were not merely rhetorical; they were understood to carry genuine force. *Yoav's* position at the *mizbe'ach* was therefore doubly significant: he was not simply claiming physical sanctuary against being killed, he was invoking a kind of legal and theological argument. The curses had been placed upon him; if *Shlomo* intended to execute him, he must also agree to lift them. Otherwise, *Yoav* would live on under the curses, and that injustice could not stand alongside his death.

### Shlomo accepts

*Shlomo* heard the report and responded: *aseh ka'asher diber* — do as he says. The *Gemara* now reads this not as a simple command to kill *Yoav* at the *mizbe'ach*, but as *Shlomo's* acceptance of *Yoav's* condition. If I am going to execute him, I accept upon myself the removal of the curses. Kill him — and the curses go with him.

### David's curses

*Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Rav*: all the curses that *David* had cursed *Yoav* with were ultimately fulfilled — not in *Yoav's* line but in the line of *David* himself. The curses boomeranged. The text of the curses, as enumerated in *Shmuel*, was: *al yikharet mibbeit Yoav zav umetzora umachazik bapelech venofel bacherev vechasar lechem* — may there not be cut off from the house of *Yoav* those afflicted with *zav*, *metzora*, those who lean on a staff, those who fall by the sword, and those who lack bread. Five categories of affliction, each directed at *Yoav* and his descendants.

### Curses boomerang

The *Gemara* then traces each of these afflictions to a descendant of *David*:

*Zav* — *Rechav'am*. The *pasuk* says that King *Rechav'am* exerted himself greatly to mount his chariot to flee to *Yerushalayim*. The word *merkava* (chariot) recalls the *pasuk* that any seat — *merkav* — upon which a *zav* rides becomes *tamei*. The verbal resonance implies that *Rechav'am* was himself a *zav*.

*Metzora* — *Uziyahu*. This case is explicit in the *navi*. *Uziyahu*, in his hubris, entered the *Heichal* to offer the *ketoret* — something reserved exclusively for *kohanim*. Immediately, *tzara'at* broke out on his forehead. This raises an obvious question: is offering the *avodah* as a non-*kohen* not itself a severe offense deserving *karet*? The answer may be that while the heavenly reckoning was still to come, the *tzara'at* was an immediate and visible sign of divine displeasure — not exhausting the punishment, but manifesting it instantaneously before the assembled priests.

*Machazik bapelech* — *Assa*. The *pasuk* says that only in his old age did *Assa's* legs become ill. *Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Rav* that he was afflicted with *podagra* — gout. The Talmud records a charming exchange: *Mar Zutra*, son of *Rav Nachman*, asked his father what gout actually feels like. *Rav Nachman* answered: like a needle in living flesh. How did he know? Three possibilities are offered: he experienced it himself; he learned it from his teacher; or it falls under the principle of *sod Hashem liyre'av* — God's secrets are revealed to those who fear Him. This last answer, the *Gemara* notes, is sometimes invoked when a rabbinic authority seems to possess knowledge that transcends ordinary means.

*Nofel bacherev* — *Yoshiyahu*. The *pasuk* describes archers shooting at King *Yoshiyahu*. *Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Rav* that they made his body like a sieve — he was pierced by a great many arrows. The word *cherev* in the curse is thus understood broadly, as death in battle rather than specifically by sword.

*Chasar lechem* — *Yechonyah*. *Nevuchadnezzar* had taken *Yechonyah* captive. The *Gemara* notes that *Rashi* flags an error in some versions of the text here — it was *Evil-Merodach*, *Nevuchadnezzar's* son, who later released *Yechonyah* and provided him with a regular daily allowance. The *Gemara's* reading is that during the period of *Nevuchadnezzar's* reign, *Yechonyah* lacked bread — thus *chasar lechem* — even though he was later provided for.

### Curser consequence

Having traced each curse to a descendant of *David*, *Rav* draws the pointed conclusion. This is what people say: *tehei luta v'lo tehei lata* — better to be the one cursed than to be the one who curses. *David* placed these imprecations upon *Yoav*; *Yoav* negotiated them away as the condition of his execution; and the curses came back to land upon *David's* own progeny. The lesson is one of cosmic irony: the act of cursing carries its own danger of blowback.

---

## Court case charges

### Sanhedrin trial

The *Gemara* now turns to the court proceedings against *Yoav*. The very fact that a trial takes place is itself exegetically derived. The *pasuk* commands *lo tikach me'im mizbechi* — you shall not take from beside my altar — and the *Gemara* reads this alongside the institution of *Shoftim v'Shotrim*, courts and officers. Where were the courts located? By the *mizbe'ach*. So *Yoav*, clinging to the *mizbe'ach*, was in fact in the immediate vicinity of the *Sanhedrin*. Rather than an extrajudicial killing — or, more precisely, rather than a purely royal prerogative execution — what transpired was a formal proceeding. The dayanim brought *Yoav* to judgment. The impression one might take from the *pesukim* alone is that this was a summary royal execution, extrajudicial if not outright vigilante. The *Gemara* insists otherwise: due process was followed, the charges were heard, *Yoav* was permitted to answer them.

### Avner murder charge

The court — or *Benayahu* acting within that framework — posed the first charge to *Yoav*: *mai ta'ama kataltei l'Avner* — why did you kill *Avner*? *Yoav's* answer was immediate: *go'el hadam havina l'Asa'el achi* — I was the blood-avenger for my brother *Asahel*. *Avner* had killed *Asahel*; *Yoav* was his brother; he had every right — perhaps even a certain obligation — to avenge the blood. The *go'el hadam* is not simply a vigilante; depending on the circumstances and the opinions in play, it is a recognized halakhic role.

### Rodeph defense

The court's counter-argument: *Asa'el rodef hayah* — *Asahel* was a *rodef*, a pursuer. He was chasing *Avner* with lethal intent. *Avner* was acting in self-defense. A killing in self-defense does not create an obligation of blood-vengeance; the *go'el hadam* has no claim. *Yoav's* rebuttal to this is that even so, the law of *rodef* itself requires that one disable the pursuer rather than kill him outright if disabling is possible. If *Avner* could have merely maimed *Asahel* and stopped the pursuit, then killing him was excessive, and *Yoav's* status as *go'el hadam* is legitimate.

### Fifth rib precision

*Yoav* offered the response: *lo yachol lei* — he could not have done otherwise, there was no opportunity to calculate so precisely. But the court immediately dismantled this defense. *Hashta b'dofen chamishit kiven lei* — in that very moment, *Avner* managed to aim with great precision at the fifth rib. *Rabbi Yochanan* explained that the fifth rib — *dofen chamishit* — is the location where the gallbladder and liver are situated, vital organs whose injury is invariably fatal. *Avner* demonstrated exact anatomical knowledge and deliberate aim. If he could strike so precisely as to hit the fifth rib of a fleet-footed man in pursuit, he could certainly have struck a less lethal target. His claim of incapacity is therefore refuted. The court has effectively established that the killing of *Asahel* was unjustified homicide, and consequently that *Yoav's* claim of *go'el hadam* was legitimate — *Yoav* could not be convicted on this count.

### Amasa murder charge

The second charge: *mai ta'ama kataltei l'Amasa* — why did you kill *Amasa*? *Yoav* answered: *Amasa mored bemalchus havah* — *Amasa* was a rebel against the king. He had been commanded to assemble the men of *Yehuda* within three days and he failed to do so. The *pasuk* records the king saying *hazeik li et ish Yehuda sheloshes yamim*, and *Amasa* went and was delayed beyond those three days.

### Amasa justified delay

The court's response to this charge is equally pointed: *Amasa ach v'rak darash* — *Amasa* was engaged in a legitimate act of *drasha*, of expounding Torah. *Ashchayu depaschu beih be-masechta* — he found the people engrossed in a tractate and did not wish to interrupt their learning. The *Gemara* derives this from a verse in *Yehoshua*: *kol ish asher yamreh et picha... yumas* — anyone who rebels against your command shall be put to death. From the word *rak* — a term of limitation — the tradition learns that this does not apply when the delay or deviation involves *divrei Torah*. *Amasa* thus had halakhic justification for his delay. The charge that he was a *mored bemalchus* collapses.

### Yoav indictment

The court's final indictment turns the tables entirely. *Yoav* himself, they declare, is the *mored bemalchus* — the rebel against the crown. The proof: *vehashmuah ba'ah ad Yoav ki Yoav natah acharei Adoniyah v'acharei Avshalom lo natah*. He sided with one of *David's* sons against the legitimate succession. Whether or not his charges against *Avner* and *Amasa* were entirely defensible, his own act of political rebellion is documented in the *navi* and is incontestable. On this charge, *Yoav* is found guilty and deserves to die.

---

## Yoav & Avshalom

### Adoniyah not Avshalom

The *Gemara* then turns to a detail embedded in the *pasuk* itself: why does the text bother to tell us that *Yoav* backed *Adoniyah* and *did not* back *Avshalom*? If the text's purpose is to establish that *Yoav* was a *mored bemalchus*, simply stating that he followed *Adoniyah* would suffice. The additional note — *v'acharei Avshalom lo natah* — invites interpretation. Three views are offered.

### Rabbi Yehoshua view

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha* says: the *pasuk* is telling us that *Yoav* had wanted to rebel behind *Avshalom* as well, but in the end he did not. *Shebikesh lintot v'lo natah* — he sought to turn aside but refrained. What held him back is then the subject of the next two opinions.

### Rabbi Eliezer view

*Rabbi Eliezer* says: *adayin lichluchit shel David kayyemet* — the moisture, the vital residue, of *David* was still present. Another version of this phrase is *adayin istagninim shel David kayyemet*. The *Gemara* explains this through a teaching of *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav*: *David* had 400 children, all of them *benei yefat to'ar* — sons born from captive women taken in war. These children were raised with the distinctive warrior's *belorit* braid, led armies, and were *ba'alei egrofin* — men of physical power and intimidation. They were *David's* janissaries, his strongmen. The phrase *lichluchit shel David* refers to this force — the vitality and power that *David* still commanded through these men. *Yoav* did not dare contend with them, and so he did not rebel during *Avshalom's* uprising.

This reading is striking because it portrays *Yoav* not as loyal but as merely prudent. He always harbored the desire to break free of *David's* authority; it was fear alone that restrained him.

### Rabbi Abba view

*Rabbi Abba bar Kahana* offers a fundamentally different picture. *Ilmalei David lo asah Yoav milchamah, v'ilmalei Yoav lo asak David baTorah* — were it not for *David*, *Yoav* would not have succeeded in war; were it not for *Yoav*, *David* would not have been able to engage in Torah. The two men had a genuine and productive partnership. *David's* Torah study and its merit sustained *Yoav* in battle; *Yoav's* military prowess gave *David* the security to learn Torah. The proof-text is the *pasuk*: *vayehi David oseh mishpat utzedakah lechol ammo veYoav ben Tzeruyah al hatzava* — *David* engaged in justice and righteousness for all his people, and *Yoav* was over the army. Why was *David* able to do *mishpat utzedakah*? Because *Yoav* carried the military burden. And why was *Yoav* so successful in his campaigns? Because *David* was doing *mishpat utzedakah* — that is, learning and teaching Torah. According to this view, *Yoav* was not merely a self-interested follower restrained by fear; he was a genuine partner in *David's* enterprise.

---

## Avner killing details

### Gate meeting

The *Gemara* returns to examine the circumstances of *Avner's* death. The *pasuk* in *Shmuel* records: *vayatzei Yoav me'im David vayishlach malachim acharei Avner vayashivu oto mi'bor haSirah* — and *Yoav* went out from *David*, sent messengers after *Avner*, and they brought him back from *Bor HaSirah*. Then: *vayattehu Yoav el toch hasha'ar ledabber ito bashali* — *Yoav* drew him aside into the gate to speak with him *bashali*, privately, on matters ostensibly of state or secrecy.

### Bor & Sira

What are *Bor* and *Sira*? *Rabbi Abba bar Kahana* explains: *bor vesira garmu l'Avner sheyehareg* — the pit and the thorn caused *Avner* to be killed. These two words encode a moral history that became *Avner's* undoing.

*Rashi* explains each in turn. *Bor* refers to the *tzapachat hamayim* — the water bowl — that *David* took from beside the sleeping *Shaul* when God had caused everyone in the camp to fall into a deep sleep. *David* could have killed *Shaul* at that moment; instead, he took only the bowl as proof. He then called out to *Shaul's* guards — including *Avner* — rebuking them for their negligence in protecting the king, displaying the bowl as evidence of how close a mortal threat had been.

### Avner's denials

What should *Avner* have said at that moment? *Hayah lo l'Avner lomar l'Shaul: re'eh kamah tzaddik hu zeh shelo hargacha* — he should have said to *Shaul*: look how righteous this man is, he could have killed you and he did not. Instead, *Avner* deflected: *shema echad mibnei hatzava netanam lo* — perhaps one of the soldiers handed it to him; perhaps *David* did not take it himself, perhaps there was some other explanation. This dismissal — the *bor* — was a failure to speak up for *David's* righteousness when it mattered.

*Sira* — the thorn — refers to the episode in the cave, where *David* cut a corner of *Shaul's* cloak with his sword. Again, *Avner* should have told *Shaul*: see how much he spared you, he was with you alone in the cave and could have killed you. Instead, *Avner* offered another dismissal: perhaps the cloak snagged on thornbushes as *Shaul* walked by, and *David*, hiding among the thorns, picked it up — it proves nothing. These two episodes of deflection and denial — *bor* and *sira* — were *Avner's* moral failures, and they were what ultimately cost him his life. *Yoav's* killing of him, the *Gemara* suggests, was not without a certain justice embedded in the narrative.

### Torah distraction

How did *Yoav* manage to catch *Avner* off guard? *Avner* was himself a capable military man. The *Gemara* explains through *Rav Yehuda's* interpretation of the word *bashali*. Extending the *yud* to a *vav* gives us *nashli*, from the root of *shal na'alecha* — remove your shoe. *Yoav* drew *Avner* aside under the pretense of discussing a halakhic question: the procedure of *chalitzah* in the case of a *yevamah* who is an amputee with no arms. How does she remove the shoe? *Yoav* began to contort himself, demonstrating how the *yevamah* might use her teeth to remove the shoe. While *Avner* was absorbed in this discussion of Torah law, *Yoav* struck him in the fifth rib.

The *Gemara* also notes that *Rabbi Yochanan* described the killing as *chabko b'chamishit* — he embraced him in the fifth, meaning the blow was to the fifth rib, the site of the liver and gallbladder, the most lethal point. This double use of the fifth rib — once when *Avner* killed *Asahel*, once when *Yoav* killed *Avner* — reinforces the moral symmetry the *Gemara* traces throughout this entire narrative.

---

## Yoav's virtues

### Avner & Amasa merit

The *Gemara* returns to the phrase from *Shlomo's* words condemning *Yoav*: *asher paga bishnei anashim tzadikim vetovim mimenu* — that he struck down two men more righteous and better than himself. In what sense were *Avner* and *Amasa* better than *Yoav*? The answer: *she'hayu dorshin achin v'rakin v'hu lo darash* — they expounded the *achin* and *rakin*, the limiting particles of the Torah — and he did not.

### Nov protest

What does this mean? *Amasa's* exposition of *ach* and *rak* we have already seen: he understood that the king's command did not override the people's engagement in Torah learning, and he acted accordingly. *Avner's* case is connected to the episode of *Nov ir hakohanim* — the city of priests that *Shaul* had slaughtered at the instigation of *Do'eg*. The *Gemara* records that *Avner* was among those who protested against the killing. He stood up and said this should not be done. *Yoav* did not protest. The ability and willingness to push back against an unjust royal command — grounded in proper halakhic *drasha* — is what distinguished them from *Yoav*.

### Uriyah execution

What did *Yoav* fail to protest? The killing of *Uriyah HaChiti*. *David* arranged for *Uriyah's* death on the battlefield, and *Yoav* was instrumental in carrying it out. The *Gemara* notes that the command was conveyed by letter — *b'igarta* — and not spoken explicitly by the king. The *Gemara* reasons that since it was written rather than verbally commanded, it should have been even easier for *Yoav* to disregard it or push back. *Avner* and *Amasa* had demonstrated that one may and should resist an unjust royal command; *Yoav* did not exercise that moral courage.

### Yoav's charity

Despite all of this, the *Gemara* does not leave *Yoav* as simply a villain. *Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Rav*: what does it mean that he was buried *b'beito bamidbar* — in his house in the desert? *Mah midbar mufkar lakol* — just as the desert is open and free to all, so too *Yoav's* house was open to all. He was generous with his wealth, supporting the poor freely. A second interpretation: just as the desert is clean of theft and licentiousness, so too *Yoav's* house was free of *gezel* and *arayot*. The *pasuk* says *v'Yoav yichaye et she'ar ha'ir* — and *Yoav* brought life to the city — and the *Gemara* understands this as referring to *Yerushalayim*: even all the delicacies he had he distributed generously.

### Execution & burial

The proceedings concluded: *Benayahu ben Yehoyada* carried out the execution, and *Yoav* was buried in his house. *Benayahu* then assumed *Yoav's* role as the military commander. The narrative arc closes: the man who had wielded military power across *David's* entire reign, who had killed two men better than himself and backed the wrong son at the succession crisis, was executed in due process by the very court that sat beside the *mizbe'ach* — and the role he had filled passed to his executioner.

---

## Four executions

### Death penalties intro

The *Gemara* now transitions to the *mishna's* framework of the four modes of capital punishment administered by *Beit Din*. The *mishna* enumerates them in a specific sequence: *sekila* (stoning), *serefa* (burning), *hereg* (beheading), and *chenek* (strangulation). *Rabbi Shimon* disagrees with this order, arranging them as *serefa*, *sekila*, *chenek*, *hereg*. The earlier discussion of the *mishna* concerned *sekila* specifically — the procedure of pushing the condemned from a height of two body-lengths.

### List order principle

*Rav Huna* said in the name of *Rav*: in general, when the Sages enumerated a list, there is no fixed order implied — *ein mukdam u'me'uchar* — unless they explicitly indicate otherwise. The primary exception he identifies is the seven cleansing agents used to test whether a stain is *dam nida*: *rok tafel* (tasteless saliva), *magisin* (chewed beans), *mei raglayim* (urine), *neter*, *borit*, *kimonia*, and *ashlag*. The *seifa* of that *mishna* states explicitly: if one applied them out of order, or applied all seven simultaneously, the act is invalid. This establishes that the sequence of those seven agents is *l'ikuva* — essential, not merely preferable.

### Additional sdarim

*Rav Papa* adds that our own *mishna's* list of the four modes of execution is also a case of fixed order — and the proof is that *Rabbi Shimon* disagrees with the order. The very fact that *Rabbi Shimon* bothers to rearrange them demonstrates that the *tanna kamma* intended a specific sequence. *Rav Papa* also adds two further exceptions to the general rule that lists lack intrinsic order: the *seder* of *Yom Kippur*, about which the *mishna* states explicitly that all the acts of *Yom Kippur* must be performed in order — *im hikdim ma'aseh lachavero lo asa velo klum* — and the *seder Tamid*, the daily sacrifice. The *Gemara* offers a qualification regarding *Yom Kippur*: it is not so much that the *seder* itself is the operative category but rather the *itzumo shel yom* — the essential nature of *Yom Kippur* itself — that demands the fixed sequence. As for the *Tamid*, *Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua* argues that the *seder Tamid* is a preference rather than an absolute requirement: obviously the animal must be slaughtered before the limbs are placed on the altar, but as between one limb and another, the order is not *me'akev*.

---

## Chalitzah order

### Chalitzah procedure

The *Gemara* then asks why the procedure of *mitzvat chalitzah* was not included in the list of fixed-order sequences. The *mishna* in *Yevamot* describes the procedure in full: the *yavam* and *yevamah* appear before the *beit din*; the judges provide advice appropriate to the situation — if, for instance, he is old and she is young or vice versa, they counsel accordingly. The *yevamah* then recites in Hebrew: *mein yevami l'hakim l'achiv shem b'Yisrael lo avah yavmi* — my *yavam* refuses to perpetuate his brother's name in Israel. The *yavam* declares: *lo chafatzti l'kachatah* — I do not wish to marry her. She then removes his shoe and spits before him, and recites: *kachah ye'aseh la'ish asher lo yivneh et beit achiv*. His name is thereafter called *beit chalutz hana'al* — the house of the removed shoe. *Rav Yehuda* described the order: she reads, he reads, she removes the shoe, she spits, she reads again.

### Chalitzah not essential

Why was this sequence not included in the enumeration of fixed-order procedures? Because although the *mishna* presents the order, and *Rav Yehuda* describes it, the sequence is not *l'ikuva* — it does not invalidate the *chalitzah* if altered. The procedure should be done in that order, but if one deviated, the *mitzvah* is nonetheless fulfilled.

### Chalitzah flexibility

The *Gemara* states this explicitly: *bein she'kidem chalitzah l'rekikah o rekikah l'chalitzah, mah she'asah asui* — whether the removal of the shoe preceded the spitting or the spitting preceded the removal, what was done is valid. This is why *chalitzah* was not placed on the list of procedures whose sequence is *me'akev*.

---

## Priestly garments

### Garment numbers

The *Gemara* concludes by addressing the priestly garments. The *mishna* states that whoever officiates in the eight garments — the *Kohen Gadol* — or the four garments — the ordinary *Kohen* — is qualified to perform the service. The four garments of the ordinary *kohen* are listed in the Torah: *ketonet*, *michnasayim*, *mitznefet*, and *avneit* — the robe, the breeches, the turban, and the belt. The *Kohen Gadol* adds four more: the *choshen*, *ephod*, *me'il*, and *tzitz*.

### Garment sequence

The *Gemara* asks: is there a required sequence for donning the priestly garments? The *baraita* states: from where do we know that something must precede the *michnasayim*? From the *pasuk*: *umichnesei vad yihyu al besaro* — the breeches of linen shall be upon his flesh. This establishes that the *michnasayim* must be first, as they are worn directly against the body, before any outer garment. Beyond this one fixed rule — undergarments before outer garments — no further sequence is mandated. The *Kohen Gadol* may don the *ephod* before the *tzitz* or the *tzitz* before the *ephod* without concern.

### Torah order logic

A natural question arises: if the *michnasayim* must be worn first, why does the Torah list the *ketonet* first? The *Gemara* answers: *mishum d'michaseh kulei gufa adifa lei* — because the *ketonet* covers the entire body, the Torah accords it pride of place in the listing. The Torah's sequence reflects which garment is most significant, not which must be donned first. The *ketonet* is preeminent in coverage and therefore in mention; the *michnasayim* are preeminent in donning sequence because they are worn against the flesh. The distinction between literary emphasis and procedural necessity is what this closing discussion turns on — and it brings the *amud* to its conclusion.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 50

## Rabbis' Hierarchy

### Four Executions

Today's daf picks up at the bottom of 49b, three lines from the end, where the *Mishnah* establishes the order of the four capital punishments: *sekila*, *sereifa*, *hereg*, *chenek*. Rabbi Shimon, notably, agrees to the two pairs—*sekila* and *sereifa* belonging together as the weightier pair, *hereg* and *chenek* as the lighter—but he reverses the order within each pair. Instead of *sekila* then *sereifa*, he has *sereifa* then *sekila*; instead of *hereg* then *chenek*, he has *chenek* then *hereg*. The entirety of today's *daf* is devoted to working out how the *rabanan* arrive at their order and how Rabbi Shimon arrives at his.

### Sekila > Sereifa

The *Gemara* opens by establishing why *sekila* is the weightiest of the four. *Sekila chamura misereifa*—*sekila* is weightier than *sereifa*—because it is the punishment prescribed for the *megadef* (blasphemer) and the *oveid avodah zarah* (idolater). And what makes those sins so grave? *Shekein posheit yado b'ikar*—they represent a direct rebellion against God Himself.

The *Gemara* immediately raises the counterargument: *adaraba*, perhaps *sereifa* is the weightier punishment, since it is the punishment given to a *bas kohen* who commits adultery, as the verse states, *ubas kohen ki tachel lehiznos es aviha hi mechalleles ba'eish tisareif*—a *bas kohen* who desecrates herself through fornication desecrates her father; she shall be burned in fire. And what makes that weighty? *Shekein mechalleles es aviha*—she brings disgrace upon her father's household, which adds a sin against persons on top of the sin against God.

### Arusa/Nesuah Proof

Here the *Gemara* introduces the core structural argument, and it is important to understand it precisely. *Kasvari rabanan*: the *rabanan* hold that the verse concerning the *bas kohen* applies only to the *nesuah* (fully married woman) and not to the *arusah* (betrothed woman). The starting point—what everyone agrees upon independently of the *bas kohen* case—is that for an ordinary *bas Yisrael*, a *nesuah* who commits adultery receives *chenek*, while an *arusah* who commits adultery receives *sekila*. This is explicit in the *pesukim*.

Then the *Gemara* says: since the *Torah* took the *arusah bas Yisrael* out of the *sekila* category and placed her into *sereifa* — *midei d'aftar rachmana arusa b'skila, shma mina skila chamura* — you learn that *sekila* is weightier. But Rashi stops the *Gemara* here and says clearly: this is not a proof. The *Gemara* sounds as though it is deriving something from the *pesukim*, but it is not. What is actually happening is that the *rabanan* began with the assumption that *sekila* is the weightiest punishment — because it is the punishment for the most severe sins, those against God directly — and then *read* that assumption into the *pesukim*, and now they are reading it back out. The reason *sekila* is assumed to be weightier is what was stated on the previous *amud*: the idolater and the blasphemer receive *sekila*, and those have to be the gravest sins. The *pesuk* passage is simply how the *rabanan* manage the *pesukim* to be consistent with their system; it proves nothing on its own.

Stated plainly: if *sereifa* applies to the *nesuah* and *sekila* is assumed to apply still to the *arusah* — an assumption the *rabanan* impose, not derive — then since the *arusah* is considered the graver case (because she brings shame to her father's house, as the *pesukim* frame it in terms of *beis aviha*), the punishment applied to the *arusah* must be the graver punishment, which confirms *sekila* over *sereifa*. But the assumption that the *arusah* is worse, and the reading of the *pas kohen* verse as limited to the *nesuah*, are both built into their starting position, not derived from it. Rashi says the *Gemara* is simply not being precise here.

On the question of whether the actual physical experience of the punishment determines the ranking: the *Gemara* never assumes this. Even if burning alive seems more painful in practice, the *Gemara*'s ranking is based entirely on the gravity of the sin for which the punishment is prescribed, not on the subjective experience of the condemned. It is worth noting that the manner of *sereifa* as practiced by *beis din* — pouring molten lead down the throat — while certainly not pleasant, is considerably more humane than burning alive.

### Sekila > Sayif

Having established the position of *sekila* relative to *sereifa*, the *Gemara* turns to proving *sekila* is weightier than *sayif* (death by the sword). Again, *sekila* is the punishment for the *megadef* and the *oveid avodah zarah*, which represents *posheit yado b'ikar*. But the *Gemara* immediately raises a challenge: *adaraba*, perhaps *sayif* is weightier — *shekein nitan l'anshei ir ha'nidachat*, it is the punishment used to destroy the entire city that committed *avodah zarah*, and moreover, *shekein mamonam avad*, their property is also destroyed, which represents an additional severity of the punishment.

The *Gemara* resolves this by asking: *eizeh koach merubeh, koach ha'madiach o koach ha'nidach* — which is the weightier force, the one who incites the city to *avodah zarah* or the people who were incited? Obviously the inciter bears greater responsibility. And a *beraitah* teaches that the *madiach ir ha'nidachat* — the one who subverts the idolatrous city — receives *sekila*. Since both cases involve *avodah zarah* but the inciter (who receives *sekila*) is the more culpable party, *sekila* is confirmed as the weightier punishment.

### Sekila > Chenek

The *Gemara* then addresses *sekila*'s superiority over *chenek* (strangulation). *Sekila* is the punishment for the *megadef* and the *oveid avodah zarah*, representing *posheit yado b'ikar*. The counterargument: *chenek chamur*, since *chenek* is the punishment for one who smites a parent (*makeh aviv ve'imo*), and what makes that weighty is *hukash kevodam li'kvod ha'makom* — the honor of parents is likened to the honor of God. Tosafos raises the point that the honor of parents cannot actually exceed the honor of God, suggesting at most they could be equal, which would mean these two punishments might be equivalent — but the *Gemara* does not pursue that line.

The resolution is the same structural move deployed earlier: since an *arusah bas Yisrael* receives *sekila* and a *nesuah bas Yisrael* receives *chenek*, and the *arusah* is assumed to represent the graver case because of the *beis aviha* context, *sekila* is confirmed as weightier than *chenek*. The *Gemara* reads this out of the *pesukim* in the same manner as before.

### Gezeira Shava

Having established that *sekila* is weightier than all three others, the *Gemara* must now show that *sereifa* is weightier than *sayif* and *chenek*. The argument for *sereifa* over *sayif* runs as follows. *Sereifa* is given to a *bas kohen* who commits adultery, which is weighty because she desecrates her father's household. Against this: *sayif* is used to wipe out an *ir ha'nidachat*, and moreover their property is destroyed. The *Gemara* resolves this through a *gezeira shava*: the word *aviha* appears in the verse concerning the *arusa* who receives *sekila* (*liznos beis aviha*) and also in the verse concerning the *bas kohen* who receives *sereifa* (*es aviha hi mechalleles*). The same way we established that *sekila* is weightier than *sayif* — via the *aviha* context — we now apply that link to *sereifa*: *mah aviha ha'amur bi'skila, skila chamur mi'sayif; af aviha ha'amur bi'sereifa, sereifa chamur mi'sayif*. Whatever *sekila* established through *aviha*, *sereifa* inherits through the parallel use of the same word.

### Sereifa Hierarchy

The proof that *sereifa* is weightier than *chenek* is more straightforward. Everyone agrees — both *rabanan* and Rabbi Shimon — that a *nesuah bas kohen* receives *sereifa* rather than the *chenek* that a *nesuah bas Yisrael* receives. This directly shows that *sereifa* is a more severe punishment than *chenek*: *midei d'amar rachmana l'nesuah bas kohen, miklal nesuah bas Yisrael me'chenek l'sereifa, shma mina sereifa chamura*. Since taking a *nesuah bas kohen* out of the *chenek* category and into the *sereifa* category represents an escalation, *sereifa* is demonstrably weightier than *chenek*. There is no controversy here; both positions agree on this point.

### Sayif > Chenek

Finally, the *Gemara* establishes that *sayif* is weightier than *chenek*. The opening move: *sayif* is the punishment for the residents of an *ir ha'nidachat*, which involves *avodah zarah* and the destruction of property — fairly weighty. Against this: *chenek* is for *makeh aviv ve'imo*, and the honor of parents is *hukash li'kvod ha'makom*. The resolution: *afilu hachi, posheit yado b'ikar adif* — even granting that comparison, a sin directly against God must outweigh a sin against parents. Since the *ir ha'nidachat* involves *avodah zarah*, which is *posheit yado b'ikar*, *sayif* is weightier than *chenek*. This is the same logic used throughout — sins against God directly occupy a categorically higher level — though one might note a certain circularity in the argument: this logic could not be invoked earlier to show that *sereifa* (given to the *bas kohen*) was secondary to *sekila*, and yet it is invoked here. The *Gemara* is working backwards from its established hierarchy and finding arguments to support each step.

---

## Rabbi Shimon's Order

### Bat Kohen Key

Turning now to Rabbi Shimon's approach, the method is essentially the mirror image. Rabbi Shimon's point of departure is the *bas kohen*, and his key claim is that *sereifa* applies to the *bas kohen* whether she is a *nesuah* or an *arusah* — this is the plain reading of the *pesukim*. For the *rabanan*, limiting *sereifa* to the *nesuah* was necessary to preserve *sekila* as the weightiest punishment. For Rabbi Shimon, that limitation is artificial. The *Torah* says *sereifa* for a *bas kohen* and means it for all cases of a *bas kohen*. This is not merely an exegetical preference; it is, for Rabbi Shimon, the natural reading. And from that reading, the entire hierarchy flows differently.

### Sereifa > Sekila

*Sereifa chamura mi'skila* — *sereifa* is weightier than *sekila* — because *sereifa* is the punishment of a *bas kohen* who commits adultery, and what makes it weighty is *mechalleles es aviha*, she desecrates her father's household. The counterargument: *adaraba, skila chamura*, *sekila* is for the *megadef* and the *oveid avodah zarah*, and what is weighty about that is *posheit yado b'ikar*, direct rebellion against God — which logically seems like a stronger claim.

Rabbi Shimon's answer is anchored in the *pesukim*: since both the *arusah* and the *nesuah* who are *bas kohen* go to *sereifa* — *de'amar achas arusah ve'achas nesuah yatze'u l'sereifa* — and since an *arusah bas Yisrael* ordinarily receives *sekila*, the *Torah* is explicitly taking a *bas kohen arusah* out of the *sekila* category and upgrading her to *sereifa*. *Ve'dhaft rachmana l'arusah bas kohen miklal arusah bas Yisrael mi'skila l'sereifa, shema mina sereifa chamura.* The *Torah* moved her upward, which means *sereifa* is the higher punishment.

It is worth pausing on the logical implication that is occasionally noted in this discussion. If one uses the hierarchy of capital punishments to infer the relative severity of sins, Rabbi Shimon's position would seem to imply that adultery by a *bas kohen* is a more severe sin than *avodah zarah*. The honest answer is that using the death-penalty hierarchy to make such inferences about sin-ranking is complicated, partly because the *Gemara* itself derives some rankings from assumptions about sin-severity and others from external textual proofs, and the results do not always yield a neat system. The practical purpose of the ranking — *nidon b'chamura*, giving the person the weightier of two applicable punishments — does not require that every ranking of punishments map onto a ranking of sins that makes intuitive sense.

### Sereifa Complete

Having established that *sereifa* is the weightiest, Rabbi Shimon must show it is weightier than *chenek* and *sayif* as well. *Sereifa chamura mi'chenek*: the opening claim is that *sereifa* goes to a *bas kohen* and is therefore weighty. The challenge: *chenek* goes to *makeh aviv ve'imo*, and *hukash kevodam li'kvod ha'makom*. The resolution: if *sereifa* is weightier than *sekila*, and *sekila* is weightier than *chenek* based on the *arusah* versus *nesuah* argument — the same proof the *rabanan* themselves use — then *sereifa* is certainly weightier than *chenek*. The proof is direct: *mi'dhaft rachmana l'nesuah bas kohen miklal nesuah bas Yisrael me'chenek l'sereifa, shema mina sereifa chamura*. A *nesuah bas kohen* is taken out of *chenek* and placed into *sereifa*, demonstrating *sereifa* is the higher punishment.

For *sereifa* over *sayif*: the initial claim is *sereifa* goes to a *bas kohen*. The challenge: *sayif* wipes out an *ir ha'nidachat*, and their property is destroyed. The resolution involves the *madiach* and *nidach* dynamic — which is weightier, the one who incites the city or the people who are incited? Obviously the inciter. For Rabbi Shimon, the *madiach ir ha'nidachat* receives *chenek* (as opposed to the *rabanan* who say *sekila*), but the principle still applies: the *madiach* receives something weightier than the *ir ha'nidachat* residents who receive *sayif*. Therefore *chenek* is weightier than *sayif*. And since *sereifa* is already established as weightier than *chenek*, by transitivity — *sereifa* is weightier than *sayif* as well.

### Sekila > Sayif

Rabbi Shimon must now rank the remaining punishments. *Sekila chamura mi'sayif*: the opening claim is that *sekila* goes to the *megadef* and *oveid avodah zarah*, so it must be weighty. The challenge: *sayif* goes to the *anshei ir ha'nidachat* and their property is destroyed. Resolution: which is weightier, the *madiach* or the *nidach*? The *madiach* is weightier, and Rabbi Shimon says the *madiach ir ha'nidachat* receives *chenek*. So *chenek* is weightier than *sayif*. And since *sekila* is weightier than *chenek* — established by the *arusah* versus *nesuah* argument — *sekila* is certainly weightier than *sayif* as well. *Kal va'chomer: umah chenek she'chamur mi'sayif, skila chamura heimenu; sayif ha'kal, lo kol sheken.*

### Sekila > Chenek

*Sekila chamura mi'chenek*: the opening claim is that *sekila* goes to the *megadef* and *oveid avodah zarah*. The challenge: *chenek* goes to *makeh aviv ve'imo*, and *hukash kevodam li'kvod ha'makom*. But this is an easy resolution: *mi'dhaft rachmana l'arusah bas Yisrael miklal nesuah bas Yisrael me'chenek l'skila, shma mina skila chamura*. The *Torah* takes an *arusah bas Yisrael* out of *chenek* (the punishment of the *nesuah*) and gives her *sekila*, showing *sekila* is the weightier punishment.

### Chenek > Hereg

The final step in Rabbi Shimon's system is establishing that *chenek* is weightier than *hereg* (death by the sword). This is somewhat surprising at first glance — one might have expected *hereg* to rank above *chenek* — but Rabbi Shimon's basis is the *madiach ir ha'nidachat*. The *madiach* receives something weightier than the ordinary residents of the *ir ha'nidachat*. The *nidachim* receive *sayif*; the *madiach* receives *chenek* according to Rabbi Shimon. Since the inciter must receive the weightier punishment, *chenek* is weightier than *sayif*. The *Gemara* then cites the *beraitah* explicitly: *madiach ir ha'nidachat b'skila* — according to the *rabanan*, the inciter receives *sekila* — *Rabbi Shimon omer b'chenek*, Rabbi Shimon says he receives *chenek*.

So Rabbi Shimon's complete hierarchy is *sereifa*, *sekila*, *chenek*, *hereg*. In practice, Rabbi Shimon's system is somewhat easier to derive than the *rabanan*'s. Once he places *sereifa* at the top, the *bas kohen* argument yields *sereifa* over the other three. Once *sekila* is established above *chenek* via the *arusah/nesuah* proof, most of the system is in place. The one surprising element — *chenek* above *hereg* — is carried by the *madiach/nidach* dynamic, which is the same structure the *rabanan* use to establish *sayif* above *chenek*, only with different punishments assigned to each role.

---

## Application & Sources

### Naara Me'orasah

The *Gemara* introduces a famous teaching cited as a pearl in the mouth of Rav Yochanan — *margla b'pumei d'Rav Yochanan* — meaning, Rashi explains, that it was Rav Yochanan's own formulation rather than a received tradition from a *mishnah* or *beraitah*. The case: *na'arah me'orasah bas Kohen she'zinsa b'skila* — a *na'arah me'orasah* who is also a *bas kohen* and who commits adultery receives *sekila*. Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *b'sereifa*. This is precisely the crux of their dispute given everything above. For the *rabanan*, *sekila* remains the weightier punishment and applies even to the *arusah bas kohen*; for Rabbi Shimon, every *bas kohen* — whether *nesuah* or *arusah* — receives *sereifa*, which is for him the weightier punishment.

### Incest Case

The *Gemara* then raises a second variant: what if this *na'arah me'orasah* — an ordinary *bas Yisrael*, not a *bas kohen* — committed her act of adultery specifically with her own father? The sin of intercourse between a father and daughter carries the punishment of *sereifa*. So she is a *na'arah me'orasah*, who by universal agreement receives *sekila*, but the particular act she committed is one for which the punishment is *sereifa*. She has, in effect, incurred two applicable punishments. According to Rabbi Shimon, who holds *sereifa* is weightier, she receives *sereifa*. According to the *rabanan*, who hold *sekila* is weightier, she receives *sekila*. The logic is parallel to the *bas kohen* case: for Rabbi Shimon, *sereifa* takes over whenever it applies because it is the heavier penalty; for the *rabanan*, *sekila* always remains the heavier penalty.

### Nifka Minah

The *Gemara* now asks: *mai kamashma lan* — what is the practical *nifka minah* of all of this? The answer: *nafka mina l'mi shenischayeiv shtei misos beis din, nidon b'chamura* — whenever a person has incurred two death penalties, the rule is that they receive the weightier one. That is the operative halachic principle that makes the entire ranking matter. The debate between Rabbi Shimon and the *rabanan* about which punishment is weightier translates directly into which punishment is administered when a person's sins make two punishments applicable simultaneously. The conclusion the *Gemara* draws is explicit: *mishum d'le'rabanan skila chamura, u'le'Rabbi Shimon sereifa chamura*.

### Braitah Analysis

The *Gemara* now asks: what is the source for Rabbi Shimon's position? *D'tanya, Rabbi Shimon omer: shtei kelalos ne'emru b'vas kohen* — two distinct categories are stated regarding a *bas kohen*, the *nesuah* and the *arusah*. The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: do only *bas kohen* cases have these two categories? A *bas Yisrael* also has the distinction of *nesuah* receiving *chenek* and *arusah* receiving *sekila*! The *Gemara* explains: the point of departure — *ima af b'vas kohen* — is that a *bas kohen* begins from the same baseline as a *bas Yisrael*, with *chenek* for the *nesuah* and *sekila* for the *arusah*. *Ve'hotzia hakatuv nesuah miklal nesuah ve'arusah miklal arusa* — the *Torah* then removed the *bas kohen* from both of those categories.

### Pesuk Reading

The mechanism of the removal is significant. The *Torah*'s statement about the *bas kohen* takes the *nesuah bas kohen* out of the *chenek* category applicable to a *nesuah bas Yisrael* and places her into *sereifa*. It simultaneously takes the *arusah bas kohen* out of the *sekila* category applicable to an *arusah bas Yisrael* and places her also into *sereifa*. *Mah keshehotzia hakatuv nesuah miklal nesuah lehachmir, af keshehotzia hakatuv arusah miklal arusah lehachmir* — just as removing the *nesuah bas kohen* from her baseline category represents an escalation (from *chenek* to *sereifa*), so too removing the *arusah bas kohen* from her baseline represents an escalation (from *sekila* to *sereifa*). This in turn establishes that *sereifa* must be weightier than *sekila*, because the *Torah* is moving the *arusah* upward by assigning *sereifa* to her.

### Zomemim Rules

The *beraitah* continues with a ruling about *edim zomemim* (false witnesses) in cases involving a *bas kohen*. *Zomemei nesuah bas kohen bikelal zomemei nesuah bas Yisrael; ve'zomemei arusah bas kohen bikelal zomemei arusah bas Yisrael.* The verse states *es aviha hi mechalleles ba'eish tisareif* — it is *she* who is burned, implying *hi b'sereifa v'lo zomemeiha b'sereifa*. The false witnesses do not receive *sereifa*; they receive the punishment that would have applied to a *bas Yisrael* in her position.

This is a striking ruling that requires explanation. In general, *edim zomemim* receive the punishment they sought to impose on the accused. Why should witnesses who tried to have a *bas kohen* executed receive a lesser punishment? The answer lies in the specific character of the *bas kohen*'s sin. The elevated punishment of *sereifa* for a *bas kohen* is grounded in *mechalleles es aviha* — she desecrates her father's household. That desecration is something only she can commit; the adulterer she was with did not desecrate her father's household, and neither did the false witnesses. The sin of *mechalleles beis aviha* is unique to the woman and cannot be imputed to the witnesses. Therefore, we strip the *bas kohen* dimension from the punishment when it comes to the *zomemim* and apply to them the penalty that would be given to a *bas Yisrael* in the equivalent situation. This also explains why the male adulterer in such a case — even if identified — would not receive *sereifa*: the elevated punishment belongs exclusively to her by virtue of her relationship to her father's household.

### Pesuk Parallels

The *Gemara* then examines the *pesukim* more carefully. The *beraitah* reads: *u'vas ish kohen ki techel liznos* — might *techel* refer to *chillul Shabbos*, desecrating the Sabbath? No: *talmud lomar liznos*, the *Torah* specifies it is the desecration that comes through sexual sin. Might it refer to an unmarried woman, a *pnuyah*? No: *ne'emar kan aviha, v'ne'emar lehalan aviha* — the word *aviha* appears here and also in the passage about the *na'arah me'orasah* (*liznos beis aviha*), establishing a *gezeira shava*. Just as there the *Torah* specifies a woman with a *zikas habaal* — a bond to a husband — so here too the *Torah* is speaking of a woman in a marital relationship: *mah lehalan znus im zikas habaal, af kan znus im zikas habaal*.

One might then ask — and the *beraitah* raises this — since we are linking the two passages through *aviha* and *liznos*, why not say this case of the *bas kohen* is also specifically a *na'arah me'orasah*? The *pshat* of *beis aviha* suggests she has not yet moved out of her father's house, which points toward betrothal. Furthermore, *im mah lehalan na'arah v'hi arusah, af kan na'arah v'hi arusah* — if the *lehalan* passage specifies a *na'arah arusah*, perhaps the *bas kohen* verse is similarly limited. The *Gemara* then asks: what about a *nesuah bas kohen*, a *bogeres bas kohen*, or even an elderly *bas kohen* who commits adultery — how do we know these are included?

### Expansion Rules

The answer is that *talmud lomar u'vas kohen ki techel liznos*: the verse describes her generically as a *bas kohen* without specifying *na'arah* or any particular marital status, in contrast to other passages that always open by specifying the woman's age and status. The generic term *bas kohen* encompasses her at any age and in any state of marriage. The *lehalan* passage established that there must be a marital bond (*zikas habaal*); the *bas kohen* verse then extends the ruling beyond the *na'arah me'orasah* case to all instances where a *bas kohen* is in some form of marital relationship and commits adultery. This is Rabbi Shimon's reading — both *nesuah* and *arusah* are included — whereas the *rabanan* limit the verse to the *nesuah* in order to preserve *sekila* as the weightier punishment for the *arusah* case.

### Bat Ish Kohen

The *beraitah* concludes with one final question about the *bas kohen*: *ein li ela she'nisas le'Kohen* — one might think the *bas kohen*'s elevated punishment of *sereifa* applies only if she has married a *kohen*. What if she married a *Levi*, a *Yisrael*, a non-Jew, a *chalal*, a *mamzer*, or a *nasin*? Do all of these still trigger the *sereifa* penalty? The *hava amina* is admittedly unusual — particularly regarding a non-Jew, where there is no halachically binding marriage at all. But the *beraitah* raises it to dismiss it: *talmud lomar u'vas ish kohen, af al pi she'eina kohenes* — the verse specifies *bas ish kohen*, a daughter of a *kohen man*, emphasizing that it is her paternal lineage that defines her status, not the identity of her husband. However her marriage may be characterized and whoever she has married, as long as she is a *bas kohen* by virtue of her father, the full weight of the *bas kohen* ruling applies to her. Her personal *kohanic* standing is not diminished by the fact that she is married to a non-*kohen*. This distinguishes her individual identity as *bas kohen* from the question of whether she herself holds the status of *kohenes*, which sometimes carries independent halachic significance.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 51

## Burning of Kohen's Daugh…

### Overview & Context

Today's daf, 51a, continues in the middle of the broader debate between the *rabbanan* and Rabbi Shimon concerning the ordering of the four court-mandated executions (*misos beis din*). The nexus of that debate, as we have seen, is the question of under what circumstances the daughter of a *kohen* who commits adultery receives the punishment of *sreifah* (burning). Which situations trigger *sreifah* — and why — illuminates how the various executions are ranked relative to one another, and so this question becomes the central battleground of the dispute. Today's daf focuses almost entirely on this issue of the *bat kohen*'s burning, not merely as a vehicle for understanding the order of executions, but as a subject worthy of thorough analysis in its own right.

## Baraita Text & Drasha

### Baraita Setup

We pick up from the top of 51a in the middle of a *baraita* that was introduced on the previous daf. The *baraita* opens with the phrase *ein li ela shenisuah l'kohen* — I know only that she is married to a *kohen*. The premise here is that we already established from the word *liznot* in the verse that the text is discussing a forbidden sexual act, not some other form of desecration. We likewise established from the word *aviha* — through a linkage to the case of the *na'arah hameurasah* — that the woman must be married. The question now becomes: to whom must she be married for the punishment of *sreifah* to apply?

The *baraita* asks how we know the law extends beyond a woman married to a *kohen* — including a woman married to a *levi*, a plain *yisrael*, an *oved kochavim*, a *chalal*, a *mamzer*, or a *nesin*. These represent a wide spectrum of marital situations. A marriage to a non-Jew (*oved kochavim*) is, as the *gemara* itself acknowledges without fully unpacking here, a case that presents particular difficulty, since halachah does not ordinarily treat such a union as a binding marriage — and if it is not binding, intercourse with another man would not technically constitute adultery. The *gemara* does not resolve this here. The *chalal* — for instance, the son of a *kohen* and a *gerushah* — represents a permissible marriage for the *bat kohen*, though it renders her a *chalalah* in the process. The *mamzer* and *nesin* represent unions that are halachically forbidden and yet binding.

The *baraita* derives that the law applies in all these cases from the phrase *u'vat ish kohen* — the daughter of a man who is a *kohen* — rather than identifying her as a *kohenet* in her own right. From this the *baraita* infers *af al pi she'eina kohenet*: even if something has acted to compromise her own *kehunah* status, she is still the daughter of a *kohen*, still subject to the unique desecration that her act represents, and therefore still subject to *sreifah*.

### Drasha on 'Hi'

The verse reads: *u'vat ish kohen ki teichel liznot et aviha hi mechalelet ba'esh tisaref* — the daughter of a *kohen* who commits an act of *znus* desecrates her father; she shall be burned in fire. The *baraita* derives from the word *hi* — "she" — that the *sreifah* is specific to her. *Hi bisreifah v'ein bo'aleha bisreifah*: the man who commits adultery with her does not receive *sreifah*. His sin is adultery in the ordinary sense, punishable by *chenek* (strangulation), or if she is a *na'arah hameurasah*, by *skilah* (stoning) — but in neither case by *sreifah*. The burning is the consequence not of the act of adultery as such, but of what she has done through that act: she has desecrated her father's house, brought shame upon her *kehunah* lineage. Though the man was the instrument through whom she did this, the desecration belongs uniquely to her. That is the force of *hi*.

### Edim Zomemim Exception

From the same word *hi*, the *baraita* further derives *v'ein zomemeha bisreifah*: conspiring witnesses (*edim zomemim*) who falsely testified that she committed this act do not receive *sreifah* either. This is striking, because the rule of *edim zomemim* ordinarily requires that the false witnesses receive precisely the punishment they sought to have inflicted on the accused — even in cases where that punishment could never technically apply to the witnesses themselves. Yet here, this is the one case where the *edim zomemim* do not receive the punishment of the accused.

The reason appears to be that *sreifah* here is not simply the punishment for adultery as a category — it is the punishment for this woman's specific act of desecrating her father's priestly household. Even in a case where *edim zomemim* could be treated as if they had committed a sin they never actually performed, there is no way to treat these male witnesses as if they brought shame upon a *kohen*'s house through an act of adultery. The desecration of the *kehunah* household is something structurally unique to a *bat kohen*. One might push back slightly: is it gender that creates the exception, or the *kehunah* status? Strictly speaking, it is a combination — gender alone is not sufficient, since a non-*kohen* woman committing adultery would not receive *sreifah* at all, and if *edim zomemim* testified falsely against such a woman their punishment would follow hers. But when the *kehunah* family status is layered atop the gendered role of this particular woman, the punishment for the witnesses cannot follow suit. However unusual this exception is in the overall framework of *edim zomemim*, the *gemara* acknowledges it as genuinely anomalous.

### Rabbi Eliezer's Statement

The *baraita* concludes with the enigmatic statement of Rabbi Eliezer: *et aviha bisreifah v'et chamiha biskilah* — with her father it is *sreifah*, with her father-in-law it is *skilah*. This is a curious formulation that the *gemara* will subject to sustained scrutiny. For now we simply note it and move on to the unpacking of the *baraita* as a whole.

## Excluding Alternatives

### Shabbat Violation

Having quoted the full *baraita*, the *gemara* now proceeds *amar mar* — that is, it goes back to examine the text piece by piece. (It is worth noting the distinction between *amar mar* and *gufa*: *amar mar* is used when the full text of a *baraita* has already been quoted and the *gemara* now unpacks it line by line; *gufa* is used when only an excerpt has been quoted and the *gemara* wishes to return to the whole *baraita*.)

The first phrase examined is *yachol afilu chillul Shabbos* — perhaps the verse applies even to a *bat kohen* who desecrates Shabbat. After all, the root *techal* in *ki teichel liznot* could be read as *challel*, desecrate, and the verse also says *et aviha hi mechalelet*, she desecrates her father — so perhaps the theme of desecration extends to Shabbat violation. Setting aside for a moment the word *liznot*, which obviously rules it out, the *gemara* entertains what the *hava amina* might have been.

The response is that *chillul Shabbos* is punishable by *skilah* — and the question is immediately raised: how could one ever have thought that *chillul Shabbos* would bring *sreifah*? The answer is that this *baraita* follows the view of Rabbi Shimon, who holds *sreifah chamurah* — that *sreifah* is a more severe punishment than *skilah*. Within that framework, a theoretical argument could be constructed: since the Torah is particularly stringent with *kohanim*, burdening them with many additional *mitzvos* and prohibitions (*derabi behu mitzvos yeseros*), perhaps a *bat kohen* who violates Shabbat should be punished at an elevated level.

The *gemara* then refines this *hava amina* with a further wrinkle. One might have thought that specifically the *bat kohen* — rather than the male *kohen* himself — would receive *sreifah* for Shabbat desecration. Why not the male *kohen*? Because male *kohanim* are themselves obligated to perform the *avodah* in the *beis hamikdash*, which involves overriding Shabbat. The Torah already permits Shabbat violation for the *kohen*'s sacred service, so the Torah would presumably not impose the most severe punishment on him for Shabbat desecration. But the *bat kohen* has no such Shabbat override — she is burdened by the weight of her family's elevated standard without the corresponding allowance. So perhaps she receives *sreifah*. This is immediately dismissed — *ka mashma lan* that she does not, because the verse says *liznot*, referring exclusively to forbidden sexual activity.

### Unmarried Status

The *gemara* next asks: *yachol afilu pnuyah* — perhaps the verse applies even to an unmarried woman. If *liznot* means something like general promiscuity or loose sexual behavior, maybe the *bat kohen* need not be married at all for the verse to apply. The *gemara* rejects this: the word *aviha* in this verse links to its usage by the *na'arah hameurasah*, making clear that the woman is in the state of marriage. The *hava amina*, then, is that the word *liznot* might refer to sexual activity in a broader sense that does not require a state of marriage.

### Znus Definition

This leads directly into a rich discussion of what *znus* means. In common usage, *zonah* and *znus* do not immediately connote adultery — they suggest promiscuity or prostitution more generally, not specifically intercourse that violates a marital bond. Yet the *gemara* initially proceeds on the assumption that *liznot* implies some form of *issur* — a forbidden sexual act — not merely sex outside of marriage.

Here it is worth digressing briefly on the two biblical terms for a prostitute: *zonah* and *kedeshah*. The conventional explanation of *kedeshah*, following Rashi and others, is that it means "designated" — one set apart for the role of hired sex. But an alternative reading, developed by the commentator Robert Alter in his analysis of the story of Judah and Tamar, proposes that the two terms are actually distinct in kind: *zonah* denotes an ordinary prostitute, while *kedeshah* refers to a cult prostitute — one who performs sexual acts in the context of religious temple ritual. This reading elegantly explains the textual details: when Judah sees Tamar, he takes her for a *zonah*, and later, when his friend is sent to retrieve the pledge, he asks around for a *kedeshah* — a more respectable category of woman — precisely to avoid the embarrassment of publicly announcing that Judah had consorted with an ordinary prostitute. The locals deny any knowledge of a *kedeshah* in the area, which is why she cannot be found. This is an illuminating piece of biblical philology, though its direct halachic relevance here is tangential.

What is halachically central is the position of Rabbi Eliezer, which the *gemara* now introduces as the basis for the *hava amina* that the verse could apply to a *pnuyah*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that *panui haba al pnuyah* — even a single man who has intercourse with a single woman, where no marital bond exists on either side and there is no technical *issur* — if they do so *she'lo l'shem ishus*, without the context of marriage, *asa'ah zonah*, he has made her into a *zonah* in the sense relevant to the prohibition on a *kohen* marrying a *zonah* (*ishah zonah vechalalah lo yikachu*). According to Rabbi Eliezer, *znus* encompasses all sex outside of marriage, not only sex that violates a specific prohibition.

This contrasts with the normative *halacha* as formulated, for example, by the Rambam: a *zonah* in the technical sense is a woman who has had intercourse with a man she is prohibited to marry. Sex while a *niddah*, for instance, does not create *zonah* status, since the prohibition is not about the identity of the man but about her ritual state. But any act of sex with a man she is forbidden to marry renders her a *zonah*. Rabbi Eliezer's broader definition would encompass even sex between two entirely unmarried and otherwise permitted individuals.

The *gemara* explains that the *hava amina* behind *yachol afilu pnuyah* was constructed following the view of Rabbi Eliezer: since *liznot* means, according to Rabbi Eliezer, any sex outside of marriage, the verse might apply even to an unmarried *bat kohen* engaged in casual promiscuity. The *gemara* then answers that *beis aviha* — through its parallel to the *na'arah hameurasah* context — establishes that the woman must be married, and thus *liznot* here must refer to *zikkas habaal*, the bond of marriage, specifically an adulterous violation of that bond. The linkage to *aviha* elsewhere indicates not that she literally had relations with her father, but rather that she is in a marital state parallel to the *meorasah* — in her father's domain — and has committed adultery against that bond.

A further *hava amina* is then considered: perhaps *aviha* in this context means she committed the sin *with her father* — incest — and that is the unique case that generates *sreifah*. The *gemara* quickly disposes of this: if so, *mai irya bat kohen* — why speak specifically of a *bat kohen*? The rule that a daughter who commits incest with her father receives *sreifah* applies to all Jewish women. The *gemara* cites the tradition of Rava in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi, who derives through the linkage of *hena-hena* and *zima-zima* that a daughter's incest with her father carries *sreifah*: the Torah's prohibition on sleeping with a woman and her daughter uses the word *zima* and specifies *ba'esh yisrefu*, which links via *hena* to the case of granddaughter, and from there encompasses daughter as well. Since *sreifah* for father-daughter incest applies universally, the verse by the *bat kohen* must be teaching something else. The *gemara* then clarifies: *et aviha hi mechalelet* — *hi* being the operative word — means that *she* is the one desecrating, not that he is desecrating her. The *bat kohen* is the one who has done the active wrong, and the wrong she has done is committing adultery with *another man* — not with her father. This interpretation is confirmed and the *hava amina* of father-daughter incest is ruled out.

## Marriage Scope

### Non-Kohen Husbands

The *baraita* then resumes: *ein li ela sheniset l'kohen* — I know only that she is married to a *kohen*. How do I extend the law to a *bat kohen* married to a *levi*, a *yisrael*, an *oved kochavim*, a *chalal*, a *mamzer*, or a *nesin*? The *baraita* derives the extension from *bat ish kohen* — the daughter of a *kohen*, emphasizing that what matters is her paternal lineage, even if her own *kehunah* status has been compromised.

One might wonder why any extension is needed at all: a *bat kohen* is free to marry whomever she chooses — there is no obligation that she marry a *kohen*. Why would we ever have thought that her marriage to a non-*kohen* changes the law? The *gemara* addresses this directly.

### Forbidden Marriages

The *hava amina* is constructed from the verse *ki teichel liznot* — the root *techal* carrying the double meaning of *lehatchil* (to begin) and *lechalel* (to desecrate). Perhaps the punishment of *sreifah* applies when this act represents the *first* desecration of her *kehunah* status. If she has already compromised that status through her marriage, then the act of adultery — however grave — is not the inaugural desecration.

The *gemara* supports this *hava amina* from established *halacha*: *v'vat kohen ki tihye l'ish zar hi bi'trumat ha'kodashim lo tochel* — a *bat kohen* who marries a non-*kohen* may no longer eat *terumah*. She is no longer embedded in a *kehunah* household: she has left her father's house through marriage, and her husband's house is not a *kohanic* household. As long as she remains in that marriage, her *kehunah* connection is severed for purposes of *terumah*. Only if she is widowed or divorced without children can she return to her father's house and resume eating *terumah*. Thus marriage to a *levi* or *yisrael* temporarily displaces her from *kehunah* status, and marriage to a *mamzer*, *nesin*, or non-Jew does so permanently.

This distinction matters enormously. If she marries a man she is forbidden to be with — a *mamzer*, a *nesin*, a non-Jew — not only is she currently barred from *terumah*, but she can never return to her father's household for that purpose. Having had sexual relations with someone who renders her permanently disqualified (*keivan sheniv'ala le-psula, pasla*), her *kehunah* status is fundamentally altered. She can no longer marry a *kohen*; she becomes a *chalalah* or *zonah* in the relevant sense. The same applies, interestingly, to a *chalal*, even though marriage to a *chalal* is technically permissible for her: the *chalal* status is contagious. A male *kohen* who sins by marrying a *gerushah* retains his own *kohen* identity — we may withhold the right to *duchen* from him as a form of penalty, but halachically his status is unchanged. It is his children who suffer the consequence: they are born *chalalin*. And when the *chalal* has intercourse with a woman — even in a fully permitted marriage — she acquires *chalalah* status. So a *bat kohen* married to a *chalal* becomes a *chalalah* and can no longer eat *terumah* or marry a *kohen*.

Given all this, the *hava amina* runs: once a *bat kohen* has already permanently forfeited her *kehunah* status through her marriage to a forbidden man, perhaps the subsequent act of adultery, terrible as it is, no longer constitutes the unique desecration of *et aviha hi mechalelet*. Her *kehunah* status has already been violated. Maybe *sreifah* should not apply. This is not a weak *hava amina* — especially for the cases of *mamzer*, *nesin*, and the rest where the compromise is permanent and complete.

### Rabbi Meir Position

The *baraita* continues with the opinion of Rabbi Meir, recorded in a separate *baraita*. A *bat kohen* who marries a *yisrael* and eats *terumah* inadvertently pays the principal but not the added fifth (*chomesh*), because despite being forbidden to eat *terumah* in her present circumstances, she came from a household where she was entitled to eat it — and were her husband to die without leaving children, she would return to that entitlement. She is therefore not treated as a full *zar* vis-à-vis *terumah*, and does not pay the *chomesh* penalty a complete outsider would. And her execution, if she commits adultery, is *sreifah* — that much is not in dispute for this case.

But if she married one of the disqualifying men — a *mamzer* or the like — Rabbi Meir holds: *misalemes keren v'chomesh*, she pays both principal and fifth, because she is now a complete *zara* in every sense; *u'misasa b'chenek* — if she commits adultery, her execution is *chenek*, not *sreifah*. Rabbi Meir maintains that once her *kehunah* status has been permanently compromised through her forbidden marriage, she no longer falls within the category of *bat ish kohen* that triggers *sreifah*.

### Rabbanan Consensus

The *rabbanan* disagree. *V'Chachamim omrim*: both women — the one married to a *yisrael* and the one married to a man who permanently disqualifies her — pay principal but not the *chomesh*, and both receive *sreifah* if they commit adultery. The reason is that the *kohanic* connection established by birth is never entirely severed. Even after a *bat kohen* has been permanently excluded from *terumah* and permanently disqualified from marrying a *kohen*, she remains the daughter of a *kohen*. The sanctity that status confers — with its attendant demands and consequences — does not dissolve. Having that *kedushah* status has, as the shiur puts it, its pluses and minuses. The *rabbanan*'s position is explicit: our *baraita* was articulated precisely to reject Rabbi Meir.

## Avihah/Chamihah Debate

### Literal Reading

We turn now to the final and most puzzling line of the *baraita*: the statement of Rabbi Eliezer, *et aviha bisreifah v'et chamiha biskilah* — with her father it is *sreifah*, with her father-in-law it is *skilah*. What does this mean?

The most literal reading would be: if the *bat ish kohen* commits adultery with her father (incest), she receives *sreifah*; if she commits adultery with her father-in-law, she receives *skilah*. This reading is immediately challenged: *mai irya bat kohen* — why speak of a *bat kohen* at all? The rule that father-daughter incest is *sreifah* applies to every Jewish daughter, as we already established. And the rule that adultery with a father-in-law is *skilah* is equally unremarkable — it is simply standard adultery by a *nesuah*, which gets *chenek*, or by an *arusah*, which gets *skilah*, depending on the marital stage. The *baraita* would be saying nothing specifically about the *bat kohen*. This reading must be abandoned.

### Domain Reading

A second approach interprets *aviha* and *chamiha* not as the identity of her partner in the act, but as the domain (*reshut*) she occupies. *Birshut aviha bisreifah* — when she is in her father's domain (i.e., she is an *arusah*, betrothed but living at home), she receives *sreifah*. *Birshut chamiha biskilah* — when she is in her father-in-law's domain (i.e., she has moved into her husband's family household as a *nesuah*), she receives *skilah*. This is an appealing reading. An *arusah* who commits adultery receives *skilah* as a *bat yisrael*; as a *bat kohen*, Rabbi Eliezer elevates this to *sreifah*, the weightier punishment. A *nesuah* who commits adultery receives *chenek* as a *bat yisrael*; as a *bat kohen*, Rabbi Eliezer elevates this one degree to *skilah*.

But there is an immediate problem: which of the Tannaitic opinions does this match? The *gemara* systematically tests it against each position. If it follows the *rabbanan* — who hold that *sreifah* is assigned to the *nesuah* (because *skilah*, being worse in their view, belongs to the *arusah*) — then the domain reading is precisely backwards; the *rabbanan* say *sreifah* is *birshut chamiha*, not *birshut aviha*. If it follows Rabbi Shimon — who holds *sreifah chamurah* and says both *arusah* and *nesuah* receive *sreifah* — then Rabbi Eliezer's differentiation between *arusah* and *nesuah* is already a departure from Rabbi Shimon's own stated position. And if it follows Rabbi Yishmael — who also holds *sreifah chamurah* and limits *sreifah* to the *arusah* while the *nesuah* reverts to *chenek* — it is the closest match, but Rabbi Eliezer says *skilah*, not *chenek*, for the *nesuah*.

### Rabbi Yishmael Analogy

The answer that comes closest to working is attributed to Rava, following a version of Rabbi Shimon's approach. Rava proposes: *vekasavar Rabbi Eliezer nesuah ke'arusah* — Rabbi Eliezer treats the *nesuah* analogously to the *arusah*. The argument runs as follows. By a regular *bat yisrael*, an *arusah* receives *skilah* and a *nesuah* receives *chenek* — the *arusah* case is elevated one degree above the *nesuah*. Now apply that structural relationship to the *bat kohen*: since *sreifah* (in Rabbi Shimon's ordering: *sreifah*, *skilah*, *chenek*, *hereg*) is one degree more severe than *skilah*, and since the *arusah* case is where *sreifah* applies, the *nesuah* case for the *bat kohen* should be elevated by one degree above *chenek* — which yields *skilah*. This is an argument by analogy: *mah arusah chad darga maskinan la miskila lisreifah, af nesuah chad darga maskinan la michenek liskilah* — just as the *arusah* goes up one level from *skilah* to *sreifah*, so the *nesuah* goes up one level from *chenek* to *skilah*.

This is a genuinely elegant answer. But the *gemara* objects: Rabbi Chanina notes that Rabbi Shimon himself said explicitly that both *arusah* and *nesuah* receive *sreifah* — so this position, while structurally similar to Rabbi Shimon's framework, departs from Rabbi Shimon's actual ruling.

### Rabbanan Reading

The final answer is given by Ravina: *le'olam kerabanan* — in truth it follows the *rabbanan*. But the *rabbanan*, as we established, hold *skilah* to be more severe and assign it to the *arusah* case, not to the *nesuah*. The *rabbanan*'s position is thus the exact inverse of what Rabbi Eliezer's statement appears to say. Ravina resolves this by proposing that the text of Rabbi Eliezer's statement has been accidentally reversed. It should read: *et aviha biskilah, v'et chamiha bisreifah* — in her father's domain (*reshut aviha*), meaning as an *arusah*, she receives *skilah*; in her father-in-law's domain (*reshut chamiha*), meaning as a *nesuah*, she receives *sreifah*. This is precisely the *rabbanan*'s position. How did the text get inverted? Because the verse itself says *et aviha hi mechalelet ba'esh tisaref* — the word *aviha* naturally associates with *sreifah* in the reader's mind, and so a copyist or transmitter naturally wrote *et aviha bisreifah* when it should have said *et aviha biskilah*. The slip was understandable, but the text is reversed.

### Practical Relevance

Rav Nachman then rules: the *halacha* follows the reading sent from Eretz Yisrael by Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yose bar Chanina — which was the first proposed interpretation. Rav Yosef objects: *hilchasa limshicha*? What is the point of ruling on a matter of court executions that has no practical application today? Abaye responds sharply: do we refrain from learning and ruling on all matters pertaining to *shechitas kodashim* — the tractates of *Zevachim*, *Menachos*, and so forth — because they apply only when the Temple stands? Clearly not. *Ela derush vekabel sachar* — we study it and receive reward for the study. *Hacha nami derush vekabel sachar*.

But Rashi points out a further dimension to Rav Yosef's objection. His concern was not merely that executions are not carried out nowadays — it was a more pointed critique: the entire discussion of *aviha* and *chamiha* was never a *halachic* debate in the first place. It was a question of *peshat* — how to interpret an obscure phrase in Rabbi Eliezer's statement. All of the competing readings ultimately arrive at the same substantive outcome; they differ only in how they parse the words. To issue a *psak halacha* on what is really a question of textual exegesis — *sugya dishma'ta hilchasa ka'amar*? — is itself the anomaly. If all one wanted to know was what Rabbi Eliezer actually meant, the answer, as Rashi wryly observes, can wait: when the time of *techiyas hameisim* comes, we can ask Rabbi Eliezer himself. With that, we have completed the full unpacking of this *baraita*, and the *gemara* will continue from here.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 52

## Srefah Hierarchy Deb (II)

### Three Positions

The daf begins in the middle of 51b, in the context of a *braita* exploring the case of a *bat kohen* — a daughter of a *kohen* — who commits adultery and receives the distinctive punishment of *srefah*. The discussion has centered on determining precisely which cases of a *bat kohen* fall under this ruling: is she *nesu'ah* (fully married), *arusah* (betrothed), or some combination? Three positions have emerged from the preceding discussion. The *chachamim* hold that a *nesu'ah* receives *srefah* because it is weightier than *chenek*, while the *arusah* receives *skila* because *skila* is the weightiest punishment. A second view, associated with Rabbi Shimon, holds that both the *arusah* and the *nesu'ah* receive *srefah*, treating *srefah* as the weightiest of all. Now the *Gemara* introduces a third position: that of Rabbi Yishmael.

### Rabbi Yishmael

The *braita* states: *u'vas kohen ki techel liznot — b'na'ara ham'urasa hakatuve medaber* — "when a daughter of a *kohen* commits adultery, the verse is speaking of a *na'ara ham'urasa*." One might ask: perhaps the verse refers even to a *nesu'ah*? The *Gemara* responds with a chain of reasoning. The verse *ish asher yinaf et eshet re'ehu — mot yumat hano'ef v'hano'efes* establishes *chenek* as the default punishment for adultery — all adulterers, male and female, were encompassed within this rule. Then the Torah created an exception: a *na'ara m'urasa* receives the weightier punishment of *skila* rather than the default *chenek*. When the Torah subsequently creates another exception for a *bat kohen* — assigning her *srefah* — the logic dictates that this exception, like the prior one, applies only to the analogous case: the *na'ara m'urasa*. All other cases of a *bat kohen* revert to the default of *chenek*, just as all other non-betrothed women revert to *chenek* as well.

### Analogy Comparison

The *braita* makes this explicit: *k'shem shehotzi hakatuve bas Yisrael b'skila arusah v'lo nesuah* — just as the Torah assigned the weightier punishment of *skila* specifically to an *arusah* and not to a *nesuah*, so too *af k'shem shehotzi hakatuve bat kohen l'srefah arusah v'lo nesuah* — when the Torah assigned the special punishment of *srefah* to a *bat kohen*, it similarly applies only to the *arusah* and not the *nesuah*.
