This is reinforced by the *pshat* of the verse itself, which says *et aviha hi mechalelet* — "she has desecrated her father" — with the focus on the father suggesting that she is still living in her father's house, which is the condition of a *na'ara m'urasa* and not a *nesuah*. This constitutes a third distinct position regarding who receives *srefah*.

---

## Zomemim Witnesses

### False Witnesses

The *braita* continues by addressing the men implicated in the adultery case — specifically the *edim zomemim*, the false witnesses who had sought to frame her — and asking what punishment they would receive.

### Bo'el Punishment

The *Gemara* interjects with a textual question: the *braita* cites the verse *va'asitem lo ka'asher zamam*, the standard formula for *edim zomemim*, but applies it to the *bo'el*, the man who actually committed the act. This is imprecise, and the text is accordingly corrected. The principle is that the *edim zomemim* would receive not the punishment of the *bat kohen* herself, but the punishment that the *bo'el* would have received — which is *chenek*, the standard punishment for adultery by a non-*kohen* male. The source is the verse *la'asos leachiv* — what the witnesses intended to do to their "brother" — and not to their "sister." It is the punishment designated for the man that serves as the model for the *zomemim*.

### Gender Distinction

This ruling underscores the gender-specific character of *srefah* in this context. As the *Gemara* makes clear: *lechacho* — "for her" — the particular punishment is *srefah*, and that punishment does not transfer to the male participants, whether the *bo'el* or the *edim zomemim*. The *bat kohen*'s *srefah* is categorically her own; neither the man who sinned with her nor the witnesses who sought to convict her share in it.

---

## Srefah Hierarchy Deb (II)

### Rabbi Akiva

Having established Rabbi Yishmael's position — that *srefah* is limited to the *na'ara m'urasa* case — the *Gemara* now turns to Rabbi Akiva's opposing view. Rabbi Akiva states: *achas arusa ve-achas nesua yatze'u le-sreifah* — both the *arusah* and the *nesuah* receive *srefah*. This aligns with the position of Rabbi Shimon, which was noted earlier. Rabbi Akiva then raises a potential further expansion: *yachol afilu pnuya* — perhaps even an unmarried woman receives *srefah*? To exclude this possibility, Rabbi Akiva employs a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *aviah* (her father) appears both in the verse about the *bat kohen* and in the context of the *na'ara m'urasa*, where it is part of the phrase *beis aviah*. Just as there the *na'ara m'urasa* is connected to a man through *zikas ha-ba'al* — the bond of a husband — so too the *bat kohen* subject to *srefah* must have such a bond. The *gezeirah shavah* thus excludes an unmarried woman, while the verse itself still encompasses both the *arusah* and the *nesuah*.

### Extra Vav Dispute

Rabbi Yishmael pushes back. He argues: *im ma le-halan na'ara ve-arusa af kan na'ara ve-arusa* — if you are going to learn from the *na'ara m'urasa* case, then the comparison should fully track that case, limiting *srefah* to a *na'ara m'urasa* specifically. Rabbi Akiva responds: *u-vas u-vas ani doresh* — "I expound 'daughter' and 'daughter.'" The verse says *u'vas ish kohen*, with the additional *vav* at the beginning of *u'vas*. Had the verse simply said *bas ish kohen*, Rabbi Akiva would have limited the ruling to the *arusah* by analogy to *beis aviah*. But the extra *vav* of *u'vas* extends the ruling to include the *nesuah* as well.

### Dibra Torah Principle

Rabbi Yishmael's response is one of the most striking passages in this section: *ve-chi mipnei she-atah doresh bas u-vas notzi zo le-sreifah?* — "Just because you expound 'daughter' and 'daughter,' shall we take this woman out to be burned?" This is the beautiful distillation of the broader methodological debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva is famous for deriving legal consequences from every additional letter, every superfluous word. Rabbi Yishmael operates by the principle of *dibra Torah k'lashon bnei adam* — the Torah speaks in the manner of ordinary human speech — and therefore resists hyper-interpretation of minor textual variations. His objection has both logical and rhetorical force: logically, the comparison to the *na'ara m'urasa* case points toward limiting *srefah* to the *arusah*; rhetorically, he is saying that burning a woman on the basis of a single extra *vav* demands a justification far more substantial than Rabbi Akiva has offered.

Rabbi Yishmael presses further. He argues that if one takes the extra *vav* of *u'vas* as a genuinely expansive word — one that broadens the category of women subject to *srefah* beyond the *arusah* — then by the same token it should include even an unmarried woman, a *pnuya*. But if instead we rely on the link to *beis aviah* to exclude the *pnuya*, then by that same logic we should exclude the *nesuah*, since the most direct comparison is to the *na'ara m'urasa*. Rabbi Yishmael is arguing that the two interpretive moves Rabbi Akiva is making are in tension: you cannot use the *vav* to expand the category to include the *nesuah* while simultaneously using the *gezeirah shavah* to exclude the *pnuya*, unless you have principled grounds for each. The *Gemara* resolves this from Rabbi Akiva's perspective: the *gezeirah shavah* of *aviah* does the work of excluding the *pnuya*, and the extra *vav* does the independent work of including the *nesuah*. Each device serves a distinct function.

However, the *Bavli* frames Rabbi Yishmael's response not as a full-throated disagreement but rather as a possible misreading: *sh'ma mina hadar bei m'gezeirah shavah* — perhaps Rabbi Yishmael thought Rabbi Akiva was abandoning the *gezeirah shavah* by appealing to the extra *vav*, and it was on that basis that he challenged him. Whether or not this framing fully captures the depth of their dispute, it is clear that for Rabbi Yishmael, the *gezeirah shavah* and the overall logical analogy together point toward limiting *srefah* to the *na'ara m'urasa*, and the extra *vav* is not a sufficient counter-argument.

### Vav as Exclusion

This raises an obvious question: if Rabbi Yishmael dismisses the extra *vav* as insufficient to expand the ruling, what does *he* do with it? The *Gemara* asks directly: *hai bas u'vas mai darish bei?* Rabbi Yishmael uses the extra *vav* to address the teaching of Avuha d'Shmuel bar Avin. The concern goes as follows: since we know that male *kohanim* are distinguished between those who are unblemished (*temimim*) and those who have blemishes (*ba'alei mumim*) — the latter being disqualified from performing the *avodah* in the *Beis HaMikdash* — one might have thought (*yachol nachlok bivnoseihem*) that a similar distinction applies to daughters of *kohanim*, so that a blemished *bat kohen* would not receive *srefah*. The *Gemara* acknowledges this is a strange *hava amina* — why would a physical blemish bear on the adultery penalty? — but the idea is that perhaps a blemish compromises her *kehunah* status in some way, thereby affecting the punishment.

The extra *vav* of *u'vas* answers this: it teaches that the ruling applies to all daughters of *kohanim* equally, blemished or unblemished, and that a blemish is entirely irrelevant to the law of *srefah*. For his part, Rabbi Akiva learns this same point from the principle of *v'hayu kodesh* — "they shall be holy" — which indicates that the *kedushah* of *kohanim* is not compromised by the presence of a blemish; the blemish restricts them only from *avodah*, not from their essential sanctified status. The *vav*, freed from this usage by Rabbi Akiva, is then available to expand *srefah* to the *nesuah*.

The section concludes by touching on the verse *et aviha hi mechalelet* and what Rabbi Yishmael learns from it. Since Rabbi Yishmael arrives at the limitation to *na'ara m'urasa* by analogy rather than by *gezeirah shavah*, the words *et aviha hi mechalelet* are available for a different teaching. A *braita* expounds: if the *bat kohen* commits this act, we are not merely noting the natural shame that falls on her father; rather, the verse instructs the community in how to respond. *Im hayu nogim bo kodesh nogim bo chol* — if the community had been treating him with honor as befitting a *kohen*, they should now treat him with ordinary disregard; *im hayu nogim bo kavod nogim bo bizayon* — if they treated him with distinction, they should now treat him with contempt. The community is meant to say: *arur shezo yaldu, arur shezo gildo, arur sheyatza zo mechalatzav* — cursed is the one who gave birth to her, cursed is the one who raised her, cursed is the one from whose loins she came.

Rav Ashi notes that an echo of this practice persists: *k'man karinan rashia bar rashia va'afilu l'rashia bar tzadika* — when we call someone a wicked person, we call them "wicked, son of the wicked," even if their parents are in fact righteous. The *Gemara* identifies this as following the view of this *tanna* — Rabbi Meir. The underlying social logic is that communal censure of the parents creates pressure that may deter such conduct from arising in the first place. The tension between that social function and the genuine injustice of shaming parents for the independent choices of their children is real, and not easily resolved.

---

## Srefah Method

### Initial Setup

Having established who receives *srefah* and the debate surrounding it, the *Gemara* transitions to a new *Mishnah* describing how *srefah* is actually carried out. The transition is introduced with the phrase *zo mitzvat haniskalin* — "this is the procedure of those who are stoned" — which signals the close of the *skila* material and the opening of the *srefah* section. The logical question of why the *Mishnah* was structured this way — describing *skila* first, then interrupting with the list of *arba misos*, rather than presenting the four executions in a single orderly sequence from the outset — is noted but not definitively resolved.

The *Mishnah* on *srefah* begins: *hayu mashki'in oso bezevel ad arkovosav* — they would immerse the condemned person in dung up to his knees. This is understood by the *meforshim* not primarily as a form of degradation but as a means of restraining the person and holding him stable. A hard rope (*sudar kasha*) is placed inside a soft scarf (*haraka*). The soft wrapping serves two purposes: it avoids leaving visible marks or lacerations on the neck, and — as the *Yerushalmi* explains — it prevents actual strangulation, since the goal is to force open the mouth, not to kill by *chenek*. The scarf-wrapped rope is then placed around the condemned person's neck: *ze moshech etzlo veze moshech etzlo* — one person on each side pulls in opposite directions, *ad sheposayach pivo* — until the person's mouth is forced open. The molten substance, the *ptilah*, is then lit and cast into his mouth, descending into his innards where it burns them internally.

### Mouth Opening

Rabbi Yehuda raises an objection to this method. If one wraps a rope inside a scarf and pulls on it from both sides, the condemned person will effectively be strangled by the scarf, which is exactly the procedure of *chenek* — strangulation. The result would be that *mitzvas srefah* has not been fulfilled; the person has been executed by *chenek* instead. Rabbi Yehuda therefore proposes an alternative: *posayach es pivo betzavas* — one forces open the mouth using tongs (*tzavas*), *shelo betovaso* — even against the person's resistance. Once the mouth is held open by the tongs, the *ptilah* is lit and cast in, descending and burning the innards in the same fashion as described by the first view.

### Historical Case

At this point, Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok offers testimony: *ma'aseh b'vas kohen achas she'zinasa* — he witnessed a case of a *bat kohen* who committed adultery, and what was done to her was *v'hekifuha chavilei zmoros u'serafuha* — they surrounded her with bundles of branches and burned her. This is literal external burning, entirely unlike what the *Mishnah* prescribes. The response given to him is that the *beis din* of that time simply did not know what they were doing. This case, as will be discussed further, raises significant questions about the divergence between the prescribed procedure and historical practice.

### Ptilah Identity

The *Mishnah* refers to lighting the *ptilah* and casting it into the mouth. The identity of the *ptilah* is now examined. Rav Masna says: *ptilah shel avar* — it is lead. Rashi explains that this does not mean one lights a piece of lead on fire, since lead does not ignite in that manner. Rather, one melts the lead and pours the molten metal down the throat. The *Yerushalmi* offers two additional possibilities: a mixture of lead and tin, or *neft* — a type of oil or petroleum-derived substance, heated and poured in. All three options produce the same essential result — burning of the internal organs — though they differ in the specific substance used.

---

## Srefah Sources

### Two Models

Having established the procedure, the *Gemara* now asks: from where do we know that *srefah* is performed in this manner — burning the inside of the body while leaving the outside intact — rather than by external burning? The answer is: *atya sreifa sreifa me'adas Korach* — one derives the method of *srefah* by means of a *gezeirah shavah* from the case of the congregation of Korach: *mah le'halan sreifas neshamah v'guf kayam af kan sreifas neshamah v'guf kayam* — just as there, the soul was burned while the body remained intact, so too here, *srefah* by the court means burning the inner soul-fire while the body remains. Rabbi Eliezer disputes the source: *atya sreifa sreifa mi'bnei Aharon* — the model should be derived instead from the case of Nadav and Avihu, the sons of Aaron, where the same principle applies: *mah le'halan sreifas neshamah v'guf kayam af kan sreifas neshamah v'guf kayam*.

### Korach Analysis

How does one know that the burning of Korach's congregation was *sreifas neshamah v'guf kayam* rather than literal external burning? The verse says: *es machtos hachata'im ha'eleh b'nafshosam* — "the fire-pans of these sinners against their souls." Reading *b'nafshosam* as indicating the soul-dimension of the punishment, the *Gemara* derives that it was their inner souls — *nishmasam* — that were burned, while their bodies remained. This is reinforced by Reish Lakish's reading of another verse: *b'chanfei la'agei ma'og charak alai shinemo* — which he interprets as referring to the flattery Korach used by means of food and feasting to seduce the leaders of Israel. *Bishvil chanufah she'hechanifu l'Korach al iskei legimah* — through the flattery associated with eating, *chireka alav sar shel Gehenom shinav* — the officer of *Gehinnom* was given license to sharpen his teeth against them. The word *nefesh* or *nafshosam* carries an appetitive connotation in Semitic languages — it can denote the throat, or one's appetitive desires — and so *b'nafshosam* is read as: they were punished through the very appetitive faculty with which they sinned, having been seduced by Korach's feasts.

Those who reject the Korach model read *b'nafshosam* differently: not as a reference to soul-versus-body, but rather as explaining the *cause* of their punishment — *she'nischayvu sreifa al iskei nafshosam* — they became liable to *srefah* on account of what they did with their appetitive souls. The burning itself was literal and physical.

### Nadav Avihu

What about the case of Nadav and Avihu? Those who derive from *bnei Aharon* that it was *sreifas neshamah v'guf kayam* point to the verse *vayamutu lifnei Hashem* — "and they died before God" — reading *ke'ein mita*, "like death." In natural death, the body remains intact while the soul departs; therefore the verse's use of *mita* language implies that their bodies were left intact while the fire consumed only their inner being. Those who reject this model read *vayamutu* differently: the fire began on the inside (*de'itchilu behu migavai*) in a death-like fashion, but ultimately consumed their bodies as well. A *braita* cited by Abba Yose ben Dosai provides additional detail: *shnei chutin shel esh yatz'u mibeit kodesh hakodashim v'nechleku le'arba* — two strands of fire emerged from the Holy of Holies and split into four; two entered the nostrils of Nadav and two entered the nostrils of Avihu, *v'sarfu osam* — and burned them. The use of *sarfu osam* — "burned them" — suggests their bodies were ultimately consumed, supporting the view that the external body was destroyed as well. Tosafot notes that the verse *vayisa'um b'chutonotam* — they removed them in their garments — indicates the bodies were still present, and suggests that perhaps at minimum the skeletal remains survived, accounting for the *tumas meis* incurred by those who carried them.

### Human Models

Why not derive the method of court *srefah* instead from the *parim hanisrafim* — the bulls that are burned as part of certain *chatat* offerings? In that case, the body of the animal is genuinely burned externally on a pyre. The *Gemara* answers: *mistabra me'adam hava lei lemeilaf* — it is more appropriate to derive the method of executing a human being from cases involving human beings rather than from cases involving animals. The points of similarity between the court *srefah* and the cases of Korach and Nadav v'Avihu are: both involve a person (*adam*); both involve a sinner (*chotei*); and in both cases the act of burning is itself the act of killing — unlike the *parim*, which were already slaughtered before being burned. Additionally, the issue of *pigul* is irrelevant in the human context. The *Gemara* entertains the counter-argument that the *parim* model has its own advantages: both burning a *korban* and court execution are fulfilling a *mitzvah* (*machshir*), and both are practices given *ledoros* — for all future generations — rather than being one-time historical events, as the divine punishments of Korach and Nadav v'Avihu were. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* concludes: *haneich nefishi* — the points of similarity between the human cases are more numerous, and those models take precedence.

### Mercy Principle

Once it is established that there are two valid models — Korach (body intact) and Nadav v'Avihu (body burned, on one reading) — the question arises: the one who derives from Korach that the body was intact, why does he not instead derive from Nadav v'Avihu's case (on the reading that the body was burned) the opposite conclusion? And vice versa: the one who derives from Nadav v'Avihu that the body was intact, why does he not derive from Korach's case (on the reading that the body was burned) the opposite conclusion? Each disputant, in other words, has access to both models — one showing the body intact and one showing the body burned. Why does each choose the model where the body is intact as the paradigm for court *srefah*?

The answer comes from Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avuha: the verse *ve'ahavta lerei'acha kamocha* — "love your neighbor as yourself" — generates the principle *beror lo misa yafa* — choose for the condemned person the most pleasant available death. Given two viable models of *srefah*, one must choose the less painful and less disfiguring option. Pouring molten lead down the throat, as horrifying as it sounds, is far preferable to external burning of the body, which would be agonizing and disfiguring in the extreme.

However, the *Gemara* then asks: once we have the principle of *ve'ahavta lerei'acha kamocha* operating, why did we need the *gezeirah shavah* at all? Why not simply derive from *ve'ahavta lerei'acha kamocha* directly that we should use the less painful method? The answer is that without the *gezeirah shavah*, the very possibility of internal burning as a form of *srefah* would never have been considered a valid option. The *pshat* of the verse commanding *srefah* points toward literal external burning. One would simply have tried to fulfill the external burning as quickly as possible — by building a very large fire, for instance — so as to minimize suffering, all within the framework of *ve'ahavta lerei'acha kamocha*. The *gezeirah shavah* is what opens up the option of internal burning as a valid form of *srefah* at all. Once that option is established as halachically legitimate, *ve'ahavta lerei'acha kamocha* then compels us to choose it over external burning. The two principles operate in tandem: the *gezeirah shavah* defines the range of available options; *ve'ahavta lerei'acha kamocha* determines which option within that range must be chosen.

---

## Theological Themes

### Body Image Approach

Two modern scholars have offered complementary frameworks for understanding the larger themes animating the *arba misos* system. Aaron Shemesh's work focuses on the principle that the human body was created *b'tzelem Elokim* — in the image of God — and that a core organizing theme across all four methods of execution is the minimization of bodily disfigurement. On this reading, the entire elaborated procedure of *srefah* — immersing in dung to hold the person steady, wrapping the rope in a soft cloth to avoid lacerations, pouring molten lead rather than external burning — reflects a sustained effort to carry out the required punishment while preserving the integrity of the body as far as possible. The system's insistence on internal rather than external burning, the various protections built into *skila* (pushing from a height rather than direct stoning, the care taken with the body afterward), and analogous details in the other executions all point, on Shemesh's account, to this unifying concern.

### Divine Death Model

Dvora Steinmetz offers a different framework, centered on the phrase *ke'ein mita* — "like death" — which the *Gemara* uses to describe what the fire accomplished in the case of Nadav and Avihu. Steinmetz asks the foundational question of what authorizes a human community to take another human life at all. Her answer emphasizes the concept of executing God's judgment: the court, in carrying out a death penalty, acts as an instrument of divine will. If that is the case, then the form of death brought about by the court should as closely as possible replicate the form of death that God himself brings about. In natural death — and in the divinely ordained deaths of Korach's assembly and of Nadav and Avihu — the body remains and the soul departs. By insisting on *ke'ein mita*, by modeling court *srefah* on these paradigms of divinely inflicted death, the court aligns its act of execution as closely as possible with divine action. On this reading, what is at stake is not primarily the preservation of the body's image, but the theological legitimacy of the court's authority to act as the executor of divine judgment.

---

## Nadav Avihu Backstory

### Ambition

Having mentioned Nadav and Avihu in the context of the *srefah* discussion, the *Gemara* offers a digression on the backstory of their deaths. The scene is set: Moses and Aaron walked in front, with Nadav and Avihu behind them, and all of Israel behind them. It was a position of extraordinary honor — only Moses and Aaron preceded them. Yet it was not enough. *Amar lo Nadav l'Avihu: eimasai yamusu shnei zkeinim halalu v'ani v'atah nanhig es hador?* — "When will these two old men die," Nadav said to Avihu, "so that you and I can lead the generation?" God's response: *nireh mi kover es mi* — "We shall see who buries whom."

### Camel Proverb

Rav Pappa cites a popular saying that captures this dynamic: *nefishei gamli sabei d'teini mashkei d'huganei* — there are many old camels carrying on their backs the hides of young camels. The proverb cautions against assuming the young will naturally outlast and replace the old. Rashi notes that a young camel's recklessness and excess energy can lead to its premature death, while the old camel endures. Nadav and Avihu, for all their brilliance and position, did not survive Moses and Aaron.

### Seduction Strategy

The *Gemara* then turns to Korach. Rabbi Elazar opens with a question: to what is a *talmid chacham* compared in the eyes of an *am ha'aretz*? Initially, *domeh l'kiton shel zahav* — he appears like a vessel of gold, something precious and untouchable, evoking deep respect and deference. If the *am ha'aretz* begins to converse with him, *siper heimenu domeh l'kiton shel kesef* — the *talmid chacham* is now like a silver vessel: still valuable, but somewhat diminished. If the *am ha'aretz* then provides the *talmid chacham* with some benefit — a loan of money, an invitation to a Shabbat meal — *domeh l'kiton shel cheres* — he has become a vessel of earthenware. And an earthenware vessel, once broken, *shuv ein lo takanah* — can never be repaired. Once that familiarity crosses a certain threshold, no subsequent effort can restore the original aura of authority and reverence.

This parable explains the strategy Korach employed. By inviting the great figures of Israel — *kru'ei eidah, anshei shem* — to his feast and seducing them through hospitality and flattery, *bishvil chanufah she'hechanifu l'Korach al iskei legimah*, he made them his beneficiaries and eliminated the natural distance that would otherwise have protected them from his influence. Having become recipients of his generosity, they could no longer view him with the critical detachment needed to resist his arguments. The same relationship that stripped the *talmid chacham* of his untouchable golden status stripped these leaders of their judgment.

---

## Execution Authority

### Requirements

The *Mishnah* notes the structural prerequisites for legitimate court executions. The *braita* derives from the verse *u'vasa el hakohanim haleviyim v'el hashoftim asher yiheyeh bayamim hahem* — "you shall come to the priests, the Levites, and to the judge who will be in those days" — that *srefah* requires three simultaneous conditions: the presence of a functioning *kohen* class (meaning a *Beis HaMikdash*), and a *Sanhedrin* seated within the *Beis HaMikdash*. *Bizman sheyesh Kohen — yesh mishpat*; *bizman she-ain Kohen — ain mishpat*. Outside these conditions, the formal death penalties cannot be administered.

### Rav Chama Case

Against this background, the case of the *Amoraic*-period figure Rav Chama bar Tuvia is deeply troubling. Imrasa bat Tali, a *bat kohen* who had committed adultery, was wrapped by Rav Chama in bundles of branches and burned alive — *akphsah chavilei zemoros v'sarfah*. This was carried out in the *Amoraic* period, long after the *Sanhedrin* had ceased to function and court executions could no longer be administered. Rav Yosef's verdict: *ta'ah b'tarti* — he made two errors. First, he violated the ruling of Rav Masna (which reflects the *Mishnah*) that *srefah* is carried out by pouring molten lead internally, not by external burning. Second, and more fundamentally, he violated the *braita*'s requirement that formal executions can only be carried out *bizman sheyesh Kohen* — when the *Beis HaMikdash* is standing and the *Sanhedrin* is in place. Neither condition obtained in his time. What Rav Chama did was an extra-legal act of execution that bore no resemblance to the *halachically* prescribed procedure, carried out at a time when no such execution was permissible.

### Testimony Dismissal

Returning to Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's testimony in the *Mishnah* — that he witnessed a *bat kohen* who had committed adultery being wrapped in bundles and burned — the *Gemara* notes that the response he received was: *mipnei she'lo hayah beis din shel osah sha'ah baki* — the *beis din* of that time did not know what it was doing. Rav Yosef adds: *beis din shel tzedukim havay* — this was a *Sadducean* court. The *Tzadukim* were known as literalists who read the Torah's *srefah* command as mandating actual external burning. This explains the practice without vindicating it; from the Rabbinic perspective, the *Sadducean* courts were executing in a manner that violated the correct *halakhah*.

### Halakha Divergence

The incident points to a striking divergence. The *halakhah* as laid out in this *Mishnah* and *Gemara* prescribes an elaborate, carefully constrained procedure. Historical practice — whether by *Sadducean* courts during the *Beis HaMikdash* period, or by figures like Rav Chama bar Tuvia in the *Amoraic* period — sometimes involved literal external burning with none of the procedural safeguards described. The Rabbinic tradition consistently dismisses such practices as error, whether due to ignorance of the proper method or to the absence of the prerequisite institutional framework. This gap between the *halakhah* as theorized and execution as historically practiced is one of the notable features of this entire tractate, and scholars have debated at length how much of the *Gemara*'s elaborate procedural system ever actually governed real judicial behavior.

### Two Accounts

The *Gemara* harmonizes the two accounts attributed to Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok. In the *Mishnah*, he speaks as an adult witness and is told the *beis din* did not know what it was doing. In a *baraita*, he recalls the same kind of incident as something he witnessed as a child (*tinok*), riding on his father's shoulders, and is told: *katan hayisa v'ein mevi'in raayah min hakatan* — you were a minor; testimony from a minor cannot be relied upon. These are two distinct stories, two distinct incidents. The *Gemara* then notes that the order in which Rabbi Elazar must have presented them: he could not have first described what he saw as an adult and been dismissed, and then tried to prove the same point with a childhood memory. Had the adult testimony been rejected, appealing to a childhood recollection would have been pointless. The logical order must therefore be: he first described what he saw as a child; was told he was too young; and then offered his adult testimony — which was in turn dismissed by attributing the incident to a *beis din* that simply did not know the correct procedure. Both accounts were dismissed, and the *Gemara*'s picture of *srefah* as described in the *Mishnah* stands as the authoritative normative prescription, regardless of how executions may or may not have actually been carried out in practice.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 53

## Hereg / Sword

### Hereg Mishna

The present daf opens at the *mishna* in the middle of 52b, immediately following the discussion of *sreifah* — the execution by pouring molten lead down the throat, derived from the principle of *ke'ein misa*, resembling natural death. The *mishna* now turns to *hereg*, execution by sword.

*Mitzvas haneheragim*: the method of decapitation. The *mishna* states: *hayu matizin es rosho besayif kederech shehamalchus osa* — they would decapitate him with a sword, in the manner that the government does. Rabbi Yehuda objects: *nival hu lo* — this is a disfiguring of the body. His preferred alternative is to place the condemned man's head on a chopping block and sever it with an axe. The *chachamim* respond with what seems like an obvious rejoinder: *ein misa menuvelet mizu* — there is no more disfiguring death than this. If Rabbi Yehuda's concern is disfigurement, the axe is hardly an improvement.

### Roman Execution

The *mishna*'s phrase *kederech shehamalchus osa* — like the government does — invites a brief historical note. Roman execution methods were not uniform: crucifixion was largely reserved for non-citizens. For citizens condemned to death, execution was carried out by the sword, though early Roman practice apparently employed the axe. The transition from axe to sword seems to have reflected a judgment that the sword was the more honorable death — associated with battle and warfare, while the axe was associated with inanimate objects or animals. Both methods, then, were attested in Roman practice, though the sword came to predominate. This historical context is significant, as it clarifies why the *chachamim* describe their method as *kederech shehamalchus osa*, and it also clarifies what Rabbi Yehuda is reacting against.

### Secular Mimicry

A *tosefta* now makes Rabbi Yehuda's true concern explicit. In the *braita*, he says to the *chachamim*: *af ani yodeia shemisa menuvelet hi* — I too know that the axe is a disfiguring form of death. *Aval ma e'eseh sheharei amra Torah: uvchukoseihem lo seleichu* — but what choice do I have? The Torah commands that we not follow in their ways. For Rabbi Yehuda, adopting an execution method that directly parallels the practice of the Roman government constitutes a violation of *lo titnu bechukoteihem*. His use of the word *nival* in the *mishna* is thus somewhat oblique; his real objection is not aesthetic but halakhic. A condemned man executed by *beis din* should not be made to feel like someone being put to death by the Romans. The axe, whatever its own aesthetic disadvantages, at least avoids that association — at least at the time Rabbi Yehuda was writing, when the sword had become the dominant Roman method.

### Torah-Derived Practice

The *chachamim*'s response cuts to the heart of the matter: *keivan dechsiv sayif baTorah, lav minaihu ka gamrinan* — since the Torah itself speaks of execution by sword, we are not learning this from them. The parallel between our practice and theirs is coincidental; its source is internal to Torah law, and therefore the prohibition of *lo titnu bechukoteihem* does not apply.

The *gemara* supports this principle with a parallel case. A *braita* teaches: *sorefin al hamelachim velo midarchei ha'emori* — one may conduct a funeral pyre for deceased kings, and this is not considered an Amorite practice. The question arises immediately: *heichi sarfinan? Ve'hachtiv uvchukoseihem lo telechu* — how can we do this, given the prohibition against following their practices? If the *gemara* had to specify that it is *not* an Amorite practice, this implies that the pagans themselves did the same thing. So why is it permitted?

The *gemara* answers: *ella keivan de'chtiv sreifa b'Oraita* — since burning funeral pyres appears in the Torah itself, as the verse states *uv'misrefot avoteicha* — in the burnings of your forefathers — this practice has independent Jewish sanction. *Lav minaihu ka gamrinan* — we are not deriving it from them. The governing principle is clear: where our practice parallels that of the gentiles but derives independently from a Torah source, there is no violation of *lo titnu bechukoteihem*.

### Bechukoteihem Parameters

This *sugya* opens an important window onto the parameters of *lo titnu bechukoteihem*. One might ask: is the prohibition purely about intent — that one must not consciously adopt gentile practices — or does it extend even to practices that merely *look* like theirs, regardless of intent? Must the Jewish practice be explicitly written in the Torah, or is it sufficient that it developed independently? These questions generate genuine complexity. For example, visiting graves or reciting formal prayers — practices found across religious cultures — raise the question of whether they represent parallel developments or problematic mimicry.

The *rishonim* identify two categories that may be subject to a stricter standard: practices rooted in *avoda zara*, and practices associated with sexual licentiousness. For these, some *rishonim* suggest it may not matter whether one intends to imitate — the practices themselves carry an intrinsically non-Jewish or idolatrous character, and that alone may render them problematic under *bechukoteihem*. For practices that are merely coincidentally shared — like the manner of execution — the decisive question is whether one is deriving and learning from them, or whether the source is genuinely internal. This *sugya* is thus a foundational text for the entire discussion of *bechukoteihem*.

---

## Hereg Sources

### Hereg Categories

The *gemara* now identifies who receives *hereg* and where its scriptural basis lies. The *mishna* later in the chapter will state: *elu hen ha'neheragin* — the following receive the sword: *ha'rotzei'ach ve'anshei ir ha'nidachat* — the murderer, and the inhabitants of an *ir ha'nidachat*, a city that has gone over to idolatry collectively.

The case of *ir ha'nidachat* is straightforward: the Torah explicitly states *lefi charev* — by the edge of the sword — in describing that punishment. One might have thought this itself a sufficient response to Rabbi Yehuda's objection, since a hatchet is not a sword. That question — how precisely the Torah's specification of *cherev* controls the instrument of execution — remains open, and it seems that within the general category of death by sword, some latitude exists. In any case, *lefi charev* for *ir ha'nidachat* is explicit. The more interesting case is the murderer.

### Nekem Yinakeim

For the murderer, the *gemara* asks: *minalan* — from where do we derive this? A *braita* is cited: *nakom yinakeim* — vengeance shall be taken — which appears in the context of killing a slave: *ki yakeh ish es avdo... u-meis tachas yado nakom yinakeim*. If a man strikes his slave and the slave dies under his hand, vengeance shall be taken. It is worth pausing on this: the fact that the Torah mandates execution for a free person who kills his own non-Jewish slave — even without intent to kill — represents a remarkable assertion of the slave's humanity in the ancient world.

But the text says only that *nekima* — vengeance — is taken. *Nekima zo eini yodeia mah hi* — I do not yet know what form this vengeance takes.

### Nekima Sword

The *gemara* resolves this through a verbal *gezeirah shavah*. The word *nekima* also appears in the curses of *Vayikra*: *veheiveisi aleichem cherev nokemes nekam bris* — I shall bring against you a sword that takes the vengeance of the covenant. Here, *nekima* is explicitly associated with the sword. Therefore, wherever the Torah says *nakom yinakeim*, it means death by sword.

A further question arises: perhaps *nekima* by sword means not cutting but stabbing — piercing the condemned through the torso? The *gemara* dismisses this: *lefi charev ksiv* — the verse specifies *the edge* of the sword, *pi* meaning the lip or edge, indicating a cutting rather than a stabbing motion.

A second question: perhaps the cutting should be done not at the neck but along the length of the body? This leads directly to the first invocation of *ve-ahavta le-reiacha kamocha*.

---

## Egla Arufa

### Ve-Ahavta

Rav Nachman said in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: the verse *ve-ahavta le-reiacha kamocha* — love your fellow as yourself — mandates *berur lo misa yafa*, that we select for the condemned person the most dignified death available. This principle is striking in its application: even in the act of execution, we are obligated to consider the dignity and experience of the condemned. Cutting at the neck is both more immediate and less disfiguring than cutting the body lengthwise; *ve-ahavta le-reiacha kamocha* therefore dictates the neck.

---

## Hereg Sources (II)

### Kal Vachomer

Having established that killing a slave is punished by the sword, the *gemara* asks: *ben chorin minalan* — what is the source for the murderer who kills a free person? The proposed answer is a *kal vachomer*: if killing a slave is punishable by the sword — a weightier form of execution than strangulation — then surely killing a free person should warrant at least as weighty a punishment. Therefore, the murderer of a free person is also executed by *hereg*.

### Severity Debate

The *kal vachomer* immediately runs into a difficulty. *Hani nicha le-man de-amar chenek kal* — this reasoning works well for the view that *chenek* is the lightest form of execution. In that case, the sword is indeed weightier, and the *kal vachomer* holds: if the killer of a slave receives the weightier punishment, the killer of a free person surely should too. *Ella le-man de-amar chenek chamur* — but according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that *chenek* is actually the *heavier* of the two, what can be said? On that view, the ordinary unspecified execution — *chenek* — is heavier than the sword, and the *kal vachomer* would run in reverse: the killer of a free person might *more* appropriately receive the heavier *chenek* rather than the sword. So the *kal vachomer* approach is insufficient on its own.

---

## Egla Arufa (II)

### Hukshu Paradigm

The *gemara* therefore turns to a different derivation. The verse *ve-ata teva'er hadam hanaki mikirbecha* — you shall cleanse the innocent blood from your midst — appears in the context of *egla arufa*, the ritual of the broken-necked calf performed when a murder victim is found and the perpetrator is unknown. This verse, which speaks generally about purging spilled blood, links all murderers conceptually to the paradigm of *egla arufa*: *hukshu kol shofchei damim le-egla arufa* — all who shed blood are associated with *egla arufa*.

### Egla Method

The *egla arufa* ceremony itself involves breaking the calf's neck with a sword, and specifically at the neck. From this: *mah lahan besayif u-min hatzavar, af kan besayif u-min hatzavar* — just as there the instrument is a sword and the location is the neck, so too in the execution of the murderer. This paradigm thus provides an independent and more comprehensive basis for *hereg* by sword at the neck, covering all murderers — not merely the killer of a slave.

A question arises: perhaps we should learn from *egla arufa* that the instrument is an axe and the location is the back of the neck, since the *egla* itself is struck from behind at the back of the neck. If so, this would actually support Rabbi Yehuda's position. Rav Nachman responds again by invoking *ve-ahavta le-reiacha kamocha* — *berur lo misa yafa*: even granting that *egla arufa* is our paradigm, it provides a general framework rather than a hyper-precise prescription. Within the latitude the paradigm provides, we optimize for the most dignified death. A cut at the front of the neck by sword is more immediate and less disfiguring than a blow with an axe at the back of the neck, so the former is the correct method.

---

## Chenek

### Chenek Method

The *gemara* now turns to the last of the four executions: *chenek*, strangulation, which is the default or generic form of execution. The *mishna* describes the method: *hayu mashki'in oto b'zevel ad arkubotav* — they would stand the condemned in dung up to his knees, apparently to keep him steady. *V'noten sudar kasheh l'toch harakah* — they would wrap a hard cord within a soft scarf, *v'korech al tzavaro* — and wrap it around his neck, *zeh moshech etzlo v'zeh moshech etzlo* — each person pulling one end in the opposite direction, *ad she'nafsho yotzeit* — until he expires. As with the other methods, the soft wrapping serves to reduce disfigurement and pain.

### Mot Yumat

The *gemara* now addresses the scriptural basis for *chenek* as the default execution. A *braita* is cited, beginning with the verse about adultery: *ish asher yinaf et eishet ish* — a man who commits adultery with a married woman. The *braita* parses this phrase before arriving at its main point.

*Ish prat l'katan* — "a man," to exclude a minor, who is not executed. However, it should be noted that if a married woman has relations with a boy over the age of nine, though the boy is not punished, the act is still halakhically considered an act of adultery with respect to the woman, who remains liable. *Prat l'eishet katan* — the phrase "a married woman" excludes the wife of a minor. Since *kiddushin* effected by a minor boy is not fully binding, such a woman does not bear the status of a married woman for purposes of adultery law.

Rashi explains that the verse is simply affirming the fact that a minor boy cannot effect binding *kiddushin*. Tosafot notes that there is one exceptional case: *yibum*. If a minor boy's older brother died leaving a widow, the minor could effect *yibum* through intercourse — since *yibum* operates through the act itself rather than through a formal act of *kinyan* that requires an adult — and in that case there would actually be a form of legally recognized marriage with a minor. Nevertheless, the verse teaches that such a marriage is not substantial enough to trigger adultery law while the boy remains a minor.

*Eishet rei'eihu* — "his fellow's wife" — *prat l'eishet acherim*, excluding the wife of a non-Jew. From a Jewish legal perspective, intercourse with a married non-Jewish woman does not constitute *niuf*, adultery. This is true in two dimensions: a Jewish woman married to a non-Jewish man (since *kiddushin* does not take effect between a Jew and a non-Jew), and a Jewish man who has relations with a married non-Jewish woman. The laws of *Bnei Noach* do recognize adultery as prohibited for non-Jews among themselves, and non-Jewish marriage is legally meaningful within that framework. The *gemara* in Rashi's reading (which corrects the censored *Kusi* to *Goy*) states: *ashmienan she'ein kiddushin l'Goy* — this teaches that there is no binding *kiddushin* with a non-Jew.

Tosafot adds an important nuance: even if adultery per se does not apply to the case of a Jewish man with a married non-Jewish woman, the Torah's express permission of *yefas to'ar* — the beautiful captive woman — even when she is married, demonstrates that absent that special dispensation some prohibition would obtain. This proves that non-Jewish marriage, while not creating adultery liability for a Jew, is not entirely without halakhic significance.

Now the *braita* reaches its main point. The verse continues: *mos yumat ha-no'ef ve-ha-no'afet* — both the adulterer and the adulteress shall be put to death. *Mot yumat* — surely put to death — in *chenek*. But is this certain? *Atah omer b'chenek o eino ela achas mikol misos ha'amuros baTorah* — perhaps it means one of the other executions that are more explicitly prescribed in the Torah, since the Torah never explicitly mentions strangulation as a form of capital punishment?

The *braita* answers: *amarta kol makom shenemar misah baTorah stam, ei atah rasha'i limshoch l'hachmir aleha ela l'hakel aleha* — wherever the Torah prescribes death without specifying the method, one has no right to impose a heavier execution; one must assume the most lenient. This is the position of Rabbi Yoshiyah.

### Lightest Default

Rabbi Yoshiyah's approach is thus: *chenek* is the default unspecified execution because it is the lightest. If the Torah leaves the method unspecified, we are bound to select the most lenient available option.

---

## Four Executions

### Logical Corollary

The logical corollary is immediate: if we may not impose a heavier execution than what the Torah specifies, and the Torah's silence is read as requiring the lightest option, then the generic cases — all those where the Torah prescribes death without further detail — must be assigned to whichever mode is least severe. This reasoning presupposes that there is a defined set of executions and a clear hierarchy among them. Without knowing what options exist and how they rank, the principle cannot be applied. This sets up the question of how we identify *chenek* as an option at all.

---

## Chenek (II)

### Natural Death

Rabbi Yonatan offers an alternative approach. *Lo mipnei shekalah* — it is not because *chenek* is the lightest that it serves as the default. That reasoning depends on the ranking debate between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis. Rabbi Yonatan's basis is different: *kol misah amurah baTorah stam einah ela chenek* — any death prescribed by the Torah without specification is simply *chenek*, not because of its relative severity but because of what the word *misah* connotes.

### Divine Death

Rabbi Yonatan's derivation, as explained by Rebbe, runs as follows. The Torah uses the language *mot yumat* — which carries the connotation of dying, of natural death — both in human execution contexts and in contexts of *misah bidei shamayim*, death at the hand of Heaven. *Mah misah amurah bidei shamayim misah she'ein bah roshem* — just as death by Heaven's hand leaves no visible mark or disfigurement on the body, so too *misah amurah bidei adam*, death at human hands designated by the same language, must be a death that leaves no mark.

Of the four executions, *chenek* — strangulation — most fully satisfies this criterion. Done properly, it leaves no external mark. Moreover, there is a deeper resonance: strangulation is death by the deprivation of breath, of *nefesh*. The word *nefesh* is etymologically connected to breathing — *vayinafash*, and he rested, carries the sense of drawing breath. Death by *chenek* strikes most directly at the *nefesh*, the breath of life, making it the most inherently natural-seeming form of death.

This frames a significant conceptual question: is the absence of *roshem* — disfigurement — valued because of inherent respect for the human body as such? Or is it valued because it mirrors *misah bidei shamayim*, divine death, and thus represents an ideal of execution that approximates God's own manner of taking life? These are two meaningfully different ways of understanding the principle.

The *gemara* then asks: why not say the default execution is *sreifah* — burning — which also, at least in its prescribed form (pouring molten lead down the throat), leaves the external body largely unmarked? The answer: since the Torah prescribes *sreifah* specifically for the *bat kohen* who commits adultery — a manifestly heavier punishment — this demonstrates by contrast that the standard case of adultery does not receive *sreifah*. *Michlal deha lav bas sreifah hi* — we infer that the ordinary adultery case falls outside the *sreifah* category. Therefore, *sreifah* cannot be the generic default, and *chenek* remains.

---

## Four Executions (II)

### Rava's Tradition

The *gemara* then asks from Rabbi Yoshiyah's perspective: how do we even know that *chenek* is among the executions? If we assign unspecified cases to the lightest execution, we still need to know what options exist. Perhaps there are only three modes of execution and the lightest of those three should be the default. *Ve'eima sayaf* — perhaps the sword is the lightest and serves as the default?

Rava resolves this: *arba misos gemara gemiri lehu* — we have a received tradition that there are exactly four modes of execution. Given this tradition, once the other three are accounted for by specific cases, the fourth — *chenek* — must exist, and the unspecified cases are assigned to it.

### Unspecified Cases

Rashi elaborates: the tradition specifies not only that there are four modes but which four they are. Since the Torah never assigns *chenek* explicitly to any particular case, and since we have a further principle that unspecified executions must be read as the most lenient, the conclusion follows: *chenek* is the lightest, and all unspecified cases receive *chenek*. Rashi puts it plainly — since we are not entitled to impose the heavier form when the Torah is silent, the entire category of unspecified cases gravitates naturally to *chenek*. The tradition and the principle together close the circle.

---

## Sekilah Basis

### Which Phrase?

The *gemara* now shifts to the question of *sekilah*, stoning, and specifically to the puzzle of which scriptural phrase marks a given transgression as warranting that execution. Rabbi Zeira poses the question to Abbaye: for those cases where *sekilah* is not stated explicitly but is derived from the paradigm case of *ov ve-yidoni* — the necromancer and the diviner — by which phrase is the derivation made? Is it from *mot yumasu* — they shall surely be put to death — or from *demeihem bam* — their blood is upon them?

This question matters because the phrase that carries the meaning of *sekilah* is the one that, when it appears elsewhere, signals that the transgressor receives stoning. The phrase *mot yumat* (or *mot yumasu*) appears in many contexts — including adultery, which we have established receives *chenek*. The phrase *demeihem bam* is far more restricted in its distribution. The answer to Rabbi Zeira's question will determine which cases receive *sekilah* through derivation.

### Ov Yidoni

The paradigm case is *ov ve-yidoni*, whose verse states explicitly: *mos yumatu ba-even yirgemu otam demeihem bam* — they shall surely be put to death; they shall be stoned; their blood is upon them (*Vayikra* 20:27). This verse contains both phrases — *mot yumasu* and *demeihem bam* — alongside the explicit mention of stoning (*ba-even yirgemu otam*). It is thus the anchor from which all other *sekilah* cases are derived. The question is which of its two non-explicit phrases carries the *sekilah* meaning when extended to other cases.

### Demihem Bam

Abbaye's answer: *bidmeihem bam gmiri* — the derivation is from *demeihem bam*. His reasoning proceeds by elimination. If *mot yumasu* were the operative phrase, what function would *demeihem bam* serve? Every phrase in a verse must be doing halakhic work, and if *mot yumasu* already communicates *sekilah*, *demeihem bam* becomes superfluous. But *demeihem bam* is a distinctively unusual expression — evoking, perhaps quite literally, the flowing blood of the victim of stoning — and it must be carrying halakhic significance.

The *gemara* immediately turns this reasoning around: if *demeihem bam* carries the meaning of *sekilah*, what does *mot yumasu* accomplish? The answer emerges from a separate *braita* about the murderer: *mos yumos hamakeh rotzei'ach hu* — he shall surely be put to death, he is a murderer. The teaching derived from *mot yumat* there is: *ein li ela be-misah haksivah bo* — I know only that you execute him by the assigned method. But *bo minayin she-im ee atah yachol la-hamiso be-misah haksivah bo she-atah memiso be-chol misah she-atah yachol la-hamiso* — from where do I know that if for some reason the standard execution cannot be carried out, you may use any available means? *Talmud lomar mos yumos hamakeh mi-kol makom* — the doubling of the death language teaches: he must be executed one way or another. This is the function of *mot yumat*: it confers a broader license to execute by other means when the prescribed method is unavailable. With this, both phrases carry distinct meanings, and the structure is coherent.

### Mot Yumasu License

To sharpen the point: *mot yumat* licenses execution by any means when the standard method fails. *Demeihem bam* identifies *sekilah* as the prescribed method for those to whom it applies. These two functions are independent and non-overlapping, which is why both phrases are necessary and neither is superfluous.

A further question is implicit: does this broader license — to execute by any available means — apply to all those under capital sentence, or only those for whom the verse explicitly states *mot yumat*? The *gemara* leaves this for another occasion, but the license itself is established.

### Mot Yumasu Disqualified

Rav Achai of Difti presses the question further in a dialogue with Ravina: what precisely is the difficulty with using *mot yumasu* as the *sekilah* indicator? The *gemara* reasons through several candidates.

If the adultery case were the concern — *ish asher yinaf et eishet ish... mos yumat ha-no'ef ve-ha-no'afet*, which says *mot yumat* and yet receives *chenek* — one might say: let us simply derive from *ov ve-yidoni* that *mot yumat* means *sekilah*! But the response is: *mide'amar rachmana arusah bi-skila miklal de-nesuah lav bi-skila* — since the Torah prescribes *sekilah* for the *na'arah me'orasah* (the betrothed maiden), we infer that the ordinary *eshet ish* (the married woman) does not receive *sekilah*. The contrast between the two cases does the work; we can therefore absorb the adultery case without difficulty.

What about hitting a father or mother, where the verse also says *mot yumat* yet the execution is *chenek*? The *gemara* suggests: derive by contrast from the *eshet ish* case, which establishes *chenek* as the meaning of *mot yumat* in its non-*sekilah* application. This too can be absorbed.

The *gemara* ultimately identifies the core problem. If *mot yumasu* were the *sekilah* phrase, and we tried to limit its *sekilah* meaning only to some cases by learning the others out from lenient precedents, we would face an impossible situation: either every case with *mot yumasu* gets *sekilah*, or every case gets *chenek* by analogy to the lenient comparator. There is no stable middle ground. The only clean solution is that *mot yumasu* does not carry *sekilah* at all — it carries the broader execution license — and *demeihem bam* is the sole marker of *sekilah*. That phrase appears only in a narrow, consistent set of cases, all of which do in fact receive *sekilah*, and its distinctiveness — including the vivid image of blood flowing from stoning — makes it the natural and unambiguous indicator.

---

## Sekilah Categories

### Full List

The *mishna* now presents the full list of those who receive *sekilah*. The cases fall into several recognizable clusters, though the *mishna*'s ordering passes between them twice in a way that is somewhat irregular.

The first cluster is sexual transgressions: one who has intercourse with his mother (*haba al ha-eim*), with his father's wife (*eshet ha-av*), with his daughter-in-law (*ha-kallah*), with another male (*ha-zachar*), or with an animal (*ha-beheimah*); and a woman who brings an animal upon herself. The second cluster is offenses against God: the blasphemer (*ha-migadef*), the idolator (*oveid avodah zarah*), one who gives his offspring to *Molech* — listed separately from idolatry, suggesting it is treated as its own category — and the practitioner of *ov ve-yidoni*, whose verse is the very paradigm case. Also in this cluster: *mechalel Shabbat*, the Sabbath violator, whose gravity is comparable to idolatry. The third cluster is offenses against parents: *ha-mekalel aviv ve-imo*, cursing one's father or mother, and the *ben sorer u-moreh*, the wayward and rebellious son.

Then the *mishna* adds the *na'arah me'orasah* and the cases involving *masit* and *madiach* — those who seduce an individual or an entire city into idolatry — and the *mechashef*, the sorcerer. The *mishna* appears to pass through its thematic clusters twice, a structural feature that invites further analysis.

### Cursing Parents

Rashi notes an implicit difficulty: why does *mekalel aviv ve-imo* — cursing one's parents — receive *sekilah*, the weightiest execution, while *makeh aviv ve-imo* — *striking* one's parents, seemingly a graver physical act — receives *chenek*, a lighter execution? Rashi explains: *hichmir mibemakah mishum de'ika tarti* — the cursing is treated more severely because it involves two elements simultaneously. First, *kalon aviv ve-imo* — a disgracing of the parents' honor. Second, *umotzi shem shamayim l'vatalah* — the invocation and misuse of God's name, since one who curses a parent does so by invoking a divine curse, making God's name complicit in this desecration of parental honor. The comparison is apt: just as *birkat Hashem* — cursing God — represents the apex of religious offense, cursing parents with God's name approaches that same register. The double gravity — dishonoring parents who represent divine authority, and doing so through God's name — explains the elevated punishment.

### Mother Case

The *mishna* then examines the case of intercourse with one's mother in detail: *haba al ha-em chayav aleiha mishum em u-mishum eshet ha-av* — if the mother is also the father's wife, the son is liable for two distinct prohibitions simultaneously: the prohibition of the mother and the prohibition of the father's wife. These are recognized as genuinely independent prohibitions, since each can exist without the other: one can have a stepmother who is not one's mother, or a mother who was never married to the father. When a single woman instantiates both, both prohibitions are violated. The practical significance includes: if the warning (*hasra'ah*) addressed only one of the two prohibitions, that is sufficient for the relevant execution; and if the act were done unintentionally, two separate *korbanot* would be required.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda dissents: *eino chayav ela mishum ha-em bilvad* — one is liable only for the mother category, not for the father's wife category. For Rabbi Yehuda, the term *eshet av* — father's wife — is definitionally limited to a woman who is *not* the man's mother. It refers exclusively to a stepmother. A biological mother, in Rabbi Yehuda's view, simply does not fall within the *eshet av* prohibition, even when she was in fact married to the father.

---

## Braita Debate

### Braita Version

A *braita* now presents Rabbi Yehuda's position in what appears to be a more restricted form. Rather than the sweeping claim of the *mishna* — that a mother is categorically excluded from *eshet av* — the *braita*'s Rabbi Yehuda says: *im lo hayesa imo reuia le-aviv eino chayav ela mishum ha-em bilvad* — if the mother was not fit for the father, the son is liable only for the mother category. The *braita* thus suggests Rabbi Yehuda's position applies only in cases where the mother was somehow unfit for the father's marriage; in normal cases, presumably, Rabbi Yehuda would agree that both categories apply.

### Not Fit

The *gemara* asks: *mai eina reuia lo* — what does "not fit" mean? The first possibility: she was forbidden to him through *chayavei krisos* or *chayavei misos beis din* — relatives or others whose marriage is biblically invalid at the most serious level. But this cannot be the case, because in such a situation *kiddushin* would not take effect at all — *harei leis kiddushin begavah* — and the woman would simply not be the father's wife in any sense. The *chachamim* surely would not need to argue that both prohibitions apply in a case where the marriage was never binding. Both sides of the debate would agree she is not the *eshet av* in that scenario.

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ela chayavei lavin* — the debate concerns prohibitions involving only a negative commandment. The father married a woman who was forbidden to him by a *lav* alone — for example, a *mamzeres* — a marriage that went through formal ceremonies but that some hold is not fully binding at the biblical level.

### Rabbi Akiva

The connection becomes clear: *Rabbi Yehuda savar lah ke-Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi Akiva, who rules *ein kiddushin tofsin bechayavei lavin* — *kiddushin* does not take effect even with women forbidden by a simple negative prohibition. If Rabbi Akiva's position is that such a marriage is not binding, then the woman in question was never legally the father's wife, and therefore cannot be in the *eshet av* category. Rabbi Yehuda's position in the *braita* is thus not really a dispute about the *eshet av* prohibition per se; it is a dispute about when *kiddushin* is valid.

### Rav Oshaia

Rav Oshaia challenges this interpretation. If Rabbi Yehuda truly holds like Rabbi Akiva that *kiddushin* is not binding in cases of *chayavei lavin*, there is a significant practical consequence: women in that category would not require *chalitza* and would not be eligible for *yibum*. They would be completely outside the framework of *yibum* entirely, just as women forbidden with *karet* are. Yet a *mishna* teaches: *issur mitzvah ve-issur kedusha, choletzes velo misyabemes* — women in the lighter prohibition categories must perform *chalitza* but may not do *yibum*. These women — including, for example, an *almanah* to a *kohen gadol*, or a *gerushah* to a regular *kohen*, both cases of negative prohibitions — are still within the *yibum* framework sufficiently to require *chalitza*. If *kiddushin* were not binding in their cases, they would be wholly outside the framework and *chalitza* would not apply.

### Terminology

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty: *le-divrav de-Tanna Kama ka-amar ve-lav sevira lei* — Rabbi Yehuda is speaking according to the first *tanna*'s framework, not expressing his own view. Rabbi Yehuda's actual dispute with the *mishna* is purely terminological. He agrees with the *tanna kama* that these women require *chalitza* but not *yibum*; he disagrees only about what the two categories should be *called*. The *mishna* calls the rabbinic-prohibition category *issur mitzvah* and the *kehuna*-based prohibition category *issur kedusha*. Rabbi Yehuda reverses the labels, calling the *kehuna* category *issur mitzvah* (since the *kohen* is commanded in holiness) and the rabbinic category *issur kedusha* (since the rabbinic enactments extend biblical *kedusha*). He agrees entirely with the underlying *halacha* — he simply contests the nomenclature. Whether the *halacha* reflects his own view or he is merely noting what *the other view* would call these categories is left as a curiosity, but the practical dispute about *chalitza* dissolves entirely.

---

## Mother Exception

### Rav Yitzchak

The *gemara* now sets aside the *braita*'s more restricted debate and returns to the plain reading of the *mishna* — that Rabbi Yehuda's position is a categorical one. When Rav Yitzchak came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he brought with him a *braita* that matches the *mishna*'s formulation: *Rabbi Yehuda omer eino chayav ela mishum ha-em bilvad* — in any case where the woman is the man's mother, Rabbi Yehuda holds the liability is for *mother* only, not for *eshet av*. This is not a limited ruling about marriages that were unfit; it is the general position that a biological mother is categorically excluded from the *eshet av* prohibition.

### Imcha Hi

Abbaye provides the scriptural basis for this view. The verse states: *imcha hi, lo segaleh ervatah* — she is your mother; do not uncover her nakedness (*Vayikra* 18). The emphasis of the phrase *imcha hi* — she is your mother — operates as a halakhic limitation: *mishum ima atah mechayvo ve-ei atah mechayvo mishum eshes av* — the verse defines her exclusively through the lens of motherhood. Once the Torah says *imcha hi*, it assigns her entirely and solely to the mother category. No other prohibition applies to her through this relationship. The *eshet av* prohibition, which the Torah establishes elsewhere as a separate category, simply does not extend to cover someone who is first and foremost defined as *imcha* — your mother.

This will serve as the foundation for Rabbi Yehuda's position, and the *gemara* will continue to develop the implications and alternative explanations in subsequent discussion.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 54

## Mother vs. Eshet Av

### Opening: Dual Identity

Daf 54 continues the discussion of those liable to *sekilah*, working through a range of capital sexual transgressions. We pick up at the bottom of 53b with the debate between Reb Yehuda and the *chachamim* regarding a man who has intercourse with his mother — where his mother is simultaneously his father's wife. Is he liable for two distinct identities, or only one? Reb Yehuda maintains he is liable only for the category of *ema* — mother — and not for the category of *eshet av*, father's wife. His implicit reasoning is that the prohibition of *eshet av* concerns a stepmother specifically, and the overlap with one's biological mother does not multiply the liability.

### Reb Yehuda's View

The *Gemara* asks: *ta'ama mai?* — what is the basis for Reb Yehuda's position? Abaye answers that the verse states *imcha hi* — "she is your mother" (Vayikra 18:7). The word *hi* functions to limit the transgression: you hold him liable *mishum ima*, on account of her being his mother, *v'ei ata mechayvo mishum eshet av* — and you do not hold him liable on account of her being his father's wife.

### Contradiction in Verses

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this reading. The verse concerning *eshet av* states: *ervat eshet avicha lo tegaleh, ervat avicha hi* — "the nakedness of your father's wife you shall not uncover, for she is your father's nakedness" (Vayikra 18:8). Here too, the word *hi* appears. If the *hi* in the verse about the mother excludes the *eshet av* identity, then by the same logic the *hi* in the verse about the father's wife would exclude the mother identity.

The result is a direct contradiction. When one encounters a woman who is both his mother and his father's wife, the verse about the mother would say: hold him liable only for *ima*, not for *eshet av*. The verse about the father's wife would say: hold him liable only for *eshet av*, not for *ima*. The two verses cancel each other out — the woman who is both is apparently excluded from both categories. The *Gemara* states this explicitly: *hashta imo she'einah eshet aviv mechayve, eshet aviv she'einah imo mechayve* — a plain mother and a plain father's wife are each clear cases of liability; yet *imo she'hi eshet aviv, lo mechayve klal* — the woman who is both winds up excluded from liability entirely?

Furthermore, the *Gemara* notes that even for the *rabbanan* who disagree with Reb Yehuda, the phrase *imcha hi* requires some interpretation — and so neither reading of the *hi* can simply stand in isolation.

### Ervata Reading Rejected

The *Gemara* then searches for an alternative basis for Reb Yehuda's position. Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika proposes reading the word *ervata* at the end of the verse — *lo tegaleh ervata*, "you shall not uncover her nakedness" — as restricting liability: *mishum ervah achat ata mechayvo v'ei ata mechayvo mishum shtei arayos* — you hold him liable for one identity, not two.

The *Gemara* immediately objects: the very same word *ervata* appears in the verse concerning the daughter-in-law — *ervat kalatcha lo tegaleh, eshet bincha hi, lo tegaleh ervata*. If *ervata* means liability is limited to one identity, then by the same reasoning a man who has intercourse with his daughter-in-law should be liable only for the status of *kallah* and not for the additional status of *eshet ish*, a married woman. Yet the *Mishnah* explicitly states that one who has intercourse with his daughter-in-law is liable *mishum kalato u'mishum eshet ish* — for both identities — and Reb Yehuda does not dispute that ruling.

The *Gemara* resolves the daughter-in-law case by noting: *keivan de'chad gufa hi af al gav de'trei issurei ninhu, ktiv ervata* — since it is one body, even though there are two prohibited statuses, the word *ervata* is written. The single *ervata* does not exclude a second identity; it simply reflects that we are speaking of a single person. But this resolution defeats the whole reading: if *ervata* is consistent with double liability, it cannot be the source for Reb Yehuda's limiting principle by the case of the mother either.

### Rava's Interpretation

With both the *hi* reading and the *ervata* reading rejected, Rava offers a third and ultimately successful solution. *Ela amar Rava kasvar Rav Yehuda: ervat avicha zo eshet avicha* — Reb Yehuda understands the phrase *ervat avicha* to mean *eshet avicha*, "your father's wife." This is, in fact, a natural reading: the prohibition in the verse for *eshet av* reads *ervat eshet avicha lo tegaleh, ervat avicha hi*, where the suffix *eruption of your father* is explained by the earlier phrase as referring to the father's wife. Rava proposes that this equivalence — *ervat avicha* means *eshet avicha* — is established through a *gezeirah shavah* and carries over to the prohibition verse as well.

### How Verses Align

Under Rava's reading, the verses work together as follows. The prohibition verse in *Acharei Mot* reads: *ervat avicha v'ervat imcha lo tegaleh, imcha hi, lo tegaleh ervata*. The phrase *ervat avicha* — now understood to mean *eshet avicha*, father's wife — includes all cases of father's wife: whether she is also the man's mother or not. *V'ervat imcha* continues, and *imcha hi* tells you that for all categories of mother — whether she is also the father's wife or not — the relevant liability is only *mishum ima*.

This structure cleanly accounts for the entire picture. *Ervat avicha* (= *eshet avicha*) encompasses father's wife who is also a mother, and father's wife who is not a mother. *V'ervat imcha... imcha hi* then covers all mothers, including the mother who is the father's wife and the mother who is not. For Reb Yehuda, *imcha hi* functions precisely here: once a woman who is both mother and father's wife has been drawn into the category of *ervat avicha* (because she is father's wife), the verse then says that for all such women, the only operative liability is *imcha* — mother. This is not a contradiction but a hierarchy: the verse first includes her and then specifies the exclusive category of her liability.

A natural question arises: if this is the intent, why didn't the verse simply say *ervat eshet avicha* instead of the shorter *ervat avicha*? The answer is precisely that the vaguer phrasing *ervat avicha* allows the verse to capture the mother who is the father's wife, not merely the stepmother. By leaving the phrase open, the *drasha* can then clarify that she is covered — but covered exclusively under the category of mother.

### Tannaitic Source

The *Gemara* concludes this section with *tanya kavatei d'Rava* — a *braita* is taught in accordance with Rava's interpretation. This *braita* derives from the *Sifra*, the Tannaic midrash on *Vayikra*, whose anonymous voice (*stam Sifra*) is identified by the *Gemara* as representing the position of Reb Yehuda. Rashi notes this point explicitly, making clear that this *drasha* is Reb Yehuda's own reading, which will now also allow us to understand how the *rabbanan* depart from it.

---

## Azharah & Onesh

### Braita Sources

The *braita* cited in this section moves the discussion from the prohibition verses (*acharei mot*) to the punishment verses (*kedoshim*). The key verse is: *va'ish asher yishkav et eshet aviv, ervat aviv gillah, mot yumatu, dmeihem bam* — "and a man who lies with his father's wife has uncovered his father's nakedness; they shall both be put to death, their blood is upon them" (Vayikra 20:11). This verse is the source for *sekilah* in the case of *eshet av*. However, mother is entirely absent from the punishment verses. The *braita* proceeds to establish both the punishment and prohibition for all relevant cases.

### Ervat Avicha Derivation

The *braita* begins: *ish* — a man, *prat le'katan*, excluding a minor. *Asher yishkav et eshet aviv* — this phrase encompasses *bein eshet aviv she'hi imo bein eshet aviv she'einah imo* — whether the father's wife is also the man's mother or not. The father's wife is thus included in the punishment verse regardless of the dual-identity question.

### Ervat Aviv Gila Link

What remains unaddressed is the case of a mother who is not the father's wife. She is simply absent from the punishment verse. The *braita* derives her inclusion from the extra phrase *ervat aviv gillah* — "he has uncovered his father's nakedness." This phrase, which follows the explicit prohibition of sleeping with the father's wife, is treated as containing additional meaning. Ironically — given that in the prohibition verse *ervat avicha* referred to the father's wife — in this punishment context, *ervat aviv gillah* comes to include the plain mother, the woman who is not the father's wife at all. The *braita* identifies this phrase as *mufneh* — free, available for use in a *gezeirah shavah* — and reserves it for that derivation to follow.

### Prohibition Sources

The *braita* then turns to the *azharah*, the prohibition. *Onesh shamanu, azharah minayin?* — We have the punishment, but where is the prohibition established? The answer comes from *Acharei Mot*: *talmud lomar ervat avicha lo tegaleh v'ervat imcha* — the verse that opens with *ervat avicha* and continues with *v'ervat imcha*. The *braita* asks: when the verse says *ervat avicha*, does it mean literally intercourse with the father himself, or does it mean *eshet avicha*, father's wife? To resolve this, it invokes a verbal analogy: the verse here says *ervat avicha lo tegaleh*, and the punishment verse says *ervat aviv gillah*. Since *ervat aviv gillah* in context clearly speaks of a woman — the man slept with a woman — so too *ervat avicha* in the prohibition verse speaks of a woman, specifically, one defined as *ervat avicha*, the father's nakedness, which means the father's wife. The *drasha* concludes: *u'mashma bein eshet aviv she'hi imo bein eshet aviv she'einah imo* — and this covers father's wife whether or not she is also the mother.

Mothers who are not the father's wife are then added from the continuation of the verse: *v'ervat imcha lo tegaleh* — which the *braita* takes as separately establishing that case. The *braita* then draws the equalization: the Torah has made a mother who is not the father's wife equivalent to a mother who is the father's wife. Both are prohibited. The *braita* concludes this portion by affirming: *im ken lama ne'emar* — why was it stated — meaning, what does the explicit inclusion of both cases in this single verse accomplish? It establishes that both are treated identically with respect to the prohibition.

### Gezeirah Shavah Method

The *gezeirah shavah* left pending earlier now operates: the phrase *ervat avicha lo tegaleh* in the prohibition verse and *ervat aviv gillah* in the punishment verse share the same terminology, making them formally linked. This link allows the rules of the punishment verse — including its scope — to carry over to the prohibition verse and vice versa. Specifically, just as the prohibition verse is shown to include mother who is not the father's wife, the same extension applies in the context of the punishment: *af b'onesh asa ha'katuv imo she'einah eshet aviv k'imo she'hi eshet aviv* — just as in the prohibition the Torah treated a mother who is not the father's wife like a mother who is the father's wife, so too in the punishment both receive the same consequence.

This is exactly the point the *braita* was holding in reserve when it identified *ervat aviv gillah* as *mufneh l'gezeirah shavah*. It serves double duty: first, it introduces the plain mother into the punishment verse in a preliminary way; second, it anchors the *gezeirah shavah* that formally unifies the two verses and extends punishment to the plain mother on the basis of the equalization established in the prohibition verse.

The *braita* then completes Reb Yehuda's position: *mishum imo ata mechayvo v'ei ata mechayvo mishum eshet aviv* — you hold him liable on account of his mother, and you do not hold him liable on account of the father's wife. Once the mother who is also father's wife has been included in the prohibition verse under *ervat avicha*, and the verse concludes *imcha hi* — equating all mothers — the only operative liability is the mother identity. This is Reb Yehuda's full position, and the *Gemara* confirms that it appears in the anonymous voice of the *Sifra*, which *halacha* identifies with Reb Yehuda.

---

## Rabbanan Position

### Literal Father Reading

Having established Reb Yehuda's reading in full, the *Gemara* turns to the *rabbanan*. The critical divergence concerns the phrase *ervat avicha* in the prohibition verse. For Reb Yehuda, as we have seen, *ervat avicha* means *eshet avicha* — the father's wife.
