For the *rabbanan*, however, *ervat avicha mamash* — *ervat avicha* is taken literally, as referring to intercourse with the father himself. This reading forecloses Reb Yehuda's entire structure: the *rabbanan* cannot use *ervat avicha* to include the mother who is also father's wife and then conclude *imcha hi* limits liability to one category, because for them the phrase is not about the father's wife at all.

### Double Liability Principle

As a consequence of this reading, the *rabbanan* hold that when a woman is both one's mother and one's father's wife, both identities generate independent liability. There is no verse limiting the transgression to a single status. This is the *rabbanan*'s straightforward position: *chayav shtayim* — liable twice, once for the mother prohibition and once for the *eshet av* prohibition.

### Rav Yehuda's Rule

The *Gemara* introduces the teaching of Rav Yehuda (not to be confused with Reb Yehuda the *tanna*): *nokhri ha'ba al aviv, chayav shtayim* — a non-Jew who has intercourse with his father is liable twice. Similarly, one who has intercourse with his father's brother (*achi aviv*) is liable twice — once for intercourse with a male and once under a separate prohibition derived from *ervat akhi avicha*. This is the teaching that supports the *rabbanan*'s reading of *ervat avicha mamash* as referring to literal intercourse with the father, generating a double prohibition.

This double-liability teaching raises an obvious question: why does Rav Yehuda frame this as a case involving a non-Jew? The answer, given shortly, is that the framing is a *lishna ma'alya* — a euphemism, a polite way of describing an act too disturbing to attribute directly. The actual legal ruling applies to a Jew.

Furthermore, the question of double liability is practically most significant not in the context of capital punishment — where you cannot execute a person twice — but rather in the case of *shogeg*, an unintentional transgression. If a Jew transgresses both prohibitions unintentionally in a single lapse of awareness, and the two prohibitions are legally distinct, he would be obligated to bring a separate *korban chatat* for each one.

### Rava's Clarification

Rava clarifies: *mistabra milta de'Rav Yehuda b'Yisrael, be'shogeg, u've'korban* — the practical import of Rav Yehuda's ruling is in the case of a Jew, acting unintentionally, with respect to the obligation of a sin offering. This is the context in which counting separate liabilities actually matters. The *Gemara* explains why the non-Jew reading cannot be taken literally: *dino mai nihu? katala* — the only legal consequence for a non-Jew in the *Bnei Noach* framework is execution, and there is no *hatra'ah* (formal warning) required and no *korbanot* system. Saying someone is liable twice is meaningless if the only consequence is a single execution. Therefore, the discussion must concern a Jew acting *be'shogeg*, where the number of separate liabilities determines the number of *korbanot*.

### Tannaitic Debate

The *Gemara* cites a *braita* that corroborates this: one who comes upon his father is liable twice; one who comes upon his father's brother is liable twice. The *braita* then records a dispute. One view holds this teaching goes against Reb Yehuda, since Reb Yehuda reads *ervat avicha* as *eshet avicha* and would therefore have no basis for treating intercourse with the father as a separate prohibition. A second view says even Reb Yehuda could agree that intercourse with the father is prohibited, deriving it through a *kal vachomer* from the case of the father's brother: if one is doubly liable for intercourse with the father's brother, who is merely a relative of the father, then certainly one would be doubly liable for intercourse with the father himself.

The *Gemara* identifies this as part of a broader dispute between Abaye and Rava: *onshin min hadin* — whether a punishment can be derived through a *kal vachomer*. Those who permit such derivations would allow Reb Yehuda to hold this position; those who do not would say that without an explicit verse Reb Yehuda has no basis to include the father as a separate prohibition.

### Eshet Av After Death

The *Gemara* then asks: where do the *rabbanan* derive the prohibition (*azharah*) for *eshet av*? Since for the *rabbanan* the phrase *ervat avicha* in the prohibition verse refers to literal intercourse with the father — not the father's wife — they cannot use that verse as their source for the *eshet av* prohibition. The answer is that they derive it from a separate verse: *ervat eshet avicha lo tegaleh* (Vayikra 18:8) — a verse that explicitly names the father's wife. This verse is entirely available to the *rabbanan* for that purpose precisely because they did not need to redirect it toward the literal-father reading the way Reb Yehuda does.

For Reb Yehuda, by contrast, the verse *ervat eshet avicha lo tegaleh* is needed for an additional derivation: it establishes that the prohibition of *eshet av* applies *l'achar mitat aviv* — even after the father has died. This is a significant *chiddush*: one might have assumed the prohibition ends with the marriage, i.e., when the father is alive and she is currently his wife. The separate verse teaches that even after the father's death the prohibition remains in force.

The *rabbanan*, not needing that verse for the prohibition of *eshet av* in general (since they derive it from the literal reading of *ervat avicha*), derive the post-death prohibition from elsewhere — from the end of the verse itself: *ervat avicha hi*, which for them is a superfluous phrase that extends the prohibition to the period after the father's death.

In turn, the *Gemara* asks: what does Reb Yehuda do with the phrase *ervat avicha hi* at the end of that verse, if he has already used the verse for the post-death extension through the *gezeirah shavah*? Reb Yehuda uses it for the limiting principle parallel to *imcha hi*: just as *imcha hi* says that for a mother who is also a father's wife, you are liable only for the mother identity, *ervat avicha hi* analogously says that if the father's wife is also currently a married woman (*eshet ish*), you are liable only for the *eshet av* identity, not additionally for *eshet ish*.

The *Gemara* challenges this: the *Mishnah* rules explicitly that one who has intercourse with his father's wife transgresses both *mishum eshet av u'mishum eshet ish*, whether the father is alive or dead — and Reb Yehuda does not dispute the *Mishnah* in that case. Abaye resolves this: even though Reb Yehuda did not register disagreement with the *Mishnah*, a *braita* records that he in fact holds this limiting position there as well.

The section concludes with the question of where the *rabbanan* derive the punishment (*onesh*) for *eshet av* after the father's death. For Reb Yehuda this follows from the *gezeirah shavah*: once the *gezeirah shavah* links the prohibition and punishment verses, the extension of the prohibition to the post-death period carries over to the punishment as well. For the *rabbanan*, who do not employ that *gezeirah shavah* (having used the free phrase *ervat aviv gillah* for the post-death extension of *eshet av* rather than for the *gezeirah shavah* itself), the punishment for *eshet av* after death is derived from that very phrase — *machaziki lehu l'onesh eishet aviv l'achar misa*.

This immediately raises a further question: if the *rabbanan* allocate *ervat aviv gillah* to *eshet av* after death, they no longer have it available for what Reb Yehuda used it for — namely, bringing the plain mother into the punishment verse. So where do the *rabbanan* derive the *onesh* for a mother who is not the father's wife?

---

## Azharah & Onesh (II)

### Mother's Punishment

The *Gemara* resolves this with the ruling of Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi: *amar kra, imcha hi*. The *rabbanan* use the phrase *imcha hi* — "she is your mother" — to equate all categories of mother: *asao ha'katuv l'imo she'einah eshet aviv k'imo she'hi eshet aviv* — the Torah has treated a mother who is not the father's wife identically to a mother who is the father's wife. Since the punishment verse includes the mother who is also the father's wife (by virtue of *asher yishkav et eshet aviv*), the phrase *imcha hi* — which the *rabbanan* deploy for this equalization rather than for Reb Yehuda's limiting principle — teaches that all the same laws that apply to a mother who is also the father's wife apply equally to a plain mother who is not. In this way, the *rabbanan* derive the punishment of *sekilah* for the plain mother from *imcha hi*, while Reb Yehuda uses the same phrase to restrict double liability. The two positions share a text but read its function in precisely opposite directions.

---

## Mishkav Zachor

### Actor and Passive

The *Gemara* now transitions to the prohibition and punishment for *mishkav zachor* — intercourse between males. The terminology here is notable: the word *zachur* (as distinct from *zachar*) is understood by Rashi as referring specifically to the one who is penetrated — the passive participant. The form *zachur* connotes the passive, as in *shamur* or *sagur*, suggesting one who has been "maled." When the verse or *Gemara* refers to the active penetrator, it uses *zachar*.

With that distinction in mind, the *Gemara* proceeds to examine both the source for the punishment and the source for the prohibition, and to determine which categories of person — actor, passive participant, adult, minor — are covered by each verse.

---

## Bestiality Laws (III)

### Why Stone Animal

Before continuing with *mishkav zachor*, the *Gemara* addresses the stoning of the animal involved in an act of bestiality. The question is deceptively simple: *im adam chata, behemah mah chata?* — if the human sinned, what did the animal do wrong? Two rationales are offered. The first: *lefi she'ba'ah le'adam takalah al yadah* — because it caused a stumbling block for a human being, and therefore it must be destroyed. Here the animal is not morally culpable but is treated as an instrument of harm. The second rationale: *she'lo te'he behemah overet ba'shuk v'yomru zo hi she'niskal ploni al yadah* — so that the animal not walk through the marketplace and people say, "This is the animal on account of which so-and-so was executed." The concern here is not about the animal's metaphysical status but about the memory of the sin. The two rationales point in meaningfully different directions: the first treats destruction of the animal as a response to what it caused; the second treats it as a practical measure to prevent public recollection of the transgression.

---

## Mishkav Zachor (II)

### Age Requirements

Returning to *mishkav zachor*, the *braita* begins: *ish* — a man, *prat le'katan* — excluding a minor from liability. The verse then continues: *asher yishkav et zachar* — the one being penetrated may be *bein gadol bein katan*, whether an adult or a minor. The actor must be an adult to be punishable, but the passive participant need not be. Conversely — and this is a crucial structural point — if the passive participant is the adult, the one doing the penetrating may in principle be a minor of sufficient age, since the age threshold for defining an act of intercourse with a male is nine years old (parallel to the three-year threshold for a female). Both parties need not be adults; what matters is that the act meets the minimum definition of intercourse and that the liable party is an adult.

### Types of Intercourse

The phrase *mishkevei ishah* — "the lyings of a woman" — appears in the prohibition verse and serves a broader halakhic function. The plural form *mishkevei* (rather than *mishkev*) signals that there are two modes of intercourse with a woman: vaginal and anal. *Megaleh lach ha'katuv she'shem mishkevot ishah* — the Torah reveals that the term "lyings of a woman" encompasses both. This teaches a general principle operative throughout the laws of *arayot*: intercourse is legally defined as either vaginal or anal penetration. By anal penetration being the only mode relevant in the case of two men, and the verse nonetheless designating it by the terminology of *mishkevei ishah*, the *drashot* extract the principle that both modes count as intercourse in all forbidden-relations contexts. Oral intercourse is not included in this definition.

### Punishment Derivation

For the punishment, the verse in *Kedoshim* reads: *mot yumatu, dmeihem bam* — they shall be put to death, their blood is upon them. The *braita* asks: is this *sekilah*, or might it be one of the other capital punishments listed in the Torah? The derivation proceeds through *gezeirah shavah*: *ne'emar kan dmeihem bam, v'ne'emar b'ov v'yidoni dmeihem bam* — the same phrase *dmeihem bam* appears here and by the case of *ov v'yidoni* (sorcery), which is established to be *sekilah*. *Mah lehalan be'sekilah, af kan be'sekilah* — just as there it is stoning, so here it is stoning.

### Actor's Prohibition

The prohibition for the active partner — the penetrator — is derived from the verse in *Acharei Mot*: *v'et zachar lo tishkav mishkevei ishah, to'evah hi* — you shall not lie with a male as one lies with a woman, it is an abomination. *Lamadnu azharah la'shochev* — this establishes the prohibition for the one who sleeps with, i.e., the actor.

### Passive's Prohibition

Where is the prohibition for the passive participant — the one who is penetrated? This is where Reb Yishmael and Reb Akiva diverge.

Reb Yishmael derives it from the verse *lo yihyeh kadesh mi'bnei Yisrael* — there shall be no *kadesh* among Israel (Devarim 23:18). The *kadesh* — commonly rendered "male prostitute" — is understood here as one who offers himself for penetration. This is not an arbitrary extension: male prostitutes in the ancient world characteristically served as the passive partner in male-male intercourse, and the verse prohibiting the *kadesh* is therefore understood as specifically addressing the act of being penetrated. The *Gemara* then supports this reading through an additional verse: *v'gam kadesh hayah ba'aretz, asu ke'chol to'avot ha'goyim asher horish* — there were also *kedeshim* in the land, they did like all the abominations of the nations. The keyword *to'avah* — abomination — links this to the verse on intercourse between males, which also uses *to'evah hi*. Reb Yishmael reads the connection: the *kadesh* is associated with a forbidden sexual act labeled *to'evah*, specifically the act between males, and therefore the prohibition of *kadesh* is the source for prohibiting the passive participant in *mishkav zachor*.

Reb Akiva holds that no separate verse is needed. He reads the verb of the original prohibition in both its active and passive forms: *v'et zachar lo tishkav* — *karei bei lo tishachev* — you shall also not be lain with by a male. By reading *lo tishkav* passively, Reb Akiva derives the prohibition for the passive participant from the same verse as the actor's prohibition, making the two a single unified prohibition rather than two separate ones. This will have consequences for how many *korbanot* are owed for multiple acts, as we shall see.

---

## Bestiality Laws (III)

### Bestiality Age Rules

The *braita* on bestiality follows the same structure. *Ish, prat le'katan* — a man, excluding a minor. The animal, by contrast, is subject to no age qualification: *bein gedolah bein ketanah* — whether the animal is large or small, adult or young, the act is defined as intercourse and the man is liable.

### Punishment Source

For the punishment, the verse reads *mot yumat* — he shall be put to death. A *gezeirah shavah* is applied: *ne'emar kan taharogu, v'ne'emar lehalan ki harog tahargenu* — the same language of *harog/taharogu* appears here and in *Devarim* 13 in the case of the *mesis*, the one who incites others to idolatry. That case is established as *sekilah*, and so by the verbal analogy, the punishment for bestiality is also *sekilah*. *Mah lehalan be'sekilah, af kan be'sekilah*.

### Actor's Prohibition

For the actor — the man who penetrates an animal — the prohibition is derived from: *u've'chol behemah lo tittein shechavtecha le'tum'ah bah* — you shall not give your lying with any animal to defile yourself thereby (Vayikra 18:23). *Lamadnu azharah la'shochev* — this establishes the prohibition for the penetrating party.

### Passive's Prohibition

Where is the prohibition for a man who is penetrated by an animal? Reb Yishmael uses the verse *lo yihyeh kadesh mi'bnei Yisrael* here as well, extending the *kadesh* prohibition beyond the case of *mishkav zachor* to include a man penetrated by an animal. The *to'evah* connection operates analogously. However, the *Gemara* notes that the word *to'evah* does not in fact appear directly in the verse prohibiting bestiality — unlike the case of *mishkav zachor* where *to'evah hi* is explicit. This is the opening for Abaye's subsequent correction.

Reb Akiva, consistent with his earlier reasoning, holds that no separate verse is required. The same verse that prohibits the actor — *lo tittein shechavtecha* — can be read as *lo tittein shechivtecha*, passively: you shall not allow your being lain with. Both active and passive are captured by the same *pasuk*, so there is again only a single prohibition covering both sides.

---

## Multiple Acts Analys (II)

### Male-Male Both Sides

Now that the prohibitions have been established and the debate between Reb Yishmael and Reb Akiva laid out, the *Gemara* examines a man who performs multiple acts in a single state of forgetfulness (*shogeg*) — specifically, acts on different sides of the same category. The question throughout is how many *korbanot chatat* he owes.

The first case: *haba al ha'zachur v'heivi alav zachur* — a man who both penetrates a male and is penetrated by a male (note: Rashi points out that the first is called *zachur*, the passive form, and the second *zachar*, indicating which role is meant in each phrase). How many sin offerings does he owe?

Reb Avahu states: *lidivre Reb Yishmael, chayav shtayim* — for Reb Yishmael, two. The act of penetrating a male violates *v'et zachar lo tishkav*, and the act of being penetrated violates *lo yihyeh kadesh* — two entirely separate verses and thus two separate prohibitions. He owes a separate *korban* for each. *Lidivre Reb Akiva, eino chayav ela achat* — for Reb Akiva, only one. Since both sides of the act are derived from the single verse *lo tishkav / lo tishachev*, they constitute a single prohibition done twice, yielding only one *korban*.

### Bestiality Both Sides

The second case: *haba al ha'behemah v'heivi behemah alav* — a man who both penetrates an animal and is penetrated by an animal.

Again, *lidivre Reb Yishmael, chayav shtayim*: one for *u've'chol behemah lo tittein shechavtecha* and one for *lo yihyeh kadesh* — two separate prohibitions. *Lidivre Reb Akiva, eino chayav ela achat*: both sides are subsumed in the single verse read as *shechavtecha / shechivtecha*, so only one *korban*.

---

## Multiple Acts Analys (II)

### Abaye's View

Abaye now intervenes. He maintains that even according to Reb Yishmael, the case of a man penetrated by an animal is *not* included in the prohibition of *kadesh*. *Dichi ketiv lo yihyeh kadesh, be'gavre ketiv* — when the verse says *lo yihyeh kadesh*, it is speaking about human beings, not about animals. The connection through *to'evah* that Reb Yishmael used to extend *kadesh* to *mishkav zachor* cannot work for bestiality because the verse prohibiting bestiality does not use the word *to'evah* in the same way.

If so, where does Reb Yishmael derive the prohibition for a man penetrated by an animal? From the extra verse *kol shochev im behemah mot yumet* — "whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death" (Shemot 22:18). This verse appears redundant as a punishment source (the punishment is already established from other verses), so it is redirected: *im eino inyan la'shochev, tenehu inyan la'nishkav* — if it is not needed for the actor, apply it to the passive participant. Furthermore, *v'afkeih rachmana la'nishkav b'lashon shochev* — the Torah expressed the passive participant using the language of the active one (*shochev*), and by analogy: just as for the actor there is both a prohibition and a punishment, so too for the passive participant there is both a prohibition and a punishment.

Under Abaye's reading, therefore, Reb Yishmael and Reb Akiva effectively converge on this specific case. For both of them, the prohibition of being penetrated by an animal derives from the same cluster of *pesukim* as the prohibition of penetrating an animal — not from a separate prohibition of *kadesh*. Accordingly, both would agree that a man who both penetrates and is penetrated by an animal in one lapse of awareness owes only one *korban*.

### Mixed Partners

A new case: *ha'nirba la'zachar v'ha'nirba la'behemah* — a man who is penetrated by a male and also penetrated by an animal, in one lapse of awareness.

For Reb Akiva, this is *chayav shtayim* — two *korbanot*. Being penetrated by a male is governed by *lo tishachev* (the passive read of the *mishkav zachor* verse), while being penetrated by an animal is governed by *shechivtecha* (the passive read of the *lo tittein shechavtecha* verse). These are entirely separate sources.

For Reb Yishmael — prior to Abaye's correction — it would have been only one *korban*, since both types of being-penetrated were encompassed under the single prohibition of *lo yihyeh kadesh*. But under Abaye's correction, Reb Yishmael no longer places the animal case under *kadesh*. He derives it instead from *kol shochev im behemah*. Thus for Abaye's reading of Reb Yishmael, these are now two separate sources — *lo yihyeh kadesh* for being penetrated by a male, and *kol shochev im behemah* redirected for being penetrated by an animal — and therefore Reb Yishmael too would say *chayav shtayim*.

### All Four Acts Summary

The *Gemara* concludes with the case of a man who does all four acts in a single lapse of awareness: he penetrates a male, is penetrated by a male, penetrates an animal, and is penetrated by an animal.

For Reb Yishmael (*lidivre Rabbi Avahu*, i.e., before Abaye's correction), the answer is *chayav shalosh* — three *korbanot*. The prohibition of *lo yihyeh kadesh* covers both cases of being penetrated (whether by a male or an animal): that is one. The prohibition of *v'et zachar lo tishkav* covers penetrating a male: that is two. The prohibition of *u've'chol behemah lo tittein shechavtecha* covers penetrating an animal: that is three. Three distinct prohibitions cover the four acts.

For Reb Akiva, the answer is *chayav shtayim* — two. He has no *kadesh* prohibition at all. The prohibition of *lo tishkav / lo tishachev* covers both sides of *mishkav zachor* (penetrating and being penetrated by a male): that is one. The prohibition of *shechavtecha / shechivtecha* covers both sides of the animal acts (penetrating and being penetrated by an animal): that is two. Two prohibitions, each transgressed twice in each direction, yield two *korbanot*.

---

## Bestiality Laws (III)

### Abaye's Correction

Abaye's intervention — already integrated into the discussion above — is formalized here as a direct correction to the position attributed to Reb Yishmael. Abaye insists that *lo yihyeh kadesh* applies *be'gavre* — only to human beings — and cannot be extended to the case of an animal. The *to'evah* link that Reb Yishmael used to connect *kadesh* to *mishkav zachor* does not carry over to bestiality, since the bestiality verse does not use *to'evah* in the applicable way. Reb Yishmael's source for the passive participant in the animal case must therefore be located in *kol shochev im behemah*, not in *kadesh*, bringing his position closer to Reb Akiva's than the initial presentation suggested.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 55

## Mishkav Zachar Ages

### Tanur Rabanan

The daf opens on Sanhedrin 54b, six lines from the bottom, with the passage *tanu rabbanan*. The *baraita* addresses male-on-male intercourse and notes, with reference to the word *zachor*—specifically as it appears with the *vav*, pointing to the one being penetrated—that *lo asu bo katan kegadol*: a minor is not treated the same as an adult. There is a meaningful distinction based on the age of the *nishkav*, the penetrated party.

To appreciate this distinction, it helps first to recall the framework for heterosexual *arayot*. In a heterosexual context, only one of the two parties need be an adult for that adult to be *chayav*; however, the other party must be of an age at which the act is legally considered intercourse at all. For a minor male in such a context, the threshold is nine years and a day—below that age, the act is not legally defined as intercourse, so the adult woman would bear no liability. For a minor female, the threshold is three years and a day, based on *Chazal*'s understanding of whether the hymen would regenerate and whether the act constitutes legally cognizable intercourse.

The question now concerns *mishkav zachar* specifically: if a minor male is the *nishkav* and an adult is the *shochev*, what age of the *nishkav* transforms the act into legally cognizable intercourse?

### Rav vs. Shmuel

On this question, *Rav* and *Shmuel* dispute. *Rav* holds: *lo asu biat pachat miben tesha shanim keben tesha shanim*—the threshold is nine years and a day. Below nine years and a day, the act is not defined as intercourse; above it, it is. *Shmuel* holds: *lo asu biat pachat miben shalosh shanim keben shalosh shanim*—the threshold is three years and a day.

The *Gemara* probes the conceptual basis of their disagreement. *Rav* reasons: *kol d'ita b'shochev ita b'nishkav, v'kol d'leita b'shochev leita b'nishkav*—the *shochev* and the *nishkav* are linked. Since a male is considered capable of the act of intercourse as the penetrating party at nine years and a day, the same age defines him as a meaningful participant when he is the penetrated party. *Shmuel*, by contrast, reasons from the Torah's own language: *mishkevei ishah ketiv*—the verse speaks of "the lyings of a woman." The Torah frames the role of the *nishkav* by analogy to a woman, and therefore the threshold is three years and a day, the same age that governs a female's participation in intercourse.

### Baraita kVetat Rav

The *Gemara* then cites a *baraita* that supports *Rav*: *zachar ben tesha shanim v'yom echad*—when it comes to *mishkav zachar*, the relevant threshold is nine years and a day. *Rashi* explains that this must be addressing the *nishkav*, because the nine-year threshold for the *shochev* was never in dispute—any time a male is doing the penetrating, nine years and a day is the operative standard. Since the *baraita* explicitly specifies *mishkav zachar* and declares nine years and a day, it is telling us that the same age applies to the *nishkav* as well—in accordance with *Rav*'s position.

---

## Bestiality Acts

### Baraita Behema

The *baraita* continues with the laws of bestiality. *Haba al ha-behemah bein kedarka bein shelo kedarka*—one who has intercourse with a female animal, whether vaginally or anally, is *chayav*. Likewise, *v'ishah ha-mevi'ah behemah aleha bein kedarka bein shelo kedarka*—a woman who has intercourse with a male animal, whether it penetrates her vaginally or anally, is *chayav*. No distinction is drawn between the modes of penetration in either case.

### Rav Nachman

At the opening of *amud aleph*, *Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda* offers an *explication*: *be'ishah shnei mishkavot u've-vehemah mishkav echad*—by a woman there are two *mishkavot*, vaginal and anal, as derived from the term *mishkevei ishah*, but by an animal there is only one, since the Torah does not use the plural *mishkevei* in the context of an animal. On this reading, when a man penetrates a female animal, the prohibition applies only to vaginal intercourse. The *baraita* that treated both modes as equivalent is thereby challenged.

### Rav Pappa

*Rav Pappa* presses back: one could argue the exact opposite. *Ishah de'orchah hi mishkav mechayev, amida achrina lo mechayev*—for a woman, since intercourse is the natural and expected form of sexual activity, one might reason that only the natural mode (vaginal) makes one liable, not the alternative (anal). But *be-vehemah delav orchah hi*—since intercourse with an animal is in no sense a natural act, the Torah's prohibition could be said to extend to every orifice regardless, since no particular mode is more "natural" than another. He acknowledges the slight tension in this reasoning—penetration of a woman by an animal is also not natural—but the challenge stands: the absence of the plural *mishkevei* by an animal does not necessarily restrict the prohibition; it might expand it.

### Tanya - No Chiyuv

A *baraita* is then cited—in some versions with the notation *tanya d'lo kevateivhu*, that this *baraita* sides with neither position: *zachar ben tesha shanim v'yom echad*, and then, *haba b'vehemah bein kedarka bein shelo kedarka v'ishah ha-mevi'ah behemah aleha bein kedarka bein shelo kedarka, chayav*. The *baraita* makes no distinction whatsoever in the bestiality cases—neither in the case of a man penetrating a female animal nor in the case of a male animal penetrating a woman—between vaginal and anal intercourse. Both modes are equally prohibited and equally carry liability.

---

## Me'arah Definition

### Me'arah Bevirah

*Ravina* poses a question to *Rava*: *ha-me'areh be-zachar mahu?* In a heterosexual context, the legally operative moment of intercourse is *me'arah*—initial penetration, when the tip of the penis enters the vagina. A prior stage, *neshikah*, involves contact without entry and is not legally sufficient; and *gmar bi'ah* is full penetration. The question is whether this same threshold of *me'arah* applies to *mishkav zachar*.

### Mishkevei Ishah

The *Gemara* responds almost dismissively: *mishkevei ishah ketiv bah*—the Torah itself defines the act of male-on-male intercourse through the language of "the lyings of a woman." Since the prohibition is explicitly framed by reference to heterosexual intercourse, including its anal variant, the same definition of intercourse—*me'arah*, initial penetration—carries over. What is notable, and conceptually significant, is that the *Gemara* does not reach this conclusion by appeal to a general *hekesh* linking all *arayot* to one another. The *arayot* framework does not automatically encompass *mishkav zachar*; rather, it is specifically the phrase *mishkevei ishah* that does the work of importing the standard definition of intercourse into this case.

### Me'arah Behema

The next question is whether *me'arah* also defines intercourse in the context of bestiality. *Amar lei*—the *Gemara* answers through the interpretive principle of *im eino inyan*. In *Vayikra*, the word *he'erah*—"he uncovered her source"—appears in two places in the context of *arayot*: once regarding a *niddah*, and once regarding an aunt (*achot aviv* or *achot imo*). From the *niddah* passage, we derive the definition of *me'arah* for all *arayot*, since all forbidden sexual relationships are linked to one another through a *hekesh*. Given that derivation, why does the Torah need to repeat *he'erah* in the context of an aunt? Since the verse about the aunt is redundant for the standard *arayot* application, the principle of *im eino inyan* directs us to apply it elsewhere—specifically to bestiality, a case not linked by *hekesh* to the other *arayot* and not covered by *mishkevei ishah* as *mishkav zachar* was. Thus, *me'arah* governs the act of intercourse in bestiality as well.

### Why Aunt

One might ask: if the Torah wanted to use this extra mention of *he'erah* to teach us about bestiality, why did it place it in the context of an aunt, a case of *chayvei keritot*, rather than in a case of *chayvei mitot beit din*, which would be a more natural extension to bestiality (itself a capital offense)? The *Gemara* answers: *ho'il ve'chulei kra le-drasha hu de'ata*—the entire verse concerning *achot av* and *achot em* is already replete with *drashot*. As we will see in *Yevamot*, the prohibition appears in *Acharei Mot* and the punishment in *Kedoshim*, and the verse in *Kedoshim* is in any case largely extra, making it a rich source for multiple *derashot*. Since the verse is packed with exegetical content, it accommodates one more—the extension of *me'arah* to the case of bestiality. The result is that the same definition of intercourse, *me'arah*, applies equally to heterosexual *arayot*, to *mishkav zachar*, and to bestiality.

---

## Self-Penetration

### Ha-Me'arah Be-Atzmo

*Rav Achdivoi bar Ami* poses to *Rav Sheshet* a question that the *Gemara* itself treats as bizarre: *ha-me'areh be-atzmo mahu?* If a man has an exceptionally long penis and is physically capable of bending it to insert it into his own anus, is he *chayav* for *mishkav zachar*? The underlying assumption of the question—that an act of intercourse might be committed by a single person against himself—is startling, since one would naturally expect that *mishkav zachar* requires two parties. *Rav Sheshet*'s response, *kabastan*, conveys something like "you are troubling me with an absurd question."

### Meshamesh Meit

*Rav Ashi* engages the question more analytically. *Bekoshi lo mishkachat la*—in any case where the man actually has an erection, this act is physically impossible. *Ki mishkachat la bi-mshamesh meit*—the only scenario in which it could occur is if the penis is non-erect, a state called *meshamesh meit*. The answer then follows from an existing dispute: *le-man d'amar meshamesh meit ba-arayot patur*, if one holds that intercourse with a non-erect penis is exempt in the context of *arayot*, then here too the man would be exempt. But *le-man d'amar chayav*, if one holds that even *meshamesh meit* constitutes cognizable intercourse, then *hacha nechayev tartei*—he would be liable twice: once as the *shochev* and once as the *nishkav*.

This conclusion is, as the *Gemara* presents it, quite striking. The more intuitive response would be that an act of intercourse is categorically defined as occurring between two parties, and that a person cannot constitute both simultaneously. The *Gemara* passes over that objection entirely, resolving the case instead on the axis of *meshamesh meit*. One is reminded of a well-known *Rosh Yeshiva* story in which students debate whether an *androginos* could betroth himself—after an elaborate discussion, the answer given is simply that he cannot because she is his sister. The punch line cuts through the wrong analytical frame entirely. Here too, the *Gemara*'s answer operates on a different axis than one might expect, and the result—double liability for self-penetration—remains genuinely difficult.

---

## Non-Jew & Animal

### Takala v. Kalon

The sugya now shifts focus from the liability of the person engaged in bestiality to the legal status of the animal itself. The *Mishnah* (on daf 58a) records that an animal involved in a capital sexual offense is stoned, and provides two explanations. The first: *im adam chata behemah be-mah chat'ah? ella le-fi she-ba l'adam takalah al yadah*—if a man sinned, what did the animal sin? Rather, because the animal caused the man to stumble, it is stoned. The second (*davar acher*): *shelo te-hei overet ba-shuk ve-yomru zu hi she-niskal ploni al yadah*—so that the animal should not be walking through the marketplace and people say, "This is the animal on account of which so-and-so was stoned." The first reason is *takalah*—the animal was a stumbling block to sin; the second is *kalon*—public shame and embarrassment.

With this background, *Rav Sheshet* is asked: if a non-Jew (*oved kochavim*) has intercourse with an animal that is subject to Jewish jurisdiction, what is done with the animal? The question is whether both *takalah* and *kalon* are required to trigger the stoning of the animal. *V'hacha takalah ika kalon leika*—there is clearly *takalah*, since bestiality is one of the seven *mitzvot benei Noach*, but there may be no *kalon*. *Rashi* offers two explanations for why shame may be absent: either because such conduct is, sadly, less aberrant among non-Jews and therefore less socially scandalous, or, less pejoratively, because the Torah's concern for protecting a person's honor extends only to Jews, not to non-Jews. The question therefore is: does *takalah* alone suffice, or must both elements be present?

### Rav Sheshet

*Rav Sheshet* responds: *tanituah*—the answer is taught in a *baraita*. The *baraita* concerns the obligation to destroy trees used as *asherot* (idolatrous trees). *Ma ilanos she-ein ochlim ve-ein shotim ve-ein merichim*—these trees do not eat, drink, or smell. Yet the Torah commands: *hashcheit srof ve-chaleh*—destroy, burn, and eliminate them, because *ba'u al yadam takalah*—they caused people to sin and served as the object of sin. *Kal va-chomer*, the *baraita* continues, one who actively causes another person to stray from the path of life to the path of destruction is certainly deserving of destruction. The operative logic is that *takalah* alone—having been the object through which a sin was committed—suffices as grounds for destruction. If it suffices for the *asherot*, it should suffice for the animal of a non-Jew as well.

### Ela Me'ata

The *Gemara* challenges this reasoning immediately: *ela me'ata*, if *takalah* alone is truly sufficient, then *oved kochavim ha-mishtachaveh le-vehemto titasar maktala?*—if a non-Jew bows down to his own animal in an act of *avodah zarah*, should that animal not also become forbidden and subject to death? The same logic of *takalah* would seem to apply. But this conclusion is untenable, because *de-Yisrael lo asur oved kochavim asur?*—it cannot be that the law is stricter for a non-Jew than for a Jew. In the case of a Jew who bows down to an animal, the animal does not thereby become forbidden or subject to stoning. It would be incoherent to rule that a non-Jew's act of worship does the same. Moreover, even setting aside the Jewish-non-Jewish comparison, there is a broader problem: if *takalah* from *avodah zarah* genuinely drives the logic behind destroying the *asherot*, one would expect the same reasoning to apply to a Jew's animal that was worshipped—and it does not. The *Gemara* thus concludes that something about this *avodah zarah* framework is out of sync with the *takalah* logic, and the derivation from *asherot* cannot stand as stated.

### Abaye - Shame

*Abaye* offers a resolution. *Ze klono meruba ve-ze klono mu'at*—there is a meaningful difference in the degree of shame involved. Intercourse with an animal (*bi'ah*) involves an extreme degree of degradation and shame; bowing down to an animal (*hishtachavayah*) does not carry the same level of disgrace. This is why, in the case of a Jew, we stone the animal for bestiality but not for *avodah zarah*—the threshold for killing a living animal is high, and that threshold is reached only when the act carries a particularly severe *kalon*.

One might then object: what of the *asherot*, which are destroyed even though bowing down to them is not as shameful as bestiality, and they are certainly not living? *Abaye* responds: *beva'alei chayim ka'aminan, dechas Rachmana aleihu*—we are speaking of living animals, and the Torah has particular compassion for them. Destroy inanimate objects of *avodah zarah*, yes, but to kill a living animal requires a much higher threshold. That threshold, for *Abaye*, is an elevated degree of shame—which is present in bestiality but not in *avodah zarah* contexts. As to how *Abaye*'s framework applies to the question about the non-Jew, *Rashi* preserves two possibilities: either shame is indeed required and is absent in the non-Jew's case (so the animal would not be stoned), or shame is present even in that case. *Abaye*'s primary contribution is to explain the existing evidence—why bestiality triggers stoning of the animal while *avodah zarah* does not—before the non-Jewish case is even resolved.

### Rava - Benefit

*Rava* offers an alternative explanation. *Amar Torah: behemah nehenis me'aveirah, tehareig*—the Torah's principle is that an animal that derived benefit or pleasure from the sinful act is executed. In the case of bestiality, the animal is regarded as an active and benefiting participant in the act; in the case of *avodah zarah*, the animal is merely an object of worship and derives no such benefit. By contrast, *va-harei ilanos de-ein nehenin me-aveirah*—but the trees of *asherot* did not benefit from the act either, yet they are destroyed. *Rava* gives the same answer as *Abaye* on this point: *beva'alei chayim kamina, dechas Rachmana aleihu*—we are discussing living creatures, for whom the Torah maintains a higher threshold. Trees do not implicate that threshold. For *Rava*, the operative distinction between bestiality and *avodah zarah* in the case of living animals is the animal's benefit or pleasure rather than the degree of shame. Applying this to the non-Jew: since the animal still derived benefit from the act regardless of the nationality of the human party, *Rava*'s logic would presumably lead to stoning the animal even in the case of the non-Jew—*takalah* plus the animal's benefit together suffice.

---

## Mishnah Reasons

### Seifa - Public

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Mishnah* itself to try to resolve the open question. The second reason given in the *Mishnah*—*davar acher: shelo te-hei behemah overet ba-shuk ve-yomru zu hi she-niskal ploni al yadah*—mentions that the animal caused someone to be stoned (*niskal al yadah*). The *Gemara* reads this second formulation as indicating both elements: the public shaming (*kalon*) of the animal walking through the marketplace, and the *takalah*, since the mention of *niskal al yadah* evokes the stumbling that brought about capital punishment. So the *seifa* encodes both *takalah* and *kalon*.

### Reisha - Takala

With the *seifa* carrying both elements, attention turns to the *reisha*—the first reason: *im adam chata behemah be-mah chat'ah? ella le-fi she-ba l'adam takalah al yadah*—"because a stumbling came about through it." *Mai lav*—is it not the case that since the *seifa* has both *takalah* and *kalon*, the *reisha* must be referring to just one of the two? And specifically, might the *reisha*'s mention of *takalah* be read not as a stumbling-block-to-sin but as a stumbling of shame—conveying that *kalon* alone suffices? If so, the case of a Jew who committed bestiality *be-shogeg* (without awareness that it was forbidden) would be a case of *kalon* without *takalah*, and the animal would still be stoned.

Alternatively, reading the *reisha* straightforwardly—*takalah* means a stumbling-block to sin—it would indicate that *takalah* alone suffices, and the applicable scenario would be the case of a non-Jew with an animal: *takalah* without *kalon*.

### Ketana Mezida

To test this, *Rav Yosef* introduces a famous *Mishnah* from *Niddah* enumerating the halachic ramifications of a girl who is three years and one day old. *Bas shalosh shanim ve-yom echad miskadeshes be-vi'ah*—if a girl of this age has intercourse (arranged by her father as the act of *kiddushin*), it is legally cognizable intercourse and she is halachically betrothed. *Ve-im ba aleha yabam kena'ah*—if the girl had been married and her husband died childless, and the *yabam* (the brother-in-law) performs *yibum* with her at this age, the act of *yibum* is legally effective and she becomes his wife. *Ve-chayavin aleha mishum eshet ish*—and any man who subsequently has intercourse with her is guilty of adultery, since she is a fully married woman.

The *Mishnah* continues: *u-metame et bo'alah le-tame mishkav tachton ke-elyon*—she renders the man who has intercourse with her *tamei* in the manner of a *niddah*. If she is a *niddah* and this man has intercourse with her, he becomes an *av ha-tumah*: anything he subsequently sits upon, even if ten cushions are stacked beneath him, each one has the status of a *mishkav*—though, because he himself is a *bo'el niddah* rather than a *niddah* herself, those cushions become a *rishon* rather than an *av*.

*Niset le-kohen, ochelet be-trumah*—if she is married to a *kohen*, she may eat *terumah*. Normally, by rabbinic law, a *kohen*'s wife eats *terumah* only after actual *nisuin* (cohabitation); and *nisuin* is considered to have occurred only when the couple is in a context where intercourse is possible. Once she is three years and a day, the marriage is understood to be a fully cohabitating marriage and she may eat *terumah*.

*Ba aleha echad min ha-psulim, pasla min ha-kehunah*—if a *pasul* (an invalid person, such as a *mamzer* or *chalal*) has intercourse with her, she is rendered invalid (*chalalah*), disqualified from marrying a *kohen*. And: *ve-im ba aleha echad mi-kol ha-arayot ha-amurot ba-Torah, mumatin al yadah, ve-hi peturah*—if any person in a forbidden *arayot* relationship has intercourse with her, that adult is executed; she, being a minor, is exempt.

The *Gemara* notes: *achat mi-kol ha-arayot, ve-afilu behemah*—presumably including an animal that had intercourse with her. The animal would be stoned. And *v'hacha kalon ika, takalah leika*—there is shame in the act, but the girl, as a minor, is not considered to have sinned in a legally meaningful sense, so there is no *takalah*. And yet the animal is stoned. This seems to prove that *kalon* alone suffices.

### Keivan Dezid

The *Gemara* rejects this inference: *keivan de-mezidah hi, takalah nami ika, ve-Rachmana hu de-chas alah*. Even a three-year-old minor, if she willfully engages in this act—however qualified "willful" must be for a child of that age—is considered to have sinned, even if she is exempt from punishment. The Torah had compassion on her (*chas aleha*) and exempted her from the penalty, but she was not entirely outside the category of sin. By contrast, the animal is not spared: *a-behemah lo chas*—the Torah's compassion did not extend to it. The *takalah* is therefore still present—the minor willfully caused or participated in a sinful act, and the animal was the instrument of that sin.

This is a striking position. One might have expected that an adult acting *be-shogeg*—without awareness that the act is forbidden—would constitute a lesser *takalah* than a willful act, even one performed by a minor who is technically exempt. The *Gemara* is asserting the opposite: willful sin that carries an exemption due to minority status still constitutes *takalah*, whereas *shogeg* by an adult—lacking the element of willfulness—does not rise to the same level of *takalah*. This is counterintuitive but is the *Gemara*'s position.

### Ben Tesha Shanim

*Rava* attempts the same inference from the parallel case of the nine-year-and-one-day-old boy. *Ben tesha shanim ve-yom echad ha-ba al yivimto kena'ah*—a boy of this age performing *yibum* effectuates the levirate marriage, even though *mi-de-oraita* this may only be *de-rabbanan*. *Ve-eino noten get ad she-yagdil*—he cannot give a *get* until he becomes an adult. *U-metamei k'niddah le-tamei mishkav tachton ke-elyon*—if he has intercourse with a *niddah*, he becomes an *av ha-tumah* and renders the cushions beneath him a *mishkav*, though at the level of *rishon*. *Posel ve-eino ma'achil*—if he is *pasul* (a *mamzer* or similar) and has intercourse with a woman, he disqualifies her, but if he is a *kohen* and has not yet reached the age of full intercourse, his wife cannot eat *terumah* since they are not yet in a state of *nisuin*. *U-posel et ha-behemah me-al gabei ha-mizbe'ach*—if he has intercourse with an animal, it cannot be brought as a *korban*, even if there are insufficient witnesses to stone it; ownership or a single witness admitting to the act would disqualify it from the altar.

*Ve-nisqelet al yado*—and the animal is stoned. Here the case is explicit: a nine-year-and-one-day-old boy has intercourse with an animal, and the animal is stoned. The same inference is drawn: *kalon ika, takalah leika*—there is shame, but he is a minor. Yet the animal is stoned. Does this not prove *kalon* alone suffices?

The *Gemara* gives the same answer: *keivan de-mezid hu, takalah nami ika, ve-Rachmana hu de-chasi aleih, aleih dideih chas, a-behemah lo chas*—since he acted willfully, there is *takalah*; the Torah exempted him from punishment as a minor, not the animal. We cannot prove that *kalon* alone is sufficient.

### Final Distinction

One final attempt is made by returning to the *Mishnah*'s *davar acher*: *shelo te-hei behemah overet ba-shuk ve-yomru zu hi she-niskal ploni al yadah*. If the *seifa* contains both *takalah* and *kalon*, perhaps the *reisha*—the first reason, which mentions only that a *takalah* came about through the animal—should be read as demonstrating that *kalon* without *takalah* suffices, specifically as a reference to the case of a Jew who committed bestiality *be-shogeg*: shame is present, but genuine *takalah* is not.

The *Gemara* counters: no, read the *reisha* straightforwardly—it demonstrates that *takalah* without *kalon* suffices, exemplified by the case of a non-Jew (*oved kochavim*) with an animal, exactly as *Rav Sheshet* originally inquired. The *Mishnah*'s first and second reasons can each stand alone. The *seifa* encodes both; the *reisha* shows that one suffices—but we cannot determine from the *Mishnah* alone which one, since the *reisha* is naturally read as pure *takalah* and the inference of *kalon* alone from it is forced. The *Gemara* leaves us here: both the case of the non-Jew with an animal (*takalah* without *kalon*) and the case of the Jew acting *be-shogeg* (*kalon* without *takalah*) remain unresolved as to whether they independently trigger the stoning of the animal.

---

---

# Sanhedrin 56

## Blasphemy & God's Name

### Intro to Blasphemy

The daf opens at the very end of 55b, transitioning from the category of sexual sins to sins relating to God directly. The Mishnah states: *hamigadef eino chayav ad sheyifareish hashem* — one who blasphemes God is not liable unless he explicitly articulates God's name. The immediate question is what "explicitly" means: does it require pronouncing the four-letter name, *yud-kei-vav-kei*, or does using one of the other divine names — such as *Elohim* — also suffice? The Gemara will address this in full.

### Kinuy in Examination

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha teaches that throughout the proceedings, the witnesses are cross-examined using a *kinuy* — which here, as Rashi explains at length, does not mean an alternative divine name but rather a substitution in which the content of the curse is expressed with reference to someone else entirely. The witnesses would say *yakeh Yose et Yose* — "May Yose smite Yose." Rashi notes that the name *Yose* is four letters, shares the letters *yud* and *vav* with the divine name, and even shares the *gematria* of *Elohim*, making it a transparent but formally safe stand-in. The point is that the witnesses demonstrate what they heard without themselves uttering an actual curse of God.

### Witness Procedure

When the final judgment arrives — *nigmar hadin* — indirect testimony is no longer sufficient. You cannot condemn someone to death on the basis of inference; direct testimony is required. The court therefore clears the room of everyone except the judges and the witnesses, since exposing others unnecessarily to the words of such a curse would be disrespectful. The senior witness is then asked to state explicitly what he heard — *emor mah sheshamata beferush*. When he does so, the judges rise to their feet, tear their garments, and do not sew them up, because hearing a curse of God's name — even when recounted by a witness with no blasphemous intent — obligates *keriah*. The second and third witnesses then each say *af ani kamohu*, "I too heard the same," rather than repeating the words themselves. The procedure thus limits repetition of the curse to the absolute minimum required for a capital verdict.

### Nokev Shem Source

A *braitah* states that liability requires *ad sheyivarech shem beshem* — the blasphemer must curse God *with* God's name, making God both subject and object of the imprecation. The Gemara asks: what is the scriptural source for this requirement? Shmuel derives it from the verse in Parashat Emor: *venokev shem Hashem mot yumat* — "one who *nokev* the name of God shall be put to death" — which then concludes *benokvo shem yumat*, "in his *nokev*-ing of the Name he shall die." The repetition of *shem* — name upon name — establishes the principle of *shem beshem*. The punishment is stoning, as derived from *ragom yirgemu bo kol ha'edah*. The prohibition (*azhara*) is from *elohim lo tekallel*, "do not curse God." As for knowing that *nokev* means to curse, the proof is from Bilaam's rhetorical question: *mah ekov lo kaboh El* — "how shall I curse what God has not cursed?" — where the root *kuf-bet-heh* unambiguously means cursing.

---

## Nokev Debate

### Pierce vs. Curse

The Gemara does not accept the identification of *nokev* with cursing without first exploring alternatives. The first alternative: *v'eima mivraz hu* — perhaps *nokev* means to pierce or puncture, as in *vayikov chor be-dalto*, "he pierced a hole in his door." On this reading, the offense would consist of physically destroying a written form of God's name. The *azhara* would then come from *lo ta'asun kein la'Hashem Eloheichem* — "you shall not do thus to the Lord your God" — the verse from which we derive the prohibition against erasing divine names, the foundation of all the laws of *sheimos*. Could destroying something bearing God's name be capital?

The Gemara responds: *ba'ina shem beshem ve-leika* — we require the structure of God's name acting upon God's name, and that structure is absent from this reading. The Gemara entertains a creative counter: perhaps one places two pieces of parchment inscribed with God's name on top of each other and pierces through both — that would be God's name piercing God's name. The Gemara rejects this: *hu nokev ve-chozer ve-nokev hu* — that is simply piercing God's name twice in succession; it is not using one instance of God's name as the agent to pierce another.

### Shem B'Shem Logic

The Gemara proposes a second scenario: carve God's name onto the edge of a knife and then use that knife to cut through a parchment bearing God's name. Now God's name is the instrument piercing God's name. The Gemara again rejects it: *hahu churpa de-sakina hu de-ka baza* — it is the sharpness of the knife that does the cutting, not the name engraved on it. The name merely happens to be present on the knife; it is not the operative agent. This stands in contrast to the verbal case of cursing, where one actually invokes God as the subject — calling upon God to act against God. The non-verbal scenarios cannot replicate this structure.

A closely related question presents itself at this point: if the prohibition is formulated verbally, does writing a blasphemous curse count? Normally the question of whether writing is equivalent to speech — *hirhur ke-dibbur* — is disputed. Here, the formulation *be-nokvo shem*, with its emphasis on articulation, suggests intuitively that one would have to actually utter the words; writing alone would likely not suffice. This remains an open question worth investigation.

### Articulation Issue

A third alternative: perhaps *nokev* means simply to articulate, as in *asher nikvu be-shemot* — "those who were mentioned by name" in the census narrative. On this reading, the sin would be pronouncing God's explicit name — *yud-kei-vav-kei* as it is spelled — which would normally only be done by the *kohen* in the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *azhara* would come from *et Hashem Elohecha tira* — you shall fear the Lord your God — with certain licensed contexts being exceptions.

The Gemara offers two objections. First, *ba'ina shem beshem ve-leika*: articulating God's name cannot satisfy the *shem beshem* requirement, since there is no way to have God's name function as both subject and object in a verbal act. Second — and this is where the Gemara's legal reasoning becomes particularly striking — *ve-od haveya azharat asei, ve-azharat asei lo shema azhara*: fearing God is a positive commandment, not a prohibition. A positive commandment cannot serve as the required *azhara* for a capital offense. This reflects a fundamental principle: *ein onshin ela im ken mazhirin* — punishment presupposes a prohibition. The legal logic here deserves attention. The Rabbis understood the entire framework of divine punishment as requiring a genuine act of transgression against an explicit prohibition. A positive commandment — something one is obligated to do — describes a failure of omission; the death penalty requires a violation of a *lav*, an active commission of a forbidden act. When the Gemara cannot find a negative prohibition for the "articulation" interpretation, that itself becomes proof that *nokev* cannot mean articulation.

One might note, as raised in this context, that *elohim lo tekallel* — the *azhara* for cursing — is sometimes read as a prohibition against cursing judges. This is a valid reading: *elohim* in Scripture frequently denotes judges. If the verse is used for cursing God, what happens to cursing a judge? The answer involves the principle that a *lav she-nitan le-azharat misat beit din* — a prohibition used to ground a capital offense — cannot simultaneously serve as the *azhara* for another offense that would otherwise yield lashes. So someone who curses a judge would not receive *malkut* through that verse.

### Nokev = Curse

With both alternative readings eliminated, the Gemara turns to the narrative context to confirm that *nokev* means to curse. The verse describing the incident that prompted this entire legislation reads: *vayikov et ha-shem vayikallel* — "he *nokev*-ed the name and he cursed." One might read this as two distinct acts: articulating God's name and separately cursing. The Gemara considers this possibility — *de-dilma ad d'avid tarvaihu*, perhaps both acts together constitute the offense. But the Gemara refutes this from the verdict: the Torah instructs, *hotzei et ha-mekallel* — "take out the one who cursed" — not *hotzei et ha-nokev*, and certainly not *hotzei et ha-nokev ve-ha-mekallel*. The verdict language refers solely to the *mekallel*, the curser. This demonstrates that *nokev* is not a second distinct act but a synonym for the act of cursing — more precisely, *shema mina chada hi*, they are one and the same thing. The *peshat* of the verse supports this: *nokev* here means to curse, and specifically to curse using God's explicit name — the act of articulating God's name in the context of a malediction.

---

## Explicit vs. Kinuy

### Two Clauses

Having established the meaning of *nokev*, the Gemara turns to the full structure of the verse: *ish ish ki yekallel elohav ve-nasa cheto — ve-nokev shem Hashem mot yumat*. The text presents what appears to be two distinct clauses with two distinct consequences. The first clause — *yekallel elohav*, "he curses his God" — carries the consequence *ve-nasa cheto*, he bears his sin, which the Gemara understands as *karet* without court-administered punishment. The second clause — *ve-nokev shem Hashem* — carries *mot yumat*, death by the court. The straightforward reading is that the first clause refers to cursing with a *kinuy*, an alternative divine name like *Elohim*, without using the four-letter name and without the *shem beshem* structure, while the second clause refers to cursing with God's explicit name in the full *shem beshem* formulation.

The *braitah* articulates the question explicitly: since we already know from *ve-nokev shem Hashem mot yumat* that cursing God with the explicit name incurs death, what is the purpose of *ki yekallel elohav*? The answer initially proposed is that *ki yekallel elohav* comes to include *kinuyim* — alternative divine names — within the scope of the prohibition.

### Rabbi Meir View

Rabbi Meir reads the verse expansively. The *braitah* records his position: *yachol lo yehei chayav ela al shem ha-meyuchad bilvad* — one might think that liability extends only to the explicit name; *minayin le-rabot kol ha-kinuyim? Talmud lomar: ish ki yekallel elohav mikol makom* — the verse *ki yekallel elohav* comes to include all *kinuyim*, in all cases. For Rabbi Meir, both clauses carry the death penalty. The consequence of *ve-nasa cheto* — he bears his sin — does not mean the offense is downgraded to *karet*; it means that when there are no witnesses and no warning, the offender bears his sin through divine punishment rather than court-administered death. But the act of cursing with a *kinuy* is capital in principle. This is a striking position.

### Sages View

The Sages (*chachamim*) read the two clauses as marking a genuine legal distinction: *al shem ha-meyuchad be-mita ve-al ha-kinuyim be-azhara* — using God's explicit name incurs the death penalty, while using a *kinuy* carries only the prohibition and its consequence of *karet* but not court-administered execution. This is the more straightforward reading: the verse itself presents two different formulations with two different legal consequences.

---

## Non-Jews & Blasphemy

### Ish Ish Non-Jews

The verse opens with the doubled phrase *ish ish* — "any man, any man" — which the *braitah* derives as coming *le-rabot et ha-ovdei kochavim she-muzharim al birkat hashem*: to include non-Jews, who are among those warned against blaspheming God, and who in fact carry this prohibition as one of the seven *mitzvot* of *bnei Noach*. The natural question: but isn't the source for the non-Jewish prohibition against blasphemy already derived from the verse *vayitzav Hashem Elokim al ha-adam*, which will shortly be established as the root of all seven *mitzvot*? Why is *ish ish* needed?

Rav Yitzchak Napcha answers: the *ish ish* is not needed to establish the prohibition for non-Jews as such — that is already known — but rather *le-rabot ha-kinuyim*, to include *kinuyim*, specifically *aliba de-Rabbi Meir*. That is: according to Rabbi Meir's view that cursing with a *kinuy* is a capital offense, *ish ish* extends that ruling to non-Jews. For Rabbi Meir, the placement of non-Jews within this verse means non-Jews are prohibited even when using a *kinuy*. For the Sages, the question of whether non-Jews are held to the same distinction as Jews — explicit name yielding capital punishment, *kinuy* yielding *karet* — will be explored in the view of Rav Manashia.

### Kigar Ka'Ezrach

The verse continues: *kager ka'ezrach be-nokvo shem yumat* — "like the stranger, like the native citizen, in his *nokev*-ing of the Name he shall die." Rabbi Meir uses this phrase differently from the Sages. Since for Rabbi Meir the entire verse already equalizes Jews and non-Jews in the scope of liability — *ish ish* having placed non-Jews fully within the prohibition including for *kinuyim* — the phrase *kager ka'ezrach* does not serve to create a distinction in liability. Instead, it distinguishes the *mode* of execution: *ger ve-ezrach be-skila, aval oved kochavim be-sayif* — Jews are executed by stoning, non-Jews by the sword. The principle that all capital offenses for *bnei Noach* are carried out by the sword is established elsewhere, but this verse clarifies that even though *ish ish* places non-Jews within the category of this offense, they do not thereby assume the Jewish punishment of stoning. The verse's parallel formulation might have suggested *hoa'il ve-israbu israbu* — since they are included, include them entirely — but *kager ka'ezrach* forestalls this by restricting stoning to the *ger* and *ezrach*.

### Napcha Non-Jew View

Rav Manashia argues that the debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding Jews does not apply symmetrically to non-Jews. Even according to the Sages — who hold that a Jew cursing with a *kinuy* incurs only *karet* and not the death penalty — a non-Jew cursing with a *kinuy* is liable to death. The source: *de-amar kra kager ka'ezrach* — the verse *kager ka'ezrach* establishes that the full legal distinction between *kinuy* and explicit name, with *kinuy* carrying only *karet*, applies to the *ger* and the *ezrach*, meaning those subject to the Jewish legal framework. For non-Jews, that distinction does not apply, and even a *kinuy* suffices for liability.

The Gemara then asks: if, according to this view, the distinction between *kinuy* and explicit name holds equally for Jews and non-Jews, what does *kager ka'ezrach* add for Rav Yitzchak Napcha? His answer: *ger ve-ezrach hu de-ba'inan shem beshem, aval oved kochavim lo ba'inan shem beshem* — it is for the Jew that the *shem beshem* structure is required; for the non-Jew, while the explicit name is necessary, the full double structure — God's name as both subject and object of the curse — is not required. This is a precise and somewhat technical distinction: a non-Jew who curses God using God's name is liable even without invoking God as the agent of the curse.

The Gemara further asks why *ish ish* is needed at all in Rav Yitzchak Napcha's scheme, given that the non-Jewish obligation is already derivable and the distinctions are already clear. The answer: *dibra Torah ke-lishon bnei adam* — the Torah speaks in ordinary human language, and the doubled *ish ish* is simply the stylistic form of an inclusive statement rather than a technical derivation. The practical upshot of all the positions can be summarized: for a Jew, *shem beshem* is required, and whether a *kinuy* alone triggers capital punishment or merely *karet* is debated between Rabbi Meir and the Sages. For a non-Jew, stoning is replaced by the sword, *shem beshem* is not required, and according to Rav Manashia even the Sages would agree that a *kinuy* suffices for liability. Whether Rabbi Meir's view about *kinuyim* applies symmetrically to non-Jews, or whether *ish ish* places them in the full scope of Rabbi Meir's position including *shem beshem*, remains a point within the discussion.

---

## Sheva Mitzvot Intro

### Seven List

Having discussed the prohibition against blasphemy in the context of non-Jews, and having mentioned that it is one of the seven *mitzvot* of *bnei Noach*, the Gemara now opens the extended treatment of those seven commandments. A *braitah* states: *sheva mitzvot nistavu bnei Noach* — the *bnei Noach* were commanded in seven *mitzvot*: *dinim* (a legal system), *birkat Hashem* (prohibition against cursing God), *avodah zarah* (idolatry), *giluy arayot* (sexual immorality), *shefichut damim* (murder), *gezel* (theft), and *eiver min ha-chai* (eating a limb torn from a living animal). A useful mnemonic for the seven: the three major categories — *avodah zarah*, *giluy arayot*, and *shefichut damim* — are the "big three," and the remaining four follow the acronym *alef-bet-gimel-dalet*: *eiver min ha-chai*, *birkat Hashem*, *gezel*, and *dinim*.

### Additional Opinions

Beyond the standard seven, additional opinions expand the list. Rabbi Chananya ben Gamla adds blood from a living animal — *dam* in addition to *eiver min ha-chai*. Rabbi Chidkya adds *sirus* — emasculation or sterilization, applicable to both animals and people. Rabbi Shimon adds *kishuf* — witchcraft. Rabbi Yossi elaborates on Rabbi Shimon's position: everything enumerated in the Torah's passage on witchcraft in Deuteronomy (*lo yimatzei becha ma'avir beno u-vito ba-esh, kosem kesamim, me'onen u-menachesh u-mechashef, ve-chover chaver, ve-sho'el ov ve-yidoni, ve-doresh el ha-metim*) is prohibited to a *ben Noach*. The reasoning is that the Torah states these abominations caused God to drive the nations from the land — and the principle *lo anash ha-katuv ela im ken hizhir* demands that punishment presupposes warning. If God punished the nations for witchcraft, they must have been warned against it through their own seven commandments. Rabbi Eliezer adds *kilayim* — crossbreeding of animals and grafting of trees (though planting mixed seeds is permitted to non-Jews).

The rationale for including *sirus* and *kilayim* in the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach* — even without explicit scriptural derivation — is worth considering. The human being was commanded *pru u-revu*, to be fruitful and multiply, from the very earliest chapters of Genesis; *sirus* directly frustrates this imperative. And the Torah's account of creation repeatedly emphasizes *le-minehu* — each creature reproducing according to its kind — which *kilayim* violates. These prohibitions thus connect to the fundamental structure of creation as God designed it: living things are to multiply and to do so true to their nature. As for *kishuf*, it too can be understood as related to *avodah zarah* or alternatively as a violation of the natural order.

### Vayitzav Source

The Gemara asks: *mena hani mili* — what is the scriptural basis for all seven? Rabbi Yochanan derives them from a single verse: *vayitzav Hashem Elokim al ha-adam lemor, mikol etz ha-gan achol tochel* — "and the Lord God commanded the human, saying: of every tree of the garden you may freely eat." This is a remarkable piece of hermeneutics. From a verse that on its plain reading grants permission to eat, the Rabbis extract all seven universal commandments. The method: each word of the verse is made to correspond to one of the seven, as will be detailed in the following section.

---

## Exegesis Details

### Dinim Courts

*Vayitzav* — "and He commanded" — corresponds to *dinim*, the legal system. A supporting verse: God says of Abraham *ki yedativ lemaan asher yitzaveh et banav ve-et beito ve-shamru derech Hashem la'asot tzedakah u-mishpat* — "I have known him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they will keep the way of the Lord, doing righteousness and justice." The combination of *vayitzav* with *tzedakah u-mishpat* points to the substantive content of a just legal order. This connection will bear on the later question of whether *dinim* means merely a court system or a full body of civil law.

### Birkat Hashem

*Hashem* — the divine name — corresponds to *birkat Hashem*, the prohibition against cursing God. The supporting verse is the one just analyzed: *ve-nokev shem Hashem mot yumat*.

### Avodah Zarah

*Elokim* — the word for God used in creation — corresponds to *avodah zarah*, idolatry. The supporting verse: *lo yihyeh lecha elohim acherim al panai*.

### Shfichut Damim

*Al ha-adam* — "concerning the human" — corresponds to *shefichut damim*, murder. This is the most explicit of the seven, grounded in the verse spoken directly to Noah: *shofech dam ha-adam ba-adam damo yishapech* — "one who sheds the blood of a human, by a human shall his blood be shed."

### Giluy Arayot

*Lemor* — "saying" — corresponds to *giluy arayot*, forbidden sexual relations. The supporting verse is from the prophets: *lemor, hein yishalach ish et ishto ve-halcha me-ito ve-haysah le-ish acher* — if a man sends away his wife and she goes and becomes another man's, she may not return to the first. This is admittedly a slender textual link; any verse containing *lemor* would serve equally well. The choice of *lemor* for *giluy arayot* is likely deliberate. Of the seven, certain categories of *giluy arayot* — a brother's wife after his death, a son-in-law's wife after divorce — may appear more arbitrary than others, less transparently derivable from natural intuition. The word *lemor*, with its connotation of "because I said so," may reflect that the prohibition in certain of its expressions rests on divine command rather than self-evident moral reasoning. This connects to a broader debate about the nature of the *sheva mitzvot*: Moses Mendelssohn wished to treat them as a Jewish version of natural law, which is why he was troubled by the Rambam's ruling that a *ben Noach* who observes them because they make rational sense — rather than because God commanded them through Moses — does not receive full credit. The Rambam's formulation emphasizes divine command; the Noda Bi-Yehuda was reportedly unable to identify the Rambam's precise source for this ruling.

### Ever Min Hachai

*Achol tochel* — "you may freely eat" — yields *eiver min ha-chai* through a reading offered by Rashi: the doubled form *achol tochel* — something that is already *ochel*, already in the status of food, you may eat — implies that something not yet in the status of food may not be eaten. A living animal, which is still engaged in producing offspring, giving milk, and giving wool, is not yet "food." Tearing a limb from it violates the permission structure of *mikol etz ha-gan achol tochel*. The Gemara is also working to root this commandment in the verse about Adam, even though *eiver min ha-chai* is most famously stated explicitly to Noah in the verse *ach basar be-nafsho damo lo tocheilu*. The drive is to locate all seven within a single verse addressed to the first human being.

### Gezel Theft

*Mikol etz ha-gan* — "of every tree of the garden" — carries the implicit meaning that the trees God designated are available; what is not designated is not available. The explicit grant of permission implies the existence of things for which no permission has been granted, and taking those without authorization constitutes *gezel*.

---

## Dinim for Jews

### Yitzchak Reversed

Rabbi Yitzchak, who taught when he came from Eretz Yisrael, taught *ipcha* — a reversed attribution. He maintains the same list of seven but reassigns the derivations: *vayitzav* corresponds not to *dinim* but to *avodah zarah*, and *Elokim* corresponds not to *avodah zarah* but to *dinim*.

### Making vs. Worship

The reassignment is straightforward for *Elokim* meaning *dinim* — the verse *ve-nikrav ba'al ha-bayit el ha-Elohim* shows that *Elokim* denotes judges. But how does *vayitzav* connect to *avodah zarah*? This requires explanation, which the Gemara supplies through a dispute.

### Chisda Dispute

Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi disagree over which verse links *vayitzav* to *avodah zarah*. One says the verse is *saru maher min ha-derech asher tzivitim, asu lahem eigel masecha* — "they turned quickly from the path I commanded them and made a golden calf." The word *tzivitim* — "I commanded them" — connects to *vayitzav*, and the subject is idolatry. The other says the verse is *ashuk Efrayim, retzutz mishpat, ki ho'il acharei tzav* — Ephraim has been oppressed and trampled in judgment, because they walked after the command of the false prophet and worshiped the *ba'al*. Here *tzav* again means a command, but the command of a false prophet leading to idolatry.

The practical difference between the two views is whether *akum she-asah avodah zarah ve-lo hishtachavah lah* — a non-Jew who made an idol but did not bow down to it — is liable. The verse *asu lahem eigel masecha* emphasizes the act of making: *mishe'at asiyah mechayev*, from the moment of making there is liability. The verse *ki ho'il acharei tzav* emphasizes the act of following and worshiping: *ad de-azil batra u-falach*, only once they actually go and worship do they incur liability. Normally the assumption is that *avodah zarah* for *bnei Noach* requires an act of worship rather than merely the making of an idol — but if the verse about the *eigel* is the source, even making may be prohibited.

Rava raises a challenge: can anyone truly maintain that a non-Jew is liable for making an idol without worshiping it? A *braitah* states: *be-Akum, devarim she-beit din shel Yisrael memitin aleihem, ben Noach muzhar aleihem* — regarding non-Jews, they are prohibited only for acts for which a Jewish court would execute a Jew. Since a Jewish court would not execute a Jew merely for making an idol, a non-Jew should likewise not be liable for making alone. Rav Pappa responds that the *braitah* comes to exclude *gipuf ve-nishuk* — hugging and kissing an idol as a form of adoration — which is not a mode of worship for which a Jewish court would execute, and is therefore not an act of worship that makes a non-Jew liable either. The case of making an idol is different: *gezel* is the clearest example of an act for which a non-Jew is liable by death but for which a Jewish court does not execute a Jew. So it is not a universal rule that non-Jewish liability tracks Jewish capital liability; it is a rule specific to acts of *avodah zarah*, where the qualifying criterion is whether the act constitutes genuine worship.

### Marah Ten Mitzvot

The discussion of *dinim* raises a broader question: were *bnei Noach* actually commanded in *dinim* at all? A *braitah* states that at Marah — the Israelites' first encampment after leaving Egypt — they received ten *mitzvot*: the seven they had already accepted as *bnei Noach*, plus *dinim*, *Shabbat*, and *kibud av va'em*. The inclusion of *dinim* here as something newly added at Marah implies that it was *not* among the original seven. The source for *dinim* at Marah: *sham sam lo chok u-mishpat* — "there He gave them statute and justice." The source for *Shabbat* and *kibud av va'em*: the phrase *ka'asher tzivcha Hashem Elohecha* in the second Decalogue is read as referring to a prior command, and the only prior command on record is at Marah.

---

## Jewish Court Requirements

### Nachman Court Rules

The Gemara reconciles the tension between the *braitah* placing *dinim* at Marah and the standard list that includes *dinim* among the seven. Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuha explains: *lo nitzrecha ela le-edah ve-edim ve-hatra'ah* — what was added at Marah was not the category of *dinim* as such, but its specifically Jewish requirements. For *bnei Noach*, a legal system functions without the full Jewish procedural constraints: one witness suffices, even hearsay may suffice, and no formal warning is required. What was added for Israel at Marah was that capital cases require an *edah* — a full court of twenty-three — two *edim*, formal witnesses, and *hatra'ah*, a warning administered before the act.

The Gemara objects: if only procedural refinements were added, the *braitah* should have said "they added to *dinim*," not "they added *dinim*." This implies a categorical addition, not a procedural one.

### Kenasot Fines

Rava therefore offers an alternative: *lo nitzrecha ela le-dinei kenasot* — what was added was the authority to adjudicate fines, that is, monetary penalties beyond the actual damage incurred. Rashi explains that the *dinim* of *bnei Noach*, as derived from *la'asot tzedakah u-mishpat* by Abraham, encompasses fair compensation — rectifying actual loss. But a *kenas*, a fine that exceeds the damage, goes beyond restitution into a different register of deterrence-based liability. That authority was granted to the Jewish legal system at Marah but was not part of the universal Noahide legal obligation. This interpretation also offers evidence supporting the Ramban's position: the *dinim* of *bnei Noach* appears to include substantive civil law, not merely the organizational infrastructure of courts. The fact that Jews were given expanded jurisdiction over *kenasot* implies that the underlying *dinim* obligation encompasses real legal substance.
